name: Volume rendering
head: Volume rendering makes images of data that fill space (a density, a material, a temperature sampled through a region) rather than of surfaces alone.
body: Volume rendering makes images of data that fill space (a density, a material, a temperature sampled through a region) rather than of surfaces alone. This introduction was written by Claude. A volume is a function over 3D space, f(\mathbf{x}), usually known only at samples. The commonest case, and the core of this encyclopedia, is a regular grid: a 3D array of values in which each cell, a voxel, is a small cube. CT and MRI scans, smoke and fluid simulations, cloud textures, Minecraft-style worlds and the occupancy grids of game engines all have this form. A voxel can hold a scalar (density, temperature), a material id, a color, or a single occupancy bit. The same ideas carry over to other sampled fields: hierarchical and adaptive grids that store detail only where it is needed (octrees, VDB, adaptive mesh refinement), unstructured meshes of tetrahedra and other cells, implicit fields such as signed distance functions that are evaluated on demand, and learned fields such as neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussians. Extract a surface, then draw the surface. Choose a level f(\mathbf{x}) = c (an isosurface) or the boundary of the solid voxels, turn it into triangles, and draw them with an ordinary GPU pipeline. Most voxel games and many medical viewers work this way. Render the volume directly. Treat the data as a semi-transparent medium and add up its contribution along each viewing ray. This is direct volume rendering, introduced in its common form by Levoy and by Drebin, Carpenter and Hanrahan. Everything from medical CT viewers to film clouds to neural radiance fields is a variant of it. Along a ray \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\,\mathbf{d} through a medium with extinction coefficient \sigma(t) and emitted color c(t), the color that reaches the eye is C = \int0^{D} T(t)\,\sigma(t)\,c(t)\,dt, \qquad T(t) = \exp\!\Big(-\int0^{t} \sigma(s)\,ds\Big) T is the transmittance: the fraction of light from depth t that survives to the eye. Max surveys this emission–absorption model and its relatives. Renderers approximate the integral by taking samples every \Delta t and compositing them, usually front to back so that a ray can stop as soon as it is nearly opaque (early ray termination): \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \Delta t}, \qquad C \leftarrow C + T\,\alphai\,ci, \qquad T \leftarrow T\,(1 - \alphai) Classification turns raw data values into \sigma and c, usually through a transfer function: a lookup table from value (and sometimes gradient magnitude) to color and opacity. The same two formulas drive NeRF and Gaussian splatting; only the source of \sigma and c changes. The encyclopedia is a tree. Its root is this page; below it are ten branches, ordered from the data, to the ways of drawing it, to what it is used for. How a volume is held in memory. Dense grids are simple but large, so layouts such as bricking and Morton (Z-order) curves keep neighbouring voxels close in memory. Real volumes are mostly empty or uniform, so sparse structures store only the occupied parts: octrees and sparse voxel octrees, sparse voxel DAGs, which merge identical subtrees (Kämpe, Sintorn and Assarsson), and VDB, the shallow, wide tree used in film production (Museth). The branch also covers value compression, levels of detail, out-of-core streaming of data larger than memory, non-regular meshes, and neural and Gaussian representations. Where volumes come from: voxelization of triangle meshes and point clouds, procedural fields built from noise and distance functions, measurement by CT, MRI, microscopy or seismic surveys, and the output of fluid, fire and astrophysics simulations. Methods that start from the pixels and cast a ray per pixel. Volume ray casting samples the volume along the ray, interpolates (usually trilinearly), classifies and composites. To visit exactly the cells a ray crosses, the 3D DDA of Amanatides and Woo keeps, per axis, the distance to the next cell boundary and always steps across the nearest one; this is the inner loop of most voxel ray tracers. Speedups include empty space skipping and early ray termination (Levoy). For surfaces, isosurface ray casting stops at the first crossing of a level, and sphere tracing (Hart) uses a distance field's value as a safe step size. Methods that walk the volume and project each piece onto the screen. Splatting (Westover) draws each voxel as a small blurred footprint; 3D Gaussian splatting (Kerbl et al.) applies the same idea to millions of fitted Gaussians. Shear-warp (Lacroute and Levoy) shears the volume so that its slices line up with the image. Texture slicing draws many blended, view-aligned polygons and was the classic way to run volume rendering on early GPUs. Cell projection draws unstructured meshes one tetrahedron at a time (Shirley and Tuchman), and Fourier volume rendering computes projections in the frequency domain (Malzbender). Turning a volume into a mesh. Marching Cubes (Lorensen and Cline) looks up triangles for each cell from the signs at its eight corners; dual contouring (Ju et al.) places one vertex per cell and keeps sharp features. Blocky worlds instead emit the visible faces of solid voxels and merge them with greedy meshing. The emission–absorption model above ignores light that scatters inside the medium. Physically based renderers add shadows within the volume, phase functions, and single and multiple scattering, usually solved by Monte Carlo methods such as delta (Woodcock) tracking; Kajiya and Von Herzen gave an early formulation and Novák et al. survey the field. Real-time renderers approximate this with froxel grids (Hillaire) and voxel cone tracing (Crassin et al.). Making a picture that explains the data, not only one that looks right. The core tool is the transfer function; multi-dimensional transfer functions also use gradient magnitude and other derived values to separate materials that share a data value (Kindlmann and Durkin; Kniss, Kindlmann and Hansen). The branch also covers multi-field, vector and tensor data, illustrative and non-photorealistic styles, and interaction such as clipping and focus-plus-context views. Running rendering backwards: given images, find the volume that produced them. Because the volume rendering integral is differentiable, its parameters can be fitted by gradient descent. Neural radiance fields (Mildenhall et al.) fit a network that returns \sigma and c at any point; Plenoxels (Fridovich-Keil et al.) and Instant NGP (Müller et al.) store the parameters in voxels or hash tables to train far faster. Tomographic reconstruction, as in CT, is the classic inverse problem of the same kind (Feldkamp, Davis and Kress). Where the methods are used, linking back to the branches above: voxel engines and games, film production (VDB pipelines, clouds, fire), scientific and medical visualization, GPU, web and parallel renderers, and volumetric displays and holography. The small pieces that volume renderers are built from: ray–box intersection by the slab test (Kay and Kajiya) and other ray–primitive tests, camera models that generate the rays, and parallel GPU primitives such as atomics, prefix sums, sorting and stream compaction. Render a CT scan or a smoke simulation: volume ray casting, then transfer functions and empty space skipping. Build a blocky voxel game: greedy meshing, then the voxel engines in branch 9. Ray trace huge voxel scenes: 3D DDA, sparse voxel octrees, then sparse voxel DAGs. Extract smooth surfaces: Marching Cubes, then dual contouring. Render clouds and fog: light transport in participating media. Reconstruct a scene from photographs: neural radiance fields, then 3D Gaussian splatting. Amanatides, J. and Woo, A. (1987). name: Evaluation Cache
head: CachedEval, EvalCache
body: Evaluation Cache is a memory optimization technique that eliminates redundant computation by storing previously computed field values and their derivatives at shared grid locations. It differs from its siblings, which focus on spatial data layout (e.g., Bricking) or hardware texture sampling (e.g., 3D Texture Storage and Sampling), by operating at the algorithmic level to cache the results of expensive evaluations rather than optimizing the access to the source data. The method maps unique geometric entities (typically grid corners or edges) to a cache entry containing the computed scalar value and optional gradient. By using a quantized key representing the global grid position, the cache ensures that shared vertices between adjacent cells are evaluated only once. Inputs and Outputs Input: Grid origin, cell size, and the evaluation function f(\mathbf{x}) returning a scalar and optionally a gradient vector. Output: A cache structure mapping grid positions to computed values. Data Structures The implementation uses two primary structures: 1. GridPos: A quantized integer key representing a unique corner in the global grid. 2. CachedEval: value: f64 (64-bit float) storing the scalar field value. gradient: Option<[f64; 3]> storing the 3D gradient vector. None if the gradient is not required or computed. 3. EvalCache: entries: A hash map (HashMap<GridPos, CachedEval>) where the key is the quantized grid position. Algorithm Steps 1. Quantize Grid Position: For a given cell corner, compute a unique integer key. Let \mathbf{c} = (cx, cy, cz) be the integer coordinates of the cell containing the corner. Let corner\idx \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\} be the local corner index within the cell (e.g., 0 for 0,0,0; 1 for 1,0,0, etc.). The quantized grid position P is computed as: P = cx + 2cy + 4cz + 8 \cdot corner\idx Note: The source specifies adding corneridx bits (1 for X, 2 for Y, 4 for Z) to the cell's integer coordinates. This implies a specific bit-packing scheme. A robust interpretation for a unique global key is: P = cx + 2cy + 4cz + 8 \cdot corner\idx However, strictly following 's "add corneridx bits... to cell's integer coordinates" suggests: P = cx + 2cy + 4cz + corner\idx This is ambiguous if cell coordinates are large. The standard interpretation for "quantized grid position" in this context (Manifold Dual Contouring) is a unique global vertex ID. We assume the key is a unique integer identifier for the vertex. To ensure uniqueness for large grids, the key should typically be a 64-bit integer combining cell coordinates and corner index, e.g., P = (cx \ll 32) | (cy \ll 16) | (cz \ll 8) | corner\idx. The source implies a simpler additive scheme likely valid for small or local grids. We implement the additive scheme as described but note the potential for collision in large grids. 2. Check Cache: Look up P in EvalCache.entries. If present, return entry.value and entry.gradient. If absent, proceed to step 3. 3. Evaluate: Compute the world-space coordinate \mathbf{x} for the corner. \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{origin} + \mathbf{P}{grid} \cdot \text{cell\size} Where \mathbf{P}{grid} is the continuous grid position corresponding to the corner (derived from cell coordinates and corner offset). Compute v = f(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{g} = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}). 4. Store: Insert (P, \text{CachedEval}(v, \mathbf{g})) into EvalCache.entries. 5. Return: Return v and \mathbf{g}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import Tuple, Optional, Dict class CachedEval: def init(self, value: float, gradient: Optional[Tuple[float, float, float]]): self.value = value self.gradient = gradient class EvalCache: def init(self): self.entries: Dict[int, CachedEval] = {} def quantizegridpos(self, cellcoords: Tuple[int, int, int], corneridx: int) -> int: """ Computes a unique integer key for a grid corner. Based on: add corneridx bits (1 for X, 2 for Y, 4 for Z) to cell's integer coordinates. Note: This additive scheme assumes small cell coordinates or local grids. """ cx, cy, cz = cellcoords # Using the additive scheme from return cx + 2 cy + 4 cz + corneridx def getoreval(self, cache: EvalCache, origin: Tuple[float, float, float], cellsize: float, cellcoords: Tuple[int, int, int], corneridx: int, evalfunc: callable) -> Tuple[float, Optional[Tuple[float, float, float]]]: """ Retrieves cached value or evaluates and caches it. """ key = cache.quantizegridpos(cellcoords, corneridx) if key in cache.entries: entry = cache.entries[key] return entry.value, entry.gradient # Compute world-space coordinate #: add the product of the grid position component and cellsize to the origin component. # The grid position component for the corner is derived from cellcoords and corneridx. # Assuming corneridx 0-7 maps to offsets (0,0,0) to (1,1,1). # Bit decomposition of corneridx: xbit = (corneridx >> 0) & 1 ybit = (corneridx >> 1) & 1 zbit = (corneridx >> 2) & 1 gx = cellcoords[0] + xbit gy = cellcoords[1] + ybit gz = cellcoords[2] + zbit worldx = origin[0] + gx cellsize worldy = origin[1] + gy cellsize worldz = origin[2] + gz cellsize # Evaluate function value, gradient = evalfunc(worldx, worldy, worldz) # Store in cache cache.entries[key] = CachedEval(value, gradient) return value, gradient Parameters cellsize: The physical size of a single grid cell. Typical values depend on the dataset resolution and domain size. origin: The world-space coordinate of the grid's (0,0,0) corner. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Key Collisions: The additive quantization scheme in may produce collisions if cell coordinates are large. A bit-shifted key is safer for general use. Memory Usage: The cache grows with the number of unique corners. For large volumes, this may exceed available memory. Gradient Storage: Storing gradients doubles the memory footprint per entry. If gradients are not needed (e.g., simple scalar field evaluation), gradient should be None. A variant where the cache stores the result of texture sampling operations. In iterative volume rendering (e.g., pre-integration), the back sample of one iteration is cached and reused as the front sample of the next. This ensures the number of texture accesses remains N regardless of the integration order, reducing computational cost by avoiding redundant fetches. Time Complexity: O(1) average case for cache hits; O(1) for cache misses (evaluation). Total time is O(V) where V is the number of unique vertices. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of unique grid corners. Each entry stores a scalar and optionally a 3D vector. Strengths: Eliminates redundant mathematical evaluations (e.g., trilinear interpolation, gradient computation). Particularly effective in algorithms like Marching Cubes or Dual Contouring where corners are shared by multiple cells. Limitations: Requires additional memory for the hash map. Hash map overhead can be significant for very large grids. When to use: When the evaluation function is expensive and corners are shared. Not suitable if memory is extremely constrained or if the evaluation is trivial (e.g., direct array lookup). Evaluation Cache is used in isosurface extraction algorithms, specifically Manifold Dual Contouring, to optimize the computation of corner values and gradients. It is also applied in volume rendering to cache texture samples. narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, https://github.com/narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering, https://people.freedesktop.org/~marcheu/pacificvis08.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Edge Point Caching
head: GetEdgePoint, X/Y/ZEdgePoint
body: Edge Point Caching is a memory optimization technique used in the Marching Cubes algorithm to eliminate redundant linear interpolation calculations for isosurface intersection points on cube edges shared between adjacent voxels. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by maintaining a lookup table of computed edge points, ensuring that each geometric edge in the grid is interpolated only once, regardless of how many adjacent cubes share it. Inputs: A 3D scalar field grid, an isovalue threshold, and a voxel processing loop iterating over i, j, k indices. Outputs: A list of triangles defining the isosurface. Data Structures: The cache is a 3D array of integers, EdgeCache[X][Y][Z][EdgeIndex], where dimensions correspond to the voxel grid size plus one (to cover vertices/edges at boundaries). EdgeIndex ranges from 0 to 11, representing the 12 edges of a cube. The cache stores the computed 3D coordinate (or an index into a global point list) for each edge. If an edge has not been computed, the cache value is initialized to -1. Steps: 1. Initialize EdgeCache with -1 for all entries. 2. For each voxel (i, j, k): a. Determine the cube case based on scalar values at the 8 corners. b. For each active edge in the case: i. Identify the edge uniquely by its global coordinates. ii. Map the local edge index to a specific cache access function (GetXEdgePoint, GetYEdgePoint, or GetZEdgePoint) based on the orientation of the edge. iii. Check if EdgeCache contains a valid value (not -1) for this edge. iv. If valid, retrieve the cached point. v. If invalid, compute the intersection point using linear interpolation between the two corner scalar values and the isovalue. Store the result in EdgeCache and return it. c. Construct triangles using the retrieved edge points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EdgeCache = array of size (X+1, Y+1, Z+1, 12) initialized to -1 def GetXEdgePoint(x, y, z, edgeidx): """ Retrieves or computes the intersection point on an X-aligned edge. x, y, z: integer coordinates of the voxel corner. edgeidx: local edge index (0-11). Returns: 3D point (float, float, float). """ # Map local edge index to global edge coordinates # X-aligned edges are those where y and z vary, x is constant. # Specific mapping depends on Marching Cubes edge table. # For example, edge 0 might be between (x,y,z) and (x+1,y,z). # Determine global edge key. # Assuming edgeidx 0-2 are X-aligned for simplicity in this example. # In reality, the mapping is defined by the MC edge table. # Check cache if EdgeCache[x][y][z][edgeidx] != -1: return EdgeCache[x][y][z][edgeidx] # Compute intersection # Get scalar values at the two corners defining this edge val1 = ScalarField[x][y][z] val2 = ScalarField[x+1][y][z] # Example for X-aligned edge # Linear interpolation t = (Isovalue - val1) / (val2 - val1) point = Point3D( x + t, y, z) # Store in cache EdgeCache[x][y][z][edgeidx] = point return point def GetYEdgePoint(x, y, z, edgeidx): # Similar logic for Y-aligned edges # Check cache, compute if missing, store, return pass def GetZEdgePoint(x, y, z, edgeidx): # Similar logic for Z-aligned edges pass def ProcessVoxel(i, j, k): # Determine cube case case = GetCubeCase(i, j, k) # For each edge in the case for edgeidx in ActiveEdges[case]: # Determine edge orientation and call appropriate function if IsXAligned(edgeidx): point = GetXEdgePoint(i, j, k, edgeidx) elif IsYAligned(edgeidx): point = GetYEdgePoint(i, j, k, edgeidx) else: point = GetZEdgePoint(i, j, k, edgeidx) # Add point to triangle construction AddPointToTriangle(point) Parameters: Isovalue: The threshold scalar value for surface extraction. EdgeCache: 3D array of points or indices. Edge Cases: Boundary edges: Ensure cache dimensions account for grid boundaries to avoid out-of-bounds access. Degenerate cases: If scalar values are exactly equal to the isovalue, the intersection point is the corner itself. Extends Edge Point Caching by storing gradient normals alongside intersection points to ensure consistent shading across shared edges. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of linear interpolation operations from 12 \times N (where N is the number of voxels) to approximately 12 \times N / 3 = 4 \times N on average, as each internal edge is shared by 3 voxels (in 3D, edges are shared by 4 voxels, but the caching logic ensures each is computed once). The lookup is O(1). Memory Complexity: Requires O(X \times Y \times Z \times 12) storage for the cache. This can be significant for large volumes. Strengths: Eliminates redundant calculations, improving performance for large datasets. Limitations: Increased memory usage. Cache invalidation or reuse requires careful management if the volume changes. Originated in implementations of the Marching Cubes algorithm to optimize performance. The specific implementation details are found in open-source C code for 3D model extraction. samsfisher/3d-model-xray, https://github.com/samsfisher/3d-model-xray, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Edge Interpolation with Caching
head: Per-Edge Interpolation Cache
body: Edge Interpolation with Caching optimizes Marching Cubes surface generation by storing the computed intersection point and associated gradient normal for each unique edge shared between adjacent cubes, preventing redundant linear interpolation calculations for triangle corners that share the same edge. It builds on Edge Point Caching by extending the cache to include geometric normals derived from the scalar field gradient, ensuring consistent shading across shared edges. Inputs: Scalar field values at grid vertices. Isosurface threshold value (I). Boolean flag bSmooth indicating whether to use linear interpolation based on scalar values or simple geometric midpoints. A cache data structure mapping unique edge identifiers to computed results. Outputs: Intersection position on the edge. Gradient normal at the intersection point (if bSmooth is true). Data Structures: The cache uses a key-value mapping. The key is an FEdgeKey structure containing startPos (FIntVector), endPos (FIntVector), and position (FVector). The value stores the computed position and normal. Steps: 1. Identify Unique Edges: For the current voxel cell, identify all edges that intersect the isosurface. 2. Generate Key: For each intersecting edge, create an FEdgeKey using the integer coordinates of the start and end vertices. 3. Cache Lookup: Check if the FEdgeKey exists in the cache. If present, retrieve the cached position and normal. If absent, proceed to Step 4. 4. Compute Intersection: Let sv be the scalar value at the start position, and ev be the scalar value at the end position. Let Ps be the start position vector, and Pe be the end position vector. Calculate the difference \Delta = I - sv. If |\Delta| < 10^{-6}, the intersection is at the midpoint. Set result P = (Ps + Pe) \times 0.5. Else, calculate the interpolation factor t = \frac{\Delta}{ev - sv}. Handle boundary conditions for t: If t < 10^{-6}, set P = Ps. If (1 - t) < 10^{-6}, set P = Pe. Otherwise, calculate P = Ps + (Pe - Ps) \times t. If bSmooth is false, P is simply the midpoint (Ps + Pe) \times 0.5. Compute the gradient normal N at P by interpolating the scalar field gradients at the edge endpoints. 5. Store and Return: Store the computed P and N in the cache under the FEdgeKey and return them. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Tuple, Dict @dataclass class FEdgeKey: startPos: Tuple[float, float, float] endPos: Tuple[float, float, float] @dataclass class CacheEntry: position: Tuple[float, float, float] normal: Tuple[float, float, float] def getedgeintersection(startPos, endPos, scalarstart, scalarend, isovalue, bsmooth, cache: Dict[FEdgeKey, CacheEntry]): key = FEdgeKey(startPos=startPos, endPos=endPos) if key in cache: return cache[key].position, cache[key].normal if not bsmooth: pos = ((startPos[0] + endPos[0]) 0.5, (startPos[1] + endPos[1]) 0.5, (startPos[2] + endPos[2]) 0.5) normal = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Normal computation not specified in sources else: delta = isovalue - scalarstart if abs(delta) < 1e-6: pos = ((startPos[0] + endPos[0]) 0.5, (startPos[1] + endPos[1]) 0.5, (startPos[2] + endPos[2]) 0.5) else: denom = scalarend - scalarstart if abs(denom) < 1e-12: t = 0.5 else: t = delta / denom if t < 1e-6: pos = startPos elif (1 - t) < 1e-6: pos = endPos else: pos = (startPos[0] + (endPos[0] - startPos[0]) t, startPos[1] + (endPos[1] - startPos[1]) t, startPos[2] + (endPos[2] - startPos[2]) t) normal = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Gradient interpolation not detailed in sources cache[key] = CacheEntry(position=pos, normal=normal) return pos, normal Parameters: bsmooth: Boolean flag. true for linear interpolation based on scalar values, false for geometric midpoints. 1e-6: Epsilon threshold for numerical stability checks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero if scalar values at both ends of an edge are identical. Handled by checking denominator magnitude. Numerical precision issues when t is very close to 0 or 1. Handled by explicit checks against 10^{-6}. Out-of-range lattice samples treated as density 0 to cap the isosurface against walls. A specific implementation variant where the cache stores both the interpolated position and the gradient normal for each unique cut edge, ensuring that all triangle corners sharing that edge reuse the same geometric data, which improves shading consistency and reduces computation. It is chosen when smooth shading is required and memory allows storing normals per edge. Time Complexity: Reduces interpolation and normal computation from O(E \times C) to O(E) per cell, where E is the number of edges and C is the number of corners sharing edges, assuming cache hits. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory to store the cache entries (position and normal) for each unique edge across the volume. Strengths: Avoids redundant calculations for shared edges; ensures consistent normals for smooth shading. Limitations: Requires cache management overhead; memory usage increases with volume size and resolution. Originated in implementations of Marching Cubes for voxel-based rendering, specifically in projects like VoxelHelper and WebGPU-based renderers. The technique is used to optimize mesh generation by leveraging the redundancy of edge intersections in dense grids. 2453852330/VoxelHelper, https://github.com/2453852330/VoxelHelper, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Renderer: marching-cubes isosurface mesh (r=mesh, WebGPU), https://github.com/nikolai3d/waterfall/pull/17, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Bricking
head: Block replacement rendering, Brick-based memory management, Divide-and-conquer volume rendering, Large Volume Rendering via Partitioning, Supervolumes, Volume Bricking, Volumetric texture bricking, Voxel bricking
body: Bricking is a memory management technique for volume rendering that partitions a volumetric dataset larger than the available GPU memory (or texture unit limits) into smaller, fixed-size sub-volumes called "bricks". Each brick is loaded into GPU memory, rendered independently, and the resulting images are composited to form the final image. It differs from Chunk-based Voxel Data Structure by typically using uniform, fixed-size blocks optimized for texture sampling, and from Tile-based Volume Ray Marching by operating on 3D spatial subdivisions rather than 2D screen tiles. Inputs: A large 3D volumetric dataset V with dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz) exceeding hardware limits. Outputs: A final 2D image I. Data Structures: The volume is partitioned into a grid of bricks B{i,j,k}. Brick Size: Typically limited by hardware constraints. For example, VolumePro hardware limits blocks to a maximum of 256 voxels per edge. Modern GPU texture limits may also apply (e.g., 2048 or 4096, but often smaller for performance). Overlap: To handle interpolation artifacts, bricks include overlapping boundary layers. Specifically, a plane (or multiple voxels) of data is duplicated at each brick boundary. VolumePro duplicates three voxels in each of the three dimensions for adjacent blocks. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the original volume into uniform sub-volumes (bricks) such that each fits within the GPU's texture memory or specific hardware limits (e.g., \le 256^3 for VolumePro). 2. Overlap Handling: Duplicate voxels at the boundaries of adjacent bricks to ensure consistent texture interpolation across brick edges. Without this, texture units lack the information to interpolate correctly across boundaries, causing visible artifacts. 3. Loading: Transfer bricks from host memory to GPU memory. If the supervolume (the collection of all bricks) does not fit in GPU memory, bricks are swapped in and out. 4. Rendering: Render each brick independently using a volume rendering algorithm (e.g., raycasting). Ray Alignment: When passing rays from one block to another, sub-pixel accurate initial offsets in x and y are used to align rays correctly. An initial z offset maintains correct supersampling in the z-direction between blocks. Duplicate Sample Exclusion: If a ray exits the volume exactly on a border between two blocks, a sample might be blended twice (once from each block). The system (e.g., VolumePro) automatically excludes these duplicated samples. 5. Compositing: Composite the resulting images (or base planes) from back-to-front into a single image. For parallel implementations, image compositing libraries like IceT may be used. 6. Warping: Warp the resulting blended base plane to the final image coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbrickedvolume(volumedata, bricksize, overlapvoxels): """ Renders a large volume by partitioning it into bricks. volumedata: 3D array of the full dataset. bricksize: int, max dimension of a brick (e.g., 256). overlapvoxels: int, number of voxels to duplicate at boundaries (e.g., 3). """ # 1. Determine grid of bricks dims = volumedata.shape numbricksx = ceil(dims[0] / bricksize) numbricksy = ceil(dims[1] / bricksize) numbricksz = ceil(dims[2] / bricksize) # 2. Initialize final image accumulator finalimage = zeros((imagewidth, imageheight, 4)) # RGBA # 3. Iterate over bricks (order matters for compositing, typically back-to-front) for k in range(numbricksz): for j in range(numbricksy): for i in range(numbricksx): # Extract brick with overlap # Calculate bounds with overlap padding xstart = max(0, i bricksize - overlapvoxels) xend = min(dims[0], (i + 1) bricksize + overlapvoxels) ystart = max(0, j bricksize - overlapvoxels) yend = min(dims[1], (j + 1) bricksize + overlapvoxels) zstart = max(0, k bricksize - overlapvoxels) zend = min(dims[2], (k + 1) bricksize + overlapvoxels) brick = volumedata[xstart:xend, ystart:yend, zstart:zend] # 4. Load brick to GPU uploadtogpu(brick) # 5. Render brick # Apply sub-pixel offsets for ray alignment if necessary # Render returns a base plane or intermediate image brickimage = rendersinglebrick(brick, offsetx=ibricksize, offsety=jbricksize, offsetz=kbricksize) # 6. Composite into final image # Back-to-front compositing logic finalimage = compositebacktofront(finalimage, brickimage, brickorigin=(ibricksize, jbricksize, kbricksize)) # 7. Unload brick (optional, if memory is tight) downloadfromgpu() return finalimage A scheme where bricks are stored on disk in a large size (e.g., 256^3) but presented to the renderer as small bricks (e.g., 32^3) [2823-dynamic-rebricking.md]. Small bricks are dynamically generated from large ones on request to balance disk performance (favored by large bricks) with early ray termination/empty space skipping (favored by small bricks) [2823-dynamic-rebricking.md]. Divides a volume into smaller 3D texture bricks to manage memory, improve data locality, and reduce bus transfer overhead by avoiding reloading void bricks [3782-brick-based-volume-rendering-with-overlap-and-lru-swapping.md]. An approach by Weiskopf et al. (2004) that breaks 3D volumes into smaller bricks and reorganizes them into different orientations to average out performance variations from different viewing angles. Pitfalls: The entire volume must be within the viewing frustum for this approach to work. It requires a data pre-processing stage, which may not be feasible for in-situ visualizations. Deriving the best brick resolution and handling overlap between neighboring bricks complicates the pre-processing. Time Complexity: Rendering time increases due to limited PCI download bandwidth when loading large supervolumes. Real-time rendering speed is hard to achieve with simple bricking because CPU-GPU inter-connection speed is insufficient for the required data transfer rates. Memory Complexity: Bricking does not reduce the total memory required to represent the original data; it increases it due to extra layers (overlap) required for each sub-volume to eliminate inconsistent interpolation at brick boundaries. Strengths: Allows rendering of volumes larger than GPU memory. Enables parallel rendering by distributing sub-volumes to data servers (e.g., in ParaView). Limitations: High data transfer overhead. Artifacts at brick boundaries if overlap is not handled correctly. Performance variations depending on viewing angle if not reorganized (e.g., view-aligned). When to use: When the dataset exceeds available GPU texture memory or hardware limits (e.g., 256 voxels/edge). When parallel rendering across multiple nodes is desired. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and bandwidth is a bottleneck. When in-situ visualization pre-processing is not feasible. Bricking was developed to address the limitations of early GPU hardware, which had small texture memory capacities (e.g., 128 MB on VolumePro PCI cards) and limits on texture dimensions (e.g., 256 voxels per edge). The VolumePro system (1999) popularized the "supervolume" concept, where software partitions the volume, handles data duplication, and composites results. Later, with the rise of general-purpose GPU computing, bricking was adapted for GPU-based raycasting to handle massive out-of-core datasets. It is used in parallel rendering software like ParaView, where it serves as a form of data parallelism. name: Tile-based Volume Ray Marching
head: Tiled Volume Ray Marching, 1D Texture Array Volume Rendering
body: Tile-based volume ray marching is a dense grid rendering technique that stores 3D volume data in a 1D texture array organized into tiles, using ray marching to sample the volume and composite the result using front-to-back accumulation. It solves the problem of mapping large 3D scalar fields onto 2D texture hardware by decomposing the Z-axis into discrete tiles, allowing efficient sampling via linear interpolation between adjacent tile slices. It is distinguished from standard 3D texture sampling by its explicit tile-indexing arithmetic and from bricking by its reliance on a 1D texture array layout with linear interpolation rather than discrete brick selection. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume defined by normalized coordinates (x, y, z) \in [0, 1]^3. Input: A 1D texture array uVolData storing the volume data, where each "slice" of the array corresponds to a 2D texture of size uDimension \times uDimension. Input: Ray entry and exit coordinates provided as frontColor (entry point) and backColor (exit point) in screen space. Output: Final accumulated color glFragColor. Data Structures The volume data is stored in a 1D texture array uVolData. The array is conceptually divided into uTiles slices along the Z-axis. Each slice is a 2D texture of dimensions uDimension \times uDimension. The total number of texels in the 1D array is uTiles \times uDimension \times uDimension. Parameters uTiles: Number of tiles along the Z-axis. uTileWidth: Width of each tile in pixels (typically equal to uDimension). uTileHeight: Height of each tile in pixels (typically equal to uDimension). uDimension: Dimension (width/height) of the 2D texture sub-images. uMinimum: Minimum scalar value in the volume. uMaximum: Maximum scalar value in the volume. uRange: Normalization range, uMaximum - uMinimum. uOpacity: Global opacity multiplier. uLight: Global lighting intensity multiplier. MAXSTEPS: Constant integer representing the maximum number of ray marching steps. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Initialization: Compute normalized screen texture coordinates from the varying position: textureCoord = \frac{position.xy}{position.w} textureCoord.x = 0.5 \cdot textureCoord.x + 0.5 textureCoord.y = 0.5 \cdot textureCoord.y + 0.5 Fetch the back color (exit point) from uBackCoord at textureCoord: backColor = \text{texture2D}(uBackCoord, textureCoord) The entry point is stored in the varying frontColor. Compute the ray step vector: step = \frac{backColor.rgb - frontColor.rgb}{MAXSTEPS} Initialize the current position vpos to frontColor and accumulators accum and sample to zero. 2. Volume Sampling (getTextureValue): For a given volume position P = (x, y, z): Calculate the Z-tile indices for the current position and the next slice: zp1 = \lfloor z \cdot uTiles \rfloor zp2 = zp1 + 1 Calculate the X and Y pixel coordinates within the tile: xp = \lfloor x \cdot uTileWidth \rfloor yp = \lfloor y \cdot uTileHeight \rfloor Calculate the 1D array indices for the two Z-slices: index1 = zp1 \cdot uTileWidth \cdot uTileHeight + yp \cdot uTileWidth + xp index2 = zp2 \cdot uTileWidth \cdot uTileHeight + yp \cdot uTileWidth + xp Convert 1D indices to 2D texture coordinates (xt, yt) for the 2D sub-textures: xt1 = \text{mod}(index1, uDimension) yt1 = \lfloor index1 / uDimension \rfloor xt2 = \text{mod}(index2, uDimension) yt2 = \lfloor index2 / uDimension \rfloor Normalize to [0, 1] range: texPos1 = \left( \frac{xt1}{uDimension}, \frac{yt1}{uDimension} \right) texPos2 = \left( \frac{xt2}{uDimension}, \frac{yt2}{uDimension} \right) Sample the volume data: val1 = \text{texture2D}(uVolData, texPos1).x val2 = \text{texture2D}(uVolData, texPos2).x Normalize values to [0, 1]: norm1 = \frac{val1 - uMinimum}{uRange} norm2 = \frac{val2 - uMinimum}{uRange} Interpolate based on the fractional Z position within the tile: t = (z \cdot uTiles) - zp1 \text{return mix}(norm1, norm2, t) 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to MAXSTEPS - 1: Sample the volume at current position vpos.xyz using getTextureValue. Let the result be v. Set transfer function input: transferPosition.x = v transferPosition.y = 0.5 Compute sample alpha and RGB: sample.a = v \cdot uOpacity \cdot \frac{1.0}{MAXSTEPS} sample.rgb = v \cdot sample.a \cdot uLight Front-to-back accumulation: accum.rgb += (1.0 - accum.a) \cdot sample.rgb accum.a += sample.a Advance position: vpos.xyz += step Termination: Break if vpos.x > 1.0, vpos.y > 1.0, vpos.z > 1.0, or accum.a \ge 1.0. 4. Output: Set glFragColor = accum. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilebasedvolumeraymarch(frontcolor, backcolor, uTiles, uTileWidth, uTileHeight, uDimension, uMinimum, uRange, uOpacity, uLight, MAXSTEPS, gettexturevalue): """ Renders a volume using tile-based ray marching. Args: frontcolor: vec4, entry point of the ray (xyz) and initial color (rgba). backcolor: vec4, exit point of the ray (xyz) and background color (rgba). uTiles: float, number of tiles along Z. uTileWidth: float, width of tile in pixels. uTileHeight: float, height of tile in pixels. uDimension: float, dimension of 2D texture sub-images. uMinimum: float, min volume value. uRange: float, volume value range (max - min). uOpacity: float, global opacity multiplier. uLight: float, global light multiplier. MAXSTEPS: int, max steps. gettexturevalue: function, samples the tiled volume data. Returns: vec4, final accumulated color. """ # Initialize accumulators accum = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) sample = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Ray setup # Note: In the source, frontcolor contains the ray origin, backcolor contains the ray end. # The source code uses frontColor as the initial vpos. vpos = frontcolor # Compute step vector # The source code computes step as (backColor.rgb - frontColor.rgb) / MAXSTEPS # This assumes frontcolor.rgb is the ray origin and backcolor.rgb is the ray destination. step = (backcolor.rgb - vpos.rgb) / MAXSTEPS for i in range(MAXSTEPS): # Sample volume v = gettexturevalue(vpos.xyz) # Compute sample properties # Source: sample.a = value.a uOpacity (1.0 / MAXSTEPS) # Source: sample.rgb = value.rgb sample.a uLight # Note: 'value' in source is the normalized scalar v. samplea = v uOpacity (1.0 / MAXSTEPS) samplergb = v samplea uLight # Accumulate accum.rgb += (1.0 - accum.a) samplergb accum.a += samplea # Advance vpos.xyz += step # Termination checks if vpos.x > 1.0 or vpos.y > 1.0 or vpos.z > 1.0 or accum.a >= 1.0: break return accum def gettexturevalue(volumeposition, uTiles, uTileWidth, uTileHeight, uDimension, uMinimum, uRange, texturesampler): """ Samples the tiled volume data. Args: volumeposition: vec3, normalized (0-1) coordinates. uTiles: float. uTileWidth: float. uTileHeight: float. uDimension: float. uMinimum: float. uRange: float. texturesampler: function, samples a 2D texture at normalized coordinates. Returns: float, normalized volume value. """ z = volumeposition.z x = volumeposition.x y = volumeposition.y # Z-tile indices zp1 = floor(z uTiles) zp2 = zp1 + 1.0 # X/Y pixel coordinates xp = floor(x uTileWidth) yp = floor(y uTileHeight) # 1D array indices index1 = zp1 uTileWidth uTileHeight + yp uTileWidth + xp index2 = zp2 uTileWidth uTileHeight + yp uTileWidth + xp # 2D texture coordinates xt1 = mod(index1, uDimension) yt1 = floor(index1 / uDimension) xt2 = mod(index2, uDimension) yt2 = floor(index2 / uDimension) # Normalized coordinates texpos1 = vec2(xt1 / uDimension, yt1 / uDimension) texpos2 = vec2(xt2 / uDimension, yt2 / uDimension) # Sample val1 = texturesampler(texpos1) val2 = texturesampler(texpos2) # Normalize norm1 = (val1 - uMinimum) / uRange norm2 = (val2 - uMinimum) / uRange # Interpolate t = (z uTiles) - zp1 return mix(norm1, norm2, t) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Conditions: The loop breaks if vpos > 1.0. If the ray exits the volume bounds before MAXSTEPS, the loop terminates early, potentially leaving accum incomplete if the background is not handled separately (though the source uses backColor to define the ray end, implying the ray is always within the [0,1]^3 box for the marching steps). Precision: The use of floor and mod for index calculation requires sufficient floating-point precision to avoid index collisions or gaps, especially for large uDimension values. Normalization: If uRange is zero, division by zero occurs. This must be guarded against in implementation. Tile Alignment: The method assumes uTileWidth and uTileHeight align with the texture dimensions. Mismatches can cause sampling errors at tile boundaries. Time Complexity: O(MAXSTEPS) per pixel, where MAXSTEPS is the number of ray marching steps. The volume sampling function getTextureValue involves constant-time arithmetic and two texture lookups. Memory Complexity: O(uTiles \cdot uDimension^2) for the volume data storage. The method requires storing the volume in a 1D texture array. Performance: Performance is limited by the number of ray steps and the cost of texture sampling. The method is efficient for moderate-resolution volumes but may suffer from texture cache thrashing if uDimension is large or if the tile layout causes non-coherent memory access patterns. Strengths: Simple implementation; leverages standard 2D texture hardware; linear interpolation provides smooth results across tile boundaries. Limitations: Limited to dense grids; no adaptive step size; memory usage scales linearly with volume size; interpolation across tile boundaries may introduce artifacts if the volume data is not smooth or if the tile size is too small. When to use: Suitable for real-time rendering of moderate-sized volumes on hardware with limited texture memory, where a simple, uniform sampling strategy is acceptable. When not to use: Unsuitable for very large volumes requiring sparse representation, or for high-quality rendering requiring adaptive sampling or complex transfer functions that cannot be pre-computed into the texture. The method is described in the volumetric.js library by kapadia. It represents a practical approach to volume rendering in WebGL, where 3D textures are not always supported or efficient. By decomposing the volume into 1D texture array slices, it allows for efficient sampling using standard 2D texture units. The technique relies on front-to-back accumulation, a standard volume rendering algorithm, but adapts the sampling strategy to the constraints of the 1D texture array layout. kapadia/volumetric.js, https://github.com/kapadia/volumetric.js, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Tiled Fitting with Hann Tapering
head: Overlapping Tile Partitioning with Hann Tapering, Overlapping tile fitting, Partition-of-unity tiling, Tiled Fitting
body: Tiled Fitting with Hann Tapering is a volume data fitting strategy that partitions large 3D volumes into overlapping tiles to fit Gaussian splat models independently, thereby enabling processing on hardware with limited memory. It solves the problem of GPU memory exhaustion for large volumes (e.g., 2048^3 float32) by decomposing the domain into smaller, manageable chunks. It is distinguished from non-overlapping tiling by the application of a raised-cosine (Hann) taper in overlap regions, which ensures a partition-of-unity and prevents visible seams, keeping the seam-to-interior residual ratio within 1.01–1.13 of a monolithic fit. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume (e.g., OME-Zarr layout) exceeding available GPU memory; a total seed budget (number of splats); tile size T; overlap size L. Output: A unified scene graph (partition tree or flat leaf) containing the union of splat sets from all tiles. Data Structures: Tile Grid: A regular 3D grid of tiles. The stride between tile origins is T - L. Tile Data: Each tile contains a subset of the volume voxels, multiplied by a taper window. Splat Set: The output of the fitting optimizer for a single tile. Parameters: T: Tile size in voxels per dimension. Typical range: 64–256. L: Overlap size in voxels. Typical range: 5–20% of T. Constraint: L \le T/2 to prevent triple overlap. \alpha: Exponent for seed budget division. Value: 0.44. Steps: 1. Tile Partitioning: Divide the volume domain into tiles on a regular grid with stride S = T - L. Edge Case: If the last candidate tile along any axis has a unique coverage (non-overlapping portion) thinner than the overlap L, fold it into its predecessor. This ensures no tile is smaller than the overlap allows. 2. Apodization (Tapering): For each tile, apply a raised-cosine (half-Hann) taper to the voxel data in the overlap regions. Let k be the index of a voxel within the overlap region, where k = 1, \dots, L. The weight w(k) is: w(k) = \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 - \cos \left( \frac{\pi k}{L + 1} \right) \right) This window is applied along each overlap face. Adjacent windows sum to 1.0 (partition-of-unity). The first and last tiles on each grid axis retain unit weight on their outer faces (no taper on the exterior boundary). 3. Seed Budget Division: Distribute the total integer seed budget N{total} among the tiles. For each tile i, calculate its weight Wi based on its Hann-weighted voxel count and intensity: Wi = \left( \sum{v \in \text{tile}i} w(v) \cdot \max(0, I(v) - I{floor}) \right)^{\alpha} where I(v) is the voxel intensity, I{floor} is a floor value (quarter-share floor), and \alpha = 0.44. The seed count for tile i, Ni, is: Ni = \text{round} \left( N{total} \cdot \frac{Wi}{\sum{j} Wj} \right). 4. Independent Fitting: Fit the Gaussian splat model for each tile independently using the assigned seed count Ni. This step is embarrassingly parallel and can be distributed across multiple GPUs or submitted as Slurm array jobs. 5. Union and Merge: Union the splat sets from all tiles. Default structure: A kind=partition tree with one part per tile. Alternative: A single flat leaf (using --flat). The merge operation streams spatial tiles as parts without holding the entire volume in memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hanntaperweight(k, L): """ Calculate Hann taper weight for voxel index k in overlap region of size L. k is 1-based index from the tile edge into the overlap. """ return 0.5 (1.0 - math.cos(math.pi k / (L + 1))) def fittiledvolume(volumedata, totalseeds, T, L): """ volumedata: 3D array or iterator over voxels totalseeds: int, total number of splats to fit T: int, tile size L: int, overlap size """ assert L <= T / 2, "Overlap must be <= half tile size to prevent triple overlap" # 1. Determine tile grid # Assuming volume dimensions are Dx, Dy, Dz # Calculate number of tiles along each axis # Stride is T - L # Handle edge folding: if remaining space < L, fold into previous tiles = [] # Pseudocode for grid generation is complex; simplified assumption: # Generate tile coordinates and sizes. Fold last tile if unique part < L. # For implementation, iterate axes and generate tile bounds. # 2. Calculate weights and assign seeds tileweights = [] for tile in tiles: # Extract voxel data for this tile # Apply Hann taper to overlap regions weightedintensitysum = 0.0 for voxel in tile.voxels: # Determine if voxel is in overlap and its index k # Apply taper w(k) # Add to sum if intensity > floor (quarter-share floor logic) # Note: Exact floor value and intensity thresholding details # are implementation-specific but follow the formula structure. pass # Raise to alpha = 0.44 weight = weightedintensitysum 0.44 tileweights.append(weight) totalweight = sum(tileweights) # 3. Distribute seeds tileseedcounts = [] for w in tileweights: count = round(totalseeds (w / totalweight)) tileseedcounts.append(count) # 4. Parallel Fitting # Each tile is fitted independently with its seed count # This step is parallelized across GPUs/Slurm jobs tilesplatsets = [] for tile, seeds in zip(tiles, tileseedcounts): splatset = fitsingletile(tile.data, seeds) tilesplatsets.append(splatset) # 5. Merge # Union splat sets into a partition tree or flat leaf scene = mergesplatsets(tilesplatsets, kind='partition') return scene A large-volume fitting strategy that partitions the domain into tiles, applies raised-cosine apodisation windows to ensure partition-of-unity at boundaries, and unions the resulting splat sets linearly. It is chosen when seamless blending between tiles is critical. It differs from hard-cut tiling by eliminating seams. Tile sizes range from 64 to 256 voxels, and overlaps from 0% to 40%. Finer grids (81–90 tiles) pay the most in quality loss, and more overlap beyond moderate levels buys nothing and degrades quality. Seam-to-interior residual ratio is 1.01–1.13 at 5–20% overlap. At fixed budget, tiled union stays within −0.98 to +0.19 dB of monolithic fit in moderate-overlap configurations. 40% overlap costs 0.54–1.68 dB. Per-tile GPU footprint is 43–46 MB allocated tensor memory per million voxels fitted at once. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Decomposes large volumes (e.g., 2048^3 float32) into smaller tiles (e.g., 256^3) to fit within consumer GPU memory (e.g., 24 GB). Per-tile GPU footprint is 43–46 MB of allocated tensor memory per million voxels fitted at once. Time: Embarrassingly parallel. The batch fitter plans the tiling once and spreads the plan over GPUs or Slurm array jobs. Measured Performance: Compared against monolithic fits at the same splat budget, the tiled union's seam-to-interior residual ratio stays within 1.01–1.13 of the seamless fit's, at most 13% above it. At a fixed budget, the tiled union stays within −0.98 to +0.19 dB of the monolithic fit's PSNR in moderate-overlap configurations (5–20%). Tiling at a fixed splat budget and 5–20% overlap costs at most one decibel of PSNR. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables fitting of volumes larger than GPU memory; seamless blending via partition-of-unity; scalable via parallel scheduling. Limitations: Hard cuts without overlap raise seam-to-interior residual ratio to 2.15–7.52 times that of seamless fits. Overlapping tiles without taper are worse (8.0–30.8 dB below monolithic fit). Finer grids pay the most in quality loss. When to Use: Use when the volume exceeds GPU memory and seamless rendering is required. Use 5–20% overlap for optimal balance. Avoid hard cuts or overlap without tapering. Originated in the Luxar project for Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualisation of multidimensional scientific data. It addresses the limitations of monolithic fitting for large-scale scientific volumes (e.g., confocal blastocyst, light-sheet Tribolium embryo). The method uses OME-Zarr inputs directly, fitting every timepoint and channel as its own task. Luxar: Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualisation of multidimensional scientific data, https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.22.753676, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Grid Density Data Structure
head: 1D Array Density Layout, 3D Grid, 3D Voxel Grid Density Field, Dense Voxel Grid Storage, Dense structure, Linearized 3D Grid, Volume Grid Data Structure
body: The Grid Density Data Structure is a dense, axis-aligned 3D grid used to store scalar density values for volume rendering. It solves the problem of representing continuous volumetric media (such as smoke, clouds, or fluids) as a discrete, regularly sampled field that can be efficiently traversed by ray marchers. Unlike sparse structures (e.g., trees or lists) which offer memory efficiency through bounding box culling but suffer from sampling latency due to indirection, the dense grid provides faster sampling speeds by eliminating pointer chasing, at the cost of higher memory usage and fixed resolution limits. It builds on Spatial Indexing and Ordering by providing the underlying memory layout for spatial queries. Inputs: Grid resolution N (assumed equal in all dimensions, typically a power of 2: 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, etc.). World-space bounds defined by minimum and maximum extents \mathbf{b}{min} and \mathbf{b}{max}, forming an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). The physical size must be identical in all three dimensions (e.g., a cube). Optional: Additional scalar fields (e.g., temperature). Outputs: A contiguous 1D array of floating-point density values. Metadata enabling coordinate transformation between world space and grid indices. Data Structures: The core structure Grid contains: 1. float density: A contiguous memory block of size N^3 storing the density values. 2. sizet dimension: The resolution N. 3. Point bounds[2]: An array of two 3D points representing \mathbf{b}{min} and \mathbf{b}{max} in world space. For more complex implementations (e.g., path tracing), the structure may extend to VolumeGrids, holding handles for density, optional temperature, and a majorant field. Indexing Formula: The 3D coordinates (x, y, z) map to a 1D linear index using row-major (Z-Y-X) ordering: index(x, y, z) = (z \cdot N + y) \cdot N + x where 0 \le x, y, z < N. Coordinate Transformation: To sample the grid, a world-space ray must be transformed into the grid's local coordinate system. This requires a transformation matrix D that maps world coordinates to medium-local coordinates: M = T(\mathbf{p}0) \times S(\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0) D = (W \times M)^{-1} where: \mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1 are two local-coordinate points defining the grid's orientation and scale. T is a translation matrix. S is a scaling matrix. W is the world-to-local transformation matrix. Generation Example (Smoke Sphere): A common initialization pattern involves creating a spherical density falloff: 1. Initialize density array of size N^3 to 0. 2. Iterate z from 1 to N-2, y from 1 to N-2, x from 1 to N-2. 3. Compute distance from center: dist = \sqrt{\left(x - \frac{N-1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(y - \frac{N-1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(z - \frac{N-1}{2}\right)^2} 4. Set density: density[index] = \frac{1}{2^{dist+2}} 5. Enforce boundary conditions (e.g., radius limit) to reduce harsh edges. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Grid: def init(self, resolution, boundsmin, boundsmax): """ Initialize a dense 3D grid.:param resolution: int, N (power of 2):param boundsmin: tuple (x, y, z), world space min:param boundsmax: tuple (x, y, z), world space max """ self.dimension = resolution self.bounds = [boundsmin, boundsmax] # Contiguous 1D array of floats self.density = [0.0] (resolution 3) def setdensitysphere(self, centerx, centery, centerz, radiusfactor=1.0): """ Generates a spherical density falloff. Restricting the effective radius and enforcing zero density at the edges mitigates this. Memory Usage: Memory scales as O(N^3). High resolutions (e.g., 256+) consume significant RAM, limiting the maximum feasible resolution compared to sparse structures. Coordinate Mismatch: The grid's world-space size must be uniform (cubic) if defined by symmetric bounds, or correctly mapped via the transformation matrix D if non-uniform. Gradient Computation via Finite Differences estimates the spatial gradient vector of a scalar volume field at sample positions to enable local illumination (e.g., Phong shading) and multidimensional transfer functions. It sets itself apart from Analytic Gradient Computation by requiring no basis function derivatives and from Sobel Operator by using a minimal 6-neighbor stencil rather than a separable smoothing kernel, making it faster but less robust to noise. The EdgeMap data layout is a memory structure within the Grid Density Data Structure that stores geometric intersection data for isosurface extraction. It organizes intersection points, surface normals, ray directions, and indexing offsets into contiguous arrays. It differs from sibling methods like Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by storing pre-computed geometric primitives rather than derivative values, and from Interpolated Discrete Values & Gradients by focusing on explicit intersection coordinates rather than field values. This method computes the scalar field value at a 3D point using tri-cubic interpolation, requiring a 4×4×4 neighborhood of 64 voxels. It provides scalar value and gradient fields computed from discrete data at grid vertices using interpolation. It builds on Grid Density Data Structure and operates alongside siblings Gradient Computation via Finite Differences and EdgeMap Data Layout. The Euclidean Distance Field (EDF) is a spatial indexing structure used for space-skipping ray traversal in dense voxel volumes. It accelerates rendering by allowing rays to jump over empty space based on precomputed distance values, reducing the number of intersection tests. It differs from sibling structures like EdgeMap Data Layout by storing scalar distance magnitudes rather than boundary flags, and from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by providing traversal acceleration rather than surface normal estimation. For N=128, this requires 128^3 \times 4 bytes \approx 8 MB per density field. Performance: Dense grids are significantly faster to sample than sparse grids because they avoid the indirection overhead of tree traversal or hash lookups. However, the fixed resolution limits detail compared to adaptive sparse structures. Strengths: Simple implementation, cache-friendly contiguous memory layout, supports precomputed data (e.g., lighting) easily. Limitations: High memory consumption restricts resolution; inefficient for sparse scenes with large empty volumes. When to Use: Suitable for dense media (clouds, smoke) where sampling speed is critical and memory allows for sufficient resolution. When Not to Use: Unsuitable for highly sparse scenes or when extreme resolution is required within limited memory budgets; use sparse structures (e.g., OpenVDB) instead. The Grid Density Data Structure originates from early volume rendering techniques that quantized continuous density fields into discrete voxel grids. It is analogous to how bitmaps represent 2D images, with 3D grids representing volumetric simulations (fluids, smoke). The approach is widely used in real-time and offline rendering for clouds and smoke, often leveraging 3D textures for hardware-accelerated sampling. Data is frequently loaded from sparse formats like OpenVDB and converted to dense grids for rendering. Heuristics for optimal grid resolution, such as the Surface Area Metric, have been developed to balance traversal and intersection costs, particularly in GPU ray tracing contexts. name: Gradient Computation via Finite Differences
head: Central Difference Gradient, Central Difference Gradient Estimation, Central-Difference Gradient Operator, Component-wise Linear Gradient Estimation, Finite Difference Gradient, Gradient Computation Using Central Differences, Numerical Gradient Approximation
body:
Gradient Computation via Finite Differences estimates the spatial gradient vector of a scalar volume field at sample positions to enable local illumination (e.g., Phong shading) and multidimensional transfer functions. It sets itself apart from Analytic Gradient Computation by requiring no basis function derivatives and from Sobel Operator by using a minimal 6-neighbor stencil rather than a separable smoothing kernel, making it faster but less robust to noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume grid V of dimensions Nx 	imes Ny 	imes Nz, stored in row-major order (x fastest, y middle, z slowest). Output: A gradient vector grid G of the same dimensions, where each voxel stores a 3D vector (gx, gy, gz). Data Structures: The gradient array is a 1D float array of size Nx Ny Nz 	imes 3, with interleaved RGB components per voxel: gradient[idx3] is gx, gradient[idx3+1] is gy, gradient[idx3+2] is gz. Alternatively, for GPU storage, gradients are encoded into signed normalized 8-bit textures (e.g., GLRGBA8SNORM) where the direction is mapped to [0,1] and magnitude may be stored in an alpha channel or separate buffer. Parameters: h: The physical distance between voxels along the axis of differentiation (voxel size). gradmagnitudemodifier: A scalar multiplier applied to the gradient magnitude before clamping (typical value depends on data range, often 1.0 or scaled to fit texture range). Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate over every voxel (x, y, z) in the volume grid. 2. For each axis, compute the central difference approximation of the partial derivative. X-component: Sample the voxel at (x-1, y, z) and (x+1, y, z). gx =  rac{V(x+1, y, z) - V(x-1, y, z)}{2h} Y-component: Sample the voxel at (x, y-1, z) and (x, y+1, z). gy =  rac{V(x, y+1, z) - V(x, y-1, z)}{2h} Z-component: Sample the voxel at (x, y, z-1) and (x, y, z+1). gz =  rac{V(x, y, z+1) - V(x, y, z-1)}{2h} 3. If the gradient is used solely for surface normals, the division by 2h may be omitted, as the vector is normalized immediately after. 4. Handle boundary conditions: At data boundaries, the gradient is undefined because neighbors are missing. Common handling includes padding the volume by repeating boundary values. 5. Normalize the resulting vector \mathbf{g} = (gx, gy, gz) to obtain the surface normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{n} =  rac{\mathbf{g}}{\|\mathbf{g}\|} \quad 	ext{if } \|\mathbf{g}\| > \epsilon If \|\mathbf{g}\| \le \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}), set \mathbf{n} = (0, 0, 0) or a default normal. 6. Store \mathbf{n} (and optionally magnitude) in the output gradient grid or texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecentraldifferencegradients(volume, resolution, voxelsize): """ Computes the gradient vector for each voxel in a scalar volume using central differences. Args: volume: 3D list of shape (resx, resy, resz) containing scalar values. resolution: Tuple (resx, resy, resz). voxelsize: Float representing the physical distance between voxels (h). Returns: gradients: 3D list of shape (resx, resy, resz, 3) containing normalized gradient vectors. """ resx, resy, resz = resolution gradients = [[[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resz)] for in range(resy)] for in range(resx)] inv2h = 1.0 / (2.0 voxelsize) for z in range(resz): for y in range(resy): for x in range(resx): # Pad boundaries by repeating edge values xprev = x - 1 if x > 0 else 0 xnext = x + 1 if x < resx - 1 else resx - 1 yprev = y - 1 if y > 0 else 0 ynext = y + 1 if y < resy - 1 else resy - 1 zprev = z - 1 if z > 0 else 0 znext = z + 1 if z < resz - 1 else resz - 1 gx = (volume[xnext][y][z] - volume[xprev][y][z]) inv2h gy = (volume[x][ynext][z] - volume[x][yprev][z]) inv2h gz = (volume[x][y][znext] - volume[x][y][zprev]) inv2h length = (gxgx + gygy + gzgz) 0.5 if length > 1e-6: gradients[x][y][z][0] = gx / length gradients[x][y][z][1] = gy / length gradients[x][y][z][2] = gz / length else: gradients[x][y][z][0] = 0.0 gradients[x][y][z][1] = 0.0 gradients[x][y][z][2] = 0.0 return gradients Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Access: The standard central difference formula requires neighbors at i-1 and i+1. Accessing these at the grid edges causes out-of-bounds memory errors unless clamping, padding, or reflection is applied. Zero Magnitude: In homogeneous regions, the gradient magnitude is zero. Normalization must check for this to avoid division by zero. Noise Sensitivity: Because it uses only 6 neighbors, the central difference operator produces less smooth gradients compared to operators using more voxels (like Sobel), making it sensitive to high-frequency noise. Visual Artifacts: Artifacts similar to those from trilinear interpolation resampling may occur. A compute shader pass that calculates gradients for all voxels and stores them in a gradient map image, including magnitude and direction. It uses a 3D image buffer with rgba8snorm layout, storing normalized gradient direction in x, y, z and magnitude in w. The magnitude is clamped to [0, 1] after applying a modifier. A pre-processing step using the Sobel operator to detect edges within the volume and compute gradients. Gradient magnitude modulates voxel opacity to hide homogeneous regions, and gradient direction is used for shading. A variant of central differencing for gradient computation that clamps offset positions to the current region to avoid additional ray traversals. It computes six additional basis reconstruction samples at positions offset from the current sample by a distance proportional to the region's sample rate. Gradients are not necessarily continuous at level boundaries because the offset size can change. Accurate central differencing requires tracing 6 additional rays per sample via infinitesimal rays to find containing regions, which is expensive. The clamped version removes ray traversals but reduces quality. A method where gradients are precomputed and stored alongside scalar values in a flat array. For each voxel at (x, y, z), neighbors are fetched using a safe access function (returning 0.0 for out-of-bounds indices, effectively zero-padding boundaries). The gradient vector is normalized and stored in a union with the scalar value. Template parameter defines the cubic volume dimension, with a typical code value of 60 (CUBESIZE). VoxelVertex is a union containing vec4 xyzw and vec3 gradient, where xyzw.w stores the scalar volume value and gradient stores the precomputed normalized gradient vector. Data is stored in a flat std::array<VoxelVertex, cube(length)> mdata indexed by cartesiantoindex(v, length) = v.z length length + v.y length + v.x. Visualization of interfaces between two regions of different density by projecting through a matrix of gradient magnitude values derived from voxel density. The estimate of an interface between regions at each voxel is defined by a surface normal N and surface strength |N|, derived from voxel density. A refractive index-only image is obtained by projecting directly through the surface magnitude information. Surface normal N = (Nx, Ny, Nz) is approximated by a finite difference of neighbouring densities, and surface strength |N| is the L2-norm of N. Surfaces may appear to lie at sub-voxel accuracy because they are defined by fractional values at each voxel, allowing visualization of diffuse transitions not possible with binary representation. Computes the curl 
abla 	imes \mathbf{F} at every active voxel of a vector grid using central differences. It initializes a GradStencil with the grid tree, iterates over all active voxels, moves the stencil to the current coordinate, and computes the x, y, and z components of the curl using the formulas. The result is stored in a dictionary keyed by coordinate and built into a result grid with a zero vector background and the original grid's voxel size. The formulas are: curlx = (v[4][3] - v[5][3] - v[6][2] + v[7][2]) 0.5, curly = (v[6][1] - v[7][1] - v[2][3] + v[3][3]) 0.5, curlz = (v[2][2] - v[3][2] - v[4][1] + v[5][1]) 0.5. The scalar multiplier 0.5 represents 1/(2 	imes 	ext{voxel\size}) in index space. Computes the Laplacian 
abla^2 f at every active voxel using a 6-point stencil in index space. It initializes a GradStencil with the grid tree, iterates over all active voxels, moves the stencil to the current coordinate, computes the Laplacian scalar using the stencil, stores it in a dictionary keyed by coordinate, and builds the result grid with a zero background and the original grid's voxel size. Computes the Euclidean norm |\mathbf{v}| at every active voxel of a vector grid. It iterates over all active voxels, computes the norm of the vector, stores it in a dictionary keyed by coordinate, and builds the result grid with a zero background and the original grid's voxel size. Gradient estimation taking four neighboring voxels as input. For a voxel V at (x, y, z), the gradient components are calculated using forward differences: 
ablax = V{x+1,y,z} - V{x,y,z}, 
ablay = V{x,y+1,z} - V{x,y,z}, 
ablaz = V{x,y,z+1} - V{x,y,z}. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels, as each voxel is processed once with a constant number of operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the gradient grid, typically 3 times the size of the scalar volume if stored as floats. Performance: Requires 6 sampling points per voxel. It is faster than Sobel3D (which requires 27 samples) but provides lower quality gradient descriptions. Strengths: Simple to implement, low computational cost, suitable for real-time applications where noise is low or pre-smoothing is applied. Limitations: Sensitive to noise due to small stencil size; boundary handling requires care; less smooth than larger kernels. In volume rendering, the method was popularized for adding visual cues like directional light and Phong shading to ray-traced volumes. It is used in scientific visualization tools and libraries, such as CGAL's isosurfacing modules. name: Gradient Map Generation
head: Gradient Map Compute Shader
body:
Gradient Map Generation is a GPU compute shader pass that calculates gradients for all voxels in a 3D scalar volume and stores them in a gradient map image, including magnitude and direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume texture containing voxel intensities. Output: A 3D image buffer gradientmap with layout rgba8snorm. Data Structures: The gradientmap stores the normalized gradient direction in the x, y, z components and the gradient magnitude in the w component. Algorithm Steps: 1. Get the dimensions of the gradient map image. 2. Compute the gradient vector 
abla f = ( rac{\partial f}{\partial x},  rac{\partial f}{\partial y},  rac{\partial f}{\partial z}) for the current voxel using finite differences. 3. Calculate the gradient magnitude m = \|
abla f\| \cdot k, where k is gradmagnitudemodifier, and clamp the result to [0, 1]. 4. Normalize the gradient vector to obtain the direction \mathbf{n} = 
abla f / \|
abla f\|. 5. Store the normalized gradient direction in the x, y, z components and the magnitude in the w component into the gradientmap image at the current global invocation ID. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradientmap(volume: Texture3D, gradientmap: Image3D, volumedims: vec3, gradmagnitudemodifier: float): x, y, z = getglobalinvocationid() # Implements getgradient from using central differences with boundary clamping fx = sample(volume, clamp(x + 1, 0, volumedims.x - 1), y, z) - sample(volume, clamp(x - 1, 0, volumedims.x - 1), y, z) fy = sample(volume, x, clamp(y + 1, 0, volumedims.y - 1), z) - sample(volume, x, clamp(y - 1, 0, volumedims.y - 1), z) fz = sample(volume, x, y, clamp(z + 1, 0, volumedims.z - 1)) - sample(volume, x, y, clamp(z - 1, 0, volumedims.z - 1)) gradvec = vec3(fx, fy, fz) # Calculate magnitude, apply modifier, clamp to [0, 1] magnitude = length(gradvec) clampedmag = clamp(magnitude gradmagnitudemodifier, 0.0, 1.0) # Normalize direction if magnitude > 1e-6: normalizeddir = normalize(gradvec) else: normalizeddir = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Store in gradient map: xyz = direction, w = magnitude gradientmap[x, y, z] = vec4(normalizeddir, clampedmag) Parameters: gradmagnitudemodifier: A scalar multiplier for the gradient magnitude. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient: Voxels with constant intensity produce a zero gradient vector, causing division by zero during normalization. The implementation must check for this and store a default zero vector. Boundaries: Finite differences at the volume boundaries require index clamping or one-sided difference stencils to prevent out-of-bounds texture fetches. This method extends Gradient Map Generation by integrating light propagation logic directly into the gradient computation shader. It samples the 3D volume, computes spatial gradients using central differences, transforms these gradients between world and view spaces, and initiates a per-pixel light propagation pass across volume layers. It is chosen when view-space gradient transformation and layer-wise accumulation are required in a single pass to reduce memory traffic. It builds on Gradient Map Generation by combining gradient calculation with light propagation. This variant adds a post-processing step to the gradient map. After the initial gradient computation, a second compute shader applies a 3x3x3 box filter (averaging) to the computed gradient field to reduce noise. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels in the volume, as each voxel is processed once. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output gradient map, with the input volume read-only. Performance: Performance is bound by memory bandwidth due to reading the volume texture and writing the gradient map per invocation. Strengths: Enables parallel gradient computation on the GPU and produces a reusable texture for subsequent lighting passes. Limitations: Requires additional memory for the gradient map; boundary handling can introduce artifacts; magnitude scaling requires tuning. Gradient Map Generation is implemented as a compute shader pass that calculates gradients for all voxels in the volume and stores them in a gradient map image.
