name: Volume Gradient Computation and Light Propagation Compute Shader
head: Gradient Computation & Light Propagation Compute Shader
body: This method is a compute shader pass that samples a 3D volume texture, computes spatial gradients using central differences, transforms gradients between world and view spaces, and initiates a per-pixel light propagation pass across volume layers. It builds on Gradient Map Generation by extending the gradient calculation to include light propagation logic within the same shader invocation, allowing for efficient view-space gradient transformation and layer-wise accumulation. Inputs and Outputs: The shader takes a 3D volume texture as input and produces multiple output images (lighting, depth, color, etc.) via storage images. It operates on a per-pixel basis for a specific layer of the volume, dispatched via a compute shader. Data Structures: Uniform Buffer Object (UBO) (binding 0, std140 layout): mat4 viewmatrix, mat4 inverseviewmatrix, vec3 middleoffrontplanevs, vec3 lightcolor, ivec2 planepixelsize, vec2 planeextentvs, vec3 lightVSPos, float voxelDepth, float distancebetweenplanes, int planecount. Push Constants (binding 0): int layerindex. Input Samplers (binding 1-6): lbin, ldbin, cbin, mbin, vpbin, vdbin (all sampler2D). Output Images (binding 7-12): lbout, ldbout, cbout, mbout, vpbout, vdbout (all rgba32f image2D). Volume Texture (binding 13): sampler3D volume. Transfer Functions (binding 14-16): sampler2D volumetransfer, sampler2D mediumtransfer, sampler1D refractiontransfertex. Numbered Steps: 1. Thread Dispatch Setup: The shader uses a local group size of 2x2 with derivative group quads enabled for efficient gradient computation. 2. UV Coordinate Computation: Compute the UV coordinates for the current pixel based on the global invocation ID and plane pixel size. 3. Layer Z Position Computation: Determine the current layer's Z position in view space. 4. World Space Position Computation: Convert the plane UV and Z position to world space. 5. Volume Texture Sampling: Sample the volume texture at the computed world position, applying the necessary coordinate transformation. 6. Central Difference Gradient Computation: Compute spatial gradients using central differences along the X, Y, and Z axes. 7. Gradient Transformation: Transform the world-space gradient to view space. 8. Refraction Gradient Computation: Compute the refraction gradient by transforming the difference vector to view space and normalizing it. 9. Light Propagation: Initiate the per-pixel light propagation pass across volume layers. Formulas: UV coordinates: uv = (global\id.xy + 0.5) / plane\pixel\size Layer Z position: current\z = middle\of\front\plane\vs.z - layer\index \times distance\between\planes View-space position: pos\vs = (2.0 \times plane\extent\vs \times (middle\of\front\plane\vs.xy + uv - 0.5), current\z) World-space position: pos\ws = (inverse\view\matrix \times (pos\vs, 1.0)).xyz + 0.5 Volume texture coordinates: coord = (pos\ws - 0.5) \times (voxelDepth, voxelDepth, 1.0) + 0.5 Central differences: s1 = sample(volume, coord - dist), s2 = sample(volume, coord + dist) for each axis, where dist = distance\between\planes World-space gradient: grad\ws = (s2 - s1) / (2.0 \times dist) View-space gradient: grad\vs = view\matrix \times grad\ws Volume gradient difference: diff = s2 - s1 Transformed volume gradient: diff = inverse(transpose(view\matrix)) \times diff Normalized volume gradient: diff = safe\normalize(diff) Parameters: ubo.voxelDepth: Scaling factor applied to X and Y dimensions when transforming world positions to volume texture coordinates. ubo.distancebetweenplanes: Spacing between volume layers in world space, used as the step size for central difference gradient computation. ubo.planepixelsize: Resolution of the output plane in pixels, used to normalize globalid.xy to UV coordinates. ubo.middleoffrontplanevs.z: View-space Z coordinate of the front plane, used as the base Z for layer indexing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero in Intersect Plane: When the direction vector's Z component is near zero, division by zero can occur. This is handled by clamping the denominator to 1e-5 with sign preservation. Zero-Length Vector Normalization: When normalizing vectors, if the length is less than 1e-6, the function returns vec3(0.0) to avoid division by zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradientandlightpropagation(globalid, layerindex, ubo, volume): # 1. Thread dispatch uses 2x2 local groups with derivative group quads # layout(localsizex = 2, localsizey = 2) in; layout(derivativegroupquadsNV) in; # 2. Compute UV coordinates uv = (globalid.xy + 0.5) / ubo.planepixelsize # 3. Compute current layer Z position currentz = ubo.middleoffrontplanevs.z - layerindex ubo.distancebetweenplanes # 4. Convert plane UV and Z to world space posvs = vec3(2.0 ubo.planeextentvs (ubo.middleoffrontplanevs.xy + uv - 0.5), currentz) posws = (ubo.inverseviewmatrix vec4(posvs, 1.0)).xyz + 0.5 # 5. Sample volume texture with coordinate transform coord = (posws - 0.5) vec3(ubo.voxelDepth, ubo.voxelDepth, 1.0) + 0.5 density = sample(volume, coord).r # 6. Compute central differences for x, y, z axes dist = ubo.distancebetweenplanes s1x = sample(volume, coord + vec3(-dist, 0, 0)).r s2x = sample(volume, coord + vec3(dist, 0, 0)).r s1y = sample(volume, coord + vec3(0, -dist, 0)).r s2y = sample(volume, coord + vec3(0, dist, 0)).r s1z = sample(volume, coord + vec3(0, 0, -dist)).r s2z = sample(volume, coord + vec3(0, 0, dist)).r # 7. Compute refraction gradient gradws = vec3(s2x - s1x, s2y - s1y, s2z - s1z) / (2.0 dist) gradvs = mat3(ubo.viewmatrix) gradws # 8. Compute volume gradient diff = vec3(s2x - s1x, s2y - s1y, s2z - s1z) diff = inverse(transpose(mat3(ubo.viewmatrix))) diff diff = safenormalize(diff) # 9. Light propagation pass across volume layers # The sources do not specify the exact light propagation logic. store(lbout, globalid.xy, vec4(density, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0)) store(ldbout, globalid.xy, vec4(gradvs, 1.0)) store(cbout, globalid.xy, vec4(diff, 1.0)) # Other outputs (mbout, vpbout, vdbout) would be populated similarly. def safenormalize(v): length = vectorlength(v) if length < 1e-6: return vec3(0.0) return v / length Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Gradient-based Diffuse Lighting with Alpha Blending
head: Gradient-based Diffuse Lighting
body: This method computes diffuse lighting for a scalar volume by estimating surface normals from voxel gradients and compositing the lit color into a framebuffer using front-to-back alpha blending. It integrates gradient estimation, lighting application, and compositing into a single per-voxel step rather than storing precomputed gradients separately. Inputs: parent: Volume data structure containing: width: Integer width of the volume grid (bounds for x and y dimensions). zSize: Integer depth (z-dimension) of the volume grid. v2: 1D array of voxel values (integers, typically 0-255). transfera: 1D array of 32-bit integers storing alpha values indexed by voxel value. transferrgb: 1D array of 32-bit integers storing RGB values indexed by voxel value. light: 3D vector (light[0], light[1], light[2]) representing the light direction. outa: Accumulated alpha (float, initialized to 0.0). rgb: Accumulated color (array of 3 floats, initialized to 0.0). Outputs: Updated outa: Accumulated alpha. Updated rgb: Accumulated color. Data Structures: Voxel values are accessed via linear indexing using coordinates ida, idb, idc. The memory layout follows v(idc, ida + idb width), implying a linear index of idc (width width) + ida + idb width. Neighbor indices are clamped to valid ranges: lower bounds to 0, ida2 and idb2 to width - 1, and idc2 to zSize - 1. Steps: 1. Gradient Estimation: Calculate the 3D gradient vector \mathbf{g} = (gx, gy, gz) using central differences on the least significant byte (0-255) of voxel values, normalized by 255.0. gx = \frac{V(idc, id{a2}, idb) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} - \frac{V(idc, id{a1}, idb) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} gy = \frac{V(idc, ida, id{b2}) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} - \frac{V(idc, ida, id{b1}) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} gz = \frac{V(id{c2}, ida, idb) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} - \frac{V(id{c1}, ida, idb) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} where V(idc, ida, idb) returns the clamped voxel value. 2. Gradient Normalization: Calculate magnitude |\mathbf{g}| = \sqrt{gx^2 + gy^2 + gz^2}. If |\mathbf{g}| > 0, divide each component by |\mathbf{g}|; otherwise, set all components to 0. 3. Diffuse Lighting Factor: Calculate D = \max(gx lx + gy ly + gz lz, 0). 4. Transfer Function Lookup: Extract alpha: \alpha{src} = \frac{\text{parent.transfer\a}[v] \ \& \ 0x000000FF}{255}. Extract RGB from rgbval = parent.transferrgb[v]: R{src} = \frac{(rgb\val \ \& \ 0x00FF0000) \gg 16}{255.0}, \quad G{src} = \frac{(rgb\val \ \& \ 0x0000FF00) \gg 8}{255.0}, \quad B{src} = \frac{rgb\val \ \& \ 0x000000FF}{255.0}. 5. Lighting Application: Apply diffuse lighting with an ambient term of 0.25, clamped to 1.0: R{lit} = \min(D \cdot R{src} + 0.25 \cdot R{src}, 1.0) G{lit} = \min(D \cdot G{src} + 0.25 \cdot G{src}, 1.0) B{lit} = \min(D \cdot B{src} + 0.25 \cdot B{src}, 1.0). 6. Alpha Blending (Front-to-Back): Composite the lit color: R{out} = (1.0 - \alpha{out}) \cdot R{lit} \cdot \alpha{src} + R{out} G{out} = (1.0 - \alpha{out}) \cdot G{lit} \cdot \alpha{src} + G{out} B{out} = (1.0 - \alpha{out}) \cdot B{lit} \cdot \alpha{src} + B{out}. Update accumulated alpha: \alpha{out} = (1.0 - \alpha{out}) \cdot \alpha{src} + \alpha{out}. 7. Output Packing: Convert final RGB to 8-bit integers and pack into a 32-bit integer with opaque alpha: R{final} = \lfloor R{out} \cdot 255 \rfloor, \quad G{final} = \lfloor G{out} \cdot 255 \rfloor, \quad B{final} = \lfloor B{out} \cdot 255 \rfloor. Pixel = (255 \ll 24) \ | \ (R{final} \ll 16) \ | \ (G{final} \ll 8) \ | \ B{final}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientbaseddiffuselightingwithalphablending( parent, light, outa, rgb, ida, idb, idc): width = parent.width zsize = parent.zSize height = width # Derived from clamping rule: idb2 clamped to width - 1 def getvoxel(a, b, c): a = max(0, min(a, width - 1)) b = max(0, min(b, height - 1)) c = max(0, min(c, zsize - 1)) idx = c (width height) + a + b width return (parent.v2[idx] & 0xFF) / 255.0 # 1. Gradient Estimation gx = getvoxel(ida + 1, idb, idc) - getvoxel(ida - 1, idb, idc) gy = getvoxel(ida, idb + 1, idc) - getvoxel(ida, idb - 1, idc) gz = getvoxel(ida, idb, idc + 1) - getvoxel(ida, idb, idc - 1) # 2. Gradient Normalization gradl = (gx2 + gy2 + gz2)0.5 if gradl > 0: nx, ny, nz = gx / gradl, gy / gradl, gz / gradl else: nx, ny, nz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # 3. Diffuse Lighting Factor diffuse = max(nx light[0] + ny light[1] + nz light[2], 0) # 4. Transfer Function Lookup currentidx = idc (width height) + ida + idb width currentval = parent.v2[currentidx] aa = (parent.transfera[currentval] & 0x000000FF) / 255 rgbval = parent.transferrgb[currentval] vvred = ((rgbval & 0x00FF0000) >> 16) / 255.0 vvgreen = ((rgbval & 0x0000FF00) >> 8) / 255.0 vvblue = (rgbval & 0x000000FF) / 255.0 # 5. Lighting Application vvred = min(diffuse vvred + 0.25 vvred, 1.0) vvgreen = min(diffuse vvgreen + 0.25 vvgreen, 1.0) vvblue = min(diffuse vvblue + 0.25 vvblue, 1.0) # 6. Alpha Blending rgb[0] = (1.0 - outa) vvred aa + rgb[0] rgb[1] = (1.0 - outa) vvgreen aa + rgb[1] rgb[2] = (1.0 - outa) vvblue aa + rgb[2] outa = (1.0 - outa) aa + outa return outa, rgb Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel for the lighting and blending step, requiring 6 neighbor lookups for gradient estimation and constant-time transfer function access. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per voxel for the current step, plus storage for the transfer functions and volume data. Performance: The method is computationally lightweight per voxel, suitable for CPU-based direct volume rendering as indicated by the source repository. The 6 neighbor lookups and transfer function accesses add overhead compared to simple alpha blending. Strengths: Provides surface-like shading effects without explicit surface extraction and is straightforward to implement. Limitations: Gradient estimation via central differences can be noisy in low-resolution volumes, and boundary clamping may distort normals at edges. The method assumes a specific memory layout and transfer function format. The method originates from a direct volume rendering implementation on the CPU, specifically documented in the browarsoftware/directvolumerenderingcpu repository. It combines gradient-based normal estimation with standard front-to-back alpha compositing to render scalar volumes. browarsoftware/directvolumerenderingcpu, https://github.com/browarsoftware/directvolumerenderingcpu, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Analytic Gradient Computation
head: Analytic Basis Gradients, Analytic Derivatives of Basis Reconstruction
body: Analytic Gradient Computation computes gradient vectors for local shading (BRDF) in volume rendering using analytic derivatives of the basis reconstruction function, avoiding additional samples or ray traversals. It sets itself apart from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by requiring no additional sample evaluations or ray traversals, relying solely on the data values already loaded for the scalar reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The scalar volume data values Cv and basis function parameters (cell width Cw, control point coordinates Cp) used for the current sample evaluation at position p. Output: The gradient vector \nabla B(p) = [\frac{\partial B}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial B}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial B}{\partial z}]. Data Structures: The method operates on the same buffers used for scalar reconstruction. No additional storage is required for gradient samples. The gradient is computed per sample point during ray traversal. Formulas: The gradient of the reconstructed scalar field B(p) is derived from the quotient rule applied to the basis reconstruction equation. For the x-component: \frac{\partial B(p)}{\partial x} = \frac{\sumC \hat{H}C(p) \sumC \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} Cv - \sumC \hat{H}C(p) Cv \sumC \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x}}{(\sumC \hat{H}C(p))^2} The partial derivative of the individual basis function component \hat{H}C(p) with respect to x is: \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} = \hat{h}\left(\frac{|C{py} - py|}{Cw}\right) \hat{h}\left(\frac{|C{pz} - pz|}{Cw}\right) \chi(x) \frac{1}{Cw} Where: \hat{h}(\cdot) is the 1D basis function component. Cw is the cell width. C{py}, C{pz} are the y and z coordinates of the control point C. \chi(t) is the sign function defined as: \chi(t) = \begin{cases} -1, & \text{if } C{pt} - pt \geq 0 \\ 1, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} In the context of \frac{\partial B}{\partial x}, the argument t corresponds to the x-dimension relative to the control point, i.e., C{px} - px. The source text explicitly writes \chi(x) in the derivative formula but defines \chi(t) with a generic argument. The sign depends on the relative position of the sample point to the control point in the dimension being differentiated. Steps: 1. For each contributing control point C, evaluate the 1D basis function \hat{h} for the absolute normalized distances in all three dimensions: hx = \hat{h}(|C{px} - px|/Cw), hy = \hat{h}(|C{py} - py|/Cw), hz = \hat{h}(|C{pz} - pz|/Cw). 2. Compute the basis function value \hat{H}C(p) = hx hy hz and accumulate SH = \sum \hat{H}C(p) and S{Hv} = \sum \hat{H}C(p) Cv. 3. Compute the partial derivative \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} using hy, hz, and \chi(C{px} - px), then accumulate S{dHx} = \sum \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} and S{dHx\v} = \sum \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} Cv. Repeat for y and z dimensions to get S{dHy}, S{dHy\v}, S{dHz}, S{dHz\v}. 4. Compute the final gradient component using the quotient rule: \frac{\partial B}{\partial x} = \frac{SH S{dHx\v} - S{Hv} S{dHx}}{SH^2}. Repeat for y and z. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeanalyticgradient(p, controlpoints, Cw, basisfunch): sumH = 0.0 sumHv = 0.0 sumdHx = 0.0 sumdHxv = 0.0 sumdHy = 0.0 sumdHyv = 0.0 sumdHz = 0.0 sumdHzv = 0.0 for C in controlpoints: dx = C.px - p.x dy = C.py - p.y dz = C.pz - p.z hx = basisfunch(abs(dx) / Cw) hy = basisfunch(abs(dy) / Cw) hz = basisfunch(abs(dz) / Cw) HC = hx hy hz sumH += HC sumHv += HC C.v chix = -1 if dx >= 0 else 1 chiy = -1 if dy >= 0 else 1 chiz = -1 if dz >= 0 else 1 dHCx = hy hz chix (1.0 / Cw) sumdHx += dHCx sumdHxv += dHCx C.v dHCy = hx hz chiy (1.0 / Cw) sumdHy += dHCy sumdHyv += dHCy C.v dHCz = hx hy chiz (1.0 / Cw) sumdHz += dHCz sumdHzv += dHCz C.v if sumH == 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) dHdx = (sumH sumdHxv - sumHv sumdHx) / (sumH sumH) dHdy = (sumH sumdHyv - sumHv sumdHy) / (sumH sumH) dHdz = (sumH sumdHzv - sumHv sumdHz) / (sumH sumH) return (dHdx, dHdy, dHdz) Parameters: Cw: Cell width. Typical values depend on the grid resolution and level of detail. Basis function \hat{h}: Typically a cubic B-spline or similar smooth function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Analytic gradients are not continuously differentiable, leading to shading artifacts at cell and level boundaries. Division by zero if \sum \hat{H}C(p) = 0; guard against this. Precision issues near cell boundaries where the sign function \chi changes. Computes exact gradient vectors for local shading by evaluating analytic derivatives of the underlying box-spline basis function. It sets itself apart from this method by specifically exploiting the symmetry and structure of Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) box-spluses to reuse the 19 samples already fetched for scalar evaluation, whereas finite difference methods require six additional full spline evaluations. Choose it when rendering FCC-structured data to maximize sample reuse. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, same as scalar evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample for gradient components. Performance: Much faster than both central difference variants, which require 6 additional basis reconstruction samples and ray traversals. Quality: Provides superior quality to clamped central differences. May be slightly worse than accurate central differences due to discontinuities in the derivative at boundaries, but the trade-off favors speed. When to use: When performance is critical and the discontinuities at cell boundaries are acceptable or mitigated by other means. Default in the ExaBricks renderer. When not to use: When continuous gradients are strictly required and performance is not a constraint. Originated in the context of ray tracing structured AMR data using ExaBricks. The method was introduced to enable efficient local shading with BRDFs without the prohibitive cost of additional samples required by finite difference methods. It leverages the mathematical structure of the basis reconstruction function to provide analytic derivatives. Ray Tracing Structured AMR Data Using ExaBricks, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~wald/Publications/2020/exabrick/exabrick.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Analytic Gradient Computation via Box-Spline Derivatives
head: Derivative Spline Evaluation, Exact Gradient for FCC
body: This method computes exact gradient vectors for local shading in volume rendering by evaluating analytic derivatives of the underlying box-spline basis function, avoiding the inaccuracies and extra memory bandwidth of finite differences. It sets itself apart from Analytic Gradient Computation by specifically exploiting the symmetry and structure of Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) box-splines to reuse the 19 samples already fetched for scalar evaluation, whereas finite difference methods require six additional full spline evaluations. Inputs: Volume data V defined on an FCC grid. Evaluation point x in continuous space. The set of direction vectors \Xi{\text{fcc}} defining the FCC box-spline M{\text{fcc}}. Outputs: Gradient vector \nabla(V M{\text{fcc}})(x). Data Structures: The scalar value is computed as s(x) = V M{\text{fcc}}(x). The gradient is computed using three directional derivatives d{110}, d{101}, d{011} along vectors \xi{110}, \xi{101}, \xi{011}. Derivative kernels M\xi are defined as sums of two box-splines. Due to symmetry, only the BB-coefficients for M{110} are explicitly stored/computed; others are derived via permutation. M{110} requires handling three polynomial piece types: \tau0, \tau2, \tau4. Steps: 1. Fetch Samples: Retrieve the 19 voxel values V required for the evaluation of the FCC box-spline M{\text{fcc}} at point x. These samples cover the support of M{\text{fcc}}. The support of each derivative kernel M\xi is a subset of the support of M{\text{fcc}}, so no additional texture fetches are needed. 2. Compute Directional Derivatives: Calculate the three directional derivatives d\xi = V M\xi for \xi \in \{\xi{110}, \xi{101}, \xi{011}\}. The directional derivative of the spline s = V M{\text{fcc}} along \xi is given by D\xi(V M{\text{fcc}}) = V M\xi. The kernel M\xi is defined as M\xi(x) = 2M{\Xi{\text{rec}} \setminus \{\xi\}}(x + \xic) - 2M{\Xi{\text{rec}} \setminus \{\xi\}}(x + \xic - \xi), where \Xi{\text{rec}} is the set of directions for the reconstructed spline, and \xic is a centering vector. Evaluate M\xi using the de Casteljau algorithm. Since M\xi is quadratic, this is computationally efficient. For M{110}, determine the polynomial piece type (\tau0, \tau2, \text{or } \tau4) based on the local grid position. Apply the corresponding precomputed BB-coefficients for that piece type to the fetched samples. Use permutational symmetries to compute M{101} and M{011} from the coefficients of M{110}. 3. Reconstruct Gradient: Combine the directional derivatives to form the Cartesian gradient vector: \nabla(V M{\text{fcc}}) = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} d{110} + d{101} - d{011} \\ d{110} + d{011} - d{101} \\ d{101} + d{011} - d{110} \end{bmatrix} where d\xi = V M\xi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeanalyticgradientfcc(V, x, gridinfo): # Map continuous point x to the 19 FCC grid indices covering the support of Mfcc. indices = maptofccsupport(x, gridinfo) samples = [V[idx] for idx in indices] # Determine polynomial piece type for M110 based on local fractional coordinates. # Not given in the sources. piecetype = getpolynomialpiecetype(x, gridinfo) # Retrieve BB-coefficients for M110 from Table 1 in based on piecetype. # Not given in the sources. coeffs110 = getbbcoefficientsM110(piecetype) # Evaluate d110 = V M110 using the dot product of samples and coefficients. d110 = sum(s c for s, c in zip(samples, coeffs110)) # Evaluate d101 and d011 using permutational symmetries of M110. # Not given in the sources. coeffs101 = permutecoefficients(coeffs110, '101') coeffs011 = permutecoefficients(coeffs110, '011') d101 = sum(s c for s, c in zip(samples, coeffs101)) d011 = sum(s c for s, c in zip(samples, coeffs011)) # Reconstruct Cartesian gradient vector. gradient = ( (d110 + d101 - d011) / 2.0, (d110 + d011 - d101) / 2.0, (d101 + d011 - d110) / 2.0) return gradient Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Finite difference methods suffer from rounding errors if the offset \delta is too small, or poor approximation if \delta is too large. The analytic method avoids this entirely. Polynomial Piece Identification: Correctly identifying the polynomial piece type (\tau0, \tau2, \tau4) is critical for using the correct BB-coefficients. Support Mismatch: While the support of M\xi is a subset of M{\text{fcc}}, care must be taken to align the coefficients with the correct fetched samples. This variant uses the analytic gradient to compute normal vectors for isosurface rendering. It is preferred over finite difference normals because it always yields accurate results regardless of step size, whereas finite difference normals are sensitive to offset selection (too small causes rounding errors, too large causes approximation errors). It offers a speed-up of 1.2x to 1.3x on standard datasets (MRI-Head, VisMale, CT-Head) due to lower data fetch overhead. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is dominated by the evaluation of the quadratic derivative kernels using the de Casteljau algorithm. Memory complexity is identical to scalar evaluation as it reuses the same 19 samples. Measured Performance: The analytic method is faster than finite difference because it avoids six additional spline evaluations. Speed-ups observed: MRI-Head 1.3x, VisMale 1.3x, CT-Head 1.2x, Carp 1.0x. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Exact gradients, lower memory bandwidth usage than finite differences, superior isosurface quality. Limitations: Requires precomputed BB-coefficients for derivative kernels and polynomial piece types. The method is specific to FCC box-spluses. When to Use: Use when high-quality normals are required for shading or isosurface rendering and performance is a concern. Do not use if the volume data is not represented by FCC box-spluses. This method was introduced by Minho Kim and Jürgen Peters in their 2012 paper "GPU Isosurface Raycasting of FCC Datasets". It addresses the limitations of finite difference gradient estimation in the context of FCC grid volume rendering, leveraging the mathematical properties of box-spluses to provide exact derivatives. GPU Isosurface Raycasting of FCC Datasets, https://minho-kim-uos.github.io/papers/kim12gpu.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Analytic Gradient Computation for Triangle Distributions
head: Analytical Triangle FT, Closed-Form Triangle Fourier Transform and Gradients, Triangle FT
body: This method computes the exact Fourier Transform \hat{u}\mathcal{T} and its spatial gradients for a single triangle \mathcal{T} defined by vertices (\mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3). It enables differentiable rendering by providing analytic derivatives of the basis reconstruction function, avoiding additional samples or ray traversals. It sets itself apart from Analytic Gradient Computation via Box-Spline Derivatives by operating on explicit mesh geometry (triangles) rather than implicit grid-based basis functions, making it suitable for sparse or structured surface representations in volume rendering contexts like fluorescence microscopy. Inputs: Triangle vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 \in \mathbb{R}^3; frequency vector \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: Fourier Transform value \hat{u}\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{\xi}); Gradient of the transform with respect to vertex positions \frac{\partial \hat{u}\mathcal{T}}{\partial \mathbf{v}p}. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 3 vectors, each 3 floats. Edges: Derived vectors \mathbf{e}p. Intermediate scalars: Lengths lp, Area A\mathcal{T}, dot products \mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}. Steps: 1. Index Permutation: Set \mathbf{v}4 = \mathbf{v}1 and \mathbf{v}0 = \mathbf{v}3. For p \in \{1, 2, 3\}, define indices p^- = p-1 and p^+ = p+1. 2. Edge Computation: Compute edge vectors opposite to vertex p: \mathbf{e}p = \mathbf{v}{p^-} - \mathbf{v}{p^+}. Compute edge lengths lp = \|\mathbf{e}p\|. 3. Normal and Area: Compute the unnormalized area vector \mathbf{A}{vec} = \mathbf{e}3 \times \mathbf{e}1. The area is A\mathcal{T} = \|\mathbf{A}{vec}\| / 2. The unit normal is \mathbf{N}\mathcal{T} = \mathbf{A}{vec} / (2 A\mathcal{T}). 4. Outward Normals: For each p, compute the non-normalized outward normal to the triangle on edge \mathbf{e}p: \mathbf{w}p = \mathbf{e}p \times \mathbf{N}\mathcal{T}. 5. Gradient of Area: The gradient of the triangle area with respect to vertex \mathbf{v}p is \frac{\partial A\mathcal{T}}{\partial \mathbf{v}p} = -\frac{\mathbf{w}p}{2}. 6. Fourier Transform Calculation: Compute the auxiliary function f\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) using the closed-form expression below. The Fourier Transform is then \hat{u}\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = 2 A\mathcal{T} f\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{\xi}). 7. Gradient of Transform: The gradient of the density function f\mathcal{T} with respect to vertex \mathbf{v}p is given by the specific term arrangement in Equation 10 of the source. Note that the source text contains a complex bracket structure; implementers must follow the exact term arrangement, particularly the last two terms which appear split or duplicated in the garbled text representation. Formulas: The auxiliary function f\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) is defined as: f\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \sum{p=1}^3 \frac{e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^2 (\mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})} - \frac{e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})(\mathbf{e}{p+} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^2} - \frac{i e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}{p-} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})(\mathbf{e}{p+} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})} + \frac{e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}{p-} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^2 (\mathbf{e}{p+} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})} - \frac{e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}{p-} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})(\mathbf{e}{p+} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^2} (Note: The source text for Eq 10 contains a complex bracket structure; the implementer must follow the source's specific term arrangement carefully, particularly the last two terms which appear duplicated or split in the garbled text). The gradient of f\mathcal{T} w.r.t \mathbf{v}p is: \frac{\partial f\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{\xi})}{\partial \mathbf{v}p} = \boldsymbol{\xi} \left[ \frac{e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^2 (\mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})} - \frac{e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})(\mathbf{e}{p+} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^2} - \frac{i e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}{p-} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})(\mathbf{e}{p+} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})} + \frac{e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}{p-} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^2 (\mathbf{e}{p+} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})} - \frac{e^{-i \mathbf{v}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}}}{(\mathbf{e}{p-} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})(\mathbf{e}{p+} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^2} \right] (Note: The source text for Eq 10 contains a complex bracket structure; the implementer must follow the source's specific term arrangement carefully, particularly the last two terms which appear duplicated or split in the garbled text). Parameters: \boldsymbol{\xi}: Frequency vector. \mathbf{v}p: Vertex positions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Divergence: The Fourier Transform of a Dirac distribution on a triangle is C^\infty, but significant computational errors arise from numerical approximations. Singularities: Denominators involving (\mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) can approach zero. The source mentions numerical approximations to prevent divergence (Eq 12a, 12b) but does not provide the full algorithmic logic for handling these singularities in the provided text. Implementers must handle cases where \mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \approx 0 using the provided limits: \lim{t \to u} \frac{e^{-it} - e^{-iu}}{(t-u)^2} \quad \text{and} \quad g(u, u, u) = \frac{e^{-iu}}{2}. Precision: Overflow can occur with large box sizes or high frequencies without proper parallelization or normalization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Index Permutation v = np.array([v1, v2, v3]) v4 = v[0] # v1 v0 = v[2] # v3 # 2. Edge Computation # ep = v{p-} - v{p+} # p=1: v0 - v2 # p=2: v1 - v0 # p=3: v2 - v1 e = np.zeros((3, 3)) e[0] = v0 - v[2] # p=1: v{1-}=v0, v{1+}=v2 e[1] = v[0] - v0 # p=2: v{2-}=v1, v{2+}=v0 e[2] = v[1] - v[0] # p=3: v{3-}=v2, v{3+}=v1 # 3. Normal and Area Avec = np.cross(e[2], e[0]) # e3 x e1 AT = np.linalg.norm(Avec) / 2.0 if AT < 1e-12: return 0.0, np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3) # Degenerate triangle NT = Avec / (2.0 AT) # 4. Outward Normals w = np.zeros((3, 3)) for p in range(3): w[p] = np.cross(e[p], NT) # 5. Gradient of Area gradA = -w / 2.0 # 6. Fourier Transform # Compute fT(xi) fT = 0.0 for p in range(3): pminus = (p - 1) % 3 pplus = (p + 1) % 3 dotep = np.dot(e[p], xi) dotepminus = np.dot(e[pminus], xi) dotepplus = np.dot(e[pplus], xi) dotvp = np.dot(v[p], xi) expterm = np.exp(-1j dotvp) # Term 1: exp / (ep. xi)^3 term1 = expterm / (dotep 3) if dotep != 0 else 0.0 # Handle singularity in practice # Term 2: - exp / (ep. xi (e{p+}. xi)^2) term2 = -expterm / (dotep (dotepplus 2)) if (dotep != 0 and dotepplus != 0) else 0.0 # Term 3: - i exp / (e{p-}. xi e{p+}. xi) term3 = -1j expterm / (dotepminus dotepplus) if (dotepminus != 0 and dotepplus != 0) else 0.0 # Term 4: exp / ((e{p-}. xi)^2 e{p+}. xi) term4 = expterm / ((dotepminus 2) dotepplus) if (dotepminus != 0 and dotepplus != 0) else 0.0 # Term 5: - exp / (e{p-}. xi (e{p+}. xi)^2) term5 = -expterm / (dotepminus (dotepplus 2)) if (dotepminus != 0 and dotepplus != 0) else 0.0 fT += term1 + term2 + term3 + term4 + term5 uhat = 2.0 AT fT # 7. Gradient of Transform # The gradient of fT w.r.t vp is xi [same bracket as fT sum term] # Note: The source formula for grad fT is xi multiplied by the sum terms. # We need to compute the gradient for each vertex. gradv = np.zeros((3, 3)) for p in range(3): pminus = (p - 1) % 3 pplus = (p + 1) % 3 dotep = np.dot(e[p], xi) dotepminus = np.dot(e[pminus], xi) dotepplus = np.dot(e[pplus], xi) dotvp = np.dot(v[p], xi) expterm = np.exp(-1j dotvp) # Same terms as fT calculation term1 = expterm / (dotep 3) if dotep != 0 else 0.0 term2 = -expterm / (dotep (dotepplus 2)) if (dotep != 0 and dotepplus != 0) else 0.0 term3 = -1j expterm / (dotepminus dotepplus) if (dotepminus != 0 and dotepplus != 0) else 0.0 term4 = expterm / ((dotepminus 2) dotepplus) if (dotepminus != 0 and dotepplus != 0) else 0.0 term5 = -expterm / (dotepminus (dotepplus 2)) if (dotepminus != 0 and dotepplus != 0) else 0.0 bracketsum = term1 + term2 + term3 + term4 + term5 gradv[p] = xi bracketsum return uhat, gradv[0], gradv[1], gradv[2] A custom CUDA implementation for forward and backward passes of the mesh FT to leverage GPU parallelization. It achieves a \approx 10^3 speedup on an NVIDIA V100 GPU compared to a vectorized CPU implementation. The forward pass complexity is O(N \cdot nt), where N is the number of voxels and nt is the number of triangles. The gradient complexity is O(N \cdot nv), where nv is the number of vertices. Time Complexity: Forward pass is O(N \cdot nt), where N is the number of voxels and nt is the number of triangles. Gradient computation is O(N \cdot nv), where nv is the number of vertices. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA V100 GPU, the CUDA implementation achieves a \approx 10^3 speedup compared to a vectorized CPU implementation. For a 500^3 image (125 million voxels) and a mesh with 10^3-10^4 triangles, the computation is feasible with GPU acceleration but prohibitive on CPU. Scaling: The forward pass scales linearly with the number of triangles for a fixed image size. Strengths: Enables differentiable rendering for 3D fluorescence microscopy; allows for large box sizes before overflow with GPU implementation. Limitations: High computational cost without parallelization; numerical instability near singularities (\mathbf{e}p \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \approx 0) requires careful handling. When to use: When differentiable rendering of triangle meshes in a volume rendering context is required, especially for large-scale 3D microscopy data. When not to use: When computational resources are limited to CPU and the scene is very large; when high precision near singularities is not critical and approximate methods suffice. Originated in the paper "Differentiable Rendering for 3D Fluorescence Microscopy". The method addresses the high computational cost of spectral methods in 3D, which was previously a limitation preventing their widespread use. The authors introduced GPU parallelization and narrow-band approximation to make the computation feasible for large images. name: Gradient Estimation from Samples
head: Gradient-based Volume Shading, Multi-Volume Ray Casting Gradient Estimation and Shading, vtkGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper shading logic
body: This method computes gradient vectors for volume shading by sampling the 3D texture at positions offset from the current reconstruction sample, thereby avoiding the expensive computation of a separate pre-calculated gradient field. It performs the finite difference approximation implicitly during the ray-casting shading pass rather than storing the result in a dedicated array. It differs from the Sobel Operator by using simple forward/backward offsets along axes rather than a 3x3x3 kernel, and from Jacobian Estimation via Central Differences by relying on specific hardware texture sampling offsets provided by the rendering pipeline context. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current sample position in texture coordinates (posX[volNumber-1]), the 3D volume texture (dataSetTexture), color mapping texture (colorTexture), light source parameters (position, attenuation, spot cutoff/exponent/direction), material parameters (shininess), and transformation matrices (eyeToTexture4, transposeTextureToEye). Output: A vec4 final color value for the sample. Data Structures: dataSetTexture: Array of sampler3D objects. Index volNumber accesses the texture for the current volume. colorTexture: Array of sampler1D objects. Max size is 4 on Apple platforms and 5 otherwise. xvec, yvec, zvec: Vectors defining the sampling offsets for the gradient components. cellScale: Scalar scaling factor for coordinate conversion. transposeTextureToEye: Matrix for transforming normals from texture space to eye space. Steps: 1. Gradient Sampling (Forward): Compute the gradient vector g1 by sampling the volume data at positions offset by xvec, yvec, and zvec from the current sample position posX[volNumber-1]. g1.x = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] + xvec[volNumber]).x g1.y = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] + yvec[volNumber]).x g1.z = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] + zvec[volNumber]).x 2. Gradient Sampling (Backward): Compute the gradient vector g2 by sampling the volume data at positions offset by the negative of xvec, yvec, and zvec. g2.x = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] - xvec[volNumber]).x g2.y = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] - yvec[volNumber]).x g2.z = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] - zvec[volNumber]).x 3. Scale Gradient: Convert the gradient from texture coordinates to eye coordinates by scaling g2 with cellScale. g2 = g2 \times cellScale 4. Normalize and Transform Gradient: Calculate length: L = \text{length}(g2). If L > 0.0: Normalize: g2{norm} = \text{normalize}(g2). Transform to eye space: g2 = \text{transposeTextureToEye} \times g2{norm}. Else: Set g2 = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0). 5. Initialize Color: Set finalColor to (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0). 6. Light Direction Calculation: If the light is positional (glLightSource[0].position.w != 0.0): Transform vertex position hPos to texture coordinates: tmp = eyeToTexture4 \times hPos. Convert to eye coordinates: ldir = tmp.xyz / tmp.w. Calculate light direction: ldir = lightPos - ldir. Calculate squared distance: sqrDistance = \text{dot}(ldir, ldir). Normalize: ldir = \text{normalize}(ldir). Calculate half vector: h = \text{normalize}(ldir + wReverseRayDir). Else (directional light): ldir is derived directly from the light source direction (implementation detail: typically glLightSource[0].position.xyz normalized). sqrDistance = 0.0 (or irrelevant). h = \text{normalize}(ldir + wReverseRayDir). 7. Attenuation: If positional: att = \frac{1.0}{C + L\sqrt{sqrDistance} + Q \cdot sqrDistance} Where C, L, Q are glLightSource[0].constantAttenuation, linearAttenuation, and quadraticAttenuation respectively. Else: att = 1.0. 8. Spot Illumination: If glLightSource[0].spotCutoff == 180.0: spot = 1.0. Else: coef = -\text{dot}(ldir, gl\LightSource[0].spotDirection). If coef \ge gl\LightSource[0].spotCosCutoff: spot = coef^{gl\LightSource[0].spotExponent}. Else: spot = 0.0. 9. Shading Calculation: If spot > 0.0: Calculate dot products: nDotL = \text{dot}(g2, ldir). nDotH = \text{dot}(g2, h). Two-sided shading: If nDotL < 0.0, negate nDotL. If nDotH < 0.0, negate nDotH. Ambient: finalColor += gl\FrontLightProduct[0].ambient. Diffuse: If nDotL > 0.0: finalColor += (gl\FrontLightProduct[0].diffuse \times nDotL) \times color. Where color is obtained from colorFromValue(volNumber, value). Specular: shininessFactor = nDotH^{gl\FrontMaterial.shininess}. finalColor += gl\FrontLightProduct[0].specular \times shininessFactor. Apply Light Factors: finalColor = att \times spot. Scene Ambient: finalColor += gl\FrontLightModelProduct.sceneColor \times color. 10. Clamping: finalColor = \text{clamp}(finalColor, clampMin, clampMax). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shadevolumesample(volnumber, value, postexture, hpos, lightsource, frontmaterial, eyetotexture, transposetexturetoeye, cellscale, xvec, yvec, zvec, clampmin, clampmax, wreverseraydir, isonecomponent, volumedata, colortexture): """ Computes the shaded color for a volume sample using gradient estimation from samples. """ # 1. Sample Gradient Components (Forward) g1x = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture + xvec[volnumber]) g1y = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture + yvec[volnumber]) g1z = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture + zvec[volnumber]) # 2. Sample Gradient Components (Backward) g2x = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture - xvec[volnumber]) g2y = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture - yvec[volnumber]) g2z = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture - zvec[volnumber]) # 3. Construct and Scale Gradient g2 = vec3(g2x, g2y, g2z) cellscale[volnumber] # 4. Normalize and Transform Gradient normallength = length(g2) if normallength > 0.0: g2normalized = normalize(g2) # Transform to eye coordinates g2 = transposetexturetoeye[volnumber] @ g2normalized else: g2 = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 5. Initialize Final Color finalcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 6. Light Direction and Properties lightpos = lightsource.position ispositional = lightpos.w != 0.0 if ispositional: # Transform vertex position to texture coords then to eye coords tmp = eyetotexture[volnumber] @ hpos ldir = tmp.xyz / tmp.w ldir = lightpos.xyz - ldir sqrdistance = dot(ldir, ldir) ldir = normalize(ldir) else: # Directional light ldir = normalize(lightpos.xyz) sqrdistance = 0.0 # Half vector calculation h = normalize(ldir + wreverseraydir) # 7. Attenuation att = 1.0 if ispositional: c = lightsource.constantattenuation l = lightsource.linearattenuation q = lightsource.quadraticattenuation att = 1.0 / (c + l sqrt(sqrdistance) + q sqrdistance) # 8. Spot Illumination spot = 1.0 if lightsource.spotcutoff != 180.0: coef = -dot(ldir, lightsource.spotdirection) if coef >= lightsource.spotcoscutoff: spot = pow(coef, lightsource.spotexponent) else: spot = 0.0 # 9. Shading if spot > 0.0: # Get color from value color = getcolorfromvalue(volnumber, value, isonecomponent, colortexture) nDotL = dot(g2, ldir) nDotH = dot(g2, h) # Two-sided shading if nDotL < 0.0: nDotL = -nDotL if nDotH < 0.0: nDotH = -nDotH # Ambient finalcolor += lightsource.frontambient # Diffuse if nDotL > 0.0: finalcolor += lightsource.frontdiffuse nDotL color # Specular shininessfactor = pow(nDotH, frontmaterial.shininess) finalcolor += lightsource.frontspecular shininessfactor # Apply attenuation and spot finalcolor = att spot # Scene Ambient finalcolor += lightsource.sceneambient color # 10. Clamping finalcolor = clamp(finalcolor, clampmin, clampmax) return finalcolor def getcolorfromvalue(volnumber, value, isonecomponent, colortexture): """ Converts the raw volume value to a color. Handles 1-component (uses color map) and 4-component (uses RGBA directly) datasets. """ if isonecomponent: scalar = value.x return colortexture[volnumber].sample(scalar) else: # Four-component dataset return vec4(value.x, value.y, value.z, 1.0) Parameters: clampMin, clampMax: Float values defining the lower and upper bounds for clamping the final color to prevent black spots. cellScale: Scalar used to scale the gradient vector from texture coordinates to eye coordinates. transposeTextureToEye: Matrix used to transform the normalized gradient from texture space to eye coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Black Spots: Occur if the final color is not clamped or if negative dot products are not handled for two-sided shading. The algorithm mitigates this by negating nDotL and nDotH if negative and clamping the result. Zero Gradient: If the gradient length is zero, the normal is set to (0,0,0), resulting in no diffuse/specular contribution (only ambient). Texture Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Focuses on combining gradient-based diffuse lighting with alpha blending for transparency. Choose when transparency is required. Uses a 3x3x3 kernel for gradient estimation. Choose when higher accuracy or smoother gradients are needed at the cost of more samples. Computes the Jacobian matrix. Choose when deformation or anisotropic scaling is involved. Averages gradients over regions. Choose when noise reduction is prioritized over sharp feature preservation. Computes mean curvature grids for surface rendering. Choose when curvature-based shading is required. Computes divergence grids for vector field visualization. Choose when analyzing flow fields is required. Pre-computes a shading volume (SHADING) from the CT density volume (CT) by calculating the surface normal via central finite differences and applying a diffuse lighting model. This avoids per-ray normal computation during rendering. Iterate over the volume grid for z from 1 to SLCS-2, y from 1 to ROWS-2, and x from 1 to COLS-2, skipping boundary layers. Compute partial derivatives using central differences: dx = \frac{CT[z][y][x+1] - CT[z][y][x-1]}{2.0}, dy = \frac{CT[z][y+1][x] - CT[z][y-1][x]}{2.0}, dz = \frac{CT[z+1][y][x] - CT[z-1][y][x]}{2.0}. Compute gradient magnitude: D = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2}. Compute normalized normal vector N = (dx/D, dy/D, dz/D) and diffuse shading value: S = Ip \cdot kd \cdot (N \cdot \hat{L}), where \hat{L} is the normalized light direction. Store as unsigned char. If gradient magnitude D is less than epsilon (7.25), set shading to 0 to avoid division by zero or noise amplification in flat regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficient for interactive visualization on GPU workstations, as it avoids pre-computing and storing large gradient fields. Strengths: Low memory footprint, simple implementation, suitable for adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data where gradient fields might be complex to pre-calculate. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Interactive volume rendering where memory is constrained or data is adaptive (AMR). When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method was described in the context of ray tracing structured AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) data using ExaBricks. It was introduced to support high-quality cell interpolation and interactive visualization on individual GPU workstations for highly complex models. The implementation details are found in the VTK source code for vtkOpenGLGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper. bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, https://github.com/bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Ray Tracing Structured AMR Data Using ExaBricks, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~wald/Publications/2020/exabrick/exabrick.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 kkhese/Volume-Rendering, https://github.com/kkhese/Volume-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gradient-Based Surface Shading
head: Gradient Shading, Gradient-based Volume Shading
body:
Gradient-based surface shading approximates the surface normal of a volume at a given point by computing the normalized gradient of the scalar field value at that location. This method is primarily used to enhance the perception of shape and boundaries between materials in volume-rendered images. It differs from direct lighting models by deriving illumination cues from the data's intrinsic spatial variation rather than external light sources, though it is computationally more expensive than simple dot-product shading due to gradient evaluation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar field V(\mathbf{x}) defined over a 3D domain, where \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) is the spatial coordinate. The field values are typically obtained via trilinear interpolation of voxel data. Output: A surface normal vector \mathbf{n} at \mathbf{x}, used for shading calculations (e.g., diffuse reflection). Data Structures The scalar field is stored as a dense 3D grid. To compute the gradient, the method requires access to neighboring voxel values. If the field is stored as a 1D array of size Nx 	imes Ny 	imes Nz, the value at index (i, j, k) is accessed as V[i][j][k]. Algorithm Steps 1. Evaluate Field Value: Determine the scalar value V(\mathbf{x}) at the query point \mathbf{x} using trilinear interpolation from the surrounding 8 voxels. 2. Compute Gradient Components: Calculate the partial derivatives  rac{\partial V}{\partial x},  rac{\partial V}{\partial y}, and  rac{\partial V}{\partial z} using central finite differences. For a grid with uniform spacing \Delta, the gradient 
abla V at \mathbf{x} is: 
abla V(\mathbf{x}) =  egin{bmatrix}  rac{V(x+\Delta, y, z) - V(x-\Delta, y, z)}{2\Delta} \  rac{V(x, y+\Delta, z) - V(x, y-\Delta, z)}{2\Delta} \  rac{V(x, y, z+\Delta) - V(x, y, z-\Delta)}{2\Delta} \end{bmatrix} If \mathbf{x} lies on a boundary where neighbors are missing, use one-sided differences or clamp to the boundary value. 3. Normalize: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} by normalizing the gradient vector: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla V(\mathbf{x})}{\|
abla V(\mathbf{x})\|} 4. Shade: Use \mathbf{n} in a standard lighting model (e.g., Phong or Blinn-Phong) to compute the final color. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradientshading(field, x, y, z, delta): """ Computes the surface normal for gradient-based shading. field: 3D array (Nx, Ny, Nz) of voxel values. x, y, z: Continuous coordinates in grid space. delta: Grid spacing (assumed uniform). """ # 1. Interpolate scalar value at (x, y, z) # Note: Trilinear interpolation is required for V(x,y,z) # but for gradient, we sample neighbors. # Helper to get clamped voxel value def getvoxel(ix, iy, iz): ix = max(0, min(ix, field.shape[0] - 1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, field.shape[1] - 1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, field.shape[2] - 1)) return field[ix, iy, iz] # 2. Compute partial derivatives using central differences # Sample neighbors in grid indices. Assuming integer coordinates for simplicity # or mapping continuous x,y,z to nearest grid indices for derivative estimation. # In practice, x,y,z are often fragment coordinates. # Map continuous coordinates to integer grid indices for neighbor access ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) # Central differences dx = (getvoxel(ix + 1, iy, iz) - getvoxel(ix - 1, iy, iz)) / (2 delta) dy = (getvoxel(ix, iy + 1, iz) - getvoxel(ix, iy - 1, iz)) / (2 delta) dz = (getvoxel(ix, iy, iz + 1) - getvoxel(ix, iy, iz - 1)) / (2 delta) # 3. Normalize gradnorm = sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if gradnorm < 1e-6: # Degenerate case: homogeneous region return [0, 0, 1] # Default normal, e.g., up return [dx / gradnorm, dy / gradnorm, dz / gradnorm] Parameters Delta (\Delta): The physical or logical spacing between voxels. Typical value: 1.0 if using grid indices, or the physical resolution of the CT/MRI scan. Lighting Model: Standard diffuse/specular coefficients are applied to the resulting normal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Homogeneous Regions: In areas where the gradient magnitude is very low or zero (e.g., uniform tissue in CT data), the normal is undefined or noisy. The method is not robust here. Noise Sensitivity: Finite differences amplify high-frequency noise in the scalar field, leading to speckled shading artifacts. Multivariate Fields: This method is unsuitable for multivariate fields. While the eigenvector e1 (direction of greatest change) can be derived from the tensor G, it represents only orientation, not absolute direction. The sign of e1 can flip in neighboring regions, causing interpolation issues and making it a poor choice for surface normals. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment/pixel, but involves 6 additional texture fetches (or memory accesses) for central differences and a normalization step. It is significantly slower than simple dot-product shading with pre-computed normals, being much as three times slower than evaluating dot products for a limited number of light sources in the fragment shader stage. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample, as no extra data structures are required beyond the scalar field itself. Strengths: Provides intuitive shape cues for boundaries between materials without requiring explicit isosurface extraction. Limitations: Fails in homogeneous regions and is sensitive to noise. Not applicable to multivariate data. When to use: When visualizing boundaries in scalar volumes and explicit surface extraction is too expensive or unnecessary. When not to use: For multivariate volumes, noisy data, or homogeneous regions where shadows or other techniques are preferred. Gradient-based surface shading was published by Hohne and Bernstein in 1986, utilizing the gray-level gradient to perform shading of surfaces rendered from 3D CT data. This approach was part of early efforts in medical visualization to extract and visualize 3D hard and soft tissue surfaces. It preceded the widespread adoption of Marching Cubes (1987) and volume raycasting (1988).
