name: Gradient-based Surface Projection
head: Refractive index-only image, Surface projections
body: Gradient-based surface projection visualizes interfaces between regions of different density by projecting through a matrix of gradient magnitude values derived from voxel density. It differs from standard volume rendering by treating the volume as a collection of internal surfaces defined by normals and strengths, rather than a continuous medium with absorption and emission. This method allows for the visualization of diffuse transitions and sub-voxel surface accuracy that binary representations cannot achieve. Inputs: Scalar volume data V containing density values. Pre-computed 3D gradient vectors N = (Nx, Ny, Nz) for each voxel, derived from finite differences of neighboring densities. Optional color information associated with the volume. Outputs: A 2D image representing the projected surface magnitudes (refractive index-only image) or shaded colored surface projections. Data Structures: A 3D array storing the surface normal vectors N at each voxel, approximated via finite differences of neighboring densities. A 3D array storing the surface strength |N| as floats at each voxel. Steps: 1. Compute Surface Normal and Strength: For each voxel, approximate the surface normal N using finite differences of neighboring densities. Calculate the surface strength (magnitude) |N| as the L2-norm of N: |N| = \sqrt{Nx^2 + Ny^2 + Nz^2} 2. Project Surface Magnitude: Generate a refractive index-only image by projecting directly through the surface magnitude values |N| along the view ray. Because surfaces are defined by fractional values at each voxel, this projection visualizes diffuse transitions that binary representations cannot. Surfaces may appear to lie at sub-voxel accuracy. 3. Shaded Surface Projection: Enhance depth perception by applying 3D lighting cues to the dataset. Use the finite difference gradient N as the surface normal direction for the lighting model. Light enters the voxel from the back with intensity I and exits with intensity I'. Modulate the intensity and color of the light by three voxel-dependent effects: translucency, luminosity, and refraction. Use the surface normal direction to modulate the intensity of the transmitted light refracted to the next voxel. Render a shaded colored refractive index image by using color information modulated by the gradient with a shading model in the projection pipeline. Edge cases and pitfalls: Surfaces may appear to lie at sub-voxel accuracy because they are defined by fractional values at each voxel. This enables visualization of diffuse transitions but may mislead if precise geometric location is required. An enhancement of depth perception by applying 3D lighting cues to the data set. It modulates transmitted light intensity by translucency, luminosity, and refraction. It uses the finite difference gradient as the surface normal direction for the lighting model, where light enters from the back and is modulated by voxel-dependent effects before being refracted to the next voxel. Strengths: Visualizes interfaces between regions of different density. Allows visualization of diffuse transitions not possible with binary representation. Provides sub-voxel accuracy perception. Limitations: Relies on gradient magnitude derived from voxel density. When to use: When the goal is to visualize internal interfaces and boundaries within a volume, especially for medical data where tissue boundaries are of interest. Originated in the context of volumetric rendering of medical data, specifically for stereotactic neurosurgery planning. The method is based on the concept that visualizing interfaces between regions of different density yields sufficient information about the volume. It builds on Gradient Computation via Finite Differences to identify these interfaces. Volumetric rendering of medical data: applications to stereotactic neurosurgery planning, https://doi.org/10.82308/10070, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Per-Region Gradient Averaging
body: Per-Region Gradient Averaging computes the 3D gradient vector for each voxel in a scalar volume by averaging directional gradients across multiple discrete scalar regions, using a binary neighbor check to detect region boundaries. It builds on Gradient Computation via Finite Differences but replaces continuous interpolation with discrete region membership checks. Inputs: A 3D volume grid of scalar values, a list of scalar regions (integers or identifiers), and the volume dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz). Outputs: A 3D grid of gradient vectors (gx, gy, gz) and their magnitudes. Data Structures: self.data: A flat list or array of VoxelGradient objects of size Dx \times Dy \times Dz. VoxelGradient: A structure containing prevgx, prevgy, prevgz (floats) and magnitude (computed). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize self.data with VoxelGradient objects for all voxels. 2. Replace the original volume data with a boolean mask or integer label map indicating region membership for each voxel. 3. For each voxel (x, y, z) in the volume: a. Initialize prevgx = 0, prevgy = 0, prevgz = 0, and n = 0. b. For each region R in the list of regions: i. Compute the directional gradient components (gx, gy, gz) for region R at (x, y, z): gx = \frac{x{plus} - x{minus}}{2} gy = \frac{y{plus} - y{minus}}{2} gz = \frac{z{plus} - z{minus}}{2} where x{plus} = 1000 if V(x+1, y, z) \in R else 0, x{minus} = 1000 if V(x-1, y, z) \in R else 0, and similarly for y and z. The value 1000 is a binary weight assigned to neighbors belonging to the current region to amplify boundary detection. ii. If (gx, gy, gz) is non-zero: new\gx = \frac{prev\gx \times n + gx}{n + 1} new\gy = \frac{prev\gy \times n + gy}{n + 1} new\gz = \frac{prev\gz \times n + gz}{n + 1} Update prevgx, prevgy, prevgz to newgx, newgy, newgz respectively, and increment n by 1. c. Set the voxel's gradient to (prev\gx, prev\gy, prev\gz). d. Compute the magnitude: \sqrt{prev\gx^2 + prev\gy^2 + prev\gz^2}. 4. Compute the maximum gradient magnitude lazily on the first call to getmaxgradientmagnitude by scanning self.data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeperregiongradients(volumedata, regions, dimx, dimy, dimz): # Data structure initialization class VoxelGradient: def init(self): self.prevgx = 0.0 self.prevgy = 0.0 self.prevgz = 0.0 self.magnitude = 0.0 voxels = [VoxelGradient() for in range(dimx dimy dimz)] # Replace volume data with boolean mask/region labels (assumed prepared externally) # regionmap[x, y, z] stores the region ID for each voxel regionmap = volumedata # Assumed to be a 3D array of region IDs for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): prevgx = 0.0 prevgy = 0.0 prevgz = 0.0 n = 0 for region in regions: # Boundary handling: clamp coordinates or return 0 for out-of-bounds def getvoxel(cx, cy, cz): if 0 <= cx < dimx and 0 <= cy < dimy and 0 <= cz < dimz: return regionmap[cx, cy, cz] return 0 # Assumed boundary handling valplusx = getvoxel(x + 1, y, z) valminusx = getvoxel(x - 1, y, z) valplusy = getvoxel(x, y + 1, z) valminusy = getvoxel(x, y - 1, z) valplusz = getvoxel(x, y, z + 1) valminusz = getvoxel(x, y, z - 1) weight = 1000.0 gx = ((weight if valplusx == region else 0.0) - (weight if valminusx == region else 0.0)) / 2.0 gy = ((weight if valplusy == region else 0.0) - (weight if valminusy == region else 0.0)) / 2.0 gz = ((weight if valplusz == region else 0.0) - (weight if valminusz == region else 0.0)) / 2.0 if gx != 0 or gy != 0 or gz != 0: newgx = (prevgx n + gx) / (n + 1) newgy = (prevgy n + gy) / (n + 1) newgz = (prevgz n + gz) / (n + 1) prevgx = newgx prevgy = newgy prevgz = newgz n += 1 idx = x dimy dimz + y dimz + z voxels[idx].prevgx = prevgx voxels[idx].prevgy = prevgy voxels[idx].prevgz = prevgz voxels[idx].magnitude = (prevgx2 + prevgy2 + prevgz2)0.5 return voxels Calculates a weight w = \text{weight} \times \max(\text{world\size}) / 128 and applies a total variation gradient to the density, k0, or diffuse field using totalvariationaddgrad(w, w, w, densemode). This variant is used in differentiable volume rendering contexts to regularize gradients. Time Complexity: O(Dx Dy Dz \times Nr), where Nr is the number of regions. Each voxel iterates over all regions and checks 6 neighbors. Memory Complexity: O(Dx Dy Dz) for storing the gradient vectors. Strengths: Effective for volumes with distinct, discrete scalar regions (e.g., segmented medical images, procedural volumes with sharp boundaries). Amplifies boundary gradients significantly. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large numbers of regions. Sensitive to the choice of the binary weight (1000). Not suitable for smooth, continuous scalar fields where standard finite differences are more appropriate. When to use: When the volume data is naturally segmented into discrete regions and sharp boundary detection is prioritized over smooth gradient estimation. When not to use: For continuous scalar fields or when computational efficiency is critical with many regions. Originated in the context of raycasting rendering implementations for volumes with discrete scalar regions. The method is part of a broader effort to improve gradient-based lighting and shading in volume rendering by leveraging region-aware boundary information. faviasono/raycastingrendering, https://github.com/faviasono/raycastingrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) gkouros/ref-dvgo, https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Gradient Magnitude Computation
head: Magnitude Grid Computation
body: Computes the Euclidean norm |\mathbf{v}| at every active voxel of a vector grid, producing a scalar magnitude grid. Inputs: A vector grid where each active voxel stores a 3D gradient vector \mathbf{v} = (vx, vy, vz). Outputs: A scalar grid where each active voxel stores the magnitude |\mathbf{v}|. Data Structures: The input is a hierarchical grid tree containing active voxels. The output is a scalar grid with the same topology, active voxel locations, voxel size, and a background value of zero. Steps: 1. Iterate over all active voxels (c, \mathbf{v}) in the grid tree. 2. Compute the Euclidean norm |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{vx^2 + vy^2 + vz^2} for each vector. 3. Store the computed magnitude in a dictionary keyed by coordinate c. 4. Build the result scalar grid using the computed dictionary, a background value of zero, and the original grid's voxel size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class ScalarGrid: def init(self, activevalues, backgroundvalue, voxelsize, topology): self.activevalues = activevalues self.backgroundvalue = backgroundvalue self.voxelsize = voxelsize self.topology = topology def computegradientmagnitude(inputvectorgrid): magnitudes = {} for coord, gradientvector in inputvectorgrid.activevoxels(): vx, vy, vz = gradientvector.x, gradientvector.y, gradientvector.z magnitude = math.sqrt(vxvx + vyvy + vzvz) magnitudes[coord] = magnitude outputgrid = ScalarGrid( activevalues=magnitudes, backgroundvalue=0.0, voxelsize=inputvectorgrid.voxelsize, topology=inputvectorgrid.topology) return outputgrid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Computes the squared Godunov norm for gradient components. It distinguishes itself by handling negative and positive gradient components separately to ensure monotonicity. It is chosen when solving hyperbolic conservation laws on grids. It takes a boolean isOutside flag, gradient vectors for negative and positive sides (gradientm, gradientp), or individual scalar components (dPxm, dPxp, dPym, dPyp, dPzm, dPzp). Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. tobiasosborne/Lyr.jl, https://github.com/tobiasosborne/Lyr.jl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) OpenVDB: nanovdb::math Namespace Reference, https://openvdb.org/documentation/doxygen/namespacenanovdb11math.html, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Neumann Gradient
head: Neumann Gradient Estimation
body:
The Neumann Gradient is a 3D gradient estimation method for scalar volumes that computes the gradient vector for each voxel using a 3×3×3 neighborhood of 26 surrounding voxels. It distinguishes itself from simpler finite difference methods by employing a linear regression framework that produces nearly isotropic gradients with reduced fringing artifacts. The method computes the gradient vector 
abla(x, y, z) = (
ablax, 
ablay, 
ablaz) at voxel position (x, y, z) by convolving the 26 neighboring voxel values with three specific 3×3×3 filter masks. The masks are derived from a linear regression framework. Inputs: Scalar volume data D (3D array). Target voxel coordinates (x, y, z). Outputs: Gradient vector 
abla(x, y, z) = (
ablax, 
ablay, 
ablaz). Data Structures: Three 3×3×3 kernel arrays Kx, Ky, Kz storing the filter weights. Normalization factor C = 1/52. Formulas: The gradient components are computed by applying the filter masks to the neighborhood: 
ablax =  rac{1}{52} \sum{i=-1}^{1} \sum{j=-1}^{1} \sum{k=-1}^{1} D(x+i, y+j, z+k) \cdot Kx[i+1][j+1][k+1] 
ablay =  rac{1}{52} \sum{i=-1}^{1} \sum{j=-1}^{1} \sum{k=-1}^{1} D(x+i, y+j, z+k) \cdot Ky[i+1][j+1][k+1] 
ablaz =  rac{1}{52} \sum{i=-1}^{1} \sum{j=-1}^{1} \sum{k=-1}^{1} D(x+i, y+j, z+k) \cdot Kz[i+1][j+1][k+1] The source provides the kernels as explicit 3D arrays for 
ablax and as tensor products for 
ablay and 
ablaz: Kx =  egin{pmatrix} (-2 & 0 & 2) & (-3 & 0 & 3) & (-2 & 0 & 2) \ (-3 & 0 & 3) & (-6 & 0 & 6) & (-3 & 0 & 3) \ (-2 & 0 & 3) & (-3 & 0 & 3) & (-2 & 0 & 2) \end{pmatrix} where each row in the LaTeX represents a 3×3 slice along the z-axis. For 
ablay and 
ablaz, the source provides tensor product notations: Ky =  rac{1}{52}  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ -2 & -3 & -2 \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 6 & 3 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ -3 & -6 & -3 \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ -2 & -3 & -2 \end{pmatrix} Kz =  rac{1}{52}  egin{pmatrix} (-2 & -3 & -2) \ (-3 & -6 & -3) \ (-2 & -3 & -2) \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 & 2 \ 3 & 6 & 3 \ 2 & 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix} The middle matrix in Kz is all zeros in the source, which is a typographical error in the original LaTeX; the intended structure is a separable 3×3×3 kernel. The kernels can be expanded into 3D arrays for implementation. Parameters: Normalization constant: 1/52. Neighborhood radius: 1 voxel (3×3×3 grid, 26 neighbors). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The method requires 26 neighbors. Boundary handling is not specified in the source; clamping to edge values or zero-padding are standard implementations. Computational Cost: The method has considerably high computational costs due to the 26-tap 3D convolution. Detail Fading: Applying the filter to the original voxel values (which can be computed with low additional cost using intermediate results) causes fading of small details, which is typically unsuitable for real medical applications. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeneumanngradient(volume, x, y, z, width, height, depth): # Extract 3x3x3 neighborhood centered at (x, y, z) # Handle boundaries by clamping to edge values def getvoxel(dx, dy, dz): cx = max(0, min(width - 1, x + dx)) cy = max(0, min(height - 1, y + dy)) cz = max(0, min(depth - 1, z + dz)) return volume[cx, cy, cz] neighbors = [[[getvoxel(dx, dy, dz) for dz in range(-1, 2)] for dy in range(-1, 2)] for dx in range(-1, 2)] # Kernel Kx from source (3 layers along z) kx = [ [[-2, 0, 2], [-3, 0, 3], [-2, 0, 2]], [[-3, 0, 3], [-6, 0, 6], [-3, 0, 3]], [[-2, 0, 3], [-3, 0, 3], [-2, 0, 2]] ] # Kernels Ky and Kz are given as tensor products in the source # Expanded into 3D arrays for implementation ky = [ [[ 4, 6, 4], [ 0, 0, 0], [-4, -6, -4]], [[ 6, 9, 6], [ 0, 0, 0], [-6, -9, -6]], [[ 4, 6, 4], [ 0, 0, 0], [-4, -6, -4]] ] kz = [ [[-4, -6, -4], [-6, -9, -6], [-4, -6, -4]], [[-6, -9, -6], [-9,-13.5,-6], [-6, -9, -6]], [[-4, -6, -4], [-6, -9, -6], [-4, -6, -4]] ] # Note: The source's Kz contains a zero matrix. Standard Neumann kernels are separable. # Implementers should use the exact source coefficients or standard separable expansion. def convolve(kernel): total = 0.0 for i in range(3): for j in range(3): for k in range(3): total += neighbors[i][j][k] kernel[i][j][k] return total / 52.0 gradx = convolve(kx) grady = convolve(ky) gradz = convolve(kz) return gradx, grady, gradz Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method requires a 26-tap 3D convolution per voxel, which the source describes as having "considerably high computational costs". Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Storing the gradient volume requires one float per component per voxel. Performance: Considerably high computational costs compared to central differences. Strengths: Produces nearly isotropic gradients and less fringing artifacts than other methods. Limitations: High cost; filtering for quality reduces small details, making it less suitable for medical applications where detail preservation is critical. Use Cases: High-quality rendering systems where visual accuracy is prioritized over speed. The Neumann gradient estimation method is based on linear regression and is a generalization of previous gradient estimation approaches. It was proposed by Neumann et al. [54] to achieve high gradient quality. It is used in high-quality volume rendering systems. Real-Time Mono- and Multi-Volume Rendering of Large Medical Datasets on Standard PC Hardware, https://doi.org/10.2312/diss.20058170, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Scanline Gradient Computation
head: VolPack Scanline Normals Computation, vpScanlineNormals
body: Scanline Gradient Computation is a memory-efficient method for computing 3D gradient vectors and surface normals for scalar volume data by processing one scanline at a time. It solves the problem of high memory bandwidth and storage requirements when computing derivatives for large volumes by maintaining only a sliding window of three slices in memory, making it suitable for volumes that exceed available RAM. It sets itself apart from batch processing methods like VolPack Volume Normals Computation by streaming data slice-by-slice rather than requiring the entire scalar array in memory. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume. The method requires the current scanline, the scanline immediately preceding it in the Y dimension, the scanline immediately following it in the Y dimension, the scanline immediately preceding it in the Z dimension, and the scanline immediately following it in the Z dimension. Output: For each voxel in the current scanline, the method computes and stores the gradient magnitude, an encoded surface normal vector, and optionally the original scalar value if the corresponding field index is provided. Data Structures: The implementation relies on a Voxel structure defined by the VolPack library, which contains fields for scalars, gradients, and normals. The exact layout and byte strides for X, Y, and Z dimensions are defined by vpSetRawVoxels. scalars: Pointer to the current scanline of input scalar data (8-bit unsigned integers). scalarsminusy: Pointer to the previous Y-slice scanline. scalarsplusy: Pointer to the next Y-slice scanline. scalarsminusz: Pointer to the previous Z-slice scanline. scalarsplusz: Pointer to the next Z-slice scanline. voxelscan: Pointer to the output voxel scanline where results are written. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the volume context and set the raw voxel layout using vpSetRawVoxels to define strides. 2. Load scalar data into a buffer. If the volume is too large for a single array, load data slice-by-slice. 3. For each scanline in the volume (typically iterating through Z and Y, then X): a. Ensure the five required scanlines (current, \pm Y, \pm Z) are loaded into memory. This requires keeping at most three slices of the volume in memory at any time. b. Call the core computation routine vpScanlineNormals for the current scanline. c. The routine computes the gradient using immediately adjacent neighbors in the Y and Z dimensions. d. Store the computed gradient magnitude and encoded normal into the voxelscan output buffer at the specified field indices. 4. Repeat until all scanlines are processed. Formulas: The sources describe the use of "immediately-adjacent neighbors" in the Y and Z dimensions to compute the gradient. For a voxel at (x,y,z), the gradient components are computed from the Y and Z neighbors using standard central differences. The gradient vector \mathbf{g} is then \left[ \frac{\partial S}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial S}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial S}{\partial z} \right]. The normal is derived from the normalized gradient. The specific encoding of the normal vector into the normalfield is handled internally by the VolPack library. Parameters: size: The length in bytes of one scanline of scalar data (equal to the X dimension of the volume). scalarfield, gradientfield, normalfield: Integer indices specifying which fields within the Voxel structure to populate. Use VPSKIPFIELD if a specific field should not be stored. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The method requires neighbors in \pm Y and \pm Z. At the boundaries of the volume, these neighbors do not exist. The VolPack documentation does not specify the boundary handling strategy (e.g., clamping, reflection, or zero-padding) in the provided text. Implementers must check the VolPack source or assume a specific behavior (often clamping or treating out-of-bounds as the boundary value). Memory Management: The method requires careful management of the sliding window of slices. Failing to update the pointers for scalarsminusy, etc., correctly will result in incorrect gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computescanlinenormals(volumedims, scalarslices, voxelfields): """ Processes a 3D volume slice-by-slice using the scanline approach. volumedims: (X, Y, Z) scalarslices: list of 2D arrays [Z][Y][X] voxelfields: (scalarfield, gradientfield, normalfield) """ X, Y, Z = volumedims gradients = [[[0.0]X for in range(Y)] for in range(Z)] normals = [[[0.0]X for in range(Y)] for in range(Z)] # Maintain a sliding window of 3 Z-slices: prev, curr, next prevslice = scalarslices[0] currslice = scalarslices[1] nextslice = scalarslices[2] for z in range(Z): for y in range(Y): # Extract 1D scanlines (X dimension) scanlinecurr = currslice[y] scanlineyminus = currslice[max(0, y - 1)] scanlineyplus = currslice[min(Y - 1, y + 1)] scanlinezminus = prevslice[y] scanlinezplus = nextslice[y] # Call core routine for this scanline # vpScanlineNormals(vpc, X, scanlinecurr, scanlineyminus, # scanlineyplus, scanlinezminus, # scanlinezplus, voxelscan,...) for x in range(X): scurr = scanlinecurr[x] syminus = scanlineyminus[x] syplus = scanlineyplus[x] szminus = scanlinezminus[x] szplus = scanlinezplus[x] # Compute gradient components from Y and Z neighbors dy = (syplus - syminus) / 2.0 dz = (szplus - szminus) / 2.0 dx = 0.0 # X-derivative not provided by scanline inputs gradmag = (dx2 + dy2 + dz2)0.5 if gradmag > 0: nx, ny, nz = dx / gradmag, dy / gradmag, dz / gradmag else: nx, ny, nz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 gradients[z][y][x] = [dx, dy, dz] normals[z][y][x] = [nx, ny, nz] # Slide Z-window forward prevslice = currslice currslice = nextslice nextidx = z + 3 nextslice = scalarslices[nextidx] if nextidx < Z else currslice return gradients, normals A utility routine (vpVolumeNormals) that computes gradient-magnitude data and encoded normal vectors from a three-dimensional array of 8-bit scalar values in one pass. It differs from the scanline version by requiring the entire volume to be loaded into memory at once. It is chosen when memory is sufficient for the full volume, simplifying the data loading logic. It accepts a VPSKIPFIELD constant to omit storing scalars, gradients, or normals. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume storage, but only O(S) auxiliary memory for the scalar data, where V is total voxels and S is slice size, as it keeps at most three slices in memory at a time. This is significantly lower than loading the entire scalar array if it exceeds RAM. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels, O(V), as each voxel is processed once. Strengths: Enables processing of volumes larger than available RAM. Efficient for 8-bit scalar data. Limitations: Requires careful buffer management. Limited to 8-bit input scalars in the vpVolumeNormals variant. Boundary conditions are not explicitly defined in the high-level guide. This method is part of the VolPack library, a set of routines for volume rendering. The specific routines vpScanlineNormals and vpVolumeNormals are documented in the VolPack User's Guide. The library was developed at Stanford University. VolPack User's Guide, http://www-graphics.stanford.edu/software/volpack/vpuserguide.html, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Finite Difference Stencils (Central/Forward/Backward)
body: Finite difference stencils compute the spatial gradient of a scalar volume by approximating partial derivatives using discrete samples from neighboring voxels. This method solves the problem of estimating surface normals or density rates of change for ray marching and shading without requiring analytic derivatives of the underlying basis functions. It differs from Analytic Gradient Computation by relying on numerical approximation rather than closed-form differentiation, and from Gradient Estimation from Samples by using fixed geometric offsets rather than statistical sampling of ray hits. All finite difference stencils approximate the first derivative of a function f(\mathbf{x}) at a point \mathbf{x} using a weighted sum of function values at discrete grid points. The general form for a partial derivative with respect to coordinate i is: \frac{\partial f}{\partial xi} \approx \sum{k} wk f(\mathbf{x} + \deltak \mathbf{e}i) where wk are weights and \deltak are offsets along the axis \mathbf{e}i. The accuracy of the stencil is determined by the order of the Taylor series expansion it matches. Lower-order stencils (like forward/backward) use fewer samples but suffer from bias or lower accuracy, while higher-order stencils (like central or 4th-order) use more samples to reduce truncation error. The choice of stencil dictates the number of memory accesses (samples) required per gradient component. Central differences approximate the derivative using points on both sides of the target voxel. For a 1D function f, the first-order central difference is: f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x + h) - f(x - h)}{2h} In 3D, this requires 2 samples per axis (6 total for the full gradient vector). It is second-order accurate (O(h^2)) and unbiased for interior points. It is the standard choice for smooth volumes where boundary effects are minimal or handled separately. Forward differences approximate the derivative using the current voxel and the next voxel in the positive direction: f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} This requires 2 samples per axis (6 total). It is first-order accurate (O(h)) and introduces a directional bias. It is typically used when memory bandwidth is constrained or when computing gradients at boundaries where backward points are unavailable, though Neumann Gradient offers a more robust boundary handling strategy. Backward differences approximate the derivative using the current voxel and the previous voxel in the negative direction: f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x) - f(x - h)}{h} This requires 2 samples per axis (6 total). Like forward differences, it is first-order accurate and biased. It is the mirror counterpart to forward differences and is rarely used in isolation for volume rendering unless specific directional constraints exist. A variant of central differencing for gradient computation that clamps offset positions to the current region to avoid additional ray traversals. Compute six additional basis reconstruction samples at positions offset from the current sample by a distance proportional to the region's sample rate. Clamp the offset positions to the current region before evaluating them. Gradients are not necessarily continuous at level boundaries because the offset size can change. Accurate central differencing requires tracing 6 additional rays per sample via infinitesimal rays to find containing regions, which is expensive. Clamped version removes ray traversals but reduces quality. Computes the curl ∇×F at every active voxel of a vector grid using central differences. Initialize a GradStencil with the grid tree. Iterate over all active voxels (c,) in the grid tree. Move the stencil to the current coordinate c. Compute the x, y, and z components of the curl using the formulas and store the tuple (cx, cy, cz) in a dictionary keyed by coordinate. Build the result grid using the computed data, a background value of zero vector (0,0,0), and the original grid's voxel size. curlx = (v[4][3] - v[5][3] - v[6][2] + v[7][2]) 0.5 curly = (v[6][1] - v[7][1] - v[2][3] + v[3][3]) 0.5 curlz = (v[2][2] - v[3][2] - v[4][1] + v[5][1]) 0.5 half: The scalar multiplier 0.5, representing 1/(2voxelsize) in index space. Implementation of nominally fifth-order finite-difference WENO that returns the numerical flux for interpolation. Given v1 = f(x-2dx), v2 = f(x-dx), v3 = f(x), v4 = f(x+dx) and v5 = f(x+2dx), return an interpolated value f(x+dx/2) with the special property that ( f(x+dx/2) - f(x-dx/2)) / dx = df/dx (x) + error, where the error is fifth-order in smooth regions: O(dx) \le error \le O(dx^5) scale2: A scaling factor for the weights, default value is 1.0. v1, v2, v3, v4, v5: Five input values for the stencil. RealT: Type for scale2, defaults to ValueType. Introduced by Chi-Wang Shu. Referenced in 'High Order Finite Difference and Finite Volume WENO Schemes and Discontinuous Galerkin Methods for CFD' (ICASE Report No 2001-11, page 6) and ICASE No 97-65 (Shu, 1997). More complex calculation than Central-Difference, requiring 54 sampling points, but offers significantly improved image quality. Finite difference methods are a cornerstone of numerical analysis, dating back to the early 20th century. In the context of volume rendering, they serve as a practical alternative to analytic gradients for complex basis functions or sparse data structures like AMR. The ExaBricks framework documents accurate central differencing for ray-traced AMR data, which requires tracing infinitesimal rays through a region BVH to find containing regions for offset positions. The trade-off between computational cost and visual quality, particularly regarding the number of samples required (e.g., 6 for central vs. 54 for Zucker-Hummel), is a key consideration in real-time rendering systems. name: Sobel Operator
head: Sobel Gradient Estimation, Sobel edge detector, Sobel gradient operator
body: The Sobel Operator is a gradient estimation method used in volume rendering to compute the spatial gradient vector for each voxel in a scalar volume. It solves the problem of determining the rate of change of data values to generate opacity functions and shading normals, emphasizing regions of high spatial frequency corresponding to edges. Unlike general edge detection where spatial location is critical, in volume rendering opacity functions are applied uniformly regardless of position, so the goal is to locate boundaries in the data value domain rather than the spatial domain. It is distinguished from its sibling Gradient-based Diffuse Lighting with Alpha Blending by being a fundamental gradient computation primitive rather than a lighting model, and from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by using separable smoothing weights that make it less sensitive to noise than the Roberts Cross operator. The method computes the gradient \mathbf{G} = (Gx, Gy, Gz) at a voxel by convolving the local neighborhood with separable kernels that combine differentiation and smoothing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume texture V, the current voxel coordinate (x, y, z), and the voxel size h. Output: A 3D gradient vector \mathbf{G}. Data Structures: Derivative weights k: A 1D array of size 3, k = [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0]. Smoothing weights s: A 1D array of size 3, s = [1.0, 2.0, 1.0]. Gradient accumulator: Three floating-point variables Gx, Gy, Gz, initialized to 0.0. Steps: 1. Determine the voxel size h from the texture properties. 2. Initialize Gx = 0.0, Gy = 0.0, Gz = 0.0. 3. Iterate over the 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood defined by offsets dx, dy, dz \in \{-1, 0, 1\}. 4. For each offset, calculate the spatial offset vector \mathbf{offset} = (dx \cdot h, dy \cdot h, dz \cdot h). 5. Sample the volume data at the offset position: v = V(x + dx, y + dy, z + dz). 6. Calculate the separable weights for each axis based on the current indices ix, iy, iz (mapped from \{-1, 0, 1\} to \{0, 1, 2\}): wx = k[ix] \cdot s[iy] \cdot s[iz] wy = s[ix] \cdot k[iy] \cdot s[iz] wz = s[ix] \cdot s[iy] \cdot k[iz] 7. Accumulate the weighted contributions: Gx \leftarrow Gx + wx \cdot v Gy \leftarrow Gy + wy \cdot v Gz \leftarrow Gz + wz \cdot v 8. Normalize the accumulated gradients by multiplying by \frac{1}{16.0} and a normalization constant NORM. 9. Return \mathbf{G} = (Gx, Gy, Gz) \cdot NORM. Formulas: The separable weight calculation effectively implements the convolution with the Sobel kernels. For a 2D slice, the horizontal gradient E(H) and vertical gradient E(V) are computed as: E(H) = (a0 + 2a1 + a2) - (a4 + 2a5 + a6) E(V) = (a2 + 2a3 + a4) - (a0 + 2a7 + a6) Where a0 \dots a7 are the pixel intensities in the 3 \times 3 window arranged around the current pixel. The diagonal kernels are defined as: E(DL) = (a1 + 2a2 + a3) - (a7 + 2a6 + a5) E(DR) = (a1 + 2a0 + a7) - (a3 + 2a4 + a5) Parameters: NORM: Not given in the sources. applies a multiplication by NORM after the 1/16.0 scaling but does not define its value. Isotropy: The operator aims for uniform response in all directions. Localization: Good precision in edge positioning. Signal-to-Noise: High resistance to noise due to smoothing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sobelgradient(volumetexture, coord, voxelsize): """ Computes the 3D gradient at coord using the Sobel operator. Args: volumetexture: Object with method sampledata(offset) returning scalar value. coord: Tuple (x, y, z) of the current voxel. voxelsize: Float scalar h. Returns: Tuple (Gx, Gy, Gz) representing the gradient vector. """ # Derivative weights k = [-1, 0, 1] # Smoothing weights s = [1, 2, 1] Gx = 0.0 Gy = 0.0 Gz = 0.0 # Loop over the 3x3x3 neighborhood for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: # Map index -1,0,1 to array index 0,1,2 idxx = dx + 1 idxy = dy + 1 idxz = dz + 1 # Calculate spatial offset offsetx = dx voxelsize offsety = dy voxelsize offsetz = dz voxelsize # Sample data at offset # Boundary conditions (e.g., clamping, mirroring, zero-padding) # must be handled by sampledata if coord is near the volume edge. v = volumetexture.sampledata(coord + (offsetx, offsety, offsetz)) # Calculate separable weights # k = [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0], s = [1.0, 2.0, 1.0] kx = -1.0 if idxx == 0 else (1.0 if idxx == 2 else 0.0) ky = -1.0 if idxy == 0 else (1.0 if idxy == 2 else 0.0) kz = -1.0 if idxz == 0 else (1.0 if idxz == 2 else 0.0) sx = 1.0 if idxx == 0 or idxx == 2 else 2.0 sy = 1.0 if idxy == 0 or idxy == 2 else 2.0 sz = 1.0 if idxz == 0 or idxz == 2 else 2.0 wx = kx sy sz wy = sx ky sz wz = sx sy kz # Accumulate Gx += wx v Gy += wy v Gz += wz v # Normalize # Source specifies division by 16.0 and multiplication by NORM. # NORM value not given in the sources. NORM = 1.0 # Placeholder for implementation-specific normalization scale = 1.0 / 16.0 NORM return (Gx scale, Gy scale, Gz scale) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overflow: Output values can overflow the maximum allowed pixel value for image types with small integer ranges (e.g., 8-bit). The standard practice is to clamp overflowing pixels to the maximum allowed value, or use a larger pixel value range. Edge Width: Natural edges often result in output lines several pixels wide due to the smoothing effect of the Sobel operator. Boundary Conditions: The method requires sampling neighbors. If the voxel is on the boundary of the volume, sampling must be handled (e.g., clamping, mirroring, or zero-padding). Approximates the Euclidean norm of the gradient vector using a linear combination of the maximum gradient component and the perpendicular component to avoid square root calculations. Choose this when performance is critical and exact magnitude is not required. It builds on the Sobel Operator by extracting the scalar magnitude. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel, as it involves a fixed 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27 sample convolution. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per voxel for the gradient vector. Performance: The Sobel operator is slower to compute than the Roberts Cross operator. Strengths: Less sensitive to noise than Roberts Cross or simple central differences due to the smoothing component. Produces considerably higher output values for similar edges, aiding in thresholding. Good localization and signal-to-noise characteristics. Limitations: Slower than Roberts Cross. Edges may be wider than 1 pixel due to smoothing. Potential for overflow in fixed-point integer representations. When to use: When noise reduction is important and a good balance between edge localization and smoothness is required for opacity function generation or shading. When not to use: When maximum computational speed is the only constraint (use Roberts Cross) or when exact edge width is critical without post-processing. The Sobel operator is an efficient edge detecting operator used for gradient measurement in volume rendering, specifically for opacity function generation and shading. It is a 2-D spatial gradient measurement operator that emphasizes regions of high spatial frequency corresponding to edges. In the context of volume rendering, it is used to locate boundaries in the data value domain rather than the spatial domain, as opacity functions are applied uniformly. It is one of several edge detection kernels, alongside Prewitt, Kirsch, and Robinson, which calculate the 1st derivative. name: Sobel Gradient Magnitude Approximation
head: Euclidian normal approximation, K-value approximation
body: This method approximates the Euclidean norm of a gradient vector using a linear combination of the maximum gradient component and the perpendicular component to avoid square root calculations. It builds on Sobel Operator by extracting the scalar magnitude required for subsequent processing steps. Inputs: Gradient components: x (the larger absolute gradient component) and y (the smaller absolute gradient component). Threshold T: A value to determine if the gradient represents an edge. Outputs: Approximated gradient magnitude A. Binary edge mask based on thresholding. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values derived from Sobel kernel convolutions. No complex data structures are required beyond the input components x and y. Steps: 1. Identify Components: Determine the absolute values of the gradient components in the primary direction (x) and the perpendicular direction (y), ensuring x \ge y. 2. Apply Approximation Formula: Calculate the magnitude A using the linear approximation A = x + K y. 3. Thresholding: If the calculated magnitude A exceeds a specified threshold T, classify the pixel as an edge. 4. Assignment: Assign a foreground value (255) to edge pixels and a background value (0) to non-edge pixels. Formula Details: The exact Euclidean magnitude is A(\theta) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}. The approximation assumes the gradient direction \theta falls within a specific range relative to the grid axes, specifically 0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{4} where x > y. The error percentage E(\theta, K) of this approximation relative to the true Euclidean norm is E(\theta, K) = 100 \left( \frac{\tan \theta}{\tan \theta + K} + K - 1 \right). This formula assumes normalized components or derives from the geometric relationship where the error depends on the angle \theta and the constant K. Parameters: K: The optimal value for K is 1/4 (0.25). This value minimizes the maximum error for both the 0–22.5° range (associated with four Sobel operators) and the 0–45° range (associated with two Sobel operators). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sobelgradientmagnitudeapprox(xabs, yabs, k=0.25, threshold=None): # Ensure x is the larger component if xabs < yabs: xabs, yabs = yabs, xabs # Calculate approximation magnitude = xabs + k yabs # Thresholding and assignment if threshold is not None: if magnitude > threshold: return 255 else: return 0 return magnitude Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The formula assumes x \ge y. If the components are equal, the error is maximized for the given K. Degenerate Input: If both x and y are zero, the magnitude is zero. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel/voxel. Gradient Magnitude Modulation is a post-processing step that uses the computed gradient magnitude to modulate sample opacity and illumination values. It emphasizes surface boundaries by increasing opacity and brightness where gradients are high, while de-emphasizing homogeneous regions and noise where gradients are small. It differs from the underlying Sobel Gradient Magnitude Approximation by adding a lookup-based mapping and the final multiplication step, rather than just computing the raw magnitude value. Choose this when you need to enhance surface detail in volume rendering. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel/voxel. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Significantly faster than exact Euclidean norm calculation on hardware without dedicated square root units or when integer arithmetic is preferred. Strengths: Low computational cost, simple implementation, isotropic response when combined with appropriate Sobel kernels. Limitations: Approximate nature introduces error that varies with the gradient angle, though K=1/4 minimizes the peak error. When to use: Real-time volume rendering, hardware implementations, or scenarios where square root operations are prohibitively expensive. When not to use: Applications requiring high-precision gradient magnitudes for scientific visualization where error bounds are strict. The method originates from early volume rendering systems, specifically the Shear-warp factorization approach. It was developed to optimize the computation of gradient magnitudes for edge detection and shading in real-time visualization. The specific choice of K=1/4 was derived from error analysis to balance accuracy across different gradient orientations. name: Gradient Magnitude Modulation
head: Gradient Magnitude Approximation, Gradient Magnitude Illumination Modulation, Gradient Magnitude Opacity Modulation
body: Gradient Magnitude Modulation is a post-processing step in volume rendering that uses the computed gradient magnitude to modulate sample opacity and illumination values. It emphasizes surface boundaries by increasing opacity and brightness where gradients are high, while de-emphasizing homogeneous regions and noise where gradients are small. It differs from the underlying Sobel Gradient Magnitude Approximation by adding a lookup-based mapping and the final multiplication step, rather than just computing the raw magnitude value. Inputs: Gradient magnitude approximation M, an 8-bit approximation in the range [0, 2^{20}] derived from the previous stage. Current sample opacity \alpha and illumination I (diffuse/specular). Three control registers: Gmimd (Gradient Magnitude Illumination Modulation for diffuse), Gmims (for specular), and Gmom (Gradient Magnitude Opacity Modulation). Gradient Magnitude Lookup Table (GmLUT). Outputs: Modulated opacity \alpha' and illumination I'. Modulation value m \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: GmLUT: A table of eight entries specifying points of a piece-wise linear function at equal intervals along the gradient magnitude axis. The output values of the table entries represent the modulation factor. Steps: 1. Compute Squared Magnitude: Calculate the sum of the squares of the gradient components (gx, gy, gz). Each component has signed 8-bit precision in the range [-127, 127]. S = gx^2 + gy^2 + gz^2 2. Approximate Square Root: Use a Newton-Raphson iteration to compute the square root of S, resulting in the 8-bit approximation M in the range [0, 2^{20}]. 3. Map to Lookup Index: Map the magnitude M into the range [0, 255] using the piece-wise linear function defined by GmLUT. Since GmLUT has 8 entries at equal intervals, the input domain [0, 2^{20}] is divided into 7 segments. The index i for the table is determined by scaling M to [0, 255] and identifying the segment. 4. Interpolate Modulation Value: Perform linear interpolation between the two nearest table values in GmLUT to compute the 8-bit repeating-fraction modulation value m. This value represents a float in the range [0, 1]. 5. Apply Modulation: If Gmom is enabled, compute \alpha' = \alpha \times m. If Gmimd is enabled, compute I'{diffuse} = I{diffuse} \times m. If Gmims is enabled, compute I'{specular} = I{specular} \times m. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientmagnitudemodulation(gx, gy, gz, alpha, Idiffuse, Ispecular, Gmimd, Gmims, Gmom, GmLUT): """ gx, gy, gz: signed 8-bit integers representing gradient components in [-127, 127]. alpha: current sample opacity. Idiffuse, Ispecular: current illumination values. Gmimd, Gmims, Gmom: boolean flags enabling modulation for diffuse, specular, and opacity respectively. GmLUT: list of 8 floats representing the piece-wise linear function values. Returns: modulatedalpha, modulatedIdiffuse, modulatedIspecular """ # Step 1: Compute squared magnitude S = gxgx + gygy + gzgz # Step 2: Newton-Raphson square root approximation # Result M is an 8-bit approximation in range [0, 2^20] x = S / 2.0 if S > 0 else 0.0 for in range(4): if x == 0: break x = 0.5 (x + S / x) M = x # Step 3 & 4: Map M to [0, 255] and interpolate using GmLUT # GmLUT has 8 entries at equal intervals along the gradient magnitude axis. maxmag = 220 numentries = 8 step = maxmag / (numentries - 1) idx = int(M / step) idx = min(idx, numentries - 2) # Clamp to valid interpolation pair frac = (M - idx step) / step vallow = GmLUT[idx] valhigh = GmLUT[idx + 1] # Linear interpolation yields the 8-bit repeating-fraction value in [0, 1] m = vallow + frac (valhigh - vallow) m = max(0.0, min(1.0, m)) # Step 5: Apply modulation modalpha = alpha modIdiffuse = Idiffuse modIspecular = Ispecular if Gmom: modalpha = alpha m if Gmimd: modIdiffuse = Idiffuse m if Gmims: modIspecular = Ispecular m return modalpha, modIdiffuse, modIspecular Parameters: GmLUT: 8-entry table defining the piece-wise linear mapping. Gmimd, Gmims, Gmom: Boolean registers enabling the modulation. Edge Cases: Zero gradient: Results in m=0 (if LUT maps 0 to 0) or the base LUT value, effectively removing the sample from view if opacity is modulated. Noise: Small gradients in noisy data result in low modulation values, reducing visual impact. Time Complexity: Constant time per sample, involving a few arithmetic operations and a table lookup/interpolation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the GmLUT (8 entries) and 3 control registers. Strengths: Effectively emphasizes surface boundaries and reduces noise artifacts by attenuating samples with small gradients. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the gradient magnitude approximation; incorrect LUT configuration can lead to over- or under-emphasis of features. When to use: When surface definition is critical and noise reduction is desired. Gradient Magnitude Modulation is part of the VolumePro real-time ray-casting system. It was introduced in the VolumePro architecture to provide flexible control over surface appearance and noise handling. The method builds on the Sobel Gradient Magnitude Approximation to provide a computationally efficient way to modulate rendering parameters. name: Jacobian Estimation via Central Differences
head: Central Difference Jacobian, Finite Difference Jacobian
body: Estimates the 3x3 Jacobian matrix of a deformation field by computing central differences of the simpleBrush function. It differs from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by returning the full matrix of partial derivatives rather than a single gradient vector, and from Sobel Operator by using isotropic central differences on the raw function rather than convolution kernels on sampled data. Inputs and outputs: Input: A position vector pos and a force/deformation parameter force passed to the deformation function simpleBrush. Output: A 3x3 matrix J where columns are the partial derivatives with respect to x, y, z. Data structures: mat3: A 3x3 matrix stored as three column vectors gradx, grady, gradz. vec3: 3D vectors for positions and differences. Parameters: EPSILON: The step size for finite differences. Steps: 1. Define the difference vectors along each axis: diff\x = (\epsilon, 0, 0) diff\y = (0, \epsilon, 0) diff\z = (0, 0, \epsilon) 2. Compute the partial derivative with respect to x by evaluating the deformation function at pos + diff\x and pos - diff\x: grad\x = \frac{simpleBrush(pos + diff\x, force) - simpleBrush(pos - diff\x, force)}{2 \cdot \epsilon} 3. Compute the partial derivative with respect to y: grad\y = \frac{simpleBrush(pos + diff\y, force) - simpleBrush(pos - diff\y, force)}{2 \cdot \epsilon} 4. Compute the partial derivative with respect to z: grad\z = \frac{simpleBrush(pos + diff\z, force) - simpleBrush(pos - diff\z, force)}{2 \cdot \epsilon} 5. Construct and return the Jacobian matrix J using these vectors as columns: J = \begin{bmatrix} | & | & | \\ grad\x & grad\y & grad\z \\ | & | & | \end{bmatrix} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def truediv(self, scalar): return vec3(self.x / scalar, self.y / scalar, self.z / scalar) class mat3: def init(self, c1, c2, c3): self.c1, self.c2, self.c3 = c1, c2, c3 def simpleBrush(pos, force): # Computes the 3D displacement vector for a given position and force parameter. # Implementation is external to this method. return vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def estimatejacobian(pos, force, epsilon): diffx = vec3(epsilon, 0.0, 0.0) diffy = vec3(0.0, epsilon, 0.0) diffz = vec3(0.0, 0.0, epsilon) dispplusx = simpleBrush(pos + diffx, force) dispminusx = simpleBrush(pos - diffx, force) dispplusy = simpleBrush(pos + diffy, force) dispminusy = simpleBrush(pos - diffy, force) dispplusz = simpleBrush(pos + diffz, force) dispminusz = simpleBrush(pos - diffz, force) gradx = (dispplusx - dispminusx) / (2.0 epsilon) grady = (dispplusy - dispminusy) / (2.0 epsilon) gradz = (dispplusz - dispminusz) / (2.0 epsilon) return mat3(gradx, grady, gradz) Edge cases and pitfalls: If EPSILON is too small, numerical precision errors may dominate the subtraction. If EPSILON is too large, the approximation deviates from the true derivative due to non-linearity. Boundary conditions for simpleBrush must handle positions outside the valid domain. Evaluates the derivative for the ODE solver by normalizing the inverse Jacobian times the direction vector w. It is chosen when a normalized direction is required for integration steps. The formula is: \text{result} = \text{normalize}(\text{inverse}(J) \cdot w) where J is the Jacobian estimated by the parent method. Time complexity: O(1) per evaluation, requiring 6 calls to simpleBrush. Memory complexity: O(1), storing only temporary vectors and the resulting matrix. Strengths: Simple to implement; isotropic accuracy for small steps. Limitations: Requires the deformation function to be differentiable; sensitive to step size choice. When to use: When the full deformation gradient is needed for physics or ray marching adjustments. When not to use: When the function is not smooth or when performance is critical and approximate gradients suffice. name: Jacobian Normalization for ODE Step
head: Normalize Inverse Jacobian Step, ODE Evaluation
body: This method computes the normalized direction vector for an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) solver by applying the inverse of an estimated Jacobian matrix to a base direction vector. It differs from raw Jacobian estimation by performing the matrix inversion and vector normalization required for stable stepping. Inputs: pos: The current 3D position in the volume. w: The base direction vector for the ODE step. force: A parameter passed to the Jacobian estimator. Outputs: stepdir: The normalized direction vector for the next ODE step. Data Structures: The Jacobian matrix J is a 3 \times 3 matrix estimated by the parent method Jacobian Estimation via Central Differences. J^{-1} is the inverse of this matrix. Steps: 1. Estimate the Jacobian matrix J at pos using estimateJacobian(pos, force). 2. Compute the inverse J^{-1}. 3. Multiply the inverse Jacobian by the direction vector: v = J^{-1} w. 4. Normalize v to obtain stepdir. Formula: step\dir = \text{normalize}\left( J^{-1} \cdot w \right) Where J = \text{estimateJacobian}(pos, force). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimatejacobiancentraldifferences(pos, force): # Parent method implementation # Computes 3x3 matrix of partial derivatives via central differences return [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] # Placeholder for parent def jacobiannormalizationodestep(pos, w, force): J = estimatejacobiancentraldifferences(pos, force) det = (J[0][0](J[1][1]J[2][2] - J[1][2]J[2][1]) - J[0][1](J[1][0]J[2][2] - J[1][2]J[2][0]) + J[0][2](J[1][0]J[2][1] - J[1][1]J[2][0])) if abs(det) < 1e-8: return w # Fallback for singular Jacobian invdet = 1.0 / det Jinv = [ [(J[1][1]J[2][2] - J[1][2]J[2][1])invdet, (J[0][2]J[2][1] - J[0][1]J[2][2])invdet, (J[0][1]J[1][2] - J[0][2]J[1][1])invdet], [(J[1][2]J[2][0] - J[1][0]J[2][2])invdet, (J[0][0]J[2][2] - J[0][2]J[2][0])invdet, (J[0][2]J[1][0] - J[0][0]J[1][2])invdet], [(J[1][0]J[2][1] - J[1][1]J[2][0])invdet, (J[0][1]J[2][0] - J[0][0]J[2][1])invdet, (J[0][0]J[1][1] - J[0][1]J[1][0])invdet] ] v = [ Jinv[0][0]w[0] + Jinv[0][1]w[1] + Jinv[0][2]w[2], Jinv[1][0]w[0] + Jinv[1][1]w[1] + Jinv[1][2]w[2], Jinv[2][0]w[0] + Jinv[2][1]w[1] + Jinv[2][2]w[2] ] normv = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if normv < 1e-8: return w # Fallback for zero vector return [v[0]/normv, v[1]/normv, v[2]/normv] Parameters: force: Passed to the Jacobian estimator. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Singular Jacobian: If \det(J) = 0, the inverse does not exist. A fallback to the unnormalized direction or identity step is required. Zero Vector: If J^{-1} w results in a zero vector, normalization fails. A fallback to the original direction w is required. It differs from general numerical Jacobian estimation by using a closed-form analytical derivation based on the input vector's components and Euclidean norm, rather than finite differences. name: Jacobian Computation for Coordinate Transformation
body: Computes a 3×3 Jacobian matrix for a batch of 3D points to facilitate coordinate space transformations or derivative propagation in rendering pipelines. It differs from general numerical Jacobian estimation by using a closed-form analytical derivation based on the input vector's components and Euclidean norm, rather than finite differences. Inputs: A tensor a of shape (N, 3) containing N 3D points (ax, ay, az). Outputs: A tensor J of shape (N, 9) containing the Jacobian elements in row-major order, or (N, 3, 3) if reshaped. Data Structures: a: Float tensor, shape (N, 3). r: Float tensor, shape (N,), representing the inverse Euclidean norm. J: Float tensor, shape (N, 9) or (N, 3, 3). Parameters: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Extract components ax, ay, az from a. 2. Compute the inverse Euclidean norm: r = 1 / \sqrt{ax^2 + ay^2 + az^2}. 3. Construct the 9 elements of the Jacobian matrix J according to the formula below. Formula: The Jacobian matrix J is defined as: J = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{az} & 0 & -\frac{ax}{az^2} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{az} & -\frac{ay}{az^2} \\ ax \cdot r & ay \cdot r & az \cdot r \end{bmatrix} where r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{ax^2 + ay^2 + az^2}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computejacobian(a: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the Jacobian matrix for coordinate transformation. Args: a: Tensor of shape (N, 3) with coordinates (x, y, z). Returns: Tensor of shape (N, 9) with Jacobian elements in row-major order. """ # Unpack coordinates ax = a[:, 0] ay = a[:, 1] az = a[:, 2] # Compute inverse Euclidean norm r = 1 / sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) r = torch.rsqrt(ax2 + ay2 + az2) # Compute terms involving az # Note: Division by zero if az == 0 results in Inf/NaN invaz = 1.0 / az invazsq = invaz invaz # Construct the 9 elements in row-major order # Row 0 j00 = invaz j01 = torch.zeroslike(ax) j02 = -ax invazsq # Row 1 j10 = torch.zeroslike(ax) j11 = invaz j12 = -ay invazsq # Row 2 j20 = ax r j21 = ay r j22 = az r # Stack into (N, 9) J = torch.stack([j00, j01, j02, j10, j11, j12, j20, j21, j22], dim=1) return J Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If any point has az = 0, the terms 1/az and 1/az^2 will produce Inf or NaN. The source code does not explicitly clamp or mask these cases. Implementers must ensure az \neq 0 or add a small epsilon to the denominator. It constructs two orthogonal normal vectors n1 = (ny, -nx, 0) and n2 = \text{cross}(n, n1) relative to a primary normal n, then multiplies the Jacobian by these normalized vectors to get directional derivatives. It also provides a numerical baseline using central finite differences with \epsilon = 10^{-5}, computing J[:, i] = (\text{network}(posh)[:,:3] - \text{network}(negh)[:,:3]) / (2\epsilon) where posh and negh are points perturbed by \pm \epsilon along axis i. name: 4th-Order Finite Difference Gradient
head: 4th-Order Accurate Finite Difference Scheme, Grid Normal Computation via 4th-Order Finite Differences
body: This method computes the gradient (normal vector) of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) grid at every voxel center using a 4th-order accurate finite difference scheme. It distinguishes itself from lower-order stencils by maintaining 4th-order accuracy at grid boundaries through specific extrapolation, avoiding the noise or bias introduced by standard 2nd-order central differences near edges. Inputs: grid: A 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) containing SDF values at voxel centers. voxelsize: Scalar physical size of a single voxel. gridresx, gridresy, gridresz: Integer dimensions of the grid. Outputs: A list of three 3D arrays [gradx, grady, gradz], each of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz), representing the partial derivatives \frac{\partial S}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial S}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial S}{\partial z}. Data Structures: The grid is stored as a dense 3D array with 0-based indexing. Boundary extrapolation uses a 3-point stencil to estimate values outside the domain. Steps: 1. Define boundary indices: nx = Nx - 1, ny = Ny - 1, nz = Nz - 1. 2. Compute the x-axis gradient components: Calculate forward difference approximation X1 by concatenating the interior forward differences with a boundary term. Calculate backward difference approximation X2 by concatenating a boundary term with the interior backward differences. Compute grad\x = (X1 - X2) / (2 \cdot \text{voxel\size}). 3. Repeat step 2 for y and z axes, adjusting tensor dimensions and indexing. Formulas: The core central difference for interior points is: \frac{\partial S}{\partial x} \approx \frac{S{i+1,j,k} - S{i-1,j,k}}{2 \Delta x} At the boundaries, 4th-order accuracy is maintained using extrapolation. For the last element in a dimension with index n, the virtual value V{n+1} is: V{n+1} = 3Vn - 3V{n-1} + V{n-2} For the first element (index 0), the virtual value V{-1} is derived from the symmetry of the stencil logic applied to X2: V{-1} = -3V0 + 3V1 + V2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compute4thordergradient(grid, voxelsize, nx, ny, nz): # grid: 3D array of shape (nx, ny, nz) # Returns three 3D arrays of shape (nx, ny, nz) gradx = [[0.0] ny nz for in range(nx)] grady = [[0.0] ny nz for in range(nx)] gradz = [[0.0] ny nz for in range(nx)] # X-axis gradient for i in range(nx): if i == 0: splus = grid[1] sminus = -3 grid[0] + 3 grid[1] + grid[2] elif i == nx - 1: splus = 3 grid[nx-1] - 3 grid[nx-2] + grid[nx-3] sminus = grid[nx-2] else: splus = grid[i+1] sminus = grid[i-1] for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): gradx[i][j][k] = (splus[j][k] - sminus[j][k]) / (2.0 voxelsize) # Y-axis gradient for j in range(ny): if j == 0: splus = grid[:, 1,:] sminus = -3 grid[:, 0,:] + 3 grid[:, 1,:] + grid[:, 2,:] elif j == ny - 1: splus = 3 grid[:, ny-1,:] - 3 grid[:, ny-2,:] + grid[:, ny-3,:] sminus = grid[:, ny-2,:] else: splus = grid[:, j+1,:] sminus = grid[:, j-1,:] for i in range(nx): for k in range(nz): grady[i][j][k] = (splus[i][k] - sminus[i][k]) / (2.0 voxelsize) # Z-axis gradient for k in range(nz): if k == 0: splus = grid[:,:, 1] sminus = -3 grid[:,:, 0] + 3 grid[:,:, 1] + grid[:,:, 2] elif k == nz - 1: splus = 3 grid[:,:, nz-1] - 3 grid[:,:, nz-2] + grid[:,:, nz-3] sminus = grid[:,:, nz-2] else: splus = grid[:,:, k+1] sminus = grid[:,:, k-1] for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): gradz[i][j][k] = (splus[i][j] - sminus[i][j]) / (2.0 voxelsize) return [gradx, grady, gradz] Parameters: voxelsize: Physical size of a voxel. Used to normalize the finite difference result to physical units. Edge Cases: Grid resolution must be at least 3 in each dimension (N \ge 3) to compute the boundary extrapolation terms involving V{n-2} and V2. If the grid is smaller than 3 voxels, the method fails. Estimates the Jacobian matrix using central differences. Choose this when volume deformation or density change rates are needed, rather than just surface normals. Time Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz), as it performs a constant number of operations per voxel. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for storing the input grid and three output gradient tensors. Strengths: Maintains 4th-order accuracy at boundaries, reducing artifacts in ray marching compared to 2nd-order schemes. Limitations: Requires a minimum grid resolution of 3. More complex to implement than 2nd-order stencils due to boundary handling. When to use: High-quality SDF rendering where boundary artifacts are visible with lower-order methods. When not to use: Real-time applications with very low resolution grids where the overhead of boundary logic is disproportionate, or when N < 3. This method is implemented in the SDFDiff repository, associated with research on differentiable rendering of SDFs. It addresses the need for accurate surface normals in volume rendering pipelines that rely on Signed Distance Functions.
