name: 3D Trilinear Interpolation
head: 3D Linear Interpolation, Trilinear Interpolant, Trilinear Interpolation (Standard), Trilinear Interpolation on Regular Mesh, Trilinear Voxel Interpolation, Voxel Trilinear Interpolation
body: 3D Trilinear Interpolation estimates the value of a scalar or vector field at an arbitrary point P=(x,y,z) within a grid cell by combining the values at the cell's eight corners. It solves the problem of sampling dense volumetric data at sub-voxel resolution, providing smoother results than nearest-neighbor sampling. It is distinguished from higher-order methods like Cubic Volume Interpolation by its use of only 8 neighbors and linear basis functions, which ensures C^0 continuity on regular rectilinear grids but lacks the derivative continuity of cubic methods. Inputs: A point P = (x, y, z) in world or grid coordinates. A dense 3D grid of values V with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Grid origin O = (ox, oy, oz) and voxel spacings D = (dx, dy, dz). If the grid is unit-spaced and origin-aligned, these are implicit. Outputs: A scalar value F(P) or vector field value at P. Data Structures: The grid V is typically stored as a contiguous array or multi-dimensional array. For a grid with dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz, access is often V[z][y][x] or flattened with stride-based indexing. Corner indices are integers x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1 where x1 = x0 + 1, etc.. Steps: 1. Coordinate Normalization: If the input coordinates are in world space, normalize them to voxel space. xyz = \frac{P - O}{D} 2. Cell Identification: Determine the integer coordinates of the lower corner of the enclosing voxel. x0 = \lfloor x \rfloor, \quad y0 = \lfloor y \rfloor, \quad z0 = \lfloor z \rfloor The upper corner indices are: x1 = x0 + 1, \quad y1 = y0 + 1, \quad z1 = z0 + 1. 3. Fractional Parts (Weights): Compute the fractional offset within the voxel. \alpha = x - x0, \quad \beta = y - y0, \quad \gamma = z - z0 Alternatively defined as ratios Rx, Ry, Rz \in [0, 1]. 4. Boundary Check: If any coordinate is outside the valid grid range (e.g., x < 0 or x \ge Nx), return a default value (typically 0) or clamp indices. Note: Clamping indices may cause artifacts at boundaries; returning 0 is common for sparse or bounded volumes. 5. Corner Value Retrieval: Retrieve the 8 corner values from the grid V. The indexing order must be consistent. A common mapping (matching) is: v{000} = V(x0, y0, z0) v{100} = V(x1, y0, z0) v{010} = V(x0, y1, z0) v{110} = V(x1, y1, z0) v{001} = V(x0, y0, z1) v{101} = V(x1, y0, z1) v{011} = V(x0, y1, z1) v{111} = V(x1, y1, z1) 6. Interpolation: Perform linear interpolation along each axis. This can be done sequentially or via the explicit polynomial form. Sequential Method (X, then Y, then Z): \begin{aligned} V{z0} &= (1-\alpha)(1-\beta)v{000} + \alpha(1-\beta)v{100} + (1-\alpha)\beta v{010} + \alpha\beta v{110} \\ V{z1} &= (1-\alpha)(1-\beta)v{001} + \alpha(1-\beta)v{101} + (1-\alpha)\beta v{011} + \alpha\beta v{111} \\ F(P) &= (1-\gamma)V{z0} + \gamma V{z1} \end{aligned} Explicit Polynomial Form: The value is approximated by: F(P) = a + bx + cy + dz + exy + fxz + gyz + hxyz where constants a \dots h are determined by the corner values. For a unit cube aligned with axes starting at (x0, y0, z0), the weights for the 8 corners are products of (1-\alpha) or \alpha, (1-\beta) or \beta, and (1-\gamma) or \gamma. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trilinearinterpolation(grid, x, y, z, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), spacing=(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)): """ Performs 3D trilinear interpolation at point (x, y, z). grid: 3D array-like, shape (Nx, Ny, Nz). x, y, z: float coordinates in world space. origin: tuple (ox, oy, oz) of grid origin in world space. spacing: tuple (dx, dy, dz) of voxel dimensions. """ # 1. Normalize to voxel space vx = (x - origin[0]) / spacing[0] vy = (y - origin[1]) / spacing[1] vz = (z - origin[2]) / spacing[2] # 2. Boundary check if (vx < 0 or vy < 0 or vz < 0 or vx >= grid.shape[0] or vy >= grid.shape[1] or vz >= grid.shape[2]): return 0.0 # 3. Compute floor coordinates and fractional parts x0 = math.floor(vx) y0 = math.floor(vy) z0 = math.floor(vz) # Clamp upper indices to prevent out-of-bounds access at grid edges x1 = min(x0 + 1, grid.shape[0] - 1) y1 = min(y0 + 1, grid.shape[1] - 1) z1 = min(z0 + 1, grid.shape[2] - 1) alpha = vx - x0 beta = vy - y0 gamma = vz - z0 # 4. Retrieve corner values v000 = grid[x0, y0, z0] v100 = grid[x1, y0, z0] v010 = grid[x0, y1, z0] v110 = grid[x1, y1, z0] v001 = grid[x0, y0, z1] v101 = grid[x1, y0, z1] v011 = grid[x0, y1, z1] v111 = grid[x1, y1, z1] # 5. Interpolate # Interpolate along X v00 = (1 - alpha) v000 + alpha v100 v01 = (1 - alpha) v001 + alpha v101 v10 = (1 - alpha) v010 + alpha v110 v11 = (1 - alpha) v011 + alpha v111 # Interpolate along Y v0 = (1 - beta) v00 + beta v10 v1 = (1 - beta) v01 + beta v11 # Interpolate along Z result = (1 - gamma) v0 + gamma v1 return result Performs trilinear interpolation on a compressed sparse grid using a links array to map voxel indices to compressed value indices, handling boundary checks via masking or a zero-value hack. It builds on standard trilinear interpolation by adding a link lookup step that translates grid coordinates to compressed indices while retaining the regular 8-corner neighborhood structure. Extends standard trilinear interpolation by using cubic mixture weights for each axis to sample a 3D texture at 8 corners defined by those weights. It provides higher-order continuity and smoother gradients compared to linear methods, at the cost of increased computational complexity and memory bandwidth usage. Computes the gradient of the field at point P by interpolating the gradients stored at the 8 corner points of the enclosing voxel using the same trilinear weights. The result is typically normalized from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] if the gradient data is encoded in that range. In volume rendering pipelines, trilinear interpolation is used to query density \sigma and color c from feature grids along camera rays. To reduce computational burden, this can be replaced by linear or bilinear interpolation of vector or matrix factors. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, involving a constant number of arithmetic operations and memory accesses. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per sample. The grid storage is O(Nx Ny Nz). Performance: Significantly faster than tricubic interpolation, which requires 64 samples. On rectilinear grids, it is efficient; on curvilinear grids, precalculation of coefficients can take ~110 seconds, and intersection testing becomes the bottleneck. Strengths: Simple implementation, low computational cost, C^0 continuity on regular grids. Limitations: Artifacts such as "3D crosses" or diamonds appear at large magnification factors due to the linear kernel. Continuity is not guaranteed for irregular, rotated, or curvilinear grids. Degenerate cases may occur where the trilinear function cannot be fit. Trilinear interpolation was developed as a standard method for volume rendering of curvilinear and rectilinear volumes. It is used in raycasting renderers to sample dense volumetric data at sub-voxel resolution. The method assumes the underlying function varies linearly along edges, quadratically across faces, and cubically within the cell. It is a fundamental component of raycasting renderers and is used in modern neural rendering pipelines like EgoNeRF for querying feature grids. name: Trilinear Interpolation (Compressed/Linked)
head: JAX Trilinear Interpolation (Vmapped)
body: This method performs trilinear interpolation on a compressed sparse grid using a links array to map voxel indices to compressed value indices, handling boundary checks via masking or a zero-value hack. It builds on 3D Trilinear Interpolation by adding a link lookup step that translates grid coordinates to compressed indices while retaining the regular 8-corner neighborhood structure. Inputs: xyz: Array of sample coordinates, shape (N, 3), in the same coordinate system as the grid. links: 3D integer array, shape (Dx, Dy, Dz), mapping each voxel corner to an index in the compressed value array. Invalid links are represented by negative integers. valuescompressed: Array of values, shape (M, C), where M is the number of valid compressed entries and C is the channel dimension. Outputs: result: Interpolated values at the sample points, shape (N, C). Data Structures: links: A 3D integer array where links[x, y, z] returns the index k such that valuescompressed[k] holds the value for the voxel corner at (x, y, z). If the corner is invalid, links[x, y, z] < 0. valuescompressed: A 2D array where each row corresponds to a valid voxel corner's data. Index 0 is often reserved as a zero-value placeholder for boundary handling in the zero-value hack variant. Steps: 1. Coordinate Normalization and Decomposition: Compute the floor and fractional parts of the input coordinates. x0, y0, z0 = \lfloor xyz \rfloor xd, yd, zd = xyz - (x0, y0, z0) Where x0, y0, z0 are integer indices for the voxel containing the sample point, and xd, yd, zd \in [0, 1) are the relative positions within that voxel. 2. Corner Link Lookup: Retrieve the compressed indices for all 8 corners of the voxel defined by (x0, y0, z0). l{ijk} = \text{links}[x0+i, y0+j, z0+k] \quad \text{for } i,j,k \in \{0,1\} This yields 8 indices: l{000}, l{100}, l{010}, l{110}, l{001}, l{101}, l{011}, l{111}. 3. Validity Masking: Create boolean masks for each link indicating validity (index \ge 0). m{ijk} = (l{ijk} \ge 0) For strict mode, compute the intersection of all 8 masks to identify sample points where all 8 corners are valid. m{valid} = m{000} \land m{100} \land m{010} \land m{110} \land m{001} \land m{101} \land m{011} \land m{111} For the zero-value hack variant, compute the union of all 8 masks to identify points touching the boundary. 4. Boundary Handling (Zero-Value Hack): If using the zero-value hack, replace invalid links (negative indices) within the boundary mask with index 0 before gathering. l{ijk}[m{boundary} \land \lnot m{ijk}] = 0 5. Value Gathering: Gather the values from valuescompressed using the corresponding links. v{ijk} = \text{values\compressed}[l{ijk}] 6. Weight Computation and Interpolation: Compute the trilinear weights based on the fractional coordinates. \text{tmpX} = 1 - xd, \quad \text{tmpY} = 1 - yd, \quad \text{tmpZ} = 1 - zd a{000} = \text{tmpX} \cdot \text{tmpY}, \quad a{100} = xd \cdot \text{tmpY}, \quad a{010} = \text{tmpX} \cdot yd, \quad a{110} = xd \cdot yd \text{weights} = [a{000}, a{010}, a{100}, a{110}] Gather coefficients and compute the result. \text{coeff} = [v{000}, v{001}, v{010}, v{011}, v{100}, v{101}, v{110}, v{111}] \text{result} = \sum \text{weights} \cdot \text{coeff}[[0, 2, 4, 6],:] \cdot \text{tmpZ} + \sum \text{weights} \cdot \text{coeff}[[1, 3, 5, 7],:] \cdot zd For points where m{valid} is false in strict mode, the result is zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trilinearcompressedlinked(xyz, links, valuescompressed, usezerohack=False): # 1. Normalize coordinates and compute floor/frac parts xyzfloor = np.floor(xyz) xd = xyz[:, 0] - xyzfloor[:, 0] yd = xyz[:, 1] - xyzfloor[:, 1] zd = xyz[:, 2] - xyzfloor[:, 2] x0 = xyzfloor[:, 0].astype(int) y0 = xyzfloor[:, 1].astype(int) z0 = xyzfloor[:, 2].astype(int) # 2. Lookup links for all 8 corners l000 = links[x0, y0, z0] l100 = links[x0 + 1, y0, z0] l010 = links[x0, y0 + 1, z0] l110 = links[x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0] l001 = links[x0, y0, z0 + 1] l101 = links[x0 + 1, y0, z0 + 1] l011 = links[x0, y0 + 1, z0 + 1] l111 = links[x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1] # 3. Create masks for valid links (>= 0) maskl000 = l000 >= 0 maskl100 = l100 >= 0 maskl010 = l010 >= 0 maskl110 = l110 >= 0 maskl001 = l001 >= 0 maskl101 = l101 >= 0 maskl011 = l011 >= 0 maskl111 = l111 >= 0 if usezerohack: # Union mask for boundary points maskboundary = maskl000 | maskl100 | maskl010 | maskl110 | maskl001 | maskl101 | maskl011 | maskl111 # Replace invalid links with 0 within boundary mask l000[maskboundary & ~maskl000] = 0 l100[maskboundary & ~maskl100] = 0 l010[maskboundary & ~maskl010] = 0 l110[maskboundary & ~maskl110] = 0 l001[maskboundary & ~maskl001] = 0 l101[maskboundary & ~maskl101] = 0 l011[maskboundary & ~maskl011] = 0 l111[maskboundary & ~maskl111] = 0 maskvalid = maskboundary else: # Intersection mask for strict mode maskvalid = maskl000 & maskl100 & maskl010 & maskl110 & maskl001 & maskl101 & maskl011 & maskl111 # 4. Gather values v000 = valuescompressed[l000] v100 = valuescompressed[l100] v010 = valuescompressed[l010] v110 = valuescompressed[l110] v001 = valuescompressed[l001] v101 = valuescompressed[l101] v011 = valuescompressed[l011] v111 = valuescompressed[l111] # 5. Compute weights tmpX = 1.0 - xd tmpY = 1.0 - yd tmpZ = 1.0 - zd a000 = tmpX tmpY a100 = xd tmpY a010 = tmpX yd a110 = xd yd weights = np.stack([a000, a010, a100, a110], axis=0) # Shape: (4, N) # 6. Gather coefficients and compute result coeff = np.stack([v000, v001, v010, v011, v100, v101, v110, v111], axis=0) # Shape: (8, C) res = np.sum(weights coeff[[0, 2, 4, 6],:], axis=0) tmpZ[:, None] + np.sum(weights coeff[[1, 3, 5, 7],:], axis=0) zd[:, None] # Initialize output and assign valid results result = np.zeroslike(res) result[maskvalid] = res[maskvalid] return result Subtopics: Trilinear Interpolation (Compressed/Linked Zero): A variant where invalid links are replaced with index 0 (assumed to hold a zero value) within a boundary union mask rather than masked out. JAX Trilinear Interpolation (Vmapped): An implementation strategy using jax.vmap for batched processing and jax.jit for compilation to accelerate the linked interpolation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of sample points, with a higher constant factor than dense trilinear due to link lookup and masking operations. Memory Complexity: O(Dx Dy Dz) for the links array, plus O(M) for valuescompressed. Measured Performance: Vectorized masking and gathering operations run in parallel; performance is limited by memory bandwidth when accessing valuescompressed if links are highly scattered. Strengths: Efficient for sparse data where the bounding box is not excessively large; maintains the smoothness of trilinear interpolation. Limitations: The links array consumes memory proportional to the bounding box volume, not the number of occupied voxels; boundary handling requires careful masking or zero-padding. When to use: When the volume is sparse but the bounding box is manageable, and smooth interpolation is required. When not to use: When the bounding box is very large relative to the number of occupied voxels. This method originates from implementations of volumetric rendering in JAX, specifically for optimizing sparse grid access in neural rendering pipelines. It leverages the compressed data structure to reduce memory footprint for values while using a link array to maintain spatial locality for interpolation. szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, https://github.com/szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Trilinear Gradient Interpolation
head: Trilinear Interpolation Backward Pass
body: Trilinear Gradient Interpolation computes the gradient or surface normal at an arbitrary point within a voxel by interpolating pre-computed vector values stored at the eight corners of the surrounding unit cube. It solves the problem of obtaining smooth, continuous directional derivatives from discrete grid data, which is essential for shading and ray marching in volume rendering. It differs from standard 3D Trilinear Interpolation by operating on vector fields rather than scalar values, and from Cubic Volume Interpolation by using only corner data without higher-order derivative constraints. Trilinear Gradient Interpolation extends standard trilinear interpolation to vector fields. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D grid of pre-computed gradient or normal vectors at voxel corners; the fractional coordinates (tx, ty, tz) of the query point relative to the voxel's minimum corner, where t \in [0, 1]. For training workflows, the upstream gradients of the loss with respect to the interpolated output, gradoutputs, of size points.size() channels. Outputs: The interpolated gradient/normal vector G{interp} (forward pass); updated gradpayload array with accumulated gradients (backward pass). Data Structures: The gradient grid is stored as three separate 3D arrays (one for each component x, y, z) or a single 4D array with shape (W, H, D, 3). Indices are integer coordinates (i, j, k) identifying the voxel corner, where 0 \le i < W, 0 \le j < H, 0 \le k < D. The backward pass accumulates gradients into a gradpayload vector of size payloadrows channels, initialized to zeros. Numbered Steps: 1. Retrieve Corner Gradients: Identify the 8 corner gradients surrounding the query point. Let G{ijk} be the gradient vector at corner (i,j,k), where i,j,k \in \{0,1\} represent the relative position within the voxel (0 for min, 1 for max). 2. Compute Interpolation Weights: Calculate the trilinear weights for each corner based on the fractional coordinates. 3. Interpolate Components: Compute the interpolated gradient vector G{interp} by summing the weighted corner gradients, equivalently implemented as three sequential linear interpolations (lerps) along the x, y, and z axes. 4. Normalization (Optional): If the input gradients are unit normals, normalize the interpolated result to maintain unit length. 5. Backward Pass (Gradient Distribution): Initialize gradpayload to zeros. Loop over each point. If outside root bounds, skip. Compute weights and total weight. If weight is 0, continue. Determine neighbor voxel and lookup its payloadindex. If payloadindex < 0, continue. Get pointer to gradient row: gradrow = gradpayload.data() + payloadindex channels. Loop over each channel. Update gradient: gradrow[channel] += weight gradoutputs[pointindex channels + channel]. Formulas: The weight for corner (i,j,k) is: w{ijk} = (1-tx)^{1-i} tx^i (1-ty)^{1-j} ty^j (1-tz)^{1-k} tz^k where tx, ty, tz \in [0, 1] are the fractional coordinates and i,j,k \in \{0,1\} are the corner indices. The interpolated vector is computed as: G{interp} = \sum{i=0}^{1} \sum{j=0}^{1} \sum{k=0}^{1} w{ijk} G{ijk} which expands to the sequential lerp operations: X-axis: x1 = \text{lerp}(G{000}, G{100}, tx), x2 = \text{lerp}(G{010}, G{110}, tx), x3 = \text{lerp}(G{001}, G{101}, tx), x4 = \text{lerp}(G{011}, G{111}, tx) Y-axis: y1 = \text{lerp}(x1, x2, ty), y2 = \text{lerp}(x3, x4, ty) Z-axis: G{interp} = \text{lerp}(y1, y2, tz) For normalization: N = G{interp} / \|G{interp}\|. Parameters: tx, ty, tz: Fractional coordinates within the voxel. Must be in [0, 1]. If outside, clamp or handle boundary conditions. normalize: Boolean flag. If true, the output is a unit vector. Default: true for normals. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Vector: If the interpolated gradient is zero, normalization fails. Return a default vector (e.g., [0,0,0] or up vector). Boundary Conditions: If the query point is outside the grid, indices must be clamped or the lookup returns -1, skipping the point. Precision: Accumulating gradients in the backward pass requires careful handling of floating-point precision when many points map to the same payload index. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilineargradientforward(gridgradients, tx, ty, tz, normalize=True): """ gridgradients: list of 8 vectors [G000, G100, G010, G110, G001, G101, G011, G111] tx, ty, tz: float in [0, 1] """ G000, G100, G010, G110, G001, G101, G011, G111 = gridgradients x1 = lerp(G000, G100, tx) x2 = lerp(G010, G110, tx) x3 = lerp(G001, G101, tx) x4 = lerp(G011, G111, tx) y1 = lerp(x1, x2, ty) y2 = lerp(x3, x4, ty) Ginterp = lerp(y1, y2, tz) if normalize: norm = vectornorm(Ginterp) if norm > 0: Ginterp = Ginterp / norm else: Ginterp = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return Ginterp def trilineargradientbackward(gradoutputs, weights, payloadindices, channels, gradpayload): """ gradoutputs: upstream gradients of shape (numpoints, channels) weights: scalar trilinear weights for each point payloadindices: integer indices into gradpayload for each point channels: number of channels per gradient gradpayload: flat array of size (payloadrows, channels) """ # Initialize gradpayload to zeros for i in range(len(gradpayload)): gradpayload[i] = 0.0 for pointidx in range(len(weights)): w = weights[pointidx] if w == 0: continue pidx = payloadindices[pointidx] if pidx < 0: continue # Get pointer to gradient row start = pidx channels end = start + channels gradrow = gradpayload[start:end] outrow = gradoutputs[pointidx] for c in range(channels): gradrow[c] += w outrow[c] def lerp(v1, v2, t): return [v1[i] + t (v2[i] - v1[i]) for i in range(len(v1))] def vectornorm(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 A specific application of Trilinear Gradient Interpolation where the grid stores surface normals instead of general gradients. It is used in ray marching for SDFs or implicit surfaces to provide smooth shading. It differs from general gradient interpolation by typically requiring explicit normalization of the result to maintain unit length, as interpolation of unit vectors does not preserve length. Choose this when rendering smooth surfaces defined by implicit functions or when shading requires consistent normal directions. Link: Trilinear Gradient Interpolation. Time Complexity: O(1) per query, involving 8 vector retrievals and 12 vector additions/multiplications (lerps). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the gradient grid, where N is the number of voxel corners. Requires storing 3 components per corner. Performance: Very fast, suitable for real-time rendering. The main cost is memory bandwidth for fetching 8 vectors. Strengths: Smooth gradients, easy to implement, works well with existing trilinear infrastructure. Limitations: Discontinuities at voxel boundaries if gradients are not consistent. Normalization can introduce artifacts if the interpolated vector is near zero. Less accurate than higher-order methods like cubic interpolation for complex fields. Trilinear interpolation is a standard technique in computer graphics for dense grids. Trilinear Gradient Interpolation extends this to vector fields. The method is commonly used in volume rendering for cloud shading and in implicit surface rendering for normal estimation. The specific implementation for normals is detailed in the SDFDiff project. hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, https://github.com/hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, https://github.com/ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YueJiang-nj/CVPR2020-SDFDiff, https://github.com/YueJiang-nj/CVPR2020-SDFDiff, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cubic Volume Interpolation
head: Cubic Trilinear Interpolation, Trilinear Interpolation with Cubic Weights
body: Cubic Volume Interpolation extends standard trilinear interpolation by using cubic mixture weights for each axis to sample a 3D texture at 8 corners defined by those weights. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D coordinate texCoord (float3) within the texture space, and a 3D texture dataTex containing the volume data. Output: A single interpolated float value representing the density or color at texCoord. Data Structures: dataTex: A 3D texture object used for sampling. mixX, mixY, mixZ: Temporary float3 variables storing the fractional offsets for the two texels and the sum of weights for normalization for each axis. Steps: 1. Calculate Cubic Mixture Weights: For each axis (X, Y, Z), compute the cubic interpolation weights and fractional offsets using the cubicInterpMixture function. 2. Sample Texture Corners: Sample the 3D texture at the 8 corners defined by the mixture weights. The coordinates for these samples are derived from mixX, mixY, and mixZ. 3. Interpolate along X Axis: For each of the two Z-slices (defined by mixZ.x and mixZ.y), interpolate along the X axis between the corresponding Y-slices. For the first Z-slice (mixZ.x): vY0Z0 = lerp(vX0Y0Z0, vX1Y0Z0, mixX.z) vY1Z0 = lerp(vX0Y1Z0, vX1Y1Z0, mixX.z) For the second Z-slice (mixZ.y): vY0Z1 = lerp(vX0Y0Z1, vX1Y0Z1, mixX.z) vY1Z1 = lerp(vX0Y1Z1, vX1Y1Z1, mixX.z) 4. Interpolate along Y Axis: For each Z-slice, interpolate along the Y axis between the results of the X interpolation. vZ0 = lerp(vY0Z0, vY1Y0Z0, mixY.z) vZ1 = lerp(vY0Z1, vY1Y1Z1, mixY.z) 5. Interpolate along Z Axis: Finally, interpolate along the Z axis between vZ0 and vZ1 using mixZ.z to produce the final value. Formulas: The cubic weights are calculated as follows, where a is the fractional part of the coordinate: a2 = a \times a a3 = a \times a2 w0 = -a3 + (2 \times a2) - a w1 = a3 - (2 \times a2) + 1 w2 = -a3 + a2 + a w3 = a3 - a2 The cubicInterpMixture function returns a float3 containing: First component: i - (w0 / (w0 + w1)) (fractional offset for the first texel) Second component: i + 1 + (w3 / (w2 + w3)) (fractional offset for the second texel) Third component: w2 + w3 (sum of weights for normalization) Parameters: triCubic: A boolean flag that determines whether to use cubic interpolation (true) or trilinear interpolation (false). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary conditions: The implementation checks if the texture coordinates are within the valid range [0, dataDim - 1]. If out of bounds, it returns a default outVal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def texturesample(tex, x, y, z): # Standard 3D texture lookup operation return tex.sample(x, y, z) def cubicinterpmixture(coord): i = math.floor(coord) a = coord - i a2 = a a a3 = a a2 w0 = -a3 + (2 a2) - a w1 = a3 - (2 a2) + 1 w2 = -a3 + a2 + a w3 = a3 - a2 offset1 = i - (w0 / (w0 + w1)) offset2 = i + 1 + (w3 / (w2 + w3)) weightsum = w2 + w3 return (offset1, offset2, weightsum) def cubicinterpolate(texcoord, datatex, datadim, outval): # Boundary check if (texcoord.x < 0 or texcoord.x > datadim.x - 1 or texcoord.y < 0 or texcoord.y > datadim.y - 1 or texcoord.z < 0 or texcoord.z > datadim.z - 1): return outval mixx = cubicinterpmixture(texcoord.x) mixy = cubicinterpmixture(texcoord.y) mixz = cubicinterpmixture(texcoord.z) # Sample the 8 corners vx0y0z0 = texturesample(datatex, mixx[0], mixy[0], mixz[0]) vx0y1z0 = texturesample(datatex, mixx[0], mixy[1], mixz[0]) vx0y0z1 = texturesample(datatex, mixx[0], mixy[0], mixz[1]) vx0y1z1 = texturesample(datatex, mixx[0], mixy[1], mixz[1]) vx1y0z0 = texturesample(datatex, mixx[1], mixy[0], mixz[0]) vx1y1z0 = texturesample(datatex, mixx[1], mixy[1], mixz[0]) vx1y0z1 = texturesample(datatex, mixx[1], mixy[0], mixz[1]) vx1y1z1 = texturesample(datatex, mixx[1], mixy[1], mixz[1]) # Interpolate along X vy0z0 = lerp(vx0y0z0, vx1y0z0, mixx[2]) vy1z0 = lerp(vx0y1z0, vx1y1z0, mixx[2]) vy0z1 = lerp(vx0y0z1, vx1y0z1, mixx[2]) vy1z1 = lerp(vx0y1z1, vx1y1z1, mixx[2]) # Interpolate along Y vz0 = lerp(vy0z0, vy1y0z0, mixy[2]) vz1 = lerp(vy0z1, vy1y1z1, mixy[2]) # Interpolate along Z return lerp(vz0, vz1, mixz[2]) Computes cubic interpolation weights and fractional offsets for a 1D coordinate, used for higher-order volume interpolation. It calculates the integer part i and fractional part a of the coordinate, then derives weights w0 through w3 using cubic polynomials. The function returns a float3 containing the fractional offsets for the two texels involved in the interpolation and the sum of weights for normalization. This is a helper function for the main cubic interpolation method. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. head: Polynomial Coefficient Extraction for Trilinear Interpolation
body: This method calculates the coefficients of the multi-variate polynomial that represents a multi-linearly interpolated level set (LS) function within a grid cell. It solves the problem of efficiently converting corner LS values into polynomial coefficients for root finding, optimizing the number of arithmetic operations compared to straightforward expansion. It is distinguished from its parent, Cubic Volume Interpolation, by its specific focus on the algebraic structure of the level set equation for intersection solving rather than general value estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of size 2^n containing the level set values of all 2^n corner grid points of a cell in n dimensions. The values must be stored in lexicographical order with reversed significance. Output: The same array, now overwritten with the polynomial coefficients ck in lexicographical order (with reversed significance) with respect to x. Data Structures: Grid Cell Index Vector: Defined as the lower bound indices of all its corner grid points. Coefficient Array: A flat array of size 2^n. The index k corresponds to the binary representation of the corner indices, mapped via the "reversed significance" convention described in the source. Formulas: The level set function f(x) is multi-linearly interpolated within a grid cell. For dimension n and cell index vector i, the interpolation formula is expressed as: f(x) = \sum{k=0}^{2^n-1} ck \prod{j=1}^{n} xj^{kj} where ck are the coefficients derived from the corner LS values. The coefficients are obtained by rewriting the standard trilinear interpolation formula. The source references equations (B.5) and (B.6) as intermediate rewriting steps, resulting in the calculation rule (B.7). While the explicit algebraic expansion of (B.7) is not fully detailed in the provided text snippet, it represents the transformation from corner values to polynomial coefficients. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize an array coeffs of size 2^n with the level set values of the grid cell's corners, ordered lexicographically with reversed significance. 2. Execute the coefficient calculation function. This function uses template metaprogramming to eliminate recursive function calls at compile time. 3. The function performs a reduced number of additions and subtractions (Algorithm B.1 in the source) to transform the corner values into coefficients ck. 4. The array coeffs is updated in-place to hold the coefficients ck in the same lexicographical order with reversed significance. Pseudocode: The source describes the algorithm as being realized using template metaprogramming to eliminate recursion. The following pseudocode represents the logical flow of the in-place transformation described in Algorithm B.1, assuming n dimensions and an array of size 2^n. Note that the exact recursive structure is unrolled by the compiler in the original implementation. Unverified code. Args: cornervalues: List of size 2^n containing LS values of corners in lexicographical order with reversed significance. Returns: List of size 2^n containing coefficients ck in the same order. """ n = int(math.log2(len(cornervalues))) if n < 0 or len(cornervalues) != 2n: raise ValueError("Array size must be a power of 2") # The source states that the array is passed to a static member function # and modified in-place. name: Quantile Interpolation for Uncertain Data
head: Analytic Quantile Interpolation, Quantile Interpolation of Histograms in 1D
body: Quantile Interpolation is a method for interpolating nonparametric probability distributions (PDFs) represented as histograms or Kernel Density Estimates (KDEs) within a volume rendering pipeline. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the uncertainty distribution at arbitrary 3D positions during Direct Volume Rendering (DVR), where traditional convolution-based nonparametric approaches suffer from exponential time complexity. Unlike its siblings, it preserves the modality of probability distributions and provides a closed-form solution with linear time complexity relative to the number of quantiles, making it feasible for real-time DVR reconstruction. It builds on 3D Trilinear Interpolation by extending the spatial interpolation logic to the statistical moments (quantile widths) of the data. Inputs: A 3D grid of size L \times M \times N. At each grid vertex vi, a nonparametric PDF pdf{Xi}(x) estimated from noise samples (via histograms or KDE). A user-defined quantile value qval (e.g., 0.5 for median, 0.001 for 1000 quantiles). Outputs: For a viewing ray sample at position \mathbf{p} inside a grid cell, the interpolated PDF pdfX(x) represented as a tuple of quantile densities \{Pr(Q1), \dots, Pr(Qq)\}. The expected color and opacity for DVR, computed by integrating the interpolated PDF against a transfer function. Data Structures: Quantile Representation: At each grid vertex vi, the PDF is partitioned into q quantiles. The representation is stored as a tuple of probability densities: \{Pr(Q{i1}), Pr(Q{i2}), \dots, Pr(Q{iq})\} where Pr(Q{ij}) is the probability density of the j-th quantile. Memory Layout: The grid stores q+1 boundary values per vertex to define the quantiles, resulting in a memory footprint of L \times M \times N \times (q+1). The densities Pr(Q{ij}) are derived from these boundaries. Preprocessing (Offline/Setup): 1. For each grid vertex vi, estimate the continuous PDF pdf{Xi}(x) from noise samples using histograms or KDE. 2. Partition pdf{Xi}(x) into q quantiles based on qval. The j-th quantile Q{ij} has a width w{ij} such that the cumulative probability up to that point is j \cdot qval. 3. Compute the quantile density for each j \in \{1, \dots, q\}: Pr(Q{ij}) = \frac{qval}{w{ij}} This creates the tuple \{Pr(Q{i1}), \dots, Pr(Q{iq})\} for storage. 4. Precompute the mean intensity m{ij} for each quantile Q{ij} at every vertex. Runtime (Fragment Shader / Ray Marching): For a sample point \mathbf{p} inside a grid cell defined by vertices v1, \dots, v8: 1. Lookup: Retrieve the quantile density tuples \{Pr(Q{i1}), \dots, Pr(Q{iq})\} and mean intensities \{m{i1}, \dots, m{iq}\} for all 8 neighboring vertices vi. Let Pri denote the density Pr(Q{ij}) for the j-th quantile at vertex i. 2. Interpolation: Compute the density Pr(Qj) for the j-th quantile of the interpolated random variable X using the closed-form 3D formula: Pr(Qj) = \frac{Pr1 Pr2 Pr3 Pr4 Pr5 Pr6 Pr7 Pr8}{t1 t2 t3 t4 t5 t6 t7} where the intermediate terms tk are computed as follows, using spatial distance parameters \alpha, \beta, \gamma \in [0,1] corresponding to the position of \mathbf{p} within the cell: \begin{aligned} t1 &= \alpha Pr1 + (1-\alpha)Pr2 \\ t2 &= \alpha Pr3 + (1-\alpha)Pr4 \\ t3 &= \alpha Pr5 + (1-\alpha)Pr6 \\ t4 &= \alpha Pr7 + (1-\alpha)Pr8 \\ t5 &= \beta \frac{Pr1 Pr2}{t1} + (1-\beta)\frac{Pr3 Pr4}{t2} \\ t6 &= \beta \frac{Pr5 Pr6}{t3} + (1-\beta)\frac{Pr7 Pr8}{t4} \\ t7 &= \gamma \frac{Pr1 Pr2 Pr3 Pr4}{t1 t2 t5} + (1-\gamma)\frac{Pr5 Pr6 Pr7 Pr8}{t3 t4 t6} \end{aligned} This formula is equivalent to linearly interpolating the quantile widths wj and then computing Pr(Qj) = qval / wj. 3. Integration: Compute the expected color and opacity by integrating the interpolated PDF against the Transfer Function (TF). The piecewise constant representation allows for specific integration schemes (e.g., Quantile Range or Quantile Mean): E(\text{TF}(X)) = \int \text{TF}(x) pdfX(x) dx Pseudocode: def interpolatequantiledensity(Prvertices, alpha, beta, gamma): """Computes the interpolated probability density for a single quantile index j. Prvertices: list of 8 floats, Pri = Pr(Qij) for i in 1..8 Returns: Pr(Qj) for the interpolated point. """ Pr1, Pr2, Pr3, Pr4, Pr5, Pr6, Pr7, Pr8 = Prvertices # Step 1: Interpolate along x-axis (alpha) t1 = alpha Pr1 + (1 - alpha) Pr2 t2 = alpha Pr3 + (1 - alpha) Pr4 t3 = alpha Pr5 + (1 - alpha) Pr6 t4 = alpha Pr7 + (1 - alpha) Pr8 # Step 2: Interpolate along y-axis (beta) term12 = (Pr1 Pr2) / t1 term34 = (Pr3 Pr4) / t2 term56 = (Pr5 Pr6) / t3 term78 = (Pr7 Pr8) / t4 t5 = beta term12 + (1 - beta) term34 t6 = beta term56 + (1 - beta) term78 # Step 3: Interpolate along z-axis (gamma) face1234num = Pr1 Pr2 Pr3 Pr4 face1234den = t1 t2 t5 face5678num = Pr5 Pr6 Pr7 Pr8 face5678den = t3 t4 t6 t7 = gamma (face1234num / face1234den) + (1 - gamma) (face5678num / face5678den) # Final result per Eq. 2 numerator = Pr1 Pr2 Pr3 Pr4 Pr5 Pr6 Pr7 Pr8 denominator = t1 t2 t3 t4 t5 t6 t7 return numerator / denominator def trilinearinterpolate(v000, v001, v010, v011, v100, v101, v110, v111, alpha, beta, gamma): """Standard trilinear interpolation for scalar values like mean intensities.""" c00 = v000 (1-alpha) + v100 alpha c01 = v001 (1-alpha) + v101 alpha c10 = v010 (1-alpha) + v100 alpha # Note: v100 reused in source logic, corrected to v110 below c10 = v010 (1-alpha) + v110 alpha c11 = v011 (1-alpha) + v111 alpha t0 = c00 (1-beta) + c10 beta t1 = c01 (1-beta) + c11 beta return t0 (1-gamma) + t1 gamma def raymarchquantilevolume(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, gridquantiles, gridmeans, gridsize, qval, tfsample): """ gridquantiles: L x M x N array, each element is a list of q densities gridmeans: L x M x N array, each element is a list of q mean intensities tfsample(intensity) -> (colorrgb, opacityfloat) """ color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] opacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 # Standard front-to-back volume rendering accumulation while t < 1.0: p = rayorigin + raydirection t # Determine containing cell and fractional coordinates (alpha, beta, gamma) cellmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Assuming unit grid for simplicity; scale by gridsize if needed cellsize = 1.0 / gridsize alpha = (p[0] - cellmin[0]) / cellsize beta = (p[1] - cellmin[1]) / cellsize gamma = (p[2] - cellmin[2]) / cellsize # Clamp to [0, 1] to handle boundaries alpha = max(0.0, min(1.0, alpha)) beta = max(0.0, min(1.0, beta)) gamma = max(0.0, min(1.0, gamma)) # Quantile Mean Integration # Compute normalization constant p = sum(qval wk) = qval sum(wk) # Since wk = qval / Pr(Qk), p = qval^2 sum(1/Pr(Qk)) # However, the source defines Pr(x=mj) = (qval wj) / sum(qval wk) # which simplifies to wj / sum(wk). sumwidths = 0.0 weightedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for j in range(len(gridquantiles[0][0][0])): # Extract densities for j-th quantile from 8 vertices Prvertices = [ gridquantiles[0][0][0][j], gridquantiles[0][0][1][j], gridquantiles[0][1][0][j], gridquantiles[0][1][1][j], gridquantiles[1][0][0][j], gridquantiles[1][0][1][j], gridquantiles[1][1][0][j], gridquantiles[1][1][1][j] ] Prj = interpolatequantiledensity(Prvertices, alpha, beta, gamma) wj = qval / Prj sumwidths += wj # Get mean intensity for this quantile at interpolated point via standard trilinear interpolation mj = trilinearinterpolate( gridmeans[0][0][0][j], gridmeans[0][0][1][j], gridmeans[0][1][0][j], gridmeans[0][1][1][j], gridmeans[1][0][0][j], gridmeans[1][0][1][j], gridmeans[1][1][0][j], gridmeans[1][1][1][j], alpha, beta, gamma) # Sample Transfer Function cj, oj = tfsample(mj) # Weight by discrete probability Pr(x=mj) = wj / sumwidths prob = wj / sumwidths weightedcolor[0] += cj[0] prob weightedcolor[1] += cj[1] prob weightedcolor[2] += cj[2] prob # Accumulate into ray using standard front-to-back compositing cellopacity = sum(wj / sumwidths oj for wj, oj in zip([qval/interpolatequantiledensity([gridquantiles[x][y][z][j] for x in (0,1) for y in (0,1) for z in (0,1)] for j in range(len(gridquantiles[0][0][0]))], [tfsample(trilinearinterpolate([gridmeans[x][y][z][j] for x in (0,1) for y in (0,1) for z in (0,1)], alpha, beta, gamma)[1] for j in range(len(gridquantiles[0][0][0])))])) # Simplified opacity accumulation for clarity: cellopacity = 0.0 for j in range(len(gridquantiles[0][0][0])): Prvertices = [gridquantiles[x][y][z][j] for x in (0,1) for y in (0,1) for z in (0,1)] wj = qval / interpolatequantiledensity(Prvertices, alpha, beta, gamma) mj = trilinearinterpolate([gridmeans[x][y][z][j] for x in (0,1) for y in (0,1) for z in (0,1)], alpha, beta, gamma), oj = tfsample(mj) cellopacity += (wj / sumwidths) oj color[0] += weightedcolor[0] cellopacity (1.0 - opacity) color[1] += weightedcolor[1] cellopacity (1.0 - opacity) color[2] += weightedcolor[2] cellopacity (1.0 - opacity) opacity += cellopacity (1.0 - opacity) if opacity >= 0.99: break t += stepsize return color, opacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximation Error: As the number of quantiles q approaches infinity, the PDF converges to a closed-form continuous distribution. Finite q is an approximation. KDE Fluctuations: If the number of noise samples used to estimate the initial PDFs is small, the resulting KDE may be poor. This leads to significant fluctuations in the interpolated PDF results, especially for a high number of quantiles. Zero Densities: If any Pri is zero, the intermediate terms tk and the final result must be handled carefully to avoid division by zero or undefined behavior, though the source formula assumes non-degenerate distributions. An integration scheme for DVR where the mean intensity of each quantile is integrated with the Transfer Function (TF). It calculates the mean intensity mj for each quantile Qj, computes the discrete probability \Pr(x = mj) for each mean intensity, samples the TF at each mean intensity mj and weights by the discrete probability, then sums. The expected fragment color is computed as E(\text{TF}(X)) = \sum{j=1}^{q} \text{TF}(x = mj) \Pr(x = mj), where \Pr(x = mj) = \frac{pj}{p}, pj = qval \cdot wj, and p = \sum{k=1}^q qval \cdot wk is the normalization constant. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of quantiles q. The arithmetic operations in Eq. 2 are applied quantile-wise, making the computational cost proportional to q. This is a significant improvement over convolution-based nonparametric approaches which have exponential time complexity. Memory Complexity: L \times M \times N \times (q+1), where L, M, N are the grid dimensions. The memory requirement increases linearly with q due to the storage of q+1 boundaries per vertex. Strengths: Preserves the modality of probability distributions at cell vertices. Provides a closed-form solution, avoiding iterative sampling or expensive convolutions. Feasible for DVR reconstruction on high-performance hardware due to linear complexity. Limitations: Accuracy depends on the quality of the initial KDE/histogram estimation. High q increases memory usage and computational load linearly. Poor KDE from reduced sample sizes can cause significant fluctuations in results. When to use: When uncertainty is modeled nonparametrically and real-time or efficient DVR is required, and the data supports sufficient sampling for KDE estimation. When not to use: When the noise samples are too sparse for reliable KDE, or when exponential time complexity is acceptable for higher fidelity nonparametric interpolation. The use of quantile interpolation in uncertainty visualization was first advocated by Hollister and Pang. The method was originally proposed for 1D interpolation of histograms by Read [49]. Hollister and Pang extended this to a closed-form bilinear interpolation of histograms/nonparametric distributions on a 2D grid. The 3D extension, as described in the primary source, applies the same logic to 3D grid cells, enabling efficient Direct Volume Rendering of uncertain data. The technique is an example of order statistics, where quantiles are ranked based on the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF). name: Quantile Interpolation of Nonparametric Distributions in 3D
head: 3D Quantile Interpolation, Quantile Interpolation of Histograms in 3D
body: This method computes the interpolated Probability Density Function (PDF) of a random variable at an arbitrary 3D position within a grid cell by interpolating quantile representations from the eight vertices of the containing 3D cell. It extends 1D quantile interpolation to 3D using a bilinear interpolation logic, sequentially interpolating along edges, then faces, then the volume. It operates on probability density functions rather than scalar values, preserving the statistical nature of uncertain data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The PDFs of the j-th quantile at the 8 vertices of a 3D grid cell, denoted Pr1 through Pr8. The spatial distance parameters \alpha, \beta, \gamma \in [0,1] define the query point's position relative to the cell vertices along the three dimensions. Output: The interpolated probability density Pr(Qj) for the j-th quantile at the query point. Data Structures: The method assumes the PDFs at vertices are pre-computed piecewise constant functions where each quantile j has a constant probability density Pri at vertex i. Steps: 1. Edge Interpolation: Compute interpolated PDFs along the cell edges by applying the 1D quantile interpolation formula to the PDFs at grid vertices using parameter \alpha. 2. Face Interpolation: Compute interpolated PDFs in the interior of cell faces by applying the 1D quantile interpolation formula to the edge-interpolated PDFs using parameter \beta. 3. Volume Interpolation: Compute the final interpolated PDF in the interior of the 3D cell by applying the 1D quantile interpolation formula to the face-interpolated PDFs using parameter \gamma. Formulas: The final interpolated PDF for the j-th quantile is given by: Pr(Qj) = \frac{Pr1 Pr2 Pr3 Pr4 Pr5 Pr6 Pr7 Pr8}{t1 t2 t3 t4 t5 t6 t7} where the intermediate terms are defined as: t1 = \alpha Pr1 + (1-\alpha)Pr2 t2 = \alpha Pr3 + (1-\alpha)Pr4 t3 = \alpha Pr5 + (1-\alpha)Pr6 t4 = \alpha Pr7 + (1-\alpha)Pr8 t5 = \beta \frac{Pr1 Pr2}{t1} + (1-\beta) \frac{Pr3 Pr4}{t2} t6 = \beta \frac{Pr5 Pr6}{t3} + (1-\beta) \frac{Pr7 Pr8}{t4} t7 = \gamma \frac{Pr1 Pr2 Pr3 Pr4}{t1 t2 t5} + (1-\gamma) \frac{Pr5 Pr6 Pr7 Pr8}{t3 t4 t6} Parameters: Pri: The probability density of the j-th quantile for the random variable at the i-th vertex of the 3D grid cell (i=1..8). \alpha, \beta, \gamma: Spatial distance parameters for the vertices of the 3D grid cell along the three dimensions, each in the range [0,1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def quantileinterpolation3d(Pr, alpha, beta, gamma): """ Computes the interpolated PDF for a specific quantile in a 3D cell. Args: Pr (list of 8 floats): Probability densities Pr1 to Pr8 at the 8 vertices. alpha (float): Spatial parameter along the first dimension [0, 1]. beta (float): Spatial parameter along the second dimension [0, 1]. gamma (float): Spatial parameter along the third dimension [0, 1]. Returns: float: The interpolated probability density Pr(Qj). """ Pr1, Pr2, Pr3, Pr4, Pr5, Pr6, Pr7, Pr8 = Pr # Step 1: Edge interpolation (along dimension 1) t1 = alpha Pr1 + (1 - alpha) Pr2 t2 = alpha Pr3 + (1 - alpha) Pr4 t3 = alpha Pr5 + (1 - alpha) Pr6 t4 = alpha Pr7 + (1 - alpha) Pr8 # Step 2: Face interpolation (along dimension 2) t5 = beta (Pr1 Pr2 / t1) + (1 - beta) (Pr3 Pr4 / t2) t6 = beta (Pr5 Pr6 / t3) + (1 - beta) (Pr7 Pr8 / t4) # Step 3: Volume interpolation (along dimension 3) t7 = gamma (Pr1 Pr2 Pr3 Pr4 / (t1 t2 t5)) + (1 - gamma) (Pr5 Pr6 Pr7 Pr8 / (t3 t4 t6)) # Final result numerator = Pr1 Pr2 Pr3 Pr4 Pr5 Pr6 Pr7 Pr8 denominator = t1 t2 t3 t4 t5 t6 t7 return numerator / denominator Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If any intermediate term tk evaluates to zero (e.g., due to zero probability densities at vertices), the formula is undefined; a small epsilon or clamping is required. The parameters \alpha, \beta, \gamma must be strictly within [0,1] to maintain the convex combination structure of the interpolation. The parent method defines the 1D quantile interpolation formula and represents PDFs as piecewise constant quantile functions. It provides the foundational 1D formula used in the edge, face, and volume steps. Quantile Interpolation for Uncertain Data Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was extended from 2D by Hollister and Pang, who presented a closed-form solution for bilinear interpolation of histograms/nonparametric distributions on a 2D grid using quantile interpolation. The 3D extension follows a similar approach, applying the 1D quantile interpolation formula sequentially along edges, faces, and the volume. name: Quantile Mean Integration
head: Quantile Mean Technique
body: Quantile Mean Integration is a volume rendering integration scheme for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) that computes the expected fragment color by evaluating the Transfer Function (TF) at the mean intensity of each quantile, weighted by the discrete probability of that quantile. It differs from Quantile Range Integration by approximating the continuous distribution within each quantile with a single point mass (the mean) rather than integrating the TF over the quantile's intensity interval. This method is chosen when computational efficiency is prioritized over the accuracy of capturing intensity variance within quantiles, as it reduces the integration of a function over an interval to a single function evaluation per quantile. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of q quantiles Q1, \dots, Qq for an interpolated random variable X. Each quantile Qj is associated with a weight wj (representing the width or probability mass contribution) and a scalar value qval (a constant scaling factor for the probability mass). Input: A Transfer Function \text{TF}(x) mapping intensity x to color/opacity. Output: The expected fragment color E(\text{TF}(X)). Data Structures: Quantile List: An array of q elements. Each element j stores: wj: The width/probability weight of the j-th quantile. mj: The mean intensity of the j-th quantile. Constants: qval: The quantile value scaling factor (typically 1/q for uniform quantiles, but treated as a general parameter here). Steps: 1. Calculate Mean Intensities: Determine the mean intensity mj for each quantile Qj. This value mj represents the expected intensity value within the j-th quantile. 2. Compute Discrete Probabilities: Calculate the unnormalized probability mass pj for each quantile using the formula: pj = qval \cdot wj Compute the normalization constant p by summing the unnormalized masses: p = \sum{k=1}^{q} qval \cdot wk Calculate the discrete probability \Pr(x = mj) for each mean intensity: \Pr(x = mj) = \frac{pj}{p} = \frac{qval \cdot wj}{\sum{k=1}^{q} qval \cdot wk} Note: If qval is constant across all quantiles, it cancels out in the normalization, simplifying to \Pr(x = mj) = \frac{wj}{\sum{k=1}^{q} wk}. 3. Evaluate Transfer Function: Sample the Transfer Function at each mean intensity mj to get \text{TF}(mj). 4. Weight and Sum: Compute the expected fragment color by summing the product of the TF value and the discrete probability for each quantile: E(\text{TF}(X)) = \sum{j=1}^{q} \text{TF}(mj) \Pr(x = mj) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def quantilemeanintegration(quantiles, transferfunction): """ Compute expected fragment color using Quantile Mean Integration. Args: quantiles: List of tuples (wj, mj) where wj is the weight/width and mj is the mean intensity of the j-th quantile. transferfunction: A function TF(x) returning color/opacity for intensity x. Returns: Expected fragment color. """ q = len(quantiles) if q == 0: return 0.0 # Or default background color # Step 1 & 2: Compute probabilities # qval is assumed to be a constant scaling factor. # In many implementations, qval is uniform (e.g., 1/q), but we keep it general. # If qval is not provided explicitly, it is often implicit in wj or normalized out. # Based on, pj = qval wj. Let's assume qval is passed or derived. # For standard uniform quantiles, qval = 1/q. If wj are normalized probabilities, qval=1. # We assume qval is a scalar constant provided or 1.0 if not specified. qval = 1.0 # Default assumption if not specified; adjust based on context numerator = 0.0 weightedtfsum = 0.0 for j in range(q): wj, mj = quantiles[j] # Unnormalized probability mass pj = qval wj # Accumulate normalization constant numerator += pj # Accumulate weighted TF evaluation # We store TF(mj) pj to divide by p later weightedtfsum += transferfunction(mj) pj # Normalization constant p p = numerator if p == 0: return 0.0 # Avoid division by zero for empty or zero-weight quantiles # Step 3 & 4: Final expected value expectedcolor = weightedtfsum / p return expectedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weights: If all wj = 0, the normalization constant p is zero, leading to division by zero. Guard against this. Precision: Summing many small probabilities can lead to floating-point precision issues. Use Kahan summation or similar techniques if q is large. Mean Calculation: The accuracy of the result depends entirely on the accuracy of mj. If mj is poorly estimated (e.g., from a skewed distribution within the quantile), the integration will be biased. An integration scheme for DVR where all intensities contained within a quantile are integrated with the Transfer Function (TF). Unlike Quantile Mean Integration, which uses a single point (the mean), this method computes the integral of the TF over the entire interval [startj, endj] of each quantile. The expected fragment color is calculated as: E(\text{TF}(X)) = \sum{j=1}^{q} \frac{qval}{wj} \int{startj}^{endj} \text{TF}(x) dx where wj is the width of the j-th quantile. This is equivalent to averaging the TFs for each quantile and performing a weighted sum where the weight is qval. It is more computationally expensive due to the integration step but provides a more accurate representation of the intensity distribution within each quantile. Time Complexity: O(q) per sample, where q is the number of quantiles. This is significantly faster than Quantile Range Integration if the TF evaluation is cheaper than integration, as it avoids numerical integration over intervals. Memory Complexity: The memory consumed by input data for the nonparametric DVR framework is L \times M \times N \times (q+1), where L \times M \times N is the grid size and q+1 represents the number of boundaries defining quantiles at each grid vertex. The integration step itself requires O(1) additional memory per sample. Strengths: Computationally efficient; simple to implement; suitable for real-time rendering where integration over intervals is too slow. Limitations: Approximates the distribution within each quantile with a single value, potentially losing information about variance and skewness within the quantile. Less accurate than Quantile Range Integration for highly non-linear Transfer Functions. When to use: When performance is critical and the Transfer Function is relatively linear or smooth within quantile intervals. When not to use: When high fidelity in representing uncertainty is required, or when the Transfer Function has sharp discontinuities within quantile intervals. Quantile Mean Integration was proposed in the context of Direct Volume Rendering with Nonparametric Models of Uncertainty. It is part of a framework that uses Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) to model uncertainty at grid vertices and reduces continuous distributions to quantile representations for efficient rendering. The method was introduced to provide a computationally viable alternative to integrating the full probability density function over the Transfer Function, balancing accuracy and performance. name: iso_corners_list_f1v4
body: isocornerslistf1v4 is a GPU kernel variant that computes the values of one function at the eight corners of the grid cells enclosing a list of input points, enabling trilinear interpolation or surface extraction. It differs from its siblings by processing 256 consecutive lattice points per thread group across 2–4 neighboring bricks, sharing shell setup overhead among all points in the group rather than per-brick, which improves occupancy and reduces redundant memory accesses. Inputs: A list of input points (lattice coordinates). A set of functions (1 for f1v4, or 8/16/32/64 for variants). Grid data structures: brick hierarchy, shell definitions, and function coefficients (e.g., C matrix for Gaussian-type orbitals). Outputs: For each input point, the values of the functions at the 8 corners of the enclosing voxel. In the case of isodcorners, the values in the \phi^T D \phi form (density-like quantities). Data Structures: Brick Hash: Built on-device, mapping brick IDs to memory slots. Rejected siblings (mask 0) are kept in the octree structure to ensure consecutive bricks are neighbors in memory. Shells: Precomputed lists of lattice points or coefficients for each shell level, stored in group-shared memory for the group. Function Coefficients (C): Stored in global memory, accessed via tiled GEMM if enabled. Steps: 1. Thread Group Initialization: Each thread group processes 256 consecutive points from the input list. 2. Brick Identification: Determine the bricks enclosing the 256 points. This may span 2–4 neighboring bricks. 3. Shell Setup: Compute the shells required for the bounding box of the group's points. This setup is shared among all 256 threads, reducing overhead compared to per-brick setup (which would handle 70–125 points). 4. Point Processing: For each point in the group: identify which shells are within reach and skip shells outside the point's bounding box. Load the necessary shell data from group-shared memory. Compute the function values at the 8 corners. For isocornerslistf1v4, this involves one function. For variants, it involves 8, 16, 32, or 64 functions. If using tiled GEMM (isogcorners), perform matrix multiplication of AO values and coefficients. 5. Output: Store the computed corner values. Points that skip shells due to being out of reach simply do not access those shell data blocks. Parameters: GTOISOGEMM: Boolean flag enabling tiled GEMM for corner computation. Default value is 1. GTOISOCORNERSLIST: Switch to enable/disable the list-based processing mode. Default is 1 (enabled). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: Points near the edge of the grid or brick boundaries must correctly identify neighboring bricks. The octree structure ensures that rejected siblings are kept to maintain neighbor connectivity. Degenerate Input: If a point is far from any brick, it may skip all shells. The kernel handles this by checking shell reachability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isocornerslistf1v4kernel(points, brickids, shelldata, coeffs): groupsize = 256 sharedshells = [None] 1024 # Group-shared memory allocation # 1. Identify bricks for the 256 points (spans 2-4 neighbors) # Brick hash is built on-device; rejected siblings (mask 0) are kept for neighbor continuity # 2. Shared shell setup for the group bounding box groupshells = [s for s in shelldata if isinbox(s, points[:groupsize])] # 3. Load shells into shared memory for i, shellidx in enumerate(groupshells): sharedshells[i] = shelldata[shellidx] # 4. Process each point in the group for i in range(groupsize): point = points[i] cornervalues = [0.0] 8 # Determine which shells are within reach; skip shells out of reach reachableshells = [s for s in groupshells if distance(point, s.center) <= s.radius] for shell in reachableshells: shellentry = sharedshells[shell] # Compute contribution to corner values # For f1v4, this is one function; variants handle 8/16/32/64 contribution = shellentry.evaluate(point) for c in range(8): cornervalues[c] += contribution[c] # Store result output[i] = cornervalues def isinbox(shell, pts): return all(shell.min <= p <= shell.max for p in pts) def distance(p, center): return ((p.x - center.x)2 + (p.y - center.y)2 + (p.z - center.z)2)0.5 Computes an 8-bit integer index representing the configuration of a voxel's eight corners relative to an isolevel, determining which edges are intersected by the surface. It calculates the marching cubes case index for each voxel based on corner values relative to an iso-level. Unlike sibling methods that handle sparse point clouds or pre-gathered data, this method operates directly on the scalar values at the voxel corners to produce the topology case. Implementation of isogcorners and isogeval kernels as tiled GEMM operations. Tiled GEMM kernel for computing corners for sets of 16, 32, or 64 functions. Process 128 rows per group for corner points of the list. Alternatively, process 32 vertices x value and gradient channels per group. GTOISOGEMM: Boolean flag enabling tiled GEMM; default value is 1. Used for canonical sets of more than 64 functions (wide GEMM w128/w192/y256) or specific sizes 16/32/64. Kernel for computing value and gradient at 64 vertices per group of 256 threads, used for sets with densities. Kernel step: One warp per channel (value, d/dx, d/dy, d/dz) accumulating F function columns in registers. Kernel step: Shells are listed and rows of C are staged as for corners. Kernel step: One thread per vertex applies its field's terms from the channels staged 16 vertices at a time. Time Complexity: The kernel processes 256 points per group, with shared shell setup reducing overhead. On lavapipe, mol at h=0.2, corner kernel times reduced from 38ms to 34ms (HOMO), 168ms to 144ms (diff density), 197ms to 121ms (trans density), 315ms to 246ms (16 MOs). Memory Complexity: Uses group-shared memory for shells, reducing global memory bandwidth. The octree structure keeps rejected siblings to maintain neighbor connectivity, increasing memory usage slightly. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of threads and groups. Tiled GEMM improves performance for larger function sets. Strengths: High occupancy due to shared shell setup. Efficient for dense point lists. Limitations: Requires careful management of shared memory for shells. May not be optimal for very sparse point lists. When to use: When processing large lists of points for isosurface extraction or interpolation. When not to use: For very small point lists or sparse data where per-brick processing might be more efficient. name: Cube Index Calculation
head: Marching Cubes Cube Index Calculation
body: Computes an 8-bit integer index representing the configuration of a voxel's eight corners relative to an isolevel, determining which edges are intersected by the surface. It calculates the marching cubes case index for each voxel based on corner values relative to an iso-level. Unlike sibling methods that handle sparse point clouds or pre-gathered data, this method operates directly on the scalar values at the voxel corners to produce the topology case. Inputs: corners: A collection of 8 scalar values representing the density or signed distance at the 8 corners of a voxel. In dense implementations, these are stored in a struct VoxelCorners<T> containing 8 fields (Corner1 to Corner8) of type T. In sparse implementations, these are provided as a float tensor of shape [N, 8]. isolevel: The scalar threshold value. Outputs: cubeindex: An 8-bit integer (0–255) representing the voxel's configuration. Data Structures: Dense Layout: A struct VoxelCorners<T> containing 8 fields (Corner1 to Corner8) of type T (e.g., byte or float). Sparse Layout: Input tensor corners of shape [N, 8] where N is the number of voxels. Output tensor cubeindices of shape [N]. Algorithm: 1. Initialize cubeindex to 0. 2. For each corner i from 0 to 7 (corresponding to corners 1 to 8 in 1-based indexing): Compare the corner's scalar value vi with isolevel. If vi < \text{iso\level}, set the i-th bit of cubeindex to 1. Otherwise, the bit remains 0. 3. Return cubeindex. Formula: \text{cube\index} = \sum{i=0}^{7} \mathbb{I}(vi < \text{iso\level}) \cdot 2^i Where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function (1 if true, 0 if false). Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Comparisons use strict inequality. If vi = \text{iso\level}, the condition vi < \text{iso\level} is false, so the bit remains 0. Boundary Conditions: In sparse implementations, if a corner coordinate is missing from the point set, a default value is used (e.g., 1.0) before comparison. Degenerate Input: If all corners are equal, the index is either 0 or 255, resulting in no surface intersection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecubeindex(corners, isolevel): """ Computes the Marching Cubes cube index for a single voxel. Args: corners: List or array of 8 scalar values [v0, v1,..., v7]. isolevel: The threshold value. Returns: int: The 8-bit cube index. """ cubeindex = 0 for i in range(8): if corners[i] < isolevel: cubeindex |= (1 << i) return cubeindex Handles cases where corners are not pre-computed but derived from a list of points. It gathers values from a sparse grid, using defaults for missing points. Processes N voxels simultaneously using tensor operations, optimizing for GPU execution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Highly parallelizable. In sparse implementations, it leverages CUDA backends for high-performance execution on large datasets. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and fast. Calculates the marching cubes case index for each voxel based on corner values relative to an iso-level. Limitations: Does not handle the topology generation itself; only provides the case index. Requires valid corner values. Not given in the sources. name: UniformGrid Cell Vertex and Material Retrieval
body: This method retrieves the linear indices and associated material data for the 8 vertices of a grid cell within a uniform 3D grid, given the linear index of the cell itself. It provides the explicit arithmetic formula for linear index calculation in a uniform grid, mapping a single cell identifier to its constituent geometric corners. Inputs: cellIdx: The linear index of the target grid cell (integer). msize: The number of cells along one axis of the uniform grid (integer). Outputs: v: An array of 8 integers representing the linear indices of the 8 vertices of the cell. materials: An array of 8 material identifiers corresponding to the vertices. Data Structures: The grid is stored in a flat, contiguous memory array (linearized). Formulas: The linear index calculation relies on three stride constants derived from msize: \begin{aligned} dx &= m\size + 1 \\ dy &= (m\size + 1) \times (m\size + 1) \\ dz &= 1 \end{aligned} The 8 vertex linear indices v[0] through v[7] are computed as: \begin{aligned} v[0] &= cellIdx \\ v[1] &= cellIdx + dz \\ v[2] &= cellIdx + dx \\ v[3] &= cellIdx + dx + dz \\ v[4] &= cellIdx + dy \\ v[5] &= cellIdx + dy + dz \\ v[6] &= cellIdx + dx + dy \\ v[7] &= cellIdx + dx + dy + dz \end{aligned} Material retrieval follows the exact same indexing logic. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def retrievecellverticesandmaterials(cellIdx, msize, materialarray): dx = msize + 1 dy = (msize + 1) (msize + 1) dz = 1 v = [0] 8 v[0] = cellIdx v[1] = cellIdx + dz v[2] = cellIdx + dx v[3] = cellIdx + dx + dz v[4] = cellIdx + dy v[5] = cellIdx + dy + dz v[6] = cellIdx + dx + dy v[7] = cellIdx + dx + dy + dz materials = [0] 8 for i in range(8): materials[i] = materialarray[v[i]] return v, materials Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary conditions: Not given in the sources. Grid dimensions: The formula assumes a cubic grid where the number of cells is the same in all dimensions (msize). Precision: Linear indices are integers. name: Cube Edge Vertex Retrieval
head: Edge Retrieval
body: Retrieves all 12 edge vertex pairs for a specific cube in the voxel grid. It differs from its parent UniformGrid Cell Vertex and Material Retrieval by focusing specifically on the 12 edges rather than the 8 corner vertices. Inputs and Outputs: Input: cubeidx (linear index of the target cube), grid (data structure containing vertex data). Output: A list of 12 pairs, where each pair contains the linear indices of the two vertices defining an edge. Data Structures: CUBEEDGESFLAT: A static lookup table of size 24 (12 edges × 2 vertices) that maps edge index e to the local corner indices c0 and c1 within the cube. Layout: int CUBEEDGESFLAT[24]. Access: For edge e, corners are at indices 2e and 2e+1. grid.cubes: A 1D array or tensor storing vertex linear indices for all cubes. Access pattern: grid.cubes(cubeidx, localcornerindex). Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list edgepairs. 2. Loop e from 0 to 11 (inclusive): a. Retrieve the first local corner index: c0 = \text{CUBE\EDGES\FLAT}[2e]. b. Retrieve the second local corner index: c1 = \text{CUBE\EDGES\FLAT}[2e+1]. c. Retrieve the global linear index of the first vertex: v0 = \text{grid.cubes}(\text{cube\idx}, c0). d. Retrieve the global linear index of the second vertex: v1 = \text{grid.cubes}(\text{cube\idx}, c1). e. Append the pair \{v0, v1\} to edgepairs. 3. Return edgepairs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def retrievecubeedges(cubeidx, grid): # Standard cube edge connectivity mapping 12 edges to 24 local corner indices CUBEEDGESFLAT = [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 0, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 4, 0, 4, 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7] edgepairs = [] for e in range(12): c0 = CUBEEDGESFLAT[e 2] c1 = CUBEEDGESFLAT[e 2 + 1] v0 = grid.cubes[cubeidx][c0] v1 = grid.cubes[cubeidx][c1] edgepairs.append((v0, v1)) return edgepairs Parameters: CUBEEDGESFLAT: Standard cube edge connectivity. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Invalid cubeidx: If cubeidx is out of bounds, the grid lookup will fail. Degenerate cubes: The method returns indices regardless of whether the cube is valid or empty. Constructs the topological state of a single voxel cube for Marching Cubes by sampling a Signed Distance Field (SDF) at its eight vertices. It differs by handling degenerate cases where SDF values equal the threshold. It builds on Cube Edge Vertex Retrieval by providing the vertex data and sign flags required to identify which edges intersect the surface. Time Complexity: O(1) per cube, as it performs a fixed number of 12 lookups. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the loop and pair storage. Strengths: Extremely fast, deterministic, and cache-friendly due to small, fixed-size access patterns. Limitations: Only provides connectivity; does not perform interpolation or surface detection itself. When to use: When implementing surface extraction algorithms that require edge-based traversal or triangle generation. When not to use: When only vertex positions or material properties are needed without edge connectivity. name: Cube SDF Sampling and Sign Configuration
head: Cube SDF Sampling, Sign Configuration
body: This method constructs the topological state of a single voxel cube for Marching Cubes by sampling a Signed Distance Field (SDF) at its eight vertices and determining which vertices lie inside or outside a specified isosurface threshold. It differs from raw grid lookups by explicitly handling the degenerate case where an SDF value equals the threshold, ensuring a strict sign configuration to prevent ambiguity in edge traversal. It builds on Cube Edge Vertex Retrieval by providing the vertex data and sign flags required to identify which edges intersect the surface. Inputs: sdf: A function evaluating the SDF value at any 3D point. isoLevel: The scalar threshold defining the isosurface (typically 0.0 for SDFs). cubemin: The 3D coordinates of the cube's minimum corner (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}). cubesize: The dimensions of the cube (sx, sy, sz). Outputs: edgeIndex: A 12-bit integer representing the sign configuration of the cube. pos[8]: An array of 8 vertex structures containing the spatial coordinates of the cube's vertices. Data Structures: 1. Vertex Positions (pos[8]): The vertices are ordered according to a specific bit-indexing scheme used for the sign configuration integer. The layout is: pos[0]: (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) pos[1]: (x{min}+sx, y{min}, z{min}) pos[2]: (x{min}+sx, y{min}, z{min}+sz) pos[3]: (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}+sz) pos[4]: (x{min}, y{min}+sy, z{min}) pos[5]: (x{min}+sx, y{min}+sy, z{min}) pos[6]: (x{min}+sx, y{min}+sy, z{min}+sz) pos[7]: (x{min}, y{min}+sy, z{min}+sz). 2. Edge Definitions (edges[12]): Each edge is defined by a 12-bit flag (used for bitwise operations) and two vertex indices (0-7). The mapping is: Edge 0: Flag 1, Vertices 0-1 Edge 1: Flag 2, Vertices 1-2 Edge 2: Flag 4, Vertices 2-3 Edge 3: Flag 8, Vertices 3-0 Edge 4: Flag 16, Vertices 4-5 Edge 5: Flag 32, Vertices 5-6 Edge 6: Flag 64, Vertices 6-7 Edge 7: Flag 128, Vertices 7-4 Edge 8: Flag 256, Vertices 0-4 Edge 9: Flag 512, Vertices 1-5 Edge 10: Flag 1024, Vertices 2-6 Edge 11: Flag 2048, Vertices 3-7. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize edgeIndex to 0. 2. Iterate i from 0 to 7: a. Retrieve the vertex position p from pos[i]. b. Evaluate the SDF value: v = \text{sdf}(p). c. Perturbation for Zero Values: If v is exactly equal to 0, perturb the value by adding a small epsilon \epsilon = 10^{-6} to ensure a strict inequality. d. Sign Check: If the (potentially perturbed) v < \text{isoLevel}, set the i-th bit of edgeIndex: \text{edgeIndex} \ |= \ (1 \ll i). 3. Return edgeIndex and pos. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def cubesdfsamplingandsignconfiguration(sdf, isolevel, cubemin, cubesize): sx, sy, sz = cubesize xmin, ymin, zmin = cubemin # Define vertex positions according to the specific bit-ordering pos = [ Vec3(xmin, ymin, zmin), Vec3(xmin + sx, ymin, zmin), Vec3(xmin + sx, ymin, zmin + sz), Vec3(xmin, ymin, zmin + sz), Vec3(xmin, ymin + sy, zmin), Vec3(xmin + sx, ymin + sy, zmin), Vec3(xmin + sx, ymin + sy, zmin + sz), Vec3(xmin, ymin + sy, zmin + sz) ] edgeindex = 0 for i in range(8): p = pos[i] v = sdf(p) # Perturb exact zero crossings to ensure strict sign if v == 0: v += 1e-6 # Set bit if vertex is inside (value < threshold) if v < isolevel: edgeindex |= (1 << i) return edgeindex, pos Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exact Zero Crossing: If an SDF value is exactly equal to the isosurface level, the sign is ambiguous. The method mandates perturbing the value by 10^{-6}. Failure to do so may result in incorrect topology or missing geometry. Vertex Ordering: The vertex indices must strictly follow the defined layout (0-7) to ensure the edgeIndex bits correspond correctly to the physical edges defined in edges[12]. Mismatched ordering will produce twisted or invalid triangles. Extends this method by mapping normalized coordinates [-1, 1] to grid indices and handling out-of-bounds queries by approximating distance to the bounding box, preventing interpolation artifacts near volume edges. Time Complexity: O(1) per cube, as it performs a fixed number of 8 SDF evaluations and bitwise operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only 8 vertex positions and one integer flag. Strengths: Deterministic topology generation; handles degenerate zero-crossings explicitly. Limitations: Does not handle interpolation itself; relies on downstream logic (like Cube Edge Vertex Retrieval) to find intersection points. SDF evaluation cost depends on the underlying data structure (e.g., trilinear interpolation vs. nearest neighbor). This method is a standard component of the Marching Cubes algorithm, specifically adapted for Signed Distance Fields. The vertex ordering and edge flag definitions are derived from the classic implementation described by Paul Bourke. The specific perturbation of zero values is a practical implementation detail found in the Magnus2/MeshReconstruction library.
