name: Normalized Mesh SDF Sampling
head: 1D Array SDF Sampling, Clamped SDF Lookup
body: This method samples a 3D signed distance field (SDF) stored in a contiguous 1D array, mapping normalized coordinates in the range [-1, 1] to grid indices while applying specific boundary handling. It builds on Cube SDF Sampling and Sign Configuration by providing the underlying data retrieval and interpolation logic for the cube's vertices. Unlike raw grid lookups, it explicitly handles out-of-bounds queries by approximating the distance to the bounding box, preventing false positives from interpolation artifacts near the volume edges. Inputs: pNormalized: A 3D vector of normalized coordinates, expected to be in the range [-1, 1]^3. res: The uniform grid resolution along the X, Y, and Z axes (integer). volume.samples: A contiguous 1D array of floats storing SDF values in row-major order. Outputs: sampledDist: The interpolated signed distance value at the query point. Data Structures: volume.samples: A 1D array of size res^3. The index for a grid coordinate (x, y, z) is calculated as: \text{index} = x + res \cdot y + res^2 \cdot z where x, y, z \in [0, res-1]. Parameters: res: Grid resolution along X, Y, Z axes. Used to compute voxelSize = 2.0 / res. conservativeMargin: A constant offset subtracted from the final distance to account for interpolation errors outside the grid. Calculated as 0.5 \cdot \sqrt{3.0} \cdot \text{voxelSize}. Steps: 1. Clamp Input: Clamp pNormalized to the range [-1, 1] for each component. 2. Compute Outside Vector: For each component i \in \{0, 1, 2\}, compute the distance outside the box: \text{outside}[i] = \max(|\text{pNormalized}[i]| - 1.0, 0.0) 3. Compute Outside Length: Calculate the Euclidean distance from the clamped point to the original point (distance to the box boundary): \text{outsideLength} = \sqrt{\sum{i=0}^{2} \text{outside}[i]^2} 4. Map to Grid Indices: Convert clamped normalized coordinates to grid indices. For each component i: \text{gridCoord}[i] = \text{clamp}\left( (\text{pNormalized}[i] \cdot 0.5 + 0.5) \cdot res, 0, res - 1 \right) Note: The source uses clamp on the final float result to integer bounds, effectively flooring or clamping to the nearest valid index range. 5. Compute Corner Indices: x0 = \lfloor \text{gridCoord}[0] \rfloor, clamped to [0, res-1]. y0 = \lfloor \text{gridCoord}[1] \rfloor, clamped to [0, res-1]. z0 = \lfloor \text{gridCoord}[2] \rfloor, clamped to [0, res-1]. x1 = \min(x0 + 1, res - 1). y1 = \min(y0 + 1, res - 1). z1 = \min(z0 + 1, res - 1). 6. Compute Fractional Weights: tx = \text{clamp}(\text{gridCoord}[0] - \lfloor \text{gridCoord}[0] \rfloor, 0, 1). ty = \text{clamp}(\text{gridCoord}[1] - \lfloor \text{gridCoord}[1] \rfloor, 0, 1). tz = \text{clamp}(\text{gridCoord}[2] - \lfloor \text{gridCoord}[2] \rfloor, 0, 1). 7. Sample 8 Corners: Retrieve SDF values from volume.samples using the 8 corner indices (xi, yj, zk) where i,j,k \in \{0,1\}. c{000} = \text{volume.samples}[x0 + res \cdot y0 + res^2 \cdot z0]. c{100} = \text{volume.samples}[x1 + res \cdot y0 + res^2 \cdot z0]. c{010} = \text{volume.samples}[x0 + res \cdot y1 + res^2 \cdot z0]. c{110} = \text{volume.samples}[x1 + res \cdot y1 + res^2 \cdot z0]. c{001} = \text{volume.samples}[x0 + res \cdot y0 + res^2 \cdot z1]. c{101} = \text{volume.samples}[x1 + res \cdot y0 + res^2 \cdot z1]. c{011} = \text{volume.samples}[x0 + res \cdot y1 + res^2 \cdot z1]. c{111} = \text{volume.samples}[x1 + res \cdot y1 + res^2 \cdot z1]. 8. Trilinear Interpolation: c{00} = \text{lerp}(c{000}, c{100}, tx). c{10} = \text{lerp}(c{010}, c{110}, tx). c{01} = \text{lerp}(c{001}, c{101}, tx). c{11} = \text{lerp}(c{011}, c{111}, tx). c0 = \text{lerp}(c{00}, c{10}, ty). c1 = \text{lerp}(c{01}, c{11}, ty). \text{sampled} = \text{lerp}(c0, c1, tz). 9. Compute Voxel Size: \text{voxelSize} = \frac{2.0}{res} 10. Compute Conservative Margin: \text{conservativeMargin} = 0.5 \cdot \sqrt{3.0} \cdot \text{voxelSize} 11. Return Result: \text{sampledDist} = \text{sampled} + \text{outsideLength} - \text{conservativeMargin} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalizedmeshsdfsampling(pnormalized, res, volumesamples): def clamp(v, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, v)) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) import math # 1. Clamp input pclamped = [clamp(pnormalized[i], -1.0, 1.0) for i in range(3)] # 2. Compute outside vector absp = [abs(pclamped[i]) for i in range(3)] outside = [max(absp[i] - 1.0, 0.0) for i in range(3)] # 3. Compute outside length outsidelength = math.sqrt(sum(o2 for o in outside)) # 4. Map clamped coords to grid gridcoords = [clamp((pclamped[i] 0.5 + 0.5) res, 0.0, float(res - 1)) for i in range(3)] # 5. Compute integer grid coords x0 = clamp(math.floor(gridcoords[0]), 0, res - 1) y0 = clamp(math.floor(gridcoords[1]), 0, res - 1) z0 = clamp(math.floor(gridcoords[2]), 0, res - 1) # 6. Compute x1, y1, z1 x1 = min(x0 + 1, res - 1) y1 = min(y0 + 1, res - 1) z1 = min(z0 + 1, res - 1) # 7. Compute fractional weights tx = clamp(gridcoords[0] - math.floor(gridcoords[0]), 0.0, 1.0) ty = clamp(gridcoords[1] - math.floor(gridcoords[1]), 0.0, 1.0) tz = clamp(gridcoords[2] - math.floor(gridcoords[2]), 0.0, 1.0) # 8. Sample 8 corners def getsdf(x, y, z): idx = x + res y + res res z return volumesamples[idx] c000 = getsdf(x0, y0, z0) c100 = getsdf(x1, y0, z0) c010 = getsdf(x0, y1, z0) c110 = getsdf(x1, y1, z0) c001 = getsdf(x0, y0, z1) c101 = getsdf(x1, y0, z1) c011 = getsdf(x0, y1, z1) c111 = getsdf(x1, y1, z1) # 9. Trilinear interpolation c00 = lerp(c000, c100, tx) c10 = lerp(c010, c110, tx) c01 = lerp(c001, c101, tx) c11 = lerp(c011, c111, tx) c0 = lerp(c00, c10, ty) c1 = lerp(c01, c11, ty) sampled = lerp(c0, c1, tz) # 10. Compute voxel size voxelsize = 2.0 / res # 11. Compute conservative margin conservativemargin = 0.5 math.sqrt(3.0) voxelsize # 12. Return result return sampled + outsidelength - conservativemargin Time Complexity: O(1) per query. It involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and 8 memory accesses. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. The memory usage is dominated by the input array volume.samples which is O(res^3). Strengths: Simple to implement; handles out-of-bounds queries gracefully without requiring separate ray-box intersection logic for the SDF volume itself. Limitations: The boundary approximation is conservative and may introduce small errors near the edges of the bounding box. When to use: When a dense, uniform grid SDF is available and queries are frequent. When not to use: When the SDF is sparse or non-uniform, or when high precision at the exact boundary of the bounding box is critical. This method is derived from implementations of ray marching with signed distance fields, specifically those found in open-source ray marching tools. It represents a standard approach for sampling uniform grid-based SDFs in normalized space. name: Brick Volume Addressing with If-Else
head: Brick Addressing Logic
body: Brick Volume Addressing with If-Else is a method to compute memory offsets for accessing neighboring samples in a brick-structured volume, primarily for resampling or gradient computation. It solves the problem of efficiently determining whether adjacent samples lie within the current brick or in a neighboring brick by using explicit conditional checks. Unlike sibling methods that assume a uniform linear layout, this method uses an if-else statement to test if needed data elements are within one brick; if true, it uses fast linear addressing, otherwise it falls back to costly address calculations. It differs from its sibling Lookup Table Addressing for Resampling by using runtime if-else branches instead of precomputed lookup tables, which incurs pipeline flush penalties but avoids table memory overhead. Inputs: Volume dimensions: Dx, Dy, Dz (integers). Brick dimensions: BDx, BDy, BDz (integers). Brick volume dimensions: BVDx, BVDy, BVDz where BVDx = Dx / BDx, etc. (integers). Current resample position integer parts: i, j, k. Outputs: Base offset: SampleOffset{i,j,k}. Offsets for 7 neighbors relative to the base offset or via ComputeOffset. Data Structures: Relies on integer arithmetic and conditional logic. Steps: 1. Compute local brick coordinates: i' = i \pmod{BDx} j' = j \pmod{BDy} k' = k \pmod{BDz} 2. Compute global brick indices: i'' = \lfloor i / BDx \rfloor j'' = \lfloor j / BDy \rfloor k'' = \lfloor k / BDz \rfloor 3. Check if all 8 samples (the 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighborhood) fit within the current brick. The condition is true if the maximum local coordinate of the neighborhood is strictly less than the brick dimension minus one: i' < BDx - 1 \quad \text{AND} \quad j' < BDy - 1 \quad \text{AND} \quad k' < BDz - 1 4. If the condition is true (all samples in current brick): Compute base offset using linear addressing within the brick: SampleOffset{i,j,k} = i' + j' \cdot BDx + k' \cdot BDx \cdot BDy Compute neighbor offsets by adding constants to the base offset: SampleOffset{i+1,j,k} = SampleOffset{i,j,k} + 1 SampleOffset{i,j+1,k} = SampleOffset{i,j,k} + BDx SampleOffset{i+1,j+1,k} = SampleOffset{i,j,k} + 1 + BDx SampleOffset{i,j,k+1} = SampleOffset{i,j,k} + BDx \cdot BDy SampleOffset{i+1,j,k+1} = SampleOffset{i,j,k} + 1 + BDx \cdot BDy SampleOffset{i,j+1,k+1} = SampleOffset{i,j,k} + BDx + BDx \cdot BDy SampleOffset{i+1,j+1,k+1} = SampleOffset{i,j,k} + 1 + BDx + BDx \cdot BDy 5. If the condition is false (at least one neighbor is in a different brick): Compute base offset using linear addressing within the brick: SampleOffset{i,j,k} = i' + j' \cdot BDx + k' \cdot BDx \cdot BDy Compute each neighbor's absolute offset using ComputeOffset: SampleOffset{i+1,j,k} = ComputeOffset(i+1,j,k) SampleOffset{i,j+1,k} = ComputeOffset(i,j+1,k) SampleOffset{i+1,j+1,k} = ComputeOffset(i+1,j+1,k) SampleOffset{i,j,k+1} = ComputeOffset(i,j,k+1) SampleOffset{i+1,j,k+1} = ComputeOffset(i+1,j,k+1) SampleOffset{i,j+1,k+1} = ComputeOffset(i,j+1,k+1) SampleOffset{i+1,j+1,k+1} = ComputeOffset(i+1,j+1,k+1) 6. The ComputeOffset(i,j,k) function is defined as: ComputeOffset(i,j,k) = BlkOffset{i,j,k} \cdot (BDx \cdot BDy \cdot BDz) + OffsetWithinBlk{i,j,k} Where: BlkOffset{i,j,k} = i'' + j'' \cdot BVDx + k'' \cdot (BVDx \cdot BVDy) And: OffsetWithinBlk{i,j,k} = i' + j' \cdot BDx + k' \cdot (BDx \cdot BDy) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def brickaddressingifelse(i, j, k, Dx, Dy, Dz, BDx, BDy, BDz): # Step 1: Local coordinates ip = i % BDx jp = j % BDy kp = k % BDz # Step 2: Global brick indices im = i // BDx jm = j // BDy km = k // BDz # Step 3: Check boundary condition if (ip < BDx - 1) and (jp < BDy - 1) and (kp < BDz - 1): # Step 4: Linear addressing within brick base = ip + jp BDx + kp BDx BDy offsets = [ 0, # i, j, k 1, # i+1, j, k BDx, # i, j+1, k 1 + BDx, # i+1, j+1, k BDx BDy, # i, j, k+1 1 + BDx BDy, # i+1, j, k+1 BDx + BDx BDy, # i, j+1, k+1 1 + BDx + BDx BDy # i+1, j+1, k+1 ] return [base + off for off in offsets] else: # Step 5: Base offset uses linear addressing per base = ip + jp BDx + kp BDx BDy def computeoffset(ii, jj, kk): iip = ii % BDx jip = jj % BDy kip = kk % BDz iim = ii // BDx jmm = jj // BDy kmm = kk // BDz BVDx = Dx // BDx BVDy = Dy // BDy blkoffset = iim + jmm BVDx + kmm (BVDx BVDy) withinblk = iip + jip BDx + kip (BDx BDy) return blkoffset (BDx BDy BDz) + withinblk neighbors = [ (i, j, k), (i+1, j, k), (i, j+1, k), (i+1, j+1, k), (i, j, k+1), (i+1, j, k+1), (i, j+1, k+1), (i+1, j+1, k+1) ] # First neighbor is base, rest use computeoffset per return [base] + [computeoffset(ni, nj, nk) for ni, nj, nk in neighbors[1:]] Parameters: Brick dimensions BD{x,y,z}: Performance statistics are provided for 32 \times 32 \times 32 and 16 \times 16 \times 16 bricks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Branch prediction uncertainty causes pipeline flushes, leading to performance penalties compared to pure linear addressing. The else branch executes in 10% of cases for 32 \times 32 \times 32 bricks and 18% of cases for 16 \times 16 \times 16 bricks. Replaces the if-else branching with a direct table lookup to avoid pipeline flushes, significantly improving performance on hardware where branch prediction is costly. Time Complexity: The if branch executes simple arithmetic to address data as fast as in a linear volume. The else branch involves multiple ComputeOffset calls, each requiring division and modulo operations, making it more expensive. Performance: A speedup of ~30% is achieved compared to a solution that always uses the costly address calculations. Scaling: The frequency of the expensive else branch decreases with larger brick sizes (10% for 32^3 vs 18% for 16^3). Strengths: Simplifies address calculation for the majority of cases when samples lie within the current brick. Limitations: Incurs pipeline flushes due to branch prediction uncertainty. name: Lookup Table Addressing for Resampling
head: Brick Resampling Lookup Table
body: Lookup Table Addressing for Resampling is a method to compute memory offsets for accessing neighboring samples in a brick-structured volume without using conditional branches or expensive runtime address calculations. It solves the problem of efficiently determining whether adjacent samples lie within the current brick or in a neighboring brick by mapping the sample's local position to one of eight precomputed offset patterns. Unlike its parent method, Brick Volume Addressing with If-Else, which uses explicit if-else checks and ComputeOffset calls, this method replaces branching with a direct table lookup, significantly improving performance on hardware where branch prediction is costly or memory bandwidth is limited. The method takes the integer coordinates of the current sample (i, j, k) relative to the global volume grid, and the brick dimensions (BDx, BDy, BDz) as inputs. It outputs an array of 7 integer offsets corresponding to the memory addresses of the 7 adjacent samples: right (i+1, j, k), top (i, j+1, k), back (i, j, k+1), and their combinations (right-top, right-back, top-back, right-top-back). The core data structure is a compressed lookup table (LUT) containing 56 offsets. The table is a 1D array of 56 32-bit integers (4 bytes each). The total size is 56 \times 4 = 224 bytes. The table is organized into 8 cases (indices 0–7), where each case contains 7 offsets for the neighbors relative to the current sample (i, j, k). The order of neighbors is fixed as: 1. (i+1, j, k), 2. (i, j+1, k), 3. (i+1, j+1, k), 4. (i, j, k+1), 5. (i+1, j, k+1), 6. (i, j+1, k+1), 7. (i+1, j+1, k+1). The method assumes brick dimensions are powers of two. If they are not, a shift operation can be used to virtually satisfy the constraint, or the "power of two apart" constraint can be removed with a simple shift. The following steps assume BDx, BDy, BDz are powers of two. 1. Extract Brick Offset: Compute the local coordinates within the brick by masking the global coordinates with the brick dimensions minus one: i{local} = i \ \& \ (BDx - 1) j{local} = j \ \& \ (BDy - 1) k{local} = k \ \& \ (BDz - 1) 2. Increment: Add 1 to each local coordinate: i' = i{local} + 1 j' = j{local} + 1 k' = k{local} + 1 3. Mask with Complement: Perform a bitwise AND with the bitwise NOT of the brick dimension minus one. This maps the values to either 0 or the brick dimension itself (BDx, BDy, BDz): i{mask} = i' \ \& \ \text{NOT}(BDx - 1) j{mask} = j' \ \& \ \text{NOT}(BDy - 1) k{mask} = k' \ \& \ \text{NOT}(BDz - 1) 4. Sum Masked Values: Sum the three masked values: Sum = i{mask} + j{mask} + k{mask} 5. Compute Index: Divide the sum by the minimum brick dimension to get an index in the range [0, 7]. This division is implemented as a right bit shift: Index = \frac{(((i \ \& \ (BDx-1)) + 1) \ \& \ \text{NOT}(BDx-1)) + (((j \ \& \ (BDy-1)) + 1) \ \& \ \text{NOT}(BDy-1)) + (((k \ \& \ (BDz-1)) + 1) \ \& \ \text{NOT}(BDz-1))}{\min(BDx, BDy, BDz)} 6. Retrieve Offsets: Use the computed index to retrieve the 7 offsets from the lookup table: Offsets = LUT[Index] Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeresamplingoffsets(i, j, k, BDx, BDy, BDz, LUT): # Step 1: Extract brick offset part ilocal = i & (BDx - 1) jlocal = j & (BDy - 1) klocal = k & (BDz - 1) # Step 2: Increment all by 1 iprime = ilocal + 1 jprime = jlocal + 1 kprime = klocal + 1 # Step 3: Mask with complement of (BD-1) # In fixed-width integer arithmetic, ~ (BD-1) clears the lower log2(BD) bits. imask = iprime & ~ (BDx - 1) jmask = jprime & ~ (BDy - 1) kmask = kprime & ~ (BDz - 1) # Step 4: Sum the three masked values total = imask + jmask + kmask # Step 5: Shift right by log2(min(BD)) to get index in [0, 7] minbd = min(BDx, BDy, BDz) shiftamount = minbd.bitlength() - 1 index = total >> shiftamount # Step 6: Retrieve offsets from LUT baseoffset = index 7 offsets = [ LUT[baseoffset + 0], # Right (i+1, j, k) LUT[baseoffset + 1], # Top (i, j+1, k) LUT[baseoffset + 2], # Right-Top (i+1, j+1, k) LUT[baseoffset + 3], # Back (i, j, k+1) LUT[baseoffset + 4], # Right-Back (i+1, j, k+1) LUT[baseoffset + 5], # Top-Back (i, j+1, k+1) LUT[baseoffset + 6] # Right-Top-Back (i+1, j+1, k+1) ] return offsets The optimal brick size is 32^3. The algorithm requires dimensions to be powers of two. The compressed lookup table size is 224 bytes. The naive approach would require 32^3 \times 7 \times 4 bytes = 896 KB. The index calculation relies on brick dimensions being powers of two. If dimensions are not powers of two, a shift operation can be introduced to virtually maintain the constraint, or the "power of two apart" constraint can be removed by introducing a simple shift. The method handles brick boundaries implicitly by mapping out-of-bounds neighbors to offsets that point to neighboring bricks, and the LUT must be precomputed correctly for all 8 cases. Gradient Computation Lookup Table: A variant of the lookup table addressing method used for gradient computation instead of resampling. Gradient computation requires accessing samples in all 6 directions, resulting in 9 subsets (cases) instead of 8. Use when computing gradients for volume rendering or other operations requiring full neighborhood access. Link: Gradient Computation Lookup Table. The time complexity is O(1) for offset computation, as it involves a fixed number of bitwise operations and a single table lookup. The memory complexity for the lookup table is constant at 224 bytes for the compressed approach, regardless of brick size (assuming power-of-two dimensions). The naive approach scales with brick volume (BDx \times BDy \times BDz \times 7 \times 4 bytes). The compressed lookup table approach reduces table size by a factor of 4096 compared to the naive approach, allowing the table to fit in CPU cache. This results in faster access times and reduced branch mispredictions compared to the if-else based method. The method is designed for standard PC hardware and benefits from cache-friendly access patterns. The strengths are branchless execution, cache-friendly table size, and efficient address computation. The limitations are the requirement for brick dimensions to be powers of two (or a workaround) and the need for precomputation of the LUT. Use this method when resampling large brick-structured volumes on hardware where branch prediction is inefficient or cache misses are costly. Avoid it if brick dimensions are not powers of two and the overhead of handling non-power-of-two dimensions outweighs the benefits. The method was introduced in the context of real-time mono- and multi-volume rendering of large medical datasets on standard PC hardware. It was developed to optimize the addressing of neighboring samples in brick-structured volumes, which are commonly used in medical imaging for efficient storage and rendering. The method builds upon the concept of brick volume addressing, where volumes are divided into smaller bricks to improve cache locality and manage memory efficiently. The lookup table approach was proposed as an optimization to the if-else based addressing method, reducing the computational overhead of determining neighbor locations. The method is used in real-time volume rendering applications, particularly in medical imaging, where large datasets need to be rendered efficiently on standard hardware. name: Nearest Voxel Lookup with Periodic Boundary
head: Grid Probing, Nearest Voxel Lookup, Nearest-Neighbor Density Lookup, Nearest-Neighbor Search Interpolation, Periodic Boundary Voxel Lookup, Wrapped Nearest Neighbor Sampling
body: This method retrieves the scalar density value of the single voxel containing a sample point, without interpolating neighboring values. It differs from interpolation methods by selecting only the nearest grid vertex. The "Periodic Boundary" variant handles out-of-bounds coordinates by wrapping them via modulo arithmetic, allowing seamless tiling or robust handling of rays outside the grid volume. Inputs: grid: A structure containing bounds (a 3D vector pair [min, max] defining the world-space AABB), baseResolution (an integer scalar or 3D vector representing voxel counts per axis), and density (a 1D array storing voxel values). p: A 3D point in world space. Outputs: value: The scalar density at the nearest voxel. Data Structures: The density array follows a Z-major, Y-major, X-minor contiguous layout. The linear memory index I for coordinates (x, y, z) is calculated as I = (z \cdot Ny + y) \cdot Nx + x. Steps: 1. Transform to Local Space: Subtract the grid's minimum bound from the sample point to shift the coordinate system so the grid origin is at (0,0,0). p{local} = p - grid.bounds[0] 2. Normalize: Divide by the grid's physical size to map the point to the [0, 1] range. gridSize = grid.bounds[1] - grid.bounds[0] p{norm} = p{local} / gridSize 3. Convert to Voxel Space: Multiply normalized coordinates by the grid resolution to obtain floating-point voxel coordinates. p{voxel} = p{norm} \cdot grid.baseResolution 4. Compute Integer Indices: Apply the floor function to the voxel coordinates to determine the integer grid indices. xi = \lfloor p{voxel}.x \rfloor yi = \lfloor p{voxel}.y \rfloor zi = \lfloor p{voxel}.z \rfloor 5. Apply Periodic Boundary Conditions: If the indices fall outside the valid range [0, N-1], wrap them using modulo arithmetic. xi = xi \pmod{Nx} yi = yi \pmod{Ny} zi = zi \pmod{Nz} 6. Lookup: Calculate the linear memory index and retrieve the value. index = (zi \cdot Ny + yi) \cdot Nx + xi value = grid.density[index] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def nearestvoxellookupperiodic(grid, p): # 1. Transform to local space plocal = p - grid.bounds[0] # 2. Normalize to [0, 1] gridsize = grid.bounds[1] - grid.bounds[0] pnorm = plocal / gridsize # 3. Convert to voxel space pvoxel = pnorm grid.baseResolution # 4. Compute integer indices using floor xi = int(math.floor(pvoxel.x)) yi = int(math.floor(pvoxel.y)) zi = int(math.floor(pvoxel.z)) # 5. Apply periodic boundary conditions (modulo) nx, ny, nz = grid.baseResolution xi = xi % nx yi = yi % ny zi = zi % nz # 6. Calculate linear index (Z-major, Y-major, X-minor) index = (zi ny + yi) nx + xi # 7. Return value return grid.density[index] Parameters: grid.baseResolution: Integer or 3D vector representing voxel counts per axis. grid.bounds: Defined by the scene geometry or asset origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Coordinates: Using truncation (e.g., staticcast<int>) instead of floor returns -1 for negative coordinates, causing invalid memory access. floor must be used to correctly handle negative coordinates before wrapping. Boundary Exceedance: Coordinates in voxel space must not exceed resolution - 1, which occurs if normalized coordinates are exactly 1.0. Periodic boundary conditions via modulo handle this by wrapping N to 0. Memory Layout: The index calculation assumes a Z-major, Y-major, X-minor layout as specified by the source formula. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. This technique is referred to as "probing" in libraries like OpenVDB. The specific handling of periodic boundaries is implemented in projects like Plenoxels to manage out-of-bounds indices via modulo arithmetic. name: Nearest Integer Rounding
head: Round, Round to nearest integer
body: Nearest Integer Rounding converts continuous floating-point coordinates into discrete integer grid indices by rounding to the closest integer value. It serves as the fundamental coordinate quantization step in volume rendering, mapping sample points to voxel centers or corners. Unlike floor-based indexing which truncates towards zero or negative infinity, this method minimizes spatial quantization error by selecting the nearest grid node, which is critical for accurate gradient estimation and high-fidelity reconstruction. It differs from Ceil which always rounds up, and Floor which always rounds down, by balancing bias in both directions. Inputs: A 3D vector xyz of type Vec3<double>, Vec3<float>, or Vec3<RealT>. Outputs: A coordinate type CoordT (typically int32t or int64t) representing the rounded integer coordinates. Data Structures: The input is a 3-element vector. The output is a scalar or vector of integer type, depending on the template specialization. Steps: 1. For each component c \in \{x, y, z\} of the input vector xyz: Let v = xyz.c. Compute the rounded integer r = \text{round}(v). The standard definition of \text{round}(v) is \lfloor v + 0.5 \rfloor for positive v, and \lceil v - 0.5 \rceil for negative v, effectively rounding to the nearest integer, with ties (e.g., 0.5) typically rounding away from zero or to the nearest even integer depending on the specific hardware/standard implementation. In the context of the source, the function Round is templated to accept Vec3<double>, Vec3<float>, or Vec3<RealT> and returns a CoordT. Formulas: rc = \text{round}(xyzc) where rc is the integer result for component c. Parameters: xyz: The input floating-point coordinates. CoordT: The target integer type for the output. RealT: The floating-point type of the input (double, float, etc.). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point representation errors may cause values exactly halfway between integers (e.g., 2.5) to be represented as 2.4999999 or 2.5000001, affecting the rounding direction. The specific tie-breaking rule (round half up, round half to even) depends on the underlying C++ std::round or hardware instruction used by the implementation. Overflow: If the input coordinates exceed the range of CoordT, the result is undefined or clamped, depending on the implementation. The source does not specify overflow handling for Round. Negative Zero: Rounding -0.0 results in 0, which is standard for integer types. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Round(xyz: Vec3[RealT]) -> CoordT: """ Rounds a 3D vector to the nearest integer coordinates. Args: xyz: Input vector of type Vec3<double>, Vec3<float>, or Vec3<RealT>. Returns: CoordT: The rounded integer coordinates. """ # Implementation depends on the specific template specialization # For Vec3<double>: if isinstance(xyz, Vec3double): return CoordT(round(xyz.x), round(xyz.y), round(xyz.z)) # For Vec3<float>: elif isinstance(xyz, Vec3float): return CoordT(round(xyz.x), round(xyz.y), round(xyz.z)) # For Vec3<RealT>: else: return CoordT(round(xyz.x), round(xyz.y), round(xyz.z)) Note: The round function here refers to the standard mathematical rounding to the nearest integer. The source provides templated overloads for double, float, and generic RealT. Returns the ceiling of a floating-point value as an int32t. It always rounds up to the nearest integer greater than or equal to the input. Defined for both double and float inputs. Use when you need to ensure coverage of the entire voxel space without gaps, such as in bounding box calculations or when sampling requires including the upper boundary. Time Complexity: O(1) per component. The operation is a single arithmetic instruction or library call. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is allocated. Performance: Extremely fast, typically mapping to a single CPU instruction (e.g., cvttss2si or similar on x86) or a highly optimized library call. Strengths: Minimal quantization error compared to floor/ceil; simple implementation. Limitations: Does not handle out-of-bounds indices (that is handled by the parent Nearest Voxel Lookup with Periodic Boundary); tie-breaking behavior may vary across platforms if not explicitly standardized. The Round and Ceil functions are part of the nanovdb::math namespace in OpenVDB, a library for sparse volumetric data. They are designed for high-performance GPU and CPU execution, indicated by the hostdev qualifiers. The implementation is templated to support various floating-point precisions and coordinate types, ensuring flexibility in volume rendering pipelines that may use single or double precision. name: Piecewise Quadratic Hermite Interpolation
head: Piecewise Quadratic Bézier Hermite Interpolation, Quadratic Polynomial Interpolation for SCALIS
body: This method interpolates a normalized scalar field within a 1D interval using two piecewise quadratic Bézier curves to satisfy Hermite data (value and derivative) at both endpoints. It solves the incompatibility of single quadratic interpolation with four constraints (two values, two derivatives) by splitting the interval, providing exact interpolation in specific cases and better stability than cubic interpolation for small subdivision counts. Inputs: Interval length L. Hermite data at start: value h1, derivative h'1. Hermite data at end: value h2, derivative h'2. Outputs: A continuous, smooth interpolant defined by two quadratic Bézier segments. Data Structures: Six control points Q0, \dots, Q5 for the two Bézier curves. Each control point Qi has an abscissa (x-coordinate) and an ordinate (y-coordinate, representing the field value). The abscissas are equally spaced across the two sub-intervals. Steps: 1. Split Interval: Divide the initial interval of length L into two equal sub-intervals, each of length L/2. 2. Define Control Points: Define two quadratic Bézier curves, one for each sub-interval. A quadratic Bézier curve is defined by three control points. Thus, we have six control points Q0, \dots, Q5. 3. Constrain Abscissas: The control points are constrained to be equally spaced in abscissa. For the first sub-interval, Q0, Q1, Q2 span the first half. For the second, Q3, Q4, Q5 span the second half. 4. Set Boundary Ordinates: Set the ordinates of Q0 and Q1 based on the Hermite data at the start of the interval (h1, h'1). Set the ordinates of Q4 and Q5 based on the Hermite data at the end of the interval (h2, h'2). The specific mapping uses standard quadratic Bézier Hermite conversion: Q0.y = h1, Q1.y = h1 + \frac{L}{4}h'1, Q4.y = h2 - \frac{L}{4}h'2, Q5.y = h2. 5. Enforce Continuity and Smoothness: The shared control point between the two segments must be equal: Q2 = Q3. The shared point must lie on the line joining Q1 and Q4 to ensure smoothness. This ensures C^1 continuity or smoothness of the derivative. 6. Calculate Shared Ordinate: Calculate the ordinate y{mid} for Q2 and Q3 using the formula: y{mid} = \frac{1}{2}(h1 + h2) + \frac{L}{8}(h'1 - h'2) where h1, h'1 are the value and derivative at the start, and h2, h'2 are the value and derivative at the end. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def piecewisequadratichermiteinterpolate(h1, h1prime, h2, h2prime, L): """ Computes the control points for two piecewise quadratic Bézier curves that interpolate Hermite data (h1, h1prime) at start and (h2, h2prime) at end over an interval of length L. Returns: Q: List of 6 control points, each as a tuple (x, y). """ # Step 1: Split interval into two equal sub-intervals of length L/2 # Step 2 & 3: Define control points with equally spaced abscissas # Q0, Q1, Q2 span [0, L/2]; Q3, Q4, Q5 span [L/2, L] Q = [ (0.0, h1), (L / 4, h1 + (L / 4) h1prime), (L / 2, 0.5 (h1 + h2) + (L / 8) (h1prime - h2prime)), (L / 2, 0.5 (h1 + h2) + (L / 8) (h1prime - h2prime)), (3 L / 4, h2 - (L / 4) h2prime), (L, h2) ] return Q Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method is noted to be numerically stable. Boundaries: The method assumes a 1D interval. For 3D volume rendering, this is applied along the ray or within grid cells. Degenerate Input: If L=0, the formula for y{mid} becomes (h1+h2)/2. If h1=h2 and h'1=h'2, the interpolation is constant. Collects corner indices for grid cells. Handles periodic boundaries for voxel lookup. Time Complexity: Constant time per evaluation after control points are computed. Memory Complexity: Minimal, storing only 6 control points per interval. Performance: More efficient and simpler than cubic interpolation. Provides exact interpolation in specific cases. For Cauchy kernels, yields better interpolation for small numbers of subdivisions compared to cubic interpolation on the original field. Strengths: Numerical stability, exact interpolation in specific cases, efficiency. Limitations: Only applicable to 1D intervals. Requires Hermite data (value and derivative). This method is used in the context of ray tracing scale-invariant integral surfaces, specifically within the SCALIS framework. It was proposed as an alternative to Hermite-Birkhoff interpolation to respect Hermite data at both endpoints without ignoring derivatives. name: Cylindrical Coordinate Interpolation
head: Interpolation in cylindrical coordinates
body: Cylindrical Coordinate Interpolation maps Cartesian query points to cylindrical space before sampling the volume data, enabling efficient texture-based lookup for geometries with cylindrical symmetry. It differs from standard Cartesian interpolation by remapping the coordinate system to align with the geometry's principal axis, reducing sampling artifacts for radially symmetric data. Inputs: point: Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) of the query location. outVal: Default output value if sampling fails. triCubic: Boolean flag selecting interpolation kernel (linear vs. trilinear/tricubic). geomSize: Dimensions of the bounding geometry (Gx, Gy, Gz). dataDim: Dimensions of the volume texture (Dx, Dy, Dz). dataTex: 3D texture object containing the volume data. Data Structures: float3: A vector type with fields x, y, z. cartToCyl(point): Helper function converting Cartesian (x, y, z) to cylindrical (r, \theta, z). Standard definition: r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, \theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x), z = z. Steps: 1. Calculate step sizes (voxel sizes in the cylindrical domain): L{step} = \frac{Gx}{Dx} \Theta{step} = \frac{Gy}{Dy} Z{step} = \frac{Gz}{Dz} Note: The source code maps geometry width Gx to data width Dx for the radial/length dimension, geometry height Gy to data height Dy for the angle dimension, and geometry depth Gz to data depth Dz for the vertical dimension. 2. Convert the Cartesian point to cylindrical coordinates: \mathbf{c} = \text{cartToCyl}(\text{point}) Let \mathbf{c} = (cx, cy, cz), where cx is radius, cy is angle, and cz is height. 3. Normalize cylindrical coordinates to texture coordinates \mathbf{t} = (tx, ty, tz): tx = \frac{cx}{L{step}} ty = \frac{cy}{\Theta{step}} tz = \frac{cz}{Z{step}} 4. Boundary Check: If any component of \mathbf{t} is outside the valid range [0, Di - 1] for its respective dimension i \in \{x, y, z\}, return outVal immediately. 5. Sampling: If triCubic is true, call cubicInterpolate(t). This function performs tricubic interpolation using the 8 surrounding voxels and their gradients (or differences) to compute a smooth value. Otherwise, perform linear texture sampling: \text{value} = \text{tex3D}(\text{dataTex}, tx, ty, tz) This performs trilinear interpolation using hardware texture units. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interpolatecyl(point, outval, tricubic, geomsize, datadim, datatex): # 1. Calculate step sizes lengthstep = geomsize.x / datadim.width anglestep = geomsize.y / datadim.height heightstep = geomsize.z / datadim.depth # 2. Convert to cylindrical coordinates # cartToCyl returns (radius, angle, height) cylcoord = carttocyl(point) # 3. Normalize to texture coordinates texcoordx = cylcoord.x / lengthstep texcoordy = cylcoord.y / anglestep texcoordz = cylcoord.z / heightstep # 4. Boundary check if (texcoordx < 0 or texcoordx > datadim.width - 1 or texcoordy < 0 or texcoordy > datadim.height - 1 or texcoordz < 0 or texcoordz > datadim.depth - 1): return outval # 5. Sampling if tricubic: return cubicinterpolate(texcoordx, texcoordy, texcoordz) else: # Linear texture sampling return tex3dsample(datatex, texcoordx, texcoordy, texcoordz) Interpolation in spherical coordinates, mapping Cartesian points to spherical space before sampling. It calculates step sizes for length, longitude, and latitude, converts the point, adds a Z-offset (geomSize.z) to the spherical coordinates, and maps them to texture coordinates: X = \text{longitude}/\text{longStep}, Y = \text{latitude}/\text{latStep}, Z = \text{length}/\text{lengthStep}. It uses the same linear or cubic sampling logic as the cylindrical variant and returns the output value if texture coordinates are out of bounds. Choose this for geometries with spherical symmetry. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The conversion and normalization are constant-time arithmetic operations. The sampling cost depends on the kernel: linear is typically faster due to hardware acceleration, while cubic requires more arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. The method relies on the pre-allocated 3D texture dataTex. Strengths: Efficiently handles cylindrical geometries by aligning the sampling grid with the data structure, reducing aliasing and improving cache coherence for radially symmetric volumes. Limitations: Only suitable for data with cylindrical symmetry. Requires careful handling of the angle discontinuity at \pm \pi if the data wraps around, though the source implementation assumes a direct mapping. Out-of-bounds checks are explicit, which may branch unpredictably. This method originates from a CUDA-based volume rendering implementation for the DTU dataset, specifically designed to handle different geometric types (cylindrical and spherical) within a unified framework. It was part of an unofficial repository (ojaisnielsen/dtu-2010-cuda-volume-rendering) demonstrating GPU-accelerated ray casting with flexible coordinate transformations. ojaisnielsen/dtu-2010-cuda-volume-rendering, https://github.com/ojaisnielsen/dtu-2010-cuda-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Euclidean Distance Field (EDF) Data Structure
head: EuclideanDF, Tiled Euclidean Distance Fields
body: The Euclidean Distance Field (EDF) is a spatial indexing structure used for space-skipping ray traversal in dense voxel volumes. It accelerates rendering by allowing rays to jump over empty space based on precomputed distance values, reducing the number of intersection tests. It differs from sibling structures like EdgeMap Data Layout by storing scalar distance magnitudes rather than boundary flags, and from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by providing traversal acceleration rather than surface normal estimation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A binary volume representing occupied and empty voxels. Output: A tiled data structure containing coarse-resolution distance values and fine-resolution occupancy masks. Data Structures and Layout The structure uses a 1:4 resolution scale, meaning one distance value represents a 4^3 = 64 voxel block. Distance Field: Stores 2-byte (16-bit) unsigned integers per 4^3 voxel block. Occupancy Mask: Stores 1-bit flags per 1^3 voxel, packed to represent the 4^3 block. Total Memory Cost: 2 bytes per 4^3 voxel (distance) + 1 bit per 1^3 voxel (occupancy). Algorithm: Traversal 1. Initialization: Load the ray origin and direction, and determine the starting tile in the EDF grid. 2. Tile Query: Access the EDF tile corresponding to the current ray position. 3. Distance Check: Retrieve the precomputed Euclidean distance value D for the current tile. 4. Skip Logic: If D > 0, advance the ray position by D units along the ray direction. If D = 0 or the ray enters a region with fine geometry, query the occupancy mask for the current 4^3 block to check for occupied voxels. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–4 until the ray exits the volume or hits an occupied voxel. Formulas Ray advancement: P{next} = P{current} + D \cdot \vec{d}, where P is the ray position, D is the distance value from the EDF tile, and \vec{d} is the normalized ray direction. Mask query condition: Occupancy mask is queried whenever sampled distance values are zero. Parameters Resolution Scale: 1:4 (one distance value per 64 voxels) is the standard implementation. Bitmask Width: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Grazing Rays: Dense areas with fine geometry (e.g., foliage) cause grazing rays to advance slowly, leading to many small steps despite the EDF. Preprocessing Cost: Generating the EDF has a significant computational cost, estimated at 10x more GPU time than alternative structures like XBrickMap. Traversal Overhead: Ascending and descending the tree structure to advance positions via DDA can introduce extra iterations, potentially negating benefits for smooth surfaces. A variant of the EDF that uses Manhattan distance (L1 norm) instead of Euclidean distance (L2 norm). It uses the same tiled 256^3 structure at 1:4 resolution with 4^3 occupancy bitmasks. Its memory cost is lower: 1 byte per 4^3 voxel plus 1 bit per 1^3 voxel. It is chosen when memory bandwidth is the primary constraint and the approximation error of Manhattan distance is acceptable for the scene geometry. A method to calculate the exact Euclidean distance field from a binary volume in only 3 passes, without propagation or numerical errors. It is used to generate the scalar distance field required for isosurface extraction. Compared to the Satherley and Jones method, it is exact, parallelizable, and significantly faster (270 seconds serial, 47 seconds parallel on 8 threads vs. 722 seconds for Satherley and Jones). The trade-off is higher memory consumption during calculation. Time Complexity: Traversal is O(N) where N is the number of skipped steps, but preprocessing is expensive (10x GPU time vs. XBrickMap). Memory Complexity: 2 bytes per 4^3 voxel for distance + 1 bit per 1^3 voxel for occupancy. Performance: Space skipping is not considerably shorter than space partitioning methods (~8% improvement). Throughput for incoherent rays is comparable to other methods, possibly due to low memory bandwidth constraints. Strengths: Reduces memory bandwidth pressure by skipping empty space; simple data layout. Limitations: Poor performance on dense, fine geometry (foliage); high preprocessing cost; limited speedup over partitioning methods. When to use: Scenes with large empty volumes and coarse geometry where preprocessing time is acceptable. When not to use: Dense, high-frequency geometry or scenes requiring very fast preprocessing. The EDF structure was developed for space-skipping ray traversal in dense voxel volumes. It builds on the concept of tiled distance fields to optimize ray traversal. The Felzenswalb distance transform method, often used to generate the underlying data for EDFs, was introduced by Felzenswalb et al. in 2012. dubiousconst282/VoxelRT, https://github.com/dubiousconst282/VoxelRT, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) EXTRAÇÃO DE ISOSUPERFÍCIES DE DOMOS DE SAL EM VOLUMES BINÁRIOS MASSIVOS, https://doi.org/10.17771/pucrio.acad.51290, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Grid Resolution Heuristic
head: Expected Cost Calculation, MacDonald and Booth Metric, Surface Area Metric Cost Model, Surface Area Metric for Grid Density
body: The Grid Resolution Heuristic is a method for determining the optimal spatial resolution (number of cells) for leaf-level uniform grids in hierarchical acceleration structures, specifically to minimize the expected traversal cost for ray tracing. It differs from static resolution choices by using the Surface Area Metric to balance the cost of grid traversal against the cost of primitive intersection, adapting the grid density (\lambda) to the specific scene geometry and hardware characteristics. Unlike sibling methods that focus on data layout or gradient computation, this heuristic directly informs the structural parameters of the grid itself. The method calculates the grid dimensions (Rx, Ry, Rz) based on a user-defined grid density parameter \lambda, the scene's bounding box volume, and the number of primitives. It uses the Surface Area Metric to estimate the probability of ray intersection with grid cells and primitives, allowing for the optimization of \lambda. Inputs: N: Number of geometric primitives in the scene. V: Volume of the scene's bounding box. \tilde{d}x, \tilde{d}y, \tilde{d}z: Extents (width, height, depth) of the scene's bounding box in each dimension. \lambda: Grid density parameter (user-defined constant). Ct: Constant cost for traversing a node (grid cell). Ci: Constant cost for intersecting a geometric primitive. Outputs: Rx, Ry, Rz: Number of cells in the x, y, and z dimensions of the grid. Optimal \lambda: The value of \lambda that minimizes the expected cost Ce. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required for the calculation itself, only scalar values for scene statistics. The resulting grid is a 3D array of cells, where each cell stores a list of primitives. Formulas: The grid resolution in each dimension is calculated as: Rx = \tilde{d}x \left( \frac{3 \lambda N}{V} \right)^{1/3} Ry = \tilde{d}y \left( \frac{3 \lambda N}{V} \right)^{1/3} Rz = \tilde{d}z \left( \frac{3 \lambda N}{V} \right)^{1/3} The expected cost Ce for traversing a random ray through the acceleration structure is defined by the Surface Area Metric: Ce = Ct \sum{n \in \text{Nodes}} \text{Pr}(n) + Ci \sum{l \in \text{Leaves}} \text{Pr}(l) \text{Prim}(l) Where: \text{Pr}(n) is the probability of a random line intersecting node n (grid cell). \text{Pr}(l) is the probability of a random line intersecting leaf l. \text{Prim}(l) is the number of geometric primitives in leaf l. Parameters: Ct: Traversal cost. Tested values include 1/12, 2, and 3. A value of 1/12 was found to perform best on relatively sparse grids when performing 1/12 intersection tests per traversal step. Ci: Intersection cost. Typically set to 1 for relative comparisons. Top-level density: For hybrid intersector optimizations, the top-level grid density is often set to \lambda = 1/16 to ensure cells contain at least 16 primitives. Algorithm: 1. Compute the scene bounding box volume V and extents \tilde{d}x, \tilde{d}y, \tilde{d}z. 2. Count the total number of primitives N. 3. Select a candidate grid density \lambda. 4. Calculate grid dimensions Rx, Ry, Rz using the formulas above. Round to nearest integers. 5. Construct the grid and populate leaves with primitives. 6. Estimate \text{Pr}(n) and \text{Pr}(l) using surface area ratios (standard Surface Area Metric implementation). 7. Calculate Ce using the cost formula. 8. Repeat for a range of \lambda values to find the minimum Ce. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculategridresolution(extentx, extenty, extentz, volume, numprimitives, griddensity): """ Calculates the number of cells in each dimension for a uniform grid. Args: extentx, extenty, extentz: Extents of the bounding box. volume: Volume of the bounding box. numprimitives: Total number of primitives N. griddensity: User-defined constant lambda. Returns: tuple: (Rx, Ry, Rz) number of cells in each dimension. """ # Formula: R = d (3 lambda N / V)^(1/3) factor = (3.0 griddensity numprimitives / volume) (1.0 / 3.0) Rx = extentx factor Ry = extenty factor Rz = extentz factor # Round to nearest integer as grid dimensions must be integers return (int(round(Rx)), int(round(Ry)), int(round(Rz))) def estimateexpectedcost(gridcells, leafprimitives, Ct, Ci): """ Estimates the expected traversal cost Ce using the Surface Area Metric. Note: This is a simplified representation. Actual Pr(n) requires surface area calculations relative to the bounding volume. Args: gridcells: List of nodes/cells. leafprimitives: List of leaves with primitive counts. Ct: Traversal cost. Ci: Intersection cost. Returns: float: Expected cost Ce. """ # Pr(n) is proportional to the surface area of the cell relative to the # total scene volume or bounding box, normalized for ray direction. # For a uniform grid, Pr(n) is often approximated by the cell's surface area # divided by the total surface area of the bounding box (for isotropic rays) # or integrated over ray directions. cost = 0.0 # Sum over nodes (grid cells) for cell in gridcells: # Pr(cell) calculation depends on specific SAM implementation # Assuming a standard SAM where Pr(cell) ~ SurfaceArea(cell) / TotalSurfaceArea # This is a placeholder for the specific probability calculation logic # which is not fully detailed in the source notes but is standard for SAM. prcell = getsurfaceareaprobability(cell) cost += Ct prcell # Sum over leaves for leaf in leafprimitives: # Pr(leaf) is the probability of intersecting the leaf's bounding volume prleaf = getsurfaceareaprobability(leaf.boundingvolume) numprims = leaf.primitivecount cost += Ci prleaf numprims return cost def getsurfaceareaprobability(boundingvolume): """ Helper to calculate intersection probability based on surface area. In a uniform grid, this is typically the surface area of the cell divided by the surface area of the scene bounding box, adjusted for ray direction distribution. """ # Implementation detail not explicitly provided in source notes # Standard SAM approximation for uniform grids pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Assumptions: The optimal densities derived by Ize et al. for CPU ray tracing are sub-optimal for GPU ray tracing because their analysis assumes fast atomic operations and compute-limited traversal, which do not hold for the GPU hardware used in the referenced studies. Scene Dependency: The optimal density \lambda is scene-dependent. However, rendering performance for various scenes did not vary noticeably for \lambda values between 1/2 and 2. Top-Level Optimization: Setting the top-level density to \lambda = 1/16 is recommended for hybrid intersector optimization to ensure sufficient primitives per cell. Time Complexity: The calculation of grid resolution is O(1) given the scene statistics. Finding the optimal \lambda requires testing multiple values, but the number of tests is small (e.g., from 1/16 to 8). Memory Complexity: The memory usage is determined by the resulting grid resolution. Sparse grids (lower \lambda) use less memory but may increase traversal cost; dense grids use more memory but may reduce intersection tests. Performance: The method aims to minimize the time-to-image by balancing traversal and intersection costs. For the tested scenes (Soda, Venice, Conf., Dragon, Fairy, Sponza), specific optimal \lambda values were found for different Ct values. Strengths: Adapts to scene complexity; provides a theoretical basis for grid sizing; simple to implement. Limitations: Assumes uniform grid structure; optimal values are hardware-dependent; requires accurate estimation of Ct and Ci. The method is based on the heuristic for uniform grids introduced by Cleary et al. [CWVB83] and used by Wald et al. [WIK06]. It employs the Surface Area Metric introduced by MacDonald and Booth [MB90] to compute the expected cost. Ize et al. [ISP07] investigated optimal grid densities for uniform and two-level grids, though their CPU-optimized results were found sub-optimal for GPU implementations. Popov et al. [PGDS09] noted that treating primitives as points can limit quality in other acceleration structures like BVHs. name: Morton Code Encoding/Decoding
head: Z-order, Z-order curve, Morton Order, Z-order encoding, Z-order curve encoding
body: Morton Code Encoding/Decoding converts N-dimensional integer coordinates into a single 1D integer index (the Morton code) by interleaving the bits of each coordinate component, and reverses this process to recover the original coordinates. This linearization preserves spatial locality, mapping nearby points in N-dimensional space to nearby indices in a 1D array, which accelerates cache-coherent access in volume rendering and sparse voxel octree construction. It sets itself apart from hierarchical indexing methods (like Morton Code Generation for Octrees) by operating on flat Cartesian coordinates rather than tree paths, and from lookup-table variants by providing the fundamental bit-interleaving definition. Inputs and Outputs: Encode: Input is an N-dimensional vector of non-negative integers (x0, x1, \dots, x{N-1}). Output is a single unsigned integer (Morton code). For 3D, inputs are typically int32 and output is uint64. Decode: Input is a Morton code (unsigned integer). Output is the N-dimensional vector of integers. Data Structures: Coordinates: Array of integers. In standard 3D implementations, values are in 0, 128) or similar bounds fitting within the bit width. Morton Code: uint64t for 3D coordinates up to 21 bits each (since 3 \times 21 = 63 < 64). Algorithm (Naive [Bit Interleaving): This method directly interleaves bits from each coordinate component. It is computationally expensive (O(\log V) where V is the max coordinate value) but serves as the baseline definition. 1. Initialize result = 0. 2. For each bit position i from 0 to B-1 (where B is the number of bits per coordinate, e.g., 21 for 64-bit codes in 3D): a. Extract the i-th bit of each coordinate xk: bk = (xk \gg i) \& 1. b. Place bk into the k \cdot B + i-th position of the result? No, the standard Z-order interleaves bits at position i of each coordinate into positions i, i+N, i+2N, \dots of the code. Correction based on formula: The formula in shifts the i-th bit of x to position 2i, y to 2i+1, z to 2i+2. This implies N=3 dimensions mapped to a code where bits are interleaved sequentially. General Formula for N dimensions: \text{Morton} = \sum{i=0}^{B-1} \sum{k=0}^{N-1} \left( (xk \gg i) \& 1 \right) \ll (N \cdot i + k) Specific 3D Formula (from): \text{answer} = \sum{i=0}^{31} \left( (x \& (1 \ll i)) \ll 2i \right) \mid \left( (y \& (1 \ll i)) \ll (2i + 1) \right) \mid \left( (z \& (1 \ll i)) \ll (2i + 2) \right) (Note: uses a loop up to 31 bits for int, but for uint64t codes, the loop limit is determined by the available bits per coordinate, typically 21 for 3D 64-bit codes). Algorithm (Fast Bit Interleaving / Parallel Bits): To avoid loops, bits are spread and combined using bitwise operations and masks. Encoding Steps (3D, 64-bit): 1. Spread X: Spread the bits of x into even positions. x = (x \mid (x \ll 32)) \& 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF (for 64-bit, though uses 32-bit steps). Standard 32-bit spread (from, adapted for 64-bit context if needed, but provides full 64-bit spread): x = (x \mid (x \ll 16)) \& 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF x = (x \mid (x \ll 8)) \& 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F x = (x \mid (x \ll 4)) \& 0x3333333333333333 x = (x \mid (x \ll 2)) \& 0x5555555555555555 2. Spread Y: Same as X. 3. Spread Z: Same as X. 4. Combine: \text{Morton} = x \mid (y \ll 1) \mid (z \ll 2) (Note: describes a 2D version: (part1by1(y) << 1) + part1by1(x). For 3D, the shift amounts are 0, 1, 2 relative to the spread bits). Decoding Steps (3D, 64-bit): 1. Extract X: Reverse the spread. x = \text{morton} \& 0x5555555555555555 x = (x \oplus (x \gg 1)) \& 0x3333333333333333 x = (x \oplus (x \gg 2)) \& 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F x = (x \oplus (x \gg 4)) \& 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF x = (x \oplus (x \gg 8)) \& 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF x = (x \oplus (x \gg 16)) \& 0x00000000FFFFFFFF 2. Extract Y: y = (\text{morton} \gg 1) \& 0x5555555555555555 Apply same reverse spread as X. 3. Extract Z: z = (\text{morton} \gg 2) \& 0x5555555555555555 Apply same reverse spread as X. Alternative Decoding (Magic Bits): Uses precomputed "magic" masks to extract bits in parallel. 1. Generate Magic array based on dimensions. 2. For each dimension i: r = (\text{code} \gg i) \& \text{Magic}[0] For j from 0 to len(Magic)-2: r = (r \oplus (r \gg ((N-1) \cdot 2^j))) \& \text{Magic}[j+1] \text{coord}i = r Parameters: Bit Width: 64-bit unsigned integer is standard for 3D. Max coordinate value is 2^{21}-1. Dimensions: 2, 3, or 4 supported in dynamic implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overflow: If coordinates exceed the bit width allocated per dimension (e.g., > 2^{21}-1 for 3D in 64-bit), the Morton code will collide or overflow. Input Validation: Encode must check if input coordinates exceed the table size (if using lookup tables) or bit limits. Decoding Edge Case: If dimensions are 0 or magic array is empty, decode returns nil/error. Pseudocode (Naive 3D Encode/Decode): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mortonencodenaive(x: int, y: int, z: int) -> int: """ Encodes 3D integer coordinates into a 64-bit Morton code using naive bit interleaving. Assumes x, y, z are non-negative and fit within 21 bits. """ morton = 0 # Loop up to 21 bits for 64-bit code (3 21 = 63) for i in range(21): # Extract i-th bit of each coordinate bitx = (x >> i) & 1 bity = (y >> i) & 1 bitz = (z >> i) & 1 # Place bits in Morton code # Bit i of x goes to position 3i # Bit i of y goes to position 3i + 1 # Bit i of z goes to position 3i + 2 morton |= (bitx << (3 i)) morton |= (bity << (3 i + 1)) morton |= (bitz << (3 i + 2)) return morton def mortondecodenaive(morton: int) -> tuple: """ Decodes a 64-bit Morton code back into 3D integer coordinates. """ x = 0 y = 0 z = 0 # Loop up to 21 bits for i in range(21): # Extract bits from Morton code # Bit at position 3i is x # Bit at position 3i + 1 is y # Bit at position 3i + 2 is z bitx = (morton >> (3 i)) & 1 bity = (morton >> (3 i + 1)) & 1 bitz = (morton >> (3 i + 2)) & 1 x |= (bitx << i) y |= (bity << i) z |= (bitz << i) return (x, y, z) A method to compute the Morton (Z-order) curve index for a 3D voxel position (x, y, z) by using precomputed lookup tables for each byte of the coordinates, avoiding expensive bitwise interleaving operations. It sets itself apart from naive bitwise interleaving by trading memory access for computational simplicity, and from general Morton encoding by optimizing specifically for chunked voxel data with a hard limit of 256^3 voxels per chunk. It builds on Morton Code Encoding/Decoding. This method generates unique integer keys for octree cells by recursively concatenating octant indices to a parent key, enabling efficient hierarchical spatial indexing and neighbor lookups. It differs from its parent, Morton Code Encoding/Decoding, which uses bit-interleaving of Cartesian coordinates, by constructing keys via path-based concatenation during tree traversal. Morton Code Spatial Sorting reorders a set of 3D points (typically Gaussian splats) by their Morton codes to improve spatial locality. This ordering enhances compression ratios when quantizing and saving data as images, such as PNGs. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the global reordering of a flat list of parameters rather than constructing a hierarchical tree structure or optimizing lookup tables for index generation. A variant for 2D coordinates (x, y). Steps: 1. Spread X: x = (x \mid (x \ll 32)) \& 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF x = (x \mid (x \ll 16)) \& 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF x = (x \mid (x \ll 8)) \& 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F x = (x \mid (x \ll 4)) \& 0x3333333333333333 x = (x \mid (x \ll 2)) \& 0x5555555555555555 2. Combine: \text{Morton} = \text{spread}(x) \mid (\text{spread}(y) \ll 1) Time Complexity: Naive encoding/decoding is O(\log V) where V is the max coordinate value (number of bits). Fast bit-interleaving (parallel bits) is O(1) with a constant number of bitwise operations (typically 5-10 shifts/masks per dimension). Lookup table methods are O(1) but require memory allocation for tables. Memory Complexity: O(1) for naive/fast methods. Lookup table methods require O(D \cdot 2^B) memory where D is dimensions and B is bits per byte/segment. Performance: Fast bit-interleaving is significantly faster than naive looping. Lookup tables can be faster on CPUs with high cache hit rates for small tables, but may suffer from cache misses for large tables. Strengths: Preserves spatial locality, enabling efficient spatial hashing, grid traversal, and neighbor lookups. Simple to implement. Limitations: Limited by integer bit width (64-bit limits 3D coordinates to ~21 bits). Not suitable for very large coordinate spaces without multi-word codes. When to use: When spatial locality is critical for cache performance (e.g., sparse voxel octrees, density grid access). When coordinates are small integers. When not to use: When coordinates exceed bit limits. When hierarchical structure is needed (use Octree methods instead). Morton order was introduced by G. M. Morton in 1966. It is also known as the Z-order curve because the 2D projection of the curve resembles the letter 'Z'. It is a space-filling curve that linearizes multi-dimensional data. It is widely used in computer graphics for spatial indexing, particularly in sparse voxel octrees (SVOs) for out-of-core construction and rendering. name: Morton Index Calculation via Byte-Lookup Table
head: Morton Code Utility, Morton encoding with LUT
body: A method to compute the Morton (Z-order) curve index for a 3D voxel position (x, y, z) by using precomputed lookup tables for each byte of the coordinates, avoiding expensive bitwise interleaving operations. It sets itself apart from naive bitwise interleaving by trading memory access for computational simplicity, and from general Morton encoding by optimizing specifically for chunked voxel data with a hard limit of 256^3 voxels per chunk. It builds on Morton Code Encoding/Decoding. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D integer coordinates (x, y, z). Output: A Morton code (integer) representing the interleaved position. Data Structures: The method relies on three lookup tables, morton256x, morton256y, and morton256z. Each table contains 256 entries. Each entry maps a single byte (0–255) to its 3-bit Morton-encoded representation. The 3-bit representation interleaves the input byte's bits with zeros for the other two dimensions. For example, morton256x[b] places the bits of byte b into the X-bit positions of the 3D Morton code, with Y and Z bits set to 0. In the libmorton implementation, these are accessed via libmorton::m3DesLUT. The mortontype is uint16t for 16-bit width or uint32t for 32-bit width. The componenttype is uint8t for 16-bit width or uint16t for 32-bit width. Algorithm Steps: 1. General Case (Large Coordinates): If coordinates exceed 255, the input is processed byte-by-byte from most significant to least significant. Extract the most significant byte of x, y, z using shift and mask operations. Look up the encoded byte in the respective tables. Combine results using bitwise OR and shift operations to build the final index. Repeat for subsequent bytes. 2. Optimized Case (Chunked Data \le 256^3): For chunks limited to 256^3 voxels, coordinates fit within 8 bits per axis. Directly index the 256-entry tables with the full 8-bit coordinate components. Combine the three results using bitwise OR. Formula: \text{index} = \text{morton256\x}[x] \mid \text{morton256\y}[y] \mid \text{morton256\z}[z] This avoids shifts and masks for byte extraction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. morton256x = [0] 256 morton256y = [0] 256 morton256z = [0] 256 def encodemortonlutoptimized(x: int, y: int, z: int) -> int: """ Encodes 3D coordinates into a Morton index using byte-lookup tables. Assumes x, y, z are < 256 (fits in one byte per axis). """ index = morton256x[x] | morton256y[y] | morton256z[z] return index def encodemortonlutgeneral(x: int, y: int, z: int) -> int: """ Encodes 3D coordinates into a Morton index using byte-lookup tables. Handles coordinates up to 32-bit integers by processing bytes. """ # Process most significant byte (bits 16-23) bx = (x >> 16) & 0xFF by = (y >> 16) & 0xFF bz = (z >> 16) & 0xFF answer = morton256x[bx] | morton256y[by] | morton256z[bz] # Shift left by 48 bits to make room for the next two bytes answer = answer << 48 # OR in the middle byte (bits 8-15) bx = (x >> 8) & 0xFF by = (y >> 8) & 0xFF bz = (z >> 8) & 0xFF answer = answer | morton256x[bx] | morton256y[by] | morton256z[bz] # Shift left by 24 bits to make room for the last byte answer = answer << 24 # OR in the least significant byte (bits 0-7) bx = x & 0xFF by = y & 0xFF bz = z & 0xFF answer = answer | morton256x[bx] | morton256y[by] | morton256z[bz] return answer Parameters: AXISMAX: Defines the maximum coordinate value per axis. 32 for 16-bit width, 1024 for 32-bit width. Table Size: 256 entries per table. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Size: Creating a lookup table for every possible unsigned int value is impractical due to memory size; therefore, the table is limited to 256 entries (one byte) and applied repeatedly. Coordinate Bounds: The optimized 3-lookup version assumes coordinates are < 256. For larger coordinates, the general byte-by-byte case must be used. Precision: The method uses integer arithmetic. Ensure the output type (mortontype) is large enough to hold the interleaved bits without overflow. A method to access immediate neighbours of a voxel in Morton-ordered memory without re-encoding coordinates, using precomputed offset tables that map a coordinate component to the memory stride required to reach its neighbour. It solves the performance bottleneck of decoding a Morton index to (x,y,z), modifying coordinates, and re-encoding, which involves expensive bitwise operations. It is significantly faster than the naive decode-modify-encode approach and offers a simpler implementation alternative to bitwise manipulation methods like Fabian Giesen’s. Encodes/decodes a list of sorted sparse voxel Morton codes into a compact uint8 sparse voxel octree representation, with optional parent-delta attribute encoding. It takes a tensor of N sorted uint32 Morton codes and a depth parameter, and optionally attributes for delta encoding. Time Complexity: O(1) for the optimized chunked case (3 lookups, 2 ORs). O(\log N) for the general case where N is the number of bits in the coordinate (typically 32, so 3-4 lookups and shifts). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for the lookup tables (3 tables \times 256 entries). Measured Performance: Compared to linear indexing, computing Morton index via LUT takes ~40% longer. Compared to bitwise operations, LUT is faster. For chunk sizes \le 256^3, the optimized 3-lookup version is ~1-2% faster than linear indexing. Strengths: Fast neighbourhood access when combined with delta lookup tables; simple implementation; avoids expensive bitwise interleaving. Limitations: Requires precomputed tables; optimized version is limited to 256^3 chunks; general version is still slower than linear indexing for simple access patterns. When to Use: When spatial locality is critical and neighbourhood access is frequent. When chunk sizes are small (\le 256^3). When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained and lookup tables cannot be afforded. When coordinates are very large and the general case overhead is unacceptable compared to bitwise methods. The method originates from Jeroen Baert's extensive tests on the most performant way to determine Morton curve positions from a 3D input position, which concluded that lookup tables are faster than bitwise operations on modern hardware. It was implemented in the context of Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) rendering. The libmorton library provides a template utility for this, supporting 16-bit and 32-bit Morton widths. name: Fast Neighbourhood Access via Delta Lookup Tables
head: Morton neighbour peeking, deltaX/Y/Z lookup
body: A method to access immediate neighbours of a voxel in Morton-ordered memory without re-encoding coordinates, using precomputed offset tables that map a coordinate component to the memory stride required to reach its neighbour. It solves the performance bottleneck of decoding a Morton index to (x,y,z), modifying coordinates, and re-encoding, which involves expensive bitwise operations. It is significantly faster than the naive decode-modify-encode approach and offers a simpler implementation alternative to bitwise manipulation methods like Fabian Giesen’s. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current voxel pointer in Morton-ordered memory, current chunk-local coordinates (x, y, z), and precomputed delta lookup tables. Output: Pointer to the neighbour voxel (e.g., at x+1, y, z) or a fallback mechanism if the neighbour is outside the current chunk. Data Structures: Three lookup tables: deltaX, deltaY, and deltaZ. Size: 256 elements each (for 8-bit coordinate components, supporting chunks up to 256^3 voxels). Type: Integer offsets (e.g., int32t) representing the stride in memory. Layout: The value at index i is the Morton index difference between a voxel at coordinate i and its neighbour at i+1 along that axis, assuming the other two coordinates are constant. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize three lookup tables (deltaX, deltaY, deltaZ) of size 256. 2. Populate deltaX[i] with the difference between the Morton index of (i+1, 0, 0) and (i, 0, 0) for i \in [0, 255]. 3. Populate deltaY[i] with the difference between the Morton index of (0, i+1, 0) and (0, i, 0) for i \in [0, 255]. 4. Populate deltaZ[i] with the difference between the Morton index of (0, 0, i+1) and (0, 0, i) for i \in [0, 255]. 5. To access the neighbour at (x+1, y, z): Check if x+1 is within the current chunk boundaries. If yes, compute newptr = currentptr + deltaX[x]. If no, fallback to global coordinate calculation. 6. To access the neighbour at (x+1, y+1, z+1): Check if x+1, y+1, z+1 are within current chunk boundaries. If yes, compute newptr = currentptr + deltaX[x] + deltaY[y] + deltaZ[z]. If no, fallback to global coordinate calculation. Formulas: Let M(x, y, z) be the Morton index of voxel (x, y, z). The delta for the x-axis is defined as: \Delta Xx = M(x+1, 0, 0) - M(x, 0, 0) The delta for the y-axis is defined as: \Delta Yy = M(0, y+1, 0) - M(0, y, 0) The delta for the z-axis is defined as: \Delta Zz = M(0, 0, z+1) - M(0, 0, z) The new pointer for a neighbour at (x+\deltax, y+\deltay, z+\deltaz) is: P{new} = P{current} + \sum{axis \in \{x,y,z\}, \delta{axis}=1} \Delta{axis}[coord{axis}] Parameters: Table size: 256 (supports chunks up to 256^3). Coordinate bit-width: 8 bits per axis (implied by table size). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Chunk Boundaries: If the neighbour lies outside the current chunk, the delta lookup is invalid for the global volume. The implementation must check chunk boundaries using macros (e.g., CANGOPOSX) before using the delta. Fallback: If the boundary check fails, the method must fall back to decoding the Morton index to global coordinates, modifying them, and re-encoding or using a global lookup. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. deltaX = [0] 256 deltaY = [0] 256 deltaZ = [0] 256 def mortonencode(x, y, z): """Standard 3D Morton (Z-order) encoding.""" x = (x | (x << 16)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF x = (x | (x << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF x = (x | (x << 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F x = (x | (x << 2)) & 0x3333333333333333 x = (x | (x << 1)) & 0x5555555555555555 y = (y | (y << 16)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF y = (y | (y << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF y = (y | (y << 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F y = (y | (y << 2)) & 0x3333333333333333 y = (y | (y << 1)) & 0x5555555555555555 z = (z | (z << 16)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF z = (z | (z << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF z = (z | (z << 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F z = (z | (z << 2)) & 0x3333333333333333 z = (z | (z << 1)) & 0x5555555555555555 return x | (y << 1) | (z << 2) def mortondecode(index): """Standard 3D Morton decoding.""" index = index & 0x5555555555555555 index = (index ^ (index >> 1)) & 0x3333333333333333 index = (index ^ (index >> 2)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F index = (index ^ (index >> 4)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF index = (index ^ (index >> 8)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF index = (index ^ (index >> 16)) & 0x00000000FFFFFFFF x = index index = (index >> 1) & 0x5555555555555555 index = (index ^ (index >> 1)) & 0x3333333333333333 index = (index ^ (index >> 2)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F index = (index ^ (index >> 4)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF index = (index ^ (index >> 8)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF index = (index ^ (index >> 16)) & 0x00000000FFFFFFFF y = index index = (index >> 1) & 0x5555555555555555 index = (index ^ (index >> 1)) & 0x3333333333333333 index = (index ^ (index >> 2)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F index = (index ^ (index >> 4)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF index = (index ^ (index >> 8)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF index = (index ^ (index >> 16)) & 0x00000000FFFFFFFF z = index return x, y, z def initdeltatables(): """Initialize delta lookup tables by computing adjacent Morton index differences.""" for i in range(256): deltaX[i] = mortonencode(i + 1, 0, 0) - mortonencode(i, 0, 0) deltaY[i] = mortonencode(0, i + 1, 0) - mortonencode(0, i, 0) deltaZ[i] = mortonencode(0, 0, i + 1) - mortonencode(0, 0, i) def peekvoxelxplusone(currentptr, xposinchunk, basemortonindex): """Access voxel at (x+1, y, z) relative to current voxel.""" if xposinchunk < 255: return currentptr + deltaX[xposinchunk] else: # Fallback: decode Morton index to global coordinates, modify, and re-encode gx, gy, gz = mortondecode(basemortonindex) newmorton = mortonencode(gx + 1, gy, gz) return baseptrtoindexmap(newmorton) # Standard global lookup mapping def peekvoxelallplusone(currentptr, xposinchunk, yposinchunk, zposinchunk, basemortonindex): """Access voxel at (x+1, y+1, z+1) relative to current voxel.""" if xposinchunk < 255 and yposinchunk < 255 and zposinchunk < 255: return currentptr + deltaX[xposinchunk] + deltaY[yposinchunk] + deltaZ[zposinchunk] else: # Fallback: decode Morton index to global coordinates, modify, and re-encode gx, gy, gz = mortondecode(basemortonindex) newmorton = mortonencode(gx + 1, gy + 1, gz + 1) return baseptrtoindexmap(newmorton) # Standard global lookup mapping Time Complexity: O(1) for neighbour access within the same chunk, as it involves only array lookups and addition. Memory Complexity: O(1) extra memory for the three lookup tables (3 256 4 bytes = 3 KB for int32t). Measured Performance: Significantly faster than the naive decode-modify-encode approach. Scaling: Supports chunks up to 256^3 voxels with fixed table size. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast access, no bitwise operations during runtime. Limitations: Requires boundary checks; fallback to global lookup is needed for cross-chunk neighbours. Originated in the PolyVox project, as described in a blog post by Matt and contributors. The method was developed to efficiently handle voxel data stored in Morton-ordered chunks, addressing the complexity of neighbour access in such a layout. Implementing Morton ordering for chunked voxel data, http://www.volumesoffun.com/implementing-morton-ordering-for-chunked-voxel-data/index.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)
