name: Voxel Memory Bank Allocation and Miniblock Organization
head: Miniblock Reordering for SDRAM, Voxel Memory Layout, Voxel Memory Organization (Miniblocks and Skewing)
body: Voxel Memory Bank Allocation and Miniblock Organization is a hardware-level memory layout strategy designed to maximize memory bandwidth and eliminate bank conflicts in SDRAM-based volume rendering systems. It solves the problem of inefficient memory access patterns during ray casting by organizing voxels into fixed-size miniblocks and applying a two-level skewing scheme across memory modules and internal SDRAM banks. Unlike general-purpose texture mapping, which relies on cache hierarchies, this method ensures that any ray parallel to the coordinate axes can access a full beam of voxels in consecutive memory cycles without pipeline stalls. It is distinct from Volume Interleaving by using fixed 2x2x2 blocks rather than arbitrary interleaving, and from Memory-Insensitive Rendering by relying on strict geometric alignment rather than algorithmic tolerance to latency. Inputs: Volume data in host memory with arbitrary dimensions. View direction (used for reordering logic). Outputs: Voxel data arranged in Voxel Memory such that four adjacent miniblocks are in separate memory modules and separate SDRAM banks. Data streamed to rendering pipelines in slice order. Data Structures: 1. Miniblock: A 2x2x2 array of voxels. Stored linearly in a single memory module at consecutive memory addresses. Size: 8 voxels. 2. Voxel Memory: A collection of memory modules. Each module contains SDRAM chips. 3. SDRAM Chip: Contains 4 internal memory banks (for 64-megabit chips). Layout and Allocation: 1. Padding: The volume dimensions in Voxel Memory must be padded to multiples of 32 voxels in each dimension. This is derived from the miniblock structure: 2 \times 4 \times 4 = 32. Arbitrary host volumes are stored with these padded dimensions and automatically cropped to their original size during rendering. 2. Miniblock Distribution (Module Skewing): Miniblocks are distributed across memory modules such that any group of four adjacent miniblocks in any cardinal direction (x, y, or z) is stored in four separate memory modules. This prevents access conflicts between modules. 3. Bank Skewing: Within a memory module, miniblocks are skewed so that adjacent miniblocks never fall into the same internal memory bank of an SDRAM chip. A 4x4x4 cube of miniblocks is skewed across the four memory banks. Mapping Formulas: Let voxel coordinates be (u, v, w). 1. Calculate miniblock coordinates (um, vm, wm): um = \lfloor u / 2 \rfloor, \quad vm = \lfloor v / 2 \rfloor, \quad wm = \lfloor w / 2 \rfloor (Note: Integer division) 2. Determine Memory Module Index (M): M = (um + vm + wm) \bmod 4 This ensures that adjacent miniblocks along any axis differ in module index by 1 (mod 4), distributing them across 4 modules. 3. Determine Memory Bank Index (B) within the module: B = ((\lfloor um / 4 \rfloor) + (\lfloor vm / 4 \rfloor) + (\lfloor wm / 4 \rfloor)) \bmod 4 This ensures that a 4x4x4 block of miniblocks maps to all 4 banks, allowing back-to-back access without bank conflicts. Data Flow and Processing Steps: 1. Read: The Voxel Memory interface reads two slices of voxels at a time. Data is read in bursts of miniblocks (8 voxels) to exploit SDRAM burst capabilities. 2. Reorder (Miniblock Level): Inside each miniblock, voxels are read in a fixed sequential order. However, the order is rearranged based on the current view direction. This logic ensures that the voxels correspond to the canonical positions assumed for tri-linear interpolation (e.g., ensuring the "left-most" voxel in the beam is processed first). 3. De-skew (Global Level): The four miniblocks output by the Voxel Memory controllers are de-skewed by a global de-skewing network. This reverses the module/bank skewing so that the left-most voxel along the x-axis flows down the leftmost rendering pipeline, and adjacent voxels in x flow down neighboring pipelines. 4. Buffer: The de-skewed miniblocks are written into the voxel slice buffers of the four rendering pipelines. 5. Gradient Computation: The slice buffers store three slices worth of data. This allows the computation of z-gradients using central differences. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocatevoxelmemory(volumedims): """ Pads volume dimensions to multiples of 32 and calculates layout metadata. """ # Pad dimensions to multiples of 32 paddedu = ((volumedims.u + 31) // 32) 32 paddedv = ((volumedims.v + 31) // 32) 32 paddedw = ((volumedims.w + 31) // 32) 32 return { 'paddeddims': (paddedu, paddedv, paddedw), 'miniblocksize': 8, # 2x2x2 voxels 'sdrambanks': 4 } def getminiblocklocation(u, v, w): """ Returns the memory module and bank index for a voxel at (u, v, w). Assumes 64-megabit SDRAMs with 4 banks. """ # Integer division for miniblock coordinates um = u // 2 vm = v // 2 wm = w // 2 # Module index: ensures adjacent miniblocks are in different modules moduleidx = (um + vm + wm) % 4 # Bank index: ensures adjacent miniblocks are in different banks # Uses 4x4x4 grouping of miniblocks bankidx = ((um // 4) + (vm // 4) + (wm // 4)) % 4 return moduleidx, bankidx def reorderminiblockforview(miniblockvoxels, viewdirection): """ Rearranges the 8 voxels within a miniblock to match canonical interpolation order for the given view direction. """ # Logic depends on specific view direction (e.g., x-aligned, y-aligned) # For x-aligned view, ensure voxel with smallest x is first # This is handled by hardware logic in the memory interface return sorted(miniblockvoxels, key=lambda v: v.x) # Simplified representation def processslicebuffer(slicebuffer, viewdirection): """ Reads from slice buffer to compute interpolated samples and gradients. Requires 3 slices for central difference z-gradients. """ if len(slicebuffer) < 3: raise ValueError("Need 3 slices for z-gradient computation") # De-skewing has already occurred, so voxels are in pipeline order # Compute gradients using central differences on the z-axis zgradient = computecentraldifference(slicebuffer) # Compute tri-linear interpolation using reordered miniblock data sample = trilinearinterpolate(slicebuffer, viewdirection) return sample, zgradient Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dimension Alignment: If volume dimensions are not multiples of 32, the hardware must handle the cropping. Failure to pad correctly may lead to miniblock misalignment and bank conflicts. Supervolumes: For volumes exceeding 256 voxels per edge, software must partition the volume into blocks (supervolumes). Adjacent blocks must duplicate 3 voxels in each dimension to maintain correct interpolation and gradients at boundaries. View Direction Dependency: The reordering logic is specific to the view direction. Changing the view direction requires updating the reordering logic in the memory interface. A specific application of miniblock skewing for Cubic Frame Buffers (CFBs) that maps n^3 voxels into n memory banks to ensure conflict-free access for rays parallel to desired directions. Choose this when hardware supports CFB architecture and requires conflict-free access for arbitrary ray angles within a set of canonical directions. Time Complexity: Memory access is O(1) per miniblock with no bank conflicts for axis-aligned rays. The overhead is the fixed cost of reordering and de-skewing logic. Memory Complexity: Requires padding volume dimensions to multiples of 32 voxels. For a volume of size N^3, the memory usage is slightly higher than N^3 due to padding. Performance: Achieves burst rates of up to 532 million voxels per second with four 133 MHz memory interfaces, provided voxels are organized in miniblocks. Strengths: Eliminates memory bank conflicts for axis-aligned rays; maximizes SDRAM burst efficiency; simple hardware logic for reordering. Limitations: Restricted to axis-aligned or near-axis-aligned rays for optimal performance; requires fixed miniblock size (2x2x2); not suitable for arbitrary non-grid-aligned sampling without significant overhead. When to Use: High-performance, real-time volume rendering on hardware with SDRAM-based Voxel Memory (e.g., VolumePro). When Not to Use: When rendering non-axis-aligned rays with high angular diversity; when memory bandwidth is not the bottleneck; when using modern GPU architectures with unified memory and cache hierarchies that handle coalesced access differently. This method was developed for the VolumePro real-time ray-casting system by MERL (Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratory). It was described in the technical report "The VolumePro Real-Time Ray-Casting System" (TR99-19). The system was designed to overcome the memory bandwidth limitations of early 2000s hardware by exploiting the regularity of volumetric data and the burst capabilities of SDRAM. The approach is specific to the VolumePro hardware architecture, which includes dedicated ASICs (vg500) for memory management and rendering pipelines. The VolumePro Real-Time Ray-Casting System, https://www.merl.com/publications/docs/TR99-19.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Skewed Memory Organization for Conflict-Free Ray Access
head: Linear Skewing Scheme, Skewing Memory Schemes
body: Skewed Memory Organization is a memory layout strategy for Cubic Frame Buffers (CFBs) that maps n^3 voxels into n memory banks to enable simultaneous, conflict-free access to a full ray of n voxels in a single memory cycle. It solves the memory contention problem inherent in parallel volume rendering by ensuring that any ray parallel to a set of desired directions accesses exactly one voxel from each bank. Unlike general-purpose texture mapping, this scheme is specifically optimized for the geometric regularity of volumetric ray casting, allowing the hardware to retrieve an entire beam without bank conflicts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D voxel coordinates (x, y, z) where 0 \le x, y, z < n'; viewing direction parameters (a, b, c); modulus n' (number of banks). Output: Bank index k for storage/retrieval; de-mapped position index along the ray. Data Structures: Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB): A logical n' \times n' \times n' volume. Memory Banks: n' physical banks, each holding n'^2 voxels. Bank Index: An integer k \in [0, n'-1] identifying the bank. Bit Packing: Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Select the modulus n' and coefficients a, b, c based on the desired viewing directions. 2. Mapping (Offline/Setup): For each voxel at (x, y, z), compute the bank index k using the appropriate formula (Eq. 1 for orthographic, Eq. 4 for arbitrary). Store the voxel data in bank k. 3. De-mapping (Runtime): When a ray is processed, fetch the voxel from bank k. Compute the de-mapped position index Dz using Eq. 3 to determine the voxel's relative position along the ray. 4. Beam Scanning Optimization: During viewing, as the system scans from one beam to the next, the bank index (distance of a voxel along the beam from the viewing position) is incremented or decremented by 1 modulo n. This change is controlled locally by the local address unit of the bank, avoiding the need to re-evaluate the skewing formula (Eq. 1 or 4) for every voxel during the time-consuming viewing process. Formulas: 1. Orthographic Skewing (Primary Axes): For rays parallel to the primary axes (\pm x, \pm y, \pm z), the bank index is calculated as: k \equiv (x + y + z) \pmod{n} where n is the number of banks. 2. Linear Skewing (Arbitrary Directions): For non-orthographic directions, a linear combination is used: k = (ax + by + cz) \bmod n' where 0 \le k, x, y, z < n' - 1. The parameters a, b, c and the modulus n' are selected to guarantee conflict-free access for a specific set of directions. 3. De-mapping (Orthographic): To retrieve the voxel beam back into 3D discrete space for a ray parallel to the +x axis (where y=y0, z=z0), the position index Dz along the beam is calculated from the bank index k: Dz = [k - (y + z) \bmod n] This allows the system to reconstruct the spatial order of voxels along the ray after fetching them from different banks. Parameters: n' (Modulus): The number of memory banks. In the cited example, n' = 517 is used. a, b, c: Coefficients for the linear skewing scheme. In the example providing conflict-free access to 26 parallel directions, a=5, b=2, c=1 are used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Directional Coverage: The linear skewing scheme (Eq. 4) only guarantees conflict-free access for the "desired directions" specified during parameter selection. Modulus Selection: The choice of n' is critical and must be compatible with the coefficients a, b, c to avoid collisions. Precision: The de-mapping formula (Eq. 3) relies on modular arithmetic. Implementations must handle negative operands correctly to ensure accurate spatial reconstruction. The Ray Projection via Multiple-Write Bus (VMWB) is a hardware-accelerated mechanism for selecting the front-most non-transparent voxel along a ray in a Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB). It solves the conflict resolution problem inherent in parallel volume rendering by using a dedicated bus to race n processing units against each other, identifying the closest voxel in logarithmic time. Unlike software-based ray casting which iterates through voxels, VMWB performs this selection in parallel across the entire beam, leveraging the skewed memory organization of its parent method to ensure conflict-free data fetch. Time Complexity: The projection time complexity is O(n \log n), identical to orthographic projections, even for the 26 parallel directions supported by the linear skewing scheme. Memory Access: Enables simultaneous access to n voxels in one memory cycle, provided the ray direction matches the pre-computed conflict-free set. Strengths: Eliminates bank conflicts for a defined set of viewing directions; reduces runtime arithmetic overhead by using local address units for beam scanning. Limitations: Conflict-free access is limited to specific directions (e.g., 26 directions in the example); arbitrary viewing angles may require different coefficients or result in conflicts. Hardware Dependency: Relies on a Cubic Frame Buffer architecture with n memory banks and local address units per bank. The Skewed Memory Organization was introduced in the context of the Viewing and Rendering Processor for a Volume Visualization System. It addresses the memory bandwidth and contention issues in parallel volume rendering by structuring the Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) to align with the geometric properties of volumetric rays. The method was developed to support efficient hardware-accelerated rendering, particularly for orthographic and near-orthographic projections, and was extended to support a limited set of non-orthographic directions via linear skewing. Viewing and Rendering Processor for a Volume Visualization System, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh89/171-178, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Ray Projection via Multiple-Write Bus
head: VMWB Projection, Voxel Multiple-Write Bus Projection
body: The Ray Projection via Multiple-Write Bus (VMWB) is a hardware-accelerated mechanism for selecting the front-most non-transparent voxel along a ray in a Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB). It solves the conflict resolution problem inherent in parallel volume rendering by using a dedicated bus to race n processing units against each other, identifying the closest voxel in logarithmic time. Unlike software-based ray casting which iterates through voxels, VMWB performs this selection in parallel across the entire beam, leveraging the skewed memory organization of its parent method to ensure conflict-free data fetch. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A full beam of n voxels fetched from the CFB along a viewing direction. Each voxel contains a value (e.g., color/intensity) and a depth index. Output: Two values for the single closest non-transparent voxel: its value and its depth (distance). These are passed directly to the shading unit. Data Structures and Layout: The system consists of n identical processing modules indexed 0, 1, \dots, n-1. Module Composition: Each module includes a transparency unit, a local address unit, and a connection to the Voxel Multiple-Write Bus (VMWB). Interconnection: Modules are interconnected via a barrel shifter, enabling fast memory-to-memory transfer of beams in O(\log n) time. Voxel Placement: Upon fetching a beam, each voxel is placed into its associated processing unit. Algorithm Steps: 1. Fetch: Retrieve a full beam of n voxels from the CFB along the current viewing direction. 2. Distribute: Place each voxel into its corresponding processing unit (0 to n-1). 3. Broadcast Parameters: Broadcast transparency control parameters, interval control parameters, and depth control parameters to all modules. 4. Local Filtering: Units holding transparent voxels are excluded from the race. Interval and depth control parameters are broadcast and compared with locally computed depth measures to generate depth sections or slices. 5. Race for Bus: All remaining units holding valid non-transparent voxels "race" for the VMWB. The comparison is performed bit-by-bit, starting from the most significant bit (MSB) of the depth index. This comparison proceeds for \log n steps. 6. Selection: The unit holding the voxel with the smallest depth index (closest to the observer) wins the race. 7. Output: The winning unit outputs the voxel's value and depth to the shading unit. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vmwbprojection(beam, n): """ Selects the closest non-transparent voxel from a beam of n voxels using the Voxel Multiple-Write Bus logic. Args: beam: List of n voxel dicts/tuples with keys 'value', 'depthindex', 'istransparent'. n: Number of voxels in the beam (and number of processing units). Returns: Tuple of (value, depth) for the closest valid voxel, or (None, None) if none. """ # Step 1 & 2: beam contains n voxels, each assigned to unit index i validunits = [] # Step 3: Parameters are broadcast (assumed available globally) # transparencyparams, intervalparams, depthparams = getbroadcastparams() # Step 4: Local filtering for i, voxel in enumerate(beam): # Check transparency if voxel['istransparent']: continue # Check depth/interval controls # Local depth measure computation (Equation 3 from source) localdepthmeasure = voxel['depthindex'] # Placeholder for Equation 3 logic # The exact filtering logic for interval/depth parameters is not given in the sources # validunits.append((i, voxel)) validunits.append((i, voxel)) if not validunits: return None, None # No valid voxel found # Step 5 & 6: Race for the bus # Compare depth indices bit-by-bit from MSB to LSB # This takes log2(n) steps closestunitindex, closestvoxel = min(validunits, key=lambda x: x[1]['depthindex']) # Step 7: Output return closestvoxel['value'], closestvoxel['depthindex'] Parameters: Transparency Control Parameters: Thresholds for voxel opacity. Interval Control Parameters: Broadcast and compared with locally computed depth measures to generate depth sections or slices. Depth Control Parameters: Broadcast and compared with locally computed depth measures to generate depth sections or slices. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: All Transparent: If all voxels in the beam are transparent or filtered out, no unit wins and the mechanism returns no output. Precision: The bit-by-bit comparison assumes fixed-point or integer depth indices. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a full beam of n voxels. A memory layout that enables VMWB by ensuring each ray accesses one voxel per bank. It sets apart from standard tiling by using linear skewing formulas to guarantee conflict-free access across 26 parallel directions. Choose it when orthographic or principal diagonal views are required on specialized hardware. Skewed Memory Organization for Conflict-Free Ray Access The underlying data structure for n^3 voxels that VMWB operates upon. It sets apart from sparse representations by storing all voxels in a dense, banked grid. Choose it when hardware-accelerated parallel projection is needed. Cubic Frame Buffer Time Complexity: The selection of the closest voxel takes O(\log n) time per beam due to the bit-by-bit comparison. The overall projection time for orthographic projections is O(n^2 \log n) or effectively O(n^2) with skewing optimization. Arbitrary parallel projections take O(n^2 \log n) time. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Conflict-free access; parallel selection; logarithmic selection time. Limitations: Hardware complexity (n modules, barrel shifter); distortion if rotation is used for non-orthographic views. When to Use: High-performance volume rendering on specialized hardware (VP3) where n is manageable and orthographic or principal diagonal views are required. When Not to Use: General-purpose CPUs without specialized bus logic; scenes requiring frequent arbitrary rotations (causes distortion). The VMWB projection mechanism was developed for the VP3 (Viewing and Rendering Processor) as part of a volume visualization system. The system uses a Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) and relies on linear skewing schemes (e.g., k = (5x + 2y + z) \bmod 517) to provide conflict-free access to 26 parallel directions (6 orthographic, 8 corner, 12 edge projections). Arbitrary parallel projections can be generated by first transforming (rotating) the scene and then viewing it through a principal orthographic direction. With this technique, however, the CFB image is distorted each time a rotation is performed. Viewing and Rendering Processor for a Volume Visualization System, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh89/171-178, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Volume Interleaving
head: Bit Interleaving, Coordinate Bit Interleaving
body: Volume Interleaving is a memory layout optimization designed to reduce cache misses during volume rendering by decomposing the volume into small blocks and interleaving the bits of voxel coordinates. It maps 3D spatial coordinates to a linear memory address such that spatially adjacent voxels are stored contiguously in memory, improving spatial locality for ray-casting algorithms. Unlike standard row-major or column-major layouts, which suffer from poor cache performance when traversing 3D volumes along arbitrary ray directions, interleaving ensures that consecutive samples along a ray are closer in memory. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D voxel coordinates (X, Y, Z) within a block of size 32^3. Output: A linear memory address (index) in the interleaved buffer. Data Structures: A 32-entry lookup table for bit manipulation. 32-bit unsigned integers for coordinate storage and address generation. Method: The volume is decomposed into small blocks containing 32^3 samples (32x32x32 voxels). Within each block, the bits of the coordinates are interleaved to generate the memory address. The mapping preserves the most significant bits (MSBs) grouped by dimension while interleaving the five least significant bits (LSBs) across dimensions. The bit interleaving mapping is defined as: (X{n \dots 0}, Y{n \dots 0}, Z{n \dots 0}) \implies Z{n \dots 5} Y{n \dots 5} X{n \dots 5} Z4 Y4 X4 \dots Z0 Y0 X0 Where: n is the index of the most significant bit of the coordinate. The bits from index n down to 5 are grouped by dimension (Z, then Y, then X). The bits from index 4 down to 0 are interleaved across dimensions (Z4 Y4 X4 \dots Z0 Y0 X0). Algorithm Steps: 1. Decompose the volume into 32 \times 32 \times 32 blocks. 2. For a given voxel at coordinates (X, Y, Z): a. Extract the five lower bits of X, Y, and Z (bits 0–4). b. Use a 32-entry lookup table and binary operators to interleave these five lower bits. c. Combine the interleaved lower bits with the upper bits (n down to 5), which are kept grouped by dimension (Z{n \dots 5} Y{n \dots 5} X{n \dots 5}). 3. The resulting bit pattern forms the linear memory address. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interleavebits(val, table): """ Interleaves the 5 lower bits of a 32-bit integer using a lookup table. Assumes val is a 32-bit unsigned integer. """ # Extract the 5 lower bits lower5 = val & 0x1F # Use lookup table to interleave these 5 bits into a 15-bit pattern # The table maps each 5-bit input to its interleaved 15-bit output # (Implementation detail: the table size is 32 entries) interleavedlower = table[lower5] return interleavedlower def volumeinterleaveaddress(x, y, z, n, lookuptable): """ Generates the linear memory address for a voxel at (x, y, z) using volume interleaving. Args: x, y, z: 32-bit unsigned integer coordinates n: Index of the most significant bit of the coordinates lookuptable: 32-entry list/array for interleaving 5 bits Returns: Linear memory address (32-bit unsigned integer) """ # Extract upper bits (from n down to 5) # Mask to keep bits from n down to 5, shift to LSB position for grouping # Note: The exact bit manipulation for upper bits depends on n. # The formula groups them as Zupper, Yupper, Xupper. # Create mask for upper bits (bits 5 to n) # Assuming n >= 5. If n < 5, upper part is 0. if n < 5: xupper = 0 yupper = 0 zupper = 0 else: # Mask for bits 5 to n # Example: if n=7, mask is 0b1111100000 (bits 5-7 set) mask = ((1 << (n + 1)) - 1) ^ ((1 << 5) - 1) xupper = (x & mask) >> 5 yupper = (y & mask) >> 5 zupper = (z & mask) >> 5 # Interleave the lower 5 bits xlowerinterleaved = interleavebits(x, lookuptable) ylowerinterleaved = interleavebits(y, lookuptable) zlowerinterleaved = interleavebits(z, lookuptable) # Combine: Zupper, Yupper, Xupper, then interleaved lower bits # The interleaved lower bits are 15 bits long (5 bits 3 dimensions) # They are interleaved as Z4 Y4 X4... Z0 Y0 X0 # Construct the final address # Upper bits are shifted to the top # Lower bits are in the bottom 15 bits address = (zupper << 15) | (yupper << 10) | (xupper << 5) # The interleaved lower bits need to be combined correctly. # The lookup table output for each dimension is 15 bits. # However, the formula implies a single interleaved sequence for all 3 dimensions' lower bits. # The lookup table approach described in likely handles the 5 bits of one dimension # into a specific pattern, but the final address requires interleaving Z, Y, X lower bits together. # Re-reading: "A 32-entry table and binary operators are used to interleave the five lower bits" # This suggests the table might map the 5 bits of (X,Y,Z) combined? # Or it interleaves each dimension's 5 bits into a 15-bit slot? # The formula shows Z4 Y4 X4... Z0 Y0 X0. # This is a 15-bit sequence. # Let's assume the table interleaves the 5 bits of a single coordinate into a 15-bit pattern # where the bits are spaced out. Then we combine them. # But the formula shows them interleaved across dimensions. # Alternative interpretation: The table maps the 5 bits of X, Y, Z into a single 15-bit interleaved value? # No, the table is 32 entries, so it takes 5 bits. # Most likely: The table interleaves the 5 bits of ONE dimension into a 15-bit field with gaps. # Then we OR them together. # If Xlower is interleaved into positions 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 (for example) # Ylower into 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 # Zlower into 2, 5, 8, 11, 14 # Then ORing them gives the interleaved sequence. # Let's assume the lookup table returns a 15-bit value where the input bits are placed # at specific positions. For X, positions 0,3,6,9,12. For Y, 1,4,7,10,13. For Z, 2,5,8,11,14. # However, the source says "interleave the five lower bits" using a table. # It does not specify the exact bit positions. # We will assume a standard bit interleaving where the table handles the permutation. # To be precise and implementable, we need the exact table or formula. # Since the source only mentions a 32-entry table, we will use a placeholder for the table content # but describe the combination logic. # Let's assume the table interleave5to15 maps a 5-bit value to a 15-bit value # with bits at positions 0, 3, 6, 9, 12. # Then we need similar tables for Y and Z, or shift the result. # Given the constraint of "no placeholders", and the source's vagueness on the exact table content, # we must rely on the formula structure. # The formula is: Z4 Y4 X4... Z0 Y0 X0 # This is equivalent to: # bit 0: X0 # bit 1: Y0 # bit 2: Z0 # bit 3: X1 # bit 4: Y1 # bit 5: Z1 #... # So, Xlowerinterleaved should have X0 at bit 0, X1 at bit 3, etc. # Ylowerinterleaved should have Y0 at bit 1, Y1 at bit 4, etc. # Zlowerinterleaved should have Z0 at bit 2, Z1 at bit 5, etc. # The lookup table likely performs this spacing. # We will define the table usage as: # tablex = lookuptable[xlower] -> places X bits at 0,3,6,9,12 # tabley = lookuptable[ylower] -> places Y bits at 1,4,7,10,13 (requires shifting or separate table) # tablez = lookuptable[zlower] -> places Z bits at 2,5,8,11,14 (requires shifting or separate table) # Since the source says "A 32-entry table", it implies one table is used for all. # So we likely shift the result of the table lookup. xlowerspaced = lookuptable[xlower] ylowerspaced = lookuptable[ylower] << 1 zlowerspaced = lookuptable[zlower] << 2 # Combine lower bits lowercombined = xlowerspaced | ylowerspaced | zlowerspaced # Final address address = (zupper << 15) | (yupper << 10) | (xupper << 5) | lowercombined return address Parameters: Block size: 32^3 samples (32x32x32 voxels). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes coordinates are within the defined block. Precision issues may arise if the number of bits n is large, requiring careful handling of upper bits. The source mentions that code running on MMX-only processors may not allow line equation tests, leading to minor artifacts, but this is related to the rendering algorithm, not the interleaving itself. A parallel technique to reorder two integers containing 4-bit groups representing voxels. Specifically, it reorders interleaved groups of bits representing even voxels (0, 2, 4, 6) and odd voxels (1, 3, 5, 7) into a contiguous or specific layout. The method shifts groups of information at the same time whenever possible to achieve the reordering in parallel. This is used in solid voxelization algorithms to optimize memory access patterns for subsequent processing. Time Complexity: The address calculation involves bitwise operations and a table lookup, which is O(1) per voxel. Memory Complexity: The layout is dense, storing 32^3 samples per block. Performance: The method reduces cache misses by ensuring spatially adjacent voxels are stored contiguously in memory. This improves performance for ray-casting algorithms that traverse the volume along rays. Strengths: Improved cache locality for 3D volume traversal. Limitations: The complexity of address calculation may offset gains on hardware with very fast cache access or specific SIMD optimizations. The method is specific to block sizes of 32^3. Volume Interleaving was introduced in the context of object-order ray-casting algorithms to optimize memory access patterns. The technique is described in "A new object-order ray-casting algorithm". It is particularly useful for rendering large volumes on hardware where cache misses are a significant performance bottleneck. name: Sparse Voxel Octree Representation
head: Basic SVO in rust, Octree Representation, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO), Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) - Basic Implementation, Voxel Octrees, pointer-based sparse octree
body: A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) is a hierarchical data structure for representing 3D space that eliminates sparse memory by not storing empty volumes. It enables efficient storage and traversal of voxel data, particularly for indirect illumination calculations at geometry-independent costs. Unlike dense grids or chunk-based structures, it adapts resolution to content density, trading traversal performance for memory efficiency. Inputs: 3D coordinates (x, y, z), voxel data, and a maximum depth D. Outputs: Voxel reference or null. Data Structures: 1. SparseVoxelOctree: Contains root (Node) and maxdepth (u32). 2. Node: Enum with two variants: Branch: Contains children: Box<[Node; 8]>. Stores exactly 8 children in contiguous memory. Leaf: Contains Option<Voxel>. Represents a unitary-sized voxel or empty space. 3. Voxel: Contains index (u32). Initialization: The tree is initialized with a specific depth D. A Node::new(depth) recursively creates a full tree where depth 0 results in a Leaf(Some(Voxel::new())) and depth > 0 results in a Branch with 8 children of depth-1. Lookup (Iterative): 1. Start with this = self, coordinates x, y, z, and size s = 2^{D-1}. 2. Loop: If this is Leaf, return the voxel reference. If this is Branch, calculate child index: index = ((x \ge s) \text{ as usize}) \ll 0 \mid ((y \ge s) \text{ as usize}) \ll 1 \mid ((z \ge s) \text{ as usize}) \ll 2 Update this to children[index]. Update coordinates: x \%= s, y \%= s, z \%= s. Update size: s /= 2. Lookup (Recursive): 1. If self is Leaf, return voxel.asref(). 2. If self is Branch, calculate index: index = ((x \ge size) \text{ as usize}) \ll 0 \mid ((y \ge size) \text{ as usize}) \ll 1 \mid ((z \ge size) \text{ as usize}) \ll 2 3. Recursively call children[index].get(x % size, y % size, z % size, size / 2). Insertion: 1. If depth is 0, replace self with the new node. 2. If self is Branch, calculate index: index = ((x \ge size) \text{ as usize}) \ll 0 \mid ((y \ge size) \text{ as usize}) \ll 1 \mid ((z \ge size) \text{ as usize}) \ll 2 3. Recursively insert into children[index] with x \% size, y \% size, z \% size, size / 2, and depth - 1. 4. Leaf to Branch Conversion: If self is Leaf, clone the existing voxel. Replace self with a new Branch node where all 8 children are Leaves containing the cloned voxel. Then recursively call insert on the new Branch node with the same x, y, z, node, size, and depth. This ensures no data is lost during the split. GPU Representation (Crassin): Nodes are stored in linear GPU memory, grouped into 2 \times 2 \times 2 tiles. A single pointer stores all 8 children. Each node contains a pointer to a 3 \times 3 \times 3 voxel brick in texture memory. Voxel centers are located at node corners, not centers, allowing interpolated values to be computed inside a brick covering 2 \times 2 \times 2 nodes. This method uses less than half the memory of border-duplication methods. Neighbor pointers to spatially neighboring nodes and the parent are included. Construction: Rasterize the mesh three times along the three main axes with viewport resolution corresponding to the maximum octree subdivision level (e.g., 512 \times 512 for a 512^3 octree). Disable depth test to generate fragment shader threads for each potentially existing leaf node. Traverse the octree top-to-bottom and subdivide when needed. Write surface attributes (color, normal, material) to the leaf node. Parameters: Viewport resolution for rasterization corresponds to the maximum level of subdivision, typically 512 \times 512 pixels for a 512^3 octree. Pitfalls: Traversal involves overhead on conventional computers. Octree encoding achieves less data compression with grey-level data than with binary data. Maps poorly to GPU memory model; cannot benefit from GPU texture caching and filtering hardware in basic implementations. Empty nodes must be collapsed to gain memory. Stores filtered scene information (energy intensity, direction, occlusion, NDFs) with increasing precision by descending the hierarchy. Chosen for efficient indirect illumination. Direct memory representation using pointers for children and separate fields for leaf status and color. Chosen for simplicity. Real-time, high-fidelity novel-view synthesis using explicit, neural-free sparse voxels and a custom rasterizer. Chosen for real-time rendering without neural networks. Optimizes the dynamic update of the sparse voxel structure. Chosen for scenes with moving parts. Time Complexity: Lookup and insertion require tree traversal, which is less efficient than direct index access in 3D textures. Traversal overhead exists on conventional computers. Memory Complexity: Eliminates sparse memory by not storing empty volumes. Uses less than half the memory of border-duplication methods for the same sampling precision. Performance: Enables real-time frame rates for indirect illumination in complex scenes. Performance trade-off due to tree traversal. Strengths: Effective memory use for sparse volumes. Geometry-independent cost for indirect illumination. Limitations: Poor mapping to GPU memory model in basic implementations. Less compression for grey-level data. When to use: Scenes with large empty spaces or varying density where memory is a constraint. When not to use: When direct texture access performance is critical and memory is not. Origin: The concept extends the quadtree representation of 2D images to 3D. History: Crassin presented a GPU implementation in his paper on voxel cone tracing global illumination. name: Sparse Voxel Octree with Bricks
head: SVO with Bricks, SVOC, Sparse Voxel Octree with 3x3x3 Bricks, Voxel Cone Tracing Octree
body: Sparse Voxel Octree with Bricks is a hierarchical scene representation that stores filtered lighting information (energy intensity, direction, occlusion, and Normal Distribution Functions) in small 3x3x3 voxel volumes, called bricks, attached to octree nodes. It solves the memory inefficiency of inter-brick interpolation in sparse octrees by positioning voxel centers at node corners, allowing hardware trilinear interpolation to cover 2x2x2 nodes without expensive one-voxel borders. This method enables smooth, geometry-independent indirect illumination at real-time frame rates, differing from naive node representations by using texture volumes per node rather than single values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene mesh or volume data; viewing and lighting configuration. Output: A sparse voxel octree structure stored in linear GPU memory, with bricks stored in texture memory, enabling filtered scene queries with increasing precision. Data Structures: 1. Octree Node: Stored in linear GPU memory. Nodes are grouped into 2x2x2 tiles. Each tile shares a single pointer to its 2x2x2 children. Contains a pointer to a 3x3x3 brick in texture memory. Contains neighbor pointers (to spatially neighboring nodes and parent). Empty nodes are collapsed to save memory. 2. Brick: A 3x3x3 voxel volume stored in texture memory. Voxel centers are located at the corners of the node's bounding box, not the center. Approximates the scene section represented by the node. Allocated in a shared brick buffer. Numbered Steps: 1. Tree Construction: The root node represents the entire scene. Children represent an eighth of the parent's volume. This hierarchy allows querying filtered scene information (energy intensity, direction, occlusion, NDFs) with increasing precision by descending the tree. 2. Brick Assignment: Each non-empty node is assigned a 3x3x3 brick. The brick stores the filtered scene information for that spatial region. 3. Voxel Center Placement: To enable correct inter-brick interpolation using hardware trilinear filtering, the 3x3x3 brick is configured such that its voxel centers align with the corners of the node's bounding box. This ensures that interpolated values for any point within a 2x2x2 node group are computed entirely within a single brick covering those nodes. 4. Memory Optimization: Empty nodes are collapsed. This reduces memory occupancy but requires pointer-based traversal logic to handle the sparse nature of the tree. 5. Neighbor Pointers: Due to memory savings from the 3x3x3 brick design (using less than half the memory of border-based approaches), neighbor pointers are added to nodes. These pointers enable quick visits to spatially neighboring nodes and the parent. 6. Grouping: Nodes are grouped into 2x2x2 tiles. A single pointer stores the children for all 2x2x2 nodes in the tile, optimizing memory layout. Formulas: Memory Reduction: The 3x3x3 brick approach uses less than half the memory compared to adding a one-voxel boundary for the same sampling precision. Precision: Filtered scene information is queried with increasing precision by descending the tree hierarchy. Parameters: Brick Size: 3x3x3 voxels. Node Tile Size: 2x2x2 nodes. Max Octree Resolution: Typically 512x512 pixels for a 512^3 octree. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inter-brick Interpolation Continuity: The original approach [CNLE09] used a one-voxel border duplicating neighbors to ensure correct interpolation. This is expensive for small bricks. The 3x3x3 brick with corner-aligned voxel centers solves this by ensuring interpolated values are computed inside a brick covering 2x2x2 nodes. Empty Nodes: Collapsing empty nodes reduces memory but requires careful pointer-based traversal logic to avoid accessing invalid memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Node: def init(self): self.brickptr = None # Pointer to 3x3x3 brick in texture memory self.childrenptr = None # Single pointer to 2x2x2 children tile self.parentptr = None # Pointer to parent node self.neighborptrs = [] # Pointers to spatially neighboring nodes class Brick: def init(self): self.voxels = [[[[0.0 for in range(3)] for in range(3)] for in range(3)] for in range(3)] # 3x3x3 voxels stored in texture memory # Voxel centers are at node corners def queryscene(node, point): """ Query filtered scene information at a point. Uses hardware trilinear interpolation on the brick. """ if node is None: return None # Empty node collapsed # Determine which brick contains the point # The brick covers a 2x2x2 node group # Voxel centers are at node corners # Get brick data brick = node.brickptr # Perform trilinear interpolation using hardware texture fetch # The interpolation is guaranteed to be within the brick # because voxel centers are at node corners value = hardwaretrilinearinterpolate(brick, point) return value def buildoctree(scenedata): """ Build the sparse voxel octree with bricks. """ root = Node() root.brickptr = allocatebrick() # Recursive construction buildrecursive(root, scenedata, 0, 0) return root def buildrecursive(node, scenedata, depth, maxdepth): """ Recursively build the octree. """ if depth >= maxdepth: return # Check if region is empty if isempty(scenedata, node.boundingbox): node.childrenptr = None # Collapse empty node return # Allocate children tile (2x2x2 nodes) node.childrenptr = allocatetile() # For each child in the 2x2x2 tile for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): child = Node() child.parentptr = node child.brickptr = allocatebrick() # Add neighbor pointers addneighborpointers(child, node) # Recurse buildrecursive(child, scenedata, depth + 1, maxdepth) # Add to tile addtotile(node.childrenptr, i, j, k, child) def addneighborpointers(node, parent): """ Add pointers to spatially neighboring nodes and parent. """ node.parentptr = parent # Find and add neighbors # This requires traversing the tree to find adjacent nodes # Details omitted as per source pass Stores a single value per node. Simpler but lacks the spatial interpolation capabilities of bricks. Choose when memory is extremely constrained and interpolation is not needed. Naive Octree Node Representation A rasterization-based approach for indirect illumination. Faster for direct visibility but may lack the smoothness of cone tracing. Choose for real-time direct illumination. SVRaster Techniques for updating the octree structure efficiently. Choose when the scene changes frequently. Dynamic Update Optimization Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Uses less than half the memory of border-based approaches for the same sampling precision. Empty nodes are collapsed to save memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Handles large and complex scenes through adaptivity. Strengths: Smooth results without light undersampling or geometric LOD issues. Efficient memory usage for small bricks. Limitations: Requires pointer-based traversal logic due to collapsed empty nodes. When to Use: When smooth, geometry-independent indirect illumination is required at real-time frame rates. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained and interpolation is not needed (use Naive Octree Node Representation). The method originates from the paper "Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing" by [CNLE09] and subsequent work. It was developed to provide smooth results without missing information like light undersampling or geometric LOD, which are issues in path-tracing or photon mapping [Jen96]. The specific 3x3x3 brick design with corner-aligned voxel centers was proposed to solve the memory inefficiency of inter-brick interpolation in sparse octrees. name: Naive Octree Node Representation
head: Branch Tree Node, Direct Memory Octree Node, Octree Voxel Storage, Pointer-based Octree Node
body: The Naive Octree Node Representation is a direct memory layout for sparse voxel octrees where each non-leaf node explicitly stores an array of 8 child pointers, and leaf nodes store a single data value (typically a color or density index). It solves the problem of hierarchical spatial partitioning by providing a straightforward, pointer-chased traversal mechanism for voxel data. It is distinguished from brick-based or rasterized variants by its lack of structural compression; every internal node allocates memory for all 8 children, leading to high memory overhead for sparse or deep trees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel position (x, y, z), a depth level, and a value (e.g., color index) to insert or retrieve. Output: The octree structure with updated nodes, or the value associated with the voxel. Data Structures: The core structure is the OctreeNode. Two primary layouts are cited: 1. Standard Naive Layout: children: An array of 8 pointers to OctreeNode (or Node). isLeaf: A boolean flag indicating if the node is a leaf. value (or voxelColorIndex): If isLeaf is true, this stores the voxel data (e.g., uint32t or int8t index). If isLeaf is false, this field is unused or repurposed depending on implementation. centerX, centerY, centerZ: Coordinates defining the node's spatial extent. depth: The current depth in the octree hierarchy. 2. Template-Based Layout: Inherits from a base treenode. Contains std::array<basetype, 8> children. Memory Cost: On a 64-bit processor: 72 Bytes per node (8 pointers \times 8 bytes + 1 byte bool + 1 byte index + padding). On a 32-bit processor: 40 Bytes per node (8 pointers \times 4 bytes + 1 byte bool + 1 byte index + padding). Algorithm Steps: 1. Root Initialization: Set depth = 0. Set isLeaf = true. Set value = 0. Set centerX = centerY = centerZ = 0. 2. Non-Root Initialization: Set isLeaf = true. Set value = 0. Set childDepth = depth - 1. Set childSize = 1 << childDepth (i.e., 2^{depth-1}). Set centerX = x + childSize, centerY = y + childSize, centerZ = z + childSize. 3. Insertion (SetVoxel): Base Case: If depth == 0, set this->value = value and return. Leaf Optimization: If isLeaf is true and this->value == value, return (no change needed). Split: If isLeaf is true but the value differs (or needs expansion), call initChildren(). Copy this->value to all 8 new children. Set this->isLeaf = false. Child Selection: Compute childIndex using GetChildIndex(x, y, z). Recurse: Call children[childIndex].SetVoxel(x, y, z, value). Collapse: Call TryCollapse() to merge identical children back into a leaf if possible. 4. Retrieval (GetValue): If isLeaf, return value. Else, compute childIndex via GetChildIndex(x, y, z) and return children[childIndex].GetValue(x, y, z). 5. Child Initialization (initChildren): Set childDepth = depth - 1. Set childSize = 1 << childDepth. Allocate children = new OctreeNode[8]. Compute base coordinates: baseX = centerX - childSize, baseY = centerY - childSize, baseZ = centerZ - childSize. Initialize 8 children with offsets corresponding to the 8 octants: Indices 0-7 correspond to combinations of (0,0,0), (childSize,0,0), (0,childSize,0), (childSize,childSize,0), (0,0,childSize), (childSize,0,childSize), (0,childSize,childSize), (childSize,childSize,childSize) relative to the base. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class OctreeNode: def init(self, depth, x, y, z): self.depth = depth self.isLeaf = True self.value = 0 self.centerX = x self.centerY = y self.centerZ = z self.children = None def initchildren(self): # Calculate child dimensions childdepth = self.depth - 1 childsize = 1 << childdepth # Allocate 8 children self.children = [None] 8 self.isLeaf = False # Base coordinates for the current node's bounding box basex = self.centerX - childsize basey = self.centerY - childsize basez = self.centerZ - childsize # Initialize all 8 children # Order: x, y, z increments (0 to 7) for i in range(8): # Determine offset for this child index dx = (i & 1) childsize dy = (i & 2) childsize dz = (i & 4) childsize child = OctreeNode(childdepth, basex + dx, basey + dy, basez + dz) child.value = self.value # Inherit current leaf value self.children[i] = child def getchildindex(self, x, y, z): # Determine which octant (x,y,z) falls into relative to center # Assuming x, y, z are absolute coordinates and centerX/Y/Z is the midpoint # This logic depends on the specific coordinate system; # standard octree indexing usually checks against the center. idx = 0 if x >= self.centerX: idx |= 1 if y >= self.centerY: idx |= 2 if z >= self.centerZ: idx |= 4 return idx def setvoxel(self, x, y, z, value): # Base case: depth 0 if self.depth == 0: self.value = value return # If leaf and value is same, do nothing if self.isLeaf and self.value == value: return # If leaf and value differs, split if self.isLeaf: self.initchildren() # Recurse into child childidx = self.getchildindex(x, y, z) self.children[childidx].setvoxel(x, y, z, value) # Try to collapse children back into a leaf if they are all identical self.trycollapse() def getvalue(self, x, y, z): if self.isLeaf: return self.value childidx = self.getchildindex(x, y, z) return self.children[childidx].getvalue(x, y, z) def trycollapse(self): # Check if all 8 children are leaves with the same value if self.children is None: return firstchild = self.children[0] if not firstchild.isLeaf: return commonvalue = firstchild.value allsame = True for child in self.children[1:]: if not child.isLeaf or child.value != commonvalue: allsame = False break if allsame: self.value = commonvalue self.isLeaf = True self.children = None Parameters: Bit Mapping for Leaf Compression (Variant): In compressed variants, the highest position child represents the leftmost 8-bit strip, and the lowest position child represents the rightmost strip. Palette: Colors are often stored as indices into a palette of 256 entries, where 0 represents absence. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth 0: This is the base case. Attempting to recurse below depth 0 is prevented by the explicit depth == 0 check in SetVoxel. Undefined Helpers: GetChildIndex and TryCollapse are referenced but not fully defined in source snippets; implementation requires a specific child index mapping function and a post-insertion collapse check. Memory Overhead: For deep trees, the memory cost factor (mc) approaches 8 compared to a dense grid, as every internal node stores 8 pointers even if most children are null or identical. A compression technique that eliminates leaf nodes at the last level by packing their information (8 voxels) into a 64-bit integer in their parent node. It stores the color of the 8 voxels as an index into a palette of 256 entries, using 8 bits per voxel (where 0 represents absence). The 8 voxels are packed into a single int64t field (leafs) in the parent node. This reduces memory overhead by avoiding the allocation of leaf nodes, preventing the memory cost factor from approaching 8 for deep trees. The layout is struct Node { Node children[8]; int64t leafs; }. A specific implementation detail where the root node is stored at the end of a contiguous nodes vector, accessed via &nodes.back(). The Octree class stores global bounds (min, max, size, gridlength) and statistics (nnodes, ndata) alongside a pointer to voxel data and the vector of nodes. The default constructor initializes min to (0,0,0), max to (1,1,1), size to (1,1,1), and gridlength to 128. Time Complexity: Insertion and retrieval are O(\log N) where N is the number of voxels, assuming a balanced tree. Traversal requires pointer chasing for every level of depth. Memory Complexity: O(N) nodes, but with a high constant factor. Each internal node consumes 72 bytes (64-bit) or 40 bytes (32-bit). For sparse data, this is significantly less than a dense grid, but for dense data, the overhead of pointers makes it less efficient than brick-based or compressed representations. Strengths: Simple implementation; direct mapping of spatial hierarchy; easy to debug and visualize. Limitations: High memory overhead due to explicit child pointers; poor cache locality due to pointer chasing; significant waste if many children are null or identical. When to Use: Small to medium-sized sparse voxel datasets where implementation simplicity is prioritized over memory efficiency. When Not to Use: Large-scale scenes requiring real-time performance with limited memory, or dense voxel data where brick-based or compressed representations are superior. The naive octree node representation is a foundational concept in spatial data structures, originating from general computer science literature on octrees. It is widely used in early implementations of sparse voxel octrees for global illumination and terrain generation. The specific memory cost calculations (72/40 bytes) and the bitmask compression variant are detailed in an unofficial study on SVO compression. The template-based C++ implementation is found in the planaria/dmc repository. The recursive insertion/retrieval logic is exemplified in terrain generation projects. The contiguous vector storage variant is seen in CPU voxel raycasting implementations.
