name: SVRaster
head: Sparse Voxels Rasterization
body: SVRaster is a real-time, high-fidelity novel-view synthesis framework that renders adaptive sparse voxels using a custom rasterizer, avoiding neural networks, 3D Gaussians, and sparse-point priors. It distinguishes itself from Gaussian splatting by partitioning 3D space into disjoint voxels and using ray direction-dependent Morton ordering to ensure correct depth sorting, thereby eliminating the popping artifacts common in Gaussian-based methods. Unlike previous neural-free voxel models, it achieves over 4 dB PSNR improvement and more than 10x FPS speedup while maintaining compatibility with grid-based 3D processing techniques like Volume Fusion and Marching Cubes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of multi-view images; camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics); maximum octree level L; number of integration samples K. Output: Rendered color images for novel views. Data Structures: Voxels are stored in a 1D array containing only leaf nodes of an octree-style spatial partition. No parent-child pointers or linear octree structures are maintained. Each voxel is defined by: 1. Index: v = \{i, j, k\} \in [0, \dots, 2^{L-1}]^3. 2. Level: l \in [1, L] (where l=0 is the unused root). 3. Geometry Parameters: v{geo} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2\times2}, representing density values at the 8 corners of the voxel. Adjacent voxals share these corner values to ensure continuous density fields. 4. Appearance Parameters: Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients encoding view-dependent color. Parameters: L: Maximum level of detail. Set to 16 in the source, defining a maximum representational grid resolution of (2^{16})^3 = 65536^3. This is a limit, not a dense allocation. K: Number of evenly spaced samples inside the ray-voxel intersection segment for volume integration. Octree Size \mathbf{w}s \in \mathbb{R}^3 and Center \mathbf{w}c \in \mathbb{R}^3 in world space. Algorithm Steps: 1. Voxel Size and Center Calculation: For a voxel with index v and level l, compute its size \mathbf{v}s and center \mathbf{v}c: \mathbf{v}s = \mathbf{w}s \cdot 2^{-l} \mathbf{v}c = \mathbf{w}c - 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{w}s + \mathbf{v}s \cdot (2v + 1) (Note: The source formula \mathbf{v}c = \mathbf{w}c - 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{w}s + \mathbf{v}s \cdot \mathbf{v}c in the notes appears to contain a typo where \mathbf{v}c is on both sides. The standard octree center calculation for index v at level l relative to size \mathbf{v}s is \mathbf{w}c - 0.5\mathbf{w}s + \mathbf{v}s(2v+1). The source text says "\mathbf{v}s \cdot \mathbf{v}c" but defines \mathbf{v}c as derived from index. We interpret \mathbf{v}c in the source formula as the normalized index vector 2v+1 or similar. Given the ambiguity, we stick to the explicit variables defined: \mathbf{v}s is size, \mathbf{v}c is center. The source equation (2) is: \mathbf{v}s = \mathbf{w}s \cdot \mathbf{v}s^{-1} (likely 2^{-l}) and \mathbf{v}c = \mathbf{w}c - 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{w}s + \mathbf{v}s \cdot \mathbf{v}c (likely \mathbf{v}c on RHS is the integer index vector). To be implementable, we define the normalized position. Let u = 2v + 1. Then \mathbf{v}c = \mathbf{w}c - 0.5 \mathbf{w}s + \mathbf{v}s u.) Correction based on strict source adherence: The source states: \mathbf{v}s = \mathbf{w}s \cdot \mathbf{v}s^{-1} and \mathbf{v}c = \mathbf{w}c - 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{w}s + \mathbf{v}s \cdot \mathbf{v}c. This is recursive. However, standard interpretation of such notation in this context (and the variable definition "derived from index v") implies \mathbf{v}c on the RHS is the normalized coordinate. We will use the standard octree center formula which matches the intent: \mathbf{v}c = \mathbf{w}c - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{w}s + \mathbf{v}s (2v + 1). 2. Morton Code Mapping: Map the voxel grid index v to a Morton code using bit-interleaving operations. This is typically done in low-level CUDA for performance. 3. Adaptive Allocation (Training Phase): Pruning: Remove voxels whose maximum contribution across training views is below a threshold. Subdivision: Subdivide voxels with high loss-related priority. Suppression: Suppress subdivision if training views sample the voxel too sparsely. 4. Rasterization Preprocessing: Project voxel corners into the image space. Assign each voxel to the image tiles it covers. Preprocess density, color, and normal data for each voxel. 5. Sorting: Sort voxels per tile using ray direction-dependent Morton ordering. The Morton order is remapped based on the signs of the viewing ray's direction components. There are 8 such sign cases in 3D. This ensures voxels are rendered in the correct depth order, preventing smaller voxels from being incorrectly occluded by larger ones. 6. Density and Alpha Computation: Density Field: Modeled as trilinearly varying inside the voxel, interpolated from the 8 shared corner values v{geo}. Activation: Apply exponential-linear activation to ensure non-negative density: \text{exp\linear}(x) = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x > 1.1 \\ \exp\left(\frac{x}{1.1} - 1 + \ln 1.1\right) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Alpha Value: Evenly sample K points inside the ray-voxel intersection segment. Compute volume integration to determine the alpha contribution \alphai of the voxel. Color: Approximate the color field as constant within the voxel for efficiency, using the SH coefficients evaluated at the ray direction. 7. Compositing: Composite voxels front-to-back using the standard alpha blending equation: C = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \cdot \alphai \cdot ci Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci \in [0,1]^3 is the view-dependent color, \alphai \in [0,1] is the alpha, and Ti is the transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def exponentiallinear(x): """ Exponential-linear activation for non-negative density. """ # x is a scalar or array if x > 1.1: return x else: return math.exp(x / 1.1 - 1 + math.log(1.1)) def trilinearinterpolate(corners, t): """ Trilinearly interpolate density from 8 corners at parameter t (0 to 1). corners: array of shape (8,) representing density at corners. t: interpolation parameter along the ray segment inside the voxel. Note: The exact mapping of 't' to the 8 corners requires the ray direction and voxel geometry. This is a placeholder for the specific trilinear kernel. """ # Implementation detail: Map t to (u,v,w) in [0,1]^3 based on ray direction # and voxel bounds. Then perform trilinear interpolation. # For the purpose of this article, we assume a helper exists or is implemented # based on the ray-voxel intersection segment. pass def rendervoxelray(rayorigin, raydirection, voxel, K=16): """ Compute alpha and color contribution of a single voxel for a given ray. """ # 1. Compute intersection segment of ray and voxel # Returns tnear, tfar in world space tnear, tfar = computerayvoxelintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, voxel) if tnear is None: return 0.0, np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # 2. Sample K points inside the segment # Evenly sample K points tsamples = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, K) # 3. Compute density and color at samples # Density is trilinearly interpolated from 8 corners # Color is constant (SH evaluated at ray direction) # Get corner densities cornerdensities = voxel.corners # Shape (8,) # Get SH coefficients for color shcoeffs = voxel.shcoeffs color = evaluatesh(shcoeffs, raydirection) alphasum = 0.0 densitysum = 0.0 for t in tsamples: # Interpolate density at t # Note: t must be normalized to the voxel's local coordinate system # for trilinear interpolation. localt = normalizetovoxel(t, voxel) density = trilinearinterpolate(cornerdensities, localt) # Apply activation density = exponentiallinear(density) # Accumulate for volume integration (simplified Riemann sum) # Delta t in world space dt = (tfar - tnear) / K alphasum += density dt # Convert accumulated density to alpha (approximation) # Standard volume rendering alpha = 1 - exp(-density thickness) # Or simply alpha = min(1.0, alphasum) depending on specific implementation # The source says "compute volume integration for its alpha value contribution" # We assume the result is mapped to [0,1] alpha = min(1.0, alphasum) return alpha, color def rendertile(tilevoxels, raydirection, K=16): """ Render a tile by sorting and compositing voxels. """ # 1. Sort voxels using ray direction-dependent Morton ordering # Morton code depends on voxel index # Order depends on signs of raydirection components sortedvoxels = sortbymortonorder(tilevoxels, raydirection) # 2. Composite front-to-back transmittance = 1.0 color = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) for voxel in sortedvoxels: alpha, c = rendervoxelray(rayorigin, raydirection, voxel, K) # Alpha composition contribution = transmittance alpha c color += contribution transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break return color def computemortonordersigndependent(voxelmortoncode, raydirection): """ Remap Morton order based on ray direction signs. There are 8 sign cases. """ sx = 1 if raydirection.x >= 0 else -1 sy = 1 if raydirection.y >= 0 else -1 sz = 1 if raydirection.z >= 0 else -1 # The specific remapping logic is described as "remaps Morton order... # according to the signs". The exact permutation table is not provided # in the text, but it ensures correct depth sorting. # Implementation requires the specific permutation table from the paper's # supplementary materials or code. return voxelmortoncode # Placeholder for the remapped key Uses brick-based compression for memory efficiency. SVRaster uses a flat 1D array of leaves, trading compression for simpler rasterization logic. Stores full octree nodes. SVRaster stores only leaves, reducing overhead. Focuses on updating the structure during training. SVRaster's adaptive allocation is a specific instance of this, focusing on pruning and subdivision based on loss. Time Complexity: Rendering is rasterization-based, allowing for real-time frame rates. The paper reports 121 FPS on a 3090 Ti for Mip-NeRF360 scenes, comparable to 3DGS (131 FPS). Memory Complexity: Uses more GPU memory and produces larger models than 3DGS. The maximum representational resolution is 65536^3, but actual memory usage depends on the number of active leaf voxels. Performance: On Mip-NeRF360, SVRaster achieves LPIPS 0.219 vs 0.257 for 3DGS, and PSNR 27.33 vs 27.45 dB. On Tanks&Temples, it shows brightness boundaries and floaters due to exposure variation, with worse PSNR and FPS than 3DGS, though LPIPS is better. Strengths: Avoids popping artifacts; compatible with grid-based 3D processing (Volume Fusion, Marching Cubes); neural-free; high fidelity. Limitations: Sensitive to exposure variation in training data; higher memory usage than 3DGS; requires custom rasterizer. SVRaster was proposed by NVIDIA Research (NVlabs) and presented at CVPR 2025. It builds on the concept of sparse voxel octrees and Plenoxels, aiming to combine the efficiency of rasterization with the explicit nature of voxel representations, avoiding the limitations of Gaussian splatting (popping) and neural fields (training complexity). The code is available at github.com/NVlabs/svraster. Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01509, fetched 2026-10-26 Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity..., https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2412.04459, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Dynamic Update Optimization
head: Dynamic Voxel Cone Tracing Optimization
body: Dynamic Update Optimization is a set of heuristics and data structure modifications applied to Voxel Cone Tracing to accelerate indirect illumination calculations in scenes containing both static and dynamic geometry. It solves the performance bottleneck of re-voxelizing and re-computing lighting for the entire scene every frame by isolating dynamic updates to affected regions. It sets itself apart from static-only voxelization by maintaining a hybrid state where static geometry is pre-computed and cached, while dynamic geometry is processed with relaxed accuracy constraints and targeted re-filtering. Inputs: Scene geometry (static and dynamic meshes). Camera position, orientation, field of view (FOV), and near/far planes. Maximum cone tracing distance (D{max}). Voxel resolution (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 256). Screen resolution (W \times H). Outputs: Updated Sparse Voxel Octree (SVo) containing static and dynamic voxel data. Indirect lighting buffer (screen-space). The method modifies the standard SVo node structure to support dynamic updates: 1. Octree Node Buffer: Stores voxel data. Dynamic voxel fragments are appended to the end of this buffer rather than overwriting existing static nodes. 2. Node Flags: A bit flag stored in each node to identify if it is static or dynamic. Static nodes are never overwritten; dynamic nodes are appended. 3. Voxel Data Layout: Static Nodes: Store full attributes (diffuse color, average normal, etc.). Dynamic Nodes: Store a 1-byte counter and the normal vector. Diffuse color is computed or approximated differently (see Step 2). 4. Neighbor Offsets: Pointers/indices linking nodes to their neighbors. Static nodes pointing to dynamic neighbors require reset/update when dynamic data changes. 5. Affected Node Buffer: A queue used to store indices of static nodes that need re-filtering due to changes in adjacent dynamic voxels. 1. Initialization (Static Geometry): Perform the standard 4 steps of voxel cone tracing (voxelization, building octree, filtering, cone tracing) for all static geometry. Mark these nodes as static using the bit flag. Store them in the octree. 2. Per-Frame Dynamic Voxelization: Voxelize only dynamic objects. For each dynamic fragment, update the octree node's normal and diffuse attributes using InterlockedMax() instead of atomic averaging. Normal: Use InterlockedMax() on the normal vector components. This is faster than averaging but reduces lighting quality for small voxel volumes (e.g., 256^3), causing artifacts where light reflects incorrectly compared to average normals. To mitigate, InterlockedMax() is used only for dynamic geometry normals; static geometry retains average normal calculation. Diffuse: Use InterlockedMax() for diffuse color as well. Counter: Maintain a 1-byte counter in the voxel data to track how many fragments contributed to the node (necessary because InterlockedMax does not provide an average count). Append dynamic voxel fragments to the end of the octree node buffer. 3. View-Frustum Culling for Direct Lighting Injection: When injecting direct lighting into the octree, perform view-frustum culling to avoid filtering light far from the camera. Calculate an Extended Frustum: Move the camera backward slightly. Increase the far plane. Keep the same FOV. The extended distance is calculated as: D{ext} = D{max} + \text{filtered voxel size}. Only voxels within this extended frustum are processed for direct lighting injection. 4. Half-Resolution Cone Tracing with Edge Correction: Perform the initial cone tracing pass at half screen resolution (W/2 \times H/2). Artifact Handling: Upscaling to full resolution causes visible artifacts, especially at geometry edges. Edge Detection: Use a depth buffer edge detection filter to identify pixels at geometry boundaries. Re-tracing: Perform cone tracing at full resolution only for these detected edge pixels. Fallback: If re-tracing is too expensive, blur the edge pixels by averaging with neighbors (lower quality, higher performance). 5. Static Node Re-filtering: Identify static octree nodes affected by dynamic voxels from the previous and current frames. Dispatch threads for all nodes to check for changes and queue affected node indices into the Affected Node Buffer. Reset static octree node neighbor offsets that point to dynamic nodes. Re-filter only the static nodes listed in the buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamicupdateoptimization(scene, camera, dt): # Step 1: Initialization (One-time or when static geometry changes) if scene.needsinitialization: staticgeometry = scene.getstaticgeometry() octree = buildoctree(staticgeometry) marknodesstatic(octree) scene.needsinitialization = False # Step 2: Dynamic Voxelization dynamicgeometry = scene.getdynamicgeometry() dynamicfragments = voxelize(dynamicgeometry) for fragment in dynamicfragments: node = octree.getorcreatenode(fragment.position) # Use InterlockedMax for speed, accepting quality loss for dynamic normals node.normal = interlockedmax(node.normal, fragment.normal) node.diffuse = interlockedmax(node.diffuse, fragment.color) node.counter += 1 # Append to end of buffer if new if node.isnew: octree.appendtodynamicbuffer(node) # Step 3: View-Frustum Culling for Direct Lighting extendedfar = camera.farplane + (maxconetracingdistance + voxelsize) extendedfrustum = createextendedfrustum(camera, extendedfar) directlightingbuffer = computedirectlighting(octree, extendedfrustum) # Step 4: Cone Tracing (Half Resolution + Edge Correction) halfresbuffer = conetrace(octree, camera, resolution=(screenw/2, screenh/2)) # Detect edges using depth buffer edgemask = detectedges(camera.depthbuffer) # Re-trace edges at full resolution fullresbuffer = halfresbuffer.upsample(bilinear=True) edgepixels = getpixelindices(edgemask) for idx in edgepixels: fullresbuffer[idx] = conetracepixel(octree, camera, idx, resolution=(screenw, screenh)) # Step 5: Static Node Re-filtering affectednodes = findaffectedstaticnodes(octree, dynamicfragments) for node in affectednodes: resetnodeneighboroffsets(node) refilternode(node) return fullresbuffer Voxel Resolution: 256 \times 256 \times 256. Cone Tracing Resolution: Half screen resolution (W/2 \times H/2). Extended Frustum Distance: D{max} + \text{voxel size}. Normal Update Method: InterlockedMax for dynamic, Average for static. Lighting Artifacts: Using InterlockedMax() for normals in small voxels causes incorrect light reflection compared to average normals. Upscaling Artifacts: Half-resolution cone tracing creates visible artifacts at geometry edges when upscaled. Performance Drop: Re-tracing all edge pixels at full resolution can significantly drop frame rate. Far Objects: Limiting cone tracing distance may cause loss of sampling for far objects like the sky. Uses brick-based storage for better cache locality; choose when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. Simple node structure without dynamic optimization; choose for static scenes or simpler implementations. Rasterization-based voxelization; choose when GPU rasterization is preferred over ray-based voxelization. Time Complexity: Reduced per-frame cost for dynamic scenes. Static geometry is processed once. Dynamic updates are proportional to the number of dynamic objects and affected nodes. Memory Complexity: Increased due to appending dynamic fragments and storing counters/flags. Measured Performance: Faster than full re-voxelization. Half-resolution cone tracing with edge correction is faster than full-resolution cone tracing but may have quality trade-offs. Strengths: Real-time performance for dynamic scenes; efficient use of GPU parallelism. Limitations: Quality degradation from InterlockedMax normals and half-resolution upsampling; artifacts at geometry edges. When to Use: Real-time applications with dynamic objects and indirect lighting requirements. When Not to Use: Static scenes (use standard voxelization); high-quality offline rendering (use full-resolution cone tracing). The method was described by Simon Green in his blog post "Implementing Voxel Cone Tracing" in January 2013. It was developed as part of an experimental implementation of voxel cone tracing to achieve real-time indirect illumination. The techniques were derived from practical experience optimizing the algorithm for dynamic scenes. Implementing Voxel Cone Tracing, http://simonstechblog.blogspot.com/2013/01/implementing-voxel-cone-tracing.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Chunked Voxel Map Serialization with Visfaces
head: Visface mask computation, libvxl_kv6_block serialization
body: This method serializes a chunked voxel map into a compact file format by iterating through the spatial grid and computing a 6-bit visibility face mask (visfaces) for each block based on its immediate solid neighbors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A libvxlmap structure containing geometry data, width, height, and depth dimensions. Output: A serialized file containing a stream of libvxlkv6block structures. Data Structures: The core output unit is struct libvxlkv6block: color: uint32t, masked to 24 bits (0xFFFFFF). z: Extracted from the block's position key. normal: Fixed to 0. visfaces: uint8t, a 6-bit mask where bits correspond to neighbor directions: Bit 0 (0x01): +x face visible. Bit 1 (0x02): -x face visible. Bit 2 (0x04): +y face visible. Bit 3 (0x08): -y face visible. Bit 4 (0x10): +z face visible. Bit 5 (0x20): -z face visible. Steps: 1. Iterate y from 0 to map->height and x from 0 to map->width. 2. Retrieve the chunk at position (x, y) using chunkfposition(map, x, y). 3. Iterate through the blocks within the chunk. 4. Verify the block's x-coordinate matches the current loop variable x using keygetx(next->position) == x. 5. Create a libvxlkv6block instance. 6. Mask the block's color to 24 bits. 7. Extract the z coordinate using keygetz. 8. Set the normal field to 0. 9. Compute the visfaces mask by checking the 6 immediate neighbors (±x, ±y, ±z) using libvxlmapissolid. If a neighbor is not solid, the corresponding bit is set. 10. Write the block to the output file. 11. Increment x offset and xy offset counters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def serializechunkedmap(map, file): # Helper to retrieve chunk at x,y def getchunkat(m, cx, cy): return m.chunks[cy m.chunkwidth + cx] # Helper to extract coordinates from packed position key def getblockx(pos): return pos & 0xFF def getblockz(pos): return (pos >> 16) & 0xFF # Helper to check if a voxel is solid def issolid(m, x, y, z): if not (0 <= x < m.width and 0 <= y < m.height and 0 <= z < m.depth): return False return m.geometry[(z m.width + y) m.width + x] xoffset = 0 xyoffset = 0 for y in range(map.height): for x in range(map.width): chunk = getchunkat(map, x, y) for block in chunk.blocks: if getblockx(block.position) != x: continue kv6 = Kv6Block() kv6.color = block.color & 0xFFFFFF kv6.z = getblockz(block.position) kv6.normal = 0 mask = 0 if not issolid(map, x + 1, y, kv6.z): mask |= 0x01 if not issolid(map, x - 1, y, kv6.z): mask |= 0x02 if not issolid(map, x, y + 1, kv6.z): mask |= 0x04 if not issolid(map, x, y - 1, kv6.z): mask |= 0x08 if not issolid(map, x, y, kv6.z + 1): mask |= 0x10 if not issolid(map, x, y, kv6.z - 1): mask |= 0x20 kv6.visfaces = mask file.write(kv6.serialize()) xoffset += 1 xyoffset += 1 Parameters: LIBVXLCHUNKSIZE: 16 (internal chunk dimension). Edge Cases: The visfaces mask only tracks immediate 6-connected neighbors. Diagonal or non-adjacent occlusion is not computed. Boundary checks are required when accessing neighbors at x=0, x=width, etc., to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Retrieves the color of a voxel at a specific (x, y, z) coordinate within a chunked voxel map. It solves the problem of efficient sparse voxel access by combining global geometry culling with binary search within sorted block arrays. It is distinguished from its sibling Chunked Voxel Map Serialization with Visfaces by its read-only access pattern and lack of visibility face computation, focusing instead on direct coordinate-to-color mapping. Memory Complexity: Depends on the chunk size and map dimensions. The geometry array size is calculated as (map->width map->height map->depth + (sizeof(sizet) 8 - 1)) / (sizeof(sizet) 8) sizeof(sizet). This method is part of the libvxl library, an unofficial implementation for reading and writing.vxl maps used in the game 'Ace of Spades' (Voxel Space). xtreme8000/libvxl, https://github.com/xtreme8000/libvxl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Map Lookup
body: Retrieves the color of a voxel at a specific (x, y, z) coordinate within a chunked voxel map. It solves the problem of efficient sparse voxel access by combining global geometry culling with binary search within sorted block arrays. It is distinguished from its sibling Chunked Voxel Map Serialization with Visfaces by its read-only access pattern and lack of visibility face computation, focusing instead on direct coordinate-to-color mapping. Input: A pointer to a libvxlmap structure and integer coordinates (x, y, z). Output: A 32-bit color value (uint32t). Returns 0 if the map is null, coordinates are out of bounds, or the global geometry bitfield indicates the position is empty. Returns DEFAULTCOLOR if the position is solid but no specific block color is found. The method uses the following structures defined in the source: struct libvxlmap: width, height, depth: Map dimensions. chunks: Pointer to an array of libvxlchunk. geometry: Pointer to an array of sizet bits representing solid/empty status. streamed: Unused in lookup. struct libvxlchunk: blocks: Pointer to an array of libvxlblock. length: Total capacity of the blocks array. index: Number of valid blocks in the array. struct libvxlblock: position: 32-bit key encoding (x, y, z). color: 32-bit color value. libvxlspan and libvxlkv6 structures are defined in the source but not used in this lookup method. Coordinates are mapped to a unique 32-bit integer key using the macro poskey(x, y, z): \text{key} = (y \ll 20) \mid (x \ll 8) \mid z This layout uses 12 bits for x (bits 8–19), 12 bits for y (bits 20–31), and 8 bits for z (bits 0–7). The maximum coordinate values are therefore x, y < 4096 and z < 256. 1. Null Check: If the map pointer is null, return 0. 2. Bounds Check: Verify 0 \le x < \text{width}, 0 \le y < \text{height}, and 0 \le z < \text{depth}. If any check fails, return 0. 3. Geometry Check: Call libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, z) to check the global geometry bitfield. If the bit at the calculated offset is 0, the position is empty; return 0. 4. Chunk Selection: Calculate the chunk index using chunkfposition(x, y, z) to map global coordinates to the specific chunk containing the voxel. Retrieve the chunk pointer from map->chunks. 5. Binary Search: Perform a binary search on chunk->blocks to find a block where block.position == poskey(x, y, z). The comparison function compares the position field of libvxlblock structures against the target key. 6. Result: If a matching block is found, return block.color. If no matching block is found, return DEFAULTCOLOR(x, y, z), defined as 0x674028. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. BITWIDTH = 64 # Standard sizet bit width CHUNKSIZE = 16 # Standard chunk dimension def chunkfposition(map, x, y, z): # Exact chunk indexing formula not provided in sources; assumes standard 2D chunk layout numchunksx = (map.width + CHUNKSIZE - 1) // CHUNKSIZE chunkidx = (y // CHUNKSIZE) numchunksx + (x // CHUNKSIZE) if chunkidx < len(map.chunks): return map.chunks[chunkidx] return None def libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, z): offset = z + (x + y map.width) map.depth bitindex = offset // BITWIDTH bitmask = 1 << (offset % BITWIDTH) if bitindex >= len(map.geometry): return False return (map.geometry[bitindex] & bitmask) != 0 def poskey(x, y, z): return ((y << 20) | (x << 8) | z) def libvxlmapget(map, x, y, z): if map is None: return 0 if x < 0 or x >= map.width or y < 0 or y >= map.height or z < 0 or z >= map.depth: return 0 if not libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, z): return 0 chunk = chunkfposition(map, x, y, z) if chunk is None: return 0 targetkey = poskey(x, y, z) low = 0 high = chunk.index - 1 foundblock = None while low <= high: mid = (low + high) // 2 midblock = chunk.blocks[mid] if midblock.position == targetkey: foundblock = midblock break elif midblock.position < targetkey: low = mid + 1 else: high = mid - 1 if foundblock is not None: return foundblock.color return 0x674028 DEFAULTCOLOR: If a voxel is marked solid in the geometry bitfield but no block exists in the chunk's block array, 0x674028 is returned. This can cause visual artifacts if the background is expected to be transparent or black. Precision: The key format limits z to 8 bits (0-255). If z \ge 256, the key generation will overflow or wrap, leading to incorrect lookups or collisions. Empty Chunks: If chunk->index is 0, the binary search loop will not execute, and DEFAULTCOLOR will be returned. Copies a map's geometry bitfield and a specific chunk's block array into a libvxlchunkcopy structure for isolated access. It is used when a subset of the map needs to be processed independently without modifying the original map. It is chosen when temporary, self-contained access to a chunk's data is required. It differs from the main lookup by creating a new structure rather than reading directly from the map. Steps: 1. Check bounds for x, y. 2. Calculate geometry size: sg = \lceil \frac{\text{width} \times \text{height} \times \text{depth}}{8 \times \text{sizeof(sizet)}} \rceil \times \text{sizeof(sizet)}. 3. Allocate and copy map->geometry into copy->geometry. 4. Get the chunk via chunkfposition. 5. Allocate copy->blockssorted of size c->index sizeof(struct libvxlblock). 6. Copy c->blocks into copy->blockssorted. 7. Set copy->width, copy->height, copy->depth. Helper: libvxlcopychunkissolid: 1. If copy is null or coordinates out of bounds, return true. 2. Calculate offset: z + (x + y \times \text{copy->width}) \times \text{copy->depth}. 3. Return (copy->geometry[offset / (sizeof(sizet) 8)] & ((sizet)1 << (offset % (sizeof(sizet) 8)))) != 0. Finds the highest solid voxel at a given (x, y) column and returns its color and z-coordinate. It is used for surface detection or sky visibility checks. It differs from standard lookup by iterating or searching for the maximum z rather than a specific coordinate. Pitfall: Uses libvxlchunkgequalblock which likely performs a lower-bound search for z \ge 0. If no block exists, assertions may trigger. Time Complexity: O(\log N) where N is the number of blocks in the chunk. The geometry check is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the main lookup. Chunk Copy requires O(N) space for the copy structure. Strengths: Efficient sparse access; global geometry culling avoids unnecessary chunk searches for empty space. Limitations: Limited z range (8 bits); DEFAULTCOLOR artifact if blocks are missing but geometry is set; not suitable for dense grids where linear access might be faster. The method is part of the libvxl library for storing and accessing voxel data in a chunked format. It is designed to work with the serialization format described in Chunked Voxel Map Serialization with Visfaces. xtreme8000/libvxl, https://github.com/xtreme8000/libvxl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Span-based Column Encoding
head: VXL span serialization
body: Span-based Column Encoding encodes a single (x,y) column of a sparse voxel map into a sequence of libvxlspan structures containing air runs, top color runs, and bottom color runs. It solves the problem of efficiently serializing sparse voxel data by reducing the storage of empty space and surface boundaries to compact run-length encoded structures. Inputs: A libvxlmap structure containing width, height, depth, and sparse block storage; coordinates (x,y) defining the column to encode. Outputs: A sequence of libvxlspan structures written to a buffer. Data Structures: libvxlspan: Contains fields colorstart, colorend, airstart, length, and offset. libvxlblock: Contains position (packed key) and color (uint32t). position key: Packed integer where z is extracted via keygetz() and the rest via keydiscardz(). Steps: 1. Initialize firstrun = true, get starting z from the first block in the chunk. 2. Determine topstart: if libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, z) is true, topstart = z, else topstart = keygetz(firstblock->position). 3. Call findsuccessivesurface to find topend and lastsurfaceblock. 4. Determine bottomstart: if topend == map->depth or !libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, topend), bottomstart = topend. Else if lastsurfaceblock points to a block at z=0, bottomstart = keygetz(lastsurfaceblock->position). 5. Write desc->colorstart = topstart, desc->colorend = topend - 1, desc->airstart = firstrun ? 0: z. Advance offset. 6. Write top colors: loop k from topstart to topend, write (block->color & 0xFFFFFF) | 0x7F000000. Advance offset. 7. If bottomend < map->depth, set desc->length = 1 + topend - topstart + bottomend - bottomstart, write bottom colors, and set z = bottomend. Else set desc->length = 1 + topend - topstart and z = bottomstart. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodecolumn(map, x, y): firstrun = True chunk = getchunk(map, x, y) if chunk.index == 0: return [] firstblock = getgequalblock(chunk, x, y, 0) z = keygetz(firstblock.position) if libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, z): topstart = z else: topstart = keygetz(firstblock.position) topend = topstart lastsurfaceblock = None while topend < map.depth and libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, topend): lastsurfaceblock = getblockat(map, x, y, topend) topend += 1 if topend == map.depth or not libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, topend): bottomstart = topend elif lastsurfaceblock and keygetz(lastsurfaceblock.position) == 0: bottomstart = keygetz(lastsurfaceblock.position) else: bottomstart = topend desc = libvxlspan() desc.colorstart = topstart desc.colorend = topend - 1 desc.airstart = 0 if firstrun else z desc.offset = 0 spans = [desc] for k in range(topstart, topend): block = getblockat(map, x, y, k) if block: colors.append((block.color & 0xFFFFFF) | 0x7F000000) # Determine bottomend bottomend = bottomstart while bottomend < map.depth and libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, bottomend): bottomend += 1 if bottomend < map.depth: desc.length = 1 + (topend - topstart) + (bottomend - bottomstart) for k in range(bottomstart, bottomend): block = getblockat(map, x, y, k) if block: colors.append(block.color) z = bottomend else: desc.length = 1 + (topend - topstart) z = bottomstart return spans, colors class libvxlspan: colorstart = 0; colorend = 0; airstart = 0; length = 0; offset = 0 class libvxlblock: position = 0; color = 0 def poskey(x, y, z): return (x << 24) | (y << 16) | z def keygetz(pos): return pos & 0xFFFF def libvxlgeometryget(map, x, y, z): return map.geometry.get((x, y, z), False) def getchunk(map, x, y): return map.chunks[y map.width + x] def getgequalblock(chunk, x, y, z): target = poskey(x, y, z) for b in chunk.blocks: if b.position >= target: return b return None def getblockat(map, x, y, z): chunk = getchunk(map, x, y) for b in chunk.blocks: if b.position == poskey(x, y, z): return b return None colors = [] Parameters: map->depth: Total height of the voxel map. 0x7F000000: Alpha mask for surface blocks. Edge Cases: Empty Column: If no blocks exist in the chunk, the function returns an empty list. Boundary Conditions: topend can equal map->depth. bottomstart logic depends on whether the surface touches the bottom (z=0) or ends at the top. Precision: Color packing uses bitwise AND with 0xFFFFFF to mask RGB, preserving only the lower 24 bits. Voxel Map Streaming is a sequential I/O method for dense voxel maps that outputs fixed-size binary chunks by iterating over (x,y) columns. It solves the problem of efficient bulk transfer of voxel data by buffering encoded columns into a sliding window, allowing consumers to read data in predictable, fixed-size blocks without managing individual column boundaries. It differs from direct column access by abstracting the underlying Span-based Column Encoding into a continuous byte stream with internal buffering and chunking logic. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of blocks in the column, as it iterates through surface blocks to determine runs. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of runs in the column. Strengths: Efficiently compresses sparse columns by ignoring large air gaps. Explicitly handles surface colors with alpha masking. Limitations: Requires random access to blocks within a column to determine geometry and colors. Not suitable for horizontal traversal without re-encoding. When to Use: When serializing voxel maps for storage or network transmission where column-wise access is natural. When Not to Use: When horizontal slicing or face-based mesh generation is required. Span-based Column Encoding is part of the libvxl library, an implementation of the Voxel Space map format used in the game Ace of Spades. It was developed by xtreme8000 to provide an efficient internal representation for sparse voxel data. The method derives from the.vxl file format specifications, focusing on compact serialization of columnar data. xtreme8000/libvxl, https://github.com/xtreme8000/libvxl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Map Streaming
head: chunked serialization
body: Voxel Map Streaming is a sequential I/O method for dense voxel maps that iterates over (x,y) coordinates, encodes columns into a buffer, and outputs fixed-size chunks for sequential reading. It builds on Span-based Column Encoding to abstract variable-length columns into a continuous byte stream with internal buffering and chunking logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A libvxlmap structure containing the voxel data, width, height, and depth; a chunksize parameter defining the output buffer granularity. Output: A sequence of bytes written to an output buffer, returned in chunks of up to chunksize. Data Structures: The method relies on the internal state of a libvxlstream object, which maintains: map: Pointer to the source libvxlmap. chunksize: The target size for each read operation's output. pos: A coordinate key representing the current (x,y) position, initialized via poskey(0, 0, 0). buffer: A dynamically allocated byte array of size chunksize 2. bufferoffset: The number of valid bytes currently residing in buffer from the start. chunkoffsets: An auxiliary array passed to the column encoder. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set stream->map to the target map, stream->chunksize to the desired size, stream->pos to poskey(0, 0, 0), and stream->bufferoffset to 0. Allocate stream->buffer with size chunksize 2 and allocate stream->chunkoffsets as required. 2. Streaming Loop: While stream->bufferoffset < stream->chunksize and keygety(stream->pos) < stream->map->height, call libvxlcolumnencode for the current (x,y) coordinates, then advance stream->pos to the next x or wrap to the next y. 3. Output and Buffer Management: Copy min(length, chunksize) bytes to the output. If length < chunksize, reset stream->bufferoffset to 0. Otherwise, memmove the remaining bytes to the start of the buffer and update stream->bufferoffset. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def poskey(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def keygetx(pos): return pos[0] def keygety(pos): return pos[1] def libvxlstreamread(stream, outbuffer): if stream is None or outbuffer is None or keygety(stream.pos) >= stream.map.height: return 0 while stream.bufferoffset < stream.chunksize and keygety(stream.pos) < stream.map.height: # libvxlcolumnencode implements Span-based Column Encoding # and appends encoded data to stream.buffer, updating stream.bufferoffset stream.bufferoffset = libvxlcolumnencode( stream.map, stream.chunkoffsets, keygetx(stream.pos), keygety(stream.pos), stream.buffer, stream.bufferoffset) if keygetx(stream.pos) + 1 < stream.map.width: stream.pos = poskey(keygetx(stream.pos) + 1, keygety(stream.pos), 0) else: stream.pos = poskey(0, keygety(stream.pos) + 1, 0) length = stream.bufferoffset bytestocopy = min(length, stream.chunksize) outbuffer[:bytestocopy] = stream.buffer[:bytestocopy] if length < stream.chunksize: stream.bufferoffset = 0 else: remaining = length - stream.chunksize stream.buffer[:remaining] = stream.buffer[stream.chunksize:length] stream.bufferoffset -= stream.chunksize return bytestocopy Parameters: chunksize: Determines the granularity of the output. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: End of Map: When all columns are processed, keygety(stream->pos) equals stream->map->height, causing the function to return 0 immediately on the next call. Buffer Overflow: The buffer is allocated as chunksize 2 to hold the encoded column plus the remainder from the previous read, preventing overflow during the memmove shift. Coordinate Wrapping: The transition from the last x to the next y must be handled atomically within the loop to avoid encoding the same column twice or skipping one. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as each voxel is encoded exactly once. The per-read cost is O(1) amortized, dominated by the buffer copy and shift operations. Memory: O(\text{chunk\size}) for the streaming buffer. The chunkoffsets array size depends on the column encoding details. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with map size. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth for buffer copying and the efficiency of libvxlcolumnencode. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides fixed-size output chunks, simplifying network transmission or disk I/O. Hides the variable length of encoded columns from the consumer. Limitations: Requires a double-sized buffer for efficient shifting. Not suitable for random access; strictly sequential. When to use it: Use when streaming voxel data over a network or to a file where fixed-size blocks are required. When not to use it: Do not use for random access queries or when memory is extremely constrained and chunksize 2 is prohibitive. Voxel Map Streaming is part of the libvxl library, an unofficial voxel engine library. It builds on Span-based Column Encoding to provide a higher-level I/O abstraction. The method was developed by xtreme8000 as part of the libvxl project. xtreme8000/libvxl, https://github.com/xtreme8000/libvxl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: 3D Texture Proxy Geometry
head: 3D Texture Proxy, 3D Texture-Based Volume Rendering, VR Basado en Texturas 3D, VR con texturas tridimensionales, texturas 3D con planos orientados al plano de proyección
body: 3D Texture Proxy Geometry is a GPU-accelerated volume rendering technique where the volumetric dataset is uploaded as a 3D texture object, and polygonal slices are rasterized and blended back-to-front to form the final image. It differs from ray casting by relying on hardware-accelerated texture sampling and interpolation rather than explicit ray marching, and from 2D texture mapping by using a single 3D texture to eliminate popping artifacts and support arbitrary viewing orientations without pre-computing multiple 2D slices. Unlike ray casting, it cannot skip unseen voxels, rendering all voxels within the view frustum. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric scalar field data, camera position and orientation, transfer function (mapping scalar values to color and opacity). Output: 2D color buffer (image). Data Structures: 1. 3D Texture Object: A GPU texture object storing the volume data. Format: Depends on data type. For unsigned short data, the sampler must be usampler3D. Using sampler3D results in all values being 0. Dimensions: Width, Height, Depth. In glTexImage3D, the depth parameter corresponds to the first dimension of the array. Passing the wrong dimension causes index confusion. Filters: GLTEXTUREMINFILTER and GLTEXTUREMAGFILTER must be chosen carefully as they affect the interpolation performed by the GPU texture mapping hardware. Linear filtering is used for trilinear interpolation. Wrapping: Typically GLCLAMPTOEDGE to prevent artifacts at boundaries. 2. View-Port Aligned Slices: Polygonal meshes representing the intersection of the 3D texture cube with arbitrarily oriented planes. 3. Minimum Texture (Optional/Advanced): A luminance-alpha texture map used in specific dependent texture lookup setups, with the alpha channel set to 1 to allow for the addition of scalar values. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-classification (Optional): Pre-classify the volume data to assign optical properties (color/opacity) before upload, or perform post-classification in the fragment shader. 2. Texture Upload: Upload the pre-classified (or raw) volume data as a 3D texture to the GPU. Pitfall: If the volume is too large for texture memory, it must be partitioned into subvolumes swapped in and out during rendering. 3. Compute View-Port Aligned Slices: Calculate polygons formed by the intersection of the 3D texture cube and arbitrarily oriented planes. Traditionally computed by the CPU. Can be offloaded to a vertex shader program. The vertex shader recognizes all 12 edges of a cube as 6 different sets of edges. For each set, it finds at most one coordinate representing the intersecting point of the edge to an arbitrary plane. 4. Rasterization: Rasterize the polygonal slices through the volume parallel to the viewpoint. 5. Fragment Processing (Texture Lookup): The fragment program accesses the 3D texture object. Perform texture fetching and transfer function lookup. Advanced Dependent Lookup (nVidia Texture Shader Extension): Stage 1: Perform lookup in the minimum texture based on computed ray parameters, normalized using the fourth texture coordinate. Stage 2: Reconstruct the scalar value on the back face (sb) using the scalar product with the gradient in view direction (gd) and the scalar on the front face (sf). If only a 2D texture lookup is required, replace this stage with DOTPRODUCTTEXTURE2DNV. Stage 3: Supply sf as a texture coordinate. Stage 4: Look up color and opacity using the denormalized ray parameter (scaled length l/w multiplied by scaling factor w), sf, and sb. Vertex program provides suitable texture coordinates for stages 2-4 to combine necessary parameters. 6. Blending: Blend the slices in back-to-front order to form the final image. Optimization: Empty space skipping can be performed in the vertex or fragment program to improve performance. Occlusion clipping can also be applied, reporting an average of 2.8 speedup. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolume(volumedata, camera, transferfunction, width, height, numslices): # 1. Setup 3D Texture # Upload volumedata to GPU as a 3D texture object. # Dimensions must be the smallest powers of two that can contain the volume data. # In glTexImage3D, the depth parameter corresponds to the first dimension of the array. texture = create3dtexture(volumedata) settextureparameters(texture, minfilter="linear", magfilter="linear") # Linear filtering for trilinear interpolation # 2. Compute View-Port Aligned Slices # Intersect volume bounding box with arbitrarily oriented planes slices = computeviewportalignedslices(camera, volumedata.bounds, numslices) # Initialize output buffers outcolor = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height width)] outalpha = [0.0] (height width) # 3. Render Loop (Back-to-Front) for slice in reversed(slices): # 4. Rasterize Slice screencoords = projecttoscreen(slice["vertices"], camera) pixels = pixelscoveredby(screencoords, width, height) # 5. Fragment Processing for y, x in pixels: texcoords = computetexturecoords(x, y, slice, camera) if texcoords is None: continue scalar = texturesample(texture, texcoords) color, opacity = transferfunction(scalar) # 6. Back-to-Front Blending idx = y width + x outalpha[idx] = outalpha[idx] + opacity (1.0 - outalpha[idx]) outcolor[idx] = [ outcolor[idx][0] (1.0 - opacity) + color[0] opacity, outcolor[idx][1] (1.0 - opacity) + color[1] opacity, outcolor[idx][2] (1.0 - opacity) + color[2] opacity ] return outcolor, outalpha def create3dtexture(data): # Allocate texture memory with smallest power-of-two dimensions containing data # Fill with zeros, copy data, upload # Note: Original data is copied without resizing; resizing is handled by the GPU return {"type": "3D", "data": data} def settextureparameters(texture, minfilter, magfilter): # Set interpolation mode: nearest neighbor or linear (trilinear) pass def computeviewportalignedslices(camera, bounds, numslices): # Generate planes arbitrarily oriented to intersect the volume bounding box # Vertices are computed by intersecting the plane with the 12 cube edges grouped into 6 sets planes = [] for i in range(numslices): t = i / numslices planes.append({ "vertices": [], # Computed by plane-cube intersection "normal": camera.viewdir, "dist": bounds.min + t (bounds.max - bounds.min) }) return planes def projecttoscreen(vertices, camera): # Transform vertices to normalized device coordinates return [v.project(camera) for v in vertices] def pixelscoveredby(screencoords, width, height): # Bounding box rasterization minx, maxx = int(min(v.x for v in screencoords)), int(max(v.x for v in screencoords)) miny, maxy = int(min(v.y for v in screencoords)), int(max(v.y for v in screencoords)) return [(y, x) for y in range(miny, maxy + 1) for x in range(minx, maxx + 1)] def computetexturecoords(x, y, slice, camera): # Compute 3D texture coordinates from ray intersection with slice ray = camera.rayat(x, y) denom = dot(ray.direction, slice["normal"]) if abs(denom) < 1e-6: return None # Ray parallel to slice t = (slice["dist"] - dot(ray.origin, slice["normal"])) / denom point = ray.origin + ray.direction t # The GPU handles scaling to [0,1] via texture matrices; we return the raw intersection point return point def texturesample(texture, coords): # Trilinear interpolation at coords # Note: GPU texture mapping hardware performs the interpolation return texture["data"].trilinear(coords) def transferfunction(scalar): # Map scalar to color and opacity return [1.0, 1.0, 1.0], 0.5 def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) Parameters: Interpolation Method: Nearest neighbor or trilinear. Trilinear is preferred for better image quality. Filters: GLTEXTUREMINFILTER and GLTEXTUREMAGFILTER. Texture Memory: A single 3D texture suffices if memory allows. Texture Dimension: 256^3 due to OpenGL texture dimension limitations. The original data volume is copied without resizing; resizing is handled by the GPU. Memory Usage: 16 MiB in main memory for the textures in this implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limit: Large volumes exceed texture memory capacity. Must be partitioned and swapped. Data Type Mismatch: Using sampler3D for unsigned short data results in all values being 0. Dimension Confusion: In glTexImage3D, the depth parameter corresponds to the first dimension of the array. Passing the wrong dimension causes index confusion. Unseen Voxels: All voxels within the slice are rendered; unseen voxels cannot be skipped. Center Misalignment: If the volume does not occupy the entire 3D texture, the volume center does not coincide with the texture center. Translations must be added to the texture matrix to align the volume center with the polygon set center. Primitive Size: Primitives must be large enough to contain the entire volume during any rotation. The minimum size is the diagonal of the volume. Performance Degradation: Increasing primitive size to fit the volume can negatively affect rendering performance unless alpha testing is applied to avoid drawing transparent fragments to the framebuffer. Banding Artifacts: Projection-oriented polygons introduce horizontal or vertical bands depending on the number of polygons used. A GPU-based tri-linear interpolation method using the LRP (linear interpolation) instruction, fetching 8 nearest neighbors via pre-computed texture coordinates. It sets itself apart by leveraging specific GPU instructions for efficient interpolation, suitable when hardware supports LRP. Choose it when maximizing interpolation performance on compatible GPUs. A technique that utilizes the GPU's capability to handle multiple texture units simultaneously, assigning one 3D texture to each data class or volume. It sets itself apart by enabling simultaneous visualization of multiple classes without blending them into a single texture, avoiding texture memory limits for single large volumes. Choose it when rendering multi-class datasets or when hardware supports multiple active texture units. A scheme to store volume data and proxy geometry locally in graphics hardware to avoid CPU-GPU bandwidth bottlenecks, using compression to fit within limited memory. It sets itself apart by reducing memory footprint and transfer overhead, making it suitable for constrained hardware. Choose it when texture memory is insufficient or bandwidth is a bottleneck. Time Complexity: Not explicitly stated in the sources, but performance scales with pixel count and slice count, with optimizations like occlusion clipping yielding a 2.8× speedup. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to volume size, constrained by available texture memory. Measured Performance: Li et al. reported an average of 2.8 speedup using optimization techniques like occlusion clipping in fragment programs. Scaling: Scaling to higher resolutions is limited by texture memory, requiring paging or out-of-core techniques for large datasets. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated trilinear interpolation eliminates bands from 2D texturization and supports arbitrary viewing orientations. Limitations: Cannot skip unseen voxels, limited by texture memory size, and projection-oriented polygons may introduce horizontal or vertical bands depending on polygon count. When to Use: Moderate-sized volumes fitting in texture memory, when hardware interpolation is preferred. When Not to Use: Volumes exceeding texture memory capacity, or when skipping unseen voxels is critical for performance. Origin: Popularized by Cabral et al. in 1994 for nonshaded volume rendering. History: Examined by Cabral et al. on the SGI RealityEngine, the first hardware to implement 3D texture mapping. The algorithm was initially inaccessible for common usage due to the high cost of the RealityEngine. Development: Rezk-Salama et al. proposed GPU vertex shader optimization to offload computation of view-port aligned polygons from CPU to GPU, balancing workload and improving performance. Usage: Became a mainstream algorithm after the introduction of affordable and powerful GPUs with 3D texture mapping support. name: Tri-linear Interpolation via LRP
head: Tri-linear Interpolation, LRP-based Interpolation
body: Tri-linear interpolation via LRP is a GPU-accelerated method for estimating scalar values at arbitrary floating-point coordinates within a 3D volume grid by interpolating the eight surrounding voxel values. It solves the problem of sampling continuous volume data from discrete voxel grids, providing smooth rendering compared to direct voxel rendering which exhibits less structural detail. It is distinguished from other interpolation methods by its specific implementation using the GPU's LRP (linear interpolation) instruction, leveraging hardware rasterization to interpolate texture coordinates "for free" between vertices, thereby optimizing memory bandwidth usage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume texture (or array) with dimensions W \times H \times D, and a query point (x, y, z) in continuous space. Output: A single interpolated scalar value SX at (x, y, z). Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array or 3D texture storing voxel values. Indices are integer coordinates (i, j, k) where 0 \le i < W, 0 \le j < H, 0 \le k < D. Texture Coordinates: 3D coordinates (u, v, w) in the range [0, 1] representing the position within the volume. Blending Factors: Three fractional values (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) representing the relative distance to the corner voxels along each axis. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the continuous query point (x, y, z) to integer floor and ceiling coordinates: \begin{aligned} xf &= \lfloor x \rfloor, & xc &= \lceil x \rceil \\ yf &= \lfloor y \rfloor, & yc &= \lceil y \rceil \\ zf &= \lfloor z \rfloor, & zc &= \lceil z \rceil \end{aligned} 2. Boundary Clamping: Ensure indices are within valid bounds. If any ceiling coordinate exceeds the volume dimension (e.g., xc \ge W), clamp it to the maximum index (W - 1). This prevents out-of-bounds array access. 3. Voxel Fetching: Retrieve the eight corner voxel values surrounding the query point: \begin{aligned} S{000} &= \text{Volume}[xf, yf, zf] \\ S{001} &= \text{Volume}[xf, yf, zc] \\ S{010} &= \text{Volume}[xf, yc, zf] \\ S{011} &= \text{Volume}[xf, yc, zc] \\ S{100} &= \text{Volume}[xc, yf, zf] \\ S{101} &= \text{Volume}[xc, yf, zc] \\ S{110} &= \text{Volume}[xc, yc, zf] \\ S{111} &= \text{Volume}[xc, yc, zc] \end{aligned} 4. Blending Factor Calculation: Compute the fractional offsets (blending factors) for each axis: \alpha = x - xf, \quad \beta = y - yf, \quad \gamma = z - zf GPU-Specific Implementation (LRP): In the context of the LRP instruction implementation, blending factors are derived from 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w) of the resampling point. The texture coordinates are multiplied by the original texture resolution (W, H, D). The fractional parts of these products serve as the blending factors: \alpha = \text{frac}(u \cdot W), \quad \beta = \text{frac}(v \cdot H), \quad \gamma = \text{frac}(w \cdot D) 5. Interpolation: Calculate the final value SX using the trilinear formula: \begin{aligned} SX = & (1-\alpha)(1-\beta)(1-\gamma)S{000} + \alpha(1-\beta)(1-\gamma)S{100} \\ & + (1-\alpha)\beta(1-\gamma)S{010} + \alpha\beta(1-\gamma)S{110} \\ & + (1-\alpha)(1-\beta)\gamma S{001} + \alpha(1-\beta)\gamma S{101} \\ & + (1-\alpha)\beta\gamma S{011} + \alpha\beta\gamma S{111} \end{aligned} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterpolation(volume, x, y, z, width, height, depth): """ Performs tri-linear interpolation on a 3D volume. Args: volume: 3D array or texture object supporting indexing. x, y, z: Continuous coordinates to sample. width, height, depth: Dimensions of the volume. Returns: Interpolated scalar value. """ # Step 1: Compute floor and ceiling coordinates xf = int(x) xc = xf + 1 yf = int(y) yc = yf + 1 zf = int(z) zc = zf + 1 # Step 2: Boundary Clamping # Clamp ceiling coordinates to max index to prevent out-of-bounds access if xc >= width: xc = width - 1 if yc >= height: yc = height - 1 if zc >= depth: zc = depth - 1 # Step 3: Fetch 8 corner voxel values S000 = volume[xf, yf, zf] S001 = volume[xf, yf, zc] S010 = volume[xf, yc, zf] S011 = volume[xf, yc, zc] S100 = volume[xc, yf, zf] S101 = volume[xc, yf, zc] S110 = volume[xc, yc, zf] S111 = volume[xc, yc, zc] # Step 4: Calculate blending factors (fractional parts) alpha = x - xf beta = y - yf gamma = z - zf # Step 5: Trilinear Interpolation Formula # Interpolate along X axis first S00 = (1 - alpha) S000 + alpha S100 S01 = (1 - alpha) S001 + alpha S101 S10 = (1 - alpha) S010 + alpha S110 S11 = (1 - alpha) S011 + alpha S111 # Interpolate along Y axis S0 = (1 - beta) S00 + beta S10 S1 = (1 - beta) S01 + beta S11 # Interpolate along Z axis result = (1 - gamma) S0 + gamma S1 return result def trilinearinterpolationlrp(volume, u, v, w, width, height, depth): """ GPU-style tri-linear interpolation using LRP instruction logic. Assumes u, v, w are texture coordinates in [0, 1]. """ # Step 4 (LRP variant): Calculate blending factors from texture coordinates alpha = (u width) % 1.0 beta = (v height) % 1.0 gamma = (w depth) % 1.0 # Convert to integer indices for fetching # Note: In hardware, these indices are pre-computed and interpolated during rasterization xf = int(u width) xc = min(xf + 1, width - 1) yf = int(v height) yc = min(yf + 1, height - 1) zf = int(w depth) zc = min(zf + 1, depth - 1) # Step 3: Fetch 8 corner voxel values S000 = volume[xf, yf, zf] S001 = volume[xf, yf, zc] S010 = volume[xf, yc, zf] S011 = volume[xf, yc, zc] S100 = volume[xc, yf, zf] S101 = volume[xc, yf, zc] S110 = volume[xc, yc, zf] S111 = volume[xc, yc, zc] # Step 5: Trilinear Interpolation Formula S00 = (1 - alpha) S000 + alpha S100 S01 = (1 - alpha) S001 + alpha S101 S10 = (1 - alpha) S010 + alpha S110 S11 = (1 - alpha) S011 + alpha S111 S0 = (1 - beta) S00 + beta S10 S1 = (1 - beta) S01 + beta S11 result = (1 - gamma) S0 + gamma S1 return result Parameters: texcoord: 3D texture coordinates of the resampling point, range [0, 1]. resolution: Original dimensions of the 3D texture (W, H, D). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Bandwidth: Trilinear interpolation requires at least eight memory reads per sample point. For real-time rendering, this creates a high demand for memory bandwidth. If memory latency is high, rendering speed can be severely slowed down. Boundary Handling: If the ceiling coordinate exceeds the volume dimension, it must be clamped to the maximum index to prevent out-of-bounds access. Precision: The calculation of blending factors using fractional parts of multiplied coordinates relies on floating-point precision. Ensure that texture coordinates are normalized correctly to avoid off-by-one errors at boundaries. A method for computing the value of a coarser-side octant vertex by performing trilinear interpolation on the coarsest level involved for any of the inputs [2770-coarsest-level-lerp.md]. It is chosen when working with multi-resolution volume data (mipmaps) to ensure consistency across levels. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and memory accesses regardless of volume size. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample, but requires access to 8 neighboring voxels. Measured Performance: Requires at least eight million memory reads per frame for typical resolutions, making memory bandwidth a critical bottleneck. Strengths: Provides smooth rendering of volumetric data, preserving structural details better than direct voxel rendering. Hardware-accelerated via LRP instructions and texture sampling units. Limitations: High memory bandwidth consumption can limit frame rates on hardware with limited memory throughput. When to Use: When smooth visualization of volume data is required and memory bandwidth is sufficient. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth is severely constrained and performance is critical, or when the volume data is sparse and sparse data structures (like Octrees) are more appropriate. Tri-linear interpolation is the primary interpolation method for volume rendering, providing smooth rendering of volumetric data. It is a method of multivariate interpolation on a 3-D regular grid that approximates the value of a function at an intermediate point linearly, using function data on the lattice points. The GPU-based implementation using the LRP instruction was described by Viola et al. [2002] in the context of hardware-accelerated frequency domain volume rendering. It is widely used in real-time volume rendering systems to handle the interpolation of millions of sample points per frame. name: Multi-Volume Rendering with Multiple Textures
head: Composición de 4 clases simultáneamente, Visualización de múltiples volúmenes utilizando texturas 3D, Viv multi-channel rendering
body: This method renders multiple distinct volumetric classes (e.g., tissue types) simultaneously by storing each class in a separate 3D texture and combining them during the fragment shader execution. It solves the problem of visualizing heterogeneous data where different channels require independent transfer functions and opacities. It sets itself apart from single-volume approaches by allowing independent control of each channel's appearance, and from out-of-core techniques by relying entirely on GPU memory residency for all active channels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N 3D textures, where each texture stores the scalar field (opacity/density) for one specific class. Each texture is bound to a distinct texture unit. Input: A set of N transfer function parameters (colors and opacities) for each class. Input: Ray coordinates (texture coordinates) generated by the proxy geometry. Output: A single RGBA color value per fragment, representing the accumulated color of all classes along the ray. Data Structures: Textures: N instances of sampler3D. The internal format is not strictly defined by the method but is constrained by hardware limits. Uniforms: An array of color vectors, tissueColor[N], where each element contains the RGB color and alpha opacity for the corresponding class. Steps: 1. Texture Binding: Assign an independent texture unit for each class in the rendering context. In OpenGL, this is done using glActiveTextureARB followed by binding the specific 3D texture to the active unit. 2. Primitive Drawing: Draw the proxy geometry (e.g., view-aligned slices or quads) that covers the volume of interest. 3. Sampling: For each fragment, sample the scalar value (luminance/opacity) from each of the N textures using the fragment's texture coordinates. 4. Color Computation: Multiply the sampled scalar value by the pre-defined color and opacity for that class. 5. Accumulation: Sum the resulting color vectors from all classes to produce the final output color. Formulas: Let Ci be the color vector (RGB) and \alphai be the opacity scalar for class i. Let Li be the sampled scalar value (luminance/opacity) from texture i at the current coordinate. The contribution color Ki for class i is: Ki = \text{float4}(Ci.rgb \cdot Li.r, Ci.a \cdot Li.r) The final output color K{final} is: K{final} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ki Parameters: Number of Channels (N): Limited by the number of available texture bind points. WebGL 2.0 guarantees a minimum of 8. Older hardware like GeForce FX supports up to 4 with ARB multitexture or up to 16 with NV fragment program extensions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: The method does not employ out-of-core techniques. It is strictly limited by the available GPU memory. Large-scale datasets may not fit if the number of channels is high. Hardware Limits: The maximum number of simultaneous textures is hardware-dependent. Shader Adaptation: Unlike some modern frameworks, this method may require manual adaptation of the fragment shader to handle different numbers of channels or specific channel switching at runtime. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermultivolume(texCoord, tissueColor, textures): finalcolor = float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Iterate over all active classes for i in range(len(textures)): # Sample the scalar value (opacity/luminance) from the i-th texture # Note: tex3D returns a float4, we use the red channel as the scalar value luminance = tex3D(textures[i], texCoord).r # Calculate color contribution for this class # Color = BaseColor Luminance # Alpha = BaseAlpha Luminance colorcontribution = float4( tissueColor[i].rgb luminance, tissueColor[i].a luminance) # Accumulate finalcolor = finalcolor + colorcontribution return finalcolor A web-based implementation using this method. It supports runtime channel switching by changing texture bindings but lacks out-of-core support. Uses the same multi-texture accumulation technique but adds bricking for data management. It chooses a global resolution level per frame, which can lead to suboptimal working sets. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of channels N per fragment, as N texture fetches and additions are performed. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot V), where V is the volume of the data. All N textures must reside in GPU memory simultaneously. Strengths: Simple implementation; allows independent transfer functions per class; supports runtime channel switching. Limitations: Strictly limited by GPU memory capacity; no out-of-core support; hardware-dependent maximum channel count. When to use: Small to medium-sized datasets where all channels fit in GPU memory and independent class visualization is required. When not to use: Large-scale datasets requiring out-of-core streaming or when the number of channels exceeds hardware texture unit limits. The technique originates from early GPU volume rendering research, specifically utilizing OpenGL's multitexturing capabilities. It was documented in the context of visualizing biomedical data with multiple tissue classes (gray matter, muscle, skin, fat, bone) using GeForce FX hardware. It is also referenced in modern web-based volume renderers like Viv and Neuroglancer. name: Proxy Geometry Compression
head: Retained-Mode Rendering with Proxy Geometry Compression, Retained-mode scheme with proxy geometry compression
body: Proxy Geometry Compression is a technique for storing volume data and proxy geometry locally in graphics hardware to avoid CPU-GPU bandwidth bottlenecks associated with immediate mode rendering. It sets itself apart from immediate-mode splatting by pre-loading compressed proxy geometry templates into GPU memory, leveraging the regularity of rectilinear volumes to achieve high compression ratios (e.g., 171:1). This allows the entire volume representation to reside in local graphics memory, enabling interactive rendering speeds that are significantly faster than sending each splat separately. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D rectilinear volume dataset and a traversal order (X, Y, or Z axis). Output: Compressed 32-bit vertex data stored in GPU memory, and decompressed texture coordinates for splatting. Data Structures: The method uses three proxy geometry templates, one for each of the three possible traversal orders (X, Y, Z). Vertex Template: Represents a single slice of the volume. For a 256^3 volume, this requires 768k vertices instead of 192M. Packed Vertex Format: Each vertex is packed into a 32-bit integer. Volume Texture Coordinates (tx, ty): Stored as integers. tx = mx \times 256 + ix ty = my \times 256 + iy mx, my (Major): 7 bits each. Supports slices up to 2^{15} \times 2^{15} voxels. ix, iy (Minor): 8 bits each. Gaussian Texture Coordinates (fx, fy): 1 bit each. Values are strictly 0 or 1. Total: 7+8+7+8+1+1 = 32 bits. Index Buffer: Uses 2-byte indices (unsigned short) to keep patch sizes under 65,535 vertices, reducing index buffer memory usage. Steps: 1. Pre-computation (CPU): Omit vertex positions because they can be calculated from volume texture coordinates. Maintain three proxy geometry templates for the three traversal orders. Pack the vertex attributes into 32-bit integers using the formula above. Upload the packed vertex data and index buffers to GPU memory. 2. Rendering (GPU Vertex Shader): For each vertex in the proxy geometry template, retrieve the packed 32-bit integer. Decompress the integer to extract mx, my, ix, iy, fx, fy. Use a lookup table (stored in constant registers) to efficiently extract these components. Recover the full volume texture coordinates: tx = mx \times 256 + ix and ty = my \times 256 + iy. Recover the Gaussian texture coordinates fx, fy (0 or 1). Pass tx, ty, fx, fy to the fragment shader. 3. Fragment Shader: Use the passed texture coordinates to sample the volume texture and the 2D Gaussian texture for EWA splatting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packvertex(mx, my, ix, iy, fx, fy): """Pack vertex attributes into a 32-bit integer.""" return (mx << 25) | (my << 18) | (ix << 10) | (iy << 2) | (fy << 1) | fx def decompressvertex(packedint): """Decompress a 32-bit integer to recover texture coordinates.""" fx = (packedint >> 0) & 1 fy = (packedint >> 1) & 1 iy = (packedint >> 2) & 0xFF ix = (packedint >> 10) & 0xFF my = (packedint >> 18) & 0x7F mx = (packedint >> 25) & 0x7F tx = mx 256 + ix ty = my 256 + iy return tx, ty, fx, fy def rendervolume(compressedvertices, indices): """Simulate vertex shader processing for each vertex in the index buffer.""" for idx in indices: packed = compressedvertices[idx] tx, ty, fx, fy = decompressvertex(packed) # Pass tx, ty, fx, fy to fragment shader for splatting Parameters: Slice Size: The method supports slices up to 2^{15} \times 2^{15} voxels due to the 7-bit major coordinate. Patch Size: Index buffers are sized to contain no more than 65,535 vertices to allow 2-byte indexing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voxel Count: The compression assumes rectilinear/regular volumes. Memory Usage: While vertex memory is compressed, index buffers can still be large. For most datasets, only 5-20% of voxels are non-transparent, limiting index buffer size to ~115.2M bytes in typical cases. Precision: The 7-bit major coordinate limits the maximum slice dimension. If a volume exceeds 2^{15} in a dimension, this compression scheme cannot represent it directly without modification. Compression Ratio: 171:1 for a 256^3 volume dataset (12M bytes vs 2048M bytes for vertices). Vertex Count Reduction: Reduces vertex count from 192M to 768k for a 256^3 volume by sharing templates across slices. Performance: Significant improvement over immediate mode rendering. Bonsai (274,866 splats): 7.53 fps (Retained) vs 0.53 fps (Immediate). Engine (247,577 splats): 10.28 fps (Retained) vs 1.40 fps (Immediate). Checkerboard (786,432 splats): 6.88 fps (Retained) vs 0.47 fps (Immediate). Lobster (555,976 splats): 10.60 fps (Retained) vs 1.19 fps (Immediate). UNC Head (2,955,242 splats): 2.86 fps (Retained) vs 0.12 fps (Immediate). Strengths: Eliminates CPU-GPU bandwidth bottleneck; fits large volumes in local GPU memory; fast decompression in vertex shader. Limitations: Requires regular/rectilinear volumes; limited slice size (2^{15}); index buffer memory can still be significant for very large transparent-heavy volumes. When to use: Interactive volume rendering on hardware with limited CPU-GPU bandwidth and sufficient local GPU memory. When not to use: Irregular grids; extremely large slices exceeding 2^{15}; scenes where index buffer memory exceeds available GPU memory. Originated in the paper "Hardware-Accelerated Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting" by Wei Chen et al. (2004). The method was developed to address the memory bandwidth bottleneck of immediate-mode splatting, which sends each quad separately to the pipeline. It builds on 3D Texture Proxy Geometry by adding compression to the proxy geometry representation.
