name: 3D Texture Proxy Geometry — 3D Texture Proxy, View-Aligned Slices, 3D-Texture Volume Rendering, 3D Texture-Based Volume Rendering
head: 3D-Texture Volume Rendering, 3D Texture-Based Volume Rendering, GPU Volume Rendering with View-Aligned Slices
body: 3D Texture Proxy Geometry is a direct volume rendering method that represents a rectilinear volume as a stack of parallel planar polygons (slabs) textured with 3D texture maps, leveraging hardware-accelerated tri-linear interpolation to sample volume data at arbitrary locations. It solves the problem of efficient hardware-accelerated volume rendering with directional lighting by pre-computing color and opacity per voxel and storing them in 3D textures, allowing the graphics pipeline to handle interpolation and compositing. Unlike shear-warp methods which fix plane counts to volume resolution, this method allows the number of rendering planes to be adjusted at runtime independent of volume resolution, and unlike coherent projection, it supports perspective views without a time penalty, though perspective projection causes irregular sampling along rays. Inputs: Rectilinear volume data (scalar field values), voxel spacing (Ax, Ay, Az), voxel counts (nx, ny, nz), client-supplied gradient-magnitude threshold, transfer function, and lighting model parameters. Outputs: Final composited image. Data Structures: 1. Volume Data: Array of size nx \times ny \times nz. 2. Lookup Table (LUT): Array of size (m+1) \times g, where m is the number of materials and g is the number of quantized gradient directions. Entries store RGBA values (color and opacity). 3. 3D Texture Maps: 3D arrays of resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz), where Ni are powers of two \ge ni. Each texel stores pre-computed RGBA values for one voxel. Large volumes are partitioned into multiple texture maps due to texture memory limits. 4. Bounding Cube: Defined by side length d, centered at the origin. Preprocessing Steps: 1. Classification and Gradient Quantization: For each voxel, compute the gradient magnitude. Classify the voxel as "reflecting" or "ambient" based on the client-supplied gradient-magnitude threshold and material field value range. Compute a quantized gradient index for reflecting voxels. 2. Lookup Table Creation: Create the LUT. For each combination of quantized gradient and reflecting material, assign appropriate color and opacity (RGBA) accounting for depth integration. Ambient material colors are computed independently of the gradient. 3. Texture Map Filling: Fill 3D texture maps with pre-computed color values, one texel per volume voxel, using the LUT indices. This involves integer operations from the volume array to the texture buffers. Rendering Steps: 1. Plane Generation: Determine the number of planes. The default is d/Az (where Az is voxel size along view direction), ensuring one sample per data point when viewed straight on. Typically, 2–4 times the default is used for accuracy. 2. Coordinate Transformation: Construct a bounding cube centered on the origin with side length d = \sqrt{Lx^2 + Ly^2 + Lz^2}, where Li = Ni Ai. Define texture coordinates (s,t,r) for the cube corners. For arbitrary viewing angles defined by rotation matrix R, transform texture coordinates using (s,t,r) = (x,y,z) D^{-1} R^{-1} S T, where D is uniform scale by d, S is non-uniform scale by (d/Lx, d/Ly, d/Lz), and T is translation by (\frac{1}{2}nx/Nx, \frac{1}{2}ny/Ny, \frac{1}{2}nz/Nz). Rotation must precede scaling to avoid shearing distortion if dimensions differ. 3. Clipping: Position six programmable world-space clipping planes at the volume faces to clip regions outside the volume. 4. Rasterization and Interpolation: Apply each texture map to parallel planes orthogonal to screen-z (squares in screen space). Texture coordinates are specified only at the four corners. Hardware interpolates texture coordinates across the square; coordinates outside [0, 1.0] are interpolated (not clamped), creating in-range values precisely when the pixel is within the volume. 5. Compositing: Render planes back-to-front. Combine via hardware blending using the slab thickness \Delta. Formulas: Slab Thickness: \Delta = \frac{\text{total distance covered by stack}}{\text{number of planes}}. Color and Opacity Integration: For slab thickness \Delta, color emission per unit distance E(p), and opacity per unit distance \alphai (for color p) and \alpha (total): Cp = E(p) \frac{1 - e^{-\alpha \Delta}}{\alpha} A = 1 - e^{-\alpha \Delta} Where Cp is the color contribution for primary p, and A is the opacity contribution. Texture Coordinates (Initial): s(x) = \frac{x + \frac{1}{2}nx Ax}{Nx Ax}, \quad t(y) = \frac{y + \frac{1}{2}ny Ay}{Ny Ay}, \quad r(z) = \frac{z + \frac{1}{2}nz Az}{Nz Az} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def nextpoweroftwo(n): if n <= 1: return 1 return 1 << (n - 1).bitlength() def computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z, nx, ny, nz): dx = (volume[x+1][y][z] - volume[x-1][y][z]) / 2.0 if 0 < x < nx-1 else 0.0 dy = (volume[x][y+1][z] - volume[x][y-1][z]) / 2.0 if 0 < y < ny-1 else 0.0 dz = (volume[x][y][z+1] - volume[x][y][z-1]) / 2.0 if 0 < z < nz-1 else 0.0 return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) def classifyvoxels(volumedata, threshold): nx, ny, nz = len(volumedata), len(volumedata[0]), len(volumedata[0][0]) materialindices = [[[-1 for in range(nz)] for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] gradientindices = [[[0 for in range(nz)] for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] for x in range(nx): for y in range(ny): for z in range(nz): gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(volumedata, x, y, z, nx, ny, nz) if gradmag > threshold: materialindices[x][y][z] = 1 gradientindices[x][y][z] = 0 else: materialindices[x][y][z] = 0 gradientindices[x][y][z] = 0 return materialindices, gradientindices def createlut(materialindices, gradientindices, transferfunc, lightingmodel): m = max(max(row) for row in materialindices) + 1 g = max(max(row) for row in gradientindices) + 1 lut = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(g)] for in range(m)] for mat in range(m): for grad in range(g): rgba = transferfunc(mat, grad, lightingmodel) lut[mat][grad] = rgba return lut def filltexturemaps(volumedata, materialindices, gradientindices, lut, Nx, Ny, Nz): nx, ny, nz = len(volumedata), len(volumedata[0]), len(volumedata[0][0]) chunksize = 64 texturemaps = [] for x0 in range(0, nx, chunksize): for y0 in range(0, ny, chunksize): for z0 in range(0, nz, chunksize): x1, y1, z1 = min(x0+chunksize, nx), min(y0+chunksize, ny), min(z0+chunksize, nz) texmap = [[[lut[materialindices[x][y][z]][gradientindices[x][y][z]] for z in range(z0, z1)] for y in range(y0, y1)] for x in range(x0, x1)] texturemaps.append(texmap) return texturemaps def setupclippingplanes(volumefaces): # Position six programmable world-space clipping planes at volume faces pass def computetexturetransform(Rinv, d, Lx, Ly, Lz, nx, ny, nz, Nx, Ny, Nz): # D: uniform scale by d, S: non-uniform scale by (d/Lx, d/Ly, d/Lz), T: translation # Correct order: rotation then scaling to avoid shearing return Rinv def rendervolume(texturemaps, rotationmatrix, numplanes, d, Az, imageheight, imagewidth): slabthickness = d / numplanes setupclippingplanes() transform = computetexturetransform(rotationmatrix, d, d, d, d, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1) finalimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight imagewidth)] for texmap in texturemaps: for planeidx in range(numplanes): # Hardware rasterizes square with texture coordinates at corners # Interpolation creates in-range values precisely when pixel is within volume # Back-to-front compositing with hardware blending pass return finalimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Projection: Causes irregular sampling (non-constant distance) along rays, leading to artifacts during internal navigation. Requires spherical support geometries which are expensive. Effective slab thickness increases with off-axis angle; ignoring this causes up to 4% error for 600-pixel windows and 14% for 1000-pixel windows. Nonlinear Transfer Functions: Hardware interpolates color, not data. This causes inaccuracies with nonlinear mappings, especially in close-up views. Aliasing: Discontinuous transfer functions (single material per voxel) cause aliasing artifacts, though not sensitive to orientation. Texture Memory: Large volumes exceed texture memory limits, requiring partitioning. Transferring maps to texture memory is not parallelizable and serial. Order of Operations: Scaling does not commute with rotation. Rotation must precede scaling to avoid shearing distortion. Few Planes: Artifacts may be visible where clipped edges of rendered squares are visible. Time Complexity: Lookup table size is independent of volume size (O(m \cdot g)). Texture map filling is proportional to volume size (O(nx ny nz)) but involves few integer operations. Rendering time depends on the number of planes and texture map transfers. Memory Complexity: Requires texture memory for 3D textures. Large volumes require partitioning, increasing memory management overhead. Performance: On Silicon Graphics Reality Engine II with 2MB 3D texture hardware, rendering times are nearly interactive. Without directional lighting, times are ~10x faster. Using four processors reduces times by 1.2–2.5x due to serial graphics pipeline bottlenecks. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated, supports perspective views without a time penalty, allows runtime adjustment of plane count, good integration with surface geometry via Z-buffer. Limitations: High geometric cost (primitives generated/rasterized) becomes limiting as hardware focuses on fragment processing. Inaccurate with nonlinear transfer functions. Aliasing from discontinuous transfer functions. Perspective artifacts if not compensated. When to Use: Suitable for moderate-sized volumes (\approx 256^3) where interactive performance with lighting is needed and hardware supports 3D textures. Not suitable for very large volumes without partitioning or when high accuracy with nonlinear transfer functions is required. The method was introduced by Cullip and Neumann in 1993 [CN94] and improved by Cabral et al. in 1994 [CCF94] to exploit hardware 3D texture interpolation (trilinear). It was implemented in the Voltx system on Silicon Graphics Reality Engine II hardware. It supports orthographic, perspective, and stereo views. name: Sm2D (2D Volume Texture Experiment)
head: 2D Volume Texture Experiment
body: Sm2D is a two-dimensional test application implemented as a 2D ray tracer to investigate the applicability of a texture-based approach for smoke volumes. It simplifies the three-dimensional volume rendering problem into a one-dimensional viewport function where tetrahedra are represented by triangles. It sets itself apart from its siblings by serving as a diagnostic tool to demonstrate the precision limits and rotational artifacts inherent in texture-based approximations compared to explicit geometric calculations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of triangles tk representing the smoke volume, a camera-aligned two-dimensional grid G (equivalent to a three-dimensional texture), and a set of viewing rays rj. Output: An absorption coefficient \alpha(rj) for each ray rj, visualized as a one-dimensional function across the viewport edge. Data Structures: Grid G: A two-dimensional array of cells ci. In the reference implementation, G is a 16 \times 16 grid. Each cell ci has a defined area \text{area}(ci). Triangles: A list of Nt triangles tk. Each triangle tk has a defined area \text{area}(tk). Rays: A list of Nr rays rj entering the grid from below at equally spaced points along the viewport edge. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Triangle Density: For each triangle tk, compute its base density: \sigma(tk) = \sigmak = \frac{1}{\text{area}(tk)} where \text{area}(t) returns the area of triangle t. 2. Accumulate Cell Density: For each cell ci in grid G, compute the accumulated density by summing contributions from all triangles: \sigma(ci) = \sum{k=0}^{Nt-1} \frac{\text{overlap}(ci, tk)}{\text{area}(ci)} \sigma(tk) where \text{overlap}(x0, x1) returns the common area (or length) of objects x0 and x1, and \sigma(x0) returns the density assigned to object x0. 3. Compute Ray Absorption: For each ray rj, sum the cell densities multiplied by the interval length (distance between entry and exit points of rj in ci): \alpha(rj) = \sum{i=0}^{Nc-1} \sigma(ci) \cdot \text{overlap}(rj, ci) where Nc is the number of grid cells. 4. Output: Visualize \alpha(rj) for all j as a graph across the viewport. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesm2d(triangles, gridrows, gridcols, numrays): # Grid covers unit square [0,1]x[0,1] cellarea = 1.0 / (gridrows gridcols) sigmagrid = [[0.0] gridcols for in range(gridrows)] # 1. Map triangles to grid for t in triangles: tarea = trianglearea(t) if tarea == 0: continue tdensity = 1.0 / tarea for r in range(gridrows): for c in range(gridcols): x0, y0 = c / gridcols, r / gridcols x1, y1 = (c + 1) / gridcols, (r + 1) / gridcols overlaparea = trianglerectangleoverlap(t, x0, y0, x1, y1) sigmagrid[r][c] += (overlaparea / cellarea) tdensity # 2. Ray tracing rayxs = [i / numrays for i in range(numrays)] absorptioncoeffs = [] for xray in rayxs: alpha = 0.0 colidx = int(xray gridcols) if colidx >= gridcols: colidx = gridcols - 1 for r in range(gridrows): y0 = r / gridrows y1 = (r + 1) / gridrows overlaplen = linerectangleoverlap(xray, 0.0, xray, 1.0, colidx/gridcols, y0, (colidx+1)/gridcols, y1) alpha += sigmagrid[r][colidx] overlaplen absorptioncoeffs.append(alpha) return absorptioncoeffs def trianglearea(t): # Standard formula for triangle area given 3 vertices return 0.5 abs(t.p1.x(t.p2.y - t.p3.y) + t.p2.x(t.p3.y - t.p1.y) + t.p3.x(t.p1.y - t.p2.y)) def trianglerectangleoverlap(t, x0, y0, x1, y1): # Computes area of intersection between triangle t and axis-aligned rectangle [x0,x1]x[y0,y1] cliprect = [(x0, y0), (x1, y0), (x1, y1), (x0, y1)] poly = [(t.p1.x, t.p1.y), (t.p2.x, t.p2.y), (t.p3.x, t.p3.y)] for edge in cliprect: poly = clippolygon(poly, edge) if not poly: return 0.0 return polygonarea(poly) def clippolygon(poly, edge): # Standard Sutherland-Hodgman clip step output = [] if not poly: return output for i in range(len(poly)): curr = poly[i] prev = poly[i-1] if isinside(curr, edge): if not isinside(prev, edge): output.append(intersect(prev, curr, edge)) output.append(curr) elif isinside(prev, edge): output.append(intersect(prev, curr, edge)) return output def isinside(p, edge): # Checks if point p is inside the half-plane defined by edge return (edge[1][0] - edge[0][0]) (p[1] - edge[0][1]) - (edge[1][1] - edge[0][1]) (p[0] - edge[0][0]) >= 0 def intersect(p1, p2, edge): # Computes intersection of line p1-p2 with edge line dx, dy = p2[0]-p1[0], p2[1]-p1[1] if edge[0][0] == edge[1][0]: t = (edge[0][0] - p1[0]) / dx return (edge[0][0], p1[1] + tdy) else: t = (edge[0][1] - p1[1]) / dy return (p1[0] + tdx, edge[0][1]) def polygonarea(poly): # Shoelace formula return 0.5 abs(sum(poly[i][0]poly[i+1][1] - poly[i+1][0]poly[i][1] for i in range(len(poly)-1)) + poly[-1][0]poly[0][1] - poly[0][0]poly[-1][1]) def linerectangleoverlap(x, y0, x, y1, rx0, ry0, rx1, ry1): # Computes length of intersection between vertical line segment and axis-aligned rectangle if x < rx0 or x > rx1: return 0.0 clipy0 = max(y0, ry0) clipy1 = min(y1, ry1) return max(0.0, clipy1 - clipy0) Parameters: Grid Resolution: The example uses a 16 \times 16 grid. Number of Rays: The example uses 64 rays. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: Triangles with zero area cause division by zero in \sigma(tk) = 1/\text{area}(tk). Rotational Artifacts: The texture-based approach produces unstable and faulty results during rotation, unlike explicit calculations which remain smooth. Spikes: Unpleasant spikes across the viewport can occur, especially for degenerated triangles or unfavorable ray angles. Precision: A texture-based approach will never get close to the precision of an explicit calculation without considerably increasing the number of grid cells. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Demonstrates precision limits and rotational artifacts of texture-based approximations. Limitations: Low precision compared to explicit methods; suffers from spikes and rotational artifacts; requires high resolution for acceptable accuracy. When to use: As a diagnostic tool to evaluate texture-based volume rendering suitability. When not to use: When high precision or smooth rotational transitions are required. Sm2D was introduced in a 2012 thesis by Dirk Sowinski as part of research on real-time smoke volume rendering. It serves as a simplified two-dimensional test case to evaluate the applicability of texture-based approaches for smoke volumes, highlighting the trade-offs between hardware-accelerated texture sampling and explicit geometric ray tracing. name: AR mapping to 3D texture
head: Linear alpha blending mapping, SIV texture coordinate mapping
body: AR mapping to 3D texture is a technique for volume visualization that maps scalar data and associated attributes (color and opacity) into a 3D texture using a linear coordinate system, thereby avoiding non-linear transformation formulas during rendering. It solves the performance bottleneck of recalculating texture coordinates for every rotation of parallel polygons by defining coordinates once and storing the geometry in a display list. It is distinguished from Wilson's depth integration by its reliance on linear estimation, which is noted to be less accurate but sufficient for effective visualization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of parallel polygons representing the volume or isosurface, and a 3D texture space. Output: A rendered image where color and opacity are composited using linear alpha blending. Data Structures: 3D Texture: A volumetric texture object capable of storing RGBA values. The mapping places color and opacity directly into this texture. Display List: A precomputed group of OpenGL commands cached for execution, used to store the rotated polygon set. Steps: 1. Define Texture Coordinates: Calculate the linear mapping from the 3D spatial coordinates of the volume to the 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w). This mapping is defined once for the entire set of parallel polygons. Let the volume bounds be [x{min}, x{max}] \times [y{min}, y{max}] \times [z{min}, z{max}]. For a point P = (x, y, z), the texture coordinates are: u = \frac{x - x{min}}{x{max} - x{min}} v = \frac{y - y{min}}{y{max} - y{min}} w = \frac{z - z{min}}{z{max} - z{min}} Clamp u, v, w to [0, 1] to handle boundary cases. 2. Populate Texture: Fill the 3D texture with the scalar data converted to color and opacity values based on the transfer function. 3. Rotate Polygons: Apply the desired rotation to the parallel polygons. Because the texture coordinates are defined in the local space of the linear mapping, they do not need to be recalculated for each rotation step. 4. Render: Use linear alpha blending to composite the fragments. The hardware interpolates the pre-stored color and opacity values from the 3D texture. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The linear estimation method is noted to be likely worse than Wilson's depth integration. Performance: Recalculating texture coordinates at each rotation is slow; this method avoids that cost. Visual Quality: Despite the estimation error, visualizations remain effective, especially given the context of the goals. A data layout strategy where gradients are stored in the RGB components of a 3D volume texture, and the original isovalue is stored in the Alpha component. This allows using a single texture for both data and shading. Röttger et al. Rendering is a technique that mitigates the high computational cost of volume integration by approximating the rendering integral and moving the computation to a pre-process. It computes a 3D lookup table of colors and opacities parameterized by front scalar value, back scalar value, and distance, which is stored in a 3D texture for hardware-accelerated lookups during rendering. This method builds on AR mapping to 3D texture by using the 3D texture not just for static data storage, but to evaluate the volume composition operator directly via texture interpolation. It is distinguished from standard ray casting by replacing per-voxel integration with texture lookups, and from pure pre-classification by supporting arbitrary transfer functions including isosurface effects through the parameterization of the lookup table. A variant implementation detail where the underlying data structure is a uniform grid. Step: setvalues accepts a (X, Y, Z) float32 tensor to update scalar values. Parameters: aabbmin: The minimum corner of the bounding box. Default is [-1, -1, -1]. aabbmax: The maximum corner of the bounding box. Default is [1, 1, 1]. defaultvalue: Initial scalar value for all points. Default is float max. Layout: getpoints returns a (X, Y, Z, 3) float32 tensor containing 3D coordinates of all grid points. getvalues returns a (X, Y, Z) float32 tensor containing scalar values. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids non-linear formulae; allows texture coordinates to be defined once; enables use of display lists for performance improvement. Limitations: The estimation method is likely worse than Wilson's depth integration. When to use: When rendering parallel polygons and performance is critical, and high precision is secondary to effective visualization. The method originates from Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration. It was developed to improve the performance of interactive volume visualization by leveraging OpenGL display lists and linear texture mapping. name: Röttger et al. Rendering
head: Pre-integration, Pre-integrated Volume Rendering, Texture-based VR, Texture-Based Volume Rendering with Pre/Post-Classification
body: Röttger et al. Rendering is a technique that mitigates the high computational cost of volume integration by approximating the rendering integral and moving the computation to a pre-process. It computes a 3D lookup table of colors and opacities parameterized by front scalar value, back scalar value, and distance, which is stored in a 3D texture for hardware-accelerated lookups during rendering. This method builds on AR mapping to 3D texture by storing pre-computed integration results in texture memory to avoid per-voxel evaluation. It is distinguished from standard ray casting by replacing per-step integration with texture lookups, and from pure pre-classification by supporting arbitrary transfer functions including isosurface effects through the parameterization of the lookup table. The method consists of two phases: a pre-processing phase to generate the lookup table and a rendering phase to use it. Inputs: Volume scalar data, transfer function (mapping scalar to color and opacity), and camera/view parameters. Outputs: A 3D texture containing pre-integrated color and opacity values, and the final rendered image. The core data structure is a 3D texture cube. Dimensions: The sources specify a tested limit of 512^3 voxels. A specific implementation used a 256^3 cube. Format: 4-component float texture (RGBA). Content: X-axis: Discrete front scalar values. Y-axis: Discrete back scalar values. Z-axis: Distances (thickness) between front and back faces. Color Channel: Stores the pre-integrated color values. Alpha Channel: Stores the pre-integrated opacity values. The lookup table is computed offline or at initialization. For a given transfer function, the integral of the volume rendering equation is computed for all combinations of front scalar, back scalar, and thickness. 1. Iterate over all discrete values of front scalar (x-axis). 2. Iterate over all discrete values of back scalar (y-axis). 3. Iterate over all discrete distances (z-axis). 4. Compute the integrated color and opacity for the triplet using the current transfer function. 5. Store the computed color and opacity in the 3D texture at coordinates corresponding to the triplet. Partial Pre-integration: To avoid recomputing the table when the transfer function changes, static components (exponentiation of distances) can be stored separately from dynamic components (color and opacity). During rendering, the pre-computed 3D table is used for lookups at each step in the volume. The method interpolates scalar values and ray segment lengths across the projected geometry to address the 3D texture. 1. Projection: Project the volume cells (e.g., tetrahedra or subdivision polygons) onto the image plane. 2. Interpolation: For each fragment or pixel covered by a projected cell, interpolate three values across the polygon: sf: The scalar function value on the front face. sb: The scalar function value on the back face. l: The ray segment length (thickness) through the cell. 3. Lookup: Use the interpolated values (sf, sb, l) as texture coordinates (addresses) into the 3D texture. 4. Retrieval: Sample the 3D texture to retrieve the pre-integrated color and opacity. 5. Compositing: The retrieved color and opacity are blended into the framebuffer using standard alpha blending to simulate the volume composition operator. The following pseudocode illustrates the rendering lookup and blending process. It assumes the 3D texture texture is already populated and parameter ranges are known. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterpolate(texture, u, v, w): # Performs standard trilinear interpolation over a 3D texture array. # texture is a 3D array of (color, opacity) tuples. # u, v, w are normalized coordinates in [0, 1]. # Returns (color, opacity) u0, u1 = int(u (texture.shape[0] - 1)), min(int(u (texture.shape[0] - 1)) + 1, texture.shape[0] - 1) v0, v1 = int(v (texture.shape[1] - 1)), min(int(v (texture.shape[1] - 1)) + 1, texture.shape[1] - 1) w0, w1 = int(w (texture.shape[2] - 1)), min(int(w (texture.shape[2] - 1)) + 1, texture.shape[2] - 1) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) c00 = lerp(texture[u0][v0][w0], texture[u1][v0][w0], u - u0 / (texture.shape[0] - 1)) c01 = lerp(texture[u0][v0][w1], texture[u1][v0][w1], u - u0 / (texture.shape[0] - 1)) c10 = lerp(texture[u0][v1][w0], texture[u1][v1][w0], u - u0 / (texture.shape[0] - 1)) c11 = lerp(texture[u0][v1][w1], texture[u1][v1][w1], u - u0 / (texture.shape[0] - 1)) c0 = lerp(c00, c01, v - v0 / (texture.shape[1] - 1)) c1 = lerp(c10, c11, v - v0 / (texture.shape[1] - 1)) return lerp(c0, c1, w - w0 / (texture.shape[2] - 1)) def renderfragment(sf, sb, l, sfmax, sbmax, lmax, texture, framebuffercolor, framebufferopacity): # 1. Normalize interpolated parameters to [0, 1] range for texture addressing u = max(0.0, min(1.0, sf / sfmax)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, sb / sbmax)) w = max(0.0, min(1.0, l / lmax)) # 2. Lookup pre-integrated color and opacity color, opacity = trilinearinterpolate(texture, u, v, w) # 3. Blend with existing framebuffer color using the over-operator finalcolor = color opacity + framebuffercolor (1.0 - opacity) finalopacity = opacity + framebufferopacity (1.0 - opacity) return finalcolor, finalopacity Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to color and opacity. Lighting Model Components (Variant): In object-space implementations using gradients, parameters include Ambient (Ka), Diffuse (Kd), Specular (Ks), Shininess, Light Color, Light Position, and Eye Position. Transfer Function Changes: Recomputing the lookup table is costly. Gradient Sign Preservation (Variant): If gradients are stored in the texture (as in the object-space variant), negative gradients must be normalized to [-1, 1] and shifted to [0, 1] for storage: \text{stored} = (\nabla f + 1.0) / 2.0. Texture Access Performance: 3D texture access is slower than 2D due to irregular memory access patterns and the cost of trilinear interpolation (8 texture accesses vs 4 for bilinear). Fill Rate Limitation: Performance is primarily limited by fill rate. Alpha Test Effectiveness: The benefit of alpha testing (skipping transparent fragments) is inversely proportional to data density. What it is: A variant where volume data (gradient and opacity) is loaded into a 3D texture, and rendering is performed by rotating the camera and drawing texture slices (object-space) rather than ray casting. Difference: Uses hardware interpolation of gradients for shading and blending, rather than pre-integrated color lookup for composition. It supports object-oriented geometry rendering. When to choose: When shading quality is prioritized over the physical accuracy of volume composition, or when implementing specific lighting models on the GPU. Link: Object-Space Texture Rendering What it is: A technique that separates the static, computationally expensive components of the integration (exponentiation of distances) from the dynamic components (color and opacity). Difference: Allows interactive changes to the transfer function with virtually no overhead, unlike full pre-integration which requires table regeneration. When to choose: When the user needs to interactively adjust the transfer function during rendering. Link: Partial Pre-integration What it is: Pre-classification applies the transfer function to voxel samples before interpolation; post-classification interpolates samples first, then applies the transfer function. Difference: Pre-classification results in well-defined images; post-classification results in diffuse images because interpolation is not commutative with the transfer function. When to choose: Use pre-classification for sharp, well-defined boundaries. Link: Classification Techniques Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by texture lookups and blending, which is O(N) where N is the number of fragments/pixels. Memory Complexity: The 3D texture requires Dx \cdot Dy \cdot Dz \cdot 4 floats. Measured Performance: Performance is primarily limited by fill rate. On a GeForce FX chip (1.6 billion texels/sec), high zoom levels significantly decreased FPS due to increased fragment generation. Scaling: Performance degrades with higher zoom levels and higher data density (for alpha testing benefits). Strengths: Substantial performance improvements over standard ray casting; supports arbitrary transfer functions including isosurface effects; leverages hardware interpolation. Limitations: 3D texture access is slower than 2D; fill rate limited; pre-processing cost for transfer function changes; image quality can suffer from banding if 2D textures are used instead of 3D. When to use: When interactive performance is required and the transfer function is static or can be handled via partial pre-integration. When not: When the transfer function changes frequently without partial pre-integration, or when fill rate is the bottleneck and high zoom levels are expected. The method was introduced by Röttger et al.. It is part of the broader development of texture-based volume rendering techniques that utilize GPU hardware for acceleration. The approach builds on the idea of pre-integration to approximate the volume rendering integral, moving computation from the per-voxel ray casting step to a pre-process. It is often compared with other texture-based methods such as those by Engel, Kraus & Ertl and Weiler et al.. name: GPU Data Layout
body: GPU Data Layout defines the host-side memory structures and OpenGL resource IDs required to manage volumetric rendering state on the GPU. It solves the problem of organizing heterogeneous resources—3D scalar textures, 1D transfer function tables, and offscreen framebuffers—into a unified configuration object for raycasting mappers. It differs from Volume Texture Creation by focusing on the logical grouping and ID management of these resources rather than the API calls to generate them, and from Volume Texture Setup by handling the broader context including color tables and depth buffers. The layout organizes rendering state into specific arrays and integer IDs. The implementation must initialize these structures before passing them to the raycasting shader or framebuffer objects. Inputs and Outputs Input: Volumetric data dimensions, component count, and data type (constrained by mapper requirements). Output: A populated TextureObjects array and associated framebuffer/texture IDs. Data Structures The core layout is defined by the following fields: 1. TextureObjects: An array of 5 unsigned int values storing OpenGL texture IDs. Index 0: 3D scalar texture (volume data). Index 1: 1D color table (transfer function). Index 2: 1D opacity table (transfer function). Index 3: 2D grabbed depth buffer. Index 4: 2D color buffer. 2. MaxValueFrameBuffer and MaxValueFrameBuffer2: Two unsigned int framebuffer IDs used for ping-pong accumulation in MIP (Maximum Intensity Projection) mode. 3. BoundingBox: A double array of size 8 \times 3 storing the world coordinates of the 8 corners of the dataset bounding box. 4. FrameBufferObject: An unsigned int ID for the primary offscreen framebuffer object. 5. DepthRenderBufferObject: An unsigned int ID for the depth renderbuffer attached to the framebuffer. 6. NoiseTexture: A float array storing procedural noise data for speckle reduction. 7. NoiseTextureSize: An int specifying the 1D dimension size of the noise texture. 8. NoiseTextureId: An unsigned int OpenGL ID for the noise texture. 9. TextureCoord1toN: An array of vtkTransform pointers mapping texture coordinates from the primary volume to additional volumes. The size is MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES. Constraints and Validation Before finalizing the layout, the following constraints must be met: Scalar data must be single-component or four-component with non-independent components. If four-component data is used, the data type must be VTKUNSIGNEDCHAR (RGBA). Additive blend mode is only supported with single-component scalars. Pseudocode The following pseudocode demonstrates the initialization and validation of the GPU data layout structure. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializegpudatalayout(volumedata, blendmode): """ Initialize the GPU data layout structure for volume rendering. Args: volumedata: Object containing GetNumberOfComponents() and GetDataType(). blendmode: Integer constant for the blend mode (e.g., ADDITIVEBLEND). Returns: dict: The populated layout dictionary or None if validation fails. """ numcomponents = volumedata.GetNumberOfComponents() datatype = volumedata.GetDataType() # Validation: Component and Type Constraints # Only one component scalars, or four component with non-independent components, are supported. validcomponents = (numcomponents == 1) or (numcomponents == 4) # If 4 components, it must be unsigned char (RGBA) if numcomponents == 4 and datatype != VTKUNSIGNEDCHAR: return None # Additive mode only works with 1-component scalars if blendmode == ADDITIVEBLEND and numcomponents != 1: return None if not validcomponents: return None # Initialize Texture Objects Array (Size 5) # Indices: 0=3D Scalar, 1=1D Color, 2=1D Opacity, 3=2D Depth Grab, 4=2D Color Buffer textureobjects = [0] 5 # Initialize Framebuffer IDs for MIP ping-pong maxvalueframebuffer = 0 maxvalueframebuffer2 = 0 # Initialize Bounding Box (8 corners, 3 coords each) boundingbox = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(8)] # Initialize Framebuffer and Renderbuffer IDs framebufferobject = 0 depthrenderbufferobject = 0 # Initialize Noise Texture for speckle reduction noisetexturesize = 0 # Not given in the sources. noisetexture = [] # Float array noisetextureid = 0 # Initialize Coordinate Transforms for additional volumes # Size depends on MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES texturecoord1ton = [None] MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES layout = { "TextureObjects": textureobjects, "MaxValueFrameBuffer": maxvalueframebuffer, "MaxValueFrameBuffer2": maxvalueframebuffer2, "BoundingBox": boundingbox, "FrameBufferObject": framebufferobject, "DepthRenderBufferObject": depthrenderbufferobject, "NoiseTexture": noisetexture, "NoiseTextureSize": noisetexturesize, "NoiseTextureId": noisetextureid, "TextureCoord1toN": texturecoord1ton } return layout Transfers volumetric scalar data from host memory or binary files into GPU-accessible 3D textures. It differs by focusing on the data transfer mechanism rather than the logical layout organization. Stores 3D scalar fields in 2D textures using a tiling scheme. It differs by using 2D texture objects instead of native 3D textures for memory layout. Memory Complexity: The layout itself is lightweight, storing only IDs and small metadata arrays. The actual memory consumption is determined by the textures referenced by TextureObjects and NoiseTexture. Performance: Accessing the layout is O(1). The performance impact comes from the GPU operations referenced by the IDs (texture sampling, framebuffer blitting). Strengths: Centralizes resource management, simplifying the shader interface by using a single array of texture IDs. Limitations: Tightly coupled to OpenGL (uses unsigned int IDs). Not given in the sources. This layout structure originates from the VTK (Visualization Toolkit) Multi Volume Ray Caster implementation, specifically within the vtkGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper and related classes. It was developed to support multi-volume rendering and MIP accumulation on the GPU. bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, https://github.com/bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Texture Loading
head: LoadScalarField, Raw Volumetric Data Loading (8/16-bit)
body: GPU Texture Loading transfers volumetric scalar data from host memory or binary files into GPU-accessible 3D textures for raycasting. It solves the problem of efficiently moving dense grid data to the GPU while managing memory constraints and avoiding redundant transfers. It differs from Tiled 2D Texture Storage for 3D Fields by using native 3D texture objects rather than packing 3D data into 2D tile arrays, and from CUDA-accelerated Vector Field Reading with Magnitude by focusing on scalar fields rather than vector fields with magnitude pre-computation. Inputs: 1. Source data: Either a vtkImageData pointer containing point or cell scalars or a raw binary file path. 2. Extent: An array of six integers textureExtent[6] specifying the requested subextent in dataset coordinates. 3. Bit depth: A boolean flag is16Bits determining if data is 8-bit (uint8) or 16-bit (uint16). 4. Source type: An integer type where 0 indicates starting from GetAdditionalTransformedInput and 1 from GetInput. Outputs: A bound 3D texture object ready for sampling, with internal state variables LoadedExtent, LoadedBounds, LoadedCellFlag, and LoadedTime updated. Data Structures: Buffer: A std::vector<uint8t> or std::vector<uint16t> sized to the exact file size or data volume. Texture (OpenGL): Internal format GLRED, swizzle mask (R, R, R, R), data type GLUNSIGNEDBYTE or GLUNSIGNEDSHORT, filter GLLINEAR, wrapping GLCLAMPTOBORDER. Texture (CUDA): cudaArray with cudaChannelFormatDesc for ushort (or appropriate type), bound to a cudaTextureObject. Steps: 1. Cache Check: If the input pointer has not changed, the cell flag is unchanged, and the requested textureExtent is enclosed within the currently LoadedExtent, return success immediately without reloading. 2. Data Acquisition: VTK Path: Retrieve scalars from the input using GetScalars. Validate that scalars exist and are not field data (only point or cell scalars are supported). Binary Path: Open the file in binary mode. Determine size using file.tellg(). Allocate a buffer of that size. Read the entire file into the buffer. 3. Texture Creation & Upload: OpenGL: Create a 3D texture with GLRED internal format. Set filtering to GLLINEAR and wrapping to GLCLAMPTOBORDER. Set the swizzle mask to (R, R, R, R) to ensure all components return the scalar value. Upload the buffer data to the texture. CUDA: Copy dimensions to device symbol dataDim. Create a 3D array using cudaMalloc3DArray with the appropriate channel format (e.g., ushort). Copy host data to the 3D array using cudaMemcpy3D with cudaMemcpyHostToDevice. Set texture parameters: cudaFilterModeLinear, address modes cudaAddressModeClamp for all axes. Bind the array to the texture object using cudaBindTextureToArray. 4. State Update: Update LoadedExtent, LoadedBounds, LoadedCellFlag, and LoadedTime to reflect the new data. Pseudocode (OpenGL Variant): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def loadvolumetexturegl(filepath, is16bits, textureextent, loadedextent, cellflag): # Cache check: if input unchanged, cell flag unchanged, and extent enclosed, succeed # Sources do not specify exact caching comparison logic if inputunchanged and cellflagunchanged and enclosed(textureextent, loadedextent, cellflag): return True # Binary path: open file, get size, allocate buffer, read filesize = os.path.getsize(filepath) buffer = bytearray(filesize) with open(filepath, 'rb') as f: f.readinto(buffer) # Texture creation gltype = GLUNSIGNEDSHORT if is16bits else GLUNSIGNEDBYTE internalformat = GLRED datatypecode = GLRED texid = glGenTextures(1) glBindTexture(GLTEXTURE3D, texid) glTexStorage3D(GLTEXTURE3D, 1, internalformat, textureextent[1] - textureextent[0] + 1, textureextent[3] - textureextent[2] + 1, textureextent[5] - textureextent[4] + 1) glTexSubImage3D(GLTEXTURE3D, 0, textureextent[0], textureextent[2], textureextent[4], textureextent[1] - textureextent[0] + 1, textureextent[3] - textureextent[2] + 1, textureextent[5] - textureextent[4] + 1, datatypecode, gltype, buffer) glTexParameteri(GLTEXTURE3D, GLTEXTUREMINFILTER, GLLINEAR) glTexParameteri(GLTEXTURE3D, GLTEXTUREMAGFILTER, GLLINEAR) glTexParameteri(GLTEXTURE3D, GLTEXTUREWRAPS, GLCLAMPTOBORDER) glTexParameteri(GLTEXTURE3D, GLTEXTUREWRAPT, GLCLAMPTOBORDER) glTexParameteri(GLTEXTURE3D, GLTEXTUREWRAPR, GLCLAMPTOBORDER) glTexParameterIiv(GLTEXTURE3D, GLTEXTURESWIZZLERGBA, [GLRED, GLRED, GLRED, GLRED]) # Sources do not specify state update implementation updateloadedstate(textureextent, is16bits) return True Pseudocode (CUDA Variant): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def loadvolumetexturecuda(hostdata, dim): # Copy dimensions to device symbol cudaMemcpyToSymbol(dataDim, dim, sizeof(cudaExtent)) # Create 3D array with ushort channel format channeldesc = cudaCreateChannelDescushort() cudaMalloc3DArray(dataArray, channeldesc, dim) # Copy data from host to 3D array copyparams = makecudaMemcpy3DParms() copyparams.srcPtr = makecudaPitchedPtr(hostdata, dim.width sizeof(ushort), dim.width, dim.height) copyparams.dstArray = dataArray copyparams.extent = dim copyparams.kind = cudaMemcpyHostToDevice cudaMemcpy3D(copyparams) # Set texture parameters dataTex.normalized = False dataTex.filterMode = cudaFilterModeLinear dataTex.addressMode[0] = cudaAddressModeClamp dataTex.addressMode[1] = cudaAddressModeClamp dataTex.addressMode[2] = cudaAddressModeClamp # Bind array to texture object cudaBindTextureToArray(dataTex, dataArray, channeldesc) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: VRAM Exhaustion: Returns false if GPU memory allocation fails. Extent Validation: If CellFlag is true, extent bounds use <= comparison; if false, strict < comparison is required for all three axes. Data Type Mismatch: Using GLRED internal format requires matching swizzle and data type to avoid interpretation errors. Field Scalars: Field data scalars are not supported; only point or cell scalars are valid. A technique to read 3D vector field values at arbitrary positions using CUDA 3D textures with linear interpolation, storing vector magnitude in the fourth component of a float4 to avoid recomputation. It differs from standard scalar loading by encoding vector magnitude directly into the texture's alpha channel during loading, allowing shaders to access magnitude without computing length() at runtime. Choose this when performance-critical shaders require frequent magnitude checks. See CUDA-accelerated Vector Field Reading with Magnitude. Loads 3D volume data into a CUDA 3D array and binds it to a texture object for GPU access. Steps include copying data dimensions to a device symbol dataDim, creating a 3D array with a ushort channel format, copying host data to the 3D array using cudaMemcpy3D, setting texture parameters to linear filter and clamp address mode, and binding the 3D array to a texture object dataTex. Time Complexity: O(N) for data transfer, where N is the number of voxels. Cache hit is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the GPU texture storage. Performance: Depends on PCIe bandwidth for host-to-device transfer. CUDA cudaMemcpy3D may offer optimized paths for aligned data. Strengths: Simple API, direct mapping to volume raycasting shaders. Limitations: Loads entire subextents; not suitable for extremely large volumes without tiling. VRAM constrained. When to use: Small to medium volumes, or when subextents are fully enclosed in memory. When not to use: Volumes exceeding available VRAM, or when dynamic streaming of sparse data is required. Used in scientific visualization and medical imaging applications requiring real-time volume rendering. Developed alongside VTK's multi-volume raycasting implementations, raw binary loading for custom OpenGL/Cinder-based raycasters, and CUDA-based volume rendering pipelines. bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, https://github.com/bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, https://github.com/jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ojaisnielsen/dtu-2010-cuda-volume-rendering, https://github.com/ojaisnielsen/dtu-2010-cuda-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: CUDA-accelerated Vector Field Reading with Magnitude
head: Float4 Vector Texture Binding, Vector Field Texture Loading
body: This method enables fast, linearly interpolated reading of 3D vector field values at arbitrary positions using CUDA 3D textures. It differs from standard scalar texture loading by storing precomputed vector magnitudes in the fourth component of a float4 structure to avoid redundant calculations during rendering. Inputs: A host-side 3D vector field dataset (typically from an NRRD file) containing (x, y, z) components per grid point, along with grid dimensions (width, height, depth). Outputs: A bound CUDA texture object (vectorFieldTex) ready for sampling in device kernels. Data Structures: 1. Host Data Buffer: A 1D array of float4 with size N = width \times height \times depth. Each element stores (vx, vy, vz, |v|), where |v| is the precomputed magnitude. 2. Device Array: A cudaArray allocated with a channel descriptor for float4. 3. Texture Object: A texture<float4, cudaTextureType3D, cudaReadModeElementType> object. Steps: 1. Precompute Magnitude: Iterate through the raw vector data. For each vector \mathbf{v} = (vx, vy, vz), compute the magnitude m = \sqrt{vx^2 + vy^2 + vz^2} and store it in the w component of a float4 structure. 2. Allocate Device Memory: Create a channel descriptor for float4 and allocate a 3D array on the GPU using cudaMalloc3DArray. 3. Copy Data to GPU: Use cudaMemcpy3D with a pitched source pointer to copy the host float4 array to the device 3D array. The pitch is width sizeof(float4). 4. Configure Texture Object: Set normalized = false (coordinates in texel space), filterMode = cudaFilterModeLinear (trilinear interpolation), and addressMode[0..2] = cudaAddressModeClamp (clamp to boundaries). 5. Bind Texture: Bind the device array to the texture object using cudaBindTextureToArray. 6. Sample Vector: In a device kernel, read the vector at position (x, y, z) using tex3D(vectorFieldTex, x, y, z), which returns a float4 containing the interpolated direction and precomputed magnitude. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def prepareandloadvectorfield(hostvectors3d, width, height, depth): # 1. Precompute magnitude and pack into float4 array totalsize = width height depth hostfloat4array = [None] totalsize for i in range(totalsize): vx = hostvectors3d[i 3] vy = hostvectors3d[i 3 + 1] vz = hostvectors3d[i 3 + 2] mag = math.sqrt(vx vx + vy vy + vz vz) hostfloat4array[i] = (vx, vy, vz, mag) # 2. Allocate device 3D array with float4 channel format channeldesc = 'float4' volumesize = (width, height, depth) dvolumearray = cudaMalloc3DArray(channeldesc, volumesize) # 3. Copy host data to device using pitched pointer pitch = width 16 # sizeof(float4) is 16 bytes srcptr = makecudaPitchedPtr(hostfloat4array, pitch, width, height) copyparams = { 'srcPtr': srcptr, 'dstArray': dvolumearray, 'extent': volumesize, 'kind': 'cudaMemcpyHostToDevice' } cudaMemcpy3D(copyparams) # 4. Configure texture object vectorfieldtex = createtextureobject() vectorfieldtex.normalized = False vectorfieldtex.filtermode = 'linear' vectorfieldtex.addressmode = ['clamp', 'clamp', 'clamp'] # 5. Bind 3D array to texture cudaBindTextureToArray(vectorfieldtex, dvolumearray, channeldesc) return vectorfieldtex def samplevectorfield(tex, x, y, z): # 6. Sample vector at arbitrary position return tex3D(tex, x, y, z) Parameters: Memory Overhead: Increases memory consumption by 1/3 compared to storing only float3 vectors. Interpolation: Linear (trilinear). Boundary Handling: Clamp. Pitfalls: CUDA Texture Type Limitations: CUDA 3D textures do not support float3 channel formats directly; only float1, float2, or float4 are supported. This necessitates the use of float4 with the fourth component used for magnitude (or padding). Memory Constraints: The 1/3 memory increase can be significant for large datasets on GPUs with limited memory. Time Complexity: Reading a vector is O(1) per query, involving a single texture fetch with hardware-accelerated trilinear interpolation. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of grid points, but with a constant factor of 4 floats per point instead of 3. Performance: Significantly speeds up visualization compared to CPU-side interpolation or magnitude computation per sample. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated interpolation; precomputed magnitude avoids redundant square root calculations in the rendering loop. Limitations: Increased memory footprint; requires pre-processing step to compute magnitudes. When to use: Real-time visualization of 3D vector fields where performance is critical and GPU memory is sufficient. When not to use: When GPU memory is extremely constrained and magnitude is not needed for visualization. This technique was described by Marek Fiser in the context of real-time visualization of 3D vector fields using CUDA. It leverages the CUDA runtime API's support for 3D textures to handle the discrete nature of volumetric data, which requires interpolation for arbitrary query points. The approach of storing magnitude in the fourth component is a workaround for the lack of float3 texture support in CUDA at the time of writing. name: Tiled 2D Texture Storage for 3D Fields
head: 2D Texture Tiling for 3D Fields, Tiled 2D Texture Storage
body: A technique to store a 3D scalar field in a 2D texture by tiling the 3D volume into 2D slices, allowing efficient GPU access via texture lookups. It maps 3D coordinates to 2D texture coordinates using a tiling scheme where the Z-coordinate determines the tile position, enabling standard 2D texture sampling hardware to access volumetric data. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar field of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Input: tilesX, the number of tiles along the X-axis of the 2D texture. Output: A 2D texture of dimensions W \times H containing the tiled volume data. Data Structures The 2D texture is organized as a grid of tiles. Each tile corresponds to a slice of the 3D volume. Bit packing and exact field layouts are not given in the sources. Parameters tilesX: The number of tiles along the X-axis of the 2D texture. It determines the tiling layout. gridSize: The resolution of the volume in the X and Y dimensions, used to calculate texture coordinates. Mapping Formula To map a 3D coordinate (x, y, z) to 2D texture coordinates (u, v): 1. Calculate the tile indices for the Z-coordinate: tileX = z \pmod{tilesX} tileY = \lfloor z / tilesX \rfloor 2. Calculate the texture coordinates: u = tileX \cdot gridSize + x v = tileY \cdot gridSize + y Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def map3dto2dtexture(x, y, z, tilesX, gridSize): """ Maps 3D volume coordinates to 2D texture coordinates. Args: x: X coordinate in volume (0 <= x < gridSize) y: Y coordinate in volume (0 <= y < gridSize) z: Z coordinate in volume (0 <= z < Nz) tilesX: Number of tiles along X-axis of the 2D texture gridSize: Spatial resolution of the volume in X and Y dimensions Returns: (u, v): 2D texture coordinates """ # Bounds checking not given in sources tileX = z % tilesX tileY = z // tilesX u = tileX gridSize + x v = tileY gridSize + y return u, v Edge Cases and Pitfalls Not given in the sources. What it is: Renders a 3D scalar field by storing Z-slices in a tiled 2D texture grid, allowing 3D sampling via 2D texture lookups and trilinear interpolation. What sets it apart: Differs from standard 3D texture sampling by mapping 3D coordinates to a 2D atlas, requiring explicit slice indexing and offset calculation in the shader. When to choose: Choose it when leveraging 2D texture hardware for volume rendering is required. Link: 2D Texture-Based Volume Rendering with Z-Slice Packing What it is: A real-time GPU-accelerated technique for rendering 3D volumetric data (specifically point clouds or scalar fields) by storing the volume in a 2D texture atlas and rendering it as a point cloud where each point represents a voxel/sample. What sets it apart: Differs from standard volume rendering by encoding the depth of each sample in the atlas layout to allow correct sorting and rendering order without traditional depth buffering for the volume itself. When to choose: Choose it for real-time point cloud or scalar field rendering on constrained hardware. Link: Point Cloud Volumetric Rendering via 2D Atlas Not given in the sources. name: 2D Texture-Based Volume Rendering with Z-Slice Packing
head: 2D Texture Z-Slice Packing, Z-Slice Packing
body: This method renders a 3D scalar field by storing its Z-slices in a tiled 2D texture grid, allowing 3D sampling via 2D texture lookups and trilinear interpolation. It differs from standard 3D texture sampling by mapping 3D coordinates to a 2D atlas, requiring explicit slice indexing and offset calculation in the shader. It builds on Tiled 2D Texture Storage for 3D Fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume of Nz slices (typically 256), stored in a 2D texture of size W \times H. Input: Camera matrices (projection, model-view) and ray marching parameters. Output: Final color and opacity per fragment. Data Structures: cubeTex: A 2D texture containing the volume data. For 256 slices arranged in a 16 \times 16 grid within a 256 \times 256 texture, each slice occupies a 16 \times 16 pixel region. transferTex: A 1D or 2D texture mapping opacity (alpha) to RGB color. rtTexture: A render target texture storing world-space coordinates of the ray entry point (back face). Numbered Steps: 1. First Pass (Back Face): Render the back face of the volume bounding box to rtTexture to store world-space coordinates of the ray entry point. 2. Second Pass (Front Face & Ray Marching): a. Ray Initialization: Determine the ray origin (front face) and direction. Retrieve the back position from rtTexture using NearestFilter to avoid interpolation artifacts at edges. If the back position is invalid ((0,0,0)), discard the fragment. b. Step Calculation: Calculate the step size. The maximum distance through the volume is \sqrt{3} (normalized cube diagonal). The step size in world units is derived from the total ray length and the number of steps. c. Loop: Iterate through the ray steps up to a fixed limit. d. Texture Coordinate Mapping: For the current ray position, calculate the 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w). e. Slice Indexing: Determine the integer Z-slice index and the next slice index for interpolation: z1 = \lfloor w \cdot 255.0 \rfloor and z2 = \min(z1 + 1.0, 255.0). f. Z-Interpolation Factor: Compute the fractional Z-distance: z{diff} = \text{mod}(w \cdot 255.0, 1.0). g. 2D Coordinate Offset: Map the 3D coordinates to the 2D texture atlas by dividing the base UV by the grid size (16.0) and adding offsets based on the slice index: u1 = \frac{u}{16.0} + \frac{\text{mod}(z1, 16.0)}{16.0}, v1 = \frac{v}{16.0} + \frac{\lfloor \frac{255.0 - z1}{16.0} \rfloor}{16.0}, and similarly for (u2, v2). h. Sampling: Sample the volume texture at (u1, v1) and (u2, v2) using bilinear filtering to get colors/alphas C1 and C2. i. Z-Interpolation: Interpolate between C1 and C2 using z{diff}. j. Transfer Function: Map the resulting alpha to the transfer function texture to get RGB color. k. Alpha Accumulation: Update accumulated alpha and color using front-to-back blending with a correction factor. Formulas: Ray Direction Increment: \Delta \vec{d} = \text{normalize}(\vec{d}) \cdot \delta, where \delta = 1.0 / \text{steps}. Alpha Correction: \alpha{sample} = \alpha{raw} \cdot \alpha{correction} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{accumulated}) \cdot \alpha{scale\factor}, where \alpha{scale\factor} = 25.6 \cdot \delta. Parameters: steps: Number of ray marching steps. Default 256.0, range 0.0–512.0. MAXSTEPS: Loop limit to prevent clipping. Set to 887 to handle diagonal viewing. alphaCorrection: User-adjustable transparency intensity. Default 1.0, range 0.01–5.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderfragment(frontpos, backpos, steps, alphacorrection): # Pitfall: Discard if back position is invalid if backpos == (0.0, 0.0, 0.0): return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Guard against division by zero if steps <= 0: steps = 1.0 # Ray setup dirvec = (backpos[0] - frontpos[0], backpos[1] - frontpos[1], backpos[2] - frontpos[2]) dist = math.sqrt(dirvec[0]2 + dirvec[1]2 + dirvec[2]2) delta = 1.0 / steps stepdir = (dirvec[0] / dist delta, dirvec[1] / dist delta, dirvec[2] / dist delta) acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 MAXSTEPS = 887 for i in range(MAXSTEPS): if accalpha >= 1.0: break pos = (frontpos[0] + stepdir[0] i, frontpos[1] + stepdir[1] i, frontpos[2] + stepdir[2] i) zcoord = pos[2] z1 = math.floor(zcoord 255.0) z2 = min(z1 + 1.0, 255.0) zdiff = math.fmod(zcoord 255.0, 1.0) u, v = pos[0], pos[1] uv1 = (u / 16.0 + math.fmod(z1, 16.0) / 16.0, v / 16.0 + math.floor((255.0 - z1) / 16.0) / 16.0) uv2 = (u / 16.0 + math.fmod(z2, 16.0) / 16.0, v / 16.0 + math.floor((255.0 - z2) / 16.0) / 16.0) # Standard 2D texture lookup with bilinear filtering color1 = texturelookup(cubeTex, uv1) color2 = texturelookup(cubeTex, uv2) colorslice = (color1[0] + (color2[0] - color1[0]) zdiff, color1[1] + (color2[1] - color1[1]) zdiff, color1[2] + (color2[2] - color1[2]) zdiff, color1[3] + (color2[3] - color1[3]) zdiff) tfcolor = texturelookup(transferTex, (colorslice[3], 1.0)) finalcolor = (tfcolor[0], tfcolor[1], tfcolor[2]) alpha = colorslice[3] alphascalefactor = 25.6 delta alphasample = alpha alphacorrection (1.0 - accalpha) alphascalefactor acccolor = (acccolor[0] + finalcolor[0] alphasample, acccolor[1] + finalcolor[1] alphasample, acccolor[2] + finalcolor[2] alphasample) accalpha += alphasample return (acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accalpha) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Edge Interpolation: Interpolated world coordinates from the first pass can produce bogus ray directions at cube edges. Use NearestFilter for rtTexture. Invalid Back Position: If the back position is (0,0,0), the fragment is discarded. Diagonal Clipping: The loop limit must exceed the maximum number of steps along the diagonal (\sqrt{3} \times \text{steps}). 887 is used for 512 max steps. Time Complexity: O(N{steps}) per fragment, where N{steps} is the number of ray marching steps. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the 2D texture, where W \cdot H = N{slices} \cdot \text{slice\width} \cdot \text{slice\height}. Performance: Efficient on GPUs due to 2D texture cache coherence and bilinear filtering. However, the overhead of calculating 2D offsets for 3D coordinates can be higher than direct 3D texture sampling. Strengths: Compatible with hardware that lacks efficient 3D texture support; leverages standard 2D texture units. Limitations: Requires two-pass rendering; manual slice indexing logic; potential precision issues at slice boundaries. This method is implemented in the provided codebase. It is an adaptation of tiled 2D texture storage for 3D fields, specifically tailored for web-based rendering where 3D textures may have limited support or performance characteristics. name: Point Cloud Volumetric Rendering via 2D Atlas
head: Point Cloud Volume, Volumetric Viewer
body: A real-time GPU-accelerated technique for rendering 3D volumetric data (specifically point clouds or scalar fields) by storing the volume in a 2D texture atlas and rendering it as a point cloud where each point represents a voxel/sample. The depth of each sample is encoded in the atlas layout to allow correct sorting and rendering order without traditional depth buffering for the volume itself. It achieves 60Hz on GTX1080 for a 4k atlas, while Intel 630 graphics render a 2k atlas at ~20fps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (volume) represented as a sequence of 2D slices (images) or a mathematical function. Output: A rendered point cloud visualization of the volume, where points are colored based on scalar value and positioned in 3D space. Data Structures: Atlas Texture: A 2D texture (GLTEXTURE2D) with GLRGBA format and GLNEAREST filtering. Atlas Layout: The 3D volume is tiled into a 2D grid. The atlas dimensions are defined by constants: SAMPLEWIDTH (2048) and WIDTH (128). The atlas is tiled into a grid of TILING x TILING blocks, where TILING is calculated as int(math.sqrt(len(volume))) or hardcoded as 16. Depth LUT: A lookup table (int depthLUT[TILING][TILING]) mapping tile coordinates to their linear depth index in the volume. Parameters: cutoffThreshold: A uniform float used as the minimum value for the RGB channels of the atlas sample to be considered part of the volume. Default initial value is 0.05 7 = 0.35. Can be adjusted with keys 'R' and 'T'. pointSize: A uniform float controlling the size of the rendered points. Default initial value is 1.0. Can be adjusted with keys 'Y' and 'H'. minVal and maxVal: Uniform floats defining the range for color remapping. maxVal is np.max(img) / 256.0. minVal is either cutoff (if minValAbsolute is false) or np.min(img) / 256.0 (if minValAbsolute is true). Steps: 1. Generate the Atlas: Convert the 3D volume data into a 2D texture atlas. If using an image sequence, read files sorted by name, create a tiling grid, and save the result. The viewer reads the data from bottom to up, left to right. The generated atlas must be rotated -90 degrees before use. 2. Load Atlas: Load the atlas image (e.g., brainatlas2k.png) and upload it to a 2D texture (GLTEXTURE2D) with GLRGBA format and GLNEAREST filtering. 3. Vertex Shader Processing: For each vertex (representing a pixel in the atlas), compute the 3D position. Calculate sample coordinate sCoord from glVertexID. Calculate tile coordinate tCoord and volume coordinate vCoord. Sample the atlas texture at sCoord. If the sample values (RGB) exceed the THRESHOLD (cutoffThreshold), return a 3D position: x = (u \mod 128 - 64) \times 2 y = (v \mod 128 - 64) \times 2 z = \text{depth}(\lfloor u/128 \rfloor, \lfloor v/128 \rfloor) - 128 where \text{depth}(x, y) is the linear index of the tile (x, y) in the atlas grid. 4. Color Remapping: In the vertex shader, if the sample is above threshold, remap its color. The grayscale value s (from sColor.x) is divided into three thirds based on minVal and maxVal. If s is in the first third, color is (s, 0, 0, alpha). If in the second third, (0, s, 0, alpha). If in the third third, (0, 0, s, alpha). Otherwise, white. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. SAMPLEWIDTH = 2048 WIDTH = 128 TILING = 16 maxVal = max(imgdata) / 256.0 minVal = min(imgdata) / 256.0 # or cutoffThreshold if minValAbsolute is false cutoffThreshold = 0.35 pointSize = 1.0 depthLUT = [[0] TILING for in range(TILING)] currentdepth = 0 for x in range(TILING): for y in range(TILING): depthLUT[x][y] = currentdepth currentdepth += 1 def getdepth(tilex, tiley): return depthLUT[tilex][tiley] def getsamplecoordinate(vertexid): x = vertexid % SAMPLEWIDTH y = vertexid // SAMPLEWIDTH return (float(x), float(y)) def getvolumecoordinate(scoord): x = int(scoord[0]) % WIDTH y = int(scoord[1]) % WIDTH return (float(x), float(y)) def gettile(samplecoord): x = int(samplecoord[0]) y = int(samplecoord[1]) tilex = x // WIDTH tiley = y // WIDTH return (tilex, tiley) def remapcolor(scolor, minval, maxval): s = scolor[0] alpha = scolor[3] third = (maxval - minval) / 3.0 fstthird = minval + third sndthird = minval + 2 third if s < fstthird: return (s, 0.0, 0.0, alpha) elif s < sndthird: return (0.0, s, 0.0, alpha) elif s <= maxval: return (0.0, 0.0, s, alpha) else: return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, alpha) # white def mainrenderloop(atlasarray): # For each vertex in the atlas (total pixels = SAMPLEWIDTH SAMPLEWIDTH) for vertexid in range(SAMPLEWIDTH SAMPLEWIDTH): scoord = getsamplecoordinate(vertexid) vcoord = getvolumecoordinate(scoord) tcoord = gettile(scoord) # Sample the atlas texture (direct array access for pseudocode) scolor = atlasarray[int(scoord[1])][int(scoord[0])] # Check threshold if scolor[0] > cutoffThreshold and scolor[1] > cutoffThreshold and scolor[2] > cutoffThreshold: # Compute 3D position x = (vcoord[0] - 64.0) 2.0 y = (vcoord[1] - 64.0) 2.0 z = float(getdepth(tcoord[0], tcoord[1])) - 128.0 # Remap color finalcolor = remapcolor(scolor, minVal, maxVal) # Emit point primitive outputpoint(x, y, z, finalcolor, pointSize) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: On Windows, depth rendering might fail due to a known bug in the implementation. Linux with supported hardware is recommended. Changing between 2k and 4k atlases doesn't change the quality drastically, but reduces the framerate significantly. Use what you can get away with. The program requires GLSL 3.30 ES support. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering, achieving 60Hz on GTX1080 for a 4k atlas. Memory Complexity: Depends on the atlas size. 2k atlas renders at ~20fps on Intel 630 graphics. Strengths: Real-time performance, simple implementation using point clouds, no need for complex ray marching or volume accumulation. Limitations: Quality does not improve significantly with larger atlases, but performance degrades. Windows compatibility issues with depth rendering. When to use: When real-time visualization of volumetric data is required and hardware supports GLSL 3.30 ES. When not to use: When high-quality volume rendering (e.g., ray marching) is needed, or on Windows systems with known depth rendering bugs. This method is part of "A Real-Time GPU Accelerated 3D Point Cloud Based Volumetric Viewer" done with python and OpenGL. It was tested on Ubuntu 19.04, Manjaro and OpenSuse Tumbleweed with the latest (43x) NVidia drivers. teo3n/pointcloudvolumetric, https://github.com/teo3n/pointcloudvolumetric, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: ClearView Unified Buffer Construction
head: ClearView Buffer Construction
body: ClearView Unified Buffer Construction is a preprocessing technique that converts a hexahedral mesh (positions, connectivity, scalars) into four GPU-friendly texture buffers (vertices, edges, faces, cellScalar) for the ClearView volume rendering pipeline. It sets itself apart from siblings like GPU Data Layout by explicitly organizing topology into a "unified" set of textures optimized for the specific gather/resolve passes of the ClearView renderer, rather than generic storage. Inputs: Hexahedral mesh with Nc cells. Vertex positions: array of size Nv \times 3 (floats). Cell connectivity: array of size Nc \times 8 (uint32 vertex indices). Cell scalars: array of size Nc (floats). Outputs: Four 2D textures: 1. vertexTex: Stores vertex indices for faces. 2. edgeTex: Stores edge attributes and LOD. 3. faceTex: Stores vertex and edge indices for faces. 4. cellScalarTex: Stores average scalar values for faces. Data Structures and Layouts: Edges Texture (edgeTex): Format: RG32F (Float32Array). Dimensions: Width We, Height He determined by texDims(edgeCount). Total texels: Ne = Nc \times 12. Linear index for edge e in cell c: L = c \times 12 + e. Column: col = L \pmod{We}. Row: row = \lfloor L / We \rfloor. Texel index: ti = (row \times We + col) \times 2. Values: edgeTex[ti] = \max(\text{scalars}[p{ia}], \text{scalars}[p{ib}]) where p{ia}, p{ib} are the two vertices of the edge. edgeTex[ti+1] = 1 - \text{normScalar} (computed below). Faces Texture (faceTex): Format: RG32UI (Uint32Array). Dimensions: Width Wf = 2, Height Hf = Nf = Nc \times 6. Two texels per face. Linear texel index for face f in cell c: t{linear} = (c \times 6 + f) \times 2. Texel 0 (Vertex Indices):.r,.g,.b,.a store the 4 vertex indices of the face. Texel 1 (Edge Indices):.r,.g,.b,.a store the 4 edge indices of the face. Mapping: Vertex indices: c \times 8 + \text{face.corners}[0..3]. Edge indices: c \times 12 + \text{face.edges}[0..3]. Cell Scalar Texture (cellScalarTex): Format: R32F (Float32Array). Dimensions: Width Ws, Height Hs determined by texDims(faceCount). 1 texel per face. Linear index: Ls = c \times 6 + f. Column: col = Ls \pmod{Ws}. Row: row = \lfloor Ls / Ws \rfloor. Value: cellScalarTex[row Ws + col] = \text{cellScalarAvg}. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Scalar Range: s{min} = \min(\text{mesh.scalars}) s{max} = \max(\text{mesh.scalars}) s{range} = \max(s{max} - s{min}, 10^{-9}) 2. Compute Edge LOD and Cell Scalar Average: For each cell c: \text{cellScalarAvg}c = \frac{1}{8} \sum{i=0}^{7} \text{scalars}[\text{cell.corners}[i]] \text{normScalar}c = \frac{\text{cellScalarAvg}c - s{min}}{s{range}} \text{edgeLod}c = 1 - \text{normScalar}c Note: The source notes imply edgeLod is constant per cell for all its edges, or potentially per edge if corner scalars vary, but the formula uses cellScalarAvg. The edge texture stores 1 - normScalar. 3. Populate Edge Texture: For each cell c and its 12 edges e: Identify vertices p{ia}, p{ib} of edge e. Calculate linear index L = c \times 12 + e. Calculate texture coordinates (col, row) from L. Calculate texel index ti = (row \times We + col) \times 2. Set edgeTex[ti] = \max(\text{scalars}[p{ia}], \text{scalars}[p{ib}]). Set edgeTex[ti+1] = \text{edgeLod}c. 4. Populate Face Texture: For each cell c and its 6 faces f: Calculate face ID: faceId = c \times 6 + f. Get face geometry: face = HEXFACES[f]. Calculate linear texel indices: t0{linear} = faceId \times 2 + 0 t1{linear} = faceId \times 2 + 1 Calculate texture coordinates for t0{linear}: col = t0{linear} \pmod{Wf} row = \lfloor t0{linear} / Wf \rfloor ti = (row \times Wf + col) \times 4 Set faceTex[ti+0..3] = [c \times 8 + \text{face.corners}[0], c \times 8 + \text{face.corners}[1], c \times 8 + \text{face.corners}[2], c \times 8 + \text{face.corners}[3]]. Calculate texture coordinates for t1{linear}: col = t1{linear} \pmod{Wf} row = \lfloor t1{linear} / Wf \rfloor ti = (row \times Wf + col) \times 4 Set faceTex[ti+4..7] = [c \times 12 + \text{face.edges}[0], c \times 12 + \text{face.edges}[1], c \times 12 + \text{face.edges}[2], c \times 12 + \text{face.edges}[3]]. 5. Populate Cell Scalar Texture: For each cell c and its 6 faces f: Calculate linear index Ls = c \times 6 + f. Calculate texture coordinates: col = Ls \pmod{Ws} row = \lfloor Ls / Ws \rfloor Set cellScalarTex[row Ws + col] = \text{cellScalarAvg}c. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clearviewbufferconstruction(mesh): """ mesh: object with attributes positions: list of [x,y,z] for each vertex cells: list of [v0, v1,..., v7] vertex indices for each cell scalars: list of float scalar values for each cell """ Nc = len(mesh.cells) Nv = len(mesh.positions) # Hexahedral face definitions (indices into cell corners 0..7) # Standard hexahedron faces: # 0: 0,1,2,3 (bottom) # 1: 4,5,6,7 (top) # 2: 0,1,5,4 (front) # 3: 2,3,7,6 (back) # 4: 0,3,7,4 (left) # 5: 1,2,6,5 (right) HEXFACES = [ [0, 1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6, 7], [0, 1, 5, 4], [2, 3, 7, 6], [0, 3, 7, 4], [1, 2, 6, 5] ] # Hexahedral edge definitions (indices into cell corners) # 12 edges per cell HEXEDGES = [ [0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 0], # Bottom ring [4, 5], [5, 6], [6, 7], [7, 4], # Top ring [0, 4], [1, 5], [2, 6], [3, 7] # Verticals ] # Step 1: Scalar Range smin = min(mesh.scalars) smax = max(mesh.scalars) srange = max(smax - smin, 1e-9) # Precompute cell scalar averages and LODs cellavgscalars = [] celledgelods = [] for c in range(Nc): corners = mesh.cells[c] avg = sum(mesh.scalars[corners[i]] for i in range(8)) / 8.0 cellavgscalars.append(avg) normscalar = (avg - smin) / srange celledgelods.append(1.0 - normscalar) # Determine texture dimensions # Helper to find power-of-two or suitable dimension def texdims(count): # Simple implementation: find width/height such that widthheight >= count # For simplicity, assume square-ish or specific layout as per source # Source implies width/height determined by texDims(edgeCount) etc. # We will assume a simple row-major packing where width is chosen to fit # For exact implementation, one might use a specific texture dimensioning function. # Here we assume a generic function that returns (w, h) return gettexturedimensions(count) # Step 2: Edge Texture Ne = Nc 12 We, He = texdims(Ne) edgetex = [0.0] (Ne 2) # RG32F -> 2 floats per texel for c in range(Nc): lod = celledgelods[c] for e in range(12): vindices = HEXEDGES[e] v0 = mesh.cells[c][vindices[0]] v1 = mesh.cells[c][vindices[1]] scalarmax = max(mesh.scalars[v0], mesh.scalars[v1]) linearidx = c 12 + e col = linearidx % We row = linearidx // We ti = (row We + col) 2 edgetex[ti] = scalarmax edgetex[ti + 1] = lod # Step 3: Face Texture Nf = Nc 6 Wf = 2 Hf = Nf facetex = [0] (Nf 2 4) # RG32UI -> 2 texels per face, 4 uints per texel for c in range(Nc): for f in range(6): faceid = c 6 + f facecorners = HEXFACES[f] faceedges = HEXEDGES[f] # Note: source says face.edges[0..3], mapping to HEXEDGES indices # Vertex indices texel (Texel 0) t0linear = faceid 2 + 0 col0 = t0linear % Wf row0 = t0linear // Wf ti0 = (row0 Wf + col0) 4 vbase = c 8 facetex[ti0 + 0] = vbase + facecorners[0] facetex[ti0 + 1] = vbase + facecorners[1] facetex[ti0 + 2] = vbase + facecorners[2] facetex[ti0 + 3] = vbase + facecorners[3] # Edge indices texel (Texel 1) t1linear = faceid 2 + 1 col1 = t1linear % Wf row1 = t1linear // Wf ti1 = (row1 Wf + col1) 4 ebase = c 12 facetex[ti1 + 0] = ebase + faceedges[0] facetex[ti1 + 1] = ebase + faceedges[1] facetex[ti1 + 2] = ebase + faceedges[2] facetex[ti1 + 3] = ebase + faceedges[3] # Step 4: Cell Scalar Texture # 1 texel per face Ws, Hs = texdims(Nf) cellscalartex = [0.0] (Nf) for c in range(Nc): for f in range(6): faceid = c 6 + f col = faceid % Ws row = faceid // Ws cellscalartex[row Ws + col] = cellavgscalars[c] return { 'edgeTex': edgetex, 'faceTex': facetex, 'cellScalarTex': cellscalartex, 'vertexTex': None, # Vertex positions are typically stored separately or implied 'smin': smin, 'smax': smax } def gettexturedimensions(count): # Placeholder for specific texture dimensioning logic # In WebGL, textures are often 2D. A simple approach is sqrt(count) import math dim = math.ceil(math.sqrt(count)) return dim, dim Parameters: srange minimum: 10^{-9}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Scalar Range: If s{max} == s{min}, s{range} is clamped to 10^{-9} to prevent division by zero. Texture Dimensions: The exact method for determining texDims (width/height) is not specified beyond "determined by texDims". Implementers must ensure the texture dimensions can hold the required number of texels without overflow. Edge Indexing: The mapping of face.edges to the global edge array assumes a consistent ordering of the 12 edges per cell. The HEXEDGES definition must match the renderer's expectations. Time Complexity: O(Nc), where Nc is the number of cells. Each cell processes a constant number of faces (6) and edges (12). Memory Complexity: O(Nc). The textures store data proportional to the number of faces and edges. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Organizes hexahedral topology into a format directly consumable by the ClearView gather/resolve shaders. Uses standard GPU texture formats (RG32F, RG32UI, R32F) for efficient sampling. Limitations: Specific to hexahedral meshes. Requires preprocessing step before rendering. When to use: When using the ClearView volume rendering pipeline with hexahedral data. When not to use: For tetrahedral meshes or non-hexahedral volumes. It is part of a larger pipeline that includes focus controls and ray-marching shaders.
