name: 3D Texture Upload
head: 3D Texture Upload for Volume Data, GL_TEXTURE_3D volume upload, Volume Texture Binding
body: This method transfers classified volume data from host memory to GPU memory by populating an OpenGL GLTEXTURE3D object. It solves the problem of preparing dense voxel grids for GPU-accelerated raycasting or slicing by ensuring correct memory layout, alignment, and filtering parameters. Inputs: Classified volume data: A contiguous block of memory containing voxel values, typically GLRGBA (4 bytes per voxel) or GLRED (1 byte per voxel). Dimensions: Width (W), height (H), depth (D) representing the volume grid dimensions. Outputs: A bound OpenGL texture object (GLTEXTURE3D) ready for sampling in shaders. Data Structures: 1. Host Buffer: If the source is a nested array (e.g., stack[x][y][z]), it must be flattened into a 1D array. Layout: x is the fastest varying index, y is the middle, and z is the slowest. Stride: stridey = W, stridez = W \times H. Total size: W \times H \times D bytes for 8-bit data. 2. GPU Texture: Target: GLTEXTURE3D. Internal Format: GLRGBA for classified RGBA data or GLR8 for scalar density. Format: GLRGBA or GLRED. Type: GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. Steps: 1. Generate and Bind: Generate a texture ID and bind it to GLTEXTURE3D. 2. Set Wrapping: Configure wrap modes for S, T, and R coordinates to GLCLAMP or GLCLAMPTOEDGE. 3. Set Filtering: Set magnification filter to GLLINEAR and minification filter to GLLINEARMIPMAPLINEAR or GLLINEAR. 4. Set Mipmap Levels: Set base level to 0 and max level to 4. 5. Set Unpack Alignment: Set GLUNPACKALIGNMENT to 1 to match the host array's byte alignment. 6. Upload Data: Call glTexImage3D with the dimensions and data pointer. 7. Generate Mipmaps: If the minification filter requires mipmaps, call glGenerateMipmap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uploadvolumetexture(gl, data, width, height, depth, internalformat, format, typeenum, usemipmaps=False): # 1. Generate and bind texture texid = gl.glGenTextures(1) gl.glBindTexture(gl.GLTEXTURE3D, texid) # 2. Set wrapping modes # Sources disagree: uses GLCLAMP, uses GLCLAMPTOEDGE. gl.glTexParameteri(gl.GLTEXTURE3D, gl.GLTEXTUREWRAPS, gl.GLCLAMPTOEDGE) gl.glTexParameteri(gl.GLTEXTURE3D, gl.GLTEXTUREWRAPT, gl.GLCLAMPTOEDGE) gl.glTexParameteri(gl.GLTEXTURE3D, gl.GLTEXTUREWRAPR, gl.GLCLAMPTOEDGE) # 3. Set filtering # Sources disagree: uses GLLINEARMIPMAPLINEAR, uses GLLINEAR. gl.glTexParameteri(gl.GLTEXTURE3D, gl.GLTEXTUREMINFILTER, gl.GLLINEAR) gl.glTexParameteri(gl.GLTEXTURE3D, gl.GLTEXTUREMAGFILTER, gl.GLLINEAR) # 4. Set mipmap levels gl.glTexParameteri(gl.GLTEXTURE3D, gl.GLTEXTUREMAXLEVEL, 4) # 5. Set unpack alignment gl.glPixelStorei(gl.GLUNPACKALIGNMENT, 1) # 6. Upload data gl.glTexImage3D( gl.GLTEXTURE3D, 0, # level internalformat, # internalformat width, # width height, # height depth, # depth 0, # border format, # format typeenum, # type data # pixels) # 7. Generate mipmaps if required if usemipmaps: gl.glGenerateMipmap(gl.GLTEXTURE3D) return texid Parameters: width, height, depth: Dimensions of the volume grid. internalformat: GLRGBA for 4-channel classified data or GLR8 for single-channel scalar data. format: GLRGBA or GLRED. type: GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. GLUNPACKALIGNMENT: Set to 1 for byte-aligned data. Edge Cases: Alignment: GLUNPACKALIGNMENT must be set to 1 to match host array byte alignment. Mipmap Consistency: If GLLINEARMIPMAPLINEAR is used, mipmaps must be generated; otherwise, sampling may fail or return undefined values. Data Flattening: If the source data is a nested array (e.g., stack[x][y][z]), it must be flattened to a 1D buffer before upload with x-fastest, y-middle, z-slowest memory order. This variant specifically addresses the host-side data preparation when the source volume is stored as a nested array structure (e.g., stack[x][y][z]) rather than a flat buffer. It converts the nested structure into a flat Uint8Array with a specific memory layout: x is the fastest varying index, y is the middle, and z is the slowest. The output is a Uint8Array of length W \times H \times D, where W = \text{stack.length}, H = \text{stack}[0].\text{length}, and D = \text{stack}[0][0].\text{length}. This step is a prerequisite for the actual glTexImage3D call if the renderer does not handle nested arrays internally. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated interpolation and coordinate transformation; simple API. Limitations: Mipmaps increase memory usage; GLLINEARMIPMAPLINEAR requires mipmaps to be generated. Origin: Not given in the sources. History: Not given in the sources. Usage: This method is standard in OpenGL-based volume rendering applications. It builds on Volume Texture Setup by performing the actual data transfer. name: Texture Uniting (Multi-Channel Packing)
body: Texture Uniting is a technique to combine four separate 3D textures (e.g., noise, detail, light, mask) into a single RGBA 3D texture to optimize memory bandwidth and sampling. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like 3D Texture Proxy Geometry by focusing on data consolidation for sampling efficiency rather than geometric approximation. Unlike Volume Texture Creation which may handle single-channel data, this method explicitly manages multi-channel alignment and resolution differences using linear clamping. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Four source 3D textures: noisetexture, detailtexture, lighttexture, masktexture. Each has an integer dimension (N{noise}, N{detail}, N{light}, N{mask}). Outputs: A single unified RGBA 3D texture (unitedtexture) with dimension N{united} (assumed cubic). Data Structures: unitedtexture: 3D texture of format RGBA. Each texel stores four floating-point values (x, y, z, w). Source textures: 3D textures of format R (single channel). Parameters: N{united}: Integer dimension of the output unified texture. N{noise}, N{detail}, N{light}, N{mask}: Integer dimensions of the source textures. Steps: 1. Initialize unitedtexture with dimensions N{united} \times N{united} \times N{united}. 2. Iterate through every voxel coordinate (i, j, k) in the unified texture, where 0 \le i, j, k < N{united}. 3. Compute normalized coordinates for sampling: u = \frac{i}{N{united}}, \quad v = \frac{j}{N{united}}, \quad w = \frac{k}{N{united}} 4. Sample the noise channel from noisetexture using linear clamping sampling at normalized coordinates (u, v, w): x = \text{SampleLevel}(\text{sampler\linear\clamp}, (u, v, w), 0).r 5. Sample the detail channel from detailtexture using linear clamping sampling at normalized coordinates (u, v, w): y = \text{SampleLevel}(\text{sampler\linear\clamp}, (u, v, w), 0).r 6. Sample the light channel from lighttexture using linear clamping sampling at normalized coordinates (u, v, w): z = \text{SampleLevel}(\text{sampler\linear\clamp}, (u, v, w), 0).r 7. Sample the mask channel from masktexture using linear clamping sampling at normalized coordinates (u, v, w) and normalize the result: w{val} = \frac{\text{SampleLevel}(\text{sampler\linear\clamp}, (u, v, w), 0).r}{32.0} 8. Write the packed vector to the unified texture: \text{unitedtexture}[i, j, k] = (x, y, z, w{val}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def unitetextures(noisetex, detailtex, lighttex, masktex, unitedsize): """ Combines four 3D scalar textures into one RGBA 3D texture. Args: noisetex: 3D texture object, dimension Nnoise detailtex: 3D texture object, dimension Ndetail lighttex: 3D texture object, dimension Nlight masktex: 3D texture object, dimension Nmask unitedsize: int, dimension of the output texture Returns: unitedtex: 3D texture object, dimension unitedsize x unitedsize x unitedsize, format RGBA """ # Initialize output texture unitedtex = create3dtexture(width=unitedsize, height=unitedsize, depth=unitedsize, format=RGBA) # Pre-calculate inverse sizes for normalized coordinate conversion invunited = 1.0 / unitedsize for i in range(unitedsize): for j in range(unitedsize): for k in range(unitedsize): # Compute normalized coordinates [0, 1] u = i invunited v = j invunited w = k invunited # Sample noise channel (R) # Uses linear clamping to handle resolution differences between source textures x = samplelinearclamp(noisetex, u, v, w) # Sample detail channel (R) y = samplelinearclamp(detailtex, u, v, w) # Sample light channel (R) z = samplelinearclamp(lighttex, u, v, w) # Sample mask channel (R) and normalize maskval = samplelinearclamp(masktex, u, v, w) wval = maskval / 32.0 # Write to unified texture unitedtex.setpixel(i, j, k, float4(x, y, z, wval)) return unitedtex def samplelinearclamp(tex, u, v, w): """ Samples a 3D texture at normalized coordinates [0,1] using linear filtering and clamp wrapping. This mimics HLSL SampleLevel with samplerlinearclamp. """ # Convert normalized coordinates to texture space coordinates # Assuming tex has dimensions D x D x D dim = tex.getdimension() tx = u dim ty = v dim tz = w dim # Perform trilinear interpolation # Note: In a real implementation, this involves fetching 8 neighboring texels and interpolating. # For the purpose of this algorithm description, we assume a standard hardware or library function # that performs this operation given normalized coordinates and a linear clamp sampler. return tex.samplelinearclamp(tx, ty, tz) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Mismatch: The method uses normalized coordinates and linear clamping to handle cases where source textures have different resolutions (N{noise} \neq N{detail}, etc.). This allows for bilinear filtering across resolution boundaries. Mask Normalization: The mask channel is divided by 32.0. If the source mask values are not in the expected range, this normalization may produce incorrect weights. Precision: Arithmetic operations are performed in 32-bit floating point, but results are truncated when written to the destination texture if the texture format uses lower precision (e.g., 16-bit). Packs PBR material properties into standard texture formats to optimize storage and sampling. BaseColor and Alpha are packed into RGBA, while Metallic and Roughness are packed into RGB (R=0, G=Roughness, B=Metallic). This is chosen when rendering PBR materials with limited texture slots. Pitfalls include ensuring alphaMode is 'OPAQUE' and doubleSided is set correctly if not remeshing. Avoids packing multiple cell attributes into a single texture if it increases memory bandwidth usage unnecessarily. Frequently accessed attributes (like inside-outside for pressure solve) should be kept in their own scalar textures to minimize bandwidth. A key pitfall is that packing inside-outside and velocity into a single RGBA texture increases memory transfer by 4x, which is inefficient if velocity is unused during pressure solving. Time Complexity: O(N{united}^3), where N{united} is the dimension of the unified texture. Each voxel requires four samples from source textures. Memory Complexity: O(N{united}^3 \times 4 \times \text{bytes\per\channel}). The unified texture uses 4x the memory of a single-channel texture of the same resolution, but reduces the number of texture objects and potentially improves cache locality during sampling. Performance: Optimizes memory bandwidth by reducing the number of texture fetches per pixel during rendering from four separate textures to one. However, if the source textures have vastly different resolutions, the linear clamping sampling may introduce artifacts or require more complex filtering. Strengths: Reduces texture object overhead, simplifies shader code (single texture lookup), and can improve cache efficiency if the unified texture is accessed frequently. Limitations: Increases memory usage for the unified texture compared to individual scalar textures if not carefully managed. Not suitable if attributes have vastly different access patterns or if bandwidth is not the primary bottleneck. When to use: When rendering requires frequent access to multiple scalar fields (e.g., density, temperature, velocity components) and memory bandwidth is a constraint. When not to use: When attributes have very different access frequencies or when memory usage is more critical than bandwidth. Originated in the context of volumetric smoke rendering and fluid simulation, specifically in the implementation of VolumetricSmoke. The technique is also discussed in the context of real-time fluid simulation and rendering, where memory bandwidth optimization is critical. It is a practical adaptation of multi-channel packing techniques used in computer graphics to optimize texture sampling performance. furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) quantaji/o-voxel-gpu, https://github.com/quantaji/o-voxel-gpu, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) PDF Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Brick Caching with LRU Replacement
head: Block Memory Management Unit (MMU) with LRU Eviction, Brick Pool Manager, Dynamic Brick Cache, Volume Block Cache
body: Brick Caching with LRU Replacement manages a fixed-size pool of volume data blocks, mapping brick coordinates to pool indices and evicting least-recently-used blocks when the pool is full. It solves the problem of limited GPU memory capacity and transfer bandwidth by ensuring that expensive data transfers from slower host memory are minimized. Unlike general-purpose CPU caches, this approach explicitly manages the cache lifecycle using a Last Recently Used (LRU) policy, often requiring CPU-side coordination due to the limitations of standard shader models regarding random memory writes. It differs from Brick-based Volume Raycasting by decoupling the volume size from GPU resolution restrictions through a re-arranged brick structure and a resident cache texture. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dimensions, brick size, brick pool ratio, file handle to volume data, optional transfer function (for active brick determination). Output: A block pointer (or nullptr if empty/not resident) for a given 3D brick coordinate (x, y, z). Data Structures: The cache is managed by a Block Memory Management Unit (MMU) containing the following fields: 1. dims: Vector3i, total volume dimensions. 2. brickdims: Vector3i, number of bricks in each dimension, calculated as \lceil \text{dims} / \text{brick\size} \rceil. 3. bricksize: Vector3i, dimensions of each brick in voxels. 4. entries: Array of Entry structures, size brickdims.x brickdims.y brickdims.z. Entry layout: { bool valid; int blkidx; }. valid: Indicates if the entry maps to a resident block. blkidx: Index into the blocks array. 5. blocks: Array of Block structures, size blknums. blknums: Total number of blocks in the pool, calculated as brickdims.x brickdims.y brickdims.z bricknumratio. 6. data: uchar, contiguous memory pool of size blknums (bricksize.x+1) (bricksize.y+1) (bricksize.z+1). Bricks are stored with size (n+1)^3 to include neighbor samples for filtering. 7. cntbuf: int, count buffer of size brickdims.x brickdims.y brickdims.z 256. Used to skip empty bricks. Loaded from disk. 8. clockpos: int, position in the LRU clock for eviction. 9. blkused: int, number of currently used blocks in the pool. 10. mutex: pthreadmutext, for thread-safe access. 11. fin: ifstream, file handle for loading bricks. Parameters: bricknumratio: Fraction of total bricks to keep in memory (e.g., 0.5 for 50%). bricksize: Dimensions of each brick in voxels. Small blocks fit the isosurface tightly for empty space skipping, while larger bricks avoid excessive storage overhead. GPU Resolution Limit: Example 512³ on NVIDIA GeForce 6. Memory Limit: Example 256MB. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Calculate brickdims from volume dims and bricksize. Allocate entries array of size brickdims.x brickdims.y brickdims.z. Calculate blknums using bricknumratio. Allocate blocks array of size blknums. Allocate data buffer of size blknums (bricksize.x+1) (bricksize.y+1) (bricksize.z+1). Load cntbuf of size brickdims.x brickdims.y brickdims.z 256 from disk. Initialize clockpos = 0, blkused = 0, and all entries as invalid. 2. Get Block (x, y, z): Boundary Check: If x \ge \text{brick\dims}.x or y \ge \text{brick\dims}.y or z \ge \text{brick\dims}.z, return nullptr. Empty Brick Check: If a transfer function tf1d is provided, check cntbuf. Let cntbase = (x brickdims.y + y) brickdims.z + z. Iterate idx from 0 to 255: If cntbuf[cntbase + idx] != 0 and tf1d->sampleSimple(idx).w != 0, break loop. If idx == 256, return nullptr (brick is empty). Cache Hit: Check entries at index (x, y, z). If valid is true: Mark block as used (update LRU timestamp/position). Return pointer to block data at blocks[entries[idx].blkidx].data. Cache Miss / Eviction: Lock mutex. If blkused < blknums: Assign next free slot (find first invalid entry in blocks or maintain a free list). Else (pool full): Use clockpos to find the first unused block (LRU-like eviction). Mark the old entry in entries as invalid. Update clockpos to the next position. Load block data from file into the assigned slot in data. Mark entries at (x, y, z) as valid, store blkidx. Increment blkused if a new slot was assigned. Unlock mutex. Return pointer to the loaded block data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class BrickCache: def init(self, dims, bricksize, bricknumratio, filepath): self.bricksize = bricksize self.brickdims = Vector3i( ceil(dims.x / bricksize.x), ceil(dims.y / bricksize.y), ceil(dims.z / bricksize.z)) self.totalbricks = self.brickdims.x self.brickdims.y self.brickdims.z self.blknums = int(self.totalbricks bricknumratio) # Data structures self.entries = [Entry(valid=False, blkidx=-1) for in range(self.totalbricks)] self.blocks = [Block() for in range(self.blknums)] self.data = bytearray(self.blknums (bricksize.x+1) (bricksize.y+1) (bricksize.z+1)) self.cntbuf = loadcntbuffromdisk(self.brickdims) # Size: totalbricks 256 self.blkused = 0 self.clockpos = 0 self.file = open(filepath, 'rb') self.mutex = Mutex() def getblock(self, x, y, z, tf1d=None): # Boundary check if x >= self.brickdims.x or y >= self.brickdims.y or z >= self.brickdims.z: return None # Empty brick check if tf1d is not None: cntbase = (x self.brickdims.y + y) self.brickdims.z + z isempty = True for idx in range(256): if self.cntbuf[cntbase + idx] != 0 and tf1d.samplesimple(idx).w != 0: isempty = False break if isempty: return None # Calculate entry index entryidx = (x self.brickdims.y + y) self.brickdims.z + z entry = self.entries[entryidx] # Cache hit if entry.valid: self.updatelru(entry.blkidx) return self.getblockdata(entry.blkidx) # Cache miss / Eviction self.mutex.lock() try: if self.blkused < self.blknums: # Find free slot blkidx = self.findfreeslot() self.blkused += 1 else: # LRU Eviction blkidx = self.clockpos oldentryidx = self.blocks[blkidx].entryidx # Assuming Block tracks its entry if oldentryidx != -1: self.entries[oldentryidx].valid = False self.clockpos = (self.clockpos + 1) % self.blknums # Load block self.loadblockfromfile(blkidx, x, y, z) # Update entry self.entries[entryidx].valid = True self.entries[entryidx].blkidx = blkidx self.blocks[blkidx].entryidx = entryidx finally: self.mutex.unlock() return self.getblockdata(blkidx) def updatelru(self, blkidx): # Update timestamp or move to front of LRU list pass def findfreeslot(self): # Find first block with valid=False or unused pass def loadblockfromfile(self, blkidx, x, y, z): # Read from self.file into self.data at offset corresponding to blkidx pass def getblockdata(self, blkidx): # Return pointer/offset to data for blkidx pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Brick coordinates must be correctly mapped to entry indices to avoid out-of-bounds access. Boundaries: Bricks at the volume boundary may have incomplete neighbor samples if the volume size is not a multiple of brick size. The (n+1)^3 storage helps with filtering but requires careful boundary handling during reconstruction. Concurrency: The mutex ensures thread safety but may become a bottleneck. The LRU clock position must be updated atomically or protected by the mutex. Empty Bricks: The cntbuf check is critical for performance. If not used, the cache may fill with empty bricks, wasting memory. The Brick Cache is a single-channel 3D texture cache that stores bricks from a multi-resolution multi-volume hierarchy. It is agnostic to the number of data channels. It differs from general-purpose CPU caches by being implemented as a GPU-resident texture managed via LRU replacement using WebGPU compute passes. It uses a low-resolution floating-point reference texture (e.g., 16³ for a 512³ volume with 32³ bricks) to store texture coordinate offsets to the brick cache, allowing the fragment shader to transform volume coordinates into brick cache texture coordinates. White/null references indicate bricks not in the cache. LRU Cache Management for Voxel Bricks is a memory management strategy that prioritizes reusing voxel brick data that has not been accessed for the longest time, thereby optimizing memory reuse while retaining useful data in the cache. It solves the problem of limited GPU memory capacity and transfer bandwidth by ensuring that expensive data transfers from slower host memory are minimized. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on hardware-specific features or different replacement policies, this approach explicitly manages the cache lifecycle using a Last Recently Used (LRU) policy, often requiring CPU-side coordination due to the limitations of standard shader models regarding random memory writes. After a block is reconstructed, it is buffered in cache memory instead of being discarded. To access a voxel, the cache is searched using a buffered-block list; if the voxel is within a cached block, it is retrieved immediately, otherwise reconstruction is invoked. The replacement policy substitutes the oldest block with the new block when the cache is full. The cache size requirement in 3D for image resolution N \times N and block size s \times s \times s is 2 \times s \times N \times N (two layers of sub-volumes). For N=256, cache size is 0.5 MB (S=16) or 1 MB (S=32); for N=1024, it is 2 MB (S=16) or 4 MB (S=32). Cache size grows at rate 2^2 while original data grows at 2^3, making caching efficient for high-resolution data. If no cache slot is available, the least recently accessed brick is evicted using an LRU scheme. After eviction, all leaf nodes whose spatial extent overlaps the evicted brick's spatial extent are checked to see if they are still partially mapped (i.e., if any other brick in the same resolution level is resident). If no other brick in that resolution level is resident, the corresponding bit in the node's bitmask is reset. Non-leaf nodes are updated by setting their bitmasks to the bitwise OR of their child nodes' bitmasks. A method where the GPU steers data loading by indicating which nodes were helpful, using spatial and temporal coherence to update an LRU cache on the CPU without significant overhead. Nodes and bricks are subdivided or fused in an LRU manner, with timestamps reset upon usage. The CPU updates timestamps of pool elements in its mirrored data structure based on GPU feedback and triggers loading of needed data. Three MRTs are used to store node usage information, allowing 12 nodes per pixel (3 x 4). A user-defined number of brick data is uploaded from the file server to the GPU each frame. Each brick comprises its global brick ID and either the EMPTY value (if all zeros) or the pre-processed brick. The global brick ID is translated to a local brick ID. If the brick's channel is not represented by the multi-channel page-table hierarchy, the brick is discarded. If EMPTY, the corresponding page is marked EMPTY; otherwise, it is marked MAPPED and added to the brick cache using the LRU buffer to find free or unused entries. When a brick is removed, its page is marked UNMAPPED. Two lists of local brick IDs (EMPTY/MAPPED and UNMAPPED) are passed to the residency octree. Time Complexity: O(1) average for cache hit, O(1) for eviction search (amortized), O(256) worst-case for empty brick check. Memory Complexity: O(blknums × brickvolume + brickcount × 256 × sizeof(int)). Performance: The method allows rendering of volumes larger than GPU memory (e.g., 512³ on 256MB VRAM) by streaming bricks. Strengths: Efficient memory usage for large volumes; effective empty space skipping via cntbuf; decouples volume size from GPU constraints. Limitations: Requires CPU-side coordination for LRU updates in some implementations; mutex contention may limit parallelism; overhead of (n+1)^3 storage for bricks. When to use: When rendering large volumes that exceed GPU memory, especially with dynamic isovalue changes requiring active brick determination. When not to use: For small volumes that fit entirely in GPU memory, where a simple resident texture is more efficient. The concept of brick-based caching with LRU replacement originated in the context of real-time ray-casting of discrete isosurfaces, where decoupling volume size from GPU resolution restrictions was necessary. The specific implementation details, including the MMU structure and cntbuf optimization, are documented in open-source projects and academic works on parallel volume rendering. The integration with residency octrees and GPU-steered management further evolved the technique to handle multi-resolution hierarchies and web-based rendering scenarios. name: Block-based Ray Cache
head: Buffered-block list, Cache Data Structure for Ray Tracing
body: The Block-based Ray Cache is a memory optimization technique for volume rendering that reduces reconstruction overhead by retaining reconstructed voxel blocks in memory for reuse by adjacent rays. It solves the problem of redundant computation in high-resolution volume rendering where data exceeds physical memory, allowing rendering times to drop from days to minutes. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly maintaining a sorted list of blocks along the ray depth to facilitate immediate lookup, rather than relying solely on generic LRU eviction without spatial locality awareness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray trace request for a specific voxel coordinate; the current state of the cache (buffered blocks). Output: The voxel value (if cached) or a newly reconstructed block added to the cache. Data Structures: The core structure is an auxiliary list called the buffered-block list. Node Layout: Each node in the list represents a reconstructed block. blockid: Identifier for the block. boundaries: The 3D spatial boundaries (min/max coordinates) of the block. data: The voxel values of the reconstructed block. timestamp or position: Used to determine the "oldest" block for replacement. Ordering: The list is maintained in sorted order according to the depth of the blocks along the current ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Tracing Initiation: Begin tracing a projection ray through the volume. 2. Cache Lookup: For each voxel access along the ray: a. Search the buffered-block list for a node whose boundaries contain the requested voxel coordinate. b. Hit: If found, retrieve the voxel value immediately from the cached block data. c. Miss: If not found, invoke the block reconstruction procedure to generate the block containing the voxel. 3. Buffering: After a block is reconstructed, buffer it in cache memory instead of discarding it. Add a new node to the buffered-block list with the block's boundaries and data. 4. List Maintenance: Ensure the buffered-block list remains sorted by depth along the ray. 5. Replacement: If the cache is full: a. Identify the oldest block in the buffered-block list (based on the replacement policy). b. Remove the oldest node from the list. c. Substitute the oldest block with the newly reconstructed block. d. Update the buffered-block array with the new block's boundaries. 6. Completion: After the ray tracing is complete, the sequence of blocks reconstructed along that ray remains in the cache for potential use by adjacent rays. Formulas: Cache Size Requirement: In 3D, for an image resolution of N \times N and a block size of s \times s \times s, the total number of blocks to store in the cache is: \text{Total Blocks} = 2 \times s \times N \times N This accounts for two layers of sub-volumes sufficient to cover worst-case access patterns. Parameters: N: Volume data dimension (e.g., 256, 1024). s: Block size dimension (e.g., 16, 32). Typical Cache Sizes: For N=256: 0.5 MB (s=16) or 1 MB (s=32). For N=1024: 2 MB (s=16) or 4 MB (s=32). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Size Too Small: If the cache memory size is too small, the hit rate becomes very small, degrading performance. Redundant Reconstruction: Failing to cache blocks leads to significant performance loss, as voxels reconstructed along one ray are likely used by adjacent rays. Boundary Conditions: The block-wise reconstruction method must handle extended block boundaries correctly to ensure seamless access across block edges. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class BufferedBlockNode: def init(self, blockid, boundaries, data): self.blockid = blockid self.boundaries = boundaries # Tuple of (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) self.data = data self.depth = calculatedepth(boundaries) # Depth along the ray def searchcache(bufferedblocklist, voxelcoord): """ Search the buffered-block list for a block containing the voxel. Returns the block data if found, else None. """ for node in bufferedblocklist: if isvoxelinblock(voxelcoord, node.boundaries): return node.data return None def isvoxelinblock(voxel, boundaries): minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = boundaries return (minx <= voxel.x <= maxx and miny <= voxel.y <= maxy and minz <= voxel.z <= maxz) def replaceoldest(bufferedblocklist, newnode): """ Remove the oldest block (lowest depth) and insert the new node. Assumes list is sorted by depth. """ if len(bufferedblocklist) > 0: # Remove the first element (oldest) bufferedblocklist.pop(0) # Insert new node maintaining sorted order by depth insertsorted(bufferedblocklist, newnode) def insertsorted(blocklist, newnode): """ Insert newnode into blocklist maintaining sort order by depth. """ # Simple insertion sort for demonstration for i, node in enumerate(blocklist): if newnode.depth < node.depth: blocklist.insert(i, newnode) return blocklist.append(newnode) def renderray(ray, cachecapacity): """ Render a single ray using the block-based ray cache. """ bufferedblocklist = [] # The cache structure voxelvalues = [] for voxel in ray.voxels: # Step 1: Search cache cacheddata = searchcache(bufferedblocklist, voxel) if cacheddata is not None: # Hit: Retrieve immediately voxelvalues.append(cacheddata[voxel.relativeindex]) else: # Miss: Reconstruct block blockid = getblockid(voxel) reconstructedblock = reconstructblock(blockid) boundaries = getblockboundaries(blockid) # Create new cache node newnode = BufferedBlockNode(blockid, boundaries, reconstructedblock) # Step 2: Buffer and manage cache if len(bufferedblocklist) >= cachecapacity: replaceoldest(bufferedblocklist, newnode) else: insertsorted(bufferedblocklist, newnode) # Retrieve from newly cached block voxelvalues.append(reconstructedblock[voxel.relativeindex]) return accumulate(voxelvalues) A technique to reduce reconstruction overhead by caching reconstructed voxel blocks in memory. It leverages the observation that voxels reconstructed along one ray are likely used by adjacent rays, retaining these blocks to avoid re-reconstruction. Using this cache technique reduces rendering time from a few days to a few minutes. It saves approximately 50% of the reconstruction time compared to point-wise reconstruction. Time Complexity: Lookup is O(B) where B is the number of blocks in the cache, assuming linear search of the buffered-block list. Reconstruction is avoided for cached blocks, significantly reducing total rendering time. Memory Complexity: The cache size grows at a rate of 2^2 (quadratic) with respect to resolution N, while the original data grows at 2^3 (cubic). This makes caching efficient for high-resolution data that exceeds physical memory. Measured Performance: For N=256 and s=16, cache size is 0.5 MB; for N=1024 and s=16, cache size is 2 MB. Rendering time can be reduced from days to minutes. Strengths: Efficient for high-resolution data; reduces redundant computation; small memory footprint relative to original data. Limitations: Performance degrades if cache size is too small; requires sorted list maintenance; not given in the sources whether parallel access to the cache is supported. When to use: Scientific visualization applications with high-resolution volume data that exceeds physical memory. When not to use: Low-resolution data where reconstruction overhead is negligible; scenarios where cache hit rates are expected to be very low due to poor spatial locality. The method originates from research on direct rendering of multiresolution decomposed volume data. It was proposed to address issues related to volume rendering of multiresolution data, introducing a novel abstract mathematical definition of the volume rendering equation. The technique builds on the observation that block-wise reconstruction is more efficient than point-wise reconstruction. name: LRU Cache Eviction with Residency Update
head: Residency-aware LRU eviction, Bitmask-consistent LRU eviction
body: This method manages the consistency between a Least Recently Used (LRU) brick cache and a hierarchical residency octree. When the cache is full, it evicts the least recently accessed brick and propagates the resulting change in spatial coverage up the octree by resetting bits in leaf and non-leaf node masks. It ensures that the residency structure accurately reflects which resolution levels are partially mapped in memory, preventing rendering artifacts from accessing non-resident data. It differs from standard LRU caches by coupling eviction side-effects with hierarchical metadata updates. Inputs: A brick cache with a fixed capacity (number of slots). An LRU tracking structure (e.g., a doubly linked list or timestamp array) mapping bricks to their access recency. A residency octree where each node (leaf or non-leaf) maintains a bitmask indicating which resolution levels have at least one resident brick in its spatial extent. The spatial extent (AABB) and resolution level of the evicted brick. Outputs: The cache state with one fewer brick (the LRU brick removed). The residency octree with updated bitmasks reflecting the removal. Data Structures: Cache Slot: Stores brick ID, spatial AABB, resolution level, and access timestamp/pointer. LRU List: Doubly linked list of cache slots ordered by access time (head = least recent, tail = most recent). Octree Node: bitmask: Integer or bitset where bit i is 1 if any brick at resolution level i within this node's spatial extent is resident. children: Array of child nodes (for non-leaf nodes). spatialextent: AABB defining the node's 3D volume. Algorithm Steps: 1. Eviction Trigger: If a new brick requires a cache slot and no slots are free, identify the brick at the head of the LRU list as the victim. 2. Remove from Cache: Remove the victim brick from the cache storage. Remove the victim from the LRU list. 3. Identify Affected Leaf Nodes: Traverse the residency octree to find all leaf nodes whose spatialextent overlaps with the victim brick's spatialextent. 4. Update Leaf Node Bitmasks: For each affected leaf node: Determine the resolution level L of the evicted brick. Check all other bricks in the cache that belong to the same resolution level L and fall within the leaf node's spatial extent. If no other brick at resolution level L is resident within this leaf node's extent, reset bit L in the leaf node's bitmask to 0. If bit L was already 0, no change is needed for this node. 5. Propagate Updates to Non-Leaf Nodes: For each affected leaf node whose bitmask changed in Step 4: Move up the tree to the parent node. Recalculate the parent's bitmask as the bitwise OR of its children's bitmasks: \text{parent.bitmask} = \bigvee{c \in \text{children}} c.\text{bitmask} If the parent's bitmask has changed, repeat the propagation for the parent's ancestors. If the parent's bitmask remains unchanged, terminate propagation for this branch. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evictlruandupdateresidency(cache, lrulist, octreeroot, evictedbrick): # Step 1 & 2: Evict LRU brick if not lrulist.isempty(): victim = lrulist.pophead() # Remove least recently used cache.remove(victim.brickid) else: return # No eviction needed # Step 3: Find affected leaf nodes affectedleaves = octreeroot.findleavesoverlapping(evictedbrick.spatialextent) # Step 4 & 5: Update bitmasks for leaf in affectedleaves: resolutionlevel = evictedbrick.resolutionlevel # Check if any other brick at this resolution level is resident in this leaf isresident = False for brick in cache.getbricksinextent(leaf.spatialextent): if brick.resolutionlevel == resolutionlevel: isresident = True break # Reset bit if not resident if not isresident: leaf.bitmask &= ~(1 << resolutionlevel) # Propagate up if bitmask changed if leaf.bitmaskchanged: propagateupdate(leaf) def propagateupdate(node): parent = node.parent if parent is None: return # Recalculate parent bitmask newparentbitmask = 0 for child in parent.children: newparentbitmask |= child.bitmask if newparentbitmask != parent.bitmask: parent.bitmask = newparentbitmask propagateupdate(parent) Parameters: Cache capacity: Not given in the sources. Bitmask size: Determined by the maximum number of resolution levels in the octree. Edge Cases: Precision: Bitwise operations assume integer bitmasks. Ensure no overflow if resolution levels exceed standard integer width. Boundaries: Spatial overlap checks must be inclusive of brick boundaries to avoid missing adjacent bricks. Degenerate Input: If the evicted brick was the only resident brick for a resolution level in a leaf, the bit must be reset. If the leaf had no bricks at that level initially, the bit is already 0. A variant addressing memory pile-up in WebGL2 environments. It sets a strict residency budget of 1.25 GB, deliberately below the plan budget, to force LRU eviction during refocus operations. Previous implementations allowed up to 8 GB requests against a 2 GB plan budget, causing bricks to accumulate (e.g., 1.67 GB across 177 bricks on hoaheart L0) without eviction. This fix ensures the LRU scheme effectively manages GPU memory by capping the total resident data size. Time Complexity: Eviction is O(1) with a doubly linked list. Updating the octree depends on the number of affected leaf nodes and the depth of the tree. In the worst case, a single eviction may trigger updates up to the root, but typically only a small subtree is affected. Memory Complexity: O(N) for cache storage and O(M) for the octree, where N is the number of bricks and M is the number of octree nodes. Strengths: Maintains strict consistency between cache state and rendering metadata, preventing access to non-resident data. Efficiently updates only affected parts of the octree. Limitations: Requires traversal of the octree to find affected leaves. Bitmask updates must be propagated carefully to avoid unnecessary work. When to use: When rendering requires accurate residency information for mixed-resolution volumes and cache capacity is limited. When not to use: If the octree is very deep and evictions frequently affect large spatial areas, the update cost may become significant. Originating from the Residency Octree approach for scalable web volume rendering, this method integrates LRU cache management with hierarchical residency tracking. It was developed to handle mixed-resolution multi-volume rendering where ray-guided traversal relies on accurate bitmask information to skip empty regions or access resident data. The GPU Residency Budget Fix variant addresses specific implementation issues in WebGL2 environments, as documented in unofficial repository updates. name: Brick Cache Implementation
head: Brick Cache, Brick Cache Layout
body: The Brick Cache is a single-channel 3D texture cache that stores bricks from a multi-resolution multi-volume hierarchy. It is agnostic to the number of data channels in the underlying dataset. It differs from general-purpose CPU caches by being implemented as a GPU-resident texture managed via LRU replacement using WebGPU compute passes. Inputs: Csize: Cache dimensions (Csizex, Csizey, Csizez), chosen by the user at initialization. Bsize: Brick dimensions (Bsizex, Bsizey, Bsizez). m: Number of data channels. k: Number of resolution levels. Usage Buffer: A 3D texture in r32uint format storing the current global timestamp for each brick-cache entry. Outputs: Brick Cache: A single-channel 3D texture in r8unorm format containing the brick data. LRU Buffer: A storage buffer in GPU memory containing an array of linear indices into the brick cache, sorted by most recent access time. 1. Brick Cache: Implemented as a single-channel 3D texture in r8unorm format. Each entry corresponds to a single brick in the multi-resolution multi-volume hierarchy. The cache size Csize is rounded up to be a multiple of the brick size Bsize. 2. Usage Buffer: A 3D texture in r32uint format with one voxel per brick-cache entry. Its size Usize is defined as: Usize = \left( \frac{Csizex}{Bsizex}, \frac{Csizey}{Bsizey}, \frac{Csizez}{Bsizez} \right) 3. LRU Buffer: A storage buffer in GPU memory containing an array of linear indices into the brick cache. The array is sorted by the most recent access time of the corresponding brick-cache entry. The LRU buffer is updated after each frame using WebGPU compute passes. 1. Process Usage Buffer: Process the usage buffer to produce a mask of brick-cache entries accessed at the current timestamp. 2. Compute Exclusive Scan: Use a sequence of compute passes to compute the exclusive scan of this mask. 3. Move Indices: Use the result of the scan to move all indices in the LRU buffer referencing brick-cache entries that have been used at the current timestamp to the front of the LRU buffer while preserving the order of the remaining elements. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatelrubuffer(usagebuffer, lrubuffer, currenttimestamp): # Step 1: Produce mask of accessed entries # The usage buffer stores the timestamp of the last access per entry. mask = [1 if val == currenttimestamp else 0 for val in usagebuffer] # Step 2: Compute exclusive scan of the mask # scanresult[i] holds the count of used entries before index i. scanresult = [0] len(mask) currentsum = 0 for i in range(len(mask)): scanresult[i] = currentsum currentsum += mask[i] # Step 3: Move indices referencing used entries to the front # Used entries (mask[cacheidx]==1) are placed at indices given by scanresult. # Unused entries (mask[cacheidx]==0) are placed after all used entries, preserving order. newlrubuffer = [0] len(lrubuffer) destunused = sum(mask) for i in range(len(lrubuffer)): cacheidx = lrubuffer[i] if mask[cacheidx] == 1: newlrubuffer[scanresult[cacheidx]] = lrubuffer[i] else: newlrubuffer[destunused] = lrubuffer[i] destunused += 1 return newlrubuffer The sequential Python logic mirrors the parallel WebGPU compute passes described in the source. The exclusive scan determines destination indices for used entries, while unused entries are appended sequentially to maintain stability. Csize: Cache size, chosen by the user at initialization. Bsize: Brick size. m: Number of channels. k: Number of resolution levels. Cache Size Alignment: Csize must be rounded up to be a multiple of Bsize. Precision: The usage buffer uses r32uint for timestamps, which must be sufficient to avoid overflow over the lifetime of the cache. Boundary Conditions: The usage buffer size Usize is derived from Csize/Bsize. If Csize is not a multiple of Bsize, the division may not be integer, but the source states Csize is rounded up. Stores ray segments in blocks rather than individual bricks [2260-block-based-ray-cache.md]. Chosen when ray coherence is high and block-level access patterns dominate. Updates residency metadata during eviction rather than maintaining a strict LRU list [3115-lru-cache-eviction-with-residency-update.md]. Chosen when metadata overhead must be minimized. Uses GPU-computed access statistics to drive eviction decisions [3654-gpu-steered-lru-cache-management.md]. Chosen when CPU-GPU synchronization latency is a bottleneck. Manages LRU state specifically for voxel-level brick granularity [4571-lru-cache-management-for-voxel-bricks.md]. Chosen when fine-grained access tracking is required. Time Complexity: The LRU update requires processing the usage buffer and computing an exclusive scan, which is O(Csize) per frame. Memory Complexity: The cache uses Csize entries in r8unorm format. The usage buffer uses Usize entries in r32uint format. The LRU buffer uses Csize entries in u32 format. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: GPU-resident, agnostic to data channels, efficient LRU updates via compute shaders. Limitations: Single-channel texture format requires channel multiplexing or external metadata for native multi-channel storage. When to use: Use when rendering large biomedicine datasets on WebGPU with strict memory constraints. When not to use: Avoid when native multi-channel texture storage is required without additional mapping overhead. The Brick Cache implementation is part of a scalable web-based volume rendering system for large biomedicine datasets. It was developed to manage memory efficiently on the GPU using WebGPU. The approach uses a residency octree for managing multi-channel data. name: GPU-Steered LRU Cache Management
head: Combining Rendering and Visibility, GPU-Steered Data Loading, Unified Management of Brick and Node Pool
body: This method enables the GPU to steer CPU-side data loading for voxel rendering by reporting node usage, thereby eliminating the overhead of CPU-driven visibility queries and tree traversal. It differs from sibling methods by unifying the management of the brick pool and node pool into two LRU-controlled caches where the GPU determines refinement needs and missing data, rather than relying on occlusion queries or frustum containment checks performed on the CPU. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray traversal results from the GPU (node indices, usage status). Output: Updated LRU timestamps in CPU memory; texture updates sent to GPU for new bricks/nodes. Data Structures: CPU Mirrored Data Structure: Maintains timestamps for all pool elements (nodes and bricks). GPU Framebuffer: Uses Multiple Render Targets (MRTs) to store node usage information. Layout: 3 MRTs are used. Capacity: Each pixel stores 3 \times 4 = 12 node indices. Steps: 1. Ray Traversal and Data Collection: During rendering, each ray traverses the N^3-tree. The GPU records the trajectory of used nodes. To handle spatial coherence, rays are grouped into packages (e.g., 2 \times 2). Within a package, different rays store different sets of the 12 traversed nodes (e.g., upper-left ray stores the first 12, upper-right the second 12). A 2 \times 2 package thus collects 48 node indices total (4 \text{ rays} \times 12 \text{ nodes/ray}). 2. GPU Feedback: The GPU outputs supplementary information about data usage and update needs alongside the color. This includes which nodes were visited and potentially which need refinement or coarsening. 3. CPU Update: The CPU reads the GPU feedback. It updates the timestamps of the corresponding pool elements (nodes and bricks) in its mirrored data structure. Elements with older timestamps are considered for eviction. 4. Cache Management: The CPU manages the LRU policy. When a new element is added, it replaces the oldest element (lowest timestamp). The CPU triggers the loading of needed data and stores bricks in the pool using the host-memory timestamps. 5. Synchronization: Necessary modifications (new bricks/nodes) are transferred to the GPU via texture-update calls. Parameters: MRT Count: 3. Nodes per Pixel: 12. Ray Package Size: 2 \times 2 (example). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparency: Rays may traverse a large number of nodes, exceeding the fixed output capacity of the framebuffer. The method relies on spatial coherence to mitigate this, but ad-hoc solutions may be needed for extreme cases. Precision: Timestamps must be reset upon usage to accurately reflect recency. This variant exploits spatial coherence by grouping rays in packages in the image plane to collect node traversal information, reducing the amount of data sent to the CPU. Rays are grouped (e.g., 2 \times 2), and different node sets are assigned to rays within the package based on their position (e.g., upper-left stores first 12 nodes, upper-right stores second 12 nodes). A 2 \times 2 package results in 48 node indices total (4 \text{ rays} \times 12 \text{ nodes/ray}). Time Complexity: Reduces CPU overhead by eliminating explicit tree traversal and occlusion queries for visibility. Memory Complexity: Requires additional GPU memory for MRTs (3 targets per pixel) to store node indices. Strengths: Unified management of brick and node pools; leverages spatial and temporal coherence; offloads visibility and LOD selection from CPU. Limitations: Limited by framebuffer output capacity (12 nodes/pixel); may require ad-hoc handling for transparent scenes with long traversal paths. When to use: Complex scenes where CPU-driven visibility queries are too costly; when spatial coherence is high. Originated in the paper "Ray-Guided Streaming for Efficient and Detailed Voxel Rendering" (2009) by Crassin et al.. The method was developed to address the significant overhead of CPU-side visibility determination (via occlusion queries and tree traversal) in previous approaches. It builds on the insight that the GPU already possesses traversal information at the end of ray tracing, allowing it to steer data loading efficiently. name: LRU Cache Management for Voxel Bricks
head: Brick Cache Management, Gestion du cache de briques, LRU Brick Cache, Last Recently Used cache strategy, Stratégie LRU
body: LRU Cache Management for Voxel Bricks is a memory management strategy that prioritizes reusing voxel brick data that has not been accessed for the longest time, thereby optimizing memory reuse while retaining useful data in the cache. It solves the problem of limited GPU memory capacity and transfer bandwidth by ensuring that expensive data transfers from slower host memory are minimized. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on hardware-specific features or different replacement policies, this approach explicitly manages the cache lifecycle using a Last Recently Used (LRU) policy, often requiring CPU-side coordination due to the limitations of standard shader models regarding random memory writes. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: The current visibility state of bricks (determined by a visibility determination phase), the current frame number (global timestamp), and the brick data to be loaded. Outputs: An updated GPU brick cache containing the most recently used bricks, and an updated LRU buffer reflecting the access order. Data Structures The implementation requires maintaining parallel structures on the CPU and GPU. 1. CPU-side Structures: Parallel N3-tree Indirection: A copy of the hierarchical storage structure (N3-tree) in central memory to allow CPU-side manipulation and notification of node destruction. Usage Flag: A flag maintained for each loaded brick at each Level of Detail (LOD). It stores the last time of use to determine priority in the LRU cache. Ordered List: A list sorted by last usage time, used to identify the next free cache slot or the victim slot for eviction. Owner Node Structure: A structure similar to the brick indirection storage, allowing direct access to owner node data to notify them of data destruction. 2. GPU-side Structures: Brick Cache: A single-channel 3D texture in r8unorm format. Each entry corresponds to a single brick. The cache size C{size} is chosen by the user at initialization and rounded up to be a multiple of the brick size B{size}. LRU Buffer: A GPU storage buffer containing an array of linear indices into the brick cache, sorted by most recent access time. Usage Buffer: A 3D texture in r32uint format with one voxel per brick-cache entry. Its size U{size} is defined as: U{size} = \left( \frac{C{sizex}}{B{sizex}}, \frac{C{sizey}}{B{sizey}}, \frac{C{sizez}}{B{sizez}} \right) This buffer stores the timestamp (frame number) when a brick-cache entry was last accessed. Numbered Steps 1. Visibility Determination: During the visibility determination phase, the system identifies which bricks are needed for the current frame. 2. Update Usage Flags (CPU) / Usage Buffer (GPU): CPU Approach: The usage flag for each loaded brick is updated with the current time/frame number. GPU Approach: During rendering, whenever a brick-cache entry is accessed, the current global timestamp (frame number) is written into the corresponding voxel in the Usage Buffer. 3. Check Cache Status: When a new brick or brick resolution is needed: If the cache is not full, transfer the brick to the next free slot. If the cache is full, identify the slot containing the brick that has not been used for the longest time. 4. Eviction and Update: If a slot is reused because it contains an old brick, and that brick is still referenced by the storage structure, update the hierarchical structure to invalidate the corresponding LOD level in the leaf containing the brick. GPU LRU Update: After each frame, a series of WebGPU compute passes update the LRU Buffer. The Usage Buffer is processed to produce a mask of accessed entries, which are then sorted to update the LRU Buffer array. 5. Data Transfer: Transfer the new brick data to the GPU using the graphics API (e.g., glTexSubImage in OpenGL). Asynchronous transfers can be managed using Pixel Buffer Objects (PBOs). Pseudocode The following pseudocode illustrates the CPU-side logic for cache management, as described in. Note that GPU-side management (as in) uses compute shaders to update the LRU buffer based on the usage buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def managelrucache(brickneeded, cacheslots, usageflags, hierarchicalstructure): """ brickneeded: The brick data and metadata (LOD, position) to be loaded. cacheslots: List of available cache slots. usageflags: Dictionary mapping brickid -> lastusedtime. hierarchicalstructure: The N3-tree copy for invalidation. """ # Step 1: Check if cache has free space if len(cacheslots) > 0: # Case: Cache is not full slot = cacheslots.pop(0) # Take next free slot transferbricktogpu(slot, brickneeded) usageflags[brickneeded.id] = currenttime() return slot else: # Case: Cache is full # Find the brick with the oldest usage time victimid = min(usageflags, key=usageflags.get) victimslot = getslotforbrick(victimid) # Check if victim brick is still referenced if isbrickreferenced(victimid, hierarchicalstructure): # Invalidate the corresponding LOD level in the leaf hierarchicalstructure.invalidatelod(victimid) # Reuse the slot cacheslots.append(victimslot) # Or manage slot list appropriately transferbricktogpu(victimslot, brickneeded) # Update usage flags del usageflags[victimid] usageflags[brickneeded.id] = currenttime() return victimslot Parameters Cache Size (C{size}): Chosen by the user at initialization. It must be rounded up to be a multiple of the brick size B{size}. Usage Flag: Maintained on the CPU (or in a GPU Usage Buffer) for each loaded brick at each LOD level, storing the last time of use. Edge Cases and Pitfalls GPU Random Writes: Standard shader stream processing models do not allow random memory writes, making pure GPU-side LRU management difficult without specific APIs like CUDA or compute shaders with atomic operations. The solution is to manage the cache on the CPU or use compute passes to update buffers. Invalidation: If a reused brick is still referenced by the storage structure, the hierarchical structure must be updated to invalidate the corresponding LOD level; failure to do so leads to rendering artifacts or stale data. Time Complexity: The LRU update step requires sorting or scanning the usage buffer. In the CPU approach, finding the minimum usage time is O(N) where N is the number of cached bricks. In the GPU approach, compute passes are required each frame to update the LRU buffer. Memory Complexity: Requires maintaining parallel structures on CPU (N3-tree copy, ordered list, owner node structure) and GPU (Brick Cache, LRU Buffer, Usage Buffer). Strengths: Optimizes memory reuse by prioritizing data that is likely to be reused soon, effectively managing limited GPU memory transfer speeds and capacity. Limitations: The CPU-side management adds overhead for synchronization and flag updates. The GPU-side approach requires additional compute passes and buffer management. When to Use: When GPU memory is constrained and data access patterns exhibit temporal locality, making LRU an effective replacement policy. When Not to Use: If the access pattern is random or if the overhead of maintaining LRU state outweighs the benefits of cache hits. The LRU strategy for voxel bricks was introduced in the context of interactive exploration of procedural volumetric data. It addresses the bottleneck of transferring data from slow host memory to fast GPU memory. The approach was further implemented in web-based volume rendering systems for large biomedicinal datasets, utilizing WebGPU compute passes for LRU buffer updates. name: Sparse structures
head: Sparse volume data structures, Sparse voxel representations
body: Sparse structures are data structures designed to store volumetric data where a significant portion of the domain is empty or homogeneous, thereby reducing memory usage and computational overhead compared to dense grids. They solve the problem of storing large 3D domains by omitting empty space or merging identical values, often at the cost of increased traversal complexity or construction time. What sets them apart from sibling methods like Value compression (which compresses values in dense grids) or Run-Length Encoding for Voxel Data (which exploits 1D coherence) is their explicit representation of spatial sparsity, either through hierarchical subdivision, hashing, or specialized geometric layouts. All sparse structures in this family share the following mechanism: 1. Sparsity Exploitation: The core principle is to avoid storing data for empty or redundant regions. This is achieved by either not allocating memory for empty voxels (e.g., Hash Grids, SparseGrid) or by merging adjacent voxels with identical values into larger logical units (e.g., Tree-based structures, Stack-Based Representation). 2. Implicit or Explicit Domain Mapping: The structures map continuous 3D coordinates or logical grid indices to stored data. This mapping can be explicit (via tree nodes or linear indices) or implicit (via hash functions). 3. Default Values: Unset or empty regions are typically represented by a default value (e.g., zero density, FLTMAX, or null pointers), allowing the renderer to skip these regions during traversal or ray marching. 4. Traversal Overhead: Accessing data in sparse structures generally requires more computation per voxel than in dense grids, as the structure must be traversed (e.g., tree descent, hash lookup, or stack iteration) to locate the relevant data. A flat, index-based sparse grid that allocates memory only for explicitly added cells, suitable for large domains with small active regions. It differs from tree-based structures by using a linear index layout rather than hierarchical pointers, and from Hash Grids by not using spatial hashing for coordinate mapping. Choose it when you need random access to specific cells in a large, mostly empty domain without the overhead of tree traversal. Maps continuous 3D coordinates to discrete bucket indices in a hash table using a multiplicative hash with prime constants. It differs from SparseGrid by using spatial hashing for coordinate mapping, allowing it to handle arbitrary continuous positions rather than just integer grid indices. Choose it for neural rendering or applications requiring fast lookup of arbitrary 3D points in a sparse field. Decomposes a voxel grid into vertical columns, compressing each column via run-length encoding of attribute values along the depth axis. It differs from siblings like SparseGrid or Hash Grids by being specialized for datasets with strong vertical anisotropy (e.g., terrain or layered scenes), achieving linear construction complexity. Choose it for layered volumetric data where vertical coherence is high. A compression technique for child pointers using entropy encoding and a lookup table of common pointers to reduce memory usage, applied similarly to offset compression. It is a sub-component of tree-based structures rather than a standalone storage format. Choose it when implementing tree-based structures to minimize the memory footprint of internal node pointers. Not given in the sources. A volume rendering technique that represents 3D scenes as CSG trees of SDF primitives, evaluates distances on the CPU, compresses the resulting 3D distance field into a Brickmap structure, and raymarches through it on the GPU. It differs from general sparse structures by being specifically designed for Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) derived from CSG operations. Choose it for rendering complex hard-surface geometry defined by SDFs. A process to reduce the bandwidth of node information sent to the CPU by removing duplicate node references using spatial coherence and HistoPyramids. It is a data reduction technique for update streams rather than a static storage structure. Choose it for dynamic scenes where frequent updates need to be transmitted efficiently. Organize sparse volumetric data into a hierarchical graph where internal nodes define spatial subdivisions and leaf nodes store voxel values. They differ from sibling structures like Hash Grids by providing explicit spatial hierarchy for culling, and from Brick-based Hierarchical Storage by operating on individual voxel granularity rather than fixed-size blocks. Choose them for general-purpose sparse volume rendering where adaptive resolution and efficient empty-space culling are required. A strategy for managing large-scale data uploads using virtual page tables and on-demand brick transfers, where volumes are preprocessed, mipmapped, and bricked to be uploaded to GPU with dynamic requests. It is a memory management strategy for sparse structures rather than a storage format itself. Choose it for rendering extremely large volumes that exceed GPU memory capacity. Definition: A data structure for representing curvilinear grids with nonplanar faces, supporting view-dependent subdivision. Step: If a cell is subdivided (subdivided is true) and was not previously subdivided (oldsubdivided is false), it takes a block from pre-allocated arrays (pyramids, prisms, hexahedra requiring 5 or 6 tetrahedra) and revises shared pointers. If subdivided is false and oldsubdivided is true, it uses the parent pointer to restore pointers and places the block on a free list. Exterior quadrilateral faces are divided into triangles for XMPVO/BSP-XMPVO sorting. For BSP-MPVO, each exterior triangle points to a subface structure. Layout: NewCell struct contains flags (subdivided, oldsubdivided, numbInbound, type, actual, cycleTestBit, notVisited, nverts), UsedTIndex, parent pointer, face pointer array, and vertex array. NewFace struct contains concave flag, nsubfaces, and Subface array. Subface struct contains shared pointers to two cells, plane equation coefficients (A, B, C, D), and an arrow flag. BlockOfCells struct contains type, used, kind, next pointer, and tets array. Usage: Used in the SILO visualization toolkit for rendering complex curvilinear grids. Definition: A two-level-deep hierarchical data structure that allocates memory more intelligently than dense buffers by subdividing the domain into coarse blocks, addressing the problem of unused voxels occupying memory. Step: A block remains unallocated (storing just a single value) until the first write-access to one of its voxels. Once the first write happens, all of the block's voxels are allocated. Layout: Two-level-deep hierarchical data structure. Domain subdivided into coarse blocks. Each block contains either: 1) A single value (usually zero, or a different value for level sets), OR 2) An N^3 array of voxels representing actual voxel data in the block. Common block size is between 8^3 and 32^3. Complexity: Voxel read and write access is O(k), or constant time, though with a larger k than an ordinary dense buffer. Allocation on first write is amortized over all subsequent accesses. Usage: Implemented in Field3D's SparseField class. Sparse volume representations were developed to address the memory inefficiency of dense voxel grids, particularly in fluid simulations and cloud rendering where large portions of the domain are empty or homogeneous. The concept of merging identical voxels into larger blocks dates back to early adaptive octree implementations, where 2x2x2 blocks were recursively merged if they shared the same density value. Modern implementations include OpenVDB, which uses octrees for upper levels and 32x32x32 blocks for lower levels to balance cache coherency and sparsity. The Block-based Sparse Buffer was introduced as a simpler alternative for applications like Field3D, offering constant-time access with amortized allocation costs. Hash Grids have gained popularity in neural rendering (e.g., Instant NGP) for their ability to map continuous coordinates to sparse feature grids efficiently. Stack-Based Representation was developed to exploit vertical coherence in layered scenes, such as terrain or architectural volumes. name: SparseGrid
head: SparseGrid Data Structure
body: SparseGrid is a sparse adaptive grid that allocates memory only for cells explicitly added to the structure, making it suitable for large domains containing small active regions. It differs from dense grids by storing only active cell indices and their associated values on the device, and differs from tree-based structures by using a flat, index-based layout rather than hierarchical pointers. Inputs and Outputs: The structure is initialized with a global shape (uint3, number of sample points per dimension), an axis-aligned bounding box (aabbmin, float3, default [-1, -1, -1]), aabbmax (float3, default [1, 1, 1]), and a defaultvalue (float, default FLTMAX) for unset points. The primary inputs are 1D int32 tensors of linear cell indices for adding or removing cells, and the outputs are tensors of corner coordinates, scalar values, and connectivity information. Data Structures: The core data structure resides on the GPU and consists of the following private members: thrust::devicevector<float> values: Stores scalar values at cell corners. thrust::devicevector<uint> cellindices: Stores the linear indices of all active cells. uint3 shape: The dimensions of the implied lattice (Nx, Ny, Nz). float3 aabbmin: Minimum corner of the bounding box. float3 aabbmax: Maximum corner of the bounding box. float defaultvalue: Value for unset points. Linear Indexing: Cells are identified by linear indices within the implied lattice defined by shape. A cell at integer coordinates (x, y, z) maps to a linear index i calculated as: i = x + y \cdot Nx + z \cdot Nx \cdot Ny where 0 \le x < Nx, 0 \le y < Ny, and 0 \le z < Nz. Operations: 1. Add Cells: addcells accepts a 1D int32 tensor of linear indices. These indices are added to the cellindices vector. 2. Remove Cells: removecells accepts a 1D int32 tensor of linear indices. These are removed from the cellindices vector. 3. Get Points: getpointsbycellindices takes a 1D int32 tensor of cell indices and returns an (N, 8, 3) float32 tensor containing the 3D coordinates of the 8 corners for each of the N active cells. The coordinates are derived by mapping the integer cell indices to the continuous space defined by aabbmin and aabbmax. 4. Get Values: getvalues returns an (N, 8) float32 tensor of scalar values at the corners of the active cells. If a corner value is not explicitly set, it defaults to defaultvalue. 5. Filter Cell Indices: filtercellindices takes cellindices, values (shape N, 8), and a level (default 0.0). It returns a 1D int32 tensor containing only the indices of cells where the iso-surface (defined by level) intersects the cell volume. 6. Get Cell Count: Returns cellindices.size(). 7. Get Point Count: Returns cellindices.size() 8. 8. Get Grid View: Returns a GridView struct containing shape, aabbmin, aabbmax, pointers to values.data().get() and cellindices.data().get(), and a boolean flag set to true. 9. Get Dual Quads: Returns a tuple of thrust::devicevector<int4>, thrust::devicevector<bool>, and thrust::devicevector<uint2>. It takes NDArray<uint2> edges and NDArray<bool> isout as input to construct dual mesh geometry. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode illustrates the data access and basic operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class SparseGrid: def init(self, shape: tuple, aabbmin: tuple, aabbmax: tuple, defaultvalue: float = float('inf')): self.shape = shape self.aabbmin = aabbmin self.aabbmax = aabbmax self.defaultvalue = defaultvalue self.cellindices = [] self.values = {} def addcells(self, indices: list): for idx in indices: if idx not in self.cellindices: self.cellindices.append(idx) if idx not in self.values: self.values[idx] = [self.defaultvalue] 8 def removecells(self, indices: list): for idx in indices: if idx in self.cellindices: self.cellindices.remove(idx) if idx in self.values: del self.values[idx] def getpointsbycellindices(self, indices: list): points = [] dx = (self.aabbmax[0] - self.aabbmin[0]) / (self.shape[0] - 1) dy = (self.aabbmax[1] - self.aabbmin[1]) / (self.shape[1] - 1) dz = (self.aabbmax[2] - self.aabbmin[2]) / (self.shape[2] - 1) for idx in indices: x = idx % self.shape[0] y = (idx // self.shape[0]) % self.shape[1] z = idx // (self.shape[0] self.shape[1]) cellpoints = [] for i in range(8): cx = (i >> 0) & 1 cy = (i >> 1) & 1 cz = (i >> 2) & 1 px = self.aabbmin[0] + (x + cx) dx py = self.aabbmin[1] + (y + cy) dy pz = self.aabbmin[2] + (z + cz) dz cellpoints.append((px, py, pz)) points.append(cellpoints) return points def getvalues(self, indices: list): vals = [] for idx in indices: if idx in self.values: vals.append(self.values[idx]) else: vals.append([self.defaultvalue] 8) return vals def filtercellindices(self, indices: list, values: list, level: float = 0.0): crossingindices = [] for i, idx in enumerate(indices): cellvals = values[i] if min(cellvals) < level < max(cellvals): crossingindices.append(idx) return crossingindices def getcellcount(self): return len(self.cellindices) def getpointcount(self): return len(self.cellindices) 8 def getgridview(self): return { "shape": self.shape, "aabbmin": self.aabbmin, "aabbmax": self.aabbmax, "valuesptr": self.values, "cellindicesptr": self.cellindices, "valid": True } def getdualquads(self, edges, isout): # Returns tuple of device vectors for dual mesh construction. # The sources do not specify the internal traversal logic. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear indexing assumes integer coordinates fit within the uint range. For very large shape values, overflow may occur. Boundaries: The shape defines the number of sample points, meaning there are shape[0]-1 cells in the x-dimension. Indices must be strictly within [0, Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz - 1]. Default Value: Unset points default to FLTMAX (or defaultvalue). This can affect iso-surface filtering if the level is high. Time Complexity: Adding or removing cells is O(1) amortized per cell if using hash-based lookup, or O(N) if using linear scan. getpoints and getvalues are O(N) where N is the number of active cells. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of active cells. Memory usage is proportional to the number of active cells, not the total domain size. Performance: Suitable for large domains with sparse active regions. Not given in the sources for specific hardware benchmarks. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of active cells. Strengths: Low memory overhead for sparse data; simple flat layout allows for efficient GPU parallel processing. Limitations: No hierarchical traversal acceleration; requires explicit management of active cells. When to use: Ideal for large domains where only small iso-surface regions are active. When not: Unsuitable for dense volumes or when hierarchical traversal acceleration is required. SparseGrid is a sparse adaptive grid implementation that inherits from a base Grid class and stores values and cell indices on the device. It is designed to support efficient iso-surface extraction on GPU by providing a flexible sparse data structure. The implementation leverages Thrust for device-side memory management and parallel operations. GuangyanCai/isoext, https://github.com/GuangyanCai/isoext, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hash Grids
head: Coordinate Hashing, Vertex Hashing for Voxel Grid
body: Hash Grids map continuous 3D vertex positions to discrete bucket indices in a hash table using a multiplicative hash with prime constants. Inputs and Outputs: Input: coords, a list or array of coordinates supporting up to 7 dimensions. Input: log2hashmapsize, the logarithm of the hash table size T with respect to 2. Output: Hashed bucket index. Data Structures: primes: An array of prime constants used for the hash function with values [1, 2654435761, 805459861, 3674653429, 2097192037, 1434869437, 2165219737]. BOXOFFSETS: A tensor defining 3D offsets as [[[i,j,k] for i in [0, 1] for j in [0, 1] for k in [0, 1]]]. Formula: The hash value is computed using a multiplicative hash with prime constants: \text{hash} = ((\text{pos}.x \times 73856093) \oplus (\text{pos}.y \times 19349663) \oplus (\text{pos}.z \times 83492791)) \pmod n where \oplus denotes bitwise XOR and n is the table size. Pseudocode: The implementation body is cut off in the provided text. The following pseudocode implements the available signature, constants, and formula in standard Python. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hash(coords, log2hashmapsize): """ coords: list or array of coordinates (supports up to 7 dimensions) log2hashmapsize: logarithm of hash table size T w.r.t 2 """ primes = [1, 2654435761, 805459861, 3674653429, 2097192037, 1434869437, 2165219737] tablesize = 1 << log2hashmapsize h = 0 for i, coord in enumerate(coords): h ^= int(coord) primes[i] return h % tablesize Parameters: log2hashmapsize: Typical values are not given in the sources. The source formula uses specific prime constants for x, y, and z, but the general function supports up to 7 dimensions. The handling of dimensions 4–7 is not specified in the source formula. Precision issues may arise if coordinate values are large, affecting the modulo operation. It efficiently tracks which grid-aligned positions contain solid geometry without allocating memory for empty space. It differs from its parent Hash Grids by operating on discrete world coordinates for voxel placement rather than hashing continuous vertex positions for feature extraction, and it serves as the foundational sparse storage layer for Multi-type Voxel Storage. Hash Grid Loss is a regularization term used in compressive neural volume rendering to minimize the bit consumption of the binary occupancy structure of a hash grid during training. It operates by modeling the probability distribution of the binary hash grid values and optimizing the negative log-likelihood, effectively driving the model to create a more concentrated (sparse) hash grid structure. It is distinct from sibling methods like Voxel World Data Structure which manage spatial indexing, and from Entropy Loss which focuses on the continuous or quantized attribute values stored within active cells rather than the occupancy bits themselves.
