name: Voxel World Data Structure
head: Hash Grid for Voxel World, HashSet of IVec3
body: The Voxel World Data Structure is a sparse representation for voxel worlds that stores voxel existence using a hash set of integer-based 3D vectors. It efficiently tracks which grid-aligned positions contain solid geometry without allocating memory for empty space. It differs from its parent Hash Grids by operating on discrete world coordinates for voxel placement rather than hashing continuous vertex positions for feature extraction, and it serves as the foundational sparse storage layer for Multi-type Voxel Storage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera position (floating-point 3D vector) and a set of initial voxel coordinates. Output: A World data structure containing a set of occupied voxel positions, and a rendered scene where cubes are drawn at these positions. Data Structures: The core structure is a World object containing a single field: voxels: A HashSet of IVec3 (integer 3D vectors). Each IVec3 represents the integer grid coordinates (x, y, z) of an occupied voxel. The use of IVec3 ensures that all voxel positions are strictly aligned to the integer grid, preventing floating-point alignment errors. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the World structure and populate it with initial voxels by iterating over desired ranges and inserting IVec3 coordinates into the hash set. 2. Runtime Interaction (Toggle): To add or remove a voxel at the camera's current location: a. Convert the camera's floating-point position to an integer IVec3 using truncation. b. Check if this IVec3 exists in the voxels hash set. c. If it exists, remove it. If it does not exist, insert it. 3. Rendering: Iterate through every IVec3 in the voxels hash set and invoke a rendering primitive to draw a cube centered at that integer coordinate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. IVec3 = tuple def drawcube(pos: IVec3) -> None: # The sources do not specify the rendering implementation. pass class World: def init(self): self.voxels: set[IVec3] = set() def initializeplatform(self, width: int, depth: int, y: int) -> None: """Populate the world with an initial flat platform.""" for z in range(depth): for x in range(width): self.voxels.add((x, y, z)) def togglevoxelatcamera(self, cameraposition: tuple) -> None: """Add or remove a voxel at the camera's grid-aligned position.""" voxelpos = (int(cameraposition[0]), int(cameraposition[1]), int(cameraposition[2])) if voxelpos in self.voxels: self.voxels.remove(voxelpos) else: self.voxels.add(voxelpos) def render(self) -> None: """Draw a cube at every occupied voxel position.""" for voxelpos in self.voxels: drawcube(voxelpos) Parameters: Grid Alignment: Voxels are strictly integer-aligned. Floating-point positions are converted to integers before storage. Initial Platform: Example uses a 32 \times 32 platform at y=0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Naively drawing individual cubes for every voxel in the hash set results in poor performance due to high vertex upload overhead. The source notes that increasing platform size causes significant performance suffering if instancing is not used. Data Type: Using Vec3 (float) instead of IVec3 (int) in the hash set is discouraged because it fails to ensure grid alignment, which is critical for consistent voxel placement. Existence Check: The structure only tracks existence. It does not store material properties or geometry details beyond position. Extends this binary existence model by associating a discrete material identifier with each occupied voxel, allowing distinction between material kinds (e.g., dirt, stone). It builds on this structure by introducing an enumeration-based type system for voxel content. Time Complexity: Insertion, removal, and existence checks in the HashSet are O(1) on average. Rendering is O(V) where V is the number of voxels, as it iterates over the entire set. Memory Complexity: O(V), storing only the coordinates of occupied voxels. Performance: Naive rendering (one draw call per voxel) scales poorly with voxel count due to CPU-GPU communication overhead. Instancing is required for larger worlds. Strengths: Simple implementation, efficient sparse storage for existence checks, easy runtime modification of the world. Limitations: No support for multiple voxel types or complex geometry per voxel in this base form; rendering performance degrades without optimization (instancing). When to use: When a simple, sparse voxel world with binary existence (solid/empty) is needed, and performance requirements are low or instancing is employed. When not to use: When multiple material types are required (use Multi-type Voxel Storage) or when rendering large numbers of voxels without GPU instancing. This structure is presented in the tutorial "Make yourself a Voxel Engine THIS weekend" as a foundational step in building a voxel engine. It introduces the concept of using a hash set for sparse voxel storage and highlights the importance of integer grid alignment. name: Multi-type Voxel Storage
head: HashMap-based Voxel Storage, VoxelKind Enum Storage
body: Multi-type Voxel Storage associates a discrete material identifier with each occupied voxel in a sparse grid, allowing a voxel world to distinguish between different material kinds (e.g., dirt, stone) rather than treating all voxels as identical solid entities. Inputs: World state, world position (P \in \mathbb{Z}^3), voxel kind (K \in \text{VoxelKind} or None). Outputs: Updated chunk state. Data Structures: VoxelKind: An enumeration defining material types (e.g., Dirt, Stone). Chunk: A structure containing a HashMap mapping 3D integer coordinates to VoxelKind, and a mesh reference (or None). The absence of a key in the HashMap represents air/nothing. World: A collection of Chunk objects indexed by their global chunk position. Algorithm: 1. Chunk Addressing: Calculate the chunk position C and local position L using Euclidean division by the fixed chunk size of 32: C = P \div 32, L = P \pmod{32}. The source uses diveuclid and remeuclid to ensure consistent behavior for negative coordinates. 2. Chunk Retrieval: Retrieve or create the Chunk at C. If creating a new chunk, initialize voxels as an empty HashMap. 3. Voxel Update: If K is None, remove L from chunk.voxels. If K is a valid type, insert (L, K) into chunk.voxels. Invalidate the chunk's mesh by setting chunk.mesh = None. 4. Chunk Generation: When a new chunk is created, iterate local coordinates x, y, z \in [0, 31]. Calculate world position W = C \times 32 + L. If W.y == 0, insert VoxelKind::Dirt at L. If W.y < 0, insert VoxelKind::Stone at L. Otherwise, leave the position absent (air). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setvoxel(world: dict, position: tuple[int, int, int], kind: str | None): """Sets or removes a voxel at the given world position.""" # Euclidean division for chunk and local coordinates chunkposition = tuple(p // 32 for p in position) localposition = tuple(p % 32 for p in position) chunk = getorcreatechunk(world, chunkposition) chunk.mesh = None if kind is None: chunk.voxels.pop(localposition, None) else: chunk.voxels[localposition] = kind def getorcreatechunk(world: dict, chunkposition: tuple[int, int, int]) -> 'Chunk': """Retrieves an existing chunk or creates a new one with procedural generation.""" if chunkposition not in world.chunks: voxels = {} for z in range(32): for y in range(32): for x in range(32): offset = (x, y, z) worldvoxelposition = tuple(c 32 + o for c, o in zip(chunkposition, offset)) if worldvoxelposition[1] == 0: voxels[offset] = "Dirt" elif worldvoxelposition[1] < 0: voxels[offset] = "Stone" world.chunks[chunkposition] = Chunk(chunkposition, voxels) return world.chunks[chunkposition] class Chunk: def init(self, position: tuple[int, int, int], voxels: dict): self.position = position self.voxels = voxels self.mesh = None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Coordinates: Standard modulo operators can return negative remainders in some languages. diveuclid and remeuclid must be used to ensure L is always in [0, 31]. Mesh Invalidation: Setting mesh = None is mandatory after any voxel modification to prevent stale geometry from rendering. Typed Voxels extends this storage by enforcing a strict enumeration-based type system for voxel content, ensuring type safety and potentially optimizing lookups for specific material categories. It is chosen when material variety is required but strict type enforcement is preferred over dynamic kind assignment. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Memory usage scales proportionally to the number of occupied voxels plus the overhead of the HashMap entries, as empty space is not stored. Each entry stores a 3D integer key and a VoxelKind value. Iteration over voxels requires traversing the HashMap, which lacks the cache locality of dense arrays. This method is described in the blog post "Make yourself a Voxel Engine THIS weekend". It is presented as a practical implementation focusing on simplicity and correctness, combining sparse storage via HashMaps with material typing via enums. name: Typed Voxels
body: Typed Voxels associate a discrete type identifier (enum) with each voxel in a sparse grid to distinguish between different material kinds, such as dirt or stone. It differs from Voxel Flag System & Filled State Logic by focusing on material type enumeration rather than binary geometric classification [2040-voxel-flag-system-filled-state-logic.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A chunk coordinate system and voxel placement commands specifying position and material type. Output: A chunk data structure containing a mapping from local voxel coordinates to material types. Data Structures: The core change is replacing the binary existence set with a typed hash map. 1. VoxelKind Enum: Defines available material types (e.g., Dirt, Stone). 2. Chunk Structure: Field voxels is a HashMap<IVec3, VoxelKind> mapping local 3D integer coordinates to the corresponding enum value. Steps: 1. Define Types: Create an enum VoxelKind listing supported material types. 2. Update Chunk Storage: Replace HashSet<IVec3> with HashMap<IVec3, VoxelKind> in the Chunk struct. 3. Placement: When placing a voxel at global position P, calculate chunk position C = P / CHUNKSIZE and local offset L = P % CHUNKSIZE, then insert (L, Type) into Chunk(C).voxels. 4. Retrieval: To get the type at P, locate Chunk(C), lookup L in Chunk(C).voxels, and return the associated VoxelKind or a default "empty" type if not found. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VoxelKind: Dirt = 0 Stone = 1 Empty = 2 class Chunk: def init(self): self.voxels = {} # Maps IVec3 tuples to VoxelKind def placevoxel(world, globalpos, kind): chunksize = 32 chunkpos = tuple(p // chunksize for p in globalpos) localoffset = tuple(p % chunksize for p in globalpos) if chunkpos not in world: world[chunkpos] = Chunk() chunk = world[chunkpos] chunk.voxels[localoffset] = kind def getvoxeltype(world, globalpos): chunksize = 32 chunkpos = tuple(p // chunksize for p in globalpos) localoffset = tuple(p % chunksize for p in globalpos) if chunkpos not in world: return VoxelKind.Empty chunk = world[chunkpos] return chunk.voxels.get(localoffset, VoxelKind.Empty) Parameters: CHUNKSIZE: 32. VoxelKind variants: Defined by the application; the source uses Dirt and Stone. Edge Cases: Empty Space: Voxels not present in the HashMap are implicitly empty. Hash Collisions: Standard hash map behavior applies. Manages topological and geometric state of individual voxels via a compact bitmask of five properties to determine solid, surface, or empty space without separate metadata arrays [2040-voxel-flag-system-filled-state-logic.md]. It differs from Typed Voxels by focusing on binary geometric classification rather than material type enumeration, allowing rapid updates during mesh voxelization [2040-voxel-flag-system-filled-state-logic.md]. Choose it when tracking surface topology and fill state is required instead of material variety. Voxel Flag System & Filled State Logic Time Complexity: Lookup and insertion are O(1) average case for hash map operations. Memory Complexity: Higher than a simple HashSet or bitfield because each voxel stores an additional integer/enum value for the type. The overhead is proportional to the number of placed voxels, not the total chunk volume. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; directly supports material-specific rendering or logic; flexible number of types. Limitations: Hash map overhead (pointers, hash entries) is higher than compact bit arrays. Not suitable if memory is extremely constrained and types are few (bit packing might be better). When to use: When the number of material types is moderate and simplicity of implementation is prioritized over extreme memory density. This method originates from the "Voxel Engine THIS weekend" tutorial series, which demonstrates building a basic voxel engine from scratch. It represents a natural evolution from binary voxel grids to typed grids, allowing for more visually and logically diverse worlds. The approach is common in early-stage voxel engine implementations due to its ease of integration with existing hash-based sparse storage structures. name: Adaptive Bit-Packed Voxel Array
head: SectionStorage, SectionStorage Adaptive Bit-Packed Voxel Array, Voxel Section
body: The Adaptive Bit-Packed Voxel Array is a storage structure for a fixed-size 16×16×16 voxel section (4096 voxels) that dynamically adjusts its memory layout based on the number of unique voxel IDs present. It supports Empty, Uniform, and Palette states to optimize memory usage for homogeneous or sparse sections. Unlike Typed Voxels, which may use fixed-size arrays or more complex sparse structures, this method uses a single palette and bit-packed indices, allowing it to collapse to zero heap memory for empty or uniform data. Input: A sequence of voxel updates (position, id) or a bulk array of 4096 VoxelIds. Output: A SectionStorage object that resolves to VoxelId values at any local position, or an iterator over all 4096 voxels. The structure uses a Representation enum (mapped to StorageKind) to manage state: 1. Empty: No heap memory. Represents all voxels as VoxelId::AIR. 2. Uniform: Stores a single VoxelId inline. No heap memory. 3. Palette: Stores a Palette struct on the heap. entries: Vec<PaletteEntry>. Each contains id: VoxelId and count: u16 (number of voxels referencing this entry, enabling uniform/empty collapse checks without scanning all 4096 voxels). words: Vec<u64>. Bit-packed indices. bits: u8. Bits per index (1 to 12). Memory accounting fields include inlinebytes, heapusedbytes, heapcapacitybytes, paletteentries, and bitsperindex. SECTIONVOLUME: 4096 (total voxels). SECTIONEDGE: 16 (side length). bitsperindex: Capped at 12 bits, supporting up to 2^{12} = 4096 unique IDs. 1. Initialization: SectionStorage::default() creates an Empty section with 0 heap capacity. SectionStorage::filled(id) creates a Uniform section if id != AIR, or Empty if id == AIR, using 0 heap capacity. 2. Bulk Construction (fromvoxels): If all 4096 voxels are identical, return Uniform or Empty. Otherwise, scan all voxels to build a Palette: Count occurrences of each VoxelId. Assign a slot index (0 to N-1) to each unique ID. Calculate bits = ceil(log2(N)). Allocate words vector of size ceil(4096 bits / 64). Write indices into words using bit-packing. 3. Single Update (set): Calculate index = position.x + position.y 16 + position.z 256. If Representation is Empty or Uniform: If the new id matches the current value, return false (no change). If id is AIR and current is Uniform, switch to Empty. Otherwise, transition to Palette with the current id and new id as the two entries, set bits = 1, and write the new index. If Representation is Palette: Read current slot: oldslot = readindex(words, bits, index). If palette.entries[oldslot].id == id, return false. If palette.entries[oldslot].count == 1: Replace palette.entries[oldslot].id with id in place. Return true. Else, check if id exists in palette.entries: If yes, update count for old slot (decrement) and new slot (increment). If no, check for a dead slot (count == 0) to reuse without repacking. If a dead slot exists, reuse it; otherwise, add id to palette.entries. Update counts, write the new index, and if the palette crosses a bit-width boundary, trigger repacking (increase bits, resize words, rewrite all indices). Return true. 4. Batch Update (setbatch): Apply set for each (position, id) in the list. Return the count of voxels that actually changed value. 5. Compaction (compact): Scan palette.entries to find entries with count > 0 (live entries). Remove entries with count == 0 (dead slots). Rebuild the palette mapping: Create a new entries vector with only live entries. Calculate new bits = ceil(log2(livecount)). If bits < oldbits, resize words and rewrite indices. If bits == oldbits, rewrite indices to reflect new slot positions. Return true if changes were made. 6. Iteration (iter / copyvoxels): For each index i from 0 to 4095: slot = readindex(words, bits, i). id = palette.entries[slot].id. Yield id. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. SECTIONVOLUME = 4096 SECTIONEDGE = 16 MAXBITS = 12 def indexbits(nunique): if nunique <= 1: return 1 bits = 1 while (1 << bits) < nunique: bits += 1 return min(bits, MAXBITS) def wordcount(bits): return (SECTIONVOLUME bits + 63) // 64 def readindex(words, bits, index): bitoffset = index bits wordidx = bitoffset // 64 bitinword = bitoffset % 64 val = words[wordidx] >> bitinword if bitinword + bits > 64: val |= words[wordidx + 1] << (64 - bitinword) return val & ((1 << bits) - 1) def writeindex(words, bits, index, slot): bitoffset = index bits wordidx = bitoffset // 64 bitinword = bitoffset % 64 mask = (1 << bits) - 1 words[wordidx] &= ~(mask << bitinword) words[wordidx] |= (slot & mask) << bitinword if bitinword + bits > 64: words[wordidx + 1] &= ~(mask >> (64 - bitinword)) words[wordidx + 1] |= (slot & mask) << (64 - bitinword) class SectionStorage: def init(self): self.data = None # None, ("Uniform", id), or ("Palette", entries, words, bits) @staticmethod def default(): return SectionStorage.filled(0) # 0 represents AIR @staticmethod def filled(id): s = SectionStorage() s.data = ("Uniform", id) if id != 0 else None return s def set(self, position, id): index = position[0] + position[1] SECTIONEDGE + position[2] SECTIONEDGE SECTIONEDGE if self.data is None: # Empty if id == 0: return False entries = [{"id": 0, "count": SECTIONVOLUME - 1}, {"id": id, "count": 1}] words = [0] wordcount(1) writeindex(words, 1, index, 1) self.data = ("Palette", entries, words, 1) return True elif self.data[0] == "Uniform": currentid = self.data[1] if currentid == id: return False if id == 0: self.data = None return True entries = [{"id": currentid, "count": SECTIONVOLUME - 1}, {"id": id, "count": 1}] words = [0] wordcount(1) writeindex(words, 1, index, 1) self.data = ("Palette", entries, words, 1) return True else: # Palette entries, words, bits = self.data[1], self.data[2], self.data[3] oldslot = readindex(words, bits, index) oldid = entries[oldslot]["id"] if oldid == id: return False newslot = next((i for i, e in enumerate(entries) if e["id"] == id), None) if newslot is not None: entries[oldslot]["count"] -= 1 entries[newslot]["count"] += 1 writeindex(words, bits, index, newslot) return True # Dead slot reuse or append deadslot = next((i for i, e in enumerate(entries) if e["count"] == 0), None) if deadslot is not None: newslot = deadslot entries[newslot]["id"] = id entries[newslot]["count"] = 1 else: newslot = len(entries) entries.append({"id": id, "count": 1}) entries[oldslot]["count"] -= 1 writeindex(words, bits, index, newslot) if len(entries) > (1 << bits): newbits = indexbits(len(entries)) if newbits > bits: newwords = [0] wordcount(newbits) for i in range(SECTIONVOLUME): s = readindex(words, bits, i) writeindex(newwords, newbits, i, s) self.data = ("Palette", entries, newwords, newbits) return True return False def setbatch(self, edits): return sum(1 for pos, id in edits if self.set(pos, id)) def compact(self): if self.data is None or self.data[0] != "Palette": return False entries, words, bits = self.data[1], self.data[2], self.data[3] live = [e for e in entries if e["count"] > 0] if len(live) == len(entries): return False slotmap = {i: newi for newi, i in enumerate([idx for idx, e in enumerate(entries) if e["count"] > 0])} newentries = [{"id": e["id"], "count": e["count"]} for e in live] newbits = indexbits(len(newentries)) newwords = [0] wordcount(newbits) for i in range(SECTIONVOLUME): oldslot = readindex(words, bits, i) writeindex(newwords, newbits, i, slotmap.get(oldslot, 0)) self.data = ("Palette", newentries, newwords, newbits) return True def get(self, position): index = position[0] + position[1] SECTIONEDGE + position[2] SECTIONEDGE SECTIONEDGE if self.data is None: return 0 if self.data[0] == "Uniform": return self.data[1] entries, words, bits = self.data[1], self.data[2], self.data[3] return entries[readindex(words, bits, index)]["id"] def copyvoxels(self, outarray): if self.data is None: outarray[:] = [0] SECTIONVOLUME return if self.data[0] == "Uniform": outarray[:] = [self.data[1]] SECTIONVOLUME return entries, words, bits = self.data[1], self.data[2], self.data[3] for i in range(SECTIONVOLUME): outarray[i] = entries[readindex(words, bits, i)]["id"] Palette Width Limit: The implementation caps bitsperindex at 12 bits. If more than 4096 unique IDs are introduced, the behavior is constrained by this limit. Dead Slot Reuse: When a palette entry is no longer referenced, its slot is marked dead (count=0) but not removed immediately. New unique IDs can reuse dead slots without repacking the indices. Boundary Conditions: Indices 0, 63, 64, 2048, 4095 are tested to ensure bit-packing handles word boundaries and edge indices correctly. Uniform Collapse: If all voxels become identical after updates or compaction, the section collapses to Uniform state, freeing heap memory. Empty Collapse: If all voxels become AIR, the section collapses to Empty state with 0 heap capacity. Memory: Empty and Uniform states use 0 heap bytes. Palette state uses heap for entries (N × sizeof(PaletteEntry)) and words (ceil(4096 × bits / 64) × 8 bytes). Memory is optimized for homogeneous sections, which are common in voxel worlds. Time Complexity: get: O(1). set: O(1) amortized, O(N) if repacking is triggered (rare). compact: O(N) where N is the number of palette entries. iter: O(4096). Strengths: Extremely low memory overhead for empty or uniform sections. Efficient for sections with a small number of unique voxel types. Supports fast bulk updates and iteration. Limitations: High memory usage if all 4096 voxels are unique (12 bits × 4096 / 8 = 6144 bytes for indices + palette overhead). Repacking can be expensive if triggered frequently. Not suitable for highly heterogeneous sections with many unique IDs. The Adaptive Bit-Packed Voxel Array is implemented in the voxel-forge repository as an unofficial voxel engine implementation. It is designed to efficiently store and manage voxel data in a 3D grid, leveraging the sparsity and homogeneity often found in voxel-based games and simulations. name: Brick-based Sparse Voxel Lookup with Open-Addressing Hash
head: BrickLookup, Hash Grid with Bricks
body: A GPU-friendly sparse voxel storage and lookup scheme that groups active voxels into 8x8x8 bricks, stores brick occupancy as 512-bit bitsets, and maps brick coordinates to compact voxel/QEF arrays via an open-addressing hash table. It builds on Voxel World Data Structure by replacing flat IVec3 hashing with a hierarchical brick-based layout to improve memory locality and reduce hash table size. Unlike Multi-type Voxel Storage which focuses on data type variety, this method optimizes for spatial coherence and efficient GPU-side ray traversal by exposing brick-level occupancy. Inputs: GridSpec: Contains voxelsize (float3), gridmin (Int3), and gridmax (Int3) defining the spatial bounds and resolution. Active voxel coordinates (x, y, z) within the grid bounds. Outputs: A BrickLookup structure containing hash tables and brick data. For a given voxel, the index of its data row in the compact arrays, or -1 if inactive or out of bounds. Data Structures: 1. Int3: Three integers x, y, z. Access via &x[i]. 2. GridSpec: voxelsize (float3), gridmin (Int3), gridmax (Int3). 3. SymQEF10: 10 floats (q00..q33) storing the upper-triangle of a symmetric 4x4 QEF matrix. 4. BrickLookup: hashkeys (const uint64t), hashvals (const uint32t), brickbits (const uint32t), brickbase (const int64t), hashcapacity (uint64t, must be a power of two). Parameters: kBrickSize: 8 (brick dimension in voxels). kBrickLocalCells: 512 (8x8x8). kBrickBitWords: 16 (512/32). kEmptyBrickKey: UINT64MAX. kEmptyBrickVal: UINT32MAX. kOverflowBrickVal: UINT32MAX - 1u. Steps: 1. Pack Voxel Key: Convert 3D voxel coordinates to a dense row-major 64-bit integer key relative to gridmin. \begin{aligned} sx &= grid\max.x - grid\min.x \\ sy &= grid\max.y - grid\min.y \\ ux &= x - grid\min.x \\ uy &= y - grid\min.y \\ uz &= z - grid\min.z \\ key &= ux + sx \times (uy + sy \times uz) \end{aligned} 2. Unpack Voxel Key: Inverse of packing. Recovers x, y, z and adds gridmin. \begin{aligned} z &= key // (sx \times sy) \\ rem &= key - z \times (sx \times sy) \\ y &= rem // sx \\ x &= rem - y \times sx \\ x{final} &= x + grid\min.x \\ y{final} &= y + grid\min.y \\ z{final} &= z + grid\min.z \end{aligned} 3. Lookup Brick Bits and Base: a. Compute brick coordinates: bx = \lfloor x / 8 \rfloor, by = \lfloor y / 8 \rfloor, bz = \lfloor z / 8 \rfloor. b. Hash brick coordinates to a slot in the open-addressing hash table using a splitmix64-like mix. c. Probe linearly: slot = (hash + i) & (hashcapacity - 1) until hashkeys[slot] == kEmptyBrickKey or hashkeys[slot] == brickkey. d. Return brickbits pointer and brickbase index from hashvals[slot]. 4. Lookup Voxel Row in Bricks: a. Check bounds: if voxel outside gridmin/gridmax, return -1. b. Compute brick coords and local voxel ID: local\id = lx + 8 \times (ly + 8 \times lz), where lx, ly, lz are local coordinates within the brick. c. Call lookupbrickbitsandbase to get bits and base. d. Check occupancy: bits[word] & (1u << bit), where word = localid // 32 and bit = localid % 32. If 0, return -1. e. Compute rank (number of active voxels before localid): rank = \sum{i=0}^{word-1} \text{popc}(bits[i]) + \text{popc}(bits[word] \& ((1u << bit) - 1)) f. Return base + rank. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packvoxelkey(x, y, z, gridmin, gridmax): sx = gridmax.x - gridmin.x sy = gridmax.y - gridmin.y ux = x - gridmin.x uy = y - gridmin.y uz = z - gridmin.z return ux + sx (uy + sy uz) def unpackvoxelkey(key, gridmin, gridmax): sx = gridmax.x - gridmin.x sy = gridmax.y - gridmin.y z = key // (sx sy) rem = key - z (sx sy) y = rem // sx x = rem - y sx return (x + gridmin.x, y + gridmin.y, z + gridmin.z) def hashbrickkey(bx, by, bz): # Combine brick coordinates into a 64-bit key key = (bx << 42) | (by << 21) | bz # Splitmix64-like mix key ^= key >> 33 key = 0xff51afd7ed558ccd key ^= key >> 33 key = 0xc4ceb9fe1a85ec53 key ^= key >> 33 return key def lookupbrickbitsandbase(bx, by, bz, hashkeys, hashvals, hashcapacity): brickkey = hashbrickkey(bx, by, bz) slot = brickkey & (hashcapacity - 1) while True: if hashkeys[slot] == brickkey: return hashvals[slot] elif hashkeys[slot] == 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF: return -1 slot = (slot + 1) & (hashcapacity - 1) def lookupvoxelrowinbricks(x, y, z, gridmin, gridmax, brickbits, hashkeys, hashvals, hashcapacity): if not (gridmin.x <= x < gridmax.x and gridmin.y <= y < gridmax.y and gridmin.z <= z < gridmax.z): return -1 bx, by, bz = x // 8, y // 8, z // 8 lx, ly, lz = x % 8, y % 8, z % 8 localid = lx + 8 (ly + 8 lz) base = lookupbrickbitsandbase(bx, by, bz, hashkeys, hashvals, hashcapacity) if base == -1: return -1 word = localid // 32 bit = localid % 32 if not (brickbits[word] & (1 << bit)): return -1 rank = 0 for i in range(word): rank += bin(brickbits[i]).count('1') rank += bin(brickbits[word] & ((1 << bit) - 1)).count('1') return base + rank Stores a sparse voxel world using an outer grid of cells pointing to fixed-size inner bricks of packed voxels. The outer grid is GRIDSIZE³ cells, each null or pointing to an 8×8×8 brick of packed uint32t voxels. Parameters: WORLDSIZE (default 512), GRIDSIZE (default 64, calculated as WORLDSIZE/BRICKSIZE). The dynamic brick pool grows automatically when capacity is exceeded, safety-clamped to GRIDSIZE³. Time Complexity: Lookup is O(1) average case for hash table access, plus O(1) for bitset rank calculation. Memory Complexity: Hash table size depends on capacity (power of two). Brick bitsets are 16 words (64 bytes) per brick. Performance: Efficient for GPU ray casting due to low contention in concurrent inserts via hashing. Strengths: Reduces hash table size by hashing bricks instead of voxels; improves memory locality. Limitations: Requires power-of-two hash capacity; returns -1 for inactive voxels, requiring caller checks. Originated in the o-voxel-gpu project by quantaji, providing a sparse voxel storage and lookup scheme for GPU-based volume rendering and mesh conversion. It is used in real-time rendering applications requiring efficient sparse voxel access, such as the bad-apple-voxel-raytracer. The method addresses the need for efficient communication of ray guidance information (missing brick identifiers) from GPU to CPU I/O layers. quantaji/o-voxel-gpu, https://github.com/quantaji/o-voxel-gpu, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) NiekMSoftware/bad-apple-voxel-raytracer, https://github.com/NiekMSoftware/bad-apple-voxel-raytracer, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: GPU-based Hash Table for Ray Guidance
head: concurrent brick request table, lock-free hash table
body: This method provides an efficient mechanism for communicating ray guidance information (specifically, missing brick identifiers) from the GPU, where ray casting occurs, to the CPU I/O layer, which manages volume data residency. It functions as a concurrent set where keys and values are identical (brick IDs), indicating the presence of a non-resident brick required for rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 4D index representing a requested brick, composed of spatial coordinates (x, y, z) and a Level of Detail (LoD) index. Output: An update to a GPU-resident hash table marking the brick ID as present/needed. The table is read back to the CPU at the end of the frame to trigger data loading. Data Structures: The hash table is a 1D array of integers. Each entry stores a brick ID, and the value 0 is reserved to indicate an empty slot. Algorithm Steps: 1. Index Mapping: Convert the 4D brick index (x, y, z, \text{LoD}) into a unique 1D hash index by treating the 4D index as if it were stored in a contiguous 1D array. 2. Offset Adjustment: Increment the calculated 1D index by 1 so that the value 0 can be used to indicate that there is no entry at a location. 3. Concurrent Insert: Attempt to insert the brick ID into the table at the calculated index using lock-free atomic primitives. 4. Probing: If the concurrent insert fails due to a race condition (another thread wrote to the slot), probe the table a fixed number of times before giving up. 5. Readback: At the end of the rendering frame, read the hash table from GPU memory to the CPU. The CPU processes the non-zero entries as a list of bricks to fetch into the volume pool. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MAXPROBES = 10 EMPTYVALUE = 0 DIMX = 1 DIMY = 1 DIMZ = 1 DIMLOD = 1 def atomicload(table, idx): return table[idx] def atomiccompareandswap(table, idx, expected, desired): if table[idx] == expected: table[idx] = desired return True return False def map4dto1d(x, y, z, lod): # Converts 4D index to 1D form as if stored in a 1D array. index = x + y DIMX + z DIMX DIMY + lod DIMX DIMY DIMZ return index def insertmissingbrick(table, brickid, x, y, z, lod): # Step 1 & 2: Map and offset index = map4dto1d(x, y, z, lod) index = index + 1 # Offset by 1 to allow 0 as empty # Step 3 & 4: Lock-free insert with probing for probe in range(MAXPROBES): # Attempt to swap EMPTYVALUE with brickid if atomiccompareandswap(table, index, EMPTYVALUE, brickid): return True # Success # If failed, probe to next index index = index + 1 return False # Gave up after MAXPROBES Parameters: Probe Count: 10 attempts before giving up on a concurrent insert. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GLSL Lock Limitations: GLSL lacks native lock primitives, necessitating lock-free structures. Concurrent Write Hazards: Multiple rays may attempt to write the same or adjacent slots. The implementation handles this via probing rather than locking. Incomplete Recording: It is not an error if a missing brick is not recorded in the hash table due to probe exhaustion. The system invariant ensures progress as long as some missing bricks are recorded, ensuring at least one ray can continue. Memory: The table is described as "small" and requires significantly less memory than multi-render-target approaches. Not given in the sources. Performance: Lock-free design reduces contention compared to locked structures. Probing on failure handles collisions without stalling threads. Strengths: Efficient communication from GPU to CPU; low memory overhead; handles concurrency without locks. Limitations: Potential for missed requests if probes are exhausted (though acceptable per invariant); requires readback from GPU to CPU each frame. This method is part of a scalable GPU-based ray-guided volume rendering system. It addresses the bottleneck of transferring ray guidance data (missing brick IDs) from the GPU renderer to the CPU I/O layer. It contrasts with Crassin et al.'s approach which uses multiple render targets to avoid write hazards, offering a more memory-efficient solution at the cost of implementing lock-free logic. An Analysis of Scalable GPU-Based Ray-Guided Volume Rendering, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4260263/, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hash Grid Loss
body: Hash Grid Loss is a regularization term used in compressive neural volume rendering to minimize the bit consumption of the binary occupancy structure of a hash grid during training. It operates by modeling the probability distribution of the binary hash grid values and optimizing the negative log-likelihood, effectively driving the model to create a more concentrated hash grid structure. It is distinct from sibling methods like Voxel World Data Structure which manage spatial indexing, and from Entropy Loss which focuses on the continuous or quantized attribute values stored within active cells rather than the occupancy bits themselves. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Binary hash grid values (specifically counts of +1 and -1 values). Output: A scalar loss value L{\text{hash}} representing the estimated bit cost of encoding the hash grid structure. Data Structures: The method operates on the binary hash grid generated by the parent Hash Grids method. The grid consists of binary flags indicating occupancy. Parameters: hf: Occurrence frequency of the +1 value in the hash grid. M+: Total number of +1 values in the hash grid. M-: Total number of -1 values in the hash grid. Formula: The loss is defined as the sum of the negative log-probabilities of the observed values: L{\text{hash}} = M+ (-\log2(hf)) + M- (-\log2(1 - hf)) Where hf is the occurrence frequency of the +1 value. The terms -\log2(hf) and -\log2(1 - hf) represent the self-information (bit cost) of occupied and empty cells, respectively. Steps: 1. Count the total number of +1 values (M+) and -1 values (M-) in the hash grid. 2. Compute the occurrence frequency of +1 values: hf = M+ / (M+ + M-). 3. Compute the loss using the formula above. 4. Add L{\text{hash}} to the total training loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computehashgridloss(Mplus, Mminus): """ Compute the Hash Grid Loss for a binary hash grid. Args: Mplus: Total number of +1 values (occupied cells). Mminus: Total number of -1 values (empty cells). Returns: float: The computed hash grid loss Lhash. """ totalcells = Mplus + Mminus if totalcells == 0: return 0.0 hf = Mplus / totalcells # Clamp hf to avoid log(0) if the grid is perfectly empty or full epsilon = 1e-9 hfclamped = max(min(hf, 1.0 - epsilon), epsilon) log2hf = math.log2(hfclamped) log21minushf = math.log2(1.0 - hfclamped) loss = Mplus (-log2hf) + Mminus (-log21minushf) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If hf = 0 or hf = 1, the logarithm becomes undefined (negative infinity), indicating a perfectly empty or perfectly full grid. The definition assumes binary values +1 and -1. If the hash grid uses different encodings, the counts must be adjusted accordingly. Entropy Loss is a regularization term used in compressive neural volume rendering to minimize the bit consumption of anchor attributes during training. It operates by modeling the probability distribution of quantized attributes and optimizing the negative log-likelihood, effectively driving the model to represent data with fewer bits. It is distinct from the Hash Grid Loss, which optimizes the binary occupancy of the hash grid structure itself, whereas Entropy Loss focuses on the continuous or quantized attribute values stored within those active cells. Not given in the sources. Hash Grid Loss was introduced in the context of ECoNGS (Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats for Volume Visualization). It is part of a two-stage optimization process where the hash grid component is optimized for compression alongside anchor attributes. The method leverages the concept of entropy coding, where the bit cost of a symbol is proportional to the negative logarithm of its probability. By minimizing this loss, the model learns to distribute the hash grid values in a way that minimizes the expected bit length of the encoded structure. ECoNGS: Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats for Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2607.18466, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Entropy Loss
body: Entropy Loss is a regularization term used in compressive neural volume rendering to minimize the bit consumption of anchor attributes during training. It operates by modeling the probability distribution of quantized attributes and optimizing the negative log-likelihood, effectively driving the model to represent data with fewer bits. It is distinct from the Hash Grid Loss, which optimizes the binary occupancy of the hash grid structure itself, whereas Entropy Loss focuses on the continuous or quantized attribute values stored within those active cells. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Quantized anchor attributes \hat{\mathbf{f}}i for each attribute type \mathbf{f} \in \{\mathbf{A}\}. Input: Context model parameters: mean \mui and variance \sigmai for each attribute. Input: Quantization step Q (typically 1, 0.001, or 0.2 depending on the attribute component). Output: Scalar loss value L{\text{entropy}} representing the estimated bit cost. Data Structures: Attributes \mathbf{A}: A set of attribute vectors associated with each anchor. Quantized Attributes \hat{\mathbf{f}}i: The discrete representation of the original attribute \mathbf{f}i, obtained via rounding after scaling by Q. Context Model Output: For each anchor i, the model outputs a scalar mean \mui and a scalar variance \sigmai. Steps: 1. Quantization: For each attribute component in \mathbf{A}, apply a predefined quantization step Q to produce \hat{\mathbf{f}}i, enabling quantization-aware training. 2. Probability Modeling: The context model predicts the mean \mui and variance \sigmai for the quantized attribute \hat{\mathbf{f}}i. 3. Probability Calculation: Compute the probability p(\hat{\mathbf{f}}i) of the quantized value under the modeled Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(\mui, \sigmai). 4. Loss Aggregation: Sum the negative log-likelihood (in bits) over all attributes and all anchors. Formula: The entropy loss is defined as: L{\text{entropy}} = \sum{\mathbf{f} \in \{\mathbf{A}\}} \sum{i=1}^{N^{\text{at}}} \left( -\log2 p(\hat{\mathbf{f}}i) \right) where: N^{\text{at}} is the number of anchors. p(\hat{\mathbf{f}}i) is the probability of the quantized attribute \hat{\mathbf{f}}i given the Gaussian parameters \mui, \sigmai. \mathbf{f} iterates over the attribute types in the set \{\mathbf{A}\}. Parameters: Quantization Step Q: Varies by attribute component due to different numerical scales. Typical values cited are Q=1 for attribute fa, Q=0.001 for ls and lr, and Q=0.2 for \Delta xg. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance Zero: If \sigmai approaches zero, the Gaussian probability density becomes numerically unstable. Clamp \sigmai to a small minimum (e.g., 10^{-6}) to prevent division by zero or NaN gradients. Boundary Conditions: The Gaussian model assumes unbounded support, but quantized attributes are discrete. Evaluate the probability density function at the exact quantized point \hat{\mathbf{f}}i to maintain accuracy. This variant describes the mechanism of estimating the probability distribution for the attributes. The context model outputs individual mean \mui and variance \sigmai for each quantized attribute \hat{\mathbf{f}}i to formulate respective Gaussian distributions \mathcal{N}(\mui, \sigmai). This approach is chosen because the anchor attributes exhibit Gaussian-like distributions. It relies on parametric density estimation rather than histogram-based or non-parametric methods. Strengths: Directly optimizes for compression efficiency by minimizing the theoretical bit rate required to encode the attributes. It adapts to the data distribution via the context model. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of quantization steps Q for different attributes. When to use: When the goal is to compress neural Gaussian splats or similar volume representations by reducing the bit depth of stored attributes. Entropy Loss was introduced in the context of ECoNGS (Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats) for volume visualization. The method was developed to address the high memory footprint of neural Gaussian splats by integrating compression directly into the training process through entropy minimization. It builds on the principle that minimizing the negative log-likelihood of a probabilistic model approximates the minimum bit rate required for lossless compression of the modeled variables. name: Dual Point Map Insertion with Linear Probing
head: Dual Point Map, Linear Probing Hash Map Insertion
body: This method stores dual points in a hash table using linear probing to handle collisions, mapping unique point identifiers to their 3D positions via a combined 64-bit key-value pair. It builds on the hashing strategy of Hash Grids by hashing vertex positions to bucket indices. Inputs and Outputs: A point identifier id (integer), a 3D position p (float3), and a global counter CachedPointCounter (integer) are provided as inputs. The DualPointMap hash table is updated with the new entry, and the PrecalculatedDualPoints array is extended with p. Data Structures: DualPointMap is an array of 64-bit unsigned integers where each entry stores a key-value pair. The upper 32 bits store the point id (masked to 18 bits) and the lower 32 bits store the pointIdx (index into PrecalculatedDualPoints). The sentinel value ~0ull (all bits set, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) indicates an empty bucket. PrecalculatedDualPoints is an array of 3D vectors (float3) where index i corresponds to the pointIdx stored in the hash map. CachedPointCounter is a global integer variable initialized to 0, incremented upon each successful insertion. Constants: MASK = 0x3ffff (binary 111111111111111111, 18 bits) and SENTINEL = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF. Numbered Steps: 1. Mask the input id with 0x3ffff to keep only the lower 18 bits. 2. Loop indefinitely to find an empty bucket in DualPointMap. 3. Read the value kv from DualPointMap[id]. 4. If kv equals 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, the bucket is empty. Proceed to insertion. 5. Assign the current CachedPointCounter value to pointIdx and increment CachedPointCounter by 1. 6. Store the key-value pair in DualPointMap[id]: upper 32 bits are id, lower 32 bits are pointIdx (masked to 32 bits). 7. Store the point position p in PrecalculatedDualPoints at index pointIdx. 8. If the bucket is not empty (kv != 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF), increment id by 1, masked with 0x3ffff, and continue the loop from step 3. Formulas: Masking: id = id & 0x3ffff. Key-Value Packing: kv = (id << 32) | pointIdx. Linear Probing: id = (id + 1) & 0x3ffff. Where id is the point identifier, pointIdx is the assigned slot index, and kv is the 64-bit packed value. Parameters: Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Table Full: If the table becomes full, the loop will cycle indefinitely. The implementation assumes the table has sufficient capacity or handles fullness externally (not specified in sources). ID Masking: The 18-bit mask limits the number of unique IDs to 2^{18} = 262,144. IDs outside this range collide before hashing. Sentinel Value: The sentinel ~0ull must not be a valid key-value pair. Since valid id values are masked to 18 bits, the upper 14 bits of the upper 32 bits are always 0, ensuring ~0ull is distinct from any valid entry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. DualPointMap = [] # Array of uint64, size not given in sources PrecalculatedDualPoints = [] # Array of float3 CachedPointCounter = 0 MASK = 0x3FFFF SENTINEL = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF def insertdualpoint(id: int, p: tuple) -> None: # Mask ID to 18 bits id = id & MASK while True: kv = DualPointMap[id] # Check if bucket is empty if kv == SENTINEL: # Assign current counter to point index pointIdx = CachedPointCounter CachedPointCounter += 1 # Construct 64-bit value: upper 32 bits = id, lower 32 bits = pointIdx kv = (id << 32) | (pointIdx & 0xFFFFFFFF) # Store in hash map DualPointMap[id] = kv # Store position in separate array PrecalculatedDualPoints.append(p) return # Collision: linear probe id = (id + 1) & MASK Retrieves a dual point position given its ID using linear probing. It follows the same hashing and probing logic as insertion but checks for key equality rather than emptiness. It returns a boolean indicating success and the position via an output parameter. This variant is chosen when retrieving existing points or verifying point existence is required. Time Complexity: Average case O(1) for insert and lookup. Worst case O(N) due to linear probing collisions. Memory Complexity: O(M) for the hash table, where M is the number of buckets. Each bucket uses 64 bits and the position array uses 96 bits (3 floats) per point. Measured performance, scaling, strengths, limitations, and usage guidelines: Not given in the sources. name: Multi-Level Hashed Grid Construction
head: Grid Encoding (Hash Grid), Hash Grid, Hashed grid with macrocells, Multi-Level Hashed Grid, Row Displacement Compressed Grid
body: Multi-Level Hashed Grid Construction is a method for rapidly building a sparse acceleration structure for volume rendering and ray tracing that combines the memory efficiency of hashed grids with the traversal speed of multi-level structures. It solves the problem of high memory consumption in classic multi-level array grids and the poor traversal performance of one-level hashed grids by using row displacement compression to eliminate empty cells and macrocells to skip large empty regions. Unlike its sibling Hash Grids, which uses a single resolution level, this method employs multiple resolutions to balance detail and coverage, and unlike Voxel World Data Structure, it avoids storing explicit empty voxels by compressing the grid topology. The method constructs a hierarchical grid structure in two main phases: building the compressed hash table for the finest level and constructing macrocells for coarser levels. Inputs: Scene geometry (e.g., triangles or points). Grid density parameter \rho (empirically 32 for typical scanned scenes). Hash grid parameters: baseres (lowest level resolution), level (number of levels), perlevelscales (scaling factor, typically 1.3195079565048218), maxparams (max entries per level, 2^{\log2 T}), and numofhashfeet (feature dimensions, typically 2). Macrocell downscaling factor (empirically 6). Outputs: A compressed hash table H and item list L for the finest level. Macrocell bit arrays for coarser levels. Hash embedding buffer containing feature vectors for all levels. 1. Offset Array O Layout: Array of integers. Purpose: Stores computed offsets for rows (y, z) to map 3D coordinates to 1D indices. Size: Depends on grid dimensions My (y-dimension) and Mz (z-dimension). 2. Hash Table H Layout: Array of machine words (integers). Purpose: Stores item counts (initially) and starting indices for item lists (after prefix sum). Size: NH, determined by the position of the last non-empty bit in the temporary bit array bH plus one. 3. Item List L Layout: Linear array of object indices (integers). Purpose: Stores indices of scene items (e.g., triangles) intersecting each cell. Size: H[NH - 1]. Items for cell i are stored contiguously, indexed by H[i]. 4. Macrocells Layout: 3D bit array. Purpose: Indicates if a region of space is empty. Construction: Downscaled by a factor of 6 on each extent from the finest grid bitmap. 5. Hash Table Metadata (Multi-Level) offsets: Vector of 16 int32, storing cumulative offsets for each level. hashmapsizes: Vector of 16 uint32, storing the size of the hash map for each level. hashmapindicator: Vector of 16 int32, indicator (1 if resolution^3 \le params\in\level, else 0). hashembedding: 1D field of datatype, size equal to total parameters across all levels. 1. Determine Grid Dimensions: Use Heuristic 1 with density parameter \rho (e.g., 32) to determine the grid dimensions Mx, My, Mz. 2. Compute Row Offsets: Calculate offsets for each (y, z) row to compress the 3D grid into a 1D structure. o(y, z) = (My \times z) + y Store these in array O. 3. Identify Non-Empty Cells: Iterate through scene items. For each item intersecting cell i=(x,y,z), mark the corresponding bit in a temporary bit array bH at index h(x,y,z). h(x,y,z) = O[(My \times z) + y] + x 4. Allocate Hash Table H: Determine NH as the position of the last non-empty bit in bH plus one. Allocate H of size NH and initialize to zero. 5. Count Items: For each item intersecting cell j, increment H[j]. After this pass, H[j] contains the count of items in cell j. 6. Prefix Sum: Compute prefix sums to determine starting indices. python for i in range(1, NH): H[i] += H[i-1] After this, H[NH - 1] holds the total number of items, and H[j] points to the end of the item list for cell j. 7. Allocate Item List L: Allocate L of size H[NH - 1]. 8. Insert Items: Iterate through items in reverse order (to maintain sorted indices) and insert them into L. python # intersectedcells[i] is a precomputed list of cell indices j for object i for i in range(NI - 1, -1, -1): for j in intersectedcells[i]: H[j] -= 1 L[H[j]] = i. 1. Calculate Level Parameters: For each level i from 0 to level - 1: Calculate resolution: \text{resolution}i = \lceil \text{base\res} \times \exp(i \times \log(\text{per\level\scales})) - 1.0 \rceil + 1 Calculate paramsinlevel = \text{resolution}i^3, rounded up to the nearest multiple of 8, capped at maxparams. Determine hashmapindicator: 1 if \text{resolution}i^3 \le \text{params\in\level}, else 0. Accumulate offsets for the embedding buffer. 2. Verify Initialization: Assert that the final accumulated offset equals the shape of the hashembedding array. 1. Create Finest Bitmap: Generate a 3D bitmap D representing the occupancy of the finest hashed grid cells. 2. Downscale: Downscale D by a factor of 6 on each extent using a quick 3D bitmap scaling operation to create coarser macrocell levels. 3. Store Macrocells: Store the resulting 3D bit arrays for each level. These are used during traversal to skip empty regions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inithashtable(baseres, level, perlevelscales, maxparams, hashembeddingsize): offsets = [0] 16 hashmapsizes = [0] 16 hashmapindicator = [0] 16 currentoffset = 0 for i in range(level): scalefactor = perlevelscales i resolution = int(math.ceil(baseres scalefactor - 1.0)) + 1 rawparams = resolution 3 if rawparams % 8 != 0: paramsinlevel = ((rawparams // 8) + 1) 8 else: paramsinlevel = rawparams if paramsinlevel > maxparams: paramsinlevel = maxparams if rawparams <= paramsinlevel: indicator = 1 else: indicator = 0 hashmapsizes[i] = paramsinlevel hashmapindicator[i] = indicator offsets[i] = currentoffset currentoffset += paramsinlevel assert currentoffset == hashembeddingsize return offsets, hashmapsizes, hashmapindicator Grid Density (\rho): 32 (for Buddha scene, balances render time and build time). perlevelscales: 1.3195079565048218. Macrocell Downscaling Factor: 6. numofhashfeet: 2. baseres: Variable, depends on scene scale. maxparams: 2^{\log2 T}. Memory Exhaustion: Non-compressed multi-level array grids can exhaust system memory for large scenes (e.g., Lucy scene), whereas hashed grids reduce memory footprint by roughly one order of magnitude. Hash Collisions: The row displacement compression assumes a perfect hash function for static data, avoiding collisions in the compressed structure. Small Non-Uniform Scenes: For small scenes with non-uniform density (e.g., Office, Conference), classic adaptive multi-level array grids may outperform this method. An algorithm to generate compression headers for a multigrid volume representation. It determines the dominant label and constant subregion status for each node in the hierarchy by analyzing child elements. It initializes a constant flag, iterates through 8 children (skipping those with label 0xFFFFFFFF), counts label occurrences to find the max label, and updates the constant flag only if all children are constant and share the same label. It writes the max label and constant flag to the output array and updates the LOD start index by adding currentdim^3. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of scene items NI, except for hash function computation which has a worst-case complexity of O(M \times 4/3), where M is the number of cells in the grid. Memory Complexity: Roughly one order of magnitude lower than regular, non-compressed multi-level array grids. Multi-level hashed grids have slightly higher memory consumption than one-level hashed grids due to the macrocell structures. Performance: Multi-level hashed grids provide around twice the render time performance of one-level hashed grids for large scanned scenes with many empty cells, due to macrocells. Build times are short and roughly linear with the number of triangles. Strengths: Low memory footprint, fast build time, good render performance for large sparse scenes. Limitations: Less effective for small, non-uniform density scenes compared to adaptive array grids. The method was introduced to address the limitations of one-level hashed grids (poor render time) and classic multi-level grids (high memory usage) in the context of interactive ray tracing of large scanned models. It builds on row displacement compression techniques and macrocell concepts from Wald et al. (2006). The multi-level hash grid encoding variant is also used in neural graphics primitives (NGP) for feature encoding. name: Universal Hash Optimization
head: Universal Hash Function for Hash Grids
body: Universal Hash Optimization is a technique used within Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) structures to mitigate hash collisions in the underlying hash table. It replaces standard deterministic hashing with a randomized universal hash function, ensuring that distinct non-isomorphic nodes are distributed uniformly across hash table buckets. This reduces the average number of equality checks required during lookups, thereby improving search performance compared to naive hashing methods that may cluster nodes in specific buckets. The method operates on a node n within an octree structure. It computes a hash value k recursively for internal nodes and directly from metadata for leaf nodes (voxels), then applies a linear congruential transformation to map this value to a bucket index. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A node n in the octree. Output: An integer hash value representing the bucket index. Data Structures: Node n: Represents a voxel or an internal octree node. info(n): A function returning the unique identifier or metadata hash associated with a voxel node n. Children: For non-voxel nodes, a list of 8 child nodes. Parameters: p: A prime number. m: The number of buckets in the hash table. a, b: Integers such that a, b \in \{0, \dots, p-1\}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize accumulator k = 0. 2. Check if n is a voxel (leaf node). 3. If n is not a voxel: iterate through all children c of node n. Recursively compute the hash for each child c. XOR the child's hash into the accumulator: k \leftarrow k \oplus \text{recursive}(c). Apply the universal hash transformation to the accumulator: k \leftarrow (a \cdot k + b) \pmod p. 4. If n is a voxel: set k \leftarrow \text{info}(n). 5. Return the final hash value: ((a \cdot k + b) \pmod p) \pmod m. Formula: The bucket index is computed as H{ab}(k) = ((a \cdot k + b) \pmod p) \pmod m, where p is a prime, m is the number of buckets, and a, b are integers in \{0, \dots, p-1\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def universalhash(n, a, b, p, m): # n: node to hash # a, b: integers in [0, p-1] # p: prime modulus # m: number of buckets # n.isvoxel: boolean attribute indicating leaf status # n.children: iterable of child nodes # n.info: metadata/identifier value for voxel nodes k = 0 if n.isvoxel: k = n.info else: for c in n.children: childhash = universalhash(c, a, b, p, m) k = k ^ childhash k = (a k + b) % p return ((a k + b) % p) % m Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameter Selection: The choice of a and b is critical. They must be chosen from the specified range to ensure the probability of collision between distinct nodes is low. Modulus Arithmetic: The intermediate calculations (a \cdot k + b) can overflow standard integer types if p is large. Implementation must handle modular arithmetic carefully to prevent overflow before the modulo operation. Voxel Info: The info(n) value must effectively distinguish between different voxel contents or states. An optimization to avoid redundant recursive hash computations by caching results in an external hash table. When searching for a node, the system checks an external hash table using the node's memory address as the key. If the address is found, the cached hash value is returned immediately. If not found, the recursive hash computation is executed, the result is stored in the external hash table, and then returned. If the structure of a node is modified, its entry must be removed from the external hash table to ensure consistency. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The universal hash function reduces the clustering of nodes in hash table buckets, leading to fewer collisions and faster average-case lookup times compared to non-universal hashing. Strengths: Uniform distribution of nodes minimizes worst-case collision scenarios. Limitations: Requires storing parameters a, b, p and potentially maintaining the memoization table. This method originates from research into the compression and efficiency of Sparse Voxel Octrees for Global Illumination calculations. The specific implementation was developed to address the inefficiency of standard hash tables in SVO structures, where naive hashing caused a significant percentage of nodes to accumulate in single buckets, slowing down searches. The universal hash function used is adapted from the family of universal hash functions described by Braverman et al. (cited as [BB11] in the source). name: SpatialHash3D
head: Uniform 3D Hash Grid
body: SpatialHash3D is a spatial index structure using a uniform 3D hash grid to enable efficient nearest-neighbor and radius-based queries for static datasets, providing O(1) cell lookup. It differs from its siblings by prioritizing implementation simplicity and predictable performance for static data over the adaptive granularity of octrees or the complex balancing of KD-trees, making it suitable for straightforward radius queries where data does not change during the query phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A static array of 3D points, where each point contains coordinates (x, y, z) and an associated value. Output: A hash table mapping cell indices to lists of points, supporting queries for points within a radius or the k-nearest neighbors. Data Structures: Hash Table: A dictionary or array mapping integer cell indices to a list of point references. Cell Index: An integer derived from the 3D coordinates. Point Structure: Contains center: [x, y, z] and associated data. Parameters: cellSize: The size of each cell in the hash grid, determining the granularity of the spatial partition. queryRadius: The search radius for radius-based queries. k: The maximum number of nearest neighbors to return. Steps: 1. Build: Iterate through all input points. For each point at (x, y, z), calculate the cell index. Insert the point into the list associated with that cell index in the hash table. 2. Query Radius: Given a query point (qx, qy, qz) and a radius r: Calculate the cell index of the query point. Determine the range of neighboring cells that intersect with the sphere of radius r centered at the query point. Iterate through all points in these neighboring cells. Calculate the Euclidean distance di from the query point to each candidate point. Return all points where di \le r. 3. Query K-Nearest: Similar to radius query, but maintain a priority queue or sorted list of the k closest points found within the relevant cells, capped at k. Formulas: Cell Index Calculation: The specific hash function is not detailed, but it maps 3D coordinates to a unique integer index based on cellSize. Distance: di = \sqrt{(xi - qx)^2 + (yi - qy)^2 + (zi - qz)^2} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class SpatialHash3D: def init(self, cellsize): self.cellsize = cellsize self.grid = {} # Map from cellindex to list of points def getcellindex(self, x, y, z): # Calculate cell coordinates cx = int(x / self.cellsize) cy = int(y / self.cellsize) cz = int(z / self.cellsize) # Hash the cell coordinates to a single integer # Note: Specific hash function not provided in sources return hash((cx, cy, cz)) def build(self, points): for point in points: x, y, z = point['center'] cellidx = self.getcellindex(x, y, z) if cellidx not in self.grid: self.grid[cellidx] = [] self.grid[cellidx].append(point) def queryradius(self, x, y, z, radius): results = [] # Determine range of cells to check # Note: Exact neighbor cell calculation logic not provided in sources # Iterate through relevant cells for cellidx in self.getneighborcells(x, y, z, radius): if cellidx in self.grid: for point in self.grid[cellidx]: px, py, pz = point['center'] dist = ((px - x)2 + (py - y)2 + (pz - z)2)0.5 if dist <= radius: results.append(point) return results def getneighborcells(self, x, y, z, radius): # Placeholder for neighbor cell iteration logic # This would calculate the bounding box of cells intersecting the sphere return [] # Not given in the sources. def queryknearest(self, x, y, z, k): # Similar to queryradius but limits results to k nearest # Note: Specific implementation details not provided in sources return [] This method optimizes spatial hash lookups in temporal volume rendering by reusing hash indices from the previous frame, thereby reducing the frequency of expensive atomic memory operations on the hash grid. It differs from standard spatial hash lookups by decoupling the index computation from the final shading pass, using a texture-based history buffer to validate and propagate indices across frames. Time Complexity: O(1) average case for cell lookup during build and query, assuming uniform distribution and efficient hashing. Query time depends on the number of points in the relevant cells and the search radius. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of points and the number of occupied cells. Performance: Predictable performance for static datasets. Strengths: Simple implementation, easy radius queries, suitable for static data. Limitations: Not adaptive to data density; performance degrades if points are not uniformly distributed or if cellSize is poorly chosen. When to use: Static datasets where simplicity and predictable performance are prioritized. When not to use: Dynamic datasets requiring frequent updates or highly non-uniform data distributions where adaptive structures like octrees might be better. SpatialHash3D is part of a pipeline for generating scalar fields from drill-hole sample data and rendering them as voxel volumes, specifically within the context of 3D IDW interpolation. It was introduced as a recommended v1 implementation for spatial indexing in this context due to its straightforward nature and suitability for static data. feat: 3D IDW interpolation volume and voxel visualisation, https://github.com/darkmine-oss/baselode/pull/50, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Reprojected Spatial Hash Map Indices
head: Temporal Reprojection of Hash Indices
body: This method optimizes spatial hash lookups in temporal volume rendering by reusing hash indices from the previous frame, thereby reducing the frequency of expensive atomic memory operations on the hash grid. It differs from standard spatial hash lookups by splitting the Ray Traced Ambient Occlusion (RTAO) pass into a reprojection step and a fullscreen shading step, using a texture-based history buffer to validate and propagate indices across frames. Inputs: Previous frame’s history texture containing hash indices and checksums. Current frame’s scene state and camera parameters for reprojection and fallback computation. Hash grid data structure for fallback index lookups. Frame counter uniform (uniforms.frameindex). Touch mask parameter derived from VXAOHASHTOUCHPERIOD. Outputs: Current frame’s hash index texture written to GPU memory. Updated hash grid frame counters modified via atomic operations. The method relies on a texture storing the hash indices from the previous frame. The history buffer contains at least two fields per entry: the spatial hash index and a checksum value used to validate that the spatial location and scene state have not changed significantly. The hash grid maintains a frame counter array to track entry freshness. 1. Reproject: Look up the hash index from the previous frame. If the history and checksum are valid, use the reprojected index. Otherwise, compute the new hash index. 2. Write: Write the current frame’s hash index to a texture. 3. Render: Perform a fullscreen RTAO pass using the gbuffer and the hashmap index texture. 4. Update Frame Counter: Atomically update the frame counter for the hash entry. To reduce atomic traffic, this update is performed only periodically based on a touch mask. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. VXAOHASHTOUCHPERIOD = 8 # Example value; source uses VXAOHASHTOUCHPERIOD touchmask = VXAOHASHTOUCHPERIOD - 1 class Texture: def read(self, pos): return (0, 0) def write(self, pos, val): pass class HashGrid: def compute(self, pos): return 0 framecounters = {} def atomicexchange(addr, newvalue): """Simulates GPU atomic exchange for frame counter update.""" oldvalue = addr.value addr.value = newvalue return oldvalue def checkchecksum(prevchecksum, currentscenestate): """Validates that the spatial location and scene state have not changed significantly.""" # Exact validation logic is not detailed in source return True def computespatialhash(position, hashgrid): """Computes the new hash index using the standard spatial hash function.""" # Exact hash function details are in SpatialHash3D return hashgrid.compute(position) def reprojecthashindex(previousindextexture, currentscenestate, hashgrid, frameindex, screenposition): """Determines the hash index for the current frame.""" previndex, prevchecksum = previousindextexture.read(screenposition) isvalid = checkchecksum(prevchecksum, currentscenestate) if isvalid: return previndex, True else: newindex = computespatialhash(currentscenestate.position, hashgrid) return newindex, False def updateframecounter(hashframes, hashindex, frameindex, touchmask): """Atomically updates the frame counter for a hash entry using a touch mask.""" if (frameindex & touchmask) == (hashindex & touchmask): atomicexchange(hashframes[hashindex], frameindex) def rtaoindexpass(previousindextexture, hashgrid, frameindex, screenposition): # Step 1: Reproject currentindex, = reprojecthashindex(previousindextexture, currentscenestate, hashgrid, frameindex, screenposition) # Step 2: Write index to texture currentindextexture.write(screenposition, currentindex) # Step 3: Update frame counter updateframecounter(hashgrid.framecounters, currentindex, frameindex, touchmask) return currentindextexture VXAOHASHTOUCHPERIOD: Determines the frequency of frame counter updates. The touch mask is derived as VXAOHASHTOUCHPERIOD - 1. The source does not specify the exact value used, but implies it is a power of two to facilitate bitwise masking. Atomic Traffic: Atomic reads and writes to the hash map cause high MMU activity and latency. Without reprojection, the index pass can take over 6 milliseconds on hardware like the MacBook Air (M2). Invalid History: If the history is invalid due to camera movement or scene changes, the fallback to computing a new hash index incurs the full cost of atomic operations. Checksum Mismatch: A mismatching checksum triggers a recomputation, which is more expensive than a reprojected lookup. A spatial index structure using a uniform 3D hash grid to enable efficient nearest-neighbor and radius-based queries for static datasets [Parent]. It provides O(1) cell lookup and serves as the fallback mechanism when reprojection fails [Parent]. Choose it when static spatial queries are required without temporal dependencies [Parent]. SpatialHash3D A fullscreen shading pass that consumes the reprojected hash index texture to compute ambient occlusion. It is decoupled from the index computation to improve shader occupancy and reduce atomic contention. Choose it when decoupling shading from index generation improves performance. RTAO Measured Performance: monu2.vox: Average GPU walltime reduced from 6.46 ms to 5.88 ms (-9.01%). FPS remained stable at ~144. sponza-1024.vox: Average GPU walltime reduced from 26.17 ms to 24.95 ms (-4.68%). FPS increased from 64.81 to 67.72 (+4.49%). Memory Usage Reduction: Device Atomic Bytes Read dropped from 309.19 MiB to 4 KiB. Device Atomic Bytes Written dropped from 617.13 MiB to 19.16 MiB. Strengths: Significantly reduces atomic memory traffic and MMU activity, leading to lower latency in the index pass. Limitations: The performance gain is modest in heavy scenes (e.g., Sponza) and depends on the validity of the history buffer. When to Use: When atomic operations on the hash grid are a bottleneck and the scene/camera motion is smooth enough to allow valid history reprojection. This optimization was introduced in the development of the vxray voxel raytracer, specifically in commit c41b366 dated 2026-09-01. It was developed to address high MMU activity and latency observed during the spatial hash lookup pass on Apple Silicon hardware (MacBook Air M2). The technique is part of a broader effort to optimize sparse voxel rendering by reducing the cost of hash map interactions.
