name: Stack-Based Representation (SBR)
head: Stacks
body: Stack-Based Representation (SBR) is a sparse volume data structure that decomposes a voxel grid into vertical columns, compressing each column via run-length encoding of attribute values along the depth axis. It solves the problem of storing layered volumetric data by exploiting vertical coherence, separating geometric layer boundaries from attribute values. Unlike sibling structures like SparseGrid or Hash Grids that rely on spatial hashing or tree traversal for arbitrary sparsity, SBR is specialized for datasets with strong vertical anisotropy, such as terrain or layered scenes, achieving linear construction complexity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid V of resolution w \times h \times d, where each voxel v{x,y,z} stores one or more attributes (e.g., color, density, material). Output: A set S of vertical stacks, one for each (x,y) position in the grid. Data Structures: Each stack S{x,y} is a sequence of intervals i1, i2, \dots, in sorted by height. Interval ik: A tuple \langle ak, hk \rangle. ak: The attribute value (e.g., material ID, color) shared by all voxels in the interval. hk: The cumulative height (z-coordinate) of the top voxel of this interval. Implicit Geometry: The interval ik covers voxels from z = 1 + h{k-1} to z = hk. For the first interval (k=1), h0 is assumed to be 0. Formulas: The stack S{x,y} is the union of all voxels in the column: S{x,y} \cong V{x,y} = \bigcup{i=1}^d v{x,y,i} An interval ik represents the space of voxels with identical attribute ak: ik \cong \bigcup{i=1+h{k-1}}^{hk} v{x,y,i} Intervals are strictly sorted by height: hk < h{k+1} \quad \text{for any given } k \text{ such that } 1 \le k \le n Algorithm: 1. Iterate through every voxel v{x,y,z} in the grid V for x \in [0, w-1], y \in [0, h-1], z \in [0, d-1]. 2. For each column (x,y), maintain a current attribute currattr and current height currh. Initialize currattr to the attribute of the first voxel v{x,y,0} and currh to 0. 3. For each subsequent voxel v{x,y,z} (where z > 0): Let newattr be the attribute of v{x,y,z}. If newattr == currattr: Increment currh by 1. Else: Append a new interval \langle \text{curr\attr}, \text{curr\h} \rangle to the stack S{x,y}. Update currattr = newattr. Update currh = z. 4. After processing all z for a column, append the final interval \langle \text{curr\attr}, \text{curr\h} \rangle to S{x,y}. 5. Store the resulting stack S{x,y} in the set S. Pitfalls: Precision: Height values hk must be stored with sufficient bits to represent the maximum depth d. Boundary Conditions: The first interval always starts at z=1 (or z=0 in 0-indexed logic) with h0=0. Degenerate Input: If a column contains only one attribute value, the stack contains a single interval with height d. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildsbr(grid, width, height, depth): """ Builds the Stack-Based Representation for a voxel grid. grid: 3D array [width][height][depth] storing attribute values. Returns: A dictionary mapping (x, y) to a list of intervals. """ stacks = {} for x in range(width): for y in range(height): stackintervals = [] if depth == 0: stacks[(x, y)] = stackintervals continue # Initialize with the first voxel currentattr = grid[x][y][0] currenth = 0 for z in range(1, depth): newattr = grid[x][y][z] if newattr == currentattr: # Extend the current interval currenth = z else: # Finalize the previous interval and start a new one stackintervals.append((currentattr, currenth)) currentattr = newattr currenth = z # Append the final interval for this column stackintervals.append((currentattr, currenth)) stacks[(x, y)] = stackintervals return stacks Extends SBR by organizing stacks into a quadtree to compress regions with identical interval sequences, achieving higher compression for layered data. A building block for QuadStack that groups rectangular regions of stacks sharing identical attributes and interval counts, compressing geometry as heightfields. Time Complexity: Construction is O(n), where n = w \times h \times d, because each voxel is processed exactly once. Parallelism: Construction is embarrassingly parallel as stack construction for one column does not depend on neighboring columns. Memory: Memory usage depends on the number of layers (intervals) per stack. In the worst case (alternating attributes every voxel), it uses more memory than the raw voxel grid due to interval overhead. In best-case layered scenarios, it is highly compact. Strengths: Optimal for vertically layered data (e.g., terrain, geological strata); simple construction; fast parallelization. Limitations: Poor compression for isotropic or horizontally layered data; does not inherently handle arbitrary 3D sparsity without hierarchical extensions like QuadStack. The Stack-Based Representation was introduced as a foundational method for compressing layered volumetric datasets. It was developed to address the inefficiency of standard voxel storage for data with strong vertical coherence, such as terrain models or atmospheric layers. The method serves as the basis for more advanced structures like QuadStack. QuadStack: An Efficient Representation and Direct Rendering of Layered Datasets | DCGI, https://dcgi.fel.cvut.cz/publications/2021/graciano-tvcg-quadstack/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: QuadStack
head: QuadStack Construction
body: QuadStack is a data structure and algorithm for the compression and direct rendering of layered volumetric datasets. It exploits directional anisotropy and spatial coherence in the vertical sequence of layer attributes to decouple attribute data (color, density) from geometric data (layer heights). Unlike Stack-Based Representation (SBR), which stores stacks in a flat list, QuadStack organizes similar stacks into a quadtree to identify and compress regions with constant layer topology, achieving significantly higher compression rates while maintaining real-time rendering performance. Inputs: A 3D voxel grid V of resolution w \times h \times d, where layers are parallel to the xy-plane. Each voxel has an associated attribute value (e.g., material type, density). Outputs: A QuadStack data structure consisting of a quadtree of gstacks, where each gstack contains an ordered sequence of attribute intervals and corresponding heightfields. Stack: A vertical column of voxels at position (x, y). Represented as a run-length encoded list of intervals. intervals: List of tuples (attrid, startz, endz). attrid: Integer identifier for the material/attribute. startz, endz: Integer voxel coordinates defining the vertical extent of the interval. Gstack (Group of Stacks): A collection of similar stacks grouped together. intervals: List of tuples (attrid, heightfield). attrid: The attribute identifier for this interval. heightfield: A 2D array (or compressed representation) storing the z-coordinates of the layer boundary for each (x, y) position within the gstack's domain. If the interval is a wildcard, the heightfield stores the boundary for the "next" attribute in the sequence or is null/ignored. QuadStack Node: isleaf: Boolean. gstack: Gstack object (if leaf). children: List of 4 QuadStack Node objects (if internal). domain: Bounding box (x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}) in the xy-plane. The construction proceeds in two phases: Top-Down Subdivision and Bottom-Up Merging. 1. Convert to Stacks: For every (x, y) in the grid, extract the vertical stack. Run-length encode the stack to produce a list of (attrid, zstart, zend) intervals. 2. Build Quadtree: Recursively subdivide the xy-plane into four quadrants. 3. Leaf Criterion: A node is a leaf if all stacks within its domain have the same attribute sequence. That is, for all stacks Si, Sj in the node's domain, the list of attrids is identical. 4. Create Gstacks: For each leaf node, group the stacks. Since the attribute sequence is identical, the gstack's intervals list contains the common attrids. The heightfield for each interval stores the z-boundary between that attribute and the next one for all (x, y) in the leaf's domain. This phase merges duplicate intervals from leaf nodes up to ancestor nodes to increase compression. 1. Traverse Bottom-Up: Process nodes from leaves to root. 2. Map Attributes: For an internal node with four children C1, C2, C3, C4, each having a gstack with intervals I{Ck}, map the attribute values to a common sequence. Use a wildcard to represent non-matching attributes. The goal is to find a mapping that maximizes the number of terminal intervals (intervals where all four children agree on the attribute, i.e., no). 3. Find Optimal Mapping: The problem is equivalent to finding a common motif with gaps. Use a brute-force search to determine the permutation of child intervals that yields the maximum number of matching terminal intervals. Let the optimal mapping produce a new sequence of attributes A{parent} for the parent node. 4. Merge Gstacks: If the derived gstack for the parent has at least one terminal interval, create a new gstack for the parent node. Heightfield Generation: Pack the heightfields from the children's intervals into the parent's heightfield. For a terminal interval, the parent's heightfield is the common boundary. For wildcard intervals, the heightfield may store the boundary from one child or be marked as invalid/merged. 5. Cleanup Children: Delete the derived gstacks from the children. Convert every propagated interval in the children's gstacks to a (wildcard) interval. Group adjacent intervals if necessary. 6. Pruning: If a child gstack ends up as a single interval, it provides no information and can be safely deleted from the node. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildquadstack(voxelgrid, width, height, depth): """ voxelgrid: 3D array [x][y][z] containing attribute IDs. Returns: QuadStack root node. """ # Phase 1: Top-Down Subdivision root = QuadStackNode(domain=(0, width, 0, height)) buildsubdivision(root, voxelgrid, width, height, depth) # Phase 2: Bottom-Up Merging mergebottomup(root) return root def buildsubdivision(node, voxelgrid, w, h, d): """Recursively subdivide and create leaf gstacks.""" xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax = node.domain # Base case: 1x1 block if xmax - xmin == 1 and ymax - ymin == 1: x, y = xmin, ymin stack = extractstack(voxelgrid, x, y, d) node.isleaf = True node.gstack = creategstackfromstack(stack) return # Recursive step midx = (xmin + xmax) // 2 midy = (ymin + ymax) // 2 children = [] for i in range(2): for j in range(2): childdomain = ( xmin + i (midx - xmin), xmin + (i + 1) (midx - xmin), ymin + j (midy - ymin), ymin + (j + 1) (midy - ymin)) child = QuadStackNode(domain=childdomain) buildsubdivision(child, voxelgrid, w, h, d) children.append(child) # Check if all children have the same attribute sequence if aresequencesidentical(children): # Merge children into a single leaf gstack at this node node.isleaf = True node.gstack = mergechildrengstacks(children) # Remove children node.children = [] else: node.isleaf = False node.children = children def aresequencesidentical(children): """Check if all leaf children have the same list of attrids.""" if not children: return False refseq = children[0].gstack.intervalsattrids for child in children[1:]: if child.gstack.intervalsattrids != refseq: return False return True def mergechildrengstacks(children): """Merge 4 children gstacks into one leaf gstack.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def mergebottomup(node): """Process node after children have been processed.""" if node.isleaf: return # Recursively merge children first for child in node.children: mergebottomup(child) # Attempt to merge children into this node # 1. Map attributes to find common intervals # 2. Maximize terminal intervals parentgstack, wildcardintervals = findoptimalmapping(node.children) if parentgstack.hasterminalintervals(): node.gstack = parentgstack node.isleaf = True # Promote to leaf if merged successfully # Cleanup children: convert propagated intervals to '' for child in node.children: converttowildcards(child.gstack, wildcardintervals) # If child gstack is only '', delete it if child.gstack.isallwildcards(): # Remove from parent's children list pass else: # No merge possible, keep as internal node node.isleaf = False def findoptimalmapping(childrengstacks): """ Find mapping of 4 children gstacks to maximize terminal intervals. Returns (newgstack, setofwildcardintervals). Uses brute-force search over permutations of child intervals. """ # Brute-force search over permutations to maximize terminal intervals. # Not given in the sources. pass def alignsequences(gstacks): """ Align 4 gstacks. Use '' for non-matching attributes. Returns a list of intervals with attrids or ''. """ # Not given in the sources. pass def converttowildcards(gstack, wildcardintervals): """Convert specific intervals in gstack to ''.""" for interval in gstack.intervals: if interval in wildcardintervals: interval.attrid = '' To retrieve the attribute at (x, y, z): 1. Traverse the quadtree from the root to the leaf corresponding to (x, y). 2. In the leaf gstack, sample the heightfields to determine which interval contains z. 3. Total access time is O(\log n + m), where n = w \times h and m is the maximum stack size. In practice, m \ll n, so the method is assumed to run in logarithmic time. Layer Direction: Assumes layers are parallel to the xy-plane. Wildcards: If a gstack consists entirely of intervals, it is deleted. Complexity: Construction time is O(n \log n) for subdivision and O(n \times (m!)^4) for merging, where n is the number of stacks and m is the max intervals per gstack. Compression: Achieves 4× to 54× compression of the original voxel memory footprint. Uses 66% to 99% less memory than uncompressed data. Rendering Performance: 18-79 MRays/s on an NVIDIA 970 GTX. Comparable to state-of-the-art algorithms. Access Time: O(\log n + m) for value retrieval. Strengths: High compression for layered data; direct rendering without mesh conversion; decoupled attributes and geometry allow transfer function optimization. Limitations: Only effective for data with strong directional anisotropy and spatial coherence in layer sequence. QuadStack was introduced by Alejandro Graciano, Antonio J. Rueda, Adam Pospíšil, Jiří Bittner, and Bedřich Benes. It builds upon the Stack-Based Representation (SBR) [1081-stack-based-representation-sbr.md], extending it with quadtree compression. It is applied to datasets from geology, industrial models, microstructural data, and magnetic reconnection simulations. name: Group of Stacks (gstack)
head: Gstack
body: A gstack is a compact data structure that represents a rectangular region of vertical stacks in a voxel grid, where all stacks share an identical sequence of attribute values and the same number of intervals. It solves the problem of redundant storage in sparse volume representations by compressing the common attribute information while storing the varying geometry as a set of non-intersecting heightfields. Unlike standard spatial decompositions that subdivide solely based on geometric complexity, gstacks specifically exploit attribute uniformity to reduce memory footprint, serving as the fundamental building block for the QuadStack hierarchy. Input: A rectangular region of stacks S defined by coordinates [x{min}, y{min}, x{max}, y{max}] within the volume grid. Each stack S{x,y} in this region must have the same number of intervals n and an identical sequence of attribute values a1, a2, \dots, an. Output: A gstack structure G consisting of a sequence of n intervals. A gstack G is encoded as a sequence of n intervals i1, i2, \dots, in. Each interval ik is a tuple: ik = \langle ak, Hk \rangle Where: ak: The attribute value (scalar or vector) common to all stacks in the region for the k-th interval. Hk: A heightfield (2D array) with dimensions (x{max} - x{min} + 1) \times (y{max} - y{min} + 1). The heightfield Hk stores the geometric extent (height) of the k-th interval for each stack in the region. The height h{x,y} of a specific stack S{x,y} is mapped to the heightfield coordinate (x - x{min}, y - y{min}). Specifically: Hk[x - x{min}, y - y{min}] = h{x,y,k} where h{x,y,k} is the height of the k-th interval in stack S{x,y}. 1. Attribute Uniformity: All stacks covered by the gstack share the exact same attribute sequence a1, \dots, an. 2. Non-Intersecting Heightfields: Because the intervals are ordered consistently for all stacks, the heightfields never intersect. For any coordinate (i, j) in the heightfield domain and any interval index k: h{i,j,k} < h{i,j,k+1} This ensures that the k-th interval is always below the (k+1)-th interval for every stack in the region. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class GStack: def init(self, xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax, attributesequence): self.xmin = xmin self.ymin = ymin self.xmax = xmax self.ymax = ymax self.n = len(attributesequence) self.attributes = attributesequence width = xmax - xmin + 1 height = ymax - ymin + 1 # Initialize heightfields for each interval self.heightfields = [[[0] height for in range(width)] for in range(self.n)] def setstackheight(self, x, y, k, heightval): localx = x - self.xmin localy = y - self.ymin if not (0 <= localx < len(self.heightfields[0][0]) and 0 <= localy < len(self.heightfields[0])): raise ValueError("Coordinates out of GStack bounds") self.heightfields[k][localx][localy] = heightval def getstackheight(self, x, y, k): localx = x - self.xmin localy = y - self.ymin return self.heightfields[k][localx][localy] Boundary Conditions: The heightfield dimensions are strictly determined by the bounding box. Accessing coordinates outside [x{min}, x{max}] \times [y{min}, y{max}] is invalid. Attribute Mismatch: A gstack cannot represent a region where stacks have different attribute sequences. If attributes differ, the region must be subdivided or represented by multiple gstacks. Height Ordering: The implementation must ensure that h{i,j,k} < h{i,j,k+1} holds for all i, j. Violating this implies a logical error in the volume data or the stacking process. A wildcard interval is a special type of interval used in internal nodes of the QuadStack hierarchy to represent gaps between terminal intervals. It corresponds to intervals stored elsewhere in descendant or ancestor nodes. Defined as iw = \langle, Hw \rangle, it has an associated heightfield Hw. If iw represents intervals ik, \dots, i{k+j} in a descendant node nd, Hw combines the heightfields of the top intervals of all sets of intervals in descendant nodes grouped by iw, such that H{k+j} corresponds to a quadrant of Hw. If iw refers to intervals in an ancestor node na, Hw corresponds to a quadrant of the ancestor's heightfield H{k+j}, as the ancestor covers a larger part of the xy-plane. This allows flexible gstacks that combine terminal intervals with areas lacking information at the current level. Compression: Compresses attribute information significantly when large rectangular regions share identical attribute sequences. Geometry is stored as heightfields, which can be further compressed using standard heightfield encoding methods. Memory: Space complexity is proportional to the number of intervals n times the area of the region (x{max}-x{min}+1)(y{max}-y{min}+1). It is more space-efficient than storing individual stacks when attribute redundancy is high. Performance: Building gstacks requires identifying regions of identical attribute sequences. Querying a stack's height is O(1) given the coordinates. Limitations: Only compresses attributes; geometric variations are still stored explicitly in heightfields. Not suitable for regions with high attribute variability. The gstack was introduced as part of the QuadStack representation for efficient encoding and direct rendering of layered datasets. It builds on the Stack-Based Representation (SBR) by adding a layer of attribute-based compression. The method was developed to address the inefficiencies of standard spatial decompositions that do not exploit attribute uniformity. name: Pointer Compression
head: Frequency-Based Pointer Encoding, Pointer Table Encoding
body: Pointer compression is a sparse structure optimization that reduces the memory footprint of child pointers in tree-based representations (such as Sparse Voxel DAGs) by replacing absolute addresses with indices into a frequency-ordered lookup table. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Offset Compression by targeting the high-value pointers at upper tree levels, where absolute pointers consume the most memory, whereas offset compression targets the frequent small deltas in lower levels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse voxel structure (e.g., DAG) containing child pointers, typically 32-bit absolute addresses. Output: A compressed representation where pointers are stored as variable-length indices into a global or per-level lookup table. Data Structures: 1. Pointer Table: A list of absolute pointers, sorted by occurrence frequency in descending order. One table is maintained per tree level to maximize hit rates for common subtrees. 2. Compressed Pointer Field: A variable-length bit field stored in the node. It uses a 2-bit type header followed by the payload. Numbered Steps: 1. Frequency Analysis: Traverse the structure and count the occurrences of each unique child pointer value for each tree level. 2. Table Construction: Sort the unique pointers for each level by frequency in descending order. The most frequent pointer is assigned index 0, the next index 1, etc.. 3. Bit-Length Assignment: Determine the bit length required for the index based on the table size and the chosen encoding scheme. The method uses a fixed set of payload sizes: 6, 14, or 22 bits for table indices, and 30 bits for absolute pointers. 4. Encoding: Replace each absolute pointer in the node with a compressed value: If the pointer exists in the table, store its index using the appropriate bit length (6, 14, or 22) indicated by the type header. If the pointer is not in the table (or the table is full), store the absolute pointer value using the 30-bit absolute type. 5. Decoding: At runtime, read the 2-bit type header. If it indicates a table index, look up the absolute address in the level-specific pointer table. If it indicates an absolute pointer, use the remaining 30 bits directly. Formulas: Let P be the absolute pointer value. Let Tl be the pointer table for level l. Let idx(P, Tl) be the index of P in Tl. The compressed value C is structured as: C = \{ \text{type} \}{2\text{-bits}} \parallel \{ \text{payload} \}{k\text{-bits}} Where k \in \{6, 14, 22, 30\} and type mapping is: Type 0: 6-bit index into Tl Type 1: 14-bit index into Tl Type 2: 22-bit index into Tl Type 3: 30-bit absolute pointer P. Parameters: Table Size: Determined by the number of unique pointers per level. The sources note that 30-bit absolute pointers are sufficient for DAG nodes in tested examples. Bit Lengths: Fixed at 6, 14, 22, and 30 bits for the payload. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Entropy encoding decreases rendering performance due to the overhead of table lookups and variable-length decoding. Memory vs. Speed: While compression improves memory usage, the trade-off is increased computational cost during traversal. Table Overflow: If a pointer is not in the table, it falls back to the 30-bit absolute representation, which uses more bits than a 6-bit index but ensures correctness. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class PointerTable: def init(self): self.entries = [] # List of absolute pointers self.indexmap = {} # Map absolute pointer -> index def addpointer(self, ptr): if ptr not in self.indexmap: self.indexmap[ptr] = len(self.entries) self.entries.append(ptr) return self.indexmap[ptr] def getpointer(self, index): return self.entries[index] class CompressedPointer: def init(self, ptr, table, level): self.ptr = ptr self.table = table self.level = level self.compressedbits = self.encode() def encode(self): # Check if pointer is in table if self.ptr in self.table.indexmap: idx = self.table.indexmap[self.ptr] # Determine bit length based on index size and type # Note: The source specifies fixed types for 6, 14, 22 bits # In practice, one might choose the smallest type that fits the index # However, the source implies a specific setup was found effective. # We assume the encoder selects the type based on the index value # or a pre-defined mapping. For simplicity, we map index ranges to types. if idx < 64: # 2^6 return (0, idx, 6) elif idx < 16384: # 2^14 return (1, idx, 14) elif idx < 4194304: # 2^22 return (2, idx, 22) else: # Fallback to absolute if index is too large for 22 bits # Or if the source implies 22 is the max index size return (3, self.ptr, 30) else: # Not in table, store absolute return (3, self.ptr, 30) def decode(self): typecode, payload, bitlen = self.compressedbits if typecode == 3: return payload else: return self.table.getpointer(payload) A related technique that compresses the offset from a node to its first child, exploiting the fact that offsets are often small and start at +1. It is typically applied alongside pointer compression to maximize memory savings in lower tree levels. Memory Complexity: Reduces the average bits per pointer from 32 to a weighted average of 6, 14, 22, or 30 bits, depending on the frequency distribution of pointers in the scene. Performance: Decreases rendering performance due to the overhead of entropy decoding and table lookups. Strengths: Significant memory reduction for scenes with repetitive subtrees or common pointer patterns. Limitations: Performance hit; less effective if pointer distribution is uniform or random. Pointer compression was introduced in the context of geometry and attribute compression for voxel scenes, specifically for Sparse Voxel DAGs. It builds on the observation that certain subtrees are used significantly more often than others, making entropy encoding a suitable candidate for memory reduction. The method was evaluated on architectural structures, complex geometry, and real-life 3D models. Geometry and Attribute Compression for Voxel Scenes, https://timothykol.com/pub/compression.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Offset Compression
body: Offset Compression is a technique for compressing tree offsets in sparse voxel structures. It exploits the fact that the offset from a node to its first child is always +1, allowing it to be stored implicitly, and that offsets are typically small in lower tree levels due to depth-first assignment. It sets itself apart from general entropy encoding by using fixed-width, level-adaptive bit-packing for offsets, which aligns with GPU texture lookup granularity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse voxel tree or DAG structure containing nodes with child pointers and sibling offsets. Output: A compressed representation where offsets use level-adaptive bit-packing and the first-child offset is implicit. Data Structures: The method modifies the storage of the offset field within a node. Instead of a fixed-size integer, the offset is stored in a variable number of bits determined by the node's depth level. First Child Offset: Implicitly defined as +1. Sibling Offset: Stored in BL bits, where L is the tree level. BL is the smallest integer byte-aligned value that can represent the maximum offset at level L. Steps: 1. Analyze Tree Levels: Iterate through all nodes in the tree to find the maximum offset value for each level. 2. Calculate Bit Depth: Determine the minimum number of bits required to encode offsets for that specific level. 3. Round to Bytes: Round the calculated bit count up to the nearest byte for GPU performance, as a texture lookup on the GPU retrieves at least a single byte. 4. Store Offsets: For the first child of any node, the offset is implicitly +1. For subsequent children, store the offset relative to the previous child using the calculated byte-aligned bit width. Parameters: Offset Size: In typical examples, a two-byte offset is sufficient for the lowest five levels. Four or five bytes are required for the highest levels. Level Thresholds: The highest levels (near the root) contain very few nodes (\approx 0.1\%), making the increased bit-width non-critical for overall memory usage. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Implicit First Child: The assumption that the first child offset is always +1 relies on a specific depth-first assignment order. GPU Performance: Failing to round up to byte boundaries can lead to inefficient memory access patterns on GPUs, where texture lookups typically retrieve at least one byte. A variant of Offset Compression applied to Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) structures where attribute decoupling introduces additional offsets. It compresses both DAG offsets and child pointers to reduce memory consumption. The method stores the offset from a node to its first child implicitly as +1, analyzes each level to determine the minimum bit depth, and rounds up to bytes for GPU performance. In examples, a two-byte offset is sufficient for the lowest five levels, while four or five bytes are required for the highest levels, which represent \approx 0.1\% of nodes. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Reduces the storage size of offsets from a fixed width to a level-dependent width, leading to a significant improvement in typical examples. Time: The compression process requires a single pass to analyze levels and calculate bit depths. Measured Performance: In typical datasets, using two-byte offsets for the lowest five levels leads to significant memory improvement. The highest levels require 4-5 bytes, but since they represent only \approx 0.1\% of nodes, the impact on total memory is minimal. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient for GPU access due to byte-aligned storage, significant memory reduction for deep trees. Limitations: Less effective for pointer compression compared to offset compression, as pointers often require full 4 bytes even at lower levels. When to Use: Use when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and the tree structure follows a depth-first assignment. Ideal for GPU-based rendering where texture lookups benefit from byte-aligned data. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Offset Compression was introduced in the context of geometry and attribute compression for voxel scenes, specifically to reduce the memory consumption of DAG structures where attribute decoupling increases the size of the structure. It builds on the observation that offsets in depth-first trees are typically small in lower levels, allowing for efficient bit-packing. Geometry and Attribute Compression for Voxel Scenes, https://timothykol.com/pub/compression.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: ExaBricks Hierarchy
head: ExaBricks, ExaBricks data structure
body: ExaBricks is a rendering method for Block-Structured Adaptive Mesh Refinement (BS-AMR) data that re-organizes input cells into compact, non-overlapping bricks and uses a secondary spatial partitioning called Active Brick Regions (ABRs) to enable smooth, high-quality interpolation across level boundaries. It sets itself apart from prior methods by eliminating costly per-sample cell location kernels (required by the basis method [37]) and deep AMR hierarchy traversals, instead relying on ABRs for fast sample reconstruction and an RTX BVH for hardware-accelerated ray marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of AMR cells, each defined by lower-left unit coordinates (i, j, k), level l, and a scalar data value Cv. Level 0 is the finest level (implicit cell size 1^3); level l has cell size 2^l. Output: A set of bricks, a hierarchy of Active Brick Regions (ABRs), and an RTX Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) over the ABRs, enabling ray traversal and volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. Brick: lowerleft: Tuple (i, j, k) of integer coordinates. level: Integer l. dims: Tuple (N, M, K) representing the number of cells in each dimension. scalars: A 3D array of size N \times M \times K storing the data values. 2. Active Brick Region (ABR): bbox: Bounding box of the region. activebricks: List of brick IDs that influence this region. minval: Minimum scalar value of any cell whose support overlaps the region. maxval: Maximum scalar value of any cell whose support overlaps the region. finestcellwidth: Cell width of the finest AMR level influencing the region. Algorithm Steps: 1. Brick Generation: Build a k-d tree top-down from the input AMR cells. For a current node, check if all cells are on the same AMR level and completely fill their combined bounding box. If yes, create a leaf node (a brick). If no, split the node along the longest axis of its bounding box. Round split positions to an integer multiple of the current coarsest cell width. Limit leaf size to at most 32 cells wide on any axis to ensure fine granularity for space skipping. Discard the internal hierarchy; store only the leaf bricks. 2. ABR Construction: Create a list of "brick support fragments". Each fragment is a box representing the support of a brick and its brick ID. Compute the bounding box of all fragments. Recursively subdivide the bounding box: For the current region and its overlapping fragments, find a partitioning plane from the fragment boundaries closest to the region's spatial center. Prefer the widest dimension for the split. If no valid plane exists, create a leaf ABR containing the current list of brick IDs. Otherwise, partition the region, sort fragments into left/right subtrees, and recurse. For each leaf ABR, compute minval, maxval, and finestcellwidth from the active bricks. 3. BVH Construction: Build an RTX BVH over the leaf ABRs. 4. Ray Traversal and Rendering: Use the RTX BVH to iterate over ABRs a ray intersects, skipping those it is safe to ignore. For samples within an ABR leaf, retrieve the list of active bricks. Perform basis reconstruction using the cells within those bricks. Reconstruction Formula: The method uses the basis function by Wald et al. [37] for smooth interpolation. For a cell C of width Cw, the basis function is: \hat{H}C(p) = \hat{h}\left(\frac{|C{px} - px|}{Cw}\right) \hat{h}\left(\frac{|C{py} - py|}{Cw}\right) \hat{h}\left(\frac{|C{pz} - pz|}{Cw}\right) where \hat{h}(x) = \max(1 - x, 0). The reconstruction at position p is: B(p) = \frac{\sum{Ci} \hat{H}{Ci}(p) C{vi}}{\sum{Ci} \hat{H}{Ci}(p)} where Ci are cells with non-zero support at p, and C{vi} is the data value. Cell Support Definition: The support of a cell C is a rectangular box extending exactly half a cell width beyond the cell itself. The support of a brick B is the union of the supports of its cells, resulting in a box exactly half the brick's cell width larger than the brick. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatebricks(cells): """ Re-organize AMR cells into non-overlapping bricks. cells: List of dicts with keys 'i', 'j', 'k', 'l', 'bbox' Returns: List of Brick objects """ # Build k-d tree top-down root = KDNode(cells) bricks = [] stack = [root] while stack: node = stack.pop() # Check if leaf condition is met if isleaf(node): bricks.append(createbrick(node)) else: # Split along longest axis splitaxis = node.longestaxis() # Round split position to integer multiple of coarsest cell width splitpos = roundtomultiple(node.bbox.center()[splitaxis], node.coarsestcellwidth) leftcells, rightcells = splitcells(node.cells, splitaxis, splitpos) if leftcells: stack.append(KDNode(leftcells)) if rightcells: stack.append(KDNode(rightcells)) return bricks def isleaf(node): """ Leaf if all cells are same level, fill bounding box, and size <= 32 on any axis. """ if not node.cells: return False levels = set(c['l'] for c in node.cells) if len(levels) > 1: return False # Check if cells completely fill bounding box if not cellsfillbbox(node.cells, node.bbox): return False # Check size limit dims = node.bbox.size() if any(d > 32 for d in dims): return False return True def createbrick(node): """ Create Brick object from leaf node cells. """ cells = node.cells # Assume all cells are same level and contiguous l = cells[0]['l'] # Determine lower-left and dimensions from cells # Implementation detail: Sort cells to find min coordinates and max dimensions mini = min(c['i'] for c in cells) minj = min(c['j'] for c in cells) mink = min(c['k'] for c in cells) # Determine N, M, K by counting unique coordinates or bounding box size / cellsize cellsize = 2 l maxi = max(c['i'] for c in cells) maxj = max(c['j'] for c in cells) maxk = max(c['k'] for c in cells) N = (maxi - mini) // cellsize + 1 M = (maxj - minj) // cellsize + 1 K = (maxk - mink) // cellsize + 1 # Extract scalar values into 3D array scalars = zeros((N, M, K)) for c in cells: idxi = (c['i'] - mini) // cellsize idxj = (c['j'] - minj) // cellsize idxk = (c['k'] - mink) // cellsize scalars[idxi, idxj, idxk] = c['value'] return Brick(lowerleft=(mini, minj, mink), level=l, dims=(N, M, K), scalars=scalars) def constructabrs(bricks): """ Build Active Brick Regions from bricks. """ # Create support fragments fragments = [] for brick in bricks: supportbox = computebricksupport(brick) fragments.append({'box': supportbox, 'brickid': brick.id}) # Compute global bounding box globalbbox = unionboxes([f['box'] for f in fragments]) # Recursive subdivision abrs = [] buildabrrecursive(globalbbox, fragments, abrs) return abrs def computebricksupport(brick): """ Support is brick bbox extended by half cell width. """ cellsize = 2 brick.level halfcell = cellsize / 2.0 bbox = brick.bbox # Derived from lowerleft and dims # Extend bbox by halfcell in all directions return bbox.extend(halfcell) def buildabrrecursive(regionbbox, overlappingfragments, abrs): """ Recursively subdivide region to create ABRs. """ if not overlappingfragments: return # Find partitioning plane plane = findbestsplitplane(regionbbox, overlappingfragments) if plane is None: # Create leaf ABR abrs.append(ABR( bbox=regionbbox, activebricks=[f['brickid'] for f in overlappingfragments], minval=computeminval(overlappingfragments), maxval=computemaxval(overlappingfragments), finestcellwidth=computefinestwidth(overlappingfragments))) else: leftfrags, rightfrags = splitfragments(overlappingfragments, plane) leftbbox, rightbbox = splitbbox(regionbbox, plane) if leftfrags: buildabrrecursive(leftbbox, leftfrags, abrs) if rightfrags: buildabrrecursive(rightbbox, rightfrags, abrs) def findbestsplitplane(region, fragments): """ Find fragment boundary closest to region center, preferring widest dimension. """ center = region.center() bestplane = None bestdist = infinity bestdim = -1 # Iterate fragment boundaries for frag in fragments: for dim in [0, 1, 2]: # Get min and max of fragment in dim minval = frag['box'].min[dim] maxval = frag['box'].max[dim] # Check if boundary is inside region if minval > region.min[dim] and minval < region.max[dim]: dist = abs(minval - center[dim]) if dist < bestdist: bestdist = dist bestplane = {'dim': dim, 'pos': minval} bestdim = dim if maxval > region.min[dim] and maxval < region.max[dim]: dist = abs(maxval - center[dim]) if dist < bestdist: bestdist = dist bestplane = {'dim': dim, 'pos': maxval} bestdim = dim # Prefer widest dimension if distances are equal? # Note: Sources say "prefer widest dimension" but also "closest to center". # Implementation: If multiple planes have same min distance, pick widest. # Simplified: Just pick closest. If tie, pick widest. return bestplane def basisreconstruct(p, abrs, bricks): """ Reconstruct value at point p using ABRs and bricks. """ # Find ABR leaf containing p abr = findabrleaf(abrs, p) totalweight = 0.0 totalvalue = 0.0 for brickid in abr.activebricks: brick = bricks[brickid] # Find cells in brick that influence p # Determine which cells in the 3D array have non-zero support cellwidth = 2 brick.level halfcell = cellwidth / 2.0 # Iterate over relevant cells in brick # Optimization: Only iterate cells whose support overlaps p # Support of cell (i,j,k) is [i-half, i+half] x... # p is in support if |pcoord - cellcenter| < halfcell for i in range(brick.dims[0]): for j in range(brick.dims[1]): for k in range(brick.dims[2]): cellcenter = brick.lowerleft + (i + 0.5) cellwidth # Check if p is in cell support if isinsupport(p, cellcenter, cellwidth): # Compute basis function hx = max(1.0 - abs(p.x - cellcenter.x) / cellwidth, 0.0) hy = max(1.0 - abs(p.y - cellcenter.y) / cellwidth, 0.0) hz = max(1.0 - abs(p.z - cellcenter.z) / cellwidth, 0.0) weight = hx hy hz value = brick.scalars[i, j, k] totalweight += weight totalvalue += weight value if totalweight == 0: return 0.0 # Or handle as empty space return totalvalue / totalweight def isinsupport(p, cellcenter, cellwidth): half = cellwidth / 2.0 return (abs(p.x - cellcenter.x) < half and abs(p.y - cellcenter.y) < half and abs(p.z - cellcenter.z) < half) A reconstruction strategy for cell-centered Block-Structured Adaptive Mesh Refinement (BS-AMR) data that maps a sample point p=(x,y,z) to a scalar value F(p) by decomposing the domain into non-overlapping rectilinear octants, ensuring continuity across level boundaries and supporting fast implicit ray-isosurface intersections. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by ray traversal through the RTX BVH and basis reconstruction. The ABR structure allows O(1) retrieval of influencing bricks for a given region, avoiding the O(\log N) or worse per-sample k-d tree traversals required by prior methods. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of bricks and ABRs. Bricks store only the necessary cells, and ABRs store metadata and lists of brick IDs. The structure avoids storing the full AMR hierarchy. Measured Performance: The method supports interactive high-quality direct volume rendering with smooth AMR reconstruction and gradient-based shading. It enables adaptive sampling that adapts to the finest level cell size while keeping total sample counts tractable. Strengths: Smooth interpolation across level boundaries using the basis method. Fast sample reconstruction without costly cell location kernels. Hardware-accelerated ray marching and space skipping via RTX BVH. Supports interactive transfer function and iso-surface editing. Limitations: The basis method's support is not truncated at the first sample on the neighboring side, leading to larger support overlap between cells from neighboring blocks compared to some prior methods. Requires re-organizing input data into bricks, discarding the original AMR hierarchy. When to use: When rendering BS-AMR data with smooth interpolation requirements and hardware-accelerated ray tracing capabilities (RTX) are available. When not to use: When the input data is Tree-Based AMR and the overhead of brick generation is prohibitive, or when nearest-neighbor interpolation is sufficient and the complexity of ABR construction is not justified. ExaBricks was introduced by Wald et al. in 2020. It builds on the brick-based organization proposed by Kähler et al. [17] and the basis reconstruction method by Wald et al. [37]. The method addresses the limitations of prior AMR rendering work, such as the costly cell location kernels used in [37] and the lack of smooth interpolation in methods like [21]. It is designed for Block-Structured AMR layouts but can be applied to a wide range of AMR refinement schemes. name: Octant Method
head: BS-AMR reconstruction strategy
body: The Octant Method is a reconstruction strategy for cell-centered Block-Structured Adaptive Mesh Refinement (BS-AMR) data that maps a sample point p=(x,y,z) to a scalar value F(p) by decomposing the domain into non-overlapping rectilinear octants. It solves the problem of discontinuous interpolation at level boundaries in AMR grids, which standard interpolants (nearest neighbor, linear, basis functions) fail to handle due to topology changes. Unlike dual cell methods that require stitching unstructured meshes and may cross level boundaries, the Octant Method uses octants that do not extend beyond parent cell bounds, tile the domain without gaps or overlap, and remain rectilinear. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sample point P=(x,y,z) in 3D space. Output: A scalar value F(P). Data Structures: Bricks: Grids of cells, typically 16 \times 16 \times 16, containing cell-centered data values associated with a refinement level L. Cell (C): A logical cell in the AMR hierarchy. Octant (O): One of eight sub-volumes of C, defined by the direction from C's center (\pm \hat{X}, \pm \hat{Y}, \pm \hat{Z}). Dual Cell (D): A logical cell centered at the same location as C, used to determine neighbor values. Refinement Factor (R): Each coarser cell is covered by exactly R \times R \times R finer cells. Vertex Naming Convention: Each octant has 8 vertices. Vertices are named based on the direction from the cell center C(0): O(0): Coincides with the cell center C. O(X), O(Y), O(Z): Face vertices, lying on the cell faces. O(XY), O(YZ), O(XZ): Edge vertices, lying on the cell edges. O(XYZ): Corner vertex, lying on the cell corner. Algorithm Steps: 1. Find Leaf Octant: Locate the leaf cell C and the specific octant O containing point P. Identify the corresponding dual cell D for level L of C. 2. Center Vertex: Set the value of the center vertex O(0) to the cell center value C.v. 3. Compute Boundary Vertices: For each boundary vertex (face, edge, corner), determine if it lies on a level boundary. Non-Boundary Case: If all required dual cell corners (e.g., D(0), D(X) for vertex O(X)) are at the same level as C, compute the value using averaging rules. Fine-Side Boundary Case: If at least one input dual corner lies on a coarser level than C, the vertex is on the fine side. Set its value by recursively calling the sample function for the vertex position minutely moved along the direction away from the cell center (towards the coarse side). Coarse-Side Boundary Case: If the vertex is on the coarse side (inputs are inner nodes or coarser), determine the interpolant locally using one of the coarser side interpolant options. 4. Trilinear Interpolation: Once all 8 vertex values of octant O are set, perform trilinear interpolation within O to find F(P). Non-Boundary Averaging Rules: Let D(v) denote the dual cell vertex value. 1. O(0).v = C.v. 2. Face Vertex: O(X).v = \frac{1}{2} (D(0).v + D(X).v). 3. Edge Vertex: O(XY).v is the average of the values of the four cells spanning the face: C(0), C(X), C(Y), C(XY). In terms of dual vertices, this corresponds to the average of the four relevant dual vertices defining that face. 4. Corner Vertex: O(XYZ).v is the average of the eight vertices of the dual cell D. Coarser Side Interpolant Options: When computing the value for a vertex on the coarse side (or the shifted position on the fine side), four options exist: 1. Coarsest-Level Lerp: Perform trilinear interpolation on the coarsest level involved for any of the inputs. 2. Current-Level Lerp: Perform trilinear interpolation on the current level L. 3. Basis Function: Use a specific basis function interpolation. 4. Finest-Level Lerp: Perform trilinear interpolation on the finest level involved. Parameters: eps: A small epsilon value used to minutely shift the vertex position away from the cell center to find the coarsest level neighbor. Pitfalls: Accuracy Sacrifice: Setting fine-side vertex values based on the coarse-side interpolant ensures continuity but sacrifices some accuracy at the boundary. Precision: The epsilon shift must be small enough to remain within the same logical cell but large enough to cross the level boundary numerically. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def octant(P): # 1. Find the leaf cell C and octant O containing P oct = findleafoctant(P) C = oct.cell D = finddualcell(oct) # 2. Set center vertex value oct.vertices[0].v = C.value # 3. Compute Face Vertices (e.g., O(X)) # Symmetric logic applies to O(Y), O(Z) l0 = D.vertices[0].level lX = D.vertices[X].level lmin = min(l0, lX) lmax = max(l0, lX) if lmin == lmax: # Non-boundary: average of dual vertices oct.vertices[X].v = (D.vertices[0].v + D.vertices[X].v) / 2.0 elif lmin < oct.level: # Fine side: fill FROM coarse side # Shift vertex position away from cell center towards coarse side shiftdir = oct.directionvector[X] # Unit vector pointing to vertex X shiftedP = oct.vertices[X].position + eps shiftdir oct.vertices[X].v = octant(shiftedP) else: # Coarse side: compute locally oct.vertices[X].v = computecoarsersidevertex(D.vertices[0], D.vertices[X], oct.level) # 4. Compute Edge Vertices (e.g., O(XY)) # Symmetric logic applies to O(YZ), O(XZ) # Requires checking levels of D[0], D[X], D[Y], D[XY] # If all same level: average of 4 cells/dual vertices # If boundary: recursive call or coarse side computation # 5. Compute Corner Vertex (O(XYZ)) # Symmetric logic applies # If all same level: average of 8 dual vertices # If boundary: recursive call or coarse side computation # 6. Trilinear Interpolation within Octant O return trilinearinterpolate(oct, P) def computecoarsersidevertex(v1, v2, level): # Implements one of the four coarser side interpolant options # e.g., coarsest-level lerp, current-level lerp, etc. # Not given in the sources. pass An optimization for isosurface extraction on AMR data that reduces redundant computation by merging 'inner' octants into dual cells, while preserving crack-free continuity at level boundaries. Choose this when performance is critical and the scene allows for pre-processing or specific traversal patterns. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The recursive nature for boundary vertices suggests potential overhead, but the rectilinear nature allows for efficient traversal. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the storage of bricks and the recursion depth for boundary resolution. Performance: The method yields better rendering quality and performance compared to sample-based isosurface methods in OSPRay, which suffer from poor quality and performance on AMR data. Strengths: Continuous interpolation across level boundaries; rectilinear octants simplify ray-triangle intersection tests; no need for unstructured mesh stitching; adaptive to refinement levels. Limitations: Sacrifices accuracy at boundaries to maintain continuity; requires careful handling of epsilon shifts; implementation complexity in managing level boundaries. When to use: When continuous, high-quality isosurface rendering of BS-AMR data is required, particularly for ray tracing. When not to use: When maximum accuracy at level boundaries is prioritized over continuity, or when the overhead of recursive boundary resolution is prohibitive. The Octant Method was introduced in a paper by Feng et al. (2018) titled "CPU Isosurface Ray Tracing of Adaptive Mesh Refinement Data". It addresses the limitations of existing interpolation methods (nearest neighbor, linear, basis functions) when applied to Block-Structured Adaptive Mesh Refinement (BS-AMR) data, which exhibit topology changes at level boundaries. The method builds on the concept of dual cells but reformulates the problem in terms of octants to ensure rectilinear tiling and continuity. name: Optimized Octant Generation
head: Merged Dual Cell Octant Method
body: An optimization for isosurface extraction on Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data that reduces redundant computation by merging 'inner' octants into dual cells, while preserving crack-free continuity at level boundaries. It builds on the Octant Method by avoiding the recomputation of vertex values for shared inner octants, which the naïve approach computes eight times. Inputs and outputs: Input: AMR-KDTree structure, isovalue, cell-centered scalar field data. Output: List of active octants encoded as 64-bit references, ready for ray tracing. Data structures: AMR-KDTree: Hierarchical structure where leaf nodes store the value range of their finest level cells. Octant Reference: A 64-bit integer encoding the octant identity. Bits 0–31: AMR-KDTree leaf index. Bits 32–63: Octant ID within the leaf. Steps: 1. Filter Leaves: Traverse all leaves of the AMR-KDTree. Ignore leaves whose stored value range does not contain the isovalue. 2. Identify Inner Octants: For remaining leaves, identify 'inner' octants within non-boundary regions. An 'inner' octant is defined as an octant that is also an octant of the corresponding dual cell. 3. Merge Octants: Merge identified inner octants into dual cells. Do not merge octants touching a level boundary. 4. Set Vertex Values: For merged dual cells, set vertex values to the cell values. The merged dual cell's vertices coincide with the cell centers. 5. Compute Active Octants: Compute the list of active octants in parallel using TBB's parallelfor. 6. Encode References: Encode each active octant into a 64-bit reference for the VoxelSource using the layout defined above. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizedoctantgeneration(amrkdtree, isovalue): activeoctants = [] # Step 1: Filter leaves candidateleaves = [] for leaf in amrkdtree.leaves: if leaf.minvalue <= isovalue <= leaf.maxvalue: candidateleaves.append(leaf) # Step 5: Parallel computation # Using a pseudo-parallel loop structure def processleaf(leaf): leafoctants = [] # Step 2 & 3: Identify and merge inner octants # Decompose finest brick into 8 octants for octantid in range(8): octant = decomposeoctant(leaf, octantid) # Check if octant touches a level boundary if octant.toucheslevelboundary: # Step 4: Naive computation for boundary octants # Vertex values must be computed explicitly to ensure continuity vertexvalues = computeoctantverticesnaive(octant) leafoctants.append((leaf.index, octantid, vertexvalues)) else: # Inner octant: merge into dual cell # Step 4: Set vertex values to cell values # Vertices coincide with cell centers cellvalue = leaf.cellvalue # Vertices of the dual cell are set to this single value # This avoids recomputing shared vertices 8 times vertexvalues = [cellvalue] 8 leafoctants.append((leaf.index, octantid, vertexvalues)) return leafoctants # Parallel execution results = parallelfor(candidateleaves, processleaf) # Step 6: Encode and collect for leafresults in results: for leafidx, octantid, vertexvalues in leafresults: # Encode 64-bit reference reference = (leafidx << 32) | octantid activeoctants.append({ 'reference': reference, 'vertexvalues': vertexvalues }) return activeoctants Parameters: Isosurface Value: The scalar threshold for extraction. Parallelism: TBB parallelfor is used for computing active octants. Edge cases and pitfalls: Level Boundaries: Octants touching a level boundary cannot be merged into dual cells; they must be processed individually to maintain continuity. Redundant Computation: The naïve approach recomputes vertex values for shared 'inner' octants eight times. In the naïve approach, all leaves of the AMR-KDTree are traversed, ignoring those that do not contain the isovalue. Each cell of the finest brick in the leaf is decomposed into eight octants using the octant method to compute vertex values. A key pitfall in this initialization is that 'inner' octants (not touching a boundary) have vertex values re-computed eight times as they are shared with eight other octants, leading to significant redundant computation. Time and memory complexity: The optimization reduces the number of processed octants by 70.6%, from roughly 2 billion to 616 million on the LandingGear dataset. This yields a 64.76% improvement in performance on the LandingGear data. Strengths and limitations: Strengths: Eliminates redundant computation of shared vertex values for inner octants. Maintains crack-free continuity. Simple to implement within existing ray tracing frameworks like OSPRay. Limitations: Requires careful handling of level boundaries to avoid cracks. Performance gain is dependent on the ratio of inner to boundary octants. When to use: Use when extracting isosurfaces from large AMR datasets with significant internal regions (non-boundary areas) to reduce computational overhead. When not to use: Not suitable if the dataset is dominated by level boundaries, as the optimization provides less benefit and adds complexity in handling boundary cases. Originated in the context of CPU isosurface ray tracing of AMR data, specifically within the OSPRay framework. The method was developed to improve upon the naïve octant generation approach by leveraging the structure of dual cells in non-boundary regions. It is evaluated on datasets such as LandingGear. name: Tree-based structures (Octree, Pointer Tree, Sparse Voxel DAG)
head: Sparse Voxel Trees, Hierarchical Sparse Volumes
body: Tree-based structures organize sparse volumetric data into a hierarchical graph where internal nodes define spatial subdivisions and leaf nodes store voxel values. This family solves the memory inefficiency of dense grids by omitting empty space and the traversal overhead of flat sparse lists by leveraging spatial locality. They differ from sibling structures like Hash Grids by providing explicit spatial hierarchy for culling, and from Brick-based Hierarchical Storage by operating on individual voxel granularity rather than fixed-size blocks. All structures in this family share the following mechanism: 1. Recursive Subdivision: The 3D domain is recursively divided into sub-volumes. In standard octrees, each node has 8 children. In pointer trees, the branching factor N varies (N^3 children). 2. Sparsity Encoding: Empty regions are represented by null pointers or absence of children, rather than storing zero-valued voxels. This provides compression proportional to the sparsity of the data. 3. Hierarchical Traversal: Rendering or access requires traversing from the root to the leaf. This allows skipping large empty volumes (culling) and adapting resolution to view distance or detail requirements. 4. Spatial Locality: Children of a node are spatially contiguous. This locality is often exploited via Morton ordering (Z-order curve) to map 3D coordinates to 1D keys, enabling efficient neighbor lookups and linear array representations in implicit variants. Uses variable branching factors (N^3) and 8-bit relative offsets for compact storage. Choose when memory footprint is critical and data has high redundancy. Merges identical subtrees into a Directed Acyclic Graph to eliminate topological redundancy. Choose when the volume contains repeated geometric patterns. Fixed 8-way branching with implicit or explicit storage. Choose for standard spatial indexing and neighbor queries. Refines interval trees to manage scene complexity for large volumes. Choose for complex scene culling. Standard sparse voxel octree implementation. Choose for general-purpose ray marching. Tree-based sparse structures originated in the early 1990s for efficient storage of 3D medical and scientific data. The Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) was popularized for volume rendering by Levoy et al.. The concept of merging identical subtrees into DAGs was introduced to reduce memory usage for complex geometries. Modern variants like the Compact Pointer Tree address the pointer overhead of traditional trees by compressing indices and integrating data compression into the hierarchy. name: Compact pointer tree
head: Hierarchical Voxel Compression with Wavelet Transform, Terabyte-scale volumetric compression
body: The Compact Pointer Tree is a tree-based data structure for volumetric RGBA data that enables interactive visualization of terabyte-scale datasets by compressing color values using wavelet transforms and allowing on-demand voxel reconstruction. It sets itself apart from sibling sparse structures by storing N^3 children per internal node (where N \in [2, 6]) and using 8-bit offsets relative to a 32-bit base address, which allows for compact storage at the cost of requiring sequential child export during construction. Unlike Pointer Compression which generally reduces pointer size, this method integrates compression into the tree hierarchy itself, using local wavelet transforms on color attributes. Inputs: Terabyte-scale volumetric RGBA data. Outputs: A compressed tree structure stored on disk/GPU memory, enabling interactive rendering at 8K resolution. Internal Node Layout: Children: N^3 child pointers. Each pointer is an 8-bit offset relative to a 32-bit base address stored within the node. If a child is null, it is marked as such. The maximum branching factor N is 6 because 6^3 = 216 fits within 8 bits (max value 255). Color Attributes: Minimum color, average color, and maximum color. These are used for wavelet compression. Sign Bit: A stored bit indicating which reconstruction formula to use. Bottom Level: Arrays of voxel color values. Supports storage of values starting from 4-bit channels. The construction occurs in two passes. First Pass (Bottom-Up Structure Building): 1. Initialize a hashmap with keys (level, index.x, index.y, index.z) to track created nodes. 2. Build Level 0 nodes: Process N images per thread to build a Level 0 node. Compute max, min, average, and child masks for the children. Store node data via hashmap lookup. 3. Build higher levels recursively: Launch jobs equal to the dense grid node count for the next level. Threads iterate over children to compute max, min, average, and child masks. Repeat until the root node is reached. Pitfall: Children exporting to a linear buffer at each level must be sequential. This is handled by the hashmap during the first pass to manage node creation efficiently, allowing parallel processing of different branches. Second Pass (Compression): 1. Parallelize over nodes at any level to compress max, min, and average values. 2. For each node: The preprocessor seeks file handles to determined positions. Recursively calculate the wavelet compressed value. This is local; it only requires knowledge of the level above. 3. After compression, the structure is ready for traversal. 1. Implement hierarchical DDA to skip empty space. 2. Scale down and modulate voxel position at each level while descending. 3. Keep a stack of computed values from the first traversal to the bottom. 4. For subsequent accesses, backtrack the structure to find the node to start descending from, avoiding full root traversal. 5. Store all data except the bottom level on GPU memory. 6. Register host memory for the bottom level. name: Sparse Voxel DAGs
head: SVDAG, Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph
body: Sparse Voxel DAGs (SVDAGs) are a memory-efficient 3D data structure that extends the Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by merging identical subtrees into shared nodes, forming a Directed Acyclic Graph. While SVOs efficiently encode spatial sparsity, they store redundant copies of identical non-empty geometry, leading to high memory consumption at high resolutions. SVDAGs solve this by allowing multiple parent nodes to share pointers to the same child instance, achieving lossless compression of topological redundancy without decompression overhead during traversal. This sets them apart from siblings like Compact pointer tree or OpenVDB (VDB), which focus on spatial sparsity or pointer compression rather than structural isomorphism. The core mechanism of the SVDAG family is the conversion of a tree structure into a DAG to eliminate duplicate subtrees. 1. Node Identity: Two nodes are considered identical if they have the same childmask (encoding the existence of 8 children) and identical pointers to their respective children. 2. Bottom-Up Reduction: The reduction process iterates from the leaves up to the root. At each level, nodes are sorted by their identity key (childmask + child pointers) to group identical nodes together. 3. Compaction and Indirection: Identical nodes are compacted into a single unique instance. An indirection table maps original node positions to their unique counterparts, and parent pointers are updated to reference these unique instances. 4. Memory Layout: Nodes store a childmask (8-bit integer) followed by an array of pointers to non-empty children. Node size varies between 8 and 36 bytes depending on the number of children (1 to 8). 5. Traversal: Ray traversal leverages the DAG structure to traverse voxels in ray order, eliminating the need for contour intersection tests and distance maintenance required in standard SVOs. A method for compressing an SVO into a minimal DAG by merging identical subtrees. It handles memory constraints by processing sub-DAGs for large resolutions and guarantees the smallest possible DAG within L iterations. Choose this when geometry has high topological redundancy. A variant defined by BNF where nodes are either Inner or Leaf nodes, removing explicit pointer storage. Choose this for cache-friendly, pointer-free traversal at the cost of indirection logic. A GPU-based traversal method for visibility queries and primary ray intersection. It simplifies the SVO loop by removing contour tests and extends beam optimization to soft shadows via reverse beam tracing. Choose this for real-time rendering on GPUs. A compression method that reuses structurally identical nodes by converting the Octree into a Directed Acyclic Octal Graph. Choose this as an alternative implementation of the DAG reduction principle. The Sparse Voxel DAG was introduced by Laine and Karras in 2010 as an extension of the Sparse Voxel Octree. It addresses the memory bottleneck of SVOs at high resolutions (e.g., 128K^3 grids) by exploiting the fact that complex 3D scenes often contain repeated geometric patterns. The structure is widely used in high-performance ray tracing and volume rendering where memory bandwidth is a limiting factor. Laine, S., & Karras, T. (2010). "Efficient Sparse Voxel Octrees." IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics. Laine, S., & Karras, T. (2010). "Progressive Refinement of Sparse Voxel Octrees." High-Performance Graphics.

name: Bottom-up SVO to DAG Reduction
head: SVO to DAG reduction, SVO to DAG transformation, SVO to Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Reduction, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Reduction, Sparse Voxel DAG Reduction, Reducing a Sparse Voxel Tree to a DAG, SVO reduction
body: Bottom-up SVO to DAG Reduction is a method for compressing a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) into a Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG) by merging identical subtrees into shared nodes. While an SVO efficiently encodes empty regions of space, it stores redundant copies of identical non-empty geometry, leading to high memory consumption at high resolutions. This method solves that problem by generalizing the tree structure to a DAG, allowing multiple parent nodes to share pointers to the same child instance, thereby encoding identical regions of space efficiently. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Compact pointer tree or OpenVDB (VDB) by focusing on topological redundancy (identical geometry) rather than just spatial sparsity or pointer compression, achieving lossless compression without decompression overhead during traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) representing a 3D voxel grid. The SVO may be too large to fit in memory entirely. Output: A minimal Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representing the same geometry with minimal node count. Data Structures: SVO Node: Defined by a traversal path from the root. Contains a childmask and pointers to children. DAG Node Layout: childmask: 8-bit integer encoding the existence of child pointers (bit i is 1 if child i exists, 0 otherwise). pointers: Array of pointers stored consecutively in memory immediately after the mask. Only pointers to non-empty children are stored. Size: Between 8 and 36 bytes per node, depending on the number of children (1 to 8). Indirection Table: A table mapping each original node's position in a level to its position in the compacted (unique) list of that level. Algorithm Steps: The reduction is performed iteratively from the leaves up to the root. The algorithm is guaranteed to find the smallest possible DAG within L iterations, where L is the maximum level of the octree. 1. Initialization: If the SVO is too large to fit in memory, construct the top L-10 levels top-down using triangle/cube intersection tests. For each leaf node in this top tree, construct a subtree to the maximum depth using a CPU-assisted algorithm (e.g., depth-peeling). Reduce each subtree to a DAG independently before inserting it into the top tree, creating a partially reduced DAG. 2. Leaf Reduction: Leaf nodes are uniquely defined by their childmasks (describing 8 voxels). There are at most 2^8 = 256 unique leaf nodes. Identify all unique leaf nodes. Update child-pointers in the level above the leaves to reference these new unique leaf instances. 3. Iterative Level Reduction: For each level l from the leaves up to the root: Identify all nodes at level l. Two nodes are identical if they have the same childmask AND identical pointers to their children. Sorting: Sort the nodes of level l using their child-pointers (and childmask) as a key. A 256-bit key is used (8 pointers \times 32 bits, or optimized for lower levels). Optimization: For the two lowest levels (where the majority of nodes reside), store subtrees of resolution 4^3 without pointers in a 64-bit integer to improve sorting performance. Compaction: Compact the sorted list to contain only unique nodes. Identical nodes become adjacent in the sorted list. Indirection: Maintain a table of indirections. For each original node, store its position in the compacted list. Pointer Update: Update the child-pointers of nodes in level l-1 using the indirection table to point to the unique instances in level l. Repeat until the root level is processed. 4. Finalization: Apply the reduction one last time to the top-SVO (if sub-DAGs were used) to generate the final DAG. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reducesvotodag(svolevels): """ Reduces a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to a minimal DAG. Input: svolevels is a list of lists, where svolevels[l] contains all nodes at level l. Level 0 is the root, Level L is the leaves. Output: The root node of the resulting DAG. """ numlevels = len(svolevels) # Process from leaves (highest level) up to the root (level 0) for level in range(numlevels - 1, -1, -1): nodes = svolevels[level] # Step 1: Sort nodes to group identical ones together # Key is the combination of childmask and child pointers # In practice, a parallel sort like tbb::parallelsort is used sortednodes = sorted(nodes, key=lambda n: (n.childmask, tuple(n.pointers))) # Step 2: Compact unique nodes and build indirection map uniquenodes = [] indirectionmap = {} # Maps original node ID to index in uniquenodes uniqueindex = 0 currentunique = None for node in sortednodes: # Check if current node is identical to the last added unique node if currentunique is None or (node.childmask == currentunique.childmask and node.pointers == currentunique.pointers): currentunique = node uniquenodes.append(node) indirectionmap[node.id] = uniqueindex uniqueindex += 1 else: # Node is a duplicate, map to the existing unique node indirectionmap[node.id] = uniqueindex - 1 # Step 3: Update pointers in the level above if level > 0: parentlevelnodes = svolevels[level - 1] for parentnode in parentlevelnodes: # Update each child pointer to point to the unique instance for childidx in range(8): if parentnode.childmask & (1 << childidx): childid = parentnode.pointers[childidx] newuniqueindex = indirectionmap[childid] # Update pointer to reference the unique node's ID/address parentnode.pointers[childidx] = uniquenodes[newuniqueindex].id # Replace the current level with the unique nodes for the next iteration svolevels[level] = uniquenodes return svolevels[0] Parameters: Max Level (L): The depth of the octree. The algorithm runs in O(L) iterations. Resolution: Demonstrated at 128K^3 (131,072^3) voxel grids. Sub-DAG Threshold: For resolutions over 1K^3, generate sub-DAGs of that size first to manage memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: The complete SVO may be orders of magnitude larger than the final DAG. The method must support streaming or chunk-based processing (constructing sub-DAGs) to handle scenes that do not fit in RAM or on disk. Attribute Compression: The method focuses on geometry (visibility). It does not compress material or reflectance properties (color, normal). Decoupling attributes is handled by Voxel Attribute Decoupling. Precision: Pointer indirection must be exact to preserve geometry. The resulting data structure. It shares identical subtrees, enabling lossless compression and efficient traversal without decompression. Choose this when memory footprint is critical and geometry has high redundancy. A technique to separate attributes from geometry. Use this in conjunction with SVO to DAG reduction to compress attributes independently, as the base reduction method does not handle material properties. Time Complexity: The reduction is guaranteed to find the minimal DAG within L iterations. The dominant operation is sorting, which is O(N \log N) per level, where N is the number of nodes at that level. Parallel sorting (e.g., tbb::parallelsort) is used on CPU. GPU parallelization is suggested using parallel prefix sums for compaction. Memory Complexity: The final DAG requires significantly less memory than the SVO. In the EPICTTADEL scene (128K^3, 19 billion voxels), the DAG requires 945MB, while the SVO requires 5.1GB (excluding pointers). Node count reduction is 1-3 orders of magnitude. Measured Performance: Reduction Time: On an Intel Core i7 3930K, reducing a 1K^3 SVO takes ~33ms, and an 8K^3 SVO takes ~4.5s. Traversal: On an NVIDIA GTX680, traversal speeds for the EPICTTADEL scene are 170 MRays/sec for ambient occlusion and 240 MRays/sec for shadows. Strengths: Lossless compression; no decompression overhead during traversal; handles extremely high resolutions (>1K^3) that would otherwise exceed memory limits; effective on irregular data. Limitations: Does not compress material properties; requires significant memory during construction if not using sub-DAGs; sorting large keys (256-bit) can be costly. When to Use: Ray tracing hard/soft shadows, ambient occlusion, and primary rays in high-resolution scenes with redundant geometry. When Not to Use: Scenes with no geometric redundancy; dynamic scenes requiring real-time compression (the method is static). The method was introduced by Viktor Kampe, Erik Sintorn, and Ulf Assarsson from Chalmers University of Technology in the paper "High Resolution Sparse Voxel DAGs". It builds on earlier work by Webber and Dillencourt [1989] on quadtrees and Parker et al. [2003] on 3D voxel data, but distinguishes itself by decoupling voxel content from geometry, allowing successful compression of irregular data. The bottom-up approach was chosen over top-down recursive testing for its efficiency. It is used primarily for GPU ray tracing of visibility queries in extremely high-resolution voxel grids.
