name: Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG)
head: Sparse Voxel DAG
body: A Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG) is a hierarchical data structure for representing 3D voxelized scenes that reduces memory footprint by identifying and merging identical subtrees, allowing multiple parent nodes to share the same child node instance. Unlike a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) which only encodes empty regions efficiently, the SVDAG additionally encodes identical regions of space by sharing pointers to identical subtrees. This allows for lossless compression without decompression overhead during traversal, making it suitable for real-time rendering and interactive editing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary voxel grid R of size N^3 voxels, where N \ge 2 and N = 2^m. The grid contains active (filled) and passive (empty) voxels. Output: A root node of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representing the voxel grid, where identical subvolumes are merged into shared nodes. Data Structures: The SVDAG consists of two node types: Internal Nodes (INODE) and Leaf Nodes (LNODE). 1. Internal Node (INODE): Child Node Mask (CHNM): An 8-bit field where each bit is a Header Tag (HT) corresponding to one of the 8 potential children (octants). If HT = 0: The subDAG is homogenously filled with passive voxels (pruned); no pointer is needed. If HT = 1: At least one voxel is active; a child node pointer is present. Reserved Bits (p): Concatenated after CHNM for alignment. Pointers (PTS): An array of 1 to 8 pointers (PT), each r bits long, pointing to child nodes. The order of pointers corresponds to the linearization order (e.g., Morton order). Layout: CHNM (8 bits) + p (reserved) + PTS (variable). Standard alignment uses p=24 and r=32, ensuring 32-bit alignment. 2. Leaf Node (LNODE): Represents a homogeneous subvolume (all passive or all active) or the base resolution. Algorithm (Bottom-Up Reduction): The construction transforms an SVO into a DAG by searching for common subtrees and referencing only unique instances, proceeding from leaves upward. 1. Root Construction: If N=2, the root is a leaf node. If N>2, the root is an internal node. 2. Recursive Build: For a given grid section: a. Check if the section is homogeneous (all voxels identical) or if the base resolution is reached. b. If homogeneous/passive: Create a Leaf Node (LNODE). If active, it represents the filled volume; if passive, it is pruned. c. If not homogeneous: Create an Internal Node (INODE). d. For each of the 8 octants: i. Extract the sub-grid. ii. Recursively build the child node. iii. If the child is a leaf representing passive voxels, set the corresponding HT in CHNM to 0 and do not add a pointer to PTS. iv. If the child is active, set HT to 1 and add the pointer to PTS. 3. Common Subtree Merging (CSM): a. Generate a unique key for the current subtree configuration (e.g., based on child pointers and structure). b. Check a cache of existing nodes. If a node with the same key exists, return the existing node's pointer instead of creating a new one. c. If not in cache, insert the new node into the cache and return its pointer. 4. Propagation: Merging opportunities propagate from leaf nodes upward. Identical subtrees at any level are merged into a single instance, and all parents point to this single instance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VoxelNode: isleaf: bool value: int # 0 for passive, 1 for active children: list[VoxelNode] # 8 elements, None if leaf chnm: int # 8-bit header tag mask pts: list[VoxelNode] # pointers to active children def getoctant(grid: list[list[list[int]]], octantidx: int, size: int) -> list[list[list[int]]]: half = size // 2 x0 = (octantidx & 1) half y0 = (octantidx & 2) half // 2 z0 = (octantidx & 4) half // 4 return [[[grid[z0+z][y0+y][x0+x] for x in range(half)] for y in range(half)] for z in range(half)] def ishomogeneous(grid: list[list[list[int]]]) -> bool: val = grid[0][0][0] for z in grid: for y in z: for x in y: if x != val: return False return True def builddag(grid: list[list[list[int]]], depth: int, size: int, cache: dict) -> VoxelNode: # Generate unique key from grid content key = str(tuple(grid[z][y][x] for z in range(size) for y in range(size) for x in range(size))) if key in cache: return cache[key] node = VoxelNode() if depth == 0 or ishomogeneous(grid): node.isleaf = True node.value = grid[0][0][0] node.children = [None]8 node.chnm = 0 node.pts = [] else: node.isleaf = False node.children = [None]8 node.chnm = 0 node.pts = [] newsize = size // 2 for i in range(8): octant = getoctant(grid, i, newsize) child = builddag(octant, depth - 1, newsize, cache) node.children[i] = child if child.isleaf and child.value == 0: pass # HT=0, pruned else: node.chnm |= (1 << i) node.pts.append(child) cache[key] = node return node def traceray(node: VoxelNode, origin: list[float], direction: list[float], bounds: list[float]) -> tuple[int, int, int]: # Standard SVDAG ray traversal # 1. Compute ray-box intersection with current node bounds # 2. If no intersection, return None # 3. If leaf: return voxel coordinates if active, else None # 4. If internal: iterate i in 0..7 # if (node.chnm >> i) & 1: # res = traceray(node.pts[i], origin, direction, childbounds[i]) # if res: return res # 5. Return None pass Parameters: N: Grid dimension size, N \ge 2, N=2^m. p: Reserved bits for alignment. Typical value: 24 bits (for 32-bit alignment). r: Length of child node pointer. Typical value: 32 bits (for 32-bit alignment). gridDepth: Maximum recursion depth. Default 4 (implies 16^3 base, but typically scaled to higher resolutions like 128K^3 via depth 16-17). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Attributes: Adding extra bits of information (e.g., color) to leaf nodes reduces the number of identical elements, abolishing compression because previously identical leaves become unique. Memory Layout: Identical pointers exist because nodes can have multiple parents. Rearranging nodes could potentially share pointers and amortize their cost, but this is an open issue. Key Generation: The caching mechanism relies on a unique key for subtree content. Incorrect key generation leads to failure to merge identical subtrees. SSVDAG is a compact, lossless volume representation that merges subtrees identical through reflective symmetries (planar reflections along principal grid axes) and employs variable bit-rate encoding for child pointers to minimize memory footprint while maintaining GPU-friendly traversal performance. It differs from its parent Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG) by recognizing geometric similarity via transformations rather than requiring exact node identity, and from Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG) by explicitly detailing the binary layout and tagged pointer encoding [1349-ssvdag-node-layout-and-tagged-pointer-encoding.md]. The PSVDAG–SVDAG Conversion Algorithm transforms a Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG) into a Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG). While PSVDAGs use variable-length Labels/Callers and intermittent binary encoding to save space, SVDAGs use constant-length 32-bit pointers and uninterrupted binary sequences to enable efficient rendering and editing. This conversion replaces the pointerless structure with a pointer-based one, allowing for Child Subtree Merging (CSM) and random access, at the cost of increased memory usage (inflation factor 3.01x–3.70x). Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The DAG consumes 8 to 36 bytes per node. It reduces total memory consumption by up to 38x compared to ESVO and up to 26x compared to a minimal pointer-less SVO. Node Reduction: In the CRYSPONZA scene, a 576x reduction in node count was achieved. In the HAIRBALL scene, a 28x reduction was achieved despite lacking obvious regularities. Build Time: Building the DAG for CRYSPONZA at 512^3 takes 8.4ms total (1.9ms sorting). At 8K^3, it takes 4.5s total (0.6s sorting). For HAIRBALL at 8K^3, it takes 40.6s total (4.5s sorting). Measured Performance: In the EPICCITADEL scene voxelized to 128K^3 resolution, the SVDAG stores 19 billion voxels in 945MB of GPU memory. An SVO would require 5.1GB (excluding pointers). On an NVIDIA GTX680, ray tracing in the sparse voxel DAG achieves 170 MRays/sec for ambient occlusion and 240 MRays/sec for shadows. The new encoding (Modisett & Billeter) reduces geometric data size by 13%-18% compared to the original SVDAG. The new encoding improves rendering time by around 10%-12% for static models and by up to 20%-25% for editable voxel models. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: No decompression overhead; efficient traversal; handles extremely high resolutions (up to 128K^3) in real-time. Limitations: Higher memory usage per node compared to pointerless structures due to pointers. Adding attributes to leaves destroys compression benefits. High Resolution Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs (SVDAGs) were proposed in 2013 by Kämpe, Sintorn, and Assarsson. The method was introduced to address the limitations of Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) and Efficient Sparse Voxel Octrees (ESVOs) by exploiting geometric similarity (identical subtrees) in addition to sparsity (empty regions). It allows for the storage and rendering of voxel geometry at resolutions as high as (128k)^3 in real time. name: Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG)
body: SSVDAG is a compact, lossless volume representation that merges subtrees identical through reflective symmetries (planar reflections along principal grid axes) and employs variable bit-rate encoding for child pointers to minimize memory footprint while maintaining GPU-friendly traversal performance. It differs from its parent Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG) by recognizing geometric similarity via transformations rather than requiring exact node identity, and from its child article by explicitly detailing the binary layout and tagged pointer encoding [1349-ssvdag-node-layout-and-tagged-pointer-encoding.md]. Inputs: A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) or an existing SVDAG. Outputs: A Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG) stored in a compressed binary format. Data Structures: 1. Indexing Structure: Contains the maximum level L and three 32-bit offsets indicating the start of each level in the inner level array. 2. Inner Node Header: A 16-bit header containing a 2-bit code for each of the 8 potential children. Tag 00: Reserved for null pointers (not stored). Tag 01: Child pointer is 16 bits. Tag 10: Child pointer is 32 bits. Tag 11: Child pointer is 32 bits. 3. Child Pointer Formats: Tag 01 (16 bits): Leftmost 3 bits encode the transformation T (reflection codes). Remaining 13 bits encode the offset in number of level-words from the beginning of the next level. A level-word is 2 bytes for an inner level and 8 bytes for the leaf level. This allows encoding reflections and references to nodes in the first 2^{14} bytes of an inner level or first 2^{16} bytes of the leaf level. Tag 10/11 (32 bits): Leftmost 3 bits encode the transformation T. Remaining 29 bits encode the lowest 29 bits of the offset. The highest bit of the offset is stored in the header or a subsequent byte. Algorithm Steps: The construction is a bottom-up external-memory process that reduces an SVO to a minimal SSVDAG by alternating phases at each level, starting from the finest level L-1 up to the root at level 0. 1. Leaf Grouping (Coarsening): The construction graph is coarsened by one level. 4^3 grids are encoded as simple grids in a single array of bricks, each occupying 64 bits. This is done by grouping the 2^3 leaves from the bottom-up process into 4^3 inner nodes at level L-2 without performing new matches. 2. Leaf Node Clustering: Each small voxel grid G of size 2^3 is represented by a binary number B(G) by concatenating occupancy bits. The canonical representation G^? is defined as G^? = T{x,y,z}(G) where T{x,y,z} = \arg \max{T{x,y,z}} B(T{x,y,z}(G)). This is the reflection with the largest integer value. Two leaf nodes are similar if their canonical representations are identical. A precomputed table of 256 entries maps all possible 2^3 voxel combinations to the canonical transformation and the unique canonical representation (one of 46 possible ones). 3. Inner Node Clustering: Inner nodes n1 and n2 are merged if they represent the same subtrees under a transformation T. First, sort inner nodes by the lexicographically sorted set of child pointers. During a streaming pass, verify similarity: for every tagged pointer (tag, p) of n1, it must map to (T(tag), p) in n2 if p is not invariant to T, or to (T(tag) \neg T(tag), p) if p is invariant. Repeat for all 8 reflection combinations, stopping at the first match. Replace pointers to the clustered nodes in the immediately higher level with tagged pointers to the single representative, where the tag encodes the specific transformation required to recover the original subtree. 4. Frequency-based Pointer Compaction: Nodes at each level are reordered by reference count (most referenced first). Pointers are replaced by offsets from the beginning of the level array. The number of bits for each offset is chosen as the smallest available in the encoded format (16-bit or 32-bit). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildssvdag(svolevels): # svolevels: list of lists of Node objects. # Node has:.children (list of 8 tuples (tag, ptr)),.refcount,.parent,.parentidx L = len(svolevels) - 1 processed = [set() for in range(L + 1)] # Precomputed table for 2^3 leaf grids: maps 256 occupancy patterns to (canonicalrep, transformbits) LEAFTABLE = buildleafcanonicaltable() for level in range(L - 1, -1, -1): nodes = svolevels[level] representatives = [] for i, node in enumerate(nodes): if i in processed[level]: continue cluster = [node] processed[level].add(i) transforms = [0] for j in range(i + 1, len(nodes)): if j in processed[level]: continue other = nodes[j] T = findsymmetrymatch(cluster[0], other) if T is not None: cluster.append(other) processed[level].add(j) transforms.append(T) representatives.append((cluster[0], transforms)) # Update parent pointers for merged nodes for k, other in enumerate(cluster[1:], start=1): T = transforms[k] other.parent.children[other.parentidx] = (T, cluster[0]) # Frequency-based compaction representatives.sort(key=lambda x: x[0].refcount, reverse=True) for offset, (rep,) in enumerate(representatives): rep.offset = offset rep.header = encodeheader(rep.children) rep.pointers = encodepointers(rep.children, offset) svolevels[level] = [rep for rep, in representatives] # Leaf coarsening: group 2^3 leaves into 4^3 bricks (64 bits each) bricks = [] leafnodes = svolevels[L-1] for i in range(0, len(leafnodes), 8): brickdata = packleafbrick(leafnodes[i:i+8]) bricks.append(brickdata) return buildindex(svolevels), bricks def findsymmetrymatch(n1, n2): # Check 8 reflections. Returns transform bits or None. for Tbits in range(8): match = True for i in range(8): tag1, ptr1 = n1.children[i] tag2, ptr2 = n2.children[i] mappedtag = applyreflectiontag(tag1, Tbits) if ptr1 != ptr2: if not isinvariant(ptr1, Tbits): match = False break else: if mappedtag != tag2: match = False break if match: return Tbits return None def applyreflectiontag(tag, Tbits): # Standard octree child index permutation under axis reflections # Tags are 2-bit codes representing child indices 0-7 return tag # Actual permutation depends on specific child indexing scheme def isinvariant(ptr, Tbits): # Checks if the subtree pointed to by ptr is symmetric under T return ptr.issymmetricunder(Tbits) def encodeheader(children): header = 0 for i in range(8): tag, ptr = children[i] if ptr is None: code = 0 else: offset = ptr.offset if offset < (1 << 13): code = 1 else: code = 2 header |= (code << (2 i)) return header def encodepointers(children, baseoffset): packed = [] for i in range(8): tag, ptr = children[i] if ptr is None: continue offset = ptr.offset - baseoffset T = ptr.tag if offset < (1 << 13): # 16-bit format: 3 bits T, 13 bits offset val = (T << 13) | offset packed.append(val & 0xFFFF) else: # 32-bit format: 3 bits T, 29 bits offset val = (T << 29) | (offset & 0x1FFFFFFF) packed.append(val & 0xFFFFFFFF) return packed def buildleafcanonicaltable(): # Returns dict mapping 256 occupancy patterns to (canonicalrep, transformbits) # Uses precomputed 2^3 voxel reflection table return {} def packleafbrick(leaves): # Packs 8 leaves into a 64-bit brick return 0 def buildindex(svolevels): # Returns indexing structure with max level L and 3 offsets return {} Parameters: Symmetry Transforms: Planar reflections along the main grid directions (X, Y, Z). Leaf Size for Construction: 2^3 voxels. Transformation Encoding: 3 bits corresponding to reflections along the X, Y, and Z axes. The transformation T{x,y,z} is its own inverse: T{x,y,z}^{-1} = T{x,y,z}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invariant Pointers: When checking similarity, if a child pointer p is invariant to the transformation T, the tag mapping logic differs from non-invariant pointers. The source specifies mapping to (T(tag) \neg T(tag), p) if invariant, requiring careful implementation of the invariant check. Precision: The method relies on exact bitwise comparison of canonical representations for leaves and exact pointer matching for inner nodes. Defines the binary layout of inner nodes, replacing fixed-size child pointers with variable-length tagged pointers (2 or 4 bytes) that embed transformation codes, solving the memory overhead problem of standard SVDAGs where all pointers are fixed at 4 bytes. Compression: In the PowerPlant scene (64K^3 resolution, ~6 billion non-empty voxels), SSVDAG stores data in <86MB (0.123 bits/voxel), compared to 16.2GB for SVO (without pointers) and 167MB for SVDAG. Performance: Real-time GPU in-core visualization with shading and shadows is achieved for the full Boeing 777 model at sub-millimetric precision. The tracing overhead for SSVDAG compared to standard SVO/SVDAG is less than 15%. Memory Distribution: In the Powerplant dataset, the most common 10% of nodes account for nearly 90% of references at level 14 and nearly 50% at level 11, justifying the frequency-based pointer compaction. Strengths: High compression ratio for scenes with reflective symmetry; transparent to standard ray-casting algorithms; GPU-friendly traversal. Limitations: Construction is complex and requires external-memory processing; limited to reflective symmetries (other similarity transforms not supported). SSVDAG was introduced by Alberto Jaspe Villanueva, Fabio Marton, and Enrico Gobbetti from CRS4 in 2016. It extends the concept of Sparse Voxel DAGs (SVDAGs) by incorporating symmetry-aware merging, building on prior work in DAG compression for SVOs. SSVDAGs: Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAGs, https://www.crs4.it/vic/data/papers/i3d2016-symmetry-dags.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SSVDAG Node Layout and Tagged Pointer Encoding
head: Compact representation, Tagged pointer encoding
body: This method defines the binary layout of inner nodes in a Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG) to minimize memory footprint while supporting GPU-friendly traversal. It replaces fixed-size child pointers with variable-length tagged pointers (2 or 4 bytes) that embed transformation codes, solving the memory overhead problem of standard SVDAGs where all pointers are fixed at 4 bytes. It differs from its parent Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG) by explicitly detailing the bit-packing scheme for these pointers and the associated traversal state management. Input: A voxelized scene represented as a Sparse Voxel DAG with symmetry-aware compression. Output: A memory layout for inner nodes where child pointers are encoded as variable-length tagged pointers, and a traversal algorithm that maintains a cumulative transformation status. Each inner node begins with a 16-bit header. This header contains 8 entries, each 2 bits wide, corresponding to the 8 potential children in octant order. Tag 00: Null pointer. No child data follows. Tag 01: 16-bit child pointer. Tag 10: 32-bit child pointer. Tag 11: 32-bit child pointer. Child pointers are stored immediately after the header. The size and format depend on the header tag. 1. 16-bit Pointer (Tag 01) Size: 2 bytes (16 bits). Layout: Bits [15:13]: Transformation code (3 bits). Bits [12:0]: Offset in number of level-words (13 bits). Addressing: For inner levels: Level-word size is 2 bytes. Max addressable offset is 2^{13} \times 2 = 2^{14} bytes (16 KB). For leaf levels: Level-word size is 8 bytes. Max addressable offset is 2^{13} \times 8 = 2^{16} bytes (64 KB). 2. 32-bit Pointers (Tags 10 and 11) Size: 4 bytes (32 bits). Layout: Bits [31:29]: Transformation code (3 bits). Bits [28:0]: Lowest 29 bits of the offset. The highest bit of the full offset (bit 29) is not stored in the pointer; it is reconstructed from the least significant bit of the 2-bit header tag for that child. If Tag is 10 (binary 10), the header's LSB is 0, so the offset high bit is 0. If Tag is 11 (binary 11), the header's LSB is 1, so the offset high bit is 1. Addressing: For inner levels: Max addressable offset > 2 GB. For leaf levels: Max addressable offset > 8 GB. During ray traversal, a 3-bit Transformation Status variable is maintained. Initialization: 0. Update: When descending to a child, XOR the current status with the 3-bit transformation code extracted from the child's pointer. Restoration: The status must be pushed to a stack along with the current node index to allow restoration upon backtracking. Application: This status indicates which reflections must be applied to indices when accessing child pointers in inner nodes or voxel contents in leaf nodes. Accessing the i-th child requires computing the byte offset within the node's data stream. Unlike SVDAG, where pointers are either 0 or 4 bytes, SSVDAG pointers are 0, 2, or 4 bytes. 1. Read the 16-bit header. 2. Extract the 2-bit tag for child i. 3. Compute the byte offset from the start of the child pointer array: \text{Offset} = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} \text{Size}(\text{Tag}j) Where \text{Size}(\text{Tag}j) is 0 if \text{Tag}j = 00, 2 if \text{Tag}j = 01, and 4 if \text{Tag}j \in \{10, 11\}. 4. Read the pointer data at this offset. 5. Extract the transformation code from the top 3 bits. 6. Decode the offset based on the pointer size (see formulas below). 16-bit Pointer Offset Decoding: Let P{16} be the 16-bit integer value of the pointer. \text{Transform} = P{16} \gg 13 \text{WordOffset} = P{16} \ \& \ 0x1FFF \text{ByteOffset} = \text{WordOffset} \times \text{LevelWordSize} Where \text{LevelWordSize} = 2 for inner levels, 8 for leaf levels. 32-bit Pointer Offset Decoding: Let P{32} be the 32-bit integer value of the pointer. \text{Transform} = P{32} \gg 29 \text{LowOffset} = P{32} \ \& \ 0x1FFFFFFF \text{HighBit} = (\text{HeaderTag} \ \& \ 1) \text{FullOffset} = (\text{HighBit} \ll 29) \ | \ \text{LowOffset} \text{ByteOffset} = \text{FullOffset} \times \text{LevelWordSize} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodechildpointer(header16bit, childindex, levelwordsize, buffer): """ Decodes the child pointer for a specific child index in an SSVDAG inner node. buffer: list of bytes containing the node data starting immediately after the header. """ # Extract the 2-bit tag for the specific child tag = (header16bit >> (childindex 2)) & 0x3 if tag == 0x0: # Null pointer return (0, None) # Calculate byte offset within the child pointer array # Sum sizes of all previous children byteoffsetinarray = 0 for j in range(childindex): prevtag = (header16bit >> (j 2)) & 0x3 if prevtag == 0x0: byteoffsetinarray += 0 elif prevtag == 0x1: byteoffsetinarray += 2 else: # 0x2 or 0x3 byteoffsetinarray += 4 # Read pointer data based on size if tag == 0x1: # 16-bit pointer ptrval = (buffer[byteoffsetinarray] << 8) | buffer[byteoffsetinarray + 1] transformcode = ptrval >> 13 wordoffset = ptrval & 0x1FFF byteoffset = wordoffset levelwordsize return (transformcode, byteoffset) else: # 32-bit pointer (tags 0x2 or 0x3) ptrval = (buffer[byteoffsetinarray] << 24) | (buffer[byteoffsetinarray + 1] << 16) | (buffer[byteoffsetinarray + 2] << 8) | buffer[byteoffsetinarray + 3] transformcode = ptrval >> 29 lowoffset = ptrval & 0x1FFFFFFF # Determine high bit from header tag headertaglowbit = tag & 0x1 highbit = headertaglowbit << 29 fulloffset = highbit | lowoffset byteoffset = fulloffset levelwordsize return (transformcode, byteoffset) def traversessvdagray(rayorigin, raydirection, nodebuffer, levelwordsize, leveloffsets): """ Demonstrates traversal logic with transformation status management. """ # Stack for backtracking stack = [] # Current transformation status currenttransform = 0 # Start at root (index 0) currentnodeidx = 0 currentlevel = 0 # Track current tree level for offset lookup while True: # Read node header header = (nodebuffer[currentnodeidx] << 8) | nodebuffer[currentnodeidx + 1] # Compute childidx from ray-node intersection logic childidx = None if childidx is None: # No intersection with this node's children, backtrack if not stack: break # Ray escaped # Restore state prevnodeidx, prevtransform = stack.pop() currentnodeidx = prevnodeidx currenttransform = prevtransform continue # Decode child pointer # Buffer for child pointers starts after the header bytes. childbuffer = nodebuffer[currentnodeidx + 2:] transformcode, childbyteoffset = decodechildpointer(header, childidx, levelwordsize, childbuffer) # Update transformation status # XOR with the pointer's reflection tag newtransform = currenttransform ^ transformcode # Push current state to stack for backtracking stack.append((currentnodeidx, currenttransform)) # Move to child # Absolute child address requires adding the level start offset from leveloffsets. currentnodeidx = leveloffsets[currentlevel] + childbyteoffset currenttransform = newtransform Variable Size Access: Accessing the i-th child requires summing the sizes of all preceding pointers [0, i-1]. This differs from SVDAG, which only had sizes 0 and 4. This computation must be performed in the shader, typically via a manually unrolled loop. Precision: The 13-bit offset in 16-bit pointers limits addressing to the first 16 KB of inner levels and 64 KB of leaf levels. If a node is located beyond this range, it must use a 32-bit pointer (Tag 10 or 11). Transformation Accumulation: The transformation status is cumulative. It must be XOR-ed with each pointer's transformation code as the traversal descends. It must be saved to the stack to be restored upon backtracking. Memory Footprint: Significantly reduced compared to fixed-pointer SVDAGs. Null children consume 0 bytes, common children consume 2 bytes, and rare/distant children consume 4 bytes. Complexity: Time: Traversal requires computing variable offsets via a loop for each child access. Space: Inner node headers are fixed at 16 bits. Child data is variable. Performance: Designed for GPU efficiency. The variable-length encoding allows compact storage, improving cache utilization. The transformation status is a simple 3-bit integer, minimizing register pressure. Limitations: The 16-bit pointer is limited to small offsets. Large scenes may require more 32-bit pointers, reducing the compression benefit. The SSVDAG node layout was introduced by Kämpe et al. in 2016 as an extension of the Sparse Voxel DAG (SVDAG). The original SVDAG used fixed 4-byte pointers. The SSVDAG method was developed to further reduce memory consumption by exploiting the fact that many child pointers are null or point to nearby nodes, allowing for variable-length encoding. It also integrates symmetry-aware compression, storing transformation codes directly in the pointers. SSVDAGs: Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAGs - CRS4, https://www.crs4.it/vic/data/papers/i3d2016-symmetry-dags.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Compact SSVDAG Encoding
head: Frequency-based pointer compaction, Leaf grouping, Memory-aligned encoding
body: Compact SSVDAG Encoding is a GPU-friendly memory layout for Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs that minimizes pointer overhead while enabling fast, decompression-free ray tracing. It distinguishes itself from standard SVDAGs by combining leaf grouping, frequency-based pointer compaction, and half-word memory alignment to reduce the memory footprint of high-resolution scenes. The technique relies on highly skewed reference distributions, where in a 64K³ Powerplant dataset, the most common 10% of nodes account for nearly 90% of pointers at level 14 and nearly 50% at level 11. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A constructed SVDAG (typically from bottom-up construction using 2^3 leaf matching). Output: A compact binary representation consisting of an indexing structure, an inner node array, and a leaf node array. Data Structures: 1. Indexing Structure: maxlevel: 32-bit integer, the maximum depth L of the tree. leveloffsets: Array of three 32-bit integers. Each offset points to the start of a specific level's inner node array within the inner level array. 2. Inner Node Array: A contiguous array of inner nodes. Nodes are reordered by reference count (descending) before encoding. Each node is encoded as a variable-length sequence of 16-bit half-words. 3. Leaf Node Array: A contiguous array of leaf nodes (bricks). Each leaf is fixed at 64 bits (8 bytes). Inner Node Layout: Each inner node begins with a 16-bit header containing eight 2-bit tags, one for each of the 8 potential children. Tag 00 (Null): The child is not stored. No pointer data follows. Tag 01 (16-bit Child): Followed by a 16-bit child pointer. Bits [15:13]: 3-bit transformation code. Bits [12:0]: 13-bit offset (in level-words) from the start of the next level's array. Tag 10 (32-bit Child): Followed by a 32-bit child pointer. Bits [31:29]: 3-bit transformation code. Bits [28:0]: Lowest 29 bits of the offset. Tag 11 (32-bit Child with MSB): Followed by a 32-bit child pointer. Bits [31:29]: 3-bit transformation code. Bit [28]: Highest bit of the offset (MSB). Bits [27:0]: Lowest 28 bits of the offset. Note: The source states "highest bit of offset in rightmost header bit" for tags 10/11. This implies the header tag itself indicates the MSB: Tag 10 has MSB=0 in the header, Tag 11 has MSB=1 in the header. The 32-bit payload contains the remaining 29 bits. Level-Word Size: For inner levels: 1 level-word = 2 bytes (16 bits). For leaf level: 1 level-word = 8 bytes (64 bits). Algorithm Steps: 1. Leaf Grouping: Coarsen the construction graph by one level. Instead of storing 2^3 leaves as individual nodes, group 4^3 grids into simple grids (bricks) stored in a single array. Each brick occupies 64 bits. This avoids new matching passes; it operates on the graph from the bottom-up construction. 2. Frequency Analysis: Count the reference count for every node at each level in the DAG. 3. Reordering: Sort the nodes at each level in descending order of their reference counts. Most referenced nodes appear first in the level's array. 4. Offset Calculation: Replace absolute pointers with offsets from the beginning of the respective level's array. Calculate the offset in level-words. 5. Pointer Compaction: Determine the number of bits required for each offset based on its magnitude and the available bit slots in the encoding format (16-bit or 32-bit child pointers). Assign the smallest valid tag (01, 10, or 11) that can represent the offset. 6. Encoding: Write the 16-bit header with the 2-bit tags for each of the 8 children. Write the child pointer data (transformation + offset) immediately after the header for each non-null child. Pack the resulting bytes into 16-bit half-words for memory alignment. 7. Indexing: Construct the indexing structure with maxlevel and the starting offsets for each level in the inner node array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodecompactssvdag(nodesbylevel): """ nodesbylevel: List of lists. nodesbylevel[l] contains node objects. Each node has: children: list of 8 child references (or None) refcount: integer transformcode: 3-bit integer (0-7) """ innerarrays = [] leafarray = [] leveloffsets = [] for levelidx, levelnodes in enumerate(nodesbylevel): # Step 2 & 3: Frequency Analysis and Reordering levelnodes.sort(key=lambda n: n.refcount, reverse=True) if levelidx == len(nodesbylevel) - 1: # Leaf Level: Encode leaves as 64-bit bricks for node in levelnodes: leafarray.append(node.data) # 64-bit voxel data else: # Inner Level innerarrays.append([]) nextlevelnodes = nodesbylevel[levelidx + 1] # Build a map from node ID to its new sorted index for offset calculation nodetoidx = {id(n): i for i, n in enumerate(nextlevelnodes)} for node in levelnodes: header = 0 childpayloads = [] for childidx in range(8): child = node.children[childidx] if child is None: # Tag 00: Null header |= (0x00 << (childidx 2)) else: # Calculate offset in level-words (2-byte units) childidxinnext = nodetoidx[id(child)] offsetwords = childidxinnext # Check if offset fits in 13 bits (Tag 01) if offsetwords < (1 << 13): tag = 0x01 # 16-bit payload: 3-bit transform, 13-bit offset payload = ((child.transformcode & 0x7) << 13) | (offsetwords & 0x1FFF) childpayloads.append(payload) else: # Use 32-bit payload (Tag 10 or 11) # MSB of offset goes to header tag LSB msb = (offsetwords >> 28) & 0x1 tag = 0x02 | msb # 10 or 11 # Payload: 3-bit transform, 29-bit offset (lower 29 bits) payload = ((child.transformcode & 0x7) << 29) | (offsetwords & 0x1FFFFFF) childpayloads.append(payload) # Set tag in header header |= (tag << (childidx 2)) # Pack header and payloads into 16-bit half-words words = [header] for p in childpayloads: if p < (1 << 16): words.append(p) else: # 32-bit payload split into two 16-bit words words.append(p & 0xFFFF) words.append((p >> 16) & 0xFFFF) innerarrays[-1].append(words) # Step 7: Indexing (accumulate offsets) leveloffsets.append(sum(len(n) for n in innerarrays[-1])) # Finalize indexing structure indexing = { 'maxlevel': len(nodesbylevel) - 1, 'leveloffsets': leveloffsets } return indexing, innerarrays, leafarray Parameters: Encoding Basis: 16-bit half-words. Leaf Size: 64 bits (8 bytes). Addressable Space: >2 GB for inner levels, 8 GB for leaves. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Offset Overflow: If a node's offset exceeds 29 bits (for inner) or the leaf limit, it cannot be encoded with the current scheme. Precision & Boundaries: Offsets are measured in level-words; misinterpreting level-word size (2 bytes vs 8 bytes) will cause traversal failures. Degenerate Input: Nodes with all null children still consume a 16-bit header word. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Addressable Space: >2 GB for inner levels, 8 GB for leaves. Performance: Optimized for GPU ray tracing. The memory-aligned encoding simplifies decoding on GPUs. Strengths: Low memory footprint, fast tracing, no decompression overhead. Limitations: Addressable space limits, encoding complexity due to reordering and offset calculation. Origin: Introduced in the paper "Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAGs (SSVDAGs) for compression-domain tracing of high-resolution geometric scenes". Development: Builds upon the SVDAG structure [Kämpe et al. 2013] and the bottom-up construction method described in the same paper. Usage: Used in high-resolution geometric scene compression and ray tracing. Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAGs (SSVDAGs) for compression-domain tracing of high-resolution geometric scenes, https://albertojaspe.net/publications/2017-JCGT-ssvdags.pdf, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: SVDAG Parameter Configurations
head: SVDAG Configurations, SVDAG1-6
body: SVDAG Parameter Configurations define the specific bit-widths for Child Node Masks (CHNM), Child Node Pointers (PT), and Addressing Words (addr. word) within a Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG) node layout. They solve the problem of optimizing memory footprint versus addressable space in hierarchical data structures by allowing variable-length pointers. Unlike the base SVO configuration which uses fixed 32-bit pointers, these configurations (SVDAG1–6) enable the use of shorter pointers (8-bit or 16-bit) for nodes located closer to the root, significantly reducing memory consumption for large scenes while maintaining the ability to address distant nodes via longer pointers. The method configures the binary layout of SSVDAG nodes. The core inputs are the desired scene resolution and the target balance between memory size and addressable space. The output is a specific configuration (SVDAG1–6) that dictates the bit-lengths of the node components. Each configuration defines the size of three key fields within the node header and pointer structure: 1. CHNM (Child Node Mask): A bitmask indicating which of the 8 suboctants are active. 2. PT (Child Node Pointer): The pointer to the child node. In configurations with multiple pointer types, different bits are used for different types. 3. Addressing Word: The word size used for memory addressing calculations. The following table lists the exact bit layouts for each configuration: | Configuration | CHNM [bits] | PT1 [bits] | PT2 [bits] | PT3 [bits] | Addressing Word [bits] | Notes | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | SVO | 8 (aligned to 32) | 32 | - | - | 32 | Baseline SVO layout | | SVDAG1 | 8 (aligned to 32) | 32 | - | - | 32 | Identical to SVO | | SVDAG2 | 16 | 8 | 8 | - | 8 | Two 8-bit pointer types | | SVDAG3 | 16 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 8 | Three pointer types | | SVDAG4 | 16 | 16 | 16 | 32 | 8 | Three pointer types | | SVDAG5 | 16 | 16 | 16 | 32 | 16 | Three pointer types | | SVDAG6 | 16 | 16 | 16 | 32 | 32 | Three pointer types | Note: For SVO and SVDAG1, the 8-bit CHNM is aligned to 32 bits using 24 reserved bits. The choice of Addressing Word and Pointer Length determines the maximum addressable memory space. The relationship is defined by the formula: \text{Addressable Space} = \text{Addressing Word Size} \times 2^{\text{Pointer Length}} The specific addressable spaces for the tested configurations are: | Pointer Length | Addressing Word 8b | Addressing Word 16b | Addressing Word 32b | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | 8b | 256 B | 64 KB | 4 GB | | 16b | 512 B | 128 KB | 8 GB | | 32b | 1024 B | 256 KB | 16 GB | When encoding a node, the system selects the shortest pointer type (PT1, PT2, or PT3) that can address the target child node's location within the addressable space defined by the configuration's addressing word. 1. Calculate Offset: Determine the byte offset of the child node from the current node's base address. 2. Check PT1: If the offset fits within the addressable space of PT1 (e.g., 256 B for 8b pointer/8b word), use PT1. 3. Check PT2: If not, check if it fits within PT2's space (e.g., 64 KB for 16b pointer/8b word). If yes, use PT2. 4. Use PT3: If neither, use PT3 (32b), which typically addresses the largest space (e.g., 4 GB or 16 GB depending on the addressing word). Alignment: In SVO and SVDAG1, the 8-bit CHNM must be padded with 24 reserved bits to align to a 32-bit boundary. Failure to do so causes misalignment in subsequent fields. Pointer Type Mismatch: In configurations like SVDAG2, PT1 and PT2 are both 8 bits. The distinction between them is handled by the Header Tags (HT) in the parent node's mask or a separate tag field, not by pointer length. Addressing Word Limitation: Using an 8-bit addressing word limits the total addressable space significantly compared to 32-bit addressing, even if 32-bit pointers are used. For example, SVDAG6 uses 32-bit pointers but an 8-bit addressing word, limiting its addressable space to 4 GB, whereas SVDAG6 with a 32-bit addressing word would address 16 GB. A technique in Sparse Voxel DAGs (SVDAG) where child node pointers (PT) have varying bit lengths (8b, 16b, or 32b) to optimize address space usage based on scene size and detail requirements. An optimization where the Child Node Mask (CHNM) Header Tags (HT) are 2 bits long instead of 1 bit. This allows four distinct codes (00, 01, 10, 11) to distinguish between passive suboctants and three different types of active child node pointers (PT1, PT2, PT3), enabling compression by using shorter pointers for closer nodes. Memory Efficiency: SVDAG configurations significantly reduce memory usage compared to SVO and SVDAG1. For the Angel Lucy model at 4096³ resolution, SVO size is 59,581.0 KB, while SVDAG3 achieves the lowest size at 7,637.6 KB. Compression Ratio: Compared to a 1-bit-per-voxel grid, SVDAG configurations achieve a compression ratio of approximately 16.1 for Angel Lucy at 4096³. Success Rate: SVDAG3 shows the highest compression success rate (1.95x better than SVDAG1) for Angel Lucy at 4096³. Pointer Distribution: In SVDAG2 at 4096³, PT1 (8b) accounts for 51.13% of pointers, and PT2 (8b) accounts for 77.99% (Note: The source table lists PT2 count for SVDAG2 as 77.99%, but this seems to refer to the cumulative or specific type distribution in SVDAG3; for SVDAG2, PT1 is 51.13% and PT2 is the remaining active pointers, though the exact PT2 percentage for SVDAG2 is not explicitly separated from PT3 in the provided text snippet, SVDAG3 PT1 is 51.11% and PT2 is 20.53%). Hardware: Tests were conducted on an AMD Ryzen 7 7435HS, nVidia GeForce RTX3060, 12 GB RAM. The SVDAG parameter configurations were introduced in the context of optimizing Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs for efficient geometry representation of voxelized 3D scenes. The configurations SVDAG1–6 were tested on three polygonal surface models: Angel Lucy (489k triangles), Porsche (22k triangles), and Skull (80k triangles), voxelized at resolutions from 128³ to 4096³. The study aimed to determine the optimal balance between pointer length, addressing word size, and memory footprint. name: Variable-Length Child Node Pointers
head: Combinations of Child Node Pointer Lengths
body: Variable-Length Child Node Pointers is a memory optimization technique for Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs (SVDAG) that employs child node pointers (PT) of varying bit lengths (8b, 16b, or 32b) to tailor the addressable space to the specific size and detail requirements of the scene. Unlike fixed-length pointer schemes, this method allows the data structure to minimize binary overhead by using shorter pointers for nodes within smaller address ranges and longer pointers for those requiring larger offsets, thereby optimizing compression ratios at the cost of increased traversal complexity due to mixed alignment. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Sparse Voxel DAG structure with a defined Child Node Mask (CHNM) length (typically 16b or 32b) and a target address word length (8b, 16b, or 32b). Output: A node layout where each child node pointer is encoded with a variable bit length (PT1, PT2, or PT3) based on the target node's address relative to the current node. Data Structures: The core data structure relies on the alignment of the Child Node Mask (CHNM) and the pointer types: 1. CHNM Alignment: The CHNM must be aligned to the size of the largest pointer type used. For 8b/16b mixed pointers, CHNM is typically 16b (aligned with 8 reserved bits if originally 8b). For 32b pointers, CHNM is aligned to 32b, which increases the binary representation size of the mask by a factor of 4 compared to an 8b mask. 2. Pointer Types: PT1: Short pointer (8b or 16b). PT2: Medium pointer (16b). PT3: Long pointer (32b). Numbered Steps: 1. Determine Address Word Length: Select the addressing word length (8b, 16b, or 32b) based on the maximum scene size and required detail. 2. Define Pointer Ranges: Assign specific address ranges to each pointer type to ensure non-overlapping coverage within the address word limits: Case A: 8b Address Word Length PT1 (8b): Addresses in range [0, 255] bytes. PT2 (16b): Addresses in range [0, 65,535] bytes. PT3 (32b): Addresses in range [0, 4,294,967,295] bytes. Case B: 16b Address Word Length with Mixed Pointers (16b PT1, 16b PT2, 32b PT3) PT1 (16b): Addresses in range [0, 131,071] bytes (first 128 KB). PT2 (16b): Addresses in range [131,072, 262,143] bytes (subsequent 128 KB). PT3 (32b): Addresses in range [0, 8,589,934,591] bytes (8 GB). 3. Encode Pointers: For each child node, compare its address against the defined ranges. Encode the pointer using the shortest type (PT1, then PT2, then PT3) that can represent the address. 4. Align CHNM: Ensure the CHNM is padded or aligned to the bit-width of the largest pointer type (e.g., 32b) to maintain structural integrity during memory access. Formulas: Address Space Limit (8b Pointer): 2^8 = 256 bytes. Address Space Limit (16b Pointer): 2^{16} = 65,536 bytes. Address Space Limit (32b Pointer): 2^{32} = 4,294,967,296 bytes (4 GB). Binary Size Augmentation: Aligning CHNM to 32b increases its size by a factor of 4 compared to 8b. Parameters: PT1 Length: 8b (for 8b word) or 16b (for 16b word). PT2 Length: 16b. PT3 Length: 32b. CHNM Length: 16b (for mixed 8b/16b/32b pointers with 8b word) or 32b (for 32b pointers). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and Boundaries: The ranges for PT1 and PT2 in the 16b word length case must be strictly non-overlapping. PT2 starts at 131,072 to avoid overlapping PT1's [0, 131,071] range. Memory Waste: Aligning CHNM to 32b significantly increases memory usage (factor of 4), and a significant portion of the 32b address space often remains unused for smaller scenes. Impracticality of 8b Pointers: Using 8b pointers is generally impractical even for very small 3D scenes due to the limited addressable space (256 bytes). Traversal Overhead: Mixed pointer lengths require additional decoding operations (shifting) during traversal, particularly when using 8b alignment, which reduces traversal speed by 15% to 25% compared to fixed 32b alignment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodevariablelengthpointer(address, addresswordbits): """ Encodes a node address into a variable-length pointer based on the address word length configuration. Args: address (int): The byte offset of the target node. addresswordbits (int): The addressing word length (8, 16, or 32). Returns: tuple: (pointerbits, pointervalue, pointertype) """ if addresswordbits == 8: # Case A: 8b Address Word Length if address <= 255: return (8, address, 'PT1') elif address <= 65535: return (16, address, 'PT2') else: return (32, address, 'PT3') elif addresswordbits == 16: # Case B: 16b Address Word Length with Mixed Pointers # PT1: 16b, Range [0, 131071] # PT2: 16b, Range [131072, 262143] # PT3: 32b, Range [0, 8589934591] if address <= 131071: return (16, address, 'PT1') elif address <= 262143: return (16, address, 'PT2') else: return (32, address, 'PT3') else: # Fallback for other configurations or errors return (32, address, 'PT3') def decodevariablelengthpointer(pointerbits, pointervalue, addresswordbits): """ Decodes a variable-length pointer back to its address. Args: pointerbits (int): The bit length of the stored pointer. pointervalue (int): The value of the pointer. addresswordbits (int): The addressing word length used during encoding. Returns: int: The decoded address. """ # In mixed pointer schemes, the value is the direct offset within the # specific range defined by the pointer type. # For PT1 and PT2 in 16b word case, PT2 addresses are shifted. # However, the source defines the ranges as absolute byte offsets. # Assuming the stored value is the absolute address for simplicity # unless relative offset logic is specified. # Based on S1, PT2 range is <131,072; 262,143>, implying absolute addressing. return pointervalue Local addressing uses separate address spaces for each node layer, where pointers are offsets from the start of that specific layer. Global addressing uses a single address space for the entire data structure. Local addressing is preferred when using Frequency-Based Compaction (FBC) to ensure that short and medium pointer address spaces are created separately for each node layer, preventing a single global short/medium space for the entire HDS. An optimized Sparse Voxel DAG structure using three child node pointer types (PT1: 8b, PT2: 16b, PT3: 32b) with an 8b address word length. It is identified as the most compact HDS configuration for all tested models and resolutions. It uses a 16b CHNM with no reserved bits. While it offers superior compression (1.88x to 3.06x compared to conventional SVDAG), it is slower to traverse than SVDAG1 (ratio 0.81 on Angel Lucy 4096^3) due to 8b alignment requiring shifting operations [S1, 5950-local-vs-global-addressing-in-svdag.md]. An optimization that sorts nodes by referencing frequency and assigns addresses to utilize shorter pointer address spaces for frequently referenced nodes, keeping less frequent nodes in longer pointer address spaces. It requires sorting nodes in descending order of referencing frequency and assigning addresses in ascending order. It is advantageous to use separate addressing spaces for each HDS layer rather than a global continuous addressing space [S1, 5950-local-vs-global-addressing-in-svdag.md]. Time Complexity: Traversal is slower than fixed-length pointer schemes. Optimized SVDAGs using variable-length pointers are 15% to 25% slower than SVDAG1 (32b fixed). For example, SVDAG3 traversal time is 0.81 times that of SVDAG1 for Angel Lucy 4096^3. Memory Complexity: Provides significant compression gains. Compression enhancement ranges from 1.88x (at 4096^3 resolution) to 3.06x (at 128^3 resolution) compared to conventional SVDAG HDS. Strengths: Maximizes compression for scenes of varying sizes by matching pointer length to address range. SVDAG3 is the most compact configuration for tested models. Limitations: Increased traversal overhead due to mixed alignment and decoding. Aligning CHNM to 32b increases binary size by a factor of 4, and large portions of the 32b address space may remain unused. When to Use: When memory footprint is critical and the scene size allows for efficient packing of frequently accessed nodes in shorter pointer ranges. When Not to Use: When traversal speed is the primary constraint and the scene size fits comfortably within a fixed 32b pointer scheme without significant waste. This method originates from research on parameter optimization in Sparse Voxel DAGs for efficient geometry representation of voxelized 3D scenes. It was developed to address the limitations of fixed-length pointer schemes, which either waste memory (32b for small scenes) or lack sufficient address space (8b/16b for large scenes). The technique was empirically tested on models such as Angel Lucy, Porsche, and Skull at various resolutions (128^3 to 4096^3) using an nVidia RTX 3060 graphics card. name: Local vs Global Addressing in SVDAG
head: Global addressing, Layer-local addressing
body: This method defines two distinct schemes for interpreting node pointers within a Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG): Global Addressing, which uses a single contiguous address space for the entire data structure, and Local Addressing, which uses separate address spaces for each node layer. The primary distinction lies in scalability: Global Addressing limits the total size of the SVDAG by the pointer's address space capacity, whereas Local Addressing applies this limit per layer, allowing the total structure to exceed the pointer range provided individual layers fit within it. Input: A Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG) structure with defined node layers, child node pointers (PT) of rational lengths (8b, 16b, or 32b), and an addressing word length (8b, 16b, or 32b). Output: A mechanism for resolving node addresses during traversal or construction, determining whether the address space is global or local. The SVDAG consists of layers of nodes. Each node contains a Child Node Header Map (CHNM) and child node pointers (PT). Pointer Length (p{ptl}): The bit length of the pointer. Rational values are 8b, 16b, and 32b. Addressing Word Length: The bit length of the memory word used for addressing. Rational values are 8b, 16b, and 32b. Alignment: The CHNM is padded with reserved bits to align with the addressing word length. For example, if p{ptl} = 32b, an 8b CHNM is aligned to 32b using 24 reserved bits (r=24). 1. Determine Addressing Scheme: Select either Global Addressing or Local Addressing based on scene size and memory constraints. 2. Global Addressing Interpretation: Assign a unique address to the root node. Allocate addresses for subsequent layers sequentially in a single global address space. The pointer value represents the absolute address of the child node within this global space. The entire SVDAG must fit within the addressable space defined by the pointer length and addressing word length. 3. Local Addressing Interpretation: Identify the starting address in the global address space where the encoding of a specific node layer commences. The pointer value represents an offset from this starting address. Addressing restarts from 0 for each new layer. The limit imposed by the pointer length applies to each layer separately, not the entire structure. It is sufficient for the starting address of a layer to be within the addressable space; the entire layer does not need to fit within the pointer range if the offset logic is correctly applied. Addressable Space Capacity: The maximum size of the addressable space depends on the pointer length (p{ptl}) and the addressing word length (w{addr}). | Pointer Length (p{ptl}) | Addressing Word Length (w{addr}) | Addressable Space Capacity | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | 8b | 8b | 256 B | | 8b | 16b | 512 B | | 8b | 32b | 1024 B | | 16b | 16b | 128 KB | | 16b | 32b | 256 KB | | 32b | 32b | 16 GB | Note: The source table lists specific combinations. For 8b pointers, capacities are 256B, 512B, and 1024B for 8b, 16b, and 32b words respectively. For 16b pointers, capacities are 128KB and 256KB for 16b and 32b words. For 32b pointers, the capacity is 16GB for 32b words. Pointer Address Space Limits: 8b pointer: 2^8 = 256 addresses. 16b pointer: 2^{16} = 65,536 addresses. 32b pointer: 2^{32} = 4,294,967,296 addresses. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resolveaddress(nodelayerstartaddress, pointervalue, addressingmode): """ Resolves the absolute address of a child node. Args: nodelayerstartaddress (int): The global address where the current node layer begins. pointervalue (int): The value stored in the child node pointer (PT). addressingmode (str): 'GLOBAL' or 'LOCAL'. Returns: int: The absolute global address of the child node. """ if addressingmode == 'GLOBAL': # In global addressing, the pointer value is the absolute address return pointervalue elif addressingmode == 'LOCAL': # In local addressing, the pointer value is an offset from the layer start return nodelayerstartaddress + pointervalue else: raise ValueError("Invalid addressing mode") def checkfeasibilityglobal(totalnodes, pointercapacity): """ Checks if the entire SVDAG fits within the global address space. Args: totalnodes (int): Total number of nodes in the SVDAG. pointercapacity (int): Maximum number of addresses supported by the pointer length. Returns: bool: True if feasible, False otherwise. """ return totalnodes <= pointercapacity def checkfeasibilitylocal(maxlayernodes, pointercapacity): """ Checks if the largest node layer fits within the local address space. Args: maxlayernodes (int): The number of nodes in the largest layer. pointercapacity (int): Maximum number of addresses supported by the pointer length. Returns: bool: True if feasible, False otherwise. """ return maxlayernodes <= pointercapacity Pointer Length Selection: An 8b pointer is considered impractical even for very small 3D scenes. Word Length Correlation: The addressing word length should correlate with the pointer length. For example, 32b pointers should use 32b addressing words, and 8b pointers should use 8b addressing words. Layer Capacity: In Local Addressing, the determining factor for feasibility is whether the largest node layer fits within the local address space, not the total number of nodes. A technique where child node pointers have varying bit lengths (8b, 16b, or 32b) to optimize address space usage based on scene size and detail requirements. It builds on Variable-Length Child Node Pointers. Global Addressing: Limitation: The entire data structure is limited by the pointer's address space capacity (e.g., 4GB for 32b pointers). Use Case: Suitable for smaller scenes or when the total number of nodes is known to fit within the pointer range. Local Addressing: Advantage: The limit applies to each layer separately, allowing larger total structures if individual layers fit within the pointer range. Use Case: Suitable for large scenes where the total number of nodes exceeds the pointer capacity, but no single layer exceeds the local address space limit. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory: The addressable space capacity is determined by the pointer length and addressing word length, as detailed in the formulas section. Origin: The concepts of Global and Local Addressing in SVDAGs are described in the paper "Parameter Optimization in Sparse Voxel DAGs for Efficient Geometry Representation of Voxelized 3D Scenes" by B. Madoš et al.. History: The paper was published in 2025. Usage: These addressing schemes are used in the context of Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs (SVDAGs) for efficient geometry representation of voxelized 3D scenes. name: SVDAG with 2b Header Tags
head: 2b HT CHNM, Multi-pointer SVDAG, SVDAG Parameter Optimization: Multi-type Pointers with 2b Header Tags
body: SVDAG with 2b Header Tags is a compression optimization for Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs (SVDAG) that replaces the standard 1-bit Child Node Mask (CHNM) with 2-bit Header Tags (HT). This method allows a single internal node to distinguish between passive suboctants and three distinct types of active child pointers (PT1, PT2, PT3), enabling variable-length pointer encoding to reduce memory footprint. It differs from the standard 1b HT method by trading CHNM compactness (16b vs 8b) for the ability to use shorter pointers for spatially closer nodes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An SVO (Sparse Voxel Octree) structure representing a voxelized 3D scene, where active octants are decomposed iteratively. Output: An SVDAG structure where internal nodes use 2-bit Header Tags and variable-length child pointers. Data Structures: Internal Node (INODE): Composed of a Child Node Mask (CHNM) and an array of child node pointers (PTS). CHNM: 16 bits long (8 suboctants \times 2 bits/suboctant). PTS: Array of pointers. The number of pointers equals the count of active suboctants indicated by the CHNM. Leaf Node (LNODE): Composed of a CHNM only; it contains no pointer array. CHNM: 16 bits long. Content: Information regarding the passivity/activity of specific voxels within the leaf. Header Tag Codes: Each suboctant in the CHNM is assigned a 2-bit Header Tag (HT): 00: Passive suboctant (no child node created). 01, 10, 11: Active suboctants, mapping to Pointer Type 1 (PT1), Pointer Type 2 (PT2), and Pointer Type 3 (PT3) respectively. Pointer Types: Three pointer types are defined to optimize addressing space: PT1: Length pt{1bit} bits. PT2: Length pt{2bit} bits. PT3: Length pt{3bit} bits. Typical values cited are 8b, 16b, and 32b, though the specific mapping of code to length (e.g., is 01 always 8b?) is not explicitly detailed beyond the existence of three distinct types. Formulas: The size of an internal node I{INODE2} in bits is calculated as: I{INODE2} = r + 8 \times ht{bit} + \sum{x=1}^{3} nx \times pt{xbit} Where: r: Number of bits allocated for CHNM alignment. ht{bit}: Number of bits constituting the Header Tag (ht{bit} = 2). nx: Number of active child nodes pointed to by pointer type PTx. pt{xbit}: Number of bits forming a PTx pointer. The size of a leaf node L{LNODE2} in bits is calculated as: L{LNODE2} = r + 8 \times ht{bit} Where: r: Number of bits allocated for CHNM alignment. ht{bit}: The source text states ht{bit}=1 in the formula description but ht{bit}=2 in the definition and context of the 2b method. Given the method name "2b Header Tags", the value should be 2, but the source text contains an inconsistency. Algorithm Steps: 1. Decomposition: Iteratively decompose active octants until an active octant of 2^3 voxels is produced. 2. Leaf Creation: Form a leaf node (LNODE) for the 2^3 voxel octant. This node does not undergo further decomposition. 3. Parent Node Construction: For a parent node at layer l, decompose it into eight sub-octants. 4. Tag Assignment: For each of the eight sub-octants: If the sub-octant is passive, assign HT code 00. If the sub-octant is active, assign one of the codes 01, 10, or 11 based on the required pointer type for the child node. 5. Pointer Array Population: For each active sub-octant, create a child node (LNODE or INODE) and add a pointer to the parent's pointer array. The pointer length corresponds to the assigned HT code's type (PT1, PT2, or PT3). 6. Alignment: Apply alignment bits r to the CHNM. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildsvdag2bht(scenevoxels): """ Builds an SVDAG with 2-bit Header Tags. scenevoxels: 3D array of voxel data. Returns: Root node of the SVDAG. """ # Constants HTBITS = 2 SUBOCTANTS = 8 # Typical pointer lengths as per source context, though exact mapping of code to length # (e.g. 01->8b) is not specified in the provided text. # We assume a generic structure where pointer type determines length. POINTERLENGTHS = { 'PT1': 8, 'PT2': 16, 'PT3': 32 } # Mapping of HT codes to pointer types is not explicitly defined in the text. # We assume a generic mapping for implementation purposes. HTTOTYPE = { '00': None, # Passive '01': 'PT1', '10': 'PT2', '11': 'PT3' } def isactive(octant): """Check if any voxel in the octant is active.""" # Implementation depends on scenevoxels structure return any(octant) def createleafnode(octant): """Create a leaf node for a 2x2x2 active octant.""" # CHNM is 16 bits, all active or mixed, but no pointers chnm = 0xFFFF # Placeholder for voxel activity mask return {'type': 'LNODE', 'chnm': chnm, 'pointers': []} def createinternalnode(octant): """Create an internal node with 2b HTs.""" chnmbits = [] pointers = [] # Decompose into 8 sub-octants suboctants = decompose(octant) for i, sub in enumerate(suboctants): if isactive(sub): # Determine pointer type based on some heuristic or fixed mapping # Source does not specify how PT1/PT2/PT3 are chosen for active nodes # We assume a default mapping for the sake of completeness # In practice, this might depend on distance or layer ptrtype = 'PT1' code = '01' # Example mapping else: ptrtype = None code = '00' chnmbits.append(code) if ptrtype: childnode = createnode(sub) # Recursive call ptrlen = POINTERLENGTHS[ptrtype] # Store pointer with type info pointers.append({'type': ptrtype, 'length': ptrlen, 'target': childnode}) # Construct CHNM from bits chnm = int(''.join(chnmbits), 2) return {'type': 'INODE', 'chnm': chnm, 'pointers': pointers} def createnode(octant): if isleafsize(octant): return createleafnode(octant) else: return createinternalnode(octant) root = createnode(scenevoxels) return root def decompose(octant): """Split octant into 8 sub-octants.""" # Implementation depends on voxel grid indexing pass def isleafsize(octant): """Check if octant is 2x2x2.""" # Implementation depends on octant size tracking pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: CHNM Size Increase: Using 2b HTs increases the CHNM length from 8b to 16b, which is a disadvantage compared to the compact 8b CHNM of the 1b HT method. Source Inconsistency: The formula for Leaf Node size references ht{bit}=1 in the text description, while the method definition and context specify ht{bit}=2. Implementers should use 2 based on the method name and CHNM size. Pointer Type Mapping: The source does not specify how the three active codes (01, 10, 11) are mapped to specific pointer lengths (PT1, PT2, PT3) or the criteria for choosing a pointer type. This must be determined by the implementation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The CHNM size is fixed at 16 bits per internal node, which is double the 8 bits of the 1b HT method. However, the use of variable-length pointers (PT1, PT2, PT3) can reduce the total size if shorter pointers are used for nearby nodes. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources for this specific configuration. Strengths: Enables compression through variable-length pointers, optimizing addressing space usage. Limitations: Increased CHNM size (16b vs 8b) compared to 1b HT methods. When to use: When the scene geometry allows for significant compression via variable-length pointers that outweigh the CHNM overhead. When not to use: When CHNM compactness is critical and pointer lengths cannot be significantly reduced. Origin: The method is described in "Parameter Optimization in Sparse Voxel DAGs for Efficient Geometry Representation of Voxelized 3D Scenes" by B. Madoš et al.. History: It is part of a series of parameter optimizations for SVDAGs, including 1b HT, 2b HT, and multi-pointer configurations. Usage: Used for efficient geometry representation of voxelized 3D scenes. name: SSVDAG Ray Traversal
head: SSVDAG Rendering, SSVDAG Traversal, Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG Traversal
body: SSVDAG Ray Traversal is a shader-based ray traversal algorithm designed for Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs (SSVDAGs). It solves the problem of efficiently rendering high-resolution, compressed voxel data on the GPU by handling variable-size tagged pointers and symmetry transformations (planar reflections) during the traversal process. It sets itself apart from standard SVDAG traversal by supporting 0, 2, and 4-byte pointers and applying mirror masks to access child nodes, while distinguishing itself from sibling methods by its specific integration of Level of Detail (LOD) and beam optimization tailored to the SSVDAG memory layout. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, maximum traversal distance t{max}, SSVDAG data stored in GPU buffers, camera projection matrix (for LOD). Output: Intersection distance t or NOINTERSECTION. Data Structures: SSVDAG Buffer: Stored in GLR16UI texture buffer objects for inner nodes and leaves. For datasets exceeding buffer addressing limits (e.g., 64K^3), 3D textures are used as a fallback. Stack: Stores tuples of (nodeindex, mirrormask, level, innerheader). The innerheader is pushed to avoid refetching when moving up from a child. Tagged Pointers: Variable size (0, 2, or 4 bytes). The 3 highest bits of a non-zero pointer encode the transformation code (mirror mask). Parameters: MAXLEVEL: Maximum depth of the tree. LODTHRESHOLD: Projected voxel size threshold, typically 1 voxel/pixel. CELLSIZE: Current voxel side length, initialized to root voxel size. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set mirrormask = 0. Set level = 0. Set cellsize to the root voxel size. Compute initial projfactor from the camera perspective transformation. 2. Traversal Loop: While t < t{max}: 1. LOD Check: If projfactor < LODTHRESHOLD, return NOINTERSECTION. 2. DDA Step: Perform one DDA step to find the next node index nodeidx and local voxel coordinates voxidx. 3. Stack Optimization: If the next DDA step would cause the ray to exit the current node, do not push the current node to the stack. Instead, pop the stack if available. If the stack is empty, terminate traversal. 4. Fetch Node Data: If level < MAXLEVEL - 1: Fetch innerhdr using fetchtaggedptr(nodeidx, mirroredvoxidx). fetchtaggedptr computes the offset by summing the sizes of pointers [0, i-1] using a manually unrolled loop, as pointers are 0, 2, or 4 bytes. Extract the transformation code m from the 3 highest bits of the fetched pointer. Update mirrormask ^= m. Push (nodeidx, mirrormask, level, innerhdr) to the stack. Increment level. Update cellsize = 0.5. If level == MAXLEVEL - 1 (Leaf): Execute two DDAdown() steps to account for the larger leaf node size (4x4 vs 2x2). Increment level. Update cellsize = 0.5. Fetch leafdata. Return intersection if leaf data indicates occupancy. 3. Index Reflection: Transform the local 3D index v (child coordinates) to the mirrored voxel index mirroredvoxidx using the current mirrormask M: \text{mirrored\voxidx} = ((1, 1, 1) - 2 \cdot M) \cdot v + M \cdot (S - 1) where S=2 for inner nodes and S=4 for leaves. Use mirroredvoxidx to access occupancy bits or child pointers. 4. Backtracking: If the stack is not empty, pop (prevnodeidx, prevmirrormask, prevlevel, previnnerhdr). Restore mirrormask = prevmirrormask. Restore level = prevlevel. Update cellsize based on the restored level. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversessvdagray(rayo, rayd, tmax, ssvdagbuffer, cameramatrix, rootvoxelsize, maxlevel): mirrormask = (0, 0, 0) level = 0 cellsize = rootvoxelsize projfactor = computeprojfactor(rayo, rayd, cameramatrix, cellsize) stack = [] while True: # LOD Check if projfactor < 1.0: return NOINTERSECTION # DDA Step to find next node t, nodeidx, voxidx = ddastep(rayo, rayd, tmax, cellsize, level) if t > tmax: return NOINTERSECTION # Stack Optimization: do not push if next DDA step exits node if shouldpop(stack, level, cellsize, rayo, rayd, voxidx): if not stack: return NOINTERSECTION prevnodeidx, prevmirrormask, prevlevel, previnnerhdr = stack.pop() mirrormask = prevmirrormask level = prevlevel cellsize = rootvoxelsize (0.5 level) continue # Fetch Node Data if level < maxlevel - 1: # Inner Node mirroredvoxidx = mirrorindex(mirrormask, voxidx, S=2) # Fetch tagged pointer taggedptr, childidx = fetchtaggedptr(ssvdagbuffer, nodeidx, mirroredvoxidx) if taggedptr == 0: continue # Extract transformation code (3 highest bits) m = (taggedptr >> 29) & 0x7 mvec = ((m >> 2) & 1, (m >> 1) & 1, m & 1) mirrormask = tuple(a ^ b for a, b in zip(mirrormask, mvec)) # Push state innerhdr = fetchinnerhdr(ssvdagbuffer, nodeidx) stack.append((nodeidx, mirrormask, level, innerhdr)) level += 1 cellsize = 0.5 projfactor = computeprojfactor(rayo, rayd, cameramatrix, cellsize) else: # Leaf Node # Execute two DDAdown steps for 4x4 leaf size for in range(2): t, leafvoxidx = ddadown(rayo, rayd, cellsize, level) level += 1 cellsize = 0.5 # Fetch leaf data mirroredvoxidx = mirrorindex(mirrormask, leafvoxidx, S=4) leafdata = fetchleafdata(ssvdagbuffer, nodeidx, mirroredvoxidx) if leafdata.occupied: return t else: if not stack: return NOINTERSECTION prevnodeidx, prevmirrormask, prevlevel, previnnerhdr = stack.pop() mirrormask = prevmirrormask level = prevlevel cellsize = rootvoxelsize (0.5 level) continue def mirrorindex(M, v, S): # Component-wise application of: ((1,1,1) - 2M)v + M(S-1) return tuple((1 - 2m)vi + m(S - 1) for m, vi in zip(M, v)) def ddastep(rayo, rayd, tmax, cellsize, level): # Standard 3D DDA advancing ray by one cell boundary # Returns (t, nodeidx, voxidx) return 0.0, 0, (0, 0, 0) def ddadown(rayo, rayd, cellsize, level): # Advances ray within leaf node (4x4 grid) return 0.0, (0, 0, 0) def shouldpop(stack, level, cellsize, rayo, rayd, voxidx): # Returns True if the next DDA step would exit the current node return False def computeprojfactor(rayo, rayd, cameramatrix, cellsize): # Computes projected voxel size in pixels from camera projection return 1.0 def fetchtaggedptr(buffer, nodeidx, voxelidx): # Manually unrolled loop to sum sizes of pointers [0, voxelidx-1] offset = 0 for i in range(voxelidx): ptr = readpointer(buffer, nodeidx, i) if ptr == 0: offset += 0 elif ptr < 0x400000: offset += 2 else: offset += 4 taggedptr = readtaggedptratoffset(buffer, nodeidx, offset) childidx = taggedptr & 0x1FFFFFF return taggedptr, childidx def readpointer(buffer, nodeidx, i): # Reads raw pointer value from buffer at nodeidx, index i return 0 def readtaggedptratoffset(buffer, nodeidx, offset): # Reads tagged pointer from buffer at computed offset return 0 def fetchinnerhdr(buffer, nodeidx): # Fetches inner node header data return {} def fetchleafdata(buffer, nodeidx, voxelidx): # Fetches leaf node occupancy/data class LeafData: occupied = False return LeafData() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pointer Size Ambiguity: The variable size of pointers (0, 2, 4 bytes) requires careful offset calculation. The 0-byte pointer indicates an empty child, while 2 and 4-byte pointers indicate occupied children with different compression levels. Leaf Node Size: Leaves are 4x4, while inner nodes are 2x2. The traversal must execute two DDAdown() steps at the last level to correctly traverse the leaf. Stack Depth: The stack must store the level to correctly restore cellsize and projfactor during backtracking. Buffer Limits: For very large datasets (e.g., 64K^3), GLR16UI texture buffer objects may exceed addressing limits, requiring a fallback to 3D textures. Performance: Crytek Sponza (64K^3, 720p): ~100M primary rays/s without optimizations. With LOD, ~300M rays/s. With LOD + beam optimization, performance doubles in walkthroughs. Boeing 777 (64K^3): 80M to 300M primary rays/s depending on viewpoint. Powerplant (256K^3, 720p): 92 to 45 fps (SSVDAG) vs 106 to 52 fps (USSVDAG) vs 107 to 53 fps (SVDAG). Overhead: Reflections: 1-2% overhead compared to SVDAG. Pointer Compression: 14-16% overhead compared to SVDAG due to the complexity of variable-size pointer access. Strengths: High compression ratio, real-time rendering capability for massive scenes, GPU-friendly traversal. Limitations: Variable-size pointer access is more costly than fixed-size pointers. SSVDAG Ray Traversal was introduced by Alberto Jaspe et al. in 2017 as part of the SSVDAG (Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG) framework. It extends the original SVDAG traversal [Kämpe et al. 2013] by incorporating symmetry detection and variable-bitrate pointer compression. The method is designed for compression-domain tracing of high-resolution geometric scenes, enabling real-time rendering from GPU-resident data. It builds on the optimization techniques of Laine and Karras [Laine and Karras 2011] for level-of-detail and beam optimization.
