name: PSVDAG–SVDAG Conversion Algorithm
head: Hierarchical Data Structure conversion, PSVDAG to SVDAG conversion, PSVDAG to SVDAG transformation, Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph to Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph conversion
body: The PSVDAG–SVDAG Conversion Algorithm transforms a Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG) into a Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG). While PSVDAGs use variable-length Labels/Callers and intermittent binary encoding to minimize storage, SVDAGs use constant-length 32-bit pointers and uninterrupted binary sequences to enable efficient rendering and editing. This conversion replaces the pointerless structure with a pointer-based one, allowing for Child Subtree Merging (CSM) and random access, at the cost of increased memory usage (inflation factor 3.01x–3.70x). The algorithm processes the linearized binary representation of the PSVDAG (obtained via depth-first traversal) in a single pass, progressively generating SVDAG nodes. It performs four main tasks: 1. Extract PSVDAG internal node binary representations and transform them into compact uninterrupted sequences. 2. Transform PSVDAG Child Node Masks (CHNM) into SVDAG CHNM, converting 2-bit Header Tags (HT) to 1-bit indicators [HT]. 3. Generate child node pointers for SVDAG internal nodes, replacing missing PSVDAG pointers. 4. Replace PSVDAG Labels and Callers with SVDAG pointers using a Label Transformation Table (LTT) to allow CSM. SVDAG Internal Node Layout Each SVDAG internal node is stored as a contiguous block of bytes. The layout is: CHNM: 8 bits (1-bit [HT] for each of the 8 children). Reserved: 24 bits (for 32-bit alignment of the CHNM part). PTS: Array of pointers, size 1 to 8, each 32 bits long. The total size of an SVDAG internal node in bytes is calculated as: SVDAG{nodesize} = (ACHNC + 2) \times 4 \text{ [B]} Where ACHNC is the number of active child nodes decremented by 1 (i.e., ACHNC = \text{ActiveChildren} - 1). In bits, the size is (ACHNC + 2) \times 32. Operating Memory Structure During conversion, each node is represented in memory by a 336-bit structure node: adr: 32-bit target address in the output SVDAG. achnc: 8-bit number of active child nodes. chnm: 32-bit node CHNM (stores the 8-bit mask). pts: Array of 8 pointers, 32-bit each. ptpt: 8-bit pointer count (number of pointers actually stored in pts). An array nodes holds one node structure for each level of internal nodes. Label Transformation Table (LTT) The LTT maps PSVDAG Labels and Callers to SVDAG addresses. It stores triplets [level, SIZ, VAL] mapped to the 32-bit address adr assigned to the child node. Semi-out-of-core: LTT stored in main memory (RAM). Out-of-core: LTT stored in secondary storage (disk). maxl: Number of node levels in the PSVDAG input. Range: maxl > 0. lmax: Maximum level index, defined as maxl - 1. Leaf nodes are at level maxl - 1. Internal nodes are at levels 0 to maxl - 2. nnadr: Next Node Address. Tracks the next free 32-bit aligned address in the output SVDAG stream. Initialized to 0. level: Current processing level. Initialized to 0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. outputbuffer = [] nnadr = 0 level = 0 lmax = maxl - 1 nodes = [None] maxl LTT = {} def convertpsvdagtosvdag(inputstream, maxl): """Main entry point. inputstream: Bit stream of linearized PSVDAG.""" global nnadr, level, lmax if maxl == 1: processleafnode(inputstream) elif maxl > 1: processinternalnode(inputstream) def processleafnode(stream): """Step 2: Process a leaf node.""" global nnadr leafbits = readbits(stream, 8) writebits(outputbuffer, leafbits, 8) writebits(outputbuffer, 0, 24) # Reserved bits nnadr += 4 def processinternalnode(stream): """Step 3: Process an internal node.""" global nnadr, level, lmax level += 1 currentnode = {'adr': 0, 'achnc': 0, 'chnm': 0, 'pts': [0]8, 'ptpt': 0} nodes[level] = currentnode achncraw = readbits(stream, 3) currentnode['achnc'] = achncraw + 1 currentnode['adr'] = nnadr nnadr += (currentnode['achnc'] + 1) 4 currentnode['ptpt'] = 0 currentnode['chnm'] = 0 while currentnode['ptpt'] < currentnode['achnc']: ht = readbits(stream, 2) idx = currentnode['ptpt'] if ht == 0: # Case 0: HT '00' - Passive Child updatechmnbit(currentnode['chnm'], idx, 0) currentnode['ptpt'] += 1 # No pointer added, no recursion. elif ht == 1: # Case 1: HT '01' - Active Child / Label updatechmnbit(currentnode['chnm'], idx, 1) currentnode['pts'][idx] = nnadr currentnode['ptpt'] += 1 siz, val = readlabel(stream) # Reads variable-length [siz, val] LTT[(level, siz, val)] = nnadr if level < lmax - 2: processinternalnode(stream) elif level == lmax - 2: processleafnode(stream) elif ht == 2: # Case 2: HT '10' - Caller / Shared Child updatechmnbit(currentnode['chnm'], idx, 1) siz, val = readcaller(stream) # Reads variable-length [siz, val] adr = LTT.get((level, siz, val)) currentnode['pts'][idx] = adr currentnode['ptpt'] += 1 elif ht == 3: # Case 3: HT '11' - Active Child / Unique updatechmnbit(currentnode['chnm'], idx, 1) currentnode['pts'][idx] = nnadr currentnode['ptpt'] += 1 if level < lmax - 2: processinternalnode(stream) elif level == lmax - 2: processleafnode(stream) writeinode(currentnode) def updatechmnbit(chnm, index, value): if value: chnm |= (1 << index) else: chnm &= ~(1 << index) return chnm def readbits(stream, n): """Read n bits from stream. """ pass def writebits(buffer, value, n): """Write n bits to buffer. """ pass def readlabel(stream): """Read variable-length Label [siz, val]. """ pass def readcaller(stream): """Read variable-length Caller [siz, val]. """ pass def writeinode(node): """Write finalized internal node to output.""" writebits(outputbuffer, node['chnm'] & 0xFF, 8) writebits(outputbuffer, 0, 24) for i in range(node['achnc']): writebits(outputbuffer, node['pts'][i], 32) Intermittent vs. Uninterrupted Encoding: PSVDAG internal nodes are encoded as intermittent binary sequences (with child nodes inserted), while SVDAG nodes are uninterrupted. The algorithm must compact these sequences during extraction. HT Mapping: PSVDAG HT '00' becomes SVDAG [HT] '0'. PSVDAG HT '01', '10', '11' become SVDAG [HT] '1'. Omitted HTs in PSVDAG are inserted as [HT] '0' in SVDAG. Unique Child Pointer: For HT '11' (unique child), the address nnadr is stored in the node but not kept in operating memory after generation, as it is referenced only once. Label vs. Caller: For HT '01' (Label), nnadr is stored in both the SVDAG pointer and the LTT. For HT '10' (Caller), the address is retrieved from the LTT. ACHNC Definition: ACHNC is the number of active child nodes decremented by 1. This value determines the size of the SVDAG node. Time Complexity: The algorithm processes the PSVDAG in a single pass. Performance depends on whether the LTT is in RAM (semi-out-of-core) or disk (out-of-core). Memory Complexity: The algorithm uses a small amount of memory for the nodes array (one per level) and the LTT. The LTT size varies by scene complexity. Measured Performance: Angel Lucy (128³): SOoC 0.28s (112 KB/s), OoC 0.30s (106 KB/s). Skull (512³): SOoC 0.81s (124 KB/s), OoC 0.85s (118 KB/s). Porsche (512³): SOoC 0.44s (129 KB/s), OoC 0.47s (129 KB/s). Scaling: Higher voxelization resolutions lead to smaller inflation rates (memory increase). Strengths: Enables CSM and random access; semi-out-of-core version is faster due to higher data throughput. Limitations: SVDAG size is larger than PSVDAG (inflation 3.01x–3.70x). The PSVDAG–SVDAG Conversion Algorithm was proposed to bridge the gap between the space-efficient but hard-to-access PSVDAG structure and the rendering-friendly SVDAG structure. The algorithm allows the use of PSVDAG for storage and SVDAG for rendering, converting on the fly or as a preprocessing step. It is used in volume rendering applications where sparse voxel grids are processed. Transforming Hierarchical Data Structures – a PSVDAG–SVDAG Conversion Algorithm, https://doi.org/10.12700/aph.18.8.2021.8.3, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Voxel Attribute Decoupling
head: DAG-based attribute decoupling
body: Voxel Attribute Decoupling is a technique that separates voxel attributes (such as color or normals) from the geometric topology of a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to enable independent, specialized compression of each component. Unlike standard SVOs or naive colored DAGs that store attributes redundantly with every node, this method achieves significant memory reduction by storing attributes in a dense array and encoding geometric offsets within child pointers, allowing subtrees with identical topology to be merged into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Inputs: An initial Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) with voxel attributes. Outputs: A DAG-based geometric structure and a dense attribute array. Data Structures: 1. DAG Nodes: Each node stores child pointers. Each child pointer contains an offset value instead of a direct index. 2. Attribute Array: A dense 1D array storing voxel attributes in depth-first order. Steps: 1. Index Assignment: Virtually assign unique indices to all nodes in the initial SVO using a depth-first traversal order. 2. Offset Calculation: For every child pointer in the SVO, calculate an offset equal to the difference between the child's index and the parent's index associated with that pointer. \text{offset} = \text{index}{\text{child}} - \text{index}{\text{parent}} 3. Storage: Store these calculated offsets together with each child pointer in the DAG structure. 4. Attribute Extraction: Extract all node attributes from the SVO and store them in a dense attribute array, maintaining the same depth-first order used for index assignment. 5. Traversal and Retrieval: During rendering or traversal, reconstruct a node's original index by summing the offsets along the path from the root to that node. Use this reconstructed index to retrieve the corresponding attribute from the dense attribute array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead: The mapping introduces storage overhead in the form of an additional offset for every child pointer. Compression: While offsets add overhead, they can be compressed very efficiently using entropy-based encoding, which amortizes the additional storage cost. DAG Merging: This method allows subtrees with identical topology to be merged into a DAG because depth-first indexing automatically results in identical offsets for geometrically identical subtrees. Decoupled SVO Compression is a memory optimization technique for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) that separates the geometric topology from voxel attributes (such as color, normals, or reflectance) to allow independent, specialized compression of each component. Unlike standard SVOs or naive colored DAGs that store attributes redundantly with every node, this method achieves significant memory reduction by compressing the sparse geometry structure and applying lossless palette-based compression to the decoupled attribute array, outperforming existing methods like PSVOs, ESVOs, and CDAGs in both memory footprint and visual quality. A technique to decouple attributes (like color) from the DAG geometry to allow independent compression, using a leaf counter to map voxel indices to attribute data without altering DAG node uniqueness. Definition: Uses a leaf counter to determine the position of a node's attributes within the dense attribute array based on the number of leaf nodes in preceding siblings. Steps: 1. For DAG resolutions larger than 1024^3, store an offset for the upper levels into a separate 32-bit counter array. 2. Use the leaf counter to calculate the attribute index by summing the leaf counts of preceding child nodes during traversal. Layout: The DAG node structure is stored in a 32-bit array consisting of an 8-bit child mask and 24-bit padding. The 24-bit padding is repurposed as the leaf counter. Parameters: Leaf counter size is 24 bits, which is sufficient for DAG resolutions up to 1024^3. Pitfalls: Using per-node counters requires reading preceding child counters for each node, resulting in extra memory reads compared to per-pointer counters. Comparison: Per-pointer counter lookups are 1.2x-1.9x faster than per-node counter lookups. However, per-node counters have negligible memory overhead (<0.1%) compared to per-pointer counters, which result in a 1.5x-1.8x larger DAG. Memory: Introduces overhead for offsets in child pointers. Per-pointer counters increase DAG size by 1.5x-1.8x, while per-node counters add <0.1% overhead. Performance: Per-pointer counter lookups are 1.2x-1.9x faster than per-node counter lookups due to reduced memory reads. Compression: Offsets can be compressed efficiently using entropy-based encoding. Attributes can be compressed using palette-based methods after decoupling. Scalability: Per-node counters require a separate 32-bit counter array for resolutions larger than 1024^3, though the overhead remains minimal. The concept of decoupling attributes from geometry in voxel structures was introduced to address the inefficiency of storing redundant attributes in standard SVOs and the limitations of naive DAG compression. The method builds on the principles of space-filling curves, such as the Morton curve, which allow for efficient mapping between 1D arrays and N-dimensional voxel grids. The specific technique of using depth-first indexing to generate identical offsets for identical subtrees enables the re-application of DAG compression to decoupled structures. name: Decoupled SVO Compression
head: Palette Compression for SVOs, SVO Compression Scheme
body: Decoupled SVO Compression is a memory optimization technique for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) that separates the geometric topology from voxel attributes (such as color, normals, or reflectance) to allow independent, specialized compression of each component. Unlike standard SVOs or naive colored DAGs that store attributes redundantly with every node, this method achieves significant memory reduction by compressing the sparse geometry structure and applying lossless palette-based compression to the decoupled attribute array, outperforming existing methods like PSVOs, ESVOs, and CDAGs in both memory footprint and visual quality. Input: A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) or Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representing a voxel scene, where each leaf or internal node may possess associated attributes (e.g., RGB color, surface normals). Output: A compressed data structure consisting of a compacted geometry array and a separate, compressed attribute array, along with metadata required for traversal and index reconstruction. The topology is stored in a linearized array to minimize overhead. Each node in the geometry array contains: Child Pointers: Compressed using implicit first-child offsets and per-level byte-precise offset compression. Childmasks: Reduced from the standard 24-bit padding to 8-bit masks, indicating the presence of children. Layout: The geometry array contains nodes with fields for the compressed child pointer offset, the 8-bit childmask, and an index pointing to the attribute array if the node is a leaf or contains attributes. Attributes are decoupled from the geometry and stored in a dense array. Attribute Array: A linear array of attribute values (e.g., 24-bit colors, 32-bit normals). Indexing: Each geometry node that has an attribute stores an index into this attribute array. In the context of the parent method Voxel Attribute Decoupling, this index is often stored as a child index minus parent index offset, but the core compression here focuses on the attribute array itself. 1. Decoupling: Traverse the original SVO/DAG and separate the geometric topology (child pointers, masks) from the voxel attributes (colors, normals). Store attributes in a linear array during traversal to exploit spatial coherence. 2. Topology Compression: Apply the following compression techniques to the geometry array: Implicit First Child Offset: Store the offset to the first child implicitly rather than explicitly for every node. Per-Level Byte-Precise Offset Compression: Compress the offsets for child pointers on a per-level basis. Pointer Compression: Further compress the pointer values. 8-bit Childmasks: Replace 24-bit padding masks with 8-bit masks. Pointer Entropy Encoding: Apply entropy encoding to the compressed pointer data. 3. Attribute Compression: Compress the decoupled attribute array using a lossless palette compression scheme: Quantization: Quantize attribute values (e.g., 12-bit or 24-bit colors, 32-bit normals) to a manageable precision. Palette Construction: Identify unique attribute values within localized blocks of the attribute array. Indexing: Replace attribute values with indices pointing to a global or local palette of unique values. 4. Storage Assembly: Combine the compressed geometry array and the compressed attribute array (palette + indices) into the final data structure. Compression Rate: Calculated as the ratio of the compressed size to the original uncompressed SVO size. \text{Compression Rate} = \frac{\text{Compressed Size}}{\text{Original SVO Size}} \times 100\% Memory Footprint: The total memory is the sum of geometry size and attribute size. \text{Total Size} = \text{Geometry Size} + \text{Attribute Size} Typical Parameters: Color Precision: 12-bit colors are used for the main comparison in Table 4 and Figure 6. For attribute precision in ESVO comparison, 24-bit colors and 32-bit ONV normals are used for palette compression to ensure better quality than ESVO's lossy schemes. SVO Levels: Supports up to 17 levels (128K^3 resolution). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decoupledsvocompression(svotree): """ Compresses an SVO by decoupling geometry and attributes. Returns: compressedgeometrybytes, compressedattributesbytes """ geometrynodes = [] attributelist = [] # Step 1: Decoupling via traversal queue = [svotree.root] while queue: node = queue.pop(0) # Extract geometry components childmask = node.childmask children = node.children # Store geometry info geometrynodes.append({ 'childmask': childmask, 'children': children, 'hasattribute': node.hasattribute, 'attributevalue': node.attributevalue if node.hasattribute else None }) # Extract attribute if present if node.hasattribute: # Quantize attribute if necessary (e.g., to 12-bit or 24-bit) quantizedattr = quantize(node.attributevalue) attributelist.append(quantizedattr) # Add children to queue for traversal for child in children: if child is not None: queue.append(child) # Step 2: Topology Compression # Apply implicit offsets, per-level compression, 8-bit masks, and entropy encoding # Note: Exact entropy coding and offset packing algorithms are not specified in the sources. compressedgeometry = packtopology(geometrynodes) # Step 3: Attribute Compression # Use palette compression compressedattributes = compressattributespalette(attributelist) return compressedgeometry, compressedattributes def quantize(value, bits=12): """ Quantizes a value to a specified bit depth. """ # Implementation depends on the data type (color, normal) # Standard quantization logic return int(value (2bits - 1)) def packtopology(geometrynodes): """ Compresses the geometry nodes using specific techniques. """ # 1. Implicit first child offset # 2. Per-level byte-precise offset compression # 3. Pointer compression # 4. 8-bit childmasks # 5. Pointer entropy encoding # The sources do not specify the exact bit-packing or entropy coder implementation. # This function returns the byte stream of the compressed geometry. return b"" def compressattributespalette(attributelist): """ Compresses attributes using a lossless palette approach. """ # 1. Identify unique values (palette) # 2. Map each attribute to an index in the palette # 3. Compress the palette and the indices # The sources do not specify the exact palette construction or index encoding algorithm. palette = list(dict.fromkeys(attributelist)) indices = [palette.index(attr) for attr in attributelist] return palette, indices ESVO Compatibility: ESVO implementations require contour data to avoid cutting off attributes during traversal. Without contours, quality degrades significantly. The decoupled method avoids this by storing attributes separately and using palette compression, which does not rely on contour-based traversal cuts. Dense Data: While designed for sparse data, the method can compress dense data. For example, a dense Christmas tree dataset achieved a lossless compression rate of 38.6% compared to the original input file. When applying a simple filtering to remove scanning noise in the air, additional sparsity benefits achieve rates below 10%. Precision: Using lower precision (12-bit) for colors reduces memory further but may impact visual quality. Higher precision (24-bit colors, 32-bit normals) ensures better quality but increases attribute size. A variable-length compression scheme for the attribute array that reduces memory footprint by exploiting spatial coherence through global material arrays and local palettes. It differs from fixed-width indexing by allowing the bit-width of indices to adapt to the number of unique attributes within localized blocks, achieving higher compression ratios for scenes with large homogeneous regions. A method to compress arbitrary voxel data (colors, normals, reflectance) by decoupling geometry topology from voxel attributes. It uses a DAG to encode the topology (geometry) and a palette-based compression scheme for the extracted attributes, allowing efficient GPU storage and real-time raytracing. It outperforms Moxel DAGs by requiring less memory and supporting multi-resolution level-of-detail rendering, whereas Moxel DAGs store empty leaf counts and use two running sums that become prohibitive at quadrillion-scale resolutions. Memory Footprint: The method significantly reduces memory usage compared to standard SVOs, PSVOs, ESVOs, and CDAGs. Citadel: 0.65 bytes/voxel (22% compression rate vs standard SVO). City: 0.59 bytes/voxel (21% compression rate). San Miguel: 0.24 bytes/voxel (8.7% compression rate). Arena: 0.33 bytes/voxel (11% compression rate). (Note: ESVO failed to load this scene). Performance: The method supports real-time rendering of colored SVOs with up to 17 levels (128K^3 resolution) on GPU. It enables applications such as hard shadows, reflections (secondary rays), and color bleeding (single-bounce global illumination) with interactive rates (e.g., 8 secondary rays per pixel). Strengths: Outperforms state-of-the-art SVO compression methods in memory footprint. Lossless attribute compression ensures higher quality than lossy schemes like ESVO's DXT1 compression. Flexible attribute handling allows for various data types (colors, normals). Limitations: Requires separate compression pipelines for geometry and attributes, increasing implementation complexity. Performance on very dense datasets may vary, though it still achieves good compression rates (e.g., 38.6% for dense tree data). The method was introduced in the paper "Geometry and Attribute Compression for Voxel Scenes". It builds upon the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representation of SVOs [KSA13] and addresses the limitations of existing compression techniques like PSVOs [SK06] and ESVOs [LK10]. The approach was developed to enable real-time rendering of large, detailed voxel scenes with full attribute data, such as colors and normals, on GPU hardware. It is used in applications requiring high-fidelity voxel rendering, including global illumination and reflection effects. Geometry and Attribute Compression for Voxel Scenes, https://timothykol.com/pub/compression.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Palette Compression
head: Block-based palette compression, Variable-length palette compression
body: Palette compression is a lossless compression scheme for the attribute array in decoupled Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) that reduces memory footprint by exploiting spatial coherence and attribute redundancy. It replaces full attribute storage with variable-length indices into local palettes, which in turn point to a global material array. Unlike fixed-width indexing, this method adapts the bit-width per block based on the number of unique attributes present, achieving higher compression ratios for homogeneous regions while maintaining fast random access via a block directory. Inputs: An uncompressed attribute array A of size \Lambda, where \Lambda equals the total voxel count in the original SVO. Outputs: An array of blocks \{B0, \dots, B{\gamma-1}\}, an array of palettes \{P0, \dots, P{\rho-1}\}, and a block directory. Data Structures: 1. Global Material Array (M): An array of size \lambda storing all unique attributes found in A. 2. Indexed Attribute Array (A^e): An array of size \Lambda where each entry mi is an index into M. 3. Block (B): A contiguous sub-segment of A^e. 4. Palette (P): An array of unique indices into M required to retrieve all attributes in a specific block. The maximum size of P is 2^\omega, where \omega is the bit-width, but it only stores the unique indices actually present in the block. 5. Block Directory: An array of entries ordered by the starting node index of each block to enable binary search. Algorithm Steps: 1. Global Indexing: Construct M containing all \lambda unique attributes from A. Replace A with A^e, where each mi \in [0, \lambda-1]. 2. Block Partitioning (Greedy Heuristic): Partition A^e into blocks using two phases. Phase 1 (Large Homogeneous Blocks): Iterate \omega from 0 to 3. Find the largest contiguous block in the current unassigned range that contains 2^\omega unique indices. If \text{MEMORY}(B, \omega) < (l - k + 1) \cdot (\omega + 1), create a palette for this block, replace the indices with local palette indices, and recursively process the remaining unassigned data on both sides of the block. If the criterion fails, increment \omega. Terminate Phase 1 when \omega \ge 4. Phase 2 (Remaining Data): For the remaining unassigned data, consider blocks starting at the current position for \omega \in \{0, \dots, 8\}. Select the block that minimizes the memory per entry metric S\omega = \text{MEMORY}(B\omega, \omega) / (k\omega - i + 1). Create a palette, replace indices, and recursively process the remainder. 3. Palette Management: Palettes are stored in a global array \{P0, \dots, P{\rho-1}\} and can be shared by multiple blocks. 4. Directory Construction: Create the block directory ordered by the starting node index to enable binary search during decoding. Memory Formula: The memory cost for a block B spanning indices mi to mj with bit-width \omega is: \text{MEMORY}(\{mi, \dots, mj\}, \omega) = (j - i + 1) \cdot \omega + 2^\omega \cdot \lceil \log2 \lambda \rceil + \text{size}(\text{directory entry}) Where: (j - i + 1) \cdot \omega: Bits for the block indices. 2^\omega \cdot \lceil \log2 \lambda \rceil: Bits for the palette entries (each entry is an index into M). \text{size}(\text{directory entry}): Overhead for the directory record. startidx + 1 palettebits = (1 << omega) math.ceil(math.log2(lambdaval)) return numentries omega + palettebits + DIRENTRYSIZE def createpalette(blockindices): uniqueindices = sorted(list(set(blockindices))) key = tuple(uniqueindices) if key in palettemap: return palettemap[key] newpaletteidx = len(palettes) palettes.append(uniqueindices) palettemap[key] = newpaletteidx return newpaletteidx def findlargeblocks(start, end): if start > end: return omega = 0 while omega < 4: maxunique = 1 << omega bestblock = None bestlen = 0 i = start while i <= end: j = i currentunique = set() while j <= end and len(currentunique) < maxunique: currentunique.add(Ae[j]) j += 1 currentlen = j - k + 1) (omega + 1) costwithpalette = memorycost(bstart, bend, omega) costwithoutpalette = (bend - bstart + 1) (omega + 1) if costwithpalette < costwithoutpalette: paletteidx = createpalette(bindices) blocks.append((bstart, bend, paletteidx, omega)) for k in range(bstart, bend + 1): val = Ae[k] localidx = palettes[paletteidx].index(val) Ae[k] = localidx findlargeblocks(start, bstart - 1) directory = [] for bstart, bend, pidx, omega in blocks: directory.append({'start': bstart, 'paletteid': pidx, 'omega': omega, 'length': bend - bstart + 1}) directory.sort(key=lambda x: x['start']) return blocks, palettes, directory Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Combinatorial Complexity: Finding the optimal block partitioning is a hard combinatorial problem, so a greedy heuristic is used instead. Phase 1 Infeasibility: Phase 1 becomes computationally infeasible for large \omega, so it terminates when \omega \ge 4 (16 unique indices). Precision: The memory formula assumes fixed sizes for directory entries and material indices. Variations in \lambda affect \lceil \log2 \lambda \rceil. A variant for discrete voxel data (e.g., Minecraft) that uses BlockStorage and variable-bit-length indices. It balances memory usage by using fewer bits for low-entropy regions and more for high-entropy regions, similar to GIF palettes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Allows fast random access because the block directory supports binary search, and palettes are small enough to fit in cache. Strengths: High compression ratio for scenes with spatially coherent attributes (e.g., large areas of same material). Decouples geometry from attributes. Limitations: Compression is lossless but computationally intensive during encoding. Random access requires two lookups (directory then palette). name: Palette-based compression for chunked discrete voxel data
head: BlockStorage, Minecraft 1.13 compression
body: Palette-based compression for chunked discrete voxel data is a lossless compression technique for discrete voxel data (e.g., Minecraft blocks) that separates block groups/chunks from their actual storage using a structure called BlockStorage. It uses a palette of block types/states and variable-bit-length indices pointing to that palette, similar to GIF color palettes. It achieves memory reduction where regions with few block types (e.g., air/stone) use only 1-2 bits per block, while high-entropy regions (forests, structures) use more bits, balanced by the palette size. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A chunk of discrete voxel data of size N = \text{CHUNK\SIZE}^3. Output: A compressed representation consisting of a bit buffer of indices and a palette array. Data Structures: 1. Chunk: Contains a static constant CHUNKSIZE and a BlockStorage instance initialized with size \text{CHUNK\SIZE}^3. Methods setBlock(x,y,z,type) and getBlock(x,y,z) convert coordinates to an index and delegate to storage. 2. BlockStorage: size (int): Total number of blocks in the chunk (N). data (BitBuffer): A buffer holding variable-bit-length indices. palette (PaletteEntry[]): Array of palette entries. paletteCount (int): Number of active entries in the palette. indicesLength (int): Bit width of each index in the BitBuffer. Starts at 1. Grows exponentially (powers of two) when palette fills. Shrinks when palette is less than half full. 3. PaletteEntry: refcount (int): Default 0. Tracks usage frequency. type (BlockType): The actual block type/state data. Recommended to be implemented as a struct/value-type. 4. BitBuffer: Represents a memory region (array of bytes/ints/longs) allowing arbitrary bit-range access. Methods: set(int bitIndex, int bitLength, int bits) and get(int bitIndex, int bitLength). Initialization: BlockStorage is initialized with indicesLength=1, paletteCount=0, palette size 2^1, and data size size \times 1 bits. Algorithm Steps: 1. Reading a Block (getBlock): 1. Read palette index from data at index indicesLength with length indicesLength. 2. Return palette[paletteIndex].type. 2. Writing a Block (setBlock): 1. Read current palette index from data at index indicesLength with length indicesLength. 2. Get current PaletteEntry from palette[paletteIndex]. 3. Decrement current entry's refcount. 4. Search palette for existing entry matching type. 5. If found: Update data at index indicesLength with that index, length indicesLength. Increment its refcount. Return. 6. If not found and current entry refcount is 0: Overwrite current entry with type. Set refcount to 1. Return. 7. If not found and current refcount > 0: Call newPaletteEntry() to get a free slot (growing if necessary). Create new PaletteEntry with refcount 1 and type. Set data at index indicesLength to new entry index, length indicesLength. Increment paletteCount. 3. Finding a New Palette Entry (newPaletteEntry): 1. Find first free entry in palette (entry is null or refcount is 0). 2. If found, return its index. 3. If not found, call growPalette(). 4. Recursively call newPaletteEntry() to find the new free slot. 4. Growing the Palette (growPalette): 1. Decode all indices from current data into an int array indices of size size. 2. Double indicesLength (indicesLength << 1). 3. Create new palette array of size 2^{\text{indicesLength}}. 4. Copy existing palette entries to new array. 5. Allocate new BitBuffer of size size indicesLength bits. 6. Encode all indices from indices array into new data buffer. 5. Fitting/Shrinking the Palette (fitPalette): 1. Iterate palette, setting entries with refcount 0 to null and decrementing paletteCount. 2. If paletteCount is not less than half of its closest power of two, return (do not shrink). 3. Decode all indices from current data into indices. 4. Halve indicesLength (indicesLength >> 1). 5. Create new palette array of size 2^{\text{indicesLength}}. 6. Iterate old palette, copying non-null entries to new palette at paletteCounter. 7. For each moved entry, re-encode indices: if old index matches current old palette index, update indices[di] to paletteCounter and increment fc (found count) until fc equals entry's refcount. 8. Allocate new BitBuffer of size size indicesLength bits. 9. Encode all indices from indices array into new data buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Chunk: CHUNKSIZE = 32 # Example value def init(self): self.storage = BlockStorage(self.CHUNKSIZE 3) def setblock(self, x, y, z, blocktype): index = self.xyztoindex(x, y, z) self.storage.setblock(index, blocktype) def getblock(self, x, y, z): index = self.xyztoindex(x, y, z) return self.storage.getblock(index) def xyztoindex(self, x, y, z): # Standard 3D-to-1D mapping for row-major layout size = self.CHUNKSIZE return x + y size + z size size class BlockStorage: def init(self, size): self.size = size self.indiceslength = 1 self.palettecount = 0 self.palette = [None] (2 self.indiceslength) self.data = BitBuffer(self.size self.indiceslength) def setblock(self, index, blocktype): paletteindex = self.data.get(index self.indiceslength, self.indiceslength) currententry = self.palette[paletteindex] # Whatever block is there will cease to exist in but a moment... currententry.refcount -= 1 # Is the block-type already in the palette? replace = -1 for i, entry in enumerate(self.palette): if entry is not None and entry.type == blocktype: replace = i break if replace != -1: # YES: Use the existing palette entry. self.data.set(index self.indiceslength, self.indiceslength, replace) self.palette[replace].refcount += 1 return # If not found and current refcount is 0, overwrite current entry if currententry.refcount == 0: currententry.type = blocktype currententry.refcount = 1 return # A new palette entry is needed! newentryindex = self.newpaletteentry() self.palette[newentryindex] = PaletteEntry(refcount=1, type=blocktype) self.data.set(index self.indiceslength, self.indiceslength, newentryindex) self.palettecount += 1 def getblock(self, index): paletteindex = self.data.get(index self.indiceslength, self.indiceslength) return self.palette[paletteindex].type def newpaletteentry(self): firstfree = -1 for i, entry in enumerate(self.palette): if entry is None or entry.refcount == 0: firstfree = i break if firstfree != -1: return firstfree # No free entry? Grow the palette, and thus the BitBuffer self.growpalette() # Just try again now! return self.newpaletteentry() def growpalette(self): # Decode the indices indices = [] for i in range(self.size): indices.append(self.data.get(i self.indiceslength, self.indiceslength)) # Create new palette, doubling it in size self.indiceslength = self.indiceslength << 1 newpalette = [None] (2 self.indiceslength) # We gotta compress the palette entries! palettecounter = 0 for pi in range(len(self.palette)): entry = self.palette[pi] if entry is not None: newpalette[palettecounter] = entry # Re-encode the indices (find and replace; with limit) fc = 0 for di in range(len(indices)): if fc < entry.refcount and indices[di] == pi: indices[di] = palettecounter fc += 1 palettecounter += 1 self.palette = newpalette # Allocate new BitBuffer self.data = BitBuffer(self.size self.indiceslength) # Encode the indices for i in range(len(indices)): self.data.set(i self.indiceslength, self.indiceslength, indices[i]) def fitpalette(self): # Iterate palette, setting entries with refcount 0 to null and decrementing paletteCount newpalettecount = 0 for i, entry in enumerate(self.palette): if entry is None or entry.refcount == 0: self.palette[i] = None else: newpalettecount += 1 self.palettecount = newpalettecount # If paletteCount is not less than half of its closest power of two, return (do not shrink) if self.palettecount >= (2 (self.indiceslength - 1)): return # Decode all indices from current data into indices indices = [] for i in range(self.size): indices.append(self.data.get(i self.indiceslength, self.indiceslength)) # Halve indicesLength self.indiceslength = self.indiceslength >> 1 # Create new palette array newpalette = [None] (2 self.indiceslength) # Iterate old palette, copying non-null entries to new palette at paletteCounter palettecounter = 0 for pi in range(len(self.palette)): entry = self.palette[pi] if entry is not None: newpalette[palettecounter] = entry # Re-encode the indices fc = 0 for di in range(len(indices)): if fc < entry.refcount and indices[di] == pi: indices[di] = palettecounter fc += 1 palettecounter += 1 self.palette = newpalette # Allocate new BitBuffer self.data = BitBuffer(self.size self.indiceslength) # Encode all indices from indices array into new data buffer for i in range(len(indices)): self.data.set(i self.indiceslength, self.indiceslength, indices[i]) class PaletteEntry: def init(self, refcount=0, type=None): self.refcount = refcount self.type = type class BitBuffer: def init(self, sizeinbits): # Standard bit buffer implementation self.size = sizeinbits self.buffer = [0] ((sizeinbits + 31) // 32) def get(self, bitindex, bitlength): # Extract bitlength bits starting at bitindex val = 0 for i in range(bitlength): wordidx = (bitindex + i) // 32 bitoffset = (bitindex + i) % 32 val |= ((self.buffer[wordidx] >> bitoffset) & 1) << i return val def set(self, bitindex, bitlength, bits): # Set bitlength bits starting at bitindex to value bits for i in range(bitlength): wordidx = (bitindex + i) // 32 bitoffset = (bitindex + i) % 32 mask = 1 << bitoffset if (bits >> i) & 1: self.buffer[wordidx] |= mask else: self.buffer[wordidx] &= ~mask Parameters: indicesLength: The bit width of each index in the BitBuffer. Starts at 1. Grows exponentially (powers of two) when palette fills. Shrinks when palette is less than half full. CHUNKSIZE: The dimension of the chunk. Recommended limit is 32^3 or 64^3. Larger chunks reduce performance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Using a Dictionary/HashMap for the palette is discouraged. Linear search over a small array of structs is faster than dictionary index calculation. Delta-compression is pointless because block types fit the bit-length of indices, and it would make reading blocks O(n) in the worst case. Chunk size must be limited. Too large chunks reduce performance and increase memory usage worse than plain arrays. Time Complexity: Reading blocks (getBlock) is O(1) time. Writing blocks (setBlock) involves linear search through the palette (O(P) where P is palette size) to find existing types or free slots. Palette growth/shrinkage involves O(N) bit operations where N is chunk size. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory footprint for low-entropy regions (air/stone) to 1-2 bits per block, while supporting thousands of block types. Strengths: Massively reduces memory footprint of blocks as a whole. A single block ideally takes up one single bit of memory. The common case is three to four bits. This leads to less RAM usage and faster transmission of block groups (chunks) across network connections. Supports practically infinite block types & states as long as not every single block in a block group is completely different from one another. Limitations: Writing blocks is more expensive than reading due to palette management. Performance degrades if chunk size is too large. When to use: When discrete voxel data has high spatial coherence (large areas of identical block types) and a need for lossless compression with variable block types. When not to use: When block types are completely random (high entropy) or when chunk sizes are very large. Origin: Implemented in Minecraft 1.13 for lossless compression of voxel/block data. History: Released with Minecraft 1.13 by Mojang. Usage: Used in Minecraft for storing chunk data. Palette-based compression for chunked discrete voxel data, https://www.longor.net/articles/voxel-palette-compression-reddit, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Decoupled DAG with Palette Compression
head: Decoupled DAG, Geometry and Attribute Compression for Voxel Scenes
body: Decoupled DAG with Palette Compression is a method for compressing arbitrary voxel data (colors, normals, reflectance) by separating geometry topology from voxel attributes. It uses a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to encode the topology and a palette-based compression scheme for the extracted attributes, allowing efficient GPU storage and real-time raytracing. It sets itself apart from standard DAGs, which are restricted to single-bit geometry information, and from Moxel DAGs, which require more memory for indices due to large empty leaf counts and lack multi-resolution support. Inputs: A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) containing voxel attributes (e.g., colors, normals). Outputs: A compressed DAG structure for geometry and a compressed attribute array. Data Structures: 1. DAG Node: Contains pointers to children. Unlike an SVO, pointers are not grouped consecutively in memory. The node stores an offset or index to map to the attribute array. 2. Dense Attribute Array: A linear array storing the extracted attributes for all leaf nodes in the order they appear during traversal. 3. Palette: A smaller array of unique attribute values used to replace repeated attributes in the dense array. Steps: 1. Construct DAG Topology: Start with the leaves at the lowest level of the input SVO. Compare subtrees in a greedy bottom-up fashion. If two subtrees are identical in geometry (topology), merge them by changing parent pointers to reference a single common subtree. This reduces the node count significantly, especially at low levels where the number of unique combinations is small (e.g., max 256 nodes at the second-lowest level for 8-child nodes). 2. Decouple Attributes: Extract voxel attributes from the SVO/DAG structure. Store these attributes in a dense attribute array. Store offsets or indices in the DAG node pointers to map each node to its position in the attribute array. This decoupling allows the geometry to be merged even if attributes differ, as attributes are no longer tied to the topology during the merging process. 3. Compress Attribute Array: Apply palette-based compression to the dense attribute array. Exploit spatial coherence where large blocks contain similar attributes. Replace sequences of similar attributes with indices into a local palette. Quantize attributes beforehand to improve compression performance, trading quality for memory savings. 4. Render via DAG Traversal: During raytracing, traverse the DAG. Use the accumulated offsets/indices in the node pointers to retrieve the correct attribute from the compressed attribute array. Decompress the attribute using the palette if necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class DAGNode: def init(self, isleaf=False, attrindex=-1): self.isleaf = isleaf self.attrindex = attrindex # Offset/index into the dense attribute array self.children = [None] 8 # Pointers to 8 children (standard octree layout) def constructdag(svoleaves): """Construct DAG topology bottom-up by merging identical subtrees.""" currentlevel = svoleaves while len(currentlevel) > 1: seen = {} nextlevel = [] for node in currentlevel: # Structural signature: leaf flag + tuple of child IDs sig = (node.isleaf, tuple(id(c) if c else -1 for c in node.children)) if sig in seen: # Merge: reuse the canonical node nextlevel.append(seen[sig]) else: seen[sig] = node nextlevel.append(node) currentlevel = nextlevel return currentlevel[0] if currentlevel else None def decoupleandcompress(dagroot): """Extract attributes to a dense array, store offsets in DAG nodes, and apply palette compression.""" attrarray = [] stack = [dagroot] while stack: node = stack.pop() if node.isleaf: idx = len(attrarray) node.attrindex = idx # Store offset directly in the node pointer attrarray.append(node.originalattribute) else: for child in node.children: if child: stack.append(child) # Palette-based compression exploiting spatial coherence palette = [] palettemap = {} compressedindices = [] for attr in attrarray: if attr not in palettemap: palettemap[attr] = len(palette) palette.append(attr) compressedindices.append(palettemap[attr]) return dagroot, attrarray, palette, compressedindices def raytracedag(dagroot, origin, direction, cellsize, palette, compressedindices): """Traverse DAG along a ray, using accumulated offsets in node pointers to retrieve attributes.""" x, y, z = origin dx, dy, dz = direction stepx = 1 if dx > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if dy > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if dz > 0 else -1 # Initialize DDA parameters tmaxx = (stepx 0.5 - x) / dx if dx != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = (stepy 0.5 - y) / dy if dy != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = (stepz 0.5 - z) / dz if dz != 0 else float('inf') tdeltax = abs(cellsize / dx) if dx != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = abs(cellsize / dy) if dy != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = abs(cellsize / dz) if dz != 0 else float('inf') node = dagroot while node and not node.isleaf: # Determine child index based on current cell coordinates relative to node bounding box cx = int((x - 0.5) / cellsize) % 8 cy = int((y - 0.5) / cellsize) % 8 cz = int((z - 0.5) / cellsize) % 8 childidx = (cx << 2) | (cy << 1) | cz if 0 <= childidx < 8 and node.children[childidx] is not None: node = node.children[childidx] # Advance ray to next cell boundary if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: x += stepx cellsize tmaxx += tdeltax else: z += stepz cellsize tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: y += stepy cellsize tmaxy += tdeltay else: z += stepz cellsize tmaxz += tdeltaz else: break # Empty space or invalid pointer if node and node.isleaf: idx = node.attrindex attridx = compressedindices[idx] return palette[attridx] return None Parameters: Resolution: Supports up to 17 hierarchical levels, corresponding to a 128K^3 voxel resolution (2.25 quadrillion voxels). Memory Usage: For a 128K^3 scene with 18.4 billion colored nodes, the compressed representation requires 7.63 GB of GPU memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Merging Failure: Merging subtrees fails to compress sufficiently when attributes are tightly linked to topology because adding voxel data reduces the probability of equal subtrees. The decoupling scheme solves this by separating geometry and attributes. Precision: Quantization of attributes can lead to quality loss. The trade-off between quality and memory must be managed. Boundary Conditions: The DAG construction assumes a consistent traversal order for attribute mapping. Packed Vertex Attribute Encoding is a compression scheme for vertex attributes in hardware-accelerated volume splatting that reduces memory usage by packing volume texture coordinates and Gaussian texture coordinates into 32-bit integers per vertex. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by specifically targeting the attribute storage of proxy geometry in EWA splatting, decoupling the coordinate components into fixed-width bit fields to achieve high compression ratios (e.g., 171:1) while allowing fast decompression via lookup tables. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The DAG compression gain is highest at low levels in the tree. For an SVO with 17 levels, the second-lowest level has billions of nodes, while the DAG has at most 256 nodes (the amount of possible unique combinations of eight child voxels having each one bit). Measured Performance: For a 128K^3 scene with 18.4 billion colored nodes, the compressed representation requires 7.63 GB of GPU memory. Real-time performance is achieved on commodity hardware for colored scenes with up to 17 hierarchical levels. Scaling: The method supports up to 17 hierarchical levels, corresponding to a 128K^3 voxel resolution. Strengths: Drastic memory reduction, efficient GPU storage, real-time raytracing, handles arbitrary voxel data (colors, normals, reflectance). Limitations: Merging subtrees is difficult when attributes are tightly linked to topology (solved by decoupling). The DAG overhead (pointers per node) is higher than SVOs if not compressed effectively. When to Use: When compressing arbitrary voxel data (colors, normals) is required, and real-time raytracing on GPU is needed. The method was introduced in the paper "Geometry and Attribute Compression for Voxel Scenes" by Timothy Kol et al. from Delft University of Technology. It addresses the limitation of previous DAG-based compression methods that were restricted to single-bit geometry information. The method builds on the concept of DAGs for sparse voxel scenes but extends it to arbitrary data through decoupling and palette compression. It outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, such as Moxel DAGs, which require more memory for indices and lack multi-resolution support. Moxel DAGs store the number of empty leaf voxels in the first child's subtree and use two running sums to compute indices, leading to large storage requirements for the index per node as empty leaves grow to quadrillions, whereas this method uses only one running sum and decouples attributes. name: Packed Vertex Attribute Encoding
head: 32-bit vertex packing, PackedVertex, Vertex compression
body: Packed Vertex Attribute Encoding is a compression scheme for vertex attributes in hardware-accelerated volume splatting that reduces memory usage by packing volume texture coordinates and Gaussian texture coordinates into 32-bit integers per vertex. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by specifically targeting the attribute storage of proxy geometry in EWA splatting, decoupling coordinate components into fixed-width bit fields to achieve high compression ratios while allowing fast decompression via lookup tables. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume texture coordinates (tx, ty) and Gaussian texture coordinate components (fx, fy) for a single vertex. Output: A single 32-bit unsigned integer (uint32t) containing the packed attributes. Data Structures: The packed data is stored in a 32-bit unsigned integer. The bit layout consists of six fields with fixed widths totaling 32 bits: mx (7 bits), ix (8 bits), my (7 bits), iy (8 bits), fx (1 bit), and fy (1 bit). The exact bit ordering (LSB to MSB) is not specified in the sources. Formulas: The volume texture coordinates tx and ty are decomposed into integer components: tx = mx \times 256 + ix ty = my \times 256 + iy Where: mx = \lfloor tx / 256 \rfloor ix = tx \pmod{256} my = \lfloor ty / 256 \rfloor iy = ty \pmod{256} The Gaussian components fx and fy are binary values (0 or 1). Parameters: mx, my: Stored using 7 bits each, allowing volume slices up to 2^{15} \times 2^{15} voxels. ix, iy: Stored using 8 bits each. fx, fy: Stored using 1 bit each. Steps: 1. Decompose Coordinates: For each vertex, calculate mx, ix, my, iy from the integer volume texture coordinates tx, ty using the formulas above. 2. Validate Gaussian Components: Ensure fx and fy are binary (0 or 1). 3. Pack Bits: Construct the 32-bit integer by shifting and masking the components into the defined bit fields. 4. Store: Write the resulting 32-bit integer to the vertex buffer. Decoding: 1. Extract: Retrieve the 32-bit integer from the vertex buffer. 2. Unpack: Extract ix, mx, iy, my, fx, fy using bitwise operations and masks corresponding to their bit widths. 3. Reconstruct: Calculate tx = mx \times 256 + ix and ty = my \times 256 + iy. 4. Lookup: Fast decompression can be implemented using a small lookup table, as used in Direct3D implementations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packvertexattributes(tx: int, ty: int, fx: int, fy: int) -> int: """ Packs volume texture coordinates (tx, ty) and Gaussian coordinates (fx, fy) into a single 32-bit integer according to the specified bit widths. Note: Exact bit ordering is not specified in the source. This implementation packs fields contiguously from LSB to MSB: ix, mx, iy, my, fx, fy. """ # Decompose tx and ty mx = tx // 256 ix = tx % 256 my = ty // 256 iy = ty % 256 # Validate inputs assert 0 <= mx < 128, "mx must fit in 7 bits" assert 0 <= ix < 256, "ix must fit in 8 bits" assert 0 <= my < 128, "my must fit in 7 bits" assert 0 <= iy < 256, "iy must fit in 8 bits" assert fx in (0, 1), "fx must be 0 or 1" assert fy in (0, 1), "fy must be 0 or 1" # Pack into 32-bit integer (LSB-first ordering) packed = 0 packed |= (ix & 0xFF) << 0 packed |= (mx & 0x7F) << 8 packed |= (iy & 0xFF) << 15 packed |= (my & 0x7F) << 23 packed |= (fx & 0x1) << 30 packed |= (fy & 0x1) << 31 return packed def unpackvertexattributes(packed: int) -> tuple: """ Unpacks a 32-bit integer into volume texture coordinates (tx, ty) and Gaussian coordinates (fx, fy). """ ix = (packed >> 0) & 0xFF mx = (packed >> 8) & 0x7F iy = (packed >> 15) & 0xFF my = (packed >> 23) & 0x7F fx = (packed >> 30) & 0x1 fy = (packed >> 31) & 0x1 tx = mx 256 + ix ty = my 256 + iy return (tx, ty, fx, fy) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The decomposition assumes integer coordinates. If floating-point coordinates are used, they must be scaled and rounded to integers before packing. Boundaries: mx and my are limited to 7 bits, restricting volume slices to 2^{15} \times 2^{15} voxels. Degenerate Input: fx and fy must be binary. Non-binary values will corrupt the packing. Time Complexity: Encoding is O(1) per vertex. Decoding is O(1) per vertex, potentially optimized with a lookup table. Memory Complexity: Reduces vertex memory from 16 bytes (4 floats) to 4 bytes (1 uint32) per vertex. Measured Performance: For a 256^3 volume dataset, vertex memory is reduced from 2048M bytes to 12M bytes, a compression ratio of 171:1. Strengths: High compression ratio, fast decompression, suitable for hardware-accelerated rendering. Limitations: Limited volume size (2^{15} \times 2^{15}), fixed Gaussian coordinate resolution (binary). When to Use: Hardware-accelerated volume splatting with proxy geometry where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: Volumes larger than 2^{15} \times 2^{15} slices, or when higher precision for Gaussian coordinates is required. Packed Vertex Attribute Encoding was introduced in the context of hardware-accelerated adaptive EWA volume splatting. It was developed to address the memory bottleneck of storing vertex attributes for proxy geometry in volume rendering. The method allows the volume texture data and packed proxy geometry information to be pre-loaded in the local memory of graphics hardware for interactive rendering. name: Packed Quad Vertex Format
head: PackedVertex
body: Packed Quad Vertex Format is a GPU-ready vertex structure designed to minimize memory bandwidth and VRAM usage during procedural mesh generation and hardware-accelerated volume splatting. It achieves this by packing vertex normals, texture coordinates, ambient occlusion (AO) data, and color metadata into a single 32-bit integer field per vertex, alongside a 3-component position vector. This method is distinct from floating-point attribute storage by using discrete bit-fields for metadata, allowing four vertices of a quad to share compact AO data within a single byte. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Vertex position (x, y, z), normal index, texture index, UV corner index, quad width, quad height, ambient occlusion value, and RGB color components. Output: A Vertex struct containing a 12-byte position and a 4-byte packed integer. Data Structures: The vertex is stored in a struct with #[repr(C)] layout, ensuring memory alignment compatible with GPU buffers. Struct Vertex (Total size: 16 bytes) position: [f32; 3] (Offset 0, Size 12 bytes, Type Float32x3) packed: u32 (Offset 12, Size 4 bytes, Type Uint32) Packed Field Bit Layout (32 bits): The packed field organizes metadata as follows: | Bits | Field | Size | Range/Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | 0–2 | Normal Index | 3 bits | 0–5 (Cardinal directions) | | 3–10 | Texture Index | 8 bits | 0–255 | | 11–12 | UV Corner | 2 bits | 0–3 | | 13–16 | Width - 1 | 4 bits | 0–15 (Stored as width - 1) | | 17–20 | Height - 1 | 4 bits | 0–15 (Stored as height - 1) | | 21–22 | Voxel AO | 2 bits | 0–3 (4 discrete levels) | | 23–25 | Color R | 3 bits | 0–7 | | 26–28 | Color G | 3 bits | 0–7 | | 29–31 | Color B | 3 bits | 0–7 | Parameters: AO Bits: 2 bits per vertex. Quad AO Storage: 1 byte (8 bits) total for all four vertices of a quad. AO Default: 3 (fully open). Algorithm: The packing process extracts specific bit ranges from input values and combines them into a single 32-bit integer. The function pack defaults to an AO value of 3. 1. Extract Normal Index: Mask the lower 3 bits of the normal index. n = \text{normal\idx} \ \& \ 0x7 2. Extract Texture Index: Mask the lower 8 bits of the texture index. t = \text{tex\index} \ \& \ 0xFF 3. Extract UV Corner: Mask the lower 2 bits of the corner index. uv = \text{corner\idx} \ \& \ 0x3 4. Extract Width: Saturate-subtract 1 from width, then mask the lower 4 bits. w = (\max(0, \text{width} - 1)) \ \& \ 0xF 5. Extract Height: Saturate-subtract 1 from height, then mask the lower 4 bits. h = (\max(0, \text{height} - 1)) \ \& \ 0xF 6. Extract AO: Clamp AO to a maximum of 3, then mask the lower 2 bits. ao = \min(\text{ao}, 3) \ \& \ 0x3 7. Extract Color Components: Mask the lower 3 bits of each color channel (R, G, B). cr = \text{color\r} \ \& \ 0x7 cg = \text{color\g} \ \& \ 0x7 cb = \text{color\b} \ \& \ 0x7 8. Combine: Shift and OR the components into the 32-bit integer. \text{packed} = (n \ll 0) \ | \ (t \ll 3) \ | \ (uv \ll 11) \ | \ (w \ll 13) \ | \ (h \ll 17) \ | \ (ao \ll 21) \ | \ (cr \ll 23) \ | \ (cg \ll 26) \ | \ (cb \ll 29) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pack(normalidx: int, texindex: int, corneridx: int, width: int, height: int, ao: int, colorr: int, colorg: int, colorb: int) -> int: # Extract bits with masks n = normalidx & 0x7 t = texindex & 0xFF uv = corneridx & 0x3 # Width and Height are stored as (value - 1), clamped to 0-15 w = max(0, width - 1) & 0xF h = max(0, height - 1) & 0xF # AO is clamped to max 3 aoval = min(ao, 3) & 0x3 # Color components are 3-bit (0-7) cr = colorr & 0x7 cg = colorg & 0x7 cb = colorb & 0x7 # Combine into 32-bit integer packed = (n << 0) | \ (t << 3) | \ (uv << 11) | \ (w << 13) | \ (h << 17) | \ (aoval << 21) | \ (cr << 23) | \ (cg << 26) | \ (cb << 29) return packed def packwithao(normalidx: int, texindex: int, corneridx: int, width: int, height: int, colorr: int, colorg: int, colorb: int, ao: int = 3) -> int: """ Wrapper that defaults AO to 3 (fully open). """ return pack(normalidx, texindex, corneridx, width, height, ao, colorr, colorg, colorb) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Width/Height Limits: The format supports widths and heights up to 16 (since width-1 is stored in 4 bits, max value 15 implies max dimension 16). Larger dimensions will wrap or clamp incorrectly. AO Clamping: Ambient occlusion values greater than 3 are clamped to 3, losing precision for finer AO gradients. Color Precision: RGB is limited to 3 bits per channel (8 levels), which may result in visible banding for high-fidelity rendering. Memory Usage: 16 bytes per vertex (12 bytes position + 4 bytes packed metadata). This is significantly smaller than standard vertex formats that store normals (12 bytes), UVs (8 bytes), and colors (12 bytes) separately. Bandwidth: Reduces memory bandwidth by packing multiple attributes into a single 32-bit word, accelerating mesh upload times from CPU to GPU. Strengths: Ideal for procedural mesh generation and voxel terrain where metadata (AO, texture ID, corner) is discrete and limited in range. Limitations: Low precision for color (3-bit) and AO (2-bit). Not suitable for high-fidelity shading requiring continuous normal or color data. Width/Height limited to 16x16 quads. The Packed Quad Vertex Format originates from implementations in procedural voxel generation and terrain rendering, specifically noted in the context of the "Minerust" project and dynamic ambient occlusion baking in procedural voxels. It addresses the bottleneck of memory bandwidth during high-frequency mesh updates by replacing floating-point attributes with compact bit-packed integers. name: Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG)
head: Pointerless Sparse Voxel DAG
body: The Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG) is a hierarchical data structure that represents a 3D voxel grid as a directed acyclic graph without using explicit pointers to child nodes. It combines the space-saving benefits of Pointerless Sparse Voxel Octrees (PSVOs) with the Common Subtree Merging (CSM) capabilities of Sparse Voxel DAGs (SVDAGs). By replacing fixed-width pointers with variable-length binary labels and callers, PSVDAG achieves higher compression ratios than both SVOs and SVDAGs, making it suitable for archiving and streaming. However, the absence of direct pointers makes immediate traversal more complex compared to pointer-based structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid R of size N \times N \times N voxels, where N = 2^n and n \in \mathbb{N}. Each voxel is binary: active ('1') or passive ('0'). Output: A binary stream representing the PSVDAG structure, organized into n levels. Data Structures and Layout: The structure is defined by Backus-Naur Form (BNF): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. PSVDAG::= <NODE> NODE::= <INODE> | <LNODE> INODE::= <ACHNC><CHNM> ACHNC::= (3)<BIT> CHNM::= (1)(8)<HT> HT::= "00" | "01"<LAB><NODE> | "10"<CAL> | "11"<NODE> LAB::= <SIZ><VAL> CAL::= <SIZ><VAL> SIZ::= (5)<BIT> VAL::= (1)(32)<BIT> LNODE::= (8)<BIT> BIT::= "0" | "1" Levels: Nodes are stored in n levels, indexed by l \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}. The root is at l=0. Inner nodes are at l \le n-2. Leaf nodes are at l = n-1. Inner Node (INODE): ACHNC (Active Child Node Count): A 3-bit unsigned integer storing the number of active children minus one (c-1). Range 0–7, representing 1–8 active children. CHNM (Child Node Mask): A sequence of 1 to 8 Header Tags (HT). Passive children (HT '00') appearing after the last active child are omitted to save space. Header Tags (HT): 2-bit identifiers for child references: '00': Passive child (empty). No further data follows. '01': Label (LAB) child. The node is a unique template. Followed by a Label and the full binary representation of the child node. '10': Caller (CAL) child. The node is a non-unique reference. Followed by a Caller. '11': Direct child. The node is unique. Followed by the full binary representation of the child node. Label (LAB) and Caller (CAL): Both have the structure <SIZ><VAL>. SIZ: 5-bit unsigned integer (0–31). Represents the length of VAL minus 1. VAL: Variable-length bit vector of length SIZ + 1 bits. Range 0 to 2^{SIZ+1}-1. If SIZ=0, VAL is 1 bit. Uniqueness: Labels and Callers are unique within a specific level l. The level index is not stored but derived during traversal. A Caller references the same node as a Label if they share the same level, SIZ, and VAL. Leaf Node (LNODE): An 8-bit vector representing the 8 voxels in a 2 \times 2 \times 2 octant. Bit 0 is passive, Bit 1 is active. Bits are ordered according to a space-filling curve (z-order or Hilbert). Algorithm: Construction and Compaction The construction follows the bottom-up reduction principles of SVDAGs [Parent], with specific adaptations for pointerless encoding: 1. Voxelization: Convert the input geometry into a binary voxel grid R of size 2^n \times 2^n \times 2^n. 2. Tree Construction: Build a standard Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from the grid. Identify common subtrees to form a Sparse Voxel DAG (SVDAG) using bottom-up reduction [Parent]. 3. Frequency Analysis: For each level l from n-2 down to 0: Identify all nodes at level l that are referenced more than once from level l-1. Let this set be NOD. Count the reference frequency for each node in NOD. Sort NOD in descending order of frequency: NOD = \{nod0, nod1, \dots, nod{p-1}\} where freq(nodi) \ge freq(nod{i+1}). 4. Label Assignment (Frequency-Based Compaction): Generate a set of labels LAB = \{lab0, lab1, \dots, lab{p-1}\} sorted by ascending binary length. Assign the shortest label labi to the most frequent node nodi. The label labi consists of SIZi and VALi. The first label is SIZ=0, VAL=0. Subsequent labels increment VAL until overflow, then increment SIZ. 5. Binary Encoding: Traverse the SVDAG in Depth-First order. For each node at level l: If the node is unique (referenced once), encode it with HT '11' followed by its binary representation. If the node is non-unique: The first reference (template) uses HT '01', followed by the assigned Label LAB and the node's binary representation. Subsequent references use HT '10', followed by a Caller CAL with the same SIZ and VAL as the assigned Label. Passive children use HT '00'. Omit trailing passive children from the CHNM sequence. Prepend the ACHNC to each Inner Node. 6. Leaf Encoding: At level n-1, encode Leaf Nodes as 8-bit vectors using the selected space-filling curve. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodepsvdag(voxelgrid, n): """ Encodes a 3D voxel grid into a PSVDAG binary stream. voxelgrid: 3D array of size 2^n x 2^n x 2^n, values 0 or 1. n: level count (grid size 2^n). Returns: binary stream (list of bits). """ # Step 1: Build SVO and SVDAG (Bottom-Up Reduction) # This step produces a DAG where nodes are identified by their child structure. # We assume a function buildsvodag that returns a list of nodes per level. # Each node has: id, childmask (8 bits), children (list of node ids or None), # and frequency (number of parents referencing it). svodagnodes = buildsvodag(voxelgrid, n) # Step 2: Frequency-Based Label Assignment # For each level l from n-2 down to 0 levellabels = {} # Maps level l to a list of (SIZ, VAL) tuples for l in range(n - 2, -1, -1): nodesatlevel = svodagnodes[l] # Identify nodes referenced more than once frequentnodes = [node for node in nodesatlevel if node.frequency > 1] if not frequentnodes: levellabels[l] = [] continue # Sort by frequency descending frequentnodes.sort(key=lambda x: x.frequency, reverse=True) # Generate labels sorted by length ascending # Label 0: SIZ=0, VAL=0 (length 1 bit) # Label 1: SIZ=0, VAL=1 (length 1 bit)... up to SIZ=0, VAL=1 # Then SIZ=1, VAL=0 (length 2 bits), etc. labels = [] siz = 0 val = 0 while len(labels) < len(frequentnodes): # Length of this label is siz + 1 labels.append((siz, val)) val += 1 if val >= (1 << (siz + 1)): val = 0 siz += 1 if siz > 31: raise ValueError("Label space exhausted") # Assign labels to nodes for i, node in enumerate(frequentnodes): node.label = labels[i] levellabels[l] = labels # Step 3: Encode Binary Stream stream = [] # Helper to encode a node's binary representation recursively def encodenode(nodeid, level): node = svodagnodes[level][nodeid] # Leaf Node (Level n-1) if level == n - 1: # Encode 8 voxels based on space-filling curve voxels = getvoxelsforoctant(nodeid, level, n) stream.extend(voxels) return # Inner Node # 1. Encode ACHNC activecount = countactivechildren(node) achncval = activecount - 1 stream.extend(inttobits(achncval, 3)) # 2. Encode CHNM (Header Tags) # Determine which children are active children = node.children activeindices = [i for i, c in enumerate(children) if c is not None] # Iterate through octants 0 to 7 for i in range(8): childid = children[i] # Passive child if childid is None: # Only encode '00' if it appears before the last active child # Or if it's the only child? No, passive children after last active are omitted. # We need to know if this is the last active child. if i in activeindices: # This is an active child. # Check if it's the last active one islastactive = (i == max(activeindices)) # Determine if this child is a template or a caller # In the first pass (Depth-First), we encounter the template first. # We need to know if this specific reference is the first one. # This requires tracking state or a two-pass approach. # For simplicity, assume we are building the stream in a way that # templates are encountered before callers. # Check if this node has a label assigned (it is a common subtree) if nodeid in getcommonsubtreeids(level): # It is a common subtree. # If this is the first reference (template), encode Label + Node # If this is a subsequent reference, encode Caller # Note: The source implies Depth-First traversal ensures Label comes first. # We need to track if we have already encoded the template for this nodeid. if not istemplateencoded(nodeid): marktemplateencoded(nodeid) stream.extend("01") # HT for Label siz, val = node.label stream.extend(inttobits(siz, 5)) stream.extend(inttobits(val, siz + 1)) encodenode(childid, level + 1) else: stream.extend("10") # HT for Caller siz, val = node.label stream.extend(inttobits(siz, 5)) stream.extend(inttobits(val, siz + 1)) else: # Unique node stream.extend("11") # HT for Direct Node encodenode(childid, level + 1) else: # Passive child. # Only encode if it is NOT after the last active child. if i <= max(activeindices) if activeindices else True: stream.extend("00") # HT for Passive # Else: omit else: # Active child (childid is not None) # This logic is handled inside the 'if i in activeindices' block above pass # Note: The above pseudocode simplifies the "first reference" logic. # In practice, a global state or a two-pass construction is needed to determine # which reference is the template. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Passive Child Omission: Passive children (HT '00') appearing after the last active child are omitted from the CHNM. The ACHNC is required to reconstruct the full 8-child structure or convert to SVDAG. Label Uniqueness: Labels are unique only within a level. A label at level l with (SIZ, VAL) is distinct from a label at level l' with the same (SIZ, VAL). Traversal Order: Depth-First traversal is required to ensure that a Label (template) is processed before any Callers referencing it. Precision: SIZ is limited to 5 bits, allowing VAL up to 32 bits. This limits the maximum number of unique nodes per level to 2^{32}, but practically constrained by the grid size. This variant focuses on the specific algorithm for assigning variable-length labels based on node reference frequency to minimize the total bit length of the structure. It sets itself apart by optimizing the label-to-node mapping to achieve higher compression, at the cost of increased construction complexity. Time Complexity: Construction requires bottom-up reduction and frequency analysis, similar to SVDAG construction, plus label assignment. Traversal is more complex than SVO/SVDAG due to label resolution, requiring a stack or recursion to resolve callers to templates. Memory Complexity: Significantly lower than SVDAG and PSVO. By eliminating 32-bit pointers and using variable-length labels, PSVDAG achieves compression ratios up to 5.33-fold compared to standard SVDAGs. Performance: Suitable for archiving and streaming due to compact binary representation. Unsuitable for real-time rendering or quick traversal due to the overhead of resolving labels and callers. Scaling: Compression efficiency improves with scene redundancy (common subtrees). The fixed 5-bit SIZ limits the label space per level, but this is sufficient for typical voxel grid sizes. PSVDAGs were proposed in 2020. They were developed to combine the advantages of PSVOs (space efficiency) and SVDAGs (common subtree merging). The structure addresses the high memory cost of pointers in SVDAGs while overcoming the lack of CSM in PSVOs. name: PSVDAG Label/Caller Encoding with Frequency-Based Compaction
head: Level-wise label assignment, frequency-sorted caller encoding
body: This method replaces the fixed 32-bit child node pointers used in Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs (SVDAG) with variable-length binary labels (callers) to enable pointerless traversal while minimizing memory footprint. It sets itself apart from standard SVDAG by achieving significant compression (up to 5.33-fold) through frequency-based sorting and level-wise label space reset, at the cost of requiring label reconstruction during traversal. Inputs: A PSVDAG structure where nodes are organized into levels, and each Inner Node (INODE) references child subgraph roots from the previous level. Outputs: A compacted representation where child references are encoded as variable-length binary labels. Data Structures: Label Table (per level): A mapping from subgraph root node identifiers to binary codes. Binary Code: Variable-length bit sequence with a minimum length of 6 bits. Steps: 1. Collect References: For each graph level l, identify all unique subgraph root nodes referenced by nodes at level l-1. 2. Count Frequency: Count the number of times each unique subgraph root node is referenced from level l-1. 3. Sort Nodes: Sort the unique subgraph root nodes in descending order of their frequency. 4. Assign Labels: Assign binary labels to the sorted nodes. The most frequent node receives the shortest label. The minimum label length is 6 bits. Subsequent nodes receive longer labels as needed to maintain unique codes. The length increases gradually with the number of unique labels/callers at that level. 5. Reset Label Space: Repeat steps 1–4 independently for each graph level. This resets the label assignment, ensuring that the most frequent nodes at every level get the shortest 6-bit codes rather than competing for short codes globally. Formulas: Compression Ratio: The shortest labels achieve a 5.33-fold compression rate compared to 32-bit pointers. \text{Compression Ratio} = \frac{32 \text{ bits}}{6 \text{ bits}} \approx 5.33 Space Occupancy: The shortest labels occupy 18.75% of the space of a 32-bit pointer. \text{Space Occupancy} = \frac{6}{32} = 0.1875 = 18.75\% Parameters: Minimum Label Length: 6 bits. SVDAG Pointer Size: 32 bits. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unique Subgraphs: If a subgraph is unique, the SVDAG pointer is 32 bits, but in PSVDAG it becomes 0 bits at its root node. However, references to it from other levels still require a valid label/caller with at least 6 bits. Precision and Range: The binary representation length ranges from 6 bits to 16 bits depending on the number of unique nodes per level. Auxiliary fields (ACHNC and CHNM) sum to 5–19 bits, which is significantly less than SVDAG's fixed overhead. Level-wise Reset: Failing to reset the label space per level would force a global frequency count, potentially assigning long codes to frequently occurring nodes at deeper levels if they are less frequent globally. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodelabelsperlevel(levelnodes, previouslevelreferences): """ Encodes child references for a specific level using frequency-based compaction. Args: levelnodes: List of nodes at the current level. previouslevelreferences: List of subgraph root node IDs referenced by levelnodes. Returns: labelmap: Dictionary mapping nodeid to binary string. """ # Step 1 & 2: Count frequency of each referenced subgraph root frequencymap = {} for refid in previouslevelreferences: frequencymap[refid] = frequencymap.get(refid, 0) + 1 # Step 3: Sort nodes by frequency (descending) sortednodes = sorted(frequencymap.keys(), key=lambda x: frequencymap[x], reverse=True) # Step 4: Assign binary labels labelmap = {} currentlength = 6 # Minimum label length per evidence index = 0 for nodeid in sortednodes: # Assign current index as binary code with currentlength bits labelmap[nodeid] = format(index, f'0{currentlength}b') index += 1 # Increase bit length when the current length can no longer uniquely represent the next index if index >= (1 << currentlength): currentlength += 1 return labelmap Time Complexity: Encoding requires sorting nodes by frequency per level, which is O(N \log N) where N is the number of unique references per level. Traversal requires label reconstruction, adding overhead compared to direct pointer dereferencing. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to SVDAG. The average label/caller size ranges from 0.625 to 2.375 bits per child node, depending on the scene and resolution. Measured Performance: On the tested scenes, the compression ratio ranges from 1.68 to 6.4 compared to SVDAG. The reduction in data structure size is between 15.63% and 59.38%. Strengths: High compression ratio for scenes with frequent subgraph reuse; pointerless traversal enables efficient streaming/archival. Limitations: Requires label reconstruction during traversal, which may be slower than direct pointer access; performance depends on the frequency distribution of subgraphs. When to Use: Ideal for archival, streaming, or memory-constrained environments where subgraph reuse is high. When Not to Use: When fast, direct traversal is critical and memory is not a constraint, SVDAG may be preferable. The PSVDAG structure builds on the advantages of both Pointerless SVO and SVDAG, aiming to provide a compact encoding suitable for 3D scene representation. The method addresses the need for efficient storage and traversal in voxelized 3D scenes. PSVDAG: Compact Voxelized Representation of 3D Scenes Using Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs, https://doi.org/10.31577/cai20203587, fetched 2026-10-26
