name: OpenVDB (VDB)
head: OpenVDB Hierarchical Compression, VDB
body: OpenVDB is a sparse voxel representation used for the hierarchical encoding and compression of volumetric grids, featuring fast O(1) random access for modification and retrieval operations. It solves the problem of efficiently storing and accessing large, sparse volumetric datasets by using a shallow tree structure that balances memory overhead with traversal speed. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific four-level topology and 64-bit direct access bit masks that encode topology and data pointers, making it a standard in production visual effects and scientific visualization. Inputs and Outputs: Input is a dense or sparse volumetric grid. Output is a serialized OpenVDB tree structure containing hierarchical node data and voxel values. Data Structures: The structure is a shallow tree with four levels: Root, Internal (Tile), and Leaf. 1. Bit Masks: Each level stores a 64-bit direct access bit mask. Internal Nodes (Tiles): The bit mask encodes the child ID or representative values for the entire tile. Leaf Nodes: The bit mask encodes the leaf origin using 3 \times 20 bits. Other bits encode metadata (e.g., compression status, quantization). 2. Leaf Node Payload: A bit mask indicating which voxels are active. A raw pointer to the voxel data array. 3. Voxel Data: Stored in arrays pointed to by leaf nodes. Parameters: Leaf Node Size: Default is 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxels. Bit Mask Width: Fixed at 64 bits per level. Algorithm (Tree Construction and Access): The tree is constructed to allow O(1) access. The root has a variable number of children, while internal nodes have a fixed number of children. 1. Initialization: Create the root node. 2. Insertion/Modification: Calculate the node index for the target coordinate. Use the 64-bit bit mask at the current level to determine the child node index. If the child does not exist, create it. Recurse to the next level until the Leaf level is reached. 3. Leaf Access: At the leaf level, use the 64-bit mask to decode the leaf origin (3 \times 20 bits) and metadata. Use the active voxel bit mask to locate the specific voxel within the leaf's data array. Return the value via the raw pointer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getvoxel(root, coords): """ Retrieve a voxel value from the OpenVDB tree. coords: tuple (x, y, z) representing the voxel position. """ node = root # Traverse levels 0 to 2 (Root and Internal nodes) for level in range(3): # Exact bit extraction from the 64-bit mask depends on OpenVDB version. # Standard approach: shift coordinate bits by level-specific offsets. childindex = (coords[0] >> (level 3)) & 0x7 if childindex is None or not node.haschild(childindex): return None # Voxel not present (empty space) node = node.children[childindex] # Now node is a Leaf # Decode leaf origin from the 64-bit mask (3 20 bits) # Sources do not specify exact bit positions; standard extraction assumes contiguous blocks. leaforiginx = (node.bitmask >> 40) & 0xFFFFF leaforiginy = (node.bitmask >> 20) & 0xFFFFF leaforiginz = node.bitmask & 0xFFFFF leaforigin = (leaforiginx, leaforiginy, leaforiginz) # Calculate local coordinates within the leaf localcoords = (coords[0] - leaforigin[0], coords[1] - leaforigin[1], coords[2] - leaforigin[2]) # Check if the voxel is active using the leaf's active bit mask localidx = localcoords[0] + localcoords[1] 8 + localcoords[2] 64 if not (node.activemask >> localidx) & 1: return None # Voxel is inactive (e.g., zero or background) # Retrieve value from the raw data pointer dataindex = localidx return node.dataptr[dataindex] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Space: If a child node does not exist, the traversal stops, and the value is considered background/empty. Inactive Voxels: Even if a leaf exists, individual voxels may be inactive. The active bit mask must be checked. Precision: The leaf origin is encoded in 20 bits per axis. Ensure coordinates fit within this range. Memory: The structure relies on raw pointers. The data prevails in address spaces visible to the CPU. This method enables GPU volume rendering of large, sparse volumetric datasets by combining offline fixed-rate lossy compression on the CPU (using OpenVDB) with fast, low-overhead on-the-fly decompression and sampling on the GPU (using NanoVDB). It solves the problem of rendering volumes that exceed single-GPU memory capacity by significantly reducing the memory footprint while maintaining random access patterns suitable for incoherent workloads like path tracing. Unlike hierarchical space-skipping approaches which show diminishing returns with RGBA transfer functions, this method typically employs a uniform majorant grid for traversal acceleration to facilitate direct comparison with dense texture rendering. A linear, GPU-optimized implementation of VDB that does not depend on CPU address spaces, allowing compact copying via memcpy and optimized voxel retrieval on the GPU. The VDB 3-4-5 Tree Traversal is a method for retrieving leaf node data from an OpenVDB file stored in a compressed texture atlas format using a hierarchical 3-4-5 tree topology. It solves the problem of random access to sparse volumetric data by mapping 3D coordinates to leaf values through a fixed-depth traversal of nodes with sizes 3^3, 4^4, and 5^5. It differs from standard pointer-based OpenVDB by storing the tree structure in compressed texture atlases rather than explicit pointers, and from NanoVDB by using a specific 3-4-5 hierarchy instead of a linearized or standard octree representation. This method describes the binary parsing of the OpenVDB file format to reconstruct sparse voxel grids in memory. It solves the problem of loading hierarchical, compressed volumetric data from disk into a traversable tree structure. Unlike raw voxel grids, this method handles sparse storage via Node5 and Node4 internal nodes, and Node3 leaf nodes, supporting both active mask compression and value compression. It differs from NanoVDB Linear Representation by maintaining a hierarchical tree structure in memory rather than a flat linear array, and from VDB Volume Rendering with OpenVDB/NanoVDB by focusing solely on data loading rather than rendering traversal. Time Complexity: O(1) random access for modification and retrieval. Memory Complexity: Sparse storage; only non-empty nodes and active voxels are stored. The 64-bit bit masks add a fixed overhead per node. Performance: Well-suited for visual effects rendering of volumetric data from fluid simulations. Fast access and modification allow for runtime editing. Strengths: Fast O(1) access, out-of-core streaming support, integration with production tools (Houdini, Cycles). Limitations: Data prevails in CPU-visible address spaces, requiring conversion for GPU use (e.g., NanoVDB). When to Use: Large, sparse volumetric datasets requiring random access and modification, particularly in VFX and scientific visualization. When Not to Use: When GPU-native memory layouts are required without conversion overhead, or for dense volumes where the sparse overhead is not justified. OpenVDB was introduced by Ken Museth in a paper that established the sparse voxel representation. It is an open-source library resulting from Museth's work, designed for hierarchical encoding and compression of volumetric grids. It has become well-established due to its integration into production renderers like Cycles and visual effects software such as Houdini and Cinema 4D. It is popular in industry-strength libraries optimized for construction and sampling on NVIDIA GPUs. name: VDB Volume Rendering with OpenVDB/NanoVDB
head: OpenVDB/NanoVDB rendering, NanoVDB encoding, OpenVDB structure
body: This method enables GPU volume rendering of large, sparse volumetric datasets by combining offline fixed-rate lossy compression on the CPU (using OpenVDB) with fast, low-overhead on-the-fly decompression and sampling on the GPU (using NanoVDB). It solves the problem of rendering volumes that exceed single-GPU memory capacity by significantly reducing the memory footprint while maintaining random access patterns suitable for incoherent workloads like path tracing. Unlike hierarchical space-skipping approaches which show diminishing returns with RGBA transfer functions, this method employs a uniform majorant grid for traversal acceleration to facilitate direct comparison with dense texture rendering. The method consists of two phases: CPU-side compression/conversion and GPU-side rendering. Input: A dense volumetric dataset (e.g., structured regular grid) and a user-defined quality parameter q \in [0, 1]. Output: A NanoVDB structure in GPU memory, supporting nearest-neighbor and trilinear interpolation sampling. The standard OpenVDB structure uses a hierarchical layout with three levels of internal nodes and leaf voxels. Index Space: 4096^3 (1 \ll 12). Node5 (Top): Span 32^3 (1 \ll 5). Node4 (Middle): Span 16^3 (1 \ll 4). Node3 (Bottom): Span 8^3 (1 \ll 3). Brick Size: 32 \times 32 \times 32 voxels for the standard {3,4,5} layout. NanoVDB creates a linear, pointer-free layout optimized for GPU access. The structure on GPU memory is defined as: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Volume { constants: Vec<VolumeConstants>, // Translation, scale, AABB (unique per animation frame) nodes5: Vec<Node5>, nodes4: Vec<Node4>, nodes3: Vec<Node3>, voxeldata: VoxelData, // 3D texture buffer } Node Layout: Each node (Node5, Node4, Node3) contains: childpointer: u32: Points to the start of N\CHILDREN child nodes. tilevalue: f32: Value for homogeneous regions. minvalue: f32, maxvalue: f32, meanvalue: f32: Statistical bounds. childmask: [u32; N\CHILDREN / 32]: Bitmask indicating validity of child nodes. Voxel Data: Stored in a 3D texture buffer. Layout: Voxels are stored in bricks of 8^3. Packing: Each 4 values in the Z direction are stored as RGBA components of a texel. Compression: BC7 block compression is applied to the 3D texture, resulting in 2 bits per voxel. The fixed-rate encoding algorithm achieves target compression ratios by encoding homogeneous blocks as nearly empty and voxelizing non-empty regions. 1. Background Value Identification: Compute a histogram of the input volume's values. The most frequent value is assumed to be the background value B. 2. Bricking: Divide the volume conceptually into bricks sized to match the leaf node dimensions (e.g., 32 \times 32 \times 32). 3. Brick Analysis: For each brick, compute the minimum and maximum voxel values [lo, hi]. 4. Brick Sorting: Sort bricks based on their similarity to the background value B using one of the metrics f1, f2, or f3. Bricks most similar to the background come first. Three metrics are defined: f1 = \min(|lo - B|, |hi - B|) (closest point-in-range) f2 = \max(|lo - B|, |hi - B|) (farthest point-in-range) f3 = |(lo + hi)/2 - B| (median distance) Evaluation suggests f2 and 32 \times 32 \times 32 brick size generally yield better quality. 5. Voxel Activation: Determine the target number of bricks to activate based on quality q. Iterate through the sorted list starting from the brick least similar to the background (end of list). Activate all voxels in the current brick by setting their original values. Continue until the target number of bricks is processed. Voxels in non-selected bricks remain inactive (implicitly background). 6. Finalization: Prune the resulting OpenVDB tree for memory optimization. 1. Conversion: Convert the compressed OpenVDB structure to NanoVDB. This creates a linear, pointer-free layout. Copy this block to GPU memory. 2. Traversal Acceleration: Use a uniform majorant grid for traversal acceleration. Hierarchical traversal was found to offer diminishing returns for this representation. 3. On-the-Fly Decompression: During rendering, GPU threads sample the volume using NanoVDB accessor and sampler functions. These functions handle tree traversal and voxel value retrieval directly on the GPU. Supported sampling: Nearest-neighbor and trilinear interpolation. If a sample location falls into an inactive region, the background value B is returned. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compressvolume(volume, W, H, D, quality): # 1. Background Value Identification histogram = [0] 256 # Standard histogram computation for 8-bit values for v in volume: histogram[v] += 1 B = max(range(256), key=lambda i: histogram[i]) # Standard argmax # 2. Bricking bricksize = 32 nx, ny, nz = math.ceil(W / bricksize), math.ceil(H / bricksize), math.ceil(D / bricksize) numbricks = nx ny nz # 3. Brick Analysis brickranges = [] for brickid in range(numbricks): lo = brickid bricksize hi = (brickid + 1) bricksize brickranges.append((lo, hi)) # 4. Brick Sorting (using f2 metric, ascending distance -> most similar first) def similarity(brickrange): lo, hi = brickrange return max(abs(lo - B), abs(hi - B)) sortedbricks = sorted(enumerate(brickranges), key=lambda x: similarity(x[1])) # 5. Voxel Activation openvdbtree = {} # Standard sparse dictionary/tree structure # Activate extreme corners explicitly to preserve world bounds openvdbtree[(0, 0, 0)] = volume[(0, 0, 0)] openvdbtree[(W-1, H-1, D-1)] = volume[(W-1, H-1, D-1)] brickstoactivate = int(numbricks quality) bricksactive = 0 # Iterate from the end (least similar to background) for idx, brickrange in reversed(sortedbricks): if bricksactive >= brickstoactivate: break # Iterate over 3D voxel coordinates in brick for x in range(brickrange[0], brickrange[1], bricksize): for y in range(brickrange[0], brickrange[1], bricksize): for z in range(brickrange[0], brickrange[1], bricksize): openvdbtree[(x, y, z)] = volume[(x, y, z)] bricksactive += 1 # 6. Finalization # Standard tree pruning removes empty internal nodes return openvdbtree def rendervdb(nanovdbptr, ray, uniformgrid): # 1. Traversal Acceleration cell = uniformgrid.findcell(ray.origin) # Standard uniform grid lookup # 2. On-the-Fly Decompression # NanoVDB accessor handles tree traversal and sampling # If sample falls in inactive region, returns background value B value = nanovdbptr.sample(ray.position) # Standard NanoVDB accessor call return value Compression Rates: 1:8, 1:4, 1:2, 1:1. 1:1 means zero percent targeted reduction (lossless activation of non-empty voxels). Quality: A user-defined parameter between 0 and 1 that controls the compression rate. It determines the percentage of bricks to fully activate. NanoVDB Overhead: Modest, approximately 10% for large datasets compared to raw data size. Lossless Compression: At 1:1 rate, the algorithm only activates voxels not considered empty, resulting in an actual size lower than the original even if target reduction is zero. High Compression: High compression rates may lead to missing features if the transfer function highlights regions deemed 'background' and thus deactivated during compression, resulting in block artifacts. Corner Voxels: The extreme (minimum and maximum) corners of the VDB must be explicitly activated even if they match the background value. If not, OpenVDB excludes them, causing the VDB tree's aspect ratio (world bound size) to differ from the original volume. Tile Activation: Activating a whole tile on a level higher than leaf node level 0 (using addTile) sets all voxels in that tile to the same value, providing no additional compression benefit from hierarchical encoding. Animation: Each animation frame has a unique Node5 vector. Switching frames changes only the starting point of structure traversal. Time Complexity: Rendering performance is competitive with hardware-accelerated 3D texture sampling. Memory Complexity: Significant memory savings compared to dense textures. NanoVDB overhead is ~10% for large datasets. Measured Performance: Galaxy dataset: VDB achieves 34.8 FPS on 1 GPU vs 18.6 FPS for dense textures on 3 GPUs. Aneurism dataset: VDB achieves 55.8 FPS on 1 GPU vs 75.9 FPS for dense textures on 1 GPU. WDAS dataset: VDB achieves 24.2 FPS on 1 GPU vs 25.4 FPS for dense textures on 1 GPU. Scaling: Enables rendering of datasets requiring multiple GPUs uncompressed on a single GPU. Strengths: Low memory footprint, random access suitable for path tracing, competitive performance with dense textures. Limitations: Block artifacts at high compression; hierarchical traversal offers diminishing returns. Origin: The method was proposed by Stefan Zellmann, Milan Jaros, Jefferson Amstutz, and Ingo Wald in 2025. Development: It integrates OpenVDB for CPU-side compression and NanoVDB for GPU-side rendering, integrated into the Barney ray tracer using the ANARI API. Usage: Used for scientific visualization of large, sparse volumetric data. name: VDB 3-4-5 Tree Traversal
head: OpenVDB 3-4-5 Tree, VDB345
body: The VDB 3-4-5 Tree Traversal is a method for retrieving leaf node data from an OpenVDB file stored in a compressed texture atlas format using a hierarchical 3-4-5 tree topology. It solves the problem of random access to sparse volumetric data by mapping 3D coordinates to leaf values through a fixed-depth traversal of nodes with sizes 3^3, 4^4, and 5^5. It differs from standard pointer-based OpenVDB by storing the tree structure in compressed texture atlases rather than explicit pointers, and from NanoVDB by using a specific 3-4-5 hierarchy instead of a linearized or standard octree representation. Inputs: pos: The 3D voxel coordinates to query, represented as vec3<f32> or vec3<i32>. leaff: An output structure of type VdbLeaf. Internal data structures: origins: Array of node origins. node5s, node4s, node3s: Texture atlases containing node data. kids5, vals5, kids4, vals4, vals3: Mask arrays for child and value existence. NODE5TOTALLOGD, NODE4TOTALLOGD, NODE3TOTALLOGD: Precomputed logarithmic dimensions. Outputs: leaff: A VdbLeaf struct containing the retrieved color, distance, number of parents, and parent pointers. VdbLeaf Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct VdbLeaf { color: vec3<f32> // Retrieved voxel value or default dist: u32 // Distance or level indicator numparents: u32 // Number of valid parent pointers (0-3) parents: array<Parent, 3> // Parent nodes in traversal order } Parent Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Parent { origin: vec3<i32> // Global coordinate of the parent node idx: u32 // Index within the parent's texture atlas } ArchiveHeader (File Header) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct ArchiveHeader { fileversion: u32 librarymajor: u32 libraryminor: u32 uuid: String hasgridoffsets: bool compression: Compression // ZIP or Blosc gridnumber: u32 metadata: Metadata } GridDescriptor Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct GridDescriptor { name: String gridtype: String instanceparent: String gridpos: u64 blockpos: u64 endpos: u64 compression: Compression metadata: Metadata } NODE5TOTALLOGD: u32 = 12 (Approximation for 5^5=3125, used for coordinate shifting). NODE4TOTALLOGD: u32 = 7 (\log2(4^4) = \log2(256) = 8, source states 7). NODE3TOTALLOGD: u32 = 3 (\log2(3^3) = \log2(27) \approx 4.75, source states 3). OPENVDBMINSUPPORTEDVERSION: u32 = 218. MAGICBYTES: u32 = 0x56444220. 1. File Initialization: Read the first 4 bytes. If not equal to MAGICBYTES (0x56444220), return MagicMismatch error. Read fileversion. If fileversion < OPENVDBMINSUPPORTEDVERSION (218), return UnsupportedVersion error. Read librarymajor, libraryminor, uuid, hasgridoffsets, compression, gridnumber, and metadata into ArchiveHeader. Read GridDescriptor for the target grid, including gridpos, blockpos, endpos, and compression. Decompress the grid data based on the compression type (ZIP or Blosc). 2. Traversal Entry: Call getvdbleaffromleaf(pos, leaff). 3. Leaf Check (getvdbleaffromleaf): Check leaff.numparents. If numparents == 3: Check if parents[2] matches node3global (derived from pos). If match, proceed to Node 3 logic. If no match, call getvdbleaffromnothing. If numparents == 2: Check if parents[1] matches node4global. If match, proceed to Node 4 logic. If no match, call getvdbleaffromnothing. If numparents == 1: Check if parents[0] matches node5global. If match, proceed to Node 5 logic. If no match, call getvdbleaffromnothing. If numparents == 0: Call getvdbleaffromnothing. 4. Root Lookup (getvdbleaffromnothing): Iterate through the origins array. If node5global matches origins[node5idx]: Set leaf.parents[0] = Parent(node5global, node5idx). Set leaf.numparents = 1. Call getvdbleaffromnode5. If no match is found after iterating all origins: Return VdbLeaf(vec3<f32>(0.0), 1u, 0u, leaf.parents). 5. Node 5 Traversal (getvdbleaffromnode5): Calculate node5local, node5child, and node5offset from pos and node5global. Check masks in kids5 and vals5 arrays using bit operations based on node5child. Load node4idx from the node5s texture atlas. If inval5 is true: Return VdbLeaf(vec3<f32>(0.2), 0u, 1u, leaf.parents). If !inkid5 is true: Return VdbLeaf(vec3<f32>(0.0), node4idx, 1u, leaf.parents). Else: Set leaf.parents[1] = Parent(node4global, node4idx). Set leaf.numparents = 2. Call getvdbleaffromnode4. 6. Node 4 Traversal (getvdbleaffromnode4): Calculate node4local, node4child, and node4offset from pos and node4global. Check masks in kids4 and vals4 arrays using bit operations based on node4child. Load node3idx from the node4s texture atlas. If inval4 is true: Return VdbLeaf(vec3<f32>(0.2), 0u, 2u, leaf.parents). If !inkid4 is true: Return VdbLeaf(vec3<f32>(0.0), node3idx, 2u, leaf.parents). Else: Set leaf.parents[2] = Parent(node3global, node3idx). Set leaf.numparents = 3. Call getvdbleaffromnode3. 7. Node 3 Traversal (getvdbleaffromnode3): Calculate node3local and node3offset from pos and node3global. Check mask in vals3 array based on node3local. Load voxel value from the node3s texture atlas. If inval3 is true: Return VdbLeaf(vec3<f32>(0.1), 0u, 3u, leaf.parents). Else: Return VdbLeaf(vec3<f32>(0.0), voxel, 3u, leaf.parents). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MAGICBYTES = 0x56444220 OPENVDBMINSUPPORTEDVERSION = 218 NODE5TOTALLOGD = 12 NODE4TOTALLOGD = 7 NODE3TOTALLOGD = 3 class Parent: def init(self, origin, idx): self.origin = origin # vec3<i32> self.idx = idx # u32 class VdbLeaf: def init(self, color, dist, numparents, parents): self.color = color # vec3<f32> self.dist = dist # u32 self.numparents = numparents # u32 self.parents = parents # list of Parent origins = [] # list of vec3<i32> node5s = [] # texture atlas for node 5 node4s = [] # texture atlas for node 4 node3s = [] # texture atlas for node 3 kids5 = [] # bitmask array vals5 = [] # bitmask array kids4 = [] # bitmask array vals4 = [] # bitmask array vals3 = [] # bitmask array def readvdbfile(filepath): # 1. Validate magic bytes magic = readu32(filepath, 0) if magic != MAGICBYTES: raise MagicMismatchError("Magic bytes mismatch") # 2. Validate version fileversion = readu32(filepath, 4) if fileversion < OPENVDBMINSUPPORTEDVERSION: raise UnsupportedVersionError(f"Version {fileversion} < {OPENVDBMINSUPPORTEDVERSION}") # 3. Read ArchiveHeader librarymajor = readu32(filepath, 8) libraryminor = readu32(filepath, 12) uuid = readstring(filepath, 16) hasgridoffsets = readbool(filepath, 16 + len(uuid)) compression = readcompression(filepath,...) gridnumber = readu32(filepath,...) metadata = readmetadata(filepath,...) # 4. Read GridDescriptor gridpos = readu64(filepath,...) blockpos = readu64(filepath,...) endpos = readu64(filepath,...) # 5. Decompress and load topology/data decompressandloadgriddata(gridpos, blockpos, endpos, compression) return True def getvdbleaffromleaf(pos, leaff): # Determine global node coordinates node5global = getglobalnode5(pos) node4global = getglobalnode4(pos) node3global = getglobalnode3(pos) if leaff.numparents == 3: if leaff.parents[2].origin == node3global: return getvdbleaffromnode3(pos, leaff) else: return getvdbleaffromnothing(pos, leaff) elif leaff.numparents == 2: if leaff.parents[1].origin == node4global: return getvdbleaffromnode4(pos, leaff) else: return getvdbleaffromnothing(pos, leaff) elif leaff.numparents == 1: if leaff.parents[0].origin == node5global: return getvdbleaffromnode5(pos, leaff) else: return getvdbleaffromnothing(pos, leaff) else: return getvdbleaffromnothing(pos, leaff) def getvdbleaffromnothing(pos, leaff): node5global = getglobalnode5(pos) for node5idx in range(len(origins)): if origins[node5idx] == node5global: leaff.parents[0] = Parent(node5global, node5idx) leaff.numparents = 1 return getvdbleaffromnode5(pos, leaff) return VdbLeaf(vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 1, 0, leaff.parents) def getvdbleaffromnode5(pos, leaff): node5global = leaff.parents[0].origin node5idx = leaff.parents[0].idx # Calculate local coordinates and child index node5local = pos - node5global 5 node5child = getchildindex(node5local, 5) node5offset = getoffset(node5local, 5) # Check masks inval5 = (vals5[node5idx] >> node5child) & 1 inkid5 = (kids5[node5idx] >> node5child) & 1 # Load node4 index from texture atlas node4idx = loadfromtextureatlas(node5s, node5idx, node5offset) if inval5: return VdbLeaf(vec3(0.2, 0.2, 0.2), 0, 1, leaff.parents) if not inkid5: return VdbLeaf(vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), node4idx, 1, leaff.parents) # Proceed to node 4 node4global = getglobalnode4(pos) leaff.parents[1] = Parent(node4global, node4idx) leaff.numparents = 2 return getvdbleaffromnode4(pos, leaff) def getvdbleaffromnode4(pos, leaff): node4global = leaff.parents[1].origin node4idx = leaff.parents[1].idx node4local = pos - node4global 4 node4child = getchildindex(node4local, 4) node4offset = getoffset(node4local, 4) inval4 = (vals4[node4idx] >> node4child) & 1 inkid4 = (kids4[node4idx] >> node4child) & 1 node3idx = loadfromtextureatlas(node4s, node4idx, node4offset) if inval4: return VdbLeaf(vec3(0.2, 0.2, 0.2), 0, 2, leaff.parents) if not inkid4: return VdbLeaf(vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), node3idx, 2, leaff.parents) node3global = getglobalnode3(pos) leaff.parents[2] = Parent(node3global, node3idx) leaff.numparents = 3 return getvdbleaffromnode3(pos, leaff) def getvdbleaffromnode3(pos, leaff): node3global = leaff.parents[2].origin node3idx = leaff.parents[2].idx node3local = pos - node3global 3 node3offset = getoffset(node3local, 3) inval3 = (vals3[node3idx] >> node3offset) & 1 voxel = loadfromtextureatlas(node3s, node3idx, node3offset) if inval3: return VdbLeaf(vec3(0.1, 0.1, 0.1), 0, 3, leaff.parents) else: return VdbLeaf(vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), voxel, 3, leaff.parents) def getglobalnode5(pos): return vec3(i32(pos.x // 5), i32(pos.y // 5), i32(pos.z // 5)) def getglobalnode4(pos): return vec3(i32(pos.x // 4), i32(pos.y // 4), i32(pos.z // 4)) def getglobalnode3(pos): return vec3(i32(pos.x // 3), i32(pos.y // 3), i32(pos.z // 3)) def getchildindex(localpos, blockdim): # Standard sparse voxel child index calculation return (localpos.x blockdim blockdim + localpos.y blockdim + localpos.z) def getoffset(localpos, blockdim): # Offset calculation for texture atlas indexing return (localpos.x blockdim blockdim + localpos.y blockdim + localpos.z) def loadfromtextureatlas(atlas, idx, offset): # Standard texture atlas lookup return atlas[idx atlas.stride + offset] def readu32(fp, offset): return int.frombytes(fp.read(4), byteorder='little') def readstring(fp, offset): length = int.frombytes(fp.read(4), byteorder='little') return fp.read(length).decode('utf-8') def readbool(fp, offset): return bool(int.frombytes(fp.read(1), byteorder='little')) def readcompression(fp, offset): return int.frombytes(fp.read(1), byteorder='little') def readmetadata(fp, offset): return fp.read(16) # Placeholder for metadata structure parsing def readu64(fp, offset): return int.frombytes(fp.read(8), byteorder='little') def decompressandloadgriddata(gridpos, blockpos, endpos, compression): # Standard decompression and atlas loading pass def vec3(x, y, z): return type('vec3', (), {'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': z}) def i32(val): return int(val) & 0xFFFFFFFF Unsupported Version: If fileversion < 218, the file is rejected. name: Time-Variant Volume Rendering with Octrees
head: Multi-timestep rendering, Time-Variant Volume Rendering with Octree Compression
body: This method addresses the limitation of GPU memory and bus bandwidth when rendering time-variant volume data, which often exceeds available VRAM. By compressing multiple timesteps of volume data into a sparse octree representation, the technique allows the entire sequence to reside in limited CPU main memory, enabling interactive rendering on commodity hardware. It sets itself apart from uncompressed hierarchical grids by providing significant compression ratios, trading some raw traversal speed for the ability to keep large datasets in-core. The method relies on the principles of Octree-based structures, specifically utilizing spatial subdivision to handle sparsity and compression. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of T timesteps of 3D volume data, where each timestep is a regular grid of scalar values (e.g., density). The data is typically medium-sized (e.g., 302^3 to 512^3). Output: A compressed octree structure stored in CPU memory, and a rendered image sequence at interactive frame rates. Data Structures: The core data structure is an octree where each node represents a sub-volume. Node Layout: Nodes are stored in a linear array, typically ordered by Morton codes (Z-order curve) to preserve spatial locality. Compression: Empty or uniform regions are represented by a single node (or null pointer in implicit structures) rather than storing individual voxel values. This provides compression ratios proportional to the sparsity of the data. Memory Layout: The entire sequence of timesteps is compressed into a single octree structure or a set of structures that fit within main memory. For the Utah CSAFE heptane simulation, 153 timesteps of 302^3 data (4.11 GB uncompressed) are compressed to 678 MB. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compression: For each timestep, construct an octree representation of the volume data. Empty or uniform blocks are collapsed into single nodes. The resulting octrees for all timesteps are stored in CPU main memory. 2. Traversal: To render a specific timestep, traverse the corresponding octree. The traversal complexity is O(\log N) for deep trees or O(1) for shallow trees with direct indexing, where N is the resolution. 3. Rendering: Perform ray tracing or ray casting through the octree. Rays are traced against the bounding boxes of the octree nodes. If a node is empty or uniform, the ray traversal can be accelerated or skipped. 4. Parallelization: The rendering process is parallelized using a dynamically load-balanced, tile-based parallelization scheme, leveraging the underlying Manta ray tracing architecture. Parameters: Compression Threshold: The threshold for determining if a block is uniform or empty. Not given in the sources. Max Depth: The maximum depth of the octree. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Quantization of scalar values may affect the accuracy of the rendered isosurfaces. Memory: While compressed, the data still requires significant CPU memory for large sequences. The method is designed for "medium-sized" volumes (less than 512^3). A technique to improve rendering rates for time-varying volume data by compressing the data using quantization and octree-difference encoding, allowing the renderer to skip rendering transparent or uniform blocks. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The method significantly reduces memory usage compared to uncompressed storage. For the Utah CSAFE heptane simulation, the compression ratio is approximately 6:1 (4.11 GB to 678 MB). Time: Rendering speed depends on the hardware and the complexity of the volume data. The method scales well with the number of CPU cores. Measured Performance: Performance was measured on the Utah CSAFE heptane simulation (302^3 volume, 153 timesteps). | Hardware | Resolution | Timestep | Frame Rate (fps) | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Core Duo 2.16 GHz | 512^2 | 25 | 17.0 | | Core Duo 2.16 GHz | 512^2 | 50 | 11.1 | | Core Duo 2.16 GHz | 512^2 | 75 | 5.7 | | Core Duo 2.16 GHz | 512^2 | 100 | 4.1 | | NUMA 16-core 2.4 GHz | 512^2 | 25 | 87.1 | | NUMA 16-core 2.4 GHz | 512^2 | 50 | 60.3 | | NUMA 16-core 2.4 GHz | 512^2 | 75 | 36.7 | | NUMA 16-core 2.4 GHz | 512^2 | 100 | 26.6 | | NUMA 16-core 2.4 GHz | 1024^2 | 25 | 29.2 | | NUMA 16-core 2.4 GHz | 1024^2 | 50 | 18.0 | | NUMA 16-core 2.4 GHz | 1024^2 | 75 | 9.6 | | NUMA 16-core 2.4 GHz | 1024^2 | 100 | 6.6 | Scaling: The technique scales well with the number of CPU threads. On a 2.4 GHz Opteron NUMA workstation, scalability was tested on 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 16 threads. The slight change in slope at 8 threads corresponds to the use of local NUMA memory by two cores instead of one. The octree technique scales as well as the hierarchical grid with uncompressed data. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows visualization of large time-variant volumes on machines with limited main memory. Enables interactive rendering of multiple timesteps. Limitations: Compressed data may render slightly slower than uncompressed data on high-end hardware with sufficient memory. The method is designed for medium-sized volumes. The method was introduced in the paper "Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes" by Wald et al. (2006). It was developed to address the limitations of GPU memory and bus bandwidth in the context of interactive volume rendering. The technique is based on the Manta ray tracing architecture. name: Octree-Difference Encoding for Time-Varying Volume Rendering
head: Octree-Difference Encoding with Tree Merging, compressed volume rendering, twd-renderer encoding
body: This method improves rendering rates for time-varying volume data by compressing the dataset using quantization and octree-difference encoding, allowing the renderer to skip transparent or uniform blocks. It sets itself apart from standard sparse structures by explicitly exploiting temporal coherence: identical subtrees at consecutive time steps are merged, and the rendering engine is restructured to perform selective rendering based on this merged tree representation. Unlike baseline renderers that process full volumes, this approach reduces I/O costs and inter-frame delay by up to 90%. The method consists of an encoding phase and a rendering phase. The encoding phase prepares a compressed, temporally coherent data structure. The rendering phase traverses this structure, skipping nodes that represent transparent or uniform space. Input: A sequence of volume datasets Vt for time steps t = 0, \dots, N-1. Each Vt is a 3D grid of voxels. Output: A compressed, merged octree structure (compositing tree) and the ability to render frames with reduced computational cost. The core data structure is an Octree where each node represents a block of voxels. Node Types: Leaf Node: Represents a uniform block of voxels. Stores the representative value (from quantization) and metadata indicating transparency or uniformity. Internal Node: Represents a subdivision of space. Contains pointers to its 8 children. Tree Merging: If the octree structure and voxel values of a subtree at time t are identical to the corresponding subtree at time t-1, the subtree at t is merged with t-1. This avoids storing redundant data and allows the renderer to skip recomputation. Minimum Renderable Block: The renderer is configured to stop at a minimum depth, corresponding to an 8-voxel block. Nodes smaller than this (1-voxel or 8-voxel merges) are not useful for rendering performance gains because a single voxel change forces re-rendering of surrounding voxels. The raw volume data is quantized to reduce precision and increase uniformity, facilitating compression. Methods: Uniform, Non-Uniform I, Non-Uniform II, or Adaptive. Selection: The choice depends on dataset statistics. For example, Uniform quantization yields 98% compression for the Jets dataset, while Non-Uniform II yields 98% for the Thermal dataset. Non-Uniform I performs poorly on Shear flow (-7% saving). Error: Quantization error is typically less than 1% for the studied datasets. The quantized data is encoded into an octree. Spatial Coherence: Neighboring voxels with similar values are fused into macro voxels (leaf nodes). Temporal Coherence: Subtrees at consecutive time steps are compared. If identical, they are merged. Encoding Cost: On a SUN Ultra Sparc, quantization takes ~0.5 seconds per time step, and octree-difference encoding takes 3-5 seconds per time step. For 100 time steps, total encoding takes 5-10 minutes. The encoded data is organized into a compositing tree. This tree structure supports the selective rendering strategy. During rendering, the tree is traversed. Transparent Space: If a node represents transparent space, it is skipped entirely. Uniform Space: If a node represents uniform space, it is rendered as a block without ray marching. Non-Uniform Space: If a node represents non-uniform space, standard ray marching is performed. Optimization: The renderer uses front-to-back compositing to encourage early termination of rays. Configuration: The renderer can be configured to stop at any depth in the tree and render immediately. The minimum number of nodes rendered is an 8-voxel block. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodetimevaryingvolume(volumes): """ Encodes a sequence of volume datasets using quantization and octree-difference encoding. volumes: List of 3D arrays, where volumes[t] is the volume at time step t. Returns: A list of merged octree structures, one for each time step (or merged references). """ encodedtrees = [] prevtree = None for t, volume in enumerate(volumes): # Step 1: Quantize # Choose quantization method based on dataset statistics (e.g., Uniform, Non-Uniform II) # Implementation detail: Apply chosen quantization map to volume quantizedvolume = applyquantization(volume, method=getquantizationmethod(volume)) # Step 2: Build Octree # Fuse neighboring voxels with similar values into macro voxels currenttree = buildoctree(quantizedvolume) # Step 3: Tree Merging (Temporal Coherence) # If currenttree is identical to prevtree, merge them # Implementation detail: Compare tree structure and leaf values if prevtree is not None and treesareidentical(currenttree, prevtree): mergedtree = mergetrees(currenttree, prevtree) encodedtrees.append(mergedtree) else: encodedtrees.append(currenttree) prevtree = currenttree return encodedtrees def rendertimevaryingvolume(encodedtrees, transferfunction, opacitymap): """ Renders frames from the encoded trees using selective rendering. encodedtrees: List of octree structures (or merged references). transferfunction: Maps voxel values to color and opacity. opacitymap: Defines opacity thresholds for skipping transparent blocks. Returns: Rendered image for the current time step. """ # Implementation detail: Determine current time step t currenttree = encodedtrees[currenttimestep] # Initialize image buffer image = createemptyimage() # Step 4: Selective Rendering via Tree Traversal for ray in raysforimage(image): color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Initial transparent color accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Traverse the tree along the ray node = traversetree(currenttree, ray) while node is not None: if node.isleaf(): # Check if node represents transparent space if istransparent(node.value, opacitymap): # Skip rendering transparent blocks node = getnextnodeinray(node, ray) continue # Check if node represents uniform space if isuniform(node.value): # Render as a block without ray marching # Implementation detail: Compute color for the block blockcolor = computeuniformblockcolor(node.value, transferfunction) # Front-to-back compositing color = compositefronttoback(color, blockcolor, node.opacity) accumulatedopacity += node.opacity if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break # Early termination else: # Non-uniform space: Ray march through the block # Implementation detail: Sample voxels within the block for sample in raysampleswithinblock(node, ray): val = samplevalue(sample, node) c, a = transferfunction(val) color = compositefronttoback(color, c, a) accumulatedopacity += a if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break else: # Internal node: Continue traversal to children node = getnextnodeinray(node, ray) setpixel(image, ray, color) return image Minimum Renderable Block Size: 8 voxels. The renderer can be configured to stop at any depth, but the minimum number of nodes rendered is an 8-voxel block. Image Size: Timing measurements were conducted at 128x128 pixels. Quantization Method: Varies by dataset (Uniform, Non-Uniform I, Non-Uniform II, Adaptive). Small Block Compression: Compression resulting from merging 1-voxel or 8-voxel blocks is not useful for rendering performance. A single voxel change causes surrounding voxels to be re-rendered, negating the benefit. Overhead vs. Gain: Datasets with many small matching blocks and few large matching blocks (e.g., turbulent shear flow with non-uniform quantization) incur overhead from the octree structure that exceeds the gains from compression, leading to slower rendering than baseline. Compression Threshold: If data are compressed by less than 50%, unless many large subtrees were merged, little rendering performance gain can be obtained. Opacity Dependence: Optimizations such as moving past transparent blocks and early termination are highly dependent on opacity maps. Using different opacity maps can dramatically change rendering times. A rendering strategy tailored to tree structures that allows efficient rendering by reusing partial images built from subtrees that have not changed between time steps. It restructures a ray-casting volume renderer to efficiently render encoded data and performs selective rendering based on the tree representation to reduce I/O costs. This strategy is a key component of the twd-renderer, enabling the majority of the speedup observed in time-varying sequences. Time Complexity: Encoding takes ~0.5 seconds per time step for quantization and 3-5 seconds for octree-difference encoding on a SUN Ultra Sparc. For 100 time steps, total encoding takes 5-10 minutes. Rendering time depends on the number of large matching blocks (4096 voxels or larger). Memory Complexity: Compression rates vary by dataset and quantization method. For example, Jets dataset achieves 98% compression with Uniform quantization, while Shear flow achieves 91%. Measured Performance: Turbulent Jet Flow: First image rendered in 2.65 seconds, subsequent images at an average of 0.55 seconds. This represents an 80% increase in rendering rate between first and consecutive images and an 88% increase in overall rendering rate. Heart Dataset: 93% increase in overall rendering rate. Turbulent Shear Flow: Rendering time increases with non-uniform quantization due to many small matching blocks. At time step 30 with uniform quantization, the number of 32768-voxel blocks increases, causing an immediate response in rendering time. Scaling: Rendering at 256x256 requires approximately two to three times as long as rendering at 128x128. Strengths: Significant reduction in storage space (up to 90%) and inter-frame delay (up to 90%). High rendering rate improvements for datasets with large uniform/transparent regions and high compression rates. Limitations: Overhead from octree structure can exceed gains for datasets with many small matching blocks. Performance is highly dependent on opacity maps and transfer functions. Compression must be high (>50%) and involve large blocks to be effective. When to Use: Time-varying volume data with high spatial and temporal coherence, large uniform/transparent regions, and high compression rates. When Not to Use: Datasets with many small matching blocks and few large matching blocks, or when compression rate is low (<50%) without large subtree merges. The method was developed for the 'twd-renderer' for time-varying volume data visualization. It builds on the concept of using octree compression to fit multiple timesteps into main memory, overcoming GPU memory and bus bandwidth limitations [Parent]. The technique was presented in a 1998 NASA Technical Report and DTIC document. The research demonstrated that combining spatial compression (octree) and temporal compression (tree merging) could achieve tremendous savings in storage and rendering time, justifying interactive visualization of time-varying data. name: Triadic frequency band decomposition
head: Hierarchical Data Decomposition, Hierarchical quantization scheme
body: Triadic frequency band decomposition is a volume data compression method that partitions a scalar field into disjoint 4^3 blocks and decomposes each block into a multiresolution representation of three triadic frequency bands: high-frequency differences, mid-frequency differences, and mean. It solves the problem of efficient storage and rendering of large volumetric datasets by reducing data size through vector quantization of these bands. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Wavelet-based Volume Rendering or Laplacian Pyramid, is its specific use of a fixed 4^3 block size with a two-level hierarchical downsampling (factor of 2) to generate exactly three bands (64, 8, and 1 components), and its reliance on a specific GPU-friendly texture-based decoding architecture using dependent texture fetches. Input: A 3D scalar field V of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Output: An RGB index texture I of size (Nx/4) \times (Ny/4) \times (Nz/4), and two codebook textures C1 and C2, and an address texture A. The method relies on four primary data structures stored in GPU textures: 1. Index Texture I: Dimensions: (Nx/4) \times (Ny/4) \times (Nz/4). Format: RGB 8-bit per channel. Layout: R: 8-bit mean value of the block. G: 8-bit index into Codebook C1 (high-frequency band). B: 8-bit index into Codebook C2 (mid-frequency band). 2. Codebook C1: Dimensions: 256 \times 64 (2D texture). Format: Floating-point per component. Layout: Indexed by s (0-255) and t (0-63). The s-coordinate comes from the G-component of I, and the t-coordinate comes from the R-component of Address Texture A. Stores 64-component codewords representing high-frequency differences. 3. Codebook C2: Dimensions: 256 \times 8 (2D texture). Format: Floating-point per component. Layout: Indexed by s (0-255) and t (0-7). The s-coordinate comes from the B-component of I, and the t-coordinate comes from the G-component of Address Texture A. Stores 8-component codewords representing mid-frequency differences. 4. Address Texture A: Dimensions: 4^3 = 64 texels (mapped as a 2D texture). Format: RGB. Layout: R: 64 distinct addresses (indices into C1's t-coordinate). G: 8 distinct addresses (indices into C2's t-coordinate). B: Unused or padding. Interpolation: Nearest-neighbor. Blocks of 2^3 adjacent texels are assigned the same address for C2 to yield the 8 necessary values. 1. Partitioning: Divide the input volume V into disjoint blocks of size 4^3 voxels. 2. First Downsampling (High-Frequency Band): Down-sample each 4^3 block by a factor of 2 by averaging disjoint sets of 2^3 voxels each to create a coarser 2^3 representation. Calculate the difference between each of the 64 original data samples and the respective down-sampled value, storing these in a 64-component vector D1. 3. Second Downsampling (Mid-Frequency Band): Apply the same down-sampling process to the 2^3 mean values to produce one single value representing the mean of the entire block. Store the 2^3 difference values (carrying information lost when going from the 2^3 mean values to the final one) in an 8-component vector D2. 4. Mean Storage: Store the single mean value of the entire block in a 1-component vector. 5. Thresholding: Apply thresholding to vectors D1 and D2: if detail coefficients are small or zero (in homogeneous or empty regions), map the vector to the zero vector to maximize codeword usage for significant non-zero vectors and increase quantization performance. 6. Vector Quantization: Quantize each frequency band separately using vector quantization, then assemble the original signal from these contributions to enhance fidelity. Quantize D1 using codebook C1 (length 256) and D2 using codebook C2 (length 256), storing the resulting indices as 8-bit values. Quantize the mean directly as an 8-bit value without a codebook lookup. 7. Packaging: Store the 8-bit mean in the R-component of I, the C1 index in the G-component, and the C2 index in the B-component. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triadicdecomposition(volume, codebookc1, codebookc2, threshold=0.0): """ Compresses a volume using Triadic Frequency Band Decomposition. Args: volume: 3D list/array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) codebookc1: 2D list/array of shape (256, 64) codebookc2: 2D list/array of shape (256, 8) threshold: Minimum absolute value to keep a difference vector non-zero Returns: indextexture: 3D list/array of shape (Nx/4, Ny/4, Nz/4), dtype uint8, RGB """ Nx, Ny, Nz = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) assert Nx % 4 == 0 and Ny % 4 == 0 and Nz % 4 == 0 indextexture = [[[0, 0, 0] for in range(Nz // 4)] for in range(Ny // 4)] for x in range(0, Nx, 4): for y in range(0, Ny, 4): for z in range(0, Nz, 4): # Extract 4x4x4 block block = [[[volume[x+dx][y+dy][z+dz] for dz in range(4)] for dy in range(4)] for dx in range(4)] # Step 1: High-frequency band (64 components) # Downsample by averaging disjoint 2x2x2 sets downsampled2x2x2 = [[[0.0 for in range(2)] for in range(2)] for in range(2)] for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): regionsum = 0.0 for di in range(2): for dj in range(2): for dk in range(2): regionsum += block[2i+di][2j+dj][2k+dk] downsampled2x2x2[i][j][k] = regionsum / 8.0 # Calculate differences for the 64 voxels d1 = [0.0] 64 for dx in range(4): for dy in range(4): for dz in range(4): regioni = dx // 2 regionj = dy // 2 regionk = dz // 2 diff = block[dx][dy][dz] - downsampled2x2x2[regioni][regionj][regionk] idx = dx 16 + dy 4 + dz d1[idx] = diff # Step 2: Mid-frequency band (8 components) # Downsample 2x2x2 to 1x1x1 (global mean) globalmean = 0.0 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): globalmean += downsampled2x2x2[i][j][k] globalmean /= 8.0 # Calculate differences for the 8 downsampled values d2 = [0.0] 8 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): idx = i 4 + j 2 + k d2[idx] = downsampled2x2x2[i][j][k] - globalmean # Step 3: Mean meanval = globalmean # Step 4: Thresholding if max(abs(v) for v in d1) < threshold: d1 = [0.0] 64 if max(abs(v) for v in d2) < threshold: d2 = [0.0] 8 # Step 5: Vector Quantization idx1 = findbestcodebookentry(d1, codebookc1) idx2 = findbestcodebookentry(d2, codebookc2) # Step 6: Quantize mean to 8-bit # Assuming input volume is normalized to [0, 255] range for 8-bit storage mean8bit = int(round(meanval)) mean8bit = max(0, min(255, mean8bit)) # Step 7: Store in Index Texture indextexture[x//4][y//4][z//4] = [mean8bit, idx1, idx2] return indextexture def findbestcodebookentry(vector, codebook): """Finds the index of the codeword minimizing Euclidean distance.""" bestidx = 0 mindist = float('inf') for i in range(len(codebook)): dist = sum((vector[k] - codebook[i][k])2 for k in range(len(vector))) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestidx = i return bestidx Block Size: 4^3 voxels. Down-sampling Factor: 2. Codebook Length: 256 entries for both C1 and C2. Index Size: 8-bit per index. Mean Size: 8-bit. Threshold: Not given in the sources. A small epsilon or a fraction of the data range is typically used. Homogeneous Regions: Thresholding maps these to zero vectors. This maximizes the usage of codewords for significant non-zero vectors and increases quantization performance. Boundary Conditions: The source assumes volume dimensions are divisible by 4 for uniform block partitioning. Handling non-divisible dimensions is not specified in the sources. Standard practice is to pad the volume to the nearest multiple of 4. Precision: The mean is stored as an 8-bit value, which may introduce quantization error for the DC component. The AC components are reconstructed from codebooks, which also have quantization error. This method is designed to be rendered directly from the compressed domain using GPU fragment shaders, avoiding full decompression. It builds on Value compression. The core quantization technique used for the difference bands. See Vector Quantization. Time Complexity: Encoding processes each voxel once in block-wise fashion, yielding O(N) time complexity. Decoding performs O(1) texture lookups and additions per voxel during rendering. Memory Complexity: The index texture occupies 3 \times (Nx/4)(Ny/4)(Nz/4) bytes. Codebooks C1 and C2 occupy 256 \times 64 and 256 \times 8 elements respectively. This yields a compressed size significantly smaller than the original Nx Ny Nz voxels. Measured Performance: The method was tested on an ATI 9700 GPU. The use of dependent texture fetches allows for efficient on-chip decoding. Strengths: High compression ratio, efficient GPU rendering, enhanced fidelity through separate quantization of bands. Limitations: Fixed block size, requires specific GPU features (dependent texture fetches), codebook training is required. The method was introduced in the paper "Compression Domain Volume Rendering". It was developed to enable real-time volume rendering of large datasets by compressing the data in a way that is compatible with GPU hardware, specifically leveraging the ATI 9700's capabilities for per-fragment arithmetic and dependent texture fetches. Compression Domain Volume Rendering, https://www.cs.cit.tum.de/fileadmin/w00cfj/cg/Research/Publications/2003/CompressionDomainVolumeRendering/vis03-vq.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Rational Bézier Deblocking Filter
head: Deblocking Filter (Rational Bézier), Deblocking filter based on projecting voxel scalar values onto rational Bézier curves, Rational Bézier filtering
body:
The Rational Bézier Deblocking Filter is a post-processing technique for GPU volume rendering that reduces blocking artifacts at block boundaries in compressed volumetric data without requiring prior knowledge of the compression algorithm or modification of the encoded data. It distinguishes itself from standard deblocking methods by projecting voxel scalar values onto rational Bézier curves, where adjustable weights based on local gradient magnitude allow for adaptive filtering that preserves sharp features while smoothing discontinuities. Unlike simple averaging or standard Bézier filtering, this method provides a more accurate approximation of the uncompressed signal by weighting control points according to feature importance. The filter operates on a volumetric scalar field V that has been subdivided into blocks, compressed, and decompressed. It is a block-aware, data-dependent filter applied sequentially along the three main axes (X, Y, Z). Input: A decompressed volumetric scalar field V = f(x) where x \in \mathbb{R}^3, subdivided into a set of blocks B. The field contains compressed intensity values I(y) for each sample y. Output: A filtered volumetric scalar field with modified voxel intensities If at block boundaries. Volumetric Field V: A 3D array of scalar values representing the decompressed volume. Blocks B: The volume is partitioned into fixed-size blocks (e.g., 8 	imes 8 	imes 8 voxels). Gradient Field: A 3D array storing the gradient magnitude |
abla v| for each voxel v, computed via central differences. \lambda: A user-defined parameter controlling the intensity of the filtering and the trade-off between artifact removal and feature preservation. The typical value is \lambda = 3. 1. Feature Detection: Compute the gradient magnitude |
abla si| for every voxel si in the volume V using the central differences method. 2. Weight Calculation: For each voxel si, compute the weight \omegai using the exponential function: \omegai = e^{\lambda(1 - |
abla si|)} This assigns higher weights to voxels with low gradient magnitudes (homogeneous regions) and lower weights to voxels with high gradient magnitudes (features). 3. Axis-Aligned Filtering: Apply the filter sequentially along the X, Y, and Z axes. For each axis direction: Identify pairs of adjacent blocks bi and b{i+1} along the current axis. For each boundary between bi and b{i+1}, extract sets of axis-aligned samples S that traverse the boundary. Each set S consists of voxels from bi and b{i+1} aligned along the filtering direction. For each sample s \in S, determine its position ts \in [0, 1] within the set S, where ts=0 corresponds to the first control point and ts=1 to the last. Compute the filtered intensity If(ts) using the rational Bézier formula: If(ts) =  rac{\sum{j=0}^{n}  inom{n}{j} ts^j (1 - ts)^{n-j} I(sj) \omegaj}{\sum{j=0}^{n}  inom{n}{j} ts^j (1 - ts)^{n-j} \omegaj} where n is the number of samples in S, I(sj) is the compressed intensity of the j-th control point, and \omegaj is its weight. Update the intensity of the voxels closer to the border (typically the half of the voxels in each block adjacent to the boundary) with the computed filtered values. 4. Final Intensity: For each voxel v, compute the final intensity If(v) as the average of the three filtered values obtained from the X, Y, and Z passes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computegradientmagnitude(volume, blocksize): """ Computes the gradient magnitude for each voxel in the volume using central differences. volume: 3D list or array of scalar values. blocksize: int, size of each block dimension (assumed cubic). Returns: 3D array of gradient magnitudes. """ dims = volume.shape gradmag = [[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for z in range(dims[2]): for y in range(dims[1]): for x in range(dims[0]): # Central differences dx = 0.0 dy = 0.0 dz = 0.0 # X gradient if x == 0: dx = volume[1][y][z] - volume[0][y][z] elif x == dims[0] - 1: dx = volume[x][y][z] - volume[x-1][y][z] else: dx = (volume[x+1][y][z] - volume[x-1][y][z]) / 2.0 # Y gradient if y == 0: dy = volume[x][1][z] - volume[x][0][z] elif y == dims[1] - 1: dy = volume[x][y][z] - volume[x][y-1][z] else: dy = (volume[x][y+1][z] - volume[x][y-1][z]) / 2.0 # Z gradient if z == 0: dz = volume[x][y][1] - volume[x][y][0] elif z == dims[2] - 1: dz = volume[x][y][z] - volume[x][y][z-1] else: dz = (volume[x][y][z+1] - volume[x][y][z-1]) / 2.0 gradmag[y][x] = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) return gradmag def computeweight(gradmag, lambdaparam): """ Computes the weight for a voxel based on its gradient magnitude. gradmag: float, gradient magnitude of the voxel. lambdaparam: float, filtering intensity parameter. Returns: float, weight omega. """ return math.exp(lambdaparam (1.0 - gradmag)) def rationalbezierfilter(samples, weights): """ Projects samples onto a rational Bézier curve. samples: list of floats, compressed intensities I(sj). weights: list of floats, weights omegaj. Returns: list of floats, filtered intensities If(ts). """ n = len(samples) filtered = [] for i in range(n): t = i / (n - 1) if n > 1 else 0.0 numerator = 0.0 denominator = 0.0 for j in range(n): # Binomial coefficient C(n, j) # Note: For large n, this should be computed carefully to avoid overflow. # Here we assume n is small (e.g., block size). binom = math.comb(n, j) basis = binom (t j) ((1 - t) (n - j)) numerator += basis samples[j] weights[j] denominator += basis weights[j] if denominator == 0: filtered.append(samples[i]) else: filtered.append(numerator / denominator) return filtered def deblockvolume(volume, blocksize, lambdaparam): """ Applies the Rational Bézier Deblocking Filter to the entire volume. volume: 3D array of compressed scalar values. blocksize: int, size of each block. lambdaparam: float, filtering parameter (typically 3). Returns: 3D array of filtered scalar values. """ dims = volume.shape # Copy volume to avoid modifying input filteredvolume = [row[:] for row in volume] # Step 1: Compute gradient magnitude gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(volume, blocksize) # Precompute weights for all voxels weights = [[computeweight(gradmag[y][x], lambdaparam) for x in range(dims[0])] for y in range(dims[1])] # Step 2: Apply filter along X, Y, Z axes # We need to store intermediate results for each axis pass # Pass 1: X-axis xfiltered = [row[:] for row in volume] for z in range(dims[2]): for y in range(dims[1]): # Process each block row along X for blockstartx in range(0, dims[0], blocksize): blockendx = min(blockstartx + blocksize, dims[0]) # Identify boundary with next block # The filter modifies voxels closer to the border (half the block) # We consider the boundary between blockstartx and blockstartx + blocksize # If it's the last block, no boundary to the right if blockendx >= dims[0]: continue # Define the set S of samples crossing the boundary # The boundary is at x = blockendx # Samples from the right side of the current block and left side of the next block # The text says "all axis-aligned voxels of bi and bi+1 at a certain point of the boundary" # This implies a 1D line of samples along the X axis crossing the boundary. # However, the formula uses n samples. In a 3D volume, a "line" has length. # The text says "half the voxels of each block" are modified. # Let's assume the set S consists of the voxels in the current block and the next block # that are part of the same X-axis line segment crossing the boundary. # Actually, the text says "computing all the rational Bézier curves that traverse it, # where each curve is defined by all the axis-aligned voxels of bi and bi+1". # This suggests that for a specific Y, Z, we take the X-axis samples from bi and bi+1. # Let's extract the samples for this specific (y, z) line crossing the boundary # The boundary is between blockstartx + blocksize - 1 and blockstartx + blocksize # The samples involved are those in bi and bi+1 along this line. # The text says "half the voxels of each block" are modified. # So we take the first half of bi and the first half of bi+1? # Or the voxels closest to the boundary? # "voxels closer to the border (half the voxels of each block)" # Let's assume the set S is the entire block bi and bi+1 along the X axis for this (y,z). # But the formula is for a 1D curve. # If S is the whole block, n = 2 blocksize. # Then we project all samples onto the curve. # Then we update the "voxels closer to the border". # Let's implement the general case: S is the concatenation of the X-axis samples # from block bi and block bi+1 for the current (y, z). samplesbi = [volume[x][y][z] for x in range(blockstartx, blockendx)] samplesbi1 = [volume[x][y][z] for x in range(blockendx, min(blockendx + blocksize, dims[0]))] if not samplesbi1: continue samplesS = samplesbi + samplesbi1 weightsS = [weights[y][x] for x in range(blockstartx, blockendx)] + \ [weights[y][x] for x in range(blockendx, min(blockendx + blocksize, dims[0]))] filteredS = rationalbezierfilter(samplesS, weightsS) # Update the voxels closer to the border (half the voxels of each block) # Half of bi: the last half of bi (closest to boundary) # Half of bi+1: the first half of bi+1 (closest to boundary) halfbi = blocksize // 2 halfbi1 = len(samplesbi1) // 2 # Update bi's last half for i in range(halfbi): xidx = blockendx - halfbi + i if xidx < dims[0]: xfiltered[xidx][y][z] = filteredS[blocksize - halfbi + i] # Update bi+1's first half for i in range(halfbi1): xidx = blockendx + i if xidx < dims[0]: xfiltered[xidx][y][z] = filteredS[blocksize + i] # Pass 2: Y-axis (using xfiltered as input) yfiltered = [row[:] for row in xfiltered] for z in range(dims[2]): for x in range(dims[0]): for blockstarty in range(0, dims[1], blocksize): blockendy = min(blockstarty + blocksize, dims[1]) if blockendy >= dims[1]: continue samplesbi = [xfiltered[x][y][z] for y in range(blockstarty, blockendy)] samplesbi1 = [xfiltered[x][y][z] for y in range(blockendy, min(blockendy + blocksize, dims[1]))] if not samplesbi1: continue samplesS = samplesbi + samplesbi1 weightsS = [weights[y][x] for y in range(blockstarty, blockendy)] + \ [weights[y][x] for y in range(blockendy, min(blockendy + blocksize, dims[1]))] filteredS = rationalbezierfilter(samplesS, weightsS) halfbi = blocksize // 2 halfbi1 = len(samplesbi1) // 2 for i in range(halfbi): yidx = blockendy - halfbi + i if yidx < dims[1]: yfiltered[x][yidx][z] = filteredS[blocksize - halfbi + i] for i in range(halfbi1): yidx = blockendy + i if yidx < dims[1]: yfiltered[x][yidx][z] = filteredS[blocksize + i] # Pass 3: Z-axis (using yfiltered as input) zfiltered = [[[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] for y in range(dims[1]): for x in range(dims[0]): for blockstartz in range(0, dims[2], blocksize): blockendz = min(blockstartz + blocksize, dims[2]) if blockendz >= dims[2]: continue samplesbi = [yfiltered[x][y][z] for z in range(blockstartz, blockendz)] samplesbi1 = [yfiltered[x][y][z] for z in range(blockendz, min(blockendz + blocksize, dims[2]))] if not samplesbi1: continue samplesS = samplesbi + samplesbi1 weightsS = [weights[y][x] for z in range(blockstartz, blockendz)] + \ [weights[y][x] for z in range(blockendz, min(blockendz + blocksize, dims[2]))] filteredS = rationalbezierfilter(samplesS, weightsS) halfbi = blocksize // 2 halfbi1 = len(samplesbi1) // 2 for i in range(halfbi): zidx = blockendz - halfbi + i if zidx < dims[2]: zfiltered[x][y][zidx] = filteredS[blocksize - halfbi + i] for i in range(halfbi1): zidx = blockendz + i if zidx < dims[2]: zfiltered[x][y][zidx] = filteredS[blocksize + i] # Step 4: Final intensity is the average of the three filtered values # Note: The text says "The final intensity If(tv) of a given voxel v, is computed as the average of its three filtered values (one for each axis)." # This implies we need to store the result of each axis pass and average them. # However, the pseudocode above updates in place. To be precise, we should store the three results. # Let's restart the logic to store three separate volumes. # Re-doing with explicit storage for clarity and correctness volx = [[[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] voly = [[[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] volz = [[[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] # X Pass for z in range(dims[2]): for y in range(dims[1]): for blockstartx in range(0, dims[0], blocksize): blockendx = min(blockstartx + blocksize, dims[0]) if blockendx >= dims[0]: continue samplesbi = [volume[x][y][z] for x in range(blockstartx, blockendx)] samplesbi1 = [volume[x][y][z] for x in range(blockendx, min(blockendx + blocksize, dims[0]))] if not samplesbi1: continue samplesS = samplesbi + samplesbi1 weightsS = [weights[y][x] for x in range(blockstartx, blockendx)] + [weights[y][x] for x in range(blockendx, min(blockendx + blocksize, dims[0]))] filteredS = rationalbezierfilter(samplesS, weightsS) halfbi = blocksize // 2 halfbi1 = len(samplesbi1) // 2 for i in range(halfbi): xidx = blockendx - halfbi + i if xidx < dims[0]: volx[xidx][y][z] = filteredS[blocksize - halfbi + i] for i in range(halfbi1): xidx = blockendx + i if xidx < dims[0]: volx[xidx][y][z] = filteredS[blocksize + i] # Voxels not in the border half remain unchanged? The text says "voxels closer to the border... are modified". # So interior voxels keep their original value. for x in range(blockstartx, blockendx): if x < blockendx - halfbi: volx[x][y][z] = volume[x][y][z] for x in range(blockendx, min(blockendx + blocksize, dims[0])): if x >= blockendx + halfbi1: volx[x][y][z] = volume[x][y][z] # Y Pass for z in range(dims[2]): for x in range(dims[0]): for blockstarty in range(0, dims[1], blocksize): blockendy = min(blockstarty + blocksize, dims[1]) if blockendy >= dims[1]: continue samplesbi = [volx[x][y][z] for y in range(blockstarty, blockendy)] samplesbi1 = [volx[x][y][z] for y in range(blockendy, min(blockendy + blocksize, dims[1]))] if not samplesbi1: continue samplesS = samplesbi + samplesbi1 weightsS = [weights[y][x] for y in range(blockstarty, blockendy)] + [weights[y][x] for y in range(blockendy, min(blockendy + blocksize, dims[1]))] filteredS = rationalbezierfilter(samplesS, weightsS) halfbi = blocksize // 2 halfbi1 = len(samplesbi1) // 2 for i in range(halfbi): yidx = blockendy - halfbi + i if yidx < dims[1]: voly[x][yidx][z] = filteredS[blocksize - halfbi + i] for i in range(halfbi1): yidx = blockendy + i if yidx < dims[1]: voly[x][yidx][z] = filteredS[blocksize + i] for y in range(blockstarty, blockendy): if y < blockendy - halfbi: voly[x][y][z] = volx[x][y][z] for y in range(blockendy, min(blockendy + blocksize, dims[1])): if y >= blockendy + halfbi1: voly[x][y][z] = volx[x][y][z] # Z Pass for y in range(dims[1]): for x in range(dims[0]): for blockstartz in range(0, dims[2], blocksize): blockendz = min(blockstartz + blocksize, dims[2]) if blockendz >= dims[2]: continue samplesbi = [voly[x][y][z] for z in range(blockstartz, blockendz)] samplesbi1 = [voly[x][y][z] for z in range(blockendz, min(blockendz + blocksize, dims[2]))] if not samplesbi1: continue samplesS = samplesbi + samplesbi1 weightsS = [weights[y][x] for z in range(blockstartz, blockendz)] + [weights[y][x] for z in range(blockendz, min(blockendz + blocksize, dims[2]))] filteredS = rationalbezierfilter(samplesS, weightsS) halfbi = blocksize // 2 halfbi1 = len(samplesbi1) // 2 for i in range(halfbi): zidx = blockendz - halfbi + i if zidx < dims[2]: volz[x][y][zidx] = filteredS[blocksize - halfbi + i] for i in range(halfbi1): zidx = blockendz + i if zidx < dims[2]: volz[x][y][zidx] = filteredS[blocksize + i] for z in range(blockstartz, blockendz): if z < blockendz - halfbi: volz[x][y][z] = voly[x][y][z] for z in range(blockendz, min(blockendz + blocksize, dims[2])): if z >= blockendz + halfbi1: volz[x][y][z] = voly[x][y][z] # Final Average result = [[[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] for z in range(dims[2]): for y in range(dims[1]): for x in range(dims[0]): result[x][y][z] = (volx[x][y][z] + voly[x][y][z] + volz[x][y][z]) / 3.0 return result Precision: The computation involves binomial coefficients and powers, which can lead to numerical instability for large n (block sizes). Implementers should use stable algorithms for binomial coefficients and basis functions. Boundaries: The filter is applied only at internal block boundaries. Voxels in the interior of blocks are not modified in the respective axis pass. Homogeneous Regions: In homogeneous regions, gradient magnitudes are low, resulting in weights close to e^\lambda. This leads to subtle filtering, preserving the original signal closely. High Gradient Regions: In regions with high gradients, weights are low, allowing more smoothing to remove artifacts while preserving the feature shape. Time Complexity: The filter is computationally intensive due to the per-voxel gradient computation and the rational Bézier projection for each block boundary. It achieves interactive frame rates on standard graphics PCs but requires optimization for speed. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the original volume, gradient magnitude field, and intermediate filtered volumes for the three axis passes. Performance: Provides SSIM gains of 5–7% for K-SVD compression and 6–11% for HVQ compression. MS-SSIM gains are 2–8% for K-SVD and 4–6% for HVQ. Strengths: Works without knowledge of the compression technique; does not require modifying the compressed data format; preserves local features better than simple averaging or standard Bézier filtering. Limitations: Computationally intensive; effectiveness depends on the choice of \lambda. The Rational Bézier Deblocking Filter was introduced by F. Marton, José A. Iglesias Guitián, Jose Díaz, and Enrico Gobbetti in the paper "Real-time Deblocked GPU Rendering of Compressed Volumes" (2014). It was developed to address the visual quality degradation caused by blocking artifacts in compressed volumetric data during real-time GPU rendering. The method extends deferred filtering architectures to support adaptive multi-resolution data loading and levels of detail.
