name: Vector-Matrix (VM) Decomposition
head: Tensor Decomposition, VM decomposition
body: Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition is a tensor factorization technique that relaxes the low-rank constraints for two modes of a tensor by factorizing it into compact vector and matrix factors, effectively acting as a special case of Block Term Decomposition (BTD). Unlike CP Decomposition, which uses a sum of outer products of pure vectors, VM uses a sum of vector-matrix outer products. This allows each component to express more complex tensor data of higher ranks, significantly reducing the required number of components compared to CP while maintaining a memory complexity of O(N^2) compared to the O(N^3) of dense grids. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D tensor \mathcal{T} of dimensions I \times J \times K (e.g., representing a radiance field feature grid). Output: A set of vector factors \mathbf{v} and matrix factors \mathbf{M} that approximate \mathcal{T}. Data Structures The decomposition represents the tensor as a sum of three types of components, one for each mode being the "rank-one" vector. For a tensor with modes corresponding to spatial axes X, Y, Z (with dimensions I, J, K respectively), the factors are: 1. X-mode components: A vector \mathbf{v}r^X \in \mathbb{R}^I and a matrix \mathbf{M}r^{Y,Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times K}. 2. Y-mode components: A vector \mathbf{v}r^Y \in \mathbb{R}^J and a matrix \mathbf{M}r^{X,Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times K}. 3. Z-mode components: A vector \mathbf{v}r^Z \in \mathbb{R}^K and a matrix \mathbf{M}r^{X,Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J}. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the vector factors \mathbf{v}r^X, \mathbf{v}r^Y, \mathbf{v}r^Z and matrix factors \mathbf{M}r^{Y,Z}, \mathbf{M}r^{X,Z}, \mathbf{M}r^{X,Y} with random values or via a CP decomposition initialization. 2. Optimization: Minimize the reconstruction error between the original tensor \mathcal{T} and the decomposed approximation using gradient descent. The decomposition acts as a low-rank regularization term during the optimization of the radiance field. 3. Evaluation: To evaluate the tensor at any point (or for rendering), compute the sum of the outer products of the learned factors according to the formula above. Formulas The tensor \mathcal{T} is decomposed as: \mathcal{T} = \sum{r=1}^{R1} \mathbf{v}r^1 \circ \mathbf{M}r^{2,3} + \sum{r=1}^{R2} \mathbf{v}r^2 \circ \mathbf{M}r^{1,3} + \sum{r=1}^{R3} \mathbf{v}r^3 \circ \mathbf{M}r^{1,2} Where \circ denotes the outer product between a vector and a matrix. Specifically, for scene modeling with R1=R2=R3=R and axes X,Y,Z, the formula is: \mathcal{T} = \sum{r=1}^R \mathbf{v}r^X \circ \mathbf{M}r^{Y,Z} + \mathbf{v}r^Y \circ \mathbf{M}r^{X,Z} + \mathbf{v}r^Z \circ \mathbf{M}r^{X,Y} The element \mathcal{T}{ijk} is computed as: \mathcal{T}{ijk} = \sum{r=1}^R \sum{m \in \{X, Y, Z\}} \mathcal{A}{r,ijk}^m Where the component tensors \mathcal{A} are defined as: \mathcal{A}{r,ijk}^X = \mathbf{v}{r,i}^X \mathbf{M}{r,jk}^{YZ} \mathcal{A}{r,ijk}^Y = \mathbf{v}{r,j}^Y \mathbf{M}{r,ik}^{XZ} \mathcal{A}{r,ijk}^Z = \mathbf{v}{r,k}^Z \mathbf{M}{r,ij}^{XY} Parameters R1, R2, R3: The number of components for each mode combination. These can be set differently depending on the complexity of each mode. In the context of 3D scene modeling (e.g., TensoRF), it is common to assume equal complexity along axes, setting R1 = R2 = R3 = R. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Gradient-based optimization of the factors can suffer from local minima; careful initialization (e.g., via CP) is recommended. Boundaries: The tensor represents discrete data, so trilinear interpolation is typically applied to model a continuous field during rendering. Degenerate Input: If scene complexity varies significantly across axes, setting R1=R2=R3=R may underfit or overfit specific dimensions; asymmetric R values should be used. Pseudocode The following Python-like pseudocode demonstrates the evaluation of a VM-decomposed tensor element \mathcal{T}{ijk} given the learned factors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatevmtensor(i, j, k, R, vX, MYZ, vY, MXZ, vZ, MXY): """ Evaluate the element at index (i, j, k) of a tensor decomposed via VM. Args: i, j, k: Indices along the three modes (dimensions I, J, K). R: Number of components (assumed equal for all modes). vX: List of R vectors, each of size I. vX[r] is vr^X. MYZ: List of R matrices, each of size J x K. MYZ[r] is Mr^{Y,Z}. vY: List of R vectors, each of size J. vY[r] is vr^Y. MXZ: List of R matrices, each of size I x K. MXZ[r] is Mr^{X,Z}. vZ: List of R vectors, each of size K. vZ[r] is vr^Z. MXY: List of R matrices, each of size I x J. MXY[r] is Mr^{X,Y}. Returns: The scalar value T{ijk}. """ total = 0.0 for r in range(R): # Component type X: vr^X (size I) outer product Mr^{Y,Z} (size J x K) # Element contribution: vr^X[i] Mr^{Y,Z}[j, k] termX = vX[r][i] MYZ[r][j][k] # Component type Y: vr^Y (size J) outer product Mr^{X,Z} (size I x K) # Element contribution: vr^Y[j] Mr^{X,Z}[i, k] termY = vY[r][j] MXZ[r][i][k] # Component type Z: vr^Z (size K) outer product Mr^{X,Y} (size I x J) # Element contribution: vr^Z[k] Mr^{X,Y}[i, j] termZ = vZ[r][k] MXY[r][i][j] total += termX + termY + termZ return total An application of VM decomposition to the density feature grid G\sigma and appearance feature grid Ga, which are composed of two overset tensors (Yin and Yang). The appearance grid Ga is a 4D tensor \mathbb{R}^{2Ny^r \times Ny^\theta \times Ny^\phi \times C}. For the appearance feature mode (C), only vector components \mathbf{b} are assigned instead of matrix components. The decomposition for the appearance grid is given by: \mathcal{G}a^y = \sum{n=1}^{Na} \mathbf{v}{a,n}^{y,R} \otimes \mathbf{M}{a,n}^{y,\Theta\Phi} \otimes \mathbf{b}{3n-2}^y + \mathbf{v}{a,n}^{y,\Theta} \otimes \mathbf{M}{a,n}^{y,\Phi R} \otimes \mathbf{b}{3n-1}^y + \mathbf{v}{a,n}^{y,\Phi} \otimes \mathbf{M}{a,n}^{y,R\Theta} \otimes \mathbf{b}{3n}^y where \mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times 6Na} is a matrix obtained by stacking all \mathbf{b}^y vectors columnwise. The number of decomposed components for the density grid is typically N\sigma = 16. Time Complexity: Reconstruction time is significantly faster than NeRF. TensoRF with VM decomposition achieves reconstruction in less than 10 minutes, which is about 100x faster than NeRF. Memory Complexity: Reduces space complexity from O(N^3) (dense voxel grid) to O(N^2). Model Size: Retains a compact model size of less than 75 MB for typical scenes. Note that VM increases the model size per component compared to CP, but significantly reduces the required number of components R for the same expression capacity. Strengths: Higher expressivity than CP; faster reconstruction than NeRF; lower memory footprint than dense grids. Limitations: Larger model size per component than CP; requires careful tuning of R if scene complexity varies significantly across axes. VM decomposition was proposed in the context of Tensorial Radiance Fields (TensoRF) by Chen et al. in 2022. It is inspired by CP decomposition and Block Term Decomposition (BTD). The method was introduced to address the high computational costs of radiance field reconstruction by providing a more efficient tensor factorization than CP, allowing for faster training and rendering while maintaining high quality. name: Tucker Decomposition (HOSVD)
head: Higher-Order Singular Value Decomposition, Tucker Model
body: Tucker Decomposition (HOSVD) is a global basis generation method that decomposes an N-dimensional input array into N basis matrices and an N-dimensional core tensor. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large volume datasets by reducing the reconstruction rank, thereby achieving data reduction. Unlike its sibling CP Decomposition, which sums rank-one tensors, Tucker Decomposition uses a multilinear product structure, allowing for a more compact representation of correlated data. It is distinguished from its parent Sparse Coding (K-SVD) by its specific application to global multiresolution basis generation for volume rendering, often integrated with octree hierarchies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An N-dimensional input dataset A \in \mathbb{R}^{I1 \times I2 \times \dots \times IN}. Outputs: N basis matrices U^{(n)} \in \mathbb{R}^{In \times Rn} for n=1 \dots N, and an N-dimensional core tensor B \in \mathbb{R}^{R1 \times R2 \times \dots \times RN}. Data Structures: Basis Matrices (U^{(n)}): Each matrix has In rows (corresponding to the spatial resolution in dimension n) and Rn columns (the rank). The rows are orthonormal. Core Tensor (B): An N-dimensional array of size R1 \times R2 \times \dots \times RN. It is "all-orthogonal," meaning the inner product of any two slices along the same mode is zero. Multilinear Rank: Defined as (R1, R2, \dots, RN), where Rn is the rank for dimension n. Parameters: Initial Rank (Rn): Typically chosen as half the input data size in that dimension, i.e., Rn = In / 2. This corresponds to an initial data reduction. Block Rank (for multiresolution): When applied to equally sized blocks of size B, the multilinear rank is often reduced to R1 = R2 = R3 = B/2. Quantization: 8-bit encoding for core tensor coefficients and 16-bit encoding for basis matrices. Steps: 1. Generate Basis Matrices: Apply Higher-Order Singular Value Decomposition (HOSVD) or Higher-Order Orthogonal Iteration (HOOI) to the input volume A along every data direction. HOOI is an Alternating Least Squares (ALS) algorithm that optimizes the basis matrices one after another. 2. Compute Core Tensor: Once the basis matrices U^{(n)} cannot be improved further, compute the core tensor B. B represents the projection of A onto the basis matrices U^{(n)}. The coefficients of B show the relationship between the original data and the bases. 3. Rank Truncation: Apply rank-truncation to the core tensor B. Because B is all-orthogonal, this process is similar to matrix SVD truncation, exploiting the singular values embedded in the diagonal slices of the core tensor. Further adaptive rank reductions can be applied after the initial decomposition. 4. Multiresolution Basis Generation (Optional/Contextual): For multiresolution rendering, generate lower-resolution basis matrices U^{(n)}{\downarrow k} by employing mipmap reduction on the row space of U^{(n)}. 5. Re-orthogonalization: Perform re-orthogonalization to match basis matrix row blocks to multiresolution volume octree nodes. 6. Octree Construction: Define a multiresolution volume octree with one small core tensor per node. Each node's core tensor is constructed by projecting the corresponding input volume brick onto the corresponding basis matrix rows. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tuckerdecompositionhosvd(A, initialranks=None): """ Performs Tucker Decomposition using HOSVD/HOOI. Args: A: Input N-dimensional tensor of shape (I1, I2,..., IN). initialranks: List of ranks (R1, R2,..., RN). If None, defaults to In/2. Returns: U: List of N basis matrices. B: Core tensor. """ N = A.ndim I = A.shape if initialranks is None: initialranks = [I[n] // 2 for n in range(N)] # Step 1: Generate Basis Matrices using HOOI # HOOI optimizes basis matrices one after another via ALS U = [] for n in range(N): # Mode-n unfolding of A Aunfolded = modenunfold(A, n) # Compute initial basis from SVD of unfolded matrix # Uninit, Sn, Vn = svd(Aunfolded) # Select top Rn columns Rn = initialranks[n] Un,, = truncatedsvd(Aunfolded, k=Rn) # Optimize Un using ALS (HOOI) # Iterate until convergence: # For each mode m != n: # Compute projection of A onto other bases # Update Un via SVD of the projected matrix # Standard HOOI implementation details omitted for brevity # but must ensure Un remains orthonormal. Un = hooioptimizemoden(A, U, n) U.append(Un) # Step 2: Compute Core Tensor B # B is the projection of A onto the basis matrices U # B = A x1 U1^T x2 U2^T... xN UN^T B = A for n in range(N): # Tensor-times-matrix product along mode n # B = B xn (U[n]^T) B = modentensormatrixproduct(B, U[n].T, n) # Step 3: Rank Truncation (Optional) # Exploit all-orthogonal property of B # In practice, compute singular values of core tensor slices # and truncate dimensions where singular values are small. # B = truncatecoretensor(B, targetranks) return U, B def modenunfold(A, n): """Unfolds tensor A into a matrix along mode n.""" # Reshape A such that mode n is the row dimension # and all other modes are combined into the column dimension pass def truncatedsvd(M, k): """Returns the top k left singular vectors of M.""" U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M, fullmatrices=False) return U[:,:k], S[:k], Vt[:k,:] def hooioptimizemoden(A, U, n): """ Optimizes the n-th basis matrix U[n] using Alternating Least Squares. Assumes other U[m] are fixed. """ # Compute the product of all other basis matrices # This effectively projects A into the subspace defined by other bases # Implementation involves tensor contractions or unfolding # followed by SVD to update U[n]. pass def modentensormatrixproduct(T, M, n): """ Computes the tensor-matrix product T xn M. """ # Reshape T, multiply M along mode n, reshape back pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Management: Large volumes require memory-mapped files and parallel memory-aligned matrix-matrix multiplications to handle the computational load. Coefficient Ordering: Unlike matrix SVD, the ordering of coefficients in the core tensor B is not strictly decreasing. However, progressive tensor rank truncation still works well in practice for adaptive multiscale reconstruction. Global vs. Local: The global basis approach keeps storage costs low by maintaining only one set of basis matrices, independent of the initial data resolution In. Tensor Approximation (TA) is a volume data compression method that interprets a volume dataset as a multi-dimensional tensor and factorizes it into a set of basis matrices and a core tensor. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large volume datasets by reducing the reconstruction rank, thereby achieving data reduction. Unlike wavelet transforms, rank-reduced TA captures non-axis aligned features at different scales more effectively using the same number of coefficients. It is distinguished from its parent Tucker Decomposition (HOSVD) by its specific integration into a multiresolution octree hierarchy with per-brick Tucker formulation and optimized GPU reconstruction. Time Complexity: The decomposition involves SVDs on unfolded matrices and ALS iterations. The complexity is dominated by the SVDs of the mode-n unfoldings, which are O(In \cdot \prod{m \neq n} Im \cdot Rn) per mode, plus the iterative convergence of HOOI. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N basis matrices of size In \times Rn and a core tensor of size \prod Rn. With Rn = In/2, the storage is significantly reduced compared to the original data I1 \times \dots \times IN. Measured Performance: Achieves good approximation quality and data reduction levels for volume datasets. Strengths: Global bases capture non-axis aligned features effectively. The all-orthogonal core tensor allows for efficient rank truncation. Multiresolution generation via mipmap reduction on basis rows is efficient. Limitations: The coefficient ordering in the core tensor is not strictly decreasing, requiring careful truncation strategies. Large volumes pose memory challenges. When to Use: When global basis generation is desired for multiresolution volume rendering and data reduction is critical. When Not to Use: When local adaptivity is more important than global basis efficiency, or when strict singular value ordering is required for truncation guarantees. Tucker Decomposition, also known as the Tucker Model, was introduced as a generalization of matrix SVD to higher-order tensors. It is also known as Higher-Order PCA. The method was applied to volume rendering by Suter et al. [SMP13] and [SIM11], who exploited the Tucker model for global multiresolution basis generation. This approach allows for the creation of a multiresolution volume octree where each node contains a small core tensor projected from the global basis. name: Tensor Approximation
head: Tensor decomposition, Tucker Decomposition, Tucker formulation tensor approximation
body: Tensor Approximation (TA) is a volume data compression method that interprets a volume dataset as a multi-dimensional tensor and factorizes it into a set of basis matrices and a core tensor. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large volume datasets by reducing the reconstruction rank, thereby achieving data reduction. Unlike wavelet transforms, rank-reduced TA captures non-axis aligned features at different scales more effectively using the same number of coefficients. It is distinguished from its parent Tucker Decomposition (HOSVD) by its specific integration into a multiresolution octree hierarchy with per-brick Tucker formulation and optimized GPU reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset V partitioned into bricks within a multiresolution octree hierarchy. Output: A compressed representation consisting of Tucker factors (basis matrices) and a core tensor for each brick, along with quantized indices or coefficients. Data Structures: Brick: A sub-volume block. Each brick is processed independently using a single TA. Tucker Model: For a brick represented as tensor \mathcal{X}, the approximation is defined by a core tensor \mathcal{G} and factor matrices U^{(n)} for each dimension n: \mathcal{X} \approx \mathcal{G} \times1 U^{(1)} \times2 U^{(2)} \times3 U^{(3)} where \timesn denotes the tensor-times-matrix (TTM) product. Quantization: A tensor-specific quantization scheme is applied to the factors/core to enable efficient storage. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the input volume domain into bricks using a multiresolution octree hierarchy. 2. Decomposition: For each brick, compute the Tucker decomposition. This involves learning data-specific bases (matrices U^{(n)}) and a core tensor \mathcal{G}. 3. Rank Reduction: Reduce the rank of the reconstruction to obtain data reduction. The rank M determines the size of the basis matrices and core tensor. 4. Quantization: Apply the tensor-specific quantization scheme to the decomposed components. 5. GPU Reconstruction: During rendering, decompress the data before the rendering stage using a per-brick solution. Implement TTM multiplications on the GPU. Assign each kernel thread to decompress one voxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but the complexity is linear in M. Brick Size: Determined by the multiresolution octree hierarchy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Quantization errors may affect reconstruction quality. The tensor-specific quantization scheme must be chosen carefully. Boundaries: The method assumes bricks are independent. Boundary artifacts may occur if not handled by the octree structure. Degenerate Input: If a brick has low variance, the rank reduction might discard important features. The learned bases are data-specific, so they must be computed per brick. A hierarchical tensor-based transform where the input volume domain is recursively partitioned into smaller blocks, each defined with a truncated tensor-product basis. It represents the original tensor as a summation of incomplete tensor approximations at multiple levels, where tensors at each level are subdivided into residual tensors passed from the higher levels. This approach differs from standard TA by explicitly modeling residuals across hierarchy levels, allowing for multi-scale approximation. Time and Memory Complexity: The computational complexity of the GPU reconstruction is O(M), growing linearly with the rank M, instead of O(M^3). Memory usage is reduced by the rank reduction and quantization, storing only the Tucker factors and core tensor per brick. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales with the number of bricks and the rank M. The linear complexity O(M) allows for efficient real-time rendering on GPUs. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Captures non-axis aligned features at different scales better than wavelet transforms using the same amount of coefficients. Learned bases are data-specific, enabling effective feature extraction and compression. Limitations: Pre-processing (decomposition and quantization) can be costly. The method requires storing Tucker factors for each brick, which may increase memory overhead compared to simpler methods if the rank is not sufficiently reduced. When to Use: Use when the volume data contains non-axis aligned features and efficient GPU-based rendering is required. Use when data-specific basis learning is beneficial for compression. When Not to Use: Avoid if pre-processing time is a critical constraint and the data does not benefit from learned bases. Avoid if the data is highly axis-aligned, where wavelet transforms might be more efficient. Tensor Approximation was proposed in combination with a multiresolution octree hierarchy [SIM 11]. The same work introduced a tensor-specific quantization scheme and an optimized GPU reconstruction method. The general idea behind tensor decomposition is to approximate a volume dataset with SVD/PCA-like tools, interpreting the volume as a tensor factorized into rank-one tensors (CP decomposition) or a core tensor and matrices (Tucker decomposition) [KB09]. Suter et al. [SZP10] showed that rank-reduced TA is more able to capture non-axis aligned features at different scales than wavelet transforms using the same amount of coefficients. The hierarchical tensor-based transform was proposed by Wu et al. [WXC 08]. name: Hierarchical Tensor-based Transform
head: Wu hierarchical tensor, Wu et al. hierarchical tensor
body: The Hierarchical Tensor-based Transform is a compression scheme for volume data that recursively partitions the input domain into smaller blocks, defining a truncated tensor-product basis for each block. It represents the original volume tensor as a summation of incomplete tensor approximations across multiple resolution levels, where tensors at each level are subdivided into residual tensors passed from higher levels. This method builds on Tensor Approximation by introducing a hierarchical multiresolution structure to the factorization process. Inputs: An input volume dataset represented as a 3D tensor V. Outputs: A set of hierarchical coefficients representing the volume, consisting of truncated tensor-product bases and residual tensors for each partition level. Data Structures: The method relies on a hierarchical partitioning of the domain. While specific bit-packing is not detailed in the sources, the logical structure consists of: 1. Blocks: Recursive subdivisions of the volume domain. 2. Bases: A truncated tensor-product basis defined for each block. 3. Residuals: Residual tensors passed from higher levels to lower levels. Steps: 1. Recursive Partitioning: The entire domain of the input volume is recursively partitioned into smaller blocks. 2. Basis Definition: For each block in the hierarchy, a truncated tensor-product basis is defined. 3. Residual Subdivision: Tensors at each level are subdivided into residual tensors that are passed from the higher levels. 4. Approximation Summation: The original tensor is represented as a summation of incomplete tensor approximations at multiple levels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. This implies a top-down or multi-level decomposition # where residuals are propagated. residuals = {} # Assuming a hierarchical level structure for level in sortedlevels(blocks): for block in blocksatlevel(level): # Get residual from parent (higher level) parentresidual = getparentresidual(block) # Subdivide current tensor into residual for children # The exact mathematical operation for subdivision is not given. currentresidual = subdividetensorintoresidual(block, parentresidual) residuals[block.id] = currentresidual # Step 4: Represent original tensor as summation of incomplete approximations # The original tensor V is approximated by summing contributions from all levels. # Vapprox = sum(incompleteapproximations) # The source does not provide the explicit formula for the summation or how # the bases and residuals combine to form the approximation. approximation = computesummationofincompleteapproximations(bases, residuals) return approximation Parameters: Partition Depth: The number of recursive subdivisions. name: Karhunen-Loeve Transform (KLT)
head: Eigen-vector Transform, PCA, PCA-like decorrelation
body: The Karhunen-Loeve Transform (KLT) is a linear decorrelation technique used in volume data compression to remove redundancy by estimating the covariance matrix and computing its eigenvectors. It is closely related to Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and provides superior decorrelation quality compared to the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). Unlike orthogonal basis methods like DCT, KLT bases are data-dependent and not mutually independent, which prevents the use of fast forward and inverse transforms. To mitigate the computational cost of these transforms, KLT is often combined with Vector Quantization (VQ) and block-wise decomposition, shifting the heavy reconstruction work to an offline preprocessing stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset V, typically subdivided into small blocks B. Output: Compressed data consisting of VQ indices (and potentially residual indices) and precomputed partial reprojection data (in VQ variants). Data Structures: Covariance Matrix (C): A square matrix where C{ij} = E[(xi - \mui)(xj - \muj)] for the data block. Eigenvectors (E): The columns of the transformation matrix, derived from the eigen-decomposition of C. Codebooks (Dk): A set of vectors (codewords) used for Vector Quantization. In multi-band variants, there are separate codebooks for low, band, and high-frequency components. Steps: 1. Block Decomposition: Subdivide the volume dataset into small, non-overlapping blocks. This overcomes the issue of dependent bases across large datasets. 2. Covariance Estimation: For each block (or the entire dataset if memory permits), compute the mean vector \mu and the covariance matrix C. 3. Eigen-decomposition: Compute the eigenvectors of C. These eigenvectors form the KLT basis. 4. Transform: Apply the KLT to the data blocks. Let x be a data vector in a block. The transformed vector y is: y = E^T (x - \mu) where E is the matrix of eigenvectors. 5. Vector Quantization (VQ): Encode the transformed coefficients using a VQ codebook. Find the codeword c \in D that minimizes the distance to y. 6. Residual Encoding (Multi-band variant): If the quantization error (residual) exceeds a threshold, encode the residual using a secondary dictionary. Repeat this process to identify three bands (low-, band-, high-pass) encoded with three separate dictionaries. 7. Precomputation (VQ variant): To avoid the computationally intensive inverse KLT during rendering, precompute partial reprojections and store them in the codebooks instead of the coefficients. This allows reconstruction to be performed via lookup rather than matrix multiplication. Parameters: Block Size: Not given in the sources. Small blocks are used to handle dependent bases. Threshold: Determines when a residual is encoded with a second dictionary. Not given in the sources. Number of Bands: Typically three (low, band, high) in the multi-band variant. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Intensity: The inverse KLT is computationally intensive. This is the primary motivation for using VQ and precomputed reprojections. Dependent Bases: The bases are not independent, preventing fast transforms. Block-wise decomposition is required to manage this. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kltcompress(volume, blocksize, codebooks): """ Compress volume using KLT and VQ. volume: 3D array of voxel values. blocksize: Size of each block (e.g., 4x4x4). codebooks: List of codebooks [Dlow, Dband, Dhigh]. """ compresseddata = [] # Step 1: Subdivide volume into blocks blocks = extractblocks(volume, blocksize) for block in blocks: # Step 2 & 3: Compute covariance and eigenvectors for this block # Note: In practice, eigenvectors are often computed once for the dataset # or a representative subset. Here we assume per-block for clarity, # though implies a global or block-wise basis. mu = mean(block) C = computecovariance(block, mu) E = computeeigenvectors(C) # Step 4: Transform xflat = block.flatten() y = E.T @ (xflat - mu) # Step 5: VQ Encoding bestidx = -1 bestdist = infinity for idx, codeword in enumerate(codebooks[0]): # Low band dist = sum((y - codeword)2) if dist < bestdist: bestdist = dist bestidx = idx # Step 6: Residual Encoding (Multi-band) residual = y - codebooks[0][bestidx] if bestdist > threshold: # Encode residual with second dictionary bestidxband = -1 bestdistband = infinity for idx, codeword in enumerate(codebooks[1]): # Band dist = sum((residual - codeword)2) if dist < bestdistband: bestdistband = dist bestidxband = idx residual = residual - codebooks[1][bestidxband] if bestdistband > threshold: # Encode residual with third dictionary bestidxhigh = -1 bestdisthigh = infinity for idx, codeword in enumerate(codebooks[2]): # High dist = sum((residual - codeword)2) if dist < bestdisthigh: bestdisthigh = dist bestidxhigh = idx compresseddata.append((bestidx, bestidxband, bestidxhigh)) else: compresseddata.append((bestidx, -1, -1)) return compresseddata def kltdecompress(compresseddata, codebooks, precomputedreprojections): """ Decompress using precomputed reprojections to avoid inverse KLT. """ # Reconstruction is mostly offline, prior to rendering # The codebooks store partial reprojections instead of coefficients # This implies the 'codewords' in the codebooks are already transformed # or pre-projected for rendering. reconstructedvolume = [] for indices in compresseddata: idxlow, idxband, idxhigh = indices # Retrieve precomputed reprojection data from codebooks # This step avoids the inverse KLT matrix multiplication datalow = precomputedreprojections[0][idxlow] databand = precomputedreprojections[1][idxband] if idxband != -1 else 0 datahigh = precomputedreprojections[2][idxhigh] if idxhigh != -1 else 0 reconstructedvolume.append(datalow + databand + datahigh) return reconstructedvolume KLT Decompression with VQ is a hybrid compression method for volume rendering that addresses the high memory bandwidth and computational cost of decoding decorrelated data. It sets itself apart from standard KLT decoding by precomputing the partial reprojections required for reconstruction and encoding them using Vector Quantization (VQ), thereby reducing the runtime decoding complexity. A method by Fout and Ma [FM07] that subdivides volume into blocks, applies KLT, and encodes low, band, and high-pass components with separate dictionaries. It uses a threshold to determine if a residual should be encoded with a second or third dictionary, allowing for efficient storage of low-frequency data while retaining detail for high-frequency signals. The inverse KLT is avoided by precomputing partial reprojections stored in the codebooks. Time Complexity: The forward KLT and inverse KLT are computationally intensive due to the lack of fast transforms. However, when combined with VQ and precomputed reprojections, the runtime decoding complexity is reduced. The preprocessing step (computing eigenvectors and codebooks) is performed offline. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the codebooks and the number of bands. Multi-band variants require storing multiple codebooks. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Block-wise decomposition allows for parallel processing of blocks. Strengths: Better decorrelation than DCT. Effective for volume data compression when combined with VQ. Limitations: Bases are not independent, preventing fast transforms. Computationally intensive inverse transform. When to use: When high-quality decorrelation is required and offline preprocessing is acceptable. When not to use: When fast, real-time decoding without precomputed data is required. The Karhunen-Loeve Transform is a linear transform that removes redundancy by decorrelating data, closely related to PCA. It was selected by Fout et al. [FM07] for better quality decorrelation in volume rendering. The method is part of the broader field of Tensor Approximation (TA), which uses SVD/PCA-like tools to approximate volume datasets. name: KLT Decompression with VQ
head: KLT Decoding with VQ, Karhunen-Loève Transform with Vector Quantization
body: KLT Decompression with VQ is a hybrid compression method for volume rendering that addresses the high memory bandwidth and computational cost of decoding decorrelated data. It sets itself apart from standard KLT decoding by precomputing the partial reprojections required for reconstruction and encoding them using Vector Quantization (VQ), thereby reducing the runtime decoding complexity. Inputs and Outputs Input: Compressed bitstream containing VQ indices and associated metadata; precomputed codebooks (dictionaries) C^p. Output: Reconstructed volume data or partial reprojections ready for rendering. Data Structures Codebooks (C^p): A set of dictionaries, one for each volume partition p. Each dictionary contains entries representing precomputed partial reprojections. The exact layout of entries (e.g., voxel values, coefficients) is not specified in the sources. Indices: Compact codes (VQ indices) pointing to entries in the codebooks. Steps 1. Precomputation (Processing Time): Partition the volume data into segments. For each partition p, compute the partial reprojections required for KLT decoding. Store these partial reprojections in associated dictionaries C^p. Apply Vector Quantization (VQ) to compactly encode the results of these partial reprojections. 2. Decompression (Runtime): Retrieve the VQ indices from the compressed bitstream. Use the indices to look up the corresponding precomputed partial reprojections from the codebooks C^p. Reconstruct the volume portion xi by summing the retrieved partial reprojections: xi = \sum{p=1}^{P} C^p(k{p,i}) where: xi is the reconstructed volume portion. P is the total number of volume partitions. C^p is the dictionary for the p-th volume partition. k{p,i} is the VQ index (codebook entry) for the i-th volume portion in partition p. Parameters Progressive Levels: The method supports progressive approximation. An example implementation uses four progressive levels. Precomputation: Partial reprojections are computed at processing time, not runtime. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Codebook Size: The size of the codebooks depends on the VQ resolution and the number of partitions. Large codebooks may consume significant memory. Quantization Error: VQ introduces quantization error. The choice of codebook size affects the trade-off between compression ratio and reconstruction fidelity. Partitioning: The effectiveness of the method depends on the partitioning strategy. Poor partitioning may lead to inefficient codebooks. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputecodebooks(volumedata, numpartitions): codebooks = [] for p in range(numpartitions): # Partition the volume data partitiondata = getpartition(volumedata, p) # Compute partial reprojections for KLT decoding # Note: The exact KLT decoding steps are defined in the parent article [Parent] partialreprojections = computepartialreprojections(partitiondata) # Apply Vector Quantization to compactly encode the results # Note: VQ implementation details are not provided in the sources codebook = applyvq(partialreprojections) codebooks.append(codebook) return codebooks def decompresswithvq(indices, codebooks): reconstructedvolume = 0 for p, index in enumerate(indices): # Look up the precomputed partial reprojection from the codebook partialreprojection = codebooks[p][index] # Sum the partial reprojections to reconstruct the volume portion reconstructedvolume += partialreprojection return reconstructedvolume Time Complexity: Decompression is fast as it primarily involves VQ lookups and summation, avoiding the computationally expensive KLT decoding at runtime. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the codebooks, which can be large depending on the VQ resolution and number of partitions. Strengths: Efficient runtime decoding; suitable for interactive visualization. Limitations: High preprocessing time; large codebook size may limit scalability. When to Use: When interactive rendering performance is critical and preprocessing time is acceptable. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or preprocessing time is prohibitive. The method was proposed by Fout and Ma [FM07] as a solution for efficient decoding of compressed volume data. It combines the redundancy removal capabilities of KLT with the compact representation of VQ. name: Sparse Representation (Dictionary Based)
head: Dictionary based sparse coding
body: Sparse Representation (Dictionary Based) encodes volume data blocks by finding a sparse linear combination of atoms from a pre-computed dictionary, solving an optimization problem to minimize reconstruction error under a sparsity constraint. It differs from Vector Quantization (VQ) by allowing each input block to be represented by a linear combination of multiple dictionary elements rather than a single nearest-neighbor prototype, offering higher fidelity at the cost of significantly more complex encoding. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volume dataset partitioned into cubic blocks of size M \times M \times M. A pre-computed dictionary \mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times K}, where m = M^3 is the dimension of a flattened block and K is the number of atoms in the dictionary. Output: For each block, a sparse coefficient vector \boldsymbol{\lambda}i \in \mathbb{R}^K containing at most S non-zero entries, and the indices of these non-zero entries. Data Structures Dictionary \mathbf{D}: A matrix of shape (m, K). Each column \mathbf{d}j is an atom of size m. Sparse Representation \boldsymbol{\lambda}i: A vector of size K. Stored efficiently as a list of pairs (index, value) for non-zero entries. Algorithm Steps 1. Vectorization: For each volume block i, extract the voxel values and map them to a column vector \mathbf{y}i \in \mathbb{R}^m. 2. Optimization: Solve for \boldsymbol{\lambda}i to minimize the reconstruction error subject to a sparsity constraint: \min{\boldsymbol{\lambda}i} \left\{ \| \mathbf{y}i - \mathbf{D}\boldsymbol{\lambda}i \|^2 \right\} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \| \boldsymbol{\lambda}i \|0 \leq S where \| \boldsymbol{\lambda}i \|0 denotes the number of non-zero entries in \boldsymbol{\lambda}i. 3. Approximation: Since the exact solution is NP-hard, use a greedy pursuit approximation algorithm. Specifically, Orthogonal Regularized Matching Pursuit (ORMP) via Choleski decomposition is employed for its simplicity and efficiency. 4. Compression: Store the sparse representation \boldsymbol{\lambda}i by recording the indices of the non-zero elements and their corresponding magnitudes. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodeblockdictionarybased(yi, D, S): """ Encodes a single volume block using sparse representation. Args: yi: numpy array of shape (m,), the flattened volume block. D: numpy array of shape (m, K), the dictionary matrix. S: int, maximum number of non-zero coefficients. Returns: indices: list of int, indices of non-zero coefficients. values: list of float, magnitudes of non-zero coefficients. """ m, K = D.shape # Initialize coefficients to zero lambdai = np.zeros(K) # ORMP via Choleski Decomposition # Note: Exact ORMP implementation details are not provided in sources. # The following is a placeholder for the greedy pursuit logic described. # In practice, this involves iteratively selecting the atom most correlated # with the residual, updating the coefficients via least-squares (using Cholesky), # and updating the residual. residual = yi.copy() selectedindices = [] for step in range(S): # 1. Select atom most correlated with residual correlations = np.abs(D.T @ residual) bestidx = np.argmax(correlations) if bestidx in selectedindices: break selectedindices.append(bestidx) # 2. Update coefficients using least-squares on selected atoms # Let Dselected be the submatrix of D with columns in selectedindices Dselected = D[:, selectedindices] # Solve min || yi - Dselected lambdaselected ||^2 # Using Cholesky decomposition: (Dselected^T Dselected) lambda = Dselected^T yi A = Dselected.T @ Dselected b = Dselected.T @ yi # Cholesky decomposition of A L = np.linalg.cholesky(A) # Solve L z = b z = np.linalg.solve(L, b) # Solve L^T lambdaselected = z lambdaselected = np.linalg.solve(L.T, z) # Update residual residual = yi - Dselected @ lambdaselected # Store coefficients in full vector for idx, val in zip(selectedindices, lambdaselected): lambdai[idx] = val # Extract non-zero entries indices = [i for i, val in enumerate(lambdai) if val != 0] values = [lambdai[i] for i in indices] return indices, values Parameters M: Block side length. Not given in the sources. K: Dictionary size. Not given in the sources. S: Sparsity level (max non-zero entries). Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls NP-Hardness: The optimization problem is NP-hard; greedy approximations do not guarantee global optimality. Precision: Floating-point errors in Cholesky decomposition may require regularization if the matrix is ill-conditioned. Boundaries: Blocks at the volume boundary must be handled (e.g., padding or smaller blocks). Not given in the sources. Represents a signal as a sparse linear combination of atoms from an overcomplete dictionary. Distinguished by its specific implementation of dictionary training via K-SVD and data reduction via importance sampling coresets to handle massive volumes. Decompresses volume data by reconstructing voxel blocks as linear combinations of codewords from a learned dictionary. Distinguished by focusing on the decomposition and reconstruction mechanics of voxel blocks, explicitly utilizing a linear combination of multiple codewords rather than a single best match. Complexity: Encoding is computationally expensive due to the need for iterative greedy pursuit algorithms (e.g., ORMP) and matrix decompositions (Cholesky), unlike the trivial nearest-neighbor search in VQ. Memory: Compression is achieved by storing only the indices and magnitudes of the sparse coefficients, reducing memory occupancy compared to storing full block data. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Higher reconstruction fidelity than VQ by using linear combinations of multiple atoms. Limitations: High encoding complexity; NP-hard optimization requires approximations. Sparse representation for volume data compression was introduced in the context of compressed GPU-based direct volume rendering. The method was notably employed by Gobbetti et al. [GIM12] using ORMP via Choleski decomposition [CARKD99]. It builds on the general concept of sparse coding in signal processing [Ela10]. name: Sparse Representation Modeling
head: Dictionaries for Sparse Representation Modeling, Sparse Coding
body: Sparse Representation Modeling represents a signal (such as a voxel block) as a sparse linear combination of atoms from an overcomplete dictionary matrix \mathbf{D}. It generalizes Vector Quantization (VQ) by allowing each input signal to be represented by a linear combination of multiple dictionary elements with arbitrary values, rather than a single prototype. This method is distinguished from its parent Sparse Representation (Dictionary Based) by its specific implementation of dictionary training via K-SVD and data reduction via importance sampling coresets to handle massive volumes. Inputs: A set of signal blocks extracted from the volume data. Each block is a vector \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m where m = M^3 (e.g., M=6 for 6^3 voxel blocks). Outputs: A learned dictionary \mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times K} with K atoms, and for each block, a sparse coefficient vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^K such that \mathbf{y} \approx \mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}. Data Structures: 1. Dictionary \mathbf{D}: A matrix of size m \times K. Columns \{\mathbf{d}j\}{j=1}^K are the prototype signal-atoms. The dictionary is overcomplete, meaning K > m. 2. Coefficient Vector \mathbf{x}: A vector of size K. It contains at most S non-zero entries (sparsity S). 3. Coreset: A weighted subset of the original data blocks used for training. Each element j in the coreset has a weight wj. Steps: 1. Data Reduction via Coreset Construction: To avoid the prohibitive cost of training on massive volumes, the dataset is reduced prior to dictionary learning. Calculate importance \iotai for each block i. The importance is proportional to the standard deviation of the block. Uniform subsampling is explicitly rejected because material boundaries carry more information than empty or uniform space. Select C elements using importance sampling, where the probability of picking block i is proportional to \iotai. Assign a weight wj to each selected element j to remove bias from the resampled set: wj = \frac{1}{\sqrt{pj}} where pj is the picking probability for element j. 2. Dictionary Training (K-SVD): Apply the K-SVD algorithm to the resampled and re-weighted set of blocks. K-SVD is a state-of-the-art method for dictionary learning that updates both the dictionary atoms and the sparse coefficients to minimize the reconstruction error. 3. Sparse Coding (Encoding): For each block \mathbf{y} in the volume, find the sparse coefficient vector \mathbf{x} that best represents \mathbf{y} using the learned dictionary \mathbf{D}. This is formulated as finding the sparsest solution: \min{\mathbf{x}} \|\mathbf{x}\|0 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{x} or approximately: \min{\mathbf{x}} \|\mathbf{x}\|0 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}\|2 \leq \epsilon where \|\mathbf{x}\|0 is the \ell0 "norm" (number of non-zero entries) and \epsilon is an error threshold. Parameters: Block Size: M^3. Example: 6^3 voxels. Dictionary Size (K): Number of atoms. Example: 1024. Sparsity (S): Maximum number of non-zero coefficients. Example: 8. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traindictionary(blocks, targetsparsity=8, dictsize=1024): """ Trains a dictionary using K-SVD on a coreset derived from importance sampling. Args: blocks: List of signal vectors y (shape: [N, m]). targetsparsity: Maximum number of non-zero coefficients S. dictsize: Number of atoms K in the dictionary. Returns: D: Dictionary matrix of shape [m, K]. """ # Step 1: Calculate importance for each block # Importance is proportional to the standard deviation of the block importances = [] for y in blocks: stddev = numpy.std(y) importances.append(stddev) # Normalize importances to form a probability distribution totalimportance = sum(importances) probabilities = [imp / totalimportance for imp in importances] # Step 2: Construct Coreset via Importance Sampling # Select C elements. C is a small fraction of N. # Note: The exact value of C is not specified in sources. C = int(len(blocks) 0.01) # Example fraction, not from source coresetblocks = [] coresetweights = [] coresetprobs = [] # Sample C indices with replacement or without? # Sources say "C elements are picked with probability proportional to iotai". # Assuming sampling without replacement for a fixed subset size C. indices = numpy.random.choice(len(blocks), size=C, replace=False, p=probabilities) for idx in indices: y = blocks[idx] pj = probabilities[idx] wj = 1.0 / numpy.sqrt(pj) coresetblocks.append(y) coresetweights.append(wj) coresetprobs.append(pj) # Step 3: Apply K-SVD to the weighted coreset # K-SVD minimizes reconstruction error while maintaining sparsity. # The weights are applied during the least-squares updates in K-SVD. D = ksvdalgorithm(coresetblocks, coresetweights, dictsize, targetsparsity) return D def ksvdalgorithm(data, weights, K, sparsity): """ Simplified representation of K-SVD algorithm. Initializes dictionary and iteratively updates atoms and coefficients. """ m = data[0].shape[0] # Initialize D randomly or using PCA D = numpy.random.randn(m, K) # Normalize columns of D for j in range(K): D[:, j] /= numpy.linalg.norm(D[:, j]) # Iterate until convergence for iteration in range(maxiterations): # 1. Sparse Coding Step: Find x for each data point # Solve min ||y - Dx||2 subject to ||x||0 <= sparsity # Using Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) or similar X = numpy.zeros((len(data), K)) for i, y in enumerate(data): w = weights[i] # Weighted residual # Standard OMP does not natively support weights in the same way # Implementation detail: Scale y and D by sqrt(w) or adjust cost function yscaled = y numpy.sqrt(w) xi = solvesparsecoding(yscaled, D, sparsity) X[i,:] = xi # 2. Dictionary Update Step for j in range(K): # Find indices of data points using the j-th atom indices = numpy.where(X[:, j] != 0)[0] if len(indices) == 0: continue # Compute error matrix E for these points E = numpy.zeros((len(indices), m)) for k, idx in enumerate(indices): E[k,:] = data[idx] - numpy.dot(D, X[idx,:]) # Remove the contribution of the j-th atom from the error E[k,:] += numpy.dot(D[:, j], X[idx, j]) # Perform SVD on E to update the atom U, S, Vt = numpy.linalg.svd(E, fullmatrices=False) # Update atom dj and corresponding coefficients # The first column of U is the new atom direction # The first row of Vt scaled by S[0] updates the coefficients newatom = U[:, 0] newatom /= numpy.linalg.norm(newatom) D[:, j] = newatom # Update coefficients for the affected data points for k, idx in enumerate(indices): # The coefficient is updated based on the projection of the residual # onto the new atom, scaled by the weight if necessary residual = data[idx] - numpy.dot(D, X[idx,:]) + numpy.dot(D[:, j], X[idx, j]) X[idx, j] = numpy.dot(newatom, residual) / numpy.dot(newatom, newatom) return D def solvesparsecoding(y, D, sparsity): """ Solves min ||y - Dx||2 subject to ||x||0 <= sparsity. Uses Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) as a common greedy algorithm. """ m = y.shape[0] K = D.shape[1] x = numpy.zeros(K) residual = y.copy() indices = [] for in range(sparsity): # Find the atom most correlated with the residual correlations = numpy.abs(numpy.dot(D.T, residual)) idx = numpy.argmax(correlations) if idx in indices: break indices.append(idx) # Solve least squares problem for the selected atoms selectedatoms = D[:, indices] coeffs,,, = numpy.linalg.lstsq(selectedatoms, y, rcond=None) # Update residual residual = y - numpy.dot(selectedatoms, coeffs) # Update x with the new coefficients for k, i in enumerate(indices): x[i] = coeffs[k] return x A specific algorithm for learning overcomplete dictionaries by iteratively updating atoms and coefficients to minimize reconstruction error. It is chosen for its ability to adapt to specific signal data better than fixed mathematical bases. A data reduction technique that selects a weighted subset of blocks for training based on their standard deviation (importance). It is chosen to make K-SVD feasible on massive volumes by avoiding uniform subsampling, which fails to capture material boundaries. Time Complexity: Dictionary training is computationally expensive. Direct K-SVD on massive volumes is prohibitively expensive. The coreset approach reduces this significantly, but it remains higher than fixed-basis methods. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the dictionary \mathbf{D} (m \times K) and the sparse coefficients \mathbf{x} for each block. The dictionary size K (e.g., 1024) is larger than the block dimension m (e.g., 216 for 6^3), but sparsity S (e.g., 8) keeps the coefficient storage low. Performance: Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on very large static and dynamic volumes. Strengths: Increased flexibility and adaptation to specific signal data compared to mathematical models (e.g., wavelets). Allows representation by linear combinations of atoms, providing better approximation than VQ. Limitations: Computationally intensive training. Uniform subsampling fails due to information loss at material boundaries. When to use: When high-quality reconstruction of complex, non-uniform volumes is required and computational resources allow for dictionary training. When not to use: When fast, reduced-memory implicit implementation is needed (use wavelets) or when the volume is extremely large and training time is prohibitive. Sparse Representation Modeling is a generalization of Vector Quantization (VQ) where signals are represented by linear combinations of dictionary elements rather than single prototypes. The concept of using overcomplete dictionaries (containing linearly dependent vectors) for sparse coding has gained significant interest in recent years. Gobbetti et al. [GIM12] applied this method to volume rendering, using K-SVD for dictionary training and importance sampling for data reduction. Recent architectures based on sparse representation of voxel blocks have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on very large static and dynamic volumes. name: Sparse Coding with K-SVD and Coresets
head: Coreset Subsampling, K-SVD Dictionary Training, K-SVD with Coresets, Sparse Coding Global Processing, Sparse Coding with Coresets
body: This method addresses the prohibitive computational cost of training data-specific dictionaries on massive volume datasets by combining the K-SVD algorithm with coreset-based data reduction. Unlike uniform subsampling, which fails to capture critical information at material boundaries, this approach uses importance sampling to construct a small, weighted subset of training blocks that approximates the original data distribution. It builds on Sparse Representation Modeling by providing a scalable training pipeline for dictionary-based sparse representations. Inputs: A set of N training blocks extracted from the volume data. Target coreset size C (where C \ll N). Dictionary size K for the K-SVD algorithm. Outputs: A trained dictionary matrix D \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times K}, where m is the dimensionality of a block. Sparse coefficients for the training blocks (implicit in the training process). Data Structures: Training Blocks: A list or matrix of shape (N, m). Importance Scores: An array \iota of length N, where \iotai is the importance of block i. Coreset: A subset of indices I \subset \{1, \dots, N\} with |I|=C, and associated weights w. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Importance Scores: Calculate the importance \iotai for each training block i. The sources specify that \iotai is proportional to the standard deviation of the block. \iotai \propto \sigmai where \sigmai is the standard deviation of the pixel/voxel values in block i. 2. Normalize Probabilities: Convert importance scores into picking probabilities pj for each block j. pj = \frac{\iotaj}{\sum{k=1}^{N} \iotak} 3. Construct Coreset via Importance Sampling: Select C blocks from the original N blocks. Each block j is picked with probability pj. This is typically done using a streaming method or repeated sampling with replacement. Let the selected indices be j1, j2, \dots, jC. 4. Assign Weights: For each selected block j in the coreset, assign a weight wj to remove bias introduced by the non-uniform sampling. The weight is calculated as: wj = \frac{1}{\sqrt{pj}} where pj is the probability with which block j was selected. 5. Train Dictionary with K-SVD: Apply the K-SVD algorithm [AEB06] to the resampled and re-weighted set of C blocks. The K-SVD algorithm iteratively updates the dictionary atoms and the sparse coefficients to minimize the reconstruction error, weighted by wj. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainsparsecodingcoreset(blocks, targetcoresetsize C, dictsize K): """ blocks: numpy array of shape (N, m), N training blocks of dimension m. C: integer, number of blocks to select for the coreset. K: integer, number of atoms in the dictionary. """ N, m = blocks.shape # Step 1: Compute importance scores (proportional to standard deviation) # importance is proportional to standard deviation stddevs = np.std(blocks, axis=1) importance = stddevs # Step 2: Normalize to get probabilities totalimportance = np.sum(importance) probabilities = importance / totalimportance # Step 3: Select C blocks using importance sampling # C elements are picked with probability proportional to importance # Using multinomial sampling with replacement or streaming selection selectedindices = np.random.choice(N, size=C, p=probabilities, replace=True) # Step 4: Calculate weights to remove bias # wj = 1 / sqrt(pj) selectedprobabilities = probabilities[selectedindices] weights = 1.0 / np.sqrt(selectedprobabilities) # Extract the coreset blocks coresetblocks = blocks[selectedindices] # Step 5: Train dictionary using K-SVD on the weighted coreset # Apply learning algorithm to the resampled and re-weighted set # Note: Standard K-SVD implementations may not natively support sample weights. # Implementation detail: If the K-SVD solver does not support weights, # one must either: # 1. Repeat each block in coresetblocks according to weight magnitude (approximate). # 2. Modify the K-SVD update step to include weight matrix W in the error term: # min || W (X - D A) ||F^2 # 3. Use a weighted variant of the sparse coding and dictionary update steps. dictionary, coefficients = ksvdalgorithm(coresetblocks, weights, K) return dictionary Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Uniform Subsampling Failure: Uniform sub-sampling is explicitly rejected because material boundaries carry more information than empty or uniform space. Numerical Instability: Massive datasets can lead to numerical instabilities during K-SVD calculations. The coreset approach mitigates this by reducing the dataset size. Computational Cost: Direct K-SVD on massive volumes is prohibitively expensive in time and memory. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is the K-SVD training on the coreset of size C. Since C \ll N, this is significantly faster than training on N blocks. The sampling step is O(N) for computing standard deviations and O(C \log N) or O(C) for selection. Memory Complexity: Reduced from O(N \cdot m) to O(C \cdot m) for the training data held in memory during K-SVD. Performance: Results demonstrate that extremely good approximations can be obtained using a tiny fraction of the original data. Strengths: Scalability to massive volumes; captures critical features (boundaries) better than uniform sampling. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of C; relies on the assumption that standard deviation is a good proxy for information content. Origin: The method was introduced by Gobbetti et al. [GIM12] for volume rendering compression, applying the concept of coresets [AHPV05, CS07] to K-SVD dictionary training. Development: Prior approaches for BTF compression by Ruiters and Klein [RK09] used truncated SVD for data reduction. Gobbetti et al. improved upon this by using importance sampling based on standard deviation. Context: It is part of the global processing techniques for sparse coding, aiming to improve upon vector quantization by using data-specific dictionaries. name: Sparse Coding
head: Sparse Coding Decompression, Sparse coding of voxel blocks
body: Sparse coding decompresses volume data by reconstructing voxel blocks as linear combinations of codewords from a learned dictionary, offering a balance between the simplicity of Vector Quantization (VQ) and the adaptability of Hierarchical VQ (HVQ). It distinguishes itself from its parent method Sparse Representation (Dictionary Based) by explicitly utilizing a linear combination of multiple codewords rather than a single best match, and from its sibling Sparse Representation Modeling by focusing on the decomposition and reconstruction mechanics of voxel blocks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Compressed data consisting of indices pointing to codewords in a dictionary and their associated weighting coefficients (sparse representation) for each voxel block. Output: Reconstructed 3D volume data. Data Structures: Dictionary D: A matrix where columns are codewords. The size is not explicitly defined in the sources, but it must contain enough codewords to support the sparsity S. Sparse Representation: For each block, a set of S indices into the dictionary and S corresponding scalar weights. Steps: 1. For each voxel block in the volume: a. Retrieve the S indices identifying the relevant codewords from the dictionary. b. Retrieve the S weighting coefficients associated with those indices. c. Compute the reconstructed voxel values by calculating the linear combination of the selected codewords weighted by their coefficients. d. Store or stream the reconstructed voxels. Formulas: The reconstruction of a voxel block V is given by: V = \sum{i=1}^{S} wi \cdot di Where: S is the sparsity (number of non-zero coefficients). wi is the weighting coefficient for the i-th codeword. di is the i-th codeword from the dictionary D. Parameters: N: Number of blocks. S: Sparsity (number of codewords used per block). M: Number of dictionaries (used for comparison with HVQ). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on floating-point arithmetic for the linear combination. Standard floating-point precision should be used for weights and codewords. Boundary: Not given in the sources. Degenerate input: If S=0, the block cannot be reconstructed. If S=1, the method degrades to VQ behavior. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decompresssparsecoding(volumeblocks, dictionary, sparsedata): """ Reconstructs volume data from sparse coding representation. Args: volumeblocks: List of block objects to be filled. dictionary: List of codeword vectors. sparsedata: List of tuples (indices, weights) for each block. indices: list of S integers pointing to dictionary. weights: list of S floats. """ for blockidx, block in enumerate(volumeblocks): indices, weights = sparsedata[blockidx] S = len(indices) # Initialize block voxels to zero block.voxels = [0.0] block.size # Linear combination of codewords for i in range(S): codeword = dictionary[indices[i]] weight = weights[i] # Add weighted codeword contribution to block voxels # Assuming codeword size matches block size for vidx in range(block.size): block.voxels[vidx] += weight codeword[vidx] Focuses on the statistical modeling of sparse coefficients rather than just the decomposition mechanics. Choose when the goal is to model the distribution of sparse codes for better compression or denoising. Link Time Complexity: O(N \times S), where N is the number of blocks and S is the sparsity. This is linear with respect to the number of blocks and sparsity. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The computational complexity is very similar to Hierarchical Vector Quantization (HVQ). Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of blocks and the sparsity level. Strengths: Allows parallel decompression of voxels by accessing codewords and coefficients; complexity is low compared to HVQ when S < M. Limitations: Requires storage of multiple coefficients and indices per block compared to VQ; dictionary size and sparsity selection impact performance. When to use: When a balance between compression ratio and reconstruction quality is needed, and parallel decompression is desired. When not: When minimal computational overhead is critical and VQ suffices, or when extremely high compression is needed and dictionary learning overhead is prohibitive. Sparse coding in the context of compressed GPU-based direct volume rendering was discussed in relation to Vector Quantization (VQ) and Hierarchical VQ (HVQ). The method leverages the idea that voxel blocks can be represented as a linear combination of dictionary codewords, maintaining low computational complexity during decompression. It builds on earlier work in compressed volume rendering, such as that by Gobbetti et al. [GIM12], which proposed parallel access to codewords and coefficients. name: PlenOctree Compression
head: Median-cut Quantization and DEFLATE Compression, PlenOctree Compression Strategy, SH-9 PlenOctree Compression
body: PlenOctree Compression is a file-size reduction strategy designed to make PlenOctrees feasible for in-browser rendering by minimizing occupied voxels and applying direct compression to the tree structure. It distinguishes itself from general value compression [6-value-compression.md] by specifically targeting the spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients of PlenOctrees using median-cut quantization and DEFLATE encoding, and from sparse structures [5-sparse-structures.md] by compressing the entire tree including pointers rather than just the data values. Inputs: An uncompressed PlenOctree containing SH coefficients (RGB vectors) and density (\sigma) values. Outputs: A compressed binary file containing the quantized codebooks, leaf pointers, and DEFLATE-compressed tree structure. Data Structures: 1. Codebook: A lookup table of size 2^{16} \times 3 storing RGB colors. Data type: float16 (IEEE 754 half-precision). One codebook is stored per SH basis function. 2. Leaf Pointers: For each leaf node in the PlenOctree, a pointer to an index in the corresponding SH basis function's codebook. Data type: int16 (16-bit signed integer). 3. Tree Structure: The full PlenOctree hierarchy, including internal node pointers and leaf data (pointers and \sigma), compressed as a byte stream. Parameters: SH Degree: Limited to degree 2 (SH-9). This reduces the number of coefficients per voxel compared to SH-16 or SH-25. Bounding Box: A looser bounding box is used during the initial PlenOctree construction to reduce the total number of occupied voxels. Quantization Levels: 2^{16} (65,536) colors. Steps: 1. Quantize SH Coefficients: For each voxel in the PlenOctree, retain the density value \sigma as a standard floating-point value (no quantization specified for \sigma). For each SH basis function m, extract the RGB coefficient vector \mathbf{k}m \in \mathbb{R}^3. Apply the median-cut algorithm to quantize all \mathbf{k}m vectors across the entire tree into 2^{16} representative colors. Generate a codebook of size 2^{16} \times 3 for each SH basis function. Replace each voxel's \mathbf{k}m with an index (pointer) into the corresponding codebook. The index is stored as an int16. 2. Compress Tree: Serialize the entire PlenOctree structure, including internal nodes, leaf pointers (to codebooks), and \sigma values. Apply the DEFLATE algorithm (as implemented in ZLIB) to the serialized byte stream. 3. Store: Save the DEFLATE-compressed tree stream. Save the codebooks (one per SH basis function) as float16 arrays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import zlib import numpy as np def compressplenoctree(tree): """ Compress a PlenOctree using SH-9, median-cut quantization, and DEFLATE. Args: tree: A PlenOctree object containing nodes with: sigma: density value (float) shcoeffs: list of RGB vectors for each SH basis function (degree 2 -> 9 coeffs) Returns: compresseddata: bytes, the DEFLATE-compressed tree stream codebooks: dict, mapping SHbasisindex -> numpy array of shape (65536, 3), dtype float16 """ numshbasis = 9 # SH-9 numcolors = 65536 # 2^16 # Initialize codebooks and pointers storage # codebooks[basisidx] will store the final 2^16 x 3 codebook codebooks = {i: None for i in range(numshbasis)} # Step 1: Collect all RGB coefficients for each SH basis function to build codebooks # We need to run median-cut on the global set of coefficients for each basis allcoeffs = {i: [] for i in range(numshbasis)} # Traverse tree to collect coefficients for node in tree.allleaves(): for basisidx in range(numshbasis): rgb = node.shcoeffs[basisidx] # Shape (3,) allcoeffs[basisidx].append(rgb) # Build codebooks using median-cut for each basis for basisidx in range(numshbasis): coeffsarray = np.array(allcoeffs[basisidx], dtype=np.float32) # Median-cut algorithm implementation # 1. Start with bounding box of all colors # 2. Repeatedly split the largest dimension of the largest box until 2^16 boxes # 3. Center of each box is a codebook entry codebook = mediancutquantize(coeffsarray, numcolors) codebooks[basisidx] = codebook.astype(np.float16) # Step 2: Replace coefficients with pointers # Create a new tree structure with pointers instead of raw RGB compressedtreenodes = [] for node in tree.allleaves(): newnode = Node() newnode.sigma = node.sigma # Keep sigma as is # Quantize each SH basis coefficient to nearest codebook entry newnode.pointers = [] for basisidx in range(numshbasis): rgb = node.shcoeffs[basisidx] # Find index in codebook[basisidx] closest to rgb # Euclidean distance in RGB space codebook = codebooks[basisidx] dists = np.linalg.norm(codebook - rgb, axis=1) idx = np.argmin(dists) newnode.pointers.append(idx) compressedtreenodes.append(newnode) # Step 3: Serialize and Compress # Serialize the tree structure (pointers and sigma) into a byte stream # The exact serialization format is not specified, but must include pointers and sigma # Assuming a simple binary layout: [sigma (float32), ptr0 (int16),..., ptr8 (int16)] per leaf # Plus internal node structure. For this example, we assume a flat list of leaves for simplicity # or a standard tree serialization. The source says "entire tree, including pointers". # Placeholder for tree serialization logic # In practice, this would serialize the node hierarchy. # Here we serialize just the leaf data for demonstration of the compression step. leafdata = [] for node in compressedtreenodes: leafdata.append(node.sigma) leafdata.extend(node.pointers) # Convert to bytes # sigma: float32 (4 bytes), pointers: int16 (2 bytes each) # Total per leaf: 4 + 92 = 22 bytes bytestream = np.array(leafdata, dtype=np.float32).tobytes() # Simplified: only sigma for demo # Note: The pointers must be included in the actual byte stream. # Correct serialization would pack sigma and pointers together. # Re-do serialization properly packed = bytearray() for node in compressedtreenodes: packed.extend(node.sigma.tobytes(4, byteorder='little', signed=False)) # Assuming float32 for ptr in node.pointers: packed.extend(ptr.tobytes(2, byteorder='little', signed=True)) # Step 4: Apply DEFLATE compresseddata = zlib.compress(bytes(packed)) return compresseddata, codebooks def mediancutquantize(colors, numcolors): """ Standard median-cut algorithm for color quantization. """ # Implementation of median-cut # 1. Sort colors by each dimension # 2. Create initial box containing all colors # 3. Loop until numcolors boxes: # a. Find box with largest range (max - min) in any dimension # b. Split that box along the dimension with the largest range # c. Split point is the median of the colors in that dimension # 4. Compute centroid of each box pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using float16 for codebooks reduces memory but may introduce quantization error in the codebook values themselves. The source specifies float16. Pointer Size: int16 limits the codebook size to 65,536 entries. If more colors are needed, this method cannot scale without changing the pointer type. Decompression: The entire tree must be fully decompressed before rendering in the web renderer. Compression Ratio: Reduces file size by 20-30 times compared to the uncompressed PlenOctree. Performance (SH-9): File Size: 1.00 GB Rendering FPS: 262 PSNR: 31.44 SSIM: 0.951 LPIPS: 0.065 Comparison with Higher SH Degrees: SH-16: 1.93 GB, 168 FPS, PSNR 31.57, SSIM 0.952, LPIPS 0.063 SH-25: 2.68 GB, 128 FPS, PSNR 31.56, SSIM 0.951, LPIPS 0.063 Strengths: Significant file size reduction enabling in-browser rendering; simple compression pipeline (median-cut + DEFLATE); high rendering FPS due to reduced data transfer and simpler SH evaluation. Limitations: Lossy compression (quantization); requires full decompression before rendering; SH-9 may lose high-frequency detail compared to SH-16/25, though the PSNR drop is minimal (0.13 dB). When to use: When in-browser rendering of NeRFs is required and bandwidth/storage is a constraint. When not to use: When maximum visual fidelity is required and bandwidth is not a constraint (use SH-16/25). PlenOctree Compression was introduced in the paper "PlenOctrees For Real-time Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)" by Yu et al.. The method was developed to address the large file sizes of PlenOctrees, which were originally too large for efficient in-browser viewing. The approach combines established techniques (median-cut quantization, DEFLATE compression) with specific adaptations for PlenOctree data structures (SH coefficients, tree pointers).
