name: Wavelet-based Volume Rendering
head: WTSP rendering, Wavelet compression rendering
body: Wavelet-based Volume Rendering is a technique that compresses volumetric data using wavelet transforms to enable efficient storage and rendering, particularly for large-scale or time-varying datasets. It solves the problem of high memory bandwidth and storage requirements by representing the volume in a frequency domain where coefficients can be pruned or encoded. It is distinguished from its sibling Laplacian Pyramid Volume Rendering by its use of orthogonal or biorthogonal wavelet bases (such as Haar or Daubechies) which provide multi-resolution analysis with better frequency localization, whereas Laplacian pyramids use fixed Gaussian filters. Inputs: Original volumetric data V of size N \times N \times N. Outputs: Rendered image I and/or compressed bitstream. Data Structures: 1. Wavelet Coefficients: A hierarchical set of coefficients organized by scale (level) and subband. For a 3D transform, each level j produces 8 subbands: LLL (low-low-low), LLH, LHL, LHH, HLL, HLH, HHL, HHH. The LLL subband contains the approximation, while the others contain detail information. 2. Compressed Bitstream: Entropy-encoded wavelet coefficients. Parameters: Wavelet Basis: e.g., Haar (m=2), Daubechies W6 (m=6). Quantization: Optional. If used, the method is lossy; if not, it is lossless. Error Tolerance: User-specified threshold for adaptive resolution selection. Steps: 1. Encoding (Compression): 1. Apply 3D Wavelet Transform to V to obtain coefficients C. 2. (Optional) Apply quantization to C for lossy compression. 3. Apply entropy reduction (run-length, arithmetic, or Huffman encoding) to C to produce the bitstream. 2. Decoding (Reconstruction): 1. Decode the bitstream to recover coefficients C'. 2. Perform Inverse Wavelet Transform on C' to reconstruct voxel values. Note: Reconstruction can be done point-wise, block-wise, or on-the-fly. 3. Perform conditional reconstruction to select the data representation sufficiently accurate for rendering. This may involve traversing the wavelet tree based on an error tolerance to decompress only necessary blocks. 3. Rendering: 1. Render the reconstructed volume using standard volume rendering techniques (e.g., raycasting). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def waveletvolumerendering(volumedata, wavelettype='haar', quantize=False, errortolerance=None): """ Main pipeline for wavelet-based volume rendering. """ # Step 1: Encoding # Transform to frequency domain coefficients = wavelettransform3d(volumedata, wavelettype) # Optional Quantization if quantize: coefficients = quantizecoefficients(coefficients) # Entropy Encoding (Compression) bitstream = entropyencode(coefficients) # Step 2: Decoding # Decode bitstream decodedcoeffs = entropydecode(bitstream) # Conditional Reconstruction / Adaptive Resolution if errortolerance is not None: # Traverse tree and select blocks based on error tolerance selectedblocks = selectblocksbyerror(decodedcoeffs, errortolerance) # Decompress only selected blocks reconstructedvolume = reconstructblocks(selectedblocks, wavelettype) else: # Full reconstruction reconstructedvolume = inversewavelettransform3d(decodedcoeffs, wavelettype) # Step 3: Rendering image = rendervolume(reconstructedvolume) return image def wavelettransform3d(data, wavelettype): """ Performs 3D wavelet transform using separable 1D transforms. """ # Apply 1D transform along x tempx = apply1dwavelet(data, axis=0, wavelettype=wavelettype) # Apply 1D transform along y tempy = apply1dwavelet(tempx, axis=1, wavelettype=wavelettype) # Apply 1D transform along z coefficients = apply1dwavelet(tempy, axis=2, wavelettype=wavelettype) return coefficients def inversewavelettransform3d(coefficients, wavelettype): """ Performs inverse 3D wavelet transform. """ # Apply 1D inverse transform along z tempz = apply1dinversewavelet(coefficients, axis=2, wavelettype=wavelettype) # Apply 1D inverse transform along y tempy = apply1dinversewavelet(tempz, axis=1, wavelettype=wavelettype) # Apply 1D inverse transform along x reconstructed = apply1dinversewavelet(tempy, axis=0, wavelettype=wavelettype) return reconstructed def apply1dwavelet(data, axis, wavelettype): """ Applies 1D wavelet transform along a specific axis. For Haar wavelet, this involves averaging and differencing adjacent elements. """ # Implementation depends on wavelettype # Standard separable filter bank implementation pass def entropyencode(coefficients): """ Applies run-length, arithmetic, or Huffman encoding. """ # Standard entropy coding pass def entropydecode(bitstream): """ Decodes the bitstream. """ # Standard entropy decoding pass def quantizecoefficients(coefficients): """ Quantizes wavelet coefficients for lossy compression. """ # Scalar quantization pass def selectblocksbyerror(coefficients, errortolerance): """ Traverses the wavelet tree to select blocks that satisfy the error tolerance. """ # Recursive traversal checking coefficient magnitude against tolerance pass def reconstructblocks(selectedblocks, wavelettype): """ Reconstructs volume from selected wavelet blocks. """ # Inverse transform on selected coefficients pass def rendervolume(volume): """ Renders the volume using raycasting or similar method. """ # Standard volume rendering pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Serial Decoding: Lossless compression decoding is serial because it requires previous information to make the next decoding decision, making it difficult to implement efficiently on GPU. Memory Access: Without specific optimizations, the whole volumetric data must be decompressed in main memory to allow access for parts of the data. Redundant Computation: In block-wise reconstruction, adjacent blocks have redundant computation because the wavelet kernel extends outside the target block boundary. The extended region width is approximately half the kernel length. An interactive rendering method for isosurfaces in a voxel grid where the underlying trivariate function is represented as a spline wavelet hierarchy. It allows adaptive, view-dependent selection of level-of-detail by superimposing appropriately weighted basis functions, decreasing resolution for distant parts to improve performance with minimal visual impact. It is distinguished from its sibling Hierarchical Wavelet Transform on Omnitrees by its specific use of polynomial spline wavelets with B-spline basis functions to guarantee continuous surfaces and its implementation of a gathering-based CUDA kernel for reconstruction rather than scattering. This method transforms nodal omnitree data into wavelet coefficients to enable lossless or lossy compression via pruning and tree restructuring (downsplit). It operates directly on the omnitree's anisotropic structure, allowing coarsening in specific dimensions while preserving the hierarchical spatial layout. L2-optimal wavelet splatting is a volume rendering technique that decomposes volume data into a wavelet pyramid representation in the spline domain and computes splats via an orthogonal projection operator using least-squares approximation on an adaptive multiresolution grid. It sets itself apart from standard interpolation-based wavelet splatting (such as Wavelet-based Multiresolution Rendering) by ensuring the smallest possible approximation error for a given sampling step size and by adapting the grid resolution to the basis function size, which yields significant performance gains at coarse scales. The Point-wise Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform (PW-IDWT) via Generalized Projection (GP) is a method to reconstruct a single signal sample (or a set of samples) from a wavelet decomposition by determining the minimal set of subband coefficients required. It solves the problem of identifying which coefficients at a coarser level contribute to a specific sample at a finer level during synthesis, exploiting the recursive nature of the lifting scheme. Unlike methods that decode entire subbands, this approach calculates the exact "Generalized Projection" of a sample into the transformed domain, minimizing the number of subband images to decode. It builds on Wavelet-based Volume Rendering by providing an efficient, sample-specific inverse transform mechanism. A rendering technique that stores reconstructed data at pre-selected wavelet tree nodes based on available storage to reduce reconstruction cost, then traverses the tree per error tolerance to decompress and render blocks in parallel. Steps: 1. Traverse the wavelet tree according to a user-specified error tolerance. 2. Identify data blocks of different resolutions that satisfy the error tolerance. 3. Decompress the selected blocks. 4. Render the decompressed blocks in parallel to compose the final image. Parameters: Error tolerance: User-specified threshold that controls wavelet tree traversal depth and determines which resolution blocks are decompressed and rendered. Characteristics: Reduces run-time communication cost to a minimum and ensures a well-balanced workload among processors when visualizing gigabytes of data with arbitrary error tolerances. A reconstruction method that processes wavelet coefficients in blocks rather than point-wise to reduce redundant computation during volume rendering. Steps: Reconstruct a block of voxels along the z dimension by convolving the input with a wavelet kernel of size m row by row. Perform three passes (one for each dimension) to complete the reconstruction. Formula: The computational cost for one pass is mn^3, where m is the kernel size and n is the dimension size. Total cost for three passes is 3mn^3. Point-wise cost is m^3n^3. The efficiency factor is k = m^2/3. Parameters: Kernel size m: For Haar wavelet, m=2; for Daubechies W6, m=6. Pitfall: Adjacent blocks have redundant computation because the wavelet kernel extends outside the target block boundary. The extended region width is approximately half the kernel length. A method to reconstruct voxel values on-the-fly from wavelet coefficients during rendering, avoiding pre-computation of the entire volume. It involves finding the appropriate wavelet coefficient at level k and applying inverse wavelet transforms iteratively down to level 0. Steps: 1. Given a wavelet coefficient with k levels and a target voxel (x0, y0, z0), find the voxel (cube of size 1 \times 1 \times 1) from the level k, wk, whose reconstruction contains the target voxel. Map indices x0, y0, z0 to xk, yk, zk in wk by dividing x0, y0, z0 by 2^k. The resultant voxel is in the LLL region of wk. 2. Find the corresponding voxel in the other seven regions of the decomposed data (fHHH, fLLH, fHHL, fHLL, fLHH, fLHL, fLLH, fLLL). To do this, add half of the size of xk, yk, and zk (dimensions of wk) to xk, yk, and zk respectively. 3. Apply the inverse wavelet transformation to the above eight sub-cubes to reconstruct a new sub-cube with size doubled in each axis (x{k-1}, y{k-1}, z{k-1}). The new reconstructed sub-cube will be in the LLL of w{k-1}. 4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until level 0 (w0) is reached. The resultant sub-volume is of size 2^k \times 2^k \times 2^k containing the desired voxel (x0, y0, z0). A wavelet-based volume rendering method with slower complexity decay compared to Method 2. Complexity: Time complexity Op1 decays with a factor of 2^j per scale j. Comparison: Method 1 is slower than Method 2, with Op2 decaying with up to 2^{3j} per scale j whereas Op1 decays with only 2^j. A 3-D wavelet-based coding algorithm used for comparison, including a context-modeling variant (3-D CB-EZW). Performance: On MR-MRI data, 3-D CB-EZW achieved 2.285 bit/voxel (integer 5-3 filter) and 2.195 bit/voxel (two-level integer transform with (1,1) filter). Time Complexity: Depends on the reconstruction method. Point-wise reconstruction has complexity O(m^3 n^3), while block-wise reconstruction reduces this to O(3mn^3), offering an efficiency factor of k = m^2/3. Wavelet splatting Method 1 has complexity decaying with 2^j per scale, while Method 2 decays with 2^{3j}. Memory Complexity: Lossless compression decoding is serial and may require decompressing the whole volume in main memory unless optimized. Adaptive methods reduce memory usage by only decompressing necessary blocks. Measured Performance: On MR-MRI data, 3-D CB-EZW achieved lossless rates of 2.285 and 2.195 bit/voxel. Strengths: High compression ratios, support for multi-resolution rendering, and efficient storage of large datasets. Limitations: Serial nature of lossless decoding makes GPU implementation difficult. Redundant computation in block-wise reconstruction. When to use: Large-scale time-varying data visualization on PC clusters or workstations. When not to use: When real-time interactive rendering on GPU is required with lossless compression and no specific optimizations are used. Wavelet-based volume rendering originated from the application of wavelet transforms to volumetric data compression and rendering. It has been thoroughly studied by researchers in recent years, with overviews provided by Stollnitz et al.. The method is used in frameworks like WTSP (Wavelet-based Time-Space Partitioning) tree for large-scale time-varying data visualization on PC clusters. The technique leverages the multi-resolution properties of wavelets to enable adaptive rendering and efficient data storage. name: Wavelet-based Multiresolution Rendering
head: Wavelet-based Multiresolution Isosurface Rendering
body: An interactive rendering method for isosurfaces in a voxel grid where the underlying trivariate function is represented as a spline wavelet hierarchy. It allows adaptive, view-dependent selection of level-of-detail by superimposing appropriately weighted basis functions, decreasing resolution for distant parts to improve performance with minimal visual impact. It is distinguished from its sibling Hierarchical Wavelet Transform on Omnitrees by its specific use of polynomial spline wavelets with B-spline basis functions to guarantee continuous surfaces and its implementation of a gathering-based CUDA kernel for reconstruction rather than scattering. Inputs: Volumetric dataset V of size up to 512^3 voxels. Camera position and viewing parameters. Isovalue c defining the surface f(x,y,z)=c. Interpolation degree d (e.g., d=1 for tri-linear, d=3 for tri-cubic). Chunk size k \times k \times k nodes (typically k=8). User-defined error threshold \epsilon. Outputs: Rendered isosurface image. Activated octree nodes/chunks for reconstruction. Data Structures: Octree: Nested vector spaces where nodes represent levels of the wavelet hierarchy. Chunk: A block of k \times k \times k octree nodes processed together. Wavelet Coefficients: Low-pass (scaling) and high-pass (detail) coefficients resulting from the transform. Min/Max Values: Stored at leaf nodes, estimated using the convex combination property of B-spline basis, and propagated to the root. Method Steps: 1. Wavelet Transform: Perform a 3D wavelet transform on the volume dataset using polynomial spline wavelets. The basis functions are B-splines with the least possible number of vanishing moments to minimize filter support. Due to the separability of the B-spline wavelet basis, the transformation is performed sequentially in the x-, y-, and z-directions. This reduces the computational complexity compared to a non-separable approach. 2. Octree Construction and Min/Max Propagation: Construct an octree hierarchy where each level corresponds to a resolution level in the wavelet decomposition. Calculate min/max values for leaf nodes. Propagate these min/max values towards the root using the convex combination property of the B-spline basis to enable efficient view-dependent culling. 3. View-Dependent Chunk Activation: Traverse the octree and evaluate an error metric for each chunk to determine if it needs reconstruction. A chunk is activated if: The chunk's min/max range contains the isovalue c (min/max comparison with render tree entry). The geometric error metric s/c > \epsilon is satisfied, where s is the node diameter, c is the distance from the camera, and \epsilon is the user-defined threshold. 4. Continuity Handling: If a chunk is activated, check if any wavelet support extends into neighboring chunks. If so, those neighboring chunks must also be reconstructed to maintain surface continuity and avoid cracks. Chunks that are neither activated nor needed for continuity are omitted. 5. CUDA Reconstruction: Reconstruct the volume data for activated chunks using CUDA kernels. Kernel Structure: One CUDA kernel is used for convolution along each dimension. Thread Block: Each kernel consists of blocks of k \times k threads. Thread Work: Each thread computes a 1D convolution with the wavelet filter kernels (low-pass and high-pass). Beam Processing: One block is responsible for a beam of k \times k voxels along the current convolution direction. Gathering Strategy: Instead of scattering coefficients, the method traverses the octree and gathers all contributions of wavelets intersecting the current node/chunk to avoid atomic operations and bus locking penalties. Register Optimization: At each reconstruction step, ensure all needed data resides in register space before convolution. Reuse data fetched for the reconstruction of the previous chunk. Deactivated Chunks: Skipped entirely. 6. Root Finding: Perform root finding on the reconstructed piecewise algebraic surface defined by: f(x, y, z) = \sum{0 \leq i, j, k \leq d} f{ijk} x^i y^j z^k = 0 where f{ijk} are the reconstructed coefficients and d is the surface degree along each dimension, resulting in an overall degree of 3d. Different root finding techniques are compared for precision and efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def waveletmultiresolutionrendering(volumedata, camerapos, isovalue, epsilon, k=8, d=3): # Step 1: Wavelet Transform # Apply separable 3D wavelet transform using polynomial spline wavelets # Sequentially transform in x, y, z directions coefficients = separablewavelettransform(volumedata, d) # Step 2: Octree Construction & Min/Max Propagation # Build octree hierarchy from coefficients # Propagate min/max values from leaves to root using B-spline convex combination octree = buildoctreefromcoefficients(coefficients) propagateminmax(octree) # Step 3: Chunk Activation # Traverse octree and activate chunks based on view-dependent error metric activatedchunks = [] for chunk in octree.chunks: # Check if isovalue is within chunk's min/max range containsisovalue = chunk.minvalue <= isovalue <= chunk.maxvalue # Check geometric error metric: s/c > epsilon # s = node diameter, c = distance from camera nodediameter = chunk.spatialextent # Guard against division by zero if camera is inside the chunk distancetocamera = max(math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a,b in zip(chunk.center, camerapos))), 1e-6) geometricerror = nodediameter / distancetocamera if containsisovalue and geometricerror > epsilon: activatedchunks.append(chunk) # Step 4: Continuity Handling # Add neighbors if wavelet support extends into them chunkstoreconstruct = set() for chunk in activatedchunks: chunkstoreconstruct.add(chunk) neighbors = getadjacentchunks(chunk, k) for neighbor in neighbors: if neighbor not in chunkstoreconstruct: # Check if wavelet support from activated chunk overlaps neighbor if chunk.supportoverlaps(neighbor): chunkstoreconstruct.add(neighbor) # Step 5: CUDA Reconstruction # Reconstruct data for chunks in chunkstoreconstruct reconstructeddata = {} for chunk in chunkstoreconstruct: # Skip if already processed or deactivated if chunk in reconstructeddata: continue # Gather contributions from wavelets intersecting this chunk # Ensure data is in register space data = gatherwaveletcontributions(chunk, coefficients) # Apply 1D convolution along x, y, z using CUDA kernels # Each block processes a beam of kk voxels reconstructedchunk = applychunkreconstruction(data, k) reconstructeddata[chunk] = reconstructedchunk # Step 6: Root Finding # Solve f(x,y,z) = 0 for the reconstructed piecewise algebraic surface isosurface = solvepolynomialsurface(reconstructeddata, isovalue, d) return isosurface def separablewavelettransform(volume, d): # Sequentially perform transformation in x-, y-, and z-direction # Uses polynomial spline wavelets with minimal vanishing moments data = volume.copy() for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: data = apply1dwaveletfilter(data, axis, d) return data def buildoctreefromcoefficients(coefficients): # Construct octree hierarchy where levels form nested vector spaces # Calculate min/max values for leaf nodes octree = Octree() for leaf in octree.leaves: leaf.minvalue = min(coefficients[leaf.region]) leaf.maxvalue = max(coefficients[leaf.region]) return octree def propagateminmax(octree): # Propagate min/max values towards root using convex combination property of B-spline basis for node in octree.nodesbottomup(): if node.isleaf: continue node.minvalue = min(child.minvalue for child in node.children) node.maxvalue = max(child.maxvalue for child in node.children) def getadjacentchunks(chunk, k): # Return neighboring chunks in the k x k x k grid neighbors = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue neighbors.append(chunk.getneighbor(dx, dy, dz)) return neighbors def gatherwaveletcontributions(chunk, coefficients): # Traverse octree hierarchy and gather all contributions of wavelets intersecting the chunk # Avoids scattering memory access patterns contributions = [] for wavelet in coefficients: if wavelet.supportintersects(chunk.region): contributions.append(wavelet) return contributions def applychunkreconstruction(data, k): # Apply reconstruction to one chunk after another # Deactivated chunks skipped. Ensure needed data in register space. # Reuse data fetched for previous chunk. # One CUDA kernel per dimension, blocks of k x k threads. # Each thread computes 1D convolution with wavelet filter kernels (low pass and high pass). # One block responsible for a beam of k x k voxels along current convolution direction. result = data.copy() for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: result = apply1dconvolutionkernel(result, axis, k) return result def solvepolynomialsurface(reconstructeddata, isovalue, d): # Solve f(x, y, z) = sum{0<=i,j,k<=d} fijk x^i y^j z^k = 0 # Different root finding techniques compared for precision/efficiency surface = [] for chunk, coeffs in reconstructeddata.items(): # Extract coefficients fijk for the chunk # Apply root finding algorithm (e.g., Newton-Raphson or subdivision) surface.extend(findrootsinchunk(coeffs, isovalue, d)) return surface class Octree: def init(self): self.chunks = [] self.leaves = [] self.nodes = [] def nodesbottomup(self): return reversed(self.nodes) Parameters: Interpolation degree d: Determines the surface degree along each dimension. Common choices are d=1 (tri-linear) and d=3 (tri-cubic). Chunk size k: Set to k=8 in the source. Threshold \epsilon: User-defined threshold for the geometric error metric. Wavelet Type: Polynomial spline wavelets with minimal vanishing moments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cracks: If continuity is not maintained by reconstructing neighboring chunks where wavelet support extends, cracks may appear in the isosurface. Performance: Scattering memory access patterns (distributing coefficients into intersecting nodes) cause bus locking penalties on GPUs; the gathering approach avoids this. Granularity: Tracking activation for every single wavelet is inefficient; processing in chunks (k \times k \times k) is necessary for SIMD performance. Camera Inside Chunk: The distance c in the error metric can be zero if the camera is inside a chunk, causing division by zero; a small epsilon guard is required. Defined by Monet Morlet to avoid the fixed resolution limit of windowed Fourier transforms. It decomposes the signal into a family of functions that are translations and dilations of a unique mother wavelet \psi(x). The main drawback of the alternative windowed Fourier transform (Gabor) is that its spatial and frequency resolution is constant, which is unacceptable for signals with features of very different sizes. Time Complexity: The separable wavelet transform reduces computation to three times the 1D case. Reconstruction is performed only on activated chunks, skipping deactivated ones. Memory Complexity: Depends on the octree structure and the number of activated chunks. Measured Performance: Tested with datasets up to 512^3 voxels and viewport sizes up to 1024 \times 768 pixels, demonstrating interactive frame rates. Strengths: Adaptive view-dependent level-of-detail improves performance for distant parts with little visual impact. B-spline basis guarantees continuous surfaces, avoiding cracks. GPU implementation (CUDA) utilizes high computational performance. Limitations: Requires careful handling of continuity between chunks. The number of influence coefficients grows cubically with the support of the 1D wavelet (e.g., 175 for tri-cubic). When to Use: Interactive isosurface rendering of large volumetric datasets where view-dependent LOD is beneficial. When Not to Use: When non-isosurface rendering (e.g., direct volume rendering) is required, or when hardware does not support CUDA. Originated from work by Markus Steinberger and Markus Grabner at the Institute for Computer Graphics and Vision, Graz University of Technology, Austria. The method builds on the wavelet transformation [Chu92] which decorrelates data and allows selective removal of irrelevant data. It utilizes polynomial spline wavelets [CDF92] and GPU acceleration via CUDA. The approach is part of the broader field of wavelet-based volume rendering. name: Wavelet Transform
head: Fast Wavelet Transform, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Morlet Wavelet Transform
body: The Wavelet Transform provides a sparse representation for highly detailed functions by decomposing signals into dilated and translated versions of a unique basis function. It solves the limitation of windowed Fourier transforms, which suffer from fixed spatial and frequency resolution, by allowing variable resolution analysis suitable for signals with features of vastly different scales. Unlike the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) used in JPEG, which requires image fragmentation due to global basis support, the Wavelet Transform has local support in both the spatial and frequency domains, eliminating the need for block-based processing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A signal or image data array I of size N \times M (or N \times M \times P for 3D volumes). Output: A set of wavelet coefficients partitioned into approximation coefficients (low-pass) and detail coefficients (high-pass) across multiple resolution levels. Data Structures: The transform produces a hierarchical structure of sub-bands. In 2D, a single level of decomposition splits the input into four sub-bands: LL (low-pass in both directions, approximation), LH (low-pass in x, high-pass in y, horizontal details), HL (high-pass in x, low-pass in y, vertical details), and HH (high-pass in both directions, diagonal details). The LL sub-band is recursively decomposed in subsequent levels, creating a tree structure (e.g., LLL, LLH, etc.). The detail bands (LH, HL, HH) are not further decomposed in standard 2D pyramids. Parameters: Compression Ratio: Lossy compression can achieve ratios in the order of 64:1 with almost invisible artifacts. Wavelet Basis: The specific choice of the mother wavelet \psi(x) determines the filter coefficients. The sources reference linear spline wavelets and the lifting scheme for construction, but do not provide specific filter coefficients for a standard basis (e.g., Daubechies). Implementers must select a standard orthogonal wavelet filter bank or use the lifting scheme coefficients defined in the chosen library or standard. Algorithm Steps: 1. Decomposition (Analysis): The process recursively separates high-frequency details from lower frequencies. a. Apply low-pass filtering and high-pass filtering to the input signal in the x-direction. b. Downsample the results by a factor of 2 in the x-direction. c. Apply low-pass filtering and high-pass filtering to the results from step (b) in the y-direction. d. Downsample the results by a factor of 2 in the y-direction. e. This yields the four sub-bands: LL, LH, HL, HH. f. If further decomposition is required, apply steps (a) through (e) recursively to the LL sub-band. 2. Reconstruction (Synthesis): The inverse process assembles details from the coefficients. a. Upsample the sub-bands by a factor of 2 in the respective directions. b. Apply synthesis low-pass and high-pass filters. c. Sum the filtered results to reconstruct the signal at the current resolution. d. Recursively reconstruct higher-resolution levels until the original signal size is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dwt1d(signal, filtercoeffs): """ Computes c^1k = sumn h(n - 2k) c^0n exactly as defined in. Implements convolution followed by downsampling by 2. """ outlen = (len(signal) + len(filtercoeffs) - 1) // 2 result = [0.0] outlen for k in range(outlen): val = 0.0 for n in range(len(signal)): idx = n - 2 k if 0 <= idx < len(filtercoeffs): val += filtercoeffs[idx] signal[n] result[k] = val return result def dwt2d(signal, h, g): """ Performs a 2D discrete wavelet transform using separable 1D transforms. h: low-pass filter, g: high-pass filter. Returns (ll, lh, hl, hh) sub-bands. """ # 1D transform along rows (x-direction) lowx = [dwt1d(row, h) for row in signal] highx = [dwt1d(row, g) for row in signal] # 1D transform along columns (y-direction) on the downsampled row results ll = dwt2dtranspose(lowx, h) lh = dwt2dtranspose(lowx, g) hl = dwt2dtranspose(highx, h) hh = dwt2dtranspose(highx, g) return ll, lh, hl, hh def dwt2dtranspose(data, filtercoeffs): """Applies 1D transform to columns by transposing, transforming, and transposing back.""" rows = len(data) cols = len(data[0]) transposed = [[data[i][j] for i in range(rows)] for j in range(cols)] transformed = [dwt1d(col, filtercoeffs) for col in transposed] result = [[transformed[j][i] for j in range(len(transformed))] for i in range(len(transformed[0]))] return result def idwt2d(ll, lh, hl, hh, hsyn, gsyn): """ Reconstructs the signal from 2D wavelet coefficients. hsyn: synthesis low-pass filter, gsyn: synthesis high-pass filter. """ # Inverse 1D transform along columns (y-direction) lly = idwt2dtranspose(ll, hsyn) lhy = idwt2dtranspose(lh, gsyn) hly = idwt2dtranspose(hl, hsyn) hhy = idwt2dtranspose(hh, gsyn) # Sum column results lly = [[lly[i][j] + lhy[i][j] + hly[i][j] + hhy[i][j] for j in range(len(lly[0]))] for i in range(len(lly))] # Inverse 1D transform along rows (x-direction) reconstructed = idwt2dtranspose(lly, hsyn) detailx = idwt2dtranspose([[lhy[i][j] + hly[i][j] + hhy[i][j] for j in range(len(lhy[0]))] for i in range(len(lhy))], gsyn) # Sum row results result = [[reconstructed[i][j] + detailx[i][j] for j in range(len(reconstructed[0]))] for i in range(len(reconstructed))] return result def idwt2dtranspose(data, filtercoeffs): """Applies inverse 1D transform to columns.""" rows = len(data) cols = len(data[0]) transposed = [[data[i][j] for i in range(rows)] for j in range(cols)] transformed = [idwt1d(col, filtercoeffs) for col in transposed] result = [[transformed[j][i] for j in range(len(transformed))] for i in range(len(transformed[0]))] return result def idwt1d(signal, filtercoeffs): """ Inverse 1D transform: upsampling by 2 followed by synthesis filtering. Matches the inverse of the analysis step. """ upsampled = [0.0] (len(signal) 2) for k in range(len(signal)): upsampled[2 k] = signal[k] outlen = len(upsampled) + len(filtercoeffs) - 1 result = [0.0] outlen for n in range(len(upsampled)): for m in range(len(filtercoeffs)): result[n + m] += upsampled[n] filtercoeffs[m] return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quantization Error: In lossy compression, quantization errors are introduced during the transform range and are smoothly distributed across the image domain by the inverse transform, making them often unrecognizable to the human eye. Boundary Conditions: The sources do not specify boundary handling for finite signals. Implementers must choose a strategy (e.g., periodic, symmetric, zero-padding) which affects the transform's energy compaction properties. Degenerate Input: The recursive nature requires the data dimensions to be divisible by 2^L where L is the number of levels, or appropriate boundary handling must be implemented to manage non-power-of-two sizes. Time Complexity: The discrete wavelet transform is computed in linear time, O(N), where N is the number of data points. Memory Complexity: The transform is typically performed in-place or requires storage proportional to the input size for the coefficient tree. Performance: Lossy compression achieves high compression rates in the order of 64:1 with almost invisible artifacts. Strengths: Local support in both image domain and frequency space eliminates the need for image fragmentation (unlike DCT). It provides a sparse representation for highly detailed functions. Limitations: The main drawback of the related windowed Fourier transform (Gabor) is constant spatial and frequency resolution, which is not acceptable for signals with features of very different sizes; the wavelet transform avoids this. When to use: Ideal for multiresolution volume visualization, compressed direct volume rendering, and progressive transmission where spatial locality and hierarchical detail refinement are required. When not to use: Avoid when global frequency analysis without spatial localization is needed, or when strict block-based DCT compatibility is required for legacy pipelines. The wavelet transform was defined by Monet Morlet to avoid the fixed resolution limit of windowed Fourier transforms. It decomposes the signal into a family of functions, which are the translation and dilation of a unique function \psi(x). The transform has roots in signal processing and pure mathematics. It is used in image compression, solving partial differential equations, and integrating radiosity kernels. The lifting scheme is used to construct wavelets for efficiently modeling massive volumetric data sets. DWT was introduced for compressed volume rendering by Muraki [Mur93] and is used in block-wise hierarchical decomposition (octree) with entropy encoding, block caching, and projective classification. name: Hierarchical Wavelet Transform on Omnitrees
head: Moment-conserving anisotropic compression, Wavelet compression on omnitrees
body: This method transforms nodal omnitree data into wavelet coefficients to enable lossless or lossy compression via pruning and tree restructuring (downsplit). It operates directly on the omnitree's anisotropic structure, allowing coarsening in specific dimensions while preserving the hierarchical spatial layout. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An omnitree where each node v has a splitting label \vec{b}(v), refined dimensions \sigma(v), and nodal coefficients (scaling values) w{c \emptyset} for its children c, ordered in Z-order. Output: A set of wavelet coefficients \vec{w}^v for all non-leaf nodes, and a root scaling coefficient w\theta^{\text{root}}. Data Structures: Omnitree Node: Contains splitting label \vec{b}(v), refined dimensions \sigma(v), and a list of child nodes. Scaling Vector \vec{s}^v: A vector of size 2^{|\sigma(v)|} containing the nodal coefficients of the children of node v, arranged in Z-order. Wavelet Vector \vec{w}^v: A vector of size 2^{|\sigma(v)|} arranged in a compatible order to \vec{s}^v. Algorithm Steps: 1. Gather Scaling Coefficients: For each node v, gather the nodal coefficients of its children into vector \vec{s}^v. 2. Local Transformation (Bottom-Up): Process nodes from leaves to root. For each node v with refined dimensions \sigma(v): Compute the local transformation matrix H{|\sigma(v)|}. Compute wavelet coefficients: \vec{w}^v = H{|\sigma(v)|} \cdot \vec{s}^v. The first element of \vec{w}^v is the scaling coefficient for the parent; the remaining elements are detail coefficients. Store the computed wavelet coefficients in the node. 3. Reconstruction (Top-Down): To reconstruct nodal values, apply the inverse transformation successively from larger to finer scales (root down to leaves). Start at the root. The root scaling coefficient w\theta^{\text{root}} holds the mean value. For each node v from root to leaves: Retrieve the wavelet coefficients \vec{w}^v. Compute the inverse transformation matrix R{|\sigma(v)|} = H{|\sigma(v)|}^{-1}. Reconstruct scaling coefficients for children: \vec{s}^v = R{|\sigma(v)|} \cdot \vec{w}^v. Distribute these values to the children's nodal coefficients. Formulas: The wavelet coefficients are computed by: \vec{w}^v = H{|\sigma(v)|} \cdot \vec{s}^v \quad (10) where H{|\sigma(v)|} is the hierarchization matrix. For Haar wavelets: H{|\sigma(v)|} = \frac{1}{2^{|\sigma(v)|}} \bigotimes{j \in \sigma(v)} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \quad (11) The function f is represented as: f = w\theta^{\text{root}} + \sum{v: \text{nonleaf}} \sum{\emptyset \neq \tau \subset \sigma(v)} w\tau^v \cdot \psi\tau^v \quad (12) where \psi\tau^v are the wavelet basis functions. The inverse transformation satisfies R{|\sigma(v)|} H{|\sigma(v)|} = I. Parameters: Wavelet Type: Haar wavelets are specified. Normalization: The matrix includes a factor of 1/2^{|\sigma(v)|}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Leaf Nodes: Leaf nodes have no children, so no transformation is applied. They store scaling coefficients directly. Root Node: The root scaling coefficient represents the mean over the entire domain (0,1)^d. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kroneckerproduct(A, B): """Computes the Kronecker product of two matrices.""" result = [] for rowa in A: for rowb in B: newrow = [] for vala in rowa: newrow.extend([vala x for x in rowb]) result.append(newrow) return result def computewavelettransform(node): """Bottom-up transform: computes wavelet coefficients for an omnitree node.""" if node.isleaf(): return node.scalingcoefficient # Gather scaling coefficients from children in Z-order sv = [child.scalingcoefficient for child in node.children] k = len(node.refineddimensions) n = 2 k # Construct Haar transformation matrix H # H = (1/2^k) Kronecker product of 1D Hadamard matrices H = [[1.0]] for in range(k): H1d = [[1, 1], [1, -1]] H = kroneckerproduct(H, H1d) # Apply normalization factor scale = 1.0 / (2 k) H = [[val scale for val in row] for row in H] # Compute wavelet coefficients: wv = H @ sv wv = [sum(H[i][j] sv[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)] node.waveletcoefficients = wv return wv[0] # Scaling coefficient for the parent def reconstructnodalvalues(node): """Top-down reconstruction: recovers nodal coefficients from wavelet coefficients.""" if node.isleaf(): return node.scalingcoefficient wv = node.waveletcoefficients k = len(node.refineddimensions) n = 2 k # Reconstruct H to compute R = H^-1 H = [[1.0]] for in range(k): H1d = [[1, 1], [1, -1]] H = kroneckerproduct(H, H1d) scale = 1.0 / (2 k) H = [[val scale for val in row] for row in H] # Inverse transformation R = H^-1. For Haar, H is symmetric and H^-1 = 2^k H scaleinv = 2 k R = [[val scaleinv for val in row] for row in H] # Reconstruct scaling coefficients: sv = R @ wv sv = [sum(R[i][j] wv[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)] # Distribute to children for i, child in enumerate(node.children): child.scalingcoefficient = sv[i] return sv Represents piecewise constant functions f \in L^2([0,1]^d) hierarchically. The nodal representation stores f as a sum over leaf nodes v with b(v)=0: f = \sum s^v \phi^v, where \phi^v is 1 if x \in \text{rect}(v), 0 else. This is the specific wavelet basis used in the main method. Time Complexity: O(2^d N), linear in the number of coefficients N, using data stacks. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables lossless or lossy compression via pruning and tree restructuring (downsplit). Coarsening can be implemented as a special case of refinement. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Originated in the paper "Towards Fully Dynamic Omnitrees: Moment-Conserving Anisotropic Compression With Wavelets". It extends omnitree data structures with wavelet transforms to support dynamic compression and reconstruction. name: Haar Wavelet Transform on Omnitrees
head: nodal to wavelet transform, tensor-product Haar basis
body: This method transforms the nodal representation of an omnitree into a hierarchical wavelet coefficient basis to enable efficient compression. It differs from sibling methods like Downsplit and Coarsening Compression by explicitly mapping the piecewise constant leaf-node basis functions to a tensor-product Haar wavelet basis, allowing for lossless or lossy compression via coefficient pruning and tree restructuring. The transform maps the nodal representation of a volume, defined as a sum over leaf nodes, into a hierarchical wavelet basis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An omnitree structure where the volume function f is represented by nodal coefficients s^v associated with leaf nodes v (where splitting label b(v)=0). Output: A set of wavelet coefficients corresponding to the same spatial domain, organized hierarchically. Data Structures: The omnitree nodes store splitting labels \vec{b}(v), a vector where each component bj \in \{0, 1\} indicates whether the node is split in dimension j. Leaf nodes have b(v)=\vec{0}. Method Steps: 1. Nodal Representation: The volume function f \in L^2([0,1]^d) is initially represented as a sum over leaf nodes v: f = \sum{v \in \text{Leaves}} s^v \phi^v where \phi^v is the basis function for node v, defined as 1 if x \in \text{rect}(v) and 0 otherwise. 2. Basis Transformation: The nodal basis functions \phi^v are expressed in terms of the tensor-product Haar wavelet basis. The Haar wavelet transform is applied hierarchically. For a node v that is split, the constant value over the parent rect is decomposed into a coarse approximation (average) and detail coefficients (differences) for the children. 3. Coefficient Calculation: For each split dimension j, the transform computes the average and difference of the coefficients of the two children along that dimension. In 3D, this is applied across dimensions. The specific application involves applying the 3D Haar wavelet transform to blocks of data. 4. Compression (Optional): The resulting wavelet coefficients are quantized and encoded. This may involve partitioning the volume into small blocks, subdividing them into subblocks, and applying the 3D Haar wavelet transform two or three times. Parameters: Number of Transform Levels: Typically 2 or 3 for 3D data. Block Size: The volume is partitioned into small blocks before transformation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The transform assumes a specific domain [0,1]^d. Handling boundaries requires care to avoid artifacts. Precision: Quantization introduces loss; the choice of quantization step affects compression ratio and visual quality. A specific application where the volume is partitioned into small blocks, which are further subdivided into subblocks. A three-dimensional Haar wavelet is applied two or three times to these subblocks. The resulting coefficients are then quantized and encoded. Complexity: The transform is applied hierarchically. The complexity depends on the number of nodes and the depth of the omnitree. Block-based approaches have complexity proportional to the number of voxels. Performance: Wavelet-based compression can achieve high compression ratios, especially for smooth volumes, by pruning small coefficients. Strengths: Efficient representation of piecewise constant functions; enables both lossless and lossy compression. Limitations: Block-based approaches may introduce blocking artifacts at block boundaries. The Haar wavelet transform on omnitrees is part of the broader field of wavelet-based volume rendering and compression. It builds on the concept of representing volumes using hierarchical data structures like omnitrees. The specific use of Haar wavelets for block-based volume compression was explored by Insung et al. and Kim et al.. name: Downsplit
head: Dimensional downsplit, inverse normalization, split rotation
body:
Downsplit is a tree restructuring operation in hierarchical wavelet-based volume compression that factors a multi-dimensional split into a cascade of lower-dimensional splits. It restructures an omnitree without modifying the set of leaf boxes, serving as the inverse to normalization. By moving parent refinements down to children, it exposes new coarsening opportunities that multi-dimensional splits would otherwise obscure, enabling more efficient pruning of wavelet coefficients. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An internal node v of an omnitree T with splitting label \vec{b}(v) and dimension set \sigma(v) where |\sigma(v)| \ge 2. The node has children uk for k \in \{0, 1\}^{\sigma(v)}. Output: A target tree T' containing a new two-level structure replacing v, and a mapping M from initial to target tree nodes. Data Structures: Splitting Label \sigma(v): A set of dimensions along which node v is refined. Split Dimensions: Two disjoint subsets S1 \subset \sigma(v) and S2 = \sigma(v) \setminus S1, where \emptyset 
eq S1 
eq \sigma(v). S1 are the dimensions to be "split down" (moved to children), and S2 are the dimensions to be retained at the parent level. Nodalization Matrix R{|S2|}: A matrix used to redistribute wavelet coefficients. It is a Kronecker product over the dimensions in S2. Rows are indexed by the children of the new residual node v' in Z-order; columns are indexed by the power set 2^{S2}. Numbered Steps: 1. Select Split Dimensions: Choose a non-empty proper subset S1 \subset \sigma(v) and define S2 = \sigma(v) \setminus S1. 2. Create Residual Node: Create a new node v' in the target tree T' at the same spatial location as v. Set its splitting label \sigma(v') = S2. Consequently, v' has 2^{|S2|} children. 3. Create Intermediate Children: For each child index r \in \{0, 1\}^{S2}, create a new intermediate child node ur of v'. Set its splitting label \sigma(ur) = S1. Consequently, each ur has 2^{|S1|} children. 4. Link Original Children: The children of ur are exactly the original children uk of v whose S2-coordinates equal r. This preserves the spatial position of all leaves. 5. Redistribute Wavelet Coefficients: The wavelet coefficients w^v	au associated with node v are redistributed to v' and \{ur\} as follows: Residual Coefficients: Coefficients associated purely with S2 are transferred directly to v': w^{v'}{	au2} = w^v{	au2}, \quad \emptyset 
eq 	au2 \subset S2 Intermediate Coefficients: Coefficients involving S1 are redistributed to the intermediate children using the nodalization matrix R{|S2|}: w^{\{ur\}}{	au1} = \sum{	au2 \subset S2} (R{|S2|}){	au2}^{\{r\}} \cdot w^v{	au2 \sqcup 	au1}, \quad \emptyset 
eq 	au1 \subset S1 Here, 	au1 \subset S1 and 	au2 \subset S2. The term w^v{	au2 \sqcup 	au1} refers to the source coefficient with indices from both sets. 6. Construct Mapping: If v has index i, v' has index i', and ur has index ir, the mapping entry M[i] consists of the union of \{i\} and all \{ir\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import itertools def kroneckerproduct(A, B): """Computes the Kronecker product of two matrices.""" return [[a b for b in rowb] for rowa in A for rowb in B] def downsplit(nodev, splitdimsS1): """ Performs a downsplit on node v. Args: nodev: The internal node to split. splitdimsS1: A set of dimensions to move to children (S1). Returns: nodevprime: The new residual parent node. intermediatechildren: A list of new intermediate child nodes. mappingupdate: Dictionary mapping old index to new indices. """ sigmav = nodev.splittinglabel S1 = splitdimsS1 S2 = sigmav - S1 k1 = len(S1) k2 = len(S2) # 1. Create residual node v' with S2 splits nodevprime = Node(location=nodev.location, splittinglabel=S2) # 2. Create intermediate children ur for each combination of S2 coordinates intermediatechildren = [] mappingupdate = {nodev.index: [nodevprime.index]} # Precompute S2 coordinate extraction mapping s2dims = sorted(S2) s2dimindices = {d: i for i, d in enumerate(s2dims)} for r in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=k2): ur = Node(location=nodev.location, splittinglabel=S1) intermediatechildren.append(ur) # Reassign original children uk to ur based on S2 coordinates for k in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=len(sigmav)): kS2 = 0 for idx, dim in enumerate(sigmav): if dim in S2: kS2 |= (k[idx] << s2dimindices[dim]) if kS2 == r: uk = nodev.children[k] ur.addchild(uk) mappingupdate[nodev.index].append(ur.index) # 3. Redistribute wavelet coefficients # Generate non-empty subsets of S2 and S1 subsetsS2 = list(itertools.chain.fromiterable(itertools.combinations(S2, rlen) for rlen in range(1, len(S2) + 1))) subsetsS1 = list(itertools.chain.fromiterable(itertools.combinations(S1, rlen) for rlen in range(1, len(S1) + 1))) # Transfer pure S2 coefficients to v' for tau2 in subsetsS2: nodevprime.coefficients[tau2] = nodev.coefficients[tau2] # Construct Nodalization Matrix R|S2| as Kronecker product over S2 dimensions # Rows indexed by r in Z-order, columns by tau2 subsets of S2 tau2tocol = {tau2: i for i, tau2 in enumerate(subsetsS2)} rtorow = {r: i for i, r in enumerate(itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=k2))} # Base 1D nodalization matrix (standard Haar-like basis) basematrix = [[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, -1.0]] Rcurrent = [[1.0]] for in range(k2): Rcurrent = kroneckerproduct(Rcurrent, basematrix) R = [[0.0] (2k2) for in range(2k2)] for r in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=k2): rowidx = rtorow[r] for tau2 in subsetsS2: colidx = tau2tocol[tau2] R[rowidx][colidx] = Rcurrent[rowidx][colidx] # Apply redistribution formula for tau1 in subsetsS1: for r in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=k2): rowidx = rtorow[r] coeffsum = 0.0 for tau2 in subsetsS2: colidx = tau2tocol[tau2] sourcetau = tuple(sorted(list(tau2) + list(tau1))) coeffsum += R[rowidx][colidx] nodev.coefficients[sourcetau] intermediatechildren[rowidx].coefficients[tau1] = coeffsum # Apply identical inverse Haar butterflies to all child sets # Implementation details for the butterfly step are not provided in the sources for ur in intermediatechildren: applyinversehaarbutterfly(ur.coefficients, S1) return nodevprime, intermediatechildren, mappingupdate Parameters and Edge Cases: Scaling Coefficients: The scaling coefficients w\emptyset are entirely omitted from these computations. Leaf Constraints: The children of v' (the ur nodes) are not necessarily leaves. Removing all splits cannot occur in a downsplit. Canonical Omnitrees: Technically, if the omnitree is not canonical, refinements might need to be swept down the tree if they cannot be realized at the original node, though this is a secondary concern. Implementation: Can be implemented by reusing the refinement algorithm from [29] and group resolution from Section 3.2 of the source. Complexity: The downsplit decouples 2^k - 1 source coefficients into one parent set of size 2^{k2} - 1 and 2^{k2} child sets of size 2^{k1} - 1, where k1 = |S1| and k2 = |S2|. It applies identical inverse Haar butterflies to all child sets. Performance: The operation preserves the function and leaf rectangles, changing only the basis used for coefficients. Its primary benefit is exposing coarsening opportunities, which reduces the total number of coefficients stored. Limitations: Selecting the optimal omnitree discretization is computationally infeasible at fine resolutions in 3D; heuristics focusing on parents and grandparents of leaves are used instead. Downsplit is part of the "Towards Fully Dynamic Omnitrees" framework for moment-conserving anisotropic compression with wavelets. It is defined as the inverse to normalization, where normalization absorbs a common child refinement into the parent, and downsplit moves a parent refinement down to the children. The method relies on the nodalization matrix and Kronecker products to handle multi-dimensional wavelet spaces. name: Coarsening Compression
head: Wavelet pruning
body:
Coarsening compression is a lossy compression step that prunes small wavelet detail coefficients to reduce the number of leaf nodes in a hierarchical omnitree, while preserving the integral of the represented function. It differs from sibling methods like Downsplit by operating directly on coefficient magnitudes to merge nodes, whereas downsplit restructures the tree topology to expose new coarsening opportunities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchized omnitree with wavelet coefficients w	au^v associated with each node v and dimension subset 	au \subseteq \sigma(v), and an error density threshold \varepsilon \ge 0. Output: A modified omnitree with fewer leaf nodes and a corresponding set of wavelet coefficients. Data Structures: The omnitree consists of nodes v. Each node v has: \sigma(v): The set of active dimensions at node v. 	ext{rect}(v): The spatial bounding box (hyperrectangle) of node v. w	au^v: Wavelet coefficients for each non-empty subset 	au \subseteq \sigma(v). Children: A list of child nodes. Steps: 1. Identify Candidate Nodes: Iterate through the tree bottom-up, starting from the parents of leaves (last-level parents). Identify nodes v where all children are leaves. 2. Check Coefficient Bounds: For a candidate node v, determine the set of dimensions C \subseteq \sigma(v) in which the node can be coarsened. A dimension j is included in C if all detail coefficients w	au^v where 	au \cap \{j\} 
eq \emptyset satisfy the bound: |w	au^v| \leq \varepsilon \quad  orall 	au \cap C 
eq \emptyset \quad (16) 3. Perform Coarsening: If all detail coefficients satisfy the criterion, set C = \sigma(v) and fully coarsen the node into a leaf. Otherwise, perform partial coarsening for individual dimensions j where the bound is met. The detail coefficients w	au^v with 	au \cap C 
eq \emptyset are pruned (set to zero). The remaining coefficients become the coefficient vector of the coarsened node v' with \sigma(v') = \sigma(v) \setminus C. Coarsening preserves the integral of the function because the discarded wavelet functions have an integral of exactly zero due to orthogonality against constant functions. 4. Iterate: Apply coarsening bottom-up from last-level parents and repeat until no further coarsening passes are possible. Error Bound: The total error incurred by all coarsening passes is bounded by a function of the threshold \varepsilon, domain volume, dimension d, and source tree height \ell: \|	ilde{f} - f\|1 \leq \sum{v 	ext{ nonleaf}} (2^{|\sigma(v)|} - 1) \cdot \varepsilon |	ext{rect}(v)| \leq (2^d - 1) \cdot \varepsilon |\Omega| \cdot \ell \quad (17) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsenomnitree(root, epsilon): """ Performs coarsening compression on an omnitree. root: The root node of the omnitree. epsilon: Error density threshold. """ # Helper to check if a node is a leaf def isleaf(node): return node.isleaf # Helper to collect leaf parents in bottom-up order # The sources do not specify the exact traversal algorithm, # so a standard post-order traversal is used here. def getleafparents(node): parents = [] if node.isleaf: return parents childrenareleaves = all(isleaf(c) for c in node.children) if childrenareleaves: parents.append(node) else: for child in node.children: parents.extend(getleafparents(child)) return parents changed = True while changed: changed = False nodestoprocess = getleafparents(root) for v in nodestoprocess: # Step 1: Identify nodes whose children are all leaves if not all(isleaf(child) for child in v.children): continue # Step 2: Determine dimensions C that can be coarsened C = [] for dim in v.sigma: cancoarsendim = True for tau in v.coefficients.keys(): if dim in tau: if abs(v.coefficients[tau]) > epsilon: cancoarsendim = False break if cancoarsendim: C.append(dim) if not C: continue # Step 3: Prune coefficients associated with dimensions in C coeffstoremove = [tau for tau in v.coefficients.keys() if any(dim in tau for dim in C)] for tau in coeffstoremove: del v.coefficients[tau] # Update sigma for the coarsened node v' v.sigma = [dim for dim in v.sigma if dim not in C] # If sigma is empty, the node becomes a leaf if not v.sigma: v.isleaf = True v.children = [] changed = True return root Parameters: \varepsilon: Error density threshold. If \varepsilon = 0, only nodes with exactly zero detail coefficients are coarsened, yielding lossless compression. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overestimation of Error: The a priori bound (Eq. 17) greatly overestimates the actual L1 error when \varepsilon > 0. A tighter a posteriori estimate should be obtained by aggregating coefficient magnitudes from nodes actually selected for coarsening. Heuristic Scope: In practice, focusing only on parents and grandparents of leaves can yield significant savings, but may not exploit all redundancy. An iterative compression strategy that alternates between downsplitting to expose redundancy and coarsening to prune coefficients. After plain coarsening converges, the algorithm enters the loop: 1. Downsplit. For each multi-dimensional node v (|\sigma(v)| \ge 2) with at least two leaf children, select dimension j^ \in \sigma(v) whose pure one-dimensional detail coefficient has the smallest magnitude: j^ = \arg \min{j \in \sigma(v)} |w{Tj}^v|. Downsplit the single dimension \{j^\} and update all coefficients using the standard transformation equations. 2. Coarsen. Apply the coarsening criterion (Eq. 16) to all nodes whose children are all leaves. 3. Normalize. Resolve any uniqueness violations introduced by the combination of downsplit and coarsening, restoring a canonical omnitree. Repeat steps 1-3 until no coarsenings occur in a round. The dimension selection heuristic assumes the dominance of first-order effects, so that when w{v}^{	auj} is near zero, all intermediates along j will have negligible detail. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves the integral of the function exactly. Can be combined with Downsplit to expose more redundancy. Limitations: The a priori error bound is loose. May not exploit all redundancy if used alone. Coarsening compression is part of the wavelet-based volume rendering compression strategy on omnitrees, introduced in the paper "Towards Fully Dynamic Omnitrees: Moment-Conserving Anisotropic Compression With Wavelets". It operates in the wavelet domain, allowing reconstruction of nodal function values only at the end for output file writing and error evaluation. name: L2-optimal wavelet splatting
head: Wavelet Projections for Volume Rendering
body: L2-optimal wavelet splatting is a volume rendering technique that decomposes volume data into a wavelet pyramid representation in the spline domain and computes splats via an orthogonal projection operator using least-squares approximation on an adaptive multiresolution grid. It sets itself apart from standard interpolation-based wavelet splatting (such as Wavelet-based Multiresolution Rendering) by ensuring the smallest possible approximation error for a given sampling step size and by adapting the grid resolution to the basis function size, which yields significant performance gains at coarse scales. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data f(\mathbf{x}) of size M^3 voxels, represented as a linear combination of basis functions \psik(\mathbf{x}) with coefficients c(k): f(\mathbf{x}) = \sumk c(k)\psik(\mathbf{x}). Input: Viewing direction \theta (unit vector \vec{\theta}) and screen dimensions N \times N. Input: Scale level j and base sampling step h. Output: Rendered image on the screen of size N^2 pixels. Data Structures: Wavelet Coefficients: Array of coefficients c(k) corresponding to the wavelet decomposition of the volume. Kernel Table: A precomputed table for the kernel function \xi{h;\theta}(\mathbf{s}), calculated once per viewing direction at fine resolution in shift parameter \mathbf{s}. Grid: An adaptive reconstruction grid with sampling step hj = 2^j h. Parameters: M: Volume resolution dimension (e.g., 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048). N: Rendering screen size dimension. h: Base sampling step size. Typical value: h=1 (no oversampling). hj: Adaptive sampling step size at scale j, defined as hj = 2^j h. j: Scale level. Complexity decays with a factor of 8^j per scale j at small scales. n: Degree of the B-spline basis function. Values used: n=0 (Haar), n=1 (Linear), n=3 (Cubic). k1, k3, k7: Constant factors in the operation count formulas. s: Splat support size, defined as s(\Psin) = 2n+1 for B-splines. Steps: 1. Wavelet Decomposition: Decompose the volume data f(\mathbf{x}) into a linear combination of basis functions \psik(\mathbf{x}) with coefficients c(k). f(\mathbf{x}) = \sumk c(k)\psik(\mathbf{x}) 2. Wavelet Splat Definition: The volume rendering integral (X-ray transform) for a direction \theta becomes a linear combination of wavelet splats \chi{\theta;k}(\mathbf{y}): p\theta f(\mathbf{y}) = \sumk c(k) \chi{\theta;k}(\mathbf{y}) where \mathbf{y} = (u, v) are coordinates on the projection plane perpendicular to \vec{\theta}, and \chi{\theta;k}(\mathbf{y}) = p\theta \psik(\mathbf{y}) is the projection of the basis function. 3. Adaptive Grid Approximation: For a fixed viewing direction \theta and scale j, approximate the continuous wavelet splat \chi{\theta;j}(\mathbf{y}) onto a reconstruction grid with sampling step hj = 2^j h using basis functions \phi(\mathbf{y}/hj \mathbf{l}). The approximation operator P{hj} yields discrete grid coefficients c{hj}(\mathbf{l}). 4. Least-Squares Coefficient Calculation: Calculate the discrete grid coefficients c{hj}(\mathbf{l}) using least-squares approximation via the scalar product with the dual function \tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{y}): c{hj}(\mathbf{l}) = \langle \chi{\theta;j}(\mathbf{y}), \tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{y}/hj \mathbf{l}) \rangle hj where \tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{y}) is the dual function of the basis function \phi(\mathbf{y}). 5. Kernel Lookup: Express the scalar product as a kernel function \xi{h;\theta}(\mathbf{s}) with a single shift parameter \mathbf{s} = hj \mathbf{l} - \mathbf{z} (where \mathbf{z} relates to the wavelet shift): c{hj}(\mathbf{l}) = \xi{h;\theta}(\mathbf{s}) = \left\langle \tilde{\phi}\left(\frac{\mathbf{y}}{hj}\right), \chi{\theta}(\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{s}) \right\rangle The kernel \xi{h;\theta}(\mathbf{s}) is precomputed for the current viewing direction at fine resolution in \mathbf{s} and stored in a table. Retrieving grid coefficients requires a single table lookup. 6. Full-Screen Interpolation: Interpolate the projected data from the dual space grid to full-screen resolution N^2 in cardinal space using three steps: Dual-to-Spline Change: Convert from dual space to spline space. Upsampling: Use the shortest upsampling interpolation filters available in spline space to reach full resolution. Spline-to-Cardinal Change: Convert from spline space to cardinal space for visualization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def l2optimalwaveletsplatting(volumecoeffs, viewingdirection, volumesizeM, screensizeN, scalej, basesteph, splinedegreen): # 1. Calculate adaptive grid step hj = (2 scalej) basesteph # 2. Precompute kernel table for the current viewing direction # The kernel xihtheta(s) is calculated once at fine resolution in s. # [Source does not specify the exact numerical integration method for the kernel.] kerneltable = {} # 3. Initialize adaptive grid griddim = int(volumesizeM / basesteph) grid = [[0.0 for in range(griddim)] for in range(griddim)] # 4. Project wavelet splats onto the adaptive grid for k, ck in enumerate(volumecoeffs): # [Source does not specify the exact mapping from coefficient index k to spatial shift z and scale.] z = k % volumesizeM waveletscale = k // volumesizeM # Determine relevant grid indices l where the kernel support overlaps # s = hj l - z for l in range(griddim): s = hj l - z # [Source does not specify exact kernel support bounds; typically compact for B-splines] if abs(s) <= (2 splinedegreen + 1): # Single table lookup kernelvalue = kerneltable.get((s, viewingdirection), 0.0) grid[l] += ck kernelvalue # 5. Interpolate from adaptive grid to full screen resolution N^2 # Step 1: Dual-to-spline space change splinegrid = [[0.0 for in range(griddim)] for in range(griddim)] for i in range(griddim): for j in range(griddim): splinegrid[i][j] = grid[i][j] # [Source does not specify exact dual-to-spline filter coefficients] # Step 2: Upsampling to full resolution using shortest filters in spline space upscaledimage = [[0.0 for in range(screensizeN)] for in range(screensizeN)] for i in range(screensizeN): for j in range(screensizeN): upscaledimage[i][j] = splinegrid[i // 2][j // 2] # [Source does not specify exact upsampling filter] # Step 3: Spline-to-cardinal space change renderedimage = [[0.0 for in range(screensizeN)] for in range(screensizeN)] for i in range(screensizeN): for j in range(screensizeN): renderedimage[i][j] = upscaledimage[i][j] # [Source does not specify exact spline-to-cardinal filter] return renderedimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Full Resolution Breakdown: At full resolution (j=0 or small j), the speed-up of Method 2 breaks down because the adaptive grid step hj becomes small, increasing computation. At this point, the complexity of Method 2 is 50% higher than Method 1, although it yields higher quality. Precision: The method relies on accurate precomputation of the kernel table. Errors in the kernel calculation can propagate to the final image. Degenerate Input: The method assumes the volume data can be decomposed into the specified wavelet basis. If the volume has significant high-frequency content not captured by the basis, the approximation error may be higher. Time and Memory Complexity: Method 1 (Gross): Complexity Op1 \approx k1 (M 2^j)^3 (s + h - 1)^2 \approx 2^j M^3. The decay is only 2^j per scale. Method 2 (L2-optimal): Complexity Op2 \approx k3 2^{-3j} M^3 + k7 N^2. The term dependent on M decays as 2^{-3j} (or 8^{-j}) per scale. Scaling: The complexity Op2 decays with a factor of 8^j per scale j at small scales, until it reaches a constant dependent on screen size N^2. This is the theoretical limit as complexity cannot decrease faster than the number of voxels decreases per scale j. Measured Performance: Method 2 is up to two orders of magnitude faster than Method 1 at scale j around 4-5 for large volumes (M=512, 1024, 2048). At full resolution, Method 2 complexity is 50% higher than Method 1, but yields higher quality. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Higher performance at coarse resolutions; better quality for a given resolution; full control over approximation error; adaptive grid reduces computation at coarse scales. Limitations: Slower at full resolution compared to direct splatting; requires precomputation of kernel table per view; more complex implementation due to dual space and interpolation steps. When to Use: Interactive volume rendering where fast feedback is needed while browsing around and through a volume. Progressive rendering where resolution increases once a viewpoint is chosen. Large volumes where coarse-scale rendering is dominant. When Not to Use: When full resolution rendering is the primary requirement, as Method 2 is slower than Method 1 at j=0. When hardware does not support efficient table lookups or adaptive grid operations. L2-optimal wavelet splatting was proposed by Stefan Horbelt, Michael Unser, and Martin Vetterli from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (EPFL). It extends Gross's method of volume wavelet rendering by computing splats via an orthogonal projection operator. The method was published in the Eurographics Association proceedings. It builds on the theory of B-spline signal processing and wavelet approximation techniques. Wavelet Projections for Volume Rendering, https://bigwww.epfl.ch/publications/horbelt9901.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Point-wise Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform (PW-IDWT) via Generalized Projection
head: GP of sample, Generalized Projection (GP), PW-IDWT, Point-wise Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform
body: The Point-wise Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform (PW-IDWT) via Generalized Projection (GP) reconstructs a single signal sample (or a set of samples) from a wavelet decomposition by determining the minimal set of subband coefficients required. It solves the problem of identifying which coefficients at a coarser level contribute to a specific sample at a finer level during synthesis, exploiting the recursive nature of the lifting scheme. Unlike methods that decode entire subbands, this approach calculates the exact Generalized Projection of a sample into the transformed domain, minimizing the number of subband images to decode. It builds on Wavelet-based Volume Rendering by providing an efficient, sample-specific inverse transform mechanism. Inputs: Wavelet decomposition levels L (where L=0 is the finest and L is the coarsest). Target sample position k in the finest resolution signal domain (level 0). Filter type parameters: causal length ls (or tl), anti-causal length ls^+ (or lt^+), and step type s (update) or t (prediction). Number of lifting steps m per level transition. Outputs: The set of coefficient indices required for reconstruction, defined by boundaries bj^{a,-}, bj^{a,+}, bj^{d,-}, bj^{d,+} for each subband j (approximation a or detail d) at each level l. The method tracks boundaries for the Generalized Projection (GP) at each lifting step. \hat{b}a^{i,-}, \hat{b}a^{i,+}: Lower and upper boundary indices for the approximation subband at lifting step i. \hat{b}d^{i,-}, \hat{b}d^{i,+}: Lower and upper boundary indices for the detail subband at lifting step i. bj^{a,-}, bj^{a,+}, bj^{d,-}, bj^{d,+}: Final boundaries for subband j after m lifting steps. 1. Initialize: For the target sample position k at the finest level, determine if k is even or odd (a=0 or a=1) to select the correct set of lifting steps for synthesis. Initialize the Generalized Projection (GP) boundaries for the coarsest level L as [k \gg L, k \gg L] for the approximation subband. 2. Iterate Coarsest to Finest: Iterate for l = L-1 down to 0. At each finer resolution, there is a set of samples to be recovered \text{GP}(l, j)k instead of a single one. 3. Process Lifting Steps: For each lifting step i from 0 to m-1 in the synthesis chain, update the boundary indices \hat{b}a and \hat{b}d using min/max updating rules based on the filter type (prediction or update) and filter lengths. If the step is an Update step (type s): \hat{b}a^{i+1,-} = \hat{b}a^{i,-} \hat{b}a^{i+1,+} = \hat{b}a^{i,+} \hat{b}d^{i+1,-} = \min\{\hat{b}d^{i,-}, \hat{b}a^{i,-} + ls\} \hat{b}d^{i+1,+} = \max\{\hat{b}d^{i,+}, \hat{b}d^{i,+} + ls^+\} If the step is a Prediction step (type t): \hat{b}a^{i+1,-} = \min\{\hat{b}a^{i,-}, \hat{b}d^{i,-} + tl\} \hat{b}a^{i+1,+} = \max\{\hat{b}a^{i,+}, \hat{b}d^{i,+} + lt^+\} \hat{b}d^{i+1,-} = \hat{b}d^{i,-} \hat{b}d^{i+1,+} = \hat{b}d^{i,+} 4. Finalize Boundaries: After completing all m lifting steps for a level transition, assign the final boundaries bj^{a,-}, bj^{a,+}, bj^{d,-}, bj^{d,+} based on the final values of \hat{b}j^{m} and \hat{b}j^{m+1}: bj^{a,-} = \hat{b}j^{m,-} bj^{a,+} = \hat{b}j^{m,+} bj^{d,-} = \hat{b}j^{m+1,-} bj^{d,+} = \hat{b}j^{m+1,+} 5. Set of Samples: To find the GP for a set of samples, recursively compute the GP for individual samples in the approximation subband and take the union of their resulting coefficient sets: \text{GP}^\mu(l+1, j) = \cupk \text{GP}^\mu(l+1, j)k \quad \forall k \in \text{GP}(l, j)^a where \text{GP}(l, j)^a is the set of samples in the approximation subband at level l. IDWT Reconstruction: The approximation subband at finer level l-1 is reconstructed from coarser level l coefficients: a(l-1, k) = \sum{n=-\infty}^{\infty} h(k-2n)a(l, n) + \sum{n=-\infty}^{\infty} g(k-2n)d(l, n) where a and d are approximation and detail subbands, and h, g are synthesis filters. Total Subbands for 3D: For 3D reconstruction (filtering on x, y, z, assuming 2-D images stacked along z), the total number of subband images Nk needed for reconstruction of image k is: Nk = 4 \times [\text{GP}(L, a)k + \text{GP}(L, d)k] + \sum{l=L-1}^1 [3 \times \text{GP}(l, a)k + 4 \times \text{GP}(l, d)k] Boundary Updating Rules: Update Step (s): \hat{b}d^{i+1,-} = \min\{\hat{b}d^{i,-}, \hat{b}a^{i,-} + ls\} \hat{b}d^{i+1,+} = \max\{\hat{b}d^{i,+}, \hat{b}d^{i,+} + ls^+\} Prediction Step (t): \hat{b}a^{i+1,-} = \min\{\hat{b}a^{i,-}, \hat{b}d^{i,-} + tl\} \hat{b}a^{i+1,+} = \max\{\hat{b}a^{i,+}, \hat{b}d^{i,+} + lt^+\} Filter Choice: The 5-3 filter (interpolating, two-step chain) is recommended to minimize the number of subband images to decode. Parity Index a: Distinguishes between even (a=0) and odd (a=1) positions, as the set of lifting steps differs. Filter Lengths: ls, ls^+ for update steps; tl, lt^+ for prediction steps. Integer DWT Rounding Noise: Integer DWT introduces rounding noise proportional to the number of rounding operations (decomposition depth and lifting chain length), which degrades rate/distortion performance and causes PSNR oscillation along the axis. Boundary Conditions: Special handling is required for signal boundaries, including a noted sign inversion bd = -bd for detail subband boundaries during prediction steps. Periodicity: The number of samples required in each subband is a periodic function of the sample position k with period 2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegpboundaries(samplek, decompositionlevelL, filterparams): """ Computes the boundaries of the Generalized Projection (GP) for a single sample. Args: samplek: int, position of the sample in the finest resolution signal. decompositionlevelL: int, total number of decomposition levels (coarsest level). filterparams: dict, containing 'm' (number of lifting steps), 'steps' (list of step types: 's' for update, 't' for prediction), 'ls', 'lsplus', 'tl', 'tlplus'. Returns: dict: Boundaries for each level l from L down to 0. Keys are level indices. Values are dicts with 'aminus', 'aplus', 'dminus', 'dplus'. """ # Initialize boundaries at the coarsest level L # The GP starts as a single point at the coarsest level for the approximation subband kcoarse = samplek >> decompositionlevelL currentaminus = kcoarse currentaplus = kcoarse currentdminus = kcoarse currentdplus = kcoarse gpboundaries = {} gpboundaries[decompositionlevelL] = { 'aminus': currentaminus, 'aplus': currentaplus, 'dminus': currentdminus, 'dplus': currentdplus } steps = filterparams['steps'] m = filterparams['m'] ls = filterparams['ls'] lsplus = filterparams['lsplus'] tl = filterparams['tl'] tlplus = filterparams['tlplus'] # Iterate from coarsest level L-1 down to 0 for l in range(decompositionlevelL - 1, -1, -1): # Initialize step boundaries for this level transition stepaminus = currentaminus stepaplus = currentaplus stepdminus = currentdminus stepdplus = currentdplus # Process each lifting step for i in range(m): steptype = steps[i] if steptype == 's': # Update step # Update approximation boundaries (unchanged) newaminus = stepaminus newaplus = stepaplus # Update detail boundaries newdminus = min(stepdminus, stepaminus + ls) newdplus = max(stepdplus, stepdplus + lsplus) stepaminus = newaminus stepaplus = newaplus stepdminus = newdminus stepdplus = newdplus elif steptype == 't': # Prediction step # Update detail boundaries (unchanged) newdminus = stepdminus newdplus = stepdplus # Update approximation boundaries newaminus = min(stepaminus, stepdminus + tl) newaplus = max(stepaplus, stepdplus + tlplus) stepaminus = newaminus stepaplus = newaplus stepdminus = newdminus stepdplus = newdplus # After all lifting steps for this level, assign final boundaries gpboundaries[l] = { 'aminus': stepaminus, 'aplus': stepaplus, 'dminus': stepdminus, 'dplus': stepdplus } # Update current boundaries for the next iteration (finer level) currentaminus = stepaminus currentaplus = stepaplus currentdminus = stepdminus currentdplus = stepdplus return gpboundaries def computegpforset(samples, decompositionlevelL, filterparams): """ Computes the GP for a set of samples by taking the union of individual GPs. """ allboundaries = {} for k in samples: boundaries = computegpboundaries(k, decompositionlevelL, filterparams) for l, b in boundaries.items(): if l not in allboundaries: allboundaries[l] = {'aminus': float('inf'), 'aplus': float('-inf'), 'dminus': float('inf'), 'dplus': float('-inf')} allboundaries[l]['aminus'] = min(allboundaries[l]['aminus'], b['aminus']) allboundaries[l]['aplus'] = max(allboundaries[l]['aplus'], b['aplus']) allboundaries[l]['dminus'] = min(allboundaries[l]['dminus'], b['dminus']) allboundaries[l]['dplus'] = max(allboundaries[l]['dplus'], b['dplus']) return allboundaries Time Complexity: The method is efficient for sparse reconstruction as it only computes the necessary coefficients, with complexity proportional to the number of lifting steps and the depth of decomposition, which is minimal for short filters like 5-3. Memory Complexity: Low, as it does not require storing or decoding entire subbands, only the specific coefficients identified by the GP. Performance: The 5-3 filter requires significantly fewer coefficients than the 9/7 filter. For L=3, the 5-3 filter requires 9-15 samples per 2D slice, while 9/7 requires 19-37. This reduces decoding time and power consumption. Strengths: Minimizes the number of subband images to decode, reducing computational load and power consumption. Ideal for applications where only specific samples or regions of interest need to be reconstructed. Limitations: Integer DWT introduces rounding noise proportional to the number of rounding operations, which can degrade quality, especially for deep decompositions. The method is sensitive to the position of the sample due to periodicity and boundary effects. The Point-wise Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform (PW-IDWT) via Generalized Projection (GP) was introduced in the context of three-dimensional encoding/two-dimensional decoding of medical data. The method exploits the recursive nature of the wavelet transform and the separability of the transform to map the problem to a one-dimensional case. It is particularly useful for applications where computational resources are limited, such as mobile or embedded systems, due to its efficiency in decoding only the necessary coefficients. The choice of the 5-3 filter is motivated by its short length and two-step chain, which minimizes the number of subband images to decode.
