name: Adaptive Resolution Data Generation
head: AR Data Generation
body: Adaptive Resolution (AR) Data Generation creates a multiresolution representation of volume data by combining hierarchical subsampling with error-based pruning. It solves the problem of storing and rendering large volumetric datasets by discarding redundant or low-detail regions, thereby reducing memory footprint and rendering time. Unlike static multiresolution techniques that generate full MIPmaps for all levels, AR generation selectively prunes octree nodes based on a scalar variance threshold, retaining only the resolution necessary to represent data features above a specified error bound. Inputs: A uniform scalar volume dataset V of resolution N^3 (e.g., 128^3). A pruning threshold \Delta (delta). Outputs: An octree data structure where leaf nodes store scalar values at varying resolutions, and internal nodes represent coarser aggregations. Data Structures: The method uses an octree. Each node represents a cubic region of the volume. Leaf Node: Stores the scalar value for its region. If the node is at Level L, it represents a sub-volume of size (N/2^L)^3. Internal Node: Represents the parent of 8 child octants. It does not store a single scalar value but serves as a container for its children. Pruning Condition: A node is a leaf if the difference between the maximum and minimum scalar values of its constituent vertices is less than \Delta. Steps: 1. Generate Base Level (Level 0): The finest resolution level contains the original N^3 data points. For a 128^3 input, Level 0 is 128^3. 2. Generate Coarser Levels via Subsampling: To create Level L+1 from Level L, sample every other data point in each dimension. If Level L has resolution R^3, Level L+1 has resolution (R/2)^3. Specifically, a point at (x, y, z) in Level L+1 corresponds to the point at (2x, 2y, 2z) in Level L. This process continues until the root node (Level 7 for 128^3) is reached, which contains a single value representing the entire volume. 3. Construct Octree and Prune: Build the octree hierarchy from Level 0 up to the root. For each node, calculate the error metric: the difference between the maximum and minimum scalar values of the vertices in its region. If this difference is less than \Delta, prune all children of the current node. The node becomes a leaf in the final structure, storing the aggregated value (or simply marking the region as uniform). If the difference is greater than or equal to \Delta, keep the children and recurse. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateardata(volume, delta): """ volume: 3D array of shape (N, N, N) delta: float, pruning threshold Returns: Octree structure """ N = volume.shape[0] # Determine max levels. For 128^3, levels 0 to 7. # Level L has resolution N / 2^L maxlevel = int(math.log2(N)) # Initialize octree root root = OctreeNode(level=0, bounds=(0, 0, 0, N, N, N)) # Recursive function to build tree and prune def buildnode(node, currentvol): # Calculate min and max of current volume region minval = numpy.min(currentvol) maxval = numpy.max(currentvol) # Check pruning condition if (maxval - minval) < delta: # Prune: this node is a leaf, store aggregate value node.value = (minval + maxval) / 2.0 # Or store min/max node.children = None return # If not pruned, and not at finest level, create children if node.level < maxlevel: node.children = [] # Subsample to create 8 child volumes # Child i corresponds to one of the 8 octants for i in range(8): # Determine bounds for child octant childbounds = getoctantbounds(node.bounds, i) # Extract sub-volume and subsample # Note: In AR generation, the child volume at level L+1 # is derived by sampling every other point from the parent's region childvol = subsampleregion(currentvol, childbounds) childnode = OctreeNode(level=node.level + 1, bounds=childbounds) node.children.append(childnode) buildnode(childnode, childvol) else: # At finest level, must be leaf node.value = currentvol[0,0,0] # Representative value node.children = None # Initial call with full volume buildnode(root, volume) return root def subsampleregion(vol, bounds): """ Extracts a sub-volume defined by bounds and subsamples it by taking every other element in each dimension. """ x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1 = bounds # Extract sub-volume sub = vol[x0:x1, y0:y1, z0:z1] # Subsample: take every other element # This creates the next coarser level representation return sub[::2,::2,::2] Parameters: \Delta (Delta): The threshold for pruning. Typical values depend on the data range. If data is normalized to [0,1], \Delta might be 0.01 or 0.05. Not given in the sources. N: Base resolution. Must be a power of 2 for perfect hierarchical subsampling. Edge Cases: If \Delta is too large, the tree may prune aggressively, losing detail. If \Delta is too small, the tree may remain deep, offering little memory savings. Boundary conditions: Subsampling must align correctly with octant boundaries. Hierarchical Voronoi Diagrams is an adaptive clustering method for the multiresolution representation of scattered data. It constructs a hierarchy of Voronoi diagrams from nested subsets of points to approximate scalar fields, building on Adaptive Resolution Data Generation by defining approximation regions and error metrics for multiresolution representation. It differs from mesh-reduction algorithms by not requiring a grid structure, making it suitable for unstructured datasets. Time Complexity: Generating the subsampled levels is O(N^3) for the finest level, with subsequent levels being 1/8 the size. Total generation time is proportional to the size of the finest level, O(N^3). Pruning requires a traversal of the octree, which is O(M) where M is the number of nodes in the final tree. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is proportional to the number of leaf nodes in the pruned octree. In uniform regions, memory is O(1) per region. In complex regions, it approaches O(N^3). Performance: Reduces memory space and rendering computation time by eliminating uninteresting (low-variance) cubes. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for data with large uniform regions; adaptive to local detail. Limitations: Requires power-of-2 dimensions for simple subsampling; not suitable for unstructured data without modification; error metric is local and may miss global features. The method was introduced in the context of IsoSurface Rendering of Adaptive Resolution Data. It addresses the need for efficient visualization of scientific volume data by exploiting redundancy. The approach uses an octree structure to store the volume, with Level 0 being the finest resolution and Level 7 being the coarsest root node for a 128^3 dataset. name: Hierarchical Voronoi Diagrams
head: Adaptive Voronoi clustering, Voronoi-based clustering
body: Hierarchical Voronoi Diagrams is an adaptive clustering method for the multiresolution representation of scattered data. It constructs a hierarchy of Voronoi diagrams from nested subsets of points to approximate scalar fields, building on Adaptive Resolution Data Generation by defining approximation regions and error metrics for multiresolution representation. It differs from mesh-reduction algorithms by not requiring a grid structure, making it suitable for unstructured datasets. Inputs: A set of n scattered data points P = \{\mathbf{p}i\}{i=1}^n in \mathbb{R}^k with associated scalar values fi = f(\mathbf{p}i). A target global error bound \epsilon{target} or a maximum number of points n{max}. Outputs: A hierarchy of Voronoi diagrams L0, L1, \dots, LJ and corresponding piecewise interpolants. Data Structures: Voronoi Diagram: A partition of space into tiles \taui. Each tile \taui is associated with a center point \mathbf{p}i. Residuals: For each tile \tauk^j at level j, store the squared residual (\epsilonk^j)^2 to avoid square root computations. Adjacency: A map of adjacent tiles for each tile to support efficient updates. Definitions: Voronoi Tile: Tile \taui is the subset of \mathbb{R}^k containing all points closer to \mathbf{p}i than to any \mathbf{p}j (j \neq i) with respect to the Euclidean norm. Sibson's Interpolant: For a point \mathbf{p}, the interpolated value is: \tilde{f}(\mathbf{p}) = \frac{\sumi ai fi}{\sumi ai} where ai are the areas/volumes cut away from Voronoi tiles \taui when inserting \mathbf{p} temporarily into the diagram. Domain Clipping: To avoid infinite ai, clip the Voronoi diagram against the boundary of a compact domain D, typically the convex hull of P. Local Residual: For tile \tauk^j at level j, the residual is computed using error norm (2.1) with p=2. Global Error: The global approximation error at level j is: \epsilon^j = \left( \frac{1}{n} \sum{k=1}^{nj} nk^j (\epsilonk^j)^p \right)^{\frac{1}{p}} \quad (2.2) where nj is the number of tiles at level j, and nk^j is the number of original data points contained in tile \tauk^j. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (L0): Construct the Voronoi diagram for the minimal point set defining the convex hull of all points P. The tiles of this diagram define the cluster regions \tauk^0 of level L0. 2. Initial Residuals: Compute all residuals \epsilonk^0 using Sibson's interpolant \tilde{f}k^0 and error norm (2.1) with p=2. Store (\epsilonk^0)^2. 3. Refinement Loop: a. Identify the tile \taum^j with the maximal residual \epsilonm^j in the current level Lj. b. Among all original data points \mathbf{p}i \in \taum^j, identify the point \mathbf{p}{max} with the maximal error \|\tilde{f}m^j(\mathbf{p}i) - fi\|. c. Insert \mathbf{p}{max} into the Voronoi diagram. This splits \taum^j into new tiles, one of which has center \mathbf{p}{max} (denoted \tau{max}^{j+1}). d. Update the residual \epsilon{max}^{j+1} for the new tile \tau{max}^{j+1}. e. Update residuals for all tiles adjacent to \tau{max}^{j+1} because their Sibson interpolants change due to the new neighbor. f. All other clusters remain unchanged: \taui^{j+1} = \taui^j, \tilde{f}i^{j+1} = \tilde{f}i^j, and \epsiloni^{j+1} = \epsiloni^j. 4. Termination Check: Compute the global error \epsilon^j using (2.2). Terminate if \epsilon^j \le \epsilon{target} or the number of inserted points reaches n{max}. Otherwise, increment j and repeat step 3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalvoronoiclustering(points, values, domainhull, maxerror=None, maxpoints=None): """ points: list of (x, y, z) coordinates values: list of scalar values f(p) domainhull: convex hull of points for clipping maxerror: global error threshold maxpoints: maximum number of Voronoi centers """ # Step 1: Initialize with convex hull points hullpoints = getconvexhull(points) hullvalues = getvaluesat(hullpoints, points, values) # Voronoi diagram state centers = hullpoints centervalues = hullvalues voronoi = buildvoronoi(centers, domainhull) # Compute initial residuals residuals = computeresiduals(voronoi, centers, centervalues, points, values, p=2) j = 0 while True: # Step 4: Check termination globalerror = computeglobalerror(residuals, points, p=2) if maxerror is not None and globalerror <= maxerror: break if maxpoints is not None and len(centers) >= maxpoints: break # Step 3a: Find max residual tile maxtileidx = argmax(residuals) tile = voronoi.tiles[maxtileidx] # Step 3b: Find point with max error in tile pointsintile = getpointsintile(tile, points) maxerrorpointidx = argmax([abs(sibsoninterpolate(p, tile, centers, centervalues, domainhull) - values[i]) for i, p in enumerate(pointsintile)]) pmax = pointsintile[maxerrorpointidx] fmax = values[points.index(pmax)] # Step 3c: Insert pmax centers.append(pmax) centervalues.append(fmax) voronoi = updatevoronoi(voronoi, pmax, domainhull) # Step 3d, e: Update residuals # Identify affected tiles (new tile and neighbors) affectedtiles = getaffectedtiles(voronoi, pmax) for tileidx in affectedtiles: tile = voronoi.tiles[tileidx] # Recompute Sibson interpolant for this tile's region # Recompute residual for this tile residuals[tileidx] = computetileresidual(tile, centers, centervalues, points, values, p=2) j += 1 return centers, centervalues, voronoi Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Areas: Sibson's interpolant requires clipping the Voronoi diagram against the domain boundary D (e.g., convex hull) to prevent infinite areas/volumes ai. Non-unique Delaunay: If more than three points are cocircular, the Delaunay triangulation is not unique, but the Voronoi diagram is unique. Precision: Storing squared residuals avoids square root computations but requires careful handling of the global error formula (2.2) which involves a p-th root. Adaptive clustering is a technique for generating a data-dependent hierarchy that represents the inherent topological and geometric structures of scattered data by recursively partitioning a set of samples into smaller groups (clusters) based on spatial adjacency or correlation of associated function values. Unlike mesh-reduction algorithms, it does not require a grid structure connecting the given data points, making it suitable for unstructured or scattered datasets. It builds on Hierarchical Voronoi Diagrams by using the hierarchy to define approximation regions and error metrics for multiresolution representation. Time Complexity: Each refinement step involves inserting a point into the Voronoi diagram (O(\log n) or O(n) depending on implementation) and updating adjacent tiles. The number of steps is determined by the error bound or point limit. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of Voronoi tiles and the adjacency structure. Performance: For dataset f1 with 100 Voronoi tiles, Error (p=1) is 6.0% and Error (p=2) is 7.4%. With 1000 tiles, Error (p=1) is 1.0% and Error (p=2) is 1.2%. For Crater Lake terrain data (159,272 samples), with 1000 Voronoi tiles, Error (p=\infty) is 10.8% and Error (p=2) is 0.80%. Strengths: Does not require a grid structure; suitable for unstructured/scattered data; adaptive resolution based on error. Limitations: Requires convex hull computation; Sibson's interpolant can be computationally expensive per evaluation; non-unique Delaunay triangulation in degenerate cases. Hierarchical Voronoi Diagrams were proposed as a new adaptive clustering approach for multiresolution representation of scattered data. The method uses a hierarchy of Voronoi diagrams constructed from nested subsets of the original set of points. It is based on the relationship between Voronoi diagrams and Delaunay triangulations, where Voronoi vertices are at the centers of circumscribed circles of Delaunay triangles. The approach was applied to analytical functions, Hubble images, and terrain data. name: Adaptive Clustering
head: Data-dependent hierarchical clustering, Hierarchical Adaptive Clustering
body: Adaptive clustering is a technique for generating a data-dependent hierarchy that represents the inherent topological and geometric structures of scattered data by recursively partitioning a set of samples into smaller groups (clusters) based on spatial adjacency or correlation of associated function values. Unlike mesh-reduction algorithms, it does not require a grid structure connecting the given data points, making it suitable for unstructured or scattered datasets. It builds on Hierarchical Voronoi Diagrams by using the hierarchy to define approximation regions and error metrics for multiresolution representation. Inputs: A set P of n points in s-dimensional space with associated t-dimensional function values, defined as P = \{(\mathbf{p}i, fi) \mid \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^s, fi \in \mathbb{R}^t, i = 1, \dots, n\}. The domain D \subset \mathbb{R}^s is assumed to be compact and contain all points \mathbf{p}i. Outputs: A hierarchy of levels Lj for j = 0, 1, \dots, where each level is defined as: Lj = \{(\tauk^j, \tilde{f}k^j, \varepsilonk^j) \mid k = 1, \dots, nj\} Here, \tauk^j are tiles forming a partition of domain D, \tilde{f}k^j are approximating functions for the tile, and \varepsilonk^j estimate the approximation error. Data Structures: Point Set: List of tuples (\mathbf{p}i, fi). Level Structure: List of cluster objects, each containing: tile: The spatial region (partition of D). approx: The function \tilde{f}k^j mapping points in the tile to \mathbb{R}^t. error: The scalar residual \varepsilonk^j. points: List of indices of points contained in the tile. Parameters: p: Exponent for the error norm, p \in [1, \infty]. Typical values depend on the desired sensitivity to outliers; p=2 is common for least-squares, p=\infty for max-norm. Stopping criteria: Prescribed number of clusters or a global error bound \varepsilon{target}. Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with a coarse approximation level L0. This typically involves a single cluster containing all points or a very coarse partition. 2. Error Calculation: For each cluster k in the current level j, calculate the local residual \varepsilonk^j using the Lp norm: \varepsilonk^j = \left( \frac{1}{nk^j} \sum{\mathbf{p}i \in \tauk^j} \|\tilde{f}k^j(\mathbf{p}i) - fi\|^p \right)^{\frac{1}{p}} where nk^j is the number of points in tile \tauk^j and \|\cdot\| is the Euclidean norm in \mathbb{R}^t. 3. Global Error Check: Calculate the global error for level j: \varepsilon^j = \left( \frac{1}{n} \sum{k=1}^{nj} nk^j (\varepsilonk^j)^p \right)^{\frac{1}{p}} If \varepsilon^j satisfies the prescribed error bound or the number of clusters meets the limit, terminate. 4. Refinement: Identify clusters with large residuals (high error). Refine these clusters to create level L{j+1}. Refinement involves splitting the tile \tauk^j and computing new approximations \tilde{f}k^{j+1} for the sub-clusters. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 until convergence. Convergence is reached when every tile contains exactly one data point or the number of points in every tile is sufficiently low to provide zero residuals. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveclustering(points, functionvalues, p=2, maxclusters=None, errorthreshold=None): """ points: list of numpy arrays (s-dim) functionvalues: list of numpy arrays (t-dim) p: norm exponent maxclusters: int or None errorthreshold: float or None """ n = len(points) # Initial level: one cluster with all points # Approximation could be the mean function value for simplicity, # though specific methods (like PCA) define it differently. currentlevelclusters = [Cluster(allindices=range(n))] iteration = 0 while True: # Calculate errors for current level globalerror = 0.0 clusterstorefine = [] for cluster in currentlevelclusters: # Get points in this cluster clusterpoints = [points[i] for i in cluster.indices] clusterfvals = [functionvalues[i] for i in cluster.indices] nk = len(clusterpoints) # Compute approximation ftilde for this cluster # Default approximation: mean of function values. # Specific variants (e.g., PCA) override this. if nk > 0: ftilde = sum(clusterfvals) / nk else: ftilde = 0.0 # Calculate local residual epsilonk if nk > 0: sumerrp = sum(np.linalg.norm(ftilde - fi)p for fi in clusterfvals) epsilonk = (sumerrp / nk)(1/p) else: epsilonk = 0.0 cluster.error = epsilonk # Add to global error # Formula: (1/n) sum(nk epsilonk^p) globalerror += nk (epsilonk p) # Determine if refinement is needed # Heuristic: refine if error is above a fraction of global error or max allowed # The source says "Refine only in cluster regions with large residuals" # We need a threshold. If errorthreshold is global, we might refine top N% or all above avg. # For implementation completeness, we refine if error > 0 and we haven't hit max clusters # and we haven't reached single-point clusters. if nk > 1: if maxclusters is None or len(currentlevelclusters) < maxclusters: clusterstorefine.append(cluster) globalerror = (globalerror / n)(1/p) # Check stopping criteria if errorthreshold is not None and globalerror <= errorthreshold: break if maxclusters is not None and len(currentlevelclusters) >= maxclusters: break if not clusterstorefine: break # Refine clusters nextlevelclusters = [] for cluster in currentlevelclusters: if cluster in clusterstorefine: # Split cluster into sub-clusters # Splitting strategy depends on the specific method (e.g., PCA splitting plane) # Here we assume a generic split into two sub-clusters based on spatial median # or principal component. For a generic implementation, we split indices. subclusters = splitcluster(cluster, points) nextlevelclusters.extend(subclusters) else: nextlevelclusters.append(cluster) currentlevelclusters = nextlevelclusters iteration += 1 # Safety break to prevent infinite loops in generic implementation if iteration > 1000: break return currentlevelclusters def splitcluster(cluster, points): """ Generic split: divide points into two halves based on the first dimension median. In PCA-based clustering, split is along the eigenvector with max eigenvalue. """ indices = cluster.indices if len(indices) <= 1: return [Cluster(indices=[i]) for i in indices] # Sort by first coordinate sortedindices = sorted(indices, key=lambda i: points[i][0]) mid = len(sortedindices) // 2 leftindices = sortedindices[:mid] rightindices = sortedindices[mid:] return [Cluster(indices=leftindices), Cluster(indices=rightindices)] class Cluster: def init(self, allindices=None, indices=None): if allindices is not None: self.indices = allindices else: self.indices = indices self.error = 0.0 A variant that uses Principal Component Analysis to define the approximating function and splitting plane. It constructs a local coordinate system for each cluster. The centroid \mathbf{c} is calculated as \mathbf{c} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n \mathbf{p}i. The covariance matrix a{jk} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n (p{ij} - cj)(p{ik} - ck) is eigen-decomposed. The approximating function is \tilde{f}k^j(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot \mathbf{e}{\lambda{min}}, where \mathbf{e}{\lambda{min}} is the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue, representing the local surface normal. The cluster is split by a hyperplane orthogonal to the eigenvector with the maximal eigenvalue \mathbf{e}{\lambda{max}}, ensuring splits are orthogonal to the longest axis. To incorporate function values fi, weighted PCA is used, where weights wi are defined by the approximation error, updating the centroid to \mathbf{c} = \frac{\sum wi \mathbf{p}i}{\sum wi} and covariance to a{jk} = \frac{\sum wi(p{ij} - cj)(p{ik} - ck)}{\sum wi}. Time Complexity: Depends on the splitting strategy. Top-down construction allows coarse levels to be computed faster than fine levels. PCA eigen-decomposition is O(s^3) per cluster, where s is spatial dimension. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of clusters and points. Hierarchical structure stores approximations and residuals for each tile. Strengths: Data-dependent, adapts to geometric complexity; no grid structure required; efficient for smooth manifolds. Limitations: Requires careful choice of error norm; PCA assumes local manifold structure; performance degrades if data is not well-clustered or noisy. When to use: Scattered data with smooth underlying structures (e.g., terrain, isosurfaces); when grid-based methods are inapplicable. When not to use: Highly irregular or noisy data without clear topological structure; when strict grid alignment is required. Adaptive clustering was introduced as a method for multiresolution modeling of scientific visualization data, particularly for recovering topological structures of two-manifold surfaces from scattered data points in 3D space. It was developed as an alternative to mesh-reduction algorithms, offering a "top-down" hierarchical construction. The approach is closely related to wavelet transforms for manifold geometries, providing efficient compression and visualization at different resolutions. name: PCA-based Clustering
head: Heckel et al. clustering, Principal Component Analysis clustering
body: PCA-based clustering partitions a set of scattered points into well-shaped clusters by aligning the splitting hyperplane with the principal axes of the point distribution. It solves the problem of generating data-dependent hierarchies for surface reconstruction or volume representation where cluster shape quality is critical. It is distinguished from basic adaptive clustering by its use of eigenanalysis to determine splitting directions, ensuring splits are orthogonal to the longest axis of the point cloud, and from affine-invariant approaches by its standard (non-normalized) covariance analysis which may produce elongated clusters on curved data. Inputs: A set of n points \mathbf{p}i = (p{i1}, \dots, p{ik})^T in k-dimensional space, optionally with associated scalar function values fi and weights wi. Outputs: A splitting hyperplane defined by a normal vector and a point on the plane (typically the centroid), and the partition of points into two subsets based on the hyperplane. Data Structures: Point Cloud: List of n vectors of size k. Covariance Matrix: k \times k symmetric matrix A. Eigenvectors: k orthonormal vectors \mathbf{e}1, \dots, \mathbf{e}k. Eigenvalues: k real, non-negative scalars \lambda1, \dots, \lambdak. Steps: 1. Compute Centroid: Calculate the mean position of the points. If weights wi are provided, use the weighted centroid. \mathbf{c} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n \mathbf{p}i \quad \text{(unweighted)} \mathbf{c} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^n wi \mathbf{p}i}{\sum{i=1}^n wi} \quad \text{(weighted)} 2. Compute Covariance Matrix: Calculate the scatter matrix centered at \mathbf{c}. a{jk} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n (p{ij} - cj)(p{ik} - ck) \quad \text{(unweighted)} a{jk} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^n wi(p{ij} - cj)(p{ik} - ck)}{\sum{i=1}^n wi} \quad \text{(weighted)} 3. Eigenanalysis: Compute the eigenvalues \lambda and corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors \mathbf{e} of the symmetric matrix A. Sort them such that \lambda{\min} corresponds to the smallest eigenvalue and \lambda{\max} to the largest. 4. Define Approximating Function: The local distance to the reconstructed manifold is approximated by the signed distance along the direction of the smallest eigenvalue (assumed to be the surface normal): \tilde{f}k^j(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot \mathbf{e}{\lambda{\min}} 5. Define Splitting Hyperplane: The splitting plane passes through the centroid \mathbf{c} and is orthogonal to the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue \mathbf{e}{\lambda{\max}}. This ensures the split is orthogonal to the longest axis of the cluster. \text{Normal } \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{e}{\lambda{\max}} \text{Plane Equation: } (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot \mathbf{e}{\lambda{\max}} = 0 6. Partition: Assign each point \mathbf{p}i to a subset based on the sign of (\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{c}) \cdot \mathbf{e}{\lambda{\max}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pcacluster(points, weights=None): """ Performs PCA-based clustering on a set of points. Returns the splitting normal and centroid. """ n = len(points) k = len(points[0]) # Step 1: Compute Centroid if weights is None: weights = [1.0] n sumweights = sum(weights) centroid = [0.0] k for i in range(n): for j in range(k): centroid[j] += weights[i] points[i][j] for j in range(k): centroid[j] /= sumweights # Step 2: Compute Covariance Matrix cov = [[0.0] k for in range(k)] for i in range(n): diff = [points[i][j] - centroid[j] for j in range(k)] for j in range(k): for l in range(k): cov[j][l] += weights[i] diff[j] diff[l] for j in range(k): for l in range(k): cov[j][l] /= sumweights # Step 3: Eigenanalysis # Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetric matrix 'cov' eigenvalues, eigenvectors = computeeigendecomposition(cov) # Find indices of min and max eigenvalues minidx = argmin(eigenvalues) maxidx = argmax(eigenvalues) # Step 4 & 5: Define Splitting Hyperplane # Normal is eigenvector corresponding to largest eigenvalue splittingnormal = eigenvectors[:, maxidx] return centroid, splittingnormal Parameters: Weights (wi): Not given in the sources as a default. If function values fi are to be considered, wi is defined by the approximation error. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Curved Data: The basic process ignores associated function values. If the function is curved in only one direction, this method generates long and skinny clusters. Recursive Splitting: The affine-invariant variant (scaling by \sqrt{1/\lambdai}) may work well on densely sampled, smooth data but provides poor approximation behavior in regions where clusters are recursively split along similar directions. Degenerate Input: If points are collinear or coplanar, eigenvalues may be zero, leading to undefined normals for the splitting plane. A variant that transforms points into a PCA-based coordinate system and scales coordinates by \sqrt{1/\lambdai} to achieve invariance under shear and other affine transformations. It is chosen when geometric invariance to non-uniform scaling is required, but may fail on data with recursive splitting along similar directions. Affine-Invariant Clustering Time Complexity: Dominated by the eigenanalysis of the k \times k covariance matrix. For fixed dimension k, this is O(n) per cluster for computing the matrix, plus constant time for eigen-decomposition. Memory Complexity: O(nk) to store the point cloud and O(k^2) for the covariance matrix. Strengths: Produces well-shaped clusters by splitting orthogonal to the longest axis. Invariant under translation, rotation, and uniform scaling. Limitations: Not invariant under general affine transformations (unless the affine-invariant variant is used). Ignores function values by default, leading to poor results on curved data if weights are not applied. The affine-invariant variant can produce poor approximations in specific recursive splitting scenarios. When to use: Densely sampled, smooth data sets where cluster shape quality is prioritized over function-value-aware splitting. When not to use: Data with significant curvature where function-value-aware splitting (e.g., bisector methods) yields fewer clusters or better approximation. The PCA-based clustering approach for surface reconstruction was introduced by Heckel et al.. It matches the general definition of adaptive clustering by using an approximating function to define local distance and a splitting plane for refinement. The method leverages the property that for a s-manifold, the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue of the covariance matrix is locally orthogonal to the manifold, serving as a normal estimate. name: Adaptive Clustering with Error-Bisector Splitting
head: Adaptive clustering with quadratic polynomials, Cluster subdivision by positive/negative error centers, Quadratic Polynomial Approximation Clustering, Quadratic clustering, Splitting along bisector of c+ and c-
body: Adaptive clustering with error-bisector splitting is a method for generating a data-dependent hierarchy of clusters from scattered 2D points with associated scalar values, using quadratic polynomial approximations to guide subdivision. It solves the problem of efficiently approximating smooth surfaces with a minimal number of clusters for a given error tolerance, outperforming PCA-based splitting by producing long, skinny clusters when curvature is directional. Unlike its sibling PCA-based Clustering, which ignores function values, this method weights spatial distribution by approximation residuals. Inputs: A set of points D = \{\mathbf{p}i\}{i=1}^N in the plane with associated scalar function values F = \{fi\}{i=1}^N. A global error bound \epsilon{max} and a maximum number of tiles N{max}. Outputs: A hierarchical set of clusters (tiles) \tauj^k at various levels j, each associated with a quadratic polynomial approximation \tilde{f}k^j and a residual error \epsilonj^k. Data Structures: Cluster: Contains a list of point indices, the current level j, and the fitted quadratic polynomial coefficients. Quadratic Polynomial: Defined by coefficients c{l,m} for l+m \le 2. In 2D, this is \tilde{f}(x1, x2) = c{0,0} + c{1,0}x1 + c{0,1}x2 + c{2,0}x1^2 + c{1,1}x1x2 + c{0,2}x2^2. Residual: The maximum norm error \epsilon = \maxi | \tilde{f}(\mathbf{p}i) - fi |. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (Level L0): Create a single root cluster \tau0^1 = D containing all points. Fit a quadratic polynomial \tilde{f}0^1 to all points in \tau0^1 using least-squares regression. Compute the residual for \tau0^1 using the maximum norm: \epsilon0^1 = \max{i \in \tau0^1} | \tilde{f}0^1(\mathbf{p}i) - fi |. 2. Refinement Loop: Identify the cluster \tauj^m in the current level Lj with the maximal residual \epsilonj^m such that \epsilonj^m \ge \epsilonj^k for all other clusters k in Lj. If \epsilonj^m \le \epsilon{max} or the total number of clusters exceeds N{max}, terminate. Splitting: Compute the positive error weights for each point \mathbf{p}i in \tauj^m: wi^+ = \begin{cases} \tilde{f}k^j(\mathbf{p}i) - fi & \text{if } \tilde{f}k^j(\mathbf{p}i) - fi > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Compute the negative error weights: wi^- = \begin{cases} fi - \tilde{f}k^j(\mathbf{p}i) & \text{if } \tilde{f}k^j(\mathbf{p}i) - fi < 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Calculate the weighted centers \mathbf{c}^+ and \mathbf{c}^-: \mathbf{c}^+ = \frac{\sum{i=1}^n wi^+ \mathbf{p}i}{\sum{i=1}^n wi^+}, \quad \mathbf{c}^- = \frac{\sum{i=1}^n wi^- \mathbf{p}i}{\sum{i=1}^n wi^-} where n is the number of points in the cluster. Define the splitting line as the perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting \mathbf{c}^+ and \mathbf{c}^-. If \mathbf{c}^+ = \mathbf{c}^-, choose an arbitrary subdivision direction (e.g., split along the major axis of the point distribution or a fixed axis). Partition the points in \tauj^m into two new clusters \tau{j+1}^{2m-1} and \tau{j+1}^{2m} based on which side of the bisector they fall. Re-fitting: For each new cluster, fit a new quadratic polynomial using least-squares. Compute the new residuals \epsilon{j+1}^{2m-1} and \epsilon{j+1}^{2m} using the maximum norm. Replace \tauj^m with the two new clusters in the hierarchy. Increment level j. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveclusteringerrorbisector(points, values, epsilonmax, maxtiles): """ points: list of (x, y) tuples values: list of scalar floats epsilonmax: float, global error bound maxtiles: int, maximum number of clusters Returns: list of clusters, each containing indices and polynomial coeffs """ # Initialization currentlevelclusters = [] rootindices = list(range(len(points))) # Fit initial polynomial coeffs = fitquadraticleastsquares(points, values, rootindices) residual = computemaxresidual(points, values, coeffs, rootindices) currentlevelclusters.append({ 'indices': rootindices, 'coeffs': coeffs, 'residual': residual, 'level': 0 }) totalclusters = 1 while totalclusters < maxtiles: # Find cluster with max residual maxidx = -1 maxresidual = -1.0 for i, cluster in enumerate(currentlevelclusters): if cluster['residual'] > maxresidual: maxresidual = cluster['residual'] maxidx = i # Termination check if maxresidual <= epsilonmax: break clustertosplit = currentlevelclusters[maxidx] indices = clustertosplit['indices'] coeffs = clustertosplit['coeffs'] # Compute weights wplus = [] wminus = [] for idx in indices: p = points[idx] fval = values[idx] approx = evaluatequadratic(p, coeffs) error = approx - fval if error > 0: wplus.append(error) wminus.append(0.0) elif error < 0: wplus.append(0.0) wminus.append(-error) # f - approx else: wplus.append(0.0) wminus.append(0.0) # Compute centers sumwplus = sum(wplus) sumwminus = sum(wminus) if sumwplus == 0: cplus = None else: cplus = (sum(wplus[k] points[indices[k]][0] for k in range(len(indices))) / sumwplus, sum(wplus[k] points[indices[k]][1] for k in range(len(indices))) / sumwplus) if sumwminus == 0: cminus = None else: cminus = (sum(wminus[k] points[indices[k]][0] for k in range(len(indices))) / sumwminus, sum(wminus[k] points[indices[k]][1] for k in range(len(indices))) / sumwminus) # Determine split line if cplus is None or cminus is None or cplus == cminus: # Fallback: arbitrary split, e.g., by x-coordinate median sortedindices = sorted(indices, key=lambda i: points[i][0]) mid = len(sortedindices) // 2 leftindices = sortedindices[:mid] rightindices = sortedindices[mid:] else: # Perpendicular bisector of cplus and cminus # Vector from cminus to cplus dx = cplus[0] - cminus[0] dy = cplus[1] - cminus[1] # Midpoint mx = (cplus[0] + cminus[0]) / 2.0 my = (cplus[1] + cminus[1]) / 2.0 # Points on one side satisfy: dx(x - mx) + dy(y - my) > 0 leftindices = [] rightindices = [] for idx in indices: x, y = points[idx] val = dx (x - mx) + dy (y - my) if val > 0: leftindices.append(idx) else: rightindices.append(idx) # Handle empty sets if all points fall on one side (rare but possible) if not leftindices: leftindices = indices[:len(indices)//2] rightindices = indices[len(indices)//2:] elif not rightindices: rightindices = indices[len(indices)//2:] leftindices = indices[:len(indices)//2] # Remove old cluster currentlevelclusters.pop(maxidx) totalclusters -= 1 # Add new clusters for newindices in [leftindices, rightindices]: newcoeffs = fitquadraticleastsquares(points, values, newindices) newresidual = computemaxresidual(points, values, newcoeffs, newindices) currentlevelclusters.append({ 'indices': newindices, 'coeffs': newcoeffs, 'residual': newresidual, 'level': clustertosplit['level'] + 1 }) totalclusters += 1 return currentlevelclusters def fitquadraticleastsquares(points, values, indices): # Solves for c00, c10, c01, c20, c11, c02 in: # f = c00 + c10x + c01y + c20x^2 + c11xy + c02y^2 # Using standard least squares matrix inversion or SVD # Implementation detail: Construct design matrix A where row i is [1, x, y, x^2, xy, y^2] # Solve A^T A c = A^T b pass def evaluatequadratic(point, coeffs): x, y = point c00, c10, c01, c20, c11, c02 = coeffs return c00 + c10x + c01y + c20x2 + c11xy + c02y2 def computemaxresidual(points, values, coeffs, indices): maxerr = 0.0 for idx in indices: err = abs(evaluatequadratic(points[idx], coeffs) - values[idx]) if err > maxerr: maxerr = err return maxerr Parameters: Error Norm: The maximum norm (p=\infty) is used for residual estimation to ensure the approximation stays within a prescribed tolerance. Error Bound (\epsilon{max}): The threshold for termination. Not given in the sources as a specific value, but defined as a user input. Max Tiles (N{max}): Limit on cluster count. Not given in the sources as a specific value. Pitfalls: Affine Invariance Issues: An affine-invariant variant of this approach may provide poor approximation behavior in regions where clusters are recursively split along similar directions. Degenerate Centers: If \mathbf{c}^+ and \mathbf{c}^- are identical (or one is undefined because all errors are zero or have the same sign), the splitting direction is arbitrary. Time Complexity: Each refinement step involves fitting a quadratic polynomial (constant time for fixed number of points per cluster, but depends on cluster size) and computing residuals. In the worst case, with N points and K clusters, fitting is O(N) per cluster. The total complexity depends on the convergence rate to the error bound. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the points and values, plus O(K) for the cluster hierarchy. Performance: Typically produces a lower number of clusters than PCA-based splitting for the same approximation error, particularly when the function is curved in only one direction, resulting in long and skinny clusters. Strengths: Efficient triangulation of scattered data; better representation of smooth surfaces via quadratic polynomials compared to piecewise linear; data-dependent hierarchy. Limitations: Not invariant under affine transformations (unless the specific affine-invariant variant is used, which has its own pitfalls); requires 2D plane assumption (generalization to higher dimensions requires local projection via PCA). When to use: When approximating smooth surfaces from scattered 2D data with a strict error bound and minimizing cluster count is critical. When not to use: When affine invariance is strictly required and data is not densely sampled/smooth; when 3D volumetric data is processed directly without projection. This method was introduced by as an adaptive clustering approach for efficient triangulation of scattered data in the plane. It generalizes the concept of error-weighted splitting to quadratic polynomial approximations, offering an improvement over piecewise linear approximations for smooth surfaces. The approach is part of a broader framework for multiresolution modeling in scientific visualization, where hierarchical data structures are used to generate optimal approximations with triangles. The affine-invariant variant was discussed in relation to [102] (not cited in the provided source list). name: Morphological Pyramid
head: Adjunction Pyramid, Erosion/Dilation Pyramid, Morphological Adjunction Pyramid, Morphological Pyramid Construction, Pyramid Synthesis for MIP
body: The Morphological Pyramid is a multiresolution representation scheme for volume data that uses morphological erosion and dilation combined with dyadic downsampling/upsampling to create a hierarchy of approximations and detail signals. It solves the problem of interactive rendering latency in Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) by allowing coarse approximations to be rendered during user interaction and progressively refined with detail coefficients once interaction ceases. Unlike linear pyramid-based MIP methods which rely on additive reconstruction, the Morphological Pyramid exploits the commutativity of the MIP operator with morphological dilation and upsampling, allowing the projection to be performed on coarse levels and expanded in 2-D, thereby avoiding expensive 3-D reconstruction for certain pyramid types. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3-D volume dataset f0 defined on a discrete grid domain F \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d (where d=3 for volumes, though the pyramid operators often operate in 2-D for projection purposes) taking values in a finite set of nonnegative integers. A structuring element A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d. Output: An approximation pyramid \{f0, f1, \dots, fL\} and a detail pyramid \{d0, d1, \dots, d{L-1}, fL\}, where L is the decomposition depth. Data Structures: Approximation Pyramid: A set of signals \{fj\}{j=0}^L. Each fj has a spatial resolution reduced by a factor of 2^j in each dimension compared to f0. Detail Pyramid: A set of signals \{dj\}{j=0}^{L-1} and the coarsest approximation fL. Each dj has the same spatial resolution as fj. Morphological Operators: Let f be a signal with domain F and A be the structuring element. Dilation: \deltaA(f)(x) = \max{y \in A, x-y \in F} f(x-y). Erosion: \epsilonA(f)(x) = \min{y \in A, x+y \in F} f(x+y). Opening: \alphaA(f)(x) = \deltaA(\epsilonA(f))(x). Pyramid Operators: REDUCE (Analysis): \psiA^\uparrow(f) = \text{DOWNSAMPLE}(\epsilonA(f)) for Adjunction Pyramids. For Sun-Maragos Pyramids, \psiA^\uparrow(f) = \text{DOWNSAMPLE}(\alphaA(f)). EXPAND (Synthesis): \psiA^\downarrow(f) = \deltaA(\text{UPSAMPLE}(f)). Note: In the context of MIP rendering, a 2-D variant \psi{\tilde{A}}^\downarrow is used, where \tilde{A} is the MIP of A (i.e., \tilde{A}:= M\Theta(A)). Generalized Subtraction: To ensure non-negative detail signals, the generalized subtraction operator \dot{-} is defined as: t \dot{-} s = \begin{cases} t, & \text{if } t > s \\ 0, & \text{if } t = s \end{cases} where 0 is the smallest possible image or voxel value. Parameters: Structuring Element A: A subset of \mathbb{Z}^d defining the local neighborhood. It must satisfy the pyramid condition: there exists an a \in A such that the translates of a over an even number of grid steps are never contained in A. Decomposition Depth L: The number of levels in the pyramid. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set f0 as the input volume. 2. Analysis (Decomposition): For j = 1 to L: a. Compute the approximation at level j: fj = \text{REDUCE}(f{j-1}). b. Compute the expanded version of the coarser approximation: \hat{f}j = \text{EXPAND}(fj). c. Compute the detail signal: d{j-1} = f{j-1} \dot{-} \hat{f}j. 3. Reconstruction (Synthesis): To reconstruct f0 from \{dk\} and fL: f = \psiA^{\downarrow L}(fL) \vee \bigvee{k=0}^{L-1} \psiA^{\downarrow k}(dk) where \vee denotes the maximum operation. This relies on the generalized addition being defined as t \dot{+} s = t \vee s = \max(t, s). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def morphologicalpyramiddecomposition(volume, structuringelementA, depthL): """ Constructs a morphological pyramid from a volume. Args: volume: 3D array f0. structuringelementA: Set of coordinates defining the structuring element. depthL: Number of pyramid levels. Returns: approximations: List [f0, f1,..., fL] details: List [d0, d1,..., d{L-1}] """ approximations = [volume] details = [] currentf = volume for j in range(1, depthL + 1): # 1. Erosion eroded = morphologicalerosion(currentf, structuringelementA) # 2. Downsampling (dyadic, factor of 2 in each dimension) # Implementation note: Keep every other voxel in each dimension. fj = downsample(eroded) approximations.append(fj) # 3. Upsampling (dyadic, factor of 2 in each dimension) # Implementation note: Insert zeros or replicate values? # Standard morphological pyramid upsampling typically inserts zeros # or uses nearest neighbor before dilation. The source defines # EXPAND as dilation of upsampled. We assume standard upsampling # that creates a grid of size 2x2x2 for each voxel. upscaled = upsample(fj) # 4. Dilation expanded = morphologicaldilation(upscaled, structuringelementA) # 5. Generalized Subtraction # d{j-1} = f{j-1} dot-minus expanded djminus1 = generalizedsubtraction(currentf, expanded) details.append(djminus1) currentf = fj return approximations, details def morphologicalpyramidreconstruction(approximations, details, structuringelementA): """ Reconstructs the volume from the pyramid. Args: approximations: List [f0,..., fL] details: List [d0,..., d{L-1}] structuringelementA: Structuring element for dilation. Returns: reconstructedvolume: 3D array f0 """ L = len(approximations) - 1 fL = approximations[L] # Start with the coarsest approximation expanded back to full resolution # Reconstruction formula: f = psi^L(fL) vee vee{k=0}^{L-1} psi^k(dk) # We can compute this iteratively from coarse to fine # However, the formula suggests expanding fL and then OR-ing with expanded details. # Let's compute the contribution of each level # Level L contribution: psi^L(fL) # Level k contribution: psi^k(dk) # To implement psi^k, we apply EXPAND k times. # EXPAND(f) = dilation(upsample(f)) reconstructed = expandntimes(fL, L, structuringelementA) for k in range(L): # Expand dk k times dkexpanded = expandntimes(details[k], k, structuringelementA) # Take maximum reconstructed = max(reconstructed, dkexpanded) return reconstructed def morphologicalerosion(volume, A): """ Computes erosion: min{y in A, x+y in F} f(x+y) """ # Implementation: For each voxel x, find the minimum value in the neighborhood defined by A. # Boundary handling: voxels outside F are treated as infinity for min? # Or the domain F is restricted. Source says x+y in F. # If x+y is not in F, it is not considered. # Standard implementation: pad with infinity. pass def morphologicaldilation(volume, A): """ Computes dilation: max{y in A, x-y in F} f(x-y) """ # Implementation: For each voxel x, find the maximum value in the neighborhood defined by A. # Boundary handling: voxels outside F are treated as -infinity for max. # Standard implementation: pad with -infinity. pass def downsample(volume): """ Dyadic downsampling by factor of 2 in each dimension. """ # Return volume[::2,::2,::2] pass def upsample(volume): """ Dyadic upsampling by factor of 2 in each dimension. """ # Create a new volume of size 2x. Insert zeros or original values? # Morphological upsampling usually inserts zeros (or background value) # before dilation. pass def generalizedsubtraction(t, s): """ t dot-minus s """ result = t.copy() result[t <= s] = 0 return result def expandntimes(f, n, A): """ Applies EXPAND operator n times. EXPAND(f) = dilation(upsample(f)) """ current = f for in range(n): upscaled = upsample(current) current = morphologicaldilation(upscaled, A) return current Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pyramid Condition: If the structuring element A does not satisfy the pyramid condition (existence of a \in A such that translates over even grid steps are never contained in A), perfect reconstruction may fail. Detail Signal Size: In Adjunction Pyramids, too few small features are retained in higher levels, making detail signals "too large". This can be mitigated by using the Sun-Maragos variant. Precision: The generalized subtraction relies on the smallest possible voxel value being 0. If the data contains negative values, this definition must be adjusted. Multiresolution Maximum Intensity Projection (MMIP) is a progressive rendering algorithm for 3-D volume data that computes the maximum value along lines through the data set. It solves the problem of interactive rendering latency by using a morphological pyramid to provide coarse approximations during user interaction and progressively refining the image with detail coefficients once interaction ceases. Unlike linear pyramid-based MIP methods which rely on additive reconstruction, MMIP exploits the commutativity of the MIP operator with morphological dilation and upsampling, allowing the projection to be performed on coarse levels and expanded in 2-D, thereby avoiding expensive 3-D reconstruction for certain pyramid types. The Sun-Maragos Pyramid is an alternative morphological pyramid scheme for MIP volume rendering where a morphological opening is used for pyramidal analysis instead of erosion, while the synthesis operator remains a dilation. The opening is defined as \alphaA(f)(x) = \deltaA(\epsilonA(f))(x). This variant improves approximation accuracy when rendering from higher levels of the pyramid compared to the standard Adjunction Pyramid, which uses erosion for analysis. Time Complexity: The construction of the pyramid involves L levels of erosion/dilation and downsampling/upsampling. Each level reduces the data size by a factor of 8 (in 3D). The total time is proportional to the sum of the volumes at each level, which is dominated by the finest level. Reconstruction involves upsampling and dilation, which is also efficient. Memory Complexity: The pyramid stores L+1 approximation levels and L detail levels. The total memory is roughly 2 \times \frac{8}{7} times the size of the original volume (geometric series sum). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales well with resolution due to the multiresolution nature. Coarse levels can be rendered quickly for interactive feedback. Strengths: Perfect reconstruction property; commutativity with MIP allows efficient 2-D projection; progressive refinement. Limitations: Detail signals can be large in Adjunction Pyramids; requires careful selection of structuring element to satisfy pyramid condition. When to use: Interactive MIP volume rendering where progressive refinement is beneficial. When not to use: When small features are critical and Adjunction Pyramids are used without the Sun-Maragos variant; when memory is extremely constrained. The Morphological Pyramid was introduced in the context of multiresolution algorithms for Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) volume rendering. It is widely used in the display of magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and ultrasound data due to its computational simplicity and effectiveness. The concept of adjunction pyramids was introduced by Roefer [Roe01, Roe03, Roe05]. The Sun-Maragos variant was studied by Sun and Maragos [15] and referenced in [3]. The method is categorized under Interaction techniques (I.3.6) and Image Representation, Hierarchical, Morphological (I.4.10). name: Multiresolution Maximum Intensity Projection (MMIP)
head: MIP Volume Rendering with Morphological Pyramids, Multiresolution MIP, Multiresolution MIP based on detail pyramid, Progressive refinement from detail pyramid, level-by-level MMIP
body: Multiresolution Maximum Intensity Projection (MMIP) is a progressive rendering algorithm for 3-D volume data that computes the maximum value along lines through the data set. It solves the problem of interactive rendering latency by using a morphological pyramid to provide coarse approximations during user interaction and progressively refining the image with detail coefficients once interaction ceases. Unlike linear pyramid-based MIP methods which rely on additive reconstruction, MMIP exploits the commutativity of the MIP operator with morphological dilation and upsampling, allowing the projection to be performed on coarse levels and expanded in 2-D, thereby avoiding expensive 3-D reconstruction for certain pyramid types. Inputs: 1. A detail pyramid sequence d0, d1, \dots, d{L-1} and the coarsest approximation fL of the input volume data set f. 2. A viewing orientation \Theta, defined by angles \theta, \phi (projection direction perpendicular to the view plane) and \alpha (orientation of the view plane). 3. A structuring element A for the morphological operations. Outputs: A sequence of progressively refined 2-D approximation images M\Theta^{(j)}(f) for j = L, L-1, \dots, 0. Data Structures: Pyramid Levels: The volume is decomposed into levels j=0 \dots L. Level L is the coarsest approximation fL. Levels 0 \dots L-1 contain detail signals dj. Storage: For efficient voxel projection, 'interesting' voxels are sorted by grey value using a histogram-based scheme. This involves a value-sorted array of voxel positions and an additional array containing cumulative histogram values. Structuring Element: The 2-D expand operator uses a structuring element \tilde{A}, defined as the MIP of the original 3-D structuring element A: \tilde{A}:= M\Theta(A). Definitions: MIP Operator (M\Theta): Computes the maximum value along rays defined by \Theta. Upsample (\text{UPSAMPLE}): Increases resolution by a factor of 2 in each spatial dimension, inserting zeros or interpolating (standard definition implied by context of dilation). Dilation (\deltaA): \deltaA(f)(x) = \max{a \in A} (f(x-a)). 2-D Expand Operator (\tilde{\psi}A^\downarrow): \tilde{\psi}A^\downarrow(f) = \delta{\tilde{A}}(\text{UPSAMPLE}(f)). Generalized Subtraction (Adjunction only): t \dot{-} s = \begin{cases} t, & \text{if } t > s \\ 0, & \text{if } t = s \end{cases}, where 0 is the smallest possible voxel value. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pyramid Construction: Recursively apply the REDUCE operator to compute approximations fj and detail signals dj until level L is reached. The original volume data can be discarded after construction due to the perfect reconstruction property. For Adjunction Pyramids: \PsiA^\downarrow(f) = \text{DOWNSAMPLE}(\epsilonA(f)) and dj = fj \dot{-} \PsiA^\downarrow \PsiA^\uparrow (fj). For Sun-Maragos Pyramids: \PsiA^\downarrow(f) = \text{DOWNSAMPLE}(\alphaA(f)). 2. Coarsest Approximation: Compute the MIP of the coarsest volume level fL, then expand it to the full image resolution using the 2-D expand operator applied L times: M\Theta^{(L)}(f) = \tilde{\psi}A^{\downarrow L}(M\Theta(fL)) where \tilde{\psi}A^{\downarrow L} denotes L-fold composition of \tilde{\psi}A^\downarrow. 3. Progressive Refinement: Iterate from j = L down to 1 to refine the image: For Adjunction Pyramids (2D-only refinement): Compute the next approximation by taking the maximum of the expanded MIP of the detail signal and the previous approximation: M\Theta^{(j-1)}(f) = \tilde{\psi}A^{\downarrow (j-1)}(M\Theta(d{j-1})) \vee M\Theta^{(j)}(f) Since detail signals dj are non-negative, the projections increase pointwise: M\Theta^{(j-1)}(f) \ge M\Theta^{(j)}(f). For Sun-Maragos Pyramids (3D reconstruction required): Reconstruct the volume at level j-1 from level j and the detail d{j-1}, then project and expand: f{j-1} = \psiA^\uparrow(fj) \dot{+} d{j-1} M\Theta^{(j-1)}(f) = \tilde{\psi}A^{\downarrow (j-1)}(M\Theta(f{j-1})) This requires a 3-D dilation for reconstruction, which is less efficient for value-sorted arrays. Pseudocode (Adjunction Pyramid Variant): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mmipadjunction(fL, details, L, theta, structuringelementA): """ Perform Multiresolution MIP using an adjunction pyramid. Args: fL: Coarsest approximation volume (level L). details: List of detail volumes [d0, d1,..., d{L-1}]. L: Decomposition depth. theta: Viewing orientation parameters. structuringelementA: 3D structuring element for morphological ops. Returns: List of 2D images [ML, M{L-1},..., M0] representing progressive refinement. """ # Precompute 2D structuring element for expansion # Mtheta(A) computes the MIP of the structuring element A along theta structuringelementA2d = mip2d(structuringelementA, theta) # Step 1: Coarsest approximation # Project coarse volume mipcoarse = mip3d(fL, theta) # Expand L times to full resolution currentimage = mipcoarse for in range(L): currentimage = expand2d(currentimage, structuringelementA2d) results = [currentimage] # Step 2: Progressive refinement from L down to 1 # details[j-1] corresponds to d{j-1} for j in range(L, 0, -1): detailvolume = details[j-1] # Project detail volume mipdetail = mip3d(detailvolume, theta) # Expand (j-1) times expandeddetail = mipdetail for in range(j-1): expandeddetail = expand2d(expandeddetail, structuringelementA2d) # Take maximum with previous approximation # Note: In adjunction pyramids, details are non-negative, # so this effectively adds detail without subtracting. currentimage = max(currentimage, expandeddetail) results.append(currentimage) return results def expand2d(image, structuringelement2d): """ Perform 2D expansion: Upsample by 2 in each dimension, then dilate. """ upscaled = upsample2d(image, factor=2) dilated = dilate2d(upscaled, structuringelement2d) return dilated def upsample2d(image, factor): """ Upsample image by inserting zeros/interpolating. Standard definition: newimage[x, y] = image[x/factor, y/factor] if divisible, else 0. """ newh, neww = image.height factor, image.width factor newimage = ZeroImage(newh, neww) for y in range(image.height): for x in range(image.width): newimage[y factor, x factor] = image[y, x] return newimage def dilate2d(image, structuringelement): """ 2D Morphological Dilation. """ result = ZeroImage(image.height, image.width) for y in range(image.height): for x in range(image.width): maxval = 0 # Assuming 0 is min value for dy, dx in structuringelement: ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < image.height and 0 <= nx < image.width: maxval = max(maxval, image[ny, nx]) result[y, x] = maxval return result This method performs progressive Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) volume rendering by refining the image directly in the 2D plane using an adjunction pyramid, avoiding 3D volume reconstruction. It leverages the commutativity of MIP and dilation to update the projection by taking the maximum of the expanded detail projection and the previous approximation. Unlike general detail pyramids that require 3D reconstruction, this variant exploits the specific properties of adjunction pyramids where detail signals are non-negative, allowing for simpler, purely 2D progressive refinement. Time Complexity: The complexity depends on the pyramid type. For adjunction pyramids, the refinement is purely 2D, making it significantly faster as it avoids 3D reconstruction. For Sun-Maragos pyramids, each refinement step requires a 3D dilation for reconstruction, which is computationally expensive, especially with value-sorted arrays. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the pyramid levels (fL and d0 \dots d{L-1}). The original volume can be discarded after pyramid construction. Performance: Interactive rendering is fast because only coarse levels are used during interaction. Progressive refinement adds detail incrementally. The adjunction variant is more efficient for streaming or interactive use due to the 2D-only update. Strengths: Perfect reconstruction capability; compatibility with MIP due to commutativity of dilation/upsampling with maximum; reduced data size for interaction; integer computations only (for flat pyramids). Limitations: Image quality is lower in preview mode due to loss of detail; Sun-Maragos variant is inefficient for certain data structures due to 3D reconstruction requirements. When to use: Interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets (e.g., MRA, ultrasound) where user interaction speed is critical and progressive detail addition is acceptable. When not to use: When high-fidelity static rendering is required without progressive refinement, or when the overhead of 3D reconstruction for Sun-Maragos pyramids is prohibitive. MMIP was introduced in the context of multiresolution algorithms for Maximum Intensity Projection volume rendering, widely used in magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and ultrasound data display. The method builds on the properties of morphological pyramids, specifically the commutativity of morphological operators with the MIP operator. The adjunction pyramid variant was detailed in works by Roe et al., while the Sun-Maragos pyramid variant was discussed in comparison studies. The approach addresses the major problem of data size in interactive rendering by allowing coarse previews and progressive refinement. name: Multiresolution MIP based on adjunction pyramid
head: Progressive refinement from adjunction pyramid
body: This method performs progressive Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) volume rendering by refining the image directly in the 2D plane using an adjunction pyramid, avoiding 3D volume reconstruction. It leverages the commutativity of MIP and dilation to update the projection by taking the maximum of the expanded detail projection and the previous approximation. Unlike general detail pyramids that require 3D reconstruction, this variant exploits the specific properties of adjunction pyramids where detail signals are non-negative, allowing for simpler, purely 2D progressive refinement. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An adjunction detail pyramid sequence d0, d1, \dots, d{L-1} and the coarsest approximation fL of the input volume data f. The parameter \Theta defines the viewing coordinate system orientation. Output: A sequence of progressively refined approximation images M\Theta^{(j)}(f) for j=L, \dots, 0. Data Structures: Pyramid Levels: The pyramid has depth L. Each level j corresponds to detail data d{j-1} (for j=1 \dots L) and the coarsest approximation fL. Operators: \psiA: The 3D analysis operator (REDUCE) of the adjunction pyramid. \tilde{\psi}A: The 2D synthesis operator (EXPAND) applied in the image plane, where \tilde{\psi}A^{k} denotes k-fold composition with itself. \vee: The pointwise maximum operator, defined as (g0 \vee g1)(x) = \max(g0(x), g1(x)). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Choose the viewing orientation \Theta. Compute the coarsest approximation image by applying the 2D synthesis operator \tilde{\psi}A L times to the MIP of the coarsest volume approximation fL: M\Theta^{(L)}(f) = \tilde{\psi}A^L (M\Theta(fL)) 2. Progressive Refinement: Loop from j = L down to 1. a. Compute the MIP of the detail signal at level j-1: P = M\Theta(d{j-1}). b. Expand this projection j-1 times using the 2D synthesis operator: E = \tilde{\psi}A^{j-1}(P). c. Update the current approximation by taking the maximum of the expanded detail projection and the previous approximation: M\Theta^{(j-1)}(f) = E \vee M\Theta^{(j)}(f) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiresolutionmipadjunction(detailpyramid, coarsestapprox, L, theta): # detailpyramid: list of 3D volumes [d0, d1,..., d{L-1}] # coarsestapprox: 3D volume fL # L: integer, decomposition depth # theta: viewing orientation parameter (direction vector) # Standard operations (self-contained): # maxalongrays(volume, direction): projects 3D volume along direction by taking max along rays # dilation2d(image): applies 2D dilation (synthesis operator) to image # Step 1: Coarsest approximation currentmip = maxalongrays(coarsestapprox, theta) for in range(L): currentmip = dilation2d(currentmip) # Step 2: Progressive refinement for j in range(L, 0, -1): detailproj = maxalongrays(detailpyramid[j-1], theta) expandeddetail = detailproj for in range(j-1): expandeddetail = dilation2d(expandeddetail) currentmip = max(currentmip, expandeddetail) return currentmip Parameters: L: Decomposition depth. \Theta: Viewing orientation. Determines the projection direction. Pitfalls: Monotonicity: Because detail signals d{j-1} in an adjunction pyramid are non-negative, the projections M\Theta^{(j-1)}(f) are guaranteed to be greater than or equal to M\Theta^{(j)}(f). The image intensity increases pointwise as one goes down the pyramid (from coarse to fine). A variant that uses an approximation pyramid instead of a detail pyramid. It avoids 3D reconstruction by applying MIP directly to approximation data at each level, which is suitable when 3D dilation is inefficient on compressed data. It differs from the adjunction variant by operating on approximation sequences f0 \dots fL rather than detail sequences, and requires the synthesis operator to be a dilation. It is chosen when memory allows storing all approximation levels, as it uses storage of the same order of magnitude as storing detail and coarsest approximation data. See Multiresolution Maximum Intensity Projection (MMIP). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Direct 2D refinement avoids expensive 3D reconstruction steps required by general detail pyramids. Limitations: Relies on the specific properties of adjunction pyramids (non-negative details). This method was introduced in the context of comparing different morphological pyramid structures for volume rendering. The approach builds on the commutativity of MIP and dilation, allowing the projection to be refined in the image plane. It is similar to wavelet splatting but replaces linear summation with maximum computation and linear wavelet filters with morphological filters. name: Multi-Resolution Volume Visualization (Split-and-Collapse)
head: Split-and-Collapse
body: Multi-Resolution Volume Visualization (Split-and-Collapse) is a method for interactive volume rendering that dynamically adjusts the resolution of different volume areas based on available memory bandwidth and user interaction. It solves the problem of maintaining high frame rates for large volumes by using a greedy algorithm to select between refinement (split) and reduction (collapse) operations, guided by an error measure. Unlike static LOD techniques, it continuously updates the representation during interaction (viewpoint changes, region of interest shifts) to respect hardware constraints. Inputs: A large 3D volume dataset. Hardware constraints (available memory, bandwidth limits between main memory and GPU). User interaction parameters (viewpoint, region of interest, transfer function). A set of parameters defining the multi-resolution hierarchy (object space or image space). Outputs: A multi-resolution representation of the volume optimized for current frame approximation. Rendered image using GPU ray casting or viewport-aligned planes with pre-integrated classification. The method relies on a multi-resolution hierarchy where volume areas are represented at different levels of detail (bricks or subvolumes). Bricks/Subvolumes: The volume is partitioned into bricks. Each brick has a resolution level. Error Measure: A metric used to guide the greedy algorithm, calculating the improvement in multi-resolution approximation for potential split or collapse operations. Pre-integration Tables: 2D and 3D tables used for classification and integration. 3D table construction time is reduced by reusing integrals from 2D tables. 1. Initialization: Load the volume data and initialize the multi-resolution hierarchy. Determine initial resolution levels for bricks based on available memory. 2. Error Calculation: For each brick, calculate the error associated with its current resolution level. This error measure guides the selection of the next operation. 3. Greedy Selection: Use a greedy algorithm to select the next refinement (split) or reduction (collapse) operation that provides the maximum improvement in approximation per unit of memory cost, respecting hardware constraints. Refinement (Split): Increase the resolution of a brick. Reduction (Collapse): Decrease the resolution of a brick. 4. Optimal Verification (Optional): An optimal polynomial algorithm can be used to obtain the multi-resolution representation with minimum error, verifying that the greedy results are near-optimal. 5. Out-of-Core Management: If the volume exceeds available memory, use out-of-core techniques compatible with the memory page demands of the Split-and-Collapse algorithm to stream data. 6. Rendering: Deploy using GPU-based ray casting or viewport-aligned planes with pre-integrated classification. Implement acceleration techniques: empty space skipping, early ray termination, and adaptive sampling. Adjust ray segments appropriately at subvolume or brick boundaries. For GPU ray casting, reduce artifacts between bricks with different LODs by blending weighted levels of detail of contiguous bricks. Reduce 3D pre-integration table construction time by reusing integrals from 2D pre-integration tables. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splitandcollapse(volume, memorylimit, errorthreshold): """ Main loop for dynamic multi-resolution volume visualization.
