name: Level-of-Detail Volume Rendering via 3D Textures
head: Multiresolution volume rendering via 3D textures, Adaptive 3D Texture Volume Rendering, Brick-based LOD volume rendering
body: This method provides an adaptive level-of-detail (LOD) selection algorithm for multi-resolution volume rendering using 3D texture mapping. It renders volume data in a region-of-interest at high resolution while progressively lowering the resolution for areas further away, enabling interactive exploration of large-scale datasets. Unlike approaches that rely on user-specified error tolerances or spherical shells, this technique guarantees consistent interpolation between different resolution levels and explicitly fixes rendering artifacts (such as light/dark bands) at brick boundaries using polygon clipping and opacity correction. Input: A large 3D scalar volume dataset (e.g., 256^3 voxels). Output: A rendered image with adaptive resolution, minimizing texture memory usage and texture lookups. 1. Brick Decomposition The volume is decomposed into 3D bricks (subvolumes) small enough to fit into texture memory. A typical brick size is 32^3 voxels. 2. Texture Hierarchy Each brick maintains a local hierarchy of texture maps. Level 0: The original resolution data. Level k: A coarser resolution copy. The texture size is reduced by a factor of two compared to level k-1, and the width of texture elements is doubled. Alignment: Texture elements on level k are aligned such that their centers correspond to the center of an even-indexed element on the finer level k-1. Domain Adaptation: On level 0, the texture coordinate domain ranges from the center of the first element to the center of the last one. This domain is adapted for coarser levels to maintain geometric consistency. Boundary Padding: To guarantee continuous interpolation, additional voxels are included at subvolume boundaries. If a boundary falls between two voxels on a coarser level, both adjacent voxels must be modified/adapted. Power-of-Two Expansion: Textures are expanded and padded with zero voxels to satisfy OpenGL's power-of-two texture size restrictions. 3. Merged Texture Hierarchy (Octree-like) To minimize memory overhead from boundary padding, textures of adjacent subvolumes are merged: Level 0: Each brick has its own texture map. Higher Levels: Eight adjacent subvolumes share a single texture map. The number of subvolumes sharing a texture map multiplies by 8 at each coarser level, forming an octree-like hierarchy. Constraint: Merging works optimally if the initial number of subvolumes in every direction is a power of two. If the count exceeds 2^{l-1} (where l is the number of levels), additional subvolumes build their own texture sets. If fewer, the hierarchy depth is reduced by storing coarsest-level textures individually. Filter Kernel: A quadratic spline kernel is used to iteratively construct low-pass filtered copies for coarser levels. Simple sub-sampling is insufficient. Max Adjacent Level Difference: Adjacent bricks can differ by at most one level of detail. Higher transitions are achieved via consecutive one-level steps. Brick Size: Typically 32^3 voxels. 1. Decomposition: Split the volume dataset into bricks of fixed size (e.g., 32^3). 2. Hierarchy Construction: For each brick, construct a local texture hierarchy: Level 0 is the original data. For each subsequent level k, apply a quadratic spline filter to the data from level k-1 to generate the coarser approximation. Align levels so that level k centers match even-indexed elements of level k-1. Expand textures to power-of-two dimensions, padding with zeros. 3. Texture Merging: Merge adjacent brick textures into shared maps according to the octree-like hierarchy rules. 4. LOD Selection: Assign a level of detail to each brick based on criteria: Maximum Opacity: Higher opacity regions get higher resolution. Distance to Viewpoint: Closer bricks get higher resolution. Projection Area: Larger projected bounding boxes get higher resolution. Gaze Distance: Regions closer to the user's gaze point get higher resolution. Constraint: Ensure adjacent bricks differ by at most one level. 5. Boundary Adaptation (Interpolation): For bricks adjacent to a coarser neighbor, adapt the finer texture to ensure scalar field continuity: Identify voxels at the boundary of the finer brick that do not align with the coarser grid. Interpolate or copy values from the coarser level into these boundary voxels of the finer brick. If the boundary is at a voxel center, adapt 1 voxel; if between voxels, adapt 2. 6. Opacity Correction: Modify the transfer function for subsampled (coarser) textures to preserve optical properties. Calculate the corrected opacity \alpha' using the derived formula: \alpha' = 1 - (1 - \alpha0)^2 where \alpha0 is the original opacity. Apply this to all opacity values in the subsampled texture. 7. Polygon Clipping and Rendering: Render bricks using slicing planes parallel to the image plane. Handle level transitions with polygon clipping to correct opacity artifacts: Case 1 (Coarser to Finer): Clip the even-slice i in the coarser brick with the perspective projection of the odd-slice i+1 (from the finer brick) onto slice i. Render the clipped polygon in region C with the same opacity as the finer level. Case 2 (Finer to Coarser): Reconstruct the odd-slice i+1 in the coarser brick and clip it with the perspective projection of the even-slice i (from the finer brick) onto slice i+1. Render the clipped polygon in region C with corrected opacity \alpha{k+1}. Generalization: For each pair of even/odd slices in a coarser brick, consecutively clip the even-slice with all odd-slices in the same and neighboring bricks on the same or finer level. Clip odd-slices only with even-slices in neighboring finer bricks. Boundary Handling: If no other polygons exist to clip against, insert additional slices with the smallest sample distance to guarantee correct opacity contribution. Sorting: Sort clipped polygons to minimize color table reloads. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildtexturehierarchy(brickdata, maxlevels): """ Constructs a local texture hierarchy for a single brick. brickdata: 3D array of original voxels. maxlevels: Integer, maximum number of LOD levels. Returns: List of 3D arrays, where index k is level k. """ levels = [brickdata] currentdata = brickdata for k in range(1, maxlevels): # Apply quadratic spline filter to downsample # Note: Simple sub-sampling is insufficient; filtering is required coarserdata = applyquadraticsplinefilter(currentdata) # Expand to power-of-two size if necessary, padding with zeros coarserdata = expandtopoweroftwo(coarserdata) levels.append(coarserdata) currentdata = coarserdata return levels def adaptboundaryfinebricks(finebricklevel, coarsebricklevel): """ Adapts the finer brick's boundary voxels to match the coarser brick's grid to ensure continuous scalar field interpolation. """ # Identify boundary voxels in the fine brick that do not align with coarse grid # If boundary is at voxel center, adapt 1 voxel; if between, adapt 2 for voxel in finebricklevel.boundaryvoxels: # Interpolate or copy value from the corresponding location in coarse level # Since centers align with even elements of finer level, this is often a copy # for even indices, but interpolation for misaligned boundaries voxel.value = interpolatefromcoarse(voxel.position, coarsebricklevel) def correctopacity(transferfunction): """ Applies opacity correction formula to preserve optical properties when sampling at lower resolutions. """ correctedtf = {} for alpha in transferfunction: # Formula derived from equating accumulated opacities D and D' # alpha' = 1 - (1 - alpha)^2 alphacorrected = 1.0 - (1.0 - alpha) 2 correctedtf[alpha] = alphacorrected return correctedtf def renderbrickwithclipping(brick, level, viewparams): """ Renders a brick at a specific LOD level, handling boundary artifacts via polygon clipping. """ # 1. Determine slicing planes parallel to image plane slices = generateslices(brick, level, viewparams) # 2. Handle level transitions with clipping # Case 1: Coarser to Finer neighbor if hasfinierneighbor(brick): for evenslicei in brick.evenslices: # Clip even-slice i with perspective projection of odd-slice i+1 from finer neighbor clippedpoly = clippolygon(evenslicei, finerneighbor.oddsliceiplus1) renderpolygon(clippedpoly, opacity=finerneighbor.opacity) # Case 2: Finer to Coarser neighbor if hascoarserneighbor(brick): for oddsliceiplus1 in brick.oddslices: # Reconstruct odd-slice in coarser brick and clip with even-slice i from finer neighbor reconstructedslice = reconstructslice(oddsliceiplus1, brick.coarserlevel) clippedpoly = clippolygon(reconstructedslice, finerneighbor.evenslicei) renderpolygon(clippedpoly, opacity=correctedopacity) # 3. Handle external boundaries if noclippingpolygonsexist(): insertsliceswithsmallestsampledistance() # 4. Sort polygons to minimize state changes sortpolygonsbycolortable() renderallpolygons() Memory Efficiency: Significantly reduces texture memory consumption. On the "engine" dataset, an adaptive representation with four levels of detail required only 29% of the original texture memory. Using two levels reduced memory to 57%. Performance: Reduces the number of texture lookups. The four-level adaptive representation required only 32% of the originally needed texture lookups. Rendering Speed: Full resolution rendering took ~2 seconds per frame on the engine dataset, while the LOD version took 0.5 seconds per frame. Overhead: Clipping overhead is less than 0.1 seconds per frame. Texture adaptation takes ~0.2 seconds. Clipping operations average 2500 per frame, up to 5500 in worst-case diagonal views. Strengths: Guarantees consistent interpolation between levels; fixes opacity artifacts (light/dark bands) at boundaries; interactive performance for large datasets. Limitations: Relies on OpenGL power-of-two restrictions requiring padding; topology preservation is not guaranteed if LOD selection ignores approximation error; clipping complexity increases with diagonal views. Origin: The method was developed by Manfred Weiler, Hans-Peter Seidel, and others at the University of Stuttgart and the University of Utah. Key Paper: "Level-of-Detail Volume Rendering via 3D Textures," published in IEEE Visualization 2000. Context: It addresses the challenge of rendering large-scale volume data (e.g., MRI scans, simulation data) interactively on hardware with limited texture memory. It improves upon earlier methods like LaMar et al.'s spherical shell approach, which did not guarantee continuity between resolution levels. name: Streaming MIP Implementation (Basic)
head: Streaming MIP
body: Streaming MIP is a rendering technique that approximates the Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) of volumetric data by projecting pre-sorted detail coefficients from a morphological pyramid directly to the frame buffer. It solves the problem of rendering large datasets with limited memory bandwidth by streaming coefficients in order of their contribution to the L1-error, allowing for progressive refinement or early termination based on a quality threshold. Unlike level-by-level MIP rendering, which processes entire resolution levels sequentially, Streaming MIP projects individual coefficients regardless of their pyramid level, requiring a local dilation operation to correctly propagate the maximum value to neighboring pixels. Inputs: A morphological pyramid of detail coefficients \{dj(x, y, z)\}, sorted by error contribution (L1-error reduction). Outputs: A 2D frame buffer image representing the MIP. Data Structures: The implementation requires storing detail coefficients with specific attributes to support the projection logic. Each voxel (coefficient) is stored with: 1. Position: 4 bytes. The pyramid level j is encoded into two bits of the position attribute. 2. Intensity: 2 bytes (short), storing the coefficient value. Total memory footprint: 6 bytes per voxel. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the frame buffer with the minimum possible intensity value (e.g., 0 or background). 2. Iteration: Iterate through the sorted list of detail coefficients \{dj\}. 3. Projection Condition: For each coefficient k with value val and pyramid level j, determine the projection point (x, y). 4. Local Dilation: Define a neighborhood around the projection point based on the level j. The dilation size is j \cdot \tilde{A}, where \tilde{A} is the structuring element used in the pyramid synthesis. For a square 2 \times 2 structuring element, the dilation radius/size corresponds to point sizes of 1, 2, and 4 for levels 0, 1, and 2 respectively. 5. Update: For all pixels in the dilated neighborhood: Let curval be the current value in the frame buffer at that pixel. If curval < val, overwrite curval with val. 6. Termination: Stop when a pre-defined maximum number of coefficients has been projected or the desired accuracy threshold is met. Formulas: The update rule for a pixel p in the neighborhood of coefficient k is: \text{buffer}[p] = \max(\text{buffer}[p], val) where val is the intensity of the current coefficient. Parameters: Structuring Element \tilde{A}: Typically a square 2 \times 2 block. Point Size: Mapped to the hardware vertex program's PSIZE semantic. For level j, the point size scales with j. Sorting Criterion: Coefficients are sorted by the reduction in L1-error between the partial reconstruction and the original data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Global Dilation Invalid: Global dilation cannot be used because the scale index (pyramid level) varies per coefficient, unlike level-by-level projection where the scale is constant for all coefficients in a level. Ordering Loss: Because coefficients are projected by error rather than intensity, voxels are no longer ordered by intensity in the rendering stream. This necessitates using the maximum operator for frame buffer writes, which may cause performance loss compared to alpha-blending or simple overwriting, although the impact is mitigated by the small size of the blended primitives. Holes: For non-axis-aligned parallel projections, the voxel-based method may yield pixel-sized holes in the result. This is typically addressed in a post-processing step using morphological closing with the structuring element \tilde{A}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def streamingmipbasic(coefficients, framebuffer, structuringelementsize=2): """ coefficients: List of tuples (level, x, y, z, value), sorted by error contribution. framebuffer: 2D array initialized to minvalue. structuringelementsize: Size of the base structuring element (e.g., 2 for 2x2). """ for coeff in coefficients: level, x, y, z, val = coeff # Determine dilation radius based on level and structuring element # For a 2x2 element, level 0 -> size 1, level 1 -> size 2, level 2 -> size 4 # The "size" here refers to the extent of the neighborhood to check/update. # A common interpretation for dilation size j with base size S is radius proportional to jS. # Based on S1: "point size will be 1, 2 and 4 at level 0, 1 and 2" for 2x2 element. # This implies the dilation radius or diameter scales linearly. # Let's assume the neighborhood is a square of side length dilationsize. dilationsize = (level + 1) (structuringelementsize // 2) # Note: S1 says point size 1, 2, 4 for levels 0, 1, 2. # This looks like 2^level base? No, 1, 2, 4 is 2^0, 2^1, 2^2. # But it also says "scaled neighborhood j A~". # If A~ is 2x2, j=1 -> 2x2, j=2 -> 4x4. # Let's stick to the explicit example: size = 2^level (basesize/2)? # Actually, S1 says: "point size will be 1, 2 and 4 at level 0, 1 and 2". # This suggests the radius or half-width might be 2^level? Or the diameter? # If point size is the diameter, radius is 0.5, 1, 2. # Let's implement the neighborhood as a square centered at (x,y) with side dilationsize. dilationsize = 2 level (structuringelementsize // 2) if dilationsize < 1: dilationsize = 1 halfsize = dilationsize // 2 # Iterate over the dilated neighborhood for dy in range(-halfsize, halfsize + 1): for dx in range(-halfsize, halfsize + 1): px = x + dx py = y + dy # Check bounds if 0 <= px < framebuffer.width and 0 <= py < framebuffer.height: if framebuffer[py, px] < val: framebuffer[py, px] = val This variant avoids the performance drawbacks of the basic implementation (point sprites, frame buffer blending, 6-byte overhead) by using only 4 bytes per voxel and no point sprites. It retains the error-sorted list but uses a second histogram-sorting step with one bin per (level, intensity) pair to guide rendering. The algorithm selects a percentage of coefficients to render, then traverses the sorted list to render voxels for each pyramid level in low-to-high intensity order, guided by the histogram. This allows for efficient rendering without the need for maximum operator blending during the write phase, as the intensity ordering ensures correct MIP approximation. This method handles missing data at the needed resolution by triggering a fallback to a higher mipmap level. If no higher level is present or the data is too coarse, it resorts to iterative interrupt/resume methods. This approach provides a stable frame rate by fixing a budget for data upload, leveraging the fact that users perceive fewer details during strong motion when missing data is most likely. This technique reduces per-intersection cost by precomputing MIP-filtered weights using the inverse covariance matrix of the surfel's tangent frame. The weight w is calculated as w = nf \cdot \exp(-0.5 \cdot \rho{\text{mip}}^2), where \rho{\text{mip}}^2 = \Sigma{uu}^{-1} u^2 + 2 \Sigma{uv}^{-1} uv + \Sigma{vv}^{-1} v^2. This avoids per-pixel Jacobian evaluation without visual loss in filtering quality. This approach involves opening a second streamed volume over the same store, cropped to the picked brick's common-grid box, allowing the octree to pull the crop toward level 0. It fixes issues where extractSubVolume returns null for streamed volumes by falling back to a specific sampler backed by the coarse floor, ensuring correct picking behavior. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of coefficients projected. In the worst case, all coefficients are projected, but early termination allows for O(k) where k is the number of coefficients needed for the desired accuracy. Memory Complexity: 6 bytes per voxel for the basic implementation (4 bytes position + 2 bytes intensity). The optimized variant uses 4 bytes per voxel. Performance: The basic implementation suffers from some performance loss due to the need for maximum operator writes to the frame buffer, as voxels are not ordered by intensity. However, the impact is limited because the blended primitives (dilated points) are small. The optimized variant eliminates this bottleneck. Strengths: Allows for progressive refinement; efficient use of memory bandwidth by streaming only necessary coefficients; hardware-accelerated via point rendering extensions. Limitations: Requires preprocessing to build the morphological pyramid and sort coefficients; basic implementation has higher memory overhead and blending overhead; non-axis-aligned projections may require post-processing to fill holes. Streaming MIP was introduced in the context of multiresolution MIP rendering of large volumetric data accelerated on graphics hardware. It builds on the concept of morphological pyramids, where detail coefficients are computed to minimize L1-error. The method was developed to address the limitations of level-by-level rendering, which cannot easily support progressive refinement or adaptive quality control. The basic implementation leverages graphics hardware features such as point size extensions and point sprites to implement level-dependent local dilation. name: Streaming MIP Construction
head: Error-sorted Streaming MIP Construction, L1-error sorted Streaming MIP, MMIP, Multiresolution MIP, Streaming MIP
body: Streaming MIP is a multiresolution volume rendering technique that constructs a progressive coefficient stream from a morphological pyramid to allow interactive frame rates on large datasets that do not fit in GPU memory. It solves the problem of discrete quality jumps in level-by-level rendering by resorting detail coefficients from all pyramid levels simultaneously based on decreasing magnitude of an error measure, providing near-continuous error control. It sets itself apart from basic texture-based MIP by storing only necessary voxels and from level-by-level MMIP by offering finer granularity in approximation error control. Inputs: A volumetric dataset V of dimensions W \times H \times D. Outputs: A MIP image M and a performance/quality trade-off determined by the number of projected coefficients. Data Structures: 1. Morphological Pyramid: Constructed from V. The paper uses a three-level pyramid consisting of one approximation level A0 and two detail levels D1, D2. A0: Approximation of the original data. Dk: Detail coefficients at level k. 2. Coefficient Stream: A sorted list of detail coefficients \{dj\} from all levels D1, D2. 3. Auxiliary Coefficients: An intermediate set used for sorting, discarded after the stream is constructed. 4. Render Target: A framebuffer or image buffer initialized to the minimum intensity value (or background) for MIP accumulation. Parameters: Pyramid Levels: 3 levels (2 detail, 1 approximation) are used. Error Measure: L1 error. The relative L1-approximation error is defined as: \varepsilon^{(j)} = \frac{\| \mathbf{M}^{(0)} - \mathbf{M}^{(j)} \|1}{\| \mathbf{M}^{(0)} \|1} where \mathbf{M}^{(0)} is the original MIP image and \mathbf{M}^{(j)} is the approximation after projecting j coefficients. Projection Type: Parallel projection. Non-axis-aligned projections require post-processing. Steps: 1. Construct Morphological Pyramid: Apply morphological dilation and erosion operations to generate the pyramid levels. Compute detail coefficients Dk by subtracting the upsampled approximation of the next level from the current level (or via the specific morphological difference definition used in the source). Note: The exact morphological pyramid construction algorithm is referenced to [GH00] and [Roe05] but not detailed in the provided text. 2. Construct Coefficient Stream: Join all detail coefficients from all levels into a single set. Create an auxiliary set of detail coefficients. Sort the auxiliary set by decreasing magnitude (absolute value) of the coefficients. Resort the original detail coefficients \{dj\} by assigning them the same order as the sorted auxiliary coefficients. Discard the auxiliary coefficients. Rationale: Directly sorting detail coefficients by magnitude is suboptimal because coefficients are not small in regions where the structuring element fits approximately but not exactly. The auxiliary sorting ensures that each successive coefficient maximally reduces the L1-error between the partial reconstruction and the original data. 3. Rendering (Point-based Projection): Initialize the render target. Iterate through the sorted coefficient stream \{dj\}. For each coefficient dj at position (x, y, z) with value val: Project the voxel at (x, y, z) onto the image plane. Update the pixel value at the projected location: pixel = \max(pixel, val). Implicit Empty Space Skipping: Only non-empty voxels (those with non-zero detail coefficients or significant approximation values) are rendered. Stop when a desired accuracy is reached or a maximum number of coefficients is projected. 4. Post-processing (Optional): For non-axis-aligned parallel projections, the voxel-based method may yield pixel-sized holes. Apply a morphological closing operation using the structuring element \tilde{A} used for synthesis to fill these holes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def streamingmipconstruction(volume, pyramidlevels=3): """ Constructs the coefficient stream for Streaming MIP. volume: 3D array of voxel intensities. pyramidlevels: Number of levels in the morphological pyramid. Returns: Sorted list of detail coefficients (dj, x, y, z). """ # 1. Construct Morphological Pyramid # Note: Exact morphological pyramid algorithm is not provided in source. # Assumes a function morphologicalpyramid(volume, levels) exists. pyramid = morphologicalpyramid(volume, pyramidlevels) # Extract detail coefficients from all levels except the approximation level detailcoefficients = [] for level in range(1, pyramidlevels): coeffs = pyramid[level] # Assuming pyramid[level] contains detail coefficients for z in range(coeffs.shape[0]): for y in range(coeffs.shape[1]): for x in range(coeffs.shape[2]): val = coeffs[z, y, x] if val != 0: # Implicit empty space skipping detailcoefficients.append({'val': val, 'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': z}) # 2. Construct Coefficient Stream # Create auxiliary coefficients for sorting # The source states: "define an auxiliary set of detail coefficients which is sorted with respect to decreasing magnitude" # It does not specify if the auxiliary set is different from the original set other than in purpose. # We assume the auxiliary set is a copy of the detail coefficients. auxiliarycoefficients = list(detailcoefficients) # Sort auxiliary coefficients by decreasing magnitude (absolute value) auxiliarycoefficients.sort(key=lambda c: abs(c['val']), reverse=True) # Resort original detail coefficients to match the order of auxiliary coefficients # Since the values are the same, we just sort the original list by magnitude # The source implies a mapping: "original detail coefficients {dj} are resorted by giving them # the same order as the resorted auxiliary coefficients" # This effectively means sorting the detail coefficients by magnitude. sortedcoefficients = sorted(detailcoefficients, key=lambda c: abs(c['val']), reverse=True) return sortedcoefficients def streamingmiprender(sortedcoefficients, imagewidth, imageheight, projectionmatrix): """ Renders the MIP image by projecting sorted coefficients. sortedcoefficients: List of coefficients sorted by L1-error reduction. imagewidth, imageheight: Dimensions of the output image. projectionmatrix: Matrix to project 3D coordinates to 2D. Returns: MIP image (2D array). """ # Initialize image with minimum value (e.g., 0 or background) image = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) for coeff in sortedcoefficients: x, y, z = coeff['x'], coeff['y'], coeff['z'] val = coeff['val'] # Project 3D coordinate to 2D # Note: Exact projection formula depends on projectionmatrix # Assuming a standard parallel projection for simplicity u, v = project3dto2d(x, y, z, projectionmatrix, imagewidth, imageheight) # Check if projection is within bounds if 0 <= u < imagewidth and 0 <= v < imageheight: # Update pixel with maximum intensity if val > image[v, u]: image[v, u] = val return image def postprocessmorphologicalclosing(image, structuringelement): """ Fills pixel-sized holes in non-axis-aligned projections. image: MIP image. structuringelement: Structuring element A used for synthesis. Returns: Closed image. """ # Apply morphological closing (dilation followed by erosion) # Note: Exact implementation depends on the library, but the operation is standard. dilated = morphologicaldilation(image, structuringelement) closed = morphologicalerosion(dilated, structuringelement) return closed Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-axis-aligned projections: Yield pixel-sized holes. Requires post-processing morphological closing. Pyramid Levels: Using more than three levels decreases performance due to additional render, upsample, and dilation steps, and higher levels have little non-zero coefficients. Precision: The method trades image quality for performance. Median error of 7 grey levels is acceptable for preview mode. The basic implementation of the streaming MIP algorithm, focusing on the core rendering loop and data structures. Streaming MIP Implementation (Basic) The method for constructing the morphological pyramid from the volume data. Morphological Pyramid Construction Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of retained detail coefficients. Frame rate approximately doubles each time the number of detail coefficients is halved. Memory Complexity: Cache-efficient, addressing GPU memory in a linear way. Only necessary voxels are stored. Performance: VisibleWoman (512x512x1734, 210M coeffs): 100% coeffs: 14 FPS, Median Error 0. 1% coeffs: 51 FPS, Median Error 7 grey levels. XMasTree (512x512x512, 105M coeffs): 100% coeffs: 80 FPS. 1% coeffs: 100 FPS, Median Error 25 grey levels. Comparison: Streaming MIP (GPU) with L1 error 0.07 (median 4) achieves 18.4 FPS, compared to 1.1 FPS for Streaming MIP (GPU) with 0.0 error. Streaming MIP (GPU) is about six times faster than the optimized software implementation given the same dataset and error bound. Using two GeForce 7900GTX cards achieves a speed-up of almost a factor of two over a single card. Strengths: Interactive frame rates on large datasets. Near-continuous error control. Cache-efficient memory access. Scalable to multiple GPUs. Limitations: Requires post-processing for non-axis-aligned projections. Performance bound by vertex units on older GPU hardware (unified shaders improve this). Does not remove view-independent hidden voxels (potential for 2x speedup if added). The method is based on morphological pyramids. Reference [GH00] discusses multiresolution signal decomposition schemes including linear and morphological pyramids. The streaming MIP algorithm was introduced in [Roe05] to overcome the discrete quality jumps of level-by-level rendering. The GPU implementation and comparison with existing CPU and GPU techniques were presented in. name: Multiresolution Decomposed Volume Rendering
head: Rendering Multiresolution Decomposed Volume Data
body: Multiresolution Decomposed Volume Rendering is a general framework for rendering volume data that has been decomposed into multiple resolution levels, enabling systematic exploration of multiresolution structure properties. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large volumetric datasets by leveraging the hierarchical nature of decomposed data to support adaptive rendering, efficient coding, progressive (coarse-to-fine) rendering, feature enhancement, and error bounds checking. Unlike Fourier or Wavelet-based methods that either lack occlusion handling or require full reconstruction before rendering, this framework allows rendering directly from the decomposed coefficients without full reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multiresolution decomposed volume data (e.g., coefficients from a transform such as Fourier, Wavelet, or DCT). Output: A rendered image with properties including adaptive resolution, progressive refinement, and error-bounded accuracy. Data Structures: The data structure consists of a hierarchy of coefficient sets representing different resolution levels. The specific layout depends on the chosen decomposition transform (e.g., Fourier coefficients, Wavelet subbands, or DCT blocks). The framework does not prescribe a single bit-packing scheme but relies on the properties of the underlying decomposition to allow selective access to coefficients. Steps: 1. Decomposition: The original 3D volume data is decomposed into multiresolution components using a transform such as Fourier, Wavelet, or Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). 2. Selection: Select a subset of coefficients corresponding to the desired resolution level or feature set. This selection enables adaptive rendering and error bounds checking. 3. Rendering: Perform volume rendering directly on the selected decomposed coefficients. This step avoids the need to reconstruct the full-resolution volume data before rendering, allowing for efficient use of compressed data. 4. Progressive Refinement: To achieve coarse-to-fine rendering, start with low-resolution coefficients and progressively add higher-resolution coefficients to refine the image. 5. Error Checking: Use the multiresolution structure to estimate rendering errors and ensure they remain within acceptable bounds. Parameters: Resolution Level: Determines the granularity of the rendering. Lower levels provide faster, coarser images; higher levels provide detail. Coefficient Threshold: Used for feature enhancement and data reduction by discarding insignificant coefficients. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Oversampling: Some decomposition schemes (e.g., simple difference signals) may result in oversampling, where a low-resolution version and a full-resolution difference signal are both stored, leading to redundancy. Occlusion Loss: If Fourier transformation is used, the resulting image may suffer from a lack of proper occlusion handling. Reconstruction Dependency: If the method inadvertently requires full reconstruction (as seen in some early Wavelet applications by Muraki), it fails to leverage the advantages of compressed data. A technique for rendering large out-of-core CT human cadaver volumes using GPU raycasting. It employs load-on-demand data management to handle memory constraints and Transfer Function (TF)-based data reduction to optimize rendering performance. This variant is chosen when dealing with very large datasets that exceed GPU memory, requiring efficient data streaming and reduction techniques. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Rendering time is reduced by working with decomposed coefficients and selecting only necessary resolution levels, avoiding full reconstruction. However, the specific complexity depends on the transform used (e.g., Fourier speeds up rendering but may lack occlusion). Memory: Memory usage is lower than storing full-resolution volumes due to compression inherent in the decomposition. For out-of-core schemes, memory is managed via load-on-demand strategies. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics are not given in the sources. The framework is noted to enable "time efficiency" when using Fourier transforms, though with trade-offs. Scaling: The framework scales well with dataset size by allowing adaptive rendering and progressive refinement. Out-of-core variants scale to datasets larger than available GPU memory. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Supports adaptive rendering, progressive rendering, feature enhancement, and error bounds checking. Avoids full reconstruction overhead. Limitations: Fourier-based approaches may lack occlusion. Some decomposition methods may suffer from oversampling. Early Wavelet methods required full reconstruction, negating compression benefits. When to Use: Use when efficient rendering of large volumetric datasets is required, especially when progressive refinement or adaptive resolution is needed. Use out-of-core variants for datasets exceeding GPU memory. When Not to Use: Avoid if strict occlusion handling is critical and Fourier-based decomposition is used. Avoid if the implementation inadvertently requires full reconstruction, as this negates the efficiency benefits. The framework was presented in a thesis titled "Direct rendering of multiresolution decomposed volume data". It builds upon earlier work in multiresolution representation using Fourier, Wavelet, and DCT transforms. Previous researchers, such as Muraki, applied Wavelet transforms for edge detection and compression but did not fully exploit multiresolution properties during rendering, often requiring full reconstruction. The framework systematically explores these properties to enable more efficient and flexible volume rendering. A related multiresolution scheme for out-of-core CT volumes was proposed by Ljung, utilizing GPU raycasting and load-on-demand management. name: Downscaled Grid Map Generation
body: Downscaled Grid Map Generation creates a low-resolution coordinate grid and an index map to map high-resolution coordinates to their corresponding low-resolution locations. It is used in differentiable rendering pipelines to facilitate optimization of shapes from 2D observations by providing a structured mapping between resolution levels. It differs from Mipmap Generation by focusing on coordinate indexing rather than value aggregation, and from VoxelGrid Down Sample by explicitly generating index maps for coordinate transformation rather than just reducing data density. Inputs: Original grid map dimensions (height H, width W). Scale factor s (integer or float). Stride k of the original grid map. Outputs: newgridmap: A meshgrid for the downscaled resolution. indexmap: A map where each element contains the index in the original grid map corresponding to the downscaled coordinate. Data Structures: newgridmap: Tensor of shape (H', W', 2), where H' = \lceil H/s \rceil and W' = \lceil W/s \rceil. indexmap: Tensor of shape (H', W'), containing integer indices. Steps: 1. Calculate the stride k of the original grid map. 2. Compute the new dimensions: H' = \lceil H / s \rceil W' = \lceil W / s \rceil 3. Generate a new meshgrid for the downscaled resolution (H', W'). Let this be G{new}, where each element G{new}[y, x] = (x, y) for y \in [0, H'-1], x \in [0, W'-1]. 4. Scale the new grid map by s \cdot k and shift it: G{scaled}[y, x] = G{new}[y, x] \cdot (s \cdot k) + \frac{(s \cdot k) - 1}{2} 5. Compute the index map by dividing the original grid mesh coordinates by s, adding 1, taking the ceiling, and subtracting 1. Note: The source describes dividing "original grid mesh coordinates" but the context implies using the scaled coordinates or mapping back. Based on the formula structure in the source, the index map I is computed as: I[y, x] = \lceil \frac{G{scaled}[y, x]}{s} \rceil - 1 Correction/Clarification: The source states "dividing the original grid mesh coordinates by scale". Given G{scaled} represents the mapped coordinates, the index is derived from these. The exact formula from the source is: I = \lceil \frac{G{scaled}}{s} \rceil - 1 Where the division and ceiling are element-wise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import math def generatedownscaledgridmap(originalh, originalw, scale, stride): """ Generates a downscaled grid map and an index map. Args: originalh (int): Height of the original grid. originalw (int): Width of the original grid. scale (float): Scale factor for downsampling. stride (float): Stride of the original grid map. Returns: newgridmap (np.ndarray): Downscaled grid map of shape (H', W', 2). indexmap (np.ndarray): Index map of shape (H', W'). """ # Step 2: Compute new dimensions newh = math.ceil(originalh / scale) neww = math.ceil(originalw / scale) # Step 3: Generate new meshgrid for downscaled resolution # meshgrid returns coordinates. We want (x, y) for each pixel. # np.meshgrid with indexing='xy' gives x in rows, y in cols? # Standard meshgrid(x, y) returns X, Y where X varies along columns, Y along rows. # We need a grid of shape (newh, neww, 2). xcoords = np.arange(neww) ycoords = np.arange(newh) xx, yy = np.meshgrid(xcoords, ycoords, indexing='xy') newgridmap = np.stack([xx, yy], axis=-1).astype(np.float32) # Step 4: Scale and shift shift = ((scale stride) - 1) / 2 scaledgrid = newgridmap (scale stride) + shift # Step 5: Compute index map # Divide by scale, add 1, ceiling, subtract 1 # Note: The source says "dividing the original grid mesh coordinates by scale". # In the context of the code snippet, it likely refers to the mapped coordinates # or the original coordinates mapped to the new space. # Based on "Compute the index map by dividing the original grid mesh coordinates by scale", # and the previous step scaling the NEW grid, there is ambiguity. # However, the index map is used to map HIGH to LOW. # If we are generating a map for the LOW resolution to point to HIGH, # we need to know where each LOW pixel comes from in HIGH. # The formula provided: ceil(coord / scale) - 1. # Let's assume the "original grid mesh coordinates" refers to the coordinates # in the original space that correspond to the new grid points. # But the new grid points are in [0, neww-1]. # The scaling step suggests we are creating a coordinate system in the original space. # Let's follow the source literally: "dividing the original grid mesh coordinates by scale". # If "original grid mesh coordinates" means the coordinates of the original grid (0..H-1, 0..W-1), # that doesn't make sense for a new grid. # It likely means: The coordinates in the new grid, scaled back to original space? # Or the scaledgrid from step 4? # Let's look at the shift: ((scale stride) - 1) / 2. This centers the sampling. # The index map is likely: # index = ceil( (scaledgrid / scale)) - 1 ? # Or index = ceil( (newgridmap stride)) - 1 ? # The source says: "Compute the index map by dividing the original grid mesh coordinates by scale, # adding 1, taking the ceiling, and subtracting 1." # This phrasing is tricky. "Original grid mesh coordinates" usually means the input grid. # But we are generating a NEW grid. # Let's assume the source implies: # 1. We have a coordinate system for the new grid. # 2. We map it to the old grid. # 3. We compute the index. # Given the ambiguity, we implement the literal steps described for the index map calculation # assuming "original grid mesh coordinates" refers to the coordinates being processed # (which are the new grid coordinates scaled to the original space). # Re-reading: "Scale the new grid map by scale stride... Compute the index map by dividing # the original grid mesh coordinates by scale..." # It is possible "original grid mesh coordinates" is a typo for "scaled grid coordinates" # or "new grid coordinates". # However, if we divide the NEW grid coordinates (0..W'-1) by scale, we get small numbers. # If we divide the SCALED grid coordinates (which are in original space units) by scale, # we get back to new space units stride. # Let's stick to the most logical interpretation for an index map: # We want to know which original pixel corresponds to the new pixel. # The new pixel at (y, x) corresponds to original pixel at (yscale, xscale). # The source formula: ceil(coord / scale) - 1. # If coord is the original coordinate, this maps high to low. # But we are generating a map FOR the downscaled resolution. # So the index map should contain indices into the ORIGINAL grid. # Therefore, the input to the index calculation should be the coordinates in the ORIGINAL grid. # The "scaledgrid" is in original grid units. # So: index = ceil(scaledgrid / scale) - 1? # No, that would just be ceil(newgrid stride) - 1. # Let's look at the source code context if possible. It's not provided. # We will implement the steps exactly as described in the text, assuming # "original grid mesh coordinates" refers to the coordinates of the grid # that is being indexed (i.e., the new grid, but interpreted in the original space). # Actually, the most standard way to create an index map for downsampling is: # indexy = floor(y scale) # indexx = floor(x scale) # The source uses ceil and -1. # ceil(z) - 1 is equivalent to floor(z - epsilon) or floor(z) if z is not integer? # No. ceil(1.5)-1 = 1. floor(1.5) = 1. # ceil(1.0)-1 = 0. floor(1.0) = 1. # So it handles integer boundaries differently. # We will use the scaledgrid (which is in original space) and divide by scale? # No, the source says "dividing the original grid mesh coordinates by scale". # If we assume "original grid mesh coordinates" means the coordinates of the ORIGINAL grid, # then we are not generating a map for the new grid. # We assume it means "the coordinates of the grid being processed (the new one) # expressed in original units". # Let's try: index = ceil( (newgridmap stride) / scale) - 1 ? # This simplifies to ceil( newgridmap (stride/scale)) - 1. # Given the strict instruction to follow the source: # "Compute the index map by dividing the original grid mesh coordinates by scale..." # We will assume this refers to the scaledgrid from step 4, as that represents # the coordinates in the original space. indexmap = np.ceil(scaledgrid / scale) - 1 indexmap = indexmap.astype(np.int64) # Pitfall check maxindex = np.max(indexmap) totalelements = originalh originalw if maxindex >= totalelements: raise ValueError("Maximum index in flattened index map exceeds number of elements in new grid map.") return newgridmap, indexmap Parameters: scale: Typical values depend on the desired downsampling factor (e.g., 2, 4). stride: Depends on the original grid map's spacing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the maximum index in the flattened index map exceeds the number of elements in the original grid map, a ValueError is raised. Precision issues may arise if scale is not an integer or if stride is very small. Time Complexity: O(H' \cdot W'), where H' and W' are the new dimensions. Memory Complexity: O(H' \cdot W') for the index map and grid map. Strengths: Provides explicit coordinate mapping for differentiable rendering. Limitations: Requires careful handling of boundary conditions and index validation. When to use: When optimizing shapes from 2D observations using differentiable renderers that require coordinate mapping between resolutions. When not to use: For simple visualization or when standard interpolation is sufficient. This method is used in the DIST-Renderer project for optimizing shapes from 2D observations. It is part of a pipeline that uses differentiable rendering to refine 3D shapes. B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, https://github.com/B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Index-Based Upsampling with Recalibration
head: Index-based upsampling, recalibration upsampling
body: Index-Based Upsampling with Recalibration is a technique to upsample low-resolution tensors to high resolution using an index map and a recalibration map, specifically for depth values. It sets itself apart from standard bilinear upsampling by using explicit integer indices to gather low-resolution samples and a separate scaling map to adjust for resolution changes, ensuring that samples from similar depth planes contribute correctly to the final color. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Low-resolution tensor T{low}, indexmap, recalibmap. Output: High-resolution tensor T{high}. Data Structures: indexmap: A tensor of shape (H \times W, 2) containing integer indices mapping high-resolution pixels to low-resolution pixels. recalibmap: A tensor of shape (H \times W) containing scaling factors for recalibration. H, W: Height and width of the high-resolution output. Steps: 1. Gather: For each pixel (i, j) in the high-resolution grid, retrieve the corresponding low-resolution coordinates from indexmap. Let these be (u, v). Gather the value from T{low} at (u, v). 2. Recalibrate: Retrieve the scaling factor s{i,j} from recalibmap at (i, j). 3. Scale: Multiply the gathered value by s{i,j} to produce the high-resolution value. Formula: T{high}[i, j] = T{low}[\text{index\map}[i, j, 0], \text{index\map}[i, j, 1]] \times \text{recalib\map}[i, j] Parameters: Typical values for ratio (resolution scaling) are around 1.5. Thresholds for rendering steps may be set to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise if index mapping is not integer-accurate. Boundary conditions for indexmap must be handled to avoid out-of-bounds access. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def indexbasedupsamplingwithrecalibration(Tlow, indexmap, recalibmap): """ Upsamples low-resolution tensor Tlow to high resolution using indexmap and recalibmap. Args: Tlow: Low-resolution tensor of shape (Hlow, Wlow, C). indexmap: Tensor of shape (Hhigh, Whigh, 2) with integer indices. recalibmap: Tensor of shape (Hhigh, Whigh) with scaling factors. Returns: Thigh: High-resolution tensor of shape (Hhigh, Whigh, C). """ Hhigh, Whigh = recalibmap.shape C = Tlow.shape[2] if len(Tlow.shape) > 2 else 1 # Initialize high-resolution tensor Thigh = torch.zeros((Hhigh, Whigh, C), dtype=Tlow.dtype, device=Tlow.device) # Extract indices uindices = indexmap[:,:, 0].long() vindices = indexmap[:,:, 1].long() # Gather values from low-resolution tensor # Assuming Tlow is 2D or 3D; handling 2D case for simplicity if C=1 if len(Tlow.shape) == 2: gathered = Tlow[uindices, vindices] else: gathered = Tlow[uindices, vindices,:] # Apply recalibration scaling # recalibmap needs to be broadcasted to match gathered shape recalibexpanded = recalibmap.unsqueeze(-1) if len(Tlow.shape) > 2 else recalibmap Thigh = gathered recalibexpanded return Thigh Depth-aware upsampling reduces blue noise and performance costs in volumetric rendering by rendering clouds to a low-resolution RGBA texture and a distance buffer, then upsampling to high resolution using the depth buffer. It sets itself apart from standard bilinear upsampling by weighting the interpolation of low-resolution samples based on the depth difference between the high-resolution fragment and the low-resolution depth values, ensuring that samples from similar depth planes contribute more to the final color. Time Complexity: O(H \times W), where H and W are the high-resolution dimensions, due to the linear scan of the index and recalibration maps. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) for storing the index and recalibration maps. Strengths: Explicit control over sampling locations via indices; recalibration allows for correction of resolution-induced artifacts. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of index and recalibration maps; may introduce aliasing if indices are not carefully chosen. When to use: When explicit control over upsampling is needed, particularly for depth values or when bilinear interpolation is insufficient. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and pre-computation is not feasible, or when smooth interpolation is preferred over explicit indexing. Originating from the DIST-Renderer project, this technique is part of a broader effort to optimize volumetric rendering through multiresolution representations. It builds on the concept of downscaled grid maps and index maps to efficiently upsample data. B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, https://github.com/B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Depth-Aware Upsampling
head: Depth-aware bilinear upsampling, Depth-weighted cloud upsampling
body: Depth-aware upsampling reduces blue noise and performance costs in volumetric rendering by rendering clouds to a low-resolution RGBA texture and a distance buffer, then upsampling to high resolution using the depth buffer. It sets itself apart from standard bilinear upsampling by weighting the interpolation of low-resolution samples based on the depth difference between the high-resolution fragment and the low-resolution depth values, ensuring that samples from similar depth planes contribute more to the final color. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: clouds: A low-resolution RGBA texture containing the pre-rendered cloud color and alpha. dist: A low-resolution single-channel (R) texture containing the depth/distance values corresponding to the clouds texture. depth: The high-resolution depth value of the current fragment being shaded. cloudsubsampling: Integer factor by which the low-resolution texture is smaller than the high-resolution output. overlaywidth, overlayheight: Dimensions of the low-resolution textures. depthsigma: Float parameter controlling the sensitivity of the depth weighting (standard deviation of the Gaussian). mindepthexponent: Float lower bound for clamping Gaussian exponents to prevent numerical underflow. Output: vec4: The high-resolution RGBA color value for the current fragment. Data Structures: clouds: sampler2D, format RGBA. dist: sampler2D, format R (or grayscale). Parameters: MAXEXPONENT: 20.0. Used to clamp the upper bound of Gaussian exponents. depthsigma: Typical values depend on scene scale and noise characteristics; not explicitly given in sources. mindepthexponent: Not explicitly given in sources, but used to clamp negative exponents. Steps: 1. Calculate Low-Resolution Coordinates: Convert the high-resolution fragment coordinates (glFragCoord.xy) to low-resolution space by dividing by cloudsubsampling. point = \frac{gl\FragCoord.xy}{cloud\subsampling} 2. Determine Bilinear Grid: Calculate the integer texel coordinate (texcoord) and the fractional offset (frac) for bilinear interpolation. The offset is centered by subtracting 0.5. texcoord = \lfloor point - 0.5 \rfloor + 0.5 frac = \text{fract}(point - 0.5) Where \lfloor \cdot \rfloor is the floor function and \text{fract}(x) = x - \lfloor x \rfloor. 3. Compute Neighbor Texcoords: Calculate the normalized texture coordinates for the four surrounding low-resolution texels (00, 01, 10, 11). The coordinates are adjusted by the fractional part and normalized by the overlay dimensions. texcoord{00} = \frac{texcoord + (0.0, 0.0)}{(overlay\width, overlay\height)} texcoord{01} = \frac{texcoord + (0.0, 1.0)}{(overlay\width, overlay\height)} texcoord{10} = \frac{texcoord + (1.0, 0.0)}{(overlay\width, overlay\height)} texcoord{11} = \frac{texcoord + (1.0, 1.0)}{(overlay\width, overlay\height)} 4. Sample Low-Resolution Data: Sample the color values from the clouds texture and the depth values from the dist texture at the four neighbor coordinates. value{ij} = \text{texture}(clouds, texcoord{ij}) dist{ij} = \text{texture}(dist, texcoord{ij}).r Where i,j \in \{0,1\}. 5. Calculate Depth-Weighted Exponents: Compute the Gaussian exponent for each neighbor based on the squared difference between the high-resolution depth and the low-resolution depth, normalized by depthsigma. exponent{ij} = -\frac{(depth - dist{ij})^2}{2 \cdot depth\sigma^2} 6. Clamp Exponents: Clamp the exponents to the range [min\depth\exponent, MAX\EXPONENT] to guard against numerical underflows and extreme weights. exponent'{ij} = \text{clamp}(exponent{ij}, min\depth\exponent, 20.0) 7. Compute Weights: Calculate the final weight for each neighbor by multiplying the standard bilinear interpolation factor by the exponential depth weight. weight{00} = (1.0 - frac.x) \cdot (1.0 - frac.y) \cdot \exp(exponent'{00}) weight{01} = frac.x \cdot (1.0 - frac.y) \cdot \exp(exponent'{01}) weight{10} = (1.0 - frac.x) \cdot frac.y \cdot \exp(exponent'{10}) weight{11} = frac.x \cdot frac.y \cdot \exp(exponent'{11}) 8. Return Weighted Average: Compute the final color as the weighted sum of the sampled colors, normalized by the sum of the weights. result = \frac{value{00} \cdot weight{00} + value{01} \cdot weight{01} + value{10} \cdot weight{10} + value{11} \cdot weight{11}}{weight{00} + weight{01} + weight{10} + weight{11}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def depthawareupsample(glfragcoord, cloudssampler, distsampler, cloudsubsampling, overlaywidth, overlayheight, depthsigma, mindepthexponent, currentdepth): """ Performs depth-aware upsampling of a low-res cloud texture to high-res. Args: glfragcoord: (x, y) High-resolution fragment coordinates. cloudssampler: Function to sample low-res RGBA texture. distsampler: Function to sample low-res depth texture. cloudsubsampling: Integer downsampling factor. overlaywidth: Width of low-res textures. overlayheight: Height of low-res textures. depthsigma: Standard deviation for depth weighting Gaussian. mindepthexponent: Lower bound for clamping exponents. currentdepth: Depth value of the current high-res fragment. Returns: vec4: High-resolution RGBA color. """ MAXEXPONENT = 20.0 # 1. Calculate low-res point pointx = glfragcoord[0] / cloudsubsampling pointy = glfragcoord[1] / cloudsubsampling # 2. Determine integer texcoord and fractional part # floor(point - 0.5) + 0.5 centers the grid texcoordx = math.floor(pointx - 0.5) + 0.5 texcoordy = math.floor(pointy - 0.5) + 0.5 fracx = (pointx - 0.5) - math.floor(pointx - 0.5) fracy = (pointy - 0.5) - math.floor(pointy - 0.5) # 3. Compute neighbor texcoords (normalized) # vector01.xx = (0.0, 0.0),.yx = (0.0, 1.0),.xy = (1.0, 0.0),.yy = (1.0, 1.0) texcoord00 = ((texcoordx + 0.0) / overlaywidth, (texcoordy + 0.0) / overlayheight) texcoord01 = ((texcoordx + 0.0) / overlaywidth, (texcoordy + 1.0) / overlayheight) texcoord10 = ((texcoordx + 1.0) / overlaywidth, (texcoordy + 0.0) / overlayheight) texcoord11 = ((texcoordx + 1.0) / overlaywidth, (texcoordy + 1.0) / overlayheight) # 4. Sample low-res data value00 = cloudssampler(texcoord00) # vec4 value01 = cloudssampler(texcoord01) value10 = cloudssampler(texcoord10) value11 = cloudssampler(texcoord11) dist00 = distsampler(texcoord00)[0] # Assuming.r component dist01 = distsampler(texcoord01)[0] dist10 = distsampler(texcoord10)[0] dist11 = distsampler(texcoord11)[0] # 5. Calculate Gaussian exponents denom = 2.0 depthsigma depthsigma exponent00 = -((currentdepth - dist00) 2) / denom exponent01 = -((currentdepth - dist01) 2) / denom exponent10 = -((currentdepth - dist10) 2) / denom exponent11 = -((currentdepth - dist11) 2) / denom # 6. Clamp exponents exponent00 = max(mindepthexponent, min(exponent00, MAXEXPONENT)) exponent01 = max(mindepthexponent, min(exponent01, MAXEXPONENT)) exponent10 = max(mindepthexponent, min(exponent10, MAXEXPONENT)) exponent11 = max(mindepthexponent, min(exponent11, MAXEXPONENT)) # 7. Compute weights # Bilinear factors Depth weights weight00 = (1.0 - fracx) (1.0 - fracy) math.exp(exponent00) weight01 = fracx (1.0 - fracy) math.exp(exponent01) weight10 = (1.0 - fracx) fracy math.exp(exponent10) weight11 = fracx fracy math.exp(exponent11) # 8. Return weighted average totalweight = weight00 + weight01 + weight10 + weight11 if totalweight == 0: # Fallback if all weights are zero (e.g., extreme depth differences) # Return average of neighbors or zero, depending on implementation preference. # Standard bilinear would return average. return (value00 + value01 + value10 + value11) / 4.0 resultr = (value00[0] weight00 + value01[0] weight01 + value10[0] weight10 + value11[0] weight11) / totalweight resultg = (value00[1] weight00 + value01[1] weight01 + value10[1] weight10 + value11[1] weight11) / totalweight resultb = (value00[2] weight00 + value01[2] weight01 + value10[2] weight10 + value11[2] weight11) / totalweight resulta = (value00[3] weight00 + value01[3] weight01 + value10[3] weight10 + value11[3] weight11) / totalweight return (resultr, resultg, resultb, resulta) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Underflow: If depthsigma is very small or depth differences are large, exponent can become very negative, causing exp() to underflow to zero. Clamping to mindepthexponent prevents this. Zero Total Weight: If all weights are zero (e.g., due to aggressive clamping), division by zero occurs. A fallback to simple averaging or zero is required. Boundary Conditions: The calculation assumes texcoord falls within the valid range of the low-res texture. If the high-res fragment is near the edge of the screen, texcoord might point outside the low-res texture bounds. Standard texture sampling behavior (clamp, repeat, or border color) will apply, but this may introduce artifacts at the edges of the cloud volume. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment. It performs a fixed number of texture lookups (8 total: 4 for color, 4 for depth) and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per fragment, plus the storage for the low-resolution clouds and dist textures. Measured Performance: Reduces performance cost compared to rendering clouds at full resolution with dense sampling, while reducing blue noise compared to simple low-resolution rendering. Strengths: Significantly reduces blue noise artifacts compared to naive low-resolution rendering. Avoids the performance penalty of increasing the sampling interval (number of raymarching steps) at high resolution. Simple to implement as a post-process or overlay shader. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the low-resolution depth buffer. If the low-res depth is inaccurate or lacks detail, the upsampling may blur or misplace cloud features. Requires rendering an additional distance buffer. Quality depends heavily on the choice of depthsigma. Too small a sigma makes the upsampling sensitive to depth noise; too large a sigma causes excessive blurring. When to use: When rendering volumetric clouds (or similar translucent volumes) where blue noise is visible at high resolutions, but full-resolution raymarching is too expensive. When not to use: When depth information is unavailable or unreliable, or when the volume has sharp depth discontinuities that cannot be captured by the low-res depth buffer. Depth-aware upsampling for volumetric clouds was introduced by Jan Wedekind in the context of procedural volumetric cloud rendering. It addresses the trade-off between visual quality (blue noise) and performance in real-time cloud rendering. The method builds on standard bilinear downsampling and upsampling techniques, adding a depth-aware weighting mechanism to preserve sharpness and reduce noise. name: Level of Detail for Volumetric Terrain
head: Real-time Volumetric Terrain Rendering LOD
body: This method provides a fast, GPU-friendly level of detail algorithm for the real-time rendering of volumetric terrain using arbitrary volumetric models. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering vast, complex terrain with geometric features impossible to represent with heightmaps, without requiring preprocessing and supporting infinite procedural terrain. It sets itself apart from bottom-up techniques by generating geometry on the fly, avoiding the massive memory and computation costs of full-resolution mesh generation during preprocessing. The algorithm generates a hierarchical mesh structure dynamically. Surface extraction and hierarchy updates are performed in a background thread on the CPU to offload the GPU and facilitate consistent, high frame rates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric terrain defined by a density function f(x, y, z), viewer position, and viewing parameters. Output: A triangle mesh representing the terrain surface at the appropriate level of detail. Data Structures: The volume mesh is organized into hexahedral blocks. Block Lattice Size: A single hexahedral block has a lattice size of 16 \times 16 \times 16. This size provides a balance between adaptivity and performance. Node Structure: A single node in the hierarchy consists of four 16 \times 16 \times 16 blocks. Algorithm Steps: 1. Density Sampling: Sample the density function f(x, y, z) for the active volume blocks. This is the most expensive step, dependent on the complexity of the density function. 2. Surface Extraction: Perform marching cubes on the sampled data to extract the isosurface. 3. Mesh Simplification: Simplify the extracted mesh to reduce triangle count while maintaining visual fidelity. 4. Mesh Smoothing: Apply smoothing to the simplified mesh. 5. Normal Computation: Compute vertex normals for lighting. 6. Hierarchy Update: Update the LOD hierarchy based on viewer distance and movement. 7. Rendering: Send the resulting mesh to the GPU for rendering. Parameters: Block Lattice Size: 16 \times 16 \times 16. Density Function: Arbitrary, evaluated at runtime. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatevolumetricterrainlod(viewerposition, viewervelocity, densityfunction): """ Updates the LOD hierarchy and extracts geometry for volumetric terrain. Runs in a background thread. """ # 1. Determine active blocks based on viewer position and LOD criteria activeblocks = determineactiveblocks(viewerposition, viewervelocity) # 2. Sample density function for active blocks # This step is computationally expensive and depends on densityfunction complexity sampleddata = {} for block in activeblocks: sampleddata[block] = sampledensityfunction(block, densityfunction) # 3. Extract surface using Marching Cubes rawmesh = marchingcubes(sampleddata) # 4. Simplify the mesh simplifiedmesh = simplifymesh(rawmesh) # 5. Smooth the mesh smoothedmesh = smoothmesh(simplifiedmesh) # 6. Compute normals finalmesh = computenormals(smoothedmesh) # 7. Update LOD hierarchy # Note: Delayed updates may occur if density function evaluation is too slow updatelodhierarchy(finalmesh, viewerposition) return finalmesh def sampledensityfunction(block, densityfunction): """ Samples the density function for a 16x16x16 block. """ # Implementation depends on the specific density function # Returns a 3D grid of density values pass def marchingcubes(sampleddata): """ Performs Marching Cubes on the sampled data. """ # Standard Marching Cubes algorithm pass def simplifymesh(mesh): """ Simplifies the mesh geometry. """ # Mesh simplification algorithm (e.g., Quadric Error Metrics) pass def smoothmesh(mesh): """ Applies smoothing to the mesh. """ # Mesh smoothing algorithm pass def computenormals(mesh): """ Computes vertex normals. """ # Compute normals from face normals pass def updatelodhierarchy(mesh, viewerposition): """ Updates the LOD hierarchy based on viewer position. """ # Adjust LOD levels based on distance and movement speed pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping Artifacts: LOD transitions can cause visible popping artifacts. Efficient geomorphing cannot be implemented due to possible topological changes between detail levels. Alpha blending can be used as a solution but reduces rendering performance. Image space blending is a viable alternative commonly used in industry. Delayed Updates: If the density function is complex and time-consuming to evaluate, LOD updates may be delayed, causing the hierarchy to not update rapidly enough for fast viewer movements. Parallel evaluation of the density function can mitigate this. Texturing Limitations: The algorithm does not create a parameterization of the terrain surface consistent across detail levels. This makes unique mapping of high-resolution textures and encoding geometric information in normal maps impossible. Complexity: The LOD algorithm achieves a memory and rendering complexity of O(\log n) with n being the edge length of the domain cube. Performance: Achieved an average refresh rate above 1500 Hz without any culling on a quad-core AMD Phenom II 3.2 GHz processor and NVIDIA GeForce GTX 580 with 1920x1080 resolution. Culling: Simple view frustum culling reduces triangle count by a factor of about 3 to 6 depending on scene and viewing conditions. Additional occlusion culling could further improve performance, especially in caves and deep valleys. Timings: Average timings for surface extraction per single node (four 16 \times 16 \times 16 blocks): density function sampling 1.510 ms (50.2%), marching cubes 0.102 ms (3.3%), mesh simplification 0.868 ms (28.9%), mesh smoothing 0.015 ms (0.4%), normal computation 0.507 ms (16.8%), total 3.002 ms. Strengths: High rendering speed, suitable for demanding real-time applications where terrain rendering consumes a small part of the overall frame time. Spatial coherent layout leads to vertex cache friendly triangulations and good triangle batch sizes. Limitations: No consistent parameterization across detail levels, making advanced texturing difficult. Popping artifacts during LOD transitions. Delayed LOD updates for complex density functions. The method was presented in a paper titled "Level of Detail for Real-Time Volumetric Terrain Rendering". It was implemented in C++ using the DirectX 11 API for rendering. The approach addresses limitations of previous methods, particularly bottom-up techniques that require full-resolution mesh generation during preprocessing, which consume massive memory and computation time, making them impractical for vast terrain models.
