name: Sectioning
head: Section Memory, External FIFO, VolumePro Sectioning
body: Sectioning partitions a volume dataset into smaller segments to constrain the on-chip memory usage of First-In-First-Out (FIFO) buffers within hardware pipelines. It solves the problem of limited on-chip storage for intermediate values required for ray-casting by off-loading these values to external memory between processing sections. Unlike Hardware-Assisted Volume Streaming which relies on hardware buffers for streaming, or Chunk-based spatial partitioning which divides space for load balancing, Sectioning specifically manages the recirculation of data within a single rendering pass to maintain exact numerical precision without approximation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, partitioned into sections along the x-direction. Output: A rendered image, identical to a non-sectioned render, with no visual artifacts at section boundaries. Data Structures: Section Memory: An external memory block acting as a large FIFO. It stores intermediate values (such as accumulated color and opacity, or gradient data) that would normally be passed between pipeline stages. Layout: The memory organization corresponds to the width of a section. In the VolumePro implementation, each section is 32 voxels wide. Content: Intermediate values needed for rendering near the right boundary of a section. Numbered Steps: 1. Partitioning: The volume dataset is partitioned into sections. In the VolumePro implementation, this is done only in the x-direction, with each section being 32 voxels wide. 2. Traversal Order Modification: Voxels are read in slice-by-slice order within a single section. Within slices, voxels are read in beam-by-beam order, but beams span only the width of the current section (32 voxels). 3. Section Processing (Right-Hand Pipeline): The full section is processed front-to-back. Shift registers in the right-hand pipeline are modified to optionally write intermediate values to Section Memory at the end of a section. These values are the ones that would have been passed to the next pipeline stage in a continuous stream. 4. Section Boundary Handling: At the start of a new section, the left-hand pipeline reads values from Section Memory. If not reading from Section Memory (e.g., first section), it accepts values from the right-hand pipeline. Values are passed through multiplexers to the left pipeline. 5. Recirculation: Values are read from Section Memory in the exact same order they were written. This ensures that the left-hand pipeline receives the same data it would have received if the sections were processed as one continuous block. 6. Iteration: The next section is processed, repeating steps 2-5 until the entire volume is rendered. Formulas: Let V be the volume dataset. Let S be the set of sections, where S = \{s1, s2,..., sn\}. Let W be the section width in voxels (W=32 in VolumePro). Let I{right} be the intermediate values generated by the right-hand pipeline. Let I{left} be the intermediate values consumed by the left-hand pipeline. The condition for correctness is: I{left}(si) = I{right}(s{i-1}) for i > 1, where I{right}(s{i-1}) is stored in Section Memory and retrieved as I{left}(si). Parameters: Section Width: 32 voxels (VolumePro specific). Direction: X-direction (VolumePro specific; theoretically possible in y- and/or z-directions). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: No approximation is made; the method guarantees no visual artifacts at section boundaries because the exact same values are written and read. Memory Organization: The section width must align with the underlying memory organization (e.g., 32 voxels for VolumePro). Ordering: The read order from Section Memory must exactly match the write order to ensure correct pipeline state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sectionedvolumerendering(volume, sectionwidth=32): """ Renders a volume using sectioning to manage on-chip FIFO memory. Assumes VolumePro-style architecture with left and right pipelines. """ # Partition volume into sections along x-direction numsections = ceil(volume.width / sectionwidth) # Section Memory acts as an external FIFO sectionmemory = [] for sidx in range(numsections): # Define current section bounds xstart = sidx sectionwidth xend = min((sidx + 1) sectionwidth, volume.width) sectionwidthactual = xend - xstart # Process section front-to-back for z in range(volume.depth): for y in range(volume.height): # Beams span only the width of the section for x in range(xstart, xend): # Ray casting logic for voxel (x, y, z) #... compute sample, gradient, etc.... # Right-hand pipeline generates intermediate values intermediatevalues = rightpipelineprocess(x, y, z, volume) # If at end of section, write to Section Memory if x == xend - 1: sectionmemory.append(intermediatevalues) # After processing all slices/beams in the section, # the left pipeline needs to receive the intermediate values # from the previous section (or initial values for first section) if sidx == 0: # First section: left pipeline gets initial values from right pipeline # (Handled by hardware multiplexers, no external memory read) leftpipelinereceive(initialvalues) else: # Subsequent sections: read from Section Memory # Values are read in the same order they were written previoussectionvalues = sectionmemory.pop(0) leftpipelinereceive(previoussectionvalues) # Continue rendering with updated left pipeline state #... Handles loading volume data into memory; Sectioning operates on already loaded data, partitioning it for processing Link. Uses hardware buffers for streaming; Sectioning uses external memory for FIFO recirculation Link. Determines streaming intervals based on bandwidth; Sectioning determines section boundaries based on memory limits Link. Divides space for parallel processing; Sectioning divides space for memory management within a single pass Link. Distributes work across nodes; Sectioning manages memory within a single node's pipeline Link. Uses MapReduce for parallel rendering; Sectioning is a hardware pipeline optimization Link. Loads bricks from disk; Sectioning manages intermediate values in external memory during rendering Link. Time Complexity: No additional computational complexity; the same values are calculated, just in a different order. Memory Complexity: Reduces on-chip FIFO memory requirements by off-loading intermediate values to external memory. Measured Performance: Implemented in VolumePro with 32-voxel sections. Strengths: Exact numerical precision; no visual artifacts at section boundaries. Limitations: Requires external memory access; limited to x-direction in VolumePro. When to use: When on-chip FIFO memory is insufficient for the full volume width. When not to use: When external memory bandwidth is a bottleneck or when hardware supports sufficient on-chip memory. Sectioning was introduced in the VolumePro real-time ray-casting system. It was developed to address the limitations of semiconductor processes regarding on-chip memory size. The method is detailed in the VolumePro technical report. The VolumePro Real-Time Ray-Casting System, https://www.merl.com/publications/docs/TR99-19.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volume Data Loading and Normalization
head: VolumeHandler
body: This method implements a C++ class for loading 3D and 4D volumetric data from.npy files, normalizing the scalar values, and managing frame indices for time-varying volumes. It differs from sibling methods like the Raw Volume Data Reader and DICOM loader by strictly relying on the NumPy binary format and applying a specific min-subtraction normalization strategy rather than standard min-max scaling to [0, 1]. It solves the problem of ingesting pre-saved NumPy volume arrays into a rendering pipeline while ensuring consistent data types and value ranges. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A file path to a.npy file containing 3D or 4D data. The template type T (e.g., float, uint8t) must match the data stored in the file. Output: A populated VolumeFrames structure containing normalized float data, shape metadata, and min/max values. Data Structures: The method uses the following internal state: VolumeFrames: A std::vector<VolumeData3D>. Each VolumeData3D element contains: Shape: A 3D array of uint32t representing dimensions (X, Y, Z). Data: A std::vector<float> storing the voxel values. MinValue: float, the minimum value in the original data before normalization. MaxValue: float, the maximum value in the original data before normalization. IsTimeVaryingVolume: bool. true if the input is 4D, false otherwise. FrameIndex: int. The current frame index for time-varying volumes. Steps: 1. Validation: Check if the file exists and has the.npy extension. If not, throw a runtimeerror. 2. Reading: Load the data using npy::readnpy<T>. Let the loaded shape be d.shape and data be d.data. 3. Dimensionality Check: Verify d.shape.size() is either 3 or 4. If not, throw a runtimeerror. 4. Processing 3D Volumes (Single Frame): If d.shape.size() == 3: Resize VolumeFrames to size 1. Set Shape to d.shape. Resize Data to size Shape[0] \times Shape[1] \times Shape[2]. Transform d.data to float. Find MinValue = \min(d.data) and MaxValue = \max(d.data). Normalize: For each element v in Data, v{new} = v - MinValue. Set IsTimeVaryingVolume to false. 5. Processing 4D Volumes (Time-Varying): If d.shape.size() == 4: Let N = d.shape[0] (number of frames). Let X = d.shape[1], Y = d.shape[2], Z = d.shape[3]. Resize VolumeFrames to size N. Set IsTimeVaryingVolume to true. For each frame t from 0 to N-1: Extract the sub-array for frame t from d.data. Set Shape to (X, Y, Z). Resize Data for this frame to X \times Y \times Z. Copy frame data and transform to float. Find MinValuet = \min(\text{frame}t) and MaxValuet = \max(\text{frame}t). Set MinValue and MaxValue for this frame. Normalize: For each element v in the frame's Data, v{new} = v - MinValuet. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VolumeData3D: Shape: list[int] # [x, y, z] Data: list[float] MinValue: float MaxValue: float class VolumeLoader: VolumeFrames: list[VolumeData3D] IsTimeVaryingVolume: bool FrameIndex: int def loadandnormalize(self, filepath: str, T: type): # 1. Validation if not filepath.endswith('.npy') or not fileexists(filepath): raise RuntimeError("File must exist and be.npy") # 2. Reading # npy::readnpy<T> returns an object with.shape (list) and.data (list of T) d = readnpy(filepath, T) # 3. Dimensionality Check if len(d.shape) not in (3, 4): raise RuntimeError("Shape dimensionality must be 3 or 4") self.VolumeFrames = [] self.IsTimeVaryingVolume = False if len(d.shape) == 3: # 4. 3D Volume Handling self.VolumeFrames.resize(1) frame = self.VolumeFrames[0] frame.Shape = d.shape size = d.shape[0] d.shape[1] d.shape[2] frame.Data.resize(size) # Transform to float and find min/max floatdata = [float(x) for x in d.data] frame.MinValue = min(floatdata) frame.MaxValue = max(floatdata) # Normalize: subtract MinValue frame.Data = [x - frame.MinValue for x in floatdata] self.IsTimeVaryingVolume = False elif len(d.shape) == 4: # 5. 4D Volume Handling numframes = d.shape[0] x, y, z = d.shape[1], d.shape[2], d.shape[3] self.VolumeFrames.resize(numframes) self.IsTimeVaryingVolume = True for t in range(numframes): frame = self.VolumeFrames[t] frame.Shape = [x, y, z] framesize = x y z frame.Data.resize(framesize) # Extract frame data (assuming d.data is flattened 4D array) # Note: Exact slicing logic depends on npy layout, assumed row-major here startidx = t framesize endidx = startidx + framesize frameraw = d.data[startidx:endidx] floatdata = [float(x) for x in frameraw] frame.MinValue = min(floatdata) frame.MaxValue = max(floatdata) # Normalize frame.Data = [x - frame.MinValue for x in floatdata] self.FrameIndex = 0 Parameters: T: Template type for input data (e.g., float, uint8t). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization Shift: The method subtracts MinValue from all elements. The resulting data range is [0, MaxValue - MinValue]. It does not scale to [0, 1]. Unsupported Formats: Only.npy files are supported. Other formats will trigger an error. Dimensionality: Inputs with dimensions other than 3 or 4 are rejected. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of voxels, as it requires a single pass to read, convert, and find min/max, followed by a pass to normalize. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the float data. The original integer data is converted to float, potentially increasing memory usage if the source was 8-bit or 16-bit. Strengths: Simple implementation for NumPy-based pipelines; handles both static and dynamic volumes uniformly. Limitations: Strict format dependency (.npy only); normalization preserves absolute magnitude differences rather than normalizing to a standard range, which may require downstream adjustment. This method originates from the DDVR project, an unofficial implementation of a volume rendering system. It is designed to bridge NumPy data structures with C++ rendering components. AoGao-Kedoka/DDVR, https://github.com/AoGao-Kedoka/DDVR, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Raw Volume Data Reader
head: BrickDensityRegion, Volume Slice Loading, RawReader
body: The Raw Volume Data Reader is a specialized loader for ingesting raw binary volume data files directly into memory. It solves the problem of converting high-precision raw sensor data (e.g., from CT scanners) into a usable format for volume rendering or sparse voxel construction. It differs from generic loaders by embedding specific quantization logic (scaling and thresholding) directly into the loading pipeline rather than treating data as opaque bytes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A raw binary file containing unsigned short (16-bit) values. Output: A contiguous memory block of unsigned short values representing the 3D volume, optionally normalized and clamped. Data Structures: The core data structure RawReader (or BrickDensityRegion) contains: mdata: A pointer to unsigned short (unsigned short) pointing to a contiguous memory block of size Z \times Y \times X \times \text{sizeof(unsigned short)}. Parameters: isomin, isomax: Thresholds for iso-clamping. Values outside this range are set to 0. mdensitymult: A multiplier for density calculation. max: The maximum value used for normalization scaling. volres: The target volume resolution (X, Y, Z). fileres: The source file resolution (X, Z). multiply: Scaling factor calculated as volres.x() / fileres.x(). Steps: 1. Open the file in binary read mode with the ate flag to determine file size. 2. Calculate expected file size: Size = Z \times Y \times X \times \text{sizeof(unsigned short)}. 3. Assert that the actual file size matches the expected size. 4. Allocate memory for the data buffer using malloc. 5. Seek to the beginning of the file and read the entire content into the allocated memory. 6. Close the file. 7. Iterate through the data to apply normalization and clamping: Find min and max values in the buffer to determine normalization range. For each element, apply iso-clamping: if value < iso\min or value > iso\max, set to 0. Calculate density value: val = tmp \times m\density\mult \times multiply / max. Calculate 3D voxel coordinates: x = i \times multiply y = vol\res.y() - y\val - 1 z = j \times multiply where i iterates from 0 to fileres.x() and j iterates from 0 to fileres.z(). 8. Store the processed values in mdata. 9. Free allocated memory in the destructor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def loadrawvolume(filename, volres, fileres, isomin, isomax, mdensitymult, maxval): # Step 1-3: Open file and verify size filesize = getfilesize(filename) expectedsize = volres.z volres.y volres.x 2 # 2 bytes for unsigned short if filesize != expectedsize: raise ValueError("File size mismatch") # Step 4-6: Read file into memory mdata = malloc(expectedsize) with open(filename, 'rb') as f: f.seek(0) data = f.read(expectedsize) # Convert bytes to unsigned short array buffer = unpackunsignedshorts(data) # Step 7: Process data multiply = volres.x / fileres.x processeddata = [] # Find min/max if not provided minval = min(buffer) maxvalactual = max(buffer) for j in range(fileres.z): for i in range(fileres.x): tmp = buffer[j fileres.x + i] # Iso-clamping if tmp < isomin or tmp > isomax: tmp = 0 # Density calculation val = tmp mdensitymult multiply / maxval # Coordinate calculation (for mapping if needed) x = i multiply y = volres.y - (j multiply) - 1 # Note: yval logic from source z = j multiply processeddata.append(val) # Store in mdata structure mdata = processeddata return mdata def freerawvolume(mdata): free(mdata) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: File size mismatch: The method asserts that the file size matches the expected volume size. If the file is corrupted or incomplete, this will fail. Precision: The method uses unsigned short (16-bit) for storage. If the source data has higher precision, it may be truncated during the initial read or normalization. Boundary conditions: The iso-clamping sets values outside the range to 0, which may result in loss of data if the range is not chosen carefully. Defines the procedure for ingesting raw binary volume data, applying domain-specific quantization to reduce precision, and preparing the data for GPU transfer. It differs by embedding specific quantization logic (scaling and thresholding) directly into the loading pipeline. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels, due to single-pass reading and processing. Memory Complexity: O(N), storing all voxels in memory as unsigned short. Strengths: Simple, fast, and direct loading of raw binary data without complex format parsing. Limitations: Lacks support for various medical imaging formats (e.g., DICOM, NIfTI) and does not handle coordinate system alignment or resampling. When to use: When working with raw binary volume data files and needing a quick, simple loading mechanism. When not to use: When dealing with standard medical imaging formats or requiring advanced features like resampling or coordinate alignment. The Raw Volume Data Reader is part of the VolumeLoader framework, which supports various medical imaging formats. It is used in contexts where raw binary data from CT scanners or specific model formats needs to be quickly ingested into memory for further processing or rendering. upupming/marching-cubes, https://github.com/upupming/marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel data loading and quantization
head: 16-bit voxel quantization, Stanford model loader, Volume Data Loading and Storage
body: This method defines the procedure for ingesting raw binary volume data (typically from CT scanners or specific model formats) into memory, applying domain-specific quantization to reduce precision, and preparing the data for GPU transfer or further processing. It solves the problem of converting high-precision raw sensor data (e.g., 12-bit Hounsfield units) into a format suitable for real-time raycasting or sparse voxel octree construction, often involving thresholding and bit-depth reduction. It differs from generic loaders by embedding specific quantization logic (scaling and thresholding) directly into the loading pipeline rather than treating data as opaque bytes. The method consists of two primary variants found in the literature: a specific implementation for the Stanford Bunny/CT data (S1, S2) and a general VolPack interface (S3), plus a specific 16-to-8-bit conversion for VDB data (S4). Input: Raw binary files (e.g.,.zaz slices) or a memory pointer to a voxel array. Data types are typically 16-bit integers (uint16t or short). Output: A 3D array or GPU buffer containing quantized values (8-bit or reduced 16-bit), ready for raycasting or sparse storage. 1. Raw Slice Array: A 2D array of uint16t representing a single slice (e.g., 512x512). 2. Volume Array: A 3D array or linear buffer. For the Stanford Bunny, dimensions are 512 \times 512 \times 360. 3. VolPack Voxel Structure: Defined by strides. The caller allocates memory; VolPack only stores pointers and stride values. 4. VDB Header/Data: Header: 16-bit resolution at offsets 0, 2, 4; 32-bit node count at offset 12. Coordinates: Int32 array starting at offset 32. Node Data: Uint16 array following coordinates. 1. Read Slices: Load each binary slice file into a 2D uint16t array. The file extension is typically.zaz. 2. Assemble Volume: Stack slices along the Z-axis. The value at position (x, y, z) is accessed as data[y][z depth + x]. 3. Quantize and Threshold: Apply the following transformation to each voxel value v{in}: v{out} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } v{in} < 160 \\ \lfloor \frac{v{in}}{4096} \rfloor \cdot 16 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Threshold: Values below 160 (approx. 0xa0) are set to 0. Quantization: The value is divided by 4096 (equivalent to right-shifting by 12 bits, retaining the top 4 bits of the 12-bit data), then multiplied by 16 (left-shifting by 4 bits) to align with 8-bit or 16-bit integer ranges. Note: S1 describes this as value /= 256 16; value = 16, which mathematically simplifies to dividing by 256 then multiplying by 16, but the formula provided in S1 explicitly uses 4096 (256 \times 16) as the divisor. The formula \lfloor v{in} / 4096 \rfloor \cdot 16 preserves the most significant 4 bits of the 12-bit Hounsfield data. 4. Transfer: Copy the resulting 3D array to GPU memory via OpenCL or similar API. 1. Allocate Memory: Allocate a contiguous block of memory for the voxel data. 2. Define Strides: Calculate byte strides for X, Y, and Z dimensions. xstride: Bytes between adjacent voxels along X. ystride: Bytes between adjacent voxels along Y. zstride: Bytes between adjacent voxels along Z. 3. Register Data: Call vpSetRawVoxels(vpc, voxels, size, xstride, ystride, zstride). voxels: Pointer to the data. size: Total size in bytes. Strides determine access patterns. Z-major order (xstride < ystride < zstride) is faster for some routines but not required. 4. Memory Management: The caller is responsible for freeing the voxels memory. VolPack does not free it upon context destruction. 1. Parse Header: Read resolution from offsets 0, 2, 4 as Uint16. Round each dimension to the nearest multiple of 8: R' = 8 \cdot \lceil R / 8 \rceil. This aligns with 8x8x8 voxel tiles. Read node count from offset 12 as Uint32. 2. Parse Coordinates: Read coordinates from offset 32 as Int32Array. Cast to Uint16Array for storage. Pitfall: If coordinate values exceed 65535, they wrap around or clamp, corrupting sparse coordinate data. 3. Parse Node Data: Read node data following coordinates as Uint16Array. 4. Compress Data: Allocate a Uint8Array (compressedData) of the same length as nodeData. 5. Quantize Loop: For each index i: compressedData[i] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } nodeData[i] == 0 \\ \lfloor 255 \cdot \frac{nodeData[i]}{65535} \rfloor & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This maps the full 16-bit range [0, 65535] to 8-bit [0, 255]. Threshold: 160 (for S1/S2). Quantization Divisor: 4096 (for S1/S2). Tile Alignment: 8 (for S4). File Extension: ".zaz" (for S1). Coordinate Overflow: In Variant C, casting 32-bit coordinates to 16-bit storage causes data corruption for large volumes. Memory Leaks: In Variant B, failing to free the voxel array manually leads to leaks, as VolPack does not manage this memory. Precision Loss: Variant A discards the lower 8 bits of the 12-bit Hounsfield data. This is acceptable for visualization but loses fine-grained density information. Parses HDF5 JSON (H5J) file attributes to extract volume size, voxel size, and channel specifications. It applies word alignment to volume dimensions. Unlike the raw binary loaders, this method handles structured metadata extraction from a hierarchical format. A procedure to specify volume data array, size, and strides for each dimension in bytes using vpSetRawVoxels. It differs from direct array loading by using a library context and stride-based access. It is chosen when using the VolPack library for rendering or processing.(Parent) Converts 16-bit VDB data to 8-bit format for GPU consumption. It rounds resolution to multiples of 8 and compresses coordinates and density. It is chosen when preparing sparse VDB data for WebGL or other 8-bit constrained renderers.(Parent) Time Complexity: Linear O(N) with respect to the number of voxels for loading and quantization. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the raw data. Variant B (VolPack) requires additional memory for the library context but shares the voxel data pointer. Performance: Z-major storage (Variant B) offers faster access for certain VolPack routines. Quantization (Variant A) reduces memory bandwidth requirements by lowering precision. Limitations: Variant A is specific to 12-bit Hounsfield data. Variant C is limited by 16-bit coordinate storage. The method originates from implementations of volume raycasting, specifically for the Stanford Bunny dataset and CT scans. The Stanford Bunny loader (S1, S2) was developed to visualize 12-bit Hounsfield data from CT scanners using OpenCL. VolPack (S3) is a standard library for volume rendering, providing a generic interface for raw voxel data. The VDB conversion (S4) is part of modern web-based volume rendering pipelines (e.g., volumetrics) to optimize data transfer to GPUs. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volume Raycasting mit OpenCL, https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01317v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) VolPack User's Guide, http://www-graphics.stanford.edu/software/volpack/vpuserguide.html, fetched 2026-10-28 al-ro/volumetrics, https://github.com/al-ro/volumetrics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: HDF5 JSON (H5J) File Parsing
head: H5J Attribute Parsing
body: Parses HDF5 JSON (H5J) file attributes to extract volume dimensions, voxel spacing, and channel specifications, applying word alignment to spatial dimensions. It differs from raw binary readers by interpreting the JSON metadata structure to construct the volSize, voxSize, and chanSpecs objects required for subsequent voxel loading and quantization. Inputs: A parsed JSON object representing the HDF5 file's attribute hierarchy (typically accessible via a library like web-h5j-loader or standard JSON parsing of the.h5j metadata). Outputs: An object containing: volSize: [number, number, number] representing width, height, and frames. voxSize: [number, number, number] representing voxel dimensions in physical units. chanSpecs: Array<{name: string, content: string}> mapping channel names to their data types. Data Structures: volSize: Array of 3 integers. voxSize: Array of 3 numbers (floats). chanSpecs: Array of objects with name (string) and content (string) fields. Steps: 1. Initialize volSize and voxSize arrays to [0, 0, 0]. 2. Check if the attrs object contains the key 'imagesize'. If present, assign attrs.imagesize to volSize. 3. Check if the attrs object contains the key 'voxelsize'. If present, assign attrs.voxelsize to voxSize. 4. Extract attrs.channels. If attrs.channels contains 'width', set volSize[0] to attrs.channels.width[0]. If attrs.channels contains 'height', set volSize[1] to attrs.channels.height[0]. If attrs.channels contains 'frames', set volSize[2] to attrs.channels.frames[0]. Note: If imagesize was present in step 2, these channel-specific overrides may replace or supplement the initial volSize. The sources imply a fallback or override mechanism where channel dimensions take precedence if explicitly defined in the channels object. 5. Align volSize[0] (width) and volSize[1] (height) to 8-byte word boundaries. Formula: alignedSize = Math.ceil(size / 8) 8. Apply this to volSize[0] and volSize[1]. 6. Construct chanSpecs from attrs.channels.names and attrs.channels.contenttypes. Iterate through the indices of the names array. For each index i, create an object { name: attrs.channels.names[i], content: attrs.channels.contenttypes[i] }. Append to chanSpecs. 7. Return the object { volSize, voxSize, chanSpecs }. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parseh5jattributes(attrs): # Step 1: Initialize volsize = [0, 0, 0] voxsize = [0, 0, 0] # Step 2: Check imagesize if 'imagesize' in attrs: volsize = list(attrs['imagesize']) # Step 3: Check voxelsize if 'voxelsize' in attrs: voxsize = list(attrs['voxelsize']) # Step 4: Extract channel dimensions if 'channels' in attrs: channels = attrs['channels'] if 'width' in channels: volsize[0] = channels['width'][0] if 'height' in channels: volsize[1] = channels['height'][0] if 'frames' in channels: volsize[2] = channels['frames'][0] # Step 5: Word alignment for width and height # Align to 8-byte boundaries volsize[0] = math.ceil(volsize[0] / 8) 8 volsize[1] = math.ceil(volsize[1] / 8) 8 # Step 6: Construct channel specs chanspecs = [] if 'channels' in attrs: channels = attrs['channels'] names = channels.get('names', []) contenttypes = channels.get('contenttypes', []) # Assuming names and contenttypes are aligned by index for i in range(len(names)): name = names[i] content = contenttypes[i] if i < len(contenttypes) else "unknown" chanspecs.append({ "name": name, "content": content }) # Step 7: Return result return { "volSize": volsize, "voxSize": voxsize, "chanSpecs": chanspecs } Parameters: Word alignment size: 8 bytes. Edge Cases: Missing imagesize or voxelsize: The arrays remain [0, 0, 0] unless populated by channel-specific attributes. Missing channels object: chanSpecs will be an empty array. Mismatched lengths in names and contenttypes: The pseudocode guards against index out-of-bounds by checking i < len(contenttypes). Loading H5J format volumes, which may contain HDF5 containers with 12-bit HEVC compressed 3D data, often requires the web-h5j-loader library. This library relies on multi-threaded ffmpeg.wasm via SharedArrayBuffer for efficient decoding. To enable SharedArrayBuffer, the server must serve the H5J files with the headers Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp. If these headers are missing, the browser will throw an exception: 'SharedArrayBuffer is not defined'. This is a security restriction; SharedArrayBuffer usage is prevented unless cross-origin isolation is explicitly enabled to mitigate side-channel attacks like Spectre. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of attributes and channels. Parsing JSON is generally fast, dominated by the structure traversal. Memory Complexity: Minimal, proportional to the size of the metadata object. Strengths: Provides structured access to volume metadata without loading the actual voxel data. Handles word alignment automatically, which is critical for memory alignment in subsequent GPU/CPU processing. Limitations: Does not load the voxel data itself. Requires the JSON metadata to be fully available. The alignment step may introduce padding, meaning the logical volume size may differ from the physical data size if not accounted for in the loader. When to use: When initializing a volume viewer or loader, to determine memory allocation and channel configuration before loading raw voxel data. When not to use: When only raw binary data is available without JSON metadata, or when the metadata structure differs from the Janelia standard. Originating from the Janelia Research Campus's web-based volume viewer tools, this parsing method is part of the web-vol-viewer ecosystem. It is designed to handle the specific metadata conventions used in Janelia's HDF5 JSON (H5J) format, which is commonly used for storing large-scale biological imaging data. The method ensures that volume dimensions are correctly aligned for efficient memory access, a common requirement in high-performance volume rendering. name: DICOM Volume Loading and Coordinate Reconstruction
head: DICOM File Loading and Stacking, DICOM Loader, DICOM Volume Reconstruction Loading & Density Conversion, DICOM to Density Conversion, Volume DICOM Loading and Rescaling
body: This method loads a 3D volumetric dataset from a series of DICOM image files, reconstructs the physical voxel grid by resolving coordinate system conventions, and converts raw pixel values into physical density. It specifically addresses the discrepancy between DICOM's pixel-center coordinate convention and the corner-point convention required by downstream volume rendering engines, while handling the non-cubic nature of medical voxels. It differs from generic volume loaders by explicitly managing DICOM-specific metadata (Rescale Slope/Intercept, Pixel Spacing, Slice Thickness) and orientation flips (rot90) necessary for correct anatomical alignment. Inputs: A directory of DICOM files (typically.dcm or.IMA), sorted by filename. Outputs: A 3D density array (float), a physical bounding box (min/max points), and voxel dimensions (scale). 1. DICOM Metadata Object: Extracted per file. rows: Integer (image height in pixels). cols: Integer (image width in pixels). pixelSpacing: Array of 2 floats [spacingy, spacingx] in mm. sliceThickness: Float in mm. bitsAllocated: Integer (usually 16). pixelRepresentation: Integer (0 for unsigned, 1 for signed). rescaleSlope: Float (default 1.0). rescaleIntercept: Float (default -1000.0). dataCollectionCenterPatient: Array of 3 floats [x, y, z] in mm. reconstructionTargetCenterPatient: Array of 3 floats [x, y, z] in mm. 2. Volume Data Buffer: Type: Uint16Array or Float32Array depending on intermediate processing. Size: rows cols numslices. 3. Physical Bounds: minpt: Array of 3 floats [x, y, z]. maxpt: Array of 3 floats [x, y, z]. 1. File Selection and Sorting: Scan the input directory for DICOM files. Filter by suffix (e.g.,.IMA or.dcm). Sort files alphabetically by filename to ensure correct slice ordering. 2. Metadata Extraction and Validation: For each file, decode the DICOM header. Extract rows, cols, pixelSpacing, sliceThickness, bitsAllocated, pixelRepresentation, rescaleSlope, rescaleIntercept, dataCollectionCenterPatient, and reconstructionTargetCenterPatient. Calculate bytesPerVoxel = bitsAllocated / 8. Pitfall: If bytesPerVoxel != 2, throw an error. Unsupported byte depths are not handled. 3. Pixel Data Loading and Orientation Correction: Read raw pixel data as unsigned short ('H'). Reshape raw data to [cols, rows] in C-order. Apply rotation to correct DICOM orientation: dataarray = np.rot90(dataarray, k=-1) (equivalent to 270-degree counter-clockwise or -90-degree rotation). Note: This rotation accounts for the standard DICOM display convention where the image is flipped horizontally relative to the patient's left-right axis. 4. Hounsfield Unit (HU) to Density Conversion: Convert raw pixel values to Hounsfield Units: \text{HU} = \text{RescaleSlope} \cdot \text{data\array} + \text{RescaleIntercept} Convert HU to normalized density (where water = 1.0): \text{density} = \frac{\text{HU} + 1000}{1000} \text{density} = \frac{\text{RescaleSlope} \cdot \text{data\array} + \text{RescaleIntercept} + 1000}{1000}. Note: Some implementations store intermediate values as signed integers by adding 2^{15} (32768) to handle negative HU values before conversion. 5. Volume Stacking: Initialize a 3D buffer volumeData of size rows cols numslices. Iterate through sorted slices i from 0 to N-1: Calculate sliceOffset = i (rows cols). Copy converted density values into volumeData[sliceOffset: sliceOffset + (rowscols)]. 6. Coordinate Reconstruction and Bounding Box Calculation: Voxel Size: \text{voxel\size} = [\text{pixelSpacing}[0], \text{pixelSpacing}[1], \text{sliceThickness}]. Note: pixelSpacing[0] corresponds to Y (rows) and pixelSpacing[1] to X (cols) in DICOM, but after rotation, the array dimensions map to physical axes. The scale vector is typically [pixelSpacing[0], pixelSpacing[1], sliceThickness]. Slice Distance Calculation: If numslices > 1: \text{slice\distance} = | \text{DataCollectionCenterPatient}{\text{slice1}}[2] - \text{DataCollectionCenterPatient}{\text{slice0}}[2] | If numslices == 1: \text{slice\distance} = \text{sliceThickness}. Center Point Calculation: Use ReconstructionTargetCenterPatient or DataCollectionCenterPatient of the first slice as the reference center midpt. Bounds Calculation (Corner-Point Convention): Volume rendering engines often require corner-point coordinates, whereas DICOM stores pixel centers. Calculate minpt and maxpt based on voxelsize and shape ([rows, cols, numslices]). Z-Axis Bounds: Compute raw bounds using the Z-component of DataCollectionCenterPatient for the first and last slices. Adjust for corner-point convention by subtracting/adding half the slicedistance. Pitfall: If the calculation of Z-bounds fails (e.g., min > max due to sorting or convention errors), reverse the order: use the last slice for minpt[2] and the first for maxpt[2], and log an error. Y-Axis (Axis 1) Convention: DICOM Y-axis convention is often reversed relative to standard Cartesian coordinates used in rendering. Swap minpt[1] and maxpt[1] to correct this. X-Axis (Axis 0): Typically follows standard left-to-right or right-to-left depending on the specific DICOM orientation tags (PatientLeft/Right). The rotation in Step 3 handles the in-plane flip, but the bounding box must align with the final array layout. 7. Final Volume Layout: The resulting volume data is often transposed or rearranged to match the renderer's expected memory layout (e.g., from [rows, cols, slices] to [slices, rows, cols] or similar, depending on the specific engine's VolumeLoader interface). The physical size in millimeters is stored separately from the texture dimensions to allow for anisotropic scaling during rendering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import os import glob def loaddicomvolume(folderpath, suffix='.dcm'): """ Loads a DICOM series from a folder, converts to density, and computes physical bounds. """ # 1. File Selection and Sorting files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(folderpath, f'{suffix}'))) if not files: raise ValueError("No DICOM files found.") numslices = len(files) slicesdata = [] metadatalist = [] # 2. Metadata Extraction and Pixel Loading for f in files: # Assume bacaDicom or pydicom loads the dataset ds = bacaDicom(f) rows = ds.rows cols = ds.cols pixelspacing = ds.pixelspacing # [spacingy, spacingx] slicethickness = ds.slicethickness rescaleslope = ds.rescaleslope rescaleintercept = ds.rescaleintercept datacollectioncenter = ds.datacollectioncenterpatient reconstructioncenter = ds.reconstructiontargetcenterpatient # Extract raw pixel data rawpixels = ds.pixelarray # Validate bytes per voxel bitsallocated = ds.bitsallocated bytespervoxel = bitsallocated // 8 if bytespervoxel != 2: raise Error(f"Unsupported bytes per voxel: {bytespervoxel}") # Reshape to [cols, rows] C-order dataarray = rawpixels.reshape((cols, rows)) # Rotate -90 degrees to correct orientation dataarray = np.rot90(dataarray, k=-1) slicesdata.append(dataarray) metadatalist.append({ 'pixelspacing': pixelspacing, 'slicethickness': slicethickness, 'datacollectioncenter': datacollectioncenter, 'reconstructioncenter': reconstructioncenter }) # 3. HU to Density Conversion densities = [] for i, dataarray in enumerate(slicesdata): # HU = Slope Pixel + Intercept huvalues = rescaleslope dataarray + rescaleintercept # Density = (HU + 1000) / 1000 densityslice = (huvalues + 1000) / 1000.0 densities.append(densityslice) # Stack into 3D volume [rows, cols, numslices] volumedata = np.stack(densities, axis=-1) # 4. Coordinate Reconstruction firstmeta = metadatalist[0] lastmeta = metadatalist[-1] # Voxel Size [x, y, z] in mm # Note: pixelspacing[0] is Y (rows), pixelspacing[1] is X (cols) # After rot90, the array dimensions are [rows, cols]. # We map physical dimensions to array dimensions. voxelsize = [firstmeta['pixelspacing'][1], firstmeta['pixelspacing'][0], firstmeta['slicethickness']] shape = volumedata.shape # (rows, cols, numslices) # Slice Distance if numslices > 1: z1 = metadatalist[0]['datacollectioncenter'][2] z2 = metadatalist[1]['datacollectioncenter'][2] slicedistance = abs(z2 - z1) else: slicedistance = firstmeta['slicethickness'] # Center Point midpt = firstmeta['reconstructioncenter'] # or datacollectioncenter # Calculate Bounds # Physical extent of the volume extentx = shape[0] voxelsize[0] # rows pixelspacingy extenty = shape[1] voxelsize[1] # cols pixelspacingx extentz = shape[2] slicedistance # numslices slicethickness # Initial min/max based on center and extent minpt = [midpt[0] - extentx/2, midpt[1] - extenty/2, midpt[2] - extentz/2] maxpt = [midpt[0] + extentx/2, midpt[1] + extenty/2, midpt[2] + extentz/2] # Adjust Z for corner-point convention using actual slice centers # DICOM stores center. Corner is center - halfthickness. # First slice center is z1. First corner is z1 - slicedistance/2. # Last slice center is zlast. Last corner is zlast + slicedistance/2. try: zfirstcenter = metadatalist[0]['datacollectioncenter'][2] zlastcenter = metadatalist[-1]['datacollectioncenter'][2] minpt[2] = zfirstcenter - slicedistance / 2 maxpt[2] = zlastcenter + slicedistance / 2 except Exception: # Fallback if calculation fails minpt[2], maxpt[2] = maxpt[2], minpt[2] print("Error: Z-axis bounds calculation failed, reversed min/max.") # Adjust Y-axis convention (swap min/max) minpt[1], maxpt[1] = maxpt[1], minpt[1] return volumedata, minpt, maxpt, voxelsize This variant prepares the loaded volume for GPU rendering by quantizing the continuous density values into a discrete window range (defined by lower and upper Hounsfield unit thresholds) and integer-downsampling the texture if any axis exceeds 256 voxels. It stores the physical size of the volume in millimeters separately from the texture dimensions to preserve anisotropic scaling information during the downsampling process. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R \cdot C), where N is the number of slices, and R, C are rows and columns. The dominant cost is reading and decoding DICOM headers and pixel data. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot R \cdot C) for the volume data buffer. Additional memory is required for DICOM header parsing. Performance: Loading speed depends heavily on I/O throughput and the efficiency of the DICOM parsing library (bacaDicom or similar). Conversion to density is a fast element-wise operation. Strengths: Handles the complex coordinate transformations required for medical imaging (corner-point vs. center-point, axis flips). Correctly maps HU to physical density. Limitations: Assumes all slices have the same dimensions and orientation. Does not handle missing slices or irregular spacing automatically without explicit slicedistance calculation. Unsupported bit depths (e.g., 8-bit or 32-bit) are rejected. When to use: When loading CT or MRI series for volume rendering where anatomical accuracy and correct physical scaling are critical. When not to use: For non-medical volumetric data, or when real-time streaming of irregularly spaced slices is required without pre-processing. This method originates from implementations in medical imaging visualization libraries, specifically those integrating DICOM loading with WebGL/WebGPU volume rendering engines. It addresses the specific challenges of rendering DICOM series in web-based environments, where standard image viewers often fail to represent the 3D nature of the data correctly (e.g., treating slices as cubes). The approach is documented in unofficial repositories such as Panacea (for the texture preparation and rendering pipeline), DGR (for the DICOM loading and gradient-based processing), and ossium (for the WebGPU-based DICOM loader and coordinate handling). feat(body-exposure): render a DICOM series in 3D, not a description of one, https://github.com/rizkyazhar486/Panacea/pull/1585, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) wskingdom/DGR, https://github.com/wskingdom/DGR, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) fraserlove/ossium, https://github.com/fraserlove/ossium, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: VTK Volume Loading & Normalization
head: VTK ASCII/Binary parser, VTK File Loader, VTK Structured Points Reader, VTK volume reader
body: This method parses VTK Structured Points files, extracts voxel data, and normalizes the scalar values to an 8-bit unsigned integer range [0, 255]. It solves the problem of converting arbitrary-precision medical or scientific volume data into a standardized format suitable for GPU-based raycasting or texture upload. It is distinguished from generic loaders by its specific reliance on the VTK Structured Points header format and its mandatory min-max normalization step, unlike Raw Volume Data Reader which assumes raw binary continuity, or DICOM Volume Loading and Coordinate Reconstruction which handles multi-frame DICOM series. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A file path to a VTK Structured Points file (ASCII or Binary). Output: A normalized std::vector<unsigned char> containing voxel data, and metadata (origin, spacing, dimensions). Data Structures: msize: std::vector<int> or similar, storing dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz). morigin: std::vector<double> or similar, storing (Ox, Oy, Oz). mspacing: std::vector<double> or similar, storing (Sx, Sy, Sz). imagedata: std::vector<unsigned char>, storing the final normalized 8-bit voxels. range: std::pair<double, double>, storing (min, max) of the original data. Steps: 1. Header Validation: Read the first line of the file. Verify it starts with "# vtk". If not, raise a VTKReadError. 2. Header Parsing: Read the first 10 lines of the file into a std::vector<std::string>. Identify the data format by searching for substrings "BINARY" or "ASCII" in the header lines. Parse the DIMENSIONS line using sscanf (or equivalent string parsing) to extract width, height, and depth into msize. Parse the ORIGIN line to extract Ox, Oy, Oz into morigin. Parse the SPACING line to extract Sx, Sy, Sz into mspacing. Identify the scalar data type from the SCALARS line (e.g., unsignedchar, float, unsignedshort). 3. Data Reading: Calculate total element count: N = Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Allocate a temporary buffer of type T (the parsed scalar type) of size N. If Binary: Read N \times \text{sizeof}(T) bytes from the file into the buffer. Check endianness. If the host is little-endian and the file is big-endian (or vice versa, though VTK binary is typically native or specified), swap byte order for each element if necessary. The source notes handling for "little endian host" swapping. If ASCII: Read N elements of type T sequentially from the text stream into the buffer. 4. Range Calculation: Iterate over the loaded buffer of type T. Compute min = \min(p[i]) and max = \max(p[i]) for all i \in [0, N-1]. Store in range = {min, max}. 5. Normalization and Casting: Allocate imagedata of size N. For each voxel i: \text{normalized}[i] = \text{static\cast<unsigned char>}\left( 255 \times \frac{p[i] - min}{max - min} \right) Store result in imagedata[i]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def loadandnormalizevtk(filepath): with open(filepath, 'r') as f: lines = f.readlines() # 1. Validate Magic Number if not lines[0].strip().startswith("# vtk"): raise VTKReadError("Not a valid VTK file.") # 2. Parse Header headertext = "".join(lines[:10]) # Read first 10 lines isbinary = "BINARY" in headertext isascii = "ASCII" in headertext # Parse DIMENSIONS dimsline = [l for l in lines if l.startswith("DIMENSIONS")][0] dims = list(map(int, dimsline.split()[1:4])) Dx, Dy, Dz = dims N = Dx Dy Dz # Parse ORIGIN originline = [l for l in lines if l.startswith("ORIGIN")][0] origin = list(map(float, originline.split()[1:4])) # Parse SPACING spacingline = [l for l in lines if l.startswith("SPACING")][0] spacing = list(map(float, spacingline.split()[1:4])) # Determine Data Type (Simplified: assume float for this example, # in practice parse SCALARS line to get T) # Note: The source uses a template readdata<T>. # We assume T is determined from the file header. T = float # 3. Read Data databuffer = [0.0] N if isbinary: # Read binary data # In a real implementation, open file in 'rb' mode # Read N sizeof(T) bytes # Handle endianness swap if host is little endian and file is big endian pass # Implementation depends on binary read specifics elif isascii: # Read ASCII data # Skip header lines, read N floats pass # 4. Compute Range minval = min(databuffer) maxval = max(databuffer) # 5. Normalize normalizeddata = [] rangespan = maxval - minval if rangespan == 0: # Avoid division by zero; fill with 0 or 128 depending on convention normalizeddata = [0] N else: for val in databuffer: normalizedval = 255 (val - minval) / rangespan normalizeddata.append(int(normalizedval)) return normalizeddata, origin, spacing, dims Parameters: T: Template type for input data (e.g., unsigned short, float). headerlinecount: Fixed at 10 lines for header parsing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Endianness: Binary VTK files may have different endianness than the host. The method must detect this and swap bytes for elements where sizeof(T) > 1 if the host is little-endian. Zero Range: If max == min, division by zero occurs in normalization. The source does not explicitly define the fallback, but standard practice is to clamp to 0 or 128. Invalid Header: Missing # vtk magic number or malformed dimensions/origin lines will cause parsing errors. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of voxels. The dominant cost is reading the data and iterating once to compute min/max, then iterating again to normalize. Memory Complexity: O(N). Requires storage for the raw data buffer (type T) and the normalized output buffer (type unsigned char). Performance: Normalization to 8-bit is fast but requires two passes over the data (one for min/max, one for scaling). This is slower than loading pre-normalized data but necessary for unknown input ranges. Strengths: Handles both ASCII and Binary VTK formats; robust header parsing; automatic normalization ensures consistent visualization across different data scales. Limitations: Only supports Structured Points datasets; does not handle unstructured grids or other VTK formats; normalization loses precision if the original data has a very large dynamic range relative to 8-bit resolution. This method is derived from the VTKVolume class in the open-source project "volume-raycasting" by M. Pilia. It implements a simplified VTK Structured Points reader tailored for GPU raycasting applications, where normalized 8-bit textures are often preferred for simplicity and compatibility with standard OpenGL texture units. The approach mirrors the VTK library's vtkStructuredPointsReader but is implemented from scratch to minimize dependencies. name: Volume Loading and Preprocessing
head: CT Volume Loading
body: This method handles the ingestion of volumetric data from various medical imaging formats (such as DICOM) and raw binary files, performing essential normalization, coordinate system alignment, and memory layout preparation for downstream rendering. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing on the complete pipeline from file I/O to GPU-ready tensor preparation, including specific affine matrix transformations for medical coordinate systems (RAS to IJK) and intensity scaling for Hounsfield Units (HU). Unlike Raw Volume Data Reader which assumes a fixed binary layout, or DICOM Volume Loading and Coordinate Reconstruction which focuses on geometry extraction for projection data, this method prepares the final 3D volume tensor for direct rendering. Inputs: Source files (DICOM series, raw binary slices, or SciData files), configuration parameters (spacing, intensity ranges, thresholds). Outputs: A normalized, contiguous volume tensor (typically floating-point or unsigned 8-bit integer) aligned to a specific coordinate system, ready for GPU upload. 1. Volume Tensor: A 3D array of voxels. In MONAI-based workflows, this is a PyTorch tensor with shape (1, C, D, H, W) after batch expansion. In brick-based workflows, data is stored in a BrickGrid structure indexed by (x, y, z) brick coordinates. 2. Affine Matrix: A 4x4 matrix representing the transformation from voxel indices (IJK) to world coordinates (RAS). 3. Slice List: An array of slice objects containing intensity metadata and file paths, sorted by spatial position. DICOM: Scan the directory for files with extension.IMA (or standard DICOM extensions). For each file, extract metadata including LargestImagePixelValue, SmallestImagePixelValue, and the IJK-to-RAS affine matrix. Raw/SciData: Parse the file header to determine resolution and location bounds. Apply one or more pre-processing methods to convert raw values to a standard range (typically [0, 1] or [0, 255]): Scale: Divide each value v by a user-defined constant C: v' = \frac{v}{C} ScaleToMax: Divide each value by the approximate maximum value M of the channel, determined automatically from the lowest resolution representation: v' = \frac{v}{M} LogTransform: Apply the common logarithm: v' = \log{10}(v) Thresholding: Apply user-defined thresholds min and max (in range [0, 1]). Values outside [min \times 255, max \times 255] are set to zero. This removes noise or irrelevant background values. Extract the IJK-to-RAS affine matrix A{ijk \to ras} from the volume metadata. Compute the inverse matrix A{ras \to ijk} = A{ijk \to ras}^{-1} for use in rendering shaders. For CT data, apply Hounsfield Unit (HU) calibration if raw values are not already in HU. If the source voxel spacing differs from the target spacing, resample the volume. Spacing Parameter: Define target voxel spacing in mm, e.g., [2.5, 2.5, 3.0]. Use interpolation (e.g., linear or nearest neighbor) to map source voxels to the target grid. Clip intensity values to a specified range, e.g., [-3024, 3024] for HU. Scale the clipped values to the target range, e.g., [0, 1]: v{final} = \frac{v{clipped} - v{min}}{v{max} - v{min}} Ensure the data type is suitable for the renderer (e.g., float32 for MONAI, uint8 for brick-based systems). Batch Expansion: Add a batch dimension if required by the rendering framework: V{batch} = V.unsqueeze(0) Device Transfer: Move the volume tensor to the GPU (CUDA). Brick Loading (Alternative): For out-of-core rendering, load data into a BrickGrid. Iterate over the Y-axis from 0 to \lfloor vol\res.y() \rfloor, computing offsets and loading each slice via loadVolSlice. Check index bounds before setting brick data. If a brick contains only zero values after pre-processing, transmit a special EMPTY value to optimize transfer. Unverified code. ScaleIntensityRange: Clipping and scaling range, e.g., [-3024, 3024] to [0, 1]. Thresholds: User-defined min and max in [0, 1] for filtering. isomin, isomax: Thresholds for CT data loading in brick-based systems, defaulting to 0 and USHRTMAX. mdensitymult: Multiplier applied to density values in BrickDensityRegion. It includes strict index bounds checking to prevent out-of-bounds access. name: DICOM CT Projection Loading and Geometry Extraction
head: CT Projection Geometry Extraction & Coordinate Conversion
body: This method loads raw CT projection data from a directory of DICOM files, extracts scanner geometry parameters, applies Hounsfield Unit (HU) calibration, and constructs a ConeBeamGeometry object suitable for tomographic reconstruction. It specifically addresses the challenge of interpreting non-standard or vendor-specific DICOM metadata (such as angle definitions and flying focal spot offsets) to correctly map 2D detector coordinates to 3D ray paths. It differs from standard CT loading by explicitly handling cylindrical-to-rectangular coordinate conversion for the ray transform and correcting for pixel-center vs. pixel-corner detector geometry. Inputs: A directory path containing.dcm files. indices: Optional advanced indexing (slice or list) to load specific projection angles. interp: Interpolation method string (default 'linear') used for the ray transform. Outputs: dataarray: A 3D NumPy array of shape [numprojections, detectorcolumns, detectorrows] with dtype=float32, containing calibrated projection values. angles: A 1D NumPy array of shape [numprojections] containing the corrected source angles in radians. geometry: A ConeBeamGeometry object (from odl.tomo) containing the source, detector, and ray configuration. 1. DICOM Dataset Object: Standard pydicom Dataset containing tags such as PixelData, RescaleSlope, RescaleIntercept, HUCalibrationFactor, DetectorFocalCenterRadialDistance, DetectorCentralElement, DetectorSpacing, and angular position tags. 2. Projection Array: float32 array, shape [N, C, R] where N is the number of projections, C is detector columns, R is detector rows. 3. Geometry Object: Contains srcradius, detradius, detectorshape, detectorspacing, angles, and detectorbounds. 1. File Discovery and Sorting: List all.dcm files in the input directory. Sort them to ensure consistent angular ordering. If indices are provided, filter the file list accordingly. 2. Metadata Extraction: For each DICOM file, extract the following tags: Detector dimensions: DetectorRows, DetectorCols (or inferred from PixelData shape). Calibration: RescaleSlope (m), RescaleIntercept (b), HUCalibrationFactor (H). Geometry: DetectorSpacing (pitch/spacing), DetectorFocalCenterRadialDistance (source-to-detector center distance component), DetectorCentralElement (center offset). Angular Position: The raw angle tag provided by the scanner. 3. Data Loading and Reshaping: Read PixelData as uint16. Reshape to [rows, cols] in Fortran order (column-major). Transpose the array to [cols, rows] to align with standard image coordinate systems where the first axis is horizontal (u) and the second is vertical (v). 4. HU Calibration: Apply the linear calibration to convert raw pixel values to Hounsfield Units. For each projection P{raw}: P = \frac{(P{raw} \cdot m + b)}{H} where m is RescaleSlope, b is RescaleIntercept, and H is HUCalibrationFactor. Store the result in dataarray. 5. Angle Extraction and Correction: Extract raw angles from the DICOM metadata. Apply unwrapping to handle discontinuities at \pm \pi: angles = np.unwrap(angles). Apply a global offset correction: angles = -angles - np.pi. This corrects for the specific angle definition used by the scanner. 6. Detector Geometry Calculation: Compute pixel size from DetectorSpacing. Calculate detector bounds in physical units. The method corrects for the difference between pixel centers and corners. Let S be the detector shape [cols, rows] and P be the pixel size. Let C{center} be DetectorCentralElement. Minimum corner (minp): minp = -(C{center} - 0.5) \cdot P Maximum corner (maxp): maxp = minp + S \cdot P These bounds define the physical extent of the detector plane. 7. Source and Detector Radii: Extract srcradius from DetectorFocalCenterRadialDistance. Compute detradius using a constant radial distance parameter (often derived from scanner specs or metadata if available, otherwise assumed constant) minus srcradius: det\radius = ConstantRadialDistance - src\radius The total source-to-detector distance is d = src\radius + det\radius. 8. Pitch Calculation (if missing): If axial position metadata is present but pitch is not explicitly defined, compute it manually: pitch = \frac{\Delta axial\pos}{(\theta{max} - \theta{min}) / (2\pi)} where \Delta axial\pos is the total axial travel and \theta{max/min} are the min/max angles. 9. Flying Focal Spot Correction: Extract source shifts for partial flying focal spot corrections. Apply mean offsets to the angles and detector bounds as first-order corrections. Note that this is a simplified handling; full dynamic correction may require more complex modeling. 10. Coordinate Conversion for Ray Transform: The ray transform (e.g., in ODL/TIGRE) often expects rectangular coordinates (u, v), but the geometry is defined in cylindrical coordinates relative to the rotation axis (up, vp). Convert the detector coordinates: u = d \cdot \arctan\left(\frac{up}{d}\right) v = \frac{d}{\sqrt{d^2 + up^2}} \cdot vp where d = src\radius + det\radius, up is the vertical detector coordinate, and vp is the horizontal detector coordinate. 11. Geometry Assembly: Create an odl.tomo.ConeBeamGeometry object using the computed srcradius, detradius, detectorshape, detectorspacing, detectorbounds, and angles. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import pydicom import os from odl.tomo import ConeBeamGeometry def loaddicomprojectionsandgeometry(folderpath, indices=None): """ Load CT projections from DICOM files and extract geometry. """ # 1. List and sort files dcmfiles = sorted([f for f in os.listdir(folderpath) if f.endswith('.dcm')]) if indices is not None: dcmfiles = [dcmfiles[i] for i in indices] numprojections = len(dcmfiles) if numprojections == 0: raise ValueError("No DICOM files found.") # 2. Read first file to determine shape and extract static geometry ds0 = pydicom.dcmread(os.path.join(folderpath, dcmfiles[0])) pixeldata = ds0.PixelData # Reshape to [rows, cols] in Fortran order, then transpose to [cols, rows] rows = ds0.Rows cols = ds0.Columns projraw = np.frombuffer(pixeldata, dtype=np.uint16).reshape((rows, cols), order='F').T # Extract calibration factors m = getattr(ds0, 'RescaleSlope', 1.0) b = getattr(ds0, 'RescaleIntercept', 0.0) H = getattr(ds0, 'HUCalibrationFactor', 1.0) # Extract geometry parameters srcradius = ds0.DetectorFocalCenterRadialDistance # Assuming ConstantRadialDistance is a known constant or derived from metadata # In many implementations, this is a fixed scanner parameter. # If not available, it must be provided externally. Here we assume it's available. # Note: The source notes imply 'ConstantRadialDistance' is used. # We will assume a variable 'constantradialdistance' is passed or known. # For this implementation, we assume it is a global constant or extracted similarly. # Let's assume it's extracted from the first dataset if present, otherwise a constant. if hasattr(ds0, 'ConstantRadialDistance'): constantradialdistance = ds0.ConstantRadialDistance else: # Fallback: If not in metadata, this value is scanner-specific and must be provided. # Common values might be derived from Source-to-Isocenter + Isocenter-to-Detector. constantradialdistance = srcradius + 540.0 # Example placeholder, not from source. detradius = constantradialdistance - srcradius d = srcradius + detradius # Detector spacing and central element detspacing = ds0.DetectorSpacing # Usually a tuple or scalar if isinstance(detspacing, (list, tuple)): pixelsizeu, pixelsizev = detspacing else: pixelsizeu = pixelsizev = detspacing centerelement = ds0.DetectorCentralElement # 3. Initialize arrays dataarray = np.zeros((numprojections, cols, rows), dtype=np.float32) angles = np.zeros(numprojections) # 4. Process each file for i, fname in enumerate(dcmfiles): ds = pydicom.dcmread(os.path.join(folderpath, fname)) # Read and reshape pixel data rawdata = np.frombuffer(ds.PixelData, dtype=np.uint16).reshape((rows, cols), order='F').T # Apply HU calibration: P = (raw m + b) / H calibrateddata = (rawdata.astype(np.float32) m + b) / H dataarray[i] = calibrateddata # Extract and correct angle rawangle = ds.AngularPosition # Tag name may vary; assuming standard angles[i] = rawangle # 5. Angle unwrapping and offset angles = np.unwrap(angles) angles = -angles - np.pi # 6. Compute detector bounds # minp = -(centerelement - 0.5) pixelsize # maxp = minp + shape pixelsize # Note: centerelement might be a vector or scalar. Assuming scalar for central element offset. # If it's a vector, apply per axis. if isinstance(centerelement, (list, tuple)): ceu, cev = centerelement else: ceu = cev = centerelement minpu = -(ceu - 0.5) pixelsizeu maxpu = minpu + cols pixelsizeu minpv = -(cev - 0.5) pixelsizev maxpv = minpv + rows pixelsizev detectorbounds = np.array([[minpu, maxpu], [minpv, maxpv]]) # 7. Flying focal spot correction (First-order mean offset) # Specific implementation depends on how source shifts are stored. # Assuming mean offsets are applied to angles and detector bounds. # This step is simplified as per notes: "Only mean offsets are applied". # We assume these offsets are extracted and applied here. # For now, we leave bounds and angles as computed, noting the correction step. # 8. Create Geometry # ODL ConeBeamGeometry expects: # - srcradius # - detradius # - detectorshape (cols, rows) # - detectorspacing (pixelsizeu, pixelsizev) # - angles # - detectorbounds (optional, or derived from spacing/shape) # Note: ODL's ConeBeamGeometry usually takes detectorshape and spacing. # The bounds calculation is used to define the detector plane extent. geometry = ConeBeamGeometry( srcradius=srcradius, detradius=detradius, detectorshape=(cols, rows), detectorspacing=(pixelsizeu, pixelsizev), angles=angles) return dataarray, angles, geometry indices: Optional. Slice or list of integers to select specific projections. Default is None (all). interp: String. Interpolation method for the ray transform. Default 'linear'. Angle Definition: DICOM angles often use a different reference frame or direction than expected by reconstruction libraries. The unwrapping and -pi offset are critical. Flying Focal Spot: Full correction is complex. This method applies only first-order mean offsets, which may introduce artifacts if the focal spot shift is significant or non-linear. Pixel Center vs. Corner: Detector bounds must be calculated from pixel centers to corners to avoid misalignment in the ray transform. Using pixel centers directly as bounds leads to incorrect ray origins. Missing Metadata: If HUCalibrationFactor is missing or 1, calibration is skipped. If ConstantRadialDistance is not in metadata, it must be provided externally. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of DICOM files N. Reading and calibrating each file is O(C \cdot R), where C and R are detector dimensions. Total time is O(N \cdot C \cdot R). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot C \cdot R) for the dataarray and O(N) for the angles array. The geometry object is O(1) relative to N. Performance: Depends heavily on I/O speed for reading DICOM files. NumPy operations are vectorized and efficient. Strengths: Handles non-standard DICOM metadata, applies HU calibration, and correctly maps detector coordinates for cone-beam geometry. Limitations: Simplified flying focal spot correction. Requires knowledge of ConstantRadialDistance if not in metadata. Assumes consistent detector geometry across all projections. This method is part of the DGR (Differentiable Gaussian Rasterizer) project for CT reconstruction, specifically designed to load projection data from the Mayo Clinic dataset. It addresses the specific geometry and metadata quirks of the CT scanners used in that dataset, enabling accurate forward projection and reconstruction using libraries like ODL and TIGRE. wskingdom/DGR, https://github.com/wskingdom/DGR, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: SOG Volume Reader
head: Recursive SOG Loader, Spherical Octree Grid Reader
body: The SOG Volume Reader is a recursive algorithm that loads a hierarchical volumetric format (SOG) into a dense 3D grid, utilizing internal, empty, leaf, and pseudo-leaf node types to efficiently store and retrieve data. It differs from standard raw readers by parsing a binary header and recursively traversing an octree structure to populate the output array, allowing for sparse or compressed representations within the SOG format. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary file in SOG format. Output: A 3D Volume array of dimensions (sx+1) \times (sy+1) \times (sz+1), where sx, sy, sz are read from the header. The array is filled with voxel values. Data Structures: Header: A single integer sx representing the base dimension. The volume is cubic with sy = sx and sz = sx. Node Types: Defined by a char type read from the file: 0: Internal node. 1: Empty node. 2: Leaf node. 3: Pseudo-leaf node. Volume Interface: setDataAt(int x, int y, int z, float val): Sets the voxel value at coordinates (x, y, z). Parameters: off[3]: The 3D offset of the current node's top-left corner in the global grid. len: The side length of the current node's sub-volume. It halves at each recursion level (nlen = len / 2). sg: A signed char encoding the state for empty or leaf nodes. writeData: A boolean flag. If false, data writing is skipped during pseudo-leaf traversal. Spacing: Hardcoded to 1.0 for x, y, and z axes. Algorithm Steps: 1. Open the file in binary mode. 2. Read the header integer sx. 3. Set sy = sx and sz = sx. 4. Allocate a Volume array of size (sx+1, sy+1, sz+1). 5. Call the recursive function readSOG(fin, vol, {0, 0, 0}, sx). 6. Inside readSOG(fin, vol, off, len, writeData = true): a. Read type (char) from the file. b. If type == 0 (Internal): i. Calculate nlen = len / 2. ii. Loop i, j, k from 0 to 1: 1. Compute noff[0] = off[0] + i nlen, noff[1] = off[1] + j nlen, noff[2] = off[2] + k nlen. 2. Recursively call readSOG(fin, vol, noff, nlen, writeData). c. If type == 1 (Empty): i. Read sg (char). ii. If writeData is true: 1. Loop i, j, k from 0 to len (Note: Source code implies iteration over the sub-volume, but the loop bound in the source snippet for empty nodes is len, which may cover the entire sub-block depending on implementation specifics. The source explicitly states loop i,j,k from 0 to len). 2. Call vol->setDataAt(off[0]+i, off[1]+j, off[2]+k, -sg). d. If type == 2 (Leaf): i. Read sg (char). ii. Read coord[3] (float array). iii. If writeData is true: 1. Initialize bit counter t = 0. 2. Loop i, j, k from 0 to 1: 1. Compute noff[0] = off[0] + i, noff[1] = off[1] + j, noff[2] = off[2] + k. 2. Set vol->setDataAt(noff[0], noff[1], noff[2], -((sg >> t) & 1)). 3. Increment t. e. If type == 3 (Pseudo-leaf): i. Read sg (char). ii. Read coord[3] (float array). iii. Loop i, j, k from 0 to 1: 1. Compute noff[0] = off[0] + i nlen, noff[1] = off[1] + j nlen, noff[2] = off[2] + k nlen. 2. Recursively call readSOG(fin, vol, noff, nlen, false). f. If type is not 0-3, handle error (e.g., print "Wrong! Type: %d"). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def readsog(fin, vol, off, length, writedata=True): """ Recursively reads an SOG node.:param fin: File object, current position is at the node type byte.:param vol: Volume object with method setDataAt(x, y, z, val).:param off: Tuple (x, y, z) offset of the current node's top-left corner.:param length: Side length of the current node's sub-volume.:param writedata: Boolean flag to skip data writing for pseudo-leaves. """ # Read node type typebyte = fin.read(1) if not typebyte: raise EOFError("Unexpected end of file") nodetype = typebyte[0] if nodetype == 0: # Internal node nlen = length // 2 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): noff = (off[0] + i nlen, off[1] + j nlen, off[2] + k nlen) readsog(fin, vol, noff, nlen, writedata) elif nodetype == 1: # Empty node sgbyte = fin.read(1) if not sgbyte: raise EOFError("Unexpected end of file") sg = sgbyte[0] if writedata: # Note: Source specifies loop from 0 to len. # Assuming this fills the sub-volume defined by 'length'. for i in range(length): for j in range(length): for k in range(length): vol.setdataat(off[0] + i, off[1] + j, off[2] + k, -sg) elif nodetype == 2: # Leaf node sgbyte = fin.read(1) if not sgbyte: raise EOFError("Unexpected end of file") sg = sgbyte[0] # Read 3 floats for coordinates coord = [] for in range(3): coordbytes = fin.read(4) if not coordbytes: raise EOFError("Unexpected end of file") coord.append(struct.unpack('f', coordbytes)[0]) if writedata: t = 0 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): noff = (off[0] + i, off[1] + j, off[2] + k) # Extract bit t from sg, negate it val = -((sg >> t) & 1) vol.setdataat(noff[0], noff[1], noff[2], val) t += 1 elif nodetype == 3: # Pseudo-leaf node sgbyte = fin.read(1) if not sgbyte: raise EOFError("Unexpected end of file") sg = sgbyte[0] # Read 3 floats for coordinates coord = [] for in range(3): coordbytes = fin.read(4) if not coordbytes: raise EOFError("Unexpected end of file") coord.append(struct.unpack('f', coordbytes)[0]) nlen = length // 2 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): noff = (off[0] + i nlen, off[1] + j nlen, off[2] + k nlen) # Recurse without writing data readsog(fin, vol, noff, nlen, False) else: raise ValueError(f"Wrong! Type: {nodetype}") def loadsog(filename): import struct with open(filename, 'rb') as fin: # Read header sxbytes = fin.read(4) if not sxbytes: raise EOFError("Empty file") sx = struct.unpack('i', sxbytes)[0] sy = sx sz = sx # Allocate volume (size sx+1, sy+1, sz+1) # Note: Implementation of Volume class is assumed to exist externally vol = Volume(sx + 1, sy + 1, sz + 1) # Start recursive read readsog(fin, vol, (0, 0, 0), sx) return vol Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The coordinates in leaf and pseudo-leaf nodes are stored as float. The voxel values are derived from bit manipulation of a char, resulting in binary values (0 or 1) negated. Boundaries: The volume array is allocated with size sx+1. The offsets and loops must respect this boundary. Degenerate Input: If the file ends prematurely, an EOF error should be raised. Invalid node types trigger an error. Empty Node Loop: The source specifies looping 0 to len for empty nodes. This behavior fills the sub-volume. If len is large, this is computationally expensive compared to internal nodes. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of voxels in the output grid, as every voxel is eventually visited and set. However, the traversal overhead depends on the tree depth and branching factor. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output volume array. The recursion depth is O(\log2(sx)). Strengths: Efficiently handles hierarchical data; supports sparse representations via empty and pseudo-leaf nodes. Limitations: Requires the entire output grid to be allocated in memory. The recursive nature may cause stack overflow for very deep trees if not optimized. When to use: When loading data specifically in the SOG format. Not suitable for other formats. The SOG Volume Reader is part of the dual contouring library by Tao Ju. It was developed to support the loading of volumetric data for surface reconstruction algorithms, specifically dual contouring. The format and reader are associated with Tao Ju's work on implicit modeling and surface reconstruction. jbayardo/tao-ju-dual-contouring, https://github.com/jbayardo/tao-ju-dual-contouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChessQian/DualContouring, https://github.com/ChessQian/DualContouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hardware-Assisted Volume Streaming
head: HAVS (Hardware-Assisted Volume Streaming), HAVS2, HAVS6
body: Hardware-Assisted Volume Streaming (HAVS) is an irregular volume rendering algorithm that streams volume data to perform rendering, solving the visibility sorting problem for unstructured grids by combining object-space and image-space processing. It performs more accurate visibility sorting compared to centroid sort methods like HAPT, while avoiding the high memory overhead of storing the entire volume on the GPU. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unstructured grid data (e.g., tetrahedral meshes), camera parameters, transfer functions. Output: Rendered image. Data Structures: The method relies on streaming primitives (tetrahedra) rather than storing the whole volume in GPU memory. Specific data structure layouts (fields, sizes, bit packing) are Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Object-Space Partial Sort: The CPU performs a partial sort of the primitives (tetrahedra) to reduce the sorting burden on the GPU. 2. Hardware-Assisted Sorting: The GPU completes the sorting and compositing via a fixed-depth k-buffer. This allows for incremental sorting of the fragment stream. 3. Rendering: The sorted fragments are composited to produce the final image. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Variants include HAVS2 and HAVS6. Typical values for parameters are Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues in sorting may arise if the k-buffer depth is insufficient for the scene complexity. Boundary conditions for streaming chunks are Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def havsrender(scene, camera): # 1.
