name: Hardware Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS)
body: Hardware Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS) is a volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids that combines object-space and image-space processing to handle arbitrary nonconvex meshes with low memory overhead. It solves the visibility sorting problem for unstructured data by using the CPU to perform a partial sort of primitives and the GPU to complete the sorting and compositing via a fixed-depth k-buffer. Unlike HAPT, which relies on centroid sorting, HAVS provides more accurate visibility sorting by incrementally sorting the fragment stream on the GPU [Parent]. It is distinct from pure object-space methods like ZSWEEP, which suffer from lower sorting efficiency and higher GPU burden. HAVS operates in two phases: object-space partial sorting on the CPU and image-space complete sorting/compositing on the GPU. The method relies exclusively on face information rather than explicit cell topology, requiring no topological information and resulting in very low memory overhead. Input: Unstructured mesh (e.g., tetrahedral cells) with scalar values at vertices; viewing parameters (MVP matrix, ModelView matrix); transfer function (3D pre-integrated table). Output: Composited color and opacity image in the framebuffer. k-buffer: A buffer of length k associated with each pixel. It stores k fragments. Each fragment contains a scalar value v and the distance d from the eye (viewport). In the reference implementation, k=6, storing 6 fragments plus the current incoming fragment for comparison. Textures: Tex 0: Framebuffer (2D RGBA, 16/32-bit float). Tex 1, 2, 3: k-buffer entries. Each texture stores 2 entries (scalar and distance). Tex 4: 3D pre-integrated transfer function (RGBA, 8/16-bit int). Parameters: mvp[4]: Model-View-Projection matrix (4x4 floats). mv[4]: ModelView matrix (4x4 floats). sz: Scale and bias parameters \{1/pw, 1/ph, (1-1/z{size})/max\len, 1/(2 \cdot z{size})\} for texture coordinate normalization. e: Eye position vector. 1. Mark vertices as internal or boundary to handle mesh boundaries correctly. 2. Compute the centroid for each face of the unstructured mesh (e.g., tetrahedra). 3. Sort the faces based on their centroids using a floating-point radix sort (LSD radix sort combined with counting sort). To sort floating-point coordinates, convert them to 32-bit unsigned integers using the bitwise formula: f = f \times (-(f>>31) | 0x80000000) where f is the float, >> is bitwise right shift, and | is bitwise OR. Divide the resulting integers into four 8-bit blocks and use counting sort for each block. 4. Send the sorted faces to the GPU for rasterization. The GPU rasterizes the sorted faces. For each fragment generated, the following fragment program steps are executed: 1. Transformations: Transform vertex to clip coordinates: oPos = MVP \times iPos. Transform vertex to eye coordinates: oTex1 = MV \times iPos. Pass scalar data value: oTex0 = iTex0. 2. Framebuffer Lookup: Compute texture coordinates from window position to avoid perspective interpolation errors: t = p \times sz. Lookup current framebuffer color/opacity: c0 = \text{Tex2D}(\text{Tex0}, t). 3. Early Termination: If framebuffer opacity c0.w \ge 0.99, kill the fragment. 4. Load k-buffer: Load existing k-buffer entries from textures into temporaries a1 through a6. Compute the current fragment's distance to the eye: a0.y = \text{distance}(eye, \text{fragment}) and scalar a0.x = v.x. 5. Find Nearest Fragment (r0): Use a sorting network to find the fragment with the minimum distance among the current fragment (a0) and the 6 k-buffer entries (a1 \dots a6). Example logic for comparing two entries x and y with distances x.y, y.y: python diff = x.y - y.y minfrag = (diff < 0) ? x: y maxfrag = (diff < 0) ? y: x Iteratively compare r0 with a1 \dots a6 to find the global minimum r0 and store the rest in r1 \dots r6. 6. Find Second Nearest Fragment (r7): Find the minimum distance among the remaining fragments r1 \dots r6 using the same sorting network logic. The result is r7. 7. Transfer Function Lookup: Set up coordinates for the 3D pre-integrated table: Front scalar: t.x = r0.x Back scalar: t.y = r7.x Distance: t.z = (r7.y - r0.y) \times sz.z + sz.w. Lookup color/opacity: c = \text{Tex3D}(\text{Tex4}, t). 8. Nullify Invalid Entry: If the winning fragment's scalar value r0.x < 0, nullify the color/opacity c. 9. Composite: Perform front-to-back blending with the framebuffer: result.color[0] = c \times (1 - c0.w) + c0. 10. Write Back k-buffer: Write the remaining k fragments (excluding the two used for compositing) back to the output buffers. In the reference implementation, entries r1, r3, r5 are written to result.color[1..3] after reordering. Out-of-Order Fragments: If fragments are highly out of order, the k-buffer (which only considers k fragments) may produce incorrect rendering results because it cannot resolve visibility beyond its depth. Perspective Interpolation: Texture coordinates for framebuffer lookup must be computed from the window position in the fragment shader, not from interpolated values, to avoid errors. Sorting Depth Trade-off: The depth of the fragment sorting network can be varied. Increasing the depth allows the use of a less accurate object-space sorting algorithm, shifting work from CPU to GPU. An algorithm for dynamic LOD that builds on HAVS, separating boundary and internal faces, sorting internal faces by importance, and dynamically adjusting the number of faces drawn based on frame rate. An optimization of HAVS that keeps the k-buffer sorted in ascending order of fragment distance to decrease comparison time in the fragment-level sorting process. Complexity: Object-space sorting complexity is O(n+k), where n is the number of primitives and k is the k-buffer size. The image-space comparison cost per pixel j with sj fragments is N1 = \sum{j=1}^{m \times n} (\sum{l=2}^k (2l-3) + (2k-1)(sj - k)). Performance: Tested on an ATI Radeon 9800 with a 512x512 viewport and 128^3 transfer function. With k=2, the GPU portion achieves 9.71 fps (F117 dataset) to 2.07 fps (Spx2 dataset). With k=6, performance drops to 4.42 fps (F117) to 1.70 fps (Spx2) due to increased sorting comparisons. Total time (CPU+GPU, k=2) ranges from 148ms (F117) to 773ms (Fighter). With early ray termination and high opacity, over 6 million cells/sec were achieved on the Fighter dataset. Strengths: Handles arbitrary nonconvex meshes; low memory overhead (no topological info); maximum data size bounded by main memory, not texture memory; simple implementation (<200 lines of rendering code). Limitations: Rendering accuracy depends on k; small k reduces precision for highly out-of-order fragments; performance decreases with larger k due to sorting network depth. When to use: Interactive visualization of large unstructured volumetric datasets where dynamic LOD or transfer function changes are needed. HAVS was introduced by Steven Callahan, Milan Ikits, Joao Comba, and Claudio Silva in their 2005 thesis "The K-Buffer and Its Applications to Volume Rendering". It was developed to address the limitations of previous unstructured grid rendering methods, offering a hybrid CPU/GPU approach that is simpler and more efficient than pure object-space methods like ZSWEEP. The method is particularly noted for its simplicity and adaptability to dynamic LOD and isosurface extraction. name: HAVS with Dynamic LOD
head: Hardware-Assisted Visibility Sorting with Dynamic Level of Detail
body: This method extends Hardware-Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS) by dynamically adjusting the number of internal mesh faces rendered to maintain a target frame rate during interactive exploration. It separates boundary and internal faces, sorts internal faces by importance, and selectively discards less important faces to reduce rasterization load. Unlike Optimized HAVS (Sorted k-buffer), which optimizes the sorting mechanism, this approach focuses on adaptive sampling of the geometry itself to balance interactivity and visual quality. Inputs: A tetrahedral mesh (or similar cell-based volume data). A target frame rate (typically 10 fps). A pre-integrated lookup table (LUT) for standard resolution. Outputs: A rendered image with opacity and color. A dynamic count of internal faces |I| to be rasterized. Data Structures: 1. Boundary Face List: Faces on the exterior of the mesh. 2. Internal Face List: Faces shared between adjacent cells, sorted by importance (most to least). 3. k-Buffer: A fixed-size buffer per pixel storing the k fragments closest to the viewpoint. 4. Primary LUT: 3D texture mapping front scalar, back scalar, and distance to pre-integrated color/opacity. Valid for intervals \le max edge length. 5. Secondary LUT: Scaled 3D texture mapping front scalar, back scalar, and normalized distance (spanning the entire bounding box) to handle large gaps caused by LOD. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: 1. Separate all mesh faces into boundary and internal lists. 2. Identify duplicate internal faces (neighboring faces with identical vertices and scalar values). Remove these duplicates to prevent zero-length integration intervals. 3. Sort the remaining internal faces from most important to least important using a sampling strategy (e.g., Field, Area, Topology, or View-aligned). 4. Generate the Primary LUT based on the maximum edge length of the original mesh. 5. Generate the Secondary LUT scaled to handle rays spanning the entire bounding box of the mesh. 2. Frame Loop (Dynamic LOD Adjustment): 1. Measure the render time of the previous frame. 2. Adjust the number of internal faces |I| to be drawn in the current frame to maintain the target frame rate. If the frame was too slow, decrease |I|; if too fast, increase |I|. 3. Select the first |I| faces from the sorted internal list. 4. Combine the selected internal faces with all boundary faces. 3. Rasterization and Compositing (HAVS Core): 1. CPU Sort: Sort the combined face list by their centroids in object space to provide a partial front-to-back order. 2. GPU Rasterization: For each face: a. Rasterize the face to generate fragments. b. k-Buffer Update: For each pixel, compare the new fragment with the k entries in the k-buffer. Keep the k fragments closest to the viewpoint. c. Compositing: Use the two k-buffer entries closest to the viewpoint (front and back) to look up color and opacity. If using the Secondary LUT (during dynamic LOD), use the scaled table to handle the potentially large distance between fragments caused by skipped faces. If using the Primary LUT (full quality), use the standard table. d. Composite the result into the framebuffer. e. Write the remaining k-2 fragments back to the k-buffer. 3. Quality Switch: When rendering full-quality images (non-interactive), replace the Secondary LUT with the Primary LUT and use the full internal face list. Pitfalls: Gaps: Removing internal faces creates intervals larger than the maximum edge length used to build the Primary LUT. Using the Primary LUT in this state causes visual artifacts. The Secondary LUT is required during dynamic LOD to handle these large spans. Precision: The k-buffer size k must be sufficient to capture the necessary depth information for accurate compositing, but large k increases memory bandwidth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. boundaryfaces = getboundaryfaces(mesh) internalfaces = getinternalfaces(mesh) removeduplicates(internalfaces) # Remove faces with same vertices/scalars sortinternalfacesbyimportance(internalfaces) # e.g., by area or field value primarylut = createlut(maxedgelength(mesh)) secondarylut = createlutscaledtoboundingbox(mesh) targetfps = 10.0 currentinternalfacecount = len(internalfaces) while rendering: # 1. Adjust LOD based on previous frame time if previousframetime > 1.0 / targetfps: currentinternalfacecount = max(0, currentinternalfacecount - step) else: currentinternalfacecount = min(len(internalfaces), currentinternalfacecount + step) # 2. Select faces selectedinternal = internalfaces[:currentinternalfacecount] allfaces = boundaryfaces + selectedinternal # 3. CPU Sort sortfacesbycentroid(allfaces) # 4. GPU Rasterization & Compositing clearkbuffer() clearframebuffer() # Choose LUT based on mode if interactivemode: lut = secondarylut else: lut = primarylut currentinternalfacecount = len(internalfaces) # Full quality override for face in allfaces: fragments = rasterize(face) for frag in fragments: # Update k-buffer: keep k closest to viewpoint updatekbuffer(frag, k) # Get front and back fragments from k-buffer frontfrag, backfrag = getkclosestfragments(kbuffer, k=2) # Lookup pre-integrated color/opacity # Distance is normalized in secondary LUT, absolute in primary color, opacity = lookup(lut, frontfrag.scalar, backfrag.scalar, frontfrag.dist, backfrag.dist) # Composite into framebuffer composite(framebuffer, color, opacity) # Write remaining k-2 fragments back writeremainingtokbuffer(kbuffer, k) previousframetime = measurerendertime() Time Complexity: Depends on the number of faces rasterized. Dynamic LOD reduces the number of faces |I| to maintain a constant frame rate, effectively capping the rendering time per frame. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the mesh faces, the k-buffer (size k per pixel), and two LUTs. The mesh faces can remain on the GPU. Performance: On an ATI Radeon X800 Pro, the method maintains interactivity by adjusting LOD. The bottleneck is rasterization, which is reduced by drawing fewer faces. Strengths: Operates on mesh faces rather than cells, resulting in fewer rasterizations (2n triangles for n tetrahedra) compared to projected tetrahedra (3.4n). Avoids empty space accumulation errors when dropping primitives. Limitations: Visual quality degrades as more faces are dropped. The use of the Secondary LUT introduces approximation errors for large intervals. This method was developed by Steve Callahan as part of his Master's thesis research on the k-buffer and its applications to volume rendering. It builds directly on the Hardware-Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS) algorithm described in Chapter 4 of the same work. The work was conducted around 2006-2007, utilizing hardware available at the time (ATI Radeon X800 Pro). name: Optimized HAVS (Sorted k-buffer)
head: Optimization of HAVS, Sorted k-buffer HAVS
body: Optimized HAVS is a refinement of Hardware Assisted Visibility Sorting Hardware Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS) that maintains the k-buffer in a strictly sorted state (ascending order of fragment distance) to reduce the computational cost of fragment-level visibility sorting. While standard HAVS requires 2k-1 comparisons to identify the two nearest fragments for compositing, this optimization reduces that requirement to k comparisons per fragment processing step after the buffer is full, thereby improving rendering efficiency for large unstructured grid datasets. Inputs: A stream of volume fragments projected to screen space. A k-buffer of fixed capacity k per pixel, storing the nearest fragments. A 3D pre-integrated lookup table for color and opacity retrieval. Image dimensions m \times n. Outputs: A composited color and opacity value for each pixel in the framebuffer. The k-buffer state updated for the next frame or fragment batch. Data Structures: k-buffer: An array of size k per pixel. Each element stores fragment properties (distance, color, opacity, etc.). The buffer is maintained in ascending order of distance from the camera. 3D Pre-integrated Table: A texture or lookup table mapping distance intervals and optical properties to color/opacity values. Parameters: k: The number of nearest fragments to retain. The source notes that existing HAVS restricts k to 6, but this optimization allows for analysis of k ranges to balance precision and efficiency. Typical values are small integers (e.g., k \le 6 or slightly higher depending on implementation constraints). Algorithm Steps: For each pixel j in the image (1 \le j \le m \times n), let sj be the total number of fragments projected to that pixel. The k-buffer is processed as follows: 1. Buffer Not Full (current\size < k): Insert the new fragment into the k-buffer at the correct position to maintain ascending order of distance. This requires comparing the new fragment with existing fragments to find the insertion point. 2. Buffer Full (current\size == k): Let the fragments in the buffer be f1, f2, \dots, fk, where f1 is the nearest (smallest distance) and fk is the farthest. Select f1 as the first nearest fragment candidate. Select the nearest fragment fi from the remaining k-1 fragments (f2, \dots, fk). Since the buffer is sorted, fi is simply f2. Compare f1 and fi (i.e., f1 and f2). The smaller one (nearest) is fj. Retrieve color and opacity using the pair (vi, v1) (representing the volume intervals) and the distance difference from the 3D pre-integrated table. Composite the resulting color and opacity to the framebuffer. Discard fj (the nearest fragment, which has been composited) and write the remaining k-1 fragments back to the k-buffer. Insert the new incoming fragment into the sorted buffer. Formulas: Let N2 be the total number of comparisons for the sorted k-buffer across all pixels. Let t1 be comparisons during insertion (buffer not full). Let t2 be comparisons when the buffer is full. The total comparisons N2 are given by: N2 = \sum{j=1}^{m \times n} (t1 + t2) = \sum{j=1}^{m \times n} \left( \sum{l=1}^{k-1} l + (1 + k - 1) \times (sj - k) \right) Where: \sum{l=1}^{k-1} l represents the comparisons needed to insert fragments into the buffer while it is filling up (sum of 1 to k-1). (1 + k - 1) \times (sj - k) represents the comparisons for the remaining sj - k fragments after the buffer is full. The term (1 + k - 1) simplifies to k, which is the number of comparisons per fragment when the buffer is full. The average comparisons per pixel e2 are: e2 = \frac{N2}{m \times n} = \frac{\sum{j=1}^{m \times n} (\sum{l=1}^{k-1} l + k \times (sj - k))}{m \times n} The difference in average comparisons between the original HAVS (e1) and the optimized HAVS (e2) is: \Delta e = e1 - e2 = \frac{\sum{j=1}^{m \times n} ((k-1) \times (sj - \frac{k}{2} - 1))}{m \times n} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizedhavsfragments(fragments, k, preintegratedtable, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Process fragments using Optimized HAVS with a sorted k-buffer. Args: fragments: List of fragments, each with (distance, color, opacity, etc.) k: Buffer size preintegratedtable: Function/lookup for color/opacity from distance intervals imagewidth: m imageheight: n Returns: framebuffer: Array of composited colors """ # Initialize k-buffers for each pixel # kbuffer[pixelindex] is a list of fragments, sorted by distance kbuffers = [[] for in range(imagewidth imageheight)] framebuffer = [None] (imagewidth imageheight) # Group fragments by pixel pixelfragments = [[] for in range(imagewidth imageheight)] for frag in fragments: pixelidx = frag.pixelindex pixelfragments[pixelidx].append(frag) for pixelidx in range(imagewidth imageheight): frags = pixelfragments[pixelidx] buffer = kbuffers[pixelidx] # Sort fragments by distance for processing order (nearest first) # Note: In hardware-assisted streaming, fragments might arrive in order. # Assuming we process them in distance order for correctness. frags.sort(key=lambda f: f.distance) for frag in frags: currentsize = len(buffer) if currentsize < k: # Insert into sorted position # Find insertion index insertidx = 0 while insertidx < currentsize and buffer[insertidx].distance < frag.distance: insertidx += 1 buffer.insert(insertidx, frag) else: # Buffer is full # f1 is the nearest (buffer[0]) # fi is the nearest among the rest (buffer[1]) f1 = buffer[0] fi = buffer[1] # Compare f1 and fi, get smaller one fj # Since buffer is sorted, f1 is always <= fi fj = f1 # Use (vi, v1) and distance difference to get color/opacity # vi corresponds to fi, v1 corresponds to f1 # This step assumes pre-integrated table takes volume intervals color, opacity = preintegratedtable(fi.volumeinterval, f1.volumeinterval, fi.distance - f1.distance) # Composite to framebuffer # Assuming framebuffer stores current accumulated color/opacity if framebuffer[pixelidx] is None: framebuffer[pixelidx] = (color, opacity) else: prevcolor, prevopacity = framebuffer[pixelidx] # Standard alpha compositing: Cout = Cfg alphafg + Cbg (1 - alphafg) newcolor = color opacity + prevcolor (1 - opacity) newopacity = opacity + prevopacity (1 - opacity) framebuffer[pixelidx] = (newcolor, newopacity) # Discard fj (f1) and write remaining k-1 fragments back # Remove f1 from buffer buffer.pop(0) # Insert the new fragment into the sorted buffer insertidx = 0 while insertidx < k - 1 and buffer[insertidx].distance < frag.distance: insertidx += 1 buffer.insert(insertidx, frag) return framebuffer Time Complexity: The number of comparisons per fragment after the buffer is full is k, compared to 2k-1 in the original HAVS. The total comparisons N2 are reduced, leading to improved efficiency. The improvement ratio \frac{\Delta e}{e1} increases as the dataset size (sj) increases. Memory Complexity: Requires storing k fragments per pixel in the k-buffer. Strengths: Reduces comparison overhead, especially for large datasets with many fragments per pixel. Allows for larger k values without proportional performance loss, potentially improving rendering precision. Limitations: Requires maintaining the sorted order of the k-buffer, which involves insertion operations. The benefit is most pronounced when sj is significantly larger than k. This optimization was proposed in a 2012 paper by authors associated with ICCASM 2012. It addresses the inefficiency of the original HAVS algorithm, which requires 2k-1 comparisons to find the two nearest fragments. By keeping the k-buffer sorted, the algorithm reduces this to k comparisons. The paper also investigates the optimal range for k to balance precision and efficiency, noting that standard HAVS often restricts k to 6. name: Chunk-based World Streaming
head: Chunk System, Chunk-based World Management and Streaming, Voxel Chunk Manager, dynamic chunk loading
body: Chunk-based World Streaming divides a 3D voxel world into fixed-size spatial partitions (chunks) to manage memory, generation, and rendering efficiently by loading only the chunks near the player. It differs from Chunk-based Training by focusing on runtime spatial management rather than data preparation for machine learning, and from Chunk Trees by using a flat hash map of active chunks rather than a hierarchical tree structure for spatial queries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Player position (world coordinates), render distance (in chunks), unload timeout (seconds), chunk size (world units), and maximum chunks to load per frame. Output: A set of active Chunk objects resident in memory, with states indicating generation and meshing progress. Data Structures: Chunk: An object representing a fixed-size volume of voxels. Fields: chunkcoordinatex (int), chunkcoordinatez (int), state (enum flags). State Flags: CHUNKSTATEINGENERATIONQUEUE, CHUNKSTATEINMESHINGQUEUE, CHUNKSTATEOUTOFVISION, CHUNKSTATEUNLOADED, CHUNKSTATEGENERATED, CHUNKSTATEMESHED, CHUNKSTATEINDELETINGQUEUE. chunkmap: A hash map (e.g., unorderedmap<glm::ivec2, Chunk>) mapping 2D chunk coordinates (x, z) to Chunk pointers. The y-dimension is typically handled within the chunk or implied by the world height. Queues: chunkstogeneratequeue: List of chunk coordinates pending generation. chunkstodelete: List of chunk pointers pending deletion. Renderer delete queue: List of chunk indices sent to the rendering backend for cleanup. Parameters: CHUNKSIZE: Size of a chunk in world units. Sources indicate a value of 16 units or imply 1024x1024x1024 block limits with coordinate division by CHUNKSIZE. chunkview: Radius in chunks around the player for loading checks. Typical value: 8. RENDERDISTANCE: Distance from the camera (in chunks) within which chunks are kept active. Used for bounds checks: distx >= -RENDERDISTANCE && distx < RENDERDISTANCE. UNLOADTIMEOUT: Time in seconds a chunk remains in OUTOFVISION state before deletion. loadlimiteachframe: Maximum number of new chunks loaded per frame. Typical value: 4. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Player Chunk: Determine the chunk coordinates containing the player: \text{player\chunk\x} = \lfloor \text{player\pos\x} / \text{CHUNK\SIZE} \rfloor \text{player\chunk\z} = \lfloor \text{player\pos\z} / \text{CHUNK\SIZE} \rfloor 2. Define View Bounds: Calculate the bounding box of chunks to consider for loading/unloading: \text{origin\x} = \text{player\chunk\x} - \text{chunk\view} \text{end\x} = \text{player\chunk\x} + \text{chunk\view} (Same for z). 3. Process Unloading: Iterate through chunkmap. If a chunk's coordinates are outside [originx, endx] or [originz, endz], delete the chunk object, erase it from the map, and add it to chunkstodelete. Alternatively, if a chunk is outside RENDERDISTANCE and marked OUTOFVISION, start a timer. If glfwGetTime() - c->unloadtimer >= UNLOADTIMEOUT, mark it as INDELETINGQUEUE. Note: Sources indicate chunks are deleted before new ones are created in the update loop, potentially for memory allocator reuse. 4. Process Loading: Iterate toriginx from originx to endx and toriginz from originz to endz. For each coordinate, check if the chunk exists in chunkmap. If not found, call addChunk(toriginx, toriginz) and increment loadedchunks. If loadedchunks >= loadlimiteachframe, break the loops. 5. Trigger Generation: For chunks within RENDERDISTANCE that are not yet generated (!CHUNKSTATEGENERATED) and are free, mark them as INGENERATIONQUEUE and push to chunkstogeneratequeue. 6. Trigger Meshing: If a chunk is generated but not meshed, check if all 6 neighbors are generated (or out of bounds/distance). If so, send the chunk to the meshing thread. 7. Execute Queues: Process chunkstogeneratequeue using parallel execution (e.g., oneapi::tbb::parallelfor). Process chunkstodelete: Pop from queue. If chunk exists in map, erase from map, push index to renderer delete queue, and delete object. If erase fails, reset state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateworld(playerpos, renderdistance, unloadtimeout, chunkview, loadlimiteachframe, chunksize): # 1. Calculate player chunk playerchunkx = floor(playerpos.x / chunksize) playerchunkz = floor(playerpos.z / chunksize) # 2. Define bounds originx = playerchunkx - chunkview endx = playerchunkx + chunkview originz = playerchunkz - chunkview endz = playerchunkz + chunkview # 3. Unload chunks outside bounds chunkstodelete = [] for chunkcoord, chunk in chunkmap.items(): if chunkcoord.x < originx or chunkcoord.x > endx or \ chunkcoord.z < originz or chunkcoord.z > endz: # Mark for deletion chunk.state = CHUNKSTATEINDELETINGQUEUE chunkstodelete.append(chunk) chunkmap.erase(chunkcoord) # 4. Load new chunks loadedcount = 0 for x in range(originx, endx + 1): for z in range(originz, endz + 1): if loadedcount >= loadlimiteachframe: break if (x, z) not in chunkmap: addchunk(x, z) loadedcount += 1 if loadedcount >= loadlimiteachframe: break # 5. Trigger generation for new chunks within render distance for chunk in chunkmap.values(): if not chunk.state.isgenerated(): distx = abs(chunk.coord.x - playerchunkx) distz = abs(chunk.coord.z - playerchunkz) if distx < renderdistance and distz < renderdistance: if chunk.state.isfree(): chunk.state = CHUNKSTATEINGENERATIONQUEUE chunkstogeneratequeue.push(chunk) # 6. Trigger meshing for generated chunks for chunk in chunkmap.values(): if chunk.state.isgenerated() and not chunk.state.ismeshed(): if allneighborsgenerated(chunk, chunkmap, renderdistance): sendtomeshingthread(chunk) # 7. Process deletion queue for chunk in chunkstodelete: if chunk in chunkmap: chunkmap.erase(chunk.coord) rendererdeletequeue.push(chunk.coord) delete chunk else: chunk.resetstate() # 8. Process generation queue (parallel) parallelfor(chunkstogeneratequeue, generatechunkdata) Synchronous Chunk Loading generates and applies a 3x3 grid of chunks around a world position in a single blocking call. It differs from the asynchronous queue-based approach by ensuring immediate consistency for the central chunk and its immediate neighbors, useful for initial world setup or save-game loading. When to choose: Use when immediate availability of the local chunk set is required without waiting for background threads, such as during game start or level transition. name: Chunk Lifecycle Management
head: Chunk Management, Chunk Spawning and Despawn
body: Chunk Lifecycle Management is the core mechanism for maintaining the set of active volumetric chunks in a streaming world, ensuring that only chunks within the player's vicinity are resident in memory. It solves the problem of memory exhaustion and unnecessary I/O by explicitly spawning new chunks as the player approaches and despawning distant chunks as they move away. It differs from Dynamic Chunk Generation with Radius by serving as the foundational logic for set-difference operations, whereas the radius variant optimizes the geometric query; it differs from Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner by focusing on the state transition of individual chunk objects rather than scanning discrete spatial regions for load/unload triggers. Inputs: Player position (or camera position) in world coordinates. Render distance radius R. Current set of existing chunks, stored in a hash map chunks mapping ChunkPosition to Chunk object. Chunk grid resolution (implicit in ChunkPosition definition). Outputs: Updated chunks hash map with new entries added and removed entries deleted. List of newChunks for terrain generation. List of chunksToDelete for cleanup. Data Structures: ChunkPosition: A tuple or struct representing the integer grid coordinates (x, y, z) of a chunk. chunks: A hash map (dictionary) where keys are ChunkPosition and values are Chunk objects. nearbyPositionsSet: A set of ChunkPosition objects calculated to be within the render distance. chunksAlreadyExist: A set of ChunkPosition keys extracted from the chunks hash map. Steps: 1. Calculate Nearby Positions: Determine all integer chunk positions (x, y, z) that fall within a spherical volume of radius R centered at the player's position. Store these in nearbyPositionsSet. 2. Identify Existing Chunks: Extract all keys from the chunks hash map into chunksAlreadyExist. 3. Despawn Distant Chunks: Iterate through each position p in chunksAlreadyExist. If p is not present in nearbyPositionsSet, the chunk is too far away. Remove the chunk object from the chunks hash map, remove it from frame draw calls, and add p to chunksToDelete. 4. Spawn Nearby Chunks: Iterate through each position p in nearbyPositionsSet. If p is not present in chunksAlreadyExist, the chunk does not exist. Create a new Chunk object, insert it into the chunks hash map with key p, and add the new chunk to newChunks. 5. Generate Terrain: For every chunk in newChunks, initiate asynchronous or synchronous terrain generation using Chunk::MultithreadGenerateTerrain. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def managechunklifecycle(playerpos, renderdistance, chunks): # Step 1: Identify nearby chunk positions # Assumes a function that returns all integer grid positions within radius R of playerpos nearbypositions = ChunkPositionsWithinRenderDistance(playerpos, renderdistance) nearbyset = set(nearbypositions) # Step 2: Get positions of chunks that currently exist existingpositions = set(chunks.keys()) chunkstodelete = [] newchunks = [] # Step 3: Iterate through existing chunks; delete if not nearby for pos in existingpositions: if pos not in nearbyset: # Remove from hash map and draw calls del chunks[pos] chunkstodelete.append(pos) # Step 4: Iterate through nearby positions; create if not existing for pos in nearbypositions: if pos not in existingpositions: # Create new chunk object newchunk = Chunk(pos) chunks[pos] = newchunk newchunks.append(newchunk) # Step 5: Generate terrain for new chunks for chunk in newchunks: chunk.MultithreadGenerateTerrain() return chunkstodelete, newchunks Parameters: renderdistance: The radius R in world units. Typical values depend on the scale of the volume and performance constraints. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point player positions must be correctly converted to integer chunk grid coordinates. Ensure consistent rounding or floor/ceil logic when mapping world coordinates to chunk indices. Boundaries: If the volume has hard boundaries, ChunkPositionsWithinRenderDistance must clamp results to valid volume extents. Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: If renderdistance is zero, only the chunk containing the player should exist. Not given in the sources. Manages chunk instantiation and removal based on a spherical render distance around the player, using set difference operations to determine which chunks to load or unload. It builds on Chunk Lifecycle Management by replacing static or scanner-based triggers with a continuous distance check against the player's current position. Unlike Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner, which scans discrete regions, this method evaluates every chunk within a calculated bounding box relative to the player to maintain a consistent spherical visibility volume. The Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner identifies which chunks in a volumetric world need to be loaded or unloaded based on the camera's current and previous positions, using offset grids to define load and unload areas. It differs from Dynamic Chunk Generation with Radius by explicitly tracking state transitions between frames via previous position comparison, and from Budget Plans by using a fixed-radius offset strategy rather than a dynamic priority queue. Budget Plans provide a system for managing chunk loading policies in chunk-based volume streaming, replacing the previous single octree-focused policy with configurable presets for exploration, whole-volume visualization, and frame-rate maintenance. This method allows an application to switch loading strategies mid-session to balance visual fidelity against performance constraints, addressing the limitation where a single policy was "right for exploring and wrong for a whole-volume figure or for holding a frame rate while rotating". It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Dynamic Chunk Generation with Radius by focusing on high-level policy presets and precedence rules rather than geometric radius calculations, and from Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner by managing the intent of the load queue rather than the mechanical scanning of the spatial hierarchy. Time Complexity: O(N + M), where N is the number of existing chunks and M is the number of chunks within the render distance. Set lookups are O(1) on average. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active chunks. The hash map stores references to all active chunks. Strengths: Simple logic, easy to implement, deterministic behavior based on distance. Limitations: Does not account for occlusion or view frustum culling beyond the radius. May load chunks that are not visible if the radius is large. Not given in the sources for specific performance metrics. When to use: When a simple, distance-based streaming strategy is sufficient and performance constraints allow for loading all chunks within a fixed radius. When not to use: When occlusion culling is critical, or when memory is extremely constrained and a more sophisticated priority-based system (like Budget Plans) is needed. Originating from the Cube project, this method provides a basic but effective framework for managing chunk lifecycles in volumetric worlds. It serves as the foundational logic for more advanced streaming techniques that build upon set-difference operations to optimize chunk loading and unloading. gabkhanfig/Cube, https://github.com/gabkhanfig/Cube, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Dynamic Chunk Generation with Radius
head: Chunk Lifecycle Management with Radius, Chunk Loading/Unloading (Render Distance Culling), Chunk culling, Distance-based chunk management
body: Dynamic Chunk Generation with Radius manages chunk instantiation and removal based on a spherical render distance around the player, using set difference operations to determine which chunks to load or unload. It builds on Chunk Lifecycle Management by replacing static or scanner-based triggers with a continuous distance check against the player's current position. Unlike Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner, which scans discrete regions, this method evaluates every chunk within a calculated bounding box relative to the player to maintain a consistent spherical visibility volume. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Player position (P), render radius (R), chunk size (S), and the current set of loaded chunks. Outputs: Updated set of loaded chunks (instantiated or destroyed). Data Structures: Loaded Chunks Dictionary: A hash map (dictionary) mapping chunk coordinates (keys) to chunk state or object references (values). Keys are typically integer tuples (x, y, z) representing the chunk grid index. This structure provides O(1) average access for existence checks. Chunk States: Chunks are categorized into three logical states during the update cycle: KEEP: The chunk exists and is within the render radius. DRAW (or CREATE): The chunk does not exist but is within the render radius. DONE (or DESTROY): The chunk exists but is outside the render radius. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Bounding Sphere Diameter: Determine the diameter of the render sphere in world units and convert it to chunk units. D{chunks} = \left\lfloor \frac{R \times 2}{S} \right\rfloor Where R is the render radius and S is the chunk size. 2. Determine Grid Range: Calculate the minimum and maximum chunk indices (x, y, z) that could possibly intersect the render sphere. \text{start} = \left\lfloor \frac{D{chunks}}{2} \right\rfloor \times -1 \text{end} = D{chunks} + \text{start} This defines the iteration range [\text{start}, \text{end}] for the chunk grid coordinates. 3. Identify Target Chunks: Iterate through all integer coordinates (x, y, z) within the range [\text{start}, \text{end}]. Compute the chunk's world position. Note: The exact mapping from grid index to world position depends on the coordinate system origin. A common approach is: P{chunk} = (x, y, z) \times S (If the origin is centered, adjustments may be needed, but the core logic relies on distance comparison). Calculate the Euclidean distance from the player position P to the chunk's center or relevant point P{chunk}: d = \| P{chunk} - P \| If d < R, add the chunk key (x, y, z) to a temporary set surroundingchunks. 4. Compute Set Differences: Compare surroundingchunks with the keys of the currently loaded chunks dictionary (loadedchunks). Chunks to Load: keys(surroundingchunks) - keys(loadedchunks) Chunks to Unload: keys(loadedchunks) - keys(surroundingchunks) 5. Execute Lifecycle Actions: For each chunk in Chunks to Load: Instantiate the chunk and add it to loadedchunks with state DRAW or KEEP. For each chunk in Chunks to Unload: Mark the chunk as DONE and destroy/remove it from loadedchunks. For each chunk in loadedchunks that remains in surroundingchunks: Maintain state KEEP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatechunks(playerpos, renderradius, chunksize, loadedchunksdict): # 1. Calculate bounds renderdiameterchunks = int(renderradius 2) // chunksize rangestart = (renderdiameterchunks // 2) -1 rangeend = renderdiameterchunks + rangestart surroundingchunks = {} # 2. Iterate and filter by distance for x in range(rangestart, rangeend + 1): for y in range(rangestart, rangeend + 1): for z in range(rangestart, rangeend + 1): # Compute chunk world position # Note: getchunkfrompoint logic varies by engine; # assuming standard grid alignment where chunk (0,0,0) is at origin or offset. # Simplified: chunkcenter = (x, y, z) chunksize chunkcenter = Vector3(x, y, z) chunksize # Distance check if (chunkcenter - playerpos).length() < renderradius: surroundingchunks[(x, y, z)] = True # 3. Determine load/unload sets loadedkeys = set(loadedchunksdict.keys()) targetkeys = set(surroundingchunks.keys()) chunkstoload = targetkeys - loadedkeys chunkstounload = loadedkeys - targetkeys # 4. Execute actions for key in chunkstoload: # Instantiate chunk chunk = createchunk(key) loadedchunksdict[key] = chunk for key in chunkstounload: # Destroy chunk destroychunk(loadedchunksdict[key]) del loadedchunksdict[key] # Note: Keys in both sets are implicitly kept; no action needed Parameters: Render Radius (R): The distance from the player within which chunks are generated. Typical values depend on scene scale and performance targets. Not given in the sources. Chunk Size (S): The physical dimension of a chunk. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stale Data: Dictionary keys must be cleared or replaced with a new temporary dictionary before population to avoid retaining stale data from previous frames. Performance: A naive single-threaded implementation checking every chunk in the radius can be extremely slow and inefficient for open worlds, potentially causing frame drops. Generation Latency: If generation is asynchronous, the player may move out of the generated area before new chunks are ready, leading to "falling out of the world" if the player runs faster than the generation rate. A multithreaded generation technique that uses a recursive flood fill algorithm to build chunks simultaneously around the player, significantly reducing loading and deletion time compared to the single-threaded radius check. Instead of iterating a bounding box, it initiates a search in 4 directions from the player's position, recursively calling the generation algorithm until the radius limit is reached. It employs concurrent dictionaries and queues to allow multiple threads to access chunks without deadlocks. On older CPUs with fewer cores, the player might outrun the generation; a mitigation is to slow down the player to allow the CPU time to generate chunks. Custom concurrency primitives were required in Unity 5.4 (.NET 4.6) because built-in ConcurrentQueue and ConcurrentDictionary were unavailable, though newer.NET versions provide these. A management approach that maintains the world state, including the chunk generator and a cache for chunk generation status and data. The World object contains an Arc<dyn WorldGen> trait object for chunk generation and an AHashMap mapping (ChunkPosition, ZoomLevel) to ChunkStatus. The ChunkStatus enum tracks whether a chunk is Generating, Generated (holding an Arc<ChunkInfo>), or Empty. ChunkInfo contains opaque geometry (Box<Array3Chunk>), translucent geometry (Vec<Array3Chunk>), and face data (StaticCopyMap<Direction, ChunkFace>). This structure supports efficient status checks and data sharing across threads via atomic reference counting (Arc). Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of chunks in the bounding box defined by the render radius. The bounding box size scales with R^3. Set difference operations are O(K) where K is the number of loaded chunks. Memory Complexity: O(L) where L is the number of loaded chunks. The dictionary overhead is minimal per entry. Strengths: Simple to implement; guarantees a spherical visibility volume; efficient lookups with hash maps. Limitations: Single-threaded version is inefficient for large radii; requires careful handling of generation latency to prevent players from outpacing world generation; bounding box iteration includes chunks outside the radius that are quickly discarded, wasting CPU cycles if the radius is large. When to use: Suitable for moderate render distances and when generation is fast or pre-cached. Requires multithreading or asynchronous generation for large open worlds to avoid stuttering. The method originated in voxel-based procedural terrain generation systems, specifically within the context of open-world games where static generation was insufficient. The initial implementation used a simple radius value updated as the player moved, labeling chunks as KEEP, DRAW, or DONE. This approach was found to be too slow for open worlds, leading to the development of multithreaded variants and more sophisticated caching mechanisms. The concept is implemented in various voxel engines, including Godot-based plugins and Rust-based generators like Infinigen. name: Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner
head: Scanner, ScannerPlugin
body: The Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner identifies which chunks in a volumetric world need to be loaded or unloaded based on the camera's current and previous positions, using offset grids to define load and unload areas. It differs from Dynamic Chunk Generation with Radius by explicitly tracking state transitions between frames via previous position comparison, and from Budget Plans by using a fixed-radius offset strategy rather than a dynamic priority queue. Inputs: Camera transform (translation), previous chunk position, chunk size (32 units), and sampling offsets. Outputs: Lists of chunks to load (dataload, meshload) and unload (dataunload, meshunload). Data Structures: The Scanner struct maintains the following fields: prevchunkpos: IVec3 (previous frame's chunk coordinates). checksperframe: usize (limit on chunks processed per frame). dataoffset: usize (radius for data loading). meshoffset: usize (radius for mesh loading). unresolveddataload: Vec<IVec3> (chunks pending data load). unresolvedmeshload: Vec<IVec3> (chunks pending mesh load). unresolveddataunload: VecDeque<IVec3> (chunks pending data unload). unresolvedmeshunload: VecDeque<IVec3> (chunks pending mesh unload). datasamplingoffsets: Vec<IVec3> (precomputed offsets for data). meshsamplingoffsets: Vec<IVec3> (precomputed offsets for mesh). Steps: 1. Calculate Current Chunk Position: Convert the camera's world translation to chunk coordinates. Given a chunk size of 32 and an offset of 16 (half-chunk), the position is calculated as: \text{chunk\pos} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{translation} - 16.0}{32.0} \right\rfloor In integer arithmetic: python chunkpos = ((cameratranslation - 16.0) / 32.0).asivec3() 2. Check for Movement: Compare chunkpos with prevchunkpos. If they are identical, skip processing for this frame. 3. Generate Load/Unload Areas: Create sets of chunk coordinates to consider for loading and unloading by adding sampling offsets to the current and previous positions, respectively: \text{load\data\area} = \text{chunk\pos} + \text{data\sampling\offsets} \text{unload\data\area} = \text{prev\chunk\pos} + \text{data\sampling\offsets} Similar areas are generated for mesh loading using meshsamplingoffsets. 4. Compute Differences: Determine the symmetric difference between the current load area and the previous unload area to identify chunks that need to be loaded or unloaded: \text{data\load} = \text{load\data\area} \setminus \text{unload\data\area} \text{data\unload} = \text{unload\data\area} \setminus \text{load\data\area} \text{mesh\load} = \text{load\mesh\area} \setminus \text{unload\mesh\area} \text{mesh\unload} = \text{unload\mesh\area} \setminus \text{load\mesh\area} 5. Update Queues: Add chunks from dataload and meshload to their respective unresolved queues. Remove chunks from dataload and meshload from the unload queues (if present). Remove chunks from dataunload and meshunload from the load queues (if present). 6. Sort Load Queues: Sort unresolveddataload and unresolvedmeshload by squared distance to the current chunkpos to prioritize nearby chunks. 7. Update State: Set prevchunkpos = chunkpos for the next frame. Parameters: checksperframe: Default value is 32 \times 32 \times 32. datadistance: Radius for data loading offsets, calculated as distance + 1. meshdistance: Radius for mesh loading offsets, calculated as distance. Edge Cases: If the camera does not move between frames, no chunks are loaded or unloaded. Precision issues in chunk position calculation can cause flickering if the camera is near chunk boundaries; using floor division with an offset (16.0) helps center the active chunk. A technique to determine which chunks are visible to the camera by checking if their bounding boxes intersect the view frustum, sorted by distance. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of chunks in the sampling offset area. Sorting adds O(K \log K) where K is the number of unresolved loads. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of unresolved chunks in the queues. Strengths: Simple to implement, deterministic behavior based on camera movement, effective for large worlds with limited memory. Limitations: May load unnecessary chunks if the camera moves erratically; does not account for occlusion or view frustum culling directly. When to use: When memory is constrained and the world is too large to fit in RAM. When not to use: When the world fits in memory or when occlusion culling is more critical than streaming. The Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner is part of the Binary Greedy Voxel Meshing Algorithm implementation, specifically designed for out-of-core streaming of voxel data. It was developed to manage memory usage in large-scale voxel environments by dynamically loading and unloading chunks based on camera proximity. name: Chunk Visibility Culling
head: Frustum Culling for Chunk Visibility
body: Chunk Visibility Culling determines which spatial chunks are visible to the camera by testing their bounding boxes against the view frustum, then sorting the visible set by distance. It differs from the parent Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner by focusing on geometric intersection with the camera’s view volume rather than offset-grid-based load/unload area determination. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: camera: A PerspectiveCamera instance providing projection and world matrices. renderRadius: A number specifying the radius in chunk coordinates around the center chunk to check. Chunk grid data: Implicitly accessed via camera.position and CHUNKWORLDSIZE. Outputs: A list of visible chunk coordinates, sorted by squared distance from the center chunk. Data Structures Frustum: Represented by a frustum object derived from the projection matrix. Visible List: A list of chunk coordinates (e.g., [x, y, z] tuples or vectors). Steps 1. Calculate Center Chunk Coordinates: Determine the chunk containing the camera by dividing the camera’s world position by the chunk world size and flooring the result: \text{center\chunk\coords} = \left( \left\lfloor \frac{\text{camera.position.x}}{\text{CHUNK\WORLD\SIZE}} \right\rfloor, \left\lfloor \frac{\text{camera.position.y}}{\text{CHUNK\WORLD\SIZE}} \right\rfloor, \left\lfloor \frac{\text{camera.position.z}}{\text{CHUNK\WORLD\SIZE}} \right\rfloor \right) 2. Set Up Frustum: Compute the view-projection matrix and extract the six planes of the view frustum: \text{projScreenMatrix} = \text{camera.projectionMatrix} \times \text{camera.matrixWorldInverse} \text{frustum} = \text{Frustum.setFromProjectionMatrix}(\text{projScreenMatrix}) 3. Check Frustum Intersection: For each chunk within the renderRadius of the centerchunkcoords, construct its axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Test if the frustum intersects this box: python if frustum.intersectsBox(bounds): add chunk.position to visiblelist 4. Sort Visible Chunks: Sort the visiblelist by the squared Euclidean distance from each chunk’s position to the centerchunkcoords. This prioritizes closer chunks for rendering or loading. Parameters camera: PerspectiveCamera. renderRadius: Number, radius in chunk coordinates. CHUNKWORLDSIZE: Implicit constant defining the spatial extent of a chunk. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point errors in camera.position or matrix multiplication may cause incorrect frustum extraction or intersection tests. Boundaries: Chunks at the edge of the renderRadius must be correctly included or excluded based on the radius definition (inclusive/exclusive). Degenerate Input: If camera is invalid or matrices are singular, frustum extraction fails. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def chunkvisibilityculling(camera, renderradius, chunkworldsize): # Step 1: Calculate center chunk coordinates centerchunkcoords = [ floor(camera.position.x / chunkworldsize), floor(camera.position.y / chunkworldsize), floor(camera.position.z / chunkworldsize) ] # Step 2: Set up frustum projscreenmatrix = multiplymatrices(camera.projectionmatrix, camera.matrixworldinverse) frustum = Frustum.setfromprojectionmatrix(projscreenmatrix) visiblechunks = [] # Step 3: Check frustum intersection for chunks within render radius for x in range(centerchunkcoords[0] - renderradius, centerchunkcoords[0] + renderradius + 1): for y in range(centerchunkcoords[1] - renderradius, centerchunkcoords[1] + renderradius + 1): for z in range(centerchunkcoords[2] - renderradius, centerchunkcoords[2] + renderradius + 1): chunkpos = [x, y, z] # Construct bounding box for the chunk bounds = createchunkbounds(chunkpos, chunkworldsize) # Check intersection if frustum.intersectsbox(bounds): visiblechunks.append(chunkpos) # Step 4: Sort visible chunks by squared distance from center def squareddistance(chunkpos): dx = chunkpos[0] - centerchunkcoords[0] dy = chunkpos[1] - centerchunkcoords[1] dz = chunkpos[2] - centerchunkcoords[2] return dxdx + dydy + dzdz visiblechunks.sort(key=squareddistance) return visiblechunks Helper functions multiplymatrices, Frustum.setfromprojectionmatrix, createchunkbounds, and frustum.intersectsbox are assumed to be standard graphics library operations or implemented as per standard definitions. Recursively traverses an octree to cull chunks outside the camera frustum and select appropriate LOD levels based on distance to the camera. Time Complexity: O(R^3) where R is the renderRadius, as it checks all chunks in a cubic volume around the center chunk. Sorting takes O(V \log V) where V is the number of visible chunks. Memory Complexity: O(V) to store the list of visible chunks. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades linearly with the cube of the render radius. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for uniform chunk grids. Limitations: Does not account for occlusion; checks all chunks in the radius even if far from the view frustum. When to Use: Uniform chunk grids where frustum culling is sufficient. When Not to Use: Highly occluded scenes or non-uniform chunk distributions where more sophisticated culling is needed. Origin: Implemented in the webvoxelterrain project by Andrew Bloese. History: Part of a web-based voxel terrain renderer, focusing on efficient chunk management for real-time rendering. Usage: Used in web-based voxel terrain applications to determine which chunks to render or load. webvoxelterrain, https://github.com/andrewbloese-00/webvoxelterrain, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Octree Frustum Culling & LOD Selection
head: CPU Frustum Culling, CPU-based Octree LOD & Frustum Culling
body: This method recursively traverses a chunk-based octree to determine which spatial regions are visible within the camera's view frustum and assigns an appropriate Level of Detail (LOD) based on the distance from the camera. It differs from sibling techniques by combining visibility culling and LOD selection into a single recursive traversal, deferring geometry queueing until a node is determined to be either fully visible at its current LOD or fully outside the frustum. It builds on Chunk Visibility Culling by adding distance-based LOD logic and explicit frustum plane intersection tests. Inputs: set: The chunk set structure containing octree metadata, root size, and geometry arrays. cam: Camera structure containing frustumplanes (array of 6 planes) and lodorigin (camera position). lod: Current level of detail (unsigned 8-bit integer). x, y, z: Chunk coordinates at the current lod level. Outputs: Populated geometry queues: queuegsvl, queuemesh, queuemisc. Data Structures: The chunk set (set) contains: root: Base root size of the chunk set. max[3]: Maximum chunk coordinates for each axis. maxbitw[3]: Bit width required to index the maximum coordinate for each axis. gsvl[lod][index]: Array of GeometrySVL pointers for structured volume geometry. gmesh[index]: Array of GeometryMesh pointers for mesh geometry. The queue structures contain: queuegsvl[0xFFFF]: Array of GeometrySVL pointers. queuemesh[0xFFFF]: Array of GeometryMesh pointers. queuemisc[0xFFFF]: Array of uint32t indices. queuegsvlcount, queuemeshcount, queuemisccount: Current counts of enqueued items. Parameters: wsroot: World space root size, calculated as set->root << lod. LODSCALE: Distance scale factor, value 1024. FRUSTUMRADIUSMULT: Frustum culling radius multiplier, value 0.85. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute World-Space Center: Calculate the center of the current chunk in world space. center[i] = (coord[i] \times ws\root) + \frac{ws\root}{2} where i \in \{0, 1, 2\} corresponds to x, y, z axes. 2. Boundary Check: Verify the chunk coordinates are within the defined bounds of the chunk set. \text{if } (coord[i] \ll lod) \ge set.max[i] \text{ for any } i, \text{ return.} 3. Frustum Culling: Check if the chunk intersects the camera frustum. The chunk is treated as a sphere or box with a radius scaled by 0.85 of the world-space root size. \text{if } \neg \text{gfx\fcull\visible}(cam.frustum\planes, center, ws\root \times 0.85), \text{ return.} gfxfcullvisible performs a standard sphere/box vs. 6-plane frustum intersection test. If the object is completely outside any plane, it returns false. 4. Distance Calculation: Compute the Euclidean distance from the camera's LOD origin to the chunk's world-space center. distance = \sqrt{\sum{i=0}^{2} (center[i] - cam.lod\origin[i])^2} 5. LOD Decision: If distance > lod \times 1024: The chunk is far enough to be rendered at the current LOD. Enqueue the appropriate geometry and return. Else: The chunk is close enough to require a higher resolution (lower LOD index). Decrement lod and recurse into the 8 children. 6. Geometry Enqueuing (Far Case): Calculate the bit widths for the flattened index: octree\bitw[i] = set.max\bitw[i] - \min(lod, set.max\bitw[i]) If lod == 0: Calculate the mesh index: index = \text{flatten3}((uint16t[])\{x, y, z\}, set.max\bitw). Retrieve m = set.gmesh[index]. If m.vbo exists, enqueue m into queuemesh and index into queuemisc. Return. Else: Calculate the SVL index: idx = \text{flatten3}((uint16t[])\{x, y, z\}, octree\bitw). Retrieve g = set.gsvl[lod][idx]. If g.vbo exists, enqueue g into queuegsvl. Return. 7. Recursion (Close Case): Decrement lod. Iterate nx, ny, nz \in \{0, 1\}. Recursively call the algorithm with coordinates ((x \times 2) + nx, (y \times 2) + ny, (z \times 2) + nz). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def octreecull(set, cam, lod, x, y, z): # 1. Compute World-Space Root Size wsroot = set.root << lod # 2. Boundary Check for i in range(3): coord = [x, y, z][i] if (coord << lod) >= set.max[i]: return # 3. Compute World-Space Center center = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): coord = [x, y, z][i] center[i] = (coord wsroot) + (wsroot / 2.0) # 4. Frustum Culling # gfxfcullvisible checks if the sphere at 'center' with radius 'wsroot 0.85' # intersects any of the 6 planes in cam.frustumplanes. if not gfxfcullvisible(cam.frustumplanes, center, wsroot 0.85): return # 5. Distance Calculation distance = glmvecdistance(cam.lodorigin, center) # 6. LOD Decision if distance > lod 1024: # Enqueue geometry for current LOD if lod == 0: # Mesh Geometry index = flatten3([x, y, z], set.maxbitw) m = set.gmesh[index] if m.vbo: queuemesh[queuemeshcount] = m queuemeshcount += 1 queuemisc[queuemisccount] = index queuemisccount += 1 else: # SVL Geometry octreebitw = [0, 0, 0] for i in range(3): octreebitw[i] = set.maxbitw[i] - min(lod, set.maxbitw[i]) idx = flatten3([x, y, z], octreebitw) g = set.gsvl[lod][idx] if g.vbo: queuegsvl[queuegsvlcount] = g queuegsvlcount += 1 return # 7. Recurse into children newlod = lod - 1 for nx in range(2): for ny in range(2): for nz in range(2): octreecull(set, cam, newlod, (x 2) + nx, (y 2) + ny, (z 2) + nz) def flatten3(coords, bitw): # Flattens 3D coordinates into a 1D index using provided bit widths # Assumes little-endian or specific packing order consistent with the source # Implementation detail: typically (z << (bitw[0]+bitw[1])) | (y << bitw[0]) | x # Exact packing order depends on 'set' implementation, but standard is XYZ or ZYX. # Based on source usage, it treats coords as uint16t array. x, y, z = coords b0, b1, b2 = bitw # Note: Source does not specify exact bit shift order, but standard voxel hashing is often ZYX or XYZ. # Assuming standard interleaved bit packing or simple shift. # Given 'maxbitw' is used for mesh and 'octreebitw' for SVL, the packing must be consistent. # A common safe assumption for 'flatten3' in such contexts: return (z << (b0 + b1)) | (y << b0) | x Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of nodes in the octree, but typically much less due to frustum culling skipping large portions of the tree. The traversal is depth-first. Memory Complexity: O(D) where D is the maximum depth of the octree (recursion stack). The queue sizes are bounded by 0xFFFF entries per type. Performance: Efficient for large sparse volumes as it avoids processing invisible or distant low-detail chunks. The fixed-size queues prevent memory fragmentation but may limit the number of chunks processed per frame if the scene is extremely dense. Strengths: Simple implementation, low CPU overhead per frame, effective culling. Limitations: CPU-bound traversal can become a bottleneck for very deep octrees or high frame rates. The fixed LOD scale factor (1024) may not suit all scene scales. This method is derived from the voxel platforming engine implementation in the voxplat repository by kosshi-net. It represents a practical approach to managing chunk-based voxel data in real-time applications, balancing visibility culling with LOD selection to maintain performance. kosshi-net/voxplat, https://github.com/kosshi-net/voxplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Budget Plans
head: chunk budget policies
body: Budget Plans provide a system for managing chunk loading policies in chunk-based volume streaming, replacing the previous single octree-focused policy with configurable presets for exploration, whole-volume visualization, and frame-rate maintenance. This method allows an application to switch loading strategies mid-session to balance visual fidelity against performance constraints, addressing the limitation where a single policy was "right for exploring and wrong for a whole-volume figure or for holding a frame rate while rotating". It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Dynamic Chunk Generation with Radius by focusing on high-level policy presets and precedence rules rather than geometric radius calculations, and from Chunk Loading/Unloading Scanner by managing the intent of the load queue rather than the mechanical scanning of the spatial hierarchy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current chunk state (minLevel, halo), a named preset string ('focus', 'uniform', 'interactive'), or an explicit plan object. Outputs: A resolved BudgetPlan object containing parameters for the chunk loader, including radius, minLevel, and halo settings. Data Structures: BudgetPlan: An object containing loading parameters. Specific fields depend on the variant (e.g., gridDims for Exact Lattice Grid). Presets: Three predefined configurations: 1. focus: Baseline octree-focused policy. 2. uniform: Uniform detail shrink pass. 3. interactive: Frame-rate holding policy. Parameters: Presets: focus, uniform, interactive. Precedence (lowest to highest): 1. Focus baseline. 2. Named preset. 3. Explicit plan object. 4. Individual options. targetFrameMs: Resolved and readable, but currently inert (nothing acts on it yet). Steps: 1. Resolve Plan: Call resolveBudgetPlan with the desired input. The function applies the precedence rules to determine the final configuration. If a named preset is used, it overrides the focus baseline but is overridden by explicit options. 2. Switch Plan: Call setBudgetPlan to apply the resolved plan mid-session. This function "re-folds over load options" to update the streaming state. 3. Preserve State: During the switch, minLevel and halo are taken from the current state. This prevents the switch from undoing a user-set setMaxDetail or undercutting a wider kernel already streamed. 4. Uniform Radius: If the radius parameter is set to 'volume', it enables a uniform detail shrink pass. This pass only affects levels beyond the specified radius, and the budget pass converges on the finest uniform level that fits within that radius. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resolvebudgetplan(inputconfig, currentstate): """ Resolves the final budget plan based on precedence. inputconfig: dict or string. Can be 'focus', 'uniform', 'interactive', or a dict with explicit options. currentstate: dict with 'minLevel' and 'halo'. """ # Precedence 1: Focus baseline (lowest) plan = { 'radius': 'default', 'minLevel': currentstate['minLevel'], # Inherited from state 'halo': currentstate['halo'] # Inherited from state } # Precedence 2: Named preset if isinstance(inputconfig, str): if inputconfig == 'uniform': plan['radius'] = 'volume' # Enables uniform detail shrink pass elif inputconfig == 'interactive': # Specific interactive logic not detailed in sources pass elif inputconfig == 'focus': # Remains default pass return plan # Precedence 3 & 4: Explicit plan object or individual options if isinstance(inputconfig, dict): # Override specific fields if present in inputconfig if 'radius' in inputconfig: plan['radius'] = inputconfig['radius'] if 'minLevel' in inputconfig: plan['minLevel'] = inputconfig['minLevel'] if 'halo' in inputconfig: plan['halo'] = inputconfig['halo'] return plan def setbudgetplan(newplan, currentstate): """ Switches the budget plan mid-session. """ # Re-fold over load options # Ensure minLevel and halo are preserved from current state # to prevent undoing setMaxDetail or undercutting wider kernels finalplan = resolvebudgetplan(newplan, currentstate) # Apply finalplan to the chunk loader # Note: targetFrameMs is resolved but currently inert applyloadingpolicy(finalplan) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: State Undoing: Switching plans must not reset minLevel or halo to defaults, as this would undo user controls like setMaxDetail or disrupt active streaming kernels. Inert Parameter: targetFrameMs is part of the plan but does not currently influence loading behavior. Replaces octree-based brick sizing with an exact lattice defined by gridDims, allowing specific block counts that were previously unreachable due to scalar cellEdge sizing. It sets itself apart by allowing precise control over block counts (e.g., 4, 9, 16) rather than relying on pyramid-based scalar sizing. Choose this when specific block dimensions are required for hardware or rendering constraints. Definition: Uses gridDims[a] bricks per axis, all drawn from minLevel. Steps: 1. Set real gridDims and stride on the plan so chunkAtVoxel indexes it correctly. 2. An axis grows if a brick would exceed deviceLimit, because emitBrick clamps oversize textures, which squashes sampling. 3. Callers read the built plan's own gridDims back to verify the actual dimensions. Pitfall: Previous chunkVolumeMultiLOD sized bricks from a scalar cellEdge, causing reachable counts to step irregularly (e.g., 2, 8, 12, 16, 27, 4 on hoaheart L5), making counts like 4 or 9 unreachable. maxBricks only coarsened by raising the level floor, fighting level control. Per-pane block-loading badges indicating GPU upload queue status, keyed on resident count movement rather than plan total. It sets itself apart by tracking actual stream requests rather than theoretical plan totals. Choose this for accurate UI feedback on GPU load. Definition: Badges key on resident count moving, counting against what the stream actually asked for, not the plan total. Steps: 1. Badge keys on resident count moving. 2. Counts against what the stream actually asked for, not plan total. 3. Absent/empty bricks are never fetched, and LRU evicts them. 4. Holds a per-episode high-water mark so the bar only moves forward. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows mid-session switching of loading strategies without losing user-set detail levels; supports precise block counts via Exact Lattice Grid. Limitations: targetFrameMs is currently inert; Exact Lattice Grid requires careful handling of deviceLimit to avoid texture squashing. When to use: Use when the application needs to switch between exploration (focus), full-volume visualization (uniform), or performance-critical rotation (interactive). Use Exact Lattice Grid when specific block counts are required. Budget Plans were introduced in the niivue project to address the limitations of a single octree-focused chunk loading policy. The design doc is located at docs/budget-plans.md, with remaining streaming work tracked in docs/streaming-todos.md. The implementation includes fixes for chunk eviction issues (e.g., chunk 0 eviction blanking the volume in WebGL2) and adapts to both WebGL2 and WebGPU backends. The Exact Lattice Grid variant was added to support specific block counts in demos like the Zarr demo, which uses a "Blocks control" to choose factorizations closest to cubic. feat(niivue): streamed multi-LOD rendering fixes, LOD compensation, budget plans, and block inspection, https://github.com/niivue/mono/pull/138, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Scalable Distributed Volume Rendering (SDVR)
head: Cluster-based Distributed Volume Rendering, Distributed Volume Rendering System, Distributed rendering system for unstructured data, Distributed slicing rendering, MPI-based distributed volume rendering
body: Scalable Distributed Volume Rendering (SDVR) is a distributed rendering system for unstructured data targeting large PC clusters, using OpenGL and MPI, designed for scalability where rendering time remains constant as data size and node count increase. It solves the problem of rendering massive unstructured grids that exceed the memory or processing capacity of a single machine by partitioning the dataset into load-balanced chunks and distributing them across a cluster. What sets it apart from its siblings is its specific focus on unstructured data via an out-of-core modified k-d decomposition for partitioning, and its design to run with or without graphics hardware on any platform, although not at peak performance without it. Inputs and outputs: Input: A large unstructured volume dataset (e.g., curvilinear or unstructured grids). Output: A final composited image. Data structures: The dataset is partitioned into "brick-shaped chunks". The specific internal layout of these chunks is not detailed in the sources, other than being "brick-shaped" and resulting from a "modified k-d decomposition". Subimages are generated per node and accumulated. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Partitioning): Partition the dataset into small load-balanced chunks in a preprocessing step using an out-of-core algorithm based on a modified k-d decomposition. 2. Distribution: Distribute the brick-shaped chunks to the nodes of the cluster. 3. Local Rendering: Each node slices, clips, and renders its assigned chunks. 4. Accumulation: Gather and accumulate the resulting subimages over the interconnect system. Parameters: Graphics hardware: Optional; the system runs with or without it, though peak performance requires hardware. APIs: OpenGL and MPI. Platform: LINUX/UNIX. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdvrrender(dataset, clusternodes): """ Main entry point for SDVR. dataset: The unstructured volume data. clusternodes: List of available cluster nodes. """ # Step 1: Preprocessing - Partition data # Uses an out-of-core algorithm based on modified k-d decomposition # to create load-balanced, brick-shaped chunks. chunks = partitiondatasetoutofcore(dataset) # Step 2: Distribution # Distribute chunks to cluster nodes. # Mapping logic (which chunk goes to which node) is implied by # "load-balanced" but specific assignment algorithm is not given. nodechunkmap = distributechunks(chunks, clusternodes) # Step 3: Local Rendering (Parallel) # Each node performs slicing, clipping, and rendering independently. subimages = [] for node in clusternodes: assignedchunks = nodechunkmap[node] # Initialize local renderer (OpenGL context) renderer = OpenGLRenderer() # Render assigned chunks # Note: Slicing and clipping are performed per chunk localsubimage = renderchunks(renderer, assignedchunks) # Collect subimage subimages.append((node, localsubimage)) # Step 4: Accumulation # Gather and accumulate subimages over the interconnect system (MPI) finalimage = accumulatesubimages(subimages) return finalimage def partitiondatasetoutofcore(dataset): """ Partitions dataset into load-balanced brick-shaped chunks. Uses an out-of-core algorithm based on modified k-d decomposition. Implementation details of the specific k-d decomposition variant are not provided in sources. """ # Placeholder for the specific out-of-core k-d decomposition logic. # The source mentions it is "modified" but does not specify the modification. chunks = [] #... implementation of modified k-d decomposition... return chunks def distributechunks(chunks, clusternodes): """ Distributes chunks to nodes for load balancing. Specific load-balancing metric (e.g., cell count, memory size) is not specified. """ # Placeholder for load-balancing distribution logic. nodechunkmap = {node: [] for node in clusternodes} #... distribute chunks to balance load... return nodechunkmap def renderchunks(renderer, chunks): """ Renders a set of chunks using slicing and clipping. """ # Placeholder for the specific slicing/clipping/rendering pipeline. # The source mentions "slices, clips, and renders" but does not detail the # ray-casting or projection method used for unstructured data. subimage = renderer.render(chunks) return subimage def accumulatesubimages(subimages): """ Gathers and accumulates subimages over the interconnect. """ # Placeholder for the accumulation/compositing logic over MPI. # Standard alpha compositing or similar technique would be used, # but the specific order or method is not detailed. finalimage = composite(subimages) return finalimage Edge cases and pitfalls: Communication Overhead: The sources note that speed-up curves leveled out after a certain number of threads (5 for one grid type, 18 for another), attributed to communications overhead. This suggests that for very large node counts or small chunks, interconnect latency may become a bottleneck. Hardware Dependency: While the system is designed to run without graphics hardware, peak performance requires it. Running without hardware may result in significantly lower performance. Platform Specificity: The prototype was built for LINUX/UNIX. Porting to other platforms may require significant adaptation. A distributed rendering method for load balancing where adjacent tetrahedra are scattered across nodes rather than clustered, using a global kd-tree to restore ordering during rendering. A volume rendering system that uses a single virtual memory space shared by all rendering nodes and GPUs. Each node refers to the same shared 3D virtual memory space representing the entire volume, accessed independently on each GPU. Ray-casting on each GPU determines small 3D blocks (memory pages) actually accessed. Virtual memory is managed via a two-level hierarchy of page tables, and physical memory is only mapped for the current working set of pages. Scalability: The primary goal is scalability: as the data set size increases, if additional computational nodes are provided, rendering time remains constant. Performance: A prototype ran successfully at interactive rates on up to 32 nodes of a PC cluster equipped with Nvidia GeForce-3 graphics cards. Hardware Requirements: Optional graphics hardware; the system can run on any platform, but peak performance requires hardware. Limitations: Speed-up levels out due to communications overhead when the number of threads/nodes increases beyond a certain point. When to use: Large unstructured datasets (16-1000+ node clusters) where scalability is critical and interactive rates are desired. When not to use: Small datasets that fit on a single node, or when peak performance is required on hardware without the overhead of distributed communication management. The SDVR system was developed for volume visualization of unstructured data, targeting large PC clusters. It was performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under contract no. W-7405-Eng-48. The work acknowledges contributions from Randall Frank, Mark Duchaineau (for cell slicing code), and co-authors. The system is described in the context of volume rendering for curvilinear and unstructured grids.
