name: Parallel Volume Ray Casting (PVR) Library Interface
head: Direct Volume Rendering for Parallel CFD, PVR library API, Parallel Volume Rendering (PVR) Algorithm
body: The Parallel Volume Ray Casting (PVR) Library Interface is a software design for distributed-memory systems that enables in-place rendering of rectilinear grid data without transferring large datasets to a host computer. It separates the rendering pipeline into local resampling (ray casting) and global compositing, allowing interactive monitoring of parallel CFD simulations. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on binary-swap compositing or require regular data partitioning, this interface selects direct compositing to remain independent of the specific data partitioning scheme, prioritizing generic applicability over peak compositing performance. Inputs: 1. Subvolume Pointer: A pointer to the local chunk of the 3D scalar dataset assigned to the current process. 2. Geometry Record: A data structure describing the spatial extent and dimensions of the local subvolume. 3. Rendering Specifications: Parameters including viewing and lighting parameters, image resolution, rendering rate, and transfer functions. Outputs: 1. Partial Image Pixels: The rendered color and opacity values for the subset of image pixels assigned to the current process. 2. Final Composite Image: The complete image formed after global compositing (typically handled by a host or dedicated node). The library interface expects the following structures to be passed from the application program to the renderer: 1. Subvolume Data: A contiguous array of voxel values. The size depends on the data resolution (1 to 12 bytes per voxel). 2. Geometry Record: Contains dimensions of the local block (Dx, Dy, Dz) and its spatial offset relative to the global domain. 3. Rendering Spec: Contains camera position, view direction, image plane resolution (Nx, Ny), and transfer function mappings. 1. Initialization and Broadcast: The host program reads the model and rendering specifications and broadcasts them to every node processor. The application program passes the renderer the subvolume pointer, geometry record, and rendering specifications. 2. Data Distribution (Pre-processing): The 3D domain is decomposed into blocks (preferred over slabs) to ensure sizes in all dimensions are as close as possible. This reduces communication costs for the underlying CFD simulation and makes rendering less view-dependent. Each data subset must contain spatially consecutive voxels. 3. Boundary Replication: Voxels at the boundaries of the distributed data blocks are replicated to handle interpolation near edges. This is required because most CFD codes use a finite-difference formulation, which inherently requires neighbor data. Note: This step could be removed if special boundary care were implemented, but replication is the standard approach for this library. 4. Local Resampling: On each processor, rays are cast from the eye through the image plane into the local data volume. Sampling Rate: One to two samples per voxel are computed. Interpolation: Color and opacity are computed by interpolating from data values using trilinear interpolation for parallelepiped elements (8 vertices). Constraint: No communication is required during this phase. 5. Local Compositing: The color and opacity of samples along each ray segment within the local block are composited front-to-back. The compositing operation is associative, allowing independent processing of segments. 6. Global Compositing (Direct Method): Image Subdivision: The image plane is subdivided, and subsets of image pixels are assigned to each node. Direct Transmission: Each node sends its rendered partial image pixels directly to the node assigned that specific portion of the image plane. Accumulation and Final Composite: Nodes accumulate these incoming partial image pixels in an array. After all rendering is complete, they composite them in proper depth order to form the final image. Selection Rationale: Direct compositing is selected over binary-swap compositing because binary-swap requires regular data partitioning and special data structures, making it less desirable for a generic library design. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pvrlibraryinterface(subvolumeptr, geometryrecord, renderingspecs): """ Main entry point for the PVR library. Args: subvolumeptr: Pointer to local 3D array of voxel values. geometryrecord: Object containing dimensions (dx, dy, dz) and global offset. renderingspecs: Object containing camera params, image resolution (nx, ny), transfer functions, etc. """ # 1. Local Resampling # Cast rays from eye through image plane into local volume # Image resolution is defined in renderingspecs imagewidth = renderingspecs.imageresolution.x imageheight = renderingspecs.imageresolution.y # Determine which pixels this process is responsible for # In Direct Compositing, pixels are assigned to nodes. # This process renders only its assigned subset of pixels. assignedpixels = getassignedpixelsubset(imagewidth, imageheight) localpartialimage = [] for pixel in assignedpixels: ray = createrayfromeye(pixel, renderingspecs.camera) # 2. Sample the volume along the ray # Sample rate: 1-2 samples per voxel samples = sampleray(ray, subvolumeptr, geometryrecord, samplerate=1.5, interpolation='trilinear') # 3. Local Compositing (Front-to-Back) # Compute color and opacity for each sample compositedcolor = 0.0 compositedopacity = 0.0 for sample in samples: # Interpolate value from subvolume using trilinear interpolation # at the sample's 3D coordinate value = trilinearinterpolate(subvolumeptr, geometryrecord, sample.position) # Map value to color and opacity using transfer function color, opacity = applytransferfunction(value, renderingspecs.transferfunction) # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = Cin + (1 - Ain) Csample Asample # Aout = Ain + (1 - Ain) Asample compositedcolor = compositedcolor + (1 - compositedopacity) color opacity compositedopacity = compositedopacity + (1 - compositedopacity) opacity # Early ray termination if opaque enough (optional optimization) if compositedopacity > 0.99: break localpartialimage.append({ 'pixelid': pixel.id, 'color': compositedcolor, 'opacity': compositedopacity }) # 4. Global Compositing (Direct Method) # Send partial image pixels to the node responsible for those pixel locations targetnode = getnodeforpixelsubset(assignedpixels) sendpixelstonode(targetnode, localpartialimage) # 5. Accumulate incoming pixels from other nodes # This process also receives pixels for its own assigned pixel subset incomingpixels = receivepixelsfromothernodes() # Combine local and incoming pixels for the assigned subset finalpixelset = localpartialimage + incomingpixels # Composite in proper depth order # Note: In direct compositing, the "depth order" refers to the order # of ray segments from different blocks. The library assumes the # transmission order or a specific merging strategy handles this. # The source states: "composite them in proper order after all rendering is completed" finalimageforthisnode = compositefinalimage(finalpixelset) return finalimageforthisnode def trilinearinterpolate(dataptr, geometry, position): """ Performs trilinear interpolation on the local subvolume. Requires boundary replication to be handled by the data structure or pre-processing step. """ # Map global position to local coordinates localpos = position - geometry.offset # Check bounds (should be within replicated boundaries) if not iswithinbounds(localpos, geometry.dimensions): return 0.0 # Or handle edge case # Extract 8 corner values #... implementation details of trilinear interpolation... v000 = dataptr[localpos.x, localpos.y, localpos.z] v100 = dataptr[localpos.x+1, localpos.y, localpos.z] #... other 6 vertices... # Interpolate #... standard trilinear formula... return interpolatedvalue def getassignedpixelsubset(width, height): """ Determines which pixels this process is responsible for. In direct compositing, the image plane is subdivided. """ # Implementation depends on the specific image subdivision strategy # (e.g., interleaved fashion for load balancing) pass def getnodeforpixelsubset(pixels): """ Determines which node is responsible for a given set of pixels. """ pass def sendpixelstonode(nodeid, pixels): """ Sends pixel data to the target node via MPI or native communication library. """ pass def receivepixelsfromothernodes(): """ Receives pixel data from other nodes. """ pass def compositefinalimage(pixels): """ Combines pixels from different blocks in proper depth order. """ pass Sample Rate: 1 to 2 samples per voxel. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation for parallelepiped elements. Data Type: Voxels can take 1 to 12 bytes depending on resolution and algorithm. Load Imbalance: Imbalanced load can degrade overall performance by 20-40%. Dynamic load balancing is challenging in runtime visualization because simulation and visualization steps are separated, making static preprocessing impractical. Boundary Interpolation: Without boundary replication, trilinear interpolation near block edges will fail or produce artifacts. Replication is required for finite-difference CFD codes. Memory Constraints: The renderer requires additional memory for data, parameters, and partial images. The memory space is dominated by the volume data size, final sub-image size, and partial image size. Display Bottleneck: If a host processor collects and combines subimages, the serial data stream limits display rates. Memory Space: The memory space for the renderer is calculated as: \text{Memory} = n{voxel} + 4 \times \left(\frac{n}{p} + \frac{n}{p^{1/2}}\right) \text{ bytes} Where: n{voxel} is the total number of voxels. p is the number of processors. n is the number of pixels in the final image. The term 4 \times ((n/p) + (n/p^{1/2})) accounts for the final sub-image size and partial image size. Each voxel can take from 1 to 12 bytes. Communication Cost: For parallel compositing on a bidirectional torus, the communication cost is: C1 \times p \times n \times t{trans} + C2 \times t{overhead} Where: C1, C2 are positive constants smaller than 1. t{trans} is the per-pixel transfer cost. t{overhead} is the per-message overhead. The analysis shows that communication cost decreases as the number of processors (p) increases, making the direct compositing method scalable. Scalability: The rendering phase (resampling) has no communication and scales well. The compositing phase involves inter-processor communication but scales acceptably due to decreasing communication cost with more processors. Performance Degradation: Imbalanced load degrades performance by 20-40%. Efficient dynamic load balancing could remove at least 50% of this degradation. Hardware: Tested on Intel Paragon XP/S using 8 to 216 processors. Implemented in C/C++ with Intel's native communication library NX, with potential for MPI/PVM. Strengths: Allows in-place rendering without transferring large datasets to a host. Direct compositing is independent of data partitioning, making it generic. Interactive visual response is helpful for monitoring CFD simulations. Limitations: Dynamic load balancing is non-trivial and not fully implemented in the base design. Rectilinear grids are assumed; extension to curvilinear or unstructured grids requires additional algorithms. Display rates can be limited by serial data streams if a host processor handles final combination. The Parallel Volume Ray Casting (PVR) Library Interface was designed for distributed memory message passing environments to support runtime visualization of parallel CFD simulations. It was developed to allow interactive monitoring of simulations, such as a three-dimensional Navier-Stokes solver, without the overhead of transferring data to a host computer. The library was tested on the Intel Paragon XP/S system with 8 to 216 processors. The implementation used C/C++ and Intel's native communication library NX. The design focuses on a simple API where the application passes a pointer to the subvolume, a geometry record, and rendering specifications. It is primarily used in scientific visualization for parallel CFD, specifically for visualizing flowfields from Navier-Stokes solvers. The library is designed for rectilinear grids, which are widely used in CFD, though it can be extended to other grid types. name: Parallel Distributed Axis-aligned Volume Rendering using MPI
head: Distributed Front-to-Back Volume Rendering, Distributed Ray Casting, MPI Ray Casting Volume Rendering, MPI Volume Rendering, MPI-based Ray Casting with Data Decomposition, Parallel Front-to-Back Volume Rendering, Parallel Volume Rendering via MPI, Slice-based Compositing
body: This method performs axis-aligned volume rendering by decomposing a 3D scalar dataset across multiple MPI processes, where each process renders a spatial subdomain by casting rays along the projection axis (typically Z) and compositing front-to-back. It differs from global ray casting by distributing data spatially along the view axis rather than distributing rays, which eliminates per-ray communication overhead and enables independent compositing per process. The method supports 1D (x-axis) and 2D (x and y axes) data decomposition to balance load and memory usage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset (e.g.,.raw or.vti), color and opacity transfer function definitions, decomposition parameters (px, py or pz), and rendering parameters (step size, view axis). Output: A final 2D RGB image assembled from partial images generated by each MPI rank. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored as a NumPy array. For.raw files, dimensions are extracted from the filename pattern NxNxM.raw, reshaped to (z, x, y), and axes x, y are reversed. For.vti files, data is loaded via VTK and transposed to align the view axis with the last dimension (e.g., transpose(data, (2, 1, 0)) for Z-view). Transfer Functions: Color TF: Parsed from text files into triplets (scalar, r, g, b) or VTK vtkColorTransferFunction objects. Opacity TF: Parsed into pairs (scalar, opacity) or VTK vtkPiecewiseFunction objects. Local Image Buffers: subimage: 2D array of shape (rows, cols, 3) with dtype float32, storing accumulated RGB color. subopacity: 2D array of shape (rows, cols) with dtype float32, storing accumulated opacity. Numbered Steps: 1. Data Decomposition: The volume grid is decomposed into chunks based on the partition type. 1D Decomposition (X-axis): Calculate chunk size x{chunk} = \lceil x{size} / px \rceil. Rank i receives data slice data[:, xstart:xend,:] where x{start} = i \cdot x{chunk} and x{end} = \min((i+1) \cdot x{chunk}, x{size}). 2D Decomposition (X-Y Plane): Determine grid dimensions x{num} and y{num} such that x{num} \cdot y{num} = px and y{num} is the largest factor of px less than or equal to \sqrt{px}. Calculate x{chunk} = \lceil x{size} / x{num} \rceil and y{chunk} = \lceil y{size} / y{num} \rceil. Rank (i, j) receives data[:, xstart:xend, ystart:yend]. 3D Decomposition (Alternative): Compute chunk indices: procz = rank // (px py), procy = (rank \% (px py)) // px, procx = rank \% px. Calculate chunk dimensions as x{dim}//px, etc. Determine start/end indices for each axis. 2. Data Distribution: Root rank (0) prepares the data chunks. Global parameters (step size, chunk shapes, counts, displacements) are broadcast to all ranks using comm.bcast. The flattened volume data is scattered to each rank using comm.Scatterv with calculated counts and displacements, then reshaped into subdatachunk. 3. Ray Casting and Compositing: For each pixel (i, j) in the local chunk's spatial dimensions: Initialize coloraccum = [0, 0, 0] and opacityaccum = 0. Iterate along the projection axis (Z) with step size s. Samples are generated at z = 0, s, 2s, \dots up to depth. Interpolation: If s=1, sample V = data[z, i, j]. If s>1, perform linear interpolation between grid points z1 = \lfloor z \rfloor and z2 = \min(z1+1, z{size}-1). Vp = (1 - \alpha) V1 + \alpha V2 where \alpha = z - z1, V1 is the value at z1, and V2 is the value at z2. Transfer Function Lookup: Map Vp to color C and opacity A using the transfer functions. Linear Interpolation (Text-based TFs): Find bracketing index k via searchsorted. Clamp to len(keys)-2. Compute interpolation factor \alpha{tf} = (Vp - keys[k]) / (keys[k+1] - keys[k]). Interpolate values. VTK TFs: Use vtkPiecewiseFunction or vtkColorTransferFunction to evaluate C and A. Gaussian TFs (Alternative): Model color as C(x) = \sum wi \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mui)^2}{\sigmai^2}\right) applied to log-transformed values. Front-to-Back Compositing: Update accumulated color and opacity: C{out} = C{in} + (1 - A{in}) C{sample} A{sample} A{out} = A{in} + (1 - A{in}) A{sample} where C{in}, A{in} are previous accumulations, and C{sample}, A{sample} are the current sample's color and opacity. Early Ray Termination: If A{out} \ge 1.0, increment termination counter and break the ray loop. 4. Image Assembly: Each rank sends its subimage and subopacity (combined into RGBA) to rank 0. Rank 0 gathers these images using comm.gather. Stitching: For 1D decomposition, concatenate images along the x-axis. For 2D decomposition, reconstruct the grid using x{num} and y{num}, placing each sub-image at its corresponding spatial location. Normalization: Convert final float32 image to uint8 by normalizing by max() and multiplying by 255. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from mpi4py import MPI def linearinterpolatetf(keys, values, x): """Linearly interpolate value from sorted keys/values array.""" idx = np.searchsorted(keys, x) - 1 if idx >= len(keys) - 2: idx = len(keys) - 2 if idx < 0: idx = 0 alpha = (x - keys[idx]) / (keys[idx + 1] - keys[idx]) return (1 - alpha) values[idx] + alpha values[idx + 1] def raycastchunk(subdata, stepsize, colorkeys, colors, opacitykeys, opacities): """ Perform front-to-back ray casting on a local volume chunk. subdata: numpy array (z, x, y) or (x, y, z) depending on decomposition. Assumes subdata is shaped (depth, height, width) for Z-axis view. """ depth, height, width = subdata.shape subimage = np.zeros((height, width, 3), dtype=np.float32) subopacity = np.zeros((height, width), dtype=np.float32) earlyterminations = 0 # Precompute sample positions and interpolation factors samples = np.arange(0.0, depth - 1, stepsize) intsamples = np.floor(samples).astype(int) alphas = samples - intsamples for i in range(height): for j in range(width): cacc = np.zeros(3, dtype=np.float32) aacc = 0.0 for k in range(len(samples)): zpos = samples[k] zidx = intsamples[k] frac = alphas[k] # Clamp zidx + 1 to prevent out of bounds znext = min(zidx + 1, depth - 1) # Interpolate volume value v1 = subdata[zidx, i, j] v2 = subdata[znext, i, j] vp = (1 - frac) v1 + frac v2 # Get color and opacity from transfer functions # Note: In a real implementation, colorkeys/colors and opacitykeys/opacities # would be passed or loaded. Here we assume they are available. # For brevity, assuming linear interpolation logic as per S1/S3. # Color lookup # cidx = np.searchsorted(colorkeys, vp) - 1 #... (clamping and interpolation logic)... # color =... # Opacity lookup # oidx = np.searchsorted(opacitykeys, vp) - 1 #... (clamping and interpolation logic)... # opacity =... # Placeholder for TF evaluation logic consistent with S1/S3 # color = evaluatecolortf(colorkeys, colors, vp) # opacity = evaluateopacitytf(opacitykeys, opacities, vp) # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = Cin + (1 - Ain) Csample Asample # Aout = Ain + (1 - Ain) Asample # cacc += (1 - aacc) color opacity # aacc += (1 - aacc) opacity # Early termination # if aacc >= 1.0: # earlyterminations += 1 # break subimage[i, j] = cacc subopacity[i, j] = aacc return subimage, subopacity, earlyterminations def main(): comm = MPI.COMMWORLD rank = comm.Getrank() size = comm.Getsize() # 1. Data Loading and Decomposition (Root Rank) if rank == 0: # Load data, trim, partition into subdatachunks # Calculate counts, displacements, chunkshapes pass # 2. Broadcast and Scatter # comm.bcast parameters # comm.Scatterv data # 3. Local Ray Casting # subimage, subopacity, terms = raycastchunk(...) # 4. Gather and Assemble # comm.gather to rank 0 # Assemble final image pass Time Complexity: O(N{pixels} \cdot N{samples}) per process, where N{samples} = depth / step\size. Early ray termination reduces the average sample count. Communication Overhead: O(N{processes}) for gathering sub-images and timing data to the root rank. Memory: Each process stores only its assigned volume chunk and local image buffer, scaling linearly with 1/N{processes} for volume data. Strengths: Eliminates per-ray communication overhead by distributing data; supports load balancing via 1D/2D decomposition; early ray termination optimizes performance for opaque regions. Limitations: Uneven data division if dimensions are not divisible by process count; requires root rank to assemble final image, which can be a bottleneck for very large images. When to Use: Large 3D scalar datasets that fit in aggregate memory but not in a single node's memory; axis-aligned views (X, Y, or Z). When Not to Use: Arbitrary view directions (requires more complex decomposition or ray distribution); interactive rendering with frequent view changes (decomposition overhead). This method is implemented in academic research projects using Python, mpi4py, and VTK. It is designed for parallel volume rendering workflows on HPC clusters, leveraging MPI for distributed memory communication. The approach builds on the principles of distributed computing and load balancing in volume rendering, specifically focusing on spatial decomposition [Parent]. name: Parallel DVR Algorithm (Object-Space Decomposition)
head: OS-DVR, OS-Parallel DVR Algorithm, View-Dependent Remapping DVR, Proposed OS-parallel DVR algorithm
body: The Parallel DVR Algorithm (Object-Space Decomposition), also known as OS-DVR, is a parallel direct volume rendering method that decomposes the volumetric dataset into clusters to minimize inter-processor communication and redundant ray calculations. Unlike standard domain decomposition methods that fix the data distribution, OS-DVR employs a view-dependent remapping phase to dynamically reassign clusters based on the current viewing parameters, thereby optimizing load balance and communication overhead for each visualization instance. It builds on MPI Volume Rendering (1D/2D Decomposition) by introducing a graph-partitioning-based remapping step that adapts the static data distribution to the view. The algorithm consists of four consecutive phases: Clustering, Remapping, Local Rendering, and Pixel Merging. The Clustering phase is a view-independent preprocessing step performed once. The subsequent three phases are executed for each visualization instance. Inputs: Volumetric dataset V (unstructured grid, e.g., tetrahedral cells). Number of processors K. Total number of clusters a (empirically determined). Viewing parameters (camera position, direction, etc.). Outputs: Final rendered image. 1. Visualization Graph (Qv): Nodes: Represent cells of V. Edges: Exist between nodes if cells share a face. Node Weight: Proportional to cell volume (in World Space Coordinates, WSC). This approximates the view-independent load (number of samples). Edge Weight: Proportional to the area of the shared face (in WSC). This approximates the view-independent interaction (ray intersections between cells). 2. Simulation Graph (Qs): Represents the initial distribution of V among K processors from the simulation phase. Used to initialize local clustering. 3. Cluster Data: Each cluster Ci has a unique global identifier. Each processor maintains a ClusterData structure for each of its local clusters, storing the associated tetrahedral cell data. 4. Remapping Graph: Constructed by augmenting the contracted visualization graph with the current cluster mapping. This phase is executed only once before the first visualization instance. 1. Construct Local Visualization Graphs: Each processor Pk (k=1 \dots K) constructs its local view-independent visualization graph Q{vk}, which is the subgraph of the global Qv induced by the nodes (cells) currently local to Pk. 2. Local Partitioning: Each processor Pk performs ak-way partitioning of Q{vk} using MeTiS. The local number of clusters ak is selected to be proportional to the total node weight in Q{vk} such that \sum{k=1}^{K} ak = a. 3. Global Clustering Solution: The collection of local partitions constitutes the global clustering solution C = [C1, C2, \dots, Ca]. Assign unique global cluster identifiers and determine the initial global mapping function M for these clusters. This phase is executed for each visualization instance. 1. Weight Estimation: Weight nodes and edges of the contracted visualization graph according to the current viewing parameters using efficient node and edge weight estimation schemes. Note: The specific formulas for view-dependent weighting are not detailed in the sources, but the goal is to reflect the computational cost and communication volume for the current view. 2. Construct Remapping Graph: Augment the contracted visualization graph to construct a remapping graph using the current cluster mapping M. 3. Partition Remapping Graph: Partition the remapping graph using RM-MeTiS (a modified MeTiS package) to find new mappings for the clusters. The partitioning minimizes cutsize (minimizing inter-processor communication volume and redundant ray segments) while maintaining balance (computational load balance). 4. Migration: Identify clusters whose new mappings differ from their current mappings. Migrate these clusters to their new home processors. 1. Each processor Pk concurrently renders its local subvolume (formed by the set of local clusters) using Koyamada's sequential DVR algorithm. 2. Koyamada's algorithm is a standard sequential volume ray casting method. 1. Each processor produces the final image of a distinct screen subregion. 2. Three screen decomposition and assignment schemes are implemented to minimize load imbalance and/or communication overhead due to ray-segment migration. 3. The specific schemes are not detailed in the sources, but they involve assigning screen regions to processors based on the current cluster distribution to reduce communication. Unverified code. Phase 1: Clustering (View-Independent, executed once) # Assume data is initially distributed among K processors based on simulation graph Qs clusters = [] globalclusterid = 0 for processorid in range(K): # Get local cells for this processor localcells = getlocalcells(processorid, volumetricdata) # Construct local visualization graph Qvk # Nodes: localcells, Edges: shared faces localgraph = buildvisualizationgraph(localcells) # Calculate total node weight for this processor totalnodeweight = sum(cellvolume(cell) for cell in localcells) # Determine local number of clusters ak proportional to total node weight # sum(ak) = a ak = proportionaltoweight(totalnodeweight, totalnodeweightallprocessors, a) # Perform ak-way partitioning using MeTiS localpartitions = metispartition(localgraph, ak) # Create ClusterData structures for each local partition for partition in localpartitions: cluster = Cluster( id=globalclusterid, cells=partition.cells, processorid=processorid) clusters.append(cluster) globalclusterid += 1 # Initial global mapping M mapping = {cluster.id: cluster.processorid for cluster in clusters} # Phase 2: Remapping (View-Dependent, executed for each instance) # Construct contracted visualization graph from clusters contractedgraph = buildcontractedgraph(clusters) # Weight nodes and edges based on viewingparams weightedgraph = estimateviewdependentweights(contractedgraph, viewingparams) # Construct remapping graph by augmenting with current mapping remappinggraph = augmentgraph(weightedgraph, mapping) # Partition remapping graph using RM-MeTiS newmapping = rmmetispartition(remappinggraph) # Migrate clusters if mapping changes for cluster in clusters: if newmapping[cluster.id] != mapping[cluster.id]: migratecluster(cluster, newmapping[cluster.id]) mapping[cluster.id] = newmapping[cluster.id] # Phase 3: Local Rendering # Each processor renders its local subvolume using Koyamada's algorithm localimages = [] for processorid in range(K): localsubvolume = getlocalsubvolume(processorid, clusters, mapping) image = koyamadadvr(localsubvolume, viewingparams) localimages.append(image) # Phase 4: Pixel Merging # Assign screen subregions to processors # Three schemes are available; select one based on optimization criteria screendecomposition = selectscreendecompositionscheme(clusters, mapping, viewingparams) finalimage = mergeimages(localimages, screendecomposition) return finalimage def buildvisualizationgraph(cells): """ Constructs a graph where nodes are cells and edges connect cells sharing a face. Node weight = cell volume. Edge weight = shared face area. """ graph = Graph() for cell in cells: node = graph.addnode(cell, weight=cell.volume()) for i, cell1 in enumerate(cells): for j, cell2 in enumerate(cells): if i < j and cell1.sharesface(cell2): area = cell1.sharedfacearea(cell2) graph.addedge(cell1.node, cell2.node, weight=area) return graph def proportionaltoweight(localweight, totalweight, totalclusters): """ Calculates ak proportional to localweight such that sum(ak) = totalclusters. """ return round(localweight / totalweight totalclusters) def estimateviewdependentweights(contractedgraph, viewingparams): """ Estimates node and edge weights based on viewing parameters. Specific formulas not provided in sources. """ # Placeholder for view-dependent weighting logic # Node weight might depend on ray density, cell volume, and view direction # Edge weight might depend on ray-segment migration probability pass def augmentgraph(contractedgraph, mapping): """ Augments the contracted graph with the current cluster mapping to form the remapping graph. """ # Implementation details not provided in sources pass def rmmetispartition(graph): """ Partitions the graph using RM-MeTiS to minimize cutsize and maintain balance. Returns new mapping of cluster IDs to processor IDs. """ # RM-MeTiS is a modified MeTiS package # Minimizes cutsize (communication) and maintains balance (load) return metispartition(graph, K, objective='cutsizeandbalance') def migratecluster(cluster, newprocessorid): """ Migrates the cluster data to the new processor. """ # Send cluster data to newprocessorid # Update local data structures on newprocessorid pass def koyamadadvr(subvolume, viewingparams): """ Renders the subvolume using Koyamada's sequential DVR algorithm. """ # Koyamada's algorithm implementation # Standard volume ray casting pass def selectscreendecompositionscheme(clusters, mapping, viewingparams): """ Selects one of three screen decomposition schemes to minimize load imbalance and/or communication overhead. """ # Scheme selection logic not provided in sources pass def mergeimages(localimages, screendecomposition): """ Merges local images into the final image based on screen decomposition. """ # Combine image regions pass a (Total number of clusters): Determined empirically. ak (Local number of clusters): Proportional to the total node weight in the local graph such that \sum{k=1}^{K} ak = a. RM-MeTiS: A MeTiS-based remapping tool developed by modifying and enhancing the original MeTiS package for partitioning the remapping graph. Global Clustering Overhead: Constructing the global view-independent visualization graph Qv for global clustering may be very expensive. The algorithm uses parallel local clustering to minimize this overhead. Cluster Weight Variation: The local number of clusters ak is selected to be proportional to the total node weight to reduce variations in cluster weights, which improves the efficiency of graph-partitioning based remapping. Communication Overhead: The algorithm aims to minimize inter-processor communication volume during pixel merging (due to ray-segment migration) and redundant calculations during local rendering (due to additional ray-segments generated by partitioning) by minimizing the cutsize of the partition. Time Complexity: The clustering phase is executed once, providing a preprocessing cost. The remapping, local rendering, and pixel merging phases are executed for each visualization instance. The complexity of remapping depends on the graph partitioning cost (MeTiS/RM-MeTiS). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the visualization graph, simulation graph, cluster data, and remapping graph. The use of local clustering reduces the memory overhead compared to global clustering. Performance: The algorithm minimizes cutsize to minimize both inter-processor communication volume during pixel merging and redundant calculations during local rendering. Strengths: View-dependent remapping allows for dynamic load balancing and communication optimization. Local clustering reduces preprocessing overhead. Limitations: Requires implementation of RM-MeTiS and three screen decomposition schemes. The specific view-dependent weighting formulas are not detailed. When to use: Suitable for parallel volume rendering on distributed memory systems where the viewing parameters change frequently, and dynamic load balancing is beneficial. When not to use: If the viewing parameters are static, the remapping overhead may not be justified. If the preprocessing cost is prohibitive, global clustering might be considered (though it has higher overhead). The OS-DVR algorithm was proposed in a thesis titled "Parallel direct volume rendering of unstructured grids based on object-space decomposition". The work models the OS decomposition problem for OS-parallel DVR as a Graph Partitioning (GP) problem with correct view-dependent node and edge weighting. The proposed model generates a remapping graph by node and edge augmentations to the graph representing the computational structure of the parallel application. A MeTiS-based remapping tool, RM-MeTiS, was developed by modifying and enhancing the original MeTiS package. The algorithm is designed for parallel machines where simulations are performed, leveraging the existing distribution of volumetric data from the simulation phase. name: Adaptive Subdivision in DiffTetVR
head: Adaptive Mesh Refinement, Adaptive tetrahedral subdivision, Gradient-based mesh refinement, Prism Splitting, Tetrahedral Subdivision
body: Adaptive Subdivision in DiffTetVR is a training strategy that refines a tetrahedral mesh by locally subdividing vertices with high accumulated color gradients, aiming to increase resolution in regions of high-frequency detail while avoiding wasted resolution in empty regions. It distinguishes itself from static mesh approaches by dynamically adjusting the mesh topology during optimization based on rendering error signals, and from general adaptive refinement methods by using a specific prism-splitting algorithm with Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) constraints to maintain mesh validity. Inputs and Outputs Input: A tetrahedral mesh (initially generated via regular grid or Delaunay triangulation of SfM points), a set of training images with camera poses, and optimization hyperparameters (learning rates, regularization strengths). Output: A refined tetrahedral mesh with updated vertex positions and colors, optimized for volume rendering. Data Structures The mesh is represented as an unstructured tetrahedral mesh. Vertices store 3D coordinates and color values. Tetrahedra store indices to their four vertices. Adjacency information (incident tetrahedra for each vertex, shared faces for each edge) is required to identify which tetrahedra to split and to solve the CSP for prism splitting. The CSP solver is implemented in C++ in FlipSolver.cpp. Numbered Steps The refinement process is iterative and interleaved with optimization epochs. One epoch is defined as training with 800 renderings from the dataset (e.g., the Tooth dataset). 1. Optimize Colors: For one epoch, optimize only vertex colors. 2. Optimize Colors and Positions: For the next epoch, jointly optimize vertex colors and positions. 3. Acculate Gradients: For the subsequent epoch, accumulate absolute color gradients at every vertex without performing optimization steps. Absolute gradients are used as they were found to result in better outcomes compared to other gradient metrics. 4. Select Vertices: Identify the \hat{N} vertices with the highest absolute color gradient magnitudes. In the reported experiments, \hat{N} corresponds to the 5% of vertices with the highest gradients. 5. Split Edges: For each selected vertex, split all incident edges by inserting a new vertex at the midpoint of each edge. 6. Split Tetrahedra: Split the incident tetrahedra using the newly inserted vertices. Splitting a tetrahedron incident to vertex a results in: A new tetrahedron incident with the splitting vertex a. A truncated pyramid in the form of a triangular prism formed by vertices b, c, d, b', c', d' (where b', c', d' are the new midpoints on edges ab, ac, ad). 7. Solve CSP for Prism Splitting: The triangular prism is split into exactly three tetrahedra. The split direction of the quad faces of the prism is determined by a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) to ensure compatibility with adjacent prisms. Split edges are categorized as 'Rising' (R) or 'Falling' (F) based on the direction of the tessellation edge relative to the extruded prism face in a counter-clockwise manner. Two adjacent prisms sharing a quad face are compatible if one uses an R split and the other uses an F split. CSP Constraints: 1. The splits for one prism may not be FFF or RRR. 2. Two adjacent prisms must split a shared quad face using exactly one F and one R split. A lookup table for vertex indices for different splitting patterns (FRR, RFR, FFR, RRF, FRF, RFF) is provided in the source, mapping tetrahedron indices to prism vertex indices. 8. Repeat: Repeat steps 1-7 until a target amount of tetrahedra is reached. 9. Final Optimization: In the final iteration, optimize only vertex colors to produce the final result. Formulas Midpoint Calculation: For an edge between vertices u and v, the new midpoint vertex m is calculated as: m = \frac{u + v}{2} Gradient Selection: Vertices vi are selected if their absolute gradient magnitude |gi| is among the top \hat{N} values, where \hat{N} = 0.05 \times V (for 5% selection). Parameters \hat{N}: The number of vertices with the largest gradient magnitudes selected for subdivision. In experiments, this was set to 5% of the total vertices. Learning Rate for Vertex Positions (l{rp}): Must be very low (e.g., 1e-6 or 5e-6) to avoid instability. Higher rates cause degenerate tetrahedra. Regularization Strength (\lambda): Used in vertex position optimization. Set to 10 in experiments. Softplus Parameter (\beta): Used in regularization. Set to 100 in experiments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Instability: Optimization of vertex positions is unstable, especially as the mesh becomes more subdivided and tetrahedra get smaller, increasing the chance of inversion. Recursive Subdivision: Subdivision does not sufficiently lower local error, causing recursive subdivision of the same regions. This eventually halts optimization progress as CSP solving and data structure updates dominate computation time. Incompatible Splits: Incompatible splits on shared quad faces lead to infinitesimally thin holes in the tet mesh. This occurs if adjacent prisms choose the same split direction (e.g., both R or both F) on a shared face. Performance: Unlike color-only optimization (PSNR ~33.5), vertex position optimization with fixed \beta=100 and \lambda=10 achieves a significantly lower PSNR of approx. 26.9 and is only stable at learning rates 1e-6 and 5e-6. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivesubdivision(mesh, images, cameras, targettetcount, gradientpercent=0.05): """ Performs adaptive subdivision on a tetrahedral mesh based on accumulated color gradients. Args: mesh: Initial tetrahedral mesh object with vertices and tetrahedra. images: List of training images. cameras: List of camera poses corresponding to images. targettetcount: Target number of tetrahedra to reach. gradientpercent: Percentage of vertices with highest gradients to subdivide. Returns: Refined mesh with optimized vertex colors and positions. """ # Initialize vertex colors and positions if not already done # mesh.vertices: list of [x, y, z, r, g, b] # mesh.tetrahedra: list of [v0, v1, v2, v3] indices currenttetcount = len(mesh.tetrahedra) while currenttetcount < targettetcount: # Step 1: Optimize Colors optimizecolors(mesh, images, cameras) # Step 2: Optimize Colors and Positions optimizecolorsandpositions(mesh, images, cameras, lrpos=1e-6, lambdareg=10, beta=100) # Step 3: Accumulate Gradients gradients = accumulateabsolutegradients(mesh, images, cameras) # Step 4: Select Vertices numverticestosubdivide = int(len(mesh.vertices) gradientpercent) sortedindices = argsortdescending(gradients) selectedvertexindices = sortedindices[:numverticestosubdivide] # Step 5 & 6: Split Edges and Tetrahedra newvertices = [] vertextomidpoint = {} # Map original vertex index to new midpoint vertex index for incident edges for vidx in selectedvertexindices: incidentedges = getincidentedges(mesh, vidx) for edge in incidentedges: u, w = edge # Create midpoint if not already created for this edge edgekey = tuple(sorted([u, w])) if edgekey not in vertextomidpoint: midv = createmidpointvertex(mesh, u, w) vertextomidpoint[edgekey] = midv newvertices.append(midv) else: midv = vertextomidpoint[edgekey] # Split incident tetrahedra incidenttets = getincidenttetrahedra(mesh, vidx) for tet in incidenttets: # Identify the splitting vertex 'a' and others 'b', 'c', 'd' # 'a' is vidx # 'b', 'c', 'd' are the other three vertices # Create new midpoints for edges ab, ac, ad # Split tetrahedron into one new tet and one prism # Split prism into three tets using CSP splittetrahedroncsp(mesh, tet, vidx, vertextomidpoint) # Update mesh data structures mesh.vertices.extend(newvertices) # Remove old tetrahedra and add new ones # Update adjacency information currenttetcount = len(mesh.tetrahedra) # Step 9: Final Optimization optimizecolors(mesh, images, cameras) return mesh def optimizecolors(mesh, images, cameras): """Optimize only vertex colors.""" # Gradient descent on vertex colors using rendering loss pass def optimizecolorsandpositions(mesh, images, cameras, lrpos, lambdareg, beta): """Jointly optimize vertex colors and positions.""" # Gradient descent on vertex colors and positions # Apply regularization with lambdareg and beta pass def accumulateabsolutegradients(mesh, images, cameras): """Accumulate absolute color gradients at every vertex.""" gradients = zeros(len(mesh.vertices)) for img, cam in zip(images, cameras): # Render and compute gradients # Accumulate absolute gradients pass return gradients def createmidpointvertex(mesh, u, w): """Create a new vertex at the midpoint of edge (u, w).""" upos = mesh.vertices[u][:3] wpos = mesh.vertices[w][:3] midpos = (upos + wpos) / 2.0 midcolor = (mesh.vertices[u][3:6] + mesh.vertices[w][3:6]) / 2.0 newidx = len(mesh.vertices) mesh.vertices.append([midpos, midcolor]) return newidx def splittetrahedroncsp(mesh, tet, splitvertexidx, vertextomidpoint): """ Split a tetrahedron incident to splitvertexidx. Results in one new tetrahedron and one prism. The prism is split into three tetrahedra using CSP. """ # Identify vertices: a=splitvertexidx, b, c, d a = splitvertexidx b, c, d = [v for v in tet if v != a] # Get midpoints for edges ab, ac, ad edgeab = tuple(sorted([a, b])) edgeac = tuple(sorted([a, c])) edgead = tuple(sorted([a, d])) abmid = vertextomidpoint[edgeab] acmid = vertextomidpoint[edgeac] admid = vertextomidpoint[edgead] # New tetrahedron incident with 'a' newtet1 = [a, abmid, acmid, admid] # Prism vertices: b, c, d, abmid, acmid, admid # Split prism into three tetrahedra using CSP # Determine split directions (R/F) for each quad face of the prism # Solve CSP to ensure compatibility with adjacent prisms # Add the three resulting tetrahedra to mesh pass Differentiable Mesh Refinement is a post-processing optimization step that improves the geometric fidelity of a triangular mesh by adjusting vertex positions to better fit an underlying implicit occupancy field. It distinguishes itself from topological refinement methods (such as Recursive Subdivision) by operating directly on the existing mesh topology, using face subsampling to maintain computational efficiency during the optimization loop. This method builds on Adaptive Subdivision in DiffTetVR by providing a final polishing step that decouples geometry adjustment from topological changes. Recursive Subdivision is a deterministic tetrahedral mesh generation and refinement technique used within the DiffTetVR framework to create a hierarchical volume representation. It solves the problem of inefficient resolution distribution by recursively bisecting tetrahedra based on specific geometric cases, ensuring that the resulting mesh maintains high element quality without degradation. Unlike general adaptive refinement which may produce irregular or skewed elements, this method guarantees that recursively splitting a tetrahedron three times yields smaller tetrahedra with exactly the same shape and quality as the initial one, resulting in only well-shaped tetrahedra. Time Complexity: The refinement process involves optimization epochs, gradient accumulation, and CSP solving. CSP solving and data structure updates can dominate computation time after many subdivisions, causing optimization progress to halt. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of tetrahedra and vertices. As the mesh is subdivided, memory usage increases linearly with the number of elements. Measured Performance: On the Tooth dataset, color-only optimization achieves a peak PSNR of 33.5. Vertex position optimization with fixed \beta=100 and \lambda=10 achieves a significantly lower PSNR of approx. 26.9 and is only stable at learning rates 1e-6 and 5e-6. Scaling: The method scales with the number of training images and camera poses. The number of subdivisions is controlled by the target tetrahedron count or gradient percentage. Strengths: Increases resolution in regions of high-frequency detail, avoiding wasted resolution in empty regions. Limitations: Optimization of vertex positions is unstable, especially as the mesh becomes more subdivided. Subdivision does not sufficiently lower local error, leading to recursive subdivision of the same regions. Incompatible splits can lead to infinitesimally thin holes. When to Use: When high-frequency detail is present in specific regions of the volume and a coarse initial mesh is used. When Not to Use: When vertex position optimization is required for stability, or when computational resources are limited due to CSP solving overhead. DiffTetVR was introduced in a preprint titled "DiffTetVR: Differentiable Tetrahedral Volume Rendering". The method builds on DiffDVR by Weiss and Westermann. The prism splitting algorithm is based on work by Erleben et al.. Initial tetrahedral meshes can be generated using regular grids or Delaunay triangulation of sparse point clouds from SfM algorithms like COLMAP. name: Differentiable Mesh Refinement
head: Gradient-based mesh refinement
body: Differentiable Mesh Refinement is a post-processing optimization step that improves the geometric fidelity of a triangular mesh by adjusting vertex positions to better fit an underlying implicit occupancy field. It distinguishes itself from topological refinement methods (such as Recursive Subdivision) by operating directly on the existing mesh topology, using face subsampling to maintain computational efficiency during the optimization loop. This method builds on Adaptive Subdivision in DiffTetVR by providing a final polishing step that decouples geometry adjustment from topological changes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An initial triangular mesh defined by vertex positions V0, a trained neural network implicit field model f(\cdot) (specifically its decode method), and a target threshold value (typically 0.5 for sigmoid outputs). Output: Optimized vertex positions V^ that minimize the discrepancy between the mesh surface and the implicit field's zero-level set. Data Structures: Vertices: A PyTorch torch.nn.Parameter tensor of shape (Nv, 3), where Nv is the number of vertices. This allows gradients to flow back to vertex positions. Faces: A tensor of shape (Nf, 3) containing indices into the vertex tensor. Optimizer: RMSprop optimizer instance configured for the vertex parameters. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the mesh vertices as a trainable parameter: V = \text{Parameter}(V0). Initialize an RMSprop optimizer with learning rate \eta = 10^{-5} for V. 2. Iteration: For each refinement step k from 1 to K (where K is self.refinementstep): a. Face Subsampling: Select a batch of B faces (size self.refinemaxfaces) from the mesh to manage GPU memory. b. Point Sampling: For each face in the batch, sample points on the triangle surface. Let the face vertices be v0, v1, v2. Generate barycentric coordinates \epsilon by sampling from a Dirichlet distribution with parameters (0.5, 0.5, 0.5): \epsilon \sim \text{Dirichlet}((0.5, 0.5, 0.5)) Compute the sampled point p for each face: p = \sum{i=0}^{2} \epsiloni vi c. Normal Estimation: Compute the geometric face normal n{geo} from the current vertex positions: v1' = v1 - v0, \quad v2' = v2 - v1 n{raw} = v1' \times v2' n{geo} = \frac{n{raw}}{\|n{raw}\| + \epsilon{num}} where \epsilon{num} = 10^{-10}. d. Implicit Field Query: Query the neural network for scalar field values at the sampled points p. The model output is passed through a sigmoid function: S = \sigma(f{\text{decode}}(p, c)) where c represents any conditioning inputs (e.g., camera pose or identity). Large batches are split into chunks of 20,000 points to prevent memory overflow. e. Target Normal Computation: Compute the target normal n{target} via automatic differentiation of the scalar field with respect to the point positions. This represents the gradient of the implicit field: n{raw\target} = -\nablap S Specifically, using autograd.grad with creategraph=True: n{raw\target} = -\frac{\partial \sum S}{\partial p} Normalize the target normal: n{target} = \frac{n{raw\target}}{\|n{raw\target}\| + \epsilon{num}} f. Loss Calculation: Define the loss function as a combination of field value proximity and normal alignment: L{val} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{j=1}^{B} (Sj - \tau)^2 L{norm} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{j=1}^{B} \| n{geo,j} - n{target,j} \|^2 L = L{val} + \lambda L{norm} where \tau is the threshold (e.g., 0.5) and \lambda = 0.01. g. Optimization Step: Perform backpropagation to compute gradients with respect to V, and update vertices: V \leftarrow V - \eta \cdot \text{RMSprop\update}(\nablaV L) Parameters: Learning rate \eta: 10^{-5}. Normal loss weight \lambda: 0.01. Batch size (faces per step): Determined by self.refinemaxfaces (Not given in the sources). Chunk size for field query: 20,000 points. Epsilon for normalization: 10^{-10}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Faces: If a face has zero area, the geometric normal computation may result in NaN or zero vectors. The addition of \epsilon{num} prevents division by zero but does not fix the gradient direction. Ensure input meshes do not contain degenerate triangles before optimization. Precision: The use of creategraph=True in automatic differentiation allows gradients to flow through the field query, but deep networks may suffer from vanishing gradients. Monitor gradient norms during training. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes the implicit field is well-defined in the vicinity of the mesh. If the mesh moves far from the trained region of the field, the gradients may become meaningless. Constrain vertex updates if necessary. Improves geometric fidelity by adjusting vertex positions to fit an occupancy field. Distinguishes itself by operating directly on mesh topology with face subsampling. Choose when a final polishing step is needed after topological refinement. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampled points per batch. Each iteration involves a forward pass through the neural network and an automatic differentiation pass. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the batch size of faces and the chunk size for field queries. Memory usage is managed by subsampling faces and splitting large point batches. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Decouples geometry optimization from topology changes; computationally efficient via subsampling; leverages differentiable rendering pipelines for end-to-end training. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained implicit field; sensitive to initial mesh quality; may get stuck in local minima if the initial mesh is far from the target surface. When to use: After topological refinement (e.g., Recursive Subdivision) to smooth and align the mesh with the implicit representation. When not to use: When the mesh topology itself is insufficient (e.g., missing details in empty regions), as this method only adjusts positions, not connectivity. name: Mesh Refinement via Vertex Optimization
body: Mesh Refinement via Vertex Optimization improves the geometric fidelity of a mesh by adjusting vertex positions to better fit an underlying occupancy field. It distinguishes itself from grid-based refinement methods by operating directly on the mesh topology, using face subsampling to maintain computational efficiency during the optimization loop. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Initial mesh vertex positions V0, latent code c, occupancy field representation, and optimization hyperparameters. Output: Optimized vertex positions V^. Data Structures: Vertex Parameters: A PyTorch torch.nn.Parameter tensor initialized from V0. Face DataLoader: A data structure batching faces for efficient processing. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a trainable parameter for vertex positions: v = \text{torch.nn.Parameter}(v0.\text{clone}()). 2. Latent Detachment: Detach the latent code c from the computation graph to prevent gradient retention during this phase: c = c.\text{detach}(). 3. Optimizer Setup: Initialize an RMSprop optimizer for the vertex parameters with a learning rate of 1 \times 10^{-5}: \text{optimizer} = \text{optim.RMSprop}([v], \text{lr}=1\text{e-}5). 4. Face Sampling: Create a DataLoader for the mesh faces with a batch size of refinemaxfaces and shuffle=True. 5. Optimization Loop: Iterate for refinementstep iterations, processing batches of faces from the dataloader. Parameters: refinementstep: Number of optimization iterations. Default: 0. refinemaxfaces: Maximum number of faces used as the batch size for refinement. Default: 10,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.optim as optim from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset def meshrefinementviavertexoptimization(v0, c, faces, refinementstep=0, refinemaxfaces=10000): # Step 1: Initialize vertex parameters from the mesh vertices v = torch.nn.Parameter(v0.clone()) # Step 2: Detach the latent code to prevent graph retention c = c.detach() # Step 3: Initialize RMSprop optimizer optimizer = optim.RMSprop([v], lr=1e-5) # Step 4: Create a DataLoader for faces facedataset = TensorDataset(faces) faceloader = DataLoader(facedataset, batchsize=refinemaxfaces, shuffle=True) # Step 5: Loop for refinementstep iterations for in range(refinementstep): for batchfaces in faceloader: optimizer.zerograd() # Compute differentiable rendering loss against the occupancy field # loss = computerenderingloss(v, c, batchfaces) # loss.backward() # optimizer.step() # The sources do not provide the specific loss function or rendering routine. return v.detach() TetWeave Late-Stage Optimization is a differentiable refinement phase that adjusts the Signed Distance Field (SDF) values, point positions, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients of an existing tetrahedral mesh without modifying its topological structure. name: TetWeave Late-Stage Optimization
body: TetWeave Late-Stage Optimization is a differentiable refinement phase that adjusts the Signed Distance Field (SDF) values, point positions, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients of an existing tetrahedral mesh without modifying its topological structure. It distinguishes itself from earlier stages by decoupling geometry optimization from grid updates, relying instead on multi-view rendering losses (mask, depth, normal) and SDF regularization to polish the reconstruction. This method builds on Mesh Refinement via Vertex Optimization by operating on the final mesh representation derived from the optimized points and SDF. Inputs: Target multi-view data: masks (M), depth maps (D), and normal maps (N). Current state: vertex positions (V), face connectivity (F), tetrahedra (T), SDF values (S) at vertices, and spherical harmonics coefficients (C{SH}). Configuration parameters: loss weights, optimization steps, and SH degree. Outputs: Refined vertex positions (V'), SDF values (S'), and SH coefficients (C{SH}'). The tetrahedral topology (T) remains unchanged. Data Structures: vertices: Tensor of shape (V, 3), float32. faces: Tensor of shape (F, 3), int64, defining the surface mesh. tetrahedra: Tensor of shape (T, 4), int64, defining the volume mesh. sdf: Tensor of shape (V,), float32, SDF values at vertices. shcoefficients: Tensor of shape (V, K), float32, where K is the number of SH coefficients based on the degree. buffers: Dictionary containing rendered mask, depth, and normalsface tensors. Steps: 1. Initialization and Mesh Creation: Construct a surface mesh object from the current vertices and faces. Extract unique edges from the tetrahedra for SDF regularization. python def getedges(tetrahedra): edges = [] for i in range(4): for j in range(i + 1, 4): edges.append(tetrahedra[:, [i, j]]) return torch.unique(torch.cat(edges, dim=0), dim=0) kalmesh = kal.rep.SurfaceMesh(vertices, faces) edges = getedges(tetrahedra) 2. Rendering: Render the surface mesh to the target camera views to obtain buffers. python # Actual differentiable rasterization implementation returns requested buffers buffers = render.rendermesh( kalmesh, targetcameras, self.conf.optimization.trainres, returntypes=self.returntypes, whitebg=False) 3. Loss Calculation: Compute individual loss components weighted by configuration constants. Mask Loss: Mean absolute difference between rendered and target masks. L{mask} = \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum |M{rendered} - M{target}| \right) \cdot w{mask} Where w{mask} is optimization.latestage.loss.maskreg. Depth Loss: Root mean square error between rendered and target depth, masked by the target mask. An epsilon \epsilon = 10^{-8} is added for numerical stability. L{depth} = \text{mean}\left(\sqrt{\text{sum}{c}\left((D{rendered} - D{target}) \cdot M{target}\right)^2 + \epsilon}\right) \cdot w{depth} Where w{depth} is optimization.latestage.loss.depthreg. Normal Loss: Root mean square error between rendered face normals and target normals, masked by the target mask. L{normal} = \text{mean}\left(\sqrt{\text{sum}{c}\left((N{rendered} - N{target}) \cdot M{target}\right)^2 + \epsilon}\right) \cdot w{normal} Where w{normal} is optimization.latestage.loss.normalreg. SDF Regularization Loss: Computes the SDF regularization loss on the edges (pairs of vertices). The weight is dynamic, decreasing linearly with iteration progress to prioritize geometric alignment early and smoothness later. Let t{iter} = \frac{iter}{total\iter}. The dynamic weight w{sdf} is calculated as: w{sdf} = w{sdf\base} - \left( w{sdf\base} - \frac{w{sdf\base}}{20} \right) \cdot \min(1.0, 4.0 \cdot t{iter}) Where w{sdf\base} is optimization.latestage.loss.sdfreg. The loss is: L{sdf} = \text{mean}( \text{sdf\reg\loss}(S, edges)) \cdot w{sdf} Where sdfregloss computes a regularization term over edge pairs. 4. Total Loss and Optimization Step: Sum the losses and perform the backward pass. L{total} = L{mask} + L{depth} + L{normal} + L{sdf} Update the optimizers and schedulers for both SDF and SH coefficients. python totalloss = maskloss + depthloss + normalloss + regsdfloss totalloss.backward() optimizersdf.step() schedulersdf.step() optimizersh.step() schedulersh.step() Parameters: optimization.latestage.loss.maskreg: Weight for mask loss. optimization.latestage.loss.depthreg: Weight for depth loss. optimization.latestage.loss.normalreg: Weight for normal loss. optimization.latestage.loss.sdfreg: Base weight for SDF regularization. sphericalharmonics.degree: Degree of the spherical harmonics used for appearance. optimization.trainres: Resolution of the rendered buffers. accumulationdelaunay: Number of steps before two updates of the Tetrahedral grid. Default value is 5. Setting to 1 updates Delaunay triangulation every step, slowing optimization. resampling.aggregation: Method for computing SDF and SH coefficients of newly sampled points. Options: interpolation (barycentric interpolation) or zero (initialize to 0). resampling.samplingmethod: Method to compute density for resampling. Options: errordensitygt (uses error between target's rendering and current reconstruction's rendering) or functionaldensity (uses explicit function, default constant). resampling.voxelresolution: Resolution of the voxel grid used to estimate the density function during resampling. resampling.steps: Iterations at which resampling occurs and the number of points for each step. Number of points cannot decrease during optimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topology Freeze: The tetrahedral grid topology is not updated during this phase. ODT (Oriented Delaunay Tetrahedralization) loss and fairness loss are not used because the grid is not updated. Numerical Stability: Epsilon (10^{-8}) is added to depth and normal losses to prevent division by zero or NaN gradients during the square root operation. Convergence: The dynamic SDF weight ensures that SDF regularization does not dominate the early stages of refinement where geometric alignment (mask/depth/normal) is critical. Not given in the sources. TetWeave Late-Stage Optimization is a late-stage optimization phase for TetWeave that refines the Signed Distance Field (SDF), point positions, and spherical harmonics coefficients without updating the tetrahedral grid topology, using mask, depth, normal, and SDF regularization losses. It was introduced as part of the broader TetWeave framework to address the need for precise surface alignment after the coarse geometry and topology have been established. The method leverages the differentiability of the rendering process to backpropagate errors from 2D observations to 3D vertex positions, SDF values, and appearance coefficients. name: TetWeave Optimization Pipeline
head: TetWeave implicit surface reconstruction, TetWeave training [S1, unofficial]
body: The TetWeave Optimization Pipeline is a differentiable optimization method that reconstructs a target 3D mesh from 2D multi-view images (masks, depth, and normals) by optimizing a set of 3D points, their Signed Distance Field (SDF) values, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by coupling tetrahedralization-based surface extraction with differentiable rendering, allowing for joint optimization of geometry and appearance without explicit mesh parameterization during the early stages. The pipeline operates in two distinct phases: a main stage where the tetrahedral grid topology is updated periodically, and a late stage where the topology is fixed to refine the scalar field and appearance. Inputs: A set of multi-view images providing target masks, depth maps, and surface normals, along with corresponding camera parameters. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D mesh (vertices and faces) and associated attributes (color/SH coefficients) representing the target object. The optimization maintains three primary learnable parameters stored as torch.nn.Parameter objects: 1. Point Positions (xnx3): Shape (N, 3), where N is the number of points. Stores the 3D coordinates of the optimization points. Initialized randomly within a ball of radius \sqrt{3}. 2. SDF Values (sdf): Shape (N,), scalar field values at each point. Initialized with random values. 3. Spherical Harmonic Coefficients (shcoefficients): Shape (N, \text{num\coeff}), where \text{num\coeff} = (\text{degree} + 1)^2. Stores the SH coefficients for color or feature encoding at each point. Initialized randomly. Additionally, the method maintains: Tetrahedra (tetrahedra): Shape (T, 4), indices of vertices forming each tetrahedron. Mesh Vertices/Faces (vertices, faces): The extracted mesh geometry from marching tetrahedra. accumulationdelaunay: Integer. Frequency (in iterations) to re-tetrahedralize points. Controls how often the mesh topology is updated. sphericalharmonics.degree: Integer. Degree of SH used, must be between 0 and 4. Determines numcoeff. resamplingdict: Dictionary mapping iteration numbers to target point counts. Triggers resampling when the current iteration matches a key. samplingmethod: String. Resampling strategy, either "functionaldensity" or "errordensitygt". lrsdf, lrxnx3, lrsh: Learning rates for the AdamW optimizers associated with SDF, points, and SH coefficients, respectively. maskreg, depthreg, normalreg, sdfreg, ODTreg, triangleanglefairnessreg: Weighting factors for the respective loss terms. 1. Initialization: Initialize xnx3 with shape (N, 3) in a ball of radius \sqrt{3}. Initialize sdf with shape (N,) with random values. Initialize shcoefficients with shape (N, \text{num\coeff}) with random values. Create AdamW optimizers for each parameter set with specified learning rates. 2. Main Stage Optimization: Iterate for conf.optimization.mainstage.iter iterations. Fetch target mask, depth, and normals for the current batch of cameras. Topology Update Check: If iter % accumulationdelaunay == 0, call tetrahedralize(xnx3) to recompute tetrahedra based on current point positions. Surface Extraction: Call marchingtetrahedra(xnx3, tetrahedra, sdf, shcoefficients, shdeg) to extract mesh vertices and faces. Rendering: Render the extracted mesh using rendermesh to obtain buffers: mask, depth, and normals. Loss Computation: Compute the following losses: Mask Loss: \mathcal{L}{mask} = \text{mean}(|\text{buffer}{mask} - \text{target}{mask}|) \times \text{mask\reg} Depth Loss: \mathcal{L}{depth} = \text{mean}\left(\sqrt{\sum{c} ((\text{buffer}{depth} - \text{target}{depth}) \cdot \text{target}{mask})^2 + 10^{-8}}\right) \times \text{depth\reg} Normal Loss: \mathcal{L}{normal} = \text{mean}\left(\sqrt{\sum{c} ((\text{buffer}{normals} - \text{target}{normals}) \cdot \text{target}{mask})^2 + 10^{-8}}\right) \times \text{normal\reg} SDF Regularization: Compute dynamic weight: w{sdf} = \text{sdf\reg} - \left( \text{sdf\reg} - \frac{\text{sdf\reg}}{20} \right) \cdot \min\left(1.0, 4.0 \cdot \frac{\text{iter}}{\text{total\iter}}\right) Compute loss: \mathcal{L}{sdf\reg} = \text{loss.sdf\reg\loss}(sdf, \text{edges}) \times w{sdf} ODT Loss: \mathcal{L}{ODT} = \text{loss.E\ODT}(x\nx3, tetrahedra) \times \text{ODT\reg} Triangle Angle Fairness Loss: \mathcal{L}{fairness} = \text{loss.triangle\angle\fairness}(vertices, faces) \times \text{triangle\angle\fairness\reg} Backward Pass: Perform backpropagation to update sdf, shcoefficients, and xnx3 (every accumulationdelaunay iterations). Resampling: If iter is in resamplingdict, increase point count N by concatenating new points and reassigning optimizer param groups to avoid stale gradients. Resampling methods include "functionaldensity" (using a grid-based density function) or "errordensitygt" (using error maps from ground truth comparison). 3. Late Stage Optimization: Iterate for the remaining iterations. Fix xnx3 and tetrahedra topology. Only optimize sdf and shcoefficients. Compute mesh via marchingtetrahedra and render for loss computation as in the main stage, but without topology updates or point position gradients. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tetweaveoptimizationpipeline(conf, initialpoints, targetviews): """ Main optimization loop for TetWeave. """ import torch # 1. Initialization N = initialpoints.shape[0] numcoeff = (conf.sphericalharmonics.degree + 1) 2 # Initialize parameters xnx3 = torch.nn.Parameter(initialpoints) # Shape (N, 3) sdf = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N)) # Shape (N,) shcoefficients = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N, numcoeff)) # Shape (N, numcoeff) # Create optimizers optimizerx = torch.optim.AdamW([xnx3], lr=conf.lrxnx3) optimizersdf = torch.optim.AdamW([sdf], lr=conf.lrsdf) optimizersh = torch.optim.AdamW([shcoefficients], lr=conf.lrsh) # Tetrahedra tensor (T, 4) tetrahedra = None totalmainiters = conf.optimization.mainstage.iter totaliter = totalmainiters + conf.optimization.latestage.iter for iter in range(totaliter): # Fetch target data targets, targetcameras = fetchnextbatch(targetviews, iter) targetmask = targets["mask"] targetdepth = targets["depth"] targetnormals = targets["normalsface"] # 2. Main Stage Logic if iter < totalmainiters: # Check if topology update is needed if iter % conf.optimization.mainstage.accumulationdelaunay == 0: # Re-tetrahedralize points tetrahedra = computedelaunaytetrahedra(xnx3) # Marching Tetrahedra: extract mesh vertices and faces from SDF on tetrahedra vertices, faces = marchingtetrahedra(xnx3, tetrahedra, sdf, shcoefficients, conf.sphericalharmonics.degree) # Differentiable rendering: project mesh to image space buffers = rendermesh(vertices, faces, targetcameras) # Compute Losses # Mask Loss maskloss = (buffers['mask'] - targetmask).abs().mean() conf.maskreg # Depth Loss depthdiff = buffers["depth"] - targetdepth depthloss = (((depthdiff targetmask)2).sum(-1) + 1e-8).sqrt().mean() conf.depthreg # Normal Loss normaldiff = buffers['normalsface'] - targetnormals normalloss = (((normaldiff targetmask)2).sum(-1) + 1e-8).sqrt().mean() conf.normalreg # SDF Regularization titer = iter / totaliter sdfweight = conf.sdfreg - (conf.sdfreg - conf.sdfreg/20) min(1.0, 4.0 titer) # edges: tensor of tetrahedron edges, shape (E, 2) regsdfloss = loss.sdfregloss(sdf, edges.reshape(-1, 2)).mean() sdfweight # ODT Loss odtloss = loss.EODT(xnx3, tetrahedra) conf.ODTreg # Triangle Angle Fairness Loss triangleanglefairnessloss = loss.triangleanglefairness(vertices, faces) conf.triangleanglefairnessreg # Total Loss totalloss = maskloss + depthloss + normalloss + regsdfloss + odtloss + triangleanglefairnessloss # Backward Pass optimizerx.zerograd() optimizersdf.zerograd() optimizersh.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizerx.step() optimizersdf.step() optimizersh.step() # Resampling if iter in conf.resamplingdict: targetcount = conf.resamplingdict[iter] xnx3, sdf, shcoefficients = resamplepoints(xnx3, sdf, shcoefficients, tetrahedra, conf.samplingmethod, targetcount) # Reassign optimizer param groups to include new tensors optimizerx = torch.optim.AdamW([xnx3], lr=conf.lrxnx3) optimizersdf = torch.optim.AdamW([sdf], lr=conf.lrsdf) optimizersh = torch.optim.AdamW([shcoefficients], lr=conf.lrsh) # 3. Late Stage Logic else: # Fix topology and points xnx3.requiresgrad = False # Marching Tetrahedra (using fixed tetrahedra) vertices, faces = marchingtetrahedra(xnx3, tetrahedra, sdf, shcoefficients, conf.sphericalharmonics.degree) # Render buffers = rendermesh(vertices, faces, targetcameras) # Compute Losses maskloss = (buffers['mask'] - targetmask).abs().mean() conf.maskreg depthdiff = buffers["depth"] - targetdepth depthloss = (((depthdiff targetmask)2).sum(-1) + 1e-8).sqrt().mean() conf.depthreg normaldiff = buffers['normalsface'] - targetnormals normalloss = (((normaldiff targetmask)2).sum(-1) + 1e-8).sqrt().mean() conf.normalreg titer = iter / totaliter sdfweight = conf.sdfreg - (conf.sdfreg - conf.sdfreg/20) min(1.0, 4.0 titer) regsdfloss = loss.sdfregloss(sdf, edges.reshape(-1, 2)).mean() sdfweight odtloss = loss.EODT(xnx3, tetrahedra) conf.ODTreg triangleanglefairnessloss = loss.triangleanglefairness(vertices, faces) conf.triangleanglefairnessreg totalloss = maskloss + depthloss + normalloss + regsdfloss + odtloss + triangleanglefairnessloss # Backward Pass (only for sdf and sh) optimizersdf.zerograd() optimizersh.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizersdf.step() optimizersh.step() # Re-enable gradients for xnx3 if needed for next stage or logging xnx3.requiresgrad = True return vertices, faces, shcoefficients NaN/Inf in Losses: Depth and normal losses add 10^{-8} before the square root to prevent NaN or infinity values when denominators are zero or values are negative. Resampling Stale Gradients: When resampling increases the point count, new tensors are concatenated. The optimizer param groups must be reassigned to ensure gradients are computed for the new points. Boundary Conditions: Points outside any tetrahedron receive an index of -1 and zero barycentric coordinates, which may affect interpolation if not handled correctly in the rendering step. SH Degree: The SH degree must be between 0 and 4; higher degrees are not supported by the current implementation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Resampling allows dynamic adjustment of N to balance detail and performance. Strengths: Joint optimization of geometry and appearance; flexible topology updates; differentiable rendering allows gradient-based optimization from 2D cues. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to repeated tetrahedralization and marching tetrahedra; sensitive to initialization and hyperparameters (e.g., accumulationdelaunay); requires multi-view inputs. When to use: When reconstructing 3D meshes from multi-view images with implicit surface representations and differentiable rendering is desired. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The TetWeave Optimization Pipeline is part of the TetWeave framework, which uses tetrahedralization for implicit surface reconstruction. It was developed by Alexandre Binninger. The method leverages differentiable rendering to optimize a set of points and their associated scalar fields to match 2D image observations.
