name: InstantNGP Network Architecture
head: Instant Neural Graphics Primitives Network, InstantNGP MLP, MonoSDF Network, Network Architecture and Implementation
body: This article describes the specific Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) configuration and feature encoding strategy used in the InstantNGP framework, as adapted by subsequent methods like MonoSDF and Point-NeuS. It solves the bottleneck of evaluating high-dimensional neural fields by combining sparse voxel grids with multi-resolution hash encoding. It sets itself apart from the parent NeRF MLP Architecture by replacing the raw positional encoding with a learnable, sparse hash-based feature storage system, and from Tiny NeRF by maintaining larger hidden dimensions for higher fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: The network takes 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 as input. Depending on the specific variant (e.g., MonoSDF adaptation), it may also take viewing direction \mathbf{d}, but the core InstantNGP feature encoding operates on \mathbf{x}. The outputs are latent features which are subsequently processed by specific head networks (SDF, Bias, Color) to produce signed distance values, density, or color. Data Structures: 1. Hash Table: A global hash table maps hashed coordinate indices to feature vectors. The hash function uses a prime number modulus and XOR folding to map multi-resolution grid coordinates to table indices. 2. Multi-Resolution Grids: Features are stored in a set of 3D grids with increasing resolutions. For a given resolution level l, the grid size is typically 2^l \times 2^l \times 2^l. 3. Feature Vector: Each entry in the hash table stores a fixed-size vector (e.g., 2 or 4 floats per resolution level). Network Layout: The architecture consists of three distinct MLPs, all sharing the same InstantNGP input encoder: 1. Base SDF Network: A 4-layer MLP with 256 hidden units per layer. It takes the concatenated features from the hash table and outputs the signed distance value. 2. Bias Network: A 2-layer MLP with 256 hidden units. It takes the same encoded features and outputs a bias term, often used to refine the SDF or density prediction. 3. Color Network: A 2-layer MLP with 128 hidden units. It takes the encoded features (and potentially viewing direction) to output the emitted color. Steps for Feature Encoding (InstantNGP): 1. For an input coordinate \mathbf{x}, quantize it to the grid resolution l for each level l \in \{0, \dots, L-1\}. 2. Compute the 8 corner indices of the voxel containing \mathbf{x} at resolution l. 3. Hash each corner index to a table index using a global hash function h(\cdot). 4. Retrieve the feature vectors \mathbf{v}i from the hash table for each corner. 5. Perform trilinear interpolation of the 8 feature vectors based on the fractional position of \mathbf{x} within the voxel. 6. Concatenate the interpolated feature vectors from all resolution levels l=0 to L-1 to form the final input feature vector \mathbf{f}. 7. Pass \mathbf{f} to the respective MLP heads. Parameters: Hidden Units: 256 for SDF and Bias networks; 128 for Color network. Layers: 4 layers for SDF; 2 layers for Bias and Color. Point Cloud Size: In MonoSDF/Point-NeuS implementations, the input point cloud is downsampled to 2 million points to demonstrate robustness to sparse data. Preprocessing: Depth maps and point clouds are generated using TransMVSNet, taking approximately 1 second per image. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Collisions: The hash table size must be large enough to minimize collisions, but small enough to fit in memory. Collisions cause feature mixing and artifacts. Precision: Trilinear interpolation requires careful handling of floating-point precision to avoid artifacts at voxel boundaries. Sparse Data: The method relies on the hash table being populated. If the input geometry is extremely sparse, many hash entries may be uninitialized, leading to NaNs or zeros. Initialize hash table entries to zero or a small bias value. A variant used in HybridNeRF. Instead of hash tables, it stores multi-resolution features in explicit 3D grids or triplanes as textures. It stores presummed features g' at resolution level L, where g'(v) = \sum{l=0}^{L} g(v, l) for each texel in L. This allows fetching anti-aliased features by interpolating between two levels implied by pixel area p(x). The number of texture fetches per MLP evaluation is reduced to 8, from 24 (3+3×7) in the original hash-based approach, a 3× reduction. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Dominated by the hash table size, which scales with the number of resolution levels and the hash table capacity. Typically fits in GPU memory for real-time rendering. Time: Feature lookup is O(1) per resolution level due to hashing. Trilinear interpolation is constant time. The MLP evaluation is linear in the number of hidden units. Total time per sample is very low, enabling real-time frame rates. Measured Performance: The MonoSDF/Point-NeuS implementation demonstrates robustness with downsampled point clouds (2 million points). Texture storage variant reduces fetches by 3×. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Extremely fast training and rendering due to sparse encoding and efficient memory access. High fidelity with relatively small networks. Limitations: Hash collisions can cause artifacts. Performance degrades if the hash table is too small. Not inherently bounded to a specific volume without additional techniques (e.g., Unbounded inward-facing scene parameterization). When to Use: Use when real-time rendering or fast training is required, and the scene can be bounded or parameterized appropriately. When Not to Use: Use when memory is extremely constrained and hash collisions cannot be avoided, or when infinite unbounded scenes are required without additional parameterization. The InstantNGP architecture was introduced by Müller et al. in 2022 as a method for real-time neural rendering. It was later adapted by MonoSDF for surface reconstruction and by HybridNeRF for hybrid rendering. The MonoSDF variant uses a 4-layer 256-unit SDF network, a 2-layer 256-unit bias network, and a 2-layer 128-unit color network, all using InstantNGP encoding. Point-NeuS: Point-Guided Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction by Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2310.07997, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) HybridNeRF: Efficient Neural Rendering via Adaptive Volumetric Surfaces, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01858, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SIREN Neural Field
head: Sine Neural Field, Sinusoidal Representation Network
body: The SIREN (Sinusoidal Representation Network) is a neural field that maps continuous coordinates to signal values using sine activations with a specific initialization, allowing it to represent high-frequency detail and have well-behaved derivatives. It solves the problem of spectral bias in standard Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), which struggle to learn high-frequency signals. Unlike the MLP Neural Field which typically uses ReLU or similar smooth activations, SIREN uses sine activations throughout (or in the final layer) to enable sharp reconstruction, reaching convergence in ~100 steps where ReLU-MLPs fail even after 2000 steps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Continuous coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d{in}} (typically 2D for images, 3D for volumes). Output: Signal values \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{d{out}} (e.g., intensity, density, color). Data Structures: The network is a sequential stack of layers. Each layer is defined by its input dimension, output dimension, and whether it is the first layer. SineLayer: A linear transformation followed by a sine activation. Fields: infeatures (int), outfeatures (int), isfirst (bool), omega (float). Linear: A standard linear transformation (affine if bias is True). Fields: infeatures (int), outfeatures (int), bias (bool). Parameters: infeatures: Dimensionality of input coordinates. outfeatures: Dimensionality of output values. hiddenfeatures: Width of hidden layers. hiddenlayers: Number of hidden sine layers. bias: Whether linear layers carry a bias (default: True). lastlayerlinear: If True, the final layer is linear instead of sine (default: False). firstomega0: Frequency parameter for the first layer (default: 20.0). hiddenomega0: Frequency parameter for hidden layers (default: 20.0). Initialization: The weights are initialized uniformly to ensure the sine activations operate in a regime where their derivative is non-zero and well-behaved. 1. First Layer: Weights W1 are sampled from U(-\frac{1}{n}, \frac{1}{n}), where n = \text{in\features}. 2. Hidden Layers: For layer i > 1, weights Wi are sampled from U(-\frac{\sqrt{6/n}}{\omega0}, \frac{\sqrt{6/n}}{\omega0}), where n = \text{in\features} of that layer and \omega0 is the appropriate frequency parameter (firstomega0 for the first hidden layer, hiddenomega0 for subsequent ones). 3. Final Layer (if linear): If lastlayerlinear is True, weights W{last} are sampled from U(-\frac{\sqrt{6/n}}{\omega{last}}, \frac{\sqrt{6/n}}{\omega{last}}), where n = \text{hidden\features} and \omega{last} = \text{hidden\omega\0}. 4. Final Layer (if sine): If lastlayerlinear is False, the final layer is a SineLayer initialized like a hidden layer. Forward Pass: The input coordinates are cloned and gradients are enabled on the copy to allow differentiation with respect to the input coordinates (e.g., for computing gradients or Laplacians). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class SineLayer(nn.Module): """A linear layer followed by a sine activation.""" def init(self, infeatures, outfeatures, isfirst=False, omega=30): super().init() self.omega = omega self.isfirst = isfirst self.linear = nn.Linear(infeatures, outfeatures, bias=True) self.initweights() def initweights(self): with torch.nograd(): if self.isfirst: # Uniform(-1/n, 1/n) bound = 1.0 / self.linear.infeatures self.linear.weight.uniform(-bound, bound) else: # Uniform(-sqrt(6/n)/omega, sqrt(6/n)/omega) bound = math.sqrt(6.0 / self.linear.infeatures) / self.omega self.linear.weight.uniform(-bound, bound) def forward(self, x): return torch.sin(self.linear(x) self.omega) class SIREN(nn.Module): """SIREN Neural Field.""" def init(self, infeatures, outfeatures, hiddenfeatures, hiddenlayers, bias=True, lastlayerlinear=False, firstomega0=30.0, hiddenomega0=30.0): super().init() layers = [] # First layer layers.append(SineLayer(infeatures, hiddenfeatures, isfirst=True, omega=firstomega0)) # Hidden layers for in range(hiddenlayers): layers.append(SineLayer(hiddenfeatures, hiddenfeatures, isfirst=False, omega=hiddenomega0)) # Final layer if lastlayerlinear: finallinear = nn.Linear(hiddenfeatures, outfeatures, bias=bias) # Initialize final linear layer weights similarly to hidden sine layers bound = math.sqrt(6.0 / hiddenfeatures) / hiddenomega0 with torch.nograd(): finallinear.weight.uniform(-bound, bound) layers.append(finallinear) else: layers.append(SineLayer(hiddenfeatures, outfeatures, isfirst=False, omega=hiddenomega0)) self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, x): # Clone input and enable gradients for coordinate differentiation xclone = x.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) output = self.network(xclone) return output, xclone Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Convention: Inputs should follow the [-1, 1] convention. Gradient Computation: The input must be cloned with gradients enabled if derivatives with respect to coordinates are required. Spectral Bias: Without sine activations and specific initialization, the network suffers from spectral bias, failing to learn high-frequency details. Maps low-dimensional input coordinates into a higher-dimensional space using fixed sinusoidal bases, enabling the MLP to represent high-frequency details. It differs from SIREN's native sine activations by providing explicit frequency bands as input features rather than relying on the network's internal sine layers. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly faster than ReLU-MLPs for high-frequency signals. SIREN reaches sharp reconstruction in ~100 steps, whereas ReLU-MLPs do not converge in 2000 steps. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of parameters (in\features \times hidden\features + hidden\features^2 \times hidden\layers + hidden\features \times out\features). Strengths: Well-behaved derivatives, ability to represent high-frequency details, fast convergence for smooth signals. Limitations: Sensitive to initialization, potential for exploding gradients if \omega is too large, not given in the sources for specific hardware performance metrics. When to use: When representing signals with high-frequency details or when derivatives of the signal are required. When not to use: For very noisy data or when computational resources are extremely limited and high-frequency detail is not needed. The SIREN was introduced in the paper "Implicit Neural Representations with Periodic Activation Functions" by Vincent Sitzmann, Julien N. P. Martel, Alexander W. Bergman, David B. Lindell, and Gordon Wetzstein. It addresses the limitations of standard MLPs in representing continuous signals, particularly in the context of neural fields for volume rendering and image representation. The method leverages the properties of sine functions to overcome spectral bias, a common issue in deep learning where networks tend to learn low-frequency functions first. name: Fourier Positional Encoding
head: Fourier Feature Embedding, Frequency Bands Embedding, Harmonic Embedding, NeRF Positional Encoding, Positional Encoding (Fourier Features), Positional Encoding Embedder, Sine/Cosine positional encoding, Sinusoidal Embedding, Sinusoidal Encoding
body: Fourier Positional Encoding maps low-dimensional input coordinates (and optionally view directions) into a higher-dimensional space using concatenated sinusoidal functions at exponentially increasing frequencies. This transformation enables the subsequent Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to represent high-frequency details and sharp boundaries that standard MLPs struggle to learn due to spectral bias. It differs from standard positional encoding (used in Transformers) by using fixed, non-learned sinusoidal bases rather than learned embeddings, and from SIREN's native sine activations by providing explicit frequency bands as input features rather than relying on the network's internal sine layers to generate high-frequency responses. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor of coordinates x with shape (batch, inputdims). Output: A tensor of encoded features with shape (batch, outdim). Data Structures: The method is implemented as a class or function factory that pre-computes frequency bands and stores embedding functions. freqbands: A 1D tensor of shape (numfreqs,) containing the base frequencies. embedfns: A list of callable functions that transform the input tensor. If includeinput is True, the first function is the identity function. Subsequent functions apply sine and cosine to scaled inputs for each frequency band. outdim: An integer representing the total output dimensionality. Layout: The outputs of embedfns are concatenated along the last axis. An alternative interleaved layout exists where sine and cosine channels for each input dimension are spaced by a stride of 2 numoctaves. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Embedding Functions: Create an empty list embedfns and set outdim = 0. 2. Handle Input Inclusion: If includeinput is True, append the identity function f(x) = x to embedfns and increment outdim by inputdims. 3. Generate Frequency Bands: Calculate the numfreqs frequency values. If logsampling is True, compute exponents as linspace(0, maxfreqlog2, numfreqs) and set freqbands = 2.0 exponents. If logsampling is False, set freqbands = linspace(2.00, 2.0maxfreqlog2, numfreqs). Optionally, scale frequencies by \omega0: freqbands = omega0 freqbands. 4. Create Embedding Functions for Each Frequency: For each frequency f in freqbands and each function p in periodicfns, create a function g(x) = p(x \cdot f). Bind f and p as default arguments in the lambda definition to avoid closure issues where all functions capture the final loop values. Append g to embedfns and increment outdim by the output dimension of p (typically 1 for sin/cos). 5. Encode Input: Given input tensor x, compute the output by concatenating the results of applying each function in embedfns to x along the last axis. Formulas: Output Dimension: If includeinput is True, \text{out\dim} = \text{input\dims} \times (1 + 2 \times \text{num\freqs}). If includeinput is False, \text{out\dim} = \text{input\dims} \times 2 \times \text{num\freqs}. The factor 2 comes from the sine and cosine functions. Frequency Generation (Log Sampling): \text{freq\bands} = 2.0^{\text{linspace}(0, \text{max\freq\log2}, \text{num\freqs})}. Parameters: inputdims (int): Dimensionality of the input vector (e.g., 3). numfreqs (int, also multires or nharmonicfunctions): Number of frequency bands to generate. Default is often 6 or 10. maxfreqlog2 (int): The maximum frequency exponent. The maximum frequency is 2^{\text{max\freq\log2}}. Typically set to numfreqs - 1. logsampling (bool): If True, frequencies are sampled logarithmically (powers of 2). If False, they are linearly spaced between 2^0 and 2^{\text{max\freq\log2}}. Default is True. includeinput (bool): If True, the original input coordinates are concatenated to the encoded output. Default is True. periodicfns (list of functions): List of activation functions applied to scaled inputs. Default is [sin, cos]. omega0 (float): Scaling factor for frequencies. Default is 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lambda Closure Issue: When generating embedding functions in a loop, variables like freq and pfn must be bound as default arguments (e.g., lambda x, f=freq: torch.sin(x f)). If not, all functions will capture the final value of the loop variable, resulting in incorrect encoding. Precision: For very high frequencies, the argument to sine/cosine can become large, potentially leading to precision issues in floating-point arithmetic. Boundary Conditions: The encoding is periodic. If the input domain is not periodic or if the highest frequency is too high relative to the sampling rate, aliasing may occur. The choice of numfreqs should be guided by the highest frequency detail present in the scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def getfourierembedder(inputdims, numfreqs, maxfreqlog2=None, logsampling=True, includeinput=True, omega0=1.0): """ Creates a Fourier positional encoding function and returns the output dimension. Args: inputdims (int): Dimensionality of input coordinates. numfreqs (int): Number of frequency bands. maxfreqlog2 (int): Maximum frequency exponent. Defaults to numfreqs - 1. logsampling (bool): If True, use logarithmic spacing. includeinput (bool): If True, concatenate original input. omega0 (float): Frequency scaling factor. Returns: embedfn (callable): Function to encode input tensor. outdim (int): Output dimensionality. """ if maxfreqlog2 is None: maxfreqlog2 = numfreqs - 1 embedfns = [] outdim = 0 # Step 2: Handle input inclusion if includeinput: embedfns.append(lambda x: x) outdim += inputdims # Step 3: Generate frequency bands if logsampling: exponents = torch.linspace(0, maxfreqlog2, numfreqs) freqbands = 2.0 exponents else: freqbands = torch.linspace(2.00, 2.0maxfreqlog2, numfreqs) # Scale by omega0 freqbands = freqbands omega0 # Step 4: Create embedding functions periodicfns = [torch.sin, torch.cos] for freq in freqbands: for pfn in periodicfns: # Bind freq and pfn to avoid closure issues embedfns.append(lambda x, f=freq, p=pfn: p(x f)) outdim += inputdims # Step 5: Define the encoding function def embedfn(x): # x shape: (batch, inputdims) # Apply all functions and concatenate outputs = [fn(x) for fn in embedfns] return torch.cat(outputs, dim=-1) return embedfn, outdim Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D \cdot F), where N is the batch size, D is the input dimension, and F is the number of frequency bands. The operation is element-wise and highly parallelizable on GPUs. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D \cdot F) for the output tensor. The frequency bands are pre-computed and stored once. Measured Performance: In NeRF, using 10 frequency bands for position and 4 for view directions allows the MLP to reconstruct high-frequency details like text and fine geometry that a raw MLP cannot. Strengths: Simple to implement, differentiable, and effective at overcoming spectral bias in MLPs. Limitations: The frequencies are fixed and not learned. If the scene contains frequencies outside the range of the chosen bands, details will be lost. The output dimension grows linearly with the number of bands, which can increase the size of the MLP's input layer. When to Use: When training an MLP to represent a continuous signal (like a neural radiance field) that contains high-frequency details. When Not to Use: When the signal is very smooth and low-frequency, or when memory constraints prevent the increased input dimensionality. The method is a core component of NeRF pipelines and SIREN-based architectures. It is inspired by the use of sinusoidal positional encodings in Transformer architectures, but adapted for continuous coordinate representation. It helps the network learn high-frequency scene details. name: Off-Axis Positional Encoding
head: off-axis IPE
body: Off-Axis Positional Encoding is a feature representation technique for neural radiance fields that uses a large projection matrix P to encode the shape of anisotropic Gaussians, allowing disambiguation of Gaussians with identical marginal distributions along basis axes. It solves the ambiguity where axis-aligned encodings produce identical features for distinct Gaussian shapes that share the same diagonal covariance elements. It differs from standard Fourier Positional Encoding by utilizing a non-identity basis matrix derived from the vertices of a twice-tessellated icosahedron to capture off-axis correlations, enabling accurate Kalman-like warping in the presence of highly anisotropic primitives. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix \Sigma representing the integrated Gaussian at a query point. Output: A feature vector representing the projected variances along the basis directions. Data Structures The method relies on a fixed basis matrix P. Dimensions: 20 \times 3 (20 rows, 3 columns). Content: Unit-norm vertices of a twice-tessellated icosahedron, with redundant negative copies removed. Values (row-major): P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8506508 & 0 & 0.5257311 \\ 0.809017 & 0.5 & 0.309017 \\ 0.5257311 & 0.8506508 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.809017 & 0.5 & -0.309017 \\ 0.8506508 & 0 & -0.5257311 \\ 0.309017 & 0.809017 & -0.5 \\ 0 & 0.5257311 & -0.8506508 \\ 0.5 & 0.309017 & -0.809017 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -0.5257311 & 0.8506508 & 0 \\ -0.309017 & 0.809017 & -0.5 \\ 0 & 0.5257311 & 0.8506508 \\ -0.309017 & 0.809017 & 0.5 \\ 0.309017 & 0.809017 & 0.5 \\ 0.809017 & 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.309017 & 0.809017 & -0.5 \\ 0.809017 & -0.5 & 0.309017 \\ -0.809017 & 0.5 & 0.309017 \\ -0.809017 & 0.5 & -0.309017 \end{bmatrix} Steps 1. Construct Basis: Define the 20 \times 3 matrix P as specified above. 2. Compute Projections: Calculate the projected variances for each basis vector. The naive computation is the diagonal of the projected covariance: \text{diag}(P \Sigma P^T). 3. Optimize Calculation: To avoid the computational cost of full matrix multiplication and diagonal extraction, use the equivalent element-wise operation: \mathbf{f} = \text{sum}(P^T \circ (\Sigma P^T), 0), where \circ denotes element-wise multiplication and \text{sum}(\cdot, 0) is summation over rows. Specifically, if Q = \Sigma P^T (a 3 \times 20 matrix), then the output feature vector \mathbf{f} (size 20) is computed as fj = \sum{i=1}^{3} P{i,j} \cdot Q{i,j} for j=1 \dots 20. Parameters Basis Matrix P: Fixed constants as defined. Not given in the sources as a tunable parameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Axis-Aligned Ambiguity: Using only axis-aligned IPE features (identity basis) fails to distinguish the shape of highly anisotropic Gaussians, which are frequent in distant parts of the scene, leading to inaccurate Kalman-like warping. Performance Cost: Computing \text{diag}(P \Sigma P^T) directly is prohibitively expensive for large P. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def getbasismatrix(): """ Returns the 20x3 basis matrix P derived from a twice-tessellated icosahedron. """ P = np.array([ [ 0.8506508, 0., 0.5257311], [ 0.809017, 0.5, 0.309017 ], [ 0.5257311, 0.8506508, 0. ], [ 1., 0., 0. ], [ 0.809017, 0.5, -0.309017 ], [ 0.8506508, 0., -0.5257311], [ 0.309017, 0.809017, -0.5 ], [ 0., 0.5257311, -0.8506508], [ 0.5, 0.309017, -0.809017 ], [ 0., 1., 0. ], [-0.5257311, 0.8506508, 0. ], [-0.309017, 0.809017, -0.5 ], [ 0., 0.5257311, 0.8506508], [-0.309017, 0.809017, 0.5 ], [ 0.309017, 0.809017, 0.5 ], [ 0.809017, 0.5, 0.5 ], [ 0.309017, 0.809017, -0.5 ], [ 0.809017, -0.5, 0.309017 ], [-0.809017, 0.5, 0.309017 ], [-0.809017, 0.5, -0.309017 ] ]) return P def offaxispe(covariancematrix, P): """ Computes off-axis positional encoding features for a given covariance matrix. Args: covariancematrix: 3x3 numpy array, symmetric positive-definite. P: 20x3 numpy array, the basis matrix. Returns: features: 1D numpy array of size 20, containing the projected variances. """ # Compute Sigma P^T. Result is 3x20. # Sigma is 3x3, P^T is 3x20. PT = P.T SigmaPT = covariancematrix @ PT # Compute element-wise product of P^T (3x20) and SigmaPT (3x20) # P^T is 3x20. elementwiseprod = PT SigmaPT # Sum over rows (axis 0) to get a 1x20 vector, then flatten to 20. features = np.sum(elementwiseprod, axis=0) return features Uses the identity matrix as the basis. Only diagonal elements of \Sigma are used. Fails to capture anisotropic shape information. Choose when computational budget is extremely tight and scene geometry is isotropic. 1267-fourier-positional-encoding.md Uses random projections for frequency encoding. Similar intuition to off-axis IPE for capturing shape, but stochastic. 1267-fourier-positional-encoding.md Time Complexity: The optimized calculation requires one matrix-vector multiplication (\Sigma P^T) and element-wise operations. It is modestly more expensive than axis-aligned IPE (which requires only diagonal extraction) but significantly cheaper than the naive \text{diag}(P \Sigma P^T) approach. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the fixed 20 \times 3 basis matrix. Negligible overhead. Measured Performance: In the "bicycle" scene, ablating off-axis features reduces SSIM from 0.687 to 0.664. Strengths: Disambiguates anisotropic Gaussians with identical marginal distributions. Improves warping accuracy for distant, highly anisotropic primitives. Limitations: Slightly higher computational cost than axis-aligned encoding. Requires full covariance matrix \Sigma (not just diagonal). Off-Axis Positional Encoding was introduced in the context of mip-NeRF 360 to improve the handling of anisotropic Gaussians in unbounded scenes. It addresses a limitation of the original mip-NeRF approach, which used axis-aligned encoding (identity basis). The method leverages the full covariance matrix, which is already computed for the Kalman-like warping step, to extract additional shape information via projections onto an icosahedral basis. name: Integrated Positional Encoding
head: Mip-NeRF Positional Encoding, anti-aliased positional encoding
body: Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) is a feature representation that generalizes standard positional encoding to allow a region of space to be compactly featurized, rather than encoding a single point. It solves the aliasing artifacts that occur in neural radiance fields when scene content is observed at multiple resolutions by integrating sine and cosine features over an interval (cone) instead of evaluating them at a single point. This effectively anti-aliases high-frequency features by shrinking them towards zero when the frequency period is small compared to the interval size. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mean position vector \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, the diagonal of a covariance matrix \sigma^2 \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing a multivariate Gaussian approximation of a 3D conical frustum, and a set of frequencies \omega. Output: A vector of integrated Fourier features. Data Structures: Frequencies: A tensor or array of base frequencies \omega. Covariance: The diagonal elements \sigma^2 are extracted from the covariance matrix for the attenuation calculation. Parameters: n\freqs: Number of frequency octaves. Default value is 16. L: The maximum frequency for IPE features. Unlike standard positional encoding, L can be set to an extremely large value and never tuned, as IPE naturally suppresses high frequencies. Steps: 1. Approximate the 3D conical frustum defined by a camera pixel with a multivariate Gaussian distribution. 2. For each pixel, cast a cone instead of a ray. 3. Sample n + 1 values for tk along the cone axis. 4. Compute IPE features for the interval spanning each adjacent pair of sampled tk values. 5. For each frequency \omega, compute the expected feature under the isotropic Gaussian assumption using the closed-form integral. Formulas: The expected value of the sine and cosine features under an isotropic Gaussian with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2 is given by: E[\sin(\omega x)] = \sin(\omega \mu) \exp(-\omega^2 \sigma^2 / 2) E[\cos(\omega x)] = \cos(\omega \mu) \exp(-\omega^2 \sigma^2 / 2) Where: \omega is the frequency. \mu is the mean position. \sigma^2 is the variance derived from the covariance matrix diagonal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch def integratedpositionalencoding(means, covsdiag, freqs): """ Compute Integrated Positional Encoding features. Args: means: Tensor of shape (, 3), mean positions. covsdiag: Tensor of shape (, 3), diagonal of the covariance matrix. freqs: Tensor of shape (nfreqs,), base frequencies. Returns: Tensor of shape (, 3 2 nfreqs), the integrated features. """ parts = [] for freq in freqs: # Calculate omega pi mean omegamean = freq math.pi means # (, 3) # Calculate attenuation factor: exp(-omega^2 sigma^2 / 2) w2sigma2 = (freq math.pi) 2 covsdiag # (, 3) decay = torch.exp(-0.5 w2sigma2) # (, 3) # Compute sine and cosine features attenuated by the decay factor parts.append(decay torch.sin(omegamean)) parts.append(decay torch.cos(omegamean)) return torch.cat(parts, dim=-1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cone Approximation: The method relies on approximating the conical frustum with a Gaussian. Precision: When the variance \sigma^2 is large relative to the frequency \omega, the decay factor \exp(-\omega^2 \sigma^2 / 2) approaches zero, which is the intended anti-aliasing behavior. An alternative approach to handling directional information in neural fields. Performance: Mip-NeRF using IPE reduces error rates relative to standard NeRF by 60% on average on a challenging multiresolution benchmark. Strengths: Eliminates the need to tune the maximum frequency hyperparameter L; effectively handles multi-resolution scenes by suppressing high frequencies when the sampling interval is large. Limitations: Requires casting cones and sampling multiple points along the axis, which is more complex than standard ray casting. The Gaussian approximation of the cone frustum is an approximation. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Integrated Positional Encoding was introduced in the Mip-NeRF paper by Barron et al., presented at ICCV 2021. It was developed to address the aliasing artifacts in NeRF renderings that occur when training and testing images observe scene content from different distances or resolutions. The method generalizes the positional encoding used in NeRF by integrating the features over a region of space rather than evaluating them at a single point. name: MLP Neural Field
head: Baseline MLP, Coordinate MLP, Plain MLP, Plain MLP Neural Field, ReLU-MLP
body: A plain MLP neural field maps continuous spatial coordinates to signal values (such as density and color) using a standard multi-layer perceptron with ReLU activations. It serves as the primary baseline for comparing neural implicit representations, particularly against SIREN, to demonstrate the impact of activation functions on spectral bias and high-frequency reconstruction. Unlike SIREN Neural Field, which uses sine activations to capture fine details, the plain MLP struggles with high-frequency signals due to its smooth activation properties. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor of continuous coordinates z \in \mathbb{R}^{in\features} (typically 3D spatial coordinates [x, y, z]). Output: A tensor of signal values y \in \mathbb{R}^{out\features} (e.g., density and RGB color). Data Structures: The network is a sequential stack of linear layers and activations. Layer 0: Linear(infeatures, hiddenfeatures) with bias. Layers 1 to H-1: Linear(hiddenfeatures, hiddenfeatures) with bias, followed by an activation function. Layer H: Linear(hiddenfeatures, outfeatures) with bias. Activation: Default is ReLU. Other options include Tanh or GELU. Parameters: infeatures: Dimensionality of input coordinates (default 3). outfeatures: Dimensionality of output values (default 4 for density + RGB). hiddenfeatures: Width of hidden layers. hiddenlayers: Number of hidden layers. bias: Boolean, whether linear layers carry a bias (default True). activation: String name of the activation function (default "ReLU"). steps: Number of training steps (default 2000 for image fitting). Algorithm: 1. Input Preparation: Clone the input coordinate tensor z and enable gradient tracking on the copy to allow differentiation with respect to coordinates. 2. Forward Pass: Pass the gradient-enabled coordinates through the sequential MLP layers defined above. 3. Output: Return the computed signal values and the gradient-enabled coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class MLPNeuralField(nn.Module): def init(self, infeatures, outfeatures, hiddenfeatures, hiddenlayers, bias=True, activation="ReLU"): super().init() layers = [] # First layer: input to hidden layers.append(nn.Linear(infeatures, hiddenfeatures, bias=bias)) # Activation for first layer if activation == "ReLU": layers.append(nn.ReLU()) elif activation == "Tanh": layers.append(nn.Tanh()) elif activation == "GELU": layers.append(nn.GELU()) else: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported activation: {activation}") # Hidden layers for in range(hiddenlayers - 1): layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddenfeatures, hiddenfeatures, bias=bias)) if activation == "ReLU": layers.append(nn.ReLU()) elif activation == "Tanh": layers.append(nn.Tanh()) elif activation == "GELU": layers.append(nn.GELU()) # Output layer layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddenfeatures, outfeatures, bias=bias)) self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, z): """ z: [B, infeatures] coordinates Returns: [B, outfeatures] signal values """ # Clone input and enable gradients zgrad = z.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) # Pass through network out = self.network(zgrad) return out, zgrad Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Convention: Inputs typically follow the [-1, 1] convention. Spectral Bias: The network exhibits spectral bias, meaning it learns low-frequency functions faster than high-frequency ones, leading to blurry reconstructions compared to SIREN. Gradient Computation: Gradients must be explicitly enabled on the input copy to compute derivatives like the Laplacian for visualization or regularization. An MLP architecture that concatenates the original input z to intermediate layers specified in inputskips, allowing the network to access low-level features at deeper layers. It differs from the parent MLP Neural Field by explicitly preserving high-frequency input information in hidden representations, a technique popularized by NeRF. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of hidden layers and features per forward pass. Training time is significantly longer than SIREN for high-frequency scenes; e.g., fitting a simple image may require 2000 steps for ReLU-MLP versus 1000 for SIREN, and still fail to converge to sharp details. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of parameters: (in\features \times hidden\features) + (hidden\layers \times hidden\features^2) + (hidden\features \times out\features) weights and biases. Strengths: Simple implementation; serves as a robust baseline for understanding neural field behavior; stable training for low-frequency signals. Limitations: Poor at representing high-frequency details due to spectral bias; requires more training steps to converge on complex scenes compared to sine-based activations. When to Use: As a baseline for comparison; for scenes with low-frequency content; when computational simplicity is prioritized over reconstruction fidelity. When Not to Use: For high-frequency details (e.g., sharp edges, fine textures); when fast convergence is required. The plain MLP neural field was introduced as a baseline method in the context of differentiable rendering and neural implicit representations. It is commonly used to contrast with SIREN (Sinusoidal Representation Networks) to highlight the importance of activation functions in capturing high-frequency signals. The method is implemented in various open-source differentiable rendering frameworks, such as the one by Yonghao Lee. name: MLP with Input Skips
head: Skip Connection MLP
body: An MLP architecture that concatenates the original input z to intermediate layers specified in inputskips, allowing the network to access low-level features at deeper layers. It differs from the parent MLP Neural Field by explicitly preserving high-frequency input information in hidden representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A coordinate vector z \in \mathbb{R}^{in{dim}}. Output: A value vector v \in \mathbb{R}^{output{dim}}. Data Structures: inputskips: A list of integers representing layer indices where the skip connection is applied. Weights Wi and biases bi for each linear layer i. Parameters: in{dim}: Dimensionality of the input vector z. hidden{dim}: Dimensionality of the hidden layers. output{dim}: Dimensionality of the output vector. n{layers}: Total number of linear layers in the MLP. skip{dim}: Dimensionality of the vector z to be skipped. Algorithm: 1. Initialize the hidden state y as the input z. 2. Iterate through each layer index i from 0 to n{layers} - 1: a. If i is in inputskips and i > 0: concatenate the original input z to the current hidden state y: y = [y, z]. b. Apply the linear transformation: y = Wi y + bi. c. Apply the ReLU activation function: y = \text{ReLU}(y). 3. After the final layer, apply a final linear transformation mapping hidden{dim} to output{dim} if output{dim} \neq hidden{dim}. The final output is v = y. Initialization: Layer 0: Input dimension in{dim}, output dimension hidden{dim}. Layers i \notin \text{input\skips}: Input dimension hidden{dim}, output dimension hidden{dim}. Layers i \in \text{input\skips}: Input dimension hidden{dim} + skip{dim}, output dimension hidden{dim}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F class MLPWithInputSkips: def init(self, indim, hiddendim, outputdim, nlayers, inputskips): self.inputskips = set(inputskips) self.layers = [] # Layer 0 self.layers.append(torch.nn.Linear(indim, hiddendim)) # Intermediate layers for i in range(1, nlayers): if i in self.inputskips: infeatures = hiddendim + indim else: infeatures = hiddendim self.layers.append(torch.nn.Linear(infeatures, hiddendim)) # Final output layer self.outputlayer = torch.nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim) def forward(self, z): y = z for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): if i in self.inputskips and i > 0: y = torch.cat([y, z], dim=-1) y = layer(y) y = F.relu(y) return self.outputlayer(y) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If inputskips contains 0, the skip is effectively ignored because there is no previous hidden state to concatenate to. Precision issues may arise if in{dim} is very large compared to hidden{dim}, causing the skip connection to dominate the gradient. Boundary conditions require ensuring that the concatenation dimension is consistent across all layers. A multi-layer perceptron that computes the derivative of the latent state over time, conditioned on a voxel embedding and a scalar time parameter. It iterates through layers, concatenating the latent state, voxel embedding, and time t at indices in skiplayers. The update rule is z{i+1} = \text{ReLU}(\text{Linear}(zi + \text{Concat}(\text{voxel\emb}, t))) for skip layers, and z{i+1} = \text{ReLU}(\text{Linear}(zi)) otherwise. The final output applies Tanh: z{out} = \tanh(\text{Linear}(z{last})). Parameters include latent{dim} (default 512), hidden{dim} (default 512), and skip{layers} (default [1, 3]). It is chosen when modeling continuous latent state evolution conditioned on spatial embeddings. Time Complexity: O(n{layers} \cdot hidden{dim}^2) for standard layers, O(n{layers} \cdot hidden{dim} \cdot (hidden{dim} + in{dim})) for skip layers. Memory Complexity: O(n{layers} \cdot hidden{dim}^2) for weights, plus O(hidden{dim} + in{dim}) for activations. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. name: Neural Volumes with Multi-Resolution Hash Encoding
head: Hash Encoding Neural Volume, InstantVNR, Interactive Volume Visualization Via Multi-Resolution Hash Encoding Based Neural Representation, VNR
body: Neural Volumes with Multi-Resolution Hash Encoding (InstantVNR) is a real-time volume rendering method that represents volumetric data using a neural field decoded via multi-resolution hash encoding. It solves the problem of high computational cost in neural volume rendering by leveraging GPU tensor cores and a native CUDA neural network framework to achieve interactive frame rates (10–60 fps) with high fidelity (PSNR > 30 dB) and compact memory usage (10–1000x smaller than raw data). It distinguishes itself from other neural field methods by supporting three distinct decoding paths: decoding into a dense 3D texture, sample streaming for host-side inference, and fused in-shader inference, while utilizing macro-cell acceleration for empty-space skipping. The method consists of a neural representation trained on volume data and a CUDA-based renderer that supports iterative ray marching with adaptive sampling. Inputs: Scene JSON containing camera parameters, volume dimensions, transfer functions, and neural network configuration (architecture, hash grid parameters). Outputs: Rendered image (color and alpha), training metrics (loss, PSNR, SSIM), and optionally isosurface meshes. SampleStreamingPayload Used for sample streaming mode. Layout: uint32t pixelindex float jitter RayMarchingIter iter union { vec3f color; vec3f org; } float alpha SingleShotPayload Used for single-shot heuristic mode. Layout: vec3f highestorg vec3f highestcolor float highestalpha Ray vec3f org vec3f dir float alpha (default 0.f) vec3f color (default 0.f, not used by shadow rays) Buffer Allocation (Iterative Mode) Buffers are allocated contiguously and pointers are assigned to params fields in the following order: 1. inferenceinput 2. inferenceoutput 3. alpha 4. colorororg 5. pixelindex 6. jitter 7. itercell (if adaptive sampling) 8. itertnext (if adaptive sampling) 9. iternextcellbegin 10. counter 11. jitterssh (if SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC) 12. interhighestorg 13. interhighestcolor 14. interhighestalpha 15. finalhighestorg 16. finalhighestcolor 17. finalhighestalpha 18. shadingcolor Buffer sizes: numPixelsPadded nSamplesPerCoord sizeof(vec4f) for inference input/output. numPixelsPadded sizeof(SampleStreamingPayload) for payloads. numPixelsPadded sizeof(RayMarchingIter) for iterators. sizeof(uint32t) for counter. If SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: add numPixelsPadded sizeof(SingleShotPayload) 2, numPixelsPadded sizeof(vec4f) for shadingcolor, and numPixelsPadded sizeof(float) for jitterssh. Where numPixelsPadded = nextmultiple(numPixels, 256U) and nSamplesPerCoord = 4 NITERS if mode == GRADIENTSHADING, else NITERS. 1. Initialize Ray Marching Iterator: If ADAPTIVESAMPLING is defined, use dda::DDAIter. Calculate macrocell coordinates: m{org} = org \times self.macrocell\spacings\rcp m{dir} = dir \times self.macrocell\spacings\rcp Call dda::dda3(morg, mdir, tMin, tMax, dims). 2. Iterate Over Macrocells: For each cell interval [t0, t1]: Calculate opacity upper bound r = opacityUpperBound(self, cell). If |r| \le \epsilon (where \epsilon is floatepsilon), skip the cell (return true). Calculate step size ss: ss = \frac{t1 - t0}{N} where N = \lfloor \frac{t1 - t0}{ss{base}} \rfloor + 1, and ss{base} is the input sample size from adaptiveSamplingRate(step, r). Iterate within [t0, t1] with step ss: python t = vec2f(t0, min(t1, t0 + ss)) while t.y > t.x: if not body(t): return false t.x = t.y t.y = min(t.x + ss, t1) If ADAPTIVESAMPLING is not defined, fall back to fixed-step ray marching. 3. Neural Inference: Depending on the rendering mode: Decoding Path: Decode neural volume into a dense 3D texture, then sample it. Sample Streaming: Collect coordinates, launch host-side TCNN inference, then resume kernel. In-Shader: Call fused TCNN inference directly inside the ray march (requires ENABLEINSHADER). ADAPTIVESAMPLING: CMake-defined boolean (0 or 1). Enables macrocell-based empty-space skipping and adaptive step lengths. When 0 or DISABLEADAPTIVESAMPLING=ON, uses fixed-step ray marching. ENABLEINSHADER: Preprocessor define. Enables fused in-shader TCNN inference. Required by INSHADER modes. ENABLEFVSRN: Preprocessor define. Enables fV-SRN backend instead of TCNN. Forces DISABLEADAPTIVESAMPLING=ON and KERNELDOUBLEPRECISION. MACROCELLSIZEMIP: Macrocell edge length is 2^{MACROCELL\SIZE\MIP} voxels. Default 4. Empty Cell Handling: If the opacity upper bound of a macrocell is zero (or near zero, |r| \le \epsilon), the cell is considered empty and skipped entirely. Failure to check this leads to wasted computation on empty space. Precision: When using ENABLEFVSRN, double precision is forced. A neural field method that encodes position and direction separately to predict indirect in-scattering radiance Li(x, \tilde{\omega}), decoupling their effects for view-dependent phase values. It uses a 5-layer perceptron with 64 neurons per layer, ReLU activations, and no output activation. The final radiance is obtained by decoding the log-encoded prediction L'i(x, \tilde{\omega}) using Li = \exp(L'i). It uses 16 grid levels, 8 features per level, a 2x scaling factor between levels, and a hash table size of 2^{19}. The phase coefficient g is left untouched (unitless scale) and not encoded. Inputs are 6-dimensional (position + direction), separately encoded using hashgrid method before passing to the MLP. Unlike most neural field methods that contribute to the full image appearance, photon fields produce only the indirect in-scattering term, allowing for smaller, faster networks due to lower-frequency fields. Time Complexity: Interactive frame rates (10–60 fps) are achieved by leveraging GPU tensor cores and macro-cell acceleration. Memory Complexity: Compact representation, 10–1000x smaller than raw volume data. Performance: High fidelity with PSNR > 30 dB. Scaling: Supports extreme-scale volume data via an efficient out-of-core training strategy, potentially scaling to terascale using an NVIDIA RTX 3090 workstation. Strengths: Real-time rendering, high fidelity, compact storage, out-of-core training support. Limitations: Requires CUDA-capable GPU, specific CMake flags for features like in-shader inference. When to use: Interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets where real-time feedback is needed. When not to use: Offline rendering where pre-training is acceptable and real-time is not required, or on hardware without CUDA support. The method was introduced by Qi Wu, David Bauer, Michael J. Doyle, and Kwan-Liu Ma in the paper "Interactive Volume Visualization Via Multi-Resolution Hash Encoding Based Neural Representation" published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics in 2023. It builds on the concept of neural fields and hash grid encoding. The project is available on GitHub as VIDILabs/instantvnr. name: HashGrid Encoding
head: Feature Grids, Hash Encoding, Instant-NGP Grid Encoding, Instant-NGP Hash Grid, Multi-resolution Hash Grid, Sparse Voxel Grid Hashing
body: HashGrid Encoding is a learnable feature encoding method that maps input spatial coordinates to multi-resolution grid features using spatial hashing and trilinear interpolation, enabling efficient training of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and other implicit neural representations on consumer GPUs. It differs from dense voxel grids by storing features in a sparse hash table, allowing high-resolution details to be captured with significantly less memory than a full dense grid of equivalent resolution. It builds on Hash Grid Neural Fields. Inputs and Outputs: inputs: Float array of shape [B, D], containing B input coordinates normalized to the range [0, 1]. D is the spatial dimensionality (typically 3). embeddings: Float array of shape [sO, C], where sO = \text{offsets}[L] is the total size of all hash tables across L levels, and C is the number of feature channels per level. offsets: Integer array of shape [L + 1], storing cumulative hash table sizes. The size for level l is \text{offsets}[l+1] - \text{offsets}[l]. outputs: Float array of shape [L, B, C]. The level dimension is placed first for cache efficiency. dydx: Float array of shape [B, L, D, C] (or [B, L D C] flattened), storing the gradient of the output with respect to the input coordinates. Parameters: L: Number of resolution levels. C: Number of feature channels per level. Supported values are 1, 2, 4, or 8. H: Base resolution. The grid size at level 0 is H. S: Scale factor determining resolution growth per level. aligncorners: Boolean flag. If true, input range [0, 1] maps to [0, \text{scale}]. If false, it maps to [0.5/\text{scale}, \text{scale}-0.5/\text{scale}], centering the pixels. gridtype: Hashing strategy. 0 = Hash (uses fasthash), 1 = Tiled (linear indexing). Data Structures: The embedding table is a single flat array grid of size \sum{l=0}^{L-1} \text{hashmap\size}l \times C. Access to level l is determined by offsets[l]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Boundary Check: If any coordinate in inputs is < 0 or > 1, set outputs to 0 and return immediately. The backward pass gradient dydx is initialized to 0. 2. Normalization: Normalize input coordinates to [0, 1] if not already done: \text{xyz} = \frac{\text{inputs} - \text{xyz\min}}{\text{xyz\delta}} 3. Level Iteration: For each level l from 0 to L-1: a. Calculate Scale and Resolution: \text{scale} = 2^l \times H - 1 \text{resolution} = \lceil \text{scale} \rceil + 1 b. Map to Grid Space: For each dimension d \in [0, D-1]: \text{pos}[d] = \text{xyz}[d] \times \text{scale} + (\text{align\corners} ? 0.0: 0.5) c. Compute Integer Grid Coordinates: \text{pos\grid}[d] = \lfloor \text{pos}[d] \rfloor \text{pos}[d] \leftarrow \text{pos}[d] - \text{pos\grid}[d] (Note: pos[d] now holds the fractional part for interpolation weights). d. Trilinear Interpolation: Initialize results[ch] = 0 for all ch \in [0, C-1]. Iterate over all 2^D corners of the voxel, indexed by idx \in [0, 2^D - 1]: i. Compute weight w = 1. ii. For each dimension d \in [0, D-1]: If bit d of idx is 0 (lower bound): w \leftarrow w \times (1 - \text{pos}[d]) \text{pos\grid\local}[d] = \text{pos\grid}[d] Else (upper bound): w \leftarrow w \times \text{pos}[d] \text{pos\grid\local}[d] = \text{pos\grid}[d] + 1 iii. Hash Index Calculation: Compute the hash index for the corner. If gridtype is 0 (Hash) and the stride exceeds hashmapsize, use fasthash. Otherwise, use modulo arithmetic on the stride-based index: \text{index} = \left( \sum{d=0}^{D-1} \text{pos\grid\local}[d] \times \prod{k=0}^{d-1} (\text{resolution}+1) \right) \pmod{\text{hashmap\size}} \times C + ch Or using the specific fasthash function: \text{hash}(\text{pos\grid}) = \bigoplus{i=0}^{D-1} (\text{pos\grid}[i] \times \text{primes}[i]) The final index into the grid array is offsets[l] + index. iv. Accumulate Features: For each channel ch \in [0, C-1]: \text{results}[ch] \leftarrow \text{results}[ch] + w \times \text{grid}[\text{index} + ch] e. Store Output: Store results into outputs[l,:,:]. 4. Backward Pass (Gradient w.r.t. Inputs): If dydx is requested: a. Initialize dydx to 0. b. For each level l, dimension gd \in [0, D-1], and channel ch: i. Compute partial derivative using finite differences along dimension gd. ii. Iterate over 2^{D-1} corners for the fixed dimension gd (left and right neighbors). iii. For dimensions nd \neq gd, determine corner position and weight w as in the forward pass. iv. Set \text{pos\grid\local}[gd] to \text{pos\grid}[gd] for the left index and \text{pos\grid}[gd] + 1 for the right index. v. Calculate indices for left and right neighbors. vi. Accumulate gradient: \text{results\grad}[ch] \leftarrow \text{results\grad}[ch] + w \times (\text{grid}[\text{index\right} + ch] - \text{grid}[\text{index\left} + ch]) vii. Write resultsgrad to dydx at offset l \cdot D \cdot C + gd \cdot C + ch. c. Sum gradients over levels and channels to get final dydx. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math PRIMES = [1, 2654435761, 805459861, 3674653429, 2097192037, 1434869437, 2165219737] def fasthash(posgrid): """ Hashes a grid coordinate to a uint32. posgrid: list/tuple of D integers. """ result = 0 for i, coord in enumerate(posgrid): result ^= coord PRIMES[i] return result def hashgridencode(inputs, embeddings, offsets, L, C, H, S, aligncorners=True, gridtype=0): """ Forward pass of HashGrid Encoding. Args: inputs: [B, D] float tensor, normalized to [0, 1]. embeddings: [sO, C] float tensor, the hash table. offsets: [L+1] int array, cumulative sizes. L: int, number of levels. C: int, channels per level (1, 2, 4, 8). H: float, base resolution. S: float, scale factor (unused in standard 2^l scaling, but kept for compatibility). aligncorners: bool. gridtype: int, 0 for hash, 1 for tiled. Returns: outputs: [L, B, C] float tensor. """ B, D = inputs.shape outputs = torch.zeros(L, B, C) for l in range(L): # 1. Calculate Scale and Resolution scale = (2 l) H - 1.0 resolution = math.ceil(scale) + 1 hashmapsize = offsets[l+1] - offsets[l] # 2. Map to Grid Space and Compute Integer Coordinates # pos holds fractional parts after floor pos = inputs scale if not aligncorners: pos += 0.5 posgrid = torch.floor(pos).long() posfrac = pos - posgrid.float() # 3. Trilinear Interpolation leveloutputs = torch.zeros(B, C) # Precompute grid offsets for this level gridoffset = offsets[l] for b in range(B): # Iterate over 2^D corners for idx in range(1 << D): w = 1.0 posgridlocal = [0] D for d in range(D): if (idx >> d) & 1: w = posfrac[b, d] posgridlocal[d] = posgrid[b, d] + 1 else: w = 1.0 - posfrac[b, d] posgridlocal[d] = posgrid[b, d] # Compute Hash Index if gridtype == 0: # Hash # Check if stride exceeds hashmapsize? # Standard implementation uses fasthash directly or modulo # Using fasthash as per source hashval = fasthash(posgridlocal) index = hashval % hashmapsize else: # Tiled # Linear indexing stride = 1 index = 0 for d in range(D): index += posgridlocal[d] stride stride = (resolution + 1) index = index % hashmapsize # Accumulate features # index is relative to hashmapsize, add gridoffset baseidx = gridoffset + index for ch in range(C): leveloutputs[b, ch] += w embeddings[baseidx + ch] outputs[l] = leveloutputs return outputs def hashgridbackward(inputs, embeddings, offsets, L, C, H, S, aligncorners=True, gridtype=0): """ Backward pass of HashGrid Encoding. Args: inputs: [B, D] float tensor. embeddings: [sO, C] float tensor. offsets: [L+1] int array. L, C, H, S, aligncorners, gridtype: same as forward. Returns: dydx: [B, L, D, C] float tensor. """ B, D = inputs.shape dydx = torch.zeros(B, L, D, C) for l in range(L): scale = (2 l) H - 1.0 resolution = math.ceil(scale) + 1 hashmapsize = offsets[l+1] - offsets[l] gridoffset = offsets[l] pos = inputs scale if not aligncorners: pos += 0.5 posgrid = torch.floor(pos).long() posfrac = pos - posgrid.float() for b in range(B): for gd in range(D): # Gradient dimension for ch in range(C): # Channel gradval = 0.0 # Iterate over 2^(D-1) corners for the partial derivative # We fix gd and iterate over other dimensions for idx in range(1 << (D-1)): w = 1.0 posgridlocal = [0] D # Determine corners for non-gd dimensions bitidx = 0 for nd in range(D): if nd == gd: continue if (idx >> bitidx) & 1: w = posfrac[b, nd] posgridlocal[nd] = posgrid[b, nd] + 1 else: w = 1.0 - posfrac[b, nd] posgridlocal[nd] = posgrid[b, nd] bitidx += 1 # Left neighbor (gd bit 0) posgridlocal[gd] = posgrid[b, gd] if gridtype == 0: hashvalleft = fasthash(posgridlocal) indexleft = hashvalleft % hashmapsize else: stride = 1 indexleft = 0 for d in range(D): indexleft += posgridlocal[d] stride stride = (resolution + 1) indexleft = indexleft % hashmapsize # Right neighbor (gd bit 1) posgridlocal[gd] = posgrid[b, gd] + 1 if gridtype == 0: hashvalright = fasthash(posgridlocal) indexright = hashvalright % hashmapsize else: stride = 1 indexright = 0 for d in range(D): indexright += posgridlocal[d] stride stride = (resolution + 1) indexright = indexright % hashmapsize # Accumulate gradient # Note: The source uses w (grid[right] - grid[left]) # But w here is the product of weights for OTHER dimensions. # The weight for gd dimension is effectively 1 for the difference? # Actually, standard trilinear gradient is: # d/dx ( (1-t)L + tR) = R - L # So we just need the product of weights for other dims. valleft = embeddings[gridoffset + indexleft + ch] valright = embeddings[gridoffset + indexright + ch] gradval += w (valright - valleft) dydx[b, l, gd, ch] = gradval return dydx Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out of Bounds: Input coordinates must be in [0, 1]. If out of bounds, the forward pass outputs 0 and the backward pass returns immediately (gradient is 0). AtomicAdd Performance: In GPU implementations, atomicAdd on half is very slow. The implementation uses half2 vectorization when NC \% 2 == 0 (where NC = \min(2, C)) to process two halves at once. If NC \% 2 \neq 0, it falls back to scalar atomicAdd or float. Hash Collisions: Handled by modulo arithmetic on the stride-based index, with a fallback to fasthash when the stride exceeds hashmapsize. Dimensionality: Input dimensionality D is restricted to 2 or 3 in some implementations, throwing a runtime error otherwise. The fasthash supports up to 7 dimensions. Extends hash grid encoding to volumetric data for X-ray/CT reconstruction, using hash grids to store density and opacity features. Choose when working with volumetric medical or scientific imaging data. A variant of hash grid encoding that uses Lagrangian coordinates for hashing, potentially offering better locality or collision properties for specific motion or deformation scenarios. Choose when dealing with dynamic scenes or deformable objects where spatial locality is crucial. Time Complexity: Per sample per level, the complexity is O(2^D) hash lookups and atomic additions. For a batch of size B and L levels, the total time complexity per thread block is O(B \times L \times 2^D). Memory Complexity: O(\sum{l=0}^{L-1} \text{hashmap\size}l \times C) for the embedding table, where hashmapsize scales with the number of levels and desired resolution. The total size is sO \times C, where sO = \text{offsets}[L]. Performance: Enables real-time training of NeRF on consumer GPUs by avoiding the memory overhead of dense high-resolution grids. Strengths: Memory efficient for sparse scenes, supports multi-resolution details, fast lookup via hashing. Limitations: Hash collisions can occur if the hash table is too small, leading to artifacts. Performance depends on hash function quality and collision resolution. Atomic operations can be a bottleneck on GPU if not vectorized. When to Use: When training neural implicit representations (like NeRF) with limited GPU memory but requiring high-frequency details. When Not to Use: When deterministic spatial locality is critical without hashing overhead, or when the scene is extremely dense and sparse hashing offers no advantage over dense grids. HashGrid Encoding was popularized by the Instant-NGP paper for accelerating NeRF training. It allows for the efficient storage and retrieval of features in a multi-resolution hash table, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis on consumer hardware. The method is widely used in modern neural rendering pipelines. name: Rasterization-based Voxelization
head: Cube Mesh Generation, Voxelizing a Triangle Mesh
body: Rasterization-based Voxelization converts a continuous triangle mesh into a discrete 3D occupancy grid (voxel array) or a surface mesh of cubes by projecting the geometry onto a 2D plane and using hardware or software rasterization to determine coverage. It solves the problem of representing complex surface geometry as a volume suitable for ray marching or other volume rendering techniques, distinguishing itself from ray-tracing voxelization by leveraging the efficiency of scan-conversion algorithms. Unlike Interior Voxelize which fills the volume, this method typically performs "shell voxelization," outputting only the surface voxels. The method maps mesh geometry to a fixed-resolution integer lattice. The core logic involves iterating over triangles, determining which voxels they overlap, and marking those voxels as occupied. Inputs: Input mesh vertices (V) and faces (F). Voxel size (vs): dimensions of the target voxel along each axis (voxelsizex, voxelsizey, voxelsizez). Voxel origin (vox\origin): the location of the bottom-left-back corner of the [0, 0, 0] voxel. Precision (p): a factor to reduce "holes" artifacts during rasterization. Outputs: Occupied voxel coordinates (vox\ijk): an array of integer voxel indices. Alternatively, a cube mesh (cube\v, cube\f) representing the voxelized surface. Alternatively, a point cloud where each point corresponds to a voxel center, optionally with per-voxel colors. The implementation often uses a hash table to store occupied voxel data to handle sparse grids efficiently. Hash Table Node (vxvoxeldatat): position: 3D float vector representing the voxel center. color: 3D float vector (optional). next: pointer to the next node in the linked list for collision handling. Output Mesh (vxmesht): vertices: array of size voxels \times 8, storing the 8 corners of each cube. normals: array of size 6, storing predefined face normals. colors: array of size voxels \times 8 (or NULL). indices: array of size voxels \times VOXELIZER\INDICES\SIZE. normalindices: array of size voxels \times VOXELIZER\INDICES\SIZE. nvertices, nindices, nnormals: counters for active elements. 1. Load Mesh: Load input vertices v and faces f. 2. Initialize Parameters: Define voxel size vs and origin vox\origin. Compute half-voxel sizes hvs = vs \times 0.5. 3. Rasterize: Call the internal rasterizer to populate a hash table of occupied voxel data. This step iterates over triangles, clips them against voxel boundaries, and inserts voxel centers into the hash table. Note: In GPU implementations, this step utilizes the hardware rasterization pipeline (vertex, fragment shaders) and atomic operations for concurrent writes into a 3D texture or buffer. 4. Generate Geometry (Optional): If a cube mesh is required, iterate through the hash table. For each occupied voxel, generate the 8 corner vertices relative to the voxel center using the half-voxel sizes. 5. Finalize: Free temporary structures (hash table) and return the output mesh or point cloud. The following pseudocode implements the CPU-based hash-table approach described in, adapted for clarity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizationbasedvoxelization(mesh, voxelsizex, voxelsizey, voxelsizez, precision): # 1. Initialize voxel size and half-voxel size vs = Vector3(voxelsizex, voxelsizey, voxelsizez) hvs = vs 0.5 # 2. Rasterize triangles into a hash table # The internal rasterizer handles triangle-voxel intersection hashtable = vxvoxelize(mesh, vs, hvs, precision) voxelcount = hashtable.size() # 3. Allocate output mesh arrays # Each voxel becomes a cube with 8 vertices outvertices = Array<Vector3>(voxelcount 8) outnormals = Array<Vector3>(6) # Predefined normals for cube faces outcolors = Array<Vector3>(voxelcount 8) if mesh.hascolors else None outindices = Array<uint>(voxelcount VOXELIZERINDICESSIZE) outnormalindices = Array<uint>(voxelcount VOXELIZERINDICESSIZE) # Copy predefined face normals outnormals = copy(vxnormals) # 18 floats (6 normals 3 components) # Define the 8 cube corner offsets relative to center cubeoffsets = [ Vector3(-hvs.x, hvs.y, hvs.z), Vector3(-hvs.x, -hvs.y, hvs.z), Vector3( hvs.x, -hvs.y, hvs.z), Vector3( hvs.x, hvs.y, hvs.z), Vector3(-hvs.x, hvs.y, -hvs.z), Vector3(-hvs.x, -hvs.y, -hvs.z), Vector3( hvs.x, -hvs.y, -hvs.z), Vector3( hvs.x, hvs.y, -hvs.z) ] vertexidx = 0 indexidx = 0 # 4. Iterate hash table and build cube geometry for bucket in hashtable.buckets: node = bucket.head while node is not None: voxeldata = node.data center = voxeldata.position color = voxeldata.color # Generate 8 vertices for this voxel's cube for i in range(8): outvertices[vertexidx] = center + cubeoffsets[i] if outcolors is not None: outcolors[vertexidx] = color vertexidx += 1 # Generate indices for the cube faces (6 faces, 2 tris each, 3 verts each) # Standard cube indexing pattern base = vertexidx - 8 faces = [ [0, 1, 2, 0, 2, 3], # Front [4, 6, 5, 4, 7, 6], # Back [0, 4, 5, 0, 5, 1], # Left [2, 6, 7, 2, 7, 3], # Right [0, 3, 7, 0, 7, 4], # Top [1, 5, 6, 1, 6, 2] # Bottom ] for face in faces: for vert in face: outindices[indexidx] = base + vert indexidx += 1 node = node.next # 5. Return output mesh structure return Mesh(outvertices, outnormals, outcolors, outindices) voxsize: Typically 1.0 / 256.0. voxorigin: Typically [0, 0, 0]. precision: Typical value 0.01f. gapfraction: Spacing between cubes in generated geometry, typically 0.02. Holes: Standard rasterization only covers pixels whose centers lie inside a triangle, leading to small cracks or holes at edges. This is mitigated by the precision parameter or by using conservative rasterization. Overfilling: Conservative rasterization can generate too many fragments, incorrectly filling empty cells. Using MSAA render targets can help solve this. Performance: The output mesh has significantly more vertices and faces than the input, scaling with voxel density. For a torus mesh (441 vertices, 800 faces), a voxel size of 0.75 results in 61,312 vertices and 91,968 faces. Converts a triangular mesh into a discrete 3D occupancy grid by mapping mesh geometry to a fixed-resolution integer lattice. It differs from direct cube generation by focusing on the occupancy grid itself, suitable for ray marching. Accelerates voxelization by parallelizing the iteration over the 2D XY plane of the voxel grid using a GPU compute shader. It retains explicit triangle-voxel intersection logic but distributes the workload, achieving significant speedups (e.g., 50x) for high-resolution grids. Converts a mathematical implicit surface definition into a voxel grid by rasterizing 2D rectangles within a Region of Interest (ROI) and evaluating the implicit function in the pixel shader. It handles complex, non-polygonal geometry directly, unlike triangle-based methods. Rasterizes triangles into a 2D texture buffer in UV space, storing the face ID in the alpha channel to enable per-texel face identification and subsequent 3D position interpolation. It decouples rasterization from 3D grid storage, allowing memory-friendly chunked processing of large meshes. Maps 3D triangle meshes to a voxel grid by leveraging the GPU's hardware rasterization pipeline, projecting triangles onto a 2D plane and using shaders to write occupied voxel indices into a buffer. It distinguishes itself by utilizing the GPU rendering pipeline (vertex, geometry, fragment shaders) and atomic operations. Converts a triangle mesh into a 3D grid by iterating over the bounding box of each triangle and testing each voxel center against the triangle's plane and edge constraints. It uses exact geometric intersection tests (SAT) rather than projection-based heuristics. Converts a triangle mesh into a voxelized representation by rendering the geometry into a 3D voxel buffer, supporting both simple occupancy and normal/color mapping. It explicitly iterates over triangle surfaces to calculate interpolated points and normals. Eliminates voxelization holes caused by standard rasterization by expanding the triangle in clip space and culling the expanded area in the fragment shader. It implements expansion logic manually in the geometry shader using homogeneous plane mathematics. Generates a robust 3D voxel representation by rasterizing the geometry from multiple orthogonal viewpoints, typically along the three principal axes. It resolves 3D occupancy by synthesizing data from distinct projection directions, ensuring complete coverage of complex geometry. Converts triangle meshes into voxel grids by leveraging standard 2D rasterization hardware to compute surface intersections, generating an intermediate 2D representation (position map or 2D texture worksheets) that is then transferred into the 3D voxel grid. This decouples intersection computation from volume resolution. The process of building volume data voxel-by-voxel, considered the third layer in the voxel modeling abstraction hierarchy. It pulls values into a voxel (similar to raytracing), whereas instantiation-based modeling pushes values into voxels. The main loop iterates over voxels in the discrete bounding box, transforms voxel position to world space, samples the primitive, and adds the value to the buffer if positive. A voxelization approach that utilizes the geometry shader to reduce draw calls by selecting the axis from which each triangle has the largest overall projection for fragment generation. It employs conservative rasterization to generate fragments as long as there is something inside the pixel, not only if its center is covered. Hardware support for conservative rasterization is available on Nvidia Maxwell architecture and later. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of triangles and the number of voxels they overlap. GPU implementations scale with the number of fragments generated. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of occupied voxels. Hash-table based approaches use memory proportional to the number of unique voxels. Performance: GPU-based methods achieve significant speedups (e.g., 50x) for high-resolution grids compared to CPU-based methods. Strengths: Fast, leverages existing hardware rasterization pipelines, suitable for real-time applications. Limitations: Output mesh size can be very large compared to the input mesh. Standard rasterization can produce holes or cracks. Conservative rasterization can overfill empty cells. When to use: When real-time performance is required, or when the input is a triangle mesh and a surface voxel representation is needed. When not to use: When deep voxelization (interior voxels) is required, or when exact geometric intersection tests are preferred over rasterization heuristics. The technique is implemented in libraries such as Point-Cloud-Utils and the header-only mesh voxelizer library by Karim Naaji. It is also discussed in the context of production volume rendering and real-time ray-traced voxel global illumination. The method is often compared to geometry shader-based voxelizers, with rasterization-based approaches providing better results due to more accurate surface intersection or rasterization techniques.
