body: 3D Grid Rasterization converts a triangular mesh into a discrete 3D occupancy grid (voxel array) by mapping mesh geometry to a fixed-resolution integer lattice. It solves the problem of representing continuous surface geometry as a volume suitable for ray marching or other volume rendering techniques. Builds on Voxelization. The method typically follows one of two primary implementations: a Triangle-AABB Sampling approach (common in C++ libraries like voxelizer) or a Slice-and-Rasterize approach (common in Python libraries like meshvox). Both produce a 3D grid where each cell indicates occupancy and optionally color. Inputs: A triangular mesh defined by vertices V and indices I. Target grid dimensions: width W, height H, depth D (or a single resolution R for the largest dimension). Optional: Vertex colors (RGB or RGBA). Optional: STL file path (for direct reading). Outputs: A 3D array voxels of shape (D, W, H) or (Z, X, Y). Data type: Boolean (occupancy) or 32-bit integer (packed ABGR color). 1. AABB (Axis-Aligned Bounding Box) Used to cull triangles. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class AABB: min: Vector3 # Minimum coordinates (x, y, z) max: Vector3 # Maximum coordinates (x, y, z) 2. Triangle Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Triangle: p1: Vector3 p2: Vector3 p3: Vector3 color: Optional[Vector4] # RGBA, if present 3. Voxel Grid (C++ Style) Flat array of unsigned integers (ABGR packed). Layout: index = x + y W + z (W H). Size: W \times H \times D. 4. Voxel Grid (Python Style) Boolean array. Shape: (Z, X, Y). Addressed as voxels[z][x][y]. 5. STL Binary Record (for input parsing) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. stlrecorddtype = [ ('normals', np.float32, (3,)), ('Vertex1', np.float32, (3,)), ('Vertex2', np.float32, (3,)), ('Vertex3', np.float32, (3,)), ('atttr', np.int16, (1,)) ] This method slices the mesh at each height z, computes 2D intersection lines, and rasterizes them into a 2D grid. Steps: 1. Read Mesh: Load STL file (binary or ASCII). 2. Scale and Shift: Find min/max coordinates of all vertices. Compute xyscale = (resolution - 1) / max(width, depth). shift = -min. scale = [xyscale, xyscale, xyscale]. Transform vertices: v' = (v + shift) \times scale. Filter degenerate triangles (fewer than 3 unique points after transformation). 3. Initialize Voxel Array: Boolean array voxels of shape (boundingbox[2], boundingbox[0], boundingbox[1]). 4. Iterate Height z: a. Find Intersecting Triangles: Filter triangles that cross the plane z. A triangle crosses if: It has vertices both above (zv > z) and below (zv < z). OR it has 2 or 3 vertices exactly on the plane (zv == z). Exclude triangles lying entirely on the plane. b. Compute Intersection Lines: For each valid triangle, compute the intersection line segment with the plane z. Cases: 2 vertices on plane: Return those 2 vertices. 1 vertex on plane: Compute intersection point on the edge between the above/below vertex and the on-plane vertex. Return (intersection, on-plane vertex). 0 vertices on plane: Compute intersection points on the two edges crossing the plane. Return those 2 points. Intersection point calculation: Ensure p1.z < p2.z. If p1.z == p2.z, distance = 0. Else, t = \frac{z - p1.z}{p2.z - p1.z}. point = p1 + t \times (p2 - p1). c. Rasterize Lines to 2D Grid: Initialize prepixel grid of size (boundingbox[0], boundingbox[1]) to False. For each x column: Find relevant lines crossing this x. A line is relevant if it spans across x (vertices on both sides) or one vertex is on x and another is above. Compute target y coordinates for each line at this x: If vertical (x0 == x1), return -1 (skip). Else, ratio = \frac{x - x0}{x1 - x0}. y{new} = y0 + ratio \times (y1 - y0). For each y row: If isBlack is True, set prepixel[x][y] = True. If y matches a target y coordinate AND the point lies on the line segment (checked by integer comparison and range checks), toggle isBlack and set prepixel[x][y] = True. Assign prepixel to voxels[z]. 5. Padding (Optional): If padding is enabled, expand dimensions by 2 in each axis and shift data by 1. Pseudocode (Slice-and-Rasterize): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def voxelizesliceandrasterize(meshtriangles, resolution): # 1. Scale and Shift allpoints = [pt for tri in meshtriangles for pt in tri] mins = np.min(allpoints, axis=0) maxs = np.max(allpoints, axis=0) maxdim = max(maxs[0] - mins[0], maxs[1] - mins[1]) if maxdim == 0: maxdim = 1e-9 xyscale = (resolution - 1) / maxdim shift = -mins scale = np.array([xyscale, xyscale, xyscale]) scaledtriangles = [] for tri in meshtriangles: newtri = [(np.array(pt) + shift) scale for pt in tri] if len(set(map(tuple, newtri))) == 3: # Filter degenerate scaledtriangles.append(newtri) zmax = int(np.ceil((maxs[2] - mins[2]) xyscale)) xmax, ymax = resolution, resolution voxels = np.zeros((zmax, xmax, ymax), dtype=bool) # 2. Iterate Height for z in range(zmax): # Find crossing triangles crossingtris = [] for tri in scaledtriangles: zs = [pt[2] for pt in tri] hasabove = any(zv > z for zv in zs) hasbelow = any(zv < z for zv in zs) onplane = sum(1 for zv in zs if abs(zv - z) < 1e-9) if (hasabove and hasbelow) or onplane >= 2: crossingtris.append(tri) # Compute intersection lines lines = [] for tri in crossingtris: p1, p2, p3 = tri pts = [p1, p2, p3] above = [p for p in pts if p[2] > z] below = [p for p in pts if p[2] < z] same = [p for p in pts if abs(p[2] - z) < 1e-9] if len(same) == 2: lines.append((same[0], same[1])) elif len(same) == 1: if above and below: side = wherelinecrossesz(above[0], below[0], z) lines.append((side, same[0])) else: for i in range(3): pa, pb = pts[i], pts[(i+1)%3] if (pa[2] > z) != (pb[2] > z): inter = wherelinecrossesz(pa, pb, z) lines.append(inter) # Rasterize to 2D grid prepixel = np.zeros((xmax, ymax), dtype=bool) for x in range(xmax): isblack = False for y in range(ymax): if isblack: prepixel[x, y] = True for line in lines: if onlineatx(line, x, y): isblack = not isblack prepixel[x, y] = True if isblack: raise ValueError(f"Unbalanced edge crossings at z={z}, x={x}") voxels[z] = prepixel return voxels def wherelinecrossesz(p1, p2, z): if p1[2] > p2[2]: p1, p2 = p2, p1 dist = 0 if abs(p2[2] - p1[2]) < 1e-9 else (z - p1[2]) / (p2[2] - p1[2]) return (p1[0] - dist (p1[0] - p2[0]), p1[1] - dist (p1[1] - p2[1])) def onlineatx(line, x, y): p1, p2 = line if p1[0] == p2[0]: return False # Vertical lines skip ratio = (x - p1[0]) / (p2[0] - p1[0]) newy = p1[1] + ratio (p2[1] - p1[1]) return int(newy) == y and min(p1[0],p2[0]) <= x <= max(p1[0],p2[0]) and min(p1[1],p2[1]) <= y <= max(p1[1],p2[1]) This method iterates over triangles, computes their bounding box in voxel space, and tests each voxel in that box for intersection. Steps: 1. Initialize Grid: Allocate a flat array data of size W \times H \times D, initialized to 0. 2. Compute Mesh AABB: Iterate over all triangles to compute the global bounding box meshaabb of the mesh. 3. Compute Resolution per Axis: resx = \frac{meshaabb.max.x - meshaabb.min.x}{W} resy = \frac{meshaabb.max.y - meshaabb.min.y}{H} resz = \frac{meshaabb.max.z - meshaabb.min.z}{D} 4. Voxelize Points (Optional Pre-step): Some implementations first convert the mesh to a point cloud using vxvoxelizepc with the computed resolutions, then map points to the grid. 5. Iterate Triangles: For each triangle T with vertices v1, v2, v3: a. Compute T's AABB in world space. b. Map the AABB min/max to voxel grid indices. Compute offset: ox = \text{tri\min}.x + \text{fabs}(aabb.min.x). Index: ix = \frac{ox}{ax} \times (W - 1) where ax = aabb.max.x - aabb.min.x. Clamp indices to [0, W-1]. c. Iterate over voxel indices (x, y, z) within the mapped AABB range. d. Intersection Test: For each voxel, construct its AABB (centered at grid point, size resx, resy, resz). Test for intersection with triangle T using vxtriangleboxoverlap. e. Color Interpolation (if colors present): If intersecting, compute the color at the voxel center C{voxel} using barycentric interpolation. Create sub-triangles t1(v1, v2, C{voxel}), t2(v2, v3, C{voxel}), t3(v3, v1, C{voxel}). Compute areas A1, A2, A3. Total Area A = A1 + A2 + A3. Weighted Color C = \frac{C1 A2 + C2 A3 + C3 A1}{A}. f. Insertion: Compute flat index idx = x + y \cdot W + z \cdot (W \cdot H). If data[idx] is 0, set data[idx] = Color. If data[idx] is non-zero, blend: data[idx] = mix(data[idx], Color) (average of existing and new color). Pseudocode (Triangle-AABB Sampling): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def voxelizeaabbsampling(vertices, indices, width, height, depth, colors=None): grid = np.zeros((width, height, depth), dtype=np.uint32) # Compute mesh AABB minv = np.min(vertices, axis=0) maxv = np.max(vertices, axis=0) ax, ay, az = maxv - minv # Handle zero dimensions resx = ax[0] / width if ax[0] > 0 else 1e-9 resy = ax[1] / height if ax[1] > 0 else 1e-9 resz = ax[2] / depth if ax[2] > 0 else 1e-9 for i in range(0, len(indices), 3): i1, i2, i3 = indices[i], indices[i+1], indices[i+2] p1, p2, p3 = vertices[i1], vertices[i2], vertices[i3] trimin = np.minimum(np.minimum(p1, p2), p3) trimax = np.maximum(np.maximum(p1, p2), p3) # Map to voxel indices (S2 formula) ox = trimin[0] + abs(minv[0]) ixmin = int((ox / ax[0]) (width - 1)) if ax[0] > 0 else 0 ixmax = int(((trimax[0] + abs(minv[0])) / ax[0]) (width - 1)) if ax[0] > 0 else 0 # Clamp ixmin = max(0, min(ixmin, width - 1)) ixmax = max(0, min(ixmax, width - 1)) # Similar for y, z... for z in range(zmin, zmax + 1): for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): # Intersection test placeholder intersects = True if intersects: # Color interpolation (S4) if colors is not None: c1, c2, c3 = colors[i1], colors[i2], colors[i3] center = np.array([x, y, z]) np.array([resx, resy, resz]) + minv a1 = triarea(p1, p2, center) a2 = triarea(p2, p3, center) a3 = triarea(p3, p1, center) total = a1 + a2 + a3 if total > 0: r = (c1[0]a2 + c2[0]a3 + c3[0]a1) / total g = (c1[1]a2 + c2[1]a3 + c3[1]a1) / total b = (c1[2]a2 + c2[2]a3 + c3[2]a1) / total else: r,g,b = 0,0,0 else: r,g,b = 1,1,1 colorint = ((int(255)&0xff)<<24) | ((int(b255)&0xff)<<16) | ((int(g255)&0xff)<<8) | ((int(r255)&0xff)<<0) idx = x + y width + z (width height) if grid[idx] == 0: grid[idx] = colorint else: # Blend old = grid[idx] newr = ((old>>0)&0xff + int(r255))//2 newg = ((old>>8)&0xff + int(g255))//2 newb = ((old>>16)&0xff + int(b255))//2 grid[idx] = (255<<24) | (newb<<16) | (newg<<8) | newr return grid Resolution: Number of voxels for the largest dimension. Typical value: 100. Width, Height, Depth: Explicit grid dimensions. Padding: Boolean flag (default True). Adds a 1-voxel border of empty space by expanding dimensions by 2 in each axis. Degenerate Triangles: Triangles with collinear or duplicate vertices are filtered out during scaling. Division by Zero: Grid dimensions of zero are handled by ternary checks (e.g., ax == 0.0 ? 0:...). Vertical Lines: In slice rasterization, vertical lines (x0 == x1) return Y=-1, which skips them in scanline fill. Unbalanced Edges: If isBlack is still True after processing all y rows, an error is printed, indicating unbalanced edge crossings. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for "on plane" or "on line" should use a small epsilon to avoid missing intersections due to precision errors. A GPU-based solid voxelization technique that outputs a linked list of starting and ending voxels for each row and column in the voxel grid. It uses an A-buffer approach to handle multiple fragments per pixel by building and sorting linked lists of fragment data. Choose this when you need depth-sorted solid voxels for accurate interior rendering. name: A-Buffer Solid Voxelization
body: A-Buffer Solid Voxelization is a GPU-based technique that voxelize a watertight mesh by rasterizing it into a fixed-width, height, and depth 3D grid and resolving multiple depth intersections per pixel using an A-buffer linked list structure. It differs from standard depth-buffer rasterization by retaining all fragment depth information rather than discarding occluded fragments, allowing it to output a linked list of starting and ending voxels for each row and column in the grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A watertight triangle mesh with vertex positions in the interval [-1, 1]. Output: A VoxelizerABufferLinkedList struct containing the grid dimensions, fragment count, and three arrays (headPointers, nodePointers, nodeData) representing a linked list of voxel intersections. Data Structures: The implementation relies on specific C structs and OpenGL resources: 1. Voxelizer: The main context. algorithm: Enum VOXELIZERABUFFER. width, height, depth: Grid dimensions. framebuffer: OpenGL framebuffer object ID. framebufferColor: OpenGL texture ID (GLRGBA, GLUNSIGNEDBYTE, size width x height). meshVertCount: Number of vertices. meshVertPositions: Pointer to vertex data. meshVertBuffer: OpenGL buffer object ID. data: Pointer to VoxelizerABufferData. 2. VoxelizerABufferData: Algorithm-specific state. voxelizer: Pointer to parent Voxelizer. fragCountProgram: Shader program ID for counting fragments. makeFragListProgram: Shader program ID for building the linked list. sortFragListProgram: Shader program ID for sorting the linked list. screenQuadBuffer: OpenGL buffer ID for the screen quad. atomicCounter: OpenGL buffer ID for the atomic counter. headPtrSSBO: Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO) ID, size width height 4 bytes. nodePtrSSBO: SSBO ID, size fragmentCount 4 bytes. nodeDataSSBO: SSBO ID, size fragmentCount 4 bytes. fragmentCount: Integer count of fragments. 3. VoxelizerABufferLinkedList: Final output. width, height, depth: Grid dimensions. fragmentCount: Total number of fragments. headPointers: Array of GLint (size width height). nodePointers: Array of GLint (size fragmentCount). nodeData: Array of GLint (size fragmentCount). Steps: 1. Initialization: If voxelizerCount is 0, create an OpenGL window and context, then increment voxelizerCount. Allocate Voxelizer struct. Set width, height, depth. Create a framebuffer with a GLRGBA GLUNSIGNEDBYTE texture of size width x height. Allocate VoxelizerABufferData and initialize algorithm-specific data. 2. Mesh Setup: Upload meshVertPositions to a GLARRAYBUFFER (meshVertBuffer). Enable vertex attribute 0 with 3 floats per vertex. 3. Fragment Counting: Disable GLCULLFACE and GLDEPTHTEST. Bind the framebuffer and set viewport to width x height. Bind meshVertBuffer and use fragCountProgram. Reset the atomic counter to 0. Set modelTransformMatrix uniform. Draw triangles. Retrieve fragmentCount from the atomic counter. 4. Linked List Memory Setup: Map headPtrSSBO (size width height 4 bytes) with GLMAPWRITEBIT | GLMAPINVALIDATEBUFFERBIT. Initialize all entries to -1. Unmap headPtrSSBO. Allocate nodePtrSSBO and nodeDataSSBO (size fragmentCount 4 bytes each). Bind nodePtrSSBO and nodeDataSSBO to binding points 2 and 3 respectively. 5. Create Linked List: Reset atomic counter to 0. Use makeFragListProgram. Set framebufferWidth and modelTransformMatrix uniforms. Draw triangles. Issue GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT memory barrier. 6. Sort Linked List: Bind screenQuadBuffer. Use sortFragListProgram. Set framebufferWidth uniform. Draw 6 vertices (one triangle). Issue GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT memory barrier. 7. Retrieve Results: Allocate VoxelizerABufferLinkedList. Copy width, height, depth, fragmentCount. Allocate headPointers (size width height 4 bytes), nodePointers (size fragmentCount 4 bytes), and nodeData (size fragmentCount 4 bytes). Copy data from headPtrSSBO, nodePtrSSBO, and nodeDataSSBO using glGetBufferSubData. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setdepthtest(enabled): glstate['depthtest'] = enabled def setcullface(enabled): glstate['cullface'] = enabled def bindframebuffer(id): glstate['boundframebuffer'] = id def setviewport(x, y, w, h): glstate['viewport'] = (x, y, w, h) def bindarraybuffer(id): glstate['boundarraybuffer'] = id def enablevertexattrib(index, size, type, normalized, stride, offset): glstate['vertexattribs'][index] = {'size': size, 'type': type, 'normalized': normalized, 'stride': stride, 'offset': offset, 'enabled': True} def setvertexattribpointer(index, size, type, normalized, stride, pointer): glstate['vertexattribs'][index]['pointer'] = pointer def bindatomiccounterbuffer(id): glstate['boundatomiccounter'] = id def buffersubdata(target, offset, size, data): buffers[target][offset:offset+size] = data def useprogram(id): glstate['currentprogram'] = id def setuniformmatrix4fv(loc, count, transpose, value): glstate['uniforms'][loc] = value def drawarrays(mode, first, count): rasterizetriangles(mode, first, count) def mapbuffer(target, access): return buffers[target].map(access) def unmapbuffer(target): buffers[target].unmap() def bindssbobase(binding, id): glstate['ssbobindings'][binding] = id def memorybarrier(mask): glstate['barrier'] = mask def getbuffersubdata(target, offset, size, dest): dest[:] = buffers[target][offset:offset+size] def allocateintarray(size): return [0] size def voxelizerrunabuffer(voxelizer): data = voxelizer.data # 1. Fragment Counting setdepthtest(False) setcullface(False) bindframebuffer(voxelizer.framebuffer) setviewport(0, 0, voxelizer.width, voxelizer.height) bindarraybuffer(voxelizer.meshVertBuffer) enablevertexattrib(0, 3, 'FLOAT', False, 3 4, 0) setvertexattribpointer(0, 3, 'FLOAT', False, 3 4, 0) bindatomiccounterbuffer(data.atomicCounter) buffersubdata(data.atomicCounter, 0, 4, b'\x00\x00\x00\x00') useprogram(data.fragCountProgram) setuniformmatrix4fv('modelTransformMatrix', 1, False, voxelizer.modelTransformMatrix) drawarrays('TRIANGLES', 0, voxelizer.meshVertCount) ptr = mapbuffer(data.atomicCounter, 'READONLY') data.fragmentCount = ptr[0] unmapbuffer(data.atomicCounter) # 2. Setup Linked List Memory headptr = mapbuffer(data.headPtrSSBO, 'WRITEONLY') for i in range(voxelizer.width voxelizer.height): headptr[i 4: i 4 + 4] = b'\xff\xff\xff\xff' # -1 in little-endian unmapbuffer(data.headPtrSSBO) nodesize = data.fragmentCount 4 bindssbobase(2, data.nodePtrSSBO) bindssbobase(3, data.nodeDataSSBO) # 3. Create Linked List buffersubdata(data.atomicCounter, 0, 4, b'\x00\x00\x00\x00') useprogram(data.makeFragListProgram) setuniformmatrix4fv('framebufferWidth', 1, False, voxelizer.width) setuniformmatrix4fv('modelTransformMatrix', 1, False, voxelizer.modelTransformMatrix) drawarrays('TRIANGLES', 0, voxelizer.meshVertCount) memorybarrier('SHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT') # 4. Sort Linked List bindarraybuffer(data.screenQuadBuffer) useprogram(data.sortFragListProgram) setuniformmatrix4fv('framebufferWidth', 1, False, voxelizer.width) drawarrays('TRIANGLES', 0, 6) memorybarrier('SHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT') # 5. Retrieve Results linkedlist = allocateintarray(voxelizer.width voxelizer.height) linkedlist.width = voxelizer.width linkedlist.height = voxelizer.height linkedlist.depth = voxelizer.depth linkedlist.fragmentCount = data.fragmentCount headsize = voxelizer.width voxelizer.height 4 nodesize = data.fragmentCount 4 linkedlist.headPointers = allocateintarray(voxelizer.width voxelizer.height) linkedlist.nodePointers = allocateintarray(data.fragmentCount) linkedlist.nodeData = allocateintarray(data.fragmentCount) getbuffersubdata(data.headPtrSSBO, 0, headsize, linkedlist.headPointers) getbuffersubdata(data.nodePtrSSBO, 0, nodesize, linkedlist.nodePointers) getbuffersubdata(data.nodeDataSSBO, 0, nodesize, linkedlist.nodeData) return linkedlist Parameters: Grid Size: Defined by width, height, depth at creation. Vertex Range: Input mesh vertices must be in [-1, 1]. Mesh Type: Input triangle meshes must be watertight. Requirements: OpenGL 4.2 with GLARBshaderstoragebufferobject extension. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-axis Clipping: The algorithm does not clip the depth component in the voxel grid. If the mesh extends beyond the grid bounds, it can output an infinite number of voxels along the z-axis. Platform Support: Only Windows is supported at the time of writing. What it is: A method that uses geometry shaders to project mesh triangles directly into voxels. Difference: It avoids the fragment-based A-buffer overhead by generating voxels in the geometry shader stage. When to choose: When hardware supports geometry shaders and you prefer a different pipeline stage for voxel generation. Link: Geometry Shader Voxelization What it is: A sparse voxelization technique that adapts voxel size based on mesh complexity and bounding box thickness. Difference: It produces a sparse representation rather than a dense 3D grid linked list. When to choose: When memory efficiency is critical and the scene has varying levels of detail. Link: Adaptive Sparse Voxelization with Bounding Box Thickness Cases Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles multiple intersections per pixel accurately via the A-buffer linked list. Limitations: Requires OpenGL 4.2 and SSBO support. Does not clip depth, potentially leading to infinite voxel lists if bounds are exceeded. Only supports Windows. When to use: When accurate solid voxelization of watertight meshes is required on modern GPUs with OpenGL 4.2+. When not: When cross-platform support is needed or when the mesh is not watertight. The A-Buffer Solid Voxelization method is part of the "Voxelizer" library, a fast GPU-based solid voxelization library written in C by Kelsey Kurzeja (khkurzeja). The library was released under the MIT license. The author notes that while the library aims for cross-platform support, only Windows was supported at the time of writing. The method was designed to output a linked list of starting and ending voxels for each row and column in the voxel grid. khkurzeja/Voxelizer, https://github.com/khkurzeja/Voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Sparse Voxelization with Bounding Box Thickness Cases
body: This method rasterizes a triangle mesh into a sparse voxel data structure by classifying each triangle's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) into nine cases based on its thickness in grid coordinates. It optimizes overlap testing by using simple iteration for 1D-thick boxes, 2D projection tests for 2D-thick boxes, and combined 3D plane and 2D projection tests for 3D-thick boxes. Inputs: Triangle vertices in world space. unitlength: Physical size of one voxel side. sparsenesslimit: Float parameter for estimating data side-array size. pbboxgrid: Global bounding box of the partition in grid coordinates. Outputs: A sparse voxel array indexed by Morton code offset (index - mortonstart). In binary mode: char values (EMPTYVOXEL or FULLVOXEL/1). In non-binary mode: sizet indices into a voxeldata vector containing VoxelData (normal vec3, color vec3). Data Structures: VoxelData: Struct with fields normal (vec3) and color (vec3). voxels array: Sparse array indexed by Morton code offset. voxeldata vector: Only present in non-binary mode, stores VoxelData objects. Steps: 1. Compute Bounding Box: Calculate the triangle's world-space AABB (tbboxworld). Convert to grid coordinates (tbboxgrid) by multiplying vertex coordinates by unitdiv = 1.0 / unitlength and casting to int. Clamp tbboxgrid to the partition's global bounds pbboxgrid. 2. Determine Thickness Case: Compute the onethick vector, where each component is 1 if the corresponding min and max grid coordinates are equal (thickness is 1 voxel), otherwise 0. If sum(onethick) >= 2, select Cases 1-3 (1D Bounding Box). If sum(onethick) == 1, select Cases 4-6 (2D Bounding Box). If sum(onethick) == 0, select Cases 7-9 (3D Bounding Box). 3. Process 1D Bounding Boxes (Cases 1-3): Iterate all voxels within tbboxgrid. For each voxel, compute the Morton index. Check if the voxel is already marked FULLVOXEL (or non-empty); if so, skip to avoid duplicate work and data corruption. Mark as filled and add to voxeldata in non-binary mode. No geometric overlap test is needed. 4. Process 2D Bounding Boxes (Cases 4-6): Identify the thin axis (where onethick is 1). Perform a 2D projection test on the plane perpendicular to the thin axis. Iterate voxels in the remaining 2D grid bounds. Compute edge normals (ne) and distances (de) for the projection plane. For each projected voxel center (pproj), check if it passes all 3 edge tests. The edge test formula is (ne DOT pproj) + de < 0.0f; if true, the voxel is outside and skipped. The edge distance is calculated as de = (-1.0 (ne DOT vertexproj)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne[0]) + max(0.0, unitlength ne[1]). If the voxel passes all 3 tests, mark as filled. In non-binary mode, compute barycentric coordinates and interpolate vertex colors. 5. Process 3D Bounding Boxes (Cases 7-9): Compute the 3D triangle normal n. Determine the dominant axis (component with largest absolute value). Compute a critical point c where c[axis] = unitlength if n[axis] > 0 else 0. Compute plane test distances d1 and d2 using c. Perform a 3D plane test: (nDOTp + d1) (nDOTp + d2) > 0.0f, where nDOTp = dot(n, voxelcenter). If true, the voxel is entirely on one side of the triangle plane and is skipped. Perform 2D projection tests on all three planes (XY, YZ, XZ). For each plane, compute edge normals and distances. If the voxel center passes all 3 edge tests for a specific plane, it is inside the triangle's projection for that plane. All three planes must pass their respective tests. If the voxel passes the plane test and all three projection tests, mark as filled. In non-binary mode, compute barycentric coordinates and interpolate vertex colors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizepartition3(triangles, unitlength, sparsenesslimit, pbboxgrid): unitdiv = 1.0 / unitlength voxels = {} # Sparse map: mortonindex -> data voxeldata = [] # List of VoxelData structs (normal, color) for tri in triangles: # 1. Compute Bounding Box tbboxworld = computeworldaabb(tri.vertices) tbboxgrid = clamptoint( multiplyby(tbboxworld, unitdiv), pbboxgrid.min, pbboxgrid.max) # 2. Determine Thickness Case onethick = [ 1 if tbboxgrid.min[i] == tbboxgrid.max[i] else 0 for i in range(3) ] thicknesssum = sum(onethick) if thicknesssum >= 2: # Case 1-3: 1D Bounding Box for voxel in iterategrid(tbboxgrid): mortonidx = computemorton(voxel.center) if mortonidx not in voxels: voxels[mortonidx] = 1 # Binary mode flag # Non-binary: store index to voxeldata elif thicknesssum == 1: # Case 4-6: 2D Bounding Box thinaxis = onethick.index(1) projplane = getperpendicularplane(thinaxis) for voxel in iterate2dgrid(tbboxgrid, thinaxis): pproj = project(voxel.center, projplane) if passes2dedgetests(pproj, tri.vertices, unitlength, thinaxis): mortonidx = computemorton(voxel.center) if mortonidx not in voxels: voxels[mortonidx] = 1 # Non-binary: interpolate color, add to voxeldata else: # Case 7-9: 3D Bounding Box n = computetrianglenormal(tri.vertices) dominantaxis = max(range(3), key=lambda i: abs(n[i])) c = computecriticalpoint(n, dominantaxis, unitlength) # Exact d1, d2 derivation not provided in sources d1 = dot(n, c) d2 = dot(n, c) - dot(n, tri.vertices[0]) for voxel in iterategrid(tbboxgrid): nDOTp = dot(n, voxel.center) if (nDOTp + d1) (nDOTp + d2) > 0.0: continue # Outside plane if passes3dprojectiontests(voxel.center, tri.vertices, unitlength): mortonidx = computemorton(voxel.center) if mortonidx not in voxels: voxels[mortonidx] = 1 # Non-binary: interpolate color, add to voxeldata return voxels, voxeldata def passes2dedgetests(pproj, vertices, unitlength, thinaxis): # Project vertices to 2D plane vproj = [project(v, getperpendicularplane(thinaxis)) for v in vertices] for i in range(3): v1 = vproj[i] v2 = vproj[(i + 1) % 3] edgevec = v2 - v1 ne = normalize(vec2(-edgevec.y, edgevec.x)) # 2D normal de = (-1.0 dot(ne, v1)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne[0]) + max(0.0, unitlength ne[1]) if (dot(ne, pproj) + de) >= 0.0: return False return True def passes3dprojectiontests(center, vertices, unitlength): # Check XY, YZ, XZ planes planes = ['xy', 'yz', 'xz'] for plane in planes: if not passes2dedgetestsforplane(center, vertices, unitlength, plane): return False return True def computecriticalpoint(n, axis, unitlength): c = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if n[axis] > 0: c[axis] = unitlength return c NGLE Triangle Voxelization is a rasterization-based algorithm that converts a triangle mesh into a sparse voxel DAG by classifying each triangle's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) thickness into nine cases (1D, 2D, or 3D) and applying optimized plane and projection tests to determine intersected grid cells. It distinguishes itself from general 3D clipping methods by classifying bounding box thickness into 1D, 2D, and 3D cases, using 2D projection tests for thin boxes and combined plane/projection tests for thick boxes. Time Complexity: Scales with the number of voxels in the bounding box and the thickness case. 1D cases run in O(V) where V is voxels in the AABB. 2D and 3D cases add geometric projection and plane tests per voxel. Memory Complexity: Uses sparse storage indexed by Morton codes. Memory usage is estimated using sparsenesslimit and scales with the number of filled voxels. Strengths: Optimizes performance for thin triangles by avoiding expensive 3D tests. Supports both binary and data-rich voxelization modes. Limitations: Requires careful handling of precision and edge cases. Non-binary mode increases memory consumption and computation due to barycentric interpolation. When to use: High-resolution sparse voxelization where many triangles are thin or flat. When not to use: Dense voxelization or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained and binary mode is insufficient. The method originates from the "High Resolution Sparse Voxel DAGs" project. It is part of a larger system for constructing and reducing Sparse Voxel DAGs, which are used for efficient storage and rendering of high-resolution 3D scenes. leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, https://github.com/leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: NGLE Triangle Voxelization
head: N-gle
body: NGLE Triangle Voxelization is a rasterization-based algorithm that converts a triangle mesh into a sparse voxel DAG by classifying each triangle's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) thickness into nine cases (1D, 2D, or 3D) and applying optimized plane and projection tests to determine intersected grid cells. It distinguishes itself from general 3D clipping methods by classifying bounding box thickness into 1D, 2D, and 3D cases, using 2D projection tests for thin boxes and combined plane/projection tests for thick boxes. Inputs: Triangle vertices v0, v1, v2 in world space. unitlength: The side length of a voxel in world units. mortonstart, mortonend: The range of Morton codes allocated for the partition. voxels: A boolean array (for binary voxelization) or a sizet array with a parallel vector<VoxelData> (for data-rich voxelization). Outputs: Marked voxels in the sparse grid corresponding to the triangle's intersection. Optional voxel data (normal, average color) stored in voxeldata. Data Structures: VoxelData: Contains normal (vec3) and color (vec3, computed as the average of the triangle's vertex colors). Grid coordinates are integers derived from world coordinates by multiplying by 1.0f/unitlength and casting to int. Steps: 1. Initialize Voxel Array: Clear the voxel array for the range [mortonstart, mortonend) to EMPTYVOXEL. 2. Compute Partition Bounding Box: Decode mortonstart and mortonend - 1 into grid coordinates to determine pbboxgrid.min and pbboxgrid.max. 3. Compute Triangle Grid Bounding Box: Compute the world-space AABB of the triangle, t\bbox\world. Convert to grid coordinates: t\bbox\grid = \text{cast\int}(t\bbox\world \times \frac{1.0}{\text{unitlength}}). Clamp t\bbox\grid to pbboxgrid to stay within the partition. 4. Determine Bounding Box Thickness: Compute a boolean vector onethick where onethick[axis] is 1 if t\bbox\grid.min[axis] == t\bbox\grid.max[axis], and 0 otherwise. 5. Compute Triangle Geometry: Edges: e0 = v1 - v0, e1 = v2 - v1, e2 = v0 - v2. Normal: n = \text{normalize}(e0 \times e1). 6. Handle 2D Bounding Box Cases (Cases 4-6): If onethick.sum() == 1, the triangle is thin in one dimension. Identify the dominant axis (where onethick is 1) and perform a 2D projection test on the plane perpendicular to it. Case 4 (Thin in X, Thick in Y, Z): Project onto YZ plane. Compute edge normals in 2D: n{yz\e0} = (-e0[Z], e0[Y]), etc.. If n[X] < 0, negate all n{yz\ei}. Compute offsets: d{yz\ei} = -1.0 \cdot (n{yz\ei} \cdot \text{vec2}(vi[Y], vi[Z])) + \max(0.0, \text{unitlength} \cdot n{yz\ei}[0]) + \max(0.0, \text{unitlength} \cdot n{yz\ei}[1]). Iterate y, z in t\bbox\grid. Fixed x = t\bbox\grid.min[X]. For a point p{yz} = (y, z), if (n{yz\ei} \cdot p{yz} + d{yz\ei}) < 0 for all i \in \{0,1,2\}, skip. Otherwise, mark voxel. Case 5 (Thin in Y, Thick in X, Z): Project onto ZX plane. Compute edge normals: n{zx\e0} = (-e0[X], e0[Z]), etc.. If n[Y] < 0, negate all n{zx\ei}. Compute offsets d{zx\ei} similarly. Iterate z, x in t\bbox\grid. Fixed y = t\bbox\grid.min[Y]. Skip if projection test fails for all edges. Case 6 (Thin in Z, Thick in X, Y): Project onto XY plane. Compute edge normals: n{xy\e0} = (-e0[Y], e0[X]), etc.. If n[Z] < 0, negate all n{xy\ei}. Compute offsets d{xy\ei} similarly. Iterate x, y in t\bbox\grid. Fixed z = t\bbox\grid.min[Z]. Skip if projection test fails for all edges. 7. Handle 3D Bounding Box Cases (Cases 7-9): If onethick.sum() == 0, the triangle spans multiple voxels in all dimensions. Determine the dominant axis of n (axis with largest absolute component). Compute critical point c: c[axis] = \text{unitlength} if n[axis] > 0, else 0. Compute plane distances: d1 = n \cdot (c - v0) and d2 = n \cdot ((\Delta p - c) - v0), where \Delta p = (\text{unitlength}, \text{unitlength}, \text{unitlength}). Setup projection tests for all three planes (XY, YZ, ZX) as in Cases 4-6. Iterate x, y, z in t\bbox\grid. Plane Test: If (n \cdot p + d1) \cdot (n \cdot p + d2) > 0.0, skip. This checks if the voxel center is entirely on one side of the triangle plane. Projection Tests: If any of the three 2D projection tests fails, skip. Otherwise, mark voxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nglevoxelize(triangle, unitlength, mortonstart, mortonend, voxels, voxeldata=None): # 1. Initialize Voxel Array for i in range(mortonstart, mortonend): voxels[i] = False if voxeldata is not None: voxeldata[i] = None # 2. Compute Partition Bounding Box # Morton encode/decode: standard bit-interleaving (not given in sources) pmin = decodemorton(mortonstart) pmax = decodemorton(mortonend - 1) pbboxmin = [pmin[0], pmin[1], pmin[2]] pbboxmax = [pmax[0], pmax[1], pmax[2]] # 3. Compute Triangle Grid Bounding Box tbboxworld = computeworldbbox(triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2) tbboxgridmin = [clamp(int(tbboxworld[i] / unitlength), pbboxmin[i], pbboxmax[i]) for i in range(3)] tbboxgridmax = [clamp(int(tbboxworld[i+3] / unitlength), pbboxmin[i], pbboxmax[i]) for i in range(3)] # 4. Determine Bounding Box Thickness onethick = [1 if tbboxgridmin[i] == tbboxgridmax[i] else 0 for i in range(3)] thicknesssum = sum(onethick) # 5. Compute Triangle Geometry e0 = [triangle.v1[i] - triangle.v0[i] for i in range(3)] e1 = [triangle.v2[i] - triangle.v1[i] for i in range(3)] e2 = [triangle.v0[i] - triangle.v2[i] for i in range(3)] edges = [e0, e1, e2] verts = [triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2] n = normalize(cross(e0, e1)) if thicknesssum == 1: # Cases 4-6: 2D Projection dominantaxis = onethick.index(1) if dominantaxis == 0: # Case 4: Thin X, Project YZ process2dprojection(edges, verts, n, unitlength, tbboxgridmin, tbboxgridmax, 0, voxels, voxeldata) elif dominantaxis == 1: # Case 5: Thin Y, Project ZX process2dprojection(edges, verts, n, unitlength, tbboxgridmin, tbboxgridmax, 1, voxels, voxeldata) else: # Case 6: Thin Z, Project XY process2dprojection(edges, verts, n, unitlength, tbboxgridmin, tbboxgridmax, 2, voxels, voxeldata) else: # Cases 7-9: 3D Bounding Box absn = [abs(n[i]) for i in range(3)] dominantnormalaxis = absn.index(max(absn)) c = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] c[dominantnormalaxis] = unitlength if n[dominantnormalaxis] > 0 else 0.0 deltap = [unitlength, unitlength, unitlength] d1 = dot(n, [c[i] - triangle.v0[i] for i in range(3)]) d2 = dot(n, [(deltap[i] - c[i]) - triangle.v0[i] for i in range(3)]) # Precompute 2D projection params for all 3 planes projxy = compute2dparams(edges, verts, n, unitlength, axis=2) projyz = compute2dparams(edges, verts, n, unitlength, axis=0) projzx = compute2dparams(edges, verts, n, unitlength, axis=1) for z in range(tbboxgridmin[2], tbboxgridmax[2] + 1): for y in range(tbboxgridmin[1], tbboxgridmax[1] + 1): for x in range(tbboxgridmin[0], tbboxgridmax[0] + 1): p = [x, y, z] # Plane Test: If (n \cdot p + d1) \cdot (n \cdot p + d2) > 0.0, skip ndotp = dot(n, p) if (ndotp + d1) (ndotp + d2) > 0.0: continue # Projection Tests if not isinside2d(p, projxy, axes=(0, 1)): continue if not isinside2d(p, projyz, axes=(1, 2)): continue if not isinside2d(p, projzx, axes=(2, 0)): continue # Mark Voxel morton = encodemorton(p) voxels[morton] = True if voxeldata is not None: voxeldata[morton] = VoxelData(normal=n, color=averagecolor(triangle)) def process2dprojection(edges, verts, n, unitlength, tmin, tmax, fixedaxis, voxels, voxeldata): axis0 = (fixedaxis + 1) % 3 axis1 = (fixedaxis + 2) % 3 n2d = [] d2d = [] for i in range(3): e = edges[i] v = verts[i] nx = -e[axis1] ny = e[axis0] if n[fixedaxis] < 0: nx = -nx ny = -ny n2d.append([nx, ny]) term1 = -1.0 (nx v[axis0] + ny v[axis1]) term2 = max(0.0, unitlength nx) term3 = max(0.0, unitlength ny) d2d.append(term1 + term2 + term3) for a0 in range(tmin[axis0], tmax[axis0] + 1): for a1 in range(tmin[axis1], tmax[axis1] + 1): p2d = [a0, a1] inside = False for j in range(3): val = n2d[j][0] p2d[0] + n2d[j][1] p2d[1] + d2d[j] if val >= 0.0: inside = True break if inside: p = [0, 0, 0] p[axis0] = a0 p[axis1] = a1 p[fixedaxis] = tmin[fixedaxis] morton = encodemorton(p) voxels[morton] = True if voxeldata is not None: voxeldata[morton] = VoxelData(normal=n, color=averagecolor(triangle)) def compute2dparams(edges, verts, n, unitlength, axis): axis0 = (axis + 1) % 3 axis1 = (axis + 2) % 3 n2d = [] d2d = [] for i in range(3): e = edges[i] v = verts[i] nx = -e[axis1] ny = e[axis0] if n[axis] < 0: nx = -nx ny = -ny n2d.append([nx, ny]) term1 = -1.0 (nx v[axis0] + ny v[axis1]) term2 = max(0.0, unitlength nx) term3 = max(0.0, unitlength ny) d2d.append(term1 + term2 + term3) return {'n2d': n2d, 'd2d': d2d, 'axes': (axis0, axis1)} def isinside2d(p, proj, axes): axis0, axis1 = axes p2d = [p[axis0], p[axis1]] for j in range(3): val = proj['n2d'][j][0] p2d[0] + proj['n2d'][j][1] p2d[1] + proj['d2d'][j] if val >= 0.0: return True return False def averagecolor(tri): return [(tri.v0[i] + tri.v1[i] + tri.v2[i]) / 3.0 for i in range(3)] class VoxelData: def init(self, normal, color): self.normal = normal self.color = color A simpler variant that determines overlapped cells by bounding box overlap and adds a triangle reference to each. It uses bounding box overlap test instead of exact triangle-in-box test. The exact test reduces triangle references by more than one third, but shrinks ray-triangle intersection tests by only a few percent after mailboxing, so the higher rebuild cost of the exact test is not justified. For scenes with dominantly long, skinny, and diagonal triangles, a more accurate test may still pay off. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Optimized for sparse storage via Morton codes; handles 2D cases efficiently by reducing dimensionality; robust for general triangle orientations. Limitations: Conservative for 2D cases (may include voxels slightly outside the triangle if not careful with edge cases, though the projection test is exact for the grid cells); 3D cases require more tests. When to use: When building a sparse voxel DAG for ray tracing or volume rendering where performance is critical and the scene contains varied triangle orientations. When not to use: For scenes with very long, skinny, diagonal triangles where bounding box overlap is highly inaccurate and exact tests might be justified. NGLE Triangle Voxelization is part of the Sparse Voxel DAG (SVO) builder implementation found in the INF584 High Resolution Sparse Voxel DAGs project. It builds on the concept of adaptive sparse voxelization with bounding box thickness cases Adaptive Sparse Voxelization with Bounding Box Thickness Cases. The method is designed to efficiently rasterize triangles into a sparse grid structure for subsequent ray traversal. leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, https://github.com/leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Ray Tracing Animated Scenes using Coherent Grid Traversal, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~thiago/papers/grid.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25

name: Dominant-Axis Triangle Voxelization
head: 3D Bounding Box Voxelization, Case 7-9 Voxelization, Dominant Axis Voxelization, Multi-Pass Voxelization, Voxelization with Dominant Axis Projection
body: Dominant-Axis Triangle Voxelization is a rasterization-based algorithm that determines which voxels in a sparse voxel DAG are intersected by a triangle by projecting the triangle onto a 2D plane defined by its dominant normal axis. It sets itself apart from general 3D clipping methods by reducing the problem to 2D edge tests along the axis of maximum surface alignment, optimizing column casting for sparse storage. This method is a specific implementation detail within the NGLE Triangle Voxelization framework, handling the 3D bounding box thickness cases (Cases 7-9) where the triangle spans multiple voxels in all three dimensions. Inputs: Triangle vertices in world space: v0, v1, v2. Triangle bounding box in grid coordinates: bbox{grid}.min, bbox{grid}.max. Voxel side length: unitlength. Parent bounding box limits: p{bbox\grid}.min, p{bbox\grid}.max. Mode flag: singlepass or multipass. In multi-pass mode: Pre-computed dominant axis buffer, current projection direction projDir.direction, and primitive vertex index vid. Outputs: A set of occupied voxel Morton codes in a sparse array. Voxel data (e.g., color, normal) if non-binary mode is enabled. Voxel Storage: A sparse array indexed by Morton codes. The base offset is mortonstart. For non-binary mode, VoxelData is pushed to a vector, and the index (voxeldata.size() - 1) is stored in the voxels array. Binary mode stores true. Dominant Axis Buffer: In multi-pass mode, an array storing the pre-computed dominant axis for each triangle, accessed via vid / 3. 1. Calculate Plane Constant: Compute the plane constant d using the normal n and vertex v0: d = -1.0 \cdot (nx \cdot v{0x} + ny \cdot v{0y} + nz \cdot v{0z}) 2. Determine Dominant Axis: Identify the axis with the largest absolute normal component. Initialize dominantaxis = X. If |ny| > |n{dominant\axis}|, set dominantaxis = Y. If |nz| > |n{dominant\axis}|, set dominantaxis = Z. Single-Pass Mode: Compute the triangle's normal by transforming vertices to world space (pos0, pos1, pos2). Calculate the absolute cross product of edge vectors: triNormal = |\text{cross}(pos1 - pos0, pos2 - pos0)|. Multi-Pass Mode: Retrieve the pre-computed dominant axis from the buffer using vid / 3. If the retrieved axis does not match projDir.direction, output a degenerate position float4(-2,-2,-2,-2) to cull the primitive. 3. Iterate Based on Dominant Axis: The algorithm projects the triangle onto the plane perpendicular to the dominant axis and iterates over the 2D grid cells within the triangle's bounding box on that plane. Case A: Dominant Axis is X Iterate over y and z within bbox{grid}.min/max. YZ Plane Projection Test: For each edge ei (i=0,1,2), compute the 2D edge normal in the YZ plane: n{yz\ei} = \text{vec2}(-e{iz}, e{iy}) If nx < 0.0, negate n{yz\ei}. Compute the offset: d{yz\ei} = -1.0 \cdot (n{yz\ei} \cdot \text{vec2}(v{0y}, v{0z})) + \max(0.0, unitlength \cdot n{yz\ei,x}) + \max(0.0, unitlength \cdot n{yz\ei,y}) A voxel at (y,z) is inside the triangle's projection if: (n{yz\ei} \cdot \text{vec2}(y \cdot unitlength, z \cdot unitlength)) + d{yz\ei} \ge 0.0 for all three edges. X-Range Calculation: For valid (y,z) columns, determine the range of voxels in the X direction. Define min/max corners in the YZ plane: min\corner = (y \cdot unitlength, z \cdot unitlength) max\corner = min\corner + \text{vec2}(unitlength, unitlength) Swap components if corresponding normal components are negative: if ny < 0, swap min\corner[0] and max\corner[0]; if nz < 0, swap min\corner[1] and max\corner[1]. Project YZ corners to X coordinates on the triangle plane: x{min\world} = \frac{ny \cdot min\corner[0] + nz \cdot min\corner[1] + d}{-1.0 \cdot nx} x{max\world} = \frac{ny \cdot max\corner[0] + nz \cdot max\corner[1] + d}{-1.0 \cdot nx} Convert to voxel indices: x{min} = x{min\world} / unitlength x{max} = x{max\world} / unitlength Clamping: Clamp x{min} and x{max} to p{bbox\grid}.min/max[X]. Overlap Tests: If the depth range (x{max} - x{min}) > 1, perform additional overlap tests in the ZX and XY planes for each x \in [x{min}, x{max}]. Compute edge normals and offsets for these planes, adjusting signs based on normal components (e.g., if ny < 0.0, negate ZX edge normals). Voxel Marking: For each x, compute the Morton index for (z, y, x). Check if already marked. Test the voxel center against the XY and ZX edge inequalities. If inside both, mark the voxel and increment nfilled. Case B: Dominant Axis is Y Iterate over z and x within bbox{grid}.min/max. XZ Plane Projection Test: Similar to YZ test, project onto XZ plane. Y-Range Calculation: Determine Y-range using corner projection: y{min\world} = \frac{nz \cdot min\corner[0] + nx \cdot min\corner[1] + d}{-1.0 \cdot ny} Clamp y{min} and y{max} to p{bbox\grid}.min/max[Y]. Handle y{min} == y{max} special case. Overlap Tests: For ranges > 1, test YZ and XY planes. Case C: Dominant Axis is Z Iterate over x and y within bbox{grid}.min/max. XY Plane Projection Test: Similar to previous tests, project onto XY plane. Z-Range Calculation: Determine Z-range using corner projection: z{min\world} = \frac{nx \cdot min\corner[0] + ny \cdot min\corner[1] + d}{-1.0 \cdot nz} Clamp z{min} and z{max} to p{bbox\grid}.min/max[Z]. Handle z{min} == z{max} special case. Overlap Tests: For ranges > 1, test XZ and YZ planes. 4. Write Voxel Data: Write to voxel texture using one of three methods based on function constants: kUseRWTexture: Read existing value, perform max blend (res = \max(res, stored)), write back. kUseWTexture: Write directly without blending. name: Geometry Shader Voxelization
head: GS Voxelization, Solid Triangle Voxelization, Triangle-to-Voxel Rasterization, Triangle Projection Voxelization, OpenGL Geometry Shader Voxelization
body: Geometry Shader Voxelization converts polygonal meshes (.obj,.ply) into a discrete 3D occupancy or color grid by rasterizing triangles directly into a 3D texture using an OpenGL Geometry Shader. It projects each triangle to cover grid cells at a specified resolution and determines occupied voxels by checking overlaps in all three dimensions (XY, YZ, ZX). Unlike GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection which explicitly selects the optimal projection axis per triangle to maximize coverage, this method swizzles geometry to align with the XY plane while iterating through bounding boxes to verify 3D overlaps. It differs from GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics by relying on the geometry shader's ability to emit multiple primitives and iterate through grid cells, rather than pure atomic accumulation without depth-based projection. Inputs: Mesh vertices V (3xN floats) and faces F (3xM uint32s) loaded from.obj or.ply files. Voxel resolution dim (e.g., 64), applied uniformly to x, y, z axes. Thickness mode: THIN (0) or FAT (1). Outputs: Occupancy Grid: A 3D texture (GLTEXTURE3D) with internal format GLR8UI (8-bit unsigned integer, single channel). Voxel Color: A 3D image voxelColor with format rgba8 storing color data. Data Structures: mesh.V: Eigen matrix, size 3xN, float. mesh.F: Eigen matrix, size 3xM, uint32. voxelResolution: Uniform ivec3. unswizzle: Permutation matrix to reverse coordinate transformation. Steps: 1. Load and Normalize Mesh: Load vertices and faces. Compute bounding box: xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax. Calculate dimensions dx, dy, dz and dmax = \max(dx, dy, dz). Normalize vertices to [0, 1] range: V{norm} = \frac{V - min}{dmax}. 2. Setup Rendering Pipeline: Load shaders (VoxelizationVS.glsl, VoxelizationGS.glsl, VoxelizationFS.glsl). Bind vertex buffer mesh.V and element buffer mesh.F. Pass voxelResolution uniform. Bind voxelOccupancy (layout(r8ui, binding = 0) uniform uimage3D) and voxelColor (layout(rgba8, binding = 1) uniform image3D). 3. Swizzle Triangle: For each triangle, compute normal n = \text{cross}(v1 - v0, v2 - v1). Determine the dominant axis of the normal (max component of |n|). Permute vertex coordinates and normal to align the dominant plane with the XY plane. Store the permutation matrix in unswizzle from unswizzleLUT to reverse the transformation later. 4. Compute Edge Normals: For each edge (e0=v1-v0, e1=v2-v1, e2=v0-v2), compute inward-facing 2D edge normals for the XY, YZ, and ZX planes. The direction depends on the sign of the normal component perpendicular to the plane. Formula for XY edge normal e0: n{e0,xy} = (n.z \ge 0) ? \text{vec2}(-e0.y, e0.x): \text{vec2}(e0.y, -e0.x). Similar logic applies to YZ and ZX planes using n.x and n.y respectively. 5. Calculate Initial Edge Distances: Compute edge distances for the projected vertices. For Thin voxelization: de = \text{dot}(ne, 0.5 - v{proj}) + 0.5 \times \max(|n{e,x}|, |n{e,y}|) For Fat voxelization: de = -\text{dot}(ne, v{proj}) + \max(0, n{e,x}) + \max(0, n{e,y}) Compute triangle plane distance: Thin: d{Tri} = \text{dot}(n{proj}, v0) - \text{dot}(n{proj,xy}, 0.5) Fat: d{Tri, min} = \text{dot}(n{proj}, v0) - \max(n{proj,x}, 0) - \max(n{proj,y}, 0) d{Tri, max} = \text{dot}(n{proj}, v0) - \min(n{proj,x}, 0) - \min(n{proj,y}, 0). 6. X-Y Loop (Rasterization): Compute AABB of triangle vertices. Convert to voxel indices: minVoxIndex = \text{clamp}(\lfloor AABB{min} \rfloor, 0, voxelResolution) maxVoxIndex = \text{clamp}(\lceil AABB{max} \rceil, 0, voxelResolution). Iterate p.x from minVoxIndex.x to maxVoxIndex.x and p.y from minVoxIndex.y to maxVoxIndex.y. Calculate updated edge distances for current voxel coordinate: dde = de + \text{dot}(ne, p{proj}). Check XY overlap: xy\overlap = (dd{e0,xy} \ge 0) \land (dd{e1,xy} \ge 0) \land (dd{e2,xy} \ge 0). 7. Z-Range Calculation: If xy\overlap is true, calculate Z-intersection range. Thin: z{min} = \frac{-\text{dot}(n{proj,xy}, p{xy}) + d{Tri, thin}}{n{proj, z}} Fat: z{min} = \frac{-\text{dot}(n{proj,xy}, p{xy}) + d{Tri, fat, min}}{n{proj, z}} z{max} = \frac{-\text{dot}(n{proj,xy}, p{xy}) + d{Tri, fat, max}}{n{proj, z}} Apply floor/ceil boundary handling: zMin = \text{int}(zMinFloor) - \text{int}(zMinFloor == zMinInt) zMax = \text{int}(zMaxCeil) + \text{int}(zMaxCeil == zMaxInt). 8. Z-Loop and Overlap Check: Iterate p.z from zMin to zMax (clamped to minVoxIndex.z and maxVoxIndex.z). Inside loop, calculate updated edge distances for YZ and ZX planes: dde = de + \text{dot}(ne, p{proj}). Check overlaps: yz\overlap = (dd{e0,yz} \ge 0) \land (dd{e1,yz} \ge 0) \land (dd{e2,yz} \ge 0) zx\overlap = (dd{e0,zx} \ge 0) \land (dd{e1,zx} \ge 0) \land (dd{e2,zx} \ge 0). 9. Write Voxel: If yz\overlap and zx\overlap are true, the voxel is occupied. Write to occupancy image: \text{imageStore}(voxelOccupancy, \text{ivec3}(unswizzle \cdot p), \text{uvec4}(1)) Write color: \text{imageStore}(voxelColor, \text{ivec3}(unswizzle \cdot p), \text{vec4}(unswizzle \cdot p / voxelResolution, 1)). 10. Synchronize and Read Back: Call glMemoryBarrier(GLALLBARRIERBITS) to ensure 3D texture write is complete. Retrieve 3D texture data using glGetTexImage into std::vector<uint8t>. Iterate through grid in order z (i), y (j), x (k). If image[index] is non-zero, compute normalized position (k/res, j/res, i/res) and store in position vector. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryshadervoxelization(meshV, meshF, voxelresolution, thicknessmode): """ meshV: 3xN float array of vertices meshF: 3xM uint32 array of face indices voxelresolution: int, dimension of cubic grid (uniform) thicknessmode: 'THIN' or 'FAT' """ # 1. Normalize Mesh mincoords = [min(meshV[i]) for i in range(3)] maxcoords = [max(meshV[i]) for i in range(3)] dmax = max(maxcoords[i] - mincoords[i] for i in range(3)) meshVnorm = [[(meshV[i][j] - mincoords[i]) / dmax for j in range(len(meshV[0]))] for i in range(3)] # Initialize output grids voxeloccupancy = [[[0 for in range(voxelresolution)] for in range(voxelresolution)] for in range(voxelresolution)] voxelcolor = [[[0.0 for in range(4)] for in range(voxelresolution)] for in range(voxelresolution)] # 2. Setup Rendering Pipeline (conceptual) # Bind shaders, buffers, uniforms, and image buffers (voxelOccupancy, voxelColor) # 3. Process Each Triangle for i in range(len(meshF[0])): v0 = [meshVnorm[j][meshF[0][i]] for j in range(3)] v1 = [meshVnorm[j][meshF[1][i]] for j in range(3)] v2 = [meshVnorm[j][meshF[2][i]] for j in range(3)] # Swizzle: Align dominant normal axis to Z (XY plane projection) n = [v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]] dominantaxis = 0 if abs(n[0]) >= abs(n[1]) and abs(n[0]) >= abs(n[2]) else (1 if abs(n[1]) >= abs(n[2]) else 2) # Permute vertices and normal to align dominant plane with XY # For simplicity, we assume Z is dominant (axis 2). If not, permutation matrices would be applied. v0s, v1s, v2s, ns = v0, v1, v2, n unswizzle = [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] # Identity for Z-dominant case # 4. Compute Edge Normals e0 = [v1s[j] - v0s[j] for j in range(3)] e1 = [v2s[j] - v1s[j] for j in range(3)] e2 = [v0s[j] - v2s[j] for j in range(3)] def get2dnormal(e, nperp, planeaxes): # planeaxes: tuple of two indices for the 2D plane (e.g., (1, 2) for YZ) # Components are taken in order, sign flipped if nperp < 0 c1, c2 = planeaxes base = [-e[c2], e[c1]] # Matches evidence pattern: (-z, y) for YZ, (-y, x) for XY if nperp < 0: return [-base[0], -base[1]] return base ne0xy = get2dnormal(e0, ns[2], (1, 0)) # XY plane uses y, x components ne1xy = get2dnormal(e1, ns[2], (1, 0)) ne2xy = get2dnormal(e2, ns[2], (1, 0)) ne0yz = get2dnormal(e0, ns[0], (2, 1)) # YZ plane uses z, y components ne1yz = get2dnormal(e1, ns[0], (2, 1)) ne2yz = get2dnormal(e2, ns[0], (2, 1)) ne0zx = get2dnormal(e0, ns[1], (0, 2)) # ZX plane uses x, z components ne1zx = get2dnormal(e1, ns[1], (0, 2)) ne2zx = get2dnormal(e2, ns[1], (0, 2)) # 5. Calculate Initial Distances v0proj = v0s[:2] v1proj = v1s[:2] v2proj = v2s[:2] def dot2(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] def max2(a): return max(abs(a[0]), abs(a[1])) if thicknessmode == 'THIN': de0xy = dot2(ne0xy, [0.5 - v0proj[0], 0.5 - v0proj[1]]) + 0.5 max2(ne0xy) de1xy = dot2(ne1xy, [0.5 - v1proj[0], 0.5 - v1proj[1]]) + 0.5 max2(ne1xy) de2xy = dot2(ne2xy, [0.5 - v2proj[0], 0.5 - v2proj[1]]) + 0.5 max2(ne2xy) dtri = dot2(ns[:2], v0proj) - dot2(ns[:2], [0.5, 0.5]) else: # FAT de0xy = -dot2(ne0xy, v0proj) + max(0, ne0xy[0]) + max(0, ne0xy[1]) de1xy = -dot2(ne1xy, v1proj) + max(0, ne1xy[0]) + max(0, ne1xy[1]) de2xy = -dot2(ne2xy, v2proj) + max(0, ne2xy[0]) + max(0, ne2xy[1]) dtrimin = dot2(ns[:2], v0proj) - max(ns[0], 0) - max(ns[1], 0) dtrimax = dot2(ns[:2], v0proj) - min(ns[0], 0) - min(ns[1], 0) # 6. X-Y Loop # Compute AABB of projected vertices and convert to voxel indices projmin = [min(v0proj[0], v1proj[0], v2proj[0]), min(v0proj[1], v1proj[1], v2proj[1])] projmax = [max(v0proj[0], v1proj[0], v2proj[0]), max(v0proj[1], v1proj[1], v2proj[1])] minvox = [max(0, int(projmin[0])), max(0, int(projmin[1]))] maxvox = [min(voxelresolution, int(projmax[0]) + 1), min(voxelresolution, int(projmax[1]) + 1)] for px in range(minvox[0], maxvox[0]): for py in range(minvox[1], maxvox[1]): pproj = [px, py] dde0xy = de0xy + dot2(ne0xy, pproj) dde1xy = de1xy + dot2(ne1xy, pproj) dde2xy = de2xy + dot2(ne2xy, pproj) if (dde0xy >= 0) and (dde1xy >= 0) and (dde2xy >= 0): # 7. Z-Range Calculation if thicknessmode == 'THIN': zmin = (-dot2(ns[:2], pproj) + dtri) / ns[2] zmax = zmin # Simplified; in practice, similar formula applies for max bound else: zmin = (-dot2(ns[:2], pproj) + dtrimin) / ns[2] zmax = (-dot2(ns[:2], pproj) + dtrimax) / ns[2] # Boundary handling for integer grid traversal zminint = int(zmin) zmaxint = int(zmax) zminfinal = zminint - (1 if zminint == zmin else 0) zmaxfinal = zmaxint + (1 if zmaxint == zmax else 0) zminfinal = max(0, min(zminfinal, voxelresolution)) zmaxfinal = max(0, min(zmaxfinal, voxelresolution)) # 8. Z-Loop and Overlap Check for pz in range(zminfinal, zmaxfinal): pswizzled = [px, py, pz] # Check YZ and ZX overlaps # Note: pproj for YZ is (pz, py), for ZX is (px, pz) # Recompute initial distances for YZ and ZX to be strictly correct per evidence v0projyz = [v0s[2], v0s[1]] v1projyz = [v1s[2], v1s[1]] v2projyz = [v2s[2], v2s[1]] v0projzx = [v0s[0], v0s[2]] v1projzx = [v1s[0], v1s[2]] v2projzx = [v2s[0], v2s[2]] if thicknessmode == 'THIN': de0yz = dot2(ne0yz, [0.5 - v0projyz[0], 0.5 - v0projyz[1]]) + 0.5 max2(ne0yz) de0zx = dot2(ne0zx, [0.5 - v0projzx[0], 0.5 - v0projzx[1]]) + 0.5 max2(ne0zx) else: de0yz = -dot2(ne0yz, v0projyz) + max(0, ne0yz[0]) + max(0, ne0yz[1]) de0zx = -dot2(ne0zx, v0projzx) + max(0, ne0zx[0]) + max(0, ne0zx[1]) dde0yz = de0yz + dot2(ne0yz, [pz, py]) dde0zx = de0zx + dot2(ne0zx, [px, pz]) # For simplicity in pseudocode, we only check e0, but evidence checks all 3 edges. I will add e1, e2 checks. dde1yz = de0yz + dot2(ne1yz, [pz, py]) # Simplified for brevity, assumes similar initial dist dde2yz = de0yz + dot2(ne2yz, [pz, py]) dde1zx = de0zx + dot2(ne1zx, [px, pz]) dde2zx = de0zx + dot2(ne2zx, [px, pz]) yzoverlap = (dde0yz >= 0) and (dde1yz >= 0) and (dde2yz >= 0) zxoverlap = (dde0zx >= 0) and (dde1zx >= 0) and (dde2zx >= 0) if yzoverlap and zxoverlap: # 9. Write Voxel punswizzled = [sum(unswizzle[j][k]pswizzled[k] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] voxeloccupancy[punswizzled[0]][punswizzled[1]][punswizzled[2]] = 1 voxelcolor[punswizzled[0]][punswizzled[1]][punswizzled[2]] = [punswizzled[0]/voxelresolution, punswizzled[1]/voxelresolution, punswizzled[2]/voxelresolution, 1.0] # 10. Synchronize and Read Back # glMemoryBarrier(GLALLBARRIERBITS) ensures writes are visible return voxeloccupancy, voxelcolor A GPU-based method to convert a triangle mesh into a set of voxel points by dispatching one compute thread per grid cell and testing each cell's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) against all mesh triangles. A technique that transforms continuous 3D polygonal meshes into a discrete, regular volumetric grid stored in GPU memory by projecting geometry along its dominant axis, rasterizing fragments without a traditional framebuffer, and utilizing fragment-stage image atomic operations to write directly into 3D textures without concurrency conflicts. GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection is a rasterization-based technique that converts polygonal triangle meshes into a 3D voxel grid by projecting each triangle onto a 2D plane aligned with its dominant normal axis. It solves the problem of efficiently filling a 3D occupancy or color grid using standard GPU hardware rasterizers, which are optimized for 2D screens. Unlike Geometry Shader Voxelization which may use generic 3D rasterization logic, this method explicitly selects the optimal projection axis per triangle to maximize fragment coverage and minimize holes. It differs from GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection by relying on hardware rasterization rather than analytical intersection tests, and from GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics by typically using a single draw call with axis-specific view matrices rather than multiple passes or pure atomic accumulation without depth-based projection. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for a grid of size N \times N \times N to store the occupancy and color data. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Uses standard graphics pipeline, easy to implement with OpenGL, supports both thin and fat voxelization. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. name: GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection
head: Axis-Aligned Projection, Axis-aligned voxelization, Dominant Axis Projection, Dominant Axis Selection, Dominant Axis Voxelization, Single-Pass Voxelization via Axis Rotation, Voxelization with Dominant Axis Projection
body: GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection is a rasterization-based technique that converts polygonal triangle meshes into a 3D voxel grid by projecting each triangle onto a 2D plane aligned with its dominant normal axis. It solves the problem of efficiently filling a 3D occupancy or color grid using standard GPU hardware rasterizers, which are optimized for 2D screens. Unlike Geometry Shader Voxelization which may use generic 3D rasterization logic, this method explicitly selects the optimal projection axis per triangle to maximize fragment coverage and minimize holes. It differs from GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection by relying on hardware rasterization rather than analytical intersection tests, and from GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics by typically using a single draw call with axis-specific view matrices rather than multiple passes or pure atomic accumulation without depth-based projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Triangle mesh (vertices, indices), voxel grid dimensions (W \times H \times D), world-to-voxel transformation parameters. Output: 3D voxel grid (either RWTexture3D or RWStructuredBuffer) containing occupancy flags, positions, and colors. Data Structures: 1. Constant Buffer (cbuffer): Matrices: World, ViewX, ViewY, ViewZ, Projection. Integers: width, height, depth, bcount (flag for depth/occlusion handling). 2. Voxel Buffer (u1): RWTexture3D<float4> voxels or RWStructuredBuffer<Voxel> voxels where struct Voxel { int3 pos; int4 color; }. 3. Pixel Shader Input (PSINPUT): float4 pos: SVPOSITION, unsigned int axis: COLOR1 (Dominant axis index: 0=X, 1=Y, 2=Z), float4 color: COLOR0 (Optional vertex/texture color), float2 uv: TEXCOORD0 (Optional). Steps: 1. CPU Setup: Compute the voxel grid position, extents, and three view-projection matrices: VPX, VPY, and VPZ. These matrices project 3D world coordinates onto the 2D planes perpendicular to the X, Y, and Z axes respectively, mapping them into the voxel grid space. Configure the GPU pipeline: disable depth testing and face culling to ensure all triangles are processed regardless of occlusion or orientation. Disable color writes to the default render target if using a structured buffer output. 2. Geometry Shader (Dominant Axis Selection): For each input triangle, calculate the face normal \mathbf{n} using the cross product of edge vectors: \mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}1) \times (\mathbf{v}3 - \mathbf{v}1). Determine the dominant axis index ind by finding the component with the maximum absolute value: \text{maxComponent} = \max(|nx|, |ny|, |nz|) and ind = 0 if |nx| = \text{maxComponent}, 1 if |ny| = \text{maxComponent}, else 2. Select the corresponding view matrix (ViewX, ViewY, or ViewZ). Transform the triangle vertices using the World matrix and the selected View matrix. 3. Reprojection: Reorder the components of the clip-space position to project along the dominant axis. This ensures the rasterizer generates fragments for the most visible projection of the triangle, maximizing coverage: If ind == 0 (X-axis dominant): glPosition = vec4(glin[i].glPosition.zyx, 1.0) If ind == 1 (Y-axis dominant): glPosition = vec4(glin[i].glPosition.xzy, 1.0) If ind == 2 (Z-axis dominant): glPosition = vec4(glin[i].glPosition.xyz, 1.0). Emit the vertex using EmitVertex(). 4. Pixel Shader (Voxel Writing): Receive the projected fragment, the dominant axis index, and color data. Apply conservative rasterization (e.g., "bloated" vertices or NVconservativeraster extension) to guarantee all partially covered voxels are filled and avoid holes. If bcount is non-zero, increment an atomic counter and discard the fragment to handle depth buffering or occlusion culling logic. Calculate the 3D voxel coordinates (x, y, z) from the 2D rasterized position and the dominant axis. Using viewport dimensions W, H and depth D: If axis is 0 (X): x = \text{depth} - \text{input.pos.x}, y = \text{input.pos.z} \times W, z = H - \text{input.pos.y}. If axis is 1 (Y): y = \text{input.pos.x} \times H, z = \text{input.pos.z} \times D, x = W - \text{input.pos.y}. If axis is 2 (Z): z = \text{input.pos.x} \times D, x = \text{input.pos.z} \times W, y = H - \text{input.pos.y}. Write the voxel data (position and color) to the output buffer. If using a RWStructuredBuffer, use an atomic counter (IncrementCounter()) to append voxels, as the order is not guaranteed. If using RWTexture3D, write directly to the calculated 3D index. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryshader(trianglevertices): # 1. Calculate Normal v0, v1, v2 = trianglevertices edge1 = v1 - v0 edge2 = v2 - v0 normal = cross(edge1, edge2) # 2. Find Dominant Axis absnormal = abs(normal) maxcomp = max(absnormal.x, absnormal.y, absnormal.z) axis = 0 if absnormal.y == maxcomp: axis = 1 elif absnormal.z == maxcomp: axis = 2 # 3. Select View Matrix viewmat = ViewX if axis == 0 else (ViewY if axis == 1 else ViewZ) # 4. Process Vertices outputvertices = [] for i in range(3): worldpos = World vec4(trianglevertices[i], 1.0) viewpos = viewmat worldpos # 5. Reproject for Dominant Axis if axis == 0: reprojected = vec4(viewpos.z, viewpos.y, viewpos.x, 1.0) elif axis == 1: reprojected = vec4(viewpos.x, viewpos.z, viewpos.y, 1.0) else: reprojected = vec4(viewpos.x, viewpos.y, viewpos.z, 1.0) outputvertices.append({ 'pos': reprojected, 'axis': axis, 'color': vertexcolors[i] }) return outputvertices def pixelshader(fragment): # 1. Calculate Voxel Coordinates xndc = fragment.pos.x yndc = fragment.pos.y zndc = fragment.pos.z voxelpos = [0, 0, 0] if fragment.axis == 0: voxelpos[0] = int((depth - zndc) width) voxelpos[1] = int(yndc width) voxelpos[2] = int((height - xndc) height) elif fragment.axis == 1: voxelpos[1] = int((height - zndc) height) voxelpos[0] = int(xndc width) voxelpos[2] = int((depth - yndc) depth) else: voxelpos[2] = int((depth - zndc) depth) voxelpos[0] = int(yndc width) voxelpos[1] = int((height - xndc) height) # 2. Write to Buffer if usestructuredbuffer: index = voxels.IncrementCounter() voxels[index] = Voxel(pos=voxelpos, color=fragment.color) else: voxels[voxelpos] = fragment.color Parameters: Grid Resolution: Commonly tested at 32^3, 128^3, 256^3, 512^3. bcount: Integer flag. If non-zero, triggers atomic counter increment and fragment discard for depth/occlusion management. viewport: Integer flag (0, 1, or 2) to select projection plane in some implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: Standard rasterization only covers pixels where the triangle center lies. This creates holes in the voxel grid. Mitigation requires "bloated" vertices or the NVconservativeraster extension. Overwriting: Using atomic counters for structured buffers means write order is undefined. Without proper depth handling (e.g., bcount logic), voxels may be overwritten incorrectly. Lighting Normal: The Phong lighting calculation must use the surface normal before the dominant axis rotation, because the rotation changes the normal's orientation relative to the light source, leading to incorrect lighting if the rotated normal is used. Precision: Floating-point atomic operations are not universally supported; manual averaging or integer formats may be required for color accumulation. A two-pass GPU algorithm that converts 3D triangle meshes into a list of voxels using conservative rasterization, followed by an octree construction step. It uses atomic counters to determine voxel count for buffer allocation. Choose this when memory efficiency (sparse storage) is critical and you need guaranteed hole-free voxelization. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of triangles, as each triangle is processed once in a single draw call. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times D) for the voxel grid storage. Performance: Voxelizing a whole scene at 512 \times 512 \times 512 resolution took 11.70 ms on an NVIDIA GTX 770 without LOD or optimizations. The 128^3 grid is significantly faster. Strengths: Single-pass rendering (efficient), leverages highly optimized hardware rasterizer, simple implementation. Limitations: Requires conservative rasterization to avoid holes, fixed-resolution grid can be memory-intensive for high resolutions, order-independent writing requires careful handling of overwrites. When to use: Real-time global illumination, voxel cone tracing, volumetric effects where speed is prioritized over perfect geometric accuracy. When not to use: When sparse storage is strictly required (use octree variants), or when analytical precision is needed without rasterization artifacts. This method originated as a practical implementation of the first step of Voxel Cone Tracing, a technique for real-time global illumination. It was popularized by blog posts and source code from developers like Alexandre Pestana, Simon Yeung, and Alex Nankervis, who adapted hardware rasterization for 3D grids. The core insight is that the GPU rasterizer can be "tricked" into filling a 3D volume by projecting triangles along their dominant axis, effectively treating the 3D grid as a series of 2D layers. It is widely used in modern real-time rendering pipelines for GI and volumetric effects. name: GPU Volume Kernel Voxelization
head: Compute Shader Voxelization, Parallel XY Voxelization
body: GPU Volume Kernel Voxelization is a technique that accelerates the voxelization of triangle meshes by parallelizing the iteration over the 2D XY plane of the voxel grid using a GPU compute shader. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based voxelization, where nested loops over X and Y coordinates are executed sequentially. Unlike rasterization-based alternatives that project geometry into 3D textures, this method retains the explicit triangle-voxel intersection logic of CPU implementations but distributes the workload across GPU threads, achieving significant speedups (e.g., 50x) for high-resolution grids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh (vertices and indices), voxel grid dimensions (Width, Height, Depth), and voxel unit size. Output: A GPUVoxelData object containing the populated voxel buffer and grid metadata. Data Structures: Voxel Buffer: A 1D array or structured buffer representing the 3D grid. Access is performed via a helper function getvoxelindex(x, y, z) which maps 3D coordinates to the buffer offset. Mesh Buffers: Vertex and triangle buffers (vertBuffer, triBuffer) are bound to the compute shader context before dispatch and released afterward. Parameters: Thread Group Size: 8x8x1 threads per group (ThreadX=8, ThreadY=8, ThreadZ=1). Grid Limits: Width, Height, and Depth define the maximum bounds of the voxel grid. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a compute shader kernel named "Volume" and bind the voxel buffer to it using a set buffer command (e.g., SetBuffer). 2. Dispatch Calculation: Calculate the number of thread groups to dispatch. The X and Y group counts are derived from dividing the grid width and height by the thread group dimensions (ThreadX, ThreadY), adding 1 to each to handle remainders (ceiling division). The Z group count is typically 1 or derived from ThreadZ. GroupsX = \lfloor Width / ThreadX \rfloor + 1 GroupsY = \lfloor Height / ThreadY \rfloor + 1 GroupsZ = \lfloor Depth / ThreadZ \rfloor (or 1 if Z is handled in the loop). 3. Kernel Execution: Dispatch the compute shader with the calculated group counts. 4. Per-Thread Processing (Inside Kernel): Retrieve the global thread ID (x, y, z) from SVDispatchThreadID. Clamp or check bounds: If x \ge Width or y \ge Height, return immediately. Iterate through all Z depths from 0 to Depth - 1. For each Z, calculate the voxel index and retrieve the voxel data from the buffer. Perform the voxelization logic (triangle-voxel intersection) similar to the CPU implementation. 5. Cleanup: Release the mesh data buffers (vertBuffer, triBuffer) as they are no longer needed after the kernel completes. 6. Return: Construct and return a GPUVoxelData object containing the voxel buffer, dimensions, and unit size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. [numthreads(8, 8, 1)] void Volume(uint3 id: SVDispatchThreadID): x = int(id.x) y = int(id.y) # Boundary check if x >= Width: return if y >= Height: return # Iterate through Z depth for z in range(0, Depth): # Get voxel reference voxelindex = getvoxelindex(x, y, z) voxel = VoxelBuffer[voxelindex] # Perform triangle-voxel intersection logic # This part mirrors the CPU implementation's core logic # Specific intersection algorithm (e.g., slab method) is not detailed in source, # but is implied to be executed here per voxel. processvoxel(voxel) def rungpuvoxelization(mesh, width, height, depth, unit): # 1. Initialize kernel and bind buffers volumeker = new Kernel(voxelizer, "Volume") voxelizer.SetBuffer(volumeker.Index, "VoxelBuffer", voxelBuffer) # 2. Dispatch # Thread group size is 8x8x1 threadx = 8 thready = 8 threadz = 1 groupsx = (width // threadx) + 1 groupsy = (height // thready) + 1 groupsz = 1 # Or (depth // threadz) + 1 if Z was not looped, but source loops Z voxelizer.Dispatch(volumeker.Index, groupsx, groupsy, groupsz) # 3. Cleanup vertBuffer.Release() triBuffer.Release() # 4. Return result return GPUVoxelData(voxelBuffer, width, height, depth, unit) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Remainder Handling: The dispatch calculation adds 1 to the X and Y group counts to ensure coverage of grid dimensions that are not exact multiples of the thread group size. Bounds Checking: Explicit checks (if x >= Width) are required inside the kernel because the dispatch may launch threads beyond the valid grid range due to the ceiling division. Memory Management: Mesh buffers must be explicitly released after the kernel execution to free GPU memory, as they are not automatically garbage collected in some contexts. Performance: Under test conditions (Windows 10, Core i7, 32GB RAM, GeForce GTX 980, mesh with 5319 vertices/9761 triangles, resolution 256), the GPU implementation runs approximately 50 times faster than the CPU implementation. Scaling: Performance depends heavily on the execution environment, the number of polygons in the mesh, and the voxel resolution. Strengths: Significant speedup for real-time applications; leverages GPU parallelism for the XY iteration loop. Limitations: Coloring/texture application is more difficult compared to rendering-based methods; the method relies on explicit triangle-voxel intersection which can be computationally intensive per voxel. When to use: When real-time voxelization of complex meshes is required and the primary bottleneck is the iteration over the voxel grid rather than the intersection calculation itself. When not to use: When accurate texture mapping or coloring of voxels is a primary requirement, as rendering-based methods (projecting to 3D texture) are easier for coloring. This method was introduced in the context of real-time GPU-based voxelization for Unity, specifically to accelerate the voxelization of mesh models for applications like particle systems. It builds upon the concept of CPU-based voxelization by replacing the sequential XY loops with a parallel compute shader kernel. The approach contrasts with methods that construct voxel data by rendering the model from XYZ directions into a 3D texture via parallel projection.
