name: Mesh Winding Number Voxelization
head: Hierarchical Mesh Winding Number Voxelization
body: Mesh Winding Number Voxelization determines the interior of a mesh by evaluating the Mesh Winding Number (MWN) at sample points within a voxel grid. Unlike Ray-Cast Style Voxel Filling or Front/Back Face Flagging, which rely on ray intersection parity or face orientation, MWN provides a robust signed distance-like field that handles meshes with holes and non-manifold geometry gracefully. It sets itself apart by yielding an integer value for closed meshes and a smoothly diffusing value around open boundaries, allowing for a consistent threshold-based classification. Inputs: A closed or open triangular mesh. A target voxel grid resolution (e.g., numcells per axis). The spatial bounds of the mesh (min/max coordinates). Outputs: A 3D boolean bitmap (Bitmap3) representing the interior voxels. Data Structures: Bitmap3: A 3D array of bits. Internally, bits are packed into 32-bit integers. Due to the lack of atomic read-and-flip operations on individual bits, concurrent writes require synchronization (e.g., a SpinLock) via a method like SafeSet. ShiftGridIndexer3: Maps integer grid indices (i, j, k) to 3D world coordinates (x, y, z). It requires a minimum corner vector and a cell size. Parameters: numcells: Base resolution per axis. The output grid dimensions are typically numcells + 2 in each axis to account for boundary padding or specific indexing schemes. cellsize: Derived from the mesh bounds. cellsize = \frac{\max(\text{bounds.MaxDim})}{numcells}. threshold: The value used to classify a voxel as inside. Typical value: 0.5. Higher values (e.g., 0.8) may result in missing chunks for meshes with holes. Steps: 1. Initialize Grid: Create a Bitmap3 with dimensions (numcells+2, numcells+2, numcells+2). 2. Setup Indexer: Create a ShiftGridIndexer3 using the mesh bounds' minimum corner and the calculated cellsize. 3. Seed Cache: Call the hierarchical WindingNumber function on a point known to be outside the mesh (e.g., the origin or a point far from the bounds). This initializes the internal bounding-box tree cache for efficient hierarchical evaluation. 4. Parallel Evaluation: Iterate over all grid indices in parallel. a. Map the grid index to a 3D world coordinate using indexer.FromGrid(idx). b. Compute the MWN at this coordinate using the hierarchical evaluator. c. If the MWN value is greater than the threshold (e.g., > 0.5), set the voxel to true. 5. Thread Safety: Use SafeSet (or equivalent atomic lock) when writing to the Bitmap3 to prevent race conditions caused by concurrent bit manipulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshwindingnumbervoxelization(mesh, numcells): # 1. Calculate bounds and cell size bounds = mesh.getbounds() maxdim = max(bounds.max - bounds.min) cellsize = maxdim / numcells # 2. Initialize grid and indexer # Output size is numcells + 2 in each axis griddims = Vector3i(numcells + 2, numcells + 2, numcells + 2) bitmap = Bitmap3(griddims) # Map grid indices to world coordinates indexer = ShiftGridIndexer3(bounds.min, cellsize) # 3. Seed the hierarchical cache with an outside point # Use a point guaranteed to be outside, e.g., origin or bounds.min - largeoffset outsidepoint = Vector3d(0, 0, 0) mesh.aabbtree.windingnumber(outsidepoint) # 4. Parallel evaluation def processvoxel(idx): # Map grid index to 3D world coordinate worldpos = indexer.fromgrid(idx) # Compute MWN wn = mesh.aabbtree.windingnumber(worldpos) # Threshold check if wn > 0.5: # Use SafeSet to handle race conditions on BitArray bitmap.safeset(idx, True) # Execute in parallel (e.g., using a thread pool or parallel loop) for idx in bitmap.indices(): processvoxel(idx) return bitmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Race Conditions: Writing to a BitArray from multiple threads without synchronization leads to data corruption because bits are packed into 32-bit integers and cannot be read-and-flipped atomically. SafeSet with a SpinLock is required. Threshold Selection: For meshes with holes, the MWN diffuses smoothly. A threshold of 0.5 is robust, but higher thresholds (e.g., 0.8) can cause significant parts of the interior to be missed. Performance: The hierarchical version is critical for large grids. Non-hierarchical evaluation is significantly slower (e.g., >1 minute vs. 1-2 seconds for a 64^3 grid on a 6-core machine). Time Complexity: The hierarchical evaluation reduces the cost per query from O(N) (where N is the number of triangles) to O(\log N) or better on average, depending on the tree structure. Total time is O(V \log N), where V is the number of voxels. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the output bitmap. The hierarchical tree adds O(N) overhead. Measured Performance: On a 6-core/12-thread machine in Release build, a 64^3 voxelization takes 1-2 seconds using the hierarchical method. The non-hierarchical version takes well over a minute. Strengths: Handles meshes with holes and non-manifold geometry gracefully. Provides a smooth transition around boundaries. Limitations: More computationally expensive per voxel than simple ray casting. Requires a hierarchical bounding-box tree structure for efficiency. When to use: When the mesh may have holes, is non-manifold, or when a robust "inside" definition is needed that doesn't rely on watertightness. When not to use: For simple, watertight meshes where speed is paramount and ray-casting or face-flagging suffices. The Mesh Winding Number was introduced by Alec Jacobson, Ladislav Kavan, and Olga Sorkine-Hornung in a SIGGRAPH paper in 2013. It extends the concept of the 2D polygon winding number to 3D meshes. For closed meshes, it yields an integer value (1 inside, 0 outside), while for meshes with holes, it diffuses smoothly around the boundaries. This property makes it particularly useful for voxelization tasks where mesh quality may vary or where open boundaries are present. 3D Bitmaps, Minecraft Cubes, and Mesh Winding Numbers — gradientspace, https://www.gradientspace.com/tutorials/2017/12/14/3d-bitmaps-and-minecraft-meshes, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Polyhedron Moment Integration and Voxelization
head: Polyhedron Moment Integration, R3D Polyhedron Moment Integration and Voxelization, R3D moment-based volume integration, simplicial decomposition integration
body: Polyhedron Moment Integration computes the polynomial density moments of a convex polyhedron within a voxel grid by recursively splitting the polyhedron along its longest axis until it occupies single voxels, then integrating the polynomial density field over the resulting polyhedron volume for each voxel. It differs from Stochastic Ray-Casting Voxelization and Ray-Cast Style Voxel Filling by providing exact analytic integration of density moments rather than stochastic or rasterization-based approximations, and from Mesh Winding Number Voxelization by supporting arbitrary polynomial density orders (not just binary occupancy). Inputs: poly: A convex polyhedron structure (r3dpoly) containing vertices, neighbor indices, and orientation flags. ibox: A bounding box defined by two corner indices ibox[0].ijk and ibox[1].ijk representing the grid region to process. polyorder: Integer specifying the polynomial order: 0 for constant (1 moment), 1 for linear (4 moments), 2 for quadratic (10 moments). destgrid: Output array for moments, sized according to grid dimensions and moment count. gridsz: Total grid dimensions (gridsz.i, gridsz.j, gridsz.k). Outputs: destgrid: Array filled with integration results. The order of moments is 1, x, y, z, x^2, y^2, z^2, xy, yz, zx for order 2. Data Structures: r3dpoly: Contains r3dvertex verts[R3DMAXVERTS] (vertex buffer, max 64), r3dint nverts (number of vertices), and r3dint funclip (index of any unclipped vertex). r3dvertex: Contains r3drvec3 pos (position), unsigned char pnbrs[3] (neighbor indices), and r3dorientation orient (orientation w.r.t clip planes). r3dorientation: Contains fflags (bitmask of face intersections) and fdist (distance to faces). Stack Entry: Contains r3dpoly poly and r3ddvec3 ibox[2] (bounding box). Max stack size is ceil(log2(gridsz.i)) + ceil(log2(gridsz.j)) + ceil(log2(gridsz.k)) + 1. R3DNUMMOMENTS(order): Macro calculating array size for moments: ((order + 1) (order + 2) (order + 3) / 6). Steps: 1. Initialize: Calculate grid size from ibox[1].ijk - ibox[0].ijk. Check for invalid inputs (null pointers, non-positive grid sizes). If invalid, return immediately. 2. Push Initial State: Copy input poly and ibox to stack[0]. Set nstack = 1. 3. Process Stack: While nstack > 0: a. Pop State: Decrement nstack and retrieve current state from stack[nstack]. b. Find Split Axis: Iterate i=0..2. Calculate siz = ibox[1].ijk[i] - ibox[0].ijk[i]. Track max siz (dmax) and its axis index (spax). c. Base Case (Single Voxel): If dmax == 1: i. Call r3dreduce on the poly to get moments. ii. Compute grid index using gind(ii, jj, kk, mm) = nmom ((ii - ibox[0].i) gridsz.j gridsz.k + (jj - ibox[0].j) gridsz.k + (kk - ibox[0].k)) + mm. iii. Add moments to destgrid at the voxel position ibox[0]. d. Recursive Step (Split): If dmax > 1: i. Split the poly along axis spax. Split coordinate is d.xyz[spax] (stack[nstack].ibox[0].ijk[spax] + dmax/2). ii. Store children in stack[nstack] and stack[nstack+1]. iii. Update Bounding Boxes: Copy ibox to child 1 (stack[nstack+1]). Update child 0 (stack[nstack]) ibox[1].ijk[spax] by subtracting (dmax - dmax/2). iv. Increment nstack to push child 1. Formulas: Grid Index: gind(ii, jj, kk, mm) = nmom ((ii - ibox[0].i) gridsz.j gridsz.k + (jj - ibox[0].j) gridsz.k + (kk - ibox[0].k)) + mm. Moment Order: Row-major ordering of moments. Sequence: 1, x, y, z, x^2, xy, xz, y^2, yz, z^2, x^3, x^2y.... Simplicial Decomposition Moments: For each triangle with vertices v0, v1, v2: locvol = ONESIXTH (-(v2.xv1.yv0.z) + v1.xv2.yv0.z + v2.xv0.yv1.z - v0.xv2.yv1.z - v1.xv0.yv2.z + v0.xv1.yv2.z). moments[0] += locvol. If polyorder >= 1: moments[1] += locvol 0.25 (v0.x + v1.x + v2.x). moments[2] += locvol 0.25 (v0.y + v1.y + v2.y). moments[3] += locvol 0.25 (v0.z + v1.z + v2.z). If polyorder >= 2: moments[4] += locvol 0.1 (v0.xv0.x + v1.xv1.x + v2.xv2.x + v1.xv2.x + v0.x(v1.x + v2.x)). moments[5] += locvol 0.1 (v0.yv0.y + v1.yv1.y + v2.yv2.y + v1.yv2.y + v0.y(v1.y + v2.y)). moments[6] += locvol 0.1 (v0.zv0.z + v1.zv1.z + v2.zv2.z + v1.zv2.z + v0.z(v1.z + v2.z)). moments[7] += locvol 0.05 (v2.xv0.y + v2.xv1.y + 2v2.xv2.y + v0.x(2v0.y + v1.y + v2.y) + v1.x(v0.y + 2v1.y + v2.y)). moments[8] += locvol 0.05 (v2.yv0.z + v2.yv1.z + 2v2.yv2.z + v0.y(2v0.z + v1.z + v2.z) + v1.y(v0.z + 2v1.z + v2.z)). moments[9] += locvol 0.05 (v2.xv0.z + v2.xv1.z + 2v2.xv2.z + v0.x(2v0.z + v1.z + v2.z) + v1.x(v0.z + 2v1.z + v2.z)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polyhedronmomentintegration(poly, ibox, polyorder, destgrid, gridsz): # Initialize gridszi = ibox[1].ijk[0] - ibox[0].ijk[0] gridszj = ibox[1].ijk[1] - ibox[0].ijk[1] gridszk = ibox[1].ijk[2] - ibox[0].ijk[2] if gridszi <= 0 or gridszj <= 0 or gridszk <= 0: return # Stack initialization stack = [] stack.append({'poly': poly, 'ibox': ibox}) nstack = 1 nmom = R3DNUMMOMENTS(polyorder) while nstack > 0: nstack -= 1 current = stack[nstack] poly = current['poly'] ibox = current['ibox'] # Find split axis dmax = 0 spax = 0 for i in range(3): siz = ibox[1].ijk[i] - ibox[0].ijk[i] if siz > dmax: dmax = siz spax = i if dmax == 1: # Base case: single voxel moments = r3dreduce(poly, polyorder) # Adjust moments for box offset if polyorder >= 1 or 2 if polyorder >= 1: xmin = (ibox[0].ijk[0] + 0.5) 1.0 # Assuming unit voxel size for simplicity in offset calculation ymin = (ibox[0].ijk[1] + 0.5) 1.0 zmin = (ibox[0].ijk[2] + 0.5) 1.0 moments[1] += xmin moments[0] moments[2] += ymin moments[0] moments[3] += zmin moments[0] if polyorder >= 2: xmin = (ibox[0].ijk[0] + 0.5) 1.0 ymin = (ibox[0].ijk[1] + 0.5) 1.0 zmin = (ibox[0].ijk[2] + 0.5) 1.0 moments[4] += 2.0 xmin moments[1] + xmin xmin moments[0] moments[5] += 2.0 ymin moments[2] + ymin ymin moments[0] moments[6] += 2.0 zmin moments[3] + zmin zmin moments[0] moments[7] += xmin moments[2] + ymin moments[1] + xmin ymin moments[0] moments[8] += ymin moments[3] + zmin moments[2] + ymin zmin moments[0] moments[9] += xmin moments[3] + zmin moments[1] + xmin zmin moments[0] # Add to destgrid ii = ibox[0].ijk[0] jj = ibox[0].ijk[1] kk = ibox[0].ijk[2] for mm in range(nmom): gind = nmom ((ii - ibox[0].i) gridsz.j gridsz.k + (jj - ibox[0].j) gridsz.k + (kk - ibox[0].k)) + mm destgrid[gind] += moments[mm] else: # Recursive step: split splitcoord = dmax / 2 # Integer division # Child 0 (lower half) child0poly = splitpolyalongaxis(poly, spax, splitcoord) child0ibox = copy(ibox) child0ibox[1].ijk[spax] -= (dmax - splitcoord) # Child 1 (upper half) child1poly = splitpolyalongaxis(poly, spax, splitcoord) child1ibox = copy(ibox) child1ibox[0].ijk[spax] += splitcoord stack.append(child1poly, child1ibox) stack.append(child0poly, child0ibox) nstack += 2 def r3dreduce(poly, polyorder): moments = [0.0] R3DNUMMOMENTS(polyorder) verts = poly.verts nverts = poly.nverts # Find first unclipped vertex vcur = -1 for v in range(nverts): if not (verts[v].orient.fflags & CLIPMASK): vcur = v break if vcur == -1: return moments # Stack for edge traversal nvstack = 0 vstack = [] vstack.append(vcur) vstack.append(0) emarks = [[0] 3 for in range(R3DMAXVERTS)] while nvstack > 0: nvstack -= 1 pnext = vstack.pop() vcur = vstack.pop() if emarks[vcur][pnext]: continue emarks[vcur][pnext] = 1 vstart = vcur v0 = verts[vstart].pos vnext = verts[vcur].pnbrs[pnext] vstack.append(vcur) vstack.append((pnext + 1) % 3) # Move to second edge np = 0 while np < 3 and verts[vnext].pnbrs[np] != vcur: np += 1 vcur = vnext pnext = (np + 1) % 3 emarks[vcur][pnext] = 1 vnext = verts[vcur].pnbrs[pnext] vstack.append(vcur) vstack.append((pnext + 1) % 3) # Triangle fan while vnext != vstart: v2 = verts[vcur].pos v1 = verts[vnext].pos locvol = (1.0/6.0) (-(v2.xv1.yv0.z) + v1.xv2.yv0.z + v2.xv0.yv1.z - v0.xv2.yv1.z - v1.xv0.yv2.z + v0.xv1.yv2.z) moments[0] += locvol if polyorder >= 1: moments[1] += locvol 0.25 (v0.x + v1.x + v2.x) moments[2] += locvol 0.25 (v0.y + v1.y + v2.y) moments[3] += locvol 0.25 (v0.z + v1.z + v2.z) if polyorder >= 2: moments[4] += locvol 0.1 (v0.xv0.x + v1.xv1.x + v2.xv2.x + v1.xv2.x + v0.x(v1.x + v2.x)) moments[5] += locvol 0.1 (v0.yv0.y + v1.yv1.y + v2.yv2.y + v1.yv2.y + v0.y(v1.y + v2.y)) moments[6] += locvol 0.1 (v0.zv0.z + v1.zv1.z + v2.zv2.z + v1.zv2.z + v0.z(v1.z + v2.z)) moments[7] += locvol 0.05 (v2.xv0.y + v2.xv1.y + 2v2.xv2.y + v0.x(2v0.y + v1.y + v2.y) + v1.x(v0.y + 2v1.y + v2.y)) moments[8] += locvol 0.05 (v2.yv0.z + v2.yv1.z + 2v2.yv2.z + v0.y(2v0.z + v1.z + v2.z) + v1.y(v0.z + 2v1.z + v2.z)) moments[9] += locvol 0.05 (v2.xv0.z + v2.xv1.z + 2v2.xv2.z + v0.x(2v0.z + v1.z + v2.z) + v1.x(v0.z + 2v1.z + v2.z)) # Move to next edge np = 0 while np < 3 and verts[vnext].pnbrs[np] != vcur: np += 1 vcur = vnext pnext = (np + 1) % 3 emarks[vcur][pnext] = 1 vnext = verts[vcur].pnbrs[pnext] vstack.append(vcur) vstack.append((pnext + 1) % 3) return moments Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Integer division in split: The split coordinate uses integer division dmax/2. This may introduce slight inaccuracies in split position compared to floating point midpoint, but ensures integer voxel alignment. Stack Overflow Prevention: The stack size is calculated based on log2 of grid dimensions, ensuring it never overflows for grids up to ~512^3. All vertices clipped: If all vertices have been clipped, r3dreduce returns immediately with zero moments. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by the polyhedron, due to recursive splitting. Memory Complexity: O(\log (\text{grid dimensions})) for the stack, plus O(\text{grid size} \times \text{moments per voxel}) for the output grid. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with grid resolution due to logarithmic stack depth. Strengths: Exact analytic integration of polynomial density moments; supports arbitrary polynomial orders; efficient for convex polyhedra. Limitations: Limited to convex polyhedra; integer division may introduce slight inaccuracies; stack size limits grid dimensions. When to use: When exact polynomial density moments are required for convex polyhedra. When not to use: For non-convex polyhedra or when approximate binary occupancy is sufficient. Polyhedron Moment Integration was developed as part of the r3d library by Devon Powell. It is used in volume rendering to produce volume data from polygonal meshes by integrating polynomial density fields. devonmpowell/r3d, https://github.com/devonmpowell/r3d, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Point-Containment Voxelization
head: AutoCAD Solid Voxelization, Grid-based Voxelization via Vertex Containment, VoxelizeSolid
body: Point-Containment Voxelization converts a 3D solid model into a 3D grid of voxels by determining which voxels intersect the solid's volume. It achieves this by sampling the grid vertices and checking their containment against the solid's Boundary Representation (BRep). It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on exact geometric containment queries for grid vertices rather than ray casting, winding numbers, or stochastic sampling. Inputs: A 3D solid object with a valid Boundary Representation (BRep). A recommendedVoxelSize (double), the user-provided suggested voxel edge length. Outputs: A VoxelModel containing a 3D grid of voxels, where each voxel is marked as intersecting the solid or not. Optionally, a list of new solid primitives representing the intersecting voxels. Data Structures: The method constructs two primary 3D arrays based on the grid dimensions N (where N is VoxelEdgeCount): 1. Vertices Array: Vertex[N+1, N+1, N+1] Point: Point3d (x, y, z coordinates in world space). Xi, Yi, Zi: int (grid indices). IsInside: bool (result of containment test). 2. Voxels Array: Voxel[N, N, N] Xi, Yi, Zi: int (grid indices). Extents: Extents3d (bounding box of the voxel). Intersects: bool (result of intersection test). V000 to V111: Vertex references to the 8 corner vertices. V000 corresponds to indices (i, j, k). V111 corresponds to indices (i+1, j+1, k+1). MinPoint: Derived as V000.Point. MaxPoint: Derived as V111.Point. Algorithm Steps: 1. Validate Bounds: Retrieve the bounding box (Extents3d) of the input solid. If the bounds are null, the method returns null immediately. 2. Calculate Grid Dimensions: Let L{max} be the length of the longest edge of the solid's bounding box. Compute the integer edge count N: N = \lceil L{max} / \text{recommendedVoxelSize} \rceil Compute the actual voxel edge length E: E = L{max} / N This ensures the voxels evenly fill the longest axis of the solid's extents. 3. Center Grid Extents: Let C be the center point of the solid's bounding box. Calculate half-edge length H: H = (N \times E) / 2.0 Set the grid's minimum point P{min} and maximum point P{max}: P{min} = C - (H, H, H) P{max} = C + (H, H, H) 4. Initialize Data Structures: Create the Vertices array of size (N+1, N+1, N+1). Create the Voxels array of size (N, N, N). 5. Populate Vertices: Iterate i from 0 to N, j from 0 to N, k from 0 to N. Calculate coordinates: x = P{min}.X + i \times E y = P{min}.Y + j \times E z = P{min}.Z + k \times E Create a Vertex object at (x, y, z) with indices (i, j, k). 6. Populate Voxels: Iterate i from 0 to N-1, j from 0 to N-1, k from 0 to N-1. Create a Voxel object. Link the voxel to its 8 constituent vertices from the Vertices array: V{000} = \text{Vertices}[i, j, k] V{001} = \text{Vertices}[i, j, k+1] V{101} = \text{Vertices}[i+1, j, k+1] V{100} = \text{Vertices}[i+1, j, k] V{010} = \text{Vertices}[i, j+1, k] V{011} = \text{Vertices}[i, j+1, k+1] V{111} = \text{Vertices}[i+1, j+1, k+1] V{110} = \text{Vertices}[i+1, j+1, k] Set Extents to the box defined by V{000}.Point and V{111}.Point. 7. Determine Vertex Containment: For each vertex in the grid, query the BRep for point containment. Let Containment be the result of the containment test. Set vertex.IsInside to true if Containment \neq \text{Outside}. Note: The specific definition of "Inside" vs "OnBoundary" depends on the BRep library, but typically points on the surface are considered inside or intersecting for voxelization purposes. 8. Determine Voxel Intersection: For each voxel, check its 8 constituent vertices. Set voxel.Intersects to true if at least one vertex has IsInside == true. 9. Generate Output: Iterate through all voxels. If voxel.Intersects is true, create a new solid primitive (e.g., a box) representing the voxel's extents and add it to the output model space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointcontainmentvoxelization(solid, recommendedvoxelsize): # 1. Validate Bounds bounds = solid.getbounds() if bounds is None: return None # 2. Calculate Grid Dimensions longestedge = bounds.getlongestedge() voxeledgecount = ceil(longestedge / recommendedvoxelsize) voxeledgelength = longestedge / voxeledgecount # 3. Center Grid Extents centerpoint = bounds.getcenter() halfedgelength = (voxeledgecount voxeledgelength) / 2.0 minpoint = centerpoint - (halfedgelength, halfedgelength, halfedgelength) maxpoint = centerpoint + (halfedgelength, halfedgelength, halfedgelength) # 4. Initialize Data Structures vertices = create3darray(voxeledgecount + 1, voxeledgecount + 1, voxeledgecount + 1) voxels = create3darray(voxeledgecount, voxeledgecount, voxeledgecount) # 5. Populate Vertices for xi in range(voxeledgecount + 1): for yi in range(voxeledgecount + 1): for zi in range(voxeledgecount + 1): x = minpoint.x + xi voxeledgelength y = minpoint.y + yi voxeledgelength z = minpoint.z + zi voxeledgelength vertices[xi, yi, zi] = Vertex(Point3d(x, y, z), xi, yi, zi) # 6. Populate Voxels for xi in range(voxeledgecount): for yi in range(voxeledgecount): for zi in range(voxeledgecount): v000 = vertices[xi, yi, zi] v001 = vertices[xi, yi, zi + 1] v101 = vertices[xi + 1, yi, zi + 1] v100 = vertices[xi + 1, yi, zi] v010 = vertices[xi, yi + 1, zi] v011 = vertices[xi, yi + 1, zi + 1] v111 = vertices[xi + 1, yi + 1, zi + 1] v110 = vertices[xi + 1, yi + 1, zi] extents = Extents3d(v000.point, v111.point) voxels[xi, yi, zi] = Voxel(xi, yi, zi, extents, v000, v001, v101, v100, v010, v011, v111, v110) # 7. Determine Vertex Containment brep = Brep(solid) for xi in range(voxeledgecount + 1): for yi in range(voxeledgecount + 1): for zi in range(voxeledgecount + 1): vertex = vertices[xi, yi, zi] containment = brep.getpointcontainment(vertex.point) vertex.isinside = (containment != PointContainment.Outside) # 8. Determine Voxel Intersection for xi in range(voxeledgecount): for yi in range(voxeledgecount): for zi in range(voxeledgecount): voxel = voxels[xi, yi, zi] voxel.intersects = any(v.isinside for v in voxel.vertices) # 9. Generate Output outputvoxels = [] for xi in range(voxeledgecount): for yi in range(voxeledgecount): for zi in range(voxeledgecount): voxel = voxels[xi, yi, zi] if voxel.intersects: outputvoxels.append(voxel.extents.createbox()) return VoxelModel(voxels, outputvoxels) Time Complexity: O(N^3), where N is VoxelEdgeCount. This is due to the triple nested loops required to create vertices, voxels, and check containment for every vertex in the grid. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for storing the vertex and voxel arrays. The vertex array is (N+1)^3 and the voxel array is N^3. Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages robust BRep containment queries provided by CAD kernels; produces a grid aligned with the object's bounding box. Limitations: Resolution is constrained by the longest axis of the bounding box, potentially leading to wasted voxels in non-uniform shapes; does not handle concavities or holes as precisely as ray-casting or winding number methods if the solid surface passes through a voxel without touching any vertex; performance degrades rapidly with high resolution due to cubic scaling. When to use: When working with CAD solids where BRep access is available and a coarse-to-medium resolution grid is sufficient; when exact vertex containment logic is preferred over probabilistic or ray-based approaches. When not to use: For high-resolution rendering where ray-casting or marching cubes are more appropriate; for complex meshes where vertex containment might miss thin features that pass between vertices. This method is implemented in the Voxelize-AutoCAD-Solid3d project, an unofficial tool for AutoCAD. It is designed to convert AutoCAD Solid3d objects into a grid of voxels for further processing or visualization. The method relies on the Autodesk.AutoCAD.BoundaryRepresentation namespace to perform point containment tests. dmccuaig/Voxelize-AutoCAD-Solid3d, https://github.com/dmccuaig/Voxelize-AutoCAD-Solid3d, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Point Cloud Voxelization
head: Voxelization from Point Cloud
body:
Point Cloud Voxelization converts a continuous 3D point cloud into a discrete, sparse voxel grid by mapping each point to a grid cell and aggregating data within occupied cells. Unlike mesh-based voxelization which determines occupancy via geometric intersection, this method relies on direct coordinate projection, making it suitable for unstructured point data. Inputs: points: Array of shape (N, F), where N is the number of points and F is the number of features. The first 3 features must be Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z). voxelsize: Array of shape (3,) specifying voxel dimensions (w, l, h). gridrange: Array of shape (6,) specifying the bounding box (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz). maxpointsinvoxel: Integer limit on points stored per voxel (default 60). maxnumvoxels: Integer limit on total allocated voxels (default 20000). Outputs: voxels: Pre-allocated array of shape (max
um\voxels, max\points\in\voxel, F), returned sliced to (V, max\points\in\voxel, F) containing point data for V active voxels. coordinates: Pre-allocated array of shape (max
um\voxels, 3), returned sliced to (V, 3) containing the integer grid coordinates of the V active voxels. numpointspervoxel: Pre-allocated array of shape (max
um\voxels), returned sliced to (V,) containing the count of valid points in each voxel. Data Structures: 1. coortovoxelidx: 3D NumPy array of shape (grid\size[2], grid\size[1], grid\size[0]) with dtype=int32, initialized to -1. Maps voxel coordinates to a sparse index in the output arrays. 2. voxels: Pre-allocated 3D array of shape (max
um\voxels, max\points\in\voxel, F). 3. coors: Pre-allocated 2D array of shape (max
um\voxels, 3) with dtype=int32. 4. numpointspervoxel: Pre-allocated 1D array of shape (max
um\voxels) with dtype=int32. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Grid Size: Calculate the dimensions of the voxel grid in cells: grid\size = \lfloor  rac{gridange[3:] - gridange[:3]}{voxel\size} floor Cast result to int32. 2. Compute Initial Coordinates: For each point pi with coordinates (x, y, z), compute the raw voxel index: coori = \lfloor  rac{(x, y, z) - gridange[:3]}{voxel\size} floor Cast to int32. 3. Boundary Masking: Create a boolean mask to filter points outside the grid range. A point is valid if: 0 \le coori[0] < grid\size[0] \quad \land \quad 0 \le coori[1] < grid\size[1] \quad \land \quad 0 \le coori[2] < grid\size[2] Apply this mask to both points and coor arrays. 4. Axis Reversal: Reverse the coordinate axis order of the filtered points and coordinates (e.g., [x, y, z] 	o [z, y, x]) to match memory layout conventions. 5. Initialization: Initialize voxelnum = 0. 6. Iterate and Map: Loop through each filtered point i with coordinate c: a. Look up voxelid = coortovoxelidx[tuple(c)]. b. If voxelid == -1 (new voxel): i. Set voxelid = voxelnum. ii. Increment voxelnum. iii. If voxelnum > maxnumvoxels, break the loop. iv. Set coortovoxelidx[tuple(c)] = voxelid. v. Set coors[voxelid] = c. c. Get npts = numpointspervoxel[voxelid]. d. If npts < maxpointsinvoxel: i. Store point data: voxels[voxelid, npts] = points[i]. ii. Increment numpointspervoxel[voxelid]. 7. Return Results: Slice the output arrays to the active count: voxels[:voxelnum], coors[:voxelnum], numpointspervoxel[:voxelnum]. Pseudocode (Numba JIT Version): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from numba import njit @njit def voxelizejit(points, voxelsize, gridrange, maxpointsinvoxel=60, maxnumvoxels=20000): pointscopy = points.copy() gridsize = np.floor((gridrange[3:] - gridrange[:3]) / voxelsize).astype(np.int32) coortovoxelidx = np.full((gridsize[2], gridsize[1], gridsize[0]), -1, dtype=np.int32) voxels = np.zeros((maxnumvoxels, maxpointsinvoxel, pointscopy.shape[-1]), dtype=pointscopy.dtype) coors = np.zeros((maxnumvoxels, 3), dtype=np.int32) numpointspervoxel = np.zeros(shape=(maxnumvoxels,), dtype=np.int32) coor = np.floor((pointscopy[:,:3] - gridrange[:3]) / voxelsize).astype(np.int32) mask = np.logicaland( np.logicaland( (coor[:, 0] >= 0) & (coor[:, 0] < gridsize[0]), (coor[:, 1] >= 0) & (coor[:, 1] < gridsize[1])), (coor[:, 2] >= 0) & (coor[:, 2] < gridsize[2])) coor = coor[mask,::-1] pointscopy = pointscopy[mask] voxelnum = 0 for i, c in enumerate(coor): voxelid = coortovoxelidx[c[0], c[1], c[2]] if voxelid == -1: voxelid = voxelnum voxelnum += 1 if voxelnum > maxnumvoxels: break coortovoxelidx[c[0], c[1], c[2]] = voxelid coors[voxelid] = c npts = numpointspervoxel[voxelid] if npts < maxpointsinvoxel: voxels[voxelid, npts] = pointscopy[i] numpointspervoxel[voxelid] += 1 return voxels[:voxelnum], coors[:voxelnum], numpointspervoxel[:voxelnum] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-Bounds Points: Points falling outside gridrange are discarded via the mask. Capacity Limits: If the number of unique voxels exceeds maxnumvoxels, the loop breaks, leaving subsequent points unprocessed. Point Overflow: If a voxel contains more than maxpointsinvoxel points, only the first maxpointsinvoxel are stored; subsequent points are discarded. Axis Convention: The coordinate axis order is reversed (x,y,z 	o z,y,x) to align with the memory layout of coortovoxelidx. A hierarchical spatial data structure used to organize point cloud objects for rendering, where each node contains a list of points and recursively subdivides its bounding volume into eight octants until a leaf condition is met. Choose this when memory efficiency or multi-resolution rendering is required over a flat grid. A broader pipeline context for generating voxel grid data, including preprocessing and post-processing steps beyond simple voxelization. Choose this when integrating voxelization into a larger rendering or processing workflow. A splatting method where a value at a continuous position is written to the single nearest voxel by rounding coordinates to integers. Implementation uses a continuous-to-discrete conversion function to map coordinates to voxel indices, checking bounds before accumulation. This method suffers from obvious aliasing problems. A converter that transforms point clouds into Gaussian ellipsoids using the same variance function as the mesh converter but determining distance based on point proximity. It determines dk as the distance to m nearest points of the target points, then computes \sigmak =  rac{(dk/2)^2}{\log(1/\zeta)} and \Sigmak = 	ext{diag}(\sigmak, \sigmak, \sigmak). Time Complexity: O(N) for coordinate computation and masking, where N is the number of points. The main loop iterates over the filtered points, so it is O(N{filtered}). Hashing via the dense coortovoxelidx array allows O(1) lookup per point. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the pre-allocated buffers voxels and coortovoxelidx. Memory usage is O(max
um\voxels 	imes max\points\in\voxel 	imes F + grid\size[0] 	imes grid\size[1] 	imes grid\size[2]). Performance: The Numba JIT version (voxelizejit) optimizes performance by avoiding Python overhead compared to the pure NumPy version (voxelize). Strengths: Simple implementation; supports feature aggregation. Limitations: Fixed capacity limits require careful tuning; dense coordinate map can be memory-intensive for large grids with small voxel sizes. Measured performance and scaling: Not given in the sources. Point cloud voxelization creates a voxel grid from a point cloud where occupied voxels store aggregated point data. The sparse voxel grid implementation detailed here, including the JIT-optimized version, is provided by. name: Octree Construction for Point Clouds
head: Point Cloud Octree Construction
body: This method constructs a hierarchical spatial data structure (octree) to organize point cloud objects for rendering, recursively subdividing space into eight octants until a leaf condition is met. It sets itself apart from flat voxel grids by enabling efficient CPU-based frustum culling and view-dependent sampling through aggregated node data, reducing the rendering load for large point clouds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of point cloud objects (points with position and color attributes) and a global bounding volume. Output: A root Node of the octree, which recursively contains child nodes and leaf nodes holding lists of points. Data Structures: Octant Enum: An 8-bit bitmask representing the 8 sub-volumes. O1=0x01 (0b00000001) through O8=0x80 (0b10000000). Node Structure: objects: List of points assigned to this node. aabb: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box defining the node's spatial extent. children: Array of 8 pointers to child Node objects (null if leaf). activeOctants: Bitmask indicating which children exist. depth: Current recursion depth. parent: Pointer to the parent node. averageObject: Cached average position and color of all objects in the subtree (used for culling). Parameters: MAXLEAFOBJECTS: Maximum number of objects allowed in a leaf node before subdivision stops. Value: 5. Steps: 1. Calculate Average: Compute the average position and color of all objects in the current node's list to store as averageObject. 2. Check Termination: If the number of objects in the current node is less than or equal to MAXLEAFOBJECTS (5), return without creating children. 3. Calculate Child AABBs: Iterate i from 0 to 7. Cast i to Octant via (Octant)(1 << i). Call calculateChildAABB with the parent region to generate the 8 child Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs). 4. Distribute Objects: Iterate through all objects in the current node. For each object, iterate through the 8 child AABBs. If childAABBs[j].contains(o.position) is true, push the object to childObjs[j] and break to the next object. This ensures objects on boundaries are assigned to the first containing octant (lowest index j), preventing duplication. 5. Clear List: Clear the current node's object list after distribution. 6. Create Children: Iterate i from 0 to 7. If childObjs[i].size() > 0: Create a new Node with the child's objects, child AABB, and depth + 1. Set the child's parent pointer to this. Activate the corresponding bit in activeOctants using activeOctants |= (1 << i). Recursively call build() on the new child. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Node: def init(self, aabb, depth=0, parent=None): self.aabb = aabb self.depth = depth self.parent = parent self.objects = [] self.children = [None] 8 self.activeoctants = 0 self.averageobject = None def build(self, objects): # Step 1: Calculate average if not objects: return self.objects = objects self.averageobject = calculateaverage(objects) # Step 2: Check termination if len(objects) <= 5: # MAXLEAFOBJECTS return # Step 3: Calculate child AABBs childaabbs = [] for i in range(8): octant = 1 << i childaabbs.append(calculatechildaabb(self.aabb, octant)) # Step 4: Distribute objects childobjs = [[] for in range(8)] for obj in objects: for j in range(8): if childaabbs[j].contains(obj.position): childobjs[j].append(obj) break # Assign to first containing octant to avoid duplication # Step 5: Clear current list self.objects = [] # Step 6: Create children for i in range(8): if len(childobjs[i]) > 0: childnode = Node(childaabbs[i], self.depth + 1, self) childnode.build(childobjs[i]) self.children[i] = childnode self.activeoctants |= (1 << i) def calculateaverage(objects): # Standard arithmetic mean of positions and colors sumpos = vec3(0, 0, 0) sumcol = vec3(0, 0, 0) count = len(objects) for obj in objects: sumpos += obj.position sumcol += obj.color return vec3(sumpos / count, sumcol / count) def calculatechildaabb(parentaabb, octant): # Standard octree subdivision: split each dimension in half # based on the bit flags in octant (0-7) minx, miny, minz = parentaabb.min maxx, maxy, maxz = parentaabb.max midx = (minx + maxx) / 2 midy = (miny + maxy) / 2 midz = (minz + maxz) / 2 # Determine min/max based on octant bits # Bit 0 (1): +x, Bit 1 (2): +y, Bit 2 (4): +z newmin = vec3( midx if (octant & 1) else minx, midy if (octant & 2) else miny, midz if (octant & 4) else minz) newmax = vec3( maxx if (octant & 1) else midx, maxy if (octant & 2) else midy, maxz if (octant & 4) else midz) return AABB(newmin, newmax) This method reduces the rendering load of large point clouds by traversing a pre-built octree on the CPU to perform frustum culling and view-dependent sampling before uploading data to the GPU. It sets itself apart from GPU-based culling techniques by aggregating point data into cached averages at internal octree nodes, allowing the CPU to decide exactly which subset of points to render based on distance thresholds. The octree partitions 3D space into a hierarchical grid of voxels to organize point cloud data for volume rendering and surface extraction. It recursively subdivides space into eight octants, distinguishing it from flat voxel grids. A hierarchical extension using an octree data structure for the interpolated volume to avoid problems of interpolating from curvilinear volumes with irregular sampling densities. It creates the octree by adding sample points from the original curvilinear grid one by one to the (originally empty) octree. Whenever a particular partition of the octree contains more than a user-specified number of curvilinear data samples, split that node into eight subnodes. After all curvilinear samples are added, calculate the estimated data value at the eight corners of each octree partition. Render the resulting volume using a hierarchical volume ray-tracer or the coherent projection approach. To avoid interpolation errors in creating the octree, an alternative is to use the octree together with the original curvilinear volume and render using values from the original sample values. Not given in the sources. The construction of octrees for point clouds is a foundational technique in spatial indexing for rendering. The specific implementation details regarding MAXLEAFOBJECTS and CPU culling aggregation are documented in unofficial repositories. The application of octrees to curvilinear volumes for volume rendering was introduced in research addressing interpolation errors in irregular sampling. arminkz/PointCloudRendering, https://github.com/arminkz/PointCloudRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Direct volume rendering of curvilinear volumes, https://doi.org/10.1145/99308.99318, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Octree-based Level of Detail and Culling
head: CPU Culling, LoD, CPU Frustum Culling, CPU-based Octree LOD & Frustum Culling, Distance-based LoD
body: This method reduces the rendering load of large point clouds by traversing a pre-built octree on the CPU to perform frustum culling and view-dependent sampling before uploading data to the GPU. It sets itself apart from GPU-based culling techniques by aggregating point data into cached averages at internal octree nodes, allowing the CPU to decide exactly which subset of points to render based on distance thresholds. Input: An octree structure built from a point cloud, where each node contains a bounding volume and a cached average point representing all points in its subtree. The current Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix and camera eye position. Output: A list of aggregated points (positions and colors) suitable for upload to a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) for rendering as GLPOINTS. Octree Node: Contains a bitmask activeOctants indicating which of the 8 children exist, a bounding region region (with center() and testAgainstFrustum() methods), and a cached averagepoint (position and color). PointModel: A structure containing position and color data, used to define the layout for the VBO. maxDepth: Maximum recursion depth for the LOD traversal, typically 15. worldsize: The diagonal length of the point cloud's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB), calculated as glm::length(pc.aabb.max() - pc.aabb.min()). cpuCulling: Boolean flag to enable/disable CPU-side aggregation and frustum culling. Default: false. cpuCullingEveryFrame: Boolean flag to recompute culling every frame. Default: false. 1. Preparation (Load Time): Compute worldsize from the point cloud's AABB diagonal. Build the octree. For each node, compute and cache the average position and color of all points in its subtree. 2. Traversal (Per Frame): If cpuCulling is disabled, skip this method. Start recursive traversal at the root node at depth 15 with the current MVP matrix and eye position. For each node, iterate through its 8 potential children (index i from 0 to 7): Check if the child is active: if (!(node->activeOctants & (1 << i))) continue;. Perform frustum culling: if (!node->children[i]->region.testAgainstFrustum(mvp)) continue;. Calculate distance from the child's center to the eye: dist = glm::length(node->children[i]->region.center() - eye). Determine the target emission depth for this child based on distance thresholds relative to worldsize: If dist > worldsize / 2: set target depth to 9. If worldsize / 4 < dist < worldsize / 2: set target depth to 10. Otherwise (dist <= worldsize / 4): set target depth to 15. Recurse into the child with the new target depth. Base Case (Emission): If the current traversal depth matches the target depth for the current node, emit the node's cached averagepoint to the output list and stop recursing into this branch. 3. Rendering: Upload the emitted aggregated points to a VBO using the byte size of PointModel. If the point list is empty (due to aggressive culling), return early from the draw call to prevent drawing invalid buffers. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def norm(v): """Compute Euclidean length of a 3D vector.""" return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def traverseoctree(node, currentdepth, targetdepth, mvp, eye, worldsize, outputpoints): """ Recursively traverse the octree to cull and sample points. Args: node: The current octree node. currentdepth: The current absolute depth in the octree (starts at 15). targetdepth: The absolute depth at which to emit points for this subtree. mvp: The Model-View-Projection matrix. eye: The camera eye position. worldsize: The diagonal length of the point cloud AABB. outputpoints: List to append aggregated points to. """ # Base case: If we have reached the target depth for this branch, emit the cached average point. if currentdepth == targetdepth: outputpoints.append(node.averagepoint) return # Guard against over-traversal if target depth is shallower than current if currentdepth < targetdepth: return # Iterate through all 8 possible children for i in range(8): # Check if this child exists using the bitmask if not (node.activeoctants & (1 << i)): continue child = node.children[i] # Frustum culling: Skip if the child's bounding region is outside the view frustum if not child.region.testagainstfrustum(mvp): continue # Calculate distance from child center to eye dist = norm(child.region.center() - eye) # Determine the new target depth for the child based on distance thresholds if dist > worldsize / 2: newtargetdepth = 9 elif worldsize / 4 < dist < worldsize / 2: newtargetdepth = 10 else: newtargetdepth = 15 # Recurse with the new target depth, decrementing current depth by 1 traverseoctree(child, currentdepth - 1, newtargetdepth, mvp, eye, worldsize, outputpoints) def renderpointcloudoctreelod(scene, mvp, eye): """ Main entry point for octree-based LOD and culling. """ if not scene.renderingparams.cpuculling: return [] worldsize = norm(scene.pc.aabb.max - scene.pc.aabb.min) outputpoints = [] # Start traversal at max depth (15) traverseoctree(scene.octree.root, 15, 15, mvp, eye, worldsize, outputpoints) # Edge case: Empty list after culling if not outputpoints: return [] # Upload to VBO using sizeof(PointModel) stride stride = 24 # sizeof(PointModel) as defined in the source vbo = allocatevbo(outputpoints, stride) gldrawpoints(vbo) return outputpoints def allocatevbo(points, stride): """Allocate GPU memory and upload point data.""" buffer = creategpubuffer(size=len(points) stride) uploaddata(buffer, points, stride) return buffer def gldrawpoints(vbo): """Issue a draw call for the uploaded point data.""" bindvbo(vbo) drawarray(mode=GLPOINTS, count=len(vbo.data)) Empty Output: If all nodes are culled by the frustum or distance thresholds, the output list may be empty. The draw function must check for this and return early to avoid rendering invalid buffers. Precision: Distance calculations and frustum tests should use sufficient precision to avoid jittering or incorrect culling, especially near threshold boundaries. What it is: The process of testing octree node bounding volumes against the camera's view frustum to skip subtrees that are not visible. Differentiation: Unlike GPU culling, this happens on the CPU before data transfer, reducing bandwidth usage. When to choose: When bandwidth to the GPU is a bottleneck or when the scene has large empty regions. Link: CPU Frustum Culling What it is: A technique to select the level of detail (depth) of the octree traversal based on the distance of the node from the camera. Differentiation: Uses fixed distance thresholds relative to the world size to determine sampling density, rather than screen-space error metrics. When to choose: When a simple, predictable reduction in point count is sufficient and screen-space error is not critical. Link: Distance-based LOD Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Octree Data Structure
head: CGAL::Octree, CGAL::Orthtree, RFVoxelOctree, RFVoxelOctreeNode, Voxel Octree Data Structure
body: The octree partitions 3D space into a hierarchical grid of voxels to organize point cloud data for volume rendering and surface extraction. It recursively subdivides space into eight octants, distinguishing it from flat voxel grids. Inputs: A set of 3D points (point cloud) and a bounding volume defining the spatial extent. Outputs: A tree structure where internal nodes represent partially filled space, leaf nodes represent occupied voxels, and empty leaf nodes retain a surface distance metric. Two primary implementations are cited: the RFVoxelOctree and CGAL::Orthtree. RFVoxelOctreeNode Layout: mpkChildren[8]: Array of 8 pointers to child nodes. mkBuildAabb: Axis-aligned bounding box in build space. mkWorldAabb: Axis-aligned bounding box in world space. meNodeType: Enum indicating state: NTINTERNAL, NTEMPTYLEAF, or NTLEAF. mfDistanceToSurface: Double-precision distance to the nearest surface (for empty leaves). RFVoxelOctree Layout: mpkRoot: Pointer to the root node. mkDataDimension: 3D integer vector defining the grid dimensions. mkOctreeOrigin: 3D double vector for the octree origin. mfVoxelSize: Physical size of a single voxel unit (default 1.0f). muiOctreeDim: Total dimension of the cubic voxel grid. Depth is derived as \log2(m\uiOctreeDim). muiOctreeDepth: Calculated depth. muiNumberOfNodes, muiNumberOfLeafs, muiNumberOfEmptyLeafs, muiNumberOfInternalNodes: Counters for statistics. name: Point Resampling with Neighbor Masking
head: Point Resampling
body: Point Resampling with Neighbor Masking is a strategy for managing point cloud density during the voxelization and optimization phases of volume rendering, specifically within the context of tetrahedral grid generation. It selectively activates or deactivates points based on their topological relationship to active elements (such as tetrahedra) and a user-defined resampling strategy. It distinguishes itself from its siblings by using explicit neighbor masks to control computational load and memory usage, rather than relying on error-driven metrics or structural hierarchy like octrees [1070-octree-construction-for-point-clouds.md]. The method operates on a set of points X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} and a set of tetrahedra T. It produces a boolean mask M of length N, where M[i] = \text{True} indicates the point i is active (kept) and \text{False} indicates it is inactive (discarded or compressed). Inputs: xnx3: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing point coordinates. tets: Tensor of shape (K, 4) containing tetrahedron vertex indices. sdf: Tensor of shape (N) or (K) containing signed distance values (used to determine "active" status). strategy: String, one of "partial", "percentage", or "full". Outputs: mask: Boolean tensor of shape (N). nbresampledpoints: Integer count of active points. Neighbor Map: A mapping from each tetrahedron to its constituent vertices, and vice versa. The function neighboractivepoints(sdf, tets) identifies vertices that are part of tetrahedra where the SDF indicates activity (e.g., near the isosurface). Active Points Set: The set of indices I{active} where the SDF value meets a specific criterion (e.g., |SDF| < \epsilon). 1. Identify Active Points: Determine the set of indices I{active} corresponding to points considered "active" based on the SDF and tetrahedron connectivity. 2. Identify Neighbor Active Points: Determine the set of indices I{neighbor} corresponding to points that are neighbors to the active tetrahedra. 3. Apply Strategy: Construct the mask M based on the chosen strategy: Partial: Activate only the neighbor active points. Percentage: Activate all active points, plus a subset of neighbor points to maintain a specific ratio or percentage of the total. Full: Activate all points. 4. Count: Calculate the number of resampled points as the sum of True values in M. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointresamplingwithneighbormasking(xnx3, tets, sdf, strategy="partial"): """ Resamples points based on active/neighbor status. Args: xnx3: Tensor (N, 3) point coordinates. tets: Tensor (K, 4) tetrahedron vertex indices. sdf: Tensor (N) or (K) signed distance values. strategy: 'partial', 'percentage', or 'full'. Returns: mask: Boolean tensor (N) nbresampledpoints: int """ N = xnx3.shape[0] mask = torch.zeros(N, dtype=torch.bool) # Helper to determine active tetrahedra based on SDF # Assuming SDF is defined per tetrahedron or interpolated. # For this implementation, we assume a function that returns active tet indices. activetetindices = getactivetets(sdf, tets) # Get neighbors of active tetrahedra # This function returns indices of vertices connected to activetetindices neighboractivepointsids = neighboractivepoints(sdf, tets) if strategy == "partial": # Activate only the neighbor active points mask[neighboractivepointsids] = True elif strategy == "percentage": # Get all active points (vertices of active tets) activepointsids = getactivepoints(sdf, tets) # Create mask with True at active indices mask[activepointsids] = True # Get indices where mask is currently True trueindices = torch.where(mask)[0] # Set neighbor indices to True mask[neighboractivepointsids] = True # Get all currently true indices again (active + neighbors) trueindices = torch.where(mask)[0] # Shuffle trueindices shuffledindices = trueindices[torch.randperm(len(trueindices))] # Flip first 90% of shuffled indices to False # This effectively keeps 10% of the active+neighbor points # Note: The source says "flip first 90%... to False", implying 10% remain True. # However, the context of "percentage" usually implies a specific ratio. # We follow the source literally: flip first 90% to False. numtoflip = int(0.9 len(shuffledindices)) indicestofalse = shuffledindices[:numtoflip] mask[indicestofalse] = False elif strategy == "full": # Activate all points mask[:] = True else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown strategy: {strategy}") nbresampledpoints = mask.sum().item() return mask, nbresampledpoints def getactivetets(sdf, tets): # Placeholder for specific SDF thresholding logic # Not given in the sources. # Assuming SDF is per-tetrahedron for this helper return torch.where(torch.abs(sdf) < 0.1)[0] def getactivepoints(sdf, tets): # Returns unique vertex indices from activetets activetets = getactivetets(sdf, tets) activetetsvertices = tets[activetets] uniquevertices = torch.unique(activetetsvertices) return uniquevertices def neighboractivepoints(sdf, tets): # Returns vertices that are neighbors to active tetrahedra # This includes vertices of active tets and their immediate neighbors activetets = getactivetets(sdf, tets) activetetsvertices = tets[activetets] uniqueactivevertices = torch.unique(activetetsvertices) # Get all vertices connected to active tets # This is a simplification; in practice, this might involve a neighbor lookup # Not given in the sources. # Assuming this function returns the union of active vertices and their neighbors return uniqueactivevertices Strategy: "partial", "percentage", "full". Default is not specified, but "partial" is described first. Percentage Threshold: For the "percentage" strategy, the source specifies flipping the first 90% of shuffled indices to False, leaving 10% active. This is a fixed value in the source. Precision: The source mentions converting values to float16 for compression, which may introduce precision loss. Boundaries: The definition of "neighbor" must be consistent with the tetrahedral mesh connectivity. Degenerate Input: If no active tetrahedra exist, the mask will be all False for partial/percentage strategies. This method computes a 3D error density field by accumulating per-pixel rendering discrepancies across multiple camera views into a voxel grid, then uses this density to guide the resampling of points for tetrahedral grid refinement. It distinguishes itself from its parent Point Resampling with Neighbor Masking by driving the resampling probability based on quantitative rendering error rather than topological neighbor status. Time Complexity: Depends on the neighbor lookup and sorting/shuffling operations. The source does not provide explicit Big-O notation. Memory Complexity: The mask requires O(N) bits. The source notes that discarding inactive points and converting to float16 can compress the model from 1.0MB to 345.5kB for a sample model. Strengths: Allows for controlled reduction of point cloud density, which can speed up optimization and reduce memory usage. Limitations: The quality of the resulting mesh depends heavily on the definition of "active" and "neighbor" points. The fixed 90% flip in the percentage strategy may not be optimal for all scenes. When to use: When computational resources are limited and a simplified point cloud representation is acceptable. When not to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction is required, or when the active region is sparse and neighbor masking might remove critical details. The method is part of the TetWeave framework, which performs isosurface extraction using on-the-fly Delaunay tetrahedral grids for gradient-based mesh optimization. It was introduced by Alexandre Binninger, Ruben Wiersma, Philipp Herholz, and Olga Sorkine-Hornung in their SIGGRAPH 2025 paper "TetWeave: Isosurface Extraction using On-The-Fly Delaunay Tetrahedral Grids for Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization". The codebase is available on GitHub. AlexandreBinninger/TetWeave, https://github.com/AlexandreBinninger/TetWeave, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Error-Driven Point Resampling & Grid Aggregation
body: This method computes a 3D error density field by accumulating per-pixel rendering discrepancies across multiple camera views into a voxel grid, then uses this density to guide the resampling of points for tetrahedral grid refinement. It distinguishes itself from its parent Point Resampling with Neighbor Masking by driving the resampling probability based on quantitative rendering error rather than topological neighbor status. Inputs: A set of input points (typically from a previous resampling stage or initial sampling). A list of camera views (position, orientation, intrinsics). A target voxel grid resolution (voxelresolution). Camera image resolution (resolution). Outputs: A refined set of points distributed according to the computed error density. A voxel grid containing mean error values per voxel. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D voxel grid structure. Fields: density (float tensor, shape [voxelresolution, voxelresolution, voxelresolution]), counts (int tensor, same shape), voxelresolution (int). Initialization: Grid(voxelresolution, -1.0, 2.0). The bounds -1.0 and 2.0 likely define the normalized coordinate space or scaling factors for the grid, though exact semantic meaning is not explicitly detailed beyond initialization. voxelindices: 1D integer tensor mapping 3D coordinates to flattened grid indices. Steps: 1. Initialize Grid: Create a 3D grid with resolution voxelresolution. Initialize error accumulation tensors (gridpointerrors) and count tensors (gridpointcounts) to zero. The grid bounds are set to -1.0 and 2.0. 2. Iterate Cameras: For each camera in the view list: a. Render: Render the current point cloud to obtain position masks (currentmask) and depth/position information using renderposmask. b. Filter Pixels: Identify valid pixels where currentmask.squeeze(-1) > 0.5. c. Compute Error: Calculate the per-pixel rendering error for these valid pixels. The specific error metric (e.g., L1, L2, depth difference) is not explicitly defined in the source, but it is aggregated into maskederror. d. Map to Voxel Indices: Convert the 3D positions of the filtered pixels to voxel indices using grid.pointvoxelidx. e. Validate Indices: Ensure the computed voxel indices are within the valid bounds [0, voxelresolution-1] in all dimensions. f. Flatten and Scatter: Flatten the valid voxel indices into a 1D tensor. Scatter-add the maskederror values to gridpointerrors and increment gridpointcounts at the corresponding flattened indices. 3. Accumulate Across Cameras: Repeat steps 2a-2f for all cameras. The gridpointerrors and gridpointcounts tensors accumulate values across all views. 4. Compute Mean Error: Calculate the mean error per voxel: \text{grid\point\errors} = \begin{cases} \frac{\text{grid\point\errors}}{\text{grid\point\counts}} & \text{if } \text{grid\point\counts} > 0 \\ \text{grid\point\errors} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This is implemented using torch.where. 5. Assign Density: Assign the computed mean error values to grid.density. 6. Resample Points: Use grid.samplepoints to generate a new set of points. The sampling strategy is controlled by resampledpointsmethod (default 'partial'). The probability of sampling a point in a voxel is proportional to its density value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errordrivenresampling(points, cameras, voxelresolution=32, resolution=[1024, 1024], aggregationmethod='interpolation', resampledpointsmethod='partial', device='cuda'): # Initialize grid structures grid = Grid(voxelresolution, -1.0, 2.0) gridpointerrors = torch.zeros(voxelresolution3, device=device) gridpointcounts = torch.zeros(voxelresolution3, dtype=torch.int, device=device) for camera in cameras: # Render positions and masks positions, currentmask = renderposmask(points, camera, resolution) # Filter valid pixels validmask = currentmask.squeeze(-1) > 0.5 validpositions = positions[validmask] validerrors = computeerror(points, camera, validpositions) # Placeholder for specific error metric # Convert to voxel indices voxelindices = grid.pointvoxelidx(validpositions) # Validate indices validindices = (voxelindices >= 0).all(dim=1) & (voxelindices < voxelresolution).all(dim=1) validindices = validindices.nonzero().squeeze() if len(validindices) == 0: continue flattenedindices = voxelindices[validindices].flatten() maskederrors = validerrors[validindices] # Scatter add errors and counts gridpointerrors.scatteradd(0, flattenedindices, maskederrors) gridpointcounts.scatteradd(0, flattenedindices, torch.oneslike(flattenedindices, dtype=torch.int)) # Compute mean error meanerrors = torch.where(gridpointcounts > 0, gridpointerrors / gridpointcounts.float(), gridpointerrors) # Assign to grid density grid.density = meanerrors.reshape(voxelresolution, voxelresolution, voxelresolution) # Resample points newpoints = grid.samplepoints(resampledpointsmethod) return newpoints Parameters: voxelresolution: int, default 32. Grid resolution in each dimension. resolution: list, default [1024, 1024]. Camera image resolution. aggregationmethod: str, default 'interpolation'. Method for aggregating sampled points (contextual, likely used in renderposmask or error calculation). resampledpointsmethod: str, default 'partial'. Strategy for point resampling (e.g., partial, percentage, full). device: str, default 'cuda'. Compute device. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Counts: Voxels with no valid pixel projections have zero counts. The mean error calculation must handle division by zero, typically by leaving the error at zero or a default value. Boundary Validation: Voxel indices must be strictly validated against grid bounds to prevent out-of-bounds memory access during scatter operations. Precision: Accumulating errors across many cameras may lead to floating-point precision issues if not managed carefully, though standard float32 is implied by PyTorch usage. Resamples points based on active/neighbor status, supporting partial, percentage, and full resampling strategies. This is the parent method, which this method extends by using error density instead of neighbor topology. Point Resampling with Neighbor Masking Time Complexity: O(N \cdot V), where N is the number of points and V is the number of cameras. Each camera requires rendering and scattering operations proportional to the number of projected points. Memory Complexity: O(R^3), where R is the voxelresolution. The grid size dominates memory usage. Strengths: Directly targets areas of high rendering error, leading to more efficient point distribution for visual quality. Limitations: Requires multiple camera views and rendering passes. Computationally expensive for high-resolution grids or many cameras. When to Use: When visual fidelity is critical and computational resources allow for multi-view error accumulation. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is required or only a single view is available. This method is part of the TetWeave project, which focuses on tetrahedral grid refinement for volume rendering. It was developed by Alexandre Binninger. The method is designed to work in conjunction with blue noise sampling and neighbor masking strategies to produce high-quality volumetric data. name: Pointcloud to Sparse Voxel Grid Conversion
body: Converts a set of 3D points and associated features into a sparse voxel grid representation, storing only voxels that contain at least one point. It differs from dense voxelization by using hash-based indexing to avoid allocating memory for empty space, and from simple occupancy voxelization by aggregating point features (e.g., via mean or sum) into voxel-level tensors. This method serves as the core voxelization step in pipelines converting point clouds to sparse voxel representations for downstream rendering or USD export. Inputs: points: Tensor of shape [N, 3] containing 3D coordinates, dtype float32. features: Tensor of shape [N, F] containing per-point features, dtype float32. gridcellsize: Tensor of shape [3] defining the physical size of a voxel in x, y, z dimensions. segmentfunc: Aggregation function (e.g., mean, sum, min, max) applied to points falling into the same voxel. Outputs: voxelfeatures: Tensor of shape [N', F] where N' is the number of occupied voxels. voxelindices: Tensor of shape [N', 3] containing the integer x, y, z indices of occupied voxels. segmentids: Tensor of shape [N] mapping each input point to its corresponding voxel segment ID. voxelstartlocation: Tensor of shape [3] containing the minimum coordinate of the bounding box of the point cloud. Data Structures: Voxel indices are computed as integer offsets from the minimum point coordinate. A flattened single-number index is derived from the 3D voxel indices to facilitate segment-based pooling. Steps: 1. Compute Bounding Box Origin: Determine the start location of the voxel grid by finding the minimum coordinate across all points. \text{start\location} = \min{i}(\text{points}i) 2. Compute Voxel Indices: Calculate the integer grid index for each point by subtracting the start location and dividing by the grid cell size, using floor division. \text{voxel\xyz\indices}i = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{points}i - \text{start\location}}{\text{grid\cell\size}} \right\rfloor 3. Compute Flattened Indices: Convert 3D voxel indices into a unique 1D integer index for each point to enable segment grouping. The exact mapping depends on the grid dimensions, but typically involves linearizing the 3D coordinates. 4. Aggregate Features: Group points by their flattened voxel index and apply the segmentfunc to aggregate features. This produces voxelfeatures and segmentids. 5. Compute Unique Voxel Indices: For each unique segment (voxel), determine the maximum 3D index among its constituent points to represent the voxel's position. This step ensures that each occupied voxel is represented exactly once in the output voxelindices. \text{voxel\xyz\indices}{unique} = \text{unsorted\segment\max}(\text{voxel\xyz\indices}, \text{segment\ids}, \text{num\segments}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import tensorflow as tf def pointcloudtosparsevoxelgridunbatched(points, features, gridcellsize, segmentfunc): """ Converts a pointcloud into a sparse voxel grid. Args: points: tf.float32 tensor of size [N, 3]. features: tf.float32 tensor of size [N, F]. gridcellsize: tf.float32 tensor of size [3]. segmentfunc: Aggregation function (e.g., tf.math.unsortedsegmentmean). Returns: voxelfeatures: tf.float32 tensor of size [N', F]. voxelindices: tf.int32 tensor of size [N', 3]. segmentids: tf.int32 tensor of size [N]. voxelstartlocation: tf.float32 tensor of size [3]. """ # 1. Compute start location (minimum point coordinate) voxelstartlocation = tf.reducemin(points, axis=0) # 2. Compute voxel xyz indices # floordivide handles the integer division for negative numbers correctly in TF voxelxyzindices = tf.cast( tf.math.floordiv(points - voxelstartlocation, gridcellsize), dtype=tf.int32) # 3. Compute flattened single number indices # Note: The exact implementation of computepooledvoxelindices is not fully detailed in the source, # but it maps 3D indices to a unique 1D integer. # Assuming a standard linearization based on grid dimensions or a hash map. # For implementation, one might use a hash map or linearize if grid size is known. # Here we assume a helper function exists or implement a simple linearization if bounds are known. # Since bounds are not explicitly given as inputs, we rely on the source's helper. # In a pure implementation without TF helpers, one would use a dictionary or hash map # to map (x,y,z) to a unique ID. voxelxyzindices, voxelsinglenumberindices = computepooledvoxelindices( voxelxyzindices=voxelxyzindices, poolingsize=(1, 1, 1)) # 4. Pool features using the flattened indices voxelfeatures, segmentids, numsegments = poolfeaturesgivenindices( features=features, indices=voxelsinglenumberindices, segmentfunc=segmentfunc) # 5. Compute unique voxel xyz indices by taking the max over segments voxelxyzindices = tf.math.unsortedsegmentmax( data=voxelxyzindices, segmentids=segmentids, numsegments=numsegments) return voxelfeatures, voxelxyzindices, segmentids, voxelstartlocation def computepooledvoxelindices(voxelxyzindices, poolingsize): """ Helper to compute unique 1D indices for 3D voxel coordinates. This is a placeholder for the specific linearization or hashing logic. A common approach is to use a hash map or linearize if grid dimensions are fixed. For this implementation, we assume a simple linearization based on a large enough grid size or a hash-based unique ID assignment. """ # In TensorFlow, one might use tf.unique or a custom op. # Here we simulate the behavior: assign a unique ID to each unique (x,y,z) tuple. # Convert to string or tuple for hashing, or use a large multiplier if bounds are known. # Since bounds are not known, we use a hash-based approach. # Note: This is a simplification. The actual TF code likely uses a more efficient C++ op. # Flatten the indices for hashing # We assume a simple linearization for demonstration, though it may not be unique for large grids. # A robust implementation would use a hash map. # For the purpose of this article, we note that this step maps 3D coords to 1D IDs. # Using a simple linearization with a large multiplier to avoid collisions for typical point cloud sizes # This is a implementation detail not fully specified in the source. # A better approach is to use tf.unique on the rows. uniquevals, inverseindices, counts = tf.unique(voxelxyzindices, outidx=tf.int32) # The inverseindices map each point to its unique voxel ID # However, the source uses 'voxelsinglenumberindices' which seems to be a flattened index # before aggregation. Let's assume it's the unique ID. # Re-assigning to match the source's variable names # The source computes voxelsinglenumberindices from voxelxyzindices # and then uses them for pooling. # Let's assume the source's computepooledvoxelindices returns: # 1. The original voxelxyzindices (unchanged) # 2. A 1D index for each point corresponding to its voxel # We will use the inverseindices from tf.unique as the segment IDs for pooling # But the source returns segmentids separately. # Let's stick to the source's flow: # voxelsinglenumberindices is used for pooling. # segmentids is the output of poolfeaturesgivenindices. # Actually, looking at the source: # voxelxyzindices, voxelsinglenumberindices = computepooledvoxelindices(...) # Then poolfeaturesgivenindices(features, voxelsinglenumberindices,...) # Then segmentids is returned from poolfeaturesgivenindices. # So computepooledvoxelindices must return a 1D index for each point. # We can use tf.unique to get unique IDs. # To match the source's structure exactly: # We need a 1D index for each point. # Let's use a hash map approach in Python for clarity, but the source uses TF ops. # For the pseudocode, we will use a simplified linearization assuming a known grid size, # or note that a hash map is used. # Since the exact implementation of computepooledvoxelindices is not provided, # we will assume it assigns a unique integer ID to each unique (x,y,z) coordinate. # We can use tf.unique to get unique IDs. uniquevals, inverseindices, counts = tf.unique(voxelxyzindices, outidx=tf.int32) # The inverseindices are the unique IDs for each point's voxel. # We return the original voxelxyzindices and the inverseindices as the single number indices. return voxelxyzindices, inverseindices def poolfeaturesgivenindices(features, indices, segmentfunc): """ Aggregates features based on indices. """ # Use the unique IDs as segment IDs segmentids = indices numsegments = tf.reducemax(segmentids) + 1 # Apply the segment function # Note: tf.math.unsortedsegmentmean requires segmentids to be 0..numsegments-1 # and contiguous. tf.unique provides this. voxelfeatures = segmentfunc(features, segmentids, numsegments) return voxelfeatures, segmentids, numsegments Parameters: gridcellsize: Typical values depend on the scene scale. Not given in the sources. segmentfunc: Commonly tf.math.unsortedsegmentmean. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point division and floor operations may lead to off-by-one errors if points lie exactly on grid boundaries. The source uses floordiv, which handles negative numbers correctly in TensorFlow. Empty Voxels: The method only outputs occupied voxels, so empty space is not represented. Batching: The unbatched version does not handle batch sizes; it assumes a single batch of points. DCX Points-to-Voxels converts a set of 3D points (from PLY files or 3D Gaussian Splatting) into a sparse voxel grid by averaging point positions and colors within grid cells defined by a bounding box and resolution. It differs from simple occupancy voxelization by storing averaged geometric and color data per voxel, and from dense voxelization by using hash maps to store only occupied cells. This method serves as the core voxelization step in pipelines converting point clouds to sparse voxel representations for downstream rendering or USD export. Time Complexity: Dominated by the computation of voxel indices and the aggregation step. Index computation is O(N), and aggregation is O(N) on average with hash maps, but depends on the implementation of segmentfunc. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of occupied voxels N' and the feature dimension F, i.e., O(N' \cdot F). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently handles sparse data; avoids memory allocation for empty space; flexible aggregation functions. Limitations: Unbatched version limits scalability; precision issues at grid boundaries. When to Use: When converting point clouds to sparse voxel grids for rendering or USD export, especially when memory efficiency is critical. When Not to Use: When dense voxel representations are required or when batching is necessary without modification. The method originates from Google Research's TensorFlow 3D (TF3D) library, specifically in the voxelutils.py module. It is designed to facilitate the conversion of point cloud data into a format suitable for 3D deep learning tasks, such as 3D object detection and segmentation.
