name: DCX Points-to-Voxels
head: Voxelization of Point Clouds
body: DCX Points-to-Voxels converts a set of 3D points (from PLY files or 3D Gaussian Splatting) into a sparse voxel grid by averaging point positions and colors within grid cells defined by a bounding box and resolution. It differs from simple occupancy voxelization by storing averaged geometric and color data per voxel, and from dense voxelization by using hash maps to store only occupied cells. This method serves as the core voxelization step in pipelines converting point clouds to sparse voxel representations for downstream rendering or USD export. Inputs: points: Array of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates of N points. colors: Optional array of shape (N, 3) containing RGB color values. resolution: Float defining voxel size in world units (default 0.1) or integer scaling factor. densitythreshold: Integer minimum number of points required to create a voxel (default 1). colorlevels: Integer for color quantization (0=off, 8/16/32=quantize) (default 0). Outputs: voxels: A sparse map where keys are voxel IDs and values contain averaged position and/or color. Data Structures: Auxiliary Map (aux): Hash map from CubeID (integer) to count (integer). Voxels Map (voxels): Hash map from CubeID (integer) to vector<float> of size 3 representing averaged 3D coordinates. In S2, this is a dictionary mapping grid coordinates to objects containing colorsum and count. CubeID: Linear voxel index computed from grid coordinates. Steps: 1. Calculate Bounds and Orders: Compute bounding box extents: minbounds = points.min(axis=0), maxbounds = points.max(axis=0). Adjust bounds for stability: temp0 = floor(minbounds resolution) - 3 temp1 = floor(maxbounds resolution) + 3 bboxmin = temp0 / resolution bboxmax = temp1 / resolution width[i] = temp1[i] - temp0[i] for i \in \{0, 1, 2\}. Compute strides (orders): orders[0] = width[0] orders[1] = width[0] width[1]. Alternatively, compute grid size directly: gridsize = ceil((maxbounds - minbounds) / resolution).astype(int) + 1. 2. Iterate Points and Compute Grid Indices: For each point i with position pi = (x, y, z): Compute scaled coordinates: sx = \lfloor (x - bbox\min[0]) \times resolution \rfloor sy = \lfloor (y - bbox\min[1]) \times resolution \rfloor sz = \lfloor (z - bbox\min[2]) \times resolution \rfloor. Alternatively, using minbounds: grid\coords = \lfloor (pi - min\bounds) / resolution \rfloor. 3. Compute Voxel ID: Linearize grid coordinates to a unique ID: voxel\id = sx + sy \times orders[0] + sz \times orders[1]. Or use tuple (sx, sy, sz) as key. 4. Aggregate Data: If using S1 (Position Averaging): Check if voxelid exists in aux. If not: Insert voxelid into aux with count = 1. Insert voxelid into voxels with value pi. If yes: Retrieve existing count and oldpoint. newcount = count + 1. Compute merged position: merged\pos[j] = \frac{count \times old\point[j] + pi[j]}{new\count} for j \in \{0, 1, 2\}. Update voxels[voxelid] = mergedpos. Update aux[voxelid] = newcount. If using S2 (Color Accumulation): Accumulate color sums and counts: voxeldata[key]['colorsum'] += colors[i] voxeldata[key]['count'] += 1. 5. Filter and Finalize: Filter voxels: If count < densitythreshold, skip the voxel. Compute final color: avg\color = (color\sum / count).astype(np.uint8). Apply color quantization if colorlevels > 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dcxpointstovoxels(points, colors=None, resolution=0.1, densitythreshold=1, colorlevels=0): """ Convert points to sparse voxels. points: (N, 3) array colors: (N, 3) array, optional resolution: float densitythreshold: int colorlevels: int """ # 1. Calculate Bounds minbounds = points.min(axis=0) maxbounds = points.max(axis=0) # Adjust bounds for stability (S1 style) # Note: S1 uses integer scaling for bounds adjustment, S2 uses float division. # We follow S2's simpler approach for general compatibility, but S1's padding is safer for edge cases. # Here we implement S1's padding logic for robustness. bboxmin = np.floor(minbounds resolution) - 3 bboxmax = np.floor(maxbounds resolution) + 3 bboxmin = bboxmin / resolution bboxmax = bboxmax / resolution width = np.floor(maxbounds resolution) + 3 - (np.floor(minbounds resolution) - 3) orders = np.zeros(2, dtype=int) orders[0] = int(width[0]) orders[1] = int(width[0] width[1]) # Data structures aux = {} # voxelid -> count voxels = {} # voxelid -> [x, y, z] coloraccum = {} # voxelid -> [r, g, b] sum (if colors provided) # 2. Iterate Points for i in range(len(points)): p = points[i] # Compute grid indices sx = int(np.floor((p[0] - bboxmin[0]) resolution)) sy = int(np.floor((p[1] - bboxmin[1]) resolution)) sz = int(np.floor((p[2] - bboxmin[2]) resolution)) # Compute Voxel ID voxelid = sx + sy orders[0] + sz orders[1] # 3. Aggregate if voxelid not in aux: aux[voxelid] = 1 voxels[voxelid] = p.copy() if colors is not None: coloraccum[voxelid] = colors[i].copy() else: count = aux[voxelid] oldpos = voxels[voxelid] newcount = count + 1 # Update position mergedpos = (count oldpos + p) / newcount voxels[voxelid] = mergedpos aux[voxelid] = newcount # Update color if colors is not None: coloraccum[voxelid] += colors[i] # 4. Filter and Finalize resultvoxels = {} for voxelid, count in aux.items(): if count < densitythreshold: continue voxeldata = { 'position': voxels[voxelid], 'count': count } if colors is not None and voxelid in coloraccum: avgcolor = coloraccum[voxelid] / count # Quantization if colorlevels > 0: # Simple quantization: scale to [0, colorlevels-1] and back # Assuming colors are in [0, 1] or [0, 255]. S2 uses uint8. # Assuming input colors are [0, 255] for uint8 conversion avgcolor = np.clip(avgcolor, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8) # Further quantization if needed if colorlevels < 256: step = 256 / colorlevels avgcolor = np.round(avgcolor / step) step avgcolor = avgcolor.astype(np.uint8) voxeldata['color'] = avgcolor resultvoxels[voxelid] = voxeldata return resultvoxels Parameters: resolution: Voxel size in world units. Default 0.1. densitythreshold: Minimum points per voxel. Default 1. colorlevels: Color quantization levels. Default 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point division and floor operations can cause boundary artifacts. S1 adds a padding of 3 units to the bounding box to mitigate this. Empty Voxels: Voxels with fewer points than densitythreshold are discarded. Color Quantization: If colorlevels is set, colors are quantized to reduce the number of unique materials, which is useful for USD PointInstancer optimization. Merges adjacent voxels with similar colors into larger boxes to reduce draw calls. This is a post-processing step applied after voxelization. A rendering technique that instances a single geometry prototype with per-voxel transforms and colors, leveraging the sparse voxel output for efficient rendering. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of points, as each point is processed once and hash map operations are O(1) on average. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of occupied voxels. The sparse map stores only non-empty voxels. Performance: Handles 1M+ voxels efficiently on GPU via instancing. CPU voxelization is fast due to simple averaging. Strengths: Simple, fast, produces sparse data suitable for large scenes. Limitations: Loses high-frequency detail within voxels due to averaging. Resolution is fixed per grid. DCX Points-to-Voxels is part of the DCx toolkit, which converts point clouds and 3D Gaussian Splatting data into USD formats. It is used in pipelines that require efficient rendering of large point cloud datasets by converting them into sparse voxel grids. The method is implemented in Python and C++ for performance. jjjkkyz/DCx, https://github.com/jjjkkyz/DCx, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) omolism/3DGS-to-Voxel-OpenUSD, https://github.com/omolism/3DGS-to-Voxel-OpenUSD, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Model Voxelization
head: LiDAR Voxelization, Ray Traversal Voxelization
body: Ray Model Voxelization converts sparse LiDAR point clouds into dense 3D occupancy grids by tracing rays from sensor origins to detected points, classifying voxels as free, occupied, or unobserved. It differs from Hard Voxelization by explicitly modeling the empty space between the sensor and the target points, rather than only marking voxels containing points, and from Point Cloud to Gaussian Converter by producing discrete grid states rather than continuous density fields. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: pointsorigin: Sensor origin positions, shape [N, 3]. points: LiDAR point coordinates, shape [N, 3+] (typically [N, 3] or [N, 4] with intensity). pointslabel: Semantic labels for points, shape [N]. pointcloudrange: 3D bounding box [x{min}, y{min}, z{min}, x{max}, y{max}, z{max}] in meters. voxelsize: Voxel dimensions [vx, vy, vz] in meters. Default: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2]. spatialshape: Output grid dimensions [H, W, D]. Default: [512, 256, 32]. Outputs: voxelstate: Integer grid [H, W, D] with values -1 (NOTOBSERVED), 0 (FREE), 1 (OCCUPIED). voxellabel: Integer grid [H, W, D] with semantic labels. Default label for free voxels is 0. invalidmask: Boolean grid [H, W, D] indicating unobserved voxels or voxels with no label. Data Structures The implementation uses CUDA kernels for parallel ray traversal. Key variables include: voxelocccount: Atomic counter for occupied voxels. voxelfreecount: Atomic counter for free voxels. ray[3]: Ray direction vector. step[3]: Step direction per axis (+1 or -1). tDelta[3]: Increment in t to move one voxel. tMax[3]: Next voxel boundary in t units. currentvoxel[3]: Current traversal position. targetvoxel[3]: End point voxel (LiDAR hit). Parameters voxelsize: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2] meters. pointcloudrange: [-51.2, -25.6, -2, 51.2, 25.6, 4.4] meters. spatialshape: [512, 256, 32]. apre/apost: Frames to aggregate before/after for ground truth. Default: 70/70. ppre/ppost: Input/prediction sequence lengths. Default: 10/10. freenthreshold: 0. occupiednthreshold: 1. Steps 1. Coordinate Transformation: Normalize point origins using the inverse pose matrix and rotate points based on dataset-specific conventions. For Lyft, rotate \pi around Z; for NuScenes, rotate -\pi/2 around Z. \text{points}{\text{norm}} = \text{pose\origin\inv} \times \text{points} \text{points}{\text{rot}} = \text{points}{\text{norm}} \times \text{rotation\matrix}^T 2. Temporal Aggregation: Aggregate input points from frames [index - p{pre}, index] and ground truth points from frames [index, index + p{post}]. For ground truth, further aggregate points from the window [i - a{pre}, i + a{post}] for each target frame i. 3. Ray Initialization: For each ray, calculate the direction vector from the sensor origin to the target point. Compute step (+1 or -1 per axis), tDelta (increment to move one voxel), and tMax (distance to the next voxel boundary). 4. Ray Traversal: Traverse the ray path using a while loop with bounds checks. Mark the target voxel by incrementing voxelocccount using atomicAdd. Mark all traversed voxels (excluding the target) by incrementing voxelfreecount using atomicAdd. Pitfall: Stop rays at a distance of 1 voxel to prevent over-traversal. Ignore voxels too close to the sensor or target using a distance threshold of 1.0m. 5. Voxel State Assignment: Assign states based on counts: If voxelocccount > 1, state = OCCUPIED (1). Else if voxelfreecount > 0, state = FREE (0). Else, state = NOTOBSERVED (-1). 6. Label Assignment: Calculate voxel indices for points within range: \text{pcds\voxel} = \lfloor (\text{points} - \text{range\min}) / \text{voxel\size} \rfloor Convert to scalar indices and assign point labels to voxellabelsqueeze. Default label for free voxels is 0. 7. Invalid Mask Generation: Generate a mask for voxels that are unobserved (state -1) or have no label. 8. Compression: Compress binary occupancy data using bit packing. Reshape the boolean array [H, W, D] to 1D, compress 8 bools into 1 uint8, and save as.npy. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def raymodelvoxelization(pointsorigin, points, pointslabel, pointcloudrange, voxelsize, spatialshape, rotationmatrix=None, poseorigininv=None): """ Convert point cloud to voxel grid using ray traversal. Args: pointsorigin: [N, 3] sensor origins points: [N, 3] LiDAR points pointslabel: [N] semantic labels pointcloudrange: [6] [xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax] voxelsize: [3] [vx, vy, vz] spatialshape: [3] [H, W, D] rotationmatrix: [3, 3] optional rotation poseorigininv: [4, 4] optional inverse pose Returns: voxelstate: [H, W, D] int (-1, 0, 1) voxellabel: [H, W, D] int invalidmask: [H, W, D] bool """ # 1. Coordinate Transformation if poseorigininv is not None: # Homogeneous coordinates for transformation pointsh = np.hstack([points, np.ones((points.shape[0], 1))]) pointsnorm = (poseorigininv @ pointsh.T).T[:,:3] else: pointsnorm = points if rotationmatrix is not None: pointsrot = pointsnorm @ rotationmatrix.T else: pointsrot = pointsnorm points = pointsrot # 2. Initialize Grids H, W, D = spatialshape voxelocccount = np.zeros(spatialshape, dtype=np.int32) voxelfreecount = np.zeros(spatialshape, dtype=np.int32) voxellabel = np.zeros(spatialshape, dtype=np.int32) # Default 0 # 3. Process Each Ray for i in range(points.shape[0]): origin = pointsorigin[i] target = points[i] # Direction vector raydir = target - origin dist = np.linalg.norm(raydir) # Skip if too close (1.0m threshold) if dist < 1.0: continue raydir = raydir / dist # Calculate voxel indices for origin and target rangemin = pointcloudrange[:3] rangemax = pointcloudrange[3:] # Clamp to range originvoxel = np.floor((origin - rangemin) / voxelsize).astype(np.int32) targetvoxel = np.floor((target - rangemin) / voxelsize).astype(np.int32) # Check bounds if not np.all(originvoxel >= 0) or not np.all(originvoxel < spatialshape): continue if not np.all(targetvoxel >= 0) or not np.all(targetvoxel < spatialshape): continue # Ray parameters step = np.where(raydir > 0, 1, -1).astype(np.int32) tdelta = np.abs(1.0 / raydir) # tMax: distance to next boundary tmax = np.zeros(3) for d in range(3): if raydir[d] > 0: tmax[d] = ((originvoxel[d] + 1) voxelsize[d] + rangemin[d] - origin[d]) / raydir[d] else: tmax[d] = (originvoxel[d] voxelsize[d] + rangemin[d] - origin[d]) / raydir[d] currentvoxel = originvoxel.copy() # Traverse ray # Stop 1 voxel before target to prevent over-traversal # Simplified: traverse until just before target voxel while not np.arrayequal(currentvoxel, targetvoxel): # Mark free voxel voxelfreecount[currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2]] += 1 # Find next voxel tnext = np.argmin(tmax) currentvoxel[tnext] += step[tnext] tmax[tnext] += tdelta[tnext] # Check bounds if not np.all(currentvoxel >= 0) or not np.all(currentvoxel < spatialshape): break # Mark target voxel as occupied voxelocccount[targetvoxel[0], targetvoxel[1], targetvoxel[2]] += 1 # 4. Assign States voxelstate = np.full(spatialshape, -1, dtype=np.int32) # NOTOBSERVED occupiedmask = voxelocccount > 1 freemask = (voxelfreecount > 0) & ~occupiedmask voxelstate[occupiedmask] = 1 # OCCUPIED voxelstate[freemask] = 0 # FREE # 5. Assign Labels # Calculate indices for all points pcdsvoxel = np.floor((points - rangemin) / voxelsize).astype(np.int32) # Flatten indices to 1D inds = (pcdsvoxel[:, 0] W D + pcdsvoxel[:, 1] D + pcdsvoxel[:, 2]) # Assign labels where points exist # Note: This assumes points are within range and valid validpoints = np.all((pcdsvoxel >= 0) & (pcdsvoxel < spatialshape), axis=1) validinds = inds[validpoints] validlabels = pointslabel[validpoints] # Scatter labels # Using a temporary array to avoid race conditions in simulation templabels = np.zeros(H W D, dtype=np.int32) np.add.at(templabels, validinds, validlabels) # Note: this sums, not assigns. # For assignment, we need to handle collisions. The source says "assign point label to voxellabelsqueeze[inds]". # In CUDA, this is a scatter. In numpy, we can use advanced indexing for unique indices or assume no collision for simplicity. # Given the source uses atomicAdd for counts, label assignment likely overwrites or uses the last point. # For a pure Python implementation without CUDA, we'll assume the last point wins or use a simple loop. # Reset and assign properly voxellabelflat = np.zeros(H W D, dtype=np.int32) for idx, label in zip(validinds, validlabels): voxellabelflat[idx] = label voxellabel = voxellabelflat.reshape(spatialshape) # 6. Invalid Mask invalidmask = (voxelstate == -1) # Unobserved # Also mark if no label? Source says "unobserved or have no label". # Since we assigned labels to occupied voxels, we check if label is 0 (default) and state is not free? # The source says "Default label for free voxels is 0". So 0 is ambiguous. # Let's stick to unobserved as the primary invalid mask for occupancy. # If semantic label is required, voxels with state OCCUPIED but no label might be invalid. # However, the source code snippet shows voxellabelsqueeze[inds] = pointslabelsinrange. # And invalidmask is generated for "unobserved or have no label". # We'll mark unobserved as invalid. # 7. Compression (for binary occupancy) # Not part of the main return, but for storage # binaryocc = (voxelstate == 1) # compressed = np.packbits(binaryocc.reshape(-1)) return voxelstate, voxellabel, invalidmask Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and the average ray length in voxels. The CUDA implementation uses parallel processing for rays. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W \times D) for the voxel grids. Bit packing reduces storage for binary occupancy by 8:1. Performance: Implemented using CUDA kernels with NVRTC for high performance. Atomic operations ensure thread safety. Strengths: Explicitly models free space, which is critical for occupancy prediction. Handles multi-frame temporal aggregation for dense ground truth. Limitations: Requires careful handling of coordinate transformations for different datasets. Numerical precision issues can occur if TF32 is not disabled in CUDA operations. When to use: When dense 3D occupancy grids with explicit free space are needed for LiDAR-based perception tasks. When not to use: When sparse representations are sufficient, or when semantic labels are not required for free space. The Ray Model Voxelization method is part of the Occ4cast project, specifically designed for processing LiDAR data for occupancy forecasting. It addresses the need for dense 3D representations that capture both occupied and free space, which is essential for autonomous driving applications. The implementation is optimized for GPU execution using CUDA. name: Hard Voxelization
body: Hard Voxelization converts a continuous 3D point cloud into a discrete, sparse voxel grid by assigning each point to a specific voxel cell based on its spatial coordinates and a fixed voxel size. It differs from soft voxelization by using hard assignment (no interpolation) and from sparse voxel octrees by using a fixed-axis-aligned grid structure. This method serves as the foundational step for producing volume data from raw point clouds, building on Point Cloud Voxelization. All variants in this family share the core mechanism of mapping continuous point coordinates (x, y, z) to discrete integer voxel indices (i, j, k) using floor division relative to a bounding box origin and voxel dimensions. Given a point p = [x, y, z], a voxel size v = [vx, vy, vz], and a range R = [x{min}, y{min}, z{min}, x{max}, y{max}, z{max}], the voxel coordinates are computed as: i = \left\lfloor \frac{x - x{min}}{vx} \right\rfloor, \quad j = \left\lfloor \frac{y - y{min}}{vy} \right\rfloor, \quad k = \left\lfloor \frac{z - z{min}}{vz} \right\rfloor Points with coordinates outside the range R are discarded or mapped to invalid indices (e.g., -1). The output is typically a set of tensors: voxels (point features grouped by voxel), coors (voxel indices), and numpointspervoxel (counts). Multiscale Hard Voxelization voxelizes a point cloud into multiple spatial scales simultaneously, outputting voxel features, coordinates, and point counts for each scale. It differs from standard single-scale voxelization by iterating over multiple scales and storing results in separate memory blocks indexed by scaleidx, providing convenience for multi-scale feature extraction networks. Hard Voxelization (Deterministic) converts a 3D point cloud into a fixed-size voxel grid by assigning each point to a discrete voxel based on its coordinates and a specified voxel size and range. It handles duplicate points within the same voxel and limits the number of points per voxel and total voxels. Unlike the non-deterministic variant which uses atomic operations for speed at the cost of reproducibility, this method guarantees bit-identical output by using stable sorting and explicit ordering logic. It serves as the foundational step for producing volume data from raw point clouds, building on Hard Voxelization. A visualization pipeline that renders voxelized point clouds using the Point Cloud Library (PCL), supporting axis-aligned or custom bounding boxes with three distinct rendering modes. It differs from its siblings by providing immediate visual feedback of voxel occupancy and bounding constraints through specific geometric representations (points, solid cubes, or wireframes) rather than just generating the underlying data structure. Definition: Computes only the voxel coordinates for each point, without assigning points to a fixed voxel grid structure or handling duplicates/max points. Used when maxpoints=-1. Steps: Calculate grid dimensions: gridx = \text{round}((coors\x{max} - coors\x{min}) / voxel\x), etc. Launch dynamicvoxelizekernel to compute voxel coordinates for each point and store them in the coors tensor. Parameters: NDim: Number of dimensions for coordinates, default 3. Hard voxelization is widely used in 3D object detection for autonomous driving, particularly in frameworks like MMDetection3D and OpenPCDet, to convert LiDAR point clouds into a format suitable for 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The deterministic variant was developed to address reproducibility issues in non-deterministic CUDA implementations where atomic operations could lead to race conditions and varying outputs across runs. Multiscale variants were introduced to facilitate feature extraction at different resolutions without multiple passes. name: Multiscale Hard Voxelization
body: Multiscale Hard Voxelization is a CUDA-based operator that voxelizes a LiDAR point cloud into multiple spatial scales simultaneously, outputting voxel features, coordinates, and point counts for each scale. It differs from standard single-scale voxelization by iterating over multiple scales and storing results in separate memory blocks indexed by scaleidx, providing convenience for multi-scale feature extraction networks. Inputs and Outputs Input: A point cloud tensor of shape [N, D], where N is the number of points and D is the number of features (typically 4: x, y, z, \text{reflectivity}). Parameters: voxelsizes: A nested list defining voxel dimensions [x, y, z] for each scale (e.g., [[0.16, 0.16, 4], [0.32, 0.32, 4]]). maxpointsforallscales: A list defining the maximum number of points allowed per voxel for each scale (e.g., [32, 64]). pointcloudrange: A list of 6 floats [x{min}, y{min}, z{min}, x{max}, y{max}, z{max}] defining the bounding box of the voxel grid in meters. maxvoxels: The maximum total number of voxels allowed across all scales. Outputs: voxels: Tensor of shape [S, M, P{max}, D], containing the point features within each voxel, where S is the number of scales, M is maxvoxels, and P{max} is the maximum points per voxel across all scales. coors: Tensor of shape [S, M, 3], containing voxel coordinates in [z, y, x] order. numpointspervoxel: Tensor of shape [S, M], containing the count of points in each voxel. Data Structures The implementation uses pre-allocated tensors on the GPU: 1. voxels: [S, \text{max\voxels}, \max(\text{max\points}), D] initialized to zeros. 2. coors: [S, \text{max\voxels}, 3] initialized to zeros. 3. numpointspervoxel: [S, \text{max\voxels}] initialized to zeros. 4. voxelnum: An array of size S tracking the number of allocated voxels per scale. 5. pointtopointidx: An array of size N mapping each point to the index of the previous point in the same voxel. 6. pointtovoxelidx: An array of size N mapping each point to its position (index) within its voxel (0-based). 7. coortovoxelidx: An array of size N mapping each point to the global voxel index. Algorithm Steps The operator processes each scale s from 0 to S-1. For each scale, it performs the following steps for every point i in the point cloud: 1. Grid Dimension Calculation: Calculate the grid dimensions for the current scale s using the voxel size vs = [vx, vy, vz] and range R = [x{min}, y{min}, z{min}, x{max}, y{max}, z{max}]: \text{grid}x = \left\lfloor \frac{x{max} - x{min}}{vx} \right\rfloor, \quad \text{grid}y = \left\lfloor \frac{y{max} - y{min}}{vy} \right\rfloor, \quad \text{grid}z = \left\lfloor \frac{z{max} - z{min}}{vz} \right\rfloor 2. Voxel Coordinate Computation: For each point i with coordinates pi = [xi, yi, zi], compute the voxel coordinates ci = [cx, cy, cz]: cx = \left\lfloor \frac{xi - x{min}}{vx} \right\rfloor, \quad cy = \left\lfloor \frac{yi - y{min}}{vy} \right\rfloor, \quad cz = \left\lfloor \frac{zi - z{min}}{vz} \right\rfloor 3. Boundary Check: If any coordinate is out of bounds, the point is discarded for this scale: If cx < 0 or cx \ge \text{grid}x, set cx = -1 and return. If cy < 0 or cy \ge \text{grid}y, set cy = -1 and return. If cz < 0 or cz \ge \text{grid}z, set cz = -1 and return. 4. Point Linking (Deterministic): To handle points falling into the same voxel, the implementation uses a deterministic O(N^2) approach by iterating backwards from the current point to find the previous point with identical coordinates. Initialize num = 0. Iterate j from i-1 down to 0: If cj == ci (coordinates match), increment num. If num == 1, set pointtopointidx[i] = j. If num >= maxpoints[s], stop and discard point i (return). 5. Voxel Index Assignment: Set pointtovoxelidx[i] = num (if not discarded). If num == 0: This is the first point in a new voxel. If voxelnum[s] >= maxvoxels, skip point i. Allocate a new voxel index: voxelidx = voxelnum[s]. Increment voxelnum[s]. Set coortovoxelidx[i] = voxelidx. Set numpointspervoxel[voxelidx] = 1. Set pointtopointidx[i] = i. If num > 0: This point belongs to an existing voxel. Find the first point in the same voxel: pointidx = pointtopointidx[i]. Set coortovoxelidx[i] = coortovoxelidx[pointidx]. Increment numpointspervoxel[coortovoxelidx[i]]. 6. Data Storage: Store the voxel coordinates in coors[s, voxelidx] as [cz, cy, cx]. Store the point features in voxels[s, voxelidx, num]. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiscalehardvoxelize(points, voxelsizes, maxpointsforallscales, pointcloudrange, maxvoxels): """ points: [N, D] float tensor voxelsizes: List[List[float]] of shape [S, 3] maxpointsforallscales: List[int] of shape [S] pointcloudrange: List[float] of shape [6] [xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax] maxvoxels: int Returns: voxels [S, M, Pmax, D], coors [S, M, 3], numpointspervoxel [S, M] """ S = len(voxelsizes) N = points.shape[0] D = points.shape[1] Pmax = max(maxpointsforallscales) # Initialize output tensors voxels = torch.zeros((S, maxvoxels, Pmax, D), dtype=points.dtype, device=points.device) coors = torch.zeros((S, maxvoxels, 3), dtype=torch.int32, device=points.device) numpointspervoxel = torch.zeros((S, maxvoxels), dtype=torch.int32, device=points.device) # Helper arrays for linking points (allocated per scale or reused) # Note: In the actual CUDA implementation, these are passed to the kernel. # Here we simulate the logic for clarity. voxelnum = torch.zeros(S, dtype=torch.int32, device=points.device) for s in range(S): vx, vy, vz = voxelsizes[s] maxp = maxpointsforallscales[s] xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax = pointcloudrange gridx = int((xmax - It serves as the foundational step for producing volume data from raw point clouds, building on Hard Voxelization. Maximum number of points allowed in a single voxel. maxvoxels: Integer. Maximum number of voxels to create. Points falling into voxels beyond this limit are dropped. Typical value is 20000. Outputs: voxels: A tensor of shape [M, max\points, C] containing the point features for each of the M valid voxels. coors: A tensor of shape [M, 3] containing the integer voxel indices (i, j, k) for each valid voxel. numpointspervoxel: A tensor of shape [M] containing the count of points assigned to each voxel. Unlike the standard deterministic=False path which relies on non-reproducible atomic operations, this method guarantees reproducibility by preserving original point order within voxels via stable sorting. Grid Pooling aggregates point cloud features into a fixed-size 3D voxel grid by performing max-pooling within each grid cell. It maps a set of N points with C-dimensional features to a W \times H \times D grid where each cell stores the maximum feature value among points falling into that cell. It differs from its sibling Hard Voxelization (Deterministic) by explicitly tracking the index of the point that achieved the maximum value to enable differentiable backpropagation, whereas hard voxelization typically discards this linkage or handles duplicates via simple overwriting or averaging without gradient tracking. Choose this when differentiable aggregation is required. This method generates cropped point cloud datasets by dividing a normalized 3D scene into a structured grid, applying morphological dilation to expand active voxel regions, and precomputing K-nearest neighbor (KNN) relationships for both input points and grid voxels. It solves the problem of efficiently preparing local feature grouping inputs for deep learning models by providing fixed-size, spatially coherent data structures that include relative coordinate offsets. It differs from its siblings by explicitly precomputing KNN indices and relative coordinates for both points and voxels within a cropped region, whereas Hard Voxelization (Deterministic) focuses on static assignment and Grid Pooling (Max Pooling over Points) focuses on aggregation rather than neighbor indexing. Choose this for preparing inputs for KNN-based neural networks. It filters out invalid coordinates, finds unique voxel coordinates using at::uniquedim, and uses nondisterministicgetassignpos and nondisterministicassignpointvoxel kernels for assignment. Limitations: Memory intensive for high-resolution grids, requires careful handling of boundary conditions and invalid points. Unlike the standard deterministic=False path which relies on non-reproducible atomic operations, this method guarantees reproducibility by preserving original point order within voxels via stable sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: points tensor of shape (N, D), where N is the number of points and D \ge 3 (typically 4, including intensity or time). rmin and rmax define the bounding box. voxelsize defines the grid resolution. maxvoxels is the global limit on occupied voxels. maxnumpoints is the limit on points per voxel. Outputs: voxels tensor of shape (M, max\num\points, D), coors tensor of shape (M, 3), and numpointspervoxel tensor of shape (M). M is the actual number of occupied voxels, capped at maxvoxels. Data Structures: points: Float tensor on GPU. inrange: Boolean mask of length N. voxelcoords: Integer tensor of shape (N', 3), where N' is the number of points within the range and valid grid bounds. sortkeys: Integer tensor of shape (N'), representing a linearized voxel index (e.g., z \cdot H \cdot W + y \cdot W + x) used for sorting. Parameters: voxelsize: Float scalar or vector (vx, vy, vz). rmin, rmax: Float vectors (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). maxvoxels: Integer. If the number of unique voxels exceeds this, the method falls back to the reference C++ implementation to preserve bit-identity. maxnumpoints: Integer. Maximum points retained per voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Range Filtering: Compute a boolean mask for points inside the bounding box. The condition is inclusive of the lower bound and exclusive of the upper bound: pi \in [r{min}, r{max}) for all dimensions. 2. Coordinate Computation: For each point in the filtered set, compute its voxel coordinate c for each dimension d \in \{x, y, z\}: cd = \lfloor \frac{pd - r{min,d}}{vd} + 0.5 \rfloor This formula mirrors the C++ round() behavior exactly. 3. Grid Boundary Validation: Compute the grid dimensions Gd = \lceil \frac{r{max,d} - r{min,d}}{vd} \rceil (or derived from config). Filter out points where any coordinate cd < 0 or cd \ge Gd. This step is critical to handle non-integer grid sizes or points at the upper bound that might round up to an out-of-bounds index. 4. Linearization: Compute a unique linear key for each valid voxel coordinate to enable sorting. For 3D coordinates (x, y, z) and grid dimensions (W, H, D): key = z \cdot (W \cdot H) + y \cdot W + x 5. Stable Sorting: Sort the points (and their associated data) by the linear key using a stable sort algorithm. This preserves the original relative order of points that map to the same voxel. 6. Grouping and Truncation: Identify unique voxel keys. For each unique voxel, select the first maxnumpoints points from the sorted list. Points beyond this limit are discarded. 7. Scattering: Scatter the selected points into the output voxels tensor, populate coors with the voxel coordinates, and record the count of points per voxel in numpointspervoxel.
