name: Per-Pixel Linked List Voxelization
head: A-Buffer Ray Intersection List, ABuffer Voxel Output Representation & Traversal, Atomic Counter Voxelization, Linked List Voxel Output, Shader Storage Buffer Object Linked List Voxelization
body: Per-Pixel Linked List Voxelization is a GPU-based technique that constructs a linked list of fragment depths per pixel using atomic counters and shader storage buffers, allowing for subsequent sorting and processing of depth-sorted voxels. It differs from rasterization-based voxelization by explicitly managing overlapping geometry per pixel via dynamic linked lists rather than fixed-depth buffers or conservative rasterization rules, and it avoids the memory overhead of full A-Buffer color/depth textures by using compact integer arrays. Inputs and outputs: Input: A mesh (vertices, triangles) in model space, a model-to-clip transformation matrix, and framebuffer dimensions (width, height). Output: A VoxelizerABufferLinkedList structure containing headPointers, nodePointers, and nodeData arrays, representing the sorted voxel depths per pixel. Data structures: Three Shader Storage Buffer Objects (SSBOs) are used, bound at specific locations: 1. HeadPointers (binding 1, std430): An array of int of size width height. Each element stores the index of the first node in the linked list for the corresponding pixel. Initialized to -1. 2. NodePointers (binding 2, std430): An array of int of size maxFragments. Each element stores the index of the next node in the linked list. 3. NodeData (binding 3, std430): An array of int of size maxFragments. Each element stores the depth of the fragment, scaled by framebufferWidth. A global atomic counter (counter, binding 0) is used to generate unique indices for each fragment. Parameters: framebufferWidth: Uniform integer, the width of the framebuffer. counter: Atomic unsigned integer, initialized to 0. maxFragments: The maximum number of fragments the system can handle. The sorting algorithm uses a safety limit of 1024 iterations per list traversal to prevent infinite loops. Steps: 1. Fragment Counting (Optional but implied by structure): The source code includes a FragCount.frag shader that increments the atomic counter for each fragment to determine the total fragment count, which is used to allocate the nodeData and nodePointers arrays. This step is not strictly part of the linked list construction but is necessary for memory allocation. 2. Make Fragment List: For each fragment generated by rasterizing the mesh: a. Increment the global atomic counter to get a unique index ucount. b. Calculate the head pointer index for the current pixel using fragment coordinates: headPointerIndex = int(glFragCoord.x) + int(glFragCoord.y) framebufferWidth. c. Atomically exchange the current head pointer value with the new fragment index to link the new node to the existing list: prevPtr = atomicExchange(HeadPointers[headPointerIndex], count). d. Set the next pointer of the new node to the previous head pointer: NodePointers[count] = prevPtr. e. Store the depth data in the new node, scaled by framebuffer width: NodeData[count] = int(depth framebufferWidth). 3. Sort Fragment List: For each pixel (processed via a screen quad): a. Calculate the head pointer index: headPointerIndex = int(glFragCoord.x) + int(glFragCoord.y) framebufferWidth. b. Retrieve the head pointer: headPtr = HeadPointers[headPointerIndex]. c. If headPtr == -1, discard the fragment (no nodes to sort). d. Initialize the outer loop pointer to the head of the list: outerPtr = headPtr. e. Iterate through the linked list using an outer loop with a safety counter (max 1024 iterations) to prevent infinite loops. f. Inside the outer loop, initialize smallestPtr to outerPtr and smallestData to NodeData[smallestPtr]. g. Initialize innerPtr to NodePointers[outerPtr]. h. Iterate through the rest of the list using an inner loop with a safety counter (max 1024 iterations) to find the node with the smallest data value. i. Inside the inner loop, if NodeData[innerPtr] < smallestData, update smallestPtr and smallestData. j. Advance innerPtr to NodePointers[innerPtr]. k. After the inner loop, if smallestPtr != outerPtr, swap NodeData[smallestPtr] and NodeData[outerPtr]. l. Advance outerPtr to NodePointers[outerPtr]. 4. Traversal: To access the sorted voxels for a pixel (i, j): a. Read the starting node index: curPtr = headPointers[i + j width]. b. The interval [startVoxel, endVoxel) represents the contiguous filled voxels along the ray for pixel (i, j). c. Advance the pointer by two hops: curPtr = nodePointers[nodePointers[curPtr]] (Note: This specific traversal logic is mentioned in the notes but the exact usage context is not fully detailed in the provided code snippets; it likely refers to a specific optimization or access pattern). HeadPointers = [-1] (width height) NodePointers = [0] maxFragments NodeData = [0] maxFragments atomicCounter = 0 def makefraglist(depth, fragCoordX, fragCoordY): global atomicCounter ucount = atomicCounter atomicCounter += 1 count = ucount headPointerIndex = fragCoordX + fragCoordY framebufferWidth # Atomic exchange: set HeadPointers[headPointerIndex] to count, return old value prevPtr = HeadPointers[headPointerIndex] HeadPointers[headPointerIndex] = count NodePointers[count] = prevPtr NodeData[count] = int(depth framebufferWidth) def sortfraglist(fragCoordX, fragCoordY): headPointerIndex = fragCoordX + fragCoordY framebufferWidth headPtr = HeadPointers[headPointerIndex] if headPtr == -1: return # Discard outerPtr = headPtr for in range(1024): # Safety limit if outerPtr == -1: break smallestPtr = outerPtr smallestData = NodeData[smallestPtr] innerPtr = NodePointers[outerPtr] for in range(1024): # Safety limit if innerPtr == -1: break innerData = NodeData[innerPtr] if innerData < smallestData: smallestPtr = innerPtr smallestData = innerData innerPtr = NodePointers[innerPtr] if smallestPtr != outerPtr: NodeData[smallestPtr] = NodeData[outerPtr] NodeData[outerPtr] = smallestData outerPtr = NodePointers[outerPtr] def traversepixel(i, j): curPtr = HeadPointers[i + j width] while curPtr != -1: # Process NodeData[curPtr] as depth curPtr = NodePointers[curPtr] Time Complexity: The sorting step is O(N^2) in the worst case for a single pixel with N fragments, due to the selection sort implementation. However, the safety limit of 1024 iterations caps the worst-case performance per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H + F), where W and H are framebuffer dimensions and F is the total number of fragments. Strengths: Handles overlapping geometry correctly per pixel. Efficient use of GPU parallelism for fragment processing. Limitations: Sorting is computationally expensive for pixels with many overlapping fragments. The fixed-size arrays require pre-allocation based on an estimate of fragment count. When to use: When accurate depth sorting of overlapping geometry is required per pixel, and the number of fragments per pixel is not excessively large. When not to use: For scenes with very high overdraw per pixel, where the O(N^2) sorting becomes a bottleneck. This method is implemented in the Voxelizer library by Kelsey Kurzeja (2014). name: Voxel Grid Data Generation Pipeline
head: Labeled Point Cloud Voxelization with Occlusion Handling, Voxel Grid Generation from Scans
body: This method generates labeled 3D voxel grids from sequential scan data, specifically designed to handle occlusions and temporal consistency between prior and current observations. It differs from standard voxelization by maintaining two distinct grid states (prior and past) and explicitly updating occlusion masks based on camera pose transformations, ensuring that newly observed geometry correctly occludes previous estimates. It builds on Voxelization by adding a temporal, scan-based processing loop. Inputs: A sequence of poses (poses), where each pose is a 4x4 transformation matrix. Point clouds associated with each pose (pastPoints, priorPoints). Labels associated with each point (pastLabels, priorLabels). Configuration parameters: stridenum, stridedistance. Output directory and naming convention. Outputs: Two voxel grids: priorGrid and pastGrid, saved to disk. Data Structures: VoxelGrid: Contains an occupancy map and an occlusion mask. The specific internal layout is implementation-dependent but must support updateOcclusions() and updateInvalid(). Pose: 4x4 matrix representing camera position and orientation. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize priorGrid and pastGrid with the target resolution and bounds. 2. Iteration Loop: Iterate through the scan sequence. For each current scan index current: a. Retrieve priorPoints, priorLabels, pastPoints, and pastLabels for the current index. b. Label Counting: Initialize labelCount = 0. Iterate through pastLabels. If label > 0, increment labelCount. Calculate pointCount as the total number of points in pastPoints. Calculate percentageLabeled = 100.0f labelCount / pointCount. c. Validation: If percentageLabeled <= 0.0f, skip grid generation for this step to avoid empty or invalid data. d. Occlusion Update: Call priorGrid.updateOcclusions(). Call pastGrid.updateOcclusions(). e. Invalid Voxel Marking: Iterate through pastPoints. For each point i, compute the endpoint in the anchor frame: \text{endpoint} = (\text{anchor\pose}^{-1} \times \text{pastPoints}[i].\text{pose}).\text{col}(3).\text{head}(3) where anchorpose is the reference frame transformation, col(3) extracts the translation vector, and head(3) takes the first three components. Call pastGrid.updateInvalid(endpoint) to mark voxels along the ray or at the endpoint as invalid/occluded. f. Save Grids: Call saveVoxelGrid(priorGrid, outputvoxeldirname, outname.str(), "input"). Call saveVoxelGrid(pastGrid, outputvoxeldirname, outname.str(), "target"). g. Advance Index: Initialize distance = 0, count = 0. While (count < config.stridenum || distance < config.stridedistance || count == 0) && current + 1 < poses.size(): distance += poseDistance(poses[current], poses[current + 1]). count += 1. current += 1. Break if no further scan is possible. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatevoxelgrids(poses, pastPoints, pastLabels, priorPoints, priorLabels, config, anchorpose, outputdir, outname): # Initialize grids priorGrid = VoxelGrid() pastGrid = VoxelGrid() current = 0 while current < len(poses): # Retrieve data for current index # Note: In a real implementation, these would be fetched based on 'current' # Assuming pastPoints/Labels etc. are aligned with poses[current] # Count labeled points labelCount = 0 pointCount = len(pastLabels) for label in pastLabels: if label > 0: labelCount += 1 percentageLabeled = 100.0 labelCount / pointCount # Skip if no labels if percentageLabeled <= 0.0: current += 1 continue # Update occlusions priorGrid.updateOcclusions() pastGrid.updateOcclusions() # Mark invalid voxels for i in range(len(pastPoints)): # Compute endpoint in anchor frame # Assuming pastPoints[i].pose is a 4x4 matrix or similar structure # anchorpose.inverse() pastPoints[i].pose transformed = matrixmultiply(inverse(anchorpose), pastPoints[i].pose) endpoint = transformed.getcolumn(3)[:3] # col(3).head(3) pastGrid.updateInvalid(endpoint) # Save grids saveVoxelGrid(priorGrid, outputdir, outname, "input") saveVoxelGrid(pastGrid, outputdir, outname, "target") # Advance scan index distance = 0.0 count = 0 while (count < config.stridenum or distance < config.stridedistance or count == 0) and current + 1 < len(poses): distance += posedistance(poses[current], poses[current + 1]) count += 1 current += 1 if current >= len(poses): break def posedistance(pose1, pose2): # Euclidean distance between translation components t1 = pose1.gettranslation() t2 = pose2.gettranslation() return vectornorm(t1 - t2) Parameters: stridenum: Maximum number of scans to skip in one stride. stridedistance: Maximum distance between scans to allow a stride. Edge Cases: Empty Labels: If percentageLabeled <= 0.0, the grid generation is skipped to prevent invalid output. Boundary Conditions: The loop breaks if current + 1 >= poses.size(). Generates a 3D occupancy grid of voxels representing a smoke volume, expanded over time from an origin point using CPU iteration and GPU buffer upload [2979-voxel-grid-generation-expansion.md]. Loads COLMAP camera intrinsics/extrinsics and 3D points, resizes images to a target resolution, adjusts coordinate system, and subsamples points if exceeding a hardware limit [3420-scene-data-loading-resizing.md]. A pipeline for converting point clouds to meshes using voxelization, cube type classification, thinning, and reconstruction, exposed via a Python binding module named DCXmain [3770-dcx-pipeline.md]. Scan-converts the geometry directly into the sampled array and renders the ensemble, allowing for true 3-D merge of visualizations. Prepares KITTI dataset for training by parsing camera extrinsics/intrinsics, downsampling point clouds, adding background shell, and splitting into train/validation sets. Definition: Prepares KITTI dataset for training by parsing camera extrinsics/intrinsics, downsampling point clouds, adding background shell, and splitting into train/validation sets. Steps: 1. Parse camera extrinsics from XML to get Tpointcloudcamera, label, sensorid, path. 2. Parse intrinsics to get K, width, height. 3. Load point cloud from PLY. 4. Downsample point cloud by 99% (frac=0.01). 5. Add 1000 random shell points around scene center/radius. 6. Save to parquet. 7. Split frames every 3 for train/val. 8. Save JSON metadata. Formula: Intrinsic matrix K is computed as: K = \begin{bmatrix} f & 0 & w/2 \\ 0 & f & h/2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where f is focal length, w and h are image dimensions. Parameters: frac=0.01: downsampling fraction for the point cloud. numshellpoints=1000: number of background points added around the scene center. train every 3 frames: ratio used to split data into training and validation sets. Not given in the sources. The core pipeline described in is part of the jbehley/voxelizer repository, which is an unofficial implementation likely related to 3D reconstruction or SLAM systems. The concept of direct geometry scan-conversion for merging volume and geometric data originates from earlier work on volume rendering and visualization, as cited in. The KITTI dataset preprocessing steps are derived from a Taichi-based 3D Gaussian Splatting implementation. jbehley/voxelizer, https://github.com/jbehley/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) DTIC ADA193649: Rendering of Surfaces from Volume Data,, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA193649, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Carving
body: Voxel carving is a technique to produce a dense, filled voxel grid representing the volume of a shape by intersecting geometric constraints derived from multiple camera views, typically depth maps or silhouettes. Unlike surface-only voxelization methods that populate only boundary voxels, voxel carving fills the interior, creating a solid representation of the object. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Rasterization-based Voxelization by explicitly rejecting space outside the observed silhouette or depth bounds, rather than projecting mesh geometry into the grid. Inputs: A 3D geometry (mesh or point cloud) to be reconstructed. A set of camera poses (extrinsics) and intrinsics. Depth maps or silhouette images rendered from these poses. Grid parameters: cubicsize (bounding box dimension), voxelresolution (number of voxels per side), and origin (typically center of the bounding box). Outputs: A dense voxel grid (VoxelGrid) where each voxel is marked as occupied or free. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array of boolean flags or occupancy states. In Open3D, this is represented by o3d.geometry.VoxelGrid with fields width, height, depth, voxelsize, origin, and optional color. Camera Pose: Defined by intrinsic matrix K and extrinsic matrix T (rotation R and translation t). Parameters: voxelresolution: Integer controlling grid density. cubicsize: Float defining the side length of the cubic bounding box. voxelsize: Calculated as cubicsize / voxelresolution. origin: The 3D coordinate of the grid's minimum corner, typically [-cubicsize/2, -cubicsize/2, -cubicsize/2] if centered at the origin. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute vertex normals for the input mesh. Determine the bounding box of the geometry. Calculate the center C and scale factor S such that the geometry fits within a unit sphere or normalized space if required by the specific implementation. Define the camera positions. A common approach uses vertices of a sphere (camerasphere) to distribute cameras evenly. 2. Grid Initialization: Create a dense voxel grid with dimensions cubicsize x cubicsize x cubicsize and voxelsize derived from voxelresolution. Initialize all voxels as potentially occupied (or free, depending on the specific carving logic; typically, carving starts with a full grid and removes free space, or starts empty and adds occupied space based on intersection). In the Open3D carvedepthmap context, the grid is initialized to represent the volume, and voxels outside the depth range are marked as free. 3. Iteration over Cameras: For each camera pose i in the set of camera positions: a. Compute Extrinsic Matrix: Convert spherical coordinates (r, rx, ry) of the camera position to a 4x4 transformation matrix Ti. b. Render Depth Map: Render the scene from the current camera pose to obtain a depth image Di (float buffer). c. Carve: Depth Map Method: For each pixel (u, v) in the depth image with depth value d: Compute the 3D ray from the camera center through the pixel. Mark all voxels along this ray from the camera up to distance d as occupied (or free, depending on convention; typically, space in front of the surface is free, space behind is unknown/occupied). Note: Standard visual hull carving marks space outside the silhouette as free. Depth-based carving marks space beyond the measured depth as free. Specifically, voxels with distance < d are kept as occupied (if assuming the object is in front) or free (if assuming the object is behind the surface). The Open3D implementation typically treats the volume in front of the depth surface as the object interior or exterior depending on the "carve" logic. The standard "carving" implies removing space that is not observed. Thus, voxels along the ray up to d are considered valid, and those beyond are carved out (marked free). Silhouette Method: For each pixel (u, v) in the silhouette image: If the pixel is part of the silhouette, mark all voxels along the corresponding ray as potentially occupied. If the pixel is background, mark all voxels along the ray as free (carved out). 4. Finalization: The resulting grid contains voxels that are consistent with all observed depth/silhouette constraints. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def voxelcarving(mesh, camerapositions, intrinsics, extrinsics, cubicsize, voxelresolution, origin=None): """ Perform voxel carving using depth maps. Args: mesh: Input 3D mesh. camerapositions: List of camera center positions (Nx3). intrinsics: Camera intrinsic matrix (3x3). extrinsics: List of camera extrinsic matrices (Nx4x4). cubicsize: Size of the bounding box. voxelresolution: Number of voxels per side. origin: Origin of the voxel grid. Defaults to [-cubicsize/2,...]. Returns: voxelgrid: A 3D boolean array (occupied voxels). """ if origin is None: origin = np.array([-cubicsize / 2.0, -cubicsize / 2.0, -cubicsize / 2.0]) voxelsize = cubicsize / voxelresolution # Initialize grid: True for occupied, False for free # Start with all True, then carve out free space gridshape = (voxelresolution, voxelresolution, voxelresolution) occupied = np.ones(gridshape, dtype=bool) # Precompute voxel centers or indices for ray casting # For efficiency, project voxel centers to image space or project rays to voxel space. # Here we use the ray-casting approach for clarity. for i, (campos, Tcam) in enumerate(zip(camerapositions, extrinsics)): # 1. Render depth map for this camera pose # In a real implementation, this calls a renderer. # depthmap[u, v] = distance from camera to surface along ray (u,v) depthmap = renderdepth(mesh, campos, Tcam, intrinsics) # 2. Carve using depth map # For each pixel, voxels closer than depthmap are potentially occupied. # Voxels further than depthmap are free (carved out). # Get pixel coordinates h, w = depthmap.shape u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w), np.arange(h)) # Convert pixel coords to 3D rays # Inverse intrinsic to get direction in camera space Kinv = np.linalg.inv(intrinsics) for y in range(h): for x in range(w): d = depthmap[y, x] if d == 0 or np.isnan(d): continue # No depth # Ray direction in camera space # Assuming principal point is at center, or using standard pinhole model # px = x - cx, py = y - cy # This step depends on the specific intrinsic definition. # General form: raydircam = Kinv @ np.array([x, y, 1]) raydircam = raydircam / np.linalg.norm(raydircam) # Transform ray to world space Rcam = Tcam[:3,:3] tcam = Tcam[:3, 3] raydirworld = Rcam @ raydircam rayoriginworld = tcam # Cast ray into voxel grid # Find intersection of ray with voxel grid bounds # Then step through voxels voxelsalongray = castrayintogrid(rayoriginworld, raydirworld, origin, voxelsize, gridshape) for voxelidx in voxelsalongray: dist = np.linalg.norm(voxelcenters[voxelidx] - rayoriginworld) if dist > d: occupied[voxelidx] = False # Carve out space behind surface else: occupied[voxelidx] = True # Keep space in front Note: The pseudocode above is a conceptual representation. Efficient implementations use GPU acceleration or optimized ray-voxel intersection algorithms (e.g., Amanatides & Woo). The Open3D carvedepthmap method handles the low-level ray casting and grid updates internally. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in depth rendering can cause holes or artifacts. Use epsilon tolerances when comparing distances. Boundaries: Ensure the voxel grid fully encloses the object and the camera frustums. If the object extends beyond the cubicsize, it will be clipped. Degenerate Input: If a camera is inside the object, the depth map may be invalid or misleading. Preprocessing should ensure cameras are outside the object. Occlusions: Voxel carving produces a "visual hull," which may not capture concavities hidden from all camera views. A streaming GPU-based method that creates an explicit volume using only surface voxels in a GPU-optimal 2D data representation, avoiding 3D texture drawbacks and minimizing GPU-CPU data transfer through load balancing. It differs from CPU-based methods by leveraging graphics hardware for interactive framerates. A CPU-based method using GVC-IB (Graphics Hardware-based Visual Hull) as its core, adding user-driven interactive refinement. Users assign perceptual significance to features via 2D image editing, allowing varying resolution and level of detail across the voxel structure. An algorithm that uses correspondence between arbitrary image regions to reconstruct concavities that are difficult or impossible to capture with standard silhouette-based methods. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M \cdot R), where N is the number of cameras, M is the number of pixels per image, and R is the average ray length in voxels. Highly dependent on grid resolution and number of views. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the total number of voxels in the grid. Dense grids consume significant memory for large volumes. Performance: Can take tens of seconds to minutes for high-resolution reconstructions on CPU. GPU-based variants offer interactive framerates for resolutions like 256x256x128. Strengths: Produces dense, filled volumes; robust to noise in individual views; simple to implement. Limitations: Produces visual hulls (loss of concavities); sensitive to camera calibration errors; high memory usage for dense grids. When to Use: When a dense volumetric representation is required and multiple calibrated views are available. When Not to Use: For scenes with significant occlusions or when high-fidelity concavities are critical without additional data. Voxel carving originated as a method for 3D reconstruction from multiple views, building on the concept of visual hulls. It was popularized in computer vision and graphics for creating volumetric models from depth maps or silhouettes. Open3D provides built-in support for this technique via carvedepthmap and carvesilhouette. Variants have been developed to address performance (GPU acceleration) and fidelity (multi-resolution, cell carving). name: Coordinate Grid Generation
head: Meshgrid Setup, Pixel coordinate grid, Pixel Coordinate Generation, NDC Pixel Coordinate Generation, [-1, 1] coordinate grid
body: Coordinate Grid Generation produces a structured set of spatial coordinates (typically in Normalized Device Coordinates, NDC, range [-1, 1]) that align with the discrete sampling grid of a volume or image. It solves the problem of mapping integer pixel or voxel indices to continuous physical or normalized space for neural field training, ray casting, and SDF evaluation. It differs from its sibling Rasterization-based Voxelization by generating the sample points themselves rather than determining which voxels a primitive occupies, and from 3D Coordinate Grid Generation by primarily targeting 2D image-plane coordinates for ray origin generation, though it extends to 3D. Inputs: Image dimensions: Width W, Height H (for 2D) or dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz (for 3D). Optional physical scale: scale (default 0.5) or pointsdistance (default 0.5) defining the physical extent or spacing. Optional info channels: infosize (default 4 for RGB+Alpha) for cell data. Outputs: 2D Case: A tensor of shape [W \times H, 2] containing (x, y) coordinates in NDC space [-1, 1]. 3D Case: A tensor of shape [Sx \times Sy \times Sz, 3] containing (x, y, z) coordinates, optionally paired with a cell tensor of shape [Sx, Sy, Sz, \text{info\size}]. Data Structures: Grid Tensor: A flattened 1D array of coordinates. For 2D, shape is [N, 2] where N=W \times H. For 3D, shape is [N, 3] where N=Sx Sy Sz. Cell Tensor (3D only): A tensor storing attributes per voxel, initialized with requiresgrad=True for differentiable rendering. Steps: 1. Generate Integer Indices: Create 1D arrays of integer indices for each dimension. For 2D: x{idx} \in [0, W-1], y{idx} \in [0, H-1]. For 3D: i \in [0, Sx-1], j \in [0, Sy-1], k \in [0, Sz-1]. 2. Normalize to NDC [-1, 1]: Map indices to the range [-1, 1]. The standard formula centers the grid on the origin: x{ndc} = \frac{x{idx} - \frac{W-1}{2}}{\frac{W-1}{2}} y{ndc} = \frac{y{idx} - \frac{H-1}{2}}{\frac{H-1}{2}} Alternatively, using torch.linspace from -1 to 1 with W and H steps achieves the same result. 3. Create Meshgrid: Use a meshgrid function to combine the 1D coordinate arrays into a grid. Indexing: Use "ij" indexing (row-major) which is standard in PyTorch/TensorFlow. Order: For 2D, stack y and x (or x and y depending on convention) and reverse if necessary to match image layout (x, y). Note that torch.meshgrid does not support "xy" indexing natively; if "xy" behavior is required, transpose the result. 4. Flatten: Reshape the grid tensor from [H, W, 2] (or [Sz, Sy, Sx, 3]) to [H \times W, 2] (or [Sz Sy Sx, 3]) in row-major order. 5. Physical Scaling (Optional): If physical coordinates are needed instead of NDC, scale the coordinates by the pointsdistance or scale parameter. x{phys} = x{ndc} \times \text{scale} 6. Centering (Optional): For 3D grids, explicitly center the grid by subtracting \lceil D/2 \rceil - 1 from each coordinate index before scaling. 7. Negation (Optional): Some implementations negate the final grid coordinates to align with specific camera coordinate systems (e.g., right-handed vs left-handed). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def generate2dcoordinategrid(width: int, height: int, scale: float = 1.0, negate: bool = True): """ Generates a 2D coordinate grid in NDC space [-1, 1]. Args: width: Image width W. height: Image height H. scale: Physical scale factor (default 1.0 for pure NDC). negate: Whether to negate the final coordinates. Returns: Tensor of shape [WH, 2] with coordinates [x, y]. """ # Step 1: Generate integer indices xidx = torch.arange(width, dtype=torch.float32) yidx = torch.arange(height, dtype=torch.float32) # Step 2: Normalize to [-1, 1] # Formula: (idx - center) / center xndc = (xidx - (width - 1) / 2) / ((width - 1) / 2) yndc = (yidx - (height - 1) / 2) / ((height - 1) / 2) # Step 3: Create Meshgrid with 'ij' indexing # torch.meshgrid returns (Xgrid, Ygrid) where Xgrid varies along columns, Ygrid along rows xgrid, ygrid = torch.meshgrid(xndc, yndc, indexing='ij') # Step 4: Stack and Flatten # Stack along last dimension to get [H, W, 2] grid = torch.stack([xgrid, ygrid], dim=-1) # Flatten to [WH, 2] gridflat = grid.view(-1, 2) # Step 5: Physical Scaling (if scale != 1.0) if scale != 1.0: gridflat = gridflat scale # Step 6: Negation (if required by convention) if negate: gridflat = -gridflat return gridflat def generate3dcoordinategrid(sx: int, sy: int, sz: int, pointsdistance: float = 0.5, infosize: int = 4): """ Generates a 3D coordinate grid for SDF evaluation or voxel attributes. Args: sx, sy, sz: Grid dimensions. pointsdistance: Physical spacing between points. infosize: Number of channels per cell (e.g., RGB + Alpha). Returns: gridcoords: Tensor of shape [sxsysz, 3]. gridcells: Tensor of shape [sx, sy, sz, infosize]. """ # Step 1: Create index arrays xidx = torch.arange(sx, dtype=torch.float32) yidx = torch.arange(sy, dtype=torch.float32) zidx = torch.arange(sz, dtype=torch.float32) # Step 2: Generate meshgrid of indices with 'ij' indexing xgrid, ygrid, zgrid = torch.meshgrid(xidx, yidx, zidx, indexing='ij') # Step 3: Stack meshgrid components gridindices = torch.stack([xgrid, ygrid, zgrid], dim=-1) # Shape [sx, sy, sz, 3] # Step 4: Center the grid # Subtract ceil(dim/2) - 1 to center around 0 centerx = np.ceil(sx / 2) - 1 centery = np.ceil(sy / 2) - 1 centerz = np.ceil(sz / 2) - 1 gridcentered = gridindices - torch.tensor([centerx, centery, centerz], dtype=torch.float32) # Step 5: Scale coordinates by pointsdistance gridscaled = gridcentered pointsdistance # Step 6: Reshape to flat list of coordinates gridcoords = gridscaled.view(-1, 3) # Step 7: Initialize gridcells tensor # Shape [sx, sy, sz, infosize], requires gradients for training gridcells = torch.zeros(sx, sy, sz, infosize, requiresgrad=True) return gridcoords, gridcells Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Even vs Odd Dimensions: The normalization formula \frac{x - (W-1)/2}{(W-1)/2} ensures the center pixel (at index (W-1)/2) maps to 0. If W is even, the center falls between pixels, which is standard for NDC but may require careful handling in ray origins. Indexing Convention: torch.meshgrid defaults to "ij". Using "xy" (NumPy default) requires transposing the output arrays, which is not directly supported in PyTorch's meshgrid and must be handled manually. Precision: Using float32 is standard, but for very large grids, float64 may be needed to prevent precision loss in coordinate values. Generates a 3D grid of sample points within a voxel space for Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluation. It produces a set of 3D points forming a regular grid within a unit cube, typically excluding boundary regions to ensure samples lie strictly inside the volume. It differs from its parent Coordinate Grid Generation by explicitly mapping integer grid indices to continuous 3D coordinates in world space (often [-1, 1]) using voxel size and origin parameters, rather than generating normalized 2D image coordinates. Mimics np.meshgrid(..., indexing="xy") in PyTorch, as torch.meshgrid only allows "ij" indexing. It is chosen when compatibility with NumPy's coordinate layout is required. The implementation calls torch.meshgrid(tensor1, tensor2) and returns ii.transpose(-1, -2), jj.transpose(-1, -2). Time Complexity: O(W \times H) for 2D and O(Sx \times Sy \times Sz) for 3D, as every grid point must be computed. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times D) where D is the dimensionality (2 or 3). For 3D with cell attributes, O(Sx Sy Sz \times \text{info\size}). Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPU using tensor operations. Generation is typically instantaneous for resolutions up to 1024^2 or 256^3 on modern GPUs. Strengths: Provides exact, differentiable coordinate mappings essential for neural rendering and SDF optimization. Limitations: Memory usage grows cubically for 3D grids, limiting resolution for dense volumes. It originated with the need to sample input coordinates for multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) that map spatial positions to color and density. name: 3D Coordinate Grid Generation
head: Voxel Grid Point Generation, Voxel Grid Sampling, Voxel Grid Sampling for Mesh Extraction
body: Generates a 3D grid of sample points within a voxel space for Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluation. It produces a set of 3D points forming a regular grid within a unit cube, typically excluding boundary regions to ensure samples lie strictly inside the volume. It differs from its parent Coordinate Grid Generation by explicitly mapping integer grid indices to continuous 3D coordinates in world space (often [-1, 1]) using voxel size and origin parameters, rather than generating normalized 2D image coordinates. Inputs: N: Integer resolution (number of voxels per axis). voxelorigin: List of 3 floats representing the origin of the voxel grid. Default: [-1, -1, -1]. voxelsize: Float size of each voxel. Calculated as 2.0 / (N - 1). transform: Boolean flag indicating whether to apply a transformation matrix to the points. Default: False. Outputs: samples: A tensor of shape (N^3, 4) or (N^3, 3) containing the 3D coordinates of the grid points. The fourth dimension (if present) is often initialized to zero or used for padding. Data Structures: overallindex: A 1D tensor/array of integers from 0 to N^3 - 1. points: A 2D array/tensor of shape (N^3, 3) storing the final 3D coordinates. Steps: 1. Calculate Bounds: Compute the low and high bounds for the grid coordinates to exclude boundary regions if necessary: \text{low} = \frac{0.5}{\text{res}} \text{high} = 1 - \frac{0.5}{\text{res}} where res is N. 2. Generate 1D Coordinates: Create a 1D linear space (linspace) from low to high with res points. 3. Create 3D Meshgrid: Generate a 3D meshgrid from the 1D coordinates using indexing='xy' (or equivalent standard Cartesian indexing). This produces three 3D arrays X, Y, and Z of shape (res, res, res). 4. Stack and Reshape: Stack X, Y, and Z into a single array and reshape it to (-1, 3) to flatten the grid into a list of points. Alternative Index-Based Method (from): 1. Initialize samples tensor of shape (N^3, 4) with zeros. 2. Create overallindex tensor from 0 to N^3 - 1. 3. Compute x, y, z indices from overallindex using integer division and modulo operations: z = \text{overall\index} // (N \times N) y = (\text{overall\index} // N) \% N x = \text{overall\index} \% N 4. Convert indices to coordinates: \text{coord}x = x \times \text{voxel\size} + \text{voxel\origin}[0] \text{coord}y = y \times \text{voxel\size} + \text{voxel\origin}[1] \text{coord}z = z \times \text{voxel\size} + \text{voxel\origin}[2] 5. If transform is True, apply transformpointstensor to the coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generate3dcoordinategrid(N, voxelorigin=[-1.0, -1.0, -1.0], voxelsize=None, transform=False): """ Generates a 3D grid of sample points within a voxel space. Args: N (int): Resolution (number of voxels per axis). voxelorigin (list): Origin of the voxel grid [x, y, z]. voxelsize (float): Size of each voxel. If None, calculated as 2.0 / (N - 1). transform (bool): Whether to apply a transformation. Returns: np.ndarray: Array of shape (N^3, 3) containing 3D coordinates. """ if voxelsize is None: voxelsize = 2.0 / (N - 1) # Method 1: Meshgrid approach (excludes boundaries if low/high are used) # Note: The source suggests excluding boundaries. # If strict boundary inclusion is needed, use np.linspace(-1, 1, N) low = 0.5 / N high = 1.0 - 0.5 / N # Create 1D linspace x1d = np.linspace(low, high, N) y1d = np.linspace(low, high, N) z1d = np.linspace(low, high, N) # Create 3D meshgrid with 'xy' indexing (standard for image-like coordinates) X, Y, Z = np.meshgrid(x1d, y1d, z1d, indexing='xy') # Stack and reshape points = np.stack((X, Y, Z), axis=-1) points = points.reshape(-1, 3) # Method 2: Index-based approach (from) # This method maps indices directly to world coordinates based on origin/size # It is often preferred for explicit voxel grid control. # Create index tensor overallindex = np.arange(N3) # Compute x, y, z indices zidx = overallindex // (N N) yidx = (overallindex // N) % N xidx = overallindex % N # Convert to coordinates coordsx = xidx voxelsize + voxelorigin[0] coordsy = yidx voxelsize + voxelorigin[1] coordsz = zidx voxelsize + voxelorigin[2] pointsindexbased = np.stack((coordsx, coordsy, coordsz), axis=-1) # Note: The two methods may yield slightly different coordinate ranges depending on # whether boundaries are included. The index-based method covers the full range # defined by voxelorigin and voxelsize. if transform: # Placeholder for transformation logic # In practice, this might involve multiplying by a rotation/translation matrix pass return pointsindexbased Parameters: N: Resolution. Typical values depend on the desired detail level (e.g., 64, 128, 256). voxelorigin: Default [-1, -1, -1]. voxelsize: Calculated as 2.0 / (N - 1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Exclusion: The meshgrid method with low/high adjustments excludes the outermost voxels' centers if not carefully aligned with the origin. The index-based method includes all N^3 points. Ensure consistency with downstream SDF evaluation expectations. Precision: Using floating-point arithmetic for coordinate generation can introduce small errors. For large N, consider using higher precision types if exact grid alignment is critical. Transform Application: If transform is enabled, ensure the transformation matrix is compatible with the coordinate system (e.g., homogeneous coordinates if using 4D vectors). A method to sample points from a 3D grid density field using stratified sampling guided by blue noise to reduce aliasing and ensure uniform distribution. It differs from sibling methods like Coarse-to-Fine SDF Sampling by explicitly constructing a probability distribution over a voxel grid and sampling indices via multinomial distribution, rather than refining a mesh or point cloud through geometric proximity. This method accelerates the generation of 3D meshes from implicit surface representations by reducing the number of expensive neural network inference calls required to evaluate Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It achieves this by first computing SDF values on a coarse grid, classifying regions as clearly inside or outside the surface, and only evaluating the neural network for points near the zero-crossing boundary at full resolution. This approach builds on 3D Coordinate Grid Generation to provide the necessary sample coordinates. Generates a tetrahedral decomposition of a 3D voxel grid for mesh extraction. It initializes an output tetrahedron definition matrix TF of size ((nx-1) (ny-1) (nz-1) 6, 4) filled with zeros. It iterates over grid indices i from 0 to nx-2, j from 0 to ny-2, and k from 0 to nz-2. For each cube, it calculates vertex indices v1 through v8 using linear indexing: v1=i+nx(j+nyk), v2=i+nx(j+1+nyk), v3=(i+1)+nx(j+nyk), v4=(i+1)+nx(j+1+nyk), v5=i+nx(j+ny(k+1)), v6=i+nx(j+1+ny(k+1)), v7=(i+1)+nx(j+ny(k+1)), v8=(i+1)+nx(j+1+ny(k+1)). It defines 6 tetrahedra per cube by assigning vertex indices to TF rows: (v1,v3,v8,v7), (v1,v8,v5,v7), (v1,v3,v4,v8), (v1,v4,v2,v8), (v1,v6,v5,v8), (v1,v2,v6,v8). Parallelization of the grid generation loop may cause race conditions if not handled correctly. Creates a mesh by sampling SDF values on a voxel grid and saving to a PLY file. It records start time, sets the decoder to eval mode, sets voxelorigin to [-1, -1, -1] and voxelsize to 2.0 / (N - 1), gets samples using getsamples, and infers SDF values using infersamples. The transform boolean parameter controls whether to apply point transformation, defaulting to False. Generates a sorted list of 3D integer offsets within a cubic volume, centered at origin, representing chunks to check for loading/unloading. It calculates grid dimension k = (half 2) + 1. It iterates i from 0 to kkk - 1, converts index to 3D bounds pos = indextoivec3bounds(i, k), centers the position pos -= IVec3::splat((k as f32 0.5) as i32), adds to sampling offsets vector, and sorts offsets by squared distance to origin. Calculates edge vector U from vertex currIndex to currIndex + xVerts, edge vector V from vertex currIndex to currIndex + xVerts + 1, computes normal N as cross product of U and V, creates face with vertices A=currIndex, B=currIndex+xVerts, C=currIndex+xVerts+1, and initializes plane position and rotation to zero. Time Complexity: O(N^3) to generate all points in the grid. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) to store the coordinates. Performance: The generation is generally fast and memory-bound. For very large N, memory allocation for the (N^3, 3) tensor can become significant. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and covers the entire volume uniformly. Essential for voxel-based SDF evaluation. Limitations: Does not adapt to surface complexity; generates points in empty space as well as near the surface. The meshgrid method with boundary exclusion may miss edge cases if the grid alignment is not precise. When to Use: When a uniform sampling of the entire voxel space is required, such as for initial SDF training or dense volume rendering. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or when adaptive sampling (e.g., near the surface) is more efficient. Originating from implementations in deep learning-based 3D reconstruction, such as the DeepSDF renderer and related projects, this method is a fundamental step in voxel-based implicit surface representation. It is widely used in neural field training and mesh extraction pipelines where a regular grid of query points is needed to evaluate implicit functions. name: Grid-based Density Sampling with Blue Noise
head: Blue Noise Stratified Sampling, Blue Noise Voxel Sampling
body: A method to sample points from a 3D grid density field using stratified sampling guided by blue noise to reduce aliasing and ensure uniform distribution. Inputs: resolution: Tuple of 3 integers (Rx, Ry, Rz) defining the grid dimensions. bottom: Tensor of shape (3,) defining the minimum corner of the voxel space. size: Tensor of shape (3,) defining the total extent of the voxel space. density: Tensor of shape (Rx, Ry, Rz) containing non-negative density values for each voxel. numpoints: Integer, the number of sample points to generate. bn: A BlueNoise instance providing pre-computed blue noise patterns. Outputs: points: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the sampled 3D coordinates. voxelindices: Tensor of shape (M, 3) containing the unique 3D voxel indices containing the sampled points. Data Structures: Grid: A class holding the state. resolution: tuple[int, int, int] bottom: torch.Tensor shape (3,) size: torch.Tensor shape (3,) density: torch.Tensor shape (Rx, Ry, Rz) bn: BlueNoise instance Steps: 1. Compute Voxel Centers: Calculate the voxel size vector: v{size} = \frac{size}{resolution} For each voxel index (i, j, k) where 0 \le i < Rx, 0 \le j < Ry, 0 \le k < Rz, compute the center: c{ijk} = bottom + v{size} \cdot (i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5) 2. Normalize Density to Frequencies: Clone the density tensor. Set all values \le 0 to 0. Sum all values in the tensor to get S. Divide each value by S to obtain the probability distribution P: P{ijk} = \frac{\max(D{ijk}, 0)}{\sum{all} \max(D{uv}, 0)} 3. Sample Voxel Indices: Flatten P into a 1D tensor of size Rx Ry Rz. Use torch.multinomial with replacement=True to draw numpoints indices from this distribution. Map these linear indices back to 3D coordinates (i, j, k) if necessary, or keep as linear indices for lookup. 4. Generate Sample Points: For each sampled voxel index, retrieve its center c{ijk}. Add a small random epsilon to break ties and avoid boundary issues: p = c{ijk} + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 10^{-6}) \text{ per dimension} 5. Find Containing Voxels: For the generated points p, compute the voxel index: idx = \lfloor \frac{p - bottom}{v{size}} \rfloor Filter indices to ensure they are within [0, resolution-1] for each dimension. Return the unique 3D indices. 6. Mask Density (Optional/Contextual): If masking is required (e.g., for functional density sampling), flatten the density tensor. Compute linear indices from the 3D voxel indices. Create a zero tensor of the same shape as density. Set values at the linear indices to the original density values. Reshape back. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np class Grid: def init(self, resolution, bottom, size, density, bn): self.resolution = resolution self.bottom = torch.tensor(bottom, dtype=torch.float32) self.size = torch.tensor(size, dtype=torch.float32) self.density = torch.tensor(density, dtype=torch.float32) self.bn = bn def samplepoints(self, numpoints): # 1. Compute voxel size voxelsize = self.size / torch.tensor(self.resolution, dtype=torch.float32) # 2. Normalize density densitycloned = self.density.clone() densitycloned = torch.clamp(densitycloned, min=0.0) totalsum = torch.sum(densitycloned) if totalsum == 0: probs = torch.oneslike(densitycloned) / densitycloned.numel() else: probs = densitycloned / totalsum # 3. Sample voxel indices probsflat = probs.view(-1) sampledindices = torch.multinomial(probsflat, numpoints, replacement=True) # Convert linear indices to 3D coordinates z = sampledindices // (self.resolution[0] self.resolution[1]) remainder = sampledindices % (self.resolution[0] self.resolution[1]) y = remainder // self.resolution[0] x = remainder % self.resolution[0] voxelindices3d = torch.stack([x, y, z], dim=1).to(torch.float32) # 4. Generate sample points centers = self.bottom + voxelsize (voxelindices3d + 0.5) epsilon = torch.randlike(centers) 1e-6 points = centers + epsilon return points, voxelindices3d def findcontainingvoxels(self, points): # 5. Find containing voxels voxelsize = self.size / torch.tensor(self.resolution, dtype=torch.float32) indices = torch.floor((points - self.bottom) / voxelsize) # Filter indices to be within [0, resolution-1] mask = (indices >= 0).all(dim=1) & (indices < torch.tensor(self.resolution, dtype=torch.float32)).all(dim=1) validindices = indices[mask] # Return unique 3D indices uniqueindices, = torch.unique(validindices, dim=0, returninverse=False) return uniqueindices def maskdensity(self, voxelindices3d): # 6. Mask density for containing voxels densityflat = self.density.view(-1) # Compute linear indices from 3D indices x = voxelindices3d[:, 0].long() y = voxelindices3d[:, 1].long() z = voxelindices3d[:, 2].long() Rx, Ry, Rz = self.resolution linearindices = x + y Rx + z (Rx Ry) # Create zero tensor and set values at linear indices maskeddensityflat = torch.zeroslike(densityflat) maskeddensityflat[linearindices] = densityflat[linearindices] # Reshape back maskeddensity = maskeddensityflat.view(self.density.shape) return maskeddensity class BlueNoise: def init(self, npzpath, device='cpu'): self.device = device self.noiselevels = [] data = np.load(npzpath) for key in sorted(data.files): noise = (torch.tensor(data[key], dtype=torch.float32, device=device) - 0.5) 2.0 self.noiselevels.append(noise) def aggregatenoise(self, level): if level < 0: level = 0 if level > 6: level = 6 return torch.cat(self.noiselevels[:level+1], dim=0) def aggregaterandomizedtargetednoise(self, nbpoints): if nbpoints <= 32: return self.aggregatenoise(0)[torch.randperm(32, device=self.device)[:nbpoints]] elif nbpoints <= 140: return self.aggregatenoise(1)[torch.randperm(140, device=self.device)[:nbpoints]] elif nbpoints <= 505: return self.aggregatenoise(2)[torch.randperm(505, device=self.device)[:nbpoints]] elif nbpoints <= 1738: return self.aggregatenoise(3)[torch.randperm(1738, device=self.device)[:nbpoints]] elif nbpoints <= 5898: return self.aggregatenoise(4)[torch.randperm(5898, device=self.device)[:nbpoints]] elif nbpoints <= 19938: return self.aggregatenoise(5)[torch.randperm(19938, device=self.device)[:nbpoints]] else: return self.aggregatenoise(6)[torch.randperm(67323, device=self.device)[:nbpoints]] Parameters: resolution: Typical values depend on scene complexity. The source uses 32 for the grid in functional sampling. epsilon: 10^{-6} is used to perturb points slightly from voxel centers. BlueNoise Levels: Pre-computed noise patterns are aggregated up to level 6, supporting up to 67,323 points. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Density: If the sum of density is zero, torch.multinomial will fail or produce uniform noise. The pseudocode handles this by falling back to uniform probabilities. Boundary Conditions: Points sampled near the boundary might fall outside the grid if not clamped. The findcontainingvoxels step filters indices to [0, resolution-1]. Precision: Using float32 is standard. The epsilon addition helps avoid exact integer boundary issues in floor operations. Samples new points based on a functional density defined over a grid, masks the grid density for voxels containing mesh vertices, and aggregates the new points' SDF values. It determines resampling parameters via resamplepointmethod(sdf, tets, xnx3, method=resampledpointsmethod) to get nbresampledpoints and neighboractivepointsmask. If nbresampledpoints is 0, it returns early. It creates a grid (e.g., resolution 32, bounds -1.0 to 2.0), populates it with density from a function applied to voxel centers, and masks this density using the voxels containing kalmesh.vertices. It then samples new points using grid.samplepoints(nbresampledpoints) and aggregates them with existing points using aggregation(updatedxnx3, neighboractivepointsmask, xnx3, sdf, tets, features=features, method=aggregationmethod). Time Complexity: Sampling is dominated by torch.multinomial, which is O(N \log M) or O(N) depending on implementation, where N is numpoints and M is the number of voxels (Rx Ry Rz). Finding containing voxels is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(M) for the density grid and O(N) for the output points. Performance: The source reports optimization with 32K points taking less than 4 minutes on an RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: Reduces aliasing through blue noise guidance. Ensures uniform distribution according to the density field. Limitations: Requires a pre-computed density grid. Resolution of the grid limits the detail of the sampling distribution. When to use: When you need to sample points from a volumetric density field with minimal aliasing, particularly for SDF evaluation or mesh reconstruction. When not to use: When the density field is sparse or irregular, or when higher precision is needed than the grid resolution allows. The method is implemented in the TetWeave project. TetWeave represents shapes as a point cloud with SDF values and optional spherical harmonics coefficients, reconstructing meshes via Delaunay tetrahedralization and Marching Tetrahedra. The method is used in the optimization pipeline to resample points based on functional density, aiding in the reconstruction of shapes from rendered targets. name: Coarse-to-Fine SDF Sampling for Mesh Creation
head: Speedup Mesh Creation via Coarse-to-Fine SDF Sampling
body:
This method accelerates mesh generation from implicit surfaces by reducing neural network inference calls for Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluation. It computes SDFs on a coarse grid, classifies regions as inside, outside, or near the surface, and only evaluates the network at full resolution for points near the zero-crossing boundary. This approach builds on 3D Coordinate Grid Generation to provide sample coordinates. The method takes a trained decoder network, a latent vector representing the shape, and a target resolution N as inputs, and outputs a PLY mesh file representing the isosurface. Samples Array: A 2D array of shape (M, 4), where M is the number of samples. Columns 0–2 store (x, y, z) coordinates, and column 3 stores the SDF value. Classification Indices: Integer arrays possamples, negsamples, and validsamples indexing into the samples array. N: Target resolution (e.g., 1024). voxelorigin: Minimum corner of the voxel space, set to [-1, -1, -1]. maxbatch: Maximum number of points processed per neural network inference pass. voxelsizehalf: Classification tolerance, calculated as  rac{2.0}{N/2 - 1}. 1. Initialize Coarse Grid Parameters: Set voxelorigin to [-1, -1, -1]. Calculate coarse resolution N{half} = N/2. Calculate coarse voxel size as 	ext{voxel\size}{half} =  rac{2.0}{N{half} - 1}. 2. Generate Coarse Samples: Generate sample coordinates for the half-resolution grid using getsamples(N{half}, voxel\origin, voxel\size{half}). 3. Infer Coarse SDF Values: Evaluate the decoder network on the coarse samples in batches of maxbatch to obtain 	ext{sdf\values}{half}. 4. Upsample to Full Resolution: Interpolate 	ext{sdf\values}{half} to full resolution N using cubic upsampling: 	ext{sdf\values}{upsampled} = 	ext{upsample\cubic}(	ext{sdf\values}{half}, N{half}, N). 5. Classify Regions: Compare 	ext{sdf\values}{upsampled} against voxelsizehalf. Points with values > 	ext{voxel\size}{half} are possamples, values < -	ext{voxel\size}{half} are negsamples, and values within [-	ext{voxel\size}{half}, 	ext{voxel\size}{half}] are validsamples. 6. Generate Full Resolution Coordinates: Calculate full voxel size as 	ext{voxel\size} =  rac{2.0}{N - 1}. Generate sample coordinates for the full resolution grid using getsamples(N, voxel\origin, voxel\size). 7. Assign Pre-computed SDF Values: Initialize the SDF column (index 3) of the full-resolution samples array to 0.0. Set samples[possamples, 3] to 0.1 and samples[negsamples, 3] to -0.1. Leave samples[validsamples, 3] unset for inference. 8. Infer Fine SDF Values: Evaluate the decoder network only on validsamples coordinates. Assign the returned SDF values to samples[validsamples, 3]. 9. Extract and Reshape: Extract the third column of the samples array and reshape it into an N 	imes N 	imes N tensor. 10. Mesh Generation: Convert the SDF tensor to a PLY mesh using convertsdfsamplestoply(SDF	ensor, voxel\origin, voxel\size, output ilename). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createmeshspeedup(decoder, latentvec, N, maxbatch, outputfilename): # Step 1: Initialize coarse grid parameters Nhalf = N // 2 voxelorigin = [-1.0, -1.0, -1.0] voxelsizehalf = 2.0 / (Nhalf - 1) voxelsize = 2.0 / (N - 1) # Step 2: Generate coarse sample coordinates sampleshalf = generategrid(Nhalf, voxelorigin, voxelsizehalf) # Step 3: Infer coarse SDF values sdfvalueshalf = batchinfer(decoder, latentvec, sampleshalf[:,:3], maxbatch) # Step 4: Upsample to full resolution sdfvaluesupsampled = cubicupsample(sdfvalueshalf, Nhalf, N) # Step 5: Classify regions possamples, negsamples, validsamples = classifyvalid(sdfvaluesupsampled, voxelsizehalf) # Step 6: Generate full resolution coordinates samplesfull = generategrid(N, voxelorigin, voxelsize) # Step 7: Assign pre-computed SDF values samplesfull[:, 3] = 0.0 samplesfull[possamples, 3] = 0.1 samplesfull[negsamples, 3] = -0.1 # Step 8: Infer fine SDF values for valid samples if len(validsamples) > 0: validcoords = samplesfull[validsamples,:3] sdfvaluesvalid = batchinfer(decoder, latentvec, validcoords, maxbatch) samplesfull[validsamples, 3] = sdfvaluesvalid # Step 9: Extract and reshape sdftensor = samplesfull[:, 3].reshape(N, N, N) # Step 10: Convert to mesh converttoply(sdftensor, voxelorigin, voxelsize, outputfilename) def generategrid(res, origin, size): # Standard 3D grid generation x = np.linspace(origin[0], origin[0] + (res - 1) size, res) y = np.linspace(origin[1], origin[1] + (res - 1) size, res) z = np.linspace(origin[2], origin[2] + (res - 1) size, res) coords = np.stack(np.meshgrid(x, y, z, indexing='ij'), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 3) return np.hstack([coords, np.zeros((len(coords), 1))]) def batchinfer(decoder, latent, coords, maxbatch): # Standard batched inference values = [] for i in range(0, len(coords), maxbatch): values.append(decoder(coords[i:i+maxbatch], latent)) return np.concatenate(values) def cubicupsample(grid, oldres, newres): # Standard trilinear/cubic interpolation from scipy.ndimage import zoom return zoom(grid, newres / oldres, order=3) def classifyvalid(sdfgrid, threshold): # Standard threshold classification flat = sdfgrid.flatten() pos = np.where(flat > threshold)[0] neg = np.where(flat < -threshold)[0] valid = np.where(np.abs(flat) <= threshold)[0] return pos, neg, valid def converttoply(sdftensor, origin, size, filename): # Standard marching cubes to PLY export from skimage import measure verts, faces,, = measure.marchingcubes(sdftensor, level=0.0) with open(filename, 'w') as f: f.write("ply
format ascii 1.0
element vertex {}
property float x
property float y
property float z
endheader
".format(len(verts))) for v in verts: f.write(f"{v[0]} {v[1]} {v[2]}
") Precision: Cubic upsampling may blur sharp features; threshold selection directly impacts surface fidelity. Boundaries: voxelorigin and voxelsize must align with the decoder's training domain to avoid extrapolation artifacts. Degenerate Input: If validsamples is empty, the method skips fine inference and uses the upsampled grid directly. Time Complexity: Reduces neural network inferences from N^3 to approximately (N/2)^3 + N{valid}, where N{valid} is the number of points near the surface. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the coarse SDF grid (N{half}^3), the full-resolution coordinate grid (N^3), and the final SDF tensor (N^3). Strengths: Significantly lowers computational cost of SDF evaluation, which is typically the bottleneck in implicit surface reconstruction. Limitations: Accuracy depends on upsampling quality and threshold tuning; an overly large threshold increases inference cost, while an overly small threshold risks aliasing or incomplete surfaces. When to use: Generating high-resolution meshes from neural implicit representations where inference is expensive. When not to use: Surfaces with extreme geometric complexity or thin features requiring dense sampling everywhere. This method is described in the unofficial repository B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer. It is integrated into a color training and mesh creation pipeline for 3D shapes, optimizing the mesh generation step by deferring expensive network evaluations to the surface boundary. name: Voxel Occupancy Test
head: Inclusion Test
body: The Voxel Occupancy Test determines whether a set of query points lies within any occupied voxel of a pre-existing voxel grid. It solves the problem of fast spatial containment queries for point clouds or particle systems against a discretized volume. It differs from Rasterization-based Voxelization and Interior Voxelize by not generating the grid itself, but rather querying an existing structure. It differs from VoxelGrid from Mesh (Ray Method) by operating on discrete point queries rather than continuous ray intersections. Inputs: 1. A voxel grid data structure containing occupied voxels. 2. An array of query points P with shape (N, 3), where each row is a coordinate (x, y, z). Outputs: 1. A boolean array B of length N, where B[i] is True if point P[i] is inside an occupied voxel, and False otherwise. Data Structures: The voxel grid typically stores occupancy in a sparse hash map or a dense array, indexed by voxel coordinates. Voxel coordinates (vx, vy, vz) are derived from world coordinates (x, y, z) and the voxel size s via: vx = \lfloor x / s \rfloor, \quad vy = \lfloor y / s \rfloor, \quad vz = \lfloor z / s \rfloor Note: Floor division behavior for negative coordinates must be consistent with the grid's creation method. Steps: 1. For each query point P[i] = (xi, yi, zi): 2. Compute the voxel indices (v{x,i}, v{y,i}, v{z,i}) using the voxel size s associated with the grid. 3. Check if the voxel at (v{x,i}, v{y,i}, v{z,i}) is marked as occupied in the grid's storage. 4. Set B[i] to True if occupied, False otherwise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxeloccupancytest(voxelgrid, querypoints, voxelsize): """ voxelgrid: A data structure supporting lookup by voxel index (e.g., set of tuples or hash map). querypoints: List of (x, y, z) tuples or array of shape (N, 3). voxelsize: Float, the side length of a single voxel. Returns: boolarray: List of booleans corresponding to each query point. """ results = [] for point in querypoints: x, y, z = point # Compute voxel indices # Using floor division to map continuous coordinates to discrete grid indices vx = int(x // voxelsize) vy = int(y // voxelsize) vz = int(z // voxelsize) # Check if this voxel is occupied in the grid # Implementation detail: The specific lookup mechanism depends on the grid's internal storage # (e.g., hash set, sparse array, or dense array). isoccupied = voxelgrid.contains(vx, vy, vz) results.append(isoccupied) return results Parameters: voxelsize: Must match the resolution used to create the voxelgrid. Mismatched sizes lead to incorrect index mapping. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Coordinates: Floor division for negative numbers behaves differently in some languages (e.g., Python's // vs C++'s /). Ensure the index calculation matches the grid's coordinate system origin and direction. Boundary Conditions: Points exactly on voxel boundaries may be assigned to different voxels depending on the floor/ceil implementation. Consistency with the voxelization method is critical. Empty Grid: If the grid has no occupied voxels, the output is all False. The Point-in-Box Inclusion Test determines which points from a given array lie within an orthogonal bounding box. It serves as the core primitive for Voxel Occupancy Test, filtering points to identify voxel occupancy. Unlike 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation which uses distance metrics, this method relies on strict axis-aligned boundary checks. It differs from Sparse AABB Collision Test by operating on a static point array rather than dynamic collision shapes. This method generates a 3D binary kernel (mask) where voxels within a specified Euclidean distance from the center are set to 1, and others are set to 0. It solves the problem of defining a discrete spherical occupancy region for voxel-based operations, such as smoothing, collision detection, or volume initialization. It differs from its sibling Point-in-Box Inclusion Test by using radial distance rather than axis-aligned bounds, and from its sibling Voxel Filled Check by generating a full kernel array rather than testing a single point. Not given in the sources. The Sparse AABB Collision Test determines whether an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) intersects any occupied voxels within a sparse volume representation. It solves the problem of static collision detection for volumetric objects by iterating through the voxel grid defined by the AABB's bounds. It differs from its sibling Point-in-Box Inclusion Test by evaluating a continuous volume rather than discrete points, and from Voxel Filled Check by supporting heterogeneous voxel types (solid, liquid, unknown) and caching terrain noise evaluation per column to optimize performance. Solidity Check determines if a specific voxel coordinate in a 3D world is occupied by solid geometry or is void (empty). It solves the problem of boundary condition handling during voxel traversal, ensuring that out-of-bounds regions are treated consistently to prevent rendering artifacts. It differs from its sibling Point-in-Box Inclusion Test by explicitly managing chunk-based spatial indexing and asymmetric boundary wrapping for X/Y versus Z axes, rather than simple AABB containment. Sphere-Clamped Voxel Neighbor Search finds the closest voxel cell to a query point within a specified radius, constrained to the grid boundaries. It solves the problem of locating the nearest occupied or valid material cell in a voxelized environment for operations like ray casting or neighbor lookups. It differs from Point-in-Box Inclusion Test by using a spherical distance metric and from Voxel Filled Check by returning the specific closest cell rather than a boolean occupancy status. Collision detection implemented as a simple grid check. Time Complexity: O(N) for N query points, assuming O(1) average-case lookup in the voxel grid's underlying storage (e.g., hash map). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per query point, excluding the storage of the result array. Strengths: Extremely fast for point containment queries; leverages existing voxelization structures. Limitations: Only works for point queries; does not handle partial voxel occupancy or continuous geometry directly. When to use: When you need to test if particles or points lie inside a pre-computed voxel volume. When not to use: For continuous collision detection or ray tracing; use VoxelGrid from Mesh (Ray Method) or Raycasting instead. The Voxel Occupancy Test is a fundamental operation in voxel-based graphics and simulation, often implemented as a method on voxel grid data structures. It is commonly used in point cloud processing, physics simulations, and spatial queries. The method checkifincluded is explicitly documented in the Open3D library. The concept of simple grid checks for collision is also noted in the context of voxel game engines. name: Point-in-Box Inclusion Test
head: Point Array Box Partitioning, annBoxSplit
body: The Point-in-Box Inclusion Test determines which points from a given array lie within an orthogonal bounding box. It serves as the core primitive for Voxel Occupancy Test, filtering points to identify voxel occupancy. Unlike 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation which uses distance metrics, this method relies on strict axis-aligned boundary checks. It differs from Sparse AABB Collision Test by operating on a static point array rather than dynamic collision shapes. Inputs: PP: An array of n points, where each point has 3 coordinates (x, y, z). box: An orthogonal bounding box defined by minimum bounds min and maximum bounds max for each dimension d \in \{x, y, z\}. Outputs: nin: The count of points inside or on the boundary of the box. The input array PP is partitioned such that the first nin points are inside, and the remaining are outside. Data Structures: PP: Array of points. box: Struct with fields min and max, each being a 3D vector. Algorithm: 1. Initialize two indices: l = 0 (left) and r = n - 1 (right). 2. Loop while l < n and r >= 0: a. Increment l while l < n and point PP[l] is inside the box on all dimensions. b. Decrement r while r >= 0 and point PP[r] is NOT inside the box on all dimensions. c. If l > r, break the loop. d. Swap PP[l] and PP[r]. e. Increment l and decrement r. 3. Set nin = l. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointinboxinclusiontest(PP, box): n = len(PP) l = 0 r = n - 1 while l < n and r >= 0: # Move l forward while points are inside while l < n and boxinside(box, PP[l]): l += 1 # Move r backward while points are outside while r >= 0 and not boxinside(box, PP[r]): r -= 1 # If pointers crossed, we are done if l > r: break # Swap the outside point at l with the outside point at r # (Actually, l is outside, r is outside? No: l stopped at outside, r stopped at inside? # Let's re-read S1 carefully: "while l < n and box.inside(dim, PP(l)), l++" -> l stops at first OUTSIDE. # "while r >= 0 and !box.inside(dim, PP(r)), r--" -> r stops at first INSIDE. # So we swap an OUTSIDE (at l) with an INSIDE (at r). swap(PP, l, r) l += 1 r -= 1 return l Helper boxinside: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boxinside(box, point): for dim in ['x', 'y', 'z']: if point[dim] < box.min[dim] or point[dim] > box.max[dim]: return False return True Edge Cases: Points exactly on the boundary are considered inside (inclusive check). Empty point array (n=0) returns 0. Finds the spatial dimension with the largest spread among all dimensions in a point set before partitioning. This heuristic aims to optimize the partitioning order or selection for subsequent operations by identifying the axis of maximum variance. Time Complexity: O(n) in the worst case, as each point is visited at most once by the two pointers. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if performed in-place. Strengths: Simple, fast, and cache-friendly due to linear scan. Limitations: Does not sort points, only partitions. Performance degrades if the box is very small or very large relative to the point distribution, though the linear scan remains constant time. Originated in the context of 3D reconstruction and dual contouring implementations, specifically within the DualContouring-3DRendring project. It is used to efficiently filter surfels or points against voxel boundaries during mesh generation. bouguerra-khalil/DualContouring-3DRendring, https://github.com/bouguerra-khalil/DualContouring-3DRendring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation
head: 3D Binary Sphere Kernel, 3D Radial Mask Generation
body: This method generates a 3D binary kernel (mask) where voxels within a specified Euclidean distance from the center are set to 1, and others are set to 0. It solves the problem of defining a discrete spherical occupancy region for voxel-based operations, such as smoothing, collision detection, or volume initialization. It differs from its sibling Point-in-Box Inclusion Test by using radial distance rather than axis-aligned bounds, and from its sibling Voxel Filled Check by generating a full kernel array rather than testing a single point. Inputs: size: Integer dimension of the cubic kernel (e.g., 3 for a 3x3x3 grid). radius: Float radius defining the sphere boundary. Outputs: kernel: A 3D array of shape (size, size, size) with dtype boolean or integer (0/1). Data Structures: The kernel is stored as a dense 3D array. Coordinates are indexed from 0 to size-1. Steps: 1. Define the coordinate range: Create a 1D linear space of integers from -(size // 2) to size // 2. Let this array be L. 2. Generate meshgrid: Create a 3D meshgrid from L for axes x, y, z. This produces three 3D arrays X, Y, Z of shape (size, size, size), where each element represents the coordinate offset from the center. 3. Compute radial distance: Calculate the Euclidean distance d from the center for each voxel: d = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2} 4. Apply threshold: Set the kernel value to 1 where d \le \text{radius}, and 0 otherwise. 5. Zero the center: Explicitly set the center element (where X=0, Y=0, Z=0) to 0. Parameters: size: Default 3. radius: Default 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generate3dfilledcirclekernel(size: int = 3, radius: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray: # 1. Create linear space from -(size//2) to size//2 half = size // 2 coords = np.arange(-half, half + 1) # 2. Generate 3D meshgrid of coordinates X, Y, Z = np.meshgrid(coords, coords, coords, indexing='ij') # 3. Compute radial distance d from center d = np.sqrt(X2 + Y2 + Z2) # 4. Set kernel to 1 where d <= radius, else 0 kernel = (d <= radius).astype(np.float32) # 5. Set center element to 0 centeridx = half kernel[centeridx, centeridx, centeridx] = 0.0 return kernel Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Center Exclusion: The center voxel is explicitly forced to 0, even if the radius is large enough to include it. This is a specific requirement of this method. Boundary Precision: The condition d \le \text{radius} includes voxels exactly on the boundary. Floating-point precision errors in distance calculation may cause slight variations in boundary voxels across implementations. Odd vs Even Sizes: The coordinate range -(size//2) to size//2 assumes an odd-sized kernel for perfect symmetry around the origin. For even sizes, the center is offset, which may affect symmetry. Sphere Carving removes solid voxels within a spherical radius from a center point in a voxel chunk, primarily used for destructible terrain scenarios. It differs from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by operating directly on the chunk data to modify state (removing voxels) rather than generating a static binary kernel, and from its sibling 3D Binary Sphere Kernel Generation by returning a count of removed elements rather than a mask. This method procedurally generates a 3D binary scalar field (density texture) representing a sphere centered at the origin of a voxel grid, specifically designed as input for GPU-based Marching Cubes surface extraction. Unlike static voxelization, this implementation features a time-varying radius that oscillates, creating a dynamic volume. It differs from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by explicitly targeting the DensityTexture property of a Marching Cubes component and utilizing a specific oscillating radius formula rather than a static threshold. Generates a 3D Gaussian kernel for smoothing operations, with the center element set to zero. Steps: 1. Create linear space from -(size//2) to size//2. 2. Generate 3D meshgrid of coordinates. 3. Compute radial distance d from center. 4. Compute Gaussian values: \exp(-d^2 / (2\sigma^2)). 5. Set center element to 0. 6. Normalize by sum of all elements. Parameters: size (default 3), sigma (default 1.0). Deterministic generation of cell write sets for box and sphere shapes, emitting writes in canonical (z, y, x) order. The sphere brush uses spallcore's fixed-point containscellcentre predicate over the shape's cell bounding box to determine included cells. Pitfalls: The write set and order are byte-stable, guarded by pinned BLAKE3 digests and confirmed by a brute-force reference over a wider box. Both brushes are verified to touch exactly eight bricks when centred on the corner where eight bricks meet. A cell centre exactly on the sphere radius is included in the write set. Time Complexity: O(N^3) where N is the kernel size, as every voxel must be visited to compute distance and apply the threshold. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) to store the kernel array. Performance: For small kernels (e.g., 3x3x3, 5x5x5), computation is negligible. For large kernels, the square root operation in distance calculation can be optimized by comparing squared distances (d^2 \le \text{radius}^2) to avoid expensive sqrt calls. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and easy to implement. Provides a clear binary representation of a spherical region. Limitations: The explicit zeroing of the center voxel makes it unsuitable for applications requiring a continuous or non-zero center contribution (e.g., standard convolution kernels). The binary nature does not provide partial occupancy information. This method is commonly used in voxel-based graphics and simulation for defining spherical regions of influence, such as in destructible environments or smoothing filters. The specific variant with center-zeroing is documented in the Plenoxels repository. The deterministic integer brush variant is part of the spall project's fixture and brush system.
