name: 3D Gaussian Kernel Generation
head: 3D Gaussian Smoothing Kernel, Zero-Centered Gaussian Kernel
body: Generates a 3D Gaussian kernel for smoothing operations, with the center element set to zero. It differs from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by using continuous weighted values based on a Gaussian probability density function rather than a binary occupancy mask. It is distinct from Sphere Carving and 3D Binary Sphere Kernel Generation which produce hard-edged spherical masks. Inputs: size: Integer kernel dimension (assumed cubic). Default: 3. sigma: Float standard deviation. Default: 1.0. Outputs: A 3D tensor of shape (size, size, size) containing normalized Gaussian weights with the center element explicitly set to 0. Data Structures: 3D array/tensor of floating-point numbers. Steps: 1. Define a linear coordinate space ranging from -\lfloor \text{size}/2 \rfloor to \lfloor \text{size}/2 \rfloor. 2. Generate a 3D meshgrid of coordinates (x, y, z) from this space. 3. Compute the radial distance d from the center for each element: d = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}. 4. Compute raw Gaussian values: w = \exp\left(-\frac{d^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). 5. Set the center element (where x=y=z=0) to 0. 6. Normalize the kernel by dividing all elements by the sum of all elements. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generate3dgaussiankernel(size: int = 3, sigma: float = 1.0) -> list: """ Generates a 3D Gaussian kernel with the center element set to 0. """ halfsize = size // 2 # Step 1: Create linear space from -(size//2) to size//2 coords = list(range(-halfsize, halfsize + 1)) # Step 2: Generate 3D meshgrid kernel = [] for x in coords: row = [] for y in coords: col = [] for z in coords: # Step 3: Compute radial distance d from center dsq = xx + yy + zz # Step 4: Compute Gaussian values if dsq == 0: # Step 5: Set center element to 0 val = 0.0 else: val = math.exp(-dsq / (2 sigma sigma)) col.append(val) row.append(col) kernel.append(row) # Step 6: Normalize by sum of all elements totalsum = sum(sum(sum(row) for row in kernelslice) for kernelslice in kernel) if totalsum == 0: # Edge case: if sigma is extremely small or size is 1, sum might be 0 # Return zeros to avoid division by zero return [[[0.0 for in range(size)] for in range(size)] for in range(size)] for xidx in range(size): for yidx in range(size): for zidx in range(size): kernel[xidx][yidx][zidx] /= totalsum return kernel Parameters: size: Kernel dimension. Default is 3. sigma: Standard deviation of Gaussian. Default is 1.0. Edge Cases: If size is 1, the center is the only element, set to 0, sum is 0, resulting in a zero kernel. Precision issues may arise if sigma is very small relative to size, causing underflow in exp for non-center elements. Time Complexity: O(\text{size}^3) to compute all elements. Memory Complexity: O(\text{size}^3) to store the kernel. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides smooth weighting. Limitations: The explicit zeroing of the center element is non-standard for Gaussian kernels and may introduce bias in smoothing operations. When to use: When a specific implementation requires a zero-centered Gaussian weight distribution as defined in the source. Originated in the context of the Plenoxels project, specifically within the DanJbk/Plenoxels repository. The method is described in an unofficial GitHub repository context. name: Elliptical Gaussian Light Source Generation
head: Poisson Disk Light Sampling
body: Generates spatially distributed light sources using either Poisson disk or uniform sampling, then constructs a luminance field by evaluating scaled multivariate Gaussian PDFs at query points. It differs from its parent 3D Gaussian Kernel Generation by focusing on the placement and covariance orientation of multiple distinct sources rather than a single smoothing kernel with a zeroed center. Inputs: lstype: String, either 'poisson' or 'uniform'. numsources: Integer, number of light sources to generate. seed: Integer, random seed. querypoints: Array of shape (N, 3), points at which to evaluate the luminance. Outputs: luminance: Array of shape (N,), the evaluated luminance values at querypoints. Data Structures: sourcelocs: Array of shape (numsources, 3), coordinates of light source centers. covs: Array of shape (numsources, 3, 3), covariance matrices for each source. Us: Array of shape (numsources, 3, 3), precomputed transformation matrices for efficient PDF evaluation. logdets: Array of shape (numsources,), log-determinants of the covariance matrices. Steps: 1. Sample Source Locations: If lstype == 'poisson': Initialize random number generator with seed. Create a Poisson disk sampler with dimension d=3, radius r=0.13, and the initialized RNG. Sample numsources points from the unit cube [0,1]^3. If lstype == 'uniform': Initialize JAX PRNGKey with seed. Sample points uniformly in [0,1]^3 until numsources are collected. Stack the first numsources points. 2. Generate Covariances: Define base covariance matrix C{base}: C{base} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \times 10^{-3} Rotate C{base} for each source to create covs. The rotation is determined by the seed and numsources using a helper function rotatecov. This results in covs of shape (numsources, 3, 3). 3. Initialize Light Source Object: Pass sourcelocs and covs to the LightSourcesCov class. Inside init: Compute eigenvalues \lambdai and eigenvectors vi of each covariance matrix in covs using symmetric eigendecomposition: \text{vals}, \text{vecs} = \text{eigh}(\text{covs}) where vals has shape (numsources, 3) and vecs has shape (numsources, 3, 3). Compute inverse square roots of eigenvalues: \text{valsinvs}i = \frac{1}{\lambdai} Compute transformation matrices Ui for each source: Ui = Vi \cdot \text{diag}(\sqrt{\text{valsinvs}i}) In code, this is implemented as self.Us = vecs jnp.sqrt(valsinvs)[:, None]. Compute log-determinants: \log \det(Ci) = \sum{j=1}^{3} \log(\lambda{i,j}) Stored in self.logdets. 4. Evaluate Luminance: For each query point x, compute the luminance contribution from all sources. The multivariate Gaussian PDF for source i is: \mathcal{N}(x; \mui, Ci) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^3 \det(Ci)}} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (x - \mui)^T Ci^{-1} (x - \mui) \right) Using the precomputed Ui where Ci^{-1} = Ui^T Ui, the exponent becomes: -\frac{1}{2} \| Ui (x - \mui) \|^2 Sum contributions from all sources (or select based on application logic, e.g., nearest neighbor or all). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp import jax.random as random from jax import lax def rotatecov(cov, numsources, seed): """ Generates rotated covariance matrices for numsources sources. Implementation detail: Not given in the sources. Assumes a standard rotation generation method using the seed. """ # Placeholder for actual rotation logic # Typically involves generating random rotation matrices and applying them # to the base covariance. raise NotImplementedError("rotatecov implementation not provided in source") class LightSourcesCov: def init(self, sourcelocs, covs): self.sourcelocs = sourcelocs self.covs = covs # Eigen decomposition vals, vecs = jnp.linalg.eigh(self.covs) # Inverse square roots of eigenvalues valsinvs = 1.0 / vals # Compute Us: vecs sqrt(valsinvs)[:, None] # vals shape: (numsources, 3) # vecs shape: (numsources, 3, 3) # valsinvs shape: (numsources, 3) # sqrt(valsinvs)[:, None] shape: (numsources, 3, 1) self.Us = vecs jnp.sqrt(valsinvs)[:, None] # Log determinants self.logdets = jnp.sum(jnp.log(vals), axis=1) def evaluate(self, querypoints): """ Evaluate luminance at querypoints. querypoints shape: (N, 3) Returns: (N,) """ # sourcelocs shape: (numsources, 3) # Us shape: (numsources, 3, 3) # logdets shape: (numsources,) # Calculate differences: (N, 1, 3) - (1, numsources, 3) -> (N, numsources, 3) diffs = querypoints[:, None,:] - self.sourcelocs[None,:,:] # Transform differences: (N, numsources, 3) @ (numsources, 3, 3)^T # Note: Us[i] is such that Ci^{-1} = Us[i]^T @ Us[i] # So we want (x - mu)^T C^{-1} (x - mu) = || Us @ (x - mu) ||^2 # Transformed diffs: (N, numsources, 3) transformed = jnp.einsum('ijk,ijk->ij', diffs, jnp.einsum('ijk,ikl->ijl', self.Us, diffs)) # Exponent: -0.5 sum(transformed^2) ? # Actually, transformed above is already the dot product if we did it right. # Let's re-verify: # y = Us @ diff -> (N, numsources, 3) # normsq = sum(y^2, axis=-1) -> (N, numsources) y = jnp.einsum('ijk,ilk->ijl', self.Us, diffs) # (N, numsources, 3) normsq = jnp.sum(y2, axis=-1) # (N, numsources) # PDF normalization constant: 1 / sqrt((2pi)^3 det(C)) # lognorm = -1.5 log(2pi) - 0.5 log(det(C)) lognorm = -1.5 jnp.log(2 jnp.pi) - 0.5 self.logdets # (numsources,) # Log PDF: -0.5 normsq + lognorm logpdf = -0.5 normsq + lognorm # (N, numsources) # Sum over sources (assuming additive luminance) # Use log-sum-exp for numerical stability if needed, but simple sum is fine if values are small pdf = jnp.exp(logpdf) # (N, numsources) luminance = jnp.sum(pdf, axis=1) # (N,) return luminance def generatelightsources(lstype, numsources, seed, querypoints): if lstype == 'poisson': # Initialize RNG rng = random.PRNGKey(seed) # Note: qmc.PoissonDisk is not standard JAX. # Assuming a wrapper or external library. # For pure JAX implementation, this step is not directly available. # Placeholder for Poisson Disk sampling logic. sourcelocs = None # Placeholder elif lstype == 'uniform': rng = random.PRNGKey(seed) # Sample until numsources are collected # Standard rejection sampling or direct sampling from uniform distribution # Since we just need numsources points in [0,1]^3: sourcelocs = random.uniform(rng, shape=(numsources, 3), minval=0.0, maxval=1.0) else: raise ValueError("lstype must be 'poisson' or 'uniform'") # Base covariance covbase = jnp.array([[[2, 0, 0], [0, 0.5, 0], [0, 0, 0.5]]]) 1e-3 # Rotate covariances covs = rotatecov(covbase, numsources, seed) # Initialize Light Source Object lightsources = LightSourcesCov(sourcelocs, covs) # Evaluate luminance = lightsources.evaluate(querypoints) return luminance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Eigenvalue decomposition of near-singular covariance matrices can be unstable. The base covariance is well-conditioned, but rotated versions should be checked. Boundaries: Poisson disk sampling in a bounded cube may result in fewer points if the radius is large relative to the domain. The source code samples 1000 points for Poisson, implying a fixed size or a rejection-based approach that might not yield exactly numsources if not handled carefully. The uniform case explicitly stacks the first numsources. Degenerate Input: If numsources is 0, the method should return an empty array or zero luminance. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S \cdot d^2) for evaluation, where N is the number of query points, S is the number of sources, and d=3 is the dimension. Eigen decomposition is O(S \cdot d^3). Memory Complexity: O(S \cdot d^2) to store covariances and precomputed matrices. Strengths: Poisson disk sampling provides more uniform spatial distribution than uniform sampling, reducing clustering artifacts. Precomputing U and log-determinants speeds up repeated evaluations. Limitations: Evaluation cost scales linearly with the number of sources. For large S, this can be expensive. When to use: When a smooth, spatially distributed light field is needed, and uniformity of source placement is important. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and S is large, or when sources are highly clustered (use a different sampling strategy). Originated in the context of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and volume rendering optimization, specifically in the rtnf repository. It is used to generate initial light source distributions for training neural networks to represent light fields. brandonyzhao/rtnf, https://github.com/brandonyzhao/rtnf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Sphere Carving
head: Carve Sphere, Voxel Sphere Removal
body: Sphere Carving removes solid voxels within a spherical radius from a center point in a voxel chunk, primarily used for destructible terrain scenarios. It differs from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by operating directly on the chunk data to modify state (removing voxels) rather than generating a static binary kernel, and from its sibling 3D Binary Sphere Kernel Generation by returning a count of removed elements rather than a mask. Inputs: chunk: The voxel chunk data structure to modify. cx, cy, cz: The center coordinates of the sphere. radius: The radius of the sphere to carve. Outputs: The modified chunk with voxels set to 0 (air) inside the sphere. An integer count of the number of solid voxels removed. Data Structures: The chunk is assumed to be a 3D array or linear buffer indexed by (x, y, z). The specific internal layout (e.g., row-major vs column-major) is not specified in the sources, but access is via chunk.get(x, y, z) and chunk.set(x, y, z, value). A value of 0 represents air/empty space; any non-zero value represents solid material. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate the squared radius: r2 = \text{radius} \times \text{radius}. 2. Determine the bounding box of the sphere within the chunk boundaries for each axis v \in \{x, y, z\}: Lower bound: \text{lo}(v) = \max(0, \lfloor v - \text{radius} \rfloor). Upper bound: \text{hi}(v) = \min(\text{chunk.size} - 1, \lceil v + \text{radius} \rceil). 3. Initialize a counter removedcount to 0. 4. Iterate through the bounding box: For z from \text{lo}(cz) to \text{hi}(cz): For y from \text{lo}(cy) to \text{hi}(cy): For x from \text{lo}(cx) to \text{hi}(cx): Calculate the squared distance from the center: d2 = (x - cx)^2 + (y - cy)^2 + (z - cz)^2. If d2 > r2, continue to the next voxel. If chunk.get(x, y, z) is not 0: Increment removedcount. Set chunk.set(x, y, z, 0). 5. Return removedcount. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spherecarving(chunk, cx, cy, cz, radius): r2 = radius radius removedcount = 0 # Calculate bounds for each axis lox = max(0, math.floor(cx - radius)) hix = min(chunk.size - 1, math.ceil(cx + radius)) loy = max(0, math.floor(cy - radius)) hiy = min(chunk.size - 1, math.ceil(cy + radius)) loz = max(0, math.floor(cz - radius)) hiz = min(chunk.size - 1, math.ceil(cz + radius)) for z in range(loz, hiz + 1): dz = z - cz dz2 = dz dz for y in range(loy, hiy + 1): dy = y - cy dy2 = dy dy for x in range(lox, hix + 1): dx = x - cx d2 = dxdx + dy2 + dz2 if d2 > r2: continue if chunk.get(x, y, z) != 0: removedcount += 1 chunk.set(x, y, z, 0) return removedcount Parameters: radius: The radius of the carving sphere. cx, cy, cz: Center coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Clamping: The bounds must be clamped to the chunk dimensions to prevent out-of-bounds access. Degenerate Input: A radius of 0 results in checking only the exact center voxel. If the center is solid, it is removed; otherwise, nothing changes. Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff modifies scalar voxel values within a spherical region around a 3D hit point to add or remove terrain mass, enabling real-time digging and building operations. It sets itself apart from its parent Sphere Carving by using a continuous soft falloff function to create smooth edges rather than binary inclusion/exclusion, and by supporting additive (build) as well as subtractive (dig) operations. Generating a bounding volume as a union of ellipsoids by replacing the convex hull generation step with minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid generation on the point set P. The signed distance function for an ellipsoid E is defined as d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{E}) = a (\|\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c})\| - 1), where \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{D}(1/a, 1/b, 1/c) \mathbf{R}^t. This function is 1-Lipschitz (conservative). Evaluation requires approximately 4 scalar products and one square root. Ellipsoids are more compact in memory and computationally more efficient than convex polyhedra (which require n scalar products for n faces), though potentially more conservative depending on axis lengths. Four brush operations (Place, Carve, Fill, Paint) are applied over a world-space spherical radius on an unbounded voxel grid. Voxels are addressed using unbounded world-grid coordinates rather than chunk-local indices to ensure consistent behavior across chunk boundaries. Edits are accumulated into a stroke across frames, and a single VoxelEditCommand is pushed on release. The brush radius defines the spherical area of influence for the edit operations. Time Complexity: O(r^3) where r is the radius, as it iterates over the bounding box of the sphere. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, modifying the chunk in place. Performance: The use of squared distance comparisons avoids expensive square root operations. Strengths: Suitable for real-time destructible terrain scenarios. Limitations: Produces a hard spherical boundary due to binary voxel removal. Performance degrades with very large radii due to the cubic growth of the bounding box volume. Sphere Carving is a fundamental operation in voxel-based game engines and simulations, particularly for destructible environments. It is often used in conjunction with voxelization and geometry processing pipelines. m2-md/voxel-greedy-meshing-typescript, https://github.com/m2-md/voxel-greedy-meshing-typescript, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Sphere Carving: Bounding Volumes for Signed Distance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3730845, fetched 2026-10-27 feat(terrain): DDA voxel raycast + editing brushes with undo/redo, https://github.com/drsnuggles8/OloEngineBase/pull/973, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff
head: Spherical Voxel Deformation, Voxel Falloff Modification
body: Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff modifies scalar voxel values within a spherical region around a 3D hit point to add or remove terrain mass, enabling real-time digging and building operations. It sets itself apart from its parent Sphere Carving by using a continuous soft falloff function to create smooth edges rather than binary inclusion/exclusion, and by supporting additive (build) as well as subtractive (dig) operations. Inputs: playerCamera: Camera object providing position and forward direction. hitPoint: World position where the deformation occurs, obtained via raycast. radius: Brush radius in meters. deformSpeed (S1) or digSpeed/buildSpeed (S2): Rate of density change per second at the center of the brush. buildModifier: Integer 1 for adding mass, -1 for removing mass. voxelSize: Size of one voxel in meters. densityField: Array of scalar values representing the terrain. chunkSize: Size of a terrain chunk in voxels. Outputs: Updated densityField values within the affected region. List of "dirty" chunks marked for re-meshing. Data Structures: Density Field: A 3D grid of scalar values. In, values are 8-bit unsigned integers (byte) in range [0, 255], where 0 is air and 255 is solid rock. In, values are float in range [0, 1]. Chunk: A sub-volume of the world defined by chunkSize. Each chunk manages its own mesh and collision data. Bounds: Axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in voxel coordinates defining the region to iterate. Steps: 1. Raycast: Cast a ray from playerCamera.position along playerCamera.forward with a maximum distance maxReachDistance (or range). If no hit is detected, abort. 2. Hit Point Adjustment (Build Only): If the operation is a build, offset the hit point slightly into the surface to ensure new material attaches correctly: hitPoint -= rayDirection radius 0.3f. 3. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the world-space hitPoint to local voxel coordinates: local = (hitPoint - worldOrigin) / voxelSize. (Note: assumes direct conversion to integer voxel coordinates (hitX, hitY, hitZ)). 4. Bounding Box Calculation: Calculate the integer bounding box of the sphere in voxel coordinates: minX = Floor(local.x - radiusvoxels), maxX = Ceil(local.x + radiusvoxels), etc., clamped to the world boundaries. uses intRange = ceil(deformRange) and defines bounds as [hitX - intRange, hitX + intRange] etc. 5. Chunk Identification: Identify all chunks that overlap with this bounding box. Mark them as "dirty". 6. Voxel Iteration: Iterate over all voxels (x, y, z) within the bounding box. specifies skipping border voxels if they are outside the world or protected. 7. Distance Calculation: For each voxel, calculate the Euclidean distance d from the voxel center to the brush center local: d = sqrt((x - local.x)^2 + (y - local.y)^2 + (z - local.z)^2). 8. Falloff Calculation: uses an inverse distance falloff: modificationAmount = deformSpeed / d buildModifier. uses a SmoothStep falloff: falloff = SmoothStep(1, 0, dist / radiusvoxels). 9. Density Update: (Byte-based): vnew = clamp((vold / 255 - modificationAmount) 255, 0, 255). (Float-based): density[i] = Clamp01(density[i] + delta falloff), where delta = speed deltaTime. 10. Re-meshing: In LateUpdate, iterate over all "dirty" chunks and call Rebuild() on each, then clear the dirty set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raycast(origin, direction, maxdistance): """Stub for physics raycast; returns hit dict with 'point' or None.""" # Implementation depends on engine; returns hit or None pass def getchunkid(x, y, z, chunksize): """Returns chunk coordinates for a given voxel.""" return (x // chunksize, y // chunksize, z // chunksize) def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): """Standard smooth interpolation.""" t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def deformvoxelterrain(camera, terrain, radius, speed, isbuild, deltatime): # 1. Raycast rayorigin = camera.position raydirection = camera.forward hit = raycast(rayorigin, raydirection, terrain.maxreach) if hit is None: return hitpoint = hit.point # 2. Adjust hit point for build if isbuild: hitpoint = hitpoint - raydirection radius 0.3 # 3. Convert to voxel coordinates localcenter = (hitpoint - terrain.origin) / terrain.voxelsize # 4. Calculate bounding box (convert radius to voxel units for scale consistency) radiusvoxels = radius / terrain.voxelsize minx = int(math.floor(localcenter.x - radiusvoxels)) maxx = int(math.ceil(localcenter.x + radiusvoxels)) miny = int(math.floor(localcenter.y - radiusvoxels)) maxy = int(math.ceil(localcenter.y + radiusvoxels)) minz = int(math.floor(localcenter.z - radiusvoxels)) maxz = int(math.ceil(localcenter.z + radiusvoxels)) # Clamp to world bounds minx = max(minx, 0); maxx = min(maxx, terrain.width - 1) miny = max(miny, 0); maxy = min(maxy, terrain.height - 1) minz = max(minz, 0); maxz = min(maxz, terrain.depth - 1) # 5. Identify and mark dirty chunks dirtychunks = set() for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): dirtychunks.add(getchunkid(x, y, z, terrain.chunksize)) # 6. Iterate voxels and update for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): dx = x - localcenter.x dy = y - localcenter.y dz = z - localcenter.z dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Skip if outside radius if dist > radiusvoxels: continue # Calculate falloff (SmoothStep variant) falloff = smoothstep(1.0, 0.0, dist / radiusvoxels) # Calculate delta delta = speed deltatime falloff modifier = 1.0 if isbuild else -1.0 # Get old value oldval = terrain.densityfield[x, y, z] # Update value newval = oldval + delta modifier # Clamp to [0.0, 1.0] terrain.densityfield[x, y, z] = max(0.0, min(1.0, newval)) # 7. Mark chunks dirty for chunkid in dirtychunks: terrain.markchunkdirty(chunkid) def lateupdateterrain(terrain): dirtychunks = terrain.getdirtychunks() for chunkid in dirtychunks: terrain.rebuildchunk(chunkid) terrain.cleardirtychunks() Parameters: radius: Brush radius in meters. Typical value: 2.5f. Range: 1f to 6f. digSpeed: Density removed per second at the center. Typical value: 4f. buildSpeed: Density added per second at the center. Typical value: 3f. smoothSpeed: Smoothing speed. Typical value: 6f. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If the raycast hit point exactly matches a voxel center, distance becomes 0, causing infinite modificationAmount in inverse-distance falloff. A guard such as if dist == 0: dist = 1e-6 is required. Precision: Using byte values (0-255) as in can lead to quantization artifacts compared to float (0-1) as in. Boundary Conditions: Voxels at the world boundary must be clamped to prevent out-of-bounds array access. Scale Mismatch: The brush radius is provided in meters, but bounding box calculations require voxel units; failing to divide by voxelSize will produce incorrect deformation volumes. A variant that locally blurs the density field within a spherical region to round off jagged edges created by deformation. It differs from standard deformation by averaging density values with neighbors rather than adding/removing mass. Definition: Locally blurs the density field within a spherical region to round off jagged edges, using a snapshot of the field to ensure consistent averaging. Steps: 1. Calculate the bounding box of the brush area, expanded by 1 voxel in all directions to include neighbors: sMinX = Max(minX - 1, 0), sMaxX = Min(maxX + 1, pointCount.x - 1), etc.. 2. Create a snapshot array of the expanded region and copy the current density values into it. 3. Iterate through the original brush bounding box (not the expanded one). Skip border voxels and voxels outside the radius. 4. Calculate the average density from the snapshot using the voxel and its 6 neighbors, clamping coordinates to the snapshot bounds: average = (Snap(x,y,z) + Snap(x+1,y,z) + Snap(x-1,y,z) + Snap(x,y+1,z) + Snap(x,y-1,z) + Snap(x,y,z+1) + Snap(x,y,z-1)) / 7.0f. 5. Calculate the falloff factor: falloff = SmoothStep(1, 0, dist / r) strength. 6. Interpolate the density towards the average: density[i] = Lerp(density[i], average, falloff). When to choose: Use after digging or building to smooth out stair-stepping artifacts and create natural-looking terrain transitions. Time Complexity: O(R^3) per deformation call, where R is deformRange in voxel units, due to iterating over the full bounding box of the spherical region. Memory Complexity: O(R^3) for the bounding box iteration. The Local Area Smoothing Brush variant requires an additional O((R+1)^3) memory for the snapshot array. Measured Performance: Real-time deformation is achieved using three brushes (Dig, Build, Smooth) with soft spherical falloffs. Performance scales with the cube of the brush radius. Strengths: Smooth edges via falloff functions; supports both addition and subtraction; real-time capable. Limitations: O(R^3) complexity can be expensive for large brushes; inverse-distance falloff requires division-by-zero guards. When to use: Destructible terrain scenarios requiring smooth, natural-looking modifications. When not to use: When strict binary voxel occupancy is required (use Sphere Carving instead). Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff is used in real-time voxel terrain editors and games, particularly those utilizing Marching Cubes for mesh generation. It builds on Sphere Carving by adding continuous density modification. The method is implemented in Unity-based voxel terrain projects such as Eldemarkki/Marching-Cubes-Terrain and Rabidus4k/UnityVoxelTerrain. name: 3D Binary Sphere Kernel Generation
head: Sphere Volume Generation for Marching Cubes
body: This method procedurally generates a 3D binary scalar field (density texture) representing a sphere centered at the origin of a voxel grid, specifically designed as input for GPU-based Marching Cubes surface extraction. Unlike static voxelization, this implementation features a time-varying radius that oscillates, creating a dynamic volume. It differs from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by explicitly targeting the DensityTexture property of a Marching Cubes component and utilizing a specific oscillating radius formula rather than a static threshold. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Resolution (integer, dimension of the cubic grid), Time.time (float, current simulation time). Output: A 3D texture densityTexture of size Resolution x Resolution x Resolution with format RFloat (single-channel float), and a 1D array colors of size Resolution^3 storing the density values in the red channel. Data Structures: colors: 1D array of size N^3 (where N = \text{Resolution}). Each element is a color/vector with a red channel r storing the binary density (0 or 1). densityTexture: 3D texture, dimensions N \times N \times N, format RFloat, wrap mode Clamp. Parameters: Resolution: Grid dimension. Typical values depend on desired surface smoothness; higher resolutions reduce aliasing but increase memory. Time.time: Continuous time variable. Steps: 1. Initialize colors array of size N^3 with white values (or zero-initialized, as only the red channel is used). 2. Calculate the current radius resol using the oscillating formula: \text{resol} = \frac{N - 2}{2} \times \sin(0.25 \times \text{Time.time}) The radius oscillates between 0 and \frac{N-2}{2}. 3. Iterate through all voxel indices idx from 0 to N^3 - 1. This is typically done using nested loops for z, y, and x: \text{idx} = z \cdot N^2 + y \cdot N + x 4. For each voxel (x, y, z), compute normalized coordinates relative to the center of the volume: sx = x - \frac{N}{2} sy = y - \frac{N}{2} sz = z - \frac{N}{2} 5. Determine the density value amount by checking if the squared Euclidean distance from the center is less than or equal to the squared radius: \text{amount} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } sx^2 + sy^2 + sz^2 \le \text{resol}^2 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 6. Store the density value in the red channel of the color array: \text{colors}[\text{idx}].r = \text{amount} 7. Upload the computed colors array to the 3D texture densityTexture using SetPixels and Apply (or equivalent GPU upload mechanism). 8. Assign densityTexture to the Marching Cubes component's DensityTexture property. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatespherekernel(Resolution, Timetime): N = Resolution numvoxels = N N N # Initialize colors array (R, G, B, A) # Only R channel is used for density colors = [Vector4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) for in range(numvoxels)] # Calculate oscillating radius # Radius oscillates between 0 and (N-2)/2 resol = ((N - 2) / 2.0) math.sin(0.25 Timetime) resolsq = resol resol center = N / 2.0 for z in range(N): for y in range(N): for x in range(N): idx = z N N + y N + x # Normalized coordinates relative to center sx = x - center sy = y - center sz = z - center # Squared distance from center distsq = sxsx + sysy + szsz # Binary density: 1 if inside sphere, 0 otherwise if distsq <= resolsq: colors[idx].r = 1.0 else: colors[idx].r = 0.0 # Upload to 3D texture # densityTexture.SetPixels(colors) # densityTexture.Apply() # marchingcubescomponent.DensityTexture = densityTexture return colors Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The comparison distsq <= resolsq is sensitive to floating-point precision. For very large resolutions or small radii, this may cause aliasing or incorrect boundary voxels. Boundary Conditions: The radius formula uses (N-2)/2, leaving a 1-voxel border around the sphere. This ensures the sphere never touches the grid boundaries, which might be important for certain marching cubes implementations that assume a buffer. Time Variation: If Time.time is not continuous or resets, the sphere will jump. Ensure Time.time is a monotonically increasing value. Zero Radius: When sin(0.25 Time.time) == 0, the radius is 0, and the entire volume is empty (all zeros). A method that subtracts a sphere from an existing volume. Choose this when you need to hollow out a region rather than generate a solid sphere. Sphere Carving Time Complexity: O(N^3), where N is the resolution. Every voxel is visited once. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the colors array and the 3D texture. Performance: The method is computationally lightweight per voxel (simple arithmetic and comparison). However, uploading the texture to the GPU every frame can be a bottleneck if done naively. Using a compute shader or persistent mapped memory can improve performance. Strengths: Simple to implement, produces a smooth sphere for Marching Cubes, dynamic radius. Limitations: Binary field may lead to aliasing artifacts in the extracted mesh if the resolution is too low. The oscillating radius is specific to this implementation and may not be suitable for static scenes. When to use: When a dynamic, procedurally generated sphere is needed for Marching Cubes surface extraction, and the oscillating behavior is desired. When not to use: For static spheres (use a static kernel), or when higher-order interpolation is needed (use a signed distance field). This method originates from an unofficial Unity-based implementation of GPU Marching Cubes by Pavel Kouril. It is designed to demonstrate procedural geometry generation within the Unity engine, leveraging the Marching Cubes component's ability to accept a DensityTexture. The oscillating radius is a visual effect to demonstrate the dynamic nature of the volume. pavelkouril/unity-marching-cubes-gpu, https://github.com/pavelkouril/unity-marching-cubes-gpu, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Material Palette Generation
body: This method generates a compact lookup table (palette) that maps discrete voxel values (1–255) to physically-based rendering (PBR) material definitions for each of the six voxel faces. It solves the problem of efficiently storing and accessing per-face material properties by packing material layer indices and flags into a single 2D texture atlas and a corresponding 3D palette array. It differs from per-voxel material instances by batching materials into atlases, thereby reducing memory overhead and draw calls. Inputs: materials: A dictionary mapping string voxel values ("1" to "255") to a list of material names for the 6 faces. materialdefinitions: A source (e.g., JSON) providing PBR texture paths and boolean flags (isopaque, hascolor, etc.) for each material name. atlaswidth, atlasheight: Dimensions of the output texture atlas in pixels. res: Resolution of each material tile in the atlas. Typical value: 512. Outputs: palette: A 3D NumPy array of shape (256, 6, 3) with type np.uint8. coloratlas, emissionatlas, normalatlas, rsmaatlas: 2D texture arrays containing the packed material channels. Data Structures: 1. Palette Texture: Shape (256, 6, 3). Each entry [voxel, face] contains: Index 0: layer & 255 (lower 8 bits of the material index). Index 1: layer >> 8 (upper 8 bits of the material index). Index 2: flag (bitmask of material properties). 2. Material Flags Bitmask: Bit 0: ISOPAQUE Bit 1: HASCOLOR Bit 2: HASEMISSION Bit 3: HASNORMAL Bit 4: HASRSMA. 3. Material Channels: color: RGBA texture. emission: RGB texture. normal: RGB texture (derived from RG source). rsma: RGBA texture (R=roughness, G=specular, B=metallic, A=ambient occlusion). Algorithm Steps: 1. Load and Sort Materials: Parse material definitions to extract unique material names. Sort unique names alphabetically to create a deterministic index i for each name. Calculate atlas grid dimensions: cols = \lfloor atlas\width / res \rfloor rows = \lfloor atlas\height / res \rfloor. 2. Build Atlas and Lookup Tables: Initialize empty atlas textures for color, emission, normal, and rsma with dimensions (rows res, cols res). For each unique material name name at index i: Calculate grid position: col = i \pmod{cols} row = \lfloor i / cols \rfloor. Calculate pixel coordinates: x = col \times res y = row \times res. Extract sub-region [y:y+res, x:x+res] from each atlas. Load the material's PBR channels. If a channel is missing, fill it with self.redx (default). Store the loaded textures in lists self.colortextures, etc.. Record the layer index: layers[name] = i. Compute the flag bitmask: flag = (IS\OPAQUE \text{ if } is\opaque \text{ else } 0) \ | \ (HAS\COLOR \text{ if } has\color \text{ else } 0) \ | \ (HAS\EMISSION \text{ if } has\emission \text{ else } 0) \ | \ (HAS\NORMAL \text{ if } has\normal \text{ else } 0) \ | \ (HAS\RSMA \text{ if } has\rsma \text{ else } 0). Record flags: flags[name] = flag. 3. Fill Palette: Initialize palette array of shape (256, 6, 3) with zeros. For each voxel value v (1 to 255): Get the list of material names for the 6 faces. If the list length is 1, replicate it to 6 faces: names = 6. If the list length is not 6, raise an error. For each face f (0 to 5): Get name = names[f]. Lookup layer = layers[name] and flag = flags[name]. Set palette[v, f] = [layer & 255, layer >> 8, flag]. 4. Verify Palette: Check for mixed opaque/transparent sides on a single voxel. Count opaque flags per voxel: opaquecounts = sum(flag & 1 for face in palette[v]). If 0 < opaquecounts < 6 for any voxel, raise an error. Mixed opacity on a single voxel is invalid. 5. Write Outputs: Save palette as a PNG texture. Save coloratlas, emissionatlas, normalatlas, and rsmaatlas as PNG textures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatevoxelpalette(materials, materialdefs, atlaswidth, atlasheight, res=512): # 1. Load and Sort Materials allnames = set() for facenames in materials.values(): allnames.update(facenames) names = sorted(list(allnames)) cols = atlaswidth // res rows = atlasheight // res # Initialize atlases coloratlas = np.zeros((rows res, cols res, 4), dtype=np.uint8) emissionatlas = np.zeros((rows res, cols res, 3), dtype=np.uint8) normalatlas = np.zeros((rows res, cols res, 3), dtype=np.uint8) rsmaatlas = np.zeros((rows res, cols res, 4), dtype=np.uint8) layers = {} flags = {} # 2. Build Atlas and Lookup Tables for i, name in enumerate(names): col = i % cols row = i // cols x = col res y = row res # Load material properties mat = materialdefs[name] isopaque = mat.get('isopaque', True) hascolor = mat.get('hascolor', True) hasemission = mat.get('hasemission', False) hasnormal = mat.get('hasnormal', False) hasrsma = mat.get('hasrsma', False) # Load textures: if channel missing, fill with self.redx (default) color = mat.get('color', np.full((res, res, 4), 255, dtype=np.uint8)) emission = mat.get('emission', np.full((res, res, 3), 0, dtype=np.uint8)) normal = mat.get('normal', np.full((res, res, 3), 128, dtype=np.uint8)) rsma = mat.get('rsma', np.full((res, res, 4), 0, dtype=np.uint8)) # Store in atlas coloratlas[y:y+res, x:x+res] = color emissionatlas[y:y+res, x:x+res] = emission normalatlas[y:y+res, x:x+res] = normal rsmaatlas[y:y+res, x:x+res] = rsma # Compute flags flag = 0 if isopaque: flag |= 1 # ISOPAQUE if hascolor: flag |= 2 # HASCOLOR if hasemission: flag |= 4 # HASEMISSION if hasnormal: flag |= 8 # HASNORMAL if hasrsma: flag |= 16 # HASRSMA layers[name] = i flags[name] = flag # 3. Fill Palette palette = np.zeros((256, 6, 3), dtype=np.uint8) for voxelstr, facenames in materials.items(): voxel = int(voxelstr) if voxel < 1 or voxel > 255: raise ValueError(f"Invalid voxel value: {voxel}") if len(facenames) == 1: facenames = facenames 6 if len(facenames) != 6: raise ValueError(f"Invalid material names at voxel {voxel}: {facenames}") for f, name in enumerate(facenames): layer = layers[name] flag = flags[name] palette[voxel, f] = [layer & 255, layer >> 8, flag] # 4. Verify Palette opaquecounts = np.sum(palette[:,:, 2] & 1, axis=1, dtype=np.uint8) mixed = np.logicaland(opaquecounts > 0, opaquecounts < 6) if np.any(mixed): raise ValueError("ERROR: Palette contains voxels with mixed opaque/transparent sides.") return palette, coloratlas, emissionatlas, normalatlas, rsmaatlas Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mixed Opacity: A voxel cannot have both opaque and transparent faces. The system validates this and exits with an error if detected. Missing Channels: If a material lacks a specific channel, it must be filled with self.redx (default) to prevent atlas corruption. Voxel Value Range: Only voxel values 1–255 are supported. The system explicitly validates this range and raises an error for values outside it. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R^2 + V \cdot F), where N is the number of unique materials, R is the resolution of each tile, V is the number of voxel types (255), and F is the number of faces (6). The dominant cost is loading and packing textures for N materials. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot R^2 + V \cdot F). The atlas size is N \cdot R^2 pixels per channel. The palette size is fixed at 256 \times 6 \times 3 bytes. Performance: Reduces memory overhead and draw calls by batching materials into atlases instead of using per-voxel material instances. Strengths: Efficient storage for voxel worlds with many distinct materials; fast lookup during rendering. Limitations: Fixed voxel value range (1–255); mixed opacity per voxel is not supported; atlas size grows linearly with the number of unique materials. This method is part of the voxel material classification and storage system in the Godot Voxel plugin. It enables efficient PBR rendering for voxel-based games by mapping discrete voxel IDs to a shared set of material atlases. viktor-ferenczi/godot-voxel, https://github.com/viktor-ferenczi/godot-voxel, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Sample Uniform and Occupied Cells
body: This method generates a mixed set of voxel indices for volume rendering by combining uniformly sampled cells with cells known to be occupied by geometry. It filters out cells with invalid density values (specifically -1). Inputs: self.levels: Integer, number of resolution levels in the grid hierarchy. self.cellsperlvl: Integer, number of voxels per level. self.occs: 1D array/tensor of density or occupancy values. self.binaries: List of arrays/tensors, one per level, representing occupancy masks. n: Integer, number of uniform samples to generate per level. self.device: Target device for computation. Outputs: lvlindices: List of 1D arrays/tensors, one per level, containing linear indices. Data Structures: Linear index calculation: idx = lvl \times cells\per\lvl + local\idx. Cells with value -1 are considered invalid/empty. Steps: 1. Initialize lvlindices as an empty list. 2. For each lvl in range(self.levels): a. Generate n random integers in range [0, self.cellsperlvl) using a uniform distribution. b. Compute global linear indices for these uniform samples: cell\ids = lvl \times self.cells\per\lvl + uniform\indices. c. Filter uniformindices to keep only those where self.occs[cellids] >= 0.0. d. Retrieve all occupied indices for the current level by flattening self.binaries[lvl] and collecting indices where the value is non-zero. e. Let m be the number of occupied indices. If n < m, select n random indices from occupiedindices using a uniform random integer generator over [0, m). Otherwise, use all occupiedindices. f. Concatenate the filtered uniformindices and the selected occupiedindices. g. Append the concatenated array to lvlindices. 3. Return lvlindices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleuniformandoccupiedcells(self, n): lvlindices = [] for lvl in range(self.levels): # 1. Generate n random integers in [0, self.cellsperlvl) uniformindices = [random.randint(0, self.cellsperlvl - 1) for in range(n)] # 2. Compute global linear indices cellids = [lvl self.cellsperlvl + idx for idx in uniformindices] # 3. Filter uniform samples where density >= 0.0 uniformindices = [idx for idx, cid in zip(uniformindices, cellids) if self.occs[cid] >= 0.0] # 4. Get all occupied indices for this level occupiedindices = [i for i, v in enumerate(self.binaries[lvl].flatten()) if v != 0] # 5. Select occupied indices if n < len(occupiedindices): selected = [random.randint(0, len(occupiedindices) - 1) for in range(n)] occupiedsubset = [occupiedindices[i] for i in selected] else: occupiedsubset = occupiedindices # 6. Concatenate indices = uniformindices + occupiedsubset # 7. Append to results lvlindices.append(indices) return lvlindices Edge Cases: Empty Level: If self.binaries[lvl] has no occupied cells, occupiedindices is empty and the result contains only filtered uniform samples. All Invalid Density: If self.occs contains only -1, uniformindices becomes empty and the result contains only occupied indices. Selection with Replacement: torch.randint (or equivalent uniform integer generator) selects indices with replacement, meaning the same occupied cell may be sampled multiple times. This variant returns all valid cells in the grid, filtering out cells with -1 density. It does not limit the sample count to n. It iterates through all grid indices, computes global IDs via cell\ids = lvl \times self.cells\per\lvl + self.grid\indices, and filters based on self.occs[cellids] >= 0.0. It initializes an empty list, appends the filtered indices for each level, and returns the list. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Ensures occupied regions are sampled alongside uniform exploration. Limitations: The total number of samples per level is not strictly n; it equals the number of valid uniform samples plus \min(n, m) occupied samples. This method originates from the faster-occgrid repository. It is implemented using PyTorch tensor operations for GPU acceleration. name: Sparse AABB Collision Test
head: TestAabb
body: The Sparse AABB Collision Test determines whether an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) intersects any occupied voxels within a sparse volume representation. It solves the problem of static collision detection for volumetric objects by iterating through the voxel grid defined by the AABB's bounds. It differs from its sibling Point-in-Box Inclusion Test by evaluating a continuous volume rather than discrete points, and from Voxel Filled Check by supporting heterogeneous voxel types (solid, liquid, unknown) and caching terrain noise evaluation per column to optimize performance. Inputs: aabb: A SparseCollisionAabb structure defining the test volume with min and max coordinates (floats). liquidsBlock: A boolean flag indicating if liquid voxels count as blocking collisions. Outputs: A result structure containing: blocked: Boolean, true if any blocking voxel was found. sampledVoxels: Count of voxels sampled. solidVoxels: Count of solid voxels. liquidVoxels: Count of liquid voxels. unknownVoxels: Count of unknown/blocked voxels. hasLiquid: Boolean, true if any liquid was encountered. hasUnknown: Boolean, true if any unknown voxel was encountered. firstBlockingSample: The CollisionSample of the first blocking voxel. firstBlockingX, firstBlockingY, firstBlockingZ: Integer coordinates of the first blocking voxel. Data Structures: SparseCollisionAabb: Contains min and max vectors. CollisionSample: Contains status (enum: KnownAir, KnownSolid, KnownLiquid, UnknownBlocked) and potentially other metadata. colHeight, colRelief: Arrays of floats indexed by column index, caching terrain height and relief values. Steps: 1. Validation: Check if aabb.min or aabb.max contains non-finite values (NaN or Inf). If so, return immediately with blocked = true and status UnknownBlockedVolume. 2. Voxel Range Calculation: Convert aabb.min and aabb.max to voxel indices minX, minY, minZ and maxX, maxY, maxZ using a helper TryBuildVoxelRange. This helper uses nextafter on the max coordinates to handle floating-point precision boundaries correctly. 3. Sample Limit Check: Calculate the total number of voxels: N = (maxX - minX + 1) \times (maxY - minY + 1) \times (maxZ - minZ + 1). If N > kMaxCollisionVolumeSamples (where kMaxCollisionVolumeSamples = 32768), return immediately with blocked = true and status UnknownBlockedVolume. 4. Column Cache Initialization: Determine the XZ footprint of the AABB. For each column (x, z) in the footprint, precompute and store the terrain height and relief in colHeight and colRelief arrays. This collapses the noise evaluation cost from O(voxels) to O(columns). 5. Voxel Iteration: Iterate through the voxel grid in the order: Z from minZ to maxZ, Y from minY to maxY, X from minX to maxZ. 6. Index Calculation: For each voxel (x, y, z), calculate the linear index for the column cache: idx = (x - minX) + (z - minZ) \times (maxX - minX + 1). 7. Sampling: Call SampleWithColumn(x, y, z, colHeight[idx], colRelief[idx]) to get the CollisionSample status. 8. Classification: Increment sampledVoxels. If status is KnownAir: Continue. If status is KnownSolid: Increment solidVoxels. Set sampleBlocks = true. If status is KnownLiquid: Increment liquidVoxels. Set hasLiquid = true. Set sampleBlocks = liquidsBlock. If status is UnknownBlocked (or default): Increment unknownVoxels. Set hasUnknown = true. Set sampleBlocks = true. 9. Blocking Check: If sampleBlocks is true and result.blocked is false: Set result.blocked = true. Store sample in result.firstBlockingSample. Store x, y, z in result.firstBlockingX, result.firstBlockingY, result.firstBlockingZ. 10. Return: Return the populated result structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparseaabbcollisiontest(aabb, liquidsblock): # Step 1: Validation if not isfinite(aabb.min) or not isfinite(aabb.max): return Result(blocked=True, status=UnknownBlockedVolume) # Step 2: Voxel Range Calculation minx, miny, minz = TryBuildVoxelRange(aabb.min) maxx, maxy, maxz = TryBuildVoxelRange(aabb.max) # Step 3: Sample Limit Check spanx = maxx - minx + 1 spany = maxy - miny + 1 spanz = maxz - minz + 1 totalvoxels = spanx spany spanz if totalvoxels > 32768: return Result(blocked=True, status=UnknownBlockedVolume) # Step 4: Column Cache Initialization colheight = [0.0] (spanx spanz) colrelief = [0.0] (spanx spanz) for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): idx = (x - minx) + (z - minz) spanx colheight[idx], colrelief[idx] = computeterrainnoise(x, z) # Initialize Result result = Result( blocked=False, sampledvoxels=0, solidvoxels=0, liquidvoxels=0, unknownvoxels=0, hasliquid=False, hasunknown=False) # Step 5-9: Voxel Iteration and Classification for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): idx = (x - minx) + (z - minz) spanx sample = samplewithcolumn(x, y, z, colheight[idx], colrelief[idx]) result.sampledvoxels += 1 sampleblocks = False if sample.status == KnownAir: pass elif sample.status == KnownSolid: result.solidvoxels += 1 sampleblocks = True elif sample.status == KnownLiquid: result.liquidvoxels += 1 result.hasliquid = True sampleblocks = liquidsblock else: # UnknownBlocked or default result.unknownvoxels += 1 result.hasunknown = True sampleblocks = True if sampleblocks and not result.blocked: result.blocked = True result.firstblockingsample = sample result.firstblockingx = x result.firstblockingy = y result.firstblockingz = z return result Parameters: liquidsBlock: Boolean. Default behavior in the source code suggests it is a configurable flag. If true, liquids block movement; if false, they do not. kMaxCollisionVolumeSamples: Constant 32768. Hard limit on voxel count to prevent excessive computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-finite Bounds: If the AABB contains NaN or Inf, the test returns UnknownBlockedVolume immediately. Precision Boundaries: TryBuildVoxelRange uses nextafter on the max coordinate to ensure floating-point inaccuracies do not cause off-by-one errors in voxel indexing. Excessive Volume: If the AABB spans more than 32,768 voxels, the test fails fast with UnknownBlockedVolume rather than iterating. The Sparse AABB Sweep Test is a voxel occupancy test that determines whether an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) moving along a displacement vector intersects any occupied voxels in a sparse volume. It solves the problem of continuous collision detection for volumetric objects by sampling the path at discrete intervals, offering a balance between the accuracy of continuous sweep tests and the performance of static point tests. It differs from its sibling Support Below Search by testing the entire swept volume rather than just the base support, and from its parent Sparse AABB Collision Test by handling non-zero displacement vectors through temporal sampling. Support Below Search determines if a voxel position has structural support directly beneath it within a specified vertical drop distance. It solves the problem of identifying valid standing positions for entities or objects in a voxel world by finding the first non-empty voxel (solid, liquid, or blocked unknown) below a given footprint. It differs from Sparse AABB Sweep Test by iterating through a defined volume to find the first support rather than sweeping for any collision along a path, and builds on Sparse AABB Collision Test by utilizing its collision sample semantics. Time Complexity: O(C + V), where C is the number of columns in the XZ footprint and V is the total number of voxels in the AABB. The column cache initialization is O(C), and the voxel sampling is O(V). Memory Complexity: O(C) for the colHeight and colRelief caches, plus O(1) for the result structure. Performance: The method optimizes terrain noise evaluation by caching it per column, reducing the cost from O(V) to O(C) for the noise component. Strengths: Handles heterogeneous voxel types (solid, liquid, unknown); provides detailed statistics on voxel composition; fast early exit for invalid or excessively large volumes. Limitations: Limited to static AABBs; does not handle continuous motion (use Sparse AABB Sweep Test for that); capped at 32,768 voxels per test. When to Use: Static collision detection for entities in a voxel world where terrain noise is expensive to evaluate per voxel. When Not to Use: Continuous collision detection (use Sparse AABB Sweep Test); very large volumes exceeding 32,768 voxels; simple point-in-box checks where volume sampling is unnecessary (use Point-in-Box Inclusion Test). The Sparse AABB Collision Test is part of the VENPOD voxel physics engine, developed by asajid2-cell. It is designed for high-performance voxel simulation, targeting 100M+ active voxels at 60 FPS. The method is implemented in C++ and integrated into the sandbox mode of the engine. asajid2-cell/voxelrender, https://github.com/asajid2-cell/voxelrender, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Sparse AABB Sweep Test
head: SweepAabb
body: The Sparse AABB Sweep Test is a voxel occupancy test that determines whether an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) moving along a displacement vector intersects any occupied voxels in a sparse volume. It solves the problem of continuous collision detection for volumetric objects by sampling the path at discrete intervals, offering a balance between the accuracy of continuous sweep tests and the performance of static point tests. It differs from its sibling Support Below Search by testing the entire swept volume rather than just the base support, and from its parent Sparse AABB Collision Test by handling non-zero displacement vectors through temporal sampling. The method takes an initial AABB, a displacement vector, and a step count, and returns a result indicating whether the path was blocked, along with the fraction of the path where the collision occurred. Inputs: aabb: The initial axis-aligned bounding box. deltaX, deltaY, deltaZ: Components of the displacement vector. steps: The number of intermediate probes to perform. liquidsBlock: Boolean flag indicating if liquid voxels count as solid obstacles. Outputs: blocked: Boolean indicating if a collision occurred. safeFraction: The fraction of the path traveled before the collision (0.0 to 1.0). hitFraction: The fraction of the path where the collision was detected. hitVolume: Details of the volume block that caused the collision. Data Structures: The implementation relies on a helper structure SparseCollisionAabb to represent the bounding box and SparseCollisionVolumeResult to return test outcomes. The exact internal layout of these structures is not specified in the source, but they must support translation and collision querying. Algorithm: 1. Validation: Check if the AABB dimensions or displacement components are non-finite (NaN or Inf). If so, return immediately with blocked=true, safeFraction=0.0, and hitFraction=0.0. 2. Degeneracy Check: If the absolute values of deltaX, deltaY, and deltaZ are all less than 0.0001f, the displacement is considered negligible. In this case, bypass the sweep loop and call the static TestAabb function directly on the original AABB. 3. Step Clamping: Clamp the steps parameter to the range [1, kMaxCollisionSweepSteps], where kMaxCollisionSweepSteps is a constant equal to 1024. 4. Initialization: Set lastSafeFraction = 0.0f. 5. Sweep Loop: Iterate step from 1 to steps (inclusive): a. Calculate the interpolation fraction: f = \frac{step}{steps}. b. Translate the AABB by the scaled displacement: \vec{d}{probe} = \vec{d} \times f. Let the translated box be probe. c. Call TestAabb(probe, liquidsBlock) to check for collisions at this intermediate position. d. If TestAabb returns blocked=true: Set result.blocked = true. Set result.safeFraction = lastSafeFraction. Set result.hitFraction = f. Set result.hitVolume to the result from TestAabb. Return result immediately. e. Update lastSafeFraction = f. 6. Completion: If the loop completes without blocking, set result.safeFraction = 1.0f, result.hitFraction = 1.0f, and result.blocked = false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def SparseAABBSweepTest(aabb, deltaX, deltaY, deltaZ, steps, liquidsBlock): # 1. Validate finiteness if not isfinite(aabb) or not isfinite(deltaX) or not isfinite(deltaY) or not isfinite(deltaZ): return SparseCollisionVolumeResult(blocked=True, safeFraction=0.0, hitFraction=0.0, hitVolume=None) # 2. Check for near-zero displacement if abs(deltaX) < 0.0001 and abs(deltaY) < 0.0001 and abs(deltaZ) < 0.0001: return TestAabb(aabb, liquidsBlock) # 3. Clamp steps kMaxCollisionSweepSteps = 1024 steps = max(1, min(steps, kMaxCollisionSweepSteps)) lastSafeFraction = 0.0 # 5. Loop for step in range(1, steps + 1): fraction = step / steps # Translate AABB probe = TranslateAabb(aabb, deltaX fraction, deltaY fraction, deltaZ fraction) # Test collision volume = TestAabb(probe, liquidsBlock) if volume.blocked: return SparseCollisionVolumeResult( blocked=True, safeFraction=lastSafeFraction, hitFraction=fraction, hitVolume=volume) lastSafeFraction = fraction # 6. No collision return SparseCollisionVolumeResult( blocked=False, safeFraction=1.0, hitFraction=1.0, hitVolume=None) Parameters: kMaxCollisionSweepSteps: 1024. Threshold for near-zero displacement: 0.0001f. Edge Cases: Non-finite inputs: Handled by immediate return with blocked=true and zero fractions. Near-zero displacement: Handled by falling back to static TestAabb to avoid numerical instability or unnecessary computation. Time Complexity: O(k), where k is the number of steps. Each step involves a constant-time AABB translation and a TestAabb call. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the volume data structure accessed by TestAabb. Performance: The method is slower than a single static TestAabb call due to the loop overhead, but faster than a true continuous sweep test which might require solving quadratic equations or more complex geometric intersections. The performance scales linearly with the number of steps. Strengths: Provides a simple way to detect collisions during movement without the complexity of continuous collision detection. The fallback to static testing for small displacements optimizes common cases where movement is negligible. Limitations: The accuracy depends on the number of steps. A low step count may miss narrow obstacles between samples. The method is discrete and may report a collision slightly later than the actual first contact point (within the interval defined by the last safe fraction and the hit fraction). When to use: When moving objects in a voxel volume and a balance between performance and collision accuracy is needed. Suitable for real-time applications where true continuous collision detection is too expensive. When not to use: When high precision is required for very small or fast-moving objects, or when the displacement is zero (use static test directly). The Sparse AABB Sweep Test is part of the voxel rendering and physics engine implementation found in the voxelrender repository by asajid2-cell. It is designed for use in voxel-based simulations, such as sand or liquid physics, where objects move through a sparse voxel grid. The method is an adaptation of standard sweep-and-prune or continuous collision detection techniques tailored for the discrete nature of voxel data. asajid2-cell/voxelrender, https://github.com/asajid2-cell/voxelrender, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Support Below Search
head: FindSupportBelow
body: Support Below Search determines if a voxel position has structural support directly beneath it within a specified vertical drop distance. It solves the problem of identifying valid standing positions for entities or objects in a voxel world by finding the first non-empty voxel (solid, liquid, or blocked unknown) below a given footprint. It differs from Sparse AABB Sweep Test by iterating through a defined volume to find the first support rather than sweeping for any collision along a path, and builds on Sparse AABB Collision Test by utilizing its collision sample semantics. Inputs: footprintAabb: A SparseCollisionAabb defining the XZ bounds of the search area and the starting Y coordinate. maxDrop: A float specifying the maximum downward distance to search. liquidsSupport: A boolean indicating whether liquid voxels count as valid support. Outputs: A result structure containing: found: Boolean indicating if support was found. supportX, supportY, supportZ: The voxel coordinates of the found support. voxel: The voxel data of the support. fromEdit: Boolean indicating if the voxel was from an edit operation. sampledVoxels: Count of voxels checked. solidVoxels: Count of solid voxels checked. liquidVoxels: Count of liquid voxels checked. Data Structures: SparseCollisionAabb: Defines the axis-aligned bounding box for the search footprint in X and Z, and the starting Y. CollisionSample: Returned by SampleWithColumn, containing status (enum: KnownSolid, KnownLiquid, UnknownBlocked), voxel data, and fromEdit flag. colHeight / colRelief: Precomputed per-column terrain height and relief arrays for the XZ footprint, used to optimize sampling. Parameters: kMaxCollisionSupportSamples: Constant uint64t set to 32768, limiting the maximum number of samples to prevent infinite loops or excessive computation. Steps: 1. Validate that the footprint AABB bounds are finite and maxDrop >= 0.0f. If invalid, return an empty result. 2. Convert the footprint's X and Z bounds to voxel indices (minX, maxX, minZ, maxZ). Convert the Y bounds to voxel indices, calculating startY from the AABB and endY = startY - maxDrop. 3. Check if endY > startY or if the total sample count would exceed kMaxCollisionSupportSamples. If so, return an empty result. 4. Precompute per-column terrain height and relief for the XZ footprint. 5. Iterate Y from startY down to endY. For each Y, iterate Z from minZ to maxZ, and X from minX to maxZ. 6. Sample the voxel at (x, y, z) using SampleWithColumn, passing the precomputed column height and relief. 7. Increment result.sampledVoxels. 8. If sample.status is KnownSolid: Increment result.solidVoxels. Set result.found = true. Record supportX, supportY, supportZ, voxel, and fromEdit. Return the result. 9. If sample.status is KnownLiquid: Increment result.liquidVoxels. If liquidsSupport is true: Set result.found = true. Record supportX, supportY, supportZ, voxel, and fromEdit. Return the result. 10. If sample.status is UnknownBlocked: Set result.found = true. Record supportX, supportY, supportZ, voxel, and fromEdit. Return the result. 11. If the loop completes without finding support, return an empty result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def supportbelowsearch(footprintaabb, maxdrop, liquidssupport): # 1. Validate inputs if not isfinite(footprintaabb) or maxdrop < 0.0: return emptyresult() # 2. Convert bounds to voxel indices starty = footprintaabb.starty endy = starty - maxdrop minx, maxx = voxelizexz(footprintaabb.minx, footprintaabb.maxx) minz, maxz = voxelizexz(footprintaabb.minz, footprintaabb.maxz) # 3. Check limits if endy > starty: return emptyresult() # Estimate sample count to check against kMaxCollisionSupportSamples spanx = maxx - minx + 1 spanz = maxz - minz + 1 spany = starty - endy + 1 totalsamples = spanx spanz spany if totalsamples > 32768: return emptyresult() # 4. Precompute column data colheight = precomputecolumnheights(minx, maxx, minz, maxz) colrelief = precomputecolumnrelief(minx, maxx, minz, maxz) result = { 'found': False, 'sampledVoxels': 0, 'solidVoxels': 0, 'liquidVoxels': 0, 'supportX': 0, 'supportY': 0, 'supportZ': 0, 'voxel': None, 'fromEdit': False } # 5. Iterate Y, Z, X for y in range(starty, endy - 1, -1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): # Calculate index for column data idx = (x - minx) + (z - minz) spanx # 6. Sample voxel sample = samplewithcolumn(x, y, z, colheight[idx], colrelief[idx]) result['sampledVoxels'] += 1 # 7. Check KnownSolid if sample.status == 'KnownSolid': result['solidVoxels'] += 1 result['found'] = True result['supportX'] = x result['supportY'] = y result['supportZ'] = z result['voxel'] = sample.voxel result['fromEdit'] = sample.fromedit return result # 8. Check KnownLiquid if sample.status == 'KnownLiquid': result['liquidVoxels'] += 1 if liquidssupport: result['found'] = True result['supportX'] = x result['supportY'] = y result['supportZ'] = z result['voxel'] = sample.voxel result['fromEdit'] = sample.fromedit return result # 9. Check UnknownBlocked if sample.status == 'UnknownBlocked': result['found'] = True result['supportX'] = x result['supportY'] = y result['supportZ'] = z result['voxel'] = sample.voxel result['fromEdit'] = sample.fromedit return result # 11. No support found return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid bounds or sample limit exceeded return immediately without sampling. Boundary precision uses nextafter implicitly via TryBuildVoxelRange. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the search volume, bounded by kMaxCollisionSupportSamples (32768). Memory Complexity: O(M) where M is the area of the XZ footprint, for storing colHeight and colRelief arrays. Strengths: Efficiently finds the first support below a position; handles liquids and unknown blocks as configurable support types. Limitations: Limited by kMaxCollisionSupportSamples; may miss support if the drop distance is too large or the footprint is too wide. When to use: When determining if an entity can stand on terrain below a specific position. When not to use: When sweeping for any collision along a path is required (use Sparse AABB Sweep Test). Origin: Implemented in the voxelrender project by asajid2-cell. The method is part of the voxel collision detection system, specifically designed for support checks in voxel-based simulations. asajid2-cell/voxelrender, https://github.com/asajid2-cell/voxelrender, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Solidity Check
head: Void Check with Boundary Handling
body: Solidity Check determines if a specific voxel coordinate in a 3D world is occupied by solid geometry or is void (empty). It solves the problem of boundary condition handling during voxel traversal, ensuring that out-of-bounds regions are treated consistently to prevent rendering artifacts. It differs from its sibling Point-in-Box Inclusion Test by explicitly managing chunk-based spatial indexing and asymmetric boundary wrapping for X/Y versus Z axes, rather than simple AABB containment. Inputs: x, y, z: Integer world voxel coordinates. map: A pointer or reference to a libvxlmap structure containing world dimensions and chunk data. Outputs: bool: True if the voxel is solid (occupied), False if it is void (empty). Data Structures: The implementation relies on the libvxlmap structure: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct libvxlmap { sizet width, height, depth; // World dimensions struct libvxlchunk chunks; // Array of chunks sizet geometry; // Geometry lookup table sizet streamed; // Streamed data offset }; struct libvxlchunk { struct libvxlblock blocks; // Pointer to block data sizet length, index; // Chunk metadata }; struct libvxlblock { uint32t position; // Encoded position key uint32t color; // Color/Type data }; Position keys are encoded as 32-bit integers: \text{pos\key}(x,y,z) = (y \ll 20) \mid (x \ll 8) \mid z Where x, y use 12 bits (0-4095) and z uses 8 bits (0-255). Steps: 1. Calculate Chunk Index: Determine the chunk index for the world position (x, y, z) using a helper function getchunkindex. The exact formula for getchunkindex is not provided in the sources, but it maps world coordinates to a chunk ID. 2. Boundary Check (Z-axis): If z < 0, return False (void). If map is null or z \ge \text{map->depth}, return True (solid). 3. Boundary Check (Chunk Bounds): If chunkindex is -1 (indicating out-of-bounds chunk), return False (void). Note: Source states "return False (not void)" which implies void, but Source also states "Out-of-bounds chunks are treated as non-void (solid)". This is a contradiction. Source does not mention chunkindex -1. Given the context of "preventing rendering holes", treating out-of-bounds as solid is the standard practice. However, the specific code snippet in says return False. We must cite the discrepancy. Correction based on code snippet: The code explicitly returns False for chunkindex == -1. Correction based on text: The text says "Out-of-bounds chunks are treated as non-void (solid)". Resolution: The code snippet is the implementation detail. The text describes the intent. The code returns False (void). This might be a bug or specific design choice in the unofficial repo. We will follow the code snippet for implementation but note the text contradiction. 4. Coordinate Wrapping: Calculate wrapped coordinates: x' = x \pmod{\text{map->width}} y' = y \pmod{\text{map->height}} z' = z x and y wrap around the map dimensions. z does not wrap. 5. Retrieve Voxel Data: Call libvxlgeometryget(x', y', z') to retrieve the voxel data. This function likely accesses the geometry array or chunk blocks to find the voxel at the wrapped position. 6. Determine Solidity: If the retrieved voxel data is non-zero, return True (solid). If the retrieved voxel data is zero, return False (void). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def soliditycheck(x: int, y: int, z: int, map: Map) -> bool: # Step 1: Calculate chunk index chunkindex = getchunkindex(x, y, z) # Step 2: Z-axis boundary check if z < 0: return False # Void if map is None or z >= map.depth: return True # Solid # Step 3: Chunk bounds check # Contradiction in sources: Code returns False (void), text says solid. # Following code snippet from if chunkindex == -1: return False # Void (per code snippet) # Step 4: Coordinate wrapping xwrapped = x % map.width ywrapped = y % map.height zwrapped = z # Step 5: Retrieve voxel data # libvxlgeometryget is assumed to return a value representing the voxel voxeldata = libvxlgeometryget(xwrapped, ywrapped, zwrapped) # Step 6: Determine solidity if voxeldata != 0: return True # Solid else: return False # Void Parameters: MOUSESENSITIVITY: Not relevant to this method, but present in source context. CHUNKSIZE, CHUNKAREA: Used in local index calculation in, but the primary method uses libvxlgeometryget. The local index calculation x % CHUNKSIZE + z % CHUNKSIZE CHUNKSIZE + y % CHUNKSIZE CHUNKAREA is an alternative implementation detail found in for accessing chunkvoxels. Edge Cases: Out-of-bounds X/Y: Wrapped using modulo. Out-of-bounds Z: Treated as solid if z \ge \text{depth}, void if z < 0. Out-of-bounds Chunk: Treated as void by code, solid by text description. Determines if a voxel is on the boundary by checking 6-connected neighbors. It inverts the logic of Solidity Check, confirming exposure to air rather than solidity. Time Complexity: O(1) assuming constant-time chunk lookup and modulo operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Handles asymmetric boundary conditions (wrapping X/Y, clamping Z) efficiently. Prevents rendering holes at world edges. Limitations: Contradiction in source regarding out-of-bounds chunk handling. Relies on specific libvxl data structures. When to use: When voxelizing or rendering volumes with wrapped horizontal boundaries and vertical limits. The method originates from the libvxl library by xtreme8000 and is also implemented in the StanislavPetrovV/Minecraft project. It is used in voxel-based game engines and volume rendering systems to efficiently query voxel occupancy while managing world boundaries.
