name: Explicit Surface to TSDF Conversion
head: Explicit Geometry to TSDF, Mesh to TSDF
body: This method converts explicit geometry, such as triangle meshes or oriented point clouds, into a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) voxel grid by computing the closest-surface distance for each voxel center and assigning a sign based on surface normals or an offset fallback. It differs from Projective TSDF Fusion by operating directly on geometric primitives rather than depth images, making it suitable for inputs from upstream reconstruction pipelines where calibrated camera poses are unavailable or unnecessary. Inputs: A triangle mesh \mathcal{T} (set of triangles with vertices a,b,c and normals \mathbf{n}) or an oriented point cloud; a global voxel grid definition (origin, resolution, truncation band \tau). Outputs: A TSDF volume where each voxel stores a truncated signed distance value and a validity flag. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A sparse or dense array of blocks. Each block contains N \times N \times N voxels (e.g., 8 \times 8 \times 8). Voxel Entry: Contains a float value (signed distance) and a boolean valid flag. Triangle: Defined by vertices a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and unit normal \mathbf{n}. Steps: 1. Iterate Voxels: For each voxel center \mathbf{p} in the global grid. 2. Find Closest Surface: Compute the closest point \Pi{\tau\star}(\mathbf{p}) on the surface \mathcal{T} to \mathbf{p}. For a mesh, \Pi{\tau\star}(\mathbf{p}) is the closest point on the closest triangle \tau\star. To find the closest point on a triangle, check if the orthogonal projection of \mathbf{p} lies inside the triangle. If so, that projection is the closest point. Otherwise, project \mathbf{p} onto the three edge segments and take the nearest point. The barycentric form of a point on a triangle is q(v, w) = a + v(b-a) + w(c-a), subject to v \geq 0, w \geq 0, v + w \leq 1. 3. Compute Unsigned Distance: Calculate the Euclidean distance d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \Pi{\tau\star}(\mathbf{p})\|2. 4. Assign Sign: Watertight/Oriented Case: If the mesh is watertight with consistent orientation, or if the input is an oriented point cloud with reliable normals, compute the sign using the local point-to-plane test: s(\mathbf{p}) = \text{sign}((\mathbf{p} - \Pi{\tau\star}(\mathbf{p}))^\top \mathbf{n}{\tau\star}) d(\mathbf{p}) where \mathbf{n}{\tau\star} is the unit normal of the closest triangle (or point). Non-Watertight/Unreliable Case: If the surface is non-watertight, contains thin sheets, or normals are unreliable, use the unsigned-distance offset fallback: s(\mathbf{p}) = d(\mathbf{p}) - \delta where \delta \approx 1\text{--}2 voxel sizes. This creates a stable zero level set around the geometry without requiring a global inside/outside convention. 5. Truncate and Store: If |s(\mathbf{p})| \leq \tau, store s(\mathbf{p}) in the voxel and mark it valid. Otherwise, mark it invalid or store a default value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convertmeshtotsdf(mesh, voxelgrid, truncationband, iswatertight): """ Converts a mesh to a TSDF volume. mesh: List of triangles, each triangle is (a, b, c, n) where a,b,c are vertices and n is normal. voxelgrid: Object providing voxel centers and storage. truncationband: Float, the truncation threshold tau. iswatertight: Boolean, whether the mesh is watertight with consistent orientation. """ for voxelcenter in voxelgrid.centers(): closesttriangle, closestpoint = findclosesttriangleandpoint(mesh, voxelcenter) dist = sqrt(dot(voxelcenter - closestpoint, voxelcenter - closestpoint)) if iswatertight: normal = closesttriangle.normal signval = dot(voxelcenter - closestpoint, normal) signeddist = (1.0 if signval >= 0 else -1.0) dist else: delta = 1.5 voxelgrid.voxelsize signeddist = dist - delta if abs(signeddist) <= truncationband: voxelgrid.setvalue(voxelcenter, signeddist, valid=True) else: voxelgrid.setvalue(voxelcenter, 0.0, valid=False) def findclosesttriangleandpoint(mesh, p): mindist = float('inf') besttriangle = None bestpoint = None for triangle in mesh: a, b, c, n = triangle closestpointontri = closestpointontriangle(p, a, b, c) dist = sqrt(dot(p - closestpointontri, p - closestpointontri)) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist besttriangle = triangle bestpoint = closestpointontri return besttriangle, bestpoint def closestpointontriangle(p, a, b, c): ap = p - a ab = b - a ac = c - a abab = dot(ab, ab) acac = dot(ac, ac) abac = dot(ab, ac) apab = dot(ap, ab) apac = dot(ap, ac) denom = abab acac - abac abac if denom == 0: return a v = (acac apab - abac apac) / denom w = (abab apac - abac apab) / denom if v >= 0 and w >= 0 and (v + w) <= 1: return a + v ab + w ac tab = max(0.0, min(1.0, dot(ap, ab) / abab)) closestab = a + tab ab distab = sqrt(dot(p - closestab, p - closestab)) bp = p - b bc = c - b tbc = max(0.0, min(1.0, dot(bp, bc) / dot(bc, bc))) closestbc = b + tbc bc distbc = sqrt(dot(p - closestbc, p - closestbc)) cp = p - c ca = a - c tca = max(0.0, min(1.0, dot(cp, ca) / dot(ca, ca))) closestca = c + tca ca distca = sqrt(dot(p - closestca, p - closestca)) if distab <= distbc and distab <= distca: return closestab elif distbc <= distca: return closestbc else: return closestca Parameters: Truncation Band (\tau): The maximum distance for which TSDF values are stored. Typical values depend on the application, often 1-2 voxel sizes. Offset (\delta): Used in the fallback case. Typically 1\text{--}2 voxel sizes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-watertight Surfaces: Global inside/outside signs are ill-defined. The unsigned-distance offset fallback is required. Thin Sheets: Similar to non-watertight surfaces, normals may not provide a consistent global sign. Use the offset fallback. Unreliable Normals: If normals are noisy or unoriented, the point-to-plane sign test may be incorrect. Use the offset fallback. Degenerate Triangles: Handle zero-area triangles in closestpointontriangle by returning a vertex or skipping. A method to compute signed distance values for voxels from calibrated depth images by projecting voxel centers into the camera frame and comparing projected depth with observed depth. It differs from direct mesh conversion by using depth measurements from multiple views, fused by weighted averaging, rather than explicit geometric primitives. Choose this when input is from calibrated depth cameras (e.g., Kinect) rather than a reconstructed mesh. Steps: 1. Transform voxel center \mathbf{p} to camera frame: \mathbf{p}c = R^\top (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{t}) = (x, y, z)^\top. 2. Project to 2D image coordinates: u = fx \frac{x}{z} + cx, \quad v = fy \frac{y}{z} + cy. 3. If z > 0 and (u,v) is valid, read observed depth \hat{z} and compute s(\mathbf{p}) = \hat{z} - z. 4. Fuse measurements from multiple views by weighted averaging. Formulas: Camera frame transformation: \mathbf{p}c = R^\top (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{t}). Pinhole projection: u = fx \frac{x}{z} + cx, \quad v = fy \frac{y}{z} + cy. Signed distance: s(\mathbf{p}) = \hat{z} - z. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Directly handles explicit geometry; robust to non-watertight surfaces with the offset fallback; compatible with compression pipelines designed for TSDF. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution meshes without acceleration; sign ambiguity for non-watertight surfaces requires fallback. When to Use: When input is a mesh or point cloud from a reconstruction pipeline, and camera poses are not available or relevant. When Not to Use: When input is raw depth images from calibrated cameras; use Projective TSDF Fusion instead. Originating from volumetric fusion systems like KinectFusion [Newcombe et al. 2011] and voxel hashing [Nießner et al. 2013], TSDF representation has become standard for integrating depth data. The explicit surface conversion path was formalized to support codecs and compression pipelines that accept explicit geometry (meshes/point clouds) as input, alongside depth images. It addresses the need to handle non-watertight and noisy scans common in real-world reconstruction by providing a robust fallback for sign assignment. name: Mesh-to-TSDF Sequence Encoding Pipeline
head: codec_mesh workflow
body: This method loads a sequence of triangle meshes matching a printf-style pattern, fits a single similarity transform to their union bounds, converts each frame to a TSDF voxel grid, encodes it into a codec stream, decodes it, and compares the original, uncompressed TSDF, and decoded surfaces. It differs from single-frame conversion by handling temporal sequences with a unified spatial transform and performing codec-specific compression with built-in surface verification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of triangle mesh files matching a printf-style path pattern. Output: A codec stream containing the TSDF data, plus optional output meshes for verification (input, uncompressed TSDF surface, decoded surface). Data Structures: Pattern: A struct defining the file path template with head (prefix), tail (suffix), and width (digit padding width, -1 if no number placeholder). MeshSequence: Represents the open sequence of meshes, providing frame count and global transform metadata. EncoderConfig: Configuration for the TSDF codec, including the truesdf flag and band constraints. MeshSdfParams: Parameters for SDF generation, including voxel size, truncation distance, and topology handling flags. Parameters: source.path: Printf-style pattern for frame files (e.g., %03d.ply). Must contain at most one number placeholder. source.heightm: Target height in metres used by meshio::fittransform to compute the similarity transform. source.metresperunit: Scale factor used by meshio::scaletransform as an alternative to height-based fitting. source.allowholes: Boolean flag that permits signed mode to accept meshes with topology defects (holes). codec.inspectonly: Boolean flag that skips GPU work and runs a host-only second pass to audit frames. fusion.voxelsizem: Resolution of the voxel grid. trunc: Truncation distance for the TSDF. Steps: 1. Parse source.path to extract head, tail, and width. Validate exactly one number placeholder in %d or %0Nd format. Reject %5d because printf pads with spaces while other tools pad with zeros, causing path mismatches. Handle escaped %% by converting to a single %. 2. Open the mesh sequence defined by the parsed pattern. Compute the union of bounding boxes of all meshes. Fit a single similarity transform to this union using source.heightm or source.metresperunit as an alternative scale. Store the transform for application to all frames. 3. Configure EncoderConfig and MeshSdfParams. Set config.truesdf = true because the mesh field represents a true distance that codes without an observed mask in a band that observes every voxel it codes. Validate the true SDF band constraints against the grid resolution and truncation. 4. Initialize GPU resources (Vulkan instance, physical device, device, allocator) if not in inspect-only mode. Prepare volume data structures for TSDF storage. 5. Process each frame: load the mesh, apply the similarity transform, check topology (reject in signed mode if defects exist and allowholes is false; shell mode accepts any topology), convert to TSDF voxel grid (closest-face sign for signed mode, closed surface for shell mode), truncate at trunc, and encode into the codec stream. Track statistics like triangle counts. 6. Decode the codec stream back to a TSDF grid. Extract surfaces from the input mesh, uncompressed TSDF, and decoded TSDF. Write output meshes if opt.output.prefix is set. Compare surfaces using eval::CompareOptions based on voxelsizem and trunc. Calculate and report conversion error (uncompressed TSDF vs normalized input), codec error (decoded vs uncompressed TSDF), and total error (decoded vs normalized input). 7. If codec.inspectonly is true, skip GPU work, run a host-only audit of frames, print details of the last frame, and write the input mesh if output prefix is set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parsepattern(text): head, tail, width = "", "", -1 i = 0 while i < len(text): if text[i] != '%': head += text[i] i += 1 continue rest = len(text) - i - 1 if rest >= 1 and text[i + 1] == '%': head += '%' i += 2 continue if rest >= 1 and text[i + 1] == 'd': width = 0 i += 2 elif rest >= 3 and text[i + 1] == '0' and text[i + 2].isdigit() and text[i + 3] == 'd': width = int(text[i + 2]) i += 4 else: raise ValueError("Invalid pattern: must be %d or %0Nd") tail = text[i:] break if width == -1: raise ValueError("No number placeholder") return {"head": head, "tail": tail, "width": width} def fitsimilaritytransform(boundingboxes, heightm, metresperunit=None): miny = min(b.miny for b in boundingboxes) maxy = max(b.maxy for b in boundingboxes) unionheight = maxy - miny if metresperunit is not None: scale = metresperunit else: scale = heightm / unionheight if unionheight > 0 else 1.0 center = ((boundingboxes[0].minx + boundingboxes[0].maxx) / 2, (miny + maxy) / 2, (boundingboxes[0].minz + boundingboxes[0].maxz) / 2) return {"scale": scale, "translation": center} def checktruesdfband(sdfparams, grid): assert sdfparams["voxelsize"] > 0 and sdfparams["trunc"] > 0 assert grid["width"] > 0 and grid["height"] > 0 and grid["depth"] > 0 def runmeshtotsdfpipeline(opt): pattern = parsepattern(opt.source.path) if pattern["width"] == 5: raise ValueError("Pattern %5d is refused: printf pads with spaces while ffmpeg pads with zeros") sequence = MeshSequence.open(opt.source.path, pattern) transform = fitsimilaritytransform(sequence.boundingboxes, opt.source.heightm, opt.source.metresperunit) config = {"truesdf": True} sdfparams = {"voxelsize": opt.fusion.voxelsizem, "trunc": opt.trunc, "allowholes": opt.source.allowholes, "transform": transform} checktruesdfband(sdfparams, sequence.gridresolution) if not opt.codec.inspectonly: instance = createvulkaninstance({}) gpu = selectphysicaldevice(instance, devicerequirements()) device = createvulkandevice(instance, gpu, devicerequirements()) allocator = createvulkanallocator(instance, device) else: device = None allocator = None for frameidx in range(sequence.count()): mesh = sequence.loadframe(frameidx) mesh.applytransform(transform) if not opt.source.allowholes and hastopologydefects(mesh): if opt.codec.mode == "signed": raise TopologyError(f"Frame {frameidx} has holes") tsdfgrid = voxelizemesh(mesh, sdfparams) if device is not None: encodetocodecstream(tsdfgrid, config, device, allocator) if not opt.codec.inspectonly: decodedtsdf = decodecodecstream() inputmesh = sequence.loadlastframe() inputmesh.applytransform(transform) sourcemesh = extractsurface(tsdfgrid) decodedmesh = extractsurface(decodedtsdf) if opt.output.prefix: writeply(f"{opt.output.prefix}input.ply", inputmesh) writeply(f"{opt.output.prefix}source.ply", sourcemesh) writeply(f"{opt.output.prefix}decoded.ply", decodedmesh) compareoptions = {"voxelsize": opt.fusion.voxelsizem, "trunc": opt.trunc} inputref = ReferenceMesh.create(inputmesh, compareoptions) sourceref = ReferenceMesh.create(sourcemesh, compareoptions) decodedref = ReferenceMesh.create(decodedmesh, compareoptions) conversionerror = inputref.compare(sourceref) codecerror = sourceref.compare(decodedref) totalerror = inputref.compare(decodedref) printcomparison(conversionerror) printcomparison(codecerror) printcomparison(totalerror) if opt.codec.inspectonly: inspected = inspectframes(sequence) printframe(inspected.last) if opt.output.prefix: writeply(f"{opt.output.prefix}input.ply", inspected.last.mesh) return {} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Path Pattern Mismatch: Using %5d causes issues because printf pads with spaces while other tools pad with zeros. Topology Defects: Signed mode requires valid topology (no holes) unless source.allowholes is true. True SDF Band: The pipeline uses truesdf = true, meaning it codes without an observed mask. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of frames and the number of voxels per frame. Memory Complexity: O(V) per frame for the TSDF grid. Performance: Measured performance depends on GPU hardware, resolution, and scene complexity. Strengths: Automated handling of sequences, unified transform, codec compression, verification pipeline. Limitations: Requires valid topology for signed mode (unless allowholes is set). Path pattern restrictions. When to Use: When processing animated geometry sequences into compressed TSDF volumes. When Not to Use: For single-frame conversion (use Explicit Surface to TSDF Conversion directly). This pipeline is part of the volumetric kit grid project, providing a complete workflow for mesh sequence to TSDF conversion. It integrates mesh I/O, SDF generation, and codec compression into a single tool. taojin-6/volumetrickitgrid, https://github.com/taojin-6/volumetrickitgrid, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: SDF Dataset Normalization
head: SDF Mesh Loading
body: SDF Dataset Normalization prepares a triangle mesh for Signed Distance Field (SDF) generation by loading the mesh and normalizing its vertex coordinates to the range [-1, 1]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A path to a mesh file. Output: A normalized mesh object with vertices scaled and translated to [-1, 1]. Data Structures: mesh: A mesh object containing a vertex array vs of shape (N, 3), where N is the number of vertices. vmin: A 3D vector representing the component-wise minimum of the vertices along axis 0. vmax: A 3D vector representing the component-wise maximum of the vertices along axis 0. vcenter: A 3D vector representing the centroid of the bounding box. Steps: 1. Load the mesh from the specified file path using trimesh.load with force='mesh'. 2. Extract the vertex coordinates vs from mesh.vertices. 3. Calculate v{min} as the minimum of vs along axis 0. 4. Calculate v{max} as the maximum of vs along axis 0. 5. Calculate the center v{center} of the bounding box using the formula: v{center} = \frac{v{min} + v{max}}{2}. 6. Translate the vertices by subtracting v{center} to center the mesh at the origin. 7. Compute the bounding box extent E = v{max} - v{min} and the maximum dimension E{max} = \max(E). 8. Scale the vertices by 2 / E{max} to fit within the range [-1, 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import trimesh import numpy as np def normalizesdfmesh(meshpath): # Load mesh, forcing mesh type mesh = trimesh.load(meshpath, force='mesh') # Extract vertices vs = mesh.vertices # Calculate bounds vmin = np.min(vs, axis=0) vmax = np.max(vs, axis=0) # Calculate center vcenter = (vmin + vmax) / 2.0 # Center the mesh centeredvs = vs - vcenter # Calculate scale to fit in [-1, 1] # Extent of the bounding box extent = vmax - vmin # Max dimension of the extent maxextent = np.max(extent) # Avoid division by zero for degenerate meshes if maxextent == 0: scale = 1.0 else: # Scale factor to map maxextent to 2 (from -1 to 1) scale = 2.0 / maxextent # Scale vertices normalizedvs = centeredvs scale # Update mesh vertices mesh.vertices = normalizedvs return mesh Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Meshes: If all vertices are identical, maxextent becomes zero, causing division by zero during scaling. A guard is required. Mesh normalization transforms a 3D mesh's vertex coordinates so that the geometry is centered at the origin and scaled to fit within a unit cube [-1, 1]^3. It differs from Variance Normalization, which scales based on the distribution of points rather than bounding extent. SDF Grid Resampling from File reads a raw Signed Distance Field (SDF) text file, parses its grid resolution, bounding box, and voxel size, then resamples it to a target cubic grid resolution using coordinate mapping and clamping. It differs from sibling methods by handling non-cubic source grids and normalizing the spatial extent to a centered bounding box before interpolation. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of vertices, due to a single pass for min/max computation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the vertex array. Strengths: Computationally inexpensive and standardizes input scale for downstream SDF generation. Limitations: Does not validate mesh topology or watertightness; highly anisotropic meshes may require axis-specific scaling adjustments. name: Mesh Normalization
body: Mesh normalization transforms a 3D mesh's vertex coordinates so that the geometry is centered at the origin and scaled to fit within a unit cube [-1, 1]^3. It differs from Variance Normalization, which scales based on the distribution of points rather than bounding extent. Inputs: A mesh object containing a list of vertices V = \{v1, v2, \dots, vN\} where each vi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: The same mesh object with updated vertex coordinates. Data Structures: vertices: Array of 3D vectors representing mesh vertices. bounds: Pair of 3D vectors representing the minimum and maximum coordinates of the mesh. extents: 3D vector of axis-aligned bounding box sizes. Steps: 1. Compute bounds and center: Determine the axis-aligned bounding box and its center. center = bounds.mean(axis=0) 2. Compute max extent: Find the largest dimension of the bounding box. max\extent = extents.max() 3. Compute scale factor: Determine the uniform scale factor required to fit the mesh into a unit cube. scale\factor = \frac{1.0}{max\extent} 4. Translate: Subtract the center from each vertex to move the mesh to the origin. v'i = vi - center 5. Scale: Multiply each translated vertex by the scale factor. v''i = v'i \times scale\factor Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalizemesh(mesh): bounds = mesh.bounds center = bounds.mean(axis=0) extents = mesh.extents maxextent = extents.max() if maxextent == 0.0: return mesh # Guard against division by zero scalefactor = 1.0 / maxextent mesh.vertices -= center mesh.vertices = scalefactor return mesh Parameters: None. The method is deterministic based on the input geometry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Extent: If the mesh consists of a single point or all vertices are identical, maxextent is 0, leading to division by zero. A guard clause is required. Variance normalization scales a mesh so that the mean squared distance from its center of mass is 1. Unlike Mesh Normalization which uses the bounding box extent, this method uses the covariance of the vertex positions. Steps: 1. Compute the center of mass (COM) of the vertices. 2. Translate the mesh to the origin: v'i = vi - COM. 3. Compute the covariance matrix C of the translated vertices. 4. Compute the scale factor s using the trace of the covariance matrix: s = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{tr}(C)}}. 5. Apply the scale: v''i = v'i \times s. 6. Translate back to the original center of mass: v'''i = v''i + COM. Formula: s = \frac{1}{\sqrt{C{00} + C{11} + C{22}}} where C{ij} are the diagonal elements of the covariance matrix. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of vertices. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if performed in-place. Strengths: Simple, fast, and ensures the model fits within a known canonical space [-1, 1]^3. Limitations: Does not account for the internal distribution of the mesh, only its outer bounds. Thin structures or outliers can dominate the scale factor, potentially shrinking important features. When to use: Standard preprocessing for SDF generation and voxelization where a canonical bounding box is required. Where it is used: Standard preprocessing step for Signed Distance Field (SDF) generation and voxelization, ensuring consistent scale and position for downstream tasks. name: SDF Grid Resampling from File
body: Reads a raw Signed Distance Field (SDF) text file, parses its grid resolution, bounding box, and voxel size, then resamples it to a target cubic grid resolution using coordinate mapping and clamping. It differs from sibling methods by handling non-cubic source grids and normalizing the spatial extent to a centered bounding box before interpolation. Inputs: filepath: Path to the raw SDF text file. targetgridres: Integer target cubic resolution for the output SDF grid. targetboundingboxmin: 3D vector defining the minimum corner of the target bounding box in physical space. targetboundingboxmax: 3D vector defining the maximum corner of the target bounding box in physical space. targetvoxelsize: Physical voxel size for the target grid. Outputs: targetgrid: A 3D tensor of shape (targetgridres, targetgridres, targetgridres) containing the resampled SDF values. Data Structures: Source Grid: A 3D array of size gridresx x gridresy x gridresz. Target Grid: A 3D array of size targetgridres x targetgridres x targetgridres. Points Tensor: A 2D tensor of shape (N, 3) where N = targetgridres^3, representing physical coordinates. Steps: 1. Parse Header: Read the first line to extract gridresx, gridresy, gridresz. Read the second line to extract boundingboxminx, boundingboxminy, boundingboxminz. Read the third line to extract voxelsize. 2. Compute Source Bounds: Calculate boundingboxmaxx = boundingboxminx + voxelsize (gridresx - 1). Similarly compute Y and Z bounds. 3. Normalize Extent: Compute minboundingboxmin = min(boundingboxminx, boundingboxminy, boundingboxminz) and maxboundingboxmax = max(boundingboxmaxx, boundingboxmaxy, boundingboxmaxz). Compute maxdist = max(boundingboxmaxx - boundingboxminx, boundingboxmaxy - boundingboxminy, boundingboxmaxz - boundingboxminz). 4. Initialize Source Grid: Create a 3D array of size gridresx x gridresy x gridresz initialized to 2.0. 5. Read Data: Read SDF values from the file in Z, Y, X order (outer loop Z, middle loop Y, inner loop X) and assign to grid[k][j][i]. 6. Generate Target Coordinates: Create linear spaces linearspacex, linearspacey, linearspacez from 0 to targetgridres - 1. Generate all combinations to form a 2D tensor of shape (N, 3). 7. Map to Physical Space: Construct boundingminmatrix by repeating boundingboxmin N times. Construct movetocentermatrix with offsets movex = (maxdist - (boundingboxmaxx - boundingboxminx)) / 2, similarly for Y and Z. Calculate physical points using points = boundingminmatrix + (targetvoxelsize maxdist / (targetboundingboxmax - targetboundingboxmin)) pointsindices - movetocentermatrix. 8. Clamp Points: Clamp out-of-bounds points to the nearest face of the source bounding box to prevent memory access errors. 9. Compute Indices: Calculate voxelminpointindex = floor((points - min) / voxelsize).clamp(max=gridres-2). 10. Interpolate: Call calculatesdfvalue with points and indices to perform trilinear interpolation. 11. Reshape: Reshape the result to (targetgridres, targetgridres, targetgridres). Parameters: targetgridres: Typical value 64 or higher. targetvoxelsize: Typical value 0.002. Pitfalls: Points falling outside the source bounding box must be clamped to the nearest face to prevent out-of-bounds memory access during interpolation. Round errors in bounding box calculation can be mitigated by adding a small epsilon (e.g., 0.0001) to boundingboxmax. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def readsdf(filepath, targetgridres, targetboundingboxmin, targetboundingboxmax, targetvoxelsize): with open(filepath) as file: # 1. Parse Header line = file.readline() gridres = line.split() gridresx, gridresy, gridresz = int(gridres[0]), int(gridres[1]), int(gridres[2]) line = file.readline() boundingboxmin = line.split() boundingboxminx, boundingboxminy, boundingboxminz = float(boundingboxmin[0]), float(boundingboxmin[1]), float(boundingboxmin[2]) line = file.readline() voxelsize = float(line) # 2. Compute Source Bounds boundingboxmaxx = boundingboxminx + voxelsize (gridresx - 1) boundingboxmaxy = boundingboxminy + voxelsize (gridresy - 1) boundingboxmaxz = boundingboxminz + voxelsize (gridresz - 1) # 3. Normalize Extent minboundingboxmin = min(boundingboxminx, boundingboxminy, boundingboxminz) maxboundingboxmax = max(boundingboxmaxx, boundingboxmaxy, boundingboxmaxz) maxdist = max(boundingboxmaxx - boundingboxminx, boundingboxmaxy - boundingboxminy, boundingboxmaxz - boundingboxminz) # 4. Initialize Source Grid grid = torch.full((gridresx, gridresy, gridresz), 2.0) # 5. Read Data (Z, Y, X order) for i in range(gridresz): for j in range(gridresy): for k in range(gridresx): val = file.readline() if val: grid[k, j, i] = float(val) # 6. Generate Target Coordinates N = targetgridres 3 linearspace = torch.linspace(0, targetgridres - 1, targetgridres) xx, yy, zz = torch.meshgrid(linearspace, linearspace, linearspace, indexing='ij') pointsindices = torch.stack((xx, yy, zz), dim=-1).reshape(-1, 3) # 7. Map to Physical Space minx = torch.full((N, 1), boundingboxminx) miny = torch.full((N, 1), boundingboxminy) minz = torch.full((N, 1), boundingboxminz) boundingminmatrix = torch.cat((minx, miny, minz), 1) movetocenterx = torch.full((N, 1), (maxdist - (boundingboxmaxx - boundingboxminx)) / 2) movetocentery = torch.full((N, 1), (maxdist - (boundingboxmaxy - boundingboxminy)) / 2) movetocenterz = torch.full((N, 1), (maxdist - (boundingboxmaxz - boundingboxminz)) / 2) movetocentermatrix = torch.cat((movetocenterx, movetocentery, movetocenterz), 1) scale = (targetvoxelsize maxdist) / (targetboundingboxmax - targetboundingboxmin) points = boundingminmatrix + scale pointsindices - movetocentermatrix # 8. Clamp Points points[:, 0] = torch.clamp(points[:, 0], boundingboxminx, boundingboxmaxx) points[:, 1] = torch.clamp(points[:, 1], boundingboxminy, boundingboxmaxy) points[:, 2] = torch.clamp(points[:, 2], boundingboxminz, boundingboxmaxz) # 9. Compute Indices mintensor = torch.tensor([boundingboxminx, boundingboxminy, boundingboxminz]) voxelminpointindex = torch.floor((points - mintensor) / voxelsize).clamp(max=gridresx-2) voxelminpointindex[:, 1] = voxelminpointindex[:, 1].clamp(max=gridresy-2) voxelminpointindex[:, 2] = voxelminpointindex[:, 2].clamp(max=gridresz-2) # 10. Interpolate (Trilinear) def trilinearinterpolate(grid, points, indices): i0, j0, k0 = indices[:, 0].long(), indices[:, 1].long(), indices[:, 2].long() i1, j1, k1 = i0 + 1, j0 + 1, k0 + 1 x = (points[:, 0] - (mintensor[0] + i0 voxelsize)) / voxelsize y = (points[:, 1] - (mintensor[1] + j0 voxelsize)) / voxelsize z = (points[:, 2] - (mintensor[2] + k0 voxelsize)) / voxelsize c00 = grid[i0, j0, k0] (1-x) + grid[i1, j0, k0] x c01 = grid[i0, j0, k1] (1-x) + grid[i1, j0, k1] x c10 = grid[i0, j1, k0] (1-x) + grid[i1, j1, k0] x c11 = grid[i0, j1, k1] (1-x) + grid[i1, j1, k1] x r0 = c00 (1-y) + c10 y r1 = c01 (1-y) + c11 y return r0 (1-z) + r1 z targetvalues = trilinearinterpolate(grid, points, voxelminpointindex) # 11. Reshape targetgrid = targetvalues.reshape(targetgridres, targetgridres, targetgridres) return targetgrid Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the target grid, dominated by coordinate mapping and interpolation. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the target grid and intermediate tensors. Strengths: Handles non-cubic source grids; normalizes spatial extent; robust against out-of-bounds access. Limitations: Dependent on the specific file format (Z, Y, X order); requires explicit bounding box parsing. When to use: When converting pre-computed SDF files to a uniform resolution for training or rendering. When not to use: When real-time generation from meshes is required. Originated in the SDFDiff project (Yue Jiang et al., CVPR 2020) for differentiable rendering of SDFs. It is used to load pre-computed SDF datasets into a uniform format for neural network training. name: Sparse VDB SDF Generation
head: OpenVDB SDF, meshToDistanceVdbVolume
body: A method that converts a triangle mesh into a sparse, tree-structured signed or unsigned distance grid using OpenVDB, storing only active voxels near the surface for memory efficiency. It differs from dense voxelization by dynamically allocating memory only for the narrow band around the mesh, making it suitable for large or complex models where ray-marched rendering or fast implicit queries are required. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh file (e.g., STL format). Output: A VdbVolume object containing the sparse distance field. Optionally, a reconstructed mesh can be extracted from the volume. Data Structures: MeshToVolumeParams: Configuration structure containing surfaceOffset (integer for active voxel layers), type (enum for Signed or Unsigned distance), voxelSize (Vector3f for physical voxel dimensions), and outXf (AffineXf3f for spatial shifting). GridToMeshSettings: Configuration structure for reconstruction containing voxelSize (matching generation dimensions) and isoValue (float for the isosurface threshold). Steps: 1. Load the input mesh from a file. 2. Initialize the MeshToVolumeParams configuration object. 3. Set surfaceOffset to 3 to define the active voxel band width. 4. Determine type by checking if the mesh topology is closed, assigning Signed if true and Unsigned otherwise. 5. Calculate voxelSize by querying suggestVoxelSize with a target of 10 million voxels and wrapping the result in a diagonal vector. 6. Initialize voxelsShift as an identity transformation matrix and assign it to params.outXf. 7. Call meshToDistanceVdbVolume with the mesh and parameters to generate the sparse volume. 8. Initialize GridToMeshSettings with the calculated voxelSize and an isovalue of 0.0. 9. Call gridToMesh on the volume data and settings to extract a triangle mesh. 10. Apply the shift transformation to the extracted mesh to restore its original spatial position. Formulas: voxelSize = Vector3f.diagonal(suggestVoxelSize(mesh, 1e7)). isoValue = 0.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from meshlib import mrmeshpy as mm mesh = mm.loadMesh("mesh.stl") params = mm.MeshToVolumeParams() params.surfaceOffset = 3 if mesh.topology.isClosed(): params.type = mm.MeshToVolumeParams.Type.Signed else: params.type = mm.MeshToVolumeParams.Type.Unsigned params.voxelSize = mm.Vector3f.diagonal(mm.suggestVoxelSize(mesh, 1e7)) voxelsShift = mm.AffineXf3f() params.outXf = voxelsShift vdbVolume = mm.meshToDistanceVdbVolume(mesh, params) gSettings = mm.GridToMeshSettings() gSettings.voxelSize = params.voxelSize gSettings.isoValue = 0.0 # Standard SDF isosurface threshold offMesh = mm.gridToMesh(vdbVolume.data, gSettings) offMesh.transform(voxelsShift) mm.saveMesh(offMesh, "outmesh.stl") Parameters: surfaceOffset: Integer specifying the number of voxel layers around the surface to mark as active. type: Enum indicating Signed for closed meshes or Unsigned for open meshes. voxelSize: Vector3f defining the physical size of each voxel, calculated to target approximately 10 million voxels. outXf: AffineXf3f transformation matrix applied to shift output voxels relative to the original mesh. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The input mesh must be topologically closed for Signed distance calculation, otherwise Unsigned must be selected. The isoValue for reconstruction is specified in voxel units, not world units. The shift matrix must be applied to the reconstructed mesh to align it with the original coordinate space. Converts explicit surfaces to Truncated Signed Distance Fields. Choose when truncation is required for integration. Normalizes SDF datasets for consistent scaling. Choose when preparing data for machine learning or standardized pipelines. Memory Efficiency: High. Stores only active voxels near the surface, making it suitable for large or complex models. Performance: Fast queries due to sparse tree structure. Use Cases: Ray-marched rendering, workflows requiring fast implicit queries without storing every voxel. Limitations: Not suitable for dense volume rendering where every voxel is needed. Requires closed mesh for signed distances. Originated in the MeshLib library, which provides Python and C++ bindings for mesh processing and voxelization. Developed to address the need for scalable, production-grade SDF generation for large models. name: Slice-based SDF Voxelization
head: Parity-based Voxelization, Ray-cast Voxelization
body: Slice-based SDF Voxelization computes a Signed Distance Field (SDF) for a triangulated surface mesh by iterating over a 3D grid, determining inside/outside status via ray-casting parity on 2D slices, and sampling the exact mesh distance at each voxel center. It differs from Signed Distance Field from Mesh by explicitly using 2D slice intersections to determine topological containment rather than relying on global distance field propagation or hierarchical structures for sign determination. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangulated surface mesh (e.g.,.stl format). Parameters: resolution: Grid spacing in world units. Must be a finite number greater than 10^{-6}. narrowband: Optional non-negative finite float specifying the maximum absolute SDF value for a voxel to be retained. Defaults to keeping all inside voxels if omitted. phasesphere: Optional array [cx, cy, cz, r] defining a sphere. Voxels inside this sphere are marked with phase = 1. Output: A list of ParticleData records containing voxel coordinates, SDF, phase, and auxiliary fields. Data Structures: ParticleData: A struct stored in a contiguous Vec or parallel arrays with the following fields: x: f32, y: f32, z: f32: Voxel center coordinates. sdf: f32: Signed distance value. phase: u32 (or i32): Phase indicator (0 or 1). labelid: u32: Label identifier (zero-initialized). fiberx: f32, fibery: f32: Auxiliary fields (zero-initialized). Algorithm Steps: 1. Validation: Check resolution and narrowband. If resolution \le 10^{-6}, negative, NaN, or Infinity, abort to prevent division by zero or excessive resource allocation. If narrowband is provided and is negative, NaN, Infinity, or NegInfinity, abort. Zero is valid and retains only voxels exactly on the surface. 2. Grid Bounds: Determine the bounding box of the mesh and compute grid dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz based on the bounding box and resolution. 3. Slice Processing (Parallel over Y, Z): For each fixed y and z coordinate in the grid: a. Ray Casting: Cast a ray along the +X direction from x{start} = bounds{min}.x - 1.0 to x{end} = bounds{max}.x + 1.0 at the current (y, z) plane. b. Intersection Collection: Collect all intersection X-coordinates into a list hitxs. To handle grazing intersections or precision issues, the ray origin is shifted by a small epsilon (10^{-4}) after each hit to find subsequent intersections. Limit the number of hits to 100,000 to prevent excessive memory usage. c. Sorting: Sort hitxs in ascending order to ensure consistent parity calculation. 4. Voxel Evaluation (Parallel over X): For each voxel index ix in the current slice: a. Coordinate Calculation: Compute the voxel center x = bounds{min}.x + (ix \cdot resolution) + (resolution \cdot 0.5). b. Inside/Outside Check: Calculate the number of intersections to the right of the voxel center using binary search (partition point) on the sorted hitxs list: \text{intersections\to\right} = \text{len}(\text{hit\xs}) - \text{partition\point}(|hx| \ hx \le x) Determine inside status: \text{is\inside} = (\text{intersections\to\right} \pmod 2 \neq 0) c. Distance Calculation: Compute the Euclidean distance d from the voxel center to the mesh surface using a point-to-mesh distance function. d. SDF Assignment: \text{sdf} = \begin{cases} -d & \text{if } \text{is\inside} \\ d & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} e. Filtering: If surfaceonly mode is active, check for geometric intersection between the voxel cuboid and the mesh. If no intersection, skip. If narrowband is provided, keep the voxel only if |\text{sdf}| \le \text{narrow\band}. Otherwise, keep if sdf \le 0.0 (inside). f. Phase Assignment: If phasesphere is provided, check if the voxel center lies within the sphere (\text{distance}^2 \le r^2). Set phase = 1 if inside, else phase = 0. g. Output: Push a ParticleData record with the computed values to the output list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from bisect import bisectright class ParticleData: def init(self, x, y, z, sdf, phase, labelid, fiberx, fibery): self.x = x; self.y = y; self.z = z; self.sdf = sdf self.phase = phase; self.labelid = labelid self.fiberx = fiberx; self.fibery = fibery def slicebasedsdfvoxelization(mesh, boundsmin, boundsmax, resolution, narrowband=None, phasesphere=None, surfaceonly=False): if resolution <= 1e-6 or not math.isfinite(resolution): raise ValueError("Invalid resolution") if narrowband is not None and (narrowband < 0 or not math.isfinite(narrowband)): raise ValueError("Invalid narrowband") nx = int((boundsmax.x - boundsmin.x) / resolution) ny = int((boundsmax.y - boundsmin.y) / resolution) nz = int((boundsmax.z - boundsmin.z) / resolution) outputparticles = [] for iy in range(ny): for iz in range(nz): y = boundsmin.y + (iy resolution) + (resolution 0.5) z = boundsmin.z + (iz resolution) + (resolution 0.5) startx = boundsmin.x - 1.0 maxdist = (max(boundsmax.x, mesh.boundsmax.x) - startx) + 1.0 hitxs = [] currentx = startx while True: # Cast ray along +X to find nearest triangle intersection hittoi = castrayalongx(currentx, y, z, maxdist) if hittoi is None: break hitxs.append(currentx + hittoi) currentx += hittoi + 1e-4 if len(hitxs) > 100000: break hitxs.sort() for ix in range(nx): x = boundsmin.x + (ix resolution) + (resolution 0.5) if surfaceonly: # Check if voxel cuboid intersects mesh if not checkcuboidintersection(x, y, z, resolution, mesh): continue hitsleftorat = bisectright(hitxs, x) intersectionstoright = len(hitxs) - hitsleftorat isinside = (intersectionstoright % 2 != 0) # Compute Euclidean distance from voxel center to mesh surface distance = computepointtomeshdistance(x, y, z, mesh) sdf = -distance if isinside else distance keep = False if narrowband is not None: keep = abs(sdf) <= narrowband else: keep = sdf <= 0.0 if not keep: continue phase = 0 if phasesphere is not None: dx = x - phasesphere[0] dy = y - phasesphere[1] dz = z - phasesphere[2] r = phasesphere[3] if (dxdx + dydy + dzdz) <= (rr): phase = 1 outputparticles.append(ParticleData( x=x, y=y, z=z, sdf=sdf, phase=phase, labelid=0, fiberx=0.0, fibery=0.0)) return outputparticles Time Complexity: O(Ny Nz \cdot (K \log K + Nx \log K)), where Ny, Nz are grid dimensions, K is the number of triangle intersections per slice, and Nx is the number of voxels per slice. Sorting hitxs takes O(K \log K), and binary search for each voxel takes O(\log K). Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for the output particles, plus O(K) per slice for intersection storage. Performance: Parallelization over Y and Z slices ensures fine-grained workload distribution. Iterating X sequentially within a slice optimizes spatial cache locality for BVH traversal. Strengths: Robust inside/outside determination via parity; exact SDF values; supports narrow bands and phase tracking. Limitations: Performance degrades with high triangle counts per slice (K); limited by the 100,000 hit cap per slice. The method is described in. It is designed for processing triangulated surface meshes (e.g.,.stl files) into signed distance fields for volume rendering or simulation. voxelizer-rs, https://github.com/lhemerly/voxelizer-rs, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: SDF-based Binary Voxelization
head: Level Set Voxelization, SDF Voxelization
body: SDF-based Binary Voxelization converts a continuous Signed Distance Field (SDF) into a discrete binary volume representation. It solves the problem of discretizing implicit surfaces defined by distance fields into a grid of occupied and unoccupied voxels. It differs from Dense Volume SDF Generation by discarding the continuous distance values in favor of a hard binary classification, and from Signed Distance Field (SDF) Generation from Scanned Surfaces by operating on an existing SDF rather than generating one from point clouds. Inputs: A 3D grid of signed distance values (e.g., MeshSignedDistanceGrid). Outputs: A 3D boolean bitmap (Bitmap3) where each voxel indicates occupancy. Data Structures: MeshSignedDistanceGrid: A 3D array storing float values representing the signed distance to the surface at each grid point. Bitmap3: A 3D array of bool values. Dimensions match the input SDF grid. Steps: 1. Initialize a Bitmap3 object with dimensions identical to the input MeshSignedDistanceGrid. 2. Iterate through every index (i, j, k) in the Bitmap3 grid. 3. Retrieve the signed distance value d from the SDF at the corresponding index: d = \text{SDF}[i, j, k]. 4. Evaluate the occupancy condition: If d < 0, the point is inside the surface. Set Bitmap3[i, j, k] = true. Otherwise (d \ge 0), the point is outside or on the surface. Set Bitmap3[i, j, k] = false. Args: sdfgrid: A 3D grid where each cell contains a float representing the signed distance to the nearest surface. Returns: A 3D boolean grid where True indicates inside the surface (negative distance) and False indicates outside (non-negative distance). """ # Get dimensions from the input SDF grid dimx = sdfgrid.width dimy = sdfgrid.height dimz = sdfgrid.depth # Initialize output binary grid with same dimensions # Implementation note: Initialize with False (outside) by default binarygrid = Grid3Dbool # Iterate over all indices in the grid for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): # Retrieve signed distance value at current index distance = sdfgrid.getvalue(x, y, z) # Set voxel to true (inside) if distance is negative, otherwise false if distance < 0: binarygrid.setvalue(x, y, z, True) else: binarygrid.setvalue(x, y, z, False) return binarygrid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Distance: Points exactly on the surface (d=0) are classified as outside (false). This creates a "hollow" shell if the surface thickness is negligible compared to voxel size. Precision: Floating-point comparison errors near d=0 may cause jitter in the binary boundary. A small epsilon threshold is sometimes used, but the standard method uses strict inequality d < 0. Boundary Conditions: The grid boundaries must align with the SDF domain. No extrapolation is performed; voxels outside the SDF domain are not generated. Constructs a Level-of-Detail (LOD) representation for a scene by downsampling high-resolution binary voxels and Signed Distance Fields (SDFs), extracting surface intersections along axes, and storing them in a sparse pointer/data structure per grid cell. It differs from standard binary voxelization by preserving continuous surface geometry information (intersections and normals) at lower resolutions, enabling more accurate ground truth generation for neural rendering or implicit surface reconstruction tasks. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of voxels in the grid. Each voxel requires one lookup and one comparison. Memory Complexity: O(N) bits (or bytes, depending on implementation) for the output bitmap. The input SDF requires O(N) floats. Performance: Extremely fast as it involves no geometric intersection calculations or ray marching, only array traversal. Strengths: Simple to implement; deterministic; preserves the exact resolution of the input SDF. Limitations: Loses sub-voxel geometric detail; suffers from aliasing if the SDF resolution is insufficient relative to the surface curvature. When to use: When a discrete occupancy grid is required for downstream processing (e.g., marching cubes, neural radiance fields) and the SDF is already available. When not to use: When sub-voxel accuracy is critical and the SDF resolution is low; when memory is extremely constrained and a sparse representation is preferred. This method is a standard post-processing step in pipelines that generate meshes from SDFs. It is described in the context of creating "Minecraft-style" voxel meshes from signed distance fields. name: 3D Voxel Grid Smoothing
head: 3D Box Filter, Voxel Grid Smoothing
body: 3D Voxel Grid Smoothing is a post-processing step applied to a discrete 3D voxel grid to reduce noise, aliasing artifacts, and high-frequency irregularities before subsequent operations such as isosurface extraction or gradient calculation. It works by applying a separable 3D convolution using a small kernel (typically a 1D triangular filter of size 3) to average voxel values over a local neighborhood. Unlike Binary Voxel RLE Encoding which focuses on storage compression, or Signed Distance Field Voxelization which computes geometric distance, this method operates directly on the scalar or vector values within the grid cells to produce a smoother field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid voxelValues of dimensions W \times H \times D (width, height, depth). The values can be scalars (e.g., density, alpha) or vectors (e.g., gradients). Output: A smoothed voxel grid of the same dimensions. Data Structures: voxelValues: A 1D array or contiguous memory buffer representing the 3D grid. INDEX(x, y, z): A macro or function mapping 3D coordinates to the 1D linear index. For row-major order where x is the fastest varying dimension: \text{INDEX}(x, y, z) = x + y \cdot W + z \cdot W \cdot H where W is the width, H is the height, and D is the depth. stencil: A 1D array of weights for the convolution kernel. For the standard implementation, stencil = [0.5, 1.0, 0.5]. voxelValues: A temporary buffer of the same size as voxelValues used to store intermediate results during an iteration to prevent data races or overwriting. Parameters: SmoothIterations: The number of times the smoothing filter is applied sequentially. Default is often 1, but can be higher for aggressive smoothing. If 0, smoothing is skipped. stencil: The 1D convolution kernel weights. The standard kernel is \{0.5, 1.0, 0.5\}, which corresponds to a triangular filter in 1D. Algorithm Steps: 1. If SmoothIterations is 0, return voxelValues unchanged. 2. Allocate voxelValues of size W \times H \times D. 3. Loop iter from 0 to SmoothIterations - 1: 4. For each voxel (x, y, z) where 0 \le x < W, 0 \le y < H, 0 \le z < D: 5. Initialize sum = 0.0 and weightSum = 0.0. 6. For each neighbor offset (dx, dy, dz) where dx, dy, dz \in \{-1, 0, 1\}: 7. Calculate neighbor coordinates: nx = x + dx, ny = y + dy, nz = z + dz. 8. Check boundary conditions: if 0 \le nx < W and 0 \le ny < H and 0 \le nz < D: 9. Calculate weight: w = \text{stencil}[dx+1] \times \text{stencil}[dy+1] \times \text{stencil}[dz+1]. 10. Accumulate value: sum += voxelValues[INDEX(nx, ny, nz)] w. 11. Accumulate weight: weightSum += w. 12. Normalize: If weightSum > 0, voxelValues[INDEX(x, y, z)] = sum / weightSum. Else, voxelValues[INDEX(x, y, z)] = 0.0. 13. Copy voxelValues back to voxelValues (e.g., using memcpy or element-wise assignment). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothvoxelgrid(voxelvalues, width, height, depth, stencil, iterations): """ Applies 3D voxel grid smoothing using a separable box filter. Args: voxelvalues: 1D list or array of size widthheightdepth. width: Grid width (x-dimension). height: Grid height (y-dimension). depth: Grid depth (z-dimension). stencil: 1D list of 3 floats, e.g., [0.5, 1.0, 0.5]. iterations: Number of smoothing passes. Returns: Smoothed voxelvalues array. """ if iterations <= 0: return voxelvalues # Helper to calculate linear index def index(x, y, z): return x + y width + z width height # Temporary buffer for the current iteration tempvalues = [0.0] (width height depth) for in range(iterations): for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): currentsum = 0.0 weightsum = 0.0 # Iterate over 3x3x3 neighborhood for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: nx = x + dx ny = y + dy nz = z + dz # Boundary check if 0 <= nx < width and 0 <= ny < height and 0 <= nz < depth: # Calculate separable weight w = stencil[dx + 1] stencil[dy + 1] stencil[dz + 1] # Accumulate weighted value currentsum += voxelvalues[index(nx, ny, nz)] w weightsum += w # Normalize if weightsum > 0: tempvalues[index(x, y, z)] = currentsum / weightsum else: tempvalues[index(x, y, z)] = 0.0 # Fallback for degenerate cases # Copy temp back to voxelvalues for next iteration voxelvalues = tempvalues[:] # Note: In a real implementation, swap buffers to avoid allocation/copy overhead # tempvalues = [0.0] (width height depth) # Re-initialize if reusing buffer return voxelvalues A generalization of the parent method that applies a 3D convolution using a uniform box filter or arbitrary odd-sized cubic kernel to average voxel values over a configurable receptive field. Unlike the parent method which is fixed to a size-3 triangular kernel, this variant allows for larger kernels (e.g., 5 \times 5 \times 5) to achieve broader neighborhood averaging or aggressive downsampling. It is chosen when stronger smoothing or multi-scale analysis is required. Link: 3D Box Filter for Voxel Averaging. A filtering step specifically applied to gradient vectors (RGB components of a volume texture) to smooth them out and prevent high irregularities. It averages the surrounding N^3 samples (where N is an odd number, default 3) and normalizes the resulting vector if non-zero. It is used when gradients are computed for transfer functions or lighting and need to be stabilized before further processing. Link: Volume Rendering 102: Transfer Functions. A method that removes scattered noise voxels by iteratively applying a 3D convolution with a filled circle kernel and zeroing out voxels below a threshold. It uses a kernel defined by kernelsize and radius, normalizes it, and repeats the convolution and thresholding process for a specified number of repeats (default 20). It is chosen for cleaning sparse or noisy volumetric data, such as in Plenoxels, where isolated artifacts are common. Link: DanJbk/Plenoxels. Time Complexity: O(I \cdot W \cdot H \cdot D \cdot K^3), where I is the number of iterations, W,H,D are grid dimensions, and K is the kernel size (3 for the standard method). The separable nature of the standard kernel reduces the effective constant factor compared to a full 3D convolution of the same radius. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for the input and temporary output buffers. Performance: The method is computationally inexpensive for small kernels and low iteration counts. It scales linearly with grid resolution. On modern hardware, it can be parallelized efficiently across voxels. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective at removing high-frequency noise and aliasing, handles boundaries gracefully via normalization. Limitations: Blurs sharp features and edges in the data. Large kernels or high iteration counts can lead to excessive smoothing and loss of detail. Boundary effects are handled by normalization but may cause slight intensity drops at edges if not careful. When to use: Before isosurface extraction to reduce jaggedness, or before gradient computation to stabilize normals. When not to use: When preserving sharp discontinuities or fine details is critical, or when real-time performance is constrained and the grid is very large. The method originates from implementations of isosurface extraction pipelines, specifically those involving marching cubes or similar algorithms where voxel grid quality directly impacts the resulting mesh. It is commonly used in volume rendering workflows to preprocess scalar fields. The specific implementation with a \{0.5, 1.0, 0.5\} stencil is documented in open-source repositories like mkazhdan/IsoSurfaceExtraction. Variants for gradient smoothing are discussed in educational resources on volume rendering transfer functions. Iterative noise removal techniques are found in modern neural rendering pipelines like Plenoxels. mkazhdan/IsoSurfaceExtraction, https://github.com/mkazhdan/IsoSurfaceExtraction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering 102: Transfer Functions, http://graphicsrunner.blogspot.com/2009/01/volume-rendering-102-transfer-functions.html, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) DanJbk/Plenoxels, https://github.com/DanJbk/Plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 3D Box Filter for Voxel Averaging
head: Box Filter, Voxel Averaging
body: A 3D convolution operation using a uniform box filter to average voxel values over a receptive field, typically used for smoothing or downsampling the grid. It builds on 3D Voxel Grid Smoothing by applying a separable 3D convolution with a 1D kernel of size 3, but generalizes this to an arbitrary odd-sized cubic kernel for broader neighborhood averaging. Unlike the parent method which is fixed to size 3, this method allows configurable receptive fields for varying degrees of smoothing or downsampling intensity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 4D tensor of shape [X, Y, Z, C] representing the voxel grid, where X, Y, Z are spatial dimensions and C is the channel count (typically 4 for RGBD data). Output: A 4D tensor of shape [X, Y, Z, C] containing the averaged voxel values. Data Structures: The input tensor is assumed to be in memory format [X, Y, Z, C] (HWC layout). The convolution kernel is a 5D tensor of shape [1, 1, K, K, K] where K is the receptive field size, repeated across channels if necessary depending on the implementation's grouping strategy. Parameters: receptivefieldsize (K): The spatial dimension of the averaging kernel. Must be an odd integer. Default value is 3. padding: Set to K // 2 to maintain the spatial dimensions of the output tensor. groups: Set to C (the number of channels) to apply the same kernel independently to each channel. Steps: 1. Permute and Convert: Permute the input tensor from shape [X, Y, Z, C] to [1, C, X, Y, Z] to match the standard convolution input format (NCHW). Convert data types to float if necessary. 2. Create Kernel: Construct a 3D kernel tensor of shape [1, 1, K, K, K] where every element has the uniform value 1.0 / K^3. 3. Repeat Kernel: Repeat the kernel tensor C times along the channel dimension (or use grouped convolution) to match the input channel count. In the reference implementation, the kernel is repeated 4 times for 4 channels. 4. Convolve: Apply 3D convolution (F.conv3d) using the constructed kernel, with padding equal to K // 2 and groups set to C. 5. Restore Shape: Squeeze the batch dimension (if added) and permute the result back from [1, C, X, Y, Z] to [X, Y, Z, C]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def boxfiltervoxelaveraging(tensor: torch.Tensor, receptivefieldsize: int = 3) -> torch.Tensor: """ Applies a 3D box filter to average voxel values over a receptive field. Args: tensor: Input tensor of shape [X, Y, Z, C]. receptivefieldsize: Size of the cubic kernel (must be odd). Default 3. Returns: Averaged tensor of shape [X, Y, Z, C]. """ # 1. Permute from [X, Y, Z, C] to [1, C, X, Y, Z] # Note: Assuming input is already float32 as per source context permuted = tensor.permute(3, 0, 1, 2).unsqueeze(0) # Shape: [1, C, X, Y, Z] # 2. Create kernel of size receptivefieldsize x receptivefieldsize x receptivefieldsize # with uniform value 1.0 / (receptivefieldsize 3) kernelvalue = 1.0 / (receptivefieldsize 3) kernel = torch.full( (1, 1, receptivefieldsize, receptivefieldsize, receptivefieldsize), kernelvalue, device=tensor.device, dtype=tensor.dtype) # 3. Repeat the kernel to match channels (or rely on groups parameter) # The source repeats it explicitly for 4 channels, but groups=C is more general. # We will use groups=C as per the source's F.conv3d call. # 4. Apply 3D convolution with padding = receptivefieldsize // 2 and groups=C # groups=C ensures each channel is convolved with its own copy of the kernel channels = tensor.shape[-1] result = F.conv3d( permuted, kernel, padding=receptivefieldsize // 2, groups=channels) # 5. Squeeze batch dimension and permute back to [X, Y, Z, C] # Result shape is [1, C, X, Y, Z] squeezed = result.squeeze(0) # Shape: [C, X, Y, Z] finalresult = squeezed.permute(1, 2, 3, 0) # Shape: [X, Y, Z, C] return finalresult Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The method uses padding equal to K // 2. This effectively performs zero-padding at the boundaries of the grid. If the grid represents a bounded volume, values near the edges may be biased towards zero if the surrounding voxels are not explicitly defined. The child method Receptive Field Voxel Extraction with Masking addresses this by masking out-of-bounds accesses. Kernel Size: The receptive field size must be an odd integer to ensure symmetric padding. Even sizes are not supported by the standard padding calculation K // 2 in this context. Precision: Input conversion to float is required for accurate averaging. Fixed-point or integer inputs should be cast to float before convolution. Extracts a local neighborhood of voxels around normalized sample points, masking out-of-bounds accesses and computing the mean of the valid neighborhood. It extends the planar 3×3 neighborhood by including depth neighbors, which the planar variant lacks. It builds on 3D Box Filter for Voxel Averaging by explicitly handling boundary conditions via masking rather than simple clamping or zero-padding, ensuring that partial neighborhoods at grid edges do not bias the average with invalid data. Downsamples the grid tensor using 3D average pooling with a specified receptive field size and optional stride. Steps: 1. Permute tensor from [X, Y, Z, 4] to [1, 4, X, Y, Z]. 2. Apply F.avgpool3d with kernel size (K, K, K) and optional stride. 3. Squeeze batch dimension and permute back to [X, Y, Z, 4]. Parameters: receptivefieldsize (default 3) and stride (default None, same as kernel size). Time and Memory Complexity: Time Complexity: O(X \cdot Y \cdot Z \cdot K^2) for the convolution operation, where K is the receptive field size. The constant factor is small due to the uniform kernel. Memory Complexity: O(X \cdot Y \cdot Z \cdot C) for the input and output tensors. The kernel memory is negligible (O(K^3)). Measured Performance: Performance depends on the hardware acceleration of 3D convolutions (e.g., CUDA cores in GPUs). The use of grouped convolution allows efficient parallel processing per channel. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement using standard deep learning libraries; effective for smoothing and downsampling; configurable receptive field size. Limitations: Zero-padding at boundaries can introduce artifacts; not suitable for non-uniform voxel grids without modification; computationally more expensive than simple averaging if K is large. When to Use: Use for smoothing voxel grids before isosurface extraction or rendering. Use when a configurable smoothing radius is needed. When Not to Use: Do not use when boundary accuracy is critical and masking is required (use Receptive Field Voxel Extraction with Masking instead). Do not use for downsampling with stride > 1 (use 3D Average Pooling or similar pooling methods). The method is derived from implementations in the Plenoxels project, which uses 3D convolutions for voxel grid processing. It is part of the broader family of voxelization and smoothing techniques used in neural radiance fields and 3D reconstruction. name: Receptive Field Voxel Extraction with Masking
head: Masked Voxel Averaging, Receptive Field Voxel Extraction
body: Receptive Field Voxel Extraction with Masking extracts a local neighborhood of voxels around normalized sample points, masking out-of-bounds accesses and computing the mean of the valid neighborhood. It builds on 3D Box Filter for Voxel Averaging by explicitly handling boundary conditions via masking rather than simple clamping or zero-padding, ensuring that partial neighborhoods at grid edges do not bias the average with invalid data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid and a set of normalized sample coordinates. Output: A tensor of averaged voxel values for each sample point. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Parameters: receptivefield: The size of the neighborhood to extract. Default value is 1 (implies kernelsize=0, single voxel). Steps: 1. Calculate kernelsize as receptivefield // 2. 2. Generate index tensors for x, y, z dimensions by adding offsets from -kernelsize to +kernelsize to the normalized sample coordinates. 3. Create boolean masks for each dimension indicating valid indices (\ge 0 and < dimension size). 4. Combine masks using logical AND to create a 3D validity mask. 5. Clamp indices to valid range [0, \text{dim}-1] to prevent runtime errors during indexing. 6. Extract voxel values using advanced indexing with the clamped indices. 7. Multiply extracted values by the validity mask (unsqueezed for broadcasting). 8. Compute the mean along the spatial dimensions (1, 2, 3) to get the averaged value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def receptivefieldvoxelextraction(grid, points, receptivefield=1): """ Extracts a local neighborhood of voxels around normalized sample points, masking out-of-bounds accesses and computing the mean of the valid neighborhood. Args: grid: 3D array of shape (D, H, W) containing voxel values. points: 2D array of shape (N, 3) containing normalized sample coordinates. receptivefield: Size of the neighborhood to extract. Returns: 1D array of shape (N,) containing the averaged voxel values. """ # Step 1: Calculate kernel size kernelsize = receptivefield // 2 offsets = list(range(-kernelsize, kernelsize + 1)) K = len(offsets) D, H, W = len(grid), len(grid[0]), len(grid[0][0]) results = [] for p in points: x, y, z = p # Step 2: Generate index tensors for x, y, z idxx = [x + k for k in offsets] idxy = [y + k for k in offsets] idxz = [z + k for k in offsets] # Step 3: Create boolean masks for valid indices maskx = [1 if 0 <= ix < W else 0 for ix in idxx] masky = [1 if 0 <= iy < H else 0 for iy in idxy] maskz = [1 if 0 <= iz < D else 0 for iz in idxz] # Step 5: Clamp indices to valid range [0, dim-1] clampedx = [max(0, min(W - 1, ix)) for ix in idxx] clampedy = [max(0, min(H - 1, iy)) for iy in idxy] clampedz = [max(0, min(D - 1, iz)) for iz in idxz] # Step 6 & 7: Extract voxel values and multiply by validity mask total = 0.0 validcount = 0 for i in range(K): for j in range(K): for l in range(K): # Step 4: Combine masks using logical AND valid = maskx[i] & masky[j] & maskz[l] if valid: total += grid[clampedz[l]][clampedy[j]][clampedx[i]] validcount += 1 # Step 8: Compute the mean along spatial dimensions results.append(total / validcount if validcount > 0 else 0.0) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: The masking logic ensures that out-of-bounds accesses do not contribute to the mean, preventing bias from invalid data. name: 3x3x3 Froxel Neighborhood
head: 27-tap Froxel Neighborhood
body: A spatial reconstruction method that extracts a 3×3×3 neighborhood of froxels around a sample point to incorporate spatial information from adjacent depth slices, applying additional smoothing across the volume's depth axis. It extends the planar 3×3 neighborhood by including depth neighbors, which the planar variant lacks. Inputs: A froxel grid containing volumetric data. A sampling index (uniform) defining the specific offset configuration. Outputs: A reconstructed froxel value for each sample point, derived from the 27 sampled neighbors. Data Structures: Sampling Offsets: A precomputed list of 27 integer offsets (dx, dy, dz), where each component ranges from -1 to 1. Shader Uniform: An integer index selecting the active offset list, updated per frame. Steps: 1. Retrieve the precomputed list of 27 offsets based on the current sampling index. 2. For each offset (dx, dy, dz) in the list, sample the froxel value at the corresponding neighbor position relative to the center. 3. Combine the 27 sampled values to produce the reconstructed output. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Neighborhood Size: 3×3×3, requiring exactly 27 samples per froxel. Sampling Index: A uniform integer provided each frame to select the offset list. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The method assumes valid neighbors; out-of-bounds accesses must be masked or clamped, following the parent method's masking logic. Performance: 27 samples per froxel is considered likely too many for real-time rendering contexts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sample3x3x3froxel(froxelgrid, centercoords, offsetlist): # offsetlist is a precomputed list of 27 (dx, dy, dz) tuples samples = [] for dx, dy, dz in offsetlist: nx, ny, nz = centercoords[0] + dx, centercoords[1] + dy, centercoords[2] + dz # Apply boundary masking inherited from parent method if 0 <= nx < froxelgrid.width and 0 <= ny < froxelgrid.height and 0 <= nz < froxelgrid.depth: samples.append(froxelgrid[nx, ny, nz]) # Standard averaging step return sum(samples) / len(samples) if samples else froxelgrid[centercoords] A lower-cost alternative using samples from the six nearby froxels and the center froxel (total 7 taps) to compute neighborhood bounds. It is analogous to the 4-tap nearest pixel neighborhood used in INSIDE. Implemented in Godot as precomputed lists of sampling offsets with a per-frame shader uniform for the sampling index. Used in the Frostbite engine's variance clipping bounds construction. Time Complexity: O(1) per froxel, but with a high constant factor due to 27 memory accesses and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory for offset lists; requires storage for the froxel grid. Performance: The 27-sample requirement is noted as likely too expensive for real-time rendering. Consequently, the 6-tap variant is often preferred in production engines like Frostbite for tasks such as variance clipping. Strengths: Provides superior smoothing across depth compared to planar neighborhoods. Limitations: High computational cost due to the number of samples. The method originates from research into temporal anti-aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering. It was implemented and tested in the Godot engine as part of a study on volumetric TAA algorithms. The findings were subsequently applied to the Frostbite engine, where variants of the neighborhood (specifically 6-tap) were used in variance clipping and anti-flicker implementations. name: Mean-Covered Voxel Intensity Sampling
body: Mean-Covered Voxel Intensity Sampling averages voxel intensities across mean-covered regions for each splat, explicitly handling the footprint pooling logic to smooth supervision signals. It computes bounding boxes based on scale indices and coverage masks, extracts sub-volumes, and returns their means. Inputs: volume: 3D tensor of voxel intensities (shape D \times H \times W). scales: List of scale indices or multipliers defining the footprint size for each splat. coveragemask: Boolean mask indicating valid splat centers or regions. volumemin, volumemax: Scalar bounds for normalization. normalize: Boolean flag to enable intensity normalization. Outputs: processed: Tensor of mean intensities corresponding to the splat footprints. Data Structures: volume: Stored as a contiguous 3D array or tensor. Indices are clamped to valid volume dimensions using torch.maximum and torch.minimum to prevent out-of-bounds access. coveragemask: Boolean tensor of the same spatial resolution as the base samples, identifying valid regions for pooling. Steps: 1. Base Sampling: Compute initial base samples using sampleintensitiesfromvolume with enablefootprintpooling=False to retrieve raw voxel values at specific coordinates. 2. Bounding Box Computation: If scales are valid and coveragemask exists, compute the voxel bounding boxes for each point based on the scale indices. 3. Index Clamping: Clamp the minimum indices (minidx) and maximum indices (maxidx) of the bounding boxes to the volume dimensions using torch.maximum and torch.minimum. 4. Region Mean Calculation: Iterate over each scaleindex: extract the region volume[z0:z1+1, y0:y1+1, x0:x1+1], compute its mean intensity, and update the output subset. 5. Normalization: If normalize is requested: check if volumemax > volumemin + 1e-8; if true, normalize and clamp to [0, 1]; otherwise, set processed values to 0.5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meancoveredvoxelintensitysampling(volume, scales, coveragemask, volumemin, volumemax, normalize): # Step 1: Get base samples without footprint pooling basesamples = sampleintensitiesfromvolume(volume, enablefootprintpooling=False) processed = torch.zeroslike(basesamples) # Step 2 & 3: Compute bounding boxes and clamp indices if scales is not None and coveragemask is not None: for scaleidx in scales: # The sources do not specify the exact bounding box computation logic minidx, maxidx = basesamples, basesamples # Bounding box calculation minidx = torch.maximum(minidx, torch.zeroslike(minidx)) maxidx = torch.minimum(maxidx, torch.tensor(volume.shape) - 1) # Step 4: Iterate over scaleindices to extract regions and compute means # The sources do not specify the exact iteration structure over splats for i in range(len(minidx)): z0, y0, x0 = minidx[i] z1, y1, x1 = maxidx[i] region = volume[z0:z1+1, y0:y1+1, x0:x1+1] meanval = torch.mean(region) processed[i] = meanval # Step 5: Normalization if normalize: if volumemax > volumemin + 1e-8: processed = (processed - volumemin) / (volumemax - volumemin) processed = torch.clamp(processed, 0.0, 1.0) else: processed = torch.fulllike(processed, 0.5) return processed Parameters: volumemin, volumemax: Scalar bounds for normalization. normalize: Boolean flag. Default behavior implies normalization is optional. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-bounds access: Clamping is required to prevent indexing errors when splats extend beyond volume boundaries. Zero-range volumes: If volumemax <= volumemin + 1e-8, normalization is skipped to avoid division by zero, defaulting to 0.5. An incremental algorithm to calculate the mean and standard deviation of an n \times n \times n region around each voxel in O(1) time, assuming CT values follow a normal distribution. It uses incremental updates for Sum1D, Sum2D, and Sum3D to compute averages and variance efficiently. Region size n is typically 15. Time Complexity: The incremental variant achieves O(1) time per voxel for computing mean and standard deviation of local neighborhoods. Performance: The incremental method was tested on a PC with Intel Q9550 CPU, 4 GB RAM, and GeForce GTX 1050 GPU, using 15 \times 15 \times 15 regions. Strengths: Explicit handling of footprint pooling logic. Efficient constant-time computation of local statistics using incremental sums. Limitations: Requires careful clamping and normalization logic. The incremental method assumes CT values follow a normal distribution. The method is implemented in the vgs repository for voxel-based supervision in Gaussian Splatting, specifically handling footprint pooling for volume rendering. The concept of fast local vicinity calculation for ambient occlusion in volume rendering was introduced in a 2019 paper on real-time CT visualization, which used incremental sums to compute local statistics for shading.
