name: Binvox File Parsing
head: Binvox File Parser, Binvox Header & RLE Voxel Reader, Binvox SVO Import, binvox loader
body: Binvox File Parsing is the method for importing the binary voxel (binvox) file format into a contiguous array or a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) structure. It converts a legacy run-length encoded (RLE) voxel representation into a format suitable for modern ray-casting or rasterization engines. Unlike raw voxel formats that store every voxel explicitly, binvox uses a compact binary RLE scheme, requiring specific handling to decompress the data correctly. The method consists of two phases: parsing the ASCII header and decompressing the binary RLE data into a flat array, optionally followed by constructing an SVO hierarchy. Input: A binary file or byte buffer containing the binvox data. Output: 1. A flat unsigned char array of size D^3 (where D is the dimension) representing the voxel grid. 2. (Optional) A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) structure built from the flat array. 1. Flat Voxel Array: A contiguous array of unsigned char (8-bit integers) with size D \times D \times D. 2. RLE Data Buffer: A byte array storing the raw binary RLE pairs read from the file. 3. SVO Node: Contains children (array of 8 references), occupancy (bitmask), and data.color (e.g., 0xff00ffff for internal nodes, 0 for empty leaves). 1. Header Parsing: Read the first line. It must start with "#binvox 1". If not, abort. Read the second line. It must start with "dim D D D". The sources specify D = 512 as the tested dimension. Note that the format requires cubic dimensions (width == height == depth), though exact power-of-2 enforcement is noted as a potential requirement or TODO in some implementations. Read and discard the next three lines: translate, scale, and data. 2. RLE Data Loading: Read the remainder of the file into a byte buffer rledata. Calculate rlesize as len(rledata) / 2. The data consists of pairs of bytes. 3. RLE Decompression: Allocate a flat array data of size D^3, initialized to 0. Iterate through rledata in pairs. For each pair at index i (where i ranges from 0 to rlesize - 1): value = rledata[i 2] count = rledata[i 2 + 1] If value != 0: Check if currentindex + count > D^3. If so, abort (panic). Fill data[currentindex... currentindex + count - 1] with value. Increment currentindex by count. Pitfall: Do not skip whitespace when reading the binary RLE section. Standard text parsing functions may skip zero bytes or misalign reads, corrupting the RLE stream. 4. SVO Construction (Optional): Initialize a nodes vector with one default root node. Initialize a stack with (0, 0, 0, 0, 8) representing (x, y, z, parentref, lod). The starting LOD is 8 for a 512^3 grid (512 = 2^9, so depth 8 covers the internal levels, with leaves at LOD 0). While the stack is not empty: Pop (x, y, z, parentref, lod). Get the parent node. Resize the nodes array if necessary to accommodate new children. Calculate the 8 child offsets based on x, y, z and lod. If lod == 0 (Leaf Level): Initialize a new node. Set occupancy to 0. For each of the 8 children (local indices 0-7): Calculate the flat index in data corresponding to this child's position in the 2 \times 2 \times 2 block. If data[flatindex] != 0: Set the corresponding bit in occupancy. Set children[i] to a new node reference. Increment placedvoxels. If occupancy is 0, set node.data.color to 0. If lod > 0 (Internal Node): Set node.data.color to 0xff00ffff. Set node.occupancy to 0xff (all 8 children occupied). For each of the 8 children: Set children[i] to a new node reference. Push (offset.x, offset.y, offset.z, childref, lod - 1) to the stack. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def importbinvoxsvo(filebytes: bytes): import io reader = io.BytesIO(filebytes) # 1. Header Parsing header = reader.readline() if not header.startswith(b"#binvox 1"): raise ValueError("Invalid binvox header") dimline = reader.readline() if not dimline.startswith(b"dim 512 512 512"): raise NotImplementedError("Unsupported dimension") dim = 512 capacity = dim dim dim # Discard translate, scale, data lines reader.readline() reader.readline() reader.readline() # 2. RLE Data Loading rledata = reader.read() rlesize = len(rledata) // 2 # 3. RLE Decompression data = bytearray(capacity) cur = 0 for i in range(rlesize): value = rledata[i 2] count = rledata[i 2 + 1] if value != 0: if cur + count > capacity: raise OverflowError("RLE exceeds capacity") for j in range(count): data[cur + j] = value cur += count # 4. SVO Construction class Node: def init(self): self.children = [None] 8 self.occupancy = 0 self.color = 0 nodes = [Node()] stack = [(0, 0, 0, 0, 8)] while stack: x, y, z, parentref, lod = stack.pop() parent = nodes[parentref] step = 1 << lod for i in range(8): dx = (i & 1) step dy = ((i >> 1) & 1) step dz = ((i >> 2) & 1) step cx, cy, cz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz childref = len(nodes) nodes.append(Node()) parent.children[i] = childref if lod == 0: node = nodes[childref] node.occupancy = 0 placedvoxels = 0 for k in range(8): vx = cx + (k & 1) vy = cy + ((k >> 1) & 1) vz = cz + ((k >> 2) & 1) flatidx = (vz dim + vy) dim + vx if data[flatidx] != 0: node.occupancy |= (1 << k) placedvoxels += 1 if placedvoxels == 0: node.color = 0 else: node = nodes[childref] node.color = 0xff00ffff node.occupancy = 0xff stack.append((cx, cy, cz, childref, lod - 1)) return nodes, data Dimensions: The binvox format requires cubic dimensions (W=H=D). The source examples use 512 \times 512 \times 512. RLE Pairs: Each pair consists of a value (1 byte) and a count (1 byte). Whitespace Skipping: When reading the binary RLE section, do not use text-based line reading or whitespace-skipping parsers. Zero bytes are valid RLE counts/values and must be read exactly. Dimension Support: The source implementation hardcodes 512 and panics on other dimensions. General implementations should parse the dimension from the header and validate it is cubic. Capacity Overflow: If the RLE data specifies a total count greater than D^3, the parser must abort. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of RLE pairs. Decompression is linear in the size of the RLE data. SVO construction is O(D^3) in the worst case (fully occupied) but proportional to the number of occupied voxels and tree depth. Memory Complexity: O(D^3) for the flat array. The SVO structure adds overhead for node objects, potentially reducing memory usage for sparse scenes compared to a dense grid, but increasing it for dense scenes due to node metadata. Performance: The RLE format is significantly more compact than raw voxels for sparse data. Decompression is fast. Building the SVO adds overhead but enables efficient ray traversal. Strengths: Compact storage for sparse voxel data; simple binary format. Limitations: Fixed dimension support in some implementations; RLE can be inefficient for highly complex, non-repetitive data; no color/normal data in the basic format (though extensions exist). The binvox format was developed for efficient storage and transmission of 3D voxel models, particularly in computer graphics and gaming. It uses a simple ASCII header followed by binary RLE data. The specific parsing method described here is from the svo-cpu project, which imports binvox files into a CPU-based Sparse Voxel Octree rasterizer. skyfex/svo-workbench, https://github.com/skyfex/svo-workbench, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marceline-cramer/svo-cpu, https://github.com/marceline-cramer/svo-cpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: IMS File Format & Image Stack Class
head: .ims
body: The IMS file format and imsbase class provide a mechanism for persisting and managing 3D image stacks (volumes) with typed pixel storage and extensible metadata segments. It solves the problem of storing volumetric data where pixel types are fixed at compile time via templates and metadata is stored as typed binary segments. It differs from generic binary voxel formats by embedding a rigid 16-byte header, supporting memory-mapped loading on Windows, and using a chunked write strategy to handle large volumes without buffer overflow. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume defined by width (W), height (H), and depth (D); a pixel type T; and a map of metadata segments. Output: A binary file with the.ims extension containing the header, pixel data, and segment data. Data Structures: The file layout is strictly sequential: 1. File Header (16 bytes): Bytes 0-2: ASCII 'IMS'. Byte 3: Encoding version (uint8, value 1). Bytes 4-7: Pixel type identifier (uint32, e.g., 0 for floats). Bytes 8-9: Width W (uint16). Bytes 10-11: Height H (uint16). Bytes 12-13: Depth D (uint16). Bytes 14-15: Number of segments S (uint16). 2. Pixel Data: Stored immediately after the header. Layout: Images sequentially, then rows within each image. First pixel is top-left, last is bottom-right. Total size: W \times H \times D \times \text{TPixelSize} bytes. 3. Segments (Sequential): Each segment consists of a header and data. Segment Header (8 bytes): Bytes 0-3: Segment type identifier (4 ASCII chars, packed into uint32). Bytes 4-7: Segment data size in bytes (uint32). Segment Data: Follows the segment header. Size matches the uint32 value in the segment header. Parameters: PixelTypeNo: Integer identifier for the pixel type (template argument). TPixelSize: Byte size of a single pixel (template argument, multiple of 1 byte). maxBuf: Chunk size for writing pixel data, set to 1 \ll 30 (1 GB). Steps: Save: 1. Open file for binary writing. 2. Set header segment count to current map size. 3. Write 16-byte header. 4. Write pixel data in chunks of maxBuf until exhausted. 5. Iterate segment map, write 8-byte segment header, then write segment data. Load: 1. Open file with read/write access and no buffering. 2. Create read-only file mapping. 3. Map view to memory. 4. Parse header fields. 5. Allocate pixel buffer and copy mapped data. 6. Parse segments sequentially. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct import sys import mmap import os def saveims(filename, width, height, depth, pixeldata, segments, pixelsize): """ pixeldata: flat array of pixels, size WHDpixelsize segments: list of tuples (typestr, databytes) pixelsize: byte size of a single pixel (TPixelSize) """ if not (0 <= width <= 65536 and 0 <= height <= 65536 and 0 <= depth <= 65536): raise ValueError("Dimensions must be within [0, 65536]") numsegments = len(segments) # Pixel type ID is a template argument; using 0 for floats as example pixeltypeid = 0 header = b'IMS' + struct.pack('<B', 1) + struct.pack('<I', pixeltypeid) + \ struct.pack('<HHH', width, height, depth) + struct.pack('<H', numsegments) with open(filename, 'wb') as f: f.write(header) # Write pixel data in chunks of maxBuf (1 GB) totalpixelbytes = width height depth pixelsize maxbuf = 1 << 30 offset = 0 while offset < totalpixelbytes: chunksize = min(maxbuf, totalpixelbytes - offset) f.write(pixeldata[offset: offset + chunksize]) offset += chunksize # Write segments isle = sys.byteorder == 'little' for segtypestr, segdata in segments: if len(segtypestr) != 4: raise ValueError("Segment type must be 4 chars") # Pack 4 ASCII chars into uint32 with endianness handling if isle: segtypeid = (ord(segtypestr[0]) | (ord(segtypestr[1]) << 8) | (ord(segtypestr[2]) << 16) | (ord(segtypestr[3]) << 24)) else: segtypeid = struct.unpack('<I', segtypestr.encode('ascii'))[0] segsize = len(segdata) segheader = struct.pack('<I', segtypeid) + struct.pack('<I', segsize) f.write(segheader) f.write(segdata) def loadims(filename, pixelsize): """ pixelsize: byte size of a single pixel (TPixelSize) Returns: headerdict, pixeldata, segments """ filesize = os.path.getsize(filename) with open(filename, 'r+b') as f: # Open file with read/write access and no buffering (platform-specific flags omitted for clarity) # Create read-only file mapping and map view to memory mm = mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESSREAD) if mm[0:3] != b'IMS': raise ValueError("Invalid IMS magic") if mm[3] != 1: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported version {mm[3]}") pixeltypeid = struct.unpackfrom('<I', mm, 4)[0] width, height, depth = struct.unpackfrom('<HHH', mm, 8) numsegments = struct.unpackfrom('<H', mm, 14)[0] # Allocate pixel buffer and copy mapped data totalpixelbytes = width height depth pixelsize pixeldata = mm[16: 16 + totalpixelbytes] # Parse segments sequentially segments = [] offset = 16 + totalpixelbytes for in range(numsegments): segtypeid = struct.unpackfrom('<I', mm, offset)[0] segsize = struct.unpackfrom('<I', mm, offset + 4)[0] offset += 8 segdata = mm[offset: offset + segsize] offset += segsize # Unpack type string (assuming little-endian for simplicity, or match save logic) segtypestr = bytes([segtypeid & 0xFF, (segtypeid >> 8) & 0xFF, (segtypeid >> 16) & 0xFF, (segtypeid >> 24) & 0xFF]).decode('ascii') segments.append((segtypestr, segdata)) mm.close() return {'width': width, 'height': height, 'depth': depth, 'pixeltypeid': pixeltypeid, 'numsegments': numsegments}, pixeldata, segments Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dimension Validation: Width, height, and depth must be within [0, 65536]. Values outside this range throw std::invalidargument. Windows Memory Allocation: On Windows, the stack size must be strictly less than 1 \ll 30 bytes. Exceeding this triggers an assertion failure. Endianness: Segment type strings are packed into uint32. The code detects little-endian architecture via (uint8t)(&v) == 1 and uses bitwise shifts; otherwise, it uses memcpy. Time Complexity: O(W \times H \times D) for initialization, copying, and file I/O. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times D) for the pixel buffer plus O(S) for segment storage, where S is the number of segments. Strengths: Supports memory-mapped loading on Windows for efficient access. Handles large volumes via chunked writing. Extensible metadata via segments. Limitations: Windows-specific memory mapping logic. Rigid header structure. Pixel type must be known at load time (template parameter in C++). When to Use: Suitable for tomography image stacks and metadata management where pixel types are homogeneous and known. When Not to Use: When cross-platform memory mapping is required without platform-specific code. When pixel types vary within the volume. The IMS file format and imsbase class were developed as part of the chmike/FastFDK project for loading, saving, and managing tomography image stacks and metadata segments. It provides a template-based approach to volume storage, allowing for type safety and efficient memory access. chmike/FastFDK, https://github.com/chmike/FastFDK, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Indexing and Bit Compression
head: Binary Voxel Bit Packing, Bit-packed Voxel Array
body: Voxel Indexing and Bit Compression maps 3D voxel coordinates to a 1D linear index and packs the resulting occupancy data into a compact bit-array, typically stored as an array of 64-bit integers. It solves the problem of efficiently storing sparse or dense binary voxel grids by reducing memory overhead and enabling parallel write operations via atomic bit-setting. It differs from Binary Voxel RLE Encoding by storing the raw bit-stream directly rather than compressing runs of identical values, and from RLE Index Computation by focusing on the storage format of the index itself rather than generating a lookup structure for RLE offsets. Inputs: 3D voxel grid dimensions (sizex, sizey, sizez); a set of occupied voxel coordinates (x, y, z). Outputs: A bit-packed array representing the occupancy status of the voxel grid. Data Structures: 1. Linear Index: A 1D integer representing the position of a voxel in the flattened grid. 2. Bit-Packed Array: An array of 64-bit unsigned integers (uint64t or unsigned long long) where each bit corresponds to one voxel. Steps: 1. Calculate Linear Index: For each occupied voxel at coordinates (x, y, z), compute its 1D index I using row-major ordering: I = x \cdot sizey \cdot sizez + y \cdot sizez + z where sizex, sizey, sizez are the dimensions of the voxel grid. 2. Initialize Storage: Allocate an array of 64-bit unsigned integers large enough to hold I{max} + 1 bits. The size of the array in elements is \lceil (sizex \cdot sizey \cdot sizez) / 64 \rceil. 3. Set Occupancy Bit: For each occupied voxel, set the bit at position I to 1. In a parallel implementation, this is done using atomic operations to ensure thread safety when multiple threads write to the same array concurrently. Determine the array index: arr\idx = I / 64. Determine the bit offset: bit\offset = I \pmod{64}. Perform atomic OR: atomicor(&array[arridx], 1 << bitoffset). 4. Handle Unoccupied Voxels: Voxels not explicitly set remain 0, indicating they are empty. Parameters: Bit Width: 64 bits per array element is standard for efficient alignment and atomic operations. Grid Dimensions: Must fit within the addressable range of the linear index. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The linear index must not overflow the integer type used for calculation. For large grids, 64-bit integers for the index calculation may be required even if the storage is bit-packed. Boundaries: Coordinates must be strictly within [0, sizex-1] \times [0, sizey-1] \times [0, sizez-1]. Out-of-bounds access causes undefined behavior or memory corruption. Atomicity: Without atomic operations, concurrent writes from multiple threads (e.g., in a GPU or multi-threaded CPU kernel) can result in lost updates or race conditions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def packvoxels(voxelcoords, gridsize): """ Pack a list of occupied voxel coordinates into a bit-compressed array. Args: voxelcoords: List of tuples (x, y, z) representing occupied voxels. gridsize: Tuple (sizex, sizey, sizez) defining the grid dimensions. Returns: numpy array of uint64 representing the bit-packed voxel grid. """ sizex, sizey, sizez = gridsize totalvoxels = sizex sizey sizez numuint64 = (totalvoxels + 63) // 64 # Initialize bit-packed array with zeros packedarray = np.zeros(numuint64, dtype=np.uint64) for (x, y, z) in voxelcoords: # Calculate 1D linear index index = x sizey sizez + y sizez + z # Calculate array index and bit offset arridx = index // 64 bitoffset = index % 64 # Set the bit (simulating atomic OR for single-threaded execution) # In a real parallel implementation, this would use atomic operations packedarray[arridx] |= (1 << bitoffset) return packedarray This variant reduces memory usage to 4 bytes per voxel by distributing 32 bits across X, Y, and Z coordinates in a 12+10+10 split, supporting volumes up to 4096 \times 1024 \times 1024. It packs coordinates into two GLSHORT values and unpacks them in a vertex program. For GPUs lacking bit shift operators, unpacking is emulated using multiplication by a fraction (via floor function) and subtraction. This approach trades computation for memory bandwidth efficiency, which is beneficial for large volumes. This variant extends bit packing to include dual vertices and intersection flags for efficient serialization to.vxz format. Dual vertices are packed by computing dualvertices = (dualvertices RES - voxelindices), clamping to [0, 1], and scaling to uint8. Intersection flags (3 boolean channels) are packed into a single uint8 where Bit 0 corresponds to channel 0, Bit 1 to channel 1, and Bit 2 to channel 2. This method is used in the O-Voxel library for GPU-accelerated volume rendering. Time Complexity: O(n) where n is the number of voxels in the bounding box, as each voxel requires a constant-time index calculation and bit set operation. Memory Complexity: O(V/8) bytes where V is the total number of voxels in the grid, as each voxel is stored as a single bit. Performance: Bit packing significantly reduces memory footprint compared to byte-per-voxel storage. Parallel atomic writes can achieve high throughput on multi-core CPUs and GPUs. Strengths: Extremely compact storage for binary occupancy data; simple indexing scheme; efficient for sparse data if combined with sparse access patterns. Limitations: Not suitable for storing per-voxel attributes (e.g., density, color) without additional structures; random access to specific voxels requires bit manipulation; not compressed for runs of zeros/ones like RLE. When to Use: When memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and only binary occupancy is needed; when parallel voxelization is required. When Not to Use: When per-voxel attributes are needed; when the grid is extremely sparse and RLE or sparse octrees are more efficient. Voxel indexing and bit compression is a fundamental technique in voxel-based rendering and geometry processing. It is widely used in GPU-accelerated volume rendering and mesh voxelization pipelines. The method is described in various implementations, including the topskychen/voxelizer repository, which uses atomic operations for parallel voxelization. The technique is also referenced in research on multiresolution MIP rendering and in the O-Voxel library for GPU-based volume rendering. topskychen/voxelizer, https://github.com/topskychen/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Multiresolution MIP Rendering of Large Volumetric Data Accelerated on Graphics Hardware, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/eurovis07/243-250, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) quantaji/o-voxel-gpu, https://github.com/quantaji/o-voxel-gpu, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: RLE Index Computation
head: ComputeIndex
body: RLE Index Computation generates a lookup structure that maps 3D voxel coordinates to their corresponding positions within a Run-Length Encoded (RLE) data stream. It solves the problem of efficiently locating non-zero voxel data without scanning the entire compressed volume. It differs from raw RLE storage by providing direct coordinate-to-offset mapping, enabling O(1) access to run headers, whereas sibling methods like Voxel Indexing and Bit Compression focus on the bit-level packing of the index itself. The method constructs a VoxelLocation array where each entry corresponds to a voxel in the 3D grid. Each entry stores the offset to the start of the RLE run containing that voxel and the position within that run. Inputs: rlevoxels: The RLE-encoded volume data, containing an array of run lengths. ilen, jlen, klen: The dimensions of the voxel grid along the x, y, and z axes, respectively. Outputs: voxelindex: An array of VoxelLocation structs, one for each voxel in the grid. If the grid is too large for the fixed-size index, this is set to NULL. Data Structures: The index entry is defined as VoxelLocation with the following fields: runcount: int. The number of voxels remaining in the current run. lenoffset: unsigned char. The byte offset into the runlengths array where the current run's length is stored. dataoffset: unsigned char. The byte offset into the voxel data array where the current run's data begins. Bit Packing: The least significant bit of dataoffset is a flag INDEXRUNISZERO. If set, the run consists of zero-valued voxels. Algorithm: 1. Initialize ilen, jlen, klen from the dimensions of rlevoxels. 2. Initialize a pointer RLElen to the start of rlevoxels->runlengths. 3. Initialize runiszero = 0 and runcount = 0. 4. Loop k from 0 to klen - 1: 5. Loop j from 0 to jlen - 1: 6. Assert runiszero == 0 and runcount == 0. This ensures that the previous voxel's run has been fully consumed. 7. Initialize lenoffset = 0 and dataoffset = 0. 8. Loop i from 0 to ilen - 1: 9. Check if lenoffset > 256. If true, the index cannot fit in the allocated byte-sized fields. Deallocate voxelindex, set it to NULL, and return VPERRORLIMITEXCEEDED. 10. Store index->runcount = runcount. 11. Store index->lenoffset = lenoffset. 12. Set index->dataoffset based on runiszero. If runiszero is true, OR INDEXRUNISZERO into dataoffset. 13. Increment the index pointer to the next voxel location. 14. While runcount == 0: 15. Read runcount = RLElen++. 16. Toggle runiszero (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0). 17. Increment lenoffset. 18. Decrement runcount. 19. If !runiszero, add voxelsize to dataoffset. Parameters: INDEXRUNISZERO: A bit flag (typically 0x01) OR-ed into the dataoffset field to indicate zero-valued runs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Index Overflow: If the number of RLE runs exceeds 256, lenoffset will exceed the capacity of an unsigned char. The method handles this by returning an error (VPERRORLIMITEXCEEDED) and setting the index to NULL. Run Consumption: The algorithm assumes that runs are consumed exactly as the voxel coordinates are traversed. The assertion runiszero == 0 and runcount == 0 at the start of each (j, k) loop ensures that no partial runs are carried over incorrectly between slices or rows. Time Complexity: O(N), where N = ilen \times jlen \times klen. Each voxel is visited once, and RLE pointers are advanced linearly. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the index array, with each entry being 3 bytes (1 byte runcount, 1 byte lenoffset, 1 byte dataoffset). Limitations: The fixed-size unsigned char fields limit the number of distinct RLE runs to 256. This is a hard constraint of the original VolPack implementation. This method is part of the VolPack volume rendering library, originally developed by Phil Lacroute at Stanford University in 1994. It was designed to provide efficient access to sparse volume data encoded with Run-Length Encoding, allowing renderers to skip zero-valued regions quickly. ferdymercury/volpack, https://github.com/ferdymercury/volpack, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Dense-grid to Voxlap-slab packing
body: Converts a dense 3D voxel mask and color grid into the Voxlap slab-RLE column format, seeding an all-solid VXL and carving air voxels using a column function to preserve buried-voxel-aware encoding. It differs from Binary Voxel RLE Encoding by maintaining explicit column offsets and supporting direct color attachment per column, and from Run-length encoded voxel runs by using a slab-based internal structure rather than simple run lists. Inputs: grid: A slice of u8 bytes sized VSID × VSID × MAXZDIM in (y, x, z) order. A non-zero byte marks a voxel as solid. color: A slice of u32 bytes sized VSID × VSID × MAXZDIM. The corresponding u32 is the BGRA color stored when a voxel becomes exposed. vsid: The voxel side dimension (width/depth). Outputs: A VXL struct containing the packed voxel data, column offsets, and metadata. Data Structures: VXL: Contains vsid, ipo (origin), ist (x-axis), ihe (z-axis), ifo (y-axis), data (boxed slice of bytes), columnoffset (boxed slice of u32), mipbaseoffsets, vbit, and vbiti. columnoffset: A vector of u32 with capacity ncols + 1, where ncols = vsid². Stores the byte offset into data for the start of each column. data: A vector of bytes storing the slab-RLE encoded columns. Vspan: Struct with fields x (u32), y (u32), z0 (u8), z1 (u8). z1 is inclusive. Parameters: MAXZDIM: The maximum height of the voxel grid, defined as 256 (one byte per z value). Steps: 1. Validate Input Sizes: Assert that grid.len() and color.len() equal vsid² × MAXZDIM. Panic if they do not. 2. Seed VXL Data Structures: Initialize data Vec and columnoffset Vec with capacity ncols 8 and ncols + 1 respectively, where ncols = vsid². 3. Iterate Columns: Iterate y from 0 to vsidu and x from 0 to vsidu: Push current data.len() to columnoffset. Write header [nextptr=0, z1=0, z1c=0, z0=0] (4 bytes) to data. Calculate base index in grid/color. If grid[base] is 0, set base color to 0; else set to color[base]. Write base color as 4 little-endian bytes to data. 4. Finalize Column Offsets: Push final data.len() to columnoffset. 5. Construct VXL Struct: Set vsid, ipo=[0.0,0.0,0.0], ist=[1.0,0.0,0.0], ihe=[0.0,0.0,1.0], ifo=[0.0,1.0,0.0]. Set data to data.intoboxedslice() and columnoffset to columnoffset.intoboxedslice(). Set mipbaseoffsets to Box::new([0, ncols + 1]), vbit to Box::new([]), and vbiti to 0. 6. Reserve Edit Capacity: Call vxl.reserveeditcapacity(ncols 512). 7. Build Sorted Air-Span List: Initialize empty airspans Vec. Iterate y from 0 to vsidu and x from 0 to vsidu. Calculate base index. Initialize z=0. While z < maxzdimu: If grid[base+z] == 0, set zs=z. Inner while loop: While z < maxzdimu and grid[base+z] == 0, increment z. Push Vspan { x: x as u32, y: y as u32, z0: zs as u8, z1: (z - 1) as u8 } to airspans. Else increment z. 8. Carve Air Spans: If airspans is not empty, call setspanswithcolfunc(&mut vxl, &airspans, SpanOp::Carve, closure). The closure takes x, y, z, calculates idx = (y vsidu + x) maxzdimu + z, and returns roxlapformats::VoxColor(color[idx]). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packdensegridtovxl(grid: List[u8], color: List[u32], vsid: u32) -> VXL: MAXZDIM = 256 ncols = vsid vsid # Step 1: Validate assert len(grid) == vsid vsid MAXZDIM assert len(color) == vsid vsid MAXZDIM # Step 2: Seed structures data = [] columnoffset = [] data.reserve(ncols 8) columnoffset.reserve(ncols + 1) # Step 3: Iterate columns for y in range(vsid): for x in range(vsid): columnoffset.append(len(data)) # Write header: nextptr=0, z1=0, z1c=0, z0=0 data.extend([0, 0, 0, 0]) baseidx = (y vsid + x) MAXZDIM if grid[baseidx] != 0: colval = color[baseidx] else: colval = 0 # Write base color as 4 little-endian bytes data.extend(colval.tobytes(4, byteorder='little')) # Step 4: Finalize offsets columnoffset.append(len(data)) # Step 5: Construct VXL vxl = VXL( vsid=vsid, ipo=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], ist=[1.0, 0.0, 0.0], ihe=[0.0, 0.0, 1.0], ifo=[0.0, 1.0, 0.0], data=data.toboxedslice(), columnoffset=columnoffset.toboxedslice(), mipbaseoffsets=Box([0, ncols + 1]), vbit=Box([]), vbiti=0) # Step 6: Reserve capacity vxl.reserveeditcapacity(ncols 512) # Step 7: Build air spans airspans = [] for y in range(vsid): for x in range(vsid): baseidx = (y vsid + x) MAXZDIM z = 0 while z < MAXZDIM: if grid[baseidx + z] == 0: zs = z while z < MAXZDIM and grid[baseidx + z] == 0: z += 1 airspans.append(Vspan(x=x, y=y, z0=zs, z1=z-1)) else: z += 1 # Step 8: Carve air spans if airspans: def closure(x, y, z): idx = (y vsid + x) MAXZDIM + z return VoxColor(color[idx]) setspanswithcolfunc(vxl, airspans, SpanOp::Carve, closure) return vxl Time Complexity: Linear in the number of voxels for the initial seeding and air-span detection. Carving is proportional to the number of air spans. Memory Complexity: Proportional to VSID² MAXZDIM for input, plus VSID² 8 for initial output structure, plus overhead for air spans. Strengths: Efficiently handles dense grids with large solid regions by seeding all-solid columns and only carving air. Preserves color information for exposed voxels. Limitations: Requires MAXZDIM to be 256. Panics if grid size mismatch or slab pool overflow occurs during carving. When to Use: When converting dense voxel data to a format suitable for acoustic or rendering simulations that require buried-voxel awareness. When Not to Use: For sparse data where other RLE methods might be more efficient, or when MAXZDIM exceeds 256. Originated in the Roxlap project, a portable reimplementation of Ken Perlin's work, specifically for acoustic simulation and cavity estimation. name: Out-of-Core Sparse Voxel Octree Construction
head: Out-of-core SVO construction, Streaming SVO construction
body: This method constructs a sparse voxel octree (SVO) from a triangle mesh while keeping memory usage logarithmic in the size of the SVO, by processing an intermediate high-resolution 3D voxel grid in Morton order in a streaming manner. It differs from its siblings, such as Brute Force SVO Construction, by avoiding complex sorting or streaming logic in favor of a simple recursive subdivision and depth-first search. Unlike Adaptive Voxelization of Unstructured Grids, which handles unstructured data, this method is designed for regular voxelization of triangle meshes. It is chosen when implementation simplicity is prioritized over memory efficiency and construction speed. The algorithm consists of two sequential subprocesses: (1) voxelization, which consumes a triangle mesh and produces an intermediate high-resolution 3D voxel grid in Morton order, and (2) SVO construction, which consumes the voxel grid and produces the output SVO. Input: A triangle mesh (with or without bounding box) and available memory size. Output: A sparse voxel octree written to disk/stream. Intermediate: A high-resolution 3D voxel grid in Morton order, stored on disk. 1. Subgrid Partition: A temporary file on disk storing the subset of triangles intersecting a specific subgrid. 2. Morton Code Stream: A sequence of 64-bit integers representing the Morton codes of non-empty cells in the intermediate voxel grid. 3. Level Queues: An array of queues, one for each level of the octree. Each queue holds at most 2^d nodes (where d=3 for 3D, so max 8 nodes per level). 4. SVO Node: Represents a voxel or internal node. Contains the Morton code and child pointers/flags. Grid Resolution: Power-of-two resolution (e.g., 2048^3). Subgrid Size: Determined by regularly subdividing the high-resolution grid until a subgrid fits in available memory. Queue Size: At most 2^d nodes per level. 1. Partitioning: Partition the triangle mesh according to subgrids of the high-resolution 3D voxel grid in a streaming manner by testing each triangle against the bounding box of every subgrid. Store the resulting triangle mesh partitions temporarily on disk. 2. Subgrid Sizing: Determine subgrid size by regularly subdividing the high-resolution 3D voxel grid until a subgrid fits in available memory. Use only power-of-two resolutions for the high-resolution 3D voxel grid to ensure subgrids correspond to contiguous ranges in Morton order. 3. Actual Voxelization: Sequentially process each subgrid. For each subgrid, consume its corresponding triangle mesh partition in a streaming manner. Voxelize triangles using the 6-separability surface voxelization variant of Huang et al. [1998]. Output only the Morton codes of non-empty cells, not boolean values for all cells. 4. Output Order: Ensure subgrids are processed in Morton order so that the output of the voxelization subprocess is the intermediate high-resolution 3D voxel grid in Morton order. The construction process reads the Morton code stream and builds the octree bottom-up using queues. 1. Initialize: Create an array of empty queues, one for each level of the octree (from leaf level up to root level). 2. Read Leaf Nodes: Read cells with Morton codes corresponding to the current level's leaf nodes from the input and store them in the queue for that level. 3. Create Parent Nodes: When a parent node's children (all nodes in the current level's queue) are processed, create an internal node with the parent's Morton code. Store this internal node in the queue of the parent's level. Record the parent-child relation. Write all non-empty nodes currently in the child's queue to the output. Clear the child's queue. 4. Repeat: Repeat reading leaf nodes and creating parent nodes level by level until the root is processed. Finally, write the root node to output and clear the root's queue. def outofcoresvoconstruction(trianglemesh, availablememory, gridresolution): """ Constructs an SVO from a triangle mesh using out-of-core voxelization and streaming construction. Args: trianglemesh: List of triangles. availablememory: Size of available RAM in bytes. gridresolution: Power-of-two resolution of the intermediate voxel grid (e.g., 2048). Returns: None (writes SVO to output stream/file). """ # Step 1: Determine subgrid size # Regularly subdivide the grid until a subgrid fits in availablememory. # Assume power-of-two resolution ensures contiguous Morton ranges. subgridsize = determinesubgridsize(gridresolution, availablememory) # Step 2: Voxelization - Partitioning # Partition triangle mesh by subgrid bounding boxes. # Store partitions on disk. subgridpartitions = partitionmeshbysubgrids(trianglemesh, subgridsize, gridresolution) # Step 3: Voxelization - Actual Voxelization # Process subgrids in Morton order. # Output Morton codes of non-empty cells to a stream. mortoncodestream = [] for subgrid in getsubgridsinmortonorder(subgridsize, gridresolution): partition = subgridpartitions[subgrid.id] # Voxelize triangles in partition using 6-separability method (Huang et al.) # Output only Morton codes of non-empty cells. codes = voxelizepartition(partition, subgrid) mortoncodestream.extend(codes) # Step 4: SVO Construction # Determine number of levels in the octree numlevels = log2(gridresolution) + 1 # Initialize queues for each level # Queue[i] holds nodes at level i (leaf level is numlevels - 1) queues = [Queue() for in range(numlevels)] # Process Morton codes # The stream contains Morton codes for leaf nodes first, then their parents, etc. # However, the algorithm reads leaf nodes, builds parents, and pushes parents to next level queue. # We need to track which level we are currently reading leaf nodes for. # In the basic version, we read all leaf nodes first? name: Sparse Voxel Octree Construction (Basic Version)
head: Basic SVO Construction, SVO Construction, basic version
body: This method constructs a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a stream of non-empty voxel Morton codes by maintaining fixed-size queues per depth level, merging nodes when a queue fills, and writing non-empty nodes to disk. It differs from its siblings, such as Brute Force SVO Construction, by avoiding complex sorting or streaming logic in favor of a simple recursive subdivision and depth-first search. This method is chosen when implementation simplicity is prioritized over memory efficiency and construction speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of non-empty voxel Morton codes, sorted in ascending order, generated by the voxelization process. Output: A Sparse Voxel Octree written to disk (or an output buffer), structured with good locality of reference so that siblings are stored contiguously. Data Structures: Queues: An array of queues, one for each depth level of the octree. Each queue holds node descriptors (leaf nodes or internal node references). Node Descriptor: A 24-byte representation per node consisting of a 64-bit reference to the first child of the node, a 1-byte offset for every child of the node, and a 64-bit reference to the data associated with the node. Empty Node: A special descriptor (value 0) indicating an empty subtree. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize an array of queues, one for each depth level of the octree. 2. While input exists: a. Consume a leaf node l from the input stream. b. Push the leaf node l onto the queue corresponding to its depth. c. Initialize a depth counter d to the current depth of the voxel grid. d. While d > 0 and the queue at depth d is full: i. Create an internal node p. ii. Set p.children to the child offsets of the elements in queues[d]. iii. Write the non-empty elements of queues[d] to disk. iv. Clear queues[d]. v. Push p onto queues[d-1]. vi. Decrement d. 3. Write the root node to output and clear the queue of level 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildsvobasic(inputstream, maxdepth): # Initialize queues for each depth level queues = [Queue(capacity=8) for in range(maxdepth + 1)] outputbuffer = [] for leafnode in inputstream: depth = leafnode.depth queues[depth].pushback(leafnode) d = depth while d > 0 and queues[d].isfull(): internalnode = makeinternalnode() internalnode.children = getchildoffsets(queues[d]) writetodisk(queues[d].nonemptyelements()) queues[d].clear() queues[d - 1].pushback(internalnode) d -= 1 writetodisk(queues[0].nonemptyelements()) queues[0].clear() return outputbuffer class Queue: def init(self, capacity): self.items = [] self.capacity = capacity def pushback(self, item): self.items.append(item) def isfull(self): return len(self.items) >= self.capacity def clear(self): self.items = [] def nonemptyelements(self): return self.items def makeinternalnode(): return {'children': [0] 8} def getchildoffsets(queue): return queue.nonemptyelements() def writetodisk(data): outputbuffer.extend(data) Parameters: maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. SVOSIZE: World side length in voxels, must be a power of two. Typical value: 512. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-bounds octants: If x, y, or z >= n (grid size), return 0 immediately to treat them as empty. Empty node overhead: The method spends significant time processing empty nodes, which reduces construction speed compared to optimized variants. Color packing: When creating a solid leaf, the descriptor uses a high-bit set value (0x80000000) combined with packed RGB8 color data. (Note: source code uses voxelcolorpacked(y) for the color value, which is corrected here to v). Brute Force SVO Construction is a top-down algorithm that builds a complete octree in memory and subsequently prunes empty branches to form a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO). It differs from its siblings, such as Sparse Voxel Octree Construction via Morton Code Sorting, by avoiding complex sorting or streaming logic in favor of a simple recursive subdivision and depth-first search. This method is chosen when implementation simplicity is prioritized over memory efficiency and construction speed. This method constructs a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a stream of non-empty voxel Morton codes by optimizing the handling of empty space. Unlike the basic version, which inserts empty child nodes individually, this approach calculates the number of empty nodes between consecutive input leaves and directly inserts empty parent nodes into higher-level queues. This reduces the number of queue operations significantly, as pushing back 2^d empty nodes is equivalent to pushing back a single node at the level above. It builds on Sparse Voxel Octree Construction (Basic Version). This method constructs a static Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a set of 3D points or voxels by converting them to Z-order (Morton) codes, sorting them for spatial locality, and recursively partitioning the sorted array into octree nodes and leaf voxels. It differs from dynamic insertion methods by pre-sorting all points into Morton order, which guarantees spatial locality and allows O(1) range queries via binary search instead of tree traversal during construction. The Dynamic Octree Growth Algorithm constructs a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by dynamically increasing its depth and spatial extent as new voxels are processed, rather than pre-calculating the scene's bounding box. It differs from static voxelization methods by handling out-of-bounds coordinates on-the-fly, ensuring the octree grows to encompass all input data without prior knowledge of the scene's dimensions. This method serves as the foundational growth logic for incremental SVO construction, upon which Octree Insertion with Growth builds specific recursive insertion and boundary check logic. This method constructs a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a stream of indexed leaves by maintaining a fixed-size array of queues, one per tree depth level, and collapsing homogeneous subtrees into single leaf or invalid nodes to compress the structure. It differs from brute-force or sorting-based builders by processing leaves in a single pass without requiring full in-memory tree storage or pre-sorting. The Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Builder is an algorithm that constructs a flat-array representation of a Sparse Voxel Octree from a list of input voxels or geometric primitives. It solves the problem of efficiently organizing spatial data for ray marching or pathfinding by creating a hierarchy where empty space is skipped, but internal nodes are explicitly allocated to maintain traversal continuity. It differs from its siblings by focusing on either a recursive depth-first initialization of a dense structure or a parallel, level-by-level GPU-based allocation and merging process, whereas the Brute Force method [1704-brute-force-svo-construction.md] typically relies on simpler, less memory-efficient insertion strategies. An out-of-core algorithm to build a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from voxel grid data sorted in Morton order. It reads voxels in groups of 8, generates parent nodes, and flushes buffers to disk to manage memory constraints. The buffer size is 8 \times \text{octree\depth} \times \text{node\size} bits. The resulting array structure ensures that at every level, child nodes are stored next to each other. The tree is sparse, containing only nodes for voxels that have data. This method assumes the octree spans the whole grid space, meaning 8 voxels always share the same parent, eliminating the need for a top-down search to find the parent node. Unlike point-based global illumination methods (e.g., Tabellion EGSR2011) which require a top-down search to find parents for scattered points, this method benefits from voxel data spanning the whole grid, simplifying parent lookup. An out-of-core, bottom-up external-memory algorithm that reduces an SVO to a minimal SSVDAG. The algorithm operates bottom-up, alternating phases at each level of the octree hierarchy. Phase 1: Cluster nodes representing similar subtrees (identical up to a similarity transform) and replace them with a single representative node. Phase 2: Replace pointers in the immediately higher level to the clustered nodes with tagged pointers to the single representative. The tag encodes the required similarity transform. Phase 3: Sort the representatives by their reference count to facilitate variable-bit-rate encoding of the pointers. The method assumes the original scene has geometric redundancy (many subtrees similar with respect to a reflective transformation). Time Complexity: The basic version is slower than the optimized version because it spends significant time processing empty nodes. The optimized version is over two orders of magnitude faster than the non-optimized version. Memory Complexity: The out-of-core method using 128 MB or 1 GB memory is roughly as fast as an in-core method using 8 GB memory, but uses up to 64 times less memory. The sparse voxel octree construction process consumes only roughly 1.6 MB of memory. Performance: On a Dell Precision T7500 workstation (Intel Xeon X5650 CPU, 7200 RPM SATA II disk), the out-of-core method using 128 MB or 1 GB memory is roughly as fast as an in-core method using 8 GB memory, but uses up to 64 times less memory. Strengths: Simple implementation, out-of-core capability, good locality of reference. Limitations: Slow processing of empty nodes. The method was introduced in the paper "Out-of-Core Construction of Sparse Voxel Octrees". It is based on the idea of reading voxels in groups of 8 and storing the generated parent voxels at each level, allowing for efficient out-of-core construction. The algorithm processes an intermediate high-resolution 3D voxel grid in Morton order in a streaming manner, keeping memory usage logarithmic in the size of the SVO. scarlyle0/voxel-compare, https://github.com/scarlyle0/voxel-compare, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Out-of-Core Construction of Sparse Voxel Octrees, https://graphics.cs.kuleuven.be/publications/BLD13OCCSVO/BLD13OCCSVOpaper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 Out-Of-Core construction of Sparse Voxel Octrees - Jeroen Baert's Blog, https://www.forceflow.be/2012/07/24/out-of-core-construction-of-sparse-voxel-octrees/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAGs (SSVDAGs) for compression-domain tracing of high-resolution geometric scenes, https://albertojaspe.net/publications/2017-JCGT-ssvdags.pdf, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

head: In-Memory SVO Construction, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Construction, Top-down Octree Construction with Pruning
body: Brute Force SVO Construction is a top-down algorithm that builds a complete octree in memory and subsequently prunes empty branches to form a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO). It differs from its siblings, such as Sparse Voxel Octree Construction via Morton Code Sorting, by avoiding complex sorting or streaming logic in favor of a simple recursive subdivision and depth-first search. This method is chosen when implementation simplicity is prioritized over memory efficiency and construction speed. Inputs: worldSize: The side length of the root bounding box in world units. maxDepth: The maximum recursion depth, determining the finest voxel resolution. geometries: Scene geometry objects to intersect against. Outputs: An SVO structure consisting of pruned IndirectionGrid nodes and Data nodes. Data Structures: 1. IndirectionGrid: An array of 8 Cell objects representing the 8 children of an octree node. 2. Cell: A structure containing: nodetype: Enum value DATA or INDEX. If DATA: color: Vector3f storing the geometry's color, normalized by dividing by worldSize. reallocation: Vector3f storing the geometry's real-world location, normalized by worldSize. If INDEX: textureindex: Vector3f storing the 3D texture coordinate pointing to the child IndirectionGrid. 3. IndirectionPool: A pool with capacity 8 \times \text{maxDepth}^2 used to manage IndirectionGrid allocations. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an empty list for geometries and initialize the indirectionPool with capacity 8 \times \text{maxDepth}^2. 2. Root Creation: Call createNode(0, Vector3f(0, 0, 0)) to start generation at depth 0 with the origin. 3. Recursive Subdivision (createNode): For a call createNode(depth, boxStart): a. Calculate child box size: \text{childBoxSize} = \frac{\text{worldSize}}{2^{\text{depth}+1}} b. Define child box offsets for the 8 sub-cubes relative to the parent's minimum corner. c. Iterate i from 0 to 7 for the 8 sub-nodes: i. Calculate childBoxStart using childBoxOffsets[i] childBoxSize + boxStart, and childBoxEnd = childBoxStart + childBoxSize. ii. Check for intersection between the child box and any geometry in the scene using Geometry.intersects(childBoxStart, childBoxEnd). d. Branching Logic: If \text{depth} + 1 \neq \text{maxDepth} (not leaf level): If intersection is not null: 1. Recursively call createNode(depth + 1, childBoxStart) to create a child indirection grid. 2. Create an INDEX cell pointing to the new grid's texture index. 3. Assign this cell to the corresponding child slot of the current node. If \text{depth} + 1 == \text{maxDepth} (leaf level): If intersection is not null: 1. Create a DATA cell. 2. Set color by normalizing the geometry's color by dividing by worldSize. 3. Set reallocation by normalizing the geometry's real location by worldSize. 4. Assign this cell to the corresponding child slot of the current node. e. If no intersection is found for a child, the child slot remains empty. 4. Pruning: Perform a depth-first search and grid lookup to prune empty branches. 5. Gathering: After pruning, octree nodes are spread all over memory; an extra pass is required to gather them into a sequential structure (array) for cache coherence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vector3f: def init(self, x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vector3f(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def mul(self, scalar): return Vector3f(self.x scalar, self.y scalar, self.z scalar) def truediv(self, scalar): return Vector3f(self.x / scalar, self.y / scalar, self.z / scalar) class Cell: INDEX = 0 DATA = 1 def init(self, nodetype, color=None, reallocation=None, textureindex=None): self.nodetype = nodetype self.color = color self.reallocation = reallocation self.textureindex = textureindex class IndirectionGrid: def init(self, children=None): self.children = children if children else [None] 8 class IndirectionPool: def init(self, capacity): self.capacity = capacity self.grids = [None] capacity self.used = 0 def allocate(self): if self.used < self.capacity: grid = IndirectionGrid() self.grids[self.used] = grid self.used += 1 return grid return None childboxoffsets = [ Vector3f(0,0,0), Vector3f(1,0,0), Vector3f(0,1,0), Vector3f(1,1,0), Vector3f(0,0,1), Vector3f(1,0,1), Vector3f(0,1,1), Vector3f(1,1,1) ] def buildsvo(worldsize, maxdepth, geometries): indirectionpool = IndirectionPool(capacity=8 maxdepth maxdepth) root = createnode(0, Vector3f(0, 0, 0), worldsize, maxdepth, geometries, indirectionpool) prunetree(root) gatherednodes = gathernodes(root) return gatherednodes def createnode(depth, boxstart, worldsize, maxdepth, geometries, indirectionpool): childboxsize = worldsize / (2 (depth + 1)) children = [None] 8 for i in range(8): childboxstart = boxstart + (childboxoffsets[i] childboxsize) childboxend = childboxstart + Vector3f(childboxsize, childboxsize, childboxsize) intersection = checkintersection(childboxstart, childboxend, geometries) if intersection is not None: if depth + 1 != maxdepth: childgrid = createnode(depth + 1, childboxstart, worldsize, maxdepth, geometries, indirectionpool) cell = Cell(nodetype=Cell.INDEX, textureindex=Vector3f(0, 0, 0)) else: normalizedcolor = intersection.color / worldsize normalizedlocation = intersection.location / worldsize cell = Cell(nodetype=Cell.DATA, color=normalizedcolor, reallocation=normalizedlocation) children[i] = cell else: children[i] = None return IndirectionGrid(children=children) def checkintersection(boxstart, boxend, geometries): for geom in geometries: if geom.intersects(boxstart, boxend): return geom return None def prunetree(node): if node is None: return for i in range(8): if node.children[i] is not None: if node.children[i].nodetype == Cell.INDEX: prunetree(node.children[i].grid) if node.children[i].grid.children == [None] 8: node.children[i] = None def gathernodes(node): result = [] collectrecursive(node, result) return result def collectrecursive(node, result): if node is None: return result.append(node) for child in node.children: if child is not None: if child.nodetype == Cell.INDEX: collectrecursive(child.grid, result) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: The entire octree structure must be held in memory at runtime, leading to high memory usage. Dense Scenes: The texture size calculation assumes 1/2 of the space is empty, which may break if the scene is dense. Index Limitation: Index nodes can only point to 2^8=255 values along each axis, limiting the max texture size to 256. Cache Coherence: After pruning, octree nodes are spread all over memory; an extra pass is required to gather them into a sequential structure for cache coherence. An optimized version of the brute force method, improving performance and memory layout. Uses Morton codes to build the SVO efficiently without holding the full tree in memory. Grows the octree dynamically as needed, rather than building it top-down. Uses queues to manage node construction and collapse. A general builder pattern for SVO construction. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of nodes visited during construction and pruning. Memory Complexity: O(N), requiring the entire octree to be stored in memory simultaneously. Performance: Simple to implement but suffers from high memory consumption and poor cache coherence due to scattered nodes. Strengths: Simple recursive implementation; easy to write and debug. Limitations: High memory usage; not suitable for very large scenes or out-of-core construction; requires post-processing for cache coherence. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Large-scale scenes, out-of-core processing, or when memory efficiency is critical. The brute force approach was one of the first methods proposed for constructing Sparse Voxel Octrees. It was introduced as a simple baseline to demonstrate the concept of sparsifying an octree by pruning empty branches. The method is described in Jeroen Baert's blog post on out-of-core construction of SVOs. head: SVO construction, optimized version
body:
This method constructs a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a stream of non-empty voxel Morton codes by optimizing the handling of empty space. Unlike the basic version, which inserts empty child nodes individually, this approach calculates the number of empty nodes between consecutive input leaves and directly inserts empty parent nodes into higher-level queues. This reduces the number of queue operations significantly, as pushing back 2^d empty nodes is equivalent to pushing back a single node at the level above. It builds on Sparse Voxel Octree Construction (Basic Version). Inputs: A sorted stream of non-empty leaf nodes, each containing a 64-bit Morton code. Outputs: An out-of-core SVO stored on disk, with internal structure maintained in memory queues. Data Structures: queues: An array of queues, one for each depth level d \in [0, 	ext{depth}]. Each queue holds nodes (empty or internal) waiting to be merged. currentmorton: An integer tracking the Morton code of the previously processed leaf, initialized to 0. depth: The maximum depth of the octree. Node layout: Each node uses 24 bytes: a 64-bit reference to the first child, a 1-byte offset for every child, and a 64-bit reference to the associated data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize currentmorton to 0. 2. While input exists: a. Consume the next leaf node l from the input stream. b. Calculate the number of empty nodes between the current and previous Morton code: 	ext{nb\empty
odes} = l.	ext{morton} - 	ext{current\morton}. c. While 	ext{nb\empty
odes} > 0: i. Determine the insertion depth for empty nodes. Calculate a as the largest integer such that 8^a < 	ext{nb\empty
odes}. Calculate b as the largest index such that queues[b] is not empty. Set the insertion depth di = \max(	ext{depth} - a, b). ii. Push an empty node onto queues[di]. iii. While di > 0 and queues[di] is full: 1. Create an internal node p. 2. Set p.	ext{children} to the contents of queues[di]. 3. Write non-empty elements of queues[di] to disk. 4. Clear queues[di]. 5. Push p onto queues[di - 1]. 6. Decrement di. 7. Subtract 8^{	ext{depth} - di} from 	ext{nb\empty
odes}. d. Process the non-empty leaf node l using the basic version logic: push l to the appropriate queue, and if the queue is full, merge nodes up the tree as described in the basic version. e. Update currentmorton to l.	ext{morton}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizedsvoconstruction(inputstream, depth, queuecapacity=8): queues = [[] for in range(depth + 1)] currentmorton = 0 diskoutput = [] for leaf in inputstream: nbemptynodes = leaf.morton - currentmorton while nbemptynodes > 0: a = 0 while 8 (a + 1) < nbemptynodes: a += 1 b = 0 for i in range(depth, -1, -1): if queues[i]: b = i break di = max(depth - a, b) queues[di].append({'type': 'empty'}) while di > 0 and len(queues[di]) >= queuecapacity: p = {'type': 'internal', 'children': queues[di]} for child in queues[di]: if child['type'] != 'empty': diskoutput.append(child) queues[di] = [] queues[di - 1].append(p) di -= 1 nbemptynodes -= 8 (depth - di) queues[depth].append(leaf) d = depth while d > 0 and len(queues[d]) >= queuecapacity: p = {'type': 'internal', 'children': queues[d]} for child in queues[d]: if child['type'] != 'empty': diskoutput.append(child) queues[d] = [] queues[d - 1].append(p) d -= 1 currentmorton = leaf.morton Parameters: depth: The maximum depth of the octree. Not given in the sources. Queue capacity: Not given in the sources. Node size: 24 bytes per node (64-bit reference to first child, 1-byte offset per child, 64-bit reference to data). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Morton codes are 64-bit integers; ensure no overflow when calculating differences. Boundary: If nbemptynodes is exactly a power of 8, the logic for a must handle the strict inequality 8^a < 	ext{nb\empty
odes} correctly. Empty Input: If the input stream is empty, the algorithm terminates immediately. Time Complexity: The optimized version is over two orders of magnitude faster than the non-optimized version. Memory Complexity: The process consumes only roughly 1.6 MB of memory. Scaling: Efficient for large voxel grids where the majority of cells are empty. Strengths: Significantly reduced queue operations by inserting empty parent nodes directly. Limitations: Requires sorted input of Morton codes. The optimized version was introduced by Lagae and Dutre in 2008. It addresses the inefficiency of the basic version, which spends considerable time processing empty nodes. The key insight is that pushing back 2^d empty nodes is equivalent to pushing back a single node at the level above. This method is part of the out-of-core construction of sparse voxel octrees, allowing for the handling of very large voxel grids that do not fit in main memory. name: Sparse Voxel Octree Construction via Morton Code Sorting
head: BVH Construction via Morton Code Sorting, Bottom-up SVO Construction with Morton Sort, Morton Code Sorting SVO Construction, Morton-based octree insertion, Octree Construction via Morton Code Sorting, Z-order octree builder
body: This method constructs a static Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a set of 3D points or voxels by converting them to Z-order (Morton) codes, sorting them for spatial locality, and recursively partitioning the sorted array into octree nodes and leaf voxels. It differs from dynamic insertion methods by pre-sorting all points into Morton order, which guarantees spatial locality and allows O(1) range queries via binary search instead of tree traversal during construction. Inputs and Outputs: A list of 3D points (or voxel centers) P = \{p0, p1, \dots, p{N-1}\}. An SVO consisting of an array of octreenode structures and an array of octreevoxel structures, serialized in a specific binary format. Data Structures: The output is stored in two contiguous arrays: 1. octreenode (8 bytes total): uint32t info: Bits 0-7 store the occupancy mask (8 bits for 8 children). Bit 8 is the isleaf flag. Bits 9-31 are padding. uint32t childptr: If isleaf is 0, this is an index into the octreenode array (children). If isleaf is 1, this is an index into the octreevoxel array (data). 2. octreevoxel (4 bytes total): uint32t rgb: Bits 0-7 padding. Bits 8-15 Blue, Bits 16-23 Green, Bits 24-31 Red. 3. Binary Serialization Format: sizet numnodes sizet numvoxels numnodes sizeof(octreenode) bytes numvoxels sizeof(octreevoxel) bytes Parameters: maxdepth: Maximum recursion depth for the octree. Controls grid resolution. Valid range [1, 12]. Default 8. 2^{\text{max\depth}} defines the side length in voxels. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Bounding Box: Initialize minbound and maxbound to the first point p0. Iterate through all points p \in P: \text{min\bound} = \min(\text{min\bound}, p), \text{max\bound} = \max(\text{max\bound}, p). 2. Equalize Aspect Ratio: Compute extent: \text{extent} = \text{max\bound} - \text{min\bound}. Find \text{max\extent} = \max(\text{extent}). Calculate margin: \text{margin} = (\text{vec3}(\text{max\extent}) - \text{extent}) \times 0.5. Shift bounds: \text{min\bound} \leftarrow \text{min\bound} - \text{margin}. 3. Compute Grid Scale: \text{scale} = \frac{1 \ll \text{max\depth}}{\max(\text{max\extent}, 10^{-6})}. 4. Convert to Grid Coordinates: For each point p: \text{grid\pos} = \lfloor (p - \text{min\bound}) \times \text{scale} \rfloor. 5. Clamp Grid Coordinates: \text{grid\pos} = \min(\text{grid\pos}, \text{vec3}((1 \ll \text{max\depth}) - 1)). 6. Encode Morton Codes: For each gridpos (x, y, z), compute a 64-bit Morton code M: M = 0. For i from 0 to 11: M \ |= \ ((x \ \& \ (1 \ll i)) \ll 2i) \ | \ ((y \ \& \ (1 \ll i)) \ll (2i + 1)) \ | \ ((z \ \& \ (1 \ll i)) \ll (2i + 2)). 7. Sort and Deduplicate: Sort the list of Morton codes. Remove duplicates using std::unique. 8. Recursive Construction: Call insertchildrenrecursive(minbound, 0, N, 1), where N is the number of unique Morton codes. Function insertchildrenrecursive(mincoord, startindex, endindex, depth): Compute halfsize for the current depth: \text{half\size} = 1 \ll (\text{max\depth} - \text{depth}). Initialize occupancymask = 0. For each octant i from 0 to 7: Compute child bounds: \text{child\min} = \text{min\coord} + \text{octant\offset}(i) \times \text{half\size}, \text{child\max} = \text{child\min} + \text{half\size} - 1. Find occupied range in the sorted Morton array using binary search: \text{range\start} = \text{lower\bound}(M(\text{child\min}), \text{begin} + \text{start\index}, \text{begin} + \text{end\index}), \text{range\end} = \text{upper\bound}(M(\text{child\max}), \text{range\start}, \text{begin} + \text{end\index}). If \text{range\start} < \text{range\end}: Set bit i in occupancymask. If depth == maxdepth, add voxel to childrenvoxels[depth]. Else, recurse: child = insertchildrenrecursive(childmin, rangestart, rangeend, depth + 1) and store result in childrennodes[depth]. Create octreenode: info = occupancymask | (isleaf ? 1: 0) << 8. childptr = index to first child or voxel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero is prevented by clamping maxextent to 10^{-6} if it is 0. Clamping prevents Morton code overflow. maxdepth is limited to 12 to ensure coordinates stay < 4096. childmax is decremented by 1 because zorder(childmax) must fall within the same octant as zorder(childmin). Duplicates represent multiple voxels at the same grid position; they are merged into a single leaf. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildsvo(points, maxdepth=8): if not points: return [], [] # 1. Compute Bounding Box minbound = points[0] maxbound = points[0] for p in points: minbound = min(minbound, p) maxbound = max(maxbound, p) # 2. Equalize Aspect Ratio extent = maxbound - minbound maxextent = max(extent.x, extent.y, extent.z) margin = vec3(maxextent) - extent margin = margin 0.5 minbound = minbound - margin # 3. Compute Grid Scale scale = (1 << maxdepth) / max(maxextent, 1e-6) # 4. Convert to Grid Coordinates and Clamp gridpositions = [] limit = (1 << maxdepth) - 1 for p in points: gp = floor((p - minbound) scale) gp.x = min(gp.x, limit) gp.y = min(gp.y, limit) gp.z = min(gp.z, limit) gridpositions.append(gp) # 5. Encode Morton Codes mortoncodes = [] for gp in gridpositions: m = 0 for i in range(12): m |= ((gp.x & (1 << i)) << (2 i)) m |= ((gp.y & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 1)) m |= ((gp.z & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 2)) mortoncodes.append(m) # 6. Sort and Deduplicate mortoncodes = sorted(list(set(mortoncodes))) n = len(mortoncodes) # Global storage nodes = [] voxels = [] def encodemorton(x, y, z): m = 0 for i in range(12): m |= ((x & (1 << i)) << (2 i)) m |= ((y & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 1)) m |= ((z & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 2)) return m def lowerbound(arr, val, lo, hi): while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 if arr[mid] < val: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid return lo def upperbound(arr, val, lo, hi): while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 if arr[mid] <= val: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid return lo def octantoffset(i): return vec3(i & 1, (i >> 1) & 1, (i >> 2) & 1) def insertchildrenrecursive(mincoord, startidx, endidx, depth): halfsize = 1 << (maxdepth - depth) occupancymask = 0 childindices = [] for i in range(8): childmin = mincoord + octantoffset(i) halfsize childmax = childmin + halfsize - 1 mmin = encodemorton(childmin.x, childmin.y, childmin.z) mmax = encodemorton(childmax.x, childmax.y, childmax.z) rangestart = lowerbound(mortoncodes, mmin, startidx, endidx) rangeend = upperbound(mortoncodes, mmax, rangestart, endidx) if rangestart < rangeend: occupancymask |= (1 << i) if depth == maxdepth: voxelidx = len(voxels) voxels.append([0, 0, 0, 0]) # Placeholder RGB childindices.append(voxelidx) else: childidx = insertchildrenrecursive(childmin, rangestart, rangeend, depth + 1) childindices.append(childidx) else: childindices.append(None) nodeinfo = occupancymask | ((1 if depth == maxdepth else 0) << 8) nodeidx = len(nodes) nodes.append([nodeinfo, 0]) if childindices: nodes[nodeidx][1] = childindices[0] else: nodes[nodeidx][1] = 0 return nodeidx rootidx = insertchildrenrecursive(minbound, 0, n, 1) return nodes, voxels Constructs a hierarchical octree data structure from a 3D volume grid to accelerate ray marching, where leaf nodes store a bitmask representing the presence of density values in their spatial extent. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly quantizing volume samples into discrete brackets to form compact leaf masks, rather than storing raw density values or using uniform voxel grids. This method constructs a K-D tree from a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to optimize volume rendering and mesh extraction by partitioning space based on Quadratic Error Function (QEF) variance. It differs from sibling methods like Octree Volume Construction by explicitly balancing the split plane to minimize the error difference between child nodes, rather than simply splitting at geometric centers or based on occupancy alone. This approach facilitates efficient contouring and mesh extraction by ensuring that each node's QEF solution is representative of its contained geometry. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) due to sorting the Morton codes, where N is the number of input points. The recursive construction is O(N) as each point is visited once. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the nodes and voxels. The node size is fixed at 8 bytes, and voxel size is 4 bytes. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of points, but the depth is limited to 12, which caps the resolution at 4096^3 voxels. Strengths: Simple to implement, guarantees spatial locality, efficient for static scenes. Limitations: Not suitable for dynamic scenes where points are added/removed frequently, as the entire tree must be rebuilt. The fixed depth limits resolution. When to use: Static volume data, pre-processing for ray marching. When not to use: Dynamic scenes, real-time updates. This method is a standard technique for building spatial acceleration structures for volume rendering and ray tracing. It is based on the Z-order curve (Morton order) which provides good spatial locality. The specific implementation details (8-byte nodes, 4-byte voxels, binary serialization) are from the rayferric/voxel-engine. The BVH construction variant is from mxbrt/svo. rayferric/voxel-engine, https://github.com/rayferric/voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) mxbrt/svo, https://github.com/mxbrt/svo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Octree Volume Construction
body: Constructs a hierarchical octree data structure from a 3D volume grid to accelerate ray marching, where leaf nodes store a bitmask representing the presence of density values in their spatial extent. Inputs: volume: A 3D scalar field providing density samples. settings.brackets: An array of threshold coefficients used to quantize volume samples into discrete bracket indices. levels: The maximum depth of the octree recursion. boundingbox: The spatial extent defining the node's region. Outputs: octree: The root node of the constructed octree. Data Structures: OctreeNode: Contains mask (integer bitmask), children (list of 8 child nodes or None), and boundingbox (spatial bounds). BoundingBox: Contains min and max coordinate vectors, and a midpoint() method returning the center coordinates. Vec3f: A 3D vector structure with x, y, z components. Algorithm: 1. Base Case (Leaf): If levels == 0, the node is a leaf. 2. Iterate over the bounding box coordinates expanded by 1 unit in all directions: x from round(bb.min.x - 1) to round(bb.max.x + 1), y from round(bb.min.y - 1) to round(bb.max.y + 1), and z from round(bb.min.z - 1) to round(bb.max.z + 1). 3. Sample the volume at integer coordinates (x, y, z) to get coef. 4. Determine the bracket index by incrementing bracket while settings.brackets[bracket + 1] <= coef. 5. Set the bit corresponding to the bracket index in the leaf node's mask: octree.mask |= (1 << bracket). 6. Recursive Case (Non-Leaf): If levels > 0, recursively create 8 child octants defined by splitting the current bounding box at its midpoint (bb.mid). 7. The children are indexed 0-7 corresponding to binary coordinates (x, y, z) relative to the midpoint. 8. Recursively construct each child with levels - 1. 9. After building children, aggregate their masks: octree.mask is the bitwise OR of all children's masks, and maskAll is the bitwise AND of all children's masks. 10. Compression: If octree.mask == maskAll, the current node is converted to a leaf node to compress the tree. Memory for children is not freed in this implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3f: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z class BoundingBox: def init(self, minval, maxval): self.min = minval self.max = maxval def midpoint(self): return Vec3f((self.min.x + self.max.x) / 2, (self.min.y + self.max.y) / 2, (self.min.z + self.max.z) / 2) class OctreeNode: def init(self): self.mask = 0 self.children = None self.boundingbox = None def buildoctree(volume, settings, levels, boundingbox): node = OctreeNode() node.boundingbox = boundingbox if levels == 0: node.mask = 0 startx = round(boundingbox.min.x - 1) endx = round(boundingbox.max.x + 1) starty = round(boundingbox.min.y - 1) endy = round(boundingbox.max.y + 1) startz = round(boundingbox.min.z - 1) endz = round(boundingbox.max.z + 1) for x in range(startx, endx + 1): for y in range(starty, endy + 1): for z in range(startz, endz + 1): coef = volume.sample(x, y, z) bracket = 0 while bracket + 1 < len(settings.brackets) and settings.brackets[bracket + 1] <= coef: bracket += 1 node.mask |= (1 << bracket) return node mid = boundingbox.midpoint() children = [] for i in range(8): xbit = (i >> 2) & 1 ybit = (i >> 1) & 1 zbit = i & 1 childmin = Vec3f(boundingbox.min.x, boundingbox.min.y, boundingbox.min.z) childmax = Vec3f(boundingbox.max.x, boundingbox.max.y, boundingbox.max.z) if xbit: childmin.x = mid.x else: childmax.x = mid.x if ybit: childmin.y = mid.y else: childmax.y = mid.y if zbit: childmin.z = mid.z else: childmax.z = mid.z childbox = BoundingBox(childmin, childmax) childnode = buildoctree(volume, settings, levels - 1, childbox) children.append(childnode) node.children = children combinedmask = 0 allmask = -1 for child in children: combinedmask |= child.mask allmask &= child.mask node.mask = combinedmask if combinedmask == allmask: node.children = None # Memory for children is not freed return node Parameters: levels: The maximum depth of the octree recursion; when levels == 0, the node is a leaf. settings.brackets: An array of threshold coefficients used to quantize volume samples into discrete bracket indices for the mask. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Compression Memory Handling: If all children have identical masks (octree.mask == maskAll), the current node is converted to a leaf node to compress the tree, though memory for children is not freed. Bracket Bounds: The bracket index determination relies on incrementing through settings.brackets; a bounds check is required to prevent out-of-bounds access when coef exceeds all threshold values.
