name: K-D Tree Construction for Volume Rendering
head: Kdtree::buildFromOctree, KdtreeISO build
body: This method constructs a K-D tree from a Sparse Voxel Octree to optimize volume rendering and mesh extraction by partitioning space based on Quadratic Error Function (QEF) variance. It recursively partitions octree nodes into a K-D tree structure using aggregate QEF statistics to determine optimal splitting axes and planes. Input: An Octree structure, and two PositionCode values (minCode, maxCode) defining the range of octree nodes to process. Output: A pointer to a Kdtree node (or nullptr if the range is empty or invalid). The implementation relies on the following structures (derived from): QefSolver: Aggregates statistics for solving a QEF. ATA: glm::mat4 (4x4 matrix), initialized to zero. ATb: glm::fvec3 (3D vector), initialized to zero. diagATc: float, initialized to zero. btb: float, initialized to zero. diagctc: glm::fvec3, initialized to zero. massPointSum: glm::fvec3, initialized to zero. averageNormalSum: glm::fvec3, initialized to zero. roughness: float, initialized to zero. pointCount: int, initialized to zero. RectilinearGrid (Node Content): minCode, maxCode: PositionCode (defines spatial bounds). allQef: QefSolver (aggregate statistics for the node). components: std::vector<QefSolver> (QEFs for sub-components). vertices: std::vector<Vertex> (extracted mesh vertices). approximate: Vertex (approximate solution to the QEF). cornerSigns: uint8t[8] (signs of the 8 corners). componentIndices: int8t[8] (indices of components for corners). isSigned: bool. faceVertices: std::map<RectilinearGrid, Vertex>. Kdtree Node: Contains minCode, maxCode, dir (split axis), depth, and pointers to left/right children. If leaf: stores sign and sample QEF from scalar field. If internal: stores clusterability and combined QEFs. 1. Termination Check: If minCode >= maxCode (component-wise comparison using glm::any(glm::greaterThanEqual(minCode, maxCode))), return nullptr. 2. Aggregate QEF Calculation: Call Octree::getSum(octree, minCode, maxCode, sum) to compute the aggregate QefSolver (sum) for all octree nodes in the range. 3. Empty Check: If sum.pointCount == 0, return nullptr. 4. Select Splitting Axis: Call chooseAxisDir(sum, minCode, maxCode): Calculate the bounding box size: size = maxCode - minCode. Compute variance for each axis i: variance[i] = sum.getVariance(axis[i]) size[i]. Identify maxVarDir (axis with maximum variance) and minVarDir (axis with minimum variance). If size[maxVarDir] < 2, fallback to 3 - maxVarDir - minVarDir. If the fallback size is also < 2, use minVarDir. Let dir be the selected axis. 5. Determine Split Plane: Use a binary search to find the split that minimizes the error difference between left and right children: Initialize minError = infinity, bestLeftMaxCode, bestRightMinCode. Set minAxis = minCode[dir], maxAxis = maxCode[dir]. Loop while maxAxis - minAxis > 1: mid = (maxAxis + minAxis) / 2. Define split bounds: rightMinCode[dir] = mid, leftMaxCode[dir] = mid. Recursively compute sums for left (minCode to leftMaxCode) and right (rightMinCode to maxCode) halves. Solve QEF for left and right to get leftError and rightError. If abs(leftError - rightError) < minError: minError = abs(leftError - rightError) bestLeftMaxCode = leftMaxCode bestRightMinCode = rightMinCode. If leftError > rightError, minAxis = mid; else maxAxis = mid. If leftError == rightError, break. 6. Create Node: Create a new Kdtree node with sum, minCode, maxCode, dir, and depth. 7. Recursive Build: Recursively build left child with minCode and bestLeftMaxCode, and right child with bestRightMinCode and maxCode. 8. Leaf Processing: If the node is a leaf (kd->isLeaf()), assign sign and sample QEF from the scalar field t. 9. Internal Node Processing: If not a leaf, assign sign, calculate clusterability, and combine QEFs from children. If clusterable is true, solve QEF for each component in kd->grid.components. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildkdtree(octree, mincode, maxcode, depth=0): # Step 1: Termination Check if any(mincode[i] >= maxcode[i] for i in range(3)): return None # Step 2: Aggregate QEF sumqef = octree.getsum(mincode, maxcode) # Step 3: Empty Check if sumqef.pointcount == 0: return None # Step 4: Select Splitting Axis size = [maxcode[i] - mincode[i] for i in range(3)] variance = [sumqef.getvariance(i) size[i] for i in range(3)] maxvardir = variance.index(max(variance)) minvardir = variance.index(min(variance)) if size[maxvardir] < 2: dir = 3 - maxvardir - minvardir if size[dir] < 2: dir = minvardir else: dir = maxvardir # Step 5: Determine Split Plane minaxis = mincode[dir] maxaxis = maxcode[dir] minerror = float('inf') bestleftmax = None bestrightmin = None while maxaxis - minaxis > 1: mid = (maxaxis + minaxis) // 2 leftmax = list(maxcode) leftmax[dir] = mid rightmin = list(mincode) rightmin[dir] = mid leftqef = octree.getsum(mincode, leftmax) rightqef = octree.getsum(rightmin, maxcode) lefterror = solveqeferror(leftqef) righterror = solveqeferror(rightqef) errordiff = abs(lefterror - righterror) if errordiff < minerror: minerror = errordiff bestleftmax = leftmax bestrightmin = rightmin if lefterror > righterror: minaxis = mid elif righterror > lefterror: maxaxis = mid else: break # Step 6: Create Node node = KdtreeNode(sumqef, mincode, maxcode, dir, depth) # Step 7: Recursive Build node.left = buildkdtree(octree, mincode, bestleftmax, depth + 1) node.right = buildkdtree(octree, bestrightmin, maxcode, depth + 1) # Step 8 & 9: Leaf/Internal Processing if node.isleaf(): node.sign = samplesign(node, octree.scalarfield) node.qef = sampleqef(node, octree.scalarfield) else: node.sign = combinesigns(node.left.sign, node.right.sign) node.clusterability = calclusterability(node.left, node.right, dir) node.allqef = combineqefs(node.left.allqef, node.right.allqef) if node.clusterability: for i in range(len(node.grid.components)): solveqefcomponent(node.grid.components[i]) return node class KdtreeNode: def init(self, qef, mincode, maxcode, dir, depth): self.qef = qef self.mincode = mincode self.maxcode = maxcode self.dir = dir self.depth = depth self.left = None self.right = None self.sign = 0 self.clusterability = False self.allqef = qef self.grid = type('Grid', (), {'components': []})() def isleaf(self): return self.left is None and self.right is None def solveqeferror(qef): # Solves ATA x = ATb and returns residual error return 0.0 def samplesign(node, scalarfield): # Assigns sign based on scalar field values at node corners return 1 def sampleqef(node, scalarfield): # Samples QEF from scalar field t return node.qef def combinesigns(signl, signr): # Combines signs from children return signl if signl != 0 else signr def calclusterability(left, right, dir): # Calculates clusterability using calClusterability(left, right, dir) return False def combineqefs(qefl, qefr): # Combines QEF statistics from children return qefl def solveqefcomponent(component): # Solves QEF for each component in kd->grid.components pass Parameters: The binary search in Step 5 continues until maxaxis - minaxis > 1. The fallback logic in Step 4 handles degenerate boxes where one dimension has size < 2. Edge Cases: If sum.pointCount == 0, the node is skipped. Precision issues in QEF solving may affect minError comparisons; using abs(leftError - rightError) helps balance the tree. Time Complexity: The construction is recursive. At each level, it computes QEF sums and performs a binary search over the split axis. The binary search depth is logarithmic with respect to the number of voxels in the dimension. Memory Complexity: Stores QEF statistics (QefSolver) for each node. The RectilinearGrid structure adds overhead for vertices and components. Strengths: Optimizes for mesh extraction quality by balancing QEF error. Efficient for contouring. Limitations: More complex than simple geometric splitting. Requires efficient QEF summation. This method originates from the KdtreeISO project by Danielmelody, designed for efficient volume rendering and mesh extraction from sparse voxel data. It builds upon the Sparse Voxel Octree Construction via Morton Code Sorting [2227-sparse-voxel-octree-construction-via-morton-code-sorting.md] to provide a spatial partitioning structure optimized for QEF-based surface reconstruction. name: Dynamic Octree Growth Algorithm
head: Jan Schultke's construction method, Octree expansion method
body: The Dynamic Octree Growth Algorithm constructs a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by dynamically increasing its depth and spatial extent as new voxels are processed, rather than pre-calculating the scene's bounding box. It differs from static voxelization methods by handling out-of-bounds coordinates on-the-fly, ensuring the octree grows to encompass all input data without prior knowledge of the scene's dimensions. This method serves as the foundational growth logic for incremental SVO construction, upon which Octree Insertion with Growth builds specific recursive insertion and boundary check logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree structure o (initially containing only a root node) and a sequence of voxel coordinates v. Output: The modified octree o with expanded depth and spatial extent if necessary. Data Structures: Octree Node: Each node has up to 8 children, indexed 0 to 7. Child Indexing: Child 0 (binary 000) represents the lowest position (minimum coordinates), and Child 7 (binary 111) represents the highest position (maximum coordinates). Coordinate System: The root node covers the range [-1, 0) for each axis. A voxel v is contained in an octree of depth d if v is in the range [-2^{d-1}, 2^{d-1}) for each axis. Algorithm Steps: 1. Check Containment: Determine if the incoming voxel v is contained within the current octree depth d. If v is within the bounds [-2^{d-1}, 2^{d-1}), no growth is needed. If not, trigger the growth loop. 2. Growth Loop: To expand the octree, the algorithm doubles the spatial extent by adding a new layer of nodes around the existing tree. For each child index i from 0 to 7 of the root node r: create a new node n', move the existing child n (at index i) to become the child at index 7-i of n', and make n' the new child of the root r at index i. The source pseudocode uses 1-based indexing (1 \le i \le 8) and a mirror calculation of 8-i+1, which maps to 0-based indexing as i \in [0, 7] and mirror index 7-i. 3. Bitstream Generation: To locate the voxel within the expanded tree, generate a bitstream based on the normalized position of the voxel. The bitstream is divided into strips of 3 bits. Each strip indicates which child to follow (0 to 7). The leftmost strip represents the root's child; the rightmost represents the leaf. This allows handling both positive and negative coordinates symmetrically around the origin boundary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Node: """Octree node with up to 8 children.""" def init(self): self.children = [None] 8 def checkcontainment(v, depth): """Check if voxel coordinate v is within bounds for given depth.""" lower = -2(depth - 1) upper = 2(depth - 1) return lower <= v < upper def growoctree(octree): """ Expands the octree by one level of depth around the root. Based on Algorithm 1. Source uses 1-based indexing (1..8) and mirror 8-i+1. Translated here to 0-based Python (0..7) and mirror 7-i. """ r = octree.root for i in range(8): n = r.children[i] nprime = Node() mirrorindex = 7 - i nprime.children[mirrorindex] = n r.children[i] = nprime return octree def generatebitstream(vx, vy, vz, depth): """ Generates a bitstream for voxel (vx, vy, vz) at given depth. Returns a list of 3-bit child indices (0-7) per level. Based on description of normalized position strips. """ # Normalize each coordinate to [0, 1) relative to current root bounds lower = -2(depth - 1) upper = 2(depth - 1) nx = (vx - lower) / (upper - lower) ny = (vy - lower) / (upper - lower) nz = (vz - lower) / (upper - lower) bitstream = [] for in range(depth): # Extract 3 bits: 1 bit per axis to form child index 0-7 bx = int(nx 2) % 2 by = int(ny 2) % 2 bz = int(nz 2) % 2 childindex = (bx << 2) | (by << 1) | bz bitstream.append(childindex) # Advance to next level nx = (nx 2) % 1.0 ny = (ny 2) % 1.0 nz = (nz 2) % 1.0 return bitstream Parameters and Edge Cases: Coordinate System: The root node covers the range [-1, 0) for each axis. This allows handling both positive and negative coordinates symmetrically around the origin boundary. Containment Check: A voxel v is contained if -2^{d-1} \le v < 2^{d-1} for all axes. Edge Cases: The algorithm assumes the octree starts with a root node. If the octree is empty, initialization is required. The growth loop assumes the root has 8 children (or nulls) to shift. If a child is null, it is moved as null, preserving the empty space structure. Provides the specific recursive insertion logic and boundary checks required for incremental construction, building on this growth algorithm. A variant that enforces a strict origin-centered coordinate system and power-of-two voxel dimensions, growing dynamically on insert. Time Complexity: Growth requires iterating over all 8 children of the root, making it O(1) per growth step (constant number of children). However, if growth is triggered frequently, the cost accumulates. Traversal is O(d) where d is depth. Memory Complexity: Each growth step doubles the spatial extent and adds a new layer of nodes. The memory usage scales with the number of non-empty nodes and the depth required to cover the scene. Strengths: No need to pre-calculate scene bounds; handles arbitrary coordinate ranges including negative values. Limitations: Frequent growth operations can be costly if voxels are widely scattered. The root-centric growth strategy may lead to inefficient memory usage if the scene is not centered near the origin. When to use: Ideal for streaming voxel data where the total extent is unknown or dynamic. The method follows the methodology published by Jan Schultke. It was adopted in the project "Estudio de la compresión y la eficiencia del Sparse Voxel Octree en el cálculo de la Iluminación Global" to handle.vox file formats that accept both positive and negative coordinates, avoiding the memory inefficiency of regular grids and the intersection test overhead of naive voxel models. name: Octree Insertion with Growth
head: Dynamic Octree Insertion, Recursive Voxel Insertion with Boundary Growth
body: Octree Insertion with Growth is a method for constructing a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by recursively inserting individual voxels while dynamically expanding the tree's spatial extent when a voxel falls outside the current root bounds. It differs from static voxelization by handling out-of-bounds coordinates on-the-fly, ensuring the octree grows to encompass all input data without pre-calculating the scene's bounding box. This builds on Dynamic Octree Growth Algorithm by providing the specific recursive insertion logic and boundary checks required for incremental construction. Inputs: A voxel v (containing position p and data/bitstream b), and an existing octree o with root node n and current depth d. Outputs: The updated octree o' with the voxel inserted. Data Structures: Node: Represents an octree node. A naive implementation uses 72 bytes (64-bit) or 40 bytes (32-bit). children[8]: Array of 8 pointers to child nodes (or null if not created). isLeaf: Boolean flag indicating if the node is a leaf. voxelColorIndex: Integer index storing the voxel's color/data if it is a leaf. Bitstream: The voxel data is encoded into a bitstream b to determine the path down the octree. Algorithm Steps: 1. Check Bounds: Get the position p of the voxel v and the current depth d of the octree o. 2. Grow if Necessary: If p is not within the valid range [-2^{d-1}, 2^{d-1}), call grow(o) to expand the octree's spatial extent and depth. The range limit is defined by the depth, specifically [-2^{d-1}, 2^{d-1}). 3. Recursive Insertion: Call the recursive insertion function insertvoxel(v, root(o), bitstream(v), depth(o)). Base Case: If the current depth d = 0, return a leaf node containing the voxel v. Recursive Step: 1. Determine the child index using the bitstream: idx = \text{group}(b, d, 3). This extracts 3 bits from the bitstream at the current depth level to select one of the 8 children. 2. Get or create the child node: n' = \text{child}(n, idx). If n' is null (\emptyset), create a new empty node n' = \text{node}(). 3. Recurse: Call insertvoxel(v, n', b, d - 1). 4. Update parent: Set the child of n at index idx to the result of the recursive call. 4. Return: Return the updated octree. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def insertvoxel(voxel, node, bitstream, depth): """ Recursively inserts a voxel into the octree. Args: voxel: The voxel data object. node: The current octree node. bitstream: The bitstream encoding the voxel's position/data. depth: The current depth level in the octree. Returns: The updated node. """ # Base case: leaf node if depth == 0: return createleafnode(voxel) # Determine child index from bitstream (3 bits per level) childidx = group(bitstream, depth, 3) # Get or create child child = node.children[childidx] if child is None: child = createemptynode() # Recurse newchild = insertvoxel(voxel, child, bitstream, depth - 1) # Update parent's child pointer node.children[childidx] = newchild return node def insertvoxelintooctree(voxel, octree): """ Main entry point for inserting a voxel, handling growth. Args: voxel: The voxel to insert. octree: The current octree structure. Returns: The updated octree. """ p = voxel.position d = octree.depth # Check if position is within current bounds # Range is -2^(d-1), 2^(d-1)) lowerbound = -2(d-1) upperbound = 2(d-1) if not (lowerbound <= p.x < upperbound and lowerbound <= p.y < upperbound and lowerbound <= p.z < upperbound): octree = growoctree(octree) # Insert into root octree.root = insertvoxel(voxel, octree.root, voxel.bitstream, octree.depth) return octree Parameters: Range Limit: The valid position range is defined by the depth d as [-2^{d-1}, 2^{d-1}). Bitstream Grouping: 3 bits are extracted per level to index the 8 children. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The range check uses integer arithmetic for bounds [-2^{d-1}, 2^{d-1}). Floating-point voxel positions must be converted to integer grid coordinates before comparison. Boundary Conditions: The upper bound is exclusive (<), while the lower bound is inclusive (\ge). This ensures unique mapping of positions to octree cells. Growth Overhead: Frequent growth operations can be expensive. The grow function must efficiently restructure the root and update all child pointers. A specific implementation detail for building the octree from a voxel fragment queue. It involves averaging octree leaf node values when different voxels fall into the same node. Layout: Octree Node Buffer: Stores octree/voxel node data. 8 nodes are grouped into 1 tile. Each octree node is 28 bytes: first 4 bytes store child tile index, next 24 bytes store neighbor node byte offset from start of octree node buffer. Octree Leaf Node: Stores voxel data directly, using 16 bytes. First 4 bytes store bit flag indicating if voxel is from static mesh (not overwritten by dynamic). 1 byte counter stored with voxel normal for averaging when different voxel fragments fall into same voxel. 3D Texture: Stores reflected radiance and alpha from [direct lighting at that voxel. Assumes all surface reflect light diffusely, so only 1 3D texture is used (different from paper storing incoming radiance). Indexed by child node tile index. A recursive function to activate or deactivate a voxel at a specific 3D position within the octree. Steps: 1. Check if position is within node bounds (boxMin to boxMax); if not, return false. 2. If depth >= currentDepth, set node->isActive = activate and return true if state changed. 3. Mark node as not a leaf. 4. Determine child index: childIdx = 0; if position.x >= node->position.x childIdx |= 1; if position.y >= node->position.y childIdx |= 2; if position.z >= node->position.z childIdx |= 4. 5. If child doesn't exist, create it with position = node->position + offset (calculated similarly to voxelization) and size = halfSize. 6. Recursively call placeVoxel on the child with depth + 1. A method for updating residency information in a hybrid approach for scalable web volume rendering. Steps: 1. For each new brick received by the client, select an available slot in the brick cache for storing it. 2. Determine all residency octree leaf nodes whose spatial extent overlaps the spatial extent of the brick. 3. Mark the determined leaf nodes as partially mapped in the brick’s resolution level and channel. 4. Propagate the update up the tree to the root node. Formula: For non-leaf nodes, update residency via bitwise OR of child node bitmasks: B{parent} = B{child1} \lor B{child2} \lor... \lor B{child8}, where B is the bitmask. Pitfall: Upwards propagation terminates early if a node's bitmask remains unchanged by the OR operation. A method for adding surfels to the octree, recursively descending to leaf nodes, and subdividing if the leaf exceeds MAXSURFELCOUNT. Steps: 1. Check if surfel is inside node using inside(obj); if not, return 0. 2. If node has children, loop over 8 children, recursively call add on each, sum results, increment surfelCount, and return sum. A specific implementation of the growth mechanism, detailing how the root node is restructured when expanding. Steps: 1. Call EnlargeCorners(dir) to compute newCornerIdx, oldCornerIdx, and offset based on the expansion direction. 2. Initialize an array of 8 child pointers (rootChildren) to nullptr, then assign the current root node to rootChildren[oldCornerIdx]. 3. Create a new empty octree node at rootChildren[newCornerIdx] with size msize, position mposition + offset, and depth 1. 4. Construct a new OctreeChildren struct with a bitmask containing only the old and new children, and the rootChildren array. 5. If expanding in a negative direction (xminus, yminus, or zminus), update the root position by adding the offset. 6. Double the octree size (msize = 2) and replace the root node with a new Octree initialized with the new children, updated size, and updated position. Pitfall: The offset calculation for xplus uses glm::vec3(msize, 0, 0) but is marked as unused in a comment, indicating a potential bug or placeholder that should be zeroed or properly utilized. Time Complexity: Insertion is O(d) where d is the depth of the octree, assuming the tree is grown only when necessary. Growth operations may involve restructuring the root, which is O(1) in terms of total nodes but requires pointer updates. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is proportional to the number of active nodes in the octree. A naive node structure uses 72 bytes (64-bit) or 40 bytes (32-bit) per node. Optimized structures (e.g., 28-byte nodes with tile grouping) can reduce this significantly. Strengths: Handles arbitrary input distributions without pre-computation. Dynamic growth ensures memory is only allocated for occupied space. Limitations: Frequent growth operations can lead to fragmentation or performance overhead. The naive node structure is memory-heavy. When to Use: When the scene's bounding box is unknown or dynamic, and incremental voxel insertion is preferred over batch voxelization. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained and a more compact node structure (like the 28-byte tile-based approach) is required, or when the scene is static and a pre-computed bounding box is available. The method originates from research on Sparse Voxel Octree compression and efficiency for global illumination calculation. It is a fundamental building block for dynamic SVO construction, allowing for the incremental addition of voxels without pre-defining the spatial extent. Variants and implementations can be found in various graphics research projects and open-source repositories. name: Octree-based Mesh Voxelization
head: Recursive Triangle Voxelization via Octree, Voxelization using octree spatial partitioning
body: Octree-based mesh voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a sparse voxel representation by recursively subdividing a 3D bounding box into an octree structure and marking leaf nodes that intersect with mesh triangles as active voxels. It differs from uniform grid voxelization by adapting resolution locally, ensuring that only space occupied by the mesh is stored, which significantly reduces memory usage for sparse or complex geometries compared to fixed-resolution approaches. Inputs and Outputs Input: A triangle mesh defined by a vertex array and an index array (triangles specified as triplets of indices). Output: An octree structure where nodes represent spatial subdivisions, and leaf nodes marked as active correspond to voxels occupied by the mesh. Data Structures The core data structure is the OctreeNode, defined with the following fields: isLeaf (bool): Indicates if the node has no children. isActive (bool): Indicates if the node represents a voxel occupied by the mesh. position (glm::vec3): The center coordinates of the node's bounding box. size (glm::vec3): The dimensions (width, height, depth) of the node's bounding box. color (glm::vec3): Optional attribute for visualization (not used in core voxelization logic). children (OctreeNode [8]): An array of pointers to 8 child nodes. If isLeaf is true, these are typically null or unused. Parameters currentDepth: The target depth for voxelization, controlling the resolution. Default value is 6. maxDepth: The maximum allowed depth to prevent infinite recursion. Default value is 10. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Create the root OctreeNode. Set its position to (0, 0, 0) and size to (2, 2, 2), defining a bounding box ranging from -1 to 1 in all axes. Initialize currentDepth to 6 and maxDepth to 10. 2. Mesh Iteration: Iterate through all meshes in the model. For each mesh, iterate through the index array in steps of 3 to extract triangles. 3. Triangle Extraction: For each triplet of indices (i, i+1, i+2), retrieve the corresponding vertices v0, v1, and v2 from the mesh's vertex array. 4. Recursive Voxelization: Call the recursive function voxelizeTriangle(root, v0, v1, v2, 1) to process the triangle against the octree starting at depth 1. 5. Intersection Test: Inside voxelizeTriangle(node, v0, v1, v2, depth): Calculate halfSize = node->size 0.5f. Calculate boxMin = node->position - halfSize and boxMax = node->position + halfSize. Perform a bounding box overlap test between the triangle and the node's box. This is implemented as a simplified AABB-AABB check: compute triMin = min(v0, v1, v2) and triMax = max(v0, v1, v2) component-wise. If triMin > boxMax or triMax < boxMin in any axis, the triangle does not intersect the node's bounding box, and the function returns immediately. 6. Depth Check: If depth >= currentDepth, mark the current node as a leaf (isLeaf = true) and active (isActive = true), then return. 7. Subdivision: If the depth is less than currentDepth: Mark the node as not a leaf (isLeaf = false). Iterate through 8 children (index i from 0 to 7). For each child, if the pointer is null, allocate a new OctreeNode. Calculate the child's position offset based on the bit flags of i: x-offset: +/- halfSize.x 0.5f if (i & 1) is true. y-offset: +/- halfSize.y 0.5f if (i & 2) is true. z-offset: +/- halfSize.z 0.5f if (i & 4) is true. Set child->position = node->position + offset and child->size = halfSize. Recursively call voxelizeTriangle(child, v0, v1, v2, depth + 1). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizemesh(mesh, currentdepth=6, maxdepth=10): # Initialize root node root = OctreeNode() root.position = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) root.size = vec3(2.0, 2.0, 2.0) root.isLeaf = False root.isActive = False root.children = [None] 8 # Iterate over all triangles in the mesh for i in range(0, len(mesh.indices), 3): v0 = mesh.vertices[mesh.indices[i]] v1 = mesh.vertices[mesh.indices[i+1]] v2 = mesh.vertices[mesh.indices[i+2]] voxelizetriangle(root, v0, v1, v2, 1, currentdepth, maxdepth) return root def voxelizetriangle(node, v0, v1, v2, depth, currentdepth, maxdepth): # Prevent infinite recursion if depth > maxdepth: return # Calculate bounding box of the current node halfsize = node.size 0.5 boxmin = node.position - halfsize boxmax = node.position + halfsize # Simplified AABB-AABB intersection test trimin = min(v0, v1, v2) trimax = max(v0, v1, v2) # Check for separation along any axis if (trimin.x > boxmax.x or trimax.x < boxmin.x or trimin.y > boxmax.y or trimax.y < boxmin.y or trimin.z > boxmax.z or trimax.z < boxmin.z): return # If target depth reached, mark as active leaf if depth >= currentdepth: node.isLeaf = True node.isActive = True return # Subdivide node.isLeaf = False for i in range(8): # Allocate child if null if node.children[i] is None: node.children[i] = OctreeNode() child = node.children[i] # Calculate child position and size child.size = halfsize offset = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Bit flags determine octant position if i & 1: offset.x += halfsize.x 0.5 else: offset.x -= halfsize.x 0.5 if i & 2: offset.y += halfsize.y 0.5 else: offset.y -= halfsize.y 0.5 if i & 4: offset.z += halfsize.z 0.5 else: offset.z -= halfsize.z 0.5 child.position = node.position + offset # Recurse voxelizetriangle(child, v0, v1, v2, depth + 1, currentdepth, maxdepth) class OctreeNode: def init(self): self.isLeaf = False self.isActive = False self.position = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.size = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.color = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.children = [None] 8 Edge Cases and Pitfalls The intersection test used is a simplified bounding box overlap test, not a precise triangle-box intersection. This may result in false positives where a node is marked active even if the triangle only passes through the node's bounding box without intersecting the actual triangle surface within that volume. The algorithm relies on a fixed initial bounding box of size (2,2,2) centered at (0,0,0). If the mesh lies outside this range, it will not be voxelized. Pre-processing to scale or translate the mesh into this canonical space is required. Uses Morton codes for efficient spatial indexing and memory layout, differing from the basic pointer-based octree by optimizing cache locality and enabling faster traversal. Choose when memory efficiency and traversal speed are critical. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. In the worst case, each triangle may traverse all nodes down to currentDepth, leading to O(N \cdot 8^{D}) where N is the number of triangles and D is the depth. However, due to the bounding box culling, only nodes intersecting the triangle's bounding box are processed. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory usage is proportional to the number of active nodes in the octree. Since it is a sparse structure, it uses significantly less memory than a uniform grid for the same resolution, especially for thin or complex surfaces. Strengths: Adaptive resolution; memory efficient for sparse data; simple implementation. Limitations: The simplified intersection test can lead to over-voxelization (false positives); fixed initial bounding box requires pre-processing; pointer-based structure may have poor cache performance compared to array-based or Morton-coded structures. When to use: Suitable for applications where memory efficiency is more important than absolute geometric precision, or when the mesh is sparse. When not to use: When high geometric fidelity is required without post-processing, or when the mesh is dense and fills the bounding box uniformly (a uniform grid might be simpler and faster). This method is described in the context of a 3D model voxelization tool that allows importing models, converting them to voxels using octree spatial partitioning, and exporting the result. The specific implementation details, including the recursive triangle voxelization algorithm and data structures, are derived from the source code and documentation of the modelvoxelizer project. name: Voxel Placement in Octree
head: SVO set, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) insertion with collapse/expand, octree voxel placement, placeVoxel
body: Voxel Placement in Octree inserts a colored voxel into a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) at a specific 3D coordinate. It handles recursive descent through the tree hierarchy, creating intermediate nodes as necessary, and marks the target leaf node with the voxel's color. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit handling of the collapse/expand state of internal nodes, ensuring that previously collapsed uniform regions can be correctly subdivided when new non-uniform data is inserted. Inputs: node: The current octree node (initially the root). nx, ny, nz: The 3D coordinates of the center of the current node's bounding box. size: The side length of the current node's bounding box. depth: The current recursion depth (0 for root). x, y, z: The 3D coordinates of the voxel to be placed. color: The color or density value of the voxel. maxDepth: The maximum allowed depth of the octree. Outputs: Modifies the octree structure in place: creates child nodes if they do not exist, sets isLeaf flags, and assigns color to the target leaf. Returns void or a boolean indicating success/bounds status. The implementation relies on an OctreeNode structure. While exact memory layouts vary by language, the logical fields required are: isLeaf: Boolean flag indicating if the node is a leaf. color: The value stored in the voxel. children: An array or pointer to 8 child nodes (indexed 0-7). If isLeaf is true or the node is collapsed, this may be null or None. position: The 3D center coordinates of the node. size: The side length of the node. 1. Base Case (Max Depth): If depth equals maxDepth, the current node is the target leaf. Set node.isLeaf = true, set node.color = color, set node.children = null, and return. 2. Boundary Check: If the voxel position (x, y, z) is outside the current node's bounding box defined by (nx, ny, nz) and size, return immediately or return false. 3. Collapse/Expand Check: If depth < maxDepth and node.isLeaf is true (indicating a previously collapsed node), the node must be expanded. Create 8 new child nodes, initialize each as a leaf with isLeaf = true, assign each child the node.color to propagate the uniform value, set node.isLeaf = false, and set node.children to the array of new children. 4. Calculate Child Index: Determine which of the 8 octants contains the voxel. Calculate half = size / 2. Determine bit flags based on the voxel's position relative to the node's center: ix = 1 if x >= nx + half, else 0; iy = 1 if y >= ny + half, else 0; iz = 1 if z >= nz + half, else 0. Compute childIdx = ix + (iy << 1) + (iz << 2). 5. Create Child if Missing: If node.children[childIdx] does not exist, create a new OctreeNode. Set its position to (nx + ixhalf, ny + iyhalf, nz + izhalf) and its size to half. Assign it to node.children[childIdx]. 6. Recurse: Call placeVoxel (or set) on node.children[childIdx] with depth + 1. Child Index: \text{childIdx} = ix + 2 \cdot iy + 4 \cdot iz Where ix, iy, iz \in \{0, 1\} are determined by: ix = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x \ge nx + \frac{s}{2} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} (Analogous for iy, iz with ny, nz, y, z). Half Size: h = \frac{s}{2}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class OctreeNode: def init(self): self.isLeaf = False self.color = None self.children = None self.position = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.size = 0.0 def placeVoxel(node, nx, ny, nz, size, depth, maxDepth, x, y, z, color): # 1. Base Case: Reached maximum depth if depth == maxDepth: node.isLeaf = True node.color = color node.children = None return # 2. Boundary Check: Position outside current node bounds half = size / 2 if not (nx - half <= x <= nx + half and ny - half <= y <= ny + half and nz - half <= z <= nz + half): return False # 3. Collapse/Expand Check: If node is currently a leaf but we need to go deeper if node.isLeaf: node.isLeaf = False node.children = [None] 8 for i in range(8): child = OctreeNode() child.isLeaf = True child.color = node.color ix = i & 1 iy = (i >> 1) & 1 iz = (i >> 2) & 1 child.position = (nx + (2ix - 1)half, ny + (2iy - 1)half, nz + (2iz - 1)half) child.size = half node.children[i] = child # 4. Calculate Child Index ix = 1 if x >= nx + half else 0 iy = 1 if y >= ny + half else 0 iz = 1 if z >= nz + half else 0 childIdx = ix + (iy << 1) + (iz << 2) # 5. Create Child if Missing if node.children[childIdx] is None: child = OctreeNode() child.position = (nx + (2ix - 1)half, ny + (2iy - 1)half, nz + (2iz - 1)half) child.size = half node.children[childIdx] = child # 6. Recurse placeVoxel(node.children[childIdx], node.children[childIdx].position[0], node.children[childIdx].position[1], node.children[childIdx].position[2], node.children[childIdx].size, depth + 1, maxDepth, x, y, z, color) return True maxDepth: The maximum recursion depth. Not given in the sources. color: The data value. Not given in the sources. Collapsed Node Access: If a collapse() operation previously set children = null on an internal node (at depth < maxDepth), a subsequent set() will throw an error when accessing node.children[childIdx]. The implementation must check node.isLeaf or !node.children before descending and expand the node if necessary. Null Color Removal: Using set(x, y, z, null) to remove voxels leaves leaf nodes with color = null, which prevents effective pruning/collapsing and can permanently "materialize" empty regions. A dedicated delete(x, y, z) function is recommended to remove nodes and prune upward when a branch becomes entirely empty. Out of Bounds: If the voxel position is outside the current node's bounding box, the function should return early to avoid infinite recursion or invalid memory access. What it is: A method that converts a triangle mesh into a voxel grid using an octree structure. Difference: Focuses on rasterizing geometry into voxels rather than inserting individual voxels into a sparse structure. When to choose: When starting from a mesh model. Link: Octree-based Mesh Voxelization What it is: An SVO implementation that uses Morton codes (Z-order curves) for efficient spatial indexing and traversal. Difference: Uses linearized indices for memory layout and traversal, whereas this method uses explicit tree pointers. When to choose: When memory locality and cache efficiency are critical, or for out-of-core storage. Link: Dynamic Sparse Voxel Octree with Morton Codes Time: Not given in the sources. The specific logic for handling collapse/expand states and the pitfalls of null-color removal are documented in community-driven development projects. SVOs were popularized for ray marching in real-time graphics. The specific "placeVoxel" implementation with explicit collapse handling appears in modern web-based voxel editors and tools. head: rapid-svo
body: A single-header C++ implementation of a dynamic sparse voxel octree using integer coordinates and Morton codes, designed for micro-optimized CPU-based voxel physics simulations in chunked procedural game worlds. It distinguishes itself by providing bulk allocation and deallocation operations alongside point queries, optimized for high-throughput voxel manipulation rather than just static storage. It builds on Octree Insertion with Growth by providing the concrete data structures and Morton code integration required for efficient spatial indexing. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes voxel positions (integer coordinates) and metadata as input. It outputs a tree structure supporting allocbulk (batch insertion), get (point query returning a pointer or nullptr), and dealloc (removal). Data Structures: The tree is templated on three parameters: <MortonType, VoxelFormat, DetailsInfo>. DetailsInfo (rapidsvo::detailsinfo): A struct containing discardoverflow (bool) and limitmaxbounds (array of 3 integers). name: Sparse Voxel Octree (Dynamic, Origin-Centered)
head: bit-svo
body: A sparse voxel octree implementation where voxel widths are powers of 2, positions are integer multiples of their widths (ensuring alignment to widths), the tree is always centered at (0,0,0), and the tree expands dynamically on insert. It differs from static SVOs by growing its depth and spatial extent only when necessary, and from general dynamic octrees by enforcing a strict origin-centered coordinate system and power-of-two voxel dimensions. Inputs: A voxel defined by integer coordinates (x, y, z) and a logarithmic size lg\size (where width w = 2^{lg\size}). The tree stores values of type T. Outputs: A reference to the TreeBody node corresponding to the voxel, or None if the voxel is outside the current bounds. Data Structures: VoxelTree<T>: lgsize: u8: The log2 of the total tree size (width). contents: Branches<T>: The root node, always a Branches struct. Branches<T>: A struct with 8 fields of type TreeBody<T>, named lll, llh, lhl, lhh, hll, hlh, hhl, hhh in xyz ordering. Memory layout is #[repr(C)], allowing direct indexing via coordinate bits. TreeBody<T>: Empty: No data. Leaf(T): Contains the value T. Branch(Box<Branches<T>>): Points to a child Branches node. VoxelBounds: x: i32, y: i32, z: i32: Integer coordinates. lgsize: i32: Logarithmic size. Algorithm Steps: 1. Bounds Check (containsbounds): Determine if a voxel fits within the current tree bounds. If voxel.lgsize < 0, return true. Calculate high = (1 << self.lgsize) >> voxel.lgsize. Calculate low = -high. If voxel.x < low or voxel.y < low or voxel.z < low, return false. If (voxel.x + 1) <= high and (voxel.y + 1) <= high and (voxel.z + 1) <= high, return true. Otherwise, return false. 2. Mask Calculation (findmask): Determine the traversal mask for the voxel's size relative to the tree. Initialize mask = (1 << self.lgsize) >> 1. If voxel.lgsize >= 0, shift mask right by voxel.lgsize: mask = mask >> voxel.lgsize. If voxel.lgsize < 0, shift mask left by -voxel.lgsize: mask = mask << (-voxel.lgsize). 3. Traversal (mutfind): Traverse or create nodes to reach the target voxel. Initialize mask using findmask and branches pointer to &self.contents. First Iteration: Use condition |x| x >= 0 to select the branch, determining the most significant bit (sign) of the coordinates. If mask == 0, return the current branch. Otherwise, call step(branch) to get the next Branches node. Subsequent Iterations: Loop while mask > 0. Use condition |x| (x & mask) != 0 to select the branch, determining the remaining bits of the coordinates. Update mask = mask >> 1. Step into the child branch. 4. Branch Selection (getbranch): Map coordinates (x, y, z) to one of the 8 children using a choosebranch function. The bits determine the index: x bit selects l (low) or h (high), y bit selects l or h, z bit selects l or h. Example: lll corresponds to (false, false, false), hhh to (true, true, true). 5. Retrieval (get): If !containsbounds(voxel), return None. Define getstep closure: if branch is Branch(ref branches), return Ok(branches.deref()), else Err(()). Call self.find(voxel, getstep). If result is Ok(&TreeBody::Leaf(ref t)), return Some(t), else None. 6. Ray Casting (castray): Calculate coords array where each element is 1 if origin[i] >= 0.0 else 0. Set childlgsize = self.lgsize as i16. Define makebounds closure: returns VoxelBounds with x = coords[0] - 1, y = coords[1] - 1, z = coords[2] - 1, lgsize = childlgsize. Call raycast::castraybranches with &self.contents, origin, direction, None, coords, &mut makebounds, and the action function act. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Branches: def init(self): self.lll = TreeBody('Empty') self.llh = TreeBody('Empty') self.lhl = TreeBody('Empty') self.lhh = TreeBody('Empty') self.hll = TreeBody('Empty') self.hlh = TreeBody('Empty') self.hhl = TreeBody('Empty') self.hhh = TreeBody('Empty') @staticmethod def empty(): return Branches() class TreeBody: def init(self, kind, value=None, children=None): self.kind = kind # 'Empty', 'Leaf', 'Branch' self.value = value self.children = children # Branches instance class VoxelTree: def init(self): self.lgsize = 0 self.contents = Branches.empty() def containsbounds(self, voxel): if voxel.lgsize < 0: return True high = (1 << self.lgsize) >> voxel.lgsize low = -high if voxel.x < low or voxel.y < low or voxel.z < low: return False if (voxel.x + 1) <= high and (voxel.y + 1) <= high and (voxel.z + 1) <= high: return True return False def findmask(self, voxel): mask = (1 << self.lgsize) >> 1 if voxel.lgsize >= 0: mask = mask >> voxel.lgsize else: mask = mask << (-voxel.lgsize) return mask def getbranch(self, branches, choosefunc, x, y, z): xbit = choosefunc(x) ybit = choosefunc(y) zbit = choosefunc(z) if not xbit and not ybit and not zbit: return branches.lll if not xbit and not ybit and zbit: return branches.llh if not xbit and ybit and not zbit: return branches.lhl if not xbit and ybit and zbit: return branches.lhh if xbit and not ybit and not zbit: return branches.hll if xbit and not ybit and zbit: return branches.hlh if xbit and ybit and not zbit: return branches.hhl return branches.hhh def mutfind(self, voxel, step): mask = self.findmask(voxel) branches = self.contents # First iteration: sign bit branch = self.getbranch(branches, lambda x: x >= 0, voxel.x, voxel.y, voxel.z) if mask == 0: return branch branches = step(branch) while mask > 0: branch = self.getbranch(branches, lambda x: (x & mask) != 0, voxel.x, voxel.y, voxel.z) if mask == 0: return branch branches = step(branch) mask >>= 1 return branch def getmutorcreatestep(self, branch): if branch.kind == 'Empty': branch.kind = 'Branch' branch.children = Branches.empty() elif branch.kind == 'Leaf': branch.kind = 'Branch' branch.children = Branches.empty() return branch.children def get(self, voxel): if not self.containsbounds(voxel): return None def getstep(branch): if branch.kind == 'Branch': return branch.children raise StopIteration try: node = self.mutfind(voxel, getstep) if node.kind == 'Leaf': return node.value except StopIteration: pass return None Pitfalls: Negative voxel lgsize: containsbounds returns true immediately if voxel.lgsize < 0, treating it as always within bounds. Leaf replacement: when inserting into a Leaf node during getmutorcreatestep, the leaf is erased and replaced with 8 empty sub-branches, which is noted as debatable but done for easier debugging of accidental replacements. Time Complexity: Insertion is O(D) where D is the depth of the tree. Benchmarks show approximately 1 microsecond per insert through 30 levels of depth (world width of 2^{30} voxels). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of non-empty nodes, with each branch node consuming memory for 8 child pointers. Strengths: Dynamic growth avoids pre-allocating memory for empty space, and the origin-centered design simplifies coordinate arithmetic for symmetric scenes. Limitations: The strict power-of-two width and alignment requirements limit flexibility, and leaf replacement on insertion may cause unnecessary memory churn if leaves are frequently replaced by branches. This implementation is part of the bit-svo project by bfops. It is designed for efficient sparse voxel storage with a focus on performance and simplicity, leveraging bit manipulation for branch selection. bfops/bit-svo, https://github.com/bfops/bit-svo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

body: This method constructs a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a stream of indexed leaves by maintaining a fixed-size array of queues, one per tree depth level, and collapsing homogeneous subtrees into single leaf or invalid nodes to compress the structure. It differs from brute-force or sorting-based builders by processing leaves in a single pass without requiring full in-memory tree storage or pre-sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of indexed leaves, where each leaf contains an index and a leaf data structure. The stream is assumed to be sorted by index. Output: A serialized SVO written to disk via a BlockWriter, consisting of Voxel and Leaf nodes. Data Structures: Node: A union-based structure representing either a Voxel or a Leaf. python class Node: def init(self, leaf=None, voxel=None): self.leaf = leaf self.voxel = voxel self.isleaf = leaf is not None self.isvalid = leaf is not None or voxel is not None Voxel: A non-leaf node structure. python class Voxel: def init(self): self.child = 0 # Offset to children in block self.valid = 0 # 8-bit mask for visible children self.leaf = 0 # 8-bit mask for leaf children Leaf: A leaf node structure. python class Leaf: def init(self, rgba=None): self.rgba = rgba if rgba else [0, 0, 0, 0] def valid(self): return self.rgba[3] != 0x00 NodeQueue: A fixed-size queue for nodes at a specific depth level. python class NodeQueue: def init(self): self.data = [None] 8 self.size = 0 def push(self, node): self.data[self.size] = node self.size += 1 def full(self): return self.size == 8 def empty(self): return self.size == 0 def clear(self): self.size = 0 def getitem(self, index): return self.data[index] Builder: The main builder class. python class Builder: def init(self, queuecount, writer): self.queues = [NodeQueue() for in range(queuecount)] self.queuecount = queuecount self.streamindex = 0 self.writer = writer Parameters: queuecount: The number of queues used for the tree construction, typically 8 for an octree. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize streamindex to 0 and all queues to empty. 2. Processing a Leaf (addleaf): Calculate leafcount = ileaf.index - streamindex. Loop while leafcount > 0: Calculate power: if leafcount >= 8, power = floor(log(leafcount) / log(8)); else power = 0. Find nonemptyi: index of the first non-empty queue in queues[0..queuecount-1]. If all empty, nonemptyi = queuecount. Calculate inserti = min(power, nonemptyi). If inserti >= queuecount, throw error "Homogenous model" and write the leaf directly. Create topush Node: if ileaf.leaf.valid() is true, topush = Node(ileaf.leaf); else topush = Node() (invalid). Call pushat(topush, inserti). Subtract pow(8, inserti) from leafcount. Set streamindex = ileaf.index. 3. Pushing to Queue (pushat): Push node to queues[index] and call collapse(index). 4. Collapse Logic (collapse): If queues[index] is not full, return immediately. Initialize parentisleaf = true. Initialize parent Voxel: parent.valid = 0, parent.leaf = 0, parent.child = writer.pos(). Loop j from 0 to 7 over queues[index]: If queues[index][j].isleaf is false, set parentisleaf = false. Update masks: If queues[index][j].isvalid is false, update parent.valid mask accordingly. If queues[index][j].isleaf is true, update parent.leaf mask accordingly. Determine topush: If parentisleaf, topush = Node(queues[index][0].leaf). Else if parent.valid == 0, topush = Node() (invalid). Else, write children to writer (leaf if node.isleaf, voxel if node.isvalid), then topush = Node(parent). After processing all 8 children, push topush to the parent queue and clear queues[index]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Homogenous Model: If inserti >= queuecount, the algorithm throws an error and writes the leaf directly to bypass the tree structure for that segment. Truncated Logic: The exact logic for updating parent.valid and parent.leaf masks, as well as queue advancement after collapse, is not fully specified in the source. Precision: log and floor operations for power calculation should use floating-point arithmetic with care for large leafcount values. Unverified code. Standard logic would update parent.valid and parent.leaf masks here. if parentisleaf: topush = Node(leaf=self.queues[index][0].leaf) elif parent.valid == 0: topush = Node() else: # Write children to writer # For each child, if it is a leaf, write the Leaf; if it is a valid voxel, write the Voxel. # Not given in the sources. Standard logic would push topush to queues[index-1] (if index > 0) and clear queues[index]. topush = Node(voxel=parent) self.queues[index].clear() Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. body: The Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Builder is an algorithm that constructs a flat-array representation of a Sparse Voxel Octree from a list of input voxels or geometric primitives. It solves the problem of efficiently organizing spatial data for ray marching or pathfinding by creating a hierarchy where empty space is skipped, but internal nodes are explicitly allocated to maintain traversal continuity. It differs from its siblings by focusing on either a recursive depth-first initialization of a dense structure or a parallel, level-by-level GPU-based allocation and merging process, whereas the Brute Force method [1704-brute-force-svo-construction.md] typically relies on simpler, less memory-efficient insertion strategies. The method exists in three primary implementations: a CPU-based recursive dense builder, a GPU-based parallel level-by-level builder, and a recursive subdivision with merging variant for pathfinding. Both the CPU and GPU variants produce a flat array of nodes but differ in memory management and traversal logic. Inputs: A list of voxels (occupied cells) or geometric primitives to be voxelized. maxDepth (or octreeresolution): The maximum depth of the octree. volumesize: The dimensions of the bounding box in voxels. Outputs: A flat array tree (or octreebuffer) containing node metadata. The tree array stores nodes as uint32t values. Bits 0-16 (17 bits): Index of the first child node in the tree array. Bit 17 (1 bit): Leaf flag. If set, the node is a leaf. Empty Node Value: 0x0000FFFF (Child index 0, Leaf flag 0). Solid Leaf Node Value: 0x00004200 (Child index 0, Leaf flag 1, plus specific marker bits). Nodes may also be stored in a struct format for metadata: 1 Byte Total: Bits 0-6 (7 bits): Depth. Bit 7 (1 bit): IsLeaf flag. Additional Fields: Position, Size, Parent Index, Children Indices (stored separately or in extended structs). This method initializes a dense octree up to maxDepth, marking leaves as solid. Parameters: maxDepth: Maximum subdivision depth. Steps: 1. Initialize tree array. 2. Set offset = 0, index = 0. 3. Push StackEntry{0, 0} to stack. 4. Push initial root node 0x0000FFFF to tree. 5. Loop while stack is not empty: 1. Calculate offset = tree.size() - index. 2. Set tree[index] |= offset << 17. 3. Increment index by offset. 4. If depth < maxDepth: 1. Increment depth. 2. Loop 8 times: push 0x0000FFFF to tree, push StackEntry{index + (8 - i), depth} to stack. 5. Else: loop 8 times: push 0x00004200 to tree. 6. Pop top of stack into current. 7. Set index = current.index, depth = current.depth. 8. Pop stack. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildrecursivedense(maxdepth): tree = [] stack = [] index = 0 depth = 0 # Initial root stack.append({'index': 0, 'depth': 0}) tree.append(0x0000FFFF) # Empty node while stack: # Calculate offset for child pointer offset = len(tree) - index # Set child pointer in current node (bits 17-31) currentnodeval = tree[index] tree[index] = (currentnodeval & 0x1FFFF) | (offset << 17) index += offset if depth < maxdepth: depth += 1 for i in range(8): # Push placeholder empty nodes tree.append(0x0000FFFF) # Push stack entry for the child stack.append({'index': index + (8 - i), 'depth': depth}) else: # Leaf level: push solid leaf placeholders for i in range(8): tree.append(0x00004200) # Pop and backtrack if stack: current = stack.pop() index = current['index'] depth = current['depth'] This method processes the voxel list level-by-level using compute shaders. Parameters: octreeresolution: Derived from maxvolumeside via ceil(log2(maxvolumeside)). Steps: 1. Voxelization: Convert scene primitives to a voxellist. 2. Initialization: Clear memory for the first 8 nodes (root children) using nodeinit shader. Set start = 0, count = 8. 3. Level Loop: Iterate from level 1 to octreeresolution - 1: 1. Flagging: Execute nodeflag shader to determine which nodes at the current level are internal (have children) or leaves. Binds octree buffer and voxel list. 2. Allocation: Execute nodealloc shader to allocate memory for children of internal nodes. Uses an atomic counter. Output start address is allocstart, count is alloccount 8. 3. State Update: start becomes allocstart. count becomes alloccount 8. allocstart becomes start + count. 4. Initialization of New Nodes: Clear memory for newly allocated nodes using nodeinit shader. 4. Leaf Storage: After the loop, execute storeleaf shader to store leaf node data based on the voxel list size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildparallelgpu(voxellist, octreeresolution): # Initialize root children start = 0 count = 8 allocstart = start + count # Clear initial nodes nodeinit(start, count) for level in range(1, octreeresolution): # Determine which nodes are internal/leaf nodeflag(octreebuffer, voxellist) # Allocate memory for children of internal nodes alloccount = nodealloc(octreebuffer, voxellist) # Update state start = allocstart count = alloccount 8 allocstart = start + count # Clear new nodes nodeinit(start, count) # Store leaf data storeleaf(octreebuffer, voxellist) This variant handles collision detection and dynamic subdivision. Parameters: MaxDepth: Maximum subdivision depth. SVOObstacle: Custom collision trace channel. Steps: 1. Start with Root node at Depth 0. 2. If root collides with SVOObstacle: 1. Recursively subdivide to MaxDepth. 2. For each child index 0-7: 1. Compute position using binary mapping: 0 = minus direction, 1 = plus direction relative to center. 2. Run recursive build task. 3. Merge: 1. Calculate total size of child results. 2. Insert root node into Node Array. 3. Iterate through child results. 4. If child's root index is invalid (Blocked), skip it. 5. Merge valid subtree into Node Array. 6. Update ParentIndex for all newly merged subtree nodes. Pitfalls: Work Imbalance: ParallelFor distribution may cause bottlenecks due to SVO sparsity. Mitigate by using Unbalanced scheduling. Time Complexity: Recursive Dense: O(8^{maxDepth}) worst-case, as it initializes all nodes up to the max depth regardless of occupancy. Parallel Level-by-Level: O(N \cdot R) where N is the number of voxels and R is the resolution/depth, dependent on the number of internal nodes. Memory Complexity: Dense: Fixed size array of 8^{maxDepth} nodes. High memory usage for sparse scenes. Sparse/Parallel: Proportional to the number of non-empty nodes and their children. Significantly more memory-efficient for sparse data. Strengths: Dense builder is simple to implement and provides fast, predictable traversal for dense volumes. Parallel builder leverages GPU compute for high throughput on large voxel lists. Recursive merging integrates well with collision detection systems. Limitations: Dense builder wastes memory on empty space. Parallel builder requires complex shader management and atomic operations. Recursive merging can suffer from load imbalance if not scheduled correctly. The Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) is a fundamental data structure in volume rendering and pathfinding. The recursive dense builder approach is often used in ray marching engines for its simplicity. The GPU-based level-by-level construction is associated with modern voxelization pipelines for real-time rendering. Initialization: Clear memory for the first 8 nodes (root children) using nodeinit shader. Set start = 0, count = 8. 3. Level Loop: Iterate from level 1 to octreeresolution - 1: 1. Flagging: Execute nodeflag shader to determine which nodes at the current level are internal (have children) or leaves. Binds octree buffer and voxel list. 2. Allocation: Execute nodealloc shader to allocate memory for children of internal nodes. Uses an atomic counter. Output start address is allocstart, count is alloccount 8. 3. State Update: start becomes allocstart. count becomes alloccount 8. allocstart becomes start + count. 4. Initialization of New Nodes: Clear memory for newly allocated nodes using nodeinit shader. 4. Leaf Storage: After the loop, execute storeleaf shader to store leaf node data based on the voxel list size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Parameters: MaxDepth: Maximum subdivision depth. SVOObstacle: Custom collision trace channel. Steps: 1. Start with Root node at Depth 0. 2. If root collides with SVOObstacle: 1. Recursively subdivide to MaxDepth. 2. For each child index 0-7: 1. Compute position using binary mapping: 0 = minus direction, 1 = plus direction relative to center. 2. Run recursive build task. 3. Merge: 1. Calculate total size of child results. 2. Insert root node into Node Array. 3. Iterate through child results. 4. If child's root index is invalid (Blocked), skip it. 5. Merge valid subtree into Node Array. 6. Update ParentIndex for all newly merged subtree nodes. Pitfalls: Work Imbalance: ParallelFor distribution may cause bottlenecks due to SVO sparsity. Mitigate by using Unbalanced scheduling. Time Complexity: Recursive Dense: O(8^{maxDepth}) worst-case, as it initializes all nodes up to the max depth regardless of occupancy. Parallel Level-by-Level: O(N \cdot R) where N is the number of voxels and R is the resolution/depth, dependent on the number of internal nodes. Memory Complexity: Dense: Fixed size array of 8^{maxDepth} nodes. High memory usage for sparse scenes. Sparse/Parallel: Proportional to the number of non-empty nodes and their children. Significantly more memory-efficient for sparse data. Strengths: Dense builder is simple to implement and provides fast, predictable traversal for dense volumes. Parallel builder leverages GPU compute for high throughput on large voxel lists. Recursive merging integrates well with collision detection systems. Limitations: Dense builder wastes memory on empty space. Parallel builder requires complex shader management and atomic operations. Recursive merging can suffer from load imbalance if not scheduled correctly. The Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) is a fundamental data structure in volume rendering and pathfinding. The recursive dense builder approach is often used in ray marching engines for its simplicity. The GPU-based level-by-level construction is associated with modern voxelization pipelines for real-time rendering. name: GPU-based Octree Generation
head: Fixed-Partition Octree Generation, GPU Octree Construction
body: This method generates a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) data structure directly on the GPU by partitioning the input volume into fixed-size cubes of 32 \times 32 \times 32 voxels. Unlike standard SVO builders that only subdivide non-empty regions, this approach subdivides the entire volume space uniformly down to the minimum node size, which simplifies the compute shader logic by avoiding dynamic branching for empty regions. It solves the problem of constructing a hierarchical acceleration structure for raycasting by mapping every non-empty voxel to a path in a pre-allocated array-based octree. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid of size n \times n \times n, where each voxel contains a density or occupancy value. Output: A flat array of OctreeEntry structures representing the octree. The array simulates a linked list where each node points to its children. Data Structures: OctreeEntry: A 64-bit structure consisting of two integers (32-bit each). data: A bitmask where the least significant bit indicates the presence of data (non-empty children or leaf data). childrenStartIndex: The index in the output array where the children of this node begin. Parameters: size: The dimension of the volume n. minNodeSize (\epsilon): The minimum side length of a node, set to 32. maxDepth: Derived from size and minNodeSize. Specifically, maxDepth = \log2(\frac{size}{minNodeSize}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Dispatch: Launch a compute shader with a thread group size of 4 \times 4 \times 4 (64 threads per group). The total number of threads dispatched equals the number of voxels in the volume (n^3). 2. Empty Check: Each thread identifies its voxel coordinate currentVoxel via SVDispatchThreadID. It samples the voxel data. If the value is less than 1 (empty), the thread returns immediately. 3. Update Path: If the voxel is non-empty, call updateOctree(currentVoxel). 4. Traverse and Mark: Inside updateOctree: Calculate the relative octant index at depth 1 using calculateRelativeOctant. Mark the root node (outputOctree[0]) as having data by setting the first bit of its data field. Initialize nextIndex as relativeIndex + 1. Loop from depth = 1 to maxDepth: Retrieve the current OctreeEntry at nextIndex. Mark the current node as having data by setting the first bit of its data field. Calculate the relative octant index for the next depth (depth + 1). Update nextIndex to current.childrenStartIndex + relativeIndex. Formulas: Array Size: The total number of elements in the octree array for a volume of size n and partition size 32 is given by the geometric series sum: \sum{i=0}^{n/32} \frac{1 - 8^{n/32 + 1}}{1 - 8} For a 512^3 volume with \epsilon=32, this results in 4681 elements. Octant Mapping: The mapping from 3D coordinates to an octant index in a 2 \times 2 \times 2 child array is defined as: f{2,2}(\vec{p}) = pi + pj \times 2 + pk \times 2 \times 2 where pi, pj, pk are the relative coordinates within the child block. Relative Octant Calculation: The relative position within a block at depth d is calculated as: g(\vec{x}) = \left( \frac{\vec{x}1}{s} \bmod (2 \times s), \frac{\vec{x}2}{s} \bmod (2 \times s), \frac{\vec{x}3}{s} \bmod (2 \times s) \right) where s = \frac{size}{2^n}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. SIZE = 512 # Example volume dimension MINNODESIZE = 32 MAXDEPTH = log2(SIZE / MINNODESIZE) class OctreeEntry: data: int # 32-bit bitmask childrenStartIndex: int # 32-bit index def calculaterelativeindex(v: int, d: int) -> int: # Division by power of two is implemented as bit shift return v >> d def calculateoctant(pos: int3, d: int) -> int: # Map 3D coordinates to 0-7 octant index # Note: Source uses pos.x, pos.z, pos.y order for i, j, k i = calculaterelativeindex(pos.x, d) k = calculaterelativeindex(pos.z, d) j = calculaterelativeindex(pos.y, d) return i + (k 2) + (j 4) def calculaterelativeoctant(pos: int3, d: int) -> int: # Calculate position modulo block size at previous depth blocksize = SIZE >> (d - 1) relativepos = pos % blocksize return calculateoctant(relativepos, d) def updateoctree(currentvoxel: int3, outputoctree: list[OctreeEntry]): # Calculate relative octant at depth 1 relativeindex = calculaterelativeoctant(currentvoxel, 1) # Mark root node (index 0) outputoctree[0].data |= 1 # Initialize next index to traverse nextindex = relativeindex + 1 # Traverse down to max depth for depth in range(1, MAXDEPTH + 1): currententry = outputoctree[nextindex] # Mark current node as having data currententry.data |= 1 outputoctree[nextindex] = currententry # Calculate relative octant for next deeper level relativeindex = calculaterelativeoctant(currentvoxel, depth + 1) # Move to child node nextindex = currententry.childrenStartIndex + relativeindex def CS(currentvoxel: int3): # Check if voxel is empty if getdata(currentvoxel) < 1: return # Update octree path for this voxel updateoctree(currentvoxel, outputoctree) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division Cost: The algorithm performs divisions with remainders (modulo operations). Although divisions by powers of two are optimized to bit shifts, the modulo operations remain expensive on GPU hardware. False Positives: The fixed-partition approach may create nodes for empty regions if the partitioning boundaries do not align perfectly with sparse data, leading to potential false positives during ray traversal if not handled carefully. Initialization: The childrenStartIndex for all nodes must be initialized to 0 or a valid offset before the shader runs, as the shader only sets the data bit and traverses existing indices. The source implies a pre-allocated array structure where indices are calculated based on the octant position, but does not explicitly detail the initialization of childrenStartIndex for internal nodes in the provided snippet. Time Complexity: O(n^3), where n is the volume dimension. This is considered inefficient for large volumes because every voxel is processed by a thread, regardless of sparsity. Memory Complexity: The array size is determined by the fixed partitioning. For a 512^3 volume with a minimum node size of 32, the array contains 4681 elements, occupying approximately 37 KB. Strengths: Simplifies GPU implementation by avoiding complex dynamic memory allocation or branching for empty regions. The fixed partitioning makes the traversal logic predictable. Limitations: High computational cost due to O(n^3) complexity and expensive modulo operations. It is not suitable for dynamic updates; the entire octree must be reconstructed if the volume changes significantly. When to use: Initial construction of the octree for static volumes. It is recommended to use this method only for initial build, and then potentially switch to a more efficient traversal or update strategy for dynamic scenes. This method was described by Enes Hergül in a thesis on raycasting-based voxel rendering. It is presented as an alternative to standard Sparse Voxel Octree construction, specifically designed to be easier to implement in a GPU compute shader by using fixed-size partitions. The approach contrasts with the basic SVO builder, which dynamically allocates nodes only for non-empty regions. name: Monte Carlo 2D Voxelization
head: Differentiable 2D Voxelization (Forward/Backward Mode), Monte Carlo 3D Voxelization, Monte Carlo Voxelization
body: Monte Carlo 2D Voxelization is a differentiable method for converting a 2D triangle mesh (defined by vertices and edges) into a volumetric occupancy grid using Monte Carlo integration of the generalized winding number. It sets itself apart from Analytic Voxelization by using stochastic sampling rather than exact geometric intersection, allowing for adaptive sampling strategies and gradient propagation through the sampling process. It differs from Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) by specifically implementing the 2D case with a focus on the generalized winding number boundary term. Inputs and Outputs: vertices: Array of shape (n, 2) containing vertex coordinates in \mathbb{R}^2, type Float. edges: Array of shape (m, 2) containing vertex indices for each edge, type uint32t. grid: Voxel grid dimensions (h, w). numsamplespervoxel: Number of Monte Carlo samples per voxel. samplingflags: Bitmask controlling strategy (Adaptive, Stratified). filterradius: Radius for the box filter. Output: occupancy array of shape (h, w) containing smoothed winding numbers. Data Structures: Bitset: Used in adaptive mode to mark boundary voxels. Stores bits for each voxel index. Filter: Box filter with radius filterradius and evaluation method eval(distance). Parameters: numsamplespervoxel: Typical value determined by user; default logic adjusts for stratified sampling. samplingflags: Default is Adaptive | Stratified. Flags: Adaptive (1<<0), Stratified (1<<1). Coordinate system: Volume is [-1, 1]^2. Grid covers this volume exactly. Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute voxelsize from grid dimensions and volume [-1, 1]^2. Specifically, voxelsize = 2.0 / griddim for each dimension. Compute voxelvolume = voxelsize[0] voxelsize[1]. Initialize random engine and uniform distribution std::uniformrealdistribution<Float>. If Adaptive flag is set, create a bitset mask and call markboundaryvoxels to identify voxels near the surface. 2. Sampling Loop: Total samples: numsamplestotal = numsamplespervoxel grid.numelements(). Iterate sampleindex from 0 to numsamplestotal - 1. Determine voxelindex = sampleindex / numsamplespervoxel. Determine samplelane = sampleindex % numsamplespervoxel. Adaptive Check: If Adaptive is set and the voxel at voxelindex is not marked in the mask (constant voxel), set numsamplesthisvoxel = 1. If samplelane > 0, skip this sample. Otherwise, numsamplesthisvoxel = numsamplespervoxel. 3. Sample Generation: Generate local sample position in [0, 1]^2: samplelocal = {distribution(engine), distribution(engine)}. Convert voxelindex to coordinates (vx, vy). Compute voxel origin in global space: voxelorigin = {vx voxelsize[0] - 1, vy voxelsize[1] - 1}. Stratified Sampling: If Stratified flag is set and numsamplesthisvoxel > 1: Compute numsamplessqrt = ceil(sqrt(numsamplesthisvoxel)). Compute stratum index: stratum = {samplelane % numsamplessqrt, samplelane / numsamplessqrt}. Compute stratumsize = voxelsize / numsamplessqrt. Sample position: sample = voxelorigin + (stratum + samplelocal) stratumsize. Non-Stratified: sample = voxelorigin + voxelsize samplelocal. 4. Generalized Winding Number (GWN): Compute GWN for the sample point against the mesh: sampleoccupancy = generalizedwindingnumber(vertices, edges, sample). The GWN is computed by summing contributions from all edges. For each edge (v0, v1), the contribution is based on the angle subtended by the edge at the sample point. 5. Filtering and Accumulation: Compute sample grid coordinate: samplegridcoord = Point2<Float>(voxel) + samplelocal. Determine filter support range using getgridsupport(samplegridcoord, filter.radius / voxelsize, mincoord, maxcoord). Iterate over neighbor voxels (nx, ny) in the support box, clamped to grid dimensions 0, width) and [0, height). Compute neighbor voxel center in [world space: ncenter = {nx voxelsize[0] + halfvoxelsize[0] - 1, ny voxelsize[1] + halfvoxelsize[1] - 1}. Compute filter weight: filterweight = filter.eval(ncenter - sample). If filterweight > 0: Compute sample weight: sampleweight = voxelvolume / numsamplesthisvoxel. Update occupancy: occupancy[coordstolinearindex(nx, ny, grid)] += filterweight sampleoccupancy sampleweight. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def montecarlo2dvoxelization(vertices, edges, grid, numsamplespervoxel, samplingflags, filterradius): """ vertices: list of [x, y] coordinates edges: list of [v0idx, v1idx] grid: (height, width) numsamplespervoxel: int samplingflags: dict with 'adaptive' and 'stratified' booleans filterradius: float """ h, w = grid voxelsizex = 2.0 / w voxelsizey = 2.0 / h voxelsize = (voxelsizex, voxelsizey) voxelvolume = voxelsizex voxelsizey halfvoxelsize = (voxelsizex / 2.0, voxelsizey / 2.0) # Initialize occupancy grid occupancy = [0.0] (h w) # Adaptive mask mask = [False] (h w) if samplingflags.get('adaptive', False): # markboundaryvoxels is a helper to identify voxels near edges mask = markboundaryvoxels(vertices, edges, grid, filterradius) numsamplestotal = numsamplespervoxel h w engine = random.Random() for sampleindex in range(numsamplestotal): voxelindex = sampleindex // numsamplespervoxel samplelane = sampleindex % numsamplespervoxel # Adaptive logic if samplingflags.get('adaptive', False): if not mask[voxelindex]: numsamplesthisvoxel = 1 if samplelane > 0: continue else: numsamplesthisvoxel = numsamplespervoxel else: numsamplesthisvoxel = numsamplespervoxel # Sample generation samplelocalx = engine.random() samplelocaly = engine.random() vx = voxelindex // h vy = voxelindex % h voxeloriginx = vx voxelsizex - 1.0 voxeloriginy = vy voxelsizey - 1.0 if samplingflags.get('stratified', False) and numsamplesthisvoxel > 1: numsamplessqrt = math.ceil(math.sqrt(numsamplesthisvoxel)) stratumx = samplelane % numsamplessqrt stratumy = samplelane // numsamplessqrt stratumsizex = voxelsizex / numsamplessqrt stratumsizey = voxelsizey / numsamplessqrt samplex = voxeloriginx + (stratumx + samplelocalx) stratumsizex sampley = voxeloriginy + (stratumy + samplelocaly) stratumsizey else: samplex = voxeloriginx + samplelocalx voxelsizex sampley = voxeloriginy + samplelocaly voxelsizey # Generalized Winding Number sampleoccupancy = generalizedwindingnumber2d(vertices, edges, (samplex, sampley)) # Filter support samplegridx = vx + samplelocalx samplegridy = vy + samplelocaly minnx = max(0, int(samplegridx - filterradius / voxelsizex)) maxnx = min(w - 1, int(samplegridx + filterradius / voxelsizex)) minny = max(0, int(samplegridy - filterradius / voxelsizey)) maxny = min(h - 1, int(samplegridy + filterradius / voxelsizey)) sampleweight = voxelvolume / numsamplesthisvoxel for ny in range(minny, maxny + 1): for nx in range(minnx, maxnx + 1): ncenterx = nx voxelsizex + halfvoxelsizex - 1.0 ncentery = ny voxelsizey + halfvoxelsizey - 1.0 distx = ncenterx - samplex disty = ncentery - sampley # Box filter evaluation filterweight = 1.0 if abs(distx) <= filterradius and abs(disty) <= filterradius else 0.0 if filterweight > 0: nvoxelindex = ny w + nx occupancy[nvoxelindex] += filterweight sampleoccupancy sampleweight return occupancy def generalizedwindingnumber2d(vertices, edges, point): """ Computes the 2D generalized winding number for a point against a set of edges. """ gwn = 0.0 for v0idx, v1idx in edges: v0 = vertices[v0idx] v1 = vertices[v1idx] # Vector from point to vertices p0 = (v0[0] - point[0], v0[1] - point[1]) p1 = (v1[0] - point[0], v1[1] - point[1]) # Angle subtended by the edge at the point # Using atan2 to compute the angle angle0 = math.atan2(p0[1], p0[0]) angle1 = math.atan2(p1[1], p1[0]) # Difference in angles, normalized to [-pi, pi] diff = angle1 - angle0 while diff <= -math.pi: diff += 2 math.pi while diff > math.pi: diff -= 2 math.pi gwn += diff return gwn / (2 math.pi) Computes backward-mode gradients of voxel occupancy with respect to vertex positions using Monte Carlo sampling. It validates inputs and dispatches to the 2D or 3D backward-mode implementation with DifferentiationMode::Backward. Inputs include doccupancy (gradients of occupancy) and outputs dvertices (gradients of vertices). Time Complexity: O(Ns \cdot Nv \cdot R^2), where Ns is the number of samples, Nv is the number of voxels, and R is the filter radius in voxels. The GWN computation is O(Ne) per sample, where Ne is the number of edges. Memory Complexity: O(Nv) for the occupancy grid and mask. Performance: Depends on the number of samples and the adaptive mask efficiency. Adaptive mode reduces samples for constant voxels. Strengths: Differentiable, supports adaptive sampling, handles complex meshes via GWN. Limitations: Stochastic noise, requires many samples for smooth gradients, restricted to [-1, 1]^2 volume. Originated from the paper "Differentiable Voxelization of Surface Representations" by Djuren, Finnendahl, Worchel, Meyer, and Alexa (2026). The method is implemented in C++ and exposed to Python via PyTorch. It is used for shape optimization, intersection avoidance, and differentiable rendering.
