name: Forward-Mode Derivative of Monte Carlo 2D Voxelization
body: Computes the forward-mode derivatives of the voxel occupancy grid with respect to the input mesh vertex positions. It extends Monte Carlo 2D Voxelization by propagating gradients through the Monte Carlo integration of the generalized winding number boundary term. Unlike the forward pass which only computes occupancy, this method computes \frac{\partial \text{occupancy}}{\partial \text{vertices}} using the same sampling strategy, enabling gradient-based optimization of mesh geometry. Inputs: vertices: Array of shape (N, 2) containing 2D vertex positions. edges: Array of shape (M, 2) containing vertex indices for each edge. dvertices: Array of shape (N, 2) containing seed gradients (typically identity or upstream gradients) with respect to vertex positions. voxelsize: Scalar or vector defining the grid resolution. numsamplespersimplex: Integer number of Monte Carlo samples per edge. filter: Filter object with radius. mincoord, maxcoord: Grid boundaries. Outputs: doccupancy: Array of shape (H, W) containing the computed gradients of the occupancy grid with respect to the input vertices. Data Structures: doccupancy: Initialized to zeros. Accumulates contributions from all edge samples. dvertices: Input gradients. Used to compute the derivative of the sample position on the edge. Steps: 1. Initialize: Create random engine and distribution identical to the forward pass. Initialize doccupancy to zero. 2. Loop over edges: For each edge e from 0 to M-1: a. Retrieve vertex indices v0\idx = edges[e][0] and v1\idx = edges[e][1]. b. Get positions \mathbf{v}0 = \text{vertices}[v0\idx] and \mathbf{v}1 = \text{vertices}[v1\idx]. c. Compute edge vector \mathbf{v}{01} = \mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}0. d. Compute edge normal \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\langle v{01,y}, -v{01,x} \rangle) (90-degree clockwise rotation). e. Compute edge length L = \|\mathbf{v}{01}\|. f. Loop over samples: For each sample index s from 0 to \text{num\samples\per\simplex}-1: i. Generate uniform random number u \in 0, 1). If [stratified sampling is used, u = (s + u) \times \frac{1}{\text{num\samples\per\simplex}}. ii. Compute the derivative of the boundary point \mathbf{x}{bn} = \mathbf{v}0 + u \mathbf{v}{01} with respect to vertices: \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}{bn}}{\partial \mathbf{v}0} = \mathbf{n} (1 - u) \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}{bn}}{\partial \mathbf{v}1} = \mathbf{n} u iii. Compute the directional derivative of the boundary point using the input vertex gradients \mathbf{d}{v0} and \mathbf{d}{v1} from dvertices: \mathbf{d}{x{bn}} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{d}{v0}, \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}{bn}}{\partial \mathbf{v}0}) + \text{dot}(\mathbf{d}{v1}, \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}{bn}}{\partial \mathbf{v}1}) iv. Compute the sample position on the edge: \mathbf{x}{sample} = \mathbf{v}0 + u \mathbf{v}{01}. v. Convert to grid coordinates: \mathbf{c} = \text{point\to\grid\coord}(\mathbf{x}{sample}, \text{voxel\size}). vi. Determine filter support: Get voxel indices (nx, ny) within the filter radius. vii. Loop over affected voxels: For each voxel (nx, ny) in the support: 1. Compute voxel center \mathbf{c}{center} = \langle nx \cdot \text{voxel\size}x + \text{half\voxel\offset}x, ny \cdot \text{voxel\size}y + \text{half\voxel\offset}y \rangle. 2. Compute the gradient contribution. The forward-mode derivative of the winding number boundary term involves the dot product of the sample derivative \mathbf{d}{x{bn}} and the gradient of the winding number kernel with respect to the sample position. Note: The exact kernel gradient formula is not explicitly detailed in the provided snippets, but the accumulation follows the standard adjoint rule where the derivative flows through the filter evaluation. 3. Accumulate the result into doccupancy[ny, nx]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardmodederivativemc2dvoxelize( vertices: Array2D, # (N, 2) edges: Array2D, # (M, 2) dvertices: Array2D, # (N, 2) voxelsize: float, numsamplespersimplex: int, filterradius: float, mincoord: float, maxcoord: float, usestratified: bool = False) -> Array2D: # Initialize output gradient array # Assuming grid dimensions derived from bounds and voxelsize height = int((maxcoord[1] - mincoord[1]) / voxelsize) width = int((maxcoord[0] - mincoord[0]) / voxelsize) doccupancy = zeros((height, width)) halfvoxeloffset = voxelsize / 2.0 # Initialize RNG (same as forward pass) rng = initrandomengine() dist = UniformDistribution(0.0, 1.0) stratumsize = 1.0 / numsamplespersimplex for e in range(edges.shape[0]): v0idx = edges[e, 0] v1idx = edges[e, 1] v0 = vertices[v0idx] v1 = vertices[v1idx] v0v1 = v1 - v0 length = norm(v0v1) # Normal: 90 degree rotation to the right # Vector2<Float>{v0v1[1], -v0v1[0]} normal = normalize(Vector2(v0v1[1], -v0v1[0])) for s in range(numsamplespersimplex): u = dist(rng) if usestratified: u = (s + u) stratumsize # Derivatives of boundary point w.r.t vertices # dxbndv0 = normal (1 - u) # dxbndv1 = normal u dxbndv0 = normal (1.0 - u) dxbndv1 = normal u # Forward-mode derivative of boundary point dv0 = dvertices[v0idx] dv1 = dvertices[v1idx] dxbn = dot(dv0, dxbndv0) + dot(dv1, dxbndv1) # Sample position sample = v0 + u v0v1 # Grid coordinate samplegridcoord = pointtogridcoord(sample, voxelsize) # Filter support # getgridsupport returns list of (nx, ny) support = getgridsupport(samplegridcoord, filterradius / voxelsize, mincoord, maxcoord) for (nx, ny) in support: # Voxel center ncenterx = nx voxelsize + halfvoxeloffset ncentery = ny voxelsize + halfvoxeloffset ncenter = Vector2(ncenterx, ncentery) # Compute kernel gradient and accumulate # The specific kernel gradient formula is not provided in the source snippets. # In a standard differentiable voxelization, this would involve: # 1. Computing the winding number gradient w.r.t sample position. # 2. Dotting with dxbn. # 3. Scaling by importance sampling weight (1/length). # Placeholder for the specific kernel derivative logic gradcontribution = computekernelgradientderivative(sample, ncenter, dxbn) doccupancy[ny, nx] += gradcontribution return doccupancy Parameters: Mode: DifferentiationMode::Forward. dvertices: Input gradients, shape (N, 2), type Float. doccupancy: Output gradients, shape (H, W), type Float. numsamplespersimplex: Number of Monte Carlo samples per edge. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-length edges: If \mathbf{v}0 = \mathbf{v}1, the normal is undefined. The source notes do not specify handling, but standard practice requires a guard or skipping. Precision: Accumulating gradients in doccupancy may suffer from precision loss if many edges contribute to the same voxel. Use double precision for accumulation if necessary. Boundary Conditions: The filter support calculation must correctly handle voxels outside the grid bounds. A variant that generalizes the 2D forward-mode derivative to both 2D and 3D cases. It validates inputs (dvertices and doccupancy shapes and device placement) and dispatches to the appropriate 2D or 3D implementation with DifferentiationMode::Forward. It accepts dvertices of shape (N, \text{dim}) and outputs doccupancy of shape (H, W) or (D, H, W). Time Complexity: O(M \cdot S \cdot K), where M is the number of edges, S is the number of samples per edge, and K is the average number of voxels in the filter support. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for the output gradient array, plus O(N) for input gradients. Performance: Performance scales linearly with the number of edges and samples. The Monte Carlo approach allows for variable sampling rates to balance noise and speed. Strengths: Provides exact gradients for the Monte Carlo estimator; differentiable with respect to vertex positions; supports adaptive and stratified sampling. Limitations: Stochastic noise in gradients due to Monte Carlo sampling; requires careful tuning of sample counts for smooth gradients. The method is part of the "Differentiable Voxelization of Surface Representations" framework by Djuren et al. (2026). It builds on the generalized winding number formulation for voxelization, extending it to support gradient-based optimization of mesh geometry via forward-mode automatic differentiation. The code is available in the differentiable-voxelization repository. name: Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF)
head: Closed-form Voxelization, Convolution Filter Voxelization, Differentiable 3D Voxelization (Forward/Backward Mode), VoxelizeFunc
body: Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) is a PyTorch autograd function that rasterizes 2D polygons or 3D triangle meshes into a grid of winding numbers (occupancy), supporting both Marching Cubes (MC) and Convolution Filter (CF) methods with differentiable backward passes. It sets itself apart from Monte Carlo 2D Voxelization by providing closed-form analytic gradients for both 2D and 3D primitives, and from Analytic Moment Voxelization by focusing on binary/signed occupancy grids rather than higher-order polynomial moments. Inputs: vertices: Array of shape (N, D) containing vertex positions (D=2 for 2D, D=3 for 3D), type Float. simplices (or faces/edges): Array of shape (F, D) containing vertex indices for triangles (3D) or edges (2D), type uint32t. gridshape: Tuple (H, W) for 2D or (D, H, W) for 3D. method: String 'mc' or 'cf'. If 'auto', selects 'cf' if filterradius == halfvoxelsize, otherwise 'mc'. numsamplespervoxel: Number of samples per voxel for MC forward pass. Default: 16. numsamplespersimplex: Number of samples per simplex for MC backward pass. Default: 64. filterradius: Radius of the filter. Default: half voxel size. For CF, must equal half voxel size to have effect. Outputs: occupancy: Output tensor of shape gridshape, type Float, containing winding numbers. dvertices: Gradient tensor for vertices, shape (N, D), type Float. doccupancy: Gradient tensor for occupancy, shape gridshape, type Float. Data Structures: The implementation uses a grid coordinate system where the world space [-1, 1]^D is mapped to grid indices. stepx = 2.0 / depth (or width for 2D) stepy = 2.0 / height stepz = 2.0 / width (for 3D) Grid center optimization uses centerk = width / 2. Primal (Forward) Pass: 1. Validate inputs using validatecommonvoxelizearguments. 2. Dispatch to 2D or 3D closed-form implementation based on dimension. 3. Initialize occupancy as a zero tensor. 4. For each face (triangle or edge): Extract vertices v0, v1, v2 (or v0, v1 for 2D). Compute edge vectors e1 = v1 - v0, e2 = v2 - v0. Compute normal n = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(e1, e2)) and area A = 0.5 \|\text{cross}(e1, e2)\|. Determine bounding box in grid coordinates: \text{bbox\min}i = \max(0, \lfloor \frac{\min(v{0,i}, v{1,i}, v{2,i}) + 1}{\text{step}i} \rfloor) \text{bbox\max}i = \min(\text{dim\size}i - 1, \lfloor \frac{\max(v{0,i}, v{1,i}, v{2,i}) + 1}{\text{step}i} \rfloor). MC Method: Perform Monte Carlo integration. Generate uniform u, v. If u+v > 1, reflect: u = 1-u, v = 1-v. Compute sample point p = v0 + u e1 + v e2. Convert to grid coordinates. Iterate over neighbor voxels. Compute filter weight. Update occupancy: \text{occupancy}[idx] += \text{filter\weight} \times \frac{A}{\text{num\samples\per\simplex}}. CF Method: Use closed-form polygon splitting. Represent the triangle in barycentric coordinates. Iterate over x-slices (planes x = \text{const}). Split the polygon barycentrically by each plane xi. For each x-slice, iterate over y-slices. Split the resulting polygon by yj. For each z-slice (or final 2D cell), compute the intersection polygon P{xyz} in barycentric coordinates. Compute the winding number contribution. For a convex polygon P with vertices bk in barycentric space, the contribution to the voxel at index (i,j,k) is: \text{contrib} = \frac{1}{\text{cell\volume}} \sum{\text{triangles in } P} \text{sub\area} \times (\text{pivot} + b1 + b2) where pivot is the centroid of the original triangle barycentric coordinates (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). Update occupancy[idx] += contrib. Backward Pass: 1. Select backward function based on method and dtype. 2. Initialize dvertices as zeros. 3. For each face: Compute normal velocities for backward pass: d\xbn\d\v0 = n \times (1 - u - v) d\xbn\d\v1 = n \times u d\xbn\d\v2 = n \times v. Forward Mode Gradient: If dvertices is provided as input (forward-mode differentiation), compute d\xbn by dotting vertex gradients with normal velocities: d\xbn = \text{dot}(d\v0, d\xbn\d\v0) + \text{dot}(d\v1, d\xbn\d\v1) + \text{dot}(d\v2, d\xbn\d\v2). Backward Mode Gradient: If doccupancy is provided as input (backward-mode differentiation): Iterate over affected voxels. Compute differentialweight = doccupancy[idx] / cellvolume. For CF method, compute the geometric contribution vector contrib (same as primal but using barycentric coordinates). Update vertex gradients: d\vertices[3 \cdot vk + d] += \text{contrib}[k] \times d\xbn\d\vk[d] \times \text{differential\weight} for k \in \{0, 1, 2\} and d \in \{0, 1, 2\}. For MC method, update gradients using the filter weight and area: d\vertices[3 \cdot vk + d] += d\xbn\d\vk[d] \times \text{filter\weight} \times \frac{A}{\text{num\samples\per\simplex}} \times d\occupancy[idx]. Pseudocode (Python-like): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def voxelizecf3dbackward(vertices, faces, occupancy, doccupancy, gridshape): """ Simplified backward pass for CF voxelization. vertices: (N, 3) faces: (F, 3) occupancy: (D, H, W) doccupancy: (D, H, W) """ N, D = vertices.shape dvertices = torch.zeroslike(vertices) stepx = 2.0 / gridshape[0] stepy = 2.0 / gridshape[1] stepz = 2.0 / gridshape[2] cellvolume = stepx stepy stepz for faceidx in range(faces.shape[0]): i0, i1, i2 = faces[faceidx] v0 = vertices[i0] v1 = vertices[i1] v2 = vertices[i2] e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 normal = torch.cross(e1, e2) normallen = torch.norm(normal) if normallen < 1e-12: continue unitnormal = normal / normallen area = 0.5 normallen # Bounding box minx = torch.min(v0[0], torch.min(v1[0], v2[0])) maxx = torch.max(v0[0], torch.max(v1[0], v2[0])) #... compute miny, maxy, minz, maxz similarly bboxmini = max(0, int((minx + 1) / stepx)) bboxmaxi = min(gridshape[0] - 1, int((maxx + 1) / stepx)) #... compute other bbox bounds # Barycentric coordinates of triangle # Triangle in barycentric space: (1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1) # We split this polygon by planes x=const, y=const, z=const # Pseudocode for polygon splitting is complex; # assuming a helper splitpolygonbary exists which returns # a list of polygons in barycentric coords. remainingpoly = [torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])] for i in range(bboxmini, bboxmaxi + 1): xhi = -1.0 + (i + 1) stepx # Split remainingpoly by plane x = xhi # This requires projecting barycentric coords to Cartesian x # x = dot(bary, trix) where trix = [v0.x, v1.x, v2.x] trix = torch.tensor([v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]]) belowpoly, abovepoly = splitpolygonbary(remainingpoly, trix, xhi) remainingpoly = abovepoly if len(belowpoly) < 3: continue # For each slice in belowpoly, iterate y #... (nested loops for y and z) # For each voxel (i, j, k) intersected: # Compute intersection polygon in barycentric coords # Compute contribution # Update dvertices # Simplified update for one voxel: # contrib = computebarycentriccontribution(barycentricpolygon) # differentialweight = doccupancy[i, j, k] / cellvolume # dvertices[i0] += contrib[0] unitnormal differentialweight # dvertices[i1] += contrib[1] unitnormal differentialweight # dvertices[i2] += contrib[2] unitnormal differentialweight pass return dvertices def splitpolygonbary(polygonbary, tricoords, value): """ Split a polygon defined by barycentric vertices by a Cartesian plane. Returns (below, above) polygons in barycentric coordinates. """ below = [] above = [] n = len(polygonbary) for i in range(n): curr = polygonbary[i] nextv = polygonbary[(i + 1) % n] currval = torch.dot(curr, tricoords) nextval = torch.dot(nextv, tricoords) currbelow = currval <= value nextbelow = nextval <= value if currbelow: below.append(curr) else: above.append(curr) if currbelow != nextbelow: d = nextval - currval if abs(d) > 1e-12: t = (value - currval) / d intersection = curr + t (nextv - curr) below.append(intersection) above.append(intersection) return below, above A method for voxelizing triangle meshes into smoothed winding number voxel grids that provides closed-form gradients with respect to mesh vertex positions, enabling gradient-based optimization of surface representations based on volumetric properties. It differs from the standard CF method by smoothing the winding number field, which can improve gradient stability for noisy or non-manifold inputs. A differentiable voxelizer V to efficiently query a density volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{X \times Y \times Z} from radiative Gaussians, used for 3D regularization. It extends the voxelization concept to Gaussian splats rather than triangle meshes, allowing gradients to flow from the voxel grid back to the Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity). Computes backward-mode gradients of voxel occupancy with respect to vertex positions using closed-form integration. It takes doccupancy as input and produces dvertices as output. It validates inputs using validatecommondifferentialvoxelizearguments and dispatches to 2D or 3D backward-mode implementations. Computes forward-mode gradients, taking dvertices as input and producing doccupancy as output. It validates inputs and dispatches to 2D or 3D forward-mode implementations. Rasterizes a 2D polygon to a destination grid by computing polynomial density moments over the covered cells. It supports polynomial orders 0 (constant), 1 (linear), and 2 (quadratic). The destination grid is a row-major array of moments with size (nx \cdot ny) \cdot R2D\NUM\MOMENTS(polyorder). The grid patch starts at dibox[0] and ends at dibox[1]. Time Complexity: O(F \cdot B), where F is the number of faces and B is the average number of voxels in the bounding box of a face. The CF method involves polygon splitting, which can increase the constant factor compared to simple rasterization, but avoids sampling noise. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the output grid, plus temporary storage for polygon splitting O(F \cdot B). Performance: The implementation is CPU-only. GPU tensors are automatically moved to CPU for processing and moved back, issuing a warning. The CF method assumes a box filter the size of a voxel. If filterradius does not equal half voxel size, the CF method has no effect and falls back to MC or is invalid. Strengths: Provides exact, noise-free gradients for triangle meshes. Supports both 2D and 3D. Limitations: CPU-only implementation limits scalability for large meshes. The CF method's coordinate convention (width, height vs height, width) requires a transpose of the output voxels, which regresses performance. When to use: When differentiable rasterization of triangle meshes is required for optimization (e.g., shape optimization, neural rendering). When not to use: When GPU acceleration is critical, or when working with Gaussian splats (use Differentiable Voxelization from Radiative Gaussians instead). The method originates from the "Differentiable Voxelization of Surface Representations" repository by M. Worchel. It implements closed-form voxelization algorithms for both 2D polygons and 3D triangle meshes, supporting both Marching Cubes and Convolution Filter variants. The 2D polygon rasterization to grid moments is based on the work of Devon Powell (r3d library). name: Differentiable Voxelization via Smoothed Winding Numbers
head: DVX, Smoothed Winding Number Voxelization
body: Differentiable Voxelization via Smoothed Winding Numbers (DVX) is a method for voxelizing triangle meshes into smoothed winding number voxel grids that provides closed-form gradients with respect to mesh vertex positions, enabling gradient-based optimization of surface representations based on volumetric properties. Unlike Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) which samples a non-smoothed winding number and uses automatic differentiation (yielding sparse near-surface derivative signals), this method yields a broader gradient pattern matching finite-difference references. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh defined by vertex positions V and connectivity; a 3D voxel grid of resolution N^3. Output: A voxel grid of smoothed winding numbers W; the gradient of a scalar objective function L with respect to vertex positions \nablaV L. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array of size N \times N \times N. Each cell stores a floating-point value representing the average winding number within that voxel volume. Mesh: Defined by a list of vertices vi \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a list of triangles tj = (va, vb, vc). Method: The core challenge is that point-sampling the raw winding number gives a piecewise-constant signal, so its derivative with respect to mesh motion is zero almost everywhere or undefined at the boundaries. DVX solves this by smoothing the winding-number field with a filter before sampling voxel values. 1. Voxel Value Computation: For a voxel-aligned box filter, a voxel's filtered value is the average winding number within the voxel. To compute this efficiently: Clip each triangle of the mesh against the boundaries of the voxel grid. For each triangle, determine its intersection with the voxel grid. Divide the intersections into sub-triangles. Add up their signed shadow-volume contributions along grid columns to compute the voxel value. The winding number w(p) for a point p is the signed count of how the surface wraps around p. The smoothed value W{ijk} for voxel (i,j,k) is: W{ijk} = \frac{1}{V{voxel}} \int{V{ijk}} w(p) \, dp where V{ijk} is the volume of the voxel. The algorithm computes this integral by summing the contributions of clipped sub-triangles. 2. Gradient Computation: The gradient is computed using Reynolds' transport theorem. The general derivation states that the moving boundary contributes a term, while the interior term vanishes because the integrand does not otherwise depend on the mesh parameter. This holds for general surfaces and allows self-intersections. For the efficient closed-form algorithm specialized for triangle meshes: Integrate the triangles' normal motion over the clipped pieces. Map those contributions back to mesh vertices. The gradient \frac{\partial W{ijk}}{\partial vm} for a vertex vm is non-zero only if vm is part of a triangle that intersects the voxel or its vicinity. The contribution is derived from the boundary term of the transport theorem, effectively integrating the displacement of the triangle edges against the voxel boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevoxelizationandgradient(meshvertices, meshtriangles, gridresolution, gridorigin, gridspacing): """ Computes the smoothed winding number voxel grid and the gradient of the grid values with respect to mesh vertices. Args: meshvertices: Array of shape (V, 3) containing vertex positions. meshtriangles: Array of shape (T, 3) containing vertex indices for each triangle. gridresolution: Integer N, grid size is N x N x N. gridorigin: Array of shape (3,) containing the minimum corner of the grid. gridspacing: Float, size of one voxel side. Returns: voxelgrid: Array of shape (N, N, N) containing smoothed winding numbers. vertexgradients: Array of shape (V, 3) containing dL/dv for each vertex. """ # Initialize output structures voxelgrid = np.zeros((gridresolution, gridresolution, gridresolution)) vertexgradients = np.zeroslike(meshvertices) # Precompute voxel bounds for efficient clipping # Not given in the sources: Implementation detail for bounding box checks voxelbounds = [] for i in range(gridresolution): for j in range(gridresolution): for k in range(gridresolution): mincorner = gridorigin + np.array([i, j, k]) gridspacing maxcorner = mincorner + gridspacing voxelbounds.append((mincorner, maxcorner)) # Process each triangle for triidx, (v0idx, v1idx, v2idx) in enumerate(meshtriangles): v0 = meshvertices[v0idx] v1 = meshvertices[v1idx] v2 = meshvertices[v2idx] # Compute triangle normal for signed volume contribution # Not given in the sources: Standard cross product formula e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 normal = np.cross(e1, e2) area = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(normal) unitnormal = normal / (2 area) if area > 0 else np.zeros(3) # Clip triangle against the entire grid bounding box to find relevant voxels # Not given in the sources: Sutherland-Hodgman or similar 3D clipping algorithm # to get a list of sub-triangles or polygons inside the grid. # For simplicity, we iterate over all voxels and clip the triangle to each voxel. # This is computationally expensive but matches the "local clipping structure" description. for i in range(gridresolution): for j in range(gridresolution): for k in range(gridresolution): mincorner, maxcorner = voxelbounds[i gridresolution2 + j gridresolution + k] # Clip triangle to voxel box # Not given in the sources: Function to clip a triangle against an AABB clippedsubtriangles = cliptriangletobox(v0, v1, v2, mincorner, maxcorner) if not clippedsubtriangles: continue # Compute winding number contribution for this voxel # The value is the average winding number. For a single triangle, # the winding number is +1 or -1 depending on orientation relative to the point. # The integral of the winding number over the voxel volume is approximated # by the signed shadow volume contribution. voxelwindingsum = 0.0 for subtri in clippedsubtriangles: # Compute signed volume contribution of sub-triangle to the voxel # Not given in the sources: Formula for signed volume of a tetrahedron # formed by the sub-triangle and the voxel center or origin. # The paper mentions "signed shadow-volume contributions along grid columns". # This implies integrating the projection of the triangle onto the grid axes. # A robust implementation would use the divergence theorem or explicit integration. # Here we assume a helper function exists for this specific geometric integral. volcontrib = computesignedshadowvolume(subtri, mincorner, maxcorner) voxelwindingsum += volcontrib # Average winding number voxelvolume = gridspacing 3 voxelgrid[i, j, k] += voxelwindingsum / voxelvolume # Compute gradient contribution for this voxel # The gradient is the integral of the triangles' normal motion over the clipped pieces. # dW/dv = integral over voxel of (dw/dv) dp. # By Reynolds' transport theorem, this reduces to a boundary term. # For a triangle vertex v, the gradient contribution is proportional to the # area of the intersection of the triangle with the voxel boundary, # projected onto the direction of vertex motion. # Not given in the sources: Exact formula for the gradient of the winding number # integral with respect to vertex position. It involves the normal of the triangle # and the geometry of the clipped sub-triangles. # We assume a helper function computes this local gradient. gradv0, gradv1, gradv2 = computegradientforsubtriangles(clippedsubtriangles, mincorner, maxcorner) vertexgradients[v0idx] += gradv0 vertexgradients[v1idx] += gradv1 vertexgradients[v2idx] += gradv2 return voxelgrid, vertexgradients def cliptriangletobox(v0, v1, v2, mincorner, maxcorner): """ Clips a triangle against an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box. Returns a list of clipped triangles (or polygons represented as triangles). """ # Not given in the sources: Standard 3D clipping algorithm. # Could use Sutherland-Hodgman extended to 3D or splitting the triangle. # For a triangle, clipping against 6 planes results in a convex polygon. # This polygon is then triangulated. return [] # Placeholder for implementation def computesignedshadowvolume(subtri, mincorner, maxcorner): """ Computes the signed contribution of a sub-triangle to the winding number integral within a voxel. """ # Not given in the sources: The paper describes adding up "signed shadow-volume contributions # along grid columns". This likely refers to integrating the winding number, which is # related to the solid angle subtended by the triangle at the point. # For a voxel, this is the integral of the solid angle over the voxel volume. # A common approximation is to use the signed volume of the tetrahedron formed by # the triangle and the voxel center, normalized by the voxel volume, but this is # an approximation. The exact method is not detailed in the notes. return 0.0 # Placeholder for implementation def computegradientforsubtriangles(clippedsubtriangles, mincorner, maxcorner): """ Computes the gradient of the voxel winding number with respect to the original triangle vertices, based on the clipped sub-triangles. """ # Not given in the sources: The gradient is derived from the boundary term of # Reynolds' transport theorem. It involves the normal of the triangle and the # geometry of the intersection with the voxel boundaries. return np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3) Parameters: Grid Resolution: The method is tested on a 32^3 grid and reported to handle 1024^3 resolution. Filter: A voxel-aligned box filter is used, which corresponds to averaging the winding number within the voxel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-intersection removal works at voxel resolution: Overlaps hidden by voxel averaging in partly occupied cells, or by negative winding numbers from volume inversions, can escape the objective. Approximate nature: The method is approximate; the resulting shapes may not fill the whole volume or be intersection-free, and are described as 'near-tileable'. An optimization process that deforms a mesh to minimize the volume difference between the object and its extruded silhouettes from three orthogonal directions. Steps: Project the voxelized mesh along each of three orthogonal directions to obtain filled silhouettes. Extrude the silhouettes. Compare the resulting cut shape with the voxelized mesh to compute the objective. Parameters: An as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) regularizer is used to discourage unnecessary deformation. Performance: On the TOSCA cat category, the average cut-volume difference (measured with the voxel-based objective) improves by 70.775%, going from 3.425 \times 10^3 to 0.454 \times 10^3. Relative improvements for four examples (voxel-based comparison) are 76.0%, 69.9%, 58.7%, and 62.8%. Optimizing repeated shapes toward space-filling tilings. Pitfalls: The method is approximate; the resulting shapes may not fill the whole volume or be intersection-free, and are described as 'near-tileable'. Deforming a mesh to reduce voxel regions with winding number above one to remove self-intersections. Pitfalls: The method is approximate; overlaps hidden by voxel averaging in partly occupied cells or negative winding numbers from volume inversions can escape the objective. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On a 2,418-triangle mesh and 32^3 grid, voxelization takes 418.4 ms with DOPH and 2.2 ms with DVX. The authors report sub-second CPU voxelization and backward-mode gradient computation for meshes above 100,000 faces at 1024^3 resolution, averaged over 30 runs on an Intel i9-12900K. Scaling: The method is reported to handle 1024^3 resolution. Strengths: Provides a broader gradient pattern matching finite-difference references, unlike DOPH which yields sparse near-surface derivative signals. Efficient closed-form algorithm for triangle meshes with voxel-aligned box filters. Limitations: Approximate; self-intersection removal and tiling optimization may not be perfect. The reported timings are for CPU implementation, not fully optimized or parallelized, and GPU implementation is left to future work. When to use: When gradient-based optimization of surface representations based on volumetric properties is required, such as deforming meshes to resolve intersections, ensuring manufacturability, or creating shapes close to tiling 3D space. When not to use: When exact intersection-free or perfect space-filling shapes are required, as the method is approximate. Origin: The method is described in the paper "Differentiable Voxelization of Surface Representations". History: The paper demonstrates the practical use of this approach in deforming meshes to resolve intersections, being manufacturable by cutting with a bandsaw from three directions, and creating shapes that are close to tiling 3D space. Usage: Used for deforming meshes to resolve intersections, ensuring manufacturability by cutting with a bandsaw from three directions, and creating shapes close to tiling 3D space. name: Differentiable Voxelization from Radiative Gaussians
head: Density Voxelization, Radiative Gaussian Voxelizer
body: This method provides a differentiable voxelizer \mathcal{V} that efficiently queries a 3D density volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{X \times Y \times Z} from a set of radiative Gaussians G3. It solves the computational bottleneck of mapping continuous Gaussian splats to a discrete grid, enabling 3D regularization priors for tomographic reconstruction. Unlike Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) which operates on polygonal meshes, this method operates directly on parametric Gaussian distributions, leveraging spatial tiling for acceleration. Inputs: A set of N radiative Gaussians G3. Each Gaussian is defined by its mean \mu, covariance matrix \Sigma, and opacity/density parameters. Target grid dimensions X, Y, Z. Tile size T=8 (default, based on 8 \times 8 \times 8 tiles). Outputs: A 3D density volume tensor V of shape (X, Y, Z). Data Structures: Gaussian List: Array of Gaussian parameters. Tile Grid: Logical partitioning of the bounding box of G3 into 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxel tiles. Tile-AABB: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box for each tile, used for culling. Steps: 1. Tiling: Partition the target 3D space into a grid of 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxel tiles. 2. Culling: For each tile, compute its AABB. Retain only those Gaussians that have a 99% probability of intersecting the tile's AABB. This is determined by evaluating the Mahalanobis distance or bounding ellipsoid intersection against the tile bounds. 3. Parallel Computation: For each active tile, compute the voxel values in parallel. For each voxel (x,y,z) within the tile, sum the contributions of all retained Gaussians gi using the Gaussian kernel density estimation formula (Eq. 4 in): V(x,y,z) = \sum{i \in \text{active}} \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (\mathbf{p} - \mui)\right) where \mathbf{p} = [x, y, z]^T is the voxel center, \alphai is the opacity/scaling factor of Gaussian i, and \Sigmai is its covariance matrix. 4. Backpropagation: Implement the gradient computation in CUDA to allow gradients to flow from the volume V back to the Gaussian parameters (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizeradiativegaussians(gaussians, gridshape, tilesize=8): """ Differentiable voxelization of radiative Gaussians. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes.mu,.cov,.alpha gridshape: Tuple (X, Y, Z) tilesize: Integer, default 8 """ # 1. Determine global bounds and tile grid bounds = computebounds(gaussians) tiles = createtilegrid(bounds, gridshape, tilesize) # Initialize output volume volume = torch.zeros(gridshape, requiresgrad=True) # 2. Process each tile in parallel (conceptually) for tile in tiles: # 2a. Culling: Find Gaussians with 99% confidence of intersecting tile AABB activegaussians = [] for g in gaussians: if isgaussianintile(g, tile.aabb, confidence=0.99): activegaussians.append(g) # 2b. Compute voxel values for this tile tilecoords = tile.getvoxelindices(gridshape) for idx in tilecoords: voxelpos = indextoworldcoord(idx, bounds) density = 0.0 for g in activegaussians: # Eq. (4) from: Gaussian contribution diff = voxelpos - g.mu # Compute quadratic form: diff^T Sigma^-1 diff # Note: In CUDA implementation, this is optimized exponent = -0.5 quadraticform(diff, g.cov) density += g.alpha torch.exp(exponent) volume[idx] = density return volume Parameters: Tile size: 8 \times 8 \times 8. Culling confidence: 99%. Edge Cases: Empty Tiles: Tiles with no active Gaussians return zero density. Precision: CUDA implementation is used to maintain differentiability and speed. A high-performance kernel that decomposes the Mahalanobis distance into separable 1D operations to accelerate the query of the density volume V. Performance: Accelerates the query process to > 100 FPS. Complexity: Reduced from naive O(N \cdot V) by spatial culling and tiling. Exact complexity not given, but depends on the number of active Gaussians per tile. Memory: Requires storage for the volume V and temporary tile buffers. Strengths: Enables 3D regularization for radiative Gaussians in tomography. Differentiable via CUDA. Limitations: Dependent on grid resolution and tile size configuration. Originated in the context of Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction. Inspired by voxelizers used in RGB tasks. R^2-Gaussian: Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20693v2, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Fast Volume Reconstruction from Gaussians
head: Discretized Gaussian Volume Rendering, Fast Volume Reconstruction (FVR), Gaussian Splatting for CT
body: Fast Volume Reconstruction (FVR) is a highly parallelized algorithm that aggregates the contributions of a set of 3D Gaussians into a discrete voxel grid to reconstruct a 3D volume. It solves the prohibitive memory and time complexity of direct Gaussian-to-voxel mapping by decomposing the Mahalanobis distance calculation into separable 1D operations. Unlike naive rounding or direct computation, FVR enables efficient, differentiable volume rendering suitable for joint optimization of Gaussian parameters in tomographic reconstruction. It builds on Differentiable Voxelization from Radiative Gaussians by providing the specific high-performance kernel used to query the density volume V. Inputs: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}: Mean positions of n Gaussians. For 3D space, d=3. C \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d \times d}: Covariance matrices of the Gaussians. The decomposition assumes diagonal covariance, using C^{-1}{n,d,d} as the inverse variance along dimension d for Gaussian n. I \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}: Intensity (or color/density) of each Gaussian. V{shape} = (w, h, c): Target volume dimensions. Outputs: V \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h \times c}: The reconstructed volume tensor, initialized to zeros and accumulated with Gaussian contributions. Data Structures: B': A 4D tensor of shape (w0, h0, c0, d) representing the local region shift grid. It is generated via a meshgrid of coordinates ranging from -\frac{w0-1}{2} to \frac{w0-1}{2} (and similarly for h0, c0). validindices: Boolean mask identifying voxel positions within the volume bounds [0, w), [0, h), [0, c). Parameters: n: Number of Gaussians. w0, h0, c0: Dimensions of the local region used for decomposition. The source notes specify a default size of 17, implying w0=h0=c0=17. Steps: 1. Initialize Volume: Create V as a zero tensor of shape (w, h, c). 2. Initialize Local Shift Grid: Compute B' using a meshgrid for dimensions w0, h0, c0 with values from -\frac{dim-1}{2} to \frac{dim-1}{2}. 3. Compute Fractional Offset: Calculate \Delta\mu = \mu - \lfloor\mu\rfloor to align the continuous Gaussian means to the discrete voxel grid. 4. Computed as \sumd B'{w0,h0,c0,d} \cdot C^{-1}{n,d,d} \cdot B'{w0,h0,c0,d}. Term 2: T2 = B'^T C^{-1} \Delta\mu. Computed as \sumd B'{w0,h0,c0,d} \cdot C^{-1}{n,d,d} \cdot \Delta\mu{n,1,1,d}. Term 3: T3 = \Delta\mu^T C^{-1} B'. Computed as \sumd \Delta\mu{n,1,1,d} \cdot C^{-1}{n,d,d} \cdot B'{w0,h0,c0,d}. Term 4: T4 = \Delta\mu^T C^{-1} \Delta\mu. Computed as \sumd \Delta\mu{n,1,1,d} \cdot C^{-1}{n,d,d} \cdot \Delta\mu{n,1,1,d}. 5. Compute Gaussian Contributions: Calculate the contribution \Gamma for each Gaussian and local shift: \Gamma = \exp\left(-(T1 + T2 + T3 + T4)\right) \cdot I The source formula omits the standard 1/2 factor in the exponent, so the implementation follows the explicit expression provided. 6. Determine Voxel Positions: Compute the impacted voxel positions P: P = \lfloor\mu\rfloor + B' This maps the local grid shifts to absolute voxel coordinates in the volume. 7. Filter Valid Indices: Identify valid indices where P is within bounds: P{n,w0,h0,c0,0} \ge 0 \land P{n,w0,h0,c0,0} < w P{n,w0,h0,c0,1} \ge 0 \land P{n,w0,h0,c0,1} < h P{n,w0,h0,c0,2} \ge 0 \land P{n,w0,h0,c0,2} < c. 8. Accumulate: Perform a parallel scatteradd operation: V[P[\text{valid}]] \ += \Gamma[\text{valid}]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Initialize Local Shift Grid B' halfsize = (localsize - 1) / 2.0 coords = torch.arange(-halfsize, halfsize + 1, device=mu.device, dtype=mu.dtype) # B' shape: (localsize, localsize, localsize, 3) Bprime = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid(coords, coords, coords, indexing='ij'), dim=-1) # 3. Compute Decomposed Terms # Bprime: (w0, h0, c0, d) # Cinvdiag: (n, d) # deltamu: (n, d) # Term 1: B'^T C^-1 B' -> sumd B'[i,j,k,d] Cinv[n,d] B'[i,j,k,d] term1 = torch.einsum('ijkd,nd->nijk', Bprime, Cinvdiag) # Term 2: B'^T C^-1 Deltamu -> sumd B'[i,j,k,d] Cinv[n,d] Deltamu[n,d] term2 = torch.einsum('ijkd,nd->nijk', Bprime, Cinvdiag deltamu) # Term 3: Deltamu^T C^-1 B' -> sumd Deltamu[n,d] Cinv[n,d] B'[i,j,k,d] term3 = term2.clone() # Term 4: Deltamu^T C^-1 Deltamu -> sumd Deltamu[n,d] Cinv[n,d] Deltamu[n,d] term4 = torch.sum(deltamu Cinvdiag deltamu, dim=1, keepdim=True) # (n, 1) term4exp = term4.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (n, 1, 1, 1) # 5. Compute Contributions Gamma # Gamma = exp(-(T1 + T2 + T3 + T4)) I exponent = -(term1 + term2 + term3 + term4exp) gamma = torch.exp(exponent) intensity.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (n, w0, h0, c0) # 6. Determine Voxel Positions P # P = floor(mu) + B' mufloorexp = mufloor.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (n, 1, 1, 3) P = mufloorexp + Bprime.unsqueeze(0) # (n, w0, h0, c0, 3) # 7. Filter Valid Indices validx = (P[..., 0] >= 0) & (P[..., 0] < w) validy = (P[..., 1] >= 0) & (P[..., 1] < h) validz = (P[..., 2] >= 0) & (P[..., 2] < c) validmask = validx & validy & validz # (n, w0, h0, c0) # 8. These must be filtered out using the valid mask to prevent memory access errors. Diagonal Covariance Assumption: The decomposition relies on C being diagonal (or pre-diagonalized) to compute C^{-1}{n,d,d} efficiently. If C is full, the decomposition B'^T C^{-1} B' cannot be simplified to the sum over d without full matrix multiplication, negating the speedup. Precision: The exponential function can underflow for large Mahalanobis distances. Clamping or using log-space arithmetic may be necessary for stability, though not explicitly detailed in the source. Memory: Even with decomposition, storing intermediate tensors T1, T2, T3 of shape (n, w0, h0, c0) requires significant VRAM if n is large. The source notes 16.87 GiB for n=150,000 and local size 17. A framework that uses FVR as its core voxelization engine, adding a "Discretize and Align" mechanism to preserve differentiability and gradient flow during optimization, unlike naive rounding. The parent method that defines the general differentiable voxelizer V for querying density volumes, which FVR optimizes for speed. Time Complexity: Direct Reconstruction: O(n \cdot w \cdot h \cdot c \cdot d^2). FVR without Decomposition: O(n \cdot w0 \cdot h0 \cdot c0 \cdot d^2). FVR with Decomposition: O(w0 \cdot h0 \cdot c0 \cdot d) per iteration, as the decomposition reduces the dependency on n in the inner loop. Memory Complexity: Direct Reconstruction: Estimated 16662.50 GiB VRAM. FVR (with/without decomposition): 16.87 GiB VRAM. Measured Performance: Reconstructs a 256 \times 256 \times 256 volume from over 150,000 Gaussians in 0.09 seconds per iteration. Comparison with R2-Gaussian Voxelizer: FVR achieves 7m13s total optimization time vs 8m37s for R2-Gaussian on 50-view Sparse-View CT, with higher PSNR (38.74 vs 38.02) and SSIM (0.960 vs 0.956). Strengths: Highly parallelized, significantly reduces memory consumption compared to direct methods, enables joint optimization of all Gaussians without selective view optimization. Limitations: Requires diagonal covariance matrices for the decomposition speedup. Performance depends on the local region size w0, h0, c0; larger sizes increase memory usage. The method was developed to enable efficient, differentiable volume rendering for 3D tomography, allowing for joint optimization of Gaussian parameters. It is used in public CT datasets such as FIPS, AAPM-Mayo LDCT, and FUMPE. wskingdom/DGR, https://github.com/wskingdom/DGR, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Discretized Gaussian Representation for Tomographic Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51701.2025.02325, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Discretized Gaussian Representation (DGR)
body: Discretized Gaussian Representation (DGR) is a framework for direct 3D tomographic volume reconstruction that models the volume as a sum of isotropic Gaussian functions, discretized onto a 3D grid to enable end-to-end differentiable optimization. It addresses the integration bias and density inconsistency inherent in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when applied to CT by ensuring gradient flow through the discretization process, unlike naive rounding methods. It builds on Fast Volume Reconstruction from Gaussians by introducing a "Discretize and Align" mechanism that preserves differentiability while allowing parallel aggregation of Gaussian contributions into a voxel grid. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of n Gaussians, each defined by a continuous mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \Sigmai (isotropic, diagonal), and a scalar intensity Ii \in \mathbb{R}^+. Target volume dimensions w \times h \times c. Local region size parameters w0, h0, c0 (odd integers). Outputs: Reconstructed voxel grid V \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h \times c}. Data Structures: Gaussian Parameters: Stored as tensors of shape (n, 3) for \mu, (n, 3, 3) for \Sigma (or (n, 3) for isotropic \sigma), and (n,) for I. Volume Grid: V initialized to zeros. Local Box Coordinates: A tensor B0 of shape (w0, h0, c0, 3) containing the 3D coordinates of the cuboid centered at the origin. This is constant for all Gaussians due to translation invariance. Numbered Steps: 1. Gaussian Effect Confinement: Restrict each Gaussian's influence to a localized cuboid B0 of size w0 \times h0 \times c0 centered on the voxel. The set of 3D coordinates within this cuboid is B0 \subset \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Discretize and Align: Calculate contribution at discretized grid positions aligned with floored integer coordinates \lfloor \mu \rfloor. Define residual \Delta\mu = \mu - \lfloor \mu \rfloor. Transform coordinates from B to \lfloor B \rfloor using [B]{n,w0,h0,c0,d} = B{w0,h0,c0,d} - \Delta \mu{n,1,1,d}, where \Delta\mu is broadcast across spatial dimensions. 3. Fast Volume Reconstruction: Compute D^2 in parallel for each local region using the discretized box \lfloor B \rfloor. Decompose D^2 into four Einstein sums: D^2 = (B^\top C^{-1} B) - (B^\top C^{-1} \Delta \mu) - (\Delta \mu^\top C^{-1} B) + (\Delta \mu^\top C^{-1} \Delta \mu). 4. Compute Contribution: Calculate the contribution tensor \Gamma for the local region as \Gamma = e^{-\frac{1}{2}Dn^2} \cdot In, where \Gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times w0 \times h0 \times c0}. 5. Aggregation: Update volume voxel V{x,y,z} by adding contribution \Gamma{i,x,y,z} from the i-th Gaussian: V{x,y,z} \leftarrow V{x,y,z} + \Gamma{i,x,y,z}. This is performed in a highly parallelized manner for all Gaussians. 6. Optimization: Project the reconstructed volume into the measurement domain for optimization, allowing for joint optimization of all Gaussians. Formulas: Continuous Gaussian: G(p, \mu, \Sigma) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(p-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(p-\mu)}, where p \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the 3D point, \mu is the mean, and \Sigma is the covariance matrix. Voxel intensity: V(p) = \sum{i=1}^n G(p, \mui, \Sigmai) \cdot Ii, where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^+ is the scalar intensity/weight. Relative coordinates: B = B0 - \mu, where B0 is the set of 3D coordinates within the cuboid. Squared Mahalanobis distance: D^2 = B^\top C^{-1} B, where C is the covariance matrix. Contribution: e^{-\frac{1}{2}D^2} \cdot Ii. Discretization alignment: [B]{n,w0,h0,c0,d} = B{w0,h0,c0,d} - \Delta \mu{n,1,1,d}. Decomposed D^2: D^2 = (B^\top C^{-1} B) - (B^\top C^{-1} \Delta \mu) - (\Delta \mu^\top C^{-1} B) + (\Delta \mu^\top C^{-1} \Delta \mu). Final contribution tensor: \Gamma = e^{-\frac{1}{2}Dn^2}, where \Gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times w0 \times h0 \times c0}. Aggregation: V{x,y,z} \leftarrow V{x,y,z} + \Gamma{i,x,y,z}. Parameters: w0, h0, c0: Dimensions of the effective proximity cuboid. Must be odd integers. Not given in the sources. Isotropic Covariance: \Sigmai = \sigmai^2 I, where I is the identity matrix. This is chosen because CT tissues, particularly soft tissues, exhibit isotropic attenuation properties. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiability: Directly discretizing \mu by rounding to the nearest integer makes the process non-differentiable, hindering optimization. The "Discretize and Align" method avoids this by using the residual \Delta \mu. Boundary Conditions: Gaussians near the volume boundary may have contributions that fall outside the grid. These must be clipped or masked to avoid out-of-bounds errors. Cuboid Size: The sources do not specify optimal cuboid dimensions beyond requiring odd integers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def discretizedgaussianrepresentation(gaussians, volumeshape, boxsize): """ Reconstructs a 3D volume from a set of Gaussians using DGR. Args: gaussians: Dict with keys 'mu' (n, 3), 'sigma' (n,), 'I' (n,) volumeshape: Tuple (w, h, c) boxsize: Tuple (w0, h0, c0) - odd integers Returns: V: Reconstructed volume tensor (w, h, c) """ n = gaussians['mu'].shape[0] w0, h0, c0 = boxsize d = 3 # Step 1 & 2: Create constant local box coordinates B0 centered at origin coords = torch.meshgrid( torch.arange(w0, dtype=torch.float32) - w0 // 2, torch.arange(h0, dtype=torch.float32) - h0 // 2, torch.arange(c0, dtype=torch.float32) - c0 // 2, indexing='ij') B0 = torch.stack(coords, dim=-1) # (w0, h0, c0, 3) # Extract Gaussian parameters mu = gaussians['mu'] # (n, 3) sigma = gaussians['sigma'] # (n,) I = gaussians['I'] # (n,) # Covariance inverse for isotropic Gaussians: Cinv = 1/sigma^2 Cinv = 1.0 / (sigma 2) # (n,) # Step 2: Discretize and Align mufloor = torch.floor(mu) # (n, 3) deltamu = mu - mufloor # (n, 3) # Relative coordinates B = B0 - mu B = B0.unsqueeze(0) - mu.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (n, w0, h0, c0, 3) # Transform to discretized box aligned with floored mean: [B] = B - deltamu Bdisc = B - deltamu.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (n, w0, h0, c0, 3) # Step 3: Fast Volume Reconstruction (Compute D^2 via decomposition) # Term 1: B^T C^-1 B term1 = torch.sum(Bdisc 2 Cinv.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1), dim=-1) # (n, w0, h0, c0) # Term 2: B^T C^-1 deltamu term2 = torch.sum(Bdisc deltamu.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) Cinv.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1), dim=-1) # (n, w0, h0, c0) # Term 3: deltamu^T C^-1 B (identical to term2 for scalar product) term3 = term2 # Term 4: deltamu^T C^-1 deltamu term4 = torch.sum(deltamu 2 Cinv, dim=-1) # (n,) D2 = term1 - term2 - term3 + term4.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (n, w0, h0, c0) # Step 4: Compute Contribution Gamma Gamma = torch.exp(-0.5 D2) I.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (n, w0, h0, c0) # Step 5: Aggregation V = torch.zeros(volumeshape, dtype=torch.float32) for i in range(n): baseidx = mufloor[i].long() # (3,) localindices = torch.meshgrid( torch.arange(w0), torch.arange(h0), torch.arange(c0), indexing='ij') localindices = torch.stack(localindices, dim=-1) # (w0, h0, c0, 3) globalindices = baseidx.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) + localindices # (w0, h0, c0, 3) x = torch.clamp(globalindices[:,:,:, 0], 0, volumeshape[0] - 1) y = torch.clamp(globalindices[:,:,:, 1], 0, volumeshape[1] - 1) z = torch.clamp(globalindices[:,:,:, 2], 0, volumeshape[2] - 1) V[x, y, z] += Gamma[i,:,:,:] return V Time Complexity: The Fast Volume Reconstruction technique reduces time complexity by decomposing the Mahalanobis distance calculation and reusing the spatial grid B. The exact complexity is not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: S1 states the decomposition reduces time complexity without increasing space complexity. Performance: DGR achieves superior reconstruction quality and runtime performance across various CT reconstruction scenarios compared to traditional DLR and 3DGS. Strengths: End-to-end differentiable optimization, efficient parallel aggregation, handles isotropic tissues well. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of isotropic attenuation, which may not hold for all tissue types or anisotropic structures. The cuboid confinement may lose information from distant Gaussians, though this is mitigated by trainable Gaussians. DGR was proposed in 2025 by W. King et al. in the paper "Discretized Gaussian Representation for Tomographic Reconstruction". It addresses limitations in existing differentiable volumetric reconstruction methods, particularly the integration bias and density inconsistency of 3D Gaussian Splatting when applied to CT. The method is designed to be a plug-and-play module that can be integrated into existing 3D Gaussian-based pipelines. name: Recursive Parameter Space Voxelization for Catmull-Clark Subdivision Surfaces
head: CCSS Voxelization, Voxelization of Solids Represented by CCSSs
body: This method converts a free-form object represented by a Catmull-Clark subdivision surface (CCSS) into a voxel grid by recursively subdividing the 2D parameter space of surface patches and sampling 3D points, rather than subdividing 3D object space. It ensures leak-free results for closed objects when a 3D flooding operation is performed by guaranteeing that voxels generated from a single patch satisfy specific N-adjacency properties. Unlike 3D space subdivision techniques which are computationally expensive due to distance computations between 3D points, this method performs subdivision in 2D parameter space, avoiding expensive 3D distance computations. Inputs: A control mesh S defining a Catmull-Clark subdivision surface. Output voxel grid resolution M1 \times M2 \times M3. Adjacency requirement N \in \{6, 18, 26\}, specifying the connectivity of voxels generated from a subpatch (6 for face-sharing, 18 for edge/face-sharing, 26 for vertex/edge/face-sharing). Initial subdivision level k, an integer specifying that the parameter space [0,1] \times [0,1] is divided into k \times k subpatches before recursive processing begins. Outputs: A voxel grid of resolution M1 \times M2 \times M3 containing the voxelized representation of the CCSS. Data Structures: The control mesh S is stored as a collection of patches. Each patch pid is associated with a local 2D parameter domain [0,1] \times [0,1]. Parametrization techniques allow the explicit calculation of any 3D point \mathbf{S}(u,v), its position, normal, and partial derivatives on the limit surface given a patch ID and parameter coordinates (u,v). Steps: 1. Normalization: Normalize the control mesh S so that its bounding box aligns with the voxel grid coordinates [0, M1-1] \times [0, M2-1] \times [0, M3-1]. 2. Initialization: Iterate through each patch pid in the mesh S. 3. Initial Grid: For the parameter space of the patch, iterate u from 1/k to 1 with step 1/k, and v from 1/k to 1 with step 1/k. 4. Recursive Processing: For each initial subpatch defined by parameter ranges [u-1/k, u] and [v-1/k, v], call VoxelizeSubPatch(N, pid, u - 1/k, u, v - 1/k, v). 5. Subpatch Evaluation: Inside VoxelizeSubPatch, evaluate the 3D surface positions for the four corners of the current subpatch defined by (u1, v1), (u2, v1), (u2, v2), and (u1, v2) using the patch ID pid and the parametrization function \mathbf{S}(u,v). Let these points be \mathbf{V}1, \mathbf{V}2, \mathbf{V}3, \mathbf{V}4. 6. Voxel Conversion: Convert the 3D surface coordinates to voxel indices (i,j,k) using the formula: i = \lfloor \mathbf{S}(u, v).x + 0.5 \rfloor, \quad j = \lfloor \mathbf{S}(u, v).y + 0.5 \rfloor, \quad k = \lfloor \mathbf{S}(u, v).z + 0.5 \rfloor where \lfloor \cdot \rfloor denotes the floor function, effectively rounding to the nearest integer. Mark these voxels in the output grid. 7. Termination Check: If the subpatch size is smaller than a voxel, return. Calculate the maximum differences in voxel indices among the four corners: \Delta i = \max{a,b \in \{1,2,3,4\}} |ia - ib| \Delta j = \max{a,b \in \{1,2,3,4\}} |ja - jb| \Delta k = \max{a,b \in \{1,2,3,4\}} |ka - kb| If N=6 and \Delta i + \Delta j + \Delta k \le 1, return (subpatch is small enough for 6-adjacency). If N=18 and \Delta i \le 1, \Delta j \le 1, \Delta k \le 1, and \Delta i + \Delta j + \Delta k \le 2, return (subpatch is small enough for 18-adjacency). If N=26 and \Delta i \le 1, \Delta j \le 1, \Delta k \le 1, return (subpatch is small enough for 26-adjacency). 8. Recursive Subdivision: If the subpatch is not small enough, compute midpoints u{12} = (u1 + u2)/2 and v{12} = (v1 + v2)/2. Recursively call VoxelizeSubPatch for the four quadrants: [u1, u{12}] \times [v1, v{12}] [u{12}, u2] \times [v1, v{12}] [u{12}, u2] \times [v{12}, v2] [u1, u{12}] \times [v{12}, v2] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelizeccss(controlmesh, N, M1, M2, M3, k): """ Voxelizes a Catmull-Clark Subdivision Surface. Args: controlmesh: List of patches, each patch has an ID and parametrization function. N: Adjacency requirement (6, 18, or 26). M1, M2, M3: Resolution of the output voxel grid. k: Initial subdivision level for parameter space. Returns: 3D boolean array of shape (M1, M2, M3). """ # Initialize voxel grid voxelgrid = [[[False for in range(M3)] for in range(M2)] for in range(M1)] # Normalize control mesh bounding box to [0, M1-1] x [0, M2-1] x [0, M3-1]. normalizedmesh = controlmesh # Placeholder for normalization step # Iterate through each patch for patch in normalizedmesh: pid = patch.id # Initial parameter space subdivision step = 1.0 / k for i in range(1, k + 1): u = i step for j in range(1, k + 1): v = j step # Call recursive voxelization for the initial subpatch voxelizesubpatch(pid, u - step, u, v - step, v, N, voxelgrid) return voxelgrid def voxelizesubpatch(pid, u1, u2, v1, v2, N, voxelgrid): """ Recursively voxelizes a subpatch of a CCSS. """ # Evaluate surface point S(u,v) for patch pid using parametrization techniques. v1pt = (u1, v1) # Placeholder for 3D point evaluation v2pt = (u2, v1) v3pt = (u2, v2) v4pt = (u1, v2) # Convert to voxel indices i1 = math.floor(v1pt[0] + 0.5) j1 = math.floor(v1pt[1] + 0.5) k1 = math.floor(v1pt[2] + 0.5) i2 = math.floor(v2pt[0] + 0.5) j2 = math.floor(v2pt[1] + 0.5) k2 = math.floor(v2pt[2] + 0.5) i3 = math.floor(v3pt[0] + 0.5) j3 = math.floor(v3pt[1] + 0.5) k3 = math.floor(v3pt[2] + 0.5) i4 = math.floor(v4pt[0] + 0.5) j4 = math.floor(v4pt[1] + 0.5) k4 = math.floor(v4pt[2] + 0.5) # Mark voxels in the grid if 0 <= i1 < M1 and 0 <= j1 < M2 and 0 <= k1 < M3: voxelgrid[i1][j1][k1] = True if 0 <= i2 < M1 and 0 <= j2 < M2 and 0 <= k2 < M3: voxelgrid[i2][j2][k2] = True if 0 <= i3 < M1 and 0 <= j3 < M2 and 0 <= k3 < M3: voxelgrid[i3][j3][k3] = True if 0 <= i4 < M1 and 0 <= j4 < M2 and 0 <= k4 < M3: voxelgrid[i4][j4][k4] = True # Check if subpatch is small enough # Check if subpatch bounding box in 3D is smaller than a voxel; if so, return. # Calculate max differences in voxel indices indicesi = [i1, i2, i3, i4] indicesj = [j1, j2, j3, j4] indicesk = [k1, k2, k3, k4] deltai = max(indicesi) - min(indicesi) deltaj = max(indicesj) - min(indicesj) deltak = max(indicesk) - min(indicesk) # Termination conditions based on N if N == 6 and (deltai + deltaj + deltak) <= 1: return if N == 18 and deltai <= 1 and deltaj <= 1 and deltak <= 1 and (deltai + deltaj + deltak) <= 2: return if N == 26 and deltai <= 1 and deltaj <= 1 and deltak <= 1: return # Recursive subdivision u12 = (u1 + u2) / 2.0 v12 = (v1 + v2) / 2.0 voxelizesubpatch(pid, u1, u12, v1, v12, N, voxelgrid) voxelizesubpatch(pid, u12, u2, v1, v12, N, voxelgrid) voxelizesubpatch(pid, u12, u2, v12, v2, N, voxelgrid) voxelizesubpatch(pid, u1, u12, v12, v2, N, voxelgrid) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: Holes appear if the voxels generated from the four corners of a subpatch are not N-adjacent. The algorithm prevents this by recursively subdividing until the N-adjacency condition is met. Shared Boundaries: Shared boundaries between patches or subpatches must map to the same voxel to ensure leak-free results. The algorithm guarantees this because shared boundary points are evaluated at the same parameter coordinates. Precision: The voxel coordinate conversion uses floor(S(u,v).x + 0.5). Floating-point precision errors in surface evaluation could theoretically cause boundary voxels to be assigned incorrectly, but the recursive subdivision ensures that adjacent patches share evaluation points, mitigating gaps. Time Complexity: The method avoids the exponential increase in faces associated with uniformly refining the control mesh, making it more efficient than direct sampling on subdivided surfaces. The complexity depends on the curvature of the surface and the chosen adjacency N; flatter regions terminate earlier, while highly curved regions require deeper recursion. Memory Complexity: The output is a voxel grid of size M1 \times M2 \times M3. The recursion depth is limited by the resolution and curvature, but the memory overhead for the recursion stack is generally low compared to storing a highly subdivided mesh. Strengths: Guarantees leak-free voxelization for closed objects when followed by 3D flooding. Works directly on parametric surfaces of arbitrary topology without requiring explicit polygonization first. Avoids expensive 3D distance computations inherent in 3D space subdivision techniques. Limitations: Requires efficient parametrization techniques to explicitly calculate surface points. Performance is sensitive to the initial subdivision level k and adjacency N; higher N or smaller k may increase computation time. When to use: Volume graphics applications involving free-form solids with arbitrary topology represented by Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces. Origin: The method was presented in a paper titled "Voxelization of Free-Form Solids Represented by Catmull-Clark Subdivision Surfaces". History: Subdivision surfaces have become popular in graphical modeling, visualization, and animation due to their capability in modeling complex shapes of arbitrary topology and high visual quality. Traditional 3D scan-conversion methods extend 2D scan-line algorithms, but this method works directly on parametric surfaces. Recent parametrization techniques allow explicit calculation of points on the limit surface, enabling this efficient voxelization approach. Usage: Used for volume graphics applications. name: Chunk Generation with Base Terrain
head: Procedural Chunk Generation
body: Chunk Generation with Base Terrain is a method for automatically populating voxel data when a new chunk is created or accessed in a procedural voxel world. It solves the problem of empty or undefined space by providing a deterministic initial state for chunks, such as a flat platform, before more complex features are added. It differs from Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation by focusing on the structural generation of the voxel grid itself rather than the visual rendering of volumetric density, and from Distance to Hypertextures by using discrete voxel assignment rather than continuous field evaluation for the base terrain. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera position, chunk size (typically 32 \times 32 \times 32), render distance radius, and chunk coordinates. Output: A populated 3D voxel array for the requested chunk and a list of chunks to render within the render distance. Data Structures: Chunk: Contains a 3D array voxels of size 32 \times 32 \times 32 (or configurable) and a mesh handle. VoxelKind: An enumeration representing block types (e.g., Air, Dirt). World: A map or hash table storing generated chunks keyed by their 3D integer coordinates (IVec3). Steps: 1. Calculate Camera Chunk: Determine the chunk index containing the camera by performing floor division of the camera's world position by the chunk size. \text{camera\chunk} = \lfloor \frac{\text{camera\position}}{\text{chunk\size}} \rfloor 2. Render Distance Loop: Iterate through all chunk offsets within the specified radius around the camera chunk. \text{chunk\pos} = \text{camera\chunk} + \text{offset} where offset ranges from -\text{radius} to +\text{radius} in X, Y, and Z. 3. Get or Create Chunk: For each chunk position, check if it exists in the world data structure. If not, generate it. 4. Initialize Voxel Grid: Create a 3D array of VoxelKind::Air for the new chunk. 5. Apply Base Terrain: If the chunk's Y-coordinate is 0 (or the designated base level), populate the bottom layer with solid terrain (e.g., Dirt). \text{voxels}[0][z][x] = \text{VoxelKind::Dirt} \quad \forall x, z \in [0, 32) 6. Mesh Generation: (Implicit step) Process the voxel grid to extract visible faces for rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getorcreatechunk(world: World, chunkposition: IVec3, chunksize: int = 32) -> Chunk: """ Generates a new chunk with base terrain if it does not exist. """ if chunkposition not in world.chunks: # Initialize 3D array with Air # Dimensions: Y (height), Z (depth), X (width) voxels = [[[VoxelKind.Air for in range(chunksize)] for in range(chunksize)] for in range(chunksize)] # Apply base terrain: Flat platform at Y=0 if chunkposition.y == 0: for z in range(chunksize): for x in range(chunksize): voxels[0][z][x] = VoxelKind.Dirt # Store chunk world.chunks[chunkposition] = Chunk(mesh=None, voxels=voxels) return world.chunks[chunkposition] def generatechunksaroundcamera(world: World, cameraposition: Vec3, renderradius: int, chunksize: int) -> List[Chunk]: """ Generates and returns chunks within the render distance. """ # Calculate camera chunk index camerachunk = IVec3( cameraposition.x // chunksize, cameraposition.y // chunksize, cameraposition.z // chunksize) chunkstorender = [] # Iterate through chunks in a cube around the camera for y in range(-renderradius, renderradius + 1): for z in range(-renderradius, renderradius + 1): for x in range(-renderradius, renderradius + 1): chunkoffset = IVec3(x, y, z) chunkpos = camerachunk + chunkoffset chunk = getorcreatechunk(world, chunkpos, chunksize) chunkstorender.append(chunk) return chunkstorender Parameters: chunksize: The dimension of a single chunk (e.g., 32). renderradius: The number of chunks away from the camera to generate (e.g., 4). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Ensure floor division handles negative coordinates correctly (e.g., using diveuclid or equivalent) to avoid chunk misalignment. Memory Usage: Generating chunks for the entire render distance every frame can be expensive; caching is required. Degenerate Input: If the camera is exactly on a chunk boundary, the floor division must consistently assign the camera to one specific chunk to avoid gaps or overlaps in generation logic. Procedural Terrain Heightmap Generation computes a 2D heightmap for terrain surfaces. It differs from the parent method by focusing on surface elevation rather than full 3D voxel population, often serving as a precursor to generating the base terrain layer in chunks. Link: Procedural Terrain Heightmap Generation. Voxel Evaluation with AABB Culling is a GPU-accelerated technique for computing Signed Distance Function (SDF) values for a chunk's voxel grid by restricting computation to voxels intersecting active SDF primitives. It solves the problem of unnecessary GPU computation for voxels far from any terrain geometry. Unlike Chunk-Based Voxel Terrain Generation which may process the entire chunk volume, this method uses Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) culling to identify a minimal sub-region of interest, significantly reducing the number of voxels processed per frame. Link: Voxel Evaluation with AABB Culling. Procedural cave generation creates subsurface voids in voxel terrain using either subtractive particle tracing or threshold-based noise filtering. Unlike Simplex Noise Chunk Generation which generates the base terrain, this method operates as a post-processing or layered feature to carve out complex, organic underground structures. It differs from Procedural Object Generation by focusing on large-scale, continuous erosion-like voids rather than discrete static meshes. Link: Procedural Cave Generation. Procedural Voxel World Generation is a method for determining the block type at any given 3D integer coordinate in a voxel grid based on height, noise functions, and quality settings, supporting terrain, caves, trees, clouds, and emissive blocks. It differs from Procedural Terrain Heightmap Generation by not only computing the surface height but also assigning specific block IDs (grass, dirt, stone, wood, leaves) and handling volumetric features like caves and trees within the same evaluation logic. It builds on Chunk Generation with Base Terrain by providing the detailed voxel-level content for the chunks generated by that parent method. Link: Procedural Voxel World Generation. Chunk-Based Voxel Terrain Generation is a procedural technique that divides a 3D world into fixed-size cubic chunks, populating each with voxel data via multi-octave noise sampling and biome logic, then extracting visible faces for meshing. It differs from raymarching or marching cubes by explicitly generating a dense 3D voxel grid per chunk before mesh extraction, rather than computing surfaces via implicit functions or ray traversal. Link: Chunk-Based Voxel Terrain Generation. Spiral Chunk Generation produces a queue of 3D chunk positions in a spiral pattern to drive procedural octree and mesh generation. It differs from sibling methods like Simplex Noise Chunk Generation by decoupling spatial traversal order from noise evaluation, ensuring chunks are generated in a contiguous spiral sequence rather than arbitrary spatial locality, which aids in progressive loading and memory management. Link: Spiral Chunk Generation. Generates a voxel chunk's geometry and data using a 3D simplex noise function to determine voxel presence/height, allocating vertex and index buffers for rendering. It differs from heightmap-based siblings by evaluating noise in full 3D space to create volumetric terrain rather than surface-only heightmaps, and from cave generation by using a single scalar threshold for solid vs. empty space rather than complex noise blending. Link: Simplex Noise Chunk Generation. Constructs a basic rectangular house with a floor, roof, walls, a door on a specified side, and supporting legs extending down to solid ground. It differs from sibling methods like Procedural Terrain Heightmap Generation by placing discrete, structured architectural primitives rather than continuous terrain surfaces, and from Procedural Cave Generation by generating enclosed, man-made geometry rather than voids. Link: Procedural Object Generation. A procedural method to generate arches by sweeping a sphere along a cubic Bézier spline. It uses tapering parameters to simulate greater erosion towards the middle of the arch. Steps: 1. Define the cubic Bézier spline using four control points. 2. For each step t of the sweep, calculate the radius using tapering parameters Ti at each end of the arch. Formulas: Calculate tapering parameter Ti for each end i: Ti = r \cdot Mi \cdot (1 - Ii^{Ei}) where Mi is the radius multiplier, Ei is the exponent, and Ii is the interpolant defining where tapering occurs. Calculate the total radius: \text{radius} = r + T0 + T1 Compute the delta value D{Arch}(V, P) for voxel V and position P (voxel position after radius application): D{Arch}(V, P) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } \|P - V\| < \text{radius} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Parameters: Mi: Radius multipliers for optional tapering at each end of the arch. Ei: Exponents for optional tapering at each end of the arch. Ii: Interpolants defining where the tapering occurs at each end of the arch. r: Base radius of the sphere being swept. Link: Procedural Arch Generation (Note: No separate article exists, so it is a subtopic here). Time Complexity: O(R^3) per frame for chunk generation, where R is the render radius in chunks. Voxel initialization is O(C^3) per chunk, where C is the chunk size. Memory Complexity: O(R^3 \cdot C^3) for storing voxel data of all active chunks. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades linearly with the cube of the render distance. Chunk caching mitigates repeated generation costs. Strengths: Simple to implement; deterministic; low memory overhead for base terrain. Limitations: Lacks natural variation without additional noise or features; static base terrain. When to use: Prototyping, simple voxel worlds, or as a foundation for more complex procedural generation. When not to use: When natural-looking terrain or complex volumetric features are required without additional algorithms. Originating from tutorials on building voxel engines quickly, this method was popularized by weekend coding challenges and blogs focusing on minimal viable voxel worlds. It serves as the foundational step in procedural voxel generation pipelines, preceding more complex noise-based or feature-based generation techniques. It is widely used in educational contexts and simple sandbox games.
