name: Fixed-Step Raymarching with Beer's Law
head: Fixed-Step Raymarcher, MarchDensity, Volumetric Cloud Density Marching, Volumetric Cloud Renderer
body: Fixed-Step Raymarching with Beer's Law is a real-time volumetric rendering technique that simulates cloud-like structures by tracing rays through a 3D density field and integrating light attenuation using Beer's Law. It differs from its parent Volumetric Cloud Raymarching by explicitly decoupling the density sampling (often via Worley and Perlin noise) from the radiative transfer calculation, applying a fixed step size for deterministic traversal rather than adaptive stepping. It differs from its child Volumetric Ray Marching with Noise by relying on scalar density thresholds and Beer's Law for transmittance, whereas the child uses normalized noise vectors to modulate density and light accumulation directly. Inputs: Camera position (P{cam}), ray direction (\vec{d}) derived from UV coordinates. Cloud volume bounding box (AABB) defined by \vec{B}{min} and \vec{B}{max}. Sun direction (\vec{S}{dir}) and Sun color (C{sun}). Noise textures or procedural functions for Worley (NW) and Perlin (NP) noise. Parameters: STEP\SIZE, LIGHT\STEP\SIZE, MAX\STEPS, uUserDensity, \vec{uUserScale}, \DensityThreshold, \AbsorptionCoefficient, \ScatterFactor. Outputs: Final pixel color (C{final}) and alpha/transmittance. Data Structures: ray: Struct containing origin (\vec{o}) and direction (\vec{d}). hitData: Struct containing entry distance (t{entry}) and exit distance (t{exit}) from AABB intersection. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Calculate the view ray direction \vec{d} from the camera position and screen UV coordinates. Apply any camera rotation matrix if required. 2. AABB Intersection: Intersect the view ray with the cloud volume AABB. If no intersection, return the sky color. Let t{entry} and t{exit} be the distances to the entry and exit points along the ray. Calculate the total distance to march: D{total} = t{exit} - t{entry}. Set initial ray position: \vec{p}{start} = \vec{o} + \vec{d} \cdot t{entry}. Edge Case: If the camera is inside the volume, t{entry} may be negative or zero; the march starts from the camera position or the calculated entry point. 3. Initialization: Initialize densityTotal = 0.0. Initialize brightness = 0.0. Initialize globalTransmittance = 1.0. Initialize cloudColor = (0, 0, 0). Initialize distanceTravelled = t{entry}. 4. Main Raymarch Loop: Loop for i from 0 to stepLimit (exclusive): Calculate current march point: \vec{p}{march} = \vec{o} + \vec{d} \cdot \text{distanceTravelled}. Check Exit: If distanceTravelled > t{exit}, break loop. Check Max Steps: If i \ge MAX\STEPS, break loop. 4.1. Density Sampling: Calculate world-scaled position: \vec{p}{world} = \vec{p}{march} \cdot \CloudScale. Sample Worley noise NW and Perlin noise NP at \vec{p}{world}. Note: In some implementations, Worley noise is accumulated over octaves with halving amplitude and doubling frequency, then normalized. Note: Perlin noise may be summed over multiple octaves (e.g., frequencies 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32). Calculate raw density: \rho{raw} = NW \cdot NP. Normalize density: \rho = \rho{raw} / uUserDensity. 4.2. Density Thresholding: If \rho < 0.05, skip to next step (continue). If \rho < \DensityThreshold, skip accumulation. 4.3. Accumulate Density: densityTotal += \rho \cdot STEP\SIZE. 4.4. Light Ray Marching (Secondary Ray): Define light ray origin: \vec{o}{light} = \vec{p}{march}. Define light ray direction: \vec{d}{light} = \text{normalize}(\vec{S}{dir}). Intersect light ray with AABB to find max light distance t{light\max}. Initialize currentLightRayT = 1.0. Loop for light step lS from STEP\SIZE to MAX\STEPS with increment LIGHT\STEP\SIZE: If lS \ge t{light\max}, break. Calculate light march point: \vec{p}{light} = \vec{o}{light} + \vec{d}{light} \cdot lS. Sample density \rho{light} at \vec{p}{light} (using same noise/scale logic). If \rho{light} < 0.05, continue. Update light transmittance: currentLightRayT = \exp(-\rho{light} \cdot LIGHT\STEP\SIZE). 4.5. Scattering and Color Accumulation: Calculate local transmittance: T{local} = \exp(-\rho \cdot STEP\SIZE). Calculate scattering term: S = (1.0 - T{local}) \cdot \text{currentLightRayT}. Alternative Implementation: Some sources use Henyey-Greenstein phase function HG(\vec{d}, \vec{S}{dir}, \ScatterFactor) and Beer's Law explicitly: T{cam} = \exp(-\text{densityTotal} \cdot \AbsorptionCoefficient). S = HG(\vec{d}, \vec{S}{dir}, \ScatterFactor). Accumulate brightness: brightness += \rho \cdot \text{currentLightRayT} \cdot T{cam} \cdot S \cdot STEP\SIZE \cdot 0.5. Accumulate cloud color: cloudColor += globalTransmittance S C{sun}. Note: globalTransmittance may be updated as globalTransmittance = T{local}. 4.6. Step Increment: distanceTravelled += STEP\SIZE. 5. Final Compositing: Calculate final cloud color: C{cloud} = \text{brightness} \cdot C{sun} or C{cloud} = \text{cloudColor}. Calculate final transmittance: T{final} = \exp(-\text{densityTotal} \cdot \AbsorptionCoefficient). Sun Glare: If the dot product of the view direction and sun direction is > 0.9995, mix in a special sun glare color. Return C{final} = C{cloud} + C{sky} \cdot T{final}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fixedstepraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax, sundir, suncolor, noisefunc, params): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 boxmin: vec3 boxmax: vec3 sundir: vec3 suncolor: vec3 noisefunc: function(vec3) -> float params: dict containing STEPSIZE, LIGHTSTEPSIZE, MAXSTEPS, uUserDensity, DensityThreshold, AbsorptionCoefficient, ScatterFactor, CloudScale """ # 1. Intersect ray with AABB hit = intersectaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax) if not hit.hit: return skycolor tentry = hit.tmin texit = hit.tmax totaldist = texit - tentry # 2. Initialize accumulators densitytotal = 0.0 brightness = 0.0 globaltransmittance = 1.0 cloudcolor = vec3(0.0) distancetravelled = tentry stepsize = params['STEPSIZE'] lightstepsize = params['LIGHTSTEPSIZE'] maxsteps = params['MAXSTEPS'] densitythreshold = params['DensityThreshold'] absorptioncoeff = params['AbsorptionCoefficient'] cloudscale = params['CloudScale'] userdensity = params['uUserDensity'] # 3. Main Loop for i in range(maxsteps): if distancetravelled > texit: break # Current position marchpos = rayorigin + raydirection distancetravelled # Density Sampling worldpos = marchpos cloudscale densityraw = noisefunc(worldpos) density = densityraw / userdensity # Thresholding if density < 0.05 or density < densitythreshold: distancetravelled += stepsize continue # Accumulate Density densitytotal += density stepsize # Secondary Light Ray lightorigin = marchpos lightdir = normalize(sundir) lighthit = intersectaabb(lightorigin, lightdir, boxmin, boxmax) maxlightdist = lighthit.tmax if lighthit.hit else 0.0 lighttransmittance = 1.0 lightt = stepsize while lightt <= maxsteps and lightt < maxlightdist: lightpos = lightorigin + lightdir lightt lightdensityraw = noisefunc(lightpos cloudscale) lightdensity = lightdensityraw / userdensity if lightdensity >= 0.05: lighttransmittance = exp(-lightdensity lightstepsize) lightt += lightstepsize # Scattering Calculation (Method 1: Simplified) localtransmittance = exp(-density stepsize) scattering = (1.0 - localtransmittance) lighttransmittance cloudcolor += globaltransmittance scattering suncolor # Update Global Transmittance globaltransmittance = localtransmittance # Step Increment distancetravelled += stepsize # 4. Final Output # Method 2 (Alternative from S2) for final color/transmittance calculation: # cameratransmittance = exp(-densitytotal absorptioncoeff) # cloudcolour = brightness suncolor # return float4(cloudcolour, 1.0 - cameratransmittance) # Using Method 1 accumulation: finalcolor = cloudcolor + skycolor globaltransmittance return finalcolor Uses normalized noise vectors to modulate density and light, differing from the scalar density/Beer's Law approach of this method. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of steps in the main raymarch loop and M is the number of steps in the secondary light raymarch loop per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, excluding the storage for noise textures if pre-computed. Performance: Real-time capable on modern GPUs. Performance scales with resolution and the number of steps. Higher quality settings increase stepLimit and decrease stepSize, significantly increasing cost. Strengths: Deterministic step size simplifies implementation and debugging. Beer's Law provides physically plausible attenuation. Noise-based density allows for detailed, organic cloud structures without large 3D textures. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missing thin cloud details if steps are too large. Requires careful tuning of STEPSIZE and LIGHTSTEPSIZE to balance quality and performance. The secondary light ray adds significant computational overhead per sample. When to use: Real-time cloud rendering in games or interactive applications where performance is critical but visual quality needs to be higher than simple billboard clouds. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring high-fidelity global illumination or very large-scale atmospheric effects where adaptive stepping or pre-computed lighting might be more efficient. The technique originates from real-time WebGL volumetric cloud rendering projects, specifically those utilizing fixed-step raymarchers to simulate cloud-like structures. It builds upon the principles of volumetric rendering and Beer's Law, adapting them for real-time execution by using procedural noise (Worley and Perlin) for density definition. The specific implementation details, such as the use of Worley and Perlin noise combination and the fixed-step light marching, are documented in unofficial GitHub repositories. name: Volumetric Ray Marching with Noise
head: Noise Volume Rendering
body: A real-time volumetric rendering technique that samples a 3D noise texture along a ray passing through a spherical cloud volume to compute opacity and color. It differs from its parent Fixed-Step Raymarching with Beer's Law by using a normalized noise vector to modulate density and light accumulation, rather than relying solely on scalar density and Beer's Law attenuation. Inputs: fragPos: Fragment position in world space. viewRay: Normalized view direction vector. center: Center of the spherical cloud volume. radius: Radius of the spherical cloud volume. fNoiseSizeAdjust: Scaling factor to convert world space to local texture space. numOctaves: Number of octaves for the noise function. noiseOpacity: Scaling factor for accumulated opacity. minNoiseSteps, maxNoiseSteps: Clamping bounds for step count. minNoiseColor: Base color for the noise volume. noiseColorScale: Scaling factor for the noise color contribution. Outputs: color: Final RGBA color of the fragment. Data Structures: noise3D(pos, octaves): A 3D noise function returning a vec4 (or vec3 with alpha) where.xyz represents the noise vector and.a represents the noise magnitude/alpha. saturate(x): Clamps x to [0, 1]. normalize(v): Normalizes vector v. dot(a, b): Dot product of vectors a and b. length(v): Euclidean length of vector v. vec2(0.5): Constant vector for alpha calculation. Steps: 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection: Compute the intersection of the ray fragPos + t viewRay with the sphere defined by center and radius. Obtain tnear and tfar (the smallest and largest positive t values). If no intersection exists, discard the fragment. 2. World Space Bounds: Calculate the world-space start and end points of the ray segment inside the sphere: \text{worldNear} = \text{fragPos} + \text{viewRay} \times \text{tnear} \text{worldFar} = \text{fragPos} + \text{viewRay} \times \text{tfar} 3. Local Texture Coordinates: Convert world-space points to local texture coordinates: \text{localTexNear} = \text{worldNear} \times \text{fNoiseSizeAdjust} \text{localTexFar} = \text{worldFar} \times \text{fNoiseSizeAdjust} 4. Step Count Calculation: Calculate the number of steps based on the distance in texture space: \text{iSteps} = \frac{\|\text{localTexFar} - \text{localTexNear}\|}{\text{stepSize}} Clamp iSteps to the range [minNoiseSteps, maxNoiseSteps]. Note: stepSize is an implicit parameter derived from the desired resolution or fixed value in the implementation context. 5. Initialization: Initialize the marching variables: \text{currentTex} = \text{localTexNear} \text{localTexDelta} = \frac{\text{localTexFar} - \text{localTexNear}}{\text{iSteps} - 1} \text{opacityAdjust} = \frac{\text{noiseOpacity}}{\text{iSteps} - 1} \text{lightAdjust} = \frac{1.0}{\text{iSteps} - 1} \text{runningOpacity} = 0 \text{runningLight} = 0 \text{unitTex} = \text{localTexNear} 6. Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to iSteps - 1: a. Sample the noise: \text{noiseCell} = \text{noise3D}(\text{currentTex}, \text{numOctaves}) b. Adjust noise by normal: \text{noiseCell.xyz} += \text{normalize}(\text{unitTex}) c. Accumulate opacity: \text{runningOpacity} += \text{noiseCell.a} \times (1.0 - \text{dot}(\text{unitTex}, \text{unitTex})) d. Accumulate light: \text{runningLight} += \text{saturate}(\text{dot}(\text{noiseCell.xyz}, \text{vec3}(0, 1, 0)) \times 0.5 + 0.5) e. Advance texture coordinates: \text{currentTex} += \text{localTexDelta} \text{unitTex} += \text{localTexDelta} 7. Final Color and Alpha Computation: \text{col} = \text{minNoiseColor} + (\text{noiseColorScale} \times \text{runningLight} \times \text{lightAdjust}) \text{alpha} = 1 - \|\text{fragTex} - \text{vec2}(0.5)\| \times 2 \text{runningOpacity} = \text{saturate}(\text{runningOpacity} \times \text{opacityAdjust}) \text{color} = \text{vec4}(\text{col}, \text{runningOpacity} \times \text{alpha}) Parameters: noiseOpacity: Scaling factor for accumulated opacity. minNoiseSteps: Minimum number of steps. maxNoiseSteps: Maximum number of steps. minNoiseColor: Base color for the noise volume. noiseColorScale: Scaling factor for the noise color contribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero in localTexDelta and adjustments if iSteps is 1. The clamping of minNoiseSteps should ensure iSteps >= 2 to avoid this, or a guard is required. dot(unitTex, unitTex) in opacity accumulation can exceed 1.0 if unitTex is not normalized, leading to negative opacity contributions. The source uses unitTex as a position vector, not a normalized direction, so this term acts as a radial falloff. fragTex in the alpha calculation is not defined in the source steps. It is assumed to be the texture coordinate of the fragment in screen or local space, or potentially localTexNear or currentTex at the end of the march. Given the context of vec2(0.5), it likely refers to a 2D projection or screen-space coordinate. Not given in the sources. This method is part of a procedural cloud rendering pipeline, specifically utilizing noise-based density modulation. It is implemented in the Cloud-Renderer project. jaafersheriff/Cloud-Renderer, https://github.com/jaafersheriff/Cloud-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Procedural Volume Cloud Modeling
head: Cloud Density Field Generation, Density Sampling and Weather
body: Procedural Volume Cloud Modeling constructs the volumetric density field of clouds by evaluating mathematical noise functions and weather parameters at arbitrary world-space coordinates. It solves the problem of generating realistic, infinite-extent cloud geometry without storing massive pre-baked 3D textures, allowing for dynamic control over cloud type, coverage, and erosion via 2D maps. It differs from Volumetric Cloud Raymarching by focusing on the generation of the density value rather than the integration of light through it, and from Atmospheric Height Gradient by incorporating specific cloud-type logic and erosion mechanics beyond simple vertical falloff. Inputs: World-space position P{world} = (x, y, z). Time t for animation. Wind vector \vec{W} = (wx, wy, wz). 2D Weather Map texture T{weather} (RGBA). 3D Shape Noise texture T{shape} (Perlin-Worley). 3D Detail Noise texture T{detail} (Perlin). Cloud LUT texture T{lut} (RGB). Outputs: Scalar cloud density \rho \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: 1. Weather Map (T{weather}): A 2D texture where channels store: R: Cloud Coverage (0.0–1.0). G: Cloud Type (0.0–1.0). B: Cloud Erosion (0.0–1.0). A: Cloud Wetness (0.0–1.0). 2. Cloud LUT (T{lut}): A 1D or 2D texture mapping Cloud Type and Height to: R: Density multiplier. G: Erosion multiplier. B: Ambient Occlusion. Steps: 1. Sample Weather Map: Sample T{weather} at the projected 2D horizontal position of P{world} (typically x, z coordinates, possibly scaled by a world size factor). Let the result be C{weather} = (c{cov}, c{type}, c{ero}, c{wet}). 2. Determine Cloud Type: Map c{type} to a specific cloud layer using the following ranges: [0.0, 0.125): Cirrus (High-level). [0.125, 0.25): Cirrus + Cumulus (Multi-layer). [0.25, 0.5): Cumulus. [0.5, 1.0]: Cumulonimbus. 3. Apply Height Gradient: Calculate a vertical attenuation factor H{grad} based on the height y of P{world} relative to the cloud layer's base and top. This enforces flat bases and rounded tops. H{grad} = \text{RemapVertical}(y, y{base}, y{top}) Note: Specific remap function is not given in sources [G: Typically a smoothstep or polynomial curve that is 0 below base, rises to 1, and falls to 0 above top.] 4. Sample Base Shape Noise: Compute the sampling coordinate for the shape noise. This coordinate must tile across kilometers. P{shape} = P{world} \cdot S{shape} + \vec{W}{shape} \cdot t where S{shape} is a scaling factor for tiling. Sample the Perlin-Worley texture: N{shape} = \text{SamplePerlinWorley}(T{shape}, P{shape}) 5. Sample Detail Noise: Compute the sampling coordinate for detail noise. This is scaled up by frequency to erode edges. P{detail} = P{world} \cdot S{detail} + \vec{W}{detail} \cdot t Sample the Perlin texture: N{detail} = \text{SamplePerlin}(T{detail}, P{detail}) 6. Calculate Erosion: The erosion factor E is influenced by the Weather Map's erosion channel, the Cloud LUT's erosion channel (G), and the detail noise. E = \text{Lerp}(1.0, N{detail}, c{ero} \cdot \text{SampleLUT}(T{lut}, c{type}, y).G) Note: Sources indicate Cloud LUT G channel affects both detail and shape noise calculations. 7. Combine Density: The final density \rho is a product of coverage, height gradient, shape noise, and erosion. \rho = c{cov} \cdot H{grad} \cdot N{shape} \cdot (1.0 - E) Note: For Cumulonimbus (high complexity), adjust coverage and erosion based on height: high altitude has low coverage and high erosion; low altitude has high coverage and low erosion. 8. Output: Return \rho. If a color is required, replicate \rho to RGB or modulate by wetness. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def SampleCloudDensity(Pworld, time, wind, Tweather, Tshape, Tdetail, Tlut): # 1. Project to 2D and sample weather map # Assuming Pworld.xz are the horizontal coordinates uvweather = Pworld.xz WORLDSCALE ccov, ctype, cero, cwet = Tweather.sample(uvweather) # 2. Determine cloud type index for LUT lookup # Map ctype to a representative value or use directly if LUT is 2D cloudtypeval = ctype # 3. Height Gradient # Enforce flat base and rounded top hgrad = remapvertical(Pworld.y, CLOUDBASEY, CLOUDTOPY) # 4. Base Shape Noise (Perlin-Worley) # Tiling across kilometers Pshape = Pworld SHAPESCALE + wind time nshape = Tshape.sampleperlinworley(Pshape) # 5. Detail Noise (Perlin) # Scaled up by frequency for erosion Pdetail = Pworld DETAILSCALE + wind time ndetail = Tdetail.sampleperlin(Pdetail) # 6. LUT Lookup for Density and Erosion multipliers # LUT G channel affects both detail and shape noise lutr, lutg, lutb = Tlut.sample(cloudtypeval, Pworld.y) # 7. Calculate Erosion # Combine weather erosion, LUT erosion, and detail noise erosionfactor = lerp(1.0, ndetail, cero lutg) # 8. Special handling for Cumulonimbus (complex shapes) # High altitude: low coverage, high erosion # Low altitude: high coverage, low erosion if cloudtypeval > 0.5: heightfactor = smoothstep(CLOUDBASEY, CLOUDTOPY, Pworld.y) ccov = lerp(ccov 2.0, ccov 0.5, heightfactor) erosionfactor = lerp(erosionfactor 0.5, erosionfactor 2.0, heightfactor) # 9. Final Density density = ccov hgrad nshape (1.0 - erosionfactor) return density Parameters: WORLDSCALE: Scaling factor for weather map UVs. Not given in the sources. SHAPESCALE: Scaling factor for base noise tiling. Not given in the sources. DETAILSCALE: Scaling factor for detail noise, typically higher than SHAPESCALE. Not given in the sources. CLOUDBASEY, CLOUDTOPY: Vertical bounds of the cloud layer. Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Noise Tiling: Noise textures must be tileable to avoid seams at kilometer scales. LUT Channel Usage: The Cloud LUT G channel (Erosion) affects both detail noise and shape noise calculations, which can lead to unexpected density artifacts if not carefully tuned. Precision: High-frequency erosion on large scales can cause aliasing if not mipmapped or filtered correctly. IsimCloudTexture density evaluation computes the volumetric density of a cloud at a given point in space by combining geometric primitives (text segments or implicit cloud bodies), fractal Brownian motion (FBM) noise, and depth-based fading. It differs from general procedural gas modeling by focusing on specific cloud structures (text-based or layered bodies) and from simple cloud density sampling by generating the density field procedurally via CUDA kernels rather than sampling pre-baked data. The method outputs a grayscale density value (replicated to RGB) suitable for volume rendering. Procedural Gas Modeling via Turbulence is a method for generating volumetric gas density by evaluating a turbulence function and mapping the result through a precomputed power table. It solves the problem of efficiently computing realistic gas density fields for volume rendering by replacing expensive per-sample power function calls with a lookup table. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on 3D textures or distance fields, this approach computes density analytically at any point in space using mathematical shaping functions. Cloud Density Sampling generates the base volumetric density of clouds by combining low-frequency 3D noise textures using a weighted sum (Fractal Brownian Motion, FBM) and remapping the result to control cloud shape and coverage. It differs from its siblings by explicitly separating the generation of the base cloud structure (via low-frequency textures and height gradients) from high-frequency detail (via curl noise displacement and high-frequency textures) and by using a specific channel-weighted FBM from a single RGBA texture sample rather than procedural noise functions. It builds on Procedural Volume Cloud Modeling by providing the specific evaluation routine for the density field. Uses N = 2, M = 32, and 5 octaves of Perlin noise to simulate enhanced cumulus cloud, with a virtual resolution of 2048^3. Used to encode cloud details in [BNM 08] for multiple scattering in clouds. A physical model where a constant heat source is applied at the base, representing sunlight heating the earth. Evaporation occurs until air is saturated or all liquid water is evaporated. The saturation mixing ratio is defined by qs = A \exp(-\alpha z). The liquid water mixing ratio is ql = \max(q - qs, 0). Parameters include latent heat of vaporization Lv, specific heat of air cp, and friction timescale ts. Boundary conditions are q0 = 0.02 at the bottom level and q0 = 0.002 at the top level. Coriolis effects are ignored for computational efficiency. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, as it involves a fixed number of texture lookups and noise evaluations. The cost depends on the number of octaves in the noise function. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, plus the storage for the 2D Weather Map, 3D Noise Textures, and Cloud LUT. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Infinite resolution, no storage limits for cloud extent, dynamic control over cloud types and weather patterns. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of noise parameters to avoid repetitive patterns. Performance can degrade if high-frequency noise requires many octaves. When to use: Real-time rendering of large-scale atmospheric clouds where memory bandwidth is a constraint for storing 3D textures. When not to use: When highly specific, non-repeating cloud formations are required that cannot be achieved through noise variation. Procedural volume cloud modeling has evolved from simple height-based gradients to complex noise-driven systems. Early methods relied on 3D textures storing density or distance fields. Modern approaches, such as those in Unity HDRP, utilize Perlin-Worley noise for shape and Perlin noise for detail, combined with 2D weather maps for artistic control. The technique is widely used in PC and console games for real-time sky rendering. name: IsimCloudTexture density evaluation
head: Cloud texture generation, IsimCloudTexture, Procedural Cloud Density Generation
body: IsimCloudTexture density evaluation computes the volumetric density of a cloud at a given point in space by combining geometric primitives (text segments or implicit cloud bodies), fractal Brownian motion (FBM) noise, and depth-based fading. It differs from general procedural gas modeling by focusing on specific cloud structures (text-based or layered bodies) and from simple cloud density sampling by generating the density field procedurally via CUDA kernels rather than sampling pre-baked data. The method outputs a grayscale density value (replicated to RGB) suitable for volume rendering. The method exists in two primary variants: a text-segment-based approach (Variant A) and a CUDA-generated implicit body approach (Variant B). Both variants evaluate density at a point p or grid index (x,y,z). Inputs: Point p = (p.x, p.y, p.z) in world or local space. Grid indices (x, y, z) and dimensions (width, height, depth) for Variant B. Volume bounds box{min}, box{max}. Text segments defining letter shapes (Variant A). Noise generator instance with FBM capability. Parameters: cloud\scale, letter\radius, smooth\width, segments (Variant A); thread block size, grid size (Variant B). Outputs: Density value d \in [0, 1]. RGB vector (d, d, d). Written to a 3D CUDA surface object (Variant B). Point3/Vector3: 3D vector with components x, y, z. Segment: Defined by endpoints, used for distance calculation. CUDA Surface: 3D texture surface object written to via surf3Dwrite. 1. Boundary Check: If p is outside box{min} and box{max}, return (0, 0, 0). 2. Text Density Calculation: Initialize text\density = 0.0. For each segment in segments: Compute squared distance d{sq} from p to the segment. If d{sq} < (letter\radius + smooth\width)^2: Compute d = \sqrt{d{sq}}. Update text\density = \max(text\density, \text{smoothstep}(letter\radius + smooth\width, letter\radius, d)). If text\density < 0.001, return (0, 0, 0). 3. Noise Evaluation: Compute n = \text{noise\}.fbm(p \times cloud\scale, 5). Compute cloud\noise = \text{clamp}((n - 0.3) \times 3.0, 0.0, 1.0). 4. Combine: final\density = text\density \times cloud\noise. 5. Depth Fading: Compute center\z = (box{min}.z + box{max}.z) \times 0.5. Compute depth\fade = \text{smoothstep}(1.5, 0.5, |p.z - center\z|). final\density = final\density \times depth\fade. 6. Return: (final\density, final\density, final\density). 1. Coordinate Normalization: Calculate normalized device coordinates px, py, pz \in [-1, 1] from thread indices (x, y, z) and dimensions (width, height, depth): px = 2.0 \times \frac{x}{width - 1} - 1.0 py = 2.0 \times \frac{y}{height - 1} - 1.0 pz = 2.0 \times \frac{z}{depth - 1} - 1.0 2. Upper Cloud Body: Calculate warped coordinates: upperX = px - 0.18 \times \sin(4.0 \times py) upperZ = pz - 0.12 \times \cos(5.0 \times py) Compute upper cloud density: upperCloud = \exp(-8.0 \times (upperX^2 + upperZ^2) - 3.5 \times (py - 0.35)^2) 3. Lower Cloud Body: Compute lower cloud density: lowerCloud = \exp(-4.5 \times (px^2 + pz^2) - 2.2 \times (py + 0.25)^2) 4. Detail Noise: Compute detail factor: detail = 0.68 + 0.20 \times \sin(11.0 \times px + 7.0 \times py) \times \sin(9.0 \times pz - 5.0 \times py) + 0.12 \times \sin(23.0 \times (px + pz)) 5. Boundary Fade: Compute boundary fade factor: boundaryFade = \text{saturate}((1.0 - \max(|px|, |py|, |pz|)) \times 8.0) where \text{saturate}(v) = \min(\max(v, 0.0), 1.0). 6. Final Density: Combine components: density = \text{saturate}((0.85 \times lowerCloud + 0.75 \times upperCloud - 0.18) \times detail \times boundaryFade) 7. Write Output: Write density to the 3D surface at (x, y, z) using surf3Dwrite with pitch x \times \text{sizeof(float)}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): """Standard smoothstep function.""" t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def clamp(v, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(v, maxval)) def saturate(v): return max(0.0, min(v, 1.0)) def distancepointtosegment(p, segstart, segend): """Euclidean distance from point p to line segment.""" segvec = segend - segstart pvec = p - segstart seglensq = segvec.dot(segvec) if seglensq == 0: return pvec.norm() t = clamp(pvec.dot(segvec) / seglensq, 0.0, 1.0) projection = segstart + segvec t return (p - projection).norm() def fbmnoise(p, scale, octaves): """ Placeholder for FBM noise evaluation. In source, this is noise.fbm(p cloudscale, 5). Implementation details of the noise generator are not provided in the sources. """ # Generic FBM implementation assumed for completeness value = 0.0 amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 1.0 for i in range(octaves): value += amplitude noisefunction(p frequency scale) amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 2.0 return value def noisefunction(p): """Placeholder for base noise function (e.g., Perlin, Simplex).""" # Not specified in sources return 0.0 def evaluateisimcloudvarianta(p, boxmin, boxmax, segments, letterradius, smoothwidth, cloudscale): """ Variant A: Text Segment Based Density Evaluation. """ # 1. Boundary Check if not (boxmin.x <= p.x <= boxmax.x and boxmin.y <= p.y <= boxmax.y and boxmin.z <= p.z <= boxmax.z): return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 2. Text Density textdensity = 0.0 for seg in segments: d = distancepointtosegment(p, seg.start, seg.end) if d < (letterradius + smoothwidth): densityval = smoothstep(letterradius + smoothwidth, letterradius, d) if densityval > textdensity: textdensity = densityval if textdensity < 0.001: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 3. Noise n = fbmnoise(p, cloudscale, 5) cloudnoise = clamp((n - 0.3) 3.0, 0.0, 1.0) # 4. Combine finaldensity = textdensity cloudnoise # 5. Depth Fade centerz = (boxmin.z + boxmax.z) 0.5 depthfade = smoothstep(1.5, 0.5, abs(p.z - centerz)) finaldensity = depthfade # 6. Return return (finaldensity, finaldensity, finaldensity) def evaluateisimcloudvariantb(x, y, z, width, height, depth): """ Variant B: CUDA Implicit Body Density Evaluation. """ # 1. Normalized Coordinates px = 2.0 x / (width - 1) - 1.0 py = 2.0 y / (height - 1) - 1.0 pz = 2.0 z / (depth - 1) - 1.0 # 2. Upper Cloud upperX = px - 0.18 sin(4.0 py) upperZ = pz - 0.12 cos(5.0 py) upperCloud = exp(-8.0 (upperX2 + upperZ2) - 3.5 (py - 0.35)2) # 3. Lower Cloud lowerCloud = exp(-4.5 (px2 + pz2) - 2.2 (py + 0.25)2) # 4. Detail Noise detail = 0.68 + 0.20 sin(11.0 px + 7.0 py) sin(9.0 pz - 5.0 py) + 0.12 sin(23.0 (px + pz)) # 5. Boundary Fade maxabs = max(abs(px), abs(py), abs(pz)) boundaryFade = saturate((1.0 - maxabs) 8.0) # 6. Final Density density = saturate((0.85 lowerCloud + 0.75 upperCloud - 0.18) detail boundaryFade) return density cloudscale: Scales input position for noise evaluation. letterradius: Radius for text segment influence, typically 0.25. smoothwidth: Smoothness width for text segments, typically 0.2. segments: Vector of line segments defining letter shapes. boxmin, boxmax: Volume bounds. Thread block size: 8x8x8 threads (dim3 threads{8, 8, 8}). Grid size: \lceil width/8 \rceil \times \lceil height/8 \rceil \times \lceil depth/8 \rceil blocks. Division by Zero: In smoothstep, if edge0 == edge1, division by zero occurs. The sources assume valid ranges where edge0 < edge1. Null Vector: Normalization operations throw if the vector norm is zero. Boundary Conditions: Points outside the bounding box return zero density immediately. Precision: CUDA implementation uses float (32-bit) while C++ implementation uses double (64-bit) for intermediate calculations. Time Complexity: O(N \times S) for Variant A, where N is the number of points and S is the number of segments. O(1) per voxel for Variant B. Memory Complexity: O(S) for Variant A (storing segments). O(1) auxiliary memory for Variant B, plus output texture storage. Performance: Variant B is optimized for GPU execution via CUDA, utilizing 3D surface writes. Variant A is a general-purpose CPU implementation. Strengths: Procedural generation allows infinite resolution and easy parameter tweaking. Limitations: Variant A requires explicit segment definitions. Variant B is hardcoded to specific implicit shapes. The method originates from two unofficial GitHub repositories: "Volumetric-Path-Tracing" by TakTikFR and "HZL-fluidEffectsStudio" by pvasbob. It is used in procedural volume cloud modeling to generate density fields for visualization. name: Procedural Gas Modeling via Turbulence
head: basic_gas procedural gas modeling, turbulence-based gas density function
body: Procedural Gas Modeling via Turbulence is a method for generating volumetric gas density by evaluating a turbulence function and mapping the result through a precomputed power table. It solves the problem of efficiently computing realistic gas density fields for volume rendering by replacing expensive per-sample power function calls with a lookup table. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on 3D textures or distance fields, this approach computes density analytically at any point in space using mathematical shaping functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: pnt (point in solid/world space), parms (parameter array), POWTABLESIZE (table size constant). Output: density (float, gas density value). Data Structures: powtable: A static array of floats of size POWTABLESIZE. parms: An array of floats. parms[1] is the maximum density value (range 0.0 to 1.0). parms[2] is the exponent for the power function. Steps: 1. Precompute Lookup Table: Calculate powtable once per image. For i from POWTABLESIZE-1 down to 0: \text{pow\table}[i] = \left( \frac{i}{\text{POW\TABLE\SIZE}-1} \times \text{parms}[1] \times 2.0 \right)^{\text{parms}[2]} 2. Evaluate Turbulence: Compute turb = fastturbulence(pnt). 3. Index Calculation: Compute the integer index: \text{idx} = \left\lfloor \text{turb} \times 0.5 \times (\text{POW\TABLE\SIZE}-1) \right\rfloor 4. Output Density: Set density = powtable[idx]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def basicgas(pnt, parms, powtable, powtablesize): # Precompute table if not done (logic from source) # In a real implementation, this would be handled by a static flag or initialization step # calcd = 1; if calcd:... calcd = 0;... # Evaluate turbulence turb = fastturbulence(pnt) # Compute density index # Note: Source uses (int) cast which truncates towards zero. # Assuming turb is in [0, 1] or similar range where this maps correctly. idx = int(turb 0.5 (powtablesize - 1)) # Output density density = powtable[idx] return density Parameters: parms[1]: Maximum density value. Range: 0.0 to 1.0. parms[2]: Exponent for the power function. Typical value for steam: 6.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The turbulence function must return values that map correctly to the table indices. The source implies turb is scaled such that turb 0.5 (POWTABLESIZE-1) yields a valid index. Precision issues may arise if turb is outside the expected range, leading to out-of-bounds access or incorrect density. A procedural shaping technique that applies a sine function to turbulence output to create vein-like structures in the gas density. Unlike the power function which increases contrast and separates plumes, the sine function creates continuous vein-like patterns similar to marble texturing. Code: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. turb = (1.0 + sin(fastturbulence(pnt) MPI 5)) 0.5 Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Uses a precomputed table of size 10,000 (for POWTABLESIZE=10000). Time: Replaces per-sample pow() calls with a table lookup. For a 640x480 image with 100 volume samples per pixel, this saves approximately 30,710,000 pow() function calls. Strengths and Limitations: Strength: High performance due to table lookup optimization. Limitation: Limited to simple shaping functions (power, sine) unless extended. When to Use: When rendering gases with simple, turbulent structures and performance is critical. Originated in David Ebert's work on procedural modeling of gases, fluids, and textures. The method uses a visual simulation of turbulent flow similar to Ken Perlin’s approach. It is part of a broader framework for procedural volume cloud modeling. Procedural Modeling, Animation, and Rendering of Gases, Fluids, and Textures, https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David-Ebert-4/publication/2786953ProceduralModelingAnimationandRenderingofGasesFluidsandTextures/links/00b7d51a73e42a3c4e000000/Procedural-Modeling-Animation-and-Rendering-of-Gases-Fluids-and-Textures.pdf, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Cloud Density Sampling
head: Base Cloud Density Generation, Low-Frequency Cloud Density, SampleCloudDensity, Schneider's Cloud Noise
body: Cloud Density Sampling generates the base volumetric density of clouds by combining low-frequency 3D noise textures using a weighted sum (Fractal Brownian Motion, FBM) and remapping the result to control cloud shape and coverage. It differs from its siblings by explicitly separating the generation of the base cloud structure (via low-frequency textures and height gradients) from high-frequency detail (via curl noise displacement and high-frequency textures) and by using a specific channel-weighted FBM from a single RGBA texture sample rather than procedural noise functions. It builds on Procedural Volume Cloud Modeling by providing the specific evaluation routine for the density field. Inputs: samplepoint: vec3, world or texture space coordinate for density evaluation. weatherdata: vec4, containing cloud coverage in the red channel (weatherdata.r). relativeHeight: float, normalized height of the sample point within the atmosphere. iscCheap: bool, if true, skips high-frequency sampling. winddirection: vec3, default (1.0, 0.0, 0.0). cloudspeed: float, default 10.0. cloudtopoffset: float, default 5.0. Time: float, global time variable. lowFrequencyTexture: sampler3D, precomputed noise texture. highFrequencyTexture: sampler3D, precomputed high-frequency noise texture. curlNoiseTexture: sampler2D, precomputed curl noise texture. Outputs: finalcloud: float, the computed cloud density value in the range [0.0, 1.0] (clamped). Data Structures: lowFrequencyTexture: A 3D texture where: Channel R stores base noise values. Channel G stores the component weighted by 0.625. Channel B stores the component weighted by 0.250. Channel A stores the component weighted by 0.125. highFrequencyTexture: A 3D texture sampled at a scaled coordinate. curlNoiseTexture: A 2D texture sampled at the XY coordinates of the sample point. Formulas: The remapping function is defined as: \text{Remap}(v, v{min}, v{max}, u{min}, u{max}) = u{min} + \frac{v - v{min}}{v{max} - v{min}}(u{max} - u{min}) The low-frequency FBM is computed from the RGBA sample N of the low-frequency texture: F{low} = 0.625 Ng + 0.250 Nb + 0.125 Na The base cloud density before height/coverage masking is: D{base} = \text{Remap}(Nr, -(1.0 - F{low}), 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) The high-frequency FBM is computed from the RGBA sample H of the high-frequency texture: F{high} = 0.625 Hr + 0.250 Hg + 0.125 Hb The high-frequency noise modifier is: M{high} = \text{mix}(F{high}, 1.0 - F{high}, \text{clamp}(relativeHeight \times 10.0, 0.0, 1.0)) Steps: 1. Apply Wind Skew: Adjust the sample point based on relative height and wind direction. \mathbf{p}{skewed} = \mathbf{p} + relativeHeight \times \mathbf{wind\direction} \times cloud\top\offset \times 0.005 2. Apply Time-Based Movement: Displace the sample point by wind and vertical movement over time. \mathbf{p}{time} = \mathbf{p}{skewed} + (\mathbf{wind\direction} + (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) \times Time \times cloud\speed \times 0.001 3. Sample Low-Frequency Texture: N = \text{SampleLowFrequencyTexture}(\mathbf{p}{time}) 4. Compute Low-Frequency FBM: F{low} = Ng \times 0.625 + Nb \times 0.250 + Na \times 0.125 5. Compute Base Cloud: D{base} = \text{Remap}(Nr, -(1.0 - F{low}), 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) 6. Apply Height Gradient: D{height} = D{base} \times \text{GetDensityHeightGradientForPoint}(\mathbf{p}{time}, weather\data, relativeHeight) 7. Apply Coverage Mask: D{coverage} = \text{Remap}(D{height}, weather\data.r, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) 8. Clamp and Enhance: D{enhanced} = \text{clamp}(D{coverage}, 0.0, 1.0) \times (weather\data.r \times 4.0) 9. High-Frequency Details (if !iscCheap and D{enhanced} > 0.0): a. Sample Curl Noise: C = \text{SampleCurlNoiseTexture}(\mathbf{p}{time}.xy) b. Displace UVs: \mathbf{p}{disp} = \mathbf{p}{time} + C.xy \times (1.0 - relativeHeight) c. Sample High-Frequency Texture: H = \text{SampleHighFrequencyTexture}(\mathbf{p}{disp} \times 0.1) d. Compute High-Frequency FBM and Modifier: F{high} = Hr \times 0.625 + Hg \times 0.250 + Hb \times 0.125 M{high} = \text{mix}(F{high}, 1.0 - F{high}, \text{clamp}(relativeHeight \times 10.0, 0.0, 1.0)) e. Erode by Remapping: D{final} = \text{Remap}(\text{clamp}(D{enhanced}, 0.2 \times M{high}, 1.0), 0.2 \times M{high}, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) 10. Return: D{final} if !iscCheap, else D{enhanced}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def SampleCloudDensity(samplepoint, weatherdata, relativeHeight, ischeap, winddirection, cloudspeed, cloudtopoffset, Time, lowFrequencyTexture, highFrequencyTexture, curlNoiseTexture): # Step 1: Apply Wind Skew p = samplepoint + relativeHeight winddirection cloudtopoffset 0.005 # Step 2: Apply Time-Based Movement p = p + (winddirection + vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) Time cloudspeed 0.001 # Step 3: Sample Low-Frequency Texture N = lowFrequencyTexture.sample(p) # Returns vec4 (r, g, b, a) # Step 4: Compute Low-Frequency FBM lowfreqFBM = N.g 0.625 + N.b 0.250 + N.a 0.125 # Step 5: Compute Base Cloud # Remap(N.r, -(1.0 - lowfreqFBM), 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) vmin = -(1.0 - lowfreqFBM) vmax = 1.0 umin = 0.0 umax = 1.0 basecloud = umin + (N.r - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) (umax - umin) # Step 6: Apply Height Gradient # GetDensityHeightGradientForPoint is assumed to return a float multiplier densityheightgradient = GetDensityHeightGradientForPoint(p, weatherdata, relativeHeight) basecloud = densityheightgradient # Step 7: Apply Coverage Mask cloudcoverage = weatherdata.r # Remap(basecloud, cloudcoverage, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) vmin = cloudcoverage vmax = 1.0 basecloudwithcoverage = umin + (basecloud - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) (umax - umin) # Step 8: Clamp and Enhance basecloudwithcoverage = clamp(basecloudwithcoverage, 0.0, 1.0) basecloudwithcoverage = cloudcoverage 4.0 # Step 9: High-Frequency Details if not ischeap and basecloudwithcoverage > 0.0: # Sample Curl Noise curlnoise = curlNoiseTexture.sample(vec2(p.x, p.z)) # Assuming XY mapping as per source # Displace UVs pdisp = p pdisp.x += curlnoise.x (1.0 - relativeHeight) pdisp.z += curlnoise.y (1.0 - relativeHeight) # Sample High-Frequency Texture H = highFrequencyTexture.sample(pdisp 0.1) # Compute High-Frequency FBM highfreqFBM = H.r 0.625 + H.g 0.250 + H.b 0.125 # Compute High-Frequency Noise Modifier mixfactor = clamp(relativeHeight 10.0, 0.0, 1.0) highfreqnoisemodifier = mix(highfreqFBM, 1.0 - highfreqFBM, mixfactor) # Erode by Remapping # Clamp basecloudwithcoverage against modifier clampedval = clamp(basecloudwithcoverage, 0.2 highfreqnoisemodifier, 1.0) # Remap vmin = 0.2 highfreqnoisemodifier vmax = 1.0 finalcloud = umin + (clampedval - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) (umax - umin) return finalcloud else: return basecloudwithcoverage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If relativeHeight is outside [0.0, 1.0], the clamp operations in the modifier and coverage mask may produce unexpected results if not handled by the caller. The Remap function divides by (v{max} - v{min}). If v{max} = v{min}, division by zero occurs. In Step 5, v{max}=1.0 and v{min}=-(1.0-F{low}). Since F{low} \in [0,1], v{min} \in [-1, 0], so v{max} \neq v{min}. In Step 7, v{min}=cloud\coverage. If cloudcoverage is 1.0, division by zero occurs. Guard against this by returning 0.0 or the input value if v{max} \approx v{min}. The curl noise displacement uses samplepoint.xy. If the sample point is in world space, this assumes the curl noise texture is aligned with the XZ plane (or XY depending on coordinate system convention). The source uses samplepoint.xy. Generates billowy cloud shapes by synthesizing cloud density \rho(\mathbf{x}) procedurally using inverted Worley fractal Brownian motion (FBM), vertical gradient attenuation, and coverage thresholding. It differs from standard Perlin-based cloud noise by using the distance-to-nearest-cell metric of Worley noise, inverted to create bright, puffy "billowy" structures characteristic of cumulus clouds, rather than the smooth, turbulent gradients of Perlin noise. Choose this when simulating cumulus clouds with distinct, puffy tops. See Procedural 3D Worley-Perlin Fractal Noise Density. Samples cloud density along a cone by iterating through a pre-generated noise kernel, transforming positions to weather map coordinates, and summing densities. It differs from standard ray-marching by evaluating density along a cone spread to approximate volumetric scattering or shadowing effects more efficiently than a single ray. Choose this when approximating volumetric light transport or shadowing in cloud rendering. See Cone Tracing Cloud Sampling. Uses a combination of Perlin octaves, a vertical profile texture, and a cube map for global cloud cover to compute density. It differs from the base method by using a cube map for global coverage and a separate vertical profile function, rather than a single RGBA texture with weighted FBM. Choose this when global coverage maps and distinct vertical profiles are required. See Full Cloud Density Function. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample for the base method, assuming texture lookups are O(1). The high-frequency branch adds constant overhead. Cone tracing is O(k) where k is the number of cone samples (e.g., 5). Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the precomputed textures (low-frequency, high-frequency, curl noise, weather data). Not given in the sources for specific resolutions, but mentions 64x64x64 for noise and 512x512 for cover maps. Measured Performance: reports 28.5 FPS on an AMD Ryzen 7 4700U at 640x480 resolution, using 3 deep opacity maps, one 512x512 offset layer, a 7x512x512 transmittance array, 5 octaves of 64x64x64 Worley noise for high-frequency detail, and 3 octaves of 64x64x64 Perlin-Worley noise for horizontal shapes. Strengths: Efficient evaluation using precomputed textures; flexible control over cloud shape via FBM weights and height gradients; supports time-based animation. Limitations: Requires precomputed textures; high-frequency details are skipped if iscCheap is true; coverage masking is simple and may not handle complex weather patterns without additional data. When to Use: Real-time cloud rendering where performance is critical and precomputed textures are available. When Not to Use: When procedural noise without textures is required, or when high-fidelity volumetric scattering is needed without approximation. The method originates from the "realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes" project by erickTornero. It is also associated with Jan Wedekind's work on procedural volumetric clouds. The technique is used in real-time cloud rendering to generate dense, volumetric cloud fields efficiently. erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, https://github.com/erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Procedural Volumetric Clouds · Jan Wedekind, https://www.wedesoft.de/software/2023/05/03/volumetric-clouds/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Procedural 3D Worley-Perlin Fractal Noise Density
head: Billowy fractal cumulus noise, Inverted Worley FBM Cloud Density, Multi-Octave Inverted Worley FBM
body: Generates billowy cloud shapes by synthesizing cloud density \rho(\mathbf{x}) procedurally using inverted Worley fractal Brownian motion (FBM), vertical gradient attenuation, and coverage thresholding. It differs from standard Perlin-based cloud noise by using the distance-to-nearest-cell metric of Worley noise, inverted to create bright, puffy "billowy" structures characteristic of cumulus clouds, rather than the smooth, turbulent gradients of Perlin noise. Inputs: World position \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z). Cloud volume bounds: cloudBottom and cloudTop (Y-coordinates). Cloud coverage parameter coverage (float, typically 0.52). Extinction coefficient \sigmat (float, typically 0.035–0.04). FBM parameters: octaves (default 3), scale (default 0.0008). Outputs: Cloud density \rho(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required; the method is stateless and procedural. Steps: 1. Height Culling: Check if the world Y-coordinate y is within [cloudBottom, cloudTop]. If y < \text{cloudBottom} or y > \text{cloudTop}, return density 0.0. 2. Coordinate Scaling: Scale the input coordinates by scale to define the base frequency of the noise field. 3. Inverted Worley FBM Calculation: Compute the base noise value using multi-octave inverted Worley noise (see worleyFBM pseudocode below). 4. Height Gradient: Compute the normalized height h relative to the cloud layer bounds, then apply a sinusoidal gradient to attenuate density at the top and bottom edges. 5. Coverage Thresholding: Subtract the inverse coverage term from the gradient-scaled noise to define the cloud base. 6. Normalization and Clamping: Normalize the result by the coverage parameter and clamp to 0, \infty). 7. Extinction Scaling: Multiply the final density by \sigmat to obtain the volumetric extinction coefficient. Formulas: The normalized height h is defined as: h = \frac{y - \text{cloudBottom}}{\text{cloudTop} - \text{cloudBottom}} The final density \rho(\mathbf{x}) is: \rho(\mathbf{x}) = \max\left(0, \frac{\text{FBM}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sin(\pi h) - (1 - \text{coverage})}{\text{coverage}}\right) \cdot \sigmat Where \text{FBM}(\mathbf{x}) is the multi-octave inverted Worley noise value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def worley3D(x: float, y: float, z: float) -> float: """ Computes the distance to the nearest cell center in Worley noise. Uses a 3x3 grid of integer lattice points around the input coordinate. """ # Determine the integer grid cell containing the point ix = math.floor(x) iy = math.floor(y) iz = math.floor(z) mindistsq = float('inf') # Iterate over the 3x3x3 neighborhood of cells for dx in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): for dz in range(-1, 2): # Generate a pseudo-random vector for the cell center # Using a simple hash function for determinism cellx = ix + dx celly = iy + dy cellz = iz + dz # Hash function to get a random vector in [0, 1)^3 # This is a placeholder for a specific hash implementation; # standard Worley implementations use a pre-computed lattice or hash. # For implementation from text, we assume a deterministic hash H. rx = hash3d(cellx, celly, cellz) ry = hash3d(celly, cellz, cellx) rz = hash3d(cellz, cellx, celly) # Distance from point to cell center distsq = (x - rx)2 + (y - ry)2 + (z - rz)2 if distsq < mindistsq: mindistsq = distsq return math.sqrt(mindistsq) def hash3d(x: int, y: int, z: int) -> float: """ Simple deterministic hash to generate a float in [0, 1). """ # Using a standard integer hash and mapping to float h = x 374761393 + y 668265263 + z 1274126177 h = (h ^ (h >> 13)) 1274126177 h = h ^ (h >> 16) return abs(h % 10000) / 10000.0 def worleyFBM(x: float, y: float, z: float, octaves: int = 3) -> float: """ Computes multi-octave inverted Worley FBM. """ sumval = 0.0 freq = 1.0 amp = 1.0 totalamp = 0.0 for i in range(octaves): # Compute inverted Worley value: 1.0 - distance w = 1.0 - worley3D(x freq, y freq, z freq) # Add to sum weighted by amplitude sumval += w amp # Accumulate total amplitude for normalization totalamp += amp # Update frequency and amplitude for next octave freq = 2.0 amp = 0.5 # Return normalized sum if totalamp == 0: return 0.0 return sumval / totalamp def computeclouddensity(x: float, y: float, z: float, cloudbottom: float, cloudtop: float, coverage: float, sigmat: float, scale: float = 0.0008, octaves: int = 3) -> float: """ Computes the final cloud density using Procedural 3D Worley-Perlin Fractal Noise. """ # Step 1: Height Culling if y < cloudbottom or y > cloudtop: return 0.0 # Step 2: Coordinate Scaling sx = x scale sy = y scale sz = z scale # Step 3: Base Noise basenoise = worleyFBM(sx, sy, sz, octaves) # Step 4: Height Gradient hnorm = (y - cloudbottom) / (cloudtop - cloudbottom) heightgrad = math.sin(math.pi hnorm) # Step 5: Raw Density rawdensity = (basenoise heightgrad) - (1.0 - coverage) # Step 6: Normalization and Clamping # Avoid division by zero epsilon = 1e-4 normalizeddensity = max(0.0, rawdensity / (coverage + epsilon)) # Step 7: Extinction Scaling return normalizeddensity sigmat Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The normalization step divides by coverage. If coverage is 0, the result is undefined. A small epsilon (10^{-4}) is added to the denominator. Height Normalization: If cloudBottom equals cloudTop, the height normalization h is undefined. This should be prevented by input validation. Precision: Worley noise involves square roots and distance calculations. Using single-precision floats may introduce minor artifacts in the noise field, but is generally acceptable for real-time rendering. Boundary Conditions: The height gradient \sin(\pi h) naturally goes to 0 at h=0 and h=1, ensuring smooth falloff at cloud boundaries. A cell-based noise function that uses the distance to the nearest seed point. It produces cellular, puffy structures ideal for clouds. A technique of summing multiple octaves of noise at different frequencies and amplitudes to create detailed, self-similar structures. Subtracting the Worley distance from 1.0 transforms the dark "cells" into bright "puffs," matching the visual appearance of cumulus clouds. Time Complexity: O(O \cdot N^3) per sample, where O is the number of octaves and N is the neighborhood size (typically 3^3=27 for Worley). Memory Complexity: O(1), as the method is procedural and requires no texture lookups or data structures. Performance: The method is computationally expensive per sample due to the hash function and distance calculations in Worley noise. However, it is efficient in terms of memory bandwidth compared to texture-based methods. Strengths: Produces realistic, billowy cloud shapes; fully procedural and resolution-independent; no texture memory required. Limitations: Computationally intensive; lacks the fine-scale turbulence of Perlin noise; requires careful tuning of coverage and height parameters. When to Use: Real-time [volumetric cloud rendering where procedural generation is preferred over texture-based approaches. The method is derived from the "volumetric-clouds-wgsl" repository by nff747, which implements a real-time volumetric cloud renderer using WebGPU. The use of inverted Worley noise for cloud density is a known technique in computer graphics, popularized by its ability to generate "billowy" structures. The specific combination of Worley FBM, height gradient, and coverage thresholding is presented in this repository as a practical implementation for real-time rendering. nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, https://github.com/nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF to Density Conversion
head: Glass Ball IOR Distribution, SDF to Density/Feature Volume, SDFVolume, signed distance to density conversion
body: SDF to Density Conversion maps a Signed Distance Function (SDF) value into a volumetric density field suitable for differentiable volume rendering. It solves the problem of representing continuous 3D surfaces and thin structures without explicit mesh extraction by treating the zero-level set of the SDF as a volumetric boundary. Unlike standard volume rendering which takes density directly, this method derives density from the distance to the implicit surface, enabling the representation of open surfaces and varying thickness through an exponential falloff. It sets itself apart from VolSDF Volume Rendering by providing the specific conversion function rather than the full rendering pipeline, and from Volume SDF Rendering by its specific parameterization of the density transition. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Signed distance value d (or s = -d) at a sample point, ray segment length \Delta t (or \Delta), and parameters \alpha (alpha) and \beta (beta). Output: Volumetric density \sigma (or \rho) and optionally a feature/color value. Data Structures: Parameters: \alpha (alpha): Scalar multiplier for intermediate density, controlling overall opacity. Initialized from configuration or learned. \beta (beta): Scalar controlling the exponential falloff rate. Smaller values yield sharper surfaces. rainbow: Boolean flag. If true, computes base color from position; otherwise, base color is 1.0. featureparam: Learnable tensor for color features. Steps: 1. Compute Signed Distance: Evaluate the SDF at the sample point to get d. Define s = -d. 2. Compute Intermediate Density (\psi or \rho): Apply a piecewise exponential function to s. If s \le 0 (inside surface): \psi = 0.5 \cdot \exp(s / \beta) If s > 0 (outside surface): \psi = 1 - 0.5 \cdot \exp(-s / \beta) Scale by \alpha: \rho = \alpha \cdot \psi. 3. Compute Final Density (\sigma): Normalize by the ray segment length \Delta t (or \Delta) to ensure density is independent of sampling resolution. \sigma = -\ln(1 - \rho) / \Delta t Note: This formula assumes \rho < 1. If \rho approaches 1, numerical stability issues may arise. 4. Compute Feature/Color (Optional): If rainbow is true: basecolor = clamp(|sample\points - center|, 0.02, 0.98). Else: basecolor = 1.0. feature = basecolor featureparam \rho (or \rho-derived value). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def sdftodensity(signeddistance: torch.Tensor, alpha: float, beta: float) -> torch.Tensor: """ Converts signed distance to intermediate density. Args: signeddistance: Tensor of signed distance values d. alpha: Scaling factor for density. beta: Falloff rate parameter. Returns: Intermediate density rho. """ # s = -d, where d is signeddistance s = -signeddistance # Piecewise exponential function # If s <= 0: psi = 0.5 exp(s / beta) # If s > 0: psi = 1 - 0.5 exp(-s / beta) psi = torch.where( s <= 0.0, 0.5 torch.exp(s / beta), 1 - 0.5 torch.exp(-s / beta)) # Scale by alpha rho = alpha psi return rho def computefinaldensity(rho: torch.Tensor, deltat: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes final volumetric density from intermediate density and segment length. Args: rho: Intermediate density (must be < 1). deltat: Ray segment length. Returns: Final volumetric density sigma. """ # Avoid log(0) or log(negative) by clamping rho slightly below 1 rhoclamped = torch.clamp(rho, max=0.9999) # sigma = -ln(1 - rho) / deltat sigma = -torch.log(1.0 - rhoclamped) / deltat return sigma def sdftodensitypipeline(signeddistance: torch.Tensor, deltat: torch.Tensor, alpha: float, beta: float, rainbow: bool = False, center: torch.Tensor = None, featureparam: torch.Tensor = None, samplepoints: torch.Tensor = None) -> dict: """ Full pipeline for SDF to Density Conversion. Args: signeddistance: Tensor of signed distance values d. deltat: Ray segment length. alpha: Scaling factor. beta: Falloff rate. rainbow: Boolean flag for position-based coloring. center: Center point for rainbow mode. featureparam: Learnable feature tensor. samplepoints: Sample point coordinates for rainbow mode. Returns: Dictionary with 'density' and 'feature'. """ # Step 1 & 2: Compute intermediate density rho = sdftodensity(signeddistance, alpha, beta) # Step 3: Compute final density # Handle edge case: if deltat is 0 or very small, pad with large value to prevent division by zero # This is typically handled before calling this function, but as a guard: deltatsafe = torch.where(deltat > 1e-10, deltat, torch.tensor(1e10, device=deltat.device)) sigma = computefinaldensity(rho, deltatsafe) # Step 4: Compute feature/color if rainbow and samplepoints is not None and center is not None: basecolor = torch.clamp(torch.abs(samplepoints - center), min=0.02, max=0.98) else: basecolor = torch.oneslike(samplepoints) if samplepoints is not None else torch.tensor(1.0) if featureparam is not None: feature = basecolor featureparam rho else: feature = basecolor rho return { "density": sigma, "feature": feature } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The last segment's delta is often padded with a large value (e.g., 10^{10}) to prevent division by zero when the ray exits the sampling volume. Numerical Stability: The formula \sigma = -\ln(1 - \rho) / \Delta t requires \rho < 1. If \rho \ge 1, the log is undefined. Clamp \rho to a value slightly less than 1. Parameter Sensitivity: \beta controls the sharpness of the transition. Smaller \beta yields sharper surfaces but may require more sampling points to avoid aliasing. Volume SDF Rendering is a neural rendering technique that integrates color and density along rays sampled from an implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF). It solves the problem of rendering complex 3D geometry from multi-view images by converting the continuous SDF into a volumetric density field, allowing standard volume rendering to capture both surface appearance and thin structures. Unlike standard volume rendering which takes density directly, this method derives density from the distance to the implicit surface, enabling the representation of open surfaces and varying thickness through the Laplace distribution CDF. It differs from VolSDF Volume Rendering primarily in its specific parameterization of the density transition and its integration with analytic or neural SDF backends. VolSDF Volume Rendering is a volume rendering technique that synthesizes images from a neural implicit surface representation by converting Signed Distance Function (SDF) values into volumetric density. It solves the problem of rendering continuous 3D surfaces without explicit mesh extraction by treating the zero-level set of the SDF as a volumetric boundary. It sets itself apart from its parent SDF to Density Conversion by providing the complete rendering pipeline (sampling, transmittance, aggregation) rather than just the conversion function, and from its sibling Volume SDF Rendering by using a differentiable neural SDF with stratified sampling and alpha-compositing rather than discrete voxel rasterization. This method converts a signed distance field (SDF) value into a volumetric density for a box primitive, applying a sigmoid-based erosion at the boundaries and adding Perlin noise to roughen the surface. It differs from standard SDF-to-density conversions by explicitly expanding the box geometry to create a specific "eroded" falloff zone rather than simply smoothing the existing boundary, and it integrates procedural noise directly into the density calculation. Computes the output alpha for a Signed Distance Field (SDF) given the Screen Space Ratio (SSR), Signed Distance (SD), Signed Distance Ratio (SDR), isoPerimeter (dilation/contraction), and softness. It differs from SDF to Density Conversion by operating directly on distance metrics and screen-space scaling factors rather than converting to volumetric density, and from Volume SDF Rendering by being a specific shading/compositing step rather than a full rendering pipeline. Simulating mirages by creating a non-uniform distribution of the index of refraction in air, where IOR decreases with increasing temperature. It creates a normal lapse layer (index = 0.95 \cdot 2^z) and an inversion layer (index = 0.8^z), combining them with np.minimum, and sets IOR to 1.0 for z < 0. Defines an implicit volumetric object where density \rho is derived from an FBM field f. Density is zero when f(\mathbf{p}) < v, and remapped via function h when f(\mathbf{p}) \ge v. The 0-isosurface of \rho corresponds to the v-isosurface of f. Formula: \rho(\mathbf{p}) = h(f(\mathbf{p})) when f(\mathbf{p}) \ge v, else 0. Pitfall: If h is not positive, the 0-isosurface of \rho will not correspond to the v-isosurface of f. DensityRegion extends VolumeRegion by scaling absorption, scattering, extinction, and emission coefficients by a spatially varying density function density(pt). Formulas: \sigmaa(pt) = sig\a \cdot density(pt), \sigmas(pt) = sig\s \cdot density(pt), \sigmat(pt) = (\sigmaa + \sigmas) \cdot density(pt), L{ve}(pt) = le \cdot density(pt). Phase function uses Henyey-Greenstein with parameter g\scatter. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points along the ray. The SDF evaluation is the dominant cost if the SDF is complex (e.g., neural network). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of samples per ray and the number of rays. Higher \alpha or lower \beta may require more samples to accurately resolve the density transition. Strengths: Differentiable, allowing gradient-based optimization of SDF parameters. Efficiently represents thin structures and open surfaces. Limitations: Sensitive to sampling density. If \Delta t is too large, the density approximation may be inaccurate. Numerical stability issues if \rho \ge 1. When to Use: When rendering neural implicit surfaces or when a smooth, differentiable representation of a surface is needed. When Not to Use: When explicit meshes are available and preferred, or when real-time performance is critical and SDF evaluation is too expensive. The method originates from neural volume rendering techniques, specifically those that use SDFs as implicit surface representations. It was popularized by works such as VolSDF, which demonstrated the effectiveness of converting SDFs to density for differentiable rendering. The specific piecewise exponential function is a common choice for mapping signed distances to densities, ensuring smooth transitions and differentiability. name: Volume SDF Rendering
head: Neural Volume Rendering (SDF-based), SDF Volume Rendering, SDF → density volume rendering, SDF-based Volume Rendering, Signed Distance Field Volume Rendering, VolumeSDFRenderer
body: Volume SDF Rendering is a neural rendering technique that integrates color and density along rays sampled from an implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF). It solves the problem of rendering complex 3D geometry from multi-view images by converting the continuous SDF into a volumetric density field, allowing standard volume rendering to capture both surface appearance and thin structures. Unlike standard volume rendering which takes density directly, this method derives density from the distance to the implicit surface, enabling the representation of open surfaces and varying thickness through the Laplace distribution CDF. It differs from VolSDF Volume Rendering primarily in its specific parameterization of the density transition and its integration with analytic or neural SDF backends. The method renders an image by casting rays from camera positions, sampling points along these rays, evaluating an implicit SDF to get distance and color, converting the distance to density, and aggregating the color using volume rendering weights. Inputs: raybundle: Contains ray origins, directions, and sample points. implicitfn: An object or function that computes the signed distance and color (or feature) at any 3D point. It may be analytic (e.g., sphere, box) or a neural network. alpha (\alpha): Scaling factor for the density. beta (\beta): Sharpness/Scale parameter for the SDF-to-density transition. eps: Small constant for numerical stability in transmittance calculation. Outputs: color: A tensor of shape (H, W, 3) representing the rendered RGB image. depth: (Optional) Depth map associated with the rendering. RayBundle: origins: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray origins in world space. directions: Tensor of shape (N, 3), normalized ray directions. samplepoints: Tensor of shape (N, D, 3), points sampled along each of the N rays, where D is the number of samples per ray. Implicit Function Output: distance: Tensor of shape (N, D), signed distance values at sample points. color: Tensor of shape (N, D, 3), color or feature values at sample points. 1. Ray Generation and Sampling: For each pixel in the image, generate a ray from the camera center through the pixel. Use a sampler (e.g., StratifiedRaysampler) to generate D sample points along each ray within a defined near/far range. Store these as samplepoints in the raybundle. 2. Implicit Function Evaluation: Query the implicit function at all sample points to obtain the signed distance and color/feature values. \text{distance}, \text{color} = \text{implicit\fn}(\text{sample\points}) Where distance has shape (N, D) and color has shape (N, D, 3). 3. Segment Length Calculation: Compute the length of each ray segment (\Delta t) between consecutive sample points. For D points, there are D segments. The first D-1 segments are the differences between consecutive depth values. The last segment is set to a large constant (10^{10}) to ensure rays exiting the volume do not contribute significant density, preventing artifacts from the infinite tail. \Delta ti = \begin{cases} t{i+1} - ti & \text{for } i = 0 \dots D-2 \\ 10^{10} & \text{for } i = D-1 \end{cases} In code, this is implemented by concatenating the differences with a large constant: python deltas = torch.cat((depthvalues[..., 1:] - depthvalues[...,:-1], 1e10 torch.oneslike(depthvalues[...,:1])), dim=-1)[..., None]. 4. SDF to Density Conversion: Convert the signed distance d to volumetric density \rho using the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a Laplace distribution with mean 0 and scale \beta. The density is scaled by \alpha. \rho = \alpha \cdot \text{CDF}{\text{Laplace}(0, \beta)}(-d) The explicit piecewise formula is: \rho = \begin{cases} 0.5 \alpha e^{-d/\beta} & \text{if } d > 0 \\ \alpha (1 - 0.5 e^{d/\beta}) & \text{if } d \le 0 \end{cases}. Implementation: python density = torch.where( signeddistance > 0, 0.5 torch.exp(-signeddistance / beta), 1 - 0.5 torch.exp(signeddistance / beta),) alpha. 5. Transmittance and Weight Calculation: Compute the transmittance T and rendering weights w for each sample. Initialize T0 = 1. For each sample i from 0 to D-1: T{i+1} = Ti \cdot \exp(-\rhoi \cdot \Delta ti + \epsilon) wi = Ti \cdot (1 - \exp(-\rhoi \cdot \Delta ti + \epsilon)) Where \epsilon is a small constant (10^{-10}) added to the exponent to prevent numerical instability (e.g., \exp(0)=1 leading to division by zero in subsequent steps or gradient issues). Note: Some sources define the final density \sigma used in the exponent as \sigma = -\ln(1 - \rho) / \Delta t. However, the standard implementation in the cited code uses \rho directly in the exponent with \Delta t. The code snippet in uses: python T.append(Tim1 torch.exp(-raysdensity[:, i-1] deltas[:, i-1] + eps)) weights = torch.stack(T, dim=1) (1 - torch.exp(-raysdensity deltas + eps)). We follow the code implementation which uses \rho directly. 6. Color Aggregation: Compute the final color by summing the product of the weights and the per-sample colors: C = \sum{i=0}^{D-1} wi \cdot ci. If a "rainbow" mode is enabled, the base color might be derived from the distance to the SDF center, clamped between 0.02 and 0.98, otherwise it is 1.0. The final feature output may also multiply base color, learnable feature parameters, and density. 7. Reshaping: Reshape the aggregated color tensor from (N, 3) to (H, W, 3) to form the final image. alpha (\alpha): Scaling factor for density. Default value from config cfg.alpha.val. beta (\beta): Sharpness parameter for the SDF-to-density transition. Default value from config cfg.beta.val. eps: Small constant for numerical stability, value 10^{-10}. Last Segment Delta: The last segment delta is set to 10^{10} to ensure that if a ray does not hit a surface within the sampled range, the transmittance decays sufficiently, preventing artifacts from the infinite tail of the ray. It also prevents division by zero or numerical instability at the end of the ray. Numerical Stability: The small constant \epsilon is added to the exponent in the transmittance calculation to prevent numerical instability. Open Surfaces: Standard SDF-based rendering assumes closed (watertight) surfaces. For open surfaces, this method may produce spurious surfaces in void regions unless modified (e.g., using NeUDF). NeUDF is a neural rendering framework that reconstructs surfaces with arbitrary topologies, including open surfaces, from multi-view 2D image supervision by leveraging the Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) as the implicit surface representation. Unlike Volume SDF Rendering, which is limited to closed (watertight) surfaces, NeUDF resolves the ambiguity of surface orientation in open structures by introducing a specialized "Udensity" probability density function and a normal regularization strategy. It differs from naive extensions of SDF-based rendering by avoiding spurious surfaces in void regions through an unbiased, occlusion-aware weighting paradigm tailored for UDFs. See NeUDF. A variant that processes rays in chunks to manage memory usage during rendering. It splits the total number of rays N into chunks of size chunksize, processes each chunk using the parent forward method, and concatenates the results. This is useful for high-resolution images or large batches where memory constraints prevent processing all rays at once. See VolSDF Volume Rendering for the base method. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the number of rays (pixels) and D is the number of samples per ray. The implicit function evaluation dominates the cost if it is a neural network. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D) to store sample points, distances, colors, and intermediate transmittance values. Chunked rendering reduces peak memory to O(\text{chunk\size} \cdot D). Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on the implicit function. Analytic SDFs (sphere, box) are very fast. Neural SDFs require forward passes through the network for every sample point, which is computationally expensive. Strengths: Can represent complex geometry with thin structures and open surfaces (with modifications). Smooth transitions between surface and volume via \alpha and \beta. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \alpha and \beta. Sensitive to sampling density. Standard SDF rendering struggles with open surfaces without specific modifications like NeUDF. When to use: When rendering implicit surfaces defined by SDFs, especially when analytic or neural SDFs are available. Useful for fitting geometry from multi-view images. When not to use: When high performance is critical and the geometry is simple (explicit meshes are faster). When open surfaces are required without using specialized variants like NeUDF. Volume SDF Rendering is a technique used in neural rendering to combine the benefits of implicit surface representations (SDFs) with volume rendering. It was popularized in the context of fitting neural surfaces from multi-view images, such as in the VolSDF method. The approach converts the signed distance field into a density field using a probabilistic model (Laplace distribution CDF) to allow standard volume rendering integrals to capture the surface appearance. It is widely used in academic projects and implementations for neural surface reconstruction and rendering, such as those found in CMU's Learning for 3D Vision course assignments.
