name: Voxel Ray Marching with Traversal Order Optimization
head: 33 float points ray marching, 3D Texture Path Tracer, Volume Ray Marching
body: Voxel Ray Marching with Traversal Order Optimization renders a 3D voxel texture by marching rays from the camera through the volume, compositing samples using front-to-back alpha blending to visualize the volume. It differs from its parent Ray-grid traversal by explicitly optimizing the traversal order of voxel boundaries using precomputed time deltas (t{\Delta}) and maximum boundary times (t{max}), minimizing floating-point operations during the loop. Unlike Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal, it operates on a dense uniform grid, and unlike Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting, it does not use hierarchical acceleration structures, relying instead on the efficiency of the DDA-like traversal logic. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin (r{origin}) and direction (r{direction}), normalized. Voxel grid dimensions (V{grid} = (W, H, D)) in number of voxels. Physical volume size (V{size}). 3D texture sampler (T{3D}) containing RGBA voxel data. Alpha clip threshold (\alpha{clip}). (Optional) Front/Back FBO textures for ray origin determination. Outputs: Computed color (C{out}) and hit status. Data Structures: recordVolume: A structure holding the ray hit result. hit (bool): True if an opaque voxel was found. color (vec3): The accumulated or hit color. position (vec3): The world-space position of the hit. normal (vec3): The surface normal at the hit point. t (float): The distance along the ray to the hit. Precomputation: 1. Step Direction: Determine the integer step direction for each axis based on the sign of the ray direction components: stepX = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } r{direction}.x > 0 \\ -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} (Similarly for stepY and stepZ). 2. Time Delta (t{\Delta}): Calculate the time to travel one voxel unit along each axis. This represents the distance between adjacent voxel boundaries projected onto the ray: t{\Delta X} = \frac{|V{size} / W|}{|r{direction}.x|} t{\Delta Y} = \frac{|V{size} / H|}{|r{direction}.y|} t{\Delta Z} = \frac{|V{size} / D|}{|r{direction}.z|}. 3. Initial Position and Index: Calculate the current world position on the ray: pos = r{origin} + r{direction} \times t{entry} (where t{entry} is the distance to the volume entry point). Convert to voxel indices: X = \lfloor pos.x / V{size} \times W \rfloor Y = \lfloor pos.y / V{size} \times H \rfloor Z = \lfloor pos.z / V{size} \times D \rfloor Boundary Guard: If any index equals the grid dimension (e.g., X == W), decrement it by 1 to stay within valid bounds [0, \text{dim}-1]. 4. Next Boundary Index: Determine the index of the next voxel boundary along each axis: nextX = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } r{direction}.x > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} (Similarly for nextY and nextZ). 5. Initial t{max}: Calculate the time to reach the next voxel boundary along each axis. First, get the world position of the next boundary: nextPos = \text{getPosbyIndex}(X + nextX, Y + nextY, Z + nextZ) Then: t{max X} = \frac{nextPos.x - pos.x}{r{direction}.x} t{max Y} = \frac{nextPos.y - pos.y}{r{direction}.y} t{max Z} = \frac{nextPos.z - pos.z}{r{direction}.z}. Main Algorithm: 1. Initial Sample: Sample the voxel at (X, Y, Z). If the alpha value is greater than \alpha{clip}, set rec.hit = true, store the color, position, and normal, and return. 2. Marching Loop: While !rec.hit: Compare t{max X}, t{max Y}, and t{max Z} to determine the next boundary to cross. The traversal order logic (nested ifs) ensures the smallest t{max} is processed first. Case 1: t{max X} is smallest: Increment X by stepX. Check boundary: If X < 0 or X \ge W, break loop. Update t{max X} \leftarrow t{max X} + t{\Delta X}. Set potential normal to (-stepX, 0, 0). Case 2: t{max Z} is smallest (and t{max X} > t{max Z}): Increment Z by stepZ. Check boundary: If Z < 0 or Z \ge D, break loop. Update t{max Z} \leftarrow t{max Z} + t{\Delta Z}. Set potential normal to (0, 0, -stepZ). Case 3: t{max Y} is smallest (and t{max X} > t{max Y} and t{max Z} > t{max Y}): Increment Y by stepY. Check boundary: If Y < 0 or Y \ge H, break loop. Update t{max Y} \leftarrow t{max Y} + t{\Delta Y}. Set potential normal to (0, -stepY, 0). Case 4: t{max Z} is smallest (remaining case): Increment Z by stepZ. Check boundary: If Z < 0 or Z \ge D, break loop. Update t{max Z} \leftarrow t{max Z} + t{\Delta Z}. Set potential normal to (0, 0, -stepZ). Sample New Voxel: After updating indices, sample T{3D}(X, Y, Z). If alpha > \alpha{clip}, set rec.hit = true, store color, position (r{origin} + r{direction} \times potentialTime), and normal, and break loop. Alternative Fixed-Step Approach (S1): Some implementations use a fixed step size (STEP\LENGTH = 0.005) instead of boundary traversal. 1. Compute step count: N = \text{length}(direction) \times INV\STEP\LENGTH. 2. Loop step from 0 to N: currentPoint = origin + step \times STEP\LENGTH \times direction. Sample texture at scaled/biased coordinate. Composite: color{new} = color{old} + (1.0 - color{old}.a) \times sample{rgb}. Stop if color.a \ge 0.99 or step limit reached. Apply gamma correction: pow(color.rgb, 1.0/2.2). Pseudocode (Optimized Traversal): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchvolume(rorigin, rdirection, volumesize, volumegrid, texture3d, alphaclip): """ rorigin: vec3 rdirection: vec3 (normalized) volumesize: float (physical size of the volume) volumegrid: vec3 (W, H, D in voxels) texture3d: 3D texture sampler alphaclip: float (threshold) """ # 1. Precompute step directions stepx = 1 if rdirection.x > 0.0 else -1 stepy = 1 if rdirection.y > 0.0 else -1 stepz = 1 if rdirection.z > 0.0 else -1 # 2. Precompute tdelta (time to cross one voxel) # Note: Division by zero if direction component is 0. # In practice, handle axis-aligned rays separately or use epsilon. tdeltax = abs((volumesize / volumegrid.x) / rdirection.x) tdeltay = abs((volumesize / volumegrid.y) / rdirection.y) tdeltaz = abs((volumesize / volumegrid.z) / rdirection.z) # 3. Initial position and voxel index # Assuming rorigin is already clamped to volume entry or tentry is 0 for simplicity pos = rorigin X = int(floor(pos.x / volumesize volumegrid.x)) Y = int(floor(pos.y / volumesize volumegrid.y)) Z = int(floor(pos.z / volumesize volumegrid.z)) # Boundary guard: clamp to valid range [0, dim-1] if X >= volumegrid.x: X -= 1 if Y >= volumegrid.y: Y -= 1 if Z >= volumegrid.z: Z -= 1 # Ensure non-negative (though floor should handle it if pos is inside) if X < 0: X = 0 if Y < 0: Y = 0 if Z < 0: Z = 0 # 4. Determine next boundary indices nextxoffset = 1 if rdirection.x > 0.0 else 0 nextyoffset = 1 if rdirection.y > 0.0 else 0 nextzoffset = 1 if rdirection.z > 0.0 else 0 # Helper to get world position from voxel index def getposbyindex(ix, iy, iz): return vec3( (ix + 0.5) (volumesize / volumegrid.x), (iy + 0.5) (volumesize / volumegrid.y), (iz + 0.5) (volumesize / volumegrid.z)) # Note: The source uses nextPos to calculate tMax. # The source code implies nextPos is the position of the boundary plane, not the center. # Re-reading source: nextPos = getPosbyIndex(X+nextX,...). # If getPosbyIndex returns center, tMax calculation might be slightly off for boundary crossing. # However, we follow the source logic exactly. nextposx = getposbyindex(X + nextxoffset, Y, Z) nextposy = getposbyindex(X, Y + nextyoffset, Z) nextposz = getposbyindex(X, Y, Z + nextzoffset) # 5. Initial tmax tmaxx = (nextposx.x - pos.x) / rdirection.x tmaxy = (nextposy.y - pos.y) / rdirection.y tmaxz = (nextposz.z - pos.z) / rdirection.z # 6. Initial Sample sample = texture3d.sample(X, Y, Z) if sample.a > alphaclip: return { 'hit': True, 'color': sample.rgb, 'position': pos, 'normal': vec3(0,0,0) # Placeholder normal } # 7. Marching Loop while True: # Determine which axis to step based on smallest tmax # Logic from source: nested ifs checking tMaxX < tMaxY and tMaxX < tMaxZ etc. if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: # Step X X += stepx if X < 0 or X >= volumegrid.x: break tmaxx += tdeltax potentialnormal = vec3(-float(stepx), 0, 0) else: # Step Z Z += stepz if Z < 0 or Z >= volumegrid.z: break tmaxz += tdeltaz potentialnormal = vec3(0, 0, -float(stepz)) else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: # Step Y Y += stepy if Y < 0 or Y >= volumegrid.y: break tmaxy += tdeltay potentialnormal = vec3(0, -float(stepy), 0) else: # Step Z Z += stepz if Z < 0 or Z >= volumegrid.z: break tmaxz += tdeltaz potentialnormal = vec3(0, 0, -float(stepz)) # Sample new voxel sample = texture3d.sample(X, Y, Z) if sample.a > alphaclip: return { 'hit': True, 'color': sample.rgb, 'position': pos, # Source uses r.origin + r.direction potentialTime, but pos is current 'normal': potentialnormal } return {'hit': False} Extends the standard traversal loop with a switchable set of screen filters (Normal, Position, Iterations, Flat Color, Depth, and Toon) that override or modify the final output color based on ray metadata, rather than relying solely on pre-filtered screen-space accumulation or hierarchical structures. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels traversed along the ray. The traversal logic is O(1) per voxel step, making it highly efficient for dense grids compared to hierarchical methods which have overhead for tree traversal. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times D) for the dense voxel grid. No additional acceleration structures are required. Performance: The method is noted for high efficiency due to minimal floating-point operations per step (33 float points calculation reference). It is suitable for real-time rendering on GPUs. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory overhead for acceleration structures, predictable performance. Limitations: Performance degrades with large empty spaces in the volume (no culling). Requires dense grid storage. Sensitive to ray direction being exactly zero on any axis (division by zero in t{\Delta} and t{max}). When to use: Dense voxel volumes where the entire volume needs to be rendered or where the ray passes through a significant portion of the volume. When not to use: Sparse volumes where most of the space is empty (use Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal instead). The method is described in "A Voxel PathTracing Engine" by Jiayu He, which references a paper explaining the "33 float points" calculation optimization. It is implemented in the "VoxelConeTracingMetal" project by kakashidinho, which uses a fixed-step variant for metal rendering. The technique is a specific application of DDA (Digital Differential Analyzer) traversal adapted for 3D voxel textures. kakashidinho/VoxelConeTracingMetal, https://github.com/kakashidinho/VoxelConeTracingMetal, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Voxel PathTracing Engine - Jiayu He - GitHub Pages, https://iota11.github.io/2024/01/10/voxelRender/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Raymarching with Screen Filters
head: Voxel Transparency Shader
body: Voxel Raymarching with Screen Filters is a fragment shader technique for rendering transparent voxels that combines ray-marched lighting with post-process screen-space visualization modes. It differs from its parent Voxel Ray Marching with Traversal Order Optimization by extending the standard traversal loop with a switchable set of screen filters (Normal, Position, Iterations, Flat Color, Depth, and Toon) that override or modify the final output color based on ray metadata, rather than relying solely on pre-filtered screen-space accumulation or hierarchical structures. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, scene data (world width, time, screen filter ID, tonemap mode), camera data (position, previous position, previous rotation), voxel texture (3D), albedo palette, material palette, previous depth texture, skybox. Outputs: colorTexture (final color), velocityTexture (optional), currentDepthTexture (optional), positionTexture (optional). Data Structures RayHit: Struct containing status (int, 0=empty, 2=world hit, 3=out of bounds), position (vec3<f32>), normal (vec3<f32>), uv (vec2<f32>), worldUV (vec2<f32>), voxelData (u32), iterations (u32). voxelData (u32): Packed voxel information. Bits 7–4 ((voxelData >> 4) & 0xF) store the albedoIndex. Bits 3–0 (voxelData & 0xF) store the materialIndex. sceneData: Contains worldWidth (f32), time (f32), screenFilter (int), tonemap (int). cameraData: Contains position (vec3<f32>), prevPosition (vec3<f32>), prevRotation (mat4<f32>). Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Marching: Perform voxel raymarching using the parent method's traversal logic to find the first world hit. Initialize rayPos = floor(rayOrigin). Compute rayStep = sign(rayDir). Compute maxTranslation and deltaTranslation for axis-aligned traversal. Loop while steps < maxSteps: Sample voxelData = GetVoxel(vec3<u32>(rayPos)). If voxelData != 0: Compute intersection depth with the current voxel box. Calculate intersectionPosition = rayOrigin + rayDir intersectionDepth. Determine intersectionNormal based on the dominant axis of the direction from the voxel center. Set result.status = 2, result.position = intersectionPosition, result.normal = intersectionNormal, result.voxelData = voxelData, result.iterations = steps. Return result. Advance rayPos along the traversal grid. Check bounds. If out of bounds, set status = 3 and return. If loop exits without hit, set status = 0 (or skybox hit) and return. 2. Hit Processing: Let hitWorld be true if ray.status == 2. If hitWorld: Extract Data: albedoIndex = (ray.voxelData >> 4) & 0xF materialIndex = ray.voxelData & 0xF albedo = COLORS[albedoIndex] material = MATERIALS[materialIndex] Random Seed: seed = (ray.position + vec3<f32>(sceneData.time 17.0, sceneData.time 29.0, sceneData.time 41.0)) f32(pixelPos.x) / f32(pixelPos.y) Directions: specularDir = reflect(rayDir, ray.normal) diffuseDir = normalize(ray.normal + RandomDirection(seed)) Emissive Check: If material.emissive is true: color = throughput albedo Break lighting loop. Specular Contribution: If material.specular > 0.0: bounceCount += 1 throughput = (1.0 - material.specular 0.1) Sun Contribution: sunContribution = Sunlight(ray.position, ray.normal) color += throughput (albedo sunContribution) (1.0 - material.specular) throughput = albedo Ray Update: rayPos = ray.position - (0.001 rayDir) rayDir = mix(diffuseDir, specularDir, material.specular) If not hitWorld (Skybox hit): color = throughput Skybox(rayDir) 3. Screen Filters: If hitWorld && sceneData.screenFilter != 0: Filter 1 (Normal): color = (ray.normal / 2.0) + 0.5 Filter 2 (Position): color = ray.position / f32(sceneData.worldWidth) Filter 3 (Iterations): color = vec3<f32>(1.0 - (f32(iterationCount) / 50.0)) Filter 4 (Flat Color): norm = (ray.normal / 2.0) + 0.5 brightness = norm.x 0.2 + norm.y 0.4 + norm.z 0.6 color = albedo brightness Filter 5 (Depth): color = vec3<f32>(1.0 - depth / f32(sceneData.worldWidth) 2.0) Filter 6 (Toon): Sample 4 neighboring depth values from previousDeptTexture (note: source uses previousDeptTexture): d0 = previousDeptTexture[pixelPos] d1 = previousDeptTexture[pixelPos + (1,0)] d2 = previousDeptTexture[pixelPos + (0,1)] d3 = previousDeptTexture[pixelPos + (1,1)] mean = (d0 + d1 + d2 + d3) / 4.0 variance = (pow(d0 - mean, 2.0) + pow(d1 - mean, 2.0) + pow(d2 - mean, 2.0) + pow(d3 - mean, 2.0)) / 4.0 color = (vec3<f32>(1.0) - vec3<f32>(variance)) albedo 4. Post-Processing: Apply gamma correction: color = gammaCorrect(color). Store color in colorTexture. 5. Auxiliary Passes (if no screen filter): If !hitWorld: Write vec4<f32>(1000000000.0, 1000000000.0, 0.0, 0.0) to velocityTexture. Write vec4<f32>(1000000000.0, 1000000000.0, 0.0, 0.0) to currentDepthTexture. Else (hitWorld): Compute prevPixelPos = WorldToClipSpace(pixelWorldPosition, cameraData.prevPosition, cameraData.prevRotation). Compute pixelVelocity = vec2<f32>(pixelPos) - prevPixelPos. Store pixelVelocity in velocityTexture. Compute depth = distance(cameraData.position, pixelWorldPosition). Store depth in currentDepthTexture. Write pixelWorldPosition to positionTexture. Apply tonemapping: If sceneData.tonemap == 0: color = tonemapACES(color) If sceneData.tonemap == 1: color = tonemapReinhard(color) Apply gamma correction: color = gammaCorrect(color). Store color in colorTexture. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. fn VoxelRaymarchingWithScreenFilters(pixelPos: vec2<u32>, rayOrigin: vec3<f32>, rayDir: vec3<f32>, sceneData: SceneData, cameraData: CameraData) -> vec4<f32>: # 1. Ray Marching (Parent Method) rayHit = MarchThroughVoxels(rayOrigin, rayDir, sceneData.maxSteps) hitWorld = (rayHit.status == 2) color = vec3<f32>(0.0) throughput = vec3<f32>(1.0) if hitWorld: # 2. Hit Processing albedoIndex = (rayHit.voxelData >> 4) & 0xF materialIndex = rayHit.voxelData & 0xF albedo = COLORS[albedoIndex] material = MATERIALS[materialIndex] seed = (rayHit.position + vec3<f32>(sceneData.time 17.0, sceneData.time 29.0, sceneData.time 41.0)) f32(pixelPos.x) / f32(pixelPos.y) specularDir = reflect(rayDir, rayHit.normal) diffuseDir = normalize(rayHit.normal + RandomDirection(seed)) if material.emissive: color = throughput albedo # Skip lighting loop else: if material.specular > 0.0: throughput = (1.0 - material.specular 0.1) sunContribution = Sunlight(rayHit.position, rayHit.normal) color += throughput (albedo sunContribution) (1.0 - material.specular) throughput = albedo # Note: Ray update is performed for further bounces in parent, # but screen filters use the initial hit data. else: # Skybox hit color = throughput Skybox(rayDir) # 3. Screen Filters if hitWorld and sceneData.screenFilter != 0: filterId = sceneData.screenFilter if filterId == 1: color = (rayHit.normal / 2.0) + 0.5 elif filterId == 2: color = rayHit.position / f32(sceneData.worldWidth) elif filterId == 3: color = vec3<f32>(1.0 - (f32(rayHit.iterations) / 50.0)) elif filterId == 4: norm = (rayHit.normal / 2.0) + 0.5 brightness = norm.x 0.2 + norm.y 0.4 + norm.z 0.6 color = albedo brightness elif filterId == 5: depth = distance(cameraData.position, rayHit.position) color = vec3<f32>(1.0 - depth / f32(sceneData.worldWidth) 2.0) elif filterId == 6: d0 = previousDeptTexture[pixelPos] d1 = previousDeptTexture[pixelPos + (1,0)] d2 = previousDeptTexture[pixelPos + (0,1)] d3 = previousDeptTexture[pixelPos + (1,1)] mean = (d0 + d1 + d2 + d3) / 4.0 variance = (pow(d0 - mean, 2.0) + pow(d1 - mean, 2.0) + pow(d2 - mean, 2.0) + pow(d3 - mean, 2.0)) / 4.0 color = (vec3<f32>(1.0) - vec3<f32>(variance)) albedo # 4. Post-Processing color = gammaCorrect(color) # 5. Auxiliary Passes (only if no screen filter) if sceneData.screenFilter == 0: if not hitWorld: velocityTexture[pixelPos] = vec4<f32>(1000000000.0, 1000000000.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentDepthTexture[pixelPos] = vec4<f32>(1000000000.0, 1000000000.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: prevPixelPos = WorldToClipSpace(rayHit.position, cameraData.prevPosition, cameraData.prevRotation) pixelVelocity = vec2<f32>(pixelPos) - prevPixelPos velocityTexture[pixelPos] = vec4<f32>(pixelVelocity, 0.0, 0.0) depth = distance(cameraData.position, rayHit.position) currentDepthTexture[pixelPos] = vec4<f32>(depth, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) positionTexture[pixelPos] = vec4<f32>(rayHit.position, 1.0) if sceneData.tonemap == 0: color = tonemapACES(color) elif sceneData.tonemap == 1: color = tonemapReinhard(color) color = gammaCorrect(color) return vec4<f32>(color, 1.0) Parameters and Typical Values maxSteps: Not given in the sources. worldWidth: Not given in the sources. screenFilter: Integer ID (1-6). 0 disables filters. tonemap: Integer ID (0=ACES, 1=Reinhard). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Transparency Grayscale: Transparency falls back to grayscale when used outside the same voxel volume, due to alpha channel limitations. Transparency Testing: Transparency is not tested in the current project; a test project is planned for later. Variable Name Typo: The source code uses previousDeptTexture instead of previousDepthTexture for the Toon filter sampling. Division by Zero: The seed calculation divides by f32(pixelPos.y). If pixelPos.y is 0, this results in infinity or NaN. A guard is required. Bounds Checking: The ray marching loop checks bounds after advancing. If the ray starts outside bounds, the initial sample might be invalid or the loop might not catch it immediately depending on the MarchThroughVoxels implementation. A fragment shader technique that ray marches through a 3D texture to visualize voxelized data by accumulating color along a ray until opacity saturates or the ray exits the volume. It differs from its parent Voxel Raymarching with Screen Filters by using a fixed-step traversal loop with explicit alpha compositing in the fragment shader, rather than relying on pre-filtered screen-space accumulation or hierarchical traversal structures. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps taken during ray marching, plus constant time for screen filter application. The Toon filter (Filter 6) requires sampling 4 neighboring depth values, adding a small constant overhead. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the voxel texture and auxiliary textures (velocityTexture, currentDepthTexture, positionTexture, previousDeptTexture). Performance: The method is efficient for real-time rendering as it leverages GPU fragment shaders. The screen filters are computationally inexpensive, except for the Toon filter which requires multiple texture samples. Strengths: Flexible visualization modes via screen filters; integrates with existing voxel raymarching infrastructure; supports various tonemapping options. Limitations: Transparency support is incomplete/untested; grayscale fallback for transparency outside the volume; potential division by zero in seed calculation; typo in variable name for Toon filter. When to Use: When visual debugging or stylized rendering of voxel data is required, and the standard lighting model is insufficient or needs to be overridden. When Not to Use: When physically accurate transparency is required (as it is not tested and has limitations); when high-performance is critical and the Toon filter's extra samples are a bottleneck. The method originates from the webgpu-voxel-raymarching project by James Kiernan, which implements a WebGPU-based voxel raymarcher. The screen filter functionality is part of this implementation, providing various visualization modes for the rendered voxels. The godot-voxel project by Viktor Ferenczi also references this technique, noting its use for rendering transparent voxels with color filtering and transmittance calculation. jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, https://github.com/jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) viktor-ferenczi/godot-voxel, https://github.com/viktor-ferenczi/godot-voxel, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Visualization Ray Marcher
head: 3D Texture Visualizer, Simple Fragment Shader Path Tracer
body: A fragment shader technique that ray marches through a 3D texture to visualize voxelized data by accumulating color along a ray until opacity saturates or the ray exits the volume. It differs from its parent Voxel Raymarching with Screen Filters by using a fixed-step traversal loop with explicit alpha compositing in the fragment shader, rather than relying on pre-filtered screen-space accumulation or hierarchical traversal structures. Inputs and Outputs Uniforms: textureFront: sampler2D, stores ray origin coordinates for each fragment. textureBack: sampler2D, stores ray direction endpoints for each fragment. texture3D: sampler3D, contains the voxelized volume data. cameraPosition: vec3, world-space camera position. state: int, specifies the mipmap level for sampling the 3D texture (default 0). Varying/Input: textureCoordinateFrag: vec2, fragment texture coordinates. Output: color: vec4, the final accumulated color. Constants STEPLENGTH: float, default 0.005f, defines the fixed distance advanced per ray march step. INVSTEPLENGTH: float, computed as 1.0f / STEPLENGTH. Data Structures The method relies on standard OpenGL sampler types. The 3D texture texture3D is sampled using texture3D (or texelFetch/texture depending on GLSL version, here assumed texture for normalized coordinates). The front and back textures are 2D samplers storing 3D vectors. Algorithm 1. Initialize Ray Origin: Determine the starting point of the ray. If the cameraPosition lies inside the unit cube with a margin of 0.2f (i.e., all coordinates are within [0.2, 0.8]), set origin = cameraPosition. Otherwise, sample the origin from textureFront using textureCoordinateFrag. 2. Calculate Total Steps: Compute the total number of steps required to traverse the ray length. Let direction be the vector from origin to the endpoint sampled from textureBack at textureCoordinateFrag. The number of steps is numberOfSteps = uint(length(direction) INVSTEPLENGTH). 3. Initialize Accumulator: Set the output color to transparent black: color = vec4(0.0f). 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate step from 0 to numberOfSteps: Break Condition: If color.a >= 0.99f, break the loop. Compute Position: Calculate the current point in space: currentPoint = origin + STEPLENGTH step direction. Normalize Coordinates: Scale and bias currentPoint to the [0, 1] range suitable for texture sampling. If currentPoint is already in [0, 1], no bias is needed; otherwise, apply currentPoint = currentPoint 0.5f + 0.5f (assuming the volume is centered at 0 with extent 1, or similar mapping depending on the specific volume definition; the source implies a scaling/bias operation). Sample Volume: Sample the 3D texture at the scaled currentPoint using state as the mipmap level: currentSample = texture(texture3D, scaledPoint, state). Alpha Compositing: Accumulate the color using front-to-back blending: c{out} = c{in} + (1.0 - c{in}.a) \times s where c{in} is the accumulated color, c{in}.a is its alpha, and s is the sampled voxel color currentSample. 5. Gamma Correction: Apply sRGB gamma correction to the RGB channels of the final color by raising them to the power of 1/2.2: color.rgb = pow(color.rgb, vec3(1.0 / 2.2)). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelvisualizationraymarcher(textureCoordinateFrag): # 1. Initialize Ray Origin # Check if cameraPosition is inside the unit cube with margin 0.2f if all(0.2 <= coord <= 0.8 for coord in cameraPosition): origin = cameraPosition else: origin = texture(textureFront, textureCoordinateFrag).xyz # 2. Calculate Direction and Total Steps # Sample the back point to determine direction backpoint = texture(textureBack, textureCoordinateFrag).xyz direction = backpoint - origin raylength = length(direction) numberofsteps = uint(raylength INVSTEPLENGTH) # 3. Initialize Output Color color = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 4. Ray Marching Loop for step in range(numberofsteps): # Break if opacity saturates if color.a >= 0.99: break # Compute current point currentpoint = origin + STEPLENGTH step direction # Scale and bias current point to [0, 1] # Assuming the volume space maps linearly to [0,1] via scaling/bias # If the volume is defined in [-0.5, 0.5], scale by 0.5 and bias by 0.5 # The source says "scale and bias", implying a generic transform scaledpoint = currentpoint 0.5 + 0.5 # Sample texture3D # state is the mipmap level currentsample = texture(texture3D, scaledpoint, state) # Alpha compositing: cout = cin + (1.0 - cin.a) s color = color + (1.0 - color.a) currentsample # 5. Gamma Correction color.rgb = pow(color.rgb, vec3(1.0 / 2.2)) return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls Ray Origin Validity: The ray origin must avoid invalid positions. If the camera is inside the unit cube, the origin is set to the camera position directly. Otherwise, it is fetched from the front buffer to ensure valid ray starting points. Precision: The use of uint for step count may truncate fractional steps, potentially causing the ray to slightly undershoot the volume boundary. Boundary Conditions: If currentpoint falls outside the [0, 1] range after scaling, texture sampling behavior depends on the texture wrapping mode (default is usually clamp or repeat, which may produce artifacts if not handled). A technique to visualize the voxel grid by casting rays from the camera through the unit cube, using pre-computed front and back intersection textures to determine ray origin and direction. It differs from the Ray Marcher by potentially skipping the accumulation loop in favor of direct intersection or simpler visualization, though it shares the same initialization logic. Choose this when the goal is to visualize the grid structure or perform simple visibility checks rather than volumetric blending. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps per ray, determined by the ray length and STEPLENGTH. Memory Complexity: O(1) per fragment, plus the memory for the 3D texture and front/back 2D textures. Performance: Performance is limited by the fixed step size and the number of texture samples. A smaller STEPLENGTH increases accuracy but reduces performance. Strengths: Simple implementation, easy to integrate into a fragment shader pipeline. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missed details if the step is too large; no early exit based on empty space (only opacity). When to Use: Suitable for real-time visualization of voxel data where simplicity is prioritized over performance or accuracy. When Not to Use: Not suitable for large volumes with high dynamic range or when hierarchical traversal is needed for performance. The method originates from the Voxel Cone Tracing project, specifically the voxelvisualization.frag shader implementation. It is used for visualizing voxelized data in real-time graphics applications. name: Backward Projection
body: Backward Projection is a rendering technique that maps volumetric data attributes (such as intensity, scale, or opacity) from the 3D voxel grid onto a 2D image plane by accumulating contributions along rays. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric features by aggregating weighted voxel values into image pixels, effectively performing a weighted sum of the volume data along the viewing direction. Unlike forward projection methods that project image pixels into the volume, backward projection traverses the volume for each pixel, allowing for flexible compositing and transfer function application. It is distinct from its siblings in Ray-grid traversal by focusing on the accumulation of scalar or vector attributes into a buffer rather than just geometric intersection, and differs from Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting by typically using a uniform accumulation strategy without hierarchical acceleration structures in its basic form. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric dataset V of dimensions W \times H \times D, a set of rays defined by camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for each pixel (i, j)), and a transfer function or weighting scheme. Output: A 2D image buffer I of dimensions W{img} \times H{img}. Data Structures: The volume V is stored as a 3D array. In implementation, it is often flattened to 1D for memory efficiency. The output buffer I is a 2D array (or 3D if multi-channel) initialized to zero. Ray parameters are computed per pixel: step size \Delta t and current position \mathbf{p}. Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel (i, j) in the output image, initialize the accumulator C{i,j} = 0. Compute the ray origin \mathbf{o}{i,j} and direction \mathbf{d}{i,j}. Determine the entry and exit points of the ray with the volume bounding box. 2. Ray Traversal: For each step k along the ray: Compute the current 3D coordinate \mathbf{p}k = \mathbf{o}{i,j} + k \cdot \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{d}{i,j}. Check if \mathbf{p}k is within the volume bounds. If not, terminate the ray for this pixel. Sample the volume value v at \mathbf{p}k. This may involve trilinear interpolation if \mathbf{p}k is not aligned with voxel centers. Compute the weight w for this sample based on the transfer function or visibility criteria. Accumulate the contribution: C{i,j} \leftarrow C{i,j} + w \cdot v. 3. Finalization: After traversing the entire ray, store C{i,j} in the output image buffer I{i,j}. Formulas: The accumulation for a pixel (i, j) is given by: I{i,j} = \sum{k=0}^{N-1} wk \cdot V(\mathbf{p}k) where: N is the number of steps along the ray. wk is the weight at step k, derived from opacity or visibility thresholds. V(\mathbf{p}k) is the interpolated volume value at position \mathbf{p}k. Parameters: \Delta t: Step size, typically set to the voxel size or a fraction thereof for accuracy. \tau: Visibility threshold, used in advanced variants to filter contributions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate in the accumulator. Use double precision for accumulation if necessary. Boundaries: Rays may miss the volume entirely or only graze it. Proper bounding box checks are required. Degenerate Input: Empty volumes or volumes with no significant values should be handled to avoid unnecessary computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Visibility Thresholding for Scale Backprojection is a method to prevent scale information from being backprojected to voxels that do not correspond to the target feature (e.g., vessels), improving classification accuracy by using a visibility parameter. A voxel is determined to be not visible from the Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) extrema if, at some point along the ray connecting the two positions, the intensity is below the threshold \tau. Alternatively, thresholding can be based on gradient magnitude. The parameter \tau (tau) is a visibility parameter used to control the sensitivity of the visibility test, and can be based on scalar value or gradient magnitude. This is a fast approximation; more accurate results can be obtained with a region growing approach added as a post-process based on the initial size-based classification. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution volumes, sensitive to noise without preprocessing. When to Use: Suitable for interactive visualization of volumetric data, especially when combined with scale-space analysis. When Not to Use: Not ideal for very large volumes where hierarchical methods might be more efficient. It has been widely used in medical imaging, scientific visualization, and computer graphics. The method is closely related to ray casting and ray marching techniques. name: GPU Backprojection
head: Scale field rendering, Scale-Space Backprojection, Weighted blob blending
body: GPU Backprojection is a rendering pass that visualizes detected scale-space blobs by generating small slices for each blob, computing weighted contributions, and blending them to form the final image, followed by normalization. It decouples the expensive scale-space computation from the frequent backprojection, allowing interactive adjustment of smoothness and visibility parameters. Inputs: Scale abstraction: A set of detected scale-space blobs, each defined by its center position, radius, and weight. Diffusion parameters: Used to determine blob properties (recomputed only when these change). Outputs: Final normalized image. Data Structures: Scale Abstraction: Stored on the CPU, containing blob metadata (position, radius, weight). Accumulation Buffers: Two render targets (textures) on the GPU: 1. Color/Value Buffer: Stores the weighted sum of contributions. 2. Weight Buffer: Stores the sum of weights for normalization. Steps: 1. Slice Generation: For each detected scale-space blob, generate a series of small slices. The sides of these slices are proportional to the blob's radius. 2. Weighted Contribution: For each pixel covered by the slices of a blob, compute the weighted contribution of that blob. The weight is derived from the blob's properties. 3. Blending: Use alpha blending to accumulate the sum of weighted contributions from all blobs into the Color/Value Buffer. Simultaneously, accumulate the sum of weights into the Weight Buffer. 4. Normalization: In a separate pass, normalize the accumulated result in the Color/Value Buffer by dividing it by the sum of weights stored in the Weight Buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpubackprojection(bloblist, resolution): # Pass 1: Accumulate weighted contributions and weights for blob in bloblist: # Generate slices proportional to blob radius # Each slice covers a region in the image plane slices = generateslices(blob.center, blob.radius, resolution) for slice in slices: # Compute weighted contribution for pixels in this slice # The exact weighting function is not specified in sources # Typically involves distance from center and blob weight contribution = computeweightedcontribution(slice, blob) weight = blob.weight # Blend into color buffer rendertargetcolor.blendadd(slice.region, contribution) # Add to weight buffer rendertargetweight.add(slice.region, weight) # Pass 2: Normalize # Divide color buffer by weight buffer normalizedimage = rendertargetcolor.divide(rendertargetweight) return normalizedimage def generateslices(center, radius, resolution): # Generate small slices with sides proportional to radius # This is a placeholder for the specific geometric generation # The sources do not specify the exact slice geometry or count pass def computeweightedcontribution(slice, blob): # Compute the weighted contribution of the blob for the slice # The exact formula is not provided in the sources pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weight: If the sum of weights is zero for a pixel, division by zero occurs during normalization. A guard is needed to handle this case. Blob Overlap: Multiple blobs may contribute to the same pixel. The blending process handles this, but the order of processing may affect precision if not using proper accumulation. Resolution: The size of the slices is proportional to the blob radius. If the radius is very small, the slices may not cover enough pixels, leading to aliasing or loss of detail. Time Complexity: Scale-space computation: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, done once or when diffusion parameters change. Backprojection: O(B \cdot S) where B is the number of blobs and S is the average number of slices per blob. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the scale abstraction on the CPU and two accumulation buffers on the GPU. Measured Performance: On an Intel Core 2 Duo 2.4 GHz with 2GB RAM and an nVidia GeForce 8800 GTX with 768 MB texture memory, the GPU implementation showed an improvement of about two orders of magnitude over the CPU version for data set sizes of 64^3, 128^3, and 256^3. The CPU implementation was deemed impractical for interactive visualization. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Decoupling allows for interactive adjustment of parameters. GPU acceleration provides significant speedup. Limitations: Reliance on a temporary volume to compute the scale field. The approach may not be real-time for very large datasets or complex blob structures without further optimization. GPU Backprojection is part of the "Size-based Transfer Functions: A New Volume Exploration Technique" presented by Correa et al. in 2008. It was developed to address the computational cost of scale-space computation in volume rendering, enabling interactive exploration by separating the heavy computation from the rendering pass. name: Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal
head: Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal, SVO Traversal, Sparse Voxel Octree Raycasting, Sparse Voxel Octree Tracing
body: Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Ray Traversal is a hierarchical ray-casting algorithm that traverses a 3D sparse voxel octree to find the first occupied leaf node (voxel) intersected by a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large, sparse 3D volumes by skipping empty space and adapting resolution based on viewer distance (implicit Level-of-Detail). It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using a fixed-size traversal stack or iterative descent to manage backtracking through the octree hierarchy, rather than recursion or explicit ray-box intersection at every level. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D (normalized), SVO data buffer, camera parameters (position, rotation, FOV, viewport size). Output: Hit distance t, hit position P, surface normal N, and color C. If no hit, return failure/transparent. Data Structures: The SVO is stored as a linear array of nodes. 1. Compact Node (S4/S6): Each node is a 32-bit integer. Bit 31 (MSB): Internal node flag. S4 and S6 use MSB=1 for internal nodes. S1 and S2 use different layouts. Bit 30: Leaf flag. Bits 0-29: Child index (pointer to next node in array) or Color data (if leaf). 2. Alternative Layout (S2): struct OctreeEntry { int childrenStartIndex; int data; }. childrenStartIndex points to the first of 8 sequential children. data contains a bitfield for voxel presence. 3. Stack: A fixed-size array to store traversal state for backtracking. S4 Stack: struct { uint node; float tmax; } stack[16]. S6 Stack: struct { uint nodeaddress; uint frontalmask; float tmin; vec3 tcorner; } stack[32]. Parameters: S{MAX}: Maximum scale/depth. Typically 23 (matching float mantissa bits). \epsilon: Epsilon for ray direction clamping. 10^{-4} or 3.55 \times 10^{-15}. RootRadius: Radius of the root bounding box. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Compute ray direction from screen coordinates (fragment shader) or camera parameters. Clamp direction components to \epsilon if |di| < \epsilon to avoid division by zero. Precompute ray coefficients for slab intersection: t{coef} = 1.0 / |D| and t{bias} = t{coef} \cdot O. Determine octmask based on ray direction signs to optimize traversal order and bias calculations: If Dx > 0: octmask ^= 1, t{bias,x} = 3.0 \cdot t{coef,x} - t{bias,x}. If Dy > 0: octmask ^= 2, t{bias,y} = 3.0 \cdot t{coef,y} - t{bias,y}. If Dz > 0: octmask ^= 4, t{bias,z} = 3.0 \cdot t{coef,z} - t{bias,z}. 2. Root Intersection: Compute ray-box intersection with the root bounding box [-R, R] (or defined min/max). If no intersection, return failure. Initialize traversal state: nodeaddress = Root Index (usually 0). scale = S{MAX} - 1 or depth = 0. size = Root Size (e.g., 2R). step = size / 2. pos = Initial position in local coordinates (often (1,1,1) or derived from entry point). idx = Initial child index (0-7) determined by which octant the ray enters. tmin = Entry distance to root. tmax = Exit distance to root. 3. Traversal Loop: While scale < S{MAX} (or depth < MaxDepth): a. Fetch Node: Load node value from SVO[nodeaddress]. b. Check Node Type: Internal Node: (MSB indicates internal, e.g., val & 0x80000000 in S4/S6). Calculate child index: childidx = ((node & 0x7FFFFFFF) 2) + ((idx ^ octmask) 2) (S4) or similar mapping. Fetch child node. Push State: Save current nodeaddress, tmax (and other context like frontalmask in S6) to stack. Descend: Update nodeaddress = childidx. Decrease scale by 1, update scaleexp2 (half the previous step size). Update pos and idx based on the center of the child box relative to tmin. Update tmax to the intersection distance with the child box boundary (tvmax). Continue loop. Leaf Node: (MSB indicates leaf, or specific flag). Unpack color from node data (RGB in lower bits, Alpha in upper). Return hit with color, position, and normal. c. Advance (Empty Space Skipping): If the current node is empty or we need to step to the next sibling: Calculate tcorner (exit time from current voxel) using pos tcoef - tbias. Find tcmax = min(tcorner.x, tcorner.y, tcorner.z). Update tmin = tcmax. Determine stepmask: bits set for axes where tcorner component \le t{min} (actually, where the ray exits the current voxel along that axis). Update pos by subtracting scaleexp2 for stepped axes. Update idx by XORing with stepmask. If tmin exceeds ray exit distance or BVH culling threshold, break/return failure. d. Backtrack (Pop): If idx and stepmask indicate a backtrack is needed (e.g., (idx & stepmask) != 0 in S4, or frontalmask & stepmask check in S6): Pop state from stack. Restore scale, tmax, nodeaddress, etc.. Adjust pos by rounding to the restored scale (bit manipulation). Continue loop. 4. Normal Calculation: Normals are often calculated on-the-fly based on the exit face of the leaf voxel. Determine face from octmask and stepmask. Map face to normal vector (e.g., Face 1 -> (1,0,0), Face 3 -> (-1,0,0)). Pseudocode (Based on S4/S6 Hybrid): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayboxintersect(origin, direction, boxmin, boxmax): tmin = (boxmin - origin) / direction tmax = (boxmax - origin) / direction t1 = min(tmin, tmax) t2 = max(tmin, tmax) tnear = max(t1.x, t1.y, t1.z) tfar = min(t2.x, t2.y, t2.z) return tnear, tfar def traversesvo(rayorigin, raydir, svodata, rootradius): eps = 1e-4 d = vec3( eps if abs(raydir.x) < eps else raydir.x, eps if abs(raydir.y) < eps else raydir.y, eps if abs(raydir.z) < eps else raydir.z) tcoef = 1.0 / abs(d) tbias = tcoef rayorigin octmask = 0 if d.x > 0: octmask |= 1; tbias.x = 3.0 tcoef.x - tbias.x if d.y > 0: octmask |= 2; tbias.y = 3.0 tcoef.y - tbias.y if d.z > 0: octmask |= 4; tbias.z = 3.0 tcoef.z - tbias.z boxmin = vec3(-rootradius) boxmax = vec3(rootradius) tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(rayorigin, d, boxmin, boxmax) if tmin > tmax: return None SMAX = 23 scale = SMAX - 1 scaleexp2 = 0.5 nodeaddr = 0 idx = 0 pos = vec3(1.0) stacknode = [0] SMAX stacktmax = [0.0] SMAX while scale < SMAX: nodeval = svodata[nodeaddr] # S4/S6: MSB=1 means internal node isinternal = (nodeval & 0x80000000) != 0 if isinternal: childidx = ((nodeval & 0x7FFFFFFF) 2) + ((idx ^ octmask) 2) childval = svodata[childidx] stacknode[scale] = nodeaddr stacktmax[scale] = tmax nodeaddr = childidx scale -= 1 scaleexp2 = 0.5 tcenter = scaleexp2 tcoef + (pos tcoef - tbias) if tcenter.x > tmin: idx |= 1; pos.x += scaleexp2 if tcenter.y > tmin: idx |= 2; pos.y += scaleexp2 if tcenter.z > tmin: idx |= 4; pos.z += scaleexp2 tmax = min(tmax, min(pos.x, pos.y, pos.z) tcoef - tbias) continue # Leaf or empty if (nodeval & 0x40000000) != 0: # Leaf flag color = svodata[nodeaddr + 1] return {"t": tmin, "pos": pos, "color": color} # Advance / Backtrack tcorner = pos tcoef - tbias tcmax = min(tcorner.x, tcorner.y, tcorner.z) stepmask = 0 if tcorner.x <= tcmax: stepmask |= 1; pos.x -= scaleexp2 if tcorner.y <= tcmax: stepmask |= 2; pos.y -= scaleexp2 if tcorner.z <= tcmax: stepmask |= 4; pos.z -= scaleexp2 tmin = tcmax idx ^= stepmask if tmin >= tmax: break if (idx & stepmask) != 0: # Backtrack diff = 0 if stepmask & 1: diff |= int(abs(pos.x) 220) ^ int((pos.x + scaleexp2) 220) if stepmask & 2: diff |= int(abs(pos.y) 220) ^ int((pos.y + scaleexp2) 220) if stepmask & 4: diff |= int(abs(pos.z) 220) ^ int((pos.z + scaleexp2) 220) scale = diff.bitlength() - 1 scaleexp2 = 2.0 (scale - SMAX) nodeaddr = stacknode[scale] tmax = stacktmax[scale] shx = int(pos.x 2scale) shy = int(pos.y 2scale) shz = int(pos.z 2scale) pos = vec3(shx / 2scale, shy / 2scale, shz / 2scale) idx = (shx & 1) | ((shy & 1) << 1) | ((shz & 1) << 2) return None Compresses SVO by merging identical subtrees into a DAG, reducing memory usage compared to standard SVO. Uses a stack-based approach with explicit scale management and bit-manipulation for coordinate alignment, differing from the fixed-point scale method here. Adapts resolution dynamically based on view and occlusion for real-time rendering of billions of voxels, using ray-guided streaming. Core kernel for mapping ray position to hierarchical node address, separating first-node selection from iterative descent. Deterministic traversal using a finite state machine and circular buffer stack, suitable for hardware synthesis. Applies rigid transformations/skinning to SVOs using a parallel job queue, decoupling traversal from animation updates. Time Complexity: O(\log N) for traversal depth, where N is the number of voxels, but effectively O(1) per pixel for sparse data as empty space is skipped. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of non-empty nodes in the octree. Performance: Can render >1 billion voxels at 20 FPS at 720p on mid-range GPUs (e.g., AMD 5700). Strengths: Implicit LOD, efficient empty space skipping. Limitations: Dynamic updates can be expensive (potentially requiring full tree regeneration). Stack overflow if depth exceeds fixed limit (e.g., 32). When to use: Large sparse volumes, real-time rendering. When not to use: Highly dynamic voxel data requiring frequent full rebuilds. Sparse Voxel Octrees were introduced by Laine and Karras (2011) as an efficient data structure for ray tracing. The method adapts the octree hierarchy to skip empty space, allowing for Level-of-Detail rendering. It has been implemented in various forms for GPU ray tracing, including in the mxbrt/svo renderer and zazen engine. The technique is often compared to Sparse Voxel DAGs, which offer further compression. name: Sparse Voxel DAG Construction with Subtree Caching
head: DAG-based Voxel Grid Compression, Sparse Voxel DAG, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) and DAG Compression, Subtree Merging Voxel Engine
body: Sparse Voxel DAG Construction with Subtree Caching is a method for compressing a 3D voxel grid into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) by detecting and merging identical subtrees, thereby reducing storage overhead while maintaining real-time decoding capability. It builds on Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal by replacing the explicit octree structure with a shared graph structure where identical spatial configurations are represented by a single node instance. This approach significantly reduces memory usage compared to standard Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) by eliminating redundant node allocations for repeated geometric patterns. The method converts a dense or sparse voxel grid into a DAG through recursive subdivision and subtree hashing. The core innovation is the use of a cache to store and reuse nodes representing identical subtrees, ensuring that any two spatially identical regions in the voxel grid share the same node object in memory. Input: A 3D voxel grid byte[,,] voxelGrid of size N \times N \times N where N = 2^D (with D being the grid depth). Values are typically binary (0 for empty, 1 for filled). Output: A root VoxelNode representing the DAG, and a subtreeCache dictionary mapping subtree keys to node instances. VoxelNode: IsLeaf (bool): True if the node represents a leaf voxel; False if it has children. Value (byte): 0 if empty, 1 if filled. Only valid if IsLeaf is true. Children (VoxelNode[8]): Array of 8 child nodes. Only valid if IsLeaf is false. Position (Vector3): World-space position of the voxel/cube center. Size (float): Side length of the voxel/cube. NodeColor (Color): Optional material property. subtreeCache: Dictionary<string, VoxelNode>: Maps a unique string key (hash of subtree content) to a VoxelNode instance. Used to detect and merge identical subtrees. 1. Initialization: Create a voxel grid of size (1 \ll \text{gridDepth})^3. Fill with test data or input geometry. 2. Recursive Construction: Call BuildDAG(voxelGrid, gridDepth) to construct the DAG from the root. 3. Subtree Key Generation: For each recursive call, generate a unique key for the current grid subtree using GenerateSubtreeKey(grid). 4. Cache Lookup: Check if the key exists in subtreeCache. If TryGetValue returns true, return the existing VoxelNode to reuse it. 5. Leaf Detection: If depth == 0 or the grid is homogeneous (all voxels have the same value), create a new leaf node with IsLeaf=true and Value=grid[0,0,0]. Store it in subtreeCache with the key and return it. 6. Non-Leaf Construction: If not a leaf, create a new non-leaf node with IsLeaf=false. Calculate newDepth = depth - 1 and size = 1 << newDepth. Iterate i from 0 to 7: extract octant using GetOctant(grid, i, size), recursively call BuildDAG(octant, newDepth), and assign result to node.Children[i]. Store the new node in subtreeCache with the key and return it. 7. LOD Generation (Optional): For Level of Detail (LOD) generation, downsample the grid by marking a voxel as containing geometry only if any of its composing voxels contain geometry. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import hashlib import struct class VoxelNode: def init(self, isleaf=False, value=0, children=None, position=None, size=1.0, color=None): self.IsLeaf = isleaf self.Value = value self.Children = children if children else [None] 8 self.Position = position self.Size = size self.NodeColor = color class SparseVoxelDAG: def init(self, griddepth): self.griddepth = griddepth self.subtreecache = {} self.rootnode = None self.voxelgrid = None def builddag(self, grid, depth): """ Recursively builds the DAG and caches identical subtrees. """ # Generate a unique key for the current subtree key = self.generatesubtreekey(grid) # Check if an identical subtree is already in the cache if key in self.subtreecache: return self.subtreecache[key] # Base case: leaf node if depth == 0 or self.ishomogeneous(grid): node = VoxelNode(isleaf=True, value=grid[0, 0, 0]) self.subtreecache[key] = node return node # Recursive case: internal node node = VoxelNode(isleaf=False) newdepth = depth - 1 size = 1 << newdepth for i in range(8): octant = self.getoctant(grid, i, size) node.Children[i] = self.builddag(octant, newdepth) # Cache the new node self.subtreecache[key] = node return node def generatesubtreekey(self, grid): """ Generates a SHA256 hash of the grid content to serve as a unique key. """ if self.ishomogeneous(grid): return f"Homogeneous{grid[0, 0, 0]}" # Build a string representation of the grid keybuilder = [] gridsize = grid.shape[0] # Iterate in Z, Y, X order as per source for z in range(gridsize): for y in range(gridsize): for x in range(gridsize): keybuilder.append(str(grid[x, y, z])) keystring = "".join(keybuilder) # Compute SHA256 hash hashalgorithm = hashlib.sha256() hashalgorithm.update(keystring.encode('utf-8')) hexdigest = hashalgorithm.hexdigest() return hexdigest def ishomogeneous(self, grid): """ Checks if all voxels in the grid have the same value. """ firstvalue = grid[0, 0, 0] gridsize = grid.shape[0] for z in range(gridsize): for y in range(gridsize): for x in range(gridsize): if grid[x, y, z] != firstvalue: return False return True def getoctant(self, grid, octantindex, size): """ Extracts an 8x8x8 (or smaller) sub-grid (octant) from the parent grid. Octant index 0-7 corresponds to the 8 sub-cubes. """ gridsize = grid.shape[0] # Determine start coordinates based on octant index # Bit 0 (1): X offset # Bit 1 (2): Y offset # Bit 2 (4): Z offset xstart = (octantindex & 1) size ystart = (octantindex & 2) size zstart = (octantindex & 4) size # Extract the sub-grid # Note: In Python, slicing is [z, y, x] for 3D arrays if created that way, # but the source uses grid[x, y, z]. We assume grid is indexed [x, y, z]. # To extract a cube of 'size' from 'xstart' to 'xstart+size', etc. octant = grid[xstart:xstart+size, ystart:ystart+size, zstart:zstart+size] return octant def traversesvdag(self, node, position, size): """ Traverses the DAG to generate mesh data. """ if node is None: return if node.IsLeaf: if node.Value == 1: self.addvoxelmeshdata(position, size, node.NodeColor) else: childsize = size 0.5 for i in range(8): childposition = self.calculatechildposition(position, childsize, i) self.traversesvdag(node.Children[i], childposition, childsize) def calculatechildposition(self, parentposition, childsize, octantindex): """ Calculates the world position of a child node relative to its parent. """ # offsetX = (octantIndex & 1) childSize # offsetY = (octantIndex & 2) childSize / 2 # offsetZ = (octantIndex & 4) childSize / 4 # Note: The source divides by 2 and 4, which is equivalent to shifting bits # if childSize is a power of 2, but generally it's: # offsetZ = (octantIndex & 4) (childSize / 4) offsetx = (octantindex & 1) childsize offsety = (octantindex & 2) (childsize / 2) offsetz = (octantindex & 4) (childsize / 4) return (parentposition[0] + offsetx, parentposition[1] + offsety, parentposition[2] + offsetz) def addvoxelmeshdata(self, position, size, color): """ Adds vertices and indices for a voxel cube to the mesh buffers. """ localvertices = [ (-0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (0.5, 0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, -0.5) ] vertexstartindex = len(self.vertices) for vx, vy, vz in localvertices: self.vertices.append(( position[0] + vx size, position[1] + vy size, position[2] + vz size)) # Define triangle indices for 6 faces (2 triangles each) # Front (0,2,1, 0,3,2), Top (2,3,6, 3,7,6), Right (1,2,6, 1,6,5), # Left (0,7,3, 0,4,7), Bottom (0,1,5, 0,5,4), Back (4,5,6, 4,6,7) indices = [ 0, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2, # Front 2, 3, 6, 3, 7, 6, # Top 1, 2, 6, 1, 6, 5, # Right 0, 7, 3, 0, 4, 7, # Left 0, 1, 5, 0, 5, 4, # Bottom 4, 5, 6, 4, 6, 7 # Back ] for idx in indices: self.triangles.append(vertexstartindex + idx) def initialize(self): """ Initializes the voxel grid with test data and builds the DAG. """ gridsize = 1 << self.griddepth self.voxelgrid = [[[0] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] for in range(gridsize)] for x in range(gridsize): for y in range(gridsize): for z in range(gridsize): self.voxelgrid[x][y][z] = (x + y + z) % 2 self.rootnode = self.builddag(self.voxelgrid, self.griddepth) gridDepth: The logarithm of the grid dimension. Typical values depend on resolution requirements. For a 256^3 grid, gridDepth is 8. subtreeCache: A dictionary used to cache and lookup existing nodes by their subtree key to enable reuse. Hash Collisions: The method uses SHA256 hashing for subtree keys. While extremely unlikely, hash collisions could cause incorrect node merging. The source uses SHA256 to mitigate this. Homogeneity Check: The ishomogeneous check is critical for leaf detection. If not implemented efficiently, it can dominate runtime for large homogeneous regions. Memory Overhead: The subtreeCache dictionary can consume significant memory if the voxel grid has high entropy (few identical subtrees). In such cases, the compression benefit is reduced. LOD Generation: The source mentions downsampling for LODs by marking a voxel as containing geometry if any composing voxels do. This must be applied before DAG construction if LODs are required. Time Complexity: The construction time is proportional to the number of voxels N^3 plus the cost of hashing and dictionary lookups. Hashing a subtree of size S takes O(S) time. In the worst case (no identical subtrees), the complexity is O(N^3). In the best case (highly repetitive geometry), it is faster due to cache hits. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is proportional to the number of unique subtrees in the DAG. For highly repetitive scenes, this is significantly less than O(N^3). For random noise, it approaches O(N^3) due to the overhead of the cache and node structures. Measured Performance: The source does not provide specific benchmark numbers for construction time or memory savings. It notes that SVOs reduce memory overhead compared to naive grids, and DAGs further reduce it by merging identical subtrees. Strengths: Significant memory savings for scenes with repetitive geometry. Real-time decoding is possible because the DAG structure is similar to an SVO. Limitations: Construction can be slow for large, non-repetitive grids due to hashing and dictionary overhead. The cache can grow large for high-entropy data. When to Use: Ideal for voxel-based games or simulations with repetitive structures (e.g., terrain, buildings). Not ideal for highly dynamic, non-repetitive data where construction overhead outweighs memory benefits. The concept of Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) was introduced to address the memory inefficiency of dense voxel grids. Kampe et al. [13] realized that merging identical leaves could significantly compact the final level of an SVO. The extension to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) by merging identical subtrees (not just leaves) further reduces memory usage. This method is used in voxel engines and real-time rendering applications where memory efficiency and fast traversal are critical. name: Octree Raymarching
head: Stack-based Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal with Fixed-Point Scale, Octree Voxel Raycasting for Hit and Add
body: Octree Raymarching is a ray traversal algorithm for a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) that uses a fixed-point-like scale representation to step through the tree hierarchy, computing hit position, normal, and depth. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal (State Machine) by using a stack-based approach with explicit scale management and bit-manipulation for coordinate alignment, rather than a state machine or recursive descent. It solves the problem of efficiently finding the first occupied voxel or empty space boundary in a sparse 3D volume for raycasting applications. Inputs: Ray origin rayOrigin, ray direction rayDirection, octree root node, maximum traversal scale MaxScale (23), and current target depth currentDepth. Outputs: Hit position hitPosition, surface normal normal, depth minT, and node index idx. Data Structures: StackEntry: Struct containing uint64t offset (parent node index) and float maxT (remaining ray segment length). rayStack: Array of StackEntry structs, size MaxScale + 1. BitCount: Precomputed lookup table for counting set bits in 7-bit integers (used for sibling counting). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Direction Normalization: If any component of rayDirection (dx, dy, dz) has absolute value less than 1e-4f, clamp it to ±1e-4f (preserving sign) to avoid division by zero. Calculate inverse step sizes: dTx = 1.0f / -|dx| dTy = 1.0f / -|dy| dTz = 1.0f / -|dz| 2. Initial Offset and Octant Calculation: Calculate base offsets based on ray origin (ox, oy, oz): bTx = dTx \cdot ox bTy = dTy \cdot oy bTz = dTz \cdot oz Determine octantMask based on ray direction signs: If dx > 0: octantMask ^= 1, bTx = 3.0f \cdot dTx - bTx. If dy > 0: octantMask ^= 2, bTy = 3.0f \cdot dTy - bTy. If dz > 0: octantMask ^= 4, bTz = 3.0f \cdot dTz - bTz. 3. Ray-Box Intersection (Root): Calculate entry and exit distances minT and maxT: minT = \max(2.0f \cdot dTx - bTx, \max(2.0f \cdot dTy - bTy, 2.0f \cdot dTz - bTz)) maxT = \min(dTx - bTx, \min(dTy - bTy, dTz - bTz)) Clamp minT to 0.0f. If minT > maxT, return false (no intersection). 4. Initialization: Initialize variables: current = 0, parent = 0, idx = 0, posX = 1.0f, posY = 1.0f, posZ = 1.0f, scale = MaxScale - 1, scaleExp2 = 0.5f. Determine initial child index idx and positions posX, posY, posZ by comparing ray entry points to the center of the root node: If 1.5f \cdot dTx - bTx > minT: idx ^= 1, posX = 1.5f. If 1.5f \cdot dTy - bTy > minT: idx ^= 2, posY = 1.5f. If 1.5f \cdot dTz - bTz > minT: idx ^= 4, posZ = 1.5f. 5. Main Traversal Loop: While scale < MaxScale: Load Node: If current == 0, load current = tree[parent]. If parent >= treeSize, return false (end of tree). Leaf/Target Depth Check: If depth >= currentDepth or node is a leaf: If node is active (node->isActive): Compute hit hitPosition = rayOrigin + rayDir minT. Compute normal. Set hitAdd = false. Return true. If node is not active: Compute hit hitPosition. Compute normal. Set hitAdd = true. Return true. Internal Node Processing: Calculate corner distances: cornerTX = posX dTx - bTx, cornerTY = posY dTy - bTy, cornerTZ = posZ dTz - bTz. maxTC = \min(cornerTX, \min(cornerTY, cornerTZ)). childShift = idx \oplus octantMask. childMasks = current \ll childShift. Hit Check: If (childMasks & 0x8000) (highest bit set, indicating a child exists in the target octant) AND minT <= maxT: If maxTC rayScale >= scaleExp2: Compute hit, normal, depth, index. Return true. Pruning: maxTV = \min(maxT, maxTC). half = scaleExp2 0.5f. Center Distances: centerTX = half dTx + cornerTX, etc.. If minT <= maxTV: If !(childMasks & 0x80) (no children in the current octant): Break loop. Push to Stack: rayStack[scale].offset = parent, rayStack[scale].maxT = maxT. Sibling Count: siblingCount = BitCount[childMasks & 127]. Child Offset: childOffset = current \gg 17. Update Parent: parent += childOffset + siblingCount. If current & 0x10000 (additional children flag), parent += siblingCount. Descend: Reset idx = 0, scale--, scaleExp2 = half. Update Position/Index: Based on centerTX/TY/TZ > minT, update idx and posX/Y/Z similarly to Step 4. maxT = maxTV, current = 0. Continue loop. 6. Backtracking (Step Mask): If the loop continues or exits without returning: Calculate stepMask: If cornerTX <= maxTC: stepMask ^= 1, posX -= scaleExp2. If cornerTY <= maxTC: stepMask ^= 2, posY -= scaleExp2. If cornerTZ <= maxTC: stepMask ^= 4, posZ -= scaleExp2. minT = maxTC. idx ^= stepMask. If (idx & stepMask) != 0: Calculate differingBits using floatBitsToUint on position differences to determine scale change. Update scale and scaleExp2 from differingBits. Update parent and maxT from rayStack[scale]. Calculate shift amounts shX, shY, shZ. Update posX, posY, posZ by shifting back. Update idx from shifted positions. current = 0. 7. Final Hit Calculation: If scale >= MaxScale, return false. Otherwise: rhit = rayOrigin + minT rayDirection. Add OctreeLoc to rhit (apply offset). Compute normal by comparing tcorner components: tX = dTx (posX + scaleExp2) - bTx, etc. Set normal to axis-aligned vector based on max component (e.g., if tX is max, rnormal = (1, 0, 0) or similar). Flip normal components based on octantMask: if (octantMask & 1) == 0, rnormal.x = -rnormal.x, etc.. rnormal = -rnormal. Offset hit: rhit += 1e-4f rnormal. Set rdepth = minT and ridx = idx \oplus octantMask \oplus 7 if pointers provided. Return true. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def octreeraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, tree, treesize, maxscale, currentdepth): # 1. Normalize Ray Direction dx, dy, dz = raydirection if abs(dx) < 1e-4: dx = 1e-4 if dx >= 0 else -1e-4 if abs(dy) < 1e-4: dy = 1e-4 if dy >= 0 else -1e-4 if abs(dz) < 1e-4: dz = 1e-4 if dz >= 0 else -1e-4 # 2. Inverse Step Sizes dTx = 1.0 / -abs(dx) dTy = 1.0 / -abs(dy) dTz = 1.0 / -abs(dz) ox, oy, oz = rayorigin bTx = dTx ox bTy = dTy oy bTz = dTz oz # 3. Octant Mask and Base Offsets octantMask = 0 if dx > 0: octantMask ^= 1 bTx = 3.0 dTx - bTx if dy > 0: octantMask ^= 2 bTy = 3.0 dTy - bTy if dz > 0: octantMask ^= 4 bTz = 3.0 dTz - bTz # 4. Ray-Box Intersection (Root) minT = max(2.0 dTx - bTx, max(2.0 dTy - bTy, 2.0 dTz - bTz)) maxT = min(dTx - bTx, min(dTy - bTy, dTz - bTz)) minT = max(0.0, minT) if minT > maxT: return False # 5. Initialization current = 0 parent = 0 idx = 0 posX, posY, posZ = 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 scale = maxscale - 1 scaleExp2 = 0.5 # Initial idx/pos determination if 1.5 dTx - bTx > minT: idx ^= 1 posX = 1.5 if 1.5 dTy - bTy > minT: idx ^= 2 posY = 1.5 if 1.5 dTz - bTz > minT: idx ^= 4 posZ = 1.5 # Data structures rayStack = [{'offset': 0, 'maxT': 0.0} for in range(maxscale + 1)] BitCount = [bin(i).count('1') for i in range(128)] # 6. Main Loop while scale < maxscale: if current == 0: current = tree[parent] if parent >= treesize: return False # Check Leaf/Target Depth (metadata access assumed from tree node) isleaf, isactive, depth = getnodeinfo(current) # if depth >= currentdepth or isleaf: hitpos = rayorigin + raydirection minT normal = computenormal(hitpos, current) # return True, hitpos, normal, minT, idx ^ octantMask ^ 7 # Internal Node cornerTX = posX dTx - bTx cornerTY = posY dTy - bTy cornerTZ = posZ dTz - bTz maxTC = min(cornerTX, min(cornerTY, cornerTZ)) childShift = idx ^ octantMask childMasks = current << childShift # Hit Check if (childMasks & 0x8000) and minT <= maxT: if maxTC rayScale >= scaleExp2: # rayScale is from evidence hitpos = rayorigin + raydirection minT normal = computenormal(hitpos, current) # return True, hitpos, normal, minT, idx ^ octantMask ^ 7 maxTV = min(maxT, maxTC) half = scaleExp2 0.5 centerTX = half dTx + cornerTX centerTY = half dTy + cornerTY centerTZ = half dTz + cornerTZ if minT <= maxTV: if not (childMasks & 0x80): break # Push Stack rayStack[scale]['offset'] = parent rayStack[scale]['maxT'] = maxT siblingCount = BitCount[childMasks & 127] childOffset = current >> 17 parent += childOffset + siblingCount if current & 0x10000: parent += siblingCount idx = 0 scale -= 1 scaleExp2 = half # Update idx/pos if centerTX > minT: idx ^= 1 posX = 1.5 if centerTY > minT: idx ^= 2 posY = 1.5 if centerTZ > minT: idx ^= 4 posZ = 1.5 maxT = maxTV current = 0 continue # 7. Backtracking stepMask = 0 if cornerTX <= maxTC: stepMask ^= 1 posX -= scaleExp2 if cornerTY <= maxTC: stepMask ^= 2 posY -= scaleExp2 if cornerTZ <= maxTC: stepMask ^= 4 posZ -= scaleExp2 minT = maxTC idx ^= stepMask if (idx & stepMask) != 0: # floatBitsToUint equivalent for scale alignment import struct def floattouint(f): return struct.unpack('I', struct.pack('f', f))[0] # differingBits logic from evidence: scale changes based on position differences scale = maxscale - 1 scaleExp2 = 0.5 # Pop Stack parent = rayStack[scale]['offset'] maxT = rayStack[scale]['maxT'] # Shift positions (standard bit alignment for grid boundaries) shX = int(math.log2(scaleExp2)) if scaleExp2 > 0 else 0 posX = posX >> shX posY = posY >> shX posZ = posZ >> shX idx = computeidxfrompos(posX, posY, posZ) # current = 0 # 8. Final Hit if scale >= maxscale: return False hitpos = rayorigin + raydirection minT # Compute Normal tX = dTx (posX + scaleExp2) - bTx tY = dTy (posY + scaleExp2) - bTy tZ = dTz (posZ + scaleExp2) - bTz maxt = max(tX, max(tY, tZ)) if maxt == tX: normal = [1, 0, 0] elif maxt == tY: normal = [0, 1, 0] else: normal = [0, 0, 1] if (octantMask & 1) == 0: normal[0] = -normal[0] if (octantMask & 2) == 0: normal[1] = -normal[1] if (octantMask & 4) == 0: normal[2] = -normal[2] normal = [-n for n in normal] hitpos = [hitpos[i] + 1e-4 normal[i] for i in range(3)] return True, hitpos, normal, minT, idx ^ octantMask ^ 7 A variant that tracks the closest active voxel and the closest empty space node encountered during traversal. It initializes closestHitDistance and closestEmptyDistance to infinity. If depth >= currentDepth and hitDistance < closestEmptyDistance, it updates hoverInfo to point to the empty space node and sets closestEmptyDistance. This is used for interaction/hover effects rather than simple hit detection. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of nodes traversed along the ray path. In sparse volumes, this is significantly faster than dense voxel traversal. The fixed-point scale and bit-manipulation allow for efficient navigation without recursion overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires a stack of size MaxScale + 1 (typically 24 entries). The tree itself is stored in a flat array. Performance: Efficient on GPU due to lack of recursion and use of bitwise operations. Precision issues are mitigated by fixed-point-like scale representation and bit-shifting for position alignment. Strengths: Handles large sparse volumes efficiently; supports hit and add (empty space) queries; stable precision. Limitations: Requires careful handling of ray direction near-zero components; stack depth is limited by MaxScale. This method is described in the unofficial source by cianjinks, which implements a Sparse Voxel Octree traversal in C++. The technique relies on fixed-point arithmetic principles adapted for floating-point ray tracing to maintain precision across octree levels. cianjinks/Sparse-Voxel-Octree, https://github.com/cianjinks/Sparse-Voxel-Octree, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GitHub - saurlax/modelvoxelizer: A 3D model voxelization tool that..., https://github.com/saurlax/modelvoxelizer, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation
head: SVO Ray March, SVO Ray Marcher, Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Tracing
body: SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation is a ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) that uses an explicit stack to manage traversal state, enabling efficient navigation through the hierarchical structure to find voxel intersections. It differs from parent methods by decoupling the traversal logic from the ray's parametric distance, using a fixed-point-like scale representation to step through the tree levels, and explicitly managing node validity and corner positions via a stack of nodeinfot elements. This approach allows for robust handling of empty space and early termination based on pixel error thresholds. Inputs: raypos: The origin of the ray (\mathbf{p}). raydir: The direction of the ray (\mathbf{d}), normalized. svotree: The Sparse Voxel Octree data structure. minraylength2: A minimum ray length constant added to the calculated distance. rayScale2: A parameter related to ray step size or resolution, used for pixel error calculation. Outputs: outt: The distance to the hit voxel along the ray. outnormal: The normal of the hit voxel face. bool: True if a hit was found, false otherwise. The algorithm relies on a stack to store traversal state. nodeinfot parent: Index or pointer to the parent node in the SVO. corner: A 3-bit integer (or equivalent) representing the corner of the current node within its parent. lower: A 3D vector (\mathbb{R}^3) representing the absolute lower bound of the current node in world space. Stack A dynamic array or linked list of nodeinfot elements. Operations: push, pop, back (access top element), size (get current depth). rayScale2: Used in svovoxelpixelerror to determine the threshold for pixel error. minraylength2: A minimum ray length constant added to the calculated distance. 1. Initialization: Initialize an empty stack stack. Determine the root node of the SVO. Calculate the initial lower bound for the root node (typically the origin of the SVO space). Push the root node onto the stack. Set rayisoutside = false. 2. Traversal Loop: While stack.size > 0: Let level = stack.size. Calculate scale = 1.0 / (1 << level). Let current = stack.back(). Determine node validity: Check if the node is null using svotreeisnull. Check if the node is a leaf using svotreeisleaff3. Check if the node has children using svotreehaschildren. Check if the node contains a voxel using svotreevoxelexists. If rayisoutside is true: Pop the stack: svostackpop(&stack). If the stack is empty, break and return false. Retrieve the new current from stack.back(). Adjust lower: lower -= cornerincrement0 scale, where cornerincrement0 is the unit vector corresponding to the popped node's corner. Attempt to move to the next corner in the outface direction: nextcorner1 = movecorner(current.corner, outface). If nextcorner1 is valid: Set rayisoutside = false. Update current.parent and current.corner to the popped node's parent and nextcorner1. Adjust lower: lower -= cornerincrement0 scale; lower += cornerincrement1 scale, where cornerincrement1 corresponds to nextcorner1. Continue to the next iteration. If nextcorner1 is invalid (boundary of parent): Set rayisoutside = true. Continue to the next iteration (loop will pop again). If the current node has a voxel (svotreevoxelexists) and the ray intersects the voxel data (svointersectsvoxeldataf3): Calculate direction bounds: dirbounds = svocalculatedirboundsf3(lower, lower + scale, raydir). Check for pixel error: error = svovoxelpixelerror(sdistancef3(raypos, dirlower), rayScale2, level). If error < threshold: Record hit distance: outt = minraylength2 + sdistancef3(raypos, dirlower). Compute normal from the opposite face of outface. Return true. If the node is a leaf (svotreeisleaff3): Record hit distance and normal. Return true. If the node has children (svotreehaschildren): Push the current node onto the stack: svostackpush(&stack, &current). Calculate the next corner for the child node: nextcorner = svopushcalculatenextcornerf3(cubenormalizeddir, dirlower, scale, t1). Update lower for the child node: nextlower = lower + (cornerincrement childscale), where childscale = 1.0 / (1 << (level + 1)). Get the child node descriptor: current = svotreegetchild(addressspace, current, nextcorner). Update lower = nextlower. Continue to the next iteration. 3. Termination: If the stack is empty and no hit was found, return false. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def svoraymarchstackbased(raypos, raydir, svotree, minraylength2, rayScale2): stack = [] rootnode = svotree.getroot() rootlower = svotree.getlowerbound() current = NodeInfo(parent=None, corner=0, lower=rootlower) stack.append(current) rayisoutside = False while len(stack) > 0: level = len(stack) scale = 1.0 / (1 << level) current = stack[-1] isnull = svotreeisnull(svotree, current) isleaf = svotreeisleaff3(svotree, current) haschildren = svotreehaschildren(svotree, current) hasvoxel = svotreevoxelexists(svotree, current) if rayisoutside: stack.pop() if len(stack) == 0: return False, None, None current = stack[-1] cornerincrement0 = getcornerunitvector(current.corner) current.lower -= cornerincrement0 scale outface = getoutface(raydir, current.corner) nextcorner1 = movecorner(current.corner, outface) if nextcorner1 is not None: rayisoutside = False current.corner = nextcorner1 cornerincrement1 = getcornerunitvector(nextcorner1) current.lower -= cornerincrement0 scale current.lower += cornerincrement1 scale continue else: rayisoutside = True continue if hasvoxel and svointersectsvoxeldataf3(svotree, current): dirbounds = svocalculatedirboundsf3(current.lower, current.lower + scale, raydir) error = svovoxelpixelerror(sdistancef3(raypos, dirbounds.dirlower), rayScale2, level) if error < threshold: outt = minraylength2 + sdistancef3(raypos, dirbounds.dirlower) outnormal = computenormalfromface(oppositeface(outface)) return True, outt, outnormal if isleaf: outt = minraylength2 + sdistancef3(raypos, dirbounds.dirlower) outnormal = computenormalfromface(oppositeface(outface)) return True, outt, outnormal if haschildren: stack.append(current) nextcorner = svopushcalculatenextcornerf3(cubenormalizeddir, dirbounds.dirlower, scale, t1) childscale = 1.0 / (1 << (level + 1)) nextlower = current.lower + (cornerincrement childscale) current = svotreegetchild(addressspace, current, nextcorner) current.lower = nextlower continue return False, None, None realazthat/landscapes, https://github.com/realazthat/landscapes, fetched 2026-10-26
