name: Octree Ray Marching with Brick Interpolation and Early Termination
body: This method traverses a sparse voxel octree using fixed-size bricks to render volume data, balancing GPU bus/cache and rasterization bottlenecks. It differs from single-stage bricking by storing unmodified scalar values in brick textures and computing RGB\alpha values post-interpolatively in the fragment shader, avoiding time-consuming texture regeneration when the transfer function changes. It builds on Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Tracing and differs from SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation by using brick interpolation and early termination thresholds. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, volume scalar data, octree structure, brick textures, transfer function. Outputs: Accumulated color and opacity per pixel. Data Structures: 1. Traversal State (per ray/pixel): rayWorldPosition (world space), rayBrickPosition (brick-local), octTreeNode (pointer), nodeSize (world units), voxelHalfSize (world units), traversalCount, nodeListTraversalCount, pushedNodeCount, curDepth, projVoxelSize, parentVoxelSize, accumulatedOpacity, extents (VolExtentMin/VolExtentMax). Parameters: projVoxelSize: Projected voxel size in world coordinates. Used for interpolation ratio. parentVoxelSize: Voxel size at the parent octree level. Used in interpolation denominator. kChildNodeSizeScalar: Scalar multiplier applied to nodeSize and voxelHalfSize on each descent step. MaxNodesToPushThisFrame: Maximum number of nodes allowed to be pushed to the usage list per frame. maxNodesPerPixelBlock: Threshold for nodeListTraversalCount before it resets to 0. startPushingNodes, stopPushingNodes: Range boundaries for pushing nodes to the usage list. Steps: 1. Reset traversal state: set octTreeNode to rootOctTreeNode, extents to VolExtentMin/VolExtentMax, nodeSize to 1.0f, voxelHalfSize to RootVoxelHalfSize. 2. Compute ray containment test: test1 = sign(rayWorldPosition - VolExtentMin), test2 = sign(VolExtentMax - rayWorldPosition), inside = dot(test1, test2). 3. Increment traversal counters: ++traversalCount, ++nodeListTraversalCount. If nodeListTraversalCount >= maxNodesPerPixelBlock, reset to 0. 4. Descent: compute brickOffset = rayBrickPosition kTreeN, clamp to childOffset = clamp(uvec3(brickOffset), 0u, 1u), update rayBrickPosition = brickOffset - vec3(childOffset). 5. Update extents: nodeExtentMin += (vec3(childOffset) nodeSize), nodeExtentMax -= ((vec3(1.0f) - vec3(childOffset)) nodeSize). 6. Fetch next octree node: octTreeNode = texelFetch(OctTreeSampler, octTreeNodePtr, 0). 7. name: Two-staged Space-Skipping with Bricking and Octrees
head: Bricking with octree refinement, Two-stage space-skipping
body: This method balances GPU bottlenecks by dividing space-skipping into two stages: coarse division using bricking to address bus and texture cache limitations, and fine division using octrees within bricks to address the rasterization bottleneck. It differs from Tong et al.'s bricking technique by storing unmodified scalar values in textures and using a fragment shader for post-interpolative RGB\alpha lookup, avoiding time-consuming texture regeneration when the transfer function changes. Inputs: 3D scalar volume data, transfer function, camera parameters. Outputs: 2D rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Bricks: 3D texture chunks of size b \times b \times b voxels. Content: Unmodified scalar voxel values. Overlap: n voxels in every direction to support interpolation. Memory Overhead: \approx (3 \cdot n / b) \cdot 100\%. 2. Octrees: Stored within each brick. Structure: Hierarchical subdivision of the brick volume. Content: Empty/non-empty status of sub-volumes to enable fine-grained skipping. Parameters: Brick size (b): Must be equal to or smaller than the available texture memory size. Overlap (n): Nearest neighbor: n=0. Trilinear interpolation: n=1 voxel in every direction. Pre-integrated rendering or on-the-fly gradient calculation: n increased by another voxel in every direction. Texture Memory Management: If volume exceeds texture memory, bricks are loaded sequentially from main memory into texture memory during rendering. Steps: 1. Brick Partitioning: Divide the volume data set into chunks called bricks. Ensure adjacent bricks overlap by n voxels to satisfy the interpolation kernel requirements. 2. Octree Construction: Construct an octree within each brick to identify empty regions at a finer granularity than the brick level. 3. Texture Loading: Load bricks into video memory as 3D textures. If the total data exceeds available texture memory, swap bricks between main memory and texture memory as needed. Note: Many graphics cards require 3D texture sizes to be powers of 2; handle non-divisible dimensions by adding partially empty bricks or using smaller rest-bricks. 4. Ray Traversal (Stage 1 - Coarse): Traverse the volume using the brick structure. Skip entire bricks that are empty or do not intersect the view frustum. This addresses bus and texture cache bottlenecks. 5. Early Ray Termination (Stage 1): Apply early ray termination to each brick to alleviate fragment shader load, particularly beneficial for highly-filled data sets. 6. Ray Traversal (Stage 2 - Fine): Within active bricks, use the octree to skip empty sub-volumes. This addresses the rasterization bottleneck by reducing the number of pixels accessed. 7. Rendering: For each sample point, lookup the scalar value from the brick texture. Use a fragment shader program to post-interpolatively lookup RGB\alpha values based on the current transfer function. Pitfalls: Triangle Throughput Bottleneck: Space-skipping techniques may increase the amount of triangles considerably. If the triangle count becomes too high, it becomes a limiting factor for frame rate, potentially overloading the triangle throughput bottleneck when the rasterization bottleneck is lifted. Bottleneck Balance: The two stages (bricking and octree) must be balanced because lifting one bottleneck may overload another (e.g., rasterization vs. triangle throughput). Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Addresses bus and texture cache bottlenecks via bricking, and rasterization bottlenecks via octrees. Strengths: Handles data sets exceeding texture memory; allows runtime transfer function changes without texture regeneration; reduces fragment shader load via early ray termination. Limitations: Risk of triangle throughput bottleneck if space-skipping increases triangle count too much; texture compression (S3TC, etc.) is unsuitable for 12- or 16-bit scalar medical data, necessitating this approach. When to use: When rendering large scalar volumes on GPUs with limited texture memory and when transfer function flexibility is required. When not to use: When triangle throughput is the primary bottleneck and space-skipping would significantly increase triangle count. Origin: Proposed by Danny Ruijters in 2006. History: Builds on Eckhardt's bricking technique [Eck98] and Tong et al.'s bricking technique [TWTT99]. The method analyzes bottlenecks in the graphics pipeline (bus, texture cache, rasterization, triangle throughput) to justify the two-stage approach. Usage: Used in GPU volume rendering, particularly for medical data where scalar values are 12- or 16-bit and transfer functions need frequent adjustment. Optimizing GPU Volume Rendering, Danny Ruijters, https://dannyruijters.nl/docs/OptimizingGPUVolumeRenderingfinal.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Stackless GPU Raycasting with Octree Traversal
head: Stackless octree traversal on the GPU
body: This method performs volume rendering by traversing a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) on the GPU without using a stack, computing the volume rendering integral in front-to-back order. It solves the problem of efficient memory access and traversal overhead in sparse volumetric data by combining space-skipping (via empty node detection) with adaptive sampling density. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Two-staged Space-Skipping with Bricking and Octrees by performing neighbor lookups implicitly on-the-fly using the octree's regular structure, rather than relying on precomputed neighbor pointers or a two-stage bricking pipeline. It builds on the concepts of Octree Ray Marching with Brick Interpolation and Early Termination but replaces explicit brick interpolation with adaptive sampling based on leaf resolution. The algorithm maintains the state of the current ray segment (entry point t{min}, current node pointer, current bounding box, and octree level) in registers. It traverses the octree from the root to the leaf containing the current sampling point, accumulates color/opacity if the leaf is non-empty, and moves to the next leaf via implicit neighbor calculation when the ray exits the current box. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (in texture coordinates, normalized to [0,1]^3). Spatial Index Texture: A 3D texture storing the octree structure. Each texel is a float4 (or vec4). Leaf Data Texture: A 3D texture storing the actual volume data (density/color) for non-empty leaves. Transfer Function: A 2D texture mapping density and octree level to color and opacity. Outputs: fragment.color: Accumulated RGBA color. fragment.depth: Depth of the first opaque surface encountered (or far plane). Spatial Index Texture Texel Layout (float4): xyz: Pointer to the first child node (for inner nodes) or to the leaf data (for leaf nodes). Stored as a 3D coordinate offset in the texture. w: Tag/Status. If w indicates an Inner Node: The xyz components point to children. The children are stored consecutively in the texture. The offset to the i-th child (where i \in [0,7]) is calculated as dot3(s, float3(1, 2, 4)) texelsz, where s is the child index vector. If w indicates a Leaf Node: The xyz components point to the leaf data in the Leaf Data Texture. The w component encodes the octree level of the neighbor (see Neighbor Traversal). Empty Node: A specific marker (e.g., w=0 or null pointer) indicating no children or data. Null Pointer: Used to terminate traversal. Neighbor Pointers: Neighbor pointers are not stored explicitly in the index texel for all 6 neighbors in the primary traversal path described in the code snippet, but the text notes that leaf nodes use RGB components to point to leaf information and 6 consecutive texels store pointers to neighbors. However, the stackless traversal logic described relies on implicit neighbor calculation for the exit face to avoid extra texture fetches. The text states: "computing neighbor information on-the-fly... exploiting the regular structure of the octree." The w component of a leaf node's index texel stores the octree level of the neighbor in the direction of the exit face. This allows the shader to compute the neighbor's bounding box without fetching the neighbor's index texel first. Early Termination Threshold: Opacity \alpha{thresh} = 0.99. If accumulated opacity exceeds this, the ray terminates. Box Normalization: All computations are done in texture coordinates. The octree subdivides the unit cube [0,1]^3. Sampling: Adaptive. Step size is determined by the resolution of the current leaf (box dimension). The following pseudocode implements the fragment shader logic. It assumes standard GLSL/HLSL-like syntax for vector operations and texture sampling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. fragment.color = float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) fragment.depth = FARPLANE nodeptr = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Current node position in spatial index texture octreelevel = 0 boxmin = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) boxdim = float3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) tmin = ray.tnear # Initial ray entry t while (not isnull(nodeptr) and fragment.color.a < 1.0): # 1. Find leaf containing current sampling point P P = ray.origin + ray.direction tmin # Fetch current node node = tex3d(spatialindex, nodeptr) # 2. Down Traversal: Descend to the leaf containing P while (isinner(node.w)): boxdim = boxdim / 2.0 boxmid = boxmin + boxdim # Determine child index based on P's position relative to boxmid # s[i] = 1 if P[i] >= boxmid[i], else 0 s = step(boxmid, P) # Update boxmin to the child's origin boxmin = boxmin + s boxdim # Calculate child offset in texture # Children are ordered: x, y, z bits map to 1, 2, 4 childoffset = dot3(s, float3(1.0, 2.0, 4.0)) texelsz nodeptr = node.xyz + float4(childoffset, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Fetch child node node = tex3d(spatialindex, nodeptr) octreelevel = octreelevel + 1 # Clip ray to current box to find exit face # Returns: tmax (exit t), exitfaceidx (0=x+, 1=y+, 2=z+, 3=x-, 4=y-, 5=z-), exitdir (boxtmax, exitfaceidx, exitdir) = boxclip(ray, tmin, tfar, boxmin, boxdim) # 3. Accumulate if non-empty if (not isempty(node.w)): # Access leaf data dataptr = node.xyz # Adaptive sampling: step size matches leaf resolution # Accumulate color and opacity (fragment.color, fragment.depth) = accumulate( fragment.color, ray, tmin, boxtmax, dataptr, boxmin, boxmin + boxdim) # Check for early termination if (fragment.color.a >= 0.99): break # Terminate ray # 4. Move to Neighbor if ray exits current block # Note: If ray terminated due to opacity, we break above. # If ray is still active, check if it exited the box. if (tmin >= boxtmax): # Compute neighbor offset implicitly # Shift box origin in direction of exit face # Neighbor level is stored in node.w (for leaf) or computed for inner? # The text implies neighbor level info is available. # For leaf nodes, node.w contains neighbor level neighborlevel = node.w # Update state for neighbor # Shift boxmin by exitdir boxdim boxmin = boxmin + exitdir boxdim # If neighbor is coarser, coarsen the box if (neighborlevel < octreelevel): boxdim = exp2(-neighborlevel) # Snap boxmin to neighbor grid boxmin = floor(boxmin / boxdim) boxdim octreelevel = neighborlevel # Fetch neighbor node pointer # The text mentions neighbor pointers are stored, but also says # "computing neighbor information on-the-fly". # The code snippet shows: # neighboroffset = float3(1+exitfaceidx, 0, 0) texelsz; # This implies a specific layout or lookup. # However, the text emphasizes implicit computation. # Re-reading snippet: "neighbor=tex3d(spatialindex, node.xyz+neighboroffset)" # This suggests neighbor pointers ARE stored in the index texture # adjacent to the leaf data pointer or within the leaf's index entry. # Let's follow the snippet's explicit neighbor fetch logic: # exitfaceidx 0-5 maps to neighbor directions. # The snippet uses a simplified offset calculation. # We assume the spatial index texture contains neighbor pointers # in a predictable location relative to the current node/data pointer. # Correcting based on snippet: # neighboroffset is calculated based on exitfaceidx. # The snippet uses: neighboroffset = float3(1+exitfaceidx, 0, 0) texelsz # This seems to be a placeholder or specific to a 1D neighbor array. # Given the text "6 consecutive texels storing pointers to neighbors", # we assume we fetch the neighbor index. neighborptr = getneighborptr(node, exitfaceidx) # Helper to fetch from neighbor array nodeptr = neighborptr.xyz octreelevel = neighborptr.w # Update level from neighbor tag boxdim = exp2(-octreelevel) boxmin = floor(boxmin / boxdim) boxdim tmin = boxtmax else: # Ray is still inside the current leaf, advance tmin # Adaptive step size based on boxdim tmin = tmin + boxdim.x # Assuming isotropic or max dim for step # Note: The snippet doesn't show explicit tmin update for non-exit case, # but accumulation requires stepping. # In adaptive sampling, we usually step by boxdim. # If the ray doesn't exit, we might just accumulate once per leaf? # The text says "adapting sampling density to brick resolution". # Usually this means multiple samples per leaf or one sample per leaf. # The snippet accumulates between tmin and boxtmax. # If it doesn't exit, tmin should advance. # However, the loop structure suggests we process the whole leaf segment # in one go if we don't exit? No, "while" loop continues. # If we don't exit, we stay in the same leaf. # To avoid infinite loop, tmin must advance. # Standard approach: tmin = boxtmax is wrong if not exited. # Let's assume the accumulation covers the segment [tmin, boxtmax]. # If not exited, we are done with this leaf? No, ray might continue. # Actually, if we are in a leaf, we accumulate the whole leaf segment # in one shot if we assume constant density? # Or we step. The text says "adapting sampling density". # Let's assume one accumulation pass per leaf entry. break # Exit leaf processing, next iteration handles neighbor or next leaf def boxclip(ray, tmin, tfar, boxmin, boxdim): # Standard slab method t0 = (boxmin - ray.origin) / ray.direction t1 = (boxmin + boxdim - ray.origin) / ray.direction tenter = max(min(t0), min(t1)) texit = min(max(t0), max(t1)) tmax = min(texit, tfar) # Determine exit face # Check which component caused texit #... implementation details... return (tmax, exitfaceidx, exitdir) def accumulate(color, ray, tstart, tend, dataptr, boxmin, boxmax): # Sample density at midpoint or adaptive steps # Map density to color/opacity via transfer function # Blend into color return (newcolor, newdepth) Null Pointers: The last leaf data texel always contains a NULL pointer. This is used to simplify handling of rays that do not exit from the current box (e.g., terminate due to opacity threshold). If traversal reaches a null pointer, the loop terminates. Coarser Neighbors: When moving to a neighbor with a coarser octree level, the current box must be coarsened. This is done by updating boxdim to 2^{-\text{neighbor\level}} and snapping boxmin to the neighbor's grid: \lfloor \text{box\min} / \text{box\dim} \rfloor \cdot \text{box\dim}. Precision: All computations are in texture coordinates (unit cube). Floating-point precision issues may arise at deep octree levels. Termination: Rays that terminate due to the opacity threshold (0.99) must not continue to neighbors. The null pointer check and the opacity check inside the loop handle this. Time Complexity: O(k) per ray, where k is the number of non-empty leaves traversed. The traversal is stackless, reducing memory overhead and instruction count compared to stack-based methods. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the octree structure, where N is the number of nodes. The spatial index is stored in a 3D texture. Performance: The method is efficient for sparse data because it skips empty space. Adaptive sampling reduces the number of texture fetches for large empty or uniform regions. The on-the-fly neighbor calculation reduces texture memory bandwidth usage compared to methods storing explicit neighbor pointers for all nodes. Strengths: No stack required; efficient memory access; adaptive sampling; early termination. Limitations: Requires a well-constructed octree; implicit neighbor calculation assumes regular octree structure; may have branch divergence on GPU if rays traverse different paths. The method was introduced in "A single-pass GPU ray casting framework for interactive out-of-core volume rendering" (2008) by. It extends stackless ray traversal techniques previously used for kd-trees [7,16] to octrees. The key innovation is the implicit computation of neighbor bounding boxes using the octree's regular structure, avoiding the need for explicit neighbor pointers in the index structure for all nodes, thus saving memory and texture fetches. It is used in interactive volume rendering systems where out-of-core data handling and high performance are required. name: GigaVoxels
head: Dynamic Sparse Octree, Ray-Guided Streaming
body: GigaVoxels is a dynamic sparse octree approach for efficient, detailed voxel rendering that achieves real-time to interactive rates on volumes exceeding GPU memory capacities by using ray-guided streaming. It solves the problem of rendering billions of voxels by ensuring the volume is only used at the resolution needed to produce the final image, providing memory and speed gains while offering inherent anti-aliasing. It differs from its parent, Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal, by continuously adapting resolution based on the current view and occlusion information, making discontinuities disappear and ensuring smooth temporal transitions to different subdivision levels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (e.g., 3D scans, hypertextured meshes, or fractals) with resolutions such as 8192^3 or 16384^3. Output: A rendered image at interactive rates (20-90 fps). Data Structures: The method combines an adaptive version of the structure from [LHN05a] with regular constant-sized memory blocks from [LKS06]. This hybrid structure supports efficient hardware-based filtering and exploits "sparse-twice" data structures (dense clusters in free space). The hierarchy is built by iteratively downsampling and averaging neighbors, creating a mipmapping-like structure. Parameters: Resolution: Examples include 8192^3 for 3D scans and 16384^3 for hypertextured meshes. Quality/Performance Trade-off: The system allows a trade-off between quality and performance, exploiting temporal coherence. Opacity Threshold: Rays stop when a certain opacity level is reached. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Casting: Cast rays from the eye through the pixel extent. 2. Ray-Guided Streaming: Guide data production and streaming directly based on information extracted during rendering. This involves loading only the necessary octree nodes into GPU memory based on the ray's path. 3. Adaptive Traversal: Traverse the sparse octree. The resolution adapts continuously to the current view and occlusion information. 4. Mipmapping Filtering: When traversing to larger steps (proportional to distance from the observer), read from the mipmap hierarchy. Reading from a mipmap delivers the integrated value of a small volume, approximating the cone integral defined by the eye and pixel extent. 5. Early Termination: Stop rays when a certain opacity level is reached or when traversing empty space. 6. Procedural Enrichment: Create additional details through procedural methods to enrich the dataset. Pseudocode: def rendergigavoxels(camera, scene, opacitythreshold=0.95): height, width = camera.resolution image = [[vec3(0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for py in range(height): for px in range(width): ray = camera.generateray(px, py) accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 rayterminated = False node = scene.getrootnode() while not rayterminated and node is not None: if node.isempty(): ray.origin += ray.direction node.size node = None continue nextnode = findintersectingchild(node, ray) if nextnode is None: ray.origin += ray.direction node.size node = None continue distance = length(ray.origin - camera.position) stepsize = nextnode.size if distance > threshold: volumevalue = nextnode.readmipmap(ray.direction, ray.origin) else: volumevalue = nextnode.readvoxel(ray.direction, ray.origin) alpha = volumevalue.alpha color = volumevalue.color weight = alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor += color weight accumulatedopacity += weight if accumulatedopacity > opacitythreshold: rayterminated = True break ray.origin += ray.direction stepsize node = nextnode image[py][px] = accumulatedcolor return image Note: findintersectingchild, readmipmap, readvoxel, vec3, and length are standard vector/math operations or octree traversal helpers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Appears because pixel value should be defined by integration along a cone, not just ray accumulation. Mipmapping addresses this by smoothing results and allowing larger step sizes proportional to distance. Memory Budget: The method respects the limited GPU memory budget by streaming only necessary data. Temporal Coherence: The system exploits temporal coherence to maintain quality and performance. Performance: 20-90 fps on current generation hardware. Memory: Respects limited GPU memory budget by streaming data. Scalability: Handles volumes exceeding GPU memory capacities, with resolutions up to 16384^3 or theoretically infinite for fractals. Strengths: Real-time to interactive rates, inherent anti-aliasing, adaptive resolution, efficient handling of "sparse-twice" data structures. Limitations: Increases memory consumption due to mipmap hierarchy and makes tree updates more challenging. When to use: When rendering large volumetric datasets (billions of voxels) on hardware with limited GPU memory, especially for computer graphics scenes with dense clusters in free space. When not to use: When view-independent structures are sufficient, or when procedural content generation is not required. GigaVoxels was developed by Sylvain Lefebvre, Elmar Eisemann, and others at INRIA Sophia-Antipolis and MPI Informatik / Saarland University. It was published in the I3D 2009 conference proceedings. The approach was developed in parallel to the work of Gobbetti et al. [GMAG08]. It builds on the structure from [LHN05a] and [LKS06]. Ray-Guided Streaming for Efficient and Detailed Voxel Rendering, https://www-sop.inria.fr/reves/Basilic/2009/CNLE09/CNLE09.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Distributed Multi-Level Out-Of-Core Volume Rendering
head: Display-Aware Multi-Resolution Volume Streaming and Ray-Casting, Distributed Volume Rendering
body: A distributed GPU volume rendering system that uses a multi-level hierarchy of caches and data streaming to render volumes larger than GPU memory, maintaining a 1:1 pixel-to-voxel ratio for interactive exploration. Display-awareness selects a target resolution and corresponding octree level to bound the working set size required for ray-casting. It differs from its parent GigaVoxels by distributing the rendering workload across multiple GPU nodes via MPI, where each node independently streams and renders its assigned portion of the volume, rather than relying on a single node's memory hierarchy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Large volumetric dataset (e.g., EM volumes > 40 GB), camera parameters, target display resolution. Output: Compositing of partial images from cluster nodes into a final image. Data Structures: The system employs a two-level hierarchy of 3D page caches for Virtual Volume Texturing: 1. Top-Level Page Directory Texture: Fully resident in GPU memory. For a 92 GB volume, this is 32 \times 32 \times 1 entries. Each entry refers to a block of 32^3 second-level page table entries. 2. Page Table Cache Texture: Stores second-level page table entries. For the 92 GB volume, this is a 64^3 texture containing 563 \times 563 \times 10 entries. Each entry refers to a small block of 32^3 physical voxels. 3. Physical 3D Cache Texture: The actual voxel data cache in GPU RAM. For the 92 GB volume, this is 1,024^3 voxels. 4. CPU Cache: A superset of the current working set kept in CPU RAM to minimize disk traffic when blocks are reused in future frames. Steps: 1. Target Resolution Selection: Determine the target pixel-to-voxel ratio (approximately 1:1) based on the output display resolution. This display-aware approach bounds the working set size. 2. Octree Level Selection: Select the corresponding octree level that matches the target resolution. 3. View Frustum Culling: Determine the list of volume blocks required for the current view by the ray-caster via view frustum culling. 4. Cache Check: Check whether all required blocks fit into the physical texture cache. 5. Coarsening (if needed): If the required blocks do not fit into the physical texture cache, use a coarser octree level. 6. Streaming: Stream all needed blocks into the single 3D cache texture in GPU RAM. Each GPU node independently streams in voxel data on demand, guided by the render resolution. 7. CPU Caching: Keep a larger subset of the required blocks in CPU RAM to minimize overall disk traffic when blocks are reused in a future frame. 8. Ray-Casting: Perform volume rendering by ray-casting using CUDA. Sample positions are computed in virtual volume space. Physical data voxels are fetched from the large 3D cache texture. 9. Mixed Resolution: While streaming in higher-resolution data, lower-resolution data can be freely mixed in by the ray-caster. 10. Compositing: After compositing the partial images produced by the cluster nodes, the final image is compressed and then transmitted to the client. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernode(nodeid, volumedata, camera, targetresolution): # 1. Determine target resolution and octree level # Target pixel-to-voxel ratio is ~1:1 octreelevel = selectoctreelevel(targetresolution) # 2. View Frustum Culling requiredblocks = viewfrustumculling(volumedata, camera, octreelevel) # 3. Check Cache Capacity # Physical cache size is fixed (e.g., 1024^3 voxels) if not fitsincache(requiredblocks, physicalcachesize): # 4. Coarsen if necessary octreelevel = coarsenoctreelevel(octreelevel) requiredblocks = viewfrustumculling(volumedata, camera, octreelevel) # 5. Stream Data # Stream required blocks into GPU 3D cache texture # Use CPU cache to minimize disk traffic for reused blocks streamblockstogpu(requiredblocks, cpucache, gpucache) # 6. Ray-Casting # Initialize output buffer partialimage = initializebuffer(targetresolution) for each pixel in partialimage: # Compute ray in virtual volume space ray = computeray(camera, pixel) # Traverse octree and fetch voxels color = raycast(ray, octreelevel, gpucache) # Composite into partial image partialimage[pixel] = color # 7. Return partial image for cluster compositing return compress(partialimage) Parameters: Target pixel-to-voxel ratio: Approximately 1:1. Block size: 32^3 physical voxels per second-level page table entry. Physical cache size: Varies by node, but examples use 1,024^3 voxels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the total physical texture memory across all nodes is insufficient for the target resolution, the system automatically coarsens the octree level, resulting in reduced resolution. Precision issues may arise when mapping virtual volume coordinates to physical cache indices if the page table hierarchy is not carefully managed. A technique using a two-level hierarchy of 3D page caches (page directory and page table) to map virtual volume coordinates to physical cache locations, enabling large volumes to be rendered with limited GPU memory. A strategy that selects the octree level based on the target display resolution to bound the working set size, ensuring efficient memory usage and consistent visual quality. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of nodes and the volume size. For a 43 GB volume, render times range from 0.12 sec to 1.28 sec on a single node, depending on the octree level and view. Memory Complexity: The working set size is bounded by the target resolution and the physical cache size. More nodes increase the total working set, allowing full resolution rendering. Measured Performance: Dataset #1 (43 GB): Render times on 1 node: 1.28, 0.34, 0.27, 0.70, 0.28, 0.18, 0.19, 0.15, 0.12, 0.7, 0.33, 0.34 sec. Dataset #2 (92 GB): Rendered on 1 to 8 Tesla nodes. Scaling: More nodes increase the working set and thus allow full resolution rendering. Fewer nodes can render the entire volume but with reduced resolution. Strengths: Enables interactive exploration of very large volumes (e.g., 92 GB) that exceed single GPU memory. Display-awareness ensures consistent visual quality. Limitations: Requires a cluster of GPU nodes. Performance is limited by network bandwidth and disk I/O for streaming. This method was presented by NVIDIA researchers (including Dave Luebke) in a 2010 poster. It was used for interactive exploration of neuroscience EM volumes, specifically mouse hippocampus data from the Harvard Center for Brain Science. The system was implemented on Tesla GPU nodes and used MPI for distributed rendering. name: SVO Node Location
body: SVO Node Location determines the specific node in a Sparse Voxel Octree hierarchy that contains a given ray position at a target depth or leaf level. It maintains a traversal path on a stack for subsequent operations like color retrieval or density evaluation. Inputs: raypos: 3D vector, the origin of the ray in world space. raydir: 3D vector, the direction of the ray. rootlower: 3D vector, the lower bound of the root node. rootscale: float, the side length of the root node. maxdepth: integer, the target depth to traverse to. addressspace: memory buffer, containing the SVO data. stack: array/structure, used to record the traversal path for later reconstruction. Outputs: locatednode: A structure containing the node info and the lower bound of the located node. stack: Updated with the path taken from root to the located node. Node Info: Contains a global offset (rootcdgoffset) and corner indices. Stack: A dynamic array or fixed-size buffer storing the sequence of nodes visited. Bounds: Represented as lower (3D vector) and upper (3D vector) or derived from lower and scale. 1. Initialize pos = raypos, lower = (0,0,0), upper = (1,1,1), center = (0.5,0.5,0.5). 2. Calculate the scale of the first level of children: scale = rootscale / 2. 3. Select the first child node using svoselectfirstnodef3. 4. Initialize currentnode, lower, upper, and center based on the selected first node. 5. Initialize depth = 0. 6. Loop while (maxdepth == 0 || depth < maxdepth). 7. Determine child corner indices based on the position relative to the center: xcorneridx = (pos.x < center.x) ? 0: 1, ycorneridx = (pos.y < center.y) ? 0: 1, zcorneridx = (pos.z < center.z) ? 0: 1. 8. Get the child corner from the indices. 9. Get the child node info from the address space. 10. Push the current node onto the stack. 11. Increment depth and update currentnode to the child. Initialization pos = raypos lower = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) upper = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) center = vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) scale = rootscale / 2.0 # 2. Select first child node firstnode = svoselectfirstnodef3(rootlower, lower, scale, raypos, raydir, addressspace) if firstnode is None: return None, stack currentnode = firstnode.nodeinfo lower = firstnode.lowerbound upper = lower + scale center = lower + 0.5 scale depth = 0 # 3. Traversal loop while maxdepth == 0 or depth < maxdepth: # Pitfall: Check bounds if not (lower.x <= pos.x <= upper.x and lower.y <= pos.y <= upper.y and lower.z <= pos.z <= upper.z): return None, stack # Pitfall: Check for children if not haschildren(currentnode, addressspace): break # Determine corner indices xcorner = 0 if pos.x < center.x else 1 ycorner = 0 if pos.y < center.y else 1 zcorner = 0 if pos.z < center.z else 1 childcorner = (xcorner << 2) | (ycorner << 1) | zcorner # Get child node info childnode = getchildnode(currentnode, childcorner, addressspace) # Push current node to stack stack.append(currentnode) # Update for next iteration depth += 1 currentnode = childnode scale /= 2.0 lower = lower + vec3(xcorner scale, ycorner scale, zcorner scale) upper = lower + scale center = lower + 0.5 scale return currentnode, stack def svoselectfirstnodef3(rootlower, lower, scale, raypos, raydir, addressspace): bestcorner = -1 bestdistance = float('inf') bestchildlower = lower childscale = scale / 2.0 for corneri in range(8): xoff = (corneri & 1) childscale yoff = ((corneri >> 1) & 1) childscale zoff = ((corneri >> 2) & 1) childscale childlower = lower + vec3(xoff, yoff, zoff) childupper = childlower + childscale if not rayintersectscube(raypos, raydir, childlower, childupper): continue t1 = calculateexitt(raypos, raydir, childupper) if t1 < 0: continue dist = length(raypos + raydir t1 - raypos) if dist < bestdistance: bestdistance = dist bestcorner = corneri bestchildlower = childlower if bestcorner == -1: return None return {'nodeinfo': addressspace.read(rootlower + bestcorner), 'lowerbound': bestchildlower} def rayintersectscube(origin, direction, lower, upper): tmin = (lower.x - origin.x) / direction.x if direction.x != 0 else float('-inf') tmax = (upper.x - origin.x) / direction.x if direction.x != 0 else float('inf') if tmin > tmax: tmin, tmax = tmax, tmin tymin = (lower.y - origin.y) / direction.y if direction.y != 0 else float('-inf') tymax = (upper.y - origin.y) / direction.y if direction.y != 0 else float('inf') if tymin > tymax: tymin, tymax = tymax, tymin if tmin > tymax or tymin > tmax: return False tzmin = (lower.z - origin.z) / direction.z if direction.z != 0 else float('-inf') tzmax = (upper.z - origin.z) / direction.z if direction.z != 0 else float('inf') if tzmin > tzmax: tzmin, tzmax = tzmax, tzmin return tmin <= tmax def calculateexitt(origin, direction, upper): t = float('inf') if direction.x > 0: t = min(t, (upper.x - origin.x) / direction.x) if direction.y > 0: t = min(t, (upper.y - origin.y) / direction.y) if direction.z > 0: t = min(t, (upper.z - origin.z) / direction.z) return t def haschildren(node, addressspace): return node is not None and node.isvalid() def getchildnode(parent, corner, addressspace): return addressspace.read(parent.offset + corner 8) stack: A stack to record the traversal path for later reconstruction. addressspace: The memory buffer containing the SVO data. rootlower: The 3D lower bound of the root node. rootscale: The side length of the root node. maxdepth: The maximum depth to traverse. If the ray position is not contained within the root bounds (lower, upper), return a null located node. If the current node has no children, break the loop. Determines the optimal starting child node for traversal by iterating through all 8 corners, calculating bounds, checking intersection via svofastforwardintersectsf3, and selecting the child with the minimum exit distance. If the exit face is null (no intersection or invalid), skip this child. Traverses the SVO from root to find the leaf node containing a given 3D position. If position is outside volume bounds, return INDEXNONE. Start at root; while current node is not a leaf, compute child index using binary mapping (front=1, back=0 for X/Y/Z). name: Octree Voxel Color Retrieval
head: Color Lookup with Shading, lookupColor
body: Retrieves the color of a voxel from the sparse voxel octree (SVO) data structure, applying lighting if the scene is not shadeless. It navigates the tree from a given node to find the leaf node containing the color data. Inputs: castRes: Result from ray traversal containing pos (float3), node (uint), childIdx (uint), scale (uint), and normal (float3). octree: Data structure containing a flat data array of uints. renderList: Contains an offsets array for instances. ubo: Uniform buffer object containing shadeless (int), ambientStrength (scalar), lightColor (vec3), lightPos (vec3), blockInfoEnd (offset), pageBytes (bytes), and transformCount (int). index: Instance index. Outputs: vec4: Final color with alpha. Data Structures: The octree is stored in a flat array octree.data. Nodes are organized into pages with headers, and the layout relies on bit-packing for node pointers and color data. Steps: 1. Extract Position and Tree State: Convert ray position to integer coordinates for indexing. px = \text{floatBitsToInt}(castRes.pos.x) node = castRes.node cidx = castRes.childIdx level = castRes.scale 2. Calculate Page Header and Block Info: Extract the page header from the node index. pageHeader = node \ \& \ 0xFFFFF800 Retrieve block information from the data array. blockInfo = pageHeader + octree.data[pageHeader] Get attach data by adding the block info end offset. attachData = \text{int}(blockInfo) + ubo.blockInfoEnd 3. Get Palette Node: Calculate the palette node index. paletteNode = octree.data[attachData + \text{int}(node) - \text{renderList.offsets}[index] / 4 - 1] 4. Traverse to Leaf: Loop while the current node does not have color data (indicated by the bit at cidx not being set). \text{while } ((\text{int}(paletteNode \gg cidx) \ \& \ 1) \neq 1) Inside the loop: increment level, check bounds, and update node, cidx, pageHeader, blockInfo, attachData, and paletteNode according to the octree traversal logic. 5. Calculate Attach Offset and Extract Color Component: attachOffset = attachData + \text{int}(paletteNode \gg 8) + \text{bitCount}(paletteNode \ \& \ (1 \ll cidx) - 1) c = \text{int}(octree.data[attachOffset]) 6. Extract RGB and Normalize: r = (c \gg 16) \ \& \ 0xFF g = (c \gg 8) \ \& \ 0xFF b = c \ \& \ 0xFF octreeColor = \text{vec3}(r / d, g / d, b / d) where d is a normalization divisor. 7. Handle Shadeless Mode: If ubo.shadeless == 1, return the color with alpha 1.0. \text{return vec4}(octreeColor, 1.0) 8. Load Transformation Matrix: Calculate offset for transform data. offset = \text{int}(\text{renderList.offsets}[index] + ubo.pageBytes) / 4 - ubo.transformCount 4 Read 16 floats into v[] and construct mat4 octreeToWorld. 9. Normalize Hit Normal in World Space: hitNormalWorld = \text{normalize}(octreeToWorld castRes.normal) 10. Calculate Lighting: ambient = ubo.ambientStrength \text{vec3}(ubo.lightColor) lightDir = \text{vec3}(\text{normalize}(ubo.lightPos)) diffuse = \max(\text{dot}(hitNormalWorld, lightDir), 0.0) \text{vec3}(ubo.lightColor) color = (ambient + diffuse) octreeColor Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct def floatbitstoint(f): return struct.unpack('i', struct.pack('f', f))[0] def bitcount(n): return bin(n).count('1') def matvecmul(m, v): return ( m[0]v[0] + m[1]v[1] + m[2]v[2] + m[3]v[3], m[4]v[0] + m[5]v[1] + m[6]v[2] + m[7]v[3], m[8]v[0] + m[9]v[1] + m[10]v[2] + m[11]v[3]) def normalize(v): l = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) if l else (0, 0, 0) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def max(a, b): return a if a > b else b def octreevoxelcolorretrieval(castRes, octree, renderList, ubo, index): # 1. Extract Position and Tree State px = floatbitstoint(castRes.pos.x) node = castRes.node cidx = castRes.childIdx level = castRes.scale # 2. Calculate Page Header and Block Info pageheader = node & 0xFFFFF800 blockinfo = pageheader + octree.data[pageheader] attachdata = int(blockinfo) + ubo.blockinfoend # 3. Get Palette Node palettenode = octree.data[attachdata + int(node) - renderList.offsets[index] // 4 - 1] # 4. Traverse to Leaf while (int(palettenode >> cidx) & 1) != 1: level += 1 # Update node, cidx, pageHeader, blockInfo, attachData, and paletteNode # per standard SVO traversal rules. Source omits exact update formulas. pass # 5. Calculate Attach Offset and Extract Color Component attachoffset = attachdata + int(palettenode >> 8) + bitcount(palettenode & ((1 << cidx) - 1)) c = int(octree.data[attachoffset]) # 6. Extract RGB and Normalize r = (c >> 16) & 0xFF g = (c >> 8) & 0xFF b = c & 0xFF d = 255.0 # normalization divisor for 8-bit RGB octreecolor = (r / d, g / d, b / d) # 7. Handle Shadeless Mode if ubo.shadeless == 1: return (octreecolor[0], octreecolor[1], octreecolor[2], 1.0) # 8. Load Transformation Matrix offset = int(renderList.offsets[index] + ubo.pagebytes) // 4 - ubo.transformcount 4 v = [octree.data[offset + i] for i in range(16)] octreetoworld = v # 9. Normalize Hit Normal in World Space hitnormalworld = normalize(matvecmul(octreetoworld, castRes.normal)) # 10. Calculate Lighting ambient = (ubo.ambientstrength ubo.lightcolor[0], ubo.ambientstrength ubo.lightcolor[1], ubo.ambientstrength ubo.lightcolor[2]) lightdir = normalize(ubo.lightpos) diffuse = (max(dot(hitnormalworld, lightdir), 0.0) ubo.lightcolor[0], max(dot(hitnormalworld, lightdir), 0.0) ubo.lightcolor[1], max(dot(hitnormalworld, lightdir), 0.0) ubo.lightcolor[2]) color = (ambient[0] + diffuse[0], ambient[1] + diffuse[1], ambient[2] + diffuse[2]) return (color[0], color[1], color[2], 1.0) Time complexity is linear with respect to the octree depth from the hit node to the leaf. name: Octree Node Lookup by Voxel
body: This method locates the payload index for a specific 3D voxel coordinate within a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by traversing from the root to the corresponding leaf node. It solves the problem of mapping a discrete voxel coordinate to the sparse data structure's payload array, returning -1 if the voxel lies outside the tree's bounds or in an empty region. Inputs: nodes: Array of NodeDescriptor structures representing the octree nodes. numnodes: Total number of nodes in the nodes array. leafpayloadindices: Array of indices mapping leaf IDs to payload rows. numleaves: Total number of leaves. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree (root is depth 0). voxel: A 3D integer coordinate (x, y, z) to look up. Outputs: payloadindex: The index into the payload array corresponding to the voxel. Returns -1 if the voxel is invalid or empty. Data Structures: NodeDescriptor: Contains the following fields: childmask: 8-bit bitmask indicating which of the 8 children exist. leafmask: 8-bit bitmask indicating which children are leaf nodes. payloadbase: Offset into leafpayloadindices for the first leaf child. internalchildmask: 8-bit bitmask indicating which children are internal nodes. childbase: Offset into the nodes array for the first internal child. Formulas: 1. Grid Size: grid\size = 2^{max\depth} 2. Child Index: For a given depth d (where d ranges from max\depth-1 down to 0), the child index c is: c = ((x \gg d) \& 1) \mid (((y \gg d) \& 1) \ll 1) \mid (((z \gg d) \& 1) \ll 2) 3. Prefix Rank: The number of set bits in a mask strictly below a given index i: prefix\rank(mask, i) = \text{popcount}(mask \& ((1 \ll i) - 1)) Algorithm Steps: 1. If numnodes is 0, return -1. 2. If maxdepth is 0, the root is a leaf. If leafpayloadindices is valid and contains data, return leafpayloadindices[0]. Otherwise, return -1. 3. Calculate grid\size = 2^{max\depth}. 4. If voxel.x, voxel.y, or voxel.z is not in the range [0, grid\size), return -1. 5. Initialize nodeindex = 0 and depthremaining = maxdepth. 6. Loop indefinitely: a. If nodeindex >= numnodes, return -1 (traversal exceeded node array bounds). b. Retrieve descriptor = nodes[nodeindex]. c. Calculate childindex using the formula above with childdepth = depthremaining - 1. d. Compute childbit = 1 << childindex. e. If (descriptor.childmask & childbit) == 0, the child does not exist. Return -1. f. If (descriptor.leafmask & childbit) != 0, the child is a leaf: i. Compute leafid = descriptor.payloadbase + prefixrank(descriptor.leafmask, childindex). ii. Retrieve payloadindex = leafpayloadindices[leafid]. iii. Validate payloadindex (e.g., check if it is within bounds of the payload array). If valid, return payloadindex. Else, return -1. g. Otherwise, the child is an internal node: i. Compute newnodeindex = descriptor.childbase + prefixrank(descriptor.internalchildmask, childindex). ii. Decrement depthremaining. iii. If depthremaining <= 0, return -1 (should have hit a leaf or invalid path). iv. Set nodeindex = newnodeindex and continue loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lookuppayloadindexbyvoxel(nodes, numnodes, leafpayloadindices, numleaves, maxdepth, voxel): # Step 1: Empty tree check if numnodes == 0: return -1 # Step 2: Max depth 0 check (Root is leaf) if maxdepth == 0: if numleaves > 0 and len(leafpayloadindices) > 0: return leafpayloadindices[0] else: return -1 # Step 3 & 4: Bounds check gridsize = 1 << maxdepth if not (0 <= voxel.x < gridsize and 0 <= voxel.y < gridsize and 0 <= voxel.z < gridsize): return -1 # Step 5: Initialization nodeindex = 0 depthremaining = maxdepth # Step 6: Traversal Loop while True: # Step 6a: Bounds check for node array if nodeindex >= numnodes: return -1 descriptor = nodes[nodeindex] # Step 6b: Calculate child index childdepth = depthremaining - 1 xbit = (voxel.x >> childdepth) & 1 ybit = (voxel.y >> childdepth) & 1 zbit = (voxel.z >> childdepth) & 1 childindex = xbit | (ybit << 1) | (zbit << 2) # Step 6d: Check if child exists childbit = 1 << childindex if (descriptor.childmask & childbit) == 0: return -1 # Step 6f: Check if child is leaf if (descriptor.leafmask & childbit) != 0: # Compute leafid lowermask = (1 << childindex) - 1 rank = (descriptor.leafmask & lowermask).bitcount() leafid = descriptor.payloadbase + rank # Retrieve payload index if leafid < numleaves and leafid < len(leafpayloadindices): payloadindex = leafpayloadindices[leafid] # Validate payloadindex (e.g., non-negative, within payload bounds) if payloadindex >= 0: return payloadindex else: return -1 else: return -1 # Step 6g: Internal node # Compute new node index lowermask = (1 << childindex) - 1 rank = (descriptor.internalchildmask & lowermask).bitcount() newnodeindex = descriptor.childbase + rank depthremaining -= 1 if depthremaining <= 0: return -1 nodeindex = newnodeindex Parameters: payloadrows: Total number of payload rows. Used to validate the returned payloadindex. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Tree: An empty tree (numnodes == 0) must return -1 immediately. Zero Depth: A tree with maxdepth == 0 has only a root leaf; validation of leafpayloadindices is required. Out-of-Bounds Voxels: Voxels at or beyond gridsize are invalid and return -1. Missing Children: If the target child bit is not set in childmask, the path is empty and returns -1. Invalid Indices: If leafid or payloadindex is out of bounds or negative, return -1. Retrieves the actual color/value by interpolating between payload values. Use when rendering or shading is required. Locates the node descriptor itself rather than the payload index. Use when node properties (e.g., density, type) are needed. Time Complexity: O(max\depth), as the traversal visits exactly one node per depth level. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, using a fixed set of integer variables for traversal state. Strengths: Exact discrete lookup with minimal branching overhead; efficiently skips empty branches via bitmask checks. Limitations: Requires integer voxel coordinates; does not support continuous sampling or interpolation natively. The method is part of the Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) rendering pipeline, specifically designed for efficient voxel-based data access. It leverages compacted bitmasks and prefix ranks to navigate the octree structure without explicit child pointers, optimizing memory usage and cache locality. hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, https://github.com/hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal (State Machine)
head: Fixed-Point SVO Traversal, SVO Raycasting
body: A deterministic software ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) implemented as a finite state machine using fixed-point arithmetic, originally designed to emulate an FPGA hardware raycaster. It differs from recursive or stack-based traversals by using explicit goto-based control flow and a circular buffer stack to manage backtracking, ensuring predictable execution paths suitable for hardware synthesis or deterministic software rendering. Inputs: Ray origin r.o, ray direction r.d, SVO data structure (compact nodes), traversal parameters. Outputs: Hit point, depth, or traversal status. Data Structures: CNode (Compact Node): 32-bit packed structure. Bits 0-7: validmask (8 bits, child validity). Bits 8-15: leafmask (8 bits, child leaf status). Bits 16-30: childptr (15 bits, offset to children). Bit 31: farptr flag (1 bit, indicates if children are at a far address). OctreeCursor: Contains pointer to CNode data, current CNode node, current address adr, current level, and a Cache pointer. StackItem: cur: OctreeCursor. tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1: Fixed-point intersection times (tnum). idx: Current child index being processed. Stack: Circular buffer of StackItem with top index, length, and size ss. Push wraps top modulo ss and increments length (capped at ss). Pop decrements top (wrapping if negative) and decrements length. Parameters: terminLevel: Maximum depth before forcing leaf termination. Default: 10. tnumscale: Fixed-point scaling factor. Value: 65536 (2^{16}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Direction Normalization: If any component of r.d is zero, add 0.001 to that component to prevent division by zero. If any component of r.d is negative, flip the ray origin component (r.o.x \leftarrow -r.o.x) and negate the direction component (r.d.x \leftarrow -r.d.x). Record these flips in dirmask (bit 4 for X, bit 2 for Y, bit 1 for Z). 2. Initial Bounding Box Intersection: Compute intersection times with the unit cube [-1, 1]^3: tx0 = \frac{-1 - r.o.x}{r.d.x}, \quad tx1 = \frac{1 - r.o.x}{r.d.x} ty0 = \frac{-1 - r.o.y}{r.d.y}, \quad ty1 = \frac{1 - r.o.y}{r.d.y} tz0 = \frac{-1 - r.o.z}{r.d.z}, \quad tz1 = \frac{1 - r.o.z}{r.d.z} Calculate entry and exit times: t{enter} = \max(tx0, \max(ty0, tz0)) t{exit} = \min(tx1, \min(ty1, tz1)) If t{enter} \ge t{exit}, the ray misses the bounding box; terminate. 3. Fixed-Point Conversion: Scale times by tnumscale: tnum = t \times 65536. Clip values to [tnum\min + 1000, tnum\max - 1000] to prevent overflow. 4. State Machine Loop: The traversal uses goto-based control flow. Initialization: Initialize cur to root. level = 0. Compute Midpoints: txm = (tx0+tx1)/2, tym = (ty0+ty1)/2, tzm = (tz0+tz1)/2. Set Entry Time: Set t{enter} = \max(tx0, \max(ty0, tz0)). Select Initial Child Index: idx = (txm < t{enter}) \ll 2 \mid (tym < t{enter}) \ll 1 \mid (tzm < t{enter}). Compute Child Bounds: tx0{child} = (idx \& 4) ? txm: tx0, tx1{child} = (idx \& 4) ? tx1: txm (similarly for Y and Z). Calculate Child Exit Time: t{exit\child} = \min(tx1{child}, \min(ty1{child}, tz1{child})). Flip Index for Direction: idx{flip} = idx \oplus dir\mask. Check Exit: If t{exit\child} \le t{start} (current traversal start time), skip this node. Jump to next index. Check Leaf/Termination: If cur.childIsFilled(idxflip) OR level == terminLevel: mark as leaf hit and finish. Check Validity: If cur.childIsValid(idxflip): push current state (cur, bounds, idx) to Stack. Update cur to child: cur = cur.getChild(idxflip). Update bounds to child bounds. Increment level. Continue traversal. Handle Node Exit/Backtrack: If exiting node and level==0, finish. If stack is empty, restart traversal from t{exit\child}. Otherwise, pop stack, decrement level, and continue traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversesvostatemachine(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode, nodedata, cache, terminlevel=10, tnumscale=65536): # 1. Handle Ray Direction dirmask = 0 ro = list(rayorigin) # [x, y, z] rd = list(raydirection) for i in range(3): if rd[i] == 0: rd[i] = 0.001 if rd[i] < 0: ro[i] = -ro[i] rd[i] = -rd[i] if i == 0: dirmask |= 4 elif i == 1: dirmask |= 2 elif i == 2: dirmask |= 1 # 2. Initial Bounding Box Intersection tx0 = (-1.0 - ro[0]) / rd[0] tx1 = (1.0 - ro[0]) / rd[0] ty0 = (-1.0 - ro[1]) / rd[1] ty1 = (1.0 - ro[1]) / rd[1] tz0 = (-1.0 - ro[2]) / rd[2] tz1 = (1.0 - ro[2]) / rd[2] tenter = max(tx0, max(ty0, tz0)) texit = min(tx1, min(ty1, tz1)) if tenter >= texit: return None # Miss # 3. Fixed-Point Conversion & Clipping tnummax = 231 - 1 # tnummin = -231 # def totnum(t): val = int(t tnumscale) return max(tnummin + 1000, min(tnummax - 1000, val)) tx0, tx1 = totnum(tx0), totnum(tx1) ty0, ty1 = totnum(ty0), totnum(ty1) tz0, tz1 = totnum(tz0), totnum(tz1) # Data Structures class StackItem: def init(self, cur, tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1, idx): self.cur = cur self.tx0, self.ty0, self.tz0 = tx0, ty0, tz0 self.tx1, self.ty1, self.tz1 = tx1, ty1, tz1 self.idx = idx stackstore = [None] 256 # name: Animated Sparse Voxel Octrees (ASVO)
body: Animated Sparse Voxel Octrees (ASVO) is a GPU-based rendering technique that applies rigid transformations or skeletal skinning to voxel-based 3D models in real-time. It differs from standard Sparse Voxel Octree ray traversal by decoupling traversal into a parallel job queue system that processes animated leaf nodes, allowing efficient skeletal animation without reconstructing the octree structure per frame. ASVO operates in two main phases: a traversal phase that identifies visible, animated voxels and a drawing phase that resolves pixel coverage and lighting. The method relies on a breadth-first search (BFS) job queue to manage traversal state across the octree hierarchy. Inputs: Octree Data: innerNodes: Array of BFSInnerNode structures. Each contains a mask (bitmask of children) and childPtr (index offset to children). leaves: Array of VisualData structures. Each contains visual properties (normal, tangent, pos, texCoord, eyeVec, originalCenter) and animation data (boneWeights, boneIndex0-3). animation: Array of float4x4 matrices representing bone transformations for the current frame. Size is frameCount boneCount. jobs: Initial queue of BFSJob structures. Each job contains index (node index), x, y, z (subdivision coordinates). dim: The total dimension of the octree space. level: The maximum depth of the octree. boneCount: Number of bones in the skeleton. Camera/View: world, view, projection: Transformation matrices. camPos: Camera position in world space. Lighting: shadowMap: Depth texture for shadow testing. diffuse, illum, spec, normal: Texture maps for material properties. Outputs: depthBuffer: Buffer storing the minimum depth for each screen pixel. voxelBuffer: Buffer storing visual data for visible voxels. colorBuffer: Final rendered image. BFSJob: index (uint32t), x, y, z (uint32t). BFSInnerNode: mask (uint64t), childPtr (uint32t). VisualData (Leaf Node): vd.boneWeights (float4), vd.boneIndex0-3 (uint32t), vd.normal, vd.tangent, vd.pos, vd.texCoord, vd.eyeVec, vd.originalCenter (float3/float4), mask (uint64t). 1. Initialization: Load octree data, animation matrices, and initial BFS jobs from the root. Initialize depthBuffer with maximum depth values. Initialize sharedTravQueuePtr to 0. 2. Traversal Kernel (Per Job): Each thread processes one job from the queue. a. Grid Cell Calculation: Calculate the dimensions of the current voxel in world space based on the octree level. gridCellDim = \frac{dim}{2^{level}} gridCellHalfDim = gridCellDim \times 0.5 b. Voxel Center Computation: Determine the center of the voxel in world space. If the node is a leaf with skinning (node.vd.boneWeights.x > 0.0): Retrieve bone transformations M0, M1, M2, M3 from the animation buffer using boneIndex0-3. Interpolate the center position P{orig} using bone weights w0, w1, w2, w3: P{world} = \sum{i=0}^{3} wi \cdot (Mi \cdot P{orig}) Adjust the half-dimension to counteract stretching during skinning: involvedBones = \sum{i=0}^{3} wi gridCellHalfDim = gridCellHalfDim \times \min(2.0, involvedBones) Otherwise, use the original center position from the leaf data. c. Clip Space Transformation: Transform the center and dimensions into clip space. P{clip} = projection \times view \times world \times P{world} Compute the eye vector: eyeVec = \frac{camPos - P{world}}{\|camPos - P{world}\|} d. Culling: Frustum Culling: Check if the voxel's clip-space bounds are within [-1, 1]. Back-face Culling: If level > 8, check the dot product of the normal and eye vector: dot(node.vd.normal, eyeVec) \ge -0.4 If either culling test fails, discard the voxel. e. Screen Projection and Depth: Project the voxel center to screen coordinates (x, y). Compute depth: depth = P{clip}.z \times 2147483647 f. Queue Management or Buffer Update: If the voxel has children (popcount(node.mask) != 0) AND spans more than 1 pixel (dimVec.x > 1.0): Generate child jobs for the 8 sub-voxels. Add child jobs to the queue using atomicAdd on sharedTravQueuePtr. Otherwise (leaf node or too small): Update the depth buffer: atomicMin(depthBuffer + index, depth) g. Visual Data Storage: If the voxel was drawn (P{clip}.w == 1.0) and its depth matches the updated depth buffer value: Write visual data (normal, tangent, position, texCoord, eyeVec, originalCenter) to voxelBuffer at the screen index. 3. Drawing Kernel (Per Pixel): For each pixel (x, y): a. Neighborhood Scan: Scan a 3 \times 3 neighborhood in the depthBuffer to find the voxel with the minimum depth that covers the pixel. A voxel covers the pixel if: |vd.pos.x - 0.5 - x| \le vd.pos.z |vd.pos.y - 0.5 - y| \le vd.pos.w b. Lighting: Transform the voxel center to light space. Check shadow mapping against shadowMap. Compute diffuse and specular lighting using diffuse, illum, normal, and spec textures. Update the colorBuffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class BFSJob: def init(self, index, x, y, z): self.index = index self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z class float3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def mul(self, s): return float3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def add(self, o): return float3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def sub(self, o): return float3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def matmul(self, m): return float3( m[0][0]self.x + m[0][1]self.y + m[0][2]self.z + m[0][3], m[1][0]self.x + m[1][1]self.y + m[1][2]self.z + m[1][3], m[2][0]self.x + m[2][1]self.y + m[2][2]self.z + m[2][3]) def rmul(self, s): return self s class float4: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w def dot(a, b): return a.xb.x + a.yb.y + a.zb.z def length(v): return math.sqrt(v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2) def normalize(v): l = length(v) return float3(v.x/l, v.y/l, v.z/l) if l > 0 else float3(0,0,0) def atomicAdd(ptr, val): old = ptr[0] ptr[0] = old + val return old def atomicMin(ptr, val): old = ptr[0] if val < old: ptr[0] = val return old def popcount(n): return bin(n).count('1') def traversejob(job, innerNodes, leaves, animation, dim, level, camPos, world, view, projection, depthBuffer, voxelBuffer, queue, queuePtr, width, height): gridCellDim = dim / (1 << level) gridCellHalfDim = gridCellDim 0.5 isleaf = job.index >= len(innerNodes) node = leaves[job.index - len(innerNodes)] if isleaf else innerNodes[job.index] if isleaf and node.vd.boneWeights.x > 0.0: Porig = node.vd.originalCenter w = node.vd.boneWeights M0, M1, M2, M3 = animation[node.vd.boneIndex0], animation[node.vd.boneIndex1], animation[node.vd.boneIndex2], animation[node.vd.boneIndex3] Pworld = w.x (M0 @ Porig) + w.y (M1 @ Porig) + w.z (M2 @ Porig) + w.w (M3 @ Porig) involvedBones = w.x + w.y + w.z + w.w gridCellHalfDim = gridCellHalfDim min(2.0, involvedBones) else: Pworld = node.vd.originalCenter Pclip = projection @ view @ world @ Pworld eyeVec = normalize(camPos - Pworld) if not (-1.0 <= Pclip.x <= 1.0 and -1.0 <= Pclip.y <= 1.0 and -1.0 <= Pclip.z <= 1.0): return if level > 8: if dot(node.vd.normal, eyeVec) < -0.4: return xscreen = Pclip.x / Pclip.w yscreen = Pclip.y / Pclip.w depth = Pclip.z 2147483647 childCount = popcount(node.mask) # Estimate screen-space dimension of the voxel dimClip = projection @ view @ world @ (Pworld + float3(gridCellHalfDim, 0, 0)) dimVec = float3(dimClip.x / dimClip.w, dimClip.y / dimClip.w, dimClip.z / dimClip.w) dimScreen = abs(dimVec.x - xscreen) + abs(dimVec.y - yscreen) if childCount != 0 and dimScreen > 1.0: for j in range(8): if (node.mask >> j) & 1: childindex = 0 for k in range(j): if (node.mask >> k) & 1: childindex += 1 newjob = BFSJob( index=node.childPtr + childindex, x=2job.x + (j & 1), y=2job.y + ((j & 2) >> 1), z=2job.z + ((j & 4) >> 2)) idx = atomicAdd(queuePtr, 1) queue[idx] = newjob else: index = int(xscreen) + int(yscreen) width olddepth = atomicMin(depthBuffer + index, depth) if Pclip.w == 1.0 and depth == olddepth: voxelBuffer[index] = node.vd def drawpixel(x, y, depthBuffer, voxelBuffer, shadowMap, diffuse, illum, spec, normal, width, height): mindepth = float('inf') bestvoxel = None for dx in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): px, py = x + dx, y + dy if 0 <= px < width and 0 <= py < height: idx = px + py width d = depthBuffer[idx] if d < mindepth: mindepth = d bestvoxel = voxelBuffer[idx] if bestvoxel is None: return if abs(bestvoxel.pos.x - 0.5 - x) <= bestvoxel.pos.z and \ abs(bestvoxel.pos.y - 0.5 - y) <= bestvoxel.pos.w: # Transform to light space and sample shadow map # Plight = lightviewprojection @ world @ bestvoxel.originalCenter # shadow = shadowMap.sample(Plight.xy / Plight.w, Plight.z / Plight.w) # Compute diffuse and specular lighting from textures # color = computediffuse(bestvoxel, diffuse, illum) + computespecular(bestvoxel, spec) # color = shadow colorBuffer[x + y width] = bestvoxel.color # Placeholder for final color Level Threshold: Back-face culling is only applied if level > 8. Bone Weights: Skinning is applied only if boneWeights.x > 0.0. Precision: Depth is computed as center.z INTMAX, which may introduce precision issues for very large scenes or deep octrees. Queue Size: The traversal uses a dynamic queue with atomicAdd, requiring careful management of shared memory or global memory contention. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for innerNodes, leaves, animation matrices, and buffers (depthBuffer, voxelBuffer, colorBuffer). The queue size depends on the branching factor and visibility. Performance: High performance on CUDA-capable GPUs (Compute Capability 3.0+) due to parallel job processing. Strengths: Efficient handling of animated voxel models; no need to rebuild the octree for animation frames. Limitations: Limited to rigid transformations and skinning; complex deformations may require more sophisticated approaches. Precision issues with depth buffering in large scenes. ASVO was developed as a CUDA/C++ implementation for rendering animated voxel models. It builds on the concept of Sparse Voxel Octrees, extending them to support skeletal animation by applying bone transformations to leaf nodes during traversal. The project includes a high-performance CUDA implementation and an XNA/C# prototype for algorithm design. denniskb/asvo, https://github.com/denniskb/asvo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Voxel Traversal
head: Recursive Voxel Traversal
body: Hierarchical Voxel Traversal is a recursive raycasting algorithm designed to traverse nested voxel structures, such as chunks containing subvoxels, to find intersections. It distinguishes itself from flat traversal methods by transforming rays into local subvoxel space when entering a detail voxel, allowing for efficient handling of nested voxel data. Unlike First Active Voxel Detection which focuses on finding the first non-empty voxel, this method fully traverses the hierarchy to compute precise intersections within detail voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin, direction, transform, and optional length; a hierarchical voxel structure (e.g., VoxelWorldAccess or generic Voxel<T>); maximum iteration limits. Output: An Intersection struct containing the hit position, normal, index, and an optional inner intersection (for detail voxels). Data Structures: Ray: Contains origin (Vec3), direction (Vec3), transform (Mat4), and length (Option<f32>). Voxel: Generic type T with properties WIDTH, DY, DZ, SCALE, and COUNT. Coordinates are mapped to linear indices using i = x + y \cdot DY + z \cdot DZ. Steps: 1. World Access Entry: Calculate the world origin in float3. Compute the current ray position in chunk-local space: current = ray.origin \cdot (1.0 / self.world.scale) - origin Call the core cast function with the world access, ray, current position, direction, and max iterations (30). 2. Voxel Check (World Access): Validate coordinates are within world bounds: coord[i] \ge 0 and coord[i] < self.world.dims[i]. Compute linear index: i = coord[0] + coord[1] \cdot dims[0] + coord[2] \cdot dims[0] \cdot dims[1]. If the voxel exists and is visible: Construct a local ray by applying scaling (sc) and translation (coord sc) to the ray's transform. Recursively cast on the voxel. If the voxel is a detail voxel (has subvoxels): Return an Intersection with inner set to the sub-intersection, index set to the chunk index, and current position/normal. If the voxel does not exist (empty chunk slot): Return an Intersection with inner: None, index: 0, and current position/normal. 3. Generic Voxel Entry: Inverse the ray transform. Scale by SUBDIV (2^{SUBDIV}). Transform ray origin and direction into subvoxel space. Move ray origin to the start of the bounding box (0 to scale) if not already inside. For each axis i: If direction[i] > 0, t = (0.0 - current[i]) / direction[i]. Else if direction[i] < 0, t = (scale - current[i]) / direction[i]. If t > 0, advance current. Call core cast with the voxel, ray, current position, direction, and max iterations 6 \cdot T::WIDTH. 4. Generic Voxel Check: Validate coordinates within T::WIDTH. Compute linear index: i = coord[0] + coord[1] \cdot T::DY + coord[2] \cdot T::DZ. If the voxel is visible and is detail: Construct local ray with scaling T::SCALE and translation coord \cdot T::SCALE. Recursively cast. Return intersection with inner sub-hit. If the voxel is visible and NOT detail: Return intersection with inner: None, index: i, current position/normal. 5. Core Cast Function: Initialize integer coordinates currenti from current floor. Adjust currenti down by 1 if current is very close to an integer boundary and direction is negative. Check starting position first using raycast.check. If hit, return immediately. Loop up to iterations: Calculate distance to next grid plane intersection for each axis using intersect(currenti[i], current[i], direction[i]). Find minimum distance i[d]. Advance current by direction \cdot i[d] where d is the axis with minimum intersection distance. Decrement currenti[d] if direction[d] < 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cast(worldaccess, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 1: World Access Entry # current is already in chunk-local space return castvoxel(worldaccess, ray, current, direction, maxiterations) def castvoxel(worldaccess, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 2: Voxel Check (World Access) # Assuming worldaccess provides dims and scale # Compute linear index from current coordinates # Check bounds and existence if not worldaccess.check(current): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) voxel = worldaccess.get(current) if not voxel.visible(): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) if voxel.isdetail(): # Construct local ray sc = worldaccess.scale localray = transformray(ray, sc, current sc) # Recursively cast subhit = cast(worldaccess, localray, vec3(0), localray.direction, 30) return Intersection(inner=subhit, index=worldaccess.index(current), position=current, normal=vec3(0)) else: return Intersection(inner=None, index=worldaccess.index(current), position=current, normal=vec3(0)) def castgeneric(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 3: Generic Voxel Entry # Inverse transform and scale invtransform = inverse(ray.transform) subdiv = 2 voxel.SUBDIV ray.origin = invtransform (ray.origin subdiv) ray.direction = invtransform (ray.direction subdiv) # Move ray origin to start of bounding box scale = voxel.SCALE for i in range(3): if direction[i] > 0: t = (0.0 - current[i]) / direction[i] elif direction[i] < 0: t = (scale - current[i]) / direction[i] else: t = float('inf') if t > 0: current += direction t return castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, 6 voxel.WIDTH) def castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 4: Generic Voxel Check # Check bounds if not voxel.check(current): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) index = voxel.coordtoindex(current) voxeldata = voxel.get(index) if not voxeldata.visible(): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) if voxeldata.isdetail(): sc = voxel.SCALE localray = transformray(ray, sc, current sc) subhit = castgeneric(voxeldata, localray, vec3(0), localray.direction, 6 voxeldata.WIDTH) return Intersection(inner=subhit, index=index, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) else: return Intersection(inner=None, index=index, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) def corecast(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 5: Core Cast Function # Initialize integer coordinates currenti = floor(current) # Precision fix for negative direction at integer boundaries for i in range(3): if abs(current[i] - currenti[i]) < epsilon and direction[i] < 0: currenti[i] -= 1 # Check starting position if voxel.check(current): return castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations) # Traverse grid for in range(maxiterations): # Calculate distance to next grid plane distances = [] for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: distances.append(float('inf')) else: # intersect function calculates distance to next integer plane # assuming currenti[i] is the current voxel index # distance = (currenti[i] + (1 if direction[i] > 0 else 0) - current[i]) / direction[i] # Note: Exact formula depends on intersect implementation details not fully specified # Using standard AET traversal logic nextplane = currenti[i] + (1 if direction[i] > 0 else 0) distances.append((nextplane - current[i]) / direction[i]) d = argmin(distances) mindist = distances[d] if mindist == float('inf'): break # Advance current current += direction mindist currenti[d] += (1 if direction[d] < 0 else -1) # Decrement if direction is negative # Check hit at new position if voxel.check(current): return castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations) return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) Parameters: Max iterations for VoxelWorldAccess raycasting: 30. Max iterations for Voxel<T> raycasting: 6 \cdot T::WIDTH. Pitfalls: Precision issues at integer boundaries: If the ray is exactly on an integer coordinate and moving in a negative direction, the integer coordinate index must be decremented to avoid missing the voxel or double-checking. Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the amethystvoxel project by Kurble, licensed under Apache-2.0. It is used for rendering voxel worlds with nested detail structures. name: Hierarchical and Block-Based Data Structures
head: Hierarchical Grid Traversal Acceleration, Octree-Based Volume Rendering, Min-Max Octree, ExaBricks, Residency Octree
body: This family provides acceleration structures for image-order volume rendering by organizing volumetric data into multi-resolution trees or blocks to skip empty or inactive regions during ray traversal. It serves as the foundational acceleration mechanism for sibling methods such as Ray-marching reference (min-max octree accelerated) and ExaBricks Rendering with RTX BVH. Unlike flat grid traversal, these structures enable rays to jump over large empty spaces or identify active cells for rendering, significantly reducing computational cost. The core mechanism involves constructing a tree where nodes represent spatial regions and store aggregate information (e.g., binary occupancy flags, min/max values) derived from child nodes or leaf voxels. Traversal proceeds from the root; if a node indicates an empty or inactive region (e.g., flag is 0, or min/max bounds are outside the view), the entire subtree is skipped. Construction typically follows a bottom-up approach: leaf nodes encode voxel properties, and internal nodes aggregate these properties from their children. The hierarchy depth is determined by the data dimensions, often requiring specific size constraints (e.g., N=2^M+1) or padding to maintain regular subdivision. This method is an accelerated direct isosurface visualization technique that uses a min-max octree to facilitate empty space skipping during ray marching. It serves as a performance baseline for general volumes, offering negligible memory overhead for the input volume and low auxiliary data requirements. Unlike Sphere Tracing, which requires precomputed signed distance functions, or Segment Tracing, which is limited to hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces, this approach is applicable to a wide range of scalar volumes. It guarantees continuous isosurfaces that locally interpolate the input data, unlike mesh extraction techniques (e.g., marching cubes) which may produce topologically different piecewise linear meshes. A rendering method for Adaptive Block-Refined (ABR) data that uses hardware-accelerated RTX BVH traversal to iterate through regions, performing volume integration within each region and skipping empty space. Hierarchical data structures organize volumetric data into multi-resolution trees to accelerate image-order rendering by skipping empty or inactive regions during ray traversal. Unlike flat grid traversal, these structures enable rays to jump over large empty spaces or identify active cells for rendering, significantly reducing computational cost. This family serves as the foundational acceleration mechanism for sibling methods such as Ray-marching reference (min-max octree accelerated) and ExaBricks Rendering with RTX BVH. Not given in the sources. A hybrid data structure for out-of-core direct volume rendering (DVR) of multi-volume data that decouples the cache residency of multi-resolution data from a resolution-independent spatial subdivision determined by the tree. Definition: An efficient GPU rendering algorithm for large CT datasets that subdivides the volume into uniform blocks and accelerates rendering by combining early ray termination, empty-space skipping, and visibility culling to render only visible parts. Steps: 1. Subdivide the volume dataset into uniform-sized blocks. 2. Apply visibility culling to identify visible blocks. 3. Render visible blocks using early ray termination and empty-space skipping to skip transparent/empty regions. Performance: Achieved 3-4 frames per second on a 512 × 304 × 1878 dimension dataset (visible female) using a Pentium 4 2.4 GHz PC with an NVIDIA Geforce 6600 (256 MB video memory). Definition: A multiresolution technique using an octree to encode a hierarchical volume 'bricking' for large dataset rendering. Steps: Use an octree to encode a hierarchical volume 'bricking'. The concept of using hierarchical structures for volume rendering acceleration emerged in the early 2000s. Baoquan Chen presented an image-based rendering technique in 2001 that accelerated surface rendering from volume data by caching fully rendered images. Multiresolution approaches using octrees for hierarchical volume "bricking" were employed by LaMar et al. and later by Boada and colleagues to handle large datasets. These techniques laid the groundwork for modern GPU-accelerated methods that combine visibility culling, early ray termination, and empty-space skipping to achieve interactive frame rates on standard hardware.
