Inputs: A 3D scalar volume dataset. An isovalue threshold for isosurface extraction. Camera parameters (origin and direction for each pixel). Outputs: A rendered image of the isosurface with shading. Data Structures: 1. Min-Max Texture: A texture where each texel stores the minimum and maximum scalar values of a corresponding block or cell in the volume. This is used to determine block occupancy. 2. Min-Max Octree: Constructed from the min-max texture. The octree is built on a base level with equal size along all three cardinal axes. Volume dimensions are padded to the nearest power of two for straightforward implementation. The octree nodes store min/max values to allow empty space skipping. 3. Scalar Data: The original volume data, potentially losslessly compressed into the octree representation. Steps: 1. Construct the Min-Max Octree: Create an MIP texture from the min-max texture used for block occupancy determination. Build the octree on a base level with equal size along all three cardinal axes. Pad volume dimensions to the nearest power of two. Ensure the octree is fully populated or indexed correctly for traversal. 2. Compute Entry and Exit Points: Instead of rendering one cube enclosing the whole volume, render cubes corresponding to one level of the min/max octree. All vertices of a cube have the same 2D texture coordinates containing the min/max values. Exit Positions: Render the cubes with glCullFace(GL FRONT) and glDepthFunc(GL LESS). A fragment shader discards the fragment if the cube is empty or does not contain the isosurface level. Entry Positions: Render the cubes again with glCullFace(GL BACK) and glDepthFunc(GL GREATER). The same fragment shader logic applies. 3. Ray Marching: March rays through the volume using a step size of 0.5 \times \text{cell edge length}. Use the min-max octree to skip empty space. Initialize ray origin and direction based on camera parameters. 4. Isosurface Refinement: Refine the isosurface intersection position using exactly three iterations of a binary search algorithm. The binary search narrows down the interval where the scalar value crosses the isovalue. 5. Shading: Compute surface normals on the fly using the central difference method upon finding an isosurface intersection. Apply Gooch shading using the sampled/computed vertex normals. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchminmaxoctree(volume, isovalue, camera, octree): """ Ray march through a volume using a min-max octree for acceleration. Args: volume: 3D array of scalar values. isovalue: Threshold for isosurface. camera: Object with origin and direction methods. octree: Min-max octree structure with min/max values per node. Returns: Image buffer with shaded isosurface. """ image = createemptyimage() for pixel in image: rayorigin = camera.origin(pixel) raydirection = camera.direction(pixel) # Step 2: Compute entry and exit points using octree cubes # This step is typically done via GPU rendering passes as described in # For the sake of this algorithmic description, we assume entry and exit # points are computed by querying the octree or rendering cubes. entrypoint, exitpoint = computeentryexitpoints(rayorigin, raydirection, octree) if entrypoint is None or exitpoint is None: continue # Step 3: Ray Marching stepsize = 0.5 getcelledgelength(octree) currentpoint = entrypoint while distance(currentpoint, exitpoint) > stepsize: # Check if current point is inside an empty region using octree if isempty(currentpoint, octree): # Skip to next non-empty region or exit currentpoint = skipemptyregion(currentpoint, raydirection, octree) if currentpoint is None or distance(currentpoint, exitpoint) <= 0: break continue # Sample volume value value = samplevolume(volume, currentpoint) # Check for isosurface crossing if value >= isovalue: # Assuming isovalue is the threshold # Step 4: Isosurface Refinement intersection = binarysearchrefinement(currentpoint, raydirection, volume, isovalue) # Step 5: Shading normal = computenormal(volume, intersection) color = applygoochshading(normal) image[pixel] = color break currentpoint += raydirection stepsize return image def computeentryexitpoints(rayorigin, raydirection, octree): """ Compute entry and exit points by rendering octree cubes. This is a conceptual representation of the GPU rendering passes described in. """ # In practice, this involves two rendering passes: # 1. Render cubes with glCullFace(GL FRONT) and glDepthFunc(GL LESS) to find exit. # 2. Render cubes with glCullFace(GL BACK) and glDepthFunc(GL GREATER) to find entry. # Here we assume a function that returns these points. exitpoint = renderexitpass(rayorigin, raydirection, octree) entrypoint = renderentrypass(rayorigin, raydirection, octree) return entrypoint, exitpoint def isempty(point, octree): """ Check if a point is in an empty region using the min-max octree. """ node = octree.findnodecontaining(point) return node.minvalue > isovalue or node.maxvalue < isovalue def skipemptyregion(point, direction, octree): """ Skip over empty regions using the octree. """ # Move along the ray until a non-empty node is found # This is a simplified implementation; actual implementation would use octree traversal current = point while isempty(current, octree): current += direction getcelledgelength(octree) return current def binarysearchrefinement(point, direction, volume, isovalue): """ Refine intersection using 3 iterations of binary search. """ low = point high = point + direction getcelledgelength(octree) # Approximate step for in range(3): mid = (low + high) / 2 value = samplevolume(volume, mid) if value < isovalue: low = mid else: high = mid return (low + high) / 2 def computenormal(volume, point): """ Compute normal using central difference. """ epsilon = getcelledgelength(volume) / 2.0 dx = samplevolume(volume, point + vec3(epsilon, 0, 0)) - samplevolume(volume, point - vec3(epsilon, 0, 0)) dy = samplevolume(volume, point + vec3(0, epsilon, 0)) - samplevolume(volume, point - vec3(0, epsilon, 0)) dz = samplevolume(volume, point + vec3(0, 0, epsilon)) - samplevolume(volume, point - vec3(0, 0, epsilon)) return normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) def applygoochshading(normal): """ Apply Gooch shading. """ # Simplified Gooch shading lightdir = normalize(vec3(1, 1, 1)) diff = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) return vec3(0.5 + 0.5 diff) # Example color mapping Parameters: Binary search iterations for isosurface refinement: 3. Ray step size: 0.5 \times \text{cell edge length}. Number of min/max cells: 32^3 resulted in the best performance in experiments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: A large number of small cells induces a tight bound of the isosurface but comes with a large overhead due to the primitives. A small number of large cells reduces the overhead but bounds the isosurface loosely. Precision issues may arise during binary search if the step size is too large relative to the volume gradient. Boundary conditions must be handled when sampling near the volume edges. An iso-surface rendering algorithm based on object-order ray casting that subdivides data into macro-cells to build a min/max octree, reducing traversal steps by rasterizing hexagonal footprints. It differs from its parent method Ray-marching reference (min-max octree accelerated) by processing visible volume cells directly rather than pixels, and from its sibling Object-Order Ray Casting with Min/Max Octrees by relying on pre-computed hierarchical data structures to skip empty regions. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays and the sparsity of the volume. Empty space skipping reduces the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Auxiliary octree data memory requirement is 1 to 4 megabytes for octrees with a depth of 7 or more. The lossless compression into an octree volume occupies less than one quarter the size of the original 3D array. Measured Performance: On an Intel Core Duo 2.16 GHz laptop with 2 GB RAM, frame rates were 2.4, 1.3, and 3.3 fps for three test scenes (LLNL Richtmyer-Meshkov, Utah CSAFE heptane, and a closer view). On a 16-node NUMA 2.4 GHz Opteron workstation, frame rates were 17.9, 9.8, and 22.0 fps for the same three test scenes. Performance gain up to ≈ 4.95-fold using fine-grained min/max cells for efficient empty space skipping. Scaling: The method scales well to large data, particularly when scene complexity is high relative to the number of rays that must be cast to fill a frame. Strengths: Applicable to a wide range of volumes. Low auxiliary data memory overhead. Guarantees continuous isosurfaces. Limitations: Outperformed by raster occlusion culling approaches at high resolutions (e.g., 3840×2160). Less efficient than the proposed rasterization approach for most resolutions, except for sparse datasets like Chameleon at low-to-medium resolutions. Dependent on rendering resolution for the ray-marching part, unlike the proposed rasterization approach which works largely in volume space. When to use: Suitable for general accelerated direct isosurface rendering, especially when memory overhead must be minimized and the volume is sparse. When not to use: Not suitable for very high resolutions where raster occlusion culling is more efficient. Not suitable if signed distance functions are available and Sphere Tracing is preferred. Origin: The method was introduced as a reference technique for evaluating direct isosurface rendering pipelines. It is based on the concept of using min-max octrees for empty space skipping. History: The technique has been used as a baseline for comparing new rendering approaches. It has been implemented in various research projects, including those involving large compressed structured volumes and FCC datasets. Usage: It is used as a baseline reference for direct isosurface visualization performance in evaluations. name: Object-Order Iso-Surface Rendering with Macro-Cells
head: Neubauer macro-cell octree
body: An iso-surface rendering algorithm based on object-order ray casting that subdivides data into macro-cells to build a min/max octree, reducing traversal steps by rasterizing hexagonal footprints. It builds on Ray-marching reference (min-max octree accelerated) by replacing per-pixel octree traversal with macro-cell rasterization to reuse traversal paths for multiple pixels. Inputs: Scalar volume dataset V. Macro-cell size parameter m (integer, typically 4 \le m \le 10). Image plane resolution and camera parameters (required for pixel iteration and projection). Iso-value threshold T (implied by boundary cell checks). Outputs: Final image buffer with color and depth values for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Min/Max Octree: Hierarchical tree where each node stores the minimum and maximum scalar values of its sub-volume. Leaf nodes correspond to macro-cells of size m^3. 2. Boundary Cell Flag: Boolean indicating if the iso-surface potentially intersects the sub-volume (\min < T < \max). Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Subdivide the entire dataset V into macro-cells of size m^3. Build a min/max octree from these macro-cells. 2. Octree Traversal: For each unprocessed pixel on the image plane, traverse the octree. At each traversal step, check the min/max values to determine if boundary cells (cells possibly containing the iso-surface) are in the sub-tree. 3. Macro-Cell Rasterization: At a leaf node, project the boundaries of the macro-cell onto the image plane, yielding a hexagonal footprint. 4. Local Ray Casting: For each pixel within the hexagonal footprint, use local rays to traverse the macro-cell grid. Use the Amanatides and Woo method for this traversal. 5. Intersection & Shading: If a boundary cell is encountered during macro-cell traversal, perform an intersection test with the iso-surface. If true, perform normal and shading calculations. Parameters: Macro-cell size m: Usually between 4 and 10. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in ray-voxel traversal may cause missed intersections. Use epsilon offsets for boundary checks. Degenerate Input: If T equals the min or max of a macro-cell, boundary flag logic must handle equality to avoid missing surfaces or including empty space. Hexagonal Projection: Assumes perspective projection; orthogonal projection may yield different footprints. A software-based volume rendering technique for regular grids that uses orthogonal projection and pre-computed min/max octrees to skip empty regions. It processes visible volume cells directly rather than pixels, distinguishing it from image-order methods. Choose this variant when working with regular grids and orthogonal cameras where pre-computed traversal acceleration is preferred over macro-cell rasterization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces traversal steps by rasterizing hexagonal footprints, reusing traversal paths for multiple pixels. Limitations: Hexagonal footprint calculation and rasterization add complexity. When to Use: Suitable for interactive visualization of large volume datasets where iso-surface extraction is required. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Proposed by Neubauer et al. [Neubauer02] as an alternative to image-order ray casting. It builds on the min/max octree concept introduced by Wilhelms et al. [Wilhelms92] and uses the Amanatides and Woo voxel traversal algorithm [Amanatides87]. Interactive volume ray tracing, https://doi.org/10.22028/d291-25931, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Object-Order Ray Casting with Min/Max Octrees
head: Mora orthogonal object-order
body: Object-Order Ray Casting with Min/Max Octrees is a software-based volume rendering technique for regular grids that uses orthogonal projection and pre-computed min/max octrees to skip empty (transparent) regions. It processes visible volume cells directly rather than pixels, distinguishing it from image-order methods. Inputs: Regular 3D grid of voxel data; pre-computed min/max octree; orthogonal view direction. Outputs: 2D image containing accumulated results for visible cells. Data Structures: 1. Min/Max Octree: Hierarchical structure storing minimum and maximum scalar values per sub-volume node to skip empty or transparent regions. 2. Hexagon Template: 2D projection mask of a cubic sub-volume. Orthogonal projection ensures every sub-volume projects to the same hexagon template, differing only by translation. 3. Hierarchical Occlusion Maps (HOMs): Images of different sizes used in isosurface rendering to indicate whether a ray must be traversed or a previously computed value can be reused. Steps: 1. Pre-computation: Construct the min/max octree from the input volume data. 2. Sub-volume Division & Projection: Divide the volume into sub-volumes of m^3 voxels. Project each sub-volume onto the image plane using orthogonal projection. 3. Visibility Culling: Use the min/max octree to determine if a sub-volume contains relevant data. Skip sub-volumes marked as empty or fully transparent. 4. Ray Traversal & HOM Check: For visible sub-volumes, process rays intersecting the hexagonal footprint. For isosurface rendering, check the HOMs to determine if a ray must be traversed or if a previously computed value can be reused. Parameters: m: Sub-volume side length in voxels. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on orthogonal projection to maintain the constant hexagonal footprint property. HOMs are specifically applied for isosurface rendering to enable ray reuse. Hardware-Adapted Object-Order Ray Casting adapts this software method for modern graphics hardware by generating fragments for rays intersecting volume cells, using pre-computed projection lists for orthogonal views. It is distinguished from its parent method by its explicit optimization for hardware fragment generation and pre-computed projection lists. Choose it when targeting graphics hardware for orthogonal views. Performance: Enables interactive frame rates of 2 to 5 fps for mid-sized data sets (e.g., bonsai, engine models). Memory: Uses a compact data set representation taking advantage of implicit neighbors, achieving similar performance with less memory consumption. Strengths: Efficient skipping of empty regions via min/max octrees; reduced computation via HOMs for isosurfaces; simple projection geometry due to orthogonality. Limitations: Restricted to orthogonal projection; software implementation in the original description; performance depends on min/max octree construction and traversal. Proposed by Mora et al. in 2002 as a software implementation for interactive volume ray tracing on regular grids. Designed to handle mid-sized data sets efficiently by leveraging orthogonal projection and hierarchical data structures. Interactive volume ray tracing, https://doi.org/10.22028/d291-25931, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hardware-Adapted Object-Order Ray Casting
head: Hong hardware object-order, Object-Order Ray-Casting with Efficient Ray-Cell Intersection
body: Hardware-Adapted Object-Order Ray Casting is a volume rendering technique that adapts object-order ray casting for modern graphics hardware by generating fragments for rays intersecting volume cells, with traversal order determined by min/max octrees. Unlike image-order methods that process pixels sequentially, this approach processes visible volume cells, loading vertex data and accumulating color/opacity into corresponding pixels for all intersecting rays. It is distinguished from its parent method Object-Order Ray Casting with Min/Max Octrees by its explicit optimization for hardware fragment generation and the use of pre-computed projection lists for orthogonal views. Inputs: Volume dataset (scalar field), min/max octree structure, camera viewpoint (orthogonal projection assumed for efficient projection lists), iso-surface or transfer function parameters. Outputs: Rendered image (color and opacity per pixel). Data Structures: 1. Min/Max Octree: Hierarchical structure storing min/max values for sub-volumes to cull empty or fully occluded regions. 2. Projection Lists: Pre-computed lists of relative pixel coordinates representing the template hexagon projection of a cell, associated with subdivisions of a square of four neighboring pixels. 3. Layer Lists: Pre-computed layers for sub-volumes to reduce visibility ordering complexity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Precompute Projection Lists (Viewpoint Dependent): Subdivide a square of four neighboring pixels on the image plane. For each subdivision, store a list of relative coordinates corresponding to the template hexagon projection of a cell. Store the global coordinate of the square where a cell center projects. Note: These lists are recomputed every time the viewpoint changes. 2. Traverse Octree and Determine Visibility: Use the min/max octree to implicitly determine the correct front-to-back order between sub-volumes. Divide sub-volumes into pre-computed layers to further reduce visibility ordering complexity. Identify visible cells (not transparent and not hidden). 3. For Each Visible Cell: Load the values and gradients of the 8 vertices of the cell. Determine the global coordinate of the square where the cell center projects. Identify the subdivision containing the projected center. Retrieve the relative coordinate list for that subdivision. Calculate rasterized pixel indices by adding the relative coordinates to the global coordinate of the square: P{\text{rasterized}} = P{\text{global}} + C{\text{relative}} Where P{\text{global}} is the global coordinate of the square and C{\text{relative}} is a relative coordinate from the list. Correction Step: Test line equations to filter out erroneous pixels projected due to the reuse of relative coordinate lists across different cells within the same subdivision. Generate fragments corresponding to the rays intersecting the cell. For every ray intersecting the cell: Sample colors and opacities along the ray. Accumulate the results into the equivalent pixel in front-to-back order. Store intermediate luminance and density values as 16-bit unsigned integers for sequential line integral estimation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwareadaptedobjectorderraycasting(volume, octree, viewpoint): # Step 1: Precompute projection lists (recomputed on viewpoint change) projectionlists = precomputeprojectionlists(viewpoint) # Step 2: Traverse octree to get visible cells in order visiblecells = traverseoctreeforvisibility(octree) for cell in visiblecells: # Load vertex data vertexvalues, vertexgradients = loadcelldata(cell) # Determine projection cellcenterproj = projectcellcenter(cell, viewpoint) squareglobal, subdivision = findsquareandsubdivision(cellcenterproj, projectionlists) # Get relative coordinates for this subdivision relativecoords = projectionlists[subdivision] # Generate fragments and accumulate for relcoord in relativecoords: # Calculate pixel index pixelidx = squareglobal + relcoord # Correction: Test line equations to filter erroneous pixels if isvalidpixel(cell, pixelidx): # Sample and accumulate along ray for this pixel accumulatepixel(pixelidx, cell, vertexvalues, vertexgradients) def isvalidpixel(cell, pixelidx): # Test line equations to correct for erroneous projections # Implementation detail: Check if pixelidx lies within the projected hexagon boundary # of the cell using half-plane tests. return checklineequations(cell, pixelidx) def precomputeprojectionlists(viewpoint): # Subdivide a square of four neighboring pixels # Associate list of relative coordinates (template hexagon) with each subdivision # Store global coordinate of the square where cell center projects # Return dictionary mapping (squareglobal, subdivisionid) -> list of relativecoords lists = {} # Standard implementation: grid subdivision based on viewpoint projection matrix return lists def traverseoctreeforvisibility(octree): # Use min/max octree to implicitly determine correct order # Divide sub-volumes into pre-computed layers # Return list of visible cells in front-to-back order return [] def accumulatepixel(pixelidx, cell, vertexvalues, vertexgradients): # For every ray intersecting the cell, sample colors/opacities # Update equivalent pixel in front-to-back order # Store intermediate values as 16-bit unsigned integers pass Parameters: Viewpoint: The projection lists and preprocessed rays are recomputed every time the viewpoint changes. Macro-Cell Size: While not explicitly defined for this specific hardware adaptation in the notes, related macro-cell methods use sizes m^3 where m is usually between four and ten. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Erroneous Pixels: The same relative coordinate list is used for all cells within the same subdivision, which can project erroneous pixels. This is corrected by testing line equations. Viewpoint Changes: Performance may degrade if the viewpoint changes frequently due to the need to recompute projection lists. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of visible cells and rays intersecting them. Pre-computation of projection lists is O(1) per viewpoint change but requires recomputation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the min/max octree, projection lists, and intermediate values (16-bit unsigned integers). Strengths: Efficient for orthogonal projections; leverages hardware fragment generation; reduces visibility ordering complexity with pre-computed layers. Limitations: Projection lists must be recomputed for viewpoint changes; potential for erroneous pixels requiring correction. When to Use: Orthogonal visualization scenarios where hardware acceleration is desired. When Not to Use: Perspective views (projection lists are optimized for orthogonal) or frequent viewpoint changes. Originating from Hong et al. [Hong05], this method adapts object-order ray casting for current graphics hardware. It builds on the concept of using hierarchical occlusion maps and min/max octrees for visibility determination. It is related to iso-surface rendering algorithms based on object-order ray casting, such as those by Neubauer et al. [Neubauer02]. name: Hierarchical Data Structures
body: Hierarchical data structures organize volumetric data into multi-resolution trees to accelerate image-order rendering by skipping empty or inactive regions during ray traversal. Unlike flat grid traversal, these structures enable rays to jump over large empty spaces or identify active cells for rendering, significantly reducing computational cost. This family serves as the foundational acceleration mechanism for sibling methods such as Ray-marching reference (min-max octree accelerated) and ExaBricks Rendering with RTX BVH. The core mechanism involves constructing a tree where nodes represent spatial regions and store aggregate information (e.g., binary occupancy flags, min/max values) derived from child nodes or leaf voxels. Traversal proceeds from the root; if a node indicates an empty or inactive region (e.g., flag is 0, or min/max bounds are outside the view), the entire subtree is skipped. Construction typically follows a bottom-up approach: leaf nodes encode voxel properties, and internal nodes aggregate these properties from their children. The hierarchy depth is determined by the data dimensions, often requiring specific size constraints (e.g., N=2^M+1) or padding to maintain regular subdivision. Encodes spatial coherence using a pyramid of binary volumes to skip empty space in image-order rendering. It uses a complete octree (pyramid) rather than a sparse structure, allowing rays to jump over large empty regions. Choose this when fast image-order traversal of regular grids with significant empty space is required. A hybrid object-order and image-order structure designed to locate active cells for direct and indirect visualization. It solves redundant ray marching by rendering only relevant active cells. Performance is resolution-dependent. Choose this for hybrid rendering approaches where identifying active cells is critical. Uses a mip pyramid over silhouette images to accelerate voxel/silhouette coverage queries. Each level stores min/max values of 4 texels from the next lower level, providing conservative bounds. Choose this when silhouette-based culling is the primary optimization goal. A preprocessing step that performs parallel, synchronized partitioning of volume data to produce a hierarchical spatial tree. This tree optimizes the compositing process, reduces runtime memory consumption, and speeds up cell searching for zoom-in viewing. It is used in parallel cell-projection rendering where data is distributed in round-robin fashion to disperse nearby cells among processors. The concept of hierarchical acceleration for volume rendering emerged in the mid-1990s to address the high cost of ray traversal through large datasets. Early work focused on unstructured data, where parallel cell-projection algorithms required efficient spatial partitioning to manage load balancing and memory consumption. The "Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration" approach was developed to handle regular grids by creating a binary pyramid that explicitly marks empty regions, enabling efficient skipping during ray tracing. The Jiang et al. structure [JRZ16] later introduced a hybrid approach for locating active cells, reflecting the shift towards resolution-dependent acceleration. These methods form the basis for modern block-based and octree acceleration techniques. name: Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization
head: Complete octree representation, Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration (Octree Pyramid), Pyramid of binary volumes
body: Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization is a data structure and rendering acceleration technique for image-order volume rendering that encodes spatial coherence (specifically, regions of zero opacity) using a pyramid of binary volumes. It solves the problem of efficiently skipping empty space during ray traversal by representing the volume data as a complete octree (pyramid) rather than a condensed sparse structure. Unlike sibling methods that may use condensed representations or object-order traversal, this approach enables fast image-order ray tracing by allowing rays to jump over large empty regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset of size N \times N \times N voxels, where N = 2^M + 1 for some integer M, with each voxel having an opacity value \alpha. Output: A pyramid of M+1 binary volumes V0, \dots, VM, where each volume Vm contains binary flags indicating the presence of non-zero opacity in the corresponding spatial region. Data Structures: The structure is a pyramid of M+1 binary volumes indexed by level m \in \{0, \dots, M\}. Volume Dimensions: V0 has dimensions (N-1) \times (N-1) \times (N-1) cells. Vm has dimensions \frac{N-1}{2^m} \times \frac{N-1}{2^m} \times \frac{N-1}{2^m} cells. VM is a single cell (1 \times 1 \times 1). Cell Content: Each cell Vm(\mathbf{i}) stores a binary value (0 or 1). 1: The region contains at least one voxel with non-zero opacity. 0: The region contains only voxels with zero opacity (empty). Coordinate System: Voxels are treated as point samples, while cells fill the space between them. Cell (1,1,1) at level 0 encloses the space between voxel (1,1,1) and voxel (2,2,2). Voxel (1,1,1) is placed at the front-lower-right corner of cell (1,1,1) at level 0. The size of a cell on level m is 2^m times the spacing between voxels. Construction Algorithm: The pyramid is constructed recursively from the base level V0 up to VM. 1. Base Level (V0) Construction: For each cell index \mathbf{i} = (i,j,k) where i,j,k \in \{1, \dots, N-1\}: V0(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \alpha(\mathbf{i} + \Delta\mathbf{i}) = 1 \text{ for any } \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This means cell \mathbf{i} in V0 is 1 if any of the 8 voxels at its vertices (defined by offsets \Delta\mathbf{i}) has non-zero opacity. 2. Recursive Level Construction (m > 0): For each cell index \mathbf{i} in volume Vm: Vm(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V{m-1}(\mathbf{j}) = 1 \text{ for any child cell } \mathbf{j} \text{ of } \mathbf{i} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Specifically, cell \mathbf{i} in Vm contains 0 if all 8 cells on level m-1 that form its octants contain zeros; otherwise, it contains 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildpyramid(opacityvoxels, N): """ Builds the hierarchical spatial enumeration pyramid. Args: opacityvoxels: 3D array of size N x N x N containing opacity values. Uses 1-based indexing to match the source notation. N: Side length of the voxel grid. Must satisfy N = 2^M + 1. Returns: pyramid: List of 3D binary arrays [V0, V1,..., VM]. """ import math M = int(math.log2(N - 1)) pyramid = [] # Step 1: Construct Base Volume V0 # V0 dimensions: (N-1) x (N-1) x (N-1) dim0 = N - 1 # Initialize 1-based padded arrays V0 = [[[0 for in range(dim0 + 1)] for in range(dim0 + 1)] for in range(dim0 + 1)] for i in range(1, dim0 + 1): for j in range(1, dim0 + 1): for k in range(1, dim0 + 1): hasnonzero = False for di in (0, 1): for dj in (0, 1): for dk in (0, 1): if opacityvoxels[i + di][j + dj][k + dk] != 0: hasnonzero = True break if hasnonzero: break if hasnonzero: break V0[i][j][k] = 1 if hasnonzero else 0 pyramid.append(V0) # Step 2: Construct higher levels V1 to VM currentvol = V0 for m in range(1, M + 1): prevvol = currentvol prevdim = dim0 // (2 (m - 1)) currdim = prevdim // 2 Vm = [[[0 for in range(currdim + 1)] for in range(currdim + 1)] for in range(currdim + 1)] for i in range(1, currdim + 1): for j in range(1, currdim + 1): for k in range(1, currdim + 1): hasnonzero = False for di in (0, 1): for dj in (0, 1): for dk in (0, 1): if prevvol[2i + di][2j + dj][2k + dk] == 1: hasnonzero = True break if hasnonzero: break if hasnonzero: break Vm[i][j][k] = 1 if hasnonzero else 0 pyramid.append(Vm) currentvol = Vm return pyramid Usage in Rendering: The pyramid is used to efficiently compute intersections between viewing rays and regions of interest. Ray Tracing: Rays are traced through the pyramid; if a cell in the current level is 0, the entire region is empty and the ray can skip it. Hybrid Ray Tracer: The pyramid speeds up tracing through segments of volumetric data lying between successive polygon intersections. Scan Conversion: The composite dataset including sampled polygons can be used during pyramid construction to improve efficiency for mixed geometric and volumetric data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Alignment: Voxel (1,1,1) is at the front-lower-right corner of cell (1,1,1) at level 0, and cell (1,1,1) at level 0 encloses the space between voxels (1,1,1) and (2,2,2). Misalignment here will cause incorrect empty region detection. Dataset Size: The method requires N = 2^M + 1. Not given in the sources. Opacity Threshold: The binary volume uses a threshold of 0; voxels with opacity exactly 0 are considered empty, while any non-zero opacity marks the region as occupied. A ray tracing algorithm that uses this pyramidal structure to skip empty regions and an adaptive termination criterion to stop tracing when opacity changes become negligible. It differs from geometric ray tracing by using a hierarchical binary volume structure, which is more efficient for volume data with tens of millions of spatially ordered cells. Time Complexity: The cost of ray tracing volumetric data using this hierarchical enumeration grows linearly with the size of the image, logarithmically with the length of each ray, and linearly with the depth complexity of the data. Memory Complexity: The pyramid stores M+1 binary volumes. The total number of cells is \sum{m=0}^{M} (\frac{N-1}{2^m})^3. Since N-1 = 2^M, the base volume has (2^M)^3 cells. The total size is roughly \frac{1}{7}(N-1)^3 cells, which is significantly less than the original N^3 voxels if only the hierarchy is stored, but the base volume V0 is still large. Since Vm are binary, they can be packed efficiently. Strengths: Efficiently skips large empty regions in volume data. Enables fast image-order rendering. Can be integrated with hybrid ray tracing for mixed geometric/volumetric scenes. Limitations: Requires dataset size N = 2^M + 1. Performance depends on the depth complexity of the data. Adaptive termination is needed to reduce dependence on depth complexity. When to Use: Suitable for image-order volume rendering of large datasets with significant empty space (spatial coherence). When Not to Use: If the dataset is small, or if the data has no spatial coherence (all voxels have non-zero opacity), the overhead of the pyramid may not be justified. Origin: The method was introduced by Marc Levoy in the paper "Efficient ray tracing of volume data". History: It is based on the observation that many volumetric datasets contain coherent regions of uninteresting voxels (opacity zero). The technique uses a pyramid of binary volumes to encode this spatial coherence. Comparison: It differs from prior work by rendering in image order (tracing rays through the octree) rather than object order (depth-first traversal). It also differs by using a pyramid of binary volumes/complete octree rather than a condensed representation. Applications: Medical imaging and molecular graphics. name: Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination
head: Pyramidal Volume Traversal, TraceRay2
body: Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination is a ray tracing algorithm that uses a pyramidal data structure of binary volumes to skip empty regions and an adaptive termination criterion to stop tracing when opacity changes become negligible. Unlike geometric ray tracing, which uses bounding volumes or spatial subdivision with lists of primitives, this method uses a hierarchical binary volume structure, which is more efficient for volume data because volume datasets have tens of millions of spatially ordered cells with single samples, whereas geometric scenes have hundreds of cells with many primitives. The method traverses a ray through a hierarchy of binary volumes (a pyramid) to determine which regions contain data. It adapts the traversal depth based on the content and terminates early if the accumulated opacity is sufficiently high. Input: Ray parameter \mathbf{u} (defining the ray direction and origin), the pyramidal binary volume structure \{Vm\}, the volume data (color and opacity fields), and parameters \epsilon, m{max}, m{min}, and M (total levels). Output: Final ray color \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) and accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}). The core data structure is a pyramid of binary volumes. Binary Volumes Vm: For each level m \in \{0, \dots, M\}, Vm is a 3D grid of bits. V0 is the base level, and Vm for m > 0 is derived from V{m-1}. Memory layout: (2^{M+1} - 1)/7 bits total for the pyramid. Volume Data: Monochrome color and opacity fields. Memory layout: 2N^3 bytes for color and opacity per voxel. Output Image: Memory layout: P^2 bytes. The binary volumes are defined recursively to indicate the presence of non-zero opacity in their spatial extent. Base Level (V0): V0(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \alpha(\mathbf{i} + \Delta\mathbf{i}) = 1 \\ 0 & \text{for } \mathbf{i} \in \{1, 2, \dots, N-1\}^3 \text{ and any } \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \alpha is the opacity field, \mathbf{i} is the index, and the condition checks if any of the eight voxels at the vertices of the cell have opacity equal to 1. Higher Levels (Vm, m > 0): Vm(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V{m-1}(2\mathbf{i} - \Delta\mathbf{i}) = 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} for \mathbf{i} \in \{1, 2, \dots, \frac{N-1}{m+1}\}^3 and any \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3. This means a cell at level m is 1 if any of the eight cells at level m-1 that form its octants are 1. \epsilon: Threshold for significant color change. Default value 0.05. Higher values reduce rendering time, lower values reduce artifacts. m{max}: Starting level for traversal. Set to M - 2 for all values of M to minimize traversal costs. m{min}: Lowest level to descend to before rendering. Set to 2 for the current implementation to avoid the high cost of ray-cell intersections at level zero. M: Total number of levels in the pyramid. The algorithm processes each ray \mathbf{u} as follows: 1. Initialize ray color \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) and opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}) to 0. 2. Set ray position \mathbf{x} to the entry point of the ray into the volume using First(u). 3. Set current level m to m{max}. 4. Loop while the ray position \mathbf{x} is in bounds (InBounds(x)) and accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}) is less than or equal to 1 - \epsilon: a. Calculate the cell index \mathbf{i} at current level m containing point \mathbf{x} using the Index(m, x) procedure. b. If the cell value Vm(\mathbf{i}) is 1 and m > m{min}: i. Decrement level m by 1 to descend into the hierarchy (m:= m - 1). ii. Continue to the next iteration of the loop to re-evaluate the cell at the new level. c. Else (if cell is 1 and at min level, or cell is 0): i. If the cell value Vm(\mathbf{i}) is 1: 1. Determine the exit point of the current cell along the ray using Next(m, x, u). 2. Call RenderCell(u, x, Next(m, x, u)) to render the interval from current \mathbf{x} to the next cell entry point. ii. Advance to the next cell on the same level. iii. While the parent of the new cell differs from the parent of the old cell and m < M: 1. Move up to the parent cell (\mathbf{i}:= \text{Parent}(m, \mathbf{i})). 2. Increment level m (m:= m + 1). iv. Update ray position \mathbf{x} to the entry point of the next cell at the current level m (\mathbf{x}:= \text{Next}(m, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u})). The RenderCell procedure handles the resampling and compositing for a specific interval along the ray defined by entry \mathbf{x}1 and exit \mathbf{x}2. 1. Define image bounds \mathbf{U}1 and \mathbf{U}2 for the cell interval using Image(x1) and Image(x2). 2. Loop through evenly spaced sample locations \mathbf{U} within this interval from \mathbf{U}1 to \mathbf{U}2. Evenly spaced locations are superimposed to avoid noise artifacts caused by resampling at non-uniformly spaced points determined by ray-cell intersections. 3. For each sample \mathbf{U}: a. Get object space coordinates \mathbf{x} using Object(U). b. Check if the base level binary volume V0 at the index of \mathbf{x} is 1 (V0(Index(0, x))). c. If 1: i. Resample color \hat{C}(\mathbf{U}) and opacity \alpha(\mathbf{U}) from the volume data using Sample. ii. Composite the sample into the ray: \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}):= \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) + \hat{C}(\mathbf{U})(1 - \alpha(\mathbf{u})) \alpha(\mathbf{u}):= \alpha(\mathbf{u}) + \alpha(\mathbf{U})(1 - \alpha(\mathbf{u})). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def TraceRay2(u, epsilon, mmax, mmin, M, V, InBounds, First, Index, Next, Parent, RenderCell): Cray = 0.0 alpharay = 0.0 x = First(u) m = mmax while InBounds(x) and alpharay <= 1.0 - epsilon: i = Index(m, x) if V[m][i] == 1 and m > mmin: m -= 1 continue else: if V[m][i] == 1: xnext = Next(m, x, u) RenderCell(u, x, xnext, Cray, alpharay, V) xnext = Next(m, x, u) while m < M and Parent(m, Index(m, xnext)) != Parent(m, i): i = Parent(m, i) m += 1 x = xnext return Cray, alpharay def RenderCell(u, x1, x2, Cray, alpharay, V): U1 = Image(x1) U2 = Image(x2) for U in range(U1, U2 + 1): x = Object(U) if V[0][Index(0, x)] == 1: Csample = Sample(V.color, x) alphasample = Sample(V.opacity, x) Cray = Cray + Csample (1.0 - alpharay) alpharay = alpharay + alphasample (1.0 - alpharay) return Cray, alpharay Note: Image, Object, and Sample are standard projection and resampling functions. Resampling Artifacts: Resampling at non-uniformly spaced points (determined by ray-cell intersections) adds noise artifacts to the image. The solution is to superimpose evenly spaced sample locations and only resample at those specific points. Level Zero Descent: Descending to level zero is inefficient for orthographic projections because ray-cell intersection costs exceed simple differencing. The solution is to stop descent at m{min}=2 and render level-zero cells within that higher-level cell. Time Complexity: The traversal skips empty regions, reducing the number of samples taken. The adaptive termination stops tracing when opacity is high, further reducing work. The cost of traversal is minimized by starting at m{max} = M - 2. Memory Complexity: The memory required is 2N^3 bytes for the volume data, (2^{M+1} - 1)/7 bits for the pyramid, and P^2 bytes for the output image. Strengths: Efficient for volume data with large empty regions. The hierarchical structure allows skipping large empty areas. The adaptive termination reduces work for opaque regions. Limitations: Inefficient if the volume is mostly opaque or has no empty regions, as the hierarchy may not provide significant skipping. The need for evenly spaced sampling adds complexity. When to Use: Suitable for volume datasets with significant empty space and where ray-cell intersection costs are high (e.g., orthographic projections). When Not to Use: Not suitable for geometric scenes with many primitives per cell, as the method is optimized for volume data with single samples per cell. The method was introduced in the paper "Efficient ray tracing of volume data". It is based on the observation that volume datasets contain coherent regions of uninteresting voxels (opacity zero) and can be encoded as a hierarchical spatial enumeration represented by a pyramid of binary volumes. The method is also known as Pyramidal Volume Traversal or TraceRay2. Efficient ray tracing of volume data, https://doi.org/10.1145/78964.78965, fetched 2026-10-25

name: Jiang et al. Acceleration Structure
head: JRZ*16 method
body: The Jiang et al. acceleration structure [JRZ16] is a hierarchical data structure designed to efficiently locate active cells within a scalar volume for both direct and indirect visualization approaches. It solves the problem of redundant ray marching through inactive background regions by identifying and rendering only the relevant active cells. Unlike pure image-order methods, it is classified as a hybrid object-order and image-order approach, meaning its performance and structure are dependent on the rendering resolution. It builds on Hierarchical Data Structures and differs from Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization and Silhouette Image Space Acceleration Structure (Mip Pyramid) by relying on resolution-dependent hybrid traversal rather than pure image-order or object-order enumeration. Inputs: A scalar volume dataset and a target rendering resolution. Outputs: A set of active cells identified for ray marching. Data structures: The specific internal layout, bit-packing, or hierarchical tree structure of the Jiang et al. acceleration structure is Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Traverse the acceleration structure to identify active cells within the volume. 2. Render the identified active cells using ray marching. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases: As a resolution-dependent method, performance characteristics and active cell identification boundaries may vary with the chosen rendering resolution. Pseudocode: Not given in the sources. The IsoBAS acceleration structure [LCD15] is a variant introduced by Liu et al. for faster identification of active cells. It is distinguished by requiring less memory overhead than previous methods. It is chosen when memory efficiency is a priority alongside active cell identification speed. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method is dependent on rendering resolution, implying that scaling the resolution affects the structure's utility or performance. Strengths and limitations: It efficiently locates active cells for both direct and indirect visualization. Its limitation is the dependency on rendering resolution, classifying it as a hybrid approach rather than a purely resolution-independent object-order method. When to use it: Use when efficient active cell location is required for ray marching in both direct and indirect visualization. When not: Avoid if a purely resolution-independent acceleration structure is required. Origin: Proposed by Jiang et al. [JRZ16]. History: It follows earlier methods such as those by Liu et al. [LCD09, LCD15] which utilized CPU-based sorting of volume slices for front-to-back rasterization. The Jiang et al. method is considered part of the same family of hybrid object-order and image-order approaches. name: Sparse Voxel Traversal
head: OpenVDB Ray Intersector, Sparse Voxel Traversal and Sampling, Structure sampling, VolumeRayIntersector, Voxel Tree Raycasting, getVoxel
body: Sparse Voxel Traversal is a hierarchical ray-intersection algorithm that accelerates volume rendering by navigating a spatial hierarchy (such as a Sparse Voxel Octree) to skip empty space and reduce the number of ray-casting steps. It solves the performance bottleneck of non-hierarchical voxel traversal, where every voxel along a ray must be visited, by allowing the ray to "leap" over large empty regions. Unlike its siblings, it operates on a recursive tree structure where higher-level cells cover a 2 \times 2 area of the level below, enabling larger steps through empty space. It distinguishes itself from standard grid traversal by using interval arithmetic with correct rounding modes to guarantee that no octant is missed during traversal, solving precision errors that occur when subdivision levels approach floating-point limits. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical voxel tree (e.g., VoxelTree, OpenVDB Grid) containing nodes of types Empty, Leaf, or Branch. A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Output: Intersection times (TOI) or a callback result from leaf nodes. Data Structures: VoxelBounds: Struct with fields x: i32, y: i32, z: i32 (coordinates as multiples of 2^{\text{lg\size}}) and lgsize: i16 (log2 of voxel size). The size in world units is 2^{\text{lg\size}} if \text{lg\size} \ge 0, else 1.0 / 2^{-\text{lg\size}}. TOI: A wrapper around f32 implementing Ord for sorting intersection times. Entry/Exit: Structures tracking the side index (0-5) and TOI of ray entry/exit. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the intersector with the grid and optional dilation count. Set the ray using setIndexRay (index space) or setWorldRay (world space). If the ray misses the grid's bounding box, return false. 2. Traversal Loop: Recursively traverse the tree starting from the root. Empty Node: If the current node is Empty, do nothing and fall through to calculate the exit. Leaf Node: If the current node is Leaf, call the action callback act(bounds, leaf). If it returns Some(r), return Ok(r). Otherwise, fall through to calculate the exit. Branch Node: If the current node is Branch: 1. Compute the midpoint of the current bounds: \mathbf{mid} = [(\text{bounds}.x + 0.5) \cdot \text{size}, (\text{bounds}.y + 0.5) \cdot \text{size}, (\text{bounds}.z + 0.5) \cdot \text{size}]. 2. Calculate the intersection point \mathbf{intersect} at the current entry time: \mathbf{intersect} = \mathbf{o} + \text{entry\toi} \cdot \mathbf{d}, where \text{entry\toi} is the TOI of the entry (0.0 if none). 3. Determine child coordinates: \text{coords}[i] = 1 if \text{intersect}[i] \ge \text{mid}[i], else 0. 4. Update bounds for the child: shift coordinates, decrement lgsize, and add child coordinates. 5. Recursively call castraybranches with the child branch, origin, direction, entry, new coords, and updated bounds. 3. Exit Calculation: If no return value is found in the node (Empty or Leaf without hit): 1. Define sides array: [\text{bounds}.x, \text{bounds}.y, \text{bounds}.z, \text{bounds}.x + 1, \text{bounds}.y + 1, \text{bounds}.z + 1]. 2. For each side, compute the time of intersection (TOI): Get dimension \text{dim} = \text{side} \% 3 and bound value b = \text{bound} \cdot \text{bounds.size()}. If \mathbf{d}[\text{dim}] == 0.0, return None. Compute \text{toi} = (b - \mathbf{o}[\text{dim}]) / \mathbf{d}[\text{dim}]. Accept if: if entry is None, \text{toi} \ge 0.0; if entry is Some, \text{entry.toi} \le \text{toi}. 3. Find the minimum valid TOI among the sides. If entry exists, exclude the entry side. 4. Return Err(exit) with the minimum TOI. 4. Coordinate Update (for Branches): If castray returns Err(exit): 1. Calculate dimension \text{dim} = \text{exit.side} \% 3. 2. If \mathbf{d}[\text{dim}] < 0.0: If \text{coords}[\text{dim}] == 0, return the exit error (ray exited tree boundary). Otherwise, set \text{coords}[\text{dim}] = 0. 3. If \mathbf{d}[\text{dim}] \ge 0.0: If \text{coords}[\text{dim}] == 1, return the exit error. Otherwise, set \text{coords}[\text{dim}] = 1. 4. Update entry: \text{entry} = \text{Entry::from\exit}(\text{exit}), which maps the exit side to the opposite face. 5. Loop to the next child. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castray(node, origin, direction, bounds, entry): """ Recursively traverse a voxel tree node. node: TreeBody (Empty, Leaf, or Branch) origin: [f32, f32, f32] direction: [f32, f32, f32] bounds: VoxelBounds entry: Optional[Entry] Returns: Result[R, Exit] """ if node is Empty: pass # Fall through to exit calculation elif node is Leaf: result = act(bounds, node) if result is not None: return Ok(result) # Fall through to exit calculation elif node is Branch: mid = [ (bounds.x + 0.5) bounds.size(), (bounds.y + 0.5) bounds.size(), (bounds.z + 0.5) bounds.size() ] entrytoi = entry.toi if entry else 0.0 intersect = [ origin[0] + entrytoi direction[0], origin[1] + entrytoi direction[1], origin[2] + entrytoi direction[2] ] coords = [ 1 if intersect[0] >= mid[0] else 0, 1 if intersect[1] >= mid[1] else 0, 1 if intersect[2] >= mid[2] else 0 ] # Update bounds for child childbounds = VoxelBounds( x=(bounds.x << 1) + coords[0], y=(bounds.y << 1) + coords[1], z=(bounds.z << 1) + coords[2], lgsize=bounds.lgsize - 1) # Recursive call res = castray(node.child, origin, direction, childbounds, entry) if res.isok(): return res exit = res.error() dim = exit.side % 3 # Update coordinates for next iteration if direction[dim] < 0.0: if coords[dim] == 0: return Err(exit) coords[dim] = 0 else: if coords[dim] == 1: return Err(exit) coords[dim] = 1 entry = Entry.fromexit(exit) # Loop to next child (simplified as recursive call with updated coords) # In practice, this is a loop in castraybranches return castray(node.child, origin, direction, childbounds, entry) # Exit calculation sides = [bounds.x, bounds.y, bounds.z, bounds.x + 1, bounds.y + 1, bounds.z + 1] validexits = [] for side, bound in enumerate(sides): dim = side % 3 boundval = bound bounds.size() if direction[dim] == 0.0: continue toi = (boundval - origin[dim]) / direction[dim] if entry is None: if toi >= 0.0: validexits.append(Exit(side, toi)) else: if entry.toi <= toi: validexits.append(Exit(side, toi)) if not validexits: return None # Should not happen if ray is inside # Find min toi, excluding entry side if entry exists minexit = None for exit in validexits: if entry is not None and exit.side == entry.side: continue if minexit is None or exit.toi < minexit.toi: minexit = exit return Err(minexit) Parameters: Precision: 30 bits (NL=30). Resolution: Octree level 9 (512^3 resolution). Dilation Count: Number of voxel dilations on a boolean copy of the input grid to account for interpolation kernel sizes (default 0). NodeLevel: The tree node level at which traversal stops and hit times are resolved (default: Leaf). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Errors: When subdivision levels approach floating-point limits, standard traversals may mismatch. This is handled by using interval arithmetic with correct rounding modes (SSE2) to guarantee correctness. Division by Zero: If \mathbf{d}[\text{dim}] == 0.0, the TOI calculation is skipped for that side. Thread Safety: The ValueAccessor is not thread-safe. A copy constructor must be used to create a separate instance per computational thread. Index vs World Space: Hit times t0 and t1 are computed in index space. Client code must use getIndexPos or getWorldPos to convert. Octree Traversal is a hierarchical ray-intersection algorithm that accelerates volume rendering by navigating a spatial hierarchy (such as an Octree or Sparse Voxel Octree) to skip empty space and reduce the number of ray-casting steps. It solves the performance bottleneck of non-hierarchical voxel traversal, where every voxel along a ray must be visited, by allowing the ray to "leap" over large empty regions. Unlike its siblings, it operates on a recursive tree structure where higher-level cells cover a 2 \times 2 area of the level below, enabling larger steps through empty space. A technique to reduce model size by omitting voxels with low importance scores, based on the observation that a small percentage of voxels contribute the majority of rendering importance. Samples into a brick for deep volume raytracing, handling empty space skipping and alpha accumulation. A specialized traversal routine for cap nodes, which are leaf-like structures containing scalar values, differing from interior nodes in how child values are retrieved. A ray marching algorithm that traverses a sparse voxel hierarchy (chunks, bricks, voxels) by computing the exit plane of the current cell using precomputed axis-aligned distance fields (AADF) stored in textures, avoiding per-voxel traversal when empty. An iterator that traverses a 3D voxel volume along a ray, returning hits for voxels contained within the volume. It uses an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) test to quickly reject rays that do not intersect the volume before performing the voxel traversal. A ray marching technique that replaces a dense voxel buffer with a sparse hierarchical structure (brick-map) to skip empty regions. It uses a top-level grid of cells (stride 8 voxels) to quickly identify occupied bricks, then descends into those bricks for fine-grained DDA. This reduces memory footprint and traversal time in sparse volumes like drone airspace (>99% empty). A rendering method that uses a sparse occupancy grid (OccGrid) to accelerate volume rendering by traversing only occupied voxels, using a custom CUDA kernel traversegrids to generate sample intervals. A variant of sparse ray marching used for Ray Traced Ambient Occlusion. It marches from a surface point in a hemisphere direction, counting occlusions up to a radius limit. It starts at the floor of the ray origin, initializes local position and distance to 0, and loops up to 3 \times \text{uniforms.grid\ext} times. It checks voxel occupancy using voxelmasks; if occupied, it returns true. It loads the voxel AADF and calculates the exit plane, then advances the ray position. It accumulates distance and stops at tmax. Unlike the main sparse ray march, this version does not use the hierarchical chunk/brick structure, only checking voxelmasks and voxelaadf. Time Complexity: Logarithmic with respect to the depth of the octree, O(\log N), where N is the number of voxels, due to skipping empty branches. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of non-empty nodes in the sparse voxel tree. Performance: On a PC with a Pentium-4 2.4GHz processor and 512Mbytes of main memory, generating 512 \times 512 images for various surfaces (e.g., asterisk(9,18)) took approximately 410-445 seconds using the algorithm with SSE2 rounding modes, comparable to Gargantini's algorithm. The version without rounding modes was several seconds faster. Strengths: Guarantees correctness for all cases with minimal performance impact by using interval arithmetic with correct rounding modes. Efficiently skips empty space in sparse volumes. Limitations: Requires careful handling of floating-point precision at high subdivision levels. The ValueAccessor is not thread-safe, requiring per-thread instances. When to Use: High-resolution sparse volumes where empty space skipping is critical and precision errors are a concern. When Not to Use: Dense volumes where the overhead of tree traversal outweighs the benefit of skipping empty space, or when hardware does not support SSE2 instructions for interval arithmetic. Sparse Voxel Traversal originated from the need to efficiently render high-resolution implicit surfaces and volumetric data. The method using interval arithmetic with correct rounding modes was introduced to solve precision errors in Gargantini's algorithm, which only partially eliminated errors under restricted conditions. The implementation in OpenVDB (VolumeRayIntersector) is used in OpenVDB v13.1.0 for ray marching through density or generic volumes. The 5-4-3 node structure (Node5, Node4, Node3) is commonly used in game industry rendering for VDB data, as seen in benchmarks like Evolve. The variant for Ray Traced Ambient Occlusion (RTAO) is used in real-time path tracing pipelines. name: Octree Traversal
head: Hierarchical Octree Traversal, Octree Space Subdivision
body: Octree Traversal is a hierarchical ray-intersection algorithm that accelerates volume rendering by navigating a spatial hierarchy to skip empty space and reduce the number of ray-casting steps. It solves the performance bottleneck of non-hierarchical voxel traversal, where every voxel along a ray must be visited, by allowing the ray to leap over large empty regions. Unlike its siblings, it operates on a recursive tree structure where each parent node divides into eight equal sub-blocks (2 \times 2 \times 2 subdivision), enabling larger steps through empty space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; the root node of the octree; traversal bounds [t{enter}, t{exit}]. Output: A sorted list of intersected leaf nodes (voxels) or a termination signal upon finding the first occupied leaf (for ray casting) or completing the volume integration. Data Structures: The octree is a hierarchical indexing mechanism where each parent node contains 0 or 8 children. The 8 children achieve a 2 \times 2 \times 2 regular subdivision of the parent node into 8 equal parts or "leaves". Interior Node: Contains pointers to up to 8 children. May store metadata (e.g., min/max scalar values) to facilitate empty space skipping. Leaf Node: Represents the finest level of subdivision (single voxel or small block). Cap Node: A specific leaf type at the boundary of the finest resolution, mapping to a cell via reconstruction. Scalar Leaf: A coarser-resolution scalar embedded in a parent node. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Start at the octree root. Initialize the ray parameter range [t{enter}, t{exit}]. 2. Mid-plane Intersection: For the current node, compute the ray intersection distances with the X, Y, and Z mid-planes of the node's bounding box: t{midX}, t{midY}, t{midZ}. 3. Ordering: Sort the mid-plane intersection distances to determine the sequential order in which the ray intersects the eight child octants. A ray intersects at most 4 octants of an interior node. 4. Child Index Computation: For each child octant in the sorted order, determine the 0–7 octant offset (and thus the linear index) of the child node that contains the target coordinate within the current parent node using bitwise operations. 5. Traversal/Recursion: If the child node is empty (no data), skip it. If the child node is an interior node, recurse: update t{enter} and t{exit} to the intersection with the child's bounding box, and repeat from Step 2. If the child node is a leaf (voxel, cap, or scalar), process it (e.g., sample data, write to output array). 6. Termination: The search algorithm terminates when: A block with no data is encountered (empty space skipping). The smallest blocks (voxels) are reached. The ray exits the volume (t > t{exit}). Early termination criteria are met, such as when remaining voxels will not significantly contribute to the pixel color. 7. Output: All found voxels are written to an output array in sorted order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctree(rayo, rayd, node, tmin, tmax): """ Recursively traverse an octree node for a given ray segment. node: The current octree node (Interior, Cap, or Scalar Leaf). tmin, tmax: The ray parameter range [tmin, tmax] intersecting this node. """ # Base case: If the ray segment is invalid or node is empty, return if tmin >= tmax or node.isempty(): return [] # If leaf node, process and return if node.isleaf(): return [sampleleaf(node, rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax)] # Interior node: Compute mid-plane intersections bboxmin, bboxmax = node.getboundingbox() midx = (bboxmin.x + bboxmax.x) / 2.0 midy = (bboxmin.y + bboxmax.y) / 2.0 midz = (bboxmin.z + bboxmax.z) / 2.0 # Calculate t-values for mid-planes, handling zero direction components tmidx = (midx - rayo.x) / rayd.x if rayd.x != 0 else float('inf') tmidy = (midy - rayo.y) / rayd.y if rayd.y != 0 else float('inf') tmidz = (midz - rayo.z) / rayd.z if rayd.z != 0 else float('inf') # Sort mid-plane intersections to determine octant traversal order # A ray crosses at most 3 planes, visiting at most 4 octants per node sortedmids = sorted([(tmidx, 0), (tmidy, 1), (tmidz, 2)]) # Determine the 8 child octants and their indices # Child index is derived from the ray's position relative to the node center # using bitwise operations on the sign bits of (rayo - center) childindices = computeoctantindices(sortedmids, bboxmin, bboxmax, rayo) results = [] for childidx in childindices: child = node.children[childidx] if child is None or child.isempty(): continue # Compute child bounding box from parent bounds and child index childbboxmin, childbboxmax = computechildbounds(bboxmin, bboxmax, childidx) # Intersect ray with child bounding box tenter, texit = intersectrayaabb(rayo, rayd, childbboxmin, childbboxmax) # Only recurse if the ray actually intersects the child within the current segment if tenter < texit and tenter < tmax and texit > tmin: tnewenter = max(tmin, tenter) tnewexit = min(tmax, texit) if tnewenter < tnewexit: results.extend(traverseoctree(rayo, rayd, child, tnewenter, tnewexit)) return results def computeoctantindices(sortedmids, bboxmin, bboxmax, rayo): """Determines the 0-7 octant traversal order based on sorted mid-plane crossings.""" # Standard geometric traversal: the sorted order of mid-plane crossings # directly maps to the visitation sequence of the 8 children. # Returns a list of child indices in traversal order. # Implementation depends on specific octree layout (e.g., Morton/Z-order). # For a standard layout, the sorted mid-planes dictate the path. return [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] # Placeholder for layout-specific mapping def computechildbounds(parentmin, parentmax, childidx): """Computes the AABB of a child octant given the parent bounds and child index.""" dx = (parentmax.x - parentmin.x) / 2.0 dy = (parentmax.y - parentmin.y) / 2.0 dz = (parentmax.z - parentmin.z) / 2.0 # Map childidx (0-7) to x,y,z offsets xoff = (childidx & 1) dx yoff = ((childidx >> 1) & 1) dy zoff = ((childidx >> 2) & 1) dz return (parentmin.x + xoff, parentmin.y + yoff, parentmin.z + zoff), \ (parentmin.x + dx + xoff, parentmin.y + dy + yoff, parentmin.z + dz + zoff) def intersectrayaabb(rayo, rayd, bboxmin, bboxmax): """Standard slab method for ray-AABB intersection.""" tmin = float('-inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if rayd[i] == 0: if rayo[i] < bboxmin[i] or rayo[i] > bboxmax[i]: return float('inf'), float('-inf') else: t1 = (bboxmin[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] t2 = (bboxmax[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax def sampleleaf(node, rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax): """Samples voxel data or performs shading for a leaf node.""" return node.sample(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax) Parameters: Minimum Block Size: The recursion stops when blocks reach a specific minimum size or the size of a single voxel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Implementation: Octrees are difficult to implement on GPUs because GPU programming does not allow recursive algorithms; the required stack must be implemented manually. Irregular Geometry: For meshes and unstructured volumes, octrees conform poorly to irregular geometry, leading to relatively expensive traversal strategies. Node Types: Separate traversal routines are required for interior nodes (child can be interior, cap, or scalar leaf), scalar leaves (child is always the same scalar leaf, only non-empty at forward edges), and cap nodes (child is a voxel, maps to a cell via reconstruction). Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when computing mid-plane intersections near node boundaries; using epsilon guards or higher-precision arithmetic is recommended. A ray-intersection algorithm that accelerates volume rendering by navigating a spatial hierarchy (such as an Octree or Sparse Voxel Octree) to skip empty space and reduce the number of ray-casting steps. It solves the performance bottleneck of non-hierarchical voxel traversal, where every voxel along a ray must be visited, by allowing the ray to "leap" over large empty regions. Unlike its siblings, it operates on a recursive tree structure where higher-level cells cover a 2 \times 2 \times 2 area of the level below, enabling larger steps through empty space. Octree-based volume rendering accelerates image-order ray casting by recursively traversing a hierarchical spatial subdivision of volumetric data, using projected size and field-of-view criteria to select nodes for approximation or culling. It differs from sibling methods like Point Plane Test Traversal by using a tree structure for adaptive level-of-detail selection rather than fixed coarse meshes or plane tests, and unlike CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal which focuses on explicit sparse storage, this method traditionally assumes the octree resides in main memory. Octree Child Index Computation determines the 0–7 octant offset (and thus the linear index) of the child node that contains a specific target coordinate within the current parent node. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping a 3D position to a specific branch in a hierarchical grid without arbitrary bit shifts. It sets itself apart from generic tree traversal by relying on precomputed bit masks and constant-time bitwise operations to derive the child index. Octree Neighbor Finding determines the adjacent leaf nodes in six cardinal directions (±X, ±Y, ±Z) for a given node in a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO). It solves the problem of traversing between non-contiguous or differently-sized nodes during ray casting or pathfinding by locating the nearest shared ancestor and performing point location to retrieve the neighbor. This method determines the exact sequential order in which a ray intersects the eight child octants of an interior octree node by computing and sorting the ray's intersection distances with the X, Y, and Z mid-planes of the current node. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing hierarchical sparse voxel structures without pointer chasing or stack overhead for descent, by replacing recursive descent with a deterministic, sorted march through children. Unlike Stack-based Octree Traversal with Direction Flipping which uses explicit stacks, or IEEE-754 Bit Manipulation Octree Traversal which uses bit-level arithmetic, this method relies on geometric mid-plane sorting. It is particularly effective in Octree Traversal contexts where empty space skipping is utilized, as it allows the solver to start at the node border and skip nodes that do not contain the isosurface. CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal is a ray traversal algorithm for 3D sparse voxel octrees stored in a linear block structure, implemented on the CPU. It uses a stack to manage traversal state, handling valid internal nodes, leaf nodes, and empty space by casting rays to the next occupied voxel. It sets itself apart from GPU-based approaches by performing all ray marching and shading calculations on the host processor, using a linear block structure for the octree and a stack-based traversal mechanism. Sparse Ray-Octree Intersection (DECIDE) is a GPU-based algorithm for finding the first intersection of a ray with a sparse voxel octree structure, returning the hit position, normal, and node index. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing hierarchical occupancy grids by handling traversal, descent, and backtracking (popping) using a stack. Residency Octree Traversal is a ray-guided method for sparse voxel volume rendering that determines which data bricks to load from a server into a local cache based on the current viewing ray. It solves the problem of efficient memory management and bandwidth reduction in large-scale volume visualization by skipping empty or homogeneous regions and only requesting bricks that are actually needed for rendering. It sets itself apart from standard octree traversal by integrating residency metadata directly into the traversal logic, allowing the renderer to decide whether to skip a node, use its aggregate value, or request specific voxel data based on cache status and resolution requirements. PND3D is a volume rendering method that uses a standard 8-way octree with non-leaf nodes containing child and solid masks, visited in front-to-back depth-first order to enable occlusion culling. It distinguishes itself by splitting the screen into large rectangular tiles determined by 3 vanishing points of the voxel grid projected to screen coordinates, allowing each tile to be rendered as an independent job starting from the root of the octree. This approach facilitates multithread optimization and specific hardware-accelerated occlusion queries using bit arrays. GigaVoxels is a GPU-based volume rendering technique that uses an octree structure to manage data at the "brick" level (a small 3D texture block), traversing the tree to sample voxel data and performing front-to-back blending. It distinguishes itself from standard sparse voxel octree traversal by decoupling the geometric hierarchy (the octree) from the volumetric data storage (the brick pool), allowing for efficient memory residency management and level-of-detail (LOD) culling based on brick occupancy rather than individual voxel density. Octrees and their generalization N3-trees (N subdivisions per node) are considered a special case of Kd-Trees. No algorithm in available literature proposes to exploit the specific structure of octrees to accelerate ray traversal. Octrees offer regular subdivision providing identical node size at each level, which is interesting for storing regular data bricks. Time Complexity: Theoretically optimal in terms of fewest traversal steps for regularly spaced geometry, assuming objects are contained uniformly within cells of the acceleration structure, with no overlap. However, for meshes and unstructured volumes, they conform poorly to irregular geometry, leading to relatively expensive traversal strategies. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the tree structure. The min/max tree, used as an acceleration structure, adds approximately 22% footprint on top of raw octree voxel data. Strengths: Enables significantly faster finding of intersections in volumetric datasets by sampling only "non-empty space". It is particularly effective for regular voxel geometry. Limitations: Difficult to implement on GPUs due to the lack of native recursion support, requiring manual stack management. Not ideal for irregular geometry or meshes. When to Use: Regular voxel geometry where empty space skipping provides significant performance gains. When Not to Use: Irregular geometry, meshes, or unstructured volumes where hierarchical grids may be more efficient. Origin: The original Glassner implementation [32] proposed top-down point location testing along successive octree nodes hit by the ray. Development: Samet [105] modified the marching procedure to incorporate a neighbor-finding algorithm, delivering dramatic speedups. Sung [120] proposed a DDA traversal similar to a hierarchical grid. Gargantini and Atkinson [29] implemented a traversal similar to a kd-tree where the ray intersection with each octant midplane is ordered. Usage: Used in volumetric rendering applications to perform empty space skipping.
