name: Coarse Mesh Traversal with Dual-Ray Culling
head: Front/back face culling traversal, Two-ray coarse mesh traversal
body: A traversal algorithm for a coarse tetrahedral mesh that uses two rays (one with front-face culling, one with back-face culling) to determine the ray's position relative to the coarse mesh elements, handling non-convex shapes and holes. It builds on Coarse Mesh Traversal by explicitly resolving the entry and exit boundaries of the current coarse element using dual-ray intersection tests, enabling robust nested traversal into the fine structure. Unlike single-pass methods that compute intersections in the fragment shader, this approach uses two distinct ray traces per coarse element to establish precise t-bounds for the inner loop. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and a BVH constructed from the coarse tetrahedral mesh faces. Output: A tuple (coarseID, tBack, tNextFace) where coarseID is the identifier of the current coarse tetrahedron, tBack is the exit distance of the ray from the current coarse element, and tNextFace is the entry distance for the next coarse element. If the ray is outside the mesh, it returns (-1, 0, 0). Data Structures: BVH: Built from the coarse mesh elements. Each leaf node represents a face of a coarse tetrahedron. The BVH stores the coarse tetrahedron ID associated with each face. Ray Record: Contains the hit distance t, the hit point, and the coarseTetID of the intersected element. Algorithm Steps: 1. Front-Face Trace: Trace a ray with front-face culling enabled (ignoring back-facing triangles). If the ray misses, return (-1, 0, 0). If it hits, store the hit distance as t{Back} and the associated tetrahedron ID as coarseID. 2. Back-Face Trace: Trace the same ray with back-face culling enabled (ignoring front-facing triangles). If the ray misses, the ray is inside the last element of the mesh. Set t{NextFace} = \text{nextafterf}(t{Back}, \infty). If the ray hits, let the hit distance be t{Front} and the tetrahedron ID be hitID. 3. Boundary Resolution: If hitID equals coarseID (the ray enters and exits the same coarse element): Set t{Front} = \text{nextafterf}(t{Front}, \infty). Set t{NextFace} = \text{nextafterf}(t{Back}, \infty). If hitID differs from coarseID (the ray enters a new coarse element): Set t{NextFace} = \text{nextafterf}(t{Front}, \infty). 4. Return: Return (coarseID, tBack, tNextFace). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversecoarsemesh(ray): # Step 1: Trace with front-face culling rayrecordfront = traceray(ray, cullmode=CULLFRONTFACINGTRIANGLES) # If front ray misses, we are outside the mesh if rayrecordfront.missed: return -1, 0, 0 # Store back-face hit info (which is actually the exit from the current element # if we consider the front ray hit the entry, but the algorithm uses # front-cull ray to find the 'back' boundary of the current element in the # context of the specific BVH implementation described) # Note: The source algorithm names tBack from the front-cull ray hit. tback = rayrecordfront.t coarseid = rayrecordfront.coarsetetid # Step 2: Trace with back-face culling rayrecordback = traceray(ray, cullmode=CULLBACKFACINGTRIANGLES) if not rayrecordback.missed: tfront = rayrecordback.t hitid = rayrecordback.coarsetetid if coarseid == hitid: # Ray enters and exits the same coarse element tfront = nextafterf(tfront, INFINITY) tnextface = nextafterf(tback, INFINITY) else: # Ray exits current element and enters a new one tnextface = nextafterf(tfront, INFINITY) else: # Ray is inside the last element of the mesh tnextface = nextafterf(tback, INFINITY) return coarseid, tback, tnextface Parameters: nextafterf(t, direction): A function that returns the next representable floating-point number after t in the specified direction (usually INFINITY for advancing forward). This prevents re-intersection with the same geometry in subsequent iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Issues: When exiting faces, standard floating-point arithmetic may cause the ray to re-intersect the same geometry in the next step. Using nextafterf advances t slightly to avoid this. Non-Convex Shapes: The dual-ray approach correctly handles non-convex shapes and holes by distinguishing between entry and exit faces based on face normal orientation relative to the ray. A technique where coarse mesh elements are treated as macrocells storing pre-computed minimum and maximum density values of their child elements. This enables empty space skipping and tighter majorant estimation for Woodcock tracking. Steps: Calculate macrocell densities by applying the transfer function to scalar values of child elements. Recalculate these values using a CUDA kernel whenever the transfer function changes. Before processing a coarse element, check if its maximum macrocell density is zero. If so, skip the element and move to the next. Comparison: Macrocells allow for empty space skipping and tighter majorant extinction, reducing sample rejection rates compared to not using macrocells. A technique to early-return from refinement tree traversal based on the normalized screen space area of the tetrahedron. Steps: Calculate the total normalized screen space area of a tetrahedron by summing the areas of the four triangles created by its four vertices. Parameters: Refinement criteria: A threshold for normalized screen space size. It can be converted to true screen space area by multiplying by total screen space. Time Complexity: Requires two BVH traversals per coarse element. The cost is proportional to the depth of the BVH. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the BVH and macrocell statistics (min/max density) for each coarse element. Strengths: Robustly handles non-convex geometries and holes. Macrocell optimization significantly reduces sample rejection rates in Woodcock tracking. Limitations: Requires two ray traces per coarse element, doubling the traversal overhead compared to single-ray methods. Macrocell values must be recomputed if the transfer function changes. When to use: When rendering non-convex volumes or volumes with holes where simple bounding box culling is insufficient. Originated in the context of direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. The method was developed to efficiently traverse coarse tetrahedral meshes while supporting nested refinement trees. name: Back-Face Culling for Ray Casting
head: Backface Raycasting, Raycasting with depth buffers, Raycasting with depth pre-pass, Front/Backface Buffer Raycasting, Two-pass depth buffer raycasting, Back-face depth culling raycasting, Back-face culling for entry/exit determination, Two-Pass Raycasting with Back-Face Depth Buffering, Two-Pass Raycasting with Backface Entry/Exit Points
body: Back-face culling for ray casting is an optimization technique that determines the entry and exit points of rays into a volume by rendering the back faces of the volume's bounding box to a texture, thereby avoiding the need to compute ray-cube intersections analytically in the raycasting shader. It builds on Coarse Mesh Traversal with Dual-Ray Culling by applying the principle of using front/back face distinction to a simple bounding box primitive, offloading geometry processing to the GPU rasterizer. Unlike single-pass methods that compute intersections in the fragment shader, this approach uses a two-pass rendering pipeline: the first pass captures the back-face depth/position, and the second pass uses this data to initialize the ray march, skipping empty space outside the volume. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume density data (3D texture), transfer function (2D texture), camera view and projection matrices, and bounding box geometry (cube). Outputs: Final composited image (color buffer). Data Structures: 1. Bounding Box Geometry: A cube defined by 8 vertices and 12 triangles. Each vertex contains: VerPos (vec3): Position in object space. VerClr (vec3): Color, used to pass the 3D position of the vertex to the fragment shader. 2. Back-Face Texture (gbfTexObj / texBackFaces): A 2D texture (RGBA) storing the 3D entry point coordinates for each pixel. Dimensions: Width × Height (screen resolution). Initialization: Zeros. Filters: LINEAR for MIN/MAG, CLAMPTOEDGE for S/T. 3. Volume Texture (gvolTexObj / uVolData): A 3D texture (sampler3D) storing density values. Requires the OEStexturefloat extension in WebGL for floating-point data. 4. Transfer Function Texture (trfunctexture): A 2D texture (sampler2D) mapping density to color. 5. Frame Buffer: A framebuffer object containing a DEPTHCOMPONENT16 renderbuffer and a 2D color texture attachment. Numbered Steps: 1. Pass 1: Back-Face Depth Capture 1. Bind the auxiliary framebuffer. 2. Enable depth testing. 3. Set depth function to GEQUAL. 4. Enable front-face culling (cull front faces, render back faces). The method assumes counter-clockwise (CCW) winding order where normals point outward; back faces yield a negative dot product with the view direction. 5. Use the "back" shader program. 6. Draw the bounding box cube. Vertex Shader: Transforms VerPos to clip space via glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(VerPos, 1.0). Passes VerClr as EntryPoint to the fragment shader. Fragment Shader: Outputs the interpolated vertex color (VerClr), which encodes the 3D entry point position, as FragColor. 7. Store the resulting color buffer into gbfTexObj. 2. Pass 2: Raycasting 1. Bind the default framebuffer. 2. Enable depth testing. 3. Set depth function to LEQUAL. 4. Enable back-face culling (cull back faces, render front faces). 5. Bind gbfTexObj to texture unit 0 (uBackCoord). 6. Bind the volume texture to texture unit 1 (uVolData). 7. Use the "raycast" shader program. 8. Draw the bounding box cube again. Vertex Shader: Transforms VerPos to clip space. Passes VerClr as EntryPoint (front face position). Fragment Shader: 1. Sample uBackCoord using screen coordinates (glFragCoord.st / ScreenSize) to retrieve the 3D exit point (exitPoint). 2. If EntryPoint == exitPoint (no back-face hit, e.g., background), discard the fragment. 3. Calculate ray direction: dir = exitPoint - EntryPoint. 4. Calculate ray length: len = length(dir). 5. Calculate step vector: deltaDir = normalize(dir) StepSize. 6. Initialize accumulators: colacc = vec4(0,0,0,0), alphaacc = 0.0, lengthacc = 0.0, raypos = EntryPoint. 7. Loop for NUMRAYSTEPS iterations: 1. Sample density: density = texture(uVolData, raypos).x. 2. Map to color: colorsample = texture(trfunctexture, vec2(density, 0.5)). 3. Calculate sample alpha: alphasample = density StepSize. 4. Front-to-back blending: colacc += (1.0 - alphaacc) colorsample alphasample 40.0. 5. Update alpha: alphaacc += alphasample. 6. Update length: lengthacc += length(deltaDir). 7. Advance ray: raypos += deltaDir. 8. Termination Conditions: If lengthacc >= len, composite background (white, alpha 0) and break. If alphaacc > 1.0, clamp to 1.0 and break. 8. Output colacc as fragment color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backfacecullingraycasting(screenwidth, screenheight, volumetexture, transferfunc, stepsize, numsteps): # Pass 1: Back-Face Depth Capture # 1. Bind auxiliary framebuffer and enable depth testing. # 2. Set depth function to GEQUAL. # 3. Enable front-face culling (cull front faces, render back faces). # 4. Draw bounding box cube with back shader. # Vertex Shader: glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(VerPos, 1.0) # EntryPoint = VerClr # Fragment Shader: FragColor = vec4(EntryPoint, 1.0) # 5. Read framebuffer color buffer into backfacetexture. # Pass 2: Raycasting # 1. Bind default framebuffer and enable depth testing. # 2. Set depth function to LEQUAL. # 3. Enable back-face culling (cull back faces, render front faces). # 4. Bind backfacetexture to texture unit 0, volumetexture to unit 1. # 5. Draw bounding box cube with raycast shader. # Vertex Shader: glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(VerPos, 1.0) # EntryPoint = VerClr # Fragment Shader: # uv = glFragCoord.xy / vec2(screenwidth, screenheight) # exitpoint = texture(backfacetexture, uv).xyz # if EntryPoint == exitpoint: discard # dir = exitpoint - EntryPoint # raylen = length(dir) # deltadir = normalize(dir) stepsize # colacc = vec4(0.0) # alphaacc = 0.0 # lengthacc = 0.0 # raypos = EntryPoint # for i in range(numsteps): # density = texture(volumetexture, raypos).x # colorsample = texture(transferfunc, vec2(density, 0.5)).rgb # alphasample = density stepsize # colacc += (1.0 - alphaacc) colorsample alphasample 40.0 # alphaacc += alphasample # lengthacc += length(deltadir) # raypos += deltadir # if lengthacc >= raylen or alphaacc > 1.0: break # FragColor = colacc Parameters: StepSize: Controls the step length in ray marching. NUMRAYSTEPS: Maximum iterations per ray. Source uses 512. Source uses 1600. ScreenSize: Resolution of the screen (width, height). uBackCoord: Sampler uniform for the back-face texture. uVolData: Sampler uniform for the volume data texture. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate System Mismatch: ExitPointCoord in the vertex shader is in clip-space. Sampling the texture using glFragCoord (window coordinates) works because the rasterizer maps clip-space to window-space, and the texture was written during rasterization. AMD Debugging Issue: The VerClr input variable must be used in the shader; otherwise, debugging may fail on AMD hardware. Floating-Point Textures: WebGL implementations require the OEStexturefloat extension to support floating-point textures for volume data. Winding Order: The method assumes counter-clockwise (CCW) winding order for front faces. Volume Raycasting with MRT Endpoints is a two-pass GPU technique that determines ray entry and exit points by rendering the volume's bounding box to multiple render targets (MRT), explicitly separating front-face and back-face coordinates into distinct textures to avoid analytical ray-cube intersection calculations. It builds on Back-Face Culling for Ray Casting by using MRT to store both entry and exit points simultaneously in the first pass, rather than relying on depth buffering and a single pass for back-faces. Unlike single-pass methods that compute intersections in the fragment shader, this approach offloads geometry processing to the rasterizer, simplifying the raycasting shader at the cost of an additional rendering pass and texture lookups. In the raycasting phase, the two auxiliary buffers are bound to distinct texture units and a viewport-filling quadrilateral is projected. For each pixel, the main fragment shader fetches back-facing texture coordinates; if invalid, the fragment is discarded, otherwise front-facing coordinates are retrieved to compute the step vector along the ray according to a predefined step length d and the total number of iterations. Each slab of thickness 2d is defined by three successive samples (sf, sm, sb), with the next slab indexed by (sf, sm, sb). Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use and when not: Not given in the sources. Back-face culling for ray casting originated as a technique to optimize volume rendering by leveraging the GPU's rasterization pipeline to determine ray entry and exit points. It was popularized in early WebGL and OpenGL tutorials for volume rendering, such as those by Khizar Siddiqui, toolchainX, and others. The method is a practical application of depth buffering and face culling to avoid analytical geometry calculations in shaders. It is commonly used in educational contexts and simple real-time volume renderers where simplicity and GPU compatibility are prioritized over advanced traversal algorithms. khizarsiddiqui/Volume-Rendering, https://github.com/khizarsiddiqui/Volume-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) VolumeRenderingUsingGLSL, https://github.com/toolchainX/VolumeRenderingUsingGLSL, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 1vx-437312114/webglvolumerenderer, https://github.com/1vx-437312114/webglvolumerenderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) kapadia/volumetric.js, https://github.com/kapadia/volumetric.js, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering, https://people.freedesktop.org/~marcheu/pacificvis08.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Volume Raycasting with MRT Endpoints
head: MRT Ray Start/Stop Determination, Two-pass raycasting
body: Volume Raycasting with MRT Endpoints is a two-pass GPU technique for determining the entry and exit points of rays into a volume by rendering the volume's bounding box to multiple render targets (MRT), followed by a second pass to sample the volume along those rays. It builds on Back-Face Culling for Ray Casting by explicitly separating front-face and back-face coordinates into distinct textures to avoid analytical ray-cube intersection calculations. Unlike single-pass methods that compute intersections in the fragment shader, this approach offloads geometry processing to the rasterizer, simplifying the raycasting shader at the cost of an additional rendering pass and texture lookups. Inputs: A 3D volume texture (typically single-channel density). A model-view-projection matrix for the volume bounding box. A step length parameter defining sample spacing. Optional: A jitter texture for stochastic sampling. Outputs: A 2D color buffer containing the final composited image. Data Structures: Framebuffer Object (FBO) with two color attachments (GLCOLORATTACHMENT0 and GLCOLORATTACHMENT1). Two 2D floating-point RGB textures bound to the FBO attachments to store ray start and stop coordinates. 3D texture for volume data. Steps: 1. Pass 1: Compute Ray Endpoints Clear the two color attachments to black (zero). Enable blending with GLONE, GLONE (additive blending). Bind the FBO with two color attachments and set draw buffers: cpp GLenum renderTargets[2] = {GLCOLORATTACHMENT0, GLCOLORATTACHMENT1}; glDrawBuffers(2, &renderTargets[0]); Render a two-unit cube (vertices in range [-1, 1]) representing the volume bounding box. In the vertex shader, apply the model-view-projection transform to glPosition and pass the original object-space position vPosition to the fragment shader. In the fragment shader, determine if the current face is front-facing using glFrontFacing. If front-facing: write 0.5 (vPosition + 1.0) to FragData[0] (start point) and vec3(0) to FragData[1] (stop point). If back-facing: write vec3(0) to FragData[0] and 0.5 (vPosition + 1.0) to FragData[1]. The additive blending ensures that only one value (start or stop) is written per pixel, as the other is zero. 2. Pass 2: Volume Raycasting Render a full-screen quad covering the viewport. Bind the two endpoint textures (RayStart, RayStop) and the volume texture. For each fragment, sample the start and stop points using screen coordinates coord = 0.5 (vPosition.xy + 1.0). If rayStart == rayStop, discard the fragment (no intersection). Compute the ray vector, length, and step vector: \text{ray} = \text{rayStop} - \text{rayStart} \text{rayLength} = \|\text{ray}\| \text{stepVector} = \text{StepLength} \times \frac{\text{ray}}{\text{rayLength}} Apply stochastic jitter to the start position if a jitter texture is available: \text{rayStart} += \text{stepVector} \times \text{jitter}(\text{coord}).r Initialize position = rayStart and destination color dst = vec4(0). Loop while rayLength > 0 (and optionally dst.a < 1 for early termination): Sample the volume: density = texture(Volume, position).r (or.x). Perform front-to-back blending: \text{src} = \text{vec4}(\text{density}) \text{src}.rgb \times= \text{src}.a \text{dst} = (1.0 - \text{dst}.a) \times \text{src} + \text{dst} Advance position: position += stepVector. Decrement length: rayLength -= StepLength. Output dst as the fragment color. Parameters: StepLength: Distance between samples. Typical value: 0.01. Balances quality and speed; larger values are faster but lower quality, smaller values are slower but higher quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-intersecting rays: Handled by discarding fragments where rayStart == rayStop. Jitter: Stochastic jitter helps reduce aliasing artifacts (e.g., wood grain) but requires a pre-computed jitter texture. Pseudocode (Fragment Shader for Pass 2): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastpass2(raystarttex, raystoptex, volumetex, steplength, jittertex=None): # Screen coordinate conversion coord = 0.5 (vposition.xy + 1.0) # Sample endpoints raystart = raystarttex.sample(coord).xyz raystop = raystoptex.sample(coord).xyz # Discard non-intersecting rays if raystart == raystop: return # Fragment discarded # Compute ray properties ray = raystop - raystart raylength = length(ray) stepvector = steplength ray / raylength # Optional stochastic jitter if jittertex is not None: raystart += stepvector jittertex.sample(coord).r pos = raystart dst = vec4(0.0) # Raymarching loop while raylength > 0 and dst.a < 1.0: density = volumetex.sample(pos).r src = vec4(density) src.rgb = src.a dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst pos += stepvector raylength -= steplength return dst A variant that computes lighting normals in volume data by approximating the gradient vector, which points in the direction of greatest change and whose magnitude indicates surface intersection. It computes the gradient at position P using central differences with step size L: grad.x = texture(P + vec3(L,0,0)) - texture(P), grad.y = texture(P + vec3(0,L,0)) - texture(P), grad.z = texture(P + vec3(0,0,L)) - texture(P). The gradient is only computed if the current voxel value V is above a Threshold (typical value: 0.45) to avoid excessive texture lookups. When the threshold is met, the gradient is normalized, diffuse lighting is computed (df = abs(dot(normal, light)), color = df DiffuseMaterial), src = vec4(color, 1.0), front-to-back blending is applied, and the loop breaks. Time Complexity: Two rendering passes. The second pass performs one texture lookup per sample along the ray. Total work is proportional to the number of pixels times the average ray length in samples. Memory Complexity: Requires two additional 2D textures for ray endpoints, plus the volume texture. Performance: Simpler fragment shader than analytical intersection methods, but incurs overhead from the first pass and two extra texture samples in the second pass (RayStart, RayStop). Strengths: Easy to implement; leverages GPU rasterization for intersection; supports early termination with front-to-back blending. Limitations: Two-pass overhead; extra texture lookups make it suboptimal for performance-critical applications; requires MRT support. When to use: Simple volume rendering where bounding box is axis-aligned or easily transformed; when implementation simplicity is prioritized over performance. When not to use: When single-pass performance is critical due to pass overhead and texture sampling cost. Originated as a simple technique for volumetric raycasting on the GPU, described in blog posts and tutorials around 2018. It is often referred to as "two-pass raycasting" due to its structure. The method is used in educational contexts and simple volume renderers where ease of implementation is key. name: Two-level Nested Ray Marching
head: Front-to-back ray marching on AMR, Ray Marching with Coarse Mesh and Refinement Tree
body: Two-level nested ray marching is a volume rendering technique for Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data that decouples traversal into a coarse mesh level and a fine refinement tree level. It solves the problem of efficiently sampling hierarchical tetrahedral data by skipping empty coarse elements and performing dense front-to-back compositing only within active refinement structures. Unlike sibling methods that may use hierarchical accelerators like K-D trees or octrees for general sparse voxel data, this method is specifically tailored for tree-based tetrahedral AMR, relying on a constant step size for sampling within the finest elements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{r}{org}, direction \mathbf{r}{dir}, and current distance t. A coarse mesh structure providing TraverseCoarseMesh and macrocell density values macrocellValues. A refinement tree structure providing traverse (to find the current tetrahedron) and intersectFaces (to find exit distance). A transfer function tf mapping scalar values to color and opacity. A constant step size stepSize. An opacity threshold of 0.99. A background color bgColor. Output: The accumulated color and final alpha value. Data Structures: macrocellValues: An array indexed by coarse element ID, storing the maximum density within that coarse element. tf: A transfer function object with methods inRange(scalar) and getColor(scalar). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set accumulated color C = \{0, 0, 0\} and accumulated alpha \alpha = 0. 2. Coarse Loop: While \alpha < 0.99: a. Call TraverseCoarseMesh(ray) to obtain the current coarse element ID (coarseID), the back face distance of the coarse element (tBack), and the distance to the next face (tNextFace). b. If coarseID is -1, break the loop (ray has exited the volume). c. Check if macrocellValues[coarseID] <= 0. d. If true, the coarse element is empty; skip processing. e. If not empty, call MarchElement(ray, C, \alpha, tBack, coarseID, stepSize, tf) to process the interior. f. Update ray.t to \max(tNextFace, ray.t) to advance the ray to the start of the next coarse element. 3. Final Compositing: Return the final color: C{final} = (1 - \alpha) \times bgColor + C. Sub-algorithm: MarchElement This function handles the nested march within a single coarse element. 1. Initialize tExit = ray.t, sampleTetID = coarseTetID, and tetVertices = vertices of coarseTetID. 2. Fine Loop: While ray.t < tMax (the back face distance of the coarse element): a. Calculate the sample point: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}{org} + ray.t \times \mathbf{r}{dir}. b. Refinement Traversal: If ray.t > tExit: i. Call traverse(samplePoint, coarseTetID) to get the current tetrahedron ID (sampleTetID) and its vertices (tetVertices). ii. Calculate tExit by intersecting the ray with the faces of the current tetrahedron using intersectFaces(ray.t, samplePoint, ray.direction, tetVertices). c. Sampling: Sample the scalar value s at \mathbf{p} using sampleData(samplePoint, sampleTetID, tetVertices). d. Transfer Function Check: If s is not in the transfer function range (!tf.inRange(s)), continue to the next iteration (skip this sample). e. Advance Ray: Update ray.t = ray.t + stepSize. f. Compositing: i. Get the transfer function color and opacity: tfColor = tf.getColor(s). ii. Adjust opacity: tfColor.opacity = tfColor.opacity \times tf.opacity. iii. Accumulate color and alpha using front-to-back compositing: C = C + (1 - \alpha) \times tfColor.opacity \times tfColor.color \alpha = \alpha + tfColor.opacity \times (1 - \alpha) 3. Return the updated C and \alpha. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchcoarse(ray, macrocellvalues, stepsize, tf, bgcolor): color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 while alpha < 0.99: coarseid, tback, tnextface = traversecoarsemesh(ray) if coarseid == -1: break if macrocellvalues[coarseid] <= 0: ray.t = max(tnextface, ray.t) continue color, alpha = marchelement(ray, color, alpha, tback, coarseid, stepsize, tf) ray.t = max(tnextface, ray.t) finalcolor = (1.0 - alpha) bgcolor + color return finalcolor def marchelement(ray, color, alpha, tmax, coarsetetid, stepsize, tf): texit = ray.t sampletetid = coarsetetid tetvertices = gettetvertices(coarsetetid) while ray.t < tmax: samplepoint = ray.org + ray.t ray.dir if ray.t > texit: sampletetid, tetvertices = traverse(samplepoint, coarsetetid) texit = intersectfaces(ray.t, samplepoint, ray.dir, tetvertices) scalar = sampledata(samplepoint, sampletetid, tetvertices) if not tf.inrange(scalar): ray.t += stepsize continue ray.t += stepsize tfcolor = tf.getcolor(scalar) tfcolor.opacity = tfcolor.opacity tf.opacity color = color + (1.0 - alpha) tfcolor.opacity tfcolor.color alpha = alpha + tfcolor.opacity (1.0 - alpha) return color, alpha def traversecoarsemesh(ray): # Standard ray-AABB traversal for the coarse mesh grid tmin = (ray.boxmin - ray.org) / ray.dir tmaxval = (ray.boxmax - ray.org) / ray.dir tenter = max(min(tmin)) texitval = min(max(tmaxval)) if tenter > texitval or texitval < 0: return -1, 0.0, 0.0 return currentcoarseid, texitval, tenter + stepsize def traverse(samplepoint, coarsetetid): # Standard tree descent: walk down from coarsetetid to find containing tet node = coarsetetid while not isleaf(node): children = getchildren(node) found = False for child in children: if pointintet(samplepoint, gettetvertices(child)): node = child found = True break if not found: break return node, gettetvertices(node) def intersectfaces(rayt, samplepoint, raydir, tetvertices): # Ray-tetrahedron exit distance calculation maxt = float('inf') for face in tetfaces(tetvertices): normal = cross(face[1] - face[0], face[2] - face[0]) denom = dot(normal, raydir) if abs(denom) > 1e-8: t = dot(normal, face[0] - samplepoint) / denom if t > rayt and t < maxt: maxt = t return maxt if maxt != float('inf') else rayt def sampledata(samplepoint, sampletetid, tetvertices): # Barycentric interpolation of scalar values at tet vertices weights = barycentriccoordinates(samplepoint, tetvertices) scalar = sum(w v.scalar for w, v in zip(weights, tetvertices)) return scalar def gettetvertices(tetid): return mesh.tetrahedra[tetid].vertices def isleaf(node): return not mesh.haschildren(node) def getchildren(node): return mesh.children[node] def pointintet(point, vertices): weights = barycentriccoordinates(point, vertices) return all(w >= -1e-6 for w in weights) def tetfaces(vertices): return [ (vertices[0], vertices[1], vertices[2]), (vertices[0], vertices[1], vertices[3]), (vertices[0], vertices[2], vertices[3]), (vertices[1], vertices[2], vertices[3]) ] def barycentriccoordinates(point, vertices): v0, v1, v2, v3 = vertices vol = dot(v1 - v0, cross(v2 - v0, v3 - v0)) w0 = dot(point - v1, cross(v2 - v1, v3 - v1)) / vol w1 = dot(point - v0, cross(v3 - v0, v2 - v0)) / vol w2 = dot(point - v0, cross(v1 - v0, v3 - v0)) / vol w3 = 1.0 - w0 - w1 - w2 return [w0, w1, w2, w3] Parameters: Step Size: A constant adjustable step size. No adaptive step size adjustments are implemented. Smaller step sizes increase sample count and impact performance. Opacity Threshold: The ray marching loop continues while \alpha < 0.99. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Coarse Elements: The method explicitly checks macrocellValues[coarseID] <= 0 to skip empty elements, avoiding unnecessary refinement tree traversals. Precision: The method relies on a constant step size, which may lead to aliasing or missed features if the step size is too large relative to the finest tetrahedra. Boundary Conditions: The intersectfaces function must correctly handle the ray exiting the current tetrahedron to update tExit. Initializing tExit to ray.t prevents immediate re-traversal or numerical exit distance errors when the ray starts inside a cell. Time Complexity: The complexity depends on the number of coarse elements intersected and the number of fine tetrahedra sampled within each. The coarse traversal skips empty regions, but the fine march uses a constant step size, meaning performance degrades linearly with the number of samples required to cover the active volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the coarse mesh macrocell values and the refinement tree structure. Strengths: Efficiently handles AMR data by leveraging coarse mesh density checks to skip empty regions. Simple implementation due to the use of a constant step size. Limitations: The constant step size is not adaptive, potentially leading to inefficient sampling in regions with varying density or feature size. It is specific to tree-based tetrahedral AMR data. When to use: When rendering tree-based tetrahedral AMR data where coarse mesh density information is available and adaptive step sizing is not required or desired. When not to use: For data requiring adaptive sampling or non-tetrahedral hierarchical structures. This method was described in the context of direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement data. It builds on the concept of hierarchical traversal by explicitly separating the coarse mesh navigation from the fine element sampling. The approach allows for optimizations such as macrocell density checks to skip empty coarse elements. name: Varying Refinement Levels of Coarse Elements
head: Coarse mesh refinement level variation, Inserting refinement levels into coarse mesh
body: This method optimizes hierarchical volume rendering by controlling the granularity of the coarse mesh used for bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) construction and macrocell-based optimizations. It solves the trade-off between BVH traversal efficiency and the overhead of traversing the underlying refinement tree (e.g., TET-AMR) by selecting which level of the refinement hierarchy is promoted to the coarse mesh. Unlike sibling methods such as Leaf Collection, Point Plane Test Traversal, Coarse Mesh Traversal with Dual-Ray Culling, Two-level Nested Ray Marching, Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA), Octree-based Volume Rendering, Multi-Resolution Rendering with K-D Tree, and CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal, this approach explicitly varies the refinement level inserted into the coarse mesh to balance macrocell tightness against BVH node count. Inputs: A hierarchical dataset with a refinement tree (e.g., TET-AMR) where elements exist at multiple refinement levels (0 to L{max}). A target refinement level k for the coarse mesh. A renderer configuration (e.g., Ray Marcher, Woodcock tracking) with optional macrocell optimizations. Outputs: A coarse mesh containing elements from refinement level k (or leaves if they are finer than k). A BVH built over this coarse mesh. Rendering performance metrics. Data Structures: Coarse Mesh: A collection of geometric primitives (tetrahedra or faces) representing the bounding volumes for BVH nodes. The size of this mesh is determined by the number of elements at level k in the refinement tree. BVH: A bounding volume hierarchy built over the coarse mesh elements. The source specifies using 4 faces per element in the BVH construction. Algorithm: 1. Traverse Refinement Tree: For each root or relevant parent in the refinement tree, traverse its children. 2. Select Element: Continue traversing down the tree until an element is reached that is either at the desired refinement level k or a leaf element. 3. Add to Coarse Mesh: Insert the selected element into the coarse mesh structure. 4. Build BVH: Construct the BVH using the elements in the coarse mesh. The source notes the use of 4 faces per element for BVH construction. 5. Render: Perform volume rendering using the selected renderer (Ray Marcher or Woodcock) with or without macrocell optimizations. Parameters: Refinement Level (k): The level of the refinement tree to insert into the coarse mesh. Typical values tested are integers 0 to 5. Macrocell Optimization: A boolean flag enabling or disabling macrocell-based culling/optimizations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: BVH Efficiency: Increasing the number of elements in the coarse mesh (higher k) decreases BVH efficiency and reduces the maximum traversal depth in the TET-AMR traversal process. This can negatively impact performance if the BVH overhead outweighs the benefits of reduced refinement tree traversal. Leaf Handling: The algorithm must correctly handle leaf nodes. If a leaf is at a level finer than k, it is still added to the coarse mesh, potentially increasing the coarse mesh size more than expected. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildcoarsemesh(refinementtree, targetlevel): """ Builds a coarse mesh by traversing the refinement tree and selecting elements at the target refinement level or leaf nodes. Args: refinementtree: The root of the refinement tree structure. targetlevel: The integer refinement level to target. Returns: coarsemesh: A list of geometric elements (faces/tetrahedra) suitable for BVH construction. """ coarsemesh = [] def traverse(node, currentlevel): # If the node is a leaf, add it to the coarse mesh if node.isleaf(): coarsemesh.append(node.element) return # If the current level matches the target level, add this element if currentlevel == targetlevel: coarsemesh.append(node.element) return # If the current level is finer than target, continue to children if currentlevel < targetlevel: for child in node.children: traverse(child, currentlevel + 1) # If currentlevel > targetlevel, stop (should not happen in standard traversal) # Start traversal from root traverse(refinementtree, 0) return coarsemesh def renderwithcoarsemesh(coarsemesh, rendererconfig): """ Renders the volume using the coarse mesh and specified renderer. Args: coarsemesh: The list of elements from buildcoarsemesh. rendererconfig: Configuration including 'usemacrocell' flag. """ # Build BVH from coarse mesh using 4 faces per element # Standard BVH construction algorithm (e.g., SAH) is applied here. bvh = None # Placeholder for standard BVH build step # Perform rendering if rendererconfig.usemacrocell: # Standard ray marching integration with macrocell culling pass else: # Standard ray marching integration without macrocell culling pass Time and Memory Complexity: The number of elements in the coarse mesh (and thus the BVH) grows exponentially with the refinement level k. For the Uniform Engine dataset, the number of elements increases from 6 at level 0 to 196,608 at level 5. For the Engine dataset, it increases from 5,177 at level 0 to 14,402,140 at level 5. BVH construction and traversal time increase with the number of elements, but the efficiency of the BVH decreases as the number of elements increases. Measured Performance: Engine Dataset: Ray Marcher with macrocell: Level 0 (41.47 ms), Level 1 (45.72 ms), Level 2 (50 ms), Level 3 (53.31 ms), Level 4 (62.45 ms), Level 5 (87.77 ms). Ray Marcher without macrocell: Level 0 (41.12 ms), Level 1 (45.53 ms), Level 2 (50.43 ms), Level 3 (54.69 ms), Level 4 (54.69 ms), Level 5 (84.02 ms). Woodcock with macrocell: Level 0 (7.14 ms), Level 1 (11.07 ms), Level 2 (18.46 ms), Level 3 (33.18 ms), Level 4 (56.65 ms), Level 5 (94.97 ms). Woodcock without macrocell: Level 0 (14.70 ms), Level 1 (16.11 ms), Level 2 (16.11 ms), Level 3 (18.52 ms), Level 4 (21.00 ms), Level 5 (21.00 ms). Uniform Engine Dataset: Ray Marcher with macrocell: Level 0 (78.58 ms), Level 1 (75.8 ms), Level 2 (80.7 ms), Level 3 (93.18 ms), Level 4 (101.84 ms), Level 5 (99.81 ms). Ray Marcher without macrocell: Level 0 (77.61 ms), Level 1 (75 ms), Level 2 (79.69 ms), Level 3 (91.93 ms), Level 4 (101.16 ms), Level 5 (100.96 ms). Woodcock with macrocell: Level 0 (10.72 ms), Level 1 (9.57 ms), Level 2 (9.56 ms), Level 3 (12.80 ms), Level 4 (22.04 ms), Level 5 (43.80 ms). Woodcock without macrocell: Level 0 (24.99 ms), Level 1 (26.66 ms), Level 2 (30.91 ms), Level 3 (33.09 ms), Level 4 (32.13 ms), Level 5 (29.30 ms). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Can improve performance for specific datasets (e.g., Uniform Engine at level 1) by reducing refinement tree traversal depth, even if BVH overhead increases. Macrocell optimizations can significantly improve Woodcock tracker performance at levels 1 and 2 for Uniform Engine due to tighter majorants. Limitations: Increasing coarse mesh elements generally decreases BVH efficiency and can hurt performance (e.g., Engine dataset). The optimal level depends heavily on the dataset structure and renderer type. When to Use: Use when the refinement tree has a large depth and reducing traversal depth is beneficial (e.g., Uniform Engine at level 1). Use with Woodcock tracking and macrocell optimizations when smaller macrocells can provide tighter majorants (e.g., Uniform Engine at levels 1 and 2). When Not to Use: Avoid for datasets where BVH efficiency is critical and increasing coarse mesh elements leads to significant performance degradation (e.g., Engine dataset). This method was proposed in the context of direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (TET-AMR) data. The research explores how different levels of the refinement hierarchy can be used to construct a coarse mesh for BVH-based acceleration, balancing the costs of BVH traversal against refinement tree traversal. The work is part of a broader effort to optimize volume rendering for complex, multi-resolution scientific data. name: Node Omission in Ray-Tree Traversal
head: Omisión de nodos no intersecables, Pruning non-intersectable nodes
body: Node omission is an optimization for hierarchical ray-tree traversal that prevents adding child nodes to the traversal stack if it is known they will not intersect the current ray, reducing the number of intersection tests. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Leaf Collection and Point Plane Test Traversal by operating on the spatial relationship between the ray's entry/exit parameters and the node's bounding box midpoints, rather than relying on leaf-level data structures or plane-based splitting planes. The method determines which of the eight children of a current octree node are intersected by a ray by analyzing the ray's intersection interval with the parent node's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray r, current node n. Output: A list of valid child node indices to be added to the traversal stack. Data Structures: Child nodes are indexed 1 through 8. The pruning logic relies on set membership of children relative to the midpoint planes, assuming a standard octree indexing convention where \{1,2,3,4\} and \{5,6,7,8\} occupy opposite halves along each axis. Parameters: tx0, ty0, tz0: The entry intersection factors of the ray with the node's bounding box along the x, y, and z axes, respectively. tx1, ty1, tz1: The exit intersection factors of the ray with the node's bounding box along the x, y, and z axes, respectively. txm, tym, tzm: The midpoint factors separating the children, calculated as ((tx0, ty0, tz0) + (tx1, ty1, tz1)) \times 0.5. t{min}: The entry point of the intersection between the ray and the node, calculated as \max(tx0, ty0, tz0). t{max}: The exit point of the intersection between the ray and the node, calculated as \min(tx1, ty1, tz1). Steps: 1. Calculate the intersection factors (tx0, ty0, tz0) and (tx1, ty1, tz1) for the node's bounding box with respect to the ray. 2. Calculate the midpoint factors: txm = (tx0 + tx1) \times 0.5 tym = (ty0 + ty1) \times 0.5 tzm = (tz0 + tz1) \times 0.5 3. Calculate the effective entry and exit distances for the node: t{min} = \max(tx0, ty0, tz0) t{max} = \min(tx1, ty1, tz1) 4. Initialize a list l containing the indices of all 8 children, sorted by their traversal order. 5. Apply pruning rules based on the comparison of midpoint factors (txm, tym, tzm) against t{min} and t{max}: If txm < t{min}: Mark children \{5, 6, 7, 8\} as invalid. If txm > t{max}: Mark children \{1, 2, 3, 4\} as invalid. If tym < t{min}: Mark children \{3, 4, 7, 8\} as invalid. If tym > t{max}: Mark children \{1, 2, 5, 6\} as invalid. If tzm < t{min}: Mark children \{2, 4, 6, 8\} as invalid. If tzm > t{max}: Mark children \{1, 3, 5, 7\} as invalid. 6. Filter the list l to remove all entries marked as invalid (typically represented by setting their value to -1). 7. Return the filtered list of valid child indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nodeomission(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax): """ Determines which children of a node are intersected by a ray. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) origin of the ray. raydirection: (x, y, z) direction of the ray. boxmin: (x, y, z) minimum corner of the node's AABB. boxmax: (x, y, z) maximum corner of the node's AABB. Returns: List of valid child indices (1-8) to traverse, or empty list if no intersection. """ # 1. Calculate intersection factors for the node box def computefactors(origin, direction, bmin, bmax): # Handle zero direction components and compute per-axis entry/exit factors if direction[0] == 0: if not (bmin[0] <= origin[0] <= bmax[0]): return None tx0, tx1 = float('-inf'), float('inf') else: tx0 = (bmin[0] - origin[0]) / direction[0] tx1 = (bmax[0] - origin[0]) / direction[0] if tx0 > tx1: tx0, tx1 = tx1, tx0 if direction[1] == 0: if not (bmin[1] <= origin[1] <= bmax[1]): return None ty0, ty1 = float('-inf'), float('inf') else: ty0 = (bmin[1] - origin[1]) / direction[1] ty1 = (bmax[1] - origin[1]) / direction[1] if ty0 > ty1: ty0, ty1 = ty1, ty0 if direction[2] == 0: if not (bmin[2] <= origin[2] <= bmax[2]): return None tz0, tz1 = float('-inf'), float('inf') else: tz0 = (bmin[2] - origin[2]) / direction[2] tz1 = (bmax[2] - origin[2]) / direction[2] if tz0 > tz1: tz0, tz1 = tz1, tz0 tmin = max(tx0, ty0, tz0) tmax = min(tx1, ty1, tz1) # Standard ray-box intersection guard if tmin > tmax or tmax < 0: return None return tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1 factors = computefactors(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax) if factors is None: return [] tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1 = factors # 2. Calculate midpoints txm = (tx0 + tx1) 0.5 tym = (ty0 + ty1) 0.5 tzm = (tz0 + tz1) 0.5 # 3. Set tmin and tmax for the current node tmin = max(tx0, ty0, tz0) tmax = min(tx1, ty1, tz1) # 4. Initialize list with all 8 children, sorted by traversal order children = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] # 5. Apply pruning rules if txm < tmin: children = [c for c in children if c not in {5, 6, 7, 8}] if txm > tmax: children = [c for c in children if c not in {1, 2, 3, 4}] if tym < tmin: children = [c for c in children if c not in {3, 4, 7, 8}] if tym > tmax: children = [c for c in children if c not in {1, 2, 5, 6}] if tzm < tmin: children = [c for c in children if c not in {2, 4, 6, 8}] if tzm > tmax: children = [c for c in children if c not in {1, 3, 5, 7}] return children Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-intersection: If t{min} > t{max} or the ray origin is behind the box (t{max} < 0), the ray does not intersect the node's bounding box. The algorithm returns an empty list. Precision: The source uses exact comparisons for midpoint factors against t{min} and t{max} without epsilon tolerance. Implementers should be aware that floating-point precision errors near the midpoint boundaries may lead to incorrect pruning in degenerate cases. Child Indexing: The specific set of children marked invalid depends on the octree's child indexing scheme. The source assumes a specific mapping where \{1,2,3,4\} are on one side of the x-midplane and \{5,6,7,8\} on the other. Implementers must verify their octree's indexing convention matches the sets used in the pruning rules. Time Complexity: The pruning step involves a constant number of comparisons and list filtering operations, making it O(1) per node visited. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the list of children. Measured Performance: On the scene in Figure 17 of the source, adding this optimization (referred to as "Evasion" or "Omission") alongside sorting increased FPS from ~16 to ~30 and reduced peak intersection tests from ~150 to ~85. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of intersection tests and stack operations by eliminating branches that are geometrically impossible to intersect. Limitations: Requires calculating intersection factors for the parent node's box. The benefit is highest when the ray passes through many empty or non-intersecting branches of the tree. This optimization is described in the context of Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) traversal for global illumination calculations. It is presented as a follow-up to sorting optimizations, referred to as "Omisión de nodos no intersecables" or "Evasion". The method was implemented and tested as part of a thesis on SVO compression and efficiency for global illumination. name: Two-Pass Hierarchy Traversal
head: Two-Step Hierarchy Traversal, Two-pass traversal
body: Two-Pass Hierarchy Traversal is a spatial hierarchy traversal optimization that reduces computational cost by splitting the descent into a coarse initial pass and a fine subsequent pass. It sets itself apart from single-pass methods like Leaf Collection or Point Plane Test Traversal by explicitly decoupling the identification of relevant subtrees from the detailed node evaluation, allowing for significant reuse across pixel blocks. Inputs: A spatial hierarchy (e.g., octree) representing the volume. A set of rays to be evaluated. A stopping depth parameter d{stop}, defined as the number of levels above the leaves where the first traversal terminates. Outputs: A set of active nodes at depth d{stop} relative to the leaves, forming a "coarse subtree". The final traversal results (e.g., scattering contributions) for the rays. Data Structures: Tree Cut Buffer: A collection of nodes identified at the end of the first pass. These nodes serve as the roots for the second pass. Tile Grouping: Rays are grouped into 2 \times 2 pixel blocks to facilitate sharing of the first pass results. Parameters: Stopping Depth (d{stop}): The depth relative to the leaves where the first traversal stops. A value of 3 means the first pass stops 3 levels above the leaves, producing subtrees of depth 3. Tile Size: 2 \times 2 pixels for sharing the first pass results. Algorithm Steps: 1. Group Rays: Divide the primary rays into groups of 2 \times 2 pixels. Note: This sharing is only applied to primary rays and only when the 2 \times 2 block does not cover an edge of the material. 2. First Pass (Coarse Extraction): For each unique ray group (or individual ray if sharing is disabled), traverse the hierarchy from the root. Continue traversal until the current node's depth is d{stop} levels above the leaves. Collect all such nodes into the Tree Cut Buffer. If multiple rays share the same group, they share this buffer. 3. Second Pass (Fine Traversal): For each ray, restart the traversal starting from the nodes in the Tree Cut Buffer corresponding to its path. Continue traversing from these nodes until the node satisfies the accuracy criterion (e.g., leaf node or sufficient detail). Compute the scattering or rendering contribution for the ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stopping Depth 0: If d{stop} = 0, the first pass descends through the entire hierarchy. The second pass cost is null, and performance equals the direct implementation. Secondary Rays: Do not apply the savings (sharing or two-pass structure) to secondary rays (rays that have bounced at least once). Material Edges: Do not apply the 2 \times 2 pixel sharing when the block covers an edge of the material, as the hierarchy traversal results may differ significantly between adjacent pixels. Args: hierarchy: The spatial hierarchy (e.g., octree). rays: List of ray objects. stoppingdepth: Integer, depth relative to leaves where first pass stops. Returns: List of computed scattering contributions for each ray. """ contributions = [None] len(rays) # Group rays into 2x2 blocks for sharing # Assuming rays are indexed in raster order for simplicity numrays = len(rays) tilesize = 2 numtilesx = (numrays // tilesize) // tilesize # Approximate grid dimension # Helper to get tile index for a ray def gettileindex(rayidx, width): y = rayidx // width x = rayidx % width return (y // tilesize) (width // tilesize) + (x // tilesize) # Precompute tile indices raytileindices = [gettileindex(i, width) for i, width in [(len(rays), 0)]] # Placeholder for width # Note: Width is not explicitly given in sources, assumed known from image dimensions # Determine unique tiles to process uniquetiles = set(raytileindices) # Cache for first pass results: tileindex -> list of nodes at stoppingdepth firstpasscache = {} for tileidx in uniquetiles: # Get rays belonging to this tile tilerays = [rays[i] for i, t in enumerate(raytileindices) if t == tileidx] # Check for material edge condition # Note: Specific edge detection logic is not detailed in sources, # assumed to be a boolean check on the material boundary within the 2x2 block if hasmaterialedge(tilerays): # If edge is present, do not share; process each ray individually for ray in tilerays: subtree = extractsubtree(hierarchy, ray, stoppingdepth) contributions[ray.id] = secondpasstraverse(subtree, ray) else: # Perform first pass for the tile (shared) # Extract a coarse subtree starting from root, stopping at stoppingdepth # Since rays in a tile are close, they likely share the same path to stoppingdepth # We use the first ray in the tile as representative, or merge paths representativeray = tilerays[0] subtreenodes = extractsubtree(hierarchy, representativeray, stoppingdepth) firstpasscache[tileidx] = subtreenodes # Perform second pass for each ray in the tile for ray in tilerays: # Restart traversal from the shared subtree nodes contributions[ray.id] = secondpasstraverse(subtreenodes, ray) return contributions def extractsubtree(hierarchy, ray, stoppingdepth): """ Traverses from root to stoppingdepth relative to leaves. Returns list of nodes at that depth. """ nodesatdepth = [] currentnodes = [hierarchy.root] currentdepth = 0 # Calculate max depth of hierarchy to determine stopping depth in absolute terms maxdepth = hierarchy.getmaxdepth() targetdepth = maxdepth - stoppingdepth while currentnodes and currentdepth < targetdepth: nextnodes = [] for node in currentnodes: if node.isleaf: break # Should not happen if stoppingdepth > 0 and tree is valid children = node.getchildren() for child in children: if ray.intersectsnode(child): nextnodes.append(child) currentnodes = nextnodes currentdepth += 1 return currentnodes def secondpasstraverse(subtreenodes, ray): """ Continues traversal from subtreenodes until accuracy criterion is met. """ # Continue traversal from the nodes in the tree cut buffer # until the node satisfies our criterion for accuracy # This typically means traversing to leaves or until a specific density/opacity threshold is met result = 0.0 for node in subtreenodes: result += traversenode(node, ray) return result def traversenode(node, ray): """ Standard single-step traversal logic for a node. """ # Implementation depends on the specific hierarchy and scattering model pass def hasmaterialedge(tilerays): """ Checks if the 2x2 block covers an edge of the material. """ # Logic to detect material boundary crossing within the 2x2 pixel block pass Time Complexity: The method reduces traversal time by up to 30% compared to naive direct implementation. The gain depends on the stopping depth. Performance: At an optimal stopping depth of 3, the two-pass method alone reduces computation time by 15%. When combined with tile sharing (2x2 pixels), the reduction is up to 30%. Overall, it provides a 20% performance improvement over naive hierarchy traversal. Memory: Requires storage for the Tree Cut Buffer and potentially caching results for tile sharing. Strengths: Significant speedup for primary rays in single and multiple scattering computations. Efficient for homogeneous participating media. Limitations: Not applicable to secondary rays. Sharing is invalid near material edges. Performance gain diminishes if stopping depth is too small (approaching 0). Origin: Introduced in the GPU implementation of the point-based rendering algorithm for participating media. Paper: "Point-Based Rendering for Homogeneous Participating Media with Refractive Boundaries" (2017). Usage: Used in rendering participating media, specifically for single and multiple scattering computations. name: Adaptive Out-of-Core Single-Pass GPU Raycasting
head: Adaptive out-of-core technique, Single-pass GPU ray casting framework
body: This method enables interactive rendering of multi-gigabyte scalar volumes on desktop hardware by combining an out-of-core octree data structure with a single-pass, stackless GPU raycasting algorithm. It solves the memory capacity and bandwidth bottlenecks of in-core rendering by maintaining a view- and transfer-function-dependent working set of volumetric bricks in GPU memory, while the rest of the dataset remains on disk. Unlike separate block rendering techniques that suffer from boundary artifacts and cannot support refractive or global illumination models, this approach performs the entire volume traversal and compositing in a single fragment shader pass, adapting sampling density to the local brick resolution. Input: A massive scalar volume dataset (e.g., 2 Gvoxels, 16-bit) stored on disk. Output: A rendered 2D image (e.g., 1024 × 1024 pixels) with accumulated color and opacity, updating the frame buffer and depth buffer. The dataset is decomposed into small cubical bricks and organized into a coarse octree structure maintained out-of-core. Leaves: Store the original voxel data for the brick. Inner Nodes: Store a filtered representation of their children (aggregated data). Node Metadata: Each node stores: The range of scalar values present in the node. Optionally, precomputed gradients. Boundary Replication: To support neighbor access for interpolation and gradients, bricks are made self-contained: One layer of neighboring samples is replicated for linear interpolation support. Two layers of neighboring samples are replicated if central differences are used for gradient computation at render time. An adaptive loader on the CPU maintains a subset of bricks in GPU memory. This set is view-dependent and transfer-function-dependent. Content: Only the bricks required for the current view and transfer function are loaded. Management: Maintained via an adaptive refinement method guided by node priorities. At each frame, a compact indexing structure is encoded in a small GPU texture. Purpose: Spatially organizes the current working set into an octree hierarchy for the raycaster. Nature: It is not a multiresolution data representation; it is a spatial index. Layout: Inner Nodes: Contain pointers to children. Leaves: Refer to volume data nodes stored in the GPU memory pool (the working set). Pointers: Include neighbor pointers to facilitate on-the-fly bounding box computation and neighbor access. 1. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. Decompose the original volumetric model into small cubical bricks. 2. Organize bricks into a coarse octree structure maintained out-of-core. 3. Store original data at leaves and filtered representations at inner nodes. 4. Store value ranges and optional precomputed gradients for each node. 5. Replicate boundary samples (1 layer for linear interpolation, 2 layers for central difference gradients) to make bricks self-contained. 2. Adaptive Loading (CPU/GPU Interaction): 1. Initialize a working set of bricks in GPU memory. 2. Compute node priorities based on view and transfer function. 3. Asynchronously fetch data from the out-of-core octree to update the working set. 4. Refine the working set incrementally based on priorities. 5. Receive feedback from the renderer regarding occlusion to avoid loading/refining occluded zones. 3. Indexing (Per Frame): 1. Encode the spatial organization of the current working set into a compact texture. 2. Populate inner nodes with pointers to children and leaves with references to GPU memory locations. 4. Single-Pass Raycasting (GPU Fragment Shader): 1. For each pixel, cast a ray into the volume. 2. Traverse the compact indexing structure (stackless octree traversal). 3. Enumerate non-empty bricks in front-to-back order. 4. Adapt sampling density to the resolution of the current brick. 5. Compute the volume rendering integral (accumulating color and opacity). 6. Stop raycasting when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. 7. Update the frame buffer and depth buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessvolume(dataset): # 1. Decompose into bricks bricks = decomposeintocubicalbricks(dataset) # 2. Build out-of-core octree octree = buildoctree(bricks) # 3. Populate node data for node in octree.traverse(): if node.isleaf(): node.data = originalvoxeldata else: node.data = filterchildrendata(node.children) node.valuerange = computevaluerange(node.data) node.gradients = computeprecomputedgradients(node.data) # Optional # 4. Replicate boundaries for self-containment if node.isleaf(): replicateneighbors(node.data, layers=1) # For linear interpolation # replicateneighbors(node.data, layers=2) # If central differences needed def updateworkingset(octree, viewparams, transferfunction): # 1. Compute priorities for nodes priorities = computenodepriorities(octree, viewparams, transferfunction) # 2. Determine working set based on memory budget and priorities workingsetnodes = selectnodesbypriority(octree, priorities) # 3. Asynchronously fetch data from disk to GPU gpumemorypool = allocategpumemory(len(workingsetnodes)) for node in workingsetnodes: gpumemorypool[node.id] = fetchdatafromdisk(node) return gpumemorypool, workingsetnodes def buildindextexture(workingsetnodes, gpumemorypool): # Create a compact texture representing the spatial hierarchy of the working set indextexture = createtexture() for node in workingsetnodes: if node.haschildreninworkingset: # Inner node: pointer to children indextexture.setpointer(node.id, node.childrenids) else: # Leaf node: reference to GPU memory indextexture.setreference(node.id, gpumemorypool[node.id].address) return indextexture def raycastfragment(rayorigin, raydirection, indextexture, gpumemorypool, transferfunction): accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 threshold = 0.95 # Example threshold # Stackless traversal of the compact octree index currentnode = indextexture.root t = rayorigin while currentnode is not None and accumulatedopacity < threshold: # 1. Traverse to next non-empty brick # Compute bounding box on-the-fly using the index structure brickbounds = computeboundingbox(currentnode, indextexture) # Intersect ray with brick bounds tenter, texit = intersectraybrick(rayorigin, raydirection, brickbounds) if tenter is None: # Ray missed this brick, move to next sibling or parent currentnode = nextnodeintraversal(currentnode, indextexture) continue t = max(t, tenter) # 2. Sample within the brick # Adapt sampling density to brick resolution stepsize = computestepsize(brickbounds) while t < texit and accumulatedopacity < threshold: samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 3. Retrieve voxel data # Access GPU memory pool using the leaf reference voxelvalue = samplevoxel(samplepos, gpumemorypool[currentnode.ref]) # 4. Transfer function color, opacity = applytransferfunction(voxelvalue, transferfunction) # 5. Front-to-back compositing alpha = opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor += color alpha accumulatedopacity += alpha t += stepsize # 6. Move to next node in front-to-back order currentnode = nextnodeintraversal(currentnode, indextexture) return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity Hardware: NVIDIA 8800 Ultra graphics board. Resolution: 1024 × 1024 window size. Dataset Size: 2 Gvoxels, 16-bit. Performance: Interactive exploration achieved on a desktop PC. Block Boundaries: Unlike separate block rendering, this method avoids artifacts at block boundaries because it performs a full-volume traversal. Occlusion: Feedback from the renderer is used to avoid refinement and data loading of occluded zones, preventing unnecessary GPU stalls. Neighbor Access: Failure to replicate boundary samples correctly will break linear interpolation or gradient computation if neighbor voxels are accessed. Time Complexity: The traversal is stackless and exploits the regular structure of octrees to reduce costly texture memory accesses by computing bounding boxes on-the-fly. The adaptive refinement ensures that only relevant parts of the volume are processed. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by the size of the working set in GPU memory, which is dynamically adjusted based on view and transfer function dependencies. The rest of the data remains out-of-core. Performance: Enables interactive exploration of multi-gigabyte datasets (e.g., 2 Gvoxels) on desktop hardware. Strengths: Supports full-volume optical models, including refracting volumes and global illumination, which separate block rendering cannot easily handle. Adapts sampling density to brick resolution, providing visual quality proportional to data availability. Reduces GPU stalls via occlusion query feedback. Limitations: Requires a GPU capable of single-pass fragment shader execution for volume traversal. Performance depends on the efficiency of the adaptive loader and the compact indexing structure construction. Unlike flat multiresolution blocking, it does not have a constant number of blocks, which may complicate certain types of parallelization or fixed-size memory allocation strategies. Origin: The method was presented in the paper "A single-pass GPU ray casting framework for interactive out-of-core rendering of massive volumetric datasets" by E. Gobbetti, F. Marton, and J. Jallet. History: It builds upon earlier work on out-of-core volume octrees and stackless ray traversal methods for kd-trees [7, 16], extending them to GPUs for volume rendering. It addresses the limitations of previous GPU volume rendering techniques that were restricted to moderate-sized volumes fitting entirely in texture memory. Usage: Primarily used for interactive exploration of multi-gigabyte CT datasets in medical visualization and numerical simulation analysis. A single-pass GPU ray casting framework for interactive out-of-core rendering of massive volumetric datasets, https://www.crs4.it/vic/data/papers/cgi2008-movr.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Stackless Traversal
head: Algorithme sans pile, Parcours sans pile
body: Stackless Traversal is a method for traversing hierarchical volume structures (specifically N3-trees) that eliminates the need for a stack data structure by recalculating Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) parameters at each tree descent and ascent. It differs from sibling methods like Leaf Collection and Point Plane Test Traversal by relying on parent pointers for ascent and full DDA recalculation rather than incremental updates or explicit leaf enumeration, optimizing for GPU register usage and branch divergence. Inputs: A hierarchical volume structure (N3-tree) where each node stores a pointer to its parent and, if non-empty, an average color/value and occupancy status. A ray defined by origin and direction. Outputs: Integrated color and opacity for the ray. Data Structures: Node: Contains a pointer to the parent node, a pointer to child nodes (if internal), and metadata (average color, occupancy). DDA State: Current position, step size, and direction signs for the current voxel/brick. Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute initial DDA parameters for the root node based on the ray origin and direction. 2. Descent: Traverse down the tree. At each step, recalculate all DDA parameters for the child node based on the current ray state and the child's spatial bounds. 3. Node Evaluation: If the current node is empty, ignore it and proceed to the next candidate. If the node is not empty, extract the current cell information from the direct pointer to the exact child node within the parent's grid, avoiding recalculation. 4. Accumulation: If the node is a leaf or contains data, use the stored average color/value and accumulate it based on the distance traversed by the ray in that brick (pre-integration). If the node is a loaded brick, sample it; if it is an unloaded brick (due to dynamic loading failure or out-of-core constraints), use the stored average. 5. Ascent: Return to the parent node using the parent pointer stored in the hierarchical structure. 6. Iteration: Repeat descent and ascent until the ray exits the volume or is fully occluded. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stacklesstraverse(ray, root): # Initialize DDA for the root dda = computedda(ray, root.bounds) currentnode = root while currentnode is not None: # Descent: Recalculate DDA for the next child # This step replaces stack-based state preservation nextnode, dda = descendandrecalcdda(currentnode, dda) if nextnode is None: # Ascent: Use parent pointer to go back up currentnode = currentnode.parent if currentnode is not None: # Extract current cell info from parent's grid using direct pointer # to the exact child node, avoiding recalculation dda = extractddafromparent(currentnode, nextnodewas) continue currentnode = nextnode # Evaluate node if currentnode.isempty: # Ignore empty nodes currentnode = currentnode.parent continue # Accumulate contribution distance = computeraybrickintersectiondistance(ray, currentnode.bounds) if currentnode.isloaded: color = samplevoxeldata(ray, currentnode.data, dda) else: # Use stored average for unloaded bricks color = currentnode.averagecolor accumulate(color, distance) # Continue traversal # Logic to determine next child or ascent is handled in descendandrecalcdda # based on ray exit from current brick Parameters: Conditional Block Size: Limited to reduce divergent threads on GPU multiprocessors. Register Usage: Limited to allow multiprocessors to handle more parallel threads, better covering texture access latency. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Memory Latency: On NVIDIA G80 architecture, dynamically indexed arrays are placed in 'local' memory (device memory) by the shader compiler, which is uncached and up to 50x slower than registers. This negatively impacts performance compared to register-based stack access. Dynamic Loading Failure: If a brick fails to load dynamically (e.g., due to sudden load overload), the algorithm falls back to using the stored average color in the node. Performance: Approximately 50% faster than the mini-stack algorithm on the tested hardware (G80). Strengths: Eliminates stack memory overhead; reduces register pressure by avoiding stack storage; limits branch divergence through constrained conditional blocks. Limitations: Recalculating DDA parameters at every step increases computational cost per node compared to incremental updates; performance is sensitive to GPU memory hierarchy (local memory penalty). When to use: When stack memory is constrained or when GPU register pressure is a bottleneck; suitable for hierarchical structures with parent pointers. When not to use: On architectures where local memory latency is prohibitive and register usage cannot be sufficiently optimized; when incremental DDA updates are significantly cheaper than recalculation. Stackless Traversal was developed as part of research into interactive exploration of procedural volume data, specifically targeting N3-tree structures. It was designed to optimize GPU rendering by minimizing stack usage and branch divergence, addressing performance bottlenecks observed in stack-based traversals on early GPU architectures like the G80. name: Octree-based Volume Rendering
head: Chamberlain's algorithm, LaMar's algorithm, Weiler's smoothing
body: Octree-based volume rendering accelerates image-order ray casting by recursively traversing a hierarchical spatial subdivision of volumetric data, using projected size and field-of-view criteria to select nodes for approximation or culling. It differs from sibling methods like Point Plane Test Traversal by using a tree structure for adaptive level-of-detail selection rather than fixed coarse meshes or plane tests, and unlike CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal which focuses on explicit sparse storage, this method traditionally assumes the octree resides in main memory. Inputs: Volumetric dataset (density \sigma and color c); camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, field-of-view). Outputs: Rendered image. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains a bounding box, a pointer to children (if not a leaf), and leaf data. Leaf Data: For traditional methods, scalar density and color values. For PlenOctree, density and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Perform octree subdivision of the volumetric data. 2. Rendering: Recursively traverse the octree. 3. Selection: Compute the projected size of each octree node on the fly. If the size is smaller than a predefined threshold, consider the node sufficiently accurate to approximate all nodes below it. 4. LaMar’s Criteria: Use two filters: distance (similar to Chamberlain) and field-of-view. Discard nodes that do not intersect the view frustum. Select nodes whose projected angle is less than half the field-of-view angle. 5. Smoothing (Weiler): Apply an extension to smooth the discontinuity artifacts at LOD boundaries. PlenOctree Variant Steps: 1. Intersection: For each ray, determine ray-voxel intersections in the octree structure, producing a sequence of segments between voxel boundaries with constant density and color, of lengths \{\deltai\}. 2. Accumulation: Apply NeRF’s volume rendering model: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=0}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where transmittance Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj). 3. Early Stopping: Stop rendering when accumulated transmittance Ti < \gamma, where \gamma = 0.01. Parameters: Predefined threshold for projected size; early-stopping transmittance threshold \gamma = 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: LOD Artifacts: Substantial visual artifacts appear at the boundaries of different levels of detail due to inconsistencies of the view-plane at different levels of detail. Memory Limitation: Inability to reduce the volumetric data size in main memory, limiting the ability to render datasets larger than main memory size. A variant that converts a trained NeRF-SH model into a sparse octree representation for real-time rendering. It sets itself apart from traditional octree methods by storing density and SH coefficients to model view-dependent appearance, rather than scalar values. Choose it when real-time rendering of neural radiance fields is required. See Hierarchical Traversal. Time Complexity: Depends on octree depth and data sparsity. LaMar’s algorithm provides a considerable speedup over Chamberlain’s algorithm by using FOV culling. Memory Complexity: Traditional methods require the entire octree in main memory, limiting scalability to datasets larger than RAM. PlenOctree uses sparse storage, reducing memory footprint. Measured Performance: PlenOctree achieves ~42 FPS on Tanks and Temples scenes at 1920×1080 resolution, maintaining comparable image quality metrics (PSNR/SSIM) to standard NeRF. Strengths: FOV culling improves performance. Limitations: LOD boundary artifacts require smoothing; memory-bound for large datasets in traditional implementations. When to Use: Real-time rendering of volumetric data with significant empty space or uniform regions; when memory allows loading the octree. When Not to Use: Datasets exceeding main memory size without sparse storage extensions; scenes requiring seamless LOD transitions without post-processing smoothing. The octree spatial hierarchy was first proposed by Chamberlain et al. for rendering surface (polygonal) geometry. LaMar et al. improved selection criteria with distance and FOV filters. Weiler et al. addressed LOD artifacts with smoothing extensions. PlenOctree extends this to neural radiance fields, enabling real-time rendering of NeRFs.
