name: Octree Child Index Computation
body: Octree Child Index Computation determines the 0–7 octant offset (and thus the linear index) of the child node that contains a specific target coordinate within the current parent node. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping a 3D position to a specific branch in a hierarchical grid without arbitrary bit shifts. It sets itself apart from generic tree traversal by relying on precomputed bit masks and constant-time bitwise operations to derive the child index. Inputs: destination: The target 3D coordinate vector (xd, yd, zd). depth: The current depth level in the octree. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. Outputs: octant: An integer in the range [0, 7] representing the octant offset of the child containing the destination. Data Structures: childbitdepth: A precomputed array where childbitdepth[d] stores the bit mask for depth d. Layout: Array of integers. Size: maxdepth + 1. Formula: childbitdepth[d] = 1 << (maxdepth - d - 1). Steps: 1. Precompute Masks: Calculate childbitdepth for all depths d \in [0, \text{max\depth}] using the formula above. 2. Extract Components: Isolate the X, Y, and Z components of the destination coordinate. 3. Mask and Shift: Apply the childbitdepth[depth] mask to the corresponding destination component using bitwise AND (&). Bit-shift the masked result by constants corresponding to the X, Y, and Z components to align them into a single integer. 4. Combine: Combine the shifted components to form the 0–7 octant offset. 5. Return: Return the scalar value when encountering a leaf; either a scalar leaf in an interior node, or a voxel within a cap node. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computechildindex(destination, depth, maxdepth, childbitdepth): # Precompute bit depth mask if not already done # childbitdepth[d] = 1 << (maxdepth - d - 1) # Get the bit mask for the current depth mask = childbitdepth[depth] # Extract destination components xd = destination.x yd = destination.y zd = destination.z # Apply mask to destination coordinates xmasked = xd & mask ymasked = yd & mask zmasked = zd & mask # Determine octant bits by shifting masked values to LSB # The shift constant corresponds to the bit position of the mask shift = maxdepth - depth - 1 bitx = xmasked >> shift bity = ymasked >> shift bitz = zmasked >> shift # Combine into 0-7 octant offset octant = bitx | (bity << 1) | (bitz << 2) return octant Parameters: maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. Typical values depend on the volume resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Leaf Nodes: When a leaf is encountered, the function returns the scalar value or voxel index directly. Precision: Integer arithmetic is preferred for index computation to avoid floating-point precision issues when comparing coordinates to bit masks. Point Location maps a continuous 3D coordinate vector to a specific leaf node or voxel within a canonical octree. It solves the problem of efficiently retrieving data associated with a spatial position by traversing the tree from a given starting node to the target leaf. What sets this method apart from generic tree traversal is its reliance on precomputed bit masks to determine child indices using constant-time bitwise operations, avoiding the computational cost of arbitrary bit shifts. It builds on Octree Child Index Computation to derive the 0-7 octant offset. Fast Projection for Octree Nodes accelerates the mapping of 3D octree nodes to 2D screen space during sparse voxel octree rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which pixels are affected by a node's projection without per-pixel ray casting for every node. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using a hierarchical 2D node map to terminate redundant thread execution, achieving a speedup of > 2x compared to naive per-pixel launching. Voxel Child Address Calculation determines the linear address of a specific child octant within a block of children, based on a valid mask. It calculates the index by creating a mask to isolate the bit corresponding to the octant, and returns the count of set bits up to that position. This method operates on a single node's children rather than traversing the tree, and focuses on index compression rather than geometric culling. Direction-dependent Morton Order Mapping is a remapping function that converts a standard Octree Morton code into a sorting key aligned with the near-to-far rendering order for a specific ray direction. It solves the problem of correct occlusion culling and blending order in sparse voxel rasterization by ensuring that voxels are processed from closest to furthest relative to the camera, regardless of the viewing angle. Unlike Point Location which determines spatial containment, or Fast Projection for Octree Nodes which estimates bounding volumes, this method specifically addresses the topological sorting requirement for volume rendering by adapting the Morton space-filling curve to the ray's sign vector. Ordered Child Traversal iterates over the children of a voxel in a specific order, typically front-to-back relative to the ray direction. It uses a precomputed 8x8 table ORDEREDCHILDREN that maps the ray direction and the current voxel's octant to the sequence of child indices to visit. This ensures correct occlusion culling and blending order in volume rendering. Octree Child Bounding Box Computation calculates the AABB of a child node given its parent bounds and child index (0–7 for octree, 0–63 for wide). Uses Morton/Z-order bit packing for child indexing. Computes mid = (min + max) 0.5. Extracts bits from childindex: highx = (childindex & 1) != 0, highy = (childindex & 2) != 0, highz = (childindex & 4) != 0. Sets child min to (highx ? mid.x: min.x, highy ? mid.y: min.y, highz ? mid.z: min.z) and child max to (highx ? max.x: mid.x, highy ? max.y: mid.y, highz ? max.z: max.z). Child index bit packing: bit 0 = x, bit 1 = y, bit 2 = z. Supports standard 8-way octree and extends to 4x4x4 wide nodes by reusing the same bit logic. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Strengths include avoiding expensive arbitrary bit shifts through precomputed masks. Limitations include the requirement to precompute bit masks for all depths. The method originates from interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. It was developed to optimize the traversal of sparse voxel octrees by reducing the computational cost of child index determination. name: Point Location
head: Octree Point Location, Integer coordinate point location
body:
Point location maps a continuous 3D coordinate vector to a specific leaf node or voxel within a canonical octree. It solves the problem of efficiently retrieving data associated with a spatial position by traversing the tree from a given starting node to the target leaf. What sets this method apart from generic tree traversal is its reliance on precomputed bit masks to determine child indices using constant-time bitwise operations, avoiding the computational cost of arbitrary bit shifts. It builds on Octree Child Index Computation to derive the 0-7 octant offset. Inputs and Outputs: Input: dest: A 3D integer coordinate vector representing the target location. depth: The current depth level in the octree, starting from the root or an intermediate node. index: The index of the current node in the flat node array. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. Output: The scalar value stored in the leaf node containing dest. Data Structures: The method assumes the following data structures, typically stored in an OctreeData container: nodes: A 2D array nodes[depth][index] of type OctNode. caps: An array caps[index] of type OctCap, used for leaf voxels at the deepest level. childbitdepth: A precomputed 1D array childbitdepth[maxdepth]. OctNode layout: childscalars[8]: Array of scalar values for leaf children. childstart: Unsigned integer base pointer or index to the children of this node. childoffset[8]: Array of 8 signed chars representing the offset from childstart to the child node. A value of -1 indicates the child is a leaf (scalar). OctCap layout: childscalars[8]: Array of scalar values for the 8 voxels in the cap. Precomputation: Before traversal, the childbitdepth array is computed for each depth level d from 0 to maxdepth: 	ext{child it\depth}[d] = 1 \ll (	ext{max\depth} - d - 1) This precomputation avoids expensive arbitrary left-shift operations during traversal. Algorithm Steps: 1. Cast Coordinates: Convert continuous input coordinates to integers and ensure they fall within the canonical interval [0, 2^{	ext{max\depth}}). 2. Initialize: Start with the given depth and index. 3. Retrieve Node: Access the current node: node = nodes[depth][index]. 4. Get Mask: Retrieve the precomputed bit mask for the current depth: childbit = childbitdepth[depth]. 5. Compute Child Index: Determine the 0-7 octant index of the child containing dest by testing bits against childbit, shifting results, and combining them: 	ext{child} = ((	ext{dest}.x \ \& \ 	ext{child it}) 
eq 0) \ll 2 \ | \ ((	ext{dest}.y \ \& \ 	ext{child it}) 
eq 0) \ll 1 \ | \ ((	ext{dest}.z \ \& \ 	ext{child it}) 
eq 0) This yields the 0-7 octant offset of the child, and hence its index. 6. Check for Leaf in Interior Node: If node.childoffset[child] == -1, the child is a scalar leaf. Return node.childscalars[child]. 7. Check for Cap Node (Deepest Level): If depth == maxdepth - 2, the node is a cap node containing voxels. Calculate the final child index using the lowest bit (bit 0) of the coordinates: 	ext{child} = (	ext{dest}.x \ \& \ 1) \ll 2 \ | \ (	ext{dest}.y \ \& \ 1) \ll 1 \ | \ (	ext{dest}.z \ \& \ 1) Update index = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] and return caps[index].childscalars[child]. 8. Traverse Down: If not a leaf and not a cap: Update index to point to the child's start location: index = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child]. Increment depth: depth += 1. Repeat from Step 3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointlocate(dest: Vec3i, depth: int, index: int, maxdepth: int, nodes: List[List[OctNode]], caps: List[OctCap], childbitdepth: List[int]) -> T: while True: node = nodes[depth][index] childbit = childbitdepth[depth] # Compute child index (0-7) based on bits in dest coordinates child = ((dest.x & childbit) != 0) << 2 | \ ((dest.y & childbit) != 0) << 1 | \ ((dest.z & childbit) != 0) # Check if child is a scalar leaf in an interior node if node.childoffset[child] == -1: return node.childscalars[child] # Check if we are at the cap level (maxdepth - 2) elif depth == maxdepth - 2: # Use the lowest bit for cap nodes index = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] child = (dest.x & 1) << 2 | (dest.y & 1) << 1 | (dest.z & 1) return caps[index].childscalars[child] # Traverse to the child node index = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] depth += 1 return 0 # Fallback return, though the loop always returns for valid inputs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Range: Coordinates must be within the canonical interval [0, 2^{	ext{max\depth}}] and cast to integers. Cap Nodes: The algorithm explicitly handles the deepest level (maxdepth - 2) as a special case using the lowest bit, implying the octree structure uses "caps" for the finest resolution. Parent Pointers: Parent pointers are omitted to save memory. Neighbor finding (which may call point location) relies on a separate parenttrace array provided by the ray traversal algorithm. An algorithm to traverse and insert a voxel into an Octree using a pre-computed bitstream to determine child indices. Definition: It uses a bitstream b encoding the voxel's position to guide insertion. Steps: 1. If depth d is 0, return a new node containing the voxel v. 2. Extract the child index from the bitstream b using group(b, d, 3) and get the corresponding child n' from node n. 3. If child n' is null, create a new empty node. 4. Recursively insert the voxel into the child node with depth d-1, and set the result as the child at the index derived from the bitstream. Parameters: b: The bitstream encoding the voxel's position. When to choose: Used for dynamic insertion into an octree where a bitstream representation of coordinates is available. Time Complexity: O(d), where d is the depth of the octree, as each iteration performs constant-time bitwise operations and array lookups. Memory Complexity: O(	ext{max\depth}) for the precomputed childbitdepth array. The node structure itself is compact, using childoffset as signed chars to save space. Performance: Precomputing bit masks avoids expensive arbitrary left-shift operations, providing noticeably better performance than the original Frisken and Perry method. Strengths: Fast lookup, low memory overhead (no parent pointers), simple bitwise logic. Limitations: Requires canonical coordinate system [0, 2^{	ext{max\depth}}]. Neighbor finding requires additional infrastructure (parenttrace). Originating from the work of Frisken and Perry, this method was adapted for interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The original proposal involved creating a single-bit mask corresponding to the current depth and applying it to coordinates. The optimized version, caching childbitdepth to avoid arbitrary shifts, was introduced in subsequent implementations for performance. name: Fast Projection for Octree Nodes
body: Fast Projection for Octree Nodes computes the projected center of an octree node from its parent's projected center using a simple 2D translation. It determines the subdivisions and pixels affected by the projection using 32-bit integer arithmetic, and recursively updates hierarchical occlusion maps (HOMs). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Parent node's projected center (cxp, cyp), octree level L, and octant index i \in \{0, \dots, 7\}. Output: Child node's projected center (cxc, cyc), subdivision indices, and affected pixel ranges. Data Structures: Translation Vectors: For each octree level L, eight constant 2D integer vectors \vec{T}{L, i} are preprocessed. These vectors represent the offset from the parent's projected center to each of the eight children's projected centers in screen space. Occlusion Map (HOM): A 2D array of 32-bit integers used to track visibility. Values indicate occlusion status, such as opaque areas marked with constants like 16 (e.g., P[x, y] = 16). Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute and store eight 2D translation vectors \vec{T}{L, i} for each relevant octree level L. 2. Child Projection: For a parent node at level L-1 with projected center (cxp, cyp), compute the projected center of child i at level L using: \begin{bmatrix} cxc \\ cyc \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} cxp \\ cyp \end{bmatrix} + \vec{T}{L, i} This uses simple 2D integer translation. 3. Subdivision and Pixel Assignment: Use 32-bit integer arithmetic to determine the bounding box of the projected child node and calculate the range of pixels [x{min}, x{max}] \times [y{min}, y{max}] covered by the node. 4. Occlusion Map Update: Recursively update the Hierarchical Occlusion Map (HOM) using 32-bit integer arithmetic. If a child node is occluded or fully opaque, mark the corresponding region in the HOM. 5. Depth Cueing: Compute the depth component for fast depth cueing using the same projection logic, ensuring consistent depth values for shading. Parameters: Arithmetic: 32-bit integer arithmetic is used for subdivision determination, pixel assignment, and recursive HOM updates. Translation Vectors: Precomputed per level. The exact derivation from the camera projection matrix and octree geometry is Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundary Conditions: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. T = {} class Node: def init(self, center, level, size): self.center = center self.level = level self.size = size def projectchildcenter(parentcenter, level, octantindex): """Compute projected center of a child node from its parent's projected center.""" dx, dy = T[level][octantindex] # 32-bit integer arithmetic as specified cxc = parentcenter[0] + dx cyc = parentcenter[1] + dy return (cxc, cyc) def updatehierarchicalocclusionmap(nodecenter, nodesize, hom): """Recursively update the occlusion map for the projected node area.""" # Determine pixel bounds using 32-bit integer arithmetic xmin = nodecenter[0] - nodesize xmax = nodecenter[0] + nodesize ymin = nodecenter[1] - nodesize ymax = nodecenter[1] + nodesize # Clip to screen bounds (standard guard) xmin = max(0, xmin) xmax = min(len(hom[0]), xmax) ymin = max(0, ymin) ymax = min(len(hom), ymax) # Mark occluded/opaque pixels (e.g., P[x, y] = 16 for opaque) for y in range(ymin, ymax): for x in range(xmin, xmax): hom[y][x] = 16 def traverseoctree(node, hom): """Traverse octree nodes using fast projection and HOM updates.""" # Check occlusion before processing (standard guard) # isoccluded logic is Not given in the sources # Project children and update HOM recursively for i in range(8): childcenter = projectchildcenter(node.center, node.level + 1, i) childsize = node.size // 2 updatehierarchicalocclusionmap(childcenter, childsize, hom) # Depth cueing computed in the same way # Recursive traversal or thread launch is Not given in the sources This method reduces the number of threads launched during sparse voxel octree filtering by using a hierarchical 2D node map to detect and terminate redundant thread execution. It sets itself apart from naive per-pixel thread launching by terminating threads that target the same common ancestor node, achieving a speedup of > 2x. Time Complexity: O(1) projection per node due to precomputed translations. HOM updates are proportional to the projected area. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the HOM, where W and H are screen dimensions. Precomputed translation vectors require O(L \times 8) space, where L is the max octree depth. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient occlusion culling via HOM; fast projection using integer arithmetic. Limitations: Requires precomputation of translation vectors; 32-bit integer arithmetic may limit precision at high resolutions. When to Use: Sparse voxel octree rendering with significant occlusion. When Not to Use: Dense volumes where occlusion culling is ineffective; very high resolutions where 32-bit integer precision is insufficient. Originated in the context of object-order ray-casting algorithms for sparse voxel octrees. The method leverages hierarchical occlusion maps (HOMs) to optimize rendering. name: Sparse Octree Filtering with Node Map
head: Light-view Map Node Map, Node Map MIP-map Filtering
body: This method reduces the number of threads launched during sparse voxel octree filtering by using a hierarchical 2D node map to detect and terminate redundant thread execution. It sets itself apart from naive per-pixel thread launching by terminating threads that target the same common ancestor node, achieving a speedup of > 2x. The method constructs a 2D node map derived from the light-view map to guide thread execution during octree filtering. It uses a MIP-map pyramid structure to manage thread coordination and termination. Node Map: A 2D array with multiple levels (MIP-map pyramid). Lowest Level (Highest Resolution): Each pixel stores the index of the 3D leaf node in the sparse octree that contains the corresponding photon from the light-view map. Higher Levels (Lower Resolution): Each pixel stores the index of the lowest common ancestor (LCA) node for the nodes referenced by the corresponding pixels in the previous (higher resolution) level. 1. Initialization: Construct the node map from the light-view map. For the lowest level, map each photon to its containing leaf node index. For higher levels, compute the LCA for groups of nodes from the level below. 2. Thread Launch: Launch one thread per pixel of the lowest node map level for each MIP-mapping pass. 3. Node Lookup and Redundancy Check: Each thread traverses the octree to find the specific node it must compute the filtered value for. Before performing computation, the thread checks the current level of the node map to see if another thread is targeting the same node (a common ancestor). If a common ancestor is detected, all threads identifying this node are terminated except the "upper left" one (based on pixel coordinates). The surviving thread computes the remaining filtered values for that node. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Octree: def findleafnode(self, position): return 0 # Standard octree lookup def findlca(self, idx1, idx2): return 0 # Standard octree LCA def computefilteredvalue(self, nodeidx): pass # Standard filtering step def sparseoctreefilteringwithnodemap(lightviewmap, octree): # 1. Construct Node Map # Lowest level: map photons to leaf node indices lowestlevel = [octree.findleafnode(photon.position) for photon in lightviewmap] nodemap = [lowestlevel] currentlevel = lowestlevel # Higher levels: compute LCAs for groups of nodes from the level below while len(currentlevel) > 1: nextlevel = [] for i in range(0, len(currentlevel), 2): if i + 1 < len(currentlevel): lcaindex = octree.findlca(currentlevel[i], currentlevel[i+1]) else: lcaindex = currentlevel[i] # Fallback for odd length nextlevel.append(lcaindex) nodemap.append(nextlevel) currentlevel = nextlevel # 2. Launch threads for each MIP-mapping pass for levelidx in range(len(nodemap)): level = nodemap[levelidx] # Track which node indices are being computed to detect common ancestors activethreads = {} for pixelidx, nodeidx in enumerate(level): # Determine 2D coordinates from pixelidx for upper-left rule # Assuming standard row-major 2D layout width = len(nodemap[0]) x = pixelidx % width y = pixelidx // width # Check if another thread already targets this node if nodeidx in activethreads: prevx, prevy = activethreads[nodeidx] # Terminate current thread if it is not upper-left if y > prevy or (y == prevy and x > prevx): continue # Thread terminated # Surviving thread computes the filtered value activethreads[nodeidx] = (x, y) octree.computefilteredvalue(nodeidx) Thread Termination Heuristic: The "upper left" rule ensures deterministic termination when multiple threads target the same common ancestor node. Performance: The heuristic reduces redundant work, yielding a speedup of > 2x compared to not using it. Edge Cases: Highly irregular photon distributions may cause uneven thread termination, but the upper-left rule guarantees exactly one thread per unique node index per pass. This method generates anisotropic mipmaps from the leaf nodes of a sparse octree to support efficient cone tracing. It solves the problem of directional lighting blur by filtering voxel data anisotropically along the positive and negative XYZ axes, storing six directional values per voxel. It sets itself apart from isotropic filtering by preserving directional information required for accurate cone tracing, building on the node map structure of Sparse Octree Filtering with Node Map to reduce thread launch overhead. Speedup: Achieves a speedup of > 2x compared to not using the heuristic to terminate redundant threads. Complexity: Reduces the number of active threads by terminating redundant threads that target the same common ancestor node in the node map. Strengths: Efficiently coordinates thread execution during MIP-map generation by leveraging the hierarchical 2D node map structure. Limitations: Requires construction of the 2D node map from the light-view map; relies on the "upper left" heuristic for deterministic thread termination. This method originates from the "Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing" technique developed by NVIDIA researchers. It addresses the computational cost of filtering sparse voxel octrees for real-time global illumination by optimizing thread launch overhead through the node map structure. name: Anisotropic Voxel Filtering for Mipmap Generation
head: Anisotropic Filtering Pass, Anisotropic Mipmap Filtering, Filtering Pass
body: This method filters lighting data at the leaf nodes of an octree anisotropically along the positive and negative XYZ directions to prepare for cone tracing. It stores six directional values per voxel to preserve directional information. Inputs: Leaf node lighting data in a 3D texture (lower mip level). Outputs: Filtered lighting data in a 3D texture (upper mip level) with anisotropic directional storage. Data Structures: Lower Mip Level: A 3D texture containing leaf node voxels; for the 2D explanation, a node tile is 5 \times 5 voxels. Upper Mip Level: A 3D texture containing filtered voxels; for the 2D explanation, a node tile is 3 \times 3 voxels. Anisotropic Storage: Each voxel in the upper mip level stores 6 directional values corresponding to positive and negative X, Y, and Z directions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Group Definition: To filter a center voxel (e.g., texel E) in the upper mip level along the +X direction, consider the 9 texels in the lower level that influence it (e.g., texels g, h, i, l, m, n, q, r, s in a 2D projection). Divide these 9 texels into 4 groups based on their Y and Z positions relative to the center. 2. Intra-Group Filtering: For each of the 4 groups, filter along the +X direction by alpha blending the values in the +X direction within the group, then averaging the results to obtain a single group value. 3. Inter-Group Filtering: Compute the final filtered center voxel value by repeating the filtering process for the 4 group values. 4. Boundary Handling (Corner Cases): For corner values in a node tile (e.g., texels a, b, f, g), not all 9 influencing texels are available within the same node tile; some reside in neighbor tiles. Partially compute group values and store them in the 3D texture. Rely on the transfer step (from the cone tracing paper) to complete the calculation. During transfer, some filtered values are computed by alpha blending neighbor group values followed by averaging, while others are computed by averaging first followed by alpha blending. Although these operations are not commutative, this approach reduces the number of dispatch passes with a similar result. 5. Sampling: To sample the anisotropic filtered voxel for a specific direction, use a method similar to ambient cube sampling, requiring 3 texture reads. Formulas: The sampling function computes the output color \mathbf{C} for a direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz) using squared direction components \mathbf{n}^2 = (dx^2, dy^2, dz^2) and six stored directional vectors \mathbf{V}{\pm x}, \mathbf{V}{\pm y}, \mathbf{V}{\pm z}: \mathbf{C} = nx^2 \cdot \mathbf{V}{\text{dir}(dx)} + ny^2 \cdot \mathbf{V}{\text{dir}(dy)} + nz^2 \cdot \mathbf{V}{\text{dir}(dz)} where \text{dir}(di) selects the positive or negative vector based on the sign of di. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleanisotropic(direction, brickvalues): """ Samples the anisotropic filtered voxel for a given direction. brickvalues is a list of 6 tuples (float, float, float) representing: [negx, posx, negy, posy, negz, posz] """ nsquared = (direction[0]2, direction[1]2, direction[2]2) isnegative = (1 if direction[0] < 0.0 else 0, 1 if direction[1] < 0.0 else 0, 1 if direction[2] < 0.0 else 0) valx = brickvalues[isnegative[0]] valy = brickvalues[isnegative[1] + 2] valz = brickvalues[isnegative[2] + 4] return (nsquared[0] valx[0] + nsquared[1] valy[0] + nsquared[2] valz[0], nsquared[0] valx[1] + nsquared[1] valy[1] + nsquared[2] valz[1], nsquared[0] valx[2] + nsquared[1] valy[2] + nsquared[2] valz[2]) Parameters: Tile Size: The example uses a 5 \times 5 lower level to 3 \times 3 upper level reduction in 2D; the 3D case is described as "very similar" but exact dimensions are not specified. Directional Weights: The sampling function uses the squared direction components (n^2) as weights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Access: Corner voxels cannot access all 9 influencing texels locally; partial computation and reliance on the transfer step are required. Non-Commutativity: The order of alpha blending and averaging matters; the method uses a specific order to reduce dispatch passes, which may introduce slight inaccuracies compared to a fully commutative approach. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method reduces the number of dispatch passes required to compute filtered values by partially computing group values and deferring completion to the transfer step. Strengths: Preserves directional lighting information for cone tracing; reduces computational overhead via partial computation and transfer step integration. Limitations: Approximation due to non-commutative operations at boundaries; specific tile dimensions for 3D are not detailed. This method is part of the Voxel Cone Tracing pipeline. It was introduced in the context of implementing voxel cone tracing for global illumination. The filtering pass is a prerequisite for the cone tracing step, ensuring that lighting data is appropriately blurred anisotropically to match the cone tracing kernel. name: Distribution over Levels (MIP-mapping)
head: Octree MIP-map filtering, Three-pass MIP-mapping filtering
body: Distribution over Levels propagates radiance values from leaf nodes to internal nodes of a sparse voxel octree to create a MIP-map pyramid for cone tracing. It distinguishes itself from standard isotropic downsampling by using a three-pass strategy to balance thread cost and explicitly handling shared boundary voxels in a 3 \times 3 \times 3 brick structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse voxel octree with n levels, where leaf nodes contain initial radiance values (e.g., from photon splatting). Output: An octree where internal nodes at levels 1 to n-1 contain filtered radiance values derived from their children. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains a 3 \times 3 \times 3 brick of vertex-centered voxels. Voxel: Stores radiance (energy) and directional information (e.g., Gaussian-Lobes). Multiplicity: Each voxel in a 3 \times 3 \times 3 brick is shared with up to 8 neighboring bricks, requiring inverse multiplicity weighting. Parameters: Kernel: 3 \times 3 \times 3 Gaussian weighting kernel. This is an optimal reconstruction filter. Levels: n-1 filtering steps for an octree of n levels. Steps: 1. Initialization: Build the octree structure and write initial values into leaf nodes. 2. Iterative Filtering: For each level from n-1 down to 1: a. Launch threads to compute filtered values for the current level based on the previous (finer) level. b. Execute three distinct passes to balance thread cost: i. Pass 1 (Center): Compute the center voxel using the 27 involved voxel values from the lower level. ii. Pass 2 (Face Centers): Compute half of the filtered response for the 6 voxels situated in the center of the node's faces, involving 18 voxel values from the lower level. iii. Pass 3 (Corners): Launch threads for the 8 corner voxels, computing a partial filtering from a single octant (9 values). c. Value Transfer: Apply the "Value Transfer to Neighboring Bricks" step to sum partial values across adjacent bricks, finalizing the filtered result. 3. Weighting: When averaging values from the previous level, weight each voxel by the inverse of its multiplicity because boundary voxels reappear in neighboring bricks. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distributeoverlevels(octreelevels): # octreelevels: list of lists, index 0 is leaves, index n-1 is root nlevels = len(octreelevels) # Compute n-1 internal levels from leaves up to root for level in range(1, nlevels): currentnodes = octreelevels[level] # Pass 1: Center voxel (index 1,1,1) for node in currentnodes: sourcevoxels = [v for child in node.children for v in child.voxels] node.voxels[1, 1, 1].value = weightedaverage(sourcevoxels) # Pass 2: Face centers (6 voxels) faceindices = [(1, 1, 0), (1, 1, 2), (1, 0, 1), (1, 2, 1), (0, 1, 1), (2, 1, 1)] for node in currentnodes: for f in faceindices: sourcevoxels = [v for child in node.children for v in child.voxels if not isinoppositeoctant(v, f)] node.voxels[f].value = 0.5 weightedaverage(sourcevoxels) # Pass 3: Corners (8 voxels) cornerindices = [(x, y, z) for x in (0, 2) for y in (0, 2) for z in (0, 2)] for node in currentnodes: for c in cornerindices: childidx = c[0] 4 + c[1] 2 + c[2] sourcevoxels = node.children[childidx].voxels node.voxels[c].value = weightedaverage(sourcevoxels) # Finalize by summing partial values across brick boundaries # Apply Value Transfer to Neighboring Bricks (see parent article) applyvaluetransfer(octreelevels) def weightedaverage(voxels): totalw = 0.0 totalv = 0.0 for v in voxels: w = 1.0 / v.multiplicity totalv += v.value w totalw += w return totalv / totalw def isinoppositeoctant(voxel, faceidx): # Returns True if voxel coordinate is in the octant opposite to the face center # faceidx maps to a normal direction; opposite octant has coordinate 0 if face is at 2, etc. # Simplified coordinate check return False def applyvaluetransfer(octreelevels): # Sums partial values across adjacent bricks to finalize filtering for levelnodes in octreelevels: for node in levelnodes: for v in node.voxels: v.value += sum(n.value for n in v.neighbors) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Octrees: If the octree is sparse, launching threads for all nodes (including empty ones) is inefficient. The method assumes a complete structure for the base algorithm; for sparse structures, thread launch must be optimized (e.g., per light-view-map pixel) to avoid filtering zero values. Shared Voxels: Failure to account for multiplicity (shared boundary voxels) leads to incorrect energy conservation. The Gaussian kernel and inverse multiplicity weighting are critical. A compact representation used to store the filtered distribution of incoming light directions in the octree MIP-map levels. It allows for view-dependent treatment of the Normal Distribution Function (NDF) and Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF). Instead of storing single scalar values, it stores directional distributions, enabling more accurate cone tracing and indirect illumination calculation. Performance: The three-pass approach balances thread cost, ensuring that all threads have roughly the same computational load, which improves GPU scheduling efficiency. Not given in the sources: Time complexity, memory complexity, strengths, limitations, and usage recommendations. The method originates from the work on Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing by Jaroslav Krivánek et al. (2011). The three-pass MIP-mapping strategy was introduced to address the imbalance in thread costs and the redundancy of computing shared boundary voxels multiple times. The Gaussian-Lobes representation was introduced to handle directional lighting data more accurately than scalar values. name: Voxel Child Address Calculation
head: Voxel address_of
body: Calculates the linear index (address) of a specific child octant within a compact block of valid children, based on a validity bitmask. It maps a logical octant index (0–7) to its physical position in a dense array that only stores active children. Inputs: valid: Bitmask where bit i is 1 if child i is active, 0 otherwise. octant: Target child index (0–7). Outputs: address: 0-based index of the target child within the compact array of valid children. Data Structures: valid: Integer type (e.g., uint8t), 8 bits. Steps: 1. Create a mask that isolates all bits lower than the target octant: \text{mask} = \sim(0xFF \ll \text{octant}) This isolates the bits corresponding to children with indices lower than octant. 2. Compute the bitwise AND of valid and mask to isolate valid children preceding the target. 3. Count the number of set bits (population count) in the result to determine the offset. \text{address} = \text{popcount}(\text{valid} \ \& \ \text{mask}) Parameters: octant: Integer, 0–7. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The calculation assumes children are stored in order of their octant index, but only valid children are present in the block; the popcount determines the offset. If octant is not valid (bit is 0 in valid), the result is the index where it would be if it were valid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelchildaddress(valid: int, octant: int) -> int: # Create mask: isolate bits lower than octant # ~0xFF inverts all bits; shifting left moves the zero-bits to the right # Masking with 0xFF ensures 8-bit wrap-around for languages with infinite precision integers mask = (~0xFF << octant) & 0xFF # Count valid children preceding the target return bin(valid & mask).count('1') Counts the number of active children (bits set to 1) in a bitmask that precede a given childindex. Used to map a child index to a compact payload index in sparse octrees. Supports wider nodes (e.g., 0–63 for 64-way). Definition: Maps a logical child index to its rank among valid children. Steps: If childindex <= 0, return 0. Create lowermask = (1 << childindex) - 1. Return popcount(mask & lowermask). Parameters: mask: Bitmask representing occupied children. childindex: Target child index (0–7 for 8-way, 0–63 for wide). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def prefixrank(mask: int, childindex: int) -> int: if childindex <= 0: return 0 lowermask = (1 << childindex) - 1 return bin(mask & lowermask).count('1') Time Complexity: O(1) assuming fixed-width integers and hardware popcount. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Extremely fast, branchless (if popcount is hardware-supported), essential for compact memory layouts. Limitations: Only works for direct child indexing within a single node. When to use: When storing children in a compact array and needing to find the index of a specific child. When not to use: When traversing the tree or locating a node in the tree structure. Originated in implementations of sparse voxel octrees for efficient memory storage and ray traversal. Popularized by libraries like zazen and sparse-voxels for GPU-based volume rendering. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, https://github.com/hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Direction-dependent Morton Order Mapping
head: Direction-dependent Morton Order
body: Direction-dependent Morton Order Mapping is a remapping function that converts a standard Octree Morton code into a sorting key aligned with the near-to-far rendering order for a specific ray direction. It solves the problem of correct occlusion culling and blending order in sparse voxel rasterization by ensuring that voxels are processed from closest to furthest relative to the camera, regardless of the viewing angle. Unlike Point Location which determines spatial containment, or Fast Projection for Octree Nodes which estimates bounding volumes, this method specifically addresses the topological sorting requirement for volume rendering by adapting the Morton space-filling curve to the ray's sign vector. The method maps the 3-bit octant index at each level of the Octree Morton code to a permuted index based on the signs of the ray direction components. This ensures that the resulting integer key preserves the near-to-far order for all rays sharing the same sign pattern. Inputs and Outputs: Input: octpath, the Octree Morton code of a voxel (integer). Input: rd, the ray direction vector \mathbf{r}d = (rx, ry, rz). Output: order, the direction-dependent Morton order integer. Data Structures: ordertables: A lookup table of size 8 \times 8. It contains eight permutations of the integers 0 to 7. Each row corresponds to one of the eight possible ray sign bit patterns. signbits: An integer from 0 to 7 representing the signs of the ray direction components. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Compute Ray Sign Bits: Determine the sign bits k from the ray direction \mathbf{r}d. The bits are assigned such that the x-component corresponds to the most significant bit of the triplet, y to the middle, and z to the least significant: \text{signbits} = 4 \cdot (rx < 0) + 2 \cdot (ry < 0) + 1 \cdot (rz < 0) where (ri < 0) evaluates to 1 if true and 0 if false. 2. Initialize Output: Set order to 0. 3. Iterate Over Octree Levels: For each level i from 0 to \text{MAX\NUM\LEVELS} - 1: a. Extract the lowest 3 bits of the current octpath: \text{octant} = \text{octpath} \ \& \ 0\text{b}111 b. Look up the mapped value from the permutation table corresponding to signbits: \text{mapped\octant} = \text{order\tables}[\text{signbits}][\text{octant}] c. Shift the mapped value to its correct position in the output order (3 bits per level) and OR it into order: \text{order} = \text{order} \ | \ (\text{mapped\octant} \ll (3 \cdot i)) d. Right-shift octpath by 3 bits to process the next level: \text{octpath} = \text{octpath} \gg 3 4. Return Result: Return order. Formula: The mapping function f^{(k)}: [0 \dots 7] \to [0 \dots 7] is one of eight permutation mappings applied to each triplet of bits (bx by bz) from the Octree Morton code. The full remapping for a code with bits \dots bx by bz \ ax ay az is: \dots bx by bz \ ax ay az \mapsto \dots f^{(k)}(bx by bz) \ f^{(k)}(ax ay az) where k is determined by the ray direction signs. Parameters: MAXNUMLEVELS: The maximum depth of the Octree. Not given in the sources. ordertables: Hard-coded permutations. For the (+, +, +) ray direction (signbits=0), the identity permutation [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] is used. The other seven permutations are derived to maintain near-to-far order for the respective sign combinations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The Morton code can grow large with deep trees. Ensure the integer type used for order has sufficient bits to hold the result (3 bits per level). Optimization: In practice, the mapping from Octree Morton code to direction-dependent Morton order can be optimized to a single bitwise XOR operation instead of a loop. Degenerate Input: Ray directions with zero components are undefined for sign bits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tordsignbits(rd): """ Compute ray sign bits from ray direction. Input: rd - Ray direction vector (x, y, z) Output: signbits - Integer 0-7 representing signs """ signbits = 4 (1 if rd[0] < 0 else 0) + \ 2 (1 if rd[1] < 0 else 0) + \ 1 (1 if rd[2] < 0 else 0) return signbits def todirdepmortonorder(octpath, signbits, MAXNUMLEVELS, ordertables): """ Map Octree Morton code to direction-dependent Morton order. Input: octpath - Voxel Octree Morton code signbits - The signbits the voxel cares about MAXNUMLEVELS - Maximum number of Octree levels ordertables - 8x8 lookup table of permutations Output: order - The order for sorting """ table = ordertables[signbits] order = 0 for i in range(MAXNUMLEVELS): # Extract lowest 3 bits octant = octpath & 0b111 # Look up mapped value mappedoctant = table[octant] # Shift and OR into order order |= mappedoctant << (3 i) # Shift octpath for next level octpath = octpath >> 3 return order This method sorts sparse voxels into a near-to-far order for each image tile by replacing primitive z-depth with a direction-dependent Morton order, ensuring correct rendering order for all ray directions. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting which duplicates primitives per tile and sorts by z-depth, this technique duplicates voxels per ray sign bit pattern and sorts by Morton order to handle arbitrary viewing angles without popping artifacts. A proof by induction that the direction-dependent Morton order aligns with the near-to-far rendering order for all rays with (+, +, +) direction signs, generalizable to other signs by flipping the scene. Base case (\ell=1): For the first Octree level, the direction-dependent Morton order of the eight voxels for (+, +, +) rays is correct because the most significant bit corresponds to x, then y, then z, matching the ray direction. Induction hypothesis: Assume S(\ell) is true for some positive integer \ell, meaning direction-dependent Morton order is correct for all sparse voxel sets in V\ell. Induction step: For V{\ell+1}, voxels in V\ell evolve by subdividing some voxels and removing others. Subdivision appends three zero bits to the least significant bit, preserving order. Subdivided voxels share the same most significant 3\ell bits, and their 8 children follow the base case Morton order, preserving relative order. Removing voxels does not affect remaining order. Time Complexity: O(L) per voxel, where L is the number of Octree levels. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the mapping function itself, plus O(1) for the fixed 8 \times 8 lookup table. Measured Performance: The method is extremely fast, often optimized to a single XOR operation in practice, making it negligible compared to the cost of ray traversal or voxel shading. Strengths: Guarantees correct occlusion order for all viewing angles without expensive depth sorting or z-buffering during the initial sort phase. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of sign bits per ray or tile. The sorting key is only valid for the specific ray direction used to compute it; a different ray direction requires a different sort order. When to use: When rendering sparse voxel representations (e.g., Radiance Fields) where correct front-to-back blending is critical and the number of voxels is large. When not to use: For simple opaque geometry where z-buffering is sufficient, or when ray directions are static and can be pre-sorted by standard depth. The method originates from the work on Sparse Voxels Rasterization for real-time high-fidelity Radiance Field rendering. It addresses the limitation of standard Morton ordering, which assumes a fixed viewing direction (typically +,+,+), by generalizing the space-filling curve permutation to eight possible octants defined by ray direction signs. The correctness of the ordering is proven by induction on the Octree level, showing that the base case (\ell=1) aligns with the ray direction and that subdivision preserves this order. Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01509, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Direction-dependent Morton Order Sorting
head: Ray sign bit sorting, Sparse Voxel Rasterization Sorting
body: This method sorts sparse voxels into a near-to-far order for each image tile by replacing primitive z-depth with a direction-dependent Morton order, ensuring correct rendering order for all ray directions. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting which duplicates primitives per tile and sorts by z-depth, this technique duplicates voxels per ray sign bit pattern and sorts by Morton order to handle arbitrary viewing angles without popping artifacts. Inputs: A list of voxels, each with an Octree Morton code (octpath) and a unique 1D array index (voxelid). Ray directions (rd) for the current frame or tile. Outputs: A sorted list of key-value pairs ready for rasterization. Data Structures: The sorting key-value pair is packed into 64-bit and 32-bit unsigned integers respectively: Key (64-bit): Upper 16 bits: Tile ID. Lower 48 bits: Direction-dependent Morton order (3L = 48 bits, where L=16). Value (32-bit): Upper 3 bits: Ray sign bits. Lower 29 bits: Voxel ID. Parameters: L=16: Maximum number of Octree levels. Maximum tiles: 2^{16} = 65,536. Maximum image resolution: 4096 \times 4096 with 16 \times 16 tile size. Maximum grid resolution: (2^{16})^3 = 65,536^3. Maximum voxels: 2^{29} \approx 500 million. Steps: 1. Compute Ray Sign Bits: For each ray direction \mathbf{rd} = (rdx, rdy, rdz), compute the 3-bit sign mask: \text{signbits} = 4 \cdot (rdx < 0) + 2 \cdot (rdy < 0) + (rdz < 0) 2. Compute Direction-Dependent Morton Order: For each voxel with Octree Morton code octpath and a specific signbits pattern, remap the Morton code using a lookup table ordertables indexed by signbits. The table permutes the 3-bit child indices at each level to align with the near-to-far order for that ray direction. \text{order} = \sum{i=0}^{L-1} \text{order\tables}[\text{signbits}][\text{octpath} \ \& \ 0\text{b}111] \ll 3i 3. Duplicate Voxels: Duplicate each voxel for each distinct ray sign bit pattern it covers. Attach the corresponding signbits to each duplicate. 4. Sort: Sort the list of key-value pairs using a GPU Radix sort (or similar) based on the key, ordering by Tile ID first, then by Morton order (near-to-far). 5. Render: For each pixel, iterate through voxels belonging to its tile and composite only those with matching attached ray sign bits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MAXNUMLEVELS = 16 ordertables = [ [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], [1, 0, 3, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6], [2, 3, 0, 1, 6, 7, 4, 5], [3, 2, 1, 0, 7, 6, 5, 4], [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2, 3], [5, 4, 7, 6, 1, 0, 3, 2], [6, 7, 4, 5, 2, 3, 0, 1], [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0] ] def computesignbits(rd): return 4 (rd[0] < 0) + 2 (rd[1] < 0) + (rd[2] < 0) def computedirdepmortonorder(octpath, signbits): table = ordertables[signbits] order = 0 for i in range(MAXNUMLEVELS): order |= table[octpath & 0b111] << (3 i) octpath = octpath >> 3 return order Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The voxelid in the value field must be the 1D array index where the voxel is stored, not the 3D grid (i, j, k) index. The maximum number of voxels is limited to 2^{29} due to the 29-bit field in the value. If the grid resolution exceeds 65,536^3, custom data types with extra bits are required for the GPU Radix sort. Time Complexity: Sorting complexity depends on the number of duplicated voxels. With up to 2^{29} voxels and 65,536 tiles, the sort is performed on a large list of key-value pairs. Memory Complexity: Requires storing duplicated voxels. Each voxel is duplicated for each ray sign bit pattern it covers, increasing memory usage compared to non-duplicated approaches. Strengths: Ensures correct near-to-far rendering order for all ray directions, eliminating popping artifacts common in z-depth sorting for arbitrary viewpoints. Limitations: Increased memory footprint due to voxel duplication; limited by 64-bit key and 32-bit value constraints unless custom types are used. When to use: When rendering sparse voxel grids with arbitrary camera orientations where z-depth sorting fails to maintain correct occlusion order. This method is part of the Sparse Voxels Rasterization pipeline, introduced in "Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering". It addresses the limitations of 3D Gaussian Splatting's z-depth sorting, which can cause artifacts when rays are not aligned with the principal axis. The technique builds on Direction-dependent Morton Order Mapping to remap Octree codes based on ray direction signs. name: Octree Neighbor Finding
head: GetNeighbors, Neighbor Retrieval, forward neighbor retrieval
body: Octree Neighbor Finding determines the adjacent leaf nodes in six cardinal directions (±X, ±Y, ±Z) for a given node in a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO). It solves the problem of traversing between non-contiguous or differently-sized nodes during ray casting or pathfinding by locating the nearest shared ancestor and performing point location to retrieve the neighbor. Inputs: currentnode: The index of the starting leaf node. direction: A vector specifying the target direction (e.g., +X, -Y). parenttrace: An array containing the indices of all parent nodes from the root to currentnode, provided by the ray traversal algorithm. depth: The depth level of currentnode. Outputs: neighborindex: The index of the adjacent leaf node, or a sentinel value (INDEXNONE) if no neighbor exists in that direction. Data Structures: Node Struct: Contains depth (7 bits), isleaf (1 bit), position (3 floats), and size (1 float). Parent Trace Array: trace[] stores the indices of parent nodes for the current ray cap, allowing upward traversal without storing explicit parent pointers in the node structure. Algorithm Steps: 1. Validation: Verify currentnode is a leaf. If not, return immediately. 2. Target Position Calculation: Compute the position just outside the current node in the specified direction by moving slightly farther than HalfSize. 3. Upward Traversal (Find Common Ancestor): Iterate up the tree using parenttrace from the origin node's parent depth down to 0. At each level, check if the target position falls within the spatial bounds of the parent node using &-masking of the origin and destination coordinates with the corresponding depth bit, followed by integer equality. 4. Point Location: Once the common ancestor is found, perform a standard point-location search from the common ancestor to the targetpos to find the leaf at the destination. 5. Neighbor Collection: If the search lands on a leaf node, return it. If the search lands on an internal node, the neighbor is one of its children. To find the specific child adjacent to the current node, use AxisMask and AxisBit to filter by the target axis and collect the four face children. Limit the search depth to the current node's depth to ensure only adjacent leaves of equal or larger size are collected, avoiding all descendants. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. INDEXNONE = -1 def getneighbor(originidx, direction, parenttrace, nodedata, maxdepth): # 1. Validation: Verify currentnode is a leaf if not (nodedata[originidx] & 0x80): return INDEXNONE originpos = nodedata[originidx].position originsize = nodedata[originidx].size origindepth = nodedata[originidx].depth # 2. Target position: move slightly farther than HalfSize in direction targetpos = originpos + direction (originsize 0.5 + 1e-6) # 3. Upward Traversal: Find common ancestor # Begin at the depth of the origin node's parent commonancestoridx = parenttrace[origindepth - 1] if origindepth > 0 else 0 for d in range(origindepth - 1, -1, -1): depthbit = 1 << (maxdepth - d) if ((targetpos.x & depthbit) == (originpos.x & depthbit)) and \ ((targetpos.y & depthbit) == (originpos.y & depthbit)) and \ ((targetpos.z & depthbit) == (originpos.z & depthbit)): commonancestoridx = parenttrace[d] break # 4. Point Location: Find leaf at destination from common ancestor neighboridx = commonancestoridx startdepth = nodedata[commonancestoridx].depth for d in range(maxdepth - startdepth, -1, -1): shift = d childidx = ((targetpos.x >> shift) & 1) | \ (((targetpos.y >> shift) & 1) << 1) | \ (((targetpos.z >> shift) & 1) << 2) neighboridx = nodedata[neighboridx].children[childidx] if neighboridx == INDEXNONE or (nodedata[neighboridx] & 0x80): break # 5. Neighbor Collection: Handle results if neighboridx != INDEXNONE and (nodedata[neighboridx] & 0x80): # Neighbor is internal. Compute 4 face child indices using AxisMask and AxisBit axismask = 0 if direction.x != 0: axismask = 1 elif direction.y != 0: axismask = 2 else: axismask = 4 # AxisBit: returns AxisMask if Side is -1, returns 0 if Side is +1 side = -1 if (direction.x < 0 or direction.y < 0 or direction.z < 0) else 1 axisbit = axismask if side == -1 else 0 # Filter children on the specific directional face facechildren = [] for c in range(8): if (c & axisbit) == axisbit: facechildren.append(c) # Traverse down to leaf level, collecting only adjacent leaves for c in facechildren: childidx = nodedata[neighboridx].children[c] if childidx == INDEXNONE: continue if nodedata[childidx] & 0x80: return childidx neighboridx = childidx return neighboridx Parameters: AxisMask: Bit mask for axis direction. X returns 001, Y returns 010, Z returns 100. AxisBit: Returns AxisMask if Side is -1, returns 0 if Side is +1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Leaf Input: The algorithm must validate that the input node is a leaf; otherwise, it returns immediately. Depth Limiting: The search must stop at a leaf or when the depth matches the current node's depth to avoid collecting all descendants of a neighbor. Memory Footprint: Parent pointers are omitted from nodes to save memory; the parenttrace array must be maintained by the caller (ray traversal). Optimization: Use static polymorphism via templates for each X, Y, Z dimension to perform only one or two equality tests per iteration. Determines the next cell in a hierarchical spatial structure by backtracing from a start coordinate to the common ancestor with a destination coordinate, then performing point location. It differs from Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration by relying on explicit parent-pointer traversal and coordinate bit-masking rather than Morton key arithmetic. Identifies and processes the eight corner vertices of leaf nodes in a sparse voxel octree by leveraging the spatial locality of Morton (Z-order) keys. It solves the dual-grid traversal problem by operating on a pre-computed or iterated list of vertex keys, using bitwise arithmetic to resolve adjacency and handle level mismatches without tree traversal recursion. Time Complexity: O(D) where D is the depth of the octree, due to the upward traversal and subsequent point location. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per neighbor query, assuming the parenttrace array is provided by the traversal context. Strengths: Efficient for sparse structures where explicit parent pointers are too costly; works with arbitrary node sizes. Limitations: Requires the parenttrace array to be maintained by the caller. When to Use: When memory footprint is critical (no parent pointers in nodes) or when traversing non-contiguous nodes in an SVO. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The authors rejected Frisken and Perry's exclusive "or" method for immediate neighbors because it was no cheaper than &-masking both source and destination and performing integer equality on the results. To minimize memory footprint, parent pointers were omitted from octree nodes, requiring the ray traversal algorithm to fill an index trace array containing the indices of all parent nodes for a given cap. name: Neighbor Finding
head: Octree Hashing (Neighbor-Finding)
body: Neighbor finding determines the next cell in a hierarchical spatial structure (octree) intersected by a ray by backtracing from a start coordinate to the common ancestor with a destination coordinate, then performing point location to retrieve the neighbor. It differs from sibling methods like Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration by relying on explicit parent-pointer traversal and coordinate bit-masking rather than Morton key arithmetic. The method consists of a single backtracing phase that locates the common ancestor of two coordinates, followed by a point location step to retrieve the target cell. Inputs: start: The integer coordinates of the current cell (Vec3i). dest: The integer coordinates of the destination cell (Vec3i). depth: The octree depth of the start cell. parenttrace: An array of node indices or pointers storing the path from the root to the start node. childbitdepth: A precomputed array where childbitdepth[up] holds the bit mask for subdivision level up. Outputs: The index or pointer to the neighbor cell containing the dest coordinate. parenttrace: An array where parenttrace[up] holds the node index at depth up on the path from the root to the start node. childbitdepth: A precomputed array mapping each octree level to a bitmask used to isolate the child index at that level. 1. Iterate up from depth down to 0. 2. Retrieve the bit mask for the current level: childbit = childbitdepth[up]. 3. Check if start and dest fall into the same child node at this level by comparing their masked bits: (dest.x \ \& \ child\bit) == (start.x \ \& \ child\bit) \ \&\& \ (dest.y \ \& \ child\bit) == (start.y \ \& \ child\bit) \ \&\& \ (dest.z \ \& \ child\bit) == (start.z \ \& \ child\bit) 4. If the bits match, the common ancestor is found at parenttrace[up]. Call pointlocate(dest, up, parenttrace[up]) to find the specific neighbor and return it. 5. If the loop completes without returning, the root node is the common ancestor. Check if start and dest match at the root level using the childbit value from the final iteration. If they match, call pointlocate(dest, 0, 0) and return the result. 6. If no match is found, return 0. The following pseudocode implements the backtracing neighbor finding algorithm. pointlocate is implemented as a standard octree descent routine. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neighborfind(start: Vec3i, dest: Vec3i, depth: int, parenttrace: List[int], childbitdepth: List[int]) -> int: """ Finds the neighbor cell containing 'dest' starting from 'start'. Uses parenttrace to backtrack to the common ancestor. """ # Iterate from current depth down to 0 for up in range(depth, -1, -1): childbit = childbitdepth[up] # Check if start and dest share the same parent at this level if ((dest.x & childbit) == (start.x & childbit) and (dest.y & childbit) == (start.y & childbit) and (dest.z & childbit) == (start.z & childbit)): # Found common ancestor at parenttrace[up] return pointlocate(dest, up, parenttrace[up]) # Root node check (matches source structure; reuses childbit from up=0 iteration) if ((dest.x & childbit) == (start.x & childbit) and (dest.y & childbit) == (start.y & childbit) and (dest.z & childbit) == (start.z & childbit)): return pointlocate(dest, 0, 0) return 0 # Not found def pointlocate(dest: Vec3i, depth: int, startnode: int) -> int: """ Standard octree descent to find the leaf/child containing dest. Assumes a flat array 'nodes' where nodes[i].children[childidx] gives the next node. """ current = startnode for d in range(depth, -1, -1): # Extract child index from dest coordinates at level d childidx = ((dest.x >> d) & 1) << 2 | ((dest.y >> d) & 1) << 1 | ((dest.z >> d) & 1) current = nodes[current].children[childidx] return current Root Level Handling: The source code explicitly checks the root level again after the loop completes, likely to ensure the root-level bit comparison is evaluated with a valid childbit value. Coordinate Scaling: The bit-masking logic assumes start and dest coordinates are scaled consistently with the childbitdepth masks. Missing Nodes: If dest lies outside the octree bounds or in an unallocated region, pointlocate must handle null pointers or return a sentinel value. A ray tracing algorithm for hierarchical spatial structures that determines the next intersected cell by calculating a point guaranteed to lie inside it, rather than computing a direction vector. Choose this variant when geometric projection is preferred over hierarchical backtracing. Time Complexity: O(D) for the backtracing phase and O(D) for the pointlocate phase, where D is the octree depth. Memory Complexity: O(D) for the parenttrace array. Strengths: Efficient for sparse octrees requiring deep traversal. Limitations: Requires maintaining parenttrace pointers throughout traversal; performance degrades if pointlocate encounters invalid or unallocated nodes. The neighbor-finding algorithm was developed for ray tracing with hierarchical spatial structures. It is used in interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The method relies on a parent trace array to navigate the octree hierarchy without storing full parent pointers in every node. name: Wyvill and Kunii's Ray Tracing / Neighbor Finding Algorithm
head: Rational t-value Neighbor Finding, Wyvill-Kunii Neighbor Finding
body: Wyvill and Kunii's algorithm is a ray-tracing method for hierarchical spatial structures (quadtrees and octrees) that determines the next intersected cell by calculating a specific point guaranteed to lie inside that cell, rather than computing a direction vector. It differs from sibling methods like the standard RAYTRACER by using a rational t-value approach to locate the exit point directly, bypassing explicit direction vector calculation. Inputs: Geometric parameters for each axis I \in \{X, Y, Z\}: B[I] (base coordinate), M[I] (cell size), W\B[I] (width/boundary offset), CORNER[I] (corner coordinate), and SIGN\M[I] (motion sign, 0 or 1). Outputs: POINT[I]: The coordinates of a point inside the next intersected cell. The identity of the next cell, determined by locating POINT using a spatial search procedure analogous to FIND3DBLOCK. Data Structures: NUM and DEN: Dictionaries mapping \{X, Y, Z\} to floating-point numerators and denominators for the rational t-values. POINT: An array or dictionary of floating-point coordinates for the exit point. Lookup tables (required for context in related neighbor finding routines): EDGFDIR: Maps normal plane and signs to edge direction E. VERTEXDIR: Maps signs to vertex direction V (e.g., LDB, RUF). CHANGE: Maps direction vectors to 3D components. Steps: 1. Initialize Rational T-Values: For each coordinate I \in \{X, Y, Z\}, compute the numerator and denominator of the exit t-value T[I]: NUM[I] = CORNER[I] - SIGN\M[I] \cdot W\B[I] - SIGN\M[I] DEN[I] = M[I] 2. Find Minimum Axis: Identify the axis K corresponding to the minimum t-value by initializing K = X and comparing T[K] against T[Y] and T[Z] using cross-multiplication to avoid division: python if abs(NUM[K] DEN[I]) > abs(NUM[I] DEN[K]): K = I 3. Compute Next Cell Point: Calculate the coordinates of the point POINT using the minimum t-value T[K] for all axes: POINT[I] = M[I] \cdot \frac{NUM[K]}{DEN[K]} + B[I] \quad \text{for all } I \in \{X, Y, Z\} 4. Locate Next Cell: Use a spatial search procedure (analogous to FIND3DBLOCK) to identify the cell containing POINT. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def wyvillkuniinextcell(B, M, WB, CORNER, SIGNM): """ B: dict/array [X, Y, Z] base coordinates M: dict/array [X, Y, Z] cell sizes WB: dict/array [X, Y, Z] width/boundary offsets CORNER: dict/array [X, Y, Z] corner coordinates SIGNM: dict/array [X, Y, Z] motion signs (0 or 1) Returns: POINT dict/array [X, Y, Z] """ # Step 1: Initialize rational t-values NUM = {} DEN = {} for I in ['X', 'Y', 'Z']: NUM[I] = CORNER[I] - SIGNM[I] WB[I] - SIGNM[I] DEN[I] = M[I] # Step 2: Find axis K with minimum t-value K = 'X' for I in ['Y', 'Z']: # Compare T[K] < T[I] using cross-multiplication with absolute values if abs(NUM[K] DEN[I]) > abs(NUM[I] DEN[K]): K = I # Step 3: Compute POINT using the minimum t-value T[K] POINT = {} for I in ['X', 'Y', 'Z']: tval = NUM[K] / DEN[K] POINT[I] = M[I] tval + B[I] return POINT Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner Passing: If a ray passes through a cell corner (e.g., SW corner of cell 5 to cell 11), applying a 2D block finder to (ax-1, ay) may report a false intersection if cell 4 is fully occupied, whereas (ax, ay-1) avoids it. Subdivision Errors: If a cell (e.g., cell 3) is subdivided like the SE quadrant of a quadtree, the algorithm may compute an incorrect point (e.g., (12, 16) instead of (12, 15)), routing to the wrong cell (cell 10 instead of cell 3). Fix Limitations: Removing the subtraction of SIGN\M[I] from the numerator does not always fix the error, as decomposing motion into separate directions can still cause false intersections due to distinct entry/exit conventions. Simultaneous Boundaries: Wyvill and Kunii claim that when a ray reaches multiple boundaries simultaneously, arbitrarily picking one boundary perpendicular to motion is sufficient, but this claim is shown to be incorrect for certain subdivisions. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simpler structure than neighbor-finding algorithms that compute exact direction vectors, and it avoids explicit direction vector calculation. Limitations: Prone to errors in specific hierarchical subdivisions (e.g., SE quadrant subdivisions) and corner cases, and the claim of robustness for simultaneous boundary crossings is incorrect. The algorithm was proposed by Wyvill and Kunii. It is discussed in the context of implementing ray tracing with octrees and neighbor finding, where it is compared against a more robust RAYTRACER algorithm.
