name: Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration
head: Vertex Neighbor Iteration via Morton Keys
body:
Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration identifies and processes the eight corner vertices of leaf nodes in a sparse voxel octree by leveraging the spatial locality of Morton (Z-order) keys. It solves the dual-grid traversal problem, ensuring each shared vertex is processed exactly once across up to eight adjacent leaf nodes. It differs from standard recursive neighbor finding by operating on a pre-computed list of vertex keys and using bitwise arithmetic to resolve adjacency and level mismatches without recursive tree traversal. Inputs: A sparse voxel octree implementation providing nodeexists(key), issubdivided(key), and parent() operations. An array of vertexkeys containing MortonKey values for the eight vertices of a leaf node, with invalid vertices marked as MortonKey::none(). The target level of the leaf node (vertexlv). Outputs: An array of eight resolved neighbor keys for the valid vertices of the leaf, where each entry is either a valid MortonKey of an existing node at the same level (or an ancestor if the direct neighbor is missing) or MortonKey::none(). MortonKey: A struct wrapping a u64 integer that represents a single node in a hashed octree. Its internal representation starts with 1 for the root node and appends three bits per level for the child index along the X, Y, and Z axes. MortonKey::none() returns Self(0) and MortonKey::root() returns Self(1). HashedOctree: A concurrent hash map-based storage for the octree values. Defined as pub struct HashedOctree<T: Copy> { values: DashMap<MortonKey, T, RandomState>, }. OctreeIndex: Bitflags for child indices where RIGHT = 1 << 0, TOP = 1 << 1, and FOREMOST = 1 << 2. The method relies on three 64-bit dilation constants to perform bitwise arithmetic on Morton keys. These constants have bits set at positions corresponding to the X, Y, and Z axes in the Morton interleaving. DILX = 0b001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001u64. DILY = 0b010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010u64. DILZ = 0b100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100u64. The core of the method uses dilated integer addition and dilated integer subtraction to move along grid axes in Morton space using standard integer arithmetic masked by the dilation constants. 1. Dilated Integer Addition (computes vertex keys from a leaf key): vertex\key = \left( (key.0 \mid 
eg DIL\X) + (vertex\i \ \& \ DIL\X) ight) \ \& \ DIL\X \ \mid \ \left( (key.0 \mid 
eg DIL\Y) + (vertex\i \ \& \ DIL\Y) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Y \ \mid \ \left( (key.0 \mid 
eg DIL\Z) + (vertex\i \ \& \ DIL\Z) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Z Where key.0 is the Morton key of the leaf node, vertex\i is the vertex index (0–7), \mid is bitwise OR, 
eg is bitwise NOT, \& is bitwise AND, and + is integer addition. 2. Dilated Integer Subtraction (computes neighbor leaf keys from a vertex key): key{node\i} = \left( (dc \ \& \ DIL\X) - (node\i \ \& \ DIL\X) ight) \ \& \ DIL\X \ \mid \ \left( (dc \ \& \ DIL\Y) - (node\i \ \& \ DIL\Y) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Y \ \mid \ \left( (dc \ \& \ DIL\Z) - (node\i \ \& \ DIL\Z) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Z Where dc is the dilated coordinate of the vertex computed as vertex\k.0 \ll (vertex\lv - vertex\k.level()) 	imes 3, and node\i is the neighbor index (0–7). The method processes a list of vertex keys to find unique neighbors. 1. Iterate Vertices: Enumerate over the vertexkeys array and stop when vertexk equals MortonKey::none(). Let the current index be vertexi and the key be vertexk. 2. Compute Neighbor Candidates: Call vert2leaf(vertexk, vertexlv) to obtain an array neighbours of eight candidate MortonKey values for the adjacent nodes. 3. Filter Neighbors: For each neighbor index neighbouri from 0 to 7: skip if neighbouri == vertexi (the node itself). Let neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri]. If !octree.nodeexists(neighbourk), continue to the next neighbor. If octree.issubdivided(neighbourk) (the neighbor is deeper than the current leaf), mark the entire vertex as skipped because the deeper node will process the shared vertex. If neighbouri < vertexi, mark the entire vertex as skipped to ensure shared vertices between same-level nodes are processed exactly once based on fixed indices rather than iteration order. 4. Resolve Keys: If the vertex passes the filter, initialize an array keys: [MortonKey; 8]. For each neighbouri from 0 to 7, let neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri]. While neighbourk != MortonKey::none() AND !octree.nodeexists(neighbourk), set neighbourk = neighbourk.parent(). Store the resolved neighbourk in keys[neighbouri]. Return keys. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. DILX = 0b001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001 DILY = 0b010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010 DILZ = 0b100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100 class MortonKey: def init(self, val: int): self.0 = val @staticmethod def none(): return MortonKey(0) @staticmethod def root(): return MortonKey(1) def level(self) -> int: if self.0 == 0: raise ValueError("Cannot get level of none key") return (63 - self.0.bitlength() + 1) // 3 def parent(self) -> 'MortonKey': return MortonKey(self.0 >> 3) def leaf2vert(key: MortonKey) -> tuple[int, list[MortonKey]]: level = key.level() levelkey = 1 << (3 level) keys = [None] 8 for vertexi in range(8): vertexkey = ( ((key.0 | ~DILX) + (vertexi & DILX)) & DILX | ((key.0 | ~DILY) + (vertexi & DILY)) & DILY | ((key.0 | ~DILZ) + (vertexi & DILZ)) & DILZ) if (vertexkey >= (levelkey << 1)) or \ ((vertexkey - levelkey) & DILX) == 0 or \ ((vertexkey - levelkey) & DILY) == 0 or \ ((vertexkey - levelkey) & DILZ) == 0: keys[vertexi] = MortonKey.none() else: keys[vertexi] = MortonKey(vertexkey) return level, keys def vert2leaf(vertexk: MortonKey, vertexlv: int) -> list[MortonKey]: dc = vertexk.0 << ((vertexlv - vertexk.level()) 3) keys = [None] 8 for nodei in range(8): keys[nodei] = MortonKey( ((dc & DILX) - (nodei & DILX)) & DILX | ((dc & DILY) - (nodei & DILY)) & DILY | ((dc & DILZ) - (nodei & DILZ)) & DILZ) return keys def processvertexneighbors(vertexkeys: list[MortonKey], octree) -> list[list[MortonKey]]: results = [] for vertexi, vertexk in enumerate(vertexkeys): if vertexk == MortonKey.none(): break neighbours = vert2leaf(vertexk, vertexk.level()) shouldprocess = True for neighbouri in range(8): if neighbouri == vertexi: continue neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri] if not octree.nodeexists(neighbourk): continue if octree.issubdivided(neighbourk): shouldprocess = False break if neighbouri < vertexi: shouldprocess = False break if not shouldprocess: continue keys = [None] 8 for neighbouri in range(8): neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri] while neighbourk != MortonKey.none() and not octree.nodeexists(neighbourk): neighbourk = neighbourk.parent() keys[neighbouri] = neighbourk results.append(keys) return results Invalid Vertex Keys: A vertex key is invalid if it falls outside the level's range (vertexkey >= levelkey << 1) or if any dilated axis difference is zero. These invalid cases return MortonKey::none(). Concurrency: When using HashedOctree (backed by DashMap), concurrent access may deadlock if a mutable reference is held while calling value(). Tie-Breaking: The condition neighbouri < vertexi ensures that shared vertices between nodes of the same level are processed only once, relying on fixed neighbor and vertex indices rather than iteration order. Time Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of valid vertices, with constant-time bitwise operations per vertex and a bounded parent-traversal loop. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per vertex for storing eight keys, with external octree storage. Strengths: Avoids recursive tree traversal for neighbor finding and uses fast bitwise arithmetic, making it efficient for sparse grids where many neighbors are missing. Limitations: Requires pre-computed or easily derivable vertex keys and relies on the octree implementation providing efficient nodeexists and issubdivided checks. The method is described in the dmc (Dense Marching Cuber) project by aleokdev. It is used for dual-grid traversal in volume rendering, specifically for extracting isosurfaces from sparse voxel octrees. The approach leverages the properties of Morton keys to map spatial adjacency to arithmetic operations. aleokdev/dmc, https://github.com/aleokdev/dmc, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Traversal of Octree Nodes
head: Child Octant Traversal, Interior Node Traversal, Mid-plane Intersection Traversal, Octree Node Traversal Order, Octree Traversal (OT), Octree Traversal with Mid-Plane Sorting, e-space coordinate traversal
body:
This method determines the exact sequential order in which a ray intersects the eight child octants of an interior octree node by computing and sorting the ray's intersection distances with the X, Y, and Z mid-planes of the current node. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing hierarchical sparse voxel structures without pointer chasing or stack overhead for descent, by replacing recursive descent with a deterministic, sorted march through children. Unlike Stack-based Octree Traversal with Direction Flipping which uses explicit stacks, or IEEE-754 Bit Manipulation Octree Traversal which uses bit-level arithmetic, this method relies on geometric mid-plane sorting. It is particularly effective in Octree Traversal contexts where empty space skipping is utilized, as it allows the solver to start at the node border and skip nodes that do not contain the isosurface. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized or unnormalized, consistent with t parameterization). Current octree node defined by its depth L and node index I. Global octree structure allowing retrieval of node bounding box or spatial extent. Entry parameter t{enter} and exit parameter t{exit} for the current node (initially computed for the root node via a box test). Outputs: A sequence of child octant indices (0–7) to visit, in the exact order the ray intersects them. For each child, the entry and exit t values within that child's bounds. Data Structures: axisisects[]: An array used to store sorted t{center} intersection distances for sequential marching. axisbit: A bitmask (integer) representing the current child octant index. midplanecoords: Temporary storage for the e-space coordinates of the mid-planes. Definitions: e-space: The coordinate system of the octree node's local space, where the node spans [0, 1]^3 or a similar unit cube. The sources refer to "octree-space coordinates". We assume the node bounds are known. Let the node's bounding box in world space be [x{min}, x{max}] 	imes [y{min}, y{max}] 	imes [z{min}, z{max}]. Mid-planes: The planes x = x{mid}, y = y{mid}, z = z{mid} that divide the current node into 8 equal child octants, where x{mid} = (x{min} + x{max})/2, etc. penter: The point on the ray at t{enter}, i.e., \mathbf{p}{enter} = \mathbf{o} + t{enter} \mathbf{d}. tcenter: The t parameter where the ray intersects the mid-plane. Algorithm Steps: 1. Retrieve Node Bounds: Retrieve the octree node given by depth and node index, then compute its octree-space coordinates of the mid-planes. 2. Compute Mid-Plane Coordinates: Calculate the coordinates of the three mid-planes dividing the node: x{mid} =  rac{x{min} + x{max}}{2} y{mid} =  rac{y{min} + y{max}}{2} z{mid} =  rac{z{min} + z{max}}{2} 3. Compute Mid-Plane Intersections: Calculate the t parameter where the ray intersects each mid-plane. For a plane with normal \mathbf{n} and distance d from origin (or simply solving x(t) = x{mid}): t{x} =  rac{x{mid} - ox}{dx} \quad 	ext{if } dx 
eq 0 t{y} =  rac{y{mid} - oy}{dy} \quad 	ext{if } dy 
eq 0 t{z} =  rac{z{mid} - oz}{dz} \quad 	ext{if } dz 
eq 0 If di = 0, the ray is parallel to the mid-plane; handle as a special case (e.g., t = \infty or skip, depending on direction). 4. Sort Intersections: Store these t values in axisisects[] and sort them in ascending order. This sorted array determines the sequence in which the ray crosses the mid-planes. 5. Determine First Child Octant: Compute the index of the first child octant intersected by the ray. This is done using the same constant shifting and binary-or operations as point location. Determine which side of each mid-plane the entry point \mathbf{p}{enter} lies on: bitx = 0 	ext{ if } p{enter,x} < x{mid} 	ext{ else } 1 bity = 0 	ext{ if } p{enter,y} < y{mid} 	ext{ else } 1 bitz = 0 	ext{ if } p{enter,z} < z{mid} 	ext{ else } 1 The child index is computed using constant shifting and binary-or as in point location. 6. Traverse Children Sequentially: Initialize currentchild = child. For each step in the sorted axisisects[] array: Identify which axis (X, Y, or Z) corresponds to the current smallest intersection distance in axisisects[]. Update currentchild by flipping the bit corresponding to that axis. This is achieved by inverting the axisbit along the corresponding mid-plane axis traversed. current\child = current\child \oplus (1 \ll axis\index) The new currentchild is the next octant to visit. Compute the new entry t for this child as the intersection distance just processed (from axisisects[]) and the exit t as the next intersection in the sorted list or t{exit} of the parent node. Stop when all children have been visited or the ray has exited the node (t > t{exit}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctreenode(rayorigin, raydir, nodebounds, tenter, texit): """ Traverses the 8 child octants of a node in the order the ray intersects them. Args: rayorigin: (ox, oy, oz) raydir: (dx, dy, dz) nodebounds: (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax) tenter: float, entry t for the current node texit: float, exit t for the current node Returns: List of tuples: (childindex, childtenter, childtexit) """ xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax = nodebounds # 1. Compute mid-planes xmid = (xmin + xmax) / 2.0 ymid = (ymin + ymax) / 2.0 zmid = (zmin + zmax) / 2.0 # 2. Compute intersection t values with mid-planes def safediv(num, den): return float('inf') if den == 0.0 else num / den tx = safediv(xmid - rayorigin[0], raydir[0]) ty = safediv(ymid - rayorigin[1], raydir[1]) tz = safediv(zmid - rayorigin[2], raydir[2]) # 3. Filter and sort mid-plane crossings that occur strictly within the node axisisects = [] if tenter < tx < texit: axisisects.append((tx, 0)) if tenter < ty < texit: axisisects.append((ty, 1)) if tenter < tz < texit: axisisects.append((tz, 2)) axisisects.sort(key=lambda item: item[0]) # 4. Determine first child octant based on entry point penter = ( rayorigin[0] + tenter raydir[0], rayorigin[1] + tenter raydir[1], rayorigin[2] + tenter raydir[2]) bitx = 0 if penter[0] < xmid else 1 bity = 0 if penter[1] < ymid else 1 bitz = 0 if penter[2] < zmid else 1 currentchild = (bitz << 2) | (bity << 1) | bitx # 5. Sequentially march through children visitedchildren = [] prevt = tenter for tcross, axis in axisisects: visitedchildren.append((currentchild, prevt, tcross)) # Invert the bitmask along the corresponding mid-plane axis traversed currentchild ^= (1 << axis) prevt = tcross # Last segment to texit if prevt < texit: visitedchildren.append((currentchild, prevt, texit)) return visitedchildren Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If the ray direction component is zero, the ray is parallel to the mid-plane. The intersection t is infinite. These should be handled by sorting such that they are effectively ignored or processed last, as they do not define a boundary crossing within the node. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in computing t values can lead to incorrect sorting or order of traversal. Use epsilon comparisons if necessary. Empty Nodes: The method assumes the node is an interior node. If the node is empty, the traversal should skip it entirely using the "empty octree strategy". Degenerate Input: If t{enter} \ge t{exit}, the ray does not intersect the node. A single-ray octree traversal algorithm that determines the exact order of child octant intersection by sorting the ray's crossings with the X, Y, and Z mid-planes of the current node. It builds on Ray Traversal of Octree Nodes by fully sorting these mid-plane intersections to march through children sequentially, exploiting binary arithmetic on integer coordinates for efficient child index updates. Unlike coherent techniques (SIMD, packets, frustum-based traversal), it avoids unnecessary work in highly variant scenes where a pixel covers multiple voxels. This method performs ray traversal through a sparse voxel octree by interpreting the IEEE-754 bit representation of floating-point coordinates to determine node depth and child indices, thereby avoiding explicit pointer chasing or coordinate division. It differs from sibling methods like Ray-Octree Traversal (Gargantini and Atkinson variant) by replacing arithmetic division and modulo operations with bitwise shifts and masks on the mantissa, and from Stack-based Octree Traversal with Direction Flipping by using a deterministic bit-indexing scheme that inherently encodes the traversal path without requiring a dynamic stack for descent. A stack-based algorithm for traversing an octree structure along a ray, handling arbitrary ray directions by flipping the coordinate system and ray parameters to ensure positive traversal direction. It differs from Ray Traversal of Octree Nodes by using an explicit stack to manage non-linear traversal paths and direction flipping to simplify child selection logic, and from IEEE-754 Bit Manipulation Octree Traversal by relying on floating-point comparisons and explicit stack management rather than bit-level integer arithmetic for step determination. Time Complexity: The initial cost per node is moderate due to the computation and sorting of mid-plane intersections (constant time for 8 children, but involves 3 divisions and a sort of 3 elements). Subsequent traversal within the node is trivial, involving only bitwise operations. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires only a small fixed-size array (axisisects[]) and a few scalar variables per node traversal. No stack is needed for descent. Measured Performance: In comparisons with Sphere Marching (SM), Octree Traversal (OT) was found to be faster on average despite requiring more iterations, because it utilizes empty octree nodes with smaller average depth. The method produces a grid pattern in iteration counts due to dependence on node location. Strengths: Efficient for sparse data; avoids stack overhead; deterministic order; good for isosurface extraction where empty space skipping is critical. Limitations: Moderate initial cost per node. When to Use: When traversing sparse voxel octrees for isosurface rendering or empty space skipping. When Not to Use: When ray coherence is high and packet-based traversal is more efficient, or when the overhead of sorting mid-plane intersections outweighs the benefits of empty space skipping. The method originates from the work on Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes by Wald et al. (2006). It was developed to efficiently traverse large octree structures for isosurface rendering, leveraging the hierarchical nature of the octree to skip empty space. The approach was further refined and applied in various contexts, including rendering piecewise approximations of SDFs and implicit surface ray tracing. The duality between voxels and cells, mapping voxels to the lower-left corner of a cell, was also observed in this context. name: Ray-Octree Traversal (Gargantini and Atkinson variant)
head: Atkinson traversal, Gargantini and Atkinson Octree Ray Traversal, Gargantini and Atkinson Octree Traversal, Gargantini and Atkinson Ray-Octree Traversal, Gargantini and Atkinson variant, Gargantini traversal
body: A single-ray octree traversal algorithm that determines the exact order of child octant intersection by sorting the ray's crossings with the X, Y, and Z mid-planes of the current node. It builds on Ray Traversal of Octree Nodes by fully sorting these mid-plane intersections to march through children sequentially, exploiting binary arithmetic on integer coordinates for efficient child index updates. Unlike coherent techniques (SIMD, packets, frustum-based traversal), it avoids unnecessary work in highly variant scenes where a pixel covers multiple voxels. Inputs: rayorig: Ray origin coordinates (list of 3 floats). raydir: Ray direction coordinates (list of 3 floats). depth: Current octree depth (integer). nodeindex: Index of the current node in the nodes array (integer). parenttrace: Array storing the traversal path (list of integers). cell: Current node's base coordinate in octree space (list of 3 integers). tenter: Ray entry parameter for the current node (float). texit: Ray exit parameter for the current node (float). isovalue: Target isovalue for scalar comparison (float). nodes: Octree node storage nodes[depth][nodeindex]. childbitdepth: Precomputed bitmask array for each depth. maxdepth: Maximum octree depth (integer). Outputs: Returns true if an isosurface intersection is found within the current node's volume; false otherwise. Data Structures: nodes[depth][nodeindex]: Accesses the current OctNode containing childmins, childmaxs, childoffset, and childstart fields. childbitdepth[depth]: Precomputed bitmask for the current depth (e.g., 2^{d{max}-depth}). axistable: Constant array {4, 2, 1} mapping sorted axis indices to bit positions. Steps: 1. Ray-Bounding Box Test: Generate rays in canonical octree space [0, 2^{d{max}}]. Perform a standard ray-bounding box test on the root to discard non-intersecting rays, yielding tenter and texit. 2. Retrieve Node: Access node = nodes[depth][nodeindex] and store nodeindex in parenttrace[depth]. 3. Compute Mid-Planes: Calculate childbit = childbitdepth[depth]. Compute the center of the current cell as floats: center = (cell.x | childbit, cell.y | childbit, cell.z | childbit). Compute intersection distances to the mid-planes: tcenter = (center - rayorig) / raydir. Compute the entry point: penter = rayorig + raydir tenter. 4. Determine First Child: Compare penter coordinates to center to determine the entry octant bits: tc.x = (penter.x \ge center.x) tc.y = (penter.y \ge center.y) tc.z = (penter.z \ge center.z) Compute the first child index: child = (tc.x << 2) | (tc.y << 1) | tc.z. Update childcell: childcell = cell | (tc.x ? childbit: 0, tc.y ? childbit: 0, tc.z ? childbit: 0). 5. Sort Mid-Plane Intersections: Create axisisects array containing the sorted indices of tcenter such that tcenter[axisisects[0]] < tcenter[axisisects[1]] < tcenter[axisisects[2]]. This represents the order of crossing the X, Y, and Z mid-planes. 6. Traverse Children: Initialize childtenter = tenter. Iterate through the sorted axisisects array while tcenter[axisisects[i]] < texit: a. Calculate Exit: childtexit = min(tcenter[axisisects[i]], texit). b. Scalar Check: If isovalue >= node.childmins[child] OR isovalue <= node.childmaxs[child]: i. If node.childoffset == -1: Traverse scalar leaf (see Subtopics). ii. Else if depth == maxdepth - 2: Traverse cap node (see Subtopics). iii. Else: Recursively call traverse(rayorig, raydir, depth+1, node.childstart + node.childoffset[child], parenttrace, childcell, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue, nodes, childbitdepth, maxdepth). c. Exit Check: If childtexit == texit, return false (ray has exited the volume). d. Update Entry: childtenter = childtexit. e. Move to Next Child: i. Get axisbit = axistable[axisisects[i]]. ii. If child & axisbit is true: child &= ~axisbit and childcell[axisisects[i]] &= ~childbit. iii. Else: child |= axisbit and childcell[axisisects[i]] |= childbit. Return false if the loop completes without finding an intersection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. handles 8-voxel neighborhood and isosurface intersection return False def traversecap(childcell, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue): # Sources do not provide full implementation; handles cap node scalar retrieval return False A specialized traversal routine for cap nodes, which are leaf-like structures containing scalar values, differing from interior nodes in how child values are retrieved. Cap intersection is identical to interior nodes, except the isovalue check and recursive call are replaced by determining the values of the eight voxels composing the cell. To optimize neighbor retrieval, given a child octant child (0-7) and a neighbor direction dir (0-7), check if (child & dir) is false; if so, the neighbor value is cap.scalars[dir]. If true, proceed with standard neighbor-finding. A scalar leaf is traversed recursively to the same depth as caps, despite having no children and a homogeneous value. When traversal reaches cap depth, if the neighborhood of identical voxels within the scalar leaf is encountered, no isosurface is present. At the borders of the scalar leaf node, neighbor-finding is performed as for cap nodes to obtain eight voxel values. If the isovalue lies within the minimum and maximum of these eight values, an isosurface intersection is computed using trilinear interpolation. Time Complexity: Moderate initial cost for computing and sorting mid-plane intersections; subsequent child traversal is trivial via bitmask inversion. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for nodes, childbitdepth, and parenttrace. Performance: Avoids SIMD/packet/frustum techniques because highly variant scenes and pixels covering multiple voxels cause unnecessary work and performance decreases compared to single-ray techniques. Wald et al. reported little performance gain from coherent techniques on large data. Strengths: Efficient single-ray traversal using binary arithmetic; no additional transform required for canonical space. Limitations: Scalar leaves and cap nodes require special handling routines. Originated from the technique of Gargantini and Atkinson [5, 6], adapted for octree structures and hashing schemes by Wald et al. in "Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes" (2006). It was chosen over Sung [19, 22, 23] and Samet [17, 19, 20] methods as the fastest traversal for their implementation. Used for interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes, such as LLNL Richtmyer-Meshkov instability and Utah CSAFE heptane fire simulations. name: Scalar Leaf Traversal
body: Scalar Leaf Traversal is a node-handling strategy for ray traversal in sparse voxel octrees where leaf nodes store a single homogeneous scalar value rather than a full voxel grid. It differs from standard leaf traversal by recursively traversing to the cap depth, performing boundary neighbor-finding to gather eight corner voxel values, and only computing a trilinear isosurface intersection when the isovalue lies within their minimum and maximum range. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D (3D tuples/lists). Scalar leaf node L with homogeneous value vL, spatial bounding box, and depth. Isosurface threshold v. Cap depth d{cap}. Current traversal depth d{curr}. Neighbor context containing child bit-mask and capscalars array of eight values. Outputs: Intersection distance t{hit} if the isosurface intersects the cell defined by the eight corner voxels. None if no intersection is found. Data Structures: Scalar leaf node stores a single scalar value, spatial bbox, and depth. Neighbor context provides access to capscalars and a child bit-mask indicating the current octree child. Steps: 1. Traverse to Cap Depth: Recursively traverse the octree until d{curr} = d{cap}. A scalar leaf is traversed to this depth even though it has no children and a homogeneous value. 2. Uniformity Check: If the traversal encounters a neighborhood of identical voxels within the scalar leaf, no isosurface is encountered. Since the leaf is homogeneous, the interior contains no surface; an intersection can only occur at the boundary if adjacent nodes differ in value. 3. Neighbor Finding: At the borders of the scalar leaf node, perform neighbor-finding to retrieve the values of the eight corner voxels of the cell. For a desired neighbor direction dir (0–7), check if (child & dir) is false. If false, the neighbor value is directly retrieved from capscalars[dir]. If true, proceed with standard recursive neighbor-finding to retrieve the value. 4. Containment Test: Once eight voxel values v{ijk} are obtained, check that the isovalue v lies within their minimum and maximum. If v < \min(v{ijk}) or v > \max(v{ijk}), return None. 5. Isosurface Intersection: If the containment test passes, perform the isosurface intersection with the eight voxels as corners of the cell. Solve the trilinear interpolant equation for the ray parameter t. The hit position is given by evaluating the ray at the first positive root of the resulting cubic polynomial. Formulas: The implicit surface is defined by the trilinear Lagrangian interpolant: f(x, y, z) = \left( \sum{i, j, k \in \{0,1\}} xi yj zk v{ijk} \right) - v = 0 where (i, j, k) is the minimum coordinate of the cell, v is the isovalue, v{ijk} is the value at the cell vertex, and x0 = 1-x, x1 = x (similarly for y, z). Substituting the ray equation r(t) = O + tD yields a cubic polynomial a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + d = 0. The intersection distance is the smallest positive real root t > 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def scalarleaftraversal(rayO, rayD, childmask, capscalars, isovalue, capdepth, currentdepth): """ Traverses a scalar leaf node to find isosurface intersection. rayO, rayD: 3-tuples/lists for origin and direction. childmask: int bit-mask indicating current octree child. capscalars: list of 8 neighbor scalar values. isovalue: float threshold. capdepth: int max traversal depth. currentdepth: int current octree depth. """ # Step 1: Traverse to Cap Depth if currentdepth < capdepth: return None # Handled by parent traversal logic # Step 2 & 3: Neighbor Finding at Boundaries cornervalues = [] for dir in range(8): if not (childmask & (1 << dir)): # Neighbor is in a sibling/parent node, value stored in capscalars val = capscalars[dir] else: # Neighbor is in the same child node, proceed with recursive neighbor-finding val = recursiveneighborlookup(dir, childmask, capscalars) cornervalues.append(val) # Step 4: Isosurface Containment Test vmin = min(cornervalues) vmax = max(cornervalues) if isovalue < vmin or isovalue > vmax: return None # No intersection # Step 5: Isosurface Intersection # Compute cubic coefficients for trilinear interpolation along ray coeffs = computetrilinearcubiccoeffs(rayO, rayD, cornervalues) roots = solvecubic(coeffs) # Find first positive root thit = None for t in roots: if t > 0: thit = t break return thit def recursiveneighborlookup(diridx, childmask, capscalars): """Standard recursive octree neighbor traversal.""" # In a full implementation, this updates childmask and calls the parent traversal routine return 0.0 # Simplified for pseudocode completeness def computetrilinearcubiccoeffs(O, D, v): """Computes coefficients a,b,c,d for f(O+tD) - isovalue = 0 using standard trilinear expansion.""" dx, dy, dz = D[0], D[1], D[2] ox, oy, oz = O[0], O[1], O[2] # Standard trilinear coefficient calculation for unit cell aligned at origin # a = dxdydz (v[7]-v[6]-v[5]+v[4]-v[3]+v[2]+v[1]-v[0]) # b, c, d follow standard trilinear expansion return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Exact expansion omitted for brevity def solvecubic(coeffs): """Solves a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + d = 0 using Cardano's method.""" a, b, c, d = coeffs if a == 0: if b == 0: return [] if c == 0 else [-d / c] disc = cc - 4bd return [] if disc < 0 else [(-c + disc0.5)/(2b), (-c - disc0.5)/(2b)] b /= a; c /= a; d /= a p = c - bb/3 q = 2bbb/27 - bc/3 + d disc = qq/4 + ppp/27 roots = [] if disc > 0: u = (-q/2 + disc0.5)(1/3) v = (-q/2 - disc0.5)(1/3) roots.append(u + v - b/3) elif disc == 0: u = (-q/2)(1/3) roots.append(2u - b/3) roots.append(-u - b/3) else: r = (-p/3)0.5 theta = (q/(2rrr)) theta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, theta)) theta = math.acos(theta) roots.append(2rmath.cos(theta/3) - b/3) roots.append(2rmath.cos((theta + 2math.pi)/3) - b/3) roots.append(2rmath.cos((theta + 4math.pi)/3) - b/3) return roots Time Complexity: O(1) per scalar leaf node for neighbor lookups and cubic solve. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per node, as no voxel grid is stored. Strengths: Significantly reduces memory usage for large uniform regions by storing a single value instead of a full voxel grid. Efficiently skips large volumes of uniform data. Limitations: Requires careful neighbor-finding at boundaries to ensure correct surface reconstruction. The cubic polynomial solution can be numerically unstable if not implemented carefully. When to Use: Ideal for volumes with large homogeneous regions, such as medical imaging with large uniform background or synthetic volumes with large empty spaces. Scalar leaf traversal is part of the broader field of interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. It was introduced in the context of optimizing ray traversal for sparse voxel octrees where leaf nodes can be either cap nodes (storing a grid of voxels) or scalar leaves (storing a single homogeneous value). The method is described in the thesis "Ray Tracing Implicit Surfaces for Interactive Visualization" by Knoll and the paper "Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes". The approach builds on the Gargantini and Atkinson variant of ray-octree traversal, adapting it to handle the unique properties of scalar leaves. head: Cap intersection, Ray-Octree Traversal
body: Cap node traversal is a specialized recursive algorithm used within the Gargantini and Atkinson ray-octree traversal scheme to handle the leaf-level boundary of the octree structure. It solves the problem of determining isosurface intersections when a ray reaches the deepest level of the hierarchy, where explicit child pointers are absent and data is stored in "cap" nodes. Cap intersection is identical to interior node traversal, except it replaces the recursive child traversal block with logic to determine the values of eight forward-neighbor voxels and perform a local isosurface intersection check. Scalar leaf traversal uses the same routine at the cap depth. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: The current ray (ray), the current depth (depth), the current node index (node\index), a parent trace array (parent\trace), the current cell coordinates (cell), the entry time (tenter), and the exit time (texit). Outputs: A boolean indicating whether an isosurface intersection was found. Data Structures OctNode: Contains fields childmins, childmaxs, and childoffset, accessed via node.childmins[child], node.childmaxs[child], and node.childoffset. Cap Node: Contains an array scalars storing voxel values, indexed via diridx. Axis Table: A constant array mapping sorted axis indices to bit masks: axistable = {4, 2, 1}. Child Bit Depth: An array childbitdepth where childbit = childbitdepth[depth]. Pseudocode The following pseudocode implements the cap node traversal logic, integrated into the main traversal loop as described in and. It assumes the caller has determined that depth == maxdepth - 2 (or equivalent boundary condition) and node.childoffset == -1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversecap(ray, depth, nodeindex, parenttrace, cell, tenter, texit, isovalue, maxdepth, nodes, childbitdepth, axistable, capscalars): """ Traverses a cap node to find isosurface intersections. Returns True if intersection found, False otherwise. """ # 1. Retrieve current node and store trace node = nodes[depth][nodeindex] parenttrace[depth] = nodeindex # 2. Calculate child bit for this depth childbit = childbitdepth[depth] # 3. Calculate center of current cell center = Vec3(cell.x | childbit, cell.y | childbit, cell.z | childbit) # 4. Calculate intersection distances to center planes tcenter = Vec3( (center.x - ray.orig.x) / ray.dir.x, (center.y - ray.orig.y) / ray.dir.y, (center.z - ray.orig.z) / ray.dir.z) # 5. Calculate entry point penter = Vec3( ray.orig.x + ray.dir.x tenter, ray.orig.y + ray.dir.y tenter, ray.orig.z + ray.dir.z tenter) # 6. Initialize child cell coordinates childcell = Vec3i(cell.x, cell.y, cell.z) # 7. Determine octant of entry point tcx = 1 if penter.x >= center.x else 0 tcy = 1 if penter.y >= center.y else 0 tcz = 1 if penter.z >= center.z else 0 # 8. Encode octant index (0-7) child = (tcx << 2) | (tcy << 1) | tcz # 9. Update child cell coordinates childcell.x |= childbit if tcx else 0 childcell.y |= childbit if tcy else 0 childcell.z |= childbit if tcz else 0 # 10. Perform 3-way minimum to sort axis intersections axes = [0, 1, 2] axes.sort(key=lambda i: tcenter[i]) axisisects = axes childtenter = tenter childtexit = 0.0 # 11. Iterate through sorted axis intersections for i in range(3): axisidx = axisisects[i] # Guard: stop if the next plane is beyond the exit time if tcenter[axisidx] >= texit: break # 12. Calculate child exit time childtexit = min(tcenter[axisidx], texit) # 13. Cap node specific logic replaces recursive child traversal # Determine values of eight forward-neighbor voxels neighborvals = [] for diridx in range(8): if not (child & diridx): # Neighbor is within the same cap node val = capscalars[diridx] else: # Neighbor is outside; perform neighbor-finding # Standard sparse voxel neighbor lookup: compute target cell coordinates # by adding/subtracting childbit based on diridx bits, then hash/lookup. val = lookupneighbor(cell, diridx, childbit) neighborvals.append(val) # Check isovalue against min/max range of the 8 neighbors minval = min(neighborvals) maxval = max(neighborvals) if minval <= isovalue <= maxval: # Standard trilinear isosurface intersection on the 8 voxel corners if intersecttrilinear(neighborvals, isovalue): return True # 14. If ray has exited the volume if childtexit == texit: return False # 15. Update entry time for next iteration childtenter = childtexit # 16. Update child index and cell coordinates based on axis crossing axisbit = axistable[axisidx] if child & axisbit: child &= ~axisbit childcell[axisidx] &= ~childbit else: child |= axisbit childcell[axisidx] |= childbit return False Parameters axistable: {4, 2, 1}. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. The condition for cap traversal is depth == maxdepth - 2. Note: The source contains a typo maxdepth -- 2, which is interpreted as maxdepth - 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Typo in Depth Check: The source code snippet uses maxdepth -- 2, which is a decrement operator in C-like languages. This is likely a typo for maxdepth - 2 or maxdepth == 2 depending on context. Neighbor Finding: The exact algorithm for finding neighbors when child & dir is true is not provided in the sources. It requires accessing voxels outside the current cap node. Isosurface Check Logic: The source code uses || in the condition isovalue >= node.childmins[child] || isovalue <= node.childmaxs[child]. This is logically unusual for a bounding box check (which typically uses &&). If childmins and childmaxs are valid, this condition is almost always true. Time Complexity: The traversal is recursive and depends on the ray path length through the octree. At the cap level, it performs a constant number of operations per ray segment, specifically eight neighbor lookups and an isosurface check. Memory Complexity: Cap nodes store scalar values for the voxels they represent. Strengths: Efficiently handles the boundary of the octree without requiring explicit child pointers for the deepest level. Limitations: Requires complex neighbor-finding logic for voxels at the boundary of cap nodes. The exact performance impact of neighbor finding is not quantified in the sources. Origin: The method is part of the "Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes" paper by Knoll et al.. History: It is an adaptation of Gargantini and Atkinson's ray-octree traversal technique, specifically modified to handle the leaf-level "cap" nodes in their sparse voxel octree representation. Usage: Used in real-time isosurface rendering of large volumetric datasets. head: Bitwise Octree Traversal, IEEE-754 Voxel Traversal, Mantissa-based Octree Traversal, Octree Ray Tracing with Bitwise Cell Indexing, Ray Traversal in Octree using IEEE-754 Bit Manipulation
body: This method performs ray traversal through a sparse voxel octree by interpreting the IEEE-754 bit representation of floating-point coordinates to determine node depth and child indices, avoiding explicit pointer chasing or coordinate division. It replaces arithmetic division and modulo operations with bitwise shifts and masks on the mantissa. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} in camera space (normalized device coordinates, range [-1, 1]). Octree data structure containing nodes and voxels (see Data Structures). Maximum traversal depth MAXDEPTH (default 12). Maximum iteration count MAXITERS (default 128). Epsilon EPSILON (default 10^{-4}). Outputs: Hit result: boolean hit, and if true, the color of the first occupied voxel encountered. The octree is stored in a flat array (e.g., SSBO in GPU implementations). OctreeNode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct OctreeNode { uint info; // Bit 0: leaf flag (1 if leaf, 0 if internal). Bits 1-8: child occupancy mask (8 bits). uint childPtr; // Index into the nodes or voxels array. }; If info & 1 is set, the node is a leaf. If info & 1 is clear, the node is internal. The occupancy mask in info (bits 1-8) indicates which of the 8 children exist. The offset to the i-th child is calculated by counting the number of set bits in mask & ((1 << i) - 1). OctreeVoxel Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct OctreeVoxel { uint rgb; // Packed RGB color. R in bits 24-31, G in 16-23, B in 8-15. }; Color components are extracted by shifting right by 24, 16, and 8 bits, masking with 0xFF, and dividing by 255.0. 1. Ray Initialization: Scale ray origin from camera space [-1, 1] to world space [1, 2]. Fix zero direction components: if any component of \mathbf{d} is zero, replace it with \pm \text{EPSILON} preserving the original sign. Clamp the magnitude of each component to at least EPSILON. Normalize \mathbf{d} and compute inverse direction \mathbf{invDir} = 1.0 / \mathbf{d}. Intersect ray with root AABB [1, 2]^3. Calculate t{enter} and t{exit}. If t{exit} < t{enter} or t{exit} < 0, return miss. Advance origin: \mathbf{o} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \max(t{enter}, 0.0). Clamp \mathbf{o} to [1, 1.9999999]^3 to prevent precision issues at the exact boundary. 2. Traversal Loop: Initialize mantissaBitIdx = 22 (corresponding to the root level, as the mantissa has 23 bits, index 22 is the MSB of the fractional part). Initialize nodeIdx to the root node index (last element in OctreeNodesSSBO). Loop for iter from 0 to MAXITERS: a. Quantize Position: Convert current position \mathbf{pos} to unsigned integer representation: u = \text{floatBitsToUint}(\mathbf{pos}). Create mask to zero out lower bits: mask = \sim(0u \ll \text{mantissaBitIdx}). Quantize position to cell minimum: \mathbf{cellMin} = \text{uintBitsToFloat}(u \ \& \ mask). b. Compute Cell Size: Calculate cell size using IEEE-754 exponent manipulation: \text{cellSize} = \text{uintBitsToFloat}((127 + \text{mantissaBitIdx} - 23) \ll 23) This effectively computes 2^{\text{mantissaBitIdx} - 23}. c. Calculate Child Index: Extract child index from the mantissa bits of \mathbf{pos}: \text{childIdx} = \text{getCellIdx}(\mathbf{pos}, \text{mantissaBitIdx}) This extracts 3 bits (X, Y, Z) at the current mantissa position to form a 0-7 index. d. Descend or Hit: Check if current node is a leaf (node.info & 1). If leaf: Check if the specific child voxel is occupied using the occupancy mask or direct index. If occupied, return hit with color from OctreeVoxel[nodeIdx + childIdx] (or appropriate offset). If not leaf: Check if child childIdx exists in node.info mask. If child exists: Calculate childPtr offset: offset = popcount(node.info.mask & ((1 << childIdx) - 1)). Update nodeIdx = node.childPtr + offset. Push nodeIdx to stack shStack[glLocalInvocationIndex][22 - mantissaBitIdx] if using stack-based backtracking. Decrement mantissaBitIdx by 1. Recompute childIdx for the new level. If child does not exist: Ascend: Find the common ancestor between the previous position (cellMin) and the new position (pos) using XOR and findMSB on their IEEE-754 representations. Update mantissaBitIdx to the level of the common ancestor. Update nodeIdx to the ancestor node. Continue loop. e. Advance Ray: Compute the position of the plane exiting the current cell along the ray direction: \mathbf{planePos} = \mathbf{cellMin} + \text{step}(0.0, \mathbf{d}) \cdot \text{cellSize} Where step(0.0, d) is 1.0 if di > 0 else 0.0 for each component. Calculate distance to exit plane t{max} using inverse ray direction: t{max} = (\mathbf{planePos} - \mathbf{pos}) \cdot \mathbf{invDir}. Clamp new position \mathbf{pos} to this distance: \mathbf{pos} \leftarrow \mathbf{pos} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t{max}. Clamp \mathbf{pos} to the neighbor cell's AABB to avoid precision issues at boundaries. Calculate neighborMin and neighborMax using bit manipulation to subtract the smallest epsilon. 3. Termination: If loop completes without finding a hit, return miss. Unverified code. Traversal mantissabitidx = 22 nodeidx = len(octreenodes) - 1 # Root per source pos = rayorigin stack = [] for in range(MAXITERS): # Quantize position to cell min upos = (floattouint(pos[0]), floattouint(pos[1]), floattouint(pos[2])) mask = ~((1 << mantissabitidx) - 1) & 0xFFFFFFFF cellmin = (uinttofloat(upos[0] & mask), uinttofloat(upos[1] & mask), uinttofloat(upos[2] & mask)) # Compute cell size expbits = (127 + mantissabitidx - 23) << 23 cellsize = uinttofloat(expbits) # Calculate child index childidx = getcellidx(pos, mantissabitidx) node = octreenodes[nodeidx] info = node['info'] childptr = node['childptr'] occupancymask = (info >> 1) & 0xFF # Check if leaf if info & 1: if occupancymask & (1 << childidx): voxel = octreevoxels[childptr + childidx] r = ((voxel['rgb'] >> 24) & 0xFF) / 255.0 g = ((voxel['rgb'] >> 16) & 0xFF) / 255.0 b = ((voxel['rgb'] >> 8) & 0xFF) / 255.0 return {"hit": True, "color": (r, g, b)} else: # Leaf but empty, ascend pass else: # Internal node if not (occupancymask & (1 << childidx)): # Child does not exist, ascend pass else: # Descend offset = popcount(occupancymask & ((1 << childidx) - 1)) stack.append(nodeidx) nodeidx = childptr + offset mantissabitidx -= 1 if mantissabitidx < 0: break # Recompute childIdx for new level upos = (floattouint(pos[0]), floattouint(pos[1]), floattouint(pos[2])) childidx = getcellidx(pos, mantissabitidx) continue # Ascend logic cellminuint = (floattouint(cellmin[0]), floattouint(cellmin[1]), floattouint(cellmin[2])) xorval = upos[0] ^ cellminuint[0] commonlevel = findmsb(xorval) mantissabitidx = commonlevel if stack: nodeidx = stack.pop() else: nodeidx = len(octreenodes) - Fixed by replacing zeros with \pm \text{EPSILON} while preserving sign. Boundary Precision: Ray origin must be clamped to [1, 1.9999999] to prevent floating-point precision issues at the exact AABB boundary. Precision at Boundaries: Clamping the new position to the neighbor cell's AABB avoids precision issues when the ray exits a cell exactly on a boundary. Time Complexity: O(D) where D is the depth of the octree, as each iteration moves one level deeper or ascends. The bitwise operations are O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if stack is not used, or O(D) if stack is used for backtracking. The octree itself is stored in a flat array. Strengths: Avoids expensive division and modulo operations by using bitwise manipulations on IEEE-754 floats. Efficient for GPU implementation due to predictable memory access patterns and lack of dynamic branching for pointer chasing. Limitations: Requires the octree to be built with a specific coordinate system and depth. Precision issues can arise at cell boundaries if not handled carefully. When to Use: Ideal for GPU-based ray tracing of sparse voxel octrees where performance is critical and the octree depth is limited (e.g., 12 levels). When Not to Use: Not suitable for very deep octrees or when dynamic node allocation is required. This method is derived from implementations in modern voxel engines and ray tracers, specifically those utilizing GPU shaders for efficient traversal. It leverages the properties of IEEE-754 floating-point numbers to encode spatial hierarchy in the mantissa bits. rayferric/voxel-engine, https://github.com/rayferric/voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Stack-based Octree Traversal with Direction Flipping
head: Octree Ray Traversal with Direction Flipping, Stack-based Octree Traversal, TreeTraverser
body: A stack-based algorithm for traversing an octree structure along a ray, handling arbitrary ray directions by flipping the coordinate system and ray parameters to ensure positive traversal direction. It differs from Ray Traversal of Octree Nodes by using an explicit stack to manage non-linear traversal paths and direction flipping to simplify child selection logic, and from IEEE-754 Bit Manipulation Octree Traversal by relying on floating-point comparisons and explicit stack management rather than bit-level integer arithmetic for step determination. Inputs: Octree: An octree structure with fields min, max, size, gridlength, and a vector of Node objects. Each Node has methods hasChild(i), isLeaf(), and isNull(). Ray: A ray defined by origin (vec3) and direction (vec3). Outputs: A sequence of visited nodes in traversal order, accessible via the stack state. The current node and its associated t-intervals during traversal. TraversalNodeInfo A struct representing a node on the traversal stack. const Node node: Pointer to the current octree node. vec3 t0: Entry t-values for the current node's bounding box (x, y, z components). vec3 t1: Exit t-values for the current node's bounding box (x, y, z components). vec3 tm: Midpoint t-values for the current node's bounding box (x, y, z components). int nextchild: Index of the next child to visit. -1: First visit to this node; children not yet determined. 0-7: Index of the next child octant to visit. 8: All children visited; node is done. TreeTraverser The main traversal class. unsigned char a: Direction flip mask. Bits 0, 1, 2 correspond to Z, Y, X axes respectively. If bit i is set, the corresponding axis was flipped. Octree const octree: Pointer to the octree being traversed. Ray ray: The modified ray with flipped origin/direction if necessary. Ray originalray: The original ray before any flips, used for final position calculation. std::vector<TraversalNodeInfo> stack: The stack of nodes to visit. int stepcount: Counter for traversal steps. 1. Set stepcount = 0, a = 0. 2. Store originalray. 3. For each axis i \in \{0, 1, 2\} (corresponding to X, Y, Z): Check ray direction sign. The source code uses specific logic: if ray.direction[i] < 0 for X and Y, or ray.direction[i] > 0 for Z (note: this Z check is non-standard and specific to the source implementation). If the condition is met: Flip ray.origin[i] = octree->size[i] - ray.origin[i]. Flip ray.direction[i] = -ray.direction[i]. Set the corresponding bit in a: bit 0 for Z, bit 1 for Y, bit 2 for X. 4. Calculate entry/exit t-values for the octree bounding box using the modified ray: tx0 = (octree->min[0] - ray.origin[0]) \times (1.0f / ray.direction[0]). tx1 = (octree->max[0] - ray.origin[0]) \times (1.0f / ray.direction[0]). Similarly for ty0, ty1 (Y axis) and tz0, tz1 (Z axis). 5. Check if the ray intersects the octree: t{enter} = \max(\max(tx0, ty0), tz0). t{exit} = \min(\min(tx1, ty1), tz1). If t{enter} < t{exit}: Create TraversalNodeInfo for the root node. Set t0 = (tx0, ty0, tz0), t1 = (tx1, ty1, tz1), tm = 0.5f (t0 + t1). Set nextchild = -1. Push onto stack. Else: Stack remains empty; no traversal occurs. Repeatedly call until the stack is empty or traversal is complete. 1. POP Check: If stack is empty, return. Let top = stack.back(). If top.nextchild == 8 (all children visited) or top.node->isLeaf(), pop stack and return. 2. PUSH (First Visit): If top.nextchild == -1: Calculate tm = 0.5f (top.t0 + top.t1). Determine the first child to visit using firstNode(top.t0, tm). Set top.nextchild to the result of firstNode. Update stack.back() with the new nextchild. 3. ADVANCE (Visit Child): Let currentcase = top.nextchild. Calculate childindex = currentcase ^ a. This maps the logical child index to the physical child index based on the direction flip mask. Check if the child exists: if (top.node->hasChild(childindex)). If it exists: Calculate the new t0 and t1 bounds for the child voxel using standard interval subdivision logic. Create TraversalNodeInfo for the child with updated t0, t1, tm = 0.5f (t0 + t1), and nextchild = -1. Push the new TraversalNodeInfo onto stack. Set top.nextchild to currentcase + 1 to visit the next child in sequence. Given t0 and tm for the current node: 1. If tx0 > ty0 and tx0 > tz0 (entering via YZ plane, i.e., X-axis first): If tym < tx0, set bit 1. If tzm < tx0, set bit 0. Result is the combined bit value. 2. Else if ty0 > tz0 (entering via XZ plane, i.e., Y-axis first): If txm < ty0, set bit 2. If tzm < ty0, set bit 0. Result is the combined bit value. 3. Else (entering via XY plane, i.e., Z-axis first): If txm < tz0, set bit 2. If tym < tz0, set bit 1. Result is the combined bit value. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = list(origin) # [x, y, z] self.direction = list(direction) # [x, y, z] def getraypoint(self, t): return [self.origin[i] + t self.direction[i] for i in range(3)] class TraversalNodeInfo: def init(self, node, t0, t1, tm, nextchild): self.node = node self.t0 = list(t0) self.t1 = list(t1) self.tm = list(tm) self.nextchild = nextchild class TreeTraverser: def init(self, octree, ray): self.octree = octree self.originalray = Ray(list(ray.origin), list(ray.direction)) self.ray = Ray(list(ray.origin), list(ray.direction)) self.a = 0 self.stack = [] self.stepcount = 0 def inittraversal(self): self.stepcount = 0 self.a = 0 for i in range(3): dirval = self.ray.direction[i] shouldflip = False if i < 2: # X or Y if dirval < 0: shouldflip = True else: # Z if dirval > 0: shouldflip = True if shouldflip: self.ray.origin[i] = self.octree.size[i] - self.ray.origin[i] self.ray.direction[i] = -self.ray.direction[i] if i == 2: self.a |= 1 elif i == 1: self.a |= 2 elif i == 0: self.a |= 4 invdir = [1.0 / self.ray.direction[i] for i in range(3)] tx0 = (self.octree.min[0] - self.ray.origin[0]) invdir[0] tx1 = (self.octree.max[0] - self.ray.origin[0]) invdir[0] ty0 = (self.octree.min[1] - self.ray.origin[1]) invdir[1] ty1 = (self.octree.max[1] - self.ray.origin[1]) invdir[1] tz0 = (self.octree.min[2] - self.ray.origin[2]) invdir[2] tz1 = (self.octree.max[2] - self.ray.origin[2]) invdir[2] t0 = [tx0, ty0, tz0] t1 = [tx1, ty1, tz1] tenter = max(max(t0[0], t0[1]), t0[2]) texit = min(min(t1[0], t1[1]), t1[2]) if tenter < texit: tm = [0.5 (t0[i] + t1[i]) for i in range(3)] rootnode = self.octree.getrootnode() info = TraversalNodeInfo(rootnode, t0, t1, tm, -1) self.stack.append(info) else: self.stack = [] def firstnode(self, t0, tm): tx0, ty0, tz0 = t0 txm, tym, tzm = tm child = 0 if tx0 > ty0 and tx0 > tz0: if tym < tx0: child |= 2 if tzm < tx0: child |= 1 elif ty0 > tz0: if txm < ty0: child |= 4 if tzm < ty0: child |= 1 else: if txm < tz0: child |= 4 if tym < tz0: child |= 2 return child def step(self): if not self.stack: return False top = self.stack[-1] if top.nextchild == 8 or top.node.isleaf(): self.stack.pop() return True if top.nextchild == -1: tm = [0.5 (top.t0[i] + top.t1[i]) for i in range(3)] firstchild = self.firstnode(top.t0, tm) top.nextchild = firstchild self.stack[-1] = top currentcase = top.nextchild childindex = currentcase ^ self.a if top.node.haschild(childindex): newt0 = list(top.t0) newt1 = list(top.t1) for i in range(3): bit = (childindex >> i) & 1 if bit == 0: newt0[i] = top.tm[i] else: newt1[i] = top.tm[i] newtm = [0.5 (newt0[i] + newt1[i]) for i in range(3)] childnode = top.node.getchild(childindex) newinfo = TraversalNodeInfo(childnode, newt0, newt1, newtm, -1) self.stack.append(newinfo) top.nextchild = currentcase + 1 self.stack[-2] = top else: top.nextchild = currentcase + 1 self.stack[-1] = top return True def getcurrentposition(self): if not self.stack: return None top = self.stack[-1] t = max(top.t0) pos = self.originalray.getraypoint(t) pos[2] = -pos[2] return pos a: Direction flip mask, computed during initialization. stepcount: Traversal step counter. Ray Direction Handling: The code assumes specific sign checks for each axis (negative for X and Y, positive for Z) to determine flipping. This is non-standard and must be replicated exactly. Position Calculation: getCurrentPosition uses originalray.getRayPoint(t) where t = stack.back().t0.max(), and then negates the z-coordinate: answer[2] = -answer[2]. This compensates for the z-flip during traversal. Division by Zero: If a ray direction component is zero, the t-calculation will result in division by zero. The source code does not explicitly handle this, so it is assumed that rays with zero direction components are either pre-filtered or handled elsewhere. Child Order: The exact logic for determining the "next" child to visit after the current one is not fully specified in the source. The implementation uses a simple increment, which matches the sequential visitation implied by the stack-based design. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of nodes visited along the ray path. Each node is visited once. Memory Complexity: O(D) where D is the depth of the octree, due to the stack. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the depth of the octree and the number of nodes intersected by the ray. Strengths: Handles arbitrary ray directions efficiently by flipping coordinates. Simple stack-based implementation. Limitations: Non-standard direction flipping logic for Z-axis. Child order logic is not fully specified. When to Use: When traversing an octree with arbitrary ray directions and a simple stack-based approach is preferred. When Not to Use: When bit-manipulation based traversal is preferred for performance, or when the non-standard Z-flip logic is a concern. The method is derived from an unofficial CPU voxel raycaster implementation. The specific direction flipping logic for the Z-axis (positive direction check) is unique to this implementation and not standard in ray tracing literature. name: CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal
head: Stack-based Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal
body: CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal is a ray traversal algorithm for 3D sparse voxel octrees stored in a linear block structure, implemented on the CPU. It uses a stack to manage traversal state, handling valid internal nodes, leaf nodes, and empty space by casting rays to the next occupied voxel. It sets itself apart from GPU-based approaches by performing all ray marching and shading calculations on the host processor, using a linear block structure for the octree and a stack-based traversal mechanism. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) stored in a linear block structure, camera parameters (screen width, height, field of view), and a ray origin/direction for each pixel. Output: A rendered image (pixel colors) where leaf nodes contribute to the final color based on ray distance. Data Structures: Voxel: Represents an internal node. Contains bitmasks for valid (which children exist) and leaf (which children are leaf nodes), and an address pointing to children in the block. Leaf: Represents a leaf node. Contains color data. VoxelStack: Manages the traversal state. entries: Array of StackEntry objects. top: Current stack depth (index of the top entry). boxsize: Size of the bounding box at the current stack level. StackEntry: Represents a node on the traversal stack. voxel: Pointer to the current Voxel or Leaf in the block. octant: The index (0-7) of the child within the parent node that this entry represents. corner: The 3D coordinate of the corner of the current node's bounding box. ray: The ray being traced, potentially mirrored for intersection tests. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Screen Coordinates: For each pixel (i, j) in the image: \text{screen\x} = \frac{i \times \text{fov}}{\text{WIDTH}} - 0.5 \text{screen\y} = \frac{j \times \text{fov}}{\text{HEIGHT}} - 0.5 Where WIDTH is 1280, HEIGHT is 720, and fov is 1.2 (default). 2. Compute Ray Direction: \text{direction} = \text{Vector}(\text{screen\x} \times \text{scale}.x, -1 \times \text{scale}.y, \text{screen\y} \times \text{scale}.z). 3. Push Root to Stack: Initialize the stack with the root node: \text{stack.push\root}(\&\text{block}.\text{back}<\text{Voxel}>(), \text{Vector}(-1, -1, -1), \text{ray}) The initial corner is (-1, -1, -1) and the ray is the camera ray. 4. Traversal Loop: While the stack is not empty: a. Get Current Octant: Retrieve the current octant index from the top of the stack: \text{oct} = \text{stack}.\text{octant} b. Check Validity and Leaf Status: \text{valid} = (\text{stack}.\text{voxel}.\text{valid} \gg \text{oct}) \& 1 \text{leaf} = (\text{stack}.\text{voxel}.\text{leaf} \gg \text{oct}) \& 1 c. If Leaf: i. Get leaf pointer: \text{Leaf}^ \text{leaf} = \&\text{block}.\text{at}<\text{Leaf}>(\text{stack}.\text{voxel}.\text{address\of}(\text{oct})) ii. Compute lightness: \text{lightness} = \frac{1}{\text{ray.square\distance}() + 1} iii. Set pixel color: \text{leaf}.\text{set\color}(\text{pixel}, \text{lightness}) iv. Break loop. d. If Valid (Internal Node): i. Push child to stack: \text{stack.push}(\&\text{block}.\text{at}<\text{Voxel}>(\text{stack}.\text{voxel}.\text{address\of}(\text{oct})), \text{ray}) ii. Update pixel green channel (visual feedback/accumulation): \text{pixel}[1] += \frac{0\text{xff} - \text{pixel}[1]}{64} iii. Continue loop. e. If Invalid (Empty Space): i. Compute child corner: \text{child\corner} = \text{stack}.\text{corner} \text{child\corner}.\text{adjust\corner}(\text{child\size}, \text{oct}) Where \text{child\size} = \text{stack.box\size} \times 0.5. ii. Compute mask: \text{mask} = \text{ray.octant\mask}() iii. Mirror ray and corner for ray-box intersection: \text{mirror\origin} = \text{ray.origin.mirror}(\text{mask}) \text{mirror\direction} = \text{ray.direction.mirror}(\text{mask}) \text{mirror\corner} = \text{child\corner.mirror}(\text{mask}) \text{mirror\corner}.\text{adjust\corner}(-\text{child\size}, \text{mask}) iv. Compute intersection distances: tx = \frac{\text{mirror\corner}.x - \text{mirror\origin}.x}{\text{mirror\direction}.x} ty = \frac{\text{mirror\corner}.y - \text{mirror\origin}.y}{\text{mirror\direction}.y} tz = \frac{\text{mirror\corner}.z - \text{mirror\origin}.z}{\text{mirror\direction}.z} v. Find smallest positive t and hit face: Initialize t = \infty, \text{hit\face} = 0. If tx > 0, t = tx, \text{hit\face} = 4. If ty > 0 and ty < t, t = ty, \text{hit\face} = 2. If tz > 0 and tz < t, t = tz, \text{hit\face} = 1. vi. March ray: \text{ray.march}(t) vii. Transfer to sibling: \text{stack}.\text{octant} \oplus= \text{hit\face} viii. Continue loop. 5. Edge Case: If the stack is empty after popping, the ray is outside the root octree. Set pixel blue channel to 0xc0 and break. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cpusparsevoxeloctreetraversal(block, width, height, fov): # Constants WIDTH = 1280 HEIGHT = 720 FOV = fov SCALEX, SCALEY, SCALEZ = 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 class Vector: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def lengthsquared(self): return self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2 def mirror(self, mask): return Vector( self.x if not (mask & 1) else -self.x, self.y if not (mask & 2) else -self.y, self.z if not (mask & 4) else -self.z) class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction def squaredistance(self): return self.origin.lengthsquared() def octantmask(self): mask = 0 if self.direction.x < 0: mask |= 1 if self.direction.y < 0: mask |= 2 if self.direction.z < 0: mask |= 4 return mask def march(self, t): self.origin = Vector( self.origin.x + self.direction.x t, self.origin.y + self.direction.y t, self.origin.z + self.direction.z t) class Voxel: def init(self, valid=0, leaf=0, address=0): self.valid = valid self.leaf = leaf self.address = address def addressof(self, oct): return self.address + oct class Leaf: def init(self): self.color = [0, 0, 0] def setcolor(self, pixel, lightness): self.color = [int(c lightness) for c in pixel] class StackEntry: def init(self, voxel, octant, corner, ray): self.voxel = voxel self.octant = octant self.corner = corner self.ray = ray class VoxelStack: def init(self): self.entries = [] self.top = -1 self.boxsize = 2.0 def pushroot(self, voxel, corner, ray): self.entries.append(StackEntry(voxel, 0, corner, ray)) self.top = 0 def push(self, voxel, ray): self.top += 1 self.entries.append(StackEntry(voxel, self.entries[self.top].octant, self.entries[self.top].corner, ray)) def pop(self): if self.top >= 0: self.top -= 1 return self.entries.pop() return None def isempty(self): return self.top < 0 @property def octant(self): return self.entries[self.top].octant @property def voxel(self): return self.entries[self.top].voxel @property def corner(self): return self.entries[self.top].corner @property def ray(self): return self.entries[self.top].ray def adjustcorner(corner, size, oct): corner.x += size if (oct & 1) else -size corner.y += size if (oct & 2) else -size corner.z += size if (oct & 4) else -size return corner stack = VoxelStack() for i in range(width): for j in range(height): # 1. Initialize Screen Coordinates screenx = (i FOV) / WIDTH - 0.5 screeny = (j FOV) / HEIGHT - 0.5 # 2. Compute Ray Direction direction = Vector(screenx SCALEX, -1 SCALEY, screeny SCALEZ) ray = Ray(origin=Vector(0, 0, 0), direction=direction) # 3. Push Root to Stack stack.pushroot(Voxel(), Vector(-1, -1, -1), ray) pixel = [0, 0, 0] # 4. Traversal Loop while not stack.isempty(): # Get current octant oct = stack.octant # Check validity and leaf status valid = (stack.voxel.valid >> oct) & 1 leaf = (stack.voxel.leaf >> oct) & 1 if leaf: # If leaf leafptr = Leaf() lightness = 1.0 / (ray.squaredistance() + 1) leafptr.setcolor(pixel, lightness) break if valid: # If valid internal node childvoxel = Voxel() stack.push(childvoxel, ray) # Update pixel green channel pixel[1] += (0xff - pixel[1]) / 64.0 continue # If invalid childcorner = Vector(stack.corner.x, stack.corner.y, stack.corner.z) childsize = stack.boxsize 0.5 adjustcorner(childcorner, childsize, oct) mask = ray.octantmask() mirrororigin = ray.origin.mirror(mask) mirrordirection = ray.direction.mirror(mask) mirrorcorner = childcorner.mirror(mask) adjustcorner(mirrorcorner, -childsize, mask) tx = (mirrorcorner.x - mirrororigin.x) / mirrordirection.x ty = (mirrorcorner.y - mirrororigin.y) / mirrordirection.y tz = (mirrorcorner.z - mirrororigin.z) / mirrordirection.z t = float('inf') hitface = 0 if tx > 0: t = tx hitface = 4 if ty > 0 and ty < t: t = ty hitface = 2 if tz > 0 and tz < t: t = tz hitface = 1 ray.march(t) stack.entries[self.top].octant ^= hitface if stack.isempty(): pixel[2] = 0xc0 # Write pixel # writepixel(i, j, pixel) Parametric Octree Traversal is a top-down ray-octree traversal algorithm that uses parametric interval arithmetic to determine which child nodes of an octree node are intersected by a ray, handling non-uniform octree depths. It sets itself apart from bottom-up approaches (like DDA traversal) by performing a depth-first search that computes entry and exit parametric times (t) for the bounding box, allowing it to skip empty subtrees without requiring a fixed tree depth or explicit stack management for the traversal order itself. Iterative Octree Traversal is a CPU-based ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) that uses a fixed-size stack to manage traversal state, handling valid internal nodes, leaf nodes, and empty space by casting rays to the next occupied voxel. It employs a two-phase approach: a register-based DDA with bit-masked coordinate tracking for upper octree levels, and a slab-boundary-based stack traversal for deeper nodes. Recursive Octree Traversal is a depth-first algorithm for processing a 3D sparse voxel octree by visiting every node in the tree structure. It serves as the foundational traversal logic for both volume rendering (rendering active leaf nodes as cubes) and isosurface extraction (generating vertex buffers via contouring). It differs from its siblings by explicitly using the call stack to manage recursion depth, whereas Iterative Octree Traversal uses an explicit stack, and Parametric Octree Traversal uses parametric ray-marching logic. It builds on CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal by replacing the stack-based state machine with direct recursive function calls. Compact Voxel Octree Raycasting is a CPU-based ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees that optimizes memory layout and traversal logic by compacting active ray-voxel interactions and decoding node masks on-the-fly. It solves the problem of inefficient traversal in sparse structures by using an explicit stack to manage non-sequential memory layouts and a parallel "COMPACTIFY" step to filter out non-intersecting rays, ensuring that only valid ray-voxel pairs are processed in subsequent levels. Unlike recursive or parametric approaches, it relies on a linear block structure with explicit state management, making it suitable for high-performance CPU implementations where memory bandwidth and cache locality are critical. It builds on CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal and differs from Parametric Octree Traversal, Iterative Octree Traversal, Recursive Octree Traversal, and Sparse Voxel Octree Path Tracing by explicitly managing traversal state and compacting active ray lists between levels. Sparse Voxel Octree Path Tracing is a rendering technique that traverses a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) structure on the CPU to perform path tracing, writing results to a texture displayed via OpenGL. It differs from GPU-based SVO rendering by performing all ray marching and shading calculations on the host processor, using a linear block structure for the octree and a stack-based traversal mechanism. It builds on CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal by integrating the traversal logic into a full path tracing loop that handles light bounces and material reflectivity.
