name: PND3D Octree Rendering
head: PND3D
body: PND3D is a volume rendering method that uses a standard 8-way octree with non-leaf nodes containing child and solid masks, visited in front-to-back depth-first order to enable occlusion culling. It distinguishes itself by splitting the screen into large rectangular tiles determined by 3 vanishing points of the voxel grid projected to screen coordinates, allowing each tile to be rendered as an independent job starting from the root of the octree. This approach facilitates multithread optimization and specific hardware-accelerated occlusion queries using bit arrays. Inputs and Outputs: Input: a sparse voxel octree where non-leaf nodes are 64-bit structures, screen resolution, and camera parameters. Output: a rendered image. Intermediate Output: a 64-bit pixel buffer containing position and leaf node index. Data Structures: Non-leaf nodes are packed 64-bit structures with the following layout: chi (char): child byte mask (1=has children, 0=pure air/solid). sol (char): solid byte mask (1=pure solid, 0=not pure solid). mrk (char): alignment padding. mrk2 (char): alignment padding. ind (int): index pointer to the first child. Numbered Steps: 1. Tile Division: Divide the screen into large rectangular tiles determined by 3 vanishing points of the voxel grid projected to screen coordinates. 2. Bounding Box Calculation: For each tile, calculate the bounding box of the cubes more quickly by using only 4 of the 8 vertices of a cube, which are known in advance based on the tile's position relative to the vanishing points. 3. Tile Rendering Job: Render each tile as an independent job, clipped to the tile like a viewport, starting from the root of the octree, allowing for multithread optimization. 4. Occlusion Query: For every non-leaf node containing some solid, perform an occlusion query on its projected bounding box. If the width is larger than 32 pixels, assume it is visible and visit its children. If the bounding box width is 32 pixels or less, use a bit array (cover buffer) with 1 bit per pixel to test if the region is fully occluded using an 'and' instruction. If fully occluded, skip the node and its children. 5. Leaf Node Processing: For leaf nodes (solid surface voxels), visit each pixel of the bounding rectangle and perform 6 dot products in the inner loop using 2 'addps' and 2 'movmskps' instructions to determine if the pixel falls inside the projected cube (a 4- or 6-sided convex polygon). 6. First Pass (CPU): Write a 64-bit pixel to the screen containing 12 bits x, 12 bits y, 12 bits z, and a 28-bit index to the leaf node holding surface voxel information. 7. Second Pass (GPU): The GPU receives the voxel position and a pointer to its surface structure, raytraces to the known cube, determines the face, and performs texture mapping with filters like bilinear and mip mapping. Formulas: Pixel packing formula: P = (x \ \& \ 0xFFF) \ | \ ((y \ \& \ 0xFFF) \ll 12) \ | \ ((z \ \& \ 0xFFF) \ll 24) \ | \ ((idx \ \& \ 0xFFFFFFF) \ll 36), where x, y, z are 12-bit coordinates and idx is the 28-bit leaf index. Parameters: Occlusion query threshold: 32 pixels width. Nodes with projected bounding box width larger than this are assumed visible. Tile count: typically 16-48 tiles per screen. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Older ATI or Intel video cards may require overriding the default rendering mode with /arbasm for full GPU acceleration or /cpu for CPU-based emulation, which lacks trilinear filtering. Precision limits are imposed by the 12-bit coordinate storage in the 64-bit pixel format. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertile(tileid, screenwidth, screenheight, rootnode): tilebounds = computetilebounds(tileid, screenwidth, screenheight) bbox = computebbox4vertices(tilebounds) traversenode(rootnode, tilebounds, bbox) def traversenode(node, tilebounds, bbox): if not node.issolid(): return if bbox.width > 32: visitchildren(node, tilebounds) else: if isfullyoccluded(tilebounds): return visitchildren(node, tilebounds) def visitchildren(node, tilebounds): for child in node.children: childbbox = computechildbbox(child, tilebounds) traversenode(child, tilebounds, childbbox) def processleafnode(leaf, tilebounds): for pixel in leaf.boundingrectanglepixels: if ispixelinsidecube(pixel, leaf): writepixel(pixel.x, pixel.y, leaf.x, leaf.y, leaf.z, leaf.index) def isfullyoccluded(tilebounds): coverbuffer = allocatecoverbuffer(tilebounds) return coverbuffer.isfullyzero() def computetilebounds(tileid, screenwidth, screenheight): return {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": screenwidth, "h": screenheight} def computebbox4vertices(bounds): return {"x": bounds["x"], "y": bounds["y"], "w": bounds["w"], "h": bounds["h"]} def computechildbbox(child, tilebounds): return {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 16, "h": 16} def ispixelinsidecube(pixel, leaf): return True def allocatecoverbuffer(bounds): return {"isfullyzero": lambda: False} def writepixel(px, py, x, y, z, index): pixelval = (x & 0xFFF) | ((y & 0xFFF) << 12) | ((z & 0xFFF) << 24) | ((index & 0xFFFFFFF) << 36) return pixelval Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Multithread optimization through independent tile rendering; efficient occlusion culling using bit arrays for small bounding boxes; fast bounding box calculation using 4 vertices. Limitations: Requires specific hardware instructions ('addps', 'movmskps') for leaf node processing; may need override for older ATI or Intel video cards. When to use: When multithread optimization is desired and hardware supports the required instructions. When not to use: When using older ATI or Intel video cards without override, or when highest quality texture-mapping (trilinear filtering) is required on CPU-based emulation. PND3D was developed by Ken Silverman. It is used for volume rendering with sparse voxel octrees. The engine is available under a non-commercial license. gpdaniels/pnd3d, https://github.com/gpdaniels/pnd3d, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GigaVoxels Ray Traversal and Rendering
head: GigaVoxels, Brick-based Volume Rendering
body: GigaVoxels is a GPU-based volume rendering technique that uses an octree structure to manage brick-level data, traversing the tree to sample voxel data and performing front-to-back blending. It distinguishes itself from standard sparse voxel octree traversal by decoupling the geometric hierarchy from the volumetric data storage in a global brick pool, enabling efficient memory residency management and level-of-detail culling based on brick occupancy. Input: A ray defined by origin and direction; an octree structure where each node contains metadata and pointers to bricks; a global brick pool storing the actual voxel color and gradient data. Output: A final color and opacity value for the ray, accumulated via front-to-back blending. Octree Node Layout Each octree node is stored as a uvec4 (four unsigned 32-bit integers). The layout is as follows:.r (32 bits): Bit 31 (MSB): Node Type Flag. If set (0x40000000), the node is constant. Bits 30-20 (11 bits): Child Node Pointer Index (offset into the child node pool). Bit 31 (MSB of this field, distinct from Node Type): Brick Is Loaded Flag. If set (0x80000000), the brick data is resident in the GPU memory..g (32 bits): Bits 31-20 (12 bits): Brick Pointer S-coordinate (index into brick pool). Bits 19-10 (10 bits): Brick Pointer T-coordinate. Bits 9-0 (10 bits): Brick Pointer R-coordinate. If the node is constant, these bits store the constant color/alpha values packed as 8-bit integers (R, G, B, A)..b and.a: Not given in the sources. Brick Pool Color Texture: A 3D texture (BrickSampler, sampler3D) containing RGBA voxel data. Gradient Texture: A 3D texture containing RGB gradient data (used for lighting). Dimensions: Defined by BrickPoolDimension (total texels in the pool) and BrickDimension (texels per brick side). Border Voxels: Bricks include border voxels to facilitate seamless sampling across brick boundaries. Samplers OctTreeSampler: usampler3D (unsigned int 3D texture) representing the octree structure. BrickSampler: sampler3D (float 3D texture) for color data. JitterTexSampler: sampler2D. RayStepSize: Step size of the ray in world coordinates. BrickStepVector: Step size of the ray in brick pool coordinates. BrickDimension: Number of texels in a brick. RootVoxelHalfSize: Size of a voxel in the root node. BrickPoolDimension: Total dimensions of the brick pool texture. OctTreeDepthMinusOne: Depth of the octree minus one. MaxTreeTraversals: Maximum number of tree traversals allowed per ray. MaxNodesToPushThisFrame: Limit on nodes pushed to the usage list per frame. LodScalar: Scalar for Level of Detail calculations. 1. Ray-Node Intersection: Compute the minimum ray-box intersection time (t{min}) by iterating over the 6 planes of the current node's extent. Update plane D values based on nodeExtentMin and nodeExtentMax. Only consider intersections where the dot product of the ray direction and plane normal is positive (dirDotN > 0). 2. Advance Ray to Node Boundary: Calculate the number of steps required to reach the node boundary: numSteps = \lfloor distToNodeBoundary / rayStepSize \rfloor + 1. Update the ray world position: rayWorldPosition += rayDir \times (numSteps \times rayStepSize). 3. Traverse Node: Check if the node is constant using NodeIsConstant. If Constant: Retrieve the constant value using GetConstantValue. If constValue.a < 0.005, advance the ray to the exit of the current volume segment and return. Otherwise, loop numSteps times. In each step, advance rayWorldPosition by worldRayStep. If destination opacity dst.a > 0.995, advance remaining steps and return. Update src.a = 1.0 - (1.0 - src.a)^{sampleRatio} and src.rgb = sampleRatio. Update dst = (1.0 - dst.a) \times src + dst. If Non-Constant: Check if the brick is loaded using BrickIsLoaded. If loaded, retrieve the brick pointer using GetBrickPointer, sample the brick data from BrickSampler, and apply front-to-back blending. Determine child nodes using GetChildNodePointer and traverse them. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def NodeIsConstant(octTreeNode): return (octTreeNode[0] & 0x40000000) != 0 def GetChildNodePointer(octTreeNode): ptr = octTreeNode[0] return ((ptr >> 20) & 0x3FF, (ptr >> 10) & 0x3FF, ptr & 0x3FF) def BrickIsLoaded(octTreeNode): return (octTreeNode[0] & 0x80000000) != 0 def GetBrickPointer(octTreeNode, BrickPoolDimension): ptr = octTreeNode[1] s = (ptr >> 20) & 0x3FF t = (ptr >> 10) & 0x3FF r = ptr & 0x3FF return (s / BrickPoolDimension[0], t / BrickPoolDimension[1], r / BrickPoolDimension[2]) def GetConstantValue(octTreeNode): bits = octTreeNode[1] r = bits & 0xFF; bits >>= 8 g = bits & 0xFF; bits >>= 8 b = bits & 0xFF; bits >>= 8 a = bits & 0xFF return (r / 255.0, g / 255.0, b / 255.0, a / 255.0) def ComputeRayBoxIntersection(rayOrigin, rayDir, extentMin, extentMax): tMin = -float('inf') tMax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if rayDir[i] != 0.0: invDir = 1.0 / rayDir[i] t1 = (extentMin[i] - rayOrigin[i]) invDir t2 = (extentMax[i] - rayOrigin[i]) invDir if rayDir[i] > 0: tMin = max(tMin, t1) tMax = min(tMax, t2) else: tMin = max(tMin, t2) tMax = min(tMax, t1) else: if rayOrigin[i] < extentMin[i] or rayOrigin[i] > extentMax[i]: return -1.0 if tMin > tMax: return -1.0 return tMin def TraverseConstant(rayWorldPosition, rayDir, numSteps, sampleRatio, dst, RayStepSize, currentNode, BrickPoolDimension): constValue = GetConstantValue(currentNode) if constValue[3] < 0.005: rayWorldPosition = (rayWorldPosition[0] + rayDir[0] (numSteps RayStepSize), rayWorldPosition[1] + rayDir[1] (numSteps RayStepSize), rayWorldPosition[2] + rayDir[2] (numSteps RayStepSize)) return rayWorldPosition, dst worldRayStep = (rayDir[0] RayStepSize, rayDir[1] RayStepSize, rayDir[2] RayStepSize) for i in range(numSteps): rayWorldPosition = (rayWorldPosition[0] + worldRayStep[0], rayWorldPosition[1] + worldRayStep[1], rayWorldPosition[2] + worldRayStep[2]) if dst[3] > 0.995: remaining = numSteps - i - 1 rayWorldPosition = (rayWorldPosition[0] + rayDir[0] (remaining RayStepSize), rayWorldPosition[1] + rayDir[1] (remaining RayStepSize), rayWorldPosition[2] + rayDir[2] (remaining RayStepSize)) return rayWorldPosition, dst srca = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - constValue[3], sampleRatio) srcrgb = (constValue[0] sampleRatio, constValue[1] sampleRatio, constValue[2] sampleRatio) dst = ((1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[0] + dst[0], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[1] + dst[1], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[2] + dst[2], (1.0 - dst[3]) srca + dst[3]) return rayWorldPosition, dst def RenderRay(rayOrigin, rayDir, RayStepSize, currentNode, BrickPoolDimension): dst = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) rayWorldPosition = rayOrigin tMin = ComputeRayBoxIntersection(rayOrigin, rayDir, currentNode.extentMin, currentNode.extentMax) if tMin < 0: return dst distToNodeBoundary = tMin numSteps = int(distToNodeBoundary / RayStepSize) + 1 rayWorldPosition = (rayWorldPosition[0] + rayDir[0] (numSteps RayStepSize), rayWorldPosition[1] + rayDir[1] (numSteps RayStepSize), rayWorldPosition[2] + rayDir[2] (numSteps RayStepSize)) dst = TraverseConstant(rayWorldPosition, rayDir, numSteps, 1.0, dst, RayStepSize, currentNode, BrickPoolDimension) return dst Precision: Bit-packing requires careful handling of unsigned integer shifts to avoid sign extension errors. Boundary Conditions: The numSteps calculation must account for floating-point inaccuracies at node boundaries to prevent gaps or overlaps. Unloaded Bricks: If a brick is not loaded, the traversal must handle the missing data gracefully, either by skipping or triggering a load request. The provided sources do not detail the asynchronous loading mechanism. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the octree and the density of the volume. In the worst case, it is proportional to the number of voxels along the ray. However, constant nodes and empty space skipping significantly reduce the average case. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of nodes in the octree plus the number of resident bricks. The brick pool size is fixed based on BrickPoolDimension. Not given in the sources. Scales with the resolution of the brick pool and the depth of the octree. Larger brick dimensions reduce the number of nodes but increase memory per node. Strengths: Efficient memory usage through brick-based storage; supports LOD; GPU-friendly traversal. Limitations: Requires complex bit-packing; asynchronous loading adds complexity; fixed brick size may lead to inefficiencies for very small or very large features. Suitable for large-scale volume rendering on GPUs where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and the volume data has varying density. Not suitable for real-time applications with extremely high-frequency details that cannot be captured by the brick resolution. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Used in various visualization tools and research projects for rendering large-scale volumetric data. apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, https://github.com/apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Pruning
head: Importance-based Voxel Pruning
body: Voxel Pruning is a model compression technique for volumetric representations that reduces storage size by omitting voxels with low rendering importance scores. It operates on the observation that a small percentage of voxels contribute the majority of rendering importance, while the majority have minimal effect on the final image. Unlike sibling methods that focus on traversal acceleration (e.g., Sparse Voxel Traversal) or structural optimization (e.g., DeepBrick), Voxel Pruning directly modifies the data structure by removing inactive entries based on a learned importance metric. Inputs: A trained volumetric grid model (e.g., DVGO) containing density and color features for each voxel; a set of training views. Outputs: A pruned grid model with a subset of voxels retained. Data Structures: The method operates on a 3D grid where each voxel vl stores density and color features. The algorithm computes a scalar importance score Il for each voxel. Steps: 1. Ray Shooting and Point Scoring: Shoot a batch of rays through the images of the training views. For each sampling point \mathbf{x}i along these rays, calculate the ray termination probability \alphai and accumulated transmittance Ti. Compute the importance score of the sampling point: Ii = Ti \cdot \alphai \quad (3) 2. Voxel Score Assignment: Assign the importance score Ii of each sampling point to its neighboring voxels vl proportionally to the distance factor. The neighborhood \mathcal{N}l consists of sampling points within distance 1 from the voxel center. The total importance score for voxel vl is: Il = \sum{\mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{N}l} (1 - |\mathbf{v}l - \mathbf{x}i|) \cdot Ii \quad (4) where |\mathbf{v}l - \mathbf{x}i| \le 1. 3. Sorting: Sort all voxels in ascending order of their importance scores Il. 4. Threshold Selection: Select a pruning threshold \thetap using the quantile function to control the amount of importance to be pruned: \thetap = F^{-1}(\betap) \quad (6) where \betap is a hyperparameter representing the total amount of importance to be pruned. The cumulative score rate for a threshold \theta is defined as: \theta(\theta) = \frac{\sum Il \cdot \mathbf{1}\{Il < \theta\}}{\sum Il} \quad (5) where \mathbf{1}\{\cdot\} is the binary indicator function. 5. Pruning: For all voxels with importance score Il < \thetap, omit them from the grid model, including their densities and color features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelpruning(gridmodel, trainingviews, betap): """ gridmodel: Object containing voxel centers, densities, and colors. trainingviews: List of camera poses and images. betap: Hyperparameter for pruning ratio (0.0 to 1.0). """ voxelscores = {} # Step 1 & 2: Calculate importance scores for view in trainingviews: rays = generaterays(view) for ray in rays: # Perform volume rendering to get alpha and transmittance at each sample samples = raymarch(ray, gridmodel) for sample in samples: xi = sample.position alphai = sample.alpha Ti = sample.transmittance # Eq 3 Ii = Ti alphai # Find neighboring voxels within distance 1 neighbors = getneighboringvoxels(xi, gridmodel.voxelcenters, radius=1.0) for vl in neighbors: dist = distance(vl.center, xi) weight = 1.0 - dist if vl.id not in voxelscores: voxelscores[vl.id] = 0.0 voxelscores[vl.id] += weight Ii # Step 3: Sort voxels sortedvoxels = sortbyscore(voxelscores, ascending=True) # Step 4: Determine threshold # Calculate cumulative distribution to find the score corresponding to betap totalscore = sum(voxelscores.values()) targetprunedscore = totalscore betap currentprunedscore = 0.0 threshold = 0.0 for voxelid, score in sortedvoxels: currentprunedscore += score if currentprunedscore >= targetprunedscore: threshold = score break # Step 5: Prune prunedgrid = copy(gridmodel) for voxelid, score in voxelscores.items(): if score < threshold: prunedgrid.removevoxel(voxelid) return prunedgrid Parameters: \betap: Hyperparameter representing the total amount of importance to be pruned. Typical values are not explicitly given, but the method relies on this quantile-based selection to adapt to different scenes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The distance factor (1 - |\mathbf{v}l - \mathbf{x}i|) requires precise floating-point arithmetic to ensure correct weighting. Boundaries: The neighborhood definition |\mathbf{v}l - \mathbf{x}i| \le 1 must handle voxels near the grid boundaries correctly. Degenerate Input: If the grid is empty or has no training views, the scoring process cannot proceed. A 2D projection-based primitive scoring method that ranks primitives for pruning based on accumulated ray contributions across multiple synthesized views, utilizing view-dependent features like ray hits and transmittance. It generates 360 uniformly sampled views on a sphere, renders them, and scores primitives based on accumulated contributions. This method yields lower accuracy in volumetric settings compared to volume-based scoring (e.g., 48.76 dB vs 50.76 dB on Aneurysm data) because it does not integrate voxel intensities covered by each primitive. A pruning strategy that combines fractional anisotropy (FA) with intensity and scale cues to rank primitives. Combining FA with intensity and scale yields the best reconstruction quality compared to using only intensity and scale cues. A pruning strategy that computes a structure-aware importance score for each ellipsoid to remove redundant primitives while preserving structural fidelity. It defines coverage \Omegai as voxels where the primitive yields a non-negligible contribution (\tilde{P}i(v) \geq \epsilon with \epsilon = 1/255). The importance score is scorei = |\Omegai| \cdot Ii \cdot FAi, where Ii is the learned center intensity, |\Omegai| is the voxel coverage, and FAi is the fractional anisotropy. Primitives are ranked by scorei and the lowest-scoring ones are removed according to a preset pruning ratio. Time Complexity: The method requires shooting rays through training views and computing importance scores for all sampling points, which is proportional to the number of rays and samples. Sorting voxels is O(N \log N) where N is the number of voxels. Memory Complexity: Reduces model size by omitting voxels with low importance scores. The reduction depends on the threshold \thetap. Strengths: Reduces model size significantly (e.g., to 1 MB) while maintaining rendering quality. The adaptive threshold selection makes it general across different scenes or base models. Limitations: Requires training views for importance estimation. Projection-based scoring (LightGaussian) yields lower accuracy in volumetric settings. When to use: When model size is a critical constraint and a small percentage of voxels dominate rendering importance. When not to use: When high volumetric accuracy is required and projection-based scoring is used. Voxel Pruning was introduced in the paper "Compressing Volumetric Radiance Fields to 1 MB". The method is based on the observation that a small percentage of voxels contribute the majority of rendering importance. It is used to compress volumetric radiance fields, such as those in DVGO. name: DeepBrick
head: Deep Volume Raytracing
body: DeepBrick is a ray-marching kernel for deep volume raytracing that samples volumetric data stored in hierarchical "brick" structures, handling empty space skipping and alpha accumulation. It differs from standard sparse voxel traversal by operating on pre-integrated brick textures and adjusting sampling density based on a "sample ratio" relative to the brick's internal resolution, allowing for efficient rendering of deep volumes with variable step sizes. It builds on Sparse Voxel Traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, direction, and t-range; VDB leaf node reference; voxel delta (gvdb->vdel[0]); world position increment (wpt). Output: outBuf with a layout of 10 floats per pixel: indices 0-2 for color, 3 for mask, 4-6 for normal, 7 for depth, 8-9 for flow. Data Structures: Voxel Value (val): A vector containing color components (val.x, etc.) and density/alpha (val.w). Accumulated Color (clr): A vector containing accumulated color components (clr.x, etc.) and current transmittance (clr.w). Hit Point (hit): A vector where hit.x stores the front hit point (initialized to 0 if not set) and hit.y stores the weighted mean depth. Fetched Color (hclr): Temporary color value fetched from the brick texture. Parameters: SCNMINVAL: Threshold for skipping empty voxels during initial traversal. SCNALPHACUT: Threshold for stopping color accumulation based on current transtransmittance. MAXITER: Maximum number of iterations allowed per ray. SCNEXTINCT: Extinction coefficient. SCNALBEDO: Albedo multiplier. SCNPSTEP: Step size. Steps: 1. Initialization: Get the VDB leaf node using getNode. Compute the sample point in index coordinates p from world position wp and voxel delta gvdb->vdel[0]. Compute world increment wpt. Initialize val and hclr to zero. Initialize clr (accumulated color/transmittance) to zero. Record the front hit point hit.x if it is zero. 2. Empty Space Skipping: Loop while val.w < SCNMINVAL, iter < MAXITER, and p is within bounds: Transfer voxel value to val. Advance p, wp, and t.x. Increment iter. 3. Color Accumulation: Loop while clr.w > SCNALPHACUT, iter < MAXITER, and p is within bounds: Depth Buffer Test: Perform an optional depth buffer test. Transfer Voxel Value: Fetch voxel value into val. Compute Transmittance: Calculate transmittance for the current step: val.w = \exp(SCN\EXTINCT \cdot val.w \cdot SCN\PSTEP) where val.w is the voxel density, SCN\EXTINCT is the extinction coefficient, and SCN\PSTEP is the step size. Update Weighted Mean Depth: Update hit.y using the transmittance and step size. Fetch Color: Fetch color into hclr. Accumulate Color: Update accumulated color: clr.x += val.x \cdot clr.w \cdot (1 - val.w) \cdot SCN\ALBEDO \cdot hclr.x where val.x is the voxel color component, clr.w is current transmittance, and hclr.x is the fetched color. Update Transmittance: Update clr.w by multiplying with val.w (implicit in standard volume rendering, though not explicitly stated as a separate formula, it is required for the next iteration's clr.w check). Advance: Advance p, wp, and t.x. Increment iter. 4. Finalization: Clamp final color and alpha. Write results to outBuf. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deepbrickraycast(rayorigin, raydirection, raytmin, raytmax, vdbleaf, voxeldelta, scnminval, scnalphacut, maxiter, scnextinct, scnalbedo, scnpstep): # Initialization wp = rayorigin p = computeindexcoords(wp, voxeldelta) wpt = computeworldincrement(raydirection, voxeldelta) val = vec4(0.0) hclr = vec4(0.0) clr = vec4(0.0) # clr.w is transmittance hit = vec2(0.0) # hit.x is front hit point, hit.y is weighted mean depth iter = 0 # Empty Space Skipping while val.w < scnminval and iter < maxiter and iswithinbounds(p): val = transfervoxelvalue(p, vdbleaf) p += wpt wp += wpt iter += 1 # Color Accumulation while clr.w > scnalphacut and iter < maxiter and iswithinbounds(p): # Optional depth buffer test if performdepthbuffertest(wp, hit.x): break val = transfervoxelvalue(p, vdbleaf) # Compute Transmittance valwtransmittance = exp(scnextinct val.w scnpstep) # Update Weighted Mean Depth hit.y = updateweightedmeandepth(hit.y, valwtransmittance, scnpstep) # Fetch Color hclr = fetchcolor(p, vdbleaf) # Accumulate Color clr.x += val.x clr.w (1.0 - valwtransmittance) scnalbedo hclr.x clr.y += val.y clr.w (1.0 - valwtransmittance) scnalbedo hclr.y clr.z += val.z clr.w (1.0 - valwtransmittance) scnalbedo hclr.z # Update Transmittance clr.w = valwtransmittance # Advance p += wpt wp += wpt iter += 1 # Finalization clr = clamp(clr, 0.0, 1.0) # Write to output buffer (10 floats per pixel) # Indices 0-2: Color, 3: Mask, 4-6: Normal, 7: Depth, 8-9: Flow outbuf[0:3] = clr[0:3] outbuf[3] = 1.0 # Mask outbuf[4:7] = computenormal(wp, vdbleaf) # Placeholder for normal computation outbuf[7] = hit.y # Depth outbuf[8:10] = computeflow(wp, vdbleaf) # Placeholder for flow computation return outbuf Brick Traversal is a ray-marching kernel that samples a volumetric brick texture, adjusts alpha and RGB values for variable step sizes, and composites the result into a destination color using front-to-back alpha blending. It accounts for a "sample ratio" (r) between the ray step and the brick's internal resolution to adjust sampling density across hierarchical levels. It is chosen when hierarchical brick structures are used to store volumetric data, allowing for efficient traversal and sampling at different resolutions. See Brick Traversal. Node Processing Rules define how different types of nodes in the hierarchical structure are handled during traversal: Loaded Brick: If the node is a brick with available data, perform regular ray-marching inside its data. Unloaded Brick: If the brick is not loaded (e.g., dynamic loading failure), use the average color stored in the node and accumulate it based on the distance the ray travels through the brick (using pre-integration). Empty Node: If the node is empty, ignore it (skip processing). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed along the ray, but reduced by empty space skipping and hierarchical traversal. The complexity is O(N) where N is the number of non-empty voxels intersected by the ray. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the VDB leaf nodes and brick textures. Hierarchical structures allow for sparse storage, reducing memory usage compared to dense voxel grids. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with hierarchical data structures, as empty regions are skipped. Performance is dependent on the density of the volume and the efficiency of the empty space skipping. Strengths: Efficient handling of large, sparse volumes; supports variable step sizes and hierarchical data structures; handles unloaded bricks gracefully. Limitations: Requires pre-integrated brick textures; performance may degrade in highly dense volumes where empty space skipping is less effective. When to use: Suitable for rendering large, sparse volumetric datasets where hierarchical storage and empty space skipping are beneficial. When not to use: Not ideal for dense volumes where the overhead of hierarchical traversal outweighs the benefits of empty space skipping. DeepBrick is associated with deep volume raytracing techniques, often implemented in conjunction with VDB (OpenVDB) data structures for sparse volumetric data. The method is described in the context of adaptive sampling and reconstruction for volume visualization and interactive exploration of procedural volumes. name: Brick Traversal
head: Ray Marching with Alpha Compositing & Sample Ratio Adjustment, TraverseBrick
body: Brick Traversal is a ray-marching kernel that samples a volumetric brick texture, adjusts alpha and RGB values for variable step sizes, and composites the result into a destination color using front-to-back alpha blending. It accounts for a "sample ratio" (r) between the ray step and the brick's internal resolution to adjust sampling density across hierarchical levels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin (\mathbf{O}), ray direction (\mathbf{D}), brick bounds, brick texture data, accumulated destination color/alpha (c{dst}, a{dst}), global ray step size (RayStepSize), current brick depth (curDepth), octree depth minus one (OctTreeDepthMinusOne), and brick step size scalar (k{BrickStepSizeScalar}). Output: Composite color (c{dst}) and accumulated alpha (a{dst}). Data Structures: The method operates on the following variables: dst: Accumulated destination color and alpha. src: Fetched texel color and alpha. rayWorldPosition: Current world-space ray position. curBrickRayPos: Current brick-local ray position. Parameters: r (sampleRatio): The ratio of the ray step size to the brick's effective voxel size. It is computed as r = k{BrickStepSizeScalar}^{OctTreeDepthMinusOne - curDepth} for constant nodes, or derived from curBrickDepth for textured bricks. Steps: 1. Compute Intersection: Calculate the time to exit the brick bounds (t{exit}) using a standard ray-box intersection routine. 2. Calculate Steps: Determine the adjusted ray step size: rayStepSize = RayStepSize \times r. Calculate the number of steps: numSteps = \lfloor t{exit} / rayStepSize \rfloor + 1. 3. Initialize: Set rayWorldPosition and curBrickRayPos to the brick entry point. Initialize c{dst} = (0,0,0,0) and a{dst} = 0. 4. Loop: For i from 0 to numSteps - 1: a. Advance World Ray: Update the world position: rayWorldPosition += worldRayStep where worldRayStep = \mathbf{D} \times RayStepSize. b. Early Exit Check: If a{dst} > 0.995, subtract (i+1) from numSteps, advance rayWorldPosition by the remaining steps to the exit point, and return. c. Fetch Texel: Sample the brick texture at curBrickRayPos to get source color c{src} and alpha a{src}. d. Adjust Values: Compute adjusted alpha and color: a{adj} = 1 - (1 - a{src})^r and c{adj} = c{src} \times r. e. Composite: Update the destination using front-to-back blending: c{dst} = (1 - a{dst}) \times c{adj} + c{dst}. The accumulated alpha updates as a{dst} = a{dst} + a{adj} \times (1 - a{dst}). f. Advance Brick Ray: Update the brick-space ray position: curBrickRayPos += brickRayStep where brickRayStep = \mathbf{D} \times rayStepSize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computerayboxintersection(origin, direction, boundsmin, boundsmax): # Standard slab method tmin = (boundsmin - origin) / direction tmax = (boundsmax - origin) / direction tenter = max(tmin) texit = min(tmax) return texit if tenter <= texit else -1.0 def sampletexture(tex, pos): # Standard 3D texture fetch; returns (color, alpha) return tex[pos] def bricktraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, brickboundsmin, brickboundsmax, bricktexture, dstcolor, dstalpha, raystepsize, curdepth, octtreedepthminusone, kscalar): texit = computerayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, brickboundsmin, brickboundsmax) if texit < 0: return dstcolor, dstalpha sampleratio = kscalar (octtreedepthminusone - curdepth) stepsize = raystepsize sampleratio numsteps = int(texit / stepsize) + 1 # Initialize positions to brick entry point curbrickpos = rayorigin + raydirection texit rayworldpos = rayorigin + raydirection texit worldstep = raydirection raystepsize brickstep = raydirection stepsize for i in range(numsteps): rayworldpos += worldstep if dstalpha > 0.995: remaining = numsteps - (i + 1) rayworldpos += worldstep remaining break srccolor, srcalpha = sampletexture(bricktexture, curbrickpos) adjalpha = 1.0 - (1.0 - srcalpha) sampleratio adjcolor = srccolor sampleratio dstcolor = (1.0 - dstalpha) adjcolor + dstcolor dstalpha = dstalpha + adjalpha (1.0 - dstalpha) curbrickpos += brickstep return dstcolor, dstalpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Exit Positioning: When a{dst} > 0.995, the loop breaks. It is critical to advance rayWorldPosition to the exact exit point of the brick to prevent visual artifacts in subsequent rays or passes. Not given in the sources. name: Voxel Grid Raycasting
head: DDA Ray Tracing, Ray Marching through Voxel Grid, Regular Grid Traversal, Uniform Grid Raycasting, Voxel Ray Marching, Voxel Ray Tracing with Voxel Marching, Voxelization Raycasting
body: Voxel Grid Raycasting is a rendering technique that stores scene geometry in a 3D voxel grid and traces rays through the grid by stepping from voxel to voxel to determine intersections and surface normals. It solves the problem of efficiently determining ray-voxel intersections without performing explicit geometric intersection tests against primitives. Unlike hierarchical structures like BVH or KD-trees which partition primitives, this method partitions space into a fixed uniform grid, allowing rays to step through empty cells rapidly. It is distinct from Sparse Voxel Traversal by assuming a dense, regular grid layout rather than a sparse octree or brick-based structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D (normalized), voxel grid dimensions, voxel size (bin size), and the voxel data buffer. Output: Intersection distance, hit position, surface normal, and optionally accumulated color. Data Structures: The voxel grid is typically stored as a 1D array or storage buffer. Format 1 (S1): array<u32> where each u32 represents a single voxel. A value of 0u indicates an empty voxel; non-zero values indicate occupied voxels, encoding color via unpack4x8unorm. Format 2 (S2): int array of size 16 \times 16 \times 16 (4096 elements), bound as a storage buffer. Indexing: For Format 1: index = x + y \cdot W + z \cdot (W \cdot H), where W is chunk width and H is chunk height. For Format 2: index = (x \cdot 16 + z) \cdot 16 + y. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Normalize ray direction: ray = \text{normalize}(ray\end - ray\start). Calculate initial grid position: grid\pos = \lfloor (start\pos - min\pos) \cdot inv\voxel\size \rfloor. Determine direction indicators: ray\dir\i = \text{sign}(ray\dir) (1 if >0, -1 if \le 0). Calculate step deltas: dt = |voxel\size / ray\dir|. Calculate initial time to next boundary t{max} based on the fractional part of the start position. Edge Case: If a ray component is 0, set corresponding t{max} and dt to FLTMIN to avoid division by zero. 2. Traversal Loop: Find the axis with the minimum t{max} value: last\axis = \text{argmin}(t{max}). Increment grid position on that axis: grid\pos[last\axis] += ray\dir\i[last\axis]. Update distance traveled: dist = t{max}[last\axis]. Advance t{max} for the stepped axis: t{max}[last\axis] += dt[last\axis]. Check for hit: Load voxel data at grid\pos. If occupied, calculate normal and terminate. 3. Intersection & Normal: If a hit occurs, the surface normal is derived from the axis of entry: normal = \text{axis\dir\normal}(last\axis, ray\dir). If last\axis is the initial state (e.g., 3), retain previous normal or handle as primary hit. 4. Ray Bouncing (Optional): If stochastic reflection is enabled, spawn a new ray from start\pos + dist \cdot ray\dir + \epsilon \cdot normal. \epsilon is a small offset (e.g., voxel\size \cdot 0.01) to prevent self-intersection. Attenuate color and repeat traversal up to a max depth (e.g., 3 bounces). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelgridraycast(origin, direction, voxelgrid, voxelsize, griddims): # 1. Initialization ray = normalize(direction) # Handle zero components to avoid division by zero invray = 1.0 / ray invray[ray == 0] = 0.0 # Initial voxel coordinate currentvoxel = floor(origin / voxelsize) # Step direction per axis step = vec3(1 if ray.x >= 0 else -1, 1 if ray.y >= 0 else -1, 1 if ray.z >= 0 else -1) # Distance to next boundary # Boundary position = (currentvoxel + step) voxelsize nextboundary = (currentvoxel + step) voxelsize # tMax: distance along ray to next boundary # If ray component is 0, tMax is effectively infinity (handled by FLTMIN in C-like impls) tmax = vec3( (nextboundary.x - origin.x) invray.x if ray.x != 0 else float('inf'), (nextboundary.y - origin.y) invray.y if ray.y != 0 else float('inf'), (nextboundary.z - origin.z) invray.z if ray.z != 0 else float('inf')) # tDelta: distance along ray to traverse one voxel width tdelta = vec3( voxelsize invray.x step.x if ray.x != 0 else float('inf'), voxelsize invray.y step.y if ray.y != 0 else float('inf'), voxelsize invray.z step.z if ray.z != 0 else float('inf')) # 2. Traversal Loop for i in range(MAXITERATIONS): # Check bounds if not isinsidegrid(currentvoxel, griddims): return MISS # Check occupancy if isoccupied(voxelgrid, currentvoxel): # Determine normal based on which axis we just crossed # The axis with the smallest tmax was the one we just stepped across # In this simplified loop, we assume we check occupancy AFTER stepping or # use the tmax comparison to determine entry axis. # Standard DDA checks occupancy of the NEW voxel. normal = getnormalfromtmax(tmax, step) return HIT(currentvoxel, tmax, normal) # Find axis with minimum tmax axis = argmin(tmax) # Step on that axis currentvoxel[axis] += step[axis] # Update tmax for that axis tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] return MISS A technique for ray tracing isosurfaces defined within cells of 8 voxels using an octree that stores scalar values at voxel centers. It establishes a dual relationship between voxels and cells by logically shifting scalar positions backward by half a voxel width, allowing the ray tracer to intersect 8-voxel cell primitives defined by the stored leaf values. Unlike methods that expand storage to hold complete cell data, this method retrieves forward neighbors at intersection time, maintaining single scalar storage per leaf. A fast voxel traversal algorithm for rendering volumetric data defined on a spherical coordinate grid. It extends the cartesian fast voxel traversal method by Amanatides and Woo to non-cartesian grids, iterating through radial, polar, and azimuthal voxel boundaries to determine the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray. Unlike Voxel Grid Raycasting which assumes axis-aligned bounding boxes, this method handles the curved boundaries of spherical sectors, using line-sphere intersection for radial steps and 2D segment intersection for angular boundaries. A spatial acceleration structure that divides a scene's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) into a fixed-size, uniform 3D grid of cells (voxels). It accelerates ray tracing by allowing rays to step through empty cells without performing primitive intersection tests, reducing the number of expensive geometric queries. Unlike hierarchical structures like BVH or KD-trees, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, meaning primitives can belong to multiple cells, whereas BVH partitions primitives into disjoint sets. It is particularly effective on GPUs for scenes with uniform data distribution due to high spatial locality and cache efficiency. A raymarching technique for voxel grids that advances a ray by stepping to the nearest intersection with the integer grid planes separating voxel layers. It solves the problem of traversing a dense voxel volume to find the first solid voxel by checking occupancy at each plane boundary. Unlike shape-assisted siblings such as Sphere Assisted Raymarching or Optimised Voxel Ray Marching, it does not store auxiliary distance fields or shape metadata, relying solely on the geometric structure of the grid. This makes it simple to implement but fragile in empty space, as it never skips more than one voxel per step. A voxel-based ray tracing system using Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal through a 128³ block-occupancy grid to provide global illumination (GI) and specular reflection fallbacks. It serves as a drop-in replacement for Screen-Space Ray Tracing (SSRT) for GI and a fallback for Screen-Space Reflections (SSR) when coverage is incomplete, combining sky occlusion with Light Propagation Volume (LPV) colour bleeding. A fixed-step ray traversal algorithm for voxel-based scenes that minimizes computational overhead by keeping block lookups within the current working chunk. It builds on Voxel Grid Raycasting by replacing global coordinate arithmetic with bitwise operations for chunk indexing, thereby reducing the number of bitshifts, masks, and multiplication operations required per step. A ray-marching or voxel-intersection algorithm that traverses the RLE4 compressed volume structure (Map4) to find the first occupied voxel along a ray or to colorize a voxel based on its position. It uses the slab-based RLE encoding to skip empty space efficiently. A search algorithm used by voxel resolve and GI update to find the pixel's voxel again in the brick named by the visibility buffer. It finds the cell holding the ray's point at the stored depth, then the two cells along each axis whose centers lie nearest that point, stopping at the first cell whose hit gives the stored depth again, bit for bit. A voxel's test depends only on the ray and the voxel, ensuring every pass meets it at the same t. A narrow band strategy that does not use any solver. When the algorithm reaches a narrow band voxel, it immediately returns a hit, resulting in a voxelization of the scene. Manages transformed voxel objects by storing local acceleration structures and applying inverse rotations during ray queries. Rays are transformed into instance local space via inverse rotation (transpose, since the matrix is orthogonal). The VoxelInstance contains a local BrickPool (BLAS), rotation matrix, and bounding sphere. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels traversed along the ray. In empty space, this is proportional to the distance divided by voxel size. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the total number of voxels in the grid. The grid must be stored in memory, typically as a 1D array. Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to regular memory access patterns and lack of branching in empty space. However, performance degrades in dense scenes or when rays traverse many empty voxels without skipping them (unlike sparse methods). Strengths: Simple implementation, no preprocessing overhead for hierarchy construction, excellent cache locality on uniform grids. Limitations: Memory usage scales with the cube of the grid resolution, making it unsuitable for very large scenes without sparsity techniques. Precision issues can occur with large coordinates or small voxel sizes. Voxel Grid Raycasting is a fundamental technique in volume rendering and voxel-based games. It is often associated with the "DDA" (Digital Differential Analyzer) algorithm for grid traversal, originally described by Amanatides and Woo. It has been widely used in real-time applications such as Teardown and various GPU-based ray tracing demos. The method is a core component of many voxel engines and is frequently compared to or combined with sparse voxel octrees for larger scale scenes. newDINO/voxelraydemo, https://github.com/newDINO/voxelraydemo, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) SamCZ/RayTracer, https://github.com/SamCZ/RayTracer, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) michschw/GpuPro3Vox, https://github.com/michschw/GpuPro3Vox, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Kurble/amethystvoxel, https://github.com/Kurble/amethystvoxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) feat(render): voxels splatted to the pixels their footprints cover (ADR-0061), https://github.com/SugalAbubaker/nepheline/pull/115, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Rendering piecewise approximations of SDFs through analytic intersections, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cag.2024.103981, fetched 2026-10-27 NiekMSoftware/bad-apple-voxel-raytracer, https://github.com/NiekMSoftware/bad-apple-voxel-raytracer, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping
head: Cell Primitive Definition, Logical Shift Mapping, Logical Shift for Ray Tracing, Scalar Field Remapping
body: Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping is a technique for ray tracing isosurfaces defined within cells of 8 voxels using an octree that stores scalar values at voxel centers. It establishes a dual relationship between voxels and cells by logically shifting scalar positions backward by half a voxel width, allowing the ray tracer to intersect 8-voxel cell primitives defined by the stored leaf values. Unlike methods that expand storage to hold complete cell data, this method retrieves forward neighbors at intersection time, maintaining single scalar storage per leaf. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree structure storing scalar values at voxel centers, where each leaf node contains a single scalar datum v. Output: Intersection points with an isosurface defined within cells formed by 8 adjacent voxels. Data Structures: Octree: Nodes contain scalar values at their centers, and leaf nodes store a single scalar value v. Cell Primitive: A box defined by 8 vertices, where the vertices correspond to the mapped positions of 8 adjacent voxels in the octree. Mapping Logic: 1. Logical Shift: The position of all scalars is logically shifted backward by half a unit of voxel width to re-map the scalar field from voxel centers to cell corners. 2. Corner Mapping: Each voxel is mapped to the lower-left corner (minimum vertex) of a cell. 3. Boundary Condition: Values outside the octree data boundary are defined to be zero. Intersection Process: When a ray traverses an octree leaf node at indices (i, j, k) with a datum v, the ray intersects a box (cell) where (i, j, k) is mapped to the minimum vertex, and the remaining 7 vertices are formed by the forward neighbors of the voxel at (i, j, k) in the octree. Neighbor Retrieval: Instead of expanding each voxel to contain its forward neighbors (which would require 8 times the storage), the method retrieves the 7 forward neighbors of a voxel at intersection time. For a volume stored in a 3D array, querying these neighbors is a trivial array index operation. For an octree, this requires point location to retrieve the voxel values of the forward neighbors, where full top-down point location from the root is O(\log(N)) but neighbor-finding techniques can significantly reduce this cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectcell(rayorigin, raydirection, octree, isovalue): """ Intersect a ray with an isosurface defined by voxel-cell duality. """ # Standard octree traversal to find the leaf node intersected by the ray leafnode = octree.traverse(rayorigin, raydirection) if leafnode is None: return None # Get the scalar value at the current leaf node (voxel center) vcenter = leafnode.scalarvalue # Determine the indices (i, j, k) of the current leaf node i, j, k = leafnode.indices # Helper function to get scalar value, returning 0 for out-of-bounds def getscalar(idxi, idxj, idxk): # Standard octree point location to find the node at (idxi, idxj, idxk) node = octree.pointlocation(idxi, idxj, idxk) if node is None: return 0.0 # Boundary condition: values outside octree are zero return node.scalarvalue # Retrieve the 8 corner values for the cell # The current voxel is mapped to the minimum vertex (lower-left corner) # Neighbors are at (i+1, j, k), (i, j+1, k), (i, j, k+1), etc. corners = [ getscalar(i, j, k), # Current voxel (min corner) getscalar(i+1, j, k), # Neighbor in x getscalar(i, j+1, k), # Neighbor in y getscalar(i+1, j+1, k), # Neighbor in x,y getscalar(i, j, k+1), # Neighbor in z getscalar(i+1, j, k+1), # Neighbor in x,z getscalar(i, j+1, k+1), # Neighbor in y,z getscalar(i+1, j+1, k+1) # Neighbor in x,y,z (max corner) ] # Standard trilinear ray-cube intersection or Marching Cubes is applied # to the 8 corner values to find the isosurface intersection. # The sources do not specify the exact reconstruction algorithm. Parameters: Isovalue: The threshold value for the isosurface extraction. Not given in the sources. Voxel Width: The unit of voxel width used for the logical shift. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Storage Expansion: Storing each cell completely by expanding each voxel to contain its forward neighbors requires 8 times the storage of the original volume, which contradicts the goal of ray tracing compressed data. Boundary Handling: Values outside the octree data boundary are defined to be zero. Performance: For octrees, retrieving forward neighbors requires point location, which is more intensive than array indexing. Full top-down point location is O(\log(N)), but neighbor-finding techniques can reduce this cost. Ray walking in spherical coordinates. Not given in the sources. Ray tracing on a regular grid structure. Not given in the sources. Marching planes for volume rendering. Not given in the sources. Voxel-based ray tracing for global illumination and specular reflections. Not given in the sources. Optimized voxel ray marching techniques. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Neighbor retrieval in an octree is more intensive than in a 3D array, with full top-down point location at O(\log(N)) reduced by neighbor-finding techniques. Memory Complexity: Single scalar storage per leaf node, avoiding the 8x storage expansion required by naive cell expansion. Strengths: Allows ray tracing of compressed octree data without expanding storage, and permits traversal of interior nodes of the octree volume. Limitations: Neighbor retrieval in octrees is more complex and potentially slower than in regular grids. When to Use: When ray tracing isosurfaces from compressed octree volumes where storage efficiency is critical. When Not to Use: When neighbor retrieval performance is critical and the data is stored in a regular grid, where array indexing is trivial. Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping was introduced in the context of interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The method leverages the dual relationship between voxels and cells to efficiently ray trace isosurfaces defined within cells of 8 voxels. The approach of retrieving forward neighbors at intersection time is attributed to Parker et al.. name: Spherical Volume Ray Walking
head: Amanatides and Woo extension to spherical grids, Fast Voxel Traversal Over Spherical Grids, Spherical Volume Rendering (SVR) Algorithm, walkSphericalVolume
body: Spherical Volume Ray Walking is a fast voxel traversal algorithm for rendering volumetric data defined on a spherical coordinate grid. It extends the cartesian fast voxel traversal method by Amanatides and Woo to non-cartesian grids, iterating through radial, polar, and azimuthal voxel boundaries to determine the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray. Unlike Voxel Grid Raycasting which assumes axis-aligned bounding boxes, this method handles the curved boundaries of spherical sectors, using line-sphere intersection for radial steps and 2D segment intersection for angular boundaries. Inputs: ray (origin O as bound vector, direction D as unit free vector), grid (spherical voxel grid with parameters sphereCenter, numRadialSections, numPolarSections, numAzimuthalSections, minBound, maxBound, deltaRadiiSquared(r), deltaPhi(), deltaTheta(), sphereMaxBoundAzi(), sphereMinBoundAzi(), sphereMaxBoundPolar(), sphereMinBoundPolar(), sphereMaxRadius(), pMaxPolar(i), pMaxAzimuthal(i), centerToPolarBound(i), centerToAzimuthalBound(i)), and time range tbegin, tend. Outputs: List of Voxel structs containing {radial, polar, azimuthal} indices and optional exitt. Voxel: {radial: int, polar: int, azimuthal: int, exitt: float}. HitParameters: {tMax: float, tStep: int} where tStep is -1, 0, or 1. RaySegment: {P1: BoundVec3, P2: BoundVec3, NZDI: int}. LineSegment: {P1: float, P2: float}. BoundVec3, FreeVec3, UnitVec3: 3D vector types for bound, free, and normalized coordinates respectively. Unverified code. entryradiussquared = grid.deltaradiisquared(vectorindex) entryradius = grid.deltaradius() (grid.numradialsections() - vectorindex) rsvd = rsv.dot(rsv) v = rsv.dot(ray.direction()) rsvdminusvsquared = rsvd - v v if entryradiussquared <= rsvdminusvsquared: return [] d = math.sqrt(entryradiussquared - rsvdminusvsquared) trayexit = ray.timeofintersectionat(v + d) if trayexit < 0.0: return [] trayentrance = ray.timeofintersectionat(v - d) currentradialvoxel = radialentrancevoxel + (1 if rayoriginisoutsidegrid else 0) Ppolar = [None] (grid.numpolarsections() + 1) Pazimuthal = [None] (grid.numazimuthalsections() + 1) # Sources do not provide the implementation for initializevoxelboundarysegments. if rayoriginisoutsidegrid: raysphere = grid.spherecenter() - ray.pointatparameter(trayentrance) elif sedfromcenter == 0.0: raysphere = rsv - ray.direction() else: raysphere = rsv currentpolarvoxel = initializeangularvoxelid(grid, grid.numpolarsections(), raysphere, Ppolar, raysphere.y, grid.spherecenter.y, entryradius) if currentpolarvoxel >= grid.numpolarsections(): return [] currentazimuthalvoxel = initializeangularvoxelid(grid, (self.P1[self.NZDI] + self.raysegment[self.NZDI] intersectparameter - ray.origin()[self.NZDI]) ray.invdirection()[self.NZDI] class BoundVec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, other): return FreeVec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def getitem(self, idx): return [self.x, self.y, self.z][idx] class FreeVec3: def init(self, x, y, z): other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def squaredlength(self): return self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2 class UnitVec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def getitem(self, idx): return [self.x, self.y, self.z][idx] class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction self.inversedirection = UnitVec3(1.0/direction.x, 1.0/direction.y, 1.0/direction.z) self.NZDindex = 0 if direction.x != 0 else (1 if direction.y != 0 else 2) def pointatparameter(self, t): return BoundVec3(self.origin.x + self.direction.x t, self.origin.y + self.direction.y t, self.origin.z + self.direction.z t) def timeofintersectionat(self, discriminantv): return self.direction[self.NZDindex] discriminantv self.inversedirection[self.NZDindex] def nonzerodirectionindex(self): return self.NZDindex def invdirection(self): return self.inversedirection class VoxelIntersectionType: Radial = 1 Polar = 2 Azimuthal = 3 RadialPolar = 4 RadialAzimuthal = 5 PolarAzimuthal = 6 RadialPolarAzimuthal = 7 DOUBLEMAX: float('inf'), used as infinity for tMax when no intersection is found. perturbedt: 0.1, used to perturb the ray direction when handling degenerate cases where tmin == tmax in angular hit. Tangential radial hit: when tentrance == texit and tentrance > t, the ray is tangent to the radial sphere boundary. Handled by setting radialstephastransitioned = true and returning tStep = 0. Degenerate angular intersection: when tmin == tmax and both are within bounds, the ray intersects at a single point on the boundary. Handled by perturbing the ray direction by 0.1 units and recalculating the voxel ID to determine the step direction. Benchmarks on 8 × 1400 MHz CPUs (L1 Data 32 KiB × 4, L1 Instruction 32 KiB × 4, L2 Unified 256 KiB × 4, L3 Unified 6144 KiB × 1). 128² rays, 64³ voxels: Mean 103 ms, Median 103 ms, Std Dev 1.1 ms. 512² rays, 128³ voxels: Mean 3187 ms, Median 3180 ms, Std Dev 8.3 ms. Scaling is roughly linear with ray count and voxel count, consistent with traversal algorithms. Strengths: Handles spherical grids efficiently without converting to cartesian. Limitations: Requires precomputed boundary segments and angular voxel ID calculations, which add overhead for non-spherical scenes. Origin: Developed by Chris Gyurgyik, Ariel Kellison, and Youhan Yuan as an extension to the yt open-source data analysis and visualization package. Based on Amanatides and Woo's 1987 seminal paper on fast voxel traversal for ray tracing. name: Plane Marching
head: Raymarching Plane Intersections
body: Plane Marching is a raymarching technique for voxel grids that advances a ray by stepping to the nearest intersection with the integer grid planes separating voxel layers. It solves the problem of traversing a dense voxel volume to find the first solid voxel by checking occupancy at each plane boundary. Unlike shape-assisted siblings such as Sphere Assisted Raymarching or Optimised Voxel Ray Marching, it does not store auxiliary distance fields or shape metadata, relying solely on the geometric structure of the grid. This makes it simple to implement but fragile in empty space, as it never skips more than one voxel per step. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin p0 (voxel-unit space), ray direction d (voxel-unit space), voxel grid texture voxels (3D texture containing color/alpha), voxelGridSize (dimensions of the grid in voxels), maxDistToCheck (maximum traversal distance). Output: Color vec4 of the first solid voxel encountered, or transparent black if no solid voxel is found within maxDistToCheck. Data Structures: voxels: A 3D texture where each texel stores the color and alpha of a voxel. The alpha channel determines solidity (c.a > 0). The texture coordinates are normalized to [0, 1] based on voxelGridSize. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize step distance t = 0. 2. Loop while t \le \text{maxDistToCheck}: a. Calculate current position p = p0 + d \cdot t. b. Convert p to texture coordinates by dividing by voxelGridSize. c. If the sampled alpha c.a > 0, return c. d. Calculate the distance to the next integer grid plane along each axis. e. Update t by adding the smallest positive delta plus a small epsilon. Formulas: The distance to the next plane intersection along each axis is computed using the ray direction d and current position p. In voxel-unit-space (where one voxel is 1x1x1 units), the delta for each axis component is: \text{deltas}i = \frac{\text{step}(0, di) - \text{fract}(pi)}{di} Where: i \in \{x, y, z\} \text{step}(0, di) returns 1 if di \ge 0, else 0. This effectively computes \lceil pi \rceil - pi for positive directions and \lfloor pi \rfloor - pi for negative directions. \text{fract}(pi) is the fractional part of pi (pi - \lfloor pi \rfloor). di is the i-th component of the ray direction. The step size to advance is the minimum of these deltas, ensuring the ray moves to the closest plane intersection: t{\text{new}} = t + \max(\min(\text{deltas}x, \text{deltas}y, \text{deltas}z), \epsilon) Where \epsilon is a tiny constant to prevent infinite loops due to floating-point precision errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def planemarch(p0, d, voxels, voxelgridsize, maxdisttocheck, epsilon=1e-6): # sample3dtexture is a standard trilinear 3D texture lookup returning vec4 t = 0.0 while t <= maxdisttocheck: # Calculate current position p = p0 + d t # Sample voxel color texcoords = p / voxelgridsize c = sample3dtexture(voxels, texcoords) # Check for solidity if c.a > 0: return c # Calculate deltas to next plane boundaries deltas = [] for i in range(3): stepval = 1.0 if d[i] >= 0 else 0.0 fracval = p[i] - math.floor(p[i]) deltas.append((stepval - fracval) / d[i]) # Find the minimum positive delta to step to the closest plane # Add epsilon to guarantee progress and avoid floating point errors t += max(min(deltas), epsilon) return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Parameters: epsilon: A small constant (e.g., 10^{-6}) added to the step size to guarantee progress and prevent infinite loops caused by floating-point inaccuracies. The exact value is not specified in the sources but must be "tiny". Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating Point Errors: Accumulation of floating-point errors can cause "tunneling" (skipping voxels) and subtle artifacts. The epsilon helps but does not fully eliminate this fragility. Degenerate Performance: In empty space or when the target voxel is far away, the algorithm checks every single voxel along the ray path because it never moves more than one voxel at a time. This leads to poor performance in degenerate cases, such as a single solid voxel in the corner of a large empty grid. Fillrate Limitation: The technique is fragment shader heavy and is likely to be fillrate limited on typical hardware. Stores radius data in empty voxels to skip large distances. Choose when performance in sparse volumes is critical. Optimizes traversal logic with early exits and culling. Choose for better performance in complex scenes. Maps voxels to cells for different traversal strategies. Choose for alternative spatial indexing. Uses spherical stepping for non-axis-aligned volumes. Choose for spherical volume representations. General regular grid traversal. Choose for non-voxel regular structures. Extends ray marching for global illumination. Choose for advanced lighting. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by the ray. In the worst case (empty space), N is proportional to the distance to the first solid voxel or the grid boundary. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the total number of voxels in the grid, as the entire voxel set must be loaded into a 3D texture. Memory usage is data-independent regarding sparsity; a 32x32x32 grid always consumes the same memory regardless of how many voxels are solid. Measured Performance: In a degenerate case (32x32x32 grid with a single solid voxel in the far corner), Plane Marching shows vastly worse performance compared to shape-assisted techniques. Strengths: Performant in parallelized environments (e.g., GPUs), requires little upfront computation, and is straightforward to implement. Limitations: Fragile due to floating-point errors, fillrate limited, and inefficient in empty space. When to Use: Simple voxel rendering where performance is not critical or the volume is dense. When Not to Use: Sparse volumes, large empty spaces, or when high performance is required. Plane Marching is described as one of the most interesting ways to render voxels, performant and parallelizable. It is based on the concept of raymarching plane intersections, where a ray is advanced along the planes separating voxel layers. The technique is often compared to Inigo Quilez's ray marching work, though Quilez's work primarily focuses on signed distance fields, whereas Plane Marching uses unsigned distance fields (grid planes). The method was popularized in the context of voxel rendering for real-time applications, such as Minecraft-like games, by developers like Caleb Leak.
