name: RLE4 Ray Tracing
head: Map4 Traversal
body: RLE4 Ray Tracing is a ray-marching and voxel-intersection algorithm that traverses an RLE4 (Run-Length Encoded 4D) compressed volume structure, also known as Map4, to locate the first occupied voxel along a ray or to colorize a voxel based on its position. It distinguishes itself from standard voxel grid traversal by using slab-based RLE encoding to skip empty space efficiently, reducing the number of memory accesses required to find occupied regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by a target voxel coordinate (x, y, z) within the volume bounds, and the RLE4 compressed volume data structure (map4). Output: The color value of the voxel at (x, y, z) if occupied, or termination if empty. Data Structures: The map4 structure contains: sx: The width of the volume in voxels (X dimension). slabs: A pointer to an array of ushort (16-bit unsigned integers) representing the slab map. The layout is indexed by x + z sx. texture: A pointer to the start of the texture/color data, which follows the slab map in memory. Each entry in the slabs array for a specific (x, z) coordinate consists of a sequence of ushort values: 1. len1: The number of slab segments in the first run. 2. len2: The number of slab segments in the second run (if applicable, though the algorithm primarily iterates through len1). 3. len1 slab entries, each encoded as a ushort. Slab Entry Encoding: Each slab entry slab is a ushort packed with Y-range information: Lower 10 bits (slab & 1023): The starting Y coordinate (y{start}) of the slab segment. Upper 6 bits (slab >> 10): The length of the slab segment in Y. The ending Y coordinate is y{end} = y{start} + \text{length}. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Conversion: Calculate integer voxel coordinates x, y, z from the ray's float position, scaled by the volume dimensions vx, vy, vz. 2. Bounds Check: Verify that 0 \le x < vx, 0 \le y < vy, and 0 \le z < vz. If any coordinate is out of bounds, terminate the search. 3. Slab Pointer Access: Compute the index into the slab map: idx = x + z \cdot vx. Access the slab pointer: p = \text{map4.slabs} + idx. 4. Read Lengths: Read the first two ushort values from p: len1 = p p \leftarrow p + 1 len2 = p p \leftarrow p + 1 5. Initialize Variables: Set y1 = 0, y2 = 0. Set texture pointer pt = p + len1. (Note: The source implies skipping the first len1 slab entries in the map to align with the texture data start, or this is a specific implementation detail where texture data follows the map. The source says pt = p + len1 after reading lengths, but then iterates len1 times reading from p. This suggests p points to the start of the slab entries for this (x,z), and pt is calculated relative to the end of the slab map or a specific offset. Based on the loop, p is used to read slab entries, and pt is used to write color. The source states pt = p + len1 initially, but then inside the loop, it reads from p. This implies pt might be an offset into the texture array, not a pointer to memory. Let's re-read carefully: ushort pt = p+len1; then pt[texture+y-y1]. This suggests pt is a pointer to the texture data, and texture is an index. The source is slightly ambiguous on memory layout. We will follow the source's variable usage: pt is a pointer to the texture data buffer, and texture is an integer offset into that buffer.) Initialize texture = 0. 6. Iterate Slabs: Loop s from 0 to len1 - 1: a. Read slab entry: slab = p; p \leftarrow p + 1. b. Decode Y-range: y1 \leftarrow y1 + (slab \ \& \ 1023) y2 \leftarrow y1 + (slab \gg 10) c. Check if target y is in [y1, y2): If y2 > y and y1 \le y: The voxel is found. Retrieve the color value col from the texture data at pt[texture + y - y1]. (Note: The source does not specify how col is retrieved from pt. It assumes col is available. We will assume col is a 32-bit integer or similar packed color value stored in the texture array.) Decode color components (5 bits per channel, range 0-31): r = \text{clamp}((col \ \& \ 0x1F) \cdot 15 + 16, 0, 31) g = \text{clamp}(((col \gg 5) \ \& \ 0x1F) \cdot 15 + 16, 0, 31) b = \text{clamp}(((col \gg 10) \ \& \ 0x1F) \cdot 15 + 16, 0, 31) Store packed RGB back into the texture array: pt[\text{texture} + y - y1] = (r \ | \ (g \ll 5) \ | \ (b \ll 10)) Return. d. If not found, advance: \text{texture} \leftarrow \text{texture} + (y2 - y1) y1 \leftarrow y2 7. Termination: If the loop completes without finding the voxel, the voxel is empty or out of bounds (though bounds were checked). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rle4traverse(map4, x, y, z, vx, vy, vz): # 1. Bounds Check if x < 0 or x >= vx or y < 0 or y >= vy or z < 0 or z >= vz: return None # 2. Access Slab Map idx = x + z vx p = map4.slabs[idx] # 3. Read Lengths len1 = p[0] len2 = p[1] p = p[2:] # Move pointer past lengths # 4. Initialize y1 = 0 y2 = 0 pt = map4.texture # Assuming map4.texture points to the start of color data textureoffset = 0 # 5. Iterate Slabs for s in range(len1): slab = p[0] p = p[1:] # Decode Y-range ystart = slab & 1023 ylen = slab >> 10 y1 = y1 + ystart y2 = y1 + ylen # Check if y is in [y1, y2) if y2 > y and y1 <= y: # Voxel found # Retrieve color from texture data # Note: The source implies col is read from pt[textureoffset + y - y1] # We assume pt is an array of uint32 or similar col = pt[textureoffset + y - y1] # Decode 5-bit RGB rraw = col & 0x1F graw = (col >> 5) & 0x1F braw = (col >> 10) & 0x1F # Quantize to 0-31 range (source formula: val 15 + 16, clamped) r = clamp(rraw 15 + 16, 0, 31) g = clamp(graw 15 + 16, 0, 31) b = clamp(braw 15 + 16, 0, 31) # Store packed RGB back newcol = r | (g << 5) | (b << 10) pt[textureoffset + y - y1] = newcol return newcol # Advance textureoffset += (y2 - y1) y1 = y2 return None def clamp(val, minval, maxval): if val < minval: return minval if val > maxval: return maxval return val Parameters: Color Quantization: 5 bits per channel (RGB), resulting in a 31-level intensity range (0-31). Slab Encoding: 10 bits for Y-start, 6 bits for Y-length. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bounds: The algorithm assumes the target Y is within volume bounds, checked at the start. If the ray passes through multiple slabs, it iterates until the Y range is found. Precision: The Y-coordinate decoding uses integer arithmetic. Ensure that the accumulation of y1 does not overflow if the volume is very large, though ushort limits the max Y-length to 64 (6 bits) and Y-start to 1024 (10 bits), suggesting a limited Y-range per slab or a specific encoding scheme. The source uses int for y1, y2, so overflow is unlikely for typical volume sizes. Empty Space: The RLE4 structure efficiently skips empty space by only storing occupied slab segments. If a voxel is not found in the loop, it is considered empty. Time Complexity: O(k), where k is the number of slab segments along the ray's path in the XZ plane. In sparse volumes, k is much smaller than the total number of voxels, providing significant speedup over dense grid traversal. Memory Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of occupied slab segments. The RLE4 compression reduces memory footprint compared to a full 3D grid. Strengths: Efficiently handles sparse volumes by skipping empty space. Simple implementation with minimal branching. Limitations: Performance degrades in dense volumes where most slabs are occupied. The fixed 5-bit color quantization may lead to color banding. When to Use: Ideal for sparse voxel volumes where empty space is prevalent. When Not to Use: Not suitable for dense volumes or when high-precision color is required. RLE4 Ray Tracing, also known as Map4 Traversal, was introduced in the context of OpenGL voxel splatting and real-time volume rendering. It is associated with the work by sp4cerat on GitHub, which provides an unofficial implementation for real-time voxel rendering using OpenGL. The method leverages run-length encoding to optimize ray traversal in 3D voxel grids. sp4cerat/OpenGL-Voxel-Splatting, https://github.com/sp4cerat/OpenGL-Voxel-Splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Shadow Volume Raycast
head: raycastShadowVolumeSparse
body: A hierarchical raycasting algorithm that traverses a sparse shadow volume texture to find the first intersection with a shadow-casting volume. It differs from fixed-step hierarchical variants by dynamically adjusting its traversal step size and level of detail (LOD) based on occupancy bits, allowing it to skip empty space efficiently in sparse representations. Inputs: origin: Ray origin in world space. dir: Ray direction (normalized). dist: Maximum ray distance. uVolOffset: Offset vector for the shadow volume texture coordinates. uVolTexelSize: Physical size of a texel in the shadow volume. uVolResolution: Resolution of the shadow volume texture (vec3). uShadowVolume: The sparse shadow volume texture (likely a sparse voxel octree or similar structure). Outputs: d: Distance to the first occupied voxel. Returns dist if no intersection is found within the limit. Data Structures: uShadowVolume: A texture where each texel contains occupancy information. The algorithm samples this texture at different LODs. The exact internal structure (e.g., sparse voxel octree encoding) is abstracted by the textureLod call, but the algorithm relies on the x component of the sampled value being non-zero to indicate occupancy. Steps: 1. Initialization: Translate origin: origin = origin + uVolOffset. Compute step size: step = uVolTexelSize. Compute step direction in texture space: stepDir = dir (1.0 / uVolResolution). Compute initial position in texture space: pos = origin (1.0 / uVolTexelSize) (1.0 / uVolResolution). Halve step parameters: stepDir = stepDir 0.5, step = step 0.5. Initialize LOD: lod = -1. Initialize distance: d = 0.0. 2. Traversal Loop: While d < dist: Sample texture: c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod).x. If lod == -1 (Coarse Search): If c != 0: Calculate bit index from fractional parts of pos: bit = (fract(pos.x uVolResolution.x) > 0.5 ? 1: 0) + (fract(pos.y uVolResolution.y) > 0.5 ? 2: 0) + (fract(pos.z uVolResolution.z) > 0.5 ? 4: 0). Create mask: mask = 1 << bit. If (mask & c) != 0: Return d. Else: Advance pos += stepDir, d += step. If c == 0: Increment lod. Double stepDir and step. Advance pos += stepDir, d += step. If lod != -1 (Refinement): If c != 0: Halve stepDir and step. Decrement lod. Backtrack: pos -= stepDir, d -= step. If c == 0: If lod < 2: Sample c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod + 1).x. If c == 0: Increment lod. Double stepDir and step. Advance pos += stepDir, d += step. Else (lod == 2): Do not go deeper. Rely on coarse search or distance limit. Parameters: uVolResolution: vec3, resolution of the shadow volume texture. uVolTexelSize: float, physical size of a texel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The algorithm assumes a maximum LOD of 2. If lod is already 2 and the sample is empty, it does not attempt to go deeper, relying on the coarse search or returning the distance limit. Precision issues may arise when calculating bit indices from fractional parts of pos if pos values are very large or small. The algorithm assumes the shadow volume texture supports textureLod with varying LOD levels. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastshadowvolumesparse(origin, dir, dist, uVolOffset, uVolTexelSize, uVolResolution, uShadowVolume): origin = origin + uVolOffset step = uVolTexelSize stepDir = dir (1.0 / uVolResolution) pos = origin (1.0 / uVolTexelSize) (1.0 / uVolResolution) stepDir = stepDir 0.5 step = step 0.5 lod = -1 d = 0.0 while d < dist: c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod).x if lod == -1: if c != 0: bit = (1 if fract(pos.x uVolResolution.x) > 0.5 else 0) + \ (2 if fract(pos.y uVolResolution.y) > 0.5 else 0) + \ (4 if fract(pos.z uVolResolution.z) > 0.5 else 0) mask = 1 << bit if (mask & c) != 0: return d else: pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step else: lod = lod + 1 stepDir = stepDir 2.0 step = step 2.0 pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step else: if c != 0: stepDir = stepDir 0.5 step = step 0.5 lod = lod - 1 pos = pos - stepDir d = d - step else: if lod < 2: c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod + 1).x if c == 0: lod = lod + 1 stepDir = stepDir 2.0 step = step 2.0 pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step # If lod == 2 and c == 0, do nothing, loop continues return dist A hierarchical raycasting algorithm for shadow volumes that uses fixed step sizes and LODs, traversing from base distance to further distances using specific LOD levels (0, 1, 2). It differs from the sparse variant by not dynamically adjusting step sizes based on occupancy bits, instead using predefined distance thresholds (baseDistance) to switch between LOD levels. It is chosen when the shadow volume is not sparse or when a simpler, fixed-step traversal is preferred. Performs a directional shadow raycast against the sparse shadow volume, including screen-space blocking check and position jittering. It first checks if the ray is blocked in screen space; if so, it returns 0.0. Otherwise, it jitters the position and calls raycastShadowVolumeSparse with the jittered position and direction. It is used to reduce aliasing and improve shadow quality. Not given in the sources. Origin: The method is described in the context of a voxel rendering project, specifically in the mainsv.cpp file of the TTFH/Voxel-Render repository. It is part of a broader set of voxel grid raycasting techniques. TTFH/Voxel-Render, https://github.com/TTFH/Voxel-Render, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Regular Grid Traversal
head: 3D-DDA, Voxel Grid Traversal, Sparse Voxel Grid Traversal
body: Regular Grid Traversal accelerates ray-scene intersection by stepping through a uniform 3D grid of cells, skipping empty space without primitive tests. It differs from hierarchical methods (e.g., Sparse Voxel Traversal) by using a fixed-size array, offering high cache efficiency on GPUs for uniform data but requiring O(N^3) memory. All children use a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (3D-DDA) to traverse the grid. The ray origin is mapped to an initial cell (X, Y, Z). Distances to the next grid boundary in each axis are tracked via tMax and tDelta. tDelta is constant per axis: tDeltaX = dx / |dirx|. tMax is updated by adding tDelta when the ray crosses a boundary. The ray advances to the nearest boundary (min(tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ)). Uses a 1D array of linked lists for primitives. Conservative mapping ensures no primitive is missed. Handles intersections outside the current cell by continuing traversal. Uses a 128³ occupancy grid for GI/Reflection fallbacks. Integrates with Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) and requires GLARBshaderimageloadstore. Uses bitwise operations for chunk indexing to minimize arithmetic overhead. Optimized for fixed-step traversal within working chunks. Regular grids are a foundational spatial acceleration structure in ray tracing. They partition space into disjoint sub-blocks, unlike BVH which partitions primitives. Effective on GPUs due to spatial locality. name: Regular Grid
head: Grilles régulières, Regular Grid Spatial Subdivision
body: A Regular Grid is a spatial acceleration structure that divides a scene's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) into a fixed-size, uniform 3D grid of cells (voxels). It accelerates ray tracing by allowing rays to step through empty cells without performing primitive intersection tests, reducing the number of expensive geometric queries. Unlike hierarchical structures like BVH or KD-trees, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, meaning primitives can belong to multiple cells, whereas BVH partitions primitives into disjoint sets. It is particularly effective on GPUs for scenes with uniform data distribution due to high spatial locality and cache efficiency. Input: A set of scene primitives, each with an associated AABB; the global scene bounding box defined by minimum corner p1 and maximum corner p2; and a grid resolution parameter N (GRIDSIZE). Output: A 1D array representing the grid, enabling efficient ray traversal and primitive intersection testing. The grid is stored as a 1D array mGrid of size N^3. Indexing: A cell at integer coordinates (x, y, z) is accessed via index: idx = x + y \cdot N + z \cdot N^2 Cell Content: Each entry in mGrid is a pointer to an ObjectList. ObjectList: A linked list structure where each node contains: A pointer to a primitive. A pointer to the next ObjectList node. A flag or ID to track if a primitive has already been tested by the current ray to avoid redundant calculations. The construction phase maps primitives to the cells they intersect. This mapping must be conservative: it may include more primitives than strictly necessary but must never exclude a primitive that intersects a cell. 1. Initialize Grid: Allocate mGrid of size N^3 and set all pointers to NULL. 2. Define Bounds: Set the scene bounds p1 (min) and p2 (max). 3. Calculate Cell Dimensions: Compute the width, height, and depth of a single cell, and their reciprocals for fast coordinate conversion: dx = \frac{p{2x} - p{1x}}{N}, \quad dx{reci} = \frac{1}{dx} dy = \frac{p{2y} - p{1y}}{N}, \quad dy{reci} = \frac{1}{dy} dz = \frac{p{2z} - p{1z}}{N}, \quad dz{reci} = \frac{1}{dz} 4. Map Primitives: For each primitive p: a. Retrieve its AABB bounds: bv1 (min corner) and bv2 (max corner). b. Calculate the grid cell coordinates (x1, y1, z1) containing bv1 and (x2, y2, z2) containing bv2: x1 = \lfloor (bv{1x} - p{1x}) \cdot dx{reci} \rfloor, \quad x2 = \lfloor (bv{2x} - p{1x}) \cdot dx{reci} \rfloor + 1 y1 = \lfloor (bv{1y} - p{1y}) \cdot dy{reci} \rfloor, \quad y2 = \lfloor (bv{2y} - p{1y}) \cdot dy{reci} \rfloor + 1 z1 = \lfloor (bv{1z} - p{1z}) \cdot dz{reci} \rfloor, \quad z2 = \lfloor (bv{2z} - p{1z}) \cdot dz{reci} \rfloor + 1 c. Clamp Coordinates: Clamp x1, y1, z1 to a minimum of 0, and x2, y2, z2 to a maximum of N-1 to handle primitives outside or on the boundary of the grid. d. Iterate Candidate Cells: Loop over x from x1 to x2-1, y from y1 to y2-1, and z from z1 to z2-1: i. Calculate cell index idx = x + y \cdot N + z \cdot N^2. ii. Construct the AABB for the current cell: cell\min = p1 + (x \cdot dx, y \cdot dy, z \cdot dz) cell\max = cell\min + (dx, dy, dz) iii. If the primitive's AABB intersects the cell's AABB, add the primitive to the ObjectList at mGrid[idx]. Traversal uses a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (3D-DDA) algorithm to step through cells. 1. Determine Start Cell: Find the initial cell (X, Y, Z) containing the ray origin. If the origin is outside the grid, advance the ray to the first intersection with the grid's bounding box. If the ray misses the grid entirely, terminate. 2. Calculate Step Distances: Compute the distance along the ray to cross one full cell in each axis (tDelta): tDeltaX = \frac{dx}{|ray\dirx|}, \quad tDeltaY = \frac{dy}{|ray\diry|}, \quad tDeltaZ = \frac{dz}{|ray\dirz|} 3. Calculate Initial Boundary Distances: Compute the distance to the first cell boundary in each axis (tMax) from the ray origin (or the entry point into the grid): tMaxX = \frac{(X + (ray\dirx > 0 ? 1: 0)) \cdot dx - ray\originx}{ray\dirx} tMaxY = \frac{(Y + (ray\diry > 0 ? 1: 0)) \cdot dy - ray\originy}{ray\diry} tMaxZ = \frac{(Z + (ray\dirz > 0 ? 1: 0)) \cdot dz - ray\originz}{ray\dirz} 4. Determine Steps: Set step directions stepX, stepY, stepZ to 1 if the corresponding ray direction component is positive, and -1 otherwise. Repeat until the ray exits the grid or a hit is found: 1. Process Current Cell: a. Check if mGrid[X + YN + ZNN] is NULL. If not, iterate through the ObjectList. b. For each primitive in the list, perform an intersection test. c. Handling Out-of-Cell Intersections: If an intersection is found, check if the intersection point lies within the current cell's bounds. If the intersection point is outside the current cell (e.g., the primitive spans multiple cells), advance the ray to the next cell(s) and continue testing. To avoid redundant tests, mark primitives that have already been tested by the current ray (e.g., using a unique ray ID). d. If the intersection point is inside the current cell, return the hit. 2. Advance Ray: Compare tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ. Advance the ray to the nearest cell boundary: If tMaxX < tMaxY and tMaxX < tMaxZ: tMaxX += tDeltaX X += stepX Else if tMaxY < tMaxZ: tMaxY += tDeltaY Y += stepY Else: tMaxZ += tDeltaZ Z += stepZ 3. Boundary Check: If any coordinate (X, Y, Z) goes out of bounds [0, N-1], terminate the ray. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, o): return Vec3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def sub(self, o): return Vec3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) class ObjectList: def init(self, primitive, nextnode=None): self.primitive = primitive self.next = nextnode def buildregulargrid(primitives, p1, p2, N): grid = [None] (N N N) dx = (p2.x - p1.x) / N dy = (p2.y - p1.y) / N dz = (p2.z - p1.z) / N dxr, dyr, dzr = 1.0/dx, 1.0/dy, 1.0/dz for prim in primitives: bv1, bv2 = prim.aabbmin, prim.aabbmax x1 = int((bv1.x - p1.x) dxr); x2 = int((bv2.x - p1.x) dxr) + 1 y1 = int((bv1.y - p1.y) dyr); y2 = int((bv2.y - p1.y) dyr) + 1 z1 = int((bv1.z - p1.z) dzr); z2 = int((bv2.z - p1.z) dzr) + 1 x1 = max(0, x1); x2 = min(N-1, x2) y1 = max(0, y1); y2 = min(N-1, y2) z1 = max(0, z1); z2 = min(N-1, z2) for x in range(x1, x2): for y in range(y1, y2): for z in range(z1, z2): idx = x + y N + z N N cmin = Vec3(p1.x + xdx, p1.y + ydy, p1.z + zdz) cmax = cmin + Vec3(dx, dy, dz) if (cmin.x < bv2.x and cmax.x > bv1.x and cmin.y < bv2.y and cmax.y > bv1.y and cmin.z < bv2.z and cmax.z > bv1.z): grid[idx] = ObjectList(prim, grid[idx]) return grid def traceray(origin, direction, grid, p1, p2, N): dx = (p2.x - p1.x) / N dy = (p2.y - p1.y) / N dz = (p2.z - p1.z) / N invd = Vec3(1.0/abs(direction.x), 1.0/abs(direction.y), 1.0/abs(direction.z)) # Grid AABB intersection t1 = (p1.x - origin.x) invd.x; t2 = (p2.x - origin.x) invd.x t3 = (p1.y - origin.y) invd.y; t4 = (p2.y - origin.y) invd.y t5 = (p1.z - origin.z) invd.z; t6 = (p2.z - origin.z) invd.z tenter = max(max(min(t1,t2), min(t3,t4)), min(t5,t6)) texit = min(min(max(t1,t2), max(t3,t4)), max(t5,t6)) if tenter > texit or texit < 0: return None tentry = max(tenter, 0.0) entrypos = origin + direction tentry X = int((entrypos.x - p1.x) / dx) Y = int((entrypos.y - p1.y) / dy) Z = int((entrypos.z - p1.z) / dz) X = max(0, min(N-1, X)); Y = max(0, min(N-1, Y)); Z = max(0, min(N-1, Z)) tdeltax = dx / abs(direction.x) tdeltay = dy / abs(direction.y) tdeltaz = dz / abs(direction.z) stepx = 1 if direction.x > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if direction.y > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if direction.z > 0 else -1 tmaxx = ((X + (1 if direction.x > 0 else 0)) dx - origin.x) / direction.x tmaxy = ((Y + (1 if direction.y > 0 else 0)) dy - origin.y) / direction.y tmaxz = ((Z + (1 if direction.z > 0 else 0)) dz - origin.z) / direction.z while 0 <= X < N and 0 <= Y < N and 0 <= Z < N: node = grid[X + Y N + Z N N] while node is not None: hitt = node.primitive.intersect(origin, direction) if hitt is not None: hitpt = origin + direction hitt cmin = Vec3(p1.x + Xdx, p1.y + Ydy, p1.z + Zdz) cmax = cmin + Vec3(dx, dy, dz) if cmin.x <= hitpt.x < cmax.x and cmin.y <= hitpt.y < cmax.y and cmin.z <= hitpt.z < cmax.z: return hitt node.primitive.rayid = origin.id node = node.next if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: tmaxx += tdeltax; X += stepx else: tmaxz += tdeltaz; Z += stepz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: tmaxy += tdeltay; Y += stepy else: tmaxz += tdeltaz; Z += stepz return None GRIDSIZE (N): The number of cells along each axis. The total number of cells is N^3. Typical values are not given in the sources. Intersection Outside Cell: A primitive stored in cell F may be intersected by a ray while traversing cell F, but the intersection point lies outside cell F (e.g., in cell G). Testing only the current cell misses this or requires redundant checks. The solution is to continue advancing the ray to subsequent cells until the intersection point is within the current cell or a closer intersection is found. Redundant Tests: A single triangle may span multiple voxels. To avoid redundant intersection tests, mark primitives that have already been tested by the current ray (e.g., using a unique ray ID). Dynamic Scenes: The Regular Grid is not suitable for dynamic scenes if using acceleration methods like Proximity Clouds, as pre-calculating distance information to the nearest full element is too costly. Boundary Handling: Primitives outside or on the boundary of the grid must be clamped to the grid indices to avoid out-of-bounds access. Memory: Memory usage is O(N^3), where N is the grid resolution. This is high for sparse scenes because the grid is uniform and cannot adapt to primitive density. Many triangles may cluster in a small area but occupy many empty voxels. Construction: O(P \cdot N^3) in the naive implementation (checking all primitives for all cells), but optimized to O(P \cdot k) where k is the average number of cells a primitive intersects, by only iterating over candidate cells defined by the primitive's AABB. Traversal: O(C), where C is the number of cells intersected by the ray. Intersection tests are performed only for primitives in visited cells. On GPUs, the Regular Grid is considered optimal for scenes with uniform data distribution due to high probability of cached texture accesses, offering up to 100x faster performance compared to non-optimized structures. GPU rasterization can find primary ray intersections by reading pixel colors, but it cannot handle secondary rays (reflections/refractions) effectively and has limits on primitive count and supersampling. The Regular Grid helps accelerate these secondary rays. Strengths: Simple implementation; constant-time access to elements and neighbors; good data locality (successively accessed elements are spatially close in memory); effective for uniform scenes on GPU. Limitations: High memory usage for sparse scenes; no adaptivity to primitive density; construction can be slow for large numbers of primitives if not optimized; stepping through the grid is not free, especially setup costs. Use for scenes with uniform data distribution, especially on GPU where cache locality is critical. Use when simplicity of implementation is prioritized over memory efficiency. Not suitable for highly sparse or highly dynamic scenes without additional acceleration structures like Proximity Clouds (which are costly for dynamic scenes). The Regular Grid was one of the first spatial acceleration structures used in ray tracing, particularly in early GPU experiments. The traversal algorithm (3D-DDA) is heavily based on the paper by Amanatides & Woo. The structure has been widely used in various forms, including "Grilles régulières" in French literature. Early implementations checked all primitives for all cells, which was slow. Optimizations involved mapping primitives to cells based on their AABBs, reducing the number of intersection tests during construction. The handling of intersections outside the current cell was addressed by Amanatides & Woo, who proposed advancing the ray to subsequent cells and marking tested primitives to avoid redundancy. The Regular Grid is used in various ray tracing applications, particularly where uniform scene distribution allows for efficient caching on GPUs. It serves as a baseline for more complex hierarchical structures like KD-trees and BVHs. flipcode - Raytracing Topics & Techniques, https://flipcode.com/archives/RaytracingTopicsTechniques-Part4SpatialSubdivisions.shtml, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) 光线追踪小记:空间加速结构Regular Grid与3DDDA, https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/415869768, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Représentation et algorithmes pour l'exploration interactive de volumes procéduraux étendus et détaillés, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00598406v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel-based Ray Tracing for GI and Specular Reflections
head: ApplyVoxelRT, Voxel RT, VoxelDDA, VoxelReflectionFallback
body: A voxel-based ray tracing system using Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal through a 128³ block-occupancy grid to provide global illumination (GI) and specular reflection fallbacks. It serves as a drop-in replacement for Screen-Space Ray Tracing (SSRT) for GI and a fallback for Screen-Space Reflections (SSR) when coverage is incomplete, combining sky occlusion with Light Propagation Volume (LPV) colour bleeding. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 128³ block-occupancy voxel grid stored in imgVoxelMask (populated each frame in the shadow pass) and LPV data for indirect lighting. Output: Indirect lighting contribution for GI and reflected colour for specular fallbacks. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 128³ block-occupancy grid stored in imgVoxelMask. LPV Data: Propagated light buffer accessed via image load/store operations. Parameters: VOXELGISAMPLES: Number of cosine-weighted hemisphere rays for GI sampling; default value is 4. VOXELGISTEPS: Configurable parameter for the number of steps in voxel GI ray traversal. VOXELREFLSTEPS: Configurable parameter for the number of steps in voxel reflection ray traversal. VOXELRTREFLECTIONS: Feature flag to enable specular reflection fallback; commented out by default. VOXELGI: Indirect effect mode identifier, value 6, added to the indirecteffect enum. Algorithm Steps: 1. VoxelDDA(): Perform 3-D DDA traversal over the voxel grid, handling grid bounds and sign-safe boundary distances, returning face-centre position and axis-aligned normal. Include ray bias in DDA traversal to avoid self-intersection and handle near-parallel rays gracefully. 2. SampleVoxelLighting(): Read the LPV data half a block in front of the hit face to obtain indirect colour at the surface from propagated light. 3. ApplyVoxelRT(): Trace VOXELGISAMPLES cosine-weighted hemisphere rays, blending sky contribution with LPV colour bounce at hit surfaces. Acts as a drop-in replacement for ApplySSRT(). 4. VoxelReflectionFallback(): Perform a single specular DDA ray trace; activated only when screen-space reflection misses (environmentReflection.a < 1). Scale voxel lighting to match typical sky-reflection brightness ranges to avoid visual mismatch. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def readvoxelmask(x, y, z): """Simulates sampling imgVoxelMask for occupancy.""" # Actual implementation fetches from GLARBshaderimageloadstore buffer return True def samplelpv(position): """Simulates reading LPV data at a world-space position.""" # Actual implementation fetches from LPV volume buffer return [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] def VoxelDDA(origin, direction, gridsize=128.0, maxsteps=1000): """ Perform 3-D DDA traversal over the voxel grid. Returns: (hitposition, hitnormal, hitdistance) or None if no hit. """ raybias = 1e-4 # Handle zero direction components gracefully invdir = [1.0 / d if abs(d) > 1e-6 else 0.0 for d in direction] step = [1 if d > 0 else -1 for d in direction] # Initial voxel coordinates currentvoxel = [math.floor(o gridsize) for o in origin] # Calculate initial t values for crossing voxel boundaries tmax = [] for i in range(3): boundary = currentvoxel[i] + (0.5 if step[i] > 0 else -0.5) if abs(direction[i]) > 1e-6: tmax.append((boundary - origin[i]) invdir[i]) else: tmax.append(float('inf')) # tdelta represents distance between boundaries tdelta = [abs(invdir[i]) for i in range(3)] # Apply ray bias to initial tmax to start traversal slightly forward tmax = [t + raybias for t in tmax] for in range(maxsteps): # Find axis with smallest tmax minidx = 0 if tmax[1] < tmax[minidx]: minidx = 1 if tmax[2] < tmax[minidx]: minidx = 2 # Advance along that axis currentvoxel[minidx] += step[minidx] tmax[minidx] += tdelta[minidx] # Check bounds if not all(0 <= v < gridsize for v in currentvoxel): return None # Check occupancy if readvoxelmask(currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2]): # Return face-centre position and axis-aligned normal hitpos = [currentvoxel[i] + 0.5 for i in range(3)] normal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] normal[minidx] = -step[minidx] dist = math.sqrt(sum((hitpos[i] - origin[i])2 for i in range(3))) return hitpos, normal, dist return None def ApplyVoxelRT(origin, normal, skycolour, numsamples=4, maxsteps=100): """ Drop-in replacement for ApplySSRT(). Traces VOXELGISAMPLES cosine-weighted hemisphere rays. """ totalindirect = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(numsamples): # Cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling u1, u2 = random.random(), random.random() theta = 2.0 math.pi u1 phi = math.acos(math.sqrt(u2)) localdir = [math.sin(phi)math.cos(theta), math.sin(phi)math.sin(theta), math.cos(phi)] # Transform localdir to world space aligned with surface normal raydir = localdir hit = VoxelDDA(origin, raydir, maxsteps=maxsteps) if hit is not None: hitpos, hitnorm, = hit lpvcol = samplelpv(hitpos) totalindirect = [totalindirect[i] + lpvcol[i] for i in range(3)] else: totalindirect = [totalindirect[i] + skycolour[i] for i in range(3)] return [c / numsamples for c in totalindirect] def VoxelReflectionFallback(origin, viewvector, normalatorigin, environmentreflection, maxsteps=100): """ Single specular DDA ray trace. Activated only when environmentreflection.a < 1. """ if environmentreflection[3] >= 1.0: return environmentreflection[:3] # Reflect view vector dot = sum(viewvector[i]normalatorigin[i] for i in range(3)) reflectdir = [viewvector[i] - 2.0dotnormalatorigin[i] for i in range(3)] hit = VoxelDDA(origin, reflectdir, maxsteps=maxsteps) if hit is not None: hitpos, hitnorm, = hit lpvcol = samplelpv(hitpos) # Scale voxel lighting to match typical sky-reflection brightness return [c 0.5 for c in lpvcol] return environmentreflection[:3] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Support: Requires LPV (Light Propagation Volumes) and GLARBshaderimageloadstore support; gracefully degrades to SSRT if these are not met. Division by Zero: Epsilon guards are required to prevent division by zero in invTonemap(), FastCatmulRom(), and TAA blending calculations, especially on hardware with aggressive FP16 FTZ behaviour (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 5000 series). Self-Intersection: Ray bias must be included in DDA traversal to avoid self-intersection. Near-Parallel Rays: DDA traversal must handle near-parallel rays gracefully. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the voxel grid (128³) and LPV data; no new buffers are needed beyond the existing imgVoxelMask. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of GI samples and steps. Strengths: Provides GI and specular reflections in areas where screen-space methods fail; drop-in replacement for SSRT. Limitations: Requires LPV and specific GPU features; quality depends on the resolution of the voxel grid (128³) and LPV accuracy. When to use: When screen-space GI/Reflections are insufficient or unavailable. When not to use: When hardware lacks LPV or image load/store support; when performance is critical and SSRT is sufficient. Origin: Implemented by nyzxor as a pull request to the Eclipse-Shader (an edit of Chocapic13 V9 / Bliss) for Minecraft, integrated via Iris. History: Added in May 2026. Usage: Used in the Eclipse-Shader for Minecraft. Add voxel-based ray tracing for GI and specular reflections, https://github.com/nyzxor/Eclipse-Shader/pull/1, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Optimised Voxel Ray Marching
head: Chunk-based Voxel Traversal, Fixed-step voxel ray marching, Optimised CPU Ray Marching, Sector's Edge, Voxel Volume Ray Tracing, VoxelsRayTracingTutorial
body: Optimised Voxel Ray Marching is a fixed-step ray traversal algorithm for voxel-based scenes that minimizes computational overhead by keeping block lookups within the current working chunk. It builds on Voxel Grid Raycasting by replacing global coordinate arithmetic with bitwise operations for chunk indexing, thereby reducing the number of bitshifts, masks, and multiplication operations required per step. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin start (world/voxel space), ray direction velocity (normalized), maximum march distance max, and a hierarchical voxel map structure Map containing chunks. Outputs: Boolean hit indicating if a non-empty block was encountered, and axis indicating the surface normal direction of the hit. Data Structures: Map: A 3D array Chunk[,,] chunks indexed by [chunkIndexX, chunkIndexY, chunkIndexZ]. CHUNKAMOUNTX = 16, CHUNKAMOUNTY = 5, CHUNKAMOUNTZ = 16. Chunk: Contains a 1D array Block[] data of size CHUNKSIZECUBED (32,768). Block: A struct with a single byte field byte kind. Layout is sequential with pack size 1. kind == 0 indicates empty space. Constants: MAPSIZEX = 512, MAPSIZEY = 160, MAPSIZEZ = 512. CHUNKSIZE = 32. SHIFT = 5 (since 2^5 = 32). MASK = 0x1f (31, equivalent to CHUNKSIZE - 1). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Convert ray start position to integer grid coordinates: x = (int)start.X, y = (int)start.Y, z = (int)start.Z. Calculate chunk indices using right shift: chunkIndexX = x >> SHIFT, chunkIndexY = y >> SHIFT, chunkIndexZ = z >> SHIFT. Calculate chunk-relative coordinates using bitwise AND: i = x & MASK, j = y & MASK, k = z & MASK. Retrieve the current working chunk: c = chunks[chunkIndexX, chunkIndexY, chunkIndexZ]. Calculate the linear index in the chunk data array: access = j + i CHUNKSIZE + k CHUNKSIZESQUARED. Calculate the ray end position: end = start + velocity. 2. Edge Case: Single Block Trace: If x == (int)end.X AND y == (int)end.Y AND z == (int)end.Z: If c is null OR c.data[access].kind == 0, set hit = false and return. Otherwise, set hit = true and return. 3. Edge Case: Out of Bounds: If start is outside map bounds (y < 0 or y >= MAPSIZEY, etc.), set hit = false and return. 4. Direction-Dependent Variable Initialization: Normalize velocity. Calculate inverse absolute velocity components: xInverted = |1 / velocity.X| yInverted = |1 / velocity.Y| zInverted = |1 / velocity.Z| If a velocity component is 0, its inverted distance is PositiveInfinity. Initialize step, comparison, reset, and access increment variables based on the sign of velocity components: X Axis: If velocity.X > 0: iStep=1, iComparison=CHUNKSIZE, iReset=0, xAccessReset=-CHUNKSIZESQUARED, xAccessIncrement=CHUNKSIZE, xDist=x-start.X+1. Else: iStep=-1, iComparison=-1, iReset=CHUNKSIZE-1, xAccessReset=CHUNKSIZESQUARED, xAccessIncrement=-CHUNKSIZE, xDist=start.X-x. Y Axis: If velocity.Y > 0: jStep=1, jComparison=CHUNKSIZE, jReset=0, yAccessReset=-CHUNKSIZE, yDist=y-start.Y+1. Else: jStep=-1, jComparison=-1, jReset=CHUNKSIZE-1, yAccessReset=CHUNKSIZE, yDist=start.Y-y. Z Axis: If velocity.Z > 0: kStep=1, kComparison=CHUNKSIZE, kReset=0, zAccessIncrement=CHUNKSIZESQUARED, zAccessReset=-CHUNKSIZECUBED, zDist=z-start.Z+1. Else: kStep=-1, kComparison=-1, kReset=CHUNKSIZE-1, zAccessIncrement=-CHUNKSIZESQUARED, zAccessReset=CHUNKSIZECUBED, zDist=start.Z-z. 5. Distance Calculation: Calculate initial distance to the next voxel boundary in t-units: xDistance = (velocity.X == 0) ? PositiveInfinity: xInverted xDist yDistance = (velocity.Y == 0) ? PositiveInfinity: yInverted yDist zDistance = (velocity.Z == 0) ? PositiveInfinity: zInverted zDist. Initialize t = 0.0. 6. Ray Marching Loop: While t <= max: Hit Check: If c is not null AND c.data[access].kind != 0, set hit = true and return. Determine Closest Boundary: If yDistance is smallest: Advance Y: j += jStep, access += jStep. Chunk Exit Check (Y): If j == jComparison: Reset j = jReset. Update access += yAccessReset. Increment chunkIndexY += jStep. If chunkIndexY is out of bounds (< 0 or >= CHUNKAMOUNTY), set hit = false and return. Load new chunk c = chunks[chunkIndexX, chunkIndexY, chunkIndexZ]. Update Y progress: t = yDistance, yDistance += yInverted, axis = Axis.Y. Else If zDistance is smallest: Advance Z: k += kStep, access += zAccessIncrement. Chunk Exit Check (Z): If k == kComparison: Reset k = kReset. Update access += zAccessReset. Increment chunkIndexZ += kStep. If chunkIndexZ is out of bounds, set hit = false and return. Load new chunk c = chunks[chunkIndexX, chunkIndexY, chunkIndexZ]. Update Z progress: t = zDistance, zDistance += zInverted, axis = Axis.Z. Else (X is smallest): Advance X: i += iStep, access += xAccessIncrement. Chunk Exit Check (X): If i == iComparison: Reset i = iReset. Update access += xAccessReset. Increment chunkIndexX += iStep. If chunkIndexX is out of bounds, set hit = false and return. Load new chunk c = chunks[chunkIndexX, chunkIndexY, chunkIndexZ]. Update X progress: t = xDistance, xDistance += xInverted, axis = Axis.X. 7. Completion: If the loop completes without hitting a block, set hit = false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarch(start, velocity, maxdist, chunks): CHUNKSIZE = 32 CHUNKSIZESQUARED = 1024 CHUNKSIZECUBED = 32768 SHIFT = 5 MASK = 31 CHUNKAMOUNTY = 5 CHUNKAMOUNTX = 16 CHUNKAMOUNTZ = 16 MAPSIZEY = 160 x = int(start[0]) y = int(start[1]) z = int(start[2]) chunkindexx = x >> SHIFT chunkindexy = y >> SHIFT chunkindexz = z >> SHIFT i = x & MASK j = y & MASK k = z & MASK c = chunks[chunkindexx][chunkindexy][chunkindexz] access = j + i CHUNKSIZE + k CHUNKSIZESQUARED endx = start[0] + velocity[0] endy = start[1] + velocity[1] endz = start[2] + velocity[2] if x == int(endx) and y == int(endy) and z == int(endz): if c is None or c.data[access].kind == 0: return False, "None" else: return True, "None" if y < 0 or y >= MAPSIZEY: return False, "None" if chunkindexx < 0 or chunkindexx >= CHUNKAMOUNTX: return False, "None" if chunkindexz < 0 or chunkindexz >= CHUNKAMOUNTZ: return False, "None" # Normalize velocity length = (velocity[0]2 + velocity[1]2 + velocity[2]2)0.5 vx, vy, vz = velocity[0]/length, velocity[1]/length, velocity[2]/length xinv = abs(1.0 / vx) if vx != 0 else float('inf') yinv = abs(1.0 / vy) if vy != 0 else float('inf') zinv = abs(1.0 / vz) if vz != 0 else float('inf') if vx > 0: istep, icomparison, ireset = 1, CHUNKSIZE, 0 xaccessreset, xaccessincrement = -CHUNKSIZESQUARED, CHUNKSIZE xdist = x - start[0] + 1 else: istep, icomparison, ireset = -1, -1, CHUNKSIZE - 1 xaccessreset, xaccessincrement = CHUNKSIZESQUARED, -CHUNKSIZE xdist = start[0] - x if vy > 0: jstep, jcomparison, jreset = 1, CHUNKSIZE, 0 yaccessreset, ydist = -CHUNKSIZE, y - start[1] + 1 else: jstep, jcomparison, jreset = -1, -1, CHUNKSIZE - 1 yaccessreset, ydist = CHUNKSIZE, start[1] - y if vz > 0: kstep, kcomparison, kreset = 1, CHUNKSIZE, 0 zaccessincrement, zaccessreset = CHUNKSIZESQUARED, -CHUNKSIZECUBED zdist = z - start[2] + 1 else: kstep, kcomparison, kreset = -1, -1, CHUNKSIZE - 1 zaccessincrement, zaccessreset = -CHUNKSIZESQUARED, CHUNKSIZECUBED zdist = start[2] - z t = 0.0 xdistance = xinv xdist if vx != 0 else float('inf') ydistance = yinv ydist if vy != 0 else float('inf') zdistance = zinv zdist if vz != 0 else float('inf') hitaxis = "None" while t <= maxdist: if c is not None and c.data[access].kind != 0: return True, hitaxis if ydistance < xdistance: if ydistance < zdistance: j += jstep access += jstep if j == jcomparison: j = jreset access += yaccessreset chunkindexy += jstep if chunkindexy < 0 or chunkindexy >= CHUNKAMOUNTY: return False, "None" c = chunks[chunkindexx][chunkindexy][chunkindexz] t = ydistance ydistance += yinv hitaxis = "Y" else: k += kstep access += zaccessincrement if k == kcomparison: k = kreset access += zaccessreset chunkindexz += kstep if chunkindexz < 0 or chunkindexz >= CHUNKAMOUNTZ: return False, "None" c = chunks[chunkindexx][chunkindexy][chunkindexz] t = zdistance zdistance += zinv hitaxis = "Z" else: if xdistance < zdistance: i += istep access += xaccessincrement if i == icomparison: i = ireset access += xaccessreset chunkindexx += istep if chunkindexx < 0 or chunkindexx >= CHUNKAMOUNTX: return False, "None" c = chunks[chunkindexx][chunkindexy][chunkindexz] t = xdistance xdistance += xinv hitaxis = "X" else: k += kstep access += zaccessincrement if k == kcomparison: k = kreset access += zaccessreset chunkindexz += kstep if chunkindexz < 0 or chunkindexz >= CHUNKAMOUNTZ: return False, "None" c = chunks[chunkindexx][chunkindexy][chunkindexz] t = zdistance zdistance += zinv hitaxis = "Z" return False, "None" Time Complexity: O(L), where L is the number of voxels traversed along the ray. The cost per step is very low due to bitwise operations for chunk indexing. Memory Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of voxels, stored in a sparse chunk structure. Measured Performance: On a Ryzen 5 1600 CPU, ray lengths of 1-10 blocks take 250 nanoseconds (64,000 rays per 16ms frame). Ray lengths of 200-400 blocks take 3,400 nanoseconds (4,700 rays per 16ms frame). Strengths: High performance for short-to-medium range ray marches due to reduced arithmetic overhead. Efficient memory access patterns within chunks. Limitations: Fixed-step nature means it does not skip empty space as effectively as hierarchical methods (like Sparse Voxel Traversal) for very long rays. Precision issues may arise with floating-point coordinates if not handled carefully, though the algorithm uses integer grid coordinates for traversal. When to use: Ideal for real-time collision detection for particles and projectiles in voxel worlds where rays are relatively short. When not to use: For global illumination or long-distance ray tracing where skipping large empty volumes is critical. The algorithm is based on the classic grid traversal algorithm by John Amanatides and Andrew Woo. It was optimized by Vercidium to keep block lookups within the current working chunk, minimizing bitshifts, masks, and multiplication operations. It is used in the game Sector's Edge for particle and projectile collision detection. name: Sparse Voxel Grid Raycasting with Occupancy Grid
head: Occupancy Grid Culling, empty block skipping
body: A volume rendering estimator that accelerates ray traversal and sampling by using a hierarchical sparse voxel grid (often implemented via VDB/NanoVDB structures) to skip empty space along rays, returning only sample locations within occupied cells. It differs from standard Voxel Grid Raycasting by replacing dense texture lookups with a hierarchical occupancy check that reduces texture reads by a factor of 3, and from Octree Traversal by using a fixed-resolution sparse grid with hierarchical levels rather than a dynamic tree structure for the primary traversal logic. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins tensor of shape (N, 3). raysd: Normalized ray directions tensor of shape (N, 3). estimator: An OccGridEstimator object containing: binaries: Boolean tensor of shape (L, Rx, Ry, Rz) storing occupancy masks for each level L. Must be contiguous on CPU before transfer to GPU. aabbs: Tensor of shape (L, 6) storing the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) for each level, where level i is enlarged by 2^i relative to the base. resolution: 3D resolution (Rx, Ry, Rz), default 128. levels: Number of hierarchical levels L. nearplane, farplane: Scalar distances, defaults 0.0 and 10^{10}. renderstepsize: Step size for marching, default 10^{-3}. coneangle: Cone angle for linearly-increased step size, default 0.0. alphathre: Alpha threshold for skipping empty space, default 0.0. earlystopeps: Early stop threshold, default 10^{-4}. sigmafn or alphafn: Optional callables taking (t{starts}, t{ends}, ray\indices) and returning density or opacity values, used to skip invisible space. Only one should be provided. renderbkgd: Background color tensor. timestamps: Optional tensor for dynamic scenes. Outputs: rgb: Rendered RGB image. opacity: Accumulated opacity. depth: Accumulated depth. nrenderingsamples: Number of samples used. Data Structures: DensityGrid (or OccGridEstimator): Manages the VDB/NanoVDB structure. tree: The underlying VDB grid object. binaries: The occupancy mask. gridcoords: Integer coordinates for voxels. gridindices: Indices for voxels. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create nearplanes and farplanes tensors of shape (N) filled with nearplane and farplane respectively. If tmin is provided, clamp nearplanes to \max(t{min}, near\plane). If tmax is provided, clamp farplanes to \min(t{max}, far\plane). If stratified is True, add uniform random noise in 0, render\step\size) to nearplanes. Update alphathre to \min(alpha\thre, mean\occupancy) if visibility skipping is enabled. 2. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute intersections for all rays against all level AABBs: t{mins}, t{maxs}, hits = \text{ray\aabb\intersect}(rays\o, rays\d, aabbs) If L > 1, concatenate t{mins} and t{maxs} along the last dimension and sort them to get t{sorted} and t{indices}. If L = 1, use unsorted concatenation and identity indices to maintain kernel compatibility. 3. Iterative Ray Marching: Initialize raymask as a boolean tensor of shape (N) with all True. Initialize opacity, depth, and rgb tensors of shape (N, 1) and (N, 3) with zeros. Loop while itersamples < maxsamples and raymask.sum() > 0: a. Calculate nalive = raymask.sum(). b. Determine samples per alive ray: n{samples} = \max\left(\min\left(\frac{N}{n{alive}}, 64\right), min\samples\right) where min\samples = 1 if cone\angle == 0 else 4. c. Call traversegrids [CUDA kernel with rays, binaries, aabbs, bounds, renderstepsize, coneangle, nsamples, raymask, and pre-computed t{sorted}/t{indices}/hits. This returns intervals, samples, and terminationplanes. The kernel traverses the sparse VDB structure, skipping empty blocks. d. Extract sample intervals: t{starts} = intervals.vals[intervals.is\left] t{ends} = intervals.vals[intervals.is\right] e. Extract valid ray indices: ray\indices = samples.ray\indices[samples.is\valid] f. Visibility Skipping (if sigmafn or alphafn is provided and alphathre > 0 or earlystopeps > 0): If sigmafn is provided, compute sigmas: positions = rays\o[ray\indices] + rays\d[ray\indices] \times \frac{t{starts} + t{ends}}{2} sigmas = \sigma\fn(t{starts}, t{ends}, ray\indices) (Handle dynamic scenes with timestamps if present). If alphafn is provided (and sigmafn is not), compute alphas similarly. Compute masks using rendervisibilityfromdensity or rendervisibilityfromalpha with packedinfo (stacked chunkindices and chunkcounts) and thresholds. Filter rayindices, tstarts, tends using the masks. g. Query radiance field for RGB and sigma: rgbs, sigmas = \text{rgb\sigma\fn}(t{starts}, t{ends}, ray\indices) (Handle dynamic scenes with timestamps if present). h. Compute rendering weights: prefix\trans = 1 - opacity[ray\indices].squeeze(-1) weights = \text{render\weight\from\density}(sigmas, prefix\trans) i. Accumulate results: rgb = rgb + weights \times rgbs opacity = opacity + weights depth = depth + weights \times \frac{t{starts} + t{ends}}{2} j. Update itersamples by adding nsamples. 4. Finalization: Add background color: rgb = rgb + render\bkgd \times (1.0 - opacity) Compute final depth: depth = \frac{depth}{\max(opacity, \epsilon)} where \epsilon is machine epsilon. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersparsevoxelgrid(rayso, raysd, estimator, sigmafn=None, alphafn=None, nearplane=0.0, farplane=1e10, renderstepsize=1e-3, renderbkgd=None, coneangle=0.0, alphathre=0.0, earlystopeps=1e-4, timestamps=None): numrays = rayso.shape[0] device = rayso.device # 1. Initialization nearplanes = torch.full((numrays,), nearplane, device=device) farplanes = torch.full((numrays,), farplane, device=device) # Clamp near/far planes if needed (omitted tmin/tmax for brevity) # Update alphathre with mean occupancy if visibility skipping is active if (alphathre > 0.0 or earlystopeps > 0.0) and (sigmafn is not None or alphafn is not None): alphathre = min(alphathre, estimator.binaries.float().mean().item()) minsamples = 1 if coneangle == 0 else 4 # 2. Ray-AABB Intersection tmins, tmaxs, hits = rayaabbintersect(rayso, raysd, estimator.aabbs) ngrids = estimator.binaries.size(0) if ngrids > 1: tsorted, tindices = torch.sort(torch.cat([tmins, tmaxs], -1), -1) else: tsorted = torch.cat([tmins, tmaxs], -1) tindices = torch.arange(0, ngrids 2, device=device, dtype=torch.int64).expand(numrays, ngrids 2) # 3. Iterative Marching raymask = torch.ones(numrays, device=device).bool() opacity = torch.zeros(numrays, 1, device=device) depth = torch.zeros(numrays, 1, device=device) rgb = torch.zeros(numrays, 3, device=device) itersamples = 0 maxsamples = 10000 # Example limit while itersamples < maxsamples: nalive = raymask.sum().item() if nalive == 0: break nsamples = max(min(numrays // nalive, 64), minsamples) itersamples += nsamples # Traverse sparse grid intervals, samples, terminationplanes = traversegrids( rayso, raysd, estimator.binaries, estimator.aabbs, nearplanes, farplanes, renderstepsize, coneangle, nsamples, raymask, tsorted, tindices, hits) tstarts = intervals.vals[intervals.isleft] tends = intervals.vals[intervals.isright] rayindices = samples.rayindices[samples.isvalid] # Visibility Skipping if (alphathre > 0.0 or earlystopeps > 0.0) and (sigmafn is not None or alphafn is not None): if tstarts.shape[0] == 0: continue if sigmafn is not None: sigmas = sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) masks = rendervisibilityfromdensity(tstarts, tends, sigmas, torch.stack([intervals.chunkindices, intervals.chunkcounts], -1), earlystopeps, alphathre) elif alphafn is not None: alphas = alphafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) masks = rendervisibilityfromalpha(alphas, torch.stack([intervals.chunkindices, intervals.chunkcounts], -1), earlystopeps, alphathre) rayindices = rayindices[masks] tstarts = tstarts[masks] tends = tends[masks] if rayindices.numel() == 0: continue # Query Radiance Field rgbs, sigmas = rgbsigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices, rayso, raysd, timestamps) # Accumulate prefixtrans = 1.0 - opacity[rayindices].squeeze(-1) weights = renderweightfromdensity(sigmas, prefixtrans) rgb = rgb + weights[:, None] rgbs opacity = opacity + weights[:, None] depth = depth + weights[:, None] (tstarts + tends)[:, None] / 2.0 # 4. Finalization if renderbkgd is not None: rgb = rgb + renderbkgd (1.0 - opacity) depth = depth / torch.clampmin(opacity, torch.finfo(rgbs.dtype).eps) return rgb, opacity, depth, itersamples Accelerates the method by decoupling counting of occupied steps from sample generation, solving variable-length buffer issues in batched CUDA kernels. Time Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the grid and the number of occupied intervals. The hierarchical traversal reduces the number of texture reads significantly compared to dense grids. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the binaries tensor of shape (L, Rx, Ry, Rz) and the VDB structure overhead. For L=4, R=128, this is manageable on modern GPUs. Performance: Reduces texture reads by a factor of 3. In a specific implementation (lava-lamp), texture reads dropped from 17.6M to 5.9M per frame at 1080p in a default view, and from 138M to 46M in a full-screen lamp view. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space; compatible with hierarchical grids; reduces memory bandwidth pressure. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of occupancy grid; sorting of intersection times adds overhead for multi-level grids; precision issues may arise with very small step sizes or large bounding boxes. When to use: When the scene has large empty regions and the occupancy grid can be pre-computed or updated efficiently. When not to use: When the scene is fully dense, or when the overhead of maintaining the occupancy grid outweighs the traversal savings. The method originates from the use of hierarchical VDB (OpenVDB/NanoVDB) grids for volume rendering, specifically adapted for GPU acceleration. It is widely used in neural radiance field (NeRF) rendering pipelines, such as those in the nerfacc library and unofficial implementations like faster-occgrid. The concept of using an occupancy grid to cull empty blocks is also found in traditional volume rendering, such as in the lava-lamp simulation. name: Two-pass chunked ray traversal for occupancy grids
head: Chunked ray traversal with occupancy grid, Two-pass occupancy grid traversal
body: This method accelerates sparse voxel grid raycasting using a two-pass CUDA kernel launch that first counts the number of traversal steps per ray to allocate exact sample buffers, then fills those buffers with sample intervals and ray indices. It solves the problem of variable-length sample buffers per ray in a batched kernel by computing the exact number of occupied intervals each ray intersects, allocating a contiguous buffer, and then populating it with precise sample intervals. The method consists of two sequential CUDA kernel launches. The first pass counts the number of occupied voxel intervals (chunks) each ray traverses to determine buffer sizes. The second pass writes the actual sample data into pre-allocated tensors using the computed offsets. Inputs: grids: int64 array of pointers to nanovdb::MaskGrid (device memory). rayso: float array of shape [nrays, 3], ray origins. raysd: float array of shape [nrays, 3], ray directions. resolution: int32 array of shape [3], grid resolution per axis. aabbs: float array of shape [ngrids, 6], axis-aligned bounding boxes for each grid. hits: bool array of shape [nrays, ngrids], pre-computed ray-grid intersection flags. tsorted: float array of shape [nrays, ngrids2], sorted entry/exit distances per grid. tindices: int64 array of shape [nrays, ngrids2], indices into tsorted. nearplanes: float array of shape [nrays]. farplanes: float array of shape [nrays]. Outputs (allocated before launch): chunkcounts: int64 array of shape [nrays], number of occupied chunks per ray. chunkindices: int64 array of shape [nrays], starting index in the sample buffer for each ray. rayindices: int64 array of shape [nsamples], maps each sample to its originating ray. tleft: float array of shape [nsamples], entry distance of each sample interval. tright: float array of shape [nsamples], exit distance of each sample interval. The core data structure is the occupancy grid (nanovdb::MaskGrid), accessed via pointers in grids. The traversal relies on sorted entry/exit distances (tsorted) and their corresponding grid indices (tindices) to efficiently skip empty regions. The output buffers are flattened 1D arrays where samples from all rays are concatenated. chunkindices acts as an exclusive prefix sum of chunkcounts to determine write offsets. stepsize: float, fixed step length for traversal. coneangle: float, cone angle for frustum traversal. threads: int, threads per block. Typical value: 256. n: int, grid update frequency. Default: 16. 1. First Pass (Counting): Launch traversekernel with firstpass=true to compute ntrav per ray and store in chunkcounts. 2. Prefix Sum: Compute the cumulative sum of chunkcounts to get total sample count nsamples and starting indices for each ray's chunk. 3. Second Pass (Filling): Launch traversekernel with firstpass=false to write chunkindices, rayindices, tleft, and tright into pre-allocated tensors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversekernel(rayso, raysd, resolution, aabbs, hits, tsorted, tindices, nearplanes, farplanes, chunkcounts, chunkindices, rayindices, tleft, tright, firstpass, nrays, ngrids): # Standard CUDA thread indexing threadidx = (blockIdx.x blockDim.x) + threadIdx.x if threadidx >= nrays: return rayid = threadidx count = 0 offset = 0 if not firstpass: offset = chunkindices[rayid] # Iterate through pre-sorted grid intervals for this ray # The exact occupancy check logic over tsorted/tindices is implementation-specific for i in range(0, ngrids 2, 2): tentry = tsorted[rayid, i] texit = tsorted[rayid, i + 1] gridid = tindices[rayid, i] # Skip grids the ray does not hit if not hits[rayid, gridid]: continue # Clamp interval to camera near/far planes tl = max(tentry, nearplanes[rayid]) tr = min(texit, farplanes[rayid]) if tl < tr: if firstpass: count += 1 else: tleft[offset] = tl tright[offset] = tr rayindices[offset] = rayid offset += 1 if firstpass: chunkcounts[rayid] = count Pre-allocation: The second pass requires pre-allocated output tensors for tleft, tright, and rayindices. Passing nullptr for these pointers in the first pass avoids overwriting or invalid memory access. Precision: Floating-point precision in tsorted and tleft/tright can cause gaps or overlaps if not handled carefully. Ensure consistent clamping to nearplanes and farplanes. Empty Rays: Rays with no hits should result in chunkcounts[rayid] = 0 and no writes in the second pass. Degenerate Input: If nrays is 0 or ngrids is 0, the kernel should handle this gracefully without launching. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{grids}) for the first pass (counting) and O(N{samples}) for the second pass (filling), where N{samples} is the total number of occupied intervals. The prefix sum is O(N{rays}). Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{grids}) for tsorted and tindices, plus O(N{samples}) for the output buffers. This is more memory-efficient than fixed-step methods if occupancy is sparse. Performance: Measured performance depends on hardware and scene density. The two-pass approach adds overhead for the counting pass but reduces memory bandwidth usage in the second pass by avoiding redundant writes. It is most beneficial when occupancy is highly variable across rays. Strengths: Exact buffer allocation, reduced memory waste, coalesced memory accesses in the second pass. Limitations: Requires two kernel launches and a prefix sum operation. Not suitable for real-time applications with strict latency constraints where the overhead of the first pass is prohibitive. This method is derived from implementations in the faster-occgrid repository, which adapts techniques from neural radiance field (NeRF) rendering to sparse occupancy grids. It addresses the inefficiency of fixed-step ray marching in sparse environments by dynamically allocating memory based on actual occupancy. name: Empty Space Skipping via Data Structures
head: Empty Space Skipping, Volume Culling, Active Cell Identification
body: Empty space skipping accelerates volume rendering by identifying and bypassing regions of the volume that do not contribute to the final image, thereby reducing the number of sample evaluations and shading calculations. It differs from its siblings by focusing on the identification of "active" or "significant" volume data using various data structures (bounding geometry, 2D slices, BVHs, or HistoPyramids) to define ray entry and exit bounds, whereas Hierarchical Grid Traversal focuses on the traversal logic of the grid itself. It sets itself apart from Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping by typically using pre-computed or coarse structural bounds rather than adaptive step sizes based on local density gradients. The core mechanism of empty space skipping is the reduction of the ray marching domain. Instead of sampling the entire volume extent [t{start}, t{exit}], the method computes a reduced interval [t{entry}, t{exit}] or a set of disjoint intervals where the volume data is non-empty or contributes to the transfer function. 1. Active Region Identification: A data structure is used to represent the spatial extent of non-empty or significant voxels. This structure allows for efficient queries to determine if a ray segment intersects active data. 2. Ray Bounding: For each pixel, the ray is tested against the active region data to find the entry point t{entry} and exit point t{exit}. 3. Culling: Samples outside these bounds are discarded. If the ray does not intersect any active region, the pixel is rendered as background. 4. Integration: The volume rendering integral is computed only over the active segments: C = \int{t{entry}}^{t{exit}} \rho(\mathbf{p}(t)) \cdot T(t) \, dt where \rho is the emission/scattering coefficient and T(t) is the transmittance. A GPU-based technique that uses view-dependent bounding geometry of block min-max structures to determine ray entry and exit depths per pixel. It differs from image-order methods by rasterizing block boundaries to establish search ranges, making it highly efficient for real-time isosurface rendering. Choose this when rendering isosurfaces with significant empty space and when GPU rasterization capabilities can be leveraged for culling. This method accelerates direct volume rendering by using 2D textures and OpenGL alpha/depth tests to discard non-contributing intervals. It determines near and far intersection points by leveraging the GPU's depth buffer. Unlike sibling methods that may use complex data structures like octrees, this technique relies on standard OpenGL pipeline tests. It is particularly effective when the volume has significant external empty space. An acceleration technique for transparent volumes that combines empty-space skipping with analytic integration of optical depth. It solves the problem of expensive ray marching inside semi-transparent objects by allowing the ray to skip empty regions outside the volume and then analytically compute the contribution of the segment inside the volume based on its length. It sets itself apart from opaque empty-space skipping by using lower bounds for sphere tracing inside objects and from full volumetric rendering by avoiding numerical integration for constant-density materials. A rendering technique for volumetric videos that uses a hybrid representation of multi-level hash tables and 2D CNN-generated MLP maps, combined with empty space skipping via an occupancy volume to achieve real-time performance. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. A technique achieving extremely fine-grained empty space skipping by marching rays only through active volume cells, located efficiently with a HistoPyramid texture and rendered as point primitives. It is considered a hybrid object-order and image-order approach, meaning it is dependent on rendering resolution. The steps involve: 1. Locating active volume cells using a HistoPyramid texture; 2. Rendering active cells as point primitives to create rays close to the isosurface; 3. Accelerating by exploiting early-depth testing (comparing fragment's interpolated z-coordinate with the depth buffer value to discard occluded fragments); 4. Rasterizing primitives in front-to-back order to increase discarded fragments, achieved via CPU-based sorting of volume slices. Empty space skipping has been a central topic in GPU-driven visualization of large-scale volumes. Liu et al. [LCD09] achieved extremely fine-grained empty space skipping by only marching rays through active volume cells, efficiently located with a HistoPyramid texture [ZTTS06]. The authors later introduced the IsoBAS acceleration structure [LCD15], yielding faster identification of active cells and requiring less memory overhead. Jiang et al. [JRZ16] also proposed an acceleration structure that can efficiently locate active cells for both direct and indirect visualization approaches. These methods [LCD09, LCD15, JRZ16] are considered hybrid object-order and image-order approaches. For an in-depth review of GPU-driven visualization of large-scale volumes, we refer to the work of Beyer et al. [BHP15]. name: Object-Order Empty Space Skipping
head: Block min-max culling, Front-to-back ray-casting with bounding box culling, GPU-based Ray-Casting with Object-Order Empty Space Skipping
body: Object-Order Empty Space Skipping is a GPU-based ray-casting acceleration technique that reduces the computational overhead of traversing transparent regions in a volume by culling entire blocks of voxels before sample evaluation. It differs from image-order methods by using view-dependent bounding geometry to determine ray entry and exit depths per pixel, thereby skipping large portions of empty space with minimal per-pixel overhead. Unlike macrocell or BSP-tree approaches that require complex tree traversal logic, this method relies on simple rasterization of block boundaries to establish search ranges, making it highly efficient for real-time isosurface rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D texture storing the volume data, camera parameters (position c, screen coordinates (x, y)), and a block min-max structure storing the minimum and maximum scalar values for each block in the volume. Output: A rendered image with isosurface shading, where rays are terminated early if they traverse inactive (transparent) blocks. Data Structures: Block Min-Max Structure: For a regular subdivision of the volume into blocks of size B^3 (e.g., 4^3 or 8^3 voxels), this structure stores two values per block: min and max. These represent the minimum and maximum scalar values present in the block's voxel data. Bounding Geometry: A set of 3D primitives representing the bounding boxes of active blocks. This geometry is kept in GPU memory and updated when the isovalue changes. Steps: 1. Ray Direction Computation: For each pixel (x, y), compute the ray direction vector d(x, y) in volume coordinates based on the camera position c: p(t, x, y) = c + t \cdot d(x, y) where t is the distance along the ray. 2. Ray Depth Range Initialization: Determine the initial search range [t{start}(x, y), t{exit}(x, y)] for each ray by rasterizing the block bounding geometry: t{start}: Rasterize the front faces of the active block bounding geometry. Use a depth test (e.g., GLLESS) to retain the closest intersection point, which corresponds to the entry point into the first active block. t{exit}: Rasterize the back faces of the active block bounding geometry. Use an inverted depth test (e.g., GLGREATER) to retain the farthest intersection point, which corresponds to the exit point from the last active block. 3. Ray Casting Loop: Iterate through the volume in front-to-back order within the fragment shader: Sample the volume at the current ray position. Object-Order Skip: If the current ray segment falls within a region covered by inactive blocks (blocks where the isovalue is outside [min, max]), skip the sampling process for that segment. This is handled by the depth range computed in Step 2, which excludes inactive blocks from the initial search range unless they are enclosed by active blocks. Image-Order Skip: For samples within active blocks but in transparent regions, use adaptive sampling or early termination based on accumulated opacity. Refine the isosurface intersection position using iterative bisection if the ray crosses the isovalue. Parameters: Block Size: The volume is subdivided into blocks of size 4^3 or 8^3 voxels. Smaller blocks increase culling precision but increase memory overhead for the min-max structure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Enclosed Inactive Blocks: Inactive blocks enclosed by active blocks are not excluded from the search range by the bounding geometry because the rasterization only captures the outer boundary of active regions. Samples in these enclosed inactive blocks are skipped on a per-sample basis early in the ray-casting loop, incurring a small overhead. Precision: Depth values for t{start} and t{exit} must be computed with sufficient precision to avoid gaps or overlaps in the bounding geometry, which could lead to incorrect ray ranges. A variant of block min-max culling designed for pre-integrated volume rendering. It modifies the region covered by each block so that each block covers a region of thickness at least the sampling distance, creating overlaps between adjacent blocks. This allows a line segment formed by two sampling points to be tested for transparency using only one block, avoiding the overhead of determining which of multiple intersecting blocks are transparent. Unlike previous methods where a line segment may intersect at most three blocks and requires testing all intersecting blocks, this method tests only one block due to the overlapping region design. Time Complexity: The culling overhead is minimal, as it relies on rasterization of bounding geometry, which is highly optimized on GPUs. The main cost is the ray casting loop, which is reduced by skipping inactive blocks. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory for the block min-max structure, proportional to the number of blocks in the volume. For large volumes that do not fit in GPU memory, a second level of coarser bricks is maintained, increasing memory usage. Performance: In empty regions, this approach results in a considerable speed-up because only one texture fetch is needed to check the mean value of the block. However, in complex scenes with many active blocks, the overhead of maintaining the bounding geometry and min-max structure may reduce performance gains. Strengths: Simple implementation, low per-pixel overhead, effective for real-time isosurface rendering. Limitations: Enclosed inactive blocks are not fully excluded, leading to per-sample overhead in those regions. Performance may degrade with complex shaders and texture indirections. Object-Order Empty Space Skipping was introduced in the context of GPU-based ray-casting for real-time volume rendering. It builds on earlier approaches that used multiple rendering passes for ray casting, replacing them with a single pass and front-to-back looping in the fragment shader. The technique was developed to overcome limitations of earlier empty space skipping methods, such as high overhead and poor performance with complex shaders. It is widely used in real-time volume rendering applications, particularly for isosurface visualization. name: Early Shader Termination
head: Early End of Computation, Early z-test optimization, Two-pass empty space culling
body: Early Shader Termination is an optimization technique that discards the execution of complex decoding shaders for fragments likely to represent empty space by using an early z-test in a two-pass rendering approach. It builds on Object-Order Empty Space Skipping by adding a lightweight pre-check to avoid expensive shader execution in empty regions. Compared to rendering uncompressed data, this approach initially perceives a loss in performance of a factor of 2-3 due to complex shaders and texture indirections; however, in empty regions, it results in a considerable speed-up because only one texture fetch is needed to check the mean. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A compressed volume dataset where each block (macro-cell) has an associated index texture I storing metadata (specifically the mean value in the R-component) and dependent data textures C1, C2. A slicing polygon representing the current view frustum or volume boundary. Output: A rendered image where empty space fragments are skipped, and depth values are correctly updated to allow subsequent fragments to pass depth tests. Data Structures: Index Texture I: Stores block metadata. The R-component holds the mean value of the block. Dependent Textures C1, C2: Store difference information or raw data, addressed using components of I. Steps: 1. First Pass (Empty Space Detection): Render the slicing polygon twice. In the first pass, issue a simple pixel shader program. In the shader, access index texture I and check the mean value stored in the R-component. If the mean value is zero, render the fragment with color and opacity set to zero. This does not affect the color buffer but sets the depth value in the depth buffer. If the mean value is not zero, discard the fragment using a kill instruction. This prevents the fragment from affecting the color or depth buffer. 2. Second Pass (Complex Rendering): Render the slicing polygon again with the complex shader. Set the depth test to GLGREATER in the second pass. The early z-test only lets fragments pass that were discarded in the first pass (where mean \neq 0). All other fragments (where mean = 0) are discarded before entering the complex shader. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyshadertermination(fragments, indextextureI, complexdecodefunc): """ Simulates the two-pass early shader termination optimization. fragments: list of objects with.coords,.blockid,.z (depth) indextextureI: dict mapping blockid to objects with.R (mean value) complexdecodefunc: callable that returns decoded color for non-empty blocks """ depthbuffer = {} # Maps fragment coordinates to depth from pass 1 pass1discarded = [] # Pass 1: Simple pixel shader for frag in fragments: meanval = indextextureI[frag.blockid].R if meanval == 0: # Empty space: write depth, zero color/opacity depthbuffer[frag.coords] = frag.z pass1discarded.append(False) else: # Non-empty space: discard via kill instruction # Depth buffer retains the last valid depth for this coordinate pass1discarded.append(True) # Pass 2: Complex shader with GLGREATER depth test finaloutput = [] for i, frag in enumerate(fragments): if not pass1discarded[i]: # Early z-test fails: GLGREATER requires frag.z > depthbuffer[frag.coords] # Since pass 1 wrote frag.z, frag.z > frag.z is false. Fragment discarded. continue # Early z-test passes for discarded fragments (mean != 0) lastdepth = depthbuffer.get(frag.coords, -float('inf')) if frag.z > lastdepth: # GLGREATER decoded = complexdecodefunc(frag, indextextureI) finaloutput.append(decoded) return finaloutput Parameters: Depth Test Function: Must be set to GLGREATER in the second pass to leverage the early z-test correctly. Mean Threshold: Zero is used as the threshold for empty space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Buffer Consistency: If a fragment is discarded in the shader (via kill), the depth value of the fragment rendered last is still valid in the depth buffer. This must be accounted for when using depth tests, as the discarded fragment does not update the depth buffer. Performance Overhead: The two-pass approach introduces overhead. The initial performance loss compared to uncompressed rendering is a factor of 2-3 due to the complexity of the shaders and texture indirections. Adds spatial coherence checks along the scanline direction to skip entire segments of empty space within a macro-cell projection. It builds on Early Shader Termination by optimizing the scope of the termination check. Time Complexity: In empty regions, the complexity is reduced to one texture fetch per block to check the mean. In non-empty regions, the full complex shader is executed. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the index texture I and dependent textures C1, C2. Measured Performance: On an Intel P4 1900 MHz machine, this approach saves another 5 percent of overall rendering time on average when combined with other optimizations like Early End of Computation. Strengths: Considerable speed-up in empty regions, which are frequent in numerical simulation results. Limitations: Initial performance loss of 2-3x compared to uncompressed rendering due to shader complexity and indirections. Requires hardware support for early z-test. The technique was proposed in the context of compression domain volume rendering to address performance losses caused by complex shader programs and texture indirections. It leverages the early z-test feature available on target graphics architectures to avoid executing pixel shaders for fragments that are likely to decode empty space. The concept of terminating computation early is also discussed in the context of cell-based first-hit ray casting, where rendering ends as soon as all pixels are covered, saving approximately 5 percent of overall rendering time.
