name: Early Scanline Termination
body: Early Scanline Termination is an optimization that stops processing a scanline as soon as a local ray through a pixel does not intersect any iso-surfaces, reducing the number of local rays cast per pixel. It builds on Early Shader Termination by adding a spatial coherence check along the scanline direction, allowing the renderer to skip entire segments of empty space within a macro-cell projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projected macro-cell, set of surface cells within the macro-cell, current scanline (row or column of pixels), and the image buffer. Output: Updated image buffer with colors for intersected pixels; identification of erroneous blank pixels (holes) for post-processing. Data Structures: Image Buffer: Stores color values for each pixel. Sequence Flags: Two flags per pixel indicating whether the pixel was recently dropped due to horizontal or vertical early scanline termination. Flags are set to 1 for all empty dropped pixels. The bounds of each new sequence of dropped pixels are marked by setting the sequence flag of the pixel immediately preceding the sequence and the pixel immediately following the sequence to 0. A pixel through which a regular local ray has been cast has its sequence flags reset to 0. Steps: 1. Identify all scanlines intersecting the macro-cell projection. 2. Check for problem cases by calculating a representative surface normal for each surface cell and checking dot products with two reference vectors. If a boundary cell prohibits termination, project its center point. The collection of these projections forms a critical region. 3. Iterate through pixels of a scanline from one boundary to the other. If a local ray does not intersect any iso-surface and the pixel is outside the critical region, stop processing the scanline. Mark all remaining empty pixels as dropped, setting the appropriate sequence flag (horizontal or vertical) to 1. Set the sequence flag of the pixel immediately preceding the first dropped pixel and the pixel immediately following the last dropped pixel to 0 to mark the sequence bounds. If a regular local ray is cast through a pixel, reset its sequence flags to 0. 4. After frame completion, identify sequences of blank pixels with sequence flags set, bounded on both sides by non-blank pixels with unset flags. Cast rays from these pixels through the complete volume to fill the holes. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Left-facing surface normals: If projected surface normals point towards the left, early termination is disallowed for scanlines intersecting those parts until all such intersections are processed. Dangerous faces: Certain surface orientations can cause errors if termination is applied. Errors: Early scanline termination can lead to errors in about 0.017 percent of pixels on average, resulting in visible holes. These holes must be identified and filled after frame completion. Sequence Flag Management: Flags must be carefully managed to correctly identify erroneous sequences. Pixels erroneously dropped will never be part of a dropped sequence again. body: This method exploits hardware-accelerated rasterization to skip over empty space in volume rendering, avoiding the overhead of explicit tree traversal on the GPU. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Early Shader Termination by using the fragment positions of rasterized bounding geometry faces as the start and end points for ray casting, which can lead to fewer look-ups into the empty-space skipping data structure compared to traditional octree structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume texture, coarse grid dimensions, threshold iso value, and bounding geometry (e.g., leaf node bounding boxes). Output: Ray casting start and end points derived from fragment positions. Data Structures: gridTex: 3D texture where each voxel contains the maximum iso value of a coarse grid cell. Bounding Geometry: Triangle mesh (quads) generated at boundaries between active and inactive grid cells. Depth Buffers: Offscreen buffers storing minimum and maximum depth values per fragment/pixel. Steps: 1. Initialization: Generate gridTex by downsampling the volume texture, storing the maximum iso value per coarse cell. 2. Thresholding: Mark a grid cell as active if its maximum iso value exceeds the threshold. 3. Geometry Generation: For each pair of neighboring cells in gridTex, generate a quad if one is active and the other is inactive. 4. First Pass: Rasterize the bounding geometry to an offscreen buffer, computing and storing the minimum and maximum depth values for each pixel. 5. Second Pass: Rasterize the front faces of the geometry to the main buffer. Discard fragments that are not at the minimum depth value. 6. Ray Setup: Compute the ray start and end positions from the minimum and maximum depth values stored in the first pass. 7. Marching: Cast and march the ray through the volume using the computed start and end points. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. name: Ray Casting with Depth/Alpha Test for Empty Space Skipping
head: Westermann & Sevenich method, Ray Casting using Alpha and Depth Tests, Empty Space Skipping via OpenGL Tests, Westermann & Sevenich Empty Space Skipping
body: This method accelerates direct volume rendering by skipping empty space intervals in the volume integral, using 2D textures and OpenGL alpha/depth tests to discard non-contributing intervals. It determines the near and far intersection points of rays with the volume by leveraging the GPU's depth buffer, allowing samples to be taken only between these points. Unlike sibling methods that may use complex data structures like octrees or BSP trees, this technique relies on standard OpenGL pipeline tests to bound the ray segment, reducing the number of samples and framebuffer writes. It is particularly effective when the volume has significant external empty space, though its benefit diminishes with high internal data dispersion. Inputs: 3D volume data (scalar field). Camera parameters including projection matrix P, modelview matrix V, and model matrix M. Rendering context supporting OpenGL alpha and depth tests. Outputs: Final color image in the framebuffer. Data Structures: 2D Textures: The volume is sliced into 2D planes parallel to the X, Y, and Z axes. Display Lists: Created for each set of textures ordered front-to-back and back-to-front. Depth Buffer: Used to store normalized device coordinates (NDC) of the nearest and farthest visible fragments. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (CPU): Calculate the gradient of each volume element using central differences. Perform illumination and shading based on lighting model variables and store the result in main memory. This step is performed once on the CPU, unlike methods that compute shading dynamically on the GPU. 2. Texture Preparation (CPU/GPU): For each axis (X, Y, Z): For each plane parallel to the axis: Create a 2D texture from the slice data. Load the texture into GPU memory. Create a display list for the set of textures, ordered front-to-back and back-to-front. 3. Determine Ray Bounds (GPU Passes): The goal is to find the entry (P) and exit (Q) points of the ray through the volume. Pass 1 (Near Point): Initialize the depth buffer to 1.0 (maximum NDC depth). Enable the Alpha Test with GLGREATER and a reference value > 0 to discard fragments with zero opacity. Set the Depth Test criterion to GLLESS. Render the volume slices so the depth buffer stores the distance of the closest significant fragment to the projection plane for each pixel. Pass 2 (Far Point): Initialize the depth buffer to 0.0 (minimum NDC depth). Keep the Alpha Test enabled (GLGREATER, ref > 0). Set the Depth Test criterion to GLGREATER. Render the volume slices so the depth buffer stores the distance of the farthest significant fragment from the projection plane for each pixel. 4. Coordinate Transformation: Read the depth values from the depth buffer for each pixel (xs, ys, zs) in NDC. Transform these NDC coordinates to world coordinates to obtain the ray origin P and ray end Q. The transformation uses the inverse of the projection and model matrices applied to the view-transformed NDC point: \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ w \end{bmatrix} = (P M)^{-1} V \begin{bmatrix} xs \\ ys \\ zs \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where P is the projection matrix, M is the model matrix, and V is the view matrix. 5. Ray Casting and Compositing: For each pixel, cast a ray between P (near) and Q (far). Sample the volume along the ray segment defined by t \in [0, 1] using parametric equations: X(t) = Px + (Qx - Px)t, \quad Y(t) = Py + (Qy - Py)t, \quad Z(t) = Pz + (Qz - Pz)t The increment in t is determined by the number of samples n per ray (e.g., \Delta t = 1/n). Composite the samples using the reduced volume rendering integral (empty space outside [P, Q] is skipped): L(x) = \int{xA'}^{xB'} \left[ e^{-\int{xA'}^{x0'} \phit(x'')dx''} \epsilon(x0') dx0' \right] where xA' and xB' correspond to points P and Q, \phit is the extinction coefficient, and \epsilon is the color. Draw the final composed color to the framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Find Near Point (P) neardepthbuffer = renderpass(textures, depthinit=1.0, alphatest='GREATER', alpharef=0.0, depthfunc='LESS') # Step 4: Pass 2 - Find Far Point (Q) fardepthbuffer = renderpass(textures, depthinit=0.0, alphatest='GREATER', alpharef=0.0, depthfunc='GREATER') # Step 5: Coordinate Transformation & Ray Casting invprojmodel = invertmatrix(multiplymatrices(cameraparams['projectionmatrix'], cameraparams['modelmatrix'])) viewmatrix = cameraparams['viewmatrix'] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): znearndc = neardepthbuffer[y][x] zfarndc = fardepthbuffer[y][x] Pworld = ndctoworld(x, y, znearndc, invprojmodel, viewmatrix) Qworld = ndctoworld(x, y, zfarndc, invprojmodel, viewmatrix) color = compositeray(Pworld, Qworld, volumedata, numsamples) framebuffer[y][x] = color def ndctoworld(xndc, yndc, zndc, invpm, viewmatrix): ndcpoint = [xndc, yndc, zndc, 1.0] worldpoint = multiplymatrixvector(invpm, ndcpoint) worldpoint = multiplymatrixvector(viewmatrix, worldpoint) return worldpoint def compositeray(P, Q, volume, nsamples): tstep = 1.0 / nsamples alphaaccum = 0.0 coloraccum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(nsamples): t = i tstep pos = [P[0] + (Q[0] - P[0]) t, P[1] + (Q[1] - P[1]) t, P[2] + (Q[2] - P[2]) t] density = samplevolume(pos, volume) colorsample, opacity = transferfunction(density) weight = (1.0 - alphaaccum) opacity coloraccum = [coloraccum[0] + weight colorsample[0], coloraccum[1] + weight colorsample[1], coloraccum[2] + weight colorsample[2]] alphaaccum += weight if alphaaccum >= 1.0: break return coloraccum An optimization for primary rays in volumetric ray tracing that creates a polygonal representation of all objects and projects them into two Z-buffers (nearest and farthest distances). It ensures polygonal models completely contain the actual volumetric objects to bound the ray segment. If no Z-buffer information exists for a pixel, intersection calculations are skipped. It typically reduces primary ray computation by a factor of four. It can also be extended to shadow rays by creating Z-buffer projections from light locations. Time Complexity: Reduces ray casting time to approximately one-quarter of a naive ray caster that samples the entire ray extension. Performance improvements of 3 to 4 times faster are observed when using alpha and depth tests compared to not using them. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 2D textures for all slices along the optimal axis, plus display lists. Strengths: Simple to implement using standard OpenGL features; effective for volumes with large empty regions outside the object; avoids complex data structure traversal. Limitations: Only skips external empty spaces; high internal data dispersion reduces effectiveness as the ray length with skipping becomes similar to the unoptimized length. Illumination is calculated on the CPU in a single pass, preventing dynamic lighting updates without recomputation. When to use: When the volume has significant transparent regions outside the object and dynamic lighting is not required. When not to use: When the volume has high internal dispersion (many small opaque regions throughout) or when dynamic lighting is needed (consider Engel, Kraus & Ertl instead). The method was introduced by Westermann and Sevenich in their work [WS01]. It is a hybrid volume rendering technique that leverages the GPU's depth buffer to skip empty spaces, allowing ray casting to sample only non-transparent material. It differs from Engel, Kraus & Ertl's method by performing illumination calculation uniquely and in the initial phase on the CPU, whereas Engel's method computes it on the GPU. The technique is part of the broader family of empty-space skipping methods aimed at accelerating volume rendering by avoiding regions in the volume that are completely transparent [Parent]. body: Semi-transparent Empty-Space Skipping is a rendering approach for transparent or semi-transparent objects with constant density material where the ray continues inside toward the exit point, and the optical contribution of the inner ray segment is evaluated analytically from its length. It solves the problem of expensive ray marching inside semi-transparent objects by allowing the ray to skip empty regions outside the volume and then analytically compute the contribution of the segment inside the volume based on its length, rather than sampling it discretely. It sets itself apart from opaque empty-space skipping by using lower bounds for sphere tracing inside objects and from full volumetric rendering by avoiding numerical integration for constant-density materials. The method adapts the BVH-based sphere tracing approach used for opaque volumes to handle transparency. The core distinction lies in how the ray interacts with the volume boundaries and how the optical depth is computed. Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), volume density function \rho(\mathbf{p}), transfer function (opacity \alpha per unit length), and a BVH representing the volume's spatial extent. Output: Final color C and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} for the pixel. The method relies on a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). For sphere tracing, each node in the BVH must store bounds that allow for lower-bound distance queries. BVH Node: Contains bounding volume (e.g., AABB or Sphere) and children indices. Bounds: For semi-transparent skipping, the bounds must support querying the minimum distance from the ray origin to the volume interior, rather than the maximum distance to the surface. 1. Ray Initialization: Initialize accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0 and color C = (0,0,0,0). Normalize \mathbf{d} if not already normalized. 2. Empty-Space Skipping (Outside): While the ray is outside the volume: Perform sphere tracing using the BVH. Use lower bounds to determine the distance to the nearest point inside the volume. This allows the ray to quickly advance to the entry point. If the ray misses the volume entirely, terminate and return background color. 3. Entry Point Detection: Identify the entry point \mathbf{p}{in} where the ray intersects the volume boundary. 4. Inside Volume Processing: Case A: Constant Density (\rho(\mathbf{p}) = \rho0): Determine the exit point \mathbf{p}{out} by continuing sphere tracing inside the volume using lower bounds to find the farthest exit or by solving the intersection analytically if the shape is simple. Calculate the segment length L = \|\mathbf{p}{out} - \mathbf{p}{in}\|. Compute the optical depth \tau = \rho0 \cdot L. Compute the transmittance T = e^{-\tau}. Update accumulated opacity: \alpha{acc} = 1 - T. Compute color contribution: C = C{in} \cdot (1 - T), where C{in} is the color of the volume material. Terminate ray. Case B: Varying Density (\rho(\mathbf{p}) varies): Switch to constant-size ray-marching to numerically integrate density when inside of volumes, as full volumetric rendering is required. Numerically integrate density along the segment: \tau = \int{\mathbf{p}{in}}^{\mathbf{p}{out}} \rho(\mathbf{p}(t)) dt. This part is not optimized by the skipping technique and requires full volumetric rendering. 5. Termination: If \alpha{acc} \ge 1 or ray length exceeds max distance, terminate. Optical Depth (Constant Density): \tau = \rho0 \cdot L Where \rho0 is the constant density and L is the length of the ray segment inside the volume. Transmittance: T = e^{-\tau} Accumulated Opacity: \alpha{acc} = 1 - T Density Function: \rho(\mathbf{p}). Can be constant \rho0 or varying (e.g., FBM noise). Sphere Tracing Step Size: For varying density, a constant step size h is used for numerical integration. Not given in the sources. Precision: Quadratic bounds allow the ray to quickly move away from the entry surface, performing significantly better than naive approaches. Exit Point Calculation: For complex shapes, determining the exact exit point \mathbf{p}{out} may require additional sphere tracing steps or analytical solutions. Unverified code. name: Distance Map Acceleration

body: Distance Map Acceleration is a ray traversal technique that uses a precomputed Chebyshev distance map to skip sampling points in empty regions of a volumetric image, reducing texture memory bandwidth and improving frame rates for volume and isosurface rendering. It builds on Occupancy Grid and Map-Based Empty Space Skipping by replacing simple binary occupancy checks with distance-based leapfrogging, allowing rays to jump directly to the nearest occupied region boundary. Unlike Two-stage Ray Marching with Empty-Space Skipping which may use hierarchical structures or multiple passes, this method performs a single-pass ray cast accelerated by a 3D distance field. Inputs: Volume data texture (scalar values). Transfer function parameters (intensity and gradient thresholds). Camera ray origin and direction. Block size B (integer, typically 4^3). Outputs: Rendered image with empty space skipped. Data Structures: 1. Volume Texture: 3D texture containing voxel intensities. Dimensions d{\text{vol}} = (dx, dy, dz). 2. Gradient Map: 3D texture storing precomputed gradient magnitudes. Generated via compute shader if useprecomputedgradient is true. 3. Occupancy Map: 3D texture of binary flags (occupied/unoccupied). Dimensions d{\text{occ}} = (dx/B, dy/B, dz/B). 4. Distance Map: 3D texture storing Chebyshev distance to the nearest occupied block. Dimensions same as Occupancy Map. 5. Transfer Function Uniform: Buffer containing imin, imax, gmin, gmax. Preprocessing Steps: 1. Gradient Map Generation: If enabled, dispatch a compute shader to calculate gradient magnitudes for all voxels using the tetrahedron method. 2. Occupancy Map Generation: Dispatch a compute shader to evaluate each block of size B \times B \times B. For volume rendering: A block is occupied if any voxel within it has non-zero alpha according to the transfer function. For isosurface rendering: A block is occupied if the isosurface threshold lies between the min and max voxel values in the block. A single-voxel halo around the block is also checked. 3. Distance Map Generation: Convert the occupancy map to a Chebyshev distance map using a compute shader. The Chebyshev distance between two points (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) is \max(|x1-x2|, |y1-y2|, |z1-z2|). Ray Traversal Algorithm: 1. Ray-Volume Intersection: Compute entry t{\text{entry}} and exit t{\text{exit}} of the ray with the volume bounding box. If the ray does not intersect, return background. 2. Sampling Parameters: Calculate the number of samples n and step size \Delta t: n = \lceil \max \vec{x}(\mathbf{d}) \cdot \| \mathbf{t}{\text{exit}} - \mathbf{t}{\text{entry}} \| \cdot f \rceil \Delta t = \frac{t{\text{exit}} - t{\text{entry}}}{n - 1} where \mathbf{d} is the ray direction, f \ge 1 is a sampling factor, and \max \vec{x} returns the maximum component of the vector. 3. Ray Casting Loop: Initialize current position t = t{\text{entry}}. While t < t{\text{exit}}: Convert normalized texture coordinate t to volume voxel coordinate u{\text{vol}} and occupancy map coordinate u{\text{occ}}: u{\text{vol}} = d{\text{vol}} \cdot t u{\text{occ}} = \frac{d{\text{vol}}}{B} \cdot t Sample the occupancy map at u{\text{occ}}. If the block is empty: Sample the distance map at u{\text{occ}} to get distance D to the nearest occupied block. Calculate the step \Delta i in occupancy map indices to reach the next occupied region. For dimension j \in \{x, y, z\}: \Delta ij = \begin{cases} \lceil (1 + \lfloor u{\text{occ},j} \rfloor - u{\text{occ},j}) / \Delta uj \rceil & \text{if } \Delta uj > 0 \\ \lceil (\lfloor u{\text{occ},j} \rfloor - u{\text{occ},j}) / \Delta uj \rceil & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \Delta uj is the change in occupancy map coordinate per sample step along the ray. Convert \Delta i to normalized distance \Delta t{\text{skip}} and advance t \leftarrow t + \Delta t{\text{skip}}. If the block is occupied: Sample the volume and gradient map at u{\text{vol}}. Apply transfer function using imin, imax, gmin, gmax to compute color and opacity. Composite the sample into the ray buffer. Check for early ray termination. Advance t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. 4. Clipping: The volume is clipped at a specified clipdistance from the camera. If the viewpoint enters the volume, the intersection vertices are computed in a vertex shader. Volumes are also clipped against the depth buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distancemapacceleratedraycast(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetex, occmap, distmap, blocksize, tfparams): # 1. Ray-Volume Intersection tentry, texit = intersectbox(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) if tentry > texit: return backgroundcolor # 2. Sampling Parameters raylen = length(raydirection) # maxx returns the maximum component of the vector n = ceil(maxcomponent(raydirection) raylen samplingfactor) if n < 1: n = 1 deltat = (texit - tentry) / (n - 1) if n > 1 else 0.0 # 3. Precompute occupancy map step sizes per sample # uocc = (dvol / B) t # deltauocc = (dvol / B) deltat dvol = volumetex.dimensions deltauocc = (dvol / blocksize) deltat t = tentry color = vec3(0.0) alpha = 0.0 while t < texit: # Map t to occupancy map coordinates uocc = (dvol / blocksize) t # Check occupancy if not occmap.sample(uocc): # Empty block: skip using distance map dist = distmap.sample(uocc) # Calculate steps to next occupied block # For each dimension, calculate steps to exit current block or reach neighbor steps = vec3(0) for j in {x, y, z}: if deltauocc[j] > 0: steps[j] = ceil((1.0 + floor(uocc[j]) - uocc[j]) / deltauocc[j]) else: steps[j] = ceil((floor(uocc[j]) - uocc[j]) / deltauocc[j]) # Convert steps to normalized distance # The skip distance is determined by the dimension requiring the fewest steps to hit an occupied block # Note: The source defines deltaij but implies using the distance map for the actual leap # In Chebyshev distance, the distance is in block units. # We advance t by the distance to the nearest occupied block in normalized coords skipdistnormalized = dist (blocksize / dvol[j]) # Approximation, exact mapping depends on ray direction # More robustly: find the smallest tadvance such that the new uocc is occupied # Using the distance map value directly as a bound for skipping t += dist (blocksize / dvol[j]) # Simplified leap based on Chebyshev distance in block units else: # Occupied block: sample volume uvol = dvol t val = volumetex.sample(uvol) grad = gradientmap.sample(uvol) if gradientmap else 0.0 # Apply Transfer Function alphaval = tfapply(val, grad, tfparams) # Composite color = color + alphaval (1.0 - alpha) samplecolor alpha = alpha + alphaval (1.0 - alpha) if alpha >= 1.0: break t += deltat return color Runtime assembly of partitioned distance maps to enable empty space skipping without recomputing the distance transform on transfer function changes. GPU compute shader routine to produce binary occupancy maps from volume data for empty-space skipping. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(V) where V is the number of voxels for gradient and occupancy map generation. Ray traversal is O(N{\text{samples}}) in the worst case, but significantly reduced by skipping empty space. The skip step calculation is O(1) per block. Memory Complexity: Occupancy map requires 1/B^3 of the volume memory. For B=4, this is 1/64th. Distance map requires similar memory to occupancy map. Gradient map requires additional memory if precomputed. Performance: Reduces texture samples in empty regions, improving frame rates. Performance depends on the sparsity of the volume and the block size B. Strengths: Efficient empty space skipping; simple implementation; works well with GPU compute shaders. Limitations: Requires preprocessing; distance map generation can be costly for large volumes; Chebyshev distance may overestimate skip distances in some cases compared to Euclidean. When to use: Volume rendering with significant empty space; isosurface rendering. When not to use: Dense volumes with little empty space; dynamic volumes where preprocessing cost outweighs benefits. Distance Map Acceleration was introduced by Lachlan Deakin and Mark Knackstedt in 2019 in "Accelerated Volume Rendering with Chebyshev Distance Maps". It is an extension of their earlier work on empty space skipping. The method is implemented in the open-source Vulkan renderer VkVolume. Efficient ray casting of volumetric images using distance maps for empty space skipping, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-019-0155-y, fetched 2026-10-24 GitHub - LDeakin/VkVolume: Vulkan-based volume renderer with efficient..., https://github.com/LDeakin/VkVolume, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Partitioned Distance Map Combination
body: Partitioned Distance Map Combination is the runtime assembly phase that merges a selected subset of precomputed partitioned distance maps into a single global distance map for empty space skipping. It uses a ping-pong buffer strategy with two swap textures to iteratively combine maps, allowing more maps to be processed than can be bound simultaneously as shader inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of precomputed partitioned distance maps (texturePartitionedDistanceMaps), a boolean array indicating which maps are active for the current transfer function (partitionedDistanceMapsToUse), and the occupancy map dimensions (sizeOccupancyMap). Output: A single combined distance map stored in textureIntermediateDistanceMapOutput. Data Structures: textureSwapArray: An array of two textures with format GLR8UI (8-bit unsigned integer, single channel) and GLREADWRITE access, acting as ping-pong buffers. texturePartitionedDistanceMaps: An array of textures, each representing a distance map for a specific intensity partition, accessed with GLREADONLY. partitionedDistanceMapsToUse: A boolean array indicating which partitioned maps are currently relevant. UBO: An 8-byte Uniform Buffer Object used to pass control flags to the compute shader. Parameters: numMapsToCombinePerLaunch: The maximum number of partitioned maps to combine in a single compute dispatch. The source specifies a constant value of 6. Numbered Steps: 1. Count Active Maps: Iterate through partitionedDistanceMapsToUse to calculate numMapsToCombineTotal, the total number of active partitioned maps. 2. Calculate Iterations: Compute numIterations as \lceil \text{numMapsToCombineTotal} / \text{numMapsToCombinePerLaunch} \rceil. 3. Iterative Combination Loop: For each iteration j from 0 to numIterations - 1: a. Bind Swap Buffers: Bind textureSwapArray[j % 2] to image unit 0 and textureSwapArray[(j + 1) % 2] to image unit 1 with GLREADWRITE access. b. Determine Maps to Combine: Calculate numMapsToUse as \min(\text{numMapsToCombinePerLaunch}, \text{numMapsToCombineTotal} - j \times \text{numMapsToCombinePerLaunch}). c. Bind Partitioned Maps: Loop through i from 0 to numMapsToUse - 1. Skip inactive maps in partitionedDistanceMapsToUse by incrementing idxMapProcessed until a true value is found. Bind the corresponding texturePartitionedDistanceMaps[idxMapProcessed] to image unit 2 + i with GLREADONLY access. Increment idxMapProcessed. d. Setup UBO: Create an 8-byte UBO. Set the first 4 bytes to useDistanceValueFromPreviousPass (1 if j > 0, else 0). Set the next 4 bytes to numMapsToUse. Bind this UBO to binding point 0. e. Dispatch Compute: Calculate work groups based on sizeOccupancyMap dimensions divided by 8. Dispatch the compute shader with dimensions (numWorkGroups[0], numWorkGroups[1], numWorkGroups[2]). Issue a memory barrier to ensure completion. 4. Final Copy: After the loop, copy the final result from the active swap buffer to textureIntermediateDistanceMapOutput using glCopyImageSubData with dimensions from sizeOccupancyMap. 5. Cleanup: Delete the UBO. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct numMapsToCombineTotal = sum(1 for active in partitionedDistanceMapsToUse if active) numIterations = (numMapsToCombineTotal + numMapsToCombinePerLaunch - 1) // numMapsToCombinePerLaunch idxMapProcessed = 0 for j in range(numIterations): readbufferidx = j % 2 writebufferidx = (j + 1) % 2 remainingmaps = numMapsToCombineTotal - j numMapsToCombinePerLaunch numMapsToUse = min(numMapsToCombinePerLaunch, remainingmaps) for i in range(numMapsToUse): while not partitionedDistanceMapsToUse[idxMapProcessed]: idxMapProcessed += 1 # Bind texturePartitionedDistanceMaps[idxMapProcessed] to image unit 2 + i idxMapProcessed += 1 # Setup UBO (8 bytes) useprev = 1 if j > 0 else 0 ubodata = struct.pack('II', useprev, numMapsToUse) # Bind UBO to binding point 0 # Calculate work groups numWorkGroups = tuple(sizeOccupancyMap[k] // 8 for k in range(3)) # Dispatch compute shader with numWorkGroups and issue memory barrier Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Active Maps: If numMapsToCombineTotal is 0, numIterations is 0, and the loop is skipped. The output distance map may need to be initialized to a maximum value to indicate no occupied space. Precision: The use of GLR8UI implies 8-bit unsigned integer distance values, which may lead to quantization errors or overflow if distances exceed 255. Boundary Conditions: The compute shader must handle boundary checks correctly when reading from partitioned maps and writing to the swap buffers. Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) with Partitioned Distance Maps (PDM) based Empty Space Skipping (ESS) is an acceleration technique for distance-field ray marching that subdivides the volume's intensity range into n partitions to precompute individual distance maps. When a transfer function (TF) changes, only the relevant PDMs are merged to form the final distance map D', avoiding a full recomputation of the distance transform. Unlike the base method Partitioned Distance Map Combination which recomputes the global distance map on every TF change, PDM-based ESS trades higher memory usage and one-time initialization cost for significantly faster TF update times, maintaining high frame rates during frequent TF adjustments. Time Complexity: The combination process scales with the number of active partitioned maps and the volume size, with iterations bounded by \lceil N / 6 \rceil where N is the number of active maps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing n partitioned distance maps plus two swap buffers, resulting in O(n \cdot V) memory usage where V is the number of voxels. Strengths: Avoids full distance transform recomputation on transfer function changes. Limitations: Higher memory usage due to storing multiple partitioned maps and precision limitations due to 8-bit distance maps. The method originates from an unofficial implementation of Partitioned Distance Map based Empty Space Skipping for Direct Volume Rendering. It builds on the principles of Distance Map Acceleration [972-distance-map-acceleration.md] and Occupancy Map Generation [1197-occupancy-map-generation.md]. CalamityMichL/DVRESSPDM, https://github.com/CalamityMichL/DVRESSPDM, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Partitioned Distance Map (PDM) Acceleration
head: Partitioned Distance Map (PDM) Update, PDM-based Empty Space Skipping, Direct Volume Rendering with Partitioned Distance Maps (PDM) based Empty Space Skipping, Accelerating Transfer Function Update for Distance Map based Volume Rendering
body: Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) with Partitioned Distance Maps (PDM) based Empty Space Skipping (ESS) is an acceleration technique for distance-field ray marching that subdivides the volume's intensity range into n partitions to precompute individual distance maps. When a transfer function (TF) changes, only the relevant PDMs are merged to form the final distance map D', avoiding a full recomputation of the distance transform. Unlike the base method Partitioned Distance Map Combination which recomputes the global distance map on every TF change, PDM-based ESS trades higher memory usage and one-time initialization cost for significantly faster TF update times, maintaining high frame rates during frequent TF adjustments. Inputs: Volume dataset V with intensity values. Number of intensity partitions n. Block size b for block-reduction (typically b=4). Transfer Function (TF) mapping intensities to RGBA. Camera parameters (position, view matrix). Outputs: Final distance map D' used for ESS during ray casting. Rendered image via ray casting. Partitioned Occupancy Maps (POMs) and Partitioned Distance Maps (PDMs): Type: uint8 (unsigned 8-bit integer). Layout: Block-reduced dimensions. If the volume has dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz, the map dimensions are \lceil Dx/b \rceil \times \lceil Dy/b \rceil \times \lceil Dz/b \rceil. Content: POM: Stores occupancy status. Value 0 indicates occupied (contains at least one voxel in the partition's intensity range), 1 indicates empty. PDM: Stores Chebyshev distance to the nearest non-empty block within that specific intensity partition. Distances > 255 are clamped to 255. Uniform Buffer Object (UBO) Layout (std140, binding 1): | Offset | Size | Field | Type | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | 0 | 64 | model | mat4 | | 64 | 64 | view | mat4 | | 128 | 64 | inverseModelView | mat4 | | 192 | 4 | samplingfactor | float | | 196 | 4 | renderContentType | int | | 200 | 4 | ditheringMode | int | | 204 | 4 | earlyRayTermination | bool | | 208 | 4 | essType | int | | 212 | 4 | gradientType | int | | 216 | 4 | itfgammacorrection | bool | | 220 | 4 | gamma | float | | 224 | 4 | enablebicubicfiltering | bool | | 228 | 4 | reusenormals | bool | | 232 | 4 | lightshadingfactor | float | | 240 | 12 | lightDirection | vec3 | | 252 | 4 | lightambientfactor | float | | 256 | 4 | lightdiffusefactor | float | | 260 | 4 | lightspecularfactor | float | | 264 | 4 | lightspecularshininess | float | Texture Bindings: texVolume (binding 0): sampler3D texGradient (binding 1): sampler3D texNoise (binding 2): sampler2D texITF (binding 3): mediump sampler2D texOccupancyMap (binding 4): mediump usampler3D texDistanceMap (binding 5): mediump usampler3D 1. Partition Definition: Subdivide the total intensity range of the volume into n partitions. Each partition p is defined by lower and upper integer intensity borders \rho{min}^p and \rho{max}^p. 2. POM Computation: Compute n Partitioned Occupancy Maps (POMs). The original volume is block-reduced into non-overlapping blocks of size b^3. A block is considered occupied in partition p if it contains at least one voxel with an intensity value within [\rho{min}^p, \rho{max}^p]. 3. PDM Computation: Compute n Partitioned Distance Maps (PDMs) from the POMs. Each PDM encodes the Chebyshev distance to the nearest non-empty voxel block within that specific intensity partition. This is typically done using a multi-pass distance transform algorithm on the GPU. When the TF is updated, the final distance map D' is assembled without recomputing the underlying PDMs: 1. Determine Active Partitions: Identify the set S of partition indices p such that the TF maps at least one intensity value in partition p to a non-zero alpha value. 2. Merge PDMs: Compute the element-wise minimum of the corresponding PDMs to form D': D'(x, y, z) = \min{p \in S} (PDMp(x, y, z)) This merging is performed in a GLSL Compute Shader. Up to a maximum of 6 PDMs are bound as input textures per pass, aggregating distances to produce D'. If more PDMs are needed, multiple passes are used with flip-flopping input/output textures. 1. Ray Origin and Direction: Get camera position in object coordinates: rayorigin = inverseModelView vec4(view[0][3], view[1][3], view[2][3], 1.0f). Intersect ray with bounding box (AABB: minBB=(-0.5,-0.5,-0.5), maxBB=(0.5,0.5,0.5)) using the slab method to find entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances. 2. Normalize to Texture Coordinates: raystart = (rayorigin + raydirection t0 - minBB) / (maxBB - minBB). raystop = (rayorigin + raydirection t1 - minBB) / (maxBB - minBB). 3. Calculate Step Parameters: ray = raystop - raystart. raylength = length(ray). Check for degenerate rays: If raylength is infinite, NaN, or > \sqrt{3} (~1.732051f), return immediately. nsteps = int(ceil(float(dimmax) raylength samplingfactor)) where dimmax is the maximum dimension of the volume texture. stepvector = normalize(ray) raylength / (float(nsteps) - 1.0f). 4. Ray Marching Loop: For each step i from 0 to n\steps - 1: Calculate sampling position: samplingPos = raystart + stepvector float(i). Empty Space Skipping: Use D' to determine the step size. The distance map value at the current block position indicates how many blocks can be skipped. Convert this block distance to world/texture space distance and advance the ray. Volume Sampling: Sample intensity from texVolume at samplingPos. Gradient Calculation: If gradientType == 0 (on-the-fly): Approximate gradient using tetrahedron technique. Sample 4 voxels at offsets k.xyy, k.yyx, k.yxy, k.xxx where k=ivec2(-1,1). Compute gradientVec = 0.25 sum(ki valuei). Normalize and store magnitude in alpha channel. If gradientType == 1 (precomputed): Sample from texGradient at samplingPos + 0.5/vec3(volumeSize). Normalize xyz components and store original magnitude in alpha. Interpolation: If enablebicubicfiltering is true, calculate tricubic interpolation weights and mix samples. Transfer Function: Map intensity to RGBA using texITF. Apply gamma correction if itfgammacorrection is true. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity. If earlyRayTermination is true, break loop if accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computepom(volume, blocksize, partitionmin, partitionmax): """ Computes a Partitioned Occupancy Map for a specific intensity partition. volume: 3D list of voxel intensities. blocksize: int, side length of blocks (e.g., 4). partitionmin, partitionmax: int, intensity range. Returns: 3D list of uint8 (0=occupied, 1=empty). """ dimz, dimy, dimx = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) pomdimz = (dimz + blocksize - 1) // blocksize pomdimy = (dimy + blocksize - 1) // blocksize pomdimx = (dimx + blocksize - 1) // blocksize pom = [[[1 for in range(pomdimx)] for in range(pomdimy)] for in range(pomdimz)] for z in range(pomdimz): for y in range(pomdimy): for x in range(pomdimx): xstart, xend = x blocksize, min((x + 1) blocksize, dimx) ystart, yend = y blocksize, min((y + 1) blocksize, dimy) zstart, zend = z blocksize, min((z + 1) blocksize, dimz) occupied = False for vz in range(zstart, zend): for vy in range(ystart, yend): for vx in range(xstart, xend): if partitionmin <= volume[vz][vy][vx] <= partitionmax: occupied = True break if occupied: break if occupied: break pom[z][y][x] = 0 if occupied else 1 return pom def computepdm(pom): """ Computes Chebyshev Distance Map from POM. pom: 3D list of uint8 (0=occupied, 1=empty). Returns: 3D list of uint8 (distance to nearest 0, clamped to 255). """ dimz, dimy, dimx = len(pom), len(pom[0]), len(pom[0][0]) dist = [[[255 for in range(dimx)] for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimz)] # Multi-pass distance transform (simplified logic for demonstration) # Pass 1: Forward for z in range(dimz): for y in range(dimy): for x in range(dimx): if pom[z][y][x] == 0: dist[z][y][x] = 0 else: d = 255 if x > 0: d = min(d, dist[z][y][x-1] + 1) if y > 0: d = min(d, dist[z][y-1][x] + 1) if z > 0: d = min(d, dist[z-1][y][x] + 1) dist[z][y][x] = d # Pass 2: Backward for z in range(dimz-1, -1, -1): for y in range(dimy-1, -1, -1): for x in range(dimx-1, -1, -1): d = dist[z][y][x] if x < dimx - 1: d = min(d, dist[z][y][x+1] + 1) if y < dimy - 1: d = min(d, dist[z][y+1][x] + 1) if z < dimz - 1: d = min(d, dist[z+1][y][x] + 1) dist[z][y][x] = d return dist def mergepdms(pdms, activeindices): """ Merges selected PDMs into a final distance map D'. pdms: list of 3D lists (PDMs). activeindices: list of indices into pdms. Returns: 3D list of uint8 (D'). """ if not activeindices: dimz, dimy, dimx = len(pdms[0]), len(pdms[0][0]), len(pdms[0][0][0]) return [[[255 for in range(dimx)] for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimz)] dprime = [row[:] for row in pdms[activeindices[0]]] for idx in activeindices[1:]: for z in range(len(dprime)): for y in range(len(dprime[0])): for x in range(len(dprime[0][0])): dprime[z][y][x] = min(dprime[z][y][x], pdms[idx][z][y][x]) return dprime def raycast(volume, dprime, cameramatrix, tf, params): """ Performs direct volume rendering using PDM-based ESS. volume: 3D list of intensities. dprime: 3D list of uint8 (final distance map). cameramatrix: 4x4 list of lists (inverseModelView). tf: Transfer function function/intensity map. params: dict with samplingfactor, earlyRayTermination, etc. Returns: 2D list of RGBA tuples. """ dimz, dimy, dimx = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) height, width = params.get('height', 100), params.get('width', 100) # Ray origin from camera matrix rayorigin = [cameramatrix[0][3], cameramatrix[1][3], cameramatrix[2][3]] minBB = [-0.5, -0.5, -0.5] maxBB = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] image = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Simplified ray direction calculation for front face raydir = [x / width - 0.5, y / height - 0.5, -1.0] raylen = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in raydir)) raydir = [c/raylen for c in raydir] # Intersect with Bounding Box (slab method) t0, t1 = intersectslab(rayorigin, raydir, minBB, maxBB) if t0 > t1: continue raystart = [(rayorigin[i] + raydir[i] t0 - minBB[i]) / (maxBB[i] - minBB[i]) for i in range(3)] raystop = [(rayorigin[i] + raydir[i] t1 - minBB[i]) / (maxBB[i] - minBB[i]) for i in range(3)] rayvec = [raystop[i] - raystart[i] for i in range(3)] raylength = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in rayvec)) if raylength <= 0 or raylength > math.sqrt(3.0) or math.isnan(raylength): continue dimmax = max(dimz, dimy, dimx) nsteps = int(math.ceil(dimmax raylength params['samplingfactor'])) stepvector = [rayvec[i] / raylength raylength / (nsteps - 1.0) for i in range(3)] accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for i in range(nsteps): samplingpos = [raystart[i] + stepvector[i] i for i in range(3)] # ESS Step bx = int(samplingpos[0] dimx / params['blocksize']) by = int(samplingpos[1] dimy / params['blocksize']) bz = int(samplingpos[2] dimz / params['blocksize']) bx = max(0, min(bx, dimx // params['blocksize'] - 1)) by = max(0, min(by, dimy // params['blocksize'] - 1)) bz = max(0, min(bz, dimz // params['blocksize'] - 1)) dist = dprime[bz][by][bx] skipdistance = dist params['blocksize'] / dimmax samplingpos = [samplingpos[j] + stepvector[j] (nsteps - 1.0) skipdistance / raylength for j in range(3)] intensity = samplevolume(volume, samplingpos, params) rgba = applytf(tf, intensity, params) if params['earlyRayTermination'] and accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break c = [rgba[k] rgba[3] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) for k in range(3)] accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[k] + c[k] for k in range(3)] accumulatedalpha += rgba[3] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) image[y][x] = accumulatedcolor return image def intersectslab(origin, direction, minBB, maxBB): t0, t1 = -math.inf, math.inf for i in range(3): if direction[i] != 0: t1 = min(t1, (maxBB[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i]) t0 = max(t0, (minBB[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i]) else: if origin[i] < minBB[i] or origin[i] > maxBB[i]: return (math.inf, -math.inf) return (t0, t1) def samplevolume(volume, pos, params): # Standard volume sampling (e.g., trilinear or tricubic interpolation) return 0.5 def applytf(tf, intensity, params): # Standard TF lookup and compositing return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.5] Block size b: Side length of non-overlapping voxel blocks. Number of partitions n: Number of intensity subranges. samplingfactor: Float parameter scaling the number of sampling steps. Typical values depend on resolution/quality. essType: Integer selecting ESS algorithm (e.g., distance ESS). earlyRayTermination: Boolean enabling/disabling early termination. enablebicubicfiltering: Boolean enabling/disabling tricubic interpolation. gradientType: Integer (0: on-the-fly, 1: precomputed). MAXSEGMENTS: Compile-time constant, value 64. Approximation Error: D' is an element-wise lower limit of the standard non-partitioned distance map D (D' \le D). This means ESS may skip fewer voxels (worse performance) if different intensity values in the same partition are mapped to both zero and non-zero alpha by the TF. However, it never skips more voxels than allowed, ensuring correctness. Degenerate Rays: If raylength is infinite, NaN, or greater than \sqrt{3} (~1.732051f), the ray is degenerate (e.g., start and endpoint coinciding or outside bounds). The shader returns immediately to prevent performance regressions. Data Type Clamping: PDM/POM data types are uint8. Distances higher than 255 are clamped. Time Complexity: Preprocessing: O(n \cdot V) where V is the number of voxels and n is the number of partitions. One-time initialization cost increases with n (e.g., 905.2ms for 256 partitions on Manix dataset). TF Update: O(k \cdot V{blocks}) where k is the number of active partitions and V{blocks} is the number of blocks. Significantly faster than full distance map recomputation (e.g., 0.20ms to 1.30ms for 16-256 partitions vs 58.1ms for original method on Manix). Rendering: O(R \cdot S) where R is the number of rays and S is the average number of steps per ray. ESS reduces S. Memory Complexity: O(n \cdot V{blocks}) for storing n PDMs. Higher memory usage compared to a single distance map. Measured Performance: Manix (512x512x460): Original distance map: 58.1ms. PDM (16 partitions) update: 0.20ms. PDM (256 partitions) update: 1.30ms. Stag Beetle (832x832x494): Original: 146.4ms. PDM (16 partitions) update: 0.41ms. PDM (256 partitions) update: 2.58ms. Kingsnake (1024x1024x795): Original: 228.2ms. PDM (16 partitions) update: 0.80ms. PDM (256 partitions) update: 6.71ms. Scaling: Performance gain in TF update time is consistent across datasets, but initialization cost scales with n and volume size. Strengths: Fast TF updates, high frame rates during interactive TF adjustment, correctness guaranteed (no over-skipping). Limitations: Higher memory usage, slower one-time initialization, potential performance degradation in rendering if ESS skips fewer voxels due to approximation. When to use: Interactive volume rendering with frequent TF changes. When not to use: Static TFs, memory-constrained environments, or when one-time initialization time is critical. Origin: Proposed by Michael Rauter in "Accelerating Transfer Function Update for Distance Map based Volume Rendering" (IEEE VIS 2024). History: Extends the work of Deakin and Knackstedt on distance map based ESS. The original approach required full distance map recomputation on TF change, which was a limiting performance factor. Faludi et al. [5] used an octree of bitfields, reporting ray marching times 35% slower than Deakin’s approach. PDM-based ESS improves upon this by using partitioned distance maps for faster updates. Usage: Used in GPU-based direct volume rendering, particularly in virtual reality and interactive visualization applications. name: Occupancy Map Generation
head: Compute Occupancy Map, ITF Occupancy Compute
body: Occupancy Map Generation is a GPU compute shader dispatch routine that produces an occupancy map from input volume, gradient, and ITF textures to enable efficient empty-space skipping in volume rendering. It differs from its sibling, Partitioned Distance Map Combination, by generating a single-resolution occupancy map rather than a continuous distance field or partitioned data. Inputs and Outputs: Input Volume: 3D texture bound to image unit 0, formatted as GLR8 or GLR16 with GLREADONLY access. Gradient Texture: 3D texture bound to image unit 1, formatted as GLRGBA8 with GLREADONLY access. ITF Texture: 2D texture bound to image unit 2, formatted as GLRGBA8 with GLREADONLY access. Output Occupancy Map: 3D texture bound to image unit 3, formatted as GLR8UI with GLREADWRITE access. Uniform Buffer (Binding 0): 20 bytes total. Offset 0: reductionBlockSize packed as glm::vec4 (16 bytes). Offset 16: useITF2D as int (4 bytes). Data Structures: The output occupancy map is bound as GLR8UI with GLREADWRITE access. The exact semantic meaning of the stored values (binary indicators vs. voxel counts) is not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Calculate the 3D workgroup dimensions for the compute shader dispatch. For each axis i \in \{0, 1, 2\}, the workgroup size Wi is computed by dividing sizeOccupancyMap[i] by 8 and rounding up: Wi = \left\lceil \frac{\text{sizeOccupancyMap}[i]}{8} \right\rceil 2. Dispatch the compute shader with the calculated workgroup counts (W0, W1, W2). 3. Issue a full memory barrier to ensure the written image data is visible to subsequent rendering passes. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateoccupancymap(volumetex, gradienttex, itftex, occupancytex, sizeoccupancymap, reductionblocksize, useitf2d): """ Host-side dispatch logic for occupancy map generation. """ # Step 1: Calculate workgroup dimensions workgroupx = (sizeoccupancymap[0] + 7) // 8 workgroupy = (sizeoccupancymap[1] + 7) // 8 workgroupz = (sizeoccupancymap[2] + 7) // 8 # Step 2: Dispatch the compute shader # bindprogram(programname) represents standard shader program binding bindprogram("shadercomputeoccupancy") # setuniform(name, value) represents standard uniform upload setuniform("reductionBlockSize", reductionblocksize) setuniform("useITF2D", useitf2d) # bindimageunit(unit, tex, access) represents standard image unit binding bindimageunit(0, volumetex, access="GLREADONLY") bindimageunit(1, gradienttex, access="GLREADONLY") bindimageunit(2, itftex, access="GLREADONLY") bindimageunit(3, occupancytex, access="GLREADWRITE") # dispatchcompute(x, y, z) represents standard compute shader dispatch dispatchcompute(workgroupx, workgroupy, workgroupz) # Step 3: Memory barrier # memorybarrier(mask) represents standard synchronization primitive memorybarrier(GLSHADERIMAGEACCESSBARRIERBIT) Parameters: reductionBlockSize: Controls the granularity of the occupancy reduction. Typical value not given in the sources. useITF2D: Flag to select between 2D and 3D ITF lookup modes. Typical value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The output format GLR8UI limits stored values to 0–255. If the reduction logic accumulates counts, overflow may occur for large reduction blocks. Boundaries: The sources do not specify padding or boundary handling for occupancy map dimensions that are not divisible by 8. A GPU compute shader dispatch routine that generates a partitioned occupancy map from volume, gradient, and partitioned occupancy textures using a reduction block size and intensity partition bounds. It differs from standard occupancy map generation by incorporating intensity partition boundaries to produce a partitioned map rather than a single binary map. Inputs and Outputs: Input Volume: 3D texture bound to image unit 0, formatted as GLR8 or GLR16 with GLREADONLY access. Gradient Texture: 3D texture bound to image unit 1, formatted as GLRGBA8 with GLREADONLY access. Output Partitioned Occupancy Map: 3D texture bound to image unit 2, formatted as GLR8UI with GLREADWRITE access. Uniform Buffer (Binding 0): 24 bytes total. Offset 0: reductionBlockSize packed as glm::vec4 (16 bytes). Offset 16: partitionintensitymin as float (4 bytes). Offset 20: partitionintensitymax as float (4 bytes). Steps: 1. Calculate the 3D workgroup dimensions by dividing sizeOccupancyMap[i] by 8 and rounding up for each axis i=0,1,2. 2. Dispatch the compute shader with the calculated workgroup counts. 3. Issue a full memory barrier to ensure visibility of written image data. 4. Bind the compute shader shadercomputepartitionedoccupancy. 5. Call the helper function ComputePOM passing the input volume texture, output datatype, texture gradient, output partitioned occupancy map, occupancy map size, reduction block size, and intensity partition boundaries. """ # Step 1: Calculate workgroup dimensions workgroupx = (sizeoccupancymap[0] + 7) // 8 workgroupy = (sizeoccupancymap[1] + 7) // 8 workgroupz = (sizeoccupancymap[2] + 7) // 8 # Step 2: Bind the specific shader bindprogram("shadercomputepartitionedoccupancy") setuniform("reductionBlockSize", reductionblocksize) setuniform("partitionintensitymin", partitionintensitymin) setuniform("partitionintensitymax", partitionintensitymax) bindimageunit(0, volumetex, access="GLREADONLY") bindimageunit(1, gradienttex, access="GLREADONLY") bindimageunit(2, partitionedoccupancytex, access="GLREADWRITE") # Step 3: Dispatch the compute shader dispatchcompute(workgroupx, workgroupy, workgroupz) # Step 4: Memory barrier memorybarrier(GLSHADERIMAGEACCESSBARRIERBIT) # Step 5: Call helper function # ComputePOM helper implementation details are not provided in the sources A compute shader routine where each thread block handles one brick to recompute occupancy in dynamic voxel worlds. It differs from standard occupancy map generation by operating on fixed-size bricks and using shared memory to aggregate counts without atomic operations. Steps: 1. Launch a compute shader where each thread block handles one brick. The block has exactly 32 threads. 2. Each thread reads 16 voxels from its assigned part of the brick. 3. Each thread counts the number of non-air voxels it read and writes this count to its own unsigned integer in shared memory. 4. Synchronize all threads within the block. 5. The first thread in the block sums the values from shared memory and writes the total to the brickmap entry for that brick. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Assumes 32 threads per block, each processing 16 voxels (512 voxels per brick). """ # threadid represents glLocalInvocationIndex (0-31) threadid = getthreadid() startvoxel = threadid 16 endvoxel = startvoxel + 16 count = 0 for v in range(startvoxel, endvoxel): # 0 represents air voxel per source description if brickdata[v] != 0: count += 1 # sharedcounts represents a shared memory array of 32 unsigned integers sharedcounts = [0] 32 sharedcounts[threadid] = count # syncthreads() represents syncthreads() syncthreads() if threadid == 0: total = sum(sharedcounts) # brickindex represents the global index of the current brick brickindex = getbrickindex() brickmap[brickindex] = total Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The brick recomputation is described as fast because it avoids atomic operations and uses shared memory, which is faster than global memory. Strengths: Efficient empty-space skipping via precomputed maps. The brick recomputation is suitable for dynamic voxel worlds where occupancy changes frequently. Limitations: The occupancy map generation assumes a static volume or requires regeneration if the volume changes. The brick recomputation is limited to fixed-size bricks and requires a specific thread block size of 32 threads. When to use: Use when empty-space skipping is needed for volume rendering. Use brick recomputation when the voxel world is dynamic and changes frequently. name: Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage)

body: A GPU compute shader dispatch routine that computes a distance map from an occupancy map, using a swap buffer for iterative or multi-pass distance calculation. It enables empty space skipping during volume ray marching by providing the distance to the nearest occupied voxel for any given position. Unlike Occupancy Mipmap Generation which creates hierarchical mipmaps, this method produces a single-resolution distance field via a specific three-stage dispatch sequence. Inputs and Outputs: Input: textureOccupancyMap (GLR8UI, GLREADWRITE). Output: textureDistanceMap (GLR8UI, GLREADWRITE). Temporary: textureSwap (GLR8UI, GLREADWRITE). Uniform: UBO (4 bytes) storing the current stage index. Data Structures: textureOccupancyMap: 3D texture, format GLR8UI. textureDistanceMap: 3D texture, format GLR8UI. textureSwap: 3D texture, format GLR8UI. UBO: 4-byte integer, binding point 0. Steps: 1. Bind textureDistanceMap to image unit 0 and textureOccupancyMap to image unit 1, both with GLR8UI format and GLREADWRITE access. 2. Create a Uniform Buffer Object (UBO) of size 4 bytes, bind it to binding point 0, and use glBindBufferRange to map the entire buffer. 3. Calculate the number of work groups for the 3D grid based on sizeOccupancyMap dimensions divided by 8, using ceiling division. 4. Stage 1: Set UBO stage value to 0, dispatch compute with dimensions (numWorkGroups[1], numWorkGroups[2], 1), and issue a memory barrier. 5. Stage 2: Bind textureSwap to image unit 1, set UBO stage value to 1, dispatch compute with dimensions (numWorkGroups[0], numWorkGroups[2], 1), and issue a memory barrier. 6. Stage 3: Set UBO stage value to 2, dispatch compute with dimensions (numWorkGroups[0], numWorkGroups[1], 1), and issue a memory barrier. 7. Clean up by unbinding the UBO and deleting the buffer object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedistancemapmultistage(occupancymap, distancemap, swapbuffer, volumesize): # 1. Bind textures bindimageunit(0, distancemap, format="GLR8UI", access="GLREADWRITE") bindimageunit(1, occupancymap, format="GLR8UI", access="GLREADWRITE") # 2. Create UBO ubo = createubo(size=4) bindubo(binding=0, buffer=ubo) bindbufferrange(binding=0, buffer=ubo, offset=0, size=4) # 3. Calculate work groups # Assuming occupancy map dimensions are known dim = texturesize(occupancymap) blocksize = 8 numworkgroupsx = ceil(dim.x / blocksize) numworkgroupsy = ceil(dim.y / blocksize) numworkgroupsz = ceil(dim.z / blocksize) # 4. Stage 1 setubovalue(ubo, 0) dispatchcompute(numworkgroupsy, numworkgroupsz, 1) memorybarrier() # 5. Stage 2 bindimageunit(1, swapbuffer, format="GLR8UI", access="GLREADWRITE") setubovalue(ubo, 1) dispatchcompute(numworkgroupsx, numworkgroupsz, 1) memorybarrier() # 6. Stage 3 setubovalue(ubo, 2) dispatchcompute(numworkgroupsx, numworkgroupsy, 1) memorybarrier() # 7. Cleanup unbindubo(binding=0) deletebuffer(ubo) Parameters: Block size: 8 (implied by division by 8 in work group calculation). UBO size: 4 bytes. Precision issues may arise if the distance map format (GLR8UI) cannot represent the maximum distance in the volume. name: Empty Space Map Generation
head: Empty Space Skipping Map, Ray Marching with Empty Space Map, Visibility Map Generation
body: Empty Space Map Generation is a preprocessing optimization for volume ray marching that creates a boolean map indicating which voxels contain no visible geometry based on a transfer function threshold. It allows the renderer to skip entire empty regions during ray traversal, significantly reducing the number of density samples and transfer function evaluations. The method integrates the transfer function's density criteria directly into the skipping logic, ensuring that only voxels contributing to the final image are processed. Inputs: Scalar field data for a volume of dimensions W \times H \times D. Transfer function definition (control points and evaluation method). Threshold density value (T). Outputs: emptyspacemap: A boolean array of size (W-1) \times (H-1) \times (D-1). Data Structures: emptyspacemap: 3D boolean array where index (i, j, k) corresponds to the voxel with minimum corner at grid coordinates (i, j, k). tfvertices: Temporary array of 8 floats, storing the transfer function output for the 8 vertices of the current voxel. Steps: 1. Initialize Map: Allocate emptyspacemap with dimensions (W-1) \times (H-1) \times (D-1). 2. Iterate Voxels: Loop over all voxel indices i from 0 to W-2, j from 0 to H-2, and k from 0 to D-2. 3. Sample Vertices: For the current voxel (i, j, k), identify its 8 vertices. The vertex indices are encoded as v = vi + vj \cdot 2 + vk \cdot 4, where vi, vj, vk \in \{0, 1\} represent the corner offsets. 4. Evaluate Transfer Function: For each vertex v, retrieve the scalar field value at the corresponding grid position (i + vi, j + vj, k + vk) and evaluate the transfer function. \text{tf\vertices}[v] = \text{transfer\function}(\text{field}(i + vi, j + vj, k + vk)) 5. Determine Emptiness: Check if any vertex has a transfer function density value greater than the threshold T. \text{is\empty} = \max(\text{tf\vertices}) \le T 6. Store Result: Set the map value for the current voxel. \text{empty\space\map}[\text{Offset}(i, j, k)] = \text{is\empty} Ray Marching Integration: When rendering, the ray marcher uses this map to skip empty voxels: 1. Compute current 3D voxel indices (vi[0], vi[1], vi[2]) from the ray position p. 2. Check emptyspacemap at these indices. 3. If empty: Compute the voxel minimum (v{min}) and maximum (v{max}) points in world space. Compute the intersection interval (t{min}, t{max}) of the ray with the voxel bounding box. Advance the ray parameter t by the maximum of (t{max} - t) and a minimum marching delta to ensure progress and avoid precision stalls. t \leftarrow t + \max(t{max} - t, \delta{march}) 4. If not empty, proceed with standard volume integration. Parameters: tolerance (T): Threshold density value. If any vertex of a voxel has a transfer function density > T, the voxel is considered non-empty. Pitfalls: Precision Problems: Computing voxel intersections can suffer from floating-point precision issues, potentially causing the ray to stall or skip incorrectly. The travel value must be clamped using FMax to ensure strict progress along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateemptyspacemap(field, transferfunction, width, height, depth, threshold, controlpoints): """ Generates a boolean map indicating empty voxels based on a transfer function threshold. """ # Initialize map with dimensions (W-1) x (H-1) x (D-1) emptyspacemap = [[[False for in range(depth - 1)] for in range(height - 1)] for in range(width - 1)] # Iterate over all voxels for i in range(width - 1): for j in range(height - 1): for k in range(depth - 1): # Evaluate transfer function at 8 vertices tfvalues = [0.0] 8 for vi in (0, 1): for vj in (0, 1): for vk in (0, 1): v = vi + vj 2 + vk 4 # Get scalar value at vertex and evaluate TF scalarval = field[i + vi][j + vj][k + vk] tfvalues[v] = transferfunction(scalarval, controlpoints) # Determine if voxel is empty # If max tf value <= threshold, the voxel is empty isempty = max(tfvalues) <= threshold # Store result emptyspacemap[i][j][k] = isempty return emptyspacemap def raymarchstepwithemptyspace(rayorigin, raydirection, emptyspacemap, voxelsize, marchingdelta): """ Single ray marching step using empty space map for skipping. Assumes uniform voxel size and axis-aligned grid. """ t = 0.0 # Compute current voxel indices from ray position x = rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0] t y = rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1] t z = rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2] t vi = int(x / voxelsize) vj = int(y / voxelsize) vk = int(z / voxelsize) # Check bounds if not (0 <= vi < len(emptyspacemap) and 0 <= vj < len(emptyspacemap[0]) and 0 <= vk < len(emptyspacemap[0][0])): return t, False # Out of bounds # Check if empty if emptyspacemap[vi][vj][vk]: # Compute voxel bounds in world space vminx = vi voxelsize vmaxx = (vi + 1) voxelsize vminy = vj voxelsize vmaxy = (vj + 1) voxelsize vminz = vk voxelsize vmaxz = (vk + 1) voxelsize # Compute intersection interval of ray with voxel bounding box tenter = t texit = float('inf') if raydirection[0] != 0: t1 = (vminx - rayorigin[0]) / raydirection[0] t2 = (vmaxx - rayorigin[0]) / raydirection[0] tenter = max(tenter, min(t1, t2)) texit = min(texit, max(t1, t2)) if raydirection[1] != 0: t1 = (vminy - rayorigin[1]) / raydirection[1] t2 = (vmaxy - rayorigin[1]) / raydirection[1] tenter = max(tenter, min(t1, t2)) texit = min(texit, max(t1, t2)) if raydirection[2] != 0: t1 = (vminz - rayorigin[2]) / raydirection[2] t2 = (vmaxz - rayorigin[2]) / raydirection[2] tenter = max(tenter, min(t1, t2)) texit = min(texit, max(t1, t2)) # Advance t by the maximum of (texit - t) and marchingdelta # This ensures progress and avoids precision stalls delta = max(texit - t, marchingdelta) t = t + delta return t, True # Skipped else: # Not empty, proceed with standard volume integration step t += marchingdelta return t, False # Processed This method accelerates volume ray casting by pre-computing a Chebyshev distance map from an occupancy map, allowing rays to skip multiple empty blocks in any dimension. It improves upon standard occupancy map skipping by enabling larger, dimension-independent skips, though it requires more complex generation and higher memory overhead. Performance: Significant speedup in sparse volumes where large empty regions exist, as it reduces the number of density samples and transfer function evaluations. Strengths: Simple to implement, low memory overhead compared to distance maps, effective for sparse data. Limitations: Only skips entire voxels; does not skip partial empty regions within a voxel. When to use: Sparse volumes with large empty regions, real-time rendering where preprocessing cost is acceptable. When not to use: Dense volumes with little empty space, or when partial voxel skipping is required. Not given in the sources. name: Chebyshev Distance Map Empty Space Skipping
head: Chebychev distance maps for empty-space skipping, Isotropic Chebyshev distance map
body: This method accelerates volume ray casting by pre-computing a Chebyshev distance map from an occupancy map, allowing rays to skip multiple empty blocks in any dimension. It improves upon standard occupancy map skipping by enabling larger, dimension-independent skips, though it requires more complex generation and higher memory overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An occupancy map where occupied voxels are marked (e.g., value 255) and empty voxels are 0. Output: A distance map texture storing the Chebyshev distance to the nearest occupied block for every voxel. Auxiliary: A swap image (texture) of the same dimensions as the distance map, required during generation. Data Structures: Distance Map: A 3D texture (uimage3D) with r8ui format (unsigned 8-bit integer per channel). Swap Image: A 3D texture with the same format and dimensions as the distance map, used to store intermediate results during the second transformation. Chebyshev Distance Definition: The Chebyshev distance between two points \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2 is defined as: D{\text{Chebyshev}}(\mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2) = \max (|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2|) where the maximum is taken over all dimensions. Generation Algorithm: The distance map is generated from the occupancy map using three sequential 1D passes, adapted from Saito and Toriwaki [12] for GPU parallelization. Each pass operates independently on rows, columns, or slices. 1. First Transformation (X-axis): Processes rows. It performs a forward pass followed by a backward pass to compute distances along the x-axis. The occupancy map can be read directly and written to the distance map in this stage. 2. Second Transformation (Y-axis): Processes columns. It reads from the output of the first transformation and writes to the swap image. It uses a zig-zag search from each voxel outwards until the minimum distance is found. 3. Third Transformation (Z-axis): Processes slices. It is identical to the second transformation but operates on the z-axis. It reads from the swap image and writes the final Chebyshev distance to the distance map. Ray Skipping Calculation: When a ray is at parameter u and the current voxel has distance D, the number of steps \Delta \mathbf{i} to the next sampling point D blocks away is calculated per dimension j \in \{x, y, z\}: \Delta{ij} = \begin{cases} \lceil (D + \lfloor \mathbf{u}j \rfloor - \mathbf{u}j) / \Delta \mathbf{u}j \rceil, & \text{if } \Delta \mathbf{u}j > 0 \\ \lceil (1 - D + \lfloor \mathbf{u}j \rfloor - \mathbf{u}j) / \Delta \mathbf{u}j \rceil, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (13) This can be vectorized as: \Delta \mathbf{i} = \lceil (\text{step}(-\Delta \mathbf{u}) + \text{sgn}(\Delta \mathbf{u}) \cdot D + \lfloor \mathbf{u} \rfloor - \mathbf{u}) / \Delta \mathbf{u} \rceil \quad (14) where \text{step}(x) is 0 if x < 0 and 1 otherwise, and \text{sgn}(x) is the sign function. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements the generation of the Chebyshev distance map. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computechebyshevdistancemap(occupancy, dimx, dimy, dimz): """ Computes the Chebyshev distance map from an occupancy map. occupancy: 3D array of size (dimx, dimy, dimz). Occupied voxels are 255, empty are 0. Returns: dist, the Chebyshev distance map. """ dist = [[[0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] swap = [[[0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] # First Transformation: X-axis (Rows) # Forward pass for z in range(dimz): for y in range(dimy): D1 = occupancy[0][y][z] dist[0][y][z] = D1 for x in range(1, dimx): D = min(D1 + 1, occupancy[x][y][z]) dist[x][y][z] = D D1 = D # Backward pass for z in range(dimz): for y in range(dimy): D1 = dist[dimx - 1][y][z] for x in range(dimx - 2, -1, -1): D = min(D1 + 1, dist[x][y][z]) dist[x][y][z] = D D1 = D # Second Transformation: Y-axis (Columns) # Reads from dist, writes to swap for z in range(dimz): for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): D = dist[x][y][z] for n in range(1, D): if y >= n: Dn = dist[x][y - n][z] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) if (y + n) < dimy and n < D: Dn = dist[x][y + n][z] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) swap[x][y][z] = D # Third Transformation: Z-axis (Slices) # Reads from swap, writes to dist for y in range(dimy): for x in range(dimx): for z in range(dimz): D = swap[x][y][z] for n in range(1, D): if z >= n: Dn = swap[x][y][z - n] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) if (z + n) < dimz and n < D: Dn = swap[x][y][z + n] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) dist[x][y][z] = D return dist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overhead: The generation process requires a swap image, doubling the memory requirements compared to using only an occupancy map. Distance Limit: Distances are stored as unsigned 8-bit integers, limiting the maximum distance to 255. Transfer Function Changes: The distance map must be regenerated every time the transfer function changes, as the occupancy map depends on the transfer function threshold. Time Complexity: The generation of the distance map involves three passes over the volume. The zig-zag search in the second and third transformations reduces the number of IO operations and is faster than the original algorithm. The ray casting step itself is O(1) per skip, allowing multiple blocks to be skipped with a single sample. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the occupancy map, the distance map, and the swap image during generation. The distance map uses r8ui, so 1 byte per voxel. Performance: The method is faster than the original approach which resumed occupancy map sampling after a set length of empty voxels. Strengths: Enables skipping multiple blocks in any dimension, not constrained by the block size B as with the occupancy map method. Limitations: Computational complexity of generating the distance map, which must be done every time the transfer function changes. Memory overhead due to the swap image. Limited maximum distance of 255. The method is based on the Chebyshev distance metric, which is the greatest difference between two points along any dimension. The algorithm for transforming an occupancy map into a Chebyshev distance map was adapted from Saito and Toriwaki [12] for efficient GPU parallelization. name: Occupancy Mipmap Generation
body: Occupancy Mipmap Generation computes a hierarchical occupancy mipmap for a 3D grid using JAX convolutions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: mat, a 3D array of shape (xdim, ydim, zdim) containing density or occupancy values. Output: mipmap, a list of JAX arrays representing the occupancy pyramid levels, followed by a scalar tensor containing the total number of occupied points. Data Structures: occupancymat: A 3D array of shape (xdim, ydim, zdim) with float32 values, initialized to zeros and set to 1.0 where mat > 0. data: A 4D JAX array of shape (1, xdim, ydim, zdim, 1) created by adding batch and channel dimensions to occupancymat. kernel: A 5D JAX array of shape (2^i, 2^i, 2^i, 1, 1) for level i. Steps: 1. Calculate the number of mipmap levels: L = \lfloor \log2(\text{xdim}) \rfloor. 2. Create the base occupancy mask: Initialize occupancymat with zeros. Set occupancymat[x, y, z] = 1.0 if mat[x, y, z] > 0, otherwise 0.0. 3. Convert to JAX array and reshape: Cast occupancymat to float32 and add batch and channel dimensions to form data of shape (1, xdim, ydim, zdim, 1). 4. Initialize mipmap as an empty list. 5. For each level i from 0 to L-1: a. Create a kernel of ones with shape (2^i, 2^i, 2^i, 1, 1). b. Define convolution dimension numbers for input (NHWDC) and kernel (HWDIO) to output (NHWDC). c. Apply lax.convgeneraldilated with stride (2^i, 2^i, 2^i) and padding 'SAME'. d. Remove batch and channel dimensions from the result. e. Append the resulting 3D array to mipmap. 6. Compute the total number of occupied points: N = \sum \text{occupancy\mat}. 7. Append N as a scalar tensor to mipmap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp from jax.lax import convgeneraldilated, convdimensionnumbers def generateoccupancymipmap(mat): xdim, ydim, zdim = mat.shape levels = int(jnp.log2(xdim)) occupancymat = jnp.zeros((xdim, ydim, zdim), dtype=jnp.float32) occupancymat = jnp.where(mat > 0, 1.0, occupancymat) data = occupancymat[None,:,:,:, None] mipmap = [] for i in range(levels): kernelsize = 2i kernel = jnp.ones((kernelsize, kernelsize, kernelsize, 1, 1)) dn = convdimensionnumbers(data.shape, kernel.shape, ('NHWDC', 'HWDIO', 'NHWDC')) convout = convgeneraldilated( data, kernel, windowstrides=(kernelsize, kernelsize, kernelsize), padding='SAME', dimensionnumbers=dn) levelgrid = convout[0,:,:,:, 0] mipmap.append(levelgrid) totaloccupied = jnp.sum(occupancymat) mipmap.append(totaloccupied) return mipmap Parameters: mat: Input 3D grid array. Dimensions xdim, ydim, zdim are used to determine the number of levels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The number of levels is computed as \lfloor \log2(\text{xdim}) \rfloor, which assumes xdim is a power of 2 for exact downsampling. The kernel size grows exponentially as 2^i, which increases memory requirements for the convolution at higher levels. Periodically refreshes a single-resolution 3D occupancy grid by querying a NeRF model for density values at voxel centers, marking voxels as occupied if density exceeds a threshold. It differs from this method by using direct thresholding on a single resolution rather than hierarchical convolutional smoothing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources.
