name: Occupancy Grid Update
head: Density-Based Grid Update, Grid Density Thresholding, Occupancy Grid Update from Density
body: This method periodically refreshes a 3D occupancy grid by querying a neural radiance field (NeRF) model for density values at voxel centers, marking voxels as occupied if the density exceeds a specified threshold. It solves the problem of stale acceleration structures in evolving NeRF training by ensuring the empty-space skipping mechanism reflects the current neural network's predictions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained or partially trained NeRF model, the current training iteration count, the 3D grid resolution, the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defining the scene bounds, and a density threshold. Output: A 3D boolean occupancy grid of shape (R, R, R) where R is the resolution. Data Structures: grid: A 3D array of shape (R, R, R) containing boolean values (True for occupied, False for empty). aabbmin, aabbmax: 3D vectors defining the lower and upper bounds of the scene in world coordinates. resolution: Integer R, the number of voxels along each axis. Steps: 1. Generate Grid Coordinates: Create a meshgrid of integer indices for the 3D grid. x, y, z = \text{linspace}(0, R-1, R) \text{grid\coords} = \text{meshgrid}(x, y, z, \text{indexing}='ij').\text{reshape}(-1, 3) 2. Convert to World Positions: Map grid indices to world coordinates using the AABB. \text{positions} = \text{aabb\min} + \left( \frac{\text{grid\coords} + 0.5}{R} \right) \times (\text{aabb\max} - \text{aabb\min}) 3. Query Densities: Batch the world positions and query the NeRF model for density values \sigma. If the model supports a forwardwithdensityonly method, call it with the positions. Otherwise, call the model with dummy view directions and extract the density output. 4. Update Grid: Compare densities against the threshold. \text{occupied} = \sigma > \text{threshold} Reshape the boolean array to (R, R, R) and update grid. Parameters: resolution (R): Integer, default 128. densitythreshold: Float, default 0.01. updategridevery: Integer, iteration interval for updates (e.g., 500). occupancythreshold: Float, synonym for density threshold in some implementations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateoccupancygrid(model, aabbmin, aabbmax, resolution, threshold, batchsize=10000): # 1. Generate grid coordinates (matches meshgrid(..., indexing='ij').reshape(-1, 3)) gridcoords = [] for x in range(resolution): for y in range(resolution): for z in range(resolution): gridcoords.append([x, y, z]) # 2. Convert to world positions positions = [] for idx in gridcoords: pos = [aabbmin[d] + ((float(idx[d]) + 0.5) / resolution) (aabbmax[d] - aabbmin[d]) for d in range(3)] positions.append(pos) # 3. Query densities in batches densities = [] numvoxels = len(positions) for i in range(0, numvoxels, batchsize): batchpositions = positions[i:i+batchsize] if hasattr(model, 'forwardwithdensityonly'): batchdensities = model.forwardwithdensityonly(batchpositions) else: dummydirs = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in batchpositions] output = model(batchpositions, dummydirs) # Assumes density is first output channel batchdensities = [out[0] for out in output] densities.extend(batchdensities) # 4. Update grid occupied = [d > threshold for d in densities] grid = [[[occupied[i resolution2 + j resolution + k] for k in range(resolution)] for j in range(resolution)] for i in range(resolution)] return grid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure gridcoords are converted to float before world position calculation to avoid integer division errors. Boundaries: The formula uses + 0.5 to sample at voxel centers, ensuring coverage of the entire AABB. Degenerate Input: If the NeRF model is not yet trained (all densities near zero), the grid will remain empty. Uses Exponential Moving Average of densities for smoother transitions and better gradient flow during training. Choose this when training stability and continuous density representation are prioritized over binary occupancy speed. Time Complexity: O(R^3) per update, where R is the grid resolution. The cost is dominated by the NeRF inference queries. Memory Complexity: O(R^3) for the occupancy grid storage. Measured Performance: In Instant-NGP implementations, a resolution of 128 with updates every 500 iterations provides a good balance between acceleration speed and update overhead. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively skips empty space in static scenes; low memory overhead compared to hierarchical structures. Limitations: Stale grid if updates are infrequent; binary thresholding can lead to aliasing artifacts at boundaries; requires periodic full-grid queries which can be costly if done too frequently. When to Use: Static or slowly changing scenes; training phases where the geometry is stabilizing. When Not to Use: Highly dynamic scenes requiring per-frame updates; scenes with fine details smaller than the voxel size. The specific implementation details cited here are from the FLASH project, an experimental implementation of Instant-NGP. It is used in modern NeRF training pipelines to accelerate ray marching by skipping empty space. InanXR/FLASH, https://github.com/InanXR/FLASH, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Density Grid Update with EMA
head: EMA Occupancy Grid Update
body: This method updates a 3D density grid using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of newly queried densities to stabilize training and refine the representation of occupied space. It builds on Occupancy Grid Update by maintaining a continuous density value per voxel rather than just binary occupancy, allowing for smoother transitions and better gradient flow during neural radiance field training. The method periodically refreshes the density grid by sampling points in world space, querying a neural network for density, and updating the grid using an EMA maximum operation. Inputs: step: Current training step integer. occevalfn: Callable taking (N, 3) coordinates and returning (N, 1) occupancy values. densitynet: Callable (neural network) taking (N, 3) coordinates and returning (N, 1) density values. self.densitygrid: 3D tensor of shape [resolution, resolution, resolution] storing current density values. self.binaries: 3D tensor of shape [resolution, resolution, resolution] storing binary occupancy flags. self.occs: 1D tensor of shape [cellsperlvl levels] storing continuous occupancy estimates. self.aabbs: 2D tensor of shape [levels, 6] storing axis-aligned bounding boxes [minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz] for each level. self.resolution: Integer, the base resolution of the grid. self.levels: Integer, number of mipmap levels. self.cellsperlvl: Integer, total number of cells per level. self.bound: Float, the side length of the world-space bounding box. self.gridcoords: 2D tensor of shape [totalcells, 3] storing cell indices. occthre: Float threshold for binarization. emadecay: Float decay factor for EMA. warmupsteps: Integer number of initial steps to sample all cells. n: Integer, update frequency (every n steps). Outputs: Updated self.densitygrid. Updated self.binaries. Updated self.occs. Updated self.meandensity. Data Structures: densitygrid: torch.float32 tensor, shape [res, res, res] for single level or [levels, res, res, res] for hierarchy. binaries: torch.bool tensor, same shape as densitygrid. occs: torch.float32 tensor, shape [cellsperlvl levels]. gridcoords: torch.int64 tensor, shape [N, 3], indices of sampled cells. Parameters: occthre: Default 0.01. emadecay: Default 0.95. warmupsteps: Default 256. n: Update every n steps. Default 16. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatedensitygridwithema(self, step, occevalfn, densitynet): # 1. Check update condition if step % self.n != 0 or not self.training: return # 2. Sample cells if step < self.warmupsteps: indices = self.getallcells() else: N = self.cellsperlvl // 4 indices = self.sampleuniformandoccupiedcells(N) # 3. Update occupancy grid (per level) for lvl in range(self.levels): gridcoords = self.gridcoords[indices] # Jitter within voxels x = (gridcoords + torch.randlike(gridcoords, dtype=torch.float32)) / self.resolution # Transform to world space x = self.aabbs[lvl,:3] + x (self.aabbs[lvl, 3:] - self.aabbs[lvl,:3]) # Evaluate occupancy occ = occevalfn(x).squeeze(-1) # Compute global cell IDs cellids = lvl self.cellsperlvl + indices # Update occupancy estimates with EMA maximum self.occs[cellids] = torch.maximum(self.occs[cellids] self.emadecay, occ) # Compute threshold and update binaries thre = torch.clamp(self.occs[self.occs >= 0].mean(), max=self.occthre) self.binaries = (self.occs > thre).view(self.binaries.shape) # 4. Update density grid resolution = self.densitygrid.shape[0] halfgridsize = self.bound / resolution # Generate coordinate lines split into chunks of 128 xs, ys, zs = [], [], [] for axis in range(3): line = torch.linspace(-self.bound + halfgridsize, self.bound - halfgridsize, resolution) chunks = torch.split(line, 128) if axis == 0: xs = chunks elif axis == 1: ys = chunks else: zs = chunks tmpgrid = torch.zeroslike(self.densitygrid) for xi, xchunk in enumerate(xs): for yi, ychunk in enumerate(ys): for zi, zchunk in enumerate(zs): xx, yy, zz = torch.meshgrid(xchunk, ychunk, zchunk, indexing="ij") pts = torch.cat([xx.reshape(-1, 1), yy.reshape(-1, 1), zz.reshape(-1, 1)], dim=-1) # Add uniform noise in [-halfgridsize, halfgridsize] pts += (torch.randlike(pts) 2 - 1) halfgridsize # Pad to multiple of 128 padn = (128 - (len(pts) % 128)) % 128 if padn > 0: pts = torch.cat([pts, torch.zeros(padn, 3, device=pts.device)], dim=0) npts = len(pts) - padn # Query density and detach gradients densityvals = densitynet(pts.to(tmpgrid.device))[:npts].reshape(len(xchunk), len(ychunk), len(zchunk)).detach() tmpgrid[xi128:xi128+len(xchunk), yi128:yi128+len(ychunk), zi128:zi128+len(zchunk)] = densityvals # Update density grid using EMA maximum self.densitygrid = torch.maximum(self.densitygrid self.emadecay, tmpgrid) self.meandensity = torch.mean(self.densitygrid).item() # Reinitialize density grid tree with current resolution and levels # Set values of the density grid tree from the binary occupancy grid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The implementation uses torch.maximum instead of scattermax for updating occupied cells, noting that empirically the results are almost the same. Boundaries: The jittering ensures points are sampled within voxels, avoiding boundary issues. Padding: Points must be padded to a multiple of 128 for the chunked processing. name: Brick Occupancy Recomputation
head: Brick Occupancy Compute
body: Brick Occupancy Recomputation is a GPU-based method for updating the occupancy status of volumetric bricks after dynamic changes to the underlying voxel data. It solves the problem of stale occupancy maps in interactive voxel environments where the world state changes frequently, such as in voxel-based games or simulations. Unlike static generation methods, this approach recomputes occupancy per brick using a lightweight compute shader, avoiding atomic operations by leveraging shared memory for intra-brick reduction. It builds on Occupancy Map Generation but is specifically optimized for incremental updates in dynamic scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A texture or buffer containing the current voxel data for a specific brick. Output: A single unsigned integer representing the occupancy count for that brick, written to a global "brickmap" or occupancy texture. Data Structures: Shared Memory Array: An array of 32 unsigned integers (uint), one per thread in the block. Voxel Data: Read from global memory. The source specifies reading 16 voxels per thread. Brickmap Entry: A single uint in global memory corresponding to the brick being processed. Parameters: Threads per Block: Exactly 32. Voxels per Thread: 16. Total Voxels per Brick: 32 \times 16 = 512 voxels. Air Threshold: Voxels are considered "non-air" if they are not air. The exact definition of "air" depends on the voxel format (e.g., density < threshold or specific material ID). Steps: 1. Thread Identification: Each thread in the 32-thread block identifies its unique index tid (0 to 31). 2. Voxel Reading: Each thread reads 16 voxels from its assigned portion of the brick's voxel data. The mapping of threads to voxel indices is not explicitly detailed, but it implies a partitioning of the 512 voxels among the 32 threads. 3. Counting: Each thread counts the number of non-air voxels in its 16-voxel chunk. Let this count be c{tid}. 4. Shared Memory Write: Each thread writes c{tid} to sharedcounts[tid] in shared memory. 5. Synchronization: All threads in the block execute a barrier synchronization (syncthreads()) to ensure all counts are written. 6. Reduction: The first thread (tid == 0) sums all values in sharedcounts to compute the total occupancy count C = \sum{tid=0}^{31} c{tid}. 7. Global Write: Thread 0 writes C to the brickmap entry for the current brick. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. tid = getthreadidinblock() # 0 to 31 localcount = 0 voxelsperthread = 16 startvoxelindex = tid voxelsperthread for i in range(voxelsperthread): voxelindex = startvoxelindex + i voxel = readvoxelfromglobalmemory(voxeldata, voxelindex) if not isair(voxel): # Implementation of isair depends on voxel format localcount += 1 sharedcounts[tid] = localcount syncthreadsinblock() # syncthreads() if tid == 0: totaloccupancy = 0 for i in range(32): totaloccupancy += sharedcounts[i] writetobrickmap(brickmap, brickid, totaloccupancy) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The occupancy count is an unsigned integer. For a 512-voxel brick, the maximum count is 512, which fits in a standard uint. Boundaries: The method assumes the brick data is fully available in global memory. Degenerate Input: If the voxel data is not properly loaded or the brick ID is invalid, the write to the brickmap may be incorrect. A two-level hierarchical structure for procedural volume exploration combining an N3-tree (an N-ary tree with N^3 children) for hierarchy and regular voxel bricks stored in the leaves. It links the compactness of a hierarchical structure with the efficient traversal and trilinear/quadrilinear filtering capabilities of regular grids on GPU. Time Complexity: O(1) per brick, as the number of threads and voxels per thread is fixed. Memory Complexity: O(1) per brick for shared memory (32 uints). Performance: Fast, as it avoids atomic operations and uses shared memory for reduction. Strengths: Low latency, no contention on global memory for reduction, suitable for dynamic scenes. Limitations: Fixed brick size (512 voxels), requires a compute shader. When to use: Dynamic voxel environments where occupancy needs frequent updates. When not to use: Static volumes where occupancy is computed once. Originated in the context of voxel-based game development, specifically for handling dynamic voxel worlds where players can modify the terrain. The method was described by Joris Rijsdijk in an unofficial blog post discussing voxel simulation and occupancy map updates. name: N3-tree with regular mipmapped bricks
head: N3-tree with regular voxel bricks, N3-tree+briques de voxels
body: The N3-tree with regular mipmapped bricks is a two-level hierarchical data structure for procedural volume exploration that combines an N-ary tree (N3-tree) for hierarchy with regular voxel bricks stored in the leaves. It links the compactness of a hierarchical structure with the efficient traversal and trilinear/quadrilinear filtering capabilities of regular grids on GPU. It generalizes the original octree-based Brick Maps to allow arbitrary subdivision of nodes (N-ary instead of binary octree) to enable efficient GPU traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A procedural volume defined by a total maximum resolution Rt on each axis, a maximum brick resolution Rb, and a node subdivision resolution N. Output: A GPU-accessible structure consisting of an indirection texture (the tree), a brick storage texture (the data), and a brick indirection storage (mip-level mapping). Data Structures: 1. Indirection Storage (The Tree): Format: 3D texture using GLRGBA32IEXT (unsigned integer RGBA, 32 bits per component). Layout: Each node in the N3-tree is stored as a small N^3 grid of indirection cells within this texture. Spatial Locality: The N^3 grids are organized using a Peano curve (Swizzled Walk) layout to maximize cache efficiency during tree traversal. Cell Encoding (Sub-node information): Each cell contains 32 bits packed as follows: Red (R): 3D address (X, Y, Z) of the child node or the regular brick in the brick storage. Encoded in binary. 10 bits per coordinate (30 bits total). Green (G): 3D address of the parent node. Encoded similarly (10 bits per coordinate). Blue (B): Reserved for future use. Alpha (A): Average value of all voxels in the node's covered space. Flags: 1 bit identifies the sub-node type (brick or tree node). 1 bit identifies an empty node flag (no descendants). Addressable Dimension: The 10-bit address allows addressing elements in a storage of maximum dimension 1024^3. 2. Brick Storage (The Data): Format: 3D texture storing regular scalar density data (or gradients). Layout: Divided into zones grouping bricks of identical resolution. Brick Structure: Each brick includes its data plus a 1-voxel border surrounding the data to allow trilinear filtering without artifacts from adjacent bricks. Filtering: Accessed in the shader by floating-point coordinates; integer coordinates from the indirection storage are transformed on the fly. 3. Brick Indirection Storage: Purpose: Links the hierarchical tree to brick data. Content: A list of addresses for each brick's data for every mip-mapping level in the brick storage. Unloaded Data: Entries marked with a negative value indicate unloaded data. Manual Mip-mapping: Hardware mip-mapping requires duplicating the 1-voxel border 2^n times for a stack of n levels and halving it at each sub-level, which is memory expensive. This method implements 3D mip-mapping manually to achieve identical performance cost but with lower memory overhead. Number of Nodes: In the worst case (full resolution, no empty space skipping), the number of nodes to store in the tree is calculated as: \sum{i=0}^{n} \left( \frac{Nb}{N^i} \right)^3 Where: n = \frac{\log(Nb)}{\log N} Nb = \frac{Rt}{Rb} Rt: Total maximum resolution on each axis. Rb: Maximum resolution of a brick. N: Resolution of each node (e.g., N=2 for octree). Parameters: Example: Rt = 1024^3, N = 4, Rb = 16. Result: An indirection storage of 64^3 is nearly sufficient. A practical recommended size is 128^3. Degrees of Freedom: Node subdivision resolution (N) and regular brick resolution. These impact traversal performance and update efficiency. Assumes x, y, z < 1024. """ return (x << 20) | (y << 10) | z def decodeaddress3d(addr30bit): """ Decodes a 30-bit integer into x, y, z. Green (G): 3D address of parent...". # If R is 30 bits + flags, it fits in 32 bits. # If G is 30 bits + flags, it fits in 32 bits. # So R and G are 32-bit integers. B and A are 32-bit integers. rchannel = (brickaddr30 << 2) | (nodetypebit << 1) | emptyflag # Assuming 2 bits for flags? # Source: "1 bit for sub-node type... 1 bit for empty node flag." # So 2 bits for flags. 30 bits for address. Total 32 bits. gchannel = (encodeaddress3d(parentx, parenty, parentz) << 2) | 0 # Parent address, no flags mentioned for parent? # Source: "Green (G): 3D address of the parent node... encoded similarly." bchannel = 0 # Reserved # Alpha: Average value. Source doesn't specify bit depth for average. # Assuming 32-bit integer or float representation as per texture format. achannel = int(avgvalue 255) if avgvalue <= 1.0 else avgvalue texture.setpixel(px, py, pz, (rchannel, gchannel, bchannel, achannel)) if not isleaf: # Recursively populate children for dx in range(N): for dy in range(N): for dz in range(N): childx = x N + dx childy = y N + dy childz = z N + dz populatenode(childx, childy, childz, level + 1, rchannel) # Start traversal from root # Root address is typically (0,0,0) populatenode(0, 0, 0, 0, 0) return texture def buildbrickstorage(Rt, Rb): """ Constructs the brick storage texture and brick indirection storage. """ # Brick storage texture bricktex = create3dtexture(width=Rb, height=Rb, depth=Rb, format=GLRGBA32IEXT) # Or appropriate data format # Add 1-voxel border to each brick # This requires duplicating border voxels for mip-mapping levels if hardware mip-mapping were used. # Since we use manual mip-mapping, we handle border logic in shader or pre-process. # Brick Indirection Storage # List of addresses for each brick's data for every mip-mapping level brickindirection = [] # Calculate number of bricks numbricksx = Rt / Rb numbricksy = Rt / Rb numbricksz = Rt / Rb for x in range(numbricksx): for y in range(numbricksy): for z in range(numbricksz): brickaddr = encodeaddress3d(x, y, z) # For each mip level, store address or -1 if unloaded miplevels = int(log(Rb) / log(2)) + 1 brickentry = [-1] miplevels brickentry[0] = brickaddr # Level 0 is loaded brickindirection.append(brickentry) return bricktex, brickindirection The original octree-based structure for global illumination that this method generalizes. Brick Maps The broader category of ray-grid traversal techniques that use hierarchical structures to skip empty space. Hierarchical Grid Traversal Time Complexity: Traversal is efficient on GPU due to the regular grid structure of leaves and the use of 3D textures which exploit hardware cache spatial locality (via Peano curve layout). Memory Complexity: The indirection storage size is determined by the worst-case node count. For Rt=1024^3, N=4, Rb=16, a 64^3 texture is nearly sufficient, but 128^3 is recommended for practical scenes. The manual mip-mapping reduces memory overhead compared to hardware mip-mapping by avoiding border duplication. Strengths: Combines hierarchical compactness with regular grid filtering efficiency. Manual mip-mapping saves memory. Peano curve layout optimizes cache hits. Limitations: Worst-case memory usage can be high if the volume is dense. Update efficiency is secondary to traversal performance but impacted by the choice of N and brick resolution. When to use: Procedural volume exploration on GPU where memory bandwidth and cache efficiency are critical. When not to use: If hardware mip-mapping memory overhead is not a concern and the volume is sparse enough that a simpler octree suffices. The method was developed by Sylvain Lefebvre et al. as an adaptation of the hierarchical volumetric textures model proposed by Sylvain Lefebvre [LHN05] for GPU implementation. It generalizes the Brick Maps proposed by Christensen and Batali [CB04] for global illumination. The work is part of the thesis "Représentation et algorithmes pour l'exploration interactive de volumes procéduraux étendus et détaillés". name: OpenVDB DDA
head: VDB DDA, Digital Differential Analyzer specialized for OpenVDB grids, Digital Differential Analyzer for OpenVDB
body: OpenVDB DDA is a Digital Differential Analyzer traversal algorithm specialized for OpenVDB grids, conceptually similar to Bresenham's line algorithm applied to a 3D ray intersecting OpenVDB nodes or voxels. It iterates through grid elements (voxels or tree nodes) intersected by a ray, using a fixed step-size defined by the template parameter Log2Dim. Unlike Hierarchical DDA (HDDA) which uses variable step-sizes to skip empty space, OpenVDB DDA marches through every node or voxel boundary along the ray path. It serves as the foundational traversal kernel for higher-level hierarchical methods like LevelSetHDDA and VolumeHDDA, which wrap this DDA to handle tree structures and empty space skipping. Inputs: ray: A ray object of type RayT. The RayT template class must provide: test(time): Evaluates the ray at a given time. t0(): Returns the start time parameter of the ray. t1(): Returns the end time parameter of the ray. invDir(): Returns the inverse direction vector (1/dx, 1/dy, 1/dz). operator()(time): Returns the 3D position vector at a given time parameter. startTime: The initial parameter value along the ray where traversal begins. Defaults to ray.t0() if not provided. maxTime: The maximum parameter value along the ray, limiting the traversal distance. Defaults to ray.t1() if not provided. Log2Dim: An integer template parameter specifying the log2 of the grid element dimension. Log2Dim = 0: Traverses individual voxels. Log2Dim > 0: Traverses tree nodes (or tiles) of size 2^{\text{Log2Dim}}. Outputs: Iterative access to the current intersected voxel/node index via voxel(). Iterative access to the current hit time via time(). Iterative access to the next hit time via next(). Boolean return from step() indicating if traversal is within bounds. The DDA class maintains the following private member variables: mT0: Current time parameter (RealT). mT1: Maximum time parameter (RealT). mVoxel: Current voxel/node index coordinates (Coord, 3D signed integer). mStep: Step size per axis for mVoxel (Coord, 3D signed integer). mDelta: Time increment per axis for mNext (Vec3T, 3D float). mNext: Time of the next intersection per axis (Vec3T, 3D float). Type aliases used within the class: RealT: typename RayT::RealType (e.g., float or double). Vec3T: typename RayT::Vec3Type (3D vector of RealT). Coord: 3D signed integer coordinate type. The DDA state is initialized via the init() method or constructor. 1. Set mT0 = startTime and mT1 = maxTime. 2. Calculate DIM = 1 << Log2Dim. 3. Get ray position pos = ray(mT0), direction dir = ray.dir(), and inverse direction inv = ray.invDir(). 4. Compute initial voxel index mVoxel: mVoxel = \text{Coord::floor}(pos) \ \& \ (\sim(DIM - 1)) This aligns the starting voxel to the grid boundary of size DIM. 5. For each axis i in \{0, 1, 2\}: If dir[i] is zero (including \pm 0): mStep[i] = 0 (dummy value). mNext[i] = std::numericlimits<RealT>::max() (disabled). mDelta[i] = std::numericlimits<RealT>::max() (dummy value). Else if inv[i] > 0 (ray moving in positive direction): mStep[i] = DIM. mNext[i] = mT0 + (mVoxel[i] + DIM - pos[i]) inv[i]. mDelta[i] = mStep[i] inv[i]. Else (inv[i] < 0, ray moving in negative direction): mStep[i] = -DIM. mNext[i] = mT0 + (mVoxel[i] - pos[i]) inv[i]. mDelta[i] = mStep[i] inv[i]. The traversal proceeds by repeatedly stepping to the next intersected element. 1. Query current hit time: tcurrent = time() returns mT0. 2. Query current voxel index: voxelidx = voxel() returns mVoxel. 3. Process the voxel/node at voxelidx (e.g., check occupancy, sample data). 4. Step to next intersection: Find stepAxis = argmin(mNext[0], mNext[1], mNext[2]). Update mT0 = mNext[stepAxis]. Update mNext[stepAxis] += mDelta[stepAxis]. Update mVoxel[stepAxis] += mStep[stepAxis]. If mT0 <= mT1, continue; else, stop. 5. Repeat from step 1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class OpenVDBDDA: def init(self, ray, starttime=None, maxtime=None, log2dim=0): self.ray = ray self.log2dim = log2dim self.dim = 1 << log2dim if starttime is None: starttime = ray.t0() if maxtime is None: maxtime = ray.t1() self.init(ray, starttime, maxtime) def init(self, ray, starttime, maxtime): assert starttime <= maxtime self.t0 = starttime self.t1 = maxtime pos = ray(starttime) dir = ray.dir() inv = ray.invDir() # Align voxel to grid boundary self.voxel = floor(pos) & ~(self.dim - 1) self.delta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.next = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.step = [0, 0, 0] for axis in range(3): if iszero(dir[axis]): # Handle zero direction (including +/- 0) self.step[axis] = 0 self.next[axis] = float('inf') self.delta[axis] = float('inf') elif inv[axis] > 0: self.step[axis] = self.dim self.next[axis] = self.t0 + (self.voxel[axis] + self.dim - pos[axis]) inv[axis] self.delta[axis] = self.step[axis] inv[axis] else: self.step[axis] = -self.dim self.next[axis] = self.t0 + (self.voxel[axis] - pos[axis]) inv[axis] self.delta[axis] = self.step[axis] inv[axis] def step(self): # Find axis with minimum next hit time stepaxis = argmin(self.next) # Advance time and voxel index self.t0 = self.next[stepaxis] self.next[stepaxis] += self.delta[stepaxis] self.voxel[stepaxis] += self.step[stepaxis] return self.t0 <= self.t1 def time(self): return self.t0 def voxel(self): return self.voxel def next(self): # Compute time of the second hit (next after current) # This incurs computational overhead as it requires simulating one step # without modifying state, or accessing precomputed next values if available. # Based on source, next() returns the time of the second hit. # Implementation detail: The source notes next() incurs overhead, # implying it's not just a member access like time() or voxel(). # A simple implementation would be to compute the next hit time for the current state. # However, the C++ source shows next() is a const method. # The most direct interpretation from S1/S2/S3 is that it returns the # parameterized time of the second hit. # Since step() updates mNext, and next() is const, it likely calculates # the next intersection time based on current mNext values. # Specifically, it returns the minimum of the updated mNext values after a hypothetical step? # Or it returns the current mNext[stepaxis] before step? # S1 says: "Return the time... of the second (i.e. next) hit". # S2 code snippet: tester.setRange(dda.time(), dda.next()); # This implies next() is the time of the next boundary after the current one. # In the init loop, mNext[i] is the time of the first boundary on axis i. # After step(), mNext[stepaxis] is updated to the second boundary on that axis. # But next() is const. # Let's look at S1/S2/S3 descriptions again. # S1: "Return the time... of the second (i.e. next) hit". # S2: "Compute the time of the second (i.e. next) hit". # S5: "Next hit time on axis i: mNext[i] =...". # The C++ implementation of next() is not fully visible in the snippets, # but the overhead note suggests it's not trivial. # A common implementation for next() in DDA is to return the minimum of # the other axes' next times if the current step was on one axis, # or simply the minimum of all mNext values if they represent the next boundaries. # However, in the init, mNext[i] is the first boundary. # So next() likely returns the minimum of the mNext values, # assuming mNext is updated to point to the next boundary after the current t0. # But step() updates mNext[stepaxis]. # If next() is const, it cannot call step(). # It likely calculates the next hit time based on the current state. # Given the overhead, it might be: min(mNext) where mNext represents the # subsequent boundaries. # Let's assume the standard DDA behavior where next() returns the time # of the next intersection event. # Since step() updates mT0 to mNext[stepaxis], and mNext[stepaxis] to the next one, # the current mNext values (after a step) represent the next boundaries. # But before any step, mNext represents the first boundaries. # So next() should return min(mNext) if mNext is updated to "next" boundaries. # But init sets mNext to "first" boundaries. # Therefore, next() likely computes the next boundary time for the axis that # just stepped, or returns the min of all mNext if they are all "next". # Given the ambiguity and "overhead" note, we note that next() is computationally # more expensive than time() or voxel(). # For implementation, one might compute: # tempnext = copy of mNext # tempnext[stepaxis] += delta[stepaxis] # return min(tempnext) # But this is a guess. The source says it incurs overhead. # We will mark it as a method that returns the next hit time. pass # See note below Note on next(): The sources state next() returns the time of the second hit and incurs computational overhead. It is distinct from time() which returns the current hit time with no overhead. A precise implementation of next() without modifying state typically involves calculating the next intersection time for the axis that will be stepped, or the minimum of the next boundaries. Since the exact C++ implementation of next() is not fully provided in the snippets, but its behavior is defined, implementers should ensure it returns the parameterized time of the next grid boundary intersection along the ray. Log2Dim: Integer template parameter. Default is 0. Dim: Fixed step-size dimension, calculated as 2^{\text{Log2Dim}}. Default is 1. Zero Direction: If a ray direction component is zero (including \pm 0), the corresponding axis step is disabled by setting mNext and mDelta to std::numericlimits<RealT>::max() to prevent infinite loops or incorrect steps. Computational Overhead: The next() method incurs a small computational overhead, whereas time() and voxel() incur no computational overhead. Precision: The algorithm uses floating-point arithmetic for time calculations. Precision issues may arise with very large coordinates or very small step sizes, though this is not explicitly detailed in the sources. Boundary Conditions: The initial voxel is aligned to the grid boundary using bitwise AND with ~(DIM-1). This assumes integer coordinates for Coord and power-of-two dimensions. A method for traversing OpenVDB frustum grids by generalizing the 3D DDA algorithm to account for the non-linearity of the perspective transform, allowing efficient ray traversal for any ray (not just camera rays) without auxiliary grids. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of voxels/nodes intersected by the ray. Each step involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and a minimum index search. Memory Complexity: Constant space O(1) for the DDA state, independent of the grid size. Performance: The time() and voxel() methods are efficient with no computational overhead. The next() method has a small overhead. Strengths: Simple, robust, and efficient for dense grids or when hierarchical skipping is not applicable or desired. It is the foundation for hierarchical methods. Limitations: Does not skip empty space, making it less efficient for sparse grids compared to HDDA. When to use: When traversing dense grids, or as a base for hierarchical traversal algorithms. When not to use: For sparse grids where empty space skipping is critical for performance. OpenVDB DDA is part of the OpenVDB library, an open-source C++ library for the management and manipulation of sparse volumetric data. The DDA class is specialized for traversing OpenVDB grids, leveraging the grid's hierarchical structure and fixed node sizes. It is conceptually similar to Bresenham's line algorithm. The method is used in various applications within the OpenVDB ecosystem, including volume rendering and level set operations. name: Incremental Ray Traversal through OpenVDB Frustum Grids
head: Frustum Grid Ray Traversal, Incremental DDA for Frustum Grids
body: This method performs efficient ray traversal through OpenVDB frustum grids by generalizing the 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to account for the non-linearity of the perspective transform. It allows for the traversal of any ray (not just camera rays) against frustum-structured voxel data without requiring auxiliary grids or precomputed acceleration structures, solving the difficulty that standard uniform-grid DDA faces when applied to non-linearly mapped index spaces. It builds on OpenVDB DDA by replacing the linear step logic with incremental updates to rational functions derived from the inverse frustum map. Inputs: Ray in world space: origin \mathbf{r}0 and direction \hat{\omega} (unit vector). OpenVDB Grid parameters: Index space bounds: [I0, I1] \times [J0, J1] \times [K0, K1]. Leaf node size: N (typically 8, so leaf dimensions are N \times N \times N). Frustum parameters: taper \tau, depth d, aspect ratio a = (J1 - J0)/(I1 - I0). Affine transform matrix M mapping frustum space to world space. Grid hierarchy structure (to access leaf nodes). Outputs: A sequence of leaf node indices (i, j, k) visited by the ray within the valid distance range [t{entry}, t{exit}]. The OpenVDB grid is a hierarchy of nodes, commonly four levels deep, where leaf nodes hold the actual voxel data. A leaf node stores an array of N \times N \times N voxels (configurable to other powers of two). The traversal operates on integer index coordinates (i, j, k) within the global index space [I0, I1] \times [J0, J1] \times [K0, K1]. \tau (taper): Ratio between the sizes of the near rectangle and the far rectangle in frustum space. d (depth): The z-coordinate of the far plane in frustum space; the near plane is at z=0. a (aspect ratio): Ratio of grid dimensions in the j and i directions, a = (J1 - J0)/(I1 - I0). \gamma (gamma): Constant derived from taper and depth, \gamma = (1/\tau - 1)/d. 1. Transform Ray to Frustum Space: Calculate the frustum ray origin \mathbf{s}0 and direction \delta using the inverse of the affine matrix M^{-1}. \mathbf{s}0 is a point (homogeneous coordinate 1). \delta is a direction (homogeneous coordinate 0). Do not renormalize \delta. 2. Clip Ray Against Frustum Boundaries: Determine the valid distance range [t0, t1] for traversal by clipping against the six planes of the frustum. a. Z-Clipping (Near/Far Planes): Intersect with k=K0 (z=0) and k=K1 (z=d) to get initial t0 and t1: t0 = tK(0) t1 = tK(d) where tK(k) = (z - s{0z})/\deltaz and z = d(k - K0)/(K1 - K0). b. Right Plane (i=I1, x'=1/2): Calculate distance tR: tR = \frac{(\gamma s{0z} + 1)/2 - s{0x}}{\deltax - \gamma \deltaz/2} Determine entry/exit: If \deltax < \gamma \deltaz/2, the ray is entering. Update t0 = \max(t0, tR). Otherwise, the ray is leaving. Update t1 = \min(t1, tR). c. Left Plane (i=-I1? No, x'=-1/2): Calculate distance tL: tL = \frac{-(\gamma s{0z} + 1)/2 - s{0x}}{\deltax + \gamma \deltaz/2} Determine entry/exit: If \deltax > -\gamma \deltaz/2, the ray is entering. Update t0 = \max(t0, tL). Otherwise, the ray is leaving. Update t1 = \min(t1, tL). d. Top and Bottom Planes: Clip similarly to left/right, but using the factor a/2 instead of 1/2 in the plane normal and point definitions. Specifically, replace 1/2 with a/2 for the y' coordinate calculations and adjust normals accordingly. e. Check Validity: If t1 \le t0, the ray does not enter the frustum. Return immediately. 3. Determine Delta Signs: Determine the signs of integer deltas \{\Delta A = \pm N: A = I, J, K\} based on the ray direction components \deltax, \deltay, \deltaz. \Delta I = N if \deltax \ge 0, else -N. \Delta J = N if \deltay \ge 0, else -N. \Delta K = N if \deltaz \ge 0, else -N. These signs control whether coordinates are incremented or decremented during traversal. 4. Initialize Iterative State: Start at the leaf containing the ray origin (or the first leaf intersected by the ray within [t0, t1]). Let the current leaf indices be (iN, jN, kN), which are multiples of N. Initialize the distances to the next boundary crossings for each axis: For I: x' = \frac{iN - (I1 + I0)/2}{I1 - I0} PI = x'(\gamma s{0z} + 1) - s{0x} QI = \deltax - x' \gamma \deltaz tI = PI / QI For J: y' = \frac{jN - (J1 + J0)/2}{I1 - I0} PJ = y'(\gamma s{0z} + 1) - s{0y} QJ = \deltay - y' \gamma \deltaz tJ = PJ / QJ For K: z = d(kN - K0)/(K1 - K0) tK = (z - s{0z})/\deltaz Define incremental constants: \Delta'I = \frac{\Delta I}{I1 - I0} \Delta'J = \frac{\Delta J}{I1 - I0} \Delta'K = \frac{d}{\deltaz} \frac{\Delta K}{K1 - K0} Define update deltas for P and Q: \Delta PI = (\gamma s{0z} + 1) \Delta'I \Delta QI = \gamma \deltaz \Delta'I \Delta PJ = (\gamma s{0z} + 1) \Delta'J \Delta QJ = \gamma \deltaz \Delta'J. 5. Iterative Traversal: While t{current} < t1: a. Find the next crossing distance: t{next} = \min(tI, tJ, tK). b. If t{next} > t1, break. c. Process the current leaf (iN, jN, kN). d. Identify which axis caused the minimum distance (e.g., if tI is min, increment iN by \Delta I). e. Update the state for the axis that crossed: If I crossed: PI \leftarrow PI + \Delta PI QI \leftarrow QI - \Delta QI tI \leftarrow PI / QI iN \leftarrow iN + \Delta I If J crossed: PJ \leftarrow PJ + \Delta PJ QJ \leftarrow QJ - \Delta QJ tJ \leftarrow PJ / QJ jN \leftarrow jN + \Delta J If K crossed: tK \leftarrow tK + \Delta'K kN \leftarrow kN + \Delta K f. Update t{current} = t{next}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversefrustumgrid(rayoriginworld, raydirworld, gridparams, matrixMinv): """ rayoriginworld: (x, y, z) raydirworld: (dx, dy, dz) gridparams: {I0, I1, J0, J1, K0, K1, N, tau, d, a} matrixMinv: 4x4 matrix inverse of M """ # 1. Transform Ray to Frustum Space # s0 is point (w=1), delta is direction (w=0) s0 = transformpoint(matrixMinv, rayoriginworld) delta = transformvector(matrixMinv, raydirworld) s0x, s0y, s0z = s0 dx, dy, dz = delta gamma = (1.0 / gridparams['tau'] - 1.0) / gridparams['d'] # 2. Clip Ray # Z-clipping # tK(k) = (z - s0z) / dz, where z = d(k - K0)/(K1 - K0) # For k=K0, z=0 -> t0 = (0 - s0z)/dz # For k=K1, z=d -> t1 = (d - s0z)/dz # Note: dz must not be 0 for valid traversal, handled by caller or epsilon check t0 = (0.0 - s0z) / dz t1 = (gridparams['d'] - s0z) / dz # Right Plane (x' = 1/2) # tR = ((gammas0z + 1)/2 - s0x) / (dx - gammadz/2) denomR = dx - gamma dz / 2.0 if abs(denomR) > 1e-9: tR = ((gamma s0z + 1.0) / 2.0 - s0x) / denomR if dx < gamma dz / 2.0: t0 = max(t0, tR) else: t1 = min(t1, tR) else: # Parallel to plane, no intersection logic needed for clipping range if already inside/outside pass # Left Plane (x' = -1/2) # tL = (-(gammas0z + 1)/2 - s0x) / (dx + gammadz/2) denomL = dx + gamma dz / 2.0 if abs(denomL) > 1e-9: tL = (-(gamma s0z + 1.0) / 2.0 - s0x) / denomL if dx > -gamma dz / 2.0: t0 = max(t0, tL) else: t1 = min(t1, tL) else: pass # Top/Bottom Planes (y' = +/- a/2) # Similar logic to Left/Right but with a/2 factor # Right-ish Y (y' = a/2) denomYtop = dy - gamma dz (gridparams['a'] / 2.0) if abs(denomYtop) > 1e-9: tYtop = ((gamma s0z + 1.0) (gridparams['a'] / 2.0) - s0y) / denomYtop if dy < gamma dz (gridparams['a'] / 2.0): t0 = max(t0, tYtop) else: t1 = min(t1, tYtop) # Left-ish Y (y' = -a/2) denomYbot = dy + gamma dz (gridparams['a'] / 2.0) if abs(denomYbot) > 1e-9: tYbot = (-(gamma s0z + 1.0) (gridparams['a'] / 2.0) - s0y) / denomYbot if dy > -gamma dz (gridparams['a'] / 2.0): t0 = max(t0, tYbot) else: t1 = min(t1, tYbot) if t1 <= t0: return [] # No intersection # 3. Determine Deltas N = gridparams['N'] dI = N if dx >= 0 else -N dJ = N if dy >= 0 else -N dK = N if dz >= 0 else -dK # G: Typo in thought, should be -N dK = N if dz >= 0 else -N # 4. Initialize State # Find starting leaf (iN, jN, kN) containing ray origin or first intersection # This requires mapping ray origin to index space or finding the first leaf intersected. # For simplicity, assume we have a function getstartingleaf(s0, t0) iN, jN, kN = getstartingleaf(s0, t0, gridparams) # Calculate initial tI, tJ, tK # I xprime = (iN - (gridparams['I1'] + gridparams['I0']) / 2.0) / (gridparams['I1'] - gridparams['I0']) PI = xprime (gamma s0z + 1.0) - s0x QI = dx - xprime gamma dz tI = PI / QI # J yprime = (jN - (gridparams['J1'] + gridparams['J0']) / 2.0) / (gridparams['I1'] - gridparams['I0']) # Note: Denom is I1-I0 PJ = yprime (gamma s0z + 1.0) - s0y QJ = dy - yprime gamma dz tJ = PJ / QJ # K z = gridparams['d'] (kN - gridparams['K0']) / (gridparams['K1'] - gridparams['K0']) tK = (z - s0z) / dz # Incremental Constants dIprime = dI / (gridparams['I1'] - gridparams['I0']) dJprime = dJ / (gridparams['I1'] - gridparams['I0']) dKprime = (gridparams['d'] / dz) (dK / (gridparams['K1'] - gridparams['K0'])) dPI = (gamma s0z + 1.0) dIprime dQI = gamma dz dIprime dPJ = (gamma s0z + 1.0) dJprime dQJ = gamma dz dJprime visitedleaves = [] currentt = t0 # 5. Iterate while currentt < t1: # Find next crossing tnext = min(tI, tJ, tK) if tnext > t1: break # Process leaf visitedleaves.append((iN, jN, kN)) # Update state for the axis that crossed if tI <= tJ and tI <= tK: PI += dPI QI -= dQI tI = PI / QI iN += dI elif tJ <= tI and tJ <= tK: PJ += dPJ QJ -= dQJ tJ = PJ / QJ jN += dJ else: tK += dKprime kN += dK currentt = tnext return visitedleaves Parallel Rays: If \deltaz = 0, the K-index update is undefined. The ray is parallel to the frustum's depth axis. This requires special handling or is considered a degenerate case. Division by Zero: Denominators in tR, tL, tY calculations can be zero if the ray is parallel to the respective planes. The code must check for this. Precision: The rational functions for tI and tJ involve division. Accumulated floating-point errors may occur over many iterations. Renormalization or periodic recalculation from exact formulas may be necessary for long traversals. Boundary Conditions: The clipping logic must correctly handle rays starting inside or outside the frustum. The initial t0, t1 from Z-clipping assumes the ray intersects the slab z \in [0, d]. If the ray is parallel to Z, this step fails. Time Complexity: O(L) where L is the number of leaf nodes visited. Each step involves constant-time arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, excluding the grid structure itself. Performance: Efficient for frustum grids because it avoids the overhead of general-purpose acceleration structures like BVHs for the grid itself, leveraging the regular structure of OpenVDB leaves. It is particularly effective for perspective camera rays where voxel density naturally decreases with distance. Strengths: No auxiliary grids needed; handles any ray; efficient traversal of non-linear grids. Limitations: Only applicable to frustum grids; requires the inverse affine transform; sensitive to numerical precision in rational function updates. The method was introduced in "Incremental Ray Traversal through OpenVDB Frustum Grids". It addresses the limitations of standard 3D DDA [Amanatides and Woo 1987] when applied to non-uniform, perspective-mapped grids. OpenVDB, developed by DreamWorks Animation and widely adopted in production path tracing, supports frustum grids to optimize memory usage for perspective views. This method generalizes the DDA to handle the rational curve nature of rays in index space after the inverse frustum transform. Incremental Ray Traversal through OpenVDB Frustum Grids, https://jcgt.org/published/0010/01/03/paper-lowres.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: DDA
head: DDA Algorithm, DDA Raycasting Algorithm, Delta Calculation Helper, Digital Differential Analyzer
body: The Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) is a grid traversal algorithm that determines the sequence of uniform grid cells (voxels or tiles) intersected by a ray, outputting the indices of visited cells in front-to-back order. It solves the problem of efficiently enumerating grid intersections without missing thin cells or performing redundant work, which plagues naive ray marching. Unlike Amanatides and Woo Voxel Traversal which explicitly computes t-values for grid boundaries, the DDA formulation often operates by maintaining and comparing accumulated distances to the next grid line in each dimension, stepping the minimum distance at each iteration. It is distinguished by its suitability for branchless GPU implementation, where conditional logic is replaced by vector masks and arithmetic updates. Inputs: rayorigin: 3D vector (ox, oy, oz) specifying the ray start point. raydirection: 3D vector (dx, dy, dz) specifying the ray direction. It does not need to be normalized for the core traversal logic, but its sign determines the stepping direction. gridbounds: Optional bounding box (grid{min}, grid{max}) or resolution grid{res} to limit traversal. maxtime: Maximum parameter t along the ray to traverse. Outputs: A sequence of integer voxel coordinates (i, j, k) visited by the ray. For each step, the time t of entry into the current cell and the exit time into the next cell. The DDA state typically maintains the following fields: pos: Integer vector (i, j, k) representing the current voxel index. sidedist: Floating-point vector representing the distance along the ray to the next grid boundary in each dimension. deltadist: Floating-point vector representing the distance along the ray to cross one full grid cell in each dimension (i.e., 1/|dx|, 1/|dy|, 1/|dz|). stepdir: Integer vector (\pm 1, \pm 1, \pm 1) indicating the direction of increment for each axis. 1. Initialization: Compute the initial voxel index: pos = \lfloor ray\origin \rfloor. Compute the reciprocal direction components: rcp\d = 1 / ray\direction. Handle zero-direction components by setting their reciprocal to infinity to avoid division by zero. Compute deltadist as the absolute value of the reciprocal direction: delta\dist = |rcp\d|. Compute stepdir based on the sign of the ray direction: step\dir = \text{sign}(ray\direction). Compute the fractional position within the current voxel: p0 = ray\origin - pos. Compute the initial distance to the next grid boundary for each axis. If dx > 0, the next boundary is at x = posx + 1, so the distance is (1 - p{0,x}) \cdot |rcp{d,x}|. If dx < 0, the next boundary is at x = posx, so the distance is -p{0,x} \cdot |rcp{d,x}|. This can be unified as: side\dist = (step\dir \cdot (pos - ray\origin) + 0.5 \cdot step\dir + 0.5) \cdot delta\dist Note: The specific formula in uses a heuristic offset; derives it from geometric intersection. Both aim to calculate the distance to the immediate next grid line. (Optional) Clip pos to grid bounds if the ray starts outside. 2. Stepping Loop: While currenttime < maxtime and within grid bounds: Invoke a callback or process the current voxel at pos. Determine which axis to step next by finding the axis with the minimum sidedist. Create a boolean mask mask where mask[i] is true if sidedist[i] is less than or equal to the other components (handling ties deterministically). mask = (side\dist \le \min(side\dist.yzx, side\dist.zxy)) Update sidedist by adding deltadist to the components indicated by mask. Update pos by adding stepdir to the components indicated by mask. Update the current time t by adding the minimum sidedist value (the distance just traveled). (Optional) Check for termination conditions (e.g., hit detected, bounds exceeded). Distance to next grid line (X-axis, dx > 0): tx = \frac{\lceil ox \rceil - ox}{dx} Subsequent crossings are spaced by 1/dx. Scaling factor for step length: The length of the ray segment corresponding to a unit step in the x-axis is \sqrt{1 + (dy/dx)^2}. This is equivalent to |rcp{d,x}| \cdot \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2} if the direction is normalized. Safe Inverse: To handle near-axis-aligned rays without division by zero: \text{safe\inv}(x) = \begin{cases} \text{select}(-10^{20}, 10^{20}, x \ge 0) & \text{if } |x| < 10^{-8} \\ 1/x & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Dim: In some implementations (e.g., OpenVDB's HDDA/DDA), a template parameter defining the step size or tile dimension, defaulting to 1 for standard voxel traversal. startTime, maxTime: Bounds for the ray parameter t. Zero Direction Components: If a ray component is zero, the ray is parallel to the grid lines in that dimension. The reciprocal is infinite, and the distance to the next grid line is infinite, effectively disabling stepping in that axis. Ray on Grid Boundary: If the ray origin lies exactly on a grid line, the initial distance calculation may yield zero. A guard dt > 0 prevents processing zero-length segments or double-counting cells. GPU Branching: Standard implementations using if statements for axis selection cause branch divergence on GPUs. The branchless mask-based approach avoids this penalty. Negative Directions: The initial distance calculation must account for the direction of travel. If dx < 0, the next boundary is at the lower integer coordinate, not the upper. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddatraverse(rayorigin, raydirection, gridres, maxtime, callback): # 1. Initialization # Compute reciprocal direction, handling zeros safely rcpd = vec3(1.0) for i in range(3): if abs(raydirection[i]) < 1e-8: rcpd[i] = 1e20 if raydirection[i] >= 0 else -1e20 else: rcpd[i] = 1.0 / raydirection[i] # Absolute reciprocal for delta distances absrcpd = abs(rcpd) # Initial voxel position pos = floor(rayorigin) # Step direction stepdir = sign(raydirection) # Fractional position within the starting voxel p0 = rayorigin - vec3(floor(rayorigin)) # Initial distances to next grid boundaries # If direction > 0, distance to next boundary (pos + 1) is (1 - p0) rcpd # If direction < 0, distance to next boundary (pos) is -p0 rcpd # Unified: (stepdir (pos - rayorigin) + 0.5 stepdir + 0.5) absrcpd # Note: This formula from is a heuristic. Geometric derivation: sidedist = vec3(0.0) for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] > 0: sidedist[i] = (1.0 - p0[i]) absrcpd[i] elif raydirection[i] < 0: sidedist[i] = -p0[i] absrcpd[i] else: sidedist[i] = 1e20 # Infinity deltadist = absrcpd # Current time t = 0.0 # 2. Stepping Loop while t < maxtime: # Process current voxel # callback(pos, t, t + min(sidedist)) # Find axis with minimum sidedist # mask[i] is true if sidedist[i] is the minimum (with tie-breaking) minval = min(sidedist) mask = vec3(sidedist == minval) # Update distances and position sidedist += mask deltadist pos += mask stepdir # Advance time t += minval # Check bounds (optional, depends on implementation) if not (0 <= pos.x < gridres.x and 0 <= pos.y < gridres.y and 0 <= pos.z < gridres.z): break return pos The Amanatides–Woo algorithm is the canonical DDA variant for uniform grids. It explicitly computes the t-values for crossing grid boundaries in each dimension, merges them into a sorted stream, and steps through the grid. It is preferred when exact t-values are needed for shading or when the grid is not unit-sized. It avoids the pitfalls of naive marching by jumping directly to the next boundary [1068-amanatides-woo-voxel-traversal.md]. A specific implementation of DDA used in the TRFRay3 library, focusing on efficient ray representation and traversal for volume rendering. It optimizes the DDA state for cache locality and SIMD execution [2104-trfray3-dda-ray-representation.md]. A variant of the DDA loop designed for differentiable rendering. It traverses the grid while maintaining the computational graph for backpropagation, allowing gradients to flow through the traversal process itself. This is crucial for optimizing scene parameters or camera poses in neural rendering [2474-differentiable-dda-loop.md]. This variant uses DDA to step through a voxel grid but leverages multiple mip levels of a majorant texture. It dynamically selects the mip level at each step to determine the step size, balancing performance (larger steps) and accuracy (smaller steps) without branching [4086-multi-level-dda-with-adaptive-mip-selection.md]. Time Complexity: O(K), where K is the number of visited cells. The algorithm visits each intersected cell exactly once. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, storing only the current state (position, distances, deltas). Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to branchless execution. The mask-based update avoids divergence. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust, no floating-point error accumulation in position (uses integer steps), suitable for real-time raycasting. Limitations: Requires uniform grid spacing. Non-uniform grids require modifications or hierarchical variants like Hierarchical DDA with Super-brick Skipping. When to use: Uniform voxel grids, real-time raycasting, GPU shaders. When not to use: Non-uniform grids, hierarchical structures (use HDDA or VDB traversal), or when exact t-values are required for complex intersection tests (use Amanatides-Woo). The Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm originated as a line-drawing algorithm in computer graphics, attributed to Bresenham's contemporaries, but adapted for ray tracing and voxel traversal in the 1990s and 2000s. It is widely used in voxel engines (e.g., Wolfenstein 3D-style raycasting) and modern volume rendering. The branchless GPU implementation has been popularized by shader-based tutorials and libraries like OpenVDB's nanovdb. sebbooth/vkEngine, https://github.com/sebbooth/vkEngine, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) OpenVDB: DDA< RayT, CoordT, Dim > Class Template Reference, https://academysoftwarefoundation.github.io/openvdb/classnanovdb11DDA.html, fetched 2026-10-24 The DDA algorithm | Voxel Raytracing, https://ii-day-ii.github.io/voxelraytracer/2023/05/05/the-dda-algorithm.html, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) The DDA Algorithm, https://aaaa.sh/creatures/dda-algorithm-interactive/, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Super Fast Ray Casting in Tiled Worlds using DDA, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NbSee-XM7WA, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Raycasting Algorithm | dderevjanik/ts-raycasting | DeepWiki, https://deepwiki.com/dderevjanik/ts-raycasting/4.1-raycasting-algorithm, fetched 2026-10-25 The DDA Algorithm, explained interactively, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43543007, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) openvdb/nanovdb/nanovdb/math/HDDA.h at master, https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/openvdb/blob/master/nanovdb/nanovdb/math/HDDA.h, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) OpenVDB: openvdb/math/DDA.h Source File, https://www.openvdb.org/documentation/doxygen/DDA8hsource.html, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) HaouchatY/differentiablexrt, https://github.com/HaouchatY/differentiablexrt, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, https://github.com/mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Amanatides–Woo Voxel Traversal
head: 3D DDA, Amanatides-Woo 3D DDA, Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm
body: The Amanatides–Woo algorithm efficiently enumerates the uniform grid cells intersected by a ray in front-to-back order by jumping exactly from one grid boundary to the next, avoiding the pitfalls of naïve ray marching such as missing thin cells, redundant work, and arbitrary step sizes. It serves as the foundational traversal method for image-order volume rendering and voxel-based ray casting, building on Ray-grid traversal by providing an output-sensitive O(K) approach where K is the number of visited cells. Inputs: Ray origin O = (Ox, Oy, Oz), ray direction D = (Dx, Dy, Dz) (non-zero magnitude), voxel grid index bounds [x{min}, x{max}) \times [y{min}, y{max}) \times [z{min}, z{max}), and voxel size V (typically V=1 for unit grids). Outputs: A sequence of voxel indices (i, j, k) visited in front-to-back order. Optionally, the hit voxel position and the normalized face normal of the crossed boundary. Data Structures: voxel: Integer tuple (i, j, k) representing the current cell index. step: Integer tuple (sx, sy, sz) where sa \in \{-1, 0, 1\}. tdelta: Float tuple (\Delta tx, \Delta ty, \Delta tz) representing the t-distance between successive grid plane crossings on each axis. tmax: Float tuple (Tx, Ty, Tz) representing the ray parameter t at which the ray crosses the next grid boundary on each axis. Parameters: Voxel size V: Not given in the sources. Ray bounds: t{enter} (entry into grid) and t{exit} (exit or max ray length). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Clip ray to grid AABB: For each axis, compute entry and exit parameters. If the ray misses the grid, terminate. If the ray origin is inside the grid, t{enter} may be negative; start traversal at t = \max(t{enter}, 0.0). 2. Initialize Direction and Step Signs: For each axis a \in \{x, y, z\}: if Da > 0, set sa = 1; if Da < 0, set sa = -1; if Da = 0, set sa = 0. 3. Calculate \Delta t (Step Size in t): For each axis a where Da \neq 0, compute \Delta ta = V / |Da|. If Da = 0, set \Delta ta = \infty. 4. Determine Starting Voxel and Initial t{max}: Calculate the starting voxel index: i = \lfloor Px / V \rfloor, j = \lfloor Py / V \rfloor, k = \lfloor Pz / V \rfloor, where P = O + t{enter} D. Clamp indices to [x{min}, x{max}), etc.. Calculate the fractional distance into the current voxel: fa = (Pa \bmod V) / V. Calculate the distance to the next boundary in t: Ta = \begin{cases} (1.0 - fa) \cdot \Delta ta & \text{if } Da > 0 \\ fa \cdot \Delta ta & \text{if } Da < 0 \\ \infty & \text{if } Da = 0 \end{cases} Note: If the origin is exactly on a boundary, floating-point conventions must be handled carefully to avoid ambiguity. 5. Traverse: While the current voxel (i, j, k) is within the grid bounds and current t \le t{exit}: 1. Visit voxel (i, j, k). 2. Identify the axis with the smallest Ta. 3. Update the voxel index for that axis: idx{axis} += s{axis}. 4. Update the t{max} for that axis: T{axis} += \Delta t{axis}. 5. Update current t \leftarrow T{axis}. 6. (Optional) Track the last moved axis to determine the surface normal of the hit voxel if a collision is detected. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def amanatideswoo(origin, direction, gridmin, gridmax, voxelsize=1.0, maxt=float('inf')): """ Traverses a uniform voxel grid along a ray in front-to-back order. Assumes origin is already clipped to the grid's AABB if outside. gridmin and gridmax are exclusive index bounds for each axis. """ # 1. Clip ray to grid AABB tenter = -float('inf') texit = float('inf') for axis in range(3): if abs(direction[axis]) < 1e-6: if not (gridmin[axis] <= origin[axis] < gridmax[axis]): return # Ray misses grid else: inv = 1.0 / direction[axis] ta = (gridmin[axis] - origin[axis]) inv tb = (gridmax[axis] - origin[axis]) inv if ta > tb: ta, tb = tb, ta tenter = max(tenter, ta) texit = min(texit, tb) if texit < max(tenter, 0.0): return # Ray misses grid # 2. Start at entry point t = max(tenter, 0.0) pos = [origin[i] + t direction[i] for i in range(3)] # 3. Initial voxel indices voxel = [int(math.floor(pos[i] / voxelsize)) for i in range(3)] for i in range(3): voxel[i] = max(gridmin[i], min(voxel[i], gridmax[i] - 1)) # 4. Step signs step = [0, 0, 0] for i in range(3): if direction[i] > 0: step[i] = 1 elif direction[i] < 0: step[i] = -1 # 5. tdelta and tmax tdelta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if abs(direction[i]) > 1e-6: tdelta[i] = voxelsize / abs(direction[i]) fract = (pos[i] / voxelsize) - voxel[i] if direction[i] > 0: tmax[i] = (1.0 - fract) tdelta[i] else: tmax[i] = fract tdelta[i] else: tdelta[i] = float('inf') tmax[i] = float('inf') # 6. Traverse loop while True: if not (gridmin[0] <= voxel[0] < gridmax[0] and gridmin[1] <= voxel[1] < gridmax[1] and gridmin[2] <= voxel[2] < gridmax[2]): break if t > texit: break yield tuple(voxel) # Find axis with smallest tmax minaxis = 0 if tmax[1] < tmax[minaxis]: minaxis = 1 if tmax[2] < tmax[minaxis]: minaxis = 2 voxel[minaxis] += step[minaxis] tmax[minaxis] += tdelta[minaxis] t = tmax[minaxis] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ties: If two or three t{max} values are equal, the ray hits an edge or corner. A strict if/else chain may skip cells. Solutions include stepping all tied axes simultaneously, emitting all "supercover" cells, or using a deterministic half-open convention. Zero Direction Components: If Da = 0, the ray never crosses planes on that axis. Set \Delta ta and Ta to \infty to avoid branching in the loop. Avoid 0 \times \infty NaNs by initializing these axes separately. Boundary Conventions: Origins exactly on voxel planes can cause floor operations to place the origin in a neighboring cell. Define a clear half-open interval convention and test points just below, on, and above boundaries. Numerical Robustness: Large world coordinates, small direction components, and negative zero can cause precision issues. Avoid adding random epsilons; use explicit conventions and targeted tolerance. Time Complexity: O(K), where K is the number of visited cells. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, storing only a few vectors per ray. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Extremely fast per-voxel update (a few comparisons and one addition); output-sensitive; robust for uniform grids. Limitations: Only suitable for uniform grids; performance degrades if the ray traverses many empty cells (though better than marching); requires careful handling of ties and boundaries. When to use: Volume rendering, voxel-based collision detection, and any scenario requiring efficient traversal of a uniform spatial grid. When not to use: Non-uniform grids (the algorithm assumes uniform voxel sizes). The algorithm was introduced by John Amanatides and Andrew Woo in the paper "A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing," published at Eurographics in 1987. It is a classic example of transforming continuous ray geometry into a discrete event sequence, optimizing the inner loop for ray tracing performance. It is widely used in voxel engines and real-time graphics. CPU-based implementations are simpler for learning but less efficient than GPU compute shaders for large scenes. tacf/cpu-voxel-raytracer-raylib, https://github.com/tacf/cpu-voxel-raytracer-raylib, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal | 3D DDA Learning Guide, https://edukatesengkang.com/2026/08/30/how-to-learn-amanatides-woo-fast-voxel-traversal-3d-dda-tmax-tdelta-grid-crossings-and-robust-ray-marching/, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Make yourself a Voxel Engine THIS weekend, https://daymare.net/blogs/voxel-engine-in-a-weekend/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) viljanvr/VisualNifty, https://github.com/viljanvr/VisualNifty, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ApaarRaina/DiffTomo, https://github.com/ApaarRaina/DiffTomo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering
head: 3D Raycasting, Vox5
body: Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering is a real-time rendering technique for 3D voxel grids that utilizes a 2D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to cast rays per screen column, determining the first occupied voxel. It renders the voxel as a vertical stripe (line) rather than a full textured quad, handling depth via a per-column depth buffer to support multiple voxels per column (stacking). Unlike standard raycasting which draws a full vertical line for a wall, this method draws vertical stripes for each depth layer within the voxel, allowing for internal structure visibility and stacking via the depth buffer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid worldMap of dimensions mapWidth x mapHeight x mapDepth, a camera position (posX, posY, posZ), a camera direction vector (dirX, dirY), a camera plane vector (planeX, planeY) defining the field of view, and a vertical pitch offset pitch. Output: A 2D image where each screen column is filled with vertical stripes representing the visible voxel layers, updated against a depth buffer. Data Structures: worldMap: A 3D array ColorRGB worldMap[mapWidth][mapHeight][mapDepth]. Dimensions: mapWidth = 96, mapHeight = 96, mapDepth = 12. ColorRGB: A struct with 3 components (Red, Green, Blue), loaded sequentially from source data. depth: A 2D array int depth[2][384]. Size: 2 buffers of size 384 (screen height). Initialization: Values set to 100000. Purpose: Stores the Z-depth of the last drawn voxel at each screen row to handle occlusion within a column. Camera State: posX, posY, posZ: Camera position. dirX, dirY: Ray direction vector. planeX, planeY: Camera plane vector for FOV calculation. pitch: Vertical tilt offset, typically 200. Formulas: Delta Distances: deltaDistX = \frac{|1.0|}{|dirX|} deltaDistY = \frac{|1.0|}{|dirY|} Perpendicular Wall Distance (Fisheye Correction): If side == 0 (hit X-wall): perpWallDist = \frac{mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2}{dirX} If side == 1 (hit Y-wall): perpWallDist = \frac{mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2}{dirY} This projects the oblique distance onto the camera axis to prevent the fisheye effect. Line Height on Screen: lineHeight = \left\lfloor \frac{h}{perpWallDist} \right\rfloor where h is the screen height. Note: The source notes that dividing by 2 for square voxels causes a crash, so it is omitted, resulting in vertically stretched voxels. Draw Start/End for Layer b: drawStart = (lineHeight \times (b - posZ)) + pitch drawEnd = lineHeight + (lineHeight \times (b - posZ)) + pitch Values are clamped to [0, h-1]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Ray Parameters: Calculate deltaDistX and deltaDistY based on dirX and dirY. Determine initial stepX and stepY based on ray direction: If dirX < 0: stepX = -1, sideDistX = (posX - mapX) deltaDistX Else: stepX = 1, sideDistX = (mapX + 1.0 - posX) deltaDistX Same logic for Y using posY, mapY, dirY, stepY, sideDistY. 2. DDA Loop (Find First Hit): Initialize mapX, mapY to the starting grid cell. Initialize hit = 0, count = 0. While mapX < 0 || mapY < 0 || (count < 384 && hit < 900): If sideDistX < sideDistY: sideDistX += deltaDistX mapX += stepX side = 0 Else: sideDistY += deltaDistY mapY += stepY side = 1 Clamp mapX to [0, mapHeight-1] and mapY to [0, mapWidth-1]. Increment hit. If worldMap[mapX][mapY][0] is not empty (or hit condition met), break loop. (Note: Source implies loop continues until hit or bounds, then processes). 3. Calculate Geometry for Current Hit: Calculate perpWallDist using the formula above. Calculate lineHeight using the formula above. Prepare Horizontal Fill State: Copy current mapX, mapY, side, sideDistX, sideDistY to temporary variables tmapX, tmapY, tside, tsideDistX, tsideDistY. Advance one step again using the same DDA logic to determine the extent of the voxel face. Clamp tmapX, tmapY. Calculate tperpWallDist and tlineHeight using the same formulas. 4. Render Vertical Stripes (Depth Layers): Iterate through all depth layers b from 0 to mapDepth - 1: Calculate drawStart and drawEnd for layer b. Get color color = worldMap[mapX][mapY][b]. Apply shading: If side == 1, color = color / 2. If color is not black: Call verLineTriDepth(x, drawStart, drawEnd, color, depth[0], 384, &count, 0, depth[1]). This function draws the vertical line segment, updating depth[0] and depth[1] to handle occlusion within the column. 5. Render Second Pass (Horizontal Fill/Edge): Iterate through all depth layers b from 0 to mapDepth - 1: Calculate tdrawStart and tdrawEnd using tlineHeight. Get tcolor = worldMap[mapX][mapY][b]. Apply shading: tcolor = tcolor / 3. Call verLineTriDepth with drawStart or tdrawStart depending on whether b < posZ, and depth[1] as the primary buffer. 6. Swap Depth Buffers: At the end of the DDA loop iteration (per voxel hit), copy depth[1] to depth[0]: memcpy(depth[0], depth[1], 384 sizeof(int)) This prepares depth[1] for the next ray or pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervoxelcolumn(screenx, rayposx, rayposy, raydirx, raydiry, mapwidth, mapheight, mapdepth, worldmap, screenheight, pitch): # 1. Initialize DDA deltadistx = abs(1.0 / raydirx) deltadisty = abs(1.0 / raydiry) mapx = int(rayposx) mapy = int(rayposy) if raydirx < 0: stepx = -1 sidedistx = (rayposx - mapx) deltadistx else: stepx = 1 sidedistx = (mapx + 1.0 - rayposx) deltadistx if raydiry < 0: stepy = -1 sidedisty = (rayposy - mapy) deltadisty else: stepy = 1 sidedisty = (mapy + 1.0 - rayposy) deltadisty hit = 0 count = 0 side = 0 # 2. DDA Loop while mapx < 0 or mapy < 0 or (count < 384 and hit < 900): if sidedistx < sidedisty: sidedistx += deltadistx mapx += stepx side = 0 else: sidedisty += deltadisty mapy += stepy side = 1 # Clamp map coordinates mapx = max(0, min(mapx, mapwidth - 1)) mapy = max(0, min(mapy, mapheight - 1)) hit += 1 # Check for hit (simplified: assume first non-black voxel is a hit for this structure) # In practice, check worldmap[mapx][mapy][0] for occupancy if worldmap[mapx][mapy][0] != RGBBLACK: break count += 1 if hit >= 900: return # No hit within bounds # 3. Calculate Geometry if side == 0: perpwalldist = (mapx - rayposx + (1 - stepx) / 2) / raydirx else: perpwalldist = (mapy - rayposy + (1 - stepy) / 2) / raydiry lineheight = int(screenheight / perpwalldist) # Prepare horizontal fill state tmapx, tmapy, tside = mapx, mapy, side tsidedistx, tsidedisty = sidedistx, sidedisty # Advance one step for t variables if tsidedistx < tsidedisty: tsidedistx += deltadistx tmapx += stepx tside = 0 else: tsidedisty += deltadisty tmapy += stepy tside = 1 tmapx = max(0, min(tmapx, mapwidth - 1)) tmapy = max(0, min(tmapy, mapheight - 1)) if tside == 0: tperpwalldist = (tmapx - rayposx + (1 - stepx) / 2) / raydirx else: tperpwalldist = (tmapy - rayposy + (1 - stepy) / 2) / raydiry tlineheight = int(screenheight / tperpwalldist) # 4. Render Vertical Stripes for b in range(mapdepth): drawstart = (lineheight (b - rayposz)) + pitch drawend = lineheight + (lineheight (b - rayposz)) + pitch drawstart = max(0, min(drawstart, screenheight - 1)) drawend = max(0, min(drawend, screenheight - 1)) color = worldmap[mapx][mapy][b] if side == 1: color = color / 2 if color != RGBBLACK: verlinetridepth(screenx, drawstart, drawend, color, depth[0], 384, count, 0, depth[1]) # 5. Render Second Pass (Horizontal Fill/Edge) for b in range(mapdepth): tdrawstart = (tlineheight (b - rayposz)) + pitch tdrawend = tlineheight + (tlineheight (b - rayposz)) + pitch tdrawstart = max(0, min(tdrawstart, screenheight - 1)) tdrawend = max(0, min(tdrawend, screenheight - 1)) tcolor = worldmap[mapx][mapy][b] tcolor = tcolor / 3 # Determine start/end based on b < rayposz if b < rayposz: start = drawstart else: start = tdrawstart verlinetridepth(screenx, start, tdrawend, tcolor, depth[1], 384, count, 0, depth[1]) # 6. Swap Depth Buffers depth[0] = depth[1].copy() # Simulating memcpy Extends this method to support two distinct vertical layers (ceilings and floors) in a single pass using a 3D DDA, differing from the single-layer focus of the parent. A simpler technique that casts one ray per screen column using a height-map-based march, differing from this method's per-pixel/vertical-stripe approach. Performs ray casting in screen space with explicit layer index handling for multiple refractions, differing from this method's strict 3D grid traversal. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of screen columns and the maximum traversal depth (capped at 900 steps in the source). The DDA traversal is efficient, jumping directly between grid boundaries. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the 3D voxel grid worldMap and the two depth buffers. For the source dimensions, this is minimal. Performance: Designed for real-time rendering on limited hardware (implied by the C-style implementation and lack of complex shading). Strengths: Handles internal voxel structure visibility via depth buffering; avoids fisheye distortion; efficient traversal. Limitations: Vertically stretched voxels due to aspect ratio handling; limited to 2 depth buffers for occlusion; hardcoded bounds and parameters in the source implementation. When to use: Real-time voxel visualization where internal structure is important and performance is critical. When not to use: When square voxel aspect ratio is required without workarounds; when deep volume rendering with many layers is needed beyond the fixed depth buffer capacity. This method originates from the voxnine project by JCLemme, an unofficial implementation of 3D voxel raycasting using DDA. It builds on the Amanatides–Woo Voxel Traversal algorithm for efficient grid traversal. The technique is notable for its use of vertical stripes and dual depth buffers to handle voxel stacking, distinguishing it from standard Wolfenstein 3D-style raycasting.
