name: Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting
head: 3D Raycaster, 3D Raycasting with Dual-Layer DDA, DDA Raycasting, DDA impl, Digital Differential Analyzer Raycasting
body: Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting is a real-time rendering technique that extends standard voxel raycasting by supporting two distinct vertical layers (e.g., worldMap[0] for ceilings and worldMap[1] for floors) within a single ray traversal pass. Unlike its sibling Classic (Column Voxel Space), which typically handles a single layer or requires separate passes, this method simultaneously determines the first occupied cell for both layers using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA). It builds on Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering by adding the capacity to render both top and bottom surfaces of a voxel column in one go, while differing from Screen-Space Ray Casting with Layer Traversal by using a strict 3D grid traversal rather than screen-space layer iteration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D voxel grid worldMap with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times 2 (where the third dimension represents the two layers: 0 for top/ceiling, 1 for bottom/floor). Camera position (rayPosX, rayPosY, rayPosZ) and direction (rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ). Screen height h. Outputs: A rendered image where each screen column displays vertical stripes for both the ceiling (layer 0) and floor (layer 1) hits, with correct depth and texture coordinates. Data Structures: worldMap: A 3D array or flattened structure indexed as worldMap[layer][x][y] or equivalent, where layer \in \{0, 1\}. rayPos: 3D vector (rayPosX, rayPosY, rayPosZ). rayDir: 3D vector (rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ). sideDist: 3D vector tracking distance to the next grid boundary for each axis. deltaDist: 3D vector storing the distance the ray travels to cross one cell in each axis. step: 3D vector storing the direction of increment (-1 or 1) for each axis. Parameters: maxdistance: The maximum distance the ray travels before stopping if no wall is found. Typical value: 1000. h: Screen height in pixels. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Initialization: For each screen column x: a. Compute the ray direction vector (rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ) based on the camera position, direction vector, and camera plane. b. Initialize the current map cell coordinates: mapX = \lfloor rayPosX \rfloor, \quad mapY = \lfloor rayPosY \rfloor, \quad mapZ = \lfloor rayPosZ \rfloor c. Calculate the initial side distances and step directions for X, Y, and Z axes: stepX = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } rayDirX < 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad stepY = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } rayDirY < 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad stepZ = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } rayDirZ < 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} sideDistX = \begin{cases} (rayPosX - mapX) \cdot deltaDistX & \text{if } rayDirX < 0 \\ (mapX + 1.0 - rayPosX) \cdot deltaDistX & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} (Similarly for sideDistY and sideDistZ). d. Compute delta distances for each axis: deltaDistX = \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{rayDirY}{rayDirX}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{rayDirZ}{rayDirX}\right)^2} deltaDistY = \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{rayDirX}{rayDirY}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{rayDirZ}{rayDirY}\right)^2} deltaDistZ = \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{rayDirX}{rayDirZ}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{rayDirY}{rayDirZ}\right)^2} e. Initialize flags hitA = false (for layer 0) and hitB = false (for layer 1). 2. DDA Loop: Perform the DDA loop while !hitA || !hitB: a. Compare sideDistX, sideDistY, and sideDistZ. b. If sideDistX is the smallest: sideDistX += deltaDistX, \quad mapX += stepX, \quad side = 0 c. Else if sideDistY is the smallest: sideDistY += deltaDistY, \quad mapY += stepY, \quad side = 1 d. Else (if sideDistZ is the smallest): sideDistZ += deltaDistZ, \quad mapZ += stepZ, \quad side = 2 e. Check for wall hit in layer 0 (hitA): If worldMap[0][mapX][mapY] > 0 and !hitA, set hitA = true. Calculate perpendicular wall distance: perpWallDist = \begin{cases} \frac{mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2}{rayDirX} & \text{if } side == 0 \\ \frac{mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2}{rayDirY} & \text{if } side == 1 \\ \frac{mapZ - rayPosZ + (1 - stepZ) / 2}{rayDirZ} & \text{if } side == 2 \end{cases} f. Check for wall hit in layer 1 (hitB): If worldMap[1][mapX][mapY] > 0 and !hitB, set hitB = true. Calculate perpWallDist using the same logic as in step 2e. 3. Rendering: a. Render Layer 0 Stripe (Ceiling): If hitA is true: lineHeight = \left\lfloor \frac{h}{perpWallDist} \right\rfloor drawStart = \max\left(0, \left\lfloor \frac{h}{2} - \frac{lineHeight}{2} \right\rfloor\right) drawEnd = \min\left(h - 1, \left\lfloor \frac{h}{2} + \frac{lineHeight}{2} \right\rfloor\right) Draw a vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd with color based on worldMap[0][mapX][mapY], halving brightness if side == 1. b. Render Layer 1 Stripe (Floor): If hitB is true: lineHeight = \left\lfloor \frac{h}{perpWallDist} \right\rfloor drawStart = \max\left(0, \left\lfloor -\frac{lineHeight}{2} + \frac{h}{2} \right\rfloor\right) drawEnd = \min\left(h - 1, \left\lfloor \frac{h}{2} \right\rfloor\right) Draw a vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd with color based on worldMap[1][mapX][mapY], halving brightness if side == 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def duallayerddaraycasting(worldmap, camerapos, cameradir, screenheight, maxdistance): """ Renders ceiling (layer 0) and floor (layer 1) stripes for each screen column. worldmap: 3D array [2][Dx][Dy] camerapos: (rayPosX, rayPosY, rayPosZ) cameradir: (rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ) screenheight: int h maxdistance: float """ rayPosX, rayPosY, rayPosZ = camerapos rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ = cameradir # Initialize map coordinates mapX = int(rayPosX) mapY = int(rayPosY) mapZ = int(rayPosZ) # Calculate step directions stepX = -1 if rayDirX < 0 else 1 stepY = -1 if rayDirY < 0 else 1 stepZ = -1 if rayDirZ < 0 else 1 # Calculate delta distances # Note: Division by zero if rayDir is 0 along an axis; handled by guard in practice deltaDistX = math.sqrt(1 + (rayDirY / rayDirX)2 + (rayDirZ / rayDirX)2) deltaDistY = math.sqrt(1 + (rayDirX / rayDirY)2 + (rayDirZ / rayDirY)2) deltaDistZ = math.sqrt(1 + (rayDirX / rayDirZ)2 + (rayDirY / rayDirZ)2) # Calculate initial side distances if rayDirX < 0: sideDistX = (rayPosX - mapX) deltaDistX else: sideDistX = (mapX + 1.0 - rayPosX) deltaDistX if rayDirY < 0: sideDistY = (rayPosY - mapY) deltaDistY else: sideDistY = (mapY + 1.0 - rayPosY) deltaDistY if rayDirZ < 0: sideDistZ = (rayPosZ - mapZ) deltaDistZ else: sideDistZ = (mapZ + 1.0 - rayPosZ) deltaDistZ hitA = False # Layer 0 hit hitB = False # Layer 1 hit side = 0 # 0: vertical face (X), 1: horizontal face (Y), 2: depth face (Z) perpWallDist = 0.0 # DDA Loop while not (hitA and hitB): # Determine which side to step if sideDistX < sideDistY: if sideDistX < sideDistZ: sideDistX += deltaDistX mapX += stepX side = 0 else: sideDistZ += deltaDistZ mapZ += stepZ side = 2 else: if sideDistY < sideDistZ: sideDistY += deltaDistY mapY += stepY side = 1 else: sideDistZ += deltaDistZ mapZ += stepZ side = 2 # Check bounds and hits # Assuming worldmap dimensions are accessible via Dx, Dy, Dz # For simplicity, we assume valid indices or handle out-of-bounds as no hit if 0 <= mapX < worldmap.shape[1] and 0 <= mapY < worldmap.shape[2]: if not hitA and worldmap[0][mapX][mapY] > 0: hitA = True # Calculate perpWallDist for layer 0 if side == 0: perpWallDist = (mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2) / rayDirX elif side == 1: perpWallDist = (mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2) / rayDirY elif side == 2: perpWallDist = (mapZ - rayPosZ + (1 - stepZ) / 2) / rayDirZ if not hitB and worldmap[1][mapX][mapY] > 0: hitB = True # Calculate perpWallDist for layer 1 (same logic) if side == 0: perpWallDist = (mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2) / rayDirX elif side == 1: perpWallDist = (mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2) / rayDirY elif side == 2: perpWallDist = (mapZ - rayPosZ + (1 - stepZ) / 2) / rayDirZ # Optional: Break if distance exceeds maxdistance (requires tracking distance) # For simplicity, we assume the loop terminates when both hits are found or bounds are exceeded # Rendering # Layer 0 (Ceiling) if hitA: lineHeight = int(screenheight / perpWallDist) drawStart = max(0, int(screenheight / 2 - lineHeight / 2)) drawEnd = min(screenheight - 1, int(screenheight / 2 + lineHeight / 2)) # Draw vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd with color from worldmap[0][mapX][mapY] # Halve brightness if side == 1 # Layer 1 (Floor) if hitB: lineHeight = int(screenheight / perpWallDist) drawStart = max(0, int(-lineHeight / 2 + screenheight / 2)) drawEnd = min(screenheight - 1, int(screenheight / 2)) # Draw vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd with color from worldmap[1][mapX][mapY] # Halve brightness if side == 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If rayDirX, rayDirY, or rayDirZ is zero, the delta distance calculations involve division by zero, resulting in NaN or infinity values. This must be handled by checking for zero direction components and using alternative formulas or clamping. Side Flip Logic: Incorrect side flip logic leads to sheared textures or incorrect scrolling directions when rays hit opposite face types. Boundary Conditions: The algorithm must handle cases where the ray exits the map bounds without hitting a wall, potentially requiring a default background color or termination condition. Renders each voxel column as 12 distinct vertical layers, iterating through vertical indices to draw stacked horizontal stripes. Choose when internal voxel structure and thickness visualization are required. Uses a 3D DDA over dual cells for particle rendering with glossy and glass materials. Choose for particle systems requiring refraction and reflection. Time Complexity: O(N) per screen column, where N is the number of cells traversed until a hit is found. In the worst case (no hit or far hit), N is proportional to the map dimension along the ray direction. Memory Complexity: O(Dx \cdot Dy \cdot 2) for the voxel grid, where Dx, Dy are the map dimensions. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the density of occupied cells and the map size. Typical values for maxdistance are 1000 units. Strengths: Simultaneous rendering of ceiling and floor layers reduces the number of ray casts per column. Efficient traversal using DDA avoids per-pixel ray marching. Limitations: Limited to two layers. Requires careful handling of zero direction components. Texture mapping can be sheared if side logic is incorrect. When to Use: Real-time voxel rendering where both ceiling and floor visibility is required, and performance is critical. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring more than two vertical layers or complex material interactions (e.g., refraction) without additional extensions. Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting is an extension of classic voxel raycasting techniques, specifically designed to handle both ceiling and floor surfaces in a single pass. It builds upon the foundational work of Amanatides and Woo on voxel traversal. The method is commonly used in real-time voxel-based games and simulations where efficient rendering of 3D grids is necessary. The specific implementation details, such as the use of two distinct layers and the rendering of vertical stripes, are documented in various online repositories and tutorials. mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, https://github.com/mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) 3D/ray/casting/dda/main.odin, https://github.com/algo-boyz/odins-raylib/blob/52b8fddb/3D/ray/casting/dda/main.odin, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) JCLemme/voxnine, https://github.com/JCLemme/voxnine, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Raycasting with Vertical Slicing
head: 12-layer vertical raycasting, voxel4.cpp raycaster
body: Voxel Raycasting with Vertical Slicing is a 3D rendering technique that visualizes voxel thickness by treating each voxel column as 12 distinct vertical layers. Unlike standard 2D raycasting which draws a single vertical line per hit, this method draws 12 vertical stripes per hit, spaced by lineHeight intervals and centered around the intersection point, allowing for the visualization of internal structure and depth. It builds on Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting by extending the vertical dimension from 2 layers to 12, enabling more complex volumetric representation while maintaining the efficiency of DDA traversal. Inputs: worldMap: A 3D integer array int worldMap[mapWidth][mapHeight][12] representing the voxel grid. Dimensions are mapWidth = 96 and mapHeight = 96. The third dimension (size 12) represents vertical layers. Values 0-5 have specific color mappings; 6-11 default to Yellow. cameraPos: (posX, posY) representing the camera position. cameraDir: (dirX, dirY) representing the camera direction vector. cameraPlane: (planeX, planeY) where planeX = 0 and planeY = 0.66, determining the Field of View (FOV). screenWidth: Width of the output screen in pixels. screenHeight: Height of the output screen in pixels. pitch: A double constant representing the vertical tilt offset for the voxel stack. Default value is 200. Outputs: A 2D screen buffer where each column x contains 12 vertical stripes corresponding to the 12 layers of the hit voxel. World Map: int worldMap[96][96][12]. Each element stores an integer representing the layer's color or state. Depth Buffer: int depth[384]. Initialized to 100000. Used to handle occlusion between the 12 vertical slices of the same voxel or across rays. The array is reset per ray in the loop. 1. Initialize Ray Position and Direction: Set rayPosX = posX and rayPosY = posY. For each screen column x from 0 to screenWidth - 1: Calculate cameraX = 2 x / screenWidth - 1. Calculate rayDirX = dirX + planeX cameraX. Calculate rayDirY = dirY + planeY cameraX. 2. Initialize DDA State: Determine stepX and stepY (+1 or -1) based on the signs of rayDirX and rayDirY. Calculate initial sideDistX and sideDistY to the first grid boundary: If rayDirX < 0, stepX = -1, sideDistX = (rayPosX - mapX) deltaDistX. Else, stepX = 1, sideDistX = (mapX + 1.0 - rayPosX) deltaDistX. Same logic applies for Y: If rayDirY < 0, stepY = -1, sideDistY = (rayPosY - mapY) deltaDistY; else stepY = 1, sideDistY = (mapY + 1.0 - rayPosY) deltaDistY. Calculate deltaDistX = sqrt(1 + (rayDirY rayDirY) / (rayDirX rayDirX)) and deltaDistY = sqrt(1 + (rayDirX rayDirX) / (rayDirY rayDirY)). 3. Perform DDA Loop: Initialize mapX = int(rayPosX) and mapY = int(rayPosY). Initialize hit = 0. While mapX or mapY are out of bounds (clamped to 0..width-1/height-1) or hit < 100: If sideDistX < sideDistY: Add deltaDistX to sideDistX. Increment mapX by stepX. Set side = 0. Else: Add deltaDistY to sideDistY. Increment mapY by stepY. Set side = 1. Clamp mapX to [0, mapHeight-1] and mapY to [0, mapWidth-1]. Increment hit. 4. Render Voxel Layers: Calculate perpWallDist: If side == 0, perpWallDist = (mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2) / rayDirX. If side == 1, perpWallDist = (mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2) / rayDirY. Calculate lineHeight = (int)(screenHeight / perpWallDist). Note: The source code uses this formula without dividing by 2 for square voxels, despite a comment suggesting it. Initialize depth array of size 384 with 100000. Loop b from 0 to 11: Calculate drawStart = ((lineHeight)(b-6)) + pitch. Clamp drawStart to [0, screenHeight-1]. Calculate drawEnd = lineHeight + ((lineHeight)(b-6)) + pitch. Clamp drawEnd to [0, screenHeight-1]. Retrieve color from worldMap[mapX][mapY][b]. If side == 1, divide color brightness by 2. If color is not Black, call verLineDepth(x, drawStart, drawEnd, color, depth, 384, &count). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelraycastingverticalslicing(worldmap, mapwidth, mapheight, camerapos, cameradir, cameraplane, screenwidth, screenheight, pitch=200): screenbuffer = [[0 for in range(screenheight)] for in range(screenwidth)] for x in range(screenwidth): camerax = 2 x / screenwidth - 1 raydirx = cameradir[0] + cameraplane[0] camerax raydiry = cameradir[1] + cameraplane[1] camerax rayposx = camerapos[0] rayposy = camerapos[1] mapx = int(rayposx) mapy = int(rayposy) if raydirx < 0: stepx = -1 sidedistx = (rayposx - mapx) math.sqrt(1 + (raydiry raydiry) / (raydirx raydirx)) else: stepx = 1 sidedistx = (mapx + 1.0 - rayposx) math.sqrt(1 + (raydiry raydiry) / (raydirx raydirx)) if raydiry < 0: stepy = -1 sidedisty = (rayposy - mapy) math.sqrt(1 + (raydirx raydirx) / (raydiry raydiry)) else: stepy = 1 sidedisty = (mapy + 1.0 - rayposy) math.sqrt(1 + (raydirx raydirx) / (raydiry raydiry)) deltadistx = math.sqrt(1 + (raydiry raydiry) / (raydirx raydirx)) deltadisty = math.sqrt(1 + (raydirx raydirx) / (raydiry raydiry)) hit = 0 side = 0 while (0 <= mapx < mapwidth and 0 <= mapy < mapheight) and hit < 100: if sidedistx < sidedisty: sidedistx += deltadistx mapx += stepx side = 0 else: sidedisty += deltadisty mapy += stepy side = 1 hit += 1 if side == 0: perpwalldist = (mapx - rayposx + (1 - stepx) / 2) / raydirx else: perpwalldist = (mapy - rayposy + (1 - stepy) / 2) / raydiry lineheight = int(screenheight / perpwalldist) depthbuffer = [100000] 384 for b in range(12): drawstart = (lineheight (b - 6)) + pitch drawend = lineheight + (lineheight (b - 6)) + pitch drawstart = max(0, min(screenheight - 1, drawstart)) drawend = max(0, min(screenheight - 1, drawend)) color = worldmap[mapx][mapy][b] if side == 1: color = color // 2 if color != 0: # Assuming verLineDepth is a function that draws a vertical line with depth testing # This is a placeholder for the actual drawing logic for y in range(drawstart, drawend + 1): if depthbuffer[y] > hit: screenbuffer[x][y] = color depthbuffer[y] = hit return screenbuffer pitch: Default value is 200. It shifts the vertical position of the voxel layers on the screen. cameraPlaneY: Value is 0.66. The horizontal component planeX is 0. Voxel Aspect Ratio: The source code contains a comment indicating uncertainty about voxel aspect ratio: 'This needs to be divided by 2 to make square voxels, but then it crashes. ??? wait nvm'. The implementation uses h / perpWallDist without the division by 2. Boundary Conditions: The DDA loop clamps mapX and mapY to [0, mapHeight-1] and [0, mapWidth-1] respectively. If the ray goes out of bounds, the loop terminates. Depth Buffer Reset: The depth buffer is reset per ray in the loop. This suggests per-ray depth management, but the array is passed to verLineDepth, which might imply global depth management depending on its implementation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of screen columns, as each column requires a DDA traversal and 12 layer draws. Memory Complexity: O(W H) for the screen buffer and O(W) for the depth buffer per ray. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales linearly with screen width. The number of layers (12) is fixed, so it does not scale with resolution. Strengths: Visualizes voxel thickness and internal structure. Efficient DDA traversal. Limitations: Fixed number of layers (12). Potential aspect ratio issues. Unclear depth management across rays. When to Use: When visualizing voxel depth is important and performance is not critical. When Not to Use: When high performance is required or when more than 12 layers are needed. Origin: The method is described in the voxnine repository by JCLemme. History and Development: The method is an extension of 2D raycasting, adding vertical layers to represent 3D voxels. Where it is Used: Used in the voxnine project for rendering 3D voxel grids. JCLemme/voxnine, https://github.com/JCLemme/voxnine, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Dual-Cell DDA Raycasting for Particles
head: Dual-Cell DDA, Ray-Traced Mirror and Glass Particles
body: A ray-tracing optimization for particle volumes that uses a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) over dual cells to efficiently test for ray-sphere intersections, enabling real-time rendering of glossy mirrors and refractive glass particles. It distinguishes itself from standard voxel raycasting by leveraging a pre-sorted neighbor grid and a 2x2x2 cell expansion strategy to guarantee hit detection within a dual cell without exhaustive search, significantly reducing shading overhead for deep particle piles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin and direction; particle system data including sortedpositionsbuffer, sortedindicesbuffer, celloffsetsbuffer, cellsize, and gridorigin. Output: Final pixel color, accounting for reflections, refractions, and room geometry intersections. Data Structures: The method relies on additive accessors added to the FluidSimulation structure, requiring no restructuring of existing files: sortedpositionsbuffer: Array of particle positions, sorted spatially. sortedindicesbuffer: Array of indices corresponding to the sorted positions. celloffsetsbuffer: Offsets defining the neighbor grid topology. cellsize: Scalar size of a single grid cell. gridorigin: Origin point of the grid. Parameters: setrtbounces: Integer controlling ray bounce depth. Default is 2. Particle count: Default 8192 larger particles. Particle Radius: Must be less than half a cell size to guarantee the 2x2x2 test coverage. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Cast primary rays from the camera. If rt=on, assign materials: 30% glossy black mirrors, 35% glass (IOR 1.5, Fresnel), and 35% matte grey. 2. DDA Traversal: Perform a 3D DDA over the dual cells of the fluid's neighbor grid. 3. Dual Cell Testing: For each DDA step at a current dual cell, test the 8 surrounding grid cells (forming a 2x2x2 block) for ray-sphere intersections. Geometric Guarantee: Since particle radius r < \frac{1}{2} \times \text{cell\size}, any sphere intersecting the dual cell must intersect at least one of the 8 surrounding grid cells. 4. Material Interaction: If a sphere is hit, compute reflection (for mirrors) or refraction (for glass, exiting the far side). Recursively cast new rays up to setrtbounces. 5. Room Intersection: If a ray misses all spheres during traversal, it intersects the room geometry. Determine color based on the panel's mean irradiance, walls lit by the panel plus one voxel cone, or black for the open front. The sky gradient substitutes for the ceiling and open front. 6. Impostor Depth Optimization: For depth testing, render camera-facing quads at the sphere's nearest point. Do not write fragdepth to avoid running the fragment shader (including ray tracing) before the depth test, which is critical for deep piles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualcellddaraytrace(rayorigin, raydirection, bounces, maxbounces): # Initialize DDA state for dual cells currentdualcell = getdualcell(rayorigin) for bounce in range(maxbounces): # Step 1: DDA traversal over dual cells hitsphere = False hitpoint = None hitnormal = None hitmaterial = None # Step 2: Test 2x2x2 grid cells surrounding the current dual cell surroundingcells = getsurroundingcells(currentdualcell) for cell in surroundingcells: # Test all spheres in this grid cell for sphereindex in getspheresincell(cell): spherepos = sortedpositionsbuffer[sphereindex] sphereradius = getradius(sphereindex) # Ray-sphere intersection test t, normal = raysphereintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, spherepos, sphereradius) if t is not None and t > 0: hitsphere = True hitpoint = rayorigin + raydirection t hitnormal = normal hitmaterial = getmaterial(sphereindex) break if hitsphere: break if hitsphere: # Step 3: Material interaction if hitmaterial == "mirror": # Reflect ray raydirection = reflect(raydirection, hitnormal) rayorigin = hitpoint + epsilon raydirection elif hitmaterial == "glass": # Refract ray (IOR 1.5) raydirection = refract(raydirection, hitnormal, 1.0, 1.5) rayorigin = hitpoint + epsilon raydirection else: # Matte grey: diffuse shading or termination return shadediffuse(hitpoint, hitnormal) # Recurse or continue loop for bounces if bounce < maxbounces - 1: return dualcellddaraytrace(rayorigin, raydirection, bounces, maxbounces) else: return shadediffuse(hitpoint, hitnormal) else: # Step 4: Room intersection return shaderoomgeometry(rayorigin, raydirection) return shadediffuse(rayorigin, raydirection) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Testing: Writing fragdepth before the depth test causes the fragment shader (including ray tracing) to run unnecessarily for occluded layers in deep piles, degrading performance from ~16.7 ms to ~92 ms per frame. Radius Constraint: The guarantee of finding every hit relies on the particle radius being strictly less than half the cell size. Performance: Reduces frame time from approximately 92 ms to 16.7 ms (vsync) for scenes with 8192 particles by avoiding full shading for occluded layers via impostor depth quads. Complexity: Time complexity depends on the number of DDA steps and the density of spheres in the 2x2x2 neighborhood. Memory complexity is linear with the number of particles for the sorted buffers. Strengths: Efficient handling of deep particle piles; supports complex materials (mirror, glass) in real-time; additive implementation requires no core restructuring. Limitations: Limited to spherical particles; requires pre-sorted data structures; performance degrades if particle radius approaches half cell size. This method was introduced in the "voxel-gi-particles" project as a bonus ray-tracing mode for real-time global illumination with particles. It was developed to enable glossy and refractive materials in a voxel-based GI system without prohibitive performance costs, leveraging the spatial coherence of particle distributions. voxel-gi-particles: the article's lightbox look, plus its ray-traced mirror and glass bonus, https://github.com/Siroko/kansei/pull/108, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Classic (Column Voxel Space)
head: Classic rendering, Column voxel space, Per-pixel 3D column raycast, Scanline voxel rendering
body: Classic rendering is a real-time terrain visualization technique that redraws the camera frustum every frame by marching world-vertical columns from the camera to the horizon. It differs from its sibling Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering by casting one ray per screen column rather than per pixel, and from Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting by using a height-map-based column march instead of a dual-layer DDA approach. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A height map and a color map, both typically 1024 \times 1024 rasters. Camera parameters: position, orientation (yaw/pitch), field of view (FOV), and far clip distance. Outputs: A 2D image where each screen column is filled by the visible portion of the corresponding world-vertical column. Data Structures: Height Map: A 2D array of height values. Color Map: A 2D array of color values corresponding to the height map. Mip Chain: A pyramid of coarser height and color rasters derived from the base maps. The number of levels (LOD) is configurable, typically ranging from 1 to \log2(\text{map width}). For a 1024 map, this allows stops at 64 \times 64 (5 levels) or 2 \times 2 (10 levels). Screen Column Buffer: An array storing the visible height or color for each screen column index. Parameters: Delta Z: Ray step size for classic and scanline modes. Range: 0.1–2.0. (Note: Unused by voxel mode). Distance: Far clip value. Range: 100–74500 meters. The maximum is approximately 74473 meters at 640 \times 480 resolution with 90^\circ FOV. LOD: Number of mip raster levels used. Default is the middle of the range. LOD Curve: Determines switch distances. Options: Linear (equal range per level), Doubling (each switch is twice as far as the previous), or Logarithmic (log-spaced from first switch to Distance). LOD Step: Meters to the first LOD switch. Range: 10 m to Distance. Editable only for Logarithmic curve; Linear and Doubling fill 0 \dots \text{Distance} automatically. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Camera: Set up the view matrix based on camera position, yaw, pitch, and FOV. 2. Iterate Screen Columns: For each screen column x from 0 to \text{width}-1: a. Cast Ray: Construct a 3D ray originating from the camera position and passing through the center of the screen pixel at column x. b. March Column: Step along the ray in world-vertical increments (Delta Z) until the horizon or far clip is reached. c. Determine LOD: Calculate the distance from the camera. Select the appropriate mip level based on the LOD curve and LOD step. d. Sample Height/Color: i. If LOD is 0: Perform bilinear sampling on the base height/color maps. Refine the sample by snapping to the inner 1/16 \dots 1 m cell grid. Add height noise. ii. If LOD > 0: Perform nearest-neighbor sampling on the coarser mip level to keep coarse blocks flat and avoid interpolation artifacts. e. Render Stripe: Draw the vertical stripe for the column using the sampled color, handling depth via the column's visible height. 3. Repeat: Redraw the entire frustum every frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderclassic(heightmap, colormap, mipchain, camera, screenwidth, screenheight, farclip, lodcurve, lodstep): # Initialize output buffer image = emptyarray(screenwidth, screenheight) # Precompute LOD switch distances based on curve lodswitches = computelodswitches(lodcurve, lodstep, farclip) for x in range(screenwidth): # Cast ray for column x rayorigin = camera.position raydirection = getraydirection(camera, x, screenwidth, screenheight) currentz = 0.0 currentlod = 0 # March column until horizon or far clip while currentz < farclip: # Determine LOD based on distance currentlod = getlodfordistance(currentz, lodswitches) # Get step size based on LOD (not explicitly defined in sources, but implied by "growing step size") stepsize = getstepsize(currentlod) # Sample height and color if currentlod == 0: height = samplebilinearrefine(heightmap, rayorigin, raydirection, currentz) color = samplebilinearrefine(colormap, rayorigin, raydirection, currentz) # Add height noise as per notes height += addheightnoise() else: height = samplenearest(mipchain[currentlod].height, rayorigin, raydirection, currentz) color = samplenearest(mipchain[currentlod].color, rayorigin, raydirection, currentz) # Check if voxel is occupied (height < camera height + some threshold) if isoccupied(height, camera.position.y): # Render the visible part of the column rendercolumnstripe(image, x, currentz, color) break # Stop marching this column once occupied voxel is found currentz += stepsize return image def computelodswitches(lodcurve, lodstep, farclip): # Implementation depends on curve type if lodcurve == "Linear": # Equal range per level numlevels = log2(heightmapwidth) rangeperlevel = farclip / numlevels return [i rangeperlevel for i in range(1, numlevels)] elif lodcurve == "Doubling": # Each switch is twice as far as the previous switches = [] dist = lodstep while dist < farclip: switches.append(dist) dist = 2 return switches elif lodcurve == "Logarithmic": # Log-spaced from first switch to Distance # Exact formula not given in sources return [lodstep (2 i) for i in range(numlevels)] # Placeholder for log spacing return [] def getlodfordistance(distance, lodswitches): # Find the highest LOD level where distance >= switch distance lod = 0 for i, switch in enumerate(lodswitches): if distance >= switch: lod = i + 1 return lod def getstepsize(lod): # Step size grows with LOD # Exact formula not given in sources return 1.0 (2 lod) # Placeholder def samplebilinearrefine(mapdata, rayorigin, raydirection, z): # Bilinear sampling on base map # Refine by snapping to 1/16...1m cell grid # Not fully specified in sources pass def samplenearest(mapdata, rayorigin, raydirection, z): # Nearest neighbor sampling on mip level # Not fully specified in sources pass def isoccupied(height, cameray): # Check if terrain height is below camera return height < cameray def rendercolumnstripe(image, x, z, color): # Draw vertical stripe for column x starting at z # Not fully specified in sources pass def addheightnoise(): # Add noise to height # Not fully specified in sources return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation Artifacts: Higher LODs use nearest-neighbor sampling to keep coarse blocks flat and avoid interpolation artifacts at distance. Precision: LOD 0 uses bilinear sampling and refinement, which may introduce precision issues if not handled correctly. Far Clip: The far clip distance must be set appropriately to avoid performance issues or visual clipping. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot S), where W is screen width, H is screen height, and S is the average number of steps per column. The use of mipmaps and growing step sizes reduces S for distant samples. Memory Complexity: O(W{map} \cdot H{map} \cdot L), where W{map} and H{map} are the map dimensions, and L is the number of LOD levels. Measured Performance: Performance depends on hardware, resolution, and scene complexity. The technique is designed for real-time rendering. Scaling: Scales with screen resolution and map size. Mipmaps help maintain performance at distance. Strengths: Simple implementation, real-time performance, effective for terrain visualization. Limitations: Limited to height-map-based terrain, may not handle complex geometry well. When to Use: Real-time terrain visualization, games, simulations. When Not to Use: Complex 3D scenes, non-terrain geometry. Origin: The technique is based on the "Voxel Space" method used in the game Comanche. History: The method has been implemented in various forms, including CPU (JS, WASM) and GPU (WebGPU) backends. Usage: Used in real-time terrain visualization, games, and simulations. varganorbert222/VoxelSpace, https://github.com/varganorbert222/VoxelSpace, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Screen-Space Ray Casting with Layer Traversal
head: Ray Marching through Columns
body: A real-time rendering technique that performs ray casting in screen space by marching pixel by pixel along the projected ray direction to intersect voxel columns and find entry/exit points for volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from its parent Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering by explicitly handling multiple surface layers within a column via a layer index, enabling the tracing of multiple refractions and deep ambient occlusion by leveraging full knowledge of surface layers rather than just the front-most surface. Inputs: A ray origin and direction (potentially perturbed for refraction), a voxel grid with stored surface layers per column, and a starting depth hint. Outputs: A sequence of intersection events (entry/exit) with their depths and layer indices. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. Voxel Column: A vertical stack of surface layers. Each layer is identified by an integer index. The parity (LSB) of the layer index determines if the ray is entering or exiting the volume material relative to the view direction. Layer Index: An integer representing the depth layer within a column. Parameters: z\sgn: Sign of the ray direction relative to the view direction. Value is -1 if ray marching against view direction, otherwise 1. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start at the pixel containing the ray origin. Initialize a layer hint variable (typically from the previous pixel's last processed layer). 2. Column Intersection: Determine the current voxel column intersected by the ray. If no column is intersected, terminate. 3. Depth Bounds: Calculate the entry and exit depths of the ray within the current voxel column: [entry, exit]. 4. Layer Search: Find the first layer index after the entry depth, using the layer hint as a starting point: layer = first\layer\after(entry, z\sgn, start\hint = layer). 5. Validity Check: Determine if a valid layer exists within the column bounds: layer\found = (z\sgn \times layer \le exit \times z\sgn). 6. State Determination: Determine if the ray is entering the volume at this layer: entering = ((layer \& 1) \neq (z\sgn > 0)) == layer\found. 7. Marching Loop: Iterate through layers within the column bounds: If the current entering state differs from the previous wasinside state, handle the intersection (e.g., compute contribution, perturb ray for refraction). If a layer was found, increment the layer index: layer += z\sgn. Toggle the entering state: entering = !entering. Continue while z\sgn \times layer \le exit \times z\sgn. 8. Hint Update: Use the final layer value as the starthint for the next pixel to optimize the search. 9. Termination: Terminate when the voxel grid boundary is reached or no more columns are intersected. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. layer = initialhint # From previous pixel or initialization while column = nextintersected(ray, column): entry, exit = intersectiondepths(ray, column) # Find first layer after entry, using current layer as hint layer = firstlayerafter(entry, zsgn, starthint=layer) # Check if the layer is within the column bounds layerfound = (zsgn layer <= exit zsgn) # Determine if this layer represents an entry into the volume # (layer & 1) != (zsgn > 0) checks parity against view direction entering = ((layer & 1) != (zsgn > 0)) == layerfound wasinside = False # Track state across layers while zsgn layer <= exit zsgn: if entering != wasinside: handleintersection(...) # If tracing refractions, perturb ray and restart from this pixel # For simple layer traversal, just continue to next layer if layerfound: layer += zsgn entering = not entering wasinside = entering # Update state for next iteration # layer is now the hint for the next pixel Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Hits: Hits may occur on voxel column boundaries in-between stored surface values. These are detected by checking if the ray changes its state between inside and outside when entering a new column (using LSB of layer index). Precision: Depth comparisons must handle floating-point precision issues, especially when entry/exit points are very close to layer boundaries. Refraction Restart: When a surface is intersected and refraction is traced, the ray casting must restart with a new perturbed ray, potentially re-evaluating the current pixel's column. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of layers intersected per pixel. The use of a depth hint from the previous pixel optimizes the search for the next layer, reducing the average cost per pixel. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of surface layers per voxel column. The method itself is memory-efficient as it processes columns on-the-fly. Strengths: Enables deep ambient occlusion by accessing multiple surface layers. Supports multiple refractions by restarting ray casting with perturbed rays. Efficient layer traversal using hints. Limitations: Requires storing multiple layers per voxel column, which increases memory usage compared to single-layer methods. Performance degrades with high layer density or complex refraction paths. This method is described in the context of memory-efficient on-the-fly voxelization of particle data, where it is used to render complex particle systems as volumetric surfaces. It builds upon the concept of screen-space ray casting and extends it to handle multiple surface layers within a voxel column, facilitating advanced effects like refraction and deep ambient occlusion. name: Wolfenstein 3D Raycasting
head: Wolfenstein 3D technique, Wolfenstein-style rendering, Lodev-style DDA, DDA Ray Casting, Raycasting with Fisheye Correction
body: Wolfenstein 3D Raycasting is a rendering technique for first-person corridors on hardware without GPUs or z-buffers, where the world is a flat 2D grid, the camera is confined to the grid plane, and one ray is cast per screen column to reconstruct a textured 3D scene. It sets itself apart from general voxel traversal methods by operating on a strictly 2D grid map with a fixed-height camera, using the perpendicular distance to the camera plane to correct fisheye distortion and determine wall height, rather than computing full 3D intersections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D grid map (Uint8Array or number[][]), player state (posX, posY, dirX, dirY, planeX, planeY), screen dimensions (FBW, FBH), and field of view defined by the plane vector length. Output: A framebuffer image containing vertical wall strips and billboard sprites. Data Structures: Map: A 1D or 2D array representing the grid. Values: 0 (empty floor), 1-4 (wall types), 5 (sliding door). Player: Object with x, y (position), dirX, dirY (unit direction vector), planeX, planeY (camera plane vector perpendicular to dir). Textures: Procedurally generated at runtime onto a 64x64 offscreen canvas, then read into a Uint32Array for fast pixel access. Z-Buffer: A 1D array of size FBW storing the perpendicular distance to the nearest wall for each screen column, used for sprite occlusion. Parameters: FOV: Determined by the length of the plane vector relative to the direction vector. A ratio of |plane|/|dir| = 0.66 yields a horizontal FOV of ~66.8 degrees. Wall Height: Real-world height of a wall tile, typically 1 unit. Steps: 1. Initialize Camera Vectors: For each screen column x from 0 to FBW - 1: Calculate cameraX = 2 x / FBW - 1 (ranges from -1 to 1). Calculate ray direction: rayDirX = dirX + planeX \cdot cameraX rayDirY = dirY + planeY \cdot cameraX 2. DDA Grid Traversal: Initialize current grid cell: mapX = floor(posX), mapY = floor(posY). Calculate step distances: \Deltax = \left| \frac{1}{rayDirX} \right|, \quad \Deltay = \left| \frac{1}{rayDirY} \right| Handle rayDirX == 0 or rayDirY == 0 by setting \Delta to a large value (e.g., 1e30). Determine step directions and initial side distances: If rayDirX < 0: stepX = -1, sideDistX = (posX - mapX) \Deltax. Else: stepX = 1, sideDistX = (mapX + 1 - posX) \Deltax. If rayDirY < 0: stepY = -1, sideDistY = (posY - mapY) \Deltay. Else: stepY = 1, sideDistY = (mapY + 1 - posY) \Deltay. Loop until a wall is hit: If sideDistX < sideDistY: sideDistX += \Deltax mapX += stepX side = 0 (hit vertical grid line) Else: sideDistY += \Deltay mapY += stepY side = 1 (hit horizontal grid line) Check if map[mapY][mapX] > 0. If so, break. Edge Case (Sliding Doors): If the hit tile is 5, advance the ray to the center line of the door cell. If the ray exits the cell before reaching the midline or hits the closed part, continue traversal. 3. Calculate Perpendicular Distance: Compute the fisheye-corrected distance: dist = side === 0 ? sideDistX - \Deltax: sideDistY - \Deltay This value represents the distance perpendicular to the camera plane, correcting for the bowing effect of raw ray length. 4. Render Wall Strip: Calculate line height: lineHeight = \frac{FBH}{dist} Calculate draw range: drawStart = \max(0, \lfloor (FBH - lineHeight) / 2 \rfloor) drawEnd = \min(FBH - 1, \lfloor (FBH + lineHeight) / 2 \rfloor) Calculate texture coordinate wallX: If side == 0: wallX = posY + dist rayDirY - floor(posY + dist rayDirY). Else: wallX = posX + dist rayDirX - floor(posX + dist rayDirX). Mirror texture X if necessary to prevent backward textures: If (side == 0 && rayDirX > 0) || (side == 1 && rayDirY < 0): wallX = 1 - wallX. Draw vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd using wallX for texture sampling. Shade based on side for depth cues. Store dist in zbuffer[x] for sprite occlusion. 5. Render Sprites (Billboards): Sort sprites by squared distance to player (far to near). For each sprite: Transform sprite position (sx, sy) to camera space: invDet = \frac{1}{planeX \cdot dirY - dirX \cdot planeY} transformX = invDet \cdot (dirY \cdot (sx - posX) - dirX \cdot (sy - posY)) transformY = invDet \cdot (-planeY \cdot (sx - posX) + planeX \cdot (sy - posY)) If transformY <= 0.05, skip (behind camera). Calculate screen X: screenX = floor((FBW / 2) (1 + transformX / transformY)). Calculate sprite size: size = abs(floor(FBH / transformY)). For each column x in sprite range: If transformY >= zbuffer[x], skip (occluded by wall). Sample texture, skip if alpha < 128, shade and write to framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castraydda(map, posx, posy, dirx, diry, planex, planey, fbw, fbh, texsize=64): mapw = len(map[0]) maph = len(map) zbuffer = [0.0] fbw for x in range(fbw): camerax = 2.0 x / fbw - 1.0 raydirx = dirx + planex camerax raydiry = diry + planey camerax mapx = int(posx) mapy = int(posy) deltadistx = abs(1.0 / raydirx) if raydirx != 0 else 1e30 deltadisty = abs(1.0 / raydiry) if raydiry != 0 else 1e30 if raydirx < 0: stepx = -1 sidedistx = (posx - mapx) deltadistx else: stepx = 1 sidedistx = (mapx + 1 - posx) deltadistx if raydiry < 0: stepy = -1 sidedisty = (posy - mapy) deltadisty else: stepy = 1 sidedisty = (mapy + 1 - posy) deltadisty hit = False side = 0 guard = 0 while not hit and guard < 128: guard += 1 if sidedistx < sidedisty: sidedistx += deltadistx mapx += stepx side = 0 else: sidedisty += deltadisty mapy += stepy side = 1 if mapx < 0 or mapx >= mapw or mapy < 0 or mapy >= maph: hit = True continue tile = map[mapy][mapx] if tile == 0: continue if tile == 5: # Sliding door logic from: advance to center line, # check openness, continue traversal if gap not reached. hit = True continue hit = True if side == 0: perpdist = sidedistx - deltadistx else: perpdist = sidedisty - deltadisty zbuffer[x] = perpdist lineheight = int(fbh / perpdist) drawstart = max(0, (fbh - lineheight) // 2) drawend = min(fbh - 1, (fbh + lineheight) // 2) if side == 0: wallx = posy + perpdist raydiry else: wallx = posx + perpdist raydirx wallx -= int(wallx) if (side == 0 and raydirx > 0) or (side == 1 and raydiry < 0): wallx = 1.0 - wallx # Fixed-point vertical texture step step = texsize / lineheight texpos = (drawstart - (fbh - lineheight) / 2) step for y in range(drawstart, drawend + 1): texy = int(texpos) & (texsize - 1) texpos += step # Write shaded texel to framebuffer # fb[y fbw + x] = shade(tex[texy texsize + int(wallx texsize)]) return zbuffer Highly efficient on CPU-only hardware; the original engine ran on 286/386-class processors. Optimizations like drawing every second column can double FPS on low-resolution displays with negligible visual loss. Time, memory complexity, strengths, limitations, and usage guidelines are not given in the sources. Wolfenstein 3D (id Software, 1992) rendered first-person corridors on 286/386-class hardware without GPUs, z-buffers, or polygons. The technique projects a 2D grid map into a 3D perspective viewport using one ray per screen column. It is a specific application of the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm for grid traversal, popularized by Lodev's tutorial. name: Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA
head: DDA Voxel Shadow Tracing, Shadow Ray Grid Optimization, Voxel Shadow Raytracer
body: Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA is a technique for computing hard shadows in voxel-based scenes by traversing a 3D voxel grid along rays cast from surface points to light sources. It solves the problem of efficiently determining light attenuation through volumetric or opaque voxel data without resorting to slow, fixed-step ray marching. It sets itself apart from its siblings by focusing specifically on the shadow calculation phase within a rendering pipeline, often utilizing the Amanatides–Woo traversal logic to jump between grid cells rather than sampling every unit of distance. The method operates in two distinct phases: the main rendering loop (which invokes the shadow raycaster) and the DDA traversal algorithm itself. It relies on a sparse or dense voxel buffer where each voxel has a density value. Inputs: Voxel Grid: A buffer of voxelmaterial structs. Each struct contains color (unused in shadow calc) and density (float, 0.0 to 1.0, where 1.0 is opaque). Light Sources: A buffer of lightsource structs containing position (vec3), power (float, max reach distance), color (vec3), and intensity (float). Surface Data: For each pixel, the world-space position (vec4, alpha > 0 indicates valid surface) and normal (vec3). Grid Dimensions: mapsize (vec3), defining the bounds of the voxel world. Outputs: Shadow Factor: A float value between 0.0 (fully shadowed) and 1.0 (fully lit), representing the remaining light intensity after attenuation. Final Color: The base pixel color multiplied by the accumulated lighting contributions. The implementation uses specific buffer layouts, typically in a GLSL compute shader context: 1. Voxel Map (Map): layout (std430, binding = 3) buffer Map containing voxelmaterial voxels[]. 2. Lights (Lights): layout (std430, binding = 2) buffer Lights containing lightsource sources[]. 3. Position Texture (postexture): layout(rgba32f, binding = 1) storing world-space positions. 4. Normal Texture (normtexture): layout(rgba32f, binding = 4) storing voxel normals. 5. Output Image (imgoutput): layout(rgba32f, binding = 0) storing the final lit color. Coordinate to ID Conversion: To access the voxel buffer, 3D coordinates are converted to a 1D index. The coordinates are clamped to [0, mapsize]: \text{ID} = \lfloor x \rfloor + \lfloor y \rfloor \cdot \text{map\size}.x + \lfloor z \rfloor \cdot \text{map\size}.x \cdot \text{map\size}.y This assumes a row-major layout where x is the fastest varying dimension. For each pixel (x, y): 1. Load pixel color, position, and normal from textures. 2. If position.a <= 0, skip (background). 3. Initialize lightValue to ambient color vec4(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 1) and lightColor to vec3(0,0,0). 4. Iterate through each light source current in the Lights buffer: a. Calculate squared distance distanceSP = distance(current.position, position.xyz). b. Light Reach Test: If distanceSP > current.power current.power, skip this light (it cannot reach the surface). c. Compute ray direction rayPixSrc = current.position - position.xyz. d. Determine if the starting voxel should be sampled: stepThroughFirstVoxel = dot(normalize(rayPixSrc), normal) > 0. This checks if the ray originates from the surface and potentially exits it immediately. e. Call stepThroughVoxelWorld(position.xyz, rayPixSrc, stepThroughFirstVoxel) to get intensity. f. Calculate result multiplier: result = current.intensity intensity (1 - (distanceSP / current.power)). g. If result > 0, add current.color.rgb result to lightColor. 5. Add lightColor to lightValue.rgb. 6. Store pixel lightValue to imgoutput. This function traverses the voxel grid from origin along dir. Initialization Phase: 1. Normalize dir. 2. Set currPos = ivec3(floor(origin.x), floor(origin.y), floor(origin.z)). 3. Set intensity = 1.0. 4. For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: a. If dir[i] >= 0: step[i] = 1 delta[i] = 1.0 / max(0.000001, dir[i]) (prevents division by zero). Max[i] = (floor(currPos[i] + 1) - origin[i]) / dir[i] Out[i] = mapsize[i] (boundary limit). b. If dir[i] < 0: step[i] = -1 delta[i] = -1.0 / dir[i] Max[i] = (floor(currPos[i]) - origin[i]) / dir[i] Out[i] = -1 (boundary limit). 5. Calculate last = ivec3(floor(origin.x + dir.x), floor(origin.y + dir.y), floor(origin.z + dir.z)). Note: The source also calculates maxLength = dir.x^2 + dir.y^2 + dir.z^2, but since dir is normalized, this is always 1.0. The termination condition primarily relies on currPos != last. Step Loop: While intensity > 0 AND !reachedEnd AND currPos != last: 1. Sample voxel at currPos using CordtoID. 2. Subtract currentVoxel.density from intensity. 3. Determine the next axis to step: Find the axis k with the minimum Max[k]. 4. Increment currPos[k] by step[k]. 5. Update Max[k] += delta[k]. 6. Check boundary: If currPos[k] == Out[k], set reachedEnd = true. Return: Return intensity. To reduce computation, shadow status can be stored in the voxel grid. For each voxel and each light source, two bits are stored: 1. One bit indicating the voxel is completely in shadow. 2. One bit indicating nothing blocks the voxel from seeing the light source. During traversal, if these bits are set, the ray calculation is skipped. This adds a memory overhead of 2 bits per light source per voxel. Unverified code. origin[axis]) / d outbound[axis] = int(mapsize[axis]) else: step[axis] = -1 delta[axis] = -1.0 / d maxdist[axis] = (floor(currpos[axis]) - origin[axis]) / d outbound[axis] = -1 # Termination setup lastpos = ivec3(floor(origin.x + dirnorm.x), floor(origin.y + dirnorm.y), floor(origin.z + dirnorm.z)) reachedend = False # If we need to sample the starting voxel, do it now if stepthroughfirstvoxel: voxelidx = cordtoid(vec3(currpos), mapsize) intensity -= voxels[voxelidx].density # Main Loop while intensity > 0 and not reachedend and currpos != lastpos: # Determine next axis to step # Find index of minimum value in maxdist minval = min(maxdist.x, maxdist.y, maxdist.z) if maxdist.x == minval: nextaxis = 'x' elif maxdist.y == minval: nextaxis = 'y' else: nextaxis = 'z' # Step currpos[nextaxis] += step[nextaxis] maxdist[nextaxis] += delta[nextaxis] # Check boundary if currpos[nextaxis] == outbound[nextaxis]: reachedend = True break # Sample voxel voxelidx = cordtoid(vec3(currpos), mapsize) intensity -= voxels[voxelidx].density return intensity def renderpixel(x, y, postexture, normtexture, imgoutput, lights, voxels, mapsize): pixel = imageload(imgoutput, ivec2(x, y)) position = imageload(postexture, ivec2(x, y)) normal = imageload(normtexture, ivec2(x, y)).rgb if position.a <= 0: return lightvalue = AMBIENT lightcolor = vec3(0, 0, 0) castlights = 0 for light in lights: distsq = length(light.position - position.xyz) # Light reach test if distsq > light.power light.power: continue raydir = light.position - position.xyz # Check if ray exits the surface immediately stepfirst = dot(normalize(raydir), normal) > 0 intensity = stepthroughvoxelworld(position.xyz, raydir, stepfirst, mapsize, voxels) # Calculate result # Note: distanceSP is used in the formula, but distsq is squared distance. # The source uses distanceSP (linear distance) in the falloff term. result = light.intensity intensity (1.0 - (distsq / light.power)) # Correction: Source uses distanceSP, not distsq. # Re-reading source: "float distanceSP = distance(...)". So distanceSP is linear. # Let's correct the pseudocode variable name to match source logic exactly. # Corrected calculation based on source: # distanceSP is linear distance. # result = current.intensity intensity (1 - (distanceSP / current.power)) # Since I defined distsq above, let's use linear distance for the formula lineardist = sqrt(distsq) result = light.intensity intensity (1.0 - (lineardist / light.power)) if result > 0: lightcolor += light.color result castlights += 1 if castlights > 0: lightvalue.rgb += lightcolor imagestore(imgoutput, ivec2(x, y), pixel lightvalue) A WebGPU compute shader-based ray tracer for voxel models that replaces a rasterizer. It casts rays per pixel, traverses a 3D voxel grid using DDA, applies directional lighting with diffuse shading, and generates hard shadows via shadow rays. It sets itself apart from its parent Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA by implementing the entire rendering pipeline (primary rays, shading, and shadow rays) within a WebGPU compute shader, rather than relying on a GLSL rasterizer with DDA for shadow calculation only. Time Complexity: The DDA traversal is O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by the shadow ray. This is significantly faster than fixed-step marching for sparse or large grids, as it skips empty space. Memory Complexity: The base method requires storing the voxel grid. The optimized version with shadow bits requires an additional 2 bits per light source per voxel. Performance: The DDA approach avoids the "slow fallback" fixed-step algorithm which increments position by a small fixed step (e.g., 0.05) and samples every step, leading to redundant calculations. Strengths: Efficient traversal of uniform grids; handles arbitrary ray directions; simple implementation. Limitations: Requires a uniform grid structure; shadow bit optimization increases memory usage linearly with the number of lights. When to use: When rendering hard shadows in voxel worlds where performance is critical and the grid is uniform. When not to use: For non-uniform grids (use Siddon's Algorithm or adaptive grids) or when soft shadows are required (DDA provides hard shadows only). The technique is based on the Amanatides–Woo voxel traversal algorithm, which enumerates grid cells intersected by a ray in front-to-back order. The specific GLSL implementation described in the sources is an unofficial contribution to the GitHub repository Ein-Baum/Voxel-shadow-raytracer. The concept of using grids to reduce shadow ray computations by storing status bits was discussed in academic literature on fast voxel traversal. name: WebGPU Voxel Ray Tracing Renderer
head: DDA voxel grid traversal, WebGPU-based ray tracing renderer
body: A WebGPU compute shader-based ray tracer for voxel models that replaces a rasterizer. It casts rays per pixel, traverses a 3D voxel grid using DDA, applies directional lighting with diffuse shading, and generates hard shadows via shadow rays. It sets itself apart from its parent Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA by implementing the entire rendering pipeline (primary rays, shading, and shadow rays) within a WebGPU compute shader, rather than relying on a GLSL rasterizer with DDA for shadow calculation only. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid (dense or sparse), a project palette of block colors, lighting parameters (sun direction, intensity, ambient light), and camera state. Output: A 2D image buffer rendered to the canvas. Data Structures: Uniform Buffer: Expanded to 128 bytes to store lighting parameters. Storage Buffer: Contains the project palette for retrieving block colors. Voxel Data: Gathered from the voxel engine into a flat buffer. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: The renderer checks for WebGPU support. If unavailable, it displays a fallback background. 2. Primary Ray Casting: For each pixel, a primary ray is cast into the scene. 3. Voxel Traversal: The 3D voxel grid is traversed using the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to find the first intersecting voxel. 4. Diffuse Shading: If a voxel is hit, diffuse shading is calculated using the dot product of the surface normal (N) and the light direction (L). 5. Shadow Raycasting: Shadow rays are cast by performing DDA traversal from the hit point toward the sun direction to determine occlusion. 6. Color Retrieval: Block colors are retrieved from the storage buffer containing the project palette. 7. Ground Plane: A ground plane with grid lines is rendered, which receives shadows. 8. Background: A subtle sky gradient background is rendered. 9. Blitting: The compute shader output is blitted to the canvas using a fullscreen triangle render pass. Formulas: Diffuse Shading: I{diffuse} = \max(0, N \cdot L). Sun Direction: Calculated from Sun Azimuth (\theta) and Sun Elevation (\phi). Parameters: Sun Azimuth: Horizontal angle of the sun, range 0 to 360 degrees. Sun Elevation: Vertical angle of the sun, range 5 to 90 degrees. Sun Intensity: Brightness of the directional light source. Ambient Light Intensity: Intensity of the ambient light component. Shadow Strength: Intensity/opacity of the shadows. Sun Color: Presets include Warm, White, Cool, Gold, Pink. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: WebGPU Availability: WebGPU is not available in headless CI environments, so the canvas shows a fallback background instead of rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. fn renderpixel(pixelx, pixely, camera, voxelgrid, palette, lighting): # 1. Cast primary ray ray = camera.getray(pixelx, pixely) # 2. Traverse voxel grid using DDA hitpoint, hitnormal, hitvoxelid = ddatraverse(ray, voxelgrid) # 3. Calculate color if hitvoxelid is not None: # Retrieve block color from palette basecolor = palette[hitvoxelid] # Calculate diffuse shading # N is hitnormal, L is lighting.sundirection diffusefactor = max(0, dot(hitnormal, lighting.sundirection)) # Apply shadow rays # Cast ray from hitpoint towards sun isshadowed = ddatraverseshadow(hitpoint, lighting.sundirection, voxelgrid) if isshadowed: diffusefactor = 0.0 # Combine lighting finalcolor = basecolor (lighting.ambientintensity + diffusefactor lighting.sunintensity) else: # Render background (sky gradient) finalcolor = getskygradient(ray.direction) return finalcolor fn ddatraverse(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid): # Standard Amanatides-Woo DDA traversal # Returns first intersecting voxel's point, normal, and ID # Implementation details inherited from Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA pass fn ddatraverseshadow(origin, direction, voxelgrid): # DDA traversal from origin in direction # Returns true if an opaque voxel is hit before reaching light pass Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the average number of voxels traversed per ray. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the size of the voxel grid and the palette. Performance: Performance depends on the hardware's WebGPU support and the complexity of the voxel scene. Strengths: Real-time lighting and shadows in a voxel environment; interactive controls for lighting parameters. Limitations: Requires WebGPU support; not available in headless environments. When to use: When real-time voxel rendering with dynamic lighting and shadows is required in a web browser. When not to use: In headless CI environments or browsers without WebGPU support. The WebGPU Voxel Ray Tracing Renderer was developed as part of the LunaVoxel project. It was introduced as an alternative to the existing Three.js rasterizer, accessible via a dedicated Render tab in the header navigation. The implementation includes directional lighting, shadow rays, and interactive controls. It was authored by tfritzy and merged in February 2026. name: TRFRay3 (DDA Ray Representation)
head: Block picking raycast, CPU DDA raycast for picking, DDA Ray Marching, DDA Raycasting with zero-direction handling, Digital Differential Analyzer raymarching, voxel walk
body: TRFRay3 is a CPU-side Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) ray representation and traversal engine designed for picking and raycasting in voxel worlds, specifically engineered to match the toroidal GPU storage layout exactly. It solves the problem of efficiently finding the first solid voxel hit along a ray in a sparse or dense voxel grid while handling edge cases like zero-direction vectors and toroidal wrapping. It differs from the Amanatides–Woo Voxel Traversal by explicitly providing a C++ class structure (TRFRay3) that pre-computes inverse directions and origin-inverse direction (OOD) terms for SIMD-friendly, division-free traversal loops, and from the Differentiable DDA Loop by being a non-differentiable, integer-step traversal method. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{O}, ray direction \mathbf{D} (normalized), world bounds (min/max), and voxel grid metadata (brick dimensions, occupancy data). Output: The first solid voxel coordinate hit by the ray, or None if no hit occurs within bounds or steps. Data Structures: The core data structure is TRFRay3<T>, which contains five TRFVector3<T> fields arranged contiguously in memory to enable SIMD/vectorization: 1. kOrigin: The ray origin (Ox, Oy, Oz). 2. kDirection: The ray direction (Dx, Dy, Dz). 3. kInvDirection: The component-wise reciprocal (1/Dx, 1/Dy, 1/Dz). 4. kOod: The Origin-Inverse Direction product (Ox/Dx, Oy/Dy, Oz/Dz). 5. kSigns: The component-wise sign of the direction (-1 if Di < 0, else 1). The Data() method returns a pointer to kOrigin, ensuring the five vectors are contiguous. Formulas: Inverse Direction: kInvDirectioni = \frac{1}{Directioni} for i \in \{x, y, z\}. Origin-Inverse Direction (OOD): OODi = \frac{Origini}{Directioni} for i \in \{x, y, z\}. Signs: kSignsi = \text{sign}(Directioni). Parameters: MAXSTEPS: Maximum number of DDA steps allowed per raycast call to prevent infinite loops. epsilon: A small value (e.g., 10^{-3}) used to clamp the ray origin to prevent degenerate cases. Steps: 1. Initialization: Validate the ray direction. If the direction is near-zero or un-normalized, return None. Compute kSigns component-wise: -1 if Directioni < 0, else 1. Compute kInvDirection via component-wise reciprocal. Note: Division by zero is avoided by requiring floating-point types and assuming non-zero direction components, enforced by a staticassert. Compute kOod as the component-wise product of kOrigin and kInvDirection. Clamp the ray origin p with an epsilon (10^{-3}) to prevent precision issues. Calculate the initial voxel coordinate containing the ray origin. Compute tDelta for each axis: tDeltai = |kInvDirectioni|. Compute tMax for each axis: If Directioni > 0: tMaxi = (Voxeli + 1 - Origini) \times tDeltai. If Directioni < 0: tMaxi = (Origini - Voxeli) \times tDeltai. If Directioni = 0: Set tDeltai = \infty, tMaxi = \infty, and step = 0 to prevent the axis from being selected. 2. Phase 1: Skip Interior Solid Voxels: Check if the current voxel is within the world window using modulo arithmetic for toroidal wrapping. Check if the voxel is solid by computing the brick index, checking the occupancy bit, and excluding MATLEAFFRINGE. If the voxel is solid, advance the ray to the next voxel (see Step 3) and repeat until a non-solid voxel is found or the ray exits the world. 3. Phase 2: Traverse to First Solid Voxel: Loop up to MAXSTEPS: Check if the current voxel is within the world window (toroidal wrap). Check if the voxel is solid. If solid, return the current voxel coordinate as the hit. Find the axis with the minimum tMax. If no valid axis exists (e.g., all tMax are infinite), return None. Advance the ray along the selected axis: Increment the voxel coordinate in that direction by kSignsaxis. Update tMaxaxis by adding tDeltaaxis. If the new voxel is out of bounds (and not toroidally wrapped), return None. 4. Termination: If MAXSTEPS is reached, return None. If the ray exits the world window without hitting a solid voxel, return None. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class TRFRay3: def init(self, origin, direction): # Defensive normalization and validation length = math.sqrt(sum(d2 for d in direction)) if length < 1e-6: return None # Near-zero direction self.origin = origin self.direction = [d / length for d in direction] # Pre-compute constants for DDA self.invdirection = [1.0 / d if abs(d) > 1e-9 else float('inf') for d in self.direction] self.signs = [1 if d > 0 else -1 if d < 0 else 0 for d in self.direction] self.ood = [o inv for o, inv in zip(self.origin, self.invdirection)] # Handle zero-direction components for i in range(3): if self.direction[i] == 0: self.invdirection[i] = float('inf') self.ood[i] = float('inf') self.signs[i] = 0 def raycast(self, worldmin, worldmax, voxelgrid, maxsteps=1000): # Clamp origin to avoid precision issues p = [o + 1e-3 for o in self.origin] # Initial voxel voxel = [int(math.floor(p[i])) for i in range(3)] # Compute tDelta and tMax tdelta = [abs(self.invdirection[i]) for i in range(3)] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if self.direction[i] > 0: tmax[i] = (voxel[i] + 1 - p[i]) tdelta[i] elif self.direction[i] < 0: tmax[i] = (p[i] - voxel[i]) tdelta[i] else: tmax[i] = float('inf') tdelta[i] = float('inf') # Phase 1: Skip solid voxels if camera is inside one while self.issolid(voxel, voxelgrid, worldmin, worldmax): # Advance to next voxel axis = self.getmintmaxaxis(tmax) if axis is None: return None voxel[axis] += self.signs[axis] tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] # Check bounds if not self.isinworld(voxel, worldmin, worldmax): return None # Phase 2: Find first solid voxel for in range(maxsteps): if self.issolid(voxel, voxelgrid, worldmin, worldmax): return voxel axis = self.getmintmaxaxis(tmax) if axis is None: return None voxel[axis] += self.signs[axis] tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] if not self.isinworld(voxel, worldmin, worldmax): return None return None def getmintmaxaxis(self, tmax): mint = float('inf') axis = None for i in range(3): if tmax[i] < mint: mint = tmax[i] axis = i return axis def isinworld(self, voxel, worldmin, worldmax): # Toroidal wrapping check # Assuming world dimensions are known or passed # For simplicity, checking bounds without wrap for this example # In actual implementation, use modulo arithmetic for toroidal wrapping return True # Placeholder for toroidal logic def issolid(self, voxel, voxelgrid, worldmin, worldmax): # Check occupancy bit and exclude MATLEAFFRINGE # Placeholder for actual voxel grid lookup return False The foundational DDA algorithm for voxel traversal. TRFRay3 implements this logic but encapsulates it in a C++ class with pre-computed inverse directions and OOD terms for performance. A variant of DDA designed for gradient-based optimization. TRFRay3 is non-differentiable and intended for standard raycasting/picking. Uses multiple levels of detail for voxel traversal. TRFRay3 operates on a single level of voxel resolution. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels traversed along the ray, bounded by MAXSTEPS. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the ray state, plus O(1) for the voxel grid lookup. Performance: Efficient on CPU due to pre-computed constants and contiguous memory layout for SIMD. Matches GPU traversal behavior exactly. Strengths: Handles toroidal wrapping, zero-direction vectors, and solid voxel skipping efficiently. Limitations: Not differentiable. Requires floating-point precision for inverse direction calculations. When to use: CPU-side picking, shadow raycasting, and any scenario requiring exact parity with GPU voxel traversal. When not to use: Differentiable rendering or hierarchical traversal where SVOs are more appropriate. TRFRay3 originates from the voxelG engine, a hardware ray tracing experimental graphics playground. It was developed to provide a CPU-side raycasting method that matches the toroidal GPU storage layout exactly, ensuring consistency between software and hardware rendering paths. The class structure is inspired by general DDA ray representations in computer graphics, specifically those used in voxel-based games and simulations. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Voxelarchitect day 226, https://github.com/Shubham-cyber-prog/100-Days-Of-Web-Development-ECWoC26/pull/1699, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) itsyouyi/Voxelizer, https://github.com/itsyouyi/Voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable DDA Loop
head: Differentiable DDA
body: A differentiable Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) loop that traverses a grid along a ray, invoking a callback function for each visited cell. It sets itself apart from standard DDA implementations by maintaining differentiability through the traversal state, allowing gradients to flow back through the ray marching steps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray direction rayd2 (normalized or scaled), grid resolution gridres, initial ray origin (implicit in p0), and a callback function func. Outputs: The state returned by the final callback invocation. Data Structures: active: Boolean array indicating which rays are still valid. state: User-defined state object passed to the callback. dtv: Array of step sizes to the next grid line for each active ray. p0: Current position of the ray. pi: Current grid index (integer coordinates). trem: Remaining ray length to traverse. absrcpd2: Precomputed absolute reciprocal of the ray direction components. Numbered Steps: 1. Loop Initialization: Initialize active to all true. Initialize dtv based on ray direction and grid spacing. Initialize p0 to the ray origin. Initialize pi to the starting grid cell. Initialize trem to the total ray length. Initialize state to the user's initial state. 2. Step Selection: Compute the step size for this iteration: dt = \min(\min(dtv), t{rem}) Identify which grid lines are hit at this step: mask = (dtv == dt) 3. Position Update: Compute the new position using the Fused Multiply-Add (FMA) operation: p1 = \text{fma}(ray\d2, dt, p0) 4. Callback Invocation: Invoke the user callback function: state, cont = func(state, \text{ArrayNu}(pi), p0, p1, active \ \& \ (dt > 0)) Note: The callback is only invoked if dt > 0 to handle the edge case where the ray starts exactly on a grid line. 5. Grid Index Update: Update dtv for active rays: dtv[active] = \text{select}(mask, abs\rcp\d2, dtv - dt) Update p0 for active rays: p0[active] = \text{fma}(ray\d2, dt, p0) Reset p0 components for rays that crossed a grid line boundary: p0[mask \ \& \ active] = \text{select}(ray\d2 \ge 0, \text{Float}(0), \text{Float}(1)) Increment pi for rays that crossed a grid line boundary: pi[mask \ \& \ active] += \text{step} Where step is +1 or -1 depending on the direction of rayd2. Update trem for active rays: trem[active] = trem - dt 6. Activity Update: Update the active mask for the next iteration: active[active] \ \&= \ \text{all}((pi \ge 0) \ \& \ (pi < \text{ArrayNi}(grid\res))) \ \& \ (t{rem} > 0) \ \& \ cont A ray becomes inactive if it goes out of bounds, runs out of length, or if the callback returns cont=False. Pitfalls: Starting on a grid line: If the ray starts exactly on a grid line, dt can be 0. The code handles this by checking dt > 0 before invoking the callback. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiableddaloop(rayd2, gridres, func, initialstate, rayorigin, raylength): # Initialization active = True state = initialstate absrcpd2 = abs(1.0 / rayd2) dtv = computeinitialdtv(rayorigin, rayd2, absrcpd2) # Implementation detail p0 = rayorigin pi = computeinitialgridindex(rayorigin, rayd2) # Implementation detail trem = raylength while active: # Step Selection dt = min(min(dtv), trem) mask = (dtv == dt) # Position Update p1 = fma(rayd2, dt, p0) # Callback Invocation # Only invoke if dt > 0 to handle starting on grid line if dt > 0: state, cont = func(state, pi, p0, p1, active) else: cont = True # Assume continue if no step taken # Grid Index Update dtv = select(mask, absrcpd2, dtv - dt) p0 = fma(rayd2, dt, p0) p0 = select(mask & active, rayd2 >= 0, 0.0, 1.0) pi = pi + step (mask & active) # step is +1 or -1 based on rayd2 sign trem = trem - dt # Activity Update outofbounds = (pi < 0) | (pi >= gridres) active = active & ~outofbounds & (trem > 0) & cont return state Time Complexity: Linear in the number of grid cells visited by the ray. Memory Complexity: Constant per ray, proportional to the grid resolution for storing dtv, p0, pi, trem. Strengths: Differentiable, allowing gradients to be computed with respect to ray parameters or grid properties. Limitations: Requires careful handling of edge cases like starting on grid lines. Performance may be impacted by the overhead of differentiable operations. When to use: When gradients through the ray traversal are needed, e.g., in differentiable rendering or optimization. When not to use: When performance is critical and differentiability is not required; standard DDA is likely faster. The Differentiable DDA Loop is presented in the context of differentiable ray tracing, specifically within the differentiablexrt repository. It builds on the principles of the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal [2323-dda.md] but extends it to support gradient computation. name: Multi-level DDA with Adaptive Mip Selection
head: DDA-based volume sampling routine, Multi-level traversal scheme
body: This method is a ray traversal and sampling algorithm for volume rendering that combines Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) stepping with adaptive mip-level selection to optimize the trade-off between step size and sampling accuracy. It solves the problem of inefficient traversal in sparse or heterogeneous volumes by using a majorant texture at multiple resolutions to skip empty space, while dynamically adjusting the granularity of the search to locate collision points precisely. It sets itself apart from standard DDA approaches by avoiding execution divergence on GPUs through a branchless, iterative mip-level adjustment heuristic, and from pure delta tracking by providing deterministic spatial bounds for step sizes. The algorithm performs a stochastic distance sampling loop using a majorant density texture. It maintains a target optical thickness (tauToGo) and steps through the volume using a DDA that intersects against "dilated" brick boundaries. The core innovation is the dynamic selection of the mip level for the majorant lookup at every step, allowing the algorithm to start coarse (large steps) and refine (smaller steps) based on proximity to a potential collision, without using conditional branches that would cause divergence on SIMT hardware. Inputs: rayOrigin: The starting position of the ray. rayDir: The direction of the ray (assumed normalized or handled via inverse direction). majorantTexture: A multi-mipmap texture storing the maximum density (majorant) for bricks. The source uses 4 mip levels (0 to 3). densityTexture: The high-resolution density texture used for final sampling. random(): A function returning a uniform random number in [0, 1). Outputs: The algorithm returns the result of the collision handling (e.g., color contribution, new path vertex) or continues the path if a null collision occurs. Majorant Texture: A 3D texture array or volume texture organized into mip levels. The source specifies a brick size of 8 \times 2^{\text{mip}} voxels. The texture stores the majorant density value for each brick. DDA State: t: Current distance along the ray. tauToGo: Remaining optical thickness to accumulate before a collision. mip: Current floating-point mip level index (range [0.0, 3.0]). Target Optical Thickness: \tau{\text{target}} = -\ln(1 - r) where r is a uniform random number. This defines the distance to the next interaction in optical space. Brick Dimension: \text{dim} = 8 \ll \text{mip} where \text{mip} is the integer part of the current mip level. The base brick size is 8 voxels. DDA Step Distance (nextt): The distance to the next brick boundary intersection, calculated using dilated boundaries. \text{ofs} = \mathbf{ri} \odot \left( \left( \mathbf{ri} \ge 0 \right) ? (\text{dim} + 0.5): (-0.5) - \mathbf{ro} \right) \mathbf{tmax} = \lfloor \mathbf{pos} \odot (1.0 / \text{dim}) \rfloor \odot \text{dim} \odot \mathbf{ri} + \text{ofs} \text{nextt} = \min(\mathbf{tmax}x, \min(\mathbf{tmax}y, \mathbf{tmax}z)) Where: \mathbf{ri} = 1.0 / \mathbf{rayDir} (inverse ray direction). \mathbf{ro} is the ray origin offset relative to the brick grid (often 0 or derived from rayOrigin). \mathbf{pos} is the current ray position. \odot denotes component-wise multiplication. Optical Thickness Traversed: \Delta \tau = \rho{\text{majorant}} \cdot \Delta t where \rho{\text{majorant}} is the sampled majorant density and \Delta t = \text{nextt} - t.
