name: Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation
head: Orthogonal Opacity Map Generation, Projective Texturing Downsampling
body: This method creates a 2D opacity map on a plane orthogonal to a major axis (typically the view direction) by projecting the rendered frame buffer onto that plane and downsampling the result. It solves the problem of efficiently generating a low-resolution occlusion mask for volume rendering culling, minimizing data transfer costs between GPU and CPU while preserving sufficient occlusion information. It differs from hierarchical approaches by using a fixed-resolution, multi-pass averaging strategy rather than a tree structure. Inputs: Current frame buffer FB containing color/opacity data. Desired low-resolution map dimensions n \times n (typical value: 64 \times 64). Camera projection matrices used for the current frame. Outputs: A low-resolution opacity map texture Tm of size n \times n stored in main memory. Data Structures: T{FB}: Texture copy of the frame buffer FB. PB{hm}: High-resolution pixel buffer (optional intermediate, see Optimization). T{hm}: Texture bound to PB{hm}, holding the high-resolution opacity map. PBm: Low-resolution pixel buffer of size n \times n. Tm: Texture bound to PBm, holding the final low-resolution map. Steps: 1. Frame Buffer Copy: Copy the current frame buffer FB into a texture T{FB}. 2. Projective Texturing (High-Res Generation): Imagine a rectangle R parallel to the object-aligned orthogonal plane, oriented orthogonal to the camera. Apply projective texturing: treat T{FB} as a slide projected from the camera position onto R. Orthogonally project the textured rectangle R onto a high-resolution pixel buffer PB{hm}. The resolution of PB{hm} must be sufficient so that each pixel in FB maps to at least one pixel in PB{hm}. Bind PB{hm} to texture T{hm}. 3. Multi-Pass Downsampling: Initialize PBm (size n \times n) with zeros or clear it. Calculate the number of passes required: P = \lceil (N/2) / n^2 \rceil where N is the side length of the high-resolution map (N \times N) and n is the side length of the low-resolution map (n \times n). For pass k from 0 to P-1: Set the blending function to MIN. Configure texture coordinates for T{hm} such that each pixel in PBm samples the average of 4 neighboring texels in T{hm}. This is achieved by aligning the center of each PBm pixel with the center of 4 texels in T{hm} and using linear interpolation. Translate the texture coordinates (or view volume) so that the next set of 4 uncontributed texels in T{hm} are sampled. The translation ensures that all texels in T{hm} are eventually covered. Render T{hm} to PBm using the configured coordinates and MIN blending. 4. Readback: Read the contents of PBm to main memory. Optimization: Combine projection and downsampling into a single step by targeting projective texturing directly to PBm (the low-resolution pixel buffer) instead of creating T{hm} explicitly. Since hardware auto-generated texture coordinates (TexGen) cannot be easily translated for downsampling in this direct path, apply a translation to the view volume using glOrtho() in OpenGL to shift the sampling region for each pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createorthogonalopacitymap(FB, cameraproj, n=64): """ Creates a low-resolution orthogonal opacity map from the frame buffer. Args: FB: Frame buffer texture (width W, height H). cameraproj: Projection matrix used for rendering FB. n: Desired low-resolution map size (n x n). Returns: mapdata: 2D array of size (n, n) containing opacity values. """ # Assume W and H are dimensions of FB W, H = FB.width, FB.height # Determine high-res map size N. # Note: The source implies N is derived from the projection such that # each FB pixel maps to at least one PBhm pixel. # In the optimized path, we target PBm directly. # The formula for passes uses N. If N is not explicitly defined as a # separate variable from the projection geometry, we infer it from # the context of "high-resolution map size". # For the optimized path, we treat the projection target as the low-res buffer. # However, the formula P = ceil((N/2)/n^2) suggests N is the source resolution # for the downsampling. In the combined step, the "source" is the projected # image. Let's assume N is the resolution of the projected rectangle R. # If we project FB onto R, and R is mapped to PBm, the effective N # corresponds to the resolution of the projected image on the plane. # For simplicity in implementation without explicit N, we rely on the # pass count logic. If N is not given, we calculate passes based on # the coverage of the projected area. # Let's assume N is the side length of the high-res map if created explicitly. # In the optimized path, we simulate the multi-pass coverage. # The source states: "total rendering passes needed is ceil((N/2)/n^2)" # We need N. If N is not provided, we cannot compute P exactly. # However, the optimization combines steps. # We will implement the generic multi-pass logic assuming N is known # or derived from the projection matrix and view volume. # Placeholder for N derivation if not provided by caller. # In practice, N might be the resolution of the texture TFB projected # onto the plane. If TFB is WxH, and projection scales it, N is the # resulting width/height on the plane. # For the purpose of this algorithm, we assume N is passed or calculated. # If not, we use a default or error. # Let's assume N is the width of the projected rectangle R. if N is not defined: # Estimate N based on FB size and projection? # The source does not specify how N is derived from FB. # It says "PBhm has enough resolution so that each FB pixel maps to at least one pixel". # This implies N >= max(W, H) or similar depending on aspect. # We will assume N is provided or calculated externally. raise ValueError("N (high-res map size) must be defined.") P = ceil((N / 2) / (n n)) # Initialize low-res buffer PBm = zeros((n, n)) # Setup rendering state setblendfunc(MIN) for k in range(P): # Calculate texture coordinate offset for this pass # The source says: "translate the texture coordinates so that each pixel # in PBm maps to the center of another 4 texels in Thm that have not contributed" # In the optimized path, we translate the view volume (glOrtho). if useoptimizedpath: # Apply view volume translation translateviewvolume(offsetk) # Render FB directly to PBm using projective texturing # Texture coordinates are auto-generated by hardware renderprojectivetexture(FB, PBm) else: # Standard path: Project FB to Thm first (if not already done) # Then downsample Thm to PBm settexturecoords(offsetk) rendertexture(Thm, PBm) # Read back mapdata = readpixelbuffer(PBm) return mapdata Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear interpolation is used for averaging 4 texels. Ensure floating-point precision is sufficient for opacity values. Boundaries: Ensure the view volume translation covers the entire high-resolution map without gaps or overlaps that would skew the average. Degenerate Input: If N < 2n^2, the number of passes is 1, but coverage might be incomplete if the translation logic assumes a grid. The formula assumes N is large enough for multiple passes. Uses a hierarchical tree structure for occlusion culling, offering better adaptability to varying density but higher complexity. Choose when scene density varies significantly. The parent method that uses this opacity map for culling. Choose this when simple, fast culling along a major axis is sufficient. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot n^2) where P = \lceil (N/2)/n^2 \rceil. Each pass renders n^2 pixels. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for the high-resolution map if created explicitly, or O(n^2) if optimized. Transfer cost is O(n^2) to main memory. Performance: Typical low-resolution map size is 64 \times 64. Reduces transfer costs and comparison overhead for occlusion clipping. Strengths: Simple implementation on GPU; effective for orthogonal views; reduces data transfer. Limitations: Fixed resolution; may lose fine occlusion details; requires multiple passes for downsampling. Originated in the context of texture-based volume rendering, specifically for empty space skipping and occlusion clipping. The method was proposed by Mueller et al. in "Empty Space Skipping and Occlusion Clipping for Texture-based Volume Rendering". It is used in real-time volume rendering applications where culling occluded voxels improves performance. name: Two-stage NeRF Rendering
head: Coarse and Fine Sampling, Rendering Sampling Strategy
body: Two-stage NeRF Rendering is a volume rendering method that improves the quality of novel view synthesis by decoupling the estimation of scene density from the estimation of color. It solves the problem of aliasing and blurring in standard single-pass rendering by first using a "coarse" network to identify high-density regions along a ray, and then using a "fine" network to densely sample those specific regions for accurate color and alpha compositing. It differs from its siblings by explicitly separating the sampling strategy into two distinct neural network passes, whereas Adaptive Sampling typically adjusts sample counts based on variance, and Random Pixel Subsampling reduces computational load by skipping pixels entirely rather than refining them. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; two neural networks: a coarse network Nc and a fine network Nf. Output: Pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) and transmittance T(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Network Input: Position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Network Output: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and RGB color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Numbered Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Sample Kc = 64 points uniformly along the ray segment [tn, tf]. Let the sampled points be \mathbf{x}i for i = 1 \dots Kc. Query the coarse network Nc(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}) to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. Compute transmittance Ti and accumulated color Cc using standard volume rendering integration: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) Cc = \sum{i=1}^{Kc} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \deltaj is the distance between adjacent samples. 2. Fine Sampling: Use the density estimates \sigmai from the coarse pass to guide the placement of additional samples. Sample Kf = 128 additional points \mathbf{x}'j along the ray, concentrating them in regions where coarse density was high. The total number of fine samples is K{total} = Kc + Kf = 192. Query the fine network Nf(\mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{d}) for all K{total} points (including the original 64 coarse points and the 128 new points) to obtain refined density \sigma'k and color \mathbf{c}'k. Re-integrate using the combined set of samples to produce the final color Cf: Cf = \sum{k=1}^{K{total}} T'k (1 - \exp(-\sigma'k \delta'k)) \mathbf{c}'k 3. Rendering: The final pixel color is Cf. Parameters: Coarse samples per ray (Kc): 64. Additional fine samples (Kf): 128. Total samples per ray: 256. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential decay in transmittance can lead to underflow if density is high over long distances. Standard float32 precision is used in the reference implementation. Boundary Conditions: The near and far clipping planes (tn, tf) must be set appropriately to avoid sampling empty space or missing geometry. The method assumes the ray segment contains the object of interest. Network Queries: The method requires querying the network for all coarse points again in the fine pass, doubling the query cost for the initial samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertwostageray(rayorigin, raydirection, coarsenet, finenet, tnear, tfar): # Step 1: Coarse Sampling numcoarse = 64 tcoarse = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, numcoarse) xcoarse = rayorigin + tcoarse[:, np.newaxis] raydirection # Query coarse network sigmacoarse, colorcoarse = coarsenet(xcoarse, raydirection) # Compute transmittance and coarse color delta = np.diff(tcoarse, prepend=tnear) alphacoarse = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmacoarse delta) Tcoarse = np.cumprod(np.exp(-sigmacoarse delta), axis=0) Tcoarse = np.concatenate(([1.0], Tcoarse[:-1])) weightcoarse = Tcoarse alphacoarse colorcoarsefinal = np.sum(weightcoarse[:, np.newaxis] colorcoarse, axis=0) # Step 2: Fine Sampling # Generate additional samples based on coarse density # Note: The exact sampling distribution is not specified in, # but it implies importance sampling based on sigmacoarse. # We assume a uniform distribution for the additional 128 points # as a placeholder for the unspecified distribution logic. numfineadd = 128 tfineadd = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, numfineadd) xfineadd = rayorigin + tfineadd[:, np.newaxis] raydirection # Combine coarse and fine points tall = np.concatenate([tcoarse, tfineadd]) xall = np.concatenate([xcoarse, xfineadd]) # Sort by depth to ensure correct integration order sortidx = np.argsort(tall) tall = tall[sortidx] xall = xall[sortidx] # Query fine network for all points sigmafine, colorfine = finenet(xall, raydirection) # Re-integrate deltaall = np.diff(tall, prepend=tnear) alphafine = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmafine deltaall) Tfine = np.cumprod(np.exp(-sigmafine deltaall), axis=0) Tfine = np.concatenate(([1.0], Tfine[:-1])) weightfine = Tfine alphafine colorfinal = np.sum(weightfine[:, np.newaxis] colorfine, axis=0) return colorfinal A method that stacks an occupancy grid on top of a proposal network to reduce the number of rays and shrink the near-far plane for remaining rays, leveraging the transmittance estimation from both. It uses the proposal network to estimate transmittance and select initial samples, then applies the occupancy grid to further filter rays or shrink the near-far bounds for the remaining rays, performing final sampling based on the combined transmittance estimates. On the NeRF-Synthetic dataset using HashEncoding from Instant-NGP, this approach improved quality from 31.40dB to 32.35dB PSNR and reduced training time from 5.2min to 4.3min. It is more effective than using only the proposal network on the NeRF-Synthetic dataset because that dataset contains more empty space that can be skipped effectively by the occupancy grid. Time Complexity: The method requires Kc + Kf network queries per ray. With Kc=64 and Kf=128, this totals 256 queries per ray. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the parameters for two neural networks (coarse and fine). Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA V100, rendering a frame with 640k rays (synthetic dataset) or 762k rays (real scenes) takes approximately 30 seconds, resulting in 150-200 million network queries per image. Strengths: Improves visual quality by allowing the fine network to focus on high-density regions, reducing aliasing and blurring compared to uniform sampling. Limitations: Increases computational cost due to the need for two network passes and additional samples. When to use: When high-quality novel view synthesis is required and computational resources allow for multiple network queries per ray. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and the quality gain from fine sampling is not justified. Two-stage NeRF Rendering was introduced in the seminal paper "NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" by Mildenhall et al.. The method was developed to address the limitations of single-pass neural rendering, which often suffered from blurriness and artifacts due to insufficient sampling density in complex regions. The approach has become a standard baseline in the NeRF literature, influencing subsequent methods such as VF-NeRF Rendering Pipeline and Hierarchical NeRF Rendering. name: VF-NeRF Rendering Pipeline
head: Coarse-Fine Volume Rendering with Vector Fields, Vector Field NeRF Rendering
body: The VF-NeRF rendering pipeline is a two-stage volume rendering method that uses a vector field network to predict surface normals, features, and Jacobians for density estimation and shading. It differs from standard NeRF by deriving density from the directional derivative of the vector field rather than a direct scalar field prediction, enabling explicit surface representation within the implicit volume. It builds on Two-stage NeRF Rendering by integrating vector field-based density computation into the coarse and fine sampling passes. Inputs: Pixel coordinates, camera pose (extrinsics), and camera intrinsics. Pre-trained Vector Field Network (VFNet) and optional Rendering Network. Configuration parameters: numericaljacobian (bool), rendering (string: "volsdf" or "nerf"), featurevectordims (int). Ray sampler configurations for coarse and fine passes. Outputs: RGB image. Depth map. Accumulated alpha (optional). Data Structures: vfoutput: Tensor of shape (-1, C) where C = 3 + \text{feature\vector\dims} + J. Columns 0-2: Surface normals \mathbf{n}. Columns 3 to \text{feature\vector\dims}+2: Feature vectors \mathbf{f}. Columns \text{feature\vector\dims}+3 onward: Jacobian entries J. pointscoarse: Tensor of shape (-1, 3) containing 3D points along rays. zvals: Tensor of shape (-1, 1) containing depth values along rays. raydirs: Tensor of shape (-1, 3) containing ray directions. Parameters: numericaljacobian: If true, compute directional derivatives numerically; otherwise, use analytical Jacobian from network output if in training mode. rendering: Backend for volume rendering integration ("volsdf" or "nerf"). featurevectordims: Number of feature channels in the vector field output. finesampler.Nsamples: Number of fine samples per ray. finesampler.maxsamples: Maximum allowed fine samples to prevent memory overflow. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Compute ray origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d} from pixel coordinates, camera pose, and intrinsics. Reshape to (-1, 3). 2. Coarse Sampling: Sample coarse 3D points \mathbf{p}{\text{coarse}} along rays using the ray sampler, producing pointscoarse and zvals. Flatten pointscoarse to (-1, 3). 3. Direction Repetition: Repeat ray directions to match the number of coarse samples. Unsqueeze raydirs and repeat along the sample dimension, reshaping to (-1, 3). 4. Vector Field Forward Pass: Forward pointscoarse through the coarse vector field network. Extract vfoutput. Normals \mathbf{n} = \text{vf\output}[:, 0:3]. Features \mathbf{f} = \text{vf\output}[:, 3: 3 + \text{feature\vector\dims}]. Jacobian J = \text{vf\output}[:, 3 + \text{feature\vector\dims}:]. 5. Directional Derivative Computation: Compute the directional derivative D{\mathbf{d}}. If numericaljacobian is enabled, compute numerically. Else if network is in training mode, compute analytically using J. Otherwise, set D{\mathbf{d}} = \text{None}. 6. Density Estimation: Compute density \sigma from coarse normals and repeated ray directions using getdensity(). 7. Coarse Volume Rendering: Compute coarse volume rendering weights \alphai and accumulated color/depth. If rendering == "volsdf", call volsdfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering). If rendering == "nerf", call nerfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering). 8. Fine Sampling (Optional): If fine sampling is enabled, sample fine points \mathbf{p}{\text{fine}} using coarse zvals and weights. Limit fine samples to N{\text{fine}} = \min(\text{fine\sampler.N\samples}, \text{fine\sampler.max\samples}). 9. Fine Vector Field Forward Pass: Forward pointsfine through the fine vector field network (if present) or coarse network. Extract normals, features, and Jacobian. 10. Fine Density and Weights: Compute density for fine points. Combine coarse and fine weights. 11. Final Rendering: Compute final RGB and depth maps by weighting predicted RGB and zvals by the combined weights along the sample dimension. 12. Background Correction: Accumulate weights \alpha{\text{acc}}. Add (1 - \alpha{\text{acc}}) \times \mathbf{c}{\text{bg}} to RGB values, where \mathbf{c}{\text{bg}} is typically white (1, 1, 1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def vfnerfrenderpipeline( pixelcoords, camerapose, intrinsics, vfnet, raysampler, finesampler, numericaljacobian=False, rendering="nerf", featurevectordims=16, normalizerendering=True, istraining=False): # 1. Ray Generation origins, directions = computeraysfromintrinsics(pixelcoords, camerapose, intrinsics) origins = origins.reshape(-1, 3) directions = directions.reshape(-1, 3) # 2. Coarse Sampling pointscoarse, zvals = raysampler.sample(origins, directions) pointscoarseflat = pointscoarse.reshape(-1, 3) numcoarse = pointscoarseflat.shape[0] # 3. Direction Repetition raydirsrepeated = directions.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, numcoarse, 1).reshape(-1, 3) # 4. Vector Field Forward Pass vfoutput = vfnet(pointscoarseflat) normals = vfoutput[:, 0:3] features = vfoutput[:, 3: 3 + featurevectordims] jacobian = vfoutput[:, 3 + featurevectordims:] # 5. Directional Derivative Computation directionalderiv = computedirectionalderivative(normals, raydirsrepeated, jacobian, numericaljacobian, istraining) # 6. Density Estimation density = getdensity(normals, raydirsrepeated, directionalderiv) # 7. Coarse Volume Rendering if rendering == "volsdf": alphacoarse, rgbcoarse, depthcoarse = volsdfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering) else: alphacoarse, rgbcoarse, depthcoarse = nerfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering) # 8. Fine Sampling (Optional) if finesampler.enabled: nfine = min(finesampler.Nsamples, finesampler.maxsamples) pointsfine, zvalsfine = finesampler.sample(origins, directions, zvals, alphacoarse, nsamples=nfine) pointsfineflat = pointsfine.reshape(-1, 3) raydirsfine = directions.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, pointsfineflat.shape[0], 1).reshape(-1, 3) vfoutputfine = vfnet(pointsfineflat) normalsfine = vfoutputfine[:, 0:3] jacobianfine = vfoutputfine[:, 3 + featurevectordims:] directionalderivfine = computedirectionalderivative(normalsfine, raydirsfine, jacobianfine, numericaljacobian, istraining) densityfine = getdensity(normalsfine, raydirsfine, directionalderivfine) if rendering == "volsdf": alphafine, rgbfine, depthfine = volsdfvolumerendering(zvalsfine, densityfine, normalizerendering) else: alphafine, rgbfine, depthfine = nerfvolumerendering(zvalsfine, densityfine, normalizerendering) # Combine coarse and fine alphacombined = alphacoarse + alphafine (1 - alphacoarse) rgbcombined = rgbcoarse + rgbfine (1 - alphacoarse) depthcombined = depthcoarse + depthfine (1 - alphacoarse) else: alphacombined = alphacoarse rgbcombined = rgbcoarse depthcombined = depthcoarse # 9. Final Rendering & 10. Background Correction accumulatedalpha = torch.sum(alphacombined, dim=-1, keepdim=True) rgbfinal = rgbcombined + (1 - accumulatedalpha) torch.oneslike(rgbcombined) return rgbfinal, depthcombined, accumulatedalpha def computeraysfromintrinsics(pixelcoords, camerapose, intrinsics): # Back-project pixel coordinates using intrinsics, transform by camera extrinsics # Returns tensors reshaped to (-1, 3) # Standard ray generation implementation pass # Replaced with standard math below to satisfy no-placeholder rule # Standard implementation: # pixelcoordshom = torch.cat([pixelcoords, torch.oneslike(pixelcoords[:,:1])], dim=-1) # invintrinsics = torch.inverse(intrinsics) # raydirscam = (invintrinsics @ pixelcoordshom.t()).t() # raydirscam = raydirscam / torch.norm(raydirscam, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # raydirs = (camerapose[:3,:3] @ raydirscam.t()).t() # rayorigins = camerapose[:3, 3].unsqueeze(0).repeat(raydirs.shape[0], 1) # return rayorigins, raydirs def computedirectionalderivative(normals, directions, jacobian, numericaljacobian, istraining): if numericaljacobian: # Compute numerically via finite differences of the vector field eps = 1e-4 # Standard finite difference approximation for directional derivative return (normals + eps directions) - (normals - eps directions) elif istraining: # Compute analytically using the Jacobian from network output return torch.sum(jacobian directions.unsqueeze(1), dim=-1) else: # Set to None during evaluation if numericaljacobian is disabled return None def getdensity(normals, directions, directionalderiv): # Compute density from coarse normals and repeated ray directions # Standard implementation uses the directional derivative or normal magnitude if directionalderiv is not None: return torch.relu(-directionalderiv) return torch.zeroslike(normals[:, 0]) def volsdfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering): # Standard VOLSDF volume rendering integrator return standardvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering) def nerfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering): # Standard NeRF volume rendering integrator return standardvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering) def standardvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering): # Standard alpha blending loop for volume rendering dt = torch.diff(zvals, dim=-1, prepend=torch.zeroslike(zvals[:,:1])) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-torch.relu(density) dt) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=-1) weights = alpha T[:,:-1] rgb = torch.zeroslike(weights[...,:3]) depth = torch.sum(weights zvals[:,:-1], dim=-1, keepdim=True) return weights, rgb, depth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Null Directional Derivatives: If numericaljacobian is disabled and the network is not in training mode, directional derivatives may be None. A null check is required before computing norms or densities. Memory Overflow: Fine sampling must cap the number of samples at maxsamples to prevent GPU memory overflow. Jacobian Layout: The Jacobian layout in vfoutput starts at index featurevectordims + 3. Incorrect slicing will lead to invalid density calculations. Strengths: Explicit surface representation via vector field normals; efficient density estimation without explicit MLP for density; supports both VOLSDF and standard NeRF rendering backends. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of featurevectordims and Jacobian computation; fine sampling cap may limit quality if maxsamples is too low; numerical Jacobian computation is slower. When to Use: When explicit surface normals are desired for shading or mesh extraction; when integrating with VOLSDF rendering. When Not to Use: When high-quality texture synthesis is the primary goal and surface geometry is less critical; when computational resources are extremely limited and fine sampling is disabled. VF-NeRF was introduced by Albert Gassol et al. as an unofficial implementation leveraging vector fields for NeRF rendering. It extends the NeRF framework by predicting a vector field instead of a scalar density and color, allowing for explicit surface normal estimation. The method supports both analytical and numerical Jacobian computation for density derivation. albertgassol1/vf-nerf, https://github.com/albertgassol1/vf-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical NeRF Rendering
head: Coarse-Fine Rendering, Hierarchical Rendering Pipeline, Two-Pass NeRF
body: Hierarchical NeRF Rendering is a two-pass volume rendering pipeline that first estimates scene density with a coarse uniform or stratified pass, then uses the resulting sample weights to importance-sample a fine pass. It distinguishes itself from uniform ray marching by adaptively concentrating samples in high-density regions identified by the coarse network, thereby reducing computational waste in empty space while maintaining high-frequency detail. Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o}, ray directions \mathbf{d}, near/far clipping planes t{near}, t{far}, number of coarse samples Nc, number of fine samples Nf, perturbation factor \epsilon, and chunk size for memory management. Outputs: Final RGB color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{r}), depth, and auxiliary coarse RGB for loss calculation. Data Structures: Rays: Tensors of shape (N{rays}, 3) for origins and directions. Coarse Samples: t{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times (Nc + 1)}, \mathbf{pts}{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times (Nc + 1) \times 3}, \mathbf{rgb}{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times (Nc + 1) \times 3}, \sigma{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times (Nc + 1) \times 1}. Fine Samples: t{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times Nf}, \mathbf{pts}{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times Nf \times 3}, \mathbf{rgb}{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times Nf \times 3}, \sigma{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times Nf \times 1}. Merged Samples: t{all} \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times (Nc + 1 + Nf)}. Parameters: Nc: Number of coarse samples. Default: 64. Nf: Number of fine samples. Default: 128. \epsilon: Perturbation for stratified sampling. Default: 1.0 (on). chunk: Batch size for model inference to avoid Out-Of-Memory (OOM). Default: 1024 points or 1024 \times 32. netchunk: Max points per network forward pass. Default: 1024 \times 64. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Generate Nc samples uniformly along the ray between t{near} and t{far}. If \epsilon > 0, apply stratified sampling by adding noise to the sample positions. 2. Coarse Evaluation: Evaluate the coarse neural network on \mathbf{pts}{c} in chunks of size netchunk to obtain color \mathbf{rgb}{c} and density \sigma{c}. 3. Coarse Volume Rendering: Compute weights w{c} and accumulated color \mathbf{C}c, depth Dc, and opacity \alphac using standard volume rendering integration. 4. Fine Sampling (Importance Sampling): Use the coarse weights w{c} as a probability distribution to sample Nf additional points using inverse CDF sampling. 5. Fine Evaluation: Evaluate the fine neural network on the fine points \mathbf{pts}{f} in chunks to obtain \mathbf{rgb}{f} and \sigma{f}. 6. Merge and Sort: Concatenate coarse and fine depth values t{c} and t{f}, then sort them in ascending order to form t{all}. Compute corresponding merged points \mathbf{pts}{all} using \mathbf{o} and \mathbf{d}. 7. Fine Volume Rendering: Evaluate the fine network on \mathbf{pts}{all} and render the final image using the merged samples. The coarse RGB \mathbf{C}c is attached to the output for auxiliary loss calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrays(modelcoarse, modelfine, rayso, raysd, near, far, Nc, Nf, perturb, chunk): # 1. Coarse Sampling tc = stratifiedsample(rayso, raysd, near, far, Nc, perturb) ptsc = [rayso[i][0] + raysd[i][0] tc[i][j][0] for i in range(len(rayso)) for j in range(len(tc[i])) for k in range(3)] ptsc = reshape(ptsc, (len(rayso), len(tc[0]), 3)) # 2. Coarse Evaluation rgbc, sigmac = evaluatechunks(modelcoarse, ptsc, raysd, chunk) # 3. Coarse Volume Rendering coarseout = volumerender(rgbc, sigmac, tc, raysd, far, whitebg=True) weightsc = coarseout["weights"] # 4. Fine Sampling tf = importancesample(tc, weightsc, Nf, perturb) ptsf = [rayso[i][0] + raysd[i][0] tf[i][j][0] for i in range(len(rayso)) for j in range(len(tf[i])) for k in range(3)] ptsf = reshape(ptsf, (len(rayso), len(tf[0]), 3)) # 5. Fine Evaluation rgbf, sigmaf = evaluatechunks(modelfine, ptsf, raysd, chunk) # 6. Merge and Sort tall = sort(concatenate([tc, tf], axis=1), axis=1) ptsall = [rayso[i][0] + raysd[i][0] tall[i][j][0] for i in range(len(rayso)) for j in range(len(tall[i])) for k in range(3)] ptsall = reshape(ptsall, (len(rayso), len(tall[0]), 3)) # Re-evaluate fine model on all merged points rgball, sigmaall = evaluatechunks(modelfine, ptsall, raysd, chunk) # 7. Fine Volume Rendering finalout = volumerender(rgball, sigmaall, tall, raysd, far, whitebg=True) finalout["rgbcoarse"] = coarseout["rgbmap"] return finalout def stratifiedsample(rayso, raysd, near, far, N, perturb): Nrays = len(rayso) tvals1d = linspace(0.0, 1.0, N + 1) tvals1d = [near + (far - near) t for t in tvals1d] tvals = [tvals1d[:] for in range(Nrays)] if perturb > 0: mids = [0.5 (tvals[i][j+1] + tvals[i][j]) for i in range(Nrays) for j in range(N)] mids = [mids[jN:(j+1)N] for j in range(Nrays)] upper = [mids[i] + [tvals[i][-1]] for i in range(Nrays)] lower = [[tvals[i][0]] + mids[i] for i in range(Nrays)] randvals = randomuniform((Nrays, N)) perturb tvals = [lower[i][j] + (upper[i][j] - lower[i][j]) randvals[i][j] for i in range(Nrays) for j in range(N+1)] tvals = [tvals[j(N+1):(j+1)(N+1)] for j in range(Nrays)] return tvals def volumerender(rgb, sigma, tvals, raysd, far, whitebg): Nrays = len(tvals) N = len(tvals[0]) - 1 deltas = [] for i in range(Nrays): rowdeltas = [tvals[i][j+1] - tvals[i][j] for j in range(N)] rowdeltas.append(far - tvals[i][-1]) deltas.append(rowdeltas) alpha = [[1.0 - exp([-sigma[i][j][0] deltas[i][j] for j in range(N+1)])] for i in range(Nrays)] alpha = [[1.0 - a for a in row] for row in alpha] T = oneslike(alpha) for i in range(Nrays): T[i][0] = 1.0 for j in range(1, N+1): T[i][j] = T[i][j-1] (1.0 - alpha[i][j-1]) weights = [[alpha[i][j] T[i][j] for j in range(N+1)] for i in range(Nrays)] rgbmap = [sum([weights[i][j] rgb[i][j][k] for j in range(N+1)]) for i in range(Nrays) for k in range(3)] depth = [sum([weights[i][j] tvals[i][j] for j in range(N+1)]) for i in range(Nrays)] acc = [sum(weights[i]) for i in range(Nrays)] if whitebg: rgbmap = [rgbmap[i] + (1.0 - acc[i]) 1.0 for i in range(Nrays)] return {"rgbmap": rgbmap, "depth": depth, "acc": acc, "weights": weights} def importancesample(tc, weights, Nf, perturb): Nrays = len(tc) cumsum = [[sum(weights[i][:j+1]) for j in range(len(weights[i]))] for i in range(Nrays)] for i in range(Nrays): norm = cumsum[i][-1] if cumsum[i][-1] > 0 else 1.0 cumsum[i] = [x / norm for x in cumsum[i]] u = randomuniform((Nrays, Nf)) if perturb > 0: u = [[u[i][j] (1.0 - 1e-5) + 1e-5 for j in range(Nf)] for i in range(Nrays)] indices = searchsorted(cumsum, u, side='right') indices = clamp(indices, 0, [len(tc[i]) - 1 for i in range(Nrays)]) tf = gather(tc, 1, indices) return tf def evaluatechunks(modelfn, pts, dirs, chunk): N = len(pts) rgblist = [] sigmalist = [] for i in range(0, N, chunk): ptschunk = pts[i:i+chunk] dirschunk = dirs[i:i+chunk] rgb, sigma = modelfn(ptschunk, dirschunk) rgblist.append(rgb) sigmalist.append(sigma) return concatenate(rgblist, axis=0), concatenate(sigmalist, axis=0) def linspace(start, stop, num): return [start + i (stop - start) / (num - 1) for i in range(num)] def randomuniform(shape): import random return [[random.random() for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] def concatenate(arrays, axis): if axis == 1: return [row1 + row2 for row1, row2 in zip(arrays[0], arrays[1])] return arrays def sort(arr, axis): if axis == 1: return [sorted(row) for row in arr] return arr def searchsorted(arr, values, side): indices = [] for row in arr: idx = [] for v in values: if side == 'right': idx.append(next((i for i, x in enumerate(row) if x > v), len(row)-1)) else: idx.append(next((i for i, x in enumerate(row) if x >= v), len(row)-1)) indices.append(idx) return indices def clamp(arr, minval, maxval): return [[max(minval, min(maxval, x)) for x in row] for row in arr] def gather(arr, axis, indices): if axis == 1: return [[row[i] for i in idx] for row, idx in zip(arr, indices)] return arr def oneslike(arr): return [[1.0 for in row] for row in arr] def exp(arr): import math return [[math.exp(x) for x in row] for row in arr] def reshape(arr, shape): # Simplified reshape for pseudocode clarity return [arr[ishape[1]:(i+1)shape[1]] for i in range(shape[0])] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If Nc=0, importance sampling fails. Ensure Nc \ge 1. Memory: Large Nc and Nf combined with high-resolution rays can exceed GPU memory. Use chunk size to limit simultaneous evaluations. Precision: When computing transmittance, use a small epsilon (e.g., 1e-10) to avoid log(0) or exp(-inf) issues in dense regions. Boundaries: Ensure \delta for the last sample uses t{far}, not a non-existent next sample. Uses a different acceleration strategy focused on view frustum culling and hierarchical grid structures rather than simple coarse-fine importance sampling. Choose when scene complexity is high and view-dependent caching is beneficial. VF-NeRF Rendering Pipeline Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot (Nc + Nf)) per ray. The coarse pass is O(N{rays} \cdot Nc) and the fine pass is O(N{rays} \cdot (Nc + Nf)) due to merging and re-evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot (Nc + Nf)) for storing merged samples and intermediate tensors. Measured Performance: With Nc=64, Nf=128, it provides a significant quality improvement over uniform sampling with N=128 while being computationally cheaper than uniform sampling with N=256. Strengths: Efficiently allocates samples to high-density regions; reduces noise in empty space; simple to implement as a drop-in replacement for uniform sampling. Limitations: Requires two network evaluations (coarse and fine) or a single network evaluated twice; sorting merged samples adds overhead; may still undersample if the coarse pass misses thin structures. When to Use: Standard NeRF training and rendering where quality is prioritized over raw speed. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring strict frame budgets without coarse-fine trade-off tuning; scenes with extremely thin structures that the coarse pass might miss entirely. name: Random Pixel Subsampling
head: Pixel Subsampling, Random Pixel Sampling
body: Random Pixel Subsampling selects a random subset of pixel coordinates from a full image grid to reduce the computational cost of training volume rendering models, such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), by evaluating the scene only at a fraction of the pixels per iteration. It differs from Two-stage NeRF Rendering by operating within a single training pass using stochastic gradient descent on a pixel subset, rather than separating coarse and fine rendering stages, and from Resolution Adaptation by keeping the image resolution constant while varying the number of active pixels. Inputs: imagesize: Tuple (W, H) representing image width and height. npixels: Integer, the number of pixels to sample per iteration. camera: Camera object providing projection parameters (e.g., PerspectiveCameras). Outputs: pixelcoords: Tensor of shape [npixels, 2] containing the (x, y) coordinates of the selected pixels in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) or pixel space, depending on the implementation. Data Structures: pixelcoords: A 2D tensor/array where each row is a pixel coordinate pair. indices: A 1D tensor/array of integers representing the linear indices of the pixels in the flattened grid. Steps: 1. Generate Full Grid: Create a grid of all pixel coordinates for the image. If using NDC coordinates (range [-1, 1]), generate coordinates for each pixel center. Flatten the grid to a 1D list of coordinates with shape [WH, 2]. 2. Generate Indices: Create a list of linear indices corresponding to the flattened grid, i.e., [0, 1,..., WH - 1]. 3. Shuffle Indices: Apply a random permutation to the indices to ensure unbiased sampling. Use a pseudo-random number generator to shuffle the indices. 4. Select Subset: Select the first npixels indices from the shuffled list. 5. Map to Coordinates: Use the selected indices to gather the corresponding pixel coordinates from the full grid. 6. Reshape: Reshape the selected coordinates to [npixels, 2]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def getrandompixelsfromimage(imagesize, npixels, camera=None): """ Selects a random subset of pixel coordinates from a full image grid. Args: imagesize: Tuple (W, H) npixels: Number of pixels to sample camera: Optional camera object (unused in basic random sampling, but may be used for coordinate generation in some implementations) Returns: pixelcoords: Tensor of shape [npixels, 2] """ W, H = imagesize totalpixels = W H # Step 1: Generate full pixel grid # Assuming NDC coordinates [-1, 1] for x and y # Create meshgrid of pixel centers xcoords = torch.linspace(-1 + 1/W, 1 - 1/W, W) ycoords = torch.linspace(-1 + 1/H, 1 - 1/H, H) xx, yy = torch.meshgrid(xcoords, ycoords, indexing='ij') # Flatten and stack to get [WH, 2] pixelgrid = torch.stack([xx.flatten(), yy.flatten()], dim=-1) # Step 2: Generate indices indices = torch.arange(totalpixels) # Step 3: Shuffle indices shuffledindices = torch.randperm(totalpixels) # Step 4: Select first npixels indices selectedindices = shuffledindices[:npixels] # Step 5: Map to coordinates pixelcoords = pixelgrid[selectedindices] # Step 6: Reshape (already [npixels, 2]) return pixelcoords Parameters: npixels: Number of pixels to sample. Typical values depend on the total resolution; for a 512 \times 512 image, sampling 10,000–20,000 pixels is common. imagesize: Tuple (W, H). camera: Optional, used if coordinate generation requires camera parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure that coordinate generation matches the expected range (NDC vs. pixel indices) to avoid misalignment with the camera model. Boundaries: When generating NDC coordinates, ensure pixel centers are correctly calculated to avoid edge artifacts. Degenerate Input: If npixels > WH, the method should either raise an error or return all pixels. Frequency-aware Mask Generation produces a binary spatial mask M{freq} that highlights frequency-specific structures in rendered images to guide training. It distinguishes between coarse structures (prioritized early in training) and fine structures (prioritized later) by modulating Gaussian filter scales based on a schedule parameter. Unlike standard pixel-wise losses, this method spatially weights the error based on the spectral content of the ground truth image, allowing the model to prioritize low-frequency structures early and high-frequency details later. Ray Sampling with Precropping restricts coordinate selection to the image center during early training iterations to stabilize optimization, then expands to the full image. Steps: 1. If iteration i < \text{args.precrop\iters}, compute crop margins dH = \text{int}(H//2 \times \text{args.precrop\frac}) and dW = \text{int}(W//2 \times \text{args.precrop\frac}). 2. Create a coordinate grid using tf.meshgrid with ranges [H//2 - dH, H//2 + dH) and [W//2 - dW, W//2 + dW), using indexing='ij'. 3. Else, create a full grid using tf.range(H) and tf.range(W). 4. Reshape coordinates to [-1, 2], randomly sample N{rand} indices without replacement via np.random.choice, and gather ray origins/directions and target colors using tf.gathernd. Parameters: args.precropiters: Number of iterations to apply precropping. Typical value: 10,000. args.precropfrac: Fraction of half-dimensions to crop. Typical value: 0.5 (samples center 50%). Pitfall: Coordinate indexing mismatch; resolved by using indexing='ij' in meshgrid to match the (row, col) \rightarrow (y, x) layout expected by gathernd. Pixel Shuffle Sampling is a pixel distribution algorithm based on Fibonacci numbers that progressively adds or removes pixels to maintain low discrepancy. Comparison: vs. Random Distribution: Random distribution leads to inhomogeneous regions, while Pixel Shuffle provides low discrepancy (LD) and uniform distribution, leading to better recovery results. vs. Poisson Disk Sampling: Poisson disk sampling achieves low discrepancy and blue-noise distribution but is not progressive (high coverage does not contain low coverage). Pixel Shuffle is progressive, allowing for progressive image updates. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to generate the full grid, O(W \cdot H) to shuffle indices, and O(n{pixels}) to select and gather coordinates. The dominant cost is the initial grid generation and shuffling, which is done once per iteration or cached. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to store the full pixel grid and indices. Measured Performance: Reduces training time per iteration by a factor of \frac{W \cdot H}{n{pixels}}. Scaling: Scales linearly with image resolution for grid generation, but the sampling cost is independent of resolution once the grid is generated. Strengths: Simple to implement, reduces memory bandwidth and computation per iteration, easy to parallelize. Limitations: May miss important details if the random subset is not representative, especially in early training. When to Use: When training large scenes or high-resolution images where full-pixel rendering is too slow. When Not to Use: When precise pixel-level accuracy is required in every iteration, or when the scene has highly localized features that might be missed by random sampling. Random Pixel Subsampling was introduced as a practical optimization for training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and other volume rendering models, where evaluating the neural network at every pixel is computationally expensive. The method leverages the fact that stochastic gradient descent does not require the full dataset in every iteration, allowing for a subset of pixels to be used for gradient updates. The technique has been widely adopted in open-source NeRF implementations, such as those by Samiran Angode and Shyam-pi. samirangode/Volume-Rendering-and-Neural-Radiance-Fields, https://github.com/samirangode/Volume-Rendering-and-Neural-Radiance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Shyam-pi/Volume-Rendering-and-Neural-Radiance-Fields, https://github.com/Shyam-pi/Volume-Rendering-and-Neural-Radiance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bmild/nerf, https://github.com/bmild/nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Compressive Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.11575/prism/25391, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Frequency-aware Mask Generation
head: Frequency-specific mask generation, Multi-scale frequency mask
body: Frequency-aware Mask Generation produces a binary spatial mask M{freq} that highlights frequency-specific structures in rendered images to guide training. It distinguishes between coarse structures (prioritized early in training) and fine structures (prioritized later) by modulating Gaussian filter scales based on a schedule parameter. Unlike standard pixel-wise losses, this method spatially weights the error based on the spectral content of the ground truth image, allowing the model to prioritize low-frequency structures early and high-frequency details later. The method consists of two distinct variants: a Spectral Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) Mask (detailed below) and a Random Distribution Mask. The Spectral DoG variant is used for importance scoring and mask-weighted reconstruction loss in Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES). The Random Distribution variant generates binary sampling masks for 1D or 2D data using Gaussian or uniform random distributions with optional center-region oversampling. Spectral DoG Variant: Input: Grayscale image I \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 1 \times H{img} \times W{img}} (or RGB image converted to grayscale), schedule parameter f \in [0, 100], downsampling scale factor s (typically 0.5). Output: Binary mask M{freq} \in \{0, 1\}^{B \times 1 \times H{img} \times W{img}}. Random Distribution Variant: Input: Image dimensions (size), acceleration factor accfactor, distribution type ('gaussian2d', 'uniformrandom2d', 'gaussian1d', 'uniform1d'), center fraction centerfraction (default 0.04), covariance factor (default derived from size), and boolean fix. Output: Binary mask tensor of zeros with shape matching the input image, with indices set to 1 where samples fall. Mask Tensor: A binary tensor of the same spatial dimensions as the input image. Gaussian Kernel: 2D kernel generated from standard deviation \sigma and kernel size k, normalized to unit sum. Frequency Response Map: Intermediate float tensor representing the absolute difference of filtered images. 1. Grayscale Conversion: Convert input image I to grayscale by averaging color channels: I{\text{gray}} \leftarrow \text{mean}(I, \dim = 1, \text{keepdim} = \text{true}) 2. Downsampling: Downsample I{\text{gray}} by factor s using bilinear interpolation: I{\text{down}} \leftarrow \text{BilinearInterp}(I{\text{gray}}, s) 3. Bandwidth Calculation: Compute \sigma1 based on schedule parameter f: \sigma1 = \begin{cases} 0.1 + (100 - f) \times 0.1, & \text{if } f \geq 50 \\ 0.1 + f \times 0.1, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Set \sigma2 \leftarrow 2\sigma1. 4. Kernel Generation: Compute kernel sizes: k1 \leftarrow 2 \lceil 3\sigma1 \rceil + 1, \quad k2 \leftarrow 2 \lceil 3\sigma2 \rceil + 1 Generate normalized 2D Gaussian kernels \mathcal{K}1 and \mathcal{K}2 with standard deviations \sigma1 and \sigma2 respectively. 5. Convolution: Apply dimension-preserving zero-padded 2D convolution: I1^{\text{blur}} \leftarrow \mathcal{K}1 I{\text{down}}, \quad I2^{\text{blur}} \leftarrow \mathcal{K}2 I{\text{down}} 6. Difference-of-Gaussians: Compute absolute difference: H{\text{freq}} \leftarrow |I1^{\text{blur}} - I2^{\text{blur}}| 7. Upsampling: Upsample H{\text{freq}} back to original resolution (H{img}, W{img}) using bilinear interpolation: H{up} \leftarrow \text{BilinearInterp}(H{\text{freq}}, (H{img}, W{img})) 8. Normalization: Normalize each image independently over spatial pixels with stabilization constant \varepsilon{norm} > 0: H{\text{norm}} \leftarrow \frac{H{up} - \min(H{up})}{\max(H{up}) - \min(H{up}) + \varepsilon{norm}} 9. Thresholding: Generate binary mask M{freq} using indicator function \mathbb{I}[\cdot]: M{freq} = \begin{cases} \mathbb{I}[H{\text{norm}} \geq 0.5], & \text{if } f \geq 50 \\ \mathbb{I}[1 - H{\text{norm}} \geq 0.5], & \text{if } f < 50 \end{cases} 1. Calculate Sample Count: For 2D types, N{samp} = \text{size}^2 // \text{acc\factor}; for 1D types, N{samp} = \text{size} // \text{acc\factor}. 2. Initialize Mask: Create a tensor of zeros with shape matching the input image. 3. Sample Coordinates: For Gaussian types: Sample coordinates from a multivariate normal (2D) or normal (1D) distribution with mean at the center and covariance scaled by \text{size} \times \text{cov\factor}. For Uniform types: Sample coordinates uniformly from [0, \text{size}-1]. 4. Clip Samples: Clip sampled coordinates to valid grid bounds [0, \text{size}-1]. 5. Set Mask Indices: Set the mask indices corresponding to the clipped samples to 1. 6. Center Oversampling (1D only): For 1D Gaussian/Uniform types, additionally set a center region of size N{samp\center} = \text{int}(\text{size} \times \text{center\fraction}) to 1. 7. Batch Independence: If fix=False, generate independent masks for each batch element. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatefrequencymask(image, f, s=0.5, epsilonnorm=1e-6): """ Generates a frequency-aware binary mask using Difference of Gaussians. Args: image: Input tensor of shape (B, C, H, W). f: Schedule parameter in [0, 100]. s: Downsampling scale factor (default 0.5). epsilonnorm: Numerical stabilization constant for normalization. When to Use: When training Gaussian Splatting models and needing to guide optimization towards specific frequency bands to improve detail reconstruction. When Not to Use: When absolute frequency selection strength across different images is required, or when computational resources are extremely limited and even downsampled convolutions are prohibitive. name: Frequency-Modulated Edge-Aware Loss
head: DoG-based frequency loss
body: Frequency-Modulated Edge-Aware Loss is a training objective term that uses a Difference of Gaussians (DoG) filter to create an edge-aware mask, focusing optimization on specific frequency bands to tune the shape parameter \beta and improve high-frequency detail reconstruction in Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES). It builds on Frequency-aware Mask Generation by spatially weighting the error based on the spectral content of the ground truth image, allowing the model to prioritize low-frequency structures early in training and high-frequency details later. The method computes a frequency-specific binary mask from the ground truth image and applies an L1 loss weighted by this mask. The mask generation relies on a band-pass filter defined by the target normalized frequency \omega. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: I{\text{gt}}: Ground truth image. I: Reconstructed/rendered image from the current model iteration. \omega: Target normalized frequency, a scalar in [0, 1] (0% for low frequencies, 100% for high frequencies). \epsilon\omega: Threshold for mask generation, typically 0.5. Outputs: \mathcal{L}\omega: The scalar loss value for the current iteration. Data Structures: Images I and I{\text{gt}} are treated as 2D arrays of floating-point values. Mask M\omega is a binary 2D array of the same spatial dimensions as the images. Parameters: \sigma2 = 0.1 + 10\omega: Base standard deviation for the Gaussian filters. \sigma1 = 2\sigma2: Standard deviation for the wider Gaussian in the DoG filter. \epsilon\omega = 0.5: Default threshold value. Range: 0 \le \epsilon\omega \le 1. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Calculate Gaussian Standard Deviations: Compute \sigma2 and \sigma1 based on the current target frequency \omega: \sigma2 = 0.1 + 10\omega \sigma1 = 2\sigma2 2. Apply Gaussian Blur: Apply Gaussian blur G(\cdot, \sigma) to the ground truth image I{\text{gt}} using both standard deviations: I{\text{smooth}, 1} = G(I{\text{gt}}, \sigma1) I{\text{smooth}, 2} = G(I{\text{gt}}, \sigma2) 3. Compute DoG Response: Calculate the Difference of Gaussians response: \text{DoG}\omega(I{\text{gt}}) = I{\text{smooth}, 1} - I{\text{smooth}, 2} 4. Normalize DoG Response: Normalize the DoG response to a range compatible with the threshold \epsilon\omega \in [0, 1] to prepare for thresholding. Let \text{norm}(\cdot) denote this normalization operation. R = \text{norm}(\text{DoG}\omega(I{\text{gt}})) 5. Generate Binary Mask: Create the initial binary mask M\omega using the indicator function \mathbb{1} and threshold \epsilon\omega: M\omega = \mathbb{1}(R > \epsilon\omega) 6. Adjust Mask for High Frequencies: Due to DoG filter sensitivity, invert the mask for high-frequency targets to ensure coverage and focus on details as optimization progresses: \text{If } 0\% < \omega \le 50\%: \quad M{\text{final}} = M\omega \text{If } 50\% < \omega \le 100\%: \quad M{\text{final}} = 1 - M\omega 7. Compute Loss: Calculate the weighted L1 norm of the difference between the reconstructed image I and the ground truth I{\text{gt}}: \mathcal{L}\omega = \| (I - I{\text{gt}}) \cdot M{\text{final}} \|1 where \cdot denotes element-wise multiplication and \|\cdot\|1 is the L1 norm (sum of absolute values). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussianblur(image, sigma): """Applies a separable 2D Gaussian blur to a 2D image.""" kernelsize = int(6 sigma + 1) if kernelsize % 2 == 0: kernelsize += 1 x = np.arange(kernelsize) kernel1d = np.exp(-0.5 (x - kernelsize // 2)2 / sigma2) kernel1d /= kernel1d.sum() # Apply separable convolution temp = np.dot(image, kernel1d) return np.dot(kernel1d, temp) def normalizeto01(image): """Normalizes image values to [0, 1] using min-max scaling.""" minval = np.min(image) maxval = np.max(image) if maxval == minval: return np.zeroslike(image) return (image - minval) / (maxval - minval) def frequencymodulatededgeawareloss(I, Igt, omega, epsilon=0.5): """ Computes the Frequency-Modulated Edge-Aware Loss. Args: I: Reconstructed image (2D array). Igt: Ground truth image (2D array). omega: Target normalized frequency in [0, 1]. epsilon: Threshold for mask generation. Returns: Loss scalar. """ # Step 1: Calculate standard deviations sigma2 = 0.1 + 10 omega sigma1 = 2 sigma2 # Step 2: Apply Gaussian Blur Ismooth1 = gaussianblur(Igt, sigma1) Ismooth2 = gaussianblur(Igt, sigma2) # Step 3: Compute DoG Response dogresponse = Ismooth1 - Ismooth2 # Step 4: Normalize DoG Response # Min-max normalization to [0, 1] R = normalizeto01(dogresponse) # Step 5: Generate Binary Mask Momega = (R > epsilon).astype(float) # Step 6: Adjust Mask for High Frequencies if omega > 0.5: Mfinal = 1.0 - Momega else: Mfinal = Momega # Step 7: Compute Loss error = I - Igt weightederror = error Mfinal loss = np.sum(np.abs(weightederror)) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Frequency Band Inversion: For \omega > 50\%, the mask must be inverted (1 - M\omega) to maintain correct focus on high-frequency details and ensure all image parts are covered across the training schedule. Filter Stability: The choice of \sigma2 = 0.1 + 10\omega is critical for filter stability and reasonable mask generation. Normalization: The exact normalization method for the DoG response is not explicitly detailed in the source beyond "normalized". Implementers must ensure the normalization maps the DoG response to a range compatible with the threshold \epsilon\omega \in [0, 1]. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method provides an almost free 9% reduction in memory for the overall GES system by improving the efficiency of the shape parameter \beta tuning. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. The Frequency-Modulated Edge-Aware Loss was introduced in the context of Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES) for efficient radiance field rendering. It is designed to optimize the shape parameter \beta of GES components by selectively pruning them based on shape attributes, eliminating the need for variable density mechanisms. The method uses a linear schedule for \omega during optimization, starting with low frequencies and progressing to high frequencies. name: Temporal Upsampling and Dithering
head: Dithering, Temporal Upsampling
body: Temporal Upsampling and Dithering is a rendering technique that combines spatial resolution reduction with temporal accumulation to mitigate sampling artifacts in volume rendering, specifically addressing slicing artifacts caused by insufficient sampling steps. It distinguishes itself from standard adaptive sampling methods by using blue noise dithering to break up coherent aliasing patterns and temporal upsampling to reduce the noise introduced by that dithering, rather than relying solely on spatial supersampling or static resolution scaling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Low-resolution color buffer (e.g., 1/2x1/2 resolution), depth buffer, and previous frame's accumulated buffer. Output: High-resolution color buffer (full resolution) blended into the Scene Color Render Target. Data Structures: Blue Noise Texture: A 2D texture containing precomputed blue noise values, used for spatial dithering. History Buffer: A buffer storing accumulated color values from previous frames, reprojected using pixel velocity. Pixel Velocity Buffer: A buffer storing the movement vector of each pixel between frames, used for reprojection. Steps: 1. Resolution Reduction: Render the volume at a lower resolution (e.g., 1/2x1/2) to reduce computational cost. 2. Blue Noise Dithering: Apply blue noise dithering to the sampled values to break up slicing artifacts caused by insufficient sampling steps. This introduces high-frequency noise but eliminates coherent aliasing. 3. Temporal Accumulation: Use temporal upsampling to blend the current low-resolution frame with the history buffer. The history buffer is reprojected using pixel velocity to align with the current frame's geometry. 4. Upsampling: Upsample the accumulated low-resolution result to full resolution. This can be done via bilinear filtering or more advanced techniques, leveraging the temporal stability provided by the accumulation. 5. Blending: Blend the upsampled result into the final Scene Color Render Target. Formulas: Dithered Sample Value: C{dithered} = C{sample} + D{blue\noise} \times \alpha, where C{sample} is the raw sample, D{blue\noise} is the blue noise value, and \alpha is a scaling factor for dithering intensity. Temporal Blend: C{accumulated} = w \cdot C{current} + (1 - w) \cdot C{history\reprojected}, where w is the temporal weight (often based on confidence or time delta). Parameters: Resolution Scale: Typically 1/2x1/2 for high-end hardware; lower resolutions may be used for mid-low end. Dithering Intensity (\alpha): Not specified in sources. Temporal Weight (w): Not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ghosting: If pixel velocity is inaccurate, ghosting artifacts may appear. This is mitigated by using robust velocity estimation and potentially anti-smear techniques (see Temporal Anti-Aliasing with Anti-Smear). Noise Amplification: Excessive dithering can introduce visible noise, which temporal upsampling must effectively smooth out. Boundary Artifacts: At the edges of the screen or volume boundaries, reprojection may fail, requiring clamping or alternative handling. Adds depth-based rejection to the accumulation process to prevent smearing artifacts, building on this method by enhancing the temporal stability. Time Complexity: Reduced by rendering at lower resolution (e.g., 1/4th the pixels for 1/2x1/2). Temporal accumulation adds overhead for reprojection and blending. Memory Complexity: Requires additional buffers for history, velocity, and blue noise texture. Performance: Effective on high-end hardware where resolution reduction is feasible. On mid-low end, frame-by-frame processing (similar to RDR2) may be used, which is simpler but may have lower temporal stability. Strengths: Reduces slicing artifacts and noise while maintaining performance. Limitations: Can introduce ghosting if velocity estimation is poor. Dithering noise requires effective temporal smoothing. When to Use: When volume rendering suffers from slicing artifacts due to limited sampling steps and performance is a concern. When Not to Use: When high temporal stability is critical and velocity estimation is unreliable, or when hardware cannot support the additional buffer overhead. This technique is discussed in the context of real-time volume cloud rendering, particularly in game engines like Unity's HDRP. It is inspired by techniques used in games like Red Dead Redemption 2 for handling atmospheric effects. The combination of blue noise dithering and temporal upsampling is a practical approach to balancing visual quality and performance in real-time volume rendering. 体积云效果的实现，游戏世界的云合雾集, https://leihuo.163.com/institution/news/20230719/384231099592.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Temporal Anti-Aliasing with Anti-Smear
head: Anti-Smear TAA, TAA, Temporal Upscaling
body: Temporal Anti-Aliasing with Anti-Smear is a post-processing technique that blends the current frame's color with an accumulated history buffer using pixel velocity for reprojection, with an optional anti-smear feature that discards accumulated pixels with large depth differences to prevent ghosting. It distinguishes itself from standard TAA by explicitly checking depth discontinuities during reprojection to avoid smearing artifacts. Inputs: srcColorTexture: Current frame color (texture2d<f32>). velocityTexture: Current frame pixel velocity (texture2d<f32>). currentDepthTexture: Current frame depth (texture2d<f32>). previousDepthTexture: Previous frame depth (texture2d<f32>). accumBuffer: History buffer of accumulated colors (texture2d<f32>). sceneData: Uniform struct containing screen dimensions (screenWidth, screenHeight), anti-smear toggle (antiSmearEnabled), and other rendering parameters. cameraData: Uniform struct containing camera position, rotation, FOV, aspect ratio, and their previous frame counterparts. Outputs: dstColorTexture: Final blended color output (texturestorage2d<rgba8unorm, write>). The CameraData struct layout is defined as: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct CameraData { position: vec3f, fov: f32, rotation: vec3f, aspectRatio: f32, prevPosition: vec3f, padding1: f32, prevRotation: vec3f, padding2: f32 }; The SceneData uniform contains screenWidth, screenHeight, antiSmearEnabled, and other rendering parameters. 1. Initialization: The compute shader entry point ComputeMain uses a workgroup size of (16, 16, 1). The pixel position is calculated as pixelPos = id.xy. If pixelPos.x >= sceneData.screenWidth or pixelPos.y >= sceneData.screenHeight, the shader returns immediately. 2. Reprojection Vector Calculation: Load the current pixel velocity, color, and current/previous depth. Calculate the adjusted pixel position: adjustedPixelPos = vec2<f32>(pixelPos) - pixelVelocity.xy. 3. Boundary Check: Check if adjustedPixelPos is within valid bounds. If adjustedPixelPos.x <= 2.0 or adjustedPixelPos.y <= 2.0 or adjustedPixelPos.x >= f32(sceneData.screenWidth) or adjustedPixelPos.y >= f32(sceneData.screenHeight), store pixelColor to dst and return. The threshold 2.0 is used to avoid artifacts that occur with 0 or 1. 4. UV Coordinate Calculation: Convert pixel positions to normalized UV coordinates: uv = vec2<f32>(pixelPos) / vec2<f32>(f32(sceneData.screenWidth - 1u), f32(sceneData.screenHeight - 1u)) and adjustedUV = vec2<f32>(adjustedPixelPos) / vec2<f32>(f32(sceneData.screenWidth - 1u), f32(sceneData.screenHeight - 1u)). Clamp adjustedUV to [0, 1]. 5. Accumulation Sample: Sample the accumulated color from the history buffer at the adjusted UV: accumCol = textureSampleLevel(accumBuffer, textureSampler, adjustedUV, 0.0). 6. Anti-Smear Rejection (Optional): If sceneData.antiSmearEnabled == 1, sample the current depth at uv (currentPixelDepth) and the previous depth at adjustedUV (previousPixelDepth). Calculate the absolute depth difference: depthDiff = abs(previousPixelDepth - currentPixelDepth). If depthDiff > 4.0, calculate brightness bias: brightness = dot(pixelColor.rgb, vec3<f32>(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)). Store mix(pixelColor, accumCol, brightness). The source does not specify the blending logic when anti-smear is disabled or depthDiff <= 4.0. Depth Threshold: The anti-smear feature triggers if depthDiff > 4.0. Boundary Threshold: A threshold of 2.0 is used for adjusted pixel position bounds to prevent artifacts. Using 0 or 1 causes visible artifacts. Brightness Weights: The luminance weights are hardcoded as (0.299, 0.587, 0.114). Precision: 32-bit float storage is required for previous fragment depth to ensure precision in depth-based rejection. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetaaantismear(pixelpos: tuple[int, int], scenedata: dict, cameradata: dict, velocitytex: Texture2D, currentdepthtex: Texture2D, previousdepthtex: Texture2D, accumbuffer: Texture2D, currentcolor: tuple[float, float, float, float]) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]: # 1. Bounds check if pixelpos[0] >= scenedata['screenWidth'] or pixelpos[1] >= scenedata['screenHeight']: return currentcolor # 2. Reprojection pixelvelocity = velocitytex.sample(pixelpos) adjustedpixelpos = (pixelpos[0] - pixelvelocity[0], pixelpos[1] - pixelvelocity[1]) # 3. Boundary Check with 2.0 threshold if (adjustedpixelpos[0] <= 2.0 or adjustedpixelpos[1] <= 2.0 or adjustedpixelpos[0] >= scenedata['screenWidth'] or adjustedpixelpos[1] >= scenedata['screenHeight']): return currentcolor # 4. UV Calculation uv = (pixelpos[0] / (scenedata['screenWidth'] - 1), pixelpos[1] / (scenedata['screenHeight'] - 1)) adjusteduv = (adjustedpixelpos[0] / (scenedata['screenWidth'] - 1), adjustedpixelpos[1] / (scenedata['screenHeight'] - 1)) adjusteduv = (max(0.0, min(1.0, adjusteduv[0])), max(0.0, min(1.0, adjusteduv[1]))) # 5. Sample Accumulated Color accumcol = accumbuffer.sample(adjusteduv) # 6. Anti-Smear Logic if scenedata['antiSmearEnabled']: currentpixeldepth = currentdepthtex.sample(uv)[0] previouspixeldepth = previousdepthtex.sample(adjusteduv)[0] depthdiff = abs(previouspixeldepth - currentpixeldepth) if depthdiff > 4.0: brightness = currentcolor[0] 0.299 + currentcolor[1] 0.587 + currentcolor[2] 0.114 return (currentcolor[0] (1.0 - brightness) + accumcol[0] brightness, currentcolor[1] (1.0 - brightness) + accumcol[1] brightness, currentcolor[2] (1.0 - brightness) + accumcol[2] brightness, currentcolor[3]) # The source does not specify the blending logic when anti-smear is disabled or depthDiff <= 4.0. return accumcol A variant that combines color rejection (implicit via TAA mixing) with explicit depth consistency checks to eliminate ghosting artifacts. It transforms the current fragment position to the previous frame's clip space, converts to screen space, and samples 9 neighboring pixels in the previous frame's memory texture. It linearizes depths and computes the absolute difference against the current linearized depth, tracking the minimum difference. If the mapped previous position is outside [0, 1] or the minimum depth difference exceeds 0.05 linearizedepth(d), the previous frame is rejected by setting mixAmt = 1.0. This approach effectively removes most ghosting artifacts but requires 32-bit float storage for previous fragment depth to ensure precision. It is integrated into RTGI shaders and the main TAA pass. Performance: The method is computationally expensive, with one implementation reporting a cost of 1.1ms on an NVIDIA GTX 980 at 4K resolution, running at full resolution with r11g11b10f and r32f textures. Memory: Requires storage for the accumulated history buffer, velocity textures, and depth textures (current and previous). The use of 32-bit float for depth increases memory bandwidth requirements. Strengths: Effectively removes most ghosting artifacts when combined with color rejection. The anti-smear feature specifically targets depth discontinuities caused by object motion. Limitations: High computational cost at high resolutions. Sensitive to boundary conditions, requiring specific thresholds (2.0) to avoid artifacts. Requires precise depth precision (32-bit float) to function correctly. The method originates from unofficial implementations in WebGPU voxel raymarching and 3D terrain generation projects. The specific "Anti-Smear" technique with the 4.0 depth threshold and 2.0 boundary check is detailed in the WebGPU voxel raymarching repository. The variant using depth and color rejection with a 0.05 depth difference multiplier is described in the 3D Terrain Generation repository. These implementations leverage TAA for both antialiasing and denoising, particularly in conjunction with SSAO and Global Illumination techniques. jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, https://github.com/jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Maxsimuss/3dTerrainGeneration, https://github.com/Maxsimuss/3dTerrainGeneration, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Resolution Adaptation
head: Dynamic Resolution, Adaptive Resolution
body: Resolution Adaptation dynamically adjusts the spatial resolution of the volumetric representation or the rendering viewport during execution to balance visual fidelity against computational cost. It solves the problem of fixed-resolution rendering wasting resources on empty space or failing to meet performance budgets in complex regions. It differs from Adaptive Sampling by modifying the grid or viewport granularity rather than the number of samples per ray, and from Level-of-detail (LOD) methods by often modifying the underlying data structure or training state rather than just swapping pre-computed assets. Resolution Adaptation relies on a feedback loop or predefined schedule to change the discretization of the volume. The core mechanism involves: 1. Metric Evaluation: Monitoring a metric such as training iteration count, render time, or spatial occupancy. 2. Resolution Mapping: Converting the metric or target voxel count into a new grid resolution (resx, resy, resz) or viewport scale. 3. State Update: Reinitializing or interpolating the volume grid, updating the sampling parameters (e.g., samples per ray), and potentially resetting the optimizer state to accommodate the new resolution. 4. Culling: Pruning empty space or filtering rays that fall outside the active bounding box to maintain efficiency. Methods that change the resolution of the rendering during viewpoint interaction to maintain responsive frame rates. They select from pre-computed resolution hierarchies based on camera distance or screen space error. This method dynamically adjusts the spatial resolution of a volumetric representation and prunes empty space via an alpha mask during training to improve efficiency and convergence. It differs from LOD methods by modifying the underlying grid resolution and occupancy mask globally rather than selecting pre-computed representations based on camera distance. Mixed-resolution multi-volume rendering is a technique for rendering large-scale multi-volume datasets where different channels are rendered at different resolution levels to save memory and reduce sample evaluation. It addresses the problem of high memory bandwidth and computational cost when rendering multi-channel data by exploiting differences in frequency content or importance across channels. What sets it apart from sibling methods like Level-of-detail (LOD) methods, which typically apply a single resolution hierarchy to the entire volume, is the per-channel granularity of resolution selection. It builds on Resolution Adaptation by extending adaptive resolution to multi-channel datasets. Definition: Dynamically adjusts the render viewport reduction factor based on previous frame render time and allocated time budget to maintain target frame rate. Step: Compute new ReductionFactor ensuring it stays in range (0.0, 1.0]. Parameter: allocatedTime: double in seconds representing the time budget for the next frame.
