name: Dynamic Volume Resolution & Alpha Mask Update
head: Dynamic Resolution and Mask Update
body: This method dynamically adjusts the spatial resolution of a volumetric representation and prunes empty space via an alpha mask during training to improve efficiency and convergence. It differs from Level-of-detail (LOD) methods by modifying the underlying grid resolution and occupancy mask globally rather than selecting pre-computed representations based on camera distance. The method operates by monitoring the training iteration count against two predefined lists: updateAlphaMasklist and upsamplist. When the current iteration matches an entry in these lists, specific updates to the volume grid, sampling strategy, and optimizer state are triggered. Inputs: Current training iteration, current volume resolution resocur, current bounding box aabb, current ray data allrays, current ground truth colors allrgbs, and hyperparameters (args). Outputs: Updated volume grid, updated alpha mask, updated sampling parameters, and reinitialized optimizer. resocur: A tuple (resx, resy, resz) representing the current voxel resolution. tensorf: The neural field object containing the volume grid and optimization state. updateAlphaMasklist: A sorted list of integers representing iterations where the alpha mask should be updated. upsamplist: A sorted list of integers representing iterations where the resolution should be upsampled. Nvoxellist: A list of target voxel counts corresponding to upsamplist. 1. Alpha Mask Update Check: If the current iteration is in updateAlphaMasklist: Determine the mask resolution resomask. If resocur[0] resocur[1] resocur[2] < 2563, set resomask = resocur to cap mask resolution. Call tensorf.updateAlphaMask(tuple(resomask)) to generate a new alpha mask. Call tensorf.shrink(newaabb) to restrict the volume to the new active bounding box. Update the L1 regularization weight: L1regweight = args.L1weightrest. If NDC rays are not used (args.ndcray is false) and it is the second update iteration, filter rays outside the bounding box: allrays, allrgbs = tensorf.filteringrays(allrays, allrgbs). Reinitialize sampler: trainingSampler = SimpleSampler(allrgbs.shape[0], args.batchsize). 2. Resolution Upsampling Check: If the current iteration is in upsamplist: Pop next voxel count: nvoxels = Nvoxellist.pop(0). Convert voxel count to resolution: resocur = Ntoreso(nvoxels, tensorf.aabb). Update samples per ray: nSamples = min(args.nSamples, calnsamples(resocur, args.stepratio)). Upsample the volume grid: tensorf.upsamplevolumegrid(resocur). Calculate learning rate scale: if args.lrupsamplereset is true, lrscale = 1; else lrscale = args.lrdecaytargetratio (iteration / args.niters). Get new parameter groups with scaled learning rates: gradvars = tensorf.getoptparamgroups(args.lrinit lrscale, args.lrbasis lrscale). Reinitialize Adam optimizer: optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(gradvars, betas=(0.9, 0.99)). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatedynamicresolutionandmask( iteration, tensorf, allrays, allrgbs, args, updateAlphaMasklist, upsamplist, Nvoxellist, trainingSampler, resocur): # 1. Alpha Mask Update if iteration in updateAlphaMasklist: # Determine mask resolution currentvoxelcount = resocur[0] resocur[1] resocur[2] if currentvoxelcount < 2563: resomask = resocur else: # Source only specifies capping at current resolution; behavior for larger volumes is not given. resomask = resocur # Generate new alpha mask and shrink volume newaabb = tensorf.updateAlphaMask(tuple(resomask)) tensorf.shrink(newaabb) # Update L1 weight L1regweight = args.L1weightrest # Filter rays if not using NDC and it's the second update iteration if not args.ndcray and len(updateAlphaMasklist) > 1 and iteration == updateAlphaMasklist[1]: allrays, allrgbs = tensorf.filteringrays(allrays, allrgbs) trainingSampler = SimpleSampler(allrgbs.shape[0], args.batchsize) # 2. Resolution Upsampling if iteration in upsamplist and Nvoxellist: nvoxels = Nvoxellist.pop(0) # Convert voxel count to resolution # Standard helper: computes cubic resolution from target voxel count and AABB volume resocur = Ntoreso(nvoxels, tensorf.aabb) # Update samples per ray # Standard helper: computes samples per ray based on resolution and step ratio nSamples = min(args.nSamples, calnsamples(resocur, args.stepratio)) # Upsample volume grid tensorf.upsamplevolumegrid(resocur) # Calculate learning rate scale if args.lrupsamplereset: lrscale = 1 else: lrscale = args.lrdecaytargetratio (iteration / args.niters) # Get new parameter groups with scaled learning rates gradvars = tensorf.getoptparamgroups(args.lrinit lrscale, args.lrbasis lrscale) # Reinitialize optimizer # Standard PyTorch Adam optimizer reinitialization optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(gradvars, betas=(0.9, 0.99)) def Ntoreso(nvoxels, aabb): # Computes cubic resolution from target voxel count and AABB volume vol = (aabb[1][0]-aabb[0][0]) (aabb[1][1]-aabb[0][1]) (aabb[1][2]-aabb[0][2]) res = max(1, int(round((nvoxels / vol) (1/3)))) return (res, res, res) def calnsamples(reso, stepratio): # Computes samples per ray based on resolution and step ratio return int(reso[0] stepratio) def SimpleSampler(numrays, batchsize): # Standard ray sampler initialization return {"numrays": numrays, "batchsize": batchsize} class AdamOptimizer: # Standard Adam optimizer reinitialization def init(self, params, betas): self.params = params self.betas = betas updateAlphaMasklist: List of iterations triggering alpha mask updates. upsamplist: List of iterations triggering volume resolution upscaling. args.lrupsamplereset: Boolean. If true, resets learning rate to initial on upsample; otherwise applies decay. args.lrdecaytargetratio: Float. Multiplier for LR decay during upscaling if lrupsamplereset is false. args.nSamples: Maximum samples per ray before dynamic adjustment. args.stepratio: Float. Controls sample density relative to resolution during upscaling. args.lrinit, args.lrbasis: Initial learning rates for main and basis parameters. alphaMaskthres: Threshold for binarizing alpha values. Values >= this become 1, < this become 0. Default: 0.5. gridSize: Resolution of the alpha mask grid. Default: (200, 200, 200). Ray Filtering: filteringrays is only applied if args.ndcray is false. NDC rays bypass spatial bounding box culling, which may cause wasted computation on empty space. Optimizer State: The optimizer is completely reinitialized on upsample, discarding momentum states. This may cause training instability if not intended. Mask Resolution Cap: If the current volume resolution is less than 256^3, the mask resolution is capped at the current volume resolution. Generates an alpha mask from the dense density field to prune empty space, using a threshold and max pooling for smoothing. It computes dense alpha values on a grid spanning the AABB, applies 3D max pooling (kernel size 3, padding 1) to smooth the alpha mask, binarizes alpha values based on a threshold (default 0.5), creates an AlphaGridMask object, and calculates the new AABB based on the bounding box of valid (alpha > 0.5) voxels. It is chosen when the goal is to explicitly remove empty space from the training domain to save memory and compute. It differs from implicit pruning by explicitly maintaining a binary occupancy grid. Performance: Improves training efficiency by focusing compute on occupied space and allowing higher resolution in complex areas. Strengths: Reduces memory footprint, accelerates convergence by removing empty space, allows dynamic resolution scaling. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of update intervals. Reinitializing the optimizer can cause instability. NDC rays are not compatible with spatial culling. When to use: When training on scenes with significant empty space or when memory is constrained. When high resolution is needed only in specific regions. When not to use: When using NDC rays without custom filtering logic. When training stability is critical and optimizer momentum is important. name: Mixed-Resolution Multi-Volume Rendering
head: Per-channel resolution selection
body: Mixed-resolution multi-volume rendering is a technique for rendering large-scale multi-volume datasets where different channels are rendered at different resolution levels to save memory and reduce sample evaluation. It addresses the problem of high memory bandwidth and computational cost when rendering multi-channel data by exploiting differences in frequency content or importance across channels. What sets it apart from sibling methods like Level-of-detail (LOD) methods, which typically apply a single resolution hierarchy to the entire volume, is the per-channel granularity of resolution selection. It builds on Resolution Adaptation by extending adaptive resolution to multi-channel datasets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multi-volume dataset with N channels, each having a multi-resolution hierarchy (e.g., octree levels l0 to l{max}). Viewing parameters (camera position, ray direction). Transfer functions. Output: A rendered image where each pixel's color is computed using samples from the appropriate resolution level for each channel. Data Structures: Channel Resolution Constraint Function: For each channel c, a function fc(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}, \dots) that returns a valid range of resolution levels [l{min}, l{max}] or a specific level l. The function takes parameters such as: \mathbf{p}: Position in the volume (e.g., ray sample distance to camera). \mathbf{v}: Viewing parameters (e.g., camera orientation, distance). Frequency content of channel c. Transfer function for channel c. User-defined bounds. Multi-Resolution Hierarchy: Each channel has its own hierarchy of resolution levels. Level l0 is the highest resolution, and higher l values indicate lower resolution (coarser grids). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. 2. Sample Ray: For each sample point \mathbf{p} along the ray: a. For each channel c: i. Evaluate the constraint function fc(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}, \dots) to determine the appropriate resolution level lc for channel c at position \mathbf{p}. ii. Retrieve the value Vc(\mathbf{p}) from the multi-resolution hierarchy of channel c at level lc. This may involve traversing the octree to find the appropriate brick/node. iii. Apply the transfer function for channel c to Vc(\mathbf{p}) to get opacity \alphac and color Cc. b. Composite the results from all channels using volume rendering integration (e.g., front-to-back or back-to-front). 3. Output: The final color for the pixel. Formulas: Resolution level selection: lc = fc(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}, \dots) Volume rendering integration (front-to-back): C = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti \cdot \alphai \cdot Ci Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where i indexes the samples along the ray, and \alphai, Ci are the opacity and color from all channels at sample i. Parameters: Resolution Levels: Defined per channel. Typical values depend on the dataset. For example, in, levels l0 to l5 are used. Constraint Function Parameters: User-defined or automatically determined based on frequency analysis. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Channels: A channel with high-frequency content may require a higher sampling rate (lower l) to avoid aliasing. Low-Importance Channels: Channels with low importance or low frequency content can be rendered at lower resolutions (higher l) to save memory and computation. Boundary Artifacts: Switching resolution levels abruptly may cause visible artifacts. Smooth transitions or consistent level selection along the ray may be needed. Memory Management: Limiting the range of resolutions uploaded to the GPU per channel saves memory. However, managing multiple resolution levels for multiple channels can be complex. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermixedresolutionmultivolume(rays, channels, cameraparams): """ Render a multi-volume dataset with mixed resolutions per channel. Args: rays: List of rays, each with origin, direction, and t-values. channels: List of channel objects, each with: name: str hierarchy: MultiResolutionHierarchy constraintfunction: Callable[[Point, CameraParams], int] -> returns resolution level l transferfunction: Callable[[float], Tuple[float, float]] -> returns (alpha, color) cameraparams: Camera parameters (position, orientation, etc.) Returns: Image: Rendered image. """ image = createemptyimage(rays) for ray in rays: color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) transmittance = 1.0 for t in ray.tvalues: point = ray.origin + t ray.direction # Accumulate contribution from all channels channelcontributions = [] for channel in channels: # Determine resolution level for this channel at this point l = channel.constraintfunction(point, cameraparams) # Sample the channel at the determined resolution level value = channel.hierarchy.sample(point, level=l) # Apply transfer function alpha, c = channel.transferfunction(value) channelcontributions.append((alpha, c)) # Composite all channels at this sample point # This is a simplified composite; actual implementation may vary alphatotal = 0.0 colortotal = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for alpha, c in channelcontributions: alphatotal += alpha transmittance colortotal += c alpha transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) color += colortotal if transmittance < 1e-6: break image[ray.pixelindex] = color return image Determines the appropriate resolution level based on the frequency content of each channel. [Link to sibling if exists, otherwise note: Not given in the sources.] Time Complexity: Depends on the number of channels, the resolution levels chosen, and the sampling rate. Generally, rendering time is reduced compared to rendering all channels at the highest resolution. Memory Complexity: Reduced by limiting the number of resolution levels uploaded to the GPU per channel. Measured Performance: In, rendering human tissue data with 5 channels showed significant memory savings and reduced sample evaluation by using mixed resolutions (e.g., pink channel at l3, orange at l5/l4/l0, rest at l0). Scaling: Scales well with the number of channels and resolution levels, as each channel can be optimized independently. Strengths: Reduces memory usage and computational cost for multi-volume datasets. Allows for flexible resolution selection based on channel importance and frequency content. Limitations: May introduce artifacts if resolution levels are not chosen carefully. Complex to implement and manage. When to Use: Large-scale multi-volume datasets with varying frequency content or importance across channels. When Not to Use: Single-channel volumes or datasets where all channels have similar frequency content and importance. name: Adaptive Sampling Step with Early Ray Termination
head: Pas d'échantillonnage volumique et arrêt précoce
body: This method optimizes volume rendering performance by reducing sampling frequency for distant data and terminating ray evaluation once total opacity is reached. It addresses the inconsistency in opacity accumulation caused by variable step sizes by employing a 3D pre-integrated transfer function. Unlike uniform sampling, it stabilizes step calculations to prevent aliasing while maintaining constant brightness. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, volume data (bricks), 3D pre-integrated transfer function texture, viewpoint position, opacity threshold (typically 1.0). Outputs: Final pixel color. Data Structures: Brick: A 3D texture block containing pre-integrated optical properties. The brick stores a value representing the average or integrated transmittance/opacity for the entire brick volume, allowing for single-step accumulation. 3D Pre-integrated Transfer Function: A 3D texture mapping input density/value and step size to accumulated color and opacity. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set accumulated color C = 0, accumulated opacity A = 0, and current ray position p to the ray origin. 2. Loop: While A < 1.0 and the ray is within the volume bounds: a. Calculate Adaptive Step: Determine the sampling step size \Delta s based on the distance of the current sample point p from the viewpoint. The step size increases with distance to decrease sampling frequency for distant data. b. Sample Brick: Identify the brick containing p. Access the 3D pre-integrated transfer function using the local density/value at p and the calculated step size \Delta s to retrieve the accumulated color contribution \Delta C and opacity contribution \Delta A for this step. c. Accumulate: Update accumulated color and opacity: C \leftarrow C + \Delta C \cdot (1 - A) A \leftarrow A + \Delta A \cdot (1 - A) d. Early Termination Check: After accumulating each brick (not after every individual sample within a brick), check if A \ge 1.0. e. Exit Condition: If A \ge 1.0, terminate the ray evaluation immediately and return C. f. Advance Ray: Move p along the ray direction by \Delta s. Pitfalls: Using a standard transfer function with adaptive step sizes causes inconsistency in opacity accumulation because the transfer function assumes a constant step size. The 3D pre-integrated transfer function is required to handle varying sampling frequencies correctly. Performing the early termination check after every sample can negatively impact performance due to dynamic tests. Checking after each brick accumulation is the recommended approach. Uses a monotonically decreasing function of distance to determine sampling density, improving upon Weghorst et al. by stabilizing step calculations and preventing aliasing. Achieves SSIM > 0.95 with reduced execution time compared to uniform linear sampling. Performance: Provides good performance on G80 GPUs. The early exit condition significantly reduces computation for rays that reach full opacity quickly. Quality: Maintains constant brightness and provides better rendering quality compared to methods that do not account for variable step sizes. Limitations: Requires a 3D pre-integrated transfer function, which increases memory usage and complexity compared to standard 1D transfer functions. This method was developed to optimize the rendering of distant data in procedural volume exploration. It builds on the concept of adaptive sampling and early ray termination, specifically addressing the challenges of brick-based volume rendering. The approach was tested on G80 hardware. name: Adaptive Sampling with Monotonically Decreasing Density Function

body: This method determines sampling density along a ray using a monotonically decreasing function of distance from the eye, simulating photographic clarity where distant objects are vague (sparse sampling) and close objects are clear (dense sampling). It improves upon the Weghorst et al. method [15] by stabilizing the step calculation, preventing the under-sampling and aliasing artifacts that occur when using simple inverse distance functions. It achieves higher structural similarity (SSIM > 0.95) with significantly reduced execution time compared to uniform linear sampling. Inputs: Ray origin and direction. Volumetric data dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz). Parameters: k (slope scaler, typical ~4), x0 (initial step length, typical 0.01), Maxsteps (max samples, typical 100), MaxAlpha (termination threshold, typically 1.0). Outputs: Accumulated color C for the pixel. Data Structures: Unnormalized Coordinate System: The volumetric data is treated as a box where the longest edge is scaled to 1.0, and other dimensions are scaled proportionally. For example, a 128 \times 128 \times 64 volume becomes a 1 \times 1 \times 0.5 box. This prevents out-of-bound buffer reading issues common with normalized coordinates when dimensions are dissimilar. Formulas: The sampling density function is defined as: f(x) = \frac{b}{1 + kx} where x is the distance from the eye, b is a constant (fixed at 5 in experiments), and k controls the slope. The condition for constant difference in sampling density between consecutive points is: f(xi) - f(x{i+1}) = f(x{i+1}) - f(x{i+2}) \frac{b}{1 + kxi} - \frac{b}{1 + kx{i+1}} = \frac{b}{1 + kx{i+1}} - \frac{b}{1 + kx{i+2}} This simplifies to a relationship where the difference in inverse distances is constant in the base method, but the proposed method regularizes this to avoid instability. The iterative step calculation \lambdai (distance from previous point) is derived to ensure stability. The direct implementation of f(x) = 1/x leads to overflow when xi is close to the step size. The stabilized recurrence for the next position x{i+1} is determined by solving for the step \lambdai such that the density difference is preserved, regularized by k. The text notes that b does not influence the relative step differences, only the absolute density scale. The compositing equation is standard front-to-back: Ci = C{i-1}(1 - \alpha(x{i-1})) + c(x{i-1})\alpha(x{i-1}) where Ci is the accumulated color, c(x{i-1}) is the color at the previous sample, and \alpha(x{i-1}) is the opacity. No, D varies). # The text says "every continuous two sampling points have the same difference in the sampling density". # This means f(xi) - f(x{i+1}) = f(x{i+1}) - f(x{i+2}). # This implies f(x) is an arithmetic progression with respect to the sample index. # f(xn) = f(x0) - n delta. # So f(x{i+1}) = f(xi) - delta. # delta is determined by the first step. # f(x1) = f(x0) - delta. # delta = f(x0) - f(x1). # x1 is determined by initialstep. x1 = x0 + initialstep. # So delta is fixed after the first step. # Then f(x{i+1}) = f(xi) - delta. # b / (1 + k x{i+1}) = b / (1 + k xi) - delta. # 1 + k x{i+1} = b / (b / (1 + k xi) - delta). # x{i+1} = ( b / (b / (1 + k xi) - delta) - 1) / k. # This is a valid, closed-form implementation of the "constant difference in density" rule. # Calculate delta from the first step if i == 0: # x0 is currentpos (start of ray inside volume) # x1 = x0 + step xnext = currentpos + step fcurr = b / (1 + k currentpos) fnext = b / (1 + k xnext) delta = fcurr - fnext # Store delta for subsequent steps # We need to store delta in the loop state. # Update position using the constant difference rule # f(x{i+1}) = f(xi) - delta fcurr = b / (1 + k currentpos) ftarget = fcurr - delta # Avoid division by zero or negative density if ftarget <= 0: break # Solve for x{i+1} # 1 + k x{i+1} = b / ftarget # x{i+1} = (b / ftarget - 1) / k xnext = (b / ftarget - 1) / k # Update step for next iteration step = xnext - currentpos currentpos = xnext # Check bounds again for next iteration if not isinsidevolume(currentpos): break return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Instability of 1/x: Using f(x) = 1/x directly causes instability and under-sampling. If xi is too close to the current step size, the next step overflows, resulting in ill-conditioned under-sampling and noise. Weghorst Method Limitations: The Weghorst et al. [15] method results in only 32 sampling points, causing visible aliasing and low SSIM (~0.5575). Out-of-Bounds: Using normalized coordinates with dissimilar dimensions can cause out-of-bound buffer reading. The unnormalized coordinate system mitigates this. Parameter Sensitivity: The k value influences sampling quality by interfering with differences between consecutive step values. Typical optimal value is ~4. The b value does not affect the relative step differences. Time Complexity: The method reduces total sampling points compared to linear sampling. Execution time is typically < 1ms for the tested configurations, compared to > 1.6ms for linear sampling. Memory Complexity: Standard volume rendering memory requirements. The unnormalized coordinate system does not add significant overhead. Measured Performance: On an Intel quad-core 3.2GHz and NVIDIA GTX 1070, with k=4, the method achieved SSIM 0.9523, MSE 285.3498, and Time 0.908ms. Strengths: High quality (SSIM > 0.95) with fewer samples than linear methods. Stable step calculation compared to 1/x approaches. Limitations: Requires tuning of k. The unnormalized coordinate system is optional but recommended for dissimilar dimensions. Origin: The method is inspired by the work of Weghorst et al. [15], which used a monotonically decreasing function for sampling. The specific modification using f(x) = b/(1+kx) was proposed to address the instability and low sampling count of the original approach. History: The approach was tested on ultra-sound biomicroscopic (UBM) volumetric images of monkey ciliary muscles. Usage: Implemented in OpenCL kernels for GPU-based volume rendering. name: Ray-Centric Adaptive Step and Termination
head: Adaptive Ray Marching, Adaptive Step Size Control
body: Ray-Centric Adaptive Step and Termination adjusts the distance between samples along a ray based on local volume properties (such as density or gradient magnitude) to skip empty space and refine detail near boundaries. It differs from Adaptive Sampling by dynamically changing the step size \Delta t within a single ray cast rather than changing the number of rays or blocks, and from Two-stage NeRF Rendering by operating on explicit volumetric data structures rather than neural uncertainty estimates. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of varying the integration step size \Delta t along the ray parameter t. The step size is typically a function of the local scalar field value f(\mathbf{x}), its gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{x}), or the density \rho(\mathbf{x}). The general ray marching loop iterates t from t{near} to t{far}: 1. Step Calculation: Compute \Delta t based on local metrics. For density-based methods, \Delta t is often inversely proportional to density or gradient magnitude to maintain constant error bounds. 2. Termination: The loop terminates when the accumulated opacity \alpha exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1.0) or t exceeds t{far}. 3. Coherence: To maintain GPU thread coherence, step sizes are often quantized or limited to a small set of discrete values, preventing divergence in warp execution. Adaptive sampling improves rendering quality by varying the sampling rate based on local complexity, such as proximity to an isosurface or variance in the rendered result. It sets itself apart from siblings like Two-stage NeRF Rendering by often employing discrete rate changes or variance-based block analysis rather than neural network-based uncertainty estimation, and from Random Pixel Subsampling by actively increasing samples in noisy areas rather than just reducing them. Adaptive Sampling for Interaction maintains interactivity during user input by lowering the volume sampling rate, then re-rendering at a high rate once the action is completed. It differs from Adaptive Sampling and Adaptive Refinement for Volume Rendering by using a binary state switch (interaction vs. idle) rather than continuous error estimation, and from Two-stage NeRF Rendering by operating on traditional ray-casted volume data rather than neural representations. Definition Samples points along rays using adaptive sampling via nerfacc, with a fallback to uniform sampling for rays that receive too few samples. Algorithm 1. Compute t{near} and t{far} using ray-AABB intersection. Filter valid rays where t{far} > t{near}. 2. If no valid rays, return empty tensors for ts, te, ray\idx, and valid. 3. Call self.nerfaccestimator.sampling with valid ray\o, ray\d, t{near}, t{far}, and self.stepsize to get ray\idx, ts, te. 4. Convert ray\idx to torch.long. 5. If self.enablefallback is True, count samples per ray using torch.bincount(rayidx, minlength=Nv). 6. Identify rays with counts < self.fallbackwhensamples as lowids. 7. For low rays, compute uniform samples: t{s\fb} = t0[:, None] + k \cdot dt, t{e\fb} = t{s\fb} + dt, where k is range(K), dt = (t1-t0)/K, and clamp final t{e\fb} to t1. 8. Construct ray\idx\fb for the fallback samples. 9. Concatenate nerfacc samples with fallback samples. Adaptive step sizing originated in scientific visualization to handle the vast empty space in atmospheric and volumetric datasets. Early implementations used density-based heuristics to skip empty regions, while later GPU-optimized variants introduced discrete rate changes to mitigate thread divergence. It is widely used in real-time volume rendering of medical CT data and atmospheric clouds. AlanHsu314/CoroNeRFpublic, https://github.com/AlanHsu314/CoroNeRFpublic, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Sampling
head: Adaptive Sampling Rate, Adaptive Volume Sampling, Adaptive Sampling Strategy, Adaptive Sampling with Bricking
body: Adaptive sampling is a strategy that improves rendering quality and reduces computational cost by sampling non-homogeneous or high-detail regions more densely than homogeneous or low-detail regions. Unlike uniform sampling, which treats all pixels equally, adaptive sampling varies the sampling rate based on local complexity, such as proximity to an isosurface, local density, or variance in the rendered result. It sets itself apart from siblings like Two-stage NeRF Rendering by often employing discrete rate changes or variance-based block analysis rather than neural network-based uncertainty estimation, and from Random Pixel Subsampling by actively increasing samples in noisy areas rather than just reducing them. Adaptive sampling generally follows one of several patterns depending on the specific variant (e.g., variance-based, silhouette-based, or density-based). The core inputs are the volumetric dataset, ray origins/directions, and a target quality or performance metric. The output is the final pixel color and/or opacity. Block/Cell Metadata: Stores variance metrics or detail levels for regions of the volume. Film Buffer: Stores per-pixel luminance and luminance squares to estimate error. Sampling State: Tracks current sample count, zero-density counts, and convergence status. This method, often used with local solvers, reduces cost by casting rays in two steps. 1. Initial Cast: Cast a sparse set of rays (e.g., 12.5% or 32 rays per block) simultaneously for all pixels. In padded regions, 100% of rays are cast. 2. Variance Analysis: Perform variance analysis on the turned-on pixels for each block based on the initial render results. 3. Adaptive Cast: Identify blocks with high variance. Cast additional rays for these blocks. 4. Reconstruction: Run the local solver on each block to reconstruct the image, using padded region pixel information for convolution. This method uses adaptive step counts based on local density to skip empty space. 1. Initialization: Initialize colorpixel = vec3(0.0), density = 0.0, cloudtest = 0.0, zerodensitysamplecount = 0, and samplecout (e.g., 128). 2. Step Size Calculation: Calculate thick = length(endPoint - startPoint), stepsize = thick / samplecout, start = length(startPoint - rayOrigin), end = length(endPoint - rayOrigin). If end < start, swap start and end. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate t from start to end with stepsize. Calculate jittered position posInAtm using ray origin, direction, and jitter offset. Get weather data and relative height. Light Test: If cloudtest <= 0.0, perform a light test by sampling cloud density at a specific point. If cloudtest > 0.0, proceed to density accumulation. Density Accumulation: If cloudtest > 0.0: Increment samplepoint by testsize (where testsize = rayDirection / float(samplecout)) and divide by 8.0 (or 1.0 depending on implementation detail). Sample density at samplepoint using SampleCloudDensity. Track zero density samples: If sampleddensity == 0.0, increment zerodensitysamplecount. If zerodensitysamplecount != 6, add sampleddensity to density and sampleddensity 0.1 (or 0.07) to colorpixel. If sampleddensity != 0.0, calculate light energy based on precipitation and density along the light ray, then add to colorpixel. If zerodensitysamplecount == 6, reset cloudtest = 0.0 and zerodensitysamplecount = 0 to exit dense region mode. Termination: Break loop if density >= 1.0 to prevent over-saturation. 4. Return: Return colorpixel and update densityinout with final density. This method uses two discrete rates to improve intersection detection near silhouettes without diverging parallel execution pipelines. 1. Base Sampling: Cast rays at base sampling rate r0. 2. Threshold Check: For each sample, check if the sample value f is within a threshold \delta of the isovalue \rho (i.e., |f - \rho| < \delta). 3. Rate Adjustment: If the threshold is met, switch to maximum sampling rate r1 = n \cdot r0 (typically n=8). 4. Intersection Detection: Intersection is detected when f < \rho (assuming front-to-back and isosurface defined by f < \rho). This method varies sampling rate on a per-macrocell basis to maintain thread coherence on GPUs. 1. Metric Calculation: For each macrocell, compute m = \sqrt{dVar(f{cell})} / \sqrt{dVar(f{vol})}, where m is the ratio of max standard deviation of cell voxels to the entire volume. 2. Multiplier Calculation: Compute multiplier M = 2m - 1 + 1 (or similar positive integer mapping). 3. Step Size Variation: Use M to vary the sampling step size \Delta t. For uniform sampling, new rate is M\Delta t. For differential sampling, modify increments: \frac{\partial^2 TM}{\partial x^2} = \sum{i=1}^M a = \frac{M(M+1)}{2} a \frac{\partial TM}{\partial x} = Max + \frac{\partial^2 TM}{\partial x^2} + b. This method tracks per-pixel luminance squares to estimate relative standard error. 1. Tracking: Track per-pixel luminance squares in the film buffer. 2. Error Estimation: Report relative standard error for each pixel. 3. Convergence Check: In final renders, stop sampling converged pixels every 8 samples. In progressive passes, skip pixels whose 3x3 neighborhood is under the noise threshold. Target Frame Time: Desired frame budget (e.g., 32 ms). Sampling Rate: Initialized to 0.5, resets to 0.5 on new volume upload. Base Rate (r0): Specified by user; 1.0 corresponds to a single voxel. Multiplier (n): Constant multiple for max rate; typical value 8. Threshold (\delta): Quality parameter for silhouette detection; constant for distance fields, data-dependent for CT scans. Sample Count (sample\cout): Calculated as 128 - 64 \cdot \text{int}(\text{dot}(rayDirection, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0))). Pipeline Divergence: Completely adaptive sampling causes neighboring pixels in parallel pipelines to diverge, under-utilizing the texture cache. Solution: Use only two discrete rates. Missed Intersections: Discrete sampling may miss intersections if the segment between two successive samples crosses the isosurface twice. Guaranteed if gradient length is bounded by L: h = |f - \rho|/L. AMR Awareness: Standard adaptive sampling may severely under- or over-sample AMR data if not aware of the hierarchy. An optimization taking advantage of coherence in projections (often from sensing device blurring) by casting a sparse grid of rays (less than one per pixel) and adaptively increasing rays in high-complexity regions [Link to 1656-adaptive-sampling-sparse-grid.md]. A sampling strategy using two discrete rates (base r0 and max r1) to improve intersection detection near silhouettes without diverging parallel execution pipelines. It uses a threshold \delta to switch rates when |sample\value - isovalue| < \delta. Typical multiplier n=8. An adaptive sampling approach that guarantees the sampling frequency can adapt to the finest level cell size while keeping total sample counts tractable, combined with opacity correction. It is tailored for AMR data, unlike OSPRay's existing code which may under- or over-sample. An adaptive sampling strategy that tracks per-pixel luminance squares to estimate relative standard error, stopping converged pixels and skipping noisy neighborhoods. Measured relMSE on showcase scene: 0.0036 (uniform, extrapolated) vs 0.0024 (adaptive) at the same mean spp. Time Complexity: Depends on the variance/density distribution. Generally reduces total samples in low-detail regions, speeding up rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires additional buffers for variance analysis, error tracking, or block metadata. Performance: On the Asian Dragon dataset (512x256x256), with brick size 32 and adaptive sampling (r1=8r0), frame rates are 19.2 fps at sampling rate 0.25, 13.8 fps at 0.5, 10.2 fps at 1, and 6.9 fps at 2. Adaptive sampling with bricking achieves 80-85% of the performance of rendering without bricking and without adaptive sampling. Strengths: Significantly increases rendering speed for datasets with large empty or low-detail regions. Improves quality in high-detail areas. Limitations: Can cause thread divergence on GPUs if not constrained to discrete rates. Requires additional passes or analysis steps. Adaptive sampling originated as a response to the inefficiencies of uniform sampling in volume rendering, where homogeneous regions are over-sampled and detailed regions are under-sampled. It has been developed in various forms for different rendering pipelines, including GPU-based compressive rendering, real-time ray-casting of isosurfaces, and AMR data visualization. name: Adaptive Sampling for Interaction
head: Adaptive Sampling for Interactive Volume Rendering, Dynamic Sampling Rate, Interaction-aware Adaptive Sampling, Two-rate Interaction Sampling
body: Adaptive Sampling for Interaction is a technique to maintain interactivity during user input (such as transfer function editing) by lowering the volume sampling rate, then re-rendering at a high rate once the action is completed. It differs from Adaptive Sampling and Adaptive Refinement for Volume Rendering by using a binary state switch (interaction vs. idle) rather than continuous error estimation, and from Two-stage NeRF Rendering by operating on traditional ray-casted volume data rather than neural representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset, current transfer function, user interaction state (active/inactive). Output: Rendered image. Data Structures: interactionactive: Boolean flag indicating if the user is currently modifying parameters (e.g., transfer function). samplespervoxel: Integer or float specifying the sampling density. Parameters: High sampling rate: 6 to 10 samples per voxel. Low sampling rate: Not given in the sources. Algorithm: 1. Detect user interaction state. If the user is modifying the transfer function or other rendering parameters, set interactionactive = true. Otherwise, set interactionactive = false. 2. Determine the sampling rate: If interactionactive is true, use a low sampling rate (value not specified in sources). If interactionactive is false, use the high sampling rate of 6 to 10 samples per voxel. 3. Perform volume rendering using the determined sampling rate. 4. If interactionactive becomes false after being true, trigger a final re-render at the high sampling rate to restore visual quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolume(volumedata, transferfunction, userinputactive): """ Renders volume with adaptive sampling based on interaction state. Args: volumedata: The 3D scalar field. transferfunction: The current transfer function mapping. userinputactive: Boolean, True if user is currently interacting (e.g., editing TF). Returns: Image buffer. """ # Determine sampling rate based on interaction state if userinputactive: # Low sampling rate for interactivity. # Exact value not given in sources. samplespervoxel = LOWRATEVALUE # Placeholder for unspecified low rate else: # High sampling rate for quality samplespervoxel = 8.0 # Typical value from range 6-10 # Perform ray casting with the determined sampling rate image = raycast(volumedata, transferfunction, samplespervoxel) return image def handleuserinteraction(volumedata, transferfunction, userinputactive): """ Wrapper for interaction loop. """ # Render at low rate during interaction image = rendervolume(volumedata, transferfunction, userinputactive) display(image) if not userinputactive: # Re-render at high rate after action completes image = rendervolume(volumedata, transferfunction, userinputactive=False) display(image) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The transition from low to high sampling rate may cause a visible "pop-in" or latency spike if not handled smoothly. The sources do not specify a smoothing mechanism. The exact low sampling rate value is not provided, which may require empirical tuning. Uses coarse and fine neural networks for different stages, not sampling rate switching. Uses error metrics to adjust sampling, not interaction state. Subsamples pixels randomly, not based on interaction. Refines regions based on detail, not interaction. Uses temporal information, not interaction state. Changes resolution, not sampling rate. Combines sampling and ERT, not interaction-based switching. Undersamples based on content, not interaction. Time Complexity: During interaction, rendering time is reduced proportionally to the reduction in sampling rate. Post-interaction, rendering time returns to the high-rate cost. Measured Performance: At the high sampling rate (6-10 samples/voxel), frame updates take nearly two seconds on an Octane2 workstation and nearly one second on a GeForce3 GPU. Strengths: Maintains interactivity during parameter editing by reducing computational load. Limitations: Visual quality is reduced during interaction (coarser surfaces). The exact low sampling rate is not specified, making performance prediction difficult. When to use: When user interaction (e.g., transfer function editing) requires real-time feedback and high-quality rendering is not critical during the interaction phase. When not to use: When continuous high-quality visualization is required during interaction. This technique was introduced by Kindermann et al. in 2001 in the paper "Interactive Volume Rendering Using Multi-Dimensional Transfer Functions". It was developed to address the performance bottleneck of high-quality volume rendering during user interaction, specifically for transfer function exploration. The method leverages the observation that surface size and location remain apparent even with lower sampling rates, providing sufficient feedback for users. name: Kernel Selection
head: Coarse Rasterization for Ellipsoid Selection, Ellipsoid Kernel Selection, Gaussian Kernel Selection, Optional coarse rasterization stage, Ray Tracing Kernel Selection
body: Kernel selection is a pre-processing and filtering strategy used in volume rendering with Gaussian ellipsoids to reduce computational cost by tracing only a subset of primitives that contribute non-trivially to the final image. It solves the problem of expensive full-scene ray tracing by discarding distant or low-density ellipsoids before the blending stage. Unlike Ray Intersection Selector (RIS) which analytically computes precise ray-primitive intersections to identify high-density regions, kernel selection relies on a coarse rasterization of bounding boxes and density thresholds to select a fixed number of nearest kernels per pixel. Inputs: Set of N Gaussian ellipsoids, each defined by center \mathbf{c}k, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}k, and opacity/density parameters. Camera parameters: focal length F, image dimensions h \times w. Selection parameters: density threshold \eta, maximum number of kernels to trace K'. Outputs: A mapping from each pixel (or low-resolution tile) to a subset of at most K' ellipsoid indices to be traced. Data Structures: PixelKernels: A 2D array of lists, indexed by (u, v), storing indices of selected ellipsoids. Dimensions are W/8 \times H/8 (low-resolution grid). CandidateList: A list of tuples (distance, kernelindex) for ellipsoids passing the density check. Steps: 1. Projection and Bounding Box Calculation: For each ellipsoid k: a. Project the center \mathbf{c}k to screen coordinates. b. Compute the distance dz from the camera to the center of the ellipsoid. c. Compute the height bh and width bw of the maximum bounding box of the ellipsoid in 2D screen coordinates using: [bh \quad bw \quad \cdot] = \frac{\log(-\eta)}{dz} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Omega} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Omega} where \boldsymbol{\Omega} is the projection matrix from camera coordinate to screen: \boldsymbol{\Omega} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{2\cdot F}{h} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2\cdot F}{w} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} 2. Coarse Rasterization: a. Initialize PixelKernels for a resolution 8\times smaller than the final image (i.e., width W/8, height H/8). b. Rasterize the bounding boxes [bh, bw] onto this low-resolution grid. c. For each pixel (u, v) in the low-res grid, record all ellipsoids whose bounding boxes cover it. This creates a preliminary set of candidate kernels for each pixel. 3. Density Filtering: a. For each candidate kernel k associated with a pixel, evaluate if it has a non-trivial contribution. b. Record ellipsoids where the maximum density e qk > \eta. The term e qk refers to the peak density value of the Gaussian kernel. c. If the source implies qk is the density value, the condition is qk > \eta. The text states "maximum density e qk > \eta", which likely denotes the exponential density term or simply the density value qk compared against threshold \eta. Given the formula uses \log(-\eta), \eta is a small positive fraction (e.g., 0.01), so -\eta is negative, making \log(-\eta) undefined in real numbers unless \eta is treated as a magnitude or the formula implies \log(1/\eta) or similar. However, we must stick to the source text: "maximum density e qk > \eta". We interpret this as checking if the kernel's density exceeds \eta. 4. Distance Sorting and Selection: a. For each pixel, collect all recorded ellipsoids from Step 3. b. Calculate the distance lk from the ray origin (camera center) to the 1D Gaussian center of each ellipsoid. c. Sort the recorded kernels by lk in ascending order. d. Select the K' nearest ellipsoids. 5. Assignment: Assign the selected K' kernels to the corresponding pixel in PixelKernels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computeboundingboxdims(dz, eta, Omega, Sigmainv): """ Computes height and width of the bounding box in screen coordinates. dz: distance from camera to ellipsoid center eta: density threshold Omega: 3x3 projection matrix Sigmainv: 2x2 inverse covariance matrix (projected) Returns: (bh, bw) """ # Note: The source formula [bh bw.] =... suggests a vector multiplication. # Assuming Sigmainv is the relevant 2x2 part or the formula implies extracting the first two components. # The source writes: [bh bw.] = (log(-eta)/dz) Omega Sigmainv Omega # This implies Sigmainv is 3x3 or the result is projected. # We assume standard 3D covariance projection to 2D screen space for the bounding box. # However, to be strictly faithful to the provided text which uses Sigma^{-1} directly: term = math.log(-eta) / dz # The source formula is ambiguous regarding dimensions. # Omega is 3x3. Sigma^{-1} is likely 3x3 (3D covariance inverse). # The result [bh bw.] is a 3-vector where the third component is ignored or used for depth. # Let's assume Sigmainv is 3x3. # Vector v = Omega @ Sigmainv @ Omega # This results in a 3x3 matrix. The formula likely implies taking the diagonal or specific elements. # However, the text says "height bh and width bw... computed via: [bh bw.] =..." # This notation usually means the first two elements of the resulting vector/matrix diagonal. # Let's assume the operation yields a vector where the first two components are bh and bw. # Re-reading carefully: "compute the height bh and width bw... via: [bh bw.] =..." # It is highly likely that Sigma^{-1} here refers to the 2D projected covariance inverse, # or the formula is a simplified representation. # Given the constraint to implement from text, we follow the literal matrix mult. # If Sigma is 3x3, Omega is 3x3. # M = Omega @ Sigmainv @ Omega # bh = M[0,0] term ? Or is it a vector result? # The notation [bh bw.] suggests a column vector. # Let's assume the result of the matrix multiplication is treated as a vector of scales? # Actually, bounding box size is usually derived from the eigenvalues or diagonal of the projected covariance. # The source formula is specific. We implement it as written. # To avoid guessing the dimensionality mismatch, we note that in PyTorch3D-style rendering, # the bounding box is often computed from the projected covariance. # We will implement the matrix multiplication as given. res = term (Omega @ Sigmainv @ Omega) # The source says [bh bw.] = res. # This implies bh = res[0,0] and bw = res[1,1] if res is diagonal, # or perhaps res is a vector. # Given Omega is diagonal-like in the source (mostly), and Sigma is symmetric. # Let's assume the result is a vector where the first two elements are the dims. # But the RHS is a matrix. # Correction: The source might mean the diagonal elements. # "height bh and width bw... computed via: [bh bw.] =..." # We will extract the diagonal elements of the resulting matrix scaled by the term. bh = res[0, 0] bw = res[1, 1] return bh, bw def kernelselection(ellipsoids, cameraparams, eta, Kprime): """ ellipsoids: list of dicts with keys 'center', 'covariance', 'density' cameraparams: dict with 'F', 'h', 'w' eta: float, density threshold Kprime: int, max kernels per pixel """ F = cameraparams['F'] h = cameraparams['h'] w = cameraparams['w'] # Projection matrix Omega Omega = np.array([ [2F/h, 0, 0], [0, 2F/w, 0], [0, 0, 1] ]) # Low-res grid dimensions lowh = h // 8 loww = w // 8 # Initialize pixel-to-kernel mapping pixelkernels = [[] for in range(lowh loww)] # Step 1 & 2: Project and Rasterize for k, ell in enumerate(ellipsoids): center = ell['center'] # [x, y, z] in camera coords cov = ell['covariance'] # 3x3 matrix dz = center[2] # Distance from camera (assuming camera looks down -z or z is depth) # Compute inverse covariance Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(cov) # Compute bounding box dimensions # Note: log(-eta) requires eta < 0 if strictly interpreted, but eta is 0.01. # The source likely means log(1/eta) or -log(eta) or eta is negative in their convention. # Source says: "eta is the threshold for maximum volume density" and "eta = 0.01". # Formula: log(-eta). If eta=0.01, -eta=-0.01, log is complex. # This is a known issue in the source text. We assume the magnitude |eta| or 1/eta. # However, to be faithful, we use math.log(abs(eta)) or similar if allowed by. # Use abs(eta) to avoid complex numbers, assuming eta is a positive magnitude threshold. logterm = math.log(abs(eta)) / dz bh, bw = computeboundingboxdims(dz, eta, Omega, Sigmainv) # Determine screen coordinates of center # Project center using Omega centerhom = np.array([center[0], center[1], center[2]]) centerscreen = Omega @ centerhom # Map to low-res grid # Assuming centerscreen[0] and centerscreen[1] are in normalized or pixel coords? # Omega maps to screen. Usually screen coords are in pixels. # Let's assume centerscreen[0] is x-pixel, centerscreen[1] is y-pixel. cx = centerscreen[0] cy = centerscreen[1] # Convert to low-res grid index # Bounding box extends bh/2 and bw/2 from center # We need to map pixel coords to low-res indices # Low-res pixel size is 8x8 in high-res lowcx = int(cx / 8) lowcy = int(cy / 8) # Rasterize bounding box onto low-res grid # Calculate extent in low-res pixels # bh and bw are in screen coordinates (pixels). # Low-res grid cell size is 8 pixels. halfbhlr = (bh / 2) / 8 halfbwlr = (bw / 2) / 8 mincy = max(0, int(lowcy - halfbhlr)) maxcy = min(lowh - 1, int(lowcy + halfbhlr)) mincx = max(0, int(lowcx - halfbwlr)) maxcx = min(loww - 1, int(lowcx + halfbwlr)) for y in range(mincy, maxcy + 1): for x in range(mincx, maxcx + 1): idx = y loww + x pixelkernels[idx].append(k) # Step 3 & 4: Filter and Select finalselection = {} # Map from pixelidx to list of kernel indices for idx, candidates in enumerate(pixelkernels): if not candidates: continue # Filter by density validcandidates = [] for k in candidates: ell = ellipsoids[k] # Check density condition: max density e qk > eta # Assuming ell['density'] holds qk or the peak density value # Source says "maximum density e qk > eta". # We assume ell['peakdensity'] > eta. if ell.get('peakdensity', 0) > eta: # Calculate distance to 1D Gaussian center # lk is distance from camera to center center = ell['center'] lk = np.linalg.norm(center) validcandidates.append((lk, k)) # Sort by distance validcandidates.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Select K' nearest selected = [k for, k in validcandidates[:Kprime]] if selected: finalselection[idx] = selected return finalselection Parameters: K': Number of nearest kernels to select per pixel. Default: 20. \eta: Density threshold. Default: 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inadequate K': Leads to dark regions around the boundary of kernels due to hard cutoff of the boundary. Threshold \eta: Decreasing \eta makes the object appear denser (less transparent) but requires a higher K' to avoid artifacts. Formula Domain: The formula uses \log(-\eta). Since \eta is positive (0.01), this is mathematically undefined in real numbers. The implementation must use \log(1/\eta) or \log(|\eta|) with appropriate sign handling, or assume \eta is negative in the source's convention. Replaces stochastic sampling with analytical ray-primitive intersection detection. Chooses this when precise surface reconstruction is needed without auxiliary networks. Uses orthogonal projections to clip occluded geometry. Adjusts sampling density based on image variance. Stops ray marching when opacity is sufficient. Optimizes the integration step during inference. Handles missing data in voxel grids. Parallelizes sampling along a single ray. Dynamically updates acceleration structures. Uses temporal coherence for sampling. Renders differentially over time. Culls invisible primitives. Distributes rendering across devices. General optimization methods. Traverses hierarchical voxel grids. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of ray-tracing operations from O(N) to O(P \cdot K'), where P is the number of pixels and K' is the selected kernel count. The coarse rasterization step is O(N) for projection and O(P) for rasterization. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the low-resolution pixel-to-kernel mapping, O(P). Measured Performance: Selecting 10% of ellipsoids significantly reduces computational cost. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective at removing distant/low-density primitives; reduces artifacts compared to random sampling if K' is sufficient. Limitations: Hard cutoff at K' can cause boundary artifacts (dark regions); sensitive to the choice of K' and \eta; coarse rasterization may miss small but important kernels if the low-res grid is too coarse. When to Use: When rendering large scenes with many Gaussian ellipsoids and computational budget is limited. When Not to Use: When high fidelity at object boundaries is critical and K' cannot be increased; when kernels are very small and sparse. Kernel selection was introduced in the context of differentiable volume rendering using Gaussian ellipsoids, specifically in the VoGE (Volume Gaussian Ellipsoid) renderer. It is part of a coarse-to-fine rendering strategy designed to efficiently render Gaussian ellipsoids by gradually reducing the number of ellipsoids interacting with viewing rays. The method builds on standard rasterization techniques (e.g., PyTorch3D) to perform a coarse selection before the more expensive ray tracing stage. name: Ray Intersection Selector (RIS)
head: IRIS (Intersection-aware Ray-based Implicit Editable Scenes)
body: Ray Intersection Selector (RIS) is a sampling strategy for neural rendering that replaces stochastic volumetric sampling with analytical ray-primitive intersection detection to identify high-density regions for volumetric rendering. It solves the problem of empty space processing and costly 3D neighbor lookups by generating meaningful samples in a single pass, eliminating the need for auxiliary networks or voxel grids. Unlike Kernel Selection which selects a subset of Gaussoids based on density thresholds, RIS analytically determines precise intersection points between camera rays and 3D Gaussians, ensuring that every neural query contributes directly to surface reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N Neural Anchors (primitives) \mathcal{P}, a camera ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, and a distance threshold \tau{\text{dist}}. Output: A sorted sequence of intersection points (samples) \{xk\} along the ray, and aggregated neural features for volumetric rendering. Data Structures The scene is parameterized as a set of N Neural Anchors. Each anchor i consists of: 1. A 3D normal distribution defined by mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i. 2. A logit parameter \omegai \in \mathbb{R} controlling opacity. 3. A latent feature vector \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^D. The covariance is factorized into a rotation matrix Ri (stored as a quaternion) and a scaling vector Si. Algorithm Steps 1. Proxy Geometry Construction: Bound each Gaussian primitive i with an affine-transformed icosahedron to create a proxy geometry. 2. Ray-Primitive Intersection: Use the OptiX API to perform ray tracing against the proxy geometry, offloading intersection logic to dedicated RT cores. Solve the intersection equations for a ray traversing an oriented ellipsoid to determine precise interaction points. 3. Sample Generation: Generate a sorted sequence of intersection points (samples) \{xk\} only where density contribution is guaranteed to be significant, skipping empty space. 4. Ray-Coherent Aggregation (RCA): For each sample point xk, define a neighborhood window Wk of size W = 2N + 1 indices centered at k: \{k-N, \dots, k, \dots, k+N\}. 5. Validity Masking: Apply a binary validity mask M{kj} to enforce spatial locality. A neighbor j \in Wk is valid only if: It belongs to the same ray index. The Euclidean distance \|\mathbf{x}k - \boldsymbol{\mu}j\|2 is below a fixed threshold \tau{\text{dist}}. 6. Feature Aggregation: For every valid neighbor j, compute the unnormalized logit l{kj} based on the Mahalanobis distance \Delta^2(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\mu}j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j). Aggregate weights w{kj} are obtained by normalizing these logits (e.g., via softmax). Synthesize a continuous latent vector \mathbf{z}k by weighting the latent features \mathbf{f}j of valid neighbors: \mathbf{z}k = \sum{j \in Wk, M{kj}=1} w{kj} \mathbf{f}j 7. Neural Decoding: Use shallow Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to decode the aggregated continuous latent vector \mathbf{z}k into view-dependent color and material density \sigma. 8. Volumetric Rendering: The neural density \sigma is spatially modulated by the explicit Gaussian opacity \omegai and integrated via point-based volumetric rendering to produce the final image. Args: anchors: List of N Neural Anchors. Each anchor is a dict with keys: 'mu': (3,) numpy array, mean position. 'Sigma': (3,3) numpy array, covariance matrix. 'omega': float, logit opacity. 'f': (D,) numpy array, latent feature vector. 'proxyicosahedron': Object supporting ray intersection test. rayorigin: (3,) numpy array, camera ray origin. raydirection: (3,) numpy array, camera ray direction (normalized). taudist: float, Euclidean distance threshold for validity mask. Returns: samples: List of dicts, each containing: 'x': (3,) numpy array, intersection point. 'sigma': float, decoded density. 'color': (3,) numpy array, decoded color. 'opacity': float, modulated opacity. """ # Step 1 & 2: Ray-Primitive Intersection using OptiX (simulated here) # In implementation, this calls OptiX API to trace against proxy icosahedrons. # Returns a list of intersection distances t sorted in ascending order. intersectiondistances = traceoptixrays(anchors, rayorigin, raydirection) # Step 3: Generate sorted sequence of samples samples = [] for t in intersectiondistances: x = rayorigin + t raydirection # Step 4: Define neighborhood window in the sorted list # Note: In a full batch implementation, this is vectorized. # Here we assume we are processing one ray at a time for clarity, # but the window logic applies to the global sorted list of all ray intersections. # For a single ray, the window is simply the local neighbors in the list. # However, the source describes a global sorted list across all rays for RCA. # We assume 'anchors' and 'intersectiondistances' are part of a larger batch context. # For this single-ray function, we approximate the window by looking at nearby anchors # based on distance along the ray, or assume the caller provides the window indices. # Simplified RCA for single ray context: # Find neighbors in the anchor list that are close to x along the ray # The source specifies a window of indices in the SORTED SEQUENCE of intersections. # Let's assume we have access to the global sorted list 'allintersections' # and the index 'k' of the current intersection in that list. # Since this function is self-contained, we simulate the windowing by # selecting anchors whose centers are within a certain range along the ray. # This is a simplification of the strided tensor operation described. # Step 5 & 6: Ray-Coherent Aggregation validneighbors = [] for i, anchor in enumerate(anchors): mu = anchor['mu'] # Check validity mask dist = math.sqrt(np.sum((x - mu)2)) if dist < taudist: # Compute Mahalanobis distance diff = x - mu # Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(anchor['Sigma']) # Not given in sources, assumed available # mahaldistsq = diff @ Sigmainv @ diff # For implementation completeness, we assume a standard Gaussian weight # based on the source's mention of Mahalanobis distance. # Since exact Sigmainv usage isn't fully detailed in the snippet, # we use a placeholder for the weight calculation logic. weight = computemahalanobisweight(x, mu, anchor['Sigma']) validneighbors.append((i, weight, anchor['f'])) # Aggregate features if not validneighbors: # Fallback or empty feature if no neighbors zk = np.zeros(anchors[0]['f'].shape) if anchors else np.array([]) else: # Normalize weights totalweight = sum(w for, w, in validneighbors) if totalweight == 0: zk = np.zeros(anchors[0]['f'].shape) if anchors else np.array([]) else: zk = np.zeros(anchors[0]['f'].shape) if anchors else np.array([]) for, w, f in validneighbors: zk += (w / totalweight) f # Step 7: Neural Decoding # Shallow MLPs decode zk into color and density # Assuming a simple linear decode for pseudocode completeness sigma = decodedensity(zk) color = decodecolor(zk) # Step 8: Modulate by Gaussian opacity # The source says "neural density sigma is spatially modulated by the explicit Gaussian opacity omegai" # Since we aggregated features, we might have an aggregated opacity or use the anchor's opacity. # The source implies the final integration uses this modulated density. # We'll assume the decoded sigma is the base, and we modulate it. # However, the source says "modulated by... omegai". # In the aggregation step, we aggregated features fi. # We need to aggregate or select an opacity. # Let's assume we also aggregate opacity or use the primary anchor's opacity. # For simplicity, we use the opacity of the closest valid neighbor or the anchor associated with the intersection. # The source doesn't specify how omega is aggregated, only that sigma is modulated by it. # We will assume the decoded sigma is already the final density for the sample point. samples.append({ 'x': x, 'sigma': sigma, 'color': color, 'opacity': 1.0 # Placeholder for omega modulation logic }) return samples def computemahalanobisweight(x, mu, Sigma): """ Computes weight based on Mahalanobis distance. """ diff = x - mu # Inverse of covariance matrix try: Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: return 0.0 mahaldistsq = diff @ Sigmainv @ diff # Weight is typically exp(-0.5 mahaldistsq) return math.exp(-0.5 mahaldistsq) def decodedensity(z): """ Placeholder for shallow MLP decoding density. """ return max(0.0, np.dot(z, [1.0, 0.0, 0.0])) # Simplified def decodecolor(z): """ Placeholder for shallow MLP decoding color. """ return np.clip(np.dot(z, [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), 0.0, 1.0) # Simplified Parameters \tau{\text{dist}}: A fixed Euclidean distance threshold used in the validity mask to ensure spatial locality between samples. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Empty Space Processing: Standard volumetric sampling queries empty space, wasting computation. RIS handles this by only evaluating structurally meaningful intersection points. Geometric Discontinuity: Naive index-based aggregation along the sorted ray list risks blending geometrically disjoint objects (e.g., foreground and background) that are adjacent in the list but distant in 3D space. This is mitigated by the validity mask M{kj}. Precision: The method relies on analytical intersection equations. Precision depends on the accuracy of the ray-triangle intersection within the OptiX API and the numerical stability of the covariance matrix inversion for Mahalanobis distance. Time Complexity: RIS operates in a single pass, linearly scaling with the number of primitives and rays. It avoids the O(N \log N) or O(N^2) costs of KNN searches and the overhead of auxiliary network queries. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for N Neural Anchors and their proxy geometries. No auxiliary voxel grids or occupancy grids are needed. Measured Performance: On the NeRF Synthetic dataset, IRIS achieves 6.038 FPS, approximately 30x higher than EKS (0.183 FPS). Training time is reduced to 51 minutes compared to EKS's 26 hours. Strengths: Eliminates empty space processing; bypasses costly 3D KNN lookups; enables high-fidelity rendering with explicit geometry; supports topology-agnostic editing and physics simulation. Limitations: Requires GPU RT cores for optimal performance (OptiX); relies on the accuracy of the proxy geometry bounds. When to Use: When high rendering throughput is required and the scene is represented by explicit Gaussian primitives. Suitable for interactive editing and physics simulation. When Not to Use: When hardware lacks dedicated RT cores; when the scene representation is purely implicit without explicit primitives. IRIS (Intersection-aware Ray-based Implicit Editable Scenes) was introduced to address the computational inefficiencies of standard ray marching and stochastic sampling in neural rendering. It builds on the paradigms of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), combining the view-dependent effects of NeRF with the explicit, editable nature of 3DGS. The method was developed to enable efficient and interactive scene editing while maintaining high visual fidelity. name: Empty-space skipping
head: Block Empty Space Skipping, Chebyshev Empty Space Skipping, Empty Region Skipping, Occupancy Grid Pruning
body: Empty-space skipping (ESS) is a ray marching optimization that accelerates volume rendering by skipping regions of the scene that are empty or occluded, thereby reducing the number of samples required to evaluate the radiance field. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GL-NeRF or VoISDF by explicitly maintaining auxiliary data structures (occupancy grids or distance maps) to prune traversal, whereas other siblings may rely on hierarchical tree structures or adaptive sampling rates without explicit empty-region culling. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, volume dimensions, sampling factor, and precomputed occupancy/distance maps. Outputs: Accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Occupancy Grid / Distance Map: A 3D texture (texOccupancyMap or texDistanceMap) storing precomputed values, accessed via texelFetch. texOccupancyMap: Stores binary occupancy (1 if occupied, 0 if empty). texDistanceMap: Stores distance to the nearest occupied voxel. Parameters: essType: Integer flag. 1 = Block Empty Space Skipping; 2 = Chebyshev Empty Space Skipping. alphathre: Opacity threshold for empty regions. Typical value: 10^{-2}. earlystopeps: Transmittance threshold for early termination. Typical value: 10^{-4}. samplingfactor: Controls step count relative to volume dimensions. ditheringMode: Integer flag for ray dithering. 1 = procedural noise; 2 = sampled from texNoise texture. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Calculate the number of steps and the step vector. n{\text{steps}} = \lceil \text{dim}{\max} \times \text{ray\length} \times \text{sampling\factor} \rceil \text{step\vector} = \frac{\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|} \times \frac{\text{ray\length}}{n{\text{steps}} - 1} Handle degenerate rays (infinite, NaN, or length > \sqrt{3}) by terminating immediately. 2. Distance Map Coordinate Setup: Compute mapping parameters between volume space and distance map texture space. \text{dim\distance\map} = \text{textureSize}(\text{texDistanceMap}, 0).\text{xyz} \text{block\size} = \lceil \text{volumeSize} / \text{dim\distance\map} \rceil \text{volume\to\distance\map} = \text{volumeSize} / (\text{block\size} \times \text{dim\distance\map}) \text{step\dist\texel} = \text{step\vector} \times \text{volumeSize} / \text{block\size} \text{step\dist\texel\inv} = 1.0 / \text{step\dist\texel} 3. Dithering (Optional): Compute a random offset to reduce banding artifacts. If ditheringMode == 1: \text{random} = \text{fract}(\sin(\text{gl\FragCoord}.x \times 12.9898 + \text{gl\FragCoord}.y \times 78.233) \times 43758.5453) If ditheringMode == 2: \text{random} = \text{texture}(\text{texNoise}, \text{gl\FragCoord.xy} / 256).r 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate with index i. For each step: a. Sampling Position: \text{samplingPos} = \mathbf{o} + (i + \text{random}) \times \text{step\vector} b. Map to Distance Map Coordinates: \text{pos\distance\map} = \text{volume\to\distance\map} \times \text{samplingPos} u = \text{pos\distance\map} \times \text{dim\distance\map} ui = \text{clamp}(\lfloor u \rfloor, 0, \text{dim\distance\map} - 1) c. Fetch Distance/Occupancy: Determine index based on ray direction signs for directional distance maps (if applicable): \text{distance\map\idx} = (\mathbf{d}.z < 0 ? 1: 0) + (\mathbf{d}.y < 0 ? 2: 0) + (\mathbf{d}.x < 0 ? 4: 0) Fetch value: If essType == 1 (Block): \text{dist} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{texOccupancyMap}, ui, 0).x If essType == 2 (Chebyshev): \text{dist} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{texDistanceMap}, ui, 0).x d. Calculate Skip Delta: Compute fractional offset for block alignment: r = \text{clamp}(ui - u, -1.0, 0.0) If essType == 1 (Block ESS): i{\text{delta\xyz}} = (\text{step}(0.0, \text{step\dist\texel\inv}) + r) \times \text{step\dist\texel\inv} If essType == 2 (Chebyshev ESS): i{\text{delta\xyz}} = (\text{step}(0.0, -\text{step\dist\texel\inv}) + \text{sign}(\text{step\dist\texel\inv}) \times \text{dist} + r) \times \text{step\dist\texel\inv} Update loop index: i{\text{delta}} = \max(1, \lceil \min(i{\text{delta\xyz}}.x, i{\text{delta\xyz}}.y, i{\text{delta\xyz}}.z) \rceil) i \leftarrow i + i{\text{delta}} e. Backtracking / Empty Space Handling: If dist == 0 (empty space reached): i{\text{delta\backwards}} = -\lceil \text{sampling\factor} \rceil \text{skipping} = \text{false} i = \max(i + i{\text{delta\backwards}}, i{\min}) f. Volume Evaluation (if not skipped): If ESS is disabled or the region is occupied: 1. Get voxel value: voxelValue = getVolumeIntensityValue(samplingPos.xyz + 0.5/volumeSize, volumeSize, 1.0/volumeSize, false). 2. Transfer Function: color = texture(texITF, vec2(voxelValue + 0.5/dimITF[0], 0.5/dimITF[1])).rgba. 3. Gamma Correction: color.a = pow(color.a, gamma) if enabled. 4. Gradient/Lighting: Compute normal from gradient, apply diffuse/specular lighting. 5. Composite: \text{color}.a = \text{clamp}(1.0 \times (1.0 - (1.0 - \text{color}.a)^{\text{sampling\factor\inv}}), 0.0, 1.0) \text{color}.xyz \times= \text{color}.a \text{out\color} \leftarrow \text{out\color} + (1.0 - \text{out\color}.a) \times \text{color} 5. Early Ray Termination (ERT): If outcolor.a > 0.98 and ERT is enabled, set outcolor.a = 1.0 and break loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def step(edge, x): """GLSL step: 0.0 if x < edge, else 1.0""" return 1.0 if x >= edge else 0.0 def sign(x): """GLSL sign: 1.0 if x > 0, -1.0 if x < 0, else 0.0""" if x > 0: return 1.0 if x < 0: return -1.0 return 0.0 def clamp(val, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(val, hi)) def fetch3dtexture(tex, coords): """Simulates GLSL texelFetch(tex, ivec3, 0).x for a 3D list of lists of lists.""" x, y, z = coords x = clamp(x, 0, len(tex) - body: This method accelerates volume rendering by dividing the volume into coarse grid elements (macrocells) and precomputing a boolean or aggregate value for each to identify and skip regions containing only zero-density cells during ray marching. It builds on the parent Empty-space skipping by applying the concept to a fixed coarse grid hierarchy rather than dynamic traversal structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A structured volume dataset, a transfer function mapping density to opacity/color, and a set of camera rays. Output: Rendered image with reduced computational load in empty regions. Data Structures: Macrocell Grid: A 3D array aligned with the volume, where each element corresponds to a macrocell. Macrocell Values: Each macrocell stores a precomputed boolean indicating if the surface passes through it, or an aggregate density value computed from its constituent fine cells. If the value indicates zero density, the macrocell is considered empty. Steps: 1. Precomputation: For each macrocell in the coarse grid, compute the aggregate density value or boolean skip flag from its constituent fine cells based on the transfer function densities. 2. Ray Traversal: For each pixel, generate a ray and use a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (3DDDA) to traverse the macrocell grid. 3. Macrocell Check: At each macrocell intersection, fetch the precomputed boolean or aggregate value. 4. Skip Decision: If the macrocell contains only zero-density cells (boolean is false or aggregate is zero), skip processing the entire macrocell and advance the ray to the next macrocell boundary. 5. Marching: If the macrocell is not empty, perform standard ray marching within the macrocell, sampling fine cells and accumulating opacity/color. 6. Termination: Stop when the ray exits the volume. Formulas: Let M{ijk} be the aggregate density or boolean flag of macrocell at indices (i,j,k). Let C{lmn} be the density of fine cell at indices (l,m,n). Skip condition: If M{ijk} = 0 (or boolean is false), skip macrocell. Aggregation method: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Macrocell Size: The number of voxels per macrocell dimension. 23 voxels per macrocell is recommended for best performance; 13, 43, and 83 are also tested. Threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead Dominance: Performance degrades if the fraction of skippable macrocells is small, because the extra memory access for retrieving macrocell values and condition checks per coarse element adds overhead without sufficient savings. Transfer Function Dependency: Performance gains depend heavily on the transfer function, as macrocell values are computed from transfer function densities. Dataset Variability: On datasets with very few zero-density macrocells (e.g., Engine dataset with 12) or high overhead per check (e.g., Agulhas dataset with 1,395,619 skipped), macrocell skipping can be slower than standard ray marching. It solves the host-GPU transfer bottleneck and high depth complexity of prior proxy-box methods by generating the boundary geometry entirely on the GPU and using native RTX hardware for ray-triangle intersection. Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA is a ray traversal technique that accelerates volume rendering by combining a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) for coarse macrocell traversal with adaptive step sizing based on opacity upper bounds. It solves the problem of inefficient sampling in sparse or low-opacity regions by skipping empty macrocells entirely and reducing sample counts in low-opacity ones. Unlike its parent Ray Marcher with Macrocell Empty Space Skipping, which primarily focuses on binary empty-space skipping, this method introduces granularity by adapting the step size within non-empty cells. It differs from Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping by using a regular grid structure rather than a mesh. An optimization that reduces the number of local rays by trimming each macro-cell to the smallest cuboid containing its portions of the iso-surfaces, rather than projecting the entire macro-cell. It works by initializing a cuboid to size zero and iterating through all cells of the macro-cell; whenever a surface cell is encountered, the cuboid is extended to the smallest necessary size so that it contains this cell. The resulting cuboid is then projected instead of the macro-cell. This saves about 28 percent of overall rendering time on average, though this gain is dependent on the data set and viewpoint position. Time Complexity: Precomputation is O(N) where N is the number of fine cells. Ray marching time is reduced proportionally to the fraction of skipped macrocells. Memory Complexity: O(M) where M is the number of macrocells. Measured Performance: MRI Dataset: Increasing skipped macrocells from 0 to 1,190 reduces rendering time from 44.83 ms to 26.05 ms. Heptane Dataset: Improves time from 51.92 ms to 46.3 ms. Advection Dataset: Improves time from 58.14 ms to 46.29 ms. Engine Dataset: Only 12 macrocells have zero density, leading to worse performance (43.61 ms with macrocell vs 41.46 ms without). Agulhas Dataset: 1,395,619 skipped macrocells, but performance is worse (55.34 ms with macrocell vs 41.53 ms without) due to overhead. Fiber Surface Dataset: Performance without macrocells is 4x-8x slower than with 23-voxel macrocells. Strengths: Simple implementation, effective for sparse volumes with large empty regions. Limitations: Overhead can dominate if skipping fraction is low. Performance is transfer-function dependent. When to Use: Sparse volumes with significant empty space. When Not to Use: Dense volumes or when the transfer function results in few zero-density macrocells. The method originates from research on direct multifield volume ray casting of fiber surfaces and direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement data. It was developed as an optimization to handle sparse data and improve rendering performance by avoiding unnecessary computations in transparent regions. It is used in interactive fiber surface exploration and tree-based AMR volume rendering pipelines.
