name: Macro-Cell Trimming
head: Culling Empty Cap-Level Macrocells
body: Macro-cell trimming is an optimization that reduces the number of local rays by trimming each macro-cell to the smallest cuboid containing its portions of the iso-surfaces, rather than projecting the entire macro-cell. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping by operating on axis-aligned bounding boxes derived from cell occupancy rather than explicit mesh geometry, and from Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by focusing on pre-projection culling of the pixel footprint rather than adaptive step sizing during traversal. Inputs: A macro-cell containing a grid of cells (typically at the finest available octree depth, i.e., cap nodes). An isovalue threshold defining the iso-surface. The spatial bounds of the macro-cell. Outputs: A trimmed bounding cuboid (axis-aligned bounding box) that tightly encloses all cells within the macro-cell intersecting the isovalue. A reduced set of pixels (u,v slice extents) for ray casting. Data Structures: Macro-cell Grid: A 3D array of cells. Each cell contains a scalar value (density or field value). Trimmed Cuboid: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). Initialized to an invalid or zero-size state. Steps: 1. Initialize Cuboid: Set the trimmed cuboid to a size of zero or an invalid state. 2. Iterate Cells: Loop through all cells within the macro-cell. 3. Check Iso-surface Intersection: For each cell, determine if it contains the isovalue (i.e., if the cell's value crosses the threshold). 4. Extend Cuboid: If a cell contains the isovalue: Calculate the spatial bounds of the cell. Update the trimmed cuboid's min/max coordinates to include the cell's bounds. Specifically, update x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}, z{min}, z{max} to the minimum/maximum values encountered so far. 5. Compute Slice Extents: After iterating all cells, compute the u,v slice extents based on the minimum and maximum u,v coordinates of the trimmed cuboid. 6. Cull Empty Macro-cells: If the macro-cell is empty (no cells contain the isovalue), omit it from extent computation entirely. The u,v slice is clamped to tightly enclose only nodes with the desired isovalue. 7. Project: Project the resulting trimmed cuboid onto the image plane instead of the full macro-cell. 8. Cast Rays: Cast local rays only for pixels covered by the projected trimmed cuboid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trimmacrocell(macrocell, isovalue): """ Trims a macro-cell to the smallest cuboid containing iso-surface portions. Args: macrocell: A 3D grid of cells with scalar values. isovalue: The threshold value for the iso-surface. Returns: A tuple (umin, umax, vmin, vmax) representing the trimmed slice extents, or None if the macro-cell is empty. """ # Initialize cuboid bounds to None (invalid) xmin = None xmax = None ymin = None ymax = None zmin = None zmax = None # Iterate through all cells in the macro-cell for cell in macrocell: # Check if the cell contains the isovalue # Note: Implementation detail: Typically involves checking if the cell's # value (or interpolated values at corners) crosses the isovalue. if cell.containsisovalue(isovalue): # Get spatial bounds of the cell cellbounds = cell.getbounds() # Update cuboid min/max if xmin is None or cellbounds.xmin < xmin: xmin = cellbounds.xmin if xmax is None or cellbounds.xmax > xmax: xmax = cellbounds.xmax if ymin is None or cellbounds.ymin < ymin: ymin = cellbounds.ymin if ymax is None or cellbounds.ymax > ymax: ymax = cellbounds.ymax if zmin is None or cellbounds.zmin < zmin: zmin = cellbounds.zmin if zmax is None or cellbounds.zmax > zmax: zmax = cellbounds.zmax # If no cells contained the isovalue, the macro-cell is empty if xmin is None: return None # Compute u,v slice extents based on the trimmed cuboid # Note: Implementation detail: Mapping 3D bounds to 2D screen coordinates (u,v) # requires the camera projection matrix. This is assumed to be handled by the # caller or a helper function. umin, vmin, umax, vmax = projectcuboidtoscreen(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax) return (umin, umax, vmin, vmax) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Macro-cells: Must be detected and omitted to avoid unnecessary processing. Precision: Ensure that the cuboid extension logic correctly handles floating-point precision when updating min/max values. Boundary Conditions: The cuboid must be initialized correctly to handle the first surface cell encountered. Performance: Macro-cell trimming saves about 28 percent of overall rendering time on average. Dependency: The time gain is very much dependent on the data set and the position of the view point. Complexity: The trimming step adds a linear scan over the macro-cell cells, but this is offset by the reduction in ray casting operations. Strengths: Reduces unnecessary calculations and octree lookups by focusing only on relevant pixels. Limitations: Effectiveness varies with data set topology and viewpoint. Macro-cell trimming was introduced as part of cell-based first-hit ray casting techniques to optimize volume rendering performance. It is also referred to as "Culling empty cap-level macrocells" in the context of interactive ray tracing of implicit surfaces. The method leverages the coherence of octree structures to efficiently cull empty regions before ray casting begins. name: Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping
head: Active Brick Boundary Mesh, Active Region Boundary Geometry, Boundary Mesh Space Skipping, RTX-Accelerated Empty Space Skipping using Triangulated Active Region Boundary Geometry
body: A GPU-accelerated space-skipping technique for structured volumes that replaces clustered proxy boxes with a triangle mesh bounding the surface between active and inactive macrocells. It solves the host-GPU transfer bottleneck and high depth complexity of prior proxy-box methods by generating the boundary geometry entirely on the GPU and using native RTX hardware for ray-triangle intersection. Inputs: Input volume dimensions Vx \times Vy \times Vz. Brick size K (default 16), defining macrocell resolution. Transfer function (TF) defining active scalar ranges. Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Volume integration intervals [t0, t1] for active regions. Final pixel color. Data Structures: 1. Macrocell Grid: Size Mx \times My \times Mz, where Mx = \lfloor Vx/K \rfloor, etc. Each cell stores the minimum and maximum scalar values of input voxels mapping to it. 2. Active Bricks Mask: Boolean grid Mx \times My \times Mz on GPU. true if macrocell has non-zero alpha for current TF. 3. Vertex Array: Pre-allocated float3 array of size N{vtxMax} = (Mx+1)(My+1)(Mz+1). Contains all possible macrocell grid vertices. 4. Triangle Index Array: Pre-allocated int3 array of size N{triMax} (upper bound based on boundary geometry on macrocell faces). Stores indices referencing the Vertex Array. 5. numTriangles: Device-side integer counter, initialized to 0, used as an atomic offset for writing triangles. 6. OptiX BVH: Built over the generated triangle mesh using OptiX 7.2. Steps: 1. Initial Setup: Build Macrocell Grid on host, upload to GPU. Allocate GPU memory for Active Bricks Mask, Vertex Array, and Triangle Index Array. Initialize numTriangles = 0. 2. Active Cell Classification (Per TF Change): Launch CUDA kernel. Each thread maps to one macrocell (i,j,k). Check if macrocell's scalar range maps to non-zero alpha in TF. Write result to ActiveBricksMask[i][j][k]. 3. Boundary Triangle Generation (Per TF Change): Clear numTriangles = 0. Run three templated CUDA kernels for X, Y, Z orientations. For orientation D \in \{0,1,2\} (X,Y,Z): Thread maps to face perpendicular to axis D. Let curr be macrocell index on positive side of face, prev on negative side. If prev is out-of-bounds, treat as inactive. If ActiveBricksMask[prev] == ActiveBricksMask[curr], return. Get 4 vertex indices \{v0, v1, v2, v3\} spanning the face. triID = atomicAdd(&numTriangles, 2). If ActiveBricksMask[prev] is true (prev active, curr inactive): Triangles[triID] = {v0, v1, v2}, Triangles[triID+1] = {v0, v2, v3}. Else (curr active, prev inactive): Triangles[triID] = {v1, v0, v2}, Triangles[triID+1] = {v2, v0, v3}. Winding order points away from active towards inactive. Download numTriangles to host. 4. BVH Rebuild: Update OptiX geometry to reference generated mesh. Rebuild BVH with "optimize for traversal" flag. Compact BVH. 5. Ray Tracing & Integration: Initialize ray with t{min}=0, t{max}=\infty. Trace ray against BVH with DISABLEANYHIT flag. No Hit: Terminate ray. Hit: Get hit distance t{hit} and hit kind (front/back). Back-Facing Hit: Ray is inside volume. Integration interval [t0, t1] = [0, t{hit}]. Front-Facing Hit: Ray enters volume at t0 = t{hit}. Trace same ray with t{min}=t0 to find exit t1. Volume Integration: Sample volume texture at fixed rate dt=0.5 (interleaved) over [t0, t1]. Apply gradient shading and early ray termination. If ray terminated early, return. Else, trace new ray from t1 to find next segment. Repeat. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA
head: Adaptive Macrocell Ray Marching, Macrocell solution
body: Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA is a ray marching technique that traverses a volumetric grid using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) over macrocells, adapting the sampling step size based on opacity upper bounds to skip empty or low-opacity regions. It differs from its parent Ray Marcher with Macrocell Empty Space Skipping by dynamically adjusting the step size within occupied macrocells rather than only skipping entirely empty ones, and from its sibling Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping by relying on a uniform grid structure with DDA traversal rather than explicit boundary meshes. The method combines coarse-grained space skipping with fine-grained adaptive sampling. It uses a 3D DDA to traverse a grid of macrocells. For each macrocell, it estimates an opacity upper bound. If the bound is negligible, the cell is skipped. Otherwise, the step size for sampling within the cell is scaled based on the opacity, allowing larger steps in transparent regions and smaller steps in dense regions. Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D (normalized), ray interval [t{min}, t{max}], volume data structure containing macrocell metadata. Output: Accumulated color and opacity, or a boolean indicating if the ray hit an opaque surface. The volume is represented by a DeviceVolume structure containing: macrocelldims: Dimensions of the macrocell grid (e.g., Nx, Ny, Nz). macrocellspacingsrcp: Reciprocal of the macrocell spacing in world units. This allows conversion from world coordinates to macrocell indices via multiplication. opacityupperbounds: A data structure (e.g., array or hash map) storing the maximum opacity estimate for each macrocell, derived from minimum and maximum scalar values of enclosed voxels. ADAPTIVESAMPLING: A preprocessor macro or boolean flag. If enabled, adaptive logic is used; otherwise, fixed-step marching is performed. floatepsilon: A small constant used to determine if a macrocell is effectively empty. If the opacity upper bound r \le \text{float\epsilon}, the cell is skipped. step: The base sampling step size. This is the default step size before adaptive scaling is applied. Brick size is dx^n \times dy^n \times dz^n, where dx, dy, dz are the volume dimensions. The parameter n was tested from 0.1 to 0.9, with best performance at n=0.3. 1. Transform Ray to Macrocell Space: Calculate the ray origin and direction in macrocell index space: m{org} = O \times \text{macrocell\spacings\rcp} m{dir} = D \times \text{macrocell\spacings\rcp} 2. Initialize DDA: Initialize a 3D DDA iterator with m{org}, m{dir}, and the ray interval [t{min}, t{max}]. The DDA yields a sequence of macrocells (cell, t0, t1), where t0 and t1 are the entry and exit distances of the ray from the current macrocell in world units. 3. Iterate Macrocells: For each macrocell (cell, t0, t1) returned by the DDA: a. Check Opacity Bound: Retrieve the opacity upper bound r for the current cell. b. Skip Empty Cells: If |r| \le \text{float\epsilon}, the cell is considered empty. Skip to the next macrocell. c. Calculate Adaptive Step Size: Determine the scaling factor based on the opacity bound. Let ss be the adaptive step size: ss = \text{sample\size\scaler}(\text{adaptiveSamplingRate}(step, r), t0, t1) Note: adaptiveSamplingRate returns a factor that increases as r decreases. samplesizescaler ensures the step fits within the remaining interval [t0, t1]. d. Sample Within Macrocell: Initialize the current sampling interval t within the macrocell: t{start} = t0 t{end} = \min(t1, t0 + ss) While t{end} > t{start}: i. Evaluate the volume rendering body function (sample density, apply transfer function, accumulate color/opacity) at the current position defined by t{start}. ii. If the body function indicates the ray is fully opaque or terminated, return immediately. iii. Advance the interval: t{start} = t{end} t{end} = \min(t1, t{start} + ss) 4. Termination: If the ray exits the volume or is fully absorbed, return the accumulated result. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FLOATEPSILON = 1e-6 def adaptiveraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, volume): # 1. Transform to macrocell space morg = rayorigin volume.macrocellspacingsrcp mdir = raydirection volume.macrocellspacingsrcp # 2. Initialize 3D DDA iterator # Yields (cellindex, tentry, texit) for each macrocell intersected dda = DDA3(morg, mdir, tmin, tmax, volume.macrocelldims) accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # 3. Iterate macrocells for cell, t0, t1 in dda: # Get opacity upper bound for this macrocell r = volume.getopacityupperbound(cell) # Skip empty cells if abs(r) <= FLOATEPSILON: continue # Calculate adaptive step size stepfactor = adaptivesamplingrate(volume.basestep, r) ss = min(stepfactor, t1 - t0) # 4. Sample within the macrocell tcurrent = t0 tnext = min(t1, t0 + ss) while tnext > tcurrent: pos = rayorigin + raydirection tcurrent # Evaluate volume (density, color, etc.) # Updates accumulatedcolor and accumulatedopacity # Returns True if ray is terminated (fully opaque) if volumerenderbody(pos, accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity): return vec4(accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity) # Advance interval tcurrent = tnext tnext = min(t1, tcurrent + ss) return vec4(accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity) def adaptivesamplingrate(basestep, opacitybound): """ Returns a scaling factor for the step size. Higher opacity bound -> smaller step (more samples). Lower opacity bound -> larger step (fewer samples). """ if opacitybound < FLOATEPSILON: return basestep # Scale factor inversely proportional to opacity bound return basestep / max(opacitybound, FLOATEPSILON) def volumerenderbody(pos, accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity): """ Standard volume rendering step: sample density, apply transfer function, accumulate. Returns True if ray is fully opaque. # Implementation depends on specific transfer function and density field. """ pass class DDA3: """ Standard 3D Digital Differential Analyzer iterator. Traverses a uniform grid along a ray, yielding cell indices and entry/exit distances. # Standard 3D DDA implementation not detailed in sources. """ pass Precision: When t0 and t1 are very close, floating-point errors may cause t{next} \le t{current}, leading to infinite loops. A minimum step size guard or epsilon check is required. Boundary Conditions: The DDA must correctly handle rays that start or end inside a macrocell. The initial t0 and final t1 must be clamped to the ray interval [t{min}, t{max}]. Dynamic Volume Overhead: For dynamic volumes, the macrocell structure must be updated every frame, which can be costly and become a performance bottleneck, especially when the volume image ratio is large. Extends the parent by supporting interruption and resumption of ray traversal state, allowing pausing mid-ray for external operations. Extends the parent for distributed rendering by introducing block-level divergence control via blockany to manage thread synchronization across macrocell boundaries. Combines macrocell traversal with Delta Tracking (Woodcock tracking) using alpha as a majorant extinction coefficient for probabilistic free-flight distances. Uses a strict two-level DDA (macrocell cube then voxel) implemented in fragment shaders, differing from the parent's adaptive step size by using fixed-size macrocells. A mechanism to skip empty regions in sparse volume data using a uniform grid and 3DDDA algorithm. The fragment shader traverses the macrocell grid using 3DDDA in an outer loop. If a macrocell is nonempty, it enters the volume rendering loop with peak finding tests between samples. To begin sampling, it finds the first t to sample when entering a macrocell by solving for the maximum x after T{enter}: x{tenter} = (-b + \sqrt{b^2 + 2aT{enter}})/a. It then computes floor values and samples as in Equation 17 of. Coarse grids (64^3 cells) work best on GPU. A variant that uses a bitfield occupancy grid to skip empty space. For each ray, it iterates through spatial steps. It checks occupancy using a bitfield: sitybitfield[ti.u32(idx//8)] & (1 << ti.u32(idx%8)). If occupied, it stores position, direction, time, and delta into buffers and marks for network evaluation. If not occupied, it calculates the distance to the next grid boundary using txyz = (((nxyz+0.5+0.5ti.math.sign(rayd))gridsizeinv2-1)mipbound-xyz)dinv and advances time to skip empty space until the next boundary is reached. Time Complexity: O(N{macrocells} + N{samples}), where N{macrocells} is the number of macrocells traversed and N{samples} is the total number of samples taken. Adaptive sampling reduces N{samples} in transparent regions. Memory Complexity: O(N{macrocells}) for storing opacity upper bounds. Performance: Significantly faster than fixed-step marching in sparse volumes. Performance depends on the accuracy of the opacity upper bounds. Empty space skipping structures are ideal for static volumes or for dynamic volumes when the rendered image resolution is large enough to hide the structure reconstruction overheads. Warp Marching outperforms Macrocell methods when the volume image ratio is large (resolutions 256×256 or 512×512), because updating the macrocell structure every frame is a bottleneck; at 1024×1024, Macrocell performs better. Strengths: Efficient space skipping, adaptive resolution, simple implementation on GPU. Limitations: Requires precomputed opacity bounds. Construction and update overhead can dominate rendering time for high-resolution dynamic volumes. The method is based on the instantvnr project, which implements interactive volume visualization via multi-resolution hash encoding based neural representation. The core idea of using macrocells with DDA for space skipping originates from early implementations using uniform grids and 3DDDA for peak finding and differential sampling. The adaptive sampling aspect was introduced to improve performance on GPUs where purely adaptive methods based on local gradients suffer from poor thread coherence. name: Resumable Ray Marching Iterator
head: OptiX7 Adaptive Ray Marching, Resumable Ray Marching
body: The Resumable Ray Marching Iterator traverses a volumetric grid using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) over macrocells, adapting the sampling step size based on opacity upper bounds to skip empty regions. It differs from its parent Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by explicitly supporting interruption and resumption of the ray traversal state, allowing the algorithm to pause mid-ray for external operations and resume later without losing progress. Inputs: Ray origin org, ray direction dir, ray segment bounds tMin, tMax, volume dimensions dims, macrocell spacing inverse macrocellspacingsrcp, fixed step size step, and a callback body(t). Outputs: Accumulated radiance/color and opacity, computed via body(t) invoked for each sampled segment. The iterator maintains state in a payload structure to support resumption. SampleStreamingPayload (stores iteration state): iter.cell: Current macrocell coordinates (integer vector). Present only if ADAPTIVESAMPLING is defined. iter.tnext: The next time parameter to process. Present only if ADAPTIVESAMPLING is defined. iter.nextcellbegin: Offset from tMin to the next cell boundary. Always present. pixelindex: Pixel identifier. jitter: Sampling jitter. alpha: Accumulated opacity. color: Accumulated color. RadiancePayload (for ray generation): alpha: Float, initialized to 0.f. color: vec3f, initialized to 0.f. rng: Pointer to random number generator state, initialized to nullptr. ShadowPayload (for shadow rays): alpha: Float, initialized to 0.f. rng: Pointer to random number generator state, initialized to nullptr. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def resumableraymarchingiterator(org, dir, tMin, tMax, dims, macrocellspacingsrcp, step, body, ADAPTIVESAMPLING): nextcellbegin = 0.0 if ADAPTIVESAMPLING: morg = org macrocellspacingsrcp mdir = dir macrocellspacingsrcp DDAIter.init(morg, mdir, tMin, tMax, dims) # Standard 3D DDA initialization while DDAIter.next(lambda cell, t0, t1: processmacrocell(cell, t0, t1, tMin, step)): pass else: tx = max(tMin + nextcellbegin, tMin) ty = min(tx + step, tMax) while ty > tx: nextcellbegin = ty - tMin body(tx, ty) tx = ty ty = min(tx + step, tMax) nextcellbegin = float('inf') return resumablecheck(ADAPTIVESAMPLING, mdir, tMin, tMax, dims, nextcellbegin) def processmacrocell(cell, t0, t1, tMin, step): r = opacityUpperBound(cell) # Standard opacity bound estimation if abs(r) <= floatepsilon: return True ss = samplesizescaler(adaptiveSamplingRate(step, r), t0, t1) tx = t0 ty = min(t1, t0 + ss) while ty > tx: nextcellbegin = ty - tMin body(tx, ty) tx = ty ty = min(tx + ss, t1) return True def samplesizescaler(ss, t0, t1): N = math.floor((t1 - t0) / ss) + 1 return (t1 - t0) / N def resumablecheck(ADAPTIVESAMPLING, mdir, tMin, tMax, dims, nextcellbegin): if ADAPTIVESAMPLING: return DDAIter.resumable(mdir, tMin, tMax, dims) # Standard DDA resumability check else: return tMin + nextcellbegin < tMax ADAPTIVESAMPLING: Preprocessor macro. Must be defined to enable adaptive logic; compilation fails if undefined. step: Fixed step size for non-adaptive mode. adaptiveSamplingRate: Function determining base step size based on opacity bound r. samplesizescaler: Normalizes step size to fit an integer number of steps in interval [t0, t1]. nextcellbegin: Member variable tracking the offset from tMin to the next cell boundary, used for resumption. Empty Cells: If fabsf(r) <= floatepsilon, the cell is skipped to avoid unnecessary sampling. Precision: floatepsilon is used for empty space detection; its value must match the volume's density range. Resumption State: nextcellbegin must be correctly updated and stored. If interrupted, iter.cell and iter.tnext must be preserved for adaptive mode. Boundary Conditions: t.y is clamped to t1 (macrocell end) or tMax (ray end) to prevent overshooting. A ray marching technique for volume rendering that uses Woodcock collision estimation (delta tracking) to skip empty space, avoiding the need for spatial acceleration structures for sampling but requiring a global maximum density estimate. It differs from sibling methods like Adaptive Ray Marching with Voxel Skipping by avoiding the need for spatial acceleration structures for sampling, instead relying on probabilistic step sizing based on a global maximum density estimate. Adaptive Ray Marching with Voxel Skipping is a two-pass algorithm that determines the optimal sampling positions for rays traversing a volumetric density grid, skipping empty space to reduce computational load. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling in sparse volumes by dynamically adjusting step sizes based on local density. It differs from its parent, the Resumable Ray Marching Iterator, by pre-computing the exact number of steps and their locations in a dedicated pass, allowing for compact, contiguous memory storage of samples, whereas the parent yields samples on-the-fly. It differs from Woodcock Collision Estimation (Standard) by using deterministic DDA-based boundary traversal rather than probabilistic collision estimation. A method for handling missing GPU memory by stopping ray tracing when data is absent, communicating this to the CPU for loading, and resuming the ray at the last position in subsequent passes. Definition: The algorithm stops rays when data is missing, communicates this to the CPU, loads the data, and resumes ray tracing at the last position. Steps: 1. Start ray tracing; if data is missing, stop the ray and communicate to CPU. 2. CPU initiates loading of missing data. 3. Algorithm resumes ray tracing at the last ray position. 4. Block terminated pixels with the Z-Buffer to treat only active rays, relying on z-cull and early-Z GPU features. 5. Maintain ray status information in two Multiple Render Targets (MRTs): preliminary output color accumulation, missing node ID, and current marching position. 6. Download missing IDs to CPU so it can adapt the data structure. 7. In the next rendering pass, initiate with a proxy surface and use the MRTs as input textures; earlyZ ensures only active pixels execute the fragment shader. Advantages: Loaded data is directly traversed by the ray, and no data lying outside the frustum is loaded. The CPU does not need to track LODs; rays indicate required precision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Adaptive sampling reduces the number of samples in empty regions, improving performance for sparse volumes. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Low, as it processes rays on-the-fly and only stores minimal state per ray for resumption. Performance: Not given in the sources. Efficient for large volumes with significant empty space due to macrocell skipping. Performance is hardware-dependent, leveraging GPU parallelism and early-Z culling. Strengths: Resumability allows for complex data streaming and neural network integration. Adaptive sampling reduces computational load. Limitations: Requires careful management of resumption state. Adaptive sampling may introduce complexity in step size calculation. When to Use: Suitable for large volumetric datasets, especially when data streaming or neural network inference is involved. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in C++ and utilizes NVIDIA OptiX for ray tracing, found in the instantvnr and open-volume-renderer repositories. The interrupt/resume capability enables ray-guided streaming for missing GPU memory, allowing multiple passes to complete a frame by loading data on-demand. name: Woodcock Collision Estimation (Standard)
head: castRayWoodcock
body: A ray marching technique for volume rendering that uses Woodcock collision estimation (delta tracking) to skip empty space, avoiding the need for spatial acceleration structures for sampling but requiring a global maximum density estimate. It differs from sibling methods like Adaptive Ray Marching with Voxel Skipping by avoiding the need for spatial acceleration structures for sampling, instead relying on probabilistic step sizing based on a global maximum density estimate. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, ray near clip, ray far clip, volume's octree bounding box, global maximum density (or its inverse invMaxDensity), transfer function returning color and opacity out, random number generator sampler, settings stepSize and densityScale, and epsilon dT = 0.0001. Outputs: Boolean indicating if a collision occurred, and the intersection position pos if true. Data Structures: Ray: fields origin, direction, nearclip, farclip. Sampler: method nextFloat() returning uniform random float in [0, 1). Settings: fields stepSize, densityScale. out: structure with color and opacity field w. Steps: 1. Compute the bounding box intersection of the ray with the volume's octree bounding box. If invalid, return false. 2. Calculate the initial ray parameter minT by clamping the ray's near clip to the bounding box near intersection, then adding a random offset: minT += (-std::log(sampler.nextFloat())) settings.stepSize. 3. Loop while minT <= maxT (where maxT is the bounding box far intersection clamped to ray far clip). 4. Calculate position pos = ray.origin + ray.direction minT. 5. Sample the volume density at pos into coef. Evaluate the transfer function to get color and opacity out. 6. Perform the collision test: if sampler.nextFloat() < out.w invMaxDensity settings.densityScale settings.stepSize, record the intersection at pos and return true. 7. If no collision, advance minT by a random step size scaled by invMaxDensity: minT += (-std::log(sampler.nextFloat())) invMaxDensity settings.stepSize. 8. If the loop completes without a collision, return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castRayWoodcock(ray, settings, sampler, invMaxDensity, dT=0.0001): # Assumes standard functions: clamp, log, computeboundingboxintersection, # samplevolumedensity, evaluatetransferfunction, recordintersection. # 1. Compute bounding box intersection of the ray with the volume's octree bounding box. # If invalid, return false. bboxnear, bboxfar = computeboundingboxintersection(ray) if bboxnear is None or bboxfar is None: return False # 2. Calculate initial ray parameter minT by clamping the ray's near clip to the bounding box near intersection, # then adding a random offset. minT = clamp(ray.nearclip, bboxnear) minT += (-log(sampler.nextFloat())) settings.stepSize # maxT is the bounding box far intersection clamped to ray far clip. maxT = clamp(ray.farclip, bboxfar) # 3. Loop while minT <= maxT. while minT <= maxT: # 4. Calculate position pos = ray.origin + ray.direction minT # 5. Sample the volume density at pos into coef. coef = samplevolumedensity(pos) # Evaluate the transfer function to get color and opacity out. out = evaluatetransferfunction(coef) # 6. Perform the collision test. if sampler.nextFloat() < out.w invMaxDensity settings.densityScale settings.stepSize: recordintersection(pos) return True # 7. If no collision, advance minT by a random step size scaled by invMaxDensity. minT += (-log(sampler.nextFloat())) invMaxDensity settings.stepSize # 8. If the loop completes without a collision, return false. return False Parameters: dT: A small epsilon value used to prevent infinite loops or precision issues, set to 0.0001. invMaxDensity: The inverse of the maximum density in the volume, initialized to 1.0f. Used to normalize the sampling probability against the global maximum. settings.stepSize: Base step size setting. settings.densityScale: Density scale setting. Edge Cases: invMaxDensity must be strictly positive to avoid division by zero during the collision test and step advancement. dT is provided but its exact application point is not specified in the sources; it is typically used as a small additive guard to minT or maxT to prevent precision-related infinite loops. name: Adaptive Ray Marching with Voxel Skipping
head: Sparse Ray Marching
body: Adaptive Ray Marching with Voxel Skipping is a two-pass algorithm that determines optimal sampling positions for rays traversing a volumetric density grid, skipping empty space to reduce computational load. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling in sparse volumes by dynamically adjusting step sizes based on local density. It differs from its parent, the Resumable Ray Marching Iterator, by pre-computing the exact number of steps and their locations in a dedicated pass, allowing for compact, contiguous memory storage of samples, whereas the parent yields samples on-the-fly. It differs from Woodcock Collision Estimation (Standard) by using deterministic DDA-based boundary traversal rather than probabilistic collision estimation. The method operates on a 3D density grid and a set of rays, producing a compact list of sampled points. It uses a two-pass approach: the first pass estimates the number of valid steps per ray to allocate memory, and the second pass writes the actual sample data. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [N, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [N, 3]. grid: 3D density grid of shape [H, H, H], flattened to 1D. bound: Half-width of the cubic scene volume [-bound, bound]. H: Grid resolution (assumed cubic). densitythresh: Threshold for occupancy. Default: 10.0f. MAXSTEPS: Maximum steps per ray. Default: 1024. MINNEAR: Minimum near clipping distance. Default: 0.05f. DTGAMMA: Step size scaling factor. Default: 1.0f / 256.0f. perturb: Boolean flag for jittering start position. Outputs: xyzs: Sampled point positions, shape [M, 3]. dirs: Ray directions at sampled points, shape [M, 3]. deltas: Step sizes (distances) at sampled points, shape [M]. rays: Metadata buffer, shape [N, 3]. Each row i contains [rayindex, startpointindex, numsteps]. Grid: A 3D array of floats representing density. The implementation uses a single resolution 128x128x128 grid. Accessed via linear index nx H H + ny H + nz. Rays Metadata: A 1D array of size 3 N storing the start index and step count for each ray in the output buffers. bound: Scene half-width. rbound: 1.0f / bound. dtmin: Minimum step size in world units. Calculated as MINSTEPSIZE() bound, where MINSTEPSIZE() = 2 sqrt(3) / MAXSTEPS(). dtmax: Maximum step size. Calculated as 2 bound / (H - 1). dtgamma: Scaling factor for adaptive step size. If bound > 1, dtgamma = DTGAMMA(), else 0.0f. 1. Ray-Box Intersection: For each ray n with origin ox, oy, oz and direction dx, dy, dz: Compute inverse direction components: rdx = 1.0f / dx, rdy = 1.0f / dy, rdz = 1.0f / dz. Compute near and far intersections for each axis with bounding box [-bound, bound]: nearx = (-bound - ox) rdx farx = (bound - ox) rdx Swap nearx and farx if nearx > farx. Repeat for y and z. If tnear >= tfar, the ray misses the volume; set numsteps = 0 and skip to next ray. 2. Initialization: Initialize step size limits: dtmin = MINSTEPSIZE() bound and dtmax = 2 bound / (H - 1). name: Network Ray Marching Iterator
head: Distributed Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA, Networked Ray Marching
body: The Network Ray Marching Iterator is a ray marching algorithm designed for distributed or networked rendering environments, typically leveraging GPU ray tracing APIs such as NVIDIA OptiX. It extends the parent Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by introducing block-level divergence control via blockany to manage thread synchronization across macrocell boundaries. This method is distinct from its siblings because it explicitly tracks the "alive" status of rays in a distributed context, ensuring that inactive threads do not waste computation while maintaining adaptive sampling rates based on opacity upper bounds. The algorithm traverses a volume using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) over macrocells. It adapts the step size within each macrocell based on an estimated opacity upper bound and uses a device function blockany to synchronize thread divergence across the block. Inputs: Ray origin org, ray direction dir, ray segment [tMin, tMax], volume dimensions dims, macrocell spacing inverse macrocellspacingsrcp, and a lambda function defining the per-sample body logic. Outputs: The final "alive" status of the ray after traversal, and accumulated color/opacity if the body function modifies state. Macrocell Coordinates: morg and mdir are floating-point vectors representing the ray origin and direction scaled by the inverse macrocell spacing. DDA State: The DDA yields a tuple (cell, t0, t1, alive) for each macrocell intersection, where cell is the macrocell index, t0 and t1 are the entry and exit distances, and alive is the boolean status of the ray. blockany: A device function that returns true if any thread in the current block satisfies a given condition. floatepsilon: A small constant used to determine if the opacity upper bound is effectively zero. Value not given in the sources. step: The base sampling step size. Value not given in the sources. 1. Calculate Macrocell Coordinates: Compute the ray origin and direction in macrocell space: m\org = org \times macrocell\spacings\rcp, m\dir = dir \times macrocell\spacings\rcp. 2. Invoke DDA: Call the DDA traversal with morg, mdir, tMin, tMax, dims, and a lambda callback. 3. Initialize Loop Variables: Inside the lambda, initialize ss = 100.f (adaptive step size) and nonempty = true. 4. Check Opacity Upper Bound: If alive is true, calculate r = opacityUpperBound(self, cell). If fabsf(r) <= floatepsilon, set nonempty = false. 5. Calculate Adaptive Step: If alive is true, set ss = adaptiveSamplingRate(step, r). 6. Divergence Control: Evaluate blockany(nonempty && alive). If this returns false, return alive (terminate the ray for this block). 7. Initialize Sample Interval: Set t = vec2f(t0, min(t1, t0 + ss)). 8. Sample Loop: Loop while blockany(alive && (t.y > t.x)): update alive = body(t, alive), t.x = t.y, t.y = min(t.x + ss, t1). 9. Return Status: Return the final alive status. If adaptive sampling is not used, initialize t = vec2f(tMin, min(tMax, tMin + step)) and alive = (t.y > t.x). Loop while blockany(alive && (t.y > t.x)): update alive = body(t, alive), t.x = t.y, t.y = min(t.x + step, tMax). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blockany(conditionlist): """Device function: returns True if any element in the list is True.""" return any(conditionlist) def networkraymarchingiterator(org, dir, tmin, tmax, dims, macrocellspacingsrcp, step, floatepsilon, opacityupperbound, adaptivesamplingrate, body): # 1. Calculate macrocell coordinates morg = [org[i] macrocellspacingsrcp for i in range(3)] mdir = [dir[i] macrocellspacingsrcp for i in range(3)] # 2. Call DDA def lambdafunc(cell, t0, t1, alive): # 3. Initialize loop variables ss = 100.0 nonempty = True # 4. Check opacity upper bound if alive: r = opacityupperbound(cell) if abs(r) <= floatepsilon: nonempty = False # 5. Calculate adaptive step if alive: ss = adaptivesamplingrate(step, r) # 6. Divergence control if not blockany([nonempty and alive]): return False # 7. Initialize sample interval tx = t0 ty = min(t1, t0 + ss) # 8. Sample loop while blockany([alive and (ty > tx)]): alive = body(tx, ty, alive) tx = ty ty = min(tx + ss, t1) # 9. Return status return True # Standard 3D DDA implementation (replaces networkdda3) # Fixes initialization bug where cell/tmaxedge were incorrectly sized/initialized cell = [int(morg[i]) if morg[i] >= 0 else int(morg[i]) - 1 for i in range(3)] cell = [max(0, min(dims[i] - 1, cell[i])) for i in range(3)] stepdir = [1 if mdir[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] tdelta = [1.0 / abs(mdir[i]) if mdir[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tmaxedge = [ (cell[i] + 1.0 - morg[i]) if mdir[i] > 0 else (cell[i] - morg[i]) for i in range(3) ] t0 = max(tmin, min(tmaxedge)) while t0 < tmax: minidx = 0 minval = tmaxedge[0] for i in range(1, 3): if tmaxedge[i] < minval: minval = tmaxedge[i] minidx = i t1 = min(minval, tmax) alive = True if not lambdafunc(cell, t0, t1, alive): return False tmaxedge[minidx] += tdelta[minidx] cell[minidx] += stepdir[minidx] cell[minidx] = max(0, min(dims[minidx] - 1, cell[minidx])) t0 = t1 return False Precision: The use of floatepsilon for opacity checks determines when a macrocell is considered empty. Boundaries: The min(t1, t0 + ss) logic ensures that the last sample does not exceed the macrocell exit distance t1. Zero Direction Components: The DDA handles rays parallel to grid axes by using infinite deltas for those dimensions. A variant that allows ray traversal to be paused and resumed, useful for progressive rendering. Choose when memory bandwidth is limited or when integrating with progressive refinement techniques. Uses majorant densities for more accurate opacity bounds. Choose when higher accuracy in empty-space skipping is required, at the cost of increased computation per macrocell. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Optimized for distributed rendering on GPUs using ray tracing APIs like OptiX. Strengths: Efficient handling of thread divergence in distributed contexts; adaptive sampling reduces unnecessary computations. Limitations: Requires support for blockany and custom DDA implementations; may not be suitable for non-GPU or non-ray-tracing environments. The Network Ray Marching Iterator was introduced as part of the instantvnr project, a neural volume rendering framework. It builds on the principles of adaptive ray marching and macrocell traversal, extending them to support distributed rendering scenarios. The method is designed to leverage the parallelism of modern GPUs and the synchronization primitives provided by ray tracing APIs. name: Macrocell Grid Traversal with Majorant Densities
head: 3D-DDA with Woodcock tracking, Majorant-based free-flight tracking, Single-Level Macrocell + DDA Space Partitioning
body: This method accelerates volumetric path tracing by combining a coarse spatial partition (macrocells) with Delta Tracking (Woodcock tracking) to skip empty or low-opacity regions more efficiently than fixed-step marching. It sets itself apart from its parent Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by explicitly using the alpha component of the transfer function as a majorant extinction coefficient to determine probabilistic free-flight distances, allowing larger steps in homogeneous cells while maintaining unbiased Monte Carlo estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} in world space; a transfer function TF mapping density to RGBA; a macrocell grid storing min/max density ranges for each cell. Output: Accumulated radiance contribution from the volume along the ray, or a termination signal if the ray exits the volume or is canceled. Data Structures: The spatial partition is defined by DeviceSpacePartitonSingleMC: valueranges: Pointer to range1f, storing min/max density values for each macrocell. majorants: Pointer to float, storing the precomputed majorant extinction coefficient for each macrocell. dims: vec3i, dimensions of the macrocell grid in cells. spac: vec3f, spatial scaling factor (world units per macrocell). spacrcp: vec3f, reciprocal of spac, used to convert world coordinates to macrocell grid coordinates. Macrocell size is fixed at 16 (1 \ll 4), where 4 is MACROCELLSIZEMIP. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Transform the ray origin and direction into macrocell space using the reciprocal scaling factor: \mathbf{m\org} = \mathbf{o} \cdot \mathbf{spac\rcp} and \mathbf{m\dir} = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{spac\rcp}. Initialize the 3D-DDA iterator with \mathbf{m\org}, \mathbf{m\dir}, and the ray's near/far bounds [t{near}, t{far}] in macrocell space. 2. Majorant Computation: For each macrocell, retrieve the stored min/max density range [d{min}, d{max}]. Look up these values in the transfer function TF to obtain the alpha components \alpha{min} = TF(d{min}).a and \alpha{max} = TF(d{max}).a. The majorant extinction coefficient \sigmat for the cell is derived from these values. In the reference implementation, fixed constants are used for demonstration: \sigmat = 1.0 and density scale = 1.0. Majorants must be recomputed whenever the transfer function changes. 3. Traversal Loop: While the ray has not exited the grid (t < t{far}): a. Cell Access: Determine the current macrocell index idx from the DDA iterator's current cell coordinates (x, y, z): idx = x + y \cdot dims.x + z \cdot dims.x \cdot dims.y. Retrieve the majorant \sigmat = majorants[idx]. b. Empty Cell Skip: If the cell is empty (e.g., d{max} = 0 or \sigmat = 0), advance the DDA iterator to the next intersected cell and continue to step 3a. c. Woodcock Tracking: If the cell is non-empty, perform Delta Tracking within the current cell: i. Compute the distance to the next cell boundary t{cell\end} using the DDA state. ii. Sample a free-flight distance t{ff} from the exponential distribution with rate \sigmat: t{ff} = -\frac{\ln(1 - \xi)}{\sigmat}, where \xi is a uniform random number in 0, 1). iii. Determine the step size t{step} = \min(t{ff}, t{cell\end} - t{current}). iv. Advance the ray position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + (t{current} + t{step}) \mathbf{d}. v. Interaction Check: If t{step} == t{ff}, an interaction occurred. Sample the scattering event (absorption/scattering) based on the actual density at \mathbf{p} and the majorant \sigmat. If scattering occurs, contribute radiance and potentially spawn a new ray. If absorbed, terminate the path. If the interaction is virtual (density < majorant), continue tracking. vi. If t{step} == t{cell\end}, the ray reached the cell boundary. Update t{current} and advance the DDA iterator to the next cell. 4. Termination: If the ray exits the grid (t \ge t{far}) or is canceled by [Russian Roulette during scattering, return the accumulated radiance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def macrocelltraversalwithmajorants(rayo, rayd, tnear, tfar, macrocellgrid, transferfunction): """ rayo: list of 3 floats, ray origin in world space rayd: list of 3 floats, ray direction in world space tnear: float, near bound in macrocell space tfar: float, far bound in macrocell space macrocellgrid: dict with keys 'dims', 'spacrcp', 'majorants' transferfunction: callable mapping density to RGBA tuple Returns: accumulated radiance (list of 3 floats) """ import math import random # 1. Transform to macrocell space morg = [rayo[i] macrocellgrid['spacrcp'][i] for i in range(3)] mdir = [rayd[i] macrocellgrid['spacrcp'][i] for i in range(3)] # Initialize 3D-DDA state dims = macrocellgrid['dims'] ddax, dday, ddaz = int(morg[0]), int(morg[1]), int(morg[2]) ddadx = 1 if mdir[0] > 0 else -1 ddady = 1 if mdir[1] > 0 else -1 ddadz = 1 if mdir[2] > 0 else -1 tmaxx = (ddax + (1.0 if ddadx > 0 else 0.0) - morg[0]) / mdir[0] if mdir[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = (dday + (1.0 if ddady > 0 else 0.0) - morg[1]) / mdir[1] if mdir[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = (ddaz + (1.0 if ddadz > 0 else 0.0) - morg[2]) / mdir[2] if mdir[2] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltax = ddadx / mdir[0] if mdir[0] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = ddady / mdir[1] if mdir[1] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = ddadz / mdir[2] if mdir[2] != 0 else float('inf') accumulatedradiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tcurrent = tnear while tcurrent < tfar: # 2. Get current cell info idx = ddax + dday dims[0] + ddaz dims[0] dims[1] sigmat = macrocellgrid['majorants'][idx] # Skip empty cells if sigmat == 0.0: # Advance DDA to next cell if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: ddax += ddadx tmaxx += tdeltax else: ddaz += ddadz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: dday += ddady tmaxy += tdeltay else: ddaz += ddadz tmaxz += tdeltaz continue # 3. Woodcock Tracking within the cell # Compute distance to next cell boundary using the DDA state tcellend = min(tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz) # Sample free-flight distance xi = random.random() tff = -math.log(1.0 - xi) / sigmat # Determine step size tstep = min(tff, tcellend - tcurrent) # Advance ray tcurrent += tstep pworld = [rayo[i] + tcurrent rayd[i] for i in range(3)] # Interaction Check: If tstep == tff, an interaction occurred if tstep == tff: # Sample actual density at pworld (Not given in the sources. In practice, this queries the underlying VDB or texture.) density = 0.0 # Placeholder for actual density query # Compute actual extinction coefficient from transfer function alphaactual = transferfunction(density)[3] # RGBA index 3 is alpha sigmaa = alphaactual # Simplified: assuming alpha represents extinction # Russian Roulette for scattering vs absorption if sigmat > 0 and random.random() < sigmaa / sigmat: # Scattering event # If scattering occurs, contribute radiance and potentially spawn a new ray pass else: # Absorption break else: # If tstep == tcellend, the ray reached the cell boundary # Advance DDA if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: ddax += ddadx tmaxx += tdeltax else: ddaz += ddadz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: dday += ddady tmaxy += tdeltay else: ddaz += ddadz tmaxz += tdeltaz return accumulatedradiance Parameters: MACROCELLSIZEMIP: Log2 of macrocell dimension, typically 4 (size 16). densityscale: Scaling factor for density values, typically 1.0. sigmat: Majorant extinction coefficient, typically 1.0 in basic implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transfer Function Changes: Majorants must be recomputed whenever the transfer function changes, as they depend on the min/max density ranges. Homogeneity Assumption: Woodcock tracking is most efficient in homogeneous cells where the majorant closely approximates the actual density. Hierarchical Diminishing Returns: Experiments with hierarchical space skipping showed diminishing returns compared to uniform grids when using RGBA transfer functions, likely due to the overhead of managing multiple levels of majorants. A ray-marching technique for volume rendering that combines a Discrete Differential Analyzer (DDA) for traversing a coarse spatial partition (macrocells) with Delta Tracking (Russian Roulette) for sampling absorption and scattering events within those cells. It sets itself apart from standard DDA by replacing uniform step sizes with probabilistic free-flight distances derived from the majorant, allowing it to skip non-interacting regions within a macrocell more efficiently than fixed-step marching, while avoiding the overhead of full per-voxel traversal. It is chosen when the volume is sparse or heterogeneous, and the transfer function allows for effective majorant estimation. See Delta Tracking with DDA Iteration (Macrocell-based). A renderer using the ANARI API that integrates VDB optimization. It sets itself apart by hiding compression details behind an ANSI-C API, converting ANARI structured-regular fields to NanoVDB grids internally, making the optimization transparent to the user. It is chosen when interoperability with standard visualization tools like ParaView is required. See ANARI Renderer Integration. Time Complexity: O(N{cells} + N{interactions}), where N{cells} is the number of macrocells traversed and N{interactions} is the number of scattering events. The DDA traversal is linear in the number of cells, and Woodcock tracking is efficient in sparse regions. Memory Complexity: O(N{macrocells}) for storing the majorant grid and min/max ranges. This is significantly smaller than a full voxel grid for sparse volumes. Measured Performance: In the reference implementation (Barney renderer), this method reduces sample count in homogeneous regions by allowing larger steps via Woodcock tracking. Performance gains are most significant in sparse volumes where empty cells can be skipped entirely. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty regions; adapts step size to local homogeneity; unbiased Monte Carlo estimation; simple uniform grid structure avoids hierarchical overhead. Limitations: Requires recomputation of majorants if transfer function changes. When to Use: Sparse or heterogeneous volumes with well-defined transfer functions; when unbiased path tracing is required. When Not to Use: Dense volumes where the overhead of macrocell traversal outweighs benefits; when hierarchical structures are preferred (though diminishing returns were observed). This method originates from the integration of VDB optimization into the Barney renderer, a multi-GPU wavefront path tracer. It was developed to leverage the structured-regular fields supported by the ANARI standard while providing efficient volume rendering. The approach builds on earlier work in 3D-DDA for volume rendering [SKTM11] and combines it with Woodcock tracking for free-flight distance sampling. The use of a uniform grid instead of hierarchical structures was chosen due to diminishing returns observed with hierarchical space skipping in the presence of RGBA transfer functions. name: Delta Tracking with DDA Iteration (Macrocell-based)
head: DDAIter-based Delta Tracking, SpacePartition_SingleMC Delta Tracking
body: A ray-marching technique for volume rendering that combines a Discrete Differential Analyzer (DDA) for traversing a coarse spatial partition (macrocells) with Delta Tracking (Russian Roulette) for sampling absorption and scattering events within those cells. It handles sparse or heterogeneous media by skipping empty macrocells and using a majorant density. It sets itself apart from standard DDA by replacing uniform step sizes with probabilistic free-flight distances derived from the majorant, allowing it to skip non-interacting regions within a macrocell more efficiently than fixed-step marching, while avoiding the overhead of full per-voxel traversal. It builds on Macrocell Grid Traversal with Majorant Densities. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin rayorg, ray direction raydir, ray near/far bounds raytnear, raytfar, macrocell grid dimensions dims, spatial inverse scale spacrcp, majorant density accessor accessmajorant, density scale constant, total extinction coefficient sigmat, and an initial optical depth budget tau. Outputs: Boolean foundhit indicating if an interaction occurred, and the hit distance rayt. Data Structures Macrocell Iterator (DDAIter): A stateful iterator that computes the sequence of macrocells intersected by a ray. It maintains current cell coordinates and exit distances. Spatial Parameters (sp): Contains spacrcp (reciprocal of spatial scale) for normalizing coordinates to grid space. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize Macrocell Iterator: Convert ray origin and direction to macrocell grid space. Compute normalized origin: m{org} = ray{org} \times sp.spac\rcp. Compute normalized direction: m{dir} = ray{dir} \times sp.spac\rcp. Call DDAIter::init(morg, mdir, raytnear, raytfar, dims) to set up the traversal state. 2. Initialize Loop State: Set foundhit = false. Determine the starting t for the first cell segment: t = next\cell\begin + ray{tnear}. Initialize tau (optical depth budget) externally. 3. Loop over Macrocells: While DDAIter::next() returns a valid cell c with entry t0 and exit t1: a. Retrieve Majorant: Get the majorant density for cell c: majorant = sp.access\majorant(c) \times density\scale. b. Skip Empty Cells: If |majorant| \le \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small float epsilon), the cell is empty. Return true from the current lambda/function to advance to the next macrocell without processing interaction logic. c. Update Optical Depth Budget: Subtract the optical thickness of the current cell segment from tau. The segment length is (t1 - t). The optical thickness is (t1 - t) \times (majorant \times \sigmat). \tau \leftarrow \tau - (t1 - t) \times (majorant \times \sigmat) d. Check for Event: If \tau > 0.f, an interaction (scattering or absorption) occurred within the previous segment or the budget was exhausted. Return true to advance to the next macrocell. e. Calculate Hit Position: If \tau \le 0.f, the interaction occurs within the current cell segment. Calculate the exact hit position t{hit}: t{hit} = t + \frac{\tau}{majorant \times \sigmat} Warning: This division can cause a division by zero error if majorant is zero but passed the epsilon check, or if sigmat is zero. f. Record Hit: Set foundhit = true. Update nextcellbegin = t{hit} - ray{tnear}. Set output rayt = t{hit}. Return false to terminate the loop. 4. Return Result: After the loop completes (ray exits all macrocells or tau budget remains positive without hitting), return foundhit. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deltatrackingddaiter(rayorg, raydir, raytnear, raytfar, dims, spacrcp, accessmajorant, densityscale, sigmat, tau): # Step 1: Initialize Macrocell Iterator morg = [rayorg[i] spacrcp for i in range(3)] mdir = [raydir[i] spacrcp for i in range(3)] dda = DDAIter(morg, mdir, raytnear, raytfar, dims) # Step 2: Initialize Loop State foundhit = False nextcellbegin = 0.0 t = nextcellbegin + raytnear # Step 3: Loop over Macrocells while dda.next(): c = dda.currentcell t0 = dda.entryt t1 = dda.exitt # Retrieve majorant density majorant = accessmajorant(c) densityscale # Skip empty cells if abs(majorant) <= 1e-6: # floatepsilon t = t1 nextcellbegin = t1 - raytnear continue # Update optical depth budget tau -= (t1 - t) (majorant sigmat) # Check for scattering/absorption event if tau > 0.0: t = t1 nextcellbegin = t1 - raytnear continue # Calculate exact hit position within the current cell # Warning: Division by zero if majorant sigmat is zero t = t + tau / (majorant sigmat) # Record hit foundhit = True nextcellbegin = t - raytnear rayt = t return foundhit, rayt return foundhit, None class DDAIter: """Standard 3D DDA iterator for macrocell traversal.""" def init(self, org, dir, tnear, tfar, dims): self.org = org self.dir = dir self.tnear = tnear self.tfar = tfar self.dims = dims self.t = tnear self.cell = [0, 0, 0] self.step = [0, 0, 0] self.tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.initdda() def initdda(self): for i in range(3): if self.dir[i] > 0: self.step[i] = 1 self.tmax[i] = (self.cell[i] + 1 - self.org[i]) / self.dir[i] elif self.dir[i] < 0: self.step[i] = -1 self.tmax[i] = (self.cell[i] - self.org[i]) / self.dir[i] else: self.step[i] = 0 self.tmax[i] = float('inf') def next(self): if self.t > self.tfar: return False # entryt is the current t (start of this cell segment) self.entryt = self.t # Find the next boundary self.t = min(self.tmax[0], self.tmax[1], self.tmax[2]) if self.t > self.tfar: self.t = self.tfar self.exitt = self.t # Advance to next cell if self.tmax[0] <= self.tmax[1] and self.tmax[0] <= self.tmax[2]: self.cell[0] += self.step[0] self.tmax[0] += self.step[0] / self.dir[0] elif self.tmax[1] <= self.tmax[2]: self.cell[1] += self.step[1] self.tmax[1] += self.step[1] / self.dir[1] else: self.cell[2] += self.step[2] self.tmax[2] += self.step[2] / self.dir[2] return True @property def currentcell(self): return tuple(self.cell) @property def entryt(self): return self.entryt @property def exitt(self): return self.exitt Parameters densityscale: Constant multiplier for the majorant density. Typically hardcoded to 1.0. sigmat: Total extinction coefficient. Typically hardcoded to 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: The calculation tau / (majorant sigmat) is performed after checking fabsf(majorant) <= floatepsilon. If majorant is exactly zero but passes the epsilon check (or if epsilon is too large), division by zero occurs. The source code explicitly warns: // can have division by zero error. Epsilon Sensitivity: The choice of floatepsilon for skipping empty cells must be small enough to avoid skipping cells with very low but non-zero density, but large enough to handle numerical noise. Time Complexity: O(N{cells}) in the worst case, where N{cells} is the number of macrocells intersected by the ray. However, empty cells are skipped in O(1), making it efficient for sparse media. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray, assuming the macrocell grid is pre-computed and accessible. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of macrocells intersected. Performance improves with larger macrocells (fewer cells to traverse) but may lose precision in heterogeneous media. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space; handles heterogeneous media via majorants; simple implementation. Limitations: Potential for division by zero; requires pre-computed majorants; may overshoot interactions if majorant is loose. When to use: Sparse or heterogeneous volumetric data where empty space skipping is beneficial. When not to use: Dense, homogeneous media where fixed-step marching might be simpler and faster. This method is part of the Open Volume Renderer project by VIDILabs. It is an implementation detail within a larger modular volume rendering framework. The specific implementation is found in the ovr/renderermacro.h and related source files. name: Voxel Ray Marching with Cube-Level DDA
head: 2-Level DDA Voxel Rendering, DDA voxel traversal, Two-level DDA
body: Voxel Ray Marching with Cube-Level DDA is a GPU-based fragment shader technique for rendering voxel volumes by casting rays through a hierarchical grid of voxel cubes and individual voxels, using a two-level Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to skip empty space efficiently. It builds on Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by explicitly decoupling the empty-space skipping logic into a separate coarse grid layer (cubes), whereas the parent uses a fixed-size macrocell DDA that may not align with the data structure's logical blocks. Unlike its siblings, it operates on a fixed 16x16x16 cube structure with a rigid two-level traversal loop, prioritizing simplicity and shader reusability over adaptive step sizing. Inputs and Outputs: Input Geometry: A simple box mesh with 8 vertices and 12 faces, rendered with front-face culling (rendermode cullfront) to allow viewing from inside or outside. Input Data: Voxel grid stored in textures, accessed via custom samplers (getcube, getvoxel). Output: Depth, light vertex position, and PBR material properties (Albedo, Emission, Normal, Roughness, Specular, Metallic, AO) for the first opaque surface hit, or accumulated transmittance/emission for transparent passes. Data Structures: DDA State: A structure holding the current position in grid coordinates (position), the ray direction reciprocal (rayrec), the traversal step direction (step), and accumulated distance (t). The exact field layout is implementation-specific but must support initialization, stepping, and face-hit calculations. Cube Size: Fixed at 16x16x16 voxels per cube. Parameters: Max Steps: 49 steps per cube (outer loop) and 49 steps per voxel (inner loop). Model Size Reciprocal: MODELSIZEREC = 1.0 / vec3(modelsize). Algorithm Steps: 1. Vertex Shader Setup: Pass the ModelView matrix. Calculate MODELSIZEREC = 1.0 / vec3(modelsize). Store the back vertex position as BACK. Compute the ray direction in model space: RAY = safevector(VERTEX - (inverse(MODELMATRIX) vec4(CAMERAPOSITIONWORLD, 1.0)).xyz). 2. Fragment Shader Initialization: Calculate ray reciprocal: rayrec = 1.0 / ray. Calculate front face intersection: front = tofrontface(BACK, ray, rayrec). Initialize outer DDA structure for cubes: ddainit(ddc, modelsize, front, ray, rayrec). 3. Outer Loop (Cube Traversal): Loop csteps from 0 to 48 (max 49 steps). Check if the current cube contains any opaque voxels using getcube(ddc.position, layer, hasopaque). If hasopaque is true, proceed to inner traversal; otherwise, step to the next cube using ddastep(ddc) and continue. If ddastep(ddc) returns true (end of ray/cube list reached), set nomorecubes = true. 4. Inner Loop (Voxel Traversal): Initialize inner DDA state: ddainitinner(ddv, ddc, modelsize, MODELSIZEREC, ray, rayrec, origin). Calculate the exit point of the cube from the ray: exit = ddavoxelfacehit(ddc, MODELSIZEREC). Transform the cube exit point to view space: exitvertex, depth = calcvertex(exit, PROJECTIONMATRIX, MODELVIEWMATRIX). If exitvertex.z >= 0.0 (behind or on the camera plane), skip the inner loop and step to the next cube. Loop vsteps from 0 to 48 (max 49 steps). Retrieve voxel data: getvoxel(ddv.position, layer, tpos, voxel, color, opaque). If opaque is true, proceed to shading; otherwise, step to the next voxel using ddastep(ddv) and continue. Calculate the precise ray intersection hit point in model coordinates: hit = origin + ddavoxelfacehit(ddv, vec3(1.0 / 16.0)) MODELSIZEREC. Transform the hit point to view space: lightvertex, hitdepth = calcvertex(hit, PROJECTIONMATRIX, MODELVIEWMATRIX). If lightvertex.z < 0.0 (in front of the screen): Assign depth to DEPTH and hit position to LIGHTVERTEX. Compute surface geometry: ddavoxelfacenormals(ddv, NORMALS, NORMAL, TANGENT, BINORMAL) and ddavoxelfaceuv(ddv, modelsize, hit, face). Fetch material properties: getopaquematerial(tpos, voxel, color, face, uv, ALBEDO, EMISSION, normalmap, rsma). Map results to shader outputs: NORMALMAP from normalmap.xy, NORMALMAPDEPTH from normalmap.z, ROUGHNESS from rsma.r, SPECULAR from rsma.g, METALLIC from rsma.b, AO from rsma.a. Set found = true and break the inner loop. If ddastep(ddv) returns true (end of cube reached), break the inner loop. 5. Loop Termination: If found is true or nomorecubes is true, break the outer loop. 6. Finalization: If found is false, execute discard to discard the fragment (transparent background). Transparent Pass Specifics: If no opaque voxel was found (!found), discard if first is true. Otherwise, sample background from SCREENTEXTURE. Blend paint color with background using transmittance: ALBEDO = mix(paint, background, totalTrans). If no opaque voxel was hit, approximate alpha using the gray component of transmittance: ALPHA = 1.0 - gray and ALBEDO = paint + color background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def safevector(v): return v if max(abs(v)) > 1e-6 else vec3(1.0) def tofrontface(back, ray, rayrec): t = min(rayrec) (1.0 - max(back rayrec)) return back + t ray def ddainit(modelsize, front, ray, rayrec): pos = floor(front modelsize) step = sign(ray) return {'pos': pos, 'rayrec': rayrec, 'step': step, 't': 0.0} def ddainitinner(ddc, modelsize, modelsizerec, ray, rayrec, origin): return {'pos': ddc['pos'], 'rayrec': rayrec, 'step': ddc['step'], 'origin': origin, 't': 0.0} def ddavoxelfacehit(dda, stepsize): # Distance to next face in grid coordinates t = (dda['step'] - (dda['pos'] + 0.5) stepsize) / dda['rayrec'] return t def calcvertex(point, proj, view): # Transform point to view space, return vertex and depth v = view point return v, v.z def ddastep(dda): dda['pos'] += dda['step'] dda['t'] += 1.0 return dda['t'] > 48.0 def getcube(pos): # Returns (layer, hasopaque) from occupancy texture return 0, True def getvoxel(pos): # Returns (tpos, voxel, color, opaque) from voxel texture return 0, 0, vec3(0), False def getopaquematerial(tpos, voxel, color, face, uv): # Returns (ALBEDO, EMISSION, normalmap, rsma) return vec3(0), vec3(0), vec2(0), vec4(0) def gray(v): return dot(v, vec3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)) def discard(): raise StopIteration def fragmentshaderopaque(BACK, RAY, modelsize, MODELVIEWMATRIX, PROJECTIONMATRIX): ray = RAY rayrec = 1.0 / ray front = tofrontface(BACK, ray, rayrec) ddc = ddainit(modelsize, front, ray, rayrec) found = False nomorecubes = False for csteps in range(49): layer, hasopaque = getcube(ddc['pos']) if hasopaque: ddv = ddainitinner(ddc, modelsize, 1.0/modelsize, ray, rayrec, vec3(0)) exitdist = ddavoxelfacehit(ddc, 1.0/modelsize) exit = ddc['pos'] + exitdist ray exitvertex, depth = calcvertex(exit, PROJECTIONMATRIX, MODELVIEWMATRIX) if exitvertex.z < 0.0: for vsteps in range(49): tpos, voxel, color, opaque = getvoxel(ddv['pos']) if opaque: hitdist = ddavoxelfacehit(ddv, vec3(1.0 / 16.0)) hit = ddv['origin'] + hitdist ray lightvertex, hitdepth = calcvertex(hit, PROJECTIONMATRIX, MODELVIEWMATRIX) if lightvertex.z < 0.0: DEPTH = depth LIGHTVERTEX = lightvertex NORMALS, NORMAL, TANGENT, BINORMAL = ddavoxelfacenormals(ddv) face, uv = ddavoxelfaceuv(ddv, modelsize, hit) ALBEDO, EMISSION, normalmap, rsma = getopaquematerial(tpos, voxel, color, face, uv) NORMALMAP = normalmap.xy NORMALMAPDEPTH = normalmap.z ROUGHNESS = rsma.r SPECULAR = rsma.g METALLIC = rsma.b AO = rsma.a found = True break if ddastep(ddv): break else: nomorecubes = ddastep(ddc) if found or nomorecubes: break if not found: discard() def fragmentshadertransparent(BACK, RAY, modelsize, MODELVIEWMATRIX, PROJECTIONMATRIX, SCREENTEXTURE): ray = RAY rayrec = 1.0 / ray front = tofrontface(BACK, ray, rayrec) ddc = ddainit(modelsize, front, ray, rayrec) totalEmission = vec3(0.0) totalTrans = vec3(1.0) paint = vec3(0.0) first = True stop = False nomorecubes = False for csteps in range(49): layer, hasopaque = getcube(ddc['pos']) if hasopaque: ddv = ddainitinner(ddc, modelsize, 1.0/modelsize, ray, rayrec, vec3(0)) exitdist = ddavoxelfacehit(ddc, 1.0/modelsize) exit = ddc['pos'] + exitdist ray exitvertex, depth = calcvertex(exit, PROJECTIONMATRIX, MODELVIEWMATRIX) if exitvertex.z < 0.0: for vsteps in range(49): tpos, voxel, color, opaque = getvoxel(ddv['pos']) if opaque: hitdist = ddavoxelfacehit(ddv, vec3(1.0 / 16.0)) hit = ddv['origin'] + hitdist ray lightvertex, hitdepth = calcvertex(hit, PROJECTIONMATRIX, MODELVIEWMATRIX) if lightvertex.z < 0.0: DEPTH = depth LIGHTVERTEX = lightvertex stop = True found = True break # Accumulate transparent voxels if ddastep(ddv): break else: nomorecubes = ddastep(ddc) if found or nomorecubes: break if not found: if first: discard() else: background = sample(SCREENTEXTURE) ALBEDO = mix(paint, background, totalTrans) ALPHA = 1.0 - gray(totalTrans) ALBEDO = paint + color background MultiDDA is an acceleration method for volume rendering that performs incremental Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal over a two-level hierarchical grid to skip empty space more efficiently than a flat grid. It builds on Voxel Ray Marching with Cube-Level DDA by replacing the single-level voxel traversal with a nested approach: a coarse traversal over "bricks" (8³ voxel blocks) followed by a fine traversal over individual voxels only within occupied bricks. It differs from its parent by explicitly decoupling the empty-space skipping logic into a separate coarse grid layer, whereas the parent uses a fixed-size cube-level DDA that may not align with the data structure's logical blocks. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of cubes and voxels traversed along the ray, bounded by the maximum step counts (49 cubes, 49 voxels per cube). Memory Complexity: Constant per fragment, storing DDA state and a few accumulators. Performance: Designed for GPU fragment shaders, allowing for good performance and runtime changes to voxels at relatively low cost. Strengths: Simple implementation, reusable DDA algorithm, supports custom samplers for PBR materials, allows viewing from inside or outside the volume. Limitations: Fixed cube size (16x16x16) may not be optimal for all data structures; transparency handling relies on screen texture sampling which can cause limitations with color filtering and shadows. When to Use: When rendering voxel volumes on the GPU with a need for simple, reusable ray marching code and support for custom PBR materials. When Not to Use: When adaptive step sizing is required for highly sparse or variable-density volumes, or when advanced shadow casting for transparent voxels is needed. The method is based on an efficient 2-level DDA algorithm, implemented 100% on the GPU as a fragment shader, as part of the "Voxel rendering addon for Godot 4.3+". It was developed by Viktor Ferenczi and is available on the Godot Asset Library. The algorithm is designed to be reusable, allowing for custom samplers and material definitions without modifying the core raymarching logic. viktor-ferenczi/godot-voxel, https://github.com/viktor-ferenczi/godot-voxel, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: MultiDDA
head: 2-Level DDA (Brick Grid), Coarse-to-Fine Traversal, Nested DDA for hierarchical grids, Two-level DDA with brickmap
body: MultiDDA is an acceleration method for volume rendering that performs incremental Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal over a two-level hierarchical grid to skip empty space more efficiently than a flat grid. It builds on Voxel Ray Marching with Cube-Level DDA by replacing the single-level voxel traversal with a nested approach: a coarse traversal over "bricks" (8³ voxel blocks) followed by a fine traversal over individual voxels only within occupied bricks. It differs from its parent by introducing a dedicated coarse occupancy grid layer, whereas the parent uses a flat voxel grid traversal without hierarchical skipping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D, inverse direction D^{-1}, brick grid dimensions B{ext}, brick size Sb = 8, voxel grid texture V, brick grid texture Br. Output: Index of the first occupied voxel along the ray, or 0 if empty. Data Structures: 1. Brick Grid: Texture3D<uint> bricks. Each texel corresponds to an 8 \times 8 \times 8 block of voxels. A value >0 indicates the brick is occupied; 0 indicates empty. 2. Voxel Grid: Texture3D<uint> voxels. Stores the actual voxel data (e.g., density, color index). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Coarse DDA: Calculate the initial brick cell Cb and step parameters (t{next}, t{delta}, step\dir) for the brick grid based on ray origin and direction, similar to standard voxel DDA. 2. Coarse Traversal Loop: Iterate through the brick grid. The loop bound is typically 3 \times B{ext} to ensure the ray exits the volume. a. Boundary Check: If Cb is outside [min\brick\cell, max\brick\cell], return 0. b. Occupancy Test: Sample bricks[Cb]. If the value is 0, the brick is empty. c. Advance Coarse DDA: Update Cb using the DDA step logic: axis\mask = step(t{next}, \min(t{next.yzx}, t{next.zxy})) t{next} += axis\mask \cdot t{delta} Cb += int3(axis\mask) \cdot step\dir d. Fine Traversal: If bricks[Cb] > 0, call tracebrick(O, D, D^{-1}, t{delta}, Cb, V). i. Inside tracebrick, perform a standard DDA traversal within the 8 \times 8 \times 8 local coordinates of the brick. ii. If an occupied voxel is found, return its global index. iii. If the brick is traversed without finding an occupied voxel, continue the coarse loop. 3. Return: If the loop completes without finding a voxel, return 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multidda(O, D, Dinv, brickgridext, voxels, bricks): # Vector helpers def step(a, b): return [1.0 if x < y else 0.0 for x, y in zip(a, b)] def minvec(a, b): return [min(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)] def sign(x): return 1 if x > 0 else (-1 if x < 0 else 0) def floorval(x): import math return math.floor(x) # Initialize coarse DDA state brickcell = [floorval(O[0] / 8.0), floorval(O[1] / 8.0), floorval(O[2] / 8.0)] tdelta = [] tnext = [] stepdir = [] for axis in range(3): if D[axis] == 0: tdelta.append(float('inf')) tnext.append(float('inf')) stepdir.append(0) else: tdelta.append(abs(Dinv[axis]) 8.0) stepdir.append(sign(D[axis])) if D[axis] > 0: tnext.append((brickcell[axis] + 1 - O[axis] / D[axis]) abs(Dinv[axis])) else: tnext.append((brickcell[axis] - O[axis] / D[axis]) abs(Dinv[axis])) for i in range(3 brickgridext): # Boundary check if any(b < 0 or b >= brickgridext for b in brickcell): return 0 # Occupancy test brickval = bricks[brickcell[0]][brickcell[1]][brickcell[2]] if brickval > 0: # Fine traversal inside brick localorigin = [O[0] - brickcell[0] 8.0, O[1] - brickcell[1] 8.0, O[2] - brickcell[2] 8.0] localtdelta = [] localtnext = [] localcell = [] for axis in range(3): if D[axis] == 0: localtdelta.append(float('inf')) localtnext.append(float('inf')) else: localtdelta.append(abs(Dinv[axis]) 8.0) localcell.append(floorval(localorigin[axis])) if D[axis] > 0: localtnext.append((localcell[axis] + 1 - localorigin[axis] / D[axis]) abs(Dinv[axis])) else: localtnext.append((localcell[axis] - localorigin[axis] / D[axis]) abs(Dinv[axis])) for j in range(8 8 8): if any(c < 0 or c >= 8 for c in localcell): break voxelval = voxels[localcell[0]][localcell[1]][localcell[2]] if voxelval > 0: return voxelval # Advance local DDA perm1 = [localtnext[1], localtnext[2], localtnext[0]] perm2 = [localtnext[2], localtnext[0], localtnext[1]] axismask = step(localtnext, minvec(perm1, perm2)) localtnext = [localtnext[k] + axismask[k] localtdelta[k] for k in range(3)] localcell = [localcell[k] + int(axismask[k]) stepdir[k] for k in range(3)] # Advance coarse DDA perm1 = [tnext[1], tnext[2], tnext[0]] perm2 = [tnext[2], tnext[0], tnext[1]] axismask = step(tnext, minvec(perm1, perm2)) tnext = [tnext[k] + axismask[k] tdelta[k] for k in range(3)] brickcell = [brickcell[k] + int(axismask[k]) stepdir[k] for k in range(3)] return 0 Parameters: brickgridext: Side length of the brick grid. Brick size: Fixed at 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxels in the primary implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SIMD Divergence: Incoherent rays cause control-flow divergence when entering the inner traversal loop, as not all SIMD lanes hit a brick at the same time, leading to stalls. Dense Scenes: In dense scenes or when viewing from afar with loose brick sizes, the overhead of two-level traversal may not provide gains over naive DDA if the brick grid is not selective enough. Viewing Angle: Performance degrades significantly when viewing along a surface inside a brick, as the full brick and voxel traversal is required. A three-level hierarchical traversal method that separates traversal into draining the current I1 DDA, stepping the I2 DDA, and advancing to the next root entry. It differs from MultiDDA by managing three distinct node types (I2, I1, leaf) rather than two levels of DDA loops. A hybrid rendering technique where camera-facing brick faces are rasterized into a depth buffer. Ray tracing uses this depth buffer to determine the ray origin for DDA, allowing it to skip empty space much faster. Quads are regenerated every frame to support dynamic voxel grids. Tighter fitting (4x4x4) improves performance when close to the model surface; looser (8x8x8) is better when viewing from afar. Performance uplift: sponza-1024-1 FPS +28.99%, sponza-1024-2 FPS +36.64%. Time Complexity: O(N{bricks} + N{voxels\in\occupied\bricks}) in the worst case, but significantly reduced in sparse scenes. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for both the voxel grid and the brick grid. Performance: In sparse scenes (e.g., sponza-256-2), MultiDDA provides significant speedups: FPS increased by +184.93% and walltime decreased by -82.73% compared to naive DDA. In dense scenes (e.g., sponza-256-1), the impact is minimal: FPS increased by only +0.04%. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for scenes with large empty spaces. Limitations: Suffers from SIMD divergence due to nested loops, less effective in dense scenes or with poor brick granularity. MultiDDA was developed as part of the VoxelRT project, an experimental voxel rendering framework. It was introduced in commit ed4004c on 2026-07-24 as a "2-level DDA" optimization to improve empty-space skipping performance over a flat voxel grid. The method is a direct response to the limitations of naive DDA in sparse volumes, leveraging the hierarchical nature of voxel data to skip large empty regions.
