name: VRI Ray Advancement
body: VRI Ray Advancement advances a Volume Ray Intersection (VRI) state machine to the next leaf voxel intersection by managing a three-level hierarchical traversal of I2 nodes, I1 nodes, and leaf voxels using Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) stepping. It differs from its parent MultiDDA by explicitly separating the traversal into three distinct phases: draining the current I1 DDA for leaf hits, stepping the I2 DDA to find the next active I1 child, and advancing to the next pre-sorted root entry when the hierarchy is exhausted. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin O and direction D; a pre-sorted list of root entries state.roots, where each entry is a tuple (t{min}, \text{I2\node}); and the current state containing DDA iterators and node references for I2 and I1 levels. Output: A LeafIntersection object containing t{enter}, t{exit}, and the leaf voxel reference, along with the updated state; or nothing if no further intersections exist. Data Structures: I2 Node: Represents a coarse block containing a children array of I1 nodes and a childmask bitmask. I1 Node: Represents a 8^3 voxel sub-grid (brick) containing a childmask and a children array of leaf voxels. Leaf Voxel: The finest granularity of the hierarchical grid. DDA State: state.i2ndda, state.i1ndda store the current DDA iterators; state.i2node, state.i1node store the current node references; state.rootidx tracks the current root entry. Parameters: I1 brick size: 8^3 voxels. I2 node size: 128 units (implied by 16 \times 8). Root block size: 32 units (implied by DDA init). Leaf voxel size: 1 unit. Algorithm Steps: 1. Phase 3: Advance to Next Pre-Sorted Root Entry. If no I1 found, set state.i2ndda = nothing and state.i2node = nothing. Increment state.rootidx. If state.rootidx > length(state.roots), return nothing. Otherwise, get tmin, i2node = state.roots[state.rootidx]. Initialize state.i2ndda = nodeddainit(ray, tmin, o, Int32(32), Int32(128)) and set state.i2node = i2node. Loop back to Phase 1. name: Empty Space Skipping with Orthogonal BSP Tree
head: Growing boxes with orthogonal BSP, Orthogonal BSP tree empty space skipping
body: This method accelerates texture-based volume rendering by partitioning the volume into sub-volumes (boxes) based on voxel properties, reorganizing them into an orthogonal BSP tree for visibility sorting, and skipping sub-volumes that are fully transparent according to the transfer function. It extends previous 2D texture approaches to 3D textures, which produce better image quality but require new sorting strategies due to arbitrary slicing plane orientations. Unlike siblings that use uniform grids or octrees, this method uses a one-stage goal-oriented growth process to separate surface voxels from interior voxels, optimizing lit rendering by minimizing unnecessary lighting computations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset represented as one or more 3D textures. A transfer function (typically a 1D lookup table mapping density to color and opacity). The current viewpoint (for perspective projection) or view direction (for parallel projection). Output: A rendered image identical to the unaccelerated result, but computed faster. Data Structures: 1. Sub-volumes (Boxes): Arbitrary axis-aligned bounding boxes enclosing clusters of voxels. Each box is defined by its minimum and maximum coordinates in the volume domain. 2. Orthogonal BSP Tree: A binary space partitioning tree where all partitioning planes are orthogonal to one of the major axes (X, Y, or Z). Each node represents a sub-volume or a partition. 3. Opacity Map: A low-resolution map on a plane orthogonal to one of the major axes of the dataset, used for occlusion culling. Steps: 1. Partition the Volume into Sub-volumes: Group voxels with similar properties in both the volume domain (position) and the transfer function domain (densities and gradient magnitudes) into the same sub-volume. Uniform Boxes: For unilluminated rendering, partition neighboring texels whose densities vary in a small range. A typical parameter value is a density range of 32. Gradient Boxes: For lit rendering, separate voxels with non-zero gradient magnitude from the rest to avoid lighting computation on interior voxels with zero gradient. This is done via a direct one-stage goal-oriented growth process. 2. Classify and Skip Invisible Sub-volumes: Classify a sub-volume as invisible if it is comprised of only voxels mapped to empty (fully transparent) by the transfer function. These sub-volumes are skipped for rendering. 3. Reorganize into Orthogonal BSP Tree: Reorganize the arbitrary set of sub-volume bounding boxes into an orthogonal BSP tree. All partitioning planes in this tree are orthogonal to a major axis. This simplifies visibility sorting compared to arbitrary oriented planes required for 3D textures. 4. Sort and Render: Render the sub-volumes in visibility order determined by the orthogonal BSP tree. The tree must be re-sorted whenever the viewpoint (for perspective projection) or view direction (for parallel projection) changes. 5. Incremental Intersection Computation: Compute incrementally the intersection of the axis-aligned sub-volumes with the slicing planes. This avoids the overhead of intersection and texture coordinate computation introduced by the partitioning. 6. Occlusion Culling: Create an opacity map on a plane orthogonal to one of the major axes. Update the opacity map from the contents of the frame buffer during rendering using GPU functionalities such as projective texture, interpolation, and blending functions. Project sub-volumes onto the opacity map and cull occluded ones. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Step 2: Classify invisible sub-volumes visiblesubvolumes = [] for box in subvolumes: if not isfullytransparent(box, transferfunction): visiblesubvolumes.append(box) # Step 3: Reorganize into Orthogonal BSP Tree bsptree = buildorthogonalbsptree(visiblesubvolumes) # Step 4: Sort and Render sortedboxes = sortboxesbyvisibility(bsptree, viewpoint) # Initialize frame buffer for occlusion culling framebuffer = [] for box in sortedboxes: # Step 5: Incremental intersection computation intersections = computeincrementalintersection(box, viewpoint) # Render the sub-volume using 3D texture rendersubvolume(box, intersections, transferfunction, framebuffer) # Step 6: Occlusion Culling opacitymap = updateopacitymap(framebuffer) culloccludedsubvolumes(visiblesubvolumes, opacitymap) def growboxes(volumedata, transferfunction): # Groups voxels with similar properties in volume and TF domains # Returns list of boxes with min/max coordinates return [] def isfullytransparent(box, transferfunction): # Checks if all voxels in box map to empty/transparent return False def buildorthogonalbsptree(boxes): # Recursively partitions boxes using planes orthogonal to major axes # Sources do not specify the exact partitioning algorithm return None def sortboxesbyvisibility(bsptree, viewpoint): # Traverses BSP tree to return boxes in back-to-front order return [] def computeincrementalintersection(box, viewpoint): # Computes intersection of axis-aligned box with slicing planes incrementally # Sources do not specify the exact incremental algorithm return [] def rendersubvolume(box, intersections, transferfunction, framebuffer): # Rasterizes box onto frame buffer using 3D texture and transfer function pass def updateopacitymap(framebuffer): # Projects frame buffer contents onto a low-resolution plane orthogonal to a major axis return [] def culloccludedsubvolumes(visiblesubvolumes, opacitymap): # Projects boxes onto opacity map and removes occluded ones pass Parameters: Density Range for Uniform Boxes: Neighboring texels whose densities vary in a small range are partitioned into a sub-texture. A typical value is 32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewpoint Changes: The BSP tree must be re-sorted whenever the viewpoint or view direction changes. Failure to do so results in incorrect rendering order. 3D Texture Slicing: Unlike 2D textures, 3D textures require handling arbitrary slicing plane orientations, which necessitates the orthogonal BSP tree for efficient sorting. Lit vs. Unlit Rendering: For lit rendering, it is crucial to separate surface voxels (non-zero gradient) from interior voxels (zero gradient) to avoid unnecessary lighting computations. Growing Boxes Partitioning is an adaptive volume partitioning method that divides a volume into sub-volumes (boxes) by clustering voxels based on their properties in both the volume domain and the transfer function domain. It aims to ensure that the visible box subset encloses few invisible voxels, thereby accelerating texture-based volume rendering by minimizing unnecessary lighting computations and texture switches. Unlike uniform partitioning or octrees, it separates surface voxels (non-zero gradient) from interior voxels (zero gradient) to optimize lit rendering, using a direct one-stage goal-oriented growth process rather than region growing followed by division. Performance: Rendering with empty space skipping is 2 to 5 times faster than without it, with identical image quality. Hardware: Tested on commodity graphics hardware with 3D textures. Strengths: Accelerates texture-based volume rendering by skipping invisible voxels; handles 3D textures with better image quality; incremental intersection computation minimizes overhead. Limitations: Requires re-sorting the BSP tree when the viewpoint or view direction changes; partitioning adds complexity compared to uniform grids. When to Use: When rendering 3D textures with lighting where many voxels are transparent or have zero gradient, and performance is critical. When Not to Use: When the volume has few transparent regions or when the overhead of partitioning and sorting outweighs the benefits of skipping. This method was proposed by Li, Mueller, and Kaufman. It extends their previous work on empty space skipping using stacks of 2D textures. The key innovation is the use of an orthogonal BSP tree to handle the arbitrary slicing plane orientations required by 3D textures, which produce better image quality than 2D textures. The method is part of the broader field of texture-based volume rendering acceleration. name: Growing Boxes Partitioning
head: Gradient boxes partitioning, Growing boxes
body: Growing Boxes Partitioning is an adaptive volume partitioning method that divides a volume into sub-volumes (boxes) by clustering voxels based on their properties in both the volume domain and the transfer function domain. It aims to ensure that the visible box subset encloses few invisible voxels, thereby accelerating texture-based volume rendering by minimizing unnecessary lighting computations and texture switches. Unlike uniform partitioning or octrees, it separates surface voxels (non-zero gradient) from interior voxels (zero gradient) to optimize lit rendering, using a direct one-stage goal-oriented growth process rather than region growing followed by division. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset (density values). A 1D transfer function mapping density to color and opacity. A predetermined cost threshold for box growth. A minimal size constraint for uniform boxes. Outputs: A set of non-overlapping boxes covering the volume, categorized as: Gradient boxes: Enclose voxels with non-zero gradient magnitude. Uniform boxes: Enclose voxels with zero gradient magnitude and similar densities. Other boxes: Fill remaining spaces left by minimal size restrictions. Data Structures: Each box is defined by its axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) to (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}) and its type (gradient, uniform, other). Voxels are assigned to exactly one box. Border voxels are replicated to ensure proper interpolation across box boundaries. Algorithm Steps: 1. Gradient Box Creation: Compute the gradient magnitude for each voxel. Identify voxels with non-zero gradient magnitude. Cluster these voxels into gradient boxes. 2. Uniform Box Creation: Identify voxels with zero gradient magnitude. Group neighboring texels whose densities vary within a small range (e.g., 32 density units). Grow boxes to enclose these uniform regions. Apply a minimal size restriction to uniform boxes. 3. Other Box Filling: Identify any remaining spaces in the volume not covered by gradient or uniform boxes (typically due to the minimal size restriction on uniform boxes). Fill these spaces with "other" boxes. Cost Function and Growth Rule: The partitioning balances the number of boxes and the total cost. Boxes grow to enclose voxels of similar properties. The general rule is to let boxes grow as large as possible while keeping the accumulated cost function smaller than a predetermined threshold. The exact formula for the cost function is not provided in the sources. Parameters: Minimal size of a uniform box: A restriction on the minimum dimensions of a uniform box. This may leave spaces filled by other boxes. Density range for uniformity: The maximum allowed density variation within a uniform box (e.g., 32 units). Cost threshold: The maximum accumulated cost for a box before growth stops. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Minimal Size Restrictions: If the minimal size for uniform boxes is too large, significant portions of the volume may be left uncovered by uniform boxes, requiring "other" boxes, which may not offer the same optimization benefits. Overhead: Increasing the number of boxes increases overhead for setting up and switching textures and increases replicated storage at box borders for proper interpolation. Lit vs. Unlit Rendering: Uniform boxes alone are inefficient for lit rendering because they include many zero-gradient voxels for lighting computation. Gradient boxes solve this by isolating surface voxels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def growingboxespartitioning(volume, transferfunction, costthreshold, minuniformsize): """ Partitions a volume into gradient, uniform, and other boxes. Args: volume: 3D array of density values. transferfunction: 1D lookup table mapping density to color/opacity. costthreshold: Maximum accumulated cost for a box. minuniformsize: Minimum size for a uniform box. Returns: A list of Box objects. """ boxes = [] visited = set() # Step 1: Create Gradient Boxes # Compute gradient magnitude for each voxel and identify non-zero values gradientvoxels = [] for z in range(volume.shape[0]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[2]): if computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z) > 0: gradientvoxels.append((x, y, z)) visited.add((x, y, z)) # Cluster gradient voxels into boxes based on cost threshold # Note: Specific clustering algorithm not detailed in sources gradientboxes = [] boxes.extend(gradientboxes) # Step 2: Create Uniform Boxes # Identify voxels with zero gradient magnitude uniformvoxels = [] for z in range(volume.shape[0]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[2]): if (x, y, z) not in visited and computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z) == 0: uniformvoxels.append((x, y, z)) visited.add((x, y, z)) # Group uniform voxels by density similarity (range of 32) uniformregions = [] uniformboxes = [] for region in uniformregions: # Grow box as large as possible while cost < threshold box = growbox(region, costthreshold) # Check minimal size restriction if box.size() >= minuniformsize: uniformboxes.append(box) else: # If too small, it is not added as a uniform box, leaving a gap pass boxes.extend(uniformboxes) # Step 3: Fill Remaining Spaces with Other Boxes # Identify uncovered spaces remainingspaces = [] # Fill with other boxes otherboxes = [] boxes.extend(otherboxes) return boxes def computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z): # Standard gradient computation (e.g., Sobel or finite differences) pass def growbox(region, costthreshold): # Grow box to enclose region while keeping cost < threshold pass Converts the set of growing boxes into an orthogonal BSP tree for visibility sorting. It sets itself apart by imposing a strict hierarchical structure on the adaptive boxes, ensuring trivial visibility sorting for 3D texture rendering. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. The one-stage growth process is described as more direct than region growing followed by division. Memory Complexity: Increases with the number of boxes due to replicated storage at box borders for interpolation. Performance: Improves rendering speed by skipping invisible sub-volumes and reducing unnecessary lighting computations on zero-gradient voxels. Strengths: Effective for lit rendering by isolating surface voxels; adaptive to volume properties. Limitations: Overhead increases with the number of boxes; minimal size restrictions may lead to inefficient "other" boxes. When to Use: When lit rendering performance is critical and the volume has distinct surface and interior regions. When Not to Use: When the overhead of managing many small boxes outweighs the benefits, or for unilluminated rendering where uniform boxes alone may suffice. Origin: Introduced by Li and Kaufman in 2003. History: Initially experimented with 2D textures, later extended to 3D textures using an orthogonal BSP tree. Usage: Used in texture-based volume rendering for early termination and empty space skipping. name: Orthogonal BSP Tree Construction
head: BSP tree conversion, Orthogonal BSP
body: Orthogonal BSP Tree Construction converts a set of arbitrarily positioned and sized "grown boxes" into an orthogonal Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) tree where every splitting plane is object-aligned. This conversion solves the problem of non-trivial visibility sorting that arises when box sizes and positions are arbitrary, potentially creating cyclic visibility orders from specific viewpoints. By enforcing object-aligned splits, it enables trivial depth sorting for 3D texture rendering. It sets itself apart from its sibling Growing Boxes Partitioning by taking the adaptive box set as input and structuring it into a strict hierarchy for traversal, and from K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction by restricting split planes to coincide with object faces rather than allowing arbitrary positions. Inputs: A set of grown boxes, each defined by its bounding box and type (uniform, gradient, or other). Outputs: An orthogonal BSP tree where leaf nodes contain exactly one box (either an original grown box or a child box generated from splitting). Data Structures: Box: Defined by its spatial bounds. It has a type field (uniform, gradient, other) and a parent pointer. BSP Node: Contains: room: A bounding box representing the union of all boxes in the node's list. boxlist: A list of boxes associated with this node. front: Pointer to the front child node. back: Pointer to the back child node. parentbox: If this node is a non-leaf node, it may hold a "parent box" that was split to create this node. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a root BSP node. Set its room to the union of all input grown boxes. Add all input grown boxes to the root's boxlist. 2. Node Splitting: Recursively split nodes until leaf constraints are met. For a given node: Termination: If the node's boxlist contains exactly one box, it is a leaf node. Stop splitting. Plane Selection: Choose a partitioning plane aligned with the faces of at least two boxes in the boxlist to minimize the number of boxes that need to be split. The plane must split the current room into two sub-boxes. Child Creation: Create two child nodes: front and back. Room Assignment: Split the current node's room using the chosen plane. Assign the resulting front sub-box as the room of the front child, and the back sub-box as the room of the back child. Box Redistribution: Iterate through each box in the current node's boxlist: If the box is completely enclosed in the front room, move it to the front child's boxlist. If the box is completely enclosed in the back room, move it to the back child's boxlist. If the box is cut by the partitioning plane: Split the box into two new boxes along the plane. Add the front part to the front child's boxlist. Add the back part to the back child's boxlist. Parent-Child Hierarchy: If the original box has no parent (it is an original grown box), set the original box as the parentbox of the current node (or associate it with the split). If the original box has a parent, set that parent as the parent of the two new child boxes. Delete the original box from the current node's list. Recursion: Recursively call the split procedure on the front and back children. 3. Bottom-Up Merging: After the initial tree construction, reduce the tree size by merging child nodes. For a pair of sibling nodes (front and back): Merge if any of the following conditions are true: 1. Both children contain uniform boxes, and the union of their boxes forms a uniform box. 2. Both children contain "other" boxes or both contain "gradient" boxes. 3. One of the boxes is tiny or very thin (size along one axis is smaller than a threshold). Merge Action: Create a new merged box representing the union of the two child boxes. Determine the type of the merged box based on the enclosed voxel properties. If the merged node replaces the two children, update the parent's reference. If the two children had different parent boxes, delete those parent boxes and make their children parentless (if they are not leaves). Repeat merging until no more merges are possible. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Box: def init(self, bounds, boxtype, parent=None): self.bounds = bounds # AABB self.type = boxtype # 'uniform', 'gradient', 'other' self.parent = parent class BSPNode: def init(self, room, boxlist=None): self.room = room # AABB self.boxlist = boxlist if boxlist else [] self.front = None self.back = None self.parentbox = None # Box that was split to create this node def splitnode(node): if len(node.boxlist) == 1: return # Leaf node # 1. Choose partitioning plane # Criterion: Minimize splits, plane coincides with faces of at least two boxes plane = choosepartitioningplane(node.boxlist, node.room) # 2. Create children and split room frontroom, backroom = splitaabb(node.room, plane) frontnode = BSPNode(frontroom) backnode = BSPNode(backroom) node.front = frontnode node.back = backnode # 3. Process boxes boxestoprocess = list(node.boxlist) node.boxlist = [] # Clear current list as boxes are moved/split for box in boxestoprocess: if box.isenclosedin(frontroom): frontnode.boxlist.append(box) elif box.isenclosedin(backroom): backnode.boxlist.append(box) else: # Box is cut by plane frontpart, backpart = splitbox(box, plane) # Set parent hierarchy if box.parent is None: # Original grown box becomes parent of this split node.parentbox = box else: # Existing parent applies to new children frontpart.parent = box.parent backpart.parent = box.parent frontnode.boxlist.append(frontpart) backnode.boxlist.append(backpart) # Recurse splitnode(frontnode) splitnode(backnode) def mergenodes(frontnode, backnode): # Check merge conditions if not canmerge(frontnode, backnode): return False # Create merged box mergedbounds = unionaabb(frontnode.room, backnode.room) mergedtype = determinemergedtype(frontnode, backnode) mergedbox = Box(mergedbounds, mergedtype) # Handle parent boxes if frontnode.parentbox != backnode.parentbox: # Delete conflicting parent boxes if they are no longer needed # Note: Logic depends on specific implementation of "parentless" children pass # Replace children with merged node in parent # This requires access to the parent of frontnode and backnode return True def buildorthogonalbsp(grownboxes): rootroom = unionaabb([b.bounds for b in grownboxes]) root = BSPNode(rootroom, grownboxes) # Initial Splitting splitnode(root) # Bottom-Up Merging # Traverse tree bottom-up and attempt merges mergeall(root) return root Parameters: Threshold for tiny/thin boxes: Not given in the sources. (Typically a small fraction of the volume extent or voxel size). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hierarchy Constraint: No box can be both a child and a parent at the same time. There is only one level of parent-child hierarchy. Parent boxes reside on non-leaf nodes; rendering uses only leaf nodes. Texture Sharing: Child boxes share the texture of their parent with siblings to avoid replicating texels along boundaries. Replicating texels would increase memory requirements. Cyclic Visibility: The conversion is necessary because arbitrary grown boxes may have cyclic visibility orders from specific viewpoints, which trivial sorting cannot handle. Allows splitting planes to be positioned arbitrarily within a node's bounds (often via bisection) rather than being strictly object-aligned, and associates polygons with the smallest node region that completely contains them, thereby avoiding polygon subdivision. Choose when arbitrary splits are acceptable or beneficial for balance, and when avoiding polygon splitting is critical. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables trivial visibility sorting for 3D texture rendering by ensuring object-aligned splits. Keeps the total number of boxes comparable to the original set after merging. Limitations: The total number of boxes at leaf nodes after splitting can be significantly greater than the original set, necessitating the merging step. When to use: When using adaptive partitioning (grown boxes) where arbitrary box sizes and positions would otherwise prevent trivial visibility sorting. When not to use: When uniform partitioning is sufficient, or when arbitrary split planes (K-D tree) are preferred for balancing. This method is part of the "Empty Space Skipping and Occlusion Clipping for Texture-based Volume Rendering" framework. It addresses the limitations of adaptive partitioning where box sizes and positions are arbitrary, leading to non-trivial visibility sorting. The conversion to an orthogonal BSP tree allows the system to leverage the efficiency of texture-based rendering with proper depth sorting. name: K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction
head: Polygon distribution in k-d tree, Spatial partitioning with k-d trees
body: K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction is a method for building a spatial partitioning data structure to organize polygons for efficient rendering and ray traversal. It solves the problem of explicitly clipping polygons against view frustums or traversal planes by storing them in a binary tree where each node splits a region in one dimension at a time. It sets itself apart from its sibling Orthogonal BSP Tree Construction by allowing splitting planes to be positioned arbitrarily within a node's bounds (often via bisection) rather than being strictly object-aligned, and by associating polygons with the smallest node region that completely contains them, thereby avoiding polygon subdivision. Inputs: A set of polygons P, each defined by its vertices. A user-defined leaf threshold T{leaf}. Outputs: A binary tree where each node v contains a list of polygon IDs and references to left/right children. Data Structures: Tree Node v: splitdim: Integer index i \in \{0, 1, 2\} indicating the axis of splitting. splitval: Float value Xi along axis i defining the hyperplane. polyids: List of polygon identifiers. leftchild: Reference to left subtree node. rightchild: Reference to right subtree node. Polygon Storage: Polygon IDs are stored in a common array Tid arranged in prefix-order traversal order to allow passing all objects associated with a subtree in one operation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with the root node v{root} containing all input polygons P. 2. Recursive Construction: For a node v receiving a set of polygons Pv: a. Leaf Check: If |Pv| \le T{leaf}, mark v as a leaf. b. Splitting Axis Selection: Determine the splitting dimension i. The standard implementation uses a round-robin fashion (e.g., i = \text{depth} \pmod 3). More sophisticated policies may analyze variance (see Axis Selection via Variance). c. Splitting Value Selection: Determine the split value Xi. The standard implementation bisects the region along axis i. d. Polygon Classification: For each polygon p \in Pv: i. Check the xi coordinate of all vertices of p. ii. If all vertices have xi < Xi, add p to the left set P{left}. iii. If all vertices have xi > Xi, add p to the right set P{right}. iv. Otherwise, retain p in the current node's list Pv. e. Recursion: i. If P{left} is not empty, create left child v{left}, set v{left}.poly\ids = P{left}, and recursively construct v{left}. ii. If P{right} is not empty, create right child v{right}, set v{right}.poly\ids = P{right}, and recursively construct v{right}. iii. If a child set is empty, the corresponding child pointer is null. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Polygon Association: Polygons are associated with the smallest node region that completely contains them. This avoids subdividing polygons but means a polygon may be stored in an internal node rather than a leaf if it spans the split plane. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for vertex positions against Xi must be consistent to avoid ambiguity. Empty Subtrees: If all polygons fall into one side, the other child is empty. The algorithm handles this by not creating a child node or marking it as null. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ if not polygons: return None node = Node() node.isleaf = False node.leftchild = None node.rightchild = None if len(polygons) <= threshold: node.isleaf = True node.polyids = [p.id for p in polygons] return node # Round-robin axis selection splitdim = depth % 3 # Calculate bounds to find bisection point minval = float('inf') maxval = float('-inf') for p in polygons: for v in p.getvertices(): val = v[splitdim] if val < minval: minval = val if val > maxval: maxval = val # Bisection value splitval = (minval + maxval) / 2.0 node.splitdim = splitdim node.splitval = splitval leftpolys = [] rightpolys = [] currentpolys = [] for p in polygons: allless = True allgreater = True for v in p.getvertices(): val = v[splitdim] if val >= splitval: allless = False if val <= splitval: allgreater = False if allless: leftpolys.append(p) elif allgreater: rightpolys.append(p) else: currentpolys.append(p) node.polyids = [p.id for p in currentpolys] node.leftchild = buildkdtree(leftpolys, depth + 1, threshold) node.rightchild = buildkdtree(rightpolys, depth + 1, threshold) return node class Node: def init(self): self.splitdim = 0 self.splitval = 0.0 self.polyids = [] self.leftchild = None self.rightchild = None self.isleaf = False Selects the splitting axis by analyzing the variance of the QEF (Quadratic Error Function) solution along each dimension, scaled by the box size. Steps: 1. Solve QEF to get approximate solution and error. 2. Calculate variance for each axis: variance[i] = qef.getVariance(approximate) \times size[i]. 3. Find maxVarDir (index of max variance) and minVarDir (index of min variance). 4. Set dir = maxVarDir. If size[maxVarDir] < 2, fallback to 3 - maxVarDir - minVarDir. If that size < 2, fallback to minVarDir. A technique proposed by Zhou et al. for building KD tree nodes in real-time using GPU programming via breadth-first search. A hierarchical spatial partitioning structure where each node is divided into two sub-nodes by a plane orthogonal to an axis, positioned arbitrarily along that axis within the node [4575-gpu-k-d-tree-ray-traversal.md]. It is a special case of BSP-Tree [4575-gpu-k-d-tree-ray-traversal.md]. This variant focuses on the traversal efficiency on GPU hardware rather than the construction method itself. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N \log N) on average for balanced trees, where N is the number of polygons. Worst-case is O(N^2) for degenerate inputs. Limitations: Sensitive to input distribution. Round-robin splitting may not be optimal for all scenes. Requires careful handling of polygons spanning split planes. It sets itself apart from its parent method, K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction, by utilizing GPU parallelism and breadth-first search (BFS) to achieve real-time performance. It differs from GPU K-D Tree Ray Traversal by focusing on the construction phase rather than the traversal phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of primitives or voxel data to be partitioned. Output: A k-d tree structure stored in GPU memory, ready for traversal. The tree is constructed via breadth-first search rather than the prefix-order traversal used in the parent method. Steps: 1. Load input primitives or voxel data into GPU memory. 2. Perform a breadth-first search (BFS) to determine the tree structure and split planes. 3. Store the resulting node information in GPU texture memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: GPU K-D Tree Ray Traversal
head: K-D Tree GPU Traversal, Kd-Tree Ray Tracing on GPU
body: GPU K-D Tree Ray Traversal accelerates ray tracing on graphics hardware by intersecting rays with a hierarchical spatial partitioning structure (K-D tree). It efficiently skips empty space and identifies intersected primitives, avoiding the computational cost of testing every primitive in the scene. It is distinguished from CPU implementations by its adaptation to GPU architectures: early Shader Model 2.0 hardware used stackless multi-pass streaming kernels, while Shader Model 3.0 introduced single-pass traversal via dynamic branching. It builds on K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction. The K-D tree is a hierarchical spatial partitioning structure where each node is divided into two sub-nodes by a plane orthogonal to an axis, positioned arbitrarily along that axis within the node. It is a special case of a BSP-Tree. Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a K-D tree structure where each node contains a split axis, split position, and references to left/right children or leaf primitives. Output: The closest intersection point or hit primitive along the ray. The tree nodes are typically stored in a flat array. Each node contains: axis: The dimension (0, 1, or 2) along which the split occurs. split: The position of the splitting plane along the specified axis. left: Index of the left child node. right: Index of the right child node. primcount: Number of primitives in the leaf. primoffset: Offset into a global primitive array for leaf nodes. 1. Initialize the ray slab with near and far clip distances. 2. Start traversal at the root node. 3. Calculate the intersection parameter t between the ray and the current node's split plane. 4. Determine traversal order based on the ray origin's position relative to the split plane. 5. Update the slab bounds (t{min}, t{max}) if the split plane is within the current ray segment. 6. Advance to the child node index. 7. If the current node is a leaf, test contained primitives against the ray slab. 8. Terminate when a hit is found, the slab is exhausted, or the maximum depth is reached. The intersection parameter t for the ray to reach the split plane is computed as: t = \frac{s - oa}{da} where s is the split position, oa is the ray origin component along the split axis a, and da is the ray direction component along axis a. The ray-slab bounds t{min} and t{max} are updated by clamping t to the current interval. maxdepth: Maximum traversal depth to prevent infinite loops on degenerate trees; typically set to the tree height or a fixed constant like 32. tmin: Near clip distance; typically 0.0 or the camera's near plane. tmax: Far clip distance; typically 1000.0 or the camera's far plane. Zero direction component: If da = 0, the ray is parallel to the split plane; t is undefined and the ray stays on one side of the plane. Precision errors: Floating-point inaccuracies near split planes can cause rays to miss nodes or traverse incorrectly; epsilon offsets are often applied. Degenerate input: Empty nodes or zero-volume cells can cause infinite loops; handled by maxdepth or node validation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, treenodes, maxdepth): """ Traverses a K-D tree for a single ray using dynamic branching. Assumes treenodes is a flat array of node structures. Returns the closest hit primitive index or -1 if no hit. """ currentnode = 0 # Start at root tmin = 0.0 # Near clip plane tmax = 1e9 # Far clip plane for step in range(maxdepth): node = treenodes[currentnode] # Check if leaf if node.primcount > 0: closestprim = -1 for i in range(node.primcount): primidx = node.primoffset + i thit = intersectprimitive(rayorigin, raydirection, primidx) if thit is not None and tmin <= thit < tmax: tmax = thit closestprim = primidx return closestprim # Determine which child to visit first splitaxis = node.axis splitpos = node.split # Ray parameter to intersection with split plane if raydirection[splitaxis] == 0.0: tsplit = float('inf') if splitpos > rayorigin[splitaxis] else float('-inf') else: tsplit = (splitpos - rayorigin[splitaxis]) / raydirection[splitaxis] # Determine traversal order based on ray origin side if rayorigin[splitaxis] < splitpos: if tsplit < tmin: currentnode = node.right else: currentnode = node.left if tsplit < tmax: tmax = tsplit else: if tsplit < tmin: currentnode = node.left else: currentnode = node.right if tsplit < tmax: tmax = tsplit # If tmax <= tmin, we have passed the region of interest if tmax <= tmin: return -1 return -1 def intersectprimitive(origin, direction, primidx): """Standard primitive intersection routine.""" # Implementation depends on primitive type (triangle, sphere, etc.) return None Time Complexity: O(\log N) on average for balanced trees, where N is the number of primitives; worst case O(N) for degenerate trees. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the tree nodes. Performance: Early GPU implementations (Foley and Sugerman) were slower than CPU counterparts due to streaming limitations. Later implementations (Horn et al.) became competitive with CPU but were limited by SIMD divergence penalties on Shader Model 3.0 hardware. Strengths: Efficient empty-space skipping; flexible for arbitrary scenes. Limitations: Dynamic branching causes divergence penalties on SIMD GPUs; stackless methods require multiple passes or fixed-depth loops. Origin: The K-D tree was shown by Havran [Hav00] to be the most flexible and provide average best results for arbitrary scenes in CPU ray tracing. History: The first GPU ray tracing use of K-D trees was proposed by Ernst et al. [EVG04], using a stack and a heavy multi-pass algorithm, which did not achieve high performance. Foley and Sugerman [FS05] improved this with stackless multi-pass methods for Shader Model 2.0. Horn et al. [HSHH07] proposed the first efficient GPU method competitive with CPU implementations, using Shader Model 3.0 dynamic branching for a single-pass algorithm. body: Empty Space Skipping with Octree is an acceleration technique for isosurface rendering that uses an octree structure storing conservative minimum and maximum scalar value estimates to skip transparent or irrelevant regions. It solves the problem of expensive spline evaluations in empty space by allowing rays to bypass nodes that do not contain the target isovalue. Unlike standard empty-space skipping which may rely on coarse bricks, this method uses hierarchical min/max ranges to prune nodes. Inputs: Scalar volume data (typically represented as B-spline coefficients or wavelet coefficients). Target isovalue I. Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Leaf size parameter b (trade-off between skipping efficiency and memory). Outputs: Intersection points with the isosurface, or early termination if the ray passes through empty space. Data Structures: Octree Node: Stores minval and maxval representing the conservative bounds of the scalar field in the subtree. Leaf Node: Corresponds to a group of b^3 adjacent polynomials. Cube Representation: For traversal, cubic cells are represented with vertices storing 2D texture coordinates containing the min/max values of the cell. Pre-processing Steps: 1. Leaf Min/Max Estimation: For each leaf node, estimate the minimum and maximum scalar values using the convex combination property of the B-spline basis. 2. BB-Form Construction: For each cubic cell, construct Bernstein-Bézier (BB) forms of its five tetrahedral polynomial pieces. 3. BB-Value Assignment: Set the min/max values of the cubic cell to the min/max values of those BB-coefficients. 4. Propagation: Propagate the min/max values from the leaves towards the root of the octree. Each internal node stores the conservative estimate (min of children mins, max of children maxes) of the minimum and maximum value appearing in its subtree. Rendering Steps: 1. Traversal: Perform a GPU-enabled parametric octree traversal. 2. Culling: For each visited node, check if the target isovalue I lies within [node.min\val, node.max\val]. If not, skip the node. 3. Entry/Exit Point Computation: Render cubes corresponding to one level of the min/max octree instead of the whole volume. Compute exit points by rendering cubes with glCullFace(GL FRONT) and glDepthFunc(GL LESS). Compute entry points by rendering cubes again with glCullFace(GL BACK) and glDepthFunc(GL GREATER). 4. Fragment Shader Logic: In the fragment shader, discard the fragment if the cube is empty or does not contain the isosurface level. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayaabbintersect(rayo, rayd, bboxmin, bboxmax): """Returns (tmin, tmax) of ray intersection with axis-aligned bounding box, or None if no intersection.""" tmin = float('-inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if rayd[i] == 0: if rayo[i] < bboxmin[i] or rayo[i] > bboxmax[i]: return None else: t1 = (bboxmin[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] t2 = (bboxmax[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 if tmin > tmax: return None if tmax < 0: return None return (max(tmin, 0.0), tmax) def traverseoctree(rayo, rayd, isovalue, node): """Recursively traverses octree to find nearest isosurface intersection distance t.""" # Pruning check if isovalue < node.minval or isovalue > node.maxval: return None # Leaf node evaluation if node.isleaf: return evaluateleaf(rayo, rayd, isovalue, node.polynomials) # Internal node: find intersecting children closestt = None for child in node.children: tmin, tmax = rayaabbintersect(rayo, rayd, child.bboxmin, child.bboxmax) if tmin is None or tmax <= 0: continue t = traverseoctree(rayo, rayd, isovalue, child) if t is not None and (closestt is None or t < closestt): closestt = t return closestt def evaluateleaf(rayo, rayd, isovalue, polynomials): """Solves for t where f(rayo + t rayd) = isovalue using BB-coefficients or B-splines.""" return solvepolynomialintersection(rayo, rayd, isovalue, polynomials) def solvepolynomialintersection(rayo, rayd, isovalue, polynomials): # Substitute ray equation into polynomial basis to form cubic in t # Solve c3t^3 + c2t^2 + c1t + c0 = isovalue using Cardano's formula or Newton-Raphson # Return smallest real root t > 0, or None if no intersection exists return None Parameters: b: Leaf size factor. Each leaf corresponds to a group of b^3 adjacent polynomials, where b is a trade-off factor between more efficient empty space skipping and memory requirement of the tree structure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Conservative estimates must be tight enough to avoid false negatives (skipping valid regions) but loose enough to allow pruning. Boundary Conditions: Ensure ray bounding box intersection tests handle rays parallel to axes or originating inside nodes correctly. Zero Direction Component: When \mathbf{d}i = 0, the ray is parallel to the axis; the test checks if the ray origin lies within the cell bounds along that axis. Uses hierarchical min/max ranges to prune nodes that do not contain the target isovalue, allowing for interactive transfer function changes. Choose when dynamic transfer functions are required. Recursively determines if a node contains any non-empty data blocks, returning EMPTY or NONEMPTY. Choose for binary or sparse data where exact emptiness is known. Constructs a view-dependent working set of octree nodes for out-of-core rendering. Choose when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck and data exceeds GPU memory. Time Complexity: Traversal is proportional to the number of non-empty nodes intersected by the ray. Pruning reduces this significantly in sparse volumes. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of leaf nodes, plus overhead for the octree structure. Performance: Reduces the number of expensive spline evaluations by skipping empty regions. Strengths: Efficient for large datasets. Limitations: Requires pre-processing to build the octree and compute min/max values; overhead may not be justified for very small or dense volumes. The method leverages the properties of B-spline bases and octree structures to enable efficient empty space skipping. It is applied to accelerate volume animation and interactive rendering for moderately sized volumes. body: Octree Traversal with Min/Max Pruning is an acceleration technique for ray tracing isosurfaces in scalar volumes stored in an octree. It solves the problem of efficiently skipping transparent or irrelevant regions during rendering by storing the minimum and maximum scalar values of each node's children. Unlike standard empty-space skipping which may rely on coarse bricks, this method uses the hierarchical min/max ranges to prune nodes that do not contain the target isovalue, allowing for interactive transfer function changes without rebuilding the entire geometry. It sets itself apart by embedding the acceleration structure and scalar data in a single octree, leveraging the duality between voxels and cells to define cell primitives for ray intersection. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Ray entry time t{\text{enter}} and exit time t{\text{exit}} for the volume bounding box. Target isovalue I. Octree structure containing scalar data and min/max metadata. Maximum octree depth D{\text{max}}. Outputs: Boolean indicating if the ray intersects the isosurface within the volume. The octree is stored as a single structure serving as both data container and acceleration tree. Node Layout: Each node contains: childmins: Array of size 8, storing the minimum scalar value present in each of the 8 children. childmaxs: Array of size 8, storing the maximum scalar value present in each of the 8 children. childoffset: Integer. If childoffset == -1, the node is a leaf (scalar data). Otherwise, it is an internal node. Implicit state during traversal: child: Current child index (0-7). childcell: 3D integer coordinate of the current cell within the octree level. Cell Primitive: The algorithm traces rays through cells composed of 8 voxels. A duality exists between voxels and cells: each voxel is mapped to the lower-left corner of a cell by shifting the scalar field backward by half a unit of voxel width. Values outside the octree data are defined as zero. This allows the ray to intersect well-defined cell primitives at each step. 1. Initialization: Start traversal at the root of the octree with the global ray parameters (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, t{\text{enter}}, t{\text{exit}}). 2. Axis Intersection Calculation: For the current node, calculate the intersection times with the X, Y, and Z octant mid-planes. Store the corresponding axis indices (0, 1, 2) sorted by increasing intersection time in axisisects. 3. Child Traversal Loop: Initialize childtenter = t{\text{enter}}. Iterate through the valid axis intersections in axisisects while the center time t{\text{center}} < t{\text{exit}}: a. Calculate Exit Time: Compute childtexit as the minimum of the intersection time on the current axis (tcenter) and the global texit. b. Min/Max Pruning Check: Check if the isovalue I lies within the child node's scalar range: I \geq \text{node.child\mins[child]} \quad \text{AND} \quad I \leq \text{node.child\maxs[child]} If this condition is false, the node does not contain the isosurface; skip to the next iteration (update childtenter and child index). c. Node Type Handling: Leaf: If node.childoffset == -1, traverse the scalar leaf. If it returns true, the ray hit and the function returns true. Max Depth Cap: If the current depth == octdata.maxdepth and the node is not a leaf, traverse the cap geometry. If it returns true, return true. Internal Node: Recursively traverse it with updated tenter/texit bounds. If it returns true, return true. d. Early Exit: If childtexit == t{\text{exit}}, the ray has exited the volume or the current bounding region without hitting anything relevant; return false. e. Update Entry Time: Set childtenter = childtexit for the next iteration. f. Update Child Index: Determine the axis bit from axistable (e.g., {4, 2, 1} for X, Y, Z) using the current axis index. If the current child index has the axis bit set, clear the bit in child and the corresponding bit in childcell. Otherwise, set the bit in child and the corresponding bit in childcell. 4. Return: If the loop completes without a hit, return false. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseminmax(ray, node, depth, tenter, texit, isovalue, maxdepth): """ Traverses an octree using min/max pruning for isosurface rendering. """ # Compute intersection times with X, Y, Z mid-planes of the current cell. # Returns axis indices (0, 1, 2) sorted by increasing intersection time. axisorder = computeaxisorder(ray, node.cellcoord, tenter, texit) childtenter = tenter child = 0 # Initial child index childcell = node.cellcoord axistable = [4, 2, 1] # Maps axis index to bit mask for axisidx in axisorder: # Intersection time with the current axis mid-plane tcenter = computeintersectiontime(ray, node.cellcoord, axisidx, tenter, texit) if tcenter >= texit: break childtexit = min(tcenter, texit) # Min/Max Pruning Check if isovalue >= node.childmins[child] and isovalue <= node.childmaxs[child]: if node.childoffset == -1: # Traverse scalar leaf (standard ray-march/isosurface check on 8 voxels) if traversescalarleaf(ray, node, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue): return True elif depth == maxdepth: # Traverse cap geometry at max depth if traversecap(ray, node, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue): return True else: # Recursive internal node traversal if traverseminmax(ray, node.children[child], depth + 1, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue, maxdepth): return True if childtexit == texit: return False childtenter = childtexit axisbit = axistable[axisidx] childbit = 1 << axisidx if child & axisbit: child &= ~axisbit childcell[axisidx] &= ~childbit else: child |= axisbit childcell[axisidx] |= childbit return False def computeaxisorder(ray, cellcoord, tenter, texit): """Returns axis indices [0, 1, 2] sorted by intersection time with cell mid-planes.""" times = [] for axis in range(3): t = computeintersectiontime(ray, cellcoord, axis, tenter, texit) times.append((t, axis)) times.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [axis for, axis in times] def computeintersectiontime(ray, cellcoord, axis, tenter, texit): """Standard ray-plane intersection with the mid-plane of the current cell along the given axis.""" mid = cellcoord[axis] + 0.5 denom = ray.d[axis] if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return float('inf') t = (mid - ray.o[axis]) / denom if tenter <= t <= texit: return t return float('inf') def traversescalarleaf(ray, node, tenter, texit, isovalue): # Sources do not specify the exact scalar leaf traversal routine. # Standard implementation: ray-march through the 8 voxels of the cell primitive # and check for isosurface intersection within [tenter, texit]. pass def traversecap(ray, node, tenter, texit, isovalue): # Sources do not specify the exact cap traversal routine. # Standard implementation: intersect ray with the cap geometry bounding the cell. pass node.childmins[child]: Minimum scalar value in the child node. node.childmaxs[child]: Maximum scalar value in the child node. octdata.maxdepth: Maximum depth of the octree. Transfer Function (RGB\alpha map): Used to classify regions interactively. Max Depth Cap: At the maximum octree depth, the algorithm does not traverse further into children but instead calls traversecap, implying leaf nodes at max depth represent cap geometry rather than volumetric data. Transfer Function Changes: When the transfer function changes, the min/max ranges are used to reclassify regions. Empty Adaptive Block Refinement (ABR) regions can be deactivated, requiring an interactive rebuild of the BVH if used in conjunction. Precision: The min/max pruning relies on the scalar range. Boundary cases where the isovalue exactly matches a stored min or max value are handled by the inclusive range check, ensuring safe traversal at the cost of potentially reduced pruning efficiency. Memory: The octree stores min/max values for each node, adding overhead to the scalar data. The structure is lossless compressed, occupying a fraction of the original memory footprint. Time: Traversal is front-to-back, allowing early termination. Pruning efficiency depends on the variance of scalar values within nodes. Competitive frame rates on common multicore architectures for large time-variant data. Superior to using bricks' min/max values for space-skipping classification, which is reported to be of much lower quality. Strengths: Allows interactive transfer function changes by recomputing majorants from stored ranges. Efficient memory usage due to compression and single structure for data and acceleration. Limitations: Indirection of the transfer function prevents direct computation of local majorants, requiring subdivision and min/max range storage. Requires pre-processing to store min/max ranges. Use for interactive isosurface rendering of large scalar volumes where transfer function changes are frequent. Use when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and compression is beneficial. Not suitable for direct volume rendering with complex transfer functions that cannot be approximated by min/max ranges. Not suitable if the volume data is not structured or cannot be converted to an octree. The method was introduced by Knoll et al. in 2006. It is described in "Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes". The technique builds on the concept of min/max trees for empty space skipping. It embeds the acceleration tree and scalar data in a single structure, employing optimized octree hash schemes. Large-scale volume visualization. Interactive isosurface rendering. name: Min-Max Octree Rendering
head: Unclassified Volume Rendering, Unclassified Volume Rendering with Min-Max Octree, vpRenderRawVolume algorithm
body: Min-Max Octree Rendering is an acceleration technique for ray-casting unclassified scalar volumes, designed for scenarios where classification parameters change frequently. It differs from pre-classified rendering by storing raw voxel data and using a hierarchical min-max structure to prune empty space and skip nodes that do not contain the target isovalue range, avoiding the costly recomputation of classification tables. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unclassified volume data (scalar field), classification function (transfer function), view and shading parameters. Output: Rendered image. Auxiliary Input: Precomputed Min-Max Octree. Data Structures: The core structure is the Min-Max Octree, a hierarchical data structure containing minimum and maximum values for each field used to index the classification tables. The smallest nodes in the octree have a side length equal to basenodesize in voxels. Parameters: basenodesize: The side length in voxels of the smallest node in the octree. Smaller values provide better pruning resolution at the expense of increased memory usage. Typical value: 4. range: A range of table indices for a parameter considered 'small'. The opacity of a voxel should not vary much if the table index is changed by the amount specified in range. Choosing a value too small or too large may reduce performance benefit. Steps: 1. Define Volume: Initialize the unclassified volume using vpSetVolumeSize(), vpSetVoxelSize(), vpSetVoxelField(), and vpSetRawVoxels(). Initialize the volume data array. 2. Configure Thresholds: For each classification table parameter, call vpMinMaxOctreeThreshold(paramnum, range) to define the "small" range for that parameter. 3. Build Octree: Call vpCreateMinMaxOctree(rootnodesize, basenodesize) to compute the min-max octree from the raw volume data and store it in the rendering context. 4. Render Loop: a. Choose the classification function (transfer function). b. Set view and shading parameters. c. Render the volume using vpRenderRawVolume(). The octree is used automatically during this call. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Context: def init(self): self.volumesize = None self.voxelsize = None self.voxelfield = None self.rawvoxels = None self.minmaxoctree = None self.classificationtables = {} self.viewmatrix = None self.shadingmodel = None def initializevolume(ctx, size, voxelsize, field, rawdata): ctx.volumesize = size ctx.voxelsize = voxelsize ctx.voxelfield = field ctx.rawvoxels = rawdata def configurethresholds(ctx, paramnum, rangeval): ctx.classificationtables[paramnum] = rangeval def buildoctree(ctx, basenodesize): # Reads rawvoxels, computes min/max bounds per octree node, stores in ctx.minmaxoctree ctx.minmaxoctree = computeminmaxoctree(ctx.rawvoxels, basenodesize) def render(ctx): # Uses ctx.minmaxoctree automatically to prune empty space and skip nodes # during ray traversal based on classification tables and view/shading parameters image = raycastwithpruning(ctx.rawvoxels, ctx.minmaxoctree, ctx.classificationtables, ctx.viewmatrix, ctx.shadingmodel) return image ctx = Context() initializevolume(ctx, size=(W, H, D), voxelsize=(dx, dy, dz), field="scalar", rawdata=voxelarray) for paramnum, rangeval in transferfunctionparams.items(): configurethresholds(ctx, paramnum, rangeval) buildoctree(ctx, basenodesize=4) while renderingneeded: setclassificationfunction(ctx, transferfunction) setviewandshadingparameters(ctx, viewmatrix, shadingmodel) render(ctx) # If volume data changes, the octree must be rebuilt if volumedatachanged: buildoctree(ctx, basenodesize=4) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the volume data is modified, vpCreateMinMaxOctree() must be called again; otherwise, renderings will be incorrect. The rootnodesize parameter in vpCreateMinMaxOctree is currently not used but is reserved for future use. The range parameter requires experimentation; suboptimal values reduce performance benefits but do not break correctness. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory for the min-max octree. The size increases as basenodesize decreases. Strengths: Ideal for interactive applications where classification (transfer function) is adjusted frequently, as it avoids recomputing the classified volume. Limitations: Slower than pre-classified rendering for static classification scenarios. Requires precomputation step. When to use: When many renderings are made from the same volume with varying classification functions. When not to use: When only a single rendering is needed (use raw ray-casting) or when classification is static (use pre-classified rendering). Min-Max Octree Rendering is part of the VolPack library. It is specifically designed to accelerate the rendering of unclassified volumes by leveraging hierarchical min-max bounds to skip irrelevant regions during ray casting. name: Octree Empty Block Culling
head: Octree Leaf Culling, Recursive Status Check
body: Octree Empty Block Culling recursively traverses an octree to determine if a node contains any non-empty data blocks, returning a status of EMPTY or NONEMPTY to enable early ray termination or skipping of empty regions. Inputs: An octree structure where each node has a depth field and a status field. A memory management unit (MMU) or similar accessor providing a getBlock function that returns a pointer to the data block associated with a leaf node, or nullptr if the block is not loaded or does not exist. Outputs: A boolean indicating whether the node (and its subtree) contains non-empty data (true for NONEMPTY, false for EMPTY). Data Structures: Node: depth: Integer, the depth of the node in the octree. status: Enum or integer, EMPTY or NONEMPTY. children: Array of 8 pointers to child nodes (for internal nodes). MMU: getBlock(nodeindex): Returns a pointer to the data block for the leaf node identified by nodeindex, or nullptr. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the current node's status to EMPTY. 2. Check if the current node is a leaf. A node is a leaf if node->depth equals the maximum tree depth. If it is a leaf: Attempt to load the block using mmu->getBlock(nodeindex). If the returned block is nullptr, set node->status = EMPTY and return false. Otherwise, set node->status = NONEMPTY and return true. If it is an internal node: Recursively call the status check function on all 8 children. Children are accessed using linear indexing: childindex = (index << 3) + i + 1 for i from 0 to 7, where index is the index of the current node in a flat array representation. If any child returns true (indicating NONEMPTY), set node->status = NONEMPTY. Return node->status == NONEMPTY. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EMPTY = 0 NONEMPTY = 1 def checkstatus(node, mmu, maxdepth, nodeindex): """ Recursively checks if a node or its subtree contains non-empty data. """ node.status = EMPTY if node.depth == maxdepth: block = mmu.getBlock(nodeindex) if block is None: node.status = EMPTY return False else: node.status = NONEMPTY return True else: baseindex = (nodeindex << 3) + 1 for i in range(8): childindex = baseindex + i if checkstatus(node.children[i], mmu, maxdepth, childindex): node.status = NONEMPTY return node.status == NONEMPTY Parameters: maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. This must be set correctly during initialization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incorrect Depth Initialization: If the tree depth is not set correctly during initialization, the leaf check node->depth == depth may fail, causing all nodes to be treated as internal or leaf incorrectly. Empty Blocks: A leaf node may exist in the octree structure but have no associated data block (e.g., not loaded into memory). The getBlock function must return nullptr in this case, and the node should be marked as EMPTY. Octree Range Culling is a variant where shells' ranges over a node are computed once per pass for up to 4 tiles of 64 functions (each lane owns a function of every tile) instead of once per tile, only for shells reaching the node. A dropped shell has every AO below 10^{-10} over the node; fntail (2 \times 10^{-10} times the column sum of |C|) is added to every function's bound for them. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is described in the context of parallel volume rendering systems, specifically in the VolumeRenderingParallel project. It is used to optimize ray traversal by skipping empty regions of the volume, thereby reducing the number of samples taken and improving rendering performance. hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, https://github.com/hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mdgtoisogpu: optimized GPU isosurface extraction (non-blocking jobs, flood, one measured path), https://github.com/scanberg/mdlib/pull/15, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: View-Dependent Working Set Generation
head: Incremental refinement procedure
body: This method constructs a view-dependent working set of octree nodes for out-of-core volume rendering by incrementally refining a sorted set of visible, non-empty nodes. It solves the problem of GPU stalls caused by out-of-core data access latency by hiding these delays through asynchronous data loading and a hierarchical cache system. Unlike static culling methods, it dynamically adapts the working set based on projected screen-space size and visibility, ensuring that only necessary data is loaded into the GPU texture cache. Inputs: Octree structure with min/max values per node; transfer function (for volume rendering); camera parameters (view frustum, projection); current GPU cache state; system memory (CPU cache). Outputs: A sorted list of active octree nodes (the working set) present in both CPU and GPU caches. Data Structures: 1. Working Set: A list of octree nodes. 2. CPU Cache: A pool of blocks managed with LRU policy, using system memory to avoid disk I/O. 3. GPU Texture Cache: A large preallocated 3D texture managed as a pool of blocks. Value Texture: 16-bit single channel. Gradient Texture: RGBA8 texture. RGB components store normalized gradients; A component stores gradient norm. 4. Summed-Area Table (SAT): Used for volume rendering emptiness checks. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the working set with the octree root node. 2. Sorting: Sort the working set by decreasing projected screen-space size of the voxels represented by the nodes. Visibility information (frustum culling) can be incorporated here. 3. Refinement Loop: While termination conditions are not met: a. Select Node: Pick the highest-priority node from the sorted working set. b. Emptiness Check: Determine if the node is empty. Isosurface Rendering: A node is non-empty if the isovalue I satisfies min \le I \le max, where min and max are the minimum and maximum values stored in the node. Volume Rendering: Use summed-area tables of transfer function opacity. Let T{opacity} be the SAT. Let v{min} and v{max} be the minimum and maximum block values. The node is non-empty if SAT(v{max}) - SAT(v{min}) > 0. c. Terminal Check: If the node is empty or outside the view frustum, mark it as terminal and do not refine further. d. Cache Availability Check: Check if data for the node's children is immediately available in the CPU cache or system memory. e. GPU Cache Space Check: Check if there is sufficient space in the GPU texture cache to store the refined children. f. Refinement: If data is available and GPU space exists: i. Subdivide the node into its 8 children. ii. Remove the parent from the working set. iii. Add the 8 children to the working set. iv. Update the GPU texture cache using glTexSubImage to move the new data. v. Re-sort the working set based on projected screen-space size. g. Asynchronous Loading: If data is not immediately available, issue an asynchronous data access request to load the data from disk/system memory into the CPU cache. Do not refine this node in the current frame step; proceed to the next node in the sorted list. 4. Cache Management: Maintain both CPU and GPU caches using a Least Recently Used (LRU) policy. The CPU cache acts as a level-2 cache to prevent disk accesses for recently used blocks. Termination Conditions: Refinement stops when any of the following is true: 1. All nodes in the working set are adequately refined (e.g., reached maximum resolution or are terminal). 2. No data is currently available in-core to perform a refinement for any remaining node in the working set. 3. No more space is available in the GPU cache for further subdivision. Parameters: Cache Policy: LRU for both CPU and GPU caches. GPU Value Texture Format: 16-bit single channel. GPU Gradient Texture Format: RGBA8 (RGB: normalized gradients, A: gradient norm). Asynchronous Loading: Enabled to hide latency. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Nodes outside the view frustum are treated as terminal. Degenerate Input: If the octree root is empty, the working set remains empty or contains only the root as terminal. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the GPU texture cache and CPU cache. The GPU cache is a preallocated 3D texture. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method is designed for out-of-core rendering, scaling to datasets larger than GPU memory by using the CPU cache and asynchronous loading. Strengths: Hides out-of-core data access latency; reduces GPU stalls; adapts to view-dependent visibility. Limitations: Requires asynchronous loading infrastructure; cache management complexity; dependent on the effectiveness of the emptiness check. When to use: Interactive out-of-core volume rendering where data exceeds GPU memory and latency must be hidden. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method was introduced in the paper "A single-pass GPU ray casting framework for interactive out-of-core volume rendering" by Vic et al. (2008). It is part of a framework designed to reduce GPU stalls by exploiting feedback from the renderer to avoid refinement and data loading of occluded zones. The approach builds on earlier work in octree traversal and cache management. name: Spatial Skipping (Occupancy Grid)
head: Instant-NGP Sampling, Occupancy Grid, Occupancy Grid Pruning
body: Spatial Skipping (Occupancy Grid) is an acceleration technique that improves uniform sampling by identifying empty regions in the volume and skipping them, effectively creating a transmittance estimator based on the ratio of occupied steps. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a simple, explicit voxel-based occupancy grid with a conservative density threshold to binarize density, whereas alternatives like Empty Space Skipping with Octree use hierarchical structures or Transfer-Function Independent Empty-Space Skipping optimize for specific transfer functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A radiance field (implicit or explicit), a ray defined by origin o and direction d, and a set of uniformly sampled points ti along the ray interval [tn, tf]. Output: A set of valid samples with associated importance weights (PDF) and transmittance values, allowing the renderer to skip samples in empty space. Data Structures: Occupancy Grid: An explicit voxel grid storing cached density values \sigma(ti) for each spatial location. The grid is updated using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) over optimization iterations. Packed Tensors: To handle varying numbers of valid samples per ray, samples are stored in a packed tensor of shape (allsamples,...) rather than a padded (nrays, nsamples,...) tensor, with an associated rayid array mapping each sample to its originating ray. Parameters: Threshold (\tau): A conservative density threshold used to binarize density. If \sigma(ti) > \tau, the sample is considered occupied; otherwise, it is empty. EMA Decay (\gamma): The decay factor for the Exponential Moving Average update of cached densities. Typical values are close to 1 (e.g., 0.9 or 0.99) to maintain stability, though exact values are not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Uniform Sampling: Generate n uniformly spaced sample points ti along the ray. 2. Density Evaluation: Evaluate the density \sigma(ti) at each sample point using the radiance field. 3. Binarization: Compute the binarized density \hat{\sigma}(ti): \hat{\sigma}(ti) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \sigma(ti) > \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 4. PDF Estimation: Calculate the piece-wise constant probability density function (PDF) for each sample: p(ti) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}(ti)}{\sum{j=1}^{n} \hat{\sigma}(tj)} 5. Transmittance Estimation: Calculate the piece-wise linear transmittance estimator T(ti): T(ti) = 1 - \frac{\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \hat{\sigma}(tj)}{\sum{j=1}^{n} \hat{\sigma}(tj)} 6. EMA Update (Optimization Phase): During training, update the cached density in the occupancy grid using Exponential Moving Average over iteration k: \sigma(ti)^k = \gamma \cdot \sigma(ti)^{k-1} + (1 - \gamma) \cdot \sigma(ti)^k Note: The source notation \sigma(ti)^k on the RHS refers to the newly evaluated density at iteration k, while \sigma(ti)^{k-1} is the cached value from the previous iteration. 7. Sample Filtering (Optional Variant): For samples identified as potentially in empty/occluded spaces, evaluate transmittance without computing gradients (requiresgrad=False) and discard those with transmittance below 10^{-4}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spatialskippingoccupancygrid(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples, radiancefield, occupancygrid, threshold, gamma): """ Performs spatial skipping using an occupancy grid. Args: rayorigin: (3,) tensor, ray origin. raydirection: (3,) tensor, ray direction. numsamples: int, number of uniform samples. radiancefield: callable, returns density sigma at points. occupancygrid: dict or array, stores cached densities sigma. threshold: float, density threshold for binarization. gamma: float, EMA decay factor. Returns: validsamples: (M, 3) tensor, valid sample positions. pdfs: (M,) tensor, importance weights. transmittances: (M,) tensor, transmittance values. rayids: (M,) tensor, index of the ray for each sample. """ # 1. Uniform Sampling tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples) # Assuming ray is parameterized as o + t d, where t is normalized 0..1 # In practice, t might be mapped to [tn, tf] samplepoints = rayorigin.unsqueeze(0) + tvals.unsqueeze(1) raydirection.unsqueeze(0) # (numsamples, 3) # 2. Density Evaluation # Evaluate density at all sample points densities = radiancefield(samplepoints) # (numsamples,) # 3. Binarization occupied = (densities > threshold).float() # (numsamples,) # 4. PDF Estimation totaloccupied = torch.sum(occupied) if totaloccupied == 0: return None, None, None, None # No valid samples pdfs = occupied / totaloccupied # (numsamples,) # 5. Transmittance Estimation # T(ti) = 1 - sum(occupied[:i]) / sum(occupied) cumsumoccupied = torch.cumsum(occupied, dim=0) transmittances = 1.0 - (cumsumoccupied / totaloccupied) # (numsamples,) # 6. EMA Update (for optimization) # Update cached density in occupancy grid # Note: In a real implementation, occupancygrid would be indexed by spatial coordinates # Here we assume a simplified update for the evaluated points for i in range(numsamples): pos = samplepoints[i] # Get previous cached density (default to 0 if not present) prevsigma = occupancygrid.get(pos, 0.0) # Update with EMA newsigma = gamma prevsigma + (1 - gamma) densities[i] occupancygrid[pos] = newsigma # 7. Return valid samples (all samples in this simplified version, # as the grid is used for future skipping, not immediate filtering of current ray's # empty space in the basic definition. The "No Gradient Filtering" variant does immediate filtering.) # For the basic method, we return all samples with their weights. # In a packed tensor implementation, rayids would be needed if multiple rays are processed. rayids = torch.zeros(numsamples, dtype=torch.long) return samplepoints, pdfs, transmittances, rayids Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: The voxel-based representation of the transmittance estimator can suffer from aliasing issues. Occluded Areas: The method still samples uniformly within occupied but occluded areas that contribute little to the final rendering (e.g., the last sample in a ray passing through a thin object). Inaccurate Estimation: Inaccurate transmittance estimations from importance sampling can result in samples lying in empty or occluded spaces, which may require additional filtering. A technique to filter out samples lying in empty or occluded spaces by evaluating their transmittance without computing gradients, detaching the sampling process from the differentiable computational graph to maximize speed. It is chosen when training speed is prioritized over gradient accuracy in empty regions. It is approximately 10x faster than keeping all samples in the computation graph because backward passes are not required for these samples. The process involves: 1. Performing importance sampling (e.g., using Occupancy Grid). 2. Identifying samples potentially in empty/occluded spaces. 3. Evaluating transmittance for these samples using the radiance field with gradients disabled (requiresgrad=False). 4. Disregarding samples with transmittance below 10^{-4}. 5. Including remaining samples in the differentiable computation graph. The transmittance threshold is 10^{-4}. This method is inspired by Instant-NGP's implementation. Time Complexity: Faster than uniform sampling in empty scenes, but slower than PDF-based estimators in complex scenes due to uniform sampling within occupied regions. The "No Gradient Filtering" variant is approximately 10x faster than standard differentiable sampling for filtered samples. Memory Complexity: Uses an explicit voxel grid for the occupancy estimator. Voxel-based estimators are generally faster than implicit (MLP-based) estimators but use more memory for large grids. Packed tensors are used to store samples efficiently, avoiding the memory overhead of padded tensors for rays with few valid samples. Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient in empty spaces, compatible with various radiance field representations (e.g., HashEncoding in Nerfacto). Limitations: Suffers from aliasing, samples uniformly in occluded areas, and may require careful threshold tuning. When to Use: When rendering scenes with large empty spaces and computational efficiency is critical. Suitable for in-the-wild settings when combined with hybrid representations like HashEncoding. When Not to Use: When high accuracy in occluded regions is required or when the scene is densely occupied, reducing the benefit of skipping. Spatial Skipping via Occupancy Grid was introduced in Instant-NGP [17] as a method to accelerate neural volume rendering by skipping empty regions during sampling. It is part of a broader class of importance sampling techniques that view sampling through the lens of transmittance estimation. The technique has been adopted and extended in various NeRF-related methods, including NerfAcc and Nerfstudio [29], often in conjunction with other efficient representations like HashEncoding [17].
