name: Parallel Tree-Construction for Empty-Space Skipping
body: Parallel tree-construction algorithms enable the run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping, primarily to accommodate dynamic changes in the transfer function. This approach distinguishes itself from static acceleration structures by allowing the hierarchy to be rebuilt on the GPU at interactive frame rates, ensuring that the skipping logic remains consistent with the current visual parameters. The core mechanism involves constructing a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) or similar tree structure in parallel on the GPU. The construction process typically adapts algorithms originally designed for triangle geometry to sparse volumetric data. This adaptation uses the boundaries of non-empty bricks (or voxels) as the bounding geometry for the nodes. The parallel nature of the construction allows for the rapid regeneration of the tree, which is necessary when the transfer function changes, as this alters which regions are considered "empty" (transparent) versus "occupied" (opaque or semi-transparent). An adaptation of a linear bounding volume hierarchy (LBVH) construction algorithm. It uses boundaries of non-empty bricks as bounding geometry, allowing construction on the GPU at interactive frame rates for 1024^3 volumes. The technique emerged in recent years to address the limitations of static acceleration structures in dynamic volume rendering scenarios. Key contributions include work by Zellmann et al. [ZHL19], who proposed the LBVH adaptation for sparse data, and subsequent works by ZSL18, ZML19, FW20, DK19, DK20, and ZSL21, which further explored parallel tree construction for this purpose. The primary motivation is to support run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures due to changes in the transfer function. name: Transfer-Function Independent Empty-Space Skipping
head: TF-independent empty-space skipping, visibility-independent culling
body: This family of techniques accelerates volume rendering by storing visibility information in the acceleration structure independent of the transfer function, thereby avoiding the need to reconstruct the structure when the transfer function changes. Unlike sibling methods that may recompute visibility or rely on static assumptions, this approach decouples spatial culling from opacity evaluation, enabling real-time transfer function adjustments without structural overhead. The core mechanism relies on representing the data distribution within a spatial node (e.g., an octree node) as a compact, transfer-function-independent descriptor. This descriptor is typically a bitfield or histogram that encodes the presence of specific data values within the node's spatial extent. To determine if a node is empty (fully transparent) for a given transfer function, the system compares the node's descriptor against a descriptor of the transfer function's visible range. This comparison is performed using a bitwise AND operation. If the result is zero, the node contains no values that contribute to the final image under the current transfer function, and the node can be culled. Mathematically, let B{node} be the bitfield representing the values present in the node, and B{tf} be the bitfield representing the values mapped to non-zero opacity by the transfer function. The node is considered empty if: B{node} \ \& \ B{tf} = 0 where \& denotes the bitwise AND operation. This allows for efficient runtime changes to the transfer function without modifying the underlying acceleration structure. This variant uses a residency octree to store transfer-function independent culling information. It stores average values in non-empty homogeneous nodes and utilizes cache-residency information. The primary advantage is that cache-residency information does not need to be redistributed over octree nodes when the transfer function changes, combining empty-space skipping with memory access optimization. The concept of transfer-function independent culling was proposed by Faludi et al. [FZZ+ 22] as a solution to the high cost of reconstructing acceleration structures after transfer function changes. Traditional methods often store visibility information that is dependent on the transfer function, requiring expensive recomputation [ZSL18, ZHL19, ZML19, FW20, DK19, DK20, ZSL21]. Faludi et al. introduced the use of bitfields to represent the value range of an octree node, allowing for a single bitwise AND operation to test for translucency. This approach was further extended by other researchers, such as those using residency octrees to combine culling with cache-residency tracking. name: Early ray termination
head: Adaptive Ray Termination, Adaptive Termination of Ray Tracing
body: Early ray termination is an acceleration optimization for front-to-back volume rendering that stops ray traversal once the accumulated opacity exceeds a user-defined threshold, based on the observation that ray color stabilizes when sufficient opacity is accumulated. It reduces the number of samples processed per ray, thereby lowering computational cost, particularly in scenes with opaque or semi-transparent surfaces where voxels away from surfaces have zero or negligible opacity. Unlike empty-space skipping, which avoids transparent regions, early ray termination avoids redundant compositing behind opaque regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, volume data (opacity field \alpha(\mathbf{x})), transfer function mapping density to opacity, and an opacity threshold \alpha{\text{thresh}}. Output: Final pixel color C and accumulated opacity \alpha. Data Structures: Accumulated color C{\text{acc}} (RGB, initialized to 0). Accumulated opacity \alpha{\text{acc}} (float, initialized to 0). Current sample position \mathbf{x} along the ray. Sample opacity \alpha{\text{sample}} obtained from the volume at \mathbf{x}. Parameters: \alpha{\text{thresh}}: The opacity threshold for termination. Common values are 1.0 (unity) or 0.95 (95% opacity). A value of 0.95 is often used because additional contributions beyond this point are visually negligible. Steps: 1. Initialize C{\text{acc}} = (0, 0, 0) and \alpha{\text{acc}} = 0. 2. Iterate along the ray from near to far (front-to-back): a. Sample the volume at the current position \mathbf{x} to get the sample opacity \alpha{\text{sample}} and sample color C{\text{sample}}. b. Compute the contribution of the current sample to the accumulated color and opacity using front-to-back compositing: \alpha{\text{contrib}} = \alpha{\text{sample}} \cdot (1 - \alpha{\text{acc}}) C{\text{acc}} = C{\text{acc}} + C{\text{sample}} \cdot \alpha{\text{contrib}} \alpha{\text{acc}} = \alpha{\text{acc}} + \alpha{\text{contrib}} c. Check if \alpha{\text{acc}} \ge \alpha{\text{thresh}}. d. If true, terminate the ray loop. e. If false, advance to the next sample position. 3. Return C{\text{acc}} and \alpha{\text{acc}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyraytermination(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, transferfunction, alphathresh=0.95): """ Renders a single ray using early ray termination. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple, origin of the ray. raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) tuple, normalized direction of the ray. volume: Object providing sample(x) -> (color, opacity) method. transferfunction: Function mapping density to opacity (if volume stores density). alphathresh: Float, threshold for accumulated opacity to terminate ray. Returns: (finalcolor, finalopacity) tuple. """ # Initialize accumulators acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 # Current position along the ray # Note: Step size and bounds checking are assumed to be handled by the traversal logic # This pseudocode focuses on the compositing and termination logic. while True: # 1. Sample the volume at current position # Assume sampleposition is updated by the traversal loop samplecolor, sampleopacity = volume.sample(sampleposition) # 2. Composite the sample # Front-to-back compositing formula alphacontrib = sampleopacity (1.0 - accopacity) acccolor = ( acccolor[0] + samplecolor[0] alphacontrib, acccolor[1] + samplecolor[1] alphacontrib, acccolor[2] + samplecolor[2] alphacontrib) accopacity += alphacontrib # 3. Check for early termination if accopacity >= alphathresh: break # 4. Advance to next sample # This step depends on the specific traversal method (e.g., fixed step, adaptive step) sampleposition = advanceray(sampleposition, raydirection) # 5. Check if ray is out of volume bounds if not iswithinvolume(sampleposition): break return acccolor, accopacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Surfaces not explicitly detected: The method relies on stepwise accumulation; surfaces appear as a by-product. It works best when voxels away from surfaces have zero opacity. Hardware Implementation: In hardware-based rendering (e.g., using the Blend method), transparency is stored in the frame buffer, not main memory, making it difficult to implement early ray termination directly without reading the frame buffer. Adaptive Supersampling: When used with adaptive supersampling, early termination must be applied independently to the computation of each component (e.g., color Cq and quality Q) to avoid adversely affecting the supersampling process. Splatting Algorithms: For splatting, a more complex test is required to end splatting early if the region of the splat is opaque. A mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that selectively omits computations for Gaussians with negligible impact on the final rendered output, enabled by physically grounded transmittance that achieves a decay pattern similar to alpha-blending. Unlike prior sort-free Gaussian Splatting methods (e.g., LC-WSR) which lack early termination due to their sort-free design, methods like Duplex-GS achieve termination results comparable to vanilla 3DGS without requiring an explicit Gaussian order. The termination ratio is defined as r^{\text{ET}} = 1 - \frac{N^{\text{rendered}}}{N^{\text{val}}}, where N^{\text{rendered}} is the number of Gaussians contributed to the final color and N^{\text{val}} is the number of total interacted valid Gaussians along the ray. On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, enabling Early Termination results in 155 FPS compared to 212 FPS when disabled, with PSNR 27.66 vs 26.60. Time and Memory Complexity: The cost of ray tracing volumetric data using hierarchical enumeration grows linearly with the image size, logarithmically with the ray length, and linearly with the depth complexity of the data. Early ray termination reduces the dependence on depth complexity. For opaque-only environments, it eliminates this dependence entirely, making the cost nearly linear with image size. Savings of up to an order of magnitude over brute-force rendering algorithms have been observed for scenes with opaque or semi-transparent surfaces. Combining early termination with other optimizations (like adaptive sampling) can yield savings of more than two orders of magnitude. Measured Performance: For the "cube data" (480x480 image size), higher density values mapped to higher opacity values cause many rays to terminate earlier, traversing fewer elements. In Gaussian Splatting, early termination improves rendering speed significantly while maintaining competitive visual quality. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant performance improvement in scenes with opaque surfaces; reduces unnecessary computation; simple to implement in software ray casting. Limitations: Difficult to implement directly in hardware-based blending methods due to frame buffer transparency storage; less effective in scenes with high transparency or low opacity gradients where rays rarely reach the threshold. When to Use: Use when rendering volumes with opaque or semi-transparent surfaces where voxels away from surfaces have zero opacity. Use when front-to-back compositing is employed. When Not to Use: Avoid in hardware-based blending methods where frame buffer access is costly. Avoid in scenes with high transparency where rays rarely accumulate sufficient opacity to trigger termination. The idea of adaptively terminating ray tracing was first proposed in [34] (cited in). Many medical data algorithms stop after the first surface or opaque voxel, reported in [15, 30, 32] (cited in). The optimization is based on the observation that once a ray strikes an opaque object or probes sufficient distance through semi-transparent data, opacity accumulates to a level where ray color stabilizes. It is applicable when data is composited from front-to-back. name: Early Termination for Gaussian Splatting
head: Early Termination (ET)
body: Early Termination (ET) is an acceleration mechanism for Gaussian Splatting that selectively omits computations for Gaussians with negligible impact on the final rendered output. It leverages physically grounded transmittance to achieve a decay pattern similar to alpha-blending, allowing the rendering process to halt when the remaining contribution is below a threshold. Unlike sort-free Gaussian Splatting methods (e.g., LC-WSR) which lack early termination due to their design, ET enables significant speedups comparable to vanilla 3DGS without requiring an explicit Gaussian order. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray, a set of valid Gaussians intersected by the ray (N^{\text{val}}), and a termination threshold \epsilon. Output: The final pixel color and the number of Gaussians actually rendered (N^{\text{rendered}}). Data Structures: Valid Gaussians: A list of Gaussians intersected by the ray. In cell-based variants, these are grouped by cell. Transmittance: A scalar value representing the accumulated opacity along the ray. Algorithm: 1. Initialize accumulated color C = 0 and transmittance T = 1. 2. Iterate through the valid Gaussians (or cells) in front-to-back order. 3. For each Gaussian i (or cell n): a. Compute the contribution of the Gaussian to the color. b. Update the accumulated color: C \leftarrow C + \text{contribution}i \times T. c. Update the transmittance: T \leftarrow T \times (1 - \alphai), where \alphai is the opacity. d. Check termination condition: i. In standard ET, if T < \epsilon, terminate. ii. In Cell-Based ET, compute cell-level transmittance T{cell}^n. If T{cell}^n < \epsilon, halt blending for that cell and proceed to the next cell or terminate if no more cells are relevant. 4. Return C. Formulas: Termination Ratio: The efficiency of early termination is measured by the ratio of skipped computations: r^{\text{ET}} = 1 - \frac{N^{\text{rendered}}}{N^{\text{val}}} where N^{\text{rendered}} is the number of Gaussians contributed to the final color, and N^{\text{val}} is the total number of interacted valid Gaussians along the ray. Cell-Level Transmittance: In cell-based variants, the transmittance T{cell}^n decays towards zero during front-to-back rendering. Parameters: Threshold (\epsilon): The predefined threshold for early termination. For standard ET, this is maintained at the same value as used in vanilla 3DGS. For Cell-Based ET, it is an empirical threshold constrained by the opacity parameter \sigma{n,k} \in [0, 1]. The exact numerical value is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The transmittance must decay sufficiently to trigger termination. If the opacity parameters are not constrained to physically plausible ranges (e.g., [0, 1]), the transmittance may not decay correctly, leading to artifacts or failure to terminate. Order Independence: In sort-free methods, the lack of strict front-to-back ordering can affect the accuracy of transmittance decay. However, physically grounded transmittance helps mitigate popping artifacts. A rendering optimization that halts the front-to-back blending process at the cell level once the cell-level transmittance decays below a predefined threshold \epsilon, eliminating transparency artifacts and accelerating rendering. Unlike prior Weighted Splatting/Rendering (WSR) methods, this formulation constrains the opacity parameter \sigma{n,k} to the physically plausible range of [0, 1], allowing the empirical threshold to be directly transferred and facilitating more effective pruning and regularization. The cell-level transmittance T{cell}^n is the key innovation that eliminates transparency artifacts and enables early termination. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, enabling Early Termination results in 155 FPS, compared to 212 FPS when disabled (w/o ET). Quality: The PSNR with ET enabled is 27.66, compared to 26.60 when disabled. Comparison: Duplex-GS achieves termination results comparable to vanilla 3DGS without requiring an explicit Gaussian order, whereas sort-free methods like LC-WSR do not support early termination. Limitations: The efficiency of cell search rasterization is contingent upon the degree of coherence between the visible regions of a cell and its associated Gaussians. Discrepancies between spatial intervals of cells and emitted neural Gaussians can introduce redundant computations. Early Termination for Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the context of Duplex-GS, a proxy-guided weighted blending method for real-time order-independent Gaussian Splatting. The method addresses the limitations of prior sort-free Gaussian Splatting methods, which lacked early termination capabilities. By restoring explicit physical meaning to the opacity parameter and ensuring physically grounded transmittance, the method enables efficient acceleration while maintaining competitive visual quality. name: Bounding Volume Culling
head: Distance-based Culling, Ray Termination by Distance
body: Bounding Volume Culling is an acceleration technique for volume rendering and Signed Distance Field (SDF) raymarching that limits ray traversal to a specific spatial extent, dropping rays that exceed a predefined distance from the eye. It solves the problem of unnecessary computation for rays that have traveled beyond the relevant scene geometry or desired visual range. Unlike Empty-space skipping which skips empty regions, or Early ray termination which stops based on opacity accumulation, this method terminates based on absolute geometric distance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), maximum travel distance t{max}, and the scene's bounding volume parameters. Output: A boolean indicating whether the ray should continue marching, or the final accumulated color/depth if terminated. Data Structures: t: A scalar accumulator representing the total distance traveled along the ray. Initialized to 0. t{max}: A scalar constant defining the culling threshold. Steps: 1. Initialize the traveled distance t \leftarrow 0. 2. During each raymarching iteration: a. Evaluate the scene distance function at the current ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. b. Update t by adding the step size \Delta t (often derived from the distance function value). c. Check the culling condition: If t > t{max}, terminate the raymarch process immediately. Formulas: Ray position: \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} Termination condition: t > t{max} Parameters: t{max}: The maximum distance from the eye. Typical values depend on the scene scale; for fog effects, it may correspond to the far clipping plane. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If t{max} is set too low, valid geometry near the camera but far from the origin (in world space) might be incorrectly culled if the ray parameterization is not aligned with the bounding volume center. This method assumes t represents the true Euclidean distance from the ray origin. Precision errors in t accumulation can cause premature termination or infinite loops if not handled with a small epsilon. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boundingvolumeculling(rayorigin, raydirection, maxdistance, scenedistancefunc): """ Raymarch with bounding volume culling. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the ray. raydirection: vec3, normalized direction of the ray. maxdistance: float, maximum allowed distance from rayorigin. scenedistancefunc: function, returns distance to closest surface at point p. Returns: color: vec3, the final color or termination indicator. """ t = 0.0 color = vec3(0.0) while t < maxdistance: # Get current position p = rayorigin + t raydirection # Evaluate distance to scene dist = scenedistancefunc(p) # Safety check for degenerate distance if dist < 0.0001: # Hit surface break # Advance ray t += dist # Accumulate color or other properties here # color += samplecolor(p) opacity # If t >= maxdistance, the ray is culled/terminated return color Bounding Spheres Optimization is an acceleration technique that eliminates unnecessary distance computations by culling rays that miss a scene object's bounding sphere. It is a specific application of bounding volume optimization, minimizing the cost of the map function by skipping SDF evaluations for objects that do not contribute to the minimal distance field. It is chosen when the scene contains discrete objects with known spherical bounds, offering a low-overhead check compared to complex bounding volumes. Heap-based Bounding Volume Culling for Sphere Tracing is an algorithm to find the closest object in a collection by maintaining a heap of bounding volume distances. It computes distances to bounding volumes first, then contents, culling based on the smallest bounding volume distance. It is chosen when rendering a union or collection of implicit surfaces, as it avoids computing expensive content distances for objects that are farther away than the currently closest candidate. Steps: 1. Compute distances to each bounding volume in the union/collection. 2. Create a min-heap of these distances. 3. Initialize d{min} to infinity. 4. Loop: a. Let d{content} be \min(d{min}, \text{distance to contents of top BV}). b. Remove top of heap. c. Let d{bv} be the distance to the new top BV. d. Stop if d{content} < d{bv} or heap is empty. 5. Return d{content}. Parameters: d{bv}: The distance to the bounding volume currently at the top of the heap. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray for simple distance culling. For heap-based collection culling, O(N \log N) for heap construction and O(\log N) per query, where N is the number of bounding volumes. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing bounding volume distances in the heap. Performance: Reduces rendering time by avoiding expensive distance function evaluations for irrelevant geometry. However, initial tests suggest it may degrade performance in perspective cases for typical implicit surfaces if the overhead of sphere intersection computation outweighs the savings. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for fog and limited-range effects. Limitations: Ineffective for scenes where geometry extends beyond the bounding volume but is still relevant; overhead of maintaining heaps for large collections. The concept of limiting raymarching to a bounding volume to speed up rendering was discussed in early online presentations and blogs. The formalization of bounding volumes for sphere tracing, including heap-based selection for collections of implicit surfaces, was presented in the "Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces" paper. name: Bounding Spheres Optimization
body: Bounding Spheres Optimization is an acceleration technique for volume rendering and Signed Distance Field (SDF) raymarching that eliminates unnecessary distance computations during ray traversal by culling rays that miss a scene object's bounding sphere. It is a specific application of bounding volume optimization, which minimizes the cost of the map function by skipping SDF evaluations for objects that do not contribute to the minimal distance field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a scene object defined by its SDF map function f(\mathbf{p}) and its bounding sphere defined by center \mathbf{c} and radius r. Output: A boolean indicating whether the ray intersects the bounding sphere, determining whether f(\mathbf{p}) must be evaluated. Data Structures: Bounding Sphere: Defined by a 3D vector \mathbf{c} = (cx, cy, cz) and a scalar radius r. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}. Algorithm: 1. Compute the vector from the ray origin to the sphere center: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}. 2. Project \mathbf{v} onto the ray direction to find the distance to the closest point on the ray line to the sphere center: t{ca} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 3. Calculate the squared distance from the closest point on the ray line to the sphere center: d^2 = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 - t{ca}^2. 4. Check for intersection: If d^2 > r^2, the ray does not intersect the sphere. Skip the evaluation of the object's SDF map function for this ray. If d^2 \le r^2, the ray intersects the sphere. Proceed to evaluate the SDF f(\mathbf{p}) at the ray's current position. Note: If the ray originates inside the sphere, t{ca} may be negative, but the intersection check d^2 \le r^2 still holds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boundingspherecull(rayorigin, raydirection, spherecenter, sphereradius): """ Determines if a ray intersects a bounding sphere. Returns True if intersection occurs (SDF evaluation needed), False otherwise. """ # Vector from ray origin to sphere center v = rayorigin - spherecenter # Project v onto ray direction tca = dot(v, raydirection) # Squared distance from ray line to sphere center # ||v||^2 - tca^2 dsquared = dot(v, v) - (tca tca) # Check if distance is within radius squared return dsquared <= (sphereradius sphereradius) Parameters: Sphere Radius (r): Must tightly bound the object to maximize culling efficiency. Threshold: The comparison d^2 \le r^2 is exact. No tolerance is typically applied in the culling step itself, though precision issues may arise with very large coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: For scenes with large coordinate values, floating-point precision errors in d^2 calculation may lead to incorrect culling. Using double precision for the culling test may be necessary in extreme cases. Degenerate Input: If the ray direction is not normalized, the projection t{ca} is invalid. The direction must be normalized before use. Overhead: The cost of the sphere intersection test must be less than the cost of the SDF evaluation it replaces. If the SDF is trivial, the culling overhead may negate benefits. An optimization technique that minimizes the cost of the map function by skipping the evaluation of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for objects that do not contribute to the minimal distance field, using bounding volumes. Without this optimization, computation cost is uniform across the frame; with it enabled, expensive computations are localized to areas where complex geometry is present. It is chosen when a scene contains dozens or hundreds of expensive primitives. A pitfall to note is that modern GPUs are MIMD rather than pure SIMD, allowing different Streaming Multiprocessors to process different instruction streams simultaneously, which helps distribute expensive threads after cheaper parts finish early. In a scene with 20 expensive primitives at 720p, enabling this optimization reduced average frame duration from 41 ms (24 fps) to 21 ms (48 fps). Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The culling test is O(1) per object per ray. The total time saved is proportional to the number of rays that miss the bounding volumes. In the zeno logo scene, execution time was reduced from 26:29 to 5:28 (21% relative time). In a scene with 20 expensive primitives at 720p, average frame duration dropped from 41 ms (24 fps) to 21 ms (48 fps). Memory: Requires storing the center and radius for each object's bounding sphere. Measured Performance: Zeno Logo: Bounding spheres reduced execution time to 21% of the unenhanced time. 20 Primitives Scene: Frame rate doubled from 24 fps to 48 fps at 720p resolution. Scaling: Performance gains scale with the number of objects and the complexity of their SDF evaluations. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of SDF evaluations, especially in scenes with sparse geometry or large empty spaces. Modern GPUs, being MIMD, can efficiently distribute the remaining expensive threads after cheaper culling operations finish early. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of bounding volumes. If the bounding volumes are loose, culling efficiency drops. Bounding spheres optimization was introduced as part of the sphere tracing method for rendering implicit surfaces. It was demonstrated in the context of the "zeno" logo and other geometric primitives, showing significant speedups by eliminating unnecessary distance computations. The broader concept of bounding volume optimization for SDFs was further explored in CUDA-based raymarching implementations, highlighting the benefits of skipping SDF evaluations for non-contributing objects. name: Orthogonal Culling Optimization
head: Orthogonal Culling, Orthogonal Projection Culling
body: Orthogonal Culling is a pre-computation optimization for sphere tracing that reduces the number of signed distance function (SDF) evaluations per ray by determining which scene objects lie within the ray's path before the marching loop begins. It differs from its parent, Bounding Spheres Optimization, which minimizes distance calculations during traversal, and its sibling, Frustum Culling (Sphere vs Frustum), which typically relies on CPU-side broad-phase culling; Orthogonal Culling performs a geometric intersection test between the ray and object bounding volumes using orthogonal projection. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, and a list of scene objects, each defined by a bounding sphere with center \mathbf{c} and radius r. Output: A boolean mask or list of indices indicating which objects intersect the ray, allowing the renderer to skip SDF evaluations for non-intersecting objects. Data Structures Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction vector \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Bounding Sphere: Defined by center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and scalar radius r \ge 0. Algorithm Steps 1. For each object in the scene, retrieve its bounding sphere center \mathbf{c} and radius r. 2. Project the vector from the ray origin to the sphere center onto the ray direction to find the line's closest point to the object. 3. Calculate the distance between the line and the sphere using the sphere's radius. 4. Compare this distance against zero. 5. If the distance is less than zero, the ray intersects the sphere and the object is considered for distance calculation. Formulas Let \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o} be the vector from the ray origin to the sphere center. The projection of \mathbf{v} onto the ray direction \mathbf{d} is given by the dot product: t = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{d} This t represents the distance along the ray to the closest point \mathbf{p} on the line: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} The squared distance D^2 from the sphere center \mathbf{c} to the point \mathbf{p} is calculated using the Pythagorean theorem: D^2 = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 - t^2 = \|\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o}\|^2 - (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{d})^2 The distance between the line and the sphere surface is D - r. The intersection condition is D - r < 0, which is equivalent to D^2 < r^2. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orthogonalcull(rayorigin, raydirection, objects): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 objects: list of dicts with keys 'center' (vec3) and 'radius' (float) returns: list of indices of objects intersecting the ray """ activeobjects = [] for i, obj in enumerate(objects): c = obj['center'] r = obj['radius'] v = c - rayorigin t = dot(v, raydirection) distsq = dot(v, v) - t t # Source notes check if distance(line, sphere) < 0 if distsq < r r: activeobjects.append(i) return activeobjects Edge Cases and Pitfalls Implementation Efficiency: The described implementation performs this culling check for all objects in the scene for every pixel. This is suboptimal because culling should be done once per object to calculate which rays it intersects, rather than per ray determining which objects it intersects. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of objects and R is the number of rays (pixels), because the implementation checks all objects per pixel. Memory: O(1) auxiliary space per ray, assuming the object list is read-only. Measured Performance Tested on a GeForce GTX 1060M at 1920x1080 resolution. Performance gain is significant but varies with object count and scene configuration. Table 5.1 Data (FPS): 1 Object: 600 FPS (optimized) vs 350 FPS (unoptimized) 10 Objects: 500 FPS (optimized) vs 300 FPS (unoptimized) 20 Objects: 40 FPS (optimized) vs 25 FPS (unoptimized) 30 Objects: 29 FPS (optimized) vs 20 FPS (unoptimized) 40 Objects: 6 FPS (optimized) vs 4 FPS (unoptimized) 45 Objects: 4 FPS (optimized) vs 1.5 FPS (unoptimized) Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Provides a consistent performance increase by reducing the number of SDF evaluations per march step. It is particularly effective when objects are not mutually obstructing, such as spheres arranged in a plane, which represents the best-case scenario for the optimization. Limitations: The naive per-pixel, per-object check is computationally expensive for large N. It does not account for occlusion by other objects in the scene, only geometric intersection with the ray. Origin Orthogonal Culling was introduced in the context of GPU-based Sphere Tracing implementations to optimize the evaluation of signed distance functions. It was developed as part of a broader set of optimizations including Bounding Spheres and Ray Grouping. History and Development The method was evaluated using a GLSL software shader and simulated on a GPU architecture (CλaSH simulation). The research highlighted that while the optimization provided high performance gains, the initial implementation was not optimal because it repeated the culling calculation for every ray-object pair per pixel, rather than computing ray-object intersections once per object. The authors suggested that this step could be offloaded to the CPU for better efficiency. Usage The technique is used in real-time ray marching applications, specifically those rendering reflective spheres and mod fields, where reducing the number of distance queries is critical for maintaining high frame rates. name: Frustum Culling (Sphere vs Frustum)
head: Chunk Frustum Culling, SIMD Sphere/Frustum Culling, Sphere vs Frustum Culling
body: Frustum culling for spheres is a geometric rejection technique used to discard bounding volumes that do not intersect the camera's view frustum, thereby avoiding expensive ray-sphere intersection tests during volume rendering traversal. Unlike SIMD shaft culling, which is restricted to primitives with planar edges such as triangles, this method is specifically designed for spherical bounding volumes and operates by comparing the signed distance from a sphere's center to the frustum planes against the sphere's radius. It serves as an optimization within the Bounding Spheres Optimization framework, building on Bounding Spheres Optimization to eliminate unnecessary distance computations for spheres that lie outside the view volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of spheres (or chunks), each defined by a center position \mathbf{c} and a radius r. The camera frustum is defined by its origin (camera position \mathbf{p}), forward vector \mathbf{f}, up vector \mathbf{u}, right vector \mathbf{r}, and clipping distances d{near} and d{far}. Output: A subset of spheres that potentially intersect the frustum. Data Structures: The sphere is represented as a structure containing: center: A 3D vector (x, y, z). radius: A scalar float. The camera frustum is represented by: position: The camera origin \mathbf{p}. forward: Unit vector \mathbf{f} pointing along the viewing axis. up: Unit vector \mathbf{u} perpendicular to \mathbf{f}. right: Unit vector \mathbf{r} perpendicular to \mathbf{f} and \mathbf{u}, computed as \mathbf{f} \times \mathbf{u} (normalized). tanx: Tangent of the horizontal field of view angle or derived value. tany: Tangent of the vertical field of view angle. factorx: Scaling factor for the horizontal frustum width. factory: Scaling factor for the vertical frustum height. near: Near clipping plane distance d{near}. far: Far clipping plane distance d{far}. Parameters: d{near}: Near clipping plane distance. Typical value: 0.1. d{far}: Far clipping plane distance. Typical value: 2000.0. R{max}: Maximum radius of spheres considered for the "enlarged frustum" test. Spheres with r < R{max} may pass the enlarged frustum test but fail the original frustum test. In chunk-based culling, R{max} corresponds to the chunk bounding sphere radius. For a chunk of size CHUNK\SIZE, the half-size is H\CHUNK\SIZE = CHUNK\SIZE // 2. The chunk bounding sphere radius is R = H\CHUNK\SIZE \times \sqrt{3}. For CHUNK\SIZE = 48, R \approx 41.57. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute the vector from the camera position to the sphere center: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}. 2. Project \mathbf{v} onto the camera's forward, up, and right axes to get coordinates in the camera's local space: z{cam} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{f} y{cam} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u} x{cam} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{r} 3. Far/Near Plane Test: Check if the sphere is within the depth range of the frustum, accounting for its radius. The sphere is outside if z{cam} < d{near} - r or z{cam} > d{far} + r. 4. Side Plane Tests: Check if the sphere is within the horizontal and vertical extents of the frustum at depth z{cam}. The frustum width and height at depth z{cam} are proportional to z{cam} \times \tan(\theta). Calculate the maximum allowed horizontal extent at z{cam}: W{max} = r + z{cam} \times \text{tan\x} \times \text{factor\x}. Calculate the maximum allowed vertical extent at z{cam}: H{max} = r + z{cam} \times \text{tan\y} \times \text{factor\y}. The sphere is outside if |x{cam}| > W{max} or |y{cam}| > H{max}. 5. If the sphere passes all tests, it is retained for further intersection testing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def issphereinfrustum(spherecenter, sphereradius, camera): # Vector from camera to sphere center v = spherecenter - camera.position # Project onto camera axes sz = dot(v, camera.forward) sy = dot(v, camera.up) sx = dot(v, camera.right) # Far/Near plane test if sz < camera.near - sphereradius or sz > camera.far + sphereradius: return False # Side plane tests # Note: Reference implementation uses a fixed CHUNKSPHERERADIUS for the offset maxx = sphereradius + sz camera.tanx camera.factorx if sx < -maxx or sx > maxx: return False maxy = sphereradius + sz camera.tany camera.factory if sy < -maxy or sy > maxy: return False return True Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors can cause spheres on the boundary of the frustum to be incorrectly culled or retained. Using a small epsilon tolerance in comparisons can help, but the standard test is robust for most rendering scenarios. Degenerate Input: If the camera's forward, up, or right vectors are not orthogonal or normalized, the projection calculations will be incorrect. Ensure these vectors are properly normalized and orthogonalized. Small Radii: Spheres with radii smaller than R{max} (the radius used to define the "enlarged frustum" in some contexts) may pass the enlarged frustum test but fail the original frustum test. This method handles this by using the actual sphere radius r in the calculations, ensuring accurate culling for all sphere sizes. Time Complexity: O(1) per sphere. The test involves a constant number of vector operations (dot products, additions, comparisons). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sphere, as no auxiliary data structures are required. Performance: This test is significantly faster than ray-sphere intersection tests, which involve square roots and quadratic equation solving. It is particularly effective in scenes with many small spheres or chunks, where a large fraction of objects are outside the view frustum. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and effective for spherical bounding volumes. Limitations: Only applicable to spherical bounding volumes. For non-spherical volumes, other culling techniques (e.g., AABB culling) may be more appropriate. When to Use: Use this method when rendering scenes with many spherical objects or when using bounding spheres for acceleration structures in volume rendering. Frustum culling for spheres was introduced as a simpler alternative to SIMD shaft culling, which is limited to primitives with planar edges like triangles. The technique is described in the context of the Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) algorithm for visualizing particle data, where it is used to efficiently reject non-overlapping spheres during ray traversal. The method leverages the geometric properties of spheres and the camera frustum to perform a quick rejection test before more expensive intersection calculations. name: Russian Roulette
head: Break From the Ray Marching Loop When Opaque (Optimization), Monte Carlo termination, Probabilistic Path Termination, RR termination, Russian Roulette for Ray Marching Termination, Russian Roulette for Volumetric Paths, Volumetric path termination
body: Russian Roulette is a probabilistic technique used to terminate volumetric paths or ray marching loops when their contribution to the final image becomes negligible, thereby reducing computational cost while maintaining statistical unbiasedness. Unlike deterministic early termination which clamps the result and introduces bias, Russian Roulette scales the weight of surviving paths to compensate for the probability of termination, ensuring the expected value remains unchanged. It is distinct from Empty-space skipping (which avoids sampling empty regions) and Early ray termination (which stops based on opacity thresholds without compensation) by explicitly handling the variance and bias trade-off through random sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current path throughput/weight W (or transmittance T), random number generator. Output: Updated weight W' (or T') and a boolean indicating whether the path continues or terminates. Data Structures: Random number generator producing uniform samples \xi \in [0, 1]. Accumulated throughput/transmittance variable (scalar or spectral vector). Parameters: Termination probability p{rr}: The probability of killing the path. Threshold: A minimum value for transmittance/weight below which RR is considered (e.g., 10^{-3}). Depth: Current path depth, used to prevent termination at the first bounce. Steps: 1. Evaluate the current contribution weight W (or transmittance T) after a scattering event or step. 2. Determine the termination probability p{rr}. Common strategies include: Using the maximum component of the spectral weight/transmittance. Using a fixed constant (e.g., 0.5) if the weight is below a threshold. Using the transmittance value itself for pure transmittance calculations. 3. Generate a uniform random number \xi \in [0, 1]. 4. Compare \xi with p{rr}: If \xi \geq p{rr} (or \xi > 1/d in some formulations where d=1/p{rr}), terminate the path. Set W' = 0. Otherwise, continue the path. Scale the weight: W' = W / p{rr}. Formulas: The expected value of the updated weight W' is: E[W'] = (1 - p{rr}) \cdot 0 + p{rr} \cdot \frac{E[W]}{p{rr}} = E[W] This confirms the estimator remains unbiased. In spectral rendering, the termination probability q is often derived from the maximum component of the scaled beta (\beta): q = \max(0, 1 - \beta{\text{scaled}}.\text{MaxComponentValue}()) where \beta{\text{scaled}} may include transmission scaling factors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def russianroulette(weight, sampler, minthreshold=1e-3, mindepth=1, currentdepth=1): """ Applies Russian Roulette to a volumetric path. Args: weight: Current throughput/transmittance (scalar or spectral). sampler: Random number generator with Get1D() method. minthreshold: Minimum weight to consider termination. mindepth: Minimum path depth before allowing termination. currentdepth: Current path depth. Returns: newweight: Scaled weight if continuing, 0 if terminated. continue: Boolean indicating if the path continues. """ # Do not terminate at the first bounce or if weight is high if currentdepth < mindepth: return weight, True # Determine termination probability based on weight # Strategy 1: Use max component for spectral weights if isinstance(weight, Spectral): maxcomp = weight.maxcomponent() if maxcomp < minthreshold: # Probability of continuing is maxcomp # Probability of terminating q = 1 - maxcomp # Note: If maxcomp is 0, q=1, path always dies q = max(0.0, 1.0 - maxcomp) else: return weight, True else: # Strategy 2: Fixed probability if below threshold if weight < minthreshold: # d=2 implies continueProb=0.5, so prr (termination) = 0.5 # Or generally, if weight < threshold, set prr = 0.5 prr = 0.5 q = prr else: return weight, True # Sample urr = sampler.get1d() # Terminate if urr < q (where q is prob of termination) # Note: S3 uses uRR < q to break. S1 uses xi >= prr to terminate. # If q is termination prob, then terminate if urr < q. if urr < q: return 0.0, False else: # Scale weight by 1 / (1 - q) which is 1 / continueprob # If q = 1 - maxcomp, then 1-q = maxcomp newweight = weight / (1.0 - q) return newweight, True Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias from Simple Break: Simply breaking the loop when transparency drops below a threshold without compensation removes the contribution of the volume beyond that point, introducing bias. Zero Intersection: If a ray does not intersect the volume or the intersection length is zero, transmission is set to 1.0 and color contribution is 0, avoiding unnecessary computation. Spectral Balance: In spectral rendering, using the maximum component for termination probability helps maintain spectral balance. Depth Constraint: Termination should not occur at depth 1 to ensure the first scattering event is always accounted for. Avoids sampling empty regions by subdividing volumes. Choose when volumes have large empty spaces. Stops marching when opacity exceeds a threshold. Choose for simple opacity culling without unbiased guarantees. Uses BVH to skip non-intersecting volumes. Choose for complex scenes with many volumes. General term for stopping integration early. Choose when performance is critical and bias is acceptable. A safer variant of early termination. Choose when visual quality must be preserved with minimal bias. Time Complexity: Reduces the average number of ray marching steps, especially in dense volumes where transmittance drops quickly. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead beyond random number state. Measured Performance: In a cloud example, rendering with Russian Roulette took 161s (unbiased) compared to 2556s without it (biased, max depth 200). Scaling: More effective in dense volumes where transparency drops rapidly. Strengths: Maintains unbiased results while significantly speeding up rendering in scenes with high variance or dense media. Limitations: Adds variance due to the random termination; requires careful tuning of termination probability. When to Use: In path tracing or ray marching for volumes where paths can become very long or contribute negligibly. When Not to Use: When strict deterministic results are required, or in very sparse volumes where the overhead of RR is not justified. Russian Roulette originates from Monte Carlo simulation techniques, where it is used to terminate particle paths that contribute little to the final result. In computer graphics, it was adapted for volumetric rendering to handle the long paths often encountered in participating media. The technique is widely used in modern path tracers like PBRT to ensure unbiased rendering of complex volumetric scenes. name: Early Stop
head: Early stop+0, Early stop+1
body: Early Stop (ES) is an optimization for sphere tracing procedural volumes that limits the evaluation of noise frequencies (fi) by breaking the summation loop as soon as the current position is determined to be outside the bounding volume of the current octave. It solves the problem of unnecessary computational cost when higher-frequency noise terms cannot possibly influence the isosurface intersection because their bounding volumes do not contain the isovalue. Unlike Empty-space skipping which skips entire ray segments, ES reduces the per-step cost by skipping function evaluations within a single step, trading a potential increase in total step count for fewer evaluations per step. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Isosurface value v. Procedural noise function defined by octaves fi, where i ranges from 0 to n. Bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) where each level i has an upper bound function \text{BVH}{i+}(\mathbf{p}) and optionally a lower bound \text{BVH}{i-}(\mathbf{p}). Parameter k: the number of additional octaves to compute beyond the minimum required index i{min} (default k=1 for standard ES+1). Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray. Normal \mathbf{n} at the intersection point. Data Structures: BVH Bounds: For each octave i, the bounding volume is represented by inclusion functions. The upper bound \text{BVH}{i+}(\mathbf{p}) provides a value such that fi(\mathbf{p}) \le \text{BVH}{i+}(\mathbf{p}). The lower bound \text{BVH}{i-}(\mathbf{p}) satisfies fi(\mathbf{p}) \ge \text{BVH}{i-}(\mathbf{p}). These bounds are typically computed using interval arithmetic or Taylor inclusion functions. Accumulator: A variable to store the partial sum of the FBM (Fractional Brownian Motion) or similar noise function. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set current ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}, accumulated sum S = 0, and current octave index i = 0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: While \mathbf{p} has not converged to the isosurface within a tolerance \epsilon: a. Compute Bounds and Function: For the current octave i, compute the upper bound \text{BVH}{i+}(\mathbf{p}) and the function value fi(\mathbf{p}). b. Early Termination Check: Check if the position is outside the bounding volume of the current octave. Condition: If \text{BVH}{i+}(\mathbf{p}) < v, then fi(\mathbf{p}) cannot contribute to reaching the isovalue v from below (assuming the sum is monotonic or bounds are tight enough for the specific noise structure). Identify i{min}: The first index i for which \text{BVH}{i+}(\mathbf{p}) < v is i{min}. If i < i{min}, continue to next octave. If i = i{min}, this is the first octave where the bound drops below v. c. Summation with Early Stop: Compute the sum of octaves starting from i{min} up to i{min} + k. For j from i{min} to i{min} + k: Compute fj(\mathbf{p}). Add fj(\mathbf{p}) to the accumulated sum S. Break the octave loop after computing f{i{min}+k}. d. Step Size Calculation: Calculate the step size \Delta t based on the accumulated sum S and the derivative or gradient information. The exact step size formula depends on the specific sphere tracing variant (e.g., standard sphere tracing uses the distance to the nearest bounding surface, while Taylor-based methods use derivative bounds). Note: Using fewer octaves (smaller k) may result in smaller step sizes because the bounding volume of the truncated sum is tighter or the derivative estimate is less accurate. e. Advance Ray: Update \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{d}. Increment i to 0 (reset octave index for the new position, as the BVH level may change) or maintain state if the hierarchy allows. 3. Convergence Check: If the change in position or sum is below \epsilon, return \mathbf{p} and the normal. Formulas: Minimum Index Condition: i{\min} = \min\{i \mid \text{BVH}{i+}(\mathbf{p}) < v\} Alternative Condition (Inside Volume): When inside the volume and searching for the isosurface, i{min} can be defined using the lower bound: \text{BVH}{i-}(\mathbf{p}) > v Summation Limit: The loop breaks after computing: f{i{\min}+k} Parameters: v: The isovalue for the isosurface. k: The number of additional functions to compute beyond i{min}. Typical value is 1 (Early stop+1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Stop+0 (k=0): Computing only f{i{min}} causes slow convergence. The ray steps safely to the outer bounding volume and repeats, massively increasing the total number of steps, especially for grazing rays (rays passing close to but not entering a bounding volume). Step Size Reduction: Stopping early reduces the number of fi computed but may result in smaller step sizes, potentially increasing the total number of steps required to converge. This could raise the final cost if the overhead of extra steps outweighs the savings in function evaluations. Grazing Rays: ES+0 is particularly bad for grazing rays. ES+1 drastically diminishes this performance loss by considering one extra level of the BVH, making slow convergence rare. Precision: The bounds \text{BVH}{i+} and \text{BVH}{i-} must be tight enough to be useful. Loose bounds may cause premature termination or failure to detect intersections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlystopspheretrace(rayorigin, raydirection, isovalue, noisefunc, bvhs, k=1, tolerance=1e-4): """ Perform sphere tracing with Early Stop optimization. Args: rayorigin: Initial ray position. raydirection: Normalized ray direction. isovalue: The target isovalue v. noisefunc: Function to compute fi(p) for octave i. bvhs: List of BVH bound objects. bvhs[i].upperbound(p) returns BVHi+(p). bvhs[i].lowerbound(p) returns BVHi-(p). k: Number of additional octaves to compute beyond imin. tolerance: Convergence threshold. Returns: Intersection point and normal, or None if no intersection. """ p = rayorigin maxsteps = 1000 # Safety limit step = 0 while step < maxsteps: # Find imin: the first octave where the upper bound is below isovalue imin = 0 for i in range(len(bvhs)): if bvhs[i].upperbound(p) < isovalue: imin = i break else: # If all bounds are >= isovalue, we might need to compute all octaves # or handle as a special case (e.g., inside volume) imin = len(bvhs) - 1 # Compute sum from imin to imin + k accumulatedsum = 0.0 for i in range(imin, min(imin + k + 1, len(bvhs))): accumulatedsum += noisefunc(i, p) # Calculate step size based on accumulatedsum and derivative info # This is a placeholder for the specific sphere tracing step size formula # which depends on the noise function and BVH derivative bounds. # For standard sphere tracing, stepsize might be related to the distance # to the bounding surface. For Taylor-based, it uses derivative bounds. stepsize = computestepsize(accumulatedsum, bvhs, imin, p) # Advance ray pnew = p + stepsize raydirection # Check for convergence if abs(pnew - p) < tolerance: return pnew, computenormal(pnew, noisefunc, bvhs) p = pnew step += 1 return None, None def computestepsize(accumulatedsum, bvhs, imin, p): """ Placeholder for step size calculation. In practice, this uses the derivative bounds from the BVH or the function itself to determine a safe step size for sphere tracing. """ # Example: simple step size based on sum magnitude # Real implementation would use BVH derivative bounds return abs(accumulatedsum) 0.1 Early Stop + k (ES+k) is an optimization for sphere tracing procedural volumes that prevents unnecessary intermediate convergence checks during BVH traversal by computing k additional octaves per traversal step. It builds on Early Stop by trading a small increase in per-step function evaluations for a significant reduction in the total number of BVH traversal steps. Unlike standard Early Stop (ES+0), which may converge too slowly and incur high step counts, ES+k maintains a balance between step reduction and computational overhead, with ES+1 generally offering the best performance across diverse scenes. Time Complexity: The cost per step is reduced by skipping fi evaluations for i > i{min} + k. However, the total number of steps may increase due to smaller step sizes when k is small. Memory Complexity: Requires storing BVH bounds for each octave. The memory footprint is proportional to the number of octaves n. Measured Performance: ES+1 provides results very similar to full computation (computing all fi) but with significantly lower cost. ES+0 causes massive performance loss due to slow convergence. ES+k with k>1 provides diminishing returns compared to k=1. Strengths: Reduces per-step computational cost by avoiding unnecessary noise function evaluations. Effective for procedural volumes with hierarchical bounding structures. Limitations: May increase the total number of steps if step sizes become too small. Not suitable for k=0 due to grazing ray issues. When to Use: When rendering procedural volumetric noise with sphere tracing, especially in large and detailed scenes where noise evaluation is expensive. When Not to Use: When the overhead of BVH bound computation outweighs the savings from skipping noise evaluations, or when the noise function does not have well-defined bounding volumes. Early Stop was introduced in the context of fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes. It leverages the hierarchical nature of bounding volume hierarchies (BVH) used in sphere tracing to prune the computation of noise octaves. The method addresses the inefficiency of computing all noise frequencies even when higher frequencies cannot affect the isosurface intersection due to their bounding volumes. name: Early Stop + k
head: ES+k
body: Early Stop + k (ES+k) is an optimization for sphere tracing procedural volumes that prevents unnecessary intermediate convergence checks during BVH traversal by computing k additional octaves per traversal step. It builds on Early Stop by trading a small increase in per-step function evaluations for a significant reduction in the total number of BVH traversal steps. Unlike standard Early Stop (ES+0), which may converge too slowly and incur high step counts, ES+k maintains a balance between step reduction and computational overhead, with ES+1 generally offering the best performance across diverse scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, BVH structure, noise function f, maximum distance d{max}, and integer parameter k \ge 0. Output: Transmittance and color along the ray, or termination status. Data Structures: The method relies on the BVH hierarchy. No new data structures are introduced; it modifies the evaluation logic within the existing traversal loop. Parameters: k: The number of additional octaves computed per BVH node visit. Typical values: 0, 1, 2, 3. Recommended default: k=1. Note: Optimal k varies by scene and view; fixed k > 1 is risky. Algorithm: The core modification occurs during the BVH traversal loop. For each step in the BVH traversal, the algorithm computes the function value for k additional octaves beyond the current level, rather than just the current level or none. This look-ahead ensures that the distance estimate is sufficiently tight to avoid premature convergence checks that would otherwise force a re-evaluation or slow convergence. 1. Initialize ray parameters: t = 0, d{max}, k. 2. While t < d{max}: a. Traverse BVH to find the smallest bounding volume containing the point \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. b. Let L be the octave level associated with the current BVH node. c. Compute the noise function value V for octaves L, L+1, \dots, L+k. d. Determine the step size \Delta t based on the tightest bound from these k+1 octaves. e. Update t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. f. Perform convergence check (if applicable) or continue traversal. 3. Return accumulated radiance/transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretraceearlystopk(rayorigin, raydirection, bvh, noisefunc, k, maxdist): """ Sphere tracing with Early Stop + k optimization. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) raydirection: (x, y, z) normalized bvh: BVH structure with nodes containing octave levels noisefunc: Function returning noise value for a given octave and point k: Integer, number of additional octaves to compute per step maxdist: Maximum ray length Returns: transmittance, color """ t = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) epsilon = 1e-6 # Standard minimum step size guard while t < maxdist: # Traverse BVH to find the smallest bounding volume containing point # (Implementation depends on specific BVH library; assume node retrieval here) point = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) node = bvh.findnodecontaining(point) if node is None: # Ray exited the volume break # Get the base octave level for this node baseoctave = node.octavelevel # Compute k additional octaves beyond the current level # This prevents unnecessary intermediate convergences minstep = float('inf') for i in range(k + 1): currentoctave = baseoctave + i # Evaluate noise function at current point for current octave noiseval = noisefunc(point, currentoctave) # Calculate step size based on the bound provided by this octave # Standard sphere tracing uses the noise value as the step bound step = max(noiseval, epsilon) # Take the minimum step size to ensure safety if step < minstep: minstep = step # Guard against zero or negative step sizes if minstep <= epsilon: minstep = epsilon t += minstep # Accumulate radiance (simplified standard volume rendering integration) density = noisefunc(point, baseoctave) color = (color[0] + density transmittance minstep, color[1] + density transmittance minstep, color[2] + density transmittance minstep) transmittance = (1.0 - density minstep) return transmittance, color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Choosing k: A fixed k > 1 is tricky because different scenes (even views of the same object) require different optimal k values. For example, on the "Sponge" scene, k=2 is optimal, while on "Sponge (far)", k=1 is better. Performance Degradation: If k is too high, performance decreases due to excessive function evaluations per step. For instance, k=3 on the Sponge scene resulted in significantly higher time (3513.6 ms) compared to k=1 (749.6 ms). ES+0 Performance: k=0 (standard Early Stop) can perform poorly due to slow convergence and increased number of steps, sometimes worse than no Early Stop at all. Measured Performance: Sponge Scene (Sub-stepping enabled): ES+0 (k=0): 273.0 avg steps, 3.65 avg octaves, 972.0 ms, ×1.0 speedup. ES+1 (k=1): 147.8 avg steps, 5.23 avg octaves, 749.6 ms, ×1.4 speedup. ES+2 (k=2): 127.3 avg steps, 6.31 avg octaves, 782.5 ms, ×1.3 speedup. ES+3 (k=3): 279.6 avg steps, 13.45 avg octaves, 3513.6 ms, ×1.2 speedup. No ES: 116.2 avg steps, 10.22 avg octaves, 1123.6 ms, reference. Sponge (far) Scene (Sub-stepping enabled): ES+0 (k=0): 273.0 avg steps, 3.65 avg octaves, 972.0 ms, ×1.0 speedup. ES+1 (k=1): 147.8 avg steps, 5.23 avg octaves, 749.6 ms, ×1.4 speedup. ES+2 (k=2): 127.3 avg steps, 6.31 avg octaves, 782.5 ms, ×1.3 speedup. Note: Performance decreases for k > 1 on this scene. Scaling: ES+1 consistently outperforms ES+3 and no Early Stop across tested scenes. Using k > 1 was never found to be faster when using quadratic bounds. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces the number of BVH traversal steps, which can be a bottleneck in large scenes. ES+1 provides a good balance between step reduction and computational overhead. Limitations: Requires tuning k for specific scenes; a fixed k > 1 is not universally optimal. ES+0 can be slower than no Early Stop in some cases. When to Use: Use ES+1 as a default choice for most scenes. Consider tuning k for specific scenes if performance is critical, but be aware that optimal k varies. Avoid ES+0 if slow convergence is observed. Avoid k > 1 if using quadratic bounds. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". It is part of a series of optimizations for sphere tracing procedural volumes, including Early Stop and quadratic Taylor bounds. History and Development: The authors observed that standard Early Stop (ES+0) could converge slowly, leading to increased step counts and worse performance than no Early Stop in some cases. They proposed computing additional octaves per step to improve convergence speed, leading to the ES+k strategy. Experimental results showed that ES+1 provided the best performance across various scenes, while higher k values could degrade performance. Where it is used: The method is applicable to sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise, particularly in large and detailed scenes where BVH traversal is a significant cost.
