name: Adaptive Refinement for Volume Rendering
head: Adaptive Refinement Volume Rendering, Image-order adaptive refinement, Interactive Adaptive Refinement, Feedback-based Adaptive Refinement
body: Adaptive Refinement for Volume Rendering is an image-order technique that balances rendering quality and performance by iteratively refining the image resolution based on local visual error. It solves the problem of high computational cost in volume ray-casting by casting rays non-uniformly, focusing computational effort on regions with high color variation (edges, silhouettes) while interpolating homogeneous regions. Unlike brute-force ray tracing which casts rays from every pixel immediately, this method starts with a coarse approximation and incrementally adds rays, allowing for interactive frame rates during exploration. It distinguishes itself from Two-stage NeRF Rendering by operating on explicit voxel grids with FEM-based error control rather than neural field approximations, and from Adaptive Sampling by using a hierarchical quadtree structure for screen-space subdivision rather than stochastic jittering. The method operates as a reactive control loop or an iterative convergence process. Two primary implementations exist: a FEM-based GPU approach and a hierarchical CPU-based approach. Both share the core logic of estimating error, marking regions for refinement, and reconstructing the image. Inputs: Scalar field dataset (voxels with color and opacity). Camera parameters (view matrix, projection). Transfer function (mapping scalar values to color/opacity). Target frame rate (for feedback loop) or convergence criteria. Parameters: romax (max region size), romin (min region size), epsilon (error threshold); or m (number of cells to refine). Outputs: Rendered image frame. Error map (indicating regions needing refinement). 1. Quadtree (CPU/GPU): Stores image regions as quadratic cells. Each leaf node represents a cell that can be subdivided into four children. 2. F Array (Error/Ray Density Map): A 2D array of flags. F(u,v) = 1 indicates a ray has been traced at pixel (u,v); 0 indicates it has not. In, this is visualized as white (ray-traced) and black (interpolated) pixels. 3. G Array (Interpolation Flag): A 2D array of flags. G(u,v) = 1 indicates the color at (u,v) has been interpolated. 4. Heap (Marking): A data structure storing quadtree leaves sorted by estimated error contribution, used to select the top m cells for refinement. 5. Error Texture (GPU): A 1D single-channel floating-point texture storing error values for new quadtree leaves, read back to main memory for marking. The volume rendering integral for a ray parametrized by arc length w^x of length L^x is: I(x) = \int0^{L^x} E(w^x) \exp\left(-\int0^t A(w^x) ds\right) dt where E is emission and A is absorption. The approximation error is measured using the L^2 error norm: \boldsymbol{\eta} = \|u - un\|S:= \left( \intS (u - un)^2 dx \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} where u is the exact solution on the viewport S and un is the approximative solution. The nodal interpolant is given by: \mathcal{I}n(u) = \sum{q \in \mathcal{Q}} u(q) \Phiq where \mathcal{Q} is the set of evaluation points and \Phiq are basis functions. The approximative solution function is: un = \sum{q \in \mathcal{Q}} Ih(q) \Phiq where Ih(q) is the approximation of the volume rendering integral at point q. The total approximation error is bounded by: \boldsymbol{\eta} = \|\boldsymbol{u} - \boldsymbol{u}n\|S \leq \|\boldsymbol{u} - \mathcal{I}n(\boldsymbol{u})\|S + \|\mathcal{I}n(\boldsymbol{u}) - \boldsymbol{u}n\|S The local error contribution on each cell T \in \mathcal{T}n is estimated by comparing two subsequent approximations: \eta{Vn}^T \approx \|u{n-1} - un\|T = \left( \intT (u{n-1} - un)^2 dx \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} This integral is solved numerically using a Gaussian quadrature rule with N=3 points: \eta{Vn}^T \approx \sum{i=1}^N \phi(xi) wi Relative L^2 error is defined as: \eta{rel} = \|u - un\|S / \|u\|S romax: Maximum size of square regions for ray tracing/interpolation. Range: 1 \le \text{romax} \le R (image side length). Typical initial value: 16. romin: Minimum size of square regions. Subdivision stops when region size reaches romin. Range: 1 \le \text{romin} \le \text{romax}. Typical initial value: 2. epsilon (e): Threshold for local color difference. If the range of colors in a region is less than e, no further processing is performed. Value: e > 0. Typical initial value: 16–32. m: Fixed number of cells to mark for refinement in each iteration. Typical value: 1000. p: Polynomial degree for interpolation during reconstruction. Fixed value: 2 (bilinear/quadratic). W: Number of evenly spaced locations along a ray where data is resampled. targetframerate: Desired frame rate budget. Typical value: 10 fps. errorthreshold: Maximum allowable visual error metric. Typical value: 1 pixel per texel. The algorithm proceeds in iterations. The following pseudocode combines the hierarchical structure of with the error estimation and marking logic of. Note that uses a GPU-based FEM estimator and heap marking, while uses a corner-difference heuristic and recursive subdivision. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def AdaptiveRefinement(R, romax, romin, epsilon): # Loop until fully refined or convergence criteria met while romax > 1: # 1. Ray Tracing Phase # Divide image into square regions of size romax for v in range(0, R, romax): for u in range(0, R, romax): RayTraceRegion(u, v, romax, romin, epsilon) # 2. Interpolation Phase # Form intermediate image by interpolating between computed rays InterpolateImage(romax) # 3. Display DisplayImage() # 4. Clear Interpolated Colors # Prepare for next iteration: clear interpolated colors but keep ray-traced ones for v in range(R): for u in range(R): if F[u, v] == 0: # If no ray was traced C[u, v] = 0 G[u, v] = 0 # 5. Increment Level-of-Detail romax = Nextromax(romax) romin = Nextromin(romin) epsilon = Nexte(epsilon) def RayTraceRegion(u, v, w, wmin, e): # Cast rays from the four corner pixels of the current region for j in range(0, w, w): for i in range(0, w, w): pixelu = u + i pixelv = v + j if pixelu < R and pixelv < R and F[pixelu, pixelv] == 0: RayTrace(pixelu, pixelv) F[pixelu, pixelv] = 1 # Check if subdivision is needed if w > wmin and Difference(u, v, w, e): # Divide region into four subregions for j in range(0, w/2, w/2): for i in range(0, w/2, w/2): RayTraceRegion(u + i, v + j, w/2, wmin, e) def Difference(u, v, w, e): # Check if the range of intensity values for any color component # of the colors at the four corners of the region exceeds epsilon corners = [ C[u, v], C[u + w, v], C[u, v + w], C[u + w, v + w] ] for component in [R, G, B]: maxval = max(c[component] for c in corners) minval = min(c[component] for c in corners) if maxval - minval > e: return True return False def InterpolateImage(romax): # Divide image into square regions of size romax for v in range(0, R, romax): for u in range(0, R, romax): InterpolateRegion(u, v, romax) def InterpolateRegion(u, v, w): # Interpolate colors at midpoints of sides and center for j in range(0, w, w/2): for i in range(0, w, w/2): pixelu = u + i pixelv = v + j if pixelu < R and pixelv < R and F[pixelu, pixelv] == 0 and G[pixelu, pixelv] == 0: Interpolate(u, v, w, pixelu, pixelv) G[pixelu, pixelv] = 1 # Recurse if region is larger than 2x2 pixels if w/2 > 1: for j in range(0, w/2, w/2): for i in range(0, w/2, w/2): InterpolateRegion(u + i, v + j, w/2) def Interpolate(u, v, w, targetu, targetv): # Compute color using linear interpolation (boundary midpoints) # or bi-linear interpolation (region centers) # Implementation depends on position relative to region corners pass def RayTrace(u, v): # Cast ray from pixel (u, v) # Resample data at W evenly spaced locations # Tri-linearly interpolate from 8 surrounding voxels # Composite with fully opaque background pass FEM-Based Variation (GPU): In the implementation described in, the steps differ slightly: 1. Estimate Error: Compute \etaT for each new quadtree leaf using the FEM estimator (Equation 9) and Gaussian quadrature. 2. Mark Cells: Use a heap to select the m cells with the biggest impact on total error. Cost: O(m \log n). 3. Refine: Create four new quadtree leaves per marked cell. Generate up to 5 evaluation points per new leaf (1 center, 4 edge midpoints). 4. Compute Integral: Perform ray casting for new evaluation points. Use Step Doubling for error control: compute color with step size h and two steps of h/2. If squared difference < error bound, accept and increase h; otherwise, decrease h and repeat. 5. Reconstruct: Render un to screen using polynomial degree p=2 interpolation on a uniform grid. Manual Parameter Selection: Choosing romax, romin, and epsilon manually can lead to sub-optimal presentation. High romax misses features; high romin poorly resolves features; high epsilon ignores features. Latency: Reactive feedback (monitoring frame rate) introduces scheduling latency. Proactive scheduling using system timing parameters (e.g., fill rates) is recommended. Interactivity Interruption: The loop is interrupted whenever the camera moves or transfer function changes to guarantee interactivity. Precision: The error estimation relies on numerical integration (Gaussian quadrature). Insufficient points may lead to inaccurate error estimates. Degenerate Input: Linear regions with strong slopes may be unnecessarily refined by variance-based estimators (like Levoy's), but the FEM hierarchical estimator handles these better by recognizing good approximation in linear regions. Time Complexity: Rendering time grows linearly with dataset size for full ray tracing, but adaptive refinement reduces effective cost by casting fewer rays in smooth regions. Marking complexity is O(m \log n) where m is the number of marked cells and n is the number of leaves. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the quadtree, error maps (F, G arrays), and intermediate color buffers. The quadtree is stored on the CPU, while error estimation and raycasting are offloaded to the GPU in modern implementations. Measured Performance:: On a CT Head dataset (256x256x225), 7 iterations were needed for an approximation error of 10^{-2} with m=1000. A single iteration took 20–40 ms for screen resolutions 512x512 and 2048x2048 respectively, on an Intel Core 2 Duo 3.0 GHz and NVIDIA GeForce 8800GT.: On a Cytochrome B5 dataset (123x123x123), Frame 1 took 4.6 seconds with 3,870 rays (20% coverage). Frame 4 took 25.7 seconds total with 19,289 rays (100% coverage). On a Sun 4/280, subsequent images appeared at intervals of approximately five seconds each.: Tested on a GeForce3 GPU. Frame rate fluctuated above the 10 fps budget, and the system successfully added cells to reduce error below 1 pixel/texel. Strengths: Faster convergence than uniform discretization (fewer rays for desired quality). Allows interactive frame rates by focusing computational effort only where necessary. Handles discontinuities better than p-adaptive methods. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of level-of-detail parameters. Reactive feedback may cause latency. Interactivity is interrupted on camera/transfer function changes. When to Use: Interactive exploration of large volume datasets where immediate feedback is required, and the scene is static or changes slowly. When Not to Use: When offline rendering with maximum quality is required (uniform ray casting may be simpler and more predictable), or when the scene changes rapidly (interactivity interruption overhead). Origin: The concept of adaptive refinement in volume rendering was introduced by [Lev90] (Levoy), who proposed adaptive image-space subdivision combined with progressive image generation. Development: (1988): Presented an image-order volume rendering algorithm that adaptively refines image quality over time, using recursive bi-linear interpolation and hierarchical subdivision. (2002): Demonstrated an interactive volume rendering system for unstructured grids using a reactive feedback loop to maintain frame rate while bounding visual error. (2011): Introduced a GPU-based implementation using Finite Element Method (FEM) theory for error estimation, focusing on h-adaptivity and step doubling for ray integration error control. Usage: Used in interactive visualization of molecular graphics, medical imaging (CT scans), and scientific data (CFD datasets). Implemented in C++ and OpenGL/GLSL requiring Shader Model 4.0 GPU. Interactive Visualization of Unstructured Grids Using Hierarchical 3D..., https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~jjcorso/pubs/leven02unstructgrid.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 Adaptive Screen-Space Sampling for Volume Ray-Casting, https://webdoc.sub.gwdg.de/ebook/serien/ah/ZIB/ZR1104.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering by Adaptive Refinement, https://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/88-030.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Conservative Early Ray Termination
head: ERT in scan conversion phase, ERT-table scheme
body: Conservative Early Ray Termination (CERT) is an optimization for the scan conversion phase of volume rendering that prunes the processing of cells by determining if a ray is already sufficiently opaque before the cell is rasterized. It differs from standard Early Ray Termination (ERT) [1019-early-ray-termination.md], which typically requires sequential accumulation from the near plane, by using a lookup table (ERT-table) and subscreen-based aggregation to make visibility decisions based on partially accumulated opacity without per-pixel overhead. This allows the technique to be applied during the parallel scan conversion phase where global ray state is not readily available. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data (unstructured grid cells), camera parameters, screen resolution, opacity threshold \tau. Output: Rendered image; reduction in scan conversion time by skipping cells. Data Structures: The core data structure is the ERT-table, which aggregates termination status per subscreen rather than per cell or per pixel. Screen Subdivision: The screen is subdivided into N subscreens S. ERT-table Entry: For each subscreen S, the entry contains: 1. A one-bit flag indicating whether conditions C1 and C2 (defined below) are satisfied for that subscreen. 2. A value maxtermZ: the maximum depth value (rearmost depth) among all pixels in the subscreen that have a partially accumulated ray segment with opacity exceeding the threshold \tau. Parameters: Opacity Threshold (\tau): The threshold for "sufficiently high" opacity. In the source evaluation, \tau = 0.9. Algorithm Steps: 1. Subdivision: Subdivide the screen into subscreens. Initialize the ERT-table entries for all subscreens. 2. Partial Composition: During ray marching or segment processing, perform partial composition of ray segments. If a partially composed segment s{ij} has opacity O{ij} \ge \tau, mark the corresponding pixel as "terminated" for the purpose of CERT. 3. Update ERT-table: For each subscreen S: Check if there exists a nonempty ray-segment list for all pixels in S (Condition C1). Check if there exists a partially composed ray segment with opacity \ge \tau in each of these lists (Condition C2). If C1 and C2 are met, set the one-bit flag for S to true. Calculate maxtermZ for S: the maximum depth z among all pixels in S that have a terminated segment. If no pixels are terminated, maxtermZ is undefined or effectively -\infty. 4. Cell Visibility Check: For a cell c to be skipped: Compute the projection area R of cell c on the screen. Identify the subscreens S that overlap with R. Verify Condition C3: For every subscreen S overlapping R, the ERT-table flag must be true, and the maxtermZ of that subscreen must be less than the depth of the nearest vertex of cell c (nearestc). Formally, the conditions to neglect scan conversion of cell c are: (C1) There exists a nonempty ray-segment list for all pixels corresponding to the projection area R for cell c. (C2) There exists a partially composed ray segment whose opacity is sufficiently high (\ge \tau) in each of these ray-segment lists. (C3) At least one of such ray-segments in each of the lists is located in front of the cell c (i.e., its depth is less than the nearest vertex of c). If C1, C2, and C3 are satisfied for all relevant subscreens, terminate the scan conversion of cell c. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. THRESHOLD = 0.9 class ERTTableEntry: flag: bool # True if C1 and C2 are satisfied for this subscreen maxtermz: float # Rearmost depth of terminated segments in this subscreen def updateerttable(subscreens, raysegmentlists): """ Update the ERT-table based on current ray segment states. raysegmentlists: dict mapping (subscreenid, pixelid) -> list of ray segments """ for subscreen in subscreens: subscreenid = subscreen.id pixelsinsubscreen = subscreen.getpixels() allpixelshavesegments = True allpixelshaveterminatedsegment = True maxtermz = -float('inf') for pixel in pixelsinsubscreen: segments = raysegmentlists.get((subscreenid, pixel.id), []) if not segments: allpixelshavesegments = False break # Find the front-most segment with opacity >= THRESHOLD terminatedsegment = None for seg in segments: if seg.opacity >= THRESHOLD: # We want the front-most (smallest z) terminated segment # But maxtermz is the rearmost (largest z) among ALL terminated segments # Wait, the source says: "maxtermZ... is the rearmost depth among all # the subscreen's per-pixel-front-most partially accumulated ray-segments # whose opacity exceed the threshold." # This implies for each pixel, we find the front-most terminated segment, # then take the max of those depths across the subscreen. if terminatedsegment is None or seg.z < terminatedsegment.z: terminatedsegment = seg if terminatedsegment is None: allpixelshaveterminatedsegment = False break if terminatedsegment.z > maxtermz: maxtermz = terminatedsegment.z if allpixelshavesegments and allpixelshaveterminatedsegment: subscreen.ertentry.flag = True subscreen.ertentry.maxtermz = maxtermz else: subscreen.ertentry.flag = False subscreen.ertentry.maxtermz = -float('inf') def shouldskipcell(cell, subscreens, erttable): """ Determine if a cell's scan conversion can be skipped. """ projectionarea = cell.getprojectionarea() overlappingsubscreens = subscreens.getoverlappingsubscreens(projectionarea) for subscreen in overlappingsubscreens: entry = erttable[subscreen.id] # Check C1 and C2 via the flag if not entry.flag: return False # Check C3: maxtermz < nearest vertex of cell if entry.maxtermz >= cell.nearestvertex.z: return False return True Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Per-pixel Overhead: A naive implementation checking per-pixel ray-segment lists incurs significant overhead. The ERT-table aggregation is essential to mitigate this. Conservatism: CERT checks a sufficient but not necessary condition for termination. This approximation may reduce the effectiveness of ERT compared to an exact check, but it enables the technique in the scan conversion phase. Partial Composition: The efficiency of ERT relies on partial composition increasing the opacity of ray segments, making it more likely to exceed the threshold. A technique where Working Nodes (WNs) in a parallel system exchange their ERT-table information to increase the accuracy and completeness of termination decisions. Mechanism: If WNa terminates scan conversion due to ERT, WNb (holding cells behind WNa) can also terminate its scan conversion based on the shared ERT-table data. Parameter: The frequency of ERT information exchange is set far below the frequency of ERT information updates at each WN to avoid interprocessor communication overhead. Performance: In evaluations, sharing decreased scan conversion time by at most 43% for Viewpoint A and 50% for Viewpoint B. Effective parallel performance improvement was 7% for Viewpoint A and 30% for Viewpoint B. Time Complexity: The overhead of maintaining the ERT-table is reduced by subscreen aggregation compared to per-pixel checks. The exact complexity depends on the number of subscreens and pixels per subscreen. Measured Performance: On a dataset of 307,565 unstructured tetrahedral cells with 62,475 vertices, CERT provided a speedup of 3.86 times in sequential execution on a single Working Node (WN). Strengths: Enables early termination in the scan conversion phase where global ray state is unavailable; reduces scan conversion time significantly. Limitations: It is an approximation (conservative), so it may not terminate as many cells as an exact ERT check. The effectiveness depends on the opacity threshold and the distribution of opaque structures. When to Use: When using a scan conversion-based volume rendering method (like Cell-Projection) and parallel execution overhead prevents per-pixel ray state tracking. Origin: Introduced in the paper "Cell-projection Parallel Volume Rendering With Early Ray Termination" by Takeo Tomita et al. (2004). Context: Developed to address load imbalance in parallel volume rendering by applying ERT concepts to the scan conversion phase, which was previously difficult due to the lack of sequential ray accumulation state. Usage: Applied in distributed parallel volume rendering systems, specifically within the CP-PVR (Cell-Projection Parallel Volume Rendering) framework. PDF Cell-projection Parallel Volume Rendering With Early Ray Termination, http://www.tomitaken.org/project/papers/ReVolver/2004/VIIP.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Inference Ray Marching and Integration
head: Inference Ray Marching, Ray Marching for Inference, CUDA Ray Marching (Inference), Sparse Ray Marching (Inference), Ray Marching (CUDA Kernel)
body: Inference Ray Marching and Integration is a GPU-accelerated pipeline for real-time volume rendering inference, designed to generate images from trained neural radiance fields (NeRFs) or sparse density grids without gradient computation. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing sparse volumetric data to sample points and integrate radiance, utilizing density bitfields or occupancy grids for acceleration and early termination to maximize throughput. It differs from training-time marchers by disabling gradient flow, using fixed or pre-computed step sizes, and operating on pre-computed ray samples with strict early-termination logic to prioritize latency over optimization stability. It serves as the core rendering engine, bridging sparse ray traversal and final compositing. The method consists of two primary phases: Ray Marching (sampling) and Integration (compositing). The marching phase generates sample points along rays, skipping empty space using an acceleration structure. The integration phase evaluates the neural network at these points and accumulates color and depth. Inputs: rayso: Float array [N, 3], ray origins for N rays. raysd: Float array [N, 3], ray directions for N rays. near: Float array [N], near plane distances. far: Float array [N], far plane distances. densitybitfield: Uint8 array [CHHH // 8], hashed grid for density acceleration (Instant-NGP style). densitygrid: Float array [H, H, H], pre-computed 3D density grid for occupancy pruning (alternative to bitfield). meandensity: Float, average density value in the grid, used for step size estimation. bound: Float, scalar bounding box size (scene bounded in [-bound, bound]^3). dtgamma: Float, cone angle for exponential acceleration. If >0, accelerates marching but may reduce quality. Default 1/256. perturb: Bool or Int. If true (or int seed), adds jitter to sample positions for anti-aliasing. maxsteps: Int, maximum number of sampled points along each ray. Default 1024. align: Int, pad output size to multiple of align for memory alignment. Default -1 (disabled). densitythresh: Float, threshold for density grid to be considered occupied. Default 10. Outputs: xyzs: Float array [M, 3], 3D coordinates of sampled points. dirs: Float array [M, 3], ray directions corresponding to each sampled point. deltas: Float array [M, 2], two delta values per point: first for RGB contribution, second for depth contribution. image: Float array [N, 3], final rendered RGB image. depth: Float array [N, 1], final rendered depth image. Alive Ray Buffers: raysalive: Int array [N], IDs of currently alive rays. Only the first nalive entries are valid. rayst: Float array [N], current traversal position (t) along each ray. Output Tensors: xyzs, dirs, deltas: Pre-allocated zero tensors of shape [M, 3], [M, 3], [M, 2] respectively, where M is the total output size. Rendering State (for Integration): raysrgbd: Float array [N, 4], initialized to zeros, accumulates RGBA. raysT: Float array [N], initialized to ones, stores transmittance. rayscost: Float array [N], optional, initialized to zeros if cost rendering is enabled. 1. Initialization: Ensure rayso and raysd are contiguous on the CUDA device. Reshape rayso and raysd to [-1, 3]. Initialize raysalive with indices 0 to nalive - 1. Initialize rayst with near distances. Set nalive = N (total rays). If perturb is true, generate random noise [nalive] for jittering. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Loop while nalive > 0 and step count < maxsteps. Step Size Calculation: Calculate nstep per ray. A common heuristic is nstep = max(min(B N // nalive, 8), 1) where B is a batch factor, or use a fixed cap. If dtgamma > 0, apply exponential acceleration: step size decreases as rays progress, proportional to dt\gamma \times t. Output Size Calculation: Calculate total output size M = n\alive \times n\step. If align > 0, pad M to the next multiple of align: M \leftarrow M + (align - (M \% align)) \% align. CUDA Kernel Invocation: Call the backend kernel backend.marchrays (or equivalent) with parameters: nalive, nstep, raysalive, rayst, rayso, raysd, bound, densitybitfield (or densitygrid), C (hash grid channels), H (grid resolution), near, far, align, perturb, dtgamma, maxsteps. The kernel populates xyzs, dirs, and deltas for the active rays. Inside the kernel: For each alive ray, compute sample positions ti = t{current} + \Delta t. Query the density grid/bitfield at xyzi. If density < density\thresh, skip the point (empty space). If occupied, write xyzi, dir, and \Delta t to output buffers. Update rayst for the next step. Compaction: After the kernel, compact the list of alive rays. Rays that have reached far or exceeded maxsteps are removed from raysalive. Update nalive to the number of remaining active rays. 3. Integration (Compositing): Initialize raysrgbd to zeros, raysT to ones. Loop through the sampled points generated by the marching phase. For each sample point i along a ray: Evaluate the NeRF network at xyzi with stopgradient enabled to prevent backpropagation. Get density \sigmai and color ci. Compute weight wi = \sigmai \Delta ti \exp(-\sum{j<i} \sigmaj \Delta tj). Update transmittance: T{new} = T{old} \times (1 - wi). Accumulate color: C{ray} = C{ray} + ci \times wi. Accumulate depth: D{ray} = D{ray} + depthi \times wi. Early Termination: If T{ray} drops below a threshold (e.g., 0.01), terminate the ray early. Count terminated rays and update nalive for the next batch if processing in chunks. 4. Finalization: Split raysrgbd into RGB and depth buffers. Convert to final image formats (e.g., uint8). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inferenceraymarchingandintegration(rayso, raysd, near, far, densitybitfield, densitygrid, meandensity, bound, dtgamma, perturb, maxsteps, align, densitythresh): """ Main entry point for Inference Ray Marching and Integration. """ N = rayso.shape[0] nalive = N # Initialize alive ray buffers raysalive = torch.arange(N, dtype=torch.int32, device=rayso.device) rayst = near.clone() # Pre-allocate output buffers for marching # M is calculated dynamically, but we allocate a large buffer or resize per step # For clarity, we assume a loop that handles dynamic M xyzsall = [] dirsall = [] deltasall = [] stepcount = 0 while nalive > 0 and stepcount < maxsteps: # Calculate steps per ray for this iteration # Heuristic: distribute steps among alive rays nstep = max(min(8, 1024 // nalive), 1) # Calculate total output size M M = nalive nstep if align > 0: M += align - (M % align) # Allocate output tensors xyzs = torch.zeros((M, 3), dtype=torch.float32, device=rayso.device) dirs = torch.zeros((M, 3), dtype=torch.float32, device=rayso.device) deltas = torch.zeros((M, 2), dtype=torch.float32, device=rayso.device) # Call CUDA kernel # Note: In a real implementation, this calls backend.marchrays # The kernel modifies rayst and fills xyzs, dirs, deltas # It also returns the number of rays that are still alive after this step nalive = marchrayscudakernel( nalive=nalive, nstep=nstep, raysalive=raysalive, rayst=rayst, rayso=rayso, raysd=raysd, bound=bound, densitybitfield=densitybitfield, densitygrid=densitygrid, meandensity=meandensity, near=near, far=far, align=align, perturb=perturb, dtgamma=dtgamma, maxsteps=maxsteps, densitythresh=densitythresh, outxyzs=xyzs, outdirs=dirs, outdeltas=deltas) # Store results xyzsall.append(xyzs) dirsall.append(dirs) deltasall.append(deltas) stepcount += 1 # Concatenate all steps if xyzsall: xyzsall = torch.cat(xyzsall, dim=0) dirsall = torch.cat(dirsall, dim=0) deltasall = torch.cat(deltasall, dim=0) else: xyzsall = torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.float32, device=rayso.device) dirsall = torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.float32, device=rayso.device) deltasall = torch.empty((0, 2), dtype=torch.float32, device=rayso.device) # Integrate image, depth = integrateraysinference(rayso, raysd, xyzsall, dirsall, deltasall, near, far) return image, depth def integrateraysinference(rayso, raysd, xyzs, dirs, deltas, near, far): """ Integrate sampled points into final image and depth. """ N = rayso.shape[0] raysrgbd = torch.zeros((N, 4), dtype=torch.float32, device=rayso.device) # RGBA raysT = torch.ones(N, dtype=torch.float32, device=rayso.device) # Transmittance raysdepth = torch.zeros(N, dtype=torch.float32, device=rayso.device) # Group samples by ray # This requires mapping xyzs back to ray indices, which is typically done in the kernel or via sorting # For pseudocode, we assume a simplified loop over rays and their samples for i in range(N): # Get samples for ray i # In practice, this is done in parallel on GPU raysamples = getsamplesforray(i, xyzs, dirs, deltas, rayso[i], raysd[i]) T = raysT[i] color = raysrgbd[i,:3] depthacc = raysdepth[i] for sample in raysamples: xyz, dir, delta = sample # Evaluate NeRF with stopgradient sigma, rgb = evaluatenerf(xyz, dir, stopgradient=True) # Alpha alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) # Weight w = alpha T # Update color += rgb w depthacc += xyz.dot(dir) w # Approximate depth T = (1.0 - alpha) # Early termination if T < 0.01: break raysrgbd[i,:3] = color raysT[i] = T raysdepth[i] = depthacc image = raysrgbd[:,:3] depth = raysdepth.unsqueeze(1) return image, depth dtgamma: 1/256. maxsteps: 1024. densitythresh: 10. bound: 1.0. perturb: True. align: -1 (disabled). Precision: Use float32 for ray positions and densities to avoid accumulation errors. Empty Space: If the density grid is sparse, ensure the acceleration structure (bitfield/grid) correctly identifies empty regions to skip sampling. Boundary Conditions: Rays starting outside the bounding box or with near > far should be handled gracefully (e.g., skipped or rendered as background). Memory Alignment: Failing to align output sizes can cause CUDA kernel launch failures or performance degradation. The final rendering stage of the Inference Ray Marching and Integration pipeline, responsible for aggregating per-step volumetric properties (density, color, depth, ambient light, uncertainty) into final pixel buffers. It differs from training-time compositing by operating on pre-computed ray samples with strict early-termination logic to maximize throughput during real-time inference. body: Inference Ray Compositing is the final rendering stage of the Inference Ray Marching and Integration pipeline, responsible for aggregating per-step volumetric properties (density, color, depth, ambient light, uncertainty) into final pixel buffers. It differs from training-time compositing by operating on pre-computed ray samples with strict early-termination logic to maximize throughput during real-time inference. It serves as the bridge between the sparse ray marching results and the final image output, handling multiple output channels (RGB, depth, ambient, uncertainty) in parallel. Inputs: nalive: Integer, number of rays currently active (not terminated). nstep: Integer, maximum number of sampling steps per ray. raysalive: Boolean array [N], mask of active rays. rayst: Integer array [N], current step index for each ray. sigmas: Float array [M], volume densities at sampled points. rgbs: Float array [M, 3], RGB colors at sampled points. deltas: Float array [M, 2], step sizes (distances) between samples. weightssum: Float array [N], accumulated opacity (alpha) for each ray. depth: Float array [N], accumulated depth for each ray. image: Float array [N, 3], accumulated RGB color for each ray. Tthresh: Float, transparency threshold for early termination (default 10^{-2}). ambients: Float array [M, 3], ambient lighting contributions (optional, for ambient variant). uncertainties: Float array [M], uncertainty values (optional, for uncertainty variant). uncertaintysum: Float array [N], accumulated uncertainty (optional). ambientsum: Float array [N], accumulated ambient light (optional). Outputs: weightssum: Updated accumulated opacity. depth: Updated accumulated depth. image: Updated final RGB image. rayst: Updated step indices; set to -1 if terminated early, or final step count if completed. uncertaintysum: Updated accumulated uncertainty (optional). ambientsum: Updated accumulated ambient light (optional). The method operates on CUDA tensors. The layout is contiguous in memory. sigmas, deltas: Shape [M] and [M, 2] respectively, where M is the total number of samples across all alive rays. raysalive, rayst, weightssum, depth, image: Shape [N] or [N, 3], where N is the number of alive rays. Tthresh: Scalar float. The core compositing formula for each step i along a ray is: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \cdot \deltai) Ti = 1 - \sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj wi = \alphai \cdot Ti \text{weights\sum} \leftarrow \text{weights\sum} + wi \text{depth} \leftarrow \text{depth} + wi \cdot ti \text{image} \leftarrow \text{image} + wi \cdot \text{rgb}i Where: \sigmai is the density (sigmas[i]). \deltai is the step size (deltas[i]). ti is the distance of the current sample from the camera origin. Ti is the transmittance up to step i, calculated as 1 - \text{weights\sum} before adding the current weight. wi is the weight contributed by the current sample. For the ambient variant, the color equation includes an ambient term Ai: \text{image} \leftarrow \text{image} + wi \cdot (\text{rgb}i + Ai) And ambientsum accumulates wi \cdot Ai. For the uncertainty variant, uncertainty Ui is accumulated similarly: \text{uncertainty\sum} \leftarrow \text{uncertainty\sum} + wi \cdot Ui. Tthresh: Float, default 10^{-2}. Rays with transmittance T < T{thresh} are terminated early. 1. Initialization: Initialize weightssum, depth, and image to zero for all rays. Initialize rayst to 0. 2. Loop: For each step s from 0 to nstep - 1: a. Identify active rays using raysalive. b. For each active ray n: i. Retrieve \sigma, \text{rgb}, \delta for the current step s. ii. If \delta = 0, mark ray n as terminated (set rayst[n] = -1) and skip further processing for this ray. iii. Compute \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \delta). iv. Compute T = 1 - \text{weights\sum}[n]. v. Compute w = \alpha \cdot T. vi. Update \text{weights\sum}[n] \leftarrow \text{weights\sum}[n] + w. vii. Update \text{depth}[n] \leftarrow \text{depth}[n] + w \cdot t. viii. Update \text{image}[n] \leftarrow \text{image}[n] + w \cdot \text{rgb}. ix. If using ambient: Update \text{ambient\sum}[n] \leftarrow \text{ambient\sum}[n] + w \cdot \text{ambient} and add ambient to color. x. If using uncertainty: Update \text{uncertainty\sum}[n] \leftarrow \text{uncertainty\sum}[n] + w \cdot \text{uncertainty}. xi. If T < T{thresh}, mark ray n as terminated (set rayst[n] = -1) and skip further steps for this ray. c. If all rays are terminated, break loop. 3. Finalization: For rays that completed all nstep steps without early termination, set rayst[n] to the final step count. Write final weightssum, depth, and image to output buffers. Unverified code. Memory Layout: The input arrays sigmas, rgbs, deltas are typically flattened or structured to allow efficient GPU access. Misalignment can cause performance degradation. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot S) for storing intermediate ray samples, plus O(N) for accumulators. Performance: Highly optimized for GPU execution using CUDA kernels. Throughput scales with the number of alive rays and available GPU memory. Strengths: Real-time performance, supports multiple output channels (RGB, depth, ambient, uncertainty), efficient early termination. body: Sparse Ray Marching (Training) is a GPU-accelerated kernel designed to sample points along rays for the training phase of neural volume rendering, specifically within the Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (NGP) framework. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing a sparse, hashed density grid to identify occupied regions while minimizing global memory traffic. It distinguishes itself from inference marchers by supporting adaptive step sizes and perturbation for gradient-based optimization, and from static allocators by dynamically managing sample buffers based on occupancy thresholds. Inputs: raysalive: Array of active ray indices. rayst: Current distance along each ray. ox, oy, oz: Ray origins. dx, dy, dz: Ray directions. grid: Hashed density grid (resolution H \times H \times H). densitythresh: Threshold for occupancy. bound: Spatial extent of the grid. perturb: Boolean flag for jittering. dtmin, dtmax: Step size bounds. dtgamma: Step size scaling factor. nstep: Maximum steps per ray. nalive: Number of active rays. NTHREAD: Threads per CUDA block (typically 256). Outputs: xyz: Sampled coordinates. dir: Ray directions at samples. delta: Step sizes and cumulative distances. Data Structures: The density grid is stored as a 1D array of size H^3 (or hashed equivalent, but accessed via clamped indices in this specific implementation variant). Ray state is maintained in parallel arrays. Steps: 1. Initialize thread index n. If n \ge n\alive, return. 2. Load ray index from raysalive[n] and current distance t from rayst[n]. 3. If perturb is true, initialize a PCG32 random number generator with seed (n, \text{perturb}) and add dt\min \times \text{rng.next\float()} to t. 4. Loop while t < \text{far} and step count < n\step: a. Calculate current point (x,y,z) by clamping ox + t \cdot dx, oy + t \cdot dy, oz + t \cdot dz to [-\text{bound}, \text{bound}]. b. Map (x,y,z) to grid indices (nx, ny, nz) by clamping 0.5 \cdot (\text{coord} \cdot rbound + 1) \cdot H to [0, H-1], where rbound = 1/\text{bound}. c. Query grid density at index nx \cdot H^2 + ny \cdot H + nz. d. If density > \text{density\thresh}: i. Write xyz, dir, and delta to output buffers. ii. Calculate dt = \text{clamp}(t \cdot dt\gamma, dt\min, dt\max). iii. Update t \leftarrow t + dt. iv. Record delta[0] = dt and delta[1] = t - lastt. v. Update lastt = t. vi. Increment step and pointers. e. Else (empty space): i. Calculate distance to next voxel boundary in x, y, z using \text{signf}(dx), \text{signf}(dy), \text{signf}(dz). ii. Compute tt = t + \max(0, \min(tx, ty, tz)). iii. Advance t in a do-while loop until t \ge tt, using the same dt calculation as occupied space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Compute tt = t + max(0, min(tx, ty, tz))" # We assume tx, ty, tz are pre-calculated relative distances to the next grid plane intersection # Placeholder for exact boundary calculation logic not fully detailed in notes # Typically involves DDA (Digital Differential Analyzer) steps tt = t + max(0, min(tx, ty, tz)) while t < tt: dt = clamp(t dtgamma, dtmin, dtmax) t += dt Parameters: NTHREAD: 256. perturb: Boolean, enables jittering. bound: Spatial extent, inverse is rbound. H: Grid resolution. meandensity: Fallback threshold if specific function returns lower value. Edge Cases: Precision issues in boundary calculations for empty space traversal. Degenerate rays (zero direction) require handling to avoid division by zero in boundary calculations. It outputs sampled positions \mathbf{xyzs} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times n\step \times 3}, directions \mathbf{dirs} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times n\step \times 3}, and deltas \mathbf{deltas} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times n\step \times 2}, where the first delta channel stores RGB contribution weights and the second stores depth contributions. The density grid is accessed via a densitybitfield tensor of type uint8. Data Structures: The hashed density grid is stored in a uint8 tensor. The exact hashing function (e.g., hash table size, collision resolution) is not specified in the provided sources. The grid resolution is defined by resolution (a 3D vector) and a bounding box defined by bound. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each ray i \in [0, N), initialize the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{rays\o}[i] and accumulated transmittance T = 1.0. Initialize step counter k = 0. [G: Standard ray marching initialization]. 2. Ray Bounds: Determine the intersection interval [t{near}, t{far}] using \mathbf{near}[i] and \mathbf{far}[i]. [G: Clip ray segment to bounding box if necessary]. 3. Marching Loop: While t < t{far} and T > \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small threshold, e.g., 10^{-4}): a. Sampling: Compute the next sample position \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} + t \cdot \mathbf{rays\d}[i]. [G: Apply perturbation if enabled, as noted in definition]. b. Density Lookup: Query the hashed density grid at \mathbf{x} using densitybitfield. Let the retrieved density be \sigma.. c. Adaptive Step: Calculate step size \Delta t. The sources mention "adaptive step sizes" but do not provide the specific formula (e.g., based on density threshold or fixed grid spacing). [G: Typically \Delta t is derived from the grid resolution or density magnitude]. d. Accumulation: Compute opacity \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \Delta t). Update transmittance T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alpha). Store \Delta t in \mathbf{deltas}[i, k, 0] and \Delta t in \mathbf{deltas}[i, k, 1]. Store \mathbf{x} in \mathbf{xyzs}[i, k] and \mathbf{rays\d}[i] in \mathbf{dirs}[i, k]. e. Advance: t \leftarrow t + \Delta t, k \leftarrow k + 1. 4. Termination: If k \ge n\step, stop. [G: n\step is a maximum step count parameter]. Degenerate Input: Zero-length rays or invalid directions should be skipped or handled with a default value. [G: Check for zero direction vector]. body: The Ray Tracing Kernel is a CUDA kernel implementation for forward and backward ray tracing through a sparse grid volume, handling spherical harmonic (SH) evaluation and ray bounds. It serves as the core computational unit for the IDDR-NGP backend, enabling differentiable rendering by computing gradients alongside radiance accumulation. It distinguishes itself by organizing computation per-warp for SH evaluation and using shared memory for ray specification caching to minimize global memory traffic. Inputs and Outputs: Forward: Grid data, ray specifications (origin, direction), SH coefficients, temporary storage, and an output pointer for color/transmittance. Backward: Gradients of the output (gradoutput), cached color values, log transmittance, and loss terms (betaloss, sparsityloss) to compute gradients for the grid and SH coefficients. Data Structures: rayspec[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK]: Shared memory array storing ray origins and directions for all rays in the block. sphfuncval[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK][9]: Shared memory array storing spherical harmonic function values. The second dimension size is fixed at 9, implying a maximum of 2nd-order SH (9 coefficients). tempstorage[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK]: Temporary storage for warp-level reduction operations. Parameters: Warp Size: 32 threads. Lane ID: laneid = threadIdx.x & 0x1F. SH Data Dimension: grid.shdatadim. If laneid >= grid.shdatadim, the thread returns early. Block Size: Determined by TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK. Steps: 1. Initialization: Threads load ray specifications (origin, direction) into shared memory rayspec. 2. SH Evaluation: Threads compute spherical harmonic function values. If laneid < grid.shdatadim, compute calcsphfunc(grid, laneid, rayid, rayspec[rayblkid].dir, sphfuncval[rayblkid]). 3. Synchronization: Synchronize warps to ensure SH values are ready: syncwarp((1U << grid.shdatadim) - 1). 4. Ray Bounds: Find the intersection bounds of the ray with the sparse grid volume: rayfindbounds(rayspec[rayblkid], grid, opt, rayid). 5. Ray Tracing: Call the core tracing function traceraycuvol with the grid, ray spec, options, lane ID, SH values, temp storage, output pointer, and optional log transmit output. 6. Backward Pass: For gradients, the kernel takes gradoutput, colorcache, logtransmitin, betaloss, sparsityloss, and grads as inputs. name: Training Ray Marching (Forward Only)
body: Training Ray Marching is a specialized ray marching function designed to optimize the training phase of neural volume rendering by dynamically allocating memory for ray samples. It estimates the maximum number of points to allocate based on the mean sample count from previous training epochs, thereby avoiding the computational overhead of over-allocating memory while supporting a "force-all-rays" mode to ensure stability when estimates are insufficient. It differs from inference-only marchers by maintaining state (step counters) across iterations to adaptively tune memory usage, and from static allocation methods by using historical data to predict resource needs. The method prepares ray data for a CUDA backend kernel, dynamically sizing output buffers based on historical performance metrics to balance memory efficiency and correctness. Inputs: rayso: Origin positions, shape [N, 3]. raysd: Direction vectors, shape [N, 3]. densitygrid: 3D density grid, shape [H, H, H]. bound: Spatial boundary float (default 10^{-4}). meandensity: Mean density value float. iterdensity: Current iteration density value float. meancount: Estimated max points from previous epoch (int). perturb: Boolean flag for perturbation. forceallrays: Boolean flag to ignore meancount and process all rays. stepcounter: Optional int array [2] for tracking points/rays. align: Alignment padding value (int). Outputs: xyzs: Sample positions, shape [M, 3]. dirs: Sample directions, shape [M, 3]. deltas: Step sizes, shape [M]. rays: Ray metadata, shape [N, 3], dtype int32. Column 0: Ray ID. Column 1: Offset into xyzs/dirs/deltas. Column 2: Number of steps for that ray. rays: A contiguous integer array of shape [N, 3]. Each row i corresponds to ray i. The values are: rays[i, 0]: The index of the ray. rays[i, 1]: The starting index in the flattened output arrays (xyzs, dirs, deltas) where samples for this ray are stored. rays[i, 2]: The number of valid samples stored for this ray. stepcounter: An integer array of shape [2]. stepcounter[0]: Total number of points generated so far. stepcounter[1]: Number of rays processed. bound: Float, spatial boundary for ray marching. Default: 10^{-4}. meancount: Int, estimated maximum number of points. If > 0 and forceallrays is false, this overrides the default allocation size. forceallrays: Bool, if true, ignores meancount and ensures all rays are processed, preventing rays from being ignored due to underestimation. align: Int, if > 0, pads the allocated size M to the next multiple of align. 1. Reshape Inputs: Reshape rayso and raysd to contiguous views of shape [-1, 3]. 2. Determine Dimensions: Let N be the number of rays (rayso.shape[0]) and H be the grid resolution (densitygrid.shape[0]). 3. Initialize Default Allocation: Set M = N \times 1024 as the hardcoded default maximum number of points. 4. Adjust Allocation Size: If forceallrays is false and meancount > 0, set M = \text{mean\count}. If align > 0, pad M to the next multiple of align. 5. Initialize Output Tensors: Create xyzs as a zero tensor of shape [M, 3]. Create dirs as a zero tensor of shape [M, 3]. Create deltas as a zero tensor of shape [M]. 6. Initialize Rays Metadata: Create rays tensor of shape [N, 3] with dtype int32. 7. Initialize Step Counter: If stepcounter is None, initialize it as a zero tensor of shape [2] with dtype int32. 8. Execute Kernel: Call the CUDA backend kernel backend.marchraystrain with all parameters (rayso, raysd, densitygrid, bound, meandensity, iterdensity, stepcounter, meancount, perturb, forceallrays, align, xyzs, dirs, deltas, rays). 9. Retrieve Actual Count: If forceallrays is true or meancount \le 0: Retrieve the actual number of points m from stepcounter[0].item(). If align > 0, pad m to the next multiple of align. Slice xyzs, dirs, and deltas to size m. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marchraystrain( rayso, raysd, densitygrid, bound, meandensity, iterdensity, stepcounter=None, meancount=0, perturb=False, forceallrays=False, align=0): # 1. Reshape inputs to contiguous views rayso = rayso.contiguous().view(-1, 3) raysd = raysd.contiguous().view(-1, 3) # 2. Get dimensions N = rayso.shape[0] H = densitygrid.shape[0] # 3. Initialize default M M = N 1024 # 4. Adjust M based on meancount and forceallrays if not forceallrays and meancount > 0: M = meancount # Pad M if align > 0 if align > 0: M = ((M + align - 1) // align) align # 5. Initialize output tensors xyzs = torch.zeros((M, 3), dtype=rayso.dtype, device=rayso.device) dirs = torch.zeros((M, 3), dtype=rayso.dtype, device=rayso.device) deltas = torch.zeros((M,), dtype=rayso.dtype, device=rayso.device) # 6. Initialize rays metadata rays = torch.zeros((N, 3), dtype=torch.int32, device=rayso.device) # 7. Initialize stepcounter if None if stepcounter is None: stepcounter = torch.zeros((2,), dtype=torch.int32, device=rayso.device) # 8. Call CUDA backend kernel # Note: The exact signature of backend.marchraystrain is implementation-specific. # It modifies xyzs, dirs, deltas, rays, and stepcounter in-place. backend.marchraystrain( rayso, raysd, densitygrid, bound, meandensity, iterdensity, stepcounter, meancount, perturb, forceallrays, align, xyzs, dirs, deltas, rays) # 9. Slice outputs if forceallrays or meancount <= 0 if forceallrays or meancount <= 0: m = stepcounter[0].item() if align > 0: m = ((m + align - 1) // align) align xyzs = xyzs[:m] dirs = dirs[:m] deltas = deltas[:m] return xyzs, dirs, deltas, rays, stepcounter Underestimation: If meancount underestimates the required points and forceallrays is false, rays may be randomly ignored, leading to incomplete rendering or training artifacts. Precision: The method relies on the CUDA backend's precision for ray-grid intersection calculations. Ensure the backend handles floating-point comparisons consistently with the host logic. Alignment: If align is not a power of two or does not match memory alignment requirements of the GPU, performance may degrade. The sources do not specify the optimal align value. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of rays and K is the average number of steps per ray. The dynamic allocation reduces memory allocation overhead compared to static large buffers. Memory Complexity: O(M), where M is the allocated number of points. M is typically N \times 1024 or meancount, whichever is larger. Performance: Faster training due to reduced memory allocation and deallocation overhead. The use of meancount allows for tighter memory bounds, reducing cache misses. Strengths: Adaptive memory usage, stability with forceallrays, efficient for training loops where ray sample counts are relatively stable. Limitations: Requires historical data (meancount) to be effective. If scene complexity changes drastically, meancount may become inaccurate, requiring forceallrays or manual tuning. When to Use: During training of neural volume rendering models where memory efficiency is critical and ray sample counts are predictable. When Not to Use: During inference where deterministic behavior is required without historical state, or when scene complexity varies wildly between frames. Training Ray Marching is part of the optimization strategies for neural radiance fields (NeRF) and related volume rendering techniques. It was introduced in the context of efficient training pipelines, specifically within the Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (NGP) framework and its derivatives. The method addresses the bottleneck of memory allocation in ray marching kernels during the iterative training process. megvii-research/cv-master-ex, https://github.com/megvii-research/cv-master-ex, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Chunked Volume Rendering
head: VolumeRendererChunk
body: Chunked Volume Rendering is a memory-management technique for image-order volume rendering that processes rays in fixed-size batches (chunks) to bound GPU memory usage during inference. It solves the problem of out-of-memory errors when rendering high-resolution images or large ray bundles by decoupling the total ray count from the per-forward-pass memory footprint. It differs from Sparse Ray Marching (Training), which optimizes sampling density during training, and Inference Ray Compositing, which focuses on the compositing logic itself; Chunked Volume Rendering specifically addresses the batching of the entire ray processing pipeline. Inputs: raybundle: A tensor containing ray origins and directions, with shape (N, 3) for origins and (N, 3) for directions, where N is the total number of rays. chunksize: An integer specifying the maximum number of rays to process in a single forward pass. sampler: An object or function responsible for generating sample points along rays. implicitfn: A function (e.g., a neural radiance field query) that returns density and color at given 3D coordinates. Outputs: feature: A concatenated tensor of rendered features (e.g., RGB, opacity) for all N rays. depth: A concatenated tensor of depth values for all N rays. chunkfeatures: A list of tensors, where each tensor holds the feature output for one chunk. chunkdepths: A list of tensors, where each tensor holds the depth output for one chunk. 1. Initialize empty lists chunkfeatures and chunkdepths. 2. Determine the total number of rays N from raybundle.origins.shape[0]. 3. Iterate over the range of rays in steps of chunksize: For each chunkstart in range(0, N, self.chunksize): a. Slice the raybundle to extract rays for the current chunk: \text{cur\ray\bundle} = \text{ray\bundle}[\text{chunk\start}: \text{chunk\start} + \text{self.chunk\size}] b. Call the parent class's forward method (e.g., from Inference Ray Marching and Integration) to process this subset: \text{cur\feature}, \text{cur\depth} = \text{super().forward}(\text{sampler}, \text{implicit\fn}, \text{cur\ray\bundle}) c. Append curfeature to chunkfeatures and curdepth to chunkdepths. 4. Concatenate all chunk outputs along dimension 0: \text{feature} = \text{torch.cat}(\text{chunk\features}, \text{dim}=0) \text{depth} = \text{torch.cat}(\text{chunk\depths}, \text{dim}=0) 5. Return feature and depth. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forward(self, sampler, implicitfn, raybundle): # Initialize storage for chunk results chunkfeatures = [] chunkdepths = [] # Get total number of rays N = raybundle.origins.shape[0] # Process rays in chunks for chunkstart in range(0, N, self.chunksize): # Slice the current chunk of rays endindex = min(chunkstart + self.chunksize, N) curraybundle = raybundle[chunkstart:endindex] # Process the chunk using the parent implementation # The parent handles sampling, querying, and compositing for these rays curfeature, curdepth = super().forward(sampler, implicitfn, curraybundle) # Store results chunkfeatures.append(curfeature) chunkdepths.append(curdepth) # Concatenate all chunk results to form the full output feature = torch.cat(chunkfeatures, dim=0) depth = torch.cat(chunkdepths, dim=0) return feature, depth chunksize: Integer. The maximum number of rays processed in a single forward pass. Typical values are not explicitly defined in the primary source, but it is chosen to fit within available GPU memory. Memory Limits: If chunksize is too large, the forward pass may exceed GPU memory, causing an OOM error. If too small, overhead from repeated kernel launches may reduce performance. Boundary Conditions: The slicing logic must handle the last chunk, which may contain fewer rays than chunksize. The pseudocode uses min(chunkstart + self.chunksize, N) to ensure no out-of-bounds access. Concatenation Order: Results must be concatenated in the same order as the input rays to maintain spatial correspondence. The loop iterates sequentially, ensuring this order. A variant that integrates an Occupancy Grid Estimator to prune empty space before rendering. It reshapes ray origins and view directions from (H, W, 3) to (N, 3), then iterates over chunks. For each chunk, it defines a density query function (sigmafn) that samples the radiance field at midpoints between tstarts and tends. It calls estimator.sampling with parameters nearplane, farplane, renderstepsize, stratified, coneangle, and alphathre to obtain occupied ray indices and depth intervals. Finally, it composites RGB, opacity, and depth using these intervals and concatenates results. This approach reduces computation by skipping empty regions. Parameters include nearplane=0.0, farplane=1e10, renderstepsize=1e-3, coneangle=0.0, alphathre=0.0, and testchunksize=8192. During training, chunksize is set to max int32 to process all rays at once, while inference uses testchunksize. An opt-in feature for chunked volume rendering that replaces linear interpolation with tricubic B-spline reconstruction to reduce texel staircase artifacts. It requires a 2-voxel halo around chunks to function correctly. The implementation adds constants LINEARMINHALO and CUBICMINHALO to the chunking logic. The NVChunkedVolume.raiseHaloTo() method re-plans loaded volumes when the halo size changes. Cubic interpolation is gated per draw on two conditions: the halo size must be \ge 2 and the volume must not be a label volume (including coarse-floor cubes). The parameter volumeIsCubicInterpolation is a boolean, defaulting to off, and is available on both backends. The public default halo remains [1,1,1]. A bug fix for WebGL2 chunked volume rendering where the volume would blank out when chunk 0 was evicted from the cache. The root cause was an early return in the draw() function when volumeTexture or volumeGradientTexture was null. For chunked volumes, these textures are best-effort aliases of chunk 0, so evicting chunk 0 caused a silent failure. The fix removes the early return on null textures for chunked volumes. It also fixes swapChunkedVolumePlan to refresh aliases after manager.remap() destroys unmatched chunks, and prevents the single-volume path from deleting textures still owned by the chunked cache entry when switching from chunked to single volume. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of rays, as each ray is processed exactly once. The constant factor depends on the overhead of chunking and concatenation, which is negligible compared to the ray marching cost. Memory Complexity: O(C \cdot M), where C is the chunksize and M is the memory required to process one ray (including intermediate buffers for sampling and compositing). This is significantly lower than the O(N \cdot M) required for unchunked rendering. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays, but memory usage is bounded by chunksize. Strengths: Prevents out-of-memory errors on high-resolution images or large ray bundles. Allows rendering on hardware with limited VRAM. Limitations: Introduces slight overhead from chunk management and concatenation. Requires tuning chunksize for optimal performance. When to use: When rendering high-resolution volumes or large ray bundles that exceed available GPU memory. When not to use: When memory is abundant and the overhead of chunking is undesirable, or when the ray count is small enough to fit in memory without chunking. Chunked Volume Rendering was introduced in the context of neural volume rendering pipelines to enable inference on high-resolution images. It is part of a broader effort to make neural rendering methods practical for real-time or near-real-time applications by managing memory efficiently. The method builds on Inference Ray Marching and Integration, which provides the core ray processing logic. body: Spatiotemporal importance sampling is a strategy for adaptive sampling in volume rendering that assigns higher sampling probabilities to pixels occluded by tools or exhibiting extensive motion, while assigning lower probabilities to stationary tissues. It solves the problem of inefficient training and poor reconstruction quality in surgical scenes where tool occlusion leads to infrequent representation of tissue pixels, and stationary tissues cause redundant training updates. Unlike uniform sampling, it addresses the varying learning difficulty across pixels, thereby speeding up convergence and improving the rendering quality of occluded areas. Inputs: A sequence of T rendered frames (or training images) \{Ii\}{i=1}^T. A sequence of binary tool masks \{Mi\}{i=1}^T, where Mi indicates the presence of a tool in frame i. Hyper-parameters: \alpha (lower-bound for weights), \beta (balance factor), n (temporal window radius). Outputs: A sequence of sampling weight maps \{Wi\}{i=1}^T, where each Wi contains the sampling probability for each pixel/ray in frame i. Data Structures: Ii: Image tensor of shape (H, W, C), where H, W are height and width, and C is channels (typically 3 for RGB). Mi: Binary mask tensor of shape (H, W), values \{0, 1\}. Wi: Weight map tensor of shape (H, W), values \in [\alpha, \infty). \Omegai: Occlusion frequency scaling map of shape (H, W). Steps: 1. Calculate Temporal Differences: For each frame i, compute the temporal difference with respect to its neighbors within a window of size n. The difference is calculated on the tool-occluded regions of the images. 2. Compute Occlusion Frequency Scaling (\Omegai): Calculate the frequency of tool occlusion for each pixel across the entire sequence. 3. So it must be per-pixel L1? # || x ||1 for a vector is sum(|x|). # If Ii is (H,W,3), Ii o Mi is (H,W,3). # The difference is (H,W,3). # L1 norm of a (H,W,3) tensor? # If it's a scalar, Wi would be scalar. But Wi is a map. # So it must be per-pixel. # Per-pixel L1: sum over channels. diffperpixel = np.abs(Iimasked - Ijmasked) # Sum over channels (axis=2) diffsum = np.sum(diffperpixel, axis=2) / 3.0 diffs.append(diffsum) # Max over neighbors if diffs: maxdiff = np.max(diffs, axis=0) # Shape (H, W) else: maxdiff = np.zeros((H, W)) # 2. Compute Occlusion Frequency Scaling Omegai # Omegai = beta (T Mi) / sum(Mi) # Handle division by zero denom = totalocclusioncount # Avoid division by zero denomsafe = np.where(denom == 0, 1, denom) omega = beta (T M[i]) / denomsafe # 3. Combine # Formula: min(maxdiff, alpha) omega # Note: Text says alpha is lower bound. Formula says min. # Implementing formula as written. rawweight = np.minimum(maxdiff, alpha) omega # 4. Apply lower bound? # Text says alpha avoids zero weight. # If rawweight is 0, it stays 0. # To follow text intent: # rawweight = np.maximum(rawweight, alpha) # But this might conflict with the min(alpha) step. # Given the ambiguity, we stick to the formula structure but # acknowledge the text description. # Let's assume the formula meant: max(min(maxdiff, cap), alpha) # But no cap is given. # We will output the formula result. Wmaps.append(rawweight) return Wmaps Time Complexity: O(T \cdot H \cdot W \cdot n), where T is the number of frames, H, W are image dimensions, and n is the temporal window radius. The calculation involves iterating over frames and neighbors, computing L1 differences, and aggregating weights. Memory Complexity: O(T \cdot H \cdot W) to store the input frames, masks, and output weight maps. Strengths: Improves convergence speed and rendering quality for occluded tissues in surgical scenes by prioritizing difficult-to-learn pixels. Reduces redundant training on stationary tissues. Limitations: Requires accurate binary masks for tool occlusion. Performance depends on the choice of hyper-parameters \alpha and \beta. The formula's handling of zero weights and occlusion frequency scaling contains ambiguities that may require tuning. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic scenes with significant tool occlusion, such as robotic surgery, where uniform sampling leads to poor reconstruction of occluded areas. When not to use: For static scenes without occlusion, or when tool masks are unavailable. Spatiotemporal importance sampling was introduced in the context of efficient deformable tissue reconstruction in surgical scenes. It addresses the challenges posed by tool occlusion and stationary tissue redundancy, which exacerbate learning complexity and reduce efficiency in neural radiance field (NeRF) based reconstruction. The method draws inspiration from EndoNeRF. It was proposed in "Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction via Orthogonal Neural Plane". name: Adaptive Undersampling
head: Fast Adaptive Undersampling, Two-pass Adaptive Undersampling with Pre-computed Intervals
body: Adaptive Undersampling accelerates volume rendering by replacing the full volume integral calculation for a subset of pixels with interpolation, while storing pre-computed integral values over fixed intervals to allow partial recomputation for pixels where interpolation is inaccurate. It differs from standard adaptive undersampling methods that use recursive block division (which are inefficient on GPUs) by employing a fixed two-pass approach with pre-computed intervals, ensuring only necessary intervals are integrated on the second pass. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: 3D volume texture (unit cube), transfer function f, viewport resolution, block size n, maximum number of intervals M. Outputs: Final image (pixel colors). Data Structures G-buffer: Contains M+1 parallel textures (or arrays) with resolution \frac{W}{n} \times \frac{H}{n} (where W, H are viewport dimensions). Texture 0 (G[0]): Stores the final composited color C (4-component vector: RGB + Transparency A) for the representative pixel of each n \times n block. Textures 1 \dots M (G[1] \dots G[M]): Store the volume integral values Ii for each of the M equal-length intervals. Each Ii is a 4-component vector containing the color and transparency contribution of that interval. Note: The last interval may have a different length if the ray exits the volume early. Parameters n: Side length of the square blocks. One pixel is processed per n \times n block in Pass 1. M: User-selected maximum number of equal-length intervals into which the integration domain is divided. Algorithm Steps 1. Pass 1: Pre-computation For each n \times n block in the viewport: 1. Select one representative pixel (e.g., top-left). 2. Determine the ray starting point s and final point f. 3. Find the starting point v of the non-zero transfer function domain using GetDistanceForStart(s, f). If GetDistanceForStart returns -1 (no intersection with non-zero domain), skip this pixel or mark as empty. Otherwise, v is the point where the ray first meets the domain where f is not zero. 4. Calculate the interval length L. Since samples are in a unit cube, the maximum ray length is \sqrt{3}. The length of each of the M equal intervals is L = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{M}. 5. Initialize composited color C = (0,0,0,0) and transparency A = 0. 6. Initialize interval integrals Ii = (0,0,0,0) for i = 0 \dots M-1. 7. Perform volume integration along the ray from v to f, divided into M intervals of length L. For each interval i, compute the integral Ii using the compositing recurrence relation (see Formulas). Store Ii in G[i+1]. 8. Handle the last interval: If the ray exits the volume before completing the M-th equal interval, the last interval is shorter. Calculate this partial integral separately and store it. 9. Store the final composited color C in G[0]. 2. Pass 2: Interpolation and Partial Recomputation For each pixel P not processed in Pass 1: 1. Identify the four neighboring pixels N0, N1, N2, N3 that were processed in Pass 1 (their coordinates correspond to the n \times n blocks surrounding P). 2. Check if the colors of the adjacent pixels are sufficiently close. If yes, interpolate the current pixel's color CP bilinearly from the C values in G[0] of the neighbors. If no, calculate CP using the recurrence relation, leveraging the pre-computed interval integrals Ii from the neighbors. Let Ai^ and Ci^ be the transparency and color contributions for interval i. If the neighbor's interval integral is close enough, use the interpolated Ai^, Ci^. Otherwise, calculate the integral for that specific interval using the recurrence relation starting from the previous interval's result. The recurrence relation for interval i is: C{i+1} = Ci + (1 - Ai) \cdot ai \cdot ci A{i+1} = Ai + (1 - Ai) \cdot ai Where ai, ci are the sample transparency and color. In the context of the interval integrals Ii, these are treated as the accumulated contributions for that segment. Specifically, for the second pass calculation: CP{i+1} = CPi + (1 - APi) \cdot Ai^ \cdot Ci^ AP{i+1} = APi + (1 - APi) \cdot Ai^ for 0 \le i \le M-1. Here Ai^ and Ci^ are either interpolated or recomputed. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getdistanceforstart(s, f, transferfunction): """ Finds the distance from start point s to the first point v where the transfer function is non-zero. Returns -1 if no such point is found along the ray segment s->f. """ # Implementation depends on specific ray-marching or intersection logic. # For the purpose of this article, we assume this function exists # and returns the 3D coordinate v or a distance value. pass def compositingstep(Cprev, Aprev, asample, csample): """ Standard front-to-back compositing step. """ Cnew = Cprev + (1.0 - Aprev) asample csample Anew = Aprev + (1.0 - Aprev) asample return Cnew, Anew def pass1render(voxeldata, transferfunction, viewportw, viewporth, n, M): """ First pass: Render representative pixels and pre-compute interval integrals. """ # G-buffer textures # G[0] stores final color C (RGBA) # G[1..M] store interval integrals Ii (RGBA) gbuffercolor = createtexture(viewportw // n, viewporth // n, channels=4) gbufferintervals = [createtexture(viewportw // n, viewporth // n, channels=4) for in range(M)] maxraylength = 1.73205080757 # sqrt(3) intervallength = maxraylength / M for blocky in range(0, viewporth, n): for blockx in range(0, viewportw, n): # Select one pixel per block (e.g., top-left) pixelx = blockx pixely = blocky # Get ray origin and direction for this pixel rayorigin, raydirection = getrayforpixel(pixelx, pixely) # Find start of non-zero transfer function domain startpointv = getdistanceforstart(rayorigin, raydirection, transferfunction) if startpointv == -1: # No non-zero domain intersection continue # Initialize compositing variables currentcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentalpha = 0.0 # Integrate over M intervals for i in range(M): # Determine interval bounds # Note: The source implies intervals are equal length sqrt(3)/M # in texture space. We march along the ray. # Sample the volume along this interval # This involves marching from current position to current position + intervallength # Accumulate the integral for this interval intervalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) intervalalpha = 0.0 # Marching loop for the interval #... (standard volume integration steps)... # For each sample in the interval: # val = samplevolume(voxeldata, samplepos) # a, c = transferfunction(val) # intervalcolor, intervalalpha = compositingstep(intervalcolor, intervalalpha, a, c) # Store interval integral gbufferintervals[i][blocky // n, blockx // n] = (intervalcolor, intervalalpha) # Update global compositing state currentcolor, currentalpha = compositingstep(currentcolor, currentalpha, intervalalpha, intervalcolor) # Check if ray has exited volume (alpha is 0 or position > end) if currentalpha <= 0.0: break # Handle last interval if it was shorter (ray exited early) # This is handled implicitly by the loop break, but the last stored # interval might need adjustment if the source specifies separate handling. # The source mentions a 'lastStep' calculation for the shorter last interval. # Store final color gbuffercolor[blocky // n, blockx // n] = (currentcolor, currentalpha) return gbuffercolor, gbufferintervals def pass2render(gbuffercolor, gbufferintervals, viewportw, viewporth, n, M): """ Second pass: Interpolate or partially recompute for remaining pixels. """ finalimage = createtexture(viewportw, viewporth, channels=4) for y in range(viewporth): for x in range(viewportw): # Skip pixels processed in Pass 1 if x % n == 0 and y % n == 0: continue # Identify 4 neighboring blocks # Neighbors are at (x//n, y//n), (x//n+1, y//n), etc. # Need to map current pixel to the 4 surrounding G-buffer texels neighborindices = getneighborblockindices(x, y, n) # Check if neighbors' colors are sufficiently close neighborcolors = [gbuffercolor[idx] for idx in neighborindices] issimilar = checkcolorsimilarity(neighborcolors) if issimilar: # Bilinear interpolation of color finalimage[y, x] = bilinearinterpolate(gbuffercolor, x, y, n) else: # Partial recomputation # Start with zero currentcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentalpha = 0.0 for i in range(M): # Get interval integral from neighbors # Interpolate or pick from neighbors intervalval = interpolateinterval(gbufferintervals[i], neighborindices, x, y, n) # If interpolation accuracy is insufficient, recompute this specific interval # This requires re-marching the ray for just this interval segment # For simplicity, we assume intervalval is the (a, c) for this interval ai, ci = intervalval currentcolor, currentalpha = compositingstep(currentcolor, currentalpha, ai, ci) if currentalpha <= 0.0: break finalimage[y, x] = (currentcolor, currentalpha) return finalimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls Woodgrain Artifacts: Caused by high derivatives of the opacity function near the ray start. Mitigated by finding the starting point v where the transfer function becomes non-zero, rather than starting at the ray origin. This increases the probability that the first integrals I0 coincide on adjacent rays. Last Interval Length: The last interval of integration may be shorter than the others because the ray may exit the volume before completing the M-th equal interval. This is handled by a separate 'lastStep' calculation. GPU Efficiency: Recursive block division is inefficient on GPUs due to concurrent processing groups. This method avoids that overhead by using a fixed two-pass approach. This method accelerates volume integral calculation by partitioning the ray integration interval into M equal pieces and using a second pass to interpolate or recompute integrals for pixels based on neighborhood coherence. It builds on Adaptive Undersampling by increasing the undersampling factor through interval partitioning, allowing pixels to reuse integral data from neighbors rather than integrating over the entire ray. Unlike standard adaptive undersampling, it explicitly manages the granularity of integration steps to balance interpolation accuracy against recomputation cost. Performance: Accelerates adaptive undersampling by a factor of 1.5 on average. In a real dataset example, 91.7% of pixels were interpolated, 5.7% required 1 interval calculation, 2.1% required 2, 0.1% required 3, and 0.4% required >3 intervals. Memory: Requires a G-buffer with M+1 textures of resolution \frac{W}{n} \times \frac{H}{n}. Strengths: Avoids the overhead of recursive subdivision on GPUs; reduces the length of the interval of integration for most pixels; mitigates woodgrain artifacts. Limitations: Effectiveness depends on the number of intervals M being relatively small; requires two passes; interpolation accuracy may be insufficient in regions with high frequency changes. Adaptive undersampling is a method for accelerating the rendering process by replacing the calculation of a volume integral with an interpolation procedure for a number of pixels. The specific two-pass method with pre-computed intervals was proposed in. It builds on earlier work such as [KSK16] and [BSSS18] which examined methods for excluding artifacts, and [L15] which used a two-pass algorithm for GPU efficiency. The method is particularly useful for high-resolution screens and devices with low computing power.
