name: NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling)
head: NeRF Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering (NeRF), NeRF Ray Marching, Standard NeRF Rendering, NeRF Two-Stage Sampling, NeRF Coarse-to-Fine Rendering, NeRF Rendering (Coarse and Fine), NeRF Fine Sampling and Rendering
body: NeRF Volumetric Rendering synthesizes novel views by querying a neural radiance field (a coordinate MLP) along camera rays and accumulating outputs using differentiable volume rendering. It solves the view synthesis problem by optimizing a continuous 5D function (spatial location and viewing direction) to predict volume density and view-dependent color. Unlike single-stage uniform sampling, this method employs a two-stage hierarchical sampling strategy: a coarse network estimates density to guide finer sampling in high-density regions, reducing aliasing and improving geometric detail. It operates on a flat batch of rays rather than a spatial grid, enabling efficient training on randomly sampled rays. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, tensor of shape [R, 3]. raysd: Unnormalized ray directions (Blender convention: camera looks down -z), tensor of shape [R, 3]. near, far: Near and far clipping plane distances along the ray, scalars or tensors of shape [R, 1]. coarsemodel, finemodel: Two neural networks with identical architecture but independent weights. nsamples: Number of coarse samples per ray (default 64). Nimportance: Number of additional fine samples to add (default 0 or 128 depending on implementation). perturb: Boolean flag to enable stratified sampling jittering (default True). whitebackground: Boolean flag to composite over white background (default True for Blender dataset). Outputs: rgb: Rendered color, shape [R, 3]. depth: Weighted average depth, shape [R]. acc: Total accumulated opacity, shape [R]. Data Structures: The neural field maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma, using positional encoding. Samples are stored as z-values along the ray parameter t. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization and Coarse Sampling: Generate linearly spaced depths t{vals} \in [0, 1] of size n{samples}. Map to world space near/far bounds: z{vals} = \text{near} \cdot (1 - t{vals}) + \text{far} \cdot t{vals} Shape: [R, n{samples}]. If perturb is True, apply stratified sampling: Compute midpoints: mids = 0.5 \cdot (z{vals}[:, 1:] + z{vals}[:,:-1]). Define intervals: lower = [z{vals}[:, 0], mids], upper = [mids, z{vals}[:, -1]]. Jitter: z{vals} = lower + (upper - lower) \cdot \text{rand}(R, n{samples}). 2. Coarse Network Query: Compute 3D points: \mathbf{pts} = \text{rays\o} + \text{rays\d} \cdot z{vals}. Flatten points to [-1, 3] and query coarsemodel to get raw RGB \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Reshape outputs to [R, n{samples}, 3] and [R, n{samples}]. 3. Coarse Rendering (Alpha Compositing): Compute segment distances \delta: \deltai = (z{vals, i+1} - z{vals, i}) \cdot \|\text{rays\d}\| Append a large value (10^{10}) for the last segment to ensure termination. Compute alpha using softplus activation on density: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\text{softplus}(\sigmai) \cdot \deltai). Add epsilon (10^{-10}) to (1-\alpha) before cumulative product for stability. Compute transmittance T (exclusive cumulative product): Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj + \epsilon). Compute weights: wi = Ti \cdot \alphai. Render coarse maps: C{coarse} = \sum wi \mathbf{c}i, \quad D{coarse} = \sum wi z{i}, \quad A{coarse} = \sum wi. 4. Fine Sampling (Hierarchical): Use coarse weights to guide finer sampling. Exclude the first weight (index 0) as it corresponds to the start of the ray. Add epsilon (10^{-5}) to weights and normalize to form a probability distribution. Compute CDF from weights, prepend zero. Sample N{importance} values from a uniform distribution and use inverse CDF sampling to draw from the coarse weight distribution. Detach z{fine} from the computation graph to prevent gradient flow to the coarse network. 5. Interleaving and Fine Network Query: Concatenate coarse z{vals} and fine z{fine}, then sort them to interleave samples. Compute new 3D points \mathbf{pts}{all} from sorted z-values. Flatten and query finemodel to get \mathbf{c}{fine} and \sigma{fine}. 6. Fine Rendering: Recompute distances \delta and alphas \alpha for the sorted samples using the fine network outputs. Compute new weights wi and transmittance Ti. Render final maps: C{final} = \sum wi \mathbf{c}i. If whitebackground is True, add background contribution: C{final} = C{final} + (1 - A{final}) \cdot \mathbf{1}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def softplus(x): return nn.functional.softplus(x) def renderrays(rayso, raysd, near, far, coarsemodel, finemodel, nsamples=64, Nimportance=128, perturb=True, whitebackground=True, epsilonalpha=1e-10, epsilonweight=1e-5): """ Renders rays using NeRF coarse-to-fine sampling. Args: rayso: [R, 3] Ray origins raysd: [R, 3] Ray directions (unnormalized) near: [R, 1] Near plane distances far: [R, 1] Far plane distances coarsemodel: Neural network returning (color, density) finemodel: Neural network returning (color, density) nsamples: int Number of coarse samples Nimportance: int Number of fine samples perturb: bool Enable stratified sampling whitebackground: bool Composite over white epsilonalpha: float Epsilon for alpha stability epsilonweight: float Epsilon for weight normalization Returns: rgb: [R, 3] depth: [R] acc: [R] """ R = rayso.shape[0] # 1. Coarse Sampling tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nsamples, device=rayso.device) zvals = near (1.0 - tvals) + far tvals # [R, nsamples] if perturb: mids = 0.5 (zvals[:, 1:] + zvals[:,:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, zvals[:, -1:]], dim=-1) lower = torch.cat([zvals[:,:1], mids], dim=-1) randomvals = torch.randlike(zvals) zvals = lower + (upper - lower) randomvals # 2. Coarse Network Query ptscoarse = rayso[:, None,:] + raysd[:, None,:] zvals[:,:, None] # [R, nsamples, 3] ptsflat = ptscoarse.reshape(-1, 3) dirsflat = raysd[:, None,:].expand(ptscoarse.shape).reshape(-1, 3) coarseout = coarsemodel(ptsflat, dirsflat) ccoarse = coarseout[0].reshape(R, nsamples, 3) sigmacoarse = coarseout[1].reshape(R, nsamples) # 3. Coarse Rendering dists = zvals[:, 1:] - zvals[:,:-1] # [R, nsamples-1] dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.full((R, 1), 1e10, device=rayso.device)], dim=-1) # [R, nsamples] dists = dists torch.norm(raysd, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # [R, nsamples] alphacoarse = 1.0 - torch.exp(-softplus(sigmacoarse) dists) # Transmittance: exclusive cumprod ones = torch.oneslike(alphacoarse[:,:1]) Tcoarse = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([ones, 1.0 - alphacoarse + epsilonalpha], dim=-1), dim=-1)[:,:-1] weightscoarse = Tcoarse alphacoarse rgbcoarse = torch.sum(weightscoarse[:,:, None] ccoarse, dim=1) acccoarse = torch.sum(weightscoarse, dim=1) depthcoarse = torch.sum(weightscoarse zvals, dim=1) # 4. Fine Sampling # Use weights from index 1 to nsamples-1 (excluding first bin start) weightsfine = weightscoarse[:, 1:] + epsilonweight weightsfine = weightsfine / (torch.sum(weightsfine, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + epsilonweight) # CDF cdf = torch.cumsum(weightsfine, dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[:,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # Sample from uniform distribution u = torch.rand(R, Nimportance, device=rayso.device) # Inverse CDF Sampling indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, right=True) belowindices = torch.clamp(indices - 1, min=0) aboveindices = torch.clamp(indices, max=cdf.shape[-1] - 1) cdfbelow = torch.gather(cdf, 1, belowindices) cdfabove = torch.gather(cdf, 1, aboveindices) # Use mids for bin interpolation midsfine = 0.5 (zvals[:, 1:] + zvals[:,:-1]) zbelow = torch.gather(midsfine, 1, belowindices) zabove = torch.gather(midsfine, 1, aboveindices) denom = cdfabove - cdfbelow + epsilonweight t = (u - cdfbelow) / denom zfine = zbelow + t (zabove - zbelow) # Detach to stop gradient flow to coarse model zfine = zfine.detach() # 5. Interleave and Fine Query zall = torch.cat([zvals, zfine], dim=-1) zall, = torch.sort(zall, dim=-1) ptsall = rayso[:, None,:] + raysd[:, None,:] zall[:,:, None] ptsflatall = ptsall.reshape(-1, 3) dirsflatall = raysd[:, None,:].expand(ptsall.shape).reshape(-1, 3) fineout = finemodel(ptsflatall, dirsflatall) cfine = fineout[0].reshape(R, zall.shape[-1], 3) sigmafine = fineout[1].reshape(R, zall.shape[-1]) # 6. Fine Rendering distsall = zall[:, 1:] - zall[:,:-1] distsall = torch.cat([distsall, torch.full((R, 1), 1e10, device=rayso.device)], dim=-1) distsall = distsall torch.norm(raysd, dim=-1, keepdim=True) alphafine = 1.0 - torch.exp(-softplus(sigmafine) distsall) onesall = torch.oneslike(alphafine[:,:1]) Tfine = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([onesall, 1.0 - alphafine + epsilonalpha], dim=-1), dim=-1)[:,:-1] weightsfinefinal = Tfine alphafine rgbfinal = torch.sum(weightsfinefinal[:,:, None] cfine, dim=1) accfinal = torch.sum(weightsfinefinal, dim=1) depthfinal = torch.sum(weightsfinefinal zall, dim=1) if whitebackground: rgbfinal = rgbfinal + (1.0 - accfinal[:, None]) return rgbfinal, depthfinal, accfinal A standalone PyTorch library providing efficient sampling for volumetric rendering, decoupled from radiance field representation, supporting Occupancy Grid and Proposal Network. A technique to refine the sampling distribution along rays by using the weights from a coarse model to generate additional sample points, improving rendering quality with minimal overhead. It calculates midpoints between coarse samples, calls samplepdf with the coarse weights (excluding first and last samples), the number of importance samples N{importance}, and a deterministic flag based on perturb. The sampled positions are detached from the computation graph, concatenated with coarse z-values, sorted, and the fine network is evaluated at the new points. Performance: Hierarchical sampling uses the coarse model's density to guide finer sampling, reducing aliasing and improving detail compared to single-stage uniform sampling. Strengths: Differentiable end-to-end, allowing optimization from images alone; handles view-dependent appearance via directional encoding; hierarchical sampling efficiently allocates samples to dense regions. Limitations: The basic implementation is inefficient and does not converge to a sufficiently high-resolution representation for complex scenes without hierarchical refinement. NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It represents a scene as a continuous 5D function mapping spatial coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and emitted color. The method is trained by minimizing the difference between rendered images and ground truth images using gradient descent, leveraging the differentiability of the volume rendering integral. The coarse-to-fine sampling strategy was introduced to address the inefficiency and aliasing artifacts of uniform sampling, allowing the model to focus computational resources on regions with high density. name: NeRF Importance Sampling
head: Importance Sampling for NeRF
body: A technique to refine the sampling distribution along rays by using the weights from a coarse model to generate additional sample points, improving rendering quality with minimal overhead. It concentrates computational effort on regions of high opacity by resampling based on coarse alpha compositing weights. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Coarse sample positions z{\text{vals}} (depths along the ray), corresponding alpha compositing weights w from the coarse network evaluation, number of importance samples N{\text{importance}}, and a boolean perturb flag. Output: Refined sample positions z{\text{samples}} concatenated with coarse positions, sorted, and their corresponding 3D coordinates for fine network evaluation. Data Structures: z{\text{vals}}: Tensor of shape [B, N{\text{coarse}}], sorted in descending order (far to near). w: Tensor of shape [B, N{\text{coarse}}], representing the contribution weight of each coarse sample. z{\text{vals\mid}}: Tensor of shape [B, N{\text{coarse}} - 1], midpoints between adjacent coarse samples. Steps: 1. Calculate Midpoints: Compute the midpoints between adjacent coarse samples to define integration intervals. z{\text{vals\mid}} = 0.5 \times (z{\text{vals}}[..., 1:] + z{\text{vals}}[...,:-1]) 2. Prepare Weights for Sampling: Extract the weights corresponding to the intervals defined by the midpoints, excluding the first and last samples. 3. Sample PDF: Use inverse transform sampling on the normalized weights to select N{\text{importance}} sample positions z{\text{samples}} within the intervals, using a deterministic flag based on perturb. 4. Stop Gradient: Apply a stop-gradient operation on the sampled positions z{\text{samples}} to prevent gradients from flowing back through the sampling process to the coarse network during backpropagation. 5. Concatenate and Sort: Concatenate the original coarse z{\text{vals}} and the new z{\text{samples}}. Sort the combined tensor in descending order to maintain the ray traversal order (far to near). 6. Evaluate Fine Network: Compute 3D coordinates from the sorted depths and evaluate the fine neural network at these points to obtain refined color and opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def importancesampling(zvals, weights, Nimportance, perturb): # zvals: [B, Ncoarse] sorted descending # weights: [B, Ncoarse] alpha compositing weights # Nimportance: int # perturb: bool # 1. Calculate midpoints zvalsmid = 0.5 (zvals[..., 1:] + zvals[...,:-1]) # 2. Prepare weights for sampling (exclude first and last) weightsmid = weights[..., 1:-1] # Normalize weights to form a PDF eps = 1e-10 pdf = weightsmid / (weightsmid.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + eps) # 3. Sample PDF using inverse transform sampling cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # Generate uniform samples ushape = list(zvals.shape[:-1]) + [Nimportance] if perturb: u = torch.rand(ushape, device=zvals.device) else: u = torch.linspace(0, 1, Nimportance, device=zvals.device) u = u.expand(ushape) # Inverse transform sampling indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf[...,:-1], u, side='right') indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, zvalsmid.shape[-1] - 1) # Interpolate within bins loweridx = indices upperidx = torch.clamp(indices + 1, 0, zvalsmid.shape[-1] - 1) zlower = zvalsmid[loweridx] zupper = zvalsmid[upperidx] # Fraction within bin cdflower = cdf[...,:-1][loweridx] cdfupper = cdf[...,:-1][upperidx] frac = (u - cdflower) / (cdfupper - cdflower + eps) zsamples = zlower + frac (zupper - zlower) # 4. Stop gradient zsamples = zsamples.detach() # 5. Concatenate and sort zvalsall = torch.cat([zvals, zsamples], dim=-1) zvalsall, = torch.sort(zvalsall, dim=-1, descending=True) return zvalsall Parameters: N{\text{importance}}: Number of fine samples. Typical value: 128. perturb: Boolean flag for training-time jittering. Edge Cases: Empty Regions: If weights are zero everywhere, sampling fails. Mitigated by weight modification (see Subtopics). Precision: Floating point errors in CDF normalization can cause sampling bias. Use epsilon. Boundaries: Ensure indices are clamped to valid ranges when using searchsorted. A variant used in mip-NeRF to improve sampling in empty regions. It modifies the coarse weights before sampling to create a smoother, wider envelope. Method: Before sampling fine samples t^f, the weights w are modified using a 2-tap max filter followed by a 2-tap blur filter (blurpool), then a hyperparameter \alpha is added, and the result is re-normalized to sum to 1. Formula: The modified weight w'k is calculated as: w'k = \frac{1}{2}(\max(w{k-1}, wk) + \max(wk, w{k+1})) + \alpha Parameters: Number of samples: 128 coarse and 128 fine. \alpha: Hyperparameter to ensure sampling in empty regions. Default value: 0.01. When to choose: Use when rendering scenes with large empty spaces or when standard importance sampling fails to capture details in low-density regions. Time Complexity: O(N{\text{coarse}} + N{\text{importance}}) for sampling and sorting. The dominant cost is the fine network evaluation at N{\text{coarse}} + N{\text{importance}} points. Memory Complexity: O(N{\text{coarse}} + N{\text{importance}}) to store sample positions and intermediate weights. Measured Performance: In mip-NeRF, using 128 coarse and 128 fine samples yields the same number of total MLP evaluations as NeRF's configuration for fair comparison. Strengths: Reduces noise and aliasing by concentrating samples on opaque regions. Limitations: Requires two network evaluations (coarse and fine) or a hierarchical structure. Sensitive to the quality of coarse weights. When to use: High-quality rendering where noise reduction is critical. When not: Real-time applications with strict latency constraints. Originated from the NeRF paper (Mildenhall et al., 2020) and refined in mip-NeRF (Barron et al., 2021). It builds on NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling). dgsmith7/nerf-mlp, https://github.com/dgsmith7/nerf-mlp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Mip-NeRF: A Multiscale Representation for Anti-Aliasing Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.00580, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NerfAcc Rendering Pipeline
head: Efficient Sampling for Volumetric Rendering, NeRF Volume Rendering (CPU/PyTorch), NerfAcc
body: The NerfAcc Rendering Pipeline is a modular, high-performance volumetric rendering framework implemented as a PyTorch library that decouples efficient sampling from the radiance field representation. It solves the computational bottleneck of neural volume rendering by using a Transmittance Estimator (such as an Occupancy Grid or Proposal Network) to generate non-uniform sample intervals along rays, which are then integrated via differentiable rendering. Unlike standard uniform sampling or sibling methods like NeRF Importance Sampling which may sample the entire space, NerfAcc combines occupancy grids to skip empty space and proposal networks to concentrate samples on surfaces, achieving speedups of 1.5× to 20× with minimal code changes. The pipeline operates in three main phases: initialization and coarse sampling, efficient interval-based sampling, and differentiable rendering with estimator updates. Inputs: Ray origins ro \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}, ray directions rd \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} (normalized), near/far clipping planes (near, far), and a neural radiance field model nerf providing density and forward (RGB + density) functions. Outputs: Rendered color C, opacity \alpha, depth z, and auxiliary data (e.g., depth variance) for the batch of rays. Samples are represented as intervals (t0, t1, r) rather than single points x, where t0 and t1 are the start and end distances along the r-th ray. This interval representation supports cone-based anti-aliasing (e.g., Mip-NeRF) and avoids redundant queries at interval boundaries. 1. Initialize Transmittance Estimator: Create an estimator to guide sampling. This can be an Occupancy Grid (from Instant-NGP) or a Proposal Network (from Mip-NeRF 360). python estimator = nerfacc.TransmittanceEstimator() 2. Initialize Coarse Samples: Generate initial sample positions using log-space distribution, then map them to the [near, far] range. python # Generate numsteps points in [0, 1] log-space zvals = torch.logspace(0, 1, numsteps, base=2.0, device=device).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) - 1 # Map to [near, far] zvals = near + (far - near) zvals 3. Define Density Query Function: Create a wrapper that queries the neural network for density given interval endpoints and ray indices. python def densityfn(t0, t1, rid): """Query density from nerf.""" # ro and rd are batched ray origins and directions return nerf.density(ro[rid], rd[rid], t0, t1) 4. Perform Efficient Sampling: Use the estimator and density function to generate packed sample intervals (t0, t1, r\id). python # t0, t1: (allsamples,), rid: (allsamples,) t0, t1, rid = nerfacc.sampling( ro, rd, estimator, densityfn=densityfn) 5. Define RGB/Density Query Function: Create a wrapper that returns both color and density for the rendered intervals. python def rgbdensityfn(t0, t1, rid): """Query rgb and density from nerf.""" return nerf.forward(ro[rid], rd[rid], t0, t1) 6. Differentiable Volumetric Rendering: Integrate the samples to compute color, opacity, and depth. The internal rendering logic follows these formulas: Deltas: Compute interval lengths. For the last interval, use a fixed sample distance if needed. \deltai = t{i+1} - ti (Note: In implementation, deltas are computed between adjacent z values, with the last delta potentially set to a constant sampledist). Alpha: Convert density \sigma to opacity \alpha. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\deltai \sigmai) Weights: Compute rendering weights wi using the cumulative product of transmittance. wi = \alphai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) To ensure numerical stability, the cumulative product uses shifted alphas: \text{alphas\shifted} = \text{concat}([1, 1 - \alpha + 10^{-15}]) wi = \alphai \cdot \text{cumprod}(\text{alphas\shifted}){i-1} Color: Weighted sum of colors ci. C = \sumi wi ci Depth: Weighted mean of midpoints z{mid}. z = \sumi wi \frac{t{i+1} + ti}{2} Depth Variance: Weighted variance of depths. Var = \sumi wi \frac{(t{i+1}-z)^2 + (t{i+1}-z)(ti-z) + (ti-z)^2}{3} python color, opacity, depth, aux = nerfacc.rendering( t0, t1, rid, rgbdensityfn=rgbdensityfn) 7. Background Contribution: If alpha is not premultiplied, add background color based on accumulated opacity. python # weightssum is the sum of weights (opacity) if alphapremultiplied: image = color else: image = color / (weightssum + 1e-9) image = image + (1 - weightssum).unsqueeze(-1) bgcolor 8. Update Transmittance Estimator: Periodically update the estimator (e.g., every n steps) using the sampled intervals and auxiliary data to improve future sampling. python estimator.updateeverynsteps(t0, t1, rid, aux) 9. Loss and Backpropagation: Compute loss against ground truth and backpropagate. python F.mseloss(color, colorgt).backward() numsteps: Number of coarse samples per ray (e.g., 64, 128). near, far: Clipping distances (scene-dependent). updateeverynsteps: Frequency of estimator updates (e.g., 10, 100). bound: Clamping bound for hashgrid encoders to prevent NaNs (e.g., 1.0, 2.0). NaN in HashGrid Encoders: Points must be clamped to [-bound, bound] before querying hashgrid-based encoders to prevent NaN gradients. python pts = pts.clamp(-self.bound, self.bound) Numerical Stability: When computing cumulative products for transmittance, add a small epsilon (10^{-15}) to 1 - \alpha to prevent underflow and NaNs. Interval Boundaries: The interval-based representation (t0, t1) avoids querying the same point twice at boundaries, but requires careful handling of the last interval's delta if it extends beyond the last sampled point. A variant that refines coarse samples by resampling around high-weight intervals. It computes deltas and alphas from coarse samples, derives weights for PDF sampling, calculates midpoints, and samples new z values using samplepdf. New points are queried for density and RGB, and results are gathered using sort indices to maintain order. This step is typically performed after the coarse pass to improve detail without excessive sampling density. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples generated by the estimator. By skipping empty space (Occupancy Grid) and concentrating on surfaces (Proposal Network), it reduces the number of neural network queries compared to uniform sampling. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active samples. The interval-based representation (t0, t1, r) is memory-efficient as it avoids storing redundant point coordinates. Performance: Reported speedups of 1.5× to 20× over baseline NeRF implementations with minor code modifications. Strengths: Modular design allows easy integration with various radiance fields (density-based or SDF-based, static or dynamic). Combines the strengths of Occupancy Grids and Proposal Networks. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the estimator parameters. The interval-based approach may complicate direct point-wise analysis if not handled correctly. NerfAcc was introduced in the paper "NerfAcc: Efficient Sampling Accelerates NeRFs" (ICCV 2023). It was designed to address the computational inefficiency of neural radiance field rendering by providing a universal, decoupled sampling framework. The library fuses operations into CUDA kernels for maximum speed while exposing flexible Python APIs. It builds on techniques from Instant-NGP (Occupancy Grids) and Mip-NeRF 360 (Proposal Networks). name: VF-NeRF
head: Vector Field NeRF
body: VF-NeRF is a neural volume rendering method that represents indoor scenes using learned vector fields rather than standard scalar density fields, trained from multi-view posed images and their associated monocular depth maps. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by modeling scene geometry and appearance through a vector field representation integrated along rays, leveraging structural priors from depth supervision. Inputs: Multi-view posed RGB images and corresponding monocular depth maps. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: The model state consists of the following components: 1. vectorfieldnetwork: A neural network (instance of VectorFieldNetwork) that outputs the local vector field at a 3D coordinate. 2. renderingnetwork: A neural network (instance of RenderingNetwork) that maps intermediate features to RGB color and opacity. 3. density: A density function (instance of LaplaceDensity) used to convert vector field magnitudes or auxiliary outputs into volumetric density \sigma. 4. finevectorfieldnetwork: Optional secondary vector field network used during fine sampling; defaults to sharing the instance of vectorfieldnetwork if not explicitly configured. 5. raysampler: Primary sampler (instance of UniformSampler) generating coarse samples. 6. finesampler: Optional sampler (instance of RangeFineSampler) generating fine samples based on coarse results. Parameters: nsamples: Number of coarse samples per ray. nimportance: Number of additional fine samples per ray. near, far: Near and far clipping planes for ray sampling. perturb: Boolean flag for jittering sample positions. range: Range parameter for the fine sampler. maxsamples: Maximum total samples allowed. betabounds: Bounds for the Laplace density beta parameter, default [1e-4, 1e9]. meanbounds: Bounds for the Laplace density mean parameter, default [0.6, 1.0]. scalemin: Minimum scale for density, default 0.1. lr: Learning rate for the optimizer. weightdecay: Weight decay for the optimizer. lrdecayfactor, lrdecaysteps: Parameters for the learning rate scheduler. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize vectorfieldnetwork and renderingnetwork using configuration objects vfnetconfig and renderingnetconfig respectively. Initialize density as LaplaceDensity with parameters from densityconfig.todict(). If fine sampling is enabled (config.raysamplerconfig.finesampling()), initialize finevectorfieldnetwork. If not explicitly configured, set finevectorfieldnetwork = vectorfieldnetwork. Create raysampler (UniformSampler) with nsamples, near, far, and perturb (inverted from config). If fine sampling is enabled, create finesampler (RangeFineSampler) with nimportance, near, far, perturb (inverted), range (config.raysamplerconfig.finerange), and maxsamples (config.raysamplerconfig.maxsamples). If config.cossimweightsanneal is not 'none', initialize LinearAnnealing with the number of weight steps, duration annealend - annealstart, and soft mode determined by cossimweightsanneal == 'soft'. Initialize optimizer with lr and weightdecay. Initialize scheduler with decay factor lrdecayfactor (1. / lrdecaysteps). If numgpus > 1, wrap networks in nn.DataParallel. Move all networks and samplers to the specified device. 2. Training Loop: Not given in the sources. Standard differentiable volume rendering integration and optimization steps apply. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def initializevfnerf(config): # Initialize vector field network vfnet = VectorFieldNetwork(config.vfnetconfig) # Initialize rendering network rendernet = RenderingNetwork(config.renderingnetconfig) # Initialize density function densityfn = LaplaceDensity(config.densityconfig.todict()) # Initialize fine vector field network if fine sampling is enabled if config.raysamplerconfig.finesampling(): finevfnet = VectorFieldNetwork(config.vfnetconfig) else: finevfnet = vfnet # Create primary ray sampler raysampler = UniformSampler( nsamples=config.raysamplerconfig.nsamples, near=config.raysamplerconfig.near, far=config.raysamplerconfig.far, perturb=not config.raysamplerconfig.perturb) # Create fine sampler if enabled finesampler = None if config.raysamplerconfig.finesampling(): finesampler = RangeFineSampler( nimportance=config.raysamplerconfig.nimportance, near=config.raysamplerconfig.near, far=config.raysamplerconfig.far, perturb=not config.raysamplerconfig.perturb, range=config.raysamplerconfig.finerange, maxsamples=config.raysamplerconfig.maxsamples) # Initialize annealer if configured annealer = None if config.cossimweightsanneal != 'none': annealer = LinearAnnealing( numsteps=config.cossimweights.shape[0], duration=config.annealend - config.annealstart, soft=(config.cossimweightsanneal == 'soft')) # Initialize optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.Adam( parameters=list(vfnet.parameters()) + list(rendernet.parameters()) + list(finevfnet.parameters()), lr=config.schedulerconfig.lr, weightdecay=config.schedulerconfig.weightdecay) # Initialize learning rate scheduler scheduler = torch.optim.lrscheduler.ExponentialLR( optimizer=optimizer, gamma=config.schedulerconfig.lrdecayfactor (1.0 / config.schedulerconfig.lrdecaysteps)) # Wrap in data parallel if multiple GPUs are configured if config.cudaconfig.numgpus > 1: vfnet = torch.nn.DataParallel(vfnet) rendernet = torch.nn.DataParallel(rendernet) densityfn = torch.nn.DataParallel(densityfn) finevfnet = torch.nn.DataParallel(finevfnet) # Move to device device = config.cudaconfig.device vfnet = vfnet.to(device) rendernet = rendernet.to(device) densityfn = densityfn.to(device) finevfnet = finevfnet.to(device) # Training loop, loss computation, and optimization steps are not given in the sources. return { 'vfnet': vfnet, 'rendernet': rendernet, 'densityfn': densityfn, 'finevfnet': finevfnet, 'raysampler': raysampler, 'finesampler': finesampler, 'optimizer': optimizer, 'scheduler': scheduler, 'annealer': annealer } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The Laplace density parameters beta and mean have wide bounds (1e-4 to 1e9 and 0.6 to 1.0 respectively), requiring careful initialization to avoid numerical instability in the exponential term of the opacity calculation. Fine Sampling: If fine sampling is disabled, the finevectorfieldnetwork is not used, and the model relies solely on the coarse network, potentially reducing detail. Depth Supervision: The method relies on monocular depth maps. Inaccurate depth maps can lead to incorrect vector field learning and poor geometry reconstruction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Tested on Python 3.9, PyTorch 1.10.0, CUDA 11.3. Strengths: Leverages monocular depth for better geometry learning in indoor scenes. Limitations: Requires posed images and depth maps. When to use: Indoor scene reconstruction where monocular depth is available and accurate. When not to use: Unposed images or scenes without reliable depth priors. VF-NeRF was introduced by Albert Gassol et al. as an implementation of a neural volume rendering method using vector fields for indoor scene representation. It builds on the NeRF framework but replaces the scalar density field with a vector field, aiming to improve geometry learning through depth supervision. albertgassol1/vf-nerf, https://github.com/albertgassol1/vf-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Iterative Ray Marching with Neural Volume Inference
body: Iterative Ray Marching with Neural Volume Inference is a CUDA-based rendering method that splits the volume integration of a neural radiance field into multiple kernel launches to handle rays that do not fully converge (reach alpha \ge 1) in a single pass. It distinguishes itself from in-shader neural volume ray marching by decoupling the neural network inference from the shading logic, using a counter-based compaction mechanism to track and process only active rays across iterations. The method processes rays in batches of size N\ITERS. It separates the computation into three distinct phases per iteration: intersection (sample coordinate generation), inference (neural network evaluation), and composition (shading and alpha blending). A host-side loop manages the execution, checking for remaining active rays between kernel launches. Inputs: params: A structure containing rendering configuration, including: counter: A device integer buffer tracking the number of active rays. frameindex: Current frame ID for random number generation. renderingmode: Enum indicating shading type (e.g., SHADOW, NOSHADING, GRADIENTSHADING, SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC). densityscale: Scalar multiplier for volume density. samplingrate: Controls step size. volume: Neural volume context providing the network and transfer function. camera: Camera parameters (origin, direction, projection). framebuffersize: Width and height of the output image. clipbox: Lower and upper bounds of the volume of interest. network: The trained neural network (e.g., TCNN) used to predict density and color. tfn: Transfer function mapping network output to color and alpha. Outputs: framebuffer: A buffer of vec4f (RGBA) pixels. params.inferenceoutput: A temporary device buffer of floats storing network outputs for the current batch. Layout is [numRays k + i] where k is the sample index and i is the ray index. RayPayload (RayMarchingIter): Stores ray state. origin: vec3f Ray origin. direction: vec3f Ray direction. alpha: float Current accumulated alpha. color: vec3f Current accumulated color. tmin, tmax: float Intersection interval. Shadow Heuristic State (ssh): Used in SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC mode. highestorg: vec3f Origin of the highest alpha sample. highestcolor: vec3f Color of the highest alpha sample. highestalpha: float Maximum alpha encountered. NITERS: Number of samples processed per kernel launch iteration. Typical values depend on memory bandwidth and network batch size. numCoordsPerSample: Number of coordinate values written per sample to the inference input buffer. If GRADIENTSHADING is enabled: 4 \times N\ITERS (1 position + 3 gradient components per sample). Otherwise: N\ITERS (1 position per sample). nearlyone: Threshold for alpha convergence (e.g., 0.999). gradientStep: Step size for finite difference gradient estimation. shadingScale: Weight for blending gradient-based shading with sample color. opacityCorrection: Correction factor applied to sample alpha. 1. Initialization: Reset params.counter to zero using cudaMemsetAsync. Launch iterativeraygenkernel (either camera or shadow mode) to generate initial rays. Camera Mode: Generate jitter using RandomTEA seeded by frameindex and ray index. Compute ray origin/direction. If the ray intersects the volume, initialize RayMarchingIter and save payload. Otherwise, write default color. Shadow Mode: Use pre-computed highestorg and jitterssh from the previous camera pass. Create shadow ray. If it intersects and highestalpha > 0, save payload; otherwise, write existing shading color. Set params.counter to the number of rays saved in the payload. 2. Main Iteration Loop: Check Active Rays: Asynchronously copy params.counter to host memory and synchronize. If count > 0, continue. Reset Counter: Set params.counter to zero for the next iteration's compaction. Intersection Kernel: Launch iterativeintersectkernel<MODE> with N\ITERS threads. For each sample k in the batch: Compute object space position c using linear interpolation: c = \text{lerp}(jitter, t.x, t.y). If GRADIENTSHADING: Compute gradient sample points gx, gy, gz by adding gradientStep to c. Store c and gradients in the inference input buffer. If not gradient shading: Store c in the inference input buffer. Neural Inference: If a network is provided: Call iterativesamplingbatchinference with input size numCoordsPerSample numRays. Output is written to params.inferenceoutput. If no network (Ground Truth): Launch iterativesamplinggroundtruthkernel to sample the volume directly. Composition Kernel: Launch iterativecomposekernel<MODE> with N\ITERS threads. For each ray i and sample k: Retrieve sample value v from params.inferenceoutput. Apply transfer function to get sampleColor and sampleAlpha. Apply opacityCorrection to sampleAlpha. Shading: If GRADIENTSHADING: Compute normal No from gradients and sample value. Transform to world space Nw. Calculate shadingColor (e.g., Phong). Lerp with sampleColor using shadingScale. If SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Track the highest alpha sample. If ssh.highestalpha < (1.0 - ray.alpha) sampleAlpha, update ssh.highestorg, ssh.highestcolor, and ssh.highestalpha. Volume Blending: Calculate transmittance tr = 1.0 - ray.alpha. Update ray alpha: ray.alpha += tr \times sampleAlpha. If MODE != SHADOW: Update ray color: ray.color += tr \times shadingColor \times sampleAlpha. Iteration Control: If k < N\ITERS and ray.alpha < nearlyone: Mark ray as active (increment params.counter at the corresponding index). If ray is finished (ray.alpha \ge nearlyone or not resumable): Write final result to framebuffer. For SHADOW mode: Lerp shadingColor with finalhighestcolor shadingColor.w transmittance. For SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Save final highest org/color/alpha and shadingcolor. Otherwise: Write ray.color and ray.alpha. 3. Post-Loop: If any rays remain active (counter > 0), repeat from Step 2. Finalize any pending writes to the framebuffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativeraymarching(params, network, tfn): """ Main iterative ray marching loop. params: Object containing counter, frameindex, renderingmode, etc. network: Neural network model for inference. tfn: Transfer function. """ # 1. Initialize cudamemsetasync(params.counter, 0) # Launch Ray Generation if params.renderingmode == SHADOW: launchkernel(iterativeraygenkernelshadow, params) else: launchkernel(iterativeraygenkernelcamera, params) # Get initial active ray count # Note: In practice, this involves async copy and sync activecount = getcountervalue(params.counter) while activecount > 0: # 2. Reset counter for next iteration compaction cudamemsetasync(params.counter, 0) # 3. Intersection Kernel # Computes sample coordinates and gradient points if needed launchkernel(iterativeintersectkernel, params, gridsize=activecount) # 4. Neural Inference if network is not None: # Input buffer size depends on mode inputsize = params.numCoordsPerSample activecount inferenceoutput = network.forward(params.inferenceinput, batchsize=inputsize) params.inferenceoutput = inferenceoutput else: launchkernel(iterativesamplinggroundtruthkernel, params) # 5. Composition Kernel # Shading, blending, and determining next iteration status launchkernel(iterativecomposekernel, params, gridsize=activecount) # 6. Check for remaining active rays activecount = getcountervalue(params.counter) # 7. Finalize # Ensure all writes are complete cudastreamsynchronize() Wired Error: The intersection step is separated from ray generation and composition due to an unidentified "wired error" that occurred when they were merged. Merging them did not provide obvious performance benefits. Precision: Alpha accumulation can suffer from precision issues if nearlyone is too close to 1.0 or if transmittance becomes very small. Boundary Conditions: Rays that do not intersect the volume must be handled in the ray generation kernel to avoid undefined behavior in subsequent kernels. Gradient Shading: Requires careful computation of finite differences. The gradientStep must be small enough to approximate the derivative but large enough to avoid numerical noise. Time Complexity: O(R \cdot S / N\ITERS) kernel launches, where R is the number of rays and S is the total number of samples per ray. Each launch involves N\ITERS samples. The total work is proportional to R \cdot S. Memory Complexity: O(N\ITERS \cdot \text{coords\per\sample}) for inference buffers, plus O(R) for ray payloads and counters. The iterative nature allows processing large scenes with limited GPU memory by batching rays. Performance: Performance depends heavily on the neural network inference speed and the efficiency of the counter-based compaction. The separation of kernels allows for better occupancy and memory coalescing compared to in-shader methods, but incurs kernel launch overhead. Strengths: Handles rays that require many samples to converge without infinite loops in a single kernel. Decouples network inference from shading, allowing for optimized inference batching. Limitations: Kernel launch overhead for each iteration. Complexity in managing ray state across iterations. The "wired error" suggests potential stability issues with merged kernels. The method is part of the instantvnr library by VIDILabs. It is designed for real-time neural volume rendering, leveraging CUDA and tiny-cuda-nn (TCNN) for efficient inference. The iterative approach addresses the challenge of variable convergence rates among rays in neural volume rendering. name: In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching
head: in-shader rendering
body: In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching is a direct volume rendering technique where the neural network (MLP) is evaluated directly inside the CUDA kernel for each sample point, rather than pre-decoding the volume into a 3D texture or using sample-streaming. It supports multiple shading modes including gradient shading and single-shade heuristics. Unlike NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling) which often relies on hierarchical sampling strategies, this method performs a uniform or jittered march through the volume bounding box, evaluating the neural field on-the-fly to determine density and color at each step. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained neural volume model (MLP), camera parameters (position, orientation, field of view), transfer function, and rendering parameters (shading mode, step size, gradient step). Output: A 2D image (framebuffer) with accumulated color and alpha. Data Structures: The neural volume is wrapped in a CUDA device class. Two primary implementations are supported: 1. TcnnDeviceVolume<N, NFEATURESPERLEVEL>: Wraps a standard tiny-cuda-nn MLP. Template parameters define network width (N \in \{16, 32, 64\}) and features per level. Provides init(), launch2D(), and sample(p) methods. 2. FvsrnDeviceVolume<N>: Used when NFEATURESPERLEVEL == -2 (indicating fV-SRN networks). Supports widths from 16 \times 1 to 16 \times 8. Provides init(), launch(), and sample(p) methods. Parameters: params.mode: Shading mode. Values include GRADIENTSHADING and SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC. params.scivisshadingscale: Scalar float controlling interpolation between raw sample color and shaded color in gradient mode. params.gradstep: Step size for numerical gradient estimation via finite differences. samplingrate: Controls the density of samples along the ray. densityscale: Scales the output density from the neural network. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Initialize the ray origin and direction in world space. Transform camera position to world space: ray.org = xfmPoint(wto, camera.position). Construct ray direction from camera forward, horizontal, and vertical vectors, shifted by normalized screen position (screen.x - 0.5f) and (screen.y - 0.5f), then normalized. 2. Volume Intersection: Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box using intersectVolume(t0, t1, ray.org, ray.dir, self). If no intersection is found (!blockany(...)), return the background color and alpha. Otherwise, the ray segment of interest is [t0, t1]. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate through the ray using an iterator networkraymarchingiterator. For each step interval [t.x, t.y]: Sample Position: Compute position p using jittered linear interpolation: p = \text{ray.org} + \text{lerp}(\text{jitter}, t.x, t.y) \times \text{ray.dir} Neural Inference: Sample the neural volume at p: \text{value} = \text{neuralvolume.sample}(p) This replaces traditional texture lookups with neural network inference. Gradient Estimation (Optional): If params.mode == GRADIENTSHADING, estimate the volume gradient numerically: \nabla \text{value} = \text{sampleGradient}(p, \text{value}, \text{grad\step}, \text{sampler}) Negate the gradient for shading purposes. Otherwise, gradient is zero. Transfer Function: Apply the transfer function to value to get sampleColor and sampleAlpha: (\text{sampleColor}, \text{sampleAlpha}) = \text{sampleTransferFunction}(\text{tfn}, \text{value}) Apply opacity correction for the step size \Delta t = t.y - t.x. Shading (Optional): If GRADIENTSHADING: Transform gradient to world space Nw = \text{xfmNormal}(otw, \nabla \text{value}) and ray direction to world space. Compute shaded color using shadescivislight with ambient and directional lights. Interpolate: \text{finalSampleColor} = \text{lerp}(\text{shadingScale}, \text{sampleColor}, \text{shadedColor}) If SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Track the point with the highest density (highestOrg, highestAlpha) encountered so far. Compositing: Accumulate color and alpha using front-to-back blending: \text{tr} = 1.0 - \text{alpha} \text{color} += \text{tr} \times \text{finalSampleColor} \times \text{sampleAlpha} \text{alpha} += \text{tr} \times \text{sampleAlpha} Termination: Continue while alive is true and alpha < nearlyone. The iterator callback returns alive && (alpha < nearlyone). 4. Single Shade Heuristic (Post-March): If params.mode == SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC and highestAlpha > 0.f: Calculate transmittance from the highest density point (highestOrg) to the light source using a secondary ray march networkraymarchingtransmittance towards the light direction. Apply the heuristic result by interpolating the final color: \text{color} = \text{lerp}(\text{shadingScale}, \text{color}, \text{highestColor} \times \text{alpha} \times \text{transmittance}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inshaderneuralvolumeraymarching(camera, neuralvolume, transferfunction, params): """ Renders a frame using in-shader neural volume ray marching. Args: camera: Camera object with position, forward, horizontal, vertical vectors. neuralvolume: Object with sample(p) method. transferfunction: Object mapping value to (color, alpha). params: Dict with 'mode', 'scivisshadingscale', 'gradstep', 'samplingrate', 'densityscale'. Returns: framebuffer: 2D array of (color, alpha). """ width, height = camera.framebuffersize framebuffer = zeros((width, height, 4)) # RGBA # Pre-compute world-to-camera and camera-to-world matrices if needed # wto = worldtoobject(camera.transform) # otw = objecttoworld(camera.transform) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # 1. Ray Initialization # Normalize screen coordinates to [-0.5, 0.5] nx = (x + 0.5) / width - 0.5 ny = (y + 0.5) / height - 0.5 # Construct ray direction in camera space, then transform to world space # Assuming camera vectors are already in world space or transformed appropriately raydircam = camera.forward + nx camera.horizontal + ny camera.vertical raydir = normalize(raydircam) rayorg = camera.position # Transformed to world space if necessary # 2. Volume Intersection t0, t1 = intersectvolumeboundingbox(rayorg, raydir, neuralvolume.bbox) if t0 > t1: # No intersection, return background framebuffer[y, x] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) continue # 3. Ray Marching accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 tr = 1.0 highestdensity = 0.0 highestorg = rayorg highestcolor = vec3(0.0) # Determine step size based on samplingrate # Note: The exact iteration logic depends on the specific iterator implementation # Here we simulate a loop over intervals [t.x, t.y] tcurrent = t0 stepsize = (t1 - t0) params['samplingrate'] # Simplified step logic while tcurrent < t1 and accumulatedalpha < 0.999: # nearlyone tnext = min(tcurrent + stepsize, t1) # Jittered interpolation jitter = randomfloat(0.0, 1.0) p = lerp(rayorg, rayorg + raydir tnext, jitter) # Approximation of lerp(jitter, t.x, t.y) # More accurately: p = rayorg + (tcurrent + jitter (tnext - tcurrent)) raydir p = rayorg + (tcurrent + jitter (tnext - tcurrent)) raydir # Neural Inference value = neuralvolume.sample(p) value = params['densityscale'] # Apply density scale # Transfer Function samplecolor, samplealpha = transferfunction.apply(value) # Opacity correction for step size # samplealpha = (tnext - tcurrent) # Depending on TF definition # Shading if params['mode'] == 'GRADIENTSHADING': # Numerical Gradient gradstep = params['gradstep'] eps = vec3(gradstep, 0, 0) grad = vec3( neuralvolume.sample(p + eps) - neuralvolume.sample(p - eps), neuralvolume.sample(p + vec3(0, gradstep, 0)) - neuralvolume.sample(p - vec3(0, gradstep, 0)), neuralvolume.sample(p + vec3(0, 0, gradstep)) - neuralvolume.sample(p - vec3(0, 0, gradstep))) grad = -grad # Negate for shading # Transform to world space Nw = transformnormal(otw, grad) Rw = transformvector(otw, raydir) # Ray direction in world space # Shade shadedcolor = shadescivislight(Nw, Rw, params) # Interpolate samplecolor = lerp(params['scivisshadingscale'], samplecolor, shadedcolor) elif params['mode'] == 'SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC': if value > highestdensity: highestdensity = value highestorg = p highestcolor = samplecolor # Composite accumulatedcolor += tr samplecolor samplealpha accumulatedalpha += tr samplealpha tr = (1.0 - samplealpha) tcurrent = tnext # 4. Single Shade Heuristic Post-Processing if params['mode'] == 'SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC' and highestdensity > 0.0: # Secondary ray march to light transmittance = computetransmittancetolight(highestorg, raydir, neuralvolume, params) finalshadedcolor = highestcolor transmittance accumulatedcolor = lerp(params['scivisshadingscale'], accumulatedcolor, finalshadedcolor accumulatedalpha) framebuffer[y, x] = (accumulatedcolor.x, accumulatedcolor.y, accumulatedcolor.z, accumulatedalpha) return framebuffer Uses hierarchical sampling with coarse and fine passes to optimize computational cost. Choose when scene complexity varies significantly and adaptive sampling is beneficial. Link Iteratively refines the ray marching path or density estimates. Choose when high-frequency details require adaptive refinement. Link Uses a differentiable voxel grid (DVGO) representation instead of a pure MLP. Choose for faster inference at the cost of memory. Link The underlying neural network architecture used by the in-shader method. Link Integrates radiance fields using volumetric primitives. Link Tools for visualizing the ray marching process and neural network outputs. Link Classifies volume data using neural networks. Link Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of samples per ray. Each sample requires a neural network inference, which is significantly more expensive than a texture lookup. Memory Complexity: Depends on the neural network size. TcnnDeviceVolume and FvsrnDeviceVolume store the MLP weights in GPU memory. Measured Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on the MLP width and the hardware's FP32/FP16 throughput. Standard widths (16, 32, 64) are optimized. fV-SRN supports widths up to 16 \times 8. Strengths: High-quality rendering with continuous representations; supports complex shading (gradient, single-shade) directly in the shader; no need for pre-computed 3D textures. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to per-sample neural inference; limited by MLP capacity for high-frequency details; requires specific network widths (16, 32, 64 or multiples of 16 for fV-SRN). When to Use: When high-quality, continuous volume rendering is required and computational resources allow for per-pixel neural inference. Suitable for scientific visualization and high-fidelity rendering. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the scene is simple enough for texture-based rendering; when memory is constrained and the MLP is large. In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching is part of the instantvnr (Instant Neural Volume Rendering) framework developed by Qi Wu and the VIDILabs team. name: DVGO Volume Rendering Forward Pass
head: DVGO forward, Direct Voxel Grid Optimization rendering
body: The DVGO forward pass renders a 3D scene represented by a direct voxel grid of density and color features into 2D images by casting rays and accumulating transmittance-weighted colors. It differs from NeRF by replacing the continuous MLP density query with a discrete, hardware-friendly voxel grid lookup, enabling faster training and inference while maintaining view-dependent color modeling. Inputs: rayso: Origin points of rays, shape (N, 3). raysd: Direction vectors of rays, shape (N, 3). near: Near plane distances for each ray, shape (N,). far: Far plane distances for each ray, shape (N,). stepsize: Distance between samples along the ray, scalar. renderkwargs: Dictionary containing optional flags (renderfeatures, renderdiffuse, renderdepth), background color bg, and stepsize (if not passed directly). Model parameters: density grid, diffuse grid (optional), rgbnet (optional), actshift, voxelsizeratio, fastcolorthres, usediffusecolor, rgbnetfullimplicit, rgbnetdirect. Outputs: rgbmarched: Rendered RGB image, shape (N, 3). alphainvlast: Accumulated transmittance at the end of the ray, shape (N,). weights: Per-sample transmittance weights, shape (M,) where M is the number of valid samples. rawalpha: Raw alpha values per sample, shape (M,). rawrgb: Raw RGB values per sample, shape (M, 3). rayid: Mapping from sample index to ray index, shape (M,). Optional: depth, diffusemarched, featuresmarched. Voxel Grids: 3D tensors storing density and color features. The spatial extent is defined by xyzmin and xyzmax. The resolution is determined by numvoxels. Mask Cache: Optional boolean grid or structure to skip free space. interval: Sampling interval for density-to-alpha conversion. Calculated as stepsize voxelsizeratio. actshift: Shift parameter for the density activation function. fastcolorthres: Threshold for early ray termination. If >0, samples with \alpha < \text{threshold} or \text{weight} < \text{threshold} are discarded. 1. Ray Sampling: Sample query points along rays using sampleray(rayso, raysd, near, far, stepsize). This returns: raypts: Sample positions, shape (M, 3). rayid: Ray indices for each sample, shape (M,). stepid: Step indices (or depths) for each sample, shape (M,). 2. Free Space Culling: If maskcache exists, filter raypts, rayid, and stepid to keep only points where maskcache(raypts) is true. 3. Density Query: Query the density field for the filtered points: density = densityfield(raypts). 4. Density to Alpha Conversion: Convert density to alpha using the Raw2Alpha function: \alpha = 1 - \exp\left(-\text{density} \cdot \text{interval}\right) Note: The source code implies a shift actshift is applied to density before this calculation, typically \text{density} = \text{density} + \text{act\shift}. 5. Alpha Thresholding (Optional): If fastcolorthres > 0, filter points where \alpha > \text{fast\color\thres}. Update raypts, rayid, stepid, density, and alpha. 6. Weight Computation: Compute accumulated transmittance weights using Alphas2Weights(alpha, rayid, N). This function computes: Ti = \prod{j < i, \text{ray}j = \text{ray}i} (1 - \alphaj) wi = Ti \cdot \alphai It also returns alphainvlast, the accumulated transmittance at the end of each ray: \text{alphainv\last}r = \prod{j, \text{ray}j = r} (1 - \alphaj). 7. Weight Thresholding (Optional): If fastcolorthres > 0, filter points where wi > \text{fast\color\thres}. Update weights, alpha, raypts, rayid, and stepid. 8. Color Query: If usediffusecolor is true, query the diffuse color field: diffuse = diffusefield(raypts). Compute RGB color: If rgbnet is None: rgb = sigmoid(diffuse). If rgbnet exists: Compute view-dependent color. Flatten viewdirs with positional embedding. Concatenate with k0 (if not rgbnetfullimplicit). Pass through rgbnet. Apply sigmoid. Add diffuse if not rgbnetdirect. 9. Feature Marching (Optional): If renderfeatures is true, compute featuresmarched by summing weights k0 grouped by rayid using segmentcoo. 10. RGB Marching: Compute final RGB via ray marching: \text{rgb\marched}r = \sum{i, \text{ray}i = r} wi \cdot \text{rgb}i Implemented using segmentcoo(src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros([N, 3]), reduce='sum'). 11. Background Addition: \text{rgb\marched} += \text{alphainv\last} \cdot \text{bg}. 12. Optional Outputs: If renderdiffuse is true: diffusemarched = segmentcoo(weights sigmoid(diffuse), rayid, reduce='sum'). If renderdepth is true: depth = segmentcoo(weights stepid, rayid, reduce='sum'). 13. Return: Dictionary containing alphainvlast, weights, rgbmarched, rawalpha (alpha), rawrgb (rgb), and rayid. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dvgoforwardpass(rayso, raysd, near, far, stepsize, renderkwargs, model): """ Forward pass for DVGO volume rendering. Args: rayso: (N, 3) ray origins raysd: (N, 3) ray directions near: (N,) near plane distances far: (N,) far plane distances stepsize: float, distance between samples renderkwargs: dict with keys 'bg', 'renderfeatures', 'renderdiffuse', 'renderdepth' model: object with attributes density, diffuse, rgbnet, actshift, voxelsizeratio, fastcolorthres, usediffusecolor, rgbnetfullimplicit, rgbnetdirect, maskcache, xyzmin, xyzmax, numvoxels Returns: dict with 'rgbmarched', 'alphainvlast', 'weights', 'rawalpha', 'rawrgb', 'rayid' """ # Step 1: Sample points raypts, rayid, stepid = sampleray(rayso, raysd, near, far, stepsize) M = len(raypts) # Step 2: Free space culling if model.maskcache is not None: validmask = model.maskcache(raypts) raypts = raypts[validmask] rayid = rayid[validmask] stepid = stepid[validmask] M = len(raypts) # Step 3: Density query density = model.density(raypts) # Step 4: Density to Alpha # Apply shift if present (assumed based on Raw2Alpha usage) densityshifted = density + model.actshift interval = stepsize model.voxelsizeratio rawalpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densityshifted interval) # Step 5: Alpha thresholding if model.fastcolorthres > 0: validmask = rawalpha > model.fastcolorthres raypts = raypts[validmask] rayid = rayid[validmask] stepid = stepid[validmask] density = density[validmask] rawalpha = rawalpha[validmask] M = len(raypts) # Step 6: Weight computation weights, alphainvlast = Alphas2Weights(rawalpha, rayid, len(rayso)) # Step 7: Weight thresholding if model.fastcolorthres > 0: validmask = weights > model.fastcolorthres raypts = raypts[validmask] rayid = rayid[validmask] stepid = stepid[validmask] rawalpha = rawalpha[validmask] weights = weights[validmask] M = len(raypts) # Step 8: Color query if model.usediffusecolor: diffuse = model.diffuse(raypts) if model.rgbnet is None: rgb = torch.sigmoid(diffuse) else: # View-dependent color computation viewdirs = raysd[rayid] # Positional encoding of viewdirs (simplified) viewdirspe = positionalencoding(viewdirs) # Concatenate with k0 if not full implicit if not model.rgbnetfullimplicit: k0 = model.k0(raypts) # Assuming k0 is a feature grid lookup inputtensor = torch.cat([viewdirspe, k0], dim=-1) else: inputtensor = viewdirspe rgb = model.rgbnet(inputtensor) if not model.rgbnetdirect: rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgb + diffuse) else: rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgb) # Step 9: Feature marching (optional) featuresmarched = None if renderkwargs.get('renderfeatures', False): k0 = model.k0(raypts) featuresmarched = segmentcoo(src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) k0), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros([len(rayso), k0.shape[-1]]), reduce='sum') # Step 10: RGB marching rgbmarched = segmentcoo(src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros([len(rayso), 3]), reduce='sum') # Step 11: Background addition bg = renderkwargs['bg'] rgbmarched = rgbmarched + (alphainvlast.unsqueeze(-1) bg) # Step 12: Optional outputs diffusemarched = None if model.usediffusecolor and renderkwargs.get('renderdiffuse', False): diffusemarched = segmentcoo(src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) torch.sigmoid(diffuse)), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros([len(rayso), diffuse.shape[-1]]), reduce='sum') depth = None if renderkwargs.get('renderdepth', False): depth = segmentcoo(src=(weights stepid), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros([len(rayso)]), reduce='sum') # Step 13: Return return { 'alphainvlast': alphainvlast, 'weights': weights, 'rgbmarched': rgbmarched, 'rawalpha': rawalpha, 'rawrgb': rgb, 'rayid': rayid, 'diffusemarched': diffusemarched, 'depth': depth, 'featuresmarched': featuresmarched } Precision: Floating point precision in Alphas2Weights can cause issues with very long rays or many samples. Use torch.float32 for stability, but be aware of potential underflow in transmittance products. Boundaries: Ray sampling must handle cases where rays start inside or outside the voxel grid bounds. The sampleray function should clamp points to the grid bounds or handle out-of-bounds queries gracefully. Degenerate Input: Rays with zero length or invalid directions should be handled by sampleray or filtered out before the forward pass. Check for norm(raysd) == 0 and skip or assign a default color. Time: O(M) where M is the number of samples after culling. The dominant operations are grid lookups and segmentcoo reductions. Memory: O(M) for storing intermediate tensors (raypts, density, alpha, weights, rgb). The voxel grids themselves are O(V) where V is the number of voxels. Not given in the sources. Scales linearly with the number of rays and samples. Voxel grid resolution affects memory usage and lookup speed. Strengths: Faster training and inference compared to MLP-based NeRF due to discrete grid lookups. Hardware-friendly. Limitations: Lower resolution than continuous representations. Artifacts at voxel boundaries. Use when training speed and inference speed are critical. Use when scene geometry is well-represented by a voxel grid. Use when high-frequency details are required and voxel resolution is insufficient. Use when memory is extremely constrained and voxel grid size is large. Developed as part of the ref-dvgo project. Builds on the idea of direct volume rendering with voxel grids. Used in 3D scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. name: MLP with Positional Encoding
head: MLP Render with Positional Encoding
body: A neural rendering module that predicts RGB color from input features, view directions, and spatial positions using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with positional encoding applied to both position and view direction. It differs from sibling methods like NeRF Volumetric Rendering by explicitly handling view-dependent appearance through concatenated positional encodings of the view vector, whereas simpler variants may assume view-independent color or use different encoding schemes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: features: Input feature vector from the volume representation (e.g., from a hash grid or triplane). Shape: (N, inChanel). pts: Spatial coordinates. Shape: (N, 3). viewdirs: View direction vectors. Shape: (N, 3). pospe: Number of positional encoding frequencies for position. viewpe: Number of positional encoding frequencies for view direction. Output: rgb: Predicted RGB color values. Shape: (N, 3). Data Structures: The input to the MLP is a concatenated tensor formed by combining raw features, raw view directions, and their respective positional encodings. The specific layout is: \text{input} = [\text{features}, \text{viewdirs}, \text{PE}(\text{pts}, pospe), \text{PE}(\text{viewdirs}, viewpe)] Note: In this specific implementation (MLPRenderPE), the features themselves are not positional encoded; only pts and viewdirs are. The MLP architecture consists of 3 sequential Linear layers: 1. Layer 1: Input dimension in\mlpC to hidden dimension featureC. 2. Layer 2: featureC to featureC. 3. Layer 3: featureC to 3 (RGB). Formulas: The input dimension in\mlpC is calculated as: in\mlpC = inChanel + 3 + (2 \cdot viewpe \cdot 3) + (3 + 2 \cdot pospe \cdot 3) Where: inChanel: Dimension of input features. 3: Raw view direction components. 2 \cdot viewpe \cdot 3: Positional encoded view direction components (sine/cosine for each frequency). 3: Raw position components. 2 \cdot pospe \cdot 3: Positional encoded position components. Parameters: featureC: Hidden dimension size. Default: 128. pospe, viewpe: Number of frequencies for positional encoding. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the bias of the final layer (Layer 3) to 0. 2. Positional Encoding: Apply positional encoding to pts with pospe frequencies and viewdirs with viewpe frequencies. If pospe or viewpe is 0, skip the respective encoding. 3. Concatenation: Concatenate features, viewdirs, encoded pts, and encoded viewdirs along the last dimension to form the input tensor. 4. MLP Forward Pass: Pass input through Layer 1. Apply ReLU activation. Pass result through Layer 2. Apply ReLU activation. Pass result through Layer 3. 5. Output Activation: Apply Sigmoid activation to the output of Layer 3 to constrain RGB values to [0, 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class PositionalEncoder(nn.Module): """Standard sinusoidal positional encoding.""" def init(self, numfreqs): super().init() self.numfreqs = numfreqs def forward(self, x): if self.numfreqs == 0: return x # x shape: (..., 3) # freqbands shape: (numfreqs,) freqbands = torch.logspace(0, self.numfreqs - 1, self.numfreqs, dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) # Expand dimensions for broadcasting # x: (..., 3) -> (..., 1, 3) # freqbands: (numfreqs,) -> (1, numfreqs, 1) # result: (..., numfreqs, 3) embedded = x.unsqueeze(-2) freqbands.unsqueeze(-1) # Apply sin and cos embedded = torch.cat([torch.sin(embedded), torch.cos(embedded)], dim=-1) # Flatten the last two dimensions: (..., numfreqs, 3) -> (..., numfreqs 3) return embedded.view(x.shape[:-1], -1) class MLPWithPE(nn.Module): def init(self, inChanel, featureC=128, pospe=0, viewpe=0): super().init() self.inChanel = inChanel self.pospe = pospe self.viewpe = viewpe self.featureC = featureC # Calculate input dimension # features: inChanel # viewdirs: 3 # PE(pts): 3 + 2 pospe 3 # PE(viewdirs): 2 viewpe 3 inmlpC = inChanel + 3 + (3 + 2 pospe 3) + (2 viewpe 3) self.posencoder = PositionalEncoder(pospe) self.viewencoder = PositionalEncoder(viewpe) self.layer1 = nn.Linear(inmlpC, featureC) self.layer2 = nn.Linear(featureC, featureC) self.layer3 = nn.Linear(featureC, 3) # Initialization: bias of final layer to 0 nn.init.zeros(self.layer3.bias) def forward(self, features, pts, viewdirs): # features: (N, inChanel) # pts: (N, 3) # viewdirs: (N, 3) # 1. Positional Encoding ptsenc = self.posencoder(pts) viewdirsenc = self.viewencoder(viewdirs) # 2. Concatenation # Order: [features, viewdirs, PE(pts), PE(viewdirs)] # Note: Raw viewdirs are included before PE(viewdirs) in the source logic indata = [features, viewdirs] if self.pospe > 0: indata.append(ptsenc) if self.viewpe > 0: indata.append(viewdirsenc) x = torch.cat(indata, dim=-1) # 3. MLP Forward Pass x = F.relu(self.layer1(x)) x = F.relu(self.layer2(x)) x = self.layer3(x) # 4. Output Activation rgb = torch.sigmoid(x) return rgb Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Positional encoding involves high-frequency sinusoids. Ensure input coordinates are normalized to a reasonable range (e.g., [-1, 1] or [0, 1]) to avoid numerical instability in high-frequency bands. Boundary Conditions: The Sigmoid activation ensures output is in [0, 1]. If the network outputs values outside this range before activation, they are compressed. This is standard for RGB prediction. Degenerate Input: If pospe and viewpe are both 0, the input is just features and viewdirs. The MLP must still be trained to capture view dependence if viewdirs is included. The final prediction head in neural volume rendering pipelines that use a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with positional encoding. It maps spatial and view-dependent features to final RGB color values. It differs from sibling layers by outputting only color (RGB), whereas variants like the Sigma Network Layer output density or other physical properties. It builds on MLP with Positional Encoding by consuming the encoded input vectors produced by that module. This method extends the standard neural volume rendering MLP by constraining the output to represent a physically plausible refractive index (IOR) field. While the parent MLP with Positional Encoding predicts RGB color and density, this variant predicts a scalar field (refractive index) used in ray tracing simulations for transparent or refractive media. It is distinguished by a specific post-processing activation function (ioract) that maps the MLP's raw output to a positive range 1, \infty), ensuring physical validity for light propagation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples N and the input dimension in\mlpC. The positional encoding adds a factor of O(N \cdot (pospe + viewpe)). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to N and the MLP parameters. The MLP has O(featureC \cdot in\mlpC + featureC^2 + featureC \cdot 3) parameters. Strengths: Explicitly models view-dependent effects (specular highlights, anisotropy) through view direction encoding. Simple and effective for many neural rendering tasks. Limitations: High-frequency positional encoding can lead to high-frequency artifacts (aliasing) if not filtered or if the scene contains high-frequency details. The MLP capacity is limited by the hidden dimension featureC. When to Use: When view-dependent appearance is important and the scene does not require extremely high-frequency detail that would cause aliasing with standard PE. When Not to Use: When computational efficiency is critical and view dependence is minimal, or when the scene has very high-frequency details that require more advanced encoding schemes (e.g., hash encoding with filtering). Originated in the context of [Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and related neural rendering techniques. The specific implementation details (bias initialization, concatenation order) are derived from the Collaborative-Neural-Radiance-Fields-for-Novel-View-Synthesis repository. name: RGB Network Layer
body: The RGB Network Layer is the final prediction head in neural volume rendering pipelines that use a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with positional encoding. It maps spatial and view-dependent features to final RGB color values. It differs from sibling layers by outputting only color (RGB), whereas variants like the Sigma Network Layer output density or other physical properties. It builds on MLP with Positional Encoding by consuming the encoded input vectors produced by that module. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A concatenated vector consisting of the first 16 components of the encoded view direction and 16 components of the spatial embedding (feature vector). Output: A 3-component RGB color vector with values in the range [0, 1]. Data Structures: self.rgbdepth: Integer specifying the number of hidden layers in the RGB MLP. Typical value: 2. self.rgbninput: Integer, number of input features. Derived from concatenation of direction and spatial embeddings. self.rgbnoutput: Integer, number of output features (typically 3 for RGB). self.rgblayer1base, self.rgblayer2base: Weights and biases for the respective layers. self.finalembedding: Tensor storing spatial embeddings for active rays. direncodefunc: Function producing directional encoding. self.temphit: Array mapping ray indices to processing slots. self.out3: Output buffer for RGB values. blockdim: Block dimension for parallel execution (e.g., 16 or 32). Steps: 1. Iterate over active sample indices sn within the current block. 2. Retrieve the ray ID: rayid = self.temphit[sn]. 3. Encode the ray direction: direnc = direncodefunc(raydirection). 4. Construct the input vector by concatenating the first 16 components of direnc with the 16 components of self.finalembedding[sn]. 5. Compute the first hidden layer hid1 via a dot product of the input vector and the weights of the first layer. 6. If self.rgbdepth == 2: Apply ReLU to hid1 to get intermediate values. Compute the second hidden layer hid2 using the weights of the second layer. Apply ReLU to hid2. Apply Sigmoid activation to produce the final output. 7. If self.rgbdepth != 2: Compute the output directly from hid1 using the weights of the single layer. Apply Sigmoid activation to produce the final output. 8. Store the result in self.out3[rayid]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rgbnetworklayer(inputvector, weightslayer1, biaseslayer1, weightslayer2=None, biaseslayer2=None, rgbdepth=2): """ Computes RGB color from input features using an MLP. Args: inputvector: Tensor of shape (..., 32) containing concatenated direction and spatial embeddings. weightslayer1: Tensor of shape (32, hiddendim) for first layer. biaseslayer1: Tensor of shape (hiddendim,) for first layer. weightslayer2: Tensor of shape (hiddendim, 3) for second layer (if depth=2). biaseslayer2: Tensor of shape (3,) for second layer (if depth=2). rgbdepth: Integer, 1 or 2. Returns: Tensor of shape (..., 3) with RGB values in [0, 1]. """ # First hidden layer hid1 = dot(inputvector, weightslayer1) + biaseslayer1 if rgbdepth == 2: # Second hidden layer hid2 = dot(relu(hid1), weightslayer2) + biaseslayer2 # Output layer with sigmoid rgb = sigmoid(hid2) else: # Single layer output with sigmoid rgb = sigmoid(dot(relu(hid1), weightslayer2) + biaseslayer2) return rgb Parameters: rgbdepth: Controls network depth. Value 2 is common. Input dimension: 32 (16 direction + 16 spatial). Output dimension: 3 (RGB). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If rgbdepth is not 1 or 2, behavior is undefined in the source. Precision issues may arise if hid1 or hid2 values are very large before sigmoid; however, the source uses 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) which is numerically stable for positive inputs, but standard sigmoid implementation should be used for negative inputs to avoid overflow. Boundary conditions for ray indices must be handled to ensure sn < didlaunchnum. Predicts physical fields (e.g., density, temperature) instead of RGB. It passes input positions through the neural network and unpacks raw outputs based on the reconstruction target. It reshapes the output tensor to match the input dimensions if necessary. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active samples and rays. The computation per sample is constant (fixed MLP depth). Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of active samples and the size of the weight matrices. Shared memory is used for weights in GPU implementations to reduce latency. Strengths: Simple, fast, and effective for color prediction. The use of shared memory in GPU kernels improves performance. Limitations: Limited to RGB output. Does not handle density or other physical properties directly. When to use: When only color information is needed for the final image. When not to use: When density, opacity, or other physical properties are required for volume integration. The RGB Network Layer is a component of neural volume rendering systems that utilize hash encoding and MLPs for fast rendering. It is commonly found in implementations like the Taichi NGP Renderer and CoroNeRF. The approach leverages the efficiency of MLPs with positional encoding to predict view-dependent color from spatial features.
