featurepointoffset[0])2 + (cellcoordinates[1] + localcoordinates[1] - featurepointoffset[1])2 + (cellcoordinates[2] + localcoordinates[2] - featurepointoffset[2])2) mindistance = min(mindistance, distance) return (1.0 - mindistance) noisestrength def samplemergedtexture(texcoord, useunitedtexture, unitedtexture, noisetexture, detailtexture, lighttexture, masktexture, noisetexturesize, lighttexturesize, masktexturesize, objectscale, textureoffset): if useunitedtexture: finaltexcoord = [(texcoord[i] + 0.5 + textureoffset[i] / noisetexturesize[i] + 1.0) % 1.0 for i in range(3)] data = unitedtexture[finaltexcoord] noise = data[0] detail = data[1] light = data[2] mask = data[3] 32.0 return [noise, detail, light, mask] else: minimalizedobjectscale = [objectscale[i] / max(objectscale[0], max(objectscale[1], objectscale[2])) for i in range(3)] scaledtexcoord = [texcoord[i] minimalizedobjectscale[i] + 0.5 for i in range(3)] noise = noisetexture[scaledtexcoord] detail = detailtexture[scaledtexcoord] light = lighttexture[scaledtexcoord] if uselightmap else 0.65 unscaledtexcoord = [texcoord[i] / minimalizedobjectscale[i] for i in range(3)] mask = masktexture[unscaledtexcoord] return [noise, detail, light, mask] def volumetricsmokerendering(camera, volumebounds, unitedtexture, noisetexture, detailtexture, lighttexture, masktexture, noisetexturesize, lighttexturesize, masktexturesize, objectscale, textureoffset, useunitedtexture, uselightmap, densitythreshold, godraysstrength, lightdecay, lightcolor, lightdirection, densitysamplecount, lightsamplecount, lightsampleperdensitysample, stepsize): h, w = camera.screenheight, camera.screenwidth image = [[vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(w)] for in range(h)] for y in range(h): for x in range(w): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.castray(x, y) accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) hit = rayintersectaabb(volumebounds[0], volumebounds[1], rayorigin, raydirection) raystart = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] hit[0] for i in range(3)] t = hit[0] for step in range(densitysamplecount): if accumulatedcolor[3] >= 0.96: break pos = [raystart[i] + raydirection[i] (t - hit[0]) for i in range(3)] sample = samplemergedtexture(pos, useunitedtexture, unitedtexture, noisetexture, detailtexture, lighttexture, masktexture, noisetexturesize, lighttexturesize, masktexturesize, objectscale, textureoffset) noise, detail, light, mask = sample[0], sample[1], sample[2], sample[3] density = noise + detail mask if density < densitythreshold: density = godraysstrength lightintensity = light (1.0 / (1.0 + lightdecay (t - hit[0]))) if density > godraysstrength 0.5 and lightintensity > 0.5: lightintensity = 1.5 color = [lightcolor[i] lightintensity for i in range(3)] alpha = density stepsize accumulatedcolor = blendftb(accumulatedcolor, vec4(color[0], color[1], color[2], alpha)) t += stepsize image[y][x] = [accumulatedcolor[i] / accumulatedcolor[3] if accumulatedcolor[3] > 0 else 0.0 for i in range(3)] return image densitythreshold: Threshold for density values; if density is below this, it is treated as empty/god ray area. godraysstrength: Constant density value assigned to empty areas to allow god rays to shine through. lightdecay: Exponential decay factor for light intensity over distance. densitysamplecount: Number of steps for density sampling in the ray march. lightsamplecount: Number of steps for light sampling. lightsampleperdensitysample: Ratio of light samples to density samples. lightcolor: RGB color of the light source. lightdirection: Direction vector of the light source. noisestrength: Multiplier for the Worley noise output. octavecount: Number of octaves for Worley noise generation. Default value: 5. persistence: Amplitude multiplier per octave in Worley noise generation. Default value: 0.5f. lacunarity: Frequency multiplier per octave in Worley noise generation. Default value: 2.0f. amplitude: Initial amplitude for Worley noise. Default value: 0.075f. size: Initial resolution for Worley noise texture. Default value: 16. useunitedtexture: Boolean flag (int) to switch between merged texture sampling and individual texture sampling. Default: 0. uselightmap: Boolean flag (int) to enable light map sampling. Default: 0. textureoffset: Vector3 parameter for noise animation offset. Calculated as (0, (-timems 0.003f worleynoisesize.y % worleynoisesize.y), 0). noisetexturesize: Vector3 parameter for Worley noise texture dimensions. lighttexturesize: Vector3 parameter for light map texture dimensions. masktexturesize: Vector3 parameter for density mask texture dimensions. objectscale: Vector4 parameter for object scaling, used to normalize texture coordinates. iteratezevery: Integer parameter controlling how often to iterate through Z slices for 3D slice display. Default: 1. updatelightmapevery: Integer parameter controlling how often to update the light map. Default: 1. timems: Float parameter for time in milliseconds, used for animation. Range: 0 to 128. Texture coordinate wrapping: The united texture sampling uses fmod with +1 to handle negative coordinates and ensure wrapping within 0,1). Mask scaling: The mask value from the united texture is scaled by 32.0f. Light map fallback: If uselightmap is false, the light value is hardcoded to 0.65f. Time Complexity: O(N M) where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the volume of the noise textures. Measured Performance: Real-time performance on modern GPUs using Unity Compute Shaders. Scaling: Scales with resolution and number of samples. Strengths: Real-time performance, procedural density generation, god ray effects. Limitations: Limited to smoke-like effects, requires careful tuning of parameters. When to use: Real-time smoke effects in games and simulations. When not to use: High-fidelity offline rendering, non-smoke volumes. name: Compositing
head: Composite ARGB
body: Compositing is the process of combining multiple color and opacity contributions into a final pixel value, a step required exclusively for semi-transparent volume rendering. It solves the problem of integrating optical properties along a viewing ray to produce a physically plausible image. Unlike Alpha Blending, which typically blends two distinct layers, or Pre-Integration Lookup, which approximates integration via texture lookups, standard compositing explicitly accumulates samples along the ray using the emission-absorption model. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of volume samples (ci, \alphai) encountered along a ray, where ci is the sample color (RGB) and \alphai is the sample opacity (A). The ray originates from the camera and traverses the volume. Output: A final pixel color C{final} and accumulated opacity \alpha{final}. Data Structures: Accumulators: Two variables are maintained per ray: accumColor: A 3-component vector (RGB), initialized to (0, 0, 0). accumAlpha: A scalar (A), initialized to 1.0 (representing 100% transparency/background). Note: Some implementations use a single 4-component vec4 or struct containing both. Steps: 1. Traverse: Iterate through volume samples i = 0 \dots N along the ray, from front (nearest to camera) to back (farthest), or vice versa depending on the chosen order. 2. Transfer Function: For each sample position, retrieve the scalar value from the volume, apply a transfer function to determine the sample's color ci and opacity \alphai. 3. Composite: Update accumulators based on the traversal order. Formulas: Front-to-Back Compositing (Standard): This is the most common approach for semi-transparent rendering. It simulates light emission and absorption. \begin{aligned} C{final} &= \sum{i=0}^{N-1} ci \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \\ \alpha{final} &= 1 - \prod{i=0}^{N-1} (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} In iterative form (per sample i): \begin{aligned} C{final} &\leftarrow C{final} + ci \cdot \alphai \cdot \alpha{transmitted} \\ \alpha{transmitted} &\leftarrow \alpha{transmitted} \cdot (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} Where \alpha{transmitted} is initialized to 1.0 and represents the accumulated transparency \prod (1-\alphaj). Back-to-Front Compositing: Less common for standard volume rendering but used in specific contexts. The order of accumulation is reversed. Parameters: Step Size: Determines sample density. Smaller steps increase accuracy but cost more. Thresholds: Opacity thresholds may be used for early ray termination (if \alpha{final} > 1 - \epsilon, stop) or to ignore negligible samples. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Accumulating many small opacity values can lead to precision errors in \alpha{transmitted} if it approaches zero. Using 1.0 - alpha directly is standard, but care must be taken with very small \alpha values. Order Dependency: The order of compositing matters. Front-to-back is required for the standard emission-absorption model. Back-to-front requires different weighting. Empty Space: If the ray does not intersect the volume, the output should be the background color (often black or the clear color). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackcompositing(samples): """ Composites volume samples using front-to-back alpha blending. Args: samples: List of tuples (colorrgb, opacitya) in front-to-back order. colorrgb is a 3-tuple (r, g, b) in [0, 1]. opacitya is a float in [0, 1]. Returns: finalcolor: 3-tuple (r, g, b) finalopacity: float """ # Initialize accumulators accumcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alphatransmitted = 1.0 for colorrgb, opacitya in samples: # Skip samples with zero opacity to save computation if opacitya == 0.0: continue # Contribution of current sample # ci alphai (1 - alpha0)... (1 - alpha{i-1}) contribution = ( colorrgb[0] opacitya alphatransmitted, colorrgb[1] opacitya alphatransmitted, colorrgb[2] opacitya alphatransmitted) # Add to accumulated color accumcolor = ( accumcolor[0] + contribution[0], accumcolor[1] + contribution[1], accumcolor[2] + contribution[2]) # Update transmitted alpha alphatransmitted = (1.0 - opacitya) # Early ray termination: if fully opaque, stop if alphatransmitted < 1e-6: break finalcolor = accumcolor finalopacity = 1.0 - alphatransmitted return finalcolor, finalopacity Projects a semi-transparent 3D scalar field onto a 2D image plane by integrating optical properties along viewing rays, eliminating the need for binary classification of the data. It differs from Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) by preserving internal texture and visibility through opacity-weighted accumulation rather than selecting only the highest intensity value. The process of combining color and opacity contributions from volume samples into final pixel values for semi-transparent rendering. It solves the problem that volume samples are often generated in slice-by-slice or beam-by-beam order rather than strict ray order, requiring buffering to maintain correct compositing sequence. Unlike Alpha Compositing Ray Casting, which assumes a linear ray traversal, this method handles arbitrary view directions and angled rays by using hardware buffers to align predecessor values for each sample. A compositing scheme that produces an X-ray picture by taking no opacity into account. It sends a ray through the volume and composites all found values with the same weight. 1. Send a ray through the volume. 2. Composite all found values with the same weight. Combines the raymarched result with the existing scene texture using standard alpha blending. 1. Sample the existing scene color from MainTex at the current UV. 2. Call raymarch(ro, rd) to get the raymarched color add. 3. Blend the colors: col (1.0 - add.w) + add.xyz add.w. A projection technique that composites samples along the ray using alpha blending until the ray exits the volume or becomes fully opaque. 1. Initialize contribution = 1.0f. 2. Composite each sample: outputColor.rgb += contribution transfer.a transfer.rgb. 3. Update contribution: contribution = (1 - transfer.a). Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of samples along the ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for accumulators, plus storage for the volume dataset. Performance: Highly parallelizable across pixels and rays. Performance is often limited by memory bandwidth when fetching volume data. Strengths: Physically plausible results for semi-transparent volumes; supports early ray termination for optimization. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution volumes; requires careful handling of sample order and precision. When to Use: Standard direct volume rendering of semi-transparent data (e.g., medical CT/MRI, clouds, smoke). When Not to Use: When only the highest intensity is needed (use MIP) or when opacity is irrelevant (use Average Compositing). Compositing in volume rendering originated with the development of direct volume rendering techniques in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The front-to-back and back-to-front compositing approaches were established as fundamental methods for integrating optical properties along rays. The emission-absorption model, which underpins standard alpha compositing, has been widely adopted in scientific visualization and real-time rendering. name: Alpha Compositing Ray Casting
head: Alpha Compositing with White Background, Front-to-back compositing, Front-to-back ray casting, Volume Compositing, Volumetric Compositing, White Background Compositing
body: Alpha Compositing Ray Casting projects a semi-transparent 3D scalar field onto a 2D image plane by integrating optical properties along viewing rays, eliminating the need for binary classification of the data. It differs from Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) by preserving internal texture and visibility through opacity-weighted accumulation rather than selecting only the highest intensity value. The method discretizes the volume rendering integral into a summation over sample points along a ray, performing front-to-back compositing. Inputs: volumetexture: 3D array or texture storing scalar voxel values. camera: Defines ray origins and directions for each pixel. transferfunction: Maps scalar values to RGB color; opacity is often derived directly from the sampled scalar value rather than a separate alpha channel. Implemented as a 2D texture in WebGL contexts. stepsize: Fixed distance between samples, or derived from volume dimensions. threshold: Opacity threshold for early ray termination (typically 0.95–0.99). Outputs: image: 2D array of RGB values representing the final rendered frame. Volume Texture: 3D array of scalar values. Sampled using trilinear interpolation or nearest neighbor. Transfer Function: 2D texture where the x-coordinate is the scalar value and y-coordinate is fixed (e.g., 0.5). Output is RGB. Accumulators: accumulatedcolor (C'): vec3, initialized to (0, 0, 0). accumulatedopacity (\alpha'): float, initialized to 0.0. 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, compute ray origin \bar{o} and direction \bar{d}. 2. Bounding Box Intersection: Intersect the ray with the volume bounds [0,1]^3 to find entry t0 and exit t1. If t0 > t1, discard the pixel. If the eye is inside the volume, clamp t0 to 0.0. 3. Step Size Calculation: Compute step size dt based on volume dimensions V{dim} and ray direction \bar{d}: dt = \min \left( \frac{1}{V{dim,x} |dx|}, \frac{1}{V{dim,y} |dy|}, \frac{1}{V{dim,z} |dz|} \right). 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate from t = t0 to t < t1 with increment dt: a. Sample: Evaluate scalar value s at position \bar{p} = \bar{o} + t\bar{d}. b. Transfer Function: Map s to color \bar{c}i; opacity \alphai is typically the sampled scalar value itself. c. Compositing: Update accumulators: C'i = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai \bar{c}i \alpha'i = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai. d. Early Termination: If \alpha' \ge \text{threshold} (typically 0.95 or 0.99), break the loop. 5. Gamma Correction: Apply gamma correction (typically 2.2) to the final accumulated color: \bar{C}{final} = \bar{C}'{last}^{1/2.2}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alphacompositingraycast(volumetexture, camera, transferfunction, volumedims, stepsize=None, threshold=0.99): """ Renders a volume using front-to-back alpha compositing. Args: volumetexture: 3D array or texture object supporting trilinear sampling. camera: Object with method castray(x, y) returning (origin, direction). transferfunction: Function or 2D texture mapping scalar value -> (color, opacity). volumedims: Tuple (dimx, dimy, dimz) of the volume grid. stepsize: Fixed marching distance. If None, derived from volumedims. threshold: Opacity threshold for early ray termination. Returns: image: 2D list of RGB values. """ import math H, W = camera.height, camera.width image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.castray(x, y) # Normalize ray direction length = math.sqrt(sum(dd for d in raydirection)) raydirection = [d/length for d in raydirection] accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 if stepsize is None: dirabs = [max(abs(d), 1e-6) for d in raydirection] dtvec = [1.0 / (volumedims[i] dirabs[i]) for i in range(3)] stepsize = min(dtvec) invdir = [1.0 / d if abs(d) > 1e-6 else 1e6 for d in raydirection] boxmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] boxmax = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] tmintmp = [(boxmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tmaxtmp = [(boxmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tmin = [min(tmintmp[i], tmaxtmp[i]) for i in range(3)] tmax = [max(tmintmp[i], tmaxtmp[i]) for i in range(3)] t0 = max(tmin) t1 = min(tmax) if t0 > t1: continue t0 = max(t0, 0.0) t = t0 while t < t1 and accumulatedopacity < threshold: pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] scalarvalue = volumetexture.sampletrilinear(pos) color, opacity = transferfunction(scalarvalue) accumulatedcolor[0] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity color[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity color[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity color[2] accumulatedopacity += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity t += stepsize image[y][x] = [c (1.0/2.2) for c in accumulatedcolor] return image Threshold: Typically 0.95 or 0.99. Higher thresholds improve accuracy but increase computation. Numerical Stability: In some variants, a small epsilon (\epsilon = 10^{-10}) is added to the product term to prevent instability. Zero Direction Components: If a ray direction component is zero, the step size calculation must clamp it to a small positive value to avoid division by zero. Transfer Function Alpha: Some implementations ignore the transfer function's alpha channel and use the sampled scalar value directly as opacity. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of samples per ray. M depends on volume depth and step size. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture, where V is the number of voxels. Performance: Real-time rendering is achievable with hardware acceleration (e.g., WebGL fragment shaders). Software implementations may be slow without optimization. Strengths: Preserves internal structure and texture better than MIP. No binary classification required, reducing false positives/negatives. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large volumes or high resolutions. Sensitive to transfer function design. The technique was popularized by Drebin et al., who introduced volumetric compositing to eliminate binary classification artifacts. Early software implementations were slow, taking several seconds per frame, but later hardware frameworks enabled real-time rendering. It is widely used in medical imaging and scientific visualization. name: Back-to-Front Compositing
head: Back-to-Front Blending Formula, Back-to-front rendering
body: Back-to-Front Compositing is a volume rendering technique that iteratively accumulates color and opacity along a viewing ray by processing samples from the farthest intersection with the volume to the nearest. It solves the problem of blending semi-transparent layers into a final image by applying the Over operator, which is the mathematical inverse of the Under operator used in front-to-back rendering. Unlike front-to-back compositing, this method does not require tracking accumulated opacity for the color calculation, but it does not support early ray termination. It differs from Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) by preserving translucency and internal structure rather than selecting only the highest intensity values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n samples along a ray, sorted in back-to-front order (from farthest to nearest). Each sample i (where i=1 is the farthest and i=n is the nearest) provides a color Ci (or gi in optical models) and an opacity \alphai (or Ai). In optical models, samples also provide a transparency factor ti. Output: The final accumulated color C{acc} (or intensity I) and optionally the accumulated opacity A{acc}. Data Structures: Sample Array: An array of size n. Each element contains fields for color (RGB or scalar intensity) and opacity (alpha). Accumulators: Two variables for the current ray: accumcolor (RGB) and accumopacity (scalar, optional). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the accumulated color C{acc} to black (0, 0, 0) or the background color C{bg} depending on the implementation context. In the pure optical model derivation, the initial intensity I is set to the background intensity I0. Initialize the accumulated opacity A{acc} to 0.0. 2. Segmentation (Optional, for Optical Model): If using the optical model with absorption coefficient \tau(x) and emission coefficient g(x), divide the ray interval from 0 to D into n equal segments of length \Delta x = D/n. Choose sample points xi = i\Delta x for i=1..n. Calculate segment transparency ti = \exp(-\tau(xi) \Delta x) for each segment i. Calculate source term value gi = g(xi) for each segment i. 3. Iteration (Back-to-Front): Loop through samples i from 1 to n (farthest to nearest): Retrieve source color C{src} = Ci and source opacity \alpha{src} = \alphai (or Ai). Update accumulated color: C{acc} \leftarrow Ci + (1 - Ai) C{acc} Or equivalently using the Over operator form: C{dst} \leftarrow (1 - \alpha{src})C{dst} + C{src} where C{dst} is the previous accumulated color. Update accumulated opacity: A{acc} \leftarrow Ai + (1 - Ai) A{acc} where A{acc} is the previous accumulated opacity. 4. Optical Model Specific Iteration: Alternatively, using the Riemann sum approximation for the volume rendering equation: I(D) \approx I0 \prod{i=1}^n ti + \sum{i=1}^n gi \prod{j=i+1}^n tj This can be computed iteratively as: I = I0 \text{for } i = 1 \text{ to } n: I = ti \cdot I + gi Formulas: Color Update (Over Operator): C{acc}^{new} = Ci + (1 - Ai) C{acc}^{old} Opacity Update: A{acc}^{new} = Ai + (1 - Ai) A{acc}^{old} Optical Model Iteration: I{new} = ti \cdot I{old} + gi Parameters: n: Number of samples along the ray. Typical values depend on volume resolution and ray length. Not given in the sources. \Delta x: Segment length. \Delta x = D/n. ti: Transparency of segment i. ti = \exp(-\tau(xi) \Delta x). gi: Emission coefficient at sample i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Early Ray Termination: Back-to-front rendering does not allow for early ray termination because the accumulated opacity is not tracked/updated in the same way as front-to-back, and the contribution of subsequent (closer) samples depends on the accumulated state from the back. Perspective Ray Tracing: Generally, back-to-front rendering does not work with regard to perspective ray tracing and ray casting and is therefore not discussed further in the context of interactive rendering. Precision: When using the optical model, the product of transparencies \prod ti can underflow to zero for long rays or dense volumes, potentially causing loss of distant contributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backtofrontcompositing(samples, backgroundcolor=Vector3(0, 0, 0)): """ Performs back-to-front compositing on a list of samples. Args: samples: List of sample objects/dicts, sorted from farthest to nearest. Each sample has 'color' (Vector3) and 'opacity' (float). backgroundcolor: The color to initialize accumulation with. Returns: Final accumulated color (Vector3) and opacity (float). """ # Initialize accumulators accumcolor = backgroundcolor accumopacity = 0.0 # Iterate from farthest (index 0) to nearest (index n-1) for sample in samples: csrc = sample.color asrc = sample.opacity # Update accumulated color using Over operator # Cacc = Csrc + (1 - Asrc) Cacc accumcolor = csrc + (1.0 - asrc) accumcolor # Update accumulated opacity # Aacc = Asrc + (1 - Asrc) Aacc accumopacity = asrc + (1.0 - asrc) accumopacity return accumcolor, accumopacity def backtofrontopticalmodel(samples, backgroundintensity=0.0): """ Performs back-to-front compositing using the optical model (Riemann sum). Args: samples: List of sample objects/dicts, sorted from farthest to nearest. Each sample has 'transparency' (float, ti) and 'emission' (float, gi). backgroundintensity: The initial intensity I0. Returns: Final accumulated intensity (float). """ # Initialize intensity with background intensity = backgroundintensity # Iterate from farthest (index 0) to nearest (index n-1) for sample in samples: ti = sample.transparency gi = sample.emission # Update intensity: I = ti I + gi intensity = ti intensity + gi return intensity Front-to-Back Compositing is a volume rendering technique that iteratively accumulates color and opacity along a viewing ray, processing samples from the nearest to the farthest intersection with the volume. It solves the problem of blending semi-transparent layers into a final image by applying the Under operator (also known as the front-to-back compositing equation), which is the mathematical inverse of the standard Over operator used in back-to-front rendering. Unlike back-to-front compositing, this method requires tracking accumulated opacity to modulate the contribution of subsequent samples, but it enables early ray termination when the accumulated opacity reaches unity, optimizing performance. It differs from Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) by preserving translucency and internal structure rather than selecting only the highest intensity values. Time Complexity: O(n) per ray, where n is the number of samples. No early ray termination is possible, so all samples must be processed. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for accumulators, plus O(n) to store samples if not streamed. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with the number of samples. Strengths: Simpler color calculation as it does not require tracking accumulated opacity for the color contribution. Easily implemented with hardware alpha blending by setting source blending factor to 1 and destination blending factor to (1 – source alpha). Limitations: Does not support early ray termination, leading to higher computational cost for transparent volumes. Generally not suitable for perspective ray tracing and interactive rendering due to these limitations. When to use: When hardware alpha blending is preferred and early ray termination is not critical. When not to use: In interactive rendering where performance is key and early ray termination is beneficial. Origin: The back-to-front compositing scheme is derived from reversing the traversal direction of front-to-back rendering. It is based on the Over operator, which is a standard compositing equation. History: The method is discussed in the context of volume rendering techniques, particularly in GPU Gems Chapter 39. It is also related to the Riemann sum approximation of the volume rendering equation. Usage: Used in volume rendering for blending semi-transparent layers. It is less common in interactive rendering compared to front-to-back compositing due to the lack of early ray termination. name: Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator)
head: Accumulate Compositing, Front-to-Back Accumulation, Front-to-Back Blending Formula, Front-to-Back Compositing with Alpha Correction, Front-to-back rendering, Standard Front-to-Back Volume Compositing
body: Front-to-Back Compositing is a volume rendering technique that iteratively accumulates color and opacity along a viewing ray, processing samples from the nearest to the farthest intersection with the volume. It solves the problem of blending semi-transparent layers into a final image by applying the Under operator (also known as the front-to-back compositing equation), which is the mathematical inverse of the standard Over operator used in back-to-front rendering. Unlike back-to-front compositing, this method requires tracking accumulated opacity to modulate the contribution of subsequent samples, but it enables early ray termination when the accumulated opacity reaches unity, optimizing performance. It differs from Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) by preserving translucency and internal structure rather than selecting only the highest intensity values. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D. Volume dataset V (scalar field). Transfer function TF mapping scalar values to color (C) and opacity (\alpha). Step size s (or adaptive step logic). Near and far clipping planes t{near}, t{far}. Outputs: Final pixel color C{acc} and opacity A{acc} (typically A{acc} is discarded or used for transparency compositing into the background). Data Structures: Accumulated Color: C{acc} = (0, 0, 0) Accumulated Opacity: A{acc} = 0 Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set C{acc} = \vec{0}, A{acc} = 0. Determine ray start t = t{near}. 2. Traversal Loop: While t < t{far} and A{acc} < 1.0 (early termination condition): a. Sample: Evaluate the volume at position P = O + t \cdot D. Let the scalar value be v. b. Transfer Function: Map v to base color C{base} and base opacity \alpha{base} using TF(v). c. Alpha Correction: Adjust \alpha{base} for the step size to ensure physical correctness of the emission-absorption model. A common correction factor involves the step size s and a density scaling factor (e.g., 200.0 in some implementations): \alpha{corrected} = 1.0 - (1.0 - \alpha{base})^{s \cdot k} where k is a constant (e.g., 200.0) representing the number of samples per unit density or a normalization factor. d. Lighting (Optional): Compute shaded color C{shaded} using normal estimation and lighting models, or use C{base} if lighting is disabled. e. Shadowing (Optional): Compute shadow factor \eta{shadow}. f. Compositing (Under Operator): Blend the current sample into the accumulator. The current sample acts as the "source" and the accumulator as the "destination" in hardware blending terms, but mathematically it is: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + (1 - A{acc}) \cdot C{shaded} \cdot \eta{shadow} \cdot \alpha{corrected} A{acc} \leftarrow A{acc} + (1 - A{acc}) \cdot \alpha{corrected} Note: Some implementations multiply RGB by alpha before blending: C{in} = C{shaded} \cdot \alpha{corrected}, then C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + (1 - A{acc}) \cdot C{in}. g. Advance: t \leftarrow t + s. 3. Final Output: The final color is C{acc}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackcompositing(rayorigin, raydir, volume, transferfunction, tnear, tfar, stepsize, enablelighting, enableshadow): # Initialize accumulators acccolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 t = tnear # Pre-calculate constants if needed # adjustedalphafactor is often derived from stepsize and volume dimensions # For simplicity, we assume stepsize is normalized or corrected internally while t < tfar and accalpha < 1.0: # 1. Sample Position samplepos = rayorigin + raydir t # 2. Check bounds (implementation specific, e.g., voxel grid bounds) if not isinsidevolume(samplepos): t += stepsize continue # 3. Get scalar value val = samplevolume(volume, samplepos) # 4. Transfer Function basecolor, basealpha = transferfunction(val) # 5. Alpha Correction for step size # Formula from: acorrected = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - ain, stepsize 200.0) # Note: stepsize here should be consistent with the exponent's scaling factor. # If stepsize is in world units, it may need normalization. alphacorrected = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - basealpha, stepsize 200.0) # 6. Lighting if enablelighting: normal = calculatenormal(samplepos, volume) shadedcolor = calculatelighting(normal, -raydir, samplepos, basecolor.rgb) else: shadedcolor = basecolor.rgb # 7. Shadowing if enableshadow: shadowfactor = calculateshadow(samplepos) else: shadowfactor = 1.0 # 8. Compositing (Under Operator) # Cacc = Cacc + (1 - Aacc) Cshaded shadowfactor alphacorrected # Aacc = Aacc + (1 - Aacc) alphacorrected contribution = shadedcolor shadowfactor alphacorrected acccolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accalpha) contribution accalpha = accalpha + (1.0 - accalpha) alphacorrected # 9. Advance t += stepsize return acccolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alpha Correction: The exponent multiplier (e.g., 200.0) is often hardcoded and depends on the specific volume density scaling and step size units. Incorrect scaling leads to overly transparent or opaque volumes. Early Termination: If A{acc} reaches 1.0, the loop terminates. This is valid because (1 - 1.0) = 0, so subsequent samples contribute nothing. Precision: Accumulating many small alpha values can suffer from floating-point precision issues if not handled carefully, though standard float is usually sufficient for typical ray lengths. A variant that modulates accumulated transparency based on an importance measure before blending, avoiding color clipping and complex tone-mapping. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. However, early ray termination significantly reduces the average N for opaque regions, making it faster than back-to-front rendering which must process all samples. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray (only accumulators are stored). Strengths: Supports early ray termination; naturally handles semi-transparent structures; standard hardware support via alpha blending (Under operator). Limitations: Requires tracking accumulated opacity; order-dependent (must be front-to-back); sensitive to step size and alpha correction parameters. When to use: When visualizing semi-transparent volumes with early termination benefits is desired. When not to use: When back-to-front ordering is required (e.g., for specific compositing with background geometry that must be behind the volume) or when using hardware that only supports Over operator blending efficiently without read-modify-write shaders. The front-to-back compositing equation, often referred to as the Under operator, is the inverse of the Over operator used in back-to-front rendering. It is derived from the emission-absorption model in volume rendering. The technique is widely used in direct volume ray casting to accumulate color and opacity from the front of the volume to the back, allowing for efficient early ray termination. It is a fundamental component of many volume rendering pipelines, often implemented in fragment shaders or via hardware alpha blending with specific blend factors. Chapter 39. name: Importance-Based Accumulated Transparency Modulation
head: Generalized MIDA, IBATM
body: Importance-Based Accumulated Transparency Modulation (IBATM) is a volume rendering compositing technique that highlights specific features by modulating accumulated transparency based on the difference between an importance measure of the incoming sample and the accumulated result along a viewing ray. Unlike its predecessor Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA), which modulates accumulated color, IBATM modulates only accumulated transparency, thereby avoiding color values exceeding unity and the need for complex tone-mapping within the core algorithm. It builds on Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator) by inserting a transparency modulation step before the standard over-operator blend. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray passing through a volume, defined by a sequence of samples si sorted in front-to-back order. Each sample si has color ci and opacity \alphai. An importance measure function F and an assembling function B. Output: Final accumulated color c{dst} and accumulated opacity \alpha{dst} for the ray. Data Structures: cdst: Floating-point accumulator for color (RGB). Initialized to (0, 0, 0). alphadst: Floating-point accumulator for opacity. Initialized to 0.0. facc: Floating-point accumulator for the importance measure of the accumulated result. Initialized to 0.0 (or appropriate identity for F). Parameters: F: Importance measure function. Must be designed according to application requirements (e.g., scalar intensity, gradient magnitude). B: Assembling function mapping importance difference to \beta \in (0, 1]. \Delta{imp}: Difference function between incoming importance fi and accumulated importance f{acc}. Usually subtraction, but not restricted to it. Steps: 1. Initialize cdst = (0, 0, 0), alphadst = 0.0, facc = F(\text{identity}). 2. For each sample si along the ray in front-to-back order: a. Calculate incoming importance: fi = F(si). b. Calculate accumulated importance: f{acc} = F(\text{accumulated state}). Note: The exact definition of F applied to the accumulated state depends on the specific measure F chosen. For scalar intensity, this might be the max intensity seen so far. c. Calculate importance difference: \Delta{imp} = \Delta{imp}(fi, f{acc}). d. Compute modulation factor: \beta = B(\Delta{imp}). e. Update accumulated transparency: \alpha{dst} \leftarrow \beta \cdot \alpha{dst}. f. Update accumulated color: c{dst} \leftarrow c{dst} + (1 - \alpha{dst}) \cdot ci. g. Update accumulated transparency: \alpha{dst} \leftarrow \alpha{dst} + (1 - \alpha{dst}) \cdot \alphai. h. Update accumulated importance: f{acc} \leftarrow F(\text{new accumulated state}). [G: The source does not explicitly define how f{acc} is updated after compositing. It is implied that f{acc} represents the importance of the current accumulated result. For MIDA, F is max intensity, so f{acc} would be \max(f{acc}, fi). For other measures, this update rule must be defined by the user.] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ibatmcomposite(samples, F, B, deltaimp): """ samples: list of tuples (c, alpha) in front-to-back order F: function that takes a sample or accumulated state and returns importance value B: function that takes deltaimp and returns beta in (0, 1] deltaimp: function that takes fi and facc and returns difference """ cdst = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alphadst = 0.0 # Initialize facc based on F's identity element or 0. # For max intensity, this would be -infinity or 0 if intensities are non-negative. # The source does not specify the exact initialization or update rule for facc # for general F, only that facc = F(accumulated samples). # We assume facc is updated after each step to reflect the importance of the current accumulation. # For MIDA (max intensity), facc = max(facc, fi). # For other measures, this must be defined. facc = F(identity) # Placeholder for initialization logic specific to F for csrc, alphasrc in samples: fi = F(csrc, alphasrc) # Importance of incoming sample # Calculate difference between incoming importance and accumulated importance delta = deltaimp(fi, facc) # Compute modulation factor beta = B(delta) # Modulate accumulated transparency alphadst = beta alphadst # Standard over-operator color blend cdst = cdst + (1.0 - alphadst) csrc # Standard over-operator opacity blend alphadst = alphadst + (1.0 - alphadst) alphasrc # Update accumulated importance for next iteration # The source states facc = F(accumulated samples). # For MIDA, this is max intensity, so facc = max(facc, fi). # For general F, this update rule is application-dependent. # Assuming a common pattern where accumulated importance is updated # by combining the new sample's importance with the previous accumulated importance. # For max intensity: facc = max(facc, fi) # For other measures, this step requires user-defined logic. facc = F(facc, csrc, alphasrc) # Placeholder for update logic specific to F return cdst, alphadst Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Dynamic Range: The resulting volume renderings are high dynamic range because transparency modulation can allow more light to pass through, increasing color intensity. Sophisticated tone-mapping is not included in the core algorithm; the authors use brightness/contrast and a gamma curve to adjust the result. Color Accumulation: Unlike MIDA, IBATM does not modulate accumulated color. This is because color can accumulate beyond 1 and requires tone-mapping, while transparency is bounded by 1 (full opacity). Importance Measure Design: The effectiveness of IBATM depends heavily on the choice of F and B. These must be designed according to application requirements. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of samples per ray, O(N), same as standard front-to-back compositing. The additional cost is the computation of F, \Delta{imp}, and B per sample. Memory Complexity: Constant per ray, O(1), for accumulators. Strengths: Highlights features by modifying accumulated transparency rather than manipulating transfer functions, which can be sensitive and complex to tune. It generalizes MIDA to other importance measures. Limitations: Results are high dynamic range, requiring post-processing (tone-mapping) for display. The choice of importance measure F and assembling function B is application-dependent and not specified by the core algorithm. When to use: When specific features need to be highlighted without fine-tuning transfer functions, or when extending MIDA-like behavior to other importance measures. When not to use: When standard, predictable compositing is required, or when high dynamic range results are undesirable without additional tone-mapping steps. IBATM was proposed as a generalization and extension of the Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA) technique. It was introduced to address the sensitivity of transfer functions and the complexity of fine-tuning them in direct volume rendering, which limits its widespread practical use. The method allows for fast volumetric data exploration by highlighting features through importance-based transparency modulation. It is particularly useful for datasets where features are characterized by high magnitude or high depth value along the viewing ray. The authors demonstrated that by using several common importance measures, different features of volumetric datasets can be highlighted. The results can be extended to a high-dimensional importance difference space by mixing results from an arbitrary number of importance measures with weighting factors. Fast Volumetric Data Exploration with Importance-Based Accumulated Transparency Modulation, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg10/061-068, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Subvolume Tracing
head: Ray Marching Subvolume
body: Subvolume Tracing renders a localized region of a volume by walking a fixed number of voxels deep along a ray and compositing the data from back to front. It differs from full volume ray casting by limiting the trace depth to a small, configurable fraction of the volume, making it suitable for interactive applications where rendering the entire volume is too expensive. It builds on Alpha Compositing Ray Casting by restricting the sampling range. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The position of the object in world space (objPosStart), the camera position in volume space (cameraPosVolSpace), and volume data accessible via SampleVol and ShadeVol functions. Output: A final color and alpha value for the pixel. Data Structures: curColor: A 4-component vector (RGBA) initialized to transparent black (0, 0, 0, 0). curCoord: A 3D coordinate in volume space representing the current sampling position. stepCoord: A 3D vector representing the step size between samples. Parameters: maxDepth: The depth in volume space to trace. Typical value is 0.15. numLoops: The number of sampling steps. Typical value is 10, though it can be increased to 400 on high-end hardware. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Calculate the object's position in volume space using a WorldToVolume matrix. Calculate the camera's position in volume space using the same matrix. 2. Boundary Calculation: Determine the front and back coordinates of the subvolume segment. frontCoord is the object's position in volume space. backCoord is calculated as frontCoord + (normalized camera direction maxDepth). The camera direction is normalize(cameraPosVolSpace - objPosStart). 3. Step Vector Calculation: Compute the step vector: stepCoord = \frac{frontCoord - backCoord}{numLoops} 4. Initialization: Set curCoord to backCoord. 5. Aliasing Prevention: Add a per-pixel random offset to curCoord to avoid layer aliasing. The offset is stepCoord RandomFromPositionFast(objPosStart). 6. Loop: Iterate numLoops times: Sample the volume at curCoord to get intensity. Shade the intensity to get a src color/alpha pair. Composite src into curColor using alpha blending. Increment curCoord by stepCoord. 7. Return: Return curColor. Alpha Blending Formula: The blending operation combines the source color (src) and destination color (dst) as follows: res.rgb = (src.rgb \times src.a) + (dst.rgb - dst.rgb \times src.a) res.a = src.a + (dst.a - dst.a \times src.a) [ S1] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def subvolumetrace(objposstart, cameraposvolspace, maxdepth=0.15, numloops=10): # 1. Coordinate Transformation # Assuming volspace and camerainvolspace are pre-calculated in vertex shader # volspace = mul(WorldToVolume, float4(objposstart, 1)) # camerainvolspace = mul(WorldToVolume, float4(cameraposvolspace, 1)) frontcoord = objposstart # Camera direction in volume space camdir = normalize(cameraposvolspace - objposstart) backcoord = frontcoord + (camdir maxdepth) # 3. Step Vector Calculation stepcoord = (frontcoord - backcoord) / numloops # 4. Initialization curcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) curcoord = backcoord # 5. Aliasing Prevention # RandomFromPositionFast is a pseudo-random function based on position randomoffset = stepcoord randomfrompositionfast(objposstart) curcoord += randomoffset # 6. Loop for i in range(numloops): intensity = samplevol(curcoord) shaded = shadevol(intensity) curcolor = alphablend(curcolor, shaded) curcoord += stepcoord return curcolor def alphablend(dst, src): # dst and src are (r, g, b, a) tuples resr = (src.r src.a) + (dst.r - dst.r src.a) resg = (src.g src.a) + (dst.g - dst.g src.a) resb = (src.b src.a) + (dst.b - dst.b src.a) resa = src.a + (dst.a - dst.a src.a) return (resr, resg, resb, resa) Extends subvolume tracing to render the entire volume by calculating the full path length through the volume cube. It differs by dynamically determining numLoops based on the distance through the volume rather than a fixed maxDepth. To choose this variant, use it when the entire volume must be visible. It sets maxDepth to 1.73 (\sqrt{3}), the maximum distance from a point on a unit cube to any other point. It trims front and back positions to be within the volume cube bounds. The number of loops is calculated as: distanceInVoxels = length(UnitVolumeToIntVolume(frontPos - backPos)) numLoops = min(distanceInVoxels, maxSamples) where maxSamples is typically 400 to keep within bounds. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to numLoops. Memory Complexity: Constant, storing only current color and coordinates. Performance: Typical settings use numLoops=10 for interactive performance, scalable to 400 on high-end PCs. Strengths: Fast rendering of local details; avoids aliasing with random offset. Limitations: Does not render the full volume; depth is fixed relative to object position. Originating from Microsoft's Mixed Reality development documentation, this method is designed for GPU-based volume rendering in shaders. It is used in mixed reality applications to render volume data efficiently. Volume rendering - Mixed Reality | Microsoft Learn, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/mixed-reality/develop/native/volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Ray Compositing and Accumulation
head: Hardware Ray Compositing, Ray Beam FIFO, Ray Shift Register, Ray Slice FIFO
body: Ray Compositing and Accumulation is the process of combining color and opacity contributions from volume samples into final pixel values for semi-transparent rendering. It solves the problem that volume samples are often generated in slice-by-slice or beam-by-beam order rather than strict ray order, requiring buffering to maintain correct compositing sequence. Unlike Alpha Compositing Ray Casting, which assumes a linear ray traversal, this method handles arbitrary view directions and angled rays by using hardware buffers to align predecessor values for each sample. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of color (C{sample}) and opacity (\alpha{sample}) values at sample points, presented in slice-by-slice, beam-by-beam order. Output: Final pixel values written to Pixel Memory, which are then transferred to a companion 3D graphics card for image warping. Data Structures: The method relies on three specific hardware buffers to store partially accumulated ray values: 1. Ray Slice FIFO: Stores partially accumulated pixel values for compositing with the next slice. 2. Ray Beam FIFO: Stores values for an additional beam time duration to handle downward-angled rays, allowing input from the beam above and before the current sample. 3. Ray Shift Register: Stores values for one additional cycle to handle samples to the left of the current one. Parameters: Precision: 12 bits are maintained for accumulated color (C{acc}), accumulated opacity (\alpha{acc}), and all intermediate compositing values to ensure correct alpha blending in large volumes. Steps: 1. Determine Predecessor: For a sample S(x,y,z), identify the correct predecessor value from the previous slice. The predecessor is one of S(x,y,z-1), S(x-1,y,z-1), S(x,y-1,z-1), or S(x-1,y-1,z-1), selected based on the view direction and the z value of the sample. 2. Select Predecessor: Use a Ray Alignment unit to drive two multiplexers (MUX) that select the correct predecessor value from the Ray Slice FIFO, Ray Beam FIFO, or Ray Shift Register. 3. Composite: Combine the current sample's color and opacity with the selected predecessor value using the chosen blending mode (e.g., Front-to-back blending). 4. Buffer: Store the resulting partially accumulated value back into the appropriate buffer (Ray Slice FIFO, Ray Beam FIFO, or Ray Shift Register) for the next sample in the stream. 5. Output: When a ray passes through the back of the volume (maximum z) or a side face, output the final accumulated pixel value. 6. Write: Write base plane pixel values to Pixel Memory. Formulas: For Front-to-back blending, the accumulated color C{acc} and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} are updated as follows: C{acc}^{new} = C{acc}^{old} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{old}) \cdot C{sample} \alpha{acc}^{new} = \alpha{acc}^{old} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{old}) \cdot \alpha{sample} Other blending modes supported include Minimum Intensity and Maximum Intensity, which compare C{sample} against C{acc} based on thresholds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. rayslicefifo = Buffer() raybeamfifo = Buffer() rayshiftregister = Buffer() PRECISIONBITS = 12 def compositefronttoback(cacc, alphaacc, csample, alphasample): """Perform front-to-back alpha blending.""" # Apply precision constraints if necessary cacc = quantize(cacc, PRECISIONBITS) alphaacc = quantize(alphaacc, PRECISIONBITS) cnew = cacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) csample alphanew = alphaacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) alphasample return quantize(cnew, PRECISIONBITS), quantize(alphanew, PRECISIONBITS) def getpredecessor(viewdirection, z, x, y): """ Determine which buffer holds the correct predecessor value. This is a simplified logic based on. """ # Logic depends on view direction and z value # Returns value from one of the FIFOs/Registers # Note: Exact mapping requires Ray Alignment unit logic not fully detailed in text # Placeholder for Ray Alignment unit logic return rayslicefifo.read() # Simplified assumption def processsamplestream(samples): """ Process a stream of samples. samples: list of (Csample, alphasample, x, y, z, viewdirection) """ pixelmemory = {} # Map (x,y) -> (Cacc, alphaacc) for sample in samples: csample, alphasample, x, y, z, viewdir = sample # 1. Determine Predecessor # In hardware, this is done by Ray Alignment unit driving MUXes # We assume the correct buffer is selected based on geometry cacc, alphaacc = getpredecessor(viewdir, z, x, y) # 2. Composite cnew, alphanew = compositefronttoback(cacc, alphaacc, csample, alphasample) # 3. Buffer for next steps # Logic to write back to FIFOs/Registers based on view direction # This is implicit in the hardware description updatebuffers(x, y, z, viewdir, cnew, alphanew) # 4. Output if ray ends if israyend(z, viewdir): pixelmemory[(x, y)] = (cnew, alphanew) return pixelmemory def updatebuffers(x, y, z, viewdir, cacc, alphaacc): """ Update Ray Slice FIFO, Ray Beam FIFO, and Ray Shift Register. Specific update logic depends on view direction and beam alignment """ # Simplified: always update slice FIFO for next slice rayslicefifo.write((x, y), (cacc, alphaacc)) # Ray Beam FIFO and Shift Register updates depend on specific ray angles Scatter-Add Accumulation accumulates weighted values along rays using scatter-add operations, supporting both feature accumulation and weight-only accumulation. It is used when values are provided to compute weighted features (weighted = weights[:, None] values) or when accumulating weights only (output = output + weights[:, None]). This method initializes an output buffer of shape [n\rays, C] and performs scatter-add using ray indices (output = output.at[ray\indices].add(weighted)). It is suitable for implementations where ray indices are known and random access to the output buffer is efficient. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples, as each sample is processed once. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of rays and the depth of the FIFOs/Registers, which depend on the volume size and view angle. Strengths: Handles non-ray-order sample presentation efficiently in hardware; supports multiple blending modes. Limitations: Requires significant hardware resources for FIFOs and alignment logic; precision loss can occur if bit depth is insufficient for large volumes. When to use: Real-time ray casting on hardware architectures like VolumePro. When not to use: Software implementations where memory bandwidth is limited and FIFO simulation is expensive. Ray Compositing and Accumulation was developed as part of the VolumePro real-time ray-casting system. It was designed to handle the specific data flow of slice-by-slice, beam-by-beam rendering on dedicated hardware. The method addresses the challenge of maintaining correct compositing order when samples are not generated in strict ray order. name: Pre-Integration Lookup
head: 3D Pre-integration Table, Pre-integrated Transfer Functions
body: Pre-integration lookup is a technique in direct volume ray casting that pre-computes the optical properties (color and opacity) of volume slabs, assuming linear evolution of scalar data within the slab. It solves the problem of accurately approximating the volume rendering integral for a slab without performing expensive per-slab integration during rendering. It sets itself apart from standard compositing by replacing the per-sample transfer function application with a 3D texture lookup indexed by entry density, exit density, and slab thickness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D scalar volume data, transfer functions (opacity and color), slab thickness parameter d. Output: Final pixel color via front-to-back compositing. Data Structures: Pre-integration Table: A 3D texture (or 3D lookup table) of size N \times N \times N (typically 256^3 for 8-bit scalar data). Dimensions correspond to: sf: Entry scalar value (front sample). sm: Middle scalar value. sb: Exit scalar value (back sample). Stored values: Pre-computed color (C) and opacity (\alpha) contributions for the slab defined by these three scalar values. Volume Data: 3D texture or array storing scalar values. Method Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Offline or Initialization): For every triplet (sf, sm, sb) in the domain of the transfer functions: Assume the scalar field varies linearly from sf to sb through sm over the slab thickness 2d. Compute the integrated color and opacity for this slab using the transfer functions. The integral accounts for the attenuation of light as it passes through the slab with varying density. Store the resulting (C, \alpha) in the 3D pre-integration table at index (sf, sm, sb). Note: The sources describe the table as providing "optical properties for volume slices" where data evolution is linear. The specific integral formula is not provided in the text, but the table maps the three scalar endpoints to the slab's cumulative optical effect. 2. Rendering (Per Pixel): For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. Divide the ray into slabs of thickness 2d. For each slab: Retrieve the three scalar sample values from the volume data: sf (front), sm (middle), sb (back). Perform a 3D texture lookup in the pre-integration table using (sf, sm, sb) as coordinates. Fetch the pre-computed color C{slab} and opacity \alpha{slab} for this slab. Composite the slabs using front-to-back compositing: C{out} = C{in} + C{slab} \cdot \alpha{slab} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha{slab} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) where C{in}, \alpha{in} are the accumulated color and opacity from previous slabs. Repeat for all slabs along the ray. Parameters: Slab thickness d: Defines the resolution of the pre-integration. Smaller d increases accuracy but requires more slabs and larger tables if the domain is fixed. Table size: Typically 256^3 for 8-bit data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The table size is limited by memory. For 8-bit data, 256^3 entries may be large. Linear Assumption: The method assumes linear scalar evolution within the slab. If the scalar field varies non-linearly within a slab, errors may occur. Boundary Conditions: The correlation sf = sb for adjacent slabs ensures continuity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputetable(volumeresolution, slabthickness, transfercolor, transferopacity): # Initialize 3D table of size 256x256x256 table = zeros(256, 256, 256, 4) # RGBA for sf in range(256): for sm in range(256): for sb in range(256): # Compute integrated color and opacity for slab with front=SF, mid=SM, back=SB # This involves integrating the transfer functions over the linear path # Formula not explicitly given in sources, but implied by "pre-calculated functions" c, a = integrateslabopticalproperties(sf, sm, sb, slabthickness, transfercolor, transferopacity) table[sf, sm, sb] = [c.r, c.g, c.b, a] return table def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, preinttable, slabthickness): accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] t = 0.0 while t < raylength: # Define slab boundaries slabfront = t slabback = t + 2 slabthickness # Sample scalar values at front, middle, back of slab sf = samplevolume(volumedata, rayorigin + raydirection slabfront) sm = samplevolume(volumedata, rayorigin + raydirection (slabfront + slabthickness)) sb = samplevolume(volumedata, rayorigin + raydirection slabback) # Lookup pre-integrated properties # Note: sf, sm, sb must be quantized to table indices idxf = quantize(sf) idxm = quantize(sm) idxb = quantize(sb) slabcolor, slabalpha = preinttable[idxf, idxm, idxb] # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = Cin + Cslab alphaslab (1 - alphain) # alphaout = alphain + alphaslab (1 - alphain) if slabalpha > 0: weight = slabalpha (1 - accumulatedcolor[3]) accumulatedcolor[0] += slabcolor[0] weight accumulatedcolor[1] += slabcolor[1] weight accumulatedcolor[2] += slabcolor[2] weight accumulatedcolor[3] += slabalpha (1 - accumulatedcolor[3]) t += 2 slabthickness return accumulatedcolor This method computes the diffuse component of Blinn-Phong shading in direct volume ray casting by approximating the integral of light interaction over a sampling step using non-linear gradient interpolation [4932-pre-integrated-diffuse-shading-with-non-linear-gradient-inte.md]. It decomposes the shading integral into four 2D look-up tables (LUTs) indexed by front and back scalar values, weighted by coefficients derived from light direction and gradient angles [4932-pre-integrated-diffuse-shading-with-non-linear-gradient-inte.md]. It sets itself apart from linear gradient interpolation by reducing shading errors caused by large angles between consecutive sample gradients, while avoiding the prohibitive memory cost of full 4D normal-based pre-integration [4932-pre-integrated-diffuse-shading-with-non-linear-gradient-inte.md]. Choose this when accurate shading is required but 4D tables are too large. Link: Pre-Integrated Diffuse Shading with Non-Linear Gradient Interpolation. This method approximates the non-linear path of a normalized gradient vector between front and back sample normals in pre-integrated volume rendering using a quadratic polynomial, thereby correcting the energy loss and shading errors inherent in linear interpolation. It enables the use of 2D pre-integration lookup tables instead of 3D tables, maintaining low memory usage and allowing real-time updates during transfer function changes. Choose this when shading accuracy is critical and memory is constrained. Link: Non-Linear Gradient Interpolation for Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering. A method for efficiently reconstructing 3D medical images that combines pre-integrated volume rendering with the Shear-Warp algorithm to eliminate aliasing artifacts from under-sampling and improve reconstruction quality via Phong lighting shading. It implements classification coding for volume data by utilizing the correlation of the opacity transfer function (OTF) and a min-max Octree data structure, establishing a new run-length encoded (RLE) data structure for fast reconstruction when OTF and view angle change. It incorporates pre-integrated volume rendering with Phong lighting shading calculation to eliminate aliasing artifacts. Choose this for fast, high-quality medical image reconstruction with dynamic OTF changes. A faster approximation of pre-integration that neglects color attenuation inside volume slabs, used in the first level of interaction where multiple TFs are modified. It is applied in the first level of the interface to handle actions that modify several TFs simultaneously, while full pre-integration is applied in the second level where a single TF is under modification, to maintain quality without compromising interactivity. Choose this for interactive transfer function design tools where speed is prioritized for multi-TF adjustments. Time Complexity: Pre-computation is O(N^3) where N is the number of scalar levels (e.g., 256^3). Rendering is O(1) per slab for the lookup, plus sampling cost. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the 3D pre-integration table. For 8-bit data, 256^3 entries, each storing RGBA, can be large. Measured Performance: Implemented on GPU for real-time performance. The 3D texture lookup is efficient on modern GPUs. Strengths: Accurate approximation of the volume rendering integral for slabs; efficient rendering via texture lookup; supports real-time updates if tables are small or recomputed efficiently. Limitations: High memory usage for large tables; assumes linear scalar evolution within slabs; less accurate for non-linear data. When to use: When accurate volume rendering is needed and memory allows for large 3D tables; suitable for GPU implementation. When not to use: When memory is severely constrained; when data varies non-linearly within slabs and high accuracy is required. Originated in the context of GPU-based volume rendering to accelerate the evaluation of the volume rendering integral. The concept of pre-integrated transfer functions was introduced to provide optical properties for volume slices assuming linear data evolution. It has been implemented on GPUs for real-time rendering. Variants include shading-aware pre-integration and simplified pre-integration for interactive tools. name: Pre-Integrated Diffuse Shading with Non-Linear Gradient Interpolation
head: Pre-Integrated Diffuse Shading
body: This method computes the diffuse component of Blinn-Phong shading in direct volume ray casting by approximating the integral of light interaction over a sampling step using non-linear gradient interpolation. It decomposes the shading integral into four 2D look-up tables (LUTs) indexed by front and back scalar values, weighted by coefficients derived from light direction and gradient angles. It sets itself apart from linear gradient interpolation by reducing shading errors caused by large angles between consecutive sample gradients, while avoiding the prohibitive memory cost of full 4D normal-based pre-integration. Inputs: Front scalar value Sf and back scalar value Sb for the current sampling step of length D. Front normal \mathbf{N}f and back normal \mathbf{N}b (gradients of the scalar field). Light direction \mathbf{L}. Diffuse coefficient Kd. Pre-computed 2D LUTs for I0, I1, I2, I3. Outputs: Pre-integrated diffuse color \tilde{C}d. Lookup Tables: Four 2D arrays, each of size N \times N, where N is the number of discrete bins for scalar values. LUTI0[Sfidx][Sbidx] stores I0(Sf, Sb). LUTI1[Sfidx][Sbidx] stores I1(Sf, Sb). LUTI2[Sfidx][Sbidx] stores I2(Sf, Sb). LUTI3[Sfidx][Sbidx] stores I3(Sf, Sb). Indices are derived by quantizing Sf and Sb into the table's scalar range. The pre-integrated diffuse color is calculated as: \tilde{C}d = Kd \cdot (a0(\mathbf{L})I0 + a1(\mathbf{L})I1 + a2(\mathbf{L})I2 + a3(\mathbf{L})I3) The integral terms Ik(Sf, Sb) are defined as: Ik(Sf, Sb) = d \int{Sf}^{Sb} c(s0) \cdot s^k \cdot \exp(-d \cdot \sigma(Sf, s0)) \, ds0 where: k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}. c(s0) is the classification color at scalar value s0. \sigma(Sf, s0) is the accumulated absorption from Sf to s0. d = \frac{D}{Sb - Sf} is the normalized step length. s = \frac{s0 - Sf}{Sb - Sf} is the normalized position within the step. The coefficients ak(\mathbf{L}) depend on the light direction and normals: \begin{aligned} a0(\mathbf{L}) &= \mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L} \\ a1(\mathbf{L}) &= \mathbf{N}b \cdot \mathbf{L} - (1 + r)\mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L} \\ a2(\mathbf{L}) &= r(2\mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{N}b \cdot \mathbf{L}) \\ a3(\mathbf{L}) &= r(\mathbf{N}b \cdot \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L}) \end{aligned} where r is a factor derived from the angle \alpha between the front and back normals: r = \frac{4(\cos(\alpha) - 1)}{\cos(\alpha)} \alpha = \frac{1}{2} \arccos(\mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{N}b) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputeluts(numbins, scalarmin, scalarmax, classificationfunc, absorptionfunc): """ Pre-compute the four 2D lookup tables I0, I1, I2, I3. classificationfunc(s) returns color c(s). absorptionfunc(sf, s) returns sigma(Sf, s). """ LUTI0 = zeros((numbins, numbins)) LUTI1 = zeros((numbins, numbins)) LUTI2 = zeros((numbins, numbins)) LUTI3 = zeros((numbins, numbins)) # Discretize scalar range scalars = linspace(scalarmin, scalarmax, numbins) for i, Sf in enumerate(scalars): for j, Sb in enumerate(scalars): if Sb <= Sf: continue # Degenerate case, handle as zero or skip D = 1.0 # Normalized step length for table indexing d = D / (Sb - Sf) # Numerical integration over s0 from Sf to Sb # Using simple Riemann sum or trapezoidal rule for pre-computation integralI0 = 0.0 integralI1 = 0.0 integralI2 = 0.0 integralI3 = 0.0 numsteps = 100 # Resolution for pre-computation integration ds0 = (Sb - Sf) / numsteps for k in range(numsteps): s0 = Sf + k ds0 s = (s0 - Sf) / (Sb - Sf) cs0 = classificationfunc(s0) sigma = absorptionfunc(Sf, s0) weight = exp(-d sigma) # Ik = d integral(c(s0) s^k exp(-dsigma) ds0) # Approximation: sum(c(s0) s^k exp(-dsigma) ds0) d term = cs0 (s k) weight ds0 d integralI0 += term[0] # Assuming cs0 is RGB, accumulate per channel integralI1 += term[1] integralI2 += term[2] integralI3 += term[3] LUTI0[i, j] = integralI0 LUTI1[i, j] = integralI1 LUTI2[i, j] = integralI2 LUTI3[i, j] = integralI3 return LUTI0, LUTI1, LUTI2, LUTI3 def computediffuseshading(LUTI0, LUTI1, LUTI2, LUTI3, Sf, Sb, Nf, Nb, L, Kd): """ Compute pre-integrated diffuse shading for a single step. """ # 1. Handle degenerate cases if Sb <= Sf: return zeros(3) # Or handle as no contribution # 2. Compute angle alpha and factor r cosalpha = dot(Nf, Nb) # Clamp cosalpha to [-1, 1] for numerical stability cosalpha = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosalpha)) alpha = acos(cosalpha) / 2.0 cosalphahalf = cos(alpha) if cosalphahalf == 0: # Degenerate case where alpha is 90 degrees, cos(alpha) is 0 # r becomes undefined. In practice, clamp or use limit. # Limit as alpha -> 90 deg: r -> -4. r = -4.0 else: r = 4.0 (cosalphahalf - 1.0) / cosalphahalf # 3. Compute coefficients a0 to a3 NfdotL = dot(Nf, L) NbdotL = dot(Nb, L) a0 = NfdotL a1 = NbdotL - (1.0 + r) NfdotL a2 = r (2.0 NfdotL - NbdotL) a3 = r (NbdotL - NfdotL) # 4. Access LUTs # Quantize Sf and Sb to indices idxSf = quantizetoindex(Sf, LUTI0.shape[0]) idxSb = quantizetoindex(Sb, LUTI0.shape[1]) I0 = LUTI0[idxSf, idxSb] I1 = LUTI1[idxSf, idxSb] I2 = LUTI2[idxSf, idxSb] I3 = LUTI3[idxSf, idxSb] # 5. Compute final color # Cd = Kd (a0I0 + a1I1 + a2I2 + a3I3) # Note: I0-I3 are vectors (RGB). a0-a3 are scalars. sumI = a0 I0 + a1 I1 + a2 I2 + a3 I3 Cd = Kd sumI return Cd Negative Dot Products: The dot product between the light direction and the normalized gradient may become negative, which is physically invalid for diffuse shading. Two solutions are common: 1. Single-sided illumination: Apply max(dot, 0) to the dot products before computing coefficients. This requires modifying the integral, which is difficult to pre-integrate exactly. The coefficients ak must be computed with clamped dot products. 2. Double-sided illumination: Mirror the gradient if the dot product is negative. This ensures continuity but may introduce artifacts if not handled carefully. Degenerate Normals: If \mathbf{N}f and \mathbf{N}b are identical, \alpha = 0, r = 0, and the method reduces to standard linear shading. If they are orthogonal, \alpha = \pi/4, r = -4. Precision: The factor r can become large negative values for large angles, potentially amplifying numerical errors in the coefficient calculation. Time Complexity: O(1) per sampling step for shading, as it involves four LUT lookups and a few arithmetic operations. Pre-computation is O(N^2 \cdot M) where N is LUT size and M is integration resolution. Memory Complexity: 4 \cdot N^2 \cdot \text{bytes\per\color}. For N=256 and 32-bit floats, this is 4 \cdot 65536 \cdot 4 \approx 1 MB. Strengths: Significantly reduces shading artifacts compared to linear gradient interpolation, especially for large angles between gradients. Much more memory-efficient than full 4D normal-based pre-integration. Limitations: Approximates the non-linear gradient interpolation with a polynomial expansion, which may introduce small errors for very large angles. Requires pre-computation. When to use: When high-quality diffuse shading is needed in volume rendering and memory is constrained, but linear interpolation causes visible artifacts. This method was proposed by Lum et al. in 2010 as an improvement over linear gradient interpolation in pre-integrated volume rendering. It addresses the visual discontinuities and errors that arise when gradients change significantly between sample points, which linear interpolation fails to capture accurately. The approach builds on the concept of pre-integration lookup tables introduced in earlier work, extending it to handle diffuse shading with a non-linear gradient model.
