name: Layered SDF Compositing
body: Layered SDF Compositing is a method for rendering Signed Distance Field (SDF) glyphs by compositing multiple pre-multiplied color layers (typically a face and one or more outline layers) using alpha blending. It solves the problem of rendering crisp, anti-aliased text or icons with variable-width outlines by treating each visual layer as a separate alpha channel in a single pass. It differs from standard Alpha Blending by explicitly managing pre-multiplied alpha arithmetic across multiple distinct layers to support complex outline structures, and from SDF Underlay & Inner Underlay by compositing discrete layers rather than sampling a blurred border offset. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N layers (where N \in \{1, 2, 4\}), each consisting of a color vector \mathbf{c}i (RGB) and an alpha value \alphai. The alphas are packed into a single vector \boldsymbol{\alpha} = (\alpha.x, \alpha.y, \alpha.z, \alpha.w) corresponding to layers 0, 1, 2, 3. Output: A final pre-multiplied color \mathbf{c}{out} and a final alpha \alpha{out}. Data Structures: The method assumes the input colors are not yet pre-multiplied. The algorithm performs pre-multiplication internally. Steps: 1. Pre-multiply and Scale: For each layer i, multiply the color \mathbf{c}i by its corresponding alpha component \alphai. 2. Composite: Compute the weighted sum of the pre-multiplied colors using the alpha components as weights. 3. Normalize: Divide the resulting RGB color by the total accumulated alpha to obtain the final pre-multiplied output color. Formulas: Let N be the number of layers. For N=1 (Layer1float): \mathbf{c}{out} = \mathbf{c}0 \alpha{out} = \alpha0 For N=2 (Layer2float): \mathbf{c}{out} = \frac{\mathbf{c}1 \alpha1 + \mathbf{c}0 \alpha0}{\alpha1 + \alpha0} Note: The source specifies lerp(color1, color0, alpha.x) which implies \mathbf{c}{out} = \mathbf{c}1 (1 - \alpha0) + \mathbf{c}0 \alpha0 if interpreted as standard lerp, but the text explicitly says "premultiply color0.rgb by color0.a and color1.rgb by color1.a" and then "divide outColor.rgb by outColor.a". The standard alpha compositing formula for layer 1 over layer 0 is \mathbf{c}{out} = \mathbf{c}1 \alpha1 + \mathbf{c}0 \alpha0 (1 - \alpha1). However, the source text for Layer2 says: outColor = lerp(color1, color0, alpha.x). In many graphics APIs, lerp(a, b, t) is a(1-t) + bt. If alpha.x is \alpha0, this is \mathbf{c}1(1-\alpha0) + \mathbf{c}0 \alpha0. This is non-standard compositing unless \alpha1 = 1 - \alpha0. Given the explicit instruction to "premultiply... and divide by outColor.a", the most faithful implementation of the text is: \mathbf{c}{pre} = \mathbf{c}1 \alpha1 + \mathbf{c}0 \alpha0 \alpha{out} = \alpha1 + \alpha0 \mathbf{c}{out} = \frac{\mathbf{c}{pre}}{\alpha{out}} Correction: The source says lerp(color1, color0, alpha.x). If we assume standard alpha compositing where layer 1 is on top of layer 0, the formula is \mathbf{c}{out} = \mathbf{c}1 \alpha1 + \mathbf{c}0 \alpha0 (1 - \alpha1). The source text is slightly ambiguous regarding the exact lerp parameters vs standard compositing. However, the Layer4 description uses nested lerp. We will follow the explicit "premultiply all... compute outColor = lerp... divide by outColor.a" pattern. For N=4 (Layer4float): \mathbf{c}{out} = \frac{\mathbf{c}3 \alpha3 + \mathbf{c}2 \alpha2 (1-\alpha3) + \mathbf{c}1 \alpha1 (1-\alpha3)(1-\alpha2) + \mathbf{c}0 \alpha0 (1-\alpha3)(1-\alpha2)(1-\alpha1)}{\alpha{total}} The source specifies: outColor = lerp(lerp(lerp(color3, color2, alpha.z), color1, alpha.y), color0, alpha.x). This corresponds to: 1. t1 = \text{lerp}(\mathbf{c}3, \mathbf{c}2, \alpha2) = \mathbf{c}3(1-\alpha2) + \mathbf{c}2 \alpha2 2. t2 = \text{lerp}(t1, \mathbf{c}1, \alpha1) = t1(1-\alpha1) + \mathbf{c}1 \alpha1 3. t3 = \text{lerp}(t2, \mathbf{c}0, \alpha0) = t2(1-\alpha0) + \mathbf{c}0 \alpha0 4. \mathbf{c}{out} = t3 / \alpha{total} Parameters: Number of layers: 1, 2, or 4. Edge Cases: Division by zero: If \alpha{total} = 0, the output color is undefined. Typically, return black or transparent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def layeredsdfcompositing(colors, alphas, numlayers): """ colors: list of tuples (r, g, b) for each layer alphas: list of floats for each layer numlayers: 1, 2, or 4 """ # Pre-multiply colors premultiplied = [] for i in range(numlayers): r, g, b = colors[i] a = alphas[i] premultiplied.append((r a, g a, b a, a)) if numlayers == 1: c0, a0 = premultiplied[0] return (c0, a0) elif numlayers == 2: c1, a1 = premultiplied[1] c0, a0 = premultiplied[0] # lerp(color1, color0, alpha.x) -> color1 (1 - alpha0) + color0 alpha0 # Note: Source says premultiply then lerp then divide. # Standard alpha compositing is usually c1a1 + c0a0(1-a1). # The source text is specific: lerp(color1, color0, alpha.x). # Assuming alpha.x is alpha0. r = c1[0] (1 - a0) + c0[0] a0 g = c1[1] (1 - a0) + c0[1] a0 b = c1[2] (1 - a0) + c0[2] a0 alphaout = a1 + a0 # Or 1.0 if fully opaque? Source says divide by outColor.a # Wait, source says "divide outColor.rgb by outColor.a". # If we use lerp, the resulting alpha is not simply sum. # Let's stick to the source's explicit steps: # 1. Premultiply. # 2. Lerp. # 3. Divide by outColor.a. # This implies outColor.a is the result of the lerp's alpha? # Lerp of premultiplied colors doesn't track alpha linearly in the same way. # Re-reading S1: "compute outColor = lerp(color1, color0, alpha.x); divide outColor.rgb by outColor.a" # This suggests outColor.a is computed separately or is the sum? # In Layer4, it's nested lerp. # Let's assume outColor.a is the accumulated alpha for normalization. alphaout = a1 + a0 # Approximation, or 1.0 if opaque. # Actually, if we premultiply, we lose the original alpha for the lerp weight? It differs by allowing the border to be offset in UV space independently of the glyph geometry and by supporting "inner" rendering. Choose it when you need a soft glow or inset shadow effect rather than a sharp outline. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (4-16 multiplications/additions) regardless of scene complexity. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only registers for the color and alpha values. Strengths: Extremely fast; supports variable-width outlines via the SDF sampling step (which precedes this compositing); handles multiple layers cleanly. Limitations: Limited to 1, 2, or 4 layers; assumes pre-multiplied alpha handling; precision issues may arise if alpha values are very small or very large. name: SDF Underlay & Inner Underlay
head: SDF Border Effect, TextMeshPro Underlay
body: SDF Underlay & Inner Underlay renders a blurred, colored border either behind (underlay) or inside (inner underlay) the primary glyph face by sampling the Signed Distance Field (SDF) atlas at an offset UV coordinate, scaling the distance, and blending it with the face color using pre-multiplied alpha. It differs from standard outline methods by allowing the border to be offset in UV space independently of the glyph geometry and by supporting "inner" rendering where the border appears within the filled region of the character. The method extends the layered compositing pipeline by introducing a secondary sampling pass for the underlay effect. It relies on pre-computed UV offsets and scale/bias parameters derived from user-defined softness and dilation values. Inputs: atlas: SDF texture (typically RGBA, where Alpha channel stores signed distance). faceColor: The color and alpha of the primary glyph face, already computed and pre-multiplied. underlayColor: The desired color of the underlay border. texcoord: Primary UV coordinates for the face. texcoord2: Secondary UV coordinates for the underlay sample. scale: Global scaling factor for the SDF. GradientScale: Font-specific gradient scaling. TextureWidth: Width of the SDF atlas in pixels. ScaleRatioC: A constant ratio used for normalization (often related to pixel density or font size). Parameters: UnderlayOffsetX, UnderlayOffsetY, UnderlayDilate, UnderlaySoftness. Outputs: faceColor: Updated color with the underlay blended in. The shader input structure typically contains: texcoord2.xy: The offset UV coordinates for sampling the underlay. texcoord2.z: A scalar value representing the scaled distance or weight (often scale or a derived factor). texcoord2.w: A bias value pre-computed from dilation and softness parameters. 1. Compute Offset UV: Calculate the UV offset based on user-defined X/Y offsets, scaled by the font scale and texture dimensions. bOffset = \left( \frac{-\text{UnderlayOffsetX} \times \text{ScaleRatioC} \times \text{GradientScale}}{\text{TextureWidth}}, \frac{-\text{UnderlayOffsetY} \times \text{ScaleRatioC} \times \text{GradientScale}}{\text{TextureHeight}} \right) 2. Compute Scale and Bias: Determine the effective scale and bias for the underlay distance field. bScale = \frac{\text{scale}}{1 + \text{UnderlaySoftness} \times \text{ScaleRatioC} \times \text{scale}} bBias = (0.5 - \text{weight}) \times bScale - 0.5 - (\text{UnderlayDilate} \times \text{ScaleRatioC} \times 0.5 \times bScale) Note: weight is typically a normalized alpha or coverage value associated with the face layer. 3. Sample Distance: Sample the SDF atlas at the offset UV coordinates. d = \text{tex2D}(\text{atlas}, \text{texcoord2}.xy).\alpha \times \text{texcoord2}.z Here, d represents the scaled signed distance. 4. Render Standard Underlay: Blend the underlay color behind the face. The underlay is visible where the scaled distance d exceeds the bias texcoord2.w. \text{faceColor} \leftarrow \text{faceColor} + \text{underlayColor} \times \text{saturate}(d - \text{texcoord2}.w) \times (1 - \text{faceColor}.a) 5. Render Inner Underlay: Blend the underlay color inside the face. This is active where the distance is below the bias (inside the shape) and the face alpha is not fully opaque (or to create a specific inner glow effect). \text{faceColor} \leftarrow \text{faceColor} + \text{underlayColor} \times (1 - \text{saturate}(d - \text{texcoord2}.w)) \times \text{saturate}(1 - sd) \times (1 - \text{faceColor}.a) Note: sd in the source notes likely refers to a specific distance threshold or the signed distance itself normalized. In standard implementations, this term often simplifies to checking if the point is inside the SDF contour. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. weight = 0.5 bScale = scale / (1.0 + UnderlaySoftness ScaleRatioC scale) bBias = (0.5 - weight) bScale - 0.5 - (UnderlayDilate ScaleRatioC 0.5 bScale) d = tex2D(atlas, texcoord2.xy).a texcoord2.z underlayfactor = saturate(d - bBias) faceColor = faceColor + underlayColor underlayfactor (1.0 - faceColor.a) sd = 0.0 innerfactor = (1.0 - saturate(d - bBias)) saturate(1.0 - sd) faceColor = faceColor + underlayColor innerfactor (1.0 - faceColor.a) UnderlayColor (Color, default 0,0,0,0.5): The color of the underlay border. UnderlayOffsetX (float, default 0): Horizontal UV offset for the underlay sample. UnderlayOffsetY (float, default 0): Vertical UV offset for the underlay sample. UnderlayDilate (float, default 0): Expands (>0) or shrinks (<0) the underlay region. UnderlaySoftness (float, default 0): Blur radius for the underlay edge. Precision: The bias calculation involves multiple scaling factors. If ScaleRatioC or GradientScale are very large, floating-point precision errors in bBias may cause jagged edges or incorrect cutoffs. Boundaries: If UnderlayOffsetX/Y pushes the UV coordinates outside the atlas bounds, standard texture wrapping modes (Clamp, Repeat) will determine the behavior. Clamping is recommended to avoid sampling adjacent glyphs. Degenerate Input: If scale is zero, bScale becomes zero, and the underlay distance d becomes zero, potentially rendering the underlay incorrectly depending on the bias. Alpha Overwrite: The method uses (1 - faceColor.a) to blend. If the face is fully opaque (a=1), the underlay will not be visible, which is the intended behavior for "behind" rendering. For inner underlay, this ensures the inner color blends correctly with the face. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, requiring one additional texture sample (tex2D) and a few arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel for intermediate calculations. Performance: The additional texture sample increases memory bandwidth usage. On mobile GPUs, this can be significant if the atlas is not cached in L1/L2. The arithmetic cost is negligible. Strengths: Provides a soft, blurred border effect that integrates well with the SDF's inherent anti-aliasing. The offset capability allows for creative text effects (e.g., drop shadows, glows). Limitations: The "inner underlay" implementation in the source notes is somewhat ambiguous regarding the sd variable. Performance degrades if the underlay offset causes sampling far from the primary UV, potentially missing the glyph entirely if the atlas is sparse. When to use: When a soft, blurred border is needed for text readability or aesthetic effect, especially in UI contexts where crisp outlines are too harsh. When not to use: When precise, hard-edged outlines are required (use standard SDF outlines instead) or when performance is critical and the additional texture sample is a bottleneck. The method is primarily associated with the Unity UI TextMeshPro package, where it is implemented as the "Underlay" effect. It allows designers to add a blurred background to text to improve readability against complex backgrounds. The technique leverages the signed distance field's ability to represent smooth transitions, using the distance value as a mask for the underlay color. andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, https://github.com/andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Training Ray Compositing
head: Volume Rendering Composite, Volume Rendering Composite Forward
body: Training Ray Compositing performs the forward and backward passes of volume rendering specifically for gradient-based optimization. It composites ray samples (RGB and density) into final image colors, alpha weights, and depth using the standard volume rendering integral. Unlike inference-only compositing, this method explicitly computes gradients for network outputs (sigmas and RGBs) to enable backpropagation through the rendering equation. It is distinguished from standard Compositing by its dual forward/backward CUDA kernel implementation and from Pre-Integration Lookup by its direct sample-wise accumulation rather than texture-based approximation. Inputs and Outputs: sigmas: Density values, float array of shape [M]. rgbs: RGB colors at sampled points, float array of shape [M, 3]. deltas: Step sizes (distances between samples), float array of shape [M, 2]. Note: Some implementations use a single channel for step size. rays: Ray metadata, int32 array of shape [N, 3]. Each row is [rayindex, startpointindex, numsteps], where rayindex maps to the output pixel, startpointindex is the offset in the sample arrays, and numsteps is the number of valid samples for that ray. Tthresh: Transparency threshold for early termination, float, default 10^{-4}. Outputs: image: Final RGB color per ray, float array of shape [N, 3]. weightssum: Total alpha (opacity) per ray, float array of shape [N]. depth: Depth value per ray, float array of shape [N]. Data Structures: The method operates on contiguous CUDA tensors. The rays array acts as a sparse index into the dense sigmas, rgbs, and deltas arrays, allowing variable numbers of samples per ray. Algorithm (Forward Pass): 1. Initialization: Ensure input tensors are contiguous. Initialize accumulators for the current ray: transmittance T = 1.0, and color accumulators r=0, g=0, b=0. Alternatively, initialize rgbtemp, depthtemp, opacitytemp to zero. 2. Ray Iteration: Iterate over active rays n. Retrieve ray metadata: index (pixel ID), offset (sample start), numsteps (sample count) from rays[n]. 3. Validation: Check for empty rays or buffer overflow (numsteps == 0 or offset + numsteps >= M). If invalid, set weightssum[index] = 0 and image[index] = 0, then skip. 4. Sample Loop: For each sample s from 0 to numsteps - 1: a. Alpha Calculation: Compute the probability of absorption at this step: \alpha = 1 - e^{-\sigma \delta} where \sigma = \text{sigmas}[offset + s] and \delta = \text{deltas}[offset + s]. b. Weight Calculation: Compute the contribution weight: w = \alpha \cdot T where T is the current transmittance. c. Accumulation: r \leftarrow r + w \cdot \text{rgbs}[offset + s, 0] g \leftarrow g + w \cdot \text{rgbs}[offset + s, 1] b \leftarrow b + w \cdot \text{rgbs}[offset + s, 2] \text{depth} \leftarrow \text{depth} + w \cdot \text{position}[offset + s] \quad \text{} \text{opacity} \leftarrow \text{opacity} + w \quad \text{} d. Transmittance Update: Update transmittance for the next sample: T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alpha) e. Early Termination: If T < T{\text{thresh}} (default 10^{-4}), break the loop. Mark the ray as dead if tracking alive indices. 5. Finalization: Write the accumulated color to image[index] and the final transmittance-derived opacity to weightssum[index]. Specifically, weightssum[index] = 1.0 - T. Algorithm (Backward Pass): 1. Gradient Inputs: Receive gradients from the loss function with respect to the output image (gradimage) and weightssum (gradweightssum). 2. Kernel Execution: Call the backward CUDA kernel compositeraystrainbackward. 3. Gradient Computation: The kernel computes gradients for sigmas and rgbs by reversing the compositing chain. It uses the saved forward pass values (weights, transmittance) to calculate \frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigma} and \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{rgb}}. 4. Depth Gradient: Note that gradients for depth are not propagated back to sigmas in the standard implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def compositeraystrainforward(sigmas, rgbs, deltas, rays, Tthresh=1e-4): """ Forward pass for Training Ray Compositing. sigmas: [M] float rgbs: [M, 3] float deltas: [M] float (step sizes) rays: [N, 3] int32 (rayindex, startoffset, numsteps) """ N = rays.shape[0] M = sigmas.shape[0] # Output buffers image = torch.zeros((N, 3), dtype=torch.float32) weightssum = torch.zeros((N), dtype=torch.float32) depth = torch.zeros((N), dtype=torch.float32) # Process each ray for n in range(N): rayidx = int(rays[n, 0]) startidx = int(rays[n, 1]) numsteps = int(rays[n, 2]) # Edge case: empty ray or overflow if numsteps == 0 or startidx + numsteps > M: continue T = 1.0 racc = 0.0 gacc = 0.0 bacc = 0.0 depthacc = 0.0 opacityacc = 0.0 for s in range(numsteps): sigma = sigmas[startidx + s] delta = deltas[startidx + s] rgb = rgbs[startidx + s] # Alpha calculation: alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) # Weight calculation: w = alpha T w = alpha T # Accumulate racc += w rgb[0] gacc += w rgb[1] bacc += w rgb[2] # Depth accumulation (assuming positions are stored or derived; # here we assume a placeholder for position 'pos' if not explicitly in deltas) # In many implementations, deltas are step sizes, positions are accumulated separately. # If 'deltas' contains positions, adjust accordingly. # Based on, depthtemp accumulates w ts[sn]. # We assume 'positions' tensor exists or is derived. For this generic impl: # pos =... # Derived from ray origin and accumulated deltas # depthacc += w pos opacityacc += w # Update transmittance T = T (1.0 - alpha) # Early termination if T < Tthresh: break # Write results image[rayidx] = torch.tensor([racc, gacc, bacc]) weightssum[rayidx] = 1.0 - T # Total opacity # depth[rayidx] = depthacc # If depth is tracked return image, weightssum, depth def compositeraystrainbackward(gradimage, gradweightssum, sigmas, rgbs, deltas, rays, Tthresh=1e-4): """ Backward pass stub. Computes gradients for sigmas and rgbs. In practice, this is implemented in CUDA to avoid Python loop overhead. """ # The backward pass replays the forward logic to compute: # dL/dsigma and dL/drgb using the chain rule through alpha and T. # dL/dsigma = sum(w (-delta) (1-alpha)/T dL/dC +...) # dL/drgb = sum(w dL/dC) # Placeholder for the actual CUDA kernel call or complex gradient derivation # gradsigmas =... # gradrgbs =... # Note: Gradients for depth are NOT propagated to sigmas. return gradsigmas, gradrgbs Computes gradients specifically for sigmas, RGBs, and ambient light during training. It supports a custom backward pass, allowing for specialized gradient handling for density parameters. A variant for surface splatting that caps the number of composited layers at c{max} = 16 per pixel to bound memory for backward pass statistics. It performs depth-interval grouping, MIP-filtered kernel evaluation, and Shepard normalization in a single forward kernel. The backward pass is a two-pass procedure: first replaying forward gap detection to reconstruct per-layer totals, then retraversing primitives to decompose per-layer gradients into per-surfel gradients using atomic operations to handle concurrent writes. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the total number of samples M and rays N. The forward pass is O(M) and the backward pass is O(M). Memory Complexity: O(M) for storing input tensors and O(N) for output buffers. The backward pass requires storing intermediate values (weights, transmittance) for each sample, increasing memory usage by a factor proportional to the number of samples per ray. Performance: Implemented as CUDA kernels for high performance on GPUs. Typical thread block size is 256 threads. Strengths: Enables end-to-end training of neural radiance fields by providing exact gradients through the volume rendering integral. Limitations: High memory consumption during training due to storing intermediate values for backpropagation. Early termination (T{\text{thresh}}) can introduce approximation errors if set too high, potentially affecting gradient accuracy. When to use: During the training phase of neural volume rendering methods (e.g., NeRF, Instant-NGP) where gradients are required. Not suitable for inference-only scenarios where gradient computation is unnecessary overhead. Training Ray Compositing is a fundamental component of differentiable volume rendering, enabling the optimization of neural scene representations. It was popularized by implementations in efficient NeRF frameworks such as Instant-NGP and its derivatives. The method relies on the analytical derivative of the volume rendering equation, allowing gradients to flow from the pixel loss back to the network's density and color outputs. Variants like the one in ER-NeRF extend this to handle specific training pipelines for talking portraits. name: Training Ray Compositing (Sigma)
head: Ray Compositing for Training (Sigma + Ambient)
body: Training Ray Compositing (Sigma) is a differentiable volume rendering method that composites per-ray samples of density (\sigma) and color (\mathbf{c}) into final image colors, alpha weights, and depth, while simultaneously computing gradients with respect to the input parameters for training. It extends standard alpha compositing by including ambient light contributions and supporting a custom backward pass to propagate gradients from the loss function back to the density and color fields. It is distinguished from its sibling Training Ray Compositing (Backward) by handling the forward composition and the joint forward-backward logic in a unified CUDA kernel interface, whereas the backward variant focuses specifically on the gradient computation logic. The method implements differentiable volume rendering along rays. It assumes that the scene is represented by a set of samples along each ray, characterized by density, color, and step size. The forward pass computes the accumulated color, alpha, and depth, while the backward pass computes the gradients of the loss with respect to the input densities and colors. Inputs: sigmas: Float tensor of shape [M], representing volume density for M samples. rgbs: Float tensor of shape [M, 3], representing view-dependent color for M samples. ambient: Float tensor of shape [M], representing ambient light contribution for M samples. deltas: Float tensor of shape [M, 2], representing step sizes (typically t{i+1}-ti and other geometric info) for M samples. rays: Integer tensor of shape [N, 3], containing ray indices or identifiers for N rays. Tthresh: Float, transparency threshold. Default value is 10^{-4}. Outputs: image: Float tensor of shape [N, 3], the final composited RGB color for each of the N rays. weightssum: Float tensor of shape [N], the output alpha channel (accumulated opacity) for each ray. depth: Float tensor of shape [N], the output depth for each ray. ambientsum: Float tensor of shape [N], the accumulated ambient contribution for each ray. The implementation relies on contiguous CUDA tensors. The input data is structured as follows: sigmas: [M] float32. rgbs: [M, 3] float32. ambient: [M] float32. deltas: [M, 2] float32. rays: [N, 3] int32. The output tensors are allocated with shapes: weightssum: [N] float32. ambientsum: [N] float32. depth: [N] float32. image: [N, 3] float32. 1. Validation: Ensure sigmas, rgbs, ambient, deltas, and rays are contiguous in memory. 2. Dimensions: Let M be the number of samples (sigmas.shape[0]) and N be the number of rays (rays.shape[0]). 3. Allocation: Allocate output tensors weightssum [N], ambientsum [N], depth [N], and image [N, 3] initialized to zero. 4. Kernel Execution: Call the forward CUDA kernel backend.compositeraystrainsigmaforward with inputs sigmas, rgbs, ambient, deltas, rays, and Tthresh, writing results to the output tensors. 5. Save for Backward: Save the input tensors (sigmas, rgbs, ambient, deltas, rays) and the output tensors (weightssum, ambientsum, depth, image) for use in the backward pass. 6. Save Parameters: Save the dimensions M, N, and the threshold T{thresh}. 1. Gradient Validation: Ensure gradweightssum, gradambientsum, and gradimage (gradients from the loss) are contiguous. 2. Retrieve: Load the saved tensors and dimensions from the forward pass. 3. Initialize: Initialize gradient tensors gradsigmas [M], gradrgbs [M, 3], and gradambient [M] with zeros. 4. Kernel Execution: Call the backward CUDA kernel backend.compositeraystrainsigmabackward with the saved tensors, gradients, and parameters to compute gradsigmas, gradrgbs, and gradambient. 5. Ambient Gradient: Call the CUDA backend kernel backend.compositeraysambientsigma to handle specific ambient light gradient computations if required by the implementation. The following Python-like pseudocode illustrates the PyTorch autograd.Function structure used in the implementation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import backend # Hypothetical CUDA extension module class TrainingRayCompositingSigma(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, sigmas, rgbs, ambient, deltas, rays, Tthresh=1e-4): # 1. Ensure contiguous sigmas = sigmas.contiguous() rgbs = rgbs.contiguous() ambient = ambient.contiguous() deltas = deltas.contiguous() rays = rays.contiguous() # 2. Get dimensions M = sigmas.shape[0] N = rays.shape[0] # 3. Allocate outputs weightssum = torch.zeros(N, device=sigmas.device, dtype=sigmas.dtype) ambientsum = torch.zeros(N, device=sigmas.device, dtype=sigmas.dtype) depth = torch.zeros(N, device=sigmas.device, dtype=sigmas.dtype) image = torch.zeros(N, 3, device=sigmas.device, dtype=sigmas.dtype) # 4. Call forward kernel backend.compositeraystrainsigmaforward( sigmas, rgbs, ambient, deltas, rays, weightssum, ambientsum, depth, image, Tthresh) # 5. Save for backward ctx.saveforbackward(sigmas, rgbs, ambient, deltas, rays, weightssum, ambientsum, depth, image) ctx.M = M ctx.N = N ctx.Tthresh = Tthresh return image, weightssum, ambientsum, depth @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradimage, gradweightssum, gradambientsum, graddepth): # Note: graddepth is typically not used or propagated to sigmas # 1. Retrieve saved tensors sigmas, rgbs, ambient, deltas, rays, weightssum, ambientsum, depth, image = ctx.savedtensors M = ctx.M N = ctx.N Tthresh = ctx.Tthresh # 2. Ensure gradients are contiguous gradimage = gradimage.contiguous() gradweightssum = gradweightssum.contiguous() gradambientsum = gradambientsum.contiguous() # 3. Initialize gradient tensors gradsigmas = torch.zeroslike(sigmas) gradrgbs = torch.zeroslike(rgbs) gradambient = torch.zeroslike(ambient) # 4. Call backward kernel backend.compositeraystrainsigmabackward( sigmas, rgbs, ambient, deltas, rays, weightssum, ambientsum, depth, image, gradimage, gradweightssum, gradambientsum, gradsigmas, gradrgbs, gradambient, Tthresh) # 5. Call ambient-specific kernel if needed backend.compositeraysambientsigma( sigmas, rgbs, ambient, deltas, rays, weightssum, ambientsum, depth, image, gradimage, gradweightssum, gradambientsum, gradsigmas, gradrgbs, gradambient, Tthresh) # Return gradients in order of inputs return gradsigmas, gradrgbs, gradambient, None, None, None Tthresh: Float. The transparency threshold. Rays with accumulated transparency below this value are considered fully opaque and can be skipped or terminated for efficiency. Default: 10^{-4}. Depth Gradient: The gradient for depth is not propagated back to the density (sigmas) parameters. This is a known limitation or design choice in this specific implementation. Contiguity: The method requires all input tensors to be contiguous in memory. Non-contiguous tensors must be cloned or moved before passing to the kernel. Precision: Standard float32 precision is used for all tensors. Precision issues may arise in very deep scenes or with very small step sizes, though the threshold Tthresh helps mitigate unnecessary computation for transparent regions. This variant composites rays for training including uncertainty estimation, computing gradients for sigmas, RGBs, ambient, and uncertainty. It extends the base method by adding an uncertainty input tensor and an uncertaintysum output tensor. The forward pass calls backend.compositeraystrainuncertaintyforward and the backward pass calls backend.compositeraystrainuncertaintybackward. It is chosen when the model needs to predict and train on uncertainty metrics alongside color and density. This variant composites rays for training with triplane-based ambient lighting, specifically handling auditory (ambaud) and eye-specific (ambeye) ambient components, as well as uncertainty. It computes gradients for sigmas, RGBs, and the various ambient components. The forward pass calls backend.compositeraystraintriplaneforward and handles inputs ambaud, ambeye, and uncertainty. It is chosen for models that incorporate multi-modal inputs like audio and eye tracking into the volume rendering process. Like the base method, the gradient for depth is not propagated to sigmas. A GPU-accelerated kernel that performs alpha compositing of pre-sampled RGB and sigma values along rays to produce final image and depth. It iterates through samples for each alive ray, accumulating transparency and computing weighted RGB and depth contributions. It uses inputs sigmas [n{alive} \times n{step}], rgbs [n{alive} \times n{step}, 3], and deltas [n{alive} \times n{step}, 2], with in-place outputs weightssum [N], depth [N], and image [N, 3]. It is chosen for high-performance rendering where the ray structure is flattened into alive-step pairs. Time Complexity: The forward and backward passes are O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of rays and M is the number of samples per ray, assuming uniform sampling. The use of Tthresh allows for early termination, reducing the effective M for transparent rays. Memory Complexity: The method requires storing the input tensors and the output tensors. The backward pass requires saving the forward pass inputs and outputs, leading to memory usage proportional to O(N \cdot M) for the saved tensors. Performance: As a CUDA kernel-based implementation, it is highly optimized for GPU execution. Performance scales with the number of alive rays and the number of samples. Strengths: Differentiable, supports ambient lighting and uncertainty, efficient early termination. Limitations: Gradient for depth is not propagated to sigmas. Requires contiguous tensors. Training Ray Compositing (Sigma) is part of the differentiable volume rendering pipeline used in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and related methods, specifically those involving training with ambient lighting and uncertainty. name: Training Ray Compositing (Backward)
head: Volume Rendering Composite Backward
body: This method computes the gradients of the volume rendering loss with respect to the input density (sigmas) and color (rgbs) parameters during the backward pass of differentiable volume rendering. It implements the chain rule to propagate gradients from the final rendered image and the total accumulated alpha weights back to the individual sample points along each ray. It is the backward counterpart to Training Ray Compositing (Sigma), which handles the forward pass and potentially other gradient computations. Inputs: grad: Gradient of the loss with respect to the final image RGB, shape [N, 3] where N is the number of rays. gradweightssum: Gradient of the loss with respect to weightssum (total alpha), shape [N]. weightssum: The computed total alpha values from the forward pass, shape [N]. image: The computed final RGB values from the forward pass, shape [N, 3]. sigmas: Density values for all sample points, shape [M]. rgbs: Color values for all sample points, shape [M, 3]. deltas: Distances between consecutive sample points along rays, shape [M]. raystartidx: Starting index in the sample arrays for each ray, shape [N]. numsteps: Number of valid sample steps for each ray, shape [N]. Outputs: gradsigmas: Output buffer for density gradients, shape [M]. gradrgbs: Output buffer for color gradients, shape [M, 3]. Data Structures: The method operates on flat arrays representing the ray marching data. Each ray i occupies a segment in the sample arrays from raystartidx[i] to raystartidx[i] + numsteps[i] - 1. Steps: 1. Initialization: For each ray i from 0 to N-1: Check for empty rays: If numsteps[i] == 0 or raystartidx[i] + numsteps[i] >= M, skip this ray (return/continue). Initialize accumulators for the backward pass: T = 1.0f (Transmittance, initialized to 1.0). r = 0, g = 0, b = 0 (Accumulated color components, initialized to 0). Get final values from the forward pass: rfinal = image[i, 0] gfinal = image[i, 1] bfinal = image[i, 2] Tfinal = 1.0f - weightssum[i] Set pointers to the start of the ray's sample data: stepidx = raystartidx[i]. 2. Backward Loop: Iterate step from 0 to numsteps[i] - 1: Let idx = stepidx + step. Retrieve current sample properties: sigma = sigmas[idx] rgb = rgbs[idx] (components rgb[0], rgb[1], rgb[2]) delta = deltas[idx] Compute alpha: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \delta). Compute weight: w = \alpha \cdot T. Compute RGB Gradients: The gradient of the loss with respect to the current color ci is given by: \frac{\partial L}{\partial ci} = wi \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial C} where \frac{\partial L}{\partial C} is the gradient from the final image (grad[i]). Update output buffer: gradrgbs[idx, 0] = grad[i, 0] w gradrgbs[idx, 1] = grad[i, 1] w gradrgbs[idx, 2] = grad[i, 2] w Update Accumulators: Update accumulated color: r += w rgb[0] g += w rgb[1] b += w rgb[2] Update transmittance: T = T \cdot (1 - \alpha). Compute Sigma Gradient: The gradient with respect to density \sigmai involves the derivative of the composite function. Based on the implementation trace: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigmai} = \deltai \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial R} (T \cdot rgb[0] - (r{final} - r)) + \frac{\partial L}{\partial G} (T \cdot rgb[1] - (g{final} - g)) + \frac{\partial L}{\partial B} (T \cdot rgb[2] - (b{final} - b)) + \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha{total}} \cdot T{final} \right) Note: The term (rfinal - r) represents the contribution of future samples to the final color. The term T rgb[k] represents the current sample's contribution to the next transmittance-weighted color. The implementation uses: termr = T rgb[0] - (rfinal - r) termg = T rgb[1] - (gfinal - g) termb = T rgb[2] - (bfinal - b) gradsigmas[idx] = deltas[idx] ( grad[i, 0] termr + grad[i, 1] termg + grad[i, 2] termb + gradweightssum[i] Tfinal) Advance pointers: stepidx remains fixed for the ray, but the loop index step increments. Effectively, we move to the next sample in the ray's segment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainingraycompositingbackward( grad, # [N, 3] gradweightssum, # [N] weightssum, # [N] image, # [N, 3] sigmas, # [M] rgbs, # [M, 3] deltas, # [M] raystartidx, # [N] numsteps, # [N] M, # Total number of samples N # Total number of rays): gradsigmas = torch.zeros(M) gradrgbs = torch.zeros(M, 3) for i in range(N): # Check for empty rays if numsteps[i] == 0 or raystartidx[i] + numsteps[i] >= M: continue # Initialize accumulators T = 1.0 racc = 0.0 gacc = 0.0 bacc = 0.0 # Get final values rfinal = image[i, 0] gfinal = image[i, 1] bfinal = image[i, 2] Tfinal = 1.0 - weightssum[i] # Get gradient inputs gradr = grad[i, 0] gradg = grad[i, 1] gradb = grad[i, 2] gradwsum = gradweightssum[i] # Loop through steps for step in range(numsteps[i]): idx = raystartidx[i] + step # Retrieve sample data sigma = sigmas[idx] rgb0 = rgbs[idx, 0] rgb1 = rgbs[idx, 1] rgb2 = rgbs[idx, 2] delta = deltas[idx] # Compute alpha alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) # Compute weight weight = alpha T # Compute RGB gradients gradrgbs[idx, 0] = gradr weight gradrgbs[idx, 1] = gradg weight gradrgbs[idx, 2] = gradb weight # Update accumulators racc += weight rgb0 gacc += weight rgb1 bacc += weight rgb2 # Update transmittance T = T (1.0 - alpha) # Compute Sigma gradient # Term for R: T rgb[0] - (rfinal - racc) # Note: racc here is the accumulated color before adding the current step's contribution to the next T? # Let's re-verify the formula from the notes: # gradsigmas[0] = deltas[0] ( grad[0] (T rgbs[0] - (rfinal - r)) +...) # Here 'r' in the note is the accumulated R before the current step? # In the loop, 'racc' is updated after computing weight. # So at the start of the gradient computation for step 'step', 'racc' holds the sum of weights colors for steps 0 to step-1. # The term (rfinal - racc) is the contribution of steps 'step' to 'numsteps-1' to the final color? # No, rfinal = sum{j=0}^{N-1} wj cj. # racc (before update) = sum{j=0}^{step-1} wj cj. # So rfinal - racc = sum{j=step}^{N-1} wj cj. # The formula uses (T rgb[0] - (rfinal - racc)). # Let's stick to the code trace provided in the notes. termr = T rgb0 - (rfinal - racc) termg = T rgb1 - (gfinal - gacc) termb = T rgb2 - (bfinal - bacc) gradsigmas[idx] = delta ( gradr termr + gradg termg + gradb termb + gradwsum Tfinal) return gradsigmas, gradrgbs Parameters: gradweightssum: Gradient of the loss with respect to weightssum (total alpha), shape [N]. grad: Gradient of the loss with respect to the final image RGB, shape [N, 3]. weightssum: The computed total alpha values from the forward pass, shape [N]. image: The computed final RGB values from the forward pass, shape [N, 3]. gradsigmas: Output buffer for density gradients, shape [M]. gradrgbs: Output buffer for color gradients, shape [M, 3]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Rays: Rays with numsteps == 0 or exceeding the sample buffer bounds must be skipped to avoid out-of-bounds access. Precision: The computation involves exponentials and subtractions of similar magnitudes (e.g., Tfinal and weightssum). Care should be taken with floating-point precision, especially for very small or large densities. Boundary Conditions: The transmittance T is updated sequentially. Any error in early steps propagates to later steps in the backward pass if not handled correctly, although the backward pass is independent of the forward pass's T values except for the final Tfinal. Time Complexity: O(M), where M is the total number of sample points across all rays. Each sample is processed once. Memory Complexity: O(M) for storing the output gradients gradsigmas and gradrgbs. Performance: As a CUDA kernel, it is designed for high parallelism on GPUs. Performance scales with the number of rays and samples per ray. Strengths: Efficiently computes gradients for differentiable volume rendering, enabling end-to-end training of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and similar models. Limitations: Requires the forward pass values (image, weightssum) to be stored or recomputed. Memory usage can be high for scenes with many rays and samples. When to use: When training neural volume rendering models that require gradients with respect to density and color parameters. When not to use: For inference-only scenarios where gradients are not needed. name: Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques
body: This family encompasses methods for evaluating continuous fields along rays (via polynomial composition) and resampling discrete volume data (via spatial convolution) to support direct volume ray casting. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Pre-Integration Lookup by focusing on the algebraic or spatial mechanics of data evaluation rather than lookup-table optimization or surface-based compositing. The methods in this family share the goal of mapping 3D data to 1D ray values or resampling grids, but they differ fundamentally in domain and mechanism. Composition via Convolution (Power Form) operates in the algebraic domain, composing trivariate polynomials with linear ray parameterizations to produce univariate polynomials. Feed-Backward Reconstruction operates in the spatial domain, using convolution kernels to resample discrete signals. No single mathematical formulation or data structure is shared across both; they are grouped here by their role in the reconstruction/compositing pipeline of volume rendering. Evaluates the composition of a trivariate polynomial field with a linear ray parameterization. It solves the problem of efficient numerical evaluation in direct volume ray casting by using convolution operators to reduce computation and register usage compared to naive substitution. Unlike Feed-Backward Reconstruction, which focuses on reconstruction filters, this method specifically optimizes the algebraic evaluation of the polynomial composition itself. Choose this when the volume data is represented as trivariate polynomials and high-order continuity is required. A spatial-domain convolution method that computes each output sample by gathering weighted contributions from neighboring input samples. It solves the problem of resampling discrete volume data onto a finer or different grid by centering the reconstruction kernel at the output location and summing the input values weighted by the kernel function. It is distinguished from its sibling Composition via Convolution (Power Form) by its explicit spatial gathering loop structure, which accesses each output sample once and each input sample multiple times, contrasting with feed-forward approaches that distribute input energy to multiple outputs. Choose this for standard resampling of discrete voxel grids. A technique by Vannier et al. that assigns a source strength and an attenuation coefficient (opacity) to each voxel. It traces rays through the volume array until they hit a surface, then assigns an intensity inversely proportional to the distance traveled along the ray. A surface is defined as a significant change in opacity value, making this approach threshold-based and susceptible to associated artifacts. The concept of source-attenuation reprojection originates from work by Vannier et al. in the context of stereotactic neurosurgery planning. The polynomial composition methods are described in unofficial notes regarding efficient numerical evaluation in volume rendering. These techniques are used in direct volume visualization pipelines where accurate field evaluation or resampling is critical for image quality. name: Composition via Convolution (Power Form)
head: Power Form
body: Composition via Convolution (Power Form) is a method for evaluating the composition of a trivariate polynomial field with a linear ray parameterization, transforming a 3D function into a univariate function along a ray. It solves the problem of efficient numerical evaluation in direct volume ray casting by using convolution operators to reduce computation and register usage compared to naive substitution. Unlike Feed-Backward Reconstruction, which focuses on reconstruction filters, this method specifically optimizes the algebraic evaluation of the polynomial composition itself. Inputs and Outputs Input: Trivariate polynomial coefficients f{ijk} of degree d in each dimension (total degree 3d), and ray parameters px, vx, py, vy, pz, vz defining the ray r(t) = p + t \cdot v. Output: Coefficients of the resulting univariate polynomial f(t) of degree 3d. Data Structures Ray Coefficient Sequences: For each axis, a sequence representing the linear polynomial components. For the x-axis, \mathbf{r}x = [px, vx]. Similarly, \mathbf{r}y = [py, vy] and \mathbf{r}z = [pz, vz]. Power Expressions: Incrementally computed convolution results. \mathbf{r}x^i represents the i-th power of the x-component ray polynomial. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize Ray Powers: Compute the power expressions for each axis incrementally using convolution. For i from 1 to d: \mathbf{r}x^i = \mathbf{r}x^{i-1} \mathbf{r}x Repeat for \mathbf{r}y^j and \mathbf{r}z^k. This is equivalent to the Horner scheme for polynomial evaluation. 2. Compute Inner Sum: For each pair (i, j), compute the intermediate polynomial \mathbf{f}{ij} by convolving the z-axis ray powers with the corresponding polynomial coefficients: \mathbf{f}{ij} = \sum{k=0}^d f{ijk} \cdot \mathbf{r}z^k 3. Compute Middle Sum: For each i, compute the intermediate polynomial \mathbf{g}i by convolving the y-axis ray powers with the previously computed \mathbf{f}{ij}: \mathbf{g}i = \sum{j=0}^d \mathbf{r}y^j \mathbf{f}{ij} 4. Compute Final Sum: Compute the final univariate polynomial coefficients \mathbf{f} by convolving the x-axis ray powers with the intermediate polynomials \mathbf{g}i: \mathbf{f} = \sum{i=0}^d \mathbf{r}x^i \mathbf{g}i Formulas The core composition formula using convolution operators is: \mathbf{f} = \sum{i=0}^d \sum{j=0}^d \sum{k=0}^d f{ijk} \cdot \mathbf{r}x^i \mathbf{r}y^j \mathbf{r}z^k Where \mathbf{r}x = [px, vx] is the coefficient sequence of the x-component of the ray. The reordered composition, which enables the memory-efficient iterative approach, is: \mathbf{f} = \sum{i=0}^d \mathbf{r}x^i \sum{j=0}^d \mathbf{r}y^j \underbrace{\sum{k=0}^d f{ijk} \cdot \mathbf{r}z^k}{\mathbf{f}{ij}} Parameters d: The degree of the polynomial in each dimension. Typical values in the source are d=3 (total degree 9). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Register Pressure: A naive implementation requires too many operations and registers to fit into a GPU framework. The convolution structure ensures that no more than one factor \mathbf{f}{ij} and \mathbf{g}i needs to be available at the same time, allowing memory reuse. Precision: The method exhibits lower Mean Squared Error (MSE) compared to naive substitution, indicating better numerical stability for the given test cases. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositionviaconvolutionpowerform(fcoeffs, rayp, rayv): """ Computes the composition of a trivariate polynomial with a linear ray. Args: fcoeffs: 3D array of coefficients fijk of shape (d+1, d+1, d+1). rayp: Array [px, py, pz] of ray origins. rayv: Array [vx, vy, vz] of ray directions. Returns: Array of coefficients for the resulting univariate polynomial. """ d = fcoeffs.shape[0] - 1 # Step 1: Compute ray power sequences via convolution # rx[i] is the coefficient sequence for (px + tvx)^i rx = [None] (d + 1) rx[0] = [1.0] # Constant 1 for i in range(1, d + 1): # Convolve previous power with linear term [px, vx] rx[i] = convolve(rx[i-1], [rayp[0], rayv[0]]) ry = [None] (d + 1) ry[0] = [1.0] for j in range(1, d + 1): ry[j] = convolve(ry[j-1], [rayp[1], rayv[1]]) rz = [None] (d + 1) rz[0] = [1.0] for k in range(1, d + 1): rz[k] = convolve(rz[k-1], [rayp[2], rayv[2]]) # Step 2, 3, 4: Iterative composition with memory reuse # We compute fij, then gi, then final f # To minimize register usage, we iterate in an order that allows overwriting # Initialize result accumulator finalf = [0.0] (3 d + 1) # Degree 3d # We can compute term by term or use the nested sum structure. # The nested sum structure allows reusing memory for fij and gi. # Let's implement the nested sum directly, storing intermediate results # gi will store sumj (ry[j] fij) # fij will store sumk (fijk rz[k]) # Precompute fij for all i, j # fij is a polynomial of degree d fij = [[None] (d + 1) for in range(d + 1)] for i in range(d + 1): for j in range(d + 1): # Compute fij = sumk fijk rz[k] currentfij = [0.0] (d + 1) for k in range(d + 1): coeff = fcoeffs[i, j, k] if coeff != 0: # Scale rz[k] by coeff and add to currentfij scaledrz = scale(rz[k], coeff) currentfij = addpolynomials(currentfij, scaledrz) fij[i][j] = currentfij # Now compute gi = sumj ry[j] fij[i][j] # And then finalf = sumi rx[i] gi # We can accumulate into finalf directly if we manage the convolution carefully # However, the source emphasizes that only one fij and one gi needs to be available. # This implies we can iterate i, then j, and accumulate. # Let's restructure to match the "memory reuse" claim more closely. # finalf = sumi rx[i] (sumj ry[j] fij[i][j]) # We can compute the inner sum for a fixed i, then convolve with rx[i] and add to finalf. for i in range(d + 1): # Compute gi = sumj ry[j] fij[i][j] gi = [0.0] (2 d + 1) # Degree 2d for j in range(d + 1): # Convolve ry[j] with fij[i][j] term = convolve(ry[j], fij[i][j]) gi = addpolynomials(gi, term) # Convolve gi with rx[i] and add to finalf termfinal = convolve(rx[i], gi) finalf = addpolynomials(finalf, termfinal) return finalf def convolve(poly1, poly2): """Convolution of two polynomial coefficient arrays.""" deg1 = len(poly1) - 1 deg2 = len(poly2) - 1 result = [0.0] (deg1 + deg2 + 1) for i, c1 in enumerate(poly1): for j, c2 in enumerate(poly2): result[i + j] += c1 c2 return result def addpolynomials(p1, p2): """Add two polynomial coefficient arrays.""" maxlen = max(len(p1), len(p2)) result = [0.0] maxlen for i in range(len(p1)): result[i] += p1[i] for i in range(len(p2)): result[i] += p2[i] return result def scale(poly, scalar): """Scale a polynomial by a scalar.""" return [c scalar for c in poly] Composition via Scaled Bernstein Form (SB) is a method for evaluating the composition of a trivariate polynomial field with a ray parameterization, transforming a 3D function into a univariate function along a ray. It solves the problem of efficient numerical evaluation in direct volume ray casting by leveraging the scaled Bernstein basis. Unlike Composition via Convolution (Power Form), which uses power bases and convolution operators, SB maintains a uniform data representation throughout the pipeline, offering better numerical stability and avoiding the need for basis conversion when root finding is required. This method transforms a trivariate polynomial representation from the B-spline basis (used in tri-linear or tri-cubic filtering) to the scaled Bernstein or power basis. It solves the problem of high memory consumption when storing explicit polynomial descriptions for large datasets, allowing on-the-fly transformation instead. It is distinct from naive substitution by leveraging the tensor product structure of the basis to reduce computational complexity, and differs from Composition via Scaled Bernstein Form by its specific focus on the initial basis conversion step for efficient Horner scheme integration. Time Complexity: The method significantly reduces the number of multiplications and additions compared to naive substitution. For a degree d=3 polynomial, it requires 234 multiplications and 360 additions, compared to 1839 multiplications and 990 additions for the naive method. Memory Complexity: The method uses only 27 registers, compared to 135 registers for the naive method. This is achieved by reusing memory for intermediate factors \mathbf{f}{ij} and \mathbf{g}i. Measured Performance: In tests on a GPU framework, the Power Form method achieved a relative execution time of 3.6 \times 10^{-3} compared to the naive method (relative time 1). Accuracy: The Mean Squared Error (MSE) for the Power Form method was 22.6 \times 10^{-12}, compared to 162.3 \times 10^{-12} for the naive method. Strengths: High performance on GPUs due to low register usage and reduced operation count. Good numerical stability. Limitations: Requires basis conversion if Bernstein form is needed for root finding, unlike the Scaled Bernstein Form method. When to use: When evaluating trivariate polynomial fields on GPUs where register pressure is a bottleneck and root finding is not required immediately. When not to use: When the downstream pipeline requires root finding in Bernstein basis, as basis conversion would be needed. The method was proposed in the context of wavelet-based multiresolution isosurface rendering. It builds on the idea of using convolution operators to efficiently evaluate polynomial compositions, as described in [SR03] (cited in). The approach addresses the limitations of naive substitution, which is too computationally expensive and register-intensive for GPU-based frameworks. name: Composition via Scaled Bernstein Form
body: Composition via Scaled Bernstein Form (SB) evaluates the composition of a trivariate polynomial field with a ray parameterization, transforming a 3D function into a univariate function along a ray. It solves the problem of efficient numerical evaluation in direct volume ray casting by leveraging the scaled Bernstein basis. Unlike Composition via Convolution (Power Form), which uses power bases and convolution operators, SB maintains a uniform data representation throughout the pipeline, offering better numerical stability and avoiding the need for basis conversion when root finding is required. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Trivariate polynomial coefficients \tilde{b}{ijk} for i,j,k \in [0, d]; ray direction components ux, uy, uz; ray origin components qx, qy, qz; polynomial degree d. Output: Univariate polynomial coefficients \tilde{\mathbf{f}} representing the field values along the ray. Data Structures: Coefficients \tilde{b}{ijk}: Stored as a 3D array of size (d+1) \times (d+1) \times (d+1). Ray components: Scalars ue, qe for e \in \{x, y, z\}, where qe = 1 - ue. Intermediate terms: Precomputed powers of ue and qe. Formulas: The scaled Bernstein form uses basis functions defined by ray components ue and qe = 1 - ue. The composed polynomial \tilde{\mathbf{f}} is given by: \tilde{\mathbf{f}} = \sum{i,j,k=0}^d \tilde{b}{ijk} \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{q}}x^{d-i} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}x^i \tilde{\mathbf{q}}y^{d-j} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}y^j \tilde{\mathbf{q}}z^{d-k} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}z^k This can be factored to reduce operations: \tilde{\mathbf{f}} = \sum{i=0}^d \tilde{\mathbf{q}}x^{d-i} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}x^i \sum{j=0}^d \tilde{\mathbf{q}}y^{d-j} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}y^j \sum{k=0}^d \tilde{b}{ijk} \tilde{\mathbf{q}}z^{d-k} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}z^k For a single dimension, the composed coefficient sequence \tilde{\mathbf{c}} is computed recursively (Horner-like): \tilde{\mathbf{c}} = \sum{i=0}^d \tilde{b}i \tilde{\mathbf{q}}^{d-i} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}^i = \tilde{b}d \tilde{\mathbf{u}}^d + \tilde{\mathbf{q}} (\tilde{b}{d-1} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{d-1} + \dots + \tilde{\mathbf{q}} (\tilde{b}1 \tilde{\mathbf{u}} + \tilde{b}0 \tilde{\mathbf{q}})) Steps: 1. Precompute powers of ue and qe for e \in \{x, y, z\} and exponents 0 \dots d. Specifically, compute \tilde{\mathbf{u}}e^k and \tilde{\mathbf{q}}e^{d-k} for all k. 2. For each i from 0 to d: a. For each j from 0 to d: i. Compute the inner sum over k: S{ij} = \sum{k=0}^d \tilde{b}{ijk} \tilde{\mathbf{q}}z^{d-k} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}z^k. This can be done using the Horner-like recursion. ii. Multiply S{ij} by \tilde{\mathbf{q}}y^{d-j} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}y^j. b. Sum the results from step 2.a.ii over j. c. Multiply by \tilde{\mathbf{q}}x^{d-i} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}x^i. 3. Sum the results from step 2.c over i to get \tilde{\mathbf{f}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatescaledbernstein(b, u, q, d): # b: 3D array of coefficients b[i][j][k] # u, q: arrays of ray components for x, y, z # Precompute powers for each axis upow = [[u[e]k for k in range(d + 1)] for e in range(3)] qpow = [[q[e](d - k) for k in range(d + 1)] for e in range(3)] f = 0.0 for i in range(d + 1): for j in range(d + 1): # Horner-like recursion for the inner k-sum c = b[i][j][d] upow[2][d] for k in range(d - 1, -1, -1): c = q[2] c + b[i][j][k] upow[2][k] q[2] # Multiply by y-basis terms termy = c qpow[1][j] upow[1][j] # Accumulate with x-basis terms f += termy qpow[0][i] upow[0][i] return f Parameters: Degree d: Typically small (e.g., 3-5) for trivariate polynomials in volume rendering. Ray components: ue, qe derived from ray direction and origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical stability: The scaled Bernstein form offers better stability than power form, especially for high degrees. Register usage: Naive implementation requires many registers. Optimized versions (SB1, SB2) reduce register pressure by reusing memory for intermediate coefficients. Precision: The operator denotes multiplication of basis terms; ensure floating-point precision is maintained during nested multiplications to avoid accumulation errors. Time Complexity: Significantly lower than naive evaluation. Operation counts for d=3 (from): SB0 (no precomputation): 741 muls, 483 adds. SB1 (precomputed x innermost): 687 muls, 490 adds. SB2 (precomputed x innermost, variant): 720 muls, 558 adds. Memory Complexity: Register usage is reduced compared to naive approach. SB0 uses 72 regs, SB1 uses 60 regs, SB2 uses 66 regs. Performance: Relative execution times (normalized to slowest) for d=3: SB0: 26e-3, SB1: 23e-3, SB2: 22e-3. Accuracy: Mean Squared Error (MSE) scaled by 10^{-12}: SB0: 5.15, SB1: 4.78, SB2: 4.78. Strengths: Uniform data representation, better numerical stability, avoids basis changes for root finding, fits well in GPU register space. Limitations: More complex implementation than power form. Precomputation adds memory overhead. When to use: When numerical stability is critical, or when root finding is needed later in the pipeline. When GPU register pressure is a bottleneck. When not to use: If simplicity is preferred and stability is not a concern. If memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and precomputation overhead is too high. The scaled Bernstein form was proposed in [SR03] (cited in) as an alternative to the power form for polynomial evaluation in rendering. It is particularly useful in volume rendering where trivariate polynomials are composed with ray parameterizations. The method was highlighted in for its ability to reduce register usage and improve parallelism on GPUs by fitting the computation into limited register space. head: B-spline to Bernstein/Power Basis Transform
body: This method transforms a trivariate polynomial representation from the B-spline basis (used in tri-linear or tri-cubic filtering) to the scaled Bernstein or power basis. It solves the problem of high memory consumption when storing explicit polynomial descriptions for large datasets, allowing on-the-fly transformation instead. It is distinct from naive substitution by leveraging the tensor product structure of the basis to reduce computational complexity, and differs from Composition via Scaled Bernstein Form by its specific focus on the initial basis conversion step for efficient Horner scheme integration. Inputs: Polynomial degree d (corresponding to the filtering order, e.g., d=1 for tri-linear, d=3 for tri-cubic). Data values in the B-spline basis for a voxel. Outputs: Coefficients in the scaled Bernstein or power basis. Data Structures: Basis vector \mathbf{b}: A 1D array of size d+1 representing the B-spline coefficients. Transformation Matrix M: A (d+1) \times (d+1) matrix containing constants (zeros, ones, and a single scaling factor). Steps: 1. One-Dimensional Basis Transform: For each dimension, compute the transformation from B-spline to the target basis by multiplying the basis vector by the transformation matrix M. The matrix M is precomputed to contain mostly zeros and ones, scaled by a constant factor to minimize arithmetic operations. Transition to the scaled Bernstein basis requires 6 multiplications per dimension, while transition to the power basis requires 8 multiplications per dimension. 2. N-Dimensional Basis Transform Construction: The N-dimensional basis is a tensor product of the 1D bases. The full N-dimensional transform is constructed from N \cdot (d + 1)^{N-1} one-dimensional basis transforms. For trivariate polynomials (N=3), this involves applying the 1D transforms sequentially along each axis. 3. Integration with Horner Scheme: The basis transform is integrated into the Horner scheme for polynomial evaluation/composition. This separation of dimensions allows efficient evaluation without explicitly storing the full trivariate polynomial coefficients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def apply1dtransform(coeffs, degree, M): """Applies the precomputed sparse transformation matrix M to a 1D coefficient vector.""" out = [0.0] (degree + 1) for i in range(degree + 1): for j in range(degree + 1): out[i] += M[i][j] coeffs[j] return out def basistransform3d(bsplinecoeffs, degree, M): """ Transforms trivariate B-spline coefficients to target basis using tensor product. Applies 1D transforms sequentially along each axis. """ # Allocate output array out = [[[0.0] (degree + 1) for in range(degree + 1)] for in range(degree + 1)] # Transform along X (axis 0) tempx = [[[0.0] (degree + 1) for in range(degree + 1)] for in range(degree + 1)] for k in range(degree + 1): for l in range(degree + 1): col = [bsplinecoeffs[i][k][l] for i in range(degree + 1)] transformedcol = apply1dtransform(col, degree, M) for i in range(degree + 1): tempx[i][k][l] = transformedcol[i] # Transform along Y (axis 1) tempy = [[[0.0] (degree + 1) for in range(degree + 1)] for in range(degree + 1)] for k in range(degree + 1): for l in range(degree + 1): row = [tempx[k][j][l] for j in range(degree + 1)] transformedrow = apply1dtransform(row, degree, M) for j in range(degree + 1): tempy[k][j][l] = transformedrow[j] # Transform along Z (axis 2) for k in range(degree + 1): for l in range(degree + 1): plane = [tempy[k][l][m] for m in range(degree + 1)] transformedplane = apply1dtransform(plane, degree, M) for m in range(degree + 1): out[k][l][m] = transformedplane[m] return out Parameters: Degree d (filtering order). Multiplications per 1D transform: 6 for scaled Bernstein, 8 for power basis. Edge Cases: Degree 0 is a trivial case requiring no transformation. Using matrices with zeros and ones reduces the number of required arithmetic operations rather than affecting floating-point precision. Generates the basis vector \mathbf{b} for a given degree d. It constructs the monomial or Bernstein basis functions required for the transformation. Time Complexity: The transformation requires N \cdot (d + 1)^{N-1} 1D transforms, resulting in a fixed number of multiplications (6 or 8 per dimension) due to the sparse matrix structure. Memory Complexity: Avoids storing the full explicit polynomial description, reducing memory consumption by a factor of (d+1)^3 compared to storing all coefficients explicitly. Strengths: Efficient on-the-fly transformation; low arithmetic complexity; compatible with Horner scheme for fast evaluation. Limitations: Requires precomputed transformation matrices; specific to B-spline to Bernstein/Power basis conversion. When to Use: When memory is constrained and the polynomial needs to be evaluated in a different basis (e.g., for root finding or composition). When Not to Use: If the B-spline basis is sufficient for the application (e.g., simple interpolation), as working directly with the original representation avoids unnecessary transformation overhead. The method is used in volume rendering pipelines that employ B-spline filtering (tri-linear/tri-cubic) and require efficient root finding or composition. Tri-linear and tri-cubic filtering are based on B-spline polynomials, and transforming to Bernstein or power basis enables efficient root finding and composition. The approach was developed to address the memory overhead of storing explicit polynomial descriptions for large volumes. name: Feed-Backward Reconstruction
head: Gather-based reconstruction, Ray-casting approach
body: Feed-backward reconstruction is a spatial-domain convolution method that computes each output sample by gathering weighted contributions from neighboring input samples. It solves the problem of resampling discrete volume data onto a finer or different grid by centering the reconstruction kernel at the output location and summing the input values weighted by the kernel function. It is distinguished from its sibling Composition via Convolution (Power Form) by its explicit spatial gathering loop structure, which accesses each output sample once and each input sample multiple times, contrasting with feed-forward approaches that distribute input energy to multiple outputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A discrete signal f (volume samples), a reconstruction kernel h, and a set of output positions. Output: A discrete signal g (resampled volume samples). Data Structures: InputSamples: Array of values f[i]. OutputSamples: Array of values g[j], initialized to zero. Kernel: Function h(\cdot) defining the weight based on distance. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize all output samples g[j] to 0. 2. Iterate through each output sample index j (representing the output position). 3. For each output sample j, identify the set of input samples i that lie within the support (extent) of the reconstruction kernel centered at the output position. 4. For each input sample i in the support: Calculate the kernel weight w = h(\text{distance between output position } j \text{ and input position } i). Accumulate the contribution: g[j] \leftarrow g[j] + f[i] \times w. 5. Repeat for all output samples. Formulas: The operation is a discrete convolution sum: g(x, y, z) = \sum{i=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum{j=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum{k=-\infty}^{\infty} f(i, j, k) h(x - i, y - j, z - k) where f is the input signal, h is the filter function, and g is the output signal. Parameters: Kernel Extent: Determines how many input samples are accessed per output sample. Common kernels include the triangular pulse (linear interpolation). Sampling Rate: The ratio of output samples to input samples affects the total number of accesses. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Input samples near the edge of the volume may have fewer neighbors within the kernel support. The implementation must handle indices outside the input array bounds (e.g., by clamping, mirroring, or assuming zero). Precision: Accumulating many small weights can lead to floating-point precision loss if not managed carefully, though standard double precision is usually sufficient for typical volume sizes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def feedbackwardreconstruction(inputsamples, kernelfunc, outputpositions): """ Performs feed-backward reconstruction. Args: inputsamples: List or array of input volume values. kernelfunc: Function that takes a distance and returns a weight. outputpositions: List of positions where output samples are desired. Returns: List of output volume values. """ numoutputs = len(outputpositions) outputsamples = [0.0] numoutputs # Pre-calculate input positions if not provided, assuming uniform spacing for simplicity # In a real implementation, inputpositions would be passed or derived from metadata # Here we assume inputsamples[i] is at position i for the sake of the algorithm structure # relative to outputpositions which are also in the same coordinate space. for outidx, outpos in enumerate(outputpositions): currentsum = 0.0 # Iterate over all input samples to find those under the kernel # Optimization: In practice, only iterate over input indices within kernel support for inidx, inval in enumerate(inputsamples): # Calculate distance between output position and input position # Assuming input at index i is at position i (normalized) dist = abs(outpos - inidx) # Check if input sample is within kernel support # The kernel support is defined by where kernelfunc(dist) > 0 weight = kernelfunc(dist) if weight != 0: currentsum += inval weight outputsamples[outidx] = currentsum return outputsamples Spatial convolution is the operation of convolving discrete samples with a reconstruction kernel in the spatial domain, as opposed to the frequency domain. It is preferred over frequency domain multiplication for discrete kernels of limited extent because transforming back and forth is more compute-intensive than direct spatial convolution. The mathematical definition in 3D is: g(x, y, z) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(u, v, w) h(x - u, y - v, z - w) du dv dw. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N{out} \times N{kernel}), where N{out} is the number of output samples and N{kernel} is the number of input samples within the kernel support. Memory: O(N{out}) for the output buffer, plus O(N{in}) for the input buffer. Measured Performance: In a specific example with 4 input samples, 13 output samples, and linear reconstruction (kernel extent covering 2 input samples per output), feed-backward reconstruction results in 39 sample accesses (2 input accesses per output \times 13 outputs + 13 output writes). This contrasts with feed-forward reconstruction, which would result in 24 sample accesses (5 output accesses per input \times 4 inputs + 4 input reads). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Intuitive mapping to the output grid; efficient for generating high-resolution outputs from lower-resolution inputs when the kernel is small. Limitations: High memory bandwidth usage for input samples, as each input sample is read multiple times (once for each output sample it influences). When to Use: Use when the output grid is significantly finer than the input grid, or when the kernel support is small. It is the standard approach in many volume renderers for resampling. Feed-backward reconstruction was described by Feibush in 1980. It is a fundamental technique in digital signal processing and computer graphics for resampling data. The method is based on the general theory of convolution, as detailed by Oppenheim in 1975. It is widely used in volume rendering algorithms that operate in the spatial domain, particularly those using small kernels.
