name: Alpha Blending
head: Accumulate opacity method, Porter-Duff compositing
body: Alpha blending is an image-order direct volume rendering technique that discretizes the continuous volume-rendering integral using a Riemann sum to perform front-to-back or back-to-front compositing. It is distinguished from its siblings by its direct implementation of the Porter-Duff "over" operator for digital image compositing, allowing transparent layers to be accumulated into a final color. Unlike Compositing which may refer to broader strategies, or Pre-Integration Lookup which approximates the integral for accuracy, alpha blending relies on the standard recursive accumulation of sample contributions weighted by accumulated opacity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, a viewing ray defined by origin x and direction w, and transfer functions mapping scalar values to color I(i) and opacity \alpha(i) (or transparency Ti) for each sample i along the ray. Output: The final pixel color I{out} (or Co). Data Structures: Ray Samples: A sequence of n samples i = 0 \dots n-1 along the ray. Each sample i has associated properties: I(i): The emitted/scattered color (pre-multiplied by opacity in standard implementations). \alpha(i): The opacity of the segment [i, i+1]. Ti: The transparency of the segment, where Ti = 1 - \alpha(i). Accumulators: I{in}: The accumulated intensity from samples processed so far. trans: The accumulated transparency (weight) of the remaining unprocessed samples. Formulas: The continuous light transport equation is given by: I(x, w) = \ints e^{\int0^s \sigma(t) dt} I(s) ds where \sigma(t) is the differential attenuation coefficient. The discrete approximation using equally spaced samples is: I = \sum{0 \leq i \leq n} \left( \prod{0 \leq j \leq i} e^{-\intj^{j+1} \sigma(t) dt} \right) I(i) The opacity of a ray segment [j, j+1] is defined as: \alpha(j) = 1 - e^{-\intj^{j+1} \sigma(t) dt} Consequently, the transparency of the segment is Tj = 1 - \alpha(j). Recursive Evaluation (Back-to-Front): The integral is evaluated recursively in back-to-front order (from i=n-1 down to 0) using the Porter-Duff "over" operator: I{out} = \alpha(i) I(i) + (1 - \alpha(i)) I{in} where I{in} is the intensity accumulated from samples behind the current sample i, and the initial I{in} is the ambient light (typically black, 0). Recursive Evaluation (Front-to-Back): Alternatively, front-to-back compositing can be implemented by tracking accumulated transparency. Let trans be the accumulated transparency of all samples processed so far (initially 1.0). For each sample i from front to back: I{out} += (1 - trans) \alpha(i) I(i) trans = (1 - \alpha(i)) This is equivalent to the front-to-back form Co = Ci + (1 - \taui) Ci^{pre} described in, where \taui is the transparency and Ci^{pre} is the pre-multiplied color. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode implements the back-to-front recursive evaluation, adapted from. It assumes a voxel-based traversal where Trace returns the index of the next active sample in a segment, and volume provides the color and opacity of the voxel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alphablending(x, z, volume, mask, threshold=1e-4): """ Renders a pixel at (x, z) by traversing rays in the y-dimension. Uses back-to-front accumulation logic adapted from the provided snippet. Note: The source pseudocode iterates y and uses a mask to find segments. This implementation generalizes the core accumulation logic. """ # Initial output color is ambient light (black) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # In the source, 'trans' represents accumulated transparency of # samples behind the current one in a back-to-front pass, # or samples in front in a front-to-back pass. # The source code: color += v.color v.opacity trans; trans = 1.0 - v.opacity; # This is a FRONT-TO-BACK accumulation where 'trans' is the weight # of the background (samples behind) that the current sample modulates? # Actually, standard front-to-back: color += (1 - accumulatedtransparency) alpha color. # The source code does: color += v.color v.opacity trans. # If trans starts at 1.0 and is multiplied by (1-opacity), it represents # the transparency of the remaining volume behind the current sample? # Let's trace: # Sample 1 (front): trans=1. color += c1 a1 1. trans becomes 1-a1. # Sample 2: trans=1-a1. color += c2 a2 (1-a1). # This matches the term: alpha(i) I(i) Product(1-alpha(j)) for j < i. # This is the standard front-to-back formula. trans = 1.0 # Iterate through samples along the ray. # The source uses a specific mask-based traversal for a 8x8x8 block. # We generalize to a standard sample loop. for i in range(numsamples): # Get voxel properties for sample i v = getvoxelatsample(i) # Update accumulated transparency of the volume behind the current sample # (which acts as the weight for the current sample's contribution in this specific # source's front-to-back logic where trans is the "background" transparency) trans = (1.0 - v.opacity) # Early ray termination: if the accumulated transparency is very low, # the remaining volume contributes negligibly. if trans < threshold: break # Add contribution: color opacity accumulatedtransparencyfrombehind # Note: v.color is assumed to be the emitted color I(i) color[0] += v.color[0] v.opacity trans color[1] += v.color[1] v.opacity trans color[2] += v.color[2] v.opacity trans return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors in the accumulation of trans can lead to incorrect early ray termination or color bleeding if trans underflows or accumulates error significantly over long rays. Boundaries: The initial value of I{in} must be the background color (usually black or the clear color of the framebuffer). Degenerate Input: If \alpha(i) = 0 for all samples, the result is the background color. If \alpha(i) = 1, the first sample occludes all subsequent ones in front-to-back rendering. The standard implementation where samples are processed from the camera outward. It allows for early ray termination when accumulated opacity is high. Link Samples are processed from the far end to the near end. It is mathematically equivalent but does not support early ray termination in the same way, though it can be useful for specific compositing orders or when integrating with other back-to-front techniques. Link Time Complexity: O(n) per pixel, where n is the number of samples along the ray. With early ray termination, the average case is often significantly faster. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray (excluding the volume data itself). Measured Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on the efficiency of the ray traversal and the sparsity of the volume. The source pseudocode uses a mask-based traversal to skip empty space, which can significantly reduce the number of samples processed. Strengths: Simple to implement; widely supported by graphics hardware (via fragment shaders); allows for early ray termination; produces visually plausible results for translucent volumes. Limitations: Approximates the continuous integral with a Riemann sum, which can lead to aliasing or inaccuracies in regions of high density variation compared to Pre-Integration Lookup. It does not account for lighting effects within the volume unless shading is added separately. When to use: General-purpose direct volume rendering where performance is critical and high-fidelity light transport approximation is not required. When not to use: When accurate integration of the light transport equation is needed (use Pre-Integration Lookup); when complex lighting effects like volumetric shadows are required without additional shading passes. Alpha blending was developed by Marc Levoy in 1988 as part of the "accumulate opacity method" for direct volume rendering. It is based on the Porter-Duff compositing operators used in digital image processing. The technique discretizes the continuous volume-rendering integral using a Riemann sum, resulting in front-to-back or back-to-front compositing. It is widely used in medical imaging for visualizing structures such as blood vessels, often in conjunction with shading techniques like Phong or Blinn-Phong models to enhance depth perception. name: Incremental Blending for In-scattering
head: Incremental In-scattering Blending
body: Incremental Blending for In-scattering is a method for approximating volumetric light scattering (in-scattering) in direct volume rendering by accumulating scattered light contributions from multiple directions into a single stored intensity buffer. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the integral of scattered light over a sphere of directions without storing per-direction results, by blending new directional samples into a running average. It differs from Lighting-Specific Compositing by specifically targeting the in-scattering term Is and using a harmonic mean update strategy, and from Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering by lacking the per-channel indirect attenuation and blur operations that allow light color to change with depth. The method discretizes the scattering sphere into J directions and updates the stored in-scattering intensity I{stored} incrementally for each direction j. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data (opacity \alpha, color c), transfer function domain, light source direction, number of scattering directions J. Output: A volume buffer storing the accumulated in-scattering intensity I{stored} for each voxel. Data Structures: I{stored}: A 3D volume buffer (same resolution as the volume data or a reduced resolution SVR) storing the scalar intensity value for each voxel. I{final}: A temporary scalar value computed for the current direction j and voxel. Parameters: I{bias}: A parameter in the range [0, 1] adjusting the minimum light level. Default behavior assumes a white light source. J: The total number of directions used to discretize the scattering sphere. Formulas: The eye-space intensity I{eye} is computed as a Riemann sum: I{eye} = \sum{k=0}^n gk \prod{p=0}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha(sp)) \quad (12) where gk is the emitted color at sample k, \alpha(sp) is opacity, and n is the total number of samples along the ray. The term gk is defined as: gk = I{final} \cdot c(sk) \cdot \alpha(sk) where c(sk) is the color from the transfer function at sample point sk, and I{final} is the in-scattering contribution for the current direction: I{final} = I{bias} + (1 - I{bias}) \cdot Is(sk) Here, Is(sk) is the scattered intensity at sample sk. The incremental blending step updates the stored intensity for direction j (where j ranges from 1 to J): I{blended} = \frac{1}{j} \cdot I{final} + \left(1 - \frac{1}{j}\right) \cdot I{stored} \quad (13) where I{blended} is the new value to store, I{final} is the result from the current direction j, and I{stored} is the previously accumulated intensity. Steps: 1. Initialize the I{stored} volume buffer to zero or an appropriate initial value. 2. Compute the direction of the light source first to ensure shadows are correctly approximated. 3. Determine the subsequent J-1 directions of the scattering sphere by subdividing a tetrahedron, icosahedron, or octahedron to achieve the desired number of rays J. 4. For each incremental update step j from 1 to J: a. For each voxel (or sample point sk along the ray), compute I{final} using the current direction's scattered intensity Is(sk) and the bias parameter I{bias}. b. Compute the blended intensity I{blended} using Eq. 13: I{blended} = \frac{1}{j} \cdot I{final} + \left(1 - \frac{1}{j}\right) \cdot I{stored} c. Store I{blended} as the new I{stored} for that voxel. 5. Use the final I{stored} values in the compositing equation (Eq. 12) to compute the final eye-space intensity I{eye}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalblendinginscattering(volume, transferfunction, lightdirection, J, Ibias): """ volume: 3D array of opacity alpha and color c transferfunction: function to map density to color c and opacity alpha lightdirection: vector for the primary light source J: number of scattering directions Ibias: minimum light level parameter [0, 1] """ # Initialize stored intensity buffer # Resolution may be reduced (SVR) to save space Istored = zeroslike(volume.opacity) # Compute scattering directions # Subdivide tetrahedron, icosahedron, or octahedron to get J directions scatteringdirections = computespheresampling(J, lightdirection) for j, direction in enumerate(scatteringdirections, start=1): # Compute scattered intensity Is for this direction # This requires ray casting through the volume for each voxel or sample # Is depends on the specific light propagation model Is = computescatteredintensity(volume, direction, transferfunction) # Compute Ifinal for each voxel # Ifinal = Ibias + (1 - Ibias) Is Ifinal = Ibias + (1.0 - Ibias) Is # Incremental blend # Iblended = (1/j) Ifinal + (1 - 1/j) Istored weightnew = 1.0 / j weightold = 1.0 - weightnew Istored = weightnew Ifinal + weightold Istored return Istored Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: The method generates large amounts of data if computed at full resolution. For a 512^3 volume, three additional 512^3 volumes are needed to store intermediate results (\alpha lp, \alpha g, I{final}). It is recommended to reduce the resolution of the SVR (Sparse Voxel Representation) to mitigate this. Precision: The blending formula involves division by j. For large J, the contribution of new samples becomes small. Standard floating-point precision should be sufficient, but accumulation errors may occur over many steps. Boundary Conditions: Rays originating in empty blocks (black squares) in a multi-resolution structure should be advanced to the next nonempty block to avoid incorrect sampling. Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering is a screen-space technique that approximates volumetric light scattering (translucency) by propagating and blurring indirect lighting components across volume slices. It extends the base Incremental Blending for In-scattering method by introducing per-channel indirect attenuation parameters and a blur operation, allowing light to change color as it penetrates deeper into the volume, similar to the effect of holding a flashlight under a hand. Choose this when color attenuation with depth is critical. Hardware Blending Recurrence Evaluation is a technique for evaluating the multiple forward scattering recurrence Ik = g{k-1} + T{k-1} I{k-1} by mapping the mathematical operation to GPU hardware blending and pixel read-back operations. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the incident light on a particle in a participating medium by leveraging the frame buffer as an accumulator. It differs from Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering by using explicit pixel read-back to resolve the recurrence dependency, whereas its sibling uses a different accumulation strategy. Choose this when hardware blending capabilities can be exploited for recurrence evaluation. Time Complexity: O(J \cdot N), where J is the number of scattering directions and N is the number of voxels or samples. Each direction requires a full pass over the volume. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the I{stored} buffer. Additional temporary buffers may be required for intermediate computations (\alpha lp, \alpha g, I{final}), potentially tripling the memory requirement if computed at full resolution. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of scattering directions J and the volume resolution. Reducing the SVR resolution can significantly reduce memory and computation time. Strengths: Efficiently approximates in-scattering without storing per-direction results. Simple incremental update rule. Limitations: High memory usage if not using reduced resolution. Assumes white light source by default (though easily extended to colored light). When to use: When real-time or interactive global light propagation is needed in direct volume rendering. When not to use: When high-fidelity color attenuation with depth is required (use Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering instead). The method originates from the paper "Interactive Global Light Propagation in Direct Volume Rendering using Local Piecewise Integration" by. It is part of a broader effort to incorporate global illumination effects, specifically in-scattering, into interactive volume rendering systems. The approach uses local piecewise integration to approximate the light propagation within the volume. name: Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering
head: Translucency Approximation via Indirect Attenuation
body: Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering is a screen-space technique that approximates volumetric light scattering (translucency) by propagating and blurring indirect lighting components across volume slices. It extends the base Incremental Blending for In-scattering method by introducing per-channel indirect attenuation parameters and a blur operation, allowing light to change color as it penetrates deeper into the volume, similar to the effect of holding a flashlight under a hand. This method builds on Incremental Blending for In-scattering by modifying the light buffer initialization, the compositing blend function, and the data flow to support spatial blurring of indirect attenuation. Inputs: Volume data (density, color). Indirect attenuation parameters Ai: Alpha values for each RGB color channel (distinct from the standard alpha A used in the eye-pass). Light color CL. Sample distance d. Blur angle: A user-defined parameter scaling the perturbation radius. Perturbation texture: Used to generate modified texture coordinates for blurring. Outputs: Final rendered image with translucent lighting effects. Light Buffers: Two framebuffers (or textures) are used in an alternating fashion. Let them be L{current} and L{next}. L{current}: Stores the indirect attenuation state for the current slice iteration. L{next}: The render target for the updated attenuation state after blurring and blending. Perturbation Texture: A texture containing noise or pattern data used to perturb texture coordinates for the blur sampling. The method modifies the standard incremental ray casting loop (Algorithm 39-3 in) as follows: 1. Initialization: Initialize the light buffer (L{current}) with the value 1 - CL instead of the standard light color CL. 2. Per-Slice Loop: For each volume slice (or ray step), perform the following: 3. Eye Pass (Pass 1): Sample the volume. Read the indirect attenuation value A{in} from L{current} using standard texture coordinates. Compute the fragment color C (standard direct lighting/compositing result). Modify the color by multiplying it by the remaining indirect transmission: C{final} = C \times (1 - A{in}). Output C{final} to the color buffer. 4. Light Pass (Pass 2): This pass updates the light buffer to propagate and blur indirect light for the next slice. Blending Operation: Replace the standard "Over" operator with the Light Buffer Compositing blend. Let C1 be the incoming fragment color (from the volume sample's indirect contribution). Let C0 be the color currently in the target render buffer (L{next}). Let A{in} be the incoming fragment alpha (the indirect attenuation parameter Ai for the current sample). The blended result C{out} is computed as: C{out} = C0 \times (1 - A{in}) + C1 \times (1 - C0) (Note: The source describes Equation 8 as C{out} = C{in} (1 - C{target}) + C{target} (1 - A{in}) in the notes, but the text clarifies C1 is incoming fragment color and C0 is target buffer color. The standard Over operator is C0(1-A1) + C1 A1. The specific "Light Buffer Compositing" for translucency is defined in the text as replacing Over. Based on the note's formula structure C{out} = C{in} (1 - C{target}) + C{target} (1 - A{in}), and standard alpha blending logic adapted for this specific buffer, the implementation must follow the source's Equation 8 definition. The note provides: C{out} = C{in} (1 - C{target}) + C{target} (1 - A{in}). We use this exact formula.) Blur Operation: Calculate the blur radius R using the sample distance d and the blur angle \theta: R = d \times \theta (Note: The source mentions Equation 9 for Blur Radius but does not provide the explicit LaTeX formula in the snippet, only describing it as scaling the perturbation by d and the blur angle. We assume a linear scaling or standard angular projection. If the source implies R = d \cdot \tan(\theta) or similar, it is not explicitly given. We state the dependency.) For each fragment in this pass, modify the texture coordinates for sampling L{current} using the perturbation texture. The perturbation is scaled by R. Sample L{current} multiple times using these modified coordinates. Compute the blurred attenuation as a weighted sum of the sampled values. Blend this blurred value into L{next} using the Light Buffer Compositing operation defined above. 5. Buffer Swap: After processing the slice, swap L{current} and L{next} so that the updated buffer becomes the source for the next slice's Eye Pass. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Lcurrent = Lbuffers[0] Lnext = Lbuffers[1] Lcurrent.clear() Lcurrent.setpixel(1.0 - CL) # Initialize with 1 - Light Color for slice in volumeslices: # Pass 1: Eye Pass for fragment in slice: # Standard volume sampling to get direct color C and standard alpha A Cdirect, Astandard = samplevolume(fragment) # Read indirect attenuation from current light buffer Aindirect = Lcurrent.sample(fragment.uv) # Multiply direct color by remaining indirect transmission Cfinal = Cdirect (1.0 - Aindirect) outputcolorbuffer(fragment.uv, Cfinal) # Pass 2: Light Pass (Update and Blur Light Buffer) Lnext.clear() # Determine blur radius # R = d blurangle (assuming linear scaling as per description) R = sampledistance blurangle for fragment in slice: # 1. Compute Blurred Indirect Attenuation blurredA = 0.0 weightsum = 0.0 # Sample current light buffer multiple times with perturbed coordinates for sample in blursamples: # Perturb UV using perturbation texture scaled by R perturbation = perturbationtexture.sample(sample.uv) uvperturbed = fragment.uv + perturbation R # Sample the current light buffer val = Lcurrent.sample(uvperturbed) # Weighted sum (weights depend on blur kernel, e.g., Gaussian) w = getblurweight(sample.offset, R) blurredA += val w weightsum += w blurredA /= weightsum # 2. Compute Incoming Fragment Color for Light Buffer # In the context of the light buffer, the "incoming fragment" # is the indirect contribution being propagated. # Based on the method, we are propagating the attenuation/light state. # The note says "set the fragment shader color to Ai instead of 0". # This implies Cin for the blend equation is related to Ai. # However, Equation 8 blends Cin and Ctarget. # In the Light Pass, we are updating the light buffer. # The "incoming fragment" C1 in Eq 8 refers to the value being written # by the fragment shader before blending. # The text says: "set the color in the fragment shader to Ai". # So C1 = Aindirect (the raw indirect attenuation for this sample). Cin = Aindirect # The indirect attenuation parameter for this sample # 3. Apply Light Buffer Compositing # C0 is the value currently in Lnext (target) Ctarget = Lnext.sample(fragment.uv) Ain = Aindirect # The alpha for the incoming fragment in the blend equation # Equation 8: Cout = Cin (1 - Ctarget) + Ctarget (1 - Ain) # Note: The note formula uses Cin and Ctarget. # Cin is the fragment color (Aindirect). # Ctarget is the buffer color. # Ain is the fragment alpha (Aindirect). Cout = Cin (1.0 - Ctarget) + Ctarget (1.0 - Ain) Lnext.setpixel(fragment.uv, Cout) # Swap buffers Lcurrent, Lnext = Lnext, Lcurrent Ai: Indirect attenuation parameters, alpha values for each RGB channel. Must be set independently per channel to achieve color-changing penetration. d: Sample distance, used to calculate the blur radius. Blur Angle: User-defined parameter scaling the perturbation radius. Color-Changing Penetration: To achieve effects like white light turning red as it penetrates (e.g., flashlight under hand), set the Ai value for red smaller than the Ai values for green and blue. This results in lower attenuation of the red component, allowing more red light to pass through deeper layers. Precision: The method relies on screen-space buffers. Matching the resolution of light propagation to the viewport produces crisp shadows with minimal aliasing artifacts. Decoupling: The resolution of light transport is decoupled from the 3D data grid, allowing accurate lighting of volumes without increasing the 3D sampling density. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of volume samples and slices, plus the cost of the blur operation (multiple samples per fragment in Pass 2). Memory Complexity: Requires two additional light buffers (framebuffers) in addition to standard color and depth buffers. Strengths: Produces convincing translucent effects for clouds and atmospheric phenomena. Decouples light transport resolution from 3D data grid resolution. Matches light propagation resolution to viewport, reducing aliasing in shadows. Limitations: Approximation: Relies on local neighborhood blurring, which may not capture complex global light transport accurately. Requires additional buffer management and passes. This technique is described in GPU Gems, Chapter 39, "Volume Rendering Techniques". It is part of the broader effort to compute volumetric light transport in screen space, offering advantages over purely grid-based methods for certain visual effects like clouds. name: Hardware Blending Recurrence Evaluation
head: Frame buffer read back blending
body: Hardware Blending Recurrence Evaluation is a technique for evaluating the multiple forward scattering recurrence Ik = g{k-1} + T{k-1} I{k-1} by mapping the mathematical operation to GPU hardware blending and pixel read-back operations. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the incident light on a particle in a participating medium by leveraging the frame buffer as an accumulator. It differs from Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering by using explicit pixel read-back to resolve the recurrence dependency, whereas its sibling uses a different accumulation strategy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of particles P, each with extinction \tauk, albedo ak, radius rk, and position. Light direction \mathbf{l} and light color/intensity. Outputs: The scattered light contribution c for each particle, which is then rendered toward the eye. Data Structures: Frame Buffer: Stores the accumulated incident light intensity I. Initialized to white (representing I0 = 1 or full intensity). Particle List: Sorted by distance to the light source for the preprocessing pass. Parameters: Source Blend Factor (f{src}): 1. Destination Blend Factor (f{dest}): T{k-1} = \exp(-\tau{k-1}) (transparency of the previous particle). Texture/Fragment Mode: Modulate. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Illumination Pass): 1. Clear the frame buffer to white. This represents the initial incident light I0. 2. Sort particles pk by increasing distance to the light source. 3. For each particle pk in sorted order: a. Read Back: Read the pixel color x at the projection of the particle's center from the frame buffer. This value represents I{k-1}, the incident light on the previous particle (or the transmitted light through it). b. Compute Incident Light: Calculate Ik = \text{color}(x) \times \text{light\color}. This is the light incident on the current particle pk. c. Compute Scattered Color: Calculate the scattered light contribution g{k-1} (denoted as c in the source code logic, but representing the source term for the next step) using the formula: c = ak \cdot \tauk \cdot Ik / 4\pi where ak is albedo, \tauk is extinction, and Ik is incident light. d. Set Render Parameters: Set the particle's alpha to 1 - \exp(-\tauk). Set the particle's color to c (modulated by phase function if applicable, see code). e. Render and Blend: Render the particle. The hardware blending equation is: c{result} = f{src} \cdot c{src} + f{dest} \cdot c{dest} Substituting the parameters: Ik = 1 \cdot g{k-1} + T{k-1} \cdot I{k-1} Here, c{src} is the particle's color (g{k-1}), c{dest} is the frame buffer value (I{k-1}), f{src}=1, and f{dest}=T{k-1}. This updates the frame buffer to store Ik for the next particle. 2. Runtime (Eye Scattering Pass): 1. Sort particles by decreasing distance from the eye. 2. For each particle, compute the scattering toward the eye using the precomputed Ik and the phase function phase(\omega, \mathbf{l}), where \omega is the direction to the viewer. 3. Render particles with standard compositing (e.g., Direct Volume Ray Casting principles) using the precomputed illumination. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. framebuffer.clear(value=1.0) # White, representing I0 particles.sort(key=lambda p: distance(p.position, lightposition)) for p in particles: # Read incident light I{k-1} from frame buffer # Note: In a real implementation, this requires a read-back operation # which is expensive. The source implies this is done per particle. incidentlightprev = framebuffer.readpixel(p.projectedcenter) # Compute incident light Ik Ik = incidentlightprev lightcolor # Compute scattered light contribution g{k-1} for the recurrence # Formula: c = ak tauk Ik / 4pi scatteredcontribution = p.albedo p.extinction Ik / (4 math.pi) # Apply phase function for directionality (if needed for the recurrence term) # The source code snippet shows: c = pk.color phase(omega, l) # However, the recurrence term g{k-1} is the light scattered TO the next particle. # The direction to the next particle is along the light direction l. # So phase(omega, l) where omega is direction to next particle (l) is phase(l, l). # The source code snippet seems to mix the runtime phase function with the preprocess. # Based on Eq 4 and text: g{k-1} is the scattered light. # We assume the phase function is applied to the scattered light direction. # For forward scattering along l, the phase function is phase(l, l). scatteredcontribution = phasefunction(l, l) # Set render state for blending # Source color is the scattered contribution g{k-1} # Destination factor is T{k-1} = exp(-tau{k-1}) # Source factor is 1 alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-p.extinction) # Render particle # The blending operation updates the frame buffer: # Ik = 1 g{k-1} + T{k-1} I{k-1} renderparticle( position=p.position, radius=p.radius, color=scatteredcontribution, alpha=alpha, blendsrc=1.0, blenddst=math.exp(-p.extinction) # T{k-1}) particles.sort(key=lambda p: -distance(p.position, eyeposition)) for p in particles: # Use precomputed Ik # Compute scattering toward eye omega = eyeposition - p.position omega = normalize(omega) # The source code snippet: c = pk.color phase(omega, l) # pk.color was set to ak tauk Ik / 4pi # So final color is (ak tauk Ik / 4pi) phase(omega, l) finalcolor = p.precomputedcolor phasefunction(omega, l) renderparticle( position=p.position, radius=p.radius, color=finalcolor, alpha=1.0 - math.exp(-p.extinction), blendsrc=1.0, blenddst=0.0 # Standard alpha blending for eye scattering, not recurrence) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Reading back pixels from the frame buffer for every particle is extremely slow on modern GPUs due to cache coherency and synchronization barriers. This method is primarily of theoretical or historical interest for understanding the recurrence mapping. Precision: Floating-point precision in the frame buffer may accumulate errors over many particles. Boundary Conditions: The frame buffer must be cleared to the correct initial value (I0) before each pass. Time Complexity: O(N) particles, but with a high constant factor due to N pixel read-back operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory beyond the frame buffer and particle list. Strengths: Conceptually simple mapping of the recurrence to hardware blending. Limitations: Pixel read-back is a bottleneck. Not suitable for real-time performance with large particle counts. When to use: Only for educational purposes or very small particle counts where correctness of the recurrence evaluation is prioritized over performance. The method was presented in the paper "Real-Time Cloud Rendering" by Dobashi et al. (2001). It was developed to efficiently handle multiple forward scattering in cloud rendering by leveraging existing GPU hardware features. The technique is specific to the context of particle-based cloud rendering and relies on the specific recurrence relation for forward scattering. Real-Time Cloud Rendering, https://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/01-005.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Tiled Ray Marching with Grid Sampling
head: Python-loop renderer, Tiled rendering
body: Renders a single view of a 3D volume by generating rays, sampling density via gridsample, and accumulating attenuation. It supports tiling to manage memory usage for large images. Unlike Fixed Step Ray Marching which may iterate sequentially, this method leverages batched tensor operations for sampling while using tiling to handle memory constraints that would otherwise cause out-of-memory errors in dense volume rendering. Inputs: volume: 3D density tensor of shape (D, H, W) or (C, D, H, W). cameramatrix: 4 \times 4 matrix defining camera pose. ijk2ras: 4 \times 4 transformation matrix from volume grid (IJK) to physical space (RAS). raysamples: Number of samples per ray. tileh, tilew: Tile dimensions for memory management. usebeerlambert: Boolean flag for attenuation model. densityfactor: Scaling factor for non-Beer-Lambert mode. margin: Safety margin for near/far clipping. Outputs: Rendered image tensor. Optional transmittance or optical depth (tau). Data Structures: dirscam: Buffer of shape (H, W, 3) storing normalized camera-space view directions. dirsworld: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) storing world-space view directions. originijk: Tensor of shape (3,) storing the camera origin in IJK space. dirsijk: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) storing ray directions in IJK space. ijk: Tensor of shape (ray\samples, H, W, 3) storing sample coordinates in IJK space. densityb: Tensor of shape (1, C, W, H, D) prepared for gridsample. Steps: 1. Initialize Camera Directions: Compute the vertical field of view (FOV) to populate dirscam. Generate a grid of directions in camera space, normalize them, and store in dirscam. 2. Extract Camera Pose: Extract the camera-to-world rotation (cam2world) and position (campos) from the cameramatrix. If the matrix represents world-to-camera (indicated by small translation norm), invert it to get camera-to-world. 3. Transform Directions to World Space: Transform camera-space directions to world space: \text{dirs\world} = \text{einsum}('ij,hwj->hwi', \text{cam2world}, \text{dirs\cam}) This results in shape (H, W, 3). 4. Extract Volume Transformation: Extract the RAS-to-IJK rotation (R) and translation (t) from ijk2ras. Compute the scale factor: s = \frac{2.0}{\text{vol\shape} - 1} where volshape is (D, H, W). 5. Transform to IJK Space: Transform world-space directions to IJK space: \text{dirs\ijk} = \text{dirs\world} @ R^T Transform camera position to IJK space: \text{origin\ijk} = \text{cam\pos} @ R^T + t Resulting shapes: dirsijk is (H, W, 3), originijk is (3,). 6. Compute Near and Far Clipping: Calculate near and far clipping distances by projecting the 8 corners of the volume bounding box (in IJK space, transformed to RAS) onto the view direction from the camera position. Add the margin to expand the range. 7. Generate Sample Depths: Compute sample depths along the ray: \text{depths} = \text{near} + (\text{far} - \text{near}) \times \text{linspace}(0, 1, \text{ray\samples}) Shape: (ray\samples,). 8. Compute IJK Coordinates: Compute IJK coordinates for all samples: \text{ijk} = s \times (\text{origin\ijk} + \text{dirs\ijk} \times \text{depths}[:, \text{None}, \text{None}, \text{None}]) - 1 This results in shape (ray\samples, H, W, 3). 9. Prepare Density Tensor: Prepare the density tensor for gridsample by unsqueezing to shape (1, C, W, H, D). 10. Render Tile: Define a function rendertile that: Samples density using F.gridsample(densityb, coordstile, aligncorners=False). If usebeerlambert is True: Compute optical depth: \tau = \sum (\text{dens\tile} \times \text{step\size}, \text{dim}=2). If returntau is True, apply Poisson noise to \tau. Otherwise, apply Poisson noise to \exp(-\tau) and return 1 - \text{noisy\transmission}. If usebeerlambert is False: Compute d = \text{density\factor} \times \text{dens\tile} / \text{ray\samples}. Compute transmission: \text{transmission} = \text{cumprod}(1.0 - d, \text{dim}=2). Compute weight: \text{weight} = d \times \text{transmission}. Compute alpha: \alpha = 1 - \prod (1.0 - d, \text{dim}=2). Return (\text{weight.sum(dim=2)} / (w\sum + 10^{-6})) \times \alpha. 11. Tiling Execution: If the image is smaller than 2 \times \text{tile\h} \times 2 \times \text{tile\w}, call rendertile with the full grid. Otherwise, iterate over H and W in steps of tileh and tilew. For each tile, extract the corresponding grid coordinates, call rendertile, and collect outputs. Concatenate outputs along W and H axes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def tiledraymarching(volume, cameramatrix, ijk2ras, raysamples, tileh=256, tilew=256, usebeerlambert=True, densityfactor=1.0, margin=30.0): """ Renders a volume using tiled ray marching with grid sampling. """ # 1. Initialize Camera Directions h, w = volume.shape[-2], volume.shape[-1] dirscam = torch.empty(h, w, 3) #... (populate dirscam based on FOV, normalized)... # 2. Extract Camera Pose cammatrix = torch.tensor(cameramatrix, dtype=torch.float32) ijk2rastensor = torch.tensor(ijk2ras, dtype=torch.float32) # Handle batched or single matrix if cammatrix.ndim == 3: camtoworldall = torch.inverse(cammatrix) else: camtoworldall = torch.inverse(cammatrix.unsqueeze(0)).squeeze(0) # Determine if inversion was needed based on translation norm testpos = cammatrix[:,:3, 3] if cammatrix.ndim == 3 else cammatrix[:3, 3] translationnorm = torch.norm(testpos, dim=-1) needsinvert = translationnorm < 1.0 camposras = torch.where(needsinvert, camtoworldall[:,:3, 3], cammatrix[:,:3, 3]) viewdir = torch.where(needsinvert, camtoworldall[:,:3, 2], cammatrix[:,:3, 2]) viewdir = viewdir / torch.norm(viewdir, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # 3. Transform Directions to World Space cam2world = camtoworldall[:3,:3] dirsworld = torch.einsum('ij,hwj->hwi', cam2world, dirscam) # 4. Extract Volume Transformation R = ijk2rastensor[:3,:3] t = ijk2rastensor[:3, 3] volshape = volume.shape scale = 2.0 / (torch.tensor(volshape, dtype=torch.float32) - 1) # 5. Transform to IJK Space dirsijk = dirsworld @ R.T originijk = camposras @ R.T + t # 6. Compute Near and Far Clipping I, J, K = volshape cornersijk = torch.tensor([ [0, 0, 0], [I-1, 0, 0], [0, J-1, 0], [I-1, J-1, 0], [0, 0, K-1], [I-1, 0, K-1], [0, J-1, K-1], [I-1, J-1, K-1] ], dtype=torch.float32) cornershomog = torch.cat([cornersijk, torch.ones(8, 1)], dim=1) cornersras = (ijk2rastensor @ cornershomog.T).T[:,:3] tocorners = cornersras.unsqueeze(0) - originijk.unsqueeze(1) distances = torch.sum(tocorners viewdir.unsqueeze(1), dim=2) near = torch.min(distances, dim=1).values - margin far = torch.max(distances, dim=1).values + margin near = torch.clamp(near, min=0.1) # 7. Generate Sample Depths stepsize = 0.1 (far - near) / raysamples depths = near + (far - near) torch.linspace(0, 1, raysamples) # 8. Compute IJK Coordinates ijk = scale (originijk.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) + dirsijk.unsqueeze(0) depths[:, None, None, None]) - 1 # 9. Prepare Density Tensor densityb = volume.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # Shape (1, 1, W, H, D) # 10. Render Tile Function def rendertile(coordstile): denstile = F.gridsample(densityb, coordstile, aligncorners=False) if usebeerlambert: tau = torch.sum(denstile stepsize, dim=2) # Poisson noise application would go here transmission = torch.exp(-tau) return 1.0 - transmission else: d = densityfactor denstile / raysamples transmission = torch.cumprod(1.0 - d, dim=2) weight = d transmission alpha = 1.0 - torch.prod(1.0 - d, dim=2) wsum = torch.sum(weight, dim=2) return (wsum / (wsum + 1e-6)) alpha # 11. Tiling Execution if h < 2 tileh and w < 2 tilew: return rendertile(ijk) else: outputs = [] for i in range(0, h, tileh): for j in range(0, w, tilew): tilecoords = ijk[:, i:i+tileh, j:j+tilew,:] out = rendertile(tilecoords) outputs.append(out) # Concatenate outputs #... (concatenate along H and W axes)... return torch.cat(outputs, dim=1) # Simplified concatenation Parameters: tileh, tilew: Tile dimensions used to bound peak memory. Default 256x256. Ignored if image is smaller than 2 \times \text{tile\h} \times 2 \times \text{tile\w}. usecheckpointing: Boolean flag. If True and training, use torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint to save memory during backprop. usebeerlambert: Boolean flag. If True, use Beer-Lambert law (exponential attenuation). If False, use a different accumulation model (cumulative product of (1-d)). scatter: Optional scatter function. If present, scatter channels are processed separately and concatenated with non-scatter channels. densityfactor: Scaling factor applied to density in the non-Beer-Lambert mode. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise when computing ijk coordinates if the volume is very large or the camera is very close. Boundary conditions: gridsample with aligncorners=False handles out-of-bounds coordinates by returning zero or padding values, which may affect edge pixels. Degenerate input: If near equals far, step size becomes zero, leading to division by zero or no sampling. The code clamps near to a minimum of 0.1. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W \cdot \text{ray\samples}) where N is the number of tiles. Tiling does not change the total number of samples but may introduce overhead from tile management. Memory Complexity: O(\text{tile\h} \cdot \text{tile\w} \cdot \text{ray\samples}) for the intermediate tensors during rendering. This allows rendering of large images that would otherwise exceed GPU memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with image resolution due to tiling. Performance is limited by memory bandwidth and tensor operation efficiency. Strengths: Memory efficient for large images; leverages GPU-accelerated gridsample for fast density lookup. Limitations: Tiling introduces overhead; may not be optimal for very small images where full-grid rendering is faster. When to use: When rendering high-resolution volumes that exceed available GPU memory. When not to use: For small images or when memory is not a constraint, full-grid rendering may be simpler and faster. Originated in the context of deep learning-based volume rendering, specifically in the flashdrr repository. It is designed to integrate with PyTorch's automatic differentiation and GPU acceleration capabilities. pcarnah/flashdrr, https://github.com/pcarnah/flashdrr, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Octree-based Void Culling
head: Brick Octree, Void Culling Octree
body: Octree-based void culling is a spatial acceleration technique used in direct volume ray casting to reduce rasterization load by skipping empty regions within volume bricks. It builds on Window/Level Volume Raycasting with Bricking by introducing a per-brick octree structure that describes only the geometry of visible data, allowing the renderer to bypass void areas before invoking the GPU. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on global spatial structures or GPU-side culling, this approach generates and traverses the octree on the CPU to minimize GPU workload, while the GPU handles the actual interpolation, transfer function application, and blending. Input: A volume brick (texture), a transfer function mapping scalar values to opacity (\alpha) and color, and an octree level limit. Output: A set of rasterized slices (cuboid boxes) representing the visible portion of the brick, blended into the frame buffer. The octree is stored in main memory. Each node in the octree represents a cuboid sub-region of the brick. Node Fields: ratio (r): A float representing the ratio of visible data to total data within the node's cube. children: An array of 8 child nodes (if not a leaf). isleaf: Boolean indicating if the node represents a single cell. Leaf Nodes: At the final octree level, each node represents a unique cell. If the cell is completely void, r = 0. If the cell is completely filled (visible), r = 1. Cell: The smallest unit of void detection. For trilinear interpolation, a cell is a cube defined by 8 corner adjacent voxel values. A cell is completely void if all 8 corner values are transparent (\alpha = 0) after applying the transfer function. For other interpolation kernels, the cell size is defined as (kernelsize - 1)^3. 1. Octree Construction (CPU): Initialize leaf nodes for the brick. For each leaf node, determine if it is void or filled based on the cell definition. Set r=0 or r=1 accordingly. Recursively calculate r for higher-level nodes by averaging the r values of their 8 children: r{parent} = \frac{1}{8} \sum{i=1}^{8} r{childi} This calculation is performed only when the transfer function changes. 2. Rendering Preparation (CPU): Sort bricks in front-to-back order relative to the camera. For each brick, traverse its octree starting from the root node. 3. Octree Traversal and Culling (CPU): For each node, evaluate its ratio r against a threshold T (where 0 < T \le 1). Case r = 0: The node is completely void. Do not draw and do not traverse further. Case 0 < r < T: The node contains mixed data. Sort its 8 children in front-to-back order. There are 8 possible valid orders due to axis alignment constraints (not 8!). Recursively apply this strategy to each child. Case r \ge T: The node is sufficiently filled. Draw the node completely as a cuboid box. Do not traverse further. Level Limit: To prevent excessive overhead at deep levels, an octree level limit is set. Nodes below this level that are not void (r > 0) are drawn completely without further traversal. 4. Rendering (GPU): When a node is selected for drawing (Case r \ge T or leaf nodes), the corresponding cuboid box is sliced. Slices can be axis-aligned or viewport-aligned. The brick texture is interpolated on each slice. The transfer function is applied. Slices are rasterized and blended into the previously drawn slices. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbrickoctree(bricktexture, transferfunction, threshold, maxdepth, currentdepth, node, cameradirection): """ Recursively traverse the octree for a single brick. Args: bricktexture: The texture data for the brick. transferfunction: Function mapping voxel value to (color, alpha). threshold: Float T. If node.r >= T, draw node. maxdepth: Integer. Stop traversal if currentdepth >= maxdepth. currentdepth: Integer. Current depth in the octree. node: The current octree node. cameradirection: Vector. Direction of view for sorting. """ # Base case: Leaf node or max depth reached if node.isleaf or currentdepth >= maxdepth: if node.r > 0: # Draw the cuboid box corresponding to this node rendercuboidbox(node.cuboid, bricktexture, transferfunction, cameradirection) return # Case 1: Completely void if node.r == 0: return # Case 2: Mixed data, below threshold if node.r < threshold: # Sort children in front-to-back order # There are 8 valid orders due to axis alignment sortedchildren = sortchildrenfronttoback(node.children, cameradirection) for child in sortedchildren: renderbrickoctree(bricktexture, transferfunction, threshold, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1, child, cameradirection) # Case 3: Sufficiently filled, draw completely else: rendercuboidbox(node.cuboid, bricktexture, transferfunction, cameradirection) def rendercuboidbox(cuboid, texture, transferfunction, cameradirection): """ Render a cuboid box by slicing it. """ # Determine slice orientation (axis-aligned or viewport-aligned) slices = generateslices(cuboid, cameradirection) for sliceplane in slices: # Interpolate texture on the slice slicedata = interpolatetextureonslice(sliceplane, texture) # Apply transfer function renderedslice = applytransferfunction(slicedata, transferfunction) # Rasterize and blend rasterizeandblend(renderedslice) Threshold (T): Determines the trade-off between void culling and triangle throughput. T=1: Draws only fully filled cells. Results in high triangle count at boundaries. T < 1: Allows some void data to be drawn, reducing overhead from small cubes. Octree Level Limit: Prevents traversal beyond a certain depth, drawing non-void nodes completely to avoid overhead. Boundary Artifacts: Setting the threshold too high (close to 1) creates many tiny cubes at the boundaries of visible data, increasing triangle throughput load. Transfer Function Changes: The octree ratios must be recalculated whenever the transfer function changes, as void definitions depend on \alpha. Sorting Complexity: While there are 8 children, the number of valid front-to-back sorting orders is limited to 8 due to axis alignment, not 8!. Time Complexity: Octree construction is O(N) where N is the number of cells in the brick. Traversal is proportional to the number of visible nodes. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the octree in main memory. Performance: Reduces GPU workload by avoiding rasterization of void regions. The CPU handles the traversal, offloading the GPU to pure rendering tasks. Strengths: Effective for datasets with large void regions. Reduces rasterization bottleneck. Limitations: Requires CPU-side processing. Overhead from small cubes if threshold is not tuned. When to use: When rendering large volume bricks with significant empty space and when CPU resources are available for traversal. When not to use: When the dataset is dense with little void space, or when CPU overhead outweighs the rasterization savings. Origin: Described by Danny Ruijters in "Optimizing GPU Volume Rendering". History: Developed as part of a suite of optimizations for GPU volume rendering, specifically targeting the rasterization bottleneck in direct volume ray casting with bricking. Usage: Used in high-performance volume rendering systems where large datasets are divided into bricks and efficient culling is required to maintain frame rates. Optimizing GPU Volume Rendering - Danny Ruijters, https://dannyruijters.nl/docs/OptimizingGPUVolumeRenderingfinal.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering
head: Fourier window, Interpolation Methods, Interpolation Schemes for Frequency Domain Volume Rendering, Nearest Neighbor Interpolation, Reconstruction Filters, Sample-and-hold, Zeroth-order interpolation
body: Interpolation schemes determine how scalar field values are reconstructed from discrete voxel samples during volume ray casting, directly influencing image quality and computational cost. They solve the problem of sampling a continuous volume representation at arbitrary ray positions that rarely align with integer grid coordinates. This family is distinguished from sibling techniques like Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution by focusing on the spatial reconstruction kernel rather than the statistical distribution of sample points, and from Depth to Distance Conversion by operating on the scalar field values rather than geometric depth buffers. All interpolation schemes in this family map a query position \mathbf{p} in voxel space to a scalar value V(\mathbf{p}) by combining a finite set of neighboring voxel values Vi using a set of weights wi(\mathbf{p}): V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i} wi(\mathbf{p}) Vi The weights are derived from a reconstruction kernel h(\mathbf{z}), where \mathbf{z} is the distance from the query point to the sample center. The choice of kernel defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring). A direct volume ray casting technique that performs resampling in the frequency domain using Fourier transforms to avoid blurring artifacts associated with spatial domain interpolation, particularly for large zoom factors. It exploits signal processing ideas such as the shifting theorem, the packing theorem, and the derivative theorem to achieve the best theoretical quality by using the ideal interpolation filter (sinc). Unlike standard spatial domain filters (e.g., B-spline, Catmull-Rom) or methods that zoom the intermediate image, this method resamples every volume slice in object space before projection, ensuring perfect reconstruction if the sampling meets Nyquist criteria. A GPU-based higher-order reconstruction scheme that evaluates a tri-cubic B-spline filter by reducing the number of texture fetches required for the convolution sum, leveraging GPU linear filtering capabilities. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard cubic interpolation, which requires 64 texel fetches for a 3D tri-cubic filter, by using separable filter kernels stored in 1D textures and pre-computed weight/offset functions to achieve the same result with only eight tri-linear texture fetches. It differs from Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling by operating in the spatial domain using fixed B-spline kernels rather than windowed sinc functions in the frequency domain. Estimates values at arbitrary 2D coordinates by linearly interpolating across the four nearest grid points. It sets itself apart from nearest neighbor interpolation by eliminating blocky artifacts while maintaining lower computational cost than higher-order schemes like tri-cubic interpolation. This method approximates volume rendering integration by leveraging standard graphics hardware rasterization, assuming linear interpolation along ray segments. It sets itself apart from analytical integration schemes by relying on the implicit interpolation of the GPU's rasterizer, resulting in view-dependent piecewise bilinear or trilinear interpolation depending on how the hardware subdivides polygons. Estimates the scalar field value at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the eight surrounding voxel corner values. It solves the problem of sampling continuous volume data at non-integer coordinates, which occurs because ray casting sample points rarely align exactly with voxel centers. Compared to nearest-neighbor interpolation, trilinear interpolation produces significantly smoother images with fewer aliasing artifacts, though it requires approximately five times more computation time. Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) Interpolation is a spatial interpolation method that generates a continuous 3D scalar field from discrete sample points by weighting nearby samples by the inverse of their distance raised to a power. It solves the problem of reconstructing a volume from irregular or sparse data (e.g., drill-hole assays) where grid-aligned interpolation schemes like trilinear are not directly applicable. Unlike Trilinear Interpolation, which assumes a regular grid, IDW operates on arbitrary point sets, though it does not guarantee C^0 continuity along interior faces of the grid. A reconstruction technique used to reduce visible artifacts from the discrete sampled nature of volume models, specifically false low frequencies caused by the Nyquist limit. It applies variable Gaussian blurring to the source volume models before or during reconstruction to high-resolution 2D images. The Nyquist Limit is defined as half the sampling rate, and infinite sampling of continuous surfaces is the only way to completely avoid artifacts. Interpolates vertex colors to a voxel center by treating the voxel center as a point inside the triangle and weighting the vertex colors by the areas of the sub-triangles formed with the voxel center. The formula is c = c1 (A2 / A) + c2 (A3 / A) + c3 (A1 / A), where A1 = \text{area}(v1, v2, P), A2 = \text{area}(v2, v3, P), A3 = \text{area}(v3, v1, P), A = A1 + A2 + A3, and P is the voxel center. Interpolates input volume along rays at a predetermined sampling rate. It uses non-binary classifiers to adjust the acceptable density range for an isovalue surface based on data change rate. When data values change slowly, a narrow range of acceptable values is used; when data values change rapidly, a wide range is used to avoid missing the surface. It supports user selection of interpolation: nearest-neighbor (preview), linear (day-to-day), cubic (publication-quality). The concept of interpolation in volume rendering emerged with the development of direct volume ray casting in the late 1980s. Levoy's foundational work on ray casting introduced the need to sample continuous volume data, initially relying on simple methods. The distinction between zeroth-order (nearest-neighbor), first-order (linear/trilinear), and higher-order (cubic/sinc) interpolation was formalized to address the trade-off between rendering speed and visual fidelity. Nearest-neighbor interpolation, equivalent to convolving with a rect function (sample-and-hold), was identified as a poor low-pass filter due to passband distortion and stopband leakage, leading to aliasing and blockiness. Trilinear interpolation became the standard for real-time applications due to its balance of smoothness and speed, though it introduces C^1 discontinuities (star patterns). Higher-order methods, such as tri-cubic B-splines and windowed sinc filters (e.g., Blackman window of width four), were developed to eliminate these artifacts for publication-quality imagery, albeit at higher computational cost. The introduction of frequency domain rendering techniques in the 1990s and 2000s provided an alternative approach to achieve high-quality sinc-like reconstruction without the spatial domain artifacts. name: Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling
head: FD method, Fourier volume rendering, Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Shear-Warp Factorization, Frequency domain based method, Resampling in the Frequency Domain
body:
Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling is a direct volume ray casting technique that performs resampling (zooming and shearing) in the frequency domain using Fourier transforms to avoid blurring artifacts associated with spatial domain interpolation, particularly for large zoom factors. It exploits signal processing ideas such as the shifting theorem, the packing theorem, and the derivative theorem to achieve the best theoretical quality by using the ideal interpolation filter (sinc). Unlike standard spatial domain filters (e.g., B-spline, Catmull-Rom) or methods that zoom the intermediate image, this method resamples every volume slice in object space before projection, ensuring perfect reconstruction if the sampling meets Nyquist criteria. The method integrates frequency-domain resampling into the Shear-Warp factorization pipeline. It transforms the volume to the frequency domain, applies shifts and zooms via zero-padding and phase multiplication, and transforms back to the spatial domain for compositing and warping. Input: 3D volume dataset V(i,j,k) with dimensions I 	imes J 	imes K. Output: 2D rendered image buffer of size N 	imes N. Volume Data: Real-valued array V. Frequency Domain Data: Complex-valued array \hat{V}. Due to the Hermitian symmetry of real functions, memory can be optimized to store only half the spectrum. Intermediate Image: 2D array storing color and transparency (density) values. Sampling distance in k-direction (s): Controls the resolution along the view axis. Typical value: 0.05. Zoom factor: Applied in i and j directions. Typical values: 10.0 or 20.0. Image buffer size (N): N = \sqrt{3} \cdot z \cdot M, where M is the maximal volume extension (max of i, j, k resolution) and z is the scene scale factor. 1. Global Fourier Transform: Compute the 3D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the volume V to obtain \hat{V}(u,v,w). \hat{V} = 	ext{FFT3D}(V) 2. Gradient Estimation (Optional but recommended for lighting): Create three copies of V. Compute their 3D DFTs. Apply the derivative theorem: multiply by i \cdot 2\pi u, i \cdot 2\pi v, and i \cdot 2\pi w respectively in the frequency domain to compute partial derivatives. Compute the Inverse 3D DFT to get gradient components 
abla Vx, 
abla Vy, 
abla Vz. Combine gradients at the compositing stage for lighting. 3. Shear-Warp Factorization Setup: Calculate shear coefficients (si, sj) and translation values (ti, tj) based on the viewing direction [Lac95]. The displacement of the k-th slice in i and j directions is denoted a{ik} and a{jk}. 4. Resampling in k-direction (Zoom/Scale): Calculate the desired sampling distance s' in the k-direction. Determine the new number of samples K' using the relationship:  rac{s'}{s} =  rac{K}{K'} \implies K' =  rac{sK}{s'} Round K' to the closest integer K{0 	ext{ pad}}. If K{0 	ext{ pad}} > 50, the deviation from the desired sampling distance is below \pm 1.0\%. Zero-pad \hat{V} in the w-direction (frequency domain corresponding to k) to size K{0 	ext{ pad}}. Perform an Inverse Fourier Transform (IFFT) in the k-direction only. The i and j directions remain in the frequency domain. 5. Resampling in i and j-directions (Zoom): Determine desired slice resolution (I0, J0). Calculate required padding I{0 	ext{ pad}} and J{0 	ext{ pad}} to achieve the new period. Zero-pad the data in the u and v directions (frequency domain corresponding to i and j). If I{0 	ext{ pad}} > 50 and J{0 	ext{ pad}} > 50, the zoom factor deviation is below \pm 1.0\%. 6. Shearing (Split Shift): The total shift a{xk} (for x \in \{i, j\}) is split into: a{xkSD}: Spatial domain component (integer multiple of voxel lengths). a{xkFD}: Frequency domain component (fraction of a voxel length). Frequency Domain Shift: Apply the shifting theorem to \hat{V} by multiplying by phase shifts e^{-i 2\pi a{xkFD} \cdot 	ext{freq}} to achieve the fractional shift. This limits wrapping effects caused by the periodic assumption of the DFT. Spatial Domain Shift: Perform an Inverse Fourier Transform in the i and j directions. Apply the integer shift a{xkSD} by moving the slice data in the spatial domain. This completes the transformation to sheared object space. 7. Compositing: Apply transfer functions to the resampled slices. Composite slices along the k-axis into a 2D intermediate image using the "over" operator [PD84]. Integrate gradient-based lighting information if computed. 8. Warping: Apply a 2D warping transformation to the intermediate image to produce the final image. Transform pixel coordinates from image space to sheared-object space using the inverse warping matrix. Interpolate pixel values from the intermediate image using a higher-order spatial domain filter (e.g., Catmull-Rom spline) to maintain high quality. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def frequencydomainvolumerendering(volume, viewparams): """ volume: 3D array (I, J, K) viewparams: dict containing shearcoeffs, translation, zoomfactors, samplingdistancek """ # 1. Global Fourier Transform # Vhat is complex, shape (I, J, K) Vhat = fftn(volume) # 2. Gradient Estimation (if lighting is required) # Compute gradients in frequency domain # Note: This requires 3 FFTs or careful handling of symmetry gradxhat = Vhat (1j 2 pi frequ) gradyhat = Vhat (1j 2 pi freqv) gradzhat = Vhat (1j 2 pi freqw) gradx = ifftn(gradxhat).real grady = ifftn(gradyhat).real gradz = ifftn(gradzhat).real # 3. Shear-Warp Setup si, sj = viewparams['shearcoeffs'] ti, tj = viewparams['translation'] zoomi, zoomj = viewparams['zoomfactors'] sk = viewparams['samplingdistancek'] # 4. Resampling in k-direction # Calculate new K size K = volume.shape[2] s = calculatesamplingdistancek(volume, viewparams) # Eq 1 context sprime = sk # Desired sampling distance Kprime = round((s K) / sprime) # Zero-pad in k-direction (frequency domain) Vhat = zeropad(Vhat, axis=2, newsize=Kprime) # IFFT in k-direction only # Shape becomes (I, J, Kprime) Vspatialk = ifft(Vhat, axis=2).real # 5. Resampling in i and j-directions I = volume.shape[0] J = volume.shape[1] # Calculate new sizes based on zoom Iprime = round(I zoomi) Jprime = round(J zoomj) # Zero-pad in i and j directions (frequency domain) # Note: Vspatialk is currently in mixed domain (k is spatial, i,j are freq) # We need to pad the frequency components i and j Vhatij = zeropad(Vspatialk, axis=0, newsize=Iprime) Vhatij = zeropad(Vhatij, axis=1, newsize=Jprime) # 6. Shearing # Split shifts for each slice k intermediateimage = zeros((N, N)) # N from params for k in range(Kprime): # Get current slice in mixed domain (i,j freq, k spatial) slicefreq = Vhatij[:,:, k] # Calculate shift for this slice shifti = si k + ti shiftj = sj k + tj # Split shift into integer (SD) and fractional (FD) parts shiftisd = floor(shifti) shiftifd = shifti - shiftisd shiftjsd = floor(shiftj) shiftjfd = shiftj - shiftjsd # Apply fractional shift in frequency domain (Phase shift) # Phase shift formula: exp(-i 2 pi shift freq) frequ = fftfreq(Iprime) freqv = fftfreq(Jprime) U, V = meshgrid(frequ, freqv) # Careful with grid orientation phasei = exp(-1j 2 pi shiftifd U) phasej = exp(-1j 2 pi shiftjfd V) slicefreqshifted = slicefreq phasei phasej # IFFT in i and j directions slicespatial = ifft2(slicefreqshifted).real # Apply integer shift in spatial domain slicespatial = shiftslice(slicespatial, shiftisd, shiftjsd) # Compositing: Blend into intermediate image # Apply transfer function and lighting using gradients # This step depends on specific transfer function implementation compositeslice = applytransferfunction(slicespatial, gradx[:,:,k], grady[:,:,k], gradz[:,:,k]) # Add to intermediate image (simplified accumulation) intermediateimage += compositeslice # 7. Warping # Apply 2D warping to intermediate image finalimage = warp(intermediateimage, viewparams['warpmatrix']) return finalimage def calculatesamplingdistancek(volume, viewparams): # Eq 1: s = dk sqrt(v'so,i^2 + v'so,j^2 + v'so,k^2) # This calculates the original sampling distance in the view direction pass Aliasing: Data not sampled alias-free (not meeting Nyquist criteria) will show strong ringing artifacts. Discontinuities: Data whose periodic extension introduces discontinuities requires special care, such as mirrored extension. Zoom Precision: Zooming is limited by discrete padding steps. If padding sizes are small (<50), deviation can exceed 1.0%. Memory: High memory consumption due to 3D FFTs. Mitigated by exploiting Hermitian symmetry. Performance: Non-interactive in current implementations due to global gradient estimation and full image calculation even for zoomed regions of interest. Applies distance-based attenuation entirely in the frequency domain by modifying the interpolation filter, avoiding expensive spatial convolution. The theoretical basis for the sinc filter, suppressing spectral replicas for exact reconstruction. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of volume slices and the cost of 3D FFTs. Higher than spatial domain zooming in the warping stage. Memory Complexity: High, due to storing complex frequency domain data. Can be reduced by half using Hermitian symmetry. Quality: Superior to standard spatial domain filtering (linear, B-spline, Catmull-Rom), especially for zoom factors > 2.0 and reproducing spikes. Lowest RMS error in zooming and displacement tests. Limitations: Not interactive; sensitive to aliasing artifacts; requires careful handling of boundary conditions. When to use: High-quality offline rendering of well-sampled (Nyquist-compliant) volume data where artifact-free zooming is critical. When not to use: Real-time applications, or data with significant aliasing/noise without pre-filtering. The method was developed by researchers at Simon Fraser University and published in 2005. It builds on the Shear-Warp factorization [Lac95] and applies signal processing theorems (shifting, packing, derivative) to volume rendering. It addresses the blurring artifacts of spatial domain interpolation by using the ideal sinc filter in the frequency domain. name: Frequency Domain Depth Cueing via Impulse Shifting
head: Analytic signal depth cueing, Cosine Delta Method, Frequency Domain Depth Cueing, Shifted H depth cueing, Shifted spectrum depth cueing
body: Frequency Domain Depth Cueing via Impulse Shifting is a technique for applying distance-based attenuation (depth cueing) to volume rendering entirely within the frequency domain, avoiding expensive spatial-domain convolution or repeated 3D FFTs per view. It modifies the interpolation filter H to a shifted filter H' by convolving it with the Fourier transform of the depth cueing function, allowing the cueing to be applied as a simple 2D operation on the slice plane during extraction. Unlike naive spatial approaches or hybrid methods that require multiple volume copies and per-view 3D transforms, this method leverages the precomputed 3D spectrum and small filter support to make the depth cueing cost negligible compared to interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The 3D Fourier transform of the volume data F(s), the original interpolation filter H(s), the view direction vector V, and depth cueing parameters (strength, offset, period). Output: The modified interpolation filter H'(s) and the final projected image values computed by interpolating F(s) with H'(s). Data Structures: F(s): 3D spectrum of the volume data. H(s): 3D interpolation kernel. Support is small, typically 3^3 to 5^3. H'(s): 2D complex array on the slice plane, representing the modified filter. D(s): 2D complex array representing the Fourier transform of the depth cueing function d(x) evaluated on the slice plane. Method Steps: 1. Define Depth Cueing Function: Choose a depth cueing function d(x) that weights voxels by their distance from the observer. Linear Cueing: dl(x) = C{cue}(V \cdot x) + C{avg}, where V is the view vector, x is the position, C{cue} is the strength, and C{avg} is a constant offset. Sine Wave Cueing: Model d(x) as a half-period sine wave to simplify its transform. Adjust the origin, amplitude, and period such that the value is zero at the farthest voxel and unity at the closest voxel to eliminate the need for a DC term. The period is typically made long enough so the cueing appears almost linear. 2. Compute Fourier Transform of Cueing Function D(s): For Linear Cueing: The transform Dl(s) is computed using a precomputed differential operator convolution VH(s). For Sine Wave Cueing: The transform consists of two impulses: D(s) = C1 \delta(s - sw) + C2 \delta(s + sw) where C1 and C2 are complex constants determined by amplitude and shift, and sw is determined by the period. 3. Compute Modified Filter H'(s): Convolve the original filter with the cueing transform: H'(s) = H(s) D(s) Implementation via Impulse Shifting: Since D(s) consists of impulses (for sine wave cueing), the convolution becomes a sum of shifted copies of H(s) with complex weights: H'(s) = C1 H(s - sw) + C2 H(s + sw). Optimization: To reduce kernel size, one of the impulses can be removed by doubling the weight of the remaining impulse, utilizing the analytic signal property. 4. Interpolate and Project: Use H'(s) instead of H(s) to interpolate F(s) during slice extraction. This operation is 2D, evaluated only on the plane of the slice being extracted. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshiftedfilter(H, sw, C1, C2, removenegative=False): """ Computes the modified interpolation filter H' for depth cueing. Args: H: 3D complex array, the original interpolation filter on a grid. sw: 3D float array, frequency shift vector. C1, C2: complex numbers, impulse weights. removenegative: bool, if True, removes the negative frequency impulse. Returns: Hprime: 2D complex array on the slice plane, the modified filter. """ # Standard trilinear interpolation of 3D grid H at shifted coordinates (sw and -sw), # extracting the 2D slice plane. Returns 2D complex arrays. Hpos = interpolate3dto2d(H, sw) Hneg = interpolate3dto2d(H, -sw) if removenegative: return 2.0 C1 Hpos return C1 Hpos + C2 Hneg def interpolate3dto2d(grid3d, shiftvec): # Standard trilinear interpolation of 3D grid at shifted coordinates, extracting 2D slice. # For each 2D coordinate on the slice plane, compute the weighted sum of the 8 neighboring 3D grid values # based on fractional distances, handling boundaries by zero-padding. Returns 2D complex array. # Sources do not specify the exact interpolation routine. def renderslice(F, Hprime, sliceplane): """ Renders a slice using the modified filter. Args: F: 3D complex array, volume spectrum. Hprime: 2D complex array, modified filter. sliceplane: 2D array of coordinates defining the extraction plane. Returns: projection: 2D complex array, the projected slice. """ # Standard slice extraction: samples F at the given 2D plane coordinates using trilinear interpolation. Fslice = extractslice(F, sliceplane) # Standard 2D convolution: for each output pixel, compute the weighted sum of neighboring input pixels using kernel Hprime. projection = convolve2d(Fslice, Hprime) return projection.real def extractslice(F, planecoords): # Standard slice extraction: samples F at the given 2D plane coordinates. # For each 2D coordinate, compute trilinear interpolation from the 3D spectrum F. Returns 2D complex array. # Sources do not specify the exact interpolation routine. def convolve2d(A, B): # Standard 2D convolution of array A with kernel B. # For each output pixel, compute the weighted sum of neighboring input pixels using kernel B, handling boundaries by zero-padding. # Sources do not specify the exact convolution routine. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Output: Removing one impulse (to reduce kernel size) or using a sine wave with two impulses makes the projection image complex (non-real). The imaginary part is a cosine wave (analytic signal artifact). However, the real part of the result still contains the correct projection image. Only the real part should be displayed. Kernel Size: Using a sine wave with two impulses increases the filter kernel size. Removing one impulse mitigates this but introduces complex output. Precomputation: VH (differential operator convolution) can be precomputed and stored in a table, making the computation of H' for linear cueing of insignificant cost. DC Term: Adjusting the sine wave parameters (origin, amplitude, period) to be zero at the farthest voxel and unity at the closest eliminates the DC term, simplifying D(s) to just two impulses. Time Complexity: The 3D forward FFT is performed only once. For each view, the modification of H to H' is a 2D operation on the slice plane. The cost of recomputing H' is negligible compared to the cost of interpolation itself, because the support of H is small (3^3 to 5^3) and D(s) is simple. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D spectrum F(s) and the filter H(s). No additional volume copies are needed. Performance: The depth cueing is "practically free" compared to spatial domain convolution. While asymptotically faster than conventional spatial domain volume rendering, implementation considerations make it barely superior in practice. Strengths: Avoids per-view 3D FFTs; avoids multiple volume copies; high quality due to sinc resampling (inherited from parent method); flexible depth cueing functions. Limitations: Produces complex output (requires taking real part); kernel size can increase with complex cueing functions; requires precomputation of differential operators for linear cueing. Origin: Developed as part of the frequency domain volume rendering work in 1993. Development: It extends the frequency domain volume rendering algorithm by incorporating depth cueing and directional shading entirely in the frequency domain, using properties of the Fourier transform (differentiation theorem) to avoid spatial domain multiplication. Usage: Used in fast volume rendering applications where depth cues are important for shape perception.
