name: Plenoxels Interpolation Methods
head: Plenoxel Grid with Trilinear Interpolation, Trilinear Plenoxel
body: Plenoxels interpolation methods define a continuous radiance field over a sparse 3D voxel grid by storing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients and opacity at voxel centers, enabling stable optimization and higher effective resolution than discrete voxel assumptions. It distinguishes itself from nearest-neighbor Plenoxels by providing a continuous function approximation that is critical for successful gradient-based optimization, and from tricubic methods by offering a favorable trade-off between smoothness and computational cost. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse 3D voxel grid containing optimized parameters; a 3D sample point \mathbf{p}; a viewing direction \mathbf{v}. Output: Radiance color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) and opacity \sigma(\mathbf{p}). Data Structures: The grid stores data at voxel centers. For each active voxel, the layout is: Opacity: 1 scalar value (\sigma). Spherical Harmonics Coefficients: 27 values (9 coefficients per color channel for degree 2 SH). Note: The sources specify storing RGB channels (zero-order SH) for background spheres to conserve memory. Parameters: Spherical Harmonics Degree: 2. This requires 9 coefficients per color channel, totaling 27 harmonic coefficients per voxel plus 1 opacity coefficient. Resolution: Typical synthetic scenes use 128^3 to 512^3. Steps: 1. Locate Neighbors: Identify the 8 nearest voxel centers surrounding the sample point \mathbf{p}. Let these centers be \mathbf{c}i for i \in \{0, \dots, 7\}. 2. Compute Weights: Calculate trilinear interpolation weights wi based on the relative position of \mathbf{p} within the unit cube defined by the 8 neighbors. 3. Interpolate Opacity: Compute the opacity \sigma(\mathbf{p}) by trilinearly interpolating the opacity values \sigmai from the 8 neighbors: \sigma(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=0}^{7} wi \sigmai 4. Interpolate SH Coefficients: For each color channel k \in \{R, G, B\}, trilinearly interpolate the 9 SH coefficients C{i,j,k} (where j indexes the 9 coefficients) from the 8 neighbors to obtain the interpolated coefficients \hat{C}{j,k}: \hat{C}{j,k} = \sum{i=0}^{7} wi C{i,j,k} 5. Evaluate Radiance: Evaluate the spherical harmonic basis functions Yj(\mathbf{v}) for the viewing direction \mathbf{v}. Compute the radiance for channel k as: ck(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum{j=0}^{8} \hat{C}{j,k} Yj(\mathbf{v}) The final color is \mathbf{c} = [cR, cG, cB]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearplenoxelsample(grid, p, v): # 1. Find 8 nearest voxel centers and weights # grid is a sparse structure mapping voxelindex -> (opacity, shcoeffs[27]) # p is a 3D vector neighbors = get8neighbors(grid, p) weights = computetrilinearweights(p, neighbors.corners) # 2. Interpolate opacity sigma = 0.0 for i, neighbor in enumerate(neighbors): sigma += weights[i] neighbor.opacity # 3. Interpolate SH coefficients (Degree 2 -> 9 coeffs per channel) # shcoeffs layout: [R0..R8, G0..G8, B0..B8] interpsh = [0.0] 27 for i, neighbor in enumerate(neighbors): for k in range(27): interpsh[k] += weights[i] neighbor.shcoeffs[k] # 4. Evaluate SH for viewing direction v # Y is a function returning 9 basis values for direction v yvals = evaluateshbasis(v, degree=2) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for channel in range(3): channeloffset = channel 9 radiance = 0.0 for j in range(9): radiance += interpsh[channeloffset + j] yvals[j] color[channel] = radiance return color, sigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nearest Neighbor Instability: Using nearest-neighbor interpolation produces a discontinuous model that is difficult to optimize and less stable with respect to learning rate variations. Tricubic Cost: Tricubic interpolation offers continuous and smooth approximation but incurs substantial computation with negligible quality gain compared to trilinear. Initialization: Coefficients are optimized directly without special initialization or pretraining with a neural network. This variant extends Plenoxels to real, unbounded scenes, including forward-facing and 360° settings. For forward-facing scenes, it uses normalized device coordinates (NDC) for the sparse voxel grid structure. For 360° scenes, it augments the foreground with a multisphere image (MSI) background model using learned voxel colors and opacities with trilinear interpolation. It places 64 spheres linearly in inverse radius from 1 to \infty, pre-scaling the inner scene to be approximately contained in the unit sphere. To conserve memory, the background stores only RGB channels (zero-order SH) and uses opacity thresholding for sparse storage. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Scales with the number of active voxels. Each voxel stores 28 scalars (1 opacity + 27 SH coefficients). Background spheres store only 3 scalars (RGB) per voxel. Time: Trilinear interpolation is significantly faster than tricubic, which incurs substantial computation. Measured Performance: On 8 NeRF synthetic scenes, Trilinear Plenoxels at 128^3 resolution (PSNR 28.46, SSIM 0.926, LPIPS 0.100) outperform Nearest Neighbor at 256^3 resolution (PSNR 27.17, SSIM 0.914, LPIPS 0.119). Trilinear interpolation at 256^3 achieves PSNR 30.57, SSIM 0.950, LPIPS 0.065. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Increases effective resolution by representing sub-voxel variations; produces a continuous function approximation critical for successful optimization; more stable with respect to learning rate variations than nearest neighbor. Limitations: Tricubic offers smoother approximation but with negligible quality gain and higher cost. When to Use: Use trilinear interpolation for stable optimization and higher quality than nearest neighbor at lower resolutions. Avoid nearest neighbor if optimization stability is a concern. Avoid tricubic unless smoothness is strictly required and computational budget allows, as quality gain is negligible. Plenoxels were introduced in the paper "Plenoxels: Radiance Fields without Neural Networks". The method builds on PlenOctrees but replaces the constant-voxel assumption with trilinear interpolation to enable direct optimization of opacity and SH coefficients without neural networks. The use of degree 2 spherical harmonics was adopted from PlenOctrees, as higher orders confer minimal benefit. The method supports coarse-to-fine optimization strategies, resizing grids between arbitrary resolutions using trilinear interpolation. name: Multi-Texture Trilinear Estimation
head: Axis-aligned/View-aligned slicing, Basic Slice-based Rendering with Trilinear Interpolation, Multi-Texture Trilinear Interpolation, PRI reconstruction, Rezk-Salama Multi-Texture Trilinear
body: Multi-Texture Trilinear Estimation is a direct volume ray casting technique that renders scalar field data defined on a 3D rectilinear grid by stacking parallel quads textured with scalar information and compositing them in depth order. It solves the problem of visualizing space data where grid cells are not uniform cubes by reconstructing scalar values from a Piecewise Rational (PRI) representation using a hybrid interpolation scheme. It sets itself apart from basic 2D texture rendering by substituting standard trilinear interpolation with two bilinear interpolations and one linear interpolation to improve image quality and speed, and from Trilinear Interpolation by relying on a stack of slices and dependent texturing rather than direct 3D texture mapping or software-based coordinate array interpolation. Inputs: Volumetric scalar field data. A Piecewise Rational (PRI) representation of the data, stored as two float textures: one for scalar values and one for knot distances. An index texture mapping spatial positions to spline segments. Camera view direction. Outputs: Final 2D image with color and opacity values. Data Structures: 1. Index Texture: 2D texture where each texel corresponds to a pixel on the PRI sampling plane. 2. Knots Texture: 2D texture storing the linear splines. Each texel (or set of texels) represents a spline segment. The knots within each spline are sorted in depth (z-direction). 3. Slice Geometry: A stack of parallel quads. Axis-aligned: Slices are perpendicular to the PRI sampling direction. View-aligned: Slices are parallel to the image plane. Parameters: View angle threshold: 45 degrees. If the view direction changes by more than 45 degrees, switching artifacts may occur unless multiple PRI copies are used. Number of PRIs: Minimum 1 for view-aligned; minimum 3 (orthogonal) for axis-aligned to support arbitrary views. Steps: 1. Slice Positioning: Position a stack of parallel quads. For axis-aligned slicing, align them perpendicular to the chosen PRI sampling direction. For view-aligned slicing, align them parallel to the image plane. 2. Projection: For each pixel fragment at position (x, y, z) in the PRI coordinate space, parallel project the position to the PRI's sampling plane by dropping the z coordinate. Identify the four nearest neighbor pixels on the sampling plane surrounding the projection point (x, y). 3. Index Retrieval: Axis-aligned: Map the index texture to each slice using texture coordinates (0,0), (0,h), (w,h), (w,0) where w,h are the index texture dimensions. Retrieve the four nearest texels in the index texture. View-aligned: Use inverse mapping (e.g., OpenGL TexGen) to retrieve the four nearest texels. 4. Spline Segment Search: For each of the four retrieved index texels, access the associated linear spline in the knots texture via dependent texturing. Perform a binary search on the knots (which are sorted in depth) to find the specific spline segment that overlaps the fragment's z location. 5. Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation: Perform four linear interpolations in the z direction using the four found spline segments. Perform bilinear interpolation in the x and y directions using the results of the four linear interpolations. Alternative Description: The method substitutes full trilinear interpolation with two bilinear interpolations and one linear interpolation to achieve a better and faster estimation of the scalar at an arbitrary position along the chosen axis. 6. Classification and Compositing: Classify the reconstructed scalar value (e.g., transfer function mapping to color and opacity) and composite the fragment in depth order (front-to-back or back-to-front) to the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderslicestack(slices, indextexture, knotstexture, viewdirection): # Determine slicing mode based on view direction if viewdirection is paralleltoaxes: mode = "axisaligned" # Requires 3 orthogonal PRIs; select the one most parallel to view pri = selectmostparallelPRI(viewdirection, [PRIX, PRIY, PRIZ]) else: mode = "viewaligned" # Requires at least 1 PRI pri = PRI0 for fragment in slices: x, y, z = fragment.position # Step 1: Parallel project to sampling plane by dropping z xproj, yproj = x, y # Step 2: Identify four nearest neighbors on sampling plane neighbors = getfournearestneighbors(xproj, yproj) # Step 3 & 4: Retrieve index texels, access knots via dependent texturing, binary search splinesegments = [] for neighbor in neighbors: # Access knots texture via dependent texturing splinedata = dependenttexturelookup(indextexture, knotstexture, neighbor) # Binary search on knots (sorted in depth) to find segment overlapping z segment = binarysearchknots(splinedata.knots, z) splinesegments.append(segment) # Step 5: Interpolation # Four linear interpolations in z direction zvalues = [] for segment in splinesegments: val = linearinterpolate(segment, z) zvalues.append(val) # Bilinear interpolation in x and y directions scalarvalue = bilinearinterpolate(zvalues, xproj, yproj) # Step 6: Classification and Compositing color, opacity = transferfunction(scalarvalue) compositefronttoback(color, opacity) def getfournearestneighbors(x, y): # Returns indices of four surrounding pixels on the sampling plane return [(int(x), int(y)), (int(x)+1, int(y)), (int(x), int(y)+1), (int(x)+1, int(y)+1)] def dependenttexturelookup(indextex, knotstex, neighboridx): # Retrieves spline data associated with the neighbor index return knotstex[neighboridx] def binarysearchknots(knots, z): # Finds the spline segment where knots[i].dist <= z < knots[i+1].dist for i in range(len(knots) - 1): if knots[i].dist <= z < knots[i+1].dist: return knots[i] return knots[-1] def linearinterpolate(segment, z): # Linear interpolation along the spline segment at z t = (z - segment.startdist) / (segment.enddist - segment.startdist) return segment.startval + t (segment.endval - segment.startval) def bilinearinterpolate(values, x, y): # Bilinear interpolation of four z-interpolated values # values layout: [bottomleft, bottomright, topleft, topright] dx = x - int(x) dy = y - int(y) return (values[0] (1 - dx) (1 - dy) + values[1] dx (1 - dy) + values[2] (1 - dx) dy + values[3] dx dy) def transferfunction(scalar): # Maps scalar value to color and opacity return scalar, scalar def compositefronttoback(color, opacity): # Accumulates color and opacity into the framebuffer pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Bottleneck: Binary search and dependent texturing for trilinear interpolation create a significant computational bottleneck on current GPUs. Memory Constraints: The basic algorithm requires three copies of the volumetric data set in main memory to eliminate switching artifacts when the view direction changes more than 45 degrees. This limits the algorithm to very small data sets. Precision: The knots texture should be stored as two separate textures with float format to ensure high precision, holding scalar values and distance values of the knots separately. An optimization that eliminates the need for multiple data copies by reconstructing volumetric data on-the-fly, storing only one stack of original data. It performs on-the-fly reconstruction of volumetric data to avoid switching artifacts. This approach is only beneficial when the GPU texture memory is not enough to store three copies, but enough for one copy. If the entire data is larger than the size of texture memory, more sophisticated techniques such as paging or out-of-core rendering are needed. It introduces a severe performance drop-off. Examined by Engel et al.. Time Complexity: The search time for spline segments contributes to a considerable computational bottleneck due to binary search and dependent texturing. Memory Complexity: Requires at least three copies of the volumetric data set in main memory for the basic algorithm to handle view changes >45 degrees without artifacts. The on-the-fly variant reduces this to one copy but increases CPU/GPU computation time. Measured Performance: The basic approach was found to have a bottleneck on current GPU platforms, though it was considered viable for future graphics cards. The multi-texture approach achieves improved image quality compared to plain 2D texture rendering without losing too much rendering speed. Strengths: Improves image quality over basic 2D texture rendering by reducing artifacts associated with bilinear interpolation. View-aligned slicing requires only one PRI. Limitations: High storage requirements limit data size. Dependent texturing and binary search are inefficient on GPUs. Switching artifacts occur with large view angle changes unless multiple copies are used. When to use: When data size is small enough to fit multiple copies in memory and view changes are limited. When not to use: When rendering large datasets that exceed texture memory. When real-time performance is critical due to GPU bottlenecks with dependent texturing. Multi-Texture Trilinear Estimation was introduced by Rezk-Salama et al.. It was developed to address the limitations of basic 2D texture-based rendering, which suffered from severe artifacts due to bilinear interpolation. The method was examined as an optimization for subjective image quality, mathematical accuracy, and memory consumption. The on-the-fly reconstruction variant was examined by Engel et al.. name: Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering with Trilinear Interpolation
head: Analytical Integration with Trilinear Reconstruction, Semi-Analytical Preintegration for Hexahedral Cells, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering, Trilinear Preintegration
body: Semi-analytical volume rendering with trilinear interpolation is a direct volume ray casting technique for hexahedral cells that eliminates topological artifacts such as discontinuities and holes in isosurfaces by analytically determining optimal sampling points along the ray. It sets itself apart from standard trilinear interpolation [1531-trilinear-interpolation.md] by replacing uniform sampling with a piecewise-linear approximation over monotonic intervals defined by the analytical extrema of the reconstructed signal, ensuring no isovalue is missed. Inputs: Scalar field values s{ijk} at the 8 corners (i,j,k) \in \{0,1\}^3 of a hexahedral cell. Ray entry point (x0, y0, z0) and exit point (x1, y1, z1) in normalized cell coordinates [0,1]^3. Transfer functions: color c(s) and opacity \tau(s). Outputs: Accumulated color intensity I for the ray segment traversing the cell. Data Structures: Coefficients a, b, c, d of the cubic polynomial s(t). List of valid extrema R = \{r1, r2, \dots\} within [0,1]. Monotonic intervals defined by sorted sampling points T = \{0, r1, r2, 1\}. Steps: 1. Ray Parametrization: Compute the direction vector components as differences between exit and entry coordinates: vx = x1 - x0, \quad vy = y1 - y0, \quad vz = z1 - z0 The ray is parametrized as x(t) = x0 + t vx, y(t) = y0 + t vy, z(t) = z0 + t vz for t \in [0,1]. 2. Signal Reconstruction (Cubic Polynomial): Substitute the ray parametrization into the trilinear interpolation formula to obtain s(t) = a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + d. The coefficients are linear combinations of the corner values s{ijk} and ray parameters: a = (s{100} - s{000} + s{010} + s{001} + s{111} - s{110} - s{011} - s{101}) vx vy vz b = (-x0 vy vz - vx y0 vz - vx vy z0 + vx vz) s{101} + (x0 vy vz + vx y0 vz + vx vy z0) s{111} + (vy vz - x0 vy vz - vx y0 vz - vx vy z0) s{011} + (-vx vz + vx vy z0 - vy vz + x0 vy vz + vx y0 vz) s{001} + (-vx vz + vx y0 vz + vx vy z0 - vx vy + x0 vy vz) s{100} + (-vx y0 vz - x0 vy vz + vx vy z0) s{110} + (-x0 y0 vz - vx y0 z0 - x0 vy z0 + vx vy z0) s{010} + (-y0 z0 - x0 y0 + y0 + x0 y0 z0) s{010} + (-y0 - z0 - x0 y0 z0 + x0 z0 + y0 z0) s{001} Coefficients c and d are derived similarly by collecting terms of t^1 and t^0 respectively, resulting in sums of 8 terms each involving s{ijk} multiplied by products of x0, y0, z0 and vx, vy, vz. 3. Extrema Calculation: Compute the derivative s'(t) = 3a t^2 + 2b t + c. Find the roots of this quadratic equation: t = \frac{-2b \pm \sqrt{4b^2 - 12ac}}{6a} If a=0, solve the linear equation 2b t + c = 0. If a=0 and b=0, the function is constant and has no extrema. 4. Pruning and Sorting: Discard any roots t such that t < 0 or t > 1. Sort the remaining valid extrema ri in ascending order. Define the sampling points T = [0, r1, r2, \dots, 1]. 5. Interval Approximation: For each consecutive pair of sampling points ti, t{i+1} in T, approximate the signal s(t) as a linear interpolation between the values at the endpoints: s{lin}(t') = (1-t') s(ti) + t' s(t{i+1}), \quad t' \in [0,1] where t' is the local parameter within the interval [ti, t{i+1}]. Let Li = t{i+1} - ti be the length of the interval. 6. Preintegration: Compute the contribution of each interval using preintegration functions C and \alpha. The total intensity is accumulated using front-to-back alpha compositing: I \approx C(s(0), s(r1), L0) + (1 - \alpha(s(0), s(r1), L0)) C(s(r1), s(r2), L1) + \dots where C(a, b, L) = \int0^1 c((1-t') a + t' b) L e^{-\int0^{t'} \tau((1-u) a + u b) L du} dt' \alpha(a, b, L) = 1 - e^{-\int0^1 \tau((1-t') a + t' b) L dt'} In practice, these integrals are evaluated via numerical quadrature or lookup tables. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def semianalyticaltrilinearrender(scorners, x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1, cfunc, taufunc): """ scorners: list of 8 floats [s000, s100, s010, s001, s101, s011, s110, s111] x0,y0,z0: entry point in [0,1]^3 x1,y1,z1: exit point in [0,1]^3 cfunc: color transfer function (returns RGB tuple) taufunc: opacity transfer function (returns float) """ vx, vy, vz = x1 - x0, y1 - y0, z1 - z0 a, b, c, d = computecubiccoefficients(scorners, x0, y0, z0, vx, vy, vz) roots = solvequadratic(3a, 2b, c) validextrema = sorted([r for r in roots if 0.0 <= r <= 1.0]) samplingpoints = [0.0] + validextrema + [1.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(len(samplingpoints) - 1): tstart, tend = samplingpoints[i], samplingpoints[i+1] L = tend - tstart sstart, send = evalcubic(a, b, c, d, tstart), evalcubic(a, b, c, d, tend) intervalcolor, intervalalpha = preintegrateinterval(sstart, send, L, cfunc, taufunc) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[k] + (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) intervalcolor[k] for k in range(3)] accumulatedalpha += (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) intervalalpha return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha def computecubiccoefficients(scorners, x0, y0, z0, vx, vy, vz): a, b, c, d = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): sval = scorners[i4 + j2 + k] cx = [1-x0, -vx, 0.0, 0.0] if i == 0 else [x0, vx, 0.0, 0.0] cy = [1-y0, -vy, 0.0, 0.0] if j == 0 else [y0, vy, 0.0, 0.0] cz = [1-z0, -vz, 0.0, 0.0] if k == 0 else [z0, vz, 0.0, 0.0] pc = [0.0]4 for m in range(4): for n in range(4): if m+n < 4: pc[m+n] += cx[m]cy[n] p = [0.0]4 for m in range(4): for n in range(4): if m+n < 4: p[m+n] += pc[m]cz[n] a += sval p[3]; b += sval p[2]; c += sval p[1]; d += sval p[0] return a, b, c, d def evalcubic(a, b, c, d, t): return ((at + b)t + c)t + d def solvequadratic(A, B, C): if abs(A) < 1e-9: return [-C/B] if abs(B) > 1e-9 else [] disc = BB - 4AC if disc < 0: return [] sqrtdisc = disc0.5 return [(-B - sqrtdisc)/(2A), (-B + sqrtdisc)/(2A)] def preintegrateinterval(sstart, send, L, cfunc, taufunc, steps=16): colorintegral = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tauintegral = 0.0 dt = 1.0 / steps for i in range(steps): tprime = (i + 0.5) dt sval = (1.0 - tprime)sstart + tprimesend cval = cfunc(sval) tauval = taufunc(sval) tauintegral += tauval dt accumulatedopacity = sum(taufunc((1.0 - (j+0.5)dt)sstart + (j+0.5)dtsend) dt for j in range(i+1)) weight = L (1.0 - tprime) colorintegral = [colorintegral[k] + weight cval[k] math.exp(-accumulatedopacity L) for k in range(3)] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-tauintegral L) return colorintegral, alpha This method extends semi-analytical volume rendering by incorporating local Phong diffuse shading into the integration process. It solves the problem of accurate lighting in volume rendering by reconstructing the shading function as a quadratic polynomial along the ray, allowing for analytical integration of the light contribution. It sets itself apart from scalar-only semi-analytical methods by requiring at most one additional sampling point per cell to capture the shading extremum, while maintaining the topological accuracy of the underlying trilinear interpolation. A technique to handle hybrid cells in Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) by propagating cell splits from the lower level cell to the higher level cell to ensure continuity across cell faces. It identifies hybrid cells (sharing an edge/face with a different level cell) and propagates splits by adding 'source split points' (using the higher-level cell's value) and 'destination split points' (using bilinearly interpolated values from a shared face) to the lower-level cell. This ensures continuity across cell faces either by using the neighbor's value or by matching the interpolation scheme of the neighbor cell, avoiding artifacts. Time Complexity: The method requires solving a quadratic equation and evaluating preintegration functions for each monotonic interval. The number of intervals is small (at most 3), making it faster than high-frequency uniform sampling for preserving topology. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for preintegration tables or numerical quadrature routines. Performance: Efficient on current graphics hardware when combined with a hybrid CPU-GPU mesh traversal technique. Strengths: Guarantees topological accuracy of isosurfaces; avoids missing isovalues; handles arbitrary transfer functions. Limitations: As the topology is consistent from one frame to another, the only remaining kind of artifacts is wobbling of the surfaces and structures inside the cells as the viewpoint changes. Complex coefficient calculation for the cubic polynomial. When to use: High-quality visualization of AMR datasets with hexahedral cells where topological accuracy is critical. Originated in a 2009 paper by titled "High-Quality, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering for AMR...", this method was developed to address the challenges of visualizing Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) datasets. It builds on the need for view-order cell traversal and high-quality rendering of hexahedral cells in AMR meshes, which often suffer from discontinuities in isosurfaces due to piecewise linear approximations. The method extends standard trilinear interpolation by leveraging the analytical properties of the reconstructed signal to determine sampling points. name: Local Phong Shading with Semi-Analytical Integration
head: Quadratic Shading Integration, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering with Shading
body:
This method extends semi-analytical volume rendering by incorporating local Phong diffuse shading into the integration process. It solves the problem of accurate lighting in volume rendering by reconstructing the shading function as a quadratic polynomial along the ray, allowing for analytical integration of the light contribution. It sets itself apart from scalar-only semi-analytical methods by requiring at most one additional sampling point per cell to capture the shading extremum, while maintaining the topological accuracy of the underlying trilinear interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Trilinear interpolation coefficients for the scalar field s(x,y,z) within a hexahedral cell; light direction vector \vec{L} = (lx, ly, lz); preintegration tables C{front}, C{back}, and \alpha; ray segment parameters t{start}, t{end} within the cell. Outputs: Integrated color contribution I for the ray segment, accounting for shading. Data Structures: The method relies on the trilinear coefficients s{ijk} (where i,j,k \in \{0,1\}) defining the scalar field s(x,y,z) in the unit cube. The shading function is represented by quadratic coefficients e, f, g for d(t) = e t^2 + f t + g. Steps: 1. Compute the analytical gradient 
abla s(x,y,z) from the trilinear coefficients. Compute the diffuse shading function d(x,y,z) = 
abla s(x,y,z) \cdot \vec{L}. 2. Parametrize the ray as x(t), y(t), z(t) for t \in [0, L] (local cell coordinates). Substitute into d(x,y,z) to obtain the quadratic form d(t) = e \cdot t^2 + f \cdot t + g, where e, f, g are computed from the gradient coefficients and ray parameters. For a parametrized ray inside a cell, the gradient variation over this ray is thus a quadratic form in t. 3. Find the local extremum r of d(t) by setting the derivative to zero: r = -f / (2e). Since d(t) is a quadratic polynomial, there is at most a single local extremum r. 4. Sample the shading function at the cell entry (t=0), cell exit (t=L), and the local extremum r (if 0 < r < L). This requires at most one additional sampling point per cell compared to the scalar-only method. 5. Split the ray segment [0, L] at the extremum r into [0, r] and [r, L] (if r is within the interval). The integral becomes: I = \int0^r c(s(t))d(t)e^{-\int0^t 	au(s(u))du} dt + \intr^L c(s(t))d(t)e^{-\int0^t 	au(s(u))du} dt. 6. Approximate the scalar field s(t) as linear between sample points. For the full cell with extremum r, the total integral is approximated using preintegration functions: I \approx d(s(0)) C{front}(s(0), s(r), r) + d(s(r)) C{back}(s(0), s(r), r) + (1 - \alpha(s(0), s(r), r)) [ d(s(r)) C{front}(s(r), s(L), L-r) + d(s(L)) C{back}(s(r), s(L), L-r) ]. 7. Preintegration functions are defined as: C{back}(a, b, l) = \int0^1 c((1-t') a + t' b) t' e^{-\int0^{t'} 	au((1-t') a + t' b) l du} dt' C{front}(a, b, l) = \int0^1 c((1-t') a + t' b) (1-t') e^{-\int0^{t'} 	au((1-t') a + t' b) l du} dt' \alpha(a, b, l) = 1 - e^{-\int0^1 	au((1-t') b + t' a) l dt'} where a, b are scalar values at interval endpoints, l is the interval length, and c(\cdot), 	au(\cdot) are the color and absorption transfer functions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def integratelocalphongshading(scoeffs, Lvec, tstart, tend, Cfront, Cback, alpha, cfunc, taufunc): # 1. Compute quadratic coefficients e, f, g for d(t) from gradient and ray e, f, g = computeshadingquadratic(scoeffs, Lvec) # 2. Find local extremum r of d(t) = et^2 + ft + g if abs(e) > 1e-9: r = -f / (2.0 e) else: r = None # Linear case, no internal extremum # 3. Determine integration intervals based on extremum if r is not None and tstart < r < tend: t1, t2, t3 = tstart, r, tend else: t1, t2, t3 = tstart, tend, tend # 4. Sample shading function d(t) at interval boundaries d1 = et1t1 + ft1 + g d2 = et2t2 + ft2 + g d3 = et3t3 + ft3 + g # 5. Compute scalar values s(t) at boundaries (linear interpolation assumed) s1 = samplescalar(scoeffs, t1) s2 = samplescalar(scoeffs, t2) s3 = samplescalar(scoeffs, t3) # 6. Compute interval lengths l1 = t2 - t1 l2 = t3 - t2 # 7. Evaluate preintegration functions cf1 = Cfront(s1, s2, l1) cb1 = Cback(s1, s2, l1) a1 = alpha(s1, s2, l1) cf2 = Cfront(s2, s3, l2) cb2 = Cback(s2, s3, l2) # 8. Apply split-interval approximation formula I = d1 cf1 + d2 cb1 if l2 > 0: I += (1.0 - a1) (d2 cf2 + d3 cb2) return I Pitfalls: Discontinuity: The reconstructed scalar field is only C^0 continuous across cell faces. Consequently, the gradient 
abla s is discontinuous, causing shading discontinuities across cell boundaries. Extremum Handling: If the extremum r lies outside the cell interval [0, L], the shading function is monotonic within the cell, and no split is needed. Complexity: Adds at most one additional sample per cell compared to scalar-only semi-analytical rendering. Performance: Not given in the sources for specific hardware performance metrics. Strengths: Captures local lighting variations within cells. Limitations: Shading discontinuities at cell faces may be visible due to C^0 continuity of the scalar field. This method is an extension of the semi-analytical volume rendering approach for AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) data, presented by Marchesin et al. in 2009. It builds on the trilinear interpolation-based semi-analytical integration described in the parent article. name: Inverse Distance Weighted Interpolation
head: 3D Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) Interpolation, Inverse Distance Weighting
body:
Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) Interpolation is a spatial interpolation method that generates a continuous 3D scalar field from discrete sample points by weighting nearby samples by the inverse of their distance raised to a power. It solves the problem of reconstructing a volume from irregular or sparse data (e.g., drill-hole assays) where grid-aligned interpolation schemes like trilinear are not directly applicable. While often applied to arbitrary point sets, specific implementations restrict the neighborhood to the eight vertices of the grid cell containing the query point. It does not guarantee C^0 continuity along interior faces of the grid. Inputs: A set of N sample points Pi = (xi, yi, zi) with associated scalar values Vi. A query point Q = (x, y, z) at which to estimate the value. Parameters: power (exponent, typically 2), searchRadius (optional max distance, typically 60 world units), maxNeighbors (optional limit, typically 16). Outputs: The interpolated scalar value F(Q). Data Structures: A spatial index (e.g., uniform 3D hash grid) supporting neighbor queries for O(1) or O(\log N) lookup. An array of sample objects containing coordinates and values. Steps: 1. Query Neighbors: Retrieve candidate points S from the spatial index. If searchRadius is specified, select points within that distance. If maxNeighbors is specified, cap the result to the k nearest neighbors. 2. Handle Empty Case: If S is empty, return a nodata sentinel value (e.g., < -10^{29}) to allow the renderer to skip these voxels. 3. Exact Hit Check: For each Pi \in S, calculate di = \|Q - Pi\|. If di = 0 (or < \epsilon), return Vi immediately to avoid division by zero. 4. Compute Weights: For each Pi \in S, compute wi = 1 / di^{	ext{power}}. 5. Normalize and Interpolate: Compute F(Q) =  rac{\sum{i \in S} wi Vi}{\sum{i \in S} wi}. Alternative Cell-Based Implementation: In some implementations, the neighborhood is restricted to the eight vertices of the single grid cell containing Q. The weights are computed using a product of squared distances to all other vertices in the cell: wi =  rac{\prod{\substack{k=0 \ k 
eq i}}^7 [dk(Q)]^2}{\sum{\substack{j=0 \ j 
eq i}}^7 \prod{\substack{l=0 \ l 
eq j}}^7 [dl(Q)]^2} where dj(Q) is the Euclidean distance between the j-th vertex and Q. If Q coincides with vertex j, wj=1 and wi=0 for i 
eq j, ensuring F(Q) = Vj. Parameters: power: The IDW exponent controlling the rate of decay. Typical value: 2. searchRadius: Maximum distance to consider samples. Typical value: 60 world units. maxNeighbors: Maximum number of nearest neighbors. Typical value: 16. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If Q coincides exactly with a sample point, di=0. An exact-hit short-circuit must be used. Continuity: The scheme does not guarantee C^0 continuity along interior faces. This can be minimized by using all vertices of all cells containing a point on an interior face, though this is ad hoc. Local Bias: Considering only surrounding cells ignores contributions from cells in the original volume that do not include an interpolated point, which is a problem with very local methods. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def idwinterpolate(querypoint, samples, power=2.0, searchradius=None, maxneighbors=16, epsilon=1e-6): # Step 1: Query neighbors from spatial index candidates = queryneighbors(samples, querypoint, searchradius, maxneighbors) # Step 2: Handle empty case if not candidates: return -1e29 # Nodata sentinel # Step 3 & 4: Compute weights with exact-hit check weights = [] values = [] for sample in candidates: d = math.sqrt(sum((q - c)2 for q, c in zip(querypoint, sample.coords))) if d < epsilon: return sample.value # Exact-hit short-circuit w = 1.0 / (d power) weights.append(w) values.append(sample.value) # Step 5: Normalize and interpolate numerator = sum(w v for w, v in zip(weights, values)) denominator = sum(weights) if denominator == 0: return -1e29 # Fallback for numerical issues return numerator / denominator def queryneighbors(samples, querypoint, searchradius, maxneighbors): # Standard spatial index query logic # Computes distances, filters by radius, sorts, and caps by maxneighbors dists = [] for s in samples: d = math.sqrt(sum((q - c)2 for q, c in zip(querypoint, s.coords))) dists.append((d, s)) dists.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) if searchradius is not None: dists = [x for x in dists if x[0] <= searchradius] return [s for, s in dists[:maxneighbors]] Uses sinc functions for ideal reconstruction in the frequency domain; suitable for regular grids but computationally expensive. Choose when aliasing must be eliminated and performance is secondary. Higher-order polynomial interpolation on regular grids; smoother than trilinear but more complex to implement. Choose when high-frequency detail preservation is needed on structured data. 2D linear interpolation; simpler than trilinear but not applicable to 3D volumes directly. Choose for 2D slice rendering or as a component in 3D schemes. Uses GPU texture hardware for fast, low-precision interpolation; limited by hardware constraints. Choose when maximum throughput is required and slight blurring is acceptable. Standard 3D linear interpolation on regular grids; efficient and C^0 continuous along faces, but requires structured data. Choose for uniform voxel grids where continuity and speed are prioritized over handling irregular samples. Time Complexity: O(k) per query for interpolation, plus spatial index lookup cost (O(1) for hash grids, O(\log N) for trees). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the sample points and spatial index. Performance: Depends heavily on the spatial index implementation. Uniform hash grids offer O(1) lookup for static datasets. Strengths: Works with irregular data; simple to implement; no grid structure required. Limitations: No guaranteed continuity; sensitive to parameter choice (power); local methods may ignore distant but relevant data. When to Use: Irregular or sparse data (e.g., geological assays) that must be converted to a volume grid or queried directly. When Not to Use: Regular grid data where trilinear or higher-order schemes are preferred for continuity and performance. IDW was introduced as a distance-weighted interpolation scheme in the 1980s. It has been applied to direct volume rendering of curvilinear volumes and geological data visualization. The method is particularly relevant for visualizing data from drill-hole assays or other non-uniform sampling patterns. name: Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution
head: Multi-ray AA, Multi-sample AA, Ray Distribution AA, MSAA via Ray Distribution
body: Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) via Ray Distribution reduces jagged edges in volume rendering by casting multiple rays per pixel, distributed within the pixel area, and averaging the results. Unlike single-ray casting, which suffers from aliasing artifacts at silhouette edges due to coarse per-pixel sampling granularity, this method samples the scene at a higher effective resolution. It is distinct from Supersampling in its specific implementation of fixed offset patterns derived from fragment coordinates, and from Epipolar Sampling which exploits geometric constraints along epipolar lines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Pixel coordinates (e.g., glFragCoord), an integer uniform AA selecting the sampling mode (1, 2, 3, or 4), and a rendering function render(uv) that performs the volume integration for a given normalized UV offset within the pixel. Output: A single averaged color value for the pixel. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method relies on scalar arithmetic and fixed offset vectors. Parameters: AA: Integer uniform selector. Values: 1, 2, 3, 4. Default is 4 if not explicitly set to 1, 2, or 3. Steps: 1. Select Mode: Determine the number of samples N based on the AA uniform. 2. Generate Offsets: Calculate 2D UV offsets (\delta u, \delta v) for each of the N rays relative to the pixel center. The offsets are normalized to the range [-0.5, 0.5] or [0, 1] depending on the coordinate system of getUV. The provided sources use offsets that are added to a base UV, implying they are relative to the pixel center or corner. The specific formulas below assume the offsets are added to the pixel's base UV coordinate. 3. name: Depth to Distance Conversion
head: Depth to Distance, z_vals to dists
body: Depth to Distance Conversion transforms sampled depth values (z{vals}) along a ray into segment lengths (dists) required for volume rendering integration. It accounts for the viewing angle by scaling the depth differences with the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the viewing direction. This method is distinct from Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering as it focuses on metric length calculation rather than value estimation, and from Sampling and Jittering as it operates on already sampled points. Inputs: z{vals}: Tensor of sampled depth values, shape (..., N), where N is the number of samples. cos\angle: Tensor of cosine values of the angle between the ray direction and the viewing direction, shape (..., 1). Outputs: dists: Tensor of segment distances, shape (..., N). Data Structures: z{vals}: Floating-point tensor. dists: Floating-point tensor. Steps: 1. Compute raw distances between consecutive depth samples: dists{raw} = z{vals}[:, 1:] - z{vals}[:,:-1] This results in a tensor of shape (..., N-1). 2. Append a large value to represent the distance to the last segment (often used to ensure the last sample contributes fully or to handle boundary conditions). The value 10^{10} is used as a proxy for infinity. dists = \text{concat}(dists{raw}, [10^{10}]) The appended value is expanded to match the batch dimensions. 3. Scale the distances by the cosine of the viewing angle to account for perspective projection effects: dists = dists \times cos\angle Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def depthtodistance(zvals, cosangle): """ Convert depth values to segment distances. Args: zvals (torch.Tensor): Sampled depth values, shape (..., N). cosangle (torch.Tensor): Cosine of the angle between ray and view direction, shape (..., 1). Returns: torch.Tensor: Segment distances, shape (..., N). """ # Step 1: Compute raw distances between consecutive samples # zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] computes the difference along the last dimension dists = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] # Step 2: Append a large value for the last segment # Create a tensor of shape (..., 1) with value 1e10 # The device and dtype should match dists largeval = torch.fulllike(dists[...,:1], 1e10) dists = torch.cat([dists, largeval], dim=-1) # Step 3: Scale by cosine of the angle # cosangle is assumed to be broadcastable to dists dists = dists cosangle return dists Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure z{vals} and cos\angle are on the same device and have compatible dtypes to avoid runtime errors. Boundary Conditions: The last segment is approximated with a large value (10^{10}). This assumes that the last sample is effectively at infinity or that the contribution of the last segment is negligible if the density is zero. If the last sample is not at infinity, this approximation may introduce errors. Cosine Angle: If cos\angle is zero (ray perpendicular to view direction), all distances become zero, which may lead to division by zero or incorrect integration if not handled. Computes segment distances between consecutive Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) points. It differs from the standard Depth to Distance method by using Euclidean distance in NDC space rather than depth differences. Definition: Computes Euclidean distance between consecutive NDC points and scales by cosine angle. Steps: 1. Compute Euclidean distance: dists = \text{norm}(ndc\pts[:, 1:] - ndc\pts[:,:-1], \text{dim}=-1). 2. Append large value and scale: dists = \text{concat}(dists, 10^{10} \times cos\angle), scaled by cosine. When to choose: Use when working with NDC space representations where Euclidean distance in NDC space is more appropriate than depth differences. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the output distances. Performance: Efficient for large-scale volume rendering as it involves minimal computation per sample. Strengths: Simple to implement, accounts for viewing angle, handles boundary conditions with a large value approximation. Limitations: The large value approximation for the last segment may not be accurate for all scenes. Assumes uniform sampling in depth space. When to use: Standard volume rendering pipelines where depth samples are uniformly distributed in depth space. When not to use: When non-uniform sampling is used, or when the last segment needs precise distance calculation. name: Alpha Grid Mask
head: Alpha Volume Sampling
body: Alpha Grid Mask is a module for sampling alpha (opacity) values from a precomputed 3D alpha volume using trilinear interpolation. It solves the problem of incorporating spatially varying opacity constraints into volume rendering pipelines by mapping raw mask values to a specified opacity range, preventing complete occlusion or invisibility artifacts. It differs from direct intensity sampling by applying a linear remapping to ensure sampled values fall within a valid [min\opacity, max\opacity] interval. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D point positions (xyzsampled), a precomputed 3D alpha volume (alphavolume), and an axis-aligned bounding box (aabb). Output: Sampled alpha values (alphavals) for the input points. Data Structures: The module stores the following fields: aabb: The bounding box of the volume, typically defined by minimum and maximum coordinates. aabbSize: The size of the bounding box. invgridSize: The inverse of the grid size, used for normalization. alphavolume: The 3D alpha mask volume, reshaped to dimensions (1, 1, D, H, W) for tensor operations. gridSize: A tensor containing the dimensions of the volume grid. Steps: 1. Normalize Coordinates: Transform the input 3D point coordinates from the world space (defined by aabb) to the normalized range [-1, 1]. The formula is: xyz{sampled} = (xyz{sampled} - aabb[0]) \times invgridSize - 1 where aabb[0] is the minimum corner of the bounding box. 2. Sample Alpha Values: Perform trilinear interpolation on the alphavolume using the normalized coordinates. The implementation uses a grid sampling function (e.g., F.gridsample in PyTorch) with aligncorners=True. The coordinates are reshaped to (1, N, 1, 1, 3) where N is the number of points, and the result is flattened to (N,). alpha\vals = \text{grid\sample}(alpha\volume, xyz{sampled}.view(1, -1, 1, 1, 3), align\corners=True).view(-1) Parameters: aligncorners: Boolean flag for grid sampling. Set to True to align the corners of the sampling grid with the corners of the input volume. minopacity, maxopacity: The target range for the sampled alpha values. The raw sampled values are linearly remapped to this interval. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Points outside the aabb will result in out-of-bounds sampling. The implementation assumes points are within the bounding box or handles boundary conditions via the grid sampling function's padding mode (not specified in sources). Precision issues may arise if the invgridSize is not computed accurately from the gridSize and aabbSize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F class AlphaGridMask: def init(self, aabb, alphavolume, gridSize): """ Initialize the Alpha Grid Mask module. Args: aabb: Tensor of shape (2, 3) representing the min and max corners of the bounding box. alphavolume: Tensor of shape (D, H, W) representing the 3D alpha mask. gridSize: Tensor of shape (3,) representing the dimensions (D, H, W) of the volume. """ self.aabb = aabb self.alphavolume = alphavolume.view(1, 1, gridSize) # Reshape to (1, 1, D, H, W) self.gridSize = gridSize self.invgridSize = 2.0 / gridSize # Assuming aabb is normalized to [-1, 1] after scaling? # Note: Source formula implies specific normalization. # Source: xyzsampled = (xyzsampled - self.aabb[0]) self.invgridSize - 1 # This implies invgridSize is derived from aabbSize and gridSize. # Let's stick to the source formula structure. # Recalculate invgridSize based on source logic if aabb is not [-1,1] # Source: xyzsampled = (xyzsampled - self.aabb[0]) self.invgridSize - 1 # This maps aabb[0] to -1 and aabb[1] to 1. # So, (aabb[1] - aabb[0]) invgridSize - 1 = 1 => invgridSize = 2 / (aabb[1] - aabb[0]) self.aabbSize = self.aabb[1] - self.aabb[0] self.invgridSize = 2.0 / self.aabbSize def samplealpha(self, xyzsampled): """ Sample alpha values from the alpha volume for given 3D points. Args: xyzsampled: Tensor of shape (N, 3) representing N 3D points. Returns: alphavals: Tensor of shape (N,) representing sampled alpha values. """ # Step 1: Normalize coordinates to [-1, 1] range # xyzsampled: (N, 3) # self.aabb[0]: (3,) # self.invgridSize: (3,) xyznormalized = (xyzsampled - self.aabb[0]) self.invgridSize - 1 # Step 2: Sample alpha values using grid sample # Reshape for gridsample: (1, N, 1, 1, 3) xyzreshaped = xyznormalized.view(1, -1, 1, 1, 3) # Perform trilinear interpolation # F.gridsample expects input of shape (N, C, H, W) or (N, C, D, H, W) for 3D # Here alphavolume is (1, 1, D, H, W) alphavals = F.gridsample( self.alphavolume, xyzreshaped, aligncorners=True, mode='trilinear', paddingmode='zeros' # Default padding mode if not specified, but source doesn't specify. # Using 'zeros' is a safe default for out-of-bounds.) # Reshape output to (N,) alphavals = alphavals.view(-1) return alphavals This method samples opacity values from a precomputed 3D alpha mask volume for a set of 3D point positions, mapping the raw mask values to a specified opacity range. It serves as the core sampling primitive for the Alpha Grid Mask module, enabling volume rendering to incorporate spatially varying opacity constraints derived from external supervision or geometry masks. It differs from direct intensity sampling by applying a linear remapping to the sampled values to ensure they fall within a valid [min\opacity, max\opacity] interval, preventing complete occlusion or invisibility artifacts. Inputs: mask: A 3D volume tensor representing the alpha mask. points: A tensor of 3D coordinates with shape [N, 3], where N is the number of points. minopacity: Scalar, minimum opacity value (default 0.0). maxopacity: Scalar, maximum opacity value (default 1.0). Outputs: opacities: A tensor of shape [N] containing the mapped opacity values for each point. In the reference implementation, it is treated as a tensor supporting trilinear interpolation. points are normalized or scaled to match the coordinate system of the mask volume. Steps: 1. Sample Raw Values: Call the underlying volume sampling function (e.g., sampleintensitiesfromvolume) using the mask tensor and points. Footprint pooling is enabled to handle aliasing or sparse sampling. This returns raw values vi for each point i. 2. Map to Opacity Range: Apply the linear transformation to clamp and scale the raw values to the desired opacity range: oi = \min\opacity + vi \times (\max\opacity - \min\opacity) where oi is the final opacity for point i. 3. Clamping (Implicit/Explicit): Ensure oi remains within [0, 1] or the specified bounds. The formula above naturally respects the bounds if vi \in [0, 1]. If vi falls outside, standard clamping or the linear mapping behavior applies depending on the source implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Assumes normalized coordinates compatible with gridsample. minopacity: Minimum opacity value. maxopacity: Maximum opacity value. Returns: opacities: 1D tensor [N] with sampled opacity values. """ # Normalize points to [-1, 1] for gridsample if mask is in [0, 1] space # Assuming points are in [0, 1] relative to mask dimensions # gridsample expects points in [-1, 1] pointsnormalized = 2.0 points - 1.0 # Reshape points to [1, N, 1, 2] for gridsample (batch, numpoints, 1, 2) # Note: gridsample works on 2D grids. name: Stochastic Jittering
head: Jittering Sample Positions, Stochastic Noise, Stochastic Sampling
body: Stochastic Jittering is a sampling technique in direct volume ray casting that replaces regularly spaced sample positions with random offsets within each segment to eliminate banding and "wood-grain" artifacts. Unlike Uniform Ray Sampling, which produces visible structural artifacts due to aliasing, Stochastic Jittering transforms these artifacts into high-frequency noise that is visually less noticeable. It differs from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering in that it typically applies jitter only to the sample positions along the ray rather than using complex importance sampling or stratification for the entire integral, though it is fundamentally a Monte Carlo approach. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin (ray\orig), ray direction (ray\dir), entry point t0 (isect.t0), step size (step\size), sample index (n). Output: Sample position (sample\pos). Data Structures: Noise: A boolean flag to enable or disable the technique. MaxNoiseFactor: A scalar controlling the maximum magnitude of the jitter. NoiseTexture: A 2D texture of size NoiseTextureSize × NoiseTextureSize used to generate spatially coherent jitter values. Steps: 1. Generate a random value r uniformly distributed in [0, 1]. In GPU implementations, this is typically sampled from a noise texture using screen coordinates. 2. Calculate the sample position t along the ray: t = isect.t0 + step\size \times (n + r) where n is the integer sample index (0, 1, 2, \dots). 3. Compute the 3D sample position: sample\pos = ray\orig + t \times ray\dir. Parameters: MaxNoiseFactor: Typical value 0.75. This scales the random offset r to bound the maximum inserted jitter magnitude. Standard stochastic sampling uses r \in [0,1] directly, while VTK implementations scale the noise factor. NoiseTextureSize: Typical value 64. Determines the resolution of the pre-generated noise texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hash2d(x, y): """Deterministic pseudo-random value in [0, 1) for screen-space coherence.""" return (math.sin(x 12.9898 + y 78.233) 43758.5453) % 1.0 def getsampleposition(isectt0, stepsize, n, rayorig, raydir, usenoise, maxnoisefactor, fragcoord): """ Calculates the sample position using stochastic jittering. Args: isectt0: Entry point t0 of the ray into the volume. stepsize: Distance between regular sample intervals. n: Integer sample index (0, 1, 2...). rayorig: Ray origin vector. raydir: Ray direction vector. usenoise: Boolean flag to enable jittering. maxnoisefactor: Maximum magnitude of the jitter offset. fragcoord: Screen-space coordinates (x, y) for texture lookup. Returns: samplepos: The 3D position of the sample. """ if usenoise: # Sample noise texture at screen coordinates, scaled by texture size r = hash2d(fragcoord[0], fragcoord[1]) # Scale by maximum noise factor if the implementation requires bounded jitter r = r maxnoisefactor t = isectt0 + stepsize (n + r) else: # Standard uniform sampling at the center of the segment t = isectt0 + stepsize (n + 0.5) samplepos = rayorig + t raydir return samplepos Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Without refinement, isosurface rendering errors are inevitable if the sample distance is not reduced; jittering only makes these artifacts less visible. Replaces banding artifacts with noise. The noise can be reduced using quasi-Monte Carlo methods, but this is not implemented in the basic version. name: Temporal Filtering and Jittering
head: Jittering, Temporal Filtering, Temporal Supersampling
body: This technique reduces spatial banding artifacts and noise in volume rendering by combining sub-voxel ray jittering with temporal reprojection, effectively increasing perceived resolution without additional raymarching steps. It leverages temporal coherence and camera motion vectors to blend frame data over time. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current frame’s volumetric data (stored in a 3D texture), previous frame’s 3D texture, camera motion vectors, and a pseudo-random sequence generator (e.g., blue noise or Halton sequence). Outputs: A temporally filtered 3D texture representing the accumulated volumetric light and transmittance. Data Structures: 3D Texture: Stores the integrated volumetric data (in-scattered light and transmittance). The implementation uses hardware trilinear interpolation (GLLINEAR) for sampling. Motion Vectors: A buffer storing the displacement of each pixel from the previous frame to the current frame, derived from camera transforms. Steps: 1. Depth Jittering: Each frame, calculate a sub-voxel offset derived from a pseudo-random sequence (such as blue noise or a Halton sequence) and apply it to offset ray positions to hide spatial banding artifacts caused by coarse slice resolution. 2. Ray Marching: Perform ray marching using the jittered rays to accumulate volumetric data into a temporary 3D texture for the current frame. 3. Temporal Reprojection: Execute a compute pass that blends the current frame’s 3D texture with the previous frame's 3D texture using camera motion vectors. 4. Final Composition: During post-processing or forward-lighting, retrieve the linear depth of the opaque scene fragment from the depth buffer. Convert the fragment's screen coordinates and linear depth into 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w) using an exponential depth equation. Sample the integrated 3D texture using hardware trilinear interpolation (GLLINEAR). Add the sampled in-scattered light to the scene color, and attenuate the scene color by the sampled transmittance. Formulas: Ray Offset: P{jittered} = P{base} + \Delta P{random}, where \Delta P{random} is the sub-voxel offset derived from the pseudo-random sequence. Reprojection & Blending: Not given in the sources. Scene Composition: C{out} = C{scene} \cdot T{sampled} + L{in-scattered}, where T{sampled} is the transmittance and L{in-scattered} is the in-scattered light sampled from the 3D texture. Parameters: Random Sequence Type: Blue noise or Halton sequence. Interpolation Method: Trilinear interpolation (GLLINEAR). Blending Factor: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A post-processing technique that smooths noise artifacts from blue noise dithering by calculating a new pixel value using a cubic polynomial over 16 neighboring pixels. It is chosen when residual noise patterns remain after temporal filtering and spatial jittering. Implementation involves rendering the raymarched scene into a Frame Buffer Object (FBO), passing the FBO texture as a uniform to a bicubic filtering material, and rendering a fullscreen triangle with that material to output the smoothed scene. It retains details while smoothing noise, particularly at edges and in less dense regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the current and previous frame’s 3D textures, plus motion vectors and FBOs for post-processing. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves perceived volume resolution without extra raymarching steps; effectively hides spatial banding artifacts. Limitations: Requires motion vectors for reprojection; residual noise may still require additional post-processing like bicubic filtering. When to use: When spatial banding and noise are visible due to coarse slice resolution or limited raymarching steps. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This technique is described in the context of volumetric fog rendering using 3D textures in OpenGL. It builds on the concept of stochastic jittering to reduce banding and extends it with temporal reprojection to smooth noise over time. Bicubic filtering upsampling is mentioned as a complementary post-processing step to further reduce noise artifacts in raymarched scenes. name: Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling)
head: Fine Sampling, Hierarchical Importance Sampling, Inverse CDF Sampling
body: Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) generates fine-grained depth samples along a ray by sampling from a probability density function (PDF) derived from coarse rendering weights. It uses inverse transform sampling on the cumulative distribution function (CDF) to concentrate samples in high-density regions, improving density estimation and reducing variance compared to uniform sampling. It builds on Sampling and Jittering by using importance sampling to refine coarse passes. Inputs: bins: 1D tensor of depth coordinates or midpoints for coarse samples, shape (Nc,) or (batch, Nc). weights: 1D tensor of unnormalized importance weights (typically volume density or opacity) corresponding to the coarse samples, shape (Nc,) or (batch, Nc). Note: leading and trailing columns are often excluded before passing to this method. Nsamples: Integer specifying the number of fine samples to generate per ray. deterministic: Boolean flag. If True, uses deterministic uniform spacing; otherwise uses random jitter. Outputs: finezvals: 1D tensor of interpolated depth coordinates for the fine samples, shape (Nsamples,) or (batch, Nsamples). Data Structures: The method operates on 1D tensors representing the ray's depth interval. For batched operations, dimensions are broadcasted or processed in parallel. Intermediate structures include the Probability Density Function (PDF) and Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) tensors. Steps: 1. Compute PDF: Normalize the coarse weights to form a probability density function. To prevent division by zero or NaNs, add a small epsilon (\epsilon = 10^{-5}) to all weights before normalization. \text{pdf}i = \frac{\text{weights}i + \epsilon}{\sum{j} (\text{weights}j + \epsilon)} where \text{weights} are the coarseweights. 2. Compute CDF: Calculate the cumulative distribution function by taking the cumulative sum of the PDF. Prepend a zero tensor to the CDF to represent the start of the first bin (index 0). \text{cdf}0 = 0 \text{cdf}i = \text{cdf}{i-1} + \text{pdf}{i-1} \quad \text{for } i > 0 In code, this is often implemented as cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), torch.cumsum(pdf, -1)], -1). 3. Generate Query Values: Generate uniform random numbers u in the interval [0, 1] with size Nsamples. If deterministic is True, use linearly spaced values: ui = \frac{i}{N{\text{samples}}} for i \in [0, N{\text{samples}}-1]. If deterministic is False, use random uniform samples: ui \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1). 4. Find Bin Indices: Determine which bin in the CDF each query value u falls into using binary search (searchsorted). \text{inds} = \text{searchsorted}(\text{cdf}, u, \text{side}=\text{'right'}) This returns the index k such that \text{cdf}{k-1} \le u < \text{cdf}k. 5. Determine Bin Boundaries: Identify the lower (below) and upper (above) bin indices for interpolation. Clamp these indices to valid ranges [0, \text{len}(\text{cdf})-1]. \text{below} = \max(0, \text{inds} - 1) \text{above} = \min(\text{len}(\text{cdf}) - 1, \text{inds}) 6. Gather CDF and Depth Values: Retrieve the CDF values and depth coordinates (bins, which are coarsezvals) for the lower and upper bins. \text{cdf}{\text{below}} = \text{cdf}[\text{below}] \text{cdf}{\text{above}} = \text{cdf}[\text{above}] \text{z}{\text{below}} = \text{bins}[\text{below}] \text{z}{\text{above}} = \text{bins}[\text{above}] 7. Interpolate Sample Positions: Perform linear interpolation within the identified bin to find the final sample depth z{\text{sample}}. \text{denom} = \text{cdf}{\text{above}} - \text{cdf}{\text{below}} Handle division by zero by clamping denom to a small value (e.g., 10^{-5}) if it is below the threshold. t = \frac{u - \text{cdf}{\text{below}}}{\max(\text{denom}, 10^{-5})} z{\text{sample}} = \text{z}{\text{below}} + t \cdot (\text{z}{\text{above}} - \text{z}{\text{below}}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def hierarchicalsampling(bins, weights, Nsamples, deterministic=True): """ Perform hierarchical sampling using inverse CDF. Args: bins: Tensor of shape (Nc,) or (batch, Nc) containing coarse depth samples. weights: Tensor of shape (Nc,) or (batch, Nc) containing unnormalized weights. Nsamples: int, number of fine samples to generate. deterministic: bool, if True uses linspace, else random uniform. Returns: finezvals: Tensor of shape (Nsamples,) or (batch, Nsamples). """ # Step 1: Compute PDF with epsilon to prevent NaNs eps = 1e-5 weights = weights + eps pdf = weights / torch.sum(weights, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Step 2: Compute CDF and prepend zero cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # Step 3: Generate query values u if deterministic: u = torch.linspace(0., 1., steps=Nsamples).to(cdf.device) if cdf.dim() > 1: u = u.unsqueeze(0).expand(cdf.shape[0], -1) else: u = torch.rand(cdf.shape[:-1] + (Nsamples,)).to(cdf.device) # Step 4: Find bin indices inds = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, right=True) # Step 5: Determine bin boundaries below = torch.clamp(inds - 1, min=0) above = torch.clamp(inds, max=cdf.shape[-1] - 1) # Step 6: Gather CDF and bin values indsg = torch.stack([below, above], dim=-1) # Gather CDF values cdfg = torch.gather(cdf.unsqueeze(1).expandas(indsg), 2, indsg).squeeze(1) # Gather depth values (bins) binsg = torch.gather(bins.unsqueeze(1).expandas(indsg), 2, indsg).squeeze(1) # Step 7: Interpolate denom = cdfg[..., 1] - cdfg[..., 0] denom = torch.where(denom < 1e-5, torch.oneslike(denom), denom) t = (u - cdfg[..., 0]) / denom finezvals = binsg[..., 0] + t (binsg[..., 1] - binsg[..., 0]) return finezvals Parameters: Nsamples: Integer specifying the number of fine samples to generate per ray. Typical values are 128 or 64. deterministic: Boolean flag. If True, uses deterministic linspace samples instead of random uniform samples for reproducibility. perturb: Float controlling jittering. 0 disables jittering (deterministic midpoints), 1 enables full stratified jittering. This parameter is often used in the coarse pass, but the fine pass here is strictly inverse CDF. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weights: Zero weights cause division by zero during PDF normalization. Handled by adding \epsilon = 10^{-5} to all weights before normalization. Zero-Width Bins: Zero-width bins (where cdfabove == cdfbelow) cause division by zero during interpolation. Handled by clamping the denominator denom to 10^{-5} if it falls below that threshold. Boundary Conditions: Indices must be clamped to valid ranges [0, \text{len}(\text{cdf})-1] to prevent out-of-bounds access. Inverse Opacity Calculation is a differentiable method for generating importance samples along a ray in volume rendering by inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the rendering contribution. It solves the problem of finding the ray parameter t corresponding to a target cumulative density value y, allowing samples to be drawn directly from transmittance estimates rather than computing expensive integrals. Unlike standard NeRF hierarchical sampling, which interpolates exponentiated densities (probabilities) and requires auxiliary losses, this method interpolates the density field directly (piecewise linear or constant), offering better numerical stability for end-to-end optimization. It enables Monte Carlo estimates with fewer ray points and allows gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process to the density field parameters. Proposal Network Sampling is a method for importance sampling in volume rendering that directly estimates the Probability Density Function (PDF) along a ray using a coarse neural network, known as the proposal network. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling by concentrating samples on high-contribution areas (such as surfaces) while spreading them in empty or occluded regions, providing more accurate transmittance estimation than spatial skipping methods. It builds on Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) by learning the sampling distribution dynamically rather than relying on static weights. RangeFineSampler is a hierarchical sampling technique for direct volume ray casting that refines coarse samples by generating a dense uniform grid around the coarse sample with the highest weight, supplemented by random samples across the full ray extent. It addresses missing high-frequency details between coarse samples by concentrating computational effort near the most significant signal while maintaining global coverage through random jittering. Unlike Inverse Opacity Calculation which derives samples from opacity gradients, or Proposal Network Sampling which uses learned neural networks to predict sample locations, RangeFineSampler relies on a deterministic geometric expansion around the peak weight index combined with stochastic uniform sampling. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The method involves computing the PDF and CDF (O(Nc)), generating random numbers (O(Nf)), binary search (O(Nf \log Nc)), and interpolation (O(Nf)). Overall complexity is dominated by O(Nf \log Nc), where Nc is the number of coarse samples and Nf is the number of fine samples. Memory: Requires storage for the CDF and intermediate tensors, proportional to O(Nc + Nf). Measured Performance: Performance depends on the hardware and resolution. On a single 2080 Ti, training a NeRF on a low-res scene (e.g., fern) takes approximately 8 hours for 200k iterations. The method allows for fewer ray points while maintaining accuracy, reducing the computational load compared to uniform sampling. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of rays and samples. It is suitable for large-scale volume rendering due to its efficiency in concentrating samples in high-density regions. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Differentiable, allowing gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process. Numerically stable with proper epsilon handling. Efficient importance sampling. Limitations: Requires coarse samples and weights as input. Performance may degrade if coarse weights are inaccurate. When to Use: Use when importance sampling is needed to reduce variance in volume rendering. Use when differentiable sampling is required for end-to-end optimization. When Not to Use: Avoid when computational resources are extremely limited and coarse weights are not available. Avoid when the scene has very low density variations, making importance sampling less beneficial. Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) originates from the NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) paper by Mildenhall et al.. It was introduced to improve the efficiency of volume rendering by concentrating samples in regions of high density. The method has been widely adopted in subsequent works, including.
