name: Monte Carlo Volume Rendering
head: Monte Carlo Scattering (MCS), Stochastic Volume Rendering
body: Monte Carlo Volume Rendering is a stochastic approach to volumetric visualization that avoids uniform step sampling by using random distance sampling and null-collision techniques to estimate light transport in participating media. It differs from its siblings, such as Uniform Ray Sampling and Ray Casting with Jittered Sampling, by explicitly modeling scattering events via random walks (photon tracing) or stochastic ray casting with exponential distance sampling, allowing for accurate handling of anisotropic scattering and complex light transport at the cost of convergence noise. The method is implemented in two primary variants found in the sources: a GPU-based ray casting approach using exponential distance sampling and a shader-based photon tracing approach using null-collision Monte Carlo. Both variants rely on stochastic sampling to determine interaction points within the volume. Inputs: Volume data: 3D texture (sampler3D) containing density/opacity values. Transfer function: 2D texture mapping density to color/opacity. Environment map: 2D texture for background/lighting. Camera parameters: Inverse Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix for ray unprojection. Volume parameters: Extinction coefficient (\sigmat), albedo (\omega), anisotropy bias (g), majorant ratio. Random seed: Derived from fragment position and frame offset. Outputs: Accumulated color buffer (for ray casting) or photon state buffers (position, direction, transmittance, radiance, bounces, samples) for photon tracing. Photon State (Photon Tracing Variant): Stored in output buffers as vec4 components: position: vec3 (photon position in world space). direction: vec3 (normalized scattering direction). bounces: uint (stored in direction.w or separate buffer). transmittance: vec3 (accumulated transmittance weight). radiance: vec3 (accumulated radiance estimate). samples: uint (stored in radiance.w or separate buffer). Random Number Generation: A hash-based pseudo-random number generator is used, typically defined as: rand(p) = fract( (cos(M \times p)x, sin(M \times p)y) \times D) where M is a 2x2 matrix of constants and D is a vec2 of constants. This variant traces rays from the camera, stochastically determining the first scattering event. 1. Ray Initialization: Unproject screen coordinates to get ray origin v{RayFrom} and direction endpoint v{RayTo} using the inverse MVP matrix. 2. Volume Intersection: Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box (cube). Calculate entry distance t{bounds}.x and exit distance t{bounds}.y. If t{bounds}.x \ge t{bounds}.y, the ray misses; sample the environment map and return. 3. Random Seed: Initialize random state using a hash of the pixel position and a frame offset. 4. Stochastic Distance Sampling: Determine the distance to the first scattering event using the exponential distribution: Initialize dist = 0.0. Calculate invSigmaMax = 1.0 / \sigma{max}, where \sigma{max} is the maximum extinction coefficient. Loop: Generate random number seed. Update distance: dist{new} = dist{old} - \frac{\log(1 - seed.x)}{\sigma{max}}. If dist > maxDistance (distance to volume exit), break loop. Sample volume color at P = mix(v{RayFrom}, v{RayTo}, dist \times invMaxDistance). Check for scattering: If seed.y < \alpha{sample} \times invSigmaMax, break loop and return dist. 5. Scattering Event: If dist > maxDistance, sample environment map and return. Calculate scattering point P{scatter} = mix(v{RayFrom}, v{RayTo}, dist / maxDistance). Sample diffuse color: C{diffuse} = sampleVolumeColor(P{scatter}). Sample light color from environment map in the scattering direction: C{light} = sampleEnvironmentMap(u{ScatteringDirection}). Calculate transmittance from P{scatter} to the volume exit in the scattering direction using sampleTransmittance. 6. Transmittance Calculation: Initialize T = 1.0. Loop similar to distance sampling: Generate random seed. Update distance. If dist > maxDistance, break. Update transmittance: T{new} = T{old} \times (1 - \alpha{sample} \times invSigmaMax). Return T. 7. Final Color: C{final} = C{diffuse} \times C{light} \times T. 8. Accumulation: Average the current frame with previous frames to reduce noise: AvgRender = AvgRender + \frac{NewRender - AvgRender}{numRenders} where numRenders is the current frame number. This variant uses shaders to simulate photon paths through the volume, accumulating radiance estimates via multiple bounces. 1. Photon Initialization (Reset Shader): Unproject screen position to get ray origin from and direction to. Normalize to. Intersect ray with unit cube to get entry bounds t{bounds}. Set photon.position = from + t{bounds}.x \times direction. Initialize photon.transmittance = vec3(1.0), photon.radiance = vec3(0.0), bounces = 0, samples = 0. 2. Photon Tracing Loop (Compute Shader): Loop for i from 0 to uSteps (number of integration steps): Generate random number r. Compute step size t = -\frac{\log(r.x)}{\sigma{majorant}}, where \sigma{majorant} is the majorant density. Update position: photon.position += t \times photon.direction. Sample volume color at new position to get absorption (\mu{abs}), scattering (\mu{scat}), and null collision (\mu{null}) coefficients: \mu{abs} = volumeSample.a \times uAbsorptionCoefficient. \mu{scat} = volumeSample.a \times uScatteringCoefficient. \mu{null} = \sigma{majorant} - \mu{abs} - \mu{scat}. \sigma{majorant} = \mu{abs} + \mu{scat} + |\mu{null}|. Compute probabilities: P{null} = \frac{|\mu{null}|}{\sigma{majorant}}. P{abs} = \frac{\mu{abs}}{\sigma{majorant}}. P{scat} = \frac{\mu{scat}}{\sigma{majorant}}. Bounds Check: If photon.position is outside the volume cube, sample environment map, add to radiance estimate (running average), reset photon, and continue to next step. Collision Type: If r.y < P{abs} + P{scat} (Scattering/Absorption event): Generate new random r. If r.y < P{abs}, photon is absorbed (transmittance becomes 0, stop). If r.y \ge P{abs} (Scattering): Update transmittance: T{new} = T{old} \times volumeSample.rgb \times \frac{\mu{scat}}{\sigma{majorant} \times P{scat}}. Sample new direction using Henyey-Greenstein phase function with bias g. Increment bounces. Else (Null Collision): Update transmittance: T{new} = T{old} \times \frac{|\mu{null}|}{\sigma{majorant} \times P{null}}. 3. Output: Write photon state to buffers. Radiance is accumulated over multiple samples. \sigma{max} / uSigmaMax: Maximum extinction coefficient for inverse probability sampling. Typical value: positive float representing max volume density. uExtinction: Extinction coefficient for exponential distance sampling. uAlphaCorrection: Scaling factor for sampled alpha values. uScatteringDirection: Direction vector for secondary scattering ray (ray casting variant). \sigma{majorant} / uMajorant: Majorant density for null-collision sampling. Typically \max(\mu{abs} + \mu{scat}). uAbsorptionCoefficient: Base absorption coefficient multiplier (default 1). uScatteringCoefficient: Base scattering coefficient multiplier (default 1). uScatteringBias / scatteringBias: Anisotropy parameter g for Henyey-Greenstein (default 0). uMaxBounces / maxBounces: Maximum scattering bounces (default 8). uSteps / steps: Number of integration steps per photon trace (default varies). extinction: UI input for total extinction. ratio: UI input for majorant ratio. bounces: UI input for max bounces. steps: UI input for steps per ray. resolution: Render buffer resolution (default 512). workgroup: Local workgroup size (default 8). Ray Miss: If the ray does not intersect the volume cube, the environment map must be sampled to avoid black pixels. Precision: Logarithmic sampling requires careful handling of random numbers near 0 to avoid infinite step sizes. Convergence: Monte Carlo methods converge slowly (1/\sqrt{N}). Accumulation over multiple frames is required for noise-free images. Time Complexity: O(N \times S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps/bounces per photon/ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the accumulator buffer or photon buffers. Performance: Depends heavily on the density of the volume and the majorant ratio. High density or large majorant ratios lead to more null collisions and slower convergence. Strengths: Handles anisotropic scattering (Henyey-Greenstein) naturally and avoids artifacts from uniform sampling in heterogeneous volumes. Accurate light transport is achieved through stochastic path tracing. Limitations: Noisy output requiring temporal accumulation; computationally expensive compared to deterministic ray casting for simple volumes; sensitive to parameter tuning (majorant, steps). When to use: When accurate scattering and anisotropy are required, and temporal accumulation is acceptable. When not to use: For real-time applications without accumulation buffers, or for homogeneous volumes where uniform sampling is sufficient. The Monte-Carlo approach was introduced as an alternative to uniform sampling, which may result in artifacts since a homogeneous material is assumed. The null-collision technique, also known as the virtual collision method, was introduced to handle heterogeneous media efficiently by sampling distances from a majorant distribution and rejecting non-scattering events. The specific implementation described in the sources is a GPU-based approach using fragment shaders for ray casting and photon tracing, as seen in the volumetric-ray-casting and vpt repositories. name: Random Jitter with Reprojection
head: Frame Accumulation, Temporal Reprojection
body: Random Jitter with Reprojection is a technique to reduce banding artifacts caused by low sample counts in volume rendering by introducing stochastic jitter during ray marching and subsequently reducing the resulting noise via temporal accumulation. It distinguishes itself from pure spatial jittering methods by leveraging temporal coherence, projecting a pseudo-hit position from the current frame into the previous frame's screen space to blend the current result with a history buffer, thereby allowing for lower per-frame sample counts while maintaining visual stability. The method operates within a direct volume ray casting framework. It modifies the standard marching loop to introduce jittered sampling positions and maintains a specific data structure for reprojection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current view matrix, previous view matrix, current frame's accumulated color, history buffer (previous frame's color), step size, density threshold. Output: Final accumulated color for the current pixel. Data Structures: reprojectionHitPosition: A float3 variable storing the 3D world position. This position is updated during the march loop when the accumulated density is below a specific threshold, serving as a proxy for the "hit" position in scenes without explicit geometry. Parameters: TRESHOLD: A density threshold used to determine if the ray is still within the volume (e.g., cloud) for reprojection purposes. If the accumulated density falls below this value, the current sample position is recorded as the reprojection hit. weight: A blending factor between the history buffer and the current result. This weight is typically kept relatively high because volumetric elements like clouds do not reproject accurately due to their non-rigid, volumetric nature. Steps: 1. Initialize reprojectionHitPosition to a default value (e.g., origin or previous frame's hit). 2. Iterate through the ray march loop: a. Calculate a jittered position by adding a random float multiplied by the step size to the current sample position. b. Update the base samplePosition by adding the step size (without jitter) to maintain a non-jittered progression track. c. Sample the density at the jittered position. d. Accumulate the density. e. If the accumulated density is below TRESHOLD, update reprojectionHitPosition to the current non-jittered samplePosition. 3. After the march loop completes, project reprojectionHitPosition to the previous screen space using the previous view matrix. 4. Sample the history buffer at the projected screen position to retrieve the previous frame's result. 5. Blend the history result and the current frame's result using the weight factor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpixel(currentview, prevview, historybuffer, stepsize, threshold): # Initialization reprojectionhitposition = float3(0, 0, 0) sampleposition = rayorigin accumulateddensity = 0.0 currentresult = float3(0, 0, 0) # March Loop while sampleposition is within bounds: # Jittered sampling jitterposition = sampleposition + randomfloat() stepsize # Update base position without jitter sampleposition += stepsize # Sample density at jittered position sampledensity = sampledensityfunction(jitterposition) # Accumulate density accumulateddensity += sampledensity # Update reprojection hit if inside volume threshold if accumulateddensity < threshold: reprojectionhitposition = sampleposition # Accumulate color contribution currentresult += computecolor(sampledensity) # Break if outside volume or max steps reached # Reprojection # Project 3D hit position to previous screen space prevscreenpos = worldtoscreen(reprojectionhitposition, prevview) # Sample history buffer history = historybuffer.sample(prevscreenpos) # Blend with current result # Weight must be relatively high because clouds do not reproject accurately result = lerp(history, currentresult, weight) return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clouds and Volumetrics: Since clouds lack a sharp geometric boundary, the "hit" position is an approximation. Inaccurate reprojection leads to ghosting or blurring. The blending weight must be tuned to balance noise reduction against motion artifacts. If too low, it may be set too late or not at all if the ray exits the volume quickly. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the history buffer, where W and H are the screen dimensions. Performance: Allows for a significant reduction in per-frame sample counts compared to non-jittered methods, reducing computational cost while maintaining visual quality through temporal accumulation. Strengths: Effective at reducing banding artifacts from low sample counts; leverages temporal coherence to smooth noise. Limitations: Introduces temporal latency and potential ghosting artifacts, especially with fast camera motion or dynamic volumetric changes. Requires a history buffer and reprojection logic. When to use: When rendering static or slowly moving volumetric scenes (e.g., clouds) where temporal coherence is high and banding from low sample counts is a concern. When not to use: In scenes with rapid camera motion or highly dynamic volumetric changes where ghosting artifacts would be distracting. This technique is described in the context of volumetric cloud rendering, specifically as an adaptive sampling technique to reduce the cost of high-quality cloud rendering by lowering sample counts and using temporal accumulation to mitigate noise. name: Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering
head: Non-uniform particle sampling, Stochastic Sampling for SPH Rendering, Stochastic sampling
body: Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering is a technique to increase rendering performance by reducing the number of particles used during rendering, using a non-uniform sampling strategy based on data importance and view-dependent criteria. It solves the problem of high computational cost when rendering large, unstructured Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) datasets by ensuring that particles in complex regions (e.g., phase interfaces, vortices) are sampled more densely than those in homogeneous areas. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by avoiding equal-time high-error trade-offs, and from Stochastic Jittering by using precomputed data-driven probabilities rather than simple spatial jittering to guide particle selection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: SPH particle dataset (positions, attributes, phases), camera parameters, transfer functions, and sampling parameters p{min} and p{max}. Output: Rendered image with reduced noise and artifacts in critical regions, achieved by selectively accessing a subset of particles per ray. Data Structures: Particle Data: Standard SPH structure containing position \mathbf{x}i, attributes (e.g., density, temperature), and phase identifier. Data Importance Grid/Array: A precomputed value pi for each particle i, representing the static importance of that particle based on local attribute complexity and phase interface presence. View-Dependent Criterion: A dynamic value pt calculated per pixel or ray segment based on view-dependent factors (e.g., opacity, occlusion). Parameters: p{min}: Minimal sampling probability. Controls render time significantly. Recommended value is 0.01 to avoid high sampling error at phase interfaces. p{max}: Maximal sampling probability. Controls rendering error with least effect on render times. Should be assigned to high values to increase the range of sampling probabilities. Steps: 1. Precompute Data Importance (pi): Calculate a static importance value for each particle. This value is low for homogeneous areas and high for complex regions like phase interfaces and vortices. This step is fast (<30ms) compared to volume resampling preprocessing. 2. Determine Sampling Probability (p): For each ray marching step, combine the precomputed data importance pi with the view-dependent criterion pt to determine the per-pixel particle access probability p. The specific combination formula is not provided, but it results in varying probabilities. 3. Stochastic Particle Selection: Based on the calculated probability p, randomly decide whether to access and render the current particle. If accessed, use the particle's attributes for shading. 4. Handle Phase Interfaces and Shading: If a phase transition leading to surface shading is detected during ray marching, use a constant sampling probability of one (p=1) for the iterative search for the surface position xs and the resampling of SPH attributes at xs for shading. For single scattering occlusion rays cast from a sampling point in a volumetric area, reduce the particle sampling probability by a factor of 10% (i.e., p{new} = 0.9 \times p{old}). Do not reduce the probability if an occlusion ray stems from a ray segment containing surface shading, because surfaces have higher opacity and use irradiance influenced by occlusion for shading. 5. Render: Accumulate the contributions of sampled particles to form the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersphimportancesampling(particles, camera, pmin, pmax): # Precompute static data importance pi for each particle # This is done once per frame or when data changes pi = computedataimportance(particles) image = createemptyimage() for each pixel (u, v): ray = camera.generateray(u, v) color = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 while transmittance > 0.001 and ray.t < maxdistance: # Find relevant particles near the current ray position relevantparticles = findparticlesnearray(ray, particles) if not relevantparticles: break # Select a particle based on importance and view-dependent criteria # pt is derived from view-dependent factors (e.g., current opacity) # The exact combination of pi and pt is not specified, # but it must be bounded by pmin and pmax selectedparticle = None for particle in relevantparticles: # Calculate view-dependent criterion pt # Example: pt could be related to the accumulated opacity so far pt = calculateviewdependentcriterion(ray, transmittance) # Combine pi and pt to get sampling probability p # Formula not given, but must respect bounds p = combineprobabilities(pi[particle.id], pt) p = clamp(p, pmin, pmax) # Stochastic selection if random() < p: selectedparticle = particle break if selectedparticle is None: # No particle sampled, advance ray ray.t += stepsize continue # Check for phase transition if isphasetransition(selectedparticle, ray): # Use constant probability 1 for surface shading search surfacepos = findsurfaceposition(selectedparticle, ray) # Resample attributes at surface position attributes = resamplesphattributes(surfacepos, particles) # Shade surface color += shadesurface(attributes, ray) transmittance = 0.0 # Surface is opaque break else: # Volumetric shading attributes = getparticleattributes(selectedparticle) # Calculate single scattering # If this is a secondary ray for occlusion, reduce probability if issecondaryocclusionray(ray): # Reduce probability for subsequent steps if cast from volumetric area # This affects the next iteration's selection pass # Shade volume volumecolor = shadevolume(attributes, ray) color += volumecolor transmittance transmittance = 1.0 - selectedparticle.opacity # Simplified # Advance ray ray.t += stepsize image[u, v] = color return image def combineprobabilities(pi, pt): # Specific formula not provided in sources # Must return a value between 0 and 1 # Heuristic: weighted average or product return pi pt def calculateviewdependentcriterion(ray, transmittance): # Example implementation: higher probability if transmittance is low (dark regions) # or if ray is near camera return 1.0 - transmittance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If p{min} approaches p{max}, the method collapses to uniform sampling, omitting performance advantages. Setting p{min} = 0 can lead to high sampling error at phase interfaces that were not correctly identified in the data importance pi. Therefore, p{min} should be set to at least 0.01 for high-quality renders. Temporal noise: Particle sampling and preprocessing do not currently consider temporal properties, so sampling noise may change between frames in time-dependent data. SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling is a precomputation technique that assigns sampling probabilities to SPH particles based on the local information complexity of their attributes and the presence of phase interfaces. It solves the problem of high-frequency shading errors and subsampling artifacts at phase boundaries by ensuring that regions with high attribute variation or discontinuous phase transitions are sampled more densely. It differs from naive random discarding by using a structured, data-driven importance grid that accounts for the spatial support of the SPH kernel, and it differs from its sibling Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data by explicitly computing entropy to quantify attribute variation rather than relying solely on stochastic selection heuristics. A direct volume rendering technique for large, unstructured smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) data that avoids intermediate grid representations by stochastically sampling a subset of particles during ray marching. It differs from standard DVR by using view-dependent and spatial-complexity-based probabilities to select particles, enabling continuous scaling from interactive previews to high-quality renders. It specifically addresses multi-phase flows by reconstructing interfaces between different fluid types (e.g., gas and liquid) using a combined volumetric and surface shading model. This method approximates Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) scalar fields along viewing rays using piecewise polynomial functions of higher order, rather than constant or linear approximations. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering SPH data, which consists of individual particle contributions with varying spatial resolution, by approximating each particle's contribution individually and summing the results. It sets itself apart from Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering by focusing on the geometric accuracy of the field representation along rays via higher-order polynomials, and from SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling by using a deterministic polynomial approximation strategy rather than entropy-based sampling. This variant adapts sampling probabilities based on the type of shading being performed. If a phase transition leading to surface shading is detected during ray marching, it uses a constant sampling probability of one for the iterative search for the surface position xs and the resampling of SPH attributes at xs for shading. For single scattering occlusion, it reduces particle sampling probability by a factor of 10% if an occlusion ray is cast from a sampling point in a volumetric area. However, it does not reduce the probability if an occlusion ray stems from a ray segment containing surface shading, because surfaces have higher opacity and use irradiance influenced by occlusion for shading. Single scattering occlusion is low frequency and impervious to subsampling compared to surface shading, allowing reduced sampling probability for secondary rays which perform the majority of SPH approximations. Time Complexity: Rendering time is linearly dependent on the number of particle accesses. By reducing particle accesses through non-uniform sampling, performance is significantly improved. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for particle data and precomputed importance values pi. No intermediate grid representation is needed, unlike volume resampling. Measured Performance: Spray Nozzle (43.2M particles): Fast rendering <1s, High-quality 8s, No sampling 45s. Bubble (4.3M particles): Aggressive subsampling <1s, Reference >10s. Turbine: Equal-time rendering (5.3s) with uniform sampling had significantly higher error than the non-uniform sampling method. Preprocessing: Negligible preprocessing time (<30ms) compared to volume resampling which can take several minutes. Strengths: Handles dense multi-phase data with accurate phase interface reconstruction; avoids discretization errors associated with grid-based resampling; allows interactive exploration due to low preprocessing time. Limitations: Temporal noise may be visible in time-dependent data; requires careful tuning of p{min} and p{max} to balance error and performance. When to Use: When rendering large, unstructured SPH datasets with complex phase interfaces where uniform sampling is too slow or produces high error. When Not to Use: When temporal consistency is critical and preprocessing for temporal coherence is not implemented; when the dataset is very small and preprocessing overhead dominates. Originating from the paper "Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data", this method was developed to address the challenges of rendering large, unstructured SPH data without the need for expensive intermediate grid representations. It builds on the principles of direct volume ray casting and importance sampling, adapting them to the specific characteristics of SPH data, such as varying particle densities and multi-phase interfaces. The method has been applied to various SPH datasets, including spray nozzles, bubble flows, and turbine simulations, demonstrating significant performance improvements over uniform sampling and volume resampling. name: SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling
head: Data importance precomputation, Entropy-based importance
body: SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling is a precomputation technique that assigns sampling probabilities to SPH particles based on the local information complexity of their attributes and the presence of phase interfaces. It solves the problem of high-frequency shading errors and subsampling artifacts at phase boundaries by ensuring that regions with high attribute variation or discontinuous phase transitions are sampled more densely. It differs from naive random discarding by using a structured, data-driven importance grid that accounts for the spatial support of the SPH kernel, and it differs from its sibling Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data by explicitly computing entropy to quantify attribute variation rather than relying solely on stochastic selection heuristics. The method operates in two phases: a precomputation phase that builds an importance grid from the particle data, and a runtime phase that queries this grid during ray marching to determine particle sampling probabilities. Inputs: Particle set \mathcal{P}, where each particle i has position \mathbf{x}i, phase \pii, and attribute values for the visualized SPH attribute A. Rendering SPH kernel function with finite support radius h. Importance grid resolution and bounds covering the spatial extent of the SPH data. Number of histogram bins N{\text{bins}} for entropy calculation. Dilation kernel width (in grid cells) and number of dilation iterations. Outputs: Importance grid storing scalar importance values pi(\mathbf{x}) for each cell. Runtime sampling probability p(\mathbf{x}) for any position \mathbf{x} during rendering. 1. Importance Grid: A 3D regular grid where each cell stores a single floating-point value representing the data importance pi(\mathbf{x}c) at the cell center \mathbf{x}c. The grid resolution is chosen to cover the bounding box of the particle set. 2. Histogram: A temporary array of size N{\text{bins}} used to compute the entropy of attribute values for particles within a local neighborhood. The precomputation determines the initial importance for each grid cell and then filters these values to account for the SPH kernel's spatial support and interface detection. 1. Initialize Grid: Create an importance grid of sufficient resolution to cover the particle domain. Initialize all cells to 0. 2. Compute Initial Importance: For each grid cell c with center \mathbf{x}c: a. Identify the set of particles \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) lying within this cell. b. If \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) is empty, set pi(\mathbf{x}c) = 0. c. If \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) contains particles with different phases (i.e., \exists i, j \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) such that \pii \neq \pij), set pi(\mathbf{x}c) = 1. d. Otherwise, if all particles in \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) have the same phase, compute the entropy of attribute A for these particles: i. Bin the attribute values of particles in \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) into a normalized histogram h(b) with N{\text{bins}} bins. ii. Compute the entropy: \mathbb{H}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A) = - \sum{b=0}^{N{\text{bins}}-1} h(b) \log2 h(b) iii. Normalize the entropy to be independent of histogram size: \overline{\mathbb{H}}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A) = \frac{2^{\mathbb{H}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A)}}{N{\text{bins}}} iv. Set pi(\mathbf{x}c) = \overline{\mathbb{H}}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A). 3. Filter with Maximum Dilation: Apply a 3D maximum dilation filter to the importance grid to propagate importance values to neighboring cells, compensating for the fact that SPH approximation at a sampling point depends on particles in neighboring cells. a. Define a dilation kernel with width equal to the number of grid cells covered by the finite support of the SPH kernel function used in rendering. b. For each cell in the grid, update its importance value to the maximum importance value found in any cell within the dilation kernel. c. Interface Detection: During dilation, if more than half of the cells in the dilation kernel do not contain any particles, the cell is expected to contain a free-surface interface. In this case, set the cell's importance pi(\mathbf{x}c) to 1. 4. Iterate Dilation: Repeat the dilation step for a user-specified number of iterations. In practice, 1 or 2 iterations are sufficient. During ray marching, for a sampling position \mathbf{x}: 1. Query the precomputed importance value pi(\mathbf{x}) from the importance grid cell containing \mathbf{x}. 2. Combine pi(\mathbf{x}) with the view-dependent transmittance factor pt(\mathbf{x}) to determine the particle sampling probability p(\mathbf{x}) according to Equation 9 of the parent article. Note: Equation 9 is not provided in the sources; the combination is typically a weighted product or sum normalized to [0,1]. A common implementation is p(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{pi(\mathbf{x}) \cdot pt(\mathbf{x})}{\max(pi(\mathbf{x}) \cdot pt(\mathbf{x}))} or similar normalization, but the exact formula depends on the parent article's definition of pt(\mathbf{x}). 3. Use p(\mathbf{x}) to stochastically select particles for the SPH approximation at \mathbf{x}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computeentropyhistogram(attributevalues, nbins): """ Computes normalized histogram and entropy for a set of attribute values. Returns normalized entropy. """ # Create histogram hist, = np.histogram(attributevalues, bins=nbins, range=(min(attributevalues), max(attributevalues))) # Normalize histogram hist = hist / np.sum(hist) # Compute entropy # Handle log(0) by ignoring bins with 0 probability entropy = -np.sum(hist[hist > 0] np.log2(hist[hist > 0])) # Normalize entropy normalizedentropy = (2 entropy) / nbins return normalizedentropy def precomputeimportancegrid(particles, gridresolution, gridbounds, nbins, kernelsupportcells, dilationiterations): """ Precomputes the importance grid for SPH attribute entropy sampling. Args: particles: List of particle objects with attributes: pos (x,y,z), phase, attrvalue gridresolution: Tuple (nx, ny, nz) for grid dimensions gridbounds: Tuple ((minx, maxx), (miny, maxy), (minz, maxz)) nbins: Number of histogram bins for entropy calculation kernelsupportcells: Number of grid cells covered by SPH kernel support dilationiterations: Number of dilation passes Returns: importancegrid: 3D numpy array of importance values """ nx, ny, nz = gridresolution importancegrid = np.zeros((nx, ny, nz)) # Map particles to grid cells # Assume particles have a method or attribute to determine their grid cell index # For simplicity, we assume a helper function getcellindex exists cellparticles = {} # Key: (i,j,k), Value: list of particles for p in particles: i, j, k = getcellindex(p.pos, gridbounds, gridresolution) if (i, j, k) not in cellparticles: cellparticles[(i, j, k)] = [] cellparticles[(i, j, k)].append(p) # Step 2: Compute initial importance for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): if (i, j, k) in cellparticles: cellplist = cellparticles[(i, j, k)] phases = [p.phase for p in cellplist] if len(cellplist) == 0: importancegrid[i, j, k] = 0 elif len(set(phases)) > 1: importancegrid[i, j, k] = 1.0 else: attrvalues = [p.attrvalue for p in cellplist] importancegrid[i, j, k] = computeentropyhistogram(attrvalues, nbins) else: importancegrid[i, j, k] = 0 # Step 3 & 4: Filter with Maximum Dilation # Define kernel size kernelsize = kernelsupportcells halfkernel = kernelsize // 2 for iteration in range(dilationiterations): newgrid = np.copy(importancegrid) for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): # Define kernel bounds imin = max(0, i - halfkernel) imax = min(nx - 1, i + halfkernel) jmin = max(0, j - halfkernel) jmax = min(ny - 1, j + halfkernel) kmin = max(0, k - halfkernel) kmax = min(nz - 1, k + halfkernel) # Check for interface: count empty cells in kernel emptycount = 0 maximportance = 0.0 for ii in range(imin, imax + 1): for jj in range(jmin, jmax + 1): for kk in range(kmin, kmax + 1): if importancegrid[ii, jj, kk] == 0: emptycount += 1 else: maximportance = max(maximportance, importancegrid[ii, jj, kk]) totalcells = (imax - imin + 1) (jmax - jmin + 1) (kmax - kmin + 1) # Interface detection if emptycount > totalcells / 2: newgrid[i, j, k] = 1.0 else: newgrid[i, j, k] = maximportance importancegrid = newgrid return importancegrid def getcellindex(pos, gridbounds, gridresolution): """ Helper function to map a 3D position to a grid cell index. """ x, y, z = pos (minx, maxx), (miny, maxy), (minz, maxz) = gridbounds nx, ny, nz = gridresolution dx = (maxx - minx) / nx dy = (maxy - miny) / ny dz = (maxz - minz) / nz i = int((x - minx) / dx) j = int((y - miny) / dy) k = int((z - minz) / dz) # Clamp to grid bounds i = max(0, min(nx - 1, i)) j = max(0, min(ny - 1, j)) k = max(0, min(nz - 1, k)) return (i, j, k) N{\text{bins}}: Number of histogram bins for entropy calculation. Not given in the sources. A typical value might be 256 or 512, depending on the attribute range and desired precision. Dilation kernel width: Equal to the number of grid cells covered by the finite support of the SPH kernel function used in rendering. Dilation iterations: User-specified number of iterations for the filtering process; 1 or 2 iterations are sufficient in practice. Phase Interface Discontinuity: The approximation of phases is discontinuous, leading to edge cases where false distinct phases may be assigned to a sampling point, causing poor surface shading due to high-frequency specular highlights and high opacities. Subsampling Errors at Interfaces: Regions with different phases contain phase interfaces provoking surface shading; small SPH subsampling errors lead to poor surface shading due to dependency on normals and high opacities. Empty Cells: Cells with no particles are assigned importance 0, which is handled correctly by the interface detection logic during dilation. Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling reduces overall sampling error in SPH rendering by selecting well-distributed particle subsets within an acceleration structure's cells. It differs from naive random discarding by enforcing a structured selection process based on cell and position importance, ensuring that the statistical properties of the particle neighborhood are preserved more accurately during ray marching. Time Complexity: Precomputation is O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of particles and K is the number of grid cells, plus O(K \cdot W^3 \cdot I) for the dilation, where W is the kernel width in cells and I is the number of iterations. Runtime sampling is O(1) per sampling point for grid query, plus the cost of stochastic particle selection. Memory Complexity: O(K) for the importance grid, where K is the number of grid cells. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of particles and grid resolution. Higher grid resolution increases memory and precomputation time but may improve accuracy. Strengths: Reduces sampling errors at phase interfaces and regions with high attribute variation. Precomputation allows for efficient runtime sampling. Limitations: Requires precomputation step. Accuracy depends on grid resolution and kernel support estimation. When to Use: When rendering SPH data with multiple phases or significant attribute variation, and when surface shading quality is critical. When Not to Use: When rendering simple, single-phase SPH data with uniform attributes, or when precomputation time is prohibitive. The method was introduced in the paper "Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data". It addresses the challenges of rendering SPH data with multiple phases, where traditional uniform sampling can lead to artifacts at phase boundaries. The use of entropy to measure attribute variation is based on information theory [Sha48], and the normalization of entropy follows Wei et al. [WDS18]. Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi‐Phase SPH Data, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14121, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling
head: Stratification of particle samples
body: Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling reduces overall sampling error in SPH rendering by selecting well-distributed particle subsets within an acceleration structure's cells. It differs from naive random discarding by enforcing a structured selection process based on cell and position importance, ensuring that the statistical properties of the particle neighborhood are preserved more accurately during ray marching. Inputs: Particle set \mathcal{P} organized in a uniform grid acceleration structure. Data importance grid pi(\mathbf{x}c), precomputed for each cell center \mathbf{x}c. Sampling position \mathbf{x} within the volume. Probability bounds p{\min} and p{\max}. Outputs: A subset of particles chosen from the relevant acceleration structure cells to evaluate the SPH approximation at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: Uniform Grid Acceleration Structure: Stores particles. Cells are aligned with the data importance grid. Data Importance Grid: Stores scalar importance values pi(\mathbf{x}c) for each cell center. Alignment Constraint: The acceleration structure and the data importance grid must have equal cell sizes and overlap perfectly, sharing the same center point \mathbf{x}c for any overlapping cells. Parameters: p{\min}: Minimum sampling probability bound. p{\max}: Maximum sampling probability bound. Grid Resolution: Determines cell size. Optimal cell width for efficient particle access is equal to the kernel function support. Finer grids increase the stratification factor but may decrease performance. Algorithm: 1. Identify all cells in the acceleration structure that contribute to the SPH approximation at the current sampling position \mathbf{x}. Let \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}) be the set of these cells. 2. For each cell \mathbf{x}c \in \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}): a. Retrieve the particle count in the cell: Nc = |\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)|. b. Retrieve the cell importance: pi(\mathbf{x}c). c. Compute the position importance pi(\mathbf{x}) based on the sampling location relative to the particle distribution or phase. d. Calculate the target number of particles n using the formula: n = p{\min} + (p{\max} - p{\min}) pi(\mathbf{x}c) pi(\mathbf{x}) Nc e. Determine the integer number of particles to select: n{int} = \lfloor n \rfloor. f. Select n{int} particles from \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c). g. Select one additional particle with probability p{rem} = n - n{int}. 3. Aggregate the selected particles from all cells in \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}) to perform the SPH approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stratifiedstochasticsampling(particlesgrid, importancegrid, x, pmin, pmax): """ Selects particles for SPH approximation at position x using stratification. Args: particlesgrid: Uniform grid mapping cell centers to lists of particles. importancegrid: Uniform grid mapping cell centers to importance values pi(xc). x: Sampling position vector. pmin: Minimum probability bound. pmax: Maximum probability bound. Returns: List of selected particles. """ selectedparticles = [] # 1. Identify contributing cells for SPH approximation at x # Note: The specific SPH kernel support determines which cells are accessed. # This function assumes a helper getcontributingcells exists which returns # the centers of cells overlapping the kernel support at x. contributingcellcenters = getcontributingcells(particlesgrid, x) # Precompute position importance pi(x) # The source does not specify the exact formula for pi(x), only that it is used. # Assuming a placeholder function for position importance calculation. positionimportance = computepositionimportance(x) for xc in contributingcellcenters: # 2a. Get particles in this cell cellparticles = particlesgrid.getparticlesatcenter(xc) Nc = len(cellparticles) if Nc == 0: continue # 2b. Get cell importance cellimportance = importancegrid.getvalueatcenter(xc) # 2c & 2d. Calculate target number n # Formula: n = pmin + (pmax - pmin) pi(xc) pi(x) |P(xc)| n = pmin + (pmax - pmin) cellimportance positionimportance Nc # 2e. Integer part nint = floor(n) # 2f. Select nint particles # Assuming a deterministic or random selection of nint particles from the list. # To ensure reproducibility in a real implementation, a seed based on x and xc # would be used. Here we simply slice or pick. if nint > 0: # Simple selection: take first nint particles. # In practice, this should be randomized or stratified within the cell. selectedparticles.extend(cellparticles[:nint]) # 2g. Probabilistic additional particle remainder = n - nint if remainder > 0: # Generate random number in [0, 1) r = random() if r < remainder: # Select one additional particle. # Which particle? Typically the next one or a random one. # We pick the next one in the list if available, else wrap or pick random. if nint < Nc: selectedparticles.append(cellparticles[nint]) else: selectedparticles.append(cellparticles[0]) # Fallback return selectedparticles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Cell Access: At each sampling position, multiple cells are accessed. The position importance pi(\mathbf{x}) remains constant across all accessed cells, but the cell importance pi(\mathbf{x}c) can differ between these cells during a single SPH approximation. Grid Alignment: The method assumes the acceleration structure and data importance grid have equal cell sizes and perfect overlap. If they do not, the center points \mathbf{x}c will not align, breaking the assumption. Performance vs. Stratification: Using a finer grid resolution increases the stratification factor but can decrease performance. The optimal cell width is equal to the kernel function support. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of contributing cells and particles per cell. The selection process is O(1) per cell if particle lists are indexed, but the overhead of managing the grid and calculating importance adds cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the uniform grid acceleration structure and the data importance grid. The importance grid is precomputed and stored. Strengths: Reduces overall sampling error by ensuring well-distributed samples in the neighborhood. It avoids the variance associated with purely random discarding of particles. Limitations: Performance can degrade if the grid resolution is too fine. It requires precomputation of importance values. When to use: When rendering SPH data with multi-phase interfaces where subsampling artifacts are prominent, particularly for surface shading and single scattering. The method is described in the context of stochastic volume rendering of multi-phase SPH data. It builds upon the concept of importance sampling using SPH attribute entropy [3626-sph-attribute-entropy-for-importance-sampling.md]. The technique was introduced to handle the high-frequency nature of surface shading and phase interfaces in SPH rendering. name: Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data
head: Coalesced Memory Access Sampling, GPU Ray Marching Implementation, OpenCL SPH Renderer
body: A direct volume rendering technique for large, unstructured smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) data that avoids intermediate grid representations by stochastically sampling a subset of particles during ray marching. It differs from standard DVR by using view-dependent and spatial-complexity-based probabilities to select particles, enabling continuous scaling from interactive previews to high-quality renders. It specifically addresses multi-phase flows by reconstructing interfaces between different fluid types (e.g., gas and liquid) using a combined volumetric and surface shading model. Inputs: SPH particle dataset: Each particle i has position \mathbf{p}i, mass mi, density \rhoi, phase ID, and other attributes (e.g., temperature, velocity). Camera parameters: Eye position, view direction, projection matrix. Rendering parameters: Number of ray march steps, kernel type (cubic spline or Epanechnikov), maximum number of particles to sample per cell, random seed/table. Transfer functions: For volumetric opacity and color. Light sources: For shading. Outputs: Rendered image: Color and opacity per pixel. 1. Particle Storage Flat array of particles. Particles are grouped by the grid cell they reside in. Each particle i stores: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. mi: Mass. \rhoi: Density. \phii: Phase ID (integer). Other attributes (e.g., temperature Ti). 2. Acceleration Structure (3D Uniform Grid) A 3D uniform grid covering the simulation domain. Each cell stores a reference (pointer/index) to a contiguous block of memory in the Particle Storage array containing all particles within that cell. This structure allows O(1) access to the list of particles in a specific spatial region. Note: The grid is used only for querying particles, not as a discrete signal for traversal. 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, generate a primary ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate along the ray for a fixed number of steps or until the ray exits the domain. a. Determine Sampling Position: Calculate the current sampling point \mathbf{x} on the ray. b. Identify Relevant Grid Cell: Find the grid cell containing \mathbf{x}. c. Stochastic Particle Sampling: i. Retrieve the list of particles in the current cell from the acceleration structure. ii. Select a subset of these particles using stochastic sampling. The probability of selecting a particle is determined by an importance measure based on view-dependent factors and spatial complexity. iii. To ensure coalesced memory access on GPUs, all threads in a work group share the same random offset, but their local work group index is added as an offset to the selection. The selected subset is always a contiguous block of particles in memory. d. SPH Evaluation: i. For each selected particle j, compute the kernel weight W(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}j) using the chosen kernel function (cubic spline or Epanechnikov). ii. Estimate the field value (e.g., density, phase indicator) at \mathbf{x} by summing contributions from selected particles: V(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{j \in \text{subset}} mj \frac{W(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}j)}{\rhoj} iii. Determine the dominant phase at \mathbf{x} based on the phase IDs of the contributing particles. iv. Compute gradients if needed for surface reconstruction. e. Shading: i. Volumetric Shading: If the ray segment is within a homogeneous phase, use pre-integrated transfer functions [EKE01] for opacity and color accumulation. Note: Pre-integration assumes fixed segment length and cannot handle phase transitions. ii. Surface Shading: If the ray segment crosses a phase interface, use a multi-material model. Apply Blinn-Phong BRDF for surface shading. iii. Single Scattering: Optionally perform stochastic single scattering to improve spatial perception of phase interfaces. f. Accumulation: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray using standard volume rendering integral equations. 3. Final Color: Output the accumulated color for the pixel. SPH Kernel Functions: Epanechnikov Kernel (support radius h): W(r) = \frac{3}{4\pi h^3} \left(1 - \frac{r^2}{h^2}\right) \quad \text{for } r \le h Cubic Spline Kernel (support radius 2h): W(r) = \frac{10}{7\pi h^3} \begin{cases} 1 - \frac{3}{2}q^2 + \frac{3}{4}q^3 & 0 \le q < 1 \\ \frac{1}{4}(2-q)^3 & 1 \le q < 2 \\ 0 & q \ge 2 \end{cases} where q = r/h. The cubic spline is smoother but has twice the support width, requiring more particle accesses. Importance Sampling Probability: The probability Pi of selecting particle i is proportional to an importance measure Ii. The exact formula for Ii is not provided in the sources, but it is derived from view-dependent factors and spatial complexity. Pre-integrated Transfer Function: For homogeneous segments, the transmittance T and color C are pre-computed in a 2D texture based on segment length L and optical depth \tau = \int \sigmat ds [EKE01]. This is not applicable to segments with phase transitions. Kernel Function: User-specified. Options: Cubic spline (smoother, wider support, more accesses) or Epanechnikov. Shading Model: Blinn-Phong BRDF for surface, Henyey-Greenstein phase function for volume. Number of Particles to Sample: Controls quality vs. performance. Higher values yield more accurate results. Random Values: Precomputed pseudo-random values are used instead of generating them on the GPU. Random Number Generation: Generating pseudo-random numbers on GPUs is difficult and slow. The method uses precomputed random values to avoid this. Phase Transitions: Pre-integrated transfer functions cannot be used for ray segments that cross phase boundaries because they assume fixed segment length and homogeneous material. Grid Usage: The uniform grid is only for particle querying. Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) or higher-order traversal methods are not applicable because the grid does not represent a discrete signal. Memory Coalescing: To ensure efficient GPU memory access, the selected subset of particles must be contiguous in memory. This is achieved by sharing a random offset across a work group and adding the local work group index. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of particles sampled per step. By sampling a subset, it reduces the complexity from O(N) per step to O(k) where k \ll N. The overall complexity is O(R \cdot S \cdot k) where R is the number of rays, S is the number of steps per ray, and k is the number of sampled particles per step. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing particles and the grid. The grid adds minimal overhead as it only stores references. Performance: Scales continuously from fast, interactive previews to high-quality rendering by adjusting the number of sampled particles. Strengths: Minimal preprocessing, no intermediate grid representation, handles large datasets, supports multi-phase flows, efficient GPU implementation with coalesced memory access. Limitations: Stochastic sampling introduces noise; requires careful tuning of the importance measure and number of samples for quality. Pre-integration is limited to homogeneous segments. When to Use: Large SPH datasets where preprocessing time and memory are constraints, and interactive or semi-interactive visualization is desired. Particularly suitable for multi-phase flows. When Not to Use: When exact, noise-free rendering is required without post-processing, or when the dataset is small enough that full particle evaluation is feasible. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data". History: It builds on previous work in SPH visualization and stochastic rendering. It addresses the computational complexity of rendering large, unstructured particle data by avoiding intermediate representations and using importance sampling. Usage: Used in scientific visualization for fluid dynamics, particularly for multi-phase flows like gas-liquid interactions. Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi‐Phase SPH Data, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14121, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Particle-Wise Higher-Order SPH Field Approximation for DVR
head: Higher-order SPH field approximation, Piecewise polynomial SPH approximation
body: This method approximates Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) scalar fields along viewing rays using piecewise polynomial functions of higher order, rather than constant or linear approximations. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering SPH data, which consists of individual particle contributions with varying spatial resolution, by approximating each particle's contribution individually and summing the results. It sets itself apart from Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering by focusing on the geometric accuracy of the field representation along rays via higher-order polynomials, and from SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling by using a deterministic polynomial approximation strategy rather than entropy-based sampling. The method comprises three passes: 1. For each particle, approximate its contribution to all relevant viewing rays. 2. For each ray, sort the contribution data assigned to it with respect to the distance from the viewer. 3. For each ray, accumulate the contributions along the ray, classify and composite the result. Inputs: SPH particle dataset: For each particle, position \chi, mass \mu, target field value \alpha, density \rho, and smoothing radius \zeta. Viewing rays: Defined by base point b and unit direction vector v, parameterized as x(t) = b + tv. Approximation parameters: Maximum polynomial degree D (order of approximation) and number K of non-trivial polynomial pieces per particle. Outputs: Composite scalar field values along each viewing ray, ready for classification and compositing. Lookup Table: A precomputed table containing localized difference coefficients for order-D approximations of the normalized particle contribution B\Lambda for many equidistant values of \Lambda. This allows quick access and generation of optimal approximations for any particle by translating and scaling. Knot Representation: A piecewise polynomial approximation of order D is encoded as a sequence of knots: (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}), \quad k = 0, 1, \dots where tk is the ray parameter (knot position) and \hat{a}{kd} are localized difference coefficients representing the change in polynomial behavior at tk. SPH Kernel Function: The cubic B-spline kernel is used: w(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi} \begin{cases} (2-r)^3 - 4(1-r)^3, & 0 \leq r < 1 \\ (2-r)^3, & 1 \leq r < 2 \\ 0, & 2 \leq r. \end{cases} where r is the normalized distance. Particle Contribution: A particle's contribution to a scalar field is expressed as: \frac{\mu\alpha}{\rho\zeta^3} w\left(\frac{\|x - \chi\|}{\zeta}\right) where \chi is particle position, \mu is mass, \alpha is target field value, \rho is density, and \zeta is smoothing radius. Normalized Particle Contribution: For a normalized particle (unit mass, density, field attribute, smoothing radius) and a line with base point b closest to particle position, the contribution is: B\Lambda(t) = w\left(\sqrt{\Lambda^2 + t^2}\right) where \Lambda is the distance between particle position and line. Specific Particle Contribution on a Ray: The contribution of a specific data particle on a ray is: \frac{\mu\alpha}{\rho\zeta^3} B\Lambda\left(\frac{t - t\chi}{\zeta}\right) where t\chi is the parameter of the point on the ray closest to the particle position and \Lambda = \frac{1}{\zeta} \|\chi - x(t\chi)\|. Polynomial Representation: A real polynomial function A of order D is represented by coefficients ad such that: A(t) = \sum{d=0}^D ad t^d The d^{th} derivative at t=0 is d! ad. Localized Coefficients: Localized coefficients ad at t are computed from standard coefficients aj as: a{d} = \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} aj t^{j-d} The function is expressed as: A(t) = \sum{d=0}^D a{d} (t - t)^d Localized Difference Coefficients: The localized difference coefficients \hat{a}{kd} satisfy: Ak(t) - A{k-1}(t) = \sum{d=0}^D \hat{a}{kd} (t - tk)^d where Ak is the polynomial on the right of tk and A{k-1} is the polynomial on the left. Coefficient Update Rule: When processing sorted knots, the localized coefficients a{kd} for piece k are updated from the previous piece k-1 using: a{kd} = \hat{a}{kd} + \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} a{(k-1)j} (tk - t{k-1})^{j-d} for d = 0, \dots, D. Optimality Criterion: Optimality is defined by minimizing the L^2 distance error: E\Lambda(S) = \|S - B\Lambda\|2 = \left( \int{\mathbb{R}} [S(t) - B\Lambda(t)]^2 dt \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} D: Maximum polynomial degree (order of approximation). K: Number of non-trivial polynomial pieces per particle. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple, Dict def computebinomial(n, k): """Compute binomial coefficient n choose k.""" if k < 0 or k > n: return 0 if k == 0 or k == n: return 1 if k > n // 2: k = n - k res = 1 for i in range(k): res = res (n - i) // (i + 1) return res def cubicbspline(r): """ Compute the cubic B-spline kernel value for normalized distance r. """ if r < 0: r = -r # Kernel is even if r < 1: return (1.0 / (4 math.pi)) ((2 - r)3 - 4 (1 - r)3) elif r < 2: return (1.0 / (4 math.pi)) (2 - r)3 else: return 0.0 def getnormalizedparticlecontribution(t, Lambda): """ Compute BLambda(t) = w(sqrt(Lambda^2 + t^2)) """ r = math.sqrt(Lambda2 + t2) return cubicbspline(r) def precomputelookuptable(D, K, Lambdavalues, numpiecesperlambda=None): """ Precompute localized difference coefficients for optimal approximations. This is a placeholder for the optimization process described in the source. The source states: "prepare a look-up table containing the localized difference coefficients of order-D approximations of BLambda for many equidistant values of Lambda." Returns: lookuptable: Dict mapping Lambda to a list of knots. Each knot is (tk, ahatk0,..., ahatkD) """ lookuptable = {} # Note: The actual optimization to find optimal piecewise polynomial S # minimizing ELambda(S) is not detailed in the provided text. # This function represents the precomputation step. for Lambda in Lambdavalues: # Placeholder: In a real implementation, an optimization algorithm # would find the knots and coefficients for S that minimize the L2 error. # Here we assume a dummy structure for the sake of completeness. # The source mentions K non-trivial pieces. # Dummy knots: In reality, these are determined by the optimization. # Let's assume we have K pieces, so K+1 knots (including boundaries). # The source says "sequence of knots (tk, ahatk0,..., ahatkD)". knots = [] # Example: Equidistant knots over the support of the kernel. # The support of BLambda is effectively [-2Lambda, 2Lambda] roughly, # but since it's normalized, the support of w is [0,2], so t in [-2, 2] for Lambda=0. # For general Lambda, the support is where sqrt(Lambda^2 + t^2) < 2, # i.e., t^2 < 4 - Lambda^2. So t in [-sqrt(4-Lambda^2), sqrt(4-Lambda^2)]. if Lambda >= 2: # No contribution lookuptable[Lambda] = [] continue supporthalfwidth = math.sqrt(4 - Lambda2) numknots = K + 1 tstep = (2 supporthalfwidth) / numknots for k in range(numknots): tk = -supporthalfwidth + k tstep # Dummy coefficients: In reality, these come from the optimization. # ahatkd represents the change in polynomial behavior at tk. # For a single particle, the first piece might have non-zero coefficients, # and subsequent pieces might be zero if the approximation is simple, # but generally, they accumulate. ahat = [0.0] (D + 1) # This is a placeholder. The source does not give the algorithm for # finding the optimal S. It only defines the error metric and the # representation format. # In a real implementation, this would involve solving a minimization # problem for the L2 norm. knots.append((tk, ahat)) lookuptable[Lambda] = knots return lookuptable def approximateparticlecontribution(particle, ray, D, K, lookuptable): """ Approximate a single particle's contribution to a ray. Args: particle: Dict with keys 'chi', 'mu', 'alpha', 'rho', 'zeta' ray: Dict with keys 'b', 'v' D: Order of approximation K: Number of non-trivial pieces lookuptable: Precomputed table of knots for normalized particles Returns: List of knots for this particle's contribution on this ray. Each knot is (tk, ak0,..., akD) where akd are the LOCALIZED coefficients for the piece starting at tk, not the difference coefficients. Wait, the source says the encoding is (tk, ahatk0,..., ahatkD). And the update rule uses ahat to compute the actual coefficients akd. So this function should return the knots in the format (tk, ahatk0,..., ahatkD). """ chi = particle['chi'] mu = particle['mu'] alpha = particle['alpha'] rho = particle['rho'] zeta = particle['zeta'] b = ray['b'] v = ray['v'] # Find tchi: parameter of the point on the ray closest to chi # x(t) = b + tv # We want to minimize ||b + tv - chi||^2 # Derivative w.r.t t: 2v. (b + tv - chi) = 0 # v. (b - chi) + t (v. v) = 0 # Since v is unit, v. v = 1 # tchi = v. (chi - b) # Vector subtraction chi - b dx = chi[0] - b[0] dy = chi[1] - b[1] dz = chi[2] - b[2] tchi = v[0]dx + v[1]dy + v[2]dz # Find Lambda: distance between particle position and line, normalized by zeta # Lambda = (1/zeta) ||chi - x(tchi)|| # x(tchi) xchiray = [b[0] + tchiv[0], b[1] + tchiv[1], b[2] + tchiv[2]] # Distance vector chi - x(tchi) distvec = [chi[0] - xchiray[0], chi[1] - xchiray[1], chi[2] - xchiray[2]] distnorm = math.sqrt(distvec[0]2 + distvec[1]2 + distvec[2]2) Lambda = distnorm / zeta # Scale factor for amplitude amplitude = (mu alpha) / (rho zeta3) # Get normalized approximation from lookup table # The lookup table stores knots for BLambda. # BLambda(t) = w(sqrt(Lambda^2 + t^2)) # The actual contribution is amplitude BLambda((t - tchi) / zeta) # The knots in the lookup table are for the variable t in BLambda(t). # Let tnorm be the parameter in the normalized space. # The actual parameter on the ray is tray. # tnorm = (tray - tchi) / zeta # tray = tchi + tnorm zeta # The knots in the lookup table are (tnormk, ahatk0,..., ahatkD) # We need to transform these to the ray parameter space. knotsray = [] # Find the closest Lambda value in the lookup table # The source says "many equidistant values of Lambda". # We assume linear interpolation or nearest neighbor. # For simplicity, we use nearest neighbor. Lambdavalues = list(lookuptable.keys()) if not Lambdavalues: return [] closestLambda = min(Lambdavalues, key=lambda L: abs(L - Lambda)) normalizedknots = lookuptable[closestLambda] for (tnormk, ahatnorm) in normalizedknots: # Transform knot position trayk = tchi + tnormk zeta # The coefficients ahat are for the polynomial in tnorm. # The polynomial is P(tnorm) = sum(ahatd (tnorm - tnormk)^d) # We want to express this in terms of tray. # tnorm - tnormk = (tray - tchi)/zeta - tnormk = (tray - (tchi + tnormkzeta))/zeta = (tray - trayk)/zeta # So P(tray) = sum(ahatd ((tray - trayk)/zeta)^d) # = sum(ahatd (1/zeta)^d (tray - trayk)^d) # The new localized difference coefficients ahatrayd are: # ahatrayd = ahatd (1/zeta)^d ahatray = [] for d in range(D + 1): ahatray.append(ahatnorm[d] (1.0 / zeta)d) # Scale the coefficients by the amplitude # The contribution is amplitude P(tray) # So the coefficients are scaled by amplitude. ahatray = [c amplitude for c in ahatray] knotsray.append((trayk, ahatray)) return knotsray def rendersphfield(particles, rays, D, K, lookuptable): """ Main rendering function. Args: particles: List of particle dicts rays: List of ray dicts D: Order of approximation K: Number of non-trivial pieces lookuptable: Precomputed table Returns: For each ray, a list of knots representing the total field approximation. """ # Pass 1: For each particle, approximate its contribution to all relevant viewing rays. # We collect all knots from all particles for each ray. rayknots = {i: [] for i in range(len(rays))} for particle in particles: for i, ray in enumerate(rays): # Check if particle is relevant to ray (e.g., within bounding box) # This is a placeholder for relevance check. knots = approximateparticlecontribution(particle, ray, D, K, lookuptable) rayknots[i].extend(knots) # Pass 2: For each ray, sort the contribution data assigned to it with respect to the distance from the viewer. # The knots are (tk, ahatk0,..., ahatkD). # Sort by tk. sortedrayknots = {} for i, knots in rayknots.items(): # Sort by the first element of the tuple, tk sortedknots = sorted(knots, key=lambda k: k[0]) sortedrayknots[i] = sortedknots # Pass 3: For each ray, accumulate the contributions along the ray, classify and composite the result. results = {} for i, knots in sortedrayknots.items(): if not knots: results[i] = 0.0 # Or some default value continue # Accumulate contributions # The knots are encoded as localized difference coefficients. # We need to compute the actual coefficients akd for each piece. # Initialize previous coefficients to zero preva = [0.0] (D + 1) prevt = None # We need to evaluate the field at specific points along the ray for compositing. # The source mentions "accumulate the contributions along the ray, classify and composite". # This typically involves stepping along the ray and evaluating the polynomial. # Let's assume we want to evaluate the field at the knot positions. # Or more generally, we integrate/composite. # For simplicity, let's compute the field value at each knot position. # The field value at t is given by the polynomial Ak(t) for the piece k containing t. # However, the knots are the boundaries. # Piece k is defined on [tk, t{k+1}]. # The coefficients akd are for the polynomial at tk. # To evaluate at a point t in [tk, t{k+1}], we use: # A(t) = sum(akd (t - tk)^d) # But we need to update akd from a{k-1}d. fieldvalues = [] for k, (tk, ahatk) in enumerate(knots): # Update coefficients # akd = ahatkd + sum{j=d}^D binom(j,d) a{(k-1)j} (tk - t{k-1})^{j-d} curra = [0.0] (D + 1) for d in range(D + 1): sumterm = 0.0 for j in range(d, D + 1): # binom(j, d) binomval = computebinomial(j, d) # (tk - t{k-1})^{j-d} if prevt is not None: deltat = tk - prevt powerterm = deltat(j - d) else: # First piece, prevt is None, so deltat is effectively 0? # Or rather, the previous polynomial is 0. # If prevt is None, it means we are at the first knot. # The previous polynomial is 0, so a{(k-1)j} = 0. powerterm = 0 # Since a{(k-1)j} is 0 sumterm += binomval preva[j] powerterm curra[d] = ahatk[d] + sumterm # Evaluate the polynomial at tk # A(tk) = sum(akd (tk - tk)^d) = ak0 (0)^0 +... = ak0 # Since (tk - tk)^0 = 1 and (tk - tk)^d = 0 for d > 0. valueattk = curra[0] fieldvalues.append((tk, valueattk)) # Update previous preva = curra prevt = tk # Composite the result # This step depends on the specific compositing algorithm (e.g., ray marching). # The source does not specify the compositing details beyond "accumulate... classify and composite". # Typically, this involves integrating the field values along the ray and applying transfer functions. # For the purpose of this article, we return the field values at the knots. results[i] = fieldvalues return results Continuity and Compact Support: The approximation candidates must be continuous, even functions with compact support. This is required because the target function B\Lambda also has these properties. Precision: The update rule for coefficients involves powers of (tk - t{k-1}). For very small intervals, precision issues may arise. Boundary Conditions: The first piece of the polynomial approximation has no previous piece, so the update rule simplifies to a{kd} = \hat{a}{kd} if we assume the previous polynomial is zero. Time Complexity: The summation of piecewise polynomials reduces to a sorting task. The update rule for coefficients has constant complexity per piece, irrespective of the number of particles contributing. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of particles, rays, and the size of the lookup table. The lookup table size depends on the number of equidistant \Lambda values and the number of knots per approximation. Strengths: Higher-order approximation provides better accuracy than linear or constant approximations. The encoding allows efficient summation via sorting. Limitations: Requires precomputation of the lookup table. The optimization problem for finding optimal approximations is non-trivial. When to use: When high accuracy is required for SPH data rendering and the computational cost of higher-order approximation is acceptable. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and lower-order approximations are sufficient. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) was introduced by Gingold and Monaghan (1977) and independently by Lucy (1977). The method for approximating SPH scalar fields along viewing rays with piecewise polynomial functions of higher order was presented in the source. name: Ray Casting with Jittered Sampling
head: Jittered Sampling Volume Rendering
body: Ray Casting with Jittered Sampling is a direct volume rendering technique that casts rays through a 3D voxel grid to accumulate color and opacity, using jittered sampling offsets to reduce aliasing artifacts. It distinguishes itself from uniform ray sampling by perturbing sample positions to break up regular grid patterns, and from stochastic methods by using a deterministic, pre-computed jitter texture rather than runtime random number generation. Inputs: 3D Voxel Data Texture: Stores voxel colors/opacities. Camera parameters: Projection matrix, ModelView matrix, Camera position. Volume parameters: Bounding box (min/max), translation, scale. Rendering parameters: Number of samples per ray, ray step size, lighting flag. Jitter Texture: 2D texture storing pre-computed jitter offsets. Outputs: Color buffer: Accumulated RGBA color per pixel. Voxel Data Texture (textureIDs[0]) Target: GLTEXTURE3D. Format: GLRGBA32F for floating-point data. GLRGBA8 for unsigned byte data. GLCOMPRESSEDRGBAS3TCDXT5EXT if uncompressed size > 1GB. Content: Voxel colors and opacities. Jitter Texture (textureIDs[1]) Target: GLTEXTURE2D. Size: 32x32 pixels. Content: 2D jitter offset vectors. Geometry Structure: Bounding box composed of 6 faces (front, back, left, right, top, bottom). Primitive: GLQUADS. Vertices: 4 vertices per face, defined by bounding box corners (x{min/max}, y{min/max}, z{min/max}). N{samples} (mnumSamples): Number of samples per ray. If voxel count is 0: N{samples} = \sqrt{dimX^2 + dimY^2 + dimZ^2} + 2. Clamped to minimum 32. JitterTexSize: Resolution of jitter texture. Fixed at 32x32. RayStepSize: Distance between samples along the ray. Formula: RayStepSize = \frac{\sqrt{3.0}}{N{samples}}. Normalizes step size relative to the diagonal of the unit cube. VolTranslation: Bounding box center. VolScale: Bounding box dimensions. VolExtentMin/Max: Bounding box min/max coordinates. 1. Coordinate Transformation Setup: Define transformation to normalize volume bounding box to a unit cube centered at the origin (or [0,1] range depending on implementation, note: source says "centered at origin" but formula implies [0,1] range after +0.5). Transform VolExtentMin, VolExtentMax, CameraPosition, and LightPosition into this local space using: coord{local} = \frac{coord{world} - VolTranslation}{VolScale} + 0.5 2. Near Plane Pass: Draw a near plane quad using a separate shader program (spCameraNearPlaneProg). Pass transformation matrices and parameters. 3. Stencil Test Setup: Enable stencil test. Set function to GLEQUAL with reference value 0. Set operation on pass to GLINCR. Purpose: Ensures only one pixel modifies the color buffer per fragment. 4. Blending Setup: Enable alpha blending. Set blend factors to GLONE and GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA. 5. Ray Casting Shader Execution: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. Sample the 3D voxel texture along the ray path. Apply jitter offsets from the 2D jitter texture to sample positions to reduce aliasing. Accumulate color and opacity along the ray. Optionally compute lighting if ComputeLighting flag is set. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupgeometry(boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax): """ Creates a bounding box geometry with 6 faces (quads).
