name: Warp-based Sampling
head: 1D Warp Marching, 2D Warp Marching, DBShuffle, SBShuffle, Warp Marching
body: Warp-based Sampling is a GPU optimization strategy for direct volume ray casting that improves texture cache performance by reorganizing thread warps to align sampling directions with the volume's memory strides. Unlike standard sampling where a warp processes a block of pixels, Warp Marching assigns a single warp to a single ray, marching through the volume in chunks equal to the warp size. This approach minimizes memory stride within the atomic scheduling unit (the warp), making it particularly effective for rendering large dynamic volumes at low resolutions where view-independent performance is critical. Inputs and Outputs Input: 3D volume texture (density field), transfer function (density to RGBA), viewing parameters (camera position, direction, projection). Output: Final pixel color (RGBA) for each frame. Data Structures Thread Organization: Threads are grouped into warps of 32 consecutive threads (CUDA atomic scheduling unit). Shared Memory: Used for intermediate color accumulation. SBShuffle (Single Buffer): Requires 9 float4 variables per warp (8 for thread-local samples + 1 for intermediate reduction result). DBShuffle (Double Buffer): Uses a double-buffering accumulation scheme to enhance GPU resource utilization. Binary Mask: Each thread maintains a single binary bit indicating if its current sample has non-zero alpha. Warp Shapes and Orientations A warp of 32 threads can be organized into three shapes: 32 \times 1, 16 \times 2, and 8 \times 4. 1D Warp Marching: Uses the 32 \times 1 shape. The warp takes 32 samples along the depth (Z) direction and 1 sample along the horizontal (X) direction. Orientation: zx. 2D Warp Marching: Uses 16 \times 2 or 8 \times 4 shapes. Orientation Naming: Major direction axis followed by minor direction axis (e.g., zx, xz). Generating Orientations: zx and xz are generated by changing the marching step (shuffling width) in the depth direction. For a warp size of 32: Marching 8 samples in depth creates zx orientation (8 depth, 4 horizontal). Marching 4 samples in depth creates xz orientation (8 horizontal, 4 depth). Standard sampling is a special case of Warp Marching with a marching step of 1 in depth, resulting in xy orientation (16 horizontal, 2 vertical for a 16 \times 16 block). Row-Major vs. Column-Major: Default is row-major. Changing thread-pixel mapping allows column-major sampling, generating the remaining three orientations. Optimal Alignment: The major sampling direction should always be aligned with the X dimension of the volume (viewing coordinate) because the X dimension has the smallest memory stride in 3D textures. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Intersection: Compute ray intersection with the volume bounding box. 2. Warp Initialization: Assign one warp to one ray. Initialize shared memory buffers. 3. Marching Loop: a. Sample: Each thread in the warp samples the volume along the ray. The step size corresponds to the warp shape dimensions. b. Transfer Function: Map density to RGBA color. c. Pre-integration (Optional): If using pre-integrated rendering, each thread takes two density values (front and back of a slab) and shuffles the sample to its neighbor using shfldown(). d. Binary Masking: Set binary bit to 1 if alpha > 0, else 0. e. Warp Voting: Use ballot() to determine if any thread in the warp has non-zero alpha. f. Skip Check: If ballot() returns 0, skip blending for this step. g. Reduction Blending: If not skipped, perform front-to-back alpha blending in a reduction manner within the warp, leveraging the associative property of blending. h. Accumulation: Copy the final reduction result to a "safe" place (shared memory or extra memory unit) and accumulate as rays march further. 4. Final Output: After marching through the volume, write the accumulated color to the frame buffer. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def warpmarchingkernel(): # 1. Determine ray parameters for this warp # In standard mapping, one warp = one ray. # In 2D mapping, one warp = multiple rays. # For simplicity, we assume 1D Warp Marching (one warp, one ray). rayorigin = getrayorigin(threadidinwarp) # All threads in warp share this raydirection = getraydirection(threadidinwarp) # 2. Initialize shared memory for accumulation # SBShuffle: 9 float4 variables sharedaccumulators = [float4(0,0,0,0)] 9 # 3. Marching loop while rayt < rayexitt: # 4. Sample and Transfer density = samplevolume(rayorigin, raydirection, rayt) color = transferfunction(density) # 5. Binary Mask hasalpha = (color.a > 0.0) # 6. Warp Voting warpstate = ballot(hasalpha) if warpstate != 0: # 7. Reduction Blending # Perform reduction to blend all valid samples in the warp # This is a parallel reduction over the 32 threads localcolor = color # Example reduction logic (simplified for 32 threads) # In practice, this involves multiple steps of shuffling and blending for offset in [16, 8, 4, 2, 1]: neighborcolor = shfldown(localcolor, offset) if hasalpha: localcolor = blendrgba(localcolor, neighborcolor) # 8. Accumulate to shared memory # Thread 0 writes the result of the reduction to shared memory if threadidinwarp == 0: sharedaccumulators[0] = localcolor # Or appropriate index based on step # 9. Sync syncthreads() # 10. Read accumulated result # The result from the previous step is now in shared memory # Blend current warp result with previous accumulated result prevaccum = sharedaccumulators[0] finalwarpcolor = blendrgba(prevaccum, localcolor) # Update shared memory for next step if threadidinwarp == 0: sharedaccumulators[0] = finalwarpcolor # 11. Advance ray rayt += stepsize # 12. Final Write if threadidinwarp == 0: writepixel(sharedaccumulators[0]) Parameters Warp Size: 32 threads. Warp Shapes: 32 \times 1 (1D), 16 \times 2 and 8 \times 4 (2D). Marching Step: Determines orientation. E.g., 8 samples depth for zx, 4 samples depth for xz. Dataset Examples: vhfhead (spacing 1:1:1), vhmbody (spacing 1:1:3). Resolution: 1024 × 1024. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Viewing Direction: Performance varies significantly with viewing direction. Standard sampling is best when facing the XY plane, but Warp Marching is superior when facing the ZY plane (up to 4x speedup). Cache Coherence: If the major sampling direction is not aligned with the volume's X dimension, texture cache hit rates drop. Pre-integration: Requires two density values per thread (front and back of slab) and specific shuffling logic (shfldown). Dynamic Warp Marching is a GPU sampling strategy for direct volume ray casting that optimizes texture cache performance by dynamically aligning the sampling direction of a thread warp with the volume's X-dimension, which has the minimum memory stride. It integrates the Warp Marching concept with a dynamic viewing-direction adjustment, overcoming the limitation of the original Dynamic approach which could only sample along horizontal or vertical directions. Performance: Warp Marching is view-independent and outperforms existing empty space skipping techniques in scenarios requiring rendering of large dynamic volumes in low resolution images. Speedup: When facing the ZY plane, Warp Marching achieves more than 4 times the speedup of the Standard method. When facing the XY plane, Standard method achieves higher frame rates, but Warp Marching is not extremely poor. DBShuffle vs SBShuffle: DBShuffle performs better than SBShuffle regardless of viewing direction for both tested datasets. Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to the number of samples per ray, but with reduced memory latency due to cache optimization. Memory complexity is low, relying on shared memory for intermediate results. Strengths: High texture cache hit rates, stable frame rates during volume exploration, effective for dynamic volumes. Limitations: May underperform Standard sampling when viewing direction aligns with the volume's natural memory stride (e.g., XY plane). Warp-based Sampling was introduced to address texture cache performance issues in GPU-based volume rendering. It builds on the concept of breaking a ray into segments and compositing them, as described by Ma et al. (1993). The method leverages warp-level GPU operations (voting and shuffling) introduced in the NVIDIA Kepler architecture. It is designed to replace the Standard sampling strategy in texture-based volume rendering algorithms. name: Dynamic Warp Marching
head: Dynamic approach
body: Dynamic Warp Marching is a GPU sampling strategy for direct volume ray casting that optimizes texture cache performance by dynamically aligning the sampling direction of a thread warp with the volume's X-dimension, which has the minimum memory stride. It integrates the Warp Marching concept with a dynamic viewing-direction adjustment, overcoming the limitation of the original Dynamic approach which could only sample along horizontal or vertical directions. Inputs: Volume data texture. Viewing direction (defined by the camera orientation relative to the volume axes). Ray origin and direction for each pixel. Outputs: Sampled voxel values along the ray path. Composited color and opacity for the pixel. Data Structures: Warp Shape: 32 \times 1. A single warp (32 threads) is responsible for one ray, with all 32 threads taking samples along the X-dimension of the volume. Thread Block Shape: Not explicitly defined for the Dynamic method in the sources, but the Static method uses 16 \times 16. The Dynamic method's warp shape is fixed at 32 \times 1. Steps: 1. Determine Viewing Direction: Identify the current viewing direction relative to the volume axes (e.g., XY, YZ, ZX, etc.). There are six unique viewing directions considered. 2. Adjust Sampling Direction: Unlike the Static method which aligns the major sampling direction with the horizontal direction of the view, the Dynamic method adjusts the major direction of the warp to always be parallel to the X-dimension of the volume. 3. Sample Along X: All 32 threads in the warp take samples along the X-dimension of the volume. This is done because the X-dimension has the minimum memory stride, ensuring best texture cache performance. 4. Integrate Warp Marching: The method integrates Warp Marching to allow sampling along any direction, overcoming the limitation of Standard sampling which only supports horizontal or vertical directions. This implies that while the warp's internal sampling is along X, the ray's path through the volume is determined by the viewing direction, and the warp's threads are mapped to cover the ray's path efficiently. Parameters: Warp shape: 32 \times 1. Block shape: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewing Direction XY or XZ: When the view is facing XY or XZ, the major warp sampling direction of the Static method is already aligned with the X-dimension of the volume. Therefore, the performance of the Static and Dynamic approaches is similar. Viewing Direction YX: The Dynamic approach is better than the Static approach when facing YX. Ray Distance/Volume Image Ratio: The performance difference between Dynamic and Static approaches is notable in datasets with larger ray distances (e.g., vhmbody) but marginal in datasets with smaller ray distances (e.g., vhfhead). This is due to different volume image ratios. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamicwarpmarching(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture): # Determine the viewing direction relative to volume axes viewingdirection = getviewingdirection(raydirection) # Adjust the sampling direction to be parallel to the X-dimension # This is the key difference from Static method samplingdirection = Vector(1, 0, 0) # X-dimension # Initialize sample position samplepos = rayorigin # Iterate through 32 samples (warp size) for i in range(32): # Sample along the X-dimension # Note: The actual ray path is determined by the viewing direction, # but the warp's threads are mapped to cover the ray's path efficiently # by sampling along X. This implies a transformation or mapping # of the ray's path to the X-dimension for cache efficiency. # The exact mapping is not detailed in the sources, but the # integration of Warp Marching allows sampling along any direction. # Get voxel value at samplepos voxelvalue = samplevolume(volumetexture, samplepos) # Composite the voxel value # (Standard volume rendering compositing step) color, opacity = composite(voxelvalue, color, opacity) # Move to next sample along the ray direction # The step size is adjusted to cover the ray path efficiently stepsize = getstepsize(raydirection, viewingdirection) samplepos = samplepos + raydirection stepsize # Check for exit condition (e.g., end of volume or sufficient opacity) if isexitcondition(samplepos, opacity): break return color, opacity Uses Standard sampling with a fixed thread block shape (16 \times 16) and aligns the major sampling direction with the horizontal direction of the view. Choose when the viewing direction is already aligned with the X-dimension (XY or XZ views) for similar performance to Dynamic. Static Warp Marching Only supports horizontal or vertical sampling directions. Choose when dynamic adjustment is not needed or when the viewing direction is fixed and favorable. Standard Sampling Performance: Significant performance improvements when the view is facing YZ, ZX, or ZY. When facing XY or XZ, performance is similar to the Static method. When facing YX, the Dynamic approach is better than the Static approach. Scaling: Performance difference is notable in datasets with larger ray distances (e.g., vhmbody) but marginal in datasets with smaller ray distances (e.g., vhfhead). Strengths: Optimizes texture cache performance by aligning sampling with the X-dimension, which has the minimum memory stride. Allows sampling along any direction by integrating Warp Marching. Limitations: Performance gain is dependent on the viewing direction and dataset characteristics (ray distance/volume image ratio). The Dynamic approach was introduced by Sugimoto et al. (2014) to adjust sampling direction according to viewing direction for best texture cache performance. The method integrates Warp Marching to overcome the limitation of the original Dynamic approach, which could only sample along horizontal or vertical directions due to the limitation of Standard sampling. name: Supersampling
head: Hardware Supersampling, Multi-sampling, Oversampling
body: Supersampling is a technique to minimize aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel and averaging the results, effectively sampling the scene at a higher spatial frequency than the displayed resolution. It sets itself apart from its siblings by uniformly increasing sample density across the pixel area (or slab depth) to combat the coarse granularity of per-pixel sampling, whereas Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution focuses on specific ray distribution patterns and [Adaptive Supersampling] (not a sibling article, but a variant discussed in sources) targets high-contrast areas. It builds on Interpolation and Sampling Techniques by defining sample points at a higher frequency than voxel spacing. Inputs: Volume dataset V with voxel spacing \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z. Camera parameters (viewpoint, projection matrix). Pixel grid dimensions W \times H. Supersampling factor k (number of samples per dimension or per pixel). Outputs: Final image buffer with color values C{pixel} for each pixel. Data Structures: Sample Pattern: A set of 2D offsets (\delta xi, \delta yi) for i=0 \dots N-1 within the pixel bounds, where N is the number of samples per pixel. Ray Buffer: Stores origin and direction for each sample ray. Accumulator: Stores the sum of color contributions for each pixel. Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulator: For each pixel (u, v), initialize the color accumulator C{sum}(u,v) = (0,0,0,0) and sample count N{samples}(u,v) = 0. 2. Generate Sample Offsets: Define N sample points within the pixel region. Common patterns include regular grids or jittered distributions. Let the offsets be (\delta xi, \delta yi) relative to the pixel center. 3. Cast Rays: For each pixel (u, v): a. For each sample index i from 0 to N-1: i. Calculate the sample position in screen space: xs = u + \delta xi, ys = v + \delta yi. ii. Construct the ray origin O and direction D based on the camera projection and the sample position (xs, ys). iii. Perform volume ray casting along the ray to compute the color contribution Ci. This involves integrating opacity and color along the ray using interpolation. 4. Accumulate: Add the contribution to the pixel's accumulator: C{sum}(u,v) \leftarrow C{sum}(u,v) + Ci. Increment N{samples}(u,v) \leftarrow N{samples}(u,v) + 1. 5. Average: For each pixel (u, v), compute the final color: C{pixel}(u,v) = \frac{C{sum}(u,v)}{N{samples}(u,v)}. Parameters: Samples per pixel: A common value is 5 samples per pixel (e.g., 4 corners + 1 center). Supersampling factor k: In hardware implementations (e.g., VolumePro), the maximum supersampling factor in the z-direction is 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing from Regular Spacing: Regular spacing where the distance between sample points in the x- and y-directions is uniform can result in aliasing artifacts; uniform distribution is desired. Hardware Limitations: Hardware supersampling is often supported only in the z-direction (interpolating slices), while x-y supersampling requires software-based multi-pass rendering. Performance Stall: In hardware pipelines, voxel memory stages must stall to wait for additional supersampled slices to clear, reducing rendering rate. High Contrast Artifacts: Aliasing is most notable along silhouette edges where there are abrupt changes in intensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def supersamplevolumerendering(volume, camera, width, height, samplesperpixel): """ Renders a volume using supersampling. Args: volume: 3D array of voxel values. camera: Object with methods to generate ray from screen coordinates. width: Image width in pixels. height: Image height in pixels. samplesperpixel: Integer, number of samples per pixel (N). Returns: image: 2D array of color values (RGBA). """ # Initialize output image and accumulator image = np.zeros((height, width, 4)) accumulator = np.zeros((height, width, 4)) count = np.zeros((height, width)) # Define sample offsets within a pixel (e.g., jittered or grid) # For simplicity, assume a function getsampleoffsets returns N (dx, dy) pairs # normalized to [-0.5, 0.5] relative to pixel center offsets = getsampleoffsets(samplesperpixel) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): pixelsum = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) pixelcount = 0 for dx, dy in offsets: # Calculate sample position in screen space # Pixel center is at (x + 0.5, y + 0.5) samplex = x + 0.5 + dx sampley = y + 0.5 + dy # Generate ray from camera rayorigin, raydirection = camera.generateray(samplex, sampley) # Cast ray through volume to get color contribution # This function handles ray marching, interpolation, and compositing color = castraythroughvolume(volume, rayorigin, raydirection) pixelsum += color pixelcount += 1 # Average the results if pixelcount > 0: image[y, x] = pixelsum / pixelcount else: image[y, x] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return image def getsampleoffsets(n): """ Generates n sample offsets within a unit square centered at (0,0). Uses a simple grid pattern for demonstration. """ if n == 1: return [(0.0, 0.0)] # Determine grid dimensions to approximate n samples # e.g., for n=5, use a 2x2 grid with center, or specific pattern # Here we use a simple jittered grid approach for general n # Note: Specific patterns like Hammersley or Multi-Jittered are preferred # to avoid aliasing, but this is a basic implementation. # For n=5, a common pattern is 4 corners + 1 center if n == 5: return [ (-0.25, -0.25), (0.25, -0.25), (-0.25, 0.25), (0.25, 0.25), (0.0, 0.0) ] # Fallback for other n: uniform grid cols = int(np.ceil(np.sqrt(n))) rows = int(np.ceil(n / cols)) offsets = [] for i in range(rows): for j in range(cols): if len(offsets) >= n: break dx = (j + 0.5) / cols - 0.5 dy = (i + 0.5) / rows - 0.5 offsets.append((dx, dy)) if len(offsets) >= n: break return offsets def castraythroughvolume(volume, origin, direction): """ Casts a single ray through the volume and returns the accumulated color. This is a placeholder for the actual ray marching algorithm. """ # Implementation details depend on the specific ray casting method # (e.g., Interpolation and Sampling Techniques) # For the purpose of this article, we assume this function returns # the final color for the ray. return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) # Placeholder A technique to mitigate interpolation artifacts in sliced-based volume rendering by adjusting the super-sampling level per slab based on its distance to the viewpoint. It assigns a higher super-sampling level to slabs located closer to the viewpoint and a lower level to slabs farther away. This balances image quality and rendering speed, unlike uniform super-sampling (e.g., VolumePro) which causes performance degradation across all slabs. A hardware-accelerated technique to reduce aliasing artifacts by increasing the number of sample slices per volume in the z-direction, interpolating additional sample slices between existing voxel slices. It performs several interpolations from the same pair of adjacent voxel slices before moving to the next slice pair. The maximum supersampling factor in z is typically eight. A pitfall is that voxel memory stages must stall, reducing the rendering rate (e.g., to 30 fps for a 256^3 dataset with factor k). A software-based technique to achieve supersampling in x and y directions by rendering the volume multiple times with sub-pixel offsets and blending the results. It renders the volume several times with slightly different sub-pixel accurate initial offsets of the base plane in the x and y dimensions, then blends the resulting images in software. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R \cdot V), where N is the number of samples per pixel, R is the number of rays (pixels), and V is the number of volume samples per ray. Supersampling increases the cost by a factor of N (or N^2 if 2D supersampling is used per pixel). Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot N) for storing intermediate accumulators if not done in-place, or O(W \cdot H) if accumulated per pixel sequentially. Measured Performance: In the VolumePro hardware, supersampling by a factor of k reduces the rendering rate of a 256^3 dataset to 30 frames per second due to pipeline stalls. Strengths: Significantly improves image quality by minimizing aliasing effects, especially along silhouette edges. Limitations: High computational cost; regular spacing can cause aliasing if not carefully designed; hardware support is often limited to the z-direction. When to use: When high visual quality is required and computational resources allow; particularly useful for static scenes or pre-rendered content. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and aliasing is acceptable or can be handled by other means (e.g., Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution). Supersampling originated as a general computer graphics technique to combat aliasing caused by coarse sampling. In volume rendering, it was adopted to improve the quality of ray-casted images by defining sample points at a higher spatial frequency than voxel spacing. The VolumePro system (1999) implemented hardware-accelerated supersampling in the z-direction, interpolating additional slices. Adaptive approaches using convolution to target high-contrast areas were also explored. Differential supersampling was later proposed to optimize performance in sliced-based rendering by varying the sampling level per slab. name: Epipolar Sampling
head: Epipolar Line Sampling, Cross-View Epipolar Aggregation
body: Epipolar Sampling is a technique to sample features from other views along epipolar lines for a given ray, enabling cross-view feature aggregation without full 3D volume rendering during the encoding phase. It differs from standard volume rendering by operating in 2D image space using epipolar geometry to align features from source views to a target view, rather than integrating density along 3D rays in world space. Inputs: Source view images and their camera parameters (intrinsics K, extrinsics W{cam}). Target view ray origins and directions (or pixel coordinates to generate them). Number of samples per epipolar line segment, s (Typical value: 64). Outputs: Sampled features from other views. Validity masks for the samples. Data Structures: The method produces tensors with the following layout: features: Float[Tensor, 'batch view otherview ray sample channel'] valid: Bool[Tensor, 'batch view otherview ray'] xyray: Float[Tensor, 'batch view ray 2'] xysample: Float[Tensor, 'batch view otherview ray sample 2'] xysamplenear: Float[Tensor, 'batch view otherview ray sample 2'] xysamplefar: Float[Tensor, 'batch view otherview ray sample 2'] origins: Float[Tensor, 'batch view ray 3'] directions: Float[Tensor, 'batch view ray 3'] Steps: 1. Generate Image Rays: For each pixel in the source view, generate world-space ray origins and directions. This is done by sampling an image grid and transforming pixel coordinates to world rays using intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. Let N be the number of rays (pixels) and V be the number of views. Compute origins and directions for all rays in the current view. 2. Project Rays to Other Views: Project the generated rays onto all other target views using their camera parameters (extrinsics, intrinsics, near, and far planes). For each target view v', compute the intersection of the ray with the image plane. Determine the bounding box of the projected ray segment in the target view's image coordinates: xy{min} and xy{max}. Compute an overlap mask overlapsimage indicating which rays actually intersect the target view's image bounds. 3. Clamp and Mask: Clamp xy{min} and xy{max} to zero for any infinite values resulting from parallel rays or projection artifacts. Apply the overlapsimage mask to filter out invalid projections. 4. Compute Sample Depths: Generate s sample depths linearly spaced between 0 and 1 along the epipolar line segment. Formula: di = \frac{i + 0.5}{s}, \quad i = 0, \dots, s-1 In code: sampledepth = (torch.arange(s) + 0.5) / s. 5. Interpolate Sample Coordinates: Interpolate the 2D coordinates in the target view for each sample depth. Formula: xy{sample} = xy{min} + di \cdot (xy{max} - xy{min}) This yields xysamplenear and xysamplefar if near/far clipping is applied, or simply the interpolated points along the line segment. 6. Handle View Exclusion: Transpose the sample coordinates so the 'view' dimension refers to the target view from which samples are drawn. Exclude the diagonal (self-view) using precomputed indices to avoid sampling from the source view itself. 7. Sample Features: Sample image features at the computed xysample coordinates using bilinear interpolation (gridsample in PyTorch) with zero padding for out-of-bounds coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def epipolarsampling(origins, directions, intrinsics, extrinsics, numsamples=64): """ origins: [B, V, R, 3] - Ray origins in world space directions: [B, V, R, 3] - Ray directions in world space intrinsics: [B, V, 3, 3] - Camera intrinsics extrinsics: [B, V, 4, 4] - Camera extrinsics (OpenCV-style: camera-to-world) numsamples: int - Number of samples per epipolar line """ B, V, R, = origins.shape device = origins.device # Step 1: Generate rays (already provided as input in this simplified signature) # In practice, these are derived from pixel coordinates and camera params # Step 2: Project rays to other views # We need to project each ray from view v to all other views v' # This involves transforming ray origins and directions to the target view's coordinate system xyminlist = [] xymaxlist = [] overlapslist = [] for vprime in range(V): if vprime == v: # Skip self-view for aggregation, but keep structure continue # Get target view camera params Kprime = intrinsics[:, vprime,:,:] # [B, 3, 3] Wc2wprime = extrinsics[:, vprime,:,:] # [B, 4, 4] Ww2cprime = torch.inverse(Wc2wprime) # [B, 4, 4] # Transform ray origins and directions to target view # origins: [B, V, R, 3] -> [B, V, R, 4] (homogeneous) originsh = torch.cat([origins, torch.oneslike(origins[...,:1])], dim=-1) # [B, V, R, 4] directionsh = torch.cat([directions, torch.zeroslike(directions[...,:1])], dim=-1) # [B, V, R, 4] originsw2c = (Ww2cprime.unsqueeze(1) @ originsh.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # [B, V, R, 4] directionsw2c = (Ww2cprime.unsqueeze(1) @ directionsh.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # [B, V, R, 4] originst = originsw2c[...,:3] # [B, V, R, 3] directionst = directionsw2c[...,:3] # [B, V, R, 3] # Project to 2D image coordinates # x = K (origin + t direction) # We need to find the range of t that intersects the image plane (z=1 in camera coords) # t = (1 - originz) / directionz # Avoid division by zero eps = 1e-8 tvals = (1.0 - originst[..., 2:3]) / (directionst[..., 2:3] + eps) # [B, V, R, 1] # 2D coordinates in target view xyproj = (Kprime.unsqueeze(1) @ (originst + tvals directionst).unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # [B, V, R, 3] xy2d = xyproj[...,:2] / (xyproj[..., 2:3] + eps) # [B, V, R, 2] # Compute min and max xy over the ray segment (if near/far planes are defined, use them) # For simplicity, assume full ray or use min/max of projected points # In pixelSplat, this is handled by projectrays which returns xymin, xymax, overlapsimage # Here we approximate: xymin = torch.min(xy2d, dim=-2, keepdim=True)[0] # [B, V, 1, 2] -> broadcast to [B, V, R, 2] xymax = torch.max(xy2d, dim=-2, keepdim=True)[0] # [B, V, 1, 2] -> broadcast to [B, V, R, 2] # Check if ray overlaps image (simplified) # Real implementation uses near/far planes and bounding box checks overlaps = torch.oneslike(xymin[..., 0]) # [B, V, R] xyminlist.append(xymin) xymaxlist.append(xymax) overlapslist.append(overlaps) # Stack results for all target views # Note: The actual implementation handles the 'otherview' dimension explicitly # This pseudocode is a simplified representation of the vectorized logic # Step 3: Clamp and Mask # Clamp infinite values to 0 xymin = torch.where(torch.isinf(xymin), torch.zeroslike(xymin), xymin) xymax = torch.where(torch.isinf(xymax), torch.zeroslike(xymax), xymax) # Step 4: Compute sample depths sampledepth = (torch.arange(numsamples, device=device) + 0.5) / numsamples # [s] # Step 5: Interpolate sample coordinates # xysample = xymin + sampledepth (xymax - xymin) # This needs to be broadcasted correctly # xymin: [B, V, R, 2], xymax: [B, V, R, 2], sampledepth: [s] # Result: [B, V, R, s, 2] # Step 6: Handle view exclusion and transpose # Exclude self-view and transpose so 'view' dim refers to target view # Step 7: Sample features # Use gridsample with zero padding # xysample needs to be normalized to [-1, 1] for gridsample # features = F.gridsample(image, xysamplenormalized, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') return features, valid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Values: Rays parallel to the image plane result in infinite t values. These must be clamped to zero or masked out. Out-of-Bounds: Samples falling outside the target image bounds must be handled by zero-padding in gridsample. Self-View: The diagonal (sampling from the source view itself) must be excluded to prevent identity mapping artifacts. Time Complexity: O(V^2 \cdot R \cdot s), where V is the number of views, R is the number of rays (pixels), and s is the number of samples per epipolar line. Memory Complexity: O(V^2 \cdot R \cdot s \cdot C), where C is the feature channel size. Strengths: Efficient cross-view feature aggregation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Leverages epipolar geometry for precise alignment. Limitations: Requires accurate camera parameters. Performance degrades with large baseline differences or inaccurate extrinsics. When to use: Sparse-view novel view synthesis, multi-view feature encoding. When not to use: Dense volume rendering with complex lighting, scenes with significant parallax errors. Epipolar sampling is a core component of the pixelSplat architecture, introduced by Charatan et al. in 2023. It enables scalable generalizable 3D reconstruction by aggregating features from multiple views along epipolar lines, avoiding the need for explicit 3D volume rendering during the encoding phase. The method builds on earlier work in multi-view stereo and neural rendering, adapting epipolar constraints for deep learning-based feature aggregation. dcharatan/pixelsplat, https://github.com/dcharatan/pixelsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Exponential Approximation Method
head: EAMGenerate, EAMRender, EAMRenderer, Exponential Attenuation Model
body: The Exponential Approximation Method (EAM) is a direct volume ray casting technique that approximates the continuous integral of light attenuation and emission along a ray using discrete steps and an exponential transmittance model. It differs from standard linear alpha compositing by scaling the sampled alpha values by a step-size-dependent correction factor, allowing for larger step sizes while maintaining visual fidelity to the exponential decay of light. It is typically chosen when performance is prioritized over exact physical accuracy, or when the volume data is sparse enough that early ray termination (stopping when accumulated alpha exceeds 0.99) provides significant speedup. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume texture (scalar density field), a transfer function (mapping density to color and opacity), camera parameters (origin, direction, near/far planes or volume bounds), and rendering parameters (step size, extinction coefficient, offset). Output: A 2D image pixel (RGBA color). Data Structures Volume Texture: A 3D texture object storing scalar density values. Typically sampled using linear interpolation. The specific format (e.g., R8, R16F, R32F) depends on the implementation but must support red-channel sampling. Transfer Function: A 1D or 2D texture mapping density values to RGBA color. Typically sampled at vec2(val, 0.5) or similar fixed coordinate. Ray Parameters: vRayFrom, vRayTo: Unprojected ray endpoints in volume space. tbounds: Intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] of the ray with the unit cube (or volume bounds). uStepSize: Normalized step size in the range [0, 1] representing the fraction of the total ray length per step. uAlphaCorrection / uExtinction: Correction factor applied to alpha. In, this is uAlphaCorrection. In, this is uExtinction. They serve the same purpose: scaling the sampled alpha to approximate exponential attenuation over the step. uOffset: Initial offset for the first sample, typically uStepSize uOffset or just uStepSize. Numbered Steps 1. Unproject and Intersect: Unproject the screen coordinate to obtain the ray origin and direction in world/volume space. Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box (often treated as a unit cube or normalized space). Calculate the intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}]. If no intersection is found (t{min} \ge t{max}), output black (or transparent). 2. Initialize Ray Segment: Compute the start and end points of the ray segment within the volume: \text{from} = \text{mix}(vRayFrom, vRayTo, t{min}) \text{to} = \text{mix}(vRayFrom, vRayTo, t{max}) Compute the physical length of the ray segment: L = \text{distance}(\text{from}, \text{to}) Compute the step length in world units: \text{rayStepLength} = L \times uStepSize Initialize the accumulator color acc to (0, 0, 0, 0). Initialize the normalized progress parameter t. In, t starts at 0.0. In, t starts at uStepSize \times uOffset. 3. Ray Marching Loop: While t < 1.0 (or t \times L < \text{segment length}) AND acc.a < 0.99: 1. Sample Position: \text{pos} = \text{mix}(\text{from}, \text{to}, t) 2. Sample Volume: \text{val} = \text{texture}(uVolume, \text{pos}).r 3. Sample Transfer Function: \text{colorSample} = \text{texture}(uTransferFunction, \text{vec2}(\text{val}, 0.5)) (Note: The second coordinate of the transfer function lookup may vary by implementation, but 0.5 is common for 1D functions mapped to 2D textures). 4. Compute Effective Alpha: \alpha = \text{colorSample}.a \times \text{rayStepLength} \times uAlphaCorrection (In, uAlphaCorrection is replaced by uExtinction). 5. Composite: \text{acc}.rgb += (1.0 - \text{acc}.a) \times \text{colorSample}.rgb \times \alpha \text{acc}.a += (1.0 - \text{acc}.a) \times \alpha 6. Increment: t = t + uStepSize 4. Post-Processing: If acc.a > 1.0 (due to numerical precision or large steps), normalize the RGB components: \text{acc}.rgb = \text{acc}.rgb / \text{acc}.a Set acc.a to 1.0. Output acc.rgb. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderexponentialapproximation(screenpos, camera, volumetexture, transferfunctiontexture, ustepsize, ualphacorrection, uoffset): # 1. Unproject and Intersect rayorigin, raydirection = unproject(screenpos, camera) # Intersect ray with volume bounds (assumed unit cube [0,1]^3 for simplicity, or explicit bounds) tmin, tmax = intersectraycube(rayorigin, raydirection) if tmin >= tmax: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 2. Initialize rayfrom = mix(camera.position, camera.position + raydirection tmin, 1.0) # Assuming raydirection is normalized and t is distance # Correction: The source uses vRayFrom/vRayTo which are likely pre-unprojected endpoints. # Let's stick to the source's mix logic with tbounds. # vRayFrom and vRayTo are the ray endpoints in volume space. # tbounds.x is tmin, tbounds.y is tmax. frompoint = mix(camera.vRayFrom, camera.vRayTo, tmin) topoint = mix(camera.vRayFrom, camera.vRayTo, tmax) raylength = distance(frompoint, topoint) raysteplength = raylength ustepsize accumulator = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = ustepsize uoffset # Using S2's initialization logic as it's more general for offset # 3. Loop while t < 1.0 and accumulator.a < 0.99: pos = mix(frompoint, topoint, t) # Sample volume val = texture(volumetexture, pos).r # Sample transfer function colorsample = texture(transferfunctiontexture, vec2(val, 0.5)) # Compute alpha alpha = colorsample.a raysteplength ualphacorrection # Composite weight = (1.0 - accumulator.a) alpha accumulator.rgb += weight colorsample.rgb accumulator.a += weight t += ustepsize # 4. Post-process if accumulator.a > 1.0: accumulator.rgb /= accumulator.a accumulator.a = 1.0 return accumulator.rgb Parameters uStepSize: Normalized step size (0 to 1). Typical values depend on volume resolution and desired quality; smaller values yield higher accuracy but slower performance. uAlphaCorrection / uExtinction: Correction factor. In, it is uAlphaCorrection. In, it is uExtinction. This value approximates the exponential decay e^{-\sigma \Delta s} where \sigma is the extinction coefficient and \Delta s is the step size. For small steps, \alpha \approx \sigma \Delta s, so uAlphaCorrection might be set to 1.0 if the volume data is already scaled appropriately, or to the extinction coefficient if the volume data is raw density. uOffset: Initial offset for the first sample. In, it is used as t = uStepSize uOffset. A value of 1.0 means the first sample is taken at the first step position. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Over-saturation: If the step size is too large or the correction factor is too high, accumulator.a can exceed 1.0, leading to incorrect color normalization. The method explicitly checks for this and normalizes. Early Termination: Stopping when accumulator.a > 0.99 is an optimization. If the volume has very high opacity, this can save significant computation. However, if the transfer function has high opacity at low density, this might clip details. Boundary Conditions: If the ray does not intersect the volume, the method outputs black. This assumes a black background. If a different background is desired, the background color should be composited after the ray march. Precision: Using float for accumulation can lead to precision issues in very large volumes or with many steps. R32F volume textures are recommended for high dynamic range. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps per ray. N is determined by the ray length and uStepSize. Early termination reduces the average N. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the accumulator, plus the memory for the volume and transfer function textures. Performance: Generally faster than exact exponential integration because it allows larger step sizes with the correction factor. The early termination optimization (stopping at alpha 0.99) can significantly speed up rendering of opaque regions. Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient on GPUs, good visual quality for sparse volumes, easy to parallelize. Limitations: Approximation error increases with larger step sizes. Not physically accurate for dense volumes or complex scattering. The "exponential approximation" is a linearization of the exponential integral, which can lead to artifacts if not tuned correctly. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering, sparse volumes, when performance is critical. When Not to Use: When high physical accuracy is required, dense volumes with complex lighting, or when exact transmittance is needed. The Exponential Approximation Method is a practical approach to direct volume rendering, often used in real-time applications. It is based on the principle of alpha compositing with an approximation of the transmittance integral. The method is implemented in various open-source projects, such as rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting and terier/vpt. The specific implementation details (e.g., uAlphaCorrection vs uExtinction) vary between projects, but the core algorithm remains consistent. rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting, https://github.com/rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) terier/vpt, https://github.com/terier/vpt, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Front-to-Back Volume Rendering
head: Front-to-back compositing, Front-to-back additive blending, Front-to-Back Ray Casting
body: Front-to-Back Volume Rendering is a direct volume rendering technique that generates images of 3D volumetric data sets by casting rays from the camera through each pixel and accumulating optical properties (color and opacity) along the ray from the viewer to the farthest visible point. It solves the problem of visualizing semi-transparent scalar fields without extracting explicit geometric surfaces, mapping data values to optical properties via a transfer function and integrating the emission-absorption model along the viewing ray. Unlike back-to-front methods, it allows for early ray termination when the accumulated opacity reaches unity, and it naturally supports hardware alpha blending. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (volume data) stored as a uniform 3D array of voxels or a 3D texture. A camera position and direction for each pixel. A transfer function mapping scalar values to color c(x) and opacity \alpha(x). Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains an accumulated color C. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored in graphics memory as a 3D texture object or a stack of 2D texture slices. Each voxel corresponds to a location in data space with one or more data values. Accumulators: Per-pixel variables for accumulated color C (RGB) and accumulated opacity/transparency T (or \alpha). Ray Parameters: Ray origin ro, ray direction rd, entry distance t0, exit distance t1, and step size \Delta t. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, compute the ray origin ro (camera position) and normalized ray direction rd. Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box to find the entry t0 and exit t1 distances using the slab method. If t0 > t1, discard the pixel. 2. Clamping: If the ray origin is inside the volume, clamp the start distance t{start} to \max(t0, 0.0) to prevent sampling behind the eye. 3. Initialization: Initialize accumulated color C = 0 and accumulated transparency T = 1 (or accumulated opacity \alpha = 0). 4. Marching Loop: Iterate from t = t{start} to t1 with a fixed step size \Delta t. Sampling: Compute the sample position p = ro + t \cdot rd. Sample the volume at p using trilinear interpolation of the surrounding eight voxels to get the scalar value v. Transfer Function: Map v to color c and opacity \alpha{local} using the transfer function. Compositing: Update the accumulated color and transparency using the front-to-back over operator: C{new} = C + T \cdot c \cdot \alpha{local} T{new} = T \cdot (1 - \alpha{local}) Alternatively, using accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}: C{new} = C + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot c \cdot \alpha{local} \alpha{acc, new} = \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alpha{local} Early Termination: If T < \epsilon (or \alpha{acc} \ge 1 - \epsilon), break the loop. 5. Finalization: Cast the accumulated color C to the output format (e.g., unsigned char). Formulas: The discrete volume rendering equation for front-to-back compositing is: C = \sum{i} Ci Ai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - Aj) where Ci and Ai are the color and opacity assigned by the transfer function to the data value at sample i. The continuous optical model defines transparency T and light intensity L as: T(a, b) = \exp \left( - \inta^b \tau(V(s(t))) dt \right) L(a, b) = \inta^b g(V(s(t)))T(a, t)dt where \tau is the absorption coefficient and g(v) = \tau(v)C(v) is the emission coefficient. Parameters: Step Size (\Delta t or Dt): The distance between samples. A typical value is 1.0 in world units or 1/128th the size of the volume. It inversely affects accuracy and quality. Sampling Rate (s): Inversely proportional to the distance between samples l. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Origin Inside Volume: Must clamp start distance to \ge 0.0. Precision/Overflow: Clamp transparency T to 0 if it drops below 0 to prevent negative values. Clamp accumulated color C to 255 if it exceeds 255. Aliasing: Low sampling rates cause inaccurate numerical approximations of the continuous optical model. Boundary Errors: Off-by-one errors can occur in parallel implementations when calculating slice boundaries. NaN Values: Logarithmic transformations of scalar values may produce NaN if inputs are non-positive. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackvolumerendering(volumetexture, camerapos, raydir, boxmin, boxmax, stepsize, transferfunction): # 1. Intersect ray with bounding box invdir = 1.0 / raydir tmintmp = (boxmin - camerapos) invdir tmaxtmp = (boxmax - camerapos) invdir tmin = min(tmintmp, tmaxtmp) tmax = max(tmintmp, tmaxtmp) t0 = max(tmin.x, max(tmin.y, tmin.z)) t1 = min(tmax.x, min(tmax.y, tmax.z)) if t0 > t1: return vec3(0.0) # Ray misses volume # 2. Clamp start distance tstart = max(t0, 0.0) # 3. Initialize accumulators acccolor = vec3(0.0) acctransparency = 1.0 # 4. Marching loop t = tstart while t < t1 and acctransparency > 0.01: # Early termination threshold # Sample position pos = camerapos + t raydir # Sample volume (trilinear interpolation assumed in texture lookup) scalarval = texture(volumetexture, pos).r # Transfer function colorsample, alphalocal = transferfunction(scalarval) # Compositing acccolor += acctransparency colorsample alphalocal acctransparency = (1.0 - alphalocal) # Advance t += stepsize return acccolor An algorithm that merges front-to-back traversal of data with a dynamic screen data structure and rotational transformations to produce images quickly. It performs front-to-back traversal which implicitly eliminates hidden structures. It only manipulates voxels that project to the free area of the dynamic screen, utilizing object and scan-line coherence. The dynamic screen stores, for each scanline, the free (unused) runs of pixels that can make up an image. Gradient and depth shading are applied to the resulting image, storing the depth of each projected voxel with the pixel in the image buffer. Implemented by Goldwasser et al. on a special multiprocessor architecture for real-time shaded graphics display with rotation, scaling, slice planes, and shading transformations on grey-scale data. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray, which depends on the volume depth and step size. Early ray termination can significantly reduce the average number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the volume size for storing the 3D texture. Performance: Can run at 90Hz in an OpenGL shader at 512×600 resolution with a step size of 1/128th the volume size, enabling real-time stereo in VR. Strengths: Provides high-quality rendering among DVR methods; computation scheme allows exploitation of parallel computing and memory-efficient data structures. Supports hardware alpha blending. Limitations: Quality is sensitive to sampling rate; low rates cause aliasing. General volume integrals cannot be evaluated directly and require subdivision. When to Use: When high-quality visualization of semi-transparent volumes is required and real-time performance is achievable via early termination or parallelization. When Not to Use: When the volume is extremely large and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck without acceleration structures, or when exact analytical solutions are possible (e.g., hexahedral grids with tri-linear interpolation). Front-to-back volume rendering is a core technique in Direct Volume Rendering (DVR), which generates images of 3D volumetric data sets without explicitly extracting geometric surfaces. The method relies on an optical model to map data values to optical properties (color and opacity) and accumulates these properties along each viewing ray. The term "voxel" denotes an individual "volume element". The technique is widely used in medical imaging and scientific visualization. Chapter 39. name: Ray Marching Volume Rendering with Henyey-Greenstein Scattering
head: Ray Marching with Henyey-Greenstein Scattering
body: This method renders a 3D volume defined by a density texture by accumulating scattered light along a ray, utilizing the Henyey-Greenstein phase function to model anisotropic scattering and shadow rays for self-shadowing. It distinguishes itself from standard front-to-back volume rendering by explicitly incorporating directional light transport through the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, allowing for the visualization of forward or backward scattering effects in participating media. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera parameters: origin ro, direction rd (derived from camera forward/right/up vectors and fragment UV coordinates). Volume texture uvolume: 3D texture storing density in the red channel. Velocity texture uvelocity (optional): 3D texture storing velocity vectors. Parameters: uphaseG (anisotropy g), udensityCoef (density multiplier), ulightDir (light direction), ulightColor (light color), ushowVelocity (boolean flag). Constants: STEPSIZE, MAXSTEPS, SHADOWSTEPSIZE, SHADOWFACTOR. Outputs: Final fragment color col. Data Structures Volume Texture: 3D array of floats. Density is stored in the red channel (texture(...).r). If velocity visualization is enabled, the texture stores 3D velocity vectors. Ray State: ro: vec3 (Ray origin). rd: vec3 (Ray direction, normalized). t: float (Current distance along ray). transmit: float (Accumulated transmission, initial 1.0). col: vec3 (Accumulated color, initial 0.0). Numbered Steps 1. Ray Initialization: Calculate ray origin ro from camera position. Calculate ray direction rd from camera forward, right, and up vectors combined with fragment UV coordinates. Perform ray-box intersection with the volume bounding box defined by boxMin = (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5) and boxMax = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) to find entry distance t0 and exit distance t1. 2. No Intersection Check: If t0 > t1 or t1 < 0, the ray misses the volume. Output a gradient background color based on the fragment's Y coordinate and terminate. 3. Marcher Initialization: Set initial march distance t = max(t0, 0.0). Set maximum march distance tMax = t1. Initialize accumulated color col = 0.0 and transmission transmit = 1.0. Add a random noise offset to t to reduce banding artifacts: t = t + \text{fract}(\sin(\text{dot}(\text{gl\FragCoord.xy}, \text{vec2}(12.9898, 78.233))) \times 43758.5453) \times \text{STEP\SIZE} 4. Precompute Phase Value: Calculate the dot product between the view direction rd and the light direction ulightDir. Let this be \cos\theta. Compute the Henyey-Greenstein phase value P(g, \cos\theta) using the anisotropy parameter uphaseG (g) and \cos\theta (see Formula section). 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to MAXSTEPS. If t > tMax, break the loop. 6. Position and Coordinate Calculation: Calculate world position: p = ro + rd \times t. Calculate normalized texture coordinates: \text{texCoord} = p + 0.5. 7. Sampling: If texCoord is within [0, 1] for all axes: If ushowVelocity is 1: Sample velocity texture. Compute magnitude mag of the velocity vector. Set density = mag 0.1 udensityCoef. Set sampleCol = normalize(velocity) 0.5 + 0.5 (visualize velocity direction as color). Else (Standard Density): Sample volume texture: density = texture(uvolume, texCoord).r udensityCoef. Set sampleCol = 1.0 (white base color). If texCoord is out of bounds, density = 0. 8. Lighting and Accumulation: If density > 0.01: Calculate alpha for the step: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{STEP\SIZE}). If ushowVelocity is 1: Add emissive color: col += sampleCol alpha transmit. Else (Lighting): Shadow Ray: Initialize shadowDens = 0.0. Step SHADOWSTEPS times along ulightDir with step size SHADOWSTEPSIZE. In each step, check if position is within texture bounds. If so, sample density and add to shadowDens. If out of bounds, exit shadow ray loop early. Light Attenuation: Calculate light value: \text{lightVal} = \exp(-\text{shadowDens} \times \text{SHADOW\FACTOR} \times \text{u\densityCoef} \times 0.1). Incoming Light: \text{incomingLight} = \text{u\lightColor} \times \text{lightVal} \times \text{phaseVal} + \text{ambientColor}. [Note: ambientColor is not explicitly defined in the source notes but is implied by the formula structure. It is treated as a constant or uniform input.] Accumulate: col += incomingLight alpha transmit. Update Transmission: transmit = (1.0 - alpha). If transmit < 0.01, break the loop to save computation. Increment: t += STEPSIZE. 9. Background and Tone Mapping: Add background contribution: col += bg transmit, where bg is the gradient background color calculated in Step 2. Apply Reinhard tone mapping: \text{col} = \frac{\text{col}}{\text{col} + 1.0}. Apply gamma correction: \text{col} = \text{pow}(\text{col}, 0.4545). Formulas Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: P(g, \cos\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{4\pi (1 + g^2 - 2g\cos\theta)^{1.5}} Where: g is the anisotropy parameter (uphaseG). \cos\theta is the dot product of the view direction and light direction. Alpha Calculation: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{STEP\SIZE}) Light Attenuation: \text{lightVal} = \exp(-\text{shadowDens} \times \text{SHADOW\FACTOR} \times \text{u\densityCoef} \times 0.1) Parameters SHADOWSTEPSIZE: Step size for shadow ray marching. Value: 0.02. SHADOWFACTOR: Multiplier for shadow density attenuation. Value: 5.0. uphaseG: Anisotropy parameter g for Henyey-Greenstein. Range: [-0.99, 0.99]. udensityCoef: Global multiplier for sampled density values. STEPSIZE: Step size for main ray marching. Value not given in the sources. MAXSTEPS: Maximum number of march steps. Value not given in the sources. SHADOWSTEPS: Number of steps for shadow ray. Value not given in the sources. ambientColor: Ambient light color. Value not given in the sources. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Shadow Ray Bounds: Shadow ray marching must exit early if the shadow ray position goes outside the [0,1] texture coordinate space to prevent sampling invalid memory or incorrect densities. Early Termination: The main ray marching loop terminates early if transmission drops below 0.01. This is a performance optimization but may cause slight inaccuracies in deep, highly opaque volumes. Banding: Random noise offset is added to the initial t to reduce banding artifacts caused by uniform step sizes. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchhenyeygreenstein(ro, rd, uvolume, uvelocity, uphaseG, udensityCoef, ulightDir, ulightColor, ushowVelocity, bg): # Constants STEPSIZE = 0.01 # Not given in sources, assumed typical value for implementation MAXSTEPS = 100 # Not given in sources, assumed typical value SHADOWSTEPSIZE = 0.02 SHADOWFACTOR = 5.0 SHADOWSTEPS = 10 # Not given in sources, assumed typical value AMBIENTCOLOR = vec3(0.1, 0.1, 0.1) # Assumed default ambient color # 1. Ray-Box Intersection boxMin = vec3(-0.5) boxMax = vec3(0.5) t0, t1 = intersectbox(ro, rd, boxMin, boxMax) # 2. No Intersection if t0 > t1 or t1 < 0: return gradientbackground(rd.y) # 3. Initialization t = max(t0, 0.0) tMax = t1 col = vec3(0.0) transmit = 1.0 # Random offset for banding reduction noise = fract(sin(dot(glFragCoord.xy, vec2(12.9898, 78.233))) 43758.5453) t += noise STEPSIZE # 4. Precompute Phase Value costheta = dot(normalize(rd), normalize(ulightDir)) g = uphaseG phaseVal = (1.0 - gg) / (4.0 PI pow(1.0 + gg - 2.0gcostheta, 1.5)) # 5. Marching Loop for i in range(MAXSTEPS): if t > tMax: break # 6. Position p = ro + rd t texCoord = p + vec3(0.5) density = 0.0 sampleCol = vec3(0.0) # 7. Sampling if isinside(texCoord, 0.0, 1.0): if ushowVelocity: vel = sampletexture(uvelocity, texCoord) mag = length(vel) density = mag 0.1 udensityCoef sampleCol = normalize(vel) 0.5 + 0.5 else: density = sampletexture(uvolume, texCoord).r udensityCoef sampleCol = vec3(1.0) # 8. Lighting and Accumulation if density > 0.01: alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density STEPSIZE) if ushowVelocity: col += sampleCol alpha transmit else: # Shadow Ray shadowDens = 0.0 shadowPos = p + ulightDir STEPSIZE # Start shadow ray from current position for s in range(SHADOWSTEPS): shadowTex = shadowPos + vec3(0.5) if isinside(shadowTex, 0.0, 1.0): shadowDens += sampletexture(uvolume, shadowTex).r else: break # Exit early if out of bounds shadowPos += ulightDir SHADOWSTEPSIZE lightVal = exp(-shadowDens SHADOWFACTOR udensityCoef 0.1) incomingLight = ulightColor lightVal phaseVal + AMBIENTCOLOR col += incomingLight alpha transmit transmit = (1.0 - alpha) if transmit < 0.01: break t += STEPSIZE # 9. Background and Tone Mapping col += bg transmit col = col / (col + 1.0) col = pow(col, 0.4545) return col The foundational accumulation method used here. It processes samples from near to far, blending each sample into the accumulated color. Choose this when you need standard alpha blending without complex light transport. [2350-front-to-back-volume-rendering.md] Optimizes memory access by grouping rays into tiles and sampling a grid. Choose this for large volumes where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. [2586-tiled-ray-marching-with-grid-sampling.md] Uses a constant step size along the ray. Choose this for simplicity and uniform sampling, but be aware of potential aliasing in sparse regions. [3136-fixed-step-ray-marching.md] Uses Signed Distance Fields for density instead of textures. Choose this for procedural volumes or when memory bandwidth for large textures is an issue. [4484-volumetric-raymarching-with-sdf-density.md] Time Complexity: O(N \times M), where N is the number of pixels (rays) and M is the number of steps per ray (MAXSTEPS). Shadow rays add a factor of SHADOWSTEPS to the lighting calculation per step. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the size of the volume texture. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the shadow ray casting for every sample. The early termination based on transmission (transmit < 0.01) helps optimize performance in opaque regions. Strengths: Accurately models anisotropic scattering, allowing for realistic lighting effects in participating media like fog or smoke. Simple to implement on the GPU. Limitations: Shadow rays significantly increase computation time. Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or inaccurate density integration in sparse regions. When to Use: Real-time rendering of volumetric effects where anisotropic scattering is desired and performance allows for shadow ray casting. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and anisotropic scattering is not required (use standard front-to-back rendering). When the volume is extremely sparse and fixed step size leads to poor sampling. This method is derived from real-time volume rendering techniques used in fluid simulation visualizations. It combines standard ray marching with the Henyey-Greenstein phase function to model light scattering in participating media. The specific implementation details, including the random offset for banding reduction and the shadow ray formulation, are based on a GitHub repository for fluid simulation. tzhazuma/Fluidsimulation, https://github.com/tzhazuma/Fluidsimulation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Tracing (Binary Objects)
head: Binary Object Ray Tracing, Binary Ray Casting, First-hit Ray Casting for Binary Volumes, Tuy's binary ray casting
body: A direct volume rendering method for visualizing opaque surfaces contained in binary volumetric data by determining only the first intersection points with a surface. It differs from gray-level volume rendering (e.g., Front-to-Back Volume Rendering) by stopping the ray traversal immediately upon hitting the object boundary, rather than compositing transmittance and color along the entire ray path. Inputs: Binary volumetric dataset V where V(x,y,z) \in \{0, 1\}; camera parameters (viewing direction, image plane resolution); lighting model (light direction, depth shading function). Outputs: 2D image where each pixel holds the color of the first surface point hit by the viewing ray. Data Structures: Volume V: 3D array of integers. V[i,j,k] = 1 if the voxel belongs to the object, 0 otherwise. Ray: Defined by origin O (camera center or pixel center) and direction D. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel in the image plane, construct a ray R(t) = O + tD traveling from the screen toward the object (viewing point). This is the inverse of light-source-to-object tracing. 2. Sampling: Resample the volume along the viewing ray at evenly spaced sample points. The sample value at a point is determined by the nearest voxel in V. 3. Intersection Detection: Test voxels sequentially along the ray to identify the transition from exterior (0) to interior (1). 4. Termination: Find the first sample with a value of 1. Stop traversal immediately. 5. Shading: Determine the pixel color by shading the intersected surface point. Shading uses depth, light direction, and an estimate of the surface normal. Formulas: Ray Equation: R(t) = O + tD, where t > 0. Sample Value: S(t) = V(\text{nearest\voxel}(R(t))). Intersection Condition: The first t such that S(t) = 1. Normal Estimation: Not explicitly defined in sources, but described as an "unnormalized estimate of the gradient" or derived from the binary transition. In practice, the normal is often approximated by the difference between the first hit voxel and its neighbors, or by the ray direction if surface orientation is assumed perpendicular to the view. Parameters: Sampling Step: Evenly located sample points. Size not given in the sources. Shading Model: Depth shading, light direction, surface normal estimate. Edge Cases: Precision: Boundary detection does not require interpolation, avoiding interpolation artifacts. Degenerate Input: Binary data must be strictly 0 or 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytracebinaryvolume(volume, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): image = empty array of size (imageheight, imagewidth, 3) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Construct ray from pixel to viewing point rayorigin = camera.getpixelorigin(x, y) raydirection = camera.getpixeldirection(x, y) # Traverse ray from screen toward object t = 0.0 stepsize = camera.getstepsize() # Not given in sources; must be defined by implementation hit = False hitpoint = None while t < camera.maxdistance: # Sample volume at current ray position samplevalue = volume.getnearestvoxel(rayorigin + raydirection t) if samplevalue == 1: hit = True hitpoint = rayorigin + raydirection t break t += stepsize if hit: # Estimate normal at hit point normal = estimatenormal(volume, hitpoint) # Shade based on depth, light direction, and normal color = shade(hitpoint, normal, camera.lightdirection, t) image[y, x] = color else: image[y, x] = backgroundcolor return image def estimatenormal(volume, point): # Approximate normal using finite differences on binary volume # This is a standard implementation detail not explicitly in sources dx = volume.getnearestvoxel(point + vec3(1,0,0)) - volume.getnearestvoxel(point - vec3(1,0,0)) dy = volume.getnearestvoxel(point + vec3(0,1,0)) - volume.getnearestvoxel(point - vec3(0,1,0)) dz = volume.getnearestvoxel(point + vec3(0,0,1)) - volume.getnearestvoxel(point - vec3(0,0,1)) return normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) def shade(point, normal, lightdir, depth): # Simple depth and diffuse shading diffuse = max(dot(normal, normalize(lightdir)), 0.0) # Depth shading: darker further away depthfactor = 1.0 - (depth / maxdepth) return vec3(diffuse depthfactor) Same method, emphasizing the binary nature of the data. The original 1984 method by Tuy et al., characterized by screen-to-object traversal. Emphasizes the termination condition upon first intersection. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of pixels and the average distance to the first surface hit. Worst case is O(N \cdot L) where N is pixels and L is ray length in voxels. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data. No accumulation buffers needed. Strengths: No interpolation or boundary detection required; efficient for opaque objects; direct surface visualization. Limitations: Only works for binary data; no internal structure visualization; shading quality depends on normal estimation. When to use: Visualizing opaque surfaces in binary volumetric data (e.g., segmented medical masks). When not to use: Gray-level volumes, transparent objects, or when internal structure is needed. Originated in 1984 with Tuy et al.. It was proposed as a method for visualizing surfaces in binary volumetric data, distinct from cuberille methods that recover shading from binary objects. It contrasts with Levoy's 1988 raycasting algorithm for gray-level volumes, which composites along the entire ray. Used in medical data visualization for surface rendering. Volumetric rendering of medical data: applications to stereotactic neurosurgery planning, https://doi.org/10.82308/10070, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Medical Volume Rendering Techniques, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.07710v1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Discrete Ray Tracing
head: 3D DDA Voxel Traversal, Naive Voxel-Raycasting, Raycasting ohne Beschleunigungsstruktur
body: Discrete Ray Tracing is a method for rendering voxelized datasets by traversing a 3D grid along a ray using a three-dimensional form of Digital Differential Analysis (DDA). It guarantees that voxels are visited in the exact order of intersection, limiting the number of intersection tests to Pythagorean complexity rather than cubic. Unlike methods requiring acceleration structures, it samples every voxel along the ray path sequentially. Inputs: Volume data: A 3D array of scalar values (voxels). Camera parameters: Position, view port vectors (upperLeft, upperRight, lowerLeft, lowerRight), screen dimensions (width, height). Transfer function: Maps scalar values to color (r, g, b) and opacity (a). Projection type: Orthographic (ray direction fixed along Z-axis in the example implementation) or Perspective (calculated via view port normals). Outputs: Rendered image: A 2D array of pixel colors (RGB) and opacity. Data Structures: volumedata: 3D array volumedata[x, y, z]. pixelcolor: 4-element array [r, g, b, a], initialized to [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]. ray: Structure with origin (Vec3) and direction (Vec3). Steps: 1. Initialize Camera Normals: Calculate normalized view port vectors. If view port vectors depend on camera position, subtract the camera position before normalizing. \begin{aligned} \mathbf{n}{UL} &= \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v}{UL} - \mathbf{p}{cam}) \\ \mathbf{n}{UR} &= \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v}{UR} - \mathbf{p}{cam}) \\ \mathbf{n}{LL} &= \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v}{LL} - \mathbf{p}{cam}) \\ \mathbf{n}{LR} &= \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v}{LR} - \mathbf{p}{cam}) \end{aligned} 2. Calculate Interpolation Deltas: Compute inverse screen dimensions and Y-direction deltas for the left and right normals: \begin{aligned} h{inv} &= 1.0 / \text{screenHeight} \\ w{inv} &= 1.0 / \text{screenWidth} \\ \Delta \mathbf{n}{L,y} &= (\mathbf{n}{LL} - \mathbf{n}{UL}) \cdot h{inv} \\ \Delta \mathbf{n}{R,y} &= (\mathbf{n}{LR} - \mathbf{n}{UR}) \cdot h{inv} \end{aligned} 3. Initialize Ray Origin: Set the ray origin to the camera position. This remains constant for all pixels. \mathbf{r}{origin} = \mathbf{p}{cam} 4. Iterate Screen Pixels (Top-to-Bottom, Left-to-Right): Initialize interpolation variables to the top of the screen: \mathbf{n}L = \mathbf{n}{UL}, \quad \mathbf{n}R = \mathbf{n}{UR} For each row y from 0 to \text{screenHeight} - 1: a. Set ray direction to left normal: \mathbf{r}{dir} = \mathbf{n}L. b. Calculate X-direction delta: \Delta \mathbf{n}x = (\mathbf{n}R - \mathbf{n}L) \cdot w{inv} For each column x from 0 to \text{screenWidth} - 1: a. Trace Ray through Volume: i. Determine Ray Path: If using the specific orthographic implementation from, the ray direction is fixed along the Z-axis (\mathbf{r}{dir} = [0, 0, 1]) and the origin is computed as the center of the near plane: \mathbf{r}{origin} = [x / \text{width}, y / \text{height}, \text{near\plane}] If using the general perspective DDA from, the ray is defined by \mathbf{r}{origin} and \mathbf{r}{dir}. The algorithm traverses the voxel grid using 3D DDA, stepping through voxel indices in the order the ray intersects them. ii. Sample Voxel: Convert the current ray position (or specific sample point along the ray) to voxel coordinates. For the nearest-neighbor approach in: \mathbf{c}{vox} = \lfloor \mathbf{c}{world} \cdot \mathbf{D} - 0.5 \rfloor where \mathbf{D} is the volume dimensions and \lfloor \cdot \rfloor is the floor function. The -0.5 centers the sampling at (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). Sample the scalar value without interpolation (nearest-neighbor): s = \text{volume\data}[\mathbf{c}{vox}] iii. Apply Transfer Function: Map scalar s to color (r, g, b) and opacity a. A common example uses Gaussian mixtures: \begin{aligned} r &= 1.0 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s - 9.0)^2}{1.0}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s - 3.0)^2}{0.1}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s + 3.0)^2}{0.5}} \\ g &= 1.0 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s - 9.0)^2}{1.0}} + 1.0 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s - 3.0)^2}{0.1}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s + 3.0)^2}{0.5}} \\ b &= 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s - 9.0)^2}{1.0}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s - 3.0)^2}{0.1}} + 1.0 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s + 3.0)^2}{0.5}} \\ a &= 0.6 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s - 9.0)^2}{1.0}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s - 3.0)^2}{0.1}} + 0.01 \cdot e^{-\frac{(s + 3.0)^2}{0.5}} \end{aligned} iv. Composite: Update accumulated pixel color and opacity using the standard over operator (front-to-back): \begin{aligned} \mathbf{C}{out} &= \mathbf{C}{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \cdot \mathbf{C}{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \\ \alpha{out} &= \alpha{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \cdot \alpha{sample} \end{aligned} b. Increment X: \mathbf{r}{dir} \leftarrow \mathbf{r}{dir} + \Delta \mathbf{n}x c. Set Pixel: Store the final color for pixel (x, y). d. Increment Y: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{n}L &\leftarrow \mathbf{n}L + \Delta \mathbf{n}{L,y} \\ \mathbf{n}R &\leftarrow \mathbf{n}R + \Delta \mathbf{n}{R,y} \end{aligned} 5. Finalize: Clip the final color components to [0, 255] and convert to uint8. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def discreteraytracing(volumedata, camera, screenwidth, screenheight, transferfunction): """ Renders a volume using Discrete Ray Tracing (3D DDA). Implements the perspective version from with compositing from. """ # 1. Initialize Camera Normals # Assuming camera provides vectors relative to origin or absolute positions # If vectors depend on camera position, subtract camera position before normalizing upperleft = normalize(camera.getupperleftvector()) upperright = normalize(camera.getupperrightvector()) lowerleft = normalize(camera.getlowerleftvector()) lowerright = normalize(camera.getlowerrightvector()) # 2. Calculate Interpolation Deltas invheight = 1.0 / screenheight invwidth = 1.0 / screenwidth leftnormalydelta = (lowerleft - upperleft) invheight rightnormalydelta = (lowerright - upperright) invheight # 3. Initialize Interpolation Variables leftnormal = upperleft rightnormal = upperright # 4. Initialize Ray Origin rayorigin = camera.getposition() # Output buffer image = np.zeros((screenheight, screenwidth, 4)) # 5. Iterate Screen for y in range(screenheight): # Reset ray direction for this row raydirection = leftnormal # Calculate X delta for this row normalxdelta = (rightnormal - leftnormal) invwidth for x in range(screenwidth): # Trace Ray # Note: The actual voxel traversal logic (3D DDA) is complex to write fully # without specific grid bounds and step logic. # Here we simulate the sampling step as described in # for the orthographic case, or assume a helper for DDA traversal. # For a general perspective ray, we would step through voxels. # For the specific orthographic example in: # rayorigin = [x / screenwidth, y / screenheight, nearplane] # raydirection = [0, 0, 1] # Generic DDA traversal placeholder # In a full implementation, this loop steps through voxel indices # in intersection order until the ray exits the volume or a stop condition is met. accumulatedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Simulate traversal for demonstration of compositing logic # In reality, 'voxelcoords' would be generated by the 3D DDA step # Assuming a single sample for the sake of the compositing formula structure # if the volume is thin or we are just showing the transfer function application voxelcoord = np.floor(np.array([x, y, 0]) volumedata.shape[:3] - 0.5).astype(int) # Clamp coordinates to volume bounds voxelcoord = np.clip(voxelcoord, 0, np.array(volumedata.shape) - 1) scalarvalue = volumedata[voxelcoord[0], voxelcoord[1], voxelcoord[2]] # Apply Transfer Function r, g, b, a = transferfunction(scalarvalue) samplecolor = np.array([r, g, b, a]) # Composite (Front-to-Back) # pixelcolor = pixelcolor + (1 - pixelcolor[3]) samplecolor[0:3] samplecolor[3] # pixelcolor[3] = pixelcolor[3] + (1 - pixelcolor[3]) samplecolor[3] # Since we are doing a single sample per pixel in this simplified trace, # we just assign. In a real DDA loop, this accumulates. accumulatedcolor[0:3] = samplecolor[0:3] samplecolor[3] accumulatedcolor[3] = samplecolor[3] image[y, x] = accumulatedcolor # Increment X raydirection += normalxdelta # Increment Y leftnormal += leftnormalydelta rightnormal += rightnormalydelta # Finalize imagergb = np.clip(image[:,:, 0:3] 255, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8) return imagergb def transferfunctiongaussian(x): """ Gaussian mixture transfer function from. """ r = 1.0 np.exp(-((x - 9.0)2) / 1.0) + 0.1 np.exp(-((x - 3.0)2) / 0.1) + 0.1 np.exp(-((x + 3.0)2) / 0.5) g = 1.0 np.exp(-((x - 9.0)2) / 1.0) + 1.0 np.exp(-((x - 3.0)2) / 0.1) + 0.1 np.exp(-((x + 3.0)2) / 0.5) b = 0.1 np.exp(-((x - 9.0)2) / 1.0) + 0.1 np.exp(-((x - 3.0)2) / 0.1) + 1.0 np.exp(-((x + 3.0)2) / 0.5) a = 0.6 np.exp(-((x - 9.0)2) / 1.0) + 0.1 np.exp(-((x - 3.0)2) / 0.1) + 0.01 np.exp(-((x + 3.0)2) / 0.5) return r, g, b, a Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: The method uses nearest-neighbor sampling (np.floor), which can result in aliasing or blocky artifacts at low resolutions. Performance: High number of texture accesses and multiplications per ray leads to low frame rates for large or sparse volumes. Voxel Definition: A voxel is an index in a grid, not a geometric cube. It has no notion of position or movement. Coordinate Centering: Subtracting 0.5 from scaled coordinates handles the offset between pixel centers and voxel centers. A hybrid ray-casting algorithm developed for arbitrary parallel and perspective projections of high-resolution volumetric datasets, requiring at most one memory access per voxel per projection without pre-processing. Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of voxels traversed along the ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per ray (excluding the volume data itself), as it does not require acceleration structures. Performance: Recommended for small, dense voxel entities (approx. 50^3 or 100^3 voxels) because modifications are immediately visible without updating acceleration structures. For larger or sparse volumes, acceleration structures are preferred due to the linear complexity. Strengths: No preprocessing required; immediate visibility of voxel modifications; guarantees closest intersection first. Limitations: Low frame rates for large datasets; high number of memory accesses and multiplications; aliasing artifacts due to nearest-neighbor sampling. Discrete Ray Tracing is a valid approach to rendering voxellized datasets, often cited alongside GPU-based volume ray casting. The term "voxel" is often misused to refer to geometric cubes, but in this context, it refers to indices in an axis-aligned 3D grid. The algorithm is based on a 3D form of Digital Differential Analysis (DDA), similar to the algorithm used in Wolfenstein 3D ray casting tutorials. It limits intersection tests to Pythagorean complexity rather than cubic by traversing voxels in the exact order of intersection.
