name: Cube-3 Hybrid Ray-Casting
head: Cube-3, Cube-3 Architecture, Cubic Frame Buffer rendering
body: Cube-3 is a highly parallel, pipelined hardware architecture and hybrid ray-casting algorithm designed for the real-time visualization of high-resolution volumetric datasets (e.g., 512^3 voxels). It solves the traditional memory access bottleneck in volume rendering by ensuring at most one memory access per voxel per projection without pre-processing or data-dependent optimizations. Unlike object-order methods like VIRIM or image-order methods like VOGUE, which process single ray samples per pipeline stage, Cube-3 processes all sample values belonging to a ray simultaneously, exploiting spatial coherency to achieve the largest possible degree of parallelism. The method combines discrete ray tracing with hybrid interpolation to generate continuous ray samples from a skewed memory structure, shading them, and compositing them via a hierarchical tree. Input: A volumetric dataset of size n^3 voxels, where each voxel is 16 bits. The viewing direction defines a "base-plane" (the volume face most perpendicular to the view). Output: A projected image on the base-plane, which is subsequently warped and interpolated by the host into the final view plane image. 1. Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB): The dataset is stored in n dual-access memory modules. Each module stores n^2 voxels. Mapping: A voxel at coordinates (x, y, z) is mapped to module k using: k = (x + y + z) \bmod n where 0 \leq k, x, y, z \leq n-1. Internal Layout: Within module k, the voxel is stored at indices (i, j) where i=x and j=y. This skewed organization ensures that any beam of n voxels parallel to a primary axis resides in different memory modules, preventing access conflicts. 2. Discrete Ray Buffers: Part of the TRILIN units, these store beams fetched from the CFB. 3. ABC Buffers: Three buffers storing continuous planes of ray samples: Above, Below, and Current. These are used for gradient estimation and shading. 4. Ray Projection Cone (RPC): A folded and circular binary tree of n-1 Voxel Combination Units (VCUs) with n shading units as leaves. 1. Generate Discrete Rays: Cast discrete voxel-rays from each pixel on the base-plane. Use a 3D variation of Bresenham's line drawing algorithm to generate these rays from continuous viewing rays. This guarantees constant stepping of distance 1 along the major axis (e.g., Z). Steps in non-major directions (e.g., X, Y) are determined by lookup tables called templates. These templates ensure that neighboring discrete rays do not overlap in voxels. Discrete rays belonging to a scanline form a Projection Ray Plane (PRP). 2. Fetch Beams: Fetch PRPs as a sequence of voxel beams from the CFB according to the discrete ray templates. Beams are stored in the discrete ray buffers of the TRILIN units. 3. Align and Store: Use a high-bandwidth global bus (Fast Bus) to align all discrete rays in each PRP parallel to a main axis of the 2D buffers. Use 2D skewing (similar to CFB) to support conflict-free storage of beams from the CFB and conflict-free retrieval of axis-aligned discrete rays. 4. Interpolate (TRI-LIN): Fetch consecutive discrete rays each clock cycle into n tri-linear interpolation units (TRI-LINs). Sheared Tri-linear Interpolation: Two discrete PRPs (top and bottom) are used to generate sample values for the original continuous rays. Interpolation uses voxels from neighboring discrete rays of the top and bottom PRPs. Gradient Estimation: Estimate the gradient at each resample location using central differences between samples of rays on the immediate left, right, above, below, and along the current ray. Sharing: Overlapping voxels of neighboring discrete rays are shared between neighboring TRILIN units. This allows sharing already computed ray samples between neighboring rays, avoiding additional CFB accesses. Store the interpolated continuous sample values and gradients in the ABC buffers. 5. Shade (Shaders): Forward interpolated sample and gradient values to shading units (Shaders). Opacity: Assign opacity values to each sample using a user-controlled look-up table (transfer function). Color: Calculate color value at each sample location according to a local illumination model. 6. Composite (RPC): Connect the n shading units as leaves of the Ray Projection Cone (RPC), a folded and circular binary tree containing n-1 Voxel Combination Units (VCUs). The RPC takes one ray of opacity and color samples and generates one projected pixel value per clock cycle. Projection Schemes: The RPC implements schemes such as first/last opaque projection, maximum voxel value, weighted summation, or standard compositing. 7. Output: Transmit the resulting pixel of the base-plane to the host. The host warps and stores the result in the frame-buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cube3render(dataset, n, viewingdirection, transferfunction, illuminationmodel): """ dataset: 3D array of size n^3, 16-bit voxels n: dimension size viewingdirection: vector defining the view transferfunction: LUT mapping voxel values to opacity illuminationmodel: function for local lighting """ # 1. Setup CFB Mapping # k = (x + y + z) % n # Internal index: (i, j) = (x, y) # 2. Generate Discrete Rays from Base-Plane # Base-plane is the volume face most perpendicular to viewingdirection baseplanepixels = getbaseplanepixels(viewingdirection, n) # Templates for non-major axis steps (Bresenham 3D variation) templates = generatebresenhamtemplates(viewingdirection, n) discreterays = [] for pixel in baseplanepixels: ray = generatediscreteray(pixel, viewingdirection, templates, n) discreterays.append(ray) # Group rays into Projection Ray Planes (PRPs) by scanline prps = groupraysintoprps(discreterays) # 3. Fetch and Align Beams # Fetch beams from CFB. Conflict-free due to skewed mapping. # Align rays on Fast Bus to match 2D buffer axis. alignedprps = [] for prp in prps: beams = fetchbeamsfromcfb(prp, n) alignedprp = alignbeamstoaxis(beams, viewingdirection) alignedprps.append(alignedprp) # 4. Interpolation and Gradient Estimation (TRI-LIN) # Use top and bottom PRPs for sheared tri-linear interpolation # Store in ABC buffers (Above, Below, Current) abcbuffers = initializeabcbuffers(n) for i in range(len(alignedprps) - 1): topprp = alignedprps[i] bottomprp = alignedprps[i+1] # Interpolate continuous samples from discrete beams # Share overlapping voxels between neighboring TRILIN units continuoussamples = shearedtrilinearinterpolate(topprp, bottomprp, n) # Estimate gradients using central differences from neighbors # Neighbors: left, right, above, below, along current ray gradients = estimategradients(continuoussamples, abcbuffers, n) # Store in ABC buffers updateabcbuffers(continuoussamples, gradients, abcbuffers) # 5. Shading shadedrays = [] for raysamples in continuoussamples: # Iterate over rays shadedsamples = [] for sample in raysamples: # Opacity from transfer function opacity = transferfunction(sample.value) # Color from illumination model using gradient color = illuminationmodel(sample.value, gradients[sample.location]) shadedsamples.append({ 'opacity': opacity, 'color': color, 'distance': sample.distance }) shadedrays.append(shadedsamples) # 6. Composition via Ray Projection Cone (RPC) # RPC is a binary tree of VCU nodes # Leaves are shading units, internal nodes are VCUs finalpixels = [] for rayshadedsamples in shadedrays: # Composite ray samples into one pixel value # Supports: first/last opaque, max voxel, weighted sum, compositing pixelvalue = compositeray(rayshadedsamples, projectionscheme='compositing') finalpixels.append(pixelvalue) # 7. Output # Transmit base-plane pixels to host for warping return finalpixels Dataset Size: Typically n^3 where n is a power of 2 (e.g., 128, 256, 512). Voxel Depth: 16 bits. Memory Modules: n modules required. Edge Cases: Memory Conflicts: Avoided by the skewed CFB organization and 2D skewing in buffers. If n is not chosen such that the modulo arithmetic distributes beams correctly, conflicts may arise. Ray Overlap: The use of templates in Bresenham's algorithm specifically avoids overlap of voxels between neighboring discrete rays, which is critical for the sharing mechanism in TRILINs. Precision: The method relies on fixed-point or specific hardware floating-point units for the interpolation and shading; precision limits are not explicitly detailed in the sources but are implied by the 16-bit input and hardware constraints. Extends Cube-3 to support arbitrary parallel projections by using a 2D Skewed Buffer and Ray Projection Tree, overcoming the orthographic limitation of the original Cube. The parent method providing the foundation for generating discrete voxel-rays from continuous viewing rays. Performance: Limited only by the data-transfer rate on the Fast Bus due to fully pipelined implementation. 128^3 dataset at 8MHz bus: 30Hz. 256^3 dataset at 33MHz bus: 30Hz. 512^3 dataset at 66MHz bus: 15Hz. 512^3 dataset at 125MHz bus: 30Hz. Hardware Requirements: A Cube-3 implementation for 30 projections per second of a 512^3 16-bit dataset requires 8 custom boards and a specially fabricated bus backplane. Complexity: The architecture exhibits the largest possible degree of parallelism compared to VIRIM and VOGUE. Strengths: Real-time visualization of high-resolution datasets; no pre-processing required; solves memory access bottleneck; supports 4D visualization (dynamic datasets). Limitations: Hardware-specific; requires high-bandwidth global bus (Fast Bus) which becomes a bottleneck for larger datasets or higher frame rates (leading to Cube-4 development). Cube-3 was developed at the State University of New York at Stony Brook. It was designed to enable real-time 4D visualization of dynamically changing datasets, such as in-situ fluid flow in rocks. The architecture is a hybrid ray-casting algorithm that exploits coherency to solve the traditional memory access bottleneck, contrasting with object-order (VIRIM) and image-order (VOGUE) approaches. The work is documented in publications from 1995. Three Architectures for Volume Rendering, https://vcg.seas.harvard.edu/publications/19950801-three-architectures-for-volume-rendering/paper, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Extended Cube Architecture for Arbitrary Parallel Projection
head: Arbitrary Parallel Viewing Architecture
body: The Extended Cube Architecture is a special-purpose computer architecture designed to enable real-time arbitrary parallel projection of volumetric data, overcoming the distortion limitations of rotating the Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) for non-orthographic views. It extends the original Cube architecture, which only supported orthographic projection, by introducing a 2D Skewed Buffer (2DSB) and a Ray Projection Tree (RPT) to fetch and process slanted planes of projection rays without pre-processing. Unlike the original Cube, which accesses axial beams directly, this method handles arbitrary viewing directions by shearing the data into a 2D memory structure, aligning rays, and projecting them in parallel. The method transforms arbitrary parallel projection rays into a format suitable for parallel hardware processing. It operates on a dataset stored in a Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) and produces a 2D projected image. Input: A volumetric dataset of size n \times n \times n voxels stored in the CFB. The viewing direction is arbitrary (parallel projection). Output: A 2D image where each pixel corresponds to a projection ray passing through the volume. 1. Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) Layout: A 3D modular memory organization. Size: For a 512^3 dataset, the CFB holds 128M voxels. Access: Supports conflict-free access to full beams of n voxels in any orthographic direction. 2. 2D Skewed Buffer (2DSB) Purpose: Stores the slanted Projection Ray Plane (PRP) and performs de-skewing. Layout: Physically divided into n modules, diagonally skewed to allow conflict-free writing of horizontal beams and reading of vertical rays. Dimensions: Width is at least 2n-1 columns to accommodate parallel rays entering the slanted PRP. Modules: Contains n modules. Each module connects to neighbors via conveyors (barrel shifters) with 256 lines (16 bits \times 16 shift places). Pipelining: Uses multiple planes (e.g., 4 planes) to allow concurrent loading of the next PRP while processing the current one. 3. Ray Projection Tree (RPT) Purpose: Parallel processing of viewing rays to compute pixel values. Layout: A hierarchical binary tree of n-1 Voxel Combination Units (VCUs). Leaves: Accept n voxels along a viewing ray. Root: Produces the final color for the corresponding pixel. 4. Voxel Combination Unit (VCU) Input: Two voxel values. Operation: Combines inputs into an output voxel value. Latency: 7 time units per combination. 1. Retrieve Projection Ray Plane (PRP): Identify the set of projection rays belonging to the same scan line of the projected 2D frame buffer. These rays form a slanted plane (PRP) within the CFB. 2. Fetch Beams: Retrieve the PRP from the CFB as n beams parallel to a primary axis. This takes O(n) cycles. 3. Store in 2DSB: Store the slanted PRP into the 2DSB one beam at a time, from closest to furthest. 4. De-skew (Shear): Shift each beam left or right within the 2DSB to align all viewing rays vertically (parallel to a 2D axis). This is performed using a barrel shifter (Conveyor). The 2DSB width (2n-1) accommodates the shear. 5. Retrieve Rays: Retrieve vertical viewing rays from the 2DSB in parallel. 6. Transfer to RPT: Transfer rays to the RPT. Shift rays during transfer to ensure the closest voxel appears at the desired position in the tree. 7. Process Rays: Process rays in parallel through the RPT. Standard: Each VCU combines two voxels in 7 time units. The tree processes \log n rays simultaneously in a pipeline fashion after initialization. Neighborhood (Optional): For algorithms requiring a 27-voxel neighborhood (central voxel + 26 neighbors), use multiple parallel 2DSBs. Extract the 27-voxel cube and transfer it to the RPT in parallel. 8. Pipeline: Use a fourth plane in the 2DSB to load the next slanted PRP while three planes are used for extracting the 27-voxel cube for concurrent projection. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. N = 512 # Dataset dimension NUMMODULES = N NUMPLANES = 4 # For pipelining def extendedcubeprojection(cfb, viewdirection): """ Perform arbitrary parallel projection using Extended Cube Architecture. cfb: Cubic Frame Buffer (3D array) viewdirection: Vector defining the parallel projection rays """ # 1. Identify Projection Ray Planes (PRPs) # PRPs are slanted planes of rays belonging to the same scan line. # All PRPs are made parallel to one major axis by fixing a degree of freedom. prps = getprps(cfb, viewdirection) # Initialize 2DSB with multiple planes for pipelining dsb = initialize2dskewedbuffer(width=2N-1, height=N, planes=NUMPLANES) # Initialize RPT rpt = initializerayprojectiontree(n=N) # 2. Process each PRP for i, prp in enumerate(prps): # 3. Fetch PRP as beams from CFB # Fetch n beams parallel to a primary axis in O(n) cycles beams = fetchbeamsfromcfb(cfb, prp) # 4. Store and De-skew in 2DSB # Load one beam at a time, closest to furthest for beamidx, beam in enumerate(beams): # Shift beam left/right to align viewing rays vertically shiftamount = calculateshift(beamidx, viewdirection) dsb.storebeam(beam, shift=shiftamount, plane=i % NUMPLANES) # 5. Retrieve and Transfer to RPT # Retrieve vertical viewing rays in parallel rays = dsb.retrieveverticalrays(plane=i % NUMPLANES) # Shift rays during transfer to align closest voxel processedrays = [] for ray in rays: alignedray = shiftrayforrpt(ray) processedrays.append(alignedray) # 6. Process Rays in RPT # Pipeline: RPT processes log(n) rays simultaneously # Each VCU combines 2 voxels in 7 time units pixelvalues = rpt.processrays(processedrays) # 7. Pipeline Optimization # While 3 planes are used for extraction, 4th plane loads next PRP # This is handled by the hardware scheduling of dsb planes return pixelvalues def calculateshift(beamidx, viewdirection): """ Calculate the horizontal shift required to align the beam's viewing rays vertically. The 2DSB must be at least 2n-1 columns wide to handle parallel rays entering the slanted PRP. """ # Implementation detail: The shift aligns the slanted PRP into a vertical orientation # within the 2D memory structure. # Exact formula depends on the specific skewing scheme and view direction. # Placeholder for specific geometric calculation based on view vector components. return 0 def shiftrayforrpt(ray): """ Shift the ray during transfer to ensure the closest voxel appears at the desired position. """ # Placeholder for ray alignment logic. return ray CFB Size: 128M voxels for a 512^3 dataset. 2DSB Width: At least 2n-1 columns. 2DSB Modules: n modules. VCU Latency: 7 time units. Intermodule Communication: Each conveyor connects to neighbors by 256 lines (16 bits \times 16 shift places). Implementation Scale: A 512^3 system requires 512 parallel processing units, 512 memory modules, ~18,000 lines of information operating in parallel, and up to 1,024 chips for memory alone. Routing Difficulties: Module data lines are grouped by module, while conveyor data lines are grouped by bit position, creating complex routing requirements. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The 2DSB width (2n-1) must be sufficient to handle the shear of the slanted PRP. An architecture variant using three additional 2D buffers to accommodate arbitrary parallel and perspective projections. Unlike the rotation technique which distorts the CFB image, this method generates arbitrary projections without distortion but requires fetching a whole projection ray plane and rearranging it. It fetches n beams in O(n) cycles, stores them in a 2D temporary buffer, and rearranges them into 26-connected discrete ray representations using a O(\log n) barrel shifter twice. Each ray is fed into the VMWB for selection of the first opaque voxel in O(\log n) time. Total time is O(n^2 \mod n \log n), allowing real-time arbitrary projection. Time Complexity: O(n^2 \log n) for arbitrary parallel projection, same as orthographic projection in the original Cube architecture, compared to conventional O(n^3). Memory Complexity: High. Requires significant hardware resources (e.g., 1,024 chips for memory in a 512^3 system). Performance: Enables interactive rendering rates for 512^3 datasets. Strengths: Supports real-time arbitrary parallel projection without image distortion; conflict-free access to beams and rays; pipeline-friendly. Limitations: Extremely high hardware complexity and intermodule communication requirements; difficult routing; not suitable for perspective projection without more complex architecture. When to Use: When real-time arbitrary parallel projection of high-resolution volumes is required and hardware resources are available. When Not to Use: When hardware simplicity is preferred, or for perspective projection (requires more complex architecture). The Extended Cube Architecture was developed as an extension of the original Cube architecture, which was a special-purpose computer architecture for volume visualization supporting only orthographic projection. The original Cube used a Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) and beam projection mechanisms. Arbitrary parallel projections were previously created by rotating the scene and viewing it through a principal orthographic direction, but this distorted the CFB image. The extended architecture was presented to support real-time arbitrary viewing without distortion. It builds on the Cube-3 Hybrid Ray-Casting method [3143-cube-3-hybrid-ray-casting.md]. An Extended Volume Visualization System for Arbitrary Parallel Projection, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh92/064-069, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Viewing and Rendering Processor for a Volume Visualization System, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh89/171-178, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Fixed Step Ray Marching
body:
Fixed Step Ray Marching is a direct volume rendering technique that visualizes 3D scalar fields (such as fog or smoke) by casting rays from the camera and accumulating color and opacity along a fixed-distance path. It solves the problem of rendering heterogeneous, translucent media without requiring explicit mesh extraction or adaptive traversal logic. Unlike sibling methods that may use adaptive stepping or discrete integral approximations, this method employs a uniform step size with front-to-back compositing, often integrating gradient-based shading and transfer functions for material appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D density grid (e.g., VDB or sparse voxel octree), a camera ray for each pixel, a directional light vector, and rendering parameters (stepsize, absorption, maxsteps, volcolor). Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated RGB color and opacity. Data Structures: Grid: A sparse 3D structure storing density values. Access is performed via sample(x, y, z) which returns the density at world coordinates. Scene: Contains bounding box bounds (bmin, bmax), light direction (lightdir), and volume color (volcolor). Parameters: stepsize: Distance between samples. Default: 0.15. absorption: Absorption coefficient multiplier. Default: 12.0. maxsteps: Maximum number of steps per ray. Default: 800. volcolor: Base volume color (RGB). Default: (1.0, 0.95, 0.88). Algorithm Steps: 1. Setup: Compute the active bounding box (bbox) from the grid. If the grid is empty, return the background color. Compute world bounds bmin and bmax by padding the bbox with stepsize 2.0 to ensure rays entering/exiting the volume are handled correctly. Normalize the light direction vector lightdir. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel (x, y), compute the ray origin and direction. Compute intersection parameters t{enter} and t{exit} with the bounding box using a ray-box intersection test. If the ray does not intersect the box (invalid intersection), set the pixel to the background color and continue to the next pixel. 3. Marching Loop: Initialize the ray parameter t = \max(t{enter}, 0.001). Initialize transmittance T = 1.0 and accumulated color components Cr = Cg = Cb = 0.0. Loop up to maxsteps: If t > t{exit} or T < 0.005, break the loop. Sampling: Compute the current 3D position P = (px, py, pz) using the ray equation at t. Sample the density d = 	ext{sample}(px, py, pz). If d > 0.001: Compute the optical depth for the step: ext = d 	imes 	ext{absorption} 	imes 	ext{step\size}. Gradient Calculation: Compute central differences for the gradient vector 
abla d = (gx, gy, gz) using a step size h = 	ext{step\size} 	imes 0.5: gx = 	ext{sample}(px+h, py, pz) - 	ext{sample}(px-h, py, pz) gy = 	ext{sample}(px, py+h, pz) - 	ext{sample}(px, py-h, pz) gz = 	ext{sample}(px, py, pz+h) - 	ext{sample}(px, py, pz-h) Handle boundary conditions: if px \pm h or similar coordinates fall outside the grid bounds, clamp the sample coordinates to the nearest valid voxel center or return 0 density. Shading: Normalize the gradient: \hat{n} =  rac{
abla d}{\|
abla d\|}. Compute the dot product with the light direction: ndotl = \max(0.0, -(\hat{n}x \cdot 	ext{light}x + \hat{n}y \cdot 	ext{light}y + \hat{n}z \cdot 	ext{light}z)). Note the negative sign indicates the gradient points outward, so we negate for standard lighting models or adjust light direction convention. Compute the shading factor: shade = 0.3 + 0.7 	imes ndotl. Composition: Compute step transmittance: tr\step = \exp(-ext). Update accumulated color for each channel c \in \{r, g, b\}: Cc += T 	imes (1.0 - tr\step) 	imes 	ext{vol\color}c 	imes shade Update transmittance: T = T 	imes tr\step. Increment t by stepsize. 4. Final Composition: Add the background contribution to the accumulated color: Cc += T 	imes 	ext{bg\color}c for each channel. Clamp the final RGB values to the range [0, 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fixedstepraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, scene, grid, params): """ rayorigin: (x, y, z) raydirection: (x, y, z) scene: object with bmin, bmax, lightdir, volcolor, bgcolor grid: object with sample(x, y, z) method params: object with stepsize, absorption, maxsteps """ # 1. Setup tenter, texit = rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, scene.bmin, scene.bmax) if tenter is None: return scene.bgcolor lightdir = normalize(scene.lightdir) stepsize = params.stepsize absorption = params.absorption maxsteps = params.maxsteps # 2. Initialize t = max(tenter, 0.001) transmittance = 1.0 colorr = 0.0 colorg = 0.0 colorb = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t > texit or transmittance < 0.005: break # 3. Sampling px, py, pz = rayorigin + raydirection t density = grid.sample(px, py, pz) if density > 0.001: # Optical depth ext = density absorption stepsize # Gradient Calculation h = stepsize 0.5 # Clamp coordinates to grid bounds before sampling gx = grid.sample(px + h, py, pz) - grid.sample(px - h, py, pz) gy = grid.sample(px, py + h, pz) - grid.sample(px, py - h, pz) gz = grid.sample(px, py, pz + h) - grid.sample(px, py, pz - h) # Shading gradlen = sqrt(gxgx + gygy + gzgz) if gradlen > 1e-6: nx, ny, nz = gx/gradlen, gy/gradlen, gz/gradlen else: nx, ny, nz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 ndotl = max(0.0, -(nx lightdir.x + ny lightdir.y + nz lightdir.z)) shade = 0.3 + 0.7 ndotl # Composition trstep = exp(-ext) colorr += transmittance (1.0 - trstep) scene.volcolor.r shade colorg += transmittance (1.0 - trstep) scene.volcolor.g shade colorb += transmittance (1.0 - trstep) scene.volcolor.b shade transmittance = trstep t += stepsize # 4. Final Composition colorr += transmittance scene.bgcolor.r colorg += transmittance scene.bgcolor.g colorb += transmittance scene.bgcolor.b return clamp(colorr, 0.0, 1.0), clamp(colorg, 0.0, 1.0), clamp(colorb, 0.0, 1.0) A real-time GPU technique that visualizes 3D scalar fields by casting rays and accumulating color/opacity. It distinguishes itself by often integrating gradient-based shading and transfer functions, and is implemented in frameworks like Taichi for high-performance visualization. A fixed-step DVR technique that supports configurable density ranges and early-out termination. It distinguishes itself by explicitly supporting both world-space and object-space indexing and using a modular shader define system. A direct volume ray casting technique that samples a 3D texture along a ray, accumulating color and opacity. It is distinguished by its reliance on a fixed number of steps (STEPS) and specific implementation of procedural noise (Worley and Perlin) combined with boundary fading. The numerical approximation of the continuous Volume Rendering Integral used in fixed-step ray marching. It solves the problem of integrating light emission and absorption by replacing path integrals with a Riemann sum over discrete sample points, assuming a piecewise-constant density model. A post-processing technique for rendering volumetric light shafts in Unity URP. It builds on Fixed Step Ray Marching by using a fixed step size and exponential absorption logic, specifically targeting light shafts from a single directional light. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of steps per ray (maxsteps). The complexity is linear with respect to resolution and step count. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for the marching loop state, plus the memory required to store the volume grid. Measured Performance: In benchmarks using the Lyr.jl library on CUDA hardware, Fixed Step Ray Marching with HDDA (Hierarchical Data-Driven Acceleration) and caching showed significant speedups over linear GPU rendering and CPU baselines. For example, on a "fire.vdb" complex sparse grid, HDDA+cache rendering was significantly faster than linear GPU rendering, with speedup factors varying by grid complexity. Strengths: Simple implementation, predictable memory usage, easy to parallelize on GPUs, suitable for real-time applications when combined with acceleration structures like HDDA. Limitations: Fixed step size can lead to aliasing or slow convergence if the step size is too large, or excessive computation if too small. Does not handle complex scattering or participating media with high optical depth efficiently without many steps. When to use: Real-time fog, smoke, or simple volumetric effects where performance is critical and high-fidelity scattering is not required. When not to use: Scenes requiring high-fidelity light transport, complex scattering, or highly heterogeneous volumes where adaptive stepping would be more efficient. Fixed Step Ray Marching is a foundational technique in direct volume rendering, originating from the need to efficiently visualize 3D scalar fields such as medical imaging data or atmospheric effects. It is implemented in various graphics libraries and frameworks, including Lyr.jl, which provides a volume ray marcher for fog volumes using fixed step size, exponential absorption, and gradient-based shading. The method is widely used in real-time graphics engines and scientific visualization tools due to its simplicity and parallelizability. tobiasosborne/Lyr.jl, https://github.com/tobiasosborne/Lyr.jl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching Volume Rendering
head: Volumetric Raymarching, Volumetric Raycasting
body: Ray Marching Volume Rendering is a real-time GPU technique that visualizes 3D scalar fields (such as smoke, clouds, or density volumes) by casting rays from the camera through the volume and accumulating color and opacity along the ray path. It solves the problem of rendering heterogeneous, translucent media without requiring explicit mesh extraction. Unlike sibling methods that may use adaptive stepping or discrete integral approximations, this method typically employs a fixed step size with front-to-back compositing, often integrating gradient-based shading and transfer functions for material appearance. It is distinguished by its implementation in frameworks like Taichi for high-performance real-time visualization, supporting features such as refraction, shadows, and spherical harmonics encoding. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D scalar field (density) volumetexture (or Taichi field smokedensitytaichi), an optional 3D color field smokecolortaichi, an optional 3D index of refraction (IOR) field, a 1D transfer function texture trfunctexture, camera parameters (position, direction, field of view), and light sources. Outputs: A 2D image buffer containing the accumulated color and opacity for each pixel. Data Structures: Volume Texture: A 3D texture where density values are stored in the red channel (accessed via.r). In Taichi implementations, this is a ti.field of shape (N, N, N) with dtype f32 or f16. Transfer Function: A 1D texture mapping density values to RGBA color. Light Density: A 3D field of shape (N, N, N, 3) storing pre-computed light contributions per voxel, initialized to ones or zeros depending on the shadowing model. Ray Buffers: For GPU implementations, buffers for ray origins rayso (3x f16), ray directions raysd (3x f16), and hit distances hitst (2x f16). Parameters: NUMRAYSTEPS or SAMPLECOUNT: Maximum number of steps per ray (e.g., 128, 1024). stepsize: Fixed distance between samples. Can be derived from pixelsize raytracingstepsizefactor or MAXDISTANCE / NUMSTEPS. raytracingstopthreshold: Termination threshold for transmittance (e.g., 0.01). alphaScale: Scaling factor for alpha normalization. finalGamma: Gamma correction exponent (typically 2.2 or 1/2.2). densityCoef: Global density multiplier (e.g., 50.0). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel, compute the ray origin ro (camera position) and direction rd from camera parameters. \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{d}{cam} + u \cdot \frac{\text{fov} \cdot (i - \text{width}/2)}{\text{width}} + v \cdot \frac{\text{fov} \cdot (j/\text{width} - 0.5)}{\text{width}} Normalize \mathbf{d}. 2. Ray-Box Intersection: Determine the entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max}) distances of the ray with the volume's bounding box (typically [-0.5, 0.5]^3) using the slab method. t{bot} = \frac{B{min} - ro}{rd}, \quad t{top} = \frac{B{max} - ro}{rd} t{min} = \max(t{bot}), \quad t{max} = \min(t{top}) 3. Initialization: Initialize accumulated color C{acc} = (0,0,0), accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0, and transmittance T = 1.0. 4. Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to NUMRAYSTEPS or until t > t{max}: a. Position Update: Compute sample position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}o + t \cdot \mathbf{r}d. b. Sampling: Sample density D from the volume texture. c. Alpha Calculation: Compute the opacity contribution for this step. \alpha{sample} = D \cdot \text{step\size} \cdot \text{density\coef} Or using Beer's Law approximation: \alpha{sample} = 1 - e^{-\sigmat \cdot \Delta d} where \sigmat is the extinction coefficient derived from density. d. Termination Check: If \alpha{acc} \ge 1.0 or T < 0.01, break the loop (Early Ray Termination). e. Lighting (Optional): If lighting is enabled, compute the light contribution at \mathbf{p}. L = \text{sample\light}(\mathbf{p}) f. Color Sampling: Map density to color using the transfer function. \mathbf{c}{sample} = \text{texture}(\text{trfunc\texture}, \text{vec2}(D, 0.5)).rgb Apply lighting: \mathbf{c}{sample} \leftarrow \mathbf{c}{sample} \cdot L. g. Compositing (Front-to-Back): \mathbf{c}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{c}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot \mathbf{c}{sample} \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alpha{sample} T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alpha{sample}) h. Advance: t \leftarrow t + \text{step\size}. 5. Background and Final Color: Add the background color modulated by the final transmittance. \mathbf{c}{final} = \mathbf{c}{acc} + \mathbf{c}{bg} \cdot T Apply gamma correction: \mathbf{c}{final} = \mathbf{c}{final}^{1/\gamma}. 6. Refraction (Optional): If an IOR field is provided, modify the ray direction at each step based on the gradient of the IOR field. \nabla \text{IOR} = \frac{\text{IOR}(\mathbf{p} + \Delta) - \text{IOR}(\mathbf{p} - \Delta)}{2\Delta} Use Snell's law to bend the ray. If total internal reflection occurs (\sin \theta{new} > 1), terminate the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchingvolumerendering(camerapos, cameradir, volumetexture, transferfunc, numsteps, stepsize, bgcolor, uselighting=False, lightdensityfield=None, densitycoef=50.0): # 1. Ray Generation rayorigin = camerapos raydirection = normalize(cameradir) # 2. Ray-Box Intersection (slab method for box [-0.5, 0.5]^3) boxmin = vec3(-0.5) boxmax = vec3(0.5) # Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero invdir = vec3(1.0 / raydirection.x if raydirection.x != 0 else 1e9, 1.0 / raydirection.y if raydirection.y != 0 else 1e9, 1.0 / raydirection.z if raydirection.z != 0 else 1e9) t0 = (boxmin - rayorigin) invdir t1 = (boxmax - rayorigin) invdir tmin = max(min(t0.x, t1.x), min(t0.y, t1.y), min(t0.z, t1.z)) tmax = min(max(t0.x, t1.x), max(t0.y, t1.y), max(t0.z, t1.z)) if tmin > tmax: return bgcolor # Ray misses volume # 3. Initialization acccolor = vec3(0.0) accalpha = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 t = tmin # 4. Marching Loop for i in range(numsteps): if t > tmax: break # Sample position pos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Sample Density (trilinear interpolation) density = sample3dtexture(volumetexture, pos) # Calculate Alpha for this step alphasample = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize densitycoef) # Early Ray Termination if accalpha >= 1.0 or transmittance < 0.01: break # Lighting lightcontribution = vec3(1.0) if uselighting and lightdensityfield is not None: lightcontribution = sample3dtexture(lightdensityfield, pos) # Transfer Function tfcolor = sample1dtexture(transferfunc, vec2(density, 0.5)) colorsample = tfcolor.rgb lightcontribution # Compositing (Front-to-Back) acccolor += (1.0 - accalpha) alphasample colorsample accalpha += (1.0 - accalpha) alphasample transmittance = (1.0 - alphasample) # Advance t += stepsize # 5. Final Color finalcolor = acccolor + bgcolor transmittance # Gamma Correction gamma = 2.2 finalcolor = pow(finalcolor, vec3(1.0 / gamma)) return finalcolor def sample3dtexture(tex, p): # Assumes tex is a 3D array of shape (W, H, D) # Normalize p to [0, 1] assuming box is [-0.5, 0.5] W, H, D = tex.shape pnorm = p + 0.5 ix = floor(pnorm.x (W - 1)) iy = floor(pnorm.y (H - 1)) iz = floor(pnorm.z (D - 1)) fx = pnorm.x (W - 1) - ix fy = pnorm.y (H - 1) - iy fz = pnorm.z (D - 1) - iz # Clamp indices ix = clamp(ix, 0, W-1); iy = clamp(iy, 0, H-1); iz = clamp(iz, 0, D-1) # Fetch 8 corners c000 = tex[ix, iy, iz] c100 = tex[ix+1, iy, iz] c010 = tex[ix, iy+1, iz] c110 = tex[ix+1, iy+1, iz] c001 = tex[ix, iy, iz+1] c101 = tex[ix+1, iy, iz+1] c011 = tex[ix, iy+1, iz+1] c111 = tex[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] # Lerp c00 = lerp(c000, c100, fx) c10 = lerp(c010, c110, fx) c01 = lerp(c001, c101, fx) c11 = lerp(c011, c111, fx) c0 = lerp(c00, c10, fy) c1 = lerp(c01, c11, fy) return lerp(c0, c1, fz) def sample1dtexture(tex, uv): # 1D texture lookup idx = floor(uv.x (len(tex) - 1)) idx = clamp(idx, 0, len(tex)-1) return tex[idx] A front-to-back ray marching technique that renders a 3D volume texture by stepping along rays from the camera, compositing color and opacity, and using pre-rendered opaque geometry to occlude the volume and adjust sampling rates. It solves the problem of self-occlusion in volume rendering without requiring full volumetric integration or multiple rendering passes. It is suitable for real-time applications where geometry occlusion is handled by the parent method. Volumetric Ray Marching for Fire is a GPU-friendly technique that samples a 3D volume along a ray to render fire simulation results stored in 3D textures. It distinguishes itself from smoke rendering by accumulating values based on a reaction coordinate (fuel) rather than blending density values, using an artist-defined color gradient to map these coordinates to flame colors. This method performs direct volume rendering by marching a ray through a 3D scalar field (volume texture) and accumulating color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. It distinguishes itself from basic raycasting by integrating a 1D transfer function for material mapping and gradient-based diffuse shading for surface appearance, while using jittered stepping to reduce aliasing artifacts. It serves as the core rendering loop for real-time GPU volume visualization, building on the discretization and ray setup provided by Ray Marching Volume Rendering. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture, plus O(V) for optional light density fields or hash tables. Performance: Up to 66 fps on an NVIDIA 3090 GPU at 800x800 resolution. Strengths: Real-time performance on modern GPUs; supports complex lighting, shadows, and refraction; no need for mesh extraction. Limitations: Fixed step size can cause aliasing (wood-grain artifacts) at low sample counts, mitigated by stochastic jittering. Requires tuning of step size and transfer functions. When to Use: Real-time visualization of smoke, clouds, fluids, and medical data. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Ray Marching Volume Rendering is a fundamental technique in computer graphics for visualizing volumetric data. It is based on the volume rendering integral, which approximates the light transport through a participating medium. The method has been widely implemented in various frameworks, including OpenGL shaders, CUDA engines, and high-level frameworks like Taichi for real-time applications. The Taichi NGP Renderer specifically adapts the Instant-NGP approach for volume rendering, using hash encoding and fully fused MLPs for density and color prediction, enabling real-time rendering of complex scenes. The technique is commonly used in scientific visualization, visual effects, and real-time fluid simulation. name: Ray Marching Volume Rendering with Geometry Occlusion
head: GPU Ray Marching
body: A front-to-back ray marching technique that renders a 3D volume texture by stepping along rays from the camera, compositing color and opacity, and using pre-rendered opaque geometry to occlude the volume and adjust sampling rates. It solves the problem of self-occlusion in volume rendering without requiring full volumetric integration or multiple rendering passes. It is suitable for real-time applications where geometry occlusion is handled by the parent method. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: volumedims: Dimensions of the 3D volume texture (ivec3). dtscale: Scalar multiplier for base step size. transformedeye: Camera position in world space. pos: World-space position of the current fragment. volumetexture: 3D texture containing density/scalar values. colormap: 2D texture (gl.SRGB8ALPHA8, size 180x1, LINEAR filtered) mapping scalar values to RGBA colors. depthbuffer: Pre-rendered depth buffer of opaque geometry (gl.DEPTHCOMPONENT32F). invprojviewmatrix: Inverse projection and view matrices for depth reconstruction. fragcoord: Screen-space fragment coordinates. Outputs: Final composited RGBA color for the pixel. Data Structures: Render Targets: Two textures created via gl.texStorage2D. Target 0: gl.RGBA8 format, size WIDTH x HEIGHT. Target 1: gl.DEPTHCOMPONENT32F format, size WIDTH x HEIGHT. Framebuffers: depthColorFbo: Attaches Target 0 to COLORATTACHMENT0 and Target 1 to DEPTHATTACHMENT. colorFbo: Attaches Target 0 to COLORATTACHMENT0 only. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Ray Direction: Compute the ray direction vector in the vertex shader: \text{vray\dir} = \text{pos} - \text{transformed\eye} Normalize the direction in the fragment shader. 2. Ray-Box Intersection: Intersect the ray with the unit box [0,1]^3 using the slab method to determine entry (t{hit.x}) and exit (t{hit.y}) distances. t{min} = \frac{\text{box}{min} - \text{orig}}{\text{dir}}, \quad t{max} = \frac{\text{box}{max} - \text{orig}}{\text{dir}} t{hit.x} = \max(t{min}.x, t{min}.y, t{min}.z), \quad t{hit.y} = \min(t{max}.x, t{max}.y, t{max}.z) If t{hit.x} > t{hit.y}, discard the pixel. 3. Calculate Base Step Size: Compute the base step size dt based on volume dimensions and ray direction magnitude: dt = dt\scale \times \min\left(\frac{1.0}{\text{volume\dims} \times |\text{ray\dir}|}\right) Note: In GLSL, volumedims (ivec3) is implicitly converted to vec3 during multiplication with abs(raydir).. 4. Add Jitter Offset: Add a jitter offset to the entry point t{hit.x} to reduce banding artifacts. t{hit.x} \leftarrow t{hit.x} + \text{offset} 5. Check for Geometry Occlusion: Sample the pre-rendered depth buffer z at the current pixel. If z \ge 1.0, no opaque geometry is present. The ray marches through the entire box from t{hit.x} to t{hit.y}. If z < 1.0, geometry is present. Reconstruct the geometry's world-space position from the depth value z and the inverse projection/view matrices. Calculate the distance t{geom} along the ray to the geometry surface. Adjust the exit point: t{hit.y} = \min(t{hit.y}, t{geom}). Adjust the step size dt if necessary to ensure the final sample aligns with the geometry surface. 6. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate from t = t{hit.x} to t = t{hit.y} with step dt: a. Sample Volume: Sample the 3D volume texture at the current ray position \text{orig} + t \times \text{dir} to get scalar value s. b. Lookup Color: Use s to index into the colormap texture to get sample color C{sample} and opacity a{sample}. c. Opacity Correction: Apply opacity correction to account for step size variations: a{corrected} = 1.0 - (1.0 - a{sample})^{dt{correction}} Where dt{correction} scales the sample opacity based on step size relative to a reference. d. Front-to-Back Compositing: Accumulate color and alpha: C{out} = C{in} + (1.0 - C{in}.a) \times C{sample}.a \times C{sample}.rgb A{out} = A{in} + (1.0 - A{in}.a) \times C{sample}.a e. Early Exit: If C{out}.a \ge 0.99, break the loop. 7. Final Composition with Geometry: If geometry was present (z < 1.0), take a final sample at t{hit.y} (the geometry surface) and composite it. The code composites volume data at the surface location, implying the geometry acts as an occluder for the volume march, or the volume data at the surface is used to color the geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchwithgeometryocclusion(pos, transformedeye, volumedims, dtscale, volumetexture, colormap, depthbuffer, invprojviewmatrix, fragcoord): def wanghash(coord): # Standard integer hash returning [0, 1) h = coord.x 374761393 + coord.y 668265263 h = (h ^ (h >> 13)) 1274126177 return (h & 0x7fffffff) / 2147483647.0 def argmax(vec): return max(range(len(vec)), key=lambda i: abs(vec[i])) # 1. Ray Direction raydir = normalize(pos - transformedeye) # 2. Ray-Box Intersection [0,1]^3 boxmin = vec3(0.0) boxmax = vec3(1.0) tmin = (boxmin - pos) / raydir tmax = (boxmax - pos) / raydir thitx = max(tmin.x, tmin.y, tmin.z) thity = min(tmax.x, tmax.y, tmax.z) if thitx > thity: return vec4(0.0) # 3. Base Step Size stepdenom = vec3(volumedims.x abs(raydir.x), volumedims.y abs(raydir.y), volumedims.z abs(raydir.z)) dt = dtscale min(1.0 / stepdenom) # 4. Jitter Offset offset = wanghash(fragcoord) dt thitx += offset # 5. Geometry Occlusion Check z = depthbuffer.sample(fragcoord).r geometrypresent = z < 1.0 geomt = thity if geometrypresent: # Reconstruct world position from depth z ndcdepth = z 2.0 - 1.0 clippos = vec4(fragcoord 2.0 - 1.0, ndcdepth, 1.0) worldpos = invprojviewmatrix clippos worldpos = worldpos / worldpos.w # Distance to geometry along ray axis = argmax(raydir) geomt = (worldpos[axis] - pos[axis]) / raydir[axis] thity = min(thity, geomt) # Adjust dt to align final sample with geometry surface numsteps = int((thity - thitx) / dt) if numsteps > 0: dt = (thity - thitx) / numsteps # 6. Ray Marching Loop Cin = vec4(0.0) Ain = 0.0 t = thitx while t < thity: samplepos = pos + t raydir s = volumetexture.sample(samplepos).r Csample = colormap.sample(vec2(s, 0.5)).rgba # Opacity Correction acorrected = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - Csample.a, dt) # Front-to-Back Compositing Cin = Cin + (1.0 - Cin.a) acorrected Csample.rgb Ain = Ain + (1.0 - Ain) acorrected if Ain >= 0.99: break t += dt # 7. Final Composition if geometrypresent: finalpos = pos + thity raydir finals = volumetexture.sample(finalpos).r finalC = colormap.sample(vec2(finals, 0.5)).rgba Cin = Cin + (1.0 - Cin.a) finalC.a finalC.rgb Ain = Ain + (1.0 - Ain) finalC.a return vec4(Cin.rgb, Ain) Parameters: dtscale: Scalar multiplier for base step size. Default value not explicitly stated. volumedims: Dimensions of the 3D volume texture (ivec3). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-uniform volume scaling: Requires translation adjustment. The code calculates volumetranslation = vec3(0.5) - volumescale 0.5 to center the volume in the [-0.5, 0.5] or [0,1] space, ensuring correct ray origin transformation. Geometry Occlusion Handling: If no geometry is present (z \ge 1.0), the ray marches through the entire box. If geometry is present, the ray stops at the geometry surface (t{hit.y} = geomt) and a final sample is taken at that surface point. Precision: Division by zero in ray-box intersection if ray direction components are zero. Handle by checking for zero components and using epsilon. Depth Reconstruction: Reconstructing world position from depth buffer requires accurate inverse projection and view matrices. Ensure matrices are correctly passed and in the correct coordinate system. Direct Volume Rendering with Precomputed Occlusion (DOS) is a single-pass, image-order ray marching technique that approximates volumetric attenuation from behind the current sample using precomputed 2D occlusion maps. It solves the problem of self-occlusion in volume rendering without requiring full volumetric integration or multiple rendering passes. Unlike standard front-to-back ray casting which integrates opacity along the ray, DOS decouples the occlusion estimation from the ray step, using spatial averaging of a pre-rendered occlusion texture to modulate the current slice's contribution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Real-time capable, handles geometry occlusion efficiently by stopping ray march, simple implementation. Limitations: Approximate self-occlusion handling (geometry only, not volumetric), step size artifacts if not corrected, requires pre-rendered depth buffer. When to use: Real-time applications with opaque geometry occluding volumes, where full volumetric self-occlusion is too expensive. When not to use: Scenes with complex volumetric self-occlusion where geometry occlusion is not the primary factor, or when high accuracy is required. Origin: The method is described in the context of the webgl-marching-cubes project by Twinklebear. History: Not given in the sources. Usage: Used in real-time WebGL applications for rendering volumes with geometry occlusion. name: Direct Volume Rendering with Precomputed Occlusion (DOS)
head: Direct Volume Rendering with Occlusion
body: Direct Volume Rendering with Precomputed Occlusion (DOS) is a single-pass, image-order ray marching technique that approximates volumetric attenuation from behind the current sample using precomputed 2D occlusion maps. It solves the problem of self-occlusion in volume rendering without requiring full volumetric integration or multiple rendering passes. Unlike standard front-to-back ray casting which integrates opacity along the ray, DOS decouples the occlusion estimation from the ray step, using spatial averaging of a pre-rendered occlusion texture to modulate the current slice's contribution. Inputs: uVolume: A 3D texture (sampler3D) storing volume density or scalar values. uTransferFunction: A 2D texture (sampler2D) mapping volume values to RGBA color and opacity. uColor: A 2D texture (sampler2D) storing the accumulated color and alpha from previous slices or frames. uOcclusion: A 2D texture (sampler2D) storing precomputed occlusion values. uOcclusionSamples: A 2D texture (sampler2D) storing 2D offset vectors used to sample the occlusion map. uExtinction: A float constant representing the extinction coefficient. uSliceDistance: A float constant representing the distance between volume slices or the step size along the ray. uOcclusionScale: A vec2 constant scaling the occlusion sample offsets. uOcclusionSamplesCount: A uint constant specifying the number of samples taken from the occlusion map. Outputs: oColor: A vec4 output at location 0, storing the accumulated color and alpha. oOcclusion: A float output at location 1, storing the updated occlusion value for the current pixel. The method relies on two render targets bound to the fragment shader outputs: a color buffer storing vec4 per pixel, initialized to vec4(0) by a reset shader, and an occlusion buffer storing float per pixel, initialized to 1.0. The vertex shader renders a full-screen triangle using hardcoded vertices (-1, -1), (3, -1), and (-1, 3) to ensure the fragment shader processes every pixel in the viewport. It passes a normalized 2D position vPosition2D (in [0, 1] range) and the corresponding 3D world position vPosition3D to the fragment shader. 1. Initialization: A reset shader clears the output buffers by setting oColor to vec4(0) and oOcclusion to 1.0. 2. Boundary Check: In the main shader, check if vPosition3D is outside the volume bounds [0, 1]. If any(greaterThan(vPosition3D, vec3(1))) || any(lessThan(vPosition3D, vec3(0))), output the previous color and occlusion unchanged and terminate. 3. Volume Sampling: Sample the volume value at vPosition3D using uVolume, then map this value through the transfer function uTransferFunction to get transferSample (a vec4 with RGB color and alpha). 4. Extinction Calculation: Calculate the extinction for the current step: extinction = transferSample.a \times uExtinction. 5. Alpha Contribution: Calculate the alpha contribution for the current slice: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-extinction \times uSliceDistance). 6. Occlusion Update: Calculate the new occlusion value by sampling uOcclusion at multiple offsets defined in uOcclusionSamples, averaging the results, and multiplying by the exponential attenuation of the current slice: oOcclusion = \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} texture(uOcclusion, vPosition2D + offseti \times scale).r \right) \times \exp(-extinction \times uSliceDistance), where N = uOcclusionSamplesCount and offseti is the i-th offset vector from uOcclusionSamples scaled by uOcclusionScale. 7. Color Blending: Calculate the color contribution using the previous occlusion value (prevOcclusion, sampled from uOcclusion at vPosition2D): color = transferSample.rgb \times prevOcclusion \times \alpha. Update the output color using front-to-back blending: oColor.rgb = prevColor.rgb + color \times (1.0 - prevColor.a) and oColor.a = \min(prevColor.a + \alpha, 1.0), where prevColor is sampled from uColor at vPosition2D. 8. Final Composite: After all slices are processed, a final composite shader mixes the accumulated color with a white background: oColor = mix(vec4(1), vec4(color.rgb, 1), color.a). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. uVolume = None # sampler3D uTransferFunction = None # sampler2D uColor = None # sampler2D uOcclusion = None # sampler2D uOcclusionSamples = None # sampler2D uExtinction = 1.0 # float uSliceDistance = 1.0 # float uOcclusionScale = (0.0, 0.0) # vec2 uOcclusionSamplesCount = 4 # uint oColor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # vec4 oOcclusion = 1.0 # float def fragmentshader(vPosition2D, vPosition3D): # Step 2: Boundary Check if any(vPosition3D > 1.0) or any(vPosition3D < 0.0): prevcolor = texture(uColor, vPosition2D) prevocclusion = texture(uOcclusion, vPosition2D).r oColor = prevcolor oOcclusion = prevocclusion return # Step 3: Volume Sampling volumevalue = texture(uVolume, vPosition3D).r transfersample = texture(uTransferFunction, vec2(volumevalue, 0.5)) # Step 4: Extinction Calculation extinction = transfersample.a uExtinction # Step 5: Alpha Contribution alpha = 1.0 - exp(-extinction uSliceDistance) # Step 6: Occlusion Update occlusionsum = 0.0 for i in range(uOcclusionSamplesCount): # Retrieve offset from uOcclusionSamples texture # Note: Assumes offsets are stored sequentially in the texture offset = texture(uOcclusionSamples, vec2(i / uOcclusionSamplesCount, 0.0)).xy samplepos = vPosition2D + offset uOcclusionScale occlusionsum += texture(uOcclusion, samplepos).r avgocclusion = occlusionsum / uOcclusionSamplesCount oOcclusion = avgocclusion exp(-extinction uSliceDistance) # Step 7: Color Blending prevcolor = texture(uColor, vPosition2D) prevocclusion = texture(uOcclusion, vPosition2D).r color = transfersample.rgb prevocclusion alpha oColor.rgb = prevcolor.rgb + color (1.0 - prevcolor.a) oColor.a = min(prevcolor.a + alpha, 1.0) def finalcomposite(color): return mix(vec4(1.0), vec4(color.rgb, 1.0), color.a) uExtinction: Float constant representing the extinction coefficient. uSliceDistance: Float constant representing the distance between volume slices or step size along the ray. uOcclusionScale: Vec2 constant scaling the occlusion sample offsets. uOcclusionSamplesCount: Uint constant specifying the number of samples taken from the occlusion map. Boundary Conditions: The method explicitly checks for volume bounds [0, 1] to avoid sampling outside the volume texture. Precision: The use of exp() and floating-point accumulation can lead to precision issues in high-density volumes. The parent method that provides the geometry occlusion data used by DOS. It renders opaque geometry to occlude the volume, which DOS then uses to adjust sampling rates and attenuation. Ray Marching Volume Rendering with Geometry Occlusion Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Real-time capability due to single-pass per slice design and avoidance of full volumetric integration. Limitations: Approximation of occlusion may lead to artifacts in complex volumes; dependent on the quality of precomputed occlusion maps. Direct Volume Rendering with Precomputed Occlusion (DOS) is a volume rendering technique described in the terier/vpt repository. It performs ray marching in a single pass per slice, using precomputed 2D occlusion maps to approximate the attenuation of light from rays behind the current sample, avoiding the need for full volumetric integration or multiple passes for occlusion. terier/vpt, https://github.com/terier/vpt, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Ray Marching for Fire
head: Fire Simulation Volume Rendering, Fire Volume Rendering
body: Volumetric Ray Marching for Fire is a GPU-friendly technique that samples a 3D volume along a ray to render fire simulation results stored in 3D textures. It distinguishes itself from smoke rendering by accumulating values based on a reaction coordinate (fuel) rather than blending density values, using an artist-defined color gradient to map these coordinates to flame colors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two 3D textures from the simulation result containing density and reaction coordinate (fuel) values. A bounding volume defining the fire region. Outputs: Final pixel color. Data Structures: 3D Textures: Store density and reaction coordinate values per voxel. Color Gradient: An artist-defined mapping specified by three colors: core, border, and smoke. 1D Texture (Optional): Maps reaction coordinates to colors for fire rendering. Steps: 1. Inject a shader into the post-processing stage of the main camera. 2. Generate rays starting at the center of the camera in the direction of each pixel. 3. Calculate whether the ray hits the target volume. 4. If the ray does not hit the volume, the sampled value is set to 0. 5. If the ray hits, march through the volume in small steps and sample the volume at each step. 6. Sample the density and reaction coordinate textures from the simulation result at each step. 7. Use the density value to determine the thickness of the smoke, and use the reaction coordinate to determine the color of the flame by mapping its value to the core, border, and smoke gradient. 8. Calculate the average of the samples weighted by the length of the ray inside the target volume to determine the pixel color. Formulas: The pixel color is determined by the average of samples weighted by the length of the ray inside the target volume. For smoke rendering, the pipeline borrows from existing literature on volumetric clouds. The equation uses d for density, \theta for the angle between the camera ray and the sun, and g for eccentricity which defaults to 0.2. The exact mathematical formula for the eccentricity function is not given in the sources. The end result is multiplied by the smoke color for a more realistic look. Parameters: Voxel Grid Size: 128 \times 128 \times 128. GPU Blocks: 16 \times 16 \times 16 blocks, each containing 512 threads. Eccentricity (g): 0.2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the ray does not hit the volume, the sampled value is 0. Debugging attribute propagation across timestamps is difficult due to HLSL shader limitations. Treating volume samples as point light sources can lead to severe flickering if not enough point samples are used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderfire(cameracenter, cameradirection, pixeluv, volumedensity, volumereaction, volumebounds, stepsize): # Generate ray rayorigin = cameracenter dirx = cameradirection[0] + pixeluv[0] diry = cameradirection[1] + pixeluv[1] dirz = cameradirection[2] + pixeluv[2] length = math.sqrt(dirx2 + diry2 + dirz2) raydirection = (dirx / length, diry / length, dirz / length) # Check intersection with volume bounds (AABB) # volumebounds = [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz] tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0.0: if rayorigin[i] < volumebounds[2 i] or rayorigin[i] > volumebounds[2 i + 1]: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: t1 = (volumebounds[2 i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (volumebounds[2 i + 1] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # March through volume totalweightedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] totalweight = 0.0 currentt = tmin while currentt <= tmax: currentpos = (rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0] currentt, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1] currentt, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2] currentt) # Sample textures density = volumedensity[currentpos] # Not given in the sources: exact texture sampling implementation reaction = volumereaction[currentpos] # Not given in the sources: exact texture sampling implementation # Determine color based on reaction coordinate # Map reaction to gradient: core, border, smoke flamecolor = mapreactiontocolor(reaction) # Not given in the sources: exact gradient mapping algorithm # Weight by step length (ray length inside volume) totalweightedcolor = [totalweightedcolor[i] + flamecolor[i] stepsize for i in range(3)] totalweight += stepsize # Move along ray currentt += stepsize # Calculate average if totalweight > 0: finalcolor = [totalweightedcolor[i] / totalweight for i in range(3)] # Apply smoke color multiplication for realism finalcolor = [finalcolor[i] smokecolor[i] for i in range(3)] return finalcolor else: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Distinct spurts of burning particles caused by incompletely combusted fuel advected into the air. It is integrated by simulating an additional Voxel space of ember particles. Randomly generate ember particles at the bottom of the fire with Perlin noise. Propel particles upwards through advection. Raymarching procedure detects these particles and adds a small glowing aura around them to make them appear realistic. Rendering fire by accumulating values determined by the reaction coordinate Y rather than smoke density, using an artist-defined 1D texture that maps reaction coordinates to colors to give the appearance of fire. March through the volume and accumulate values determined by the reaction coordinate Y, using the 1D texture. To use the fire volume as a light source, sample the volume at several locations and treat each sample as a point light source, using the reaction coordinate and 1D color texture to determine intensity and color. Alternative lighting approach: downsample the texture of reaction coordinates to an extremely low resolution and use every voxel as a light source. Unlike smoke rendering which blends values during marching, fire rendering accumulates values based on the reaction coordinate. The low-resolution voxel lighting approach is less prone to flickering but does not capture high-frequency lighting effects such as local lighting due to sparks. Performance: Real-time (60+ fps) on an NVIDIA RTX 2060 graphics card. Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps along the ray within the volume. Strengths: GPU-friendly, real-time performance, realistic appearance with ember effects. Limitations: Severe flickering if treating volume samples as point light sources without enough samples. May not capture high-frequency lighting effects with low-resolution voxel lighting. Debugging is difficult due to HLSL limitations. Originated from a project by CS184 students, implementing a fire simulation and rendering pipeline. The rendering technique borrows from existing literature on volumetric clouds. The fire rendering approach is similar to smoke rendering but uses reaction coordinate accumulation. A more physically based discussion of fire rendering can be found in Nguyen et al. 2002. name: Fire Rendering
head: Fire Rendering via Reaction Coordinate, Fire Volume Rendering
body: Fire rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique that renders fire by accumulating values determined by a reaction coordinate Y rather than smoke density, using an artist-defined 1D texture to map these coordinates to fire colors. Unlike smoke rendering, which blends values during the marching process, fire rendering accumulates these reaction-based values to simulate the emissive nature of flames. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume texture containing the reaction coordinate Y for each voxel. An artist-defined 1D texture mapping reaction coordinates to colors. Camera parameters for ray generation. Output: A 2D image of the rendered fire. Optionally, lighting contributions for other scene objects. Data Structures: Reaction Coordinate Volume: A 3D texture where each voxel stores a scalar value Y. The layout and resolution depend on the simulation source. Color Map: A 1D texture (or array) mapping Y \in [0, 1] (or the simulation's range) to RGBA fire colors. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray from the camera origin through the pixel's position in world space. 2. Volume Intersection: Determine the entry and exit points of the ray with the fire volume bounding box. 3. Ray Marching: Step along the ray within the volume bounds. At each step, sample the reaction coordinate Y from the 3D volume texture. Sample the color C from the 1D color map using Y as the index. Accumulate the color. Unlike smoke, where alpha blending is standard, fire rendering accumulates values based on the reaction coordinate. The specific accumulation formula is not explicitly detailed in the source beyond "accumulating values," but typically this implies additive blending or integration of emissive intensity. 4. Lighting (Optional): Point Light Approach: Sample the volume at several locations. Treat each sample as a point light source. Use Y and the 1D color texture to determine the light's intensity and color. Voxel Light Approach: Downsample the reaction coordinate texture to an extremely low resolution. Use every voxel in this low-res texture as a light source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfire(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, colormap, numsamples): # Determine intersection with volume bounding box tmin, tmax = intersectboundingbox(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return backgroundcolor # Step along the ray stepsize = (tmax - tmin) / numsamples accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) for i in range(numsamples): t = tmin + i stepsize position = rayorigin + t raydirection # Sample reaction coordinate Y from volume Y = volumetexture.sample(position) # Map Y to fire color using 1D texture color = colormap.sample(Y) # Accumulate color (additive accumulation for emissive fire) accumulatedcolor += color stepsize # Standard integration approximation return accumulatedcolor def renderfirelightingpoint(volumetexture, colormap, numsamples): """ Alternative lighting approach: treat volume samples as point lights. """ lights = [] # Sample volume at several locations for in range(numsamples): position = randompointinvolume() Y = volumetexture.sample(position) color = colormap.sample(Y) intensity = calculateintensity(Y) # Implementation detail not specified lights.append(PointLight(position, color, intensity)) return lights def renderfirelightingvoxel(volumetexture, colormap, lowresvolume): """ Alternative lighting approach: downsample volume and use voxels as lights. """ lights = [] # Downsample reaction coordinate texture to extremely low resolution lowresvol = downsample(volumetexture, resolution=(1, 1, 1)) # Specific downsampling method not specified # Use every voxel as a light source for voxel in lowresvol: Y = voxel.value color = colormap.sample(Y) intensity = calculateintensity(Y) # Implementation detail not specified lights.append(PointLight(voxel.position, color, intensity)) return lights Parameters: Reaction Coordinate Y: The primary variable driving the visual appearance. It indexes into the 1D color texture. Number of Samples: Controls the smoothness of the ray marching. Too few samples in the point light approach can lead to severe flickering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flickering: Treating volume samples as point light sources can lead to severe flickering if not enough point samples are used. Loss of High-Frequency Effects: The low-resolution voxel lighting approach is less prone to flickering but does not capture high-frequency lighting effects such as local lighting due to sparks. Precision: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of rays (pixels). Lighting calculations add complexity based on the number of light sources generated. Memory Complexity: Depends on the resolution of the 3D reaction coordinate volume and the 1D color map. Strengths: Simple to implement; allows for artistic control via the 1D color texture; can be used as a light source. Limitations: The point light approach can flicker; the voxel light approach loses high-frequency details. When to use: When a stylized or artist-controlled fire appearance is desired, or when the fire volume is already available as a simulation output. When not to use: When physically accurate fire lighting with high-frequency details is required without significant performance cost. Fire rendering is discussed in the context of real-time fluid simulation and rendering. It is similar to smoke rendering but differs in the accumulation method and the use of the reaction coordinate. A more physically based discussion of fire rendering can be found in Nguyen et al. 2002.
