name: Raycasting with Transfer Function and Shading
head: Front-to-back volume raycasting with gradient-based diffuse shading
body: This method performs direct volume rendering by marching a ray through a 3D scalar field and accumulating color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. It distinguishes itself from basic raycasting by integrating a 1D transfer function for material mapping and gradient-based diffuse shading for surface appearance, while using jittered stepping to reduce aliasing artifacts. It serves as the core rendering loop for real-time GPU volume visualization, building on the discretization and ray setup provided by Ray Marching Volume Rendering. Inputs: position (vec4): The screen-space position of the fragment, used to determine ray origin and direction via cube map sampling. cubeFront (sampler2D, binding 0): Cube map face storing the entry point of the ray into the volume bounding box. cubeBack (sampler2D, binding 1): Cube map face storing the exit point of the ray from the volume bounding box. volume (sampler3D, binding 2): The 3D scalar field texture containing density or intensity values. gradients (sampler3D, binding 3): A 3D texture storing pre-computed surface normals, encoded as 2D vectors. transferFunction (sampler1D, binding 4): A 1D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA color and opacity. bakedNoise (sampler2D, binding 5): A 2D texture containing pre-generated noise values for ray jittering. ciModelMatrixInverseTranspose (mat3): The inverse-transpose of the model matrix, used to transform normals from object space to world space. light (struct): Contains direction (vec3), ambient (vec3), and diffuse (vec3). threshold (ivec2): The range of iso-values (0-255) to render. Default is (0, 255). stepSize (vec3): The step size vector in each dimension. iterations (int): The maximum number of ray marching steps. diffuseShading (bool): Flag to enable or disable gradient-based shading. stepScale (float): A scaling factor used in opacity correction. glFragCoord (vec2): The current fragment coordinates, used for noise sampling. Outputs: oColor (vec4, location 0): The final accumulated color with alpha 1.0. oNormal (vec3, location 1): The normal at the last sampled position (or zero if no valid sample). glFragDepth: The depth of the ray's final position. The method relies on standard OpenGL sampler types. The gradients texture stores normals in a compressed 2D format to save memory. The normal decoding follows the spheremap transform attributed to Cry Engine 3 and Martin Mittring. 1. Ray Setup: Compute texture coordinates texC from position.xy / position.w. Adjust coordinates: texC.x = 0.5 texC.x + 0.5, texC.y = 0.5 texC.y - 0.5. Sample the front and back faces of the volume bounding box: front = texture(cubeFront, texC).xyz and back = texture(cubeBack, texC).xyz. Compute the ray direction: dir = normalize(back - front). Initialize the ray position pos = vec4(front, 0), destination color dst = vec4(0), source color src = vec4(0), and accumulated value value = vec4(0). Compute the step vector: step = dir stepSize. Jitter the start position to reduce aliasing: pos.xyz += step texture(bakedNoise, glFragCoord.xy / 256).x. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to iterations - 1. Set pos.w = 0. Sample the volume scalar value: value.a = texture(volume, pos.xyz).x. Convert the scalar to an integer iso-value: isoValue = int(255.0f value.a). Check if the iso-value is within the rendering threshold: if (isoValue >= threshold.x && isoValue <= threshold.y): Sample the transfer function: src = texture(transferFunction, value.a). Apply opacity correction to account for step size: src.a = 1 - pow((1 - src.a), stepScale / 0.5). If diffuseShading is true: Sample the encoded gradient: encoded = texture(gradients, pos.xyz).xy. Decode the normal using the spheremap transform: n.z = dot(encoded, encoded) 2.0 - 1.0. n.xy = normalize(encoded.xy) sqrt(1.0 - n.z n.z). value.xyz = n. Transform the normal to world space: normal = normalize(ciModelMatrixInverseTranspose value.xyz). Compute the light direction: lightDir = normalize(-light.direction). Compute the Lambertian diffuse factor: lambert = max(dot(normal, lightDir), 0.0). Apply shading to the source color: src.rgb = light.diffuse lambert src.rgb + light.ambient src.rgb. Perform front-to-back blending: src.rgb = src.a. dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst. Early Termination: If dst.a >= 0.95, break the loop. Advance the ray position: pos.xyz += step. Boundary Check: If pos.x > 1.0 || pos.y > 1.0 || pos.z > 1.0, break the loop. 3. Output: Set oColor = vec4(dst.rgb, 1.0). Set oNormal = value.xyz. Set glFragDepth = pos.z. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodenormal(enc: vec2) -> vec3: """Decode normal from 2D spheremap encoding.""" nz = dot(enc, enc) 2.0 - 1.0 nxy = normalize(enc.xy) sqrt(1.0 - nz nz) return vec3(nxy.x, nxy.y, nz) def main(): # 1. Ray Setup texc = position.xy / position.w texc.x = 0.5 texc.x + 0.5 texc.y = 0.5 texc.y - 0.5 front = texture(cubeFront, texc).xyz back = texture(cubeBack, texc).xyz dir = normalize(back - front) pos = vec4(front.x, front.y, front.z, 0.0) dst = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) src = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) value = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) step = dir stepSize # Jitter start position noiseval = texture(bakedNoise, glFragCoord.xy / 256.0).x pos.xyz += step noiseval # 2. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(iterations): pos.w = 0.0 # Sample volume value.a = texture(volume, pos.xyz).x isovalue = int(255.0 value.a) if threshold.x <= isovalue <= threshold.y: # Sample transfer function src = texture(transferFunction, value.a) # Opacity correction src.a = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - src.a, stepScale / 0.5) if diffuseShading: # Sample and decode gradient enc = texture(gradients, pos.xyz).xy value.xyz = decodenormal(enc) # Transform normal normal = normalize(ciModelMatrixInverseTranspose value.xyz) # Lighting lightdir = normalize(-light.direction) lambert = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) # Apply shading src.rgb = light.diffuse lambert src.rgb + light.ambient src.rgb # Front-to-back blending src.rgb = src.a dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst # Early termination if dst.a >= 0.95: break # Advance position pos.xyz += step # Boundary check if pos.x > 1.0 or pos.y > 1.0 or pos.z > 1.0: break # 3. Output oColor = vec4(dst.rgb, 1.0) oNormal = value.xyz glFragDepth = pos.z Normal Decoding (Spheremap Transform): Given encoded normal enc (vec2): nz = \text{dot}(enc, enc) \times 2.0 - 1.0 n{xy} = \text{normalize}(enc.xy) \times \sqrt{1.0 - nz^2} n = (n{xy}, nz) Opacity Correction: src.a = 1 - (1 - src.a)^{\frac{stepScale}{0.5}} Front-to-Back Blending: dst = (1 - dst.a) \times src + dst stepScale: Float parameter used in opacity correction. Typical value not specified, but used as divisor in exponent. threshold: ivec2 defining the range of iso values (0-255) to render. Default from TransferFunction is (0, 255). stepSize: vec3 defining the step size in each dimension. iterations: int defining the maximum number of ray marching steps. Out of Bounds: The ray position is checked against 1.0 in x, y, and z. If any coordinate exceeds 1.0, the loop breaks immediately. Early Termination: The ray marching loop breaks if the accumulated alpha dst.a reaches or exceeds 0.95, optimizing performance for opaque regions. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Real-time performance on modern GPUs. Gradient-based shading provides realistic surface appearance. Jittered stepping reduces aliasing artifacts. Simple implementation using standard OpenGL features. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or loss of detail if not tuned properly. Pre-computed gradients require additional memory and preprocessing. Limited to scalar fields; does not support vector fields or complex volume data types without modification. Use this method for real-time visualization of 3D scalar fields (e.g., medical imaging, smoke, clouds) where performance is critical and gradient-based shading is desired. It is suitable when the volume data is static or changes slowly, allowing for pre-computed gradients. Avoid for high-fidelity offline rendering where ray tracing or path tracing is preferred for accurate lighting and shadows. Not suitable for dynamic vector fields or non-scalar volume data without significant modification. This method is implemented in the VolumeRendering project by Jose Villegas. It utilizes a fragment shader to perform front-to-back volume raycasting, integrating a 1D transfer function and gradient-based diffuse shading. The normal decoding technique is attributed to the Cry Engine 3 and Martin Mittring. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, https://github.com/jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Evaluation Stepping DVR
head: Direct Volume Rendering Stepping, Ray Evaluation Stepping, Stepping DVR
body: Ray Evaluation Stepping DVR is a fixed-step ray marching technique for Direct Volume Rendering that integrates density and color along a ray, supporting configurable density ranges and early-out termination. It distinguishes itself from its siblings by explicitly supporting both world-space and object-space indexing based on the volume's capabilities, and by using a modular shader define system to swap transfer functions, blending, and BRDF evaluations at compile time. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (density or color), ray origin (rayStart), ray direction (rayDir), volume bounding box (AABB), and configuration parameters. Output: A final color (output.color), normal (output.normal), and depth (output.depth). Data Structures: The method uses a Parameters struct passed to the kernel, typically stored in constant memory for efficient access. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Parameters { float stepsize; // Distance between samples along the ray float alphaEarlyOut; // Alpha threshold for early termination float densityMin; // Minimum density value for normalization float densityMax; // Maximum density value for normalization }; Parameters and Typical Values: stepsize: Default 0.005. alphaEarlyOut: Default 1.0 - 10^{-5}. enableEarlyOut: Boolean, default true. minDensity: Default 0. maxDensity: Default 1. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Step Size Calculation: Determine the step size based on volume indexing support: If the volume supports object-space indexing: stepsize = \frac{voxelSize}{stepsPerVoxel} where stepsPerVoxel is controlled by a UI slider in the range [0.1, 10.0]. If the volume does not support object-space indexing: stepsize = \frac{maxSize}{stepsPerRay} where maxSize is the volume's bounding box size, and stepsPerRay is controlled by a UI slider in the range [10, 1000.0]. 2. Configuration and Shader Compilation: Set Parameters struct fields: stepsize, alphaEarlyOut, densityMin, densityMax. Copy Parameters to device constant memory. Generate shader defines based on configuration: RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGVOLUMEINTERPOLATIONT RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGTRANSFERFUNCTIONT RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGBLENDINGT RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGBRDFT RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGENABLEEARLYOUT: Set to 1 if enableEarlyOut is true, else 0. RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGSKIPTRANSFERFUNCTION: Set to 1 if volume output type is Density (0), else 1 if Color (1). If neither, throw runtime error. 3. Ray-Volume Intersection: Intersect the ray with the volume's AABB to get t{min} and t{max1}. Clamp t{min} to 0. Clamp t{max} to \min(t{max1}, t{max}), where t{max} is the ray's maximum extent. 4. Initialization: Initialize output: output.color = (0, 0, 0, 0), output.normal = (0, 0, 0), output.depth = 0. Initialize previousDensity = -1. Initialize terminationIndex = 0. 5. Ray Marching Loop: While the step is valid: Calculate current distance: t{current} = t{min} + terminationIndex \times stepsize. Validity Check: Condition 1: t{current} \le t{max}. Condition 2 (if RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGENABLEEARLYOUT is 1): output.color.w < alphaEarlyOut. If either condition fails, break the loop. If KERNELSYNCHRONIZEDTRACING is 0, break if the current thread is invalid. If 1, break if all threads in the warp are invalid. Sample Position: position = rayStart + rayDir \times t{current} Volume Evaluation: If RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGSKIPTRANSFERFUNCTION is 1: Evaluate volume for real4 color directly. Multiply color's alpha (w) by stepsize. Evaluate normal. Else: Evaluate volume for realt density. Normalize density: density2 = (value - densityMin) \times divDensityRange where divDensityRange = \frac{1}{densityMax - densityMin}. If requireNormal is true (and value \ge densityMin): Evaluate normal using volume.evalNormal. If KERNELSYNCHRONIZEDTRACING is 1, evaluate if any thread requires normal. Transfer Function (if not skipped): Evaluate transfer function: color1 = tf.eval(density2, n, previousDensity, stepsize, batch) Update previousDensity = density2. BRDF (if alpha > 0): If color1.w > 0: color2 = brdf.eval(color1, position, n, rayDir, batch) Else color2 = color1. Blending: Normalize normal n. Create newContribution with color2, n, and t{current}. If valid, update output: output = blending.eval(output, newContribution) Increment terminationIndex. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayevaluationsteppingdvr(raystart, raydir, volume, params): """ raystart: float3 raydir: float3 volume: Volume object with evaldensity, evalnormal, evalcolor methods params: Parameters struct with stepsize, alphaEarlyOut, densityMin, densityMax """ # 1. Intersection tmin, tmax1 = intersectaabb(raystart, raydir, volume.aabb) tmin = max(0.0, tmin) tmax = min(tmax1, raymaxextent) # raymaxextent is external input # 2. Initialization outputcolor = float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) outputnormal = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) outputdepth = 0.0 previousdensity = -1.0 terminationindex = 0 divdensityrange = 1.0 / (params.densityMax - params.densityMin) # Determine mode based on volume output type skiptf = (volume.outputtype == DENSITY) # 0 for Density, 1 for Color # 3. Loop while True: tcurrent = tmin + terminationindex params.stepsize # Validity check if tcurrent > tmax: break if params.enableearlyout and outputcolor.w >= params.alphaEarlyOut: break # Position position = raystart + raydir tcurrent # Volume Evaluation if skiptf: # Direct color evaluation colorraw = volume.evalcolor(position) colorraw.w = params.stepsize normal = volume.evalnormal(position) color1 = colorraw else: # Density evaluation densityval = volume.evaldensity(position) # Normalization density2 = (densityval - params.densityMin) divdensityrange # Normal evaluation if required normal = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if densityval >= params.densityMin: normal = volume.evalnormal(position) # Transfer Function color1 = transferfunction.eval(density2, normal, previousdensity, params.stepsize) previousdensity = density2 # BRDF if color1.w > 0: color2 = brdf.eval(color1, position, normal, raydir) else: color2 = color1 # Blending if isvalidsample: normalizednormal = normalize(normal) newcontribution = Contribution(color2, normalizednormal, tcurrent) outputcolor, outputnormal, outputdepth = blending.eval( outputcolor, outputnormal, outputdepth, newcontribution) terminationindex += 1 return outputcolor, outputnormal, outputdepth A general category of techniques sampling volume data along rays. Ray Evaluation Stepping DVR is a specific implementation within this category using fixed steps and modular shader defines. Link Focuses specifically on marching through density fields. Ray Evaluation Stepping DVR extends this by including color, BRDF, and transfer function evaluation. Link An alternative approach that pre-integrates volume data into a discrete integral. Ray Evaluation Stepping DVR performs integration on-the-fly during ray marching. Link A specialized technique for light shafts. Ray Evaluation Stepping DVR is a general-purpose DVR method, not specific to light shafts. Link Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps along the ray, determined by stepsize and ray length. Memory Complexity: O(1) per thread for the marching state, plus O(V) for the volume data storage. Performance: Depends heavily on GPU hardware (RTX series recommended) and volume resolution. Early-out can significantly reduce average step count. Strengths: Modular design allows easy swapping of transfer functions and blending modes. Supports both world-space and object-space indexing. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or excessive sampling if not tuned. Requires careful configuration of density ranges. When to use: When flexible transfer function and blending integration is needed, and the volume supports the required indexing mode. When not to use: When adaptive step size is required for high-frequency details, or when the volume does not support the required indexing mode and adaptive stepping is critical. The method is described in the context of the fV-SRN project, which uses CUDA and OpenGL for volume rendering. It is part of a larger renderer library that supports various volume formats and compression techniques. The project targets NVIDIA RTX GPUs and uses Python for configuration and training integration. shamanDevel/fV-SRN, https://github.com/shamanDevel/fV-SRN, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Density Marching
head: Simple Ray Marching
body: Density Marching is a direct volume ray casting technique that samples a 3D texture along a ray cast from the camera through a volume bounding box, accumulating color and opacity using front-to-back blending. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on a fixed number of steps (STEPS) rather than adaptive or distance-based stepping, and its specific implementation of procedural noise (Worley and Perlin) combined with boundary fading for cloud-like volumes. Unlike Ray Evaluation Stepping DVR which may use variable step sizes, Density Marching uses a uniform discretization of the ray path. Inputs and Outputs: The method operates in a fragment shader. Inputs include a vertex attribute vUVW (vec3), uniform data containing viewProj (mat4) and globalCameraPos (vec4), a 3D texture sampler volumeTex (binding 1), and push constants containing model (mat4) and localCameraPos (vec4). The output is outColor (vec4). Data Structures: rayOrigin: vec3, camera position. rayDirection: vec3, normalized direction vector. accum: vec4, accumulates RGB color and Alpha opacity. currentPos: vec3, current position along the ray. deltaStep: vec3, step vector. densityTotal: float, integrated density for transmittance. brightness: float, accumulated scattered light. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Direction Calculation: Compute the ray direction by normalizing the difference between the interpolated vertex attribute and the local camera position: \vec{rayDir} = \text{normalize}(\vec{vUVW} - \vec{localCameraPos}) 2. Ray-Box Intersection: Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box (defined as boxMin = vec3(0.0) and boxMax = vec3(1.0) in the source, though other sources use explicit min/max bounds) using the slab method to obtain entry and exit distances tNear and tFar. 3. Ray Segment Validation: Calculate tStart = max(tNear, 0.0) and tEnd = max(tFar, 0.0). Compute totalDist = tEnd - tStart. If totalDist <= 0.0, discard the fragment. 4. Ray Initialization: Calculate the starting ray position at the box entry point: \vec{rayPosition} = \vec{rayOrigin} + \vec{rayDir} \times tStart Initialize densityTotal = 0.0 and brightness = 0.0. 5. Wind Scrolling (Optional): Apply wind scrolling to the ray position if time-based animation is enabled: \vec{scrollPosition} = \vec{rayPosition} + (\vec{windTime}, 0, 0) 6. Boundary Fading (Optional): Calculate fade factors for the top and bottom boundaries to prevent abrupt cutoffs. \text{distToBot} = \frac{\vec{rayPosition}.y - \text{boxMin}.y}{\text{boxMax}.y - \text{boxMin}.y} \text{botFizzle} = \text{clamp}(\text{distToBot} \times 10.0, 0, 1) \text{topFizzle} = \text{clamp}((1.0 - \text{distToBot}) \times 10.0, 0, 1) \text{totalFizzle} = \text{botFizzle} \times \text{topFizzle} 7. Step Calculation: Compute the step size: \text{stepSize} = \frac{\text{totalDist}}{\text{STEPS}} Initialize currentPos = \vec{localCameraPos} + \vec{rayDir} \times tStart and deltaStep = \vec{rayDir} \times \text{stepSize}. 8. Procedural Density Generation (Optional): If using procedural noise instead of a 3D texture, compute Worley density using Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM): Initialize amplitude = 1.0, frequency = 1.0, amplitudeTotal = 0.0, worleyDensity = 0.0. Loop OctaveCount times: worleyDensity += ProceduralWorley(\vec{scrollPosition} \times \text{frequency}, 1.0 / \text{CloudScale}) \times \text{amplitude} amplitudeTotal += amplitude amplitude /= 2.0 frequency = 2.0 worleyDensity /= amplitudeTotal Additionally, compute Perlin density: \text{perlinDensity} = \text{ProceduralPerlin}(\vec{scrollPosition}, \text{CloudScale} \times 0.8) Combine densities: \text{density} = \text{worleyDensity} \times \text{perlinDensity} \times \text{totalFizzle} 9. Marching Loop: Loop i from 0 to STEPS - 1: Sample Density: If using texture: density = texture(volumeTex, currentPos).r. If using procedural: Use the calculated density from Step 8. Threshold Check: If density > 0.01 (texture) or density > DensityThreshold (procedural), proceed; otherwise, skip accumulation for this step. Accumulate Opacity and Color (Texture Path): color = vec3(density). alpha = density \times \text{DENSITY\MULTIPLIER} \times \text{stepSize}. Update accumulation: \vec{accum}.rgb += (1.0 - \vec{accum}.a) \times \vec{color} \times \alpha \vec{accum}.a += (1.0 - \vec{accum}.a) \times \alpha Accumulate Light (Procedural Path): Update densityTotal += density \times \text{stepSize}. Calculate sunTransmittance using a MarchLight function. Calculate cameraTransmittance = \exp(-\text{densityTotal} \times \text{AbsorptionCoefficient}). Calculate scatter using Henyey-Greenstein (HG) phase function. Add to brightness: \text{brightness} += \text{density} \times \text{sunTransmittance} \times \text{cameraTransmittance} \times \text{scatter} \times \text{stepSize} \times 0.5 Advance Position: \vec{currentPos} += \vec{deltaStep} If using procedural path, increment distanceTravelled by stepSize. 10. Final Output: If accum.a < 0.001, discard the fragment. Otherwise, output outColor = accum. Parameters: STEPS: Integer, number of samples per ray. Typical value: 128. DENSITYMULTIPLIER: Float, scales sampled density to alpha. Typical value: 5.0. StepSize: Float, step size for marching (derived from totalDist / STEPS). StepLimit: Integer, maximum number of steps. WindTime: Float, time variable for scrolling. CloudScale: Float, scale factor for procedural noise. OctaveCount: Integer, number of FBM octaves for Worley noise. DensityThreshold: Float, minimum density for contribution. AbsorptionCoefficient: Float, absorption coefficient for transmittance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The slab method for ray-box intersection must handle cases where the ray is parallel to a slab boundary. Boundaries: Without totalFizzle, volumes may exhibit hard edges at the top and bottom of the bounding box. Degenerate Input: If totalDist <= 0.0, the ray does not intersect the volume, and the fragment should be discarded to avoid undefined behavior. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. vUVW: vec3 localCameraPos: vec3 boxMin: vec3 = vec3(0.0) boxMax: vec3 = vec3(1.0) STEPS: int = 128 DENSITYMULTIPLIER: float = 5.0 AbsorptionCoefficient: float = 1.0 CloudScale: float = 1.0 WindTime: float = 0.0 OctaveCount: int = 4 DensityThreshold: float = 0.01 rayDir = normalize(vUVW - localCameraPos) invDir = 1.0 / rayDir tNear = (boxMin - localCameraPos) invDir tFar = (boxMax - localCameraPos) invDir tMin = max(min(tNear), min(tFar)) tMax = min(max(tNear), max(tFar)) tStart = max(tMin.x, 0.0) # Assuming tMin is vec3 of entry times, taking max component for entry tEnd = tMax.x # Assuming tMax is vec3 of exit times, taking min component for exit? t0 = (boxMin - localCameraPos) / rayDir t1 = (boxMax - localCameraPos) / rayDir tNear = max(max(t0.x, t0.y), t0.z) tFar = min(min(t1.x, t1.y), t1.z) totalDist = tFar - tNear if totalDist <= 0.0: discardfragment() rayPosition = localCameraPos + rayDir tNear densityTotal = 0.0 brightness = 0.0 accum = vec4(0.0) scrollPosition = rayPosition + vec3(WindTime, 0.0, 0.0) distToBot = (rayPosition.y - boxMin.y) / (boxMax.y - boxMin.y) botFizzle = clamp(distToBot 10.0, 0.0, 1.0) topFizzle = clamp((1.0 - distToBot) 10.0, 0.0, 1.0) totalFizzle = botFizzle topFizzle stepSize = totalDist / STEPS currentPos = localCameraPos + rayDir tNear deltaStep = rayDir stepSize worleyDensity = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 frequency = 1.0 amplitudeTotal = 0.0 for i in range(OctaveCount): worleyDensity += ProceduralWorley(scrollPosition frequency, 1.0 / CloudScale) amplitude amplitudeTotal += amplitude amplitude /= 2.0 frequency = 2.0 worleyDensity /= amplitudeTotal perlinDensity = ProceduralPerlin(scrollPosition, CloudScale 0.8) density = worleyDensity perlinDensity totalFizzle for i in range(STEPS): # Determine density source if usetexture: density = texture(volumeTex, currentPos).r threshold = 0.01 else: threshold = DensityThreshold if density > threshold: if usetexture: color = vec3(density) alpha = density DENSITYMULTIPLIER stepSize accum.rgb += (1.0 - accum.a) color alpha accum.a += (1.0 - accum.a) alpha else: densityTotal += density stepSize # Placeholder for MarchLight and HG scatter calculation as per S2 # sunTransmittance = MarchLight(...) # cameraTransmittance = exp(-densityTotal AbsorptionCoefficient) # scatter = HG(...) # brightness += density sunTransmittance cameraTransmittance scatter stepSize 0.5 currentPos += deltaStep if accum.a < 0.001: discardfragment() outColor = accum A broader category of techniques using ray marching for volume rendering. Density Marching is a specific implementation within this category. Link Uses variable step sizes based on density evaluation. Density Marching uses fixed steps. Link Focuses on the discrete integration of the volume rendering integral. Density Marching is a numerical approximation of this. Link Specifically targets light shafts (god rays) using raymarching. Density Marching targets general volume density. Link Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of pixels (fragments) and R is the number of steps (STEPS). Since STEPS is fixed (e.g., 128), it is linear with respect to pixel count. Memory Complexity: O(1) per fragment, plus the memory for the 3D texture or procedural noise state. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution and step count. Increasing STEPS improves quality but increases cost proportionally. Strengths: Simple to implement; fixed step count ensures predictable performance; procedural noise allows for infinite resolution without texture memory. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or slow convergence in sparse volumes; no adaptive stepping for efficiency. When to use: Real-time rendering of cloud-like volumes where performance predictability is key and high-frequency detail is generated via procedural noise. When not to use: When high accuracy in sparse volumes is required without excessive steps, or when texture memory is limited and procedural noise is too expensive. Density Marching originates from early direct volume ray casting techniques. The specific implementation described here is found in unofficial repositories for volume rendering tutorials and cloud shaders. It builds on the foundational work of Fixed Step Ray Marching. vis-magnus-2018, https://github.com/GitThirteen/vis-magnus-2018, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) volumetric-cloud-renderer, https://github.com/ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Discrete Volume Rendering Integral (VRI)
head: Pass 2 Fragment Shader VRI Evaluation
body: The Discrete Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) is the numerical approximation of the continuous Volume Rendering Integral used in fixed-step ray marching to compute pixel color from a 3D scalar field. It solves the problem of integrating light emission and absorption along a ray by replacing path integrals with a Riemann sum over discrete sample points. It sets itself apart from Classical Ray Tracing Integration by assuming a piecewise-constant density and color model within each segment, leading to a specific closed-form integration of the transmittance term that differs from higher-order or analytical approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Entry texture coordinate s{in}, exit texture coordinate s{out}, slice spacing in world coordinates \Delta x, spatial dimensions of the bounding box x{dim}, y{dim}, z{dim}, backlight color L{backlight}, 3D volume texture for attenuation \tau, and optional 1D transfer function for \tau' and kd. Output: Final pixel color L{out}. Data Structures: 3D Volume Texture: Stores attenuation values \tau(s) at 3D texture coordinates. 1D Transfer Function (Optional): Maps attenuation \tau to modified attenuation \tau' and emission coefficient kd. Gradient Texture (Optional): Stores volume gradients for shading computation of C(s). Parameters: \Delta x: Slice spacing in world coordinates (typical value depends on volume resolution and bounding box size; Not given in the sources). \Delta s: Spacing in texture coordinates along the ray, derived from \Delta x and spatial dimensions. Steps: 1. Compute \Delta s: Calculate the spatial locations of the entry and exit points from their texture coordinates. Divide the spatial segment between these points into pieces of length \Delta x. The value \Delta s is the difference in texture coordinates corresponding to one piece of length \Delta x. 2. Initialize: Set L{out} = (0,0,0) and accumulated transparency t = 1. 3. Iterate: For each step s from s{in} to s{out} with increment \Delta s: a. Lookup Attenuation: Retrieve \tau(s) from the 3D volume texture. If a transfer function exists, look up \tau' and kd from the 1D transfer function using \tau(s). b. Compute Opacity: Calculate \alpha = \tau(s) \; \Delta x. c. Compute Color: Determine C(s) using the volume gradient (e.g., Phong equation) or other shading methods, potentially using the gradient texture and kd. d. Accumulate Light: Update L{out} = L{out} + t \; C(s) \; \alpha. e. Update Transparency: Update t = t \; (1 - \alpha). 4. Finalize: Return L{out} + t \; L{backlight}, where L{backlight} is the light coming from behind the volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevri(sin, sout, deltax, xdim, ydim, zdim, Lbacklight, volumetexture, transferfunction=None, gradienttexture=None): # Step 1: Compute deltas # Compute spatial locations of entry and exit points from sin and sout # spatialin = texturetoworld(sin, xdim, ydim, zdim) # spatialout = texturetoworld(sout, xdim, ydim, zdim) # spatialsegmentlength = length(spatialout - spatialin) # numsteps = round(spatialsegmentlength / deltax) # if numsteps == 0: return Lbacklight # deltas = (sout - sin) / numsteps Lout = (0, 0, 0) t = 1.0 # Step 3: Iterate s = sin while s <= sout: # Step 3a: Lookup Attenuation tau = volumetexture.sample(s) if transferfunction is not None: tauprime, kd = transferfunction.sample(tau) alpha = tauprime deltax else: alpha = tau deltax # Step 3b: Compute Color C(s) # C(s) is computed using volume gradient or other methods # gradient = gradienttexture.sample(s) if gradienttexture else computegradient(s) # C(s) = shadingmodel(gradient, tau, kd) Cs = computecolor(s, gradienttexture, tau, kd if transferfunction else None) # Step 3c: Accumulate Light Lout = Lout + t Cs alpha # Step 3d: Update Transparency t = t (1 - alpha) s = s + deltas # Step 4: Finalize return Lout + t Lbacklight Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computing \Delta s: A common pitfall is using texture coordinate spacing directly instead of deriving it from the world-space slice spacing \Delta x. The change in texture coordinates must advance the spatial position by \Delta x. Precision: Accumulating transparency t can suffer from precision loss if many steps are taken; however, the incremental update t = t \times (1 - \alpha) is generally stable for typical volume rendering parameters. Degenerate Input: If the ray does not intersect the volume (s{in} = s{out}), the loop does not execute, and the result is L{backlight}. Volume Raycasting Discretization is the numerical approximation of the continuous Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) by replacing the path integrals with a Riemann sum over discrete sample points along a ray. It solves the problem of computing the final pixel color from a 3D scalar field by casting parallel rays from the eye through each pixel, sampling the volume at fixed intervals, and compositing the results front-to-back. It sets itself apart from Classical Ray Tracing Integration by assuming a piecewise-constant density and color model within each segment, leading to a specific closed-form integration of the transmittance term that differs from higher-order or analytical approaches. Classical Ray Tracing Integration is a volume rendering technique that computes pixel color by combining background transmission (attenuated by absorption) and uniform in-scattering. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric objects with defined boundaries or integrating geometric visibility directly into volume pipelines. Unlike standard direct volume ray casting which samples uniformly along the entire ray, this method explicitly calculates entry and exit points to limit sampling to the volume interior and applies Beer's law for transmission. It is distinguished from Alpha Compositing Ray Casting by its handling of homogeneous spheres via analytical integration, and from Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching by its assumption of uniform scattering color. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps along the ray, O(N), where N is the number of samples between s{in} and s{out}. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, excluding the storage for the 3D volume texture and optional transfer/gradient textures. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the resolution of the volume texture, the slice spacing \Delta x, and the hardware's texture sampling capabilities. Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with volume resolution and ray length. Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient on GPUs due to regular memory access patterns, and provides good visual quality for many applications. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missing details if \Delta x is too large. Requires careful computation of \Delta s to maintain spatial accuracy. When to Use: Suitable for real-time volume rendering where performance is critical and the volume data is dense. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes requiring high accuracy in sparse volumes or where adaptive stepping is beneficial. The Discrete Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) is a fundamental technique in GPU-based volume rendering, as described in educational materials on GPU volume rendering. It builds on the principles of direct volume ray casting and fixed-step ray marching, providing a practical method for evaluating the volume rendering integral in a fragment shader. name: Volume Raycasting Discretization
head: Discrete VRE, Discrete Volume Rendering Equation, Discrete Volume Rendering Integral, Discrete volume rendering, Riemann sum VRE, Volume ray marching
body: Volume Raycasting Discretization is the numerical approximation of the continuous Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) by replacing the path integrals with a Riemann sum over discrete sample points along a ray. It solves the problem of computing the final pixel color from a 3D scalar field by casting parallel rays from the eye through each pixel, sampling the volume at fixed intervals, and compositing the results front-to-back. It sets itself apart from Classical Ray Tracing Integration by assuming a piecewise-constant density and color model within each segment, leading to a specific closed-form integration of the transmittance term that differs from higher-order or analytical approaches. Inputs: A 3D scalar field f of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Camera parameters: eye position, view direction, and projection plane. Transfer function TF mapping scalar values to color C and opacity \alpha. Step size \Delta s (or number of samples W). Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel (u,v) contains the accumulated color L(u,v). Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored as a 3D array or 3D texture. For CPU implementations, a common layout is row-major: volumes[z][x + y width]. For GPU, a 3D texture stores scalar values and optionally precomputed gradients. Ray State: Accumulated color C{acc} (RGB) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} (float), initialized to 0. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel (u,v), compute the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Determine the entry point s{in} and exit point s{out} of the ray with the volume bounding box. 2. Discretization: Divide the segment [s{in}, s{out}] into W intervals of length \Delta si = s{i+1} - si. The sample positions are \mathbf{r}(si) = \mathbf{o} + si \mathbf{d}. 3. Sampling: For each sample i from 0 to W-1: Evaluate the scalar value v = f(\mathbf{r}(si)) using trilinear interpolation from the 8 surrounding voxels. Map v to color \hat{C}i and opacity \alphai using the transfer function. Note: \hat{C}i is often pre-multiplied by \alphai in the compositing formula. 4. Transmittance and Weight Calculation: Compute the transmittance Ti entering segment i. T0 = 1. For i > 0, Ti = T{i-1} \exp(-\alpha{i-1} \Delta s{i-1}). Compute the weight wi contributed by segment i. Assuming constant opacity \alphai over the segment, the integral of the extinction term yields: wi = Ti \left( 1 - \exp(-\alphai \Delta si) \right). Note: Some implementations approximate this simply as wi = Ti \alphai \Delta si (first-order Taylor expansion) or use \alphai directly if \Delta s is normalized. The exponential form is more accurate for finite step sizes. 5. Compositing (Front-to-Back): Update accumulated color and opacity: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + \hat{C}i \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + \alphai \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}). Alternatively, using weights wi and non-premultiplied color Ci: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + wi \cdot Ci \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + wi. 6. Termination: If \alpha{acc} \ge 1 - \epsilon (early ray termination) or the ray exits the volume, stop processing. 7. Final Color: If a background was not composited, the final pixel color is C{final} = C{acc} / \alpha{acc} (if \alpha{acc} > 0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeraycastingdiscretization(volumedata, transferfunction, camera, stepsize): # Initialize output image with zeros (RGB channels) image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): # 1. Ray Initialization rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(x, y) entryt, exitt = computeraybboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata.bounds) if entryt >= exitt: continue # Accumulators acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # 2. Discretization and 3. Sampling Loop t = entryt while t < exitt: # Sample position samplepos = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) # Check bounds if not isinsidevolume(samplepos, volumedata.bounds): t += stepsize continue # 3. Sampling scalarval = trilinearinterpolate(volumedata, samplepos) color, alpha = transferfunction(scalarval) # Pre-multiply color by alpha premultcolor = (color[0] alpha, color[1] alpha, color[2] alpha) # 5. Compositing (Front-to-Back) acccolor = (acccolor[0] + premultcolor[0] (1.0 - accalpha), acccolor[1] + premultcolor[1] (1.0 - accalpha), acccolor[2] + premultcolor[2] (1.0 - accalpha)) accalpha = accalpha + alpha (1.0 - accalpha) # 6. Termination if accalpha >= 0.99: break # Advance t += stepsize # 7. Final Color image[y][x] = acccolor return image def computeraybboxintersection(origin, direction, bounds): # Standard slab method to find entry and exit t values return 0.0, 1.0 def isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): return bounds.min[0] <= pos[0] <= bounds.max[0] and bounds.min[1] <= pos[1] <= bounds.max[1] and bounds.min[2] <= pos[2] <= bounds.max[2] def trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos): # Returns interpolated scalar value at pos return 0.0 def transferfunction(scalar): # Returns (color: tuple of 3 floats, alpha: float) return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0), 0.5 Parameters: stepsize: Distance between samples. Typical values range from 0.001 to 0.01 in normalized coordinates, or fixed voxel counts. Too large causes aliasing/undersampling; too small reduces performance. epsilon: Threshold for early ray termination. Typical value 0.95 or 0.99. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: If the ray entry/exit points do not align with sample positions, corner samples may be missed or double-counted, causing stepping artifacts or intensity gaps. Interpolation Bias: Integer casting of floating-point coordinates truncates toward zero, potentially causing sampling bias near boundaries. Gradient Clamping: If normals are computed via central differences, neighbor indices at volume edges must be clamped to prevent out-of-bounds access. Transmittance Initialization: The transmittance for the first segment must be explicitly 1.0. A sample placement strategy where the first sample point is calculated relative to the eye position, creating a sampling pattern that forms concentric lines across pixels. It optimizes sampling positions to reduce aliasing compared to uniform grid alignment. A technique that improves ray integration approximation by using a 2D \psi table independent of the transfer function. This allows interactive transfer function changes without recomputing the integration table, differing from standard discretization which recomputes weights per sample. A direct volume rendering technique implemented on the CPU using explicit multithreading. It distinguishes itself by using specific implementations of trilinear interpolation and early ray termination on CPU architectures, unlike GPU-based raycasting which leverages parallel shaders. A simplified alternative to front-to-back compositing that averages scalar intensities along rays. It treats the volume as a transparent medium where every sample contributes equally, ignoring opacity and absorption, making it computationally inexpensive but low contrast. A strategy that adapts sampling density along the ray based on view-dependent frequency, respecting the Nyquist limit. It uses a quadratic sampling function derived from ray differentials, providing finer steps near the viewpoint and coarser steps further away to prevent aliasing. An extension that approximates the in-scattering term of the radiative transfer equation using a Riemann sum. It explicitly evaluates the influx of scattered light via auxiliary light rays and Beer's law, unlike standard discretization which ignores scattering. The foundational approximation assuming density and color are constant within each segment. It requires no pre-computed tables or linear interpolation, relying on a piecewise-constant assumption. It is simpler than Partial Pre-Integration but suffers from visible discontinuities at low sampling rates. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot W), where P is the number of pixels and W is the number of samples per ray. Rendering time grows linearly with dataset size if all voxels are visited, but optimizations like early termination reduce this. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for the volume data. The algorithm itself uses O(1) auxiliary memory per ray. Performance: On a 500x500 resolution with a 150^3 voxel dataset, performance depends heavily on stepsize and early termination efficiency. Strengths: Simple to implement, fully differentiable (used in NeRF), handles arbitrary transfer functions interactively. Limitations: Susceptible to aliasing if step size is too large; computationally expensive for high-resolution volumes without acceleration structures; ignores scattering. When to use: Interactive visualization with dynamic transfer functions, neural rendering (NeRF), or when scattering is negligible. When not to use: When high-fidelity scattering is required, or when real-time performance is critical on very large datasets without GPU acceleration. The method was derived from the continuous volume rendering integral by Lacroute [Lac94] using the rectangle rule for numerical integration. It was popularized by Levoy's "Brute-Force" algorithm, which traced parallel rays and composited front-to-back. The specific discretization using the exponential transmittance term (1 - e^{-\tau \Delta s}) provides a more accurate approximation for finite step sizes than simple linear accumulation. It is implemented in frameworks like Inviwo and is the core rendering loop in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). name: Eye Align
head: Eye-aligned sampling, eye-origin alignment
body: Eye Align is a sample placement strategy for volume raycasting where the first sample point inside the volume is calculated relative to the eye position, creating a sampling pattern across pixels that forms concentric lines. It sets itself apart from siblings like Entry Align by aligning samples to the viewer's perspective rather than the volume entry boundary, which can introduce specific aliasing artifacts at the ray endpoints. Inputs: entryPoint: 3D vector, entry point of the ray into the volume (in texture coordinates). exitPoint: 3D vector, exit point of the ray from the volume (in texture coordinates). eyePos: 3D vector, position of the camera/eye (in texture coordinates). dim: 3D vector, dimensions of the volume grid. samplingRate: float, number of samples per unit length in texture space. Outputs: tStart: float, the parameter value for the first sample point inside the volume. tIncr: float, the step increment between consecutive samples. tEnd: float, the total length of the ray within the volume. Data Structures: Standard floating-point vectors and scalars. No complex packing required. Steps: 1. Calculate the ray vector in texture coordinates: \vec{ray} = \text{exitPoint} - \text{entryPoint} 2. Calculate the total number of samples based on ray length, volume dimensions, and sampling rate: \text{samples} = \|\vec{ray} \cdot \text{dim}\| \times \text{samplingRate} Note: The source code uses length(ray dim), implying element-wise multiplication followed by Euclidean norm. 3. Calculate the total ray length: t{\text{End}} = \|\vec{ray}\| 4. Calculate the step increment: t{\text{Incr}} = \frac{t{\text{End}}}{\text{samples}} 5. Calculate the distance from the eye to the entry point to determine the offset for the first sample: \text{numSteps} = \frac{\|\text{entryPoint} - \text{eyePos}\|}{t{\text{Incr}}} 6. Calculate the start parameter for the first sample inside the volume by removing the fractional part of the steps from the eye: t{\text{Start}} = (1 - \text{fract}(\text{numSteps})) \times t{\text{Incr}} Where \text{fract}(x) = x - \lfloor x \rfloor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def eyealign(entryPoint, exitPoint, eyePos, dim, samplingRate): # 1. Ray vector in texture coordinates ray = exitPoint - entryPoint # 2. Total number of samples # Element-wise multiplication then length rayscaled = vec3(ray.x dim.x, ray.y dim.y, ray.z dim.z) samples = length(rayscaled) samplingRate # 3. Total ray length tEnd = length(ray) # 4. Step increment tIncr = tEnd / samples # 5. Distance from eye to entry in terms of steps disteyeentry = length(entryPoint - eyePos) numSteps = disteyeentry / tIncr # 6. Start parameter # fract(x) = x - floor(x) frac = numSteps - floor(numSteps) tStart = (1.0 - frac) tIncr return tStart, tIncr, tEnd Parameters: samplingRate: Not given in the sources. Typical values depend on the desired visual fidelity and performance constraints. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Endpoint Estimation Error: The Riemann sum mid-point estimate used in conjunction with this sampling strategy tends to over- or underestimate contributions at both the first and last sample points. This is visually indicated by overshooting artifacts (e.g., red sections in comparative visualizations). Zero Ray Length: If entryPoint equals exitPoint, tEnd and tIncr become zero, leading to division by zero in step 4 and 5. This should be handled by skipping rendering or returning default values. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when numSteps is very large or very small, affecting the accuracy of tStart. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. The calculation of tStart and tIncr is O(1) per ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray. Strengths: Simple to implement; aligns sampling with the viewer's perspective, which can be beneficial for certain types of aliasing patterns. Limitations: Prone to endpoint estimation errors (over/underestimation) due to the mid-point rule interaction. The concentric line pattern may be visually noticeable or undesirable in some contexts. When to use: When viewer-centric sampling alignment is desired and endpoint artifacts are acceptable or can be mitigated by other means. When not to use: When high accuracy at volume boundaries is critical, or when the concentric aliasing pattern is undesirable. Entry Align may be preferred to mitigate endpoint errors. The method was described in the context of volume raycasting sampling strategies, specifically as a "first attempt" following work by Kruger et al. [6] (cited in). It is presented as an alternative to aligning samples with the volume entry point (Entry Align). The source is an unofficial document titled "Volume Raycasting Sampling Revisited". name: Entry Align
head: Half-step Entry Align
body: Entry Align is a sample placement strategy for fixed-step volume raycasting that shifts the first sample point half a step away from the volume entry boundary to align with the Riemann sum midpoint estimate. Unlike its sibling Eye Align, which aligns samples relative to the eye position, Entry Align aligns the sampling grid relative to the volume geometry, eliminating the boundary estimation error at the entry point. Inputs: entryPoint: The 3D position where the ray enters the volume, in texture coordinates. exitPoint: The 3D position where the ray exits the volume, in texture coordinates. dim: The dimensions of the volume texture (width, height, depth). samplingRate: The number of samples per unit length in texture space. Outputs: tStart: The starting parameter for the first sample along the ray. tIncr: The step increment between consecutive samples. tEnd: The total length of the ray in texture coordinates. Data Structures: ray: A 3D vector representing the direction and length of the ray in texture space. samples: A scalar representing the total number of samples to be taken. Steps: 1. Calculate the ray vector in texture coordinates: \text{ray} = \text{exitPoint} - \text{entryPoint} 2. Calculate the total number of samples required based on the ray length and sampling rate: \text{samples} = \|\text{ray} \times \text{dim}\| \times \text{samplingRate} Note: The multiplication ray dim scales the texture coordinate ray to world-like units if dim represents the volume resolution, or simply scales the vector. The source code implies length(ray dim) computes the magnitude of the scaled vector. 3. Calculate the total length of the ray in texture coordinates: t{\text{End}} = \|\text{ray}\| 4. Calculate the step increment (distance between samples in parameter space): t{\text{Incr}} = \frac{t{\text{End}}}{\text{samples}} 5. Set the start parameter to half a step from the entry point: t{\text{Start}} = 0.5 \times t{\text{Incr}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def entryalign(entrypoint, exitpoint, dim, samplingrate): # 1. Calculate ray vector in texture coordinates ray = exitpoint - entrypoint # 2. Calculate total number of samples # Note: ray dim scales the vector. length() computes the Euclidean norm. samples = length(ray dim) samplingrate # 3. Calculate total ray length in texture coordinates tend = length(ray) # 4. Calculate step increment tincr = tend / samples # 5. Set start parameter to half a step from entry tstart = 0.5 tincr return tstart, tincr, tend Parameters: samplingRate: Determines the density of samples. Typical values depend on the desired visual quality and performance constraints. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Back Boundary Error: While Entry Align corrects the estimation error at the entry point, the last sample may still under- or overestimate the contribution at the exit boundary, depending on how close the final sample is to the back side of the volume. This is because the step size is fixed based on the entry alignment, and the exit point is not necessarily aligned with a sample midpoint. A variant that aligns both the first and last samples to minimize boundary artifacts at both entry and exit. It adjusts the step size per ray to ensure the last sample is half a step from the exit point. Recommended as best practice for zero performance impact and minimal errors. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. The calculation of tStart and tIncr is O(1) per ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray for the parameters. Strengths: Eliminates the boundary estimation error at the entry point, which is a common artifact in naive fixed-step raycasting. Simple to implement. Limitations: Does not correct the boundary error at the exit point. The fixed step size may lead to suboptimal sampling density if the ray length varies significantly across pixels, though the step size is calculated per ray. When to use: When the entry boundary error is the primary concern and the exit boundary error is acceptable or can be mitigated by other means (e.g., Entry Exit Align). When not to use: When high accuracy at both boundaries is required; use Entry Exit Align instead. Entry Align was introduced in the context of revisiting volume raycasting sampling strategies to address Riemann sum estimation errors. It builds on the concept of midpoint Riemann sums, where sample points are shifted to the center of their respective integration intervals. The method is similar to techniques described in "Real-Time Volume Graphics" by Engel et al.. Volume Raycasting Sampling Revisited, https://osf.io/download/u9qnz/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Entry Exit Align
head: Entry Exit Align Corner, Entry Exit Align Corner Sampling, Recommended Sampling Strategy
body: Entry Exit Align is a sample placement strategy for fixed-length volume raycasting that aligns sample points with both the ray entry and exit points to minimize boundary artifacts. Unlike its sibling Entry Align, which only aligns the first sample, Entry Exit Align ensures that neither the first nor the last sample under- or overestimates the integral by adjusting the step size per ray. It is recommended as the best practice for volume raycasting due to zero performance impact and minimal errors. Inputs: entryPoint: The 3D coordinate where the ray enters the volume, given in texture coordinates. exitPoint: The 3D coordinate where the ray exits the volume, given in texture coordinates. samplingRate: The desired number of samples per unit volume dimension. dim: The dimensions of the volume texture (width, height, depth). Outputs: tStart: The starting parameter along the ray for the first sample. tIncr: The step increment (distance between samples) along the ray. tEnd: The total length of the ray vector. Data Structures: vec3: A 3D vector type holding x, y, z components. float: Standard floating-point number. Algorithm: The method calculates the number of samples required to cover the ray length while ensuring the first sample is half a step inside the entry and the last sample is half a step inside the exit. To handle corner rays where the length is smaller than the standard step size, it uses a ceiling function applied to the scaled length of the ray against the volume dimensions minus one, ensuring at least one sample is placed at the midpoint of such short rays. 1. Calculate the ray vector in texture coordinates: \text{ray} = \text{exitPoint} - \text{entryPoint} 2. Calculate the number of samples using the ceiling function applied to the scaled length of the ray against the volume dimensions minus one: \text{samples} = \lceil \text{samplingRate} \times \|\text{ray} \times (\text{dim} - \vec{1})\| \rceil Where \vec{1} is a vector (1, 1, 1) and \times denotes component-wise multiplication. 3. Calculate the total ray length: t{\text{End}} = \|\text{ray}\| 4. Calculate the step increment by dividing the total length by the number of samples: t{\text{Incr}} = \frac{t{\text{End}}}{\text{samples}} 5. Set the start parameter to half a step from the entry point: t{\text{Start}} = 0.5 \times t{\text{Incr}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def entryexitalign(entryPoint, exitPoint, samplingRate, dim): """ Calculates sampling parameters for Entry Exit Align Corner strategy. Args: entryPoint (tuple): Entry point in texture coordinates (x, y, z). exitPoint (tuple): Exit point in texture coordinates (x, y, z). samplingRate (float): Samples per unit dimension. dim (tuple): Volume dimensions (width, height, depth). Returns: tStart (float): Start parameter for first sample. tIncr (float): Step increment. tEnd (float): Total ray length. """ # 1. Ray vector in texture coordinates ray = (exitPoint[0] - entryPoint[0], exitPoint[1] - entryPoint[1], exitPoint[2] - entryPoint[2]) # 2. Number of samples adjusteddim = (dim[0] - 1.0, dim[1] - 1.0, dim[2] - 1.0) scaledray = (ray[0] adjusteddim[0], ray[1] adjusteddim[1], ray[2] adjusteddim[2]) scaledlength = math.sqrt(scaledray[0]2 + scaledray[1]2 + scaledray[2]2) samples = math.ceil(samplingRate scaledlength) # Ensure at least one sample is taken for degenerate rays if samples < 1: samples = 1 # 3. Total ray length raylength = math.sqrt(ray[0]2 + ray[1]2 + ray[2]2) tEnd = raylength # 4. Step increment tIncr = tEnd / samples # 5. Start parameter (half a step from entry) tStart = 0.5 tIncr return tStart, tIncr, tEnd Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner Rays: Standard strategies may exclude contributions at corners where the ray length is smaller than the step size. This method explicitly includes these by adjusting the step size to the ray length and placing a sample at the midpoint. Pre-integrated Rendering: Implementations using pre-integrated volume rendering reduced to two dimensions require all rays to use the same step length. Consequently, they cannot use this per-ray adaptive step size and must choose a strategy that under- or overestimates the integral. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Zero performance impact compared to simpler strategies. Strengths: Eliminates stepping artifacts and gaps at the bounding box. It does not suffer from over- or underestimation of first/last samples. Limitations: Requires per-ray calculation of step size, which may be incompatible with fixed-step pre-integrated rendering techniques. When to use: Recommended as the best practice for general volume raycasting. When not to use: When using pre-integrated volume rendering in 2D where a uniform step size across all rays is mandatory. The method was developed and evaluated in the Inviwo framework. It builds upon the "Eye Align" and "Entry Align" strategies, addressing their respective deficiencies regarding boundary estimation. The authors note that while errors due to sample placement can be significant for data at the borders, they are often marginal in real-world use cases with higher resolution volumes. However, artifacts can appear when zooming in on borders, justifying the recommendation of this method. name: Self-Attenuation Integral Evaluation
head: Proof for Equation used for Self-Attenuation
body: Self-Attenuation Integral Evaluation is a closed-form analytical solution for the volume rendering integral when the density field is modeled as a normalized 3D Gaussian and the transfer function is linear. It solves the problem of computing the self-attenuation term e^{-\int \sigma} exactly, avoiding the numerical errors and performance costs associated with discrete ray marching or Riemann sum approximations. It is distinct from Zero Order Integration (Rectangle Rule) because it provides an exact integral result rather than a discretized approximation, and from In-Scattering Integral Approximation via Riemann Sum by eliminating the need for sample accumulation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray \mathcal{R}(t) parameterized by t \in (-\infty, \infty), where \mathcal{R}(t) maps to 3D space. The ray passes through a pixel p. Input: A normalized 3D Gaussian density function \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathbf{x}, 0) centered at the origin (or transformed appropriately for the Gaussian's position and covariance). Output: The scalar value 1 - e^{-f0(p)}, where f0(p) is the integrated 2D Gaussian density (the column sum of the Gaussian along the ray). Data Structures: The method assumes the density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) is defined by \mathcal{G}3^n. No explicit lookup tables or voxel grids are required for the integration step itself, though the Gaussian parameters (mean, covariance) must be accessible. Mathematical Derivation: The volume rendering integral for a ray \mathcal{R} with color c0(\mathcal{R}) and density \sigma = \mathcal{G}3^n is given by: I(\mathbf{p}) = c0(\mathcal{R}) \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(t), 0) e^{-\int{-\infty}^t \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(\tau), 0) d\tau} dt Let the inner cumulative integral be H(t): H(t) = \int{-\infty}^t \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(\tau), 0) d\tau The derivative of H(t) with respect to t is the integrand: \frac{dH(t)}{dt} = \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(t), 0) Substituting dH(t) = \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(t), 0) dt into the outer integral: \int{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-H(t)} dH(t) Since \mathcal{G}3^n is a normalized Gaussian, H(t) converges from 0 (at t = -\infty) to f0(p) (at t = \infty), where f0(p) is the total integrated density along the ray (the 2D projection of the Gaussian). Changing the variable of integration from t to u = H(t): \int0^{f0(p)} e^{-u} du Evaluating this definite integral: \left[ -e^{-u} \right]0^{f0(p)} = -e^{-f0(p)} - (-e^0) = 1 - e^{-f0(p)} Algorithm: 1. Compute the 2D integrated density f0(p) for the ray passing through pixel p. This is the integral of the 3D Gaussian projected onto the ray direction. For a standard 3D Gaussian with covariance \Sigma, this involves projecting the covariance onto the 2D image plane and computing the integral of the resulting 2D Gaussian. 2. Compute the attenuation factor: A = 1 - e^{-f0(p)}. 3. The final color contribution is c0(\mathcal{R}) \cdot A. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If f0(p) is very large, e^{-f0(p)} underflows to 0, resulting in full opacity (A=1). If f0(p) is very small, 1 - e^{-f0(p)} \approx f0(p), which matches the linear approximation. The derivation assumes the transfer function is linear (g(s)=s) and the background is black (I0=0), consistent with the parent Volume Raycasting Discretization. An algorithm that rapidly evaluates the optical properties of each segment by eliminating the extinction coefficient from the opacity-associated color integral and computing color attenuation segment by segment instead of point by point. This approach improves lookup table generation speed and accuracy compared to point-wise integration, often used in GPU-based raycasting implementations. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian per ray, assuming the 2D integrated density f0(p) can be computed analytically or via a precomputed projection. This is significantly faster than discrete ray marching which is O(N) where N is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for the integration step. Strengths: Exact analytical solution eliminates discretization error. Extremely fast evaluation enables real-time rendering of dense Gaussian fields (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting). Limitations: Only applicable when the density field is explicitly modeled as a Gaussian (or a function with a known cumulative distribution function that allows this substitution). It does not handle arbitrary density fields or non-linear transfer functions directly without approximation. When to use: When rendering scenes represented by 3D Gaussians (e.g., 3DGS) and high performance is required. When not to use: For arbitrary voxel data or non-Gaussian primitives where the integral cannot be simplified analytically. The method originates from the analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering accuracy. It was formally proven in the supplemental material of "Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?" by Celarek et al.. The proof demonstrates that the complex volume rendering integral for a Gaussian primitive simplifies to a closed-form expression involving the exponential of the projected 2D density. This insight is critical for understanding the trade-offs between accurate volumetric rendering and the simplified splatting approximations used in real-time 3DGS.
