name: Partial Pre-Integration
body: Partial Pre-Integration is a GPU-accelerated cell projection technique that improves the accuracy of ray integration approximation in volume rendering by utilizing a 2D lookup table (\psi table) that is independent of the transfer function. Unlike Full Pre-Integration, which requires recomputing the lookup table whenever the transfer function changes, Partial Pre-Integration allows for interactive transfer function updates with minimal overhead. It builds on Volume Raycasting Discretization by replacing per-sample ray marching with a single fragment shader lookup, trading some computational speed for reduced under-sampling errors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar field values at the entry (sf) and exit (sb) points of a voxel cell, the geometric thickness of the cell along the ray (l), and a transfer function T(s) that maps scalar values to RGBA colors. Output: The final RGBA color contribution of the cell to the image. Data Structures: 2D \psi Table: A pre-compiled 2D texture or array. The dimensions and content are fixed and independent of the visualization attributes or transfer function. The table stores pre-computed integration results based on optical thickness and absorption properties derived from the scalar values. Steps: 1. Retrieve Colors: Sample the transfer function T at the entry scalar value sf and the exit scalar value sb to obtain their associated RGBA colors, denoted as Cf and Cb. 2. Compute Indices: Use the retrieved colors Cf, Cb, and the cell thickness l to compute the indices for accessing the 2D \psi table. The specific mapping from (Cf, Cb, l) to table coordinates is determined by the pre-integration formulation, typically involving the optical thickness and absorption coefficients derived from the alpha components of Cf and Cb. 3. Lookup and Compose: Retrieve the pre-computed values from the \psi table using the computed indices. Use these values to compute the final fragment color for the cell, effectively performing the integration of the volume rendering integral over the cell span. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partialpreintegration(sf, sb, l, transferfunction, psitable): """ Computes the color contribution of a voxel cell using Partial Pre-Integration. Args: sf (float): Scalar value at the entry point of the cell. sb (float): Scalar value at the exit point of the cell. l (float): Thickness of the cell along the ray. transferfunction (function): Maps scalar s to RGBA color. psitable (2D array): Pre-compiled lookup table independent of transfer function. Returns: tuple: Final RGBA color for the cell. """ # Step 1: Retrieve RGBA colors associated with sf and sb from the transfer function Cf = transferfunction(sf) Cb = transferfunction(sb) # Step 2: Compute indices into the 2D psi table # The indices are derived from the colors and thickness. # In standard partial pre-integration, this involves calculating # optical thickness and absorption parameters from Cf and Cb. # Let alphaf, alphab be the alpha components of Cf, Cb. # Let colorf, colorb be the RGB components. # Note: The exact formula for index computation depends on the specific # definition of the psi table by Moreland et al.. # Typically, indices are based on the optical thickness tau and absorption. # For implementation, one must map (Cf, Cb, l) to 2D coordinates (u, v). # Placeholder for the specific index calculation logic defined by Moreland et al. # This part is not explicitly detailed in the provided notes beyond "compute the indices". # A common approach involves normalizing the alpha values and thickness. u = computeindexu(Cf, Cb, l) v = computeindexv(Cf, Cb, l) # Step 3: Retrieve values from the psi table and use them to compute the final fragment color psivalue = psitable[u, v] # The final color is computed using the psi value and the retrieved colors. # Again, the exact composition formula is part of the Moreland et al. method. finalcolor = computefinalcolor(psivalue, Cf, Cb) return finalcolor def computeindexu(Cf, Cb, l): # Implementation detail not fully specified in notes. # Requires mapping color/thickness to table dimension. return 0 # Placeholder def computeindexv(Cf, Cb, l): # Implementation detail not fully specified in notes. return 0 # Placeholder def computefinalcolor(psivalue, Cf, Cb): # Implementation detail not fully specified in notes. return (0, 0, 0, 0) # Placeholder Parameters: \psi Table Resolution: Not given in the sources. Thickness (l): The geometric length of the ray segment within the voxel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Under-sampling: Partial Pre-Integration is less prone to under-sampling errors compared to simple average scalar methods. Performance: It is slower than the simple average scalar method (original PT by Shirley and Tuchman). Transfer Function Changes: Unlike Full Pre-Integration, the \psi table does not need to be recomputed when the transfer function changes. However, the lookup texture (if implemented as a texture) may need to be reloaded if the implementation relies on transfer-function-dependent textures, though the notes state the \psi table itself is pre-compiled and independent. A GPU-accelerated cell projection method that combines direct volume rendering with multiple isosurfaces. It uses tetrahedral discretization, requires no cell connectivity, and offers lower memory usage than hardware-accelerated ray casting variants. Improves accuracy by adaptively subdividing ray segments within a cell based on local extrema of scalar and shading polynomials, allowing lookup-based integration over smaller intervals. Time Complexity: Slower than the simple average scalar method (original PT). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 2D \psi table. The table is pre-compiled and independent of visualization attributes. Strengths: Less prone to under-sampling errors than simple averaging; allows interactive transfer function updates without full table recomputation. Limitations: Slower than basic averaging methods. When to Use: When interactive transfer function exploration is required and under-sampling artifacts are a concern, and performance is acceptable. When Not to Use: When maximum performance is critical and interactive transfer function changes are not needed (use Full Pre-Integration or simple averaging). Partial Pre-Integration was introduced by Moreland et al.. It was developed to overcome the disadvantage of Full Pre-Integration, where the pre-integration table must be recomputed every time the transfer function changes, which can be an expensive operation depending on table resolution. The 2D \psi table used in this method was computed by Moreland et al. and made available for downloading. An implementation using fragment shaders was described in a prototype programmed in C++ using OpenGL 2.0 with GLSL. GPU-Based Cell Projection for Interactive Volume Rendering, https://graphics.tudelft.nl/~marroquim/publications/pdfs/marroquim-sibgrapi2006.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Hybrid Volume and Isosurface Rendering with Partial Pre-Integration
head: PT with partial preintegration, PTINT
body: Hybrid Volume and Isosurface Rendering with Partial Pre-Integration (PTINT) is a GPU-accelerated cell projection method that combines direct volume rendering with multiple isosurfaces to achieve interactive frame rates. It builds on Partial Pre-Integration by eliminating bus transfer overhead and allowing the simultaneous rendering of opaque or semi-transparent isosurfaces within the same fragment shader passes. Unlike pure ray casting, PTINT uses a tetrahedral discretization that requires no cell connectivity, offering significantly lower memory usage than hardware-accelerated ray casting (HARC) variants. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field defined on a set of n vertices and m tetrahedra. Output: A 2D image with combined volume shading and isosurface geometry. Data Structures and Memory Layout: The method requires no explicit cell connectivity, storing data in textures to optimize GPU access. Texture Element Size: 16 bytes per element. Total Storage: 16(2n + m) bytes for n vertices and m tetrahedra. Storage per Tetrahedron: Assuming an average of 4 tetrahedra per vertex, the storage is 24 bytes per tetrahedron. Memory Usage: Approximately 24 MB for one million cells (20 MB without illumination data). Operational Variants: The algorithm supports three operational variants: 1. Basic Average Scalar Method: Standard volume rendering without pre-integration. 2. Partial Pre-Integration Technique: Uses the \psi table for improved integration accuracy. 3. Partial Pre-Integration with Isosurface Rendering: A hybrid mode combining direct volume rendering with multiple isosurfaces to achieve interactive frame rates by eliminating bus transfer overhead. Algorithm Steps: The rendering is performed in two main passes, with all isosurface computation handled in the second fragment shader to avoid additional rendering passes. 1. First Pass (Volume/Pre-integration): Render the tetrahedra to intermediate framebuffers 2 and 3. Compute gradient vectors gf and gb if lighting or isosurfaces are enabled. If isosurfaces/lighting are not desired, skip gradient computations and skip rendering to framebuffers 2 and 3. 2. Intermediate CPU Pass: Update gradient arrays if they were computed in the first pass. If gradients were skipped, this step is omitted. 3. Second Pass (Hybrid Rendering): Interpolate gradients and compute normals. If gradients were skipped, skip interpolation and normal computation. Perform isosurface detection and shading in the second fragment shader. Apply Phong shading model with controllable diffuse, specular, and ambient coefficients for isosurfaces. Render isosurfaces as fully opaque or semi-transparent fragments. Optimizations and Pitfalls: Early Tetrahedral Discard: An early discard test is applied to improve performance by skipping tetrahedra that do not contribute to the final image. Small Pixel Area Degradation: On datasets like "Liquid Oxygen Post," PTINT may lose performance compared to ray casting at viewpoints where the model occupies a small pixel area, as cell projection approaches are unaffected by pixel area size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderptint(vertices, tetrahedra, isosurfacethresholds, enablelighting, enableisosurfaces): # 1. First Pass: Volume and Gradient Computation if enablelighting or enableisosurfaces: # Compute forward and backward gradients gf and gb # Standard gradient estimation per tetrahedron gradients = estimategradients(vertices, tetrahedra) # Render volume data to intermediate framebuffers 2 and 3 rasterizevolume(vertices, tetrahedra, gradients) else: # Skip gradient computation and framebuffer 2/3 rendering rasterizevolume(vertices, tetrahedra, None) # 2. Intermediate CPU Pass if enablelighting or enableisosurfaces: # Update gradient arrays on CPU # Synchronize gradient data between GPU passes syncgradients(gradients) else: # Skip updating gradient arrays pass # 3. Second Pass: Hybrid Isosurface and Volume Shading if enablelighting or enableisosurfaces: # Interpolate gradients and compute normals # Barycentric interpolation of gradients to fragment positions normals = interpolategradients(vertices, tetrahedra, gradients) else: # Skip interpolation and normal computation normals = None # Apply early tetrahedral discard test # Cull tetrahedra outside view frustum or with zero screen projection visibletets = culltetrahedra(tetrahedra) # Render final image for tet in visibletets: if enableisosurfaces: for threshold in isosurfacethresholds: # Find intersection of scalar field with threshold inside tetrahedron if findisosurfaceintersection(tet, threshold): # Phong shading for isosurface with controllable coefficients # Standard Phong model: ambient + diffuse + specular color = applyphongshading(tet, normals, diffuse=0.8, specular=0.5, ambient=0.2) outputfragment(color, opaque=True) # Or semi-transparent # Render volume contribution # Accumulate color and opacity using partial pre-integration volumecolor = accumulatevolumeshading(tet, normals) outputfragment(volumecolor, alpha=0.5) # Blending with isosurface Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in sources, but achieves interactive frame rates on tested hardware. Memory Complexity: O(n + m) with a constant factor of 16 bytes per vertex/tet element. Total memory is 16(2n + m) bytes. Measured Performance: Hardware: Intel Pentium IV 3.6 GHz, 2 GB RAM, nVidia GeForce 6800 256 MB, PCI Express 16x. Viewport: 512 \times 512 pixels, constantly rotating model. Blunt Fin Dataset: PTINT outperforms all compared algorithms (GATOR, VICP, VICP Balanced, HARC, HARC INT, HAVIS, HAVS). Oxygen Post Dataset: PTINT loses to ray casting algorithms at certain viewpoints where the model has a small pixel area. Strengths: Low memory footprint (24 bytes/tet vs. 96-144 bytes/tet for HARC variants). No cell connectivity required, freeing GPU memory. Interactive frame rates via elimination of bus transfer overhead. Hybrid visualization allows underlying volumes to be hidden by opaque isosurfaces or enhanced by semi-transparent layers. Limitations: Performance degradation on small pixel area views compared to ray casting. Considerable performance loss if Phong shading is used for isosurfaces due to gradient computation overhead. When to Use: When interactive frame rates are required for large tetrahedral datasets and hybrid volume/isosurface visualization is desired, particularly on hardware with limited GPU memory. When Not to Use: When rendering datasets with small pixel area coverage where ray casting might be more efficient. Origin: Proposed by R. Marroquim et al. in the paper "Volume and Isosurface Rendering with GPU-Accelerated Cell Projection" (CGF 2008). Development: The method extends previous cell projection techniques (GATOR, VICP) and hardware-accelerated ray casting (HARC) by integrating partial pre-integration and isosurface rendering into a unified GPU pipeline. Usage: Tested on datasets including Blunt Fin, Combustion Chamber, Liquid Oxygen Post, Super Phoenix, Fuel Injection, and Electron Distribution Probability. Implemented in C++ with OpenGL 2.0 and GLSL under Linux. Volume and Isosurface Rendering with GPU-Accelerated Cell Projection, https://graphics.tudelft.nl/~marroquim/publications/pdfs/marroquim-CGF2008.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Semi-Analytical Fragment Shader Preintegration
body:
Semi-Analytical Fragment Shader Preintegration is a fragment shader-based technique that improves the accuracy of ray integration in volume rendering by adaptively subdividing the ray segment within a cell based on the local extrema of the scalar and shading polynomials. Unlike standard preintegration which assumes constant or linear variation over the entire interval, this method computes the roots of the derivative of the signal and shading functions to define integration boundaries, allowing for lookup-based integration over smaller, more uniform intervals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray exit point (normalized to [0,1]), cubic coefficients a,b,c,d for the scalar polynomial, and quadratic coefficients e,f,g for the shading polynomial. Output: Accumulated color and opacity for the fragment. Data Structures: Preintegration Table: A 256 × 256 × 32 RGBA texture where each component is 16-bit floating point. The dimensions correspond to scalar value, shading value, and interval length. Logarithmic table access is used for the length dimension to provide greater precision at small lengths. Offscreen Buffer: A 16-bit floating point buffer used for rendering to improve blending accuracy before copying to the front buffer. Algorithm: The fragment shader performs the following steps: 1. Find Exit Point: Compute the intersection of the ray with the back face of the cell to determine the parameter t{exit} (normalized to [0,1] relative to the cell traversal). 2. Compute Polynomial Coefficients: Calculate cubic coefficients a, b, c, d for the scalar signal polynomial s(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d and quadratic coefficients e, f, g for the shading polynomial l(t) = et^2 + ft + g. 3. Find Local Extrema: Initialize a list of points T = \emptyset. For the scalar polynomial, find roots of the derivative s'(t) = 3at^2 + 2bt + c = 0. If a 
eq 0 and b 
eq 0: Calculate discriminant \Delta = 4b^2 - 12ac. Add roots  rac{-2b + \sqrt{\Delta}}{6a} and  rac{-2b - \sqrt{\Delta}}{6a} to T. Else if a = 0 and b 
eq 0: Add root  rac{-c}{2b} to T. For the shading polynomial, find root of the derivative l'(t) = 2et + f = 0. If e 
eq 0: Add root  rac{-f}{2e} to T. 4. Prune and Sort: Remove any points t \in T such that t \le 0 or t \ge 1. Add boundary points 0 and 1 to T. Sort T in ascending order. 5. Adaptive Preintegration: For each consecutive pair (t1, t2) in T: Reconstruct scalar values s1 = d + t1(c + t1(b + t1a)) and s2 = d + t2(c + t2(b + t2a)). Reconstruct shading values l1 and l2 at t1 and t2 using the quadratic coefficients. Compute interval length l = t2 - t1. Fetch values from the front-weighted and back-weighted preintegration textures using (s1, s2, l) and (s2, s1, l) respectively. Combine the fetched textures to get the contribution for this interval. Accumulate the contribution into the final color and opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fragmentshader(texit, a, b, c, d, e, f, g): # 1. Find exit point (normalized to [0, 1]) # texit is computed externally or passed as a uniform # 2. Compute polynomial coefficients # a, b, c, d for scalar s(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d # e, f, g for shading l(t) = et^2 + ft + g # 3. Find local extrema T = [] # Scalar extrema (roots of derivative 3at^2 + 2bt + c = 0) if a != 0 and b != 0: delta = 4 b2 - 12 a c sqrtdelta = math.sqrt(max(delta, 0.0)) T.append((-2 b + sqrtdelta) / (6 a)) T.append((-2 b - sqrtdelta) / (6 a)) elif a == 0 and b != 0: T.append(-c / (2 b)) # Shading extrema (root of derivative 2et + f = 0) if e != 0: T.append(-f / (2 e)) # 4. Prune and Sort T = [t for t in T if 0 < t < 1] T.append(0.0) T.append(1.0) T.sort() # 5. Adaptive Preintegration accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 for i in range(len(T) - 1): t1 = T[i] t2 = T[i+1] # Reconstruct scalar values s1 = d + t1 (c + t1 (b + t1 a)) s2 = d + t2 (c + t2 (b + t2 a)) # Reconstruct shading values l1 = g + t1 (f + t1 e) l2 = g + t2 (f + t2 e) # Interval length length = t2 - t1 # Fetch front/back textures at (s1, s2, l) frontval = texture3dlookup(s1, s2, length) backval = texture3dlookup(s2, s1, length) # Combine textures to get interval contribution # Standard partial preintegration combination logic intervalcolor = frontval[:3] (1.0 - backval[3]) + backval[:3] frontval[3] intervalopacity = frontval[3] + backval[3] (1.0 - frontval[3]) # Accumulate value accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[j] + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) intervalcolor[j] for j in range(3)] + [accumulatedopacity] accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) intervalopacity return accumulatedcolor[:3], accumulatedcolor[3] def texture3dlookup(s, l, length): # Standard 3D texture fetch with logarithmic length mapping pass Parameters: Table Resolution: 256 × 256 × 32. Precision: 16-bit floating point per component. Length Access: Logarithmic mapping for the length dimension. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discriminant Negative: If \Delta < 0 for the scalar polynomial, no real roots exist, and no extrema are added for that polynomial. Precision: Small interval lengths require logarithmic access to maintain precision in the preintegration table lookup. Boundary Conditions: Points exactly at 0 or 1 are included to ensure full coverage of the cell. Interval Integration computes in-scattered radiance by decomposing the ray path into intervals defined by the front and back faces of a light volume. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly treating light volume boundaries as integration limits, enabling a "sum and difference" approach where contributions are added for front-face intersections and subtracted for back-face intersections. Choose this method when rendering volumetric light scattering in scenes with directional, point, or spot lights where light volume boundaries are well-defined. Memory Complexity: Requires a 256 × 256 × 32 × 4 × 2 bytes = ~128 MB texture for the preintegration table. An additional 16-bit floating point offscreen buffer is used for blending. Strengths: Improved accuracy over standard preintegration, especially for non-linear scalar fields. The method ensures perspective-correct sorting of cells in all cases. Limitations: Requires computing polynomial roots in the fragment shader. The logarithmic table access adds complexity to the texture lookup. The method was introduced in the context of high-quality volume rendering for Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. It builds upon the concept of partial pre-integration to allow for adaptive subdivision of the integration interval based on the local behavior of the scalar and shading functions. The implementation was demonstrated using OpenGL on the GPU, leveraging the fragment shader for the adaptive preintegration computation. name: Interval Integration for Volumetric Light Scattering
head: Analytic Interval Integration, Sum & Difference of Intervals
body: Interval Integration computes in-scattered radiance by decomposing the ray path into intervals defined by the front and back faces of a light volume, allowing analytical evaluation of the scattering integral for directional lights and numerical or lookup-based evaluation for point and spot lights. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly treating light volume boundaries as integration limits, enabling a "sum and difference" approach where contributions are added for front-face intersections and subtracted for back-face intersections. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, medium definition (density, optical depth, phase function), light description (position, direction, falloff), and shadow map data. Outputs: In-scattered radiance LS for the pixel. Data Structures Light Volume Geometry: Defined by front faces (Gf) and back faces (Gb), which establish the integration intervals along the ray. Exact layouts, sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. Lookup Texture: For omnidirectional lights, a texture mapping \cos^{-1}(v \cdot l) to 2D space approximates complex angular dependencies. Method Steps 1. Interval Decomposition: Identify the intersection points of the view ray with the light volume. Let tn be the distance to the n-th front face intersection and tm be the distance to the m-th back face intersection. 2. Integral Formulation: Compute the total in-scattered radiance as the sum of front-face contributions minus the sum of back-face contributions. 3. Light-Type Solvers: Directional Lights: Assume constant direction and constant power (light distance \gg medium depth). Evaluate the analytic solution L'S(d) in the pixel shader using the distance d along the ray. Omnidirectional Lights: Express terms with respect to direction and distance due to complexity. Create a lookup texture mapping \cos^{-1}(v \cdot l), evaluate the differential, and numerically integrate using a Compute Shader. Spot Lights: Handle angular falloff by clamping the interval to the cone intersection. For no falloff, treat as a point light. For fixed falloff, use a modified point light LUT. For variable falloff, perform cone intersection and numerically integrate using Newton-Cotes methods in the pixel shader. Formulas LS = \sum{n \in Gf} L'S(tn) - \sum{m \in Gb} L'S(tm) Where LS is the total in-scattered radiance, Gf and Gb are the sets of front and back face intersections, and L'S(t) is the indefinite scattering integral evaluated at distance t. For directional lights, the analytic solution is: L'S(d) = L(d, l) \rhom(xl, \omegax) \frac{1 - e^{-\tau{ex} d}}{\tau{ex}} Where d is the distance along the ray, L(d, l) is the light intensity, \rhom(xl, \omegax) is the medium scattering property (phase function), and \tau{ex} is the extinction coefficient. Parameters with Typical Values Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Shadow Map Inconsistencies: Rendering only front faces or excluding distant occluders causes incorrect integration intervals and visible artifacts. Ensure shadow map contents are consistent with scene geometry by rendering both front and back faces if needed and including distant occluders. Temporal Jitter: Temporal AA jitter causes flickering in down-sampled buffers because a 1-pixel flicker at full resolution becomes a 4x4 pixel artifact in a 1/4 resolution buffer. Add a separate TAA resolve to down-sampled buffers before compositing. High-Frequency Occluders: Dense occluders at low viewing angles (e.g., sunset through woods) cause performance drops due to high pixel coverage. Adjust tessellation factors based on view angle and pre-filter shadow maps. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of light volume intersections and solver complexity. Directional lights are O(1) per interval due to the analytic solution, while omnidirectional and spot lights require lookup textures or numerical integration. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for light volume geometry and lookup textures for non-directional lights. Strengths: Fast enough for entire specification ranges and flexible enough for almost any engine, while remaining compatible with physically-based pipelines. Limitations: Performance degrades with high-frequency occluders at grazing angles, and complex spot light falloffs require numerical integration. When to Use: Real-time volumetric scattering for directional, point, or spot lights in physically-based rendering pipelines. When Not to Use: When performance is critical with many high-frequency occluders at grazing angles, or when simple directional lighting only is needed. This method was developed by NVIDIA for use in Fallout 4, integrating with their Gameworks volumetric lighting system. It was presented in a technical talk regarding the implementation of fast, flexible, physically-based volumetric light scattering in the game. The approach builds on earlier analytic single scattering models. Volumetric Light Scattering in Fallout 4, https://www.scribd.com/document/748135006/Fast-Flexible-Physically-Based-Volumetric-Light-Scattering, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: CPU Volume Raycasting
head: CPU Ray Casting, Interactive DVR System, Pure CPU direct volume rendering, Ray Casting with Trilinear Interpolation
body: CPU Volume Raycasting is a direct volume rendering technique that computes the volume rendering integral by casting rays from the camera through each pixel into a voxel grid, accumulating color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. It is distinguished from GPU-based raycasting by its explicit multithreaded pixel processing on the CPU and from sibling discretization methods by its specific implementation of trilinear interpolation and early ray termination. Unlike Eye Align which optimizes sampling positions, or Partial Pre-Integration which approximates integration over steps, this method performs per-sample evaluation with standard compositing. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values (density/intensity). Transfer Functions: Two 1D lookup tables mapping scalar values to RGBA color and opacity. Camera Parameters: Position, orientation (Euler angles or quaternion), and field of view. Lighting: Light direction and Phong lighting coefficients (ambient + diffuse). Rendering Settings: Step size, opacity multiplier, and alpha threshold for early termination. Outputs: Image Buffer: A 2D array of RGB pixels (8-bit per channel). Volume Data Layout: The volume is stored as a 3D array. Two distinct layouts are observed in source implementations: 1. Slice-based (S1): int[zSize][] where volumes[z] is a 1D array of size width width. Values are extracted from a 2D source image by masking the alpha channel: 0x00ffffff & imageInPixels[i + idi]. 2. Flat Row-Major (S2): A std::vector<uint8t> within a Volume struct containing width, height, and depth. Data is stored in row-major order: data[x + y width + z width height]. Transfer Function Layout: Stored as two 1D integer arrays: int[] transferrgb and int[] transfera, typically loaded from 2D PNG images. In the S2 implementation, a lookup function transferFunction->lookup(val) returns a struct with.rgb and.a fields. Ray Structure: A Ray struct contains origin (Vector3) and direction (Vector3), where Vector3 has fields x, y, z (float). Pixel Buffer: A std::vector<uint8t> with 3 components per pixel (RGB). The index for pixel (i, j) in an image of width is (j width + i) 3. Rotation Matrix: Camera orientation is defined by Euler angles (roll, pitch, yaw). These are converted to a quaternion q[4]: \begin{aligned} c1 &= \cos(\text{yaw}/2), & s1 &= \sin(\text{yaw}/2) \\ c2 &= \cos(\text{pitch}/2), & s2 &= \sin(\text{pitch}/2) \\ c3 &= \cos(\text{roll}/2), & s3 &= \sin(\text{roll}/2) \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} q[0] &= c1 c2 c3 - s1 s2 s3 \\ q[1] &= c1 c2 s3 + s1 s2 c3 \\ q[2] &= s1 c2 c3 + c1 s2 s3 \\ q[3] &= c1 s2 c3 - s1 c2 s3 \end{aligned} The quaternion is then converted to a 3x3 rotation matrix M[3][3]: \begin{aligned} M[0][0] &= 2(q0^2 + q1^2) - 1, & M[0][1] &= 2(q1 q2 - q0 q3), & M[0][2] &= 2(q1 q3 + q0 q2) \\ M[1][0] &= 2(q1 q2 + q0 q3), & M[1][1] &= 2(q0^2 + q2^2) - 1, & M[1][2] &= 2(q2 q3 - q0 q1) \\ M[2][0] &= 2(q1 q3 - q0 q2), & M[2][1] &= 2(q2 q3 + q0 q1), & M[2][2] &= 2(q0^2 + q3^2) - 1 \end{aligned} Intensity Mapping (S1 Specific): Precomputed squared and cubed values for intensity mapping are stored in arrays squared[256] and cubed[256]: \text{squared}[i] = \frac{(i/256.0)^2}{3.0}, \quad \text{cubed}[i] = (i/256.0)^3 \quad \text{for } i \in [0, 255] 1. Initialization: Split the image into tiles for multithreading. A common configuration is a 4x4 grid of tiles. For each tile (a, b), define bounds: startA = a width / 4, endA = startA + width / 4, startB = b height / 4, endB = startB + height / 4. Initialize ray origin and direction for each pixel (i, j) within the tile. Check intersection with the volume's bounding sphere. If no intersection, skip the pixel. Set ray parameter t to the entry point t0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate while t < t1 (exit point) and accumulatedalpha < 0.99f (early termination threshold). Calculate sample point p = ray.origin + ray.direction t. Sampling: If using S1's nearest-neighbor approach: Map p to voxel coordinates, apply rotation matrix, and clamp to bounds. Retrieve value v from volumes[z][x + y width]. If using S2's trilinear interpolation: Calculate fractional offsets dx, dy, dz from p. Retrieve the 8 corner voxel values a through h. Perform trilinear interpolation: \begin{aligned} ab &= a(1-dx) + b(dx) \\ cd &= c(1-dx) + d(dx) \\ ef &= e(1-dx) + f(dx) \\ gh &= g(1-dx) + h(dx) \\ abc &= ab(1-dy) + cd(dy) \\ def &= ef(1-dy) + gh(dy) \\ val &= abc(1-dz) + def(dz) \end{aligned} Handle out-of-bounds coordinates by returning 0 (S2) or clamping indices (S1). Transfer Function Lookup: Map val to color c and opacity a{sample} using the transfer function. Apply global opacity multiplier: asample = asample settings.opacity. Lighting (S1 Specific): Compute gradient using central differences of neighboring voxels. Normalize gradient. Compute diffuse lighting: diffuse = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0). Combine ambient and diffuse to modulate color. Compositing (Front-to-Back): Update accumulated color Cout and alpha alphaout: \begin{aligned} C{out} &= C{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \cdot a{sample} \cdot c \\ \alpha{out} &= \alpha{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \cdot a{sample} \end{aligned} where C{in} and \alpha{in} are the accumulated values before this step. Step Advance: Increment t by settings.stepSize. Note: S1 uses a fixed step of 0.75 in its loop c += 0.75. S2 uses settings.stepSize, typically derived from rayLength / (samplingRate rayLength). 3. Finalization: Clamp final color components to [0, 1]. Convert to 8-bit integers: pixel[idx + k] = (uint8t)(min(color[k], 1.0f) 255) for k \in \{0, 1, 2\}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, scalar): return Vector3(self.x scalar, self.y scalar, self.z scalar) def rmul(self, scalar): return self.mul(scalar) def cpuvolumeraycasting(volume, transferfunc, camera, light, settings, width, height, uselighting): pixels = [0] (width height 3) rotmatrix = eulertorotationmatrix(camera.roll, camera.pitch, camera.yaw) tilesizex = width // 4 tilesizey = height // 4 threads = [] for a in range(4): for b in range(4): startx = a tilesizex endx = startx + tilesizex starty = b tilesizey endy = starty + tilesizey threads.append(lambda sx=startx, ex=endx, sy=starty, ey=endy: rendertile( volume, transferfunc, camera, light, settings, sx, ex, sy, ey, width, height, pixels, rotmatrix, uselighting)) for t in threads: t() return pixels def rendertile(volume, transferfunc, camera, light, settings, startx, endx, starty, endy, width, height, pixels, rotmatrix, uselighting): for j in range(starty, endy): for i in range(startx, endx): rayorigin, raydirection = getrayforpixel(i, j, camera, width, height) t0, t1 = intersectsphere(rayorigin, raydirection, volume.boundingsphere) if t0 is None: continue t = t0 acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 while t < t1 and accalpha < 0.99: p = rayorigin + raydirection t val = volumesampletrilinear(volume, p) sample = transferfunc.lookup(val) samplecolor = sample.rgb samplealpha = sample.a settings.opacity if uselighting: normal = volumecomputegradient(volume, p) normal = normalize(normal) diffuse = max(dot(normal, light.direction), 0.0) samplecolor = samplecolor (light.ambient + light.diffuse diffuse) weight = (1.0 - accalpha) samplealpha acccolor[0] += weight samplecolor[0] acccolor[1] += weight samplecolor[1] acccolor[2] += weight samplecolor[2] accalpha += weight t += settings.stepsize idx = (j width + i) 3 pixels[idx] = int(min(acccolor[0], 1.0) 255) pixels[idx+1] = int(min(acccolor[1], 1.0) 255) pixels[idx+2] = int(min(acccolor[2], 1.0) 255) def volumesampletrilinear(volume, p): x, y, z = p.x, p.y, p.z ix, iy, iz = math.floor(x), math.floor(y), math.floor(z) dx, dy, dz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz if not volume.isinside(ix, iy, iz): return 0.0 def getval(x, y, z): if not volume.isinside(x, y, z): return 0.0 return volume.data[x + y volume.width + z volume.width volume.height] a = getval(ix, iy, iz) b = getval(ix+1, iy, iz) c = getval(ix, iy+1, iz) d = getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz) e = getval(ix, iy, iz+1) f = getval(ix+1, iy, iz+1) g = getval(ix, iy+1, iz+1) h = getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) ab = a (1-dx) + b dx cd = c (1-dx) + d dx ef = e (1-dx) + f dx gh = g (1-dx) + h dx abc = ab (1-dy) + cd dy defval = ef (1-dy) + gh dy return abc (1-dz) + defval dz def eulertorotationmatrix(roll, pitch, yaw): c1, s1 = math.cos(yaw/2), math.sin(yaw/2) c2, s2 = math.cos(pitch/2), math.sin(pitch/2) c3, s3 = math.cos(roll/2), math.sin(roll/2) q0 = c1c2c3 - s1s2s3 q1 = c1c2s3 + s1s2c3 q2 = s1c2c3 + c1s2s3 q3 = c1s2c3 - s1c2s3 M = [[0]3 for in range(3)] M[0][0] = 2(q0q0 + q1q1) - 1; M[0][1] = 2(q1q2 - q0q3); M[0][2] = 2(q1q3 + q0q2) M[1][0] = 2(q1q2 + q0q3); M[1][1] = 2(q0q0 + q2q2) - 1; M[1][2] = 2(q2q3 - q0q1) M[2][0] = 2(q1q3 - q0q2); M[2][1] = 2(q2q3 + q0q1); M[2][2] = 2(q0q0 + q3q3) - 1 return M def getrayforpixel(i, j, camera, width, height): aspect = width / height fov = camera.fov ndcx = (2.0 (i + 0.5) / width) - 1.0 ndcy = 1.0 - (2.0 (j + 0.5) / height) raydir = Vector3(ndcx aspect math.tan(fov/2), ndcy math.tan(fov/2), -1.0) raydir = normalize(raydir) return camera.position, raydir def intersectsphere(origin, direction, sphere): oc = origin - sphere.center a = dot(direction, direction) b = 2.0 dot(oc, direction) c = dot(oc, oc) - sphere.radius sphere.radius disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return None, None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t0 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) t1 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) if t0 < 0: t0 = t1 return t0, t1 def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v.xv.x + v.yv.y + v.zv.z) if l == 0: return Vector3(0,0,0) return Vector3(v.x/l, v.y/l, v.z/l) def dot(v1, v2): return v1.xv2.x + v1.yv2.y + v1.zv2.z Step Size (settings.stepSize): Distance between samples. In S1, calculated as 1.0 when samplingRate=1. In S2, a configurable setting. Opacity Multiplier (settings.opacity): Global scalar applied to sample opacity from the transfer function. Alpha Threshold: Termination condition for early ray casting. Typically 0.99f. Ray Length: Diagonal length of the volume bounding box. In S1, approximated as width sqrt(2). Volume Distortion: If the source image is not square or height is not a multiple of width, the derived volume shape (zSize = height / width) may be distorted or truncated. Out-of-Bounds Sampling: If coordinates fall outside the volume bounds, implementations vary: S1 clamps indices, while S2 returns 0. This affects interpolation weights at edges. Aliasing: S1 explicitly states "no pixel interpolation," relying on nearest-neighbor access which causes aliasing/blocky artifacts at oblique angles. S2 uses trilinear interpolation to mitigate this. Color Overflow: Final color values must be clamped to [0, 1] before 8-bit conversion to prevent overflow. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels, M is the number of samples per ray (determined by volume depth and step size), and S is the cost of sampling/compositing per sample. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Full control over rendering pipeline on CPU; supports complex transfer functions and Phong lighting without GPU shader constraints; suitable for interactive systems where GPU resources are unavailable or insufficient. Limitations: Prone to aliasing if step size is large or interpolation is poor; no built-in acceleration structures (like BVH) in the basic implementations described, leading to uniform sampling. When to Use: Interactive direct volume rendering on CPU-only systems; educational implementations; scenarios requiring custom lighting or transfer function logic not easily expressible in shaders. When Not to Use: High-performance real-time rendering of large volumes; scenes requiring complex light transport (e.g., full in-scattering) without approximation. CPU Volume Raycasting originated as a foundational technique in Direct Volume Rendering (DVR), allowing visualization of 3D scalar fields on standard hardware before GPU compute shaders became prevalent. The specific implementations cited here represent independent open-source projects: Pure CPU Direct Volume Rendering: Developed by Tomasz Hachaj, this implementation emphasizes a pure CPU approach with quaternion-based rotation and Phong lighting, explicitly avoiding 3rd party libraries and GPU acceleration. Interactive DVR System: Developed by Manishaa1704, this system focuses on multithreaded pixel processing and trilinear interpolation for smoother visuals, serving as an educational example of CPU-based DVR. These methods build upon the theoretical framework of the Volume Rendering Integral discretization [831-volume-raycasting-discretization.md], applying it via explicit ray marching loops on the CPU. browarsoftware/directvolumerenderingcpu, https://github.com/browarsoftware/directvolumerenderingcpu, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) manishaa1704/Interactive-DVR-System, https://github.com/manishaa1704/Interactive-DVR-System, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Average Intensity Projection
head: Additive Reprojection, Average Intensity, Mean Density, Mean Density Projection, Simple Additive Projections, X-ray projection (average)
body: Average Intensity Projection (AIP) is a volume rendering technique that computes the image by averaging the scalar intensities of voxels along rays through the volume onto the image plane. It serves as a simplified alternative to front-to-back compositing, producing an image equivalent to an X-ray projection through the data. Unlike standard ray casting which accounts for opacity and absorption, AIP treats the volume as a transparent medium where every sample contributes equally to the final pixel value, making it computationally inexpensive but prone to low contrast. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values. Sources describe two common layouts: 1. 3D Texture: Dimensions X \times Y \times Z (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 109), stored in a GLTEXTURE3D with GLRGBA internal format but GLRED base format, using GLUNSIGNEDBYTE type. 2. Raw Array: 1D array of unsigned char values with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz, stored in row-major order. Camera/View: Defined by a view position (viewPos) and a bounding box for the volume (e.g., min vec3(-1.0), max vec3(1.0) or centered at volume origin). Parameters: numsteps: Fixed number of sampling steps along the ray (e.g., 256). scale: Scaling factor for output image dimensions (ImageWidth = VolumeWidth \times scale). isoSurf: Optional uniform float for isosurface extraction mode, processed as iso = isoSurf - floor(isoSurf). Outputs: Image: A 2D grid of pixel values. Format: unsigned char (0-255 range). Dimensions: Scaled width and height. Value: The arithmetic mean of the sampled voxel intensities along the ray. Ray: Defined by origin or and direction dir. Transfer Function (Optional): A 1D texture (GLTEXTURE1D) mapping scalar values to color/opacity. In pure AIP, this is often bypassed or used only for final color mapping. Accumulators: totalVoxelValue or meanSum: Accumulates the sum of sampled intensities. cnt or validSamples: Counts the number of valid samples taken. 1. Initialize: For each pixel, initialize totalVoxelValue = 0.0 and cnt = 1 (to avoid division by zero). 2. Ray Setup: Compute ray origin fpos (fragment position) and direction direction = normalize(fpos - viewPos). Alternatively, for orthographic projections, map pixel coordinates to volume space: originalX = pixelX / scale, originalY = pixelY / scale, with ray origin at (originalX, originalY, 0) and direction (0, 0, 1). 3. Intersection (Perspective): Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box to find entry (tenter) and exit (texit) distances using the slab method. 4. Step Calculation: Calculate ray length dist = distance(entry, exit) and step size stepsize = dist / numsteps. 5. Sampling Loop: Iterate i from 0 to numsteps - 1: Increment counter cnt++. Determine sample position curPos along the ray. Coordinate Transformation: Scale Z-coordinate if necessary: tmp.z = curPos.z 2.3486238532110093 (to handle non-isotropic data or texture normalization). Map to texture coordinates: texPos = (1 + tmp) / 2. Invert Y-axis: texPos.y = 1 - texPos.y (due to image data inversion). Sampling: Fetch value val = texture(texVol, texPos).x. Accumulation: If using raw array indexing (orthographic case): Translate sample to volume center, apply rotation matrix, translate back, check bounds, compute linear index, and fetch voxelIntensity = vol.data[index] / 255.0f. Add to sum: totalVoxelValue += val (or voxelIntensity). Advance: curPos = curPos + direction stepsize. 6. Finalize: Compute the average: meanValue = totalVoxelValue / cnt. 7. Color Mapping (Optional): Map meanValue to a final color using a transfer function or color map. If lighting is enabled, calculate normals from the mean position and apply lighting. Unverified code. Args: volumedata: 3D array of shape (Z, Y, X) with values in [0, 1] viewpos: Camera position (list/tuple of 3 floats) imagewidth: Output image width imageheight: Output image height numsteps: Number of samples per ray scale: Scaling factor for image dimensions relative to volume fovdeg: Field of view in degrees for perspective projection Returns: imagedata: 2D array of floats (0.0 to 1.0) representing average intensity """ imagedata = [[0.0 for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] # Define bounding box for intersection (example: unit cube centered at origin) bboxmin = [-1.0, -1.0, -1.0] bboxmax = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Calculate ray direction from pixel coordinates direction = computeraydirection(x, y, imagewidth, imageheight, fovdeg) # Ray-Bbox Intersection (Slab Method) result = intersectbox(viewpos, direction, bboxmin, bboxmax) if result is None: continue tenter, texit = result dist = texit - tenter stepsize = dist / numsteps totalvalue = 0.0 count = 1 # Avoid division by zero, matches initialization currentpos = [ viewpos[0] + direction[0] tenter, viewpos[1] + direction[1] tenter, viewpos[2] + direction[2] tenter ] for in range(numsteps): count += 1 # Coordinate transformation specific to source tmp = [currentpos[0], currentpos[1], currentpos[2] 2.3486238532110093] # Map to [0, 1] texture coordinates texpos = [(1.0 + tmp[0]) / 2.0, (1.0 + tmp[1]) / 2.0, (1.0 + tmp[2]) / 2.0] # Invert Y axis texpos[1] = 1.0 - texpos[1] # Sample volume val = samplevolume(volumedata, texpos) totalvalue += val # Advance position currentpos = [ currentpos[0] + direction[0] stepsize, currentpos[1] + direction[1] stepsize, currentpos[2] + direction[2] stepsize ] # Compute average meanvalue = totalvalue / count imagedata[y][x] = meanvalue return imagedata def computeraydirection(pixelx, pixely, imgw, imgh, fovdeg=60.0): """Computes a normalized ray direction for a given pixel in a perspective camera.""" aspect = imgw / imgh fovrad = math.radians(fovdeg) halfh = math.tan(fovrad / 2.0) halfw = halfh aspect dx = (pixelx / imgw - 0.5) 2.0 halfw dy = (0.5 - pixely / imgh) 2.0 halfh # Camera looks down -Z axis dirvec = [dx, dy, -1.0] length = math.sqrt(dirvec[0]2 + dirvec[1]2 + dirvec[2]2) return [dirvec[0]/length, dirvec[1]/length, dirvec[2]/length] def intersectbox(origin, direction, minb, maxb): """ Slab method for ray-box intersection. Returns (tenter, texit) or None if no intersection. """ tmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0.0: if origin[i] < minb[i] or origin[i] > maxb[i]: return None tmin[i] = -float('inf') tmax[i] = float('inf') else: tmin[i] = (minb[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmax[i] = (maxb[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tenter = max(tmin[0], tmin[1], tmin[2]) texit = min(tmax[0], tmax[1], tmax[2]) if tenter > texit: return None if texit < 0: return None # Box is behind the ray if tenter < 0: tenter = 0 return tenter, texit def samplevolume(volumedata, texcoords): """Samples a 3D volume using clamped nearest-neighbor for pseudocode simplicity.""" # Clamp coordinates to [0, 1] c = [max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) for v in texcoords] # Map to array indices (assuming volumedata is Z, Y, X) zidx = int(c[2] (len(volumedata) - 1)) yidx = int(c[1] (len(volumedata[0]) - 1)) xidx = int(c[0] (len(volumedata[0][0]) - 1)) return volumedata[zidx][yidx][xidx] Division by Zero: The sample counter cnt is initialized to 1 and incremented before sampling to ensure color /= cnt never divides by zero. Coordinate Inversion: The texture Y-coordinate must be inverted (1 - texPos.y) because image data is often inverted on the Y-axis. Non-Isotropic Data: The Z-coordinate may require scaling by a specific constant (e.g., 2.3486238532110093) before mapping to texture space to handle non-isotropic voxels or specific normalization requirements. Low Contrast: Additive projection techniques suffer from a confused or unclear appearance because all information is projected, resulting in very little contrast to distinguish gradual variations or small abrupt changes. Occlusion: Unlike front-to-back compositing, AIP does not handle obscuration, which can hide structural details. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Performance: Very fast due to the lack of complex compositing (opacity/alpha blending) and lighting calculations. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast rendering, useful for quick overviews or X-ray-like visualizations. Limitations: Low contrast, no depth cues from occlusion, sensitive to noise and background clutter. When to Use: When speed is critical and depth perception is not required, or for initial data exploration. When Not to Use: When detailed structural visualization, depth cues, or high contrast is needed. Average Intensity Projection, also known as additive reprojection, was developed by Hohne et al. for medical imaging applications, specifically stereotactic neurosurgery planning. It is one of their generalized projection images, designed to directly image the volume of data without surface shading. The technique is equivalent to an X-ray projection through the volume. It is often contrasted with techniques that use partial volume effects for surface shading or segmentation. name: Differential Sampling
head: Differential construction of T
body: Differential sampling is a ray discretization strategy for volume raycasting that adapts the sampling density along a ray based on the view-dependent frequency of the image plane, ensuring the sampling rate respects the Nyquist limit. Unlike uniform sampling methods, it uses a quadratic sampling function T(x) derived from ray differentials, allowing variable step sizes that are finer near the viewpoint and coarser further away, which prevents aliasing for features close to the camera. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera origin \vec{o}, central view direction \vec{w}, right vector \vec{u}, up vector \vec{v}, image plane resolution (\Delta x, \Delta y), scaling factor sk, volume data structure, and exit distance D{\text{exit}}. Outputs: A sequence of sample positions \vec{P}i along the ray and their corresponding transfer function evaluations. Data Structures: The method maintains the following state variables per ray during iteration: \vec{P}: Current 3D sample position. \vec{D}: Unitized ray direction vector. x: Current image-space coordinate index (integer). \Delta t: Current step size (derivative of T with respect to x). T: Cumulative distance along the ray corresponding to image coordinate x. maxtsampled: Greatest t value already sampled. Exact memory layouts and bit packing are not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Generate the ray direction vector \vec{d} for pixel coordinates (x, y) using the pinhole camera model. 2. Unitize the ray direction to obtain \vec{D}. 3. Compute the partial derivative of \vec{D} with respect to the image-space coordinate x. 4. Calculate the scalar coefficients k, a, and b based on the pixel footprint and differential magnitude. 5. Initialize the sampling state at x=0. 6. Iterate along the ray: sample the volume, handle macrocell entry boundaries, and increment the position and step size. Formulas: Ray generation: \vec{d}(x, y) = \vec{w} + x\vec{u} + y\vec{v}. Ray unitization: \vec{D}(x, y) = \vec{d} / \sqrt{\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d}}. Ray differential vector: \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial x} = \frac{(\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d})\vec{u} - (\vec{d} \cdot \vec{u})\vec{d}}{(\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d})^{3/2}}. Step size multiplier: k = sk |\vec{u}\Delta x + \vec{v}\Delta y|. Quadratic coefficients: a = k \left| \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial x} \right|, b = k. Sampling function: T(x) = \frac{a}{2}x^2 + bx. Step size derivative: \frac{\partial T}{\partial x} = ax + b. Position update: \vec{P}{n+1} = \vec{P}n + \Delta tn \vec{D}. Step size update: \Delta t{n+1} = \Delta tn + a. Macrocell entry coordinate: x{\text{enter}} = \frac{-b + \sqrt{b^2 + 2aT{\text{enter}}}}{a}. Parameters: sk: Scaling factor for k. Typical value: 4. Theoretical Nyquist limit requires sk < 0.5, but this is excessive in practice. k0: Constant combining k and geometric factors. If k is arbitrarily chosen, k0 = k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. d = w + xu + yv D = d / sqrt(dot(d, d)) Ddx = ((dot(d, d) u) - (dot(d, u) d)) / (dot(d, d) 1.5) magDdx = sqrt(dot(Ddx, Ddx)) k = sk sqrt(dot(udx + vdy, udx + vdy)) a = k magDdx b = k x = 0 dt = b P = o T = 0.0 maxtsampled = -inf # Guard for macrocell entry duplicates while P is inside volume and T < Dexit: # Sample volume at current position samplevolume(P) # Handle macrocell entry if crossing boundary if enteringnewmacrocell(Tenter): xenter = (-b + sqrt(b2 + 2aTenter)) / a x = floor(xenter) dt = b + a x T = 0.5 a x2 + b x P = o + T D maxtsampled = max(maxtsampled, T) # Increment per source equations P = P + dt D dt = dt + a x = x + 1 T = 0.5 a x2 + b x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Samples at Macrocell Boundaries: When entering a new macrocell, the sampling sequence might overlap with previously visited space. To avoid duplicate samples, store the greatest t already sampled and use the maximum of that value and T{\text{enter}}. Nyquist Limit: Using sk < 0.5 satisfies the Nyquist limit theoretically but is computationally expensive. sk=4 is a practical default. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. The number of samples adapts to view-dependent frequency, generally higher near the viewpoint and lower further away. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for state variables. Strengths: Respects the Nyquist frequency of the image plane, reducing aliasing artifacts for structures close to the viewpoint. Avoids adaptive branching, maintaining thread coherence on GPUs. Limitations: Requires computation of ray differentials (\partial \vec{D} / \partial x) per pixel. Purely adaptive methods based on local gradients perform poorly on GPUs due to poor thread coherence, though per-macrocell adaptation is supported. When to Use: High-quality volume rendering where aliasing is a concern, particularly for large volumes viewed from varying distances. When Not to Use: Real-time applications with strict performance constraints where uniform sampling is sufficient, or when the volume lacks high-frequency features near the camera. Differential sampling was introduced in the context of volume ray casting with peak finding, building on the concept of ray differentials originally formulated by Igehy. The method addresses the issue that regular sampling in world-space undersamples features close to the viewpoint relative to those further away, due to the convolution of the volume rendering integral during the transformation from world-space to image-space. It was implemented in a GLSL fragment shader framework for OpenGL. Volume Ray Casting with Peak Finding and Differential..., https://www.sci.utah.edu/~knolla/avrc.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: In-Scattering Integral Approximation via Riemann Sum
head: Discrete In-Scattering Integral, Riemann Sum In-Scattering
body: This method approximates the continuous in-scattering integral along a camera ray by discretizing the path into small segments and summing the contributions of rectangular areas defined by the sampled radiance and segment width. It solves the problem of computing the influx of light energy scattered toward the eye for general, non-homogeneous volumes where no analytical solution exists. Unlike Zero Order Integration (Rectangle Rule) which focuses on the general volume rendering equation, this specific approach explicitly details the evaluation of the in-scattering term Li(x, \omega) via auxiliary light rays and Beer's law. Inputs: Camera ray segment bounds t0 and t1. Step size dx (width of the rectangles). Volume density field and lighting configuration. Outputs: Approximated in-scattered radiance for the ray segment. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Discretization: Divide the camera ray segment within the volume boundaries (from t0 to t1) into sub-segments of length dx. 2. Sampling Loop: For each sub-segment, identify the sample point x (typically the middle of the interval). 3. Lighting Evaluation (Li(x, \omega)): Shoot a ray from x in the direction of the light source to determine the distance light traveled through the volume to reach x. Apply Beer's law to the light travel distance to determine the remaining light energy at point x. Note: The basic Riemann sum description does not account for the scattering phase function, which is required for the full calculation of Li(x, \omega). 4. Accumulation: Compute the area of the rectangle for the current segment as Li(x, \omega) \cdot dx. 5. Summation: Sum the areas of all rectangles to approximate the integral. Formula: The integral to approximate is: \int{x=t0}^{t1} Li(x, \omega) dx Where: Li(x, \omega) is the radiance scattered towards the eye direction \omega at point x. The integral spans the camera ray segment between parametric distances t0 and t1. dx is the width of the rectangles. Parameters: dx: The width of the rectangles. Smaller dx yields higher accuracy but increases processing time. Pitfalls: No Analytical Solution: The integral has no analytical solution for general volume shapes and lighting scenarios, necessitating numerical approximation. Missing Phase Function: The basic description does not account for the scattering phase function. Approximation Error: The result is an approximation whose accuracy depends heavily on the choice of dx. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def approximateinscattering(t0, t1, dx, volumesampler, lightdirection, lightsourceradiance): """ Approximates the in-scattering integral using a Riemann sum. Args: t0: Start parametric distance of the ray segment. t1: End parametric distance of the ray segment. dx: Step size (width of rectangles). volumesampler: Function that returns density/extinction at a 3D point. lightdirection: Normalized direction vector towards the light source. lightsourceradiance: Radiance emitted by the light source. Returns: Approximated in-scattered radiance. """ totalinscattering = 0.0 x = t0 while x < t1: currentdx = min(dx, t1 - x) xcenter = x + currentdx / 2.0 # March along lightdirection from xcenter to find distance inside volume. # Implementation details (step size, boundary checks) are omitted. dlight = 0.0 pos = xcenter step = 0.01 # Light ray step size is implementation-dependent while volumesampler(pos) > 0.0: dlight += step pos = pos + lightdirection step # Apply Beer's law to determine remaining light energy at xcenter sigmat = volumesampler(xcenter) li = lightsourceradiance math.exp(-sigmat dlight) totalinscattering += li currentdx x += currentdx return totalinscattering Time Complexity: O(N) where N \approx (t1 - t0) / dx. Processing time increases as dx decreases. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Works for any volume shape and lighting scenario. Limitations: Accuracy depends on dx; does not inherently handle phase functions. When to use: When a simple, general-purpose approximation is needed. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the practical need to compute in-scattering in volume rendering where analytical solutions are unavailable. It is based on the fundamental mathematical concept of the Riemann sum, which approximates integrals by summing rectangular areas. The specific application to volume rendering, including the use of auxiliary light rays and Beer's law, is described in "An Introduction to Volume Rendering". name: Zero Order Integration (Rectangle Rule)
head: Alpha Compositing, Discrete Volume Rendering, Piecewise-constant approximation, Quadrature Approximation, Riemann Sum Approximation, Riemann sum with rectangle rule, Uniform sampling approximation, Zero-order hold reconstruction
body: Zero Order Integration approximates the continuous volume rendering integral by decomposing it into a Riemann sum over discrete segments along a ray, assuming the scalar field (density) and color are constant within each segment. It sets apart from higher-order methods like Partial Pre-Integration by requiring no pre-computed tables or linear interpolation, relying instead on a simple piecewise-constant assumption. This simplicity comes at the cost of visible discontinuities and approximation errors, particularly when sampling rates are low. Inputs: Ray parameterization r(t) entering at t0 and exiting at tN. N sample positions ti along the ray, typically equidistant or stratified. Scalar field values \sigmai (density/extinction) and color values ci (emission) at each sample point ti. Optional noise standard deviation rawnoisestd. Outputs: Composite color C(\mathbf{r}). Accumulated opacity Acc(\mathbf{r}). Expected depth Depth(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: Arrays of size N for positions ti, densities \sigmai, and colors ci. Array of size N for segment distances \deltai. Array of size N for alphas \alphai. Array of size N for transmittance Ti. Array of size N for weights wi. Steps: 1. Compute Segment Distances: Calculate the distance between consecutive samples. For i = 0 to N-2, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. The last segment distance \delta{N-1} is set to a large value (e.g., 10^{10}) to ensure the ray exit is fully accounted for. If the ray direction \mathbf{d} is not unit length, scale distances by its magnitude: \deltai = (t{i+1} - ti) \|\mathbf{d}\| 2. Apply Noise (Optional): If regularization is enabled, add Gaussian noise to the density: \sigmai \leftarrow \sigmai + \text{randn}() \cdot \text{raw\noise\std} Typical value for rawnoisestd is 0.0. 3. Compute Opacity (\alphai): Using the zero-order hold assumption, the density is constant \sigmai over the segment \deltai. The opacity is computed as: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\max(\sigmai, 0) \cdot \deltai). The relu or max(0,...) ensures non-negative density for the exponential. 4. Compute Transmittance (Ti): Transmittance is the probability of light passing through all previous segments. It is computed using an exclusive cumulative product: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) For i=1, T1 = 1. To prevent numerical instability when \alphaj \approx 1, add a small epsilon (10^{-10}) to (1 - \alphaj) before multiplication. Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj + \epsilon) 5. Compute Weights (wi): The contribution weight for each sample is the product of transmittance and opacity: wi = Ti \cdot \alphai 6. Composite Color: Sum the weighted color contributions: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \cdot ci 7. Compute Accumulated Opacity: Acc(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi 8. Compute Expected Depth (Optional): Depth(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \cdot ti Clamp depth to a minimum of 10^{-10} to avoid division by zero in downstream disparity calculations. 9. Background Compositing (Optional): If a white background is assumed, composite the result: C{final} = C(\mathbf{r}) + (1 - Acc(\mathbf{r})) \cdot \mathbf{1} Pseudocode: import numpy as np def zeroorderintegration(tvals, sigmavals, colorvals, raydirectionnorm=1.0, rawnoisestd=0.0, whitebkgd=False, epsilon=1e-10): """ Perform zero-order integration (rectangle rule) for volume rendering. Args: tvals: Array of shape (N,) containing sample positions along the ray. sigmavals: Array of shape (N,) containing density/extinction at each sample. colorvals: Array of shape (N, 3) containing RGB color at each sample. raydirectionnorm: Scalar magnitude of the ray direction vector. rawnoisestd: Standard deviation for noise added to density. whitebkgd: Boolean, if True composite onto white background. epsilon: Small value to prevent numerical instability in transmittance. Returns: rgb: Composite RGB color. acc: Accumulated opacity. depth: Expected depth. """ N = len(tvals) # 1. Compute segment distances # Differences between consecutive samples dists = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] # Append a large value for the last segment to ensure full ray coverage dists = np.concatenate([dists, np.full(1, 1e10)]) # Scale by ray direction magnitude if not unit length dists = dists raydirectionnorm # 2. Apply optional noise to density if rawnoisestd > 0.0: sigmavals = sigmavals + np.random.randn(N) rawnoisestd # 3. Compute alpha (opacity) for each segment # Use relu for sigma to ensure non-negative density for exp sigmaclamped = np.maximum(sigmavals, 0.0) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmaclamped dists) # 4. Compute transmittance using exclusive cumulative product # Ti = product{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) # Add epsilon to (1 - alpha) to prevent instability if alpha is 1.0 oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alpha + epsilon # Cumulative product of (1 - alpha) cumprod = np.cumprod(oneminusalpha) # Transmittance is the product of all previous segments # T[0] = 1.0 (no previous segments) # T[i] = cumprod[i-1] transmittance = np.concatenate([[1.0], cumprod[:-1]]) # 5. Compute weights weights = transmittance alpha # 6. Composite RGB # weights shape (N,), colorvals shape (N, 3) rgb = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] colorvals, axis=0) # 7. Compute accumulated opacity acc = np.sum(weights) # 8. Compute expected depth # Clamp depth to min 1e-10 to avoid division by zero depth = np.sum(weights tvals) depth = np.maximum(depth, 1e-10) # 9. Background compositing if whitebkgd: rgb = rgb + (1.0 - acc) np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) return rgb, acc, depth Parameters: rawnoisestd: Float, standard deviation for noise added to density for regularization. Typical value: 0.0. epsilon: Float, small value added to (1-\alpha) to prevent numerical instability. Typical value: 10^{-10}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuities: The reconstructed signal is not C^0 continuous, leading to visible discontinuities and significant approximation errors, especially with uniform sampling. Uniform Sampling Artifacts: Assuming homogeneous material within each segment can result in artifacts if the sampling rate is insufficient to capture high-frequency details. Numerical Instability: If \alphai \approx 1.0, (1-\alphai) becomes zero, causing transmittance to drop to zero abruptly. Adding epsilon prevents this. Depth Division: When computing disparity from depth, clamp depth to a minimum value to avoid division by zero. A higher-order technique that reduces trajectory error by querying a vector field at four positions, chosen for accurate streamline visualization where zero-order integration fails due to low accuracy. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store sample values, distances, alphas, and transmittance. Performance: Faster than pre-integration methods because it avoids pre-computed tables, though it still requires scalar field interpolation. Strengths: Simple to implement, no pre-computation required. Limitations: Low accuracy due to piecewise-constant approximation; visible artifacts (jagged edges, aliasing) if sampling rate is low. Not suitable for high-quality rendering without high sampling rates. When to use: Real-time applications with limited computational resources, or as a baseline method. When not to use: High-quality offline rendering, scenes with high-frequency details, or when smooth transitions are critical. Zero Order Integration, also known as the rectangle rule or Riemann sum approximation, is one of the earliest and most fundamental methods for discretizing the volume rendering integral. The method assumes that the scalar field (density) and color are constant within each ray segment, effectively performing a zero-order hold reconstruction. It remains used in neural rendering frameworks (e.g., NeRF) as a baseline quadrature method. name: Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration
head: Fourth-order Runge-Kutta, Runge-Kutta 4 Integrator
body: Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) is a higher-order numerical integration technique for volume rendering that queries a vector field at four distinct positions to compute a single ray-marching step, significantly reducing trajectory error compared to the zero-order Zero Order Integration (Rectangle Rule) or first-order Euler methods. It solves the initial value problem for a point in an unsteady vector field by taking four samples in the neighborhood of the current point and calculating the next position using a weighted sum. It is chosen when accurate streamline visualization is required, trading approximately 4 times the computation of Euler for an order-of-magnitude reduction in local truncation error. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current position xn (3D vector), step size dt (scalar, also denoted \delta), vector field function v(x, t) returning a 3D vector at position x and time t. Output: Next position x{n+1} (3D vector). Data Structures: xn: Current position coordinates (x, y, z). ki: Intermediate slope vectors (k{ix}, k{iy}, k{iz}) representing displacement increments. dt: Step size scalar. Formulas: The method computes four slope estimates k1, k2, k3, k4 and combines them into a weighted average step: \begin{aligned} k1 &= dt \cdot v(xn) \\ k2 &= dt \cdot v\left(xn + \frac{k1}{2}\right) \\ k3 &= dt \cdot v\left(xn + \frac{k2}{2}\right) \\ k4 &= dt \cdot v(xn + k3) \\ x{n+1} &= xn + \frac{1}{6}k1 + \frac{1}{3}k2 + \frac{1}{3}k3 + \frac{1}{6}k4 + O(dt^5) \end{aligned} Where: xn is the current position. x{n+1} is the next position. dt is the time step (step size). v(x) is the vector field value at position x. O(dt^5) represents the local truncation error term. Parameters: Step size (dt or \delta): Determines the distance advanced per step. In real-time applications, this is often dynamic to maintain frame rate. Time (t{func}): Required for unsteady (time-varying) vector fields. Must be synchronized with the application's time step. For steady fields, this argument is ignored or fixed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rk4integrate(pos, dt, vectorfieldfunc, timeval=None): # 1. Sample k1 at current position v1 = vectorfieldfunc(pos, timeval) k1 = (dt v1.x, dt v1.y, dt v1.z) # 2. Sample k2 at pos + k1/2 mid1 = (pos.x + k1[0] 0.5, pos.y + k1[1] 0.5, pos.z + k1[2] 0.5) v2 = vectorfieldfunc(mid1, timeval) k2 = (dt v2.x, dt v2.y, dt v2.z) # 3. Sample k3 at pos + k2/2 mid2 = (pos.x + k2[0] 0.5, pos.y + k2[1] 0.5, pos.z + k2[2] 0.5) v3 = vectorfieldfunc(mid2, timeval) k3 = (dt v3.x, dt v3.y, dt v3.z) # 4. Sample k4 at pos + k3 end = (pos.x + k3[0], pos.y + k3[1], pos.z + k3[2]) v4 = vectorfieldfunc(end, timeval) k4 = (dt v4.x, dt v4.y, dt v4.z) # 5. Compute weighted sum: x{n+1} = xn + k1/6 + k2/3 + k3/3 + k4/6 dtsixth = dt / 6.0 nextx = pos.x + dtsixth (k1[0] + 2.0 k2[0] + 2.0 k3[0] + k4[0]) nexty = pos.y + dtsixth (k1[1] + 2.0 k2[1] + 2.0 k3[1] + k4[1]) nextz = pos.z + dtsixth (k1[2] + 2.0 k2[2] + 2.0 k3[2] + k4[2]) return (nextx, nexty, nextz) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Steady Fields: No special implementation is needed; simply ignore the time argument or pass a fixed value. Precision: RK4 has a local error of O(dt^5), whereas Euler has O(dt^2) local error. Vortices: Euler integration tends to escape vortices even at low step sizes, whereas RK4 often converges toward the vortex center or follows the streamline more accurately. A first-order vector field integrator that computes the next step using only the current position and vector field value (x{n+1} = xn + dt \cdot v(xn)). It has a local error of O(dt^2) and is significantly faster but less accurate than RK4. It is suitable for quick previews or when computational resources are extremely limited, but it tends to escape vortices and accumulates error quickly. A 2nd/3rd order Runge-Kutta method for solving ODEs with adaptive step size control. It estimates error using embedded formulas and adjusts the step size h based on relative (rtol) and absolute (atol) tolerances. Typical parameters are rtol=10^{-2}, atol=10^{-4}, and h{max}=0.1 \cdot t{span}. Time Complexity: RK4 requires four vector field evaluations per step, making it approximately 4 times slower than Euler integration. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per step (storing k1, k2, k3, k4). Accuracy: RK4 error is smaller by an order of magnitude compared to Euler. For example, RK4 with dt=1 can have less error than Euler with dt=0.5. Strengths: High accuracy for a fixed step size; robust handling of vortices; simple implementation. Limitations: Fixed step size (unless combined with adaptive logic); higher computational cost than Euler; potential instability if dt is too large for the field's curvature. When to use: When visual fidelity of streamlines is critical and real-time performance allows for 4 times the cost of Euler. When not to use: When extreme performance is required and approximate trajectories are acceptable (use Euler). The method was implemented as a standard improvement over Euler integration to reduce trajectory errors without the complexity of adaptive solvers. It is used in real-time smoke volume rendering and vector field visualization, where the step size is dynamically adjusted to maintain real-time behavior.
