name: Runge-Kutta 2/3 ODE Solver
head: RK23, Runge-Kutta 23
body: A 2nd/3rd order Runge-Kutta method for solving ODEs with adaptive step size control. It sets itself apart from its parent Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration by using a lower-order embedded pair to estimate local truncation error, enabling dynamic step size adjustment rather than fixed steps. It is distinct from the Hybrid ODE Solver for Ray Trajectory variant, which selectively falls back to Euler integration in specific geometric regimes. Inputs: y: Current state vector (position/velocity). w: Additional solver state/weights. force: Function evaluating the derivative f(t, y). t: Current time. t\span: Target end time. rtol: Relative tolerance (default 10^{-2}). atol: Absolute tolerance (default 10^{-4}). hmax: Maximum step size (default 0.1 \times t\span). Outputs: y: Updated state at t\span. t: Updated time. Data Structures: State vector y and derivative vectors ki share the same dimension as the ODE system. Scalars h, t, er, r are floating-point numbers. Algorithm: 1. Compute initial slope: k1 = force(y). 2. Estimate initial error magnitude r using k1 and rtol. 3. Initialize step size: h = 0.8 \times rtol^{1/3} / r. 4. Loop while t < t\span: a. Clamp h to [h{min}, h{max}], where h{min} = 16 \times \text{FLOAT\MIN} \times |t|. b. If 1.1 \times h \ge t\span - t, set h = t\span - t. c. Compute intermediate slopes: k2 = force(y + \frac{h}{2} k1) k3 = force(y + \frac{3h}{4} k2) d. Compute next state estimate (3rd order): y{next} = y + \frac{2h}{9} k1 + \frac{h}{3} k2 + \frac{4h}{9} k3 e. Compute final slope for error estimation: k4 = force(y{next}) f. Compute error estimate vector e: e = \frac{h}{72.0} (-5k1 + 6k2 + 8k3 - 9k4) g. Compute relative error er using e, \max(|y|, |y{next}|), and rtol. h. If er \le rtol: i. Accept step: t \leftarrow t + h, y \leftarrow y{next}, k1 \leftarrow k4. ii. Update step size: h \leftarrow h \times \min(5.0, 0.8 \times (rtol/er)^{1/3}). i. If h \le h{min}, break loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import sys def computerelativeerror(e, ymax): # Computes the maximum relative error magnitude across vector elements return max(abs(ei) / ymaxi for ei, ymaxi in zip(e, ymax)) def rk23solve(y, force, tspan, rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-4, hmax=None): t = 0.0 hmax = hmax if hmax is not None else 0.1 tspan # Initial slope k1 = force(y) # Estimate initial error to set initial step size ymaxinit = max(abs(y)) r = computerelativeerror(k1, ymaxinit) if r == 0: r = 1e-12 # Guard against division by zero h = 0.8 (rtol (1/3)) / r while t < tspan: # Clamp step size hmin = 16 sys.floatinfo.min abs(t) h = max(hmin, min(h, hmax)) # Check if step exceeds remaining time if 1.1 h >= tspan - t: h = tspan - t # Compute stages k2 = force(y + (h / 2.0) k1) k3 = force(y + (3.0 h / 4.0) k2) # 3rd order solution ynext = y + (2.0 h / 9.0) k1 + (h / 3.0) k2 + (4.0 h / 9.0) k3 # 4th stage for error estimation k4 = force(ynext) # Error estimate vector e = (h / 72.0) (-5 k1 + 6 k2 + 8 k3 - 9 k4) # Relative error check ymax = max(max(abs(y)), max(abs(ynext))) er = computerelativeerror(e, ymax) if er <= rtol: # Accept step t += h y = ynext k1 = k4 # Update step size h = h min(5.0, 0.8 (rtol / er) (1/3)) if h <= hmin: break return y, t Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: h{min} is computed as 16 \times \text{FLOAT\MIN} \times |t|. Boundaries: The check 1.1 \times h \ge t\span - t prevents overshooting the integration interval. Degenerate Input: If r=0 during initialization, division by zero occurs. A hybrid integration strategy that uses an adaptive Runge-Kutta integrator when the sphere radius S(\hat{x}) is large compared to the error threshold \hat{\epsilon}, and falls back to simple Euler integration when S(\hat{x}) is small to reduce overhead. It evaluates RKF45, DP54, and BS23, selecting BS23 for its balance of accuracy (minimum four evaluations per step) and performance. If S(\hat{x}) < a \cdot \hat{\epsilon} (where a=3), it falls back to forward Euler. Implicit solvers are avoided because the equations are not stiff, constant speed prevents runaway error, and implicit solvers incur difficult-to-control performance overhead compared to BS23's small minimum overhead. Time Complexity: Adaptive; depends on the number of function evaluations required to meet tolerance. The BS23 variant requires a minimum of four evaluations per step. Memory Complexity: O(d) where d is the dimension of the state vector, storing k1, k2, k3, k4 and current state. Strengths: Adaptive step size allows for efficiency in smooth regions and accuracy in complex regions. BS23 offers a good accuracy/performance balance for ray tracing applications. Limitations: Overhead of error estimation and step size adjustment. Not suitable for stiff equations without implicit variants. When to use: When solving ODEs for ray trajectories where computational cost must be balanced against visual accuracy. The method originates from the Bogacki-Shampine scheme, a 2nd/3rd order Runge-Kutta method. It is used in non-linear sphere tracing for rendering deformed signed distance fields to integrate ray trajectories. The algorithm steps and parameter defaults follow the specification provided in the source notes. tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, https://github.com/tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Non-linear sphere tracing for rendering deformed signed distance fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3355089.3356502, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Classical Ray Tracing Integration
head: Kajiya and Von Herzen
body: Classical Ray Tracing Integration is a volume rendering technique that computes pixel color by combining background transmission (attenuated by absorption) and uniform in-scattering. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric objects with defined boundaries or integrating geometric visibility directly into volume pipelines. Unlike standard direct volume ray casting which samples uniformly along the entire ray, this method explicitly calculates entry and exit points to limit sampling to the volume interior and applies Beer's law for transmission. It is distinguished from Alpha Compositing Ray Casting by its handling of homogeneous spheres via analytical integration, and from Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching by its assumption of uniform scattering color. The method operates in two primary modes: analytical integration for homogeneous spheres and ray marching with shading heuristics for general volume data. Both modes rely on the volume rendering integral discretized into a summation over sample points along a ray [Parent principles]. Inputs: Camera ray (origin O, direction D), volume data (3D grid or sphere parameters), transfer function, shading parameters. Outputs: Final pixel color C{final}. 1. Sphere Object (analytical mode): center: vec3 (e.g., [0, 0, -4]). radius: float (e.g., 1.0). sigmaa: float (absorption coefficient, e.g., 0.1). scatter: vec3 (uniform scatter color, e.g., [0.8, 0.1, 0.5]). 2. Volume Context (marching mode): volume: 3D texture or grid. tfn: Transfer function mapping scalar value to (C, \alpha). params: Shading mode (GRADIENTSHADING or SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC), shadingScale, gradientStep, lighting parameters. 1. Intersection Test: Compute parametric distances t0 and t1 where the ray enters and leaves the sphere. If no intersection, return backgroundcolor. 2. Distance Calculation: Compute the distance traveled through the sphere as d = t1 - t0. 3. Transmission: Apply Beer's law to compute the transmission factor T: T = e^{-\sigmaa \cdot d} where \sigmaa is the absorption coefficient. 4. Color Composition: Compute the final color as the sum of the attenuated background and the uniform scatter: C{final} = C{background} \cdot T + C{scatter} \cdot (1 - T). 1. Initialization: Initialize alpha = 0, color = 0. For SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Initialize highestOrg = 0, highestColor = 0, highestAlpha = 0. 2. Intersection Check: If the ray intersects the volume bounds [t{start}, t{end}], proceed. Otherwise, return background. 3. Jitter: Generate a random jitter value j \in [0, 1) to offset the first sample position along the ray direction. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate t from t{start} to t{end} with step size marchingStep. Position: Calculate position p = O + t \cdot D. Sample: Get scalar value d using trilinear interpolation [Parent principles]. Transfer Function: Map d to sample color Cs and opacity \alphas. Opacity Correction: Apply opacity correction based on step size to ensure slice-count invariance. Gradient Calculation: Compute gradient No = -\nabla d using a central difference operator with gradientStep. Transform to world space Nw. Transmittance: Calculate current transmittance tr = 1 - \alpha. Shading Mode: If GRADIENTSHADING: Transform ray direction to world space. Compute shaded color C{shade} using lighting model (ambient + directional) with normal Nw. Blend sample color: Cs = \text{lerp}(\text{shadingScale}, Cs, C{shade}). If SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Check if current sample density is highest: if \alphas \cdot (1 - \alpha) > \text{highestAlpha}, update highestOrg, highestColor, and highestAlpha. Use unshaded Cs for accumulation. Accumulation: Update color: C{new} = C{old} + (1 - \alpha{old}) \cdot Cs \cdot \alphas. Update alpha: \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} + (1 - \alpha{old}) \cdot \alphas. Termination: If \alpha \ge 0.99 (nearly one), break loop. 5. Final Shading (Heuristic Only): If highestAlpha > 0, compute shadow ray transmittance T{shadow} from highestOrg to light direction. Compute final color: C{final} = \text{lerp}(C{accumulated}, C{highest} \cdot \alpha{highest} \cdot T{shadow}, \text{shadingScale}). 6. Gamma Correction: Apply gamma 2.2 correction to the final color [Parent principles]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def vec3add(a, b): return (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1], a[2] + b[2]) def vec3scale(v, s): return (v[0] s, v[1] s, v[2] s) def vec3pow(v, p): return (v[0] p, v[1] p, v[2] p) def computerayexit(origin, direction, bounds): # Slab intersection for axis-aligned box t0 = max((bounds[0][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)) t1 = min((bounds[1][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)) return max(t0, t1) def trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos, dims): # Standard trilinear interpolation vx = pos[0] (dims[0] - 1) vy = pos[1] (dims[1] - 1) vz = pos[2] (dims[2] - 1) x0, y0, z0 = int(math.floor(vx)), int(math.floor(vy)), int(math.floor(vz)) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 x0 = max(0, min(x0, dims[0]-1)) x1 = max(0, min(x1, dims[0]-1)) y0 = max(0, min(y0, dims[1]-1)) y1 = max(0, min(y1, dims[1]-1)) z0 = max(0, min(z0, dims[2]-1)) z1 = max(0, min(z1, dims[2]-1)) wx = vx - x0 wy = vy - y0 wz = vz - z0 c00 = volume[x0][y0][z0] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y0][z0] wx c01 = volume[x0][y0][z1] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y0][z1] wx c10 = volume[x0][y1][z0] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y1][z0] wx c11 = volume[x0][y1][z1] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y1][z1] wx r0 = c00 (1-wy) + c10 wy r1 = c01 (1-wy) + c11 wy return r0 (1-wz) + r1 wz def classicalraytracingintegration(rayorigin, raydirection, sphere, backgroundcolor, volume=None, params=None): """ Renders a pixel using classical ray tracing integration. Supports homogeneous spheres (analytical) and general volumes (marching). """ def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) # --- Mode 1: Homogeneous Sphere (Analytical) --- if sphere is not None and volume is None: t0, t1 = sphere.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if t0 is None: return backgroundcolor distance = t1 - t0 transmission = math.exp(-sphere.sigmaa distance) finalcolor = vec3add( vec3scale(backgroundcolor, transmission), vec3scale(sphere.scatter, 1.0 - transmission)) return vec3pow(finalcolor, 1.0 / 2.2) # --- Mode 2: General Volume (Ray Marching) --- if volume is not None: tstart, tend = volume.intersectbounds(rayorigin, raydirection) if tstart is None: return backgroundcolor alpha = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) highestorg = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) highestcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) highestalpha = 0.0 jitter = random.random() stepsize = params.marchingStep if params else 0.01 tcurr = tstart + jitter stepsize while alpha < 0.99 and tcurr < tend: p = vec3add(rayorigin, vec3scale(raydirection, tcurr)) scalar = trilinearinterpolate(volume.data, p, volume.dims) samplecolor, samplealpha = volume.tfn(scalar) # Opacity correction for slice-count invariance samplealpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-samplealpha stepsize) grad = volume.samplegradient(p, scalar, params.gradientStep) normalworld = volume.transformnormal(grad) transmittance = 1.0 - alpha if params.mode == "GRADIENTSHADING": dirworld = volume.transformvector(raydirection) shadedcolor = volume.shadescivislight(dirworld, normalworld, samplecolor, params.matgradientshading, params.lightambient, params.lightdirectionalrgb, params.lightdirectionaldir) samplecolor = vec3add(vec3scale(samplecolor, 1.0 - params.shadingScale), vec3scale(shadedcolor, params.shadingScale)) elif params.mode == "SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC": currentdensity = transmittance samplealpha if currentdensity > highestalpha: highestorg = p highestcolor = samplecolor highestalpha = currentdensity contrib = vec3scale(samplecolor, transmittance samplealpha) color = vec3add(color, contrib) alpha += transmittance samplealpha tcurr += stepsize if params.mode == "SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC" and highestalpha > 0.0: # Shadow ray transmittance computation not provided in sources [Comment] shadowtransmittance = 1.0 finalshadedcolor = vec3scale(highestcolor, highestalpha shadowtransmittance) color = vec3add(vec3scale(color, 1.0 - params.shadingScale), vec3scale(finalshadedcolor, params.shadingScale)) return vec3pow(color, 1.0 / 2.2) return backgroundcolor sigmaa: Absorption coefficient. Typical value: 0.1. scatter: Uniform scatter color. Typical value: [0.8, 0.1, 0.5]. backgroundcolor: Color returned if no intersection. Typical value: [0.572, 0.772, 0.921]. shadingScale: Scalar blending unshaded and shaded colors. gradientStep: Step size for gradient estimation. marchingStep: Step size for ray marching. Redundant Distance Calculation: Computing the Euclidean distance between entry and exit points (\|\bar{p}1 - \bar{p}2\|) is correct but computationally redundant if t0 and t1 are known; use t1 - t0. Uniform Scattering Assumption: The analytical mode assumes uniform scattering color regardless of position or direction; it does not account for directional lighting or varying scattering properties. Heuristic Gradient: In SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC, gradients are not accumulated; only the highest density point is stored for deferred shading. Shadow Ray Cost: Computing shadow transmittance from the highest density point adds significant cost for the heuristic mode. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples along the ray. For analytical spheres, it is O(1) per pixel. For marching, it depends on volume density and step size. Memory Complexity: O(1) for analytical mode. O(V) for volume data storage in marching mode. Performance: Analytical integration is extremely fast and exact for homogeneous spheres. Ray marching handles complex scalar fields and supports deferred shading heuristics. Strengths: Exact solution for homogeneous volumes; integrates geometric visibility; supports shading heuristics for complex data. Limitations: Analytical mode is limited to simple shapes; uniform scattering assumption is unrealistic for many volumes; heuristic shading may produce artifacts if the highest density point is not representative. When to use: Ideal for rendering simple volumetric objects (e.g., clouds, smoke balls) or when integrating geometric surfaces with volume data. Avoid for highly anisotropic or spatially varying scattering volumes. The method originates from early volume rendering techniques that combined ray tracing with volume data. The integration of classical ray tracing into volume rendering pipelines was proposed to handle visibility and geometric merging, such as superimposing radiation treatment planning isodose surfaces over CT data. The heuristic shading approach was developed to balance performance and visual quality in scientific visualization. Recent applications include integrating ray tracing for interreflections in 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching)
head: God Rays, Light Shafts, VolumetricLightURP
body: Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching) is a post-processing or overlay technique for rendering volumetric light shafts (crepuscular rays) in the Unity Universal Render Pipeline (URP) by raymarching from the camera through a fixed-distance volume, modulated by the main light's realtime shadows. It solves the problem of simulating atmospheric fog beams and god rays in real-time 3D scenes where full volumetric path tracing is too expensive. Unlike its sibling Screen-Space God Rays, which uses radial blur on an occlusion map, this method performs actual 3D raymarching with shadow sampling, providing geometrically consistent light shafts that respect scene depth and shadows, at the cost of higher performance overhead. It builds on Fixed Step Ray Marching by using a fixed step size and exponential absorption logic, but specifically targets light shafts from a single directional light. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera world position, fragment world position (from vertex shader), main light position (LightPos), main light color/intensity (LightColor), density (Density), step count (StepCount), max distance (MaxDistance), scattering multiplier (Scattering), and base color (BaseColor). Outputs: Accumulated light color and alpha for the current pixel. Data Structures: Shader Properties (CBUFFER): BaseColor: float4 (RGBA), default (1,1,1,1). Density: Float, default 0.5, range [0, 1]. StepCount: Int, default 64, range [16, 128]. MaxDistance: Float, default 20.0. Scattering: Float, default 1.2. LightPos: float4 (xyz: world position, w: 1.0). LightColor: float4 (RGB: color intensity, A: unused). Vertex Shader Output: positionHCS: Clip space position. positionWS: World space position. Fragment Shader State: rayOrigin: Camera world position. rayDir: Normalized vector from camera to fragment world position. accum: Accumulated light contribution, initialized to 0.0. Parameters: g (Henyey-Greenstein asymmetry parameter): 0.35 (hardcoded). stepSize: Calculated as MaxDistance / steps. Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Shader: Transform input object space position to clip space and world space. Pass world space position to fragment shader via TEXCOORD0. 2. Fragment Shader Initialization: Get camera world position (camPos). Get fragment world position (posWS) from TEXCOORD0. Calculate ray direction: rayDir = normalize(posWS - camPos). Initialize accum = 0.0. Determine steps = max(StepCount, 1) to prevent division by zero. Calculate stepSize = MaxDistance / steps. 3. Raymarching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to steps - 1: Calculate distance: dist = i stepSize. Calculate sample position: samplePos = rayOrigin + rayDir dist. Shadow Sampling: Transform samplePos to shadow coordinates: shadowCoord = TransformWorldToShadowCoord(samplePos). Sample main light realtime shadow: shadow = MainLightRealtimeShadow(shadowCoord). Light Direction: Calculate vector from sample to light: lightDir = normalize(LightPos.xyz - samplePos). Phase Function: Calculate scattering angle cosine: cosTheta = dot(rayDir, lightDir). Compute Henyey-Greenstein phase function: P(\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{(1 + g^2 - 2g \cos\theta)^{1.5}} where g = 0.35. Accumulation: Add to accum: accum += shadow \times P(\theta) \times Density \times stepSize. 4. Final Color: Calculate lightAmount = accum. Output color: LightColor.rgb lightAmount Scattering. Output alpha: saturate(lightAmount). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Varyings { float4 positionHCS: SVPOSITION; float3 positionWS: TEXCOORD0; }; Varyings vert(float3 positionOS: POSITION) { Varyings OUT; // Unity URP helper to get world space and clip space positions VertexPositionInputs pos = GetVertexPositionInputs(positionOS); OUT.positionHCS = pos.positionCS; OUT.positionWS = pos.positionWS; return OUT; } float HenyeyGreenstein(float cosTheta, float g) { float g2 = g g; return (1.0 - g2) / pow(1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g cosTheta, 1.5); } float4 frag(Varyings IN): SVTARGET { // Get camera world position float3 camPos = GetCameraWorldPosition(); // Standard URP helper or equivalent float3 rayDir = normalize(IN.positionWS - camPos); float accum = 0.0; // Clamp step count to prevent division by zero int steps = max(StepCount, 1); float stepSize = MaxDistance / steps; for (int i = 0; i < steps; i++) { float dist = i stepSize; float3 samplePos = camPos + rayDir dist; // Shadow sampling float4 shadowCoord = TransformWorldToShadowCoord(samplePos); float shadow = MainLightRealtimeShadow(shadowCoord); // Light direction float3 lightDir = normalize(LightPos.xyz - samplePos); // Phase function float cosTheta = dot(rayDir, lightDir); float phase = HenyeyGreenstein(cosTheta, 0.35); // Accumulation accum += shadow phase Density stepSize; } float lightAmount = accum; float3 finalColor = LightColor.rgb lightAmount Scattering; float alpha = saturate(lightAmount); return float4(finalColor, alpha); } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If StepCount is less than 1, it is clamped to 1 to prevent division by zero or invalid loop behavior. The method only supports a single directional light (the "main light"). It does not support complex volume textures or multiple light sources. Performance cost is significant: adds ~2.30 ms to a 5.0 ms frame in benchmarked scenarios. A cheaper post-processing alternative using radial blur on an occlusion map. It fails with multiple lights or off-screen lights but is faster. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps (StepCount). Each step involves a shadow coordinate transform and a shadow texture sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for accumulation, plus standard shadow map memory. Performance: Adds approximately 2.30 ms to a 5.0 ms frame in benchmarked tests. Strengths: Geometrically consistent with scene depth and shadows; supports dynamic light movement and density changes via C# controller. Limitations: Only works with the main directional light; no support for multiple lights or volumetric textures; performance scales linearly with step count and resolution. When to use: Stylized atmospheric lighting, fog beams, or god rays where shadow accuracy is important and performance budget allows. When not to use: Scenes with multiple light sources, off-screen lights, or when performance is critical and screen-space approximation is acceptable. The technique is implemented as a custom shader and C# controller for the Unity Universal Render Pipeline (URP). It is designed for fog beams, atmospheric lighting, and stylized god ray effects. The implementation uses the Henyey-Greenstein phase function with a hardcoded asymmetry parameter g=0.35. The method is distinct from voxel-based god ray implementations (like those in the voxel engine benchmark) which march shafts from surfaces brighter than the sky. name: Screen-Space God Rays
head: Crepuscular Rays, Light Shafts, Radial Blur God Rays, Screen-Space Radial Blur, Volumetric Light Shaft
body: Screen-Space God Rays is a post-processing technique that renders screen-space crepuscular rays by accumulating radial blur from the sun's screen position, modulated by density, decay, and weight. It fakes volumetric light shafts using a radial blur on an occlusion map, dominating implementations for over a decade due to speed and simplicity. Unlike volumetric ray marching, it is cheaper (two extra passes, handful of texture samples) but less accurate, failing with multiple lights or off-screen lights. The method operates in three passes: generating an occlusion map, applying radial blur, and compositing. Inputs: tDiffuse: The main scene color buffer (sampler2D). tOcclusion: The black-and-white occlusion map generated in Pass 1 (sampler2D). sunScreenPos / uLightPos: The 3D light source projected to 2D screen coordinates in UV space [0,1] (vec2). density / uDensity: Controls the spread of the ray delta or how far each ray extends outward from the light (float). decay / uDecay: How quickly brightness falls off along each ray (float). weight / uWeight: Sample weight multiplier or initial brightness of each sample (float). exposure / uExposure: Final exposure multiplier scaling the composite brightness (float). NUMSAMPLES: Number of samples per ray (int). 64 is a common sweet spot balancing smoothness and cost. Outputs: godRaysTexture: The final radial blur result containing only the god ray light shafts. glFragColor: The final composited color. Uniforms (Pass 2): tOcclusion: sampler2D. uLightPos: vec2. uExposure: float. uDecay: float. uDensity: float. uWeight: float. NUMSAMPLES: const int. 1. Render the scene with all geometry as solid black and the light source as a bright shape (circle/sphere) to create a black-and-white occlusion map where bright pixels indicate direct light visibility. Set scene override material to black. Render scene geometry to occlusionTarget. Render light source geometry (bright) to occlusionTarget with depth testing to ensure proper occlusion by foreground geometry. 1. Project Light Position: Project the 3D sun direction to 2D screen space using the view-projection matrix. Scale sunDir by 10000.0, transform by viewProjMatrix, divide by clipW, convert to NDC, and then to [0,1] screen coordinates. Edge Case: If clipW <= 0.0001, the sun is behind the camera. Return center screen (0.5, 0.5) and set inFront = false. 2. Initialize: Set textCoord = vUv, color = texture2D(tDiffuse, textCoord) (or vec3(0.0) if accumulating only rays), illuminationDecay = 1.0 (or illumination = 1.0). 3. Radial Accumulation Loop: For i from 0 to NUMSAMPLES - 1: Calculate delta vector: deltaUV = (vUv - uLightPos) uDensity / float(NUMSAMPLES). (Note: uses (vUv - sunScreenPos) (1.0 / 64.0) density, which is equivalent if density in corresponds to uDensity/NUMSAMPLES in. We follow the explicit loop structure in for clarity). Update coordinate: uv -= deltaUV. Sample occlusion map: samp = texture2D(tOcclusion, clamp(uv, 0.0, 1.0)).rgb. Accumulate: color += samp illumination uWeight. (Note: uses sample illuminationDecay weight). Update decay: illumination = uDecay. (Note: uses illuminationDecay = decay). 4. Finalize: glFragColor = vec4(color uExposure, 1.0). (Note: uses color exposure where color included the initial diffuse texture sample). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): # Calculate the step vector for radial blur # deltaUV points from light position towards current pixel, scaled by density and sample count deltauv = (vUv - uLightPos) uDensity / float(NUMSAMPLES) uv = vUv illumination = 1.0 color = vec3(0.0) for i in range(NUMSAMPLES): # Move towards the light source (opposite to deltauv direction if deltauv is defined as pixel-to-light) # In the source, deltauv is (vUv - uLightPos)... and uv -= deltaUV. # This means we are moving AWAY from the light if deltauv is positive? # Let's re-read: "sample repeatedly along the line from that pixel toward the light's screen position". # If uv starts at vUv, and we want to go TOWARD uLightPos, we should subtract (vUv - uLightPos). # deltauv = (vUv - uLightPos)... # uv -= deltauv => uv = vUv - (vUv - uLightPos)... = vUv + (uLightPos - vUv)... # This moves towards uLightPos. Correct. uv = uv - deltauv # Clamp to screen bounds to avoid sampling outside the texture uvclamped = clamp(uv, 0.0, 1.0) # Sample the occlusion map samp = texture2D(tOcclusion, uvclamped).rgb # Apply decay and weight samp = samp illumination uWeight # Accumulate color = color + samp # Update illumination decay illumination = illumination uDecay # Final exposure glFragColor = vec4(color uExposure, 1.0) density / uDensity: Controls the spread of the ray delta. Higher values stretch rays longer. Default 0.92. weight / uWeight: Sample weight multiplier. Controls overall ray intensity. Default 0.58. decay / uDecay: How quickly brightness falls off along each ray. Values close to 1.0 (like 0.97) produce long, gradual rays.. exposure / uExposure: Final exposure multiplier. Default 0.35. NUMSAMPLES: Number of samples per ray. 64 is a common sweet spot. Sun Behind Camera: If clipW <= 0.0001 during projection, the sun is behind the camera. Return center screen (0.5, 0.5) and handle accordingly. Off-Screen Light: The technique only works for a single, visible light source. If the light moves off-screen, the rays disappear. Multiple Lights: The technique fails with multiple light sources. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is NUMSAMPLES. Constant number of texture samples (64) per pixel in Pass 2. Memory Complexity: O(WH) for the occlusion map and god rays texture, where W and H are screen dimensions. Measured Performance: Requires two extra render passes and a handful of texture samples per pixel, a fraction of the cost of volumetric ray marching. Strengths: Fast, simple, convincing results for single light sources. Limitations: Less accurate than volumetric ray marching. Fails with multiple lights or off-screen lights. When to use: Mobile or lower-end hardware, single dominant light source (sun). When not to use: Multiple light sources, physically accurate requirements, lights moving off-screen. Origin: Published by Kenny Mitchell in GPU Gems 3 in 2007. History: One of the first mainstream implementations in games, notably Crysis (2007), setting a standard expectation for high-end PC games. Dominated god ray implementations for over a decade. Usage: Used in Crysis (2007). nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, https://github.com/nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volumetric Lighting (God Rays) — How It Works - Moonjump, https://moonjump.com/game-dev-mechanics-volumetric-lighting-god-rays-how-it-works/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Image-order Ray-Casting
head: Levoy's Ray Casting, Levoy raycasting, Image-order Volume Rendering, Composite ray casting, Volume Ray Tracing
body:
Image-order Ray-Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that visualizes 3D scalar or vector data by casting primary rays from the viewpoint through a volumetric dataset, sampling values at regular intervals, and compositing colors and opacities to form a 2D projection. It solves the problem of rendering fuzzy, semi-transparent volumes without explicit geometric surface extraction, avoiding the aliasing artifacts associated with binary classification in surface extraction methods like marching cubes. Unlike surface ray tracing, it handles only primary rays (no secondary rays for shadows or reflections) and differs from object-order methods (like splatting) by processing the image pixel-by-pixel rather than projecting voxels onto the screen. Inputs: A 3D scalar voxel grid V with dimensions W 	imes H 	imes D, a viewing frustum defined by eye point E, near plane, and pixel coordinates (u,v), and a 1D transfer function mapping scalar values to color c(s) and opacity \alpha(s). Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel (u,v) contains an accumulated color C{out}. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array of scalar values. Access is typically via trilinear interpolation. Transfer Function: A lookup table or function T(s) = (c(s), \alpha(s)). Ray State: Accumulated color C, accumulated transmittance T, current position X, and step counter. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel (u,v), compute the ray origin O = E and direction D = 	ext{normalize}(P - E), where P is the 3D position of the pixel on the near plane. 2. AABB Intersection: Intersect the ray X(t) = O + tD with the volume's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defined by [\minx, \maxx] 	imes [\miny, \maxy] 	imes [\minz, \maxz] using the slab method: For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: t{i,\min} =  rac{\mini - Oi}{Di}, \quad t{i,\max} =  rac{\maxi - Oi}{Di} \quad (	ext{if } Di 
eq 0; \infty 	ext{ otherwise}) Compute entry and exit distances: t{	ext{entry}} = \max(0, \max(t{x,\min}, t{y,\min}, t{z,\min})) t{	ext{exit}} = \min(t{x,\max}, t{y,\max}, t{z,\max}) If t{	ext{entry}} > t{	ext{exit}}, the ray misses the volume; output background color and continue to next pixel. 3. Initialization: Initialize accumulated color C = (0,0,0) and transmittance T = 1.0. Set current parameter t = t{	ext{entry}}. 4. Traversal Loop: While t < t{	ext{exit}}: Step Increment: t \leftarrow t + \Delta t, where \Delta t is the fixed step size (typically proportional to voxel size, e.g., \Delta t = 	ext{voxel\size} / n). Position Update: X = O + tD. Sampling: Map X to voxel coordinates and perform trilinear interpolation to get scalar value s: Let dx = x - \lfloor x floor, dy = y - \lfloor y floor, dz = z - \lfloor z floor. s = \sum{i,j,k \in \{0,1\}} (1-dx)^{1-i}dx^i (1-dy)^{1-j}dy^j (1-dz)^{1-k}dz^k \cdot v{ijk} where v{ijk} are the 8 surrounding voxel values. Classification: Map s to color cs and opacity \alphas using the transfer function. Shading (Optional): Estimate gradient 
abla s using central differences to compute normal \mathbf{N} = 	ext{normalize}(-
abla s) for local illumination (e.g., Phong). Compositing (Front-to-Back): Update C and T: C \leftarrow C + T \cdot cs \cdot \alphas T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphas) Early Termination: If T < \epsilon (e.g., 0.01) or accumulated opacity 1-T > 0.95, break loop. 5. Output: Store C as the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imageorderraycasting(volume, transferfunction, eyepoint, nearplane, imagewidth, imageheight, stepsize, epsilon=0.01): # Precompute AABB bounds from volume aabbmin = volume.minbounds aabbmax = volume.maxbounds image = emptyarray(imagewidth, imageheight, 3) for v in range(imageheight): for u in range(imagewidth): # 1. Ray Generation pixelpos = nearplane.project(u, v) rayorigin = eyepoint raydir = normalize(pixelpos - rayorigin) # 2. AABB Intersection (Slab Method) tmin = 0.0 tmax = infinity for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: if abs(raydir[axis]) > 1e-8: t1 = (aabbmin[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) / raydir[axis] t2 = (aabbmax[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) / raydir[axis] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) else: if rayorigin[axis] < aabbmin[axis] or rayorigin[axis] > aabbmax[axis]: tmin = infinity # Ray misses break if tmin > tmax or tmin == infinity: image[u, v] = backgroundcolor continue # 3. Initialization acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) transmittance = 1.0 # 4. Traversal Loop t = tmin while t < tmax: # Position pos = rayorigin + t raydir # Sampling (Trilinear Interpolation) # Note: volume.sample() handles floor and interpolation internally scalarval = volume.sample(pos) # Classification colors, alphas = transferfunction(scalarval) # Compositing (Front-to-Back) contribution = colors alphas transmittance acccolor = acccolor + contribution transmittance = transmittance (1.0 - alphas) # Early Termination if transmittance < epsilon: break # Step t += stepsize image[u, v] = acccolor return image Parameters: Step Size (\Delta t): Fixed distance between samples. Typically \Delta t = 	ext{voxel\size} / n where n \ge 1. Epsilon (\epsilon): Threshold for early termination. Typical value 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Handled in slab method by checking Di 
eq 0. Aliasing: Undersampling causes aliasing artifacts. Supersampling (multiple rays per pixel) mitigates this but increases cost. Boundary Conditions: Interpolation must handle coordinates outside the voxel grid (clamp or repeat). Precision: Floating-point errors in t accumulation can cause gaps or overlaps; using world-space coordinates for position calculation (X = O + tD) is preferred over incremental addition. Computes ray entry/exit points by rasterizing the volume's bounding box twice with different depth tests, then uses these coordinates for ray casting. Solves efficient interval determination on GPU without complex intersection algorithms. A variant focusing on specific traversal strategies for the ray-casting pipeline. Uses image-space coherency to generate ray-segments by scan-converting front-facing faces, traversing them through the volume, and inserting composited segments into a RayBuffer. A variant that casts rays through a 3D voxel grid, sampling values using barycentric interpolation within the unit cube, and accumulating lighting contributions (ambient, diffuse, specular) along the ray path. It initializes viewing plane and volume structures, computes ray origin/direction per pixel, iterates along the ray with a fixed step size, samples via barycentric interpolation, calculates lighting, and clamps the accumulated result to [0, 1]. A volumetric rendering technique where a ray is projected through the data volume for each pixel, and intersecting voxels influence the pixel value. A variant where the volume is transformed to align with the view direction prior to ray-casting, so resample locations coincide with integer grid points. It decomposes the transformation into affine transforms (shear/scale), resamples the volume for regular access, and casts rays based on the resampled data. Produces an intermediate image aligned with one of the volume faces (via shear/scale transform) and then warps (2D transform) it to the view plane to achieve a one-to-one mapping of ray-samples onto the volume. Time Complexity: O(N{pixels} \cdot N{samples}), where N{samples} is the number of steps along the ray. Proportional to volume resolution and image resolution. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, plus O(1) per pixel for accumulation. Performance: Computationally expensive due to the large number of samples and interpolation operations per pixel. GPU acceleration (fragment shaders) enables real-time performance for moderate resolutions. Strengths: High-fidelity visualization of fuzzy boundaries, no aliasing from surface extraction, flexible viewpoint and lighting, handles partial transparency naturally. Limitations: High computational cost, sensitive to aliasing if undersampled, requires careful tuning of transfer functions. When to Use: Medical imaging (CT/MRI), scientific visualization (fluids, clouds), and entertainment (smoke, fire) where visual quality and transparency are prioritized over speed. When Not to Use: Real-time applications with very large volumes and strict latency constraints without GPU acceleration, or when simple surface visualization suffices. Developed in the late 1980s, volume ray casting builds on foundational work in optical modeling. Marc Levoy introduced a practical algorithm in 1988 for displaying surfaces from volume data without intermediate geometric primitives. James T. Kajiya and Brian P. Von Herzen developed algorithms for tracing rays through volume densities in 1984. The first ray casting algorithm for rendering was presented by Arthur Appel in 1968. It is used in medical imaging, molecular graphics, fluid dynamics, and entertainment, implemented in tools like VTK, Open Inventor, and hardware like VolumePro. name: Two-Pass Depth Ray Casting
head: Depth Peeling Ray Casting, Entry/Exit Depth Ray Casting, GPU Ray-Casting, Krüger Ray-Casting, Ray-Casting de Krüger, Volumetric Ray-Casting
body: Two-Pass Depth Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that computes ray entry and exit points by rendering the volume's bounding box twice with different face culling and depth test modes, then uses these coordinates to cast rays through the volume in a subsequent pass. It solves the problem of efficiently determining the start and end of the integration interval for each pixel on the GPU without complex ray-volume intersection algorithms. Unlike Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting which may use different traversal strategies, this method relies on hardware rasterization of the bounding box to find intersections. It differs from Koyamada's Algorithm by explicitly separating the depth determination phase from the accumulation phase using multiple render targets. Inputs: 3D volume texture (tVolume): Scalar field data. Transfer function texture (tTFFunc): Maps volume values to RGBA. Volume resolution (tDIM): Dimensions in voxels (e.g., m\DataRes). Value span (v\Min, v\Max): Minimum and maximum values in the dataset. Bounding box geometry: Cube defined by 8 vertices and 36 indices. Outputs: Final rendered image in RenderFB. Bounding Box Geometry: Vertices: 8 vertices, each with 3 floats for position (x,y,z) and 3 floats for color (r,g,b). Indices: 36 uint32s forming 12 triangles (2 per face). Framebuffers: Three framebuffers (mProjInFB, mProjOutFB, mRenderFB) resized to viewport dimensions (m\ViewportSize.x, m\ViewportSize.y). Render Targets (Textures): ProjInFB (Entry): Floating-point texture, width/height matching window, NearestFilter, ClampToEdgeWrapping, FloatType, no mipmaps. Stores world-space coordinates of the back-face intersection (ray entry). ProjOutFB (Exit): Floating-point texture, same properties as ProjInFB. Stores world-space coordinates of the front-face intersection (ray exit). 3D Texture (cubeTex): Data3DTexture with dimensions (imageStackLength, 256, 256), RedFormat, LinearFilter, no mipmaps. 1. Pass 1 (Entry Point): Render the volume's bounding box with back-face culling enabled. Set the depth test to DEPTHLESS and clear the depth buffer to 1.0. The fragment shader outputs the world-space coordinates of the intersection to ProjInFB. This captures the nearest intersection (ray entry point) for each screen pixel. 2. Pass 2 (Exit Point): Render the same bounding box with front-face culling enabled. Set the depth test to DEPTHGREATER and clear the depth buffer to 0.0. The fragment shader outputs the world-space coordinates to ProjOutFB. This captures the farthest intersection (ray exit point). 3. Pass 3+ (Ray Casting and Accumulation): Render a fullscreen quad (or front-facing cube) to RenderFB. Bind ProjInFB and ProjOutFB as textures providing ray start and end coordinates. Bind the 3D volume texture and transfer function. Calculate ray vector: \vec{ray} = \vec{backPosition} - \vec{frontPosition}. Calculate ray length: L = \|\vec{ray}\|. Calculate step parameters: \delta = 1.0 / \text{steps}, \vec{deltaDirection} = \text{normalize}(\vec{ray}) \cdot \delta, \Delta L = \|\vec{deltaDirection}\|. Initialize: \vec{currentPosition} = \vec{frontPosition}, \vec{accumulatedColor} = (0,0,0,0), L{acc} = 0. Loop for steps iterations (or up to a fixed max, e.g., 998): Sample volume: I = \text{texture}(t\Volume, \vec{currentPosition}).r. Apply contrast/brightness: I' = \text{contrast} \cdot I + \text{brightness}. Threshold: If I' \le \text{colorTreshLow} or I' \ge \text{colorTreshHigh}, set I' = 0. Compute color contribution: If I' \ge 0.5: C = (I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \delta, 0, 0, I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \delta). Else: C = (I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \delta, I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \delta, I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \delta, I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \delta). Accumulate: \vec{accumulatedColor} += C. Update: L{acc} += \Delta L, \vec{currentPosition} += \vec{deltaDirection}. Early Termination: If L{acc} \ge L or \vec{accumulatedColor}.a \ge 1.0, break loop. Output \vec{accumulatedColor} to glFragColor. 4. Early Depth Test Optimization: In passes 3 to N, write a depth value that forces fragment rejection in subsequent passes for fragments that have reached maximum opacity, utilizing the GPU's Early Depth Test feature to skip expensive fragment shader execution. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pass1entrypoint(): setdepthtest(LESS) cleardepth(1.0) setculling(BACK) renderboundingbox() # Fragment shader: glFragColor = vec4(worldSpaceCoords, 1.0) def pass2exitpoint(): setdepthtest(GREATER) cleardepth(0.0) setculling(FRONT) renderboundingbox() # Fragment shader: glFragColor = vec4(worldSpaceCoords, 1.0) def pass3raycasting(): setdepthtest(LESS) # For early rejection cleardepth(0.0) bindframebuffer(RenderFB) bindtexture("tex", ProjInFB) # Entry coords bindtexture("texOut", ProjOutFB) # Exit coords (if needed, though entry is usually sufficient for direction if origin is known, but here we use both) bindtexture("cubeTex", tVolume) # Render fullscreen quad renderquad() # Fragment Shader Logic def fragmentshader(): # Get projected coordinates projectedcoords = getfragmentposition() texc = vec2( (projectedcoords.x / projectedcoords.w + 1.0) / 2.0, (projectedcoords.y / projectedcoords.w + 1.0) / 2.0) # Retrieve entry and exit points backposition = texture2D(tex, texc).xyz frontposition = getworldspacecoords() # From vertex shader/quad geometry # Edge case: Invalid intersection if backposition.x == 0.0 and backposition.y == 0.0: return vec4(0.0) # Ray setup ray = backposition - frontposition raylength = length(ray) steps = 256 # Typical value delta = 1.0 / steps deltadirection = normalize(ray) delta deltalength = length(deltadirection) currentposition = frontposition accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) accumulatedlength = 0.0 # Parameters contrast = 1.0 brightness = 0.0 colortreshlow = 0.0 colortreshhigh = 1.0 alphacorrection = 2.0 for i in range(998): # Fixed max iterations # Sample volume textureintensity = texture(cubeTex, currentposition).r textureintensity = contrast textureintensity + brightness # Thresholding if textureintensity <= colortreshlow or textureintensity >= colortreshhigh: textureintensity = 0.0 # Color contribution if textureintensity >= 0.5: color = vec4( textureintensity 2.56 alphacorrection delta, 0.0, 0.0, textureintensity 2.56 alphacorrection delta) else: color = vec4( textureintensity 2.56 alphacorrection delta, textureintensity 2.56 alphacorrection delta, textureintensity 2.56 alphacorrection delta, textureintensity 2.56 alphacorrection delta) accumulatedcolor += color accumulatedlength += deltalength currentposition += deltadirection # Early termination if accumulatedlength >= raylength or accumulatedcolor.a >= 1.0: break # Write depth for early rejection in subsequent passes if fully opaque if accumulatedcolor.a >= 1.0: setdepth(1.0) # Force rejection return accumulatedcolor steps: Number of steps along the ray. Default: 256. tDIM (vec3): Volume resolution in voxels. vMin, vMax (float): Min/Max volume values. tCoordIn, tCoordOut (sampler2D): Textures for entry/exit coordinates. tVolume (sampler3D): 3D volume texture. tTFFunc (sampler1D/sampler2D): Transfer function. colorTreshLow, colorTreshHigh: Intensity threshold bounds. alphaCorrection: Scalar multiplier for intensity. contrast, brightness: Contrast/brightness adjustment. Scaling: Performance is greatly impacted by data volume due to the rasterization of support primitives. Zero Viewport: Invalid framebuffer operations if viewport size is zero. Check mViewportSize.x > 0.0 && mViewportSize.y > 0.0 before resizing. Invalid Intersection: If backPosition is (0,0,0), it indicates an invalid intersection (edge of cube). Return black. Accumulation Method: This implementation uses simple additive accumulation without explicit opacity weighting (1.0 - \text{accumulatedAlpha}), unlike standard front-to-back alpha compositing. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot S), where P is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps per ray. The method requires 3+ passes per frame (2 for depth, 1+ for accumulation). Memory Complexity: O(V + P), where V is the volume texture size and P is the framebuffer size for storing entry/exit coordinates. Performance: Early Depth Test allows skipping fragments that reach full opacity, improving performance in transparent regions. However, the method does not scale well with large data volumes due to the overhead of rasterizing bounding box primitives for every pass. Strengths: Simple implementation on GPU; leverages hardware depth testing; no complex ray-triangle intersection code required. Limitations: Fixed step count may lead to aliasing or slow convergence; additive accumulation is less physically accurate than alpha compositing; poor scalability with data size. When to use: Real-time rendering on Shader Model 2.0/3.0 GPUs for moderate-sized regular voxel grids. When not to use: Large-scale datasets requiring adaptive sampling or complex scene composition with surfaces. Origin: First proposed by Krüger [KW03] for Shader Model 2.0 GPUs. Development: Extended by Scharsach [Sch05] using Shader Model 3.0 features, including dynamic branching and block-based volume partitioning for selective memory loading. Usage: Used in interactive volume exploration tools, particularly for medical imaging (DICOM data) where regular voxel grids are common. name: Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting
head: Basic ray-casting model, DRR Generation via Ray Casting, Digital Radiograph Synthesis, Levoy Raycasting, Ray Casting DRR
body: Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that processes volume data without generating intermediate representations, assigning optical properties directly to voxels. It solves the problem of synthesizing 2D projections (such as Digital Radiographs) or shaded views from 3D scalar fields by casting rays from the image plane into the dataset. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Two-Pass Depth Ray Casting and Koyamada's Algorithm, is its feed-backward accumulation order and the specific early-termination optimization enabled when accumulated opacity reaches one. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V with dimensions W \times H \times D. A camera model defining the image plane and ray origins/directions. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Volume V: A 3D array of scalar values (e.g., density). Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. Accumulators: Per-ray variables for accumulated color C{acc} (RGB) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} (scalar). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel in the image plane, cast a ray into the dataset. The ray is defined by its origin and direction vector. 2. Sampling: Traverse the ray through the volume. Initially, basic equidistant sampling is used along the ray path. For higher performance, this is replaced by Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) or Bresenham-like algorithms to efficiently traverse voxel boundaries. 3. Interpolation: At each sample point along the ray, interpolate the volume data V to generate the scalar value at that specific coordinate. 4. Shading: Shade each sample point using a shading model. This model accounts for light transmission and reflection, converting the scalar value into color C and opacity \alpha. 5. Accumulation (Feed-Backward): Add the results of the shading model to the current ray's accumulators. The standard volume rendering integral is approximated using the feed-backward order: C{acc} = C{acc} + C \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) Where C is the sample color and \alpha is the sample opacity. 6. Termination: Terminate the process when the ray exits the volume boundaries or when the accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} equals one. Parameters: Sampling Interval: Determined by the DDA step size or equidistant spacing. Not given in the sources. Coordinate System: Consistency is mandatory across the pipeline. For medical applications (DRR), the DRRGeometry class must initialize spatial parameters from DICOM metadata fields 'Image Position Patient' and 'Image Orientation Patient'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vanhooklevoyraycasting(volume, rayorigin, raydirection, imageplaneparams): """ Implements the basic Van Hook-Levoy feed-backward ray casting. Args: volume: 3D array of scalar values. rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z). raydirection: 3D vector (x, y, z), normalized. imageplaneparams: Object containing camera geometry and DICOM metadata. Returns: color: 3D vector (R, G, B). opacity: Scalar. """ # Initialize accumulators acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 # Determine ray bounds within the volume # Implementation detail: Calculate intersection of ray with volume bounding box. # Let tmin and tmax be the entry and exit distances along the ray. tmin, tmax = computerayvolumeintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volume.bounds) # Set sampling step. # Basic implementation uses equidistant sampling. # Optimized implementation uses DDA/Bresenham. stepsize = computestepsize(raydirection, volume.spacing) # Traverse ray t = tmin while t <= tmax: # Calculate current sample position pos = rayorigin + t raydirection # Check if position is within volume bounds (guard against boundary errors) if not isinsidevolume(pos, volume.dimensions): break # Interpolate volume data at pos # Implementation detail: Use trilinear interpolation for smoothness. scalarvalue = interpolatevolume(volume, pos) # Shading model: Convert scalar to color and opacity # The shading model accounts for light transmission and reflection. color, opacity = shadingmodel(scalarvalue) # Feed-backward accumulation # Add results to current ray acccolor = acccolor + color (1.0 - accopacity) accopacity = accopacity + opacity (1.0 - accopacity) # Early termination optimization # When opacity is one, no other data points can affect the ray's color. if accopacity >= 1.0: break # Advance along ray t += stepsize return acccolor, accopacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Transformations: Handling coordinate system consistency is critical. Errors in mapping DICOM metadata ('Image Position Patient', 'Image Orientation Patient') to the volume coordinate system cause artifacts. Boundary Handling: Volume boundary handling involves numerous implementation details. Incorrect ray-box intersection logic leads to sampling outside the valid data range. Precision: Floating-point precision in accumulation can lead to slight inaccuracies in color blending, though early termination mitigates error propagation for opaque regions. A specific application of Van Hook-Levoy ray-casting for medical imaging. It generates 2D X-ray-like projections from 3D CT data. It is chosen when rapid visualization of bone or contrast structures is needed for surgical planning. Link to DRR Generation. Porting the algorithm to parallel hardware (CUDA/OpenCL) to achieve real-time performance. It is chosen when interactive frame rates are required, moving from offline processing (seconds) to real-time (milliseconds). Link to GPU Volume Rendering. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of samples per ray. With DDA, S is proportional to the number of voxels intersected by the ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray (excluding the volume storage). No intermediate representations are generated. Measured Performance: Python/Numba (CPU): Seconds to tens of seconds for offline processing. Python/PyCUDA (GPU): Tens to hundreds of milliseconds for real-time interaction. Strengths: Simple implementation; direct access to interior information; early termination optimization reduces computation for opaque regions. Limitations: Computationally intensive compared to surface rendering; "cloudy interiors" can be difficult to interpret. When to use: Ideal for direct volume visualization and DRR generation where intermediate geometry extraction is undesirable. When not to use: When surface-based interpretation is preferred or when hardware acceleration is unavailable and real-time performance is critical. Origin: The method was published by Marc Levoy in 1988. David Van Hook also explored the basic ray-casting model in 1986. History: It is one of the four main paradigms of volume rendering, alongside splatting, shear-warp, and cell projection. It falls under the category of direct volume rendering, which processes voxels directly without intermediate polygonal meshes. Development: Initially implemented on CPUs, the algorithm was later ported to GPUs (introduced by Kruger in 2003) to leverage parallel processing for the independent ray calculations. Usage: Widely integrated into medical imaging pipelines for therapy planning and Digital Radiograph (DRR) synthesis. 医疗影像开发实战:如何用光线投射算法快速生成DRR图像(附Python代码), https://un.csdn.net/98nhkcg5t04h, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Parallel, Feed-Forward Volume Rendering Algorithm, https://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/91-029.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Medical Volume Rendering Techniques, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.07710v1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Koyamada's Algorithm
head: Koyamada's DVR algorithm, Sequential DVR Algorithm
body: Koyamada's Algorithm is an image-order ray-casting method for unstructured tetrahedral volumes that leverages image-space coherency to generate and compose ray-segments in object space. It differs from its siblings by explicitly constructing continuous ray-segments via scan-conversion of external faces and traversing them through the volume using cell connectivity, rather than sampling fixed intervals along a pixel ray. This approach avoids the redundant ray-segment generation that occurs when local clusters are treated as independent subvolumes, ensuring that segments crossing pseudo-boundary faces are composed into single continuous segments [4496-local-rendering-phase.md]. Inputs: Volumetric dataset defined by tetrahedral cells. Camera parameters defining the projection plane and ray origins. Outputs: A composited image where each pixel contains the final color and opacity derived from the composited ray-segments stored in the RayBuffer. Data Structures: The algorithm relies on three primary data structures: 1. VertexArray: Stores per-vertex data. scalarvalue: The scalar value at the vertex. WSC: World Space Coordinates (x, y, z). NPC: Normalized Projection Coordinates (x, y, z) on the screen plane. 2. CellArray: Stores per-cell topology. Vertices: An array of 4 integers, containing the indices of the four vertices of the tetrahedron. NeighborCells: An array of 4 integers. Each entry corresponds to a face of the tetrahedron. If the face is internal, the value is the index of the neighbor cell. The index within the neighbor cell's NeighborCells array that refers back to the current cell is also stored (typically encoded or derived to avoid search). If the face is external, a sentinel value (e.g., -1) is used. 3. RayBuffer: A 2D virtual array indexed by pixel coordinates (u, v). Each entry holds a linked list of composited ray-segments. Each list element contains: ZDepth: The z-coordinate (in NPC) of the exit point of the ray-segment. Lists are maintained in increasing order of this value. Color-Opacity: The composited RGB color and opacity value for the segment. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate Ray-Segments (Scan Conversion): Iterate through all front-facing (ff) external faces of the volume in any order. For each ff-external face, scan-convert its projection onto the screen. For each pixel (u, v) covered by the face's projection: Determine the ray origin and direction corresponding to pixel (u, v). Calculate the entry point P into the volume. The entry point is the intersection of the ray with the ff-external face. Initialize the composition state at P (typically starting with background color/opacity). Traverse the ray through the volume cells until it exits through a back-facing (bf) external face. Insert the resulting composited ray-segment into the linked list of the RayBuffer at pixel (u, v). 2. Trace Ray Inside Volume (Cell Traversal): Given an entry point P and entry face F{in} for a tetrahedral cell C: Identify the three other faces of C that are candidates for the exit face. For each candidate face F{cand}: Let the vertices of F{cand} be A, C, D (where A is a common vertex with F{in} or chosen appropriately to define the triangle). Check if the ray intersects the plane of F{cand}. If the projection of vectors \vec{AC} and \vec{AD} onto the screen are parallel, the face is perpendicular to the screen; skip this face and test the next candidate. Otherwise, calculate the intersection point Q of the ray with the plane of F{cand}. Validate if Q lies inside the triangle ACD using barycentric coordinates. 3. Determine Exit Face and Point: Express vector \vec{AQ} as a linear combination of \vec{AC} and \vec{AD}: \vec{AQ} = \alpha \vec{AC} + \beta \vec{AD} Solve for \alpha and \beta using the 2x2 linear system derived from the NPC coordinates: \begin{bmatrix} xC - xA & xD - xA \\ yC - yA & yD - yA \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \alpha \\ \beta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} xr - xA \\ yr - yA \end{bmatrix} Where (xA, yA), (xC, yC), and (xD, yD) are the NPC coordinates of vertices A, C, D, and (xr, yr) are the NPC coordinates of the ray (constant for the pixel). Validate the intersection: If \alpha > 0, \beta > 0, and \alpha + \beta < 1, then Q is inside triangle ACD. This face is the exit face. No further tests are needed for this ray-segment within this cell. Otherwise, Q is not inside the triangle; test the next candidate face. If no candidate face yields a valid intersection, the ray exits through a back-facing external face (or the cell is degenerate). 4. Calculate Exit Properties: Once the exit face and point Q are identified, calculate the z-coordinate of Q in NPC space: zQ = zA + \alpha(zC - zA) - \beta(zD - zA) Note: The source formula uses a minus sign for the \beta term; ensure consistency with the vector definition \vec{AQ} = \alpha \vec{AC} + \beta \vec{AD}. If the standard barycentric form is used, the sign may vary based on vertex ordering. The source explicitly states: zQ = zA + \alpha(zC - zA) - \beta(zD - zA). Calculate the scalar value sQ at Q using 2D inverse distance interpolation (barycentric interpolation): sQ = \alpha sC + \beta sD + (1 - \alpha - \beta) sA Where sA, sC, sD are the scalar values at vertices A, C, D. The coefficients represent the area ratios of sub-triangles QAD, QAC, and QCD to the area of triangle ACD. 5. Resample and Composite: With the entry point P (known from the previous step or scan conversion) and exit point Q (just calculated), resample the scalar values along the segment PQ. Use equi-distant sampling with interval \Delta s. \Delta s must be small enough to ensure at least one sample is taken in each cell. Composite the samples using standard volume rendering integration (e.g., front-to-back compositing) to update the color and opacity. The exit point Q and its properties become the entry point for the next cell. Repeat steps 2-5 until a back-facing external face is reached. 6. Final Composition: After all ff-external faces are processed, the RayBuffer contains all composited ray-segments. For each pixel, sort the linked list of ray-segments by ZDepth (if not already sorted during insertion) and composite them from front to back to produce the final pixel color and opacity. Parameters: Sampling Interval (\Delta s): Equi-distant sampling is used. The value must be chosen such that \Delta s is small enough to guarantee at least one sample per cell. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sorting Order: The original algorithm sorts ff-external faces by centroid x-coordinates, which is an approximate order that may be incorrect. The modified approach described here avoids this by scan-converting faces in any order and generating rays per pixel, ensuring correctness. Parallel Vectors: If the projection of vectors \vec{AC} and \vec{AD} are parallel, the face is perpendicular to the screen, and the ray cannot exit through that face in the projected sense. Test another face. Precision: Barycentric coordinate validation (\alpha > 0, \beta > 0, \alpha + \beta < 1) is sensitive to floating-point precision. Use a small epsilon for comparisons. The core computation step in the Object-Space parallel implementation. It handles spatial decomposition constraints within a single processing unit by treating local clusters as a single local subvolume, ensuring continuous ray-segments across pseudo-boundary faces. A sibling method that uses two passes to determine depth and color, differing in its approach to handling occlusion and depth sorting. A sibling method that uses a different traversal strategy, often involving pre-sorted lists or different data structures for cell traversal. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of pixels, the number of cells intersected by rays, and the number of external faces. The scan-conversion step is proportional to the projected area of external faces. The traversal step is proportional to the number of cells intersected by all rays. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the RayBuffer, which stores a linked list of ray-segments per pixel. The size depends on the number of ray-segments, which in turn depends on the volume's complexity and the number of external faces. Strengths: Leverages image-space coherency, reducing redundant calculations. Handles unstructured tetrahedral grids efficiently using connectivity information. Avoids the sorting pitfalls of the original algorithm. Limitations: Requires efficient scan-conversion of external faces. The RayBuffer can become large for complex volumes with many external faces. The quality of the image depends on the sampling interval \Delta s. When to Use: Suitable for unstructured tetrahedral volumes where image-space coherency can be exploited. Particularly useful in parallel implementations where local rendering phases can be optimized. When Not to Use: Not suitable for structured grids where simpler traversal methods are more efficient. May not be optimal for very simple volumes with few external faces. Koyamada's Algorithm was introduced by Koyamada. It is a ray-casting approach that makes use of image space coherency to generate rays and follows those rays in the object space. The algorithm was originally described in a thesis or report. The method has been adapted for parallel direct volume rendering of unstructured grids based on object-space decomposition. name: Local Rendering Phase
head: Local subvolume rendering, Processor-local rendering
body: The Local Rendering Phase is the core computation step in the Object-Space (OS) parallel implementation of Koyamada's Algorithm. It solves the problem of redundant ray-segment generation that occurs when local clusters on a single processor are treated as independent subvolumes. By treating the set of local clusters assigned to a processor as a single local subvolume, it ensures that ray-segments crossing pseudo-boundary faces (shared between local clusters) are composed into a single continuous segment rather than being recomputed. This phase builds on Koyamada's Algorithm by handling the spatial decomposition constraints within a single processing unit. Inputs: The set of local clusters Cp assigned to processor Pi. The CellArray structures containing cell geometry and connectivity for these clusters. The RayBuffer structure for the current pixel row/column being processed. Outputs: Composited color and opacity values for ray-segments exiting the local subvolume, stored in the RayBuffer. Data Structures: CellArray: Contains cell data. Each cell ci has neighbor references. RayBuffer: A linked-list structure indexed by pixel location. Each entry stores a list of ray-segments sorted by their exit z-value. Steps: 1. Concurrent Traversal: Each processor Pi concurrently traverses the cells of the CellArray structures of its local clusters Cp. 2. Face Classification: For each cell ci in Cp, check each face f: Identify f as an external face if cell ci does not have a neighbor cell through face f. Identify f as a boundary face if cell ci is neighbor to a cell cj through face f such that cj belongs to a non-local cluster of Pi (i.e., cj \in Cq where Cq is not in Pi's set). Faces shared between two local clusters of Pi are pseudo-boundary faces and are not treated as external or boundary faces for ray generation purposes. 3. Ray-Segment Generation: Scan-convert each identified external and boundary face. Generate a ray-segment for each pixel covered by the face. 4. Ray Traversal: Follow each generated ray-segment through the local subvolume according to Koyamada's algorithm. The traversal uses the connectivity information preserved in ClusterData structures, allowing the ray to pass through multiple local clusters seamlessly. The ray continues until it exits from a bf-external face (boundary face that is also external) or a bf-boundary face (boundary face that is not external, i.e., exits the local subvolume to a non-local cluster). 5. Buffer Insertion: When a ray-segment exits the local subvolume, insert its composited color and opacity values into the linked-list of the respective pixel location in the RayBuffer structure. Insertion must be in sorted order according to the ray-segment's exit z-value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localrenderingphase(processorid, localclusters, raybuffer): """ Renders the local subvolume defined by localclusters for processorid. """ # Step 1 & 2: Traverse cells and identify ray origins rayorigins = [] for cluster in localclusters: for cell in cluster.cells: for face in cell.faces: # Check if face is external (no neighbor) if not face.hasneighbor(): rayorigins.append((cell, face, 'external')) # Check if face is boundary (neighbor exists but is non-local) elif face.hasneighbor(): neighborcluster = face.neighbor.clusterid if neighborcluster not in localclusters: rayorigins.append((cell, face, 'boundary')) # Else: pseudo-boundary, skip ray generation # Step 3 & 4: Generate and trace ray-segments for cell, face, facetype in rayorigins: # Scan-convert face to generate pixel coordinates pixels = scanconvertface(face) for pixel in pixels: # Generate ray-segment starting at pixel, through face raysegment = generateraysegment(pixel, face, cell) # Trace through local subvolume using Koyamada's algorithm # The traversal respects connectivity across cluster boundaries exitface, exitz = traceraythroughlocalsubvolume(raysegment, localclusters) # Step 5: Insert into RayBuffer if exitface is not None: compositedcolor = raysegment.compositedcolor compositedopacity = raysegment.compositedopacity # Insert into linked-list sorted by exitz raybuffer.insertsorted(pixel, exitz, compositedcolor, compositedopacity) def traceraythroughlocalsubvolume(ray, localclusters): """ Traces a ray through the union of localclusters. Returns (exitface, exitz) or (None, None) if ray stays within. """ currentcell = ray.startcell currentface = ray.startface while True: # Move to next cell along ray direction nextcell = currentcell.getneighborindirection(ray.direction) # If no neighbor, ray exited the local subvolume if nextcell is None: return (currentface, ray.zatexit) # If neighbor exists, check if it is part of the local subvolume if nextcell.clusterid in localclusters: # Continue traversal within local subvolume currentcell = nextcell # Update ray segment composition ray.compose(nextcell) currentface = nextcell.getexitface(ray.direction) else: # Neighbor is non-local, so we exit the local subvolume return (currentface, ray.zatexit) Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Virtual Non-Convexities: Object-Space (OS) decomposition may create local subvolumes with virtual non-convexities, even if the global dataset is convex. This increases the number of ray-segments generated per pixel compared to the sequential algorithm. RayBuffer Necessity: Due to virtual non-convexities, multiple ray-segments may exit the local subvolume for a single pixel. The RayBuffer structure is crucial for handling this multiplicity and maintaining correct depth sorting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the RayBuffer size, which scales with the number of ray-segments per pixel. Virtual non-convexities can increase this number. Strengths: Eliminates redundant computation on pseudo-boundary faces by treating local clusters as a single subvolume. Limitations: Virtual non-convexities from decomposition can lead to more ray-segments per pixel than in the sequential case, requiring robust RayBuffer management. When to use: When implementing OS parallel direct volume rendering using Koyamada's Algorithm. The Local Rendering Phase was introduced in the context of parallel direct volume rendering of unstructured grids based on object-space decomposition. It addresses the inefficiencies of rendering local clusters independently by recognizing that clusters on the same processor are highly interacting and should be rendered as a unified local subvolume.
