name: Per-primitive Ray Sampling
head: Primitive-centric ray marching
body: Per-primitive ray sampling is a rendering strategy where each geometric primitive (specifically ellipsoids) independently updates only the ray segments it intersects, avoiding redundant parameter loads and enabling accurate Transfer Function (TF) mapping by accumulating contributions in 3D space. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Fixed Step Ray Marching and Image-order Ray-Casting by organizing computation around primitives rather than rays, which eliminates the need for explicit per-tile sorting required in 2D rasterization because contributions accumulate in depth order as each ray segment corresponds to a discrete depth interval. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of primitives, each defined by center \mu, covariance \Sigma, support radius factor r{supp}, and intensity I; a sampling step size \Delta t; and a projection matrix. Outputs: Accumulated ray segments rayi for each pixel, which are subsequently traversed front-to-back for alpha blending. Data Structures: Primitive: Defined by \mu = (\mux, \muy, \muz), covariance matrix \Sigma, support radius factor r{supp}, and intensity I. Ray Segment: A 1D array rayi for pixel i, discretized with step size \Delta t. The j-th entry stores the accumulated intensity at depth t = j\Delta t. Steps: 1. Transform and Cull: Transform primitives by the projection matrix. Process only those visible in screen space. 2. Cache Parameters: Cache ellipsoid parameters in tile-level shared memory to minimize redundant global memory accesses across pixels. 3. Determine Depth Range: For a primitive with center \mu and covariance \Sigma, determine the valid depth range. Segments within |t - \muz| \le r{supp} \cdot \sqrt{\Sigma'{zz}} are considered, where \sqrt{\Sigma'{zz}} is the standard deviation along the z-axis after projection. 4. Update Ray Segments: For each primitive, calculate the start and end indices of the affected ray segments and update them with the primitive's contribution. Formulas: Ray Parameterization: In ray space, the ray for pixel (xi, yi) is ri(t) = (xi, yi, 0) + t \cdot (0, 0, 1), where t varies along the z-axis. Sample Position: The sample position for index j is rayi[j] = \hat{V}(ri(j\Delta t)) = \hat{V}(xi, yi, j\Delta t). Primitive Contribution: The contribution of a primitive to ray segment j is: \tilde{P}(xi, yi, j \cdot \Delta t) = I \cdot \frac{\sigma(k \cdot (1 - \mathbf{d}^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{d}))}{\sigma(k)} where \mathbf{d} = [xi, yi, j\Delta t] - [\mux, \muy, \muz] is the displacement from the primitive center, k is a scaling factor, and \sigma is the sigmoid function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perprimitiveraysampling(primitives, deltat, raysegments): """ primitives: List of primitives, each with attributes: mu: (mux, muy, muz) Sigma: 3x3 covariance matrix rsupp: support radius factor I: intensity k: scaling factor (assumed constant or per-primitive) deltat: float, sampling step size raysegments: Dict mapping pixelid to list of floats (accumulated intensity) """ # Step 1 & 2: Transform and Cache (Implementation detail: handled by hardware/cache) # For each primitive, determine its valid depth range and update ray segments. for prim in primitives: mu = prim.mu Sigma = prim.Sigma rsupp = prim.rsupp I = prim.I k = prim.k # Calculate projected standard deviation along z-axis # Note: Sigma'{zz} is the z-component of covariance after projection. # In the source, this is denoted as Sigma'{zz}. We assume Sigma provided is already in ray space or transformed. # If Sigma is in world space, it must be transformed by the projection matrix first. # Here we assume Sigma is the relevant covariance for the ray space calculation. sigmazzsqrt = sqrt(Sigma[2, 2]) # Determine valid depth range indices # indexstart = floor((muz - rsupp sigmazzsqrt) / deltat) # indexend = floor((muz + rsupp sigmazzsqrt) / deltat) # However, the source formula for index calculation is: # indexstart = floor((muz - r sqrt(Sigmazz)) / deltat) # indexend = floor((muz + r sqrt(Sigmazz)) / deltat) # We need to iterate over pixels that this primitive affects. # The source implies a loop over primitives, then over ray segments. # But ray segments are per-pixel. The source algorithm 1 is simplified. # A complete implementation requires mapping the primitive's screen-space bounding box to pixels. # Since the source does not provide the pixel mapping logic, we assume a helper function # that yields (pixelid, j) for all ray segments j affected by the primitive. affectedsegments = getaffectedsegments(prim, deltat, sigmazzsqrt) for pixelid, j in affectedsegments: # Calculate displacement d # Ray position at j: (xi, yi, j deltat) # We need xi, yi for the pixel. This is typically derived from pixelid. xi, yi = getpixelcoords(pixelid) dx = xi - mu[0] dy = yi - mu[1] dz = (j deltat) - mu[2] d = [dx, dy, dz] # Calculate quadratic form d^T Sigma^{-1} d # Sigmainv = inverse(Sigma) # quadratic = dot(d, dot(Sigmainv, d)) # For efficiency, if Sigma is diagonal, this simplifies. # General case: Sigmainv = inverse(Sigma) quadratic = dot(d, dot(Sigmainv, d)) # Calculate contribution # sigma(k (1 - quadratic)) / sigma(k) # sigma(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) numerator = sigmoid(k (1 - quadratic)) denominator = sigmoid(k) contribution = I (numerator / denominator) # Update ray segment raysegments[pixelid][j] += contribution def getaffectedsegments(prim, deltat, sigmazzsqrt): """ Returns a list of (pixelid, j) tuples for ray segments affected by the primitive. This function encapsulates the logic of determining which pixels and depth indices fall within the primitive's projected extent. """ mu = prim.mu rsupp = prim.rsupp # Depth range zmin = mu[2] - rsupp sigmazzsqrt zmax = mu[2] + rsupp sigmazzsqrt indexstart = floor(zmin / deltat) indexend = floor(zmax / deltat) # Determine pixel range # This requires the primitive's screen-space bounding box. # The source mentions "Transform primitives by the projection matrix". # We assume the primitive's extent in x,y is known or can be derived from Sigma. # For a full implementation, one would project the ellipsoid's bounding box. # Since the source does not provide this, we return a placeholder range. # In practice, this would be a loop over pixels in the bounding box. # Placeholder: Assume we have a function to get pixels in bounding box pixels = getpixelsinbbox(prim) segments = [] for pixelid in pixels: for j in range(indexstart, indexend + 1): segments.append((pixelid, j)) return segments def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-x)) def getpixelcoords(pixelid): # Returns (xi, yi) for the given pixel ID # Implementation depends on rasterization grid pass def getpixelsinbbox(prim): # Returns list of pixel IDs within the primitive's screen-space bounding box # Implementation depends on projection and bounding box calculation pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in calculating d^T \Sigma^{-1} d can affect the sigmoid evaluation, especially for large displacements. Boundaries: The support radius factor r{supp} determines the cutoff. If too small, contributions are truncated; if too large, unnecessary computations occur. Degenerate Input: If \Sigma is singular, \Sigma^{-1} is undefined. A small regularization term may be needed. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives and the average number of ray segments they intersect. It avoids the O(N{rays} \cdot N{steps}) complexity of naive ray marching by only processing relevant primitives for each segment. Memory Complexity: Requires storing ray segments for all pixels and caching primitive parameters in shared memory. Performance: Eliminates redundant global memory traffic by processing each primitive once and caching parameters in tile-level shared memory. Strengths: Accurate TF evaluation in 3D space, no explicit sorting required, reduced memory traffic. Limitations: Requires efficient culling and bounding box calculation to avoid processing non-intersecting primitives. Performance may degrade with high primitive density and overlap. Per-primitive ray sampling was introduced in the context of 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering (ESVR). It addresses the overhead of naively adopting ray marching for learned primitives, where each ray step requires checking intersections and fetching parameters. By organizing computation around primitives, it enables real-time rendering with accurate TF mapping. ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Layered Volume Rendering with Light Propagation
head: Layer-based volumetric ray marching, Plane-sweep volume rendering
body:
Layered Volume Rendering with Light Propagation is a compute-shader-based technique that processes a stack of parallel planes (layers) to render volumetric data. It propagates light and view rays across layers, accumulating color, alpha, and material properties while applying refraction gradients and transfer functions. It differs from standard front-to-back ray casting by decoupling light transport into a separate propagation pass across discrete Z-layers, allowing for efficient irradiance scaling and refraction updates before the final view-ray accumulation. Inputs and Outputs: The method operates on a stack of N parallel planes. Input Buffers: ldbin: Light direction buffer (sampled at UV). lbin: Light color buffer (sampled at previous light hit point). vpbin: View position buffer. vdbin: View direction buffer. cbin: Color buffer (accumulated color). mbin: Material buffer. volumetransfer: Texture mapping vec2(densityin, densityprev) to vec4(alphaout). mediumtransfer: Texture mapping vec2(densityin, densityprev) to vec4(tintout). Output Buffers: lbout: Updated light color. ldbout: Updated light direction. cbout: Final color and alpha. mbout: Updated material. vpbout: Next view position. vdbout: Next view direction. Uniforms (UBO): planepixelsize: Pixel size of rendering planes in world units. distancebetweenplanes: Constant Z-distance between consecutive layers. lightVSPos: View-space position of the light source. lightcolor: View-space color/intensity of the light source. planecount: Total number of layers. middleoffrontplanevs.z: Z-coordinate of the front plane in view space. Data Structures: All buffers are accessed via imageLoad/imageStore using ivec2 pixel coordinates derived from glGlobalInvocationID. Steps: 1. Coordinate Calculation: Compute UV and pixel coordinates from glGlobalInvocationID. Calculate the current layer's Z-coordinate in view space: z{current} = z{front} - 	ext{layer\index} 	imes d{plane} where z{front} is ubo.middleoffrontplanevs.z, 	ext{layer\index} is the current layer index, and d{plane} is ubo.distancebetweenplanes. 2. Light Propagation Intersection: Sample the current light direction L{dir} from ldbin at the current UV. Intersect a ray starting at (0.5, 0.5, z{current} + d{plane}) with direction -L{dir} to find the hit point P{lp\prev} on the current plane. 3. Light Propagation Sampling & Averaging: Sample the light color L{prev} from lbin at P{lp\prev}.xy. Sample ldbin at P{lp\prev}.xy and apply 4-tap averaging: L{dir\avg} = 0.5 	imes L{center} + 0.125 	imes (L{n} + L{s} + L{e} + L{w}) Normalize L{dir\avg} to get L{prev}. If \|L{prev}\| < 10^{-6}, set L{prev} = (0, 0, 1) to prevent NaN propagation. 4. Irradiance Scaling: Compute screen-space area factors: S{current} = |  rac{\partial u}{\partial x} | 	imes |  rac{\partial v}{\partial y} | S{prev} = |  rac{\partial u{prev}}{\partial x} | 	imes |  rac{\partial v{prev}}{\partial y} | where derivatives are computed via dFdx/dFdy. Compute irradiance scaling factor: I =  egin{cases} S{prev} / S{current} & 	ext{if } S{current} > 10^{-8} \ 1.0 & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} This prevents division by zero. 5. Transfer Function Application: Convert UV and P{lp\prev}.xy to world positions at z{current} and z{current} + d{plane}. Sample volumedensity and volumedensityprev. Sample volumetransfer with vec2(volumedensity, volumedensityprev) to get alpha \alpha. Sample mediumtransfer to get tint T via: T = 	ext{mix}((1,1,1), M{data}.rgb, M{data}.a) Compute light color for output: L{out} = L{prev} 	imes I 	imes (1.0 - \alpha) 	imes T Clamp L{out} to vec3(20.0). Store to lbout. 6. Light Refraction Update: Compute midpoint in world space: P{mid} = (P{lp\ws} + P{prev\lp\ws}) 	imes 0.5. Get refraction gradient 
abla{ref}. Update light direction: L{next} = L{prev} + 
abla{ref} 	imes d{plane} Normalize L{next} and store to ldbout. 7. Ray Propagation Setup: Sample view position V{pos} from vpbin and direction V{dir} from vdbin. Convert V{pos} to world space. Sample color buffer cbin for C{prev} and A{prev}. Sample material buffer mbin for M{prev}. Sample light buffer lbin for light ID/intensity I{light}. 8. Ray Propagation Intersection: Intersect a ray from V{pos} with direction -V{dir} to the plane at z{current} + d{plane} to get previous view point V{prev}. Convert to world space. 9. Ray Propagation Shading: Compute volume gradient N at V{ws} + 0.5. Let V = 	ext{normalize}(-V{dir}). Compute light direction L{dir} = 	ext{normalize}(	ext{ubo.lightVSPos} - V{pos}). Compute half-vector H = 	ext{normalize}(L{dir} + V). Compute specular term: S{pec} = \max(	ext{dot}(N, H), 0.0)^{128.0} Compute specular intensity: I{spec} = 	ext{ubo.light\color} 	imes S{pec} 	imes 0.05 Compute material mask: M{ask} = 	ext{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.05, 	ext{volume\density}). 10. Ray Propagation Accumulation: Update color, alpha, and material: C{current} = C{prev} + (1.0 - A{prev}) 	imes M{prev} 	imes (\alpha 	imes C{light} 	imes I{light} + I{spec} 	imes M{ask}) A{current} = A{prev} + (1.0 - A{prev}) 	imes \alpha M{current} = M{prev} 	imes (1.0 - M{data}.w) + M{prev} 	imes M{data}.xyz 	imes M{data}.w. 11. Ray Propagation Refraction & Next Step: Compute midpoint: P{mid\vp} = (V{ws} + V{prev\ws}) 	imes 0.5 + 0.5. Get refraction gradient 
abla{vd}. Update view direction: V{next} = V{dir} + 
abla{vd} 	imes d{plane} Normalize V{next}. Intersect ray from V{pos} with V{next} to plane at z{current} - d{plane} to get V{next\pos}. 12. Background Replacement: If 	ext{layer\index} == 	ext{ubo.plane\count} - 1: Draw checkerboard background: S{cale} = 16 UV{check} = V{next}.xy 	imes S{cale} F = 	ext{mod}(\lfloor UV{check}.x floor + \lfloor UV{check}.y floor, 2.0) C{bg} = 	ext{mix}((0.2, 0.2, 0.2), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), F) Blend C{bg} with C{current} using (1.0 - A{current}). Set A{current} = 1.0. 13. Output Storage: Store C{current} and A{current} to cbout, M{current} to mbout, V{next\pos} to vpbout, and V{next} to vdbout. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): # 1. Coordinate Calculation uv = vec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy) / vec2(ubo.planepixelsize) # Approximate scaling layerindex = glGlobalInvocationID.z # Or derived from invocation ID depending on dispatch zcurrent = ubo.middleoffrontplanevs.z - float(layerindex) ubo.distancebetweenplanes # 2. Light Propagation Intersection ldcurrent = imageLoad(ldbin, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy)).xyz # Ray: origin (0.5, 0.5, zcurrent + distance), dir -ldcurrent # Intersect with plane z = zcurrent + distance? # Note: Source says "Intersect a ray starting at (0.5, 0.5, currentz + distance) with direction -ldcurrent to find the hit point lpprev on the current plane." # This implies the plane is at zcurrent + distance? Or the ray goes backwards to the previous plane? # Based on "lpprev", it likely hits the previous layer's plane. # Let's assume the intersection logic finds the point on the plane z = zcurrent + distance (which is the "previous" plane in back-to-front order if layerindex increases front-to-back? # Actually, zcurrent decreases as layerindex increases. So layer 0 is front. # If we are at layerindex, the "previous" light hit is on layerindex-1? # The source says: "Intersect... to find the hit point lpprev on the current plane." # This phrasing is ambiguous. "lpprev" suggests previous layer. # Let's stick to the source's variable names. # Simplified intersection for plane z = zplane # Ray: O = (0.5, 0.5, zcurrent + distance), D = -ldcurrent # Plane: z = zcurrent + distance? No, that's the origin. # Let's assume the ray intersects the plane at z = zcurrent + distance (which is the plane "in front" of current if we are marching back?) # Actually, standard layered rendering often marches from back to front or front to back. # Let's assume the intersection calculates the point on the plane z = zcurrent + distance. # Since origin is already at zcurrent + distance, this step might be trivial or refer to the NEXT plane in the propagation direction. # However, source says "lpprev". Let's assume it hits the plane at z = zcurrent + distance. # If the ray direction is -ldcurrent, and it starts at zcurrent + distance, it goes deeper. # Let's assume the "current plane" for light propagation is the one at zcurrent + distance. lpprevxy = vec2(0.5, 0.5) # Placeholder for actual intersection result # In a real implementation, this requires a ray-plane intersection function. # Given the source's simplicity, we assume lpprevxy is computed. # 3. Light Propagation Sampling & Averaging lprev = imageLoad(lbin, ivec2(lpprevxy)).rgb ldsample = imageLoad(ldbin, ivec2(lpprevxy)).xyz # 4-tap averaging # Neighbors: up, down, left, right ldavg = ldsample 0.5 ldavg += imageLoad(ldbin, ivec2(lpprevxy + ivec2(1, 0))).xyz 0.125 ldavg += imageLoad(ldbin, ivec2(lpprevxy + ivec2(-1, 0))).xyz 0.125 ldavg += imageLoad(ldbin, ivec2(lpprevxy + ivec2(0, 1))).xyz 0.125 ldavg += imageLoad(ldbin, ivec2(lpprevxy + ivec2(0, -1))).xyz 0.125 ldprev = normalize(ldavg) if length(ldprev) < 1e-6: ldprev = vec3(0, 0, 1) # 4. Irradiance Scaling scurrent = abs(dFdx(uv.x)) abs(dFdy(uv.y)) sprev = abs(dFdx(lpprevxy.x)) abs(dFdy(lpprevxy.y)) if scurrent > 1e-8: I = sprev / scurrent else: I = 1.0 # 5. Transfer Function Application # Convert UV and lpprevxy to world positions # This requires knowing the mapping from UV to World X,Y at a given Z. # Assuming a simple orthographic projection or known camera matrix. # For pseudocode, we assume helper functions worldpos(uv, z) and worldpos(lpxy, z) poscurrws = worldpos(uv, zcurrent) posprevws = worldpos(lpprevxy, zcurrent + ubo.distancebetweenplanes) voldensity = samplevolumedensity(poscurrws) voldensityprev = samplevolumedensity(posprevws) alpha = samplevolumetransfer(vec2(voldensity, voldensityprev)).a tint = samplemediumtransfer(vec2(voldensity, voldensityprev)).rgb # Assuming tint is RGB part # Source: mix(vec3(1.0), mdata.rgb, mdata.a) # mdata is from mediumtransfer. Let's assume mediumtransfer returns vec4 where xyz is tint and a is weight? # Or mdata is the sampled vec4. mdata = samplemediumtransfer(vec2(voldensity, voldensityprev)) tint = mix(vec3(1.0), mdata.rgb, mdata.a) lout = lprev I (1.0 - alpha) tint lout = clamp(lout, vec3(0.0), vec3(20.0)) imageStore(lbout, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy), vec4(lout, 1.0)) # 6. Light Refraction Update midws = (poscurrws + posprevws) 0.5 refgrad = computerefractiongradient(midws) # Placeholder for gradient calculation ldnext = ldprev + refgrad ubo.distancebetweenplanes ldnext = normalize(ldnext) imageStore(ldbout, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy), vec4(ldnext, 1.0)) # 7. Ray Propagation Setup vpcurrent = imageLoad(vpbin, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy)).xyz vdcurrent = imageLoad(vdbin, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy)).xyz vpws = worldposfromview(vpcurrent) # Convert view to world cprev = imageLoad(cbin, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy)).rgb aprev = imageLoad(cbin, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy)).a mprev = imageLoad(mbin, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy)).xyzw idlight = imageLoad(lbin, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy)).r # Assuming ID is stored in R # 8. Ray Propagation Intersection # Intersect ray from vpcurrent with dir -vdcurrent to plane at zcurrent + distance vpprevws = intersectviewraytoplane(vpcurrent, -vdcurrent, zcurrent + ubo.distancebetweenplanes) # 9. Ray Propagation Shading n = computevolumegradient(vpws + 0.5) v = normalize(-vdcurrent) ldir = normalize(ubo.lightVSPos - vpcurrent) h = normalize(ldir + v) spec = pow(max(dot(n, h), 0.0), 128.0) isval = ubo.lightcolor spec 0.05 materialmask = smoothstep(0.0, 0.05, voldensity) # 10. Ray Propagation Accumulation # Clight is likely lout or idlight some factor. Source says "alpha c id". # c is likely the light color from lbout or similar. Let's use lout from step 5. clight = lout ccurrent = cprev + (1.0 - aprev) mprev (alpha clight idlight + isval materialmask) acurrent = aprev + (1.0 - aprev) alpha mcurrent = mprev (1.0 - mdata.w) + mprev mdata.xyz mdata.w # 11. Ray Propagation Refraction & Next Step midvpws = (vpws + vpprevws) 0.5 + 0.5 # +0.5 offset mentioned in source vdgrad = computeviewrefractiongradient(midvpws) # Placeholder vdnext = vdcurrent + vdgrad ubo.distancebetweenplanes vdnext = normalize(vdnext) vpnextws = intersectviewraytoplane(vpcurrent, vdnext, zcurrent - ubo.distancebetweenplanes) # 12. Background Replacement if layerindex == ubo.planecount - 1: scale = 16.0 checkuv = vpnextws.xy scale f = mod(floor(checkuv.x) + floor(checkuv.y), 2.0) bg = mix(vec3(0.2), vec3(0.5), f) ccurrent = mix(ccurrent, bg, 1.0 - acurrent) acurrent = 1.0 # 13. Output Storage imageStore(cbout, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy), vec4(ccurrent, acurrent)) imageStore(mbout, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy), mcurrent) imageStore(vpbout, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy), vec4(vpnextws, 1.0)) imageStore(vdbout, ivec2(glGlobalInvocationID.xy), vec4(vdnext, 1.0)) Time Complexity: O(N 	imes W 	imes H) per frame, where N is the number of layers, and W 	imes H is the resolution. Each layer requires a constant number of texture samples and arithmetic operations per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(W 	imes H) for the input and output buffers. The method requires ping-ponging buffers for light and view directions/colors across layers. Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on the number of layers and the cost of texture sampling. The use of compute shaders allows for parallel processing of pixels. The 4-tap averaging and irradiance scaling add computational overhead but improve visual quality by smoothing light propagation. Strengths: Efficient handling of light transport in volumetric scenes by decoupling light and view rays. The layer-based approach allows for easy integration of refraction and transfer functions. The use of compute shaders provides flexibility in shader logic. Limitations: The method assumes a regular stack of parallel planes, which may not fit all volumetric data structures. The refraction gradient calculation is a simplification and may not accurately model complex light bending. The background replacement is a hack for the last layer and may not be suitable for all scenes. When to use: Suitable for real-time rendering of volumetric data where light transport is important, such as clouds, smoke, or medical imaging. When not to use: Not suitable for scenes with complex geometry or non-planar layer structures. Not ideal for offline rendering where higher accuracy is required. This method is derived from the vis-magnus-2018 repository, an unofficial implementation of a volume rendering technique. The technique leverages Vulkan compute shaders for parallel processing. The specific implementation details, including the layer-based propagation and refraction updates, are documented in the source code and associated notes. name: Directional Derivative Diffuse Lighting
head: Density Gradient Diffuse Approximation, Inigo Quilez's directional derivatives
body: Directional Derivative Diffuse Lighting is an approximation for diffuse lighting in volumetric raymarching that estimates light scattering by comparing density at the current point and an offset point in the light direction, avoiding the need for normal calculation. It sets itself apart from standard surface raymarching normals by requiring only two density samples instead of multiple gradient estimates, making it significantly cheaper for the resource-intensive volumetric loop. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current 3D position p in the volume, light direction vector sunDirection (normalized), and a density function scene(p) that returns the scalar density at position p. Output: A diffuse lighting factor (scalar) and a linear lighting color vector, used to modulate the accumulated volume color. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond the density function scene(p) and standard vector types. The method relies on scalar arithmetic and vector addition. Parameters: Offset Scale: 0.3 (distance along the light direction for the second sample). Ambient Color: vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75). Ambient Multiplier: 1.1. Diffuse Color: vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3). Diffuse Multiplier: 0.8. Clamp Range: [0.0, 1.0]. Steps: 1. Sample the density at the current point p: dcurrent = scene(p). 2. Sample the density at an offset point p' located further along the light direction: doffset = scene(p + 0.3 sunDirection). 3. Calculate the diffuse factor by taking the difference between the two density samples, dividing by the offset scale, and clamping the result to [0.0, 1.0]. This approximates the rate of change of density along the light direction. Formula: diffuse = clamp((dcurrent - doffset) / 0.3, 0.0, 1.0) Interpretation: If density increases along the light path (dcurrent > doffset), the result is positive, indicating more scattering. If density decreases, the result is lower or zero, indicating less scattering. 4. Compute the linear lighting color by mixing ambient light and the calculated diffuse light: Formula: lin = ambientcolor ambientmult + diffusecolor diffuse diffusemult Specifics: lin = vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75) 1.1 + vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3) diffuse 0.8 5. Determine the base color of the volume slice by mixing white and black based on the current density dcurrent: Formula: basecolor = mix(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), dcurrent) 6. Combine the base color with the linear lighting and the density alpha, then accumulate into the final result using the over operator: Formula: color = vec4(basecolor lin, dcurrent) Accumulation: res += color.rgb color.a (1.0 - res.a) (assuming res is the accumulated result color with alpha). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directionalderivativediffuselighting(p, sundirection, scenefunc): """ Calculates diffuse lighting for a volumetric point using directional derivatives. Args: p (vec3): Current 3D position in the volume. sundirection (vec3): Normalized light direction vector. scenefunc (function): Function that returns density at a given 3D position. Returns: tuple: (diffusefactor, linearlightingcolor) """ # Step 1: Sample density at current point dcurrent = scenefunc(p) # Step 2: Sample density at offset point along light direction # Offset scale is 0.3 as per source offsetscale = 0.3 poffset = p + offsetscale sundirection doffset = scenefunc(poffset) # Step 3: Calculate diffuse factor # Formula: clamp((dcurrent - doffset) / offsetscale, 0.0, 1.0) diffusefactor = (dcurrent - doffset) / offsetscale if diffusefactor < 0.0: diffusefactor = 0.0 elif diffusefactor > 1.0: diffusefactor = 1.0 # Step 4: Compute linear lighting color # Ambient: vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75) 1.1 ambientcolor = vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75) 1.1 # Diffuse: vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3) diffuse 0.8 diffusecolor = vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3) diffusefactor 0.8 linearlighting = ambientcolor + diffusecolor return diffusefactor, linearlighting def accumulatevolumeslice(p, sundirection, scenefunc, res): """ Accumulates a single volume slice using directional derivative diffuse lighting. Args: p (vec3): Current 3D position. sundirection (vec3): Normalized light direction. scenefunc (function): Density function. res (vec4): Current accumulated result (rgb, a). Returns: vec4: Updated accumulated result. """ dcurrent = scenefunc(p) # Only process if density is present if dcurrent > 0.0: # Get lighting, linearlighting = directionalderivativediffuselighting(p, sundirection, scenefunc) # Base color: mix white and black based on density basecolor = mix(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), dcurrent) # Apply lighting coloredbase = basecolor linearlighting # Form the slice color with alpha slicecolor = vec4(coloredbase, dcurrent) # Accumulate using over operator: resnew = resold + slice (1 - resold.a) # Note: The source code does color.rgb = color.a before accumulation, # which effectively makes the contribution slice.rgb slice.a. # Standard over operator is: res += slice (1 - res.a) # The source code: color.rgb = color.a; res += color (1.0 - res.a); # This implies the slice's alpha is used to modulate its RGB contribution before blending. slicecolor.rgb = slicecolor.a res.rgb += slicecolor.rgb (1.0 - res.a) res.a += slicecolor.a (1.0 - res.a) return res Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Calculation Suboptimality: Standard normal calculation using getNormal requires 4-6 sample points to estimate the gradient, which is resource-intensive given the heavy volumetric loop. This method avoids that by using only 2 samples. Loop Inclusion: Unlike surface raymarching where diffuse is computed once at the surface, this calculation must be included inside the volumetric raymarching loop because density varies throughout the volume. Precision: The division by 0.3 can amplify noise if the density function is noisy. Clamping to [0.0, 1.0] prevents negative lighting contributions but may clip valid gradients if the density change is very steep. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, requiring exactly 2 density function evaluations per lighting calculation. This is significantly faster than gradient-based normal estimation which requires 4-6 evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory, as it only stores a few scalar and vector variables. Strengths: Low computational cost, easy to implement, provides a visually plausible approximation of diffuse lighting in volumes without explicit normals. Limitations: Approximation may not capture complex scattering effects accurately. The fixed offset scale (0.3) may not be optimal for all volume densities or scales. When to use: Real-time volumetric rendering where performance is critical and approximate diffuse lighting is sufficient. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring high physical accuracy, or volumes with very fine details where the fixed offset might miss significant density changes. The method is attributed to Inigo Quilez and presented in his article on directional derivatives. It was developed as an alternative to standard normal calculation in volumetric raymarching to reduce the computational cost associated with gradient estimation. name: Specific Material and Geometry Rendering
head: Material Parameter Setting, Surface and DRR Rendering Modes
body: Specific Material and Geometry Rendering provides mechanisms to define volumetric material properties (ambient, diffuse, specular) and rendering modes (Surface, DRR, MIP) within volume rendering pipelines, particularly in the VolPack API and real-time ray-marched implementations. It solves the problem of mapping scalar or vector volume data to visual appearance and handling geometric occlusion or specific projection requirements. It differs from general ray marching by explicitly exposing material parameter interfaces and distinct rendering modes that alter the fragment shader's output logic, rather than relying solely on the integration of the radiative transfer equation. The family shares the concept of decoupling the physical density/scattering data from the visual appearance rules. This is achieved through: 1. Material Parameterization: Defining optical properties (reflection coefficients, shininess) that are applied to voxels based on their geometric orientation (gradient direction) relative to the viewer. 2. Rendering Mode Selection: Using a uniform variable to switch the fragment shader's computation between different output definitions (e.g., Phong shading vs. attenuation-only vs. maximum intensity). 3. Gradient-Based Classification: Determining surface properties (exterior vs. interior) based on the sign of the volume gradient vector at the sample point. Procedural volumetric cloud rendering is a real-time technique that ray-marches a spherical cloud layer built from tileable 3D noise fields, lighting it with multiple-scattering approximations and Mie phase functions. It solves the problem of rendering physically plausible, large-scale cloudscapes with dynamic lighting and shadows at interactive frame rates. What sets it apart from Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering is the use of procedural noise for density generation rather than pre-computed voxel grids, and from Ray-marched Volumetric Fog by employing specific cloud physics (Mie scattering, multiple scattering approximations, and vertical density profiles) rather than generic volumetric fog. Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique implemented in the VolumeIntegrator::Li function that performs ray marching through a single volume region, accumulating emitted light and computing transmittance and scattering contributions from a single light source. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific implementation within the Mr-Voxel library's integrator, which combines an accelerated voxel data structure with a ray marching loop that handles single-volume, single-light scenarios with Russian Roulette termination. Unlike Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering which often relies on procedural noise for density, or Ray-marched Volumetric Fog which may use simplified scattering models, this method explicitly computes optical depth and direct lighting transmittance per step for a defined volume object. Ray-marched volumetric fog simulates light absorption, scattering, soft shadows, and light shafts (god rays) by treating fog as a 3D volume of participating media traced via ray-marching from the camera to the scene. It differs from backward ray-marching (scene to camera) by enabling early-out optimizations when transmittance becomes negligible, and it differs from voxel-based methods by operating directly in screen space using depth reconstruction rather than explicit volume data structures. Material parameter setting allows the configuration of volumetric material properties such as ambient, diffuse, specular reflection, and shininess. The function vpSetMaterial is used to assign these properties to specific material identifiers (VPMATERIAL0 through VPMATERIAL5). Properties include VPAMBIENT, VPDIFFUSE, VPSPECULAR (taking RGB values), and VPSHINYNESS (taking a specular exponent, ignoring G and B). The application of these properties is controlled by surfaceside, which can be VPEXTERIOR (voxels where the gradient points towards the viewer), VPINTERIOR (gradient points away), or VPBOTHSIDES. The meaning of exterior and interior can be reversed using VPREVERSESURFACESIDES. Rendering modes define how the final color C(s) is computed for a sample point s along the ray. Surface Rendering: C(s) is computed according to the Phong equation using the volume gradient. Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs): C(s) = (0,0,0), and only the backlight is attenuated by the accumulated transmittance t. Maximum Intensity Projections (MIPs): The output is the opacity \alpha of the maximum-opacity interval along the ray. A uniform variable tells the fragment shader which mode to use. The VolPack API, documented in the VolPack User's Guide, introduced specific material parameter setting and rendering modes (Surface, DRR, MIP) for volume rendering. These features allow for flexible visualization of volumetric data, ranging from surface-like shading to projection-based analyses like DRRs and MIPs, commonly used in medical imaging and scientific visualization. The concepts of material parameterization and mode switching have been adapted in various real-time implementations, such as procedural cloud rendering and volumetric fog shaders, to balance physical accuracy with performance. name: Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering
head: Nubis³, Nubis Cubed, Nubis Evolved, Volumetric Cloud Renderer, Volumetric Cloud Rendering, Real-time Volumetric Cloud Rendering
body: Procedural volumetric cloud rendering is a real-time technique that ray-marches a spherical cloud layer built from tileable 3D noise fields, lighting it with multiple-scattering approximations and Mie phase functions. It solves the problem of rendering physically plausible, large-scale cloudscapes with dynamic lighting and shadows at interactive frame rates. What sets it apart from Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering is the use of procedural noise for density generation rather than pre-computed voxel grids, and from Ray-marched Volumetric Fog by employing specific cloud physics (Mie scattering, multiple scattering approximations, and vertical density profiles) rather than generic volumetric fog. Inputs: Camera: Position, view-projection matrix, viewport dimensions. Lighting: Sun direction (spherical coordinates converted to Cartesian), sun color, sun intensity. Cloud Parameters: Base height, thickness, coverage, density multiplier, wind speed/vector, anisotropy, extinction, ambient intensity, erosion amount. Textures: uShape: 128³ sampler3D (Perlin fbm dilated by Worley, plus three Worley octaves). uDetail: 32³ sampler3D (Worley detail). uWeather: 512² sampler2D (coverage and cloud type per region). solidDepth: 2D texture for solid geometry occlusion. solidColor: 2D texture for solid geometry color. Constants: EARTHRADIUS (6,371,000 m), SHAPESCALE (1/9000 m/tile), DETAILSCALE (1/900), WEATHERSCALE (1/48,000). Outputs: outColor: vec4 with RGB as in-scattered radiance, A as transmittance. outDepth: float representing metres along the ray (0 if no cloud). Vertex Input: struct VertexInput { vec4 vertex; vec2 uv; }. Vertex Output: struct VertexOutput { vec4 screenPosition; vec2 uv; vec3 rayDirection; }. Cloud State: Per-view ownership of persistent textures (LUTs, cloud field, shadow map, history). 1. Vertex Shader Setup: Convert vertex position to clip space. Determine ray direction based on UV quadrant to cover the frustum corners: If uv.x < 0.5 && uv.y < 0.5: use FrustumCornerBL. If uv.x < 0.5 && uv.y >= 0.5: use FrustumCornerTL. If uv.x >= 0.5 && uv.y < 0.5: use FrustumCornerBR. Else: use FrustumCornerTR. Transform corners to world space using camera rotation only. 2. Ray Setup: Normalize rayDirWorldspace to get rayDirWorld. Intersect ray with the spherical cloud shell: Calculate oc = ro - vec3(0.0, -EARTHRADIUS, 0.0). rCam = length(oc). b = dot(oc, rd). c = dot(oc, oc). Compute hOuter = b b - (c - rOuter rOuter). If hOuter < 0.0, return false. Compute sOuter = sqrt(hOuter). tOuterNear = -b - sOuter. tOuterFar = -b + sOuter. Compute hInner = b b - (c - rInner rInner). If hInner > 0.0, sInner = sqrt(hInner), else sInner = 0.0. Intersection interval is [tOuterNear, tOuterFar] intersected with inner shell bounds if applicable. Intersect ray with solid geometry box (if present) to get tHitSolid. Clamp near intersection tHit.x to max(0, tHit.x) and far intersection tHit.y to min(tHit.y, tHitSolid). Calculate start point pointWorld = rayOrigWorld + tHit.x rayDirWorld. 3. Density Sampling: Transform position using high-res scaling: hiResPosition = outerProduct(position, hiResS) + outerProduct(hiResT, vec4(1.f)) where hiResT =.1f hiResNoiseTranslate and hiResS =.1f hiResNoiseScaling. Sample 4 textures from volumeHighRes at hiResPosition[0] (R), [1] (G), [2] (B), [3] (A). Compute hiResDensity = dot(hiResNoise, normalizeL1(hiResChannelWeights)). If invertDensity, hiResDensity = 1.f - hiResDensity. Apply falloff: falloff = yFalloff(position) xzFalloff(position). yFalloff: distY = min(YFALLOFFDIST, min(position.y - ymin, ymax - position.y)). Return distY / YFALLOFFDIST. xzFalloff: distX = min(XZFALLOFFDIST, min(position.x - xmin, xmax - position.x)), distZ = min(XZFALLOFFDIST, min(position.z - zmin, zmax - position.z)). Return min(distX, distZ) / XZFALLOFFDIST. hiResDensity = falloff. Add offset: hiResDensityWithOffset = hiResDensity + hiResDensityOffset. If hiResDensityWithOffset <= 0.f, return 0.f. Sample low-res: loResPosition = position loResNoiseScaling.1f + loResNoiseTranslate. loResNoise = texture(volumeLowRes, loResPosition). loResDensity = dot(loResNoise, normalizeL1(loResChannelWeights)). Invert: loResDensity = 1.f - loResDensity. Compute erosion weight: erosionWeight = getErosionWeightQuntic(hiResDensity) where getErosionWeightQuntic(d) = pow((1.f - d), 6). Final density: density = hiResDensityWithOffset - erosionWeight loResDensityWeight loResDensity. Return max(density densityMult 5.f, 0.f). 4. Lighting Optical Depth: Each march step takes six samples toward the sun to get optical depth. Intersect ray with box tHit = intersectBox(rayOrig, rayDir). tFar = max(0.f, tHit.y). dt = tFar / numStepsRecursive. ds = rayDir dt. Initialize tau = 0.f, pointWorld = rayOrig. Loop t from 0 to tFar with step dt: density = sampleDensity(pointWorld). tau -= density. pointWorld += ds. After loop: tau = (cloudLightAbsorptionMult dt). lightTransmittance = exp(tau). 5. Ray Marching Integration: Step size is derived from the ray's span through the layer. Steps are jittered per pixel with interleaved gradient noise that changes each frame. March termination: The march stops once transmittance drops below 0.5%. In-scattering is integrated analytically over each step so the result does not depend on step size. Lighting evaluation per step: Calculate sun direction sunDirSpherical using dirSph2Cart from sun latitude/longitude. Compute sun position sunPos = SUNRADIUS sunDirSpherical. Calculate light direction dirLight = normalize(sunPos - pointWorld). Calculate cosine of angle between ray and light cosRayLightAngle = dot(rayDirWorld, dirLight). Compute phase value phaseVal = phase(cosRayLightAngle). Get sun color sunColor = getSunColor(sunLongitudeRadians). Evaluate four-octave multiple-scattering approximation (attenuated extinction, contribution, phase eccentricity per octave) with a two-lobe Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Apply powder term to darken back-lit edges. Apply ambient term fading from blue at top (vec3(0.62, 0.74, 0.95)) to grey at bottom (vec3(0.36, 0.42, 0.52)). Sun/sky color shift warm as sun nears horizon. 6. Temporal Reprojection (Optional but common in real-time implementations): Render at reduced resolution (e.g., half or quarter) with sub-pixel jitter from a Halton sequence. Resolve pass reconstructs world position from cloud depth, projects through previous frame's view-projection matrix, and blends history sample at 92% (blend factor 0.08f). History is clamped to 3×3 neighbourhood to prevent ghosting from disocclusions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalizeL1(v): return v / dot(v, vec4(1.0)) def calculateyfalloff(pos, params): ymin = -0.5 params.volumescaling.y + params.volumetranslate.y ymax = ymin + params.volumescaling.y disty = min(params.yfalloffdist, min(pos.y - ymin, ymax - pos.y)) return disty / params.yfalloffdist def calculatexzfalloff(pos, params): xmin = -0.5 params.volumescaling.x + params.volumetranslate.x xmax = xmin + params.volumescaling.x zmin = -0.5 params.volumescaling.z + params.volumetranslate.z zmax = zmin + params.volumescaling.z distx = min(params.xzfalloffdist, min(pos.x - xmin, xmax - pos.x)) distz = min(params.xzfalloffdist, min(pos.z - zmin, zmax - pos.z)) return min(distx, distz) / params.xzfalloffdist def sampleclouddensity(pos, textures, params): hirespos = outerproduct(pos, params.hiress) + outerproduct(params.hirest, vec4(1.0)) hiresnoise = texture(textures.volumehighres, hirespos) hiresdensity = dot(hiresnoise, normalizeL1(params.hireschannelweights)) if params.invertdensity: hiresdensity = 1.0 - hiresdensity falloff = calculateyfalloff(pos, params) calculatexzfalloff(pos, params) hiresdensity = falloff hiresdensitywithoffset = hiresdensity + params.hiresdensityoffset if hiresdensitywithoffset <= 0.0: return 0.0 lorespos = pos params.loresnoisescaling 0.1 + params.loresnoisetranslate loresnoise = texture(textures.volumelowres, lorespos) loresdensity = dot(loresnoise, normalizeL1(params.loreschannelweights)) loresdensity = 1.0 - loresdensity erosionweight = pow(1.0 - hiresdensity, 6) density = hiresdensitywithoffset - erosionweight params.loresdensityweight loresdensity return max(density params.densitymult 5.0, 0.0) def henyeygreenstein(costheta, g): g2 = g g return (1.0 - g2) / (4.0 3.14159 pow(1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g costheta, 1.5)) def calculatesuntransmittance(point, raydir, density, textures, params): tau = 0.0 ds = raydir (params.tfar / 6.0) currentpoint = point for in range(6): d = sampleclouddensity(currentpoint, textures, params) tau -= d currentpoint += ds tau = params.cloudlightabsorptionmult (params.tfar / 6.0) return exp(tau) def calculatemultiplescattering(point, density, suntransmittance, phase, params): # Four-octave approximation after Wrenninge and Hillaire scattering = vec3(0.0) for octave in range(4): attenuation = exp(-density params.extinction (octave + 1)) contribution = params.sunintensity suntransmittance attenuation eccentricity = 1.0 - (octave 0.2) scattering += contribution phase eccentricity return scattering def raymarchclouds(rayorig, raydir, cloudparams, textures, frame): oc = rayorig - vec3(0.0, -6371000.0, 0.0) b = dot(oc, raydir) c = dot(oc, oc) houter = b b - (c - cloudparams.router 2) if houter < 0.0: return vec4(0.0), 0.0 souter = sqrt(houter) touternear = -b - souter touterfar = -b + souter hinner = b b - (c - cloudparams.rinner 2) sinner = sqrt(hinner) if hinner > 0.0 else 0.0 tstart = max(0.0, touternear) tend = touterfar raylength = tend - tstart stepsize = raylength / cloudparams.maxsteps jitter = (halton(frame % 16 + 1, 2) - 0.5) 2.0 / cloudparams.cloudwidth stepsize = (1.0 + jitter) point = rayorig + raydir tstart transmittance = 1.0 radiance = vec3(0.0) depthaccum = 0.0 transmittanceweighteddepth = 0.0 for i in range(cloudparams.maxsteps): if transmittance < 0.005: break density = sampleclouddensity(point, textures, cloudparams) if density > 0.0: suntransmittance = calculatesuntransmittance(point, raydir, density, textures, cloudparams) sundir = normalize(vec3(0.0, 100.0, 0.0) - point) cosangle = dot(normalize(raydir), normalize(sundir)) phase = henyeygreenstein(cosangle, cloudparams.anisotropy) scattering = calculatemultiplescattering(point, density, suntransmittance, phase, cloudparams) heightfactor = (point.y - cloudparams.baseheight) / cloudparams.thickness ambient = mix(vec3(0.36, 0.42, 0.52), vec3(0.62, 0.74, 0.95), heightfactor) stepradiance = scattering (1.0 - exp(-density stepsize)) radiance += stepradiance transmittance transmittance = exp(-density stepsize) depthaccum += stepsize transmittanceweighteddepth += stepsize transmittance point += raydir stepsize meandepth = transmittanceweighteddepth / (1.0 - transmittance) if transmittance < 0.999 else 0.0 return radiance, transmittance, meandepth shapenoisescale: Default 6.4 km. Sets cloud size. At this scale, cloud size measures 590-760 m on GPU noise dumps. coverage: Scales weather coverage. With physical profiles, coverage times the vertical profile is the cloud fraction. uShape: 128³ sampler3D for shape noise. uDetail: 32³ sampler3D for detail noise. uWeather: 512² sampler2D for weather map. absorptionCoefficient: Controls light absorption via Beer-Lambert law; default 1.0, range [0.0, 5.0]. densityThreshold: Minimum noise value to contribute to cloud density; range [0.0, 1.0]. scatterFactor: Controls forward light scattering strength; 0 is weakest, 1 is strongest; range [0.0, 1.0]. cloudScale: Controls zoom level into noise texture; range [0.001, 0.05]. octaveCount: Number of noise layers combined for Fractal Brownian Motion; range [1, 4]. windSpeed: Controls speed of cloud movement; range [0.0, 10.0]. uMaxSteps: Maximum marching steps, default 128. s.scale: Resolution scale factor for temporal reprojection, default 0.5. EARLYSTOPTHRESHOLD: 1e-2f. Threshold for early stopping. EARLYSTOPLOGTHRESHOLD: -4.6f. Log transmittance threshold for early stopping. MINNUMFINESTEPS: 16. Minimum number of fine steps for adaptive ray marching. COARSESTEPSIZEMULTIPLIER: 4.f. Multiplier for coarse step size relative to fine step size. MAXNUMMISSEDSTEPS: 5. Maximum number of missed steps in adaptive ray marching. STEPSIZEFINE: 0.02f. Fixed step size for fine ray marching. MAXSUNINTENSITY: 4.f. Maximum sun intensity. XZFALLOFFDIST: 1.f. Distance for XZ falloff calculation. YFALLOFFDIST: 1.f. Distance for Y falloff calculation. SUNRADIUS: 100.f. Radius of the sun in world units. AMBIENTTOP: vec3(0.62, 0.74, 0.95) ambient color at top of layer. AMBIENTBOTTOM: vec3(0.36, 0.42, 0.52) ambient color at bottom of layer. uBlend: Blending factor in temporal resolve pass, set to 0.08f. Texture History Validity: History validity is checked by texture identity. A new view, reallocation, or resize starts from an invalid history. Shadow Map Basis Error: The shadow map is traced along the view's first directional light. If every consumer looked it up for each light in that light's own basis, a second, nonparallel sun read the first one's optical depths as a displaced, wrongly oriented shadow. Viewport Depth Mismatch: Cloud raymarch and half-res haze prepass sized their pixel lattice from the depth texture (covering the whole render target) while their targets cover the viewport, reading depth without the viewport origin. An inset camera traced the wrong part of the view and the wrong depths. Both must use view.viewport for the lattice and offset depth reads by its origin. Light Sorting Flag Order: The sort key (volumetric, shadowmapsenabled, entity) is ascending, so lights without these came first. A plain directional light then took index 0, the volumetric sun lost its VOLUMETRIC flag. Reverse the two flags; the atmosphere's CPU mirror of the order does the same. Reprojection Depth Compromise: Reprojection uses the mean cloud depth per pixel. Where a thin near cloud overlaps a far one, that depth is a compromise and the history clamp does the rest. Sky Model Limitation: Sky is an analytic gradient, not an atmosphere model, so the sun's colour at low elevation is hand-tuned. Multiple Scattering Approximation: The multiple-scattering octaves are an approximation; the lit side of thick clouds is somewhat flatter than in a path-traced reference. Time Complexity: O(N M) where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of marching steps per pixel. With temporal reprojection, the effective cost is reduced by the resolution scale factor squared. Memory Complexity: O(T) where T is the size of the noise textures (128³ + 32³ + 512²) and history buffers. Per-view ownership of textures increases memory usage with multiple views. Measured Performance: On Mesa llvmpipe (CPU rasterizer) at 640×360: full-res, 128 steps, no temporal costs 927 ms total; half-res, 128 steps, temporal costs 266 ms total (29% of full-res). Scaling: Temporal reprojection allows rendering at half or quarter resolution with minimal quality loss, converging to full-resolution over roughly a dozen frames. Strengths: Real-time performance, physically plausible lighting, dynamic shadows, large-scale cloudscapes. Limitations: Approximation in multiple scattering, hand-tuned sky color, single cloud layer support in some implementations, history validity issues with view changes. When to use: Real-time games, simulations requiring dynamic cloud lighting and shadows. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring path-traced accuracy, scenes with multiple distinct cloud layers requiring separate handling (unless extended). Procedural volumetric cloud rendering originated from techniques presented in SIGGRAPH talks by Andrew Schneider (Horizon: Zero Dawn, 2015) and Sebastian Hillaire (Frostbite, 2016; Unreal Engine, 2020). The Nubis series of techniques (Nubis Evolved 2022, Nubis³ 2023) by Andrew Schneider further refined the procedural noise shaping and multiple scattering approximations. The method is implemented in engines such as Bevy and Unity. name: Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering
head: VolumeIntegrator::Li
body: Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique implemented in the VolumeIntegrator::Li function that performs ray marching through a single volume region, accumulating emitted light and computing transmittance and scattering contributions from a single light source. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific implementation within the Mr-Voxel library's integrator, which combines an accelerated voxel data structure with a ray marching loop that handles single-volume, single-light scenarios with Russian Roulette termination. Unlike Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering which often relies on procedural noise for density, or Ray-marched Volumetric Fog which may use simplified scattering models, this method explicitly computes optical depth and direct lighting transmittance per step for a defined volume object. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray ray (origin, direction, t0, t1), a scene object mScene providing access to volumes and lights, and a transmittance pointer T. Output: A Spectrum representing the accumulated radiance Lv, and the updated transmittance T. Data Structures: VolumeIntegrator: Contains member mStepSize (float/double) defining the base step size for ray marching. Scene: Provides getVolumeCount(), getVolumes() (array of volume objects), and getLightSources() (array of light objects). Volume: Provides methods tau(ray, length,...) for optical depth, Lve(p) for emitted radiance, and sigmas(p) for scattering coefficient. Ray: Has method intersect(shadRay, &surface) to check for occlusions. Parameters: mStepSize: The base step size for ray marching. Typical value not specified in sources, but used to calculate numSamples. Russian Roulette probability: Fixed at 0.5. Transmittance threshold: 10^{-3}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Samples: Compute the number of steps numSamples based on the ray segment length (t1 - t0) and mStepSize. If numSamples is 0, set it to 1. \text{numSamples} = \max\left(1, \left\lfloor \frac{t1 - t0}{\text{mStepSize}} \right\rfloor \right) 2. Calculate Step Length: Compute the actual step length step to ensure the ray covers exactly from t0 to t1. \text{step} = \frac{t1 - t0}{\text{numSamples}} 3. Random Offset: Apply a random offset to the starting position t0 to reduce banding artifacts. t0 \leftarrow t0 + \text{step} \times \frac{\text{rand()}}{\text{RAND\MAX}} 4. Initialize Accumulators: Set accumulated radiance Lv = 0 and transmittance Tr = 1. 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to numSamples: a. Update Positions: Let p{prev} be the current position. Update current position p = \text{ray}(t0 + i \times \text{step}). Create a short ray tRay from p{prev} to p with length step. b. Optical Depth: Compute the optical depth (tau) for the step. The source specifies calling volumes[0]->tau(tRay, 0.5 step, 0). c. Update Transmittance: Multiply current transmittance by the exponential of the negative optical depth. Tr \leftarrow Tr \times e^{-\tau} d. Accumulate Emission: Add the emitted radiance at point p to Lv. Lv \leftarrow Lv + L{ve}(p) e. Scattering Check: Get the scattering coefficient \sigmas = \text{volumes}[0].\sigmas(p). If \sigmas is not black (zero), proceed to compute lighting. f. Light Direction: Compute the normalized direction \omegaL from point p to the light source position. g. Shadow Ray: Create a shadow ray shadRay from p in direction \omegaL. Check if it intersects a surface closer than the light distance. The condition for being unshadowed is: no intersection, or intersection distance t{surf} is greater than the distance to the light. \text{unshadowed} = (\neg \text{mScene}.\text{intersect}(\text{shadRay}, \text{surface})) \lor (\text{surface}.t > \|p - \omegaL\|) h. Light Transmittance: If unshadowed, compute the light transmittance lT through the volume. The source specifies calling volumes[0]->tau(shadRay, mStepSize 2, 0.0). lT = e^{-\tau{light}} i. Direct Lighting: Compute the direct lighting contribution Ld using the light's color and the light transmittance. Add to accumulated radiance, scaled by scattering coefficient and current transmittance. Ld = lT \times \text{lights}[0].\text{color} Lv \leftarrow Lv + Ld \times \sigmas \times Tr j. Russian Roulette: If Tr < 10^{-3}, perform Russian Roulette. With probability 0.5, break the loop. Otherwise, continue and scale Tr by 1/0.5 (i.e., Tr \leftarrow Tr / 0.5). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def VolumeIntegratorLi(ray, scene, Tout): # Access scene data volumes = scene.getVolumes() lights = scene.getLightSources() mStepSize = scene.getIntegrator().mStepSize # Assume single volume and single light as per implementation notes volume = volumes[0] light = lights[0] # 1. Calculate number of samples t0 = ray.t0 t1 = ray.t1 numSamples = int((t1 - t0) / mStepSize) if numSamples == 0: numSamples = 1 # 2. Calculate actual step length step = (t1 - t0) / numSamples # 3. Apply random offset to starting position randomval = rand() / RANDMAX t0 += randomval step # 4. Initialize accumulators Lv = Spectrum(0, 0, 0) Tr = 1.0 # 5. Ray marching loop for i in range(numSamples): # Update positions pprev = ray(t0 + (i - 1) step) if i > 0 else ray(t0) # Note: logic in source implies pprev updates to current p, then p updates. # Source says: "update pPrev to current p, update p to ray(t0)". # This phrasing is ambiguous. Standard ray marching: pprev is start of step, p is end. # Let's interpret: pprev is position at start of step i. p is position at end of step i. # The source says: "update pPrev to current p, update p to ray(t0)". # This likely means: pprev = p; p = ray(t0 + istep). # But t0 was modified by offset. Let's assume tcurrent = t0 + istep. tcurrent = t0 + i step pprev = ray(tcurrent - step) if i > 0 else ray(t0) # Approximation for first step p = ray(tcurrent) # Create short ray for optical depth calculation # Source: tRay from pPrev to p with length step tRay = Ray(pprev, p - pprev) # Compute optical depth (tau) # Source: volumes[0]->tau(tRay, 0.5 step, 0) tau = volume.tau(tRay, 0.5 step, 0) # Update transmittance Tr = Tr exp(-tau) # Accumulate emitted light Lve = volume.Lve(p) Lv = Lv + Lve # Get scattering coefficient ss = volume.sigmas(p) # Check if scattering is non-zero if not ss.isblack(): # Compute light direction wL = normalize(light.position - p) # Create shadow ray shadRay = Ray(p, wL) # Check intersection surface = Surface() intersected = scene.intersect(shadRay, surface) # Distance to light disttolight = length(light.position - p) # Check if unshadowed # Source: !mScene->intersect(shadRay, &surface) || (surface.t > (p-wL).length()) # Note: (p-wL).length() is effectively disttolight if wL is normalized and points to light unshadowed = (not intersected) or (surface.t > disttolight) if unshadowed: # Compute light transmittance # Source: volumes[0]->tau(shadRay, mStepSize 2, 0.0) taulight = volume.tau(shadRay, mStepSize 2, 0.0) lTr = exp(-taulight) # Compute direct lighting contribution Ld = lTr light.color Lv = Lv + Ld ss Tr # Russian Roulette if Tr < 1e-3: if rand() < 0.5: break else: Tr = Tr / 0.5 Tout = Tr return Lv Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Samples: If the ray segment is shorter than mStepSize, numSamples is forced to 1 to prevent division by zero or empty loops. Single Volume/Light Assumption: The implementation explicitly accesses volumes[0] and lights[0]. It does not support multiple volumes or lights in the current form, with a TODO noting that aggregators are needed for multiple volumes. Precision: Transmittance can drop below 10^{-3}, triggering Russian Roulette to prevent unnecessary computation. Optical Depth Calculation: The source uses 0.5 step for the volume tau calculation in the main loop and mStepSize 2 for the shadow ray. These specific values are implementation details that may affect accuracy. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples numSamples, which is proportional to the ray length divided by mStepSize. Memory Complexity: Constant, as it only stores a few accumulators and temporary rays per step. Strengths: Simple implementation for single-volume, single-light scenarios; uses Russian Roulette for efficiency; combines voxel acceleration with ray marching. Limitations: Limited to single volume and single light; does not handle multiple scattering; specific tau calculation parameters (0.5step, mStepSize2) are hardcoded and may not be optimal for all scenes. When to Use: Suitable for simple volumetric effects in a controlled environment where performance is prioritized over physical accuracy for complex lighting. When Not to Use: For scenes with multiple light sources, multiple volumes, or requiring high-fidelity multi-scattering. Mr-Voxel is a combination of an accelerated voxel data-structure and volume rendering library, developed by C. Gibson. The volume rendering component is part of the author's graphics graduate thesis, which culminated in research and design surrounding voxel data structures. The lighting equations used are derived or loosely based on the volume rendering sections of "Physically Based Rendering, 2nd edition" by Matt Pharr. The long-term goal involves including importance-sampled light caches for all polygonal, implicit, and volume objects. cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray-marched Volumetric Fog
head: Forward ray-marching fog, Full-screen volumetric fog
body: Ray-marched volumetric fog simulates light absorption, scattering, soft shadows, and light shafts (god rays) by treating fog as a 3D volume of participating media traced via ray-marching from the camera to the scene. It differs from backward ray-marching (scene to camera) by enabling early-out optimizations when transmittance becomes negligible, and it differs from voxel-based methods by operating directly in screen space using depth reconstruction rather than explicit volume data structures. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera view ray direction, camera position, depth buffer (for scene intersection), light position, light intensity (\Phi), fog density (\tau), scattering coefficient (a), and step size (\Delta l). Outputs: Final pixel color (radiance L). Data Structures Depth Buffer: 2D texture or array storing depth values z for each pixel UV coordinate. Ray State: Current position x, accumulated transmittance T, accumulated radiance L{acc}. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel with UV coordinate u, shoot a ray from the camera origin C through the view direction \omega. 2. Scene Intersection: Reconstruct the 3D position of the scene intersection point x{end} by sampling the depth buffer at u and unprojecting the depth value. 3. Ray Clamping: Clamp the total ray length to a maximum distance z{far} to prevent infinite marching if the ray misses the scene geometry. 4. Jittering (Optional): Add a pseudo-random delta step \delta to the ray's starting position to fix slice artifacts. 5. Marching Loop: Iterate from n = 0 to N along the ray from camera to x{end}: a. Calculate current sample position x(ln). b. Calculate distance d from x(ln) to the light source. c. Calculate visibility v(x) from x(ln) to the light source. d. Calculate in-scattering Li. e. Calculate transmittance e^{-\tau ln} from camera to x(ln). f. Accumulate radiance: L{acc} += Li \cdot e^{-\tau ln} \cdot \Delta l. 6. Final Compositing: Combine accumulated fog radiance with the background scene color (not detailed in source, implied by "full-screen shader"). Formulas The total radiance L is approximated using a Riemann sum: L = \sum{n=0}^{N} Li(x(ln), \omega) e^{-\tau ln} \Delta l Where: L: Calculated radiance. Li(x(ln), \omega): In-scattering term at step n. e^{-\tau ln}: Transmittance for distance ln travelled from camera. \Delta l: Ray-march step size. \tau: Fog density. The in-scattering term Li for a point light is: Li(x, \omega) = \frac{a \Phi}{4\pi d^2} v(x) e^{-\tau d} P(\omega, \omega') Where: a: Scattering coefficient (probability of photon scattering). \Phi: Point light intensity. d: Distance between sample point x and light source. v(x): Visibility of sample point from light source. e^{-\tau d}: Transmittance from light to sample point. P(\omega, \omega'): Phase function describing scattering direction probability. Parameters Density (\tau): Constant for uniform fog. Visibility (v(x)): Set to 1 in the reference implementation. Can be sampled from a light's cube shadow map if available. Phase Function (P): Uses Schlick phase function approximation of Henyey-Greenstein (HG) for real-time performance. Step Size (\Delta l): Determines resolution of the march. Larger steps increase noise but reduce cost. Pitfalls Slice Artifacts: Occur when rays march with the same step size starting at the same point, causing samples to align on the same "slices". Noise: Jittering reduces slice artifacts but can make the result look noisier, especially with larger step sizes. Banding: Visible in the distance, partially mitigated by jittering every sample on a ray. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchedvolumetricfog(uv, camerapos, viewdirection, depthbuffer, lightpos, lightintensity, density, scatteringcoeff, stepsize, zfar): # 1. Reconstruct scene intersection depth = depthbuffer.sample(uv) scenepos = unproject(uv, depth) # Standard unprojection using camera matrices # 2. Calculate ray direction and length raydir = normalize(scenepos - camerapos) raylen = length(scenepos - camerapos) # 3. Clamp ray length if raylen > zfar: raylen = zfar # 4. Jitter start position to fix slice artifacts jitter = randomfloat() stepsize # Pseudo-random value in 0, stepsize) startoffset = jitter raydir # 5. Initialize accumulation accumulatedradiance = vec3(0.0) currentpos = camerapos + startoffset # 6. Marching loop numsteps = int(raylen / stepsize) for n in range(numsteps): # Current sample position samplepos = camerapos + (n stepsize + jitter) raydir # Distance from sample to light d = length(lightpos - samplepos) # Visibility (set to 1 if no shadow mapping) visibility = 1.0 # # Transmittance from camera to sample ln = length(samplepos - camerapos) transmittancecamera = exp(-density ln) # Transmittance from light to sample transmittancelight = exp(-density d) # Phase function (Schlick approximation of Henyey-Greenstein) # Simplified Schlick phase function P(g, theta) # g is asymmetry parameter, theta is angle between view and light direction # Assuming g=0 for isotropic or pre-calculated for HG approx phase = schlickphasefunction(viewdirection, normalize(lightpos - samplepos)) # In-scattering term # Li = (a Phi / (4 pi d^2)) v(x) e^(-tau d) P inscattering = (scatteringcoeff lightintensity / (4.0 3.14159 d d)) visibility transmittancelight phase # Accumulate: Li transmittancefromcamera stepsize accumulatedradiance += inscattering transmittancecamera stepsize return accumulatedradiance Renders volumetric clouds using procedural noise functions. Choose when clouds are the primary volumetric element and require complex internal structure. Renders volumes using [voxel grids and marching cubes/rays. Choose when explicit volumetric data (e.g., medical scans, smoke simulations) is available and high accuracy is needed. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of pixels and P is the number of march steps per ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel (excluding depth buffer and light shadow maps). Performance: Real-time capable on modern GPUs if step count is limited. Performance degrades with higher resolution, larger step sizes, or complex light interactions (shadow maps). Strengths: Simple implementation, works with existing scene geometry, allows dynamic lighting interactions (soft shadows, god rays). Limitations: Slice artifacts without jittering, noise with large steps, no occlusion by other volumetric objects (only scene geometry), uniform fog assumption in basic implementation. When to use: Real-time games requiring atmospheric fog with dynamic lighting. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring high accuracy, scenes with complex non-uniform volumetric data (use voxel methods), or when performance is extremely constrained and simple 2D fog is sufficient. The technique is based on the paper "Real-time Volumetric Lighting in Participating Media" by Toth and Umenhofer. It has been implemented in games such as Horizon Zero Dawn, Death Stranding, and Returnal. The implementation described is a forward ray-marching approach, deviating from the backward ray-marching in the original paper to allow for early-out optimizations. name: Volumetric Raymarching with SDF Density
head: Raymarching with a twist, Signed distance field (SDF) ray marching, Volumetric Raymarching
body: Volumetric Raymarching with SDF Density is a rendering technique that adapts sphere tracing principles to volumetric Signed Distance Fields (SDFs), encoding both interior density and exterior distance in a single continuous function. It solves the problem of rendering intricate procedural volumes, such as fractals or noise-based densities, without requiring explicit voxelization or precomputed grids. Unlike standard raymarching which stops at the first surface intersection, this method marches through the object interior using a constant step size, accumulating color and alpha via front-to-back blending based on the SDF's positive interior values. It sets itself apart from Fixed Step Ray Marching by interpreting the distance field as density rather than geometric proximity, and from Tiled Ray Marching with Grid Sampling by relying on procedural evaluation rather than grid lookups. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), SDF function f(\mathbf{p}) that returns -d (negative of Euclidean distance to surface) for points inside the volume, and 0 or positive for points outside. Outputs: Final color \mathbf{C} and accumulated alpha \alpha. Data Structures: rayOrigin: vec3 rayDirection: vec3 res: vec4 (accumulator for color and alpha) depth: float (distance along ray) p: vec3 (current sample position) Parameters: MARCHSIZE: Constant step size. Typical value: 0.08. MAXSTEPS: Maximum iterations. Typical value: 100. Steps: 1. Initialize depth to 0.0 and res to (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0). 2. Calculate initial position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \text{depth} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 3. Loop for i from 0 to MAXSTEPS - 1: a. Evaluate density D = f(\mathbf{p}). b. If D > 0.0: i. Compute sample color \mathbf{C}{sample}. A simple mapping mixes white (1,1,1) and black (0,0,0) based on density: \mathbf{C}{sample} = \text{mix}((1,1,1), (0,0,0), D). ii. Set sample alpha \alpha{sample} = D. iii. Apply alpha to color: \mathbf{C}{sample} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample}. iv. Accumulate using front-to-back blending: \mathbf{res} \leftarrow \mathbf{res} + \mathbf{C}{sample} \cdot (1.0 - \mathbf{res}.a) c. Advance depth: \text{depth} \leftarrow \text{depth} + \text{MARCH\SIZE}. d. Update position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + \text{depth} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 4. Return res. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarch(rayorigin, raydirection): # Constants MARCHSIZE = 0.08 MAXSTEPS = 100 depth = 0.0 p = rayorigin + depth raydirection res = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(MAXSTEPS): # Evaluate SDF; returns -distance inside, >= 0 outside density = scene(p) if density > 0.0: # Map density to color (white to black) # mix(a, b, t) returns a + t (b - a) samplecolor = mix(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), density) samplealpha = density # Apply alpha to color samplecolor = samplecolor samplealpha # Front-to-back blending res = res + samplecolor (1.0 - res.a) depth = depth + MARCHSIZE p = rayorigin + depth raydirection return res Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Step Size: Using a constant step size is critical. The distance returned by the SDF must NOT be used for stepping, as it represents density magnitude, not geometric clearance. SDF Sign: The SDF function must return the negative of the distance (-d) so that values are positive inside the object and zero outside. Standard SDFs return positive inside; this inversion is required for the density check D > 0.0. Precision: For complex, non-intersecting surfaces like fractals, fixed-step methods may require more iterations than sphere tracing to converge, potentially leading to aliasing in thin features if the step size is too large. A post-processing technique using cone-shaped SDFs for directional light shafts in screen space. Chosen when rendering volumetric lighting effects from specific light sources rather than general volume density. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is MAXSTEPS. Independent of scene complexity as the SDF is evaluated procedurally. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as no voxel grid or acceleration structure is stored. Performance: Efficient for real-time procedural volumes (e.g., clouds, smoke) on GPUs due to lack of precomputation. Performance scales with MAXSTEPS and MARCHSIZE; smaller steps increase accuracy but reduce frame rate. Strengths: Watertight traversal without precomputation; compact representation; avoids aliasing in thin features by refining steps near boundaries (if step size is adaptive, though this method uses fixed steps). Limitations: Fixed step size may miss thin features or require high MAXSTEPS for accuracy; no explicit handling of scattering or complex lighting beyond simple color mapping in the base method. When to use: Procedural volumes where explicit voxelization is infeasible, real-time rendering of clouds/smoke, differentiable optimization for scene fitting. When not to use: When high-fidelity light transport (multiple scattering) is required without additional shaders; when exact geometric boundaries are needed without density interpretation. Originating from the adaptation of sphere tracing principles to volumetric SDFs, this method was popularized in real-time graphics communities for rendering procedural clouds and smoke. It enables compact representation of intricate procedural volumes by evaluating the SDF on-the-fly, supporting applications like real-time procedural terrain or cloud volumes. The technique leverages the continuous nature of SDFs to encode interior density, allowing for differentiable optimization in neural reconstruction contexts.
