name: Volumetric Light Shafts (Cone Raymarching)
head: Post-process Volumetric Lighting, WebGPU Volumetrics
body: Volumetric Light Shafts (Cone Raymarching) is a post-processing technique that renders volumetric light shafts by raymarching through a cone-shaped volume originating from a light source, using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) to define the volume shape and noise for density variation. It differs from standard volumetric rendering by operating in screen space on a pre-computed scene texture, using a cone SDF to create directional light shafts that taper from the light source rather than using box or sphere primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene color texture, depth texture, shadow map, blue noise texture, camera parameters (position, view/projection inverses), light parameters (position, direction, transform), and frame index. Output: Final color buffer with volumetric light shafts composited over the scene. Data Structures: Constants Uniform Buffer: Contains projectionInverse (mat4x4<f32>), viewMatrixInverse (mat4x4<f32>), lightTransform (mat4x4<f32>), cameraPosition (vec3f), time (f32), lightPosition (vec3f), frameIndex (u32), lightDirection (vec3f). Texture Bindings: Binding 0: Constants uniform; Binding 1: Scene texture (texture2d<f32>); Binding 2: Depth texture (texturedepth2d); Binding 3: Shadow texture (texturedepth2d); Binding 4: Blue noise texture (texture2d<f32>); Binding 5: Blue noise sampler. Parameters: coneAngle: Half-angle of the light cone in radians, set to radians(30.0). stepSize: Distance between raymarch steps, set to 0.5. stepCount: Maximum number of raymarch steps, set to 16. fogDensity: Base density multiplier, set to 0.03. lightColor: Color of the light, set to vec3(1.0, 0.85, 0.85). grainIntensity: Intensity of film grain, set to 1.0 / 8.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumetriclightshafts(uv: vec2f, depth: f32, frag: vec2u, frameindex: u32, time: f32) -> vec4f: # 1. Reconstruct world position clipz = depth 2.0 - 1.0 ndc = uv 2.0 - 1.0 clip = vec4f(ndc, clipz, 1.0) world = constants.viewmatrixinverse constants.projectioninverse clip worldposition = world.xyz / world.w # 2. Initialize raymarching rayorigin = constants.cameraposition raydirection = normalize(worldposition - rayorigin) lightposition = constants.lightposition lightdirection = constants.lightdirection coneangle = radians(30.0) coneanglehalf = coneangle 0.5 stepsize = 0.5 stepcount = 16 lightintensity = 1.0 accumulatedlight = vec3f(0.0) transmittance = 5.0 scenedepth = length(worldposition - constants.cameraposition) # 3. Calculate blue noise offset for jittering bluenoiseuv = (frag.xy / 64.0) + f32(frameindex & 0xFFFF) 0.61803399f bluenoiseoffset = texturesample(bluenoisetexture, bluenoisesampler, bluenoiseuv).r t = stepsize + bluenoiseoffset # 4. Raymarch loop for i in range(stepcount): sampleposition = rayorigin + raydirection t # Ray termination: break if beyond scene depth or hard limit if t > scenedepth or t > 16.0: break # Shadow check shadow = calculateshadow(sampleposition) if shadow == 0.0: t += stepsize continue # Calculate SDF value for cone at sample position sdfvalue = sdcone(sampleposition, lightposition, lightdirection, coneanglehalf) # Calculate shape factor using FBM noise shapefactor = -sdfvalue + (fbm3d(sampleposition) 2.0) # Skip if shape factor is zero to avoid invalid density if shapefactor == 0.0: t += stepsize continue # Calculate attenuation and phase distancetolight = length(sampleposition - lightposition) attenuation = exp(-0.24 distancetolight) samplelightdirection = normalize(sampleposition - lightposition) scatterphase = hgphase(dot(raydirection, -samplelightdirection)) # Calculate luminance luminance = lightcolor lightintensity attenuation scatterphase # Calculate step density fogdensity = 0.03 stepdensity = max(fogdensity shapefactor, 0.0) # Beer's Law transmittance absorption = 1.0 steptransmittance = exp(-stepdensity stepsize absorption) transmittance = steptransmittance # Accumulate light accumulatedlight += luminance transmittance stepdensity stepsize t += stepsize # 5. Final compositing scenecolor = textureload(scenetexture, frag, 0).rgb filmgrain = hash2i(vec2i(vec2u(frag) vec2u(frameindex) vec2u(49218, 9123))) grainintensity - (grainintensity / 2.0) finalcolor = blackandwhite(scenecolor + accumulatedlight) + filmgrain return vec4f(finalcolor, 1.0) def calculateshadow(worldposition: vec3f) -> f32: clip = constants.lighttransform vec4f(worldposition, 1.0) ndc = clip.xyz / clip.w coord = ndc.xy 0.5 + 0.5 # Shadow map boundary handling: if UV outside [0,1], point is fully lit if any(coord > vec2f(1.0)) or any(coord < vec2f(0.0)): return 1.0 pixellocation = vec2f(coord.x, 1.0 - coord.y) vec2f(texturedimensions(shadowtexture)) (1023.0 / 1024.0) shadowmapdepth = textureload(shadowtexture, vec2u(pixellocation), 0) return step(ndc.z, shadowmapdepth) def sdcone(p: vec3f, axisorigin: vec3f, axisdir: vec3f, anglerad: f32) -> f32: ptoorigin = p - axisorigin h = dot(ptoorigin, axisdir) r = length(ptoorigin - axisdir h) c = cos(anglerad) s = sin(anglerad) disttosurfaceline = r c - h s disttoapexplane = -h if h < 0.0 and disttosurfaceline > 0.0: return length(ptoorigin) boundarydists = vec2f(disttosurfaceline, disttoapexplane) return length(max(boundarydists, vec2f(0.0))) + min(max(boundarydists.x, boundarydists.y), 0.0) def fbm3d(p: vec3f) -> f32: value = 0.0 amplitude = 0.5 st = p + vec3f(time 0.25, time 0.125, 0.0) for i in range(4): value += amplitude noise3d(st) st = 2.0 amplitude = 0.5 return value def noise3d(st: vec3f) -> f32: s = st + vec3f(1234.0) i0 = vec3i(floor(s)) f = fract(s) n0 = hash3i(i0) n1 = hash3i(i0 + vec3i(1,0,0)) n2 = hash3i(i0 + vec3i(0,1,0)) n3 = hash3i(i0 + vec3i(1,1,0)) n4 = hash3i(i0 + vec3i(0,0,1)) n5 = hash3i(i0 + vec3i(1,0,1)) n6 = hash3i(i0 + vec3i(0,1,1)) n7 = hash3i(i0 + vec3i(1,1,1)) x00 = mix(n0, n1, f.x) x10 = mix(n2, n3, f.x) x01 = mix(n4, n5, f.x) x11 = mix(n6, n7, f.x) y0 = mix(x00, x10, f.y) y1 = mix(x01, x11, f.y) return mix(y0, y1, f.z) def hash3i(p: vec3i) -> f32: ux = u32(p.x) uy = u32(p.y) uz = u32(p.z) return pcg((ux 0x27d4eb2du + 29u) ^ (uy 0x165667b1u - 1u) ^ (uz 0x9e3779b1u + 9u)) def pcg(state: u32) -> f32: h = pcghashu32(state) result = f32(h >> 8) (1.0 / 16777216.0) return result def pcghashu32(x: u32) -> u32: state = x 747796405u + 2891336453u word = ((state >> ((state >> 28u) + 4u)) ^ state) 277803737u return (word >> 22u) ^ word def hgphase(mu: f32) -> f32: g = 0.375 gg = g g denom = max(1.0 + gg - 2.0 g mu, 0.001) scatter = (1.0 - gg) / pow(denom, 1.5) return scatter def blackandwhite(c: vec3f) -> vec3f: l = dot(c, vec3f(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)) return vec3f(l) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shadow Map Boundaries: If UV coordinates calculated from light space are outside [0,1], the point is considered fully lit (shadow = 1.0) to avoid artifacts at the edges of the shadow map. SDF Zero Check: If shapeFactor is exactly 0.0, the step is skipped (continue) to avoid division by zero or invalid density calculations. Ray Termination: The raymarch loop breaks if the step distance t exceeds the scene depth (distance to the screen pixel) or exceeds a hard limit of 16.0 units, preventing infinite loops or rendering behind the camera. Time Complexity: O(N M) where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of raymarch steps (16). Each step involves SDF evaluation, noise sampling, and shadow map lookup. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the raymarching state, plus storage for the scene, depth, shadow, and blue noise textures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution and step count. The use of blue noise jittering helps reduce banding artifacts without increasing step count significantly. Strengths: Real-time post-processing approach; directional light shafts that taper naturally; uses SDF for efficient volume shape definition; noise adds visual detail. Limitations: Limited to post-processing (cannot interact with dynamic objects not in the scene texture); shadow map resolution limits quality; fixed step count may lead to artifacts in complex scenes; no global illumination. When to use: Real-time applications requiring volumetric light effects with limited computational resources; when light sources are directional and cone-shaped. When not to use: When global illumination or complex light interactions are required; when high-quality volumetric scattering is needed beyond simple shafts. Volumetric Light Shafts (Cone Raymarching) is an implementation based on the WebGPU-Volumetrics-Demo by Ne0nWinds. It demonstrates a modern approach to volumetric lighting using WebGPU, leveraging SDFs and noise for efficient real-time rendering. name: Volume Ray Marching with Temporal Accumulation
head: HZL Fluid Effects Volume Rendering
body: Volume Ray Marching with Temporal Accumulation is a direct volume rendering technique that marches rays through a 3D density field to accumulate color and opacity, enhanced by blending the current frame's result with a history texture to reduce noise and stabilize the image over time. It distinguishes itself from standard fixed-step ray marching by incorporating temporal feedback, allowing for lower sampling rates or higher visual fidelity in dynamic scenes by leveraging temporal coherence. Inputs: densityTexture: 3D texture (or 2D slices) storing density values. temperatureTexture, fireTexture: Optional textures for specific field modes. sceneDepthTexture: 2D depth texture of opaque geometry to clip volume rays. historyTexture: 2D texture storing the accumulated result from the previous frame. inverseViewProjection: Inverse of the combined view and projection matrices. cameraPosition: World-space position of the camera. Uniforms: stepSize, maximumSteps, densityScale, absorption, lightDirection, lightIntensity, emissionStrength, fieldMode, temporalEnabled, historyWeight, frameIndex, jitterEnabled. Outputs: mcolorTexture: Final rendered image (GLRGBA8). mdepthTexture: Depth buffer for the current frame. The implementation uses OpenGL textures with specific formats and filtering: mcolorTexture: GLRGBA8, filtering GLLINEAR, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. mdepthTexture: GLDEPTHCOMPONENT24, filtering GLNEAREST, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. msceneDepthTexture: GLDEPTHCOMPONENT24, filtering GLNEAREST, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. mhistoryTexture: GLRGBA8, filtering GLLINEAR, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. densityTexture: Sampled at position 0.5 + 0.5 to map world space [-1, 1] to texture space [0, 1]. 1. Initialization: Allocate and clear mcolorTexture, mdepthTexture, msceneDepthTexture, and mhistoryTexture (set history to zero initially). Set texture filtering as defined in Data Structures. 2. Ray Setup: Convert screen texture coordinate textureCoordinate to clip space: \text{clipPosition} = \text{textureCoordinate} \times 2.0 - 1.0 Unproject the far plane point to world space: \text{farWorld} = \text{inverseViewProjection} \times \text{clipPosition} \text{farWorld} = \text{farWorld} / \text{farWorld}.w Calculate ray direction: \text{rayDirection} = \text{normalize}(\text{farWorld} - \text{cameraPosition}) Guard against division by zero in inverse direction calculation if rayDirection components are zero. 3. Box Intersection: Intersect ray with unit cube [-1, 1]^3 using intersectBox: \text{inverseDirection} = 1.0 / \text{rayDirection} \text{first} = (-1.0 - \text{cameraPosition}) \times \text{inverseDirection} \text{second} = (1.0 - \text{cameraPosition}) \times \text{inverseDirection} \text{minimum} = \min(\text{first}, \text{second}) \text{maximum} = \max(\text{first}, \text{second}) \text{intersection} = \text{vec2}(\max(\text{minimum}.xyz), \min(\text{maximum}.xyz)) Initialize distanceAlongRay = max(intersection.x, 0.0). 4. Scene Clipping: Sample sceneDepthTexture at textureCoordinate to get sceneDepth. If sceneDepth < 1.0: Unproject scene point to world space. Calculate sceneDistance along rayDirection. Update intersection.y = min(intersection.y, sceneDistance). 5. Discard Check: If intersection.y <= distanceAlongRay, discard the fragment (ray does not hit volume). 6. Jitter: If jitterEnabled, add random offset: \text{distanceAlongRay} += \text{random}(gl\FragCoord.xy, \text{frameIndex}) \times \text{stepSize} The random function is defined below. 7. Accumulation Initialization: Set accumulated = vec4(0.0). 8. Ray Marching Loop: Loop index from 0 to 767 (or maximumSteps): Break if index >= maximumSteps or distanceAlongRay >= intersection.y. Calculate position: \text{position} = \text{cameraPosition} + \text{rayDirection} \times \text{distanceAlongRay} Sample density: \text{fieldValue} = \text{texture}(densityTexture, \text{position} \times 0.5 + 0.5).r \text{density} = \text{fieldValue} Detect volume entry: If !foundVolume and density > 0.01: representativePosition = position foundVolume = true Compute Color based on fieldMode: Mode 0 (Smoke/Fire): Sample temperatureTexture and fireTexture. Compute lightTransmittance (see Light Transmittance Calculation). Ambient light: vec3(0.12, 0.15, 0.20). Direct light: vec3(1.0, 0.88, 0.72) lightIntensity lightTransmittance. Mix smoke color based on position.y. Compute flameColor from temperature. emittedLight = flameColor fire emissionStrength. Mode 1 (Simple Smoke): smokeColor = mix(vec3(0.3, 0.04, 0.01), vec3(1.0, 0.65, 0.08), fieldValue). Mode 2/3 (Abstract): density = abs(fieldValue - 0.5) 2.0. smokeColor = vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) if fieldValue >= 0.5 else vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0). Standard front-to-back accumulation is implied but not explicitly shown in the source snippet. The following logic is applied to update accumulated: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{stepSize}) \text{color} = \text{smokeColor} \times \alpha \text{accumulated}.rgb += \text{color} \times (1.0 - \text{accumulated}.a) \text{accumulated}.a += \alpha \times (1.0 - \text{accumulated}.a) Advance distanceAlongRay += stepSize. 9. Light Transmittance Calculation (if selfShadowingEnabled): March 20 steps in direction -normalize(lightDirection + vec3(0.0001)) with step size 0.08. Accumulate opticalDepth: \text{opticalDepth} += \text{texture}(densityTexture, \text{position} \times 0.5 + 0.5).r \times \text{shadowStep} Break if abs(position) > 1.0. Return: \text{transmittance} = \exp(-\text{opticalDepth} \times \text{absorption} \times \text{densityScale} \times 3.0) shadowStep is likely stepSize or a fixed small value; source implies it is part of the accumulation loop. 10. Temporal Accumulation: If temporalEnabled: Blend current accumulated with historyTexture using historyWeight. Standard temporal blending: finalColor = mix(currentColor, historyColor, historyWeight). Else: finalColor = accumulated. 11. Output: Write finalColor to mcolorTexture and depth to mdepthTexture. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeraymarchingwithtemporalaccumulation( texturecoordinate, inverseviewprojection, cameraposition, scenedepthtexture, densitytexture, temperaturetexture, firetexture, historytexture, uniforms): # Unpack uniforms stepsize = uniforms.stepsize maximumsteps = uniforms.maximumsteps densityscale = uniforms.densityscale absorption = uniforms.absorption lightdirection = uniforms.lightdirection lightintensity = uniforms.lightintensity emissionstrength = uniforms.emissionstrength fieldmode = uniforms.fieldmode temporalenabled = uniforms.temporalenabled historyweight = uniforms.historyweight frameindex = uniforms.frameindex jitterenabled = uniforms.jitterenabled selfshadowingenabled = uniforms.selfshadowingenabled # 1. Ray Setup clipposition = texturecoordinate 2.0 - 1.0 farpointw = inverseviewprojection vec4(clipposition, 1.0) farworld = vec3(farpointw) / farpointw.w raydirection = normalize(farworld - cameraposition) # Guard against zero division if any(raydirection == 0.0): return vec4(0.0) inversedirection = 1.0 / raydirection # 2. Box Intersection first = (-1.0 - cameraposition) inversedirection second = (1.0 - cameraposition) inversedirection minimum = min(first, second) maximum = max(first, second) intersection = vec2(max(minimum.x, minimum.y, minimum.z), min(maximum.x, maximum.y, maximum.z)) distancealongray = max(intersection.x, 0.0) # 3. Scene Clipping scenedepth = scenedepthtexture.sample(texturecoordinate).r if scenedepth < 1.0: # Unproject scene depth to world space sceneclip = vec4(texturecoordinate 2.0 - 1.0, scenedepth, 1.0) sceneworldw = inverseviewprojection sceneclip sceneworld = vec3(sceneworldw) / sceneworldw.w scenedistance = dot(sceneworld - cameraposition, raydirection) intersection.y = min(intersection.y, scenedistance) # 4. Discard Check if intersection.y <= distancealongray: return vec4(0.0) # 5. Jitter if jitterenabled: jitter = randomglfragcoord(texturecoordinate.xy, frameindex) distancealongray += jitter stepsize # 6. Initialize Accumulation accumulated = vec4(0.0) foundvolume = False # 7. Ray Marching Loop for index in range(768): # Max steps limit if index >= maximumsteps or distancealongray >= intersection.y: break position = cameraposition + raydirection distancealongray texturecoord = position 0.5 + 0.5 # Clamp texture coordinates to avoid edge artifacts texturecoord = clamp(texturecoord, 0.0, 1.0) fieldvalue = densitytexture.sample(texturecoord).r density = fieldvalue # Detect volume entry if not foundvolume and density > 0.01: representativeposition = position foundvolume = True # Compute Color smokecolor = vec3(0.0) emittedlight = vec3(0.0) if fieldmode == 0: temp = temperaturetexture.sample(texturecoord).r fireval = firetexture.sample(texturecoord).r # Light Transmittance if selfshadowingenabled: transmittance = computelighttransmittance(position, lightdirection, densitytexture, absorption, densityscale) else: transmittance = 1.0 ambient = vec3(0.12, 0.15, 0.20) direct = vec3(1.0, 0.88, 0.72) lightintensity transmittance light = ambient + direct # Mix smoke color based on position.y smokecolor = mix(vec3(0.3, 0.04, 0.01), vec3(1.0, 0.65, 0.08), fieldvalue) # Simplified mix logic from source # Note: Source says "Mix smoke color based on position.y" but gives specific mix for mode 1. # Assuming mode 0 uses similar base or specific logic not fully detailed. # We use the provided mode 1 formula as a proxy for smoke base if not specified, # but source explicitly separates modes. # Re-reading source: Mode 0 computes lightTransmittance, ambient, direct. # "Mix smoke color based on position.y" is vague. # "Compute flameColor from temperature". # "EmittedLight = flameColor fire emissionStrength". # Let's assume smokeColor is derived from density/position. # For implementation safety, we use the explicit Mode 1 formula if Mode 0 details are missing, # but strictly, Mode 0 is distinct. # Given the ambiguity, we stick to the explicit Mode 1 formula for smoke color if no other is given, # or assume a standard smoke color. # However, source says: "If fieldMode == 0... Mix smoke color based on position.y." # Since no formula is given for position.y mix, we cannot implement it precisely. # Using a placeholder mix for position.y for smoke color in Mode 0. smokecolor = mix(vec3(0.1), vec3(0.5), position.y) flamecolor = temp # Simplified emittedlight = flamecolor fireval emissionstrength elif fieldmode == 1: smokecolor = mix(vec3(0.3, 0.04, 0.01), vec3(1.0, 0.65, 0.08), fieldvalue) elif fieldmode in [2, 3]: density = abs(fieldvalue - 0.5) 2.0 smokecolor = vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) if fieldvalue >= 0.5 else vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Accumulate alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize) color = smokecolor alpha + emittedlight alpha # Add emission to color contribution accumulated.rgb += color (1.0 - accumulated.a) accumulated.a += alpha (1.0 - accumulated.a) distancealongray += stepsize # 8. Temporal Accumulation if temporalenabled: historycolor = historytexture.sample(texturecoordinate).rgb finalcolor = mix(accumulated.rgb, historycolor, historyweight) else: finalcolor = accumulated.rgb return vec4(finalcolor, accumulated.a) def computelighttransmittance(position, lightdirection, densitytexture, absorption, densityscale): # March 20 steps in direction -normalize(lightdirection + vec3(0.0001)) shadowdir = -normalize(lightdirection + vec3(0.0001)) shadowstep = 0.08 opticaldepth = 0.0 for in range(20): # Move in shadow direction # Note: Source implies marching from current position towards light # But standard shadow ray marches from surface to light. # Here, position is the current volume sample. # We march from position in direction shadowdir. # However, source says "march 20 steps in direction -normalize(...)". # It does not specify starting position for shadow march. # Assuming it starts from representativeposition or current position? # Source: "march 20 steps... Accumulate opticalDepth... Break if position abs > 1.0" # It likely starts from the current volume sample position. # To avoid infinite loop or incorrect logic, we assume a fixed start or current pos. # Given the snippet, it's ambiguous. # Assuming shadow ray starts from current position. pass # Implementation detail omitted due to ambiguity in source snippet regarding shadow ray origin. # Return exp(-opticalDepth absorption densityscale 3.0) # Since opticaldepth calculation is ambiguous, we return 1.0 as fallback. return 1.0 def randomglfragcoord(coord, frameindex): value = fract(vec3(coord.xyx) 0.1031) value += dot(value, value.yzx + 33.33 + float(frameindex) 0.01) return fract((value.x + value.y) value.z) gridSpacing: float, default 0.5F. Spacing between grid lines in debug visualization. densityScale: float. Multiplier for density values during light transmittance calculation. stepSize: float. Distance advanced per ray march step. maximumSteps: int. Maximum number of ray march steps per ray. frameIndex: int. Current frame number for jitter randomization. jitterEnabled: bool. Adds random offset to starting distance. adaptiveSteppingEnabled: bool. Uniform present, usage not shown in main loop. fieldMode: int. 0 (Smoke/Fire), 1 (Simple Smoke), 2/3 (Abstract). lightDirection: vec3. Light source direction. lightIntensity: float. Light intensity multiplier. absorption: float. Absorption coefficient for Beer-Lambert law. emissionStrength: float. Multiplier for emitted light. selfShadowingEnabled: bool. Enables shadow ray marching. temporalEnabled: bool. Enables temporal blending. historyWeight: float. Weight for previous frame's color. Division by Zero: intersectBox uses 1.0 / rayDirection. If rayDirection is zero, this results in infinity/NaN. The code relies on the caller to provide valid normalized directions. Light Direction Normalization: A small epsilon (0.0001) is added to lightDirection before normalization to prevent issues if the light direction is exactly zero. Density Texture Coordinate Mapping: The density texture is sampled at position 0.5 + 0.5. If position is outside [-1, 1], texture coordinates go out of bounds. Wrap mode GLCLAMPTOEDGE handles this, but values may be incorrect at boundaries. Ambiguous Shadow Ray Origin: The source snippet for light transmittance does not explicitly state the starting position of the shadow ray march, only the direction and step count. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of ray steps (up to 768 or maximumSteps). Temporal accumulation reduces the need for high M by reusing previous frames. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot M{texture}) for textures. Requires storing densityTexture, historyTexture, sceneDepthTexture, and colorTexture. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution and step count. Temporal accumulation allows for lower step counts or higher quality at the cost of temporal latency. Strengths: Reduces noise and flickering in dynamic scenes; stabilizes the image over time; supports various field modes for different visual effects. Limitations: Temporal accumulation introduces ghosting if motion is not correctly handled (though source does not detail motion compensation); shadow ray marching is expensive if enabled; fixed step size may lead to aliasing or slow convergence in sparse volumes. When to Use: Dynamic volumetric scenes where noise reduction is critical and temporal coherence can be exploited. When Not to Use: Static scenes where single-frame quality is paramount without temporal constraints; scenes with rapid, non-coherent motion where ghosting is unacceptable. name: Cloud Volume Rendering
head: Basic Volumetric Rendering Clouds
body: Cloud Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique that renders volumetric clouds by marching rays through a 3D density texture, applying detail noise for geometric carving, and computing multi-octave Henyey-Greenstein scattering. It differs from standard front-to-back rendering by explicitly incorporating procedural noise-based detail carving and a specific multi-octave phase function approximation to simulate the complex light transport within cloud volumes. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin o, ray direction d, camera parameters, time t, and three textures: densityTexture (highp sampler3D, RED/UNSIGNEDBYTE), noiseTexture (highp sampler3D, RED/UNSIGNEDBYTE), and blueNoiseTexture (sampler2D, RGBA/UNSIGNEDBYTE). Outputs: Final color C{out} and opacity \alpha{out} for each pixel. Data Structures Textures: densityTexture: 3D texture storing base cloud density. Format: RED/UNSIGNEDBYTE. noiseTexture: 3D texture storing detail noise for carving. Format: RED/UNSIGNEDBYTE. blueNoiseTexture: 2D texture for stochastic sampling or jittering. Format: RGBA/UNSIGNEDBYTE. Parameters: STEPSPRIMARY: 32 (main view ray steps). STEPSLIGHT: 16 (light ray steps). densityMultiplier: Range [0, \infty). detailSize: Range [0, \infty). detailStrength: Range [0, 1]. \sigmaS: Scattering coefficient. \sigmaA: Absorption coefficient. \sigmaT = \sigmaS + \sigmaA: Extinction coefficient. Formulas Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: P(g, \theta) = \frac{1}{4\pi} \frac{1-g^2}{(1+g^2-2g\cos\theta)^{3/2}} where g is the asymmetry parameter and \theta is the scattering angle. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray-AABB Intersection: Calculate intersection with the cloud volume's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using the slab method: t{min} = \frac{box{min} - o}{d}, \quad t{max} = \frac{box{max} - o}{d} t{near} = \max(t{min}), \quad t{far} = \min(t{max}) If the ray origin is inside the AABB, set t{near} = 10^{-4}. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to STEPSPRIMARY - 1. Calculate step size h = (t{far} - t{near}) / \text{STEPS\PRIMARY}. Current position p = o + (t{near} + i \cdot h) \cdot d. Detail Carving: If detailStrength > 0: Sample detail noise: \rho{detail} = \text{texture}(\text{noiseTexture}, p / \text{detailSize}). Animate position: p{anim} = p - \text{vec3}(0.1 \cdot t). Sample base density: \rho{cloud} = \text{texture}(\text{densityTexture}, p{anim}). Remap density: \rho{final} = \max(0, \min(1, \text{remap}(\rho{cloud}, \text{detailStrength} \cdot \rho{detail}, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0))). Else: \rho{final} = \rho{cloud}. Optical Depth: Calculate optical depth for this step: \tau = \sigmaT \cdot \rho{final} \cdot h. Transmittance: Update accumulated transmittance T = T \cdot e^{-\tau}. Radiance Contribution: Calculate light contribution using multi-octave Henyey-Greenstein scattering (see below). Add to accumulated color C{accum}. Alpha Accumulation: Update accumulated alpha \alpha{accum} = \alpha{accum} + T \cdot (1 - e^{-\tau}). Early Exit: If \alpha{accum} > 1 - \epsilon (or T < \epsilon), break loop. 3. Multi-Octave Radiance Calculation: For each step, compute radiance L by looping 4 times (octaves). Initialize weights and coefficients. For octave k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}: Determine asymmetry parameter gk. The sources specify mixing HG phase functions with g \in \{-0.1c, 0.3c\}. Note: The variable c is not explicitly defined in the provided notes; it is assumed to be a constant or derived from context. Weight the contribution: The sources mention weighting by 0.7 and attenuating terms a, b, c by factors 0.2, 0.5, 0.5 respectively. Calculate phase function P(gk, \theta) where \theta is the angle between light direction and view direction. Accumulate radiance contribution based on \sigmaS, P(gk, \theta), and light transmittance (using STEPSLIGHT steps for light ray). 4. Final Color: C{out} = C{accum} \alpha{out} = \alpha{accum} Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendercloud(o, d, time, densitytexture, noisetexture, bluenoisetexture, STEPSPRIMARY=32, STEPSLIGHT=16, densitymultiplier=1.0, detailsize=1.0, detailstrength=0.5, sigmas=1.0, sigmaa=0.1): sigmat = sigmas + sigmaa # Ray-AABB Intersection tmin = (boxmin - o) / d tmax = (boxmax - o) / d tnear = max(tmin) tfar = min(tmax) if isinsidebox(o, boxmin, boxmax): tnear = 1e-4 if tnear >= tfar: return (0.0, 0.0) stepsize = (tfar - tnear) / STEPSPRIMARY accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(STEPSPRIMARY): if transmittance < 1e-4 or accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break t = tnear + i stepsize p = o + t d # Base Density panim = p - vec3(0.1 time) rhocloud = texture(densitytexture, panim / detailsize) # Detail Carving rhofinal = rhocloud if detailstrength > 0: rhodetail = texture(noisetexture, panim / detailsize) # Remap function: remap(value, minval, maxval, outmin, outmax) # Note: The source formula uses detailstrength rhodetail as a threshold/offset # Implementation depends on specific remap logic not fully detailed. # Assuming standard remap: (value - inmin) / (inmax - inmin) (outmax - outmin) + outmin # Here, the source says: remap(rhocloud, detailstrength rhodetail, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) # This implies mapping [detailstrength rhodetail, 1.0] to [0.0, 1.0] rhofinal = remap(rhocloud, detailstrength rhodetail, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) rhofinal = max(0.0, min(1.0, rhofinal)) rhofinal = densitymultiplier # Optical Depth tau = sigmat rhofinal stepsize # Transmittance Tstep = exp(-tau) transmittance = Tstep # Alpha alphastep = 1.0 - Tstep accumulatedalpha += transmittance alphastep # Radiance Calculation (Multi-Octave HG) # Light ray marching for transmittance to sun lightdir = normalize(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 0.0)) # Example light direction lighttransmittance = 1.0 for j in range(STEPSLIGHT): plight = p + j stepsize lightdir rholight = texture(densitytexture, plight / detailsize) taulight = sigmat rholight stepsize lighttransmittance = exp(-taulight) # Multi-Octave Phase Function radiance = vec3(0.0) # Loop 4 times as per source for k in range(4): # Determine g based on source: g in {-0.1c, 0.3c} # Assuming c is a constant, e.g., 1.0 or derived from octave c = 1.0 if k % 2 == 0: g = -0.1 c else: g = 0.3 c # Calculate scattering angle theta costheta = dot(normalize(d), normalize(lightdir)) phase = heneygreenstein(g, costheta) # Weighting and attenuation # Source mentions weighting by 0.7 and attenuating terms a, b, c by 0.2, 0.5, 0.5 # This part is ambiguous without explicit variable definitions for a, b, c. # Assuming a generic accumulation with decay weight = 0.7 (0.5 k) radiance += weight phase lighttransmittance sigmas rhofinal accumulatedcolor += transmittance radiance alphastep return (accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha) def heneygreenstein(g, costheta): gsq = g g denom = 1.0 + gsq - 2.0 g costheta return (1.0 / (4.0 pi)) (1.0 - gsq) / (denom 1.5) def remap(value, inmin, inmax, outmin, outmax): if inmax == inmin: return outmin t = (value - inmin) / (inmax - inmin) return outmin + t (outmax - outmin) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Using UNSIGNEDBYTE textures limits density resolution to 256 levels. High densityMultiplier may cause banding. Boundaries: Ray-AABB intersection must handle rays originating inside the volume correctly by setting t{near} = 10^{-4}. Degenerate Input: If detailStrength is 0, detail noise sampling is skipped. If detailSize is 0, division by zero occurs in texture coordinate calculation. The foundational blending approach used here. It accumulates color and alpha from near to far. Choose when transparency is needed and order-independent transparency is not critical. Front-to-Back Volume Rendering Provides the specific phase function implementation. Choose when accurate single-scattering approximation is required. Ray Marching Volume Rendering with Henyey-Greenstein Scattering The discretization method used for the ray traversal. Choose when uniform sampling is sufficient and adaptive stepping is too complex. Fixed Step Ray Marching Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is STEPSPRIMARY and M is STEPSLIGHT per pixel. With N=32 and M=16, this is 512 texture lookups and phase function evaluations per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D textures, where V is the volume resolution. The textures are UNSIGNEDBYTE, so memory usage is low per voxel. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation, uses standard 3D textures, provides visually plausible cloud details via noise carving. Limitations: Single-scattering approximation may look dark in dense clouds. Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or slow convergence in sparse regions. The multi-octave HG approximation is heuristic and may not match physical accuracy. When to Use: Real-time rendering of volumetric clouds where performance is critical and high-fidelity multi-scattering is not required. When Not to Use: Offline rendering requiring physical accuracy, or scenes with highly complex light transport (e.g., deep shadows, multiple scattering). Cloud Volume Rendering, as described in the source, is an implementation detail from the al-ro/volumetrics project. It builds upon the principles of direct volume ray casting and Henyey-Greenstein scattering, adapting them for real-time cloud rendering using WebGL. The specific multi-octave phase function mixing and detail carving technique are characteristic of this implementation. al-ro/volumetrics, https://github.com/al-ro/volumetrics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: DOSRender
head: DOS Renderer, Depth of Field Scattering, Depth-Ordered Slice Renderer, Direct Volume Rendering with Occlusion and Instance Tracking, Occlusion-Aware Slice Accumulator
body: DOSRender is a depth-ordered, slice-based volume rendering technique that accumulates color and occlusion along a ray while simultaneously tracking semantic instance and group IDs for segmentation. It distinguishes itself from standard front-to-back ray casting by integrating precomputed occlusion samples and hierarchical group membership buffers directly into the accumulation pass, allowing for efficient occlusion-aware rendering and semantic data extraction in a single pass. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: uMvpInverseMatrix: Inverse Model-View-Projection matrix for unprojecting screen coordinates. uDepth: Current depth value for the ray. uInstanceID, uGroupID: Textures storing instance and group IDs at 2D screen positions. uIDVolume: 3D texture mapping 3D positions to instance IDs. sGroupMembership: std430 buffer mapping instance IDs to group IDs. uAccumulator: Texture storing the accumulated color, occlusion, instance ID, and group ID from previous slices. uOcclusion: Texture or buffer containing precomputed occlusion samples. uOcclusionScale: Scale factor for occlusion sample offsets. uOcclusionSamplesCount: Number of occlusion samples to average. uExtinction: Uniform float controlling the extinction coefficient multiplier. uSliceDistance: Uniform float representing the distance between slices. uColorBias, uAlphaBias, uAlphaTransfer: Parameters for transfer function biasing. Volume Color Data: Mask/data volumes and transfer functions used to sample transferSample. Outputs (Fragment Shader): oColor: vec4 containing the accumulated color and alpha. oOcclusion: float representing the remaining occlusion/transmittance. oInstanceID: uint for the current instance ID. oGroupID: uint for the current group ID. vPosition: vec2 vertex shader output representing screen position. Data Structures bGroupMembership: A std430 storage buffer (binding 0) containing uint sGroupMembership[], which maps instance IDs to group IDs. oAccColorVolume: An rgba8 image3D (binding 1), write-only, used for accumulating color across slices. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization (Reset Pass): Reset outputs to initial values: oColor = vec4(0), oOcclusion = 1.0, oInstanceID = 0u, oGroupID = 0u. 2. Unprojection: Unproject the screen position aPosition (from vertex shader) and depth uDepth to 3D world space: vPosition3D = \frac{(uMvpInverseMatrix \times vec4(aPosition, uDepth, 1)).xyz}{w} where w is the w-component of the resulting vector. 3. Boundary Check: If any component of vPosition3D is outside the [0, 1] range, output the previous color, occlusion, instance ID, and group ID (from the accumulator or previous step) and terminate the shader execution. 4. Semantic ID Resolution: Retrieve the current instance and group IDs from 2D position textures using the screen position vPosition2D: glsl uint instanceID = texture(uInstanceID, vPosition2D).r; uint groupID = texture(uGroupID, vPosition2D).r; If groupID is 0 (indicating an unassigned instance): 1. Fetch a new instance ID from uIDVolume at vPosition3D. 2. Look up the new group ID from sGroupMembership using the fetched instance ID. 3. If the new group ID is non-zero, update oInstanceID and oGroupID with these new values; otherwise, retain the old IDs. 5. Volume Sampling: Sample the volume color at vPosition3D using mask/data volumes and transfer functions, applying biases: glsl vec4 transferSample = sampleVolumeColor(vPosition3D); The sampling incorporates uColorBias, uAlphaBias, and uAlphaTransfer. 6. Accumulator Retrieval: Sample the accumulator texture at the current screen position to get previous state: glsl vec4 color = texture(uAccumulator, vPosition); Let prevColor be this value. 7. Extinction and Alpha Calculation: Calculate extinction: extinction = transferSample.a \times uExtinction Calculate alpha (opacity) for the current slice: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-extinction \times uSliceDistance) Here, uExtinction acts as the total extinction coefficient \sigmat. 8. Occlusion Calculation: Compute occlusion attenuation by averaging precomputed occlusion samples. The samples are taken at offsets from vPosition2D: O = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ci \cdot e^{-\sigmat \cdot d} where Ci are the occlusion samples, \sigmat is the extinction, d is the slice distance (uSliceDistance), and N is the number of samples (uOcclusionSamplesCount). The samples are located at vPosition2D + occlusionSampleOffset uOcclusionScale. Update oOcclusion using this calculated value. 9. Color Blending: Calculate the color contribution: color = transferSample.rgb \times prevOcclusion \times \alpha where prevOcclusion is prevColor.a (or the stored occlusion value). Update the output color: oColor = prevColor + vec4(color \times (1.0 - prevColor.a), \alpha) Clamp the alpha component: oColor.a = \min(oColor.a, 1.0) Finally, mix the accumulated color with a white background: oColor = mix(vec4(1), vec4(color.rgb, 1), color.a). 10. Output: Write oColor, oOcclusion, oInstanceID, and oGroupID to the frame buffer or accumulator texture. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dosrenderfragment(): # 1. Unproject clippos = vec4(aPosition, uDepth, 1.0) worldposvec = uMvpInverseMatrix clippos w = worldposvec.w if w == 0: return # Error or default vPosition3D = worldposvec.xyz / w # 2. Boundary Check if not all(0.0 <= vPosition3D[i] <= 1.0 for i in range(3)): # Output previous state from accumulator or previous slice prevacc = texture(uAccumulator, vPosition2D) return prevacc.rgb, prevacc.a, prevacc.b, prevacc.c # Assuming layout matches outputs # 3. Semantic ID Resolution instanceID = texture(uInstanceID, vPosition2D).r groupID = texture(uGroupID, vPosition2D).r if groupID == 0: newinstanceID = texture(uIDVolume, vPosition3D).r newgroupID = sGroupMembership[newinstanceID] if newgroupID != 0: instanceID = newinstanceID groupID = newgroupID # 4. Volume Sampling # sampleVolumeColor applies transfer functions with biases transferSample = samplevolumecolor(vPosition3D, uColorBias, uAlphaBias, uAlphaTransfer) # 5. Retrieve Accumulator prevColor = texture(uAccumulator, vPosition2D) prevOcclusion = prevColor.a # Assuming alpha stores occlusion/transmittance # 6. Extinction and Alpha extinction = transferSample.a uExtinction alpha = 1.0 - exp(-extinction uSliceDistance) # 7. Occlusion Calculation # Average occlusion samples occlusionsum = 0.0 for i in range(uOcclusionSamplesCount): offset = getocclusionsampleoffset(i, uOcclusionScale) samplepos = vPosition2D + offset Ci = texture(uOcclusion, samplepos).r occlusionsum += Ci exp(-extinction uSliceDistance) currentocclusion = occlusionsum / uOcclusionSamplesCount # 8. Color Blending colorcontribution = transferSample.rgb prevOcclusion alpha # Update color newcolor = prevColor.rgb + colorcontribution (1.0 - prevColor.a) newalpha = prevColor.a + alpha (1.0 - prevColor.a) # Standard front-to-back alpha blend # Clamp alpha newalpha = min(newalpha, 1.0) # Mix with white background finalcolor = mix(vec4(1.0), vec4(newcolor, 1.0), newalpha) # 9. Output oColor = finalcolor oOcclusion = currentocclusion oInstanceID = instanceID oGroupID = groupID Parameters steps: Number of scattering steps or depth levels. slices: Number of slices used in the rendering process. extinction: Extinction coefficient controlling light absorption/scattering intensity. aperture: Aperture size, likely controlling depth of field blur or scattering spread. samples: Number of samples used for occlusion or scattering calculations. cutDepth: Depth cutoff value, likely for clipping or limiting scattering depth. showBoundingBox: Boolean flag to render a bounding box. showAxes: Boolean flag to render coordinate axes. boundingBoxColor: RGB color array for the bounding box. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Group ID 0: A group ID of 0 indicates an unassigned instance. The shader explicitly checks for this and remaps it using the sGroupMembership buffer to prevent rendering artifacts from uninitialized group data. Out of Bounds: If the 3D position is outside the [0,1] range, the shader must correctly output the previous accumulated state to avoid discarding valid data or introducing black artifacts. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of slices (slices) and occlusion samples (uOcclusionSamplesCount) per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the accumulator texture, instance/group ID textures, and the sGroupMembership buffer. Strengths: Integrates semantic segmentation (instance/group IDs) directly into the volume rendering pass, reducing the need for separate post-processing passes. The use of precomputed occlusion samples can accelerate depth-ordering effects. Limitations: Relies on precomputed occlusion samples, which may limit dynamic occlusion scenarios. The requirement for std430 buffers and specific texture layouts may increase implementation complexity on some hardware. When to use: When semantic segmentation is required alongside volume visualization, or when occlusion-aware depth ordering is critical and can be approximated by precomputed samples. When not to use: For scenes with highly dynamic occlusion that cannot be precomputed, or when hardware does not support std430 buffers efficiently. DOSRender is described in the context of the vpt-conductor project, an unofficial implementation or toolset related to volume rendering and visualization. The technique appears to be a specialized variant of direct volume ray casting, adapted for semantic segmentation tasks by tracking instance and group IDs. UL-FRI-LGM/vpt-conductor, https://github.com/UL-FRI-LGM/vpt-conductor, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching Volume Rendering (GLSL)
head: Fragment Shader Ray Marching, GLSL Ray Marching Volume Rendering
body: This method implements direct volume rendering within a fragment shader by marching a ray through a 3D texture volume, applying alpha blending and early ray termination. It differs from Fixed Step Ray Marching by integrating the integration loop directly into the fragment shader for per-pixel execution, and from Volume Raycasting on GPU by relying on a fixed step size rather than adaptive or grid-based traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position in world space, view direction (derived from fragment position), a 3D texture (volumeTexture) containing scalar density data, model-view-projection inverse matrix, and parameters MAXSTEPS and STEPSIZE. Outputs: A vec4 fragment color with accumulated RGBA values. Data Structures: volumeTexture: A 3D texture (e.g., sampler3D in GLSL) where the red channel (r) stores density values. The texture coordinates are expected to be in the range [0, 1]. invModel: The inverse of the model matrix, used to transform the camera position into the volume's local coordinate system. Parameters: MAXSTEPS: Integer, maximum number of iterations per ray. Typical value: 256. STEPSIZE: Float, distance between samples along the ray. Typical value: 0.01. Algorithm Steps: 1. Transform Camera Position: Transform the camera position from world space to the volume's model space using the inverse model matrix. \mathbf{rayOrigin} = \mathbf{M}^{-1} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{C}{world} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Where \mathbf{C}{world} is the camera position. 2. Compute Ray Direction: Calculate the ray direction vector from the transformed origin to the fragment's position in model space. \mathbf{rayDir} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{P}{model} - \mathbf{rayOrigin}) 3. Define Bounding Box: Define the volume's bounding box in model space. The example uses a unit cube centered at the origin: \mathbf{boxMin} = (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5) \mathbf{boxMax} = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) 4. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute the intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] using the slab method. \mathbf{invDir} = \frac{1}{\mathbf{rayDir}} \mathbf{t0s} = (\mathbf{boxMin} - \mathbf{rayOrigin}) \cdot \mathbf{invDir} \mathbf{t1s} = (\mathbf{boxMax} - \mathbf{rayOrigin}) \cdot \mathbf{invDir} \mathbf{tSmaller} = \min(\mathbf{t0s}, \mathbf{t1s}) \mathbf{tLarger} = \max(\mathbf{t0s}, \mathbf{t1s}) t{min} = \max(\max(\mathbf{tSmaller}x, \mathbf{tSmaller}y), \max(\mathbf{tSmaller}z, 0.0)) t{max} = \min(\min(\mathbf{tLarger}x, \mathbf{tLarger}y), \mathbf{tLarger}z) 5. Check Intersection: If t{min} \ge t{max}, the ray misses the volume. Discard the fragment. 6. Initialize Accumulators: Set the current ray parameter t = t{min} and initialize the accumulated color to transparent black: \mathbf{accumulatedColor} = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) 7. Marching Loop: Iterate up to MAXSTEPS times while t < t{max}: a. Sample Position: Compute the 3D position in model space: \mathbf{pos} = \mathbf{rayOrigin} + t \cdot \mathbf{rayDir} b. Sample Density: Sample the density from the volume texture. An offset of +0.5 is applied to map the model space coordinates (centered at 0) to texture coordinates (centered at 0.5): \text{density} = \text{texture}(\text{volumeTexture}, \mathbf{pos} + (0.5, 0.5, 0.5)).r c. Map to Color: Convert density to a color sample. The example uses a simple grayscale mapping where color equals density: \mathbf{colorSample} = (\text{density}, \text{density}, \text{density}, \text{density}) d. Front-to-Back Blending: Accumulate the color using standard front-to-back alpha compositing: \mathbf{accumulatedColor}.rgb += (1.0 - \mathbf{accumulatedColor}.a) \cdot \mathbf{colorSample}.rgb \cdot \mathbf{colorSample}.a \mathbf{accumulatedColor}.a += (1.0 - \mathbf{accumulatedColor}.a) \cdot \mathbf{colorSample}.a e. Early Termination: If \mathbf{accumulatedColor}.a \ge 0.95, break the loop. f. Advance Ray: Increment t by STEPSIZE: t = t + \text{STEP\SIZE} 8. Final Output: After the loop, if the final fragment alpha is negligible (\le 0.001), discard the fragment. Otherwise, output accumulatedColor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. rayOrigin = invModel vec4(cameraPos, 1.0) rayOrigin = rayOrigin.xyz rayDir = normalize(vPosition - rayOrigin) boxMin = vec3(-0.5) boxMax = vec3(0.5) invDir = 1.0 / rayDir t0s = (boxMin - rayOrigin) invDir t1s = (boxMax - rayOrigin) invDir tSmaller = min(t0s, t1s) tLarger = max(t0s, t1s) tMin = max(max(tSmaller.x, tSmaller.y), max(tSmaller.z, 0.0)) tMax = min(min(tLarger.x, tLarger.y), tLarger.z) if tMin >= tMax: discard t = tMin accumulatedColor = vec4(0.0) for i in range(MAXSTEPS): if t >= tMax: break # a. Sample position pos = rayOrigin + t rayDir # b. Sample density (offset +0.5 for texture coordinates) density = texture(volumeTexture, pos + vec3(0.5)).r # c. Map density to color colorSample = vec4(density) # d. Front-to-back blending accumulatedColor.rgb += (1.0 - accumulatedColor.a) colorSample.rgb colorSample.a accumulatedColor.a += (1.0 - accumulatedColor.a) colorSample.a # e. Early termination if accumulatedColor.a >= 0.95: break # f. Advance ray t += STEPSIZE if accumulatedColor.a <= 0.001: discard return accumulatedColor The compositing strategy used in the accumulation step. Choose when opacity is the primary visual cue. The underlying traversal technique. Choose when uniform sampling is sufficient and adaptive steps are too complex. A broader category of GPU-based volume rendering. Choose this when comparing shader-based approaches to compute-shader or voxel-based approaches. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of pixels (fragments) and P is the number of steps per ray (bounded by MAXSTEPS). Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the size of the 3D texture volume. The shader state is constant per fragment. Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on MAXSTEPS and STEPSIZE. A fixed step size of 0.01 with 256 steps results in a maximum path length of 2.56 units. If the volume is smaller than this, many steps are wasted. Early ray termination at 0.95 alpha can significantly reduce average step counts for opaque regions. Strengths: Simple to implement in a fragment shader; leverages hardware texture sampling; early termination provides optimization. Limitations: Fixed step size leads to aliasing if steps are too large or wasted computation if steps are too small; no adaptive traversal based on density gradients; limited to the resolution of the 3D texture. When to use: Real-time rendering of simple volumes where high fidelity is not critical, or as a baseline implementation. When not to use: High-quality offline rendering, volumes with high dynamic range density, or scenes requiring adaptive sampling. This method is a standard implementation of direct volume rendering in real-time graphics, often found in educational resources and hobbyist projects. The specific implementation details (unit cube, offset +0.5, fixed parameters) are derived from the HNanoSolver project. It builds on the general principles of ray casting and front-to-back compositing described in Front-to-Back Volume Rendering. name: Light Transmittance Marching
head: Light Marching, Light Transmissance March, Nested Light Ray Sampling, Nested Raymarching for Light Sampling, Secondary light march, Shadow Raymarching in Volume
body: Light Transmittance Marching is a technique to compute physically accurate lighting in a volume by casting a secondary raymarch from each sample point on the primary view ray towards the light source to calculate absorbed light (transmittance). It solves the problem of volumetric occlusion, where light passing through the volume before reaching a sample point is attenuated by the medium itself. Unlike Front-to-Back Volume Rendering, which typically assumes uniform or pre-computed lighting, this method dynamically computes the light energy arriving at each sample point by accounting for the density along the path to the light. Inputs: rayOrigin: The camera position. rayDirection: The normalized direction of the primary view ray. lightDirection: The normalized direction vector from the scene to the light source (e.g., the sun). scene(pos, isLightSample): A function that returns the density at position pos. The boolean flag distinguishes between primary ray sampling and light sampling, allowing for different density evaluation strategies or optimizations. MAXSTEPS: The number of steps in the primary raymarch loop. MAXSTEPSLIGHTS: The number of steps in the nested light sampling loop. MARCHSIZE: The step size for the primary raymarch. marchSize (or stepSize): The step size for the nested light sampling loop. ABSORPTIONCOEFFICIENT: The coefficient used in Beer's Law for light absorption. Outputs: lightEnergy: The accumulated luminance for the pixel, incorporating the attenuated light contribution from each sample point along the primary ray. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar variables for position, density, and accumulated energy. The method relies on iterative sampling of the scene function. Parameters: MAXSTEPSLIGHTS: Set to 6 to preserve frame-rate. ABSORPTIONCOEFFICIENT: Set to 0.9. marchSize (light step): Set to 0.03. MAXSTEPS: Set to 50. MARCHSIZE (primary step): Set to 0.16. Steps: 1. Initialize the primary raymarch loop. For each step i from 0 to MAXSTEPS - 1: a. Calculate the current position p along the primary ray: p = rayOrigin + (rayOrigin + depth \cdot rayDirection) where depth accumulates MARCHSIZE at each step. b. Sample the density at p using the primary scene function: density = scene(p, false) c. If density > 0.0: i. Initiate a nested light sampling loop to calculate light transmittance. ii. Initialize totalDensity = 0.0 and position = p. iii. For each step j from 0 to MAXSTEPSLIGHTS - 1: 1. Advance the position along the light direction: position = position + lightDirection \cdot marchSize \cdot j. 2. Sample the density at the new position using the light-specific scene function: lightSample = scene(position, true). 3. Accumulate the density: totalDensity = totalDensity + lightSample. Note: An alternative implementation accumulates density weighted by step size: totalDensity += density stepSize where stepSize = MAXLIGHTDISTANCE / NUMLIGHTSTEPS. iv. Calculate the light transmittance using Beer's Law: transmittance = e^{-ABSORPTION\COEFFICIENT \cdot totalDensity}. Note: Some implementations use exp(-totalDensity) directly if the absorption coefficient is incorporated into the density or step size. v. Multiply the primary ray's accumulated transmittance by the light transmittance: totalTransmittance = totalTransmittance \cdot transmittance. vi. Calculate the luminance contribution: luminance = density. vii. Add to the total light energy: lightEnergy = lightEnergy + totalTransmittance \cdot luminance. d. Advance the primary ray depth: depth = depth + MARCHSIZE. 2. Return lightEnergy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lighttransmittancemarch(rayorigin, raydirection, lightdirection, scenefunc, maxsteps=50, maxstepslights=6, marchsize=0.16, lightmarchsize=0.03, absorptioncoefficient=0.9): """ Computes light energy for a single ray using nested light transmittance marching. Args: rayorigin: vec3, camera position. raydirection: vec3, normalized view ray direction. lightdirection: vec3, normalized direction to the light source. scenefunc: function(pos, islightsample) -> float, returns density. maxsteps: int, number of steps in primary raymarch. maxstepslights: int, number of steps in nested light march. marchsize: float, step size for primary raymarch. lightmarchsize: float, step size for light march. absorptioncoefficient: float, Beer's law coefficient. Returns: float, accumulated light energy. """ lightenergy = 0.0 totaltransmittance = 1.0 depth = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): # Calculate current position on primary ray p = rayorigin + (rayorigin + depth raydirection) # Note: Source uses 'rayOrigin + depth rayDirection' but initializes depth with offset. # Correcting based on logic: p = rayOrigin + depth rayDirection where depth starts at MARCHSIZE offset. # Simplified standard march: p = rayorigin + depth raydirection # Sample density for primary ray density = scenefunc(p, False) if density > 0.0: # Nested light march totaldensitylight = 0.0 lightpos = p for j in range(maxstepslights): # Advance position along light direction lightpos = lightpos + lightdirection lightmarchsize j # Sample density for light path lightsample = scenefunc(lightpos, True) totaldensitylight += lightsample # Calculate transmittance using Beer's Law # transmittance = exp(-absorptioncoefficient totaldensitylight) # Source defines BeersLaw(totalDensity, ABSORPTIONCOEFFICIENT) transmittance = math.exp(-absorptioncoefficient totaldensitylight) # Update total transmittance for the primary ray totaltransmittance = transmittance # Accumulate light energy luminance = density lightenergy += totaltransmittance luminance # Advance primary ray depth += marchsize return lightenergy Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The nested loop significantly increases algorithmic complexity. To maintain frame-rate, MAXSTEPSLIGHTS must be kept low (e.g., 6). This may require reducing the precision of the primary raymarch (e.g., reducing FBM octaves). Precision: Using a small marchSize for the light march (0.03) helps accuracy but increases the number of samples if MAXSTEPSLIGHTS is not adjusted. Boundary Conditions: The light march assumes the light source is at infinity or the direction is constant. If the light source is point-based and close, the direction lightDirection should be recalculated for each sample point, which is not covered in the basic implementation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of steps in the primary raymarch and M is the number of steps in the nested light march. This is significantly slower than non-lit volume rendering (O(N)). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as it only requires scalar variables for accumulation. It does not require additional data structures beyond the scene function's internal storage. Measured Performance: With MAXSTEPS=50 and MAXSTEPSLIGHTS=6, the method is feasible for real-time rendering on modern GPUs, provided the scene function is efficient. Strengths: Physically accurate lighting attenuation within the volume; simple to implement as a nested loop. Limitations: High computational cost due to nested sampling; assumes uniform light direction (directional light); does not account for scattering within the volume, only absorption. When to Use: When directional lighting and volumetric occlusion are required for real-time applications, and performance constraints allow for nested sampling. When Not to Use: When point lights or complex scattering are required, or when performance is critical and approximate lighting is acceptable. Light Transmittance Marching was introduced in the context of real-time volumetric cloud rendering to address the lack of proper lighting models in early raymarching demos. It builds on the concept of Beer's Law for light absorption in participating media. The technique is commonly used in real-time graphics for clouds and fog, where dynamic lighting interaction is desired without the cost of full path tracing. name: Volume Raycasting on GPU
head: GPU-Based Raycasting, GPU-accelerated raycasting, Multi-pass Volume Raycasting, Stream model raycasting, fragment program raycasting
body: Volume Raycasting on GPU is a direct volume rendering (DVR) strategy that exploits the programmable parallelism of modern graphics processing units (GPUs) to generate and trace a single ray per screen pixel through a 3D volume dataset. Unlike fixed-pipeline Texture Mapping (TM) methods, which apply shading to every fragment regardless of contribution and suffer from striping artifacts under perspective projection due to uniform sampling steps, GPU raycasting encodes the rendering pipeline in fragment shaders, enabling adaptive sampling, early ray termination, and empty space skipping. It builds on Ray Marching and Discretization by implementing the ray traversal and compositing logic directly within the GPU's fragment processing stage. The method typically employs a multi-pass algorithm where initial passes precompute ray geometry, and subsequent passes perform parallel raymarching for each pixel. The core implementation involves storing the volume dataset as a 3D texture mapped to a colored unit cube bounding box. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D texture containing the volume scalar field; camera parameters (origin, view direction, projection); transfer function (TF) mapping scalar values to color and opacity; and a preset opacity threshold for early termination. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity of the ray traversing the volume. Data Structures: 1. 3D Texture: Stores the volume data. The bounding box is treated as a unit cube. The texture coordinates at the eight corners of this cube are encoded in the RGB color channels of a 2D texture representing the cube's faces. 2. Direction Vector Texture (2D): Stores the normalized direction vectors for the casting ray for each pixel. This is derived by subtracting the color values of the back face of the bounding cube from the front face and normalizing the result. 3. Intermediate Framebuffer/Texture: Used in multi-pass implementations to store accumulated color and opacity between raymarching steps, allowing for early termination checks. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Direction and Origin Computation: Render the front face of the colored unit cube bounding box into an intermediate texture. Render the back face of the colored unit cube bounding box into another intermediate texture. For each pixel, subtract the RGB color values of the back face from the front face. Normalize the resulting vector to obtain the ray direction v. The ray origin O is defined as the pixel position on the front face of the bounding cube. Store the normalized direction vectors in a 2D texture DIR[x][y]. 2. Raymarching Loop (Fragment Shader): For each pixel, retrieve the ray origin O and direction v (or DIR[x][y]). Initialize accumulated color C{acc} = (0,0,0,0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. Define a parametric ray equation: r(t) = O + v \times t, where t is the distance along the ray. Alternatively, using the texture coordinate formulation: r = P + d \cdot DIR[x][y], where P is the per-vertex position of the front face, d is the total raymarched distance, and r represents the 3D texture coordinates used to sample voxel data. Uniformly sample the volume along the ray. In a single-pass implementation, this is done using GPU Shader Model 3.0 loop capabilities. In a multi-pass implementation, the full raymarch is split into chunks (e.g., M steps per pass). At each sampling point r: Sample the 3D texture to get the scalar value s. Apply the Transfer Function (TF) to map s to color c and opacity \alpha. Perform front-to-back blending: C{acc} = C{acc} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) Termination Check: Terminate the ray if: The ray leaves the volume bounding box. The accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} exceeds a preset threshold. (In multi-pass) The accumulated opacity in the intermediate texture exceeds the threshold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fragmentshader(pixelcoords): # 1. Get Ray Geometry # Ray direction from the precomputed texture v = DIR[pixelcoords.x][pixelcoords.y] # Ray origin is the interpolated position of the front face of the bounding box O = FRONTFACEPOS # 2. Initialize Accumulators acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 # 3. Raymarching Loop # Determine total steps or use a loop with early exit # Note: In a real GPU shader, this might be a fixed loop or split across passes t = 0.0 while t < MAXDISTANCE: # Calculate current 3D texture coordinate # r = O + v t r = O + v t # Check if r is within the volume bounds [0,1]^3 if not isinsidevolume(r): break # Sample volume data scalarvalue = sample3dtexture(VOL, r) # Map to color and opacity color, opacity = TF(scalarvalue) # Front-to-back blending # Cnew = Cold + c alpha (1 - alphaold) # alphanew = alphaold + alpha (1 - alphaold) contribution = color opacity (1.0 - accopacity) acccolor = acccolor + contribution accopacity = accopacity + opacity (1.0 - accopacity) # Early termination check if accopacity >= THRESHOLD: break # Advance along ray t = t + STEPSIZE return acccolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Projection: Fixed-pipeline TM methods suffer from striping artifacts because uniform sampling steps in screen space do not correspond to uniform steps in world space under perspective projection. GPU raycasting handles this via adaptive sampling steps or by computing ray directions per pixel, maintaining uniformity in world space. Memory Bandwidth: Multi-pass implementations require storing intermediate results in temporary framebuffers, which can suffer from low efficiency due to bus bandwidth and latency between CPU and GPU. Precision: The encoding of texture coordinates in RGB channels for direction computation requires careful normalization to avoid precision errors in the direction vector. A raycasting framework that avoids multiple rendering passes (casting rays and storing intermediate results in temporary framebuffers) to address the low efficiency of multi-pass pipelines on current graphics hardware architectures. Compared with multi-pass rendering, single-pass solutions offer advantages in efficiency, accuracy, and flexibility. It has been extended by Stegmaier and colleagues for spectral DVR using the Kubelka–Munk theory and by Hadwiger et al. to display implicit isosurfaces from volumes on rectilinear 3D grids using hierarchical grid representations for empty space skipping. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampling steps per ray and the number of pixels. Adaptive sampling and early termination reduce the average number of steps per ray. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the 3D volume texture and the intermediate framebuffers (in multi-pass implementations). Measured Performance: Used for real-time display of fused multimodal brain datasets for neurosurgical planning and other medical imaging applications. Performance is limited by GPU memory bandwidth and the cost of 3D texture sampling. Strengths: Flexible pipeline allowing for acceleration techniques like early ray termination and empty space skipping; fragment-based shading applies computation only to contributing fragments; adaptive sampling improves image quality under perspective projection. Limitations: Multi-pass versions suffer from framebuffer read/write overhead; single-pass versions may have limited flexibility for complex acceleration structures compared to CPU-based methods. When to use: Real-time visualization of large 3D datasets, particularly in medical imaging where interactive frame rates are required. When not to use: When the volume data exceeds available GPU texture memory and efficient out-of-core streaming is not implemented; when complex light transport effects beyond simple absorption and emission are required without significant shader complexity. The general strategy of exploiting programmable GPUs for raycasting was proposed by Krüger and Westermann, and Purcell et al., who described a stream model exploiting the intrinsic parallelism and efficient communication on modern GPUs. The original GPU-based solutions were based on multiple rendering passes. Later, Stegmaier and colleagues developed single-pass frameworks to improve efficiency. The method is widely used in medical imaging, including neurosurgical planning, thoracic CT segmentation, coronary artery disease diagnosis, virtual autopsy, lung cancer screening, virtual endoscopy, and 4D cardiac dataset visualization. name: Piecewise Linear Opacity Mapping with Gradient Scaling
head: Gradient-scaled opacity mapping, Gradient-scaled piecewise linear opacity, Surface-enhanced volume rendering
body:
This method maps voxel scalar values to opacity using piecewise linear functions defined by tissue types, then scales the resulting opacity by the magnitude of the local gradient vector to suppress tissue interiors and enhance bounding surfaces. It differs from binary classification techniques by mapping all voxels to non-zero opacity, thereby rendering thin, wispy structures that would otherwise appear as holes, and by using gradient scaling to create semi-transparent surface overlays rather than solid opaque surfaces. Inputs: Scalar volume data f(xi) for voxels at positions xi. N tissue types, where N \ge 1. For each tissue type n \in \{1, \dots, N\}: Known CT number (scalar value) fvn. Target opacity \alpha{vn} assigned to tissue type n at fvn. The tissue types must be ordered such that fv1 < fv2 < \dots < fvN. Outputs: Opacity \alpha(xi) for each voxel xi. Data Structures: The source assumes a 3D grid of voxels. Gradient magnitudes |
abla f(xi)| are pre-computed and stored for all voxels to allow efficient lookup table generation. If gradient magnitudes are not pre-stored, they must be computed per voxel. Adjacency Criteria: The method requires that the scene meets specific adjacency criteria to ensure unambiguous classification: 1. Tissues of each type touch tissues of at most two other types. 2. If tissue types are ordered by CT number, each type touches only types adjacent to it in the ordering. 3. Formally, no tissue of CT number fvn touches any tissue of CT number fvm where |n - m| > 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Gradient Calculation: Compute the local gradient vector 
abla f(xi) for each voxel xi and its magnitude |
abla f(xi)|. The source references an operator described in Section 3 of the original document for this approximation. [G: Standard central difference or Sobel operators are typically used for gradient estimation in discrete volumes]. 2. Interval Determination: For each voxel xi with value f(xi), determine which tissue interval [fvn, fv{n+1}] the value falls into. If fvn \le f(xi) \le fv{n+1} for some n \in \{1, \dots, N-1\}, proceed to Step 3. If f(xi) is outside all defined intervals (i.e., f(xi) < fv1 or f(xi) > fvN), set \alpha(xi) = 0. [G: Values exactly equal to fvN may be handled by extending the last interval or clamping; the source implies N types define N-1 intervals, but typically the last type's opacity is applied for values \ge fvN. The source formula explicitly covers n=1 \dots N-1. For f(xi) > fvN, the source implies 0 or undefined behavior in the explicit formula, but standard practice often clamps. However, the source text says "otherwise... 0" in the explicit formula block in S2. We follow S2 strictly: if not in [fvn, fv{n+1}], opacity is 0]. 3. Linear Interpolation: Calculate the linear interpolation weight and base opacity. Compute the normalized position of f(xi) within the interval [fvn, fv{n+1}]: w =  rac{f(xi) - fvn}{fv{n+1} - fvn} Interpolate the base opacity between \alpha{vn} and \alpha{vn+1}: \alpha{base}(xi) = (1 - w) \alpha{vn} + w \alpha{vn+1} \alpha{base}(xi) = \alpha{vn} +  rac{f(xi) - fvn}{fv{n+1} - fvn} (\alpha{vn+1} - \alpha{vn}) 4. Gradient Scaling: Multiply the base opacity by the gradient magnitude to suppress interiors and enhance surfaces: \alpha(xi) = |
abla f(xi)| \cdot \alpha{base}(xi) \alpha(xi) = |
abla f(xi)| \left( \alpha{vn} +  rac{f(xi) - fvn}{fv{n+1} - fvn} (\alpha{vn+1} - \alpha{vn}) ight) for fvn \le f(xi) \le fv{n+1}. 5. Final Opacity: The resulting \alpha(xi) is the final opacity for the voxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeopacitygradientscaled(fvoxel, fvvalues, alphavvalues, gradientmagnitude): """ Computes opacity for a single voxel using piecewise linear mapping scaled by gradient. Args: fvoxel (float): Scalar value of the voxel f(xi). fvvalues (list[float]): Ordered CT numbers [fv1, fv2,..., fvN]. alphavvalues (list[float]): Target opacities [alphav1, alphav2,..., alphavN]. gradientmagnitude (float): |grad f(xi)|. Returns: float: Opacity alpha(xi). """ N = len(fvvalues) # Check if value is within any interval [fvn, fv{n+1}] for n in range(N - 1): fvn = fvvalues[n] fvn1 = fvvalues[n + 1] if fvn <= fvoxel <= fvn1: alphavn = alphavvalues[n] alphavn1 = alphavvalues[n + 1] # Linear interpolation weight # Note: If fvn == fvn1, this would be division by zero. # Sources assume distinct fv values for ordering. weight = (fvoxel - fvn) / (fvn1 - fvn) # Base opacity interpolation alphabase = alphavn + weight (alphavn1 - alphavn) # Gradient scaling alpha = gradientmagnitude alphabase return alpha # If fvoxel is outside all defined intervals [fv1, fvN] return 0.0 Parameters and Typical Values: N: Number of tissue types. In the medical imaging study, N was sufficient to define air-skin and tissue-bone interfaces. fvn: Known CT numbers. In the molecular graphics study, these corresponded to electron density values for atoms. \alpha{vn}: Target opacities. These are user-defined or derived from tissue properties. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Adjacency Violation: If tissue types do not touch only adjacent types in the ordered CT number list, voxels at boundaries cannot be unambiguously classified, leading to incorrect rendering. Thin Features: Binary thresholds may miss thin features of a tissue type if voxel values fall below the threshold. This method avoids that by mapping all voxels to non-zero opacity (within the defined range), rendering thin regions as faint wisps. Gradient Constancy: The thickness of the transition region around isosurface contours remains constant only if the local gradient magnitude is constant within a radius of r voxels around each point on the surface. Anisotropy and Motion: CT scanners have anisotropic spatial sensitivity, causing striping artifacts. Patient motion also causes striping because shading depends on gradient orientation, and misalignments between adjacent slices disrupt this. Non-Adjacency Handling: For datasets not meeting adjacency criteria (e.g., internal soft tissue organs), users can interactively clip or carve away unwanted tissues to isolate subsets that meet the criteria. Image Quality Improvements: Blurring: Apply slight blurring to the opacities generated by the classification procedure to soften silhouettes without affecting surface detail crispness. Super-sampling: Interpolate additional samples between acquired ones prior to compositing to improve visibility calculation accuracy and reduce aliasing. Aliasing Reduction: Non-binary classification decisions carry 3-D bandlimiting into the 2-D projection, reducing aliasing artifacts from point sampling (one ray per pixel). Rendering Optimizations: Pre-computation: Pre-compute colors and opacities and store them in intermediate 3-D datasets to simplify image generation to geometric transformation of two values per voxel and compositing. Rotation Sequence: To produce a rotation sequence efficiently, hold colors and opacities constant and alter only the direction in which rays are cast. Note that fixing shading causes light sources to appear to travel with the data. Aspect Ratio Correction: For high-resolution datasets (512x512), cast 4 rays per slice in the vertical direction to correct for aspect ratio. Interpolation Expansion: Expand the dataset using cubic B-spline interpolation in the vertical direction, then cast one ray per slice to improve detail. Extensions: Interstitial Volumes: Render interstitial volumes as semi-transparent gels by adding color and texture representing variables like gradient magnitude or anatomical tissue type. Geometric Merging: Superimpose geometric models (e.g., ball-and-stick models) onto volume data by performing a true 3-D merge, either by scan-converting geometry into the sampled array or incorporating classical ray tracing of geometry into the volume rendering pipeline. Multiple Visualizations: Perform a true 3-D merge of two or more visualizations (e.g., radiation treatment planning isodose surfaces over CT data). Segmentation Integration: Combine volume rendering with high-level object definition/segmentation algorithms. Use initial visualizations to guide segmentation, then use segmentation output (potentially with confidence levels/probabilities) to modulate opacity. Time and Memory Complexity: Opacity Computation: One lookup table reference per voxel if gradient magnitudes are pre-stored. New lookup table generation is required if classification parameters change. Ray Tracing/Compositing: For a square image of n pixels with orthographic projection and K sample locations along each ray, the cost is 3Kn^2 additions, 2Kn^2 tri-linear interpolations, and Kn^2 linear interpolations. Measured Performance: Molecular Graphics (Cytochrome B5, 113x113x113 voxels): Classification/shading took 5 minutes on a SUN 4/280 with 32MB RAM. Ray tracing/compositing took 40 minutes. Medical Imaging (CT Cadaver, 113 slices of 256x256): Computation of each set of colors/opacities took 20 minutes. Each view/compositing took an additional 20 minutes. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Renders thin, wispy surfaces instead of holes for regions not meeting strict adjacency or threshold criteria. Suppresses tissue interiors while enhancing bounding surfaces. Carries 3-D bandlimiting into 2-D projection, reducing aliasing. Limitations: Requires adjacency criteria to be met for unambiguous classification. Sensitive to acquisition artifacts (striping from anisotropy or motion). Blurring opacities softens silhouettes but may reduce sharpness. Super-sampling substantially increases computational expense. When to Use: When visualizing surfaces from volume data where thin structures are important. When semi-transparent surface overlays (e.g., skin and bone) are desired. When the data meets the adjacency criteria or can be pre-processed to meet them. When Not to Use: When the data contains non-adjacent tissue types that cannot be clipped or segmented out. When high-fidelity geometric precision is required without the "faint wisp" appearance of thin structures. When computational resources are severely limited and pre-computation of gradients is not feasible. Origin: The method was introduced by William M. Wooding and others in the late 1980s. The primary source is a paper titled "Display of Surfaces from Volume Data" (CGA 1988) and a related DTIC report "Rendering of Surfaces from Volume Data" (ADA193649). History and Development: The technique was applied to molecular graphics (Cytochrome B5 electron density map) and medical imaging (CT cadaver study) to demonstrate its effectiveness in displaying surfaces from sampled scalar functions of three dimensions. It was developed as an alternative to techniques relying on geometric primitives, aiming to generate images with approximately equivalent resolution but fewer interpretation errors. Usage: Used in molecular graphics and medical imaging studies. It is particularly suited for visualizing anatomical scenes with distinct tissue types that satisfy the adjacency criteria.
