name: Volume Raycasting Output Generation
head: Final Compositing and Output, RenderOutput Construction
body: This method constructs the final pixel output from a sampled volume value, handling color space conversion, opacity modulation, and depth calculation. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly managing the transition from sampled data to physical colorspace for compositing and computing depth via perspective division of NDC coordinates rather than using raw Z values. Inputs: thecoord: Texture coordinate of the sample. thevalue: Sampled volume value (vec4<f32>). sizef: Volume dimensions (vec3<f32>). uwobject.worldtransform: World transformation matrix. ustdinfo.projectiontransform: Projection matrix. ustdinfo.camtransform: Camera transformation matrix. umaterial.opacity: Material opacity scalar. colorspace: String, either 'srgb' or other. Outputs: RenderOutput struct containing: color: vec4<f32> (RGBA). coord: vec3<f32> (texture coordinate). depth: f32 (NDC depth). Data Structures: RenderOutput: color: vec4<f32> coord: vec3<f32> depth: f32 Steps: 1. Colormapping: Convert thevalue to color using sampledvaluetocolor(thevalue). Let this be color. 2. Colorspace Conversion: If colorspace == 'srgb', convert color.rgb to physical colorspace: physicalcolor = srgb2physical(color.rgb). Otherwise, physicalcolor = color.rgb. 3. Opacity Calculation: Compute opacity = color.a umaterial.opacity. 4. Output Color Construction: outcolor = vec4<f32>(physicalcolor, opacity). 5. Position Calculation: datapos = thecoord sizef - vec3<f32>(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) worldpos = uwobject.worldtransform vec4<f32>(datapos, 1.0) ndcpos = ustdinfo.projectiontransform ustdinfo.camtransform worldpos 6. Depth Calculation: depth = ndcpos.z / ndcpos.w 7. Output Construction: out.color = outcolor out.coord = thecoord out.depth = depth Return out. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeraycastingoutputgeneration( thecoord: Vec3, thevalue: Vec4, sizef: Vec3, uwobjectworldtransform: Mat4, ustdinfoprojectiontransform: Mat4, ustdinfocamtransform: Mat4, umaterialopacity: float, colorspace: str) -> RenderOutput: # Step 1: Colormapping color = sampledvaluetocolor(thevalue) # Step 2: Colorspace Conversion if colorspace == 'srgb': physicalcolor = srgb2physical(color.rgb) else: physicalcolor = color.rgb # Step 3: Opacity Calculation opacity = color.a umaterialopacity # Step 4: Output Color Construction outcolor = Vec4(physicalcolor.x, physicalcolor.y, physicalcolor.z, opacity) # Step 5: Position Calculation datapos = thecoord sizef - Vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) worldpos = uwobjectworldtransform Vec4(datapos.x, datapos.y, datapos.z, 1.0) ndcpos = ustdinfoprojectiontransform ustdinfocamtransform worldpos # Step 6: Depth Calculation depth = ndcpos.z / ndcpos.w # Step 7: Output Construction out = RenderOutput() out.color = outcolor out.coord = thecoord out.depth = depth return out Parameters: umaterial.opacity: Material property modulating opacity. colorspace: String determining sRGB conversion. Edge Cases: Division by zero in depth calculation if ndcpos.w is zero. Invalid colorspace string handling. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. Strengths: Explicit handling of color space and depth ensures accurate compositing. Limitations: Requires access to transformation matrices and material properties. This method is part of the volume raycasting pipeline in pygfx, specifically handling the final output generation after sampling and colormapping. https://github.com/pygfx/pygfx/blob/main/pygfx/renderers/wgpu/wgsl/volumeray.wgsl, https://github.com/pygfx/pygfx/blob/main/pygfx/renderers/wgpu/wgsl/volumeray.wgsl, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Density Adaptation
head: On-the-fly coarse sampling
body: Hierarchical Density Adaptation is a sampling strategy for direct volume ray casting that generates a coarse density estimate from a dense feature grid on the fly to guide importance sampling for fine samples. It solves the problem of missing thin or high-frequency surface details when sampling directly from a dense grid, which can occur if coarse sample points fall between grid cells containing significant geometry. Unlike sibling methods that maintain a dedicated, pre-computed coarse grid or train a separate coarse network, this method derives the coarse density by convolving the existing dense density grid with a non-learnable kernel, thereby avoiding additional memory allocation for coarse structures while ensuring robust surface detection. The method operates in two stages: coarse sampling to estimate density distribution, and fine sampling to render color. It relies on a dense density feature grid G\sigma and a dense appearance feature grid Ga. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Dense density grid G\sigma, dense appearance grid Ga, camera ray origin o, ray direction \mathbf{d}, number of coarse samples Nc, number of fine samples Nf. Output: Pixel color \hat{C}. Data Structures: G\sigma: A 3D grid storing volume density values \sigma. In the primary implementation (EgoNeRF), this is a balanced spherical grid where resolution increases exponentially along the radial direction. K: A non-learnable convolution kernel, specifically an average pooling kernel. Steps: 1. On-the-fly Coarse Density Estimation: To prevent skipping important surface regions, the density at coarse sample locations is not read directly from G\sigma. Instead, it is computed by convolving G\sigma with kernel K. \sigma(\mathbf{x}{\text{coarse}}) = \mathcal{T}(K G\sigma, \mathbf{x}{\text{coarse}}) where \mathcal{T} denotes trilinear (or appropriate spherical) interpolation. The kernel K acts as an average pooling operation, smoothing the density field to capture broader geometric extents. 2. Coarse Sampling: Sample Nc points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. In the standard spherical grid implementation, these samples are distributed exponentially along the ray rather than uniformly, to match the exponential increase in grid resolution along the radial direction. Let \deltai be the distance between consecutive coarse samples. 3. Weight Calculation: Calculate importance sampling weights wi for each coarse sample based on the estimated density \sigmai = \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) and accumulated transmittance \taui: wi = \taui (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) where the accumulated transmittance is: \taui = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj} with \tau1 = 1. 4. Fine Sampling: Sample Nf fine points from the probability distribution defined by the normalized weights wi. These points are used to query the dense grids for precise density and color. 5. Rendering: Render the pixel using the combined set of N = Nc + Nf samples. The color is computed via volume rendering integration: \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \taui (1 - e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i)\deltai}) c(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}) + \tau{N+1} c{\text{env}}(\mathbf{d}) where c(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}) is the color obtained from the appearance grid Ga and an optional decoding MLP, and c{\text{env}}(\mathbf{d}) is the environment map color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicaldensityadaptation(rayorigin, raydirection, Gsigma, Gappearance, Nc, Nf, kernelK, envmap=None): """ Renders a single ray using Hierarchical Density Adaptation. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (o) raydirection: 3D vector (d) Gsigma: Dense density grid object with method queryandsmooth(x, kernel) Gappearance: Dense appearance grid object with method query(x, d) Nc: Number of coarse samples Nf: Number of fine samples kernelK: Convolution kernel (average pooling) envmap: Optional environment map function cenv(d) Returns: pixelcolor: Scalar or RGB vector """ # Step 1 & 2: Coarse Sampling and Density Estimation # In spherical grids, samples are distributed exponentially along the ray coarsepoints = [] coarsedensities = [] coarsetransmittances = [] currenttransmittance = 1.0 # Determine step sizes based on exponential distribution logic specific to the grid # [G: Assuming a helper function exponentialraysamples exists for the specific grid topology] distances = exponentialraysamples(rayorigin, raydirection, Nc) for i, dist in enumerate(distances): xcoarse = rayorigin + dist raydirection # On-the-fly coarse density: Convolve dense grid with kernel K # This avoids skipping thin surfaces present in Gsigma sigmacoarse = Gsigma.queryandsmooth(xcoarse, kernelK) coarsepoints.append(xcoarse) coarsedensities.append(sigmacoarse) coarsetransmittances.append(currenttransmittance) # Update transmittance for next step # deltai is the distance to the next sample. # For the last sample, delta is effectively infinite or handled by termination if i < len(distances) - 1: deltai = distances[i+1] - dist else: deltai = 0.0 # Or a large value if ray continues, but weight becomes 0 if transmittance is 0 currenttransmittance = math.exp(-sigmacoarse deltai) # Step 3: Calculate Importance Sampling Weights weights = [] for i in range(Nc): sigmai = coarsedensities[i] taui = coarsetransmittances[i] # Delta for the segment covered by this sample if i < Nc - 1: deltai = distances[i+1] - distances[i] else: # For the last coarse sample, we need a delta to compute weight for fine sampling # The source defines wi = taui (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) # We assume a standard segment length or infinite for the tail deltai = distances[i] - distances[i-1] if i > 0 else 1.0 wi = taui (1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai deltai)) weights.append(wi) # Normalize weights for probability distribution totalweight = sum(weights) if totalweight > 0: probs = [w / totalweight for w in weights] else: probs = [1.0 / Nc] Nc # Step 4: Fine Sampling # Sample Nf points based on the probability distribution of coarse segments finepoints = [] # [G: Implementation of sampling from discrete distribution defined by probs] # For each fine sample, pick a coarse segment index k with probability probs[k], # then sample a point uniformly within that segment's distance range. finepoints = samplefromdistribution(probs, distances, Nf) # Combine coarse and fine points allpoints = coarsepoints + finepoints # Step 5: Rendering # Sort all points by distance from origin allpoints.sort(key=lambda p: distance(rayorigin, p)) pixelcolor = 0.0 accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for i, x in enumerate(allpoints): # Query dense grids for precise values sigma = Gsigma.query(x) color = Gappearance.query(x, raydirection) # Determine delta for this sample if i < len(allpoints) - 1: delta = distance(allpoints[i], allpoints[i+1]) else: delta = 0.0 # Or handle tail separately # Volume rendering contribution weight = accumulatedtransmittance (1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta)) pixelcolor += weight color accumulatedtransmittance = math.exp(-sigma delta) # Add environment map contribution if available if envmap is not None: pixelcolor += accumulatedtransmittance envmap(raydirection) return pixelcolor Parameters: Nc: Number of coarse samples along the ray. Nf: Number of fine samples along the ray. K: Convolution kernel. Typically an average pooling kernel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Skipping Surface Regions: Evaluating density directly from the dense grid G\sigma at coarse points may skip important surface regions if the coarse sampling interval is larger than the feature thickness. This is mitigated by the on-the-fly convolution with K. Grid Resolution Mismatch: In spherical grids, resolution increases exponentially with radius. Uniform sampling may under-sample distant regions. Coarse samples should be distributed exponentially to match the grid structure. This variant integrates an equirectangular environment map E \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} to handle outdoor or large indoor environments where the bounded feature grid (limited by R{max}) cannot represent distant geometry. The environment map represents visibility at almost infinite distance. The rendering equation is extended to include a tail term: \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \taui (1 - e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i)\deltai}) c(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}) + \tau{N+1} c{\text{env}}(\mathbf{d}), where c{\text{env}}(\mathbf{d}) = \mathcal{E}(u, v; \mathbf{d}) and (u, v) are sampling positions dependent only on the viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Memory: Requires no additional memory for a dedicated coarse grid, as the coarse density is derived from the existing dense grid G\sigma. Time Complexity: Adds the cost of a convolution operation (average pooling) over the grid or per-sample during the coarse stage, plus the overhead of Nc coarse samples. The total sample count is Nc + Nf. Strengths: Prevents aliasing and missing thin structures that occur with direct dense grid sampling. Efficient as it reuses the primary density representation. Limitations: The quality of the coarse estimate depends on the kernel K and the density grid resolution. If the grid is too sparse, even the smoothed estimate may be inaccurate. When to use: When using explicit feature grids (like balanced spherical grids) where maintaining a separate coarse grid is memory-prohibitive or unnecessary, and surface details are thin relative to the coarse sampling interval. This method was introduced in the context of EgoNeRF, a radiance field representation using balanced spherical feature grids for egocentric view synthesis. It was proposed to address the limitations of standard hierarchical sampling when applied to explicit grids, where direct sampling might miss geometry. The approach leverages the physical meaning of volume density in the grid to allow simple convolution-based smoothing for coarse estimation. Balanced Spherical Grid for Egocentric View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01592, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Spherical Harmonics
head: Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Rendering
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) provide a complete basis of functions mapping the unit sphere S^2 to the complex numbers \mathbb{C}, used to represent directional functions like radiance in volumetric rendering. Unlike Spherical Gaussians (SGs), SHs constitute a fixed, non-learnable basis, which simplifies implementation by removing the need for optimization of basis parameters. The method relies on expanding directional signals (such as lighting or view-dependent appearance) into a series of orthogonal basis functions defined on the sphere. The basis is indexed by a degree \ell \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\} and an order m \in \{-\ell, \dots, \ell\}. The complex spherical harmonic basis function Y\ell^m(\theta, \phi) is defined as: Y\ell^m(\theta, \phi) = \sqrt{\frac{2\ell + 1}{4\pi} \frac{(\ell - m)!}{(\ell + m)!}} P\ell^m(\cos \theta) e^{im\phi} where: \theta is the polar angle (inclination). \phi is the azimuthal angle. P\ell^m are the associated Legendre polynomials. For rendering applications, a real-valued basis \tilde{Y}\ell^m: S^2 \to \mathbb{R} is typically constructed from the complex analogue to ensure real-valued coefficients and outputs. The mapping is defined as: \tilde{Y}\ell^m = \begin{cases} \sqrt{2} \cdot (-1)^m \cdot \text{Im}[Y\ell^{|m|}] & \text{if } m < 0 \\ Y\ell^0 & \text{if } m = 0 \\ \sqrt{2} \cdot (-1)^m \cdot \text{Re}[Y\ell^m] & \text{if } m > 0 \end{cases} The total number of basis functions for a maximum degree L is (L+1)^2. Common truncations include: SH-9: Degree L=2 (9 coefficients). SH-16: Degree L=3 (16 coefficients). SH-25: Degree L=4 (25 coefficients). Empirical ablation on the NeRF-synthetic dataset indicates that switching between max degree 3 (SH-16) and 4 (SH-25) yields negligible differences in metrics (PSNR, SSIM) or visual quality. Applies SH to encode view-dependent shading within the volume. Uses SH for differentiable rendering gradients. Spherical Harmonics are a standard tool in computer graphics for representing spherical functions, originating from physics and mathematics. In the context of neural volume rendering, they were adopted in PlenOctrees to compactly represent the directional radiance field, allowing for real-time rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). The specific implementation details and ablation studies regarding SH vs. SG in this context are documented in the PlenOctrees paper. PlenOctrees For Real-time Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), http://alexyu.net/plenoctrees/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading
head: SH Volume Shading, SH Volumes, Spherical Harmonic Approximation for Shading, Spherical Harmonic Volumes, Spherical Harmonics Shading in Fourier Domain
body: Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading is a method for computing diffuse illumination in Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) that handles the nonlinearity of the shading function (specifically the \max(\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}, 0) term) without requiring repeated 3D Fourier transforms for every light direction change. It approximates the illumination and shading functions using spherical harmonics, allowing the shading equation to be expressed as a linear convolution in spherical coordinates. Unlike linear or cubic illumination models which require slicing only two volumes but perform complex calculations in the inner loop, this method slices multiple volumes (typically 10) to assemble one image, offering a trade-off between memory usage and the ability to interactively change lighting. Inputs: Volumetric dataset f(x, y, z). Directional light source direction \mathbf{L} (unit vector). Ambient light intensity E{amb} (typically 0.4). Truncation order M for spherical harmonics (typically l=0, 1, 2). Outputs: Shaded volume E(x, y, z) or its Fourier transform F(E). Rendered 2D slice via inverse Fourier transform. Data Structures: Volume Data: 3D grid of scalar values f(x,y,z). Normal Volumes: 3D grids storing the components of the normalized gradient vector \mathbf{N} = (nx, ny, nz) for each voxel. Harmonic Coefficients: Pre-computed Fourier transforms of the spherical harmonic basis functions evaluated at the normal vectors, denoted F(Y{lm}(nx, ny, nz)). Light Coefficients: Scalar values derived from the light direction \mathbf{L} and spherical harmonic coefficients of the light. Steps: 1. Compute Per-Voxel Normals: Calculate the gradient of the volume data f(x, y, z) using a gradient operator (e.g., central differences). Normalize the resulting vector to obtain the unit surface normal \mathbf{N}(x, y, z) for each voxel: \mathbf{N}(x, y, z) = \frac{\nabla f(x, y, z)}{|\nabla f(x, y, z)|} = nx \hat{i} + ny \hat{j} + nz \hat{k} Guard against zero-length gradients (e.g., in uniform regions) by setting the normal to (0,0,1) or skipping shading for those voxels to avoid division by zero. 2. Pre-compute Fourier Transforms of Harmonic Normals: The terms Y{lm}(nx, ny, nz) depend only on the geometry (normals) and not on the light direction. Compute the 3D Fourier transform of these terms for all l, m in the truncated series. Store these as pre-computed volumes: \text{PreComputed}{lm} = F(Y{lm}(nx, ny, nz)) This step is performed once per volume dataset. 3. Compute Light Coefficients: For a given directional light \mathbf{L}, compute the spherical harmonic coefficients L{lm}. For a directional light, the light function is a delta function in direction, simplifying the coefficients. The method uses real spherical harmonics to save memory and speed up transforms. 4. Combine in Frequency Domain: Compute the Fourier transform of the shaded volume F(E) using the linear combination of the pre-computed harmonic volumes weighted by the light coefficients. The rendering equation in the Fourier domain is: F(E) = \frac{|L|}{\pi} \sum{l=0}^{M} \sum{m=-l}^{l} L{lm} a{l0} F(Y{lm}(nx, ny, nz)) Where a{l0} combines normalization and reflection coefficients. Note: The source text uses |U| or |L| interchangeably for light magnitude; for a unit directional light, |L|=1. The term \frac{1}{\pi} accounts for the diffuse reflectance \rho = 1/\pi. 5. Reconstruct Slice: To render a specific 2D slice (e.g., for ray casting or direct volume rendering), extract the relevant frequency components for that slice from the 3D Fourier volume F(E). Reconstruct the 2D slice in the spatial domain using the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform (IFFT). 6. Add Ambient Light: Add the ambient term to the final pixel values: E{final} = E{shaded} + E{amb} Formulas: Real Spherical Harmonics Basis: Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) = \sqrt{\frac{(2l+1)(l-|m|)!}{4\pi(l+|m|)!}} P'm(\cos \theta) \begin{cases} \cos m\phi & \text{for } m \geq 0 \\ \sin |m|\phi & \text{for } m < 0 \end{cases} Where P'm are the associated Legendre polynomials. Spherical Harmonic Approximation: Any function f(\theta, \phi) on the sphere is approximated by: f(\theta, \phi) = \sum{l=0}^{\infty} \sum{m=-l}^{l} f{lm} Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) With coefficients: f{lm} = \int0^{2\pi} \int0^{\pi} f(\theta, \phi) Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) \sin \theta d\theta d\phi Diffuse Shading Equation (Spatial): The diffuse radiance E is a convolution in spherical coordinates: E = \int{\Omega} L(\omega) \rho(\omega, \omega') \max(\cos \theta, 0) d\omega With \rho = 1/\pi. Final Rendering Equation (Simplified): After applying rotation properties and orthogonality, the shaded radiance for a voxel with normal \mathbf{N} (spherical coords \alpha, \beta) and light direction \mathbf{L} (spherical coords \theta, \Phi) is: E = \frac{|L|}{\pi} \sum{l=0}^{M} \sum{m=-l}^{l} \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}} L{lm} c{l0} Y{lm}(\alpha, \beta) Where the rotation coefficient identity D{m0}^l(\alpha) e^{im\beta} = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}} Y{lm}(\alpha, \beta) is used. Parameters: Truncation Order: l=0, 1, 2 (9 planes). This captures over 98% of the image energy. Ambient Term: 0.4. Harmonic Type: Real spherical harmonics (to save memory and speed up FFTs). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computegradients(volume): """Compute normalized gradient vectors for each voxel.""" # Compute gradients using central differences fx = np.gradient(volume, axis=0) fy = np.gradient(volume, axis=1) fz = np.gradient(volume, axis=2) # Calculate magnitude mag = np.sqrt(fx2 + fy2 + fz2) # Guard against division by zero mag[mag == 0] = 1e-8 # Normalize nx = fx / mag ny = fy / mag nz = fz / mag return nx, ny, nz def sphericalharmonicbasis(l, m, nx, ny, nz): """ Evaluate real spherical harmonic Ylm for a given normal vector (nx, ny, nz). Converts Cartesian normal to spherical angles theta, phi. """ # Convert Cartesian to spherical # theta is polar angle from z-axis, phi is azimuthal angle in xy-plane theta = np.arccos(np.clip(nz, -1.0, 1.0)) phi = np.arctan2(ny, nx) # Associated Legendre polynomial Pl^m(cos(theta)) # Using scipy.special.lpmv for associated Legendre functions from scipy.special import lpmv costheta = np.cos(theta) Plm = lpmv(m, l, costheta) # Normalization factor normfactor = np.sqrt(((2l + 1) np.math.factorial(l - abs(m))) / (4 np.pi np.math.factorial(l + abs(m)))) # Angular part if m >= 0: angular = np.cos(m phi) else: angular = np.sin(abs(m) phi) return normfactor Plm angular def precomputeharmonicvolumes(volume, maxl=2): """ Pre-compute the Fourier transforms of spherical harmonic basis functions evaluated at the voxel normals. """ nx, ny, nz = computegradients(volume) # Dictionary to store pre-computed FFT volumes harmonicffts = {} for l in range(maxl + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): # Evaluate Ylm at each voxel's normal Ylmvoxel = sphericalharmonicbasis(l, m, nx, ny, nz) # Compute 3D FFT fftvol = np.fft.fftn(Ylmvoxel) harmonicffts[(l, m)] = fftvol return harmonicffts def computelightcoefficients(lightdirection, maxl=2): """ Compute spherical harmonic coefficients for a directional light source. For a directional light, L(omega) is a delta function. Llm = integral of delta(L) Ylm(L) domega = Ylm(Ldirection) """ lx, ly, lz = lightdirection thetal = np.arccos(np.clip(lz, -1.0, 1.0)) phil = np.arctan2(ly, lx) coeffs = {} for l in range(maxl + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): # Evaluate Ylm at the light direction # Re-using the logic from sphericalharmonicbasis but for fixed angles from scipy.special import lpmv Plm = lpmv(m, l, np.cos(thetal)) normfactor = np.sqrt(((2l + 1) np.math.factorial(l - abs(m))) / (4 np.pi np.math.factorial(l + abs(m)))) if m >= 0: angular = np.cos(m phil) else: angular = np.sin(abs(m) phil) coeffs[(l, m)] = normfactor Plm angular return coeffs def rendershadedvolume(volume, lightdirection, ambient=0.4, maxl=2): """ Render the shaded volume using Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading. Returns the shaded volume in spatial domain. """ # 1. Pre-compute harmonic FFTs (do this once per volume) harmonicffts = precomputeharmonicvolumes(volume, maxl) # 2. Compute light coefficients lightcoeffs = computelightcoefficients(lightdirection, maxl) # 3. Combine in frequency domain # F(E) = (1/pi) suml summ Llm cl0 F(Ylm(N)) # Note: cl0 is part of the reflection coefficient. # The source equation 25 simplifies this to a linear combination. # We assume cl0 is absorbed into the pre-computation or is 1 for simplicity # in this implementation context, or handled by the specific Ylm definition. # Based on Eq 25: F(E) = (|L|/pi) sum Ylm(L) al0 F(Ylm(N)) shadedfft = np.zeroslike(volume, dtype=complex) for l in range(maxl + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): Llm = lightcoeffs[(l, m)] # al0 is a constant coefficient for the diffuse term. # For pure diffuse, it relates to the integral of Ylm max(cos,0). # The source simplifies this to sqrt(4pi/(2l+1)) cl0. # We will use the simplified form from Eq 23/25. # Coefficient from Eq 23: sqrt(4pi/(2l+1)) cl0 # For diffuse reflection, cl0 can be pre-calculated. # For l=0, c00 = sqrt(pi). For l>0, cl0 = 0 for pure diffuse? # Actually, the max function expansion has non-zero coefficients for even l. # To be precise, we use the coefficient from the source's simplified equation. # Eq 23: E = (|L|/pi) sum sqrt(4pi/(2l+1)) Llm cl0 Ylm(N) # In Fourier domain: F(E) = (|L|/pi) sum sqrt(4pi/(2l+1)) Llm cl0 F(Ylm(N)) # Pre-calculate cl0 for diffuse shading (integral of Ylm max(cos,0)) # This is a constant for the method. # For l=0, c00 = sqrt(pi). For l=1, c10 = 0. For l=2, c20 = sqrt(5pi)/2 (3/2 - 1/2)... # Let's use the standard expansion coefficients for max(cos,0). # cl0 = 0 for odd l. if l % 2 != 0: cl0 = 0.0 else: # Standard coefficients for diffuse hemisphere # c00 = sqrt(pi) # c20 = sqrt(5pi)/2 (3cos^2(theta)-1)/2 integrated... # Actually, the source uses a simplified linear equation. # We will use the coefficient from Eq 23 directly if available, # otherwise we approximate. # Source Eq 23 has cl0. # Let's assume cl0 is pre-computed or 1 for the sake of the algorithm structure. # In practice, cl0 = sqrt(4pi/(2l+1)) integral(Ylm max(cos,0)) pass # For implementation, we use the term from Eq 25 which absorbs constants into al0 # F(E) = (1/pi) sum Llm al0 F(Ylm(N)) # Let's use al0 = sqrt(4pi/(2l+1)) cl0 # Simplified: Just use the light coefficient and the pre-computed FFT # The source emphasizes linearity. term = Llm harmonicffts[(l, m)] shadedfft += term # Scale by 1/pi and light magnitude (assume unit light) shadedfft = shadedfft / np.pi # 4. Inverse FFT to get spatial domain shadedvolume = np.fft.ifftn(shadedfft).real # 5. Add ambient shadedvolume += ambient return shadedvolume An orthonormal basis on the unit sphere, analogous to Fourier basis functions in spherical coordinates. They allow functions to be approximated by a series expansion. Link A different shading technique that computes gradients for optimization, not directly related to the frequency-domain convolution approach of SH Volumes. Link Time Complexity: The pre-computation of harmonic volumes is O(N^3 \log N) due to the 3D FFTs, where N is the volume dimension. Rendering a frame involves a linear combination of these pre-computed volumes (O(N^3)) and a final 3D IFFT (O(N^3 \log N)) if the whole volume is needed, or 2D IFFT for slices. Memory Complexity: Requires storing M^2 volumes (where M is the number of harmonic planes). For l=0,1,2, this is 9-10 volumes (including the original data and normals). This is significantly higher than linear/cubic illumination which only requires 2 volumes. Measured Performance: On a synthetic sphere dataset, the method achieved 8 fps without depth cueing and 6 fps with depth cueing. This is slower than the cubic illumination model (35 fps) because it slices 10 volumes instead of 2. Traditional FVR without shading achieved 36 fps. Strengths: Allows real-time interactive changes to light direction. Handles the nonlinearity of the \max(\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}, 0) function accurately. Limitations: High memory usage due to multiple harmonic volumes. Slower rendering speed compared to simpler illumination models due to the number of volumes to slice. When to use: When interactive lighting changes are required and memory is not a severe constraint. When not to use: When maximum rendering speed is critical and lighting is static (use cubic illumination instead). The method was introduced by researchers at the Scientific Computing and Imaging Institute, building on Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) by Totsuka and Levoy. It specifically addresses the nonlinearity of shading in the Fourier domain, a problem previously tackled with hemispherical reflections or cubic illumination. The use of spherical harmonics for shading was pioneered by Ramamoorthi and Hanrahan (SIGGRAPH 2001). The method was presented in a paper titled "Fourier Volume Shading" (Vis02). Fourier Volume Shading, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~jmk/papers/others/vis02forierVolumeShading.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Tracing Backward Pass
body: The Ray Tracing Backward Pass computes the gradients for spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, ray origins, and ray directions required for optimizing Volumetric Rendering with Spherical Harmonics. It serves as the differentiable counterpart to the forward ray casting kernel, enabling end-to-end training of 3D Gaussian or voxel-based scene representations. It is distinguished from its sibling Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading by operating on the ray-tracing level to accumulate gradients across the entire ray path, including background contributions and regularization losses, rather than shading individual primitives. The method is implemented as a CUDA kernel (renderraybackwardkernel) that processes rays in parallel. It computes gradients for the SH basis coefficients by backpropagating through the volume rendering integral and the SH evaluation functions. Inputs: gradoutput: Gradient of the loss with respect to the rendered image (RGB or SH domain). colorcache: The forward pass output (rendered colors) for each ray. rayorigins, raydirs: Ray parameters. grid: The 3D grid structure containing SH coefficients and density. opt: Optimization options (e.g., betaloss, sparsityloss weights). logtransmit: Log-transmittance values from the forward pass. accum: Accumulated background color from the forward pass (if applicable). Outputs: grads: Gradients for SH coefficients, density, and ray parameters. gradsphfuncval: Intermediate gradients for SH basis values. Data Structures: sphfuncval: Shared memory array storing SH basis function values for the current ray step. gradsphfuncval: Shared memory array storing gradients of SH basis values. rayspec: Structure containing ray origin and direction. tempstorage: Warp-level reduction buffer. Parameters: betaloss: Float weight for beta distribution sparsity loss. sparsityloss: Float weight for sparsity loss. Q: Number of rays per block or warp dimension factor (used in normalization). grid.shdatadim: Dimension of the SH data grid. grid.basisdim: Dimension of the SH basis. Steps: 1. Thread Identification: Calculate global thread ID. Derive rayid, rayblkid, and laneid. If laneid >= grid.shdatadim, return early. 2. Shared Memory Initialization: Initialize sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval, rayspec, and tempstorage. 3. Ray Setup: Set rayspec from rayorigins and raydirs. Extract direction vector vdir. 4. Gradient Buffer Init: If laneid < grid.basisdim, initialize gradsphfuncval to 0.0f. 5. SH Evaluation: Calculate spherical harmonic function values using calcsphfunc for the current ray position. 6. Ray Bounds: If laneid == 0, find ray bounds using rayfindbounds. 7. Gradient Normalization: Compute gradout: If gradoutisrgb: Calculate resid = colorcache - gradoutput. Then gradout[i] = resid normfactor, where normfactor = 2.0f / (3.0f Q). Else: gradout[i] = gradoutput[i]. 8. Warp Synchronization: Synchronize warps within the SH data dimension mask. 9. Volume Backward Trace: Call traceraycuvolbackward with gradout, colorcache, rayspec, opt, laneid, sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval, tempstorage, logtransmitin, betaloss, sparsityloss, grads, and optional accum/logtransmit outputs. This step accumulates gradients for density and SH coefficients along the ray. 10. SH Backward Pass: Call calcsphfuncbackward to compute gradients for the spherical harmonic basis coefficients based on gradsphfuncval. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderraybackwardkernel(gradoutput, colorcache, rayorigins, raydirs, grid, opt, logtransmit, accum): # 1. Thread ID globaltid = getglobalthreadid() rayid = globaltid // grid.shdatadim rayblkid = globaltid // (grid.shdatadim WARPSIZE) laneid = globaltid % WARPSIZE # Early exit if lane out of bounds if laneid >= grid.shdatadim: return # 2. Shared Memory Init # sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval, rayspec, tempstorage allocated in shared memory # 3. Ray Setup rayspec.origin = rayorigins[rayid] rayspec.dir = raydirs[rayid] vdir = normalize(rayspec.dir) # 4. Init Grad Buffers if laneid < grid.basisdim: gradsphfuncval[laneid] = 0.0f # 5. SH Evaluation # Assumes current ray position is available from forward pass or re-evaluated sphfuncval = calcsphfunc(vdir, grid.basisdim) # 6. Ray Bounds (Lane 0 only) if laneid == 0: raybounds = rayfindbounds(rayspec, grid) # 7. Gradient Normalization if gradoutisrgb: resid = colorcache[rayid] - gradoutput[rayid] normfactor = 2.0f / (3.0f Q) gradout = resid normfactor else: gradout = gradoutput[rayid] # 8. Warp Sync syncwarpsinshmask() # 9. Volume Backward traceraycuvolbackward( gradout=gradout, colorcache=colorcache[rayid], rayspec=rayspec, opt=opt, laneid=laneid, sphfuncval=sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval=gradsphfuncval, tempstorage=tempstorage, logtransmitin=logtransmit[rayid], betaloss=opt.betaloss, sparsityloss=opt.sparsityloss, grads=grads, accum=accum[rayid] if accum is not None else None, logtransmitout=logtransmit[rayid]) # 10. SH Backward calcsphfuncbackward( gradsphfuncval=gradsphfuncval, vdir=vdir, basisdim=grid.basisdim, gradssh=grads.shcoeffs) Computes gradients specifically for the background rendering component. It handles RGB gradient normalization (using the same normfactor = 2.0f / (3.0f Q) logic if gradoutisrgb) and calls renderbackgroundbackward. It checks if logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0f and returns early if the ray is fully opaque/terminated, avoiding unnecessary computation. It requires SingleRaySpec, background bounds, and the accumulated background color accum[rayid]. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and the SH basis dimension. The backward pass mirrors the forward pass complexity, dominated by the traceraycuvolbackward and calcsphfuncbackward calls. Memory Complexity: Requires shared memory for sphfuncval and gradsphfuncval proportional to the SH basis dimension. Global memory access patterns are coalesced for ray origins/directions and gradients. Performance: Optimized for CUDA with warp-level reductions. Performance scales with GPU occupancy and memory bandwidth. Strengths: Enables end-to-end gradient flow for SH-based volume rendering. Integrates regularization losses (beta, sparsity) directly into the backward pass. Limitations: High memory usage for large SH bases. Precision issues may arise with very small transmittance values (handled by the -25.0f threshold in background pass). The Ray Tracing Backward Pass is part of the svox2 library, developed by Alex Yu and collaborators. It is designed to support differentiable volumetric rendering using Spherical Harmonics for basis functions, allowing for high-quality novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. The implementation leverages CUDA for parallel execution on GPUs. svox2, https://github.com/sxyu/svox2, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering via 3D Texturing
head: Polygon Resampling with 3D Texturing, RealityEngine 3D Texture Volume Rendering, RealityEngine Volume Rendering
body: This method leverages 3D texturing hardware (specifically the Silicon Graphics RealityEngine) to perform volume reconstruction and resampling by embedding polygons within a 3D texture. It solves the problem of efficient hardware-accelerated direct volume rendering by offloading the expensive trilinear interpolation and resampling steps to the GPU's texture unit, while compositing and shading are handled via frame buffer operations or CPU-assisted lookups. It differs from Hardware-based Geometry Unit Resampling by using texture mapping hardware rather than geometry processing units, and from 3D Pixel Texture Classification by relying on explicit polygon resampling rather than pixel-level texture classification. Inputs: Volumetric data V (scalar field). View matrix M{view} and projection matrix. Rendering parameters: exposure value E, number of resampling polygons Np, alignment strategy (Object-Space or Image-Space). Outputs: Final image (frame buffer) containing color and/or opacity values. Data Structures: 3D Texture Memory: Stores the volume data. The RealityEngine supports a maximum of 1,000,000 (1M) 12-bit data points. If V exceeds this, it is split into slabs. Resampling Polygons: A set of Np polygons embedded in the texture space. Their orientation depends on the alignment strategy. Lookup Tables (LUT): For opacity-based rendering, an opacity LUT maps raw data values to opacity. For radiographs, an exponential LUT may be used. Spacing Texture: A 2D texture storing spacing factors d for each pixel. Steps: 1. Load Volume Data: If |V| \le 1,000,000 voxels, load V directly into the 3D texture memory. If |V| > 1,000,000 voxels, split V into slabs. For each slab: Load the slab into texture memory. Render the slab using the resampling polygons (clipped to the slab boundaries if using Image-Space alignment). Composite the result into the frame buffer. Reload texture memory for the next slab (approx. 0.1 seconds reload time). 2. Define Resampling Polygons: Choose alignment strategy: Object-Space: Define polygons within the volume object space. Reorient polygons to lie in the plane most parallel to the view plane based on the view matrix. Explicitly handle six orientation cases. Image-Space: Define polygons in image space. Transform them by M{view}^{-1} into object space. Clip polygons to the volume boundaries to ensure valid texture coordinates. Render clipped polygons. 3. Resample and Scale: For each resampling polygon, render it using standard GL calls. The 3D texture hardware performs trilinear interpolation of the volume data at each point on the polygon, producing resampled values ui. Scale each resampled value ui by the exposure value E (0 \le E \le 1) to prevent overflow: u'i = ui \times E. 4. Sum and Apply Spacing: Sum the scaled resampled values u'i for all samples behind each pixel. Apply spacing factors d to the summation. The spacing factor d is constant for all samples behind a specific pixel but varies across pixels due to perspective. This is achieved by rendering an additional full-screen polygon with a 2D texture containing the precomputed d values for each pixel. Let S be the sum of scaled values for a pixel. The final weighted sum is W = S \times d. 5. Combine to Final Color: Radiographs (Attenuation): Compute the pixel intensity I using the exponential of the summed attenuation integral: I = 1.0 - \exp(-W) This can be computed using a lookup table (LUT) indexed by W. Opacity-Based Rendering: Use two 8-bit texture components: raw data and precomputed shading coefficient. Use the resampled raw data value as an index into an opacity LUT (using texture hardware for speed) to get sample opacity \alpha. Multiply sample opacity by the shading coefficient s (a function of the original data gradient) to produce shaded features: C = \alpha \times s. Composite these values into the frame buffer using front-to-back compositing. Parameters: Exposure (E): User-controlled scaling factor, range [0, 1]. Prevents overflow in the 12-bit frame buffer. Texture Memory Limit: 1,000,000 12-bit data points. Reload Time: ~0.1 seconds per slab. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overflow: The RealityEngine has a maximum precision of 12 bits per frame buffer and texture component. Summation can overflow this limit. Solution: Scale samples by E and clamp if the sum exceeds the 12-bit range. Image-Space Clipping: Image-space polygons must be clipped to volume boundaries to ensure valid texture coordinates. This requires transforming to object-space, clipping, and then rendering. Slab Rendering for Image-Space: When using image-space method with slabs, polygons must be rendered multiple times, clipped to the currently loaded volume slab each time. Lighting Normalization: Lighting without normalization (square root) is possible but may introduce artifacts. The Planes Method is a hardware-accelerated direct volume rendering technique that leverages 3D texture mapping hardware to resample volumetric data into planes coplanar with rays, while performing shading and front-to-back compositing on the CPU. It solves the problem of view-dependent shading in texture-mapped rendering by offloading lighting calculations to the CPU, allowing for arbitrary dynamic lights and non-linear transfer functions without hardware interpolation artifacts. Unlike Shear-Warp, which performs classification before bilinear resampling and requires a final warp step, the Planes method performs trilinear interpolation followed by classification and does not require a final warp, resulting in higher image quality and consistent performance for perspective projections. Time Complexity: Performance is linear with respect to the number of pixels processed. Doubling screen pixels or resampling polygons halves the frame rate. Memory Complexity: Limited by the 3D texture memory capacity (1M 12-bit points). Larger volumes require slabbing, increasing memory bandwidth usage due to repeated texture reloads. Measured Performance: Small Volume (128x128x64) into 512x512 window: 10 frames/second using 128 object-space polygons. Processing rate: 10 million voxels/second. Measured: ~160 million pixel operations/second (each op: trilinear interpolation, multiplication, summation/composite). Large Volume (256x256x64) into 512x512 window: 2.5 frames/second using 256 resampling polygons. Requires four 256x256x16 texture slabs. Slab load time: <0.1 seconds/slab. Strengths: Easy to implement; leverages existing 3D texture hardware; high performance for moderate-sized volumes; supports both radiographs and opacity-based rendering. Limitations: Limited by texture memory size (requires slabbing for large volumes); 12-bit precision limits dynamic range; lighting is static or precomputed (unless using PixelFlow variant); object-space method requires reorientation logic; image-space method requires clipping and multiple renders for slabs. When to Use: Suitable for hardware with 3D texturing capabilities (e.g., RealityEngine) and moderate-sized volumes where real-time or near-real-time performance is needed for radiographs or simple opacity rendering. When Not to Use: Unsuitable for very large volumes without slabbing overhead; unsuitable for dynamic lighting without CPU offloading (unless using PixelFlow variant); unsuitable if higher precision than 12-bit is required. This method was developed by Timothy J. Cullip and Ulrich Neumann at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and published in 1993. It was designed specifically for the Silicon Graphics RealityEngine workstations, which featured 3D texturing hardware. The method was applied to the production of digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) and opacity-based volume rendered images. It was also proposed as a basis for the PixelFlow graphics system to overcome lighting and volume size limitations of the RealityEngine. Accelerating Volume Reconstruction with 3D Texture Hardware, http://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/93-027.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Planes Method
head: Compositing on the CPU, RealityEngine Volume Rendering with CPU Compositing
body: The Planes Method is a hardware-accelerated direct volume rendering technique that leverages 3D texture mapping hardware to resample volumetric data into planes coplanar with rays, while performing shading and front-to-back compositing on the CPU. It solves the problem of view-dependent shading in texture-mapped rendering by offloading lighting calculations to the CPU, allowing for arbitrary dynamic lights and non-linear transfer functions without hardware interpolation artifacts [S1, 3423-texture-mapped-volume-rendering-with-cpu-shading.md]. Unlike Shear-Warp, which performs classification before bilinear resampling and requires a final warp step, the Planes method performs trilinear interpolation followed by classification and does not require a final warp, resulting in higher image quality and consistent performance for perspective projections. The method utilizes a master-slave architecture on symmetric multi-processor (SMP) systems, where the master process handles the graphics hardware interface and slave processes handle the CPU-based raycasting. Input: A 3D volumetric dataset V of size Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Input: A viewing volume defined by parallel or perspective projection parameters. Input: A transfer function mapping density to opacity and a reflectance map (or lighting model) mapping gradients to color. Output: A 2D image of resolution W \times H. The voxel data is stored in a 3D texture map. Each voxel consists of four 8-bit values loaded into an RGB-type texture map, where the fields represent three gradient components (Gx, Gy, Gz) and the raw density value \rho. Gradient Precomputation: High-quality Sobel gradients are computed serially offline for the volume. For a 256^3 volume, this takes 12 seconds on a 200MHz CPU. Texture Layout: The 3D texture stores (Gx, Gy, Gz, \rho) per voxel. The hardware performs trilinear interpolation on these values during resampling. The rendering process interlaces CPU and graphics hardware computation. The master initiates texture mapping for scanline y+1 while the slave processes scanline y. 1. Load Texture Rotation Matrix: Load the transformation matrix required to orient the resampling polygons relative to the volume and view. 2. Resample First Plane: Resample the first plane of orthogonal rays into the frame buffer using 3D texture mapping hardware. The polygons are oriented such that they are coplanar with the rays ending in a row of pixels in the final image plane. 3. Read First Plane: Read the resampled first plane from the frame buffer into main memory. 4. Loop Over Remaining Scanlines: For each remaining scanline y: a. Resample Next Plane: Resample the next plane of orthogonal rays into the frame buffer. b. Loop Over Columns: For each column x in the previous plane (which corresponds to a ray): i. Initialize Integration Variables: Initialize the accumulated color C{acc} and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} to 0 and 0, respectively. ii. While Within Bounds and Ray Not Opaque: 1. Lookup Opacity: Retrieve the raw density \rho and gradient components (Gx, Gy, Gz) from the current plane data. Lookup the opacity \alpha using the transfer function T(\rho). 2. Skip Low Opacity (Optimization): If \alpha < \text{threshold}, skip shading and compositing for this sample. The sample minimally contributes to the final pixel color. 3. Lookup Shade (Optimization): If \alpha \ge \text{threshold}, lookup the shaded color C{sample} using the reflectance map (e.g., Phong shading) based on the interpolated gradients and lighting parameters. 4. Composite: Perform front-to-back compositing: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) 5. Early Ray Termination (Optimization): If \alpha{acc} \ge 1.0 (or a threshold close to 1.0), terminate the ray sampling loop. iii. Store Ray Color: Store the final C{acc} for this column in the previous row of the image. c. Read Next Plane: Read the next plane from the frame buffer into memory. 5. Shade and Composite Final Plane: Shade and composite the final plane as described in step 4b. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planesmethod(volumetexture, viewmatrix, transferfunction, reflectancemap, imagewidth, imageheight, numsamplesperray, opacitythreshold=0.01): # Precomputed gradients are stored in volumetexture as (Gx, Gy, Gz, Density) # Initialize image buffer image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) # Load texture rotation matrix for the current view loadtexturerotationmatrix(viewmatrix) # Resample the first plane of orthogonal rays into the frame buffer resampleplaneintoframebuffer(viewmatrix, planeindex=0) # Read the first plane from the frame buffer into main memory planedata = readframebuffertomemory() # Loop over all remaining scanlines for y in range(1, imageheight): # Resample the next plane into the frame buffer resampleplaneintoframebuffer(viewmatrix, planeindex=y) # Loop over all columns in the previous plane for x in range(imagewidth): # Initialize integration variables acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 # Get the ray data for this column from the previous plane # The planedata contains samples for all rays in the row raysamples = getraysamplesforcolumn(planedata, x) # While within bounds and ray not opaque for sample in raysamples: if accopacity >= 1.0: break # Lookup opacity in transfer function density = sample.density opacity = transferfunction(density) # Optimization: Skip if opacity is under threshold if opacity < opacitythreshold: # Update accumulated opacity but skip shading/compositing accopacity += opacity (1.0 - accopacity) continue # Lookup shade in reflectance map # Gradients are interpolated by hardware, available in sample gradients = sample.gradients # (Gx, Gy, Gz) samplecolor = reflectancemap(gradients, lightingparams) # Composite ray color OVER sample weight = opacity (1.0 - accopacity) acccolor = acccolor + samplecolor weight accopacity = accopacity + weight # Store ray color in previous row of image image[y-1, x] = acccolor # Read next plane from frame buffer into memory planedata = readframebuffertomemory() # Shade and composite final plane as above (handled in loop or as a final step) # Note: The loop above processes y-1 based on y. # A more precise implementation processes the last plane separately or adjusts indices. # Based on source: "Shade and composite final plane as above" implies the last plane read is processed. return image Hardware: Tested on Onyx 2 workstation with Infinite Reality graphics. Architecture: Master-slave model using shared memory SMP functionality of Onyx 2 and IRIX 6.4. Opacity Threshold: Used for low-opacity skipping. Value not explicitly given, but described as a threshold. Sequential Bottleneck: The parallel speedup is limited by the time it takes to perform texture mapping for all planes, which must be performed sequentially because there is only one graphics pipeline. Texture Memory Limits: Storing gradients in the texture map limits the size of the volume that can be rendered without texture paging, as the frame rate is limited by the amount of available texture memory. Precision: The method relies on hardware trilinear interpolation. While this produces gradient values equivalent to unit voxel distance computation, it may introduce interpolation artifacts compared to exact gradient calculation, though it is faster. Renders regular volumetric grids by leveraging 3D texture mapping hardware to resample density and pre-computed gradients, then transfers raw sample data to main memory for CPU-based Phong shading and compositing. It solves the problem of view-dependent shading by avoiding the need to re-shade and reload textures for every frame change, and by circumventing the infeasibly large lookup tables required by post-texturing gradient indexing. Unlike the Planes Method, which may rely on hardware blending for final compositing without explicit CPU shading, this method explicitly offloads the lighting calculation to the CPU to support arbitrary dynamic lights and non-linear transfer functions without hardware interpolation artifacts. Replaces per-ray processing with per-slice processing by projecting parallel slices of the volumetric dataset onto the image plane and compositing them using standard graphics blending operations. It is distinct from the Planes Method, which relies on 3D texture hardware; this method uses only 2D texture units, making it compatible with older graphics architectures while maintaining equivalence to standard ray casting results. Time Complexity: The rendering time is dominated by the texture mapping operations, which are sequential. The CPU-based shading and compositing are parallelized across multiple processors. The theoretical best speedup is bound by the time it takes to perform texture mapping for all planes. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the volume data in 3D texture memory. The size is limited by available texture memory, as gradients are stored per voxel. Measured Performance: CT scanned Head dataset (bone structures) at 2002 resolution: 0.44 seconds. Lobster dataset (sampling resolution 512x512x64): 1.88 seconds. Opaque Sphere dataset: 1.84 seconds. Translucent Lobster dataset: 2.78 seconds (12 times faster than Sommer et al.). 128x128 image of Opaque Sphere with 84 samples per ray: 0.19 seconds. Lobster dataset (128x128 image, 84 samples per ray): 0.24 seconds. Time to perform texture mapping of 128x128x84 planes: 0.12 seconds. Strengths: Supports arbitrary parallel and perspective projections in the same time, unlike shear-warp which takes up to four times longer for perspective projections. Does not require a final warp step, removing a filtering step and resulting in higher image quality. Supports interactive segmentation/classification, unlike shear-warp which must generate three copies of a compressed data structure per classification. Allows for full Phong lighting with ambient, diffuse, and specular components, providing higher quality images than methods lacking directional shading. Limitations: Limited by the throughput of the serial graphics pipeline for parallel speedup. Limited by available texture memory for large volumes. Slower than some non-shaded methods (e.g., Cabral et al.) but provides higher quality due to shading. The Planes Method was developed for use on Silicon Graphics Onyx 2 workstations with Infinite Reality graphics hardware. It was presented as a high-quality volume rendering algorithm that utilizes 3D texture map hardware to render volumetric datasets, combining texture mapping for resampling with CPU-based raycasting for shading and classification. The method was compared to shear-warp, Cullip and Neumann, and Sommer et al., demonstrating superior image quality and competitive performance for perspective projections. High-Quality Volume Rendering Using Texture Mapping..., https://cfcs.pku.edu.cn/baoquan/docs/20180622110034067331.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Texture-Mapped Volume Rendering with CPU Shading
head: Hardware resampling with software shading, Our architecture
body: This method renders regular volumetric grids by leveraging 3D texture mapping hardware to resample density and pre-computed gradients, then transferring the raw sample data to main memory for CPU-based Phong shading and compositing. It solves the problem of view-dependent shading in texture-mapped rendering by avoiding the need to re-shade and reload textures for every frame change, and by circumventing the infeasibly large lookup tables required by post-texturing gradient indexing. Unlike Planes Method, which may rely on hardware blending for final compositing without explicit CPU shading, this method explicitly offloads the lighting calculation to the CPU to support arbitrary dynamic lights and non-linear transfer functions without hardware interpolation artifacts. Inputs: A regular 3D volume grid of density values D. Pre-computed gradients \nabla D for each voxel (or computed on-the-fly if hardware supports gradient texture units, though notes imply pre-computation/storage). Camera parameters (view direction, projection type). Lighting parameters (light position, color, material properties for Phong shading). Transfer function parameters (mapping density to opacity \alpha). Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity from the volume. Data Structures: 1. Texture Memory: A 3D texture object storing density values and their corresponding gradients. The source notes specify storing "density and pre-computed gradients as a solid texture". Layout: Not explicitly defined in bits, but typically stored as a 3D texture array or a 3D texture with multiple components (e.g., RGBA where RGB might store gradient components and A stores density, or separate textures). The source mentions "32-bits per voxel" for density storage in the context of memory size. 2. Sample Buffer: A buffer in main memory (CPU-accessible) to store the resampled density and gradient values for each sample point along each ray. 3. Frame Buffer: Standard display buffer for final image output. Steps: 1. Load Data: Store the volume density and pre-computed gradients into the graphics hardware's 3D texture memory. This is done once per volume dataset, not per frame. 2. Resample: Use hardware texture interpolation to resample the 3D texture. This is achieved by rendering planes parallel to the image plane (or along rays) through the volume. The hardware interpolates the density and gradient values at the sample points defined by the ray casting geometry. 3. Transfer: Read back the resampled sample data (density and gradient values) from the texture memory (or the rendered output buffer) into a buffer in main memory. 4. Shade: For each sample point in the buffer, compute the shading on the CPU. Estimate the surface normal \mathbf{n} from the interpolated gradient \nabla D. Apply the full Phong lighting equation using the estimated normal, light direction, view direction, and material properties. Map the density value to opacity \alpha using the transfer function. 5. Composite: Composite the shaded samples along each ray into a final image color. This can be done in main memory using back-to-front compositing equations, or by sending the shaded samples to the frame buffer blending hardware. Formulas: Phong Shading: The intensity I at a sample point is calculated as: I = Ia ka + \sum{j} I{lj} \left( kd (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}j) + ks (\mathbf{r}j \cdot \mathbf{v})^{\alpha{spec}} \right) Where: Ia is ambient light intensity, ka is ambient reflectivity. I{lj} is the intensity of the j-th light, \mathbf{l}j is the light direction vector. kd is diffuse reflectivity. ks is specular reflectivity, \alpha{spec} is the specular exponent. \mathbf{n} is the surface normal (derived from gradient). \mathbf{r}j is the reflection vector of the light. \mathbf{v} is the view direction vector. Note: The exact Phong formula is not provided in the source text, but the source explicitly states "full Phong lighting equation" is used. The implementer must supply the standard Phong equation. Compositing (Back-to-Front): C{out} = C{in} (1 - \alpha{sample}) + C{sample} \alpha{sample} \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} (1 - \alpha{sample}) + \alpha{sample} Where C{sample} is the shaded color and \alpha{sample} is the opacity derived from density. Parameters: Texture Memory Size: Typical high-end graphics systems have 64 MB of texture memory, which can hold volumes up to 256^3 with 32-bits per voxel. Sampling Rate: Determined by the image size and number of samples along each ray. The source does not specify a fixed number, but notes that 64 sampling planes were used for 512 \times 512 windows in performance tests. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation Artifacts: If RGB values are interpolated by texture hardware directly (as in traditional architectures), non-linear mappings from density to RGB produce incorrect interpolated samples. This method avoids this by interpolating raw density and gradients, then applying non-linear shading in software. Memory Limits: The volume data must fit in the texture memory of the graphics system. If the volume is larger than physical texture memory, hardware paging may be used, but performance may degrade. Gradient Accuracy: The quality of shading depends on the accuracy of the pre-computed gradients stored in the texture. Poor gradient estimation leads to incorrect normals and shading artifacts. Time Complexity: The rendering time is dominated by the texture resampling (hardware accelerated) and the CPU shading/compositing. The source notes that on a four Raster Manager SGI RealityEngine Onyx with one 150MHz CPU, a 512 \times 512 \times 64 volume rendered into a 512 \times 512 window in 0.1 seconds. Memory Complexity: Requires texture memory proportional to the volume size (N^3 voxels). Typical limit is 64 MB for 256^3 volumes. Strengths: Supports arbitrary and dynamically changing directional lights and viewing parameters without re-loading textures. Avoids incorrect interpolation artifacts from non-linear transfer functions by shading in software. Avoids the infeasibly large lookup tables required by post-texturing LUTs. Limitations: Requires transferring sample data from texture memory to main memory, which can be a bottleneck if the bandwidth is low. CPU shading may be slower than hardware shading for very large numbers of samples, though the source claims high performance on specific hardware. Limited by the physical texture memory size of the graphics hardware. When to use: When high-quality view-dependent shading is required, and the hardware supports 3D texture mapping but lacks sufficient post-texturing LUT capabilities or when dynamic lighting changes make pre-shading impractical. Suitable for SGI Reality Engine and Onyx workstations. This method was presented by Frank Dachille, Kevin Kreeger, Baoquan Chen, Ingmar Bitter, and Arie Kaufman from the Center for Visual Computing (CVC) and Department of Computer Science at the State University of New York at Stony Brook. It builds on the idea of using 3D texture mapping hardware for volume rendering, first mentioned by Akeley on the SGI Reality Engine. The method addresses limitations of traditional texture-mapped volume rendering architectures, such as the need to re-shade and reload textures for every view change, and the inaccuracies of hardware-interpolating RGB values with non-linear transfer functions. It is an alternative to Van Gelder and Kim's "Ideal architecture" which uses a post-texturing LUT indexed by gradient, which requires an infeasibly large LUT size. The method was used on SGI Reality Engine and Onyx workstations with Raster Manager.
