name: Isosurface and first-hit ray casting
body: Isosurface and first-hit ray casting is an image-order rendering technique that determines the visible surface of a volumetric scalar field by tracing rays from the eye and stopping at the nearest point where the scalar value meets a user-defined isovalue C{iso}. It solves the problem of visualizing implicit surfaces embedded within 3D data without requiring explicit mesh extraction or hidden-surface removal. Unlike Direct volume ray casting, which accumulates color and opacity along the entire ray path, this method performs a boolean decision: it returns the first sample C{src} such that C{iso} = C{src} (or C{src} \ge C{iso}), ignoring all subsequent samples. This distinguishes it from Distance-field ray marching, which interpolates signed distance fields for smooth geometry, and Ray-grid traversal, which focuses on efficient voxel access patterns rather than the specific surface-detection logic. The family shares a common mathematical framework for detecting the intersection of a viewing ray with an implicit surface defined by f(\mathbf{x}) = C{iso}. Ray Representation and Bounds: Each pixel generates a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). The ray is parameterized as \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for t \ge 0. The volume is enclosed in an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defined by \mathbf{u}{min} and \mathbf{u}{max}. Rays are clipped to this volume. The intersection of the ray with the AABB yields entry t{min} and exit t{max} distances: t0 = (\mathbf{u}{min} - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{invD}, \quad t1 = (\mathbf{u}{max} - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{invD} t{min} = \max(\min(t{0x}, t{1x}), \min(t{0y}, t{1y}), \min(t{0z}, t{1z})) t{max} = \min(\max(t{0x}, t{1x}), \max(t{0y}, t{1y}), \max(t{0z}, t{1z})) where \mathbf{invD} = 1.0 / \mathbf{d}. If t{max} \le t{min}, the ray misses the volume entirely. Traversal and Surface Detection: The algorithm traverses the ray from near to far (t{min} to t{max}) to ensure the first hit is found, implementing the "painters algorithm" visibility sorting for implicit surfaces. At each sample point \mathbf{x}(t), a boolean check determines if the surface is found: C = \begin{cases} true & \text{if } C{iso} = C{src} \\ false & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where C{src} is the sampled scalar value f(\mathbf{x}(t)). In discrete implementations, this is often simplified to checking if the sampled value meets or exceeds the threshold (C{src} \ge C{iso}). Hit Processing and Shading: Upon finding a hit at parameter t{hit}, the algorithm computes the 3D position \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{o} + t{hit}\mathbf{d} and the surface normal \mathbf{n} (typically via the gradient \nabla f) to apply shading models. If no hit is found within t{max}, the pixel is colored with the background color. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements a fixed-step marching variant with sign-change detection and bisection refinement, as described in the literature: def samplescalarfield(p): # Performs 3D texture lookup for scalar field f(p) return texturelookup3d(p) def sampleiso(p, uIsovalue): return samplescalarfield(p) - uIsovalue def hassignchange(dprev, dcurr): return dprev dcurr <= 0.0 def refineisohitbisection(origin, dir, ta, tb, da, db, urefinementiterations): for in range(urefinementiterations): tmid = 0.5 (ta + tb) dmid = sampleiso(origin + tmid dir, uIsovalue) if hassignchange(da, dmid): tb = tmid db = dmid else: ta = tmid da = dmid return 0.5 (ta + tb) def computenormal(p, ustepsize, uIsovalue): h = ustepsize gx = samplescalarfield(p + vec3(h, 0.0, 0.0)) - samplescalarfield(p - vec3(h, 0.0, 0.0)) gy = samplescalarfield(p + vec3(0.0, h, 0.0)) - samplescalarfield(p - vec3(0.0, h, 0.0)) gz = samplescalarfield(p + vec3(0.0, 0.0, h)) - samplescalarfield(p - vec3(0.0, h, 0.0)) grad = vec3(gx, gy, gz) norm = max(length(grad), 1e-12) return -grad / norm def traceshadowray(origin, dir, stepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue): t = 2.0 stepsize while True: p = origin + t dir if p.x < udomainmin.x or p.y < udomainmin.y or p.z < udomainmin.z or \ p.x > udomainmax.x or p.y > udomainmax.y or p.z > udomainmax.z: break if samplescalarfield(p) >= uIsovalue: return 0.0 t += stepsize return 1.0 def shadeisopoint(phit, lightdirworld, uenableshadows, ustepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue): normal = computenormal(phit, ustepsize, uIsovalue) diffuse = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdirworld)) shadow = 1.0 if uenableshadows != 0: shadow = traceshadowray(phit, lightdirworld, ustepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue) basecolor = vec3(1.0) return basecolor diffuse shadow def integrateisorayworld(origin, dir, tstart, tend, ustepsize, urefinementiterations, uIsovalue, uLightAngle, uenableshadows, udomainmin, udomainmax): rescolor = vec3(0.0) reshit = False # Guard against invalid bounds if tstart >= tend: return rescolor, reshit # Initialize with the first sample inside the volume bounds tprev = tstart dprev = sampleiso(origin + tprev dir, uIsovalue) # Handle case where ray starts exactly on the surface if abs(dprev) < 1e-6: phit = origin + tprev dir lightdirworld = normalize(vec3(cos(uLightAngle 2.0 3.141592653589793), sin(uLightAngle 2.0 3.141592653589793), -1.0)) rescolor = shadeisopoint(phit, lightdirworld, uenableshadows, ustepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue) reshit = True return rescolor, reshit lightdirworld = normalize(vec3(cos(uLightAngle 2.0 3.141592653589793), sin(uLightAngle 2.0 3.141592653589793), -1.0)) tcurr = tstart + ustepsize while tcurr <= tend: dcurr = sampleiso(origin + tcurr dir, uIsovalue) if hassignchange(dprev, dcurr): thit = refineisohitbisection(origin, dir, tprev, tcurr, dprev, dcurr, urefinementiterations) phit = origin + thit dir rescolor = shadeisopoint(phit, lightdirworld, uenableshadows, ustepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue) reshit = True break tprev = tcurr dprev = dcurr tcurr += ustepsize return rescolor, reshit A zero-order interpolation ray casting algorithm for generating images of surfaces in binary volumetric data without explicit boundary detection or hidden-surface removal. It distinguishes itself by operating on binary occupancy grids (voxels are either inside or outside) rather than continuous scalar fields, relying on discrete occupancy checks rather than sign-change detection or interpolation. It is chosen when data is already binarized and high-performance, low-complexity rendering is required. Iso-surface Bisection Tracing renders implicit surfaces directly from volumetric scalar fields by tracing rays and locating the zero-crossing of the signed function g(t) = f(\mathbf{x}(t)) - c without extracting polygon meshes. It distinguishes itself from standard ray marching by using interval arithmetic to bound the function over continuous intervals, guaranteeing that no surface features (such as thin shells, cusps, or near-tangent intersections) are missed regardless of sampling density. Unlike Binary Ray Casting, which relies on discrete occupancy grids, and 1-Pass Isosurface Raycaster Adaptive, which uses adaptive step sizes, this method uses fixed-step traversal to detect sign changes followed by deterministic bisection refinement, or interval-arithmetic bisection for robust black-box functions. A single-pass compute shader raycasting method that performs isosurface extraction with adaptive step sizing. It uses a scalar field texture to find the isosurface and a gradient texture for Phong shading. It is chosen when computational resources are limited but higher accuracy than fixed-step marching is needed, adapting the step size based on local field gradients. A minor variant that visualizes the Euclidean distance between pixel coordinates and surface coordinates using a log-scale gamma correction. Definition: It computes the distance d between the pixel's projected surface coordinate \mathbf{s} and the pixel center \mathbf{p}, then applies a logarithmic transformation and gamma correction to produce a depth-aware visualization. Formula: d = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}\|2, \quad l = \log(\max(d, 10^{-2})), \quad v = \left(\frac{l - l{\min}}{l{\max} - l{\min}}\right)^{1/2.33} where l{\min} and l{\max} are the minimum and maximum log-distances across the batch. Parameters: The lower bound for the log argument is clamped to 10^{-2} to prevent \log(0), and the gamma exponent is fixed at 1/2.33 \approx 0.429. Implementation: logdists = ( pxcoords.sub(surfacecoords).norm(dim=-1, p=2, keepdim=True).clamp(1e-2, float('inf')).log()) return ( logdists.sub(logdists.min()).div(logdists.max().sub(logdists.min())).pow(1 / 2.33)) The technique originates from the foundational work on ray tracing by Appel (1968) and Whitted (1980), who established the image-order approach of shooting rays from the eye to determine visibility. Engel et al. (2006) specifically applied these principles to volume graphics, noting that iso-surface rendering in volumes is a special case of transfer function evaluation where only one non-zero solution exists. It is widely used in medical imaging for virtual endoscopy, where visualizing the interior of hollow organs (like the colon or blood vessels) requires precise surface extraction from CT or MRI scalar data. The method contrasts with rasterization by processing pixels in image order, which simplifies visibility handling but can be slower for large screen-space objects. name: Deferred Shading for Isosurfaces
head: Curvature Estimation, Deferred Shading with Differential Properties, Differential Surface Properties Computation, Gradient and Hessian Estimation, Image-Space Shading
body:
Deferred Shading for Isosurfaces is a multi-pass image-space technique that decouples surface property computation from lighting by calculating position, gradient, Hessian, and curvature in separate rendering passes before applying shading. It solves the problem of achieving high-quality, physically-based shading and non-photorealistic effects on isosurfaces extracted from discrete scalar volumes without the overhead of reconstructing explicit triangle meshes. Unlike sibling methods that compute shading during ray-casting or rely on mesh generation, this approach computes differential properties in image space, making its complexity independent of the underlying grid size. The method operates as a pipeline of five distinct rendering passes. Each pass renders a full-screen quad to invoke a fragment shader for every pixel, writing results to off-screen floating-point pixel buffers (textures). Input: A 3D scalar volume texture V. Intermediate Outputs: Position image (pos): 3D coordinates of the isosurface intersection. Gradient image (g): RGB floating-point image storing 
abla f. Hessian image (H): Stored in two RGB floating-point images, storing the six unique second partial derivatives. Curvature images: Two floating-point targets storing principal curvatures (\kappa1, \kappa2) and directions (e1, e2). Final Output: The shaded color image. Volume Texture: 3D texture containing the scalar field f(x,y,z). 1D Filter Weight Textures: Used for tri-cubic B-spline convolution weights. Off-screen Buffers: Floating-point render targets (typically RGBA32F or similar) to store vector and matrix data per pixel. 1. Pass 1: Ray-Casting (Position) Input: Volume V. Action: Perform ray-casting to find the first intersection with the isosurface. Store the 3D world position of the intersection in the position image (pos). Note: This step typically requires 3 passes if using specific brick-based skipping optimizations, but fundamentally outputs the position. 2. Pass 2: Gradient Computation Input: Position image (pos), Volume V. Action: Compute the gradient \mathbf{g} = 
abla f in three rendering passes (one for each component gx, gy, gz). Method: For each component, evaluate a tri-cubic B-spline convolution sum. This requires 8 texture fetches from the 3D volume texture and 3 fetches from 1D filter weight textures. Output: Store \mathbf{g} in a single RGB floating-point image. 3. Pass 3: Hessian Computation Input: Position image (pos), Volume V. Action: Compute the Hessian matrix \mathbf{H} = 
abla \mathbf{g} (second partial derivatives) in six rendering passes, one for each unique component (f{xx}, f{yy}, f{zz}, f{xy}, f{xz}, f{yz}) due to symmetry. Method: Analogous to gradient computation, using tri-cubic filtering. Each pass uses either 11 or 14 texture fetches. Output: Store the six coefficients in two RGB floating-point images. 4. Pass 4: Curvature Estimation Input: Gradient image (\mathbf{g}), Hessian images (\mathbf{H}). Action: Compute principal curvature magnitudes \kappa1, \kappa2 and directions \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 in a single rendering pass. Formulas: The shape operator \mathbf{S} is defined as the tangent space projection of the normalized Hessian: \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{P}^T  rac{\mathbf{H}}{|\mathbf{g}|} \mathbf{P} where \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{I} -  rac{\mathbf{g}\mathbf{g}^T}{|\mathbf{g}|^2} is the projection matrix onto the tangent plane. Let \mathbf{A} be the 2 	imes 2 representation of \mathbf{S} in the tangent basis. The principal curvatures are the eigenvalues of \mathbf{A}: \kappa{1,2} =  rac{1}{2} \left( 	ext{trace}(\mathbf{A}) \pm \sqrt{	ext{trace}(\mathbf{A})^2 - 4 \det(\mathbf{A})} ight) The principal directions \mathbf{e}i in the tangent basis (defined by basis vectors \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) are computed as: \mathbf{e}i = \kappai \mathbf{u} + (\kappai + a{22} - a{11}) \mathbf{v} Output: Store \kappa1, \kappa2 and \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 in two floating-point targets. 5. Pass 5: Shading Input: Position (pos), Gradient (\mathbf{g}), Curvatures (\kappa1, \kappa2, \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2). Action: Render the final shaded image using the pre-computed properties. Effects: Blinn-Phong/Tone Shading: Uses the normal vector \mathbf{n} = \pm \mathbf{g}/|\mathbf{g}|. Curvature Color Mapping: Maps \kappa1, \kappa2, mean curvature (\kappa1+\kappa2)/2, or Gaussian curvature \kappa1\kappa2 to colors via 1D or 2D lookup textures. Accessibility Shading: Uses a 1D or 2D curvature transfer function to darken areas with large negative maximum curvature. Curvature-Aligned Flow Advection: Projects 3D curvature direction vectors to the 2D image plane and advects flow on a per-pixel basis. Non-Photorealistic Effects: Silhouette outlining (thickness controlled by curvature) and ridge/valley line depiction (specified in the \kappa1, \kappa2 domain). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pass1raycasting(volume): # Output: posimage (3D float) for each pixel (x, y): ray = generatecameraray(x, y) intersection = raycastvolume(ray, volume) posimage[x, y] = intersection.position def pass2gradient(posimage, volume): # Output: gradimage (3D float, RGB) # Compute one component per pass (gx, gy, gz) for component in [0, 1, 2]: for each pixel (x, y): p = posimage[x, y] # Tri-cubic B-spline convolution for partial derivative # 8 fetches from volume, 3 from 1D filter weights val = tricubicpartialderivative(volume, p, component) gradimage[x, y][component] = val def pass3hessian(posimage, volume): # Output: hessimage1, hessimage2 (3D float, RGB each) # 6 unique components: fxx, fyy, fzz, fxy, fxz, fyz components = ['fxx', 'fyy', 'fzz', 'fxy', 'fxz', 'fyz'] for i, comp in enumerate(components): for each pixel (x, y): p = posimage[x, y] # 11 or 14 texture fetches depending on implementation val = tricubicsecondderivative(volume, p, comp) if i < 3: hessimage1[x, y][i] = val else: hessimage2[x, y][i-3] = val def pass4curvature(gradimage, hessimage1, hessimage2): # Output: curvmagimage (2D float), curvdirimage (2D float) for each pixel (x, y): g = gradimage[x, y] # Reconstruct Hessian matrix H from two RGB images H = reconstructhessian(hessimage1[x, y], hessimage2[x, y]) normg = length(g) if normg < epsilon: curvmagimage[x, y] = 0 curvdirimage[x, y] = 0 continue # Shape operator S = P^T (H / |g|) P # P = I - (g g^T) / |g|^2 P = identitymatrix() - outerproduct(g, g) / (normg normg) S = transpose(P) @ (H / normg) @ P # Project S to 2x2 tangent basis A # Basis vectors u, v are orthogonal to g u, v = computetangentbasis(g) a11 = dot(u, S @ u) a12 = dot(u, S @ v) a21 = dot(v, S @ u) a22 = dot(v, S @ v) traceA = a11 + a22 detA = a11 a22 - a12 a21 discriminant = traceA2 - 4 detA if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0 sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) k1 = 0.5 (traceA + sqrtdisc) k2 = 0.5 (traceA - sqrtdisc) curvmagimage[x, y] = [k1, k2] # Principal directions in tangent basis e1tangent = k1 u + (k1 + a22 - a11) v e2tangent = k2 u + (k2 + a22 - a11) v curvdirimage[x, y] = [e1tangent, e2tangent] def pass5shading(posimage, gradimage, curvmagimage, curvdirimage): # Output: finalimage for each pixel (x, y): g = gradimage[x, y] k1, k2 = curvmagimage[x, y] # Normal n = normalize(g) # Example: Blinn-Phong lightdir =... viewdir =... halfvec = normalize(lightdir + viewdir) diff = max(0, dot(n, lightdir)) spec = pow(max(0, dot(n, halfvec)), shininess) color = ambient + diff diffuse + spec specular # Example: Curvature Mapping # color = mapcurvaturetocolor(k1, k2) finalimage[x, y] = color Filter Weights: Tri-cubic B-spline filters are used for reconstruction. Precision: Floating-point render targets are required to store gradient, Hessian, and curvature data without quantization artifacts. Degenerate Input: If |\mathbf{g}| \approx 0 (flat regions or noise), the normal and curvature are undefined. A guard value (e.g., zero curvature) should be used. Flow Advection Seams: Curvature direction vectors are not uniquely oriented (sign ambiguity), which can cause visible seams in flow advection visualizations. A rendering pipeline used in conjunction with raycasting-based rasterization of elliptical splats. It implements a deferred shading stage similar to the isosurface method but adapted for surface splatting techniques. Complexity: The complexity is independent of the grid size, relying only on image-space operations. Performance: On an NVIDIA GeForce 6800, each property computation required 1 to 6 rendering passes, each rendering a single screen-aligned quad. Memory: Requires multiple floating-point off-screen buffers (position, gradient, Hessian, curvature). Strengths: High-quality shading and non-photorealistic effects; decoupled from volume sampling; real-time rates for flow advection. Limitations: High number of rendering passes (up to 19 total including ray-casting); potential seams in flow advection due to orientation ambiguity. When to use: When high-quality differential property visualization (curvature, flow) is required for isosurfaces without mesh generation overhead. The method was introduced by Christoph Schüller, Daniel Weiskopf, and Thomas Ertl in their 2005 paper "Real-Time Ray-Casting and Advanced Shading of Discrete Isosurfaces". It builds on earlier work in differential properties of volumes [SH05] and curvature estimation [KWTM03]. The technique is part of the broader field of image-space volume rendering and deferred shading. Real-Time Ray-Casting and Advanced Shading of Discrete Isosurfaces, https://cgl.ethz.ch/people/archive/siggc/publications/eg05.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, https://github.com/sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Surface shading for thresholded volumes
head: Boundary normal estimation, Z-buffer shading
body:
Surface shading for thresholded volumes applies lighting models to isosurfaces extracted from scalar volumes by determining surface geometry and illumination in image space or via rasterization hardware, distinct from direct volume rendering shading. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Deferred Shading for Isosurfaces by avoiding the high memory and computational costs of per-ray cell storage or repeated neighbor-finding, often relying on z-buffer slopes or precomputed gradients rather than deferred multi-pass normal accumulation. The method determines surface appearance for pixels where a ray intersects an isosurface defined by a threshold f(X) = c. The core challenge is estimating the surface normal \mathbf{n} and applying a lighting model, typically Lambertian, without the overhead of full deferred shading. Input: Scalar volume data f(x,y,z), threshold value c, light direction \mathbf{l}, ambient intensity Ia, diffuse intensity Id, and depth buffer (z-buffer) or position/gradient buffers. Output: Final color C for each pixel. 1. Z-Buffer: Stores depth z of the first hit for each pixel. 2. Position Buffer (Optional): Stores 3D intersection point \mathbf{p} and distance d (if available from a previous pass). 3. Gradient Buffer (Optional): Stores precomputed voxel gradients 
abla f in RGB components of a texture or frame buffer. Normals can be estimated using one of three approaches: 1. Projected Slope (Z-buffer based): Compute the slope of the projected surface using z-buffer values at neighboring pixels (x \pm 1, y) and (x, y \pm 1). nx \approx  rac{z(x+1, y) - z(x-1, y)}{2}, \quad ny \approx  rac{z(x, y+1) - z(x, y-1)}{2} The normal is \mathbf{n} = (-nx, -ny, 1) normalized. 2. Geometry (Boundary-based): Determine orientation from the cube face and its neighbors in the boundary of the opaque volume. This requires knowing which voxel face was intersected and its adjacency. 3. Gradient (Finite Differences): Compute the gradient of f(X) using finite differences at neighboring voxels. 
abla f \approx \left(  rac{f(x+h, y, z) - f(x-h, y, z)}{2h}, \dots ight) The normal is \mathbf{n} = 
abla f / \|
abla f\|. Shades distant pixels darker using only z-buffer depth values. C = Ia + Id \cdot  rac{z{max} - z}{z{max} - z{min}} where z is the depth, and z{min}, z{max} are near and far plane depths. Uses the estimated normal \mathbf{n} and light direction \mathbf{l}. I = Ia + Id (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) where \mathbf{n} is the normalized normal and \mathbf{l} is the normalized light vector. Renders a surface proximity map by normalizing the logarithmic distance to the surface. P = \left(  rac{\log(d) - \min(\log)}{\max(\log) - \min(\log)} ight)^{1/2.33} where d is the surface distance, clamped to [10^{-2}, \infty) before logging. 1. Thresholding: Render the volume to identify isosurface intersections. This can be done via raycasting or rasterization with alpha testing. 2. Buffer Population: Store depth in Z-buffer. Optionally store position \mathbf{p} and/or gradient 
abla f in auxiliary buffers. 3. Normal Computation: If using Z-buffer: Compute slopes from neighboring depth values. If using Gradient Buffer: Read 
abla f directly. If using Raycasting: Compute 
abla f via finite differences at intersection point. 4. Lighting Calculation: Compute \mathbf{n} = 	ext{normalize}(	ext{estimated normal}). Compute diffuse term D = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0). Apply material color M (from transfer function or constant). C = M \cdot (Ia + Id \cdot D). 5. Output: Write C to frame buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def surfaceshadingthresholded(volume, threshold, lightdir, ambientintensity, diffuseintensity, gradientstep): """ Computes surface shading for a thresholded volume using gradient-based normals. Assumes a previous pass has identified intersection points. """ # 1. Identify intersection points (simplified: assume we have a list of hits) # In practice, this is done via raycasting or rasterization alpha-test. hits = findisosurfacehits(volume, threshold) outputimage = zeroslike(volume.shape[:2]) # 2D image for hit in hits: pos = hit.position # 2. Compute gradient using central differences gradx = (volume[pos.x + gradientstep, pos.y, pos.z] - volume[pos.x - gradientstep, pos.y, pos.z]) / (2.0 gradientstep) grady = (volume[pos.x, pos.y + gradientstep, pos.z] - volume[pos.x, pos.y - gradientstep, pos.z]) / (2.0 gradientstep) gradz = (volume[pos.x, pos.y, pos.z + gradientstep] - volume[pos.x, pos.y, pos.z - gradientstep]) / (2.0 gradientstep) gradient = vec3(gradx, grady, gradz) normal = normalize(gradient) # 3. Compute Lambertian diffuse factor # Ensure lightdir is normalized light = normalize(lightdir) lambert = max(dot(normal, light), 0.0) # 4. Sample material color (simplified: constant or from transfer function) # For thresholded volumes, material is often uniform or based on value materialcolor = vec3(1.0) # Placeholder for transfer function lookup # 5. Final color color = materialcolor (ambientintensity + diffuseintensity lambert) # 6. Write to image outputimage[hit.screenx, hit.screeny] = color return outputimage No Hit: If no surface is intersected (e.g., closest.w <= 0.0), output a default color (e.g., white or background). Gradient Noise: Finite difference gradients can be noisy in low-resolution volumes. Smoothing or higher-order differences may be needed. Z-buffer Slopes: Estimating normals from z-buffer slopes assumes smooth surfaces; sharp edges may produce incorrect normals. Lighting Limitations: Hardware-based methods (e.g., using OpenGL color matrix) may be restricted to single light sources and monochrome displays if register space is limited. Distinct from DVR: These shading functions are applied after thresholding and are distinct from direct volume rendering shading. A method that performs fast, shadow-less Lambertian shading for isosurfaces extracted from thresholded volumes. It distinguishes itself by explicitly avoiding deferred normal computation to prevent prohibitive memory and computational costs associated with per-ray cell storage or repeated neighbor-finding. While the underlying ray traversal remains single-ray based, the shading phase aggregates rays into packets to exploit parallelism. A volume rendering technique that extracts surfaces from a 3D volume using a threshold and renders them using raycasting with Phong illumination, operating on multiple object volumes simultaneously. A visualization technique that renders a surface proximity map by normalizing the logarithmic distance to the surface. It visualizes precomputed surface distances using log normalization and gamma correction, identical in formula to Distance Shading but operating on a distance scalar field. Step: Calculate the SDF value f(pi) at the intersection point. Compute \log(f(pi)). Normalize this value to the range [0, 1]. Brighter pixels indicate rays that terminated further away from the surface. Formula: P = \left(  rac{\log(d) - \min(\log)}{\max(\log) - \min(\log)} ight)^{1/2.33}, where d is surface distance, clamped to 10^{-2}, \infty) before logging. A single-pass rendering technique for shaded isosurfaces using multi-stage rasterization, eliminating the need for frame buffer copying and allowing colored ambient and diffuse light sources. Step: Map the interpolated gradient to the first constant color register (variable A in the final combiner's primary color context). Variable A is assigned to primary color (Id) and multiplied with variable B mapped to the dot product. Compute the dot product of the light vector and the gradient in the RGB-portion of the second general combiner. Set variable C to zero and map variable D to secondary color (Ia) for the final combiner to compute the equation: Id \cdot (L \cdot N) + Ia. Pitfall: It is not possible to write initial values to the two spare registers displayed in Fig. 2, limiting the ability to add a second diffuse light source without sacrificing trilinear interpolation or separate ambient/diffuse colors. An efficient algorithm to display shaded isosurfaces by exploiting rasterization hardware, evaluating local illumination equation. Restricted to single light source and monochrome display. Step: Store voxel gradient vector components in RGB components of a 3D-texture. Store intensity values in the alpha-component. Render into frame buffer using OpenGL alpha-test to display specified isovalues. Reinsert the frame buffer (containing voxel gradient in RGB) into the rasterization pipeline. Use OpenGL color matrix to compute dot-product with light vector. This is a two-pass technique. Formula: Local illumination: I = Ia + Id 	imes (	ilde{n} \cdot 	ilde{l}), where 	ilde{l} is light direction, 	ilde{n} is isosurface normal (volume gradient), Ia is ambient intensity, Id is diffuse intensity. A shading pass that computes lighting for the isosurface found in the previous pass, using [gradient-based normals and Lambertian shading. Step: Sample the closest position buffer. Compute gradient using central differences: positive samples at pos + vec3(h,0,0), etc., negative samples at pos - vec3(h,0,0), etc. Gradient is (positive - negative) / (2.0 h). Normalize gradient to get normal. Compute Lambertian diffuse factor: float lambert = max(dot(normal, uLight), 0.0). Sample material color from transfer function using volume position. Output final color: oColor = vec4(material lambert, 1). Parameter: uGradientStep: The step size h used for finite difference gradient calculation. uLight: The light direction vector. Pitfall: If closest.w <= 0.0 (no hit), output white vec4(1). Time Complexity: Depends on the normal estimation method. Z-buffer slope estimation is O(1) per pixel (constant number of neighbors). Gradient estimation via finite differences is O(1) per hit if gradients are precomputed, or O(N) if computed on-the-fly during raycasting. Memory Complexity: Z-buffer shading requires only a depth buffer. Gradient-based methods may require storing gradients in a texture or buffer, increasing memory usage by 3 	imes the resolution (for RGB gradients). Performance: Hardware-accelerated methods (e.g., Fast Shaded Isosurfaces) can achieve interactive frame rates by leveraging rasterization pipelines. Deferred shading methods are more flexible but slower due to multiple passes. Strengths: Simple to implement for basic shading; efficient for static scenes; leverages existing graphics hardware. Limitations: Limited lighting models (often Lambertian only); single light source restrictions in some hardware implementations; normal estimation errors at boundaries or noisy data. When to Use: Real-time visualization of isosurfaces where performance is critical and complex lighting is not required. When Not to Use: When accurate, high-quality lighting with multiple light sources and shadows is needed; consider Deferred Shading for Isosurfaces or raytracing. The technique originated with the need for efficient visualization of medical and scientific data, particularly bone and tissue structures. Early methods relied on z-buffer slopes for simplicity. Later, with the advent of programmable graphics hardware, methods like Fast Shaded Isosurfaces exploited rasterization pipelines for interactive performance. The approach is distinct from direct volume rendering, focusing on the surface properties of thresholded data rather than the volumetric integration of light. name: Shading and Frame Buffer Filling
head: ISORender, Lambertian shading with no shadows, Packet Ray Casting with Lambertian Shading, Simple Lambertian shading with no shadows
body: This method performs fast, shadow-less Lambertian shading for isosurfaces extracted from thresholded volumes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly avoiding deferred normal computation to prevent prohibitive memory and computational costs associated with per-ray cell storage or repeated neighbor-finding. While the underlying ray traversal remains single-ray based, the shading phase aggregates rays into packets to exploit parallelism. Inputs and Outputs: Input: uClosest texture containing the closest hit position and distance for each pixel. Input: uLight uniform vec3 representing the light direction. Input: uDiffuse uniform vec3 representing the diffuse color/material property. Output: oColor fragment color. Data Structures: uClosest: A 2D texture where each texel stores a vec4. The components are interpreted as the 3D hit position (x, y, z) and the distance w along the ray. If w \le 0, no intersection was found. Parameters: Gradient step size h = 0.005. Steps: 1. Sample Hit Position: For each pixel, sample the closest hit position from the uClosest texture. \text{closest} = \text{texture}(uClosest, vPosition) where vPosition is the fragment coordinate. 2. Check Intersection: If \text{closest}.w > 0, an isosurface intersection exists. Proceed to normal estimation and shading. If \text{closest}.w \le 0, output white and terminate. \text{if } \text{closest}.w \le 0: \quad oColor = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) 3. Normal Estimation: Compute the surface normal using gradient-based normal estimation. The gradient is approximated using central differences on the volume data at the hit position. The step size h is fixed at 0.005. \mathbf{n} = \nabla V(\mathbf{p}) \approx \left( \frac{V(\mathbf{p} + h\mathbf{e}x) - V(\mathbf{p} - h\mathbf{e}x)}{2h}, \frac{V(\mathbf{p} + h\mathbf{e}y) - V(\mathbf{p} - h\mathbf{e}y)}{2h}, \frac{V(\mathbf{p} + h\mathbf{e}z) - V(\mathbf{p} - h\mathbf{e}z)}{2h} \right) Normalize \mathbf{n} to unit length. 4. Lambertian Shading: Compute the diffuse lighting factor using the dot product of the normal \mathbf{n} and the light direction \mathbf{l} (from uLight). \text{lambert} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0.0) 5. Output Color: Multiply the material diffuse color by the lighting factor. oColor = \text{uDiffuse} \times \text{lambert} The alpha component is set to 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) class Vec4: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w def dot(a, b): return a.xb.x + a.yb.y + a.zb.z def normalize(v): mag = (v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2)0.5 return Vec3(v.x/mag, v.y/mag, v.z/mag) def maxval(a, b): return a if a > b else b def texture2d(tex, uv): return tex[uv] def texture3d(tex, p): return tex[p] def shadingandframebufferfilling(uClosest, uLight, uDiffuse, uVolume, vPosition): # Step 1: Sample closest hit position and distance closest = texture2d(uClosest, vPosition) # Step 2: Check intersection if closest.w <= 0.0: return Vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Step 3: Compute normal via gradient-based estimation h = 0.005 p = Vec3(closest.x, closest.y, closest.z) # Central differences for gradient gx = (texture3d(uVolume, p + Vec3(h, 0.0, 0.0)).x - texture3d(uVolume, p - Vec3(h, 0.0, 0.0)).x) / (2.0 h) gy = (texture3d(uVolume, p + Vec3(0.0, h, 0.0)).x - texture3d(uVolume, p - Vec3(0.0, h, 0.0)).x) / (2.0 h) gz = (texture3d(uVolume, p + Vec3(0.0, 0.0, h)).x - texture3d(uVolume, p - Vec3(0.0, 0.0, h)).x) / (2.0 h) normal = normalize(Vec3(gx, gy, gz)) # Step 4: Compute Lambertian diffuse factor lightdir = normalize(uLight) lambert = maxval(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) # Step 5: Output color oColor = Vec4(uDiffuse.x lambert, uDiffuse.y lambert, uDiffuse.z lambert, 1.0) return oColor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Intersection: Pixels with no hit output white. Normal Computation Cost: Deferring normal computation is avoided due to the prohibitive cost of storing each cell per ray or repeating neighbor-finding. Precision: The method yields single-precision, numerically stable results. This method performs fast, shadow-less Lambertian shading for isosurfaces extracted from thresholded volumes by batching ray generation and shading operations using a packet architecture. It is distinguished from sibling methods by explicitly avoiding deferred normal computation to prevent prohibitive memory and computational costs associated with per-ray cell storage or repeated neighbor-finding. While the underlying ray traversal remains single-ray based, the shading phase aggregates rays into packets to exploit parallelism. Time Complexity: The shading pass is O(1) per pixel, dominated by texture sampling and arithmetic operations. The packet architecture allows diffuse shading to be performed in batch, likely delivering a speedup over a more conventional single-ray tracer. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Suitable for fast ray casting of isosurfaces where shadowing is not required. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory footprint, fast shading via packet batching. Limitations: No shadows, limited to Lambertian shading, normal estimation depends on gradient accuracy. name: Lambertian Shading with Packet Architecture
head: Batch diffuse shading, Batch diffuse shading with packet architecture, Packet Ray Tracing with Lambertian Shading, Packet Shading
body: This method performs fast, shadow-less Lambertian shading for isosurfaces extracted from thresholded volumes by batching ray generation and shading operations using a packet architecture. It is distinguished from sibling methods by explicitly avoiding deferred normal computation to prevent prohibitive memory and computational costs associated with per-ray cell storage or repeated neighbor-finding. While the underlying ray traversal remains single-ray based, the shading phase aggregates rays into packets to exploit parallelism. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of rays intersecting the isosurface, derived from the parent Shading and Frame Buffer Filling stage. Output: Shaded color values written to the frame buffer. Data Structures: Ray Packet: A container holding a group of rays, where each ray stores origin, direction, traversal state, hit point, and computed normal. The exact internal layout is not specified in the sources. Normal Vector: Computed immediately upon intersection, not deferred. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Generate rays for the image plane and group them into packets. 2. Traversal: Perform ray traversal against the volume data structure (e.g., octree) using single-ray processing, as traversal does not employ packets. 3. Intersection Detection: Identify when a ray intersects the isosurface during traversal. 4. Normal Computation: Compute the surface normal at the intersection point immediately. Deferring this computation is prohibited due to the prohibitive cost of storing each cell per ray or repeating the neighbor-finding process. 5. Batch Shading: Perform diffuse shading in batch for all rays in the current packet. Formula: C = kd \max(0, N \cdot L) + ka C: Final color vector kd: Diffuse reflection coefficient (scalar or vector) N: Surface normal at the intersection point L: Light direction vector ka: Ambient reflection coefficient (scalar or vector) Note: Exact coefficients and light direction are not specified in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction self.hit = False self.hitpoint = None self.normal = None self.color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.volumedata = None def normalize(v): length = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] if length > 0 else [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] def computenormal(point, volumedata): # Central finite difference gradient of the scalar field eps = 1e-4 gx = volumedata(point + [eps, 0, 0]) - volumedata(point - [eps, 0, 0]) gy = volumedata(point + [0, eps, 0]) - volumedata(point - [0, eps, 0]) gz = volumedata(point + [0, 0, eps]) - volumedata(point - [0, 0, eps]) return [gx, gy, gz] def batchlambertianshading(rays, kd, ka, L): # Packet size is not specified in the sources. packetsize = 16 # Implementation-defined packets = [rays[i:i+packetsize] for i in range(0, len(rays), packetsize)] for packet in packets: for ray in packet: if ray.hit: ray.normal = computenormal(ray.hitpoint, ray.volumedata) ray.normal = normalize(ray.normal) for ray in packet: if ray.hit: diff = max(0.0, ray.normal[0]L[0] + ray.normal[1]L[1] + ray.normal[2]L[2]) ray.color = [kd diff + ka for in range(3)] Parameters: Shading Model: Simple Lambertian, no shadows. Packet Size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Deferred Normal Computation: Do not defer normal computation. Storing each cell per ray or repeating neighbor-finding is prohibitively costly. Traversal Architecture: Traversal does not use packets. Using packet traversal is not part of this method. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The packet architecture for shading likely delivers a speedup over a more conventional single-ray tracer. Strengths: Fast ray casting of isosurfaces; batch processing of shading operations. Limitations: No shadows; normal computation must be done immediately, limiting flexibility in shading pipelines. When to use: When fast, shadow-less Lambertian shading of isosurfaces is required. When not to use: When shadow rendering is required. This method is described in the context of interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. It is part of a pipeline that includes data compression, octree construction, and ray traversal. The approach emphasizes performance for interactive applications by simplifying the shading model and optimizing the shading phase through batching. name: Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement
head: Volumetric isosurface rendering, Iso Ray Casting, Isosurface Ray Casting, Iso-Surface Rendering, Isosurface mode
body:
Volumetric isosurface rendering with intersection refinement is a real-time technique that extracts an isosurface directly from a 3D volumetric scalar field during ray traversal, avoiding explicit polygon mesh extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes). It detects the surface by checking if the sampled scalar value equals or crosses the target isovalue, stops traversal at the first hit, and refines the intersection position to reduce discretization artifacts. Unlike Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR), which composites the entire volume, this method stops at the first hit, offering higher performance for opaque surfaces. It differs from Real-Time Ray-Casting and Advanced Shading of Discrete Isosurfaces by operating on implicit continuous data rather than discrete extracted meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric scalar field texture (f), camera parameters (view/projection matrices, position), an isovalue (uIsovalue), a ray marching step size (uStepSize), and rendering parameters (refinement iterations, shadow enablement). Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the color of the first isosurface intersection, shaded with lighting and shadows. Data Structures: The method relies on Uniform Buffer Objects (UBOs) and a 3D texture sampler. 1. CameraUBO (std140, binding=0): mat4 uView: View matrix. mat4 uProj: Projection matrix. vec3 uCameraPos: Camera position in world space. float pad0: Padding to align to 16 bytes. 2. VolumeUBO (std140, binding=1): vec3 uDomainMin: Minimum bounds of the volume domain. float uStepSize: Step size for ray marching and normal computation. vec3 uDomainMax: Maximum bounds of the volume domain. float uIsovalue: The scalar threshold defining the isosurface. float uLightAngle: Angle for light direction calculation (mapped to 2\pi). int uEnableShadows: Boolean flag (0 or 1) to enable/disable shadow rays. int uRefinementIterations: Number of bisection/refinement iterations. float pad1: Padding. 3. Volume Texture: sampler3D volumeTex at binding=0. Sampled using standard trilinear interpolation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Construction and Box Intersection: For each fragment covered by the volume, construct a ray origin O and direction D from the camera. Compute the intersection parameters t{min} and t{max} for the ray with the volume domain [uDomainMin, uDomainMax]. If t{max} \le t{min}, the ray misses the volume; return empty/no hit. Set t{start} = \max(t{min}, 0.0) and t{end} = t{max}. 2. Ray Marching and Surface Detection: Initialize t{prev} = t{start}. Sample the scalar field at the start position: d{prev} = f(O + t{prev} D) - uIsovalue. Iterate t{curr} from t{start} + uStepSize to t{end} with step uStepSize. At each step, sample the field: d{curr} = f(O + t{curr} D) - uIsovalue. Check for a sign change between d{prev} and d{curr}. A sign change indicates the isosurface lies within the interval [t{prev}, t{curr}]. (Note: Some implementations simply stop when the sampled value exceeds the isovalue). 3. Intersection Refinement: If a sign change is detected, refine the hit position t{hit} using one of two methods described in the sources: Method A: Bisection Refinement Given interval [ta, tb] (initially t{prev}, t{curr}) with signs da, db: 1. Compute midpoint tm = (ta + tb) / 2. 2. Evaluate dm = f(O + tm D) - uIsovalue. 3. If da \cdot dm \le 0, set tb = tm, db = dm; else set ta = tm, da = dm. 4. Repeat for uRefinementIterations (typical range 0–10). 5. Final hit: t{hit} = (ta + tb) / 2. Method B: Linear Interpolation Refinement Let X{prev} = O + t{prev} D and X{next} = O + t{curr} D. Let f{prev} and f{next} be the raw scalar values at these points. 1. Calculate new point: X{new} = (X{next} - X{prev})  rac{uIsovalue - f{prev}}{f{next} - f{prev}} + X{prev} 2. Read volume value f{new} at X{new}. 3. If f{new} > uIsovalue, assign X{new} to X{prev} and f{new} to f{prev}. Otherwise, assign to X{next} and f{next}. 4. Iterate until convergence or a fixed iteration count (typically ~10). 4. Hit Position and Normal Computation: Compute the hit position: P{hit} = O + t{hit} D. Estimate the surface normal using central differences with step size h = uStepSize: gx = f(P{hit} + (h,0,0)) - f(P{hit} - (h,0,0)) gy = f(P{hit} + (0,h,0)) - f(P{hit} - (0,h,0)) gz = f(P{hit} + (0,0,h)) - f(P{hit} - (0,0,h)) The gradient is 
abla f = (gx, gy, gz). The normal is the normalized negative gradient: n = - rac{
abla f}{|
abla f|} The negative gradient ensures the normal points outward toward the lighter medium. Note: In some implementations (e.g., Met.3D), the gradient computation may vary based on grid type (pressure, hybrid, auxiliary). 5. Shading and Shadows: Calculate the light direction vector \ell from uLightAngle (mapped to 2\pi). Compute Lambertian diffuse term: L = \max(0, n \cdot \ell). Shadow Ray Traversal: If uEnableShadows is true, cast a shadow ray from P{hit} in direction \ell. 1. Start at t = 2 \cdot uStepSize to avoid self-intersection due to precision errors. 2. March with step uStepSize. 3. If f(O{shadow} + t \ell) \ge uIsovalue before leaving the volume, return shadow factor S = 0. 4. If the ray exits the volume without hitting, return S = 1. Color Assignment: The final color is computed as: Color = BaseColor \cdot L \cdot S BaseColor can be a fixed color, a color mapped from the isovalue via a transfer function, or a color derived from a secondary scalar field (e.g., coloring wind speed by temperature). Using the isovalue to fetch color avoids artifacts caused by transfer function interpolation at the surface. 6. Multiple Isosurfaces (Optional): If the surface is transparent or multiple isosurfaces are supported, the ray traversal continues after the first hit to composite nested surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfragment(origin, direction, domainmin, domainmax, stepsize, isovalue, refinementiterations, enableshadows, lightangle, volumedata): # 1. Ray-box intersection tmin = float('inf') tmax = float('-inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0.0: if origin[i] < domainmin[i] or origin[i] > domainmax[i]: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: t1 = (domainmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (domainmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) if tmax <= tmin: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) tstart = max(tmin, 0.0) tend = tmax # 2. Ray marching and sign change detection tprev = tstart posprev = origin + tprev direction dprev = samplevolume(posprev, volumedata) - isovalue hit = False finalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) tcurr = tstart + stepsize while tcurr <= tend: poscurr = origin + tcurr direction dcurr = samplevolume(poscurr, volumedata) - isovalue if dprev dcurr <= 0.0: # Sign change detected, refine intersection ta, tb = tprev, tcurr da, db = dprev, dcurr for in range(refinementiterations): tm = (ta + tb) / 2.0 posm = origin + tm direction dm = samplevolume(posm, volumedata) - isovalue if da dm <= 0.0: tb, db = tm, dm else: ta, da = tm, dm thit = (ta + tb) / 2.0 phit = origin + thit direction # 3. Normal computation h = stepsize gx = samplevolume(phit + (h, 0.0, 0.0), volumedata) - samplevolume(phit - (h, 0.0, 0.0), volumedata) gy = samplevolume(phit + (0.0, h, 0.0), volumedata) - samplevolume(phit - (0.0, h, 0.0), volumedata) gz = samplevolume(phit + (0.0, 0.0, h), volumedata) - samplevolume(phit - (0.0, 0.0, h), volumedata) grad = (gx, gy, gz) normlen = sqrt(gxgx + gygy + gzgz) normal = (-gx/normlen, -gy/normlen, -gz/normlen) # 4. Lighting and shadows angle = lightangle 6.28318530718 lightdir = normalize((cos(angle), sin(angle), -1.0)) diffuse = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) shadow = 1.0 if enableshadows == 1: tshadow = 2.0 stepsize while True: pshadow = phit + tshadow lightdir if pshadow.x < domainmin.x or pshadow.y < domainmin.y or pshadow.z < domainmin.z or \ pshadow.x > domainmax.x or pshadow.y > domainmax.y or pshadow.z > domainmax.z: break if samplevolume(pshadow, volumedata) >= isovalue: shadow = 0.0 break tshadow += stepsize basecolor = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Fixed color; can be mapped from isovalue or secondary field finalcolor = (basecolor[0]diffuseshadow, basecolor[1]diffuseshadow, basecolor[2]diffuseshadow) hit = True break tprev, dprev = tcurr, dcurr tcurr += stepsize return (finalcolor[0], finalcolor[1], finalcolor[2], 1.0) def samplevolume(pos, volumedata): # Performs trilinear interpolation of the 3D volume texture at pos # Implementation depends on hardware/software backend pass Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray. Refinement adds a constant factor (k iterations) only when a hit is found. Shadow rays add another traversal pass. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storage for the 3D volume texture and small UBOs. No explicit mesh geometry is stored. Performance: Real-time on modern GPUs. Performance scales with step size and number of samples. Smaller step sizes increase accuracy but reduce frame rate. Optimizations: Empty-space skipping: Using a 32x32x32 brick min/max acceleration structure allows rays to jump over regions that cannot contain the isovalue. Interaction Step Size: A coarser step size can be used during camera interaction to maintain frame rate, with refinement restoring quality. Grid Type: Performance varies by grid type; hybrid or auxiliary pressure grids are significantly more expensive than simple pressure level grids due to complex sampling requirements. Strengths: No preprocessing/mesh extraction required. Dynamic isovalue changes are instantaneous without CPU geometry rebuilds. Avoids the high computational cost of full volume rendering (DVR) for opaque surfaces. High-quality intersection refinement reduces stair-stepping artifacts. Limitations: Discretization artifacts if refinement is insufficient or step size is too large. Self-intersection in shadow rays if not handled (requires offset start). This method was developed as a real-time GPU-based implementation for scientific visualization, notably in the SciVisLab framework. It is also implemented in Met.3D for meteorological data visualization and has been integrated into the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) as vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper2 with features like refined isosurface rendering and shadow mapping. The technique addresses the limitations of traditional isosurface extraction (marching cubes) by providing a direct, flexible, and performant way to visualize scalar fields in real-time. name: Cell-Based First-Hit Ray Casting
body: Cell-based first-hit ray casting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates iso-surface visualization by dividing the volume into cubic sub-volumes called macro-cells, storing encountered cells in a buffer to exploit inter-ray coherency, and avoiding unnecessary intersection tests for rays visiting the same cells. It performs iso-surfacing with interactive threshold adjustment, reducing average ray path lengths to only a few steps per pixel through volume subdivision and early termination. It sets itself apart from conventional ray casting by processing only macro-cells containing iso-surface portions and from Surface Fitting techniques by not requiring dedicated acceleration hardware or pre-computed surface meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset, a set of iso-value thresholds (e.g., in Hounsfield Units), a camera position and orientation, and an image resolution (e.g., 512x512). Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains a color value determined by the first iso-surface intersection along the corresponding view ray. Data Structures: 1. Min-Max Octree: The volume is organized as an octree. Each node represents a cubic sub-volume. Each node stores two scalar values: minval and maxval, representing the minimum and maximum data values within that sub-volume. Leaf nodes represent macro-cells. 2. Macro-Cell: A cubic sub-volume consisting of n^3 data cells (or (n+1)^3 voxels). n is a parameter typically between 3 and 10. 3. Cell Hit Buffer: A buffer storing cells encountered along the last ray cast. Each entry includes a flag indicating if a portion of an iso-surface is contained in that cell. This buffer is used to skip intersection tests for subsequent rays visiting the same cells. Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Construction: Divide the volume data into macro-cells of size n \times n \times n cells. Build the min-max octree. For each node, compute the minimum and maximum data values of the sub-space it represents. Leaf nodes correspond to macro-cells. 2. Octree Traversal and Macro-Cell Selection: Traverse the octree starting from the root. For each node, check if any of the specified iso-value thresholds lies between the node's minval and maxval. Only process the 8 child nodes if this condition is met. This effectively skips empty space. When a leaf node (macro-cell) passes the check, it contains a part of the iso-surface. 3. Macro-Cell Trimming: Trim the found macro-cell to the smallest cuboid containing its portions of the iso-surfaces. This reduces the area projected to the screen. 4. Projection and Rasterization: Project the trimmed macro-cell onto the image plane. Rasterize the projection to identify all pixels covered by the macro-cell. 5. Local Ray Casting: For each pixel covered by the projection that has not yet been assigned a color (i.e., not yet hit by an iso-surface in the current frame), cast a local ray through the macro-cell. The ray starts at the entry point into the macro-cell and stops when it hits an iso-surface or leaves the macro-cell. Viewing Order: Macro-cells and their child nodes must be processed in correct viewing order to ensure the first intersection determines the final pixel color. This is achieved by sorting child nodes according to the viewing vector during traversal, using a representative ray direction that intersects all sub-volumes. 6. Voxel Traversal and Boundary Detection: Use a fast voxel traversal algorithm (e.g., Amanatides and Woo) to detect cells pierced by the local ray within the macro-cell. For each intersected cell, determine if it is a boundary cell (containing data values both above and below one of the specified thresholds). Coherency Check: Before performing expensive intersection tests, check the Cell Hit Buffer. If the cell was encountered in the last ray and the buffer indicates an iso-surface portion is contained there, perform the intersection test; otherwise, skip it if the buffer indicates no surface. 7. Ray-Surface Intersection: If a boundary cell is found, execute a ray-surface intersection test. Fast Intersection Algorithm: Divide the ray path through the surface cell into two equal parts. Calculate the density values at the endpoints of each part. If an intersection exists (indicated by the density values), approximate the intersection point using linear interpolation. Note: An exact intersection algorithm (inverting trilinear interpolation) exists but is computationally expensive. The fast method yields slightly less accurate results but is significantly cheaper. 8. Shading and Output: If an intersection is found, calculate the gradient vector at the intersection point using trilinear interpolation of the volume data. Calculate a color value from the gradient (e.g., using lighting models). Assign the color to the corresponding pixel. If the iso-surface is opaque, mark the pixel such that no more local rays are cast at this pixel during the current frame. 9. Early Scanline Termination (Optional Optimization): Eliminate local rays that are highly probable not to find any intersections, further reducing ray counts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cellbasedfirsthitraycasting(volume, thresholds, camera, imagewidth, imageheight, n): """ volume: 3D array of scalar values thresholds: list of iso-values camera: object with position and direction vectors imagewidth, imageheight: int n: int, macro-cell dimension (cells per side) """ # 1. Build Min-Max Octree octree = buildminmaxoctree(volume, n) # 2. Initialize Output and Coherency Buffer image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) hitbuffer = {} # Maps cellid to boolean (hassurface) # 3. Traverse Octree in Viewing Order # Sort traversal order based on camera direction to ensure first-hit correctness nodestoprocess = [octree.root] while nodestoprocess: node = nodestoprocess.pop(0) # Check if node contains any iso-surface if not any(threshold in [node.minval, node.maxval] or (node.minval < threshold < node.maxval) for threshold in thresholds): continue if node.isleaf(): # Leaf node: Macro-cell macrocell = node.data # Trim macro-cell to smallest cuboid containing iso-surfaces trimmedcuboid = trimmacrocell(macrocell, thresholds) # Project trimmed cuboid to screen coveredpixels = projecttoscreen(trimmedcuboid, camera, imagewidth, imageheight) # Cast local rays for covered pixels for pixel in coveredpixels: if image[pixel.y, pixel.x] is not empty: continue # Pixel already hit ray = getrayforpixel(pixel, camera) # Traverse voxels in the macro-cell cellspierced = fastvoxeltraversal(ray, macrocell) for cell in cellspierced: # Check coherency buffer if cell.id in hitbuffer: if not hitbuffer[cell.id]: continue # Skip if buffer says no surface # Check if cell is a boundary cell if isboundarycell(cell, thresholds): # Perform fast ray-surface intersection intersectionpoint = fastraysurfaceintersection(ray, cell, thresholds) if intersectionpoint is not None: # Calculate gradient via trilinear interpolation gradient = trilineargradient(volume, intersectionpoint) # Compute color color = computecolor(gradient, camera) # Assign color image[pixel.y, pixel.x] = color # Mark pixel as hit markpixelhit(pixel) # Update coherency buffer for this cell hitbuffer[cell.id] = True break # Stop processing this ray for this pixel else: # Internal node: Add children to queue, sorted by viewing distance children = getsortedchildren(node, camera.direction) nodestoprocess.extend(children) return image def buildminmaxoctree(volume, n): """ Recursively builds a min-max octree. Leaf nodes represent macro-cells of size n x n x n cells. """ # Implementation details omitted for brevity, but involves: # 1. Dividing volume into n^3 blocks. # 2. Computing min/max for each block. # 3. Recursing if block is too large or needs subdivision. pass def trimmacrocell(macrocell, thresholds): """ Returns the smallest cuboid within the macrocell that contains any cell crossing a threshold. """ # Find min/max x, y, z indices of boundary cells pass def projecttoscreen(cuboid, camera, width, height): """ Rasterizes the 3D cuboid onto the 2D image plane. Returns list of pixel coordinates. """ pass def fastvoxeltraversal(ray, macrocell): """ Uses Amanatides and Woo algorithm to find cells pierced by ray. """ pass def isboundarycell(cell, thresholds): """ Returns True if cell contains values both above and below any threshold. """ for t in thresholds: if cell.minval < t < cell.maxval: return True return False def fastraysurfaceintersection(ray, cell, thresholds): """ Fast approximation: 1. Split ray segment in cell into two halves. 2. Evaluate density at endpoints. 3. If sign change, linearly interpolate intersection. """ # Implementation based on S1 description pass def trilineargradient(volume, point): """ Computes gradient using trilinear interpolation of volume data. """ pass def computecolor(gradient, camera): """ Standard lighting model (e.g., Phong) using gradient as normal. """ pass Parameters: n (Macro-cell size): The number of cells along one dimension of a macro-cell. Typical values range between 3 and 10. Iso-value Threshold: Determines visibility. Values vary by application (e.g., 0 HU for soft tissue, 1100 HU for stents). Image Resolution: Fixed at 512x512 in reported experiments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Macro-cell Size Trade-offs: Small macro-cells increase octree traversal and projection time, split rays into more segments, and increase expensive ray initialization steps for rays traveling along iso-surfaces without intersecting. Large macro-cells reduce the effectiveness of early scanline termination because small critical regions are less likely to be detected. Viewing Order: Ray segments must be processed in correct viewing order to ensure the first intersection determines the final pixel color. Failure to sort child nodes by viewing vector causes visibility artifacts. Coherency Buffer: Distance coding is not used because it would require recomputation for each new iso-value. Performance Degradation: Conventional ray casting can be faster than cell-based first-hit ray casting when soft tissue (low threshold) hides the stent, because ray-surface intersection distances are very short, reducing empty space traversal time. Cell-based suffers here because almost all macro-cells must be processed and fine-structured tissue creates "peep holes" delaying termination. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of macro-cells intersecting the iso-surface and the local ray path length. The technique reduces average ray path lengths to only a few steps per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the min-max octree and the cell hit buffer. The octree size is proportional to the volume size divided by n^3. Measured Performance: In virtual angioscopy (inside stented aorta) at 512x512 resolution: Minimum frame time 1.103s vs 1.783s (conventional); Average 1.291s vs 2.119s. At 450 HU threshold (bones/stent visible): Cell-based time 1.953s, Conventional 8.563s (Speedup 4.38x). At 1100 HU threshold (only stent visible): Cell-based time 0.609s, Conventional 12.781s (Speedup 20.98x). Ray path reduction (typical fly-through): Conventional 262,144 rays, 35.494 steps/pixel. Cell-based 1,147,347 rays, 15.626 steps/pixel. With optimizations (mt, est): 396,808 rays, 3.932 steps/pixel. Strengths: Fast perspective iso-surfacing, interactive threshold adjustment, no dedicated acceleration hardware required, good cache coherency (each macro-cell accessed once per frame). Limitations: Slower than conventional ray casting when low thresholds hide surfaces behind dense tissue due to "peep holes" and high macro-cell processing overhead. When to Use: Fast perspective iso-surfacing is required, especially for high thresholds where surfaces are sparse or for virtual endoscopy. When Not to Use: When low thresholds are used and surfaces are dense/hidden, or when exact intersection accuracy is critical and the fast approximation is insufficient. Cell-based first-hit ray casting was introduced by André Neubauer, Lukas Mroz, H. Hauser, and R. Wegenkittl in 2002. It was developed as part of the AlVis project for visualization of aluminium foam samples from high-resolution industrial CT and successfully tested for post-implantation assessment of stent placement in virtual angioscopy. The technique builds on conventional ray casting and fast voxel traversal algorithms (Amanatides and Woo). It addresses the limitations of Surface Fitting techniques which require dedicated hardware and lack interactive threshold adjustment. name: Robust Iso-surface Rendering via Bisection and Newton Refinement
head: bisection trace with Newton refinement, isoray rendering pipeline
body:
This method renders implicit surfaces by tracing rays through a volume using a guaranteed-convergence bisection algorithm, followed by optional Newton refinement to achieve sub-pixel precision. It solves the problem of missing or inaccurate surface intersections in standard ray marching by using interval arithmetic (specifically Affine Arithmetic) to bound the implicit function, ensuring that the root-finding process never diverges or skips the surface. It differs from Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement by prioritizing robustness via inclusion functions over pure speed, and from Cell-Based First-Hit Ray Casting by operating continuously in ray space rather than discretely in voxel cells. The pipeline consists of camera setup, ray-AABB culling, robust bisection tracing using inclusion functions, optional Newton refinement, and shading. Inputs: f: Implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R} returning value and optionally gradient. bounds: Axis-aligned bounding box (lo, hi) where lo, hi \in \mathbb{R}^3. threshold: Iso-value (typically 0.0). cameraparams: Eye position, target, FOV, projection type. newtoniter: Number of Newton refinement steps (default 3). maxdepth: Maximum bisection iterations. lipschitz: Lipschitz constant L for the inclusion function, or 'auto'. Outputs: RenderResult: Contains hit positions p, ray distances t, hit masks, and surface normals n. Image: RGB shaded image or depth map. AffineForm Used for tight interval bounds via Affine Arithmetic. x0: (N,) central value (midpoint). xi: (N, K) partial deviations for K noise symbols. delta: (N,) accumulated non-affine error (remainder). N: Batch size. K: Number of noise symbols. TraceResult position: (N, 3) hit positions. t: (N,) ray distances. hit: (N,) boolean mask. normal: (N, 3) surface normals. margin: AABB expansion factor, typically 0.01 (1% of bounds size). newtoniter: Default 3. fovdeg: Vertical field of view, default 60.0. projection: 'perspective' or 'parallel'. lipschitz: 'auto' or float. If 'auto', estimated via gradient sampling. dtype: Default torch.float64 or np.float64. safety: Multiplier for Lipschitz estimation, default 1.5. nsamples: Samples for Lipschitz estimation, default 10000. maxsymbols: Max noise symbols for AffineInclusion, default 8. 1. Camera Setup: Generate ray origins O and directions D for each pixel. For perspective: D depends on fovdeg and pixel coordinates. For parallel: D is constant, extent is halfdiag 1.1. 2. AABB Culling: Compute margin: m = (hi - lo) 	imes 0.01. Expand bounds: aabb{lo} = lo - m, aabb{hi} = hi + m. Intersect rays with AABB to get t{min}, t{max} and hitmask. Rays missing the AABB are discarded. 3. Lipschitz Estimation (if lipschitz == 'auto'): Sample n\samples points uniformly in bounds. Evaluate gradient norms \|
abla f\|. If analytic gradient unavailable, use centered differences with step h=10^{-5}. L = \max(\|
abla f\|) 	imes safety. 4. Bisection Trace: Construct GradientInclusion or AffineInclusion object using f and L. For each ray, perform bisection within [t{min}, t{max}]. At each step, evaluate inclusion function F(t) on the current interval. If 0 \in F(t), split interval. Else, discard branch. Stop when interval width < \epsilon or maxdepth reached. Record hit position p = O + t{mid} D and t. 5. Newton Refinement (Optional): For each hit point p, iterate k times: p{new} = p -  rac{f(p)}{
abla f(p) \cdot D} D Update p \leftarrow p{new}. This refines the intersection along the ray direction. 6. Normal Computation: Evaluate 
abla f(p) at refined positions. Normalize: n =  rac{
abla f(p)}{\max(\|
abla f(p)\|, 10^{-12})}. If gradient unavailable, use centereddifferencenormals. 7. Shading/Depth: Shaded: Lambertian shading with ambient and light direction. Depth: Normalize t to [0, 1] using t{min}, t{max} of valid hits. Handle t{min}=t{max} by setting range to 1.0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def robustisosurfacerender( f, bounds, cameraparams, threshold=0.0, newtoniter=3, maxdepth=64, lipschitz='auto', mode='shaded', safety=1.5, nsamples=10000): """ Robust iso-surface rendering via bisection and Newton refinement. Args: f: Implicit function f(pos) -> (val, gradorNone) bounds: (lo, hi) tuples of (3,) arrays cameraparams: Dict with 'eye', 'target', 'fovdeg', 'projection' threshold: Iso-value newtoniter: Number of Newton steps maxdepth: Max bisection iterations lipschitz: 'auto' or float L mode: 'shaded' or 'depth' safety: Lipschitz estimation safety factor nsamples: Samples for Lipschitz estimation Returns: RenderResult object with position, t, hit, normal """ lo, hi = bounds margin = (hi - lo) 0.01 aabblo = lo - margin aabbhi = hi + margin # 1. Camera Setup if cameraparams['projection'] == 'perspective': origins, directions = generateraysperspective( cameraparams['eye'], cameraparams['target'], cameraparams['fovdeg'], aabblo, aabbhi) else: origins, directions = generateraysparallel( cameraparams['eye'], cameraparams['target'], aabblo, aabbhi) N = origins.shape[0] # 2. Ray-AABB Intersection tmin, tmax, hitmask = rayaabbintersect(origins, directions, aabblo, aabbhi) # Filter rays that hit the AABB validindices = np.where(hitmask)[0] if len(validindices) == 0: return RenderResult.empty(N) validorigins = origins[validindices] validdirs = directions[validindices] validtmin = tmin[validindices] validtmax = tmax[validindices] # 3. Lipschitz Estimation if lipschitz == 'auto': L = estimatelipschitz(f, bounds, nsamples=nsamples, safety=safety) else: L = lipschitz # 4. Bisection Trace # Create inclusion function (GradientInclusion or AffineInclusion) inclusion = GradientInclusion(f, L) # Perform bisection hitpositions, hitts = bisecttrace( validorigins, validdirs, validtmin, validtmax, inclusion, threshold, maxdepth) # 5. Newton Refinement if newtoniter > 0: hitpositions = newtonrefine( hitpositions, validdirs, f, newtoniter) # 6. Normal Computation grad = f(hitpositions)[1] # (M, 3) or None if grad is not None: norms = np.linalg.norm(grad, axis=1, keepdims=True) norms = np.maximum(norms, 1e-12) normals = grad / norms else: normals = centereddifferencenormals(f, hitpositions) # 7. Construct Result result = RenderResult.empty(N) result.position[validindices] = hitpositions result.t[validindices] = hitts result.hit[validindices] = True result.normal[validindices] = normals # 8. Shading/Depth if mode == 'shaded': image = shadelambertian(result, cameraparams) elif mode == 'depth': image = renderdepthmap(result) return result def estimatelipschitz(f, bounds, nsamples=10000, safety=1.5, h=1e-5): """Estimate Lipschitz constant L = max(||grad f||) safety.""" lo, hi = bounds rng = np.random.defaultrng() pts = rng.uniform(lo, hi, (nsamples, 3)) vals, grad = f(pts) if grad is not None: gradnorms = np.linalg.norm(grad, axis=1) else: # Centered finite differences offsets = np.array([ [h, 0, 0], [-h, 0, 0], [0, h, 0], [0, -h, 0], [0, 0, h], [0, 0, -h] ]) allpoints = (pts[None,:,:] + offsets[:, None,:]).reshape(6 nsamples, 3) allvals, = f(allpoints) v = allvals.reshape(6, nsamples) gx = (v[0] - v[1]) / (2.0 h) gy = (v[2] - v[3]) / (2.0 h) gz = (v[4] - v[5]) / (2.0 h) gradnorms = np.sqrt(gx2 + gy2 + gz2) return float(gradnorms.max() safety) def newtonrefine(positions, directions, f, iterations): """Refine intersection points using Newton's method along ray.""" p = positions.copy() for in range(iterations): val, grad = f(p) # Newton step: pnew = p - f(p)/grad(p).d d # grad(p).d is dot product of gradient and ray direction graddotd = np.sum(grad directions, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Avoid division by zero graddotd = np.maximum(np.abs(graddotd), 1e-12) np.sign(graddotd) p = p - (val / graddotd) directions return p def centereddifferencenormals(f, pos, h=1e-5): """Compute normals via centered differences.""" N = pos.shape[0] offsets = np.array([ [h, 0, 0], [-h, 0, 0], [0, h, 0], [0, -h, 0], [0, 0, h], [0, 0, -h] ]) allpoints = (pos[None,:,:] + offsets[:, None,:]).reshape(6 N, 3) allvals, = f(allpoints) v = allvals.reshape(6, N) gradx = (v[0] - v[1]) / (2.0 h) grady = (v[2] - v[3]) / (2.0 h) gradz = (v[4] - v[5]) / (2.0 h) normals = np.stack([gradx, grady, gradz], axis=1) norms = np.linalg.norm(normals, axis=1, keepdims=True) norms = np.maximum(norms, 1e-12) return normals / norms Zero Gradient: If \|
abla f\| \approx 0, normalization uses \max(\|
abla f\|, 10^{-12}) to prevent division by zero. No Hits: If no rays hit the AABB, the result is empty or filled with zeros/NaNs depending on mode. Depth Normalization: If t{min} = t{max} for valid hits, the range is set to 1.0 to prevent division by zero. Lipschitz Underestimation: If L is too small, the inclusion function may not contain the root, causing bisection to fail. The safety factor (default 1.5) mitigates this. Optional post-processing step applied after bisection to achieve sub-pixel accuracy by iteratively correcting the hit position using directional derivatives. Chosen when high precision is required beyond the bisection convergence threshold. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D) where N is number of pixels and D is max bisection depth. Newton refinement adds O(N \cdot I) where I is iterations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for ray data and results. Affine arithmetic adds overhead proportional to number of noise symbols K. Performance: Robust but slower than simple ray marching due to interval evaluations. Affine Arithmetic is tighter than Interval Arithmetic but more expensive. Strengths: Guaranteed convergence, handles complex implicit functions, sub-pixel accuracy. Limitations: Slower than non-robust methods, sensitive to Lipschitz constant estimation, higher memory for Affine forms. When to Use: When visual correctness is critical and surface topology is complex. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is paramount and approximate results are acceptable. This method is implemented in the isoray library, which provides a Python-based framework for robust iso-surface rendering using interval arithmetic. It builds on the principles of guaranteed root-finding using inclusion functions, specifically leveraging Affine Arithmetic for tighter bounds than standard Interval Arithmetic. The approach is designed to address the reliability issues of standard ray marching in scientific visualization and implicit surface rendering.
