name: Newton Refinement
head: Post-bisection refinement
body: Newton Refinement is an optional post-processing step applied after the bisection phase of robust iso-surface rendering to achieve sub-pixel hit-point accuracy. It improves the precision of the intersection point t by iteratively correcting the position using directional derivatives, refining the result beyond the convergence threshold of the bisection method. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current hit position t (from bisection), ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, the implicit function f(\mathbf{x}), and its gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) (or Lipschitz constant for bounds, but gradient is required for Newton steps). Output: Refined hit position t{new} and corresponding 3D point \mathbf{p}{new}. Data Structures: t: Scalar float representing the ray parameter. origin: Vector (x, y, z) representing the ray origin. direction: Normalized vector (dx, dy, dz) representing the ray direction. hit: Boolean flag indicating if the ray intersected the surface during bisection. Parameters: newtoniter: Number of Newton refinement iterations to perform. Default value is 3. Set to 0 to disable. Algorithm: 1. Check if the ray hit the surface (hit == True). If not, skip refinement. 2. Initialize t{curr} = t (the result from bisection). 3. For i from 0 to newtoniter - 1: a. Compute the 3D position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t{curr} \cdot \mathbf{d}. b. Evaluate the implicit function value: fp = f(\mathbf{p}). c. Evaluate the gradient (directional derivative along ray is sufficient, but full gradient is standard): \mathbf{g} = \nabla f(\mathbf{p}). d. Compute the directional derivative: f'p = \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{d}. e. Check for division by zero or near-zero f'p. If |f'p| < \epsilon, break loop. f. Update t: t{new} = t{curr} - \frac{fp}{f'p}. g. Clamp t{new} to the valid interval [t{lo}, t{hi}] to prevent stepping outside the searched region. h. Update t{curr} = t{new}. 4. Return t{curr} and \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{o} + t{curr} \cdot \mathbf{d}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def newtonrefine(t, origin, direction, hit, tlo, thi, newtoniter=3, ffunc, gradfunc): """ Refine hit position t using Newton's method. Args: t: Current hit parameter from bisection. origin: Ray origin (3D vector). direction: Ray direction (normalized 3D vector). hit: Boolean, True if bisection found an intersection. tlo: Lower bound of the bisection interval. thi: Upper bound of the bisection interval. newtoniter: Number of iterations (0 disables). ffunc: Function f(p) -> float. gradfunc: Function grad(p) -> (3D vector). Returns: Refined t and position p. """ if not hit or newtoniter <= 0: p = origin + t direction return t, p tcurr = t for in range(newtoniter): # Compute 3D position p = origin + tcurr direction # Evaluate function and gradient fval = ffunc(p) grad = gradfunc(p) # Directional derivative # Dot product of gradient and ray direction fprime = sum(g d for g, d in zip(grad, direction)) # Guard against zero derivative (grazing ray or flat region) if abs(fprime) < 1e-12: break # Newton step tnew = tcurr - fval / fprime # Clamp to bisection interval to ensure robustness tnew = max(tlo, min(thi, tnew)) tcurr = tnew pfinal = origin + tcurr direction return tcurr, pfinal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Availability: Newton refinement requires the gradient of the implicit function. If the gradient is not available or is zero, Newton's method may fail or diverge. Grazing Rays: If the ray is nearly tangent to the surface, the directional derivative f'p approaches zero, causing numerical instability or large steps. Implementation Status: In some provided code snippets (e.g., renderrobustness.py), the feature is mentioned as available but not called in the core loop; the bisection result is used directly. A Newton iteration mode that terminates a vertex step if the predicted next error is below a tenth of the tolerance, without confirming with an evaluation. The predicted error is calculated as |f'| / (2 |f|) s^2, where f' is the gradient magnitude, f is the function value, and s is the step size. This applies to exponentially decaying fields. The normal used is that of the evaluation before the step. On amide/mol datasets at h=0.2 and 0.12, this reduces evaluations per vertex from 2.0-2.6 to 1.3-2.0, with a largest vertex residual of 1.4 \times 10^{-4} h (tolerance 10^{-4} h). A bug existed where evaluators skipped a group of 64 vertices when the AND of vdone flags was set; a mix of 1 (converged) and 2 (predicted) cleared the AND, causing full runs after convergence. The fix ensures any nonzero flag counts. A ray tracing approach to find the first parameter along a ray where the field value equals the isovalue c, by isolating the root via sign change detection and localizing it precisely. The behavior is highly correlated to the chosen step size: small steps make the method computationally expensive, while larger step sizes can miss isosurface crossings. Time Complexity: Adds O(k) evaluations per hit, where k is newtoniter (typically 3). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray. Performance: Predictive termination can reduce evaluations per vertex by ~20-30% in specific GPU implementations. Strengths: Achieves sub-pixel accuracy; leverages existing gradient information. Limitations: Requires differentiable implicit functions; unstable for grazing rays or zero gradients. When to use: When high-precision hit points are required and gradients are available. When not to use: When gradients are unavailable or performance is critical and bisection precision is sufficient. Newton Refinement is part of the "Robust Iso-surface Rendering via Bisection and Newton Refinement" framework, implemented in the isoray library. It builds on the principle that bisection provides a robust, guaranteed interval, while Newton's method provides fast local convergence to higher precision. The concept of combining ray marching for isolation with Newton localization for precision is also discussed in the context of scale-invariant integral surfaces. Predictive Newton termination was introduced in optimized GPU isosurface extraction code. name: Average Intensity Projection with IsoSurface Detection
head: Exact Projection Mean Density
body: Average Intensity Projection with IsoSurface Detection is a hybrid volume rendering technique that computes the mean density of all voxels along a ray within a valid range and renders that mean value with lighting based on the mean position. It differs from standard Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) by averaging values rather than taking the maximum, and from pure isosurface rendering by incorporating background density information into the final color and lighting calculation. Inputs: Ray origin startPos and direction rayDir. Ray near tNear and far tFar bounds. 3D volume texture texVol containing scalar density values. 1D transfer function texture tf (or colorMap) mapping density to color. Isosurface threshold isoSurf. Number of steps numsteps (fixed at 256). Boolean flag enableLighting. Outputs: Fragment color FragColor. Data Structures: meanSum: float, accumulates density values. validSamples: int, count of samples within valid density range. meanPos: vec3, accumulates positions for mean position calculation. color: vec4, accumulates color contributions. cnt: int, counter initialized to 1 to avoid division by zero in compensation logic. Steps: 1. Initialize meanSum = 0.0, validSamples = 0, meanPos = vec3(0.0), color = vec4(0.0), cnt = 1. 2. Loop i from 0 to numsteps - 1: a. Calculate current position curPos along the ray. b. Transform curPos to texture coordinates: tmp = (curPos.x, curPos.y, curPos.z \times 2.3486238532110093) texPos = \frac{1 + tmp}{2} texPos.y = 1 - texPos.y c. Sample density iso1 = texture(texVol, texPos).x. d. Advance position to nextPos and transform to texPosNext similarly. e. Sample density iso2 = texture(texVol, texPosNext).x. f. Check for isosurface crossing: if iso1 < isoSurf and iso2 > isoSurf: i. Use binary search isoSurface(texPos, texPosNext, isoSurf, texIso) to find exact surface intersection. ii. Sample value at intersection: value = texture(texVol, texIso).x. iii. Add to color accumulator: color = color + value. iv. name: Terrain Raymarching
head: Heightmap Raymarching
body: Terrain Raymarching renders 2D heightmap terrains by casting rays through each pixel and stepping along the ray until the ray's height drops below the terrain surface defined by the heightmap value at the ray's xz position. It distinguishes itself from standard raycasting by its simplicity in handling high-level detail via procedural or texture-based heightmaps, and from voxel rendering by operating on a 2D height function rather than a 3D occupancy grid. Unlike Heightfield Rendering, which fills vertical screen segments from the calculated terrain height down to the horizon for each column, Terrain Raymarching typically marches a single ray per pixel to find the first hit. Inputs: Camera position and projection matrix. Heightmap data (texture sampler or procedural function) H(x, z), returning the terrain height at world coordinates x, z. Step size \Delta s for ray marching. Maximum number of steps or maximum distance. Outputs: Color buffer with terrain shading. Data Structures: Heightmap: 2D array or texture mapping (x, z) \rightarrow h. Steps: 1. For each pixel (u, v) in the image, construct a ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} from the camera. 2. Initialize ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}. 3. Loop for i = 0 to N{max}: a. Sample the terrain height at the ray's current xz coordinates: h{terrain} = H(px, pz). b. Get the ray's current height: h{ray} = py. c. If h{ray} \le h{terrain}, the ray has hit the terrain. Break loop. d. Advance the ray: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \Delta s. 4. If a hit was found, determine the color based on the height h{terrain} (e.g., white for snow at high altitudes, green for grass at lower altitudes). 5. Shade the hit point by raymarching towards a light source to compute lighting. Parameters: Step size \Delta s: Not given in the sources. Maximum steps N{max}: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the step size is too large, the ray may skip over the terrain surface, resulting in no hit or incorrect depth. Precision issues may occur if the terrain height and ray height are very close but the step size causes overshooting. Procedural heightmaps must be consistent with the coordinate system used for ray sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def terrainraymarching(camera, heightmap, stepsize, maxsteps): for each pixel (u, v): rayorigin = camera.getorigin(u, v) raydirection = camera.getdirection(u, v) p = rayorigin hit = False for i in range(maxsteps): # Get terrain height at current ray xz position terrainh = heightmap.sample(p.x, p.z) # Check if ray is below terrain if p.y <= terrainh: hit = True break # Step along the ray p = p + raydirection stepsize if hit: # Determine color based on height if terrainh > thresholdsnow: color = WHITE else: color = GREEN # Shade the point by raymarching towards a light source color = shadepoint(p, color, lightsource) setpixelcolor(u, v, color) Horizon Mapping is a technique to describe the self-occlusion of a heightfield by calculating visibility. Visibility is calculated by determining the altitude or horizon angle for a set of azimuth directions for every point in the surface. This data is stored into a horizon map. It is used to approximate shadows and ambient occlusion in terrain rendering without full ray tracing. Terrain Raymarching is computationally intensive per pixel due to the iterative stepping process, but it fits perfectly on the GPU as each pixel can be calculated independently. The performance depends heavily on the step size and the complexity of the heightmap. Larger step sizes reduce the number of iterations but may lead to inaccuracies. The method allows for high-level detail rendering, which is a major advantage. However, it may suffer from aliasing if the step size is not adaptive. Terrain Raymarching is a general application of raymarching techniques, which have been used to render a variety of complex scenes. The specific application to terrain rendering using heightmaps is discussed in the context of distance field raymarching. The technique leverages the GPU's parallel processing capabilities to achieve real-time rendering speeds. name: Heightfield Rendering
head: 2D Raycast Heightmap Renderer, Comanche Heightmap Algorithm, Scanline, View-Z slices
body: Heightfield Rendering is a CPU-driven, image-order technique for rendering 2D heightmap terrains by casting rays from the camera through discrete depth planes (view-Z slices) and projecting the intersection heights onto a 2D screen buffer. It solves the problem of real-time terrain visualization with hidden surface removal, distinguishing itself from standard raycasting by casting multiple rays per screen column at increasing depth intervals (Level of Detail) rather than one ray per pixel, and from voxel rendering by operating on a 2D height function rather than a 3D occupancy grid. Unlike Terrain Raymarching, which typically marches a single ray per pixel to find the first hit, this method fills vertical screen segments from the calculated terrain height down to the horizon (or previous occlusion buffer) for each column. Inputs: heightMap: A 2D raster image (typically square, power-of-two dimensions, e.g., 1024×1024) where pixel intensity (e.g., Red channel) encodes terrain height. colorMap: A 2D raster image (same dimensions as heightMap) encoding terrain color. camera: Position (x, y, z), rotation angle \theta (yaw), field of view (FOV), and view distance. playerPos: World coordinates (x, y, z) of the camera/observer. Outputs: screenBuffer: A 1D array of colors indexed by x + y \times \text{width}, representing the final image. Camera (vsCamera): position: vsVector3f (x, y, z). rotation: vsVector2f (x, y) or scalar angle. fov: Float, field of view in degrees. distance: Float, max view distance. Map (vsMap): width, height: Integers, dimensions of the height/color maps. shift: Integer, \log2(\text{width}), used for bitwise modulo optimization. altitude: Pointer to height data. color: Pointer to color data. Screen (vsScreenData): width, height: Integers, screen resolution. screen: Pointer to 1D color array. Occlusion Buffer (yBuffer or hiddenY): Array of integers, size equal to screen width. Initialized to screenHeight (bottom of screen). Tracks the lowest drawn pixel (highest Y value in screen coordinates, closest to camera) for each column to handle occlusion. MAXDEPTH: Maximum rendering distance in world units. Default: 1024. LODDISTANCE: Distance interval for increasing step size. Default: 256. LODAMOUNT: Multiplier for LOD step increase. Default: 1.5. FOGSTART: Distance at which fog begins. Default: 256. CLOSELOD: Multiplier for near-field column width. Default: 1.0. FOV: Field of view. Default: 90.0 degrees. WIDTH, HEIGHT: Screen resolution. Default: 800×800 or 320×200. deltaZ: Initial LOD step size. Default: 0.1f. deltaZincrement: LOD step increase per depth layer. Default: 0.00025f. invzconstant: Vertical stretch multiplier. Default: 350.0f. shrinkFactor: Safety factor for ray stepping (see Pitfalls). Calculated as \frac{1}{\sqrt{c^2+1}} where c is the bound on the heightfield's derivative. 1. Initialization: Load heightMap and colorMap. Ensure dimensions are square and power-of-two. Initialize yBuffer array of size WIDTH with all values set to HEIGHT (bottom of screen). Initialize camera parameters: position, rotation, FOV, and view distance. Calculate viewFactor = \sin(\text{FOV} / 2 \text{ radians}). Calculate zScale = (\text{WIDTH} / \text{HEIGHT}) \times 1.0 to maintain aspect ratio. 2. Depth Loop (LOD): Iterate depth d from 1 to MAXDEPTH. Calculate colWidth = \text{WIDTH} / (\text{viewFactor} \times d \times 2 \times \text{CLOSE\LOD}). If colWidth < 1, set to 1. LOD Adjustment: After processing columns for depth d, increase d by (\lfloor d / \text{LOD\DISTANCE} \rfloor \times \text{LOD\AMOUNT}) to skip distant samples. 3. Column Sampling Loop: For each column start position sx from 0 to WIDTH with step colWidth: Calculate sample position in camera space: \text{samplePos}.x = \text{Lerp}(-\text{viewFactor} \times d, \text{viewFactor} \times d, \text{sx} / \text{WIDTH}) \text{samplePos}.y = d Apply camera rotation: \text{tempX} = \cos(\text{rot}) \times \text{samplePos}.x - \sin(\text{rot}) \times \text{samplePos}.y \text{tempY} = \sin(\text{rot}) \times \text{samplePos}.x + \cos(\text{rot}) \times \text{samplePos}.y \text{samplePos}.x = \text{tempX} + \text{playerPos}.x \text{samplePos}.y = \text{tempY} + \text{playerPos}.y Sample heightmap at samplePos (using modulo or bitwise AND for wrapping): \text{heightVal} = \text{heightMap}[\text{samplePos}] \text{worldZ} = -\text{heightVal} \times \text{zScale} + \text{playerPos}.z (Note: Sign of heightVal negation depends on map encoding; S4 negates it). Calculate screen Y coordinate sy: \text{sy} = (\text{worldZ} / d) \times \text{HEIGHT} + \text{HEIGHT} / 2 (Alternative formula from S2/S3: \text{proj\height} = \lfloor (\text{camera.height} - \text{height}) / z \times \text{SCALE\FACTOR} + \text{horizon} \rfloor). Clamp sy to [0, \text{SCREEN\HEIGHT}-1]. 4. Occlusion Check and Drawing: If sy < yBuffer[sx] (meaning the terrain is closer to the camera/bottom of screen than previously drawn): Sample colorMap at samplePos. Apply fog: If d > \text{MAX\DEPTH} - \text{FOG\START}, set alpha: \text{color}.a = \lfloor 255 \times (\text{MAX\DEPTH} - d) / \text{FOG\START} \rfloor Draw vertical line from sy to yBuffer[sx] for pixels sx to sx + colWidth - 1 (clamped to WIDTH). Update yBuffer[sx + i] = sy for all drawn pixels i. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderheightfield(camera, heightmap, colormap, screenwidth, screenheight): # Constants MAXDEPTH = 1024 LODDISTANCE = 256 LODAMOUNT = 1.5 FOGSTART = 256 CLOSELOD = 1.0 FOV = 90.0 WIDTH = screenwidth HEIGHT = screenheight # Precompute viewfactor = sin(radians(FOV / 2.0)) zscale = (WIDTH / HEIGHT) 1.0 cosrot = cos(-camera.rotation) sinrot = sin(-camera.rotation) # Initialize occlusion buffer ybuffer = [HEIGHT] WIDTH # Clear screen screen = [Color(0, 0, 0, 255)] (WIDTH HEIGHT) # Depth Loop d = 1.0 while d < MAXDEPTH: # Calculate column width for LOD colwidth = int(WIDTH / (viewfactor d 2 CLOSELOD)) if colwidth < 1: colwidth = 1 # Column Loop sx = 0 while sx < WIDTH: # Calculate sample position in camera space # Lerp from -viewFactord to viewFactord based on column fraction fraction = sx / WIDTH samplexcam = lerp(-viewfactor d, viewfactor d, fraction) sampleycam = d # Apply rotation tempx = cosrot samplexcam - sinrot sampleycam tempy = sinrot samplexcam + cosrot sampleycam # Translate to world space samplexworld = tempx + camera.position.x sampleyworld = tempy + camera.position.y # Sample heightmap (wrap coordinates) hx = modulo(int(samplexworld), heightmap.width) hy = modulo(int(sampleyworld), heightmap.height) heightval = heightmap.getcolor(hx, hy).r # Assuming Red channel is height # Calculate world Z (terrain height) # Note: S4 negates heightVal, S3 uses camera.height - height worldz = -heightval zscale + camera.position.z # Calculate screen Y # S4 formula sy = (worldz / d) HEIGHT + HEIGHT / 2 # Clamp sy = max(0, min(sy, HEIGHT - 1)) # Occlusion check if sy < ybuffer[sx]: # Sample color cx = modulo(int(samplexworld), colormap.width) cy = modulo(int(sampleyworld), colormap.height) color = colormap.getcolor(cx, cy) # Fog if d > MAXDEPTH - FOGSTART: fogfactor = (MAXDEPTH - d) / FOGSTART color.a = int(255 fogfactor) # Draw vertical line for this column width for i in range(colwidth): colidx = sx + i if colidx < WIDTH: # Draw from sy to ybuffer[colidx] # Assuming drawverticalline(x, ytop, ybottom, color) # ytop is sy (closer to camera/bottom), ybottom is old buffer value drawverticalline(screen, colidx, sy, ybuffer[colidx], color, WIDTH, HEIGHT) ybuffer[colidx] = sy sx += colwidth # LOD Step Increase d += ((int(d) // LODDISTANCE) LODAMOUNT) def drawverticalline(screen, x, ytop, ybottom, color, width, height): """Draws a vertical line from ytop to ybottom (exclusive) at column x.""" # Ensure correct order starty = min(ytop, ybottom) endy = max(ytop, ybottom) for y in range(starty, endy): if 0 <= y < height: idx = x + y width screen[idx] = color Overshooting: The naive distance field D(pos) = h(pos.xz) + pos.y can overestimate distance in the ray direction, causing rays to overshoot the heightfield if a step size of D(pos) is taken. Solution: Use a shrinkFactor derived from the bound c on the heightfield's derivative: \text{shrinkFactor} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{c^2+1}}. Coordinate Wrapping: Heightmap coordinates must wrap around the grid (e.g., 1024x1024). Use modulo or bitwise AND with (N-1) for power-of-two dimensions. Screen Bounds: projheight can be negative or exceed screen height; must be clamped to [0, \text{SCREEN\HEIGHT}-1]. Map Dimensions: Height and color maps must be square, same dimensions, and powers of two for bitwise optimization. Pitch Limits: Pitch is often limited to \pm 80^\circ and roll disabled to maintain stable view-Z slicing. Offset Errors: Line drawing implementations may introduce 1-pixel offsets depending on coordinate system conventions (e.g., sx+i+1 vs sx+i). Projects heightmap onto a vertical screen buffer for occlusion, drawing horizontal slices. Software rendering for constrained hardware using discrete depth/height slices and fixed-point math. Time Complexity: O(\text{WIDTH} \times (\text{MAX\DEPTH} / \text{LOD\step})) in the worst case. Optimized by variable column width (colWidth), which reduces ray casting density at greater distances. Memory Complexity: O(\text{WIDTH} + \text{MAP\SIZE}). Requires O(\text{WIDTH}) for the occlusion buffer (yBuffer) and storage for height/color maps. Performance: CPU-driven, suitable for real-time on modest hardware (e.g., GBA, early PCs). Performance scales with screen width and max depth; LOD reduces far-field cost. Strengths: Real-time perspective, simple implementation, low memory overhead, effective hidden surface removal via per-column buffer. Limitations: Limited to heightfield terrains (no overhangs), discrete depth steps can cause aliasing or "popping" if LOD is coarse, pitch/roll restrictions. When to Use: 2D/2.5D terrain rendering where performance is critical and terrain is defined by a heightmap. When Not to Use: Complex 3D geometry with overhangs, or when full 3D raymarching precision is required. Heightfield Rendering, also known as the Comanche Heightmap Algorithm or Scanline rendering, originated in the Comanche series of flight simulation games (e.g., Comanche: Maximum Overkill) and the Voxel Space engine. It was popularized in the demoscene and indie development for its ability to render large terrains in real-time on limited hardware. The technique relies on projecting 2D height data into screen space using perspective division, a method distinct from modern GPU-based rasterization or voxel rendering. varganorbert222/VoxelSpace, https://github.com/varganorbert222/VoxelSpace, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Not-Nik/VoxelSpaceEngine, https://github.com/Not-Nik/VoxelSpaceEngine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) AndreasVlcek/Voxel-Space-Engine-Comanche-Terrain-Rendering, https://github.com/AndreasVlcek/Voxel-Space-Engine-Comanche-Terrain-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PaigePalisade/HeightmapViewer, https://github.com/PaigePalisade/HeightmapViewer, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) A Note on Ray Marching with Heightfields, https://www.peterstefek.me/ray-marching-heightfields.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Multiple Flat Shaded Opaque Isosurfaces
head: Texture-map-based isosurface extraction, View-independent cell projection with alpha testing
body: This method renders multiple opaque isosurfaces from an unstructured tetrahedral mesh without requiring explicit visibility sorting of the cells. It leverages a 2D texture map to identify isosurface fragments within each projected tetrahedron and uses a combination of the alpha test and the OpenGL z-test to guarantee correct occlusion. Unlike sibling methods that rely on geometric sorting or ray-marching refinement, this approach is view-independent and relies on fragment-level shading to handle multiple scalar values simultaneously. Inputs: A tetrahedral mesh where each tetrahedron T has four vertices v0, v1, v2, v3. A scalar field value si associated with each vertex vi. A set of isovalue thresholds \{s{\text{iso}, k}\} for the desired isosurfaces. Lighting parameters: directional light vectors and diffuse colors. Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel contains the color of the front-most isosurface fragment. Data Structures: Texture Map (M): A 2D texture used to look up material properties based on the scalar values at the vertices of the projected tetrahedron. The texture coordinates (u, v) are derived from the scalar values of the tetrahedron vertices. Specifically, the texture map is indexed by the scalar values sf (scalar at the "front" vertex relative to view) and sb (scalar at the "back" vertex). Note: The exact mapping of vertex scalars to texture coordinates is not explicitly defined in the source text, but it implies a lookup based on the range [sf, sb] or similar. The source states the texture map is "modified to 'thicken' isosurfaces" to avoid gaps. Texel Layout: Each texel stores: RGB: Ambient material color of the isosurface corresponding to the specific isovalue. Alpha: 1.0 if an isosurface is present at this scalar configuration; 0.0 otherwise. Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Processing: For each tetrahedron in the mesh: a. Project the four vertices to screen space. b. Identify the "front" vertex vf and "back" vertex vb based on the viewing direction. The source defines visibility ordering: if sf < sb, the viewer looks along the gradient, so smaller isovalues occlude greater ones. If sf > sb, the order reverses. c. Retrieve the scalar values sf and sb from vertices vf and vb. 2. Texture Lookup: a. Use sf and sb as coordinates (or indices) to sample the texture map M. b. Let the result be (C{mat}, \alpha{tex}). c. The texture map is pre-computed such that: If the isosurface condition is met (i.e., the ray through the tetrahedron intersects an isosurface), \alpha{tex} = 1.0 and C{mat} is the assigned color for that isovalue. If no isosurface is present in the tetrahedron for the current view configuration, \alpha{tex} = 0.0. d. Thickening: The texture map is slightly modified (thickened) around the isovalue boundaries to prevent gaps between adjacent tetrahedra where the isosurface might otherwise be missed due to discretization or projection artifacts. 3. Lighting Calculation: a. Since the method does not provide interpolated gradients, lighting is calculated entirely in the vertex program (flat shading). b. For each directional light Lj: Input: Light direction \mathbf{d}j (object coordinates) and diffuse color \mathbf{c}j. Operation: Compute diffuse contribution using the flat normal of the tetrahedron face or vertex. The source specifies "three vertex program operations per light". c. Combine ambient and diffuse contributions to form the final fragment color. 4. Fragment Shading and Occlusion: a. For each fragment generated by the rasterizer: Sample the texture map again (or use the interpolated value from step 2) to get \alpha{tex}. If \alpha{tex} == 0, discard the fragment. If \alpha{tex} == 1, set the fragment's alpha to 1.0 (opaque) and color to the computed lit color. b. Enable the Alpha Test to discard fragments with alpha 0. c. Enable the Z-Test (depth test) to ensure that only the front-most isosurface fragment is written to the color buffer. This guarantees correct occlusion without sorting cells. 5. Multiple Isosurfaces: a. Assign a unique material color to each isovalue in the texture map. b. The visibility ordering is implicit: for sf < sb, smaller isovalues are rendered "in front" of greater isovalues because the texture map lookup returns the color of the isosurface that satisfies the condition first or is prioritized by the "thickening" and alpha test logic. The source states: "isosurfaces for smaller isovalues occlude those for greater isovalues" when sf < sb. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. for each tetrahedron T in mesh: # 1. Identify front and back vertices based on view direction vf, vb = getfrontbackvertices(T, viewdirection) sf = T.vertices[vf].scalar sb = T.vertices[vb].scalar # 2. Texture Lookup texel = M.lookup(sf, sb) # 3. Lighting (Flat Shading) # Compute normal N for the tetrahedron face (or use vertex normal) N = computeflatnormal(T) finalcolor = ambientcolor for each light L in lights: # L.direction is object-space direction # L.diffuse is the light color # 3 operations per light: dot product, clamp, multiply diff = max(0, dot(N, L.direction)) finalcolor += diff L.diffuse # 4. Fragment Output if texel.alpha > 0: fragment.color = finalcolor fragment.alpha = 1.0 fragment.depth = computedepth(T) renderfragment(fragment) else: discardfragment() Parameters: Light Data: Per light, two entries in the vertex program's attribute vector: light direction in object coordinates and diffuse light color. Lighting Cost: Three vertex program operations per light. Texture Map Thickness: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gaps between patches: Without thickening the texture map, gaps may appear between isosurface patches in adjacent tetrahedra. No interpolated gradients: The method is limited to flat shaded isosurfaces; it cannot provide smooth shading based on interpolated vertex normals. Visibility Ordering: The occlusion behavior depends on the relative order of sf and sb. If sf < sb, smaller isovalues occlude greater ones. If sf > sb, the reverse is true. This variant addresses the rendering of multiple contour surfaces together to ensure transparency is handled correctly, particularly in engines like rgl that draw triangles in back-to-front order. Joint rendering is essential for standard and grid engines to maintain correct alpha blending when multiple isosurfaces intersect or overlap. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra and lights. Each light adds a constant number of operations (3) per vertex/tetrahedron. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the texture map size, which depends on the discretization of the scalar value space. The source does not specify the exact resolution or size of the texture map. Strengths: No need for explicit cell sorting or visibility ordering. Supports a virtually arbitrary number of directional lights. Simple implementation using standard OpenGL features (alpha test, z-test). Limitations: Limited to flat shading; no interpolated gradients. Requires a texture map lookup, which may have cache overhead. "Thickening" may introduce slight geometric inaccuracies at the isosurface boundaries. When to use: When rendering multiple opaque isosurfaces from unstructured tetrahedral meshes where view-independent performance is desired and flat shading is acceptable. When not to use: When smooth shading or high geometric precision is required, or when transparency blending is needed without joint rendering techniques. This method was demonstrated in the context of hardware-based view-independent cell projection for unstructured grids. It builds on earlier work by Röttger et al. [14] and Stein et al. [16] regarding texture-map-based isosurface extraction. The approach was shown to be effective for rendering multiple isosurfaces without the overhead of sorting cells, as illustrated in Figure 11 of the source. name: Differential Sampling and Peak Finding
head: Adaptive Surface Detection, Peak Finding, Surface Ray Marching, Surface Raycasting with Adaptive Step Size
body: Differential Sampling and Peak Finding is a volume rendering technique that combines adaptive ray stepping with explicit root finding to render sharp, Dirac-like features in transfer functions as semi-transparent isosurfaces. Unlike standard postclassification which misses these features or preintegration which skews their opacity and shading due to piecewise summation assumptions, this method solves directly for the roots of the transfer function. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a 2D lookup table to query potential peak isovales rather than precomputed integrals, allowing for correct shading and opacity handling of high-frequency transfer function components. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume scalar field V, transfer function \rho\alpha(f) (opacity as a function of field value), ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, isovalue iso, termination alpha threshold, and lookup table parameters. Outputs: Final pixel color and opacity. Data Structures: Globals: ps0, ps1: vec4 representing position (x, y, z, t) at segment entry and exit. fs0, fs1: float representing field values f(\mathbf{ps0}) and f(\mathbf{ps1}). dt: float representing step size (time parameter t). iso: float representing the target isovalue. Lookup Table (peakTable): A 2D texture where each entry stores an isovalue \upsilon (or a set of up to four sequential isovales \upsiloni) that possibly exists within the segment defined by entry and exit field values [fi, fo]. Entries are sorted from first to last peak value encountered. If no peak exists, a flag outside the range of scalar values is stored. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set step size dt = b. Set ps1.w (time t) to 0. Set ps1.xyz to ray.origin. Compute initial field value fs1 = volumefilter(ps1.xyz). 2. Ray Casting Loop: Copy current state: ps0 = ps1, fs0 = fs1. Advance position: ps1 += dt ray.direction. Differential Sampling: If DIFFERENTIALSAMPLING is defined, increment step size: dt += a. Compute new field value: fs1 = volumefilter(ps1.xyz). 3. Peak Lookup: If !DVRONLY, sample the lookup table: iso = texture2D(peakTable, float2(fs0, fs1)). If iso != invalidflag, a peak is potentially present. Proceed to Peak Finding (Step 4). Otherwise, skip to Step 5. 4. Peak Finding (Root Solving): Define implicit function f(t) = V(\mathbf{R}(t)) - iso. Compute boundary values: f0 = fs0 - iso, f1 = fs1 - iso. Sign Change Check: If f0 \cdot f1 < 0, a root exists in the segment. Set bracketing points: \mathbf{p}0 = \mathbf{ps0}, \mathbf{p}1 = \mathbf{ps1}. Bisection/Secant Iteration: Iterate k from 0 to 1 (2 iterations). Compute intermediate point using secant formula: \mathbf{p}{rt} = \mathbf{p}0 - (\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0) \frac{f0}{f1 - f0} Evaluate field at intermediate point: f{rt} = \text{volume\filter}(\mathbf{p}{rt}.xyz) - iso. Update bounds: If f{rt} \cdot f0 < 0, set \mathbf{p}1 = \mathbf{p}{rt}, f1 = f{rt}. Else, set \mathbf{p}0 = \mathbf{p}{rt}, f0 = f{rt}. Final Sample: Recompute root estimate: \mathbf{p}{rt} = \mathbf{p}0 - (\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0) \frac{f0}{f1 - f0}. Set field value f{rt} = iso (assume exact isovalue to avoid Moiré patterns). Set dt = 1.0 to scale opacity (constant segment distance). Call dvrsample(prt, frt, dt) to render the peak. Note: If multiple peaks are handled, the table returns up to four sequential isovales. The algorithm performs peak finding sequentially on all four values in precomputed order. 5. Standard DVR Sampling: If !PEAKONLY (or if PEAKXORDVR is set and no peak was found), call dvrsample(ps1, fs1, dt). 6. Termination: If color.a > terminationalpha, break loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. ps0: vec4 # Position at segment entry ps1: vec4 # Position at segment exit fs0: float # Field value at ps0 fs1: float # Field value at ps1 dt: float # Step size (time parameter) iso: float # Target isovalue color: vec4 # Accumulated color/alpha def volumefilter(pos: vec3) -> float: """Sample volume at position.""" return texture(volumetexture, pos).r def dvrsample(pos: vec4, fieldval: float, stepdt: float): """Perform standard volume rendering sample.""" # Implementation depends on specific DVR method (e.g., front-to-back compositing) # Uses fieldval to lookup color/opacity from transfer function pass def peakfind(): """Solve for root within current segment [ps0, ps1].""" f0 = fs0 - iso f1 = fs1 - iso # Check for sign change indicating a root if f0 f1 < 0: p0 = ps0 p1 = ps1 # Secant method iterations (2 iterations as per source) for k in range(2): # Secant formula for root estimation # prt = p0 - (p1 - p0) (f0 / (f1 - f0)) # Note: Vector subtraction and scalar division deltap = p1 - p0 fraction = f0 / (f1 - f0) prt = p0 - (deltap fraction) frt = volumefilter(prt.xyz) - iso # Update bracketing bounds if frt f0 < 0: p1 = prt f1 = frt else: p0 = prt f0 = frt # Final root estimate deltap = p1 - p0 fraction = f0 / (f1 - f0) prt = p0 - (deltap fraction) # Assume exact isovalue to avoid Moire patterns frt = iso # Use constant dt=1 for opacity scaling at peak dt = 1.0 # Render the peak dvrsample(prt, frt, dt) def raycast(rayorigin: vec3, raydirection: vec3): global ps0, ps1, fs0, fs1, dt, iso, color # Initialization dt = b # Initial step size parameter ps1 = vec4(rayorigin, 0.0) # w component is time t fs1 = volumefilter(ps1.xyz) while True: # Save current state ps0 = ps1 fs0 = fs1 # Advance ray ps1 = ps1 + vec4(raydirection dt, dt) # Differential sampling: adapt step size # 'a' is the increment parameter for differential sampling dt = dt + a # Sample new position fs1 = volumefilter(ps1.xyz) # Peak Finding Logic if not DVRONLY: # Query lookup table for potential isovales # peakTable is a 2D texture indexed by (fs0, fs1) iso = texture2D(peakTable, vec2(fs0, fs1)).r if iso != invalidflag: peakfind() # Standard DVR Logic if not PEAKONLY: if PEAKXORDVR: # Only sample DVR if no peak was found/processed # Note: Logic implies checking if peakfind was actually called # For simplicity, we assume if iso was invalidflag, we DVR if iso == invalidflag: dvrsample(ps1, fs1, dt) else: # DVR always, or XOR if peakfind wasn't triggered (implementation dependent) # Source says: "If !PEAKONLY (or if PEAKXORDVR is set and peakfind was not called)" # We assume standard behavior if not XOR or if peak not found dvrsample(ps1, fs1, dt) # Termination check if color.a > terminationalpha: break Parameters: b: Initial step size. a: Increment for differential sampling step size. terminationalpha: Alpha threshold for ray termination. invalidflag: Value indicating no peak found in the lookup table. iso: Target isovalue for peak detection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Moire Patterns: Evaluating the field f(\mathbf{R}(t)) at the root estimate can cause Moire patterns with sharp transfer functions. The method assumes the value is exactly iso at the root position. Opacity Scaling: Opacity \rho\alpha is not scaled by the segment distance \Delta t at the peak; a constant \Delta t = 1 is used. This biases the integral towards peaks but ensures correct rendering of sharp features regardless of sampling rate. Multiple Peaks: If multiple peaks exist in a segment, the lookup table must store up to four sequential peaks. The algorithm processes them sequentially. Handling multiple peaks costs roughly 20% more performance. Lookup Table Resolution: A coarser discretization (128 bins) is often sufficient for peak finding, whereas preintegration requires larger tables for comparable quality near isosurfaces. A two-stage search algorithm to find the approximate location of the maximum value in a volume along a ray. The first stage performs a coarse linear scan, and the second stage refines the position using a divide-by-two approach. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by combining a global linear sweep with a localized binary-search-like refinement, prioritizing robustness in finding the global maximum within a segment over pure convergence speed. Time Complexity: Building the lookup table proceeds in O(N^2) time, similarly to preintegration. Memory Complexity: Requires a 2D lookup table. The table size depends on the discretization resolution (e.g., 128 bins). Performance: Building the peak-finding table is roughly twice as fast as building a preintegrated table at the same resolution. Heptane fire scene (1024x900): Peak finding renders at 7.1 fps, postclassification at 11.6 fps, preintegration at 8.8 fps. Zebrafish optic tract (1600x512): Peak finding at 2.1 fps, Preintegration at 2.0 fps, Semi-transparent isosurfacing at 4.3 fps. Finding multiple peaks costs roughly 20% more performance. Strengths: Correctly renders sharp, Dirac-like features in transfer functions as semi-transparent isosurfaces. Avoids Moire patterns and incorrect opacity integration associated with preintegration for noisy or high-frequency data. Supports different rendering modalities (PEAKXORDVR, PEAKONLY, DVRONLY) with no performance penalty. Limitations: Introduces bias in the volume rendering integral by assuming discrete impulses at peaks. Requires construction and storage of a 2D lookup table. May miss features if the sampling rate is too low to detect sign changes, though differential sampling helps mitigate this. Origin: The method was introduced by Knoll et al. in "Volume Ray Casting with Peak Finding and Differential Sampling". History: It was developed to address the shortcomings of standard postclassified and preintegrated volume rendering when dealing with transfer functions containing sharp features approaching Dirac impulses. The technique borrows from ray differentials formulations of Igehy for sampling strategy and uses Descartes' rule of signs and secant methods for root solving, similar to other interactive ray tracing algorithms. Usage: It is used for interactive high-fidelity volume rendering of noisy or entropic data (e.g., from scanned sources in medicine or biology) where high-frequency features are critical. name: Coarse-to-Fine Volume Maximum Search
head: Two-stage volume maximum search, Coarse-fine peak localization
body: A two-stage search algorithm to find the approximate location of the maximum value in a volume along a ray. The first stage performs a coarse linear scan, and the second stage refines the position using a divide-by-two approach. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by combining a global linear sweep with a localized binary-search-like refinement, prioritizing robustness in finding the global maximum within a segment over pure convergence speed. Inputs: startcoord: The starting 3D coordinate in the volume grid. stepcoord: The step vector (direction and magnitude) for the coarse scan. nsteps: The number of steps for the coarse linear scan (integer). sizef: The dimensions of the volume grid (used for sampling bounds/normalization). samplevol(coord, sizef): A function that samples the volume at coord, returning a vec4<f32> (typically RGBA). Outputs: thecoord: The 3D coordinate of the found maximum. theref: The scalar maximum value found (extracted from the r component). thevalue: The full sampled value (vec4<f32>) at thecoord. Data Structures: theref: f32, initialized to a large sentinel value (999999.0). thecoord: vec3<f32>, initialized to startcoord. thevalue: vec4<f32>, initialized to zero. substepcoord: vec3<f32>, initialized to stepcoord. Steps: 1. Coarse Linear Scan: Initialize theref = 999999.0, thecoord = startcoord, and thevalue = vec4<f32>(0.0). Loop iter from 0.0 to nsteps (exclusive). In each iteration: a. Calculate coord = startcoord + iter stepcoord. b. Sample value = samplevol(coord, sizef). c. Extract reff = value.r. d. If reff < theref, update theref = reff, thecoord = coord, and thevalue = value. 2. Fine Refinement (Divide-by-Two): Initialize substepcoord = stepcoord. Loop iter2 from 0 to 3 (4 iterations). In each iteration: a. Halve the step: substepcoord = substepcoord 0.5. b. Calculate neighbors: coord1 = thecoord - substepcoord and coord2 = thecoord + substepcoord. c. Sample neighbors: value1 = samplevol(coord1, sizef) and value2 = samplevol(coord2, sizef). d. Extract values: ref1 = value1.r and ref2 = value2.r. e. Update logic: i. If ref1 <= theref (deliberate less-equal), update theref = ref1, thecoord = coord1, thevalue = value1. ii. Else if ref2 < theref, update theref = ref2, thecoord = coord2, thevalue = value2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsetofinemaxsearch(startcoord, stepcoord, nsteps, sizef, samplevol): # Stage 1: Coarse Linear Scan theref = 999999.0 thecoord = startcoord thevalue = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for iter in range(nsteps): coord = startcoord + iter stepcoord value = samplevol(coord, sizef) reff = value.r if reff < theref: theref = reff thecoord = coord thevalue = value # Stage 2: Fine Refinement substepcoord = stepcoord for iter2 in range(4): substepcoord = substepcoord 0.5 coord1 = thecoord - substepcoord coord2 = thecoord + substepcoord value1 = samplevol(coord1, sizef) value2 = samplevol(coord2, sizef) ref1 = value1.r ref2 = value2.r if ref1 <= theref: # Deliberate less-equal theref = ref1 thecoord = coord1 thevalue = value1 elif ref2 < theref: theref = ref2 thecoord = coord2 thevalue = value2 return thecoord, theref, thevalue Parameters: nsteps: Number of steps in the coarse linear scan. Typical values depend on ray length and desired coarse resolution. Not given in the sources. Refinement iterations: Fixed at 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The refinement loop uses a deliberate less-equal (<=) comparison for the first neighbor (coord1) to handle ties or specific boundary conditions, while using strict less-than (<) for the second neighbor (coord2). The sentinel value 999999.0 assumes volume values are significantly smaller. If values exceed this, the algorithm may fail to update. Boundary checks for coord1 and coord2 are not explicitly detailed in the source snippet; implementation must ensure samplevol handles out-of-bounds coordinates gracefully or clamps them. Time Complexity: O(N + K), where N is nsteps and K is the number of refinement iterations (4). The coarse scan dominates if N \gg 4. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Simple to implement; robustly finds the global maximum within the coarse segment; the refinement stage quickly converges to a local peak. Limitations: The coarse scan may miss narrow peaks if nsteps is too small; the refinement is local and may get stuck in a local maximum if the coarse scan lands in a basin of attraction. When to use: When a reliable estimate of the maximum location is needed before further processing (e.g., isosurface extraction), and computational cost of a full binary search is prohibitive. When not to use: When high precision is required immediately without a coarse stage, or when the volume has very high-frequency noise that could mislead the coarse scan. Originating from implementations in the pygfx library (WGPU renderer), this method is used in image-order volume rendering to efficiently locate peaks along rays for isosurface extraction or maximum intensity projection. It builds on Differential Sampling and Peak Finding. volumeray.wgsl, https://github.com/pygfx/pygfx/blob/main/pygfx/renderers/wgpu/wgsl/volumeray.wgsl, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Mode Rendering with Iso-surfaces and Meshes
head: Hybrid Ray Tracing for Iso-surfaces and Meshes, Surface-Volume Hybrid Rendering
body: Multi-Mode Rendering with Iso-sururface and Meshes is a hybrid rendering technique that combines hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection for explicit surface geometry (meshes) and implicit iso-surfaces with volume ray marching for scalar field data. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering scenes containing both dense volumetric data and sparse, high-frequency surface details by leveraging separate bounding volume hierarchies (BVHs) and shortening the volume integration range based on the nearest surface hit. Unlike pure volume rendering, it prioritizes surface geometry for occlusion and depth cues, and unlike pure mesh rendering, it retains the ability to visualize internal structures up to the surface boundary. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A scalar field dataset (structured AMR or regular grid), a set of triangle meshes, an iso-value for implicit surface generation, a transfer function for volume coloring/opacity, and a camera ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: A final color and opacity for each pixel, potentially including ambient occlusion values. Data Structures: The method maintains three distinct spatial acceleration structures: 1. Volume BVH: A BVH built over the volume data bricks/regions to accelerate empty space skipping during ray marching. 2. Iso-surface BVH: A BVH built over the implicit iso-surface geometry. This structure is rebuilt whenever the iso-value changes. 3. Mesh BVH: A BVH built over the explicit triangle meshes, utilizing hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection (e.g., RTX). Algorithm Steps: 1. Mesh Intersection: Trace the input ray against the Mesh BVH using hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection to find the nearest intersection distance t{mesh}. 2. Iso-surface Intersection: Transform the ray into the volume coordinate space. Trace the transformed ray against the Iso-surface BVH to find the nearest intersection distance t{iso}. 3. Ray Shortening: Determine the effective end of the volume integration range t{end}: If a surface hit exists (t{mesh} < \infty or t{iso} < \infty), set t{end} = \min(t{mesh}, t{iso}). If no surface hit exists, t{end} is determined by the clipping plane's ray.tmax or the volume boundary. Note: Clipping planes are implemented by constraining the ray's [ray.tmin, ray.tmax] intervals. 4. Volume Integration: Trace the shortened ray (from ray.tmin to t{end}) through the Volume BVH. Perform ray marching to integrate the volume data (color and opacity) up to the surface hit point. 5. Surface Shading (Optional): If a surface was hit, shade the surface point using local shading models and/or ambient occlusion. 6. Composite: Combine the volume contribution (from step 4) and the surface contribution (from step 5) using standard alpha compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayo, rayd, meshbvh, isobvh, volumebvh, transferfunc, clippingplanes): # 1. Clip ray based on clipping planes tmin = max(rayo.tmin, clippingplanes.tmin) tmax = min(rayo.tmax, clippingplanes.tmax) # 2. Trace against Mesh BVH (Hardware Accelerated) hitmesh = meshbvh.intersect(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax) tmesh = hitmesh.t if hitmesh else float('inf') # 3. Transform ray to volume space and trace against Iso-surface BVH rayvol = transformtovolumespace(rayo, rayd) hitiso = isobvh.intersect(rayvol, tmin, tmax) tiso = hitiso.t if hitiso else float('inf') # 4. Determine integration end point tend = min(tmesh, tiso, tmax) # 5. Volume Ray Marching volumecolor = vec3(0.0) volumeopacity = 0.0 currentt = tmin # March through volume BVH while currentt < tend: # Sample volume data at currentt sample = volumebvh.sample(rayo, rayd, currentt) color, opacity = transferfunc(sample) # Composite alpha = opacity (1.0 - volumeopacity) volumecolor += color alpha volumeopacity += alpha # Advance step size (could be adaptive or fixed) currentt += stepsize if volumeopacity >= 1.0: break # 6. Surface Shading (if hit) surfacecolor = vec3(0.0) if tmesh < tiso: # Use mesh hit point hitpoint = rayo + rayd tmesh normal = meshbvh.getnormal(hitpoint) surfacecolor = shademesh(hitpoint, normal, ambientocclusion=True) elif tiso < tmesh: # Use iso-surface hit point hitpointvol = rayvol + rayvol.d tiso hitpoint = transformtoworldspace(hitpointvol) normal = isobvh.getnormal(hitpointvol) surfacecolor = shadeisosurface(hitpoint, normal, ambientocclusion=True) # 7. Final Composite finalcolor = volumecolor + surfacecolor (1.0 - volumeopacity) return finalcolor Parameters: Iso-value: Threshold for generating the implicit surface. Changing this requires rebuilding the Iso-surface BVH. Ambient Occlusion: Supported for depth cues, typically requiring two additional rays per pixel for surface and iso-surface geometry. Clipping Planes: Defined by [ray.tmin, ray.tmax] intervals to control the integration range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Iso-value Change: The Iso-surface BVH must be fully rebuilt when the iso-value changes, which can be computationally expensive. Coordinate Space: Rays must be correctly transformed between world and volume space for accurate iso-surface intersection. Precision: Hardware-accelerated intersection may have precision limits; however, the method relies on the BVH for coarse culling and hardware for exact triangle tests. Builds a BVH for implicit surfaces defined by a scalar field threshold. Chosen when the surface topology changes frequently or is defined analytically. Links to Iso-surface and first-hit ray casting. Uses RTX hardware for triangle intersection. Chosen for explicit, static, or frequently updated mesh geometry. Links to Triangular Mesh Scene Rendering. Uses a BVH to skip empty space during ray marching. Chosen for sparse or large-scale volumetric data. Links to Cell-Based First-Hit Ray Casting. Time Complexity: Dominated by the cost of BVH traversals and ray marching. The mesh and iso-surface intersections are O(\log N) due to BVHs, while volume marching is O(K) where K is the number of samples within the shortened ray segment. Memory Complexity: Requires storing three BVHs (Volume, Iso-surface, Mesh) and the underlying scalar field data. Performance: The method leverages hardware acceleration for mesh and iso-surface intersections, which are often sparse, allowing for efficient empty space skipping. Volume marching is optimized by shortening the ray length based on surface hits. Strengths: Supports mixed content (volumes, implicit surfaces, explicit meshes) in a single pipeline. Provides accurate depth cues via surface shading and ambient occlusion. Limitations: Requires rebuilding the Iso-surface BVH when the iso-value changes. Complex to implement due to the need for multiple BVHs and coordinate space transformations. When to Use: Ideal for scientific visualization where both internal volume structures and external surface boundaries need to be rendered simultaneously. When Not to Use: When only pure volume rendering or pure mesh rendering is required, as the overhead of managing multiple BVHs is unnecessary. The method was introduced in the context of the ExaBricks renderer, which targets large-scale structured AMR data. It was developed to support realistic evaluation conditions by combining various rendering modes, including implicit isosurfaces and direct volume rendering. The approach exploits the sparsity of iso-surfaces for efficient empty space skipping and leverages modern GPU hardware for ray-triangle intersection. name: GVDB Raycasting with Binary Search Surface Tracing
head: GVDB Shading and Screen-Space Flow/Depth, custom_iso_kernel shading, flow computation, raySurfaceTrilinearBrickCustom
body: This method is a GPU raycasting kernel that traces rays through a GVDB sparse voxel dataset to find the first surface intersection using fixed-step marching followed by a binary search, then computes surface properties. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its integration of screen-space flow computation and ambient occlusion directly within the surface tracing kernel, rather than relying on separate post-processing passes or mesh extraction. It builds on Isosurface and first-hit ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: GVDB sparse voxel dataset (gvdb), view matrices (current and next), light direction (lightDir), eye direction (eyedir), isosurface threshold (SCNTHRESH), fixed step size (SCNPSTEP), binary search iterations (binarySearchSteps), specular exponent (specularExponent), viewport bounds (viewport). Outputs: Per-pixel hit point, normal, color, flow vector, depth, and ambient occlusion value. Data Structures: GVDB Dataset: Contains node structures with minimum bounds (vmin), voxel size (vdel), and resolution (res). Nodes are accessed via getNodeAtPoint. Atlas Offset: Per-node offset (o) for texture sampling. Ray State: Origin (rpos), direction (rdir), current distance (tCurrent). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel within the viewport range [minX, minY, maxX, maxY], compute ray origin rpos and direction rdir from the current view matrix. 2. Ray Marching: Call raySurfaceTrilinearBrickCustom. Get the leaf node and atlas offset o for the current ray position. Convert world position pworld to index coordinates p using: p = \frac{\text{world\pos} - v{min}}{v{del}[0]} where v{min} is node minimum bounds and v{del}[0] is voxel size. Step ray by SCNPSTEP. Check texture value tex3D against SCNTHRESH. If tex3D >= SCNTHRESH, the ray is inside the volume. Record the previous position (tLower) and current position (tUpper) to bracket the surface. If the ray exceeds volume bounds (p.x/y/z < 0 or >= gvdb->res[0]) or hits an invalid node, terminate and return no hit. 3. Binary Search Refinement: Perform binarySearchSteps iterations to find the closest point outside the isosurface. Initialize tLower to the last position outside the volume and tUpper to the first position inside. For each iteration i: tMiddle = 0.5 \cdot (tLower + tUpper) p = pStart + tMiddle \cdot dir If tex3D(p) >= SCNTHRESH, set tUpper = tMiddle. Else, set tLower = tMiddle. Final hit point: p = pStart + tLower \cdot dir. 4. Surface Property Computation: Normal: Compute via getGradient at the hit point. Color: Compute via getColorF at the hit point. 5. Shading: Start with ambientColor. Diffuse: Add diffuseColor abs(dot(norm, lightDir)). Specular: Compute reflection vector R = \text{normalize}(\text{reflect3}(lightDir, norm)). Add specular term: \text{specular} = c{spec} \cdot \frac{\alpha + 2}{6.82} \cdot \max(0, R \cdot E)^\alpha where c{spec} is specular color, \alpha is specularExponent, R is reflection vector, E is eye direction. 6. Flow Computation: Project hit point to screen space using current view matrix to get screenCurrent. Project hit point to screen space using next view matrix to get screenNext. Compute flow: \text{flow} = 0.5 \cdot (\text{screenCurrent} - \text{screenNext}) where coordinates are normalized. 7. Depth and AO: Compute depth from screenCurrent.z. Compute ambient occlusion via computeAmbientOcclusion. 8. Output: Write hit point, normal, color, flow, depth, and AO to the output buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raySurfaceTrilinearBrickCustom(gvdb, rpos, rdir, SCNPSTEP, SCNTHRESH, binarySearchSteps, viewport): # Initialize ray tCurrent = 0.0 pStart = rpos dir = rdir # Ray marching loop while True: # Check viewport bounds if not ispixelinviewport(viewport): return None # Get node and offset node = getNodeAtPoint(gvdb, pStart + tCurrent dir) if node is None: return None # Invalid node o = node.atlasoffset vmin = node.vmin vdel = node.vdel res = gvdb.res[0] # Convert to index coordinates pworld = pStart + tCurrent dir p = (pworld - vmin) / vdel[0] # Check bounds if p.x < 0 or p.x >= res or p.y < 0 or p.y >= res or p.z < 0 or p.z >= res: return None # Sample texture val = tex3D(gvdb.volIn, p.x + o.x, p.y + o.y, p.z + o.z) if val >= SCNTHRESH: # Inside volume, perform binary search tLower = tCurrent - SCNPSTEP tUpper = tCurrent for i in range(binarySearchSteps): tMiddle = 0.5 (tLower + tUpper) pmid = pStart + tMiddle dir pmididx = (pmid - vmin) / vdel[0] # Check bounds for mid point if pmididx.x < 0 or pmididx.x >= res or pmididx.y < 0 or pmididx.y >= res or pmididx.z < 0 or pmididx.z >= res: tUpper = tMiddle continue valmid = tex3D(gvdb.volIn, pmididx.x + o.x, pmididx.y + o.y, pmididx.z + o.z) if valmid >= SCNTHRESH: tUpper = tMiddle else: tLower = tMiddle # Final hit point hitpoint = pStart + tLower dir return hitpoint else: # Outside volume, step forward tCurrent += SCNPSTEP if tCurrent > MAXDISTANCE: # Max distance guard return None def computeshading(hitpoint, norm, lightDir, eyedir, specularExponent): # Diffuse diffuse = diffuseColor abs(dot(norm, lightDir)) # Specular R = normalize(reflect3(lightDir, norm)) specular = specularColor ((specularExponent + 2) / 6.82) pow(max(0.0, dot(R, eyedir)), specularExponent) return ambientColor + diffuse + specular def computeflow(hitpoint, viewCurrent, viewNext): screenCurrent = projecttoscreen(hitpoint, viewCurrent) screenNext = projecttoscreen(hitpoint, viewNext) flow = 0.5 (screenCurrent - screenNext) return flow Parameters: SCNPSTEP: Fixed step size for ray marching. SCNTHRESH: Isosurface threshold value. binarySearchSteps: Number of binary search iterations, typically 10. specularExponent: Shininess exponent for specular highlight. viewport: Valid pixel range [minX, minY, maxX, maxY]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray marching may exceed volume bounds or hit invalid nodes. Handled by checking p.x/y/z >= 0 and < gvdb->res[0], and checking if getNodeAtPoint returns nullptr. Precision issues in binary search may occur if SCNPSTEP is too large relative to voxel size. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps in ray marching plus logarithmic with respect to precision for binary search. Memory Complexity: Low, as it operates per-pixel and does not require large auxiliary buffers beyond the GVDB structure. Strengths: Efficient for sparse voxel datasets; integrates shading and flow computation in a single pass. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missed thin structures if not tuned properly. When to use: Real-time visualization of sparse volumetric data with surface properties. When not to use: Dense volumes where marching is too slow, or when high-precision surface reconstruction is required without post-processing. This method originates from the GVDB (GPU Volume Database) project, specifically the customisokernel implementation. It is used in interactive volume visualization tools that require real-time surface rendering and flow analysis.
