name: Direct Surface Rendering with Intersection Buffer
head: Direct Surface Rendering, Intersection buffer method
body: Direct Surface Rendering with Intersection Buffer is a volume rendering technique that generates an image-space representation of an isosurface defined by a threshold within a 3D volume, enabling interactive cutting operations without pre-computing a triangular mesh. Unlike methods that extract polygonal meshes (e.g., Marching Cubes) or perform single-hit ray casting, this method stores all surface intersections for each ray in an intersection buffer. This allows the user to define cutting planes interactively by comparing stored depths against near/far depth buffers, avoiding the need to retrace rays through the volume for every view change. It builds on Isosurface and first-hit ray casting by retaining multiple hits per ray. The method consists of two phases: preprocessing (ray casting and buffer construction) and image production (cutting and shading). Inputs: 3D volume dataset V with voxel values. Isosurface threshold \tau. Image plane resolution W \times H. Camera position and orientation. (Optional) Set of cutting planes C1, \dots, Cm with normals N1, \dots, Nm. Outputs: Final image pixels with intensity and depth. Intersection Buffer (stored during preprocessing). 1. Transverse Cube Bit Volume A binary volume used to accelerate traversal. Each bit corresponds to a cube in the volume grid. Layout: 1 bit per cube. Definition: A cube is transverse if it contains the isosurface. 2. Intersection Buffer An array indexed by pixel number i (from 1 to N, where N = W \times H). Layout: k[i]: Integer count of intersections for pixel i. D[i][j]: Depth of the j-th intersection for pixel i (1 \le j \le k[i]). I[i][j]: Intensity (shading value) of the j-th intersection for pixel i. (Optional) N[i][j]: Surface normal at the j-th intersection. Size: Depends on the maximum number of intersections per ray. In tests, the buffer size was 2.13 Mbytes for a 300x300 image. 1. Precompute Transverse Flags: Iterate over all cubes in the volume. For each cube, determine if it is transverse. A cube is transverse if its 8-bit flag b indicates mixed voxel states relative to threshold \tau. For voxel i in the cube: bi = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } Vi \leq \tau \\ 1 & \text{if } Vi > \tau \end{cases} The cube is transverse if the resulting 8-bit integer b satisfies 0 < b < 255 (i.e., binary 00000001 to 11111110). 2. Cast Rays: For each pixel i in the image plane: a. Construct a ray R from the camera through the pixel center. b. Traverse the volume using fast voxel traversal. c. Skip non-transverse cubes using the bit volume. d. For each transverse cube encountered: i. Calculate the ray entry point \alpha and exit point \beta on the cube facets. ii. Evaluate the scalar field F(u) at \alpha and \beta using bi-linear interpolation of the four bounding voxels on the respective facet. iii. Check if the ray span is transverse: if (F(\alpha) - \tau)(F(\beta) - \tau) < 0, the surface intersects the ray segment within the cube. iv. Calculate the intersection point \gamma: \gamma = \alpha + (\beta - \alpha) \left( \frac{\tau - F(\alpha)}{F(\beta) - F(\alpha)} \right) (Note: The source formula uses F(\gamma) in the numerator, but since \gamma is on the surface, F(\gamma) = \tau. The standard linear interpolation form is used here for clarity and correctness, derived from the source's intent). v. Compute the surface normal G at \gamma by tri-linearly interpolating the normals of the 8 bounding voxels. vi. Compute the voxel normal at (x,y,z) using central difference approximation: \begin{aligned} gx &= F(x+1, y, z) - F(x-1, y, z) \\ gy &= F(x, y+1, z) - F(x, y-1, z) \\ gz &= F(x, y, z+1) - F(x, y, z-1) \end{aligned} vii. Calculate intensity I at \gamma using shading (e.g., Phong) with G. viii. Store \gamma's depth D and intensity I in the Intersection Buffer for pixel i. Append to the list for pixel i. e. Continue until the ray exits the volume. 1. Cutting Plane Setup: If cutting planes are specified, scan-convert them to generate two depth buffers: Dnear and Dfar, both of size W \times H. Dnear initialized to 0 (or minimum depth). Dfar initialized to maximum depth (or infinity). For each pixel, Dnear[p] is the depth of the nearest intersection with any cutting plane along the ray. Dfar[p] is the depth of the farthest intersection. 2. Image Generation: For each pixel i: a. Retrieve the list of intersections from the Intersection Buffer. b. Iterate through the intersections j = 1 to k[i]. c. Check if the intersection depth D[i][j] satisfies: D{\text{near}}[i] \leq D[i][j] \leq D{\text{far}}[i] d. The first intersection satisfying this condition is the visible surface point. e. Set the pixel color to I[i][j]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessvolume(volume, threshold, imagewidth, imageheight, camera): """ Preprocesses the volume to create the intersection buffer. """ # 1. Precompute transverse cube flags # volumecubes is a grid of cubes. Each cube has 8 voxels. transverseflags = computetransverseflags(volume, threshold) # 2. Initialize Intersection Buffer # Structure: List of lists. buffer[i] = [(depth, intensity),...] intersectionbuffer = [[] for in range(imagewidth imageheight)] # 3. Cast rays for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): pixelindex = y imagewidth + x ray = camera.getray(x, y) # Fast voxel traversal currentcube = ray.startcube while ray.isinsidevolume(): # Check if transverse using bit test if istransverse(transverseflags, currentcube): # Calculate entry and exit points on cube facets alpha, beta = ray.intersectcube(currentcube) # Evaluate scalar field at entry and exit # F(u) is bi-linear interpolation of facet voxels falpha = interpolatefacet(volume, alpha) fbeta = interpolatefacet(volume, beta) # Check for surface intersection within this cube if (falpha - threshold) (fbeta - threshold) < 0: # Calculate intersection point gamma # Using linear interpolation between alpha and beta t = (threshold - falpha) / (fbeta - falpha) gamma = alpha + t (beta - alpha) # Calculate normal at gamma # Tri-linear interpolation of voxel normals normal = interpolatenormals(volume, gamma) # Calculate intensity (e.g., Phong shading) intensity = computeshading(gamma, normal, camera) # Store depth and intensity depth = ray.distanceto(gamma) intersectionbuffer[pixelindex].append((depth, intensity)) # Move to next cube ray.advancetonextcube() return intersectionbuffer def renderwithcuts(intersectionbuffer, imagewidth, imageheight, cuttingplanes, camera): """ Renders the image using the intersection buffer and cutting planes. """ # 1. Create depth buffers from cutting planes dnear = [0.0] (imagewidth imageheight) dfar = [float('inf')] (imagewidth imageheight) if cuttingplanes: for plane in cuttingplanes: # Scan-convert plane to depth buffers # For each pixel, find intersection with plane for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): idx = y imagewidth + x ray = camera.getray(x, y) t = ray.intersectplane(plane) if t is not None: depth = t if depth > dnear[idx]: dnear[idx] = depth if depth < dfar[idx]: dfar[idx] = depth # 2. Select visible intersections image = [] for y in range(imageheight): row = [] for x in range(imagewidth): idx = y imagewidth + x intersections = intersectionbuffer[idx] visibleintensity = None for depth, intensity in intersections: if dnear[idx] <= depth <= dfar[idx]: visibleintensity = intensity break # First valid intersection if visibleintensity is not None: row.append(visibleintensity) else: row.append(0) # Background image.append(row) return image def computetransverseflags(volume, threshold): """ Computes the 8-bit flag for each cube. """ flags = {} for cube in volume.cubes: flag = 0 for i, voxel in enumerate(cube.voxels): if voxel.value > threshold: flag |= (1 << i) # Transverse if flag is between 1 and 254 if 0 < flag < 255: flags[cube.id] = True else: flags[cube.id] = False return flags def interpolatefacet(volume, point): """ Bi-linear interpolation of the 4 voxels bounding the facet containing point. """ # Implementation depends on specific facet geometry # Returns scalar value F(point) pass def interpolatenormals(volume, point): """ Tri-linear interpolation of normals of 8 bounding voxels. Voxel normal at (x,y,z) is computed via central difference. """ voxelnormals = [] for voxel in point.boundingvoxels(): gx = volume[voxel.x+1, voxel.y, voxel.z] - volume[voxel.x-1, voxel.y, voxel.z] gy = volume[voxel.x, voxel.y+1, voxel.z] - volume[voxel.x, voxel.y-1, voxel.z] gz = volume[voxel.x, voxel.y, voxel.z+1] - volume[voxel.x, voxel.y, voxel.z-1] voxelnormals.append((gx, gy, gz)) # Tri-linear interpolation of these 8 vectors return trilinearinterpolate(voxelnormals, point) Threshold \tau: User-defined value separating surface from volume. Cutting Planes: User-specified planes. In tests, combinations of planes were used to reveal inner structures. Image Resolution: Tested at 300x300. Performance Degradation: The time to extract an image depends on the number of intersections along the ray before a valid one is found or the ray passes the far buffer. More intersections require more comparisons. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for transverse checks and depth buffer comparisons must handle precision limits. Boundary Conditions: Ray traversal must correctly handle rays entering/exiting the volume boundaries. Multiple Surfaces: The method supports multiple disconnected surfaces and semi-transparent surfaces if transparency and color information are stored in the buffer. Time Complexity: Preprocessing: O(N{rays} \cdot N{cubes\traversed}). Fast voxel traversal requires 2 floating point comparisons, 1 addition, 1 integer addition, 2 integer comparisons per transverse cube, and a bit test/comparison for non-transverse cubes. Image Production: O(N{pixels} \cdot N{intersections\per\pixel}). Depends on the number of stored intersections. Memory Complexity: O(N{pixels} \cdot N{max\intersections}). The intersection buffer size was 2.13 Mbytes for a 300x300 image in tests. Measured Performance: On a DEC Alpha 3000 model 400 workstation with a 300x300 image plane: Ray casting for CT Head dataset: 21.35 seconds. Image extraction from buffer: 0.057 seconds. Buffer size: 2.13 Mbytes. Strengths: Enables real-time interactive cutting operations without re-tracing rays. Avoids mesh generation overhead. Supports semi-transparent surfaces and interactive lighting via stored normals. Limitations: High memory usage for large volumes or high intersection counts. Performance degrades with many intersections per ray. Fast voxel traversal is preferred over octree-based traversal because octree entry point calculations outweigh the benefit of skipping non-transverse cubes. When to Use: Real-time cutting operations on large volume datasets in medical imaging and flow visualization. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or when only a single surface hit is needed and interactive cutting is not required. Origin: The method was presented in a paper focusing on real-time cutting operations for displaying surface interiors. History: It was implemented in C on a DEC Alpha 3000 model 400 workstation and tested on CT Head, MR Brain, and Hydrogen datasets. Comparison: Unlike Marching Cubes, which extracts a polygon mesh, this method stores ray-surface intersections directly. It is related to direct volume rendering but focuses on the surface defined by a threshold. Fast Cutting Operations on Three Dimensional Volume Datasets, https://zenodo.org/records/14173364, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Real Time Cutting Operations
head: Cutting Planes via Depth Buffers
body: Real Time Cutting Operations is a technique for clipping volume surfaces using cutting planes by maintaining near and far depth buffers per pixel, avoiding full re-rendering when planes change. It sets itself apart from siblings by pre-computing visibility intervals via scan-conversion of planes into depth buffers, allowing the renderer to discard intersections outside these intervals without re-tracing the entire volume. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of cutting planes Ci defined by normal Ni and offset; a ray R(p) for each pixel p in the image plane; a volume dataset. Outputs: A rendered image where surface points are displayed only if their depth lies within the computed near/far bounds. Data Structures: 1. Near Depth Buffer (D{near}): Array of size equal to image resolution. Stores the maximum depth of "facing same direction" planes or parallel planes in negative halfspace. 2. Far Depth Buffer (D{far}): Array of size equal to image resolution. Stores the minimum depth of "facing opposite direction" planes. 3. Intersection Buffer: Per-pixel storage for all surface intersections along the ray. Layout for pixel (i,j): k{i,j}: Count of intersections. D(i,j): Array of depths for each intersection. I(i,j): Array of intensities for each intersection. Note: The source notation S(i,k) appears to refer to the count or a specific intersection attribute, but the text clarifies k is the count and D/I are arrays indexed by intersection number. Steps: 1. Initialize Buffers: Set all elements in D{near} to 0. Set all elements in D{far} to \text{MAX\DEPTH}. 2. Classify Planes: For each pixel p, classify each cutting plane Ci relative to ray R(p): Parallel: R(p) \cdot Ni = 0. Facing Same Direction: R(p) \cdot Ni > 0. Facing Opposite Direction: R(p) \cdot Ni < 0. 3. Update Depth Buffers: If Ci is parallel to R(p) AND pixel p is in the negative halfspace of the plane (Ci(p) < 0), set D{near}(p) \leftarrow \text{MAX\DEPTH} and D{far}(p) \leftarrow 0. If Ci faces the same direction as R(p), compute intersection depth d. Update D{near}(p) = \max(D{near}(p), d). If Ci faces the opposite direction to R(p), compute intersection depth d. Update D{far}(p) = \min(D{far}(p), d). 4. Ray Casting and Intersection: Cast rays into the volume. Store all surface intersections in the Intersection Buffer, recording depth D(i,j) and intensity I(i,j) for each intersection. 5. Visibility Test: For each intersection at depth d in pixel p, display the surface point if D{near}(p) \le d \le D{far}(p). Discard points where d < D{near}(p) or d > D{far}(p). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def realtimecuttingoperations(cuttingplanes, imagewidth, imageheight, maxdepth): # Initialize depth buffers Dnear = [0.0] (imagewidth imageheight) Dfar = [maxdepth] (imagewidth imageheight) # Process each pixel for p in range(imagewidth imageheight): ray = getrayforpixel(p) for plane in cuttingplanes: # Classify plane relative to ray dotproduct = dot(ray.direction, plane.normal) if abs(dotproduct) < epsilon: # Parallel plane if evaluateplane(plane, ray.origin + ray.direction 0.0) < 0: # Pixel in negative halfspace Dnear[p] = maxdepth Dfar[p] = 0.0 elif dotproduct > 0: # Facing same direction depth = computeintersectiondepth(ray, plane) if depth is not None: Dnear[p] = max(Dnear[p], depth) else: # Facing opposite direction depth = computeintersectiondepth(ray, plane) if depth is not None: Dfar[p] = min(Dfar[p], depth) # Ray casting and filtering intersections = [] for p in range(imagewidth imageheight): ray = getrayforpixel(p) # Cast ray and collect all intersections rayintersections = castrayintovolume(ray) for intersection in rayintersections: if Dnear[p] <= intersection.depth <= Dfar[p]: intersections.append({ 'pixel': p, 'depth': intersection.depth, 'intensity': intersection.intensity }) return intersections Parameters: \text{MAX\DEPTH}: Maximum depth value for the volume or scene. Not given in the sources. \epsilon: Epsilon for floating point comparison for parallel detection. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Parallel Planes: If a plane is parallel to the ray and the pixel is in the negative halfspace, the near buffer is set to max and far to zero, effectively disabling visibility for that pixel. No Intersections: If no intersections are found, nothing is displayed. Precision: Floating point comparisons for parallel detection require an epsilon threshold. Time Complexity: Pre-processing depth buffers is O(P \cdot C) where P is number of pixels and C is number of cutting planes. Ray casting is O(R \cdot I) where R is number of rays and I is average intersections per ray. Visibility test is O(I) per ray. Memory Complexity: O(P) for depth buffers plus O(R \cdot I) for intersection buffer. Strengths: Allows interactive specification of cutting planes without re-tracing the entire volume for every change. Limitations: Requires storing all intersections before filtering, which can be memory intensive for complex volumes. When to use: When interactive cutting is required and the volume has sparse or well-defined surfaces. When not to use: When memory is constrained or the volume has extremely dense intersections. The method was introduced in "Fast Cutting Operations on Three Dimensional Volume Datasets". It addresses the need for efficient clipping in volume rendering by decoupling plane updates from ray casting. name: Distance-field ray marching
head: Sphere tracing
body: Distance-field ray marching (commonly known as sphere tracing) is a rendering method that finds surfaces by moving along a ray in repeated steps, using a signed distance field (SDF) to choose each step size adaptively, avoiding the tradeoff of fixed-step marching. Unlike naive fixed-step marching which uses a constant increment, sphere tracing uses the SDF value as the step size, ensuring the step is as large as possible without risk of overshooting. Unlike traditional rasterization, the visible shape is defined mathematically by a scene function, not by a triangle mesh. The method renders geometry by shooting a ray through each pixel and repeatedly querying a Signed Distance Function (SDF). An SDF is a formula that, given any point p in space, returns the distance from p to the nearest surface. The sign indicates position: negative inside, positive outside, zero exactly on the surface. The core loop initializes a ray with an origin point ro and a normalized direction vector v. It maintains a current position p (initially ro). In each iteration: 1. The SDF is evaluated at p to get the distance d to the nearest surface. 2. If d < 0, the ray has penetrated the surface; the algorithm returns a hit. 3. If d \le \text{HIT\THRESHOLD} (a small value such as 0.001), the ray has hit the surface. The loop terminates. 4. Otherwise, the position is advanced: p \leftarrow p + d \cdot v. This step size is guaranteed not to overshoot the surface because d is the distance to the nearest surface. 5. The loop continues while the step count is less than \text{MAX\STEPS}. If the loop terminates without a hit (e.g., t exceeds a maximum range or \text{MAX\STEPS} is reached), the ray misses. The scene is defined by combining primitive SDFs. For a sphere of radius r centered at c, the distance function is d(p) = \|p - c\| - r. Union of two objects with distance fields d1 and d2 is iso(p) = \min(d1(p), d2(p)). Intersection is iso(p) = \max(d1(p), d2(p)). Subtraction of object d2 from d1 is iso(p) = \max(d1(p), -d2(p)). Parameters include \text{MAX\STEPS} (a safety cap, typically 32 to 128 depending on implementation) and \text{HIT\THRESHOLD} (epsilon). A maximum range or accumulated travel distance limit can also bound rays that miss. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarch(ro, v, scene, maxsteps=40, hitthreshold=0.001, maxrange=100.0): p = ro for i in range(maxsteps): d = scene(p) if d < 0: return p, True, dot(p - ro, v) if d <= hitthreshold: return p, True, dot(p - ro, v) p += v d if dot(p - ro, v) > maxrange: break return p, False, dot(p - ro, v) Estimates surface normals at an SDF isosurface by numerically computing the gradient using central finite differences along the coordinate axes. Chosen when shading requires accurate normals without explicit mesh data. Uses precomputed gradient, occupancy, and distance maps for efficient empty space skipping. Chosen when rendering large voxel-based volumes where traversal overhead dominates. Applies stochastic Woodcock tracking using macrocell majorants to handle density variations. Chosen for volumetric rendering with highly heterogeneous media. Determines occlusion by sphere tracing a ray towards a light source. Chosen when accurate hard shadows are needed for implicit surfaces. Uses a 3D distance texture with dual bounding boxes to handle boundary conditions and invalid values at texture edges. Chosen when rendering implicit surfaces stored in GPU textures. Refines coarse ray-marched hits using bisection and Newton's method for precise surface intersection. Chosen when high-precision hit locations are required. Adapts step sizes to guarantee safety against overshooting, often using Lipschitz bounds or conservative scaling. Chosen when rendering non-Lipschitz or noisy distance fields. Approximates the intersection of a viewing cone with an implicit surface for antialiasing at grazing angles. Chosen when rendering smooth, alias-free edges without supersampling. Provides mathematical formulas for basic shapes (spheres, boxes, tori) and CSG operations. Chosen as the foundational building blocks for scene construction. The core technique that varies step sizes along a ray using SDF values to guarantee safe progression without penetration. Chosen as the standard baseline for implicit surface rendering. Extends sphere tracing for Fractal Brownian Motion noise using a BVH to compute valid distance bounds and adaptive steps. Chosen for rendering complex procedural fractals efficiently. Performs real-time GPU volume rendering by marching through a 3D scalar field (e.g., smoke density) to compute color and transparency. Chosen for volumetric effects like fog, clouds, or medical data. The technique was introduced as 'Sphere Tracing' by John C. Hart in 1994 in 'Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces'. It became widely used in 4k intros released in 2009, specifically in productions like 'Frequency' by xt95 and 'Potatro'. name: Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant
head: Woodcock tracker, stochastic ray marching with majorant
body: This method performs volume rendering using Woodcock tracking (null-collision) within coarse mesh elements, utilizing macrocell densities to determine the majorant extinction value. It builds on Distance-field ray marching by replacing deterministic step sizes with stochastic jumps governed by a majorant, and integrates the traversal of a coarse mesh structure to manage the underlying adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. Using macrocell majorant values provides a tighter majorant than using only transfer function opacity, reducing null collisions and improving performance. The algorithm processes a ray through a coarse tetrahedral element. It maintains the ray's parametric distance t along the direction vector. The core loop advances the ray by a stochastic step size determined by the majorant, samples the scalar field, and performs an acceptance test against the majorant to determine if a collision (interaction) occurs. Inputs: ray: Ray structure with origin ray.org, direction ray.dir, and current parametric distance ray.t. tMax: Maximum ray distance for traversal. coarseTetID: Identifier for the current coarse tetrahedral element. macrocellMajorant: Pre-computed majorant value for the macrocell containing the element. tf: Transfer function object providing inRange(scalar), getColor(scalar), and opacity. Outputs: color: The accumulated color if a collision is accepted; otherwise, the function returns false (no hit). Data Structures: tetVertices: Array of 4 vertex positions for the current tetrahedron. sampleTetID: Identifier for the specific leaf tetrahedron within the coarse element where sampling occurs. Steps: 1. Initialize Majorant: Calculate the effective majorant for the current step. M = \text{tf.opacity} \times \text{macrocellMajorant} If M \le 0, the ray skips this element; return false. 2. Initialize Traversal State: Set tExit to the next representable floating-point number below ray.t to ensure strict inequality checks for exit conditions: tExit ← nextafterf(ray.t, -INFINITY). Initialize sampleTetID ← 0 and tetVertices ← {}. 3. Stochastic Loop: Advance Ray: Generate a random number u \in (0, 1). Update the ray's parametric distance: t{new} = t{current} - \frac{\ln(1 - u)}{M} Update ray.t to t{new}. Check Bounds: If ray.t \ge tMax, the ray has exceeded the maximum range; return false. Calculate Sample Point: Compute the 3D position: p = \text{ray.org} + \text{ray.t} \times \text{ray.dir}. Check Element Exit: If ray.t > tExit, the ray has exited the current tetrahedron boundary. Traverse the mesh to find the new tetrahedron containing p: sampleTetID, tetVertices ← traverse(p, coarseTetID). Calculate the exit distance for the new tetrahedron: tExit ← intersectFaces(ray.t, p, ray.dir, tetVertices). Sample Data: Retrieve the scalar value at p using the current tetrahedron: scalar ← sampleData(p, sampleTetID, tetVertices). Transfer Function Check: If scalar is not in the transfer function's valid range (!tf.inRange(scalar)), continue to the next iteration of the loop (null collision due to empty space). Get Color: Retrieve the color and opacity from the transfer function: color ← tf.getColor(scalar). Acceptance Test: Generate a new random number u' \in (0, 1). If: \text{color.opacity} \times \text{tf.opacity} \ge u' \times M then a collision is accepted. Return color. Otherwise, continue to the next iteration (null collision). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def woodcockelem(ray, tmax, coarsetetid, macrocellmajorant, tf): # 1. Initialize Majorant majorant = tf.opacity macrocellmajorant if majorant <= 0: return False # 2. Initialize Traversal State # nextafterf(x, -inf) returns the largest representable floating point number less than x texit = nextafterf(ray.t, -float('inf')) sampletetid = 0 tetvertices = {} # 3. Stochastic Loop while True: # Advance Ray u = random() ray.t = ray.t - log(1 - u) / majorant # Check Bounds if ray.t >= tmax: return False # Calculate Sample Point samplepoint = ray.org + ray.t ray.dir # Check Element Exit if ray.t > texit: sampletetid, tetvertices = traverse(samplepoint, coarsetetid) texit = intersectfaces(ray.t, samplepoint, ray.dir, tetvertices) # Sample Data scalar = sampledata(samplepoint, sampletetid, tetvertices) # Transfer Function Check if not tf.inrange(scalar): continue # Get Color color = tf.getcolor(scalar) # Acceptance Test uprime = random() if color.opacity tf.opacity >= uprime majorant: return color Parameters: tMax: Maximum ray distance. If exceeded, the ray is terminated. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Agulhas Dataset Performance: On the Agulhas dataset, using macrocell optimizations for Woodcock tracking decreases performance. This is because processing must restart from the beginning of the next element when using macrocell values to avoid overstepping into denser regions and missing collisions. Floating Point Precision: The use of nextafterf for tExit is critical to prevent immediate re-entry or infinite loops due to floating-point equality issues at boundaries. It builds on Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant by integrating the traversal of a coarse mesh structure to manage the underlying adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. Using macrocell majorant values provides a tighter majorant than using only transfer function opacity, reducing null collisions and improving performance. However, it degrades performance on the Agulhas dataset due to the overhead of restarting element processing to prevent missing collisions in shallow trees. Comparison: In tests on unstructured mesh data, the Woodcock tracker was significantly faster than the standard Ray Marcher (e.g., 29.07s vs 112.51s on one dataset, 26.30s vs 115.71s on another). Scaling: Rendering times for the Ray Marcher grow with smaller step sizes. The Woodcock tracker's performance is less dependent on fixed step sizes but depends on the tightness of the majorant. It applies the Woodcock tracking algorithm, a standard technique in Monte Carlo radiation transport, to the context of volume rendering on AMR tetrahedral meshes. name: Woodcock Tracking with Coarse Mesh and Macrocells
head: Null-collision Woodcock with macrocell majorant, Woodcock ray casting on AMR
body: This method performs volume rendering using Woodcock tracking (null-collision) within coarse mesh elements, utilizing macrocell densities to determine the majorant extinction value. It builds on Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant by integrating the traversal of a coarse mesh structure to manage the underlying adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. Using macrocell majorant values provides a tighter majorant than using only transfer function opacity, reducing null collisions and improving performance. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, maximum ray length (t{max}), coarse mesh structure, macrocell density values, transfer function (TF), and scalar field data. Outputs: Final pixel color. Data Structures: Coarse Mesh: A hierarchy of coarse tetrahedra. Each coarse element has an associated macrocellMajorant value. Macrocell Values: An array or map where macrocellValues[coarseID] stores the maximum macrocell density for that coarse element. Transfer Function: Provides tf.opacity (scalar to opacity mapping) and tf.getColor(scalar) (scalar to RGBA color). Refinement Tree: Used to locate the specific fine tetrahedron within a coarse element. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coarse Element Traversal: Call TraverseCoarseMesh(ray) to determine the current coarse element ID (coarseID), the back face distance (tBack), and the next face distance (tNextFace). If coarseID is -1, the ray has exited the volume. Return the background color. 2. Majorant Calculation: Retrieve the macrocell majorant: macrocellMajorant = macrocellValues[coarseID]. Call WoodcockElem with this majorant. Inside WoodcockElem, calculate the effective majorant: \sigma{max} = \text{tf.opacity} \times \text{macrocellMajorant} If \sigma{max} \le 0, return false (no emission/absorption possible). 3. Free Path Sampling: Sample a free path length using the majorant \sigma{max}: t{step} = -\frac{\log(1 - \text{rand}())}{\sigma{max}} Update the ray position: t{ray} = t{ray} + t{step} If t{ray} \ge t{max}, return false. 4. Tetrahedron Location: Calculate the sample point: P = \text{ray.org} + t{ray} \times \text{ray.dir} If the sample point is outside the current tetrahedron (checked against tExit), traverse the refinement tree to find the specific fine tetrahedron (sampleTetID) and its vertices (tetVertices). Update tExit to the distance to the exit face of the new tetrahedron. 5. Scalar Sampling and Acceptance: Sample the scalar value at P using sampleTetID and tetVertices. If the scalar is not in the transfer function range, continue the loop (null collision). Get the color: color = tf.getColor(scalar). Perform the null-collision acceptance test: \text{color.opacity} \times \text{tf.opacity} \ge \text{rand}() \times \sigma{max} If accepted, return color. Otherwise, treat as a null collision and continue the loop. 6. Boundary Handling: When stepping over to the next coarse element, if the previous volume was less dense, the free path might overstep the boundary. To fix this, set ray.t to just after the next coarse element's minimum t value in front of the ray, effectively taking a step back to the beginning of the next coarse element. This step is not needed if macrocell majorant values are not used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def woodcockcoarse(ray, macrocellvalues, tf, tmax): """ Main loop for Woodcock tracking on coarse mesh. ray: object with.org,.dir,.t (current t) macrocellvalues: dict mapping coarseid to max macrocell density tf: transfer function object with.opacity(scalar),.getcolor(scalar),.inrange(scalar) tmax: maximum ray length """ while True: # 1. Traverse coarse mesh coarseid, tback, tnextface = traversecoarsemesh(ray) if coarseid == -1: return backgroundcolor # 2. Get macrocell majorant macrocellmajorant = macrocellvalues[coarseid] # 3. Process element color = woodcockelem(ray, tback, coarseid, macrocellmajorant, tf, tmax) if color is not None: return color # 4. Handle boundary crossing # If we exited the element, reset t to just after the next face to prevent overstepping # due to density changes between elements ray.t = tnextface + epsilon def woodcockelem(ray, texit, coarsetetid, macrocellmajorant, tf, tmax): """ Woodcock tracking inside a single coarse element. texit: distance to the exit face of the current tetrahedron """ # Calculate effective majorant # Note: tf.opacity is typically the opacity at the specific scalar, # but here it seems to refer to a scaling factor or the max opacity for the element. # Based on source: majorant = tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # We assume tf.opacity here refers to the opacity scaling factor for the element # or is evaluated per sample. The source code snippet suggests: # majorant <- tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # However, tf.opacity is usually scalar-dependent. # Looking at Algorithm 12 line 2: majorant <- tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # And line 24: color.opacity tf.opacity >= rand() majorant # This implies tf.opacity might be a constant for the element or the source # uses tf.opacity as a global scaling factor. # Let's follow the source literally: majorant is calculated once per element? # No, line 24 uses color.opacity tf.opacity. # If majorant is constant, then the acceptance test compares against it. # Let's assume tf.opacity in line 2 is a constant for the element, # or the source implies the majorant is based on the max opacity. # Given "maximum macrocell density... scaled with the opacity of the transfer function", # it likely means: sigmamax = maxtfopacity maxmacrocelldensity. # Re-reading Algorithm 12: # 2: majorant <- tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # This line is outside the while loop. So majorant is constant for the element. # This implies tf.opacity is a constant for the element (e.g., max opacity). sigmamax = tf.opacity macrocellmajorant if sigmamax <= 0: return None # Initialize tetrahedron info sampletetid = 0 tetvertices = [] while True: # Sample free path ray.t = ray.t - log(1 - rand()) / sigmamax if ray.t >= tmax: return None samplepoint = ray.org + ray.t ray.dir # Check if we are still in the current tetrahedron if ray.t > texit: # Traverse refinement tree to find the fine tetrahedron sampletetid, tetvertices = traverserefinementtree(samplepoint, coarsetetid) # Update texit to the exit face of the new tetrahedron texit = intersectfaces(ray.t, samplepoint, ray.dir, tetvertices) # Sample scalar scalar = sampledata(samplepoint, sampletetid, tetvertices) if not tf.inrange(scalar): continue color = tf.getcolor(scalar) # Acceptance test # Source: color.opacity tf.opacity >= rand() majorant # Note: tf.opacity here is the same constant used for sigmamax? # If so, this simplifies to: color.opacity >= rand() macrocellmajorant # But let's stick to the source formula. if color.opacity tf.opacity >= rand() sigmamax: return color Performance: Using macrocell majorant values reduces null collisions compared to using only transfer function opacity, leading to better performance. Complexity: The complexity depends on the coarse mesh traversal and the refinement tree depth. The method allows for interactive frame rates on tested datasets. Memory: Requires storing coarse mesh structures, macrocell values, and the refinement tree. The transfer function and scalars reside in GPU memory. Limitations: Only emission and absorption are implemented; secondary effects are not supported. This method is part of a volume rendering system for tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. It was implemented alongside a ray marching method. The approach leverages the fact that transfer functions and scalars reside in GPU memory, allowing recalculation during rendering. name: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians
body: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians is a volumetric rendering method that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture along camera rays to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral, contrasting with the rasterization-based splatting approach of Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of approximations in standard 3DGS, such as ignoring spatial overlap and incorrect self-attenuation, by performing adaptive sampling and integration. Unlike splatting, which projects Gaussians to screen space and blends them, this method traverses the 3D scene directly, ensuring that overlapping primitives are resolved with precision governed by the sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Scene representation: A set of M 3D Gaussians, each defined by mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color coefficients (e.g., spherical harmonics) \mathbf{c}i. Ray marching parameters: Maximum depth, minimum step size, and convergence threshold. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C} and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}. Data Structures: Gaussian Tensor: A tensor of shape (M, D) where D includes fields for position (3), scale (3 or 1), rotation (4 for quaternion), opacity (1), and color coefficients (variable, e.g., 4 \times 3 for SH order 1). Ray Buffer: Stores current ray position, accumulated transmittance T, and accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc}. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Initialize ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}, accumulated transmittance T = 1.0, and accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} = \mathbf{0}. 2. Adaptive Sampling Loop: While T > \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small threshold, e.g., 10^{-5}) and step count < N{max}: a. Step Selection: Determine the next step size \Delta t using adaptive sampling along the ray. b. Ray Advance: Update ray position: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p} + \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{d}. c. Gaussian Evaluation: For each Gaussian i in the scene (or within a spatially accelerated bounding volume): i. Distance Calculation: Compute the squared Mahalanobis distance from the ray point \mathbf{p}{new} to the Gaussian center \boldsymbol{\mu}i: di^2 = (\mathbf{p}{new} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^T \mathbf{\Sigma}i^{-1} (\mathbf{p}{new} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i) \mathbf{\Sigma}i is the 3D covariance matrix derived from scale and rotation. ii. Density/Opacity Contribution: Compute the Gaussian value at the sample point: gi = \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} di^2\right) Note that 3DGS typically uses an opacity model, while OTS uses an extinction-based model. The difference lies in how gi is integrated into the transmittance equation. iii. Color Contribution: Compute the view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{v}) for the viewing direction \mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{d} using spherical harmonics if applicable. d. Integration: Update accumulated transmittance and color. For 3DGS Marcher (Opacity Model): The contribution is blended based on the Gaussian's opacity relative to the accumulated transmittance. \alpha{contrib} = gi \mathbf{C}{acc} = \mathbf{C}{acc} + T \cdot \alpha{contrib} \cdot \mathbf{c}i T = T \cdot (1 - \alpha{contrib}) This approximates the volumetric integral using the 3DGS opacity formulation. For OTS Marcher (Extinction Model): The contribution is integrated using an extinction-based model, which more accurately handles overlap. \Delta Ti = \exp\left(-\int{t}^{t+\Delta t} \sigmai(\tau) d\tau\right) The integration is performed via adaptive sampling along each ray to compute the transmittance drop. e. Update: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}{new}. 3. Final Color: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}{acc} + T \cdot \mathbf{C}{background} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchgaussians(rayo, rayd, gaussians, maxsteps=1000, epsilon=1e-5): # Initialize ray buffer p = rayo.clone() T = torch.tensor(1.0) Cacc = torch.zeros(3) backgroundcolor = torch.zeros(3) # for step in range(maxsteps): if T < epsilon: break # Adaptive step selection along the ray deltat = 0.1 # Sources specify adaptive sampling; exact step logic is implementation-dependent # Advance ray pnew = p + deltat rayd # Evaluate Gaussian mixture for i in range(len(gaussians)): mu, sigmainv, alpha, shcoeffs = gaussians[i] v = -rayd # Viewing direction # Mahalanobis distance diff = pnew - mu dsq = diff @ sigmainv @ diff # Gaussian value gi = alpha torch.exp(-0.5 dsq) # View-dependent color ci = evaluatesphericalharmonics(shcoeffs, v) # Integration model if useextinctionmodel: # OTS Marcher # Extinction-based integration via adaptive sampling transmittancedrop = torch.exp(-gi deltat) # Approximation Cacc += T (1 - transmittancedrop) ci T = transmittancedrop else: # 3DGS Marcher # Opacity-based blending alphacontrib = gi Cacc += T alphacontrib ci T = (1 - alphacontrib) p = pnew # Final color composition C = Cacc + T backgroundcolor return C Parameters: Sample Count: Governs precision. The ray marcher performs adaptive sampling along each ray to accurately resolve Gaussian overlap to compute the volumetric integral with a precision governed by the sample count. Threshold \epsilon: Controls when to stop marching. Typical value: 10^{-5}. Max Steps: Prevents infinite loops. Typical value: 100-1000 depending on scene depth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Popping artifacts result from approximations made based only on Gaussian centers and ignoring spatial overlap, not floating-point errors. Boundaries: Ray clipping against scene bounds is required. Degenerate Input: Gaussians with zero scale or invalid rotations must be filtered out. Overlap: Standard 3DGS splatting ignores overlap; ray marching resolves it, but at higher computational cost. The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm is a volumetric rendering method for 3D Gaussians that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral using an extinction-based model. It distinguishes itself from splatting-based approaches by performing adaptive binning and analytical integration along rays, ensuring that overlapping Gaussians are resolved with precision governed by sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Unlike raytracing solutions for Gaussians, this method explicitly accounts for primitive overlap in the integration process. A ray marching-based renderer that follows the 3DGS model of opacity, reusing the data structures (tensors with weights, positions, scales, and rotations), activation functions, and learning rates of 3DGS. It differs from OTS Marcher in the model of opacity/extinction used, but shares the same ray marching pipeline structure (per-primitive pass, tiling, sorting, per-pixel kernel). A technique to model view-dependent appearance (e.g., reflections) in 3D Gaussian Splatting by representing the color of each Gaussian as a function of the viewing direction using spherical harmonics coefficients, rather than a single static color value. The color is computed by evaluating the spherical harmonics basis functions at the viewing direction vector associated with that Gaussian, using the pre-trained spherical harmonic coefficients stored for that Gaussian. The implementation uses all available spherical harmonic components from pre-trained models, with the baseline comparison using only the 0th order (DC) coefficient, which represents view-independent color. Using all spherical harmonic components produces renderings with view-dependent effects (shiny surfaces, reflections), whereas using only the DC (0th order) component results in view-independent, lower-quality renderings that lack these specular details. The core logic is implemented in the function coloursfromsphericalharmonics in model.py, which must be vectorized. A method that integrates physics-based continuum mechanics directly within 3DGS, treating each Gaussian as a discrete physical particle with volume. It allows direct simulation of the Gaussians, enabling physically accurate dynamics. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store Gaussian parameters. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades with the number of Gaussians and sample count. Strengths: Accurate handling of overlap and self-attenuation; no rasterization artifacts; consistent with volumetric rendering theory. Limitations: High computational cost due to per-ray evaluation and adaptive sampling. When to use: When accuracy is critical, such as in scientific visualization or offline rendering; when studying the impact of approximations in 3DGS. When not to use: For real-time applications where speed is paramount; standard splatting is preferred for interactive applications. Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians was introduced to systematically analyze and assess the approximations made in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), such as spatial overlap and sorting. The method was developed to clarify the differences between 3DGS and accurate volumetric rendering, specifically regarding opacity vs. extinction-based rendering. It builds on the 3DGS model but replaces the rasterization pipeline with a ray-marching one, allowing for the reuse of learned Gaussian parameters. The approach has been used to demonstrate that approximations like overlap and sorting have negligible impact on still images, especially with a large number of Gaussians. name: OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm
head: Adaptive Binning Ray Marching, OTS Marcher, OTS Marching, Ray Marching (OTS scheme)
body: The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm is a volumetric rendering method for 3D Gaussians that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral using an extinction-based model. It distinguishes itself from splatting-based approaches by performing adaptive binning and analytical integration along rays, ensuring that overlapping Gaussians are resolved with precision governed by sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Unlike raytracing solutions for Gaussians, this method explicitly accounts for primitive overlap in the integration process. The algorithm performs adaptive sampling along each viewing ray to resolve Gaussian overlap. It iterates over the Gaussian mixture twice: first to establish bin borders adapted to the Gaussian data, and second to perform analytical integration into bins of variable extent. The bins are then blended together following the volume integral equation. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, scale, rotation, and color; a viewing ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a maximum ray depth or opacity threshold. Outputs: The final pixel color I(\mathbf{x}) and accumulated transmittance. Density Section Buffer: A fixed-size buffer storing sections. Each section is defined by: start: The start parameter t along the ray. end: The end parameter t along the ray. density: The sampling density for this section. Bin: A segment of the ray defined by start and end t values, storing integrated color and extinction. 1. Adaptive Binning Initialization: Create a fixed-size density section buffer. Iterate over all Gaussians to fill the buffer. For each Gaussian, compute its intersection interval with the ray. Define the start and end of the sampling section using the Gaussian's position \pm 3 standard deviations along the ray direction. Compute the density such that a pre-defined number of bins fit within the space defined by start and end. 2. Section Merging: Add the new section to the density section buffer. Combine existing and new sections to ensure they are ordered and non-overlapping. If sections overlap, the section with the higher sampling density takes precedence in the overlap area. Combining two sections can result in up to three new sections. Sections that fall outside the buffer capacity are deferred to the next batch. 3. Bin Creation: Traverse the merged sections to create bins. The size of each bin is inversely proportional to the density of the section it belongs to. 4. Blending Integral Computation (Batching): Divide the work into batches of bins (e.g., 128 bins per batch). Initialize the first batch at t=0. Subsequent batches start at the end-border of the last bin of the previous batch. Iterate over the Gaussian mixture again to compute integrals for each bin in the current batch. For each bin, compute 4 values: Red, Green, Blue, and integrated extinction (opacity). Colors are multiplied by the per-Gaussian integrated extinction. Stop when all Gaussians are processed or accumulated opacity reaches a high threshold. 5. Blending: Blend the bin evaluations together using the following equation: I(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{\infty} \gammai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} e^{-\rhoj} + cb \prod{j=0}^{\infty} e^{-\rhoj} Where: \gammai is the color contribution of bin i. \rhoj is the integrated extinction (opacity) of bin j. The term \prod{j=0}^{i-1} e^{-\rhoj} is the transmittance factor, cached between iterations to avoid redundant computation. cb is the background color. 6. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients manually using a front-to-back strategy. Two variants exist: Attached: Considers the numerical integration procedure and border positions in the gradient calculation. Detached: Assumes the numerical method can be ignored, keeping sampling and border positions constant with respect to differentiation. The detached variant performs significantly better. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def otsmarchingraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, backgroundcolor, maxsectionsbuffer, binsperbatch=128, opacitythreshold=0.99, binspergaussian=10): """ Renders a single ray using the OTS Marching Algorithm. """ # 1. Adaptive Binning Initialization sections = [] for g in gaussians: # Compute intersection interval along ray using position +/- 3 standard deviations tstart = g.position - 3.0 g.scale tend = g.position + 3.0 g.scale if tstart > tend: tstart, tend = tend, tstart # Compute density such that a pre-defined number of bins fit in the space length = tend - tstart density = binspergaussian / length if length > 0 else 0.0 newsection = Section(start=tstart, end=tend, density=density) sections = mergesections(sections, newsection, maxsectionsbuffer) # 2. Bin Creation bins = createbins(sections) # 3. Blending Integral Computation (Batching) totalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for batchstart in range(0, len(bins), binsperbatch): batchend = min(batchstart + binsperbatch, len(bins)) currentbatchbins = bins[batchstart:batchend] for bin in currentbatchbins: bincolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] binextinction = 0.0 # Iterate over Gaussians again to compute integrals for each bin for g in gaussians: # Check overlap and compute analytical integral if g.overlapssegment(bin.start, bin.end): c, e = g.integrateoversegment(bin.start, bin.end) bincolor[0] += c[0] bincolor[1] += c[1] bincolor[2] += c[2] binextinction += e # Front-to-back blending matching Eq. 3 transmittancefactor = exp(-binextinction) totalcolor[0] += bincolor[0] transmittance totalcolor[1] += bincolor[1] transmittance totalcolor[2] += bincolor[2] transmittance transmittance = transmittancefactor # Check accumulated opacity threshold if 1.0 - transmittance >= opacitythreshold: break if 1.0 - transmittance >= opacitythreshold: break # Add background totalcolor[0] += backgroundcolor[0] transmittance totalcolor[1] += backgroundcolor[1] transmittance totalcolor[2] += backgroundcolor[2] transmittance return totalcolor, transmittance def mergesections(existing, newsec, maxsize): """ Combines newsec with existing sections ensuring order and no overlap. Higher density wins in overlap. Combining 2 sections creates up to 3 new sections. """ merged = existing + [newsec] merged.sort(key=lambda s: s.start) result = [] for sec in merged: if not result: result.append(sec) continue last = result[-1] if sec.start < last.end: # Overlap exists if sec.density >= last.density: # Higher density wins: extend last section, discard lower density part last.end = max(last.end, sec.end) else: # Lower density wins in overlap: split last section last.end = sec.start result.append(sec) else: result.append(sec) # Defer excess sections to next batch if buffer full if len(result) > maxsize: result = result[:maxsize] return result def createbins(sections): """ Traverse sections to create bins. Bin size is inversely proportional to density. """ bins = [] for sec in sections: if sec.density <= 0: continue binwidth = 1.0 / sec.density t = sec.start while t < sec.end: binend = min(t + binwidth, sec.end) bins.append(Bin(start=t, end=binend)) t = binend return bins class Section: def init(self, start, end, density): self.start = start self.end = end self.density = density class Bin: def init(self, start, end): self.start = start self.end = end Batch Size: Typically 128 bins per batch. Activation Function: Softplus with \beta = 2 is used instead of sigmoid to allow Gaussians to become fully opaque. Standard Deviation Factor: 3 standard deviations are used to define the start and end of sampling sections. Buffer Overflow: Sections that fall out of the fixed-size density section buffer are deferred to the next batch. Opacity Convergence: Using a constant opacity initialization can prevent convergence for large Gaussian counts. A power function fitting opacity to the number of Gaussians is recommended for initialization. Gradient Choice: The attached gradient variant is computationally more expensive and performs worse than the detached variant. Performance: The algorithm is considerably slower than splatting, typically between one and two orders of magnitude slower, depending on the scene. Accuracy: It provides accurate resolution of Gaussian overlap and precise perspective projection, serving as a testbed to examine the importance of these factors in 3DGS. Complexity: The algorithm requires iterating over the Gaussian mixture twice per batch (once for binning, once for integration), leading to higher computational cost compared to single-pass splatting. Strengths: Accurate volumetric rendering, handles overlap correctly, accounts for primitive overlap in integration unlike some raytracing solutions. Limitations: Low performance compared to splatting; implementation complexity is higher. The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm was introduced in the paper "Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?". It was developed as part of an implementation to study the impact of approximations like spatial overlap and sorting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The implementation builds on the original 3DGS code base to enable meaningful comparisons. name: View-dependent color with Spherical Harmonics
head: Spherical Harmonics (SH) for View-Dependent Color, Spherical Harmonics Color Evaluation, Spherical Harmonics Rendering, SH Render, Rendering with Spherical Harmonics, Spherical Harmonic Colour Model
body: This method represents the view-dependent color of a 3D Gaussian primitive as a function of the viewing direction using spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. It solves the problem of storing directional color variation (such as specular highlights and reflections) compactly without requiring per-ray neural network queries. Unlike simple point colors or view-independent diffuse shading, this model captures glossy effects by evaluating a fixed set of orthogonal basis functions on the unit sphere, allowing each Gaussian to exhibit different colors from different angles. It builds on Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians by providing the color value Cc(\mathbf{d}) used during the compositing step. Inputs and Outputs Input: For each Gaussian i, the normalized viewing direction vector \mathbf{d}i from the camera center to the Gaussian's mean position, and the stored SH coefficients. Output: An RGB color vector \mathbf{C}i(\mathbf{d}i) = [Ri, Gi, Bi]^T evaluated at direction \mathbf{d}i. Data Structures Each Gaussian stores 48 SH coefficients: 16 per color channel (Red, Green, Blue). The coefficients are stored contiguously in memory. The layout is: indices 0–2 are the degree-0 (DC) coefficients for R, G, B respectively; indices 3–47 contain the remaining coefficients for degrees 1, 2, and 3. The coefficients are scalars k{\ell,c}^m corresponding to basis functions Y{\ell}^m. Spherical Harmonic Basis Constants The evaluation uses fixed normalization constants: SH\C0 = 0.28209479177387814 SH\C1 = 0.4886025119029199 Degree 2 and 3 constants are fixed polynomials but exact values are not given in the sources. Standard values are used. Numbered Steps 1. Compute Viewing Direction: For each Gaussian, compute the normalized direction vector \mathbf{d} = [x, y, z]^T from the camera center to the Gaussian's mean position. 2. Initialize Color: Initialize the output color vector \mathbf{C} with the DC component (degree 0) scaled by SH\C0. \mathbf{C} = SH\C0 \cdot [k{0,R}^0, k{0,G}^0, k{0,B}^0]^T 3. Evaluate Degree 1 (if active): If the SH degree is \ge 1, add contributions from the first-order coefficients using the direction components x, y, z scaled by SH\C1. The specific linear combination follows the convention in the reference implementation: color = color - SHC1 y c1 + SHC1 z c2 - SHC1 x c3. 4. Evaluate Degree 2 (if active): If the SH degree is \ge 2, add contributions from second-order coefficients using quadratic direction terms (xy, yz, 2z^2-x^2-y^2, xz, x^2-y^2) scaled by degree-2 normalization constants. 5. Evaluate Degree 3 (if active): If the SH degree is \ge 3, add contributions from third-order coefficients using cubic direction terms. 6. Apply Bias and Clamping: Apply a bias of +0.5 and a ReLU activation to the resulting RGB values to ensure non-negative color values. \mathbf{C}{final} = \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{C} + 0.5) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math SHC0 = 0.28209479177387814 SHC1 = 0.4886025119029199 SHC20 = 1.0925484305920792 SHC21 = -0.3153915652525201 SHC22 = 0.5462742152960396 SHC23 = -0.3153915652525201 SHC24 = 0.10846220610920792 SHC30 = -0.5900435899266435 SHC31 = 2.890611442640554 SHC32 = -0.4570457994644658 SHC33 = 0.3731763325901154 SHC34 = -0.4570457994644658 SHC35 = 1.445305721320277 SHC36 = -0.5900435899266435 def evalsh(shcoeffs, x, y, z, maxdegree=3): """ Evaluates view-dependent color for a single Gaussian. shcoeffs: list of 48 floats [DC(3), D1(9), D2(15), D3(21)] x, y, z: components of the normalized viewing direction vector maxdegree: integer, maximum SH degree active (0-3) Returns: list of 3 floats [R, G, B] """ # Degree 0 (DC) r, g, b = shcoeffs[0], shcoeffs[1], shcoeffs[2] r = SHC0 g = SHC0 b = SHC0 if maxdegree >= 1: # Degree 1 coefficients for R, G, B r1, r2, r3 = shcoeffs[3], shcoeffs[4], shcoeffs[5] g1, g2, g3 = shcoeffs[6], shcoeffs[7], shcoeffs[8] b1, b2, b3 = shcoeffs[9], shcoeffs[10], shcoeffs[11] # Basis functions: -y, z, -x scaled by SHC1 r += SHC1 (-y r1 + z r2 - x r3) g += SHC1 (-y g1 + z g2 - x g3) b += SHC1 (-y b1 + z b2 - x b3) if maxdegree >= 2: # Degree 2 coefficients for R, G, B r1, r2, r3, r4, r5 = shcoeffs[12:17] g1, g2, g3, g4, g5 = shcoeffs[17:22] b1, b2, b3, b4, b5 = shcoeffs[22:27] # Standard SH2 basis functions xy, yz, z2 = x y, y z, z z x2, y2 = x x, y y r += SHC20 xy r1 + SHC21 yz r2 + SHC22 (2 z2 - x2 - y2) r3 + SHC23 xz r4 + SHC24 (x2 - y2) r5 g += SHC20 xy g1 + SHC21 yz g2 + SHC22 (2 z2 - x2 - y2) g3 + SHC23 xz g4 + SHC24 (x2 - y2) g5 b += SHC20 xy b1 + SHC21 yz b2 + SHC22 (2 z2 - x2 - y2) b3 + SHC23 xz b4 + SHC24 (x2 - y2) b5 if maxdegree >= 3: # Degree 3 coefficients for R, G, B r1, r2, r3, r4, r5, r6, r7 = shcoeffs[27:34] g1, g2, g3, g4, g5, g6, g7 = shcoeffs[34:41] b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7 = shcoeffs[41:48] # Standard SH3 basis functions x2, y2, z2 = xx, yy, zz r += SHC30 y (3 x2 - y2) r1 + SHC31 x y z r2 + SHC32 y (4 z2 - x2 - y2) r3 + SHC33 x z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) r4 + SHC34 y (4 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) r5 + SHC35 z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) r6 + SHC36 x (x2 - 3 y2) r7 g += SHC30 y (3 x2 - y2) g1 + SHC31 x y z g2 + SHC32 y (4 z2 - x2 - y2) g3 + SHC33 x z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) g4 + SHC34 y (4 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) g5 + SHC35 z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) g6 + SHC36 x (x2 - 3 y2) g7 b += SHC30 y (3 x2 - y2) b1 + SHC31 x y z b2 + SHC32 y (4 z2 - x2 - y2) b3 + SHC33 x z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) b4 + SHC34 y (4 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) b5 + SHC35 z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) b6 + SHC36 x (x2 - 3 y2) b7 # Apply bias and ReLU r = max(0.0, r + 0.5) g = max(0.0, g + 0.5) b = max(0.0, b + 0.5) return [r, g, b] Parameters Maximum SH Degree (L): Typically 3. This results in (L+1)^2 = 16 basis functions per color channel, totaling 48 coefficients per Gaussian. Training Schedule: Optimization begins with only the degree-0 band active. One further band is unlocked every 1,000 iterations until all four bands (degrees 0-3) are active. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Basis Functions are Fixed: The basis functions Y{\ell}^m(\mathbf{d}) are fixed polynomials of the direction components and are never updated during training. Only the coefficients k are learned via gradient descent. Direction Normalization: The direction vector \mathbf{d} must be normalized before evaluation. Precision: Standard single-precision arithmetic is used. An optimization that reduces memory bandwidth pressure by evaluating view-dependent colors over multiple frames rather than every frame, trading immediate visual fidelity for rendering performance. Time Complexity: The evaluation of SH coefficients is O(1) per Gaussian per frame, involving a fixed number of multiplications and additions. It is significantly faster than querying a neural network. Memory Complexity: Each Gaussian stores 48 additional float values (48 \times 4 bytes = 192 bytes) for the SH coefficients. This is a constant overhead per primitive. Measured Performance: The method contributes to the overall rendering speed of 3DGS, which reaches 134 fps on the Mip-NeRF360 benchmark. The SH evaluation itself is described as costing "almost nothing at display time". Strengths: Captures view-dependent effects like highlights and reflections, which simple point colors cannot. It is differentiable and can be optimized via gradient descent. Limitations: High-degree SH (degree 3) increases memory usage significantly (48 coefficients vs 3 for DC). It may struggle with very sharp, high-frequency specularities compared to other representations, though degree 3 is generally sufficient for many scenes. When to Use: When view-dependent appearance (specularities, reflections) is important for photorealism. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth is extremely constrained and view-dependent effects are not critical (use DC only). Origin: The method was introduced in the 3D Gaussian Splatting paper (Kerbl et al., 2023). It repurposes spherical harmonics from irradiance environment maps to represent the color leaving a Gaussian. History: Spherical harmonics are a well-known orthogonal basis for functions on the unit sphere, analogous to Fourier series. The specific application to 3DGS involves truncating the series at degree 3 and learning the coefficients via gradient descent. Usage: It is a core component of the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, enabling photorealistic novel view synthesis.
