name: Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking
head: Baked view-dependent color buffer, Progressive SH evaluation, Progressive Spherical Harmonics
body: Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking is an optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces memory bandwidth pressure caused by high-degree spherical harmonics (SH) by evaluating view-dependent colors over multiple frames rather than every frame. It alleviates the bottleneck where loading high-degree SH coefficients consumes more memory than the splat's geometric attributes, storing the evaluated results in a "baked" color buffer. Unlike standard per-frame SH evaluation, this method trades immediate visual fidelity for rendering performance, converging to the correct view-dependent color within a short, fixed number of frames. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian splats with stored SH coefficients (e.g., Degree 3), camera view direction, and a convergence parameter N (number of frames to fully update all visible splats). Output: A "baked" view-dependent color buffer containing the evaluated RGB color for each visible splat. Data Structures: Splat Attributes: Position, scale, orientation, base color, and flags, consuming 52 bytes per splat. SH Coefficients: For Degree 3, 45 additional floating-point values (16 coefficients times three for RGB, minus three since the base color is handled separately). Baked Color Buffer: Stores the evaluated RGB color for each splat. Size depends on the number of visible splats. For Degree 3, the SH data adds 180 bytes per splat (45 \times 4 bytes) to the staging memory load, which is more than triple the 52 bytes of geometric data. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Create a baked color buffer for all visible splats and initialize it with the base color or the previous frame's baked color. 2. Progressive Update Loop: For each frame f (where f=1, 2, \dots, N): a. Determine the subset of splats to update, targeting a fraction of 1/N of the total visible splats per frame. b. Select a subset of splats (e.g., sequential or random) comprising 1/N of the total visible splats. c. For each selected splat i: i. Evaluate the spherical harmonics function C(\mathbf{v}i) using the splat's SH coefficients and the view direction \mathbf{v}i. ii. Write the resulting RGB color to the baked color buffer for splat i. d. For splats not selected in this frame, retain their previously baked color value. 3. VR Handling: In Virtual Reality, account for different camera directions for left and right eyes. It is sufficient to progressively bake color values for only one eye and reuse them for the other, or evaluate based on the direction to the center of both eyes. 4. Rendering: Use the baked color buffer for shading during the current frame's rasterization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressiveshbaking(splats, viewdirections, numframestoconverge=10): """ splats: List of splat objects with.shcoeffs (45 floats for Degree 3) and.basecolor viewdirections: List of 3D view direction vectors numframestoconverge: N, frames to fully update all visible splats """ numsplats = len(splats) bakedcolors = [splat.basecolor for splat in splats] # Initialize with base color splatsperframe = max(1, numsplats // numframestoconverge) currentsplatidx = 0 for frame in range(numframestoconverge): for in range(splatsperframe): if currentsplatidx >= numsplats: break # Evaluate spherical harmonics: C(v) = sum{l=0}^{L} sum{m=-l}^{l} c{lm} Y{lm}(v) # Standard SH evaluation routine bakedcolors[currentsplatidx] = splats[currentsplatidx].basecolor currentsplatidx += 1 if currentsplatidx >= numsplats: break return bakedcolors Parameters: Convergence Frames (N): Number of frames to fully update all visible splats. Typical value: 10. SH Degree: Degree 3 is used, requiring 45 additional coefficients per splat (16 coefficients times three for RGB, minus three since the base color is handled separately). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: VR Eye Discrepancy: Left and right eyes have different view directions. Reusing baked colors from one eye for the other may cause slight inaccuracies, but is deemed sufficient. Motion Artifacts: Under sufficiently high frame rates, progressive updates cause little to no apparent lag even under motion. Memory Bandwidth: High-degree SH (e.g., Degree 3) adds 180 bytes per splat to staging memory, which is a significant bottleneck compared to 52 bytes of geometric data. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Storing Degree 3 SH coefficients adds 180 bytes per splat (45 \times 4 bytes) to the staging pass memory load. This is more than triple the 52 bytes used for position, scale, orientation, color, and flags. Time: Updating all harmonics per frame is expensive. On the Kinuta scene, updating all harmonics takes 1.6 ms, while updating 1/10th takes 0.6 ms and 1/30th takes 0.5 ms. On the Campus scene, updating all harmonics takes 4.4 ms, while updating 1/10th takes 1.5 ms and 1/30th takes 1.1 ms. Measured Performance: Kinuta Scene: All: 1.6 ms, 1/10th: 0.6 ms, 1/30th: 0.5 ms. Campus Scene: All: 4.4 ms, 1/10th: 1.5 ms, 1/30th: 1.1 ms. Berlin Scene: All: 0.4 ms, 1/10th: 0.2 ms, 1/30th: 0.1 ms. Garden Scene: All: 2.6 ms, 1/10th: 1.9 ms, 1/30th: 1.8 ms. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly reduces memory bandwidth pressure and staging time for high-degree SH. Convergence is typically fast enough (e.g., 10 frames) to cause barely noticeable artifacts. Limitations: Progressive updates introduce a temporary lag in view-dependent color updates, but under sufficiently high frame rates, this causes little to no apparent lag even under motion. Requires additional memory for the baked color buffer. When to Use: Use when rendering high-degree SH (e.g., Degree 3) and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Use in VR where per-eye evaluation is expensive. When Not to Use: Use when SH degree is low (e.g., Degree 0 or 1) and bandwidth is not a concern. Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking was introduced in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for large models and VR rendering. It addresses the performance bottleneck caused by the large memory footprint of high-degree spherical harmonics coefficients. The technique was developed as part of the Splatshop project, which focuses on efficiently editing large Gaussian Splat models. Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Spherical Beta View-Dependent Color
head: Spherical Beta lobes
body: Spherical Beta (SB) is a specular model that adds explicit specular lobes on top of the base or Spherical Harmonic (SH) color to model view-dependent appearance in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It is derived from Deformable Beta Splatting (Liu et al., SIGGRAPH 2025). Unlike SH, which represents the full view-dependent function, SB uses a small number of explicit lobes, offering higher PSNR and significantly smaller file sizes than SH degree 3. It builds on View-dependent color with Spherical Harmonics. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gaussian splat parameters including base color or SH coefficients, and optional SB lobe parameters (axis angles, sharpness, color). Output: Final view-dependent color for the splat. Data Structures: Lobe Parameters: Stored as half-floats (16-bit floats). Storage Layout: One 16-byte texel is stored per lobe per splat. Lobe Definition: Each lobe is defined by: Axis: Defined by spherical angles (converted to a 3D vector at load time). Sharpness (\beta): A scalar value. Color (rgb): A 3D vector. Number of Lobes: Up to 4 lobes are supported. Trainers default to 2 lobes. 2 lobes require 12 floats per splat (assuming 3 floats per lobe for color and 1 for sharpness, plus axis storage details implied by 16-byte texel). Note: The source states "2 lobes are 12 floats per splat" and "one 16-byte texel per lobe". 16 bytes = 2 half-floats. If axis is 2 angles (2 half-floats), sharpness (1 half-float), color (3 half-floats), that is 6 half-floats = 12 bytes. The source says 16-byte texel. This implies padding or specific packing. The source explicitly states "12 floats per splat" for 2 lobes. We will stick to the explicit "12 floats" and "16-byte texel" statements. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Load Time): Convert lobe parameters from PLY properties (sbparams). Convert axis from spherical angles to a 3D direction vector. Store parameters as half-floats. If a splat has lobes but no SH, mark it for dynamic re-evaluation. 2. Rendering (Shader): For each splat: Compute the view direction vector dir from the camera to the splat center. Initialize color = 0.0. If SH coefficients are present: Evaluate SH color C{SH}(dir). color = \max(C{SH}(dir), 0.0). Else if base color is present: color = \max(base\color, 0.0). For each lobe i (from 0 to N-1, where N \le 4): Get lobe axis axisi, sharpness \betai, and color rgbi. Compute dot product: d = \max(dot(dir, axisi), 0.0). Compute lobe contribution: Li = pow(d, 4 \cdot \exp(\betai)) \cdot softplus(rgbi) Where softplus(x) = \ln(1 + \exp(x)) [G, standard definition]. Add to color: color = color + Li. Return color. Formulas: Lobe Contribution: L = pow(\max(dot(dir, axis), 0), 4 \cdot \exp(\beta)) \cdot softplus(rgb) dir: View direction vector. axis: Lobe axis vector. \beta: Sharpness parameter. rgb: Lobe color vector. softplus(x) = \ln(1 + \exp(x)). Parameters: Number of lobes: 2 (default), up to 4. Sharpness (\beta): Learned parameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Base Color: The base/SH color is clamped to zero before adding lobes to prevent negative values from absorbing highlights. Dynamic Re-evaluation: Splats with lobes but no SH must re-evaluate color as the camera moves. Format Support: Only uncompressed PLY supports lobe data. Compressed PLY, SOG, and SPZ do not support lobe storage. Beta Kernel: This method only implements the color lobes, not the Beta kernel (opacity falloff). Using the Beta kernel requires additional changes to quad extent, bounds/culling, and per-splat values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatesphericalbetacolor(splat, viewdir): """ Evaluates the view-dependent color for a splat using Spherical Beta lobes. Args: splat: Object containing: shcoeffs: List of SH coefficients (optional) basecolor: RGB vector (optional) lobes: List of lobe dictionaries, each with: axis: 3D vector (unit length) beta: float (sharpness) rgb: 3D vector viewdir: 3D vector (direction from camera to splat) Returns: RGB color vector """ # Initialize color to zero color = vec3(0.0) # Add base or SH color, clamped to zero if splat.shcoeffs is not None: # Evaluate SH color (assuming a helper function exists for SH evaluation) shcolor = evaluatesh(splat.shcoeffs, viewdir) color = max(shcolor, vec3(0.0)) elif splat.basecolor is not None: color = max(splat.basecolor, vec3(0.0)) # Add lobe contributions for lobe in splat.lobes: axis = lobe.axis beta = lobe.beta rgb = lobe.rgb # Compute dot product, clamped to [0, 1] dotval = max(dot(viewdir, axis), 0.0) # Compute lobe power term # 4 exp(beta) exponent = 4.0 exp(beta) lobepow = pow(dotval, exponent) # Compute softplus of color # softplus(x) = ln(1 + exp(x)) lobergb = vec3(0.0) for i in range(3): lobergb[i] = log(1.0 + exp(rgb[i])) # Add contribution color += lobepow lobergb return color A method for baking view-dependent color, potentially using different approximations. See Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking. Memory: 2 lobes require 12 floats per splat, compared to 45 floats for SH bands 1-3. This results in approximately 45% of the PLY file size compared to SH degree 3. Performance: The shader performs one pow operation per lobe. Quality: On the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark, SH degree 0 + 2 lobes achieves +0.15 to +0.30 dB higher PSNR than SH degree 3. Strengths: Smaller file size, faster rendering (fewer operations than high-degree SH), higher PSNR than SH degree 3 for specular highlights. Limitations: Only supports uncompressed PLY. Does not include the Beta kernel (falloff). Limited to explicit lobes, may not capture complex view-dependent effects as well as high-degree SH. When to use: When specular highlights are important and file size/performance is a concern, and uncompressed PLY is acceptable. When not to use: When complex view-dependent effects beyond simple lobes are needed, or when compressed PLY/SOG/SPZ formats are required. Spherical Beta view-dependent color is based on the specular model from Deformable Beta Splatting (Liu et al., SIGGRAPH 2025). It was implemented in the PlayCanvas engine (Pull Request #9729) for WebGL2 and WebGPU. It is also integrated into SuperSplat and gsplat. Add Spherical Beta view-dependent color for PLY gaussian splats, https://github.com/playcanvas/engine/pull/9729, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Physics-based Gaussian Simulation
head: PhysGaussian, Gaussian Splashing
body: Physics-based Gaussian Simulation is a method that integrates physics-based continuum mechanics directly within 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), treating each Gaussian as a discrete physical particle with volume for direct simulation. It solves the problem of animating 3D representations by creating a unified simulation-to-rendering pipeline, allowing for physically accurate dynamics rather than relying on pre-recorded motion or simple deformation. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by embedding physical laws into the representation itself, enabling the Gaussians to behave like material particles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A static 3DGS scene (set of Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, and color) and physical parameters (e.g., density, viscosity, gravity). Output: A sequence of animated 3DGS scenes where Gaussian positions and covariances evolve according to physical laws. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is treated as a discrete physical particle. The data structure extends standard 3DGS attributes: \mathbf{p}i: Position (3D vector). \mathbf{C}i: Covariance matrix (3x3 symmetric positive definite), representing the particle's volume and orientation. \rhoi: Density (scalar, if applicable). \mathbf{v}i: Velocity (3D vector, required for physics integration). \mathbf{F}i: Force (3D vector, accumulated per step). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the 3DGS scene. Assign physical properties (mass, volume) to each Gaussian based on its covariance determinant and opacity. 2. Force Calculation: Compute external forces (e.g., gravity) and internal forces (e.g., pressure, viscosity) between neighboring Gaussians. For fluid simulations, Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) may be used. 3. Integration: Update the velocity and position of each Gaussian particle using a physics integrator (e.g., Verlet or Euler). 4. Covariance Update: Update the covariance matrix to reflect deformation and rotation induced by the physical simulation. 5. Rendering: Render the updated 3DGS scene using standard splatting techniques. Formulas: Particle Mass: mi \propto \det(\mathbf{C}i)^{1/2} \cdot \alphai (where \alphai is opacity). Force Balance: \mathbf{F}{total, i} = \mathbf{F}{ext} + \sum{j \in \text{neighbors}} \mathbf{F}{int}(i, j). Position Update: \mathbf{p}i^{t+1} = \mathbf{p}i^t + \mathbf{v}i^t \Delta t + \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{a}i^t \Delta t^2. Parameters: Time step \Delta t: Not given in the sources. Physical constants (gravity, viscosity): Scene-dependent. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Physical simulations require high precision to avoid energy drift or explosion. Boundaries: Handling collisions with scene boundaries or other objects requires additional logic (e.g., mesh-based simulation frameworks). Degenerate Input: Gaussians with zero volume or opacity may cause division by zero in physical calculations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def physicsbasedgaussiansimulation(gaussians, dt, gravity): """ Simulate physics for a set of 3D Gaussians.:param gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes p, C, alpha, etc.:param dt: Time step.:param gravity: Gravity vector. """ # Step 1: Calculate forces for g in gaussians: g.force = gravity g.mass # External force # Internal forces (e.g., pressure, viscosity) between neighbors for neighbor in getneighbors(g, gaussians): g.force += computeinternalforce(g, neighbor) # Step 2: Integrate physics for g in gaussians: # Update velocity g.velocity += g.force dt / g.mass # Update position g.position += g.velocity dt # Update covariance (simplified rotation/deformation) g.covariance = updatecovariance(g.covariance, g.velocity, dt) return gaussians Note: getneighbors, computeinternalforce, and updatecovariance are implementation-specific details not provided in the sources. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N and the neighbor search complexity. Typically O(N) to O(N \log N) with spatial hashing. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian attributes plus physics state (velocity, force). Strengths: Physically accurate dynamics; unified simulation-to-rendering pipeline. Limitations: Computationally expensive; requires careful tuning of physical parameters; may not handle complex topological changes (e.g., breaking) without additional mechanisms. When to use: When physically accurate animation is required for 3DGS scenes. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and physical accuracy is not required. Origin: PhysGaussian [41] integrates physics-based continuum mechanics directly within 3DGS. Gaussian Splashing [42] uses Position-Based Fluids. History: Developed as part of the evolution of 3DGS to support dynamic scenes and animation. Usage: Used in applications requiring physically accurate animation of 3D representations, such as urban driving scenes and fluid simulation. From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting: Theory and Applications, https://doi.org/10.1109/sibgrapi67909.2025.11223276, fetched 2026-10-26 From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://www.visgraf.impa.br/Data/RefBib/PSPDF/tutorial-sib2025/tutorial-sib2025.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Weighted Blending (Fuzzy Metaballs)
head: Fuzzy Metaballs rendering, Sort-free Gaussian rendering
body: Weighted Blending is a sort-free ray-marching technique for 3D Gaussians that computes the intersection of a ray with each Gaussian independently and combines these intersections via a weighted average of their depths. Unlike NeRF-style methods that sort intersections by depth and use closer Gaussians to attenuate further ones, this method blends all intersections simultaneously, avoiding the computational cost and complexity of sorting. It builds on Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians by providing a specific heuristic for combining ray-Gaussian intersections without explicit ordering. Inputs: A ray defined by origin \vec{o} and direction \vec{v}, and a set of N 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by its mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, inverse covariance matrix \Sigmai^{-1}, and weight \lambdai \ge 0 (where \sumi \lambdai = 1 in the original formulation). Outputs: A final intersection depth tf, and optionally the accumulated opacity \alpha, color, or normal at that depth. Data Structures: Gaussian: Stores \mui (3 floats), \Sigmai^{-1} (9 floats, symmetric), \lambdai (1 float), and potentially color/SH coefficients. Ray: Origin \vec{o} (3 floats), Direction \vec{v} (3 floats, normalized). Per-Gaussian Intersection Data: For each Gaussian i, compute and store: ti: Intersection depth along the ray. di: Unnormalized log distance (density log). wi: Weight for blending. \deltai: Unnormalized Gaussian density. Steps: 1. Compute Intersection Depth (ti): For each Gaussian i, calculate the intersection point parameter ti using the linear approach (point of maximum likelihood): ti = \frac{\mui^T \Sigmai^{-1} \vec{v}}{\vec{v}^T \Sigmai^{-1} \vec{v}} Note: This assumes the ray origin is at the camera center or the formula is adjusted for ray origin \vec{o}. The source uses \vec{v} as the ray direction vector in the numerator/denominator context implying a ray from origin or a specific linearization. Standard ray equation is \vec{p}(t) = \vec{o} + t\vec{v}. The source formula ti = (\mui^T \Sigmai^{-1} \vec{v}) / (\vec{v}^T \Sigmai^{-1} \vec{v}) appears to assume \vec{o}=0 or defines t relative to the projection of \mu onto \vec{v} in the metric defined by \Sigma^{-1}. For a general ray \vec{o} + t\vec{v}, the intersection maximizing the Gaussian density along the ray is found by solving \nablat P(\vec{o}+t\vec{v}) = 0. The source explicitly states this linear approach. 2. Compute Unnormalized Log Distance (di): Calculate the unnormalized log distance for Gaussian i at the intersection point \vec{p}i = \vec{o} + ti \vec{v}: di = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ (\vec{p}i - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (\vec{p}i - \mui) \right] + \log(\lambdai) If \lambdai = 0, di = -\infty. 3. Compute Unnormalized Density (\deltai): \deltai = \exp(di) 4. Compute Weights (wi): The weights depend on the variant used (see Subtopics). For the original model: wi = \exp \left( \beta1 di \sigma \left( \frac{\beta3}{\eta} ti \right) - \frac{\beta2}{\eta} ti \right) where \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} is the sigmoid function. 5. Compute Final Intersection Depth (tf): Blend the intersection depths using the computed weights: tf = \frac{\sumi wi ti}{\sumi wi} This same weighted average structure can be applied to other properties like color \vec{c}i or normal \vec{n}i: \vec{c}f = \frac{\sumi wi \vec{c}i}{\sumi wi}, \quad \vec{n}f = \frac{\sumi wi \vec{n}i}{\sumi wi} 6. Compute Opacity (\alpha): The final opacity is computed from the sum of unnormalized densities: \alpha = \sigma \left( \beta4 \sumi \deltai + \beta5 \right) (For the simplified model, see Subtopics). Parameters: \beta1, \beta2, \beta3, \beta4, \beta5: Hyperparameters controlling the weight and transparency functions. \eta: Shape scale factor to account for shapes of different scales. Typical values are not specified in the sources for the general case, but the Two Parameter Model simplifies this to \beta1, \beta2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If \sumi wi = 0 (e.g., all Gaussians are far away or have \lambdai=0), tf is undefined. A guard should return a default depth or handle the empty case. Precision: Computing \exp(di) can lead to overflow or underflow if di is large positive or large negative. Clamping or using log-space arithmetic is recommended. Behind Camera: Intersections with ti < 0 (behind the camera) may contribute in the original model via the sigmoid term. In practice, these are often ignored or handled by the \beta3 term. A simplified rendering model for shape reconstruction that reduces the original 5 hyperparameters to 2 (\beta1, \beta2). It removes the sigmoid term for behind-camera contributions by setting \beta3 = 0, as intersections behind the camera are not used in practice. It replaces the sigmoid alpha function with a decaying exponential, dropping \beta4 and \beta5, relying on unnormalized \lambdai for opacity control. Weight Function: wi = \exp \left( \beta1 di - \frac{\beta2}{\eta} ti \right). Alpha Function: \alpha = 1 - \exp \left( - \sumi \deltai \right). Pitfall: Losing the global normalization condition (\sum \lambdai = 1) causes minor differences in pose estimation, but these are negligible for shape estimation. A hyperparameter-free rendering variant that requires sorting intersections and uses alpha compositing (transmission) to compute weights, enabling differentiable rendering without tunable parameters. Step: Sort all ray-Gaussian intersections by depth ti. Compute accumulated transmission Ti for each intersection based on earlier (closer) intersections. Accumulated Transmission: Ti = \exp \left( -\sumj \deltaj 1[tj < ti] \right), where 1[\cdot] is the indicator function. Weight for Alpha Compositing: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\deltai)). Comparison: This approach is slower than the sort-free models but performs nearly identically in quality, while requiring no hyperparameters. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of Gaussians. No sorting is required for the original and Two Parameter models, making them faster than the Zero Parameter model which requires O(N \log N) sorting. Memory Complexity: O(N) per ray to store intersection data (ti, di, wi). Strengths: Sort-free, differentiable, simple implementation, avoids complex occlusion handling. Limitations: The original model requires tuning 5 hyperparameters plus a scale factor \eta. The Two Parameter model is simpler but still requires \beta1, \beta2. The Zero Parameter model is parameter-free but slower due to sorting. When to Use: Suitable for shape reconstruction and differentiable rendering where sorting is expensive or undesirable. The Two Parameter model is recommended for most shape reconstruction experiments. The method originates from the "Fuzzy Metaballs" paper [34], which introduced a heuristic technique for blending ray-Gaussian intersections without sorting. The specific implementation details and variants (Two Parameter, Zero Parameter) are described in "Flexible Techniques for Differentiable Rendering with 3D Gaussians". The technique is built into JAX and allows for reconstructions on both CPU and GPU. Flexible Techniques for Differentiable Rendering with 3D Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2308.14737, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching
head: 3D Texture Distance Function with Boundary Shell, Distance function for a cube sized 3D texture
body: Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching renders implicit surfaces defined by a pre-computed 3D signed distance texture by combining direct texture lookups with geometric bounding box checks to handle boundary conditions. It solves the problem of invalid or noisy distance values at the edges of a finite texture volume by defining an inner "green" region for safe lookups and an outer "red" bounding box that acts as a hard stop for the ray marcher, preventing the algorithm from sampling invalid data. Unlike primitive SDFs, this method allows complex mesh-derived data (e.g., the Stanford Bunny) to be integrated into ray marching scenes using standard boolean operators like union. Inputs and Outputs Input: A query point x in world space; a 3D texture texture containing signed distance values; parameters textureBoundary and textureShell. Output: A scalar distance value res representing the distance to the nearest surface or the boundary of the valid texture region. Data Structures 3D Texture: A voxel grid storing signed distance values. The source uses a 192 \times 192 \times 192 texture with an inner valid region of 128 \times 128 \times 128. Parameters: textureBoundary: Half-dimensions of the inner valid region. Value: (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). textureShell: Thickness of the boundary region surrounding the inner valid region. Value: (0.05, 0.05, 0.05). Algorithm Steps The distance function determines if the query point x is inside the valid texture region or outside it. 1. Calculate Distance to Inner Boundary: Compute the vector di representing the distance from x to the inner valid region box, adjusted by the shell thickness. di = |x| - \text{textureBoundary} + \text{textureShell} Here, |x| denotes the component-wise absolute value of x. 2. Calculate Distance to Outer Boundary (Red Box): If the point is outside the inner region, the distance to the outer bounding box (the "red box" in the source figures) is calculated. This serves as the SDF value for points outside the texture volume, ensuring the ray marcher stops at the texture boundary. res = \| \max(di + \text{textureShell}, 0) \| Note: The source notation \| \cdot \| refers to the norm. The term \max(di + \text{textureShell}, 0) ensures that if the point is inside the shell region, the distance contribution is zeroed out before taking the norm. 3. Check for Inner Region Entry: Determine if the point x is inside the inner valid region (the "green box"). c = \max(d{ix}, \max(d{iy}, d{iz})) If c < 0, the point is inside the inner valid region. 4. Lookup Distance: If the point is inside the inner region (c < 0): Adjust the point coordinates to align with the texture coordinate space: x = x + \text{textureBoundary} Perform the texture lookup: res = \text{lookupTexture}(\text{texture}, x) Return res. 5. Return Outer Distance: If the point is not inside the inner region (i.e., c \ge 0), return the distance to the red box calculated in Step 2. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bounded3dtexturesdf(x, texture, textureboundary=(0.5, 0.5, 0.5), textureshell=(0.05, 0.05, 0.05)): # Step 1: Calculate distance to inner boundary adjusted by shell # Component-wise absolute value of x absx = [abs(x[0]), abs(x[1]), abs(x[2])] # di = |x| - textureBoundary + textureShell di = [ absx[0] - textureboundary[0] + textureshell[0], absx[1] - textureboundary[1] + textureshell[1], absx[2] - textureboundary[2] + textureshell[2] ] # Step 2: Calculate distance to outer boundary (Red Box) # max(di + textureShell, 0) adjusteddi = [ max(di[0] + textureshell[0], 0.0), max(di[1] + textureshell[1], 0.0), max(di[2] + textureshell[2], 0.0) ] # res = norm(adjusteddi) res = (adjusteddi[0]2 + adjusteddi[1]2 + adjusteddi[2]2)0.5 # Step 3: Check if inside inner region (Green Box) # c = max(dix, max(diy, diz)) c = max(di[0], max(di[1], di[2])) # Step 4: If inside inner region, lookup texture if c < 0: # Adjust coordinates: x = x + textureBoundary xadj = [ x[0] + textureboundary[0], x[1] + textureboundary[1], x[2] + textureboundary[2] ] # Lookup distance from texture # lookupTexture assumes normalized coordinates [0,1] or similar mapping # The source implies xadj is used directly as texture coordinates res = lookuptexture(texture, xadj) # Step 5: Return result return res Edge Cases and Pitfalls Invalid Boundary Data: Texture samples outside the green box but inside the blue box (the boundary region) may contain invalid distance values. The algorithm remedies this by disregarding that region for lookups and using the red box distance instead. Scale Mismatch: The distance returned by the texture lookup must be in accordance with the scale of the scene; otherwise, an appropriate bound must be applied. Normal Estimation: When estimating normals (e.g., via finite differences), the epsilon value must be adjusted to account for the voxel spacing in the texture. If the value is too small, the representation may appear "grainy". Mesh Holes: For accurate distance field generation from meshes (e.g., Stanford Bunny), holes in the mesh must be closed before conversion to a 3D distance texture. A variant designed to mitigate artifacts caused by the bounding shell of the texture volume contributing to ambient occlusion calculations. It adjusts the distance function to prevent the outer boundary from incorrectly occluding the surface. Time Complexity: The SDF evaluation is O(1) per query, involving a few arithmetic operations and one texture lookup. Memory Complexity: Depends on the resolution of the 3D texture. The source example uses a 192^3 texture. Strengths: Allows complex, mesh-derived geometry to be used in ray marching; handles boundary conditions robustly by falling back to a geometric bounding box; supports boolean operations (union, intersection). Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the 3D distance texture; texture resolution limits detail; boundary shell thickness (textureShell) requires tuning per texture. When to Use: When rendering complex static geometry defined by a mesh that has been converted to a distance field, especially when integrating it into a larger ray marching scene. When Not to Use: For dynamic geometry or when memory bandwidth is a severe bottleneck and the geometry is simple enough for primitive SDFs. The method originates from research on GPU ray marching for ambient occlusion, specifically using 3D textures as implicit surfaces. It was applied to render the Stanford Bunny model, which required closing mesh holes before conversion to a 3D distance texture using the GEL framework. The approach enables the inclusion of texture-based representations into scenes using standard SDF boolean operators. GPU Ray Marching of Distance Fields, https://www2.compute.dtu.dk/pubdb/edoc/imm6392.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU Ray Marching for Ambient Occlusion, https://www.scribd.com/document/520755804/imm6392, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination)
head: SDF Union, Union of SDFs, Scene SDF Composition
body: Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination) is a method for composing multiple Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitives into a single implicit surface representing their geometric union. It solves the problem of defining complex scenes without triangle meshes by evaluating the minimum distance from a query point to any primitive in the scene. Unlike Boolean Operations on Distance Fields, which generalizes to intersection and complement, or Smooth SDF Composition, which blends surfaces, this method strictly enforces the nearest-surface control required for safe sphere tracing. It builds on SDF Primitive Definitions by aggregating their outputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3; a collection of N SDF primitives, where each primitive i provides a function di(\mathbf{p}) returning the signed distance to that primitive's surface. Output: A single scalar value D{scene}(\mathbf{p}) representing the signed distance to the closest surface in the composed scene. Data Structures: The scene is typically stored as a collection of primitive objects. A common layout, as seen in implementation examples, separates primitives by type into vectors: worldspheres: std::vector<Sphere> worldboxes: std::vector<Box> worldmandelbulbs: std::vector<MandelBulb> worldtoruses: std::vector<Torus> Each primitive object implements a method pointDist(point) (or similar) that computes its specific SDF. Formulas: The core operation is the minimum function: D{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min{i=0}^{N-1} (di(\mathbf{p})) Or equivalently for two primitives A and B: S{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(SA(\mathbf{p}), SB(\mathbf{p})) Parameters: N: The number of primitives in the scene. Primitive-specific parameters (e.g., sphere center \mathbf{c}, radius r; box half-sizes; torus major/minor radii) are encapsulated within the primitive objects. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize mindist to positive infinity (or a sufficiently large value, though std::numericlimits<double>::max() is preferred to avoid precision issues with far-away objects). 2. Iterate through each primitive i in the scene: a. Evaluate the primitive's SDF at the query point \mathbf{p} to get di. b. If di < \text{min\dist}, update \text{min\dist} = di. 3. Return mindist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scenesdfunion(p: Vector3, primitives: List[Primitive]) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance to the union of all primitives in the list. Args: p: The query point in 3D space. primitives: A list of objects, each implementing a 'dist(p)' method. Returns: The minimum signed distance to any primitive surface. """ # Initialize with infinity to ensure the first primitive always sets the value. # Using a hardcoded large number like 999 is a pitfall if objects are farther away. mindist = float('inf') for primitive in primitives: # Evaluate the specific SDF for this primitive d = primitive.dist(p) # Keep the smallest distance found so far if d < mindist: mindist = d return mindist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization Value: Initializing mindist to a hardcoded constant (e.g., 999) is incorrect if all scene objects are farther than that distance from the query point, leading to an incorrect return value. It must be initialized to infinity or the distance of the first object. Overshooting: Using a distance larger than the minimum (e.g., from a far object) causes the ray marcher to take a step that skips over the nearer surface, breaking the convergence guarantee of sphere tracing. Signedness: The method assumes the input SDFs are correctly signed (negative inside, positive outside) for the union to represent the solid region where either primitive is solid. Subtracts one SDF from another using negation and minimum, carving volume. Blends SDFs to create rounded edges or chamfers, preserving Lipschitz continuity. Uses smooth minimum operators to create organic, transitional volumes between objects. Time Complexity: O(N) per query point, where N is the number of primitives. Each primitive must be evaluated to find the global minimum. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the primitive definitions and their parameters. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides exact geometric union for convex primitives; guarantees safe stepping for sphere tracing because the minimum distance is a conservative lower bound. Limitations: Does not handle intersections or subtractions directly (requires Boolean Operations on Distance Fields); sharp creases at intersections of primitives; performance degrades linearly with scene complexity. When to use: Ideal for ray marching scenes composed of distinct, non-intersecting or simply unioned objects where exact distance bounds are required for convergence. The method is based on the approach described by Iñigo Quilez in his "Distance Functions" tutorials. It relies on the mathematical property that the signed distance function of a union of sets is the minimum of their individual signed distance functions, provided the distance estimators are conservative (do not underestimate the true distance). This allows sphere tracing to converge without intersecting geometry. name: CSG Difference
head: SDF Difference, Subtraction of SDFs, CSG Subtraction, difference
body: The CSG Difference operation constructs a new Signed Distance Function (SDF) by subtracting one shape from another, effectively carving the first object out of the second. Unlike the standard union (minimum) in Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination), which merges volumes, this operation removes the volume of the subtractor from the base, ensuring the resulting field represents the solid region of the base that does not overlap with the subtractor. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two scalar SDF functions, Sa(p) and Sb(p), evaluated at point p. Sa is the subtractor (shape to be removed), and Sb is the base (shape to keep). Output: A scalar value S{diff}(p) representing the distance to the surface of the difference operation. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The operation is point-wise and stateless, relying only on the scalar values returned by the constituent SDFs. Numbered Steps: 1. Evaluate the base SDF at the query point p: db = Sb(p). 2. Evaluate the subtractor SDF at the query point p: da = Sa(p). 3. Negate the subtractor distance: neg\da = -da. 4. Return the maximum of the base distance and the negated subtractor distance: result = \max(db, neg\da). Formula: The CSG difference is defined as: S{diff}(p) = \max(Sb(p), -Sa(p)) Where: Sb(p) is the signed distance to the base object at point p. Sa(p) is the signed distance to the subtractor object at point p. The negative sign on Sa(p) inverts the inside/outside convention of the subtractor, so that the interior of A becomes "far away" (positive distance) in the max operation, effectively excluding it from the result. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Near the boundary where Sb(p) \approx -Sa(p), floating-point precision errors can cause artifacts. Ensure epsilon thresholds in ray marching are appropriate for the scale of the scene. Degenerate Input: If the subtractor completely contains the base, the resulting SDF will be positive everywhere (empty solid). If they do not intersect, the result is simply the base SDF where the subtractor is outside, and the inverted subtractor where it overlaps. Normals: The normal of the resulting surface is derived from the gradient of the resulting SDF. At the boundary where the subtractor cuts the base, the normal is determined by the base. At the boundary created by the subtractor's interior (the hole), the normal is determined by the subtractor (inverted). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def csgdifference(da: float, db: float) -> float: """ Computes the CSG difference of two SDF values. Args: da: Signed distance to the subtractor shape (A). db: Signed distance to the base shape (B). Returns: Signed distance to the result of B minus A. """ # Invert the subtractor's distance negda = -da # The result is the maximum of the base distance and the inverted subtractor distance return max(db, negda) Smooth Subtraction provides a smooth approximation of the boolean difference operation (A \setminus B) for two Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It blends the subtraction of one shape from another using a smoothing parameter k. Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation, requiring two SDF queries and basic arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(1), no additional storage required. Measured Performance and Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient, allows for arbitrary complex shapes to be carved out of others. Limitations: The resulting SDF is only valid if the input SDFs are valid. Sharp corners at the intersection of the base and subtractor may require careful normal estimation for rendering. When to use: When you need to create holes, cutouts, or complex boolean combinations in SDF-based rendering. When not to use: When smooth transitions between shapes are required (use Smooth Subtraction instead). The CSG Difference is a fundamental operation in Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) applied to Signed Distance Fields. It is widely used in procedural geometry generation and ray marching shaders to create complex scenes from simple primitives. The method relies on the property that the distance to the union of two shapes is the minimum of their distances, and the distance to the difference is the maximum of the base distance and the negated subtractor distance. Origin and historical development are not given in the sources. isosurface, https://github.com/swiftcoder/isosurface, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Smooth Subtraction
head: S-Subtraction
body: Smooth Subtraction provides a smooth approximation of the boolean difference operation (A \setminus B) for two Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It blends the subtraction of one shape from another using a smoothing parameter k. Inputs: d1: SDF value of the subtracted volume. d2: SDF value of the base volume. k: Smoothing factor or blending radius (k > 0). Output: d: Smoothed SDF value for the difference. The operation is point-wise and scalar, requiring no auxiliary data structures. 1. Compute the blending factor h by clamping a linear function of the distance sum: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 - 0.5 \frac{d2 + d1}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) 2. Compute the linear interpolation between d2 and -d1 using h: \text{mix}(d2, -d1, h) = d2 \cdot (1 - h) + (-d1) \cdot h 3. Add the smoothstep correction term to the interpolation: d = \text{mix}(d2, -d1, h) + k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 - 0.5 \frac{d2 + d1}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) d = \text{mix}(d2, -d1, h) + k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) \text{mix}(a, b, t) = a \cdot (1 - t) + b \cdot t where \text{clamp}(v, \text{min}, \text{max}) restricts v to [\text{min}, \text{max}]. k: The smoothing factor or blending radius. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Division by Zero: k must be strictly positive to prevent division by zero in the h calculation. Precision: When d1 and d2 are large with opposite signs, cancellation errors may occur in d1 + d2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothsubtraction(d1: float, d2: float, k: float) -> float: if k <= 0.0: raise ValueError("k must be positive.") h = 0.5 - 0.5 (d2 + d1) / k h = max(0.0, min(1.0, h)) mixval = d2 (1.0 - h) + (-d1) h return mixval + k h (1.0 - h) Uses the min function for sharp boundaries. Choose when differentiability is not required and exact boolean operations are needed. See CSG Difference. Blends two SDFs together using a similar smoothstep approach. Choose when merging objects with rounded intersections is desired. See Smooth Union. Time Complexity: O(1) per query point. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Differentiable, allowing gradient descent on parameters. Limitations: The result is an approximation, not a true boolean difference. The smoothing radius k introduces a bias; the resulting surface is not exactly at distance 0 from the original boolean boundary. When to use: Differentiable rendering, neural implicit surface optimization, or when smooth transitions between objects are visually preferred over sharp corners. When not to use: When exact boolean geometry is required for collision detection or non-differentiable rendering. Derived from differentiable constructive solid geometry requirements in neural rendering and optimization contexts. Implemented in PyTorch-based SDF rendering libraries. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Object Combination Operators
head: SDF boolean operators, smooth minimum alternatives
body: Object Combination Operators are a family of functions that combine two signed distance functions (SDFs), a and b, to produce specific geometric features such as rounded edges, chamfers, stairs, or pipes, rather than the sharp edges produced by standard boolean operations. Unlike the standard min operator used in Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination) or the blending-focused SDF Smooth Union, these operators aim to produce correct distance values or tight distance bounds that preserve Lipschitz continuity when the gradients of the input SDFs are orthogonal. All operators in this family take two scalar distance values, a and b, and a radius parameter r (and occasionally n) as inputs, and return a single scalar distance value. The parameter r specifies the radius of the resulting feature (e.g., the fillet radius) and must be significantly smaller than the size of the objects to maintain validity. The core mathematical property distinguishing these operators from generic smooth minimums is their preservation of Lipschitz continuity. Standard smooth minimums can violate the Lipschitz condition (where the gradient magnitude exceeds 1) when combining SDFs, leading to ray marching artifacts. These operators are designed such that Lipschitz continuity is preserved provided the gradients of the two SDFs are at right angles (orthogonal). If the gradients are off by more than 30 degrees, or if the surfaces are parallel and close to each other, the Lipschitz condition may no longer hold, causing artifacts. The family includes operators for various intersection features: Chamfer: fOpUnionChamfer(a, b, r) = min(min(a, b), (a - r + b) sqrt(0.5)) Intersection Chamfer: fOpIntersectionChamfer(a, b, r) = max(max(a, b), (a + r + b) sqrt(0.5)) Difference Chamfer: fOpDifferenceChamfer(a, b, r) = fOpIntersectionChamfer(a, -b, r) Round: u = max(vec2(r - a, r - b), vec2(0)); fOpUnionRound(a, b, r) = max(r, min(a, b)) - length(u) Intersection Round: u = max(vec2(r + a, r + b), vec2(0)); fOpIntersectionRound(a, b, r) = min(-r, max(a, b)) + length(u) Difference Round: fOpDifferenceRound(a, b, r) = fOpIntersectionRound(a, -b, r) Stairs: s = r/n; u = b - r; fOpUnionStairs(a, b, r, n) = min(min(a, b), 0.5 (u + a + abs(mod(u - a + s, 2 s) - s))) Intersection Stairs: fOpIntersectionStairs(a, b, r, n) = -fOpUnionStairs(-a, -b, r, n) Difference Stairs: fOpDifferenceStairs(a, b, r, n) = -fOpUnionStairs(-a, b, r, n) Soft Union: e = max(r - abs(a - b), 0); fOpUnionSoft(a, b, r) = min(a, b) - e e 0.25 / r Pipe: fOpPipe(a, b, r) = length(vec2(a, b)) - r Engrave: fOpEngrave(a, b, r) = max(a, (a + r - abs(b)) sqrt(0.5)) Groove: fOpGroove(a, b, ra, rb) = max(a, min(a + ra, rb - abs(b))) Tongue: fOpTongue(a, b, ra, rb) = min(a, max(a - ra, abs(b) - rb)) Columns: fOpUnionColumns and fOpDifferenceColumns produce a series of columns or pillars at the intersection, controlled by n. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fOpUnionColumns(a: float, b: float, r: float, n: float) -> float: if a < r and b < r: px = a py = b sqrt2 = math.sqrt(2.0) px = (a - b) / sqrt2 py = (a + b) / sqrt2 px = px - (sqrt2 / 2.0) r columnradius = (r sqrt2) / ((n - 1) 2 + sqrt2) px = px + columnradius sqrt2 if n % 2 == 1: py = py + columnradius period = columnradius 2 py = py - math.floor(py / period) period result = math.sqrt(px2 + py2) - columnradius result = min(result, px) result = min(result, a) return min(result, b) else: return min(a, b) def fOpDifferenceColumns(a: float, b: float, r: float, n: float) -> float: aneg = -a m = min(aneg, b) if aneg < r and b < r: px = aneg py = b sqrt2 = math.sqrt(2.0) px = (aneg - b) / sqrt2 py = (aneg + b) / sqrt2 columnradius = (r sqrt2) / ((n - 1) 2 + sqrt2) py = py + columnradius px = px - (sqrt2 / 2.0) r px = px - (columnradius sqrt2) / 2.0 if n % 2 == 1: py = py + columnradius period = columnradius 2 py = py - math.floor(py / period) period result = -math.sqrt(px2 + py2) + columnradius result = max(result, px) result = min(result, aneg) return -min(result, b) else: return -m Combines two SDFs into a single smooth field using polynomial or LogSumExp approximations, avoiding sharp edges. name: SDF Smooth Union
head: LogSumExp SDF Union, S-Union, Smooth Minimum, Smooth Union, Smooth Union SDF Operator
body: SDF Smooth Union is a constructive operator that blends two Signed Distance Function (SDF) values, a and b, into a single smooth distance field, replacing the sharp edge of a boolean union with a rounded transition controlled by a parameter k. It builds on Object Combination Operators and sets itself apart from the standard min operator by providing a continuous, differentiable transition between shapes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two scalar SDF values a and b, and a smoothing parameter k > 0. Output: A single scalar smooth union distance d{union}. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the operation is element-wise on scalar distances. If material information is carried, the operator may also blend material attributes, but the core distance calculation remains scalar. Steps: 1. Compute the interpolation weight h based on the difference between b and a, scaled by k, and clamp it to [0, 1]. 2. Interpolate between b and a using h. 3. Subtract a cubic correction term k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) from the interpolated value. Formulas: There are two primary implementations found in the sources: the Cubic Smooth Minimum and the LogSumExp (Log-Sum-Exp) Smooth Minimum. 1. Cubic Smooth Minimum: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 + 0.5 \frac{b - a}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) d{union} = \text{mix}(b, a, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) Where \text{mix}(x, y, t) = x(1-t) + y \cdot t. 2. LogSumExp Smooth Minimum: d{union} = -\frac{1}{k} \ln \left( e^{-k \cdot a} + e^{-k \cdot b} \right) Or equivalently using the log-sum-exp function: d{union} = \frac{1}{-k} \text{logsumexp}(-k \cdot a, -k \cdot b). Parameters: k: The smoothing factor or blend radius. Larger values create a smoother, wider blend between the shapes. Typical values range from 0.1 to 1.0 depending on scene scale, with 1.0f cited as a typical value in and 0.5 or 0.33 used for primitive versus scene blending in. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameter k Scale: The parameter k must be significantly smaller than the size of the objects to maintain validity. Numerical Stability: In the LogSumExp implementation, direct computation of e^{-k \cdot i} can overflow if -k \cdot i is large positive. Subtracting the maximum value before exponentiation is required for stability. Pseudocode (Cubic Implementation): The cubic implementation is explicitly provided in and. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothunioncubic(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: if k <= 0: return min(a, b) h = 0.5 + 0.5 (b - a) / k if h < 0.0: h = 0.0 elif h > 1.0: h = 1.0 mixedval = b (1.0 - h) + a h correction = k h (1.0 - h) return mixedval - correction Pseudocode (LogSumExp Implementation): The LogSumExp implementation is provided in. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothunionlogsumexp(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: if k <= 0: return min(a, b) vala = -k a valb = -k b maxval = max(vala, valb) logsum = math.log(math.exp(vala - maxval) + math.exp(valb - maxval)) + maxval return -logsum / k A blending function for combining two SDFs to create organic, metaball-like merges using a cubic smoothing function, controlled by a blend radius parameter k. It sets itself apart from the standard min operator by providing a continuous, differentiable transition without branching or trigonometry, suitable for organic shapes. Choose it when creating smooth, organic merges where exact distance preservation is less critical than visual continuity. Time Complexity: O(1) per pair of SDFs. The cubic method involves basic arithmetic operations (add, multiply, clamp). The LogSumExp method involves exponentials and logarithms, which are more expensive but still constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional storage is required beyond the input scalars and the output scalar. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of SDFs to be combined if applied recursively or in a tree structure. Strengths: Produces visually smooth, organic transitions between primitives; differentiable (enabling gradient-based optimization in some contexts). Limitations: Does not preserve exact distance properties (the result is an approximation, not a true SDF in the strict sense everywhere); artifacts can occur if k is too large relative to object size. When to use: When creating organic merges, metaballs, or soft intersections where sharp boolean edges are undesirable. When not to use: When exact distance preservation is critical for ray marching stability in complex non-orthogonal configurations, or when sharp edges are desired (use standard min). The concept of smooth union in SDFs originated from the need to create organic shapes and avoid the visual artifacts of sharp boolean operations in ray marching. The cubic smooth minimum operator was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his online articles on SDFs. The LogSumExp approximation is derived from the soft-minimum function used in machine learning and optimization. name: Polynomial Smooth Minimum
head: Quilez smin, Quilez smooth min, smoothMin
body: Polynomial Smooth Minimum is a blending function for combining two Signed Distance Function (SDF) values to create organic, metaball-like merges between primitives without branching or trigonometry. It sets itself apart from the standard min operator by providing a continuous, differentiable transition controlled by a smoothing radius parameter k, allowing for smooth union operations in Constructive SDF Modeling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two scalar SDF values a and b, and a non-negative smoothing radius k. Output: A single scalar value representing the smooth minimum of a and b. Data Structures: Operates on scalar floating-point values with no auxiliary data structures. Algorithm: The method computes an intermediate blend factor h based on the distance between a and b relative to k, then adjusts the minimum value by a quadratic term. 1. Edge Case Handling: If k \le 10^{-6}, return \min(a, b) to avoid division by zero or numerical instability. 2. Compute Blend Factor: Calculate h = \max(k - |a - b|, 0.0) / k. This value ranges from 0.0 (when |a - b| \ge k) to 1.0 (when a = b). 3. Compute Result: Return \min(a, b) - h^2 \cdot k \cdot 0.25. Note: Source provides an equivalent formulation using h = \text{clamp}(0.5 + 0.5(b - a)/k, 0.0, 1.0) and \text{result} = \text{mix}(b, a, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h). Both yield identical results for the same inputs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polynomialsmoothminimum(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: if k <= 1e-6: return min(a, b) diff = abs(a - b) h = max(k - diff, 0.0) / k return min(a, b) - (h h k 0.25) Parameters: k: The blend radius parameter, exposed as a UI slider. Typical values are 0.2 or 0.3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: When |a - b| \ge k, h = 0 and the result equals \min(a, b), preserving the hard union outside the blending region. Floating-point precision may cause artifacts when subtracting close values for large k. The dual operator for smooth intersection, combining two SDF values using a smoothing factor k. It computes h = \max(k - |a - b|, 0.0) / k and returns \max(a, b) + h^2 \cdot k \cdot 0.25. Choose this when carving out material smoothly or implementing smooth subtraction, as it is implemented as smax(-d1, d2, k) for smooth subtraction and smax(d1, d2, k) for smooth intersection. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive pair. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is attributed to Inigo Quilez, a prominent graphics programmer known for his work on ray marching and SDFs. It is widely known in the procedural geometry community as "Quilez smin". The technique is used in real-time ray marching shaders for creating complex organic shapes from simple primitives. name: Smooth Intersection
head: Round Intersection, S-Intersection, Smooth SDF Operations
body: Smooth Intersection is a Constructive SDF operator that blends the boolean intersection of two signed distance fields into a rounded feature controlled by a blending radius r (or smoothing parameter k). It is distinguished from generic smooth minimums like SDF Smooth Union by its specific geometric construction aimed at preserving distance field properties. Inputs: a: Distance from the first SDF. b: Distance from the second SDF. r: Blending radius or smoothing parameter. Outputs: d: The resulting blended distance value. Data Structures: None required; scalar operations. Steps: 1. Compute m = \max(a, b). 2. Evaluate the condition -a < r and -b < r. 3. If the condition is true, compute f = \max(m, -(r - \sqrt{(r+a)^2 + (r+b)^2})). 4. If the condition is false, set f = m. 5. Return f. Formulas: The sources provide two distinct mathematical formulations for the operation. 1. Geometric/Vector Formulation (S-Intersection): This method calculates the distance to a rounded corner formed by the intersection. f = \begin{cases} \max\left(m, -\left(r - \sqrt{(r+a)^2 + (r+b)^2}\right)\right) & \text{if } -a < r \land -b < r \\ m & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 2. Polynomial/Blending Formulation: This method uses a polynomial blend based on the difference between distances. h = \max(k - |a - b|, 0.0) d = \min(a, b) - \frac{h^2}{4k} Alternative Polynomial Formulation: Source and describe a similar polynomial approach using a mixing factor h: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 - 0.5 \frac{b - a}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) d = \text{mix}(b, a, h) + k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) where \text{mix}(x, y, t) = x(1-t) + yt. Parameters: r (or k): Blending radius or smoothing factor. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Lipschitz Continuity: The operator preserves Lipschitz continuity (gradient magnitude \le 1) when the gradients of the two SDFs are orthogonal. If gradients deviate by more than 30^\circ or surfaces are parallel and close, the condition may break, causing ray marching artifacts. Usage Guidelines: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: The following implements the Geometric/Vector Formulation (S-Intersection). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothintersection(a: float, b: float, r: float) -> float: m = max(a, b) if (-a < r) and (-b < r): disttocorner = math.sqrt((r + a)2 + (r + b)2) return max(m, -(r - disttocorner)) else: return m Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves distance field validity and produces correct rounded features without sharp boolean edges. Limitations: Lipschitz continuity is not guaranteed when SDF gradients are non-orthogonal or surfaces are parallel/close. When to use: When blending two SDFs requires a smooth, rounded intersection feature while maintaining valid distance bounds. When not to use: When SDF gradients are expected to deviate by more than 30^\circ or when surfaces are parallel and close, as artifacts may occur. Smooth Intersection operators are documented in unofficial repositories related to sphere tracing and differentiable rendering. name: Multi-Material Distance Fields
head: Augmented SDF signature, Color-Coded SDFs, Material-Augmented Signed Distance Function, SDF with Material Data, SDF with material ID
body: Multi-Material Distance Fields extend standard Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) to return both a geometric distance and a material identifier, enabling per-object material assignment within Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) scenes. Unlike sibling operators like SDF Smooth Union which focus on geometric blending, this method preserves the sharp boolean logic of CSG while propagating shading data, allowing the renderer to determine surface color based on the closest object's material ID rather than just its depth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A position vector p in world space. Output: A pair (d, m), where d is the signed distance to the nearest surface and m is the material identifier (e.g., an integer index or a normalized color value) associated with that surface. Data Structures: The scene is represented as a CSG tree. Each leaf node contains: 1. An SDF function SDFi(p) returning a scalar distance. 2. A material identifier Mi. In shader implementations, the output is typically a float2 (or vec2): x component: Distance d. y component: Material data m (e.g., color index or direct color value). Algorithm: The evaluation is recursive. For a leaf node, the SDF is evaluated directly. For internal nodes (Union, Intersection, Difference), the results of the left and right children are combined. The combination logic compares the distance components (d) to determine the closest surface, then selects the corresponding material component (m) from the winning child. 1. Leaf Evaluation: For a leaf node with SDF function f and material ID m{leaf}: (d, m) = (f(p), m{leaf}). 2. Union Operation: Given left result (da, ma) and right result (db, mb): If da \le db: Return (da, ma). Else: Return (db, mb). Logic: The union takes the minimum distance. The material of the closest object is preserved. 3. Intersection Operation: Given left result (da, ma) and right result (db, mb): If da \ge db: Return (da, ma). Else: Return (db, ma). Logic: The intersection takes the maximum distance (deepest inside both). The material is taken from the left child (ma) if the left child is the limiting factor (da \ge db), otherwise it takes the right child's distance but still uses the left child's material. Note: Standard CSG intersection usually implies the material of the object being intersected into, but the provided source explicitly assigns ma in the else case. 4. Difference Operation: Given left result (da, ma) and right result (db, mb): If da \ge -db: Return (da, ma). Else: Return (-db, ma). Logic: Difference is A \setminus B. If the left object is closer to the surface (or outside the right object), keep left material. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def evaluatematerialsdf(tree: dict, p: tuple) -> tuple: if tree['type'] == 'leaf': sdffunc = tree['sdffunc'] material = tree['material'] distance = sdffunc(p) return (distance, material) lefttree = tree['left'] righttree = tree['right'] operation = tree['op'] da, ma = evaluatematerialsdf(lefttree, p) db, mb = evaluatematerialsdf(righttree, p) if operation == 'union': if da <= db: return (da, ma) else: return (db, mb) elif operation == 'intersection': if da >= db: return (da, ma) else: return (db, ma) elif operation == 'difference': if da >= -db: return (da, ma) else: return (-db, ma) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown operation: {operation}") def raymarchmaterialscene(scenetree: dict, rayorigin: tuple, raydirection: tuple, colorramp: list) -> tuple: maxsteps = 64 t = 0.0 hitmaterial = None for i in range(maxsteps): p = ( rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0] t, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1] t, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2] t) d, m = evaluatematerialsdf(scenetree, p) if d < 0.001: hitmaterial = m break t += d if hitmaterial is not None: if isinstance(hitmaterial, (int, float)) and hitmaterial < len(colorramp): color = colorramp[hitmaterial] else: color = hitmaterial if isinstance(hitmaterial, tuple) else (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) return (color, 1.0) else: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) Parameters: ColorRamp: A texture or array mapping material IDs (the y-component of the map output) to colors. Max Steps: Typically 64 or more, depending on scene complexity and required precision. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Comparing floating-point distances da and db for equality can be unstable. Using a small epsilon for the hit condition (d < 0.001) is standard. Intersection/Difference Material Logic: The specific material assignment in Intersection and Difference operations (always taking ma from the left child in the source code) is a design choice. A data structure that holds surface shading information, including color, physical properties, and texture descriptors, accessible from both host and device code. It distinguishes itself by explicitly separating geometric displacement (via heightmapTex) from shading calculations and by managing texture projection modes and normal deflection scaling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables complex multi-material scenes with CSG operations without requiring multiple render passes or complex shader branching for material selection. Shadows are straightforward to calculate using the depth buffer and the same SDF. Limitations: Material boundaries are sharp (discrete). The material assignment logic in Intersection/Difference is fixed by the tree structure (left-child dominance in the provided implementation), which may not match all artistic requirements. The technique was popularized in the context of real-time raymarching shaders, notably by Jamie Wong and Iñigo Quilez. It allows for the creation of complex, multi-colored geometric scenes using simple SDF primitives and CSG operations. The approach is detailed in tutorials on raymarching signed distance functions. sungiant/sdf, https://github.com/sungiant/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Raymarching Distance Fields: Concepts and Implementation..., https://adrianb.io/2016/10/01/raymarching.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Material Object Format
body: The Material Object Format is a data structure that holds surface shading information, including color, physical properties, and texture descriptors, accessible from both host and device code. It distinguishes itself by explicitly separating geometric displacement (via heightmapTex) from shading calculations and by managing texture projection modes and normal deflection scaling. Input: Material parameters (albedo, metalness, roughness, F0) and optional texture descriptors. Output: A Material instance containing shading and texture metadata. The Material object consists of the following fields: | Field | Type | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | albedo | vec3 (linear float) | Surface color in linear RGB. | | metalness | float | Range [0, 1]. Controls specular vs. diffuse shading contribution. | | roughness | float | Range [0, 1]. Controls smoothness of reflections and light scattering. | | F0 | vec3 (linear float) | Base reflectivity when metalness is 0. | | triplar | bool | Texture projection mode. false for XZ planar mapping, true for triplanar mapping. | | normalStrength | float | Linear scaling factor for normal deflection from normal maps. | | albedoTex | int | Texture descriptor for sRGB albedo map. Value -1 if unused. Multiplied with albedo. | | normalTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear detail normal map. Value -1 if unused. | | roughnessTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear roughness map. Value -1 if unused. Multiplied with roughness. | | metalnessTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear metalness map. Value -1 if unused. Multiplied with metalness. | | heightmapTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear displacement heightmap. Value -1 if unused. Used for geometric displacement by the object SDF, not for shading. | | ambietTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear ambient occlusion map. Value -1 if unused. | Texture descriptors are integers referencing texture objects or mipmap arrays, and only the descriptor value is needed to read a texture from device code. Two constructors initialize the Material object: 1. Full Constructor: Takes albedo, metalness, roughness, and F0 as arguments. Sets all texture descriptors (albedoTex, normalTex, roughnessTex, metalnessTex, heightmapTex, ambietTex) to -1. Sets triplar to false (planar mapping). Sets normalStrength to 1.0. 2. Simplified Constructor: Takes albedo, roughness, and metalness. Calls the Full Constructor with these values and a default F0 of [0.04, 0.04, 0.04]. The default F0 is considered the standard base reflectance for most non-metal dielectrics (e.g., plastics, organic materials). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Material: def init(self, albedo, metalness, roughness, F0=None): """ Implements both constructors: Constructor 1 (Full): F0 is provided. Constructor 2 (Simplified): F0 is None, defaults to [0.04, 0.04, 0.04]. """ if F0 is None: F0 = [0.04, 0.04, 0.04] self.albedo = albedo self.metalness = metalness self.roughness = roughness self.F0 = F0 self.triplar = False self.normalStrength = 1.0 self.albedoTex = -1 self.normalTex = -1 self.roughnessTex = -1 self.metalnessTex = -1 self.heightmapTex = -1 self.ambietTex = -1 Texture Descriptors: All texture fields default to -1 to specify the material as textureless. Heightmap vs. Shading: heightmapTex is explicitly excluded from shading calculations and is used solely by the object SDF for geometric displacement. Normal Strength: normalStrength scales normal deflection from normal map textures, which is useful when displacing a surface at a less steep angle than the normal map is designed for. name: Linear SDF Blend
head: Shape Blending
body: Linear SDF Blend creates a morphing transition between two signed distance functions by linearly interpolating their distance values. Unlike SDF Smooth Union which generates a rounded edge feature, it preserves the individual geometry of both shapes within the blend region to produce continuous shape transitions. Inputs: d1: Distance value of the first primitive at query point p. d2: Distance value of the second primitive at query point p. a: Blend factor (alpha), a scalar in [0, 1]. Outputs: d{blend}: The blended distance value. Data Structures: Scalars d1, d2, a, d{blend} are typically float or vec1. Formula: d{blend} = a \cdot d1 + (1 - a) \cdot d2 Steps: 1. Evaluate the SDF for the first primitive at point p to get d1. 2. Evaluate the SDF for the second primitive at point p to get d2. 3. Determine the blend factor a. This can be a constant, a function of time, or a function of position. 4. Compute the linear interpolation using the formula above. Parameters: a: The blend weight. a=0 yields d2, a=1 yields d1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuity: If a changes abruptly with position, the derivative of d{blend} with respect to position will be discontinuous, causing visual artifacts. Sign Ambiguity: If one shape is inside (d < 0) and the other is outside (d > 0), the blend may produce a distance value that does not correspond to a meaningful surface boundary between the two shapes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def linearsdfblend(d1: float, d2: float, a: float) -> float: """ Blends two SDF values linearly. Args: d1: Distance of the first primitive. d2: Distance of the second primitive. a: Blend factor in [0, 1]. Returns: Blended distance value. """ # Clamp alpha to [0, 1] to prevent extrapolation artifacts aclamped = max(0.0, min(1.0, a)) # Linear interpolation formula return aclamped d1 + (1.0 - aclamped) d2 def examplespherecubeblend(p: tuple, time: float) -> float: """ Example blending a sphere into a cube using time. Based on. """ # Helper to compute sphere distance def sdfsphere(point, center, radius): return math.sqrt(sum((point[i] - center[i])2 for i in range(3))) - radius # Helper to compute axis-aligned box distance def sdfbox(point, center, size): # Standard SDF for an axis-aligned box dist = 0.0 for i in range(3): diff = abs(point[i] - center[i]) - size[i] dist = max(dist, diff) return max(dist, 0.0) # Define primitives sphered = sdfsphere(p, (0,0,0), 1.0) boxd = sdfbox(p, (0,0,0), (1.0, 1.0, 1.0)) # Blend factor oscillating between 0 and 1 over time # (SinTime[3] + 1.) / 2. from a = (math.sin(time) + 1.0) / 2.0 return linearsdfblend(sphered, boxd, a) A technique to blend between two SDFs based on the distance of the query point from the origin, using a smooth interpolation factor. It uses smoothstep to create a spatially varying blend factor s that transitions from 0 to 1 as the distance from the origin increases from 0.0 to 1.0. This creates a radial blend zone. The function returns a vec2 containing the blended distance and a primitive identifier (typically 1). Definition: Blends SDFs a and b using a spatially varying smoothstep factor. Formula: s = \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 1.0, \|p\|) d = (1 - s) \cdot a.x + s \cdot b.x Parameters: The smoothstep range is fixed between 0.0 and 1.0. Layout: Returns vec2(d, 1) where d is the distance and 1 is the primitive ID. Pseudocode: python import math def smoothstepsdfblend(p: tuple, a: tuple, b: tuple) -> tuple: """ Blends two SDFs (returned as (distance, id)) based on distance from origin. Based on. """ # Calculate distance from origin distfromorigin = math.sqrt(sum(p[i]2 for i in range(3))) # Calculate smoothstep factor s # smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (distfromorigin - 0.0) / (1.0 - 0.0))) s = t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) # Interpolate distances (x-component) d = (1.0 - s) a[0] + s b[0] # Return blended distance and primitive ID return (d, 1.0) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; produces smooth morphing animations; preserves the individual geometry of both shapes within the blend region. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: For morphing animations between two shapes where the transition is temporal or spatially controlled by a smooth factor. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Linear SDF blending is a technique popularized in the ray marching community for creating smooth transitions between shapes. It is analogous to alpha blending in image compositing. The method was described by Alan Zucconi in his tutorial on Signed Distance Functions and further illustrated in the Geeks3D GLSL Hacker tutorial on primitive blending. It is often used in conjunction with time-based animation to morph between primitives like spheres and cubes.
