name: Smooth SDF Composition
head: Signed Distance Function (SDF) Scene Composition, Smooth Min SDF, Smooth Union of SDFs
body: Smooth SDF Composition blends multiple primitive Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) into a single continuous field using a smooth minimum operator, avoiding the sharp creases produced by standard constructive SDF modeling. Unlike the nearest-surface control of Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination), this method creates a transitional volume between objects, enabling organic merging effects in ray marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two or more scalar SDF values (d1, d2, \dots) evaluated at a point p, and a blending factor k \ge 0. Output: A single blended distance value d{smooth}. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required beyond the scalar values returned by individual primitive SDF evaluators (e.g., sdfTorus, sdfBox as defined in). Steps: 1. Evaluate the individual SDF for each primitive at the query point p. For example, calculate d{torus} and d{box}. 2. Select a blending factor k. A typical value is 0.5 for moderate blending. 3. Compute the smooth minimum of the distances using the formula: d{smooth} = -\frac{1}{k} \ln(e^{-k d1} + e^{-k d2}) This formula approximates the minimum while maintaining C^1 continuity. 4. Return d{smooth} as the distance to the nearest object in the blended scene. Parameters: k: Blending factor. Controls the width of the transition zone. Larger k approaches the hard minimum; smaller k creates a smoother, wider blend. Typical value: 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If k=0, the formula involves division by zero. In practice, if k is very small, the result approaches the arithmetic mean or requires a fallback to the standard minimum. Precision issues may arise if d1 and d2 differ significantly in magnitude, causing one exponential term to dominate and underflow/overflow. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothmin(d1: float, d2: float, k: float) -> float: if k == 0.0: return min(d1, d2) # Clamp to prevent exp() overflow for large positive distances kd1 = -k max(d1, -100.0) kd2 = -k max(d2, -100.0) exp1 = math.exp(kd1) exp2 = math.exp(kd2) return -1.0 / k math.log(exp1 + exp2) def evaluatescenesdf(primitives, k): if not primitives: return float('inf') currentdist = primitives[0]() for i in range(1, len(primitives)): nextdist = primitives[i]() currentdist = smoothmin(currentdist, nextdist, k) return currentdist Computes the minimum signed distance from a point to any primitive in the scene, effectively performing a union operation. It differs from Smooth SDF Composition by aggregating multiple distinct primitives into a single scene-level distance field rather than composing a single smooth blend of shapes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables organic, fluid merging of shapes without sharp edges. Limitations: The smooth transition zone can obscure the true boundary of objects, potentially causing ray marching artifacts if the step size is not adjusted for the gradient changes in the blend region. Not given in the sources. Sample - Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions, https://github.com/ComputeNode/cyfra/pull/13, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Scene SDF Evaluation
head: SDF Scene Composition, Signed Distance Function (SDF) Scene Composition
body: Scene SDF Evaluation computes the minimum signed distance from a query point to any primitive in a scene, effectively performing a union operation across all defined geometry. It differs from Smooth SDF Composition by aggregating multiple distinct primitives into a single scene-level distance field rather than composing a single smooth blend of shapes. Inputs: point: The 3D query position (p \in \mathbb{R}^3). scene: A structure containing arrays of primitives (spheres, cuboids) and their counts. Outputs: mindist: The scalar signed distance to the nearest surface in the scene. Data Structures: Sphere: Contains center (c \in \mathbb{R}^3) and radius (r \in \mathbb{R}). Cuboid: Contains center (c \in \mathbb{R}^3), halfextents (h \in \mathbb{R}^3), and potentially orientation (q \in \mathbb{R}^4) if rotated. Scene: Contains spherecount (uint), cuboidcount (uint), spheres (array of Sphere), cuboids (array of Cuboid). Steps: 1. Initialize mindist to a large positive value representing infinity, typically 10000.0. 2. Iterate through all spheres in the scene: For each sphere i, evaluate the sphere SDF: d{sphere} = \| p - ci \| - ri. Update mindist = min(mindist, d{sphere}). 3. Iterate through all cuboids in the scene: For each cuboid j, evaluate the cuboid SDF. This involves transforming p into the cuboid's local space (if rotated), computing the distance to the box, and returning the result. Update mindist = min(mindist, d{cuboid}). 4. Return mindist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatescenesdf(point, scene): # Initialize with a large value representing infinity mindist = 10000.0 # Evaluate all spheres for i in range(scene.spherecount): sphere = scene.spheres[i] # Distance from point to sphere surface disttocenter = length(point - sphere.center) spheredist = disttocenter - sphere.radius if spheredist < mindist: mindist = spheredist # Evaluate all cuboids for j in range(scene.cuboidcount): cuboid = scene.cuboids[j] # Evaluate cuboid SDF (implementation details depend on rotation) # Assuming a standard axis-aligned or rotated box SDF function cuboiddist = evaluatesdfcuboid(cuboid, point) if cuboiddist < mindist: mindist = cuboiddist return mindist def evaluatesdfsphere(sphere, point): return length(point - sphere.center) - sphere.radius def evaluatesdfcuboid(cuboid, point): # Standard cuboid SDF logic: transform point to local space, # compute distance to box, return max(0, dist) - halfextents logic. # Specifically: d = max(|plocal| - h, 0) + length(max(|plocal| - h, 0)) # This step is implied by the source's loop structure but not detailed in S1. pass Parameters: MAXSIGNEDDISTANCE: 10000.0. Edge Cases: If the scene is empty, the function returns MAXSIGNEDDISTANCE. Precision issues may arise if primitives are extremely close or overlapping, though the min operation handles overlaps correctly for unions. A boolean intersection operation for SDFs that returns the maximum distance value at any point, representing the region common to both shapes. To implement, evaluate the SDF for both shapes at point p and return \max(d1, d2). This is the dual of the union operation used in the main scene evaluation. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of primitives in the scene. Each primitive is evaluated exactly once. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the primitive data structures. Strengths: Simple to implement; allows for complex scene composition using basic primitives. Limitations: Performance degrades linearly with scene complexity. Not suitable for very large scenes without spatial acceleration structures (which are not part of this basic evaluation method). The method originates from ray marching techniques using Signed Distance Functions. The specific implementation pattern of iterating through spheres and cuboids is documented in the ray-marcher project. The theoretical basis for using min for union and max for intersection is established by Alan Zucconi. unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric Rendering: Signed Distance Functions - Alan Zucconi, https://www.alanzucconi.com/2016/07/01/signed-distance-functions/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Signed Distance Field (SDF) Primitive Definition
head: SDF Function, SDF Shapes, Signed Distance Field (SDF), Signed Distance Function (SDF), Signed Distance Function Primitives
body: A Signed Distance Field (SDF) Primitive Definition is an analytical function that returns the shortest Euclidean distance from a query point \mathbf{p} in 3D space to the surface of a geometric primitive, with a sign indicating whether the point is inside (negative) or outside (positive) the shape. It solves the problem of representing complex 3D geometry as a continuous scalar field, replacing explicit mesh topology with implicit distance evaluations. Unlike sibling Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination) which composites primitives, or SDF Transformation which modifies the input coordinate space, this method defines the fundamental geometric primitives themselves. It is distinguished from mesh-based rendering by allowing complex scenes to be constructed via simple arithmetic on scalar values, providing a conservative distance estimate that guarantees no surface is closer than d(\mathbf{p}), preventing ray overshooting. Input: A 3D point \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z) in world or local space. Output: A scalar float d = \text{SDF}(\mathbf{p}) representing the signed distance. Convention: The y-axis is up; objects are centered at the origin unless otherwise noted. Primitives are defined by parameters stored in simple structures or passed as arguments. Common layouts include: Sphere: struct sph { float r; vec3 c; } where r is radius and c is center. Box: struct box { vec3 p; vec3 size; } where p is position and size is full size (halved in calculation). Cylinder: struct cylinder { vec2 p; float r; } for infinite cylinders (center in XZ plane). Capped Cylinder: struct cylinderCapped { float r; float h; } where h is half-height. Cone: struct cone { float r; float h; vec3 c; } where c is center/offset. Plane: struct plane { vec4 k; } where k.xyz is the normal and k.w is the offset. Torus: struct tor { float inR; float outR; } where inR is tube radius and outR is major radius. GDF Vectors: An array of 19 normalized vec3 directions used for Generalized Distance Functions (GDF). The core definition for any primitive is the signed Euclidean distance. Below are the specific implementations for standard primitives. 1. Sphere The distance from \mathbf{p} to the center \mathbf{c} minus the radius r. d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\| - r For a unit sphere at the origin: f(x, y, z) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} - 1 2. Box (AABB) Let \mathbf{b} be the half-extents. Compute \mathbf{d} = |\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{b}. d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\max(\mathbf{d}, 0)\| + \min(\max(dx, \max(dy, dz)), 0) A cheaper, overestimating variant is: d{cheap}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(|\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{b}) 3. Plane Defined by normal \mathbf{n} (normalized) and distance from origin d{offset}. d(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + d{offset} For a horizontal plane at height h (normal \mathbf{y}): d(\mathbf{p}) = py + h 4. Cylinder (Infinite, along Y) d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}{xz} - \mathbf{c}{xz}\| - r where \mathbf{p}{xz} = (px, pz) and \mathbf{c}{xz} is the center in the XZ plane. 5. Cylinder (Capped, along Y) Let dx = \|\mathbf{p}{xz} - \mathbf{c}{xz}\| - r and dy = |py| - h (where h is half-height). d(\mathbf{p}) = \min(\max(dx, dy), 0) + \|\max(dx, dy, 0)\| 6. Capsule Defined by endpoints \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} and radius r. First compute distance to line segment: t = \text{saturate}\left(\frac{(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})}{\|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}\|^2}\right) d{seg}(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) - \mathbf{p}\| d(\mathbf{p}) = d{seg}(\mathbf{p}) - r 7. Torus Let R{out} be the major radius and R{in} be the tube (minor) radius. q = (\|\mathbf{p}{xz}\| - R{out}, py) d(\mathbf{p}) = \|q\| - R{in} 8. Cone Defined by radius r, height h, and center/offset \mathbf{c}. Let \phi = \arctan(r/h). d(\mathbf{p}) = \max(\sqrt{x^2+z^2}\cos(\phi) - |y|\sin(\phi), \max(y-h, -y)) More detailed implementation handles tip and base ring distances explicitly. 9. Generalized Distance Function (GDF) Uses a set of pre-normalized vectors \mathbf{v}i (e.g., 19 vectors for icosahedron-like shapes) and an exponent e. d(\mathbf{p}) = \left( \sum{i} |\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{v}i|^e \right)^{1/e} - r For sharp edges (e \to \infty), use max: d(\mathbf{p}) = \max{i} |\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{v}i| - r Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): return [x / math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) for x in v] def dot(a, b): return sum(xy for x, y in zip(a, b)) def length(v): return math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) def absvec(v): return [abs(x) for x in v] def maxvec(a, b): return [max(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)] def minvec(a, b): return [min(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)] def saturate(t): return max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) def sdfsphere(p, c, r): """Sphere SDF. p: point, c: center, r: radius.""" return length([p[i] - c[i] for i in range(3)]) - r def sdfbox(p, center, halfsize): """Box SDF. p: point, center: position, halfsize: half-extents.""" d = absvec([p[i] - center[i] for i in range(3)]) d = [d[i] - halfsize[i] for i in range(3)] # Exact distance q = maxvec(d, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) r = minvec(d, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) return length(q) + min(min(r[0], min(r[1], r[2]))) def sdftorus(p, center, majorradius, minorradius): """Torus SDF. p: point, center: position, majorradius: Rout, minorradius: Rin.""" # Vector from center to p, projected to XZ plane for major radius calc dx = p[0] - center[0] dy = p[1] - center[1] dz = p[2] - center[2] # Distance to the center ring of the torus in XZ plane distxz = math.sqrt(dxdx + dzdz) - majorradius # Vector q in the plane containing the tube center and the point q = [distxz, dy] return length(q) - minorradius def sdfcapsule(p, a, b, r): """Capsule SDF. p: point, a: start, b: end, r: radius.""" ab = [b[i] - a[i] for i in range(3)] pa = [p[i] - a[i] for i in range(3)] ablensq = dot(ab, ab) if ablensq == 0: return length(pa) - r t = saturate(dot(pa, ab) / ablensq) closest = [a[i] + t ab[i] for i in range(3)] return length([closest[i] - p[i] for i in range(3)]) - r def sdfplane(p, normal, offset): """Plane SDF. p: point, normal: normalized normal vector, offset: distance from origin.""" return dot(p, normal) + offset def sdfcylindercapped(p, center, radius, halfheight): """Capped Cylinder SDF along Y axis.""" dx = p[0] - center[0] dy = p[1] - center[1] dz = p[2] - center[2] distxz = math.sqrt(dxdx + dzdz) - radius disty = abs(dy) - halfheight d = [distxz, disty] q = maxvec(d, [0.0, 0.0]) r = minvec(d, [0.0, 0.0]) return length(q) + min(r[0], r[1]) Gradient Step Size: For normal approximation via finite differences, a step size of \epsilon = 0.0001 is typical. Lipschitz Bound: The SDF guarantees that outside all geometry, the ray can safely advance by exactly |d(\mathbf{p})| without overshooting. Precision: GDF implementations with variable exponents can be slow and may not produce correct distances on all hardware due to driver loop unrolling issues (e.g., Nvidia 350.12). Non-Closed Forms: Not every shape has a closed-form SDF. Arbitrary meshes require approximate SDFs (baked into textures or BVH traversal). Discontinuities: Taking the min/max of two SDFs yields sharp discontinuities in the derivative, affecting normal quality. Defines the fundamental geometric building blocks and Boolean compositing rules (Union, Intersection, Difference) for SDFs. It solves the problem of representing complex 3D geometry as a single continuous scalar field by combining simple analytic shapes using arithmetic operators. It is distinguished from mesh-based rendering by replacing explicit topology with implicit distance evaluations. Unlike sibling SDF Transformation which modifies the input coordinate space, this method operates on the output distance values to define the final surface. Applies geometric transformations (rotation, translation, scaling, bending, twisting, tiling) to implicit surfaces defined by SDFs. It operates in the domain of the distance function: transforming the query point \mathbf{x} before evaluating the distance function f. This builds on Signed Distance Field (SDF) Primitive Definition by allowing primitives to be manipulated spatially. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. For a scene with N primitives combined via CSG, complexity is O(N) per sample point. Memory Complexity: O(1) for analytical primitives. No mesh storage required. Performance: Raymarching using SDFs is significantly faster than triangle raytracing for complex procedural scenes because it avoids intersection tests with individual triangles, stepping instead by the distance to the nearest surface. Strengths: Exact normals (via gradient), easy CSG operations, compact representation, no tessellation artifacts. Limitations: Limited to shapes with known analytical SDFs or approximations; sharp corners from CSG can cause normal artifacts; GDF loops may suffer from driver optimization issues. When to use: Procedural rendering, real-time shaders, scenes with high complexity but simple geometry. When not to use: Scenes with highly detailed, non-analytical geometry where mesh-based raytracing or rasterization is more appropriate. Signed Distance Fields originated in the level set method for tracking interfaces, representing an orientable manifold surface as a function tracking the signed distance to the nearest point on the interface. The term "SDF" in computer graphics was popularized by Inigo Quilez's articles on distance functions and raymarching. The technique allows for efficient ray marching (sphere tracing) by using the distance value as a safe step size. It is widely used in real-time graphics, particularly in GLSL shaders for procedural geometry. name: SDF Primitives & Operations
head: Basic Shapes, Boolean operations on implicit surfaces, CSG Intersection, Implicit Function CSG, SDF Operations, Subtraction, Union
body: SDF Primitives & Operations define the fundamental geometric building blocks and Boolean compositing rules for Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). This method solves the problem of representing complex 3D geometry as a single continuous scalar field by combining simple analytic shapes (primitives) using arithmetic operators. It is distinguished from mesh-based rendering by replacing explicit topology with implicit distance evaluations, allowing complex scenes to be constructed via simple arithmetic on scalar values. Unlike sibling SDF Transformation which modifies the input coordinate space, this method operates on the output distance values to define the final surface. Inputs: Point \mathbf{p} in 3D space. Primitive parameters (e.g., radius r, box half-extents \mathbf{b}, plane normal \mathbf{n}). For composite operations: two or more SDF functions fA, fB and their respective parameters. Outputs: A scalar float representing the signed distance from \mathbf{p} to the nearest surface. Positive values indicate outside, zero on the surface, negative inside. No complex data structures are required for basic primitives. The state is defined by the function parameters. For CSG operations, the scene graph is typically a tree of function pointers or lambda expressions evaluating child SDFs. 1. Evaluate the primitive SDF f(\mathbf{p}) for the current raymarch point \mathbf{p} using the appropriate analytic formula. 2. If compositing, evaluate child SDFs fA(\mathbf{p}) and fB(\mathbf{p}). 3. Apply the Boolean operator (min for union, max for intersection, max with negation for subtraction) to combine the scalar outputs. 4. Return the resulting scalar distance value. 5. Compute the surface normal via central finite differences if lighting is required. All vectors are 3D. |\cdot| denotes component-wise absolute value, \|\cdot\| denotes Euclidean length, and \max/\min denote component-wise or scalar maximum/minimum as context dictates. 1. Sphere: Centered at origin, radius r. f{sphere}(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}\| - r 2. Box: Axis-aligned, centered at origin, half-extents \mathbf{b} = (bx, by, bz) where bi > 0. q = |\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{b} q{max} = \max(q, 0) f{box}(\mathbf{p}) = \|q{max}\| + \min(\max(qx, \max(qy, qz)), 0) 3. Round Box: Box with rounded edges of radius r{round}. f{roundbox}(\mathbf{p}) = f{box}(\mathbf{p}) - r{round} 4. Cylinder: Axis-aligned along Y, height h, radius r. d = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - r h{half} = h / 2 f{cyl}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(\max(d, |py| - h{half}), 0) 5. Round Cylinder: Cylinder with rounded edges. f{roundcyl}(\mathbf{p}) = f{cyl}(\mathbf{p}) - r{round} 6. Plane: Defined by unit normal \mathbf{n} and distance h from origin along \mathbf{n}. f{plane}(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} - h 7. Torus: Centered at origin, major radius R, minor radius r. q = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R f{torus}(\mathbf{p}) = \sqrt{q^2 + py^2} - r 8. Ellipsoid: Axis-aligned, radii \mathbf{r} = (rx, ry, rz). \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} / \mathbf{r} f{ellipsoid}(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}'\| - 1 9. Cone: Parametrized by position \mathbf{p}, surface normal \mathbf{c}, and height h. Exact formula not provided in sources. 10. Pyramid: Parametrized by position \mathbf{p} and height h. Exact formula not provided in sources. 11. Link: Produces one half of a chain-link structure. Parametrized by position \mathbf{p}, major/minor radii, and link length. Exact formula not provided in sources. 12. Elongated Torus: Variant of Torus extended in x, y, z directions. Exact formula not provided in sources. CSG Operations combine SDFs fA and fB to create new surfaces: 1. Union (A \cup B): The surface is the boundary of the combined volume. f{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(fA(\mathbf{p}), fB(\mathbf{p})) 2. Intersection (A \cap B): The surface is the boundary of the overlapping volume. f{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(fA(\mathbf{p}), fB(\mathbf{p})) 3. Subtraction (A \ B): The surface is A minus B. f{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(fA(\mathbf{p}), -fB(\mathbf{p})) Epsilon: For normal calculation, a small value. Radius/Size: Primitive-specific. Amplitude (A): Maximal amplitude of the fractal function for solid noise primitives. Precision: Near the surface (f(\mathbf{p}) \approx 0), floating-point errors can cause jitter in ray marching steps. Subtraction Artifacts: Subtracting a large object from a small one can result in inverted normals if not handled correctly by the CSG logic. Smooth Union: Not covered in basic operations, but standard min/max creates sharp edges. Fractal Density Bounds: Due to the fractal function, density may be positive outside the sphere's radius. The function has non-negative values at most A units away from the radius, requiring bounds padding. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def length(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def absvec(v): return [abs(v[0]), abs(v[1]), abs(v[2])] def maxvec(a, b): return [max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1]), max(a[2], b[2])] def sphere(p, r): return length(p) - r def box(p, b): q = absvec(p) - b qmax = maxvec(q, [0, 0, 0]) return length(qmax) + min(max(q[0], max(q[1], q[2])), 0) def plane(p, n, h): return sum(p[i] n[i] for i in range(3)) - h def union(afunc, aparams, bfunc, bparams, p): return min(afunc(p, aparams), bfunc(p, bparams)) def intersection(afunc, aparams, bfunc, bparams, p): return max(afunc(p, aparams), bfunc(p, bparams)) def subtraction(afunc, aparams, bfunc, bparams, p): return max(afunc(p, aparams), -bfunc(p, bparams)) def normalat(func, params, p, eps=1e-4): dx = func([p[0]+eps, p[1], p[2]], params) - func([p[0]-eps, p[1], p[2]], params) dy = func([p[0], p[1]+eps, p[2]], params) - func([p[0], p[1]-eps, p[2]], params) dz = func([p[0], p[1], p[2]+eps], params) - func([p[0], p[1], p[2]-eps], params) vec = [dx, dy, dz] l = length(vec) if l == 0: return [0, 1, 0] return [vec[0]/l, vec[1]/l, vec[2]/l] Computes the distance to an axis-aligned box using component-wise absolute value and max/min operators. It is computationally efficient due to the absence of square roots in intermediate steps, making it ideal for tight bounding volume hierarchies [1092-signed-box-distance-function.md]. Returns the distance from a point to a sphere surface centered at the origin. It is the simplest analytic primitive and serves as a foundational building block for ellipsoids and windowed noise primitives [1237-sphere-signed-distance-function.md]. Composites multiple primitive shapes into a single implicit surface by applying Boolean logic to their distance fields. It reduces geometric composition to arithmetic operations on scalar values, enabling normals and shadows derived from the resulting field's gradient. It is chosen when complex, multi-part geometry is required without explicit mesh topology [1329-csg-operations-on-implicit-functions.md]. Modifies the input position vector to create periodic, mirrored, or reflected spatial structures. They partition space into cells and are chosen when infinite repeating patterns (grids, tiles) are needed without increasing geometric complexity [1730-sdf-domain-manipulation-operators.md]. Provides atomic Signed Distance Functions for common geometric shapes like Sphere, Box, and Torus. These are chosen as the base layer for all procedural SDF scene construction [1731-sdf-primitives.md]. Rounds an SDF by subtracting a constant distance value from the result. It is chosen to uniformly thicken or thin surfaces, create rounded edges on boxes, or adjust collision boundaries [1829-sdf-rounding.md]. Defines a plane using a unit normal and height parameter. It is chosen for infinite planar surfaces, ground planes, or clipping boundaries in ray marching [1102-plane-signed-distance-function.md]. Creates complex geometry by subtracting domain-repeated smaller objects from a non-repeated larger object. It is chosen to generate perforated or lattice-like structures efficiently. Windows a fractal noise function within a sphere's radius to create volumetric density. It is chosen for procedural organic or gaseous volumes, requiring bounds padding due to fractal amplitude. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. CSG operations add a constant factor proportional to the number of children in the scene graph. Memory Complexity: O(1) for primitives. Scene graph size depends on the number of primitives. Measured Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to lack of branching and simple arithmetic. Performance scales linearly with the depth of the CSG tree. Strengths: Infinite resolution (analytic). Easy to implement and debug. Compact memory footprint. Natural support for smooth blending and morphing. Limitations: Cannot represent arbitrary topology (e.g., self-intersections in complex ways without CSG). Normals are approximate if computed via finite differences. When to use: Ideal for real-time rendering of stylized, geometric, or procedural scenes. When not to use: When photorealistic detail from scanned meshes is required, or when the geometry is too complex for efficient CSG evaluation. The concept of Signed Distance Fields for rendering was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his blog posts and books on ray marching. The mathematical foundations of CSG with distance fields were established by Hart. The technique has become a staple in real-time graphics for creating procedural geometry, VFX, and stylized rendering. name: SDF Domain Manipulation Operators
head: Domain Manipulation Operators, SDF Modifiers, SDF domain transformations, Space Partitioning, pSomething operators
body: SDF Domain Manipulation Operators modify the input position vector \mathbf{p} to partition space into cells, creating periodic, mirrored, or reflected spatial structures for Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). They transform the coordinate space before the primitive SDF is evaluated, allowing for the creation of complex patterns like grids and symmetries with minimal computational overhead. Unlike CSG Operations on Implicit Functions, which combines scalar fields via boolean logic, domain operators transform the geometry's location in space directly. All domain manipulation operators follow a common convention: the input position vector \mathbf{p} is passed as the first argument and modified in place (inout p). For operators acting on subsets of dimensions, specific components are supplied (e.g., <p.x> or <p.zx>). The core mechanism involves partitioning the space into cells of a defined size. The operator maps the query point \mathbf{p} to a local coordinate within its cell and returns a cell index (or identifier). This cell index can be used as a random seed for procedural variation or symmetry tracking. For cell index 0, \mathbf{p} remains unchanged, and cells are centered on the origin, meaning objects do not need to be manually translated to fit the grid. The general transformation for periodic repetition in one dimension is: c = \text{floor}\left(\frac{p + \text{size}/2}{\text{size}}\right) p' = \text{mod}(p + \text{size}/2, \text{size}) - \text{size}/2 where c is the cell index and p' is the transformed position. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): """Standard dot product for vectors of equal length.""" return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def pmod(p, size): """Maps p to the local coordinate within its cell and returns the cell index c.""" halfsize = size 0.5 c = math.floor((p + halfsize) / size) p = (p + halfsize) % size - halfsize return c def pmodmirror(p, size): """Maps p to a mirrored local coordinate within its cell and returns the cell index c.""" halfsize = size 0.5 c = math.floor((p + halfsize) / size) p = (p + halfsize) % size - halfsize # Mirror every other cell p = (c % 2) 2 - 1 return c def pmirror(p, dist): """Reflects p across a plane at distance dist and returns the sign s.""" s = 1.0 if p >= 0.0 else -1.0 p = abs(p) - dist return s def preflect(p, planenormal, offset): """Reflects p across a plane defined by normal and offset, returns sign of t.""" t = dot(p, planenormal) + offset if t < 0.0: p = p - (2.0 t) planenormal s = 1.0 if t >= 0.0 else -1.0 return s CSG Operations on Implicit Functions creates complex geometric shapes from simple SDF primitives via boolean operations: union, intersection, and difference. It combines scalar fields using binary node operations to construct complex implicit surfaces. Unlike explicit mesh-based CSG, which requires complex boolean intersection algorithms on polygonal geometry, SDF CSG reduces scene composition to simple arithmetic on distance values. This allows for the rendering of near-tangent intersections and complex composite geometries with minimal computational overhead per sample. Finite Repetition creates a bounded grid of repeated instances of a base SDF primitive, limiting the replication count to a specified range in each dimension. Unlike infinite tiling operators, it restricts the domain to a finite box, preventing geometry from extending to infinity. It is chosen when a localized, tiled structure is required without the computational cost or visual artifacts of infinite repetition. Creating complex geometry by subtracting domain-repeated smaller objects from a non-repeated larger object (e.g., domain repeated cubes subtracted from a larger sphere). This combines domain repetition with subtracting distance fields from each other to create complex objects. Reflects an SDF across the XZ plane. The step is to take the absolute value of the Y component of \mathbf{p}. Reflects an SDF across the YZ plane. The step is to take the absolute value of the X component of \mathbf{p}. Reflects an SDF across the XY plane. The step is to take the absolute value of the Z component of \mathbf{p}. name: CSG Operations on Implicit Functions
head: CSG Operations, CSG implicit surfaces, SDF Boolean Operators, SDF Boolean Operations, CSG with SDFs, Constructive Solid Geometry with SDFs
body: CSG Operations on Implicit Functions is a method of creating complex geometric shapes from simple Signed Distance Function (SDF) primitives via boolean operations: union, intersection, and difference. It combines scalar fields using binary node operations to construct complex implicit surfaces. Unlike explicit mesh-based CSG, which requires complex boolean intersection algorithms on polygonal geometry, SDF CSG reduces scene composition to simple arithmetic on distance values. This allows for the rendering of near-tangent intersections and complex composite geometries with minimal computational overhead per sample. Inputs: Two SDF functions, fA(p) and fB(p), which return the signed distance from a query point p to the surface of object A or B. Output: A composite SDF function f{scene}(p) that represents the boolean combination of the input shapes. The scene is represented as a node hierarchy where each node holds pointers to two child ScalarField objects. Nodes are evaluated recursively or iteratively to compute the final distance. The core arithmetic mappings for standard CSG operations are: 1. Union: The distance to the union is the minimum of the individual distances. A point is inside the union if it is inside at least one of the shapes. f{union}(p) = \min(fA(p), fB(p)) 2. Intersection: The distance to the intersection is the maximum of the individual distances. A point is inside the intersection only if it is inside both shapes. f{intersect}(p) = \max(fA(p), fB(p)) 3. Difference (Subtraction): The difference A \setminus B is computed by intersecting A with the complement of B. The complement of an SDF is obtained by negating its distance values. f{sub}(p) = \max(fA(p), -fB(p)) 4. XOR: Exclusive OR can be constructed from the above operations. f{xor}(p) = \max(\min(fA(p), fB(p)), -\max(fA(p), fB(p))) 1. Instantiate nodes with pointers to child SDFs: new UnionNode(a, b), new IntersectionNode(a, b), new DifferenceNode(a, b). 2. Chain nodes by passing output nodes as inputs to subsequent nodes to build the scene graph. 3. Evaluate the final root node's Value(p) method at the query point to get the combined SDF distance. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the recursive evaluation of a CSG tree. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class ScalarField: def init(self, func): self.func = func def evaluate(self, pos): return self.func(pos) class Node: def init(self, op, left, right): self.operation = op self.left = left self.right = right def evaluate(self, pos): adist = self.left.evaluate(pos) bdist = self.right.evaluate(pos) if self.operation == "Union": return min(adist, bdist) elif self.operation == "Intersection": return max(adist, bdist) elif self.operation == "Difference": return max(adist, -bdist) else: raise ValueError("Unknown operation") def evaluatecsg(node, pos): """Evaluates the CSG tree at position pos. Returns the combined signed distance.""" if isinstance(node, ScalarField): return node.evaluate(pos) return node.evaluate(pos) Smooth Union: Alternative Union with smooth transition. Takes additional float k (0 to 2) determining smoothness, typically 0.1 to 1.0. Implementation: h = clamp(0.5 + 0.5 (b - a) / k, 0.0, 1.0); return mix(b, a, h) - k h (1.0 - h). Stairs Operations: Union Stairs, Difference Stairs, and Intersection Stairs create steps between edges. Takes floats r (step width) and n (number of steps). Noise: Unary operation adding Perlin noise to signed distance. Takes float noiseProp (0 to 0.5). Uses GLSL mix function. Onion: Unary operation creating a hole inside a shape. Takes float thickness (smaller value = larger hole). Scaling: Scaling an SDF requires scaling the input coordinates by the inverse of the scale factor and scaling the output distance by the scale factor to maintain correct distance values. DeMorgan’s Theorem: DeMorgan’s theorem (A \cap B = \overline{\overline{A} \cup \overline{B}}) does not work directly with min/max operators for distance bounds because the minimum operator is not complemented properly. Using max ensures the bound holds. Subtraction Artefact: max(-a, b) is exact only when the surface of A is entirely contained within B. If A pokes through the boundary of B, the resulting SDF is not Lipschitz-1 and sphere marching may skip surfaces — add a small EPSILON correction or tighten the step size in those regions. Material Boundaries: The polygonizer does not consider materials, leading to drastic color changes between vertices at CSG boundaries. To separate colors, material changes must be treated as surface boundaries (inside/outside changes). Distance Bounds: For intersection, the resulting function is a bound on the true distance, not necessarily the exact distance. Specifically, in Case II (dA < 0, dB > 0), the closest point in A to p may not be in the intersection, but no point in the intersection can be closer than dB. An interactive editor that constructs SDFs from primitives and operations using a stack-based interface similar to Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), implicitly representing a tree with postorder traversal. It differs from explicit tree editors by deferring structure resolution until compilation, allowing users to build complex scenes by pushing operations onto a linear stack where only the top item is visible until combined. A voxel-based implementation of CSG operations on discrete level set data. Operations are performed element-wise on voxel buffers. Union: A{new}(i,j,k) = \min(A(i,j,k), B(i,j,k)). Intersection: A{new}(i,j,k) = \max(A(i,j,k), B(i,j,k)). Difference: A{new}(i,j,k) = \max(A(i,j,k), -B(i,j,k)). In user interface terms, intersection corresponds to a copy operation, union to a paste operation, and difference to a cut operation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simplicity: Boolean operations are reduced to min/max. No Mesh Booleaning: Avoids the computational complexity and numerical instability of polygonal boolean operations. Free Normals: Surface normals are derived from the gradient of the composite SDF, which is consistent with the geometry. Limitations: Approximate Distance: The resulting SDF is a bound, not the exact distance to the CSG boundary, which can affect sphere tracing step sizes (though still valid for rendering). Sharp Edges: Standard CSG produces sharp, non-smooth edges unless smooth variants are used. Material Handling: The polygonizer does not consider materials, leading to drastic color changes between vertices at CSG boundaries. CSG was introduced in the 1970s for solid modeling. The application of CSG to implicit surfaces using min/max operators was formalized by Ricci in 1974. The technique became widely popular in real-time graphics with the advent of ray marching and SDFs, notably demonstrated by Iñigo Quilez and Jamie Wong in the 2010s. It is used in voxel editors and differentiable rendering pipelines. name: Stack-Based SDF Editor
head: Post-order SDF construction, RPN-style SDF editor
body: An interactive editor that constructs Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) from primitives and operations using a stack-based interface similar to Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), implicitly representing a tree with postorder traversal. It differs from explicit tree editors by deferring structure resolution until compilation, allowing users to build complex scenes by pushing operations onto a linear stack where only the top item is visible until combined. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of operations pushed onto a stack, categorized as Shapes, Transformations, or CSG Operations. Output: A compiled GLSL shader string containing the SDF evaluation function. Data Structures: Operation Stack: A list of operation objects representing the postorder traversal of the scene graph. AST Tree: A recursive structure built from the stack where nodes are either leaves (primitive shapes annotated with domain-modifying transformations) or internal nodes (CSG operations acting on range values). Numbered Steps: 1. Push Operation: Operations are pushed onto the stack. The editor only considers the first item by default; subsequent items are not visible until joined via union or other operations. 2. Invalidate Cache: Modifying any parameter calls #invalidate, which clears the cached shader program to trigger recompilation on the next access. 3. Build SDF (Tree Reconstruction): The buildSDF function iterates over the stack, popping off previous operations according to the arity of the current operation to reconstruct the tree structure. 4. Generate GLSL: The system recursively traverses the AST, transforming nodes to appropriate calls. At leaves, it composes domain-modifying functions in the opposite order of application. Internal nodes generate range operations (e.g., min for union). 5. Compile: The generated GLSL string is spliced into a template and compiled. Formulas: Union: S{union}(p) = \min(SA(p), SB(p)). Domain Transformation Composition: If transformations T1, T2, \dots are applied to a shape, the input position p is transformed by composing them in the opposite order: Tn(\dots T2(T1(p)) \dots). Parameters: Primitive Types: Box and Sphere (e.g., radius 1.0). Transformations: Translate (vec3 offset) and Rotate (float angle). CSG Operations: Union and Intersection. Configuration: Uses lazy evaluation and caching via getter/setter methods that call #invalidate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility: Subsequent stack items remain invisible until a union or similar operation combines them with the top item. AST vs Conceptual Tree: The generated AST differs from the conceptual operation tree because domain modifications (transformations) are attached to leaves, while range modifications (CSG operations) form internal nodes. Performance: Without #invalidate caching, the shader would be reassembled and compiled on every frame, causing severe inefficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildsdf(stack): aststack = [] for op in stack: if op['type'] == 'Shape': aststack.append({'type': 'Leaf', 'shape': op['shape'], 'transforms': [], 'params': op.get('params', {})}) elif op['type'] == 'Transform': if aststack: aststack[-1]['transforms'].append(op['transform']) elif op['type'] == 'CSG': if len(aststack) >= 2: right = aststack.pop() left = aststack.pop() aststack.append({'type': 'CSG', 'op': op['op'], 'left': left, 'right': right}) return aststack[0] if aststack else None def generateglsl(node): if node['type'] == 'Leaf': p = "p" for t in reversed(node['transforms']): if t['type'] == 'Translate': p = f"opTx({p}, vec3({t['x']}, {t['y']}, {t['z']}))" elif t['type'] == 'Rotate': p = f"opRotX({p}, {t['angle']})" radius = node['params'].get('radius', '1.0') return f"sd{node['shape'].upper()}({p}, {radius})" elif node['type'] == 'CSG': leftcode = generateglsl(node['left']) rightcode = generateglsl(node['right']) if node['op'] == 'Union': return f"min({leftcode}, {rightcode})" elif node['op'] == 'Intersection': return f"max({leftcode}, {rightcode})" return f"min({leftcode}, {rightcode})" return "" Caching via #invalidate prevents recompilation on every frame, making runtime evaluation efficient. The Config class uses lazy evaluation and caching to avoid unnecessary shader recompilation. The interface is described as intuitive once the input model is understood. The Stack-Based SDF Editor was developed as a final project for COS 426, focusing on raymarching with Signed Distance Fields. It demonstrates building SDFs from primitives and operations using a stack-based interface similar to RPN notation. name: SDF Rounding
head: Distance Offset, Rounding, Rounding Transformation, SDF Offset
body: SDF Rounding is a geometric transformation that rounds the edges of a shape by a specified radius. It operates by subtracting a constant distance value from the SDF result, distinguishing it from SDF Domain Manipulation Operators which modify the coordinate space, and SDF Primitives which define base shapes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a base SDF function d(p) returning the signed distance to the primitive surface. Input: A rounding radius r \ge 0. Output: The rounded signed distance d{\text{rounded}}(p). Data Structures: The SDF function d(p) is implemented as a callable returning a scalar or tensor. The radius r is stored as a scalar float. Steps: 1. Evaluate the base SDF at the query point p to obtain the signed distance d = d(p). 2. Subtract the rounding radius r from the distance value. 3. Return the result d{\text{rounded}} = d - r. Formula: d{\text{rounded}}(p) = d(p) - r Where: d(p) is the signed distance from point p to the original primitive surface. r is the rounding radius parameter. Parameters: r: The distance at which to perform the rounding. A value of 0.1 is used as an example in reference implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If r exceeds the minimum feature size of the primitive, the zero-crossing shifts inward, potentially collapsing thin features or inverting the signed distance sign. The sign of the distance is preserved relative to the original surface, but the surface location moves inward by r. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfrounding(sdffunc, radius): """ Applies SDF rounding to a base signed distance function. Args: sdffunc: A callable that takes a point p (vec3) and returns the signed distance. radius: A float representing the rounding radius r. Returns: A callable that returns the rounded signed distance. """ def roundedsdf(p): # Evaluate the base SDF d = sdffunc(p) # Subtract the radius to round the edges return d - radius return roundedsdf Creates a hollow shell by taking the absolute value of the distance and subtracting a radius. It is a specific application of SDF Rounding that inverts the interior to create a void. Not given in the sources. name: SDF Onion
head: Onion, Onion SDF, SDF Absolute Value Offset, SDF Shell
body: The SDF Onion operation creates a hollow shell or layered structure from a solid Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitive by taking the absolute value of the distance and subtracting a specified radius. It is a specific application of SDF Rounding that inverts the interior of the shape to create a void. Inputs: 1. sdf: A callable returning the signed distance d for a query point p. 2. radius: A scalar float r \ge 0 defining the shell offset. Outputs: A callable returning the signed distance to the shell surface. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the operation is a point-wise mathematical transformation applied to the output of the parent SDF. Steps: 1. Evaluate the parent SDF at the query coordinates to obtain the signed distance d = \text{sdf}(p). 2. Compute the absolute value of the signed distance: d{abs} = |d|. 3. Subtract the radius r from the absolute distance: d{onion} = d{abs} - r. 4. Return d{onion}. Formula: d{onion}(p) = |\text{sdf}(p)| - r Where: p is the 3D query point. \text{sdf}(p) is the signed distance from p to the original solid shape. r is the shell radius/thickness. Parameters: radius (r): The shell thickness. Typical values depend on the scale of the parent primitive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Thickness: If r=0, the result is |d|, representing the unsigned distance to the surface. Large Radius: If r exceeds the distance from the center to the nearest surface of the parent shape, the resulting SDF may be positive everywhere inside the original volume, creating a large void. Degenerate Shapes: For shapes with zero volume or thin surfaces, the absolute value operation combined with subtraction may produce artifacts if the radius is not carefully chosen relative to the shape's curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfonion(sdffunc, radius): """ Creates an SDF for a hollow shell from a solid SDF. Args: sdffunc: A callable that takes a 3D point p and returns the signed distance. radius: The thickness of the shell (r >= 0). Returns: A callable that returns the signed distance to the shell surface. """ def onionsdf(p): d = sdffunc(p) dabs = abs(d) donion = dabs - radius return donion return onionsdf The operation requires O(1) time per query point, involving only absolute value and subtraction arithmetic on top of the parent SDF evaluation. Memory complexity is O(1) as no additional data structures are stored. It is computationally cheap and effective for creating hollow objects, but produces uniform shell thickness and cannot generate variable thickness without more complex operations. The interior of the shell is empty, which may require additional ray marching logic if the ray must stop at the inner surface. Use this when a hollow version of a solid primitive is required, and avoid it when variable thickness or complex internal structures are needed. The SDF Onion operation is used in ray marching and implicit surface rendering to create hollow objects. The onion function can be applied recursively to a sphere with different radii to create layered structures. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Elongation
body: Elongation modifies a base signed distance function by shifting the query point's absolute coordinates by an elongation vector, then adjusting the resulting distance with the maximum negative coordinate offset. It is a post-processing step applied to an existing SDF evaluation, distinct from coordinate-only transformations. Inputs: p: The 3D query point (vector). s: The elongation vector (vector). SDF{base}(q): The base signed distance function to be elongated. Outputs: d{out}: The elongated signed distance value. Data Structures: Standard 3D vectors for p and s. Intermediate vector q and scalar d{out}. Steps: 1. Compute the intermediate vector q by subtracting the elongation vector s from the absolute value of the query point p: q = |p| - s 2. Evaluate the base SDF at the component-wise positive part of q: d{base} = SDF{base}(\max(q, 0)) 3. Compute the component-wise negative part of q, clamped to zero, and take its maximum component: m = \max(\max(-q, 0)) 4. Add m to the base distance: d{out} = d{base} + m Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def elongation(p, s, sdfbase): # Step 1: q = |p| - s q = abs(p) - s # Step 2: Evaluate base SDF at positive part of q qpos = max(q, 0.0) # Component-wise max dbase = sdfbase(qpos) # Step 3 & 4: Add max of negative part clamped to 0 qneg = max(-q, 0.0) # Component-wise max m = max(qneg) # Maximum component dout = dbase + m return dout Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A technique to address field variation divergence near skeleton end-points in SCALIS fields. It forces an additional sampling position near end-points to increase correlation between the minima of individual primitives and the global field. It is implemented by adding a segment primitive with constant radius at the end vertices of the skeleton. name: Finite Repetition
head: Bounded Tiling, Finite Domain Repetition, Limited Repetition
body: Finite Repetition creates a bounded grid of repeated instances of a base Signed Distance Function (SDF) primitive, limiting the replication count to a specified range in each dimension. Unlike infinite tiling operators, it restricts the domain to a finite box. Inputs: p: Input position vector (\mathbb{R}^3). c: Period vector defining the cell size in each dimension (\mathbb{R}^3). l: Limit vector defining the maximum number of cells to replicate in each dimension (\mathbb{R}^3). Outputs: p': Transformed position vector mapped to the nearest valid cell within the bounds. Data Structures: Vectors p, c, l are 3-component floating-point vectors. Steps: 1. Normalize the position by the period: u = p / c. 2. Round each component of u to the nearest integer to find the cell index: q{\text{raw}} = \text{round}(u). 3. Clamp the cell indices to the limits: q = \text{clamp}(q{\text{raw}}, -l, l). 4. Map the position back to the local cell: p' = p - c \cdot q. Formula: q = \text{clamp}\left(\text{round}\left(\frac{p}{c}\right), -l, l\right) p' = p - c \cdot q Parameters: c: Must be non-zero. Typical values depend on the desired tile size. l: Non-negative values representing the radius of the grid in cells. Edge Cases: If c contains zero, division is undefined. Guard against zero components in c before division. If l is zero, the result is the identity transformation (no repetition). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def repeatfinite(p: Vec3, c: Vec3, l: Vec3) -> Vec3: # Step 1 & 2: Divide by period and round to nearest integer qraw = (p / c).round() # Step 3: Clamp cell indices to limits [-l, l] q = qraw.clamp(-l, l) # Step 4: Map position back to local cell pprime = p - c q return pprime Not given in the sources. name: Quadric SDF (First-Order Approximation)
body: Computes an approximate signed distance from a query point to a quadric surface defined by a general quadratic equation, using a first-order Taylor approximation. It enables ray marching against arbitrary quadrics without deriving closed-form distance functions, trading geometric accuracy for implementation simplicity. Inputs: Query point v = (x, y, z). Quadric coefficients a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j defining the surface ax^2 + by^2 + cz^2 + dxy + eyz + fzx + gx + hy + iz + j = 0. Outputs: Approximate signed distance d{approx}. Data Structures: Coefficients are stored as six quadratic terms (a,b,c,d,e,f), three linear terms (g,h,i), and one constant (j). Standard double-precision floats are used. Steps: 1. Evaluate the implicit function value f0 at v: f0 = ax^2 + by^2 + cz^2 + dxy + eyz + fzx + gx + hy + iz + j 2. Compute the gradient components \nabla f = (dx, dy, dz): dx = 2ax + dy + fz + g dy = 2by + ez + dx + h dz = 2cz + fx + ey + i 3. Compute the gradient magnitude f1: f1 = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2} 4. Return the approximation: d{approx} = \frac{f0}{f1} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def quadricsdffirstorder(x, y, z, a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j): # 1. Evaluate implicit function f0 = (a x x + b y y + c z z + d x y + e y z + f z x + g x + h y + i z + j) # 2. Compute gradient components dx = 2 a x + d y + f z + g dy = 2 b y + e z + d x + h dz = 2 c z + f x + e y + i # 3. Compute gradient magnitude f1 = math.sqrt(dx dx + dy dy + dz dz) # 4. Return approximation if f1 == 0.0: return 0.0 # Guard against division by zero return f0 / f1 Parameters: a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j: Coefficients of the quadric equation. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient: If the gradient magnitude f1 is near zero (e.g., at critical points or far from the surface), the distance estimate becomes unstable or incorrect. A guard against division by zero is required. Approximation Error: The first-order approximation is only accurate near the surface. Far from the surface, the error grows, potentially causing ray marching to overshoot or undershoot. Sign Ambiguity: The sign of f0 determines the side of the surface, but the approximation may flip sign incorrectly if the gradient is small. Transforms the quadric coefficients to align with principal axes, simplifying the distance calculation. Choose when the quadric is rotated or sheared. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Memory Complexity: O(1) for coefficients. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with the number of query points. Strengths: Simple to implement; works for any quadric defined by a general equation. Limitations: Approximate distance; unstable near critical points; less accurate than exact SDFs. When to use: When exact SDFs are unavailable or too complex to derive; for simple quadrics where high precision is not critical. When not to use: When high precision is required; near critical points of the quadric. Originated from the use of first-order Taylor approximations for implicit surface distance estimation. It is used in ray marching for rendering quadric surfaces. Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, https://github.com/Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Basic Primitive Definitions
head: Analytical SDF Primitives, Basic Signed Distance Functions
body: Basic Primitive Definitions provide the foundational analytical Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for simple geometric shapes, serving as the atomic building blocks for distance-field ray marching. They compute the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of a shape, guaranteeing no underestimation to prevent ray overshooting. Unlike SDF Domain Manipulation Operators which transform space or SDF Rounding which modifies surfaces, primitives define the base geometry itself. All basic primitives share a common computational framework: 1. Canonical Definition: Primitives are defined centered at the origin with specific orientations (e.g., sphere at (0,0,0), cylinder along Y-axis). 2. Transformations: To place a primitive at a different location, orientation, or scale: Translate: Replace query point p with p - c, where c is the center. Rotate: Multiply p by the inverse rotation matrix R^{-1} before evaluation: p' = R^{-1} p. Scale: Uniformly scale by s using d(p/s) \cdot s. 3. Output: A scalar signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}, where d < 0 indicates inside and d > 0 indicates outside. Analytical SDFs for basic shapes (sphere, box, torus, cylinder, capsule, plane, rhombic triacontahedron). Defines the base geometry using exact Euclidean distance formulas. Exact SDFs for convex polyhedra (prisms, pyramids). Uses symmetry folding and separation of axes to reduce 3D queries to simpler projections. Exact SDF for cones, including base cap and apex. Reduces 3D distance to a 2D problem via rotational symmetry, preserving sharp edges unlike quadric approximations. SDF for line segments. Computes distance to the closest point on a segment defined by endpoints, handling boundaries explicitly. The concept of using analytical distance functions for rendering was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his online tutorials, providing efficient, branch-free distance estimators for ray marching. These primitives form the core of modern SDF-based rendering, enabling complex scene construction through boolean operations and domain manipulation. name: SDF Primitives
head: Basic SDFs, Basic Signed Distance Functions, SDF Primitive Functions, Signed Distance Field (SDF) Primitives, Signed Distance Primitives
body: SDF Primitives are analytical Signed Distance Functions that compute the exact Euclidean distance from a query point in 3D space to the surface of a basic geometric shape, returning a negative value if the point is inside and a positive value if it is outside. They serve as the foundational building blocks for distance-field ray marching, enabling efficient step-size estimation by guaranteeing that the returned distance is never an underestimation, which prevents ray overshooting. Unlike SDF Domain Manipulation Operators which transform space, or SDF Rounding which modifies surfaces, primitives define the base geometry itself. Inputs: A query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and primitive-specific parameters (e.g., radius, half-extents, normal). Outputs: A scalar signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: vec3: 3D vector (x, y, z). vec2: 2D vector (x, y). float: Scalar real number. General Transformations: All primitives are defined centered at the origin. To place a primitive at a different location or orientation: 1. Translate: Replace p with p - c, where c is the center. 2. Rotate: Multiply p by an inverse rotation matrix R^{-1} before passing to the SDF: p' = R^{-1} p. 3. Scale: Uniformly scale by s using d(p/s) \cdot s. Formulas and Steps: 1. Sphere Parameters: Radius r. Formula: d(p) = \|p\| - r. Implementation: return length(p) - r;. 2. Axis-Aligned Box (AABB) Parameters: Half-extents b = (bx, by, bz). Steps: 1. Compute q = |p| - b (component-wise absolute value and subtraction). 2. Compute d{out} = \| \max(q, 0.0) \|. 3. Compute d{in} = \min(\max(qx, \max(qy, qz)), 0.0). 4. Result: d = d{out} + d{in}. Note: This handles faces, edges, and corners correctly without underestimation. 3. Torus Parameters: Major radius R, tube radius r. Steps: 1. Compute q = (\|p{xz}\| - R, py) where p{xz} = (px, pz). 2. Result: d = \|q\| - r. 4. Infinite Plane Parameters: Unit normal n, offset d (distance from origin along normal). Formula: d(p) = p \cdot n + d. Note: n must be normalized. 5. Cylinder (Infinite along Y) Parameters: Radius r, half-height h. Steps: 1. Compute d{vec} = (\|p{xz}\|, py). 2. Compute dist = |d{vec}| - (r, h). 3. Result: d = \min(\max(distx, disty), 0.0) + \| \max(dist, 0.0) \|. Note: This defines a cylinder capped at y = \pm h. 6. Capsule Parameters: Endpoints a, b, radius r. Steps: 1. Compute vector ab = b - a and ap = p - a. 2. Compute projection parameter t = \text{clamp}(\frac{ap \cdot ab}{ab \cdot ab}, 0.0, 1.0). 3. Compute closest point on segment c = a + ab \cdot t. 4. Result: d = \|p - c\| - r. 7. Rhombic Triacontahedron Parameters: None (fixed shape). Steps: 1. Initialize magic numbers: c = \cos(\pi/5), s = \sqrt{0.75 - c^2}. 2. Define direction n = (-0.5, -c, s). 3. Fold 1: p = |p|; p = p - 2 \cdot \min(0.0, p \cdot n) \cdot n. 4. Fold 2: p{xy} = |p{xy}|; p = p - 2 \cdot \min(0.0, p \cdot n) \cdot n. 5. Fold 3: p{xy} = |p{xy}|; p = p - 2 \cdot \min(0.0, p \cdot n) \cdot n. 6. Result: d = pz - 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vec3length(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def vec3dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def vec3abs(v): return (abs(v[0]), abs(v[1]), abs(v[2])) def vec3sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def vec3add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def vec3scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def vec3maxscalar(v, s): return (max(v[0], s), max(v[1], s), max(v[2], s)) def vec3componentmaxclamped(v): m = max(v[0], max(v[1], v[2])) return min(m, 0.0) def sdsphere(p, r): return vec3length(p) - r def sdbox(p, b): q = vec3sub(vec3abs(p), b) dout = vec3length(vec3maxscalar(q, 0.0)) din = vec3componentmaxclamped(q) return dout + din def sdtorus(p, R, r): pxzlen = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) q = (pxzlen - R, p[1]) return math.sqrt(q[0]2 + q[1]2) - r def sdplane(p, n, d): return vec3dot(p, n) + d def sdcylinder(p, r, h): pxzlen = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) dvec = (pxzlen, p[1]) dist = vec3sub(vec3abs(dvec), (r, h)) minmaxval = min(max(dist[0], dist[1]), 0.0) dout = vec3length(vec3maxscalar(dist, 0.0)) return minmaxval + dout def sdcapsule(p, a, b, r): ab = vec3sub(b, a) ap = vec3sub(p, a) abdotab = vec3dot(ab, ab) if abdotab == 0: return vec3length(ap) - r t = vec3dot(ap, ab) / abdotab t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) closest = vec3add(a, vec3scale(ab, t)) return vec3length(vec3sub(p, closest)) - r def sdrhombictriacontahedron(p): c = math.cos(math.pi / 5.0) s = math.sqrt(0.75 - cc) n = (-0.5, -c, s) p = vec3abs(p) dotpn = vec3dot(p, n) p = vec3sub(p, vec3scale(n, 2.0 min(0.0, dotpn))) pxy = (abs(p[0]), abs(p[1]), p[2]) p = pxy dotpn = vec3dot(p, n) p = vec3sub(p, vec3scale(n, 2.0 min(0.0, dotpn))) pxy = (abs(p[0]), abs(p[1]), p[2]) p = pxy dotpn = vec3dot(p, n) p = vec3sub(p, vec3scale(n, 2.0 min(0.0, dotpn))) return p[2] - 1.0 Computes exact Euclidean distance to an axis-aligned box using component-wise absolute values and max/min operations. Chosen when axis-aligned bounding volumes are needed; distinguishes itself from spheres by handling distinct geometric regions (faces, edges, corners). Computes distance to an infinite plane defined by a unit normal and height. Chosen for infinite surfaces or clipping planes. Computes exact Euclidean distance to a sphere surface. Chosen as the simplest primitive; analytically closed-form and computationally minimal compared to ellipsoids. Computes signed distance for an ellipsoid with radii r. Chosen when non-uniform scaling is required; requires solving higher-degree polynomials compared to the sphere. Computes signed distance for a capsule (cylinder with hemispherical caps) aligned with an axis or defined by endpoints. Chosen for organic shapes or limbs. A Signed Distance Function for a Rhombic Triacontahedron crystal shape, constructed by folding 3D space using specific magic numbers and directions multiple times. It distinguishes itself from standard convex primitives by using iterative space folding to create complex symmetry. Chosen for artistic or crystalline visual effects. Definition: The shape is defined by folding space along a specific direction n and axes, using magic numbers derived from \pi/5. Steps: 1. Initialize magic numbers: c = \cos(\pi/5), s = \sqrt{0.75 - c^2}. 2. Define direction n = (-0.5, -c, s). 3. Fold 1: p = |p|; p = p - 2 \cdot \min(0.0, p \cdot n) \cdot n. 4. Fold 2: p{xy} = |p{xy}|; p = p - 2 \cdot \min(0.0, p \cdot n) \cdot n. 5. Fold 3: p{xy} = |p{xy}|; p = p - 2 \cdot \min(0.0, p \cdot n) \cdot n. 6. Result: d = pz - 1.0. Formula: c = \cos(\pi/5), s = \sqrt{0.75 - c^2}, n = (-0.5, -c, s). Code: See sdrhombictriacontahedron in the main pseudocode section. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Exact and efficient, free of numerical noise for standard primitives. The Rhombic Triacontahedron is more expensive due to multiple folds and trigonometric constants. Strengths: Exact distance guarantees prevent ray overshooting in sphere tracing. Simple to implement and highly parallelizable on GPUs. Limitations: Only supports specific geometric shapes. Complex scenes require combining primitives via CSG operations, which can introduce artifacts for concave geometry. When to use: Real-time ray marching, procedural geometry, and scenes composed of basic shapes. When not to use: Scenes with highly complex, non-analytic geometry where mesh-based rendering or voxel-based methods are more appropriate. name: Signed Box Distance Function
head: Box SDF, Box SDF v2, Rectangular (Axis-Aligned Box) SDF, SDF Box, SDF Cube, Signed Box, sdBox
body: The Signed Box Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean signed distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box centered at the origin. It returns negative values for points inside the box and positive values for points outside, distinguishing interior from exterior space. It is the 3D analog of the Rectangle Signed Distance Function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: p, a 3D query point. Input: b, the half-extents of the box (vector), where each component represents half the side length along that axis. Alternatively, the box can be defined by center c and side lengths s, where b = s/2. Output: A scalar float representing the signed Euclidean distance. Data Structures: p, b, c, s: 3D vectors with components (x, y, z). Algorithm: The method exploits the symmetry of the box across the three coordinate planes. By taking the absolute value of the point coordinates, the problem is reduced to the first octant, where the box occupies the region [0, bx] \times [0, by] \times [0, bz]. 1. Shift and Scale: If the box is defined by center c and side lengths s, compute the half-extents b = s / 2 and the relative point p' = p - c. 2. Symmetry Reduction: Compute the absolute value of the relative point coordinates: q = |p'|. 3. Distance to Faces: Compute the vector d = q - b. This vector represents the signed distance to the nearest face along each axis. If di < 0, the point is inside the box along axis i. If di \ge 0, the point is outside the box along axis i. 4. Inside Distance: Calculate the distance to the interior surface. This is determined by the maximum of the components of d, clamped to zero: d{inside} = \min(\max(dx, \max(dy, dz)), 0). If the point is outside, this value is zero; if inside, it is negative. 5. Outside Distance: Calculate the Euclidean distance to the exterior surface. This is the length of the vector formed by the positive components of d (the distance to the nearest face, edge, or corner). d{outside} = \| \max(d, 0) \| = \sqrt{\max(dx, 0)^2 + \max(dy, 0)^2 + \max(dz, 0)^2} 6. Combine: The final signed distance is the sum of the inside distance and the outside distance. d(p) = \min(\max(dx, \max(dy, dz)), 0) + \| \max(d, 0) \| Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def abs(self): return Vec3(abs(self.x), abs(self.y), abs(self.z)) def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def maxscalar(self, val): return Vec3(max(self.x, val), max(self.y, val), max(self.z, val)) def maxcomponent(self): return max(self.x, max(self.y, self.z)) def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) def signedboxdistance(p: Vec3, b: Vec3) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to an axis-aligned box centered at the origin with half-extents b. """ # 1. Symmetry reduction: map to first octant q = p.abs() # 2. Distance to faces: d = q - b d = q.sub(b) # 3. Inside distance: max of components, clamped to 0 insidedist = min(d.maxcomponent(), 0.0) # 4. Outside distance: length of positive components posd = d.maxscalar(0.0) outsidedist = posd.length() # 5. Combine return insidedist + outsidedist def signedboxdistancecentered(p: Vec3, c: Vec3, s: Vec3) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to an axis-aligned box defined by center c and side lengths s. """ bx = s.x / 2.0 by = s.y / 2.0 bz = s.z / 2.0 b = Vec3(bx, by, bz) prel = p.sub(c) return signedboxdistance(prel, b) Parameters: b (half-extents): Typical values depend on scene scale. For a unit box, b = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). c (center): Default (0, 0, 0) if not specified. s (side lengths): Must be positive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Near the surface, floating-point precision errors can cause jitter in normals or distance values. Degenerate Input: If any component of b is zero, the box becomes a plane, line, or point. Underestimation vs Overestimation: The exact formula (Algorithm 3.6) provides the true Euclidean distance. Approximations that underestimate the distance (e.g., Algorithm 3.5) cause smaller ray steps and slower convergence, and can lead to incorrect ambient occlusion. Overestimation can cause the ray to pass through the surface. The Unsigned Box Distance Function computes the Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box centered at the origin, returning only non-negative values regardless of whether the point lies inside or outside the volume. Unlike its sibling, the Signed Box Distance Function, which distinguishes interior from exterior space, this method treats the box as a solid boundary where internal points are measured by their distance to the nearest face. Computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the boundary of an axis-aligned rectangle centered at the origin. It is the 2D analog of the Signed Box Distance Function. Computes the signed distance to a box with rounded edges, defined by half-extents b and edge radius e. The algorithm computes p' = |p| - b, then q = |p' + e| - e, and returns the minimum of three terms, each representing distance to a face, edge, or corner with rounding. Computes the signed distance to a 2D box with custom orientation and thickness between points a and b, where th is the full thickness perpendicular to the segment [a, b]. If the segment length is negligible, it falls back to a circle SDF. Otherwise, it rotates the query point into the local frame of the segment and calls the 2D box SDF. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. The computation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (absolute values, subtractions, max/min, and a square root). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are required. Strengths: Exact Euclidean distance, fast evaluation, supports CSG operations (union, intersection, difference) via min/max operations, provides correct normals via gradient. Limitations: Only applies to axis-aligned boxes. For oriented boxes, a transformation matrix must be applied to the query point before evaluation, which adds computational cost. The sharp corners can cause aliasing in ambient occlusion if the ray marching steps are too large. The Signed Box Distance Function is a fundamental primitive in the field of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and ray marching. It was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his online resources on distance functions. The method exploits the symmetry of the box to reduce the computation to the first octant, a technique widely used in computer graphics for efficient geometric queries. It is used in real-time rendering, implicit modeling, and collision detection.
