name: Unsigned Box Distance Function
head: Unsigned Box, udBox
body: The Unsigned Box Distance Function computes the Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box centered at the origin, returning only non-negative values regardless of whether the point lies inside or outside the volume. Unlike its sibling, the Signed Box Distance Function, which distinguishes interior from exterior space, this method treats the box as a solid boundary where internal points are measured by their distance to the nearest face. Inputs and outputs: Input: p (vec3), the query point in 3D space. Input: b (vec3), the half-extents of the box along the X, Y, and Z axes. The box is centered at (0,0,0) and spans [-bx, bx] \times [-by, by] \times [-bz, bz]. Output: d (float), the unsigned Euclidean distance from p to the box surface. Data structures: No complex data structures are required. The function operates on standard 3D vectors. Formula: The distance is calculated using the following formula: d = \|\max(|p| - b, 0)\| Where: |p| denotes the component-wise absolute value of vector p, i.e., (|px|, |py|, |pz|). \max(v, 0) denotes the component-wise maximum of vector v and the scalar 0, i.e., (\max(vx, 0), \max(vy, 0), \max(vz, 0)). \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm (length) of the resulting vector. Step-by-step derivation: 1. Compute the absolute coordinates of the point: q = |p|. 2. Subtract the box half-extents: r = q - b. 3. Clamp negative values to zero: s = \max(r, 0). This step effectively ignores the interior of the box, treating any negative distance (interior) as zero distance to the surface. 4. Compute the Euclidean length of the remaining vector: d = \sqrt{sx^2 + sy^2 + sz^2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def udBox(px, py, pz, bx, by, bz): """ Computes the unsigned distance from point p to an axis-aligned box centered at the origin with half-extents b. Args: px, py, pz: Query point coordinates bx, by, bz: Box half-extents Returns: Non-negative Euclidean distance to the box surface. """ # Step 1: Component-wise absolute value of p absx = abs(px) absy = abs(py) absz = abs(pz) # Step 2: Subtract half-extents diffx = absx - bx diffy = absy - by diffz = absz - bz # Step 3: Component-wise max with 0 (clamp negatives to zero) clampedx = max(diffx, 0.0) clampedy = max(diffy, 0.0) clampedz = max(diffz, 0.0) # Step 4: Euclidean norm (length) distance = (clampedx2 + clampedy2 + clampedz2)0.5 return distance Parameters and typical values: b: Must be positive. If any component is zero, the box degenerates into a plane, line, or point. p: Any real-valued 3D coordinate. Edge cases and pitfalls: Inside the box: If the point is strictly inside the box, the intermediate diff vector will have negative components. The clamping step sets these to 0. If the point is inside, the distance returned is the distance to the nearest face (if only one component is negative) or 0 (if the point is strictly inside all boundaries, though the formula \max(|p|-b, 0) yields a vector of zeros only if |p| \le b component-wise, resulting in distance 0). The formula provided returns 0 if the point is inside the box volume because \max(|pi| - bi, 0) = 0 for all i, leading to a zero vector and thus distance 0. Precision: Near the box edges and corners, the function is continuous but not differentiable. Floating-point precision issues may arise when |pi| \approx bi. Degenerate input: If b contains negative values, the geometric interpretation is invalid. Evaluates the signed distance from a point to an axis-aligned cuboid, handling both outside and inside distances. It transforms the point using the cuboid's 4x4 matrix, calculates distances to faces, and combines outside and inside distance components. The cuboid struct layout is: transform (Mat4, 64 bytes), dimensions (Vec3, 12 bytes), padding (u32, 4 bytes), totaling 80 bytes with 16-byte alignment. Construction uses Cuboid::new(dimensions).translate(v).rotate(v). Time complexity: O(1). The calculation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (absolute value, subtraction, comparison, square root). Memory complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are allocated. Strengths: Extremely fast evaluation, suitable for real-time ray marching and collision detection where interior/exterior distinction is not required. Limitations: Does not provide information about whether the point is inside or outside the volume. Not suitable for operations requiring signed distance properties (e.g., smooth unions, boolean operations with SDFs). The Unsigned Box Distance Function is a standard primitive in Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering, often used in GLSL-based ray marchers. It is part of the collection of SDF primitives popularized by the glsl-sdf-primitives library. While the signed variant is more common in constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations, the unsigned variant is useful for simple boundary checks or when the interior is treated as empty space. marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Box with Edge Rounding SDF
head: Rounded Box SDF, SDF Primitive: Box with Edge Rounding, sdBoxRounded
body: Computes the signed distance to an axis-aligned box with rounded edges and corners, defined by half-extents b and edge radius e. It extends the basic box distance by replacing sharp corners with spherical fillets, allowing for smooth geometric transitions in ray marching. It differs from the Unsigned Box Distance Function by providing signed interior/exterior information and from the Rectangle Signed Distance Function by supporting 3D volumes with uniform edge rounding rather than planar rectangles. Inputs: p: Query point (vec3). b: Half-extents of the box (vec3). e: Edge/corner rounding radius (float). Outputs: Signed distance value (float). Negative inside, positive outside, zero on surface. Data Structures: Standard 3D vector types for p and b. Scalar float for e. Steps: 1. Compute the absolute distance from the center: p' = |p| - b. 2. Compute the rounded corner distance: q = |p' + e| - e. 3. Determine the distance to the box faces, edges, and rounded corners: Let d{face} be the distance to the flat faces. Let d{edge} be the distance to the straight edges. Let d{corner} be the distance to the rounded corners. The final distance is \min(\text{distance to faces}, \text{distance to edges}, \text{distance to corners}). Formula: The standard implementation computes the distance by analyzing the position of p relative to the box's geometry. Let d = |p| - b. Let q = |d + e| - e. The signed distance is: \text{sd} = \begin{cases} \min(q.x, q.y, q.z) & \text{if } d.x < 0 \land d.y < 0 \land d.z < 0 \\ \min(\text{length}(q), \text{distance to edges}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} More precisely, following: 1. d = |p| - b 2. q = |d + e| - e 3. The distance is the minimum of the distances to the rounded corners, edges, and faces. The specific calculation involves checking if the point is in the corner region, edge region, or face region. If d.x < 0, d.y < 0, d.z < 0: The point is in the corner region. Distance is \min(q.x, q.y, q.z). Otherwise, the distance is calculated based on the closest feature (face, edge, or corner). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdboxrounded(p, b, e): # p: vec3, b: vec3, e: float d = abs(p) - b q = abs(d + e) - e # Determine if point is in corner, edge, or face region # Corner region: all components of d are negative if d.x < 0 and d.y < 0 and d.z < 0: return min(q.x, q.y, q.z) # Edge region: two components of d are negative # Face region: one component of d is negative # Calculate distance to the closest feature # This part is complex and depends on the specific implementation details # For a complete implementation, see # Simplified logic based on description: # The distance is the minimum of the distances to the rounded corners, edges, and faces. # The exact formula involves checking the signs of d and calculating the distance accordingly. # Note: The exact formula for the non-corner regions is not fully detailed in # but typically involves calculating the distance to the rounded edges and faces. # For the purpose of this article, we assume the standard implementation: # The distance is the minimum of the distances to the rounded corners, edges, and faces. # Return the calculated distance return 0.0 # Placeholder for the actual calculation Parameters: e: Edge radius. Must be 0 \le e \le \min(bx, by, bz). Edge Cases: e = 0: Reduces to the standard Signed Box Distance Function. e = \min(b): The box becomes a sphere with radius \min(b) if bx=by=bz, or a capsule-like shape otherwise. Precision issues near the boundaries between face, edge, and corner regions. Signed distance to a 2D rounded box with corner radius r. Formula: \text{box2d}(p, b - r) - r. Implementation: pub fn roundedbox2d(p: Vec2, b: Vec2, r: f32) -> f32 { box2d(p, b - Vec2::splat(r)) - r }. Chosen when 2D rounded rectangles are needed. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Smooth geometry, efficient ray marching, no need for mesh tessellation. Limitations: Rounding radius must be uniform. Not suitable for non-uniform rounding. When to use: When smooth, rounded boxes are required in ray marching. When not to use: When sharp corners are needed (use standard box) or when non-uniform rounding is required. Originated from Inigo Quilez's work on SDFs. name: Rectangle Signed Distance Function
head: 2D Rectangle SDF, sdRect
body: Computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the boundary of an axis-aligned rectangle centered at the origin. It is the 2D analog of the Signed Box Distance Function. Inputs: p: Query point in 2D space. hsize: Half-extents of the rectangle along the x and y axes. Outputs: d: Signed distance. Data Structures: Tuples or lists of two floating-point numbers for p and hsize. Steps: 1. Calculate the displacement vector dv from the rectangle's boundary: dvx = |px| - hsizex, \quad dvy = |py| - hsizey where |px| and |py| apply the absolute value component-wise. 2. Calculate the exterior distance using the positive components of dv: outsideDistance = \sqrt{\max(dvx, 0)^2 + \max(dvy, 0)^2} where \max(dv, 0) applies the maximum operator to each component with 0, and \|\cdot\| is the Euclidean length. 3. Calculate the interior distance using the closest edge: insideDistance = \min(\max(dvx, dvy), 0) This captures the distance to the closest edge when the point is inside the rectangle. 4. Return the sum: d = outsideDistance + insideDistance Formula: d = \|\max(dv, 0)\| + \min(\max(dvx, dvy), 0) where dv = |p| - hsize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdRect(p, hsize): dvx = abs(p[0]) - hsize[0] dvy = abs(p[1]) - hsize[1] posx = dvx if dvx > 0.0 else 0.0 posy = dvy if dvy > 0.0 else 0.0 outsidedist = (posx2 + posy2)0.5 insidedist = min(max(dvx, dvy), 0.0) return outsidedist + insidedist Parameters: hsize: Typical values depend on scene scale. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Near the boundary, floating-point precision may cause jitter. Clamping or epsilon checks are often used in ray marching loops to prevent infinite loops or z-fighting. Degenerate Input: If hsize contains zero or negative values, the geometry is invalid or degenerate. Not given in the sources. A 3D extension for a cube centered at the origin with width, height, and length equal to 2.0 (half-extents of 1.0). Definition: d = \|\max(d, 0)\| + \min(\max(dx, \max(dy, dz)), 0) where d = |p| - (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Code: Unverified code. name: Plane Signed Distance Function
head: Plane SDF, Plane distance, Signed Distance Function (SDF) for Plane, Signed Plane, sdPlane
body: The Plane Signed Distance Function (SDF) computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to an infinite plane defined by a normal vector and an offset. It serves as a fundamental building block in distance-field ray marching, often representing ground planes or infinite boundaries. Unlike its siblings such as the Sphere SDF or Box SDF, which define bounded volumes, the plane is unbounded. It is distinguished by its computational simplicity, requiring only a single dot product and addition, making it the most efficient primitive for infinite planar surfaces. Input: A query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and plane definition parameters. Output: A scalar signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. The plane is defined by two components: 1. Normal (\mathbf{n}): A 3D unit vector (nx, ny, nz) perpendicular to the plane. 2. Offset (h or d0): A scalar representing the distance from the origin to the plane along the normal. Alternatively, the plane can be represented as a 4D vector \mathbf{n}{eq} = (nx, ny, nz, nw), where nw corresponds to the offset term in the plane equation. 1. Compute the dot product of the query point \mathbf{p} and the plane normal \mathbf{n}. 2. Add the scalar offset h to the dot product result. The signed distance d is calculated as: d = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + h Where: \mathbf{p} is the query point. \mathbf{n} is the unit normal vector of the plane. h is the offset. The sign convention varies by source: In and, h is added directly (d = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + h). In, the formula is f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{n} - h, where h defines the relative placement with respect to the plane perpendicular to \mathbf{n} intersecting the origin. In, the distance is given as \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{n} - \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}, where \mathbf{r} is a point on the plane. This is equivalent to \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{n} - h' where h' = \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}. Sign Convention: d > 0: The point is on the side of the plane towards which the normal \mathbf{n} points. d < 0: The point is on the opposite side of the normal. d = 0: The point lies exactly on the plane. \mathbf{n}: Must be a unit vector (\|\mathbf{n}\| = 1). h: Scalar offset. Typical values depend on scene scale. For a ground plane at y=0 with normal (0,1,0), h=0. For a plane at y=-5 with normal (0,1,0), h=5 (using d = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + h). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdplane(p: Vector3, n: Vector3, h: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a plane defined by unit normal n and offset h. Args: p: Query point (x, y, z). n: Plane normal vector. MUST be normalized. h: Offset. The plane equation is effectively n.xx + n.yy + n.zz + h = 0. Note: Some sources use minus h. This implementation follows. Returns: Signed Euclidean distance. Positive if p is on the side of n, negative otherwise. """ # Guard: Ensure normal is normalized to guarantee Euclidean distance # In production, assert or normalize n if not guaranteed by caller. # Calculate dot product of point and normal dotproduct = p.x n.x + p.y n.y + p.z n.z # Add offset distance = dotproduct + h return distance 1. Unnormalized Normal: If \mathbf{n} is not a unit vector, the result is scaled by \|\mathbf{n}\|, breaking the "distance" property required for correct ray marching step sizes. 2. Offset Sign Convention: Sources and use different signs for the offset (+h vs -h). The implementer must align the offset definition with the rest of the scene graph or SDF library. 3. Infinite Extent: The plane is infinite. It does not have edges. If a bounded plane is required, it must be combined with other primitives (e.g., via min/max operations for union/intersection) or clipped by other SDFs. Time Complexity: O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Extremely fast; exact distance; no convergence issues for infinite surfaces. Limitations: Cannot represent bounded planar shapes (like a square tile) on its own; requires combination with other SDFs for finite planes. When to use: Infinite ground planes, skyboxes, or as a clipping boundary. When not to use: When a finite planar surface is needed without additional SDF logic. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. The plane SDF is one of the most basic primitives in implicit surface modeling. It appears in foundational ray marching literature, such as Hart's "Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces", where it is listed alongside spheres and cylinders. It is also widely implemented in GLSL-based SDF libraries, such as those by Inigo Quilez (referenced in), which popularized the sdPlane function in real-time graphics. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU Ray Marching of Distance Fields, https://www2.compute.dtu.dk/pubdb/edoc/imm6392.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, http://graphics.cs.illinois.edu/sites/default/files/zeno.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Sphere Signed Distance Function

body: The Sphere Signed Distance Function (SDF) computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point in 3D space to the surface of a sphere, returning a signed value that is negative inside the sphere, positive outside, and zero on the surface. It serves as a fundamental implicit primitive for distance-field ray marching and volume rendering, providing an analytically exact distance estimator that enables safe, large step sizes along rays. Unlike the Ellipsoid SDF, which requires solving a sixth-degree polynomial, the Sphere SDF is closed-form and rotationally invariant. Inputs: p: The query point in 3D space, represented as a vector (px, py, pz). c: The center of the sphere, represented as a vector (cx, cy, cz). Default is the origin (0, 0, 0). r: The radius of the sphere, a scalar value r > 0. Output: d: A scalar signed distance value. No complex data structures are required. The sphere is defined by two parameters: 1. Center (c): A 3D vector. In some implementations (e.g., neural implicit fields), this may be a learnable parameter stored as a tensor of shape (1, 3) or (3). 2. Radius (r): A scalar. In some implementations, this may be a learnable parameter. The signed distance d(p) from a point p to a sphere with center c and radius r is given by: d(p) = \| p - c \| - r Where: \| \cdot \| denotes the Euclidean norm (L2 norm). \| p - c \| = \sqrt{(px - cx)^2 + (py - cy)^2 + (pz - cz)^2}. If the sphere is centered at the origin (c = (0,0,0)), the formula simplifies to: d(p) = \| p \| - r 1. Compute Relative Vector: Calculate the vector from the sphere center to the query point: v = p - c. 2. Compute Euclidean Distance: Calculate the length of v: dist = \| v \|. 3. Subtract Radius: Subtract the sphere's radius from the distance: d = dist - r. 4. Return Result: Return d. If d < 0, the point is inside; if d > 0, the point is outside; if d = 0, the point is on the surface. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spheresdf(p, c, r): """Computes the signed distance from point p to a sphere with center c and radius r.""" dx = p[0] - c[0] dy = p[1] - c[1] dz = p[2] - c[2] return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) - r def spheretrace(rayorigin, raydirection, spherecenter, sphereradius, maxsteps=100, epsilon=1e-4, maxdistance=100.0): """ Marches a ray using the Sphere SDF to find the intersection distance. Returns the distance t along the ray where the surface is hit, or infinity if missed. Assumes the ray starts outside the sphere. """ t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): # Current sample point along the ray p = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) # Evaluate SDF at current point dist = spheresdf(p, spherecenter, sphereradius) # Check for surface hit if dist < epsilon: return t # Step forward by the estimated distance to the surface t += dist # Safety bound to prevent infinite loops on missed rays if t > maxdistance: return float('inf') return float('inf') Radius (r): Typically a positive float. In examples, hardcoded values like 0.5 or 1.0 are common. Center (c): Typically (0, 0, 0) for centered spheres. Can be any 3D vector. Learnability: In neural rendering contexts (e.g., NeRF variants), c and r may be treated as learnable parameters optimized during training. Precision: For points very close to the surface, floating-point precision errors may cause jitter in normal estimation if the gradient is computed numerically. Analytical gradients or epsilon stabilization are preferred. Zero Radius: If r=0, the sphere becomes a point. At r=0, the formula reduces to d(p) = \|p - c\|, returning the distance to the center. This is valid but may cause issues in ray marching if step sizes become too small near the center. Negative Radius: Radii must be positive. A negative radius is geometrically invalid for a standard sphere SDF. Definition Order: In some scripting languages (e.g., Fennel/Lua), the SDF function must be defined before the object constructor that uses it, due to top-down evaluation order. Gradient Calculation: The implicit function f(p) = \|p-c\|^2 - r^2 has a gradient \nabla f(p) = 2(p-c), which evaluates to a zero vector at the center. The SDF gradient \nabla d(p) = \frac{p-c}{\|p-c\|} is undefined at the center, requiring numerical stabilization or fallback logic. The 2D analog of the Sphere SDF, computing distance to a circle perimeter. Chose this for 2D rendering or cross-sections. Generalizes the sphere to non-uniform scaling. Chose this for stretched spheres; note it requires solving a sixth-degree polynomial. Combines a sphere with a cylinder. Chose this for rod-like shapes with rounded ends. Computes distance to a circular arc. Chose this for partial circles in 2D or 3D curves. Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation. Requires 3 subtractions, 3 multiplications, 2 additions, and 1 square root. Memory Complexity: O(1). Only stores center and radius. Performance: Extremely fast. The square root operation is the most expensive part, but modern hardware optimizes this well. Strengths: Exact distance (no approximation error). Smooth and differentiable everywhere except the center. Enables large step sizes in ray marching, reducing the number of samples needed. Limitations: Only represents perfect spheres. SDFs are amenable to composition (union, intersection, difference) via min/max operations, allowing complex shapes without external CSG libraries. Singularity at the center for gradient-based normal calculation. When to Use: When rendering spherical objects, collision detection for spheres, or as a building block for CSG operations (union, intersection, difference). When Not to Use: For non-spherical objects where an ellipsoid or more complex primitive is more appropriate. The Sphere SDF is one of the most basic and widely used distance functions in computer graphics, originating from the field of raymarching and signed distance field rendering. The mathematical foundation relies on the definition of a sphere as the locus of points equidistant from a center. The use of SDFs for ray marching (sphere tracing) was introduced by John C. Hart in 1994, who demonstrated that the distance to the nearest surface can be used to step along a ray without missing intersections. It is used in real-time rendering, procedural generation, and as a primitive in neural implicit representations. name: Circle Signed Distance Function
head: 2D Circle SDF, 2D Sphere SDF, Circle SDF, sdCircle
body: The Circle Signed Distance Function computes the signed distance from a 2D query point to the perimeter of a circle centered at the origin. It returns a negative value inside the circle, a positive value outside, and zero on the boundary. It serves as the 2D analog of the Sphere Signed Distance Function. Inputs: p: A 2D query point, represented as a vector (px, py). r: The radius of the circle, a scalar. Outputs: d: The signed distance from p to the circle boundary. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Formula: The signed distance is calculated as the Euclidean norm of the query point minus the radius: d = \|p\| - r where \|p\| = \sqrt{px^2 + py^2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdcircle(p: tuple, r: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a circle of radius r centered at origin. Args: p: Tuple (x, y) representing the 2D query point. r: Float representing the radius of the circle. Returns: Float representing the signed distance. Negative if inside, positive if outside. """ return (p[0] 2 + p[1] 2) 0.5 - r Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sign Interpretation: A negative result indicates the point is inside the circle, zero indicates it is on the boundary, and a positive result indicates it is outside. Zero Radius: If r=0, the function returns the distance to the origin. This is mathematically valid but may cause degenerate behavior in ray marching if not handled. Negative Radius: The radius r should be non-negative. If a negative radius is passed, the sign of the distance will be inverted relative to the geometric expectation. Off-Center Circles: For circles not centered at the origin, the query point must be translated by the circle's center vector before evaluation. Time Complexity: O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Extremely fast evaluation; analytically exact distance. Limitations: Only applies to circles centered at the origin. When to use: Ideal for 2D ray marching and procedural texture generation. The Circle SDF is the 2D analog of the Sphere Signed Distance Function. Its implementation relies on the standard definition of Euclidean distance. erbenpeter/sdf, https://github.com/erbenpeter/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ellipsoid Signed Distance Function
head: Ellipsoid Approximation, Ellipsoid Improved, Ellipsoid SDF
body: Computes the signed distance from a point p to an ellipsoid defined by semi-axes r. It provides a fast approximation (V1) or a more accurate iterative-free approximation (V2). Inputs: Point p \in \mathbb{R}^3, semi-axes radii r \in \mathbb{R}^3 (where ri > 0). Output: Signed distance d. Data Structures: p: 3-component vector. r: 3-component vector. Steps: 1. Compute k1 = \| p / r \|. 2. Compute k2 = \| p / (r \circ r) \|, where \circ is component-wise multiplication. 3. Return d = \frac{k1 (k1 - 1.0)}{k2}. Formula: d = \frac{\| p / r \| (\| p / r \| - 1)}{\| p / (r \circ r) \|} Parameters: r: Semi-axes lengths. Must be positive. Edge Cases: If ri = 0, the function is undefined. Clamp r to a small epsilon if necessary. If p = 0, k1=0, k2=0, resulting in 0/0. Return -\min(r) for the interior case. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ellipsoidsdf(p, r): # p: vec3, r: vec3 # Avoid division by zero when p is at the origin if p == (0.0, 0.0, 0.0): return -min(r) # Step 1: k1 = length(p / r) k1 = length(p / r) # Step 2: k2 = length(p / (r r)) rsq = r r k2 = length(p / rsq) # Step 3: Return k1 (k1 - 1.0) / k2 # Guard against k2 == 0 to prevent inf/nan if k2 == 0.0: return -min(r) d = k1 (k1 - 1.0) / k2 return d Special case where rx=ry=rz. Use for spheres. Cylinder + hemispheres. Use for tubular structures. Axis-aligned or oriented boxes. Use for rectangular volumes. Time Complexity: O(1), constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). Accuracy: V2 is significantly more accurate than V1, especially for highly anisotropic ellipsoids. However, it is still an approximation and not the exact SDF. Strengths: Fast, differentiable, smooth. Limitations: Not exact. May cause artifacts in high-precision ray marching if the error exceeds the step size. The ellipsoid SDF is a standard primitive in SDF libraries. name: Capsule Signed Distance Function
head: 3D Capsule SDF, Capsule SDF, Capsule3D SDF, Signed Capsule, sdCapsule
body: The Capsule Signed Distance Function computes the signed distance from a query point to a capsule defined by two endpoints and a radius. It provides a closed-form solution for a shape with rotational symmetry along a finite segment, building on SDF Primitives. It is distinguished from the Sphere Signed Distance Function by its linear axis and from the Signed Box Distance Function by its smooth, rounded geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3, capsule endpoints a, b \in \mathbb{R}^3, radius r \in \mathbb{R}^+. Output: Signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}, positive outside, negative inside, zero on surface. Data Structures: Vectors p, a, b are 3D Cartesian coordinates. Scalar r is a single floating-point value. Steps: 1. Compute the vector from endpoint a to the query point: pa = p - a. 2. Compute the vector representing the capsule axis: ba = b - a. 3. Compute the squared length of the axis: len\sq = ba \cdot ba. 4. Determine the projection parameter h of p onto the segment ab: If len\sq < \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-12}), set h = 0.0. Otherwise, compute h = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{pa \cdot ba}{len\sq}, 0.0, 1.0\right). 5. Compute the closest point on the segment: closest = a + ba \cdot h. 6. Compute the vector from the closest point to p: diff = p - closest. 7. Return the distance: d = \|diff\| - r. Formula: h = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{(p-a) \cdot (b-a)}{\|b-a\|^2}, 0, 1\right) d = \|(p-a) - h(b-a)\| - r Parameters: r: Radius of the capsule. a, b: Endpoints defining the central axis segment. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Capsule: If a = b, the axis length is zero and len\sq = 0; the division is guarded by clamping h to 0.0 when len\sq < 10^{-12}, effectively treating the shape as a sphere centered at a. Precision: Using squared length in the denominator avoids square roots during projection but requires a threshold guard to prevent division by zero. Single-precision length() evaluations in ray marchers may yield ~1e-3 error due to floating-point accumulation; the analytical formula is exact in double precision. Coordinate Systems: The function is general for any orientation in 3D space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, val)) def sdcapsule(p, a, b, r): """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a capsule defined by endpoints a, b and radius r. """ pa = p - a ba = b - a lensq = ba.dot(ba) if lensq < 1e-12: h = 0.0 else: h = clamp(pa.dot(ba) / lensq, 0.0, 1.0) closest = a + ba h diff = p - closest return diff.length() - r A specialized case where the capsule is aligned with a coordinate axis (typically Y), simplifying the projection to a simple clamp on the Y coordinate. The 2D equivalent, often called a "stadium" in 2D graphics, computed as the distance to a line segment minus the radius. Time Complexity: O(1), involving a constant number of vector operations (subtraction, dot product, clamp, length). Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring no auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Exact analytical solution with no approximation error and fast evaluation for arbitrary 3D orientations. Limitations: The degenerate case a=b must be handled to avoid division by zero. When to use: Rendering or ray-marching objects with cylindrical bodies and rounded ends. The capsule SDF is a standard primitive in Signed Distance Field rendering, implemented in various graphics repositories. The axis-aligned variant provides a simplified calculation for specific use cases. The 2D equivalent is used in planar graphics. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) erbenpeter/sdf, https://github.com/erbenpeter/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Arc Signed Distance Function
head: SDF Arc, sdArc
body: The Arc Signed Distance Function computes the signed distance to a 3D arc shape, defined as a tube of radius arctuberadius running along a circular arc. It is distinguished from the Capsule Signed Distance Function by its curved trajectory and from the Torus by its limited angular aperture. Inputs: p: Query point in 3D space (Vec3). depth: A global Z-coordinate value used to define the plane of the arc. arccenter: Center of the arc's circular path (Vec3). orientationangle: Angle of the arc's starting position in degrees. apatureangle: Total angular width of the arc in degrees. ra: Radius of the circle defining the arc path. rb: Radius of an inner circle, used for interesting shapes. arctuberadius: Radius of the tube running along the arc. Data Structures: The Arc struct contains the following fields: Vec3 arccenter float arctuberadius float orientationangle float apatureangle float scacos float scasin float scbcos float scbsin float ra float rb The constructor precomputes sine and cosine values for the orientation and aperture angles. Steps: 1. Construct Position: Create a 3D position vector from the query point p, replacing its Z-component with the global depth. \text{pos} = (p.x, p.y, \text{depth}) 2. Translate: Shift the position relative to the arc center. \text{pos} = \text{pos} - \text{arc\center} 3. Rotate: Rotate the position into the arc's local coordinate system using the precomputed sine and cosine of the orientation angle. x = \text{pos}.x \cdot \text{sca\cos} - \text{pos}.y \cdot \text{sca\sin} y = \text{pos}.x \cdot \text{sca\sin} + \text{pos}.y \cdot \text{sca\cos} \text{pos}.x = x, \quad \text{pos}.y = y 4. Symmetry: Take the absolute value of the X component to exploit symmetry across the arc's central axis. \text{pos}.x = |\text{pos}.x| 5. Project Distance: Compute the distance to the infinite circular ring defined by radii ra and rb. k = \begin{cases} \text{pos}.x \cdot \text{scb\sin} + \text{pos}.y \cdot \text{scb\cos} & \text{if } \text{scb\cos} \cdot \text{pos}.x > \text{scb\sin} \cdot \text{pos}.y \\ \sqrt{\text{pos}.x^2 + \text{pos}.y^2 + \text{pos}.z^2} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \text{project\distance} = \sqrt{\text{pos}.x^2 + \text{pos}.y^2 + \text{pos}.z^2 + ra^2 - 2 \cdot ra \cdot k} - rb 6. Final Distance: Combine the project distance with the Z-axis deviation (from depth) and subtract the tube radius. \text{distance} = \sqrt{\text{project\distance}^2 + p.z^2} - \text{arc\tube\radius} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def sdarc(p: Vec3, depth: float, arc: 'Arc') -> float: # 1. Construct position vector using global depth pos = Vec3(p.x, p.y, depth) # 2. Translate by arc center pos = pos - arc.arccenter # 3. Rotate by orientation angle x = pos.x arc.scacos - pos.y arc.scasin y = pos.x arc.scasin + pos.y arc.scacos pos.x = x pos.y = y # 4. Take absolute value of x pos.x = abs(pos.x) # 5. Compute intermediate value k if arc.scbcos pos.x > arc.scbsin pos.y: k = pos.x arc.scbsin + pos.y arc.scbcos else: k = math.sqrt(pos.x pos.x + pos.y pos.y + pos.z pos.z) # 6. Compute project distance to the ring projectdistance = math.sqrt(pos.dot(pos) + arc.ra arc.ra - 2.0 arc.ra k) - arc.rb # 7. Compute final distance including Z deviation return math.sqrt(projectdistance projectdistance + p.z p.z) - arc.arctuberadius Parameters: ra: Radius of the circle defining the arc path. Typical value varies by instance (e.g., 1.75). rb: Radius of an inner circle. Default is 0.0. arctuberadius: Radius of the tube running along the arc. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Angle Conversion: The constructor must convert orientationangle and apatureangle from degrees to radians by multiplying by \pi/180.0. Precision: The source code utilizes a fast square root approximation (FT::sqrt) which may introduce minor precision errors compared to standard sqrt. Aperture Logic: The conditional check for k determines if the point lies within the angular span of the arc. Not given in the sources. name: Polyhedral Primitives
head: Polyhedral SDFs, Polyhedron Signed Distance Functions
body: This family provides exact signed distance functions for convex polyhedra, prisms, and pyramids, enabling precise ray marching. It distinguishes itself from SDF Primitives, Cone Signed Distance Function, and Segment Signed Distance Function by focusing on multi-faceted shapes with planar faces rather than simple quadratic forms or domain manipulations. It provides closed-form analytic solutions that exploit geometric symmetries to reduce 3D distance queries to simpler 2D or 1D projections. All polyhedral SDFs in this family share a common computational structure based on symmetry reduction and extrusion. 1. Symmetry Folding: Most polyhedra possess reflectional symmetries across coordinate planes. The first step is typically computing the absolute value of the query point components (q = |p|). This folds the 3D space into a fundamental octant (or sector), reducing the number of cases the algorithm must handle. For shapes with rotational symmetry (like prisms), additional reflections or rotations map the point into a smaller fundamental domain (e.g., a 30° sector for hexagons). 2. Separation of Axes: For prisms, the distance calculation separates the axial component (usually Z) from the cross-sectional component (XY). The total distance is computed by combining the distance to the infinite prism (d{xy}) and the distance to the caps (dz) using the extruded shape formula: d = \min(\max(d{xy}, dz), 0) + \text{length}(\max(d{xy}, dz, 0)). 3. Fundamental Domain Projection: For non-prismatic polyhedra (octahedra, pyramids), the algorithm projects the folded point onto the closest face, edge, or vertex. This often involves comparing the point's position against linear inequalities defining the faces to determine which region of the Voronoi cell the point lies in. 4. Branch-Free Optimization: Where possible, implementations use max, min, and clamp operations to replace conditional branches, ensuring consistent performance on GPU architectures. Computes the exact signed distance to a regular octahedron. It is distinguished by its specific symmetry group and face geometry, offering a distinct aesthetic for procedural geometry. Choose this when a smooth, faceted sphere-like shape with 8 triangular faces is required. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdoctahedron(p, s): """ Computes the signed distance to an octahedron of size s. p: tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) s: float, size parameter """ # Step 1: Absolute coordinates px, py, pz = abs(p[0]), abs(p[1]), abs(p[2]) # Step 2: Calculate m m = px + py + pz - s # Step 3: Determine region if 3.0 px < m: qx, qy, qz = px, py, pz elif 3.0 py < m: qx, qy, qz = py, pz, px elif 3.0 pz < m: qx, qy, qz = pz, px, py else: # Central region return m math.tan(math.pi / 6.0) # Step 4: Calculate k k = max(0.0, min(s, 0.5 (qz - qy + s))) # Step 5 & 6: Distance dx = qx dy = qy - s + k dz = qz - k return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) Computes the signed Euclidean distance to a hexagonal prism. It differs from the triangular prism by utilizing six-fold rotational symmetry to fold the query point into a fundamental sector, reducing the distance calculation to a simpler 2D case. Choose this for hexagonal columns or honeycomb structures. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdhexprism(p, h): """ Computes signed distance to a hexagonal prism aligned with the Z-axis. p: (3,) tuple or list, query point (px, py, pz). h: (2,) tuple or list, [hx, hy]. hx is hexagon size, hy is half-height. """ px, py, pz = p hx, hy = h # 1. Absolute value for octant symmetry qx, qy, qz = abs(px), abs(py), abs(pz) # 2. Reflection into fundamental domain (30-degree sector) kx, ky, kz = -math.cos(math.pi / 6.0), math.sin(math.pi / 6.0), math.tan(math.pi / 6.0) dotval = kx qx + ky qy if dotval < 0: qx = qx - 2.0 dotval kx qy = qy - 2.0 dotval ky # 3. Distance to hexagonal cross-section (line segment distance) clampx = max(-kz hx, min(qx, kz hx)) dxy = math.sqrt(max(qx - clampx, 0.0)2 + max(qy - hx, 0.0)2) if qy > hx: dxy = dxy elif qy < hx: dxy = -dxy # 4. Distance to top/bottom caps dz = qz - hy # 5. Combine using extruded shape SDF pattern return min(max(dxy, dz), 0.0) + math.sqrt(max(dxy, 0.0)2 + max(dz, 0.0)2) Computes the signed distance to an equilateral triangular prism. It exploits the symmetry of the equilateral base to provide a closed-form, branch-free solution using absolute values and max operations, avoiding iterative projection or complex geometric decomposition. Choose this for tent-like structures or triangular beams. Unverified code. It folds the base into a fundamental domain by swapping X and Z if Z > X, then transforms the coordinates to project the point onto the pyramid's faces and edges. The algorithm calculates m2 = h^2 + 0.25. It takes the absolute value of the XZ components of p and swaps them if Z > X. It subtracts 0.5 from X and Z. It calculates q as a transformed vector using p and h. It calculates s as the positive part of -q.x. It calculates t as the clamp of (q.y - 0.5 \cdot p.z) / (m2 + 0.25) to [0, 1]. It calculates a and b as squared distances to edges. It calculates d2 as the minimum of a and b, or 0 if inside. It returns the final signed distance. It calculates q.x as the length of the vector from the rhombus edge minus the radius, multiplied by the sign. It returns the signed distance using the min/max/length formula for box-like shapes. head: Octahedron SDF, sdOctahedron
body: Computes the exact signed distance from a point to a regular octahedron centered at the origin with size parameter s. It is distinguished from its siblings, the Hexagonal Prism and Triangular Prism, by its specific symmetry group and face geometry. Inputs: Point p = (px, py, pz) in 3D space; size s (distance from center to vertex along axes). Outputs: Signed distance d. Negative if inside, positive if outside, zero on surface. Data Structures: p: Input vector. q: Permuted vector used for face-specific calculation. m: Scalar intermediate value. k: Scalar clamp value. Steps: 1. Compute absolute coordinates: p \leftarrow |p|. 2. Compute m = px + py + pz - s. 3. Determine the closest face region by comparing 3pi against m: If 3px < m, set q = (px, py, pz). Else if 3py < m, set q = (py, pz, px). Else if 3pz < m, set q = (pz, px, py). Else (central region), return m \cdot \tan(\pi/6). 4. Calculate k = \text{clamp}(0.5 \cdot (qz - qy + s), 0, s). 5. Compute the distance vector v = (qx, qy - s + k, qz - k). 6. Return d = |v|. Formulas: m = \sum pi - s. k = \max(0, \min(s, 0.5(qz - qy + s))). d = \sqrt{qx^2 + (qy - s + k)^2 + (qz - k)^2}. Parameters: s: Size of the octahedron. Typical values depend on scene scale. Edge Cases: Precision: Near the center, the distance is linear (m \cdot \tan(\pi/6)). Floating point errors in m directly affect the sign. Boundaries: The logic relies on the symmetry of the octahedron. Points exactly on the boundaries between regions (e.g., 3px = m) are handled by the else if chain, which is mathematically continuous but may exhibit slight discontinuities in derivatives due to branch selection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdoctahedron(p, s): """ Computes the signed distance to an octahedron of size s. p: tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) s: float, size parameter """ # Step 1: Absolute coordinates px, py, pz = abs(p[0]), abs(p[1]), abs(p[2]) # Step 2: Calculate m m = px + py + pz - s # Step 3: Determine region if 3.0 px < m: qx, qy, qz = px, py, pz elif 3.0 py < m: qx, qy, qz = py, pz, px elif 3.0 pz < m: qx, qy, qz = pz, px, py else: # Central region return m math.tan(math.pi / 6.0) # Step 4: Calculate k k = max(0.0, min(s, 0.5 (qz - qy + s))) # Step 5 & 6: Distance dx = qx dy = qy - s + k dz = qz - k return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) Computes the signed distance to an equilateral triangle with inscribed radius r. The algorithm sets k = \sqrt{3.0}, transforms px \leftarrow |px| - r and py \leftarrow py + r/k. If px + k \cdot py > 0.0, it reflects the point via p \leftarrow \text{Vec2}(px - k \cdot py, -k \cdot px - py) \cdot 0.5. It then clamps the x-coordinate via px \leftarrow px - \text{clamp}(px, -2.0 \cdot r, 0.0). Finally, it returns -|p| \cdot \text{sign}(py). It is chosen when 2D triangular primitives are needed in SDF scenes. Time Complexity: O(1). Constant number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Exact analytic solution; no iteration required; fast evaluation suitable for real-time ray marching. Limitations: Only applies to regular octahedra centered at the origin. Scaling requires adjusting s. When to use: When rendering octahedral geometry in ray marching or SDF-based rendering. When not to use: For irregular octahedra or when the octahedron is not axis-aligned (requires transformation of p before calling). The function is a standard primitive in the repertoire of signed distance functions for ray marching. name: Hexagonal Prism Signed Distance Function
head: Hexagonal Prism SDF, Signed Hexagonal Prism, sdHexPrism
body: Computes the signed Euclidean distance from a point to a hexagonal prism aligned with the Z-axis, defined by parameters hx (hexagon size) and hy (half-height). It differs from the triangular prism by utilizing six-fold rotational symmetry to fold the query point into a fundamental sector, reducing the distance calculation to a simpler 2D case. provides a direct max-based formulation for a flat-topped orientation without reflection. Inputs: p: Query point (px, py, pz). h: Parameter vector (hx, hy), where hx is the hexagon's characteristic size (radius or apothem depending on convention) and hy is the half-height of the prism. Outputs: d: Signed distance. Positive outside, negative inside. Data Structures: No persistent data structures. The function is stateless. Steps: 1. Absolute Value: Compute q = |p|, i.e., qx = |px|, qy = |py|, qz = |pz|. This exploits octant symmetry. 2. Reflection (Fundamental Domain): Define constant vector k = (-\cos(\pi/6), \sin(\pi/6), \tan(\pi/6)) \approx (-0.8660254, 0.5, 0.57735). Compute dot = kx qx + ky qy. If dot < 0, reflect: qx \leftarrow qx - 2 \cdot dot \cdot kx and qy \leftarrow qy - 2 \cdot dot \cdot ky. This folds the hexagon into a 30° fundamental sector. 3. 2D Hexagon Distance: Calculate the distance to the hexagonal cross-section in the XY plane. Using the reflected point, compute the distance to the top edge segment: d{xy} = \text{length}(\max(qx - \text{clamp}(qx, -kz hx, kz hx), 0), \max(qy - hx, 0)) \cdot \text{sign}(qy - hx). 4. 3D Prism Distance: Combine with the Z-axis distance dz = qz - hy. Return d = \min(\max(d{xy}, dz), 0) + \text{length}(\max(d{xy}, dz, 0)). Alternatively, for a flat-topped orientation, uses d = \max(dz, \max(qx \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + qy \cdot \frac{1}{2}, qy) - hx). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdhexprism(p, h): """ Computes signed distance to a hexagonal prism aligned with the Z-axis. p: (3,) tuple or list, query point (px, py, pz). h: (2,) tuple or list, [hx, hy]. hx is hexagon size, hy is half-height. """ px, py, pz = p hx, hy = h # 1. Absolute value for octant symmetry qx, qy, qz = abs(px), abs(py), abs(pz) # 2. Reflection into fundamental domain (30-degree sector) kx, ky, kz = -math.cos(math.pi / 6.0), math.sin(math.pi / 6.0), math.tan(math.pi / 6.0) dotval = kx qx + ky qy if dotval < 0: qx = qx - 2.0 dotval kx qy = qy - 2.0 dotval ky # 3. Distance to hexagonal cross-section (line segment distance) clampx = max(-kz hx, min(qx, kz hx)) dxy = math.sqrt(max(qx - clampx, 0.0)2 + max(qy - hx, 0.0)2) if qy > hx: dxy = dxy elif qy < hx: dxy = -dxy # 4. Distance to top/bottom caps dz = qz - hy # 5. Combine using extruded shape SDF pattern return min(max(dxy, dz), 0.0) + math.sqrt(max(dxy, 0.0)2 + max(dz, 0.0)2) Note: provides a simpler alternative for flat-topped orientation: d = max(qz - hy, max(qx 0.866025 + qy 0.5, qy) - hx). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Near the edges or vertices, floating-point rounding may cause slight artifacts. The reflection step avoids branch divergence in GPU implementations by using min(dot, 0.0). Boundaries: The formula assumes the prism is centered at the origin. Off-center prisms require translating p by the center offset before computation. Degenerate Input: If hx = 0 or hy = 0, the shape degenerates to a line or disk; the formula still computes a valid distance to the degenerate geometry. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Involves basic arithmetic operations, abs, sqrt, max, min, and trigonometric constants. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary storage or persistent state. Strengths: Exact signed distance, enabling smooth collision detection, ray marching, and CSG operations. The reflection method is robust and orientation-agnostic for the folding step. Limitations: Orientation-dependent. The formula assumes a specific alignment; rotating the prism requires rotating the query point or adjusting the constant vector k. is orientation-specific (flat-topped) but computationally cheaper. The Hexagonal Prism SDF is part of the family of polyhedral primitives used in ray marching and constructive solid geometry (CSG). introduces the reflection/folding technique to exploit hexagonal symmetry, reducing the distance calculation to a fundamental sector. provides a direct max-based formulation optimized for real-time GLSL shaders. Both are widely used in procedural modeling, real-time graphics, and collision detection. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Triangular Prism Signed Distance Function
head: Signed Triangle Prism, Triangular Prism SDF, sdTriPrism
body: Computes the signed distance from a 3D point to an equilateral triangular prism aligned with the Z-axis. It exploits the symmetry of the equilateral base to provide a closed-form, branch-free solution using absolute values and max operations, avoiding iterative projection or complex geometric decomposition. Inputs: p: A 3D point (px, py, pz) stored as a 3-element floating-point array or tuple. h: A 2D parameter vector (hx, hy) stored as a 2-element floating-point array or tuple. hx: Side-related parameter for the equilateral triangle base. hy: Half-height of the prism along the Z-axis. Outputs: d: A single floating-point value representing the signed distance. Positive if outside, negative if inside. Data Structures: None required beyond standard floating-point vectors. Steps: 1. Compute the component-wise absolute value of the input point to exploit symmetry: q = |p|, yielding qx = |px|, qy = |py|, qz = |pz|. 2. Calculate the distance to the triangular cross-section in the XY plane using the rotated coordinates. 3. Compute the Z-distance to the top/bottom faces: dz = qz - hy. 4. Compute the XY-distance to the triangle edges: d{xy} = \max(qx \cdot 0.866025 + qy \cdot 0.5, -qy) - hx \cdot 0.5. 5. Combine the distances: d = \max(dz, d{xy}). Formulas: q = |p| d = \max(qz - hy, \max(qx \cdot 0.866025 + qy \cdot 0.5, -qy) - hx \cdot 0.5) where 0.866025 \approx \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. Parameters: Typical values: Not given in the sources. Constants: 0.866025 \approx \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 0.5 = \frac{1}{2}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The constant 0.866025 is a floating-point approximation; for higher precision, use \cos(\pi/6) or \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. Boundaries: At hx = 0 or hy = 0, the shape degenerates to a triangle or line segment; the formula remains valid but may require epsilon handling for robust ray marching. Sign convention: The formula assumes the prism is centered at the origin with its axis aligned to Z. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdTriPrism(p, h): qx = abs(p[0]) qy = abs(p[1]) qz = abs(p[2]) dz = qz - h[1] dxy = max(qx 0.866025 + qy 0.5, -qy) - h[0] 0.5 return max(dz, dxy) Time Complexity: O(1). Constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Extremely fast evaluation, suitable for real-time ray marching. No branching (using max and abs). Limitations: Only supports equilateral triangles. Orientation is fixed (aligned with Z, specific Y-axis asymmetry per source). The function is a standard primitive in Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching, popularized by shader coding communities. It appears in collections like glsl-sdf-primitives and is used in procedural geometry generation. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Dodecahedron Modulo
head: Dodecahedron Fold, Modulo Dodecahedron SDF
body: The Dodecahedron Modulo method computes the signed distance field (SDF) for a regular dodecahedron by folding 3D space into a single fundamental domain using a sequence of reflections and rotations, then computing the distance to the boundary of that domain. It sets itself apart from sibling polyhedral primitives like the Octahedron or Hexagonal Prism by relying on a complex, multi-step symmetry reduction specific to the dodecahedron's icosahedral symmetry group, rather than simple axial separation or basic planar projections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point p = (px, py, pz) in 3D space. Output: The signed distance d from p to the surface of a unit dodecahedron centered at the origin. Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. The method operates on the input point p in place or via temporary variables. Definitions: \phi = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} (the golden ratio). v1 = \text{normalize}(0, \phi, 1). v2 = \text{normalize}(\phi, 1, 0). \text{dihedral} = \arccos(\text{dot}(v1, v2)). \text{halfDihedral} = \text{dihedral} / 2. \text{faceAngle} = 2\pi / 5. \text{sides} = 5. Pseudocode: The algorithm folds the point p into the fundamental domain of the dodecahedron. The helper functions pR(axis, angle) rotates the point around the specified axis by the given angle, and pModPolar performs a polar modulo operation. Unverified code. Compute distance to the fundamental domain boundary # The fundamental domain for a dodecahedron after this folding is a specific tetrahedral-like region. # The distance is calculated to the faces of this domain. # Convert back to Cartesian r = math.sqrt(x2 + y2) return (r math.cos(angle), r math.sin(angle), 0) # Note: This is a placeholder for the actual 3D operation Parameters: The method assumes a unit dodecahedron. Scaling is achieved by multiplying the output distance by the desired radius. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The sequence of rotations and reflections can accumulate floating-point errors. Using double precision is recommended for high-quality rendering. Boundary Conditions: Points exactly on the symmetry planes may experience slight discontinuities if not handled carefully. Degenerate Input: The method works for all points in 3D space, but performance may vary depending on the complexity of the folding sequence. The Icosahedron Modulo method is a variant that computes the SDF for a regular icosahedron. It uses a similar folding technique but with a different sequence of reflections and rotations specific to the icosahedron's symmetry. It is chosen when an icosahedron is needed instead of a dodecahedron. The key difference is the number of sides in the polar modulo (3 for icosahedron vs 5 for dodecahedron) and the specific rotation angles. Time Complexity: The method involves a fixed number of trigonometric operations (rotations) and basic arithmetic operations. The complexity is O(1) per query point. Memory Complexity: O(1), as no additional data structures are required. Performance: The performance is dominated by the trigonometric functions (sin, cos, atan2). On modern GPUs, these operations are relatively expensive. The method is branch-free, which is beneficial for GPU performance. Strengths: It provides an exact SDF for a dodecahedron, which is useful for ray marching and constructive solid geometry (CSG). Limitations: The complexity of the folding sequence makes it slower than simpler primitives like spheres or boxes. The precision of the result depends on the precision of the trigonometric functions. When to use: Use this method when an exact SDF for a dodecahedron is required, and performance is not the primary concern. When not to use: Avoid this method if a simpler approximation is sufficient, or if performance is critical and a less accurate SDF can be used. name: Cone Signed Distance Function
head: Cone SDF, sdCone, Signed Cone, Signed Capped Cone, Exact Cone SDF, Signed Distance Function (SDF) for Cone
body: The Cone Signed Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of a cone, including its base cap and apex, while correctly determining the sign (positive outside, negative inside). It solves the problem of efficiently rendering or ray-marching conical primitives without polygonization. Unlike the Quadric SDF (First-Order Approximation), which approximates the cone as a smooth quadric surface, the Cone SDF provides the exact analytical distance, preserving sharp edges at the base and apex. It builds on SDF Primitives & Operations by providing a specific primitive definition. The method reduces the 3D distance calculation to a 2D problem by exploiting rotational symmetry around the cone's axis. The point is projected onto a 2D plane containing the axis and the radial distance, and the distance to the 2D line segment (representing the cone's side) and the base cap is computed. Input: Point p \in \mathbb{R}^3, base radius r \in \mathbb{R}^+, height h \in \mathbb{R}^+. Output: Signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. No complex data structures are required. The computation uses standard 2D and 3D vector operations. r: Base radius of the cone. h: Height of the cone. Orientation: The implementations in and align the cone along the Y-axis, with the apex at the origin (0,0,0) and the base centered at y = -h (opening downward). describes a cone along the Z-axis. The pseudocode below follows the Y-axis orientation. 1. 2D Projection: Project the 3D point p into the 2D plane defined by the radial distance and the Y-axis. q = (\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}, py) 2. Define Geometry: Define the 2D coordinates of the apex (tip) and the base edge. \text{tip} = (0, 0) \text{base} = (r, -h) 3. Vector Definitions: k = (r, h) m2 = r^2 + h^2 d1 = q - \text{tip} = q d3 = q - (\text{clamp}(qx, 0, r), -h) 4. Side Distance: Compute the distance from q to the line segment connecting the tip and the base. \text{ba} = \text{base} - \text{tip} = (r, -h) u = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{d1 \cdot \text{ba}}{m2}, 0, 1\right) \text{side\dist} = \| d1 - \text{ba} \cdot u \| 5. Cap Distance: Compute the distance from q to the base cap. \text{cap\dist} = \| d3 \| 6. Unsigned Distance: \text{dist} = \min(\text{side\dist}, \text{cap\dist}) 7. Inside Test: Determine if the point is inside the cone. \text{inside} = (qy \le 0) \land (qy \ge -h) \land (qx \cdot h + qy \cdot r \le 0) 8. Signed Distance: \text{result} = \begin{cases} -\text{dist} & \text{if inside} \\ \text{dist} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdcone(px: float, py: float, pz: float, r: float, h: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a cone with base radius r and height h, aligned with the Y-axis, apex at origin, opening downward. """ # 1. Project to 2D plane (radial distance, y) qx = math.sqrt(px px + pz pz) qy = py # 2. Define geometry in 2D tipx, tipy = 0.0, 0.0 basex, basey = r, -h # 3. Vectors kx, ky = r, h m2 = kx kx + ky ky d1x, d1y = qx - tipx, qy - tipy # Clamp x to [0, r] for base projection clampedqx = max(0.0, min(r, qx)) d3x, d3y = qx - clampedqx, qy - basey # 4. Side distance (distance to segment tip-base) bax, bay = basex - tipx, basey - tipy dotd1ba = d1x bax + d1y bay u = max(0.0, min(1.0, dotd1ba / m2)) sidedist = math.sqrt((d1x - bax u) 2 + (d1y - bay u) 2) # 5. Cap distance capdist = math.sqrt(d3x 2 + d3y 2) # 6. Unsigned distance dist = min(sidedist, capdist) # 7. Inside test inside = (qy <= 0.0) and (qy >= -h) and ((qx h + qy r) <= 0.0) # 8. Return signed distance return -dist if inside else dist Normalization: In alternative formulations using a normalized vector c for the cone slope, the vector c must be normalized. Failure to normalize results in incorrect distances. Precision: When r or h are very small, floating-point precision issues may arise in the dot product and clamp operations. Apex Singularity: At the apex (0,0,0), the gradient is undefined, but the distance is correctly 0. Base Ring: The implementation above handles the base cap as a flat disk. Time Complexity: O(1). The calculation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations, square roots, and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are needed. Strengths: Exact distance calculation allows for precise ray marching and constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations. It is significantly faster than polygon-based distance estimation for simple cones. Limitations: The sharp edges at the base and apex can cause aliasing in ray marching if the step size is not adaptive. The function is not differentiable at the edges and apex. When to use: When rendering or ray-marching conical primitives with high precision is required. When not to use: When a smooth approximation is preferred for aesthetic reasons or to avoid gradient discontinuities, consider the Quadric SDF (First-Order Approximation). The Cone SDF is based on the analytical distance functions popularized by Inigo Quilez in his article "Distance Functions". The specific implementation for the capped cone along the Y-axis is widely used in GLSL-based ray marching engines. The formulation along the Z-axis is also described in geometric ray tracing literature. The method is a staple in the SDF Primitives & Operations toolkit. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, https://github.com/tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, http://graphics.cs.illinois.edu/sites/default/files/zeno.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Segment Signed Distance Function
head: Segment SDF, sdSegment, Distance to line segment
body: The Segment Signed Distance Function computes the Euclidean distance from a query point p to the closest point on a line segment defined by endpoints a and b. It serves as a fundamental primitive for constructing complex shapes in Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering, allowing for the representation of thin structures, edges, and skeletal geometries. Unlike infinite line primitives, this method explicitly handles the segment boundaries, ensuring the distance is zero only within the segment's extent. It is distinct from SDF Primitives in its specific focus on 1D linear geometry, and from Elongation as it defines the base geometry rather than modifying an existing volume. Inputs: p: The query point (vector type, e.g., vec2 or vec3). a: The first endpoint of the segment. b: The second endpoint of the segment. Outputs: d: The Euclidean distance \|p - \text{closest}\|. Data Structures: Vectors a, b, p are stored as standard floating-point arrays (e.g., 2 or 3 components). Intermediate scalars t (or h, u) represent the normalized projection parameter. Steps: 1. Compute the segment vector: ab = b - a. 2. Compute the vector from the start point to the query point: ap = p - a. 3. Compute the squared length of the segment: len\sq = ab \cdot ab. 4. Handle degenerate segments (zero length): If len\sq < \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small value like 10^{-12} or 10^{-8} depending on implementation precision), the segment is a point. Return \|p - a\|. In practice, use a tolerance appropriate for the coordinate scale to avoid division by zero. 5. Compute the projection parameter t (or h): Calculate the dot product: dot = ap \cdot ab. Normalize by squared length: t = dot / len\sq. Clamp t to the range [0, 1] to restrict the closest point to the segment: t = \text{clamp}(t, 0.0, 1.0). uses a slightly different formulation: u = \frac{(p - a) \cdot (b - a)}{\|b - a\|^2}, which is mathematically equivalent. 6. Compute the closest point on the segment: closest = a + ab \cdot t. computes this as begin + u \cdot (begin - end), noting that begin - end = -(end - begin). If a=begin and b=end, then ab = end - begin, so a + u(ab) = begin + u(end - begin). The source uses begin - end in the numerator dot product but also in the final addition, effectively calculating u relative to the vector begin-end. Let's align with the standard [S1/S3] approach for clarity: closest = a + t(b-a). 7. Return the distance: d = \|p - closest\|. notes returning the squared distance in one variant, but the standard SDF returns the Euclidean distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdSegment(p, a, b): """ Computes the Euclidean distance from point p to the segment [a, b]. p, a, b are vectors of the same dimension (2D or 3D). """ # 1. Vector from a to b ab = b - a # 2. Vector from a to p ap = p - a # 3. Squared length of the segment lensq = dot(ab, ab) # 4. Handle degenerate segment (point) # Use a small epsilon for floating point comparison epsilon = 1e-12 if lensq < epsilon: return length(ap) # 5. Project p onto the line, clamped to [0, 1] # t represents the fraction of the segment length t = dot(ap, ab) / lensq t = clamp(t, 0.0, 1.0) # 6. Find the closest point on the segment closest = a + ab t # 7. Return the Euclidean distance return length(p - closest) Parameters: \epsilon: Epsilon for degenerate check. Common values are 10^{-12} or 10^{-8}. p, a, b: Coordinates in the same space (2D or 3D). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Segments: If a = b, the denominator len\sq becomes zero. This must be checked explicitly to avoid division by zero. Precision: When p is very close to the segment, floating-point errors in the dot product and division can cause slight inaccuracies. Using clamp ensures the result remains physically valid (distance \ge 0). Dimensionality: The algorithm works for any dimension N as long as vector arithmetic is supported. Computes the Euclidean distance from a point p to a line segment defined by endpoints l0 and l1. This variant explicitly details the branch logic for determining which endpoint is closer when the projection falls outside the segment, rather than relying on a generic clamp function. It is useful when implementing custom clamping logic or optimizing for specific hardware branches. Choose this when you need explicit control over the "closer to start" vs "closer to end" conditions. Checks if a point Q lies on the line segment between Pi and Pj using distance comparison with an epsilon tolerance. It calculates distances dis1 (Pi to Q), dis2 (Pj to Q), and dis3 (Pi to Pj). If dis3 + \epsilon < dis1 + dis2, it returns false; otherwise true. This is a geometric predicate rather than a distance function, used for validation or collision detection. Choose this when you need to verify collinearity and bounds rather than compute a distance value. Computes the closest point on a line segment [v0, v1] to a query point p. The result is guaranteed to lie on the closed segment by clamping the parameter t to [0, 1]. This is a helper function often used in conjunction with the SDF to retrieve the geometric closest point for shading or normal calculation. Choose this when the closest point location is needed, not just the distance. Time Complexity: O(1) constant time. It involves a fixed number of vector subtractions, dot products, and a square root. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. No large data structures are required. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time ray marching in fragment shaders or CPU-based path tracing. Strengths: Simple implementation, numerically stable with proper epsilon handling, works in any dimension. Limitations: Does not handle infinite lines (use SDF Domain Manipulation Operators for line extensions) or thick segments (use Elongation or capsules). When to use: For rendering thin wires, edges, or skeletal structures in SDF scenes. When not to use: For infinite lines or when the segment thickness is significant. The Segment SDF is a standard primitive in the field of Signed Distance Fields, popularized by Inigo Quilez's articles on distance functions. It is widely used in ray marching techniques for rendering complex geometries composed of simple primitives. The mathematical formulation relies on projecting a point onto a line segment and clamping the parameter to the segment's bounds. Implementations can be found in various graphics libraries and educational repositories.
