name: Uniform Scaling of SDFs
head: Uniform Scaling of Signed Distance Functions, SDF Scaling, Scaling SDFs, SDF Scale
body: Uniform scaling of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) is a technique to transform an implicit surface by a uniform factor while preserving the correctness of the distance value for ray marching. It solves the problem that scaling is not a rigid body transformation and distorts distances; without correction, the ray marching algorithm may overestimate the distance to the surface, causing the object to disappear. Unlike Non-Uniform Scaling of SDFs, which requires conservative bounds to avoid overestimation, uniform scaling allows for an exact compensation of distance distortion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base SDF function f(p), a query point p in world space, and a uniform scaling factor s (where s > 0). Output: The signed distance from p to the scaled surface. Data Structures: The scaling factor s is typically stored as a scalar floating-point value (e.g., f32) associated with the primitive. Steps: 1. Inverse Transform Point: Divide the query point p by the scaling factor s. This compresses the evaluation space, effectively mapping the world point into the local space of the unscaled primitive. p' = \frac{p}{s} If the primitive has a center offset o, the operation is (p - o) / s. 2. Evaluate Base SDF: Query the base SDF function with the transformed point p' to get the raw distance d'. d' = f(p') 3. Rescale Distance: Multiply the returned distance d' by the scaling factor s to compensate for the distortion caused by the non-rigid scaling. d = d' \times s Formula: The general formula for a uniformly scaled SDF is: d{scaled}(p) = f\left(\frac{p}{s}\right) \times s For a specific primitive like a sphere with center o and base radius r, the scaled SDF is: d{sphere}(p) = \left( \left\| \frac{p - o}{s} \right\| - r \right) \times s where \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm. Parameters: s: The uniform scaling factor. Values s > 1 enlarge the surface footprint; values s < 1 shrink it. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Overestimation: If the distance is overestimated (e.g., scaling down without correction: sphereSDF(samplePoint / 0.5)), the ray marching algorithm may step past the surface, causing the object to disappear completely. Underestimation: If the distance is underestimated (e.g., using no correction or a smaller correction factor), the ray marching algorithm still works but requires more iterations, resulting in slower performance. Sign Preservation: The sign of the distance is preserved regardless of the scaling correction factor, so the object remains visible even with incorrect distance values, but the geometric accuracy is lost. Zero Scaling: s=0 is undefined and should be guarded against. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scalesdfuniform(sdffunc, point, scalefactor): """ Computes the signed distance to a uniformly scaled SDF. Args: sdffunc: A function that takes a point and returns the signed distance. point: The query point in world space (vector3). scalefactor: The uniform scaling factor (scalar > 0). Returns: The signed distance from point to the scaled surface. """ if scalefactor == 0: raise ValueError("Scaling factor must be non-zero.") # Step 1: Inverse transform point # If the base SDF assumes a center at origin, simple division. # If the base SDF has an offset 'center', use (point - center) / scalefactor scaledpoint = point / scalefactor # Step 2: Evaluate base SDF rawdistance = sdffunc(scaledpoint) # Step 3: Rescale distance finaldistance = rawdistance scalefactor return finaldistance Non-uniform scaling of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) is a technique to transform an SDF primitive by scaling its axes by different factors, ensuring the ray marching algorithm does not overestimate the distance to the surface. Unlike uniform scaling, which allows for exact distance compensation, non-uniform scaling distorts distances anisotropically; this method uses the minimum scaling factor as a conservative correction multiplier to guarantee distance underestimation, which is safe for ray marching convergence. Time Complexity: O(1) relative to the scaling operation itself, as it involves one division, one SDF evaluation, and one multiplication. The complexity is dominated by the base SDF evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring storage for the scalar scaling factor. Strengths: Exact distance preservation ensures optimal ray marching step sizes, leading to fast convergence and accurate rendering. Limitations: Only applicable to uniform scaling. Non-uniform scaling requires different techniques. When to use: When an SDF primitive needs to be resized uniformly in world space. When not to use: When non-uniform scaling is required, or when the scaling factor is zero or negative (negative scaling flips normals and may require additional handling depending on the renderer). Uniform scaling of SDFs is a fundamental technique in ray marching for implicit surfaces. It was popularized in the context of real-time ray marching shaders, notably by Jamie Wong. The method relies on the mathematical property that scaling a space by s and then measuring distance requires multiplying the result by s to maintain the metric properties of the signed distance field. It is widely used in procedural geometry generation and real-time rendering engines. name: Non-Uniform Scaling of SDFs
head: Anisotropic SDF Scaling, Non-Uniform Scaling of Signed Distance Functions
body: Non-uniform scaling of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) is a technique to transform an SDF primitive by scaling its axes by different factors, ensuring the ray marching algorithm does not overestimate the distance to the surface. Unlike uniform scaling, which allows for exact distance compensation, non-uniform scaling distorts distances anisotropically; this method uses the minimum scaling factor as a conservative correction multiplier to guarantee distance underestimation, which is safe for ray marching convergence. Inputs: samplePoint: The 3D coordinate in world space where the SDF is being evaluated. s: A 3D vector (sx, sy, sz) representing the non-uniform scaling factors for the X, Y, and Z axes. baseSDF: A function that evaluates the unscaled SDF. Outputs: dist: The corrected signed distance value. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Transform the sample point: Divide the samplePoint by the scaling vector s. This maps the world-space point into the local space of the unscaled primitive. p{local} = \frac{samplePoint}{s} = \left( \frac{x}{sx}, \frac{y}{sy}, \frac{z}{sz} \right) 2. Evaluate the base SDF: Compute the distance in the local space using the unscaled primitive definition. d{local} = baseSDF(p{local}) 3. Apply correction factor: Multiply the local distance by the minimum of the scaling factors. dist = d{local} \times \min(sx, sy, sz) Formula: For a general SDF someSDF scaled by vector s = (sx, sy, sz), the transformed SDF S{scaled}(x, y, z) is: S{scaled}(x, y, z) = someSDF\left(\frac{x}{sx}, \frac{y}{sy}, \frac{z}{sz}\right) \times \min(sx, sy, sz) Example Derivation (Unit Sphere): Consider a unit sphere scaled to half its size along the X-axis (sx=0.5, sy=1, sz=1). The unscaled unit sphere SDF is \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} - 1. Applying the non-uniform scaling formula: 1. Transform point: (\frac{x}{0.5}, \frac{y}{1}, \frac{z}{1}) = (2x, y, z). 2. Evaluate base SDF: \sqrt{(2x)^2 + y^2 + z^2} - 1. 3. Multiply by min scaling factor: \min(0.5, 1, 1) = 0.5. Resulting corrected SDF: sphereSDF(x, y, z) = 0.5 \times \left( \sqrt{(2x)^2 + y^2 + z^2} - 1 \right) Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Overestimation Risk: Non-uniform scaling cannot exactly compensate for distance distortion because the correction factor depends on the location of the closest point on the surface relative to the sampling point, which is unknown during evaluation. Using the minimum scaling factor is a safe approximation that ensures the returned distance is never greater than the true distance (underestimation), preventing ray marching from skipping the surface. Directional Variance: The overestimation factor varies depending on where the sampling point and the closest surface point are located. For the half-scaled sphere example, evaluating at (2, 0, 0) with the naive unscaled formula yields 3, while the true distance is 1.5. Zero/Negative Scaling: Scaling factors must be positive. Zero or negative scaling breaks the geometric interpretation of the distance field and the validity of the minimum factor heuristic. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nonuniformscaledsdf(samplepoint, scalingfactors, basesdf): """ Evaluates an SDF with non-uniform scaling. Args: samplepoint: tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) scalingfactors: tuple or list of 3 floats (sx, sy, sz) basesdf: function that takes (x, y, z) and returns float distance Returns: float: The corrected signed distance """ sx, sy, sz = scalingfactors # Step 1: Transform sample point to local space localx = samplepoint[0] / sx localy = samplepoint[1] / sy localz = samplepoint[2] / sz # Step 2: Evaluate base SDF in local space localdist = basesdf(localx, localy, localz) # Step 3: Multiply by the minimum scaling factor minscale = min(sx, sy, sz) correcteddist = localdist minscale return correcteddist This technique is described in the context of ray marching and Signed Distance Functions, specifically addressing the limitations of applying non-rigid transformations to distance fields. name: Distance to Natural Quadrics
head: Natural Quadrics SDF, SDF for Natural Quadrics
body: Distance to Natural Quadrics provides closed-form Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for standard solid modeling primitives: planes, spheres, cylinders, cones, and tori. It solves the problem of efficiently querying the Euclidean distance from a query point to these geometric surfaces, which is the core operation in ray marching (sphere tracing). Unlike constructive methods that combine simpler shapes, this method provides direct analytical solutions for complex primitives like tori and cones, which are essential for modeling organic or structural elements without approximation errors. It is distinct from Constructive SDF Modeling because it handles primitives that cannot be easily decomposed into unions/intersections of boxes or spheres, and from Distance to Superquadrics because it operates in the standard Euclidean metric rather than Lp norms. Inputs: Query point p = (px, py, pz) in 3D space. Primitive-specific parameters (e.g., radius, height, normal). Outputs: Scalar signed distance d. d < 0: point is inside the primitive. d > 0: point is outside the primitive. d = 0: point is on the surface. Data Structures: Vectors are treated as standard 3D Cartesian coordinates. Parameters are typically stored as floats or vectors (e.g., vec2 for torus radii). Formulas and Steps: 1. Plane: Defined by a unit normal vector n and a point p0 on the plane. d(p) = n \cdot (p - p0) Note: The source notation n \times (p - p0) in is interpreted as the dot product, as the cross product yields a vector, not a scalar distance. 2. Sphere: Defined by center c and radius r. d(p) = \|p - c\| - r For a unit sphere at the origin (c=0, r=1): d(p) = \|p\| - 1 3. Cylinder: The source describes a unit-radius cylinder centered about the z-axis, defined by projecting into the xy-plane. However, and provide implementations for capped cylinders or axis-aligned variants. Infinite Cylinder (z-axis, radius r): d(p) = \sqrt{px^2 + py^2} - r (Derived from projecting to the plane perpendicular to the axis). Capped Cylinder (y-axis, radius r, half-height h): Let d{radial} = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - r and d{axial} = |py| - h. d = \min(\max(d{radial}, d{axial}), 0) + \max(\sqrt{\max(d{radial}, 0)^2 + \max(d{axial}, 0)^2}, 0) Note: uses a specific formula involving maxvalues logic, but the standard closed-form for a capped cylinder aligned with Y is: d = \sqrt{\max(d{radial}, 0)^2 + \max(d{axial}, 0)^2} + \min(\max(d{radial}, d{axial}), 0) This formula returns the distance to the side, cap, or corner, whichever is nearest. 4. Cone: Defined by apex, axis, and divergence angle \theta (or sin/cos of the angle). Let the cone axis be aligned with the z-axis, apex at origin, and opening angle \theta. Let q = (\cos \theta, -\sin \theta) in the xz-plane profile. Let w = (\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}, py). The distance is calculated by projecting w onto the cone surface line defined by q: d(p) = \text{dist}{2D}(w, \text{cone profile}) Specifically, using the GLSL implementation from: q{scaled} = h \cdot \left(\frac{cx}{cy}, -1\right) a = w - q{scaled} \cdot \text{clamp}\left(\frac{w \cdot q{scaled}}{q{scaled} \cdot q{scaled}}, 0, 1\right) b = w - q{scaled} \cdot \left(\text{clamp}\left(\frac{wx}{q{scaled, x}}, 0, 1\right), 1\right) d = \sqrt{\min(\|a\|^2, \|b\|^2)} \cdot \text{sign}(s) Where s determines the inside/outside based on the cone's orientation. 5. Torus: Defined by major radius R (distance from center of tube to center of torus) and minor radius r (radius of the tube). Let q = (\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R, py). d(p) = \|q\| - r Typical values: R=0.8, r=0.3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdfplane(p, n, p0): """ Signed distance to a plane. p: query point (x, y, z) n: unit normal vector (nx, ny, nz) p0: point on the plane (x0, y0, z0) """ # Vector from p0 to p dx = p[0] - p0[0] dy = p[1] - p0[1] dz = p[2] - p0[2] # Dot product n. (p - p0) return n[0]dx + n[1]dy + n[2]dz def sdfsphere(p, c, r): """ Signed distance to a sphere. p: query point (x, y, z) c: center (cx, cy, cz) r: radius """ dx = p[0] - c[0] dy = p[1] - c[1] dz = p[2] - c[2] return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) - r def sdfcylindercapped(p, r, h): """ Signed distance to a capped cylinder aligned with Y-axis. p: query point (x, y, z) r: radius h: half-height """ # Distance to the infinite cylinder surface (radial) # Cylinder axis is Y, so we look at XZ plane radialdist = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) - r # Distance to the caps (axial) axialdist = abs(p[1]) - h # Combine radial and axial distances # If inside bounds in one dimension, distance is determined by the other # If outside bounds in both, distance is Euclidean distance to the corner/edge drad = max(radialdist, 0.0) dax = max(axialdist, 0.0) return math.sqrt(drad2 + dax2) + min(max(radialdist, axialdist), 0.0) def sdftorus(p, R, r): """ Signed distance to a torus centered at origin, spun about Z-axis. p: query point (x, y, z) R: major radius (t[0]) r: minor radius (t[1]) """ # Project to XZ plane to get distance from the major circle center line # qx is distance from the ring center in XZ plane # qy is the Y coordinate qx = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) - R qy = p[1] return math.sqrt(qx2 + qy2) - r def sdfcone(p, h, sintheta, costheta): """ Signed distance to a cone aligned with Y-axis, apex at origin. p: query point (x, y, z) h: height of the cone (used to scale the profile) sintheta: sin of the half-angle at the apex costheta: cos of the half-angle at the apex """ # Profile vector q in the radial-vertical plane (r, y) # Based on GLSL implementation adapted for Y-axis alignment # q represents the point at the base of the cone in the 2D profile # If the cone goes from y=0 to y=h, and radius at base is Rbase # Then tan(theta) = Rbase / h. # The source uses c (cos/sin) and h. # Let's use the standard 2D cone distance logic from # w is the point in the radial-vertical plane radial = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) y = p[1] w = (radial, y) # q is the vector to the base corner in the profile # If apex is at 0,0 and height is h, base radius is h tan(theta) # tan(theta) = sin/cos tantheta = sintheta / costheta baseradius = h tantheta # q vector in (radial, y) space: (baseradius, h) # However, defines q differently. Let's stick to the robust 2D projection method. # Vector from apex to base corner qvec = (baseradius, h) # Project w onto qvec dotwq = w[0]qvec[0] + w[1]qvec[1] dotqq = qvec[0]2 + qvec[1]2 # Clamp t to [0, 1] to stay on the segment t = dotwq / dotqq if t < 0.0: t = 0.0 if t > 1.0: t = 1.0 # Closest point on the segment closest = (qvec[0]t, qvec[1]t) # Distance to the segment distsq = (w[0]-closest[0])2 + (w[1]-closest[1])2 # Determine sign (inside/outside) # The cone surface normal points outward. # A simple check: if the point is "below" the cone surface in the profile # Cross product in 2D: w x qvec cross = w[0]qvec[1] - w[1]qvec[0] # If cross > 0, it's on one side, else the other. # Sign depends on orientation. Assuming standard cone opening up. sign = 1.0 if cross > 0 else -1.0 return math.sqrt(distsq) sign Generalizes natural quadrics using Lp norms to create shapes with rounded, square, or pinched cross-sections. Choose this when you need smoothable variations of primitives (e.g., squaring a cylinder) rather than exact Euclidean distances. Computes the exact Euclidean distance for a finite cylinder defined by two endpoints and a radius. Choose this for pipes and limbs where the axis is arbitrary in 3D space, whereas Natural Quadrics typically assumes axis-aligned orientations. Computes the exact Euclidean distance for a torus. While included in Natural Quadrics, this entry focuses specifically on the torus topology and its specific algebraic form, distinguishing it from other ring-like or looped primitives. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. Each SDF involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and square roots. Memory Complexity: O(1) per primitive. Only parameters (radius, height, etc.) need to be stored. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time ray marching on GPUs. The torus and capped cylinder require square roots, which are slightly more expensive than simple additions but negligible compared to iterative methods. Strengths: Exact Euclidean distance ensures stable and efficient ray marching (no overshooting or jittering). Closed-form solutions avoid numerical instability associated with iterative solvers. Limitations: Limited to specific geometric shapes. Cannot represent arbitrary meshes or complex organic shapes without CSG combination. Axis-aligned assumptions in some formulas (e.g., cylinder) require transformation of the query point p if the primitive is rotated or translated. When to use: When rendering scenes composed of standard geometric primitives (spheres, cylinders, cones, tori) and exact distance bounds are required for convergence. When not to use: When the primitive is not a natural quadric (use Distance to Superquadrics or mesh SDFs). When the primitive is arbitrarily oriented and transforming the point is too costly (consider pre-computing transformations or using Cylinder Signed Distance Function with endpoint vectors). Signed Distance Functions for natural quadrics were formalized in the context of "Sphere Tracing," a geometric method for antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces. The appendix of derives these distances to aid in the implementation of sphere tracing, noting that while they may be less efficient than closed-form solutions for simple primitives like boxes (which can be handled by min/max operations), they are essential for higher-order constructions like blends and deformations. The torus SDF is a classic result, derived from the product of two circles. The cone SDF derivation involves trigonometric projections of the query point onto the cone's profile line. These methods are foundational in procedural geometry and ray marching tutorials. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) (PDF) Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray..., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2792108SphereTracingAGeometricMethodfortheAntialiasedRayTracingofImplicitSurfaces, fetched 2026-10-27 Ray Marching with Signed Distance Fields - Scribd, https://www.scribd.com/document/831412915/1-Ray-Marching-and-Signed-Distance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Introduction to Raymarching Distance Functions, https://observablehq.com/@gre/introduction-to-raymarching-distance-functions, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Distance to Superquadrics
head: Superellipsoid distance, Superellipsoids, Superquadric Distance via p-norm, Supertori, pq-norm distance
body: Distance to Superquadrics generalizes standard natural quadrics (spheres, cylinders, cones) and tori into superquadrics and supertori by replacing the Euclidean L2 norm with the Lp (or L{pq}) norm. This method allows for the creation of shapes with rounded, square, or pinched cross-sections by varying the exponent parameter p. It is distinct from Distance to Natural Quadrics because it operates in a non-Euclidean metric space, requiring a specific conversion to Euclidean distances to ensure consistent ray marching behavior and blending with other primitives. Inputs: Point p = (x, y, z) in 3D space. Shape exponent p (scalar, p > 0). Radius r (scalar, defining the scale of the superellipsoid). Optional: Exponents p, q for asymmetric superquadrics (supertori or generalized ellipsoids). Outputs: Signed distance d(p) in Euclidean space. Data Structures: No persistent data structures required. The function is stateless and computes the distance analytically per query. Formulas: The core distance metric is the Lp norm. In 2D, the Lp norm of a vector (x, y) is defined as: ||(x, y)||p = (|x|^p + |y|^p)^{1/p} In 3D, for a superellipsoid centered at the origin, the implicit surface is defined by: (|x|^p + |y|^p + |z|^p)^{1/p} = r The raw distance in the Lp metric, denoted dp(p), is calculated as: dp(p) = (|x|^p + |y|^p + |z|^p)^{1/p} - r Euclidean Conversion: Because ray marching requires a unifying Euclidean metric space to compare distances between different primitives and to ensure the step size is safe (i.e., the ray does not pass through the surface), the Lp distance must be converted to an equivalent Euclidean distance. Let re be the radius of the largest Euclidean sphere inscribed within the Lp-norm superellipsoid of radius r (in the Lp metric). The conversion factor depends on p: re = \begin{cases} r \cdot \frac{3^{1/p}}{\sqrt{3}} & \text{if } p < 2 \\ r & \text{if } p \ge 2 \end{cases} The final Euclidean signed distance d{eucl}(p) is scaled by the ratio of the inscribed radius to the nominal radius: d{eucl}(p) = dp(p) \cdot \frac{re}{r} Substituting re/r: d{eucl}(p) = \begin{cases} \left( (|x|^p + |y|^p + |z|^p)^{1/p} - r \right) \cdot \frac{3^{1/p}}{\sqrt{3}} & \text{if } p < 2 \\ (|x|^p + |y|^p + |z|^p)^{1/p} - r & \text{if } p \ge 2 \end{cases} Parameters: p: Controls the shape. p = 2: Euclidean sphere (round). p = 1: Octahedron (diamond in 2D). p \to \infty: Cube (square in 2D, chessboard metric). 0 < p < 1: Pinched or star-shaped variations. r: Base radius. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def distancetosuperquadricsdf(x, y, z, p, r): """Computes the Euclidean signed distance to a superellipsoid.""" if p <= 0: return float('inf') sump = abs(x)p + abs(y)p + abs(z)p lpnorm = sump (1.0 / p) dlp = lpnorm - r if p < 2.0: factor = (3.0 (1.0 / p)) / math.sqrt(3.0) else: factor = 1.0 return dlp factor def raymarchsuperquadric(ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz, p, r, maxsteps=1000, maxdist=100.0, tol=1e-4): """Standard sphere tracing loop using the superquadric SDF.""" t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return float('inf') px = ox + t dx py = oy + t dy pz = oz + t dz d = distancetosuperquadricsdf(px, py, pz, p, r) if d < tol: return t t += d return float('inf') Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Metric Unification: Using Lp distances directly for blending or comparison with other primitives (like spheres or cylinders) is invalid because they exist in different metric spaces. The Euclidean conversion is mandatory for correct visual results in composite scenes. Precision: For very large p, |x|^p can overflow or underflow. Standard floating-point handling applies. Degenerate Input: p=0 is undefined. p < 0 produces non-convex, pinched shapes that may require specialized handling not covered by the standard convex superellipsoid definition. A generalization of the torus using Lp norms for both the major and minor circles. It follows the same conversion principles as superellipsoids but applies the norm to the distance evaluation of the torus's cross-section. Uses different exponents p and q for different axes (e.g., |x|^p + |y|^q + |z|^p). This allows for asymmetric shapes. The Euclidean conversion factor must be derived based on the specific p, q values, typically involving the maximum inscribed sphere in the asymmetric metric. Calculates the radius of the largest Euclidean sphere re inscribed within a pq-norm superellipsoid of radius rs in the pq-norm metric. The formula is re = rs \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt[p]{3} + \sqrt[q]{3}} if p or q < 2, otherwise re = rs \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Requires O(1) arithmetic operations (powers, roots, absolute values). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Provides a continuous family of shapes from spheres to cubes to pinched forms with a single parameter. Efficient for ray marching when the Euclidean conversion is applied. Limitations: The gradient is not always smooth at p=1 or p \to \infty boundaries in the raw metric, though the Euclidean conversion helps maintain continuity in the signed distance field. The conversion factor is an approximation based on the inscribed sphere; it ensures safety (no tunneling) but may result in slightly larger step sizes than strictly necessary for non-spherical shapes, potentially slowing convergence slightly compared to exact analytical normals for simple primitives. When to use: When a shape with adjustable "squareness" or "pinchedness" is needed, or when blending between different geometric primitives in a unified SDF framework. Superquadrics were introduced by Alan Barr in 1981. The concept arises from generalizing the distance metrics used in basic primitive definitions. While natural quadrics rely on the Euclidean L2 norm, superquadrics utilize the Lp norm to create a broader class of implicit surfaces. This method is integral to the Sphere Tracing algorithm, as it allows the rendering of complex, organic, or mechanical shapes that are not representable by simple quadratic equations. The requirement for Euclidean conversion was highlighted to ensure that the geometric method of sphere tracing remains valid across different metric spaces. name: Cylinder Signed Distance Function
head: Capped Cylinder SDF, Cylinder SDF, Finite Cylinder SDF, Signed Capped Cylinder, Signed Cylinder, Signed Distance Function (SDF) for Cylinder, sdCappedCylinder, sdCylinder
body: The Cylinder Signed Distance Function (SDF) computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to a finite cylinder defined by two endpoints and a radius. Unlike infinite cylinder variants, the capped version correctly handles the flat end caps and their corners, returning negative values inside the volume and positive values outside. It is distinct from the Torus Signed Distance Function (which models a ring) and Distance to Superquadrics (which offers smoothable variations but not exact Euclidean distance for standard primitives). Inputs: p: Query point (Vector3). c1, c2: Cylinder endpoints (Vector3). r: Cylinder radius (scalar). Outputs: d: Signed distance (scalar). Negative if inside, positive if outside, zero on surface. Data Structures: Standard 3D vector (x, y, z) and scalar types. No special bit-packing required for the core function. Steps: 1. Compute Axis Geometry: Calculate the axis direction vector dir = c2 - c1 and its squared length len\sq = dir \cdot dir. 2. Handle Degeneracy: If len\sq < \epsilon (degenerate cylinder), return length(p - c1) - r. 3. Project Point: Compute the unclamped projection parameter t = \frac{(p - c1) \cdot dir}{len\sq}. 4. Compute Closest Point: Calculate the closest point on the finite axis segment: closest = c1 + dir \cdot clamp(t, 0.0, 1.0). 5. Calculate Radial Distance: Compute the vector from the closest axis point to the query point: diff = p - closest. The radial distance is side\dist = length(diff) - r. 6. Determine Signed Distance: Apply the piecewise logic based on t and side\dist, where h = length(dir) is the cylinder height: If 0 \le t \le 1: return side\dist \ge 0 \ ? \ side\dist \: \ min(side\dist, min(h \cdot t, h \cdot (1 - t))). If t > 1: return side\dist \ge 0 \ ? \ \sqrt{side\dist^2 + h^2(t-1)^2} \: \ h(t-1). If t < 0: return side\dist \ge 0 \ ? \ \sqrt{side\dist^2 + h^2(-t)^2} \: \ h(-t). Axis-Aligned Simplification: For a cylinder aligned with the Y-axis (or Z-axis) with radius r and half-height h, the distance can be computed using a 2D projection trick structurally identical to the box SDF: 1. q = (length(p{xz}) - r, |py| - h). 2. d = max(q, 0.0). 3. inside = min(max(qx, qy), 0.0). 4. outside = length(d). 5. Return outside + inside. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdcappedcylinder(p, c1, c2, r): """ Computes signed distance to a capped cylinder. p: query point (Vec3) c1, c2: endpoints (Vec3) r: radius (float) """ axis = c2 - c1 lensq = dot(axis, axis) # Handle degenerate case (point cylinder) if lensq < 1e-12: return length(p - c1) - r # Project p onto axis pa = p - c1 t = dot(pa, axis) / lensq # Closest point on the segment tclamped = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) closest = c1 + axis tclamped # Radial distance diff = p - closest sidedist = length(diff) - r h = length(axis) # Piecewise signed distance logic if 0.0 <= t <= 1.0: if sidedist >= 0.0: return sidedist else: return min(sidedist, min(h t, h (1.0 - t))) elif t > 1.0: if sidedist >= 0.0: return sqrt(sidedist2 + h2 (t - 1.0)2) else: return h (t - 1.0) else: # t < 0.0 if sidedist >= 0.0: return sqrt(sidedist2 + h2 (-t)2) else: return h (-t) Computes the signed distance to a ring or annulus with radius r and thickness th. The formula projects the query point into 2D, measures the radial deviation from r, and subtracts half the thickness: |\|p\| - r| - th \cdot 0.5. Implementation: return (p.length() - r).abs() - th 0.5. Calculates the distance to the global offset surface of a cubic Bézier space curve. The method defines the curve parametrically as p(u) and finds the closest point p(u) to the query point x by solving the orthogonality condition (x - p(u)) \cdot p'(u) = 0. This condition converts into a degree-five 1D Bézier curve, which is solved efficiently using standard root-finding techniques. Time and Memory Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) memory per query point. The computation involves a constant number of vector operations, dot products, and square roots. Measured Performance: Runs efficiently on modern GPUs and CPUs; the axis-aligned 2D projection variant is slightly faster due to avoiding branch-heavy logic and using simpler arithmetic. Strengths and Limitations: Provides exact Euclidean distance, making it robust for ray marching, collision detection, and CSG operations. The arbitrary-axis implementation requires careful handling of degenerate inputs (zero-length cylinders) and floating-point precision near the caps. It is more expensive than infinite cylinder SDFs but necessary for finite geometry. When to Use: Use when exact distance to a finite, arbitrarily oriented cylinder is required for rendering or physics. Avoid when infinite extent is sufficient or when approximate distance fields are acceptable for performance. Originated as part of the standard set of signed distance functions for natural quadrics used in implicit surface rendering and ray marching. Popularized by GLSL shader libraries and real-time rendering pipelines for modeling pipes, limbs, and structural elements. The mathematical formulation for arbitrary-axis cylinders relies on projecting query points onto the central segment and handling cap corners via Pythagorean distance. The axis-aligned 2D projection trick generalizes the box SDF to cylindrical coordinates. It is widely used in distance-field ray marching for antialiased implicit surface rendering. name: Torus Signed Distance Function
head: Link SDF, Link Shape SDF, Signed Torus, sdTorus
body: Computes the signed distance from a query point to the surface of a torus centered at the origin and aligned with the Y-axis. It provides the primitive distance query required for distance-field ray marching and constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations. It is distinguished from sibling primitives like the Cylinder Signed Distance Function by its closed-loop topology and from Distance to Superquadrics by its specific algebraic form for a torus. Inputs: p = (px, py, pz): Query point in 3D space. R: Major radius (distance from the torus center to the tube centerline). r: Minor radius (radius of the tube cross-section). Outputs: d: Signed distance. Positive outside the torus, negative inside, zero on the surface. Data Structures: None required; scalar computation. Steps: 1. Compute the radial distance of the point's projection onto the XZ plane from the origin: \rho = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}. 2. Construct a 2D vector q = (qx, qy) representing the offset from the torus centerline: qx = \rho - R, qy = py. 3. Compute the Euclidean distance from q to the origin and subtract the minor radius: d = \sqrt{qx^2 + qy^2} - r. Formula: d = \sqrt{(\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R)^2 + py^2} - r Parameters: R > 0: Major radius. r > 0: Minor radius. Constraint: r < R yields a standard ring torus; r = R yields a horn torus; r > R yields a self-intersecting spindle torus. Edge Cases: Origin: If p=(0,0,0), \rho=0, q=(-R, 0), d = R - r. Precision: Near the surface or when \rho \approx R, standard floating-point precision is sufficient. Self-intersection: For spindle tori (r > R), the SDF remains mathematically valid but defines a complex nested inside region. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdtorus(p: tuple, R: float, r: float) -> float: """ Computes signed distance to a torus centered at origin, aligned with Y-axis. p: (px, py, pz) R: Major radius r: Minor radius """ px, py, pz = p # Radial distance in the XZ plane rho = (px2 + pz2)0.5 # 2D vector from the torus centerline to the point qx = rho - R qy = py # Signed distance: distance to centerline minus tube radius return (qx2 + qy2)0.5 - r A variation that includes a length parameter for non-circular cross-sections or deformed tori, sometimes referred to as a link shape. Use when modeling chain links or specific mechanical parts. Link SDF. A torus where r > R. The SDF formula remains the same, but the topology changes to a self-intersecting shape. Use for specific organic or abstract shapes. Spindle Torus. Time Complexity: O(1). Requires two square roots and basic arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Exact analytic solution; no iterative approximation; robust for ray marching. Limitations: Only applies to perfect tori. Cannot model tori with varying cross-sections or twists without deformation. When to use: When rendering or ray marching perfect toroidal shapes. When not to use: For complex toroidal structures with varying thickness or non-circular cross-sections. The SDF for a torus is a standard primitive in signed distance function libraries, popularized by tools like the glsl-sdf-primitives repository. It is a fundamental building block for CSG operations involving toroidal shapes. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Pyroclastic Sphere Primitive
body: The Pyroclastic Sphere Primitive is a signed distance field (SDF) primitive that creates organic, turbulent shapes suitable for pyroclastic or fluid-like visual effects by displacing a base sphere's distance function with procedural noise. It distinguishes itself from static SDF primitives by combining a low-frequency sinusoidal "breathing" modulation with high-frequency fractal Brownian motion (fBM) and sinusoidal products to generate complex, time-varying surface topology. Inputs: World-space position wsP. Primitive attributes: center wsCenter, radius radius, density density, noise amplitude amplitude, noise gamma gamma, 2D displacement flag displace2D, and a fractal noise evaluator fractal (e.g., fBM). Rasterization state: world-space voxel size wsVoxelSize. Outputs: Sample value sample.value (density). Data Structures: RasterizationState: Contains wsP and wsVoxelSize. RasterizationSample: Contains value (float). SolidNoisePoint/PyroclasticPoint attributes: radius, wsCenter, density, fractal, gamma, amplitude, displace2D. Steps: 1. Transform to Local Space: Compute the local position lsP relative to the sphere center and normalized by radius: lsP = \frac{wsP - wsCenter}{radius} 2. Determine Noise Sample Point: Determine the point nsP at which to evaluate the noise function. If 2D displacement is enabled, project lsP onto the unit sphere surface; otherwise, use the full local position: nsP = \begin{cases} \frac{lsP}{|lsP|} & \text{if } displace2D \\ lsP & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Handle the case where |lsP| \approx 0 by setting nsP to a default vector (e.g., (1,0,0)) to avoid division by zero. 3. Evaluate Fractal Noise: Evaluate the procedural noise function at nsP: rawNoise = fractal.eval(nsP) 4. Apply Gamma and Amplitude: Apply gamma correction and scale by amplitude: fractalFunc = amplitude \cdot \gamma(rawNoise) \gamma(x) is typically x^{1/\gamma{param}} or similar power function depending on the noise implementation's gamma parameter. 5. Compute Sphere Distance: Calculate the signed distance of the point from the sphere surface in local space: sphereFunc = |lsP| - 1.0 6. Compute Filter and Threshold Widths: Determine the filter width from the voxel size and the threshold width for smoothing: filterWidth = |wsVoxelSize| thresholdWidth = \frac{filterWidth \cdot 0.5}{radius} 7. Compute Pyroclastic Value: Combine the sphere distance and noise, then apply a smoothstep-like fit to create a gradual transition: pyroValue = \text{fit}(sphereFunc - fractalFunc, -thresholdWidth, thresholdWidth, 1.0, 0.0) \text{fit}(x, a, b, c, d) is equivalent to \text{smoothstep}(a, b, x) mapped to range [c, d]. Specifically: t = \frac{x-a}{b-a}, result = c + (d-c)t, clamped to [0,1]. 8. Set Sample Density: Multiply by the base density: sample.value = density \cdot pyroValue Alternative Formula Representation: Some sources define the pyroclastic density directly as: pyroclasticDensity(P) = \max(radius - |P/radius| + |m(P)|, 0) where m(P) is the noise function value. The density is then: density = \text{smoothStep}(pyroclasticDensity, 0, 0.05) This formulation uses the absolute value of the noise, whereas the step-by-step method uses subtraction (sphereFunc - fractalFunc). The step-by-step method allows for overhangs where density disconnects, while the absolute value formulation may behave differently at boundaries. Parameters: displace2D: Boolean flag. If true, noise is evaluated on the sphere surface (2D), preventing overhangs. If false, noise is evaluated in 3D space, allowing overhangs. radius: Radius of the base sphere. amplitude: Scaling factor for the noise displacement. gamma: Gamma correction exponent for the noise function. density: Base density multiplier. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhangs: Using 3D displacement (displace2D = false) can create overhangs where parts of the density disconnect from the main body. To prevent this, use 2D displacement (displace2D = true), which projects the noise lookup point onto the sphere, making displacement constant along the normal vector. Division by Zero: When lsP is near zero, nsP normalization fails. A guard is required. Precision: The smoothstep fitting requires careful handling of thresholdWidth to avoid numerical instability when radius is very small or very large. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pyroclasticspheresample(wsP, wsCenter, radius, density, amplitude, gamma, displace2D, fractaleval, wsVoxelSize): # Step 1: Transform to local space lsP = (wsP - wsCenter) / radius # Step 2: Determine noise sample point lsPlength = length(lsP) if lsPlength < 1e-6: nsP = Vector(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Default to avoid division by zero else: if displace2D: nsP = lsP / lsPlength else: nsP = lsP # Step 3: Evaluate fractal noise rawnoise = fractaleval(nsP) # Step 4: Apply gamma and amplitude # Assuming gamma is a power function: x^(1/gamma) or x^gamma depending on convention. # Common convention in graphics: gamma correction is x^(1/gammaparam). # If gamma parameter is 2.2, we raise to 1/2.2. # However, source says "gamma correction", often implemented as pow(x, 1.0/gamma). # Let's assume standard gamma correction: if rawnoise < 0: rawnoise = 0.0 # Clamp negative noise if necessary, or handle signed noise fractalfunc = amplitude pow(rawnoise, 1.0 / gamma) # Step 5: Compute sphere distance spherefunc = lsPlength - 1.0 # Step 6: Compute filter and threshold widths filterwidth = length(wsVoxelSize) thresholdwidth = (filterwidth 0.5) / radius # Step 7: Compute pyroclastic value using smoothstep-like fit # fit(x, a, b, c, d) = c + (d-c) smoothstep(a, b, x) # smoothstep(a, b, x) = clamp((x-a)/(b-a), 0, 1) x = spherefunc - fractalfunc if thresholdwidth < 1e-6: # Avoid division by zero if voxel size is negligible pyrovalue = 1.0 if x > 0 else 0.0 else: t = (x - (-thresholdwidth)) / (thresholdwidth - (-thresholdwidth)) t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) pyrovalue = t # Since c=1.0, d=0.0, fit(x, -t, t, 1.0, 0.0) = 1.0 - t? # Wait, fit(x, a, b, c, d) maps a->c, b->d. # If x < a, result c. If x > b, result d. # Here a = -thresholdWidth, b = thresholdWidth, c = 1.0, d = 0.0. # So if x < -tw, result 1.0. If x > tw, result 0.0. # t = (x - a) / (b - a) = (x + tw) / (2tw) # result = c + (d-c)t = 1.0 + (0.0-1.0)t = 1.0 - t pyrovalue = 1.0 - t # Step 8: Set sample density samplevalue = density pyrovalue return samplevalue This method defines an implicit surface by displacing the radius of a base sphere using animated procedural noise, creating a breathing, organic shape suitable for pyroclastic or fluid-like visual effects. It distinguishes itself from static SDF primitives by combining a low-frequency sinusoidal "breathing" modulation with high-frequency fractal Brownian motion (fBM) and sinusoidal products to generate complex, time-varying surface topology. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, dominated by the noise evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) for primitive attributes. Strengths: Creates complex, organic shapes with overhangs and disconnected parts (if 3D displacement is used). Simple to implement. Limitations: Aliasing artifacts if not properly antialiased (smoothstep helps). 3D displacement can lead to disconnected density islands. When to Use: When organic, turbulent, or pyroclastic shapes are needed. When Not to Use: When strict, smooth, non-overhanging spheres are required (use static SDF sphere). The Pyroclastic Sphere Primitive is described in "Production Volume Rendering". It is used in production volume rendering to create realistic pyroclastic flows and other turbulent phenomena. The technique relies on adding procedural noise to a distance function, a concept also found in other noise-based primitives. name: Deforming SDF Sphere with Noise
head: Animated Noise SDF Sphere, Animated SDF Displacement, SDF Sphere with Noise Displacement, Signed Distance Field (SDF) Sphere with Noise Displacement
body: This method defines an implicit surface by displacing the radius of a base sphere using animated procedural noise, creating a time-varying organic shape. It distinguishes itself from static SDF primitives by combining a low-frequency sinusoidal "breathing" modulation with high-frequency fractal Brownian motion (fBM) and sinusoidal products to generate complex surface topology. Inputs: \mathbf{p}: The 3D point in world space to evaluate. t: The global animation time (gtime). sphereradius: The base radius R of the sphere. noiseamplitude: The scaling factor A{noise} for the displacement magnitude. Outputs: d(\mathbf{p}): The signed distance from \mathbf{p} to the deformed surface. No auxiliary data structures are required; the method relies on scalar arithmetic and vector operations. sphereradius (R): Base radius of the sphere. noiseamplitude (A{noise}): Scaling factor for displacement magnitude. gtime (t): Global time variable, advancing per frame. The signed distance is calculated as: d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}\| - (r(t) + D(\mathbf{p}, t)) Where: 1. Base Radius r(t): r(t) = R + A{breath} \sin(\omega{breath} t) With A{breath} = 0.25 and \omega{breath} = 2.0. 2. Sinusoidal Displacement D{sin}: D{sin} = \sin(16 x + \phi) \sin(16 y + \phi) \sin(16 z + \phi) Where \phi = 6.0 t. 3. fBM Displacement D{fbm}: D{fbm} = \text{fBM}(2\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}(t)) Where \mathbf{v}(t) = (t, 0.7t, 1.3t). 4. Total Displacement D: D = A{noise} \left( 0.6 D{sin} + 0.8 (D{fbm} - 0.5) \right) The term (D{fbm} - 0.5) centers the fBM output, assuming it ranges in [0, 1]. 1. Calculate the time-varying base radius r using the sine wave modulation. 2. Calculate the phase offset \phi for the sinusoidal component. 3. Compute the sinusoidal displacement D{sin} by multiplying three sine waves modulated by the point coordinates and phase. 4. Compute the fBM displacement D{fbm} by evaluating the noise function at a scaled and time-shifted position. 5. Combine the sinusoidal and fBM components into a total displacement D, weighted by noiseamplitude. 6. Return the signed distance as the Euclidean norm of \mathbf{p} minus the sum of the displaced radius r and displacement D. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def norm(self): return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def hash3d(v): # Standard deterministic hash for value noise h = int(v.x 127.1 + v.y 311.7 + v.z 74.7) h = (h << 13) ^ h return 1.0 - 2.0 ((h (h h 15731 + 789221) + 1376312589) & 0x7fffffff) / 0x7fffffff def valuenoise(p): # Trilinear interpolation of surrounding hash values ix, iy, iz = int(math.floor(p.x)), int(math.floor(p.y)), int(math.floor(p.z)) fx, fy, fz = p.x - ix, p.y - iy, p.z - iz fx, fy, fz = fxfx(3-2fx), fyfy(3-2fy), fzfz(3-2fz) n00 = lerp(hash3d(Vec3(ix, iy, iz)), hash3d(Vec3(ix+1, iy, iz)), fx) n10 = lerp(hash3d(Vec3(ix, iy+1, iz)), hash3d(Vec3(ix+1, iy+1, iz)), fx) n01 = lerp(hash3d(Vec3(ix, iy, iz+1)), hash3d(Vec3(ix+1, iy, iz+1)), fx) n11 = lerp(hash3d(Vec3(ix, iy+1, iz+1)), hash3d(Vec3(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1)), fx) return lerp(lerp(n00, n10, fy), lerp(n01, n11, fy), fz) def fractalbrownianmotion(p, octaves=4): # Layered value noise with decreasing amplitude and frequency val = 0.0 amp = 1.0 freq = 1.0 for in range(octaves): val += amp valuenoise(p freq) amp = 0.5 freq = 2.0 return val def signeddistance(p, gtime, sphereradius, noiseamplitude): # 1. Base radius breathes over time r = sphereradius + 0.25 math.sin(gtime 2.0) # 2. Phase for sinusoidal displacement phase = gtime 6.0 # 3. Sinusoidal displacement component sindisp = math.sin(16.0 p.x + phase) math.sin(16.0 p.y + phase) math.sin(16.0 p.z + phase) # 4. Fractal Brownian Motion displacement timeshift = Vec3(gtime, gtime 0.7, gtime 1.3) scaledp = Vec3(p.x 2.0, p.y 2.0, p.z 2.0) fbm = fractalbrownianmotion(scaledp + timeshift) # 5. Total displacement displacement = noiseamplitude (0.6 sindisp + 0.8 (fbm - 0.5)) # 6. Final SDF return p.norm() - (r + displacement) def spheretrace(orig, dir, maxsteps=128, minstep=0.01, sphereradius=1.5, noiseamplitude=1.0, gtime=0.0): pos = Vec3(orig.x, orig.y, orig.z) for in range(maxsteps): d = signeddistance(pos, gtime, sphereradius, noiseamplitude) if d < 0.0: return True step = max(d 0.1, minstep) pos = Vec3(pos.x + dir.x step, pos.y + dir.y step, pos.z + dir.z step) return False fBM Range: The formula assumes fractalbrownianmotion returns values in [0, 1]; if the implementation returns [-1, 1], the centering term (D{fbm} - 0.5) will shift the displacement bias. Precision: High-frequency sine terms (16x) may cause precision issues if coordinates are large; normalizing or clamping input coordinates might be necessary for stability in large scenes. Self-Intersection: Large noiseamplitude values can cause the surface to fold over itself, leading to incorrect normals if computed via gradient, though the SDF value remains valid for ray marching. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Infinite Tiling with Modulo
head: Infinite Crystal Grid SDF, Modulo SDF, Modulo Tiling, Tiling, Tiling via Modulo
body: Infinite Tiling with Modulo is a technique for rendering infinite repeating patterns by using the modulo operator to fold space, allowing a single primitive SDF to be tiled infinitely. It enables ray-marched fractal renderers like Mandelbulbs and Menger sponges by tiling a scene infinitely at essentially zero extra cost. It sets itself apart from Constructive SDF Modeling by avoiding explicit boolean combinations for repetition, instead relying on spatial folding to handle periodicity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray position p (vec3). Input: Tile size T (float). Input: Offset O (float or vec3). Input: Base SDF function sdf(q) (float). Output: Tiled distance d (float). Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method operates on standard floating-point vectors. Steps: 1. Fold Space: Apply the modulo operation to the ray position p to map it into a local tile coordinate system. The standard formula centers the tile at the origin: q = \text{mod}(p + O, T) - O Where mod is the floating-point modulo operator. This folds the world into a box of size T centered at the origin. 2. Evaluate Base SDF: Evaluate the base signed distance function at the folded coordinate q: d = \text{sdf}(q) 3. Return Distance: Return d. Parameters: T (Tile Size): The period of the modulo operation. Typical value: 3.0. O (Offset): Added before modulo to center the tile at the origin. Typical value: 1.5 (for T=3.0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Coordinates: The standard mod function behavior depends on the language/runtime. In GLSL, mod(x, y) returns x - y floor(x/y). If the base SDF assumes positive coordinates (e.g., for certain fractal iterations), the offset O must be chosen such that q remains in the valid quadrant, or the base SDF must be symmetric/periodic-aware. Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate in deep fractal iterations if not managed, though the tiling itself is stable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def infinitetilingmodulo(p: Vec3, tilesize: float, offset: float, basesdf: Callable[[Vec3], float]) -> float: """ Tiles a base SDF infinitely using modulo folding. Args: p: Ray position. tilesize: Period of the tiling. offset: Offset to center the tile. basesdf: Function computing distance for a single tile. Returns: Signed distance to the nearest tiled surface. """ # Fold space into a tile centered at origin # q = mod(p + offset, tilesize) - offset # Note: GLSL mod(x, y) = x - y floor(x/y) q = p + offset q = q - tilesize floor(q / tilesize) q = q - offset # Evaluate base SDF at folded coordinate d = basesdf(q) return d A variant of Infinite Tiling which produces a finite number of repetitions of a shape. It takes an additional vector \vec{l} as input, where \vec{l} is the corner of the box used to limit the number of repetitions of the shape. This is useful when an infinite grid is not desired, but a bounded array of objects is needed without explicit instance management. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per ray step for the tiling operation itself. The complexity is dominated by the base SDF evaluation. Memory: O(1). No additional memory is required for the tiling logic. Measured Performance: The tiling operation adds "essentially zero extra cost". In production, tricks like bounding-volume early-outs, reduced step counts for distant geometry, and rendering at half resolution before upscaling keep frame rates real-time even as scene complexity grows. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables infinite detail and fractal geometry without explicit mesh data. Simple to implement. Limitations: Requires the base SDF to be compatible with the folding (e.g., periodic or symmetric). Can cause aliasing if the tile size is small relative to the pixel footprint and no mipmapping or supersampling is used. When to Use: Use for fractals, crystal grids, or any scene requiring infinite repetition of a primitive. Do not use when a finite, bounded array of distinct objects is needed (use Finite Tiling or Instancing). The technique is foundational for ray-marched fractal renderers such as Mandelbulbs and Menger sponges. It allows these complex, self-similar structures to be defined implicitly without explicit geometry. The method is widely used in real-time graphics and shader art for generating complex patterns from simple primitives. arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, https://github.com/arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions: Sphere Tracing..., https://www.mysimulator.uk/articles/ray-marching/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) PDF COS 426 Final Project Writeup Raymarching with Signed Distance Fields, https://jbaum98.github.io/cos426finalproject/writeup.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Boolean Operations on Distance Fields
head: SDF Boolean Operations, Boolean Operations on SDFs, SDF Boolean Operators, SDF Unions, SDF Intersections, SDF Differences, Combined SDF, Combining SDFs
body:
Boolean operations on Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) combine primitive distance functions to construct complex implicit surfaces using Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) logic. This method solves the problem of modeling arbitrary composite shapes without requiring mesh topology, by evaluating the scalar field of the resulting volume at any point in space. It is distinguished from Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination) by its strict adherence to exact set-theoretic Boolean logic (min/max) rather than smooth approximations, although smooth variants exist. Inputs: Two signed distance functions, d1(p) and d2(p), evaluated at a point p \in \mathbb{R}^3. Each function returns a scalar distance value. In implementations tracking material IDs, inputs may be vectors containing both distance and an identifier. Outputs: A new signed distance function d{result}(p) representing the Boolean combination of the two volumes. The core data structure is a scalar value representing distance. Some implementations extend this to a vector or struct to preserve material identity: Scalar: float or f32. Vector/Struct: vec2 or similar, where.x is the distance and.y is a material ID or marker. Let d1 be the distance to the first object and d2 be the distance to the second object. 1. Union (Add): The volume of the union is the set of points closest to either object. The distance is the minimum of the two distances: d{union}(p) = \min(d1(p), d2(p)) 2. Intersection: The volume of the intersection is the set of points inside both objects. The distance is the maximum of the two distances: d{intersection}(p) = \max(d1(p), d2(p)) 3. Difference (Subtraction): The volume of A - B is the set of points in A but not in B. This is implemented by negating the distance of the subtracted object (B) and taking the maximum: d{difference}(p) = \max(d1(p), -d2(p)) Note: Some sources define subtraction as B - A using \max(-d1, d2). The standard convention A - B uses \max(d1, -d2). The following Python-like pseudocode implements the three standard Boolean operations. It assumes d1 and d2 are scalar distances. If material IDs are required, the logic extends to selecting the ID corresponding to the winning distance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfunion(d1: float, d2: float) -> float: """ Computes the union of two SDFs. Returns the minimum distance. """ return min(d1, d2) def sdfintersection(d1: float, d2: float) -> float: """ Computes the intersection of two SDFs. Returns the maximum distance. """ return max(d1, d2) def sdfdifference(d1: float, d2: float) -> float: """ Computes the difference (subtraction) of d1 by d2 (d1 - d2). Negates d2 and returns the maximum. """ return max(d1, -d2) def sdfunionwithid(a: tuple, b: tuple) -> tuple: """ Computes union with material ID tracking. Input: (distance, materialid) Output: (distance, materialid) """ dista, ida = a distb, idb = b if dista < distb: return (dista, ida) else: return (distb, idb) def sdfintersectionwithid(a: tuple, b: tuple) -> tuple: """ Computes intersection with material ID tracking. """ dista, ida = a distb, idb = b if dista > distb: return (dista, ida) else: return (distb, idb) def sdfdifferencewithid(a: tuple, b: tuple) -> tuple: """ Computes difference (a - b) with material ID tracking. """ dista, ida = a distb, idb = b # Negate b's distance for subtraction negdistb = -distb if dista > negdistb: return (dista, ida) else: # Return negated distance and b's ID return (negdistb, idb) Operation Type: Enum or string specifying 'union', 'intersection', or 'difference'. Smoothness Parameter (k): For smooth unions (not strict Boolean), a blending parameter k controls the transition radius. The smooth union formula is: j = 	ext{clamp}(0.5 + 0.5(b - a)/k, 0, 1) d{smooth} = 	ext{mix}(b, a, j) - k \cdot j \cdot (1 - j) This is not a strict Boolean operation but a common extension. Discontinuities: Standard Boolean operations (min/max) create sharp, non-smooth transitions at the boundaries where the active SDF switches. This results in discontinuous derivatives (normals) at the seams. Normal Computation: Normals must be computed from the winning SDF. If d1 < d2 in a union, the normal is 
abla d1; otherwise, it is 
abla d2. For difference, if -d2 > d1, the normal is -
abla d2. Precision: Near the boundary where d1 \approx d2, floating-point precision errors can cause jitter in normals if not handled carefully. Degenerate Input: If one SDF is always positive (empty volume) or negative (full volume), the result simplifies to the other SDF or the empty/full volume respectively. Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation, requiring two SDF evaluations and one min/max operation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per operation. Performance: Extremely fast compared to mesh-based CSG, as it avoids boolean mesh intersection algorithms. Suitable for real-time ray marching. Strengths: Infinite resolution (analytical), easy composition of complex shapes, no mesh artifacts. Limitations: Sharp edges at Boolean seams (unless smoothed), difficulty in representing non-manifold geometry or thin features that require very small step sizes in ray marching. Boolean operations on SDFs were popularized in the context of ray marching and procedural graphics by Inigo Quilez and others in the early 2010s. The technique leverages the mathematical property that the signed distance function to a union of sets is the minimum of their individual distance functions, and the intersection is the maximum. It is a fundamental building block for Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination) and allows for the creation of complex scenes from simple primitives like spheres and boxes. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, https://github.com/Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, https://github.com/nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) erbenpeter/sdf, https://github.com/erbenpeter/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChadMcKinney/Dirac-Sea-Engine, https://github.com/ChadMcKinney/Dirac-Sea-Engine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 6 – Raymarching: Floor + Union of Rounded Box and Sphere, http://www.geeks3d.com/20130524/building-worlds-with-distance-functions-in-glsl-raymarching-glslhacker-tutorial-opengl/6/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Skipping Spheres: SDF Scaling & Early Ray Termination for Fast Sphere..., https://diglib.eg.org/items/7f21e58c-639e-4359-bf94-414738612006, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Further Graphics - name: FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration
head: High-level view algorithm of how step size is computed during the FBM loop, Procedural FBM Sphere Tracing
body: This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by computing valid Sphere Distance Bounds (SDB) using a dynamic Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) derived from the FBM structure itself. It enables early termination of octave summation and adaptive step sizing, reducing the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM at every step, this approach builds on Distance-field ray marching by integrating the BVH logic directly into the FBM summation loop, avoiding the memory overhead of explicit spatial trees or dynamic re-ordering. The algorithm computes a step size and the final FBM value F by iterating through the n octaves of the noise function. It maintains the current accumulated value F, the derivative along the ray dF, and the total step size step. The method uses global Lipschitz constants \lambda and \gamma initially, which can be replaced by local values for adaptive stepping. Inputs: p: Current 3D position. n: Number of octaves in the FBM sum. v: Threshold function (hypertexture), approximated by its 1st order (affine) Taylor polynomial. u: Ray direction vector. k: Early stop threshold parameter. Outputs: F: Final FBM value. step: Computed step size for the ray march. Parameters: \lambda{noise}, \gamma{noise}: Lipschitz constants for the noise function. Default values used for Perlin noise [Per85]. \lambda{Fn}, \gamma{Fn}: Global Lipschitz constants for the full FBM. Typical n: 20 (as used in Sponge scene tests). Typical k: 0, 1, 2, 3. Data Structures: inclFuncParams: Tuple (BVH, \lambda, dF, \gamma) passed to the intersection function. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize F \leftarrow 0, dF \leftarrow 0, step \leftarrow 0. 2. Set global Lipschitz constants: \lambda \leftarrow \lambda{Fn}, \gamma \leftarrow \gamma{Fn}. 3. Loop for i from 1 to n (each octave): a. Add current octave value to F: F \leftarrow F + oi(p). b. Add derivative along ray to dF: dF \leftarrow dF + (u \cdot o'i(p)). c. Compute Bounding Volume H (BVH) for remaining octaves: BVH \leftarrow F + s(i+1, n). Here s(i+1, n) represents the bound of the remaining octaves. d. Determine if step size computation is required (compStep): compStep is true if i == n (last octave) OR if the ray is outside the bounding volume (BVH - v(0) < 0). e. If compStep is true: i. Update Lipschitz constants to local values: \lambda \leftarrow \lambda{Fi}, \gamma \leftarrow \gamma{Fi} (Adaptive Lipschitz). ii. Prepare inclusion function parameters: inclFuncParams \leftarrow (BVH, \lambda, dF, \gamma). iii. Compute current step size: currstep \leftarrow intersect(inclFuncParams, v). iv. Update total step size: step \leftarrow step + currstep. v. Enforce minimum step size: step \leftarrow \max(\text{step}, \text{curr\step}) (optional if Sub-stepping is on). f. Perform Sub-stepping: i. Move ray position: p \leftarrow p + u \cdot \text{curr\step}. ii. Update F using threshold at current step: F \leftarrow v(\text{curr\step}). iii. Update threshold v at current step. iv. Update derivative: dF \leftarrow dF + \gamma \cdot \text{curr\step}. v. Clamp dF: dF \leftarrow \max(dF, \lambda). g. Apply Early Stop+k: i. Decrement k: k \leftarrow k - 1. ii. If k < 0, break the loop. 4. Return final F and step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbmspheretrace(p, n, vfunc, u, k, lambdanoise, gammanoise, lambdaFn, gammaFn): """ Computes FBM value and step size using BVH acceleration. Args: p: Current position (vec3) n: Number of octaves (int) vfunc: Threshold function (callable, approximated by 1st order Taylor) u: Ray direction (vec3) k: Early stop threshold (int) lambdanoise: Lipschitz constant for noise gammanoise: Gamma constant for noise lambdaFn: Global Lipschitz constant for FBM gammaFn: Global Gamma constant for FBM Returns: F: Final FBM value (float) step: Computed step size (float) """ F = 0.0 dF = 0.0 step = 0.0 lam = lambdaFn gam = gammaFn for i in range(1, n + 1): # Evaluate current octave and its derivative oi = octavenoise(p, i) oiprime = octavederivative(p, i) F += oi dF += dot(u, oiprime) # Compute BVH for remaining octaves # s(i+1, n) is the bound of remaining octaves srem = remainingoctavebound(i + 1, n) BVH = F + srem # Determine if step size computation is needed compstep = (i == n) or (BVH - vfunc(0) < 0) if compstep: # Adaptive Lipschitz: replace global with local lam = locallipschitz(i) gam = localgamma(i) # Compute step size using inclusion function inclparams = (BVH, lam, dF, gam) currstep = intersectinclusion(inclparams, vfunc) # Update total step step += currstep # Optional: enforce minimum step if Sub-stepping is on # step = max(step, currstep) # Sub-stepping p = p + u currstep F = vfunc(currstep) # Update threshold v at current step (handled by vfunc(currstep) above if vfunc returns value) # Note: The source says "Update threshold v at current step", # assuming vfunc handles the threshold logic or returns the updated threshold value. dF += gam currstep dF = max(dF, lam) # Early Stop+k k -= 1 if k < 0: break return F, step Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thread Divergence: The FBM sum loop may exit earlier for some threads than others due to Early Stop. However, rays from the same warp are spatially coherent, so divergence is typically limited to a single octave. GPU Memory Usage: The method avoids O(n) per-thread data storage required by dynamic re-ordering methods [WH96], making it more suitable for fast GPU implementation. Threshold Approximation: The threshold function v(p) is approximated by its 1st order (affine) Taylor polynomial. Higher order functions were not implemented as the approximation showed no noticeable error in tested scenes. Noise Parameters: The algorithm requires \lambda{noise} and \gamma{noise} for arbitrary noise functions. Default values are used for Perlin noise [Per85]. This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by treating the cascaded sum of octaves as a dynamic, implicit Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It progressively evaluates octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold, allowing for early termination and empty space skipping. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM at every step, this approach reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. It builds on FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration by replacing the explicit spatial tree with a procedural hierarchy derived from the FBM structure itself. Time Complexity: The average number of octaves computed per step is reduced from O(N) to O(k) in empty space, where k \ll N. Memory Complexity: O(1) per thread, avoiding the O(n) storage required by dynamic re-ordering methods. Performance: Tested on an Nvidia RTX 4080 Ti at 1024×1024 resolution on a 20-octave FBM Sponge scene: Early Stop (ES): Reduced avg octaves from 49596.3 to 24252.6 (close view) and 56577.8 to 10347.0 (far view). Time reduced from 770.0ms to 399.8ms (1.9x speedup) and 843.0ms to 178.4ms (4.7x speedup). Adaptive Lipschitz: Reduced avg steps from 428.1 to 331.7 (close view) and 223.7 to 154.5 (far view). Time reduced from 110.2ms to 87.1ms (1.3x speedup) and 42.4ms to 28.3ms (1.5x speedup). Sub-stepping (SS): With Adaptive Lipschitz, reduced avg steps from 331.7 to 265.2 (close view) and 154.5 to 273.0 (far view, steps increased but octaves decreased). Time reduced from 87.1ms to 72.5ms (1.2x speedup) and 28.3ms to 22.0ms (1.3x speedup). Early Stop+k (ES+k=1): With SS, reduced avg octaves from 4314.0 to 3815.0 (close view) and 1123.6 to 749.6 (far view). Time reduced from 72.5ms to 65.0ms (1.1x speedup) and 22.7ms to 16.7ms (1.4x speedup). Strengths: Significant performance gains in scenes with large empty spaces or intricate structures where FBM evaluation cost dominates. Low memory overhead suitable for GPU implementation. Limitations: Slightly smaller step sizes compared to dynamic re-ordering [WH96], but with much lower overhead. Thread divergence due to Early Stop, though limited by spatial coherence. The method was introduced in the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". It was implemented in GLSL fragment shaders and tested on scenes with 20-octave FBM of Perlin noise. The approach was developed to address the high computational cost of evaluating large FBM sums in sphere tracing, particularly for very large and detailed scenes. Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70072, fetched 2026-10-26

name: FBM Sphere Tracing with Implicit BVH
head: Dynamic Bounding Volume Hierarchy for FBM, Progressive evaluation of octaves
body: This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by treating the cascaded sum of octaves as a dynamic, implicit Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It progressively evaluates octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold, allowing for early termination and empty space skipping. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM at every step, this approach reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. It builds on FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration by replacing the explicit spatial tree with a procedural hierarchy derived from the FBM structure itself. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. FBM parameters: octave count N, amplitude Ai and frequency Fi for each octave i \in [0, N-1]. Base noise function n(\mathbf{p}) with range [-1, 1]. Isosurface threshold v (typically 0). Outputs: Distance to the nearest surface intersection or empty space indicator. Accumulated density (for volume rendering). Data Structures: No explicit tree nodes. The hierarchy is implicit in the loop order of octave evaluation. Variables: val (current accumulated FBM value), rem (remaining maximum possible contribution of uncomputed octaves). Algorithm: The core optimization occurs within the FBM evaluation loop. Instead of computing all N octaves, the algorithm maintains a bound on the maximum possible value the remaining octaves can add. If the current value plus this maximum bound cannot reach the threshold v, the point is guaranteed to be outside the object (assuming the object exists where f(\mathbf{p}) > v), and the loop terminates early. 1. Initialize val = 0. 2. Initialize rem = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ai. This represents the worst-case contribution if all remaining noise samples were at their maximum positive value (1). 3. Iterate through octaves i from 0 to N-1: a. Compute noise sample ni = n(\mathbf{p} \cdot Fi). b. Update val: val = val + Ai \cdot ni. c. Update rem: rem = rem - Ai. Since ni \in [-1, 1], the maximum possible contribution of the next octave i+1 is A{i+1}. By subtracting Ai from rem after processing octave i, rem correctly reflects the sum of amplitudes of all unprocessed octaves j > i. d. Early Termination Check: If val + rem < v, terminate the loop immediately. The point is outside the object. 4. If the loop completes, val is the full FBM value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbmwithimplicitbvh(p, octaves, threshold): """ Computes FBM with early termination based on implicit BVH bounds. Args: p: 3D point position. octaves: List of tuples (amplitude, frequency) for each octave. threshold: The isosurface threshold (typically 0). Returns: The FBM value if fully computed, or the partial value if early terminated. Note: The caller must handle the 'early terminated' state to skip ray marching steps. """ val = 0.0 # Initialize rem as the sum of all amplitudes (worst-case potential of all octaves) rem = sum(a for a, f in octaves) for i, (amplitude, frequency) in enumerate(octaves): # Evaluate base noise at scaled position # Assuming base noise returns values in [-1, 1] noiseval = basenoise(p frequency) # Add current octave contribution val += amplitude noiseval # Update remaining bound: remove current amplitude from potential max # The remaining octaves can contribute at most their sum of amplitudes rem -= amplitude # Check if it's impossible to reach the threshold # If val + rem < threshold, even if all remaining noise samples are 1, # the total will be below the threshold. if val + rem < threshold: return val, True # True indicates early termination return val, False # False indicates full computation Parameters: Threshold v: The density threshold defining the object boundary. Default is 0. Object exists where f(\mathbf{p}) > v. Octave count N: The number of noise layers. Higher counts increase complexity and the Lipschitz constant. Amplitude Ai: Typically decreases with octave index (e.g., Ai = A0 \cdot \text{lacunarity}^{-i}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accumulation of val and rem must be done with sufficient precision to avoid false positives in the early termination check, especially when rem is small. Noise Range: The method assumes the base noise function is strictly bounded in [-1, 1]. If the noise function has a different range, rem must be scaled accordingly. Gradient Calculation: For sphere tracing step sizes, gradients are still required. If early termination occurs, the gradient is undefined or incomplete. The algorithm must ensure that sphere tracing steps are only taken when the full FBM (or a sufficiently accurate approximation) is available, or use the partial value with caution. This method accelerates the ray marching of implicit surfaces defined by a sum of bounded functions Fn(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^n fi(\mathbf{p}) by exploiting the known value ranges of individual terms. It constructs an implicit hierarchy where partial sums serve as bounding volumes for the final sum, allowing early termination when the potential range of the total function excludes the isosurface threshold. It differs from explicit BVH approaches by computing bounds on-the-fly from pre-sorted function ranges rather than traversing a spatial tree structure. A technique to render hypertextures by modulating a smooth main shape function with FBM noise, while preserving the ability to use the implicit BVH and gradient-based sphere tracing optimizations. It defines a smooth base shape function S(\mathbf{p}) (e.g., a sphere or plane) and computes the FBM noise N(\mathbf{p}). Unlike naive hypertexture rendering which might require full evaluation of complex modulated functions, this method keeps the structure compatible with the progressive octave evaluation and gradient-based stepping. Time Complexity: Reduces average evaluation cost per step in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves needed to prove emptiness. In dense regions, the cost remains O(N) as all octaves must be evaluated. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as no explicit tree structure is stored. The hierarchy is implicit in the evaluation order. Measured Performance: Speedups up to 12-fold on opaque or constant semi-transparent scenes compared to classical sphere tracing, and up to 2-fold on non-constant density volumetric scenes. Gains of up to \times 1.8 are attributed specifically to the progressive octave evaluation. Strengths: Real-time performance on large, detailed scenes; no precomputation or storage overhead; compatible with animated content due to proceduralism. Limitations: Effectiveness depends on the distribution of the noise; if the object is dense and fills most of the scene, early termination opportunities are reduced. The method assumes the base noise is bounded in [-1, 1]. Originating from the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes", this method addresses the high rendering cost of procedural 3D noise in real-time applications. Precomputing volumes is storage-prohibitive for large open worlds and prevents animation. The method leverages the structure of FBM, treating cascaded sums as nested bounding volumes to enable efficient empty space skipping. It is part of a broader effort to accelerate sphere tracing for general Signed Distance Functions (SDF) by combining progressive evaluation with Lipschitz-based stepping.
