name: Implicit BVH for Sum of Bounded Functions
head: Procedural Bounding Volume Hierarchy
body: This method accelerates ray marching for implicit surfaces defined by a sum of bounded functions Fn(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^n fi(\mathbf{p}) by exploiting known value ranges of individual terms. It constructs an implicit hierarchy where partial sums act as bounding volumes for the final sum, enabling early termination when the potential range of the total function excludes the isosurface threshold. It differs from explicit spatial BVH approaches by computing bounds on-the-fly from pre-sorted function ranges rather than traversing a tree structure. Inputs: A set of n scalar functions fi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}, each bounded within [-\Delta{fi}, \Delta{fi}]. A target threshold value v (typically 0 for isosurfaces). A ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for marching. Outputs: The intersection distance t along the ray, or a failure indicator if no intersection exists within the marching bounds. Data Structures: A precomputed range sum array S of size n+1 where S[k] = s(k+1, n) = \sum{m=k+1}^{n} \Delta{fm} for k \in [0, n], with S[n] = 0. The functions fi must be sorted such that \Delta{f1} \geq \Delta{f2} \geq \dots \geq \Delta{fn}. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute \Delta{fi} for all i. Sort fi in descending order of \Delta{fi}. Compute the suffix sums s(i+1, n) for all i \in [1, n]. 2. Ray Marching Initialization: Start at t=0. 3. Iteration: For each marching step: a. Evaluate the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. b. Initialize partial sum F{current} = 0 and current index i=1. c. Early Termination Check Loop: While i \leq n: i. Evaluate fi(\mathbf{p}) and update F{current} \leftarrow F{current} + fi(\mathbf{p}). ii. Compute the inclusion interval for the final sum Fn based on the current partial sum: Fn = F{current} \pm s(i+1, n). iii. Check if the threshold v lies outside this interval. If v < F{current} - s(i+1, n) or v > F{current} + s(i+1, n), then no root exists for Fn at this \mathbf{p} in the current direction. Terminate the ray march (return failure). iv. Increment i \leftarrow i + 1. d. If the loop completes, Fn(\mathbf{p}) = F{current} is the exact function value. e. Check if |Fn(\mathbf{p}) - v| < \epsilon (convergence). If yes, return t. f. Compute step size h (e.g., using Lipschitz constants if available, or a fixed step) and advance t \leftarrow t + h. Formulas: Inclusion Function for Intermediate Sum: F{i+1} = Fi(\mathbf{p}) \pm \Delta{f{i+1}} \quad (4) where \Deltaf is the bound such that f \in [-\Deltaf, \Deltaf]. Sum of Ranges: s(i, j) = \sum{m=i}^{j} \Delta{fm} \quad \text{for } j \geq i. Inclusion Function for Final Sum from Partial Sum: Fn = Fi(\mathbf{p}) \pm s(i+1, n) \quad (6). Parameters: \epsilon: Convergence tolerance for ray marching. Not given in the sources. Step size strategy: Not given in the sources (depends on Lipschitz continuity assumptions in later sections). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unsorted Functions: If functions are not sorted by descending \Delta{fi}, the early termination guarantee is weakened or invalid, potentially leading to incorrect skips or missed intersections. Invalid Bounds: If \Delta{fi} is not a tight bound, the inclusion interval becomes loose, reducing the effectiveness of early termination but maintaining correctness. Lipschitz Continuity: This method assumes only boundedness for the inclusion logic. If the derivative is not Lipschitz continuous, standard sphere tracing step sizes may be invalid, requiring alternative marching strategies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchsumofboundedfunctions(rayorigin, raydirection, functions, deltas, threshold, epsilon, maxsteps, stepsize): """ functions: list of callable fi(p) deltas: list of float Deltafi, sorted descending threshold: float v epsilon: float convergence tolerance stepsize: float h (fixed step or computed via Lipschitz bounds) """ n = len(functions) # Precompute suffix sums s(i+1, n) for 0-indexed i # suffixsums[k] stores sum of deltas from index k to n-1 suffixsums = [0.0] (n + 1) currentsum = 0.0 for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): currentsum += deltas[i] suffixsums[i] = currentsum t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): p = rayorigin + t raydirection partialsum = 0.0 earlystop = False for i in range(n): partialsum += functionsi # Remaining range sum corresponds to s(i+2, n) in 1-based indexing # In 0-indexed: remaining sum is suffixsums[i+1] lowerbound = partialsum - suffixsums[i+1] upperbound = partialsum + suffixsums[i+1] if threshold < lowerbound or threshold > upperbound: earlystop = True break if earlystop: return None # No intersection # If loop completes, partialsum is the exact Fn(p) if abs(partialsum - threshold) < epsilon: return t # Advance ray t += stepsize return None # Max steps reached Time Complexity: O(n) per ray marching step in the worst case (evaluating all functions). Best case is O(1) if early termination occurs at the first function. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store precomputed range sums and function references. Strengths: No spatial data structure construction overhead; efficient for functions with rapidly decaying ranges (e.g., FBM octaves). Limitations: Requires prior knowledge of tight bounds \Delta{fi}; sorting overhead; less effective if bounds are loose or functions have similar ranges. When to Use: When the implicit function is a sum of many bounded terms with known, decreasing ranges (e.g., procedural noise). When Not to Use: When functions are not bounded or bounds are unknown; when spatial coherence is high and explicit BVH is more efficient. Originated in the context of fast sphere tracing for procedural volumetric noise. The method was introduced to exploit the hierarchical nature of FBM (Fractional Brownian Motion) noise, where higher-frequency octaves have smaller amplitudes, allowing them to be treated as bounding volumes for lower-frequency sums. It is used in real-time rendering of procedural landscapes and materials. name: Raymarching with Depth Buffer Occlusion
head: Depth-buffered Raymarching, Raymarching with Mesh Interaction, Z-Buffer Occlusion
body: Raymarching with Depth Buffer Occlusion is a technique that allows raymarched Signed Distance Field (SDF) objects to correctly occlude and be occluded by standard mesh-based geometry. It solves the problem where raymarched objects typically float on top of all other scene elements because the raymarching loop ignores the depth of pre-rendered meshes. By querying the scene's depth buffer to determine the distance to the nearest mesh surface, the raymarcher can terminate early if the mesh is closer, ensuring proper visual layering. This method is distinct from pure SDF rendering as it hybridizes rasterization (for meshes) with raymarching (for SDFs), whereas siblings like SDF Depth Buffer Integration may use different integration strategies or acceleration structures. The method integrates the standard sphere tracing loop Parent with a depth buffer lookup. The core modification is calculating the maximum allowable travel distance for each ray based on the nearest mesh surface and enforcing this limit within the marching loop. Inputs: Ray origin ro (camera position in world space). Ray direction rd (normalized direction in world space). Scene depth texture CameraDepthTexture. UV coordinates uv for depth sampling. SDF scene definition (implicit function). Outputs: Final pixel color, blending the raymarched SDF result with the background (mesh) color. Depth Buffer: A texture (e.g., sampler2D) storing linear or non-linear depth values. Vertex Shader Output (v2f): ray: A float3 representing the world-space ray direction. Crucially, this vector is normalized such that its z-component in eyespace is 1.0 (magnitude in z-direction) before transformation to world space. 1. Vertex Shader Preparation: Compute the ray direction rd in eyespace (view space). Normalize the ray in the z-axis to create rn. In eyespace, z < 0 is the forward direction. To avoid flipping the ray direction when dividing by a negative z-value, divide by the absolute value of the z-component: rn = \frac{rd}{|rd.z|} Transform rn from eyespace to world space using the inverse view matrix: o.ray = \text{mul}(\text{CameraInvViewMatrix}, rn) Pass o.ray to the fragment shader. 2. Fragment Shader Depth Sampling: Sample the depth buffer texture at the current UV coordinates to get the non-linear depth value. Convert the sampled depth to linear eyespace depth d using a function like LinearEyeDepth(). This d represents the distance along the z-axis from the camera plane to the mesh surface. Calculate the true Euclidean distance s from the camera origin to the mesh surface along the ray. This leverages similar triangles, using the length of the z-normalized ray vector rn (passed as i.ray.xyz in world space, but its length is invariant to rotation if we consider the projection geometry, or more precisely, the length of the vector that has unit z-component in view space): s = d \times |rn| Where |rn| is the magnitude of the vector rn computed in step 1. Note: In the source code, length(i.ray.xyz) is used, which corresponds to the length of the transformed vector. Since the transformation is a rotation (inverse view matrix), the length is preserved from the eyespace rn. 3. Raymarching Loop: Initialize current distance traveled t = 0. Iterate up to maxstep (e.g., 64): Occlusion Check: If t \ge s, the ray has reached or passed the mesh surface. Terminate the loop and return a transparent color (or the background color) to allow the mesh to show through. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF at the current position p = ro + t \cdot \hat{rd} (where \hat{rd} is the normalized world-space ray direction). Hit Check: If the SDF value d{sdf} \le \text{HIT\THRESHOLD}, a hit is found. Compute shading and return the color. Step: Advance t by d{sdf}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(appdata): # Compute ray direction in eyespace rdeyespace = normalize(appdata.position - camerapositioneyespace) # Normalize in Z-axis to create rn # Use abs() to prevent direction flip in eyespace where z < 0 is forward rneyespace = rdeyespace / abs(rdeyespace.z) # Transform to world space rayworld = mul(CameraInvViewMatrix, rneyespace) return { 'uv': appdata.uv, 'ray': rayworld, 'position': appdata.position } def fragmentshader(v2f): # 1. Get Depth Buffer Value depthtexel = tex2D(CameraDepthTexture, v2f.uv) # 2. Convert to Linear Eyespace Depth # LinearEyeDepth converts the non-linear depth buffer value to linear distance d = LinearEyeDepth(depthtexel.r) # 3. Calculate True Distance to Mesh Surface # length(v2f.ray) is the magnitude of the z-normalized ray vector # This vector has a z-component of 1.0 in eyespace before rotation s = d length(v2f.ray) # 4. Raymarch ro = CameraWS # Camera position in world space rd = normalize(v2f.ray) # Normalized world space direction t = 0.0 maxstep = 64 hitthreshold = 0.001 for i in range(maxstep): # Check against mesh depth if t >= s: # Ray hit the mesh first, return transparent to let mesh show return fixed4(0, 0, 0, 0) # Evaluate SDF p = ro + rd t dist = scenesdf(p) # Check for SDF hit if dist <= hitthreshold: # Compute normal and shading normal = computenormal(p) color = shade(p, normal, rd) return fixed4(color, 1.0) # Step forward t += dist # If loop finishes without hit or mesh occlusion, return transparent return fixed4(0, 0, 0, 0) def finalcolor(meshcolor, sdfcolor): # Alpha blend: mesh is background, SDF is foreground # Assuming sdfcolor has alpha 1.0 if hit, 0.0 if missed return meshcolor (1.0 - sdfcolor.a) + sdfcolor.xyz sdfcolor.a CameraDepthTexture: Sampler2D for the scene depth buffer. maxstep: Maximum iterations for the raymarch loop (e.g., 64). hitthreshold: Epsilon for surface hit detection (e.g., 0.001) Parent. Ray Direction Flip: In eyespace, z < 0 is forward. Dividing the ray direction by rd.z without taking the absolute value (abs()) will flip the ray direction if rd.z is negative, causing the raymarched scene to appear inverted. Depth Precision: The accuracy of occlusion depends on the depth buffer precision. Low precision may cause z-fighting or incorrect occlusion boundaries between SDF and mesh objects. Transparency: The method assumes opaque meshes for the depth buffer. Transparent meshes may require additional handling or separate depth passes. This variant addresses the specific case of scale-invariant integral surfaces (like skeleton-based sphere-cones) to guarantee correct occlusion in the depth buffer. It computes a scaling factor for the radii of sphere-cone primitives to ensure the SDF does not penetrate the occluding depth buffer. The worst-case configuration for this scaling is identified as two segment primitives aligned with the viewing direction -\mathbf{v}, both having radius \tau at point q. Due to surface scale invariance, the scaling factor is computed numerically for a unit radius case, representing the distance from q to the isosurface in direction \mathbf{v}. This worst-case configuration is independent of the actual skeleton layout, requiring no additional skeleton processing. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of raymarch steps. The depth buffer lookup is O(1) per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the depth buffer texture, where W and H are the screen dimensions. Performance: Adds minimal overhead (one depth texture sample and a few arithmetic operations) to the raymarching loop. The primary cost remains the SDF evaluations. Strengths: Enables seamless integration of SDF objects with standard rasterized meshes without complex hybrid rendering pipelines. Simple to implement in shader languages like HLSL/GLSL. Limitations: Only works for opaque meshes that write to the depth buffer. Does not handle transparent meshes or SDF objects occluding each other (unless the SDF objects are also rendered to a depth buffer first, which is not described in the primary source). Precision issues may arise with very large or very small scene scales. The technique was popularized by Adrian Buehler in a blog post titled "Raymarching Distance Fields: Concepts and Implementation". It addresses a common issue in real-time raymarching where SDF objects fail to interact with the rest of the scene's geometry. The method leverages standard graphics API features (depth buffers) to solve this interaction problem. The concept of using a depth buffer to limit raymarching is also referenced in earlier contexts, such as the "depth buffering technique using a 1D array" for 2D raycasting in embedded systems, though the 3D mesh interaction method is distinct. The radii scaling variant for sphere-cones was introduced in research on fast ray tracing of scale-invariant integral surfaces. name: SDF Depth Buffer Integration
head: Raymarching with Depth Buffer Output, Sphere Tracing for Depth Output, Sphere Tracing with Depth Buffer Output
body: SDF Depth Buffer Integration is a technique that extends sphere tracing by explicitly writing the computed surface hit point's depth to the hardware depth buffer (SVDepth). It solves the problem of incorrect occlusion between ray-marched SDF geometry and standard rasterized geometry, where the depth buffer would otherwise record the depth of the proxy mesh face rather than the actual ray-marched surface. It is distinguished from standard raymarching, which typically only outputs color, by ensuring the SDF geometry participates in standard depth testing. The method builds on Distance-field ray marching. It requires a fragment shader that outputs both color and depth, and a specific render queue configuration to ensure correct occlusion ordering. Inputs: Vertex position in object space. Camera position in world space. Scene SDF function S(p). Outputs: color (SVTARGET): The rendered surface color. depth (SVDepth): The NDC depth value of the hit point. The vertex shader output struct (v2f) layout is: position (SVPOSITION): Clip-space vertex position for rasterization. localPosition (TEXCOORD0): Object-space position, used as the ray origin. viewDirection (TEXCOORD1): Object-space view vector from camera to vertex, stored un-normalized. MAXSTEPS: Maximum ray march iterations. Typical value: 32. THICKNESS: SDF value threshold for hit detection. Typical value: 0.001. NORMALEPSILON: Offset for finite difference normal estimation. Typical value: 0.01. 1. Vertex Shader Setup: Compute clip-space position: o.position = UnityObjectToClipPos(v.vertex). Store object-space vertex position as ray origin: o.localPosition = v.vertex. Compute camera position in object space: objectSpaceCameraPos = mul(unityWorldToObject, float4(WorldSpaceCameraPos, 1)). Compute view direction: o.viewDirection = v.vertex - objectSpaceCameraPos. 2. Fragment Shader Initialization: Set ray origin pos = i.localPosition. Normalize view direction: dir = normalize(i.viewDirection.xyz). Initialize progress = 0. Initialize hitsurface = false. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate iter from 0 to MAXSTEPS - 1. Calculate sample point: samplePoint = pos + dir progress. Query SDF: distance = scene(samplePoint). If distance < THICKNESS: Set hitsurface = true. Break loop. Advance ray: progress = progress + distance. 4. Hit/Miss Handling: If !hitsurface: Execute discard to prevent writing to buffers. 5. Color Calculation: Compute surface normal using central finite differences: nx = S(p + \epsilon ex) - S(p - \epsilon ex) ny = S(p + \epsilon ey) - S(p - \epsilon ey) nz = S(p + \epsilon ez) - S(p - \epsilon ez) where \epsilon = \text{NORMAL\EPSILON}. Transform normal to world space and normalize. Compute lighting and return color. 6. Depth Calculation: Transform hit point to clip space: tracedClipPos = UnityObjectToClipPos(float4(samplePoint, 1.0)). Compute NDC depth: depth = tracedClipPos.z / tracedClipPos.w. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vert(vvertex): oposition = UnityObjectToClipPos(vvertex) olocalPosition = vvertex objectSpaceCameraPos = mul(unityWorldToObject, float4(WorldSpaceCameraPos, 1)) oviewDirection = vvertex - objectSpaceCameraPos return { 'position': oposition, 'localPosition': olocalPosition, 'viewDirection': oviewDirection } def frag(i): pos = i['localPosition'] dir = normalize(i['viewDirection'].xyz) progress = 0.0 samplePoint = float3(0, 0, 0) hitsurface = False for iter in range(MAXSTEPS): samplePoint = pos + dir progress distance = scene(samplePoint) if distance < THICKNESS: hitsurface = True break progress = progress + distance if not hitsurface: discard() # Color Calculation normal = computenormal(samplePoint) color = rendersurface(samplePoint, normal) # Depth Calculation tracedClipPos = UnityObjectToClipPos(float4(samplePoint, 1.0)) depth = tracedClipPos.z / tracedClipPos.w return color, depth def scene(pos): # Example: Sphere of radius 0.5 at origin return length(pos) - 0.5 def computenormal(pos): eps = NORMALEPSILON changeX = scene(pos + float3(eps, 0, 0)) - scene(pos - float3(eps, 0, 0)) changeY = scene(pos + float3(0, eps, 0)) - scene(pos - float3(0, eps, 0)) changeZ = scene(pos + float3(0, 0, eps)) - scene(pos - float3(0, 0, eps)) surfaceNormal = float3(changeX, changeY, changeZ) surfaceNormal = mul(unityObjectToWorld, float4(surfaceNormal, 0)) return normalize(surfaceNormal) def rendersurface(pos, normal): # Simplified lighting lightDirection = normalize(WorldSpaceLightPos0.xyz) lightAngle = max(dot(normal, lightDirection), 0.0) return Color lightAngle LightColor0 Incorrect Occlusion: Without SVDepth output, the depth buffer records the proxy mesh face depth, causing rasterized objects behind the SDF surface to appear in front, and vice versa. Early-Z Disable: Writing SVDepth disables GPU early-Z optimization for affected pixels because the hardware cannot know the depth before the fragment shader runs. Discard vs Clip: Use discard instead of clip(-1) to avoid potential driver differences in depth buffering. Precision Loss: View direction is stored un-normalized in TEXCOORD1 and normalized in the fragment shader to avoid precision loss during interpolation. Batching: DisableBatching must be set to True because batching breaks the object-to-world transform used for ray setup. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of pixels and M is MAXSTEPS. Each pixel requires up to MAXSTEPS SDF evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the ray marching state. Performance: The explicit depth write disables early-Z, potentially reducing performance compared to standard rasterization or raymarching without depth output. Strengths: Correct occlusion between SDF and rasterized geometry. Limitations: Loss of early-Z optimization; requires specific render queue settings (Geometry+1). The method was introduced in Tutorial 045 of the Ronja Tutorials series, extending previous sphere tracing tutorials (043, 044) to address depth buffer integration. It is commonly used in Unity shader development for rendering SDF geometry alongside standard meshes. name: Ray Marching with Refraction and Beer's Law Absorption
head: renderRefraction, transparent raymarching
body: This method extends distance-field ray marching to simulate transparent dielectric objects by handling refraction, total internal reflection (TIR), and exponential light absorption (Beer's Law) over multiple bounces. Unlike standard ray marching which terminates at the first surface hit, this approach continues the ray through transparent boundaries, flipping the normal direction to track interior traversal and accumulating distance for attenuation. It distinguishes itself from Approximate Refraction by explicitly computing the refracted ray direction and handling TIR, and from Cone Marching by using a single ray path rather than volumetric cone integration for absorption. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{ro}, ray direction \mathbf{rd}, scene signed distance function (SDF) sceneSDF, maximum refraction bounces MAXREFRACTIONS, and per-material absorption vector \mathbf{a} (RGB). Outputs: Final pixel color C{out}. Data Structures: SdResult: Struct containing dist (float, signed distance), mat (material struct), and potentially other metadata. dist < 0 indicates inside the object. Material: Contains refractionindex (float, IOR) and absorption (vec3). Parameters: MAXREFRACTIONS: Integer, typically 4. absorption: RGB vector controlling exponential light attenuation per unit distance inside the medium. Algorithm: 1. Initialize color = vec3(0), invert = -1.0 (indicating outside initially, but logic flips based on hit sign), absorbdist = 0.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to MAXREFRACTIONS - 1: a. Cast ray: If invert < 0, call castRayDI(ro, rd) (interior cast); else call castRayD(ro, rd) (exterior cast). Let result be sd. b. If invert < 0, add sd.dist to absorbdist. c. If sd.dist < 0: i. If invert > 0, render background and break loop. ii. Else, continue to next iteration (ray exited object, invert will flip). d. Compute intersection point: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{ro} + \mathbf{rd} \cdot sd.dist. e. Compute normal: \mathbf{n} = \text{getNormalFast}(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \text{invert}. f. Compute reflection direction: \mathbf{ref} = \text{reflect}(\mathbf{rd}, \mathbf{n}). g. Add lighting contribution: color += light(sd.mat, ro, ref, p, n). h. If invert > 0, break loop (ray exited object). i. Compute Index of Refraction (IOR): i. If invert < 0 (inside), ior = sd.mat.refractionindex. ii. If invert > 0 (outside), ior = 1.0 / sd.mat.refractionindex. j. Compute refraction direction: \mathbf{raf} = \text{refract}(\mathbf{rd}, \mathbf{n}, \text{ior}). k. If \mathbf{raf} == \mathbf{0} (Total Internal Reflection), set \mathbf{rd} = \mathbf{ref}. Else, set \mathbf{rd} = \mathbf{raf}. l. Update ray origin to prevent self-intersection: \mathbf{ro} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{rd} \cdot (0.01 / |\mathbf{rd} \cdot \mathbf{n}|). m. Update invert: If TIR occurred (tif is true), keep invert; else invert = invert -1.0. 3. Apply Beer's Law absorption: C{out} = \text{color} \cdot e^{-\mathbf{a} \cdot \text{absorb\dist}}. Formulas: Beer's Law Absorption: C{out} = C{in} \cdot e^{-\mathbf{a} \cdot d} where \mathbf{a} is the absorption vector and d is the accumulated distance traveled inside transparent media. Self-intersection offset: \mathbf{ro}{new} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{rd} \cdot \frac{0.01}{|\mathbf{rd} \cdot \mathbf{n}|} This offset prevents floating-point inaccuracies at sharp angles from causing immediate re-intersection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrefraction(ro, rd, maxrefractions=4): color = vec3(0.0) invert = -1.0 # -1 for outside, 1 for inside logic adjustment absorbdist = 0.0 for i in range(maxrefractions): # Cast ray based on current state if invert < 0: sd = castRayDI(ro, rd) else: sd = castRayD(ro, rd) # Accumulate distance if inside if invert < 0: absorbdist += sd.dist # Handle exit or background if sd.dist < 0: if invert > 0: return background(ro, rd) else: # Exited object, loop continues, invert flips next pass # Intersection point p = ro + rd sd.dist # Normal with correct orientation n = getNormalFast(p) invert # Reflection component ref = reflect(rd, n) color += light(sd.mat, ro, ref, p, n) # If we hit from outside (invert > 0 means we just entered or are outside?), # The source logic: "If invert>0, break" after lighting. # This implies if we are outside and hit, we stop refracting further? # Actually, standard transparent raymarching: # invert tracks if we are currently "inside" the material for absorption. # Let's follow the source strictly: if invert > 0: break # Compute IOR for refraction if invert < 0: ior = sd.mat.refractionindex else: ior = 1.0 / sd.mat.refractionindex # Compute refraction raf = refract(rd, n, ior) # Check for Total Internal Reflection (TIR) tif = (raf == vec3(0.0)) if tif: rd = ref else: rd = raf # Offset origin to prevent self-intersection ro = p + rd (0.01 / abs(dot(rd, n))) # Update invert state if tif: pass # Keep invert else: invert = invert -1.0 # Apply Beer's Law absorption = sd.mat.absorption # Assuming material has absorption color = exp(-dot(absorption, absorbdist)) return color The pseudocode assumes castRayDI and castRayD are distinct SDF casters handling interior/exterior distance queries appropriately, and refract returns zero vector on TIR. The source logic for invert flipping is specific to the implementation's state machine for tracking interior distance. This method extends Ray Marching with Refraction and Beer's Law Absorption by simulating chromatic dispersion, where the index of refraction (IOR) varies by wavelength. It splits the ray into Red, Green, and Blue channels, refracting each with a distinct IOR to produce spectral separation effects, while falling back to a single IOR when dispersion is negligible. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to MAXREFRACTIONS and the cost of SDF evaluation per bounce. Each bounce requires a full ray cast and normal computation. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1), as it only stores current ray state and accumulated color/distance. Strengths: Physically plausible transparency, handles complex internal reflections and absorption. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multiple bounces. Sensitive to floating-point precision at grazing angles (mitigated by offset). Does not account for subsurface scattering or volumetric scattering within the medium, only surface refraction and path absorption. When to use: Rendering transparent dielectrics like glass, water, or gems where internal reflections and color absorption are important. When not to use: Opaque objects, or when performance is critical and approximate transparency suffices. This method is implemented in the cahekp/Raymarching repository. It builds upon standard ray marching techniques by adding transparency handling. The use of Beer's Law for absorption is a standard technique in computer graphics for simulating light attenuation in participating media or transparent solids. cahekp/Raymarching, https://github.com/cahekp/Raymarching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NiekMSoftware/bad-apple-voxel-raytracer, https://github.com/NiekMSoftware/bad-apple-voxel-raytracer, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Transmission & Chromatic Dispersion Ray Marching
head: Chromatic Dispersion Ray Marching
body: This method extends Ray Marching with Refraction and Beer's Law Absorption by simulating chromatic dispersion, where the index of refraction (IOR) varies by wavelength. It splits the ray into Red, Green, and Blue channels, refracting each with a distinct IOR to produce spectral separation effects, while falling back to a single IOR when dispersion is negligible. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D. Scene SDF and material properties at the hit point: transmission T, IOR n, dispersion factor d. Scene parameters: throughHitPos, throughHitRes, transmissionSamples. Ambient light color L{amb} and base transmission color C{base}. Emission color C{emit} and strength S{emit}. Outputs: Transmitted color C{trans} = [R, G, B]. Data Structures: Material struct fields relevant to this step: transmission (float), ior (float), dispersion (float). Steps: 1. Check Transmission: If T \le 0.001, return black or handle as opaque. 2. Compute Incident Vector: Let V be the view direction (from camera to hit point). Compute incident vector I = -V. 3. Non-Dispersion Case: If d \le 10^{-4}: Compute relative IOR: \eta = \frac{1.0}{\max(n, 1.0001)}. Compute refracted direction D{refr} = \text{refract}(I, N, \eta), where N is the surface normal. TIR Check: If \|D{refr}\|^2 < 10^{-6}, set D{refr} = D{reflected} (the reflected fallback direction). March: Recursively march the ray from O' = \text{hitPos} + D{refr} \cdot (\epsilon \cdot 6.0) with direction D{refr}, using transmissionSamples. Accumulate: If a hit occurs inside the medium, compute transmitted color: C{trans} = L{amb} \cdot C{base} + C{emit} \cdot S{emit}. 4. Dispersion Case: If d > 10^{-4}: Compute IOR spread: \Delta n = d \cdot 0.35. Define channel IORs: nR = n + \Delta n, nG = n, nB = n - \Delta n. For each channel c \in \{R, G, B\}: Compute \etac = \frac{1.0}{\max(nc, 1.0001)}. Compute D{refr,c} = \text{refract}(I, N, \etac). TIR Check: If \|D{refr,c}\|^2 < 10^{-6}, set D{refr,c} = D{reflected}. March: Recursively march from O' with D{refr,c}. Accumulate: Compute Cc for the channel. Combine: C{trans} = [CR, CG, CB]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marchchromaticdispersion(hitpos, normal, viewdir, material, sceneparams): # 1. Check transmission if material.transmission <= 0.001: return vec3(0.0) # Incident vector I = -viewdir # 2. Non-dispersion path if material.dispersion <= 1e-4: eta = 1.0 / max(material.ior, 1.0001) refracteddir = refract(I, normal, eta) # TIR fallback if dot(refracteddir, refracteddir) < 1e-6: refracteddir = reflect(I, normal) # March startpos = hitpos + refracteddir (1e-4 6.0) # epsilon placeholder transcolor = marchscenetransmission(startpos, refracteddir, sceneparams.throughhitpos, sceneparams.throughhitres, sceneparams.transmissionsamples) # Accumulate return sceneparams.ambientlight sceneparams.throughbase + transcolor # 3. Dispersion path iorspread = material.dispersion 0.35 iorr = material.ior + iorspread iorg = material.ior iorb = material.ior - iorspread channels = [] for iorval in [iorr, iorg, iorb]: eta = 1.0 / max(iorval, 1.0001) refracteddir = refract(I, normal, eta) # TIR fallback if dot(refracteddir, refracteddir) < 1e-6: refracteddir = reflect(I, normal) startpos = hitpos + refracteddir (1e-4 6.0) # epsilon placeholder transcolor = marchscenetransmission(startpos, refracteddir, sceneparams.throughhitpos, sceneparams.throughhitres, sceneparams.transmissionsamples) channels.append(transcolor) return vec3(channels[0], channels[1], channels[2]) Parameters: dispersion: Chromatic dispersion factor, typically in [0, 1]. ior: Index of refraction, clamped to \ge 1.0. Edge Cases: Total Internal Reflection (TIR): Detected by checking if the squared length of the refracted direction is less than 10^{-6}. If true, the refracted ray is replaced with the reflected fallback direction to prevent NaN or invalid directions. Precision: The threshold 10^{-4} for dispersion is used to avoid unnecessary branching and floating-point noise in the IOR calculation. Not given in the sources. This method is implemented in the RayMarchingtool repository by TeoGrajqevci. It is an extension of standard ray marching with refraction, adding spectral separation to transparent materials. name: Reflected Ray Directions
head: Reflection, reflect, Vector Reflection
body: A method to determine the direction of a ray after it interacts with a surface during distance-field ray marching. It calculates the new propagation direction based on the incident ray and the surface normal, enabling specular highlights and environment mapping in volume rendering. It differs from Ray Marching with Refraction and Beer's Law Absorption by preserving the ray within the same medium (no index of refraction change) and from Approximate Refraction by providing an exact geometric reflection rather than an approximation. Inputs: Incident ray direction \vec{v} (normalized). Surface normal \vec{n} at the intersection point (normalized). Optional: Distance field value f(p) to determine if a hit occurred. Outputs: Reflected ray direction \vec{v}{new} (normalized). Data Structures: Vectors \vec{v}, \vec{n} are 3D floating-point vectors. Steps: 1. Surface Hit Detection: Determine if the ray has hit a surface. In distance-field marching, this is typically when the distance field value f(pi) \approx 0 (within a small epsilon). If no surface is hit, the direction remains unchanged: \vec{v}{i+1} = \vec{v}i. 2. Normal Retrieval: If a surface is hit, compute the surface normal \vec{N}i at the current position pi. For distance fields, this is usually the normalized gradient: \vec{N}i = \frac{\nabla f(pi)}{\|\nabla f(pi)\|}. 3. Dot Product Calculation: Compute the dot product between the incident direction and the normal: d = \vec{v} \cdot \vec{n}. 4. Reflection Vector Calculation: Apply the reflection formula. The reflected direction \vec{r} is calculated as: \vec{r} = \vec{v} - 2(\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n})\vec{n} This is equivalent to subtracting twice the projection of \vec{v} onto \vec{n} from \vec{v}. 5. Normalization: Normalize the resulting vector to ensure it remains a unit direction vector: \vec{v}{new} = \frac{\vec{r}}{\|\vec{r}\|}. Note: If \vec{v} and \vec{n} are already normalized and orthogonal components are handled correctly, the result should be normalized, but precision errors may require explicit normalization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reflectray(incidentdirection: Vector3, surfacenormal: Vector3) -> Vector3: """ Calculates the reflected ray direction. Args: incidentdirection: The incoming ray direction (normalized). surfacenormal: The surface normal at the hit point (normalized). Returns: The reflected ray direction (normalized). """ # Step 1: Calculate dot product dotproduct = dot(incidentdirection, surfacenormal) # Step 2: Calculate reflection vector # Formula: r = v - 2 (v. n) n reflectionvector = subtract( incidentdirection, multiplyvectorscalar(surfacenormal, 2.0 dotproduct)) # Step 3: Normalize the result # Although mathematically the result should be unit length if inputs are unit, # floating point errors may necessitate normalization. return normalize(reflectionvector) Parameters: No specific parameters other than the input vectors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Errors: The result of the reflection formula should theoretically be a unit vector if inputs are unit vectors. However, floating-point arithmetic may introduce small errors. Explicit normalization is recommended. Back-face Normals: Ensure the normal points in the correct direction relative to the incident ray. If the ray is exiting a surface, the normal might need to be flipped depending on the shading model, though for pure reflection direction calculation, the geometric reflection holds regardless of side. Degenerate Input: If the incident ray is parallel to the surface (\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n} = 0), the reflection is the incident ray itself. If the incident ray is anti-parallel (\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n} = -1), the reflection is the reverse of the incident ray. Calculates the refracted direction of a ray given surface normals and refractive indices, handling entry and exit from spheres. It differs from reflected directions by changing the ray's speed and direction based on Snell's Law. Choose this when rendering transparent or translucent objects. See Ray Marching with Refraction and Beer's Law Absorption. Steps: 1. Get surface normal \vec{N}. 2. Set n1 to current refractive index and n2 to object's refractive index. 3. Calculate s = \vec{ray} \cdot \vec{N}. 4. If object is a sphere and s > 0 (exiting sphere), swap n1 and n2. 5. Calculate n = n1 / n2. 6. Calculate refracted ray as n \cdot (\vec{ray} - s \cdot \vec{N}) - \vec{N} \cdot \sqrt{1 - n^2 \cdot (1 - s^2)}. 7. Normalize the result and update ref to n2. Time Complexity: O(1) per reflection event. Requires a few dot products, multiplications, and one normalization. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, provides physically accurate specular reflections for smooth surfaces. Limitations: Only handles surface reflections; does not account for diffuse interreflection or complex material properties without additional shading models. Does not handle refraction or absorption. When to use: When rendering glossy or specular surfaces in volume rendering or ray marching. When not to use: When rendering transparent objects (use refraction) or diffuse surfaces (use Lambertian shading). Originated from basic geometric optics and vector algebra. The reflection formula \vec{r} = \vec{v} - 2(\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n})\vec{n} is a standard result in computer graphics, widely used in ray tracing and ray marching implementations. It is a fundamental component of lighting models in volume rendering, particularly for simulating specular highlights on implicit surfaces defined by distance fields. hexhowells/GoTracer, https://github.com/hexhowells/GoTracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) jacklv123/Volumetric-photon-mapping, https://github.com/jacklv123/Volumetric-photon-mapping, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Approximate Refraction
head: Normal-based texture offset refraction
body: Approximate refraction is a technique to make a fluid surface appear to refract objects behind it, providing a visual effect similar to ray tracing but with significantly lower computational cost and implementation complexity. It differs from Ray Marching with Refraction and Beer's Law Absorption by avoiding the physical simulation of light paths through the volume, instead relying on a 2D texture coordinate offset derived from the surface normal. It is distinct from Reflected Ray Directions as it targets transmission rather than reflection, and from Cone Marching by using point-sampled normals rather than volume-aware cone intersections for the offset calculation. Inputs: A background scene rendered into a texture. A volume representing the fluid surface. View direction V and up vector z. Scalar parameter \beta > 0. Outputs: Final image with refracted appearance. Data Structures: 1. Background Texture: Stores the color of objects behind the fluid. 2. Hit Location Texture: Stores the 2D screen-space coordinates p of the nearest ray-surface intersection. Alpha channel: 1 if intersection exists, 0 otherwise. 3. Shading Normal Texture: Stores the surface normal N at the intersection point. Steps: 1. Render Background: Render all scene geometry located behind the fluid volume into a background texture. 2. Ray Marching: For each pixel, march through the volume to find the nearest intersection with the fluid surface. Store the screen-space hit location p in the Hit Location Texture. Store the shading normal N at the hit point in the Shading Normal Texture. Set the alpha of the Hit Location Texture to 0 if no intersection is found, 1 otherwise. 3. Compute Basis Vectors: Calculate the orthonormal basis vectors Ph and Pv for the image plane based on the view direction V and up vector z. 4. Calculate Texture Offset: For each pixel with a valid hit (alpha = 1), compute the texture coordinate offset using the surface normal N and parameter \beta. 5. Sample Background: Look up the color in the Background Texture using the calculated texture coordinate t. 6. Composite: Use the sampled background color in the shading equation for the fluid surface. Add foreground objects to create the final image. Formulas: The texture coordinate t is calculated as: t = p - \beta(N \cdot Ph, N \cdot Pv) Where: p is the location of the pixel being shaded (screen-space coordinates). N is the surface normal at the hit point. \beta is a scalar parameter controlling the severity of the refraction effect (\beta > 0). Ph and Pv are orthonormal basis vectors for the image plane. The vertical basis vector Pv is calculated as: Pv = \frac{z - (z \cdot V)V}{\|z - (z \cdot V)V\|} Where: z is the up vector. V is the view direction. The horizontal basis vector Ph is calculated as: Ph = Pv \times V Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeapproximaterefraction(backgroundtexture, hitlocationtexture, normaltexture, viewdirection, upvector, beta): """ Computes the approximate refraction effect for a fluid surface. Args: backgroundtexture: Texture containing the scene behind the fluid. hitlocationtexture: Texture containing screen-space hit locations (p) and validity (alpha). normaltexture: Texture containing surface normals (N) at hit locations. viewdirection: View vector V. upvector: Up vector z. beta: Scalar parameter controlling refraction severity. Returns: Final image texture. """ # Precompute basis vectors for the entire frame # Project up vector onto plane perpendicular to view direction zproj = upvector - dot(upvector, viewdirection) viewdirection normzproj = length(zproj) # Handle degenerate case where upvector is parallel to viewdirection if normzproj < 1e-6: # Fallback: use a default horizontal vector, e.g., (1, 0, 0) # This is a standard graphics fallback Pv = normalize(cross(viewdirection, (1, 0, 0))) else: Pv = zproj / normzproj Ph = cross(Pv, viewdirection) finalimage = emptytexturelike(hitlocationtexture) for each pixel (x, y): # Get hit location and normal p = hitlocationtexture[x, y].xy alpha = hitlocationtexture[x, y].a N = normaltexture[x, y].xyz if alpha == 0: # No intersection, use background or default color finalimage[x, y] = backgroundtexture[x, y] continue # Calculate texture coordinate offset # N dot Ph gives the horizontal component of the normal in the image plane # N dot Pv gives the vertical component offsetx = N.x Ph.x + N.y Ph.y + N.z Ph.z # Dot product N. Ph offsety = N.x Pv.x + N.y Pv.y + N.z Pv.z # Dot product N. Pv tx = p.x - beta offsetx ty = p.y - beta offsety # Sample background texture at offset coordinate refractedcolor = backgroundtexture[tx, ty] # Use refracted color in shading (simplified here as direct color) # In a full shader, this would be combined with lighting models finalimage[x, y] = refractedcolor return finalimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate View Direction: If the up vector z is parallel to the view direction V, the denominator in the Pv calculation becomes zero. A fallback basis vector must be chosen. Boundary Conditions: Texture coordinates t may fall outside the [0, 1] range. Standard texture wrapping or clamping modes should be applied when sampling the background texture. Precision: The offset magnitude depends on \beta and the magnitude of the normal's projection. Large normals or large \beta values can cause significant displacement, potentially sampling incorrect background regions. Physically based refraction with absorption. Choose when accurate light transport through the volume is required. Handles reflections. Choose when mirror-like surfaces are needed. Uses cone intersections for better volume accuracy. Choose when high-quality volume rendering is needed and performance allows. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the refraction offset calculation, assuming constant-time texture lookups. The dominant cost is the ray marching step to find the surface intersection. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the background texture, hit location texture, and normal texture. Performance: Significantly faster than ray tracing for refraction, as it avoids casting secondary rays into the scene. Strengths: Simple to implement, fast, suitable for real-time applications. Limitations: Does not account for the actual path of light through the volume; can produce artifacts if the background scene is complex or if the surface curvature is extreme. May not find intersections with other scene geometry as accurately as ray tracing. The method was described in "Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids". It was developed as a practical alternative to ray tracing for fluid animation in interactive environments, where performance is critical. The technique leverages the fact that for many fluid simulations, the visual impact of refraction can be approximated by distorting the background image based on the surface normal. Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cone Marching
body: Cone Marching is an optimization for distance-field ray marching that groups bundles of rays into a cone to skip repeated Signed Distance Function (SDF) calculations. It differs from standard ray marching by performing a coarse, vertex-shader-based march of these cones to advance the ray origin and step count before the fragment shader resumes fine-grained marching. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera position (ro), camera ray direction (rd), camera field of view tangent (u\camTanFov), plane subdivision count (u\camPlaneSubdivisions), maximum distance (u\maxDis), and maximum steps (u\maxSteps). Outputs: A March struct containing the total distance travelled (dis) and the number of steps taken (steps), passed from the vertex shader to the fragment shader. Data Structures March Struct: float dis: Total distance travelled by the cone. int steps: Number of steps taken during the cone march. Algorithm Steps 1. Geometry Setup: Create a marching plane geometry with subdivisions. The width segments are calculated as \lfloor camera.aspect \times 32 \rfloor and height segments as 32 to ensure square/evenly spaced vertices and avoid artifacts. 2. Vertex Shader Cone March: Compute the cone ray origin (cro) and direction (crd) in world space. Initialize total distance d = 0 and step counter i = 0. Loop while i < u\maxSteps: Calculate current position: p = cro + d \cdot crd. Calculate scene distance: cd = scene(p). Calculate current cone radius: ccr = \frac{d \cdot u\camTanFov \cdot 2.0}{u\camPlaneSubdivisions}. Check break condition: If cd < ccr \cdot 1.25 OR d \ge u\maxDis, break the loop. The padding factor 1.25 is used to avoid artifacts at SDF edges. Advance distance: d += cd. Increment steps: i += 1. Return March(d, i). 3. Fragment Shader Fine March: Receive vDisTravelled and vSteps from the vertex shader. If vDisTravelled \ge u\maxDis, return clear color. Compute ray origin ro and direction rd for the specific pixel. Call rayMarch(vDisTravelled, vSteps, ro, rd). The rayMarch function initializes its loop counter at vSteps and starting distance at vDisTravelled, continuing until hit or max distance. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct March: dis: float steps: int def conemarch(cro: vec3, crd: vec3) -> March: d = 0.0 i = 0 while i < umaxSteps: p = cro + d crd cd = scene(p) ccr = (d ucamTanFov 2.0) / ucamPlaneSubdivisions # Break if intersection detected (with padding) or max distance reached if cd < ccr 1.25 or d >= umaxDis: break d += cd i += 1 return March(dis=d, steps=i) def vertexshader(): # Compute cro and crd in world space #... (transform UV to clip, unproject, transform to world, normalize)... result = conemarch(cro, crd) vDisTravelled = result.dis vSteps = result.steps def raymarch(startdis: float, stepstaken: int, ro: vec3, rd: vec3) -> float: d = startdis i = stepstaken while i < umaxSteps: p = ro + d rd cd = scene(p) # Standard ray marching break condition if cd < ueps or d >= umaxDis: break d += cd i += 1 return d def fragmentshader(): if vDisTravelled >= umaxDis: return uclearColor ro = ucamPos rd = normalize(ucamToWorldMat (ucamInvProjMat vec4(uv 2.0 - 1.0, 0, 1)).xyz) dis = raymarch(vDisTravelled, vSteps, ro, rd) #... shading logic... Parameters u\camTanFov: Tangent of half the camera's field of view. Value: \tan(\frac{camera.fov}{2}). u\camPlaneSubdivisions: Number of subdivisions for the screen/marching plane. Typical value: 32. Padding Factor: 1.25 (used in break condition). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Aspect Ratio Artifacts: Using rectangular screen vertices without accounting for aspect ratio causes artifacts. Vertices must be evenly spaced/square. Padding Selection: The break condition uses a padding factor (1.25) on the cone radius to avoid artifacts at the edges of the SDF, unlike standard ray marching which uses a small epsilon. Complexity: Reduces the number of SDF evaluations in the fragment shader by advancing the ray origin in the vertex shader. Performance: Provides FPS gains by skipping repeated calculations for bundles of rays. Limitations: The simple approach described is less complex than multi-pass cone marching but may not decrease the cone size as effectively as multi-pass methods until it equals pixel size. Cone Marching in this context originates from an implementation in Three.js, described as a straightforward optimization for basic ray marching setups. It is presented as an alternative to more complex multi-pass approaches that theoretically decrease cone size until it equals pixel size. Cone Marching in Three.js, https://medium.com/@nabilnymansour/cone-marching-in-three-js-6d54eac17ad4, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Distance Color Blending
head: Depth-Cued Colors, Intensity Depth-Cuing
body: Distance Color Blending is a shading technique that enhances depth perception in volume rendering by blending the sampled voxel color with a background (sky) color based on the distance from the viewer. It solves the problem of foreground/background distinction in dense volumetric data by applying a transparency falloff that dims distant objects and shifts their hue, simulating atmospheric haze or aerial perspective. Unlike standard lighting models which compute surface reflectance, this method operates on the accumulated color along the ray, modulating it non-linearly with depth. It is distinct from Ray-marched Shadows (which occlude light) and Ambient Occlusion via SDF (which darkens crevices), as it specifically targets global depth cues rather than local geometry lighting. Inputs: cv: The color of the volume sample at the current hit point or integration step. cb: The background (sky) color. dv: The normalized distance of the sample from the viewer, typically the fraction of the total ray length or a normalized depth value in [0, 1]. k{ds}: Depth scaling factor controlling the magnitude of the blending effect. k{de}: Depth exponent controlling the rate of application (non-linearity). Alternative Inputs for Linear Variant: z: fragment depth; z{\max}: maximum depth in scene; \text{depth}: attenuation parameter. Outputs: cd: The final depth-cued color. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar variables for color (vec3 or vec4) and distance (float). Steps: 1. Calculate Distance: Determine the distance from the eye to the current sample point. In ray marching, this is the accumulated ray length t or the normalized fraction dv. 2. Compute Blending Factor: Calculate the blending factor B (or s) based on the distance and chosen falloff function (exponential or linear). 3. Blend Colors: Interpolate between the volume color cv and the background color cb using the blending factor. 4. Output: Return the resulting color cd. Formulas: Exponential Depth Cueing (Standard): The blending factor B is calculated as: B = k{ds} dv^{k{de}} The final color is: cd = (1 - B) cv + B cb Where: cd is the depth-cued color. cv is the original voxel color. cb is the background color. dv is the fraction of distance through the volume. k{ds} controls the size/magnitude of the blending effect. k{de} controls the rate of application (exponent). Note: Some implementations use a cubic exponential falloff for the fog factor F: F = 1.0 - \exp(-k d^3) C{final} = C{obj} \cdot (1 - F) + C{bg} \cdot F Where k = 10^{-7} and d is the object distance. Note: Another exponential variant uses ray distance t directly: \text{fog} = 1.0 - \exp(-0.0035 \cdot t^2) \text{col} = \text{mix}(\text{lit\color}, \text{sky\color}, \text{fog}) Clamped to [0.0, 1.0]. Linear Depth Cueing: The blending factor s is calculated as: s = \frac{1 + \text{depth} \times z}{1 + z{\max}} The final color intensity I is modified to: I{final} = s I + (1 - s) I{bg} Where: z is the z-value of the fragment. z{\max} is the maximal z-value in the scene. \text{depth} is the attenuation parameter. I is the original intensity. I{bg} is the background color intensity. Parameters: k{ds}: Typical value 1.0. k{de}: Typical value 0.5. cb: Background color. If grey (a,a,a), only intensity dimming occurs. If blue (a,b,c) with c>a,b, a cool shift is introduced to simulate aerial perspective. Fog density coefficient: 0.0035 (for the t^2 exponential variant). k: 10^{-7} (for the d^3 exponential variant). Linear depth parameter: Non-zero to enable attenuation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure dv is normalized correctly to avoid blending artifacts at the volume boundaries. Color Shift: Using a non-grey background color cb introduces a hue shift (e.g., blue shift for distance). This should be intentional to simulate atmospheric scattering; otherwise, use a grey background for pure intensity dimming. Clamping: The blending factor and final color must be clamped to [0.0, 1.0] to prevent overflow or negative values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distancecolorblending(cv, cb, dv, kds, kde): """ Exponential Distance Color Blending. Args: cv (vec3): Volume color at current sample. cb (vec3): Background color. dv (float): Normalized distance through volume [0, 1]. kds (float): Depth scaling factor. kde (float): Depth exponent. Returns: vec3: Depth-cued color. """ # Calculate blending factor B # B = kds dv ^ kde # Note: If dv is 0, B is 0. If dv is 1, B is kds. # Ensure kds is scaled if necessary to keep B in [0, 1] range for full depth. B = kds (dv kde) # Clamp B to [0, 1] B = max(0.0, min(1.0, B)) # Blend colors cd = (1.0 - B) cv + B cb return cd def lineardepthcueing(cv, cb, z, zmax, depthparam): """ Linear Depth Cueing. Args: cv (vec3): Volume color. cb (vec3): Background color. z (float): Fragment depth. zmax (float): Maximal depth in scene. depthparam (float): Attenuation parameter. Returns: vec3: Depth-cued color. """ # Calculate blending factor s s = (1.0 + depthparam z) / (1.0 + zmax) # Clamp s to [0, 1] s = max(0.0, min(1.0, s)) # Blend colors cd = s cv + (1.0 - s) cb return cd Exponential Depth Cueing is a shading technique that simulates atmospheric fog to enhance depth perception in volume rendering by dimming distant voxels. It solves the problem of foreground/background distinction in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear transparency falloff based on normalized depth. Unlike linear cueing, it uses an exponential function to control how rapidly objects recede into darkness, allowing for more natural aerial perspective effects. See Exponential Depth Cueing. Linear Depth Cueing is a technique to simulate atmospheric attenuation as depth cuing, blending colors of distant objects with the background color to indicate distance. It uses a linear interpolation factor based on the fragment's z-depth relative to the maximum scene depth. It is simpler to implement but may appear less natural than exponential variants for large depth ranges. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The blending calculation involves a few arithmetic operations (multiplication, exponentiation, addition) and is negligible compared to the ray marching or volume integration cost. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional buffers are required beyond the color and depth values. Performance: The technique is computationally inexpensive and can be applied in the fragment shader or during the final color accumulation step without significant performance impact. Strengths: Enhances depth perception significantly in dense volumes; simple to implement; adds atmospheric realism. Limitations: Does not account for actual light scattering physics (it is a heuristic); the choice of parameters (k{ds}, k{de}) is artistic and may require tuning for different scenes. When to Use: When depth perception is critical in dense volumetric data, or when simulating atmospheric effects like fog or haze. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy of light transport is required, or when the volume is sparse and depth cues are already provided by geometry. Distance Color Blending, also known as Intensity Depth-Cuing, is a well-known technique for enhancing the perception of depth in a scene, originally described in computer graphics literature [Foley96, cited in S5]. It dims the color of objects far from the viewer, creating an effect similar to viewing the scene through haze. The technique has been adapted for volume rendering to dim volume sample colors as they recede from the viewer. It has also been augmented with color modulation to increase blue in distant samples, simulating aerial perspective used by painters for centuries. The method is often extended to optical models in volume rendering to enhance depth perception. name: Exponential Depth Cueing
head: Fog Depth Cueing
body: Exponential Depth Cueing is a shading technique that simulates atmospheric fog to enhance depth perception in volume rendering by dimming distant voxels. It solves the problem of foreground/background distinction in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear transparency falloff based on normalized depth. Unlike linear cueing, it uses an exponential function to control how rapidly objects recede into darkness, allowing for more natural aerial perspective effects. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: frontfactor (fog transparency at the front plane), density (fog density parameter), and depth (normalized distance of the voxel from the viewer). Outputs: A transparency factor T used to modulate the voxel's color components. Data Structures: The method relies on scalar parameters and a single computed transparency value. No complex data structures are required beyond the standard volume rendering context. Parameters: frontfactor: Transparency of the fog at the front plane. Must be positive. Usually < 1.0. Larger values brighten the foreground. density: Controls the fog density, determining how rapidly objects recede into darkness. depth: Normalized depth value, where 0 is at the front plane of the viewing volume and 1 is at the back plane. Formula: The fog transparency T is calculated as: T = \text{front\factor} \times \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{depth}) Each voxel color component is multiplied by T during rendering. Steps: 1. Enable depth cueing in the rendering context. 2. Set the depth cueing parameters (frontfactor and density). 3. For each voxel or sample point along the ray: a. Determine the normalized depth value (0 at front, 1 at back). b. Calculate T using the formula above. c. Multiply the voxel's color components by T. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exponentialdepthcueing(frontfactor, density, depth): """ Calculate fog transparency for exponential depth cueing. Args: frontfactor (float): Transparency at the front plane (positive, usually < 1.0). density (float): Fog density controlling recession rate. depth (float): Normalized depth [0.0, 1.0]. Returns: float: Transparency factor T. """ # Guard against invalid inputs if frontfactor <= 0: raise ValueError("frontfactor must be positive") if density < 0: raise ValueError("density should be non-negative for standard fog") if depth < 0 or depth > 1: raise ValueError("depth must be normalized between 0 and 1") # Calculate transparency using exponential falloff T = frontfactor math.exp(-density depth) return T def applycueingtovoxel(color, frontfactor, density, depth): """ Apply exponential depth cueing to a voxel's color. Args: color (tuple): RGB color of the voxel. frontfactor (float): Transparency at the front plane. density (float): Fog density. depth (float): Normalized depth [0.0, 1.0]. Returns: tuple: Cueing-applied RGB color. """ T = exponentialdepthcueing(frontfactor, density, depth) cueingcolor = (color[0] T, color[1] T, color[2] T) return cueingcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure density and depth are handled with sufficient precision to avoid numerical instability when depth is large and density is high, which could result in underflow to zero. Boundaries: depth must be strictly normalized between 0 and 1 as defined by the viewing volume planes. Parameter Constraints: frontfactor must be positive. An efficient ray marching algorithm designed to accurately generate spatial-temporal points for deformable tissue reconstruction, balancing rendering speed and reconstruction quality. It outperforms the Depth-Cueing method in PSNR (33.374 vs 31.325) and SSIM (0.907 vs 0.897) on the EndoNeRF dataset, while maintaining competitive inference speed (1.73 fps vs 1.95 fps). The Depth-Cueing method suffers from suboptimal performance due to reliance on noisy and incomplete stereo depth data and is inapplicable for temporal interpolation due to the absence of stereo depth in certain contexts. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel/sample for the transparency calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for parameters. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics for Exponential Depth Cueing alone are not provided in the sources. However, comparative data for the "Depth-Cueing" method (which uses this exponential model) on the EndoNeRF dataset shows a test speed of 1.95 fps, PSNR of 31.325, SSIM of 0.897, and LPIPS of 0.132. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively distinguishes foreground from background; computationally inexpensive. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth information; performance degrades with noisy or incomplete stereo depth data; not suitable for temporal interpolation in dynamic scenes. When to Use: When enhancing depth perception in static or quasi-static volume data with reliable depth information is required. When Not to Use: In dynamic scenes requiring temporal interpolation or when stereo depth data is noisy/incomplete. Exponential Depth Cueing was introduced as part of the VolPack volume rendering library. It is designed to introduce black "fog" to make distant voxels appear darker than close ones, thereby aiding in the distinction of foreground objects from background objects. The technique is implemented via specific API calls (vpEnable and vpSetDepthCueing) within the VolPack context. name: Ray-marched Shadows
head: Hard Shadow Ray Marching, Hard Shadows, Hard Shadows via Sphere Tracing, SDF Shadow Ray Marching, SDF Shadows
body: Ray-marched shadows determine if a surface point is occluded from a light source by performing sphere tracing along a ray directed from the surface point toward the light. Unlike Distance Color Blending which blends colors based on depth, this method returns a binary occlusion factor (0 for shadow, 1 for light) by checking if the Signed Distance Field (SDF) drops below a threshold before the ray reaches the light. It differs from Shadow Casting Algorithm by leveraging the global geometric information inherent in the SDF, requiring no separate shadow map pass or rasterization overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: x: The 3D surface point being shaded (obtained from the primary ray march). lightPos: The 3D position of the light source. f: The scene's Signed Distance Function, where f(p) returns the distance to the nearest surface at point p. D: The maximal ray traversal distance (typically the distance to the light source for point lights, or a large constant for directional lights). tmin: The initial traversal distance to prevent self-shadowing. epsilon: The intersection threshold (e.g., 10^{-3} or 0.001). Outputs: shadowFactor: A scalar value, typically 1.0 if not in shadow, and 0.0 (or a small value like 0.2) if in shadow. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values and 3D vectors. Parameters: epsilon: Intersection threshold. Typical values: 0.001, 10^{-3}. tmin: Initial step. Must be > \epsilon to avoid self-intersection. Typical values: 0.1, or a small offset like 10^{-3}. D: Max traversal distance. For directional lights, this is often an arbitrary large value or the scene bounding box diameter. MAXMARCHSTEPS: Optional limit on iterations to prevent infinite loops. Typical value: 255, 20. Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: Calculate the unit direction vector toward the light: \mathbf{r}{Ld} = \text{normalize}(\text{lightPos} - \mathbf{x}). 2. Initialize Traversal: Set current distance t = t{min} and distance to surface d = 0. 3. March Loop: While t < D (and optionally t < \text{MAX\MARCH\STEPS}): a. Evaluate the SDF at the current ray position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{x} + t \cdot \mathbf{r}{Ld}. Compute d = f(\mathbf{p}). b. Check Intersection: If d < \epsilon, the ray has hit a surface. Return 0 (in shadow). c. Advance: Update t = t + d. 4. Return: If the loop completes without hitting a surface, return 1 (not in shadow). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchedshadow(x, lightpos, scenesdf, epsilon=0.001, tmin=0.1, maxdist=None): """ Computes hard shadow for point x relative to lightpos using SDF sphere tracing. Args: x: vec3, surface point. lightpos: vec3, light position. scenesdf: function, returns distance to nearest surface. epsilon: float, intersection threshold. tmin: float, initial step to avoid self-shadowing. maxdist: float, max traversal distance. If None, uses distance to light. Returns: float: 1.0 if lit, 0.0 if in shadow. """ # 1. Initialize Ray lightdir = normalize(lightpos - x) # Determine max distance if maxdist is None: maxdist = length(lightpos - x) # 2. Initialize Traversal t = tmin d = 0.0 # 3. March Loop while t < maxdist: # a. Evaluate SDF p = x + t lightdir d = scenesdf(p) # b. Check Intersection if d < epsilon: return 0.0 # In shadow # c. Advance t += d # 4. Return return 1.0 # Not in shadow Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Shadowing: If t{min} is 0, the initial point \mathbf{x} yields distance d=0 (since \mathbf{x} is on the surface). This triggers the intersection condition d < \epsilon immediately, incorrectly marking the point as in shadow. To fix this, t{min} must be > \epsilon, or the ray origin must be offset by the normal: \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{n} \cdot \text{offset}. Precision: Floating-point precision errors can cause jitter or incorrect occlusion near surfaces. Using a small t{min} and appropriate \epsilon mitigates this. Soft Shadow Ray Marching computes a soft shadow factor along a ray by accumulating the ratio of the Signed Distance Field (SDF) height to the ray step distance, simulating area light penumbra. Unlike Hard Shadow Ray Marching, which returns a binary occlusion result, this method attenuates illumination based on how close the ray passes to intervening geometry relative to the light's size. It differs from Shadow Casting Algorithm by leveraging the global geometric information inherent in the SDF, requiring no separate shadow map pass or rasterization overhead. Time Complexity: O(N) per light source per pixel, where N is the number of sphere tracing steps. N depends on the scene complexity and the distance to the light. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel per light. Performance: Hard shadows are straightforward to implement with SDFs compared to rasterization, requiring only one additional sphere trace per light source per pixel. However, they add significant computational cost proportional to the number of lights, as each light requires a separate ray march. Strengths: No aliasing artifacts associated with shadow maps (e.g., pixelation, peter-panning); shadows are resolution-independent and consistent with the SDF geometry. Limitations: Computationally expensive for multiple lights; hard shadows can appear aliased if the step size is too large relative to the geometry. Soft shadows require careful tuning of the attenuation function. Ray-marched shadows were popularized in the context of Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching for real-time graphics. The technique is described in "GPU Ray Marching of Distance Fields" (DTU, 2011) as Algorithm 3.2, attributed to IQ (Inigo Quilez). It is a standard component of SDF-based renderers, often cited alongside basic sphere tracing. name: Soft Shadow Ray Marching
head: MIP shadow, Quilez soft shadows, SDF Shadows, Soft March, Soft Shadow Calculation via SDF, Soft Shadow Casting via Raymarching, Soft Shadows, Soft Shadows via SDF
body: Soft Shadow Ray Marching computes a soft shadow factor along a ray by accumulating the ratio of the Signed Distance Field (SDF) height to the ray step distance, simulating area light penumbra. Unlike Hard Shadow Ray Marching, which returns a binary occlusion result, this method attenuates illumination based on how close the ray passes to intervening geometry relative to the light's size. It differs from Shadow Casting Algorithm by leveraging the global geometric information inherent in the SDF, requiring no separate shadow map pass or rasterization overhead. Inputs: Surface point p (position on the zero-isosurface). Light direction L (normalized vector from p to light source). Scene SDF function f(x) returning distance to nearest geometry. Light size parameter L{size} (or sharpness coefficient k). Maximum shadow distance D{max} (optional, for performance). Maximum iteration count N{max} (optional, for performance). Outputs: Shadow factor s \in [0, 1], where 1 is fully lit and 0 is fully shadowed. Data Structures: Standard floating-point variables for distance, position, and accumulation. Parameters: k (or L{size}): Controls shadow hardness/penumbra width. Typical values: k=12.0, k=16.0, k=20.0, or L{size}=0.03. D{max}: Maximum ray distance. Typical value: 60.0. N{max}: Maximum steps. Typical value: 64, 128, or 60. \epsilon: Minimum step size or occlusion threshold. Typical value: 0.0001 or 0.001. Algorithm: 1. Initialize accumulated shadow factor res = 1.0. 2. Initialize current distance along ray t = \epsilon (to avoid self-intersection). 3. Loop for i from 0 to N{max}-1: a. Evaluate sample point p{sample} = p + t \cdot L. b. Query SDF: h = f(p{sample}). c. Hard Occlusion Check: If h < \epsilon, the ray has intersected geometry. Return 0.0. d. Penumbra Calculation: Update res = \min(res, k \cdot \frac{h}{t}). Note: Some implementations use a logarithmic denominator to prevent artifacts when lights are near objects: res = \min(res, \frac{h}{\log(t \cdot w + 1.0)}) where w is a sharpness parameter. e. Step Advance: t = t + h. f. Termination Check: If t > D{max} or res < \epsilon, break loop. 4. Return \text{clamp}(res, 0.0, 1.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softshadowraymarch(p, lightdir, scenesdf, k=12.0, maxdist=60.0, maxsteps=64): """ Computes soft shadow factor using SDF ray marching. Args: p: vec3, surface point lightdir: vec3, normalized direction to light scenesdf: function, returns distance to nearest geometry k: float, shadow hardness coefficient (inverse of light size) maxdist: float, maximum ray length maxsteps: int, maximum iterations Returns: float: shadow factor in [0, 1] """ res = 1.0 t = 0.01 # epsilon to avoid self-intersection for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: break # Sample point along the ray samplepoint = p + t lightdir # Query distance field h = scenesdf(samplepoint) # Hard occlusion: if we hit geometry closely, it's fully shadowed if h < 0.0001: return 0.0 # Accumulate soft shadow factor # Quilez formula: min(res, k h / t) # Alternative logarithmic form to prevent near-light artifacts: # res = min(res, h / log(t w + 1.0)) res = min(res, k h / t) # Advance ray by the safe distance t += h # Early exit if fully shadowed if res < 0.001: break # Clamp result to valid range return max(0.0, min(1.0, res)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Shadowing: The initial step t must be greater than zero (typically \epsilon \approx 0.01) to prevent the surface point from occluding itself. Near-Light Artifacts: A linear drop-off (h/t) can cause severe artifacts when light sources are placed very close to objects. Using a logarithmic denominator or capping the ratio mitigates this. Precision: If h is extremely small but not below the threshold, the ratio h/t may underflow or cause instability. The threshold check h < \epsilon handles this by returning 0.0 (fully occluded). Alias Artifacts: Hard shadows exhibit aliasing; soft shadows naturally smooth these transitions due to the penumbra calculation. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of ray march steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Performance: Adds minimal overhead compared to hard shadows, as it reuses the same ray march loop with an additional ratio accumulation. Performance scales with scene density; denser geometry may require more steps or earlier termination. Strengths: No separate pass required; works with any SDF; naturally anti-aliased; supports dynamic geometry without update costs. Limitations: Approximate; does not simulate complex light transport (e.g., multiple bounces); quality depends on step size and k parameter tuning. The technique was popularized by Inigo Quilez, who demonstrated that SDFs provide global scene information useful for soft shadows without additional data structures. It is a standard feature in raymarched SDF renderers, often cited alongside ambient occlusion as a "free" shading effect. Variations include logarithmic adjustments for near-light stability and scale-based penumbra control.
