name: Shadow Casting Algorithm
head: cast shadows algorithm
body: The Shadow Casting Algorithm determines if a surface point is in shadow by projecting light through a volumetric dataset to compute occlusion, effectively simulating how light interacts with embedded geometric structures within volume data. It differs from standard ray-marched shadows by treating the shadow calculation as a resampling operation that integrates light attenuation through the volume, allowing for the simultaneous rendering of geometric polygons and volumetric data. The algorithm computes the total voxel colors by accounting for light attenuation caused by both the volumetric data and embedded geometric polygons. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D array of voxel opacities (density), a set of embedded geometric polygons (e.g., scan-converted surfaces), and a light source definition. Output: An array of total voxel colors representing the final illumination after shadowing. Data Structures: Voxel Array: A 3D grid storing initial light strengths or opacities. Polygon Data: Geometric definitions of embedded surfaces, often scan-converted into the volume space. Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the 2D profile geometry or polygon data into the array of initial light strengths. For volumetric data, assign all voxels a slightly non-zero opacity if simulating effects like dust-filled rooms. 2. Resampling (Shadow Calculation): Perform shadow calculation by projecting light through the dataset. The standard implementation involves three successive resampling steps to map the light field onto the volume. Note: To eliminate one resampling step and yield crisper shadows, reorganize the order of operations in the shadow casting algorithm. 3. Attenuation: Apply tri-linear interpolation during 3D scan-conversion to resample 3D data. This step accumulates opacity along the light path. 4. Final Computation: Compute the array of total voxel colors by combining the initial light strengths with the accumulated attenuation from the volume and polygons. Pitfalls: Excessive Blurring: Frequent tri-linear interpolation for resampling 3D data causes excessive blurring during 3D scan-conversion, resulting in softer polygonal edges than desired. A better filter would reduce this blurring. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shadowcastingalgorithm(voxelgrid, polygons, lightsource): """ Computes shadowed illumination for a volume with embedded polygons. """ # Initialize the light strength array # Load polygon geometry into initial light strengths if simulating specific effects lightarray = initializelightarray(voxelgrid, polygons) # Standard implementation: Three successive resampling steps # Step 1: Resample light field based on volume density lightarray = resamplestep1(lightarray, voxelgrid) # Step 2: Resample light field based on polygon occlusion lightarray = resamplestep2(lightarray, polygons) # Step 3: Final resampling to map to output space finalcolors = resamplestep3(lightarray) return finalcolors def optimizeshadowcasting(voxelgrid, polygons, lightsource): """ Optimized version that reorders operations to eliminate one resampling step. """ lightarray = initializelightarray(voxelgrid, polygons) # Reorganized order to reduce blurring and improve crispness # Perform necessary resampling steps in an optimized sequence # This eliminates one of the three successive resampling steps optimizedcolors = optimizedresamplesequence(lightarray, voxelgrid, polygons) return optimizedcolors Texture projection maps 2D textures onto geometric and volumetric data by projecting textures through space onto surfaces. It solves the difficulty of wrapping textures around volumetrically defined objects, where the defining surfaces are not explicitly known, by projecting through space rather than relying on surface parameterization. It differs from direct surface wrapping by treating the texture as a light-like projection, allowing it to be handled as a straightforward extension of the shadow casting algorithm. A strategy to render geometric objects defined by extrusion of 2D profiles using the shadow casting algorithm to simulate volumetric light shafts. The profile is loaded into the array of initial light strengths, and all voxels in the volumetric data are assigned a slightly non-zero opacity to obtain the effect of sculpted shafts of light passing through a dust-filled room. If the beam is assumed to pass through the volumetric data without attenuation, it can be rendered without a separate shadow pass and without the accompanying 3D representation. Time Complexity: Adding shadows roughly doubles the time required to compute the array of total voxel colors. However, it does not affect the time required to generate each frame in a rotation sequence when lighting and data are fixed, the observer moves, and specular highlights are absent. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The addition of textures to the algorithm increases image generation time by roughly 50%, depending on the number and size of textured polygons. Strengths: Produces images free from aliasing artifacts and handles mixtures of geometric and volumetric data efficiently. Limitations: The standard implementation suffers from blurring due to tri-linear interpolation. Computational expense can be high for complex polygonal data, potentially requiring hierarchical data structures or unified data structures for both geometric and volumetric data to speed up processing. The Shadow Casting Algorithm was developed in the context of rendering mixtures of geometric and volumetric data, particularly for applications such as radiation treatment planning. It addresses the challenge of visualizing how light (or radiation beams) interacts with both explicit geometric structures and implicit volumetric data simultaneously. The work acknowledges contributions from the Computer Science and Radiation Oncology departments, utilizing CT scans and electron density maps for validation. name: Texture Projection
head: Texture Mapping, Projective Texture Mapping
body: Texture projection maps 2D textures onto geometric and volumetric data by projecting textures through space onto surfaces. It solves the difficulty of wrapping textures around volumetrically defined objects, where the defining surfaces are not explicitly known, by projecting through space rather than relying on surface parameterization. It differs from direct surface wrapping by treating the texture as a light-like projection, allowing it to be handled as a straightforward extension of the shadow casting algorithm. Inputs: Volumetric dataset (implicit or explicit surface definition). Geometric polygons (optional, embedded in volumetric data). 2D texture map. Projection parameters (origin, direction, or projection matrix). Outputs: Textured surface appearance for the volumetric object or embedded polygons. Data Structures: Texture coordinates (u, v) generated per sample point on the surface. Sample point position \mathbf{p} in world or view space. Steps: 1. Determine Surface Location: Identify the location of the defining surface of the volumetric object. This is the primary challenge, as volumetric data does not inherently provide an explicit boundary. 2. Project Texture Coordinates: For each point \mathbf{p} on the surface, compute the corresponding 2D texture coordinates (u, v) by projecting \mathbf{p} through the texture space. This is analogous to the shadow casting process, where the texture acts as the light source. 3. Sample Texture: Retrieve the color value from the 2D texture map using the computed (u, v) coordinates. 4. Composite: Blend the sampled texture color with the underlying volumetric or geometric shading. Formulas: Let \mathbf{p} be the 3D point on the surface. The projection to 2D texture coordinates (u, v) is typically defined by a projection matrix M: \begin{bmatrix} u' \\ v' \\ w' \end{bmatrix} = M \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} u = \frac{u'}{w'}, \quad v = \frac{v'}{w'} Where (u, v) are normalized to [0, 1]. Parameters: Projection Matrix M: Defines the view frustum or orthographic projection for the texture. Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Surface Ambiguity: Wrapping textures around volumetrically defined objects is difficult because it requires knowing where their defining surfaces lie. Spectral Mismatch: Geometric, volumetric, and texture data each exhibit different spectra. Care must be taken when mixing them to avoid visual artifacts. Embedded Polygons: Mapping textures onto polygons embedded in volumetric datasets is relatively simple but requires handling the intersection of the texture projection with the polygon geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def textureprojection(surfacepoints, texturemap, projectionmatrix): """ Projects a 2D texture onto a set of 3D surface points. Args: surfacepoints: List of 3D points (x, y, z) defining the surface. texturemap: 2D array representing the texture. projectionmatrix: 3x4 or 4x4 matrix for projecting 3D to 2D texture space. Returns: List of colors corresponding to each surface point. """ colors = [] for point in surfacepoints: # Homogeneous coordinates phomogeneous = [point.x, point.y, point.z, 1.0] # Project to texture space # Note: Exact matrix multiplication details depend on the projection type # (orthographic vs perspective). Assuming standard projective transform. uvw = multiplymatrixvector(projectionmatrix, phomogeneous) # Perspective divide if uvw.w == 0: # Handle degenerate case (point at infinity or invalid projection) continue u = uvw.u / uvw.w v = uvw.v / uvw.w # Check bounds if 0 <= u <= 1 and 0 <= v <= 1: # Sample texture color = texturemap.sample(u, v) colors.append(color) else: # Point is outside the texture projection area colors.append(None) # Or handle as background/transparent return colors def multiplymatrixvector(matrix, vector): """ Standard matrix-vector multiplication. matrix: 3x4 or 4x4 vector: 4-element homogeneous vector Returns: 3-element vector (u, v, w) """ # Implementation depends on matrix dimensions. # For a 3x4 matrix: # u = M[0][0]x + M[0][1]y + M[0][2]z + M[0][3] # v = M[1][0]x + M[1][1]y + M[1][2]z + M[1][3] # w = M[2][0]x + M[2][1]y + M[2][2]z + M[2][3] # For a 4x4 matrix, use the first 3 rows. pass Triplanar texture projection maps a 2D texture onto a 3D surface by applying planar mapping in three perpendicular planes (XY, XZ, YZ) and interpolating the results based on the surface normal's alignment. It solves the problem of texture stretching that occurs with single-axis planar mapping on complex or curved surfaces, such as spheres, by ensuring the texture orientation adapts to the local geometry. Unlike its siblings, it avoids visible seams and stretching by weighting three orthogonal projections, making it suitable for shading complex volumetric surfaces. It builds on Texture Projection. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Easier to implement than surface wrapping for volumetric data; integrates with shadow casting algorithms. Limitations: Requires determining surface location for volumetric objects; potential artifacts from spectral mismatch between data types. When to use: When rendering mixtures of geometric and volumetric data where explicit surface parameterization is difficult or unavailable. Texture projection was introduced in the context of rendering mixtures of geometric and volumetric data. The approach is similar to that described by Feibush, Levoy, and Cook [1980]. A good survey of texture mapping algorithms was written by Heckbert [1986]. The technique is part of the broader field of volume rendering, which encompasses both opaque voxel overpainting and semi-transparent voxel blending. name: Triplanar Texture Projection
head: Round Cube Mapping, Trianplanar Texture Projection, Triplanar Mapping, Triplanar Texture Mapping
body: Triplanar texture projection maps a 2D texture onto a 3D surface by applying planar mapping in three perpendicular planes (XY, XZ, YZ) and interpolating the results based on the surface normal's alignment. It solves the problem of texture stretching that occurs with single-axis planar mapping on complex or curved surfaces, such as spheres, by ensuring the texture orientation adapts to the local geometry. Unlike its siblings, it avoids visible seams and stretching by weighting three orthogonal projections, making it suitable for shading complex volumetric surfaces. It builds on Texture Projection. Inputs: p: vec3 position in world or local space. n: vec3 surface normal (normalized). tex: 2D texture sampler. k: float hardness parameter (default 1.0, typical 5.0). Outputs: color: vec3 or vec4 sampled color from the texture. Data Structures: None required beyond standard vector types. Steps: 1. Compute the absolute value of the normal components: a = |n|. 2. Apply the hardness parameter k to the absolute normal components: w = a^k. 3. Normalize the weights to sum to 1.0: W = w / (wx + wy + wz). 4. Sample the texture for each of the three planes using the position components as UV coordinates, typically scaled by a texture repeat factor and offset by 0.5: XY plane (weighted by Z normal): c{xy} = \text{sample}(tex, p{xy}). XZ plane (weighted by Y normal): c{xz} = \text{sample}(tex, p{xz}). YZ plane (weighted by X normal): c{yz} = \text{sample}(tex, p{yz}). 5. Blend the sampled colors using the normalized weights: color = Wx c{yz} + Wy c{xz} + Wz c{xy}. Formulas: The general formula for triplanar mapping with hardness parameter k is: \text{texture}{\text{triplanar}}(p, n, k) = \frac{|nx|^k \cdot \text{sample}(py, pz) + |ny|^k \cdot \text{sample}(px, pz) + |nz|^k \cdot \text{sample}(px, py)}{|nx|^k + |ny|^k + |nz|^k} Where: p = (px, py, pz) is the position. n = (nx, ny, nz) is the surface normal. \text{sample}(u, v) is the texture sampling function. k is the hardness parameter. Parameters: k: Hardness parameter. Controls how sharply the texture aligns with the normal. Higher values make the texture snap more strongly to the dominant axis. Typical value: 5.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Normal: If the normal is zero, the weights are undefined. Guard against this by ensuring the normal is normalized before use. Degenerate Normals: If two components of the normal are zero (e.g., along an axis), the division by sum of weights is still valid as long as at least one component is non-zero. Memory Bandwidth: Triplanar mapping requires three texture lookups per iteration, which is significantly more expensive than biplanar mapping. It is not suitable for sampling heightmaps during ray marching iterations where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triplanartextureprojection(p: Vec3, n: Vec3, tex: Sampler2D, k: float = 5.0) -> Vec3: # Step 1: Absolute normal absn = abs(n) # Step 2: Apply hardness weights = pow(absn, k) # Step 3: Normalize weights weightsum = weights.x + weights.y + weights.z # Guard against division by zero if weightsum == 0.0: return sample(tex, p.xy) # Fallback to XY plane normalizedweights = weights / weightsum # Step 4: Sample textures # XY plane weighted by Z samplexy = sample(tex, p.xy) # XZ plane weighted by Y samplexz = sample(tex, p.xz) # YZ plane weighted by X sampleyz = sample(tex, p.yz) # Step 5: Blend color = normalizedweights.x sampleyz + \ normalizedweights.y samplexz + \ normalizedweights.z samplexy return color This variant addresses the hard edges that appear when texturing voxel models, where each face of a voxel shows a discrete texture snippet. Instead of using the geometric face normal, it calculates a smooth normal by drawing a line from the voxel's center to the ray intersection point. This centroid normal is then used with triplanar mapping to blur the hard edges between voxel faces, providing a softer transition. This is chosen when texturing voxel-based geometry to avoid the blocky appearance of standard AABB texturing. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, but requires three texture lookups instead of one or two. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for intermediate vectors. Performance: Significantly higher memory bandwidth usage than biplanar mapping due to three texture lookups per iteration. Not suitable for heightmap sampling during ray marching where bandwidth is critical. Strengths: Eliminates texture stretching on complex surfaces; no seams or stretching artifacts. Limitations: High computational cost due to multiple texture samples; not ideal for performance-critical heightmap sampling. When to Use: Shading complex curved surfaces to avoid stretching, or texturing voxel models to avoid hard edges between faces. When Not to Use: When sampling heightmaps during ray marching iterations due to high memory bandwidth overhead. Triplanar mapping, also known as round cube mapping, was introduced as a solution to texture stretching in planar mapping for complex surfaces. It is widely used in ray marching and voxel rendering to provide seamless texture application on 3D geometry. The technique is particularly relevant in real-time rendering and voxel-based environments where visual continuity is important. kushchevd/RayMarching, https://github.com/kushchevd/RayMarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Raymarching Distance Fields with CUDA, https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/10/22/2730, fetched 2026-10-27 Raycasting-basiertes Voxelrendering, https://serwiss.bib.hs-hannover.de/frontdoor/index/index/docId/2250, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Ambient Occlusion via SDF
head: AO Ray Marching, Alex Evans AO, Cheap Ambient Occlusion, Normal-direction AO, Proximity-based Occlusion, Ray Marched Ambient Occlusion, Real Ambient Occlusion, SDF AO
body: Ambient Occlusion via SDF approximates the darkening of crevices and contact points by sampling the signed distance function (SDF) along the surface normal. It detects occlusion by comparing the actual distance to nearby geometry against the expected distance if the surface were isolated; a smaller actual distance indicates an obstacle is closer, reducing the ambient light contribution. Unlike screen-space methods or shadow maps, this technique requires no separate rendering pass or auxiliary buffers, relying solely on the scene's distance function. It is computationally cheaper than full ray-marched shadows but provides a local approximation of global illumination effects. Inputs: p: The 3D position of the surface point being shaded. n: The normalized surface normal at p. map(p): The scene SDF function returning the distance to the nearest surface. Outputs: ao: A scalar value in [0, 1], where 0 is fully occluded (black) and 1 is fully lit. Data Structures: No complex structures. Standard floating-point variables. Parameters: numsteps: Number of samples along the normal. Typical values: 5, 20. stepdist: Base step size. Typical values: 0.015, 0.08, or derived via linear interpolation. decay: Exponential decay factor for sample weights. Typical values: 0.6, 0.7. multiplier: Scaling factor applied to the accumulated occlusion before clamping. Typical values: 1.4, 2.0. power: Exponent applied to the final AO term to amplify contrast. Typical value: 40. Algorithm: The method casts a ray from p along n in discrete steps. At each step i, it evaluates the SDF at position pi = p + n \cdot di. The occlusion is determined by the difference between the step distance di and the SDF value hi = \text{map}(pi). If hi < di, another surface is closer than the empty space expected, indicating occlusion. There are three common variations in implementation found in the sources: 1. Linear Step with Exponential Decay (Alex Evans style): Samples at fixed intervals with decaying weights. This is the most common "cheap" AO. 2. Squared Difference with Inverse Distance Weighting: Uses a squared difference term divided by the step index to penalize closer obstacles more heavily while reducing influence of distant samples. 3. Sum Ratio: Sums the SDF values and divides by the expected sum if no occlusion existed. Pseudocode (Linear Step with Exponential Decay): This variant is preferred for its stability and widespread use in real-time raymarching. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ambientocclusionsdf(p, n, numsteps=5, basestep=0.08, decay=0.7, multiplier=2.0): """ Computes ambient occlusion by sampling the SDF along the normal. Args: p: vec3, surface position. n: vec3, surface normal (normalized). numsteps: int, number of samples (typically 5). basestep: float, base distance increment (typically 0.08). decay: float, weight decay per step (typically 0.7). multiplier: float, scaling factor for occlusion intensity (typically 2.0). Returns: float: Ambient occlusion factor in [0, 1]. """ occ = 0.0 weight = 1.0 for i in range(1, numsteps + 1): # Calculate distance for this step dist = basestep i # Evaluate SDF at the sample point # map() is the scene SDF function h = map(p + n dist) # Accumulate occlusion: difference between expected empty space (dist) # and actual distance to geometry (h). # If h < dist, geometry is closer, adding to occlusion. occ += (dist - h) weight # Decay weight for further steps weight = decay # Scale and clamp result # 1.0 - occ gives the lit portion. # multiplier amplifies the effect. ao = 1.0 - (occ multiplier) return clamp(ao, 0.0, 1.0) Pseudocode (Squared Difference Variant): Used in some tutorials for a different falloff characteristic. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ambientocclusionsquared(p, n, stepdist=0.015, stepnbr=20): """ Computes AO using squared difference and inverse step weighting. """ occlusion = 1.0 currentstep = stepnbr while currentstep > 0: # Distance from origin dist = currentstep stepdist # Sample SDF samplepos = p + n dist sdfval = map(samplepos).d #.d implies the distance component # Calculate contribution # Numerator: squared difference between expected distance and actual SDF # Denominator: current step index (reduces influence of far samples) contribution = pow(dist - sdfval, 2) / currentstep occlusion -= contribution currentstep -= 1 return clamp(occlusion, 0.0, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distant Artifacts: If the total travel distance (numsteps stepdist) is too large, distant geometry may contribute to the occlusion term, creating incorrect darkening in open areas. Precision: In high-precision SDFs, small errors in map() can cause flickering. Using highp float precision is recommended. Normal Accuracy: The method assumes n is accurate. Incorrect normals (e.g., from low-poly meshes without smoothing) lead to sampling in empty space or into geometry incorrectly, producing noisy AO. A variant that estimates AO based on the number of raymarching steps required to hit a surface during the primary ray march, rather than a separate normal-based pass. Mechanism: During the standard sphere-tracing loop, if the surface is hit at step index i out of a maximum Steps, the AO coefficient is calculated as 1 - \frac{i}{\text{Steps}-1}. Pros: Zero additional SDF evaluations; leverages existing raymarch data. Cons: Tightly coupled with raymarch resolution; less accurate for local crevices compared to normal sampling. Estimates AO by sampling the SDF at multiple points distributed on a sphere around the surface point, providing a more isotropic occlusion estimate than normal-only sampling. Mechanism: Samples are placed using a golden-ratio-based spherical distribution to ensure uniform density. N: Number of samples (aoSamples). R: Kernel radius (aoKernelSize). For i from 0 to N-1: py = 1 - \frac{i}{N} \cdot 2 r = \sqrt{1 - py^2} \theta = \phi \cdot i, where \phi = \pi(3 - \sqrt{5}) px = \cos(\theta) \cdot r pz = \sin(\theta) \cdot r Sample position: \text{hitPos} + (px, py, pz) \cdot R Accumulate: \text{ao} += \text{saturate}(\frac{\text{SDF}}{R}) Final AO: 1 - (1 - \frac{\sum \text{saturate}(\text{SDF}/R)}{N \cdot 0.5})^2 Parameters: aoSamples typically 8 (range 0-32); aoKernelSize typically 0.075 (range 0.0-0.25). Pros: Better handles occlusion from sides, not just above/below the normal. Cons: More expensive (N SDF calls per pixel vs 5-20 for normal AO). Time Complexity: O(k), where k is the number of AO samples (typically 5-20). It adds a constant overhead to the shading cost per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1). No buffers or textures are required. Performance: Significantly faster than screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO) or ray-marched shadows because it avoids large kernel samples or secondary ray tracing through the entire scene. Strengths: Resolution-independent (unlike SSAO). Works well with procedural SDFs and fractals. Easy to tune via multiplier and decay parameters. Limitations: Approximate: Only considers the local neighborhood along the normal (or sphere). Can produce "halo" artifacts if the step size is too large or if the SDF has sharp discontinuities. Dependent on normal quality. The technique is rooted in the early days of real-time raymarching in WebGL and GLSL. Alex Evans popularized the "cheap ambient occlusion" method using normal-direction SDF sampling in his 2012 GDC talk "Real-Time Ray Tracing" and subsequent demos. It became a staple in the demoscene and indie shader communities due to its ability to add depth to simple SDF scenes without complex lighting pipelines. The squared-difference variant is often cited in educational tutorials explaining the geometric intuition of AO via SDFs. name: Iridescent Material with Perturbation
head: Iridescent Material (Cosine Palette), Iridescent Material with Specular and Shadow
body: This method renders iridescent surfaces by mapping a scalar input to a 3D color vector using a cosine palette function, simulating thin-film interference colors. It combines this base iridescent layer with specular highlights and shadowing to create a complete shading model. It differs from Distance Color Blending by using a continuous palette function driven by perturbed normals rather than discrete distance-based color mixing, and from Phong Shading with SDF Normals by explicitly modeling interference-like color shifts via the palette function rather than standard diffuse/specular reflection. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin (rayOrigin), ray direction (rayDirection), collision distance (collision.x), light position (lightPos), gamma value (GAMMA). Outputs: Final screen-space RGB color. Data Structures: vec3: 3-component floating-point vector (x, y, z). float: Single-precision floating-point scalar. vec3 pal(float t, vec3 a, vec3 b, vec3 c, vec3 d): Palette function returning a color. vec3 spectrum(float n): Spectrum function returning a color based on input n. Parameters: GAMMA: Gamma correction exponent. Typical value: 2.2. Palette coefficients for spectrum: a = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) b = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) c = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) d = (0.0, 0.33, 0.67) Steps: 1. Calculate Intersection Point: Compute the 3D position of the hit point: pos = rayOrigin + rayDirection \cdot collision.x 2. Calculate Normal: Compute the surface normal at pos. Let this be nor. 3. Calculate View and Light Directions: eyeDirection = normalize(rayOrigin - pos) lightDirection = normalize(lightPos - pos) 4. Calculate Reflection Vector: reflection = reflect(rayDirection, nor) 5. Calculate Base Iridescent Color: a. Compute perturbation vector: perturb = sin(pos \cdot 10.) b. Compute perturbed normal input for spectrum: n{input} = dot(nor + perturb \cdot 0.05, eyeDirection) \cdot 2. c. Compute base color using the spectrum function: color = spectrum(n{input}) 6. Calculate Specular Component: a. Compute initial specular term: specular = clamp(dot(reflection, lightDirection), 0., 1.) b. Modulate specular with sine wave and raise to power: specular = pow((sin(specular \cdot 20. - 3.) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5) + 0.1, 32.) \cdot specular c. Scale by 0.1: specular = specular \cdot 0.1 d. Add secondary specular component: specular = specular + pow(clamp(dot(reflection, lightDirection), 0., 1.) + 0.3, 8.) \cdot 0.1 7. Calculate Shadow: a. Define dome direction: dome = (0, 1, 0) b. Compute shadow factor: shadow = pow(clamp(dot(nor, dome) \cdot 0.5 + 1.2, 0., 1.), 3.) 8. Combine Colors: color = color \cdot shadow + specular 9. Apply Gamma Correction: finalColor = linearToScreen(color) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def pal(t: float, a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, c: np.ndarray, d: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """Cosine palette function.""" return a + b np.cos(2 np.pi (c t + d)) def spectrum(n: float) -> np.ndarray: """Spectrum function using specific palette coefficients.""" a = np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) b = np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) c = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) d = np.array([0.0, 0.33, 0.67]) return pal(n, a, b, c, d) def gamma(color: np.ndarray, g: float) -> np.ndarray: """Apply gamma correction.""" return np.power(color, g) def lineartoscreen(linearrgb: np.ndarray, gammaval: float = 2.2) -> np.ndarray: """Convert linear RGB to screen space.""" return gamma(linearrgb, 1.0 / gammaval) def iridescentmaterial(rayorigin: np.ndarray, raydirection: np.ndarray, collisionx: float, lightpos: np.ndarray, normalfunc, gammaval: float = 2.2) -> np.ndarray: """ Calculate iridescent material color. Args: rayorigin: Origin of the ray. raydirection: Direction of the ray. collisionx: Distance to the collision point. lightpos: Position of the light source. normalfunc: Function to compute normal at a given position. gammaval: Gamma value for correction. Returns: Final screen-space color. """ # Step 1: Calculate Intersection Point pos = rayorigin + raydirection collisionx # Step 2: Calculate Normal nor = normalfunc(pos) # Step 3: Calculate View and Light Directions eyedirection = (rayorigin - pos) eyedirection = eyedirection / np.linalg.norm(eyedirection) lightdirection = (lightpos - pos) lightdirection = lightdirection / np.linalg.norm(lightdirection) # Step 4: Calculate Reflection Vector # reflect(I, N) = I - 2 dot(I, N) N # Note: raydirection is incoming, so we use -raydirection for standard reflect formula if N is outward. # However, the source code uses reflect(rayDirection, nor). # In GLSL, reflect(I, N) assumes I is the incident vector. # If rayDirection is from eye to surface, it is the incident vector. reflection = raydirection - 2 np.dot(raydirection, nor) nor # Step 5: Calculate Base Iridescent Color perturb = np.sin(pos 10.0) ninput = np.dot(nor + perturb 0.05, eyedirection) 2.0 color = spectrum(ninput) # Step 6: Calculate Specular Component specular = np.dot(reflection, lightdirection) specular = np.clip(specular, 0.0, 1.0) specular = np.power((np.sin(specular 20.0 - 3.0) 0.5 + 0.5) + 0.1, 32.0) specular specular = specular 0.1 specularterm2 = np.dot(reflection, lightdirection) specularterm2 = np.clip(specularterm2, 0.0, 1.0) specular = specular + np.power(specularterm2 + 0.3, 8.0) 0.1 # Step 7: Calculate Shadow dome = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) shadow = np.dot(nor, dome) 0.5 + 1.2 shadow = np.clip(shadow, 0.0, 1.0) shadow = np.power(shadow, 3.0) # Step 8: Combine Colors color = color shadow + specular # Step 9: Apply Gamma Correction finalcolor = lineartoscreen(color, gammaval) return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of sin and pow with large exponents (32, 8) can lead to precision issues if inputs are not clamped properly. The clamp operations on dot products are critical. Boundaries: The shadow calculation involves dot(nor, dome) 0.5 + 1.2. If nor is not normalized or dome is not a unit vector, this may produce incorrect results. The source assumes nor is normalized. Degenerate Input: If collision.x is invalid (e.g., no collision), the method should not be executed. The source code checks if (collision.x > -0.5). A technique for rendering iridescence in thin films (soap bubbles, oil films) using Airy summation for s/p polarization over multiple wavelengths. It performs Airy summation for s and p polarization components, samples 9 wavelengths to compute the interference pattern, and applies the interference model over a dielectric base or a metal base. For metal bases, it derives the complex Index of Refraction (IOR) from F0 and edge tint using Gulbrandsen's inversion. A key pitfall is that thin film at zero thickness must be handled as a special case to avoid numerical instability or incorrect reflection. A technique to blend Blinn-Phong lighting with iridescent lighting to create tinted iridescent objects. It calculates Blinn-Phong specular by calling blinnPhongSpec(lightDirection, eyeDirection, nor, 0.5) to get power, multiplies by tint to get baseColor. It calculates iridescent color as defined in the base iridescent method. It calculates Blinn-Phong base color as baseColor = power tint. It blends using mix(baseColor, color, mixBaseAndIridescent). The parameter mixBaseAndIridescent is a slider controlling the blend factor between Blinn-Phong and iridescent lighting, typically in range [0,1]. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The method involves a constant number of trigonometric and power operations per hit point. The complexity is O(1) per pixel/sample, assuming normal calculation is O(1). Memory: Minimal memory usage, only storing intermediate vectors and scalars. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement, produces visually appealing iridescent effects with minimal computational cost. Limitations: The iridescence is an approximation and does not physically model thin-film interference accurately. The perturbation is based on position, which may not align with surface features. When to Use: Use when a fast, visually convincing iridescent effect is needed, such as in real-time rendering or stylized graphics. When Not to Use: Use Thin-Film Interference via Airy Summation when physical accuracy is required. The method originates from Thomas Hooper’s Crystals shader, which uses a combination of raymarching and SDF. It was popularized in the context of Shadertoy shaders, where cosine palette functions are commonly used for iridescence. The technique is often used in real-time graphics and procedural art. name: Spherical Gaussian Shading
head: SG Shading, Shading Rendering of Spherical Gaussians, Specular BRDF Approximation
body: Spherical Gaussian (SG) Shading approximates complex lighting environments and specular reflections by decomposing incident radiance into a set of Spherical Gaussians, which are then rendered as discrete point lights or integrated into microfacet BRDF models. It solves the problem of real-time, view-dependent specular shading in volume rendering and neural radiance fields (NeRFs) by replacing expensive environment map lookups or high-order spherical harmonic integrations with efficient, analytically tractable approximations. It differs from Phong Shading with SDF Normals by supporting continuous, view-dependent specular lobes rather than discrete specular highlights, and from Blinn-Phong Shading in Volume Rendering by offering a more flexible parameterization of the specular lobe width and shape via Gaussian parameters. Inputs: Surface position \mathbf{r} and normal \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}). View direction \mathbf{v}. A set of k Spherical Gaussians representing the lighting environment. Each SG k is defined by its center direction \mathbf{c}k, sharpness \sigmak, and intensity Ik. Optional: Light positions \mathbf{p}i and intensities \mathbf{I}i if using the point-light decomposition method. Outputs: Outgoing radiance Lo(\mathbf{v}) or shading color \mathbf{S}{SG}(\mathbf{r}). The lighting environment is stored as a list of Spherical Gaussians. Each SG k contains: center: 3D unit vector \mathbf{c}k representing the dominant direction of the light source. sharpness: Scalar \sigmak > 0 controlling the width of the lobe. intensity: Scalar or vector Ik representing the magnitude of the radiance. For the point-light decomposition variant, each SG is expanded into 5 point lights: centerlight: Position at \mathbf{p}k, intensity I{k,0}. samplelights: 4 positions sampled around \mathbf{c}k, intensities I{k,1} \dots I{k,4} diminishing according to Gaussian probabilities. 1. Point Light Decomposition Method To render a single SG as 5 point lights, the first light is placed at the SG center, and the remaining four are sampled around the center with intensities diminishing according to Gaussian probabilities. For HDR environments, SGs are placed far from the scene to assume distant lighting. The shading contribution \mathbf{S}{SG}(\mathbf{r}) from k point lights is calculated as: \mathbf{S}{SG}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^k \frac{\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \mathbf{L}i(\mathbf{r})}{|\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r})| |\mathbf{L}i(\mathbf{r})|} \frac{\mathbf{I}i}{\gamma \cdot \mathbf{Dis}i(\mathbf{r})^2} Where: \mathbf{L}i(\mathbf{r}) is the direction from the i-th light source to the target point \mathbf{r}. \mathbf{I}i is the intensity of the i-th light. \mathbf{Dis}i(\mathbf{r}) is the Euclidean distance between the light and the surface point. \gamma is a hyperparameter controlling luminance. 2. Microfacet BRDF Approximation Method For specular response approximation, the outgoing radiance is modeled as: Lo(\mathbf{v}) = \sumk \left[ M(\mathbf{l}k, \mathbf{v})(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}k)^+ + \int{\mathbf{l} \in \Omega} D(\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{v})Lk(\mathbf{l})d\mathbf{l} \right] Where: M(\mathbf{l}k, \mathbf{v}) combines Fresnel and mask-shadowing functions. D(\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{v}) is the normal distribution function, modeled using an anisotropic Spherical Gaussian. Lk(\mathbf{l}) is the k-th Spherical Gaussian representing incident radiance. (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}k)^+ denotes the positive part of the dot product (clamped to 0). \gamma: Hyperparameter used to control the luminance of the light. Typical values are not specified in the sources, but it acts as a scaling factor for inverse-square decay. Number of lights per SG: 5. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalgaussianshadingpointlight(r, N, lights, gamma): """ Renders shading using the point-light decomposition of Spherical Gaussians. Args: r: 3D position of the surface point. N: 3D normal vector at r. lights: List of light objects, each with 'pos' (3D vector), 'intensity' (3D vector). gamma: Luminance control hyperparameter. Returns: Shading color vector. """ shading = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Nnorm = length(N) for light in lights: # Calculate direction from light to surface Lvec = light.pos - r Dis = length(Lvec) # Avoid division by zero if Dis < 1e-6: continue Ldir = Lvec / Dis Ndir = N / Nnorm # Diffuse term: N. L dotnl = dot(Ndir, Ldir) # Only contribute if light is in front of surface if dotnl > 0: # Inverse square decay with gamma scaling # Formula: (N. L) I / (gamma Dis^2) attenuation = light.intensity / (gamma Dis Dis) shading += dotnl attenuation return shading def sphericalgaussianshadingbrdfapprox(r, N, v, sglist): """ Approximates specular response using SG-based microfacet BRDF. Note: This is a high-level representation. The integral term requires specific implementation of the anisotropic SG normal distribution D(l,v). Args: r: 3D position. N: 3D normal. v: View direction. sglist: List of Spherical Gaussians (center, sharpness, intensity). Returns: Outgoing radiance. """ Nnorm = length(N) Ndir = N / Nnorm radiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for sg in sglist: # lk is the center direction of the SG lk = sg.center # Term 1: Masking/Shadowing and Fresnel approximation # M(lk, v) is a factor combining fresnel and mask-shadowing. # For simplicity, assume a basic Fresnel approximation or precomputed M. # (n. lk)^+ dotnl = dot(Ndir, lk) if dotnl > 0: # Placeholder for M(lk, v) calculation # M depends on material properties and view angle. M = computefresnelmasking(Ndir, lk, v) radiance += M dotnl sg.intensity # Term 2: Integral of D(l,v) Lk(l) # This integral is approximated by the SG properties. # D(l,v) is modeled through anisotropic spherical Gaussian. # The integral of a Gaussian times a Gaussian is another Gaussian. # This term captures the specular highlight. # Specific implementation of the anisotropic SG integral is required. specularcontribution = computesgspecularintegral(sg, Ndir, v) radiance += specularcontribution return radiance Precision and Order: The SG approximation is not precise enough even with 3rd order spherical Gaussians. It requires a much higher number of coefficients to achieve high fidelity, making it potentially unusable in real-time scenarios if high accuracy is required. HDR Lighting: If the lighting environment is High Dynamic Range (HDR), SGs should be placed far from the scene to assume distant lighting, preventing incorrect intensity scaling. Spatial Variation: When lights are placed at 3D positions in the scene (spatially variant), their directions vary from ray to ray. The distance decay must be calculated per-ray to respect real-world lighting effects. A shadow rendering method fitting NeRFs that uses variance shadow mapping ideas to render cast shadows efficiently by comparing depth inconsistencies from light and camera views, providing soft shadows with visibility in [0, 1]. An approach where incoming radiance is represented through sparsely distributed environment maps. This results in a loss of spatial precision for increased angular resolution, often used in conjunction with SG approximations. Time Complexity: O(k) per pixel, where k is the number of Spherical Gaussians or point lights. The point-light decomposition increases the constant factor by 5x per SG. Memory Complexity: O(k) to store the SG parameters. Performance: The method is designed for real-time or near-real-time performance, but notes that high-precision requirements can make it unusable in real-time scenarios due to the need for many coefficients. Strengths: Efficient approximation of view-dependent specular effects; supports spatially variant lighting; compatible with NeRFs and volume rendering. Limitations: Lower precision compared to higher-order methods; requires careful tuning of \gamma and SG placement for HDR scenes. When to use: When real-time specular shading is needed in neural radiance fields or volume rendering, and high-fidelity global illumination is not critical. When not to use: When high-precision specular reflections are required and computational budget allows for more expensive methods. Spherical Gaussian Shading originated from techniques to approximate complex lighting environments for real-time rendering. The point-light decomposition method was proposed for relighting scenes with object insertions in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). The BRDF approximation approach, using SGs to model the normal distribution function in microfacet models, was developed by Xu et al. as part of localized environment map techniques. name: Custom Shading Models
head: Custom Shading Routines, Per-voxel Shading Callbacks
body: Custom Shading Models provide a mechanism for users to define arbitrary lighting computations per-voxel or per-hit-point, bypassing standard lookup tables or fixed-function pipelines. This family solves the problem of applying non-standard, physically based, or highly stylized lighting effects to volume-rendered or ray-marched geometry. It differs from sibling methods like Phong Shading with SDF Normals by allowing complete algorithmic freedom rather than restricting the user to a specific analytic model, and from Distance Color Blending by operating on lighting calculations rather than color accumulation. The core mechanism for implementing custom shading in volume rendering, as defined by the VolPack API, involves replacing the default shading lookup shader with a user-defined callback. The user registers this callback using vpSetCallback with the VPGRAYSHADEFUNC identifier. When invoked, the callback function computes the color for the current voxel based on the scalar field value, normal, and lighting parameters. Key implementation details: Callback Registration: The user defines a function (e.g., myshader) and registers it via vpSetCallback(vpc, VPGRAYSHADEFUNC, myshader). Lookup Table Alternative: Instead of callbacks, users can create custom routines to initialize shading lookup tables of any size, allowing the use of non-encoded normal vectors or color transfer functions. Performance: Using callback functions can lead to significant performance degradation during rendering compared to lookup table methods. Depth Cueing: An independent feature, depth cueing can be enabled via vpEnable(vpc, VPDEPTHCUE, 1) to darken distant voxels, assisting in foreground/background distinction. A physically based specular model using GGX NDF, Schlick Fresnel, and Smith geometry. Chosen for energy conservation and long-tail highlights. A GPU-based pipeline combining Lambertian diffuse, rim lighting, indirect ambient, and GGX specular for voxel worlds, integrating shadow casting and emissive handling. Combines Blinn-Phong diffuse/specular with metallic Fresnel reflections and emissive contributions, using simplified power-law specular lobes. A CPU-based algorithm modifying voxel palette indices directly based on neighbor occupancy, optimized for immediate visual feedback without ray tracing. Applies lighting (diffuse, specular, ambient) to a face color based on normal and light direction. The normal's Z component is set to its absolute value, and the light vector is normalized from the sine and cosine of LightAngle. The color is computed as max(faceColor.rgb, 0) + GetSpecular(n, light) faceColor.a, then multiplied by (1 - dot(n, light) Diffuse) and lerped between Ambient and 1 using n.z n.z. The final color is set to float4(col, faceColor.a). A procedural surface shader for roads that differentiates between asphalt, curb/shoulder, and terrain based on lateral distance to the road centerline, including emissive lane markings. The lateral distance d is calculated as p.x - roadX(p.z) with absolute value ad. If ad < ROADHALFWIDTH, albedo is dark gray, metal is 0.35, and emissive is 0.0; lane lines are calculated using smoothstep for edge lines, center lines, and dashed separators, adding emissive cyan color. If ad < ROADHALFWIDTH + SHOULDER, albedo is dark gray, metal is 0.1, and emissive is a magenta strip at the road edge. Otherwise, albedo is very dark, metal is 0.0, and emissive is 0.0. Parameters include asphalt metal 0.35, lane line color vec3(0.15, 1.0, 1.1) 1.3, edge line offset ROADHALFWIDTH - 0.3, center line offset 0.18, and dashed line frequency p.z 0.18. The concept of custom shading in volume rendering originated with the VolPack library, which provided a framework for shading volumetric data. VolPack allowed users to either initialize custom shading lookup tables or define callback routines for per-voxel shading, offering flexibility beyond its default encoded normal vectors. This approach laid the groundwork for modern custom shading models in ray marching and voxel engines, where users implement specific lighting equations (such as GGX or Blinn-Phong variants) directly in shader code or CPU routines. name: GGX Microfacet BRDF
head: GGX BRDF, GGX Microfacet Model, GGX Microfacet Specular Model, GGX Shading, Walter et al. Specular
body: The GGX Microfacet BRDF is a specular reflection model that approximates surface scattering using a Gaussian distribution of microfacet normals (GGX) combined with the Schlick Fresnel approximation and a Smith geometry function. It is chosen over simpler models like Blinn-Phong for its physically plausible long-tail specular highlights and energy conservation properties. It builds on Custom Shading Models by providing a specific analytical formulation for rough surfaces. Inputs: Surface normal N, view direction V, light direction L, roughness parameter \alpha{rough}, base specular reflectance F0. Outputs: Specular reflection coefficient fr. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required for the standard implementation. Inputs are scalar or vector values. Steps: 1. Compute the half-vector H = \text{normalize}(L + V). 2. Compute squared roughness \alpha = \alpha{rough}^2. 3. Compute the GGX Normal Distribution Function (NDF) D(N, H, \alpha): D = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi \left( (N \cdot H)^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1 \right)^2 + \epsilonD} where N \cdot H = \max(\text{dot}(N, H), 0.0) and \epsilonD = 10^{-6} prevents division by zero. 4. Compute the geometry parameter k: k = \frac{(\alpha{rough} + 1)^2}{8} Note: Source uses an alternative approximation k = 0.5 \alpha and k^2 = k \cdot k in its specific shader implementation. The standard Smith formulation uses the former. 5. Compute the single-scattering geometry term G1 for view and light directions: G1(V) = \frac{N \cdot V}{\max((N \cdot V)(1 - k) + k, \epsilonG)} G1(L) = \frac{N \cdot L}{\max((N \cdot L)(1 - k) + k, \epsilonG)} where N \cdot V = \max(\text{dot}(N, V), 0.0), N \cdot L = \max(\text{dot}(N, L), 0.0), and \epsilonG = 10^{-6}. 6. Compute the total geometry term G = G1(V) \cdot G1(L). 7. Compute the Schlick Fresnel term F(L, H, F0): F = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - L \cdot H)^5 where L \cdot H = \max(\text{dot}(L, H), 0.0). 8. Compute the final specular BRDF value: fr = \frac{D \cdot G \cdot F}{4 (N \cdot V) (N \cdot L) + \epsilon{denom}} where \epsilon{denom} = 10^{-4}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ggxmicrofacetbrdf(N, V, L, roughness, F0): # 1. Half vector H = normalize(L + V) # 2. Squared roughness alpha = roughness roughness alphasqr = alpha alpha # 3. GGX NDF dotNH = max(dot(N, H), 0.0) denomD = dotNH dotNH (alphasqr - 1.0) + 1.0 D = alphasqr / (PI denomD denomD + 1e-6) # 4. Geometry parameter k (Standard Smith) k = (roughness + 1.0) 2 / 8.0 # 5. Geometry terms dotNV = max(dot(N, V), 0.0) dotNL = max(dot(N, L), 0.0) G1V = dotNV / max(dotNV (1.0 - k) + k, 1e-6) G1L = dotNL / max(dotNL (1.0 - k) + k, 1e-6) G = G1V G1L # 6. Fresnel dotLH = max(dot(L, H), 0.0) F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) (1.0 - dotLH) 5 # 7. Final BRDF denomspec = 4.0 dotNV dotNL + 1e-4 specular = (D G F) / denomspec return specular Parameters: roughness: Surface roughness. Typical value: 0.54. F0: Base specular reflectance. Typical value: 0.14 for dielectrics. For metals, this is derived from measured refractive index data. Edge Cases: Division by zero is prevented by adding epsilon values (10^{-6} or 10^{-4}) to denominators in D and the final specular term. Degenerate inputs (e.g., N \cdot V = 0) result in zero specular contribution due to the geometry term or denominator guards. A method to ensure energy conservation for rough metals by compensating for energy lost in single-scattering GGX specular lobes. It uses a precomputed 32x32 directional albedo table E(\mu, \alpha), where \mu is cosine and \alpha is roughness. This ensures that white rough metal reflects ~100% at every roughness, correcting the energy loss inherent in single-scattering approximations. Time Complexity: O(1) per light per surface point. Requires several trigonometric and dot-product operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) for standard GGX. O(1) lookup for multi-scattering compensation if the table is baked into shader memory. Performance: Fast enough for real-time rendering. The Schlick approximation is computationally cheap compared to full Fresnel equations. Strengths: Physically plausible highlights, handles rough surfaces well, widely supported in PBR pipelines. Limitations: Single-scattering approximation loses energy for very rough metals, requiring compensation. Does not account for subsurface scattering or thin-film effects without extensions. When to use: Real-time rendering of rough surfaces where visual fidelity is important. When not to use: When exact energy conservation for rough metals is critical without post-processing compensation, or when subsurface scattering is required. The GGX distribution was introduced by Walter et al. in "Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces" (2007). It is based on the Trowbridge-Reitz distribution, which provides a better fit for many real-world materials compared to the Beckmann distribution. The Schlick Fresnel approximation is a standard simplification used in real-time graphics. The model is widely used in modern PBR engines and voxel shaders. name: Voxel Shading Pipeline
head: Block Shading, Shading and Lighting, Voxel Lighting
body: The Voxel Shading Pipeline is a fragment-shader-based lighting model for ray-marched voxel worlds that combines Lambertian diffuse shading, rim lighting, indirect ambient reflection, and a compact microfacet specular term. It solves the problem of providing visually plausible surface lighting for discrete voxel geometry without requiring explicit mesh generation or complex global illumination. It differs from sibling methods by integrating hard shadow casting and emissive block handling directly into the ray-marched hit loop, whereas GGX Microfacet BRDF focuses on analytical surface scattering and Fast Shading for Voxel Engines optimizes for engine integration. Inputs: Camera position (camPos), ray direction (rayDir), hit position (hitPosition), hit cell coordinates (hitCell), hit face normal (hitFaceNormal), block type (b), sun direction (L), and time (time) for sun rotation. Outputs: Final pixel color (finalColor). Data Structures: TraceResult: Contains hit (bool), t (float, distance), cell (ivec3), normal (vec3). BlockType: Enum including BLOCKEMISSIVE. Parameters: lightColor: vec3(1.0, 0.96, 0.85). ambient: vec3(0.12, 0.14, 0.18). roughness: 0.54. F0: 0.14. rimPower: 2.2. rimIntensity: 0.12. indirectFactor: 0.25. emissiveIndirectFactor: 0.35. emissiveDirectFactor: 0.5. rimSpecularFactor: 0.6. toneMapScale: 2.0. SUNROTSPEED: Constant for sun rotation. ENABLESHADOW: Boolean flag. ENABLEATMOSPHERE: Boolean flag. Steps: 1. Ray Hit Validation: If no hit, return sky color. If hit distance t <= 0.0, set hitPosition = camPos; else hitPosition = camPos + rayDir (t + 1e-5). 2. Normal and Vector Setup: Normalize hitFaceNormal to get surface normal N. Compute view vector V = normalize(rayDir). Compute sun direction L based on time. 3. Atmosphere/Absorption: Compute absorpColor using atmospheric scattering or absorption model. If ENABLEATMOSPHERE, compute sky color via atmosphere function; else sky = absorpColor. 4. Local Coordinates: Calculate local position within the voxel: local = hitPosition - vec3(float(hitCell.x), float(hitCell.y), float(hitCell.z)). Apply fract() to get localPos. 5. Albedo Sampling: Sample block albedo texture using hitCell and localPos. 6. Diffuse Lighting: Compute nDotL = max(0.0, dot(N, L)). Lambertian term lambert = nDotL. 7. Rim Lighting: Compute rim = pow(1.0 - max(0.0, dot(N, V)), 2.2) 0.12. 8. Shadow Casting: Initialize shadow = 1.0. If ENABLESHADOW, trace a secondary ray from hitPosition + N 0.01 in direction L. If the trace hits a voxel, set shadow = 0.0. 9. Direct and Indirect Light: directLight = lightColor lambert. indirectLight = 0.25 albedo. 10. Emissive Handling: If block type is BLOCKEMISSIVE: Get emission color and intensity. indirectLight += 0.35 emission. directLight += emission 0.5. 11. Lighting Integration: Compute diffAlbedo = albedo absorpColor. Calculate lit color: lit = (shadow \cdot directLight + ambient) \cdot diffAlbedo + (indirectLight \cdot absorpColor) + rim \cdot 0.6 \cdot absorpColor. 12. Specular Integration: Compute microfacet specular term using GGX-like distribution: alpha = roughness roughness. H = normalize(L - V). dotLH = max(0.0, dot(L, H)), dotNH = max(0.0, dot(N, H)), dotNL = max(0.0, dot(N, L)). alphaSqr = alpha alpha. denom = dotNH dotNH (alphaSqr - 1.0) + 1.0. D = alphaSqr / (PI denom denom + 1e-6). F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) pow(1.0 - dotLH, 5.0). k = 0.5 alpha, k2 = k k. Specular contribution: spec = shadow (dotNL D F / (max(1e-6, dotLH dotLH (1.0 - k2)) + k2)) absorpColor lit. lit += spec. Apply shadow to final lit value: lit = max(0.7, shadow). 13. Tone Mapping: Apply Reinhard-like tone mapping: finalColor = 1.0 - exp(-2.0 lit). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelshadingpipeline(camPos, rayDir, tr, time): # tr is TraceResult with hit, t, cell, normal if not tr.hit: return skycolor # Computed via atmosphere or absorpColor # 1. Hit Position if tr.t <= 0.0: hitPosition = camPos else: hitPosition = camPos + rayDir (tr.t + 1e-5) hitCell = tr.cell hitFaceNormal = tr.normal N = normalize(hitFaceNormal) V = normalize(rayDir) L = normalize(sunvec(time SUNROTSPEED)) # 2. Atmosphere/Sky absorpColor = computeabsorption(vec3(0,1,0), camPos, L,...) # Implementation details omitted if ENABLEATMOSPHERE: sky = 1.0 - exp(atmosphere(rayDir, camPos, L,...)) else: sky = absorpColor # 3. Local Coords & Albedo local = hitPosition - vec3(float(hitCell.x), float(hitCell.y), float(hitCell.z)) localPos = fract(local) b = getblocktype(hitCell) albedo = sampleblockalbedo(hitCell, localPos, N) # 4. Basic Lighting Terms nDotL = max(0.0, dot(N, L)) lambert = nDotL rim = pow(1.0 - max(0.0, dot(N, V)), 2.2) 0.12 lightColor = vec3(1.0, 0.96, 0.85) ambient = vec3(0.12, 0.14, 0.18) # 5. Shadow shadow = 1.0 if ENABLESHADOW: sh = tracevoxel(hitPosition + N 0.01, L, tLimit, maxSteps) if sh.hit: shadow = 0.0 # 6. Direct/Indirect Light directLight = lightColor lambert indirectLight = 0.25 albedo if b == BLOCKEMISSIVE: emission = getemissivecolor(hitCell) getemissiveintensity(hitCell) indirectLight += 0.35 emission directLight += emission 0.5 # 7. Integration diffAlbedo = albedo absorpColor lit = (shadow directLight + ambient) diffAlbedo + (indirectLight absorpColor) + rim 0.6 absorpColor # 8. Specular (GGX-like) roughness = 0.54 F0 = 0.14 alpha = roughness roughness H = normalize(L - V) dotLH = max(0.0, dot(L, H)) dotNH = max(0.0, dot(N, H)) dotNL = max(0.0, dot(N, L)) alphaSqr = alpha alpha denom = dotNH dotNH (alphaSqr - 1.0) + 1.0 D = alphaSqr / (PI denom denom + 1e-6) F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) pow(1.0 - dotLH, 5.0) k = 0.5 alpha k2 = k k spec = shadow (dotNL D F / (max(1e-6, dotLH dotLH (1.0 - k2)) + k2)) absorpColor lit lit += spec lit = max(0.7, shadow) # 9. Tone Mapping finalColor = 1.0 - exp(-2.0 lit) return finalColor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use 1e-5 offset in ray origin to avoid self-intersection artifacts. Shadow Bias: Use N 0.01 offset for shadow ray origin. Division by Zero: Add 1e-6 to denominators in specular calculation. Overbright: Atmosphere sky color is exponentiated negatively to reduce brightness. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for shading, plus O(N) for shadow ray marching where N is steps to sun. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, plus texture memory for albedo. Performance: Interactive on modern GPUs due to simple shading model and hard shadows. Strengths: Simple implementation, visually pleasing for voxel worlds, handles emissive blocks. Limitations: Hard shadows only, no soft shadows or global illumination. When to use: Interactive voxel games, real-time rendering. When not to use: Photorealistic rendering requiring soft shadows or GI. The method originates from community-driven voxel shader implementations, specifically the "Voxel-World-Shader" by razzle-reinizu and "Ray-Marched Voxel Simulation" by Joris Rijsdijk. It is used in indie voxel games and educational graphics projects. name: Blinn-Phong with Metallic Reflections
head: Neon City Lighting, Wet Asphalt Shader
body: A custom shading model combining Blinn-Phong diffuse/specular components, metallic environment reflections weighted by a Schlick-like Fresnel term, and emissive contributions for neon effects. It distinguishes itself from standard Blinn-Phong by introducing material-dependent specular power and intensity, and from GGX microfacet models by using a simplified power-law specular lobe and analytic sky reflection rather than complex microfacet distribution functions. Inputs: Surface point p and view ray direction rd (normalized). Surface normal n (normalized). Material properties: albedo (RGB), metalness (m \in [0,1]), emissive (RGB). Ambient color constant. Sky color function C{sky}(d). Outputs: Final surface color C{out}. Data Structures: sf (Surface Field): Struct containing albedo (vec3), metal (float), emissive (vec3). Parameters: Light direction: L = (-0.5, 0.8, -0.25). Light color: CL = (0.5, 0.65, 1.0). Ambient intensity: C{amb} = 0.16. Specular power base: P{low} = 32.0. Specular power metal: P{high} = 140.0. Specular intensity base: I{low} = 0.4. Specular intensity metal: I{high} = 2.0. Fresnel power: F{pow} = 5.0. Reflection intensity base: R{low} = 0.03. Reflection intensity metal: R{high} = 0.6. Fresnel reflection weight base: W{low} = 0.25. Fresnel reflection weight metal: W{high} = 0.75. Shadow sample count: N{shadow} = 12. Shadow offset: 0.03. Steps: 1. Calculate normal n = \text{calcNormal}(p). 2. Determine surface properties (albedo, metalness m, emissive) based on material ID at p. 3. Define light direction L = \text{normalize}(-0.5, 0.8, -0.25) and light color CL = (0.5, 0.65, 1.0). 4. Calculate diffuse term: diff = \max(\text{dot}(n, L), 0.0). 5. Calculate shadow factor S = \text{softShadow}(p + n \times 0.03, L, 12.0). 6. Apply shadow to diffuse: diff = diff \times S. 7. Calculate half-vector: h = \text{normalize}(L - rd). 8. Calculate specular power: P = \text{mix}(32.0, 140.0, m). 9. Calculate specular intensity: I = \text{mix}(0.4, 2.0, m). 10. Calculate specular term: spec = \text{pow}(\max(\text{dot}(n, h), 0.0), P) \times S \times I. 11. Calculate ambient occlusion ao = \text{calcAO}(p, n). 12. Calculate base color: C = sf.albedo \times (C{amb} \times ao) + sf.albedo \times CL \times diff + CL \times spec. 13. Calculate Fresnel factor: f = \text{pow}(1.0 - \max(\text{dot}(n, -rd), 0.0), 5.0). 14. Calculate reflection direction: r = \text{reflect}(rd, n). 15. Calculate reflection intensity: R = \text{mix}(0.03, 0.6, m). 16. Calculate Fresnel reflection weight: W = 0.25 + 0.75 \times f. 17. Add reflected contribution: C = C + C{sky}(r) \times R \times W \times ao. 18. Add emissive contribution: C = C + sf.emissive. 19. Return C. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blinnphongmetallic(p, rd, n, sf, calcNormal, softShadow, calcAO, skyColor): # 1. Normal calculation (assumed external or pre-calculated) # n = calcNormal(p) # 2. Material properties from sf albedo = sf.albedo metal = sf.metal emissive = sf.emissive # 3. Light setup lightdir = normalize(vec3(-0.5, 0.8, -0.25)) lightcol = vec3(0.5, 0.65, 1.0) ambient = 0.16 # 4. Diffuse diff = max(dot(n, lightdir), 0.0) # 5. Shadow shadow = softShadow(p + n 0.03, lightdir, 12.0) diff = diff shadow # 6. Specular halfvec = normalize(lightdir - rd) specpow = mix(32.0, 140.0, metal) specint = mix(0.4, 2.0, metal) spec = pow(max(dot(n, halfvec), 0.0), specpow) shadow specint # 7. Ambient Occlusion ao = calcAO(p, n) # 8. Base Color color = albedo (ambient ao) + albedo lightcol diff + lightcol spec # 9. Fresnel fresnel = pow(1.0 - max(dot(n, -rd), 0.0), 5.0) # 10. Reflection refldir = reflect(rd, n) reflint = mix(0.03, 0.6, metal) fresnelweight = 0.25 + 0.75 fresnel reflected = skyColor(refldir) color = color + reflected reflint fresnelweight ao # 11. Emissive color = color + emissive return color Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, dominated by shadow ray marching (N{shadow} steps) and AO calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Fast execution; provides stylized "neon" aesthetic with high-contrast specular highlights and wet-surface reflections. Limitations: Not physically based; specular power is fixed per material type rather than derived from microfacet theory; Fresnel term is a power approximation, not Schlick's exact formula. When to use: Stylized real-time rendering, voxel engines, or ray marching demos where performance is critical and artistic control over "wet" or "metallic" look is desired. When not to use: Physically based rendering (PBR) pipelines requiring energy conservation or accurate material response. Originated in the "neon-raymarcher" project by PIGJET, this model is designed for ray-marched cityscapes with neon aesthetics. It adapts the classic Blinn-Phong model to support metallic reflections via a simplified Fresnel term and environment mapping, suitable for the "Wet Asphalt" look in cyberpunk-style scenes. name: Fast Shading for Voxel Engines
body: Fast Shading for Voxel Engines is a CPU-based lighting algorithm designed for voxel engines that assumes vertical sun rays to simulate illumination by modifying voxel palette indices directly. It differs from standard radiometric lighting models by operating on discrete tone groups within a palette, where indices 1–32, 33–64, etc., represent dark-to-light gradients, allowing for fast, artifact-free shading without complex ray tracing or normal calculations. Unlike GGX Microfacet BRDF which computes physically based reflections, or Voxel Shading Pipeline which may involve GPU acceleration, this method is strictly CPU-bound and optimized for immediate visual feedback in simple voxel environments. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid of dimensions xsize \times ysize \times zsize, where each voxel stores a palette index. Output: The same voxel grid with modified palette indices to reflect shading. Data Structures: The voxel grid is accessed via getvoxelpal(x, y, z) and setvoxelpal(x, y, z, val). Palette indices are integers. Empty voxels are typically index 0. Indices are grouped into tone groups of 32 (e.g., 1–32, 33–64). Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate through the voxel grid from x=1 to xsize-2, y=1 to ysize-2, and z=1 to zsize-2. Boundary voxels are skipped to avoid out-of-bounds checks for neighbors. 2. Retrieve the current voxel's palette index: voxel = getvoxelpal(x, y, z). 3. Calculate the lower bound (color margin) for the current tone group: color\margin = \lfloor \frac{voxel - 1}{32} \rfloor \times 32 + 1 This ensures the shaded color remains within the same tonal band. 4. If voxel != 0 (the voxel is occupied), apply shading by subtracting values based on the occupancy of neighboring voxels: Subtract 3 if the voxel directly above (x, y+1, z) is occupied (non-zero). Subtract 2 if any of the following are occupied: (x+1, y+1, z), (x-1, y+1, z), (x+1, y+1, z+1), or (x+1, y+1, z-1). Subtract 1 if any of the following are occupied: (x+1, y, z+1), (x-1, y, z-1), (x+1, y, z-1), or (x-1, y, z+1). 5. Clamp the resulting voxel index to the lower bound: if voxel < colormargin, set voxel = colormargin. 6. Write the modified index back: setvoxelpal(x, y, z, voxel). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastshade2(xsize, ysize, zsize, getvoxelpal, setvoxelpal): for x in range(1, xsize - 1): for y in range(1, ysize - 1): for z in range(1, zsize - 1): voxel = getvoxelpal(x, y, z) # Skip empty voxels if voxel == 0: continue # Calculate tone group lower bound colormargin = ((voxel - 1) // 32) 32 + 1 shading = 0 # Check neighbors for shading contribution # Subtract 3 if directly above is occupied if getvoxelpal(x, y + 1, z) != 0: shading += 3 # Subtract 2 if specific upper neighbors are occupied if (getvoxelpal(x + 1, y + 1, z) != 0 or getvoxelpal(x - 1, y + 1, z) != 0 or getvoxelpal(x + 1, y + 1, z + 1) != 0 or getvoxelpal(x + 1, y + 1, z - 1) != 0): shading += 2 # Subtract 1 if specific side neighbors are occupied if (getvoxelpal(x + 1, y, z + 1) != 0 or getvoxelpal(x - 1, y, z - 1) != 0 or getvoxelpal(x + 1, y, z - 1) != 0 or getvoxelpal(x - 1, y, z + 1) != 0): shading += 1 # Apply shading and clamp voxel = voxel - shading if voxel < colormargin: voxel = colormargin setvoxelpal(x, y, z, voxel) Parameters: xsize, ysize, zsize: Dimensions of the voxel level. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The voxel index must not drop below the lower bound of its tone group (colormargin). Failure to clamp results in invalid palette indices or visual artifacts. Boundary voxels are excluded from processing to simplify neighbor access. A faster but less visually detailed variant of the shading algorithm, also assuming vertical sun rays. It reduces the number of neighbor checks compared to fastshade2. The shading logic subtracts 3 if (x, y+1, z) is occupied, 2 if (x+1, y+1, z) is occupied, and 1 if (x+1, y, z+1) or (x-1, y, z-1) is occupied. It uses the same tone group clamping logic and iteration bounds as fastshade2. Choose this variant when performance is critical and the reduced shading detail is acceptable. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels processed. The constant factor is low due to simple integer arithmetic and neighbor checks. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as it modifies the grid in place. Performance: Optimized for CPU execution in voxel engines like DOOMMY, which rely on CPU rendering. Strengths: Extremely fast, no floating-point operations, simple implementation, works well with palette-based rendering. Limitations: Assumes vertical sun rays, limited shading detail compared to normal-based lighting, only works with specific palette structures (tone groups of 32). When to use: Simple voxel games, CPU-only rendering pipelines, real-time shading where performance is paramount. When not to use: Physically based rendering, scenes with complex lighting angles, or when high-fidelity shading is required. Fast Shading for Voxel Engines was developed as part of the DOOMMY voxel engine, an unofficial voxel-based game engine that uses only CPU for rendering and Lua for scripting. The engine was created by jabberx and released under the GNU General Public License. The shading method is designed to provide basic lighting effects efficiently on CPU hardware, reflecting the constraints and goals of early voxel engine development. jabberx/doommy, https://github.com/jabberx/doommy, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Diffuse Lighting Models
head: Diffuse Shading, Lambertian Shading, Phong Diffuse
body: Diffuse Lighting Models calculate the scattering of light from a surface, providing the primary cue for shape and depth in ray-marched volume rendering and SDF rendering. Unlike specular models that highlight surface gloss or ambient models that provide uniform illumination, diffuse models compute light intensity based on the angle between the surface normal and the light direction. This family is distinct from Distance Color Blending by integrating directional light vectors and from Ray-marched Shadows by assuming unobstructed light paths unless combined with shadowing techniques. All models in this family rely on the geometric relationship between the surface normal \mathbf{N} and the light direction \mathbf{L}. The core mechanism involves computing the dot product \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L} to determine the projected area of the light source onto the surface. This value is clamped to [0, 1] to prevent back-face illumination and negative lighting contributions. The final color contribution is typically calculated as: C{diffuse} = C{base} \times (\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L})+ \times C{light} where (\cdot)+ denotes the positive part (clamping negatives to zero), C{base} is the material albedo, and C{light} is the light color intensity. Normals are derived either analytically from the SDF gradient or via finite differences in volume data. Calculates lighting by accumulating terms based on the Phong reflection model, using normals approximated from the SDF gradient. Choose this when specular highlights are required alongside diffuse shading. Computes diffuse illumination for SDF surfaces by evaluating the dot product between the surface normal and light direction. It solves the problem of shading ray-marched geometry without explicit mesh topology by deriving normals via finite differences. Unlike Sphere Tracing Basics, which returns a flat base color, this method integrates light direction and color. Applies Blinn-Phong lighting to volume data during ray marching. It differs from pure Phong shading by using the half-vector for specular components and integrates front-to-back compositing with lighting. Choose this for volumetric data where surface normals are approximated via central differences of intensity gradients. Computes colors for each vertex based on a lighting model and vertex normals, then linearly interpolates colors across the facet. Choose this for performance-critical applications where per-fragment normal calculation is too expensive, though it may exhibit shading artifacts on large polygons. A shading model assuming uniform lighting where light surrounds an object equally in all directions. glShadeModel(GLFLAT) Flat shading diminishes the three dimensionality of the scene. Diffuse lighting models originate from early computer graphics shading techniques, specifically within the OpenGL specification which defined flat and Gouraud (smooth) shading models. The Lambertian model, named after Johann Heinrich Lambert, is the standard for ideal diffuse reflection. In the context of volume rendering and SDFs, these models were adapted to work with implicit surfaces where normals are derived from gradients rather than mesh topology.
