name: Differentiable Silhouette Rendering
head: Soft Silhouette Rendering, Minimum Absolute SDF Silhouette
body: Differentiable Silhouette Rendering is a technique to render binary silhouettes of 3D shapes represented by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) in a way that allows gradient back-propagation to scene parameters. It solves the non-differentiability of standard binary silhouette detection (e.g., ray termination at infinity) by computing a "soft" silhouette value based on the minimum absolute SDF encountered along a ray. It sets itself apart from its parent Differentiable Sphere Tracing by focusing specifically on the silhouette supervision signal rather than full photometric or geometric rendering, and from siblings like Instant-NSR-PL Forward Pass by relying on the minimum absolute distance query rather than normal-based edge detection. Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. SDF function f(\mathbf{p}) (e.g., neural network or analytical). Convergence threshold \epsilon (typically small positive value, e.g., 10^{-4} m). Unit sphere radius R{unit}=1.0 for background handling. Outputs: Soft silhouette value Sr per pixel. Binary silhouette (derived from sign of Sr). Data Structures: No complex structures required. The method operates per-pixel during ray marching. Steps: 1. Deep Sphere Tracing: Perform sphere tracing along the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for a maximum number of steps or until a max distance is reached. Record the SDF values f(\mathbf{p}i) at each sample point \mathbf{p}i. 2. Minimum Absolute SDF: Compute the minimum absolute SDF value encountered along the ray: S{min} = \mini |f(\mathbf{p}i)| This step identifies the closest surface to the camera along the ray, leveraging the property that SDFs are nearest-surface sensitive. 3. Background Handling: Check if the ray intersects the unit sphere (or the bounding volume of interest). If the ray does not intersect the unit sphere (i.e., it misses the object entirely), set the soft silhouette value to the distance from the origin to the ray minus 1.0. This ensures the value is always > 0, consistently marking it as background. If the ray intersects, proceed to step 4. 4. Soft Silhouette Calculation: Subtract the convergence threshold \epsilon from the minimum absolute SDF: S{soft} = S{min} - \epsilon This produces a tight differentiable approximation of the silhouette. 5. Binary Silhouette Determination: If S{soft} < 0, the pixel is foreground. If S{soft} > 0, the pixel is background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiablesilhouetterendering(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunction, epsilon=1e-4, maxsteps=50): """ Renders a differentiable soft silhouette for a single ray. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera ray origin. raydirection: 3D vector, camera ray direction (normalized). sdffunction: Callable, returns SDF value for a 3D point. epsilon: float, convergence threshold. maxsteps: int, maximum number of sphere tracing steps. Returns: softsilhouette: float, the differentiable silhouette value. """ # Step 1: Deep Sphere Tracing to find minimum absolute SDF minabssdf = float('inf') t = 0.0 hitunitsphere = False # Check intersection with unit sphere for background handling # Ray-sphere intersection: |o + td|^2 = 1 # t^2 + 2o.dt + |o|^2 - 1 = 0 a = dot(raydirection, raydirection) b = 2.0 dot(rayorigin, raydirection) c = dot(rayorigin, rayorigin) - 1.0 discriminant = bb - 4ac if discriminant >= 0: hitunitsphere = True # We don't strictly need the intersection point, just the flag # However, for robustness, we might want to ensure we are inside/outside correctly # The source implies checking intersection is sufficient to distinguish foreground/background rays pass # Perform sphere tracing for i in range(maxsteps): # Sample point point = rayorigin + t raydirection # Query SDF dist = sdffunction(point) # Track minimum absolute SDF absdist = abs(dist) if absdist < minabssdf: minabssdf = absdist # Advance along ray t += dist # Safety break if t becomes too large (avoiding infinity check) if t > 100.0: # Arbitrary large bound break # Step 2 & 3: Background Handling and Soft Silhouette Calculation if not hitunitsphere: # Ray misses the unit sphere. # Set soft silhouette to distance from origin to ray minus 1.0. # Distance from origin to ray is |o x d| since d is normalized. disttoray = length(cross(rayorigin, raydirection)) softsilhouette = disttoray - 1.0 else: # Ray hits the unit sphere (foreground candidate) # Subtract threshold softsilhouette = minabssdf - epsilon return softsilhouette Loss Function: The silhouette loss \mathcal{L}s is computed against ground truth binary silhouette S{gt} (1 for foreground, 0 for background): \mathcal{L}s = S{gt} \max(0, Sr) + (1 - S{gt}) \max(0, -Sr) This formulation allows the silhouette error to back-propagate differentiably to the optimized parameters. Volumetric Silhouette Rendering is a technique to render silhouettes of volumetric data by detecting edges where the view vector is perpendicular to the surface normal, using a 3D normal map and a pre-computed cube map for view vector normalization. It sets itself apart from geometry-based silhouette extraction by operating directly on volumetric representations via rasterization of normal fields, allowing interactive rendering of complex volumetric datasets. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sphere tracing steps per ray. The method adds minimal overhead to standard sphere tracing (one absolute value and min operation per step). Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it only tracks the minimum absolute SDF value. Strengths: Fully differentiable with respect to SDF parameters and camera extrinsics. It leverages the nearest-surface property of SDFs to optimize the correct surface. It avoids the non-differentiability of checking for ray termination at infinity. Limitations: The accuracy depends on the resolution of the sphere tracing (number of steps). Aggressive marching strategies may reduce quality. It only provides silhouette supervision, not color or texture. When to use: When optimizing 3D shape from 2D silhouette masks is required, and the shape is represented by an SDF. When not to use: When full photometric rendering or texture optimization is needed. The method was introduced in the context of rendering deep implicit signed distance functions with differentiable sphere tracing. It addresses the need for differentiable silhouette supervision in 3D shape prediction and optimization. The approach was presented in the paper "DIST: Rendering Deep Implicit Signed Distance Function With Differentiable Sphere Tracing". DIST: Rendering Deep Implicit Signed Distance Function With Differentiable Sphere Tracing, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr42600.2020.00209, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Volumetric Silhouette Rendering
head: Silhouette tracing
body: Volumetric Silhouette Rendering is a technique to render silhouettes of volumetric data by detecting edges where the view vector is perpendicular to the surface normal, using a 3D normal map and a pre-computed cube map for view vector normalization. It sets itself apart from geometry-based silhouette extraction by operating directly on volumetric representations via rasterization of normal fields, allowing interactive rendering of complex volumetric datasets. Inputs: A 3D volumetric dataset. A pre-computed 3D normal map texture derived from the volume. A pre-computed cube map storing normalized view vectors for all possible interpolated coordinates. Camera position (eye point C). Outputs: A binary silhouette mask (black or white) merged with the base color (e.g., from a toon-shader). Data Structures: 1. 3D Normal Map: A 3D texture where each texel stores the surface normal vector (Nx, Ny, Nz) at that volumetric position. 2. Cube Map: A 6-face cube map texture. Each face stores pre-normalized view vectors. The coordinates used to fetch from this map are the interpolated, un-normalized view vector directions. This avoids runtime normalization costs. Steps: 1. Render Normal Map: Render the 3D normal map. At each vertex of the rendered polygons (representing the volume's isosurface or sampled points), issue the normalized view vector as an additional texture coordinate. The view vector is calculated as V = C - P, where P is the vertex position. 2. Interpolate: During rasterization, interpolate the texture coordinates (including the view vector components) on a per-fragment basis. 3. Re-normalize View Vector: Because normalization is not preserved by linear interpolation, the interpolated view vector components are used as coordinates to fetch texture values from the pre-computed cube map. This fetch returns the correctly normalized view vector V{norm} for the fragment. 4. Compute Dot Product: Use register combiners (or equivalent hardware shader logic) to compute the dot product between the normalized view vector V{norm} and the normal vector N fetched from the 3D normal map: D = N \cdot V{norm}. 5. Square Result: Square the dot product result to obtain a positive value: S = D^2. This ensures that the silhouette condition is met regardless of the sign of the dot product (front/back facing relative to the view). 6. Trigger Multiplexer: Use the squared value S to trigger a multiplexer. If the view vector is perpendicular to the normal (silhouette edge), the dot product D is near zero, so S is near zero. The multiplexer outputs black or white depending on this result. Specifically, the text implies a thresholding or direct mapping where the dot product magnitude determines the output. 7. Merge: Merge the silhouette result (black/white) with the colors produced by the toon-shader or base volume rendering. Formula: The geometric definition of a silhouette edge for a mesh is given by: ((N1 \cdot (C - V1))(N2 \cdot (C - V2))) \leq 0 where N1, N2 are face normals, V1, V2 are points on the faces, and C is the eye point. For the volumetric implementation, the condition is approximated by the dot product between the surface normal N and the view vector V: D = N \cdot V{norm} The silhouette is highlighted when D \approx 0. The squared value D^2 is used to trigger the output. Parameters: Threshold for silhouette detection: Not explicitly defined in the sources, but implied by the multiplexer trigger logic based on the dot product. Cube map resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation Error: Normalization is not preserved by interpolation, necessitating the cube map lookup. Failure to re-normalize leads to incorrect silhouette detection. Hardware Dependency: The method relies on "register combiners" and specific hardware features like 3D texture support and cube maps, which may not be available on modern hardware without shader equivalents. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for a 3D normal map and a cube map. The cube map size depends on the resolution of interpolated view vector coordinates. Measured Performance: Experiments were run on a Pentium4 processor at 1.5 GHz and a GeForce4 graphics unit with 128 MB local memory and 3D texture support. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows interactive rendering of silhouettes for volumetric data sets. Limitations: Hardware-dependent (register combiners, 3D textures); relies on pre-computed cube maps which may consume significant memory. The method was proposed in the context of interactive volume illustration, aiming to provide silhouette cues for volumetric data similar to those available in geometry-based rendering. It builds on the geometric definition of silhouette edges for polygonal meshes. Interactive volume illustration, https://openalex.org/W2147354080, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Direct Diffuse Integrator
head: sdf-direct-diff
body: The SDF Direct Diffuse Integrator is a differentiable volume rendering method that computes direct illumination for scenes defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It extends standard path tracing by incorporating a boundary integral term evaluated at grazing points, which enables accurate gradient computation for thin surfaces and silhouettes where standard sphere tracing fails. Unlike Differentiable Sphere Tracing, which relies on standard ray-marching intersections, this method explicitly handles the discontinuity of visibility at object boundaries using a relaxed boundary formulation. The method computes the radiance L for a camera ray by combining direct illumination from the primary intersection with a boundary correction term derived from grazing points. Input: Camera ray r, scene definition (SDF, BSDF, Emitter), sampling parameters. Output: Radiance L (color) and its gradients with respect to scene parameters. Interaction (itx): Contains position p, normal n, SDF value d, and emitter status. Grazing Point (grzi): The location on the surface where the ray grazes the SDF isosurface. Boolean (isgrzi): Indicates if the primary intersection is a grazing point. SDFEPS: Epsilon for sampling relaxed silhouette points. Typical value: 10^{-4}. SDFDERIVEPS: Epsilon for direction derivative sampling. Typical value: 10^{-1}. ITXEPS: Intersection threshold. Typical value: 10^{-5}. RAYEPS: Ray marching step size. Typical value: 10^{-3}. NUMGRZ: Number of refinements for grazing point. Typical value: 12. GRZMODE: Method for finding grazing points. Typical value: 'bisection'. 1. Ray Intersection: Perform ray intersection using the 'grz' method to obtain the primary intersection itx, a boolean isgrzi indicating if the intersection is a grazing point, and the grazing point location grzi. \text{itx}, \text{is\grz\i}, \text{grz\i} = \text{sdf.ray\intersect}(\text{ray}, \text{method}='grz') 2. Surface Emission: Compute the surface emission E at the intersection. E = \text{itx.emitter}(\text{scene}=\text{scene}).\text{eval}(\text{itx}) 3. Gradient Replacement Vector: Calculate a velocity vector v for gradient replacement based on the SDF value and normal n. v = -\frac{\text{sdf.at}(\text{itx}.p)}{\|n\|^2} n Here, \text{sdf.at}(p) returns the signed distance value at position p. 4. Position Adjustment: Replace the intersection position itx.p with the velocity-adjusted position using gradient replacement. \text{itx}.p = \text{dr.replace\grad}(\text{itx}.p, v) 5. Incoming Radiance: Sample the emitter direction and evaluate the BSDF to compute incoming radiance Li. \text{itxL}, Li = \text{scene.sample\emitter\direction}(\text{itx}, \text{samples}, \text{test\visibility}=\text{False}) Li = \text{bsdf} 6. Shadow Ray: Check visibility for the direct illumination path using a shadow ray intersected against the SDF. \text{itx\shadow}, \text{is\grz\o}, \text{grz\o} = \text{sdf.ray\intersect}(\text{rayL}, \text{method}='grz') 7. Grazing Point Retrieval: Compute the grazing point itxgrz for the silhouette/boundary integral by retrieving the intersection at the grazing distance. \text{itx\grz} = \text{sdf.get\intersect}(\text{ray}, t{grz}, \text{is\grz\i}) 8. Grazing Radiance: Evaluate the radiance L{grz} at the grazing point by sampling the emitter and evaluating the BSDF at itxgrz. 9. Boundary Integral: Compute the boundary integral contribution bp using the normal velocity vn = -\text{sdf.at}(\text{grz}) and the difference in radiance between the grazing point and the primary intersection. bp[\text{is\grz\i}] = vn \frac{\text{dr.detach}(L{grz} - L)}{\text{SDF\EPS}} 10. Final Radiance: Add the boundary integral to the final radiance using gradient replacement. L = \text{dr.replace\grad}(L, L + bp) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfdirectdiffuseintegrator(ray, scene, sdf, samples, SDFEPS): # Step 1: Ray Intersection with grazing detection itx, isgrzi, grzi = sdf.rayintersect(ray, method='grz') # Step 2: Surface Emission E = itx.emitter(scene=scene).eval(itx) # Step 3: Calculate velocity vector for gradient replacement n = itx.normal d = sdf.at(itx.p) v = - (d / dr.squarednorm(n)) n # Step 4: Replace intersection position itx.p = dr.replacegrad(itx.p, v) # Step 5: Sample emitter and evaluate BSDF itxL, Li = scene.sampleemitterdirection(itx, samples, testvisibility=False) Li = itx.bsdf # Step 6: Shadow ray visibility check rayL = itxL.toray() itxshadow, isgrzo, grzo = sdf.rayintersect(rayL, method='grz') # Step 7: Get grazing point for boundary integral # Note: tgrz is derived from the grazing detection logic in sdf.rayintersect itxgrz = sdf.getintersect(ray, grzi.t, isgrzi) # Step 8: Evaluate radiance at grazing point # Assuming similar sampling logic as Step 5 but at itxgrz itxLgrz, Lgrz = scene.sampleemitterdirection(itxgrz, samples, testvisibility=False) Lgrz = itxgrz.bsdf # Step 9: Compute boundary integral contribution # vn is the normal velocity at the grazing point vn = -sdf.at(grzi) bp = dr.zeroslike(Li) if isgrzi: # dr.detach is used to prevent backprop through the boundary term's radiance difference # in some implementations, but here it ensures stable gradients for the boundary term bp = vn dr.detach(Lgrz - Li) / SDFEPS # Step 10: Add boundary integral using gradient replacement L = dr.replacegrad(Li, Li + bp) return L Precision: The choice of SDFEPS is critical. Too small a value leads to numerical instability in the boundary term division; too large a value blurs the silhouette. Grazing Detection: The 'grz' method must correctly identify grazing points. If isgrzi is false, the boundary term is not applied, potentially missing silhouette gradients. Visibility: The shadow ray visibility check uses testvisibility=False in the emitter sampling, but the shadow ray itself must be intersected to determine occlusion. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of ray marching steps and the cost of the grazing point refinement. The additional grazing point calculation adds overhead compared to standard sphere tracing. Memory Complexity: Low, as it primarily stores interaction data and does not require large buffers. Strengths: Accurate gradients for silhouettes and thin surfaces; differentiable with respect to SDF parameters. Limitations: Requires a robust 'grz' intersection method; sensitive to SDFEPS. When to Use: When rendering scenes with thin objects or when silhouette gradients are important for optimization. When Not to Use: For thick, opaque objects where standard sphere tracing suffices, or when computational efficiency is prioritized over gradient accuracy at boundaries. The SDF Direct Diffuse Integrator is part of the "relaxed boundary" approach for differentiable rendering with SDFs. It was introduced to address the limitations of standard differentiable sphere tracing, which fails to provide accurate gradients at object boundaries. The method is implemented in the zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary repository. zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, https://github.com/zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching with Neural SDF
head: DeepSDF Rendering, Neural SDF Ray Marching
body: Ray Marching with Neural SDF approximates the Space Distance Field (SDF) using a deep neural network to render images by marching rays along the estimated distance field. Unlike traditional sphere tracing which relies on analytical primitive definitions, this method uses a learned implicit representation, allowing for the rendering of complex, non-analytic geometries defined by the network's latent code. It builds on Distance-field ray marching by replacing the analytical d(p) function with a neural network evaluation. The method renders a scene by initializing rays from a camera, querying a trained neural network for distance estimates, and advancing the ray position iteratively until convergence or maximum distance is reached. Inputs: Camera parameters: position, width, height, field of view (fov), aspect ratio. Neural SDF model: A neural network (e.g., a Multi-Layer Perceptron) trained to output the signed distance to the surface given a 3D coordinate and a latent code. Rendering parameters: maxsteps (default 30-40), epsilon (default 10^{-3}), maxdist (default 10.0). Lighting: Directional light vector. Outputs: A 2D image (height \times width) representing the rendered scene. Data Structures: Camera: Stores width, height, fov (default \pi/3), position (3D vector), and aspectratio (width/height). Ray Directions: A tensor of shape (width \times height, 3) containing normalized direction vectors for each pixel. Distances: A tensor of shape (width \times height, 1) initialized to zeros, tracking the remaining distance to the surface for each ray. Positions: A tensor of shape (width \times height, 3) tracking the current 3D position of each ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create ray directions by sampling a grid over the image plane and normalizing them. Initialize distances tensor to zeros with shape [width \times height, 1] on the GPU. Calculate initial ray positions: p = ro + distances \cdot v. Since distances are 0, p = ro. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate up to maxsteps times. Query SDF: Evaluate the neural SDF at the current positions p. The network takes the concatenation of the latent code and the 3D coordinates as input. Let the output be d (shape [width \times height, 1]). Convergence Check: If all elements in distances are less than epsilon (e.g., 10^{-3}), break the loop. Update: Update distances by adding the sampled SDF value d: distances \leftarrow distances + d. Recalculate Positions: Update positions: p \leftarrow ro + distances \cdot v. Max Distance Check: If all rays have either converged (distances < epsilon) or exceeded maxdist, break the loop. 3. Normal Estimation: Estimate normals at the final positions using central finite differences with step size e = 10^{-3}. For each position p, compute: nx = SDF(p + [e, 0, 0]) - SDF(p - [e, 0, 0]) ny = SDF(p + [0, e, 0]) - SDF(p - [0, e, 0]) nz = SDF(p + [0, 0, e]) - SDF(p - [0, 0, e]) n = [nx, ny, nz] Normalize n to get the surface normal. 4. Shading: Calculate brightness using a single directional light. Clamp the dot product of the normal n and light direction l to [0, 1]: brightness = \max(0, \min(1, n \cdot l)). Set brightness to 0 for pixels where the final accumulated distance exceeds maxdist. 5. Output: Reshape brightness to height \times width. Convert to numpy, scale by 255, and cast to uint8 for the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def renderneuralsdf(camera, neuralsdf, latentcode, maxsteps=30, epsilon=1e-3, maxdist=10.0, lightdir=None): """ Renders an image using ray marching with a neural SDF. Args: camera: Camera object with width, height, fov, position, and getdirections() method. neuralsdf: Neural network function/model that takes (latentcode, coords) and returns SDF values. latentcode: Tensor of shape (1, latentdim) representing the object shape. maxsteps: Maximum number of ray marching iterations. epsilon: Convergence threshold. maxdist: Maximum distance a ray can travel. lightdir: Normalized light direction vector. Returns: numpy array: Rendered image (uint8). """ device = camera.position.device dtype = camera.position.dtype # 1. Initialize Rays # Get ray directions for all pixels: shape (width height, 3) directions = camera.getdirections() # Assumes this returns normalized directions numrays = directions.shape[0] # Initialize distances tensor: shape (numrays, 1) distances = torch.zeros((numrays, 1), device=device, dtype=dtype) # Initial positions: p = ro + distances v. Since distances=0, p = ro rayorigins = camera.position.expand(numrays, -1) # Shape (numrays, 3) positions = rayorigins.clone() # 2. Ray Marching Loop for step in range(maxsteps): # Query Neural SDF: input is latentcode concatenated with positions # latentcode shape: (1, latentdim), positions shape: (numrays, 3) # Expand latentcode to match batch size expandedlatent = latentcode.expand(numrays, -1) # Concatenate: [latentcode, coords] -> shape (numrays, latentdim + 3) inputcoords = torch.cat([expandedlatent, positions], dim=-1) # Evaluate SDF: returns shape (numrays, 1) sdfvalues = neuralsdf(inputcoords) # Check convergence: if all distances < epsilon if torch.all(distances < epsilon): break # Update distances: distances += sdfvalues distances = distances + sdfvalues # Recalculate positions: p = ro + distances v # distances is (numrays, 1), directions is (numrays, 3) # Broadcast multiplication positions = rayorigins + distances directions # Check maxdist: if all rays have converged or exceeded maxdist converged = torch.all(distances < epsilon) exceededmax = torch.all(distances > maxdist) if converged or exceededmax: break # 3. Normal Estimation # Estimate normals at final positions using central finite differences e = 1e-3 dx = torch.tensor([e, 0, 0], device=device, dtype=dtype).expand(numrays, -1) dy = torch.tensor([0, e, 0], device=device, dtype=dtype).expand(numrays, -1) dz = torch.tensor([0, 0, e], device=device, dtype=dtype).expand(numrays, -1) # Compute SDF at perturbed positions # Note: This assumes the neuralsdf function can handle batched inputs sdfposdx = neuralsdf(torch.cat([expandedlatent, positions + dx], dim=-1)) sdfnegdx = neuralsdf(torch.cat([expandedlatent, positions - dx], dim=-1)) sdfposdy = neuralsdf(torch.cat([expandedlatent, positions + dy], dim=-1)) sdfnegdy = neuralsdf(torch.cat([expandedlatent, positions - dy], dim=-1)) sdfposdz = neuralsdf(torch.cat([expandedlatent, positions + dz], dim=-1)) sdfnegdz = neuralsdf(torch.cat([expandedlatent, positions - dz], dim=-1)) # Calculate normal components nx = sdfposdx - sdfnegdx ny = sdfposdy - sdfnegdy nz = sdfposdz - sdfnegdz normals = torch.stack([nx, ny, nz], dim=-1) # Normalize normals norms = torch.norm(normals, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Avoid division by zero norms = torch.clamp(norms, min=1e-8) normals = normals / norms # 4. Shading brightness = torch.zeros((numrays, 1), device=device, dtype=dtype) if lightdir is not None: # Ensure lightdir is broadcastable lightdirexpanded = lightdir.expand(numrays, -1) # Dot product: normals (numrays, 3). lightdir (numrays, 3) -> (numrays, 1) dotproduct = torch.sum(normals lightdirexpanded, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Clamp to [0, 1] brightness = torch.clamp(dotproduct, 0.0, 1.0) # Set brightness to 0 for rays that exceeded maxdist brightness = torch.where(distances > maxdist, torch.zeroslike(brightness), brightness) # 5. Output # Reshape to height x width brightness2d = brightness.reshape(camera.height, camera.width) # Convert to numpy, scale by 255, cast to uint8 image = (brightness2d.cpu().numpy() 255).astype(np.uint8) return image Parameters: maxsteps: Maximum number of ray marching iterations. Default value is 30 in rendertofile.py and 40 in rederer.py. epsilon (precision): The convergence threshold for ray marching. If the remaining distance is less than epsilon, the ray is considered to have hit the surface. Default value is 10^{-3}. maxdist: The maximum distance a ray can travel before being clipped. Default value is 10.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The normal estimation implementation in the reference code contains a bug where it only uses the first object (objects[0]) even if multiple objects are passed, and the index is hardcoded. The PyGame screen initialization in the reference code is hardcoded to 1280x720. Precision issues may arise if epsilon is too small relative to the network's output scale or if the step size e for finite differences is not chosen carefully. Time Complexity: Dominated by the neural network inference per ray per step. Total complexity is O(W \cdot H \cdot S \cdot C), where W, H are image dimensions, S is maxsteps, and C is the cost of a neural network forward pass. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for storing ray positions, distances, and normals. The neural network weights are stored separately. Performance: Performance depends heavily on the neural network architecture and hardware acceleration (GPU). The reference implementation uses PyTorch on CUDA. Strengths: Can represent complex, non-analytic geometries. No need for explicit mesh or voxel storage. Limitations: Requires training data and training time. Normal estimation via finite differences is computationally expensive (6 extra network queries per pixel). Harder to optimize with traditional acceleration structures like BVHs compared to explicit meshes. When to use: When the geometry is complex and defined implicitly by a neural network, or when learning a shape from data. When not to use: For simple analytical primitives where analytical SDFs are faster and more accurate. This method is based on the concept of DeepSDF, which approximates the Space Distance Field (SDF) using a deep neural network. The specific implementation described in the sources is from a research project exploring the possibility of approximating the SDF using deep machine learning for image rendering. The project uses Python 3.13 and PyTorch. Kulakov-Nikita/RayMarchingAI, https://github.com/Kulakov-Nikita/RayMarchingAI, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Standard Constant Step Ray Marching
head: Basic Raymarching Loop, Fixed Step Ray Marching, Raymarch, SDF Ray Marching
body: Standard Constant Step Ray Marching is an iterative algorithm for finding the intersection of a ray with an implicit surface or sampling a volume by advancing the ray position at fixed intervals. It mitigates the drawback of root-finding methods that may identify multiple intersection points by focusing on determining the first root (or accumulating volume data). Unlike Spheretracing, which uses the distance field value to determine the step size, this method uses a predefined constant step size, allowing it to work with any function that returns a boolean (inside/outside) or a scalar field, rather than requiring a strict Signed Distance Field (SDF). It builds on Ray-primitive intersection. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{r}0 (e.g., camera position). Ray direction \mathbf{r}d (normalized unit vector). Fixed step size \Delta t. Maximum step count k{\max} (or maximum distance). Implicit surface function f(\mathbf{x}) or scalar field map. (Optional) Bounding box limits t{\min}, t{\max}. Outputs: Intersection distance t (if surface hit). Accumulated radiance/color (if volume rendering). Boolean indicating hit/miss. Data Structures: Scalar variables for position, distance, and counters. No complex structures required. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize step counter k = 0 and current distance t = 0. 2. (Optional) Compute bounding box intersection parameters t{\min} and t{\max} for the ray. 3. Loop while k < k{\max} and (if bounding box is used) t \le t{\max}: a. Calculate current sample point: \mathbf{r}(k) = \mathbf{r}0 + \Delta t \cdot k \cdot \mathbf{r}d. b. Evaluate the field function at \mathbf{r}(k): d = f(\mathbf{r}(k)). c. Surface Intersection Variant: i. If d \le 0 (or d < \epsilon), the ray has hit or passed inside the surface. Return intersection distance t = k \cdot \Delta t. ii. If d > 0 and a maximum distance check is used, break if t > \text{MAX\DIST}. d. Volume Rendering Variant: i. Sample density \rho from d. ii. Evaluate transfer function to get attenuation \alpha and color contribution. iii. Update accumulated radiance: L{\text{new}} = L{\text{old}} \cdot \exp(-\rho \cdot \Delta t \cdot \alpha). iv. Advance t by \Delta t. e. Increment k. 4. If loop completes without hit (surface) or termination (volume), return miss/no intersection. Pseudocode (Surface Intersection): import math def raymarchsurface(r0, rd, stepsize, maxsteps, surfacefunc): """ r0: vec3, ray origin rd: vec3, normalized ray direction stepsize: float, fixed delta t maxsteps: int, maximum iterations surfacefunc: function, returns distance (negative if inside) """ k = 0 t = 0.0 while k < maxsteps: # Calculate current position using fixed step formula pos = r0 + rd (stepsize k) # Sample the implicit surface dist = surfacefunc(pos) # Check for intersection: d <= 0 indicates inside or on surface if dist <= 0.0: return t, True k += 1 t = stepsize k return 0.0, False Pseudocode (Volume Rendering): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raymarchvolume(r0, rd, stepsize, maxsteps, volumefunc, transferfunc): """ volumefunc: returns scalar density transferfunc: returns (density, attenuation) tuple """ t = 0.0 L = 1.0 # Incoming radiance # Optional: Compute tmin, tmax for bounding box # tmin, tmax = computeboxintersection(r0, rd, box) k = 0 while k < maxsteps: pos = r0 + rd t # Sample volume density = volumefunc(pos) # Apply transfer function tfval = transferfunc(density) densityval = tfval.density attenuation = tfval.attenuation # Accumulate radiance L = L math.exp(-densityval stepsize attenuation) t += stepsize k += 1 return L Parameters: \Delta t (Step Size): Critical parameter. Typical values range from 0.001 (high precision/volume) to 0.1 (coarse/surface). k{\max} (Max Steps): Typical value 10–64 depending on scene complexity and step size. \epsilon (Epsilon): Threshold for intersection detection. Often 0.001 or similar small value. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tunneling: If \Delta t is too large, the ray may jump over thin geometry between samples. Performance: If \Delta t is too small, excessive samples are taken in empty space, causing performance loss. Surface Definition: The algorithm assumes f(x) < 0 is inside and f(x) = 0 is the surface boundary. Precision: Fixed steps do not adapt to local geometry, potentially missing details that Spheretracing (adaptive step) would catch. A rendering technique where the pixel color is determined by the number of raymarching steps taken before hitting a surface or reaching the maximum step count, visualizing computational intensity. It serves as a debug or artistic tool rather than a physically accurate method. Time Complexity: O(k{\max}), linear with respect to the maximum number of steps. Memory Complexity: O(1), constant space per ray. Strengths: Simple to implement; works with any implicit function (boolean or scalar), not just SDFs. Limitations: Prone to tunneling if step size is not carefully chosen; inefficient in empty space if step size is small; does not guarantee finding the exact first intersection point as accurately as adaptive methods (like Spheretracing). When to use: Simple shapes, boolean volumes, or when SDF evaluation is expensive/impossible. When not to use: Complex scenes with thin geometry requiring high precision, or when SDFs are available (use Spheretracing instead). The method was indicated by [PH89] and used for rendering Hypertexture volumes. It is similar to volumetric ray-casting techniques. The ray equation \mathbf{r}(k) = \mathbf{r}0 + \Delta t k \mathbf{r}d is a standard formulation for fixed-step traversal. name: Iteration-Based Coloring
head: Iteration count, Step count coloring [S1, unofficial]
body: Iteration-Based Coloring is a rendering technique where the final pixel color is determined by the number of raymarching steps taken before the ray terminates (either by hitting a surface or reaching a maximum step count). It visualizes the computational intensity of the raymarch, highlighting regions where the ray traveled further or required more sampling iterations. Unlike standard shading which relies on material properties and lighting, this method maps algorithmic performance metrics directly to visual output. Inputs: Ray origin and direction for each pixel. Implicit surface function or voxel data structure. Maximum step count limit (N{max}). Fixed step size (\Delta t). Outputs: Pixel color value. Data Structures: Step counter: An integer tracking the number of iterations performed for the current ray. Termination flag: Boolean indicating if the ray has hit a surface or exceeded N{max}. Steps: 1. Initialize the ray for the current pixel using the camera parameters. 2. Initialize step counter k = 0. 3. While k < N{max} and ray is not terminated: a. Evaluate the distance to the nearest surface (or check voxel occupancy) at the current ray position. b. Advance the ray along its direction by the step size \Delta t. c. Increment k. 4. Determine the color based on the final value of k. Formulas: The color intensity C is mapped linearly to the step count k. A common normalization maps k to the range [0, 255]: C = \left\lfloor \frac{k}{N{max}} \times 255 \right\rfloor Where: k is the number of steps taken. N{max} is the maximum allowed steps. Parameters: N{max}: The maximum number of steps. A typical value cited is 64. \Delta t: The fixed step size. Typically set to 1.0 for standard constant step marching. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Termination: Rays that never hit a surface (e.g., background) will always result in N{max} steps, returning the maximum intensity value. Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors may cause the ray to overshoot or undershoot the surface slightly, requiring a small epsilon threshold for hit detection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterationbasedcoloring(rayorigin, raydirection, surfacefunction, maxsteps, stepsize=1.0): """ Renders a single pixel using iteration-based coloring. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the ray. raydirection: vec3, normalized direction of the ray. surfacefunction: callable, returns distance to surface at a point. maxsteps: int, maximum number of raymarching iterations. stepsize: float, fixed distance to advance per step. Returns: int: Step count taken before termination. """ currentpos = rayorigin stepcount = 0 for i in range(maxsteps): dist = surfacefunction(currentpos) if dist < 1e-4: return stepcount currentpos = currentpos + raydirection stepsize stepcount += 1 return stepcount A variant that visualizes geometric depth by mapping the z-coordinate of the first surface hit to grayscale intensity, rather than computational step count. It differs from its parent by encoding spatial distance instead of algorithmic intensity. Time Complexity: O(N \times S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of steps per ray. The complexity is dominated by the raymarching loop. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as only the step count and current position need to be stored. Performance: Visualizes computational intensity, making it useful for debugging raymarchers or creating abstract visual effects. It does not provide physically accurate shading. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides immediate feedback on raymarch efficiency and surface proximity. Limitations: Does not convey material properties or lighting. The technique was described in a 2013 blog post on raymarching distance fields, where it was presented as a simple way to "spice up" black and white renders by visualizing where the most intensive portions of the image are. name: Depth Rendering
head: Depth Map Rendering, Z-Buffer Visualization
body: Depth Rendering is a visualization technique that maps the z-coordinate (depth) of the first surface hit by a ray to grayscale intensity, producing a depth map where brightness corresponds to distance from the camera. It differs from its parent, Iteration-Based Coloring, which visualizes computational intensity (step count) rather than geometric depth. Inputs: Ray origin and direction for each pixel (x, y), provided by rc.getRayForPixel(x, y). An octree data structure representing the volume, with bounding box defined by tree->min and tree->max. A TreeTraverser object initialized with the tree and the ray. Outputs: A 4-channel texture array (texturearray) of size rc.ny rc.ny 4 (assuming square resolution). Channels: Red, Green, Blue (identical grayscale values), and Alpha (set to 1). Data Structures: VoxelData: Contains morton (uint64t), color (vec3), and normal (vec3). TreeTraverser: Manages the traversal state, providing isTerminated(), getCurrentNode(), step(), and getCurrentPosition(). Algorithm: 1. Initialize OpenMP parallelization using the number of available CPU cores. 2. Parallelize the pixel loop over y and x. 3. For each pixel (x, y): a. Initialize TreeTraverser t with the tree and the ray for (x, y). b. Traverse the tree while !t.isTerminated(): i. If t.getCurrentNode()->isLeaf() and t.getCurrentNode()->hasData(), break the loop. ii. Otherwise, call t.step(). c. Retrieve the hit position pos = t.getCurrentPosition(). d. Compute the depth factor: \text{factor} = \frac{|pos[2]|}{|tree->max[2]| - |tree->min[2]|} e. Compute grayscale intensity: r = 255 - (255 \times \text{factor}) g = 255 - (255 \times \text{factor}) b = 255 - (255 \times \text{factor}) f. Write to texturearray at index index = y (rc.ny 4) + x 4: texturearray[index] = (unsigned char) r texturearray[index+1] = (unsigned char) g texturearray[index+2] = (unsigned char) b texturearray[index+3] = (unsigned char) 1 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderdepth(tree, rc, texturearray): # Initialize OpenMP threads numthreads = getnumprocs() setnumthreads(numthreads) # Parallel pixel loop for y in range(rc.ny): for x in range(rc.ny): # Initialize ray and traverser ray = rc.getrayforpixel(x, y) t = TreeTraverser(tree, ray) # Traverse tree while not t.isterminated(): node = t.getcurrentnode() if node.isleaf() and node.hasdata(): break t.step() # Get hit position pos = t.getcurrentposition() # Compute depth factor # Note: Source uses abs() on min/max components depthrange = abs(tree.max[2]) - abs(tree.min[2]) if depthrange == 0: factor = 0.0 else: factor = abs(pos[2]) / depthrange # Compute grayscale color intensity = 255 - (255 factor) r = int(intensity) g = int(intensity) b = int(intensity) # Write to texture array index = y (rc.ny 4) + x 4 texturearray[index] = r texturearray[index + 1] = g texturearray[index + 2] = b texturearray[index + 3] = 1 Parameters: tree->min[2] and tree->max[2]: The minimum and maximum z-coordinates of the volume bounding box, used for normalization. Edge Cases: If depthrange is zero, division by zero occurs; the pseudocode guards against this. If the ray does not hit any leaf node with data, t.isTerminated() becomes true, and pos may be undefined or invalid; the source does not specify handling for this case. A visualization technique that renders a depth map by normalizing the logarithmic distance traveled by the ray, where brighter pixels indicate further travel distance. It calculates the distance d = |pi - p0| between the hit point pi and the ray origin p0, computes \log(d), and normalizes this value to the range [0, 1]. The implementation typically involves clamping the distance to avoid \log(0), subtracting the minimum log-distance, dividing by the range, and optionally applying a power function for tonemapping. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the average depth of the tree traversal. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels for the output texture array. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides immediate visual feedback on scene depth. Limitations: Sensitive to the choice of bounding box for normalization; does not account for occlusion beyond the first hit. When to use: When a quick depth visualization is needed without complex shading. When not to use: When accurate depth perception over large dynamic ranges is required (consider Logarithmic Depth Rendering). Originated in early CPU-based voxel raycasting implementations, specifically in the cpuvoxelraycaster project by Forceflow. It is used as a debugging and visualization tool for voxel-based rendering pipelines. name: Step Size Selection
head: Constant step marching, Fixed-step volume rendering, Ray Marching with Fixed Step Count, Simple ray marching, Step Size Determination, Step Size Heuristic
body: Step Size Selection determines the distance between consecutive samples along a ray during volume rendering, balancing rendering speed against the accuracy of the Riemann sum approximation of the volume integral. Unlike adaptive methods that vary step length based on local density or distance fields, this method uses a fixed number of steps or a constant step size, simplifying implementation but requiring careful heuristic selection to avoid aliasing or missed features. It is a core component of Standard Constant Step Ray Marching, where the step size dictates the sampling density relative to the projected pixel size and scene scale. Inputs: Camera field of view (fov) in degrees or radians. Image width (W) in pixels. Ray entry distance (t{min}) and exit distance (t{max}) along the ray. Fixed number of steps (N) or target step size (\Delta t). 3D texture data (density/opacity) and sampler configuration. Outputs: Accumulated color and opacity for the pixel. Data Structures: Uniforms: Contains the inverse Model-View-Projection matrix (M^{-1}) for ray generation. Texture: 3D texture (T) storing scalar density values, typically in range [0, 1]. Sampler: Linear or nearest-neighbor sampler for texture interpolation. Ray State: Current position (rayPos), step vector (step), and accumulator (result). Parameters: fov: Field of view angle. Typically provided in degrees in code, converted to radians for trigonometric functions. t{min}: Distance to the volume entry point. t{max}: Distance to the volume exit point. N: Fixed number of steps. A common value is 64. \Delta t: Step size. Typical values depend on scene scale (e.g., 1 or 2 for a 100-unit room). Formulas: 1. Projected Pixel Width (Heuristic): To estimate an appropriate step size based on perspective, calculate the projected width of a single pixel at the entry point t{min}: projPixWidth = 2 \cdot \tan\left(\frac{fov{rad}}{2 \cdot W}\right) \cdot t{min} where fov{rad} = fov{deg} \cdot \pi / 180. 2. Step Vector (Fixed Count): If using a fixed number of steps N, the step vector is computed as: step = \frac{far - near}{N} where near and far are the 3D positions of the entry and exit points. 3. Linear Interpolation (Optional): For perspective-correct sampling, one can compute projPixWidth at both t{min} and t{max} and linearly interpolate the step size along the ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Transform screen-space vertices (e.g., a full-screen quad) using the inverse MVP matrix to obtain the ray origin (near) and a point on the ray (far). Normalize by the w-component to get NDC coordinates. 2. Step Calculation: Compute the step vector using the fixed number of steps N and the distance between near and far. Alternatively, set \Delta t based on the projected pixel width heuristic. 3. Initialization: Set rayPos = near and accumulator result = 0.0. 4. Loop: Iterate i from 0 to N-1: a. Coordinate Mapping: Map rayPos from world/NDC space to texture coordinates. For a unit cube [-1, 1], use: texCoord = (rayPos + 1.0) \cdot 0.5 b. Sampling: Sample the 3D texture at texCoord. Extract the density (e.g., red channel) and normalize by N and any scaling factor (e.g., 4.0): sample = \frac{T(texCoord).r \cdot 4.0}{N} c. Boundary Check: Verify if rayPos is within the volume bounds (e.g., [-1, 1] in all dimensions). d. Compositing: If inside the volume and result < 1.0, accumulate using front-to-back alpha blending: result += (1.0 - result) \cdot sample Otherwise, add 0.0. e. Advance: Update rayPos = rayPos + step. 5. Output: Return the final accumulated color with alpha 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stepsizeselectionraymarch(near, far, fovdeg, imagewidth, numsteps, texturesample): """ Performs fixed-step ray marching with step size selection based on projected pixel size. Args: near: list[float], ray origin (entry point) far: list[float], ray point at exit distance fovdeg: float, field of view in degrees imagewidth: int, width of the image in pixels numsteps: int, fixed number of steps (e.g., 64) texturesample: callable, function(coord) -> float, standard 3D texture fetch Returns: list[float], accumulated color [R, G, B, A] """ # 1. Compute step vector step = [(far[i] - near[i]) / numsteps for i in range(3)] # 2. Initialize ray state raypos = list(near) result = 0.0 # 3. Optional: Compute projected pixel width for validation/heuristic # fovrad = fovdeg 3.141592653589793 / 180.0 # projpixwidth = 2.0 math.tan(fovrad / (2.0 imagewidth)) math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in near)) for i in range(numsteps): # 4. Map position to texture coordinates (assuming unit cube [-1, 1]) texcoord = [(raypos[j] + 1.0) 0.5 for j in range(3)] # 5. Check bounds (strict inequality as per source) inside = all(p < 1.0 for p in raypos) and all(p > -1.0 for p in raypos) if inside and result < 1.0: # 6. Sample texture # Note: Source uses red channel and multiplies by scalefactor density = texturesample(texcoord) samplecontribution = (density 4.0) / numsteps # 7. Front-to-back compositing result += (1.0 - result) samplecontribution # 8. Advance ray raypos = [raypos[j] + step[j] for j in range(3)] return [result, result, result, 1.0] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: If the step size is too large, small frequency features (e.g., clouds, smoke details) are missed, causing a filtering issue. Shadow Misses: Large step sizes may cause rays to skip over small solid objects casting shadows on the volume. Boundary Exclusion: Using strict inequalities (< and >) for bounds [-1, 1] may exclude points exactly at the boundary. However, since rays typically start inside or on the boundary, this mainly affects the last few samples outside the volume. Data Scaling: Texture data is assumed to be in [0, 1]. The multiplication by 4.0 in the sample step suggests the data may need amplification or represents a specific density scale. Uniform Media: For uniform media, the step size can be fixed proportional to the medium's optical thickness or voxel resolution to ensure consistent sampling. Computes normalized step sizes and a scaling factor to map arbitrary volume dimensions and aspect ratios into a unit cube coordinate system for uniform ray marching. It ensures that the sampling density remains consistent across axes regardless of the volume's physical aspect ratio, preventing distorted or inconsistent sampling in non-cubic volumes. It differs from adaptive methods by maintaining a fixed step size derived from the maximum dimension, scaled by aspect ratios. Determines step size dynamically based on local density or distance field gradients to optimize sampling density. It addresses the trade-off between rendering speed and geometric accuracy, ensuring that samples are dense enough to resolve high-frequency details near the camera while reducing computation cost further away. It differs from constant step methods by dynamically adjusting granularity based on spatial context. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the fixed number of steps. Independent of scene complexity or density variation. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, excluding the 3D texture storage. Performance: Fast and predictable due to fixed iteration count, suitable for real-time applications. However, it may waste samples in empty regions or undersample dense regions compared to adaptive methods. Strengths: Simple implementation, no branching for step size calculation, predictable memory usage. Limitations: Requires heuristic tuning for different scene scales. When to Use: Uniform media, simple volumes, or when implementation simplicity is prioritized over optimal sampling. When Not to Use: Complex scenes with high dynamic range in density, or when memory/bandwidth constraints require adaptive skipping. The concept of fixed-step ray marching for volume rendering originated in early computer graphics literature as a straightforward method for integrating volume density along rays. The heuristic of using the projected pixel size to determine step size was introduced to mitigate aliasing by ensuring that the sampling rate matches the spatial frequency of the image. This method is widely used in real-time rendering, including WebGL and WebGPU samples, due to its simplicity and hardware friendliness. name: Raycasting Step Size & Aspect Ratio Normalization
head: Aspect Ratio Normalized Ray Marching, Normalized Step Size Calculation
body: This method computes a normalized step size and a scaling factor to map arbitrary volume dimensions and aspect ratios into a unit cube coordinate system for uniform ray marching. It ensures that the sampling density remains consistent across axes regardless of the volume's physical aspect ratio, preventing distorted or inconsistent sampling in non-cubic volumes. It differs from adaptive methods by maintaining a fixed step size derived from the maximum dimension, scaled by aspect ratios. Inputs: dimensions: vec3 representing the volume's dimensions in voxels or world units along x, y, and z axes. aspectRatios: vec3 defining the relative scaling of volume axes. Clamped to a minimum of vec3(0). stepScale: A multiplier for the base step size. Clamped to a minimum of 0.1f. Outputs: stepSize: The normalized step size used for ray marching. scaleFactor: A vec3 used to map coordinates into the unit cube. Data Structures: maxSize: A scalar float representing the maximum value among dimensions.x, dimensions.y, and dimensions.z. scaleFactor: A vec3 where each component maps the corresponding axis to the unit cube. Steps: 1. Calculate maxSize as the maximum of the volume's x, y, and z dimensions: maxSize = \max(dimensions.x, dimensions.y, dimensions.z) 2. Compute the base stepSize for each axis. The source provides a formula that simplifies to 1.0 / maxSize for each axis, but explicitly states: stepSize = \frac{1.0f}{dimensions[i] \times \left(\frac{maxSize}{dimensions[i]}\right)} This simplifies to: stepSize = \frac{1.0f}{maxSize} 3. Compute scaleFactor to handle aspect ratios. The source formula is: scaleFactor = \frac{vec3(1)}{\left(\frac{vec3(1) \times maxSize}{dimensions \times aspectRatios}\right)} Which simplifies to: scaleFactor = \frac{dimensions \times aspectRatios}{maxSize} 4. Apply stepScale to the final step size: finalStepSize = stepSize \times stepScale 5. Clamp stepScale to a minimum of 0.1f. 6. Clamp aspectRatios to a minimum of vec3(0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computestepsizeandscale(dimensions, aspectratios, stepscale): # Clamp aspect ratios to minimum 0 aspectratios = max(aspectratios, vec3(0)) # Calculate maxSize maxsize = max(dimensions.x, dimensions.y, dimensions.z) # Compute base step size (simplified from source formula) # stepSize = 1.0f / (dimensions[i] (maxSize / dimensions[i])) # This simplifies to 1.0f / maxSize for all axes basestepsize = 1.0f / maxsize # Compute scaleFactor # scaleFactor = vec3(1) / ((vec3(1) maxSize) / (dimensions aspectRatios)) # This simplifies to (dimensions aspectRatios) / maxSize scalefactor = (dimensions aspectratios) / maxsize # Apply stepScale, clamped to minimum 0.1f clampedstepscale = max(stepscale, 0.1f) finalstepsize = basestepsize clampedstepscale return finalstepsize, scalefactor Parameters: stepScale: Multiplier for the base step size. Controls rendering speed vs. quality. Minimum value: 0.1f. aspectRatios: vec3 defining relative scaling of volume axes. Minimum value: vec3(0). Edge Cases: If maxSize is 0, division by zero occurs. Guard against zero dimensions. If aspectRatios contains zeros, scaleFactor components become zero, potentially causing degenerate mappings. Time Complexity: O(1) for precomputation of step size and scale factor. Ray marching itself is O(N) where N is the number of steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) for storing maxSize, scaleFactor, and stepSize. Strengths: Ensures consistent sampling density across non-cubic volumes. Simple to implement. Limitations: Does not adapt to local density variations, potentially leading to over-sampling in empty space or under-sampling in dense regions. When to use: When uniform sampling is required and volume aspect ratios vary. When not to use: When adaptive sampling is needed for efficiency or accuracy in complex scenes. This method is derived from the VolumeRendering project by Jose Villegas. It is used in software-based volume rendering implementations to handle non-cubic volumes. jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, https://github.com/jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Uniform Ray Marching
head: Ray-to-Sample Generation, Uniform Ray Marching for Visualization
body: Uniform Ray Marching generates 3D sample positions along rays within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a fixed spacing between samples. It serves as a dense uniform sampler for Line-of-Sight (LOS) integral visualization, replacing coarse sampling to avoid aliasing artifacts such as concentric 'sampling rings' caused by steep gradients near inner radius cuts. It is often used as a fallback strategy in hardware or environments that do not support specialized libraries like nerfacc. Inputs: rayso: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing ray origins. raysd: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing ray directions. aabbmin, aabbmax: Vectors defining the AABB boundaries. renderstepsize: Scalar float defining the fixed distance between sample points. nsamples: Integer specifying the number of uniform sub-segments per ray (alternative to renderstepsize). rmaxrsun: Optional float specifying an outer sphere radius in solar radii (R{sun}). If None, no outer sphere clipping is applied. Outputs: ts: Tensor of shape (M,) containing start times for each segment. te: Tensor of shape (M,) containing end times for each segment. rayidx: Tensor of shape (M,) mapping each segment to its parent ray index. valid: Boolean tensor of shape (N,) indicating which original rays had valid intersections. Where M is the total number of valid samples across all rays. Data Structures: Rays are represented as separate origin and direction tensors. Intersection times tmin and tmax are stored as 1D tensors of length N. Indices are managed using integer tensors broadcasted to match the maximum number of steps per ray. Steps: 1. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute the intersection of each ray with the AABB to determine the entry (tmin) and exit (tmax) distances along the ray direction. t{min}, t{max} = \text{intersect\ray\aabb}(rays\o, rays\d, aabb\min, aabb\max) 2. Initial Validity Mask: Initialize a boolean mask ok where rays are potentially valid: ok = (t{max} > t{min}) 3. Optional Outer Sphere Clipping: If rmaxrsun is provided, clip the ray interval to the intersection with a sphere of radius \rho = r{max\rsun} / aabb\scale. Calculate coefficients for the quadratic equation |o + t d|^2 = \rho^2: A = \sum{i} (rays\di)^2 B = 2.0 \sum{i} (rays\oi \cdot rays\di) C = \sum{i} (rays\oi)^2 - \rho^2 Compute the discriminant and handle numerical safety by clamping A to 10^{-20} and the discriminant to 0.0: disc = B^2 - 4.0 A C A{safe} = \max(A, 10^{-20}) disc{safe} = \max(disc, 0.0) Solve for intersection times t{in} and t{out}: t{in} = \frac{-B - \sqrt{disc{safe}}}{2.0 A{safe}} t{out} = \frac{-B + \sqrt{disc{safe}}}{2.0 A{safe}} Update interval bounds and validity: t{min} = \max(t{min}, t{in}) t{max} = \min(t{max}, t{out}) hit = (disc \ge 0) ok = ok \land hit 4. Final Validity Check: Determine final valid rays where the interval is non-empty: valid = ok \land (t{max} > t{min}) 5. Generate Uniform Segments: There are two common approaches depending on whether nsamples or renderstepsize is the primary control. Approach A: Fixed Number of Samples (nsamples) For valid rays, let a = t{min}[valid] and b = t{max}[valid]. Create n{samples} + 1 linearly spaced points in [0, 1]: u = \text{linspace}(0.0, 1.0, n{samples} + 1) Compute edge coordinates (broadcasting a, b to shape (N{valid}, 1) and u to (1, n{samples}+1)): edges = a[:, None] + (b - a)[:, None] \cdot u[None,:] Flatten edges into segment starts ts and ends te: ts = edges[:,:-1].reshape(-1) te = edges[:, 1:].reshape(-1) Generate ray indices mapping segments to valid rays: ray\idx = \text{repeat\interleave}(\text{arange}(N{valid}), n{samples}) Approach B: Fixed Step Size (renderstepsize) Compute the number of steps per ray: n{steps} = \max(1, \lceil (t{max} - t{min}) / render\step\size \rceil) Determine max\steps = \max(n{steps}). Create an index tensor idx of shape (1, max\steps) containing [0, 1, \dots, max\steps-1]. Broadcast n{steps} to shape (N, 1) and create a boolean mask where idx < n{steps}. Compute start times ts and end times te: ts = (t{min} + idx \cdot render\step\size) te = \min(t{min} + (idx + 1) \cdot render\step\size, t{max}) Flatten ts and te using the mask. Construct ray\idx by expanding ray indices [0, N-1] to shape (N, max\steps) and flattening with the mask. 6. Compute Sample Positions (Post-Processing): If sample positions are required, compute them from the generated t values: samples = rays\o[ray\idx] + ts \cdot rays\d[ray\idx] Pseudocode (PyTorch-like, Approach A): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uniformraymarching(rayso, raysd, aabbmin, aabbmax, nsamples, rmaxrsun=None, aabbscale=1.0): # 1. Ray-AABB Intersection tmin, tmax = rayaabbintersect(rayso, raysd, aabbmin, aabbmax) # 2. Initial Validity ok = tmax > tmin # 3. Optional Outer Sphere Clipping if rmaxrsun is not None: rho = rmaxrsun / aabbscale A = (raysd raysd).sum(dim=-1) B = 2.0 (rayso raysd).sum(dim=-1) C = (rayso rayso).sum(dim=-1) - rho rho # Numerical safety Asafe = torch.clamp(A, min=1e-20) disc = B B - 4.0 Asafe C discsafe = torch.clamp(disc, min=0.0) tin = (-B - torch.sqrt(discsafe)) / (2.0 Asafe) tout = (-B + torch.sqrt(discsafe)) / (2.0 Asafe) tmin = torch.maximum(tmin, tin) tmax = torch.minimum(tmax, tout) hit = disc >= 0 ok = ok & hit # 4. Final Validity valid = ok & (tmax > tmin) # 5. Generate Uniform Segments for valid rays # Filter rays validrayso = rayso[valid] validtmin = tmin[valid] validtmax = tmax[valid] # Create interpolation grid u = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nsamples + 1, device=rayso.device) # Broadcast and compute edges # validtmin shape: (Nvalid, 1) # u shape: (nsamples + 1,) edges = validtmin[:, None] + (validtmax[:, None] - validtmin[:, None]) u[None,:] # Flatten ts = edges[:,:-1].reshape(-1) te = edges[:, 1:].reshape(-1) # Ray indices Nvalid = valid.sum() rayidx = torch.arange(Nvalid, device=rayso.device).repeatinterleave(nsamples) return ts, te, rayidx, valid An oversampling technique where each fine sample owns the slab it is the midpoint of, clipped to the brick's segment, ensuring slab thicknesses tile [0, len] exactly at LOD (Level of Detail) interfaces. This addresses discontinuities at exit faces caused by previous empty-space skip implementations that probed one stride past each cube's exit face, leaving material in the last sub-stride unprobed. In CPU replicas, this corrected worst-case two-cube split errors ranging from -3.99% to +0.68%. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of rays and S is the number of samples per ray. The intersection test is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot S) to store the generated sample positions and indices. Strengths: Simple to implement; deterministic; avoids aliasing artifacts associated with coarse sampling; serves as a robust fallback when specialized libraries are unavailable. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to over-sampling in empty space or under-sampling in high-frequency regions if not adaptive. The "oversampled" variant requires careful slab ownership logic to prevent discontinuities at LOD boundaries. Performance: Measured whole-image Total Variation (TV) error improvements of -2.7% (x) and -2.2% (y) in browser-based WebGPU rendering with 64 chunks. Uniform Ray Marching is a fundamental technique in volume rendering, often implemented as a baseline or fallback method. It is cited in the context of the Jax-Volumetric-Renderer and CoroNeRFpublic. Recent implementations in niivue have refined the method to handle multi-LOD streaming and slab tiling correctly, addressing specific artifacts in browser-based visualization. szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, https://github.com/szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) AlanHsu314/CoroNeRFpublic, https://github.com/AlanHsu314/CoroNeRFpublic, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) feat(niivue): streamed multi-LOD rendering fixes, LOD compensation, budget plans, and block inspection, https://github.com/niivue/mono/pull/138, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
