name: Adaptive Step Size Calculation
head: Cone-angle based step size, Step Size Calculation
body: Adaptive Step Size Calculation determines the distance between samples during ray marching by scaling the step size based on the ray's distance from the origin and a predefined cone angle. It addresses the trade-off between rendering speed and geometric accuracy, ensuring that samples are dense enough to resolve high-frequency details near the camera while reducing computation cost further away. It differs from constant step methods by dynamically adjusting granularity based on spatial context. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: t: Current ray time (distance from ray origin). \alpha{cone}: Cone angle for volume rendering. dt{min}: Minimum step size. dt{max}: Maximum step size. Output: dt: The calculated step size for the current ray segment. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values. Steps: 1. Calculate the unconstrained step size by multiplying the current ray distance t by the cone angle \alpha{cone}. 2. Clamp the result to the range [dt{min}, dt{max}] to prevent steps from becoming too small (causing performance issues) or too large (causing aliasing or missed details). Formula: dt = \text{clamp}(t \cdot \alpha{cone}, dt{min}, dt{max}) Where: t \ge 0 is the distance along the ray. \alpha{cone} is a constant parameter representing the angular resolution or cone angle. dt{min} and dt{max} are scalar bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateadaptivestepsize(t, coneangle, dtmin, dtmax): """ Calculate adaptive step size for ray marching. Args: t (float): Current ray distance from origin. coneangle (float): Cone angle parameter. dtmin (float): Minimum allowed step size. dtmax (float): Maximum allowed step size. Returns: float: The calculated step size. """ # Calculate unconstrained step size rawstep = t coneangle # Clamp to valid range stepsize = max(dtmin, min(dtmax, rawstep)) return stepsize Parameters: t: Current ray time/distance. \alpha{cone}: Cone angle for volume rendering. dt{min}: Minimum step size. dt{max}: Maximum step size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If t=0, the step size is clamped to dt{min}, preventing zero-length steps. Precision issues may arise if t is very large and \alpha{cone} is small, potentially resulting in dt < dt{min} due to floating-point underflow before clamping. Extends adaptive step size by adapting the number of steps based on cone sampling, offering higher fidelity for complex volumes. Combines adaptive step size with temporal reprojection to reduce flickering and improve stability in animated scenes. Time Complexity: O(1) per step calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Reduces total sample count compared to constant step size for distant rays, improving performance. However, near-field rays may require more samples if dt{min} is small. Strengths: Balances accuracy and performance; simple to implement. Limitations: May still produce aliasing if \alpha{cone} is not tuned correctly for the scene's frequency content. When to Use: Suitable for general volume rendering where performance is a concern and the scene has varying density scales. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes requiring uniform resolution regardless of distance, or where strict error bounds are required. The method is derived from techniques used in efficient ray marching for volume rendering and occlusion grids. It is commonly associated with implementations that aim to optimize rendering speed by reducing sample counts at a distance. Yosshi999/faster-occgrid, https://github.com/Yosshi999/faster-occgrid, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count and Cone Sampling
head: Adaptive Step Count with Cone Sampling
body: This method performs volume rendering of volumetric clouds by adaptively selecting the number of ray march steps based on the viewing angle and using cone sampling to approximate light transport within the volume. It solves the problem of balancing rendering performance and visual quality in real-time atmospheric clouds, where top-down views require fewer steps than horizon views, and single-sample lighting causes banding artifacts. It differs from standard constant step ray marching by varying the step count dynamically and from sibling methods by using a fixed kernel of 6 offset vectors rotated towards the light source for density estimation along the light path. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D (normalized). Ray segment bounds t{start} and t{end} in world space. Pixel identifier (integer) for jittering. Time variable T for wind animation. Light direction L (normalized). Earth center position C{earth} (typically (0, R{earth}, 0)). Parameters: baseDensityFactor, jitterfactor, eccentricity, silverintensity, silverspread, brightness. Outputs: Accumulated color C{out} (RGB). Accumulated density \alpha{accum} (scalar, clamped to 1.0). The method uses a fixed kernel of 6 offset vectors. These are defined in local space and rotated to align with the light direction. Kernel Offsets (Local): 1. (0.1, 0.25, -0.15) 2. (0.2, 0.5, 0.2) 3. (-0.2, 0.1, -0.1) 4. (-0.05, 0.75, 0.05) 5. (-0.1, 1.0, 0.0) 6. (0.0, 3.0, 0.0) 1. Calculate Adaptive Step Count: Compute the dot product of the ray direction D and the world up vector U = (0, 1, 0). d = \text{dot}(D, U) Calculate the number of steps N{steps} using linear interpolation (mix) between 35 and 60 steps based on the viewing angle. Top-down views (d \approx 1) use 35 steps; horizon views (d \approx 0) use 60 steps. N{steps} = \lfloor \text{mix}(35.0, 60.0, 1.0 - d) \rfloor 2. Initialize Variables: Compute the step size: \Delta t = \frac{t{end} - t{start}}{N{steps}} Initialize transmittance T{trans} = 1.0 and accumulated density \alpha{accum} = 0.0. Initialize output color C{out} = (0, 0, 0). 3. Construct Light Rotation Matrix (TBN): To rotate the cone sampling kernel towards the light direction L, construct a rotation matrix. Find the axis with the largest absolute component in L: \text{maxComp} = \text{argmax}i |Li| Define unit vectors for the axes: Vx = (1, 0, 0), \quad Vy = (0, 1, 0), \quad Vz = (0, 0, 1) Select V{max} corresponding to \text{maxComp}. Compute the cross product to find an orthogonal vector Z{comp}: Z{comp} = \text{cross}(L, V{max}) Compute the X component: X{comp} = \text{cross}(Z{comp}, L) Normalize X{comp} and Z{comp} if necessary (though cross products of orthogonal vectors are often normalized, the source implies direct usage). Form the rotation matrix M{sun} with columns X{comp}, L, and Z{comp}: M{sun} = \begin{bmatrix} X{comp} & L & Z{comp} \end{bmatrix} 4. Precompute Cone Sampling Offsets: Transform the 6 local kernel offsets K{local}[i] into world space aligned with the light: K{world}[i] = M{sun} \times K{local}[i], \quad \text{for } i \in [0, 5] 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate j from 0 to N{steps} - 1: a. Calculate Sample Position: Compute current t: t = t{start} + j \cdot \Delta t Generate jitter offset using pixel ID and t to select an index from a pre-defined or pseudo-random set (mod 16). Let this be jitterIndex. Retrieve jitterLocation (a 2D vector or similar structure derived from the index). Calculate the perturbed ray direction component: \Delta Dx = \text{jitterLocation}.x \Delta Dy = (\text{jitterLocation}.x + \text{jitterLocation}.y) \cdot \text{jitterfactor} \Delta Dz = \text{jitterLocation}.y Update position P: P = O + t \cdot (D + (\Delta Dx, \Delta Dy, \Delta Dz)) b. Sample Density: Transform P to relative atmospheric coordinates. Divide by 8.0 to control noise frequency. Skew the sample point using wind direction and time T: P{skewed} = \text{Skew}(P, \text{wind}, T) Calculate relative height h from P and C{earth}. Sample low-frequency density: \rho{base} = \text{SampleLowFreq}(P{skewed}, P, h, C{earth}) \cdot \text{baseDensityFactor} If \rho{base} > 0.0, erode with high-frequency noise: \rho{high} = \text{ErodeCloud}(\rho{base} \cdot 1.4, D, P{skewed}, h) Update accumulated density: \alpha{accum} \leftarrow \alpha{accum} + \rho{high} \cdot 0.5 Check for early termination: If \alpha{accum} \ge 1.0, set \alpha{accum} = 1.0 and break the loop. c. Cone Sampling for Lighting: Initialize densityAlongLight = 0.0. Loop i from 0 to 5: Calculate light sample position: P{light} = P + \Delta t \cdot K{world}[i] \cdot (i + 1) (Note: Source says float(i), implying multiplication by index. If i=0, offset is 0.) Sample density at P{light}: \rho{light\base} = \text{SampleLowFreq}(P{light}, \dots) If \rho{light\base} > 0.0: \rho{light\high} = \text{ErodeCloud}(\rho{light\base} \cdot 1.4, D, P{light}, h) \text{densityAlongLight} \leftarrow \text{densityAlongLight} + \rho{light\high} d. Compute Light Energy and Update Color: Calculate total light energy using a function GetLightEnergy with parameters: Relative height h densityAlongLight \rho{base} Henyey-Greenstein phase function value p(\theta) with eccentricity eccentricity Cosine of the angle between light and view direction Step size \Delta t Brightness multiplier brightness E{light} = \text{GetLightEnergy}(h, \text{densityAlongLight}, \rho{base}, p(\theta), \Delta t, \text{brightness}) Update transmittance and color: T{trans} = \text{mix}(T{trans}, E{light}, 1.0 - \alpha{accum}) C{out} \leftarrow C{out} + T{trans} baseDensityFactor: Controls cloud density center intensity. Default: 0.380. jitterfactor: Multiplier for jitter offset in Y component. Default: 1.180. eccentricity: Henyey-Greenstein scattering parameter. Default: 0.6. silverintensity: Parameter for modified Henyey-Greenstein function. Default: 0.7. silverspread: Parameter for modified Henyey-Greenstein function. Default: 0.1. brightness: Lighting brightness multiplier. Default: 5.0. Precision: The mixing of transmittance and light energy requires careful handling of floating-point precision to avoid banding, especially at low densities. Boundaries: The ray segment bounds t{start} and t{end} must correctly clip against the volume boundaries (e.g., sphere intersection with atmosphere). Degenerate Input: If the ray direction is parallel to the world up vector, the dot product is 1 or -1. The formula handles d \approx 1 (top-down) well. If d is negative (viewing from below), the mix parameter 1.0-d exceeds 1, potentially exceeding 60 steps. The source specifies "horizon views" for d near 0, implying the method is optimized for viewing from above or the horizon. Kernel Alignment: The TBN matrix construction assumes L is not parallel to the chosen maxComp axis. If L is parallel, the cross product becomes zero. A fallback axis selection is not explicitly detailed in the source but is a standard implementation requirement. Time Complexity: O(N{steps} \cdot K), where N{steps} is the adaptive step count (35-60) and K=6 is the number of cone samples. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of steps and constant with respect to the scene size (assuming texture lookups are O(1)). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, excluding the noise texture/sampler state. Specific performance metrics (FPS, resolution) are not provided in the sources. The method is designed for real-time rendering, as indicated by the use of jittering and adaptive steps. The method scales well with resolution as it is a per-pixel operation. The adaptive step count reduces computational load for top-down views, providing a performance benefit in scenes with significant vertical viewing angles. Strengths: Reduces artifacts from single-sample lighting via cone sampling. Adaptive steps optimize performance based on viewing angle. Limitations: Fixed kernel size (6 samples) may not capture complex light transport in very dense volumes. The method relies on procedural noise, which may lack the detail of texture-based approaches. Use for real-time volumetric cloud rendering where performance is critical and visual quality needs to be maintained across varying camera angles. Not suitable for offline rendering where higher fidelity light transport (e.g., multiple scattering) is required. Not suitable for scenes with dynamic light sources that change rapidly, as the TBN matrix must be recomputed per ray. The method is derived from the implementation in the open-source project "realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes" by erickTornero. The technique combines adaptive step sizing, which is common in ray marching to optimize performance, with cone sampling, a technique used to approximate the integration of light through a volume by sampling along a cone aligned with the light direction. This approach helps to reduce the "staircase" artifacts and noise associated with single-sample lighting in volumetric rendering. The method is used in real-time graphics applications, specifically for rendering atmospheric clouds in games or simulations. erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, https://github.com/erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Ray Marching with Temporal Reprojection
head: HZL Fluid Effects Studio volume renderer, field mode shading
body: This method performs volume rendering by combining adaptive ray marching with temporal accumulation to reduce noise and flickering in animated scenes. It builds on Adaptive Step Size Calculation by using density thresholds to vary step size, and extends standard ray marching by reprojection of the previous frame's color and alpha into the current frame's screen space. It is distinct from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count and Cone Sampling by relying on spatial reprojection rather than cone-based filtering for temporal stability. Inputs: Ray origin and direction. Volume density field (accessed via ray marching). stepSize: Base step length. densityScale: Scaling factor for density in opacity calculation. absorption: Absorption coefficient multiplier. adaptiveSteppingEnabled: Boolean flag. historyTexture: Previous frame's accumulated color and alpha buffer. historyWeight: Base weight for temporal blending. emittedLight: Emissive contribution per unit step. smokeColor: Base color of the volume. fieldMode: Integer switch (0-7) for color mapping logic. Outputs: Final accumulated color (accumulated.rgb) and alpha (accumulated.a). Data Structures: accumulated: A vector or struct holding rgb (float3) and a (float). Initialized to zero. history: Sampled from historyTexture at reprojected UV coordinates. Holds rgb and a. representativePosition: World or view space position of the current ray step, used for reprojection. Parameters: stepSize: Base step length. densityScale: Scaling factor. absorption: Absorption multiplier. adaptiveSteppingEnabled: Boolean. historyWeight: Base blend weight. emissionStrength: Multiplier for emitted light (used in emittedLight calculation). fieldMode: Integer (0-7). Steps: 1. Initialize accumulated.rgb and accumulated.a to zero. 2. Loop through ray steps: a. Compute currentStep. If adaptiveSteppingEnabled is true and current density < 0.004, set currentStep = stepSize 4.0. Otherwise, currentStep = stepSize. b. Calculate opacity: opacity = 1.0 - \exp(-density \cdot densityScale \cdot currentStep \cdot absorption \cdot 4.0) c. Update accumulated color: accumulated.rgb \leftarrow accumulated.rgb + (1.0 - accumulated.a) \cdot (opacity \cdot smokeColor + emittedLight \cdot currentStep) d. Update accumulated alpha: accumulated.a \leftarrow accumulated.a + (1.0 - accumulated.a) \cdot opacity e. If accumulated.a > 0.985, break the loop. f. Increment distanceAlongRay by currentStep. 3. If accumulated.a < 0.002, discard the fragment (do not write to color buffer). 4. If temporalEnabled is true and foundVolume is true: a. Project representativePosition to previous clip space. b. Compute UV coordinates from previous clip space. c. Clamp UV to [0.0, 1.0]. d. Sample historyTexture at clamped UV to get history. e. Compute responsiveWeight: responsiveWeight = historyWeight \cdot (1.0 - |history.a - accumulated.a|) f. Blend: accumulated = mix(accumulated, history, clamp(responsiveWeight, 0.0, 0.95)) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveraymarchingwithtemporalreprojection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumesampler, historytexture, camerastate, params): # Initialize accumulation accumulatedrgb = vec3(0.0) accumulateda = 0.0 # Parameters stepsize = params.stepSize densityscale = params.densityScale absorption = params.absorption adaptiveenabled = params.adaptiveSteppingEnabled historyweight = params.historyWeight emittedlight = params.emittedLight # Pre-calculated or per-step smokecolor = params.smokeColor fieldmode = params.fieldMode # Temporal reprojection state temporalenabled = params.temporalEnabled foundvolume = False # Ray marching loop distancealongray = 0.0 while True: # Get density at current position density = volumesampler.sample(rayorigin + raydirection distancealongray) # Adaptive step size if adaptiveenabled and density < 0.004: currentstep = stepsize 4.0 else: currentstep = stepsize # Opacity calculation # Note: The source formula includes a 4.0 factor in the exponent opacity = 1.0 - exp(-density densityscale currentstep absorption 4.0) # Color accumulation accumulatedrgb += (1.0 - accumulateda) (opacity smokecolor + emittedlight currentstep) # Alpha accumulation accumulateda += (1.0 - name: Sphere Tracing
head: Classic Sphere Tracing, SDF Sphere Tracing, SDF Tracing, Signed Distance Field Ray Marching, Sphere Tracing for Ray Marching
body: Sphere Tracing is an iterative ray-marching algorithm for rendering implicit surfaces defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It solves the problem of finding the intersection between a ray and a complex geometric surface represented mathematically rather than as a polygon mesh. Unlike Standard Constant Step Ray Marching, which uses a fixed interval and risks missing thin geometry or overshooting surfaces, Sphere Tracing dynamically calculates a safe step size equal to the distance to the nearest surface. This guarantees that the ray never penetrates the surface, ensuring robust convergence for pathological shapes with discontinuous derivatives. Sphere Tracing relies on the property that an SDF f(\mathbf{x}) returns the Euclidean distance from a point \mathbf{x} to the nearest surface f^{-1}(0). For a general Lipschitz continuous function with constant \lambda, the step size is bounded by |f(\mathbf{x})|/\lambda. In the specific case of an SDF, \lambda=1, so the function value itself is the exact distance and a safe lower bound for the step. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} (3D vector). Ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized 3D vector). SDF function f(\mathbf{x}) returning signed distance. Maximum march distance D{max} (scalar). Convergence threshold \epsilon (scalar, e.g., 10^{-4}). Maximum iteration count N{max} (integer). Outputs: Intersection distance t (scalar) or hit point \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Hit mask (boolean) indicating if a surface was found within D{max}. The algorithm maintains a single scalar variable for the accumulated distance traveled along the ray, typically denoted as t or depth. No complex data structures are required for the core traversal, though implementations often batch rays into tensors of shape (N, 3) for origins and directions to leverage GPU parallelism. 1. Initialize: Set the current distance traveled t = 0.0. Initialize a hit flag or mask to false. 2. Loop: Iterate for i from 0 to N{max} - 1: a. Evaluate: Compute the current point on the ray \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. Evaluate the SDF at this point: d = f(\mathbf{p}). b. Check Hit: If |d| < \epsilon (or d < \epsilon for unsigned distance fields), the ray has hit the surface. Return t (or \mathbf{p}) and mark as hit. c. Check Max Distance: If t \ge D{max}, the ray has traveled too far without hitting the surface. Return D{max} (or a miss indicator). d. Step: Advance the ray by the distance d. Update t \leftarrow t + d. Note: If d is negative (inside the object), the ray moves backward toward the surface boundary. 3. Termination: If the loop completes without hitting the surface, return a miss indicator (e.g., t = D{max}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretrace(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunction, maxdist, epsilon, maxsteps): """ Performs sphere tracing to find the intersection of a ray with an SDF surface. Args: rayorigin (vec3): The starting point of the ray. raydirection (vec3): The normalized direction of the ray. sdffunction (func): A function f(p) returning the signed distance to the surface. maxdist (float): The maximum distance the ray will travel. epsilon (float): The threshold for considering a point as a hit. maxsteps (int): The maximum number of iterations allowed. Returns: float: The distance to the hit point, or maxdist if no hit is found. bool: True if a hit was found, False otherwise. """ t = 0.0 hit = False for i in range(maxsteps): # 1. Calculate current position currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 2. Evaluate SDF dist = sdffunction(currentpos) # 3. Check for surface hit # Using absolute value for signed distance fields to handle both inside/outside if abs(dist) < epsilon: hit = True break # 4. Check for max distance exceeded if t >= maxdist: break # 5. Step forward # The SDF value is the safe lower bound for the step size t += dist return t, hit Epsilon (\epsilon): Determines the precision of the hit. Typical values range from 10^{-4} to 10^{-6}. A larger epsilon may cause the ray to stop slightly before or after the true surface, while a smaller epsilon increases iteration count. Max Steps (N{max}): Limits the computational cost. Typical values are 10–32 for simple scenes or real-time shaders, and up to 1024 for high-quality offline rendering. Max Distance (D{max}): The far clipping plane for the ray. Typical values depend on scene scale, e.g., 100.0 or 1000.0. Overshooting: If the function used is not a true SDF (i.e., the gradient magnitude |\nabla f| \neq 1), the step size may be too large, causing the ray to pass through the surface. This is known as the "blind root-finding" problem. Thin Geometry: Rays passing near parallel surfaces or grazing angles may require many iterations because the step size is constrained by the small distance to the nearest surface. Non-Convergence: If the ray does not converge within maxsteps, the result is invalid. Implementations often zero out the position or mark the ray as a miss. Inside the Surface: If the ray starts inside an object (f(\mathbf{p}) < 0), the step size is negative, moving the ray backward toward the surface boundary. Antialiasing technique representing pixels as cones to compute fractional coverage, differing from standard sphere tracing by detecting intersections with an "inner cover" surface. Uses local Lipschitz bounds on candidate segments for adaptive step sizes, reducing SDF queries compared to global bounds. Accelerates convergence by precomputing augmented distance fields using quadric surfaces to bound geometry. Post-processing metric for evaluating geometric fidelity between predicted SDFs and ground-truth meshes. Steps further than the SDF bound allows using a relaxation parameter \omega to reduce iteration counts. Steps by a multiple of the SDF value to accelerate convergence at grazing angles and allow surface penetration. Solves ray traversal in deformed SDF spaces by integrating an ODE, correcting for invalid Euclidean metrics. Time Complexity: The number of iterations depends on the scene complexity and the ray's path. In the best case (perpendicular approach to flat surfaces), convergence is fast. In the worst case (grazing angles or parallel surfaces), the number of steps increases significantly. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, as only the current position and distance traveled are stored. Performance: Highly efficient for procedural geometry and complex implicit surfaces where explicit mesh storage would be prohibitive. Performance is limited by the cost of evaluating the SDF function, which can be complex for CSG operations or noise fields. Strengths: Robust handling of pathological surfaces, no need for mesh data, compact representation of geometry, and inherent antialiasing capabilities when combined with cone tracing. Limitations: Slow convergence near grazing angles or thin features. Requires the SDF to be Lipschitz continuous with a known constant. Not suitable for non-SDF implicit functions without modification. Sphere Tracing was introduced by John C. Hart in 1996. It was developed as a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, leveraging the properties of distance functions to guarantee convergence without overshooting. The technique has become a staple in the demoscene and real-time graphics (e.g., Shadertoy) due to its ability to render complex procedural geometry efficiently in fragment shaders. It is closely related to the broader field of Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering and is a specific instance of distance-field ray marching. name: Cone Intersection
head: Cone Tracing, Antialiased Ray Intersection, Cone Tracing with Covers, Cone-object intersection
body: Cone intersection is an antialiasing technique for sphere tracing that represents a pixel as a viewing cone rather than a point ray, allowing symbolic prefiltering to eliminate aliasing artifacts at grazing angles. It differs from standard sphere tracing by detecting intersections with an "inner cover" surface and computing the fractional coverage of the pixel by the implicit surface, whereas siblings like Segment Tracing or Quadric Tracing focus on varying step sizes or bounding volumes without necessarily computing area-based coverage fractions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A signed distance function (SDF) f(x) defining the implicit surface, a ray origin o and direction d, and camera parameters (field of view \theta, resolution Nh, Nv). Output: A final pixel color and opacity, computed by compositing shading values from representative samples along the ray. Data Structures: Ray State: Current position x, accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}, accumulated color c{acc}. Sample List: A bounded list (max 4 samples) storing representative points (xi), their distances ti, their pixel radii r{p,i}, and their coverage fractions \alphai. Parameters: rp: Pixel radius. Defined as half the diameter of a pixel. \theta: Field of view angle. Nh, Nv: Horizontal and vertical resolution. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Calculate Pixel Radius: Determine the radius of the pixel rp at the current traversal distance t. The sources provide an approximation using the maximum resolution dimension: rp(t) = t \cdot \frac{2 \tan(\theta/2)}{\max(Nh, Nv)} Note that rp grows linearly with distance t. 2. Define Inner Cover: Construct the inner cover surface f{inner}(x) by offsetting the SDF by the pixel radius: f{inner}(x) = f(x) + rp Sphere tracing is performed on this inner cover surface instead of the original surface f(x). 3. Ray Traversal (Sphere Tracing): Iterate along the ray starting from t=0. At each step, evaluate f(x) at the current point x. Step Size: The step size S{next} is determined by the radius of the unbounding sphere, defined as the sum of the pixel radius and the SDF value: S{next} = rp + f(x). (Note: describes a comparable traversal step that may take the ray through the surface). Update Position: x \leftarrow x + S{next} \cdot d. Convergence Test: If f(x) \le 0 (or a small epsilon), the ray has intersected the original surface. Terminate traversal for this ray. 4. Identify Representative Samples: During traversal, track unbounding spheres (spheres of radius rp + f(x) centered at x) that fall within the cone bounds. A cone intersection is indicated if the ray intersects the inner cover, which corresponds to the condition f(x) \le rp. The "representative" point for a cone intersection is the center of the smallest unbounding sphere (with respect to pixel size) among those inside the cone. This point is the location along the ray section closest to the surface. Keep track of up to four such representative points to maintain performance. 5. Calculate Coverage Fraction (\alpha): For each representative point x, calculate the fraction of the pixel covered by the surface. Assuming local planarity, the surface intersects the cone's cross-section (a disk of radius rp) with a straight edge at signed distance f(x) from the center. The coverage fraction \alpha is given by the formula derived by Thompson (1990): \alpha = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\pi} \left( \frac{f(x)}{rp} \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{f(x)}{rp}\right)^2} + \arcsin\left(\frac{f(x)}{rp}\right) \right) If f(x) > rp, \alpha = 0. If f(x) < -rp, \alpha = 1. This \alpha represents the opacity of the surface at this intersection. 6. Shading and Compositing: Shade the representative point x to get color c{shade} and alpha \alpha{shade} (if the surface has material properties). Accumulate the coverage \alpha as opacity. Composite the colors using the Porter-Duff "over" operator: c{out} = c{in} + c{shade} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha{shade} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) For intersection edges involving multiple surfaces, keep track of all SDFs whose unbounding spheres fit within the cone bounds. Use the SDFs of each intersecting surface to provide proportions for combining their shading properties. 7. Final Output: The final pixel color is the accumulated color after processing all representative samples and the background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def coneintersectionraytrace(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, fov, resolution): """ Performs cone intersection ray tracing for a single pixel. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple raydirection: (x, y, z) tuple (normalized) sdf: function f(x, y, z) returning signed distance fov: field of view in radians resolution: (width, height) tuple Returns: (finalcolor, finalalpha) """ nh, nv = resolution maxres = max(nh, nv) t = 0.0 maxsteps = 100 accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 # List to store representative samples: (t, fval, rp, shadecolor, shadealpha) # Limit to 4 samples for performance samples = [] for step in range(maxsteps): x = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) rp = t (2.0 math.tan(fov / 2.0)) / maxres fval = sdf(x[0], x[1], x[2]) if fval <= 0.0: shadecolor, shadealpha = shadesurface(x, sdf) newr = accumulatedcolor[0] + shadecolor[0] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newg = accumulatedcolor[1] + shadecolor[1] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newb = accumulatedcolor[2] + shadecolor[2] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newa = accumulatedalpha + shadealpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor = (newr, newg, newb) accumulatedalpha = newa break if fval <= rp: shadecolor, shadealpha = shadesurface(x, sdf) samples.append((t, fval, rp, shadecolor, shadealpha)) stepsize = rp + fval if stepsize <= 1e-6: stepsize = 1e-6 t += stepsize if t > 1000.0: break # Composite samples back-to-front for i in range(len(samples) - 1, -1, -1): ts, fs, rps, shadecolor, shadealpha = samples[i] ratio = fs / rps ratio = max(-1.0, min(1.0, ratio)) if ratio >= 1.0: alphacov = 0.0 elif ratio <= -1.0: alphacov = 1.0 else: term1 = ratio math.sqrt(1.0 - ratio ratio) term2 = math.asin(ratio) alphacov = 0.5 + (1.0 / math.pi) (term1 + term2) effectivealpha = alphacov shadealpha newr = accumulatedcolor[0] + shadecolor[0] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newg = accumulatedcolor[1] + shadecolor[1] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newb = accumulatedcolor[2] + shadecolor[2] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newa = accumulatedalpha + effectivealpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor = (newr, newg, newb) accumulatedalpha = newa return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha def shadesurface(point, sdf): """ Computes surface normal via finite differences and returns a simple diffuse color. Actual shading logic is application-specific. """ eps = 1e-4 dx = sdf(point[0]+eps, point[1], point[2]) - sdf(point[0]-eps, point[1], point[2]) dy = sdf(point[0], point[1]+eps, point[2]) - sdf(point[0], point[1]-eps, point[2]) dz = sdf(point[0], point[1], point[2]+eps) - sdf(point[0], point[1], point[2]-eps) normal = (dx, dy, dz) lenn = math.sqrt(normal[0]2 + normal[1]2 + normal[2]2) if lenn > 0: normal = (normal[0]/lenn, normal[1]/lenn, normal[2]/lenn) else: normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) lightdir = (1.0, 1.0, -1.0) lenl = math.sqrt(lightdir[0]2 + lightdir[1]2 + lightdir[2]2) lightdir = (lightdir[0]/lenl, lightdir[1]/lenl, lightdir[2]/lenl) diff = max(0.0, normal[0]lightdir[0] + normal[1]lightdir[1] + normal[2]lightdir[2]) color = (diff, diff, diff) alpha = 1.0 return color, alpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Premature Shrinking: If the SDF is expensive or approximated by a bound, the unbounding sphere radius may shrink below the pixel radius prematurely, leading to incorrect cone intersections. Distance Approximation: If the SDF is inaccurate, use the first-order approximation d(x) \approx f(x) / \|\nabla f(x)\| for distance estimation, which is asymptotic to geometric distance. Representative Point Off-Surface: The representative sample is off the implicit surface. A usable surface normal must be defined by assuming continuity in the gradient of the distance function. Performance: Tracking sample lists becomes expensive at higher resolutions, causing frame rates to drop significantly. Ellipsoid Scaling: For non-uniformly scaled objects (e.g., ellipsoids), signed distance bounds may return underestimated distances (as low as 1% of actual distance), affecting cone intersection accuracy. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of steps, but the number of steps depends on the accuracy of the distance estimate. Halving the distance estimate doubles the number of steps. Memory Complexity: Low, but requires storing a list of representative samples (limited to 4) per pixel. Performance: Achieves around 60 fps for 512x512 resolution, but drops considerably for larger resolutions due to the cost of tracking sample lists. Sphere tracing rendered a complex scene in 12:47 at 256x256 resolution. Strengths: Eliminates aliasing artifacts from point sampling, especially at silhouette edges and grazing angles. Can also prefilter texture aliasing. Limitations: Does not antialias edges projected from the camera perspective onto the object itself (maintains interactive frame rates). Convergence is entirely linear, unlike interval analysis which has a quadratically convergent refinement stage. Cone intersection was introduced as an antialiasing method by Amanatides (1984) for computing intersections of cones with spheres, planes, and polygons. Hart and DeFanti (1991) extended this to implicit surfaces using sphere tracing and the concept of "covers" (offset surfaces). The technique is implemented in the zeno rendering system. name: Segment Tracing
body: Segment Tracing is a ray marching algorithm that computes local Lipschitz bounds on candidate segments to determine adaptive step sizes, reducing the number of field function queries compared to global Lipschitz bound methods like Sphere Tracing. It works for a particular class of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces, leveraging the composition of distance functions and kernel functions to compute directional Lipschitz bounds. Unlike Sphere Tracing, which uses a global bound that limits step size efficiency, Segment Tracing allows larger, safer steps by adapting to the local gradient and field values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray \delta(t), a hierarchical skeletal implicit surface model where primitives and operators support local Lipschitz bound queries, an initial candidate step distance \varepsilon0, an amplification factor \kappa, and a threshold \mu. Output: The intersection parameter t along the ray, or the domain exit parameter. Data Structures: The method requires the implicit model to implement specific queries for each primitive and operator node: 1. Field function evaluation f(p). 2. Local Lipschitz bound over a segment \lambda(e), where e is a segment of the ray. 3. Local Lipschitz bound over a sphere \lambda(S) (used in some implementations for tighter bounds). Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the intersection between the ray and the domain [t-, t+] = \Delta \cap \Omega, and initialize t = t-. 2. Set the initial candidate stepping distance \varepsilon0. 3. While t < t+: 1. Compute the field function value f(t) at the current position. 2. If |f(t)| < \mu, an intersection has occurred; terminate and return t. 3. Define the candidate segment e(t, \varepsiloni) = [\delta(t), \delta(t + \varepsiloni)]. 4. Compute the local directional Lipschitz bound \lambda(e(t, \varepsiloni)) for the candidate segment. This step leverages the fact that primitives are defined as a composition of a distance function and a kernel function. 5. Evaluate f(pi^) (where pi^ is the current point) and compute the safe stepping increment s(t, \varepsiloni) using the formula: s(t, \varepsiloni) = \min \left( \frac{|f(t)|}{\lambda(e(t, \varepsiloni))}, \varepsiloni \right) where s is the effective stepping distance, f(t) is the field function value, \lambda(e) is the local Lipschitz bound on segment e, and \varepsiloni is the candidate distance. 6. Update the position: t \leftarrow t + s(t, \varepsiloni). 7. Compute the next candidate stepping distance \varepsilon{i+1} = \kappa \cdot s(t, \varepsiloni), where \kappa is the geometric amplification factor. Parameters: \mu: The threshold value from which an intersection is considered to have occurred (|f(t)| < \mu). \varepsilon0: The initial candidate step distance. Its value has little impact on performance; if too large, the initial Lipschitz bound is large, leading to small subsequent steps. \kappa: The geometric amplification factor for the next candidate step. Typical value is \kappa \approx 2. Must be > 1. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: If \varepsilon0 is too large, the computed Lipschitz bound \lambda(e(t0, \varepsilon0)) is large (upper bound), causing the next candidate distance \varepsilon1 to be small. If \varepsilon0 \to \infty, \lambda(e) becomes the global bound. If the computation of local bounds is too complex or computationally intensive for a given operator or primitive, the algorithm automatically reverts to the standard Sphere Tracing framework locally. The method works only for a particular class of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces and is not directly applicable to a wide range of volumes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def segmenttracing(rayorigin, raydirection, domainmin, domainmax, fieldfunction, locallipschitzsegment, epsilon0, kappa, mu): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 (normalized) domainmin: float (tmin) domainmax: float (tmax) fieldfunction: function(p) -> float locallipschitzsegment: function(t, epsilon) -> float epsilon0: float kappa: float (> 1) mu: float """ t = domainmin epsilon = epsilon0 while t < domainmax: # Evaluate field function at current position p = rayorigin + t raydirection fval = fieldfunction(p) # Check for intersection if abs(fval) < mu: return t # Compute local Lipschitz bound for candidate segment [t, t + epsilon] lambdabound = locallipschitzsegment(t, epsilon) # Compute safe stepping increment if lambdabound == 0: step = epsilon else: step = min(abs(fval) / lambdabound, epsilon) # Clamp step to domain boundary to prevent overshoot and fix boundary precision step = min(step, domainmax - t) # Update position t = t + step # Amplify candidate step for next iteration epsilon = kappa step return domainmax # No intersection within domain The parent method using a global Lipschitz bound. Choose when simplicity is preferred and local bound computation is not feasible. [1674-sphere-tracing.md] Uses cone intersection tests for tighter bounds. Choose when higher precision is needed for complex primitives. [1553-cone-intersection.md] Uses quadric approximations for step size. Choose for quadric-based implicit surfaces. [1866-quadric-tracing.md] Uses L1 distance fields. Choose for grid-based volumes where L1 metrics are appropriate. [2752-chamfer-l1-distance-computation.md] Uses over-stepping heuristics. Choose for a simple speedup over standard Sphere Tracing without local bound computation. [3805-over-relaxation-sphere-tracing.md] Reduces queries by a factor of 1.2. Choose for a minor improvement over Sphere Tracing. [3811-enhanced-sphere-tracing.md] Uses non-linear transformations. Choose for specific non-linear field representations. [4079-non-linear-sphere-tracing.md] Time Complexity: Increases the overall complexity of the shader due to the implementation of extra functions for computing the Lipschitz bound over a segment, a ray, or a spherical domain. Memory Complexity: Does not require accelerating data structures such as voxel grids or octrees for storing the local Lipschitz bound. Measured Performance: Reduces field function queries by up to three orders of magnitude compared to Sphere Tracing, resulting in accelerations of up to \times 10, despite the extra computational cost of Lipschitz bound queries. Scaling: Performance gains are most significant for hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces where local bounds can be computed efficiently. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of field function queries; no need for precomputed acceleration structures; adapts to local gradient variations. Limitations: Requires primitives and operators to implement complex local Lipschitz bound queries; not directly applicable to a wide range of volumes; overhead from bound computation can negate benefits if not optimized. When to use: When rendering hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces and field function evaluation is expensive. When not to use: When the implicit model does not support local Lipschitz bound queries, or when the overhead of computing these bounds exceeds the savings from fewer field evaluations. Introduced in, the method was developed to address the limitations of Sphere Tracing, which uses a global Lipschitz bound that limits efficiency. The method leverages the structure of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces, where primitives are defined as a composition of a distance function and a kernel function, allowing for the computation of local directional Lipschitz bounds. It has been used in the context of ray tracing compactly supported primitives combined in a Blobtree. name: Quadric Tracing
body:
Quadric tracing is a method to accelerate sphere tracing by precomputing an augmented distance field using quadric surfaces (second-degree algebraic surfaces) to bound or unbound scene geometry, reducing the number of Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluations. It solves the slowdown of sphere tracing near surfaces and with increasing scene complexity, where function evaluation time and convergence slow drastically. Unlike relaxed sphere tracing (which uses a scalar to determine step size and reverts if too large) or enhanced sphere tracing (which uses previous two radii to approximate planar surfaces), quadric tracing uses precomputed geometric bounds to accelerate convergence. It stops when the computed distance value dips below a threshold, switching to enhanced sphere tracing for final convergence. Inputs: A 3D grid of precomputed quadric parameters and SDF values; a ray defined by origin p0 and direction v (|v|2 = 1). Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray. Data Structures: The accelerator data structure is a regular 3D grid. Each cell stores: Quadric of Revolution: 96 bits (3 floats). Defined relative to the grid point pc. The axis of revolution direction n \in \mathbb{R}^3 (|n|2 = 1) is multiplied by 2 + k to store the quadric parameters. The scalar parameter k \in [-1, 1] encodes the shape (eccentricity and curvature). SDF Value: 32 bits (1 float). A signed distance function value d stored for the cell. Total: 128 bits per cell. Preprocessing: For every cell in parallel on the GPU, starting from the quadric origin pc: 1. Shoot rays in N uniformly sampled directions vi (i = 1, \dots, N). 2. Sphere trace each ray pc + t vi until the surface or the bounding box is reached. 3. For each ray-surface intersection (xi, yi, zi):= pc + ti vi, compute the unique ki \in [-1, 1] value defining the quadric of revolution touching the surface at that point. Operate in the 2D plane defined by vi and normal n. Let q = (qx, qy) \in \mathbb{R}^2 be the rotated projection where n is the y-axis. Solve for k using the quadratic equation: qx^2 k^2 + (2 \operatorname{sgn}(qy) qy^2 - qy) k - qy^2 = 0 Select the smaller solution for ki. 4. To obtain the unbounding quadric within the cell, we need the narrowest candidate unbounding quadric region from all rays; therefore, k:= \min \{ki \mid i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\}. 5. Store the axis direction n (normalized gradient -
abla f(p)/|
abla f(p)|) scaled by 2+k, and the SDF value. Rendering: 1. For each evaluation point along the ray, query the closest grid cell to get k, n, and d. 2. Intersect the ray with the precomputed quadric to accelerate tracing convergence. 3. If the quadric intersection yields a valid step that does not skip the surface, take it. Otherwise, fall back to standard sphere tracing or enhanced sphere tracing. 4. Stop when the distance value dips below a threshold. Conic Section Definitions: The quadric is a revolution of a conic section. The conic section coefficients A, B, C are functions of k: A(k) = k^2, \quad B(k) = 2(k - 1/2), \quad C(k) = -k These define the implicit equation in the 2D plane (y-axis is axis of revolution): A \cdot x^2 + B \cdot y^2 + C \cdot y = 0 \quad (1) The polar parametrization of the conic section is s(t) = [\cos(t) \cdot r(t), \sin(t) \cdot r(t)]^T, where: r(t) =  rac{-C \cdot \sin(t)}{A \cdot \cos^2(t) + B \cdot \sin^2(t)} The interval L(k) restricts the parameter t to avoid unwanted hyperbola branches: L(k) =  egin{cases}  rac{\pi}{2}, & 	ext{if } A(k) \cdot B(k) \geq 0 \ \arctan\left(\sqrt{ rac{-A}{B}}ight), & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (k \in [-1, 1]) \quad (2) The implicit equation of the unbounding quadric of revolution in 3D (z-axis is axis of revolution) is: A \cdot (x^2 + y^2) + B \cdot z^2 + C \cdot z = 0 \quad (3) Ray-Quadric Intersection: Given ray p0 + t \cdot v (p0 = (x0, y0, z0), v = (vx, vy, vz)), substitute into (3) to solve at^2 + bt + c = 0: a = A \cdot vx^2 + A \cdot vy^2 + B \cdot vz^2 b = 2A \cdot x0 vx + 2A \cdot y0 vy + 2B \cdot z0 vz + C vz c = A \cdot (x0^2 + y0^2) + B \cdot z0^2 + C \cdot z0 Let roots be t1 \leq t2. If no real roots, I:= [-\infty, +\infty]. If 0 
eq |k| < 1/2 (hyperbolas), omit the unwanted branch: I:=  egin{cases} [-\infty, t2] & 	ext{if } (z0 + t1 vz) \cdot k < 0 \ [t1, +\infty] & 	ext{if } (z0 + t2 vz) \cdot k < 0 \end{cases} If none of the conditions apply, I remains as previously defined. Selecting Intersection t: Evaluate the following conditional assignments in order to find the first valid intersection t \geq 0: 1. t:= t2 if t1 = -\infty 2. t:= t1 if 0 < t2 < +\infty 3. t:= \infty if t1 < 0 4. t:= 0 if otherwise Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def intersectquadric(p0, v, A, B, C, k): # Quadratic coefficients for ray p0 + tv against A(x^2+y^2) + Bz^2 + Cz = 0 a = A (v.x2 + v.y2) + B v.z2 b = 2 A (p0.x v.x + p0.y v.y) + 2 B p0.z v.z + C v.z c = A (p0.x2 + p0.y2) + B p0.z2 + C p0.z # Solve quadratic equation if abs(a) < 1e-9: if abs(b) < 1e-9: return float('inf') t1 = -c / b t2 = float('inf') else: disc = b2 - 4 a c if disc < 0: t1 = float('-inf') t2 = float('inf') else: sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 # Omit unwanted hyperbola branch if |k| < 0.5 and k != 0 if abs(k) < 0.5 and k != 0: z1 = p0.z + t1 v.z z2 = p0.z + t2 v.z if z1 k < 0: t1 = float('-inf') if z2 k < 0: t2 = float('inf') # Select first valid intersection t >= 0 per source assignment order t = float('inf') if t1 == float('-inf'): t = t2 elif 0 < t2 < float('inf'): t = t1 elif t1 < 0: t = float('inf') else: t = 0 return t def quadrictrace(p0, v, grid, maxsteps=100, threshold=1e-4): """ Quadric tracing algorithm. grid.query(p) returns a cell struct with.A,.B,.C,.k,.d (SDF value). """ p = p0 for in range(maxsteps): cell = grid.query(p) d = cell.d if d < threshold: return p # Query quadric parameters for current cell A, B, C, k = cell.A, cell.B, cell.C, cell.k # Compute acceleration step from quadric intersection tq = intersectquadric(p, v, A, B, C, k) # Take quadric step if valid and does not skip the surface, else fall back to SDF step if tq > 0 and tq <= d: t = tq else: t = d p = p + t v return p # Non-convergence or max steps reached Combines regular or improved quadratic Taylor bounds with enhancements: Sub-stepping, ES+1, and Adaptive computation of \gamma{Fn}. Using k > 1 was never found to be faster when using quadratic bounds. On the Sponge scene with all enhancements, Linear bounds have 362.3 avg steps, 3815.0 avg octaves, 65.0 ms time. Regular Quad has 70.0 avg steps, 651.1 avg octaves, 16.3 ms time, offering a 	imes 4.0 speedup vs Linear and 	imes 6.7 speedup vs naive. On Sponge (far) scene, Linear (far) has 147.8 avg steps, 749.6 avg octaves, 16.7 ms time. Regular Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.8 ms time (	imes 1.7 vs Linear, 	imes 4.1 vs naive). Improved Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.7 ms time (	imes 1.7 vs Linear, 	imes 4.2 vs naive). With enhancements, quadratic bounds provide massive performance gains over linear bounds with same enhancements (	imes 4.0 and 	imes 1.7 speedups on test scenes) and 	imes 6.7 and 	imes 4.1 speedups over the naive method. Quadric tracing offers a 20% to 100% speedup in rendering static scenes. It amortizes the slowdown caused by the complexity of the geometry. The method takes much larger steps along the ray, often skipping several grid cells without skipping ray-surface intersections. However, sometimes the quadric does not contain the whole cell it is assigned to, so the acceleration is zero or negligible for some positions. About 20% of expensive signed distance function evaluations are saved. Quadric tracing was introduced to accelerate sphere tracing for implicit surfaces defined by signed distance functions (SDFs). Most implicit surface representations require conversion to a triangle list for efficient, real-time visualization, but distance-based representations allow sphere tracing to enable raytracing for the whole scene within milliseconds using the GPU. The representation supports set operations such as union, intersection, subtraction, and real-time offsets, allowing any CSG tree to be constructed from a large set of primitives. However, function evaluation time and convergence slow drastically with scene complexity. The method generalizes the unbounding sphere and separating plane approach to unbounding quadrics for any SDF. It is applicable to light visibility computation such as soft shadows, ambient occlusion, and global illumination, as well as room impulse response estimation and deep learning based implicit signed distance functions. name: Chamfer-L1 Distance Computation
body: Chamfer-L1 Distance Computation evaluates geometric fidelity between a predicted Signed Distance Function (SDF) and a ground-truth mesh by measuring average nearest-neighbor distances between sampled surface points. It serves as a post-processing evaluation metric rather than a ray-marching step-size rule, distinguishing it from sibling methods like Cone Intersection that optimize traversal. Inputs: Predicted SDF field S(\mathbf{x}), ground-truth mesh M, bounding volume B, target sample count N = 2^{17} = 131,072. Outputs: Scalar Chamfer distance value. Data Structures: Point sets P{\text{pred}} and P{\text{gt}} storing 3D coordinates. Steps: 1. Uniformly sample N points \mathbf{x}i within the bounding volume B. 2. Assign each \mathbf{x}i a random spherical direction \mathbf{d}i uniformly distributed on the unit sphere. 3. Trace a ray \mathbf{r}i(t) = \mathbf{x}i + t \cdot \mathbf{d}i using sphere tracing on S. 4. Collect intersection points where S(\mathbf{p}) \approx 0 into P{\text{pred}}. 5. Repeat sampling until the minimum required number of surface points is obtained, using the same stopping criterion as defined in the parent context (A.4). 6. Sample points P{\text{gt}} from the ground-truth mesh M (e.g., via Marching Cubes extraction or direct implicit sampling). 7. Compute the Chamfer distance between P{\text{pred}} and P{\text{gt}} using the implementation provided by PyTorch3D. Formulas: The Chamfer distance is computed as the mean of the nearest-neighbor distances in both directions: D{\text{Chamfer}} = \frac{1}{|P{\text{pred}}|} \sum{p \in P{\text{pred}}} \min{q \in P{\text{gt}}} \|p - q\|2 + \frac{1}{|P{\text{gt}}|} \sum{q \in P{\text{gt}}} \min{p \in P{\text{pred}}} \|q - p\|2 \quad Parameters: N = 131,072 initial samples in B. Stopping criterion matches parent method A.4. Edge Cases: Mesh extraction via Marching Cubes introduces additional error compared to sampling the true implicit SDF directly. If the predicted SDF fails to capture the surface, intersection points may be sparse or undefined. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def computechamferl1(sdffn, meshvertices, meshfaces, boundingvolume, numsamples=131072): # 1. Sample points in bounding volume B mincoords, maxcoords = boundingvolume samples = [[random.uniform(mincoords[i], maxcoords[i]) for i in range(3)] for in range(numsamples)] # 2. Trace rays using sphere tracing to find surface intersections predictedpoints = [] for x0 in samples: # Random spherical direction d = [random.gauss(0, 1) for in range(3)] norm = math.sqrt(sum(vv for v in d)) d = [v/norm for v in d] # Sphere tracing loop t = 0.0 for in range(100): pos = [x0[i] + t d[i] for i in range(3)] dist = sdffn(pos) if abs(dist) < 1e-4: predictedpoints.append(pos) break t += dist if t > 10.0: break # 3. Sample ground truth mesh surface gtpoints = samplemeshsurface(meshvertices, meshfaces, numsamples) # 4. Compute Chamfer Distance (brute-force nearest neighbor) def nearestdist(p, points): return min(math.sqrt(sum((p[i]-q[i])2 for i in range(3))) for q in points) predtogt = sum(nearestdist(p, gtpoints) for p in predictedpoints) / len(predictedpoints) gttopred = sum(nearestdist(q, predictedpoints) for q in gtpoints) / len(gtpoints) return predtogt + gttopred def samplemeshsurface(vertices, faces, numsamples): areas = [] for f in faces: v0, v1, v2 = [vertices[v] for v in f] cross = [ (v1[1]-v0[1])(v2[2]-v0[2]) - (v1[2]-v0[2])(v2[1]-v0[1]), (v1[2]-v0[2])(v2[0]-v0[0]) - (v1[0]-v0[0])(v2[2]-v0[2]), (v1[0]-v0[0])(v2[1]-v0[1]) - (v1[1]-v0[1])(v2[0]-v0[0]) ] areas.append(0.5 math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in cross))) totalarea = sum(areas) probs = [a/totalarea for a in areas] selectedfaces = [] for in range(numsamples): r = random.random() cumulative = 0.0 for i, p in enumerate(probs): cumulative += p if r <= cumulative: selectedfaces.append(faces[i]) break pts = [] for f in selectedfaces: v0, v1, v2 = [vertices[v] for v in f] u = random.random() v = random.random() if u + v > 1: u = 1 - u v = 1 - v pts.append([ (1 - u - v) v0[0] + u v1[0] + v v2[0], (1 - u - v) v0[1] + u v1[1] + v v2[1], (1 - u - v) v0[2] + u v1[2] + v v2[2] ]) return pts Sphere Assisted Raymarching: Accelerates ray traversal in voxel grids by storing the largest empty sphere radius per voxel, decoupling shape from color and allowing large steps through empty space. It differs from this method by using exact Euclidean distances for step sizing rather than L1 approximations, and serves as a traversal optimization rather than a post-processing metric. Sampling complexity is O(N \cdot S) where N=131,072 and S is the average sphere tracing steps. Distance computation is O(|P{\text{pred}}| \cdot |P{\text{gt}}|) for brute-force nearest neighbor. The method provides a direct geometric fidelity metric for implicit surface evaluation. Ground-truth sampling via Marching Cubes introduces extraction error compared to direct implicit sampling. It does not inherently measure normal alignment, which requires separate Normal-L2 evaluation. The method was introduced in the Neural Geometric Level of Detail paper to evaluate the accuracy of predicted SDFs against ground-truth meshes in neural rendering pipelines. It leverages the Chamfer distance implementation from PyTorch3D for metric computation. Neural Geometric Level of Detail: Real-time Rendering with Implicit 3D Shapes, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.01120, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Sphere Assisted Raymarching
head: Shape Assisted Raymarching, Shape Marching, Sphere Assisted
body: Sphere Assisted Raymarching is a technique for accelerating ray traversal in voxel grids by storing the radius of the largest empty sphere centered at each voxel in a separate shape texture. This decouples shape information from color information. The technique allows rays to take large steps through empty space, significantly reducing the number of voxel lookups compared to plane marching. It sets itself apart from its parent method by using the exact Euclidean distance (sphere radius) rather than an L1 approximation to determine step sizes, providing tighter bounds on empty space. Sphere Assisted Raymarching stores the Euclidean distance to the nearest solid voxel for every empty voxel. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin p0, ray direction d (normalized), maximum check distance maxDistToCheck, voxel grid size voxelGridSize. Output: Color of the first solid voxel hit, or transparent if no voxel is hit within maxDistToCheck. Data Structures Two 3D textures are required: 1. voxels: A 3D texture storing normalized float color values, where the alpha channel indicates solidity. 2. shape: A separate 3D texture storing non-negative integers, where the red channel stores the radius of the largest empty sphere centered at that voxel. Solid Voxel Marker: The value 255 represents a solid voxel. Empty Voxel Value: The value represents the distance to the nearest solid voxel. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize ray parameter t = 0. 2. Loop while t \le maxDistToCheck: a. Calculate current position p = p0 + d \cdot t. b. Convert to grid coordinates p{grid} = p / voxelGridSize. c. Sample the shape texture at p{grid} to get shapeValue. d. If shapeValue == 255, the ray has hit a solid voxel. Return the color from the voxels texture at p{grid}. e. Calculate the distance to the next axis-aligned plane boundaries along d using \delta{plane} = \mini \frac{\mathbb{I}(di > 0) - \text{fract}(p{grid,i})}{di}, where \mathbb{I} is the indicator function and \text{fract}(x) = x - \lfloor x \rfloor. f. Update t \leftarrow t + \max(\delta{plane} + \text{shapeValue}, \epsilon). 3. If the loop terminates without hitting a solid voxel, return transparent color. Pseudocode The following pseudocode implements the method as described in. It uses standard Python syntax and explicit vector operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sphereassistedraymarch(p0, d, maxDistToCheck, voxelGridSize, shapetexture, voxelstexture): t = 0.0 epsilon = 1e-6 # Small constant to guarantee progress while t <= maxDistToCheck: # Calculate current world position p = [p0[i] + d[i] t for i in range(3)] # Convert to grid coordinates for sampling and plane calculation pgrid = [p[i] / voxelGridSize for i in range(3)] # Sample shape data shapevalue = shapetexture.samplelevel(pgrid, 0).r # Check for solid voxel if shapevalue == 255: return voxelstexture.samplelevel(pgrid, 0) # Calculate deltas to next plane boundaries # step(0, d) returns 1.0 where d > 0, else 0.0 # fract(pgrid) returns the fractional part of grid coordinates stepmask = [1.0 if d[i] > 0.0 else 0.0 for i in range(3)] fractp = [pgrid[i] - math.floor(pgrid[i]) for i in range(3)] deltas = [(stepmask[i] - fractp[i]) / d[i] for i in range(3)] # Find the minimum delta to the nearest plane boundary mindelta = min(deltas) # Step forward by the maximum of the plane distance and the sphere radius t += max(mindelta + shapevalue, epsilon) return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Parameters 255: Constant representing a solid voxel in the shape texture. epsilon: Small constant added to the step size to guarantee progress and avoid infinite loops due to floating-point precision issues. maxDistToCheck: Maximum distance the ray will travel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Upfront Cost: Generating the shape data (distance field) has a significant upfront computational cost. Memory Usage: Requires two textures (color and shape), increasing memory usage compared to single-texture methods. Precision: The shape data uses integer formats to store distances, which may limit precision for very large voxel grids or fine details. A variant that stores the size of the largest possible cube around each empty cell instead of a sphere. It is faster to compute (order of magnitude faster) but slightly suboptimal for step size compared to sphere-assisted. It uses a summed area table (SAT) to compute the area of arbitrary boxes in O(1) time, allowing binary search for the maximum cube size in O(\log n) per voxel, reducing upfront complexity from O(n^2) to O(n \log n). Time Complexity: The raymarching step itself is efficient, reducing voxel lookups in empty space. However, the upfront cost to generate the shape data is O(n^2) for sphere-assisted, where n is the number of voxels. Memory Complexity: Requires two 3D textures (color and shape), doubling memory usage compared to methods using a single texture. Performance: Reduces the number of voxel lookups, which can improve performance in sparse scenes. However, it is not always a performance win due to the overhead of texture sampling and the upfront generation cost. Strengths: Large steps through empty space; reduces ray traversal steps. Limitations: High upfront computational cost for shape generation; higher memory usage; integer precision limits. When to Use: When the scene is sparse and the cost of ray traversal is high relative to the upfront shape generation cost. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained, or when the scene is dense and the upfront cost outweighs the traversal savings. Sphere Assisted Raymarching was introduced by Caleb Leak in his blog posts on raymarching voxel rendering. It was developed as an optimization over plane marching to handle large empty spaces more efficiently. name: Cube Assisted Raymarching
head: Cube Assisted
body: Cube Assisted Raymarching is a distance-field ray marching technique that stores the size of the largest empty cube centered at each voxel instead of the largest empty sphere. It solves the problem of slow shape data generation in Sphere Assisted Raymarching by trading some step optimality for significantly faster preprocessing. While Sphere Assisted Raymarching provides optimal step sizes, Cube Assisted Raymarching is an order of magnitude faster to compute the shape data, making it suitable for larger voxel grids where preprocessing time is a bottleneck. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid where each voxel is marked as solid or empty. Output: A shape texture (or distance field) where each voxel stores the side length of the largest empty cube centered at that voxel. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A 3D array of boolean or integer values indicating occupancy. 2. Summed Area Table (SAT): A 3D array of the same dimensions as the voxel grid. Each entry SAT[x][y][z] stores the sum of all solid voxels in the rectangular prism from (0,0,0) to (x,y,z). 3. Shape Texture: A 3D array storing the computed cube side lengths. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Summed Area Table: Iterate through the voxel grid and compute the SAT. For each voxel (x,y,z), the value is the sum of the current voxel's occupancy plus the sums of its neighbors in the negative x, y, and z directions, minus the overlaps. 2. Binary Search for Cube Size: For each empty voxel (x,y,z), perform a binary search to find the maximum side length s such that a cube of side s centered at (x,y,z) contains no solid voxels. The binary search range is typically [1, maxdimension]. For a candidate side length s, define the cube boundaries. Use the SAT to check if the cube is empty in O(1) time. 3. Store Result: Store the maximum valid s in the shape texture for voxel (x,y,z). Formulas: SAT Computation: SAT[x][y][z] = V[x][y][z] + SAT[x-1][y][z] + SAT[x][y-1][z] + SAT[x][y][z-1] - SAT[x-1][y-1][z] - SAT[x-1][y][z-1] - SAT[x][y-1][z-1] + SAT[x-1][y-1][z-1] Where V[x][y][z] is 1 if the voxel is solid, 0 otherwise. Boundary checks are required for indices < 0. Cube Area Check using SAT: The number of solid voxels in a box defined by corners (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) is: Count = SAT[x2][y2][z2] - SAT[x1-1][y2][z2] - SAT[x2][y1-1][z2] - SAT[x2][y2][z1-1] + SAT[x1-1][y1-1][z2] + SAT[x1-1][y2][z1-1] + SAT[x2][y1-1][z1-1] - SAT[x1-1][y1-1][z1-1] The cube is empty if Count == 0. Cube Boundaries: For a cube of side s centered at (cx, cy, cz), the boundaries are: x1 = cx - \lfloor s/2 \rfloor, \quad x2 = cx + \lfloor (s-1)/2 \rfloor y1 = cy - \lfloor s/2 \rfloor, \quad y2 = cy + \lfloor (s-1)/2 \rfloor z1 = cz - \lfloor s/2 \rfloor, \quad z2 = cz + \lfloor (s-1)/2 \rfloor Note: The exact boundary calculation depends on whether the cube is aligned to voxel centers or edges. The sources imply a centered cube. A common implementation uses integer division for half-sizes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesat(voxelgrid, dims): """ Computes the 3D Summed Area Table for the voxel grid. voxelgrid: 3D list/array of 0 (empty) or 1 (solid). dims: tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) Returns: 3D list/array SAT """ Dx, Dy, Dz = dims sat = [[[0 for in range(Dz)] for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] for x in range(Dx): for y in range(Dy): for z in range(Dz): val = voxelgrid[x][y][z] sat[x][y][z] = val if x > 0: sat[x][y][z] += sat[x-1][y][z] if y > 0: sat[x][y][z] += sat[x][y-1][z] if z > 0: sat[x][y][z] += sat[x][y][z-1] if x > 0 and y > 0: sat[x][y][z] -= sat[x-1][y-1][z] if x > 0 and z > 0: sat[x][y][z] -= sat[x-1][y][z-1] if y > 0 and z > 0: sat[x][y][z] -= sat[x][y-1][z-1] if x > 0 and y > 0 and z > 0: sat[x][y][z] += sat[x-1][y-1][z-1] return sat def getboxsolidcount(sat, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2, dims): """ Returns the number of solid voxels in the box [x1, x2] x [y1, y2] x [z1, z2] using SAT. Indices are inclusive. """ Dx, Dy, Dz = dims # Helper to get SAT value with boundary checks def getsat(x, y, z): if x < 0 or y < 0 or z < 0: return 0 if x >= Dx or y >= Dy or z >= Dz: return 0 return sat[x][y][z] return (getsat(x2, y2, z2) getsat(x1-1, y2, z2) getsat(x2, y1-1, z2) getsat(x2, y2, z1-1) + getsat(x1-1, y1-1, z2) + getsat(x1-1, y2, z1-1) + getsat(x2, y1-1, z1-1) getsat(x1-1, y1-1, z1-1)) def computecubeassistedshape(voxelgrid, dims): """ Computes the Cube Assisted shape texture. Returns: 3D list/array of cube side lengths. """ Dx, Dy, Dz = dims sat = computesat(voxelgrid, dims) shape = [[[0 for in range(Dz)] for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] maxdim = max(Dx, Dy, Dz) for x in range(Dx): for y in range(Dy): for z in range(Dz): if voxelgrid[x][y][z] == 1: shape[x][y][z] = 0 continue # Binary search for max cube size low = 1 high = maxdim bests = 0 while low <= high: s = (low + high) // 2 # Calculate cube boundaries centered at (x,y,z) # Using integer division for half-sizes halfs = s // 2 # Adjust for even/odd sizes to keep center # For a cube of size s centered at integer coordinate, # the extent is roughly +/- s/2. # Let's define the box as [x - floor(s/2), x + floor((s-1)/2)] # This ensures the center voxel is included if s is odd, # and the center is between voxels if s is even? # Actually, for a voxel-centered cube, we want the cube to # cover the voxel. A simple approach is to check if a cube # of size s fits. # Let's use the definition: cube extends from center - s/2 to center + s/2 # In integer grid, we check voxels in range. x1 = x - (s // 2) x2 = x + ((s - 1) // 2) y1 = y - (s // 2) y2 = y + ((s - 1) // 2) z1 = z - (s // 2) z2 = z + ((s - 1) // 2) # Check boundaries if x1 < 0 or x2 >= Dx or y1 < 0 or y2 >= Dy or z1 < 0 or z2 >= Dz: high = s - 1 continue if getboxsolidcount(sat, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2, dims) == 0: bests = s low = s + 1 else: high = s - 1 shape[x][y][z] = bests return shape Parameters: epsilon: A small value added to the step size to prevent infinite loops. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The binary search must handle cubes that extend beyond the voxel grid boundaries. These are considered invalid or must be clamped. Precision: The SAT uses integer sums, so it is exact for binary voxel grids. For non-binary grids, the SAT stores sums, and the "empty" check might need a threshold. Degenerate Input: A single solid voxel in a large empty grid. The SAT handles this correctly. The binary search will find the largest cube that does not include the solid voxel. Time Complexity: Upfront shape data generation is O(n \log n), where n is the number of voxels. This is an improvement over the O(n^2) complexity of a simple sphere-assisted implementation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the SAT and the shape texture, both of size O(n). Measured Performance: In tests on a 32x32x32 voxel set, Cube Assisted Raymarching was an order of magnitude faster to compute the shape data than Sphere Assisted Raymarching. Render times were close to Sphere Assisted Raymarching on low-end sets, but Plane Marching showed a moderate lead as set size increased. Strengths: Significantly faster preprocessing than Sphere Assisted Raymarching. Still provides large steps through empty space. Limitations: Slightly suboptimal step sizes compared to Sphere Assisted Raymarching. When to Use: When preprocessing time is a bottleneck and the slight loss in step optimality is acceptable. When Not to Use: When optimal step sizes are critical and preprocessing time is not a concern. Cube Assisted Raymarching was introduced by Caleb Leak in his blog post "Raymarching Voxel Rendering". It was developed as an optimization to the Sphere Assisted Raymarching technique, which suffered from high upfront computational cost. The technique leverages Summed Area Tables, a data structure common in computer vision, to enable fast empty space queries. name: Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing
head: Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing with Screen-Space Intersection Selection, Over-relaxation sphere tracing with screen-space selection, Over-relaxed sphere tracing, Sphere tracing with over-relaxation
body: Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing accelerates the convergence of sphere tracing by stepping further than the signed distance bound allows, controlled by a relaxation parameter \omega. It solves the problem of excessive iteration counts in complex scenes by reducing the number of signed distance function (SDF) evaluations required to reach an intersection or the maximum depth. Unlike standard sphere tracing, which uses the exact distance bound, this method selects the final intersection point based on a screen-space error metric to reduce aliasing artifacts when the maximum iteration count is exceeded or when rays graze object edges. The method combines an accelerated stepping strategy with a robust fallback mechanism and screen-space-aware termination. It requires a signed distance bound function f(p) and a ray defined by origin o and normalized direction d. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d (normalized). Signed distance bound function f(p). t{min}: Minimum ray distance. t{max}: Maximum ray distance. pixelRadius: The radius of a pixel at t=1, used as a sub-pixel accuracy threshold. MAX\ITERATIONS: Maximum number of iterations (typical value: 80). omega (\omega): Relaxation parameter, range 1, 2) (typical value: 1.2). forceHit: Boolean flag; if true, returns the best candidate even if error exceeds threshold. Output: Intersection distance t, or INFINITY if no valid intersection is found within constraints. The algorithm maintains the following state variables within the iteration loop: t: Current distance along the ray. candidate\t: The best intersection distance found so far. candidate\error: The screen-space error associated with candidate\t. previousRadius: The absolute signed distance from the previous iteration. stepLength: The distance to advance in the current step. functionSign: +1 if f(o) \ge 0, -1 if f(o) < 0. 1. Initialization: Set t = t{min}. Set candidate\error = INFINITY. Set candidate\t = t{min}. Set previousRadius = 0. Set stepLength = 0. Determine functionSign: if f(o) < 0 then -1, else +1. 2. Iteration Loop (for i from 0 to MAX\ITERATIONS - 1): Evaluate SDF: Calculate current position p = o + t \cdot d. Calculate signedRadius = functionSign \cdot f(p). Calculate radius = |signedRadius|. Check Over-Relaxation Failure (SOR Fail): A failure occurs if \omega > 1 AND (radius + previousRadius) < stepLength. This condition indicates that the unbounding spheres of the current and previous steps overlap, meaning the previous step may have overshot a surface. Handle Failure or Advance: If SOR Fail: Reduce step length: stepLength = stepLength - \omega \cdot stepLength. Disable over-relaxation: Set \omega = 1. Note: The sources describe a fallback position p{fallback} = pi + d \cdot \delta{i-1} \cdot (1-\omega) for conventional tracing, but the provided pseudocode implements a step-length reduction and continues from the current position pi after resetting \omega. The sources note that checking if the fallback sphere overlaps with the current sphere to guarantee no surface was passed is possible but omitted for performance due to branching divergence. If No SOR Fail: Calculate step length: stepLength = signedRadius \cdot \omega. Update previous radius: previousRadius = radius. Calculate screen-space error: error = radius / t. Update Best Candidate: If error < candidate\error: Set candidate\t = t. Set candidate\error = error. Check Early Termination: If (error < pixelRadius) OR (t > t{max}): Break loop. Advance Ray: t = t + stepLength. 3. Post-Loop Result: If (t > t{max} OR candidate\error > pixelRadius) AND forceHit is false: Return INFINITY. Else: Return candidate\t. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def overrelaxationspheretracing(o, d, f, tmin, tmax, pixelradius, maxiterations, omega=1.2, forcehit=False): t = tmin candidateerror = float('inf') candidatet = tmin previousradius = 0 steplength = 0 # Determine sign based on initial position if f(o) < 0: functionsign = -1 else: functionsign = 1 for i in range(maxiterations): # Evaluate signed distance p = o + t d signedradius = functionsign f(p) radius = abs(signedradius) # Check for over-relaxation failure (overshoot) # Condition: omega > 1 AND sum of radii < previous step length sorfail = (omega > 1) and ((radius + previousradius) < steplength) if sorfail: # Reduce step length and disable over-relaxation steplength = steplength - omega steplength omega = 1 else: # Apply over-relaxation steplength = signedradius omega previousradius = radius # Calculate screen-space error if t > 0: error = radius / t else: error = float('inf') # Update best candidate if error < candidateerror: candidatet = t candidateerror = error # Check termination conditions if (not sorfail and error < pixelradius) or (t > tmax): break # Advance ray t = t + steplength # Final result logic if (t > tmax or candidateerror > pixelradius) and not forcehit: return float('inf') else: return candidatet \omega (omega): The relaxation parameter. Range [1, 2). Typical value is 1.2 for the best balance of performance and quality. Larger values cause earlier premature defaulting to conventional sphere tracing. pixelRadius: The radius of a pixel at t=1. Used as the threshold for sub-pixel accuracy. MAX\ITERATIONS: Maximum iterations. Typical value 80. forceHit: Boolean. If true, forces the return of candidate\t even if the error is large or t{max} is exceeded. Overshooting: Over-relaxation can cause the ray to step into or over objects, missing intersections. This is detected by the overlap of unbounding spheres. Grazing Rays: When a ray grazes an object's edge, it may terminate in mid-air if the last point is used. The screen-space error metric mitigates this by selecting the point with the smallest unbounding sphere radius. Branching Divergence: An optimization to check if the fallback position's unbounding sphere overlaps with the current position's sphere (guaranteeing no surface was passed) is omitted in the standard implementation because it introduces branching and state handling that diminishes GPU performance. Self-Intersections: Secondary rays may suffer from self-intersection artifacts. The sources mention dynamic \epsilon for prevention, but this is a separate concern from the core over-relaxation algorithm. Performance: The method reduces the number of required SDF evaluations and iterations, allowing rays to trace deeper into the scene. City Scene (1280x720, NVIDIA GTX Titan): 16.829 ms (59.421 Hz) with over-relaxation vs 20.409 ms (48.998 Hz) without. Jewel Scene (1280x720, NVIDIA GTX Titan): 2.978 ms (335.744 Hz) with over-relaxation vs 3.472 ms (288.018 Hz) without. Path Tracing (Jewel Scene, 10 bounces): 101.934 ms (9.8 Hz) with over-relaxation (\omega=1.4) vs 118.302 ms (8.453 Hz) without. Strengths: Significant performance improvement in complex scenes; reduces aliasing artifacts from grazing rays and iteration limits. Limitations: Tuning \omega is challenging; too high a value causes premature fallback to slower conventional tracing. The fallback mechanism may still miss intersections if the overlap check is not rigorous enough (as per the simplified implementation). The method was introduced in the paper "[Enhanced Sphere Tracing" by the authors of the sources. It applies the principle of over-relaxation (common in numerical analysis) to sphere tracing. The technique was implemented in DirectX/DirectCompute and demonstrated real-time performance.
