name: Enhanced Sphere Tracing
head: Aggressive Marching, Aggressive Ray Marching, Aggressive Sphere Tracing, Over-relaxed sphere tracing, Sphere tracing with over-relaxation
body: Enhanced Sphere Tracing is a ray marching strategy that accelerates convergence by stepping a multiple of the queried signed distance function (SDF) value, rather than the value itself. It solves the problem of slow convergence at grazing angles and allows the ray to penetrate the surface, enabling sampling of the interior for training supervision. It differs from Cone Intersection and Segment Tracing by using a scalar multiplier on the step size rather than geometric bounds or local Lipschitz constants to determine the step, and from Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing primarily in its implementation details regarding safety checks, though both share the core over-relaxation principle. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction \vec{v} (normalized). SDF function f(p) returning signed distance. Aggressive factor \alpha > 1 (default 1.5). Convergence threshold \epsilon (e.g., 5 \times 10^{-5}). Maximum step count k{max} (e.g., 1024). Outputs: Intersection point p or null if not found within k{max}. Data Structures: Current position p, initialized to o. Step counter s, initialized to 0. Steps: 1. Query: Evaluate d = f(p). 2. Check Convergence: If |d| < \epsilon, return p. 3. Calculate Step: Compute step size s{step} = \alpha \cdot d. Note: If d < 0 (inside), the step moves further inside; if d > 0 (outside), it moves toward the surface. 4. Advance: Update position p \leftarrow p + s{step} \cdot \vec{v}. 5. Increment: s \leftarrow s + 1. 6. Termination: If s \ge k{max}, return null. 7. Loop: Repeat from Step 1. Formulas: The convergence condition for the distance to the surface after k steps is given by: |d0 (1 - \alpha \sin \theta)^k| < \epsilon where d0 is the initial distance, \theta is the angle between the ray direction and the surface normal, and \alpha is the aggressive factor. The minimum number of steps k{min} required is: k > k{min} = \frac{\log \epsilon - \log d0}{\log |1 - \alpha \sin \theta|} This derivation assumes |1 - \alpha \sin \theta| < 1. Parameters: \alpha: Aggressive marching multiplier. Default 1.5. Range 1.2 to 1.8 is effective. \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Typical value 5 \times 10^{-5}. k{max}: Maximum steps. Typical value 1024. Pitfalls: Thin Geometry: If geometry is super thin, a single aggressive step may trespass two surfaces, leaving the ray outside the shape and causing infinite marching or small holes. Non-Conservative Fields: The method assumes the SDF is conservative (never overstates distance). If the field overstates distance, over-relaxation is unsound and may skip surfaces. Grazing Angles: While it improves performance, extremely small \theta can still lead to slow convergence if \alpha is not tuned correctly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def enhancedspheretracing(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, alpha=1.5, epsilon=5e-5, maxsteps=1024): """ Perform enhanced sphere tracing. Args: rayorigin: Vector3, origin of the ray. raydirection: Vector3, normalized direction of the ray. sdf: Function, signed distance function f(p). alpha: Float, aggressive factor (> 1). epsilon: Float, convergence threshold. maxsteps: Int, maximum number of steps. Returns: Vector3 or None: Intersection point or None if not found. """ p = rayorigin for i in range(maxsteps): d = sdf(p) # Check convergence if abs(d) < epsilon: return p # Calculate step size stepsize = alpha d # Advance position p = p + stepsize raydirection return None A technique where the ray marches a small distance further outside the Minimum Distance Sphere (MDS) edge to decrease the number of marches, increasing performance. It calculates the over-stepping distance as o(p) = (1 + \frac{\sigma}{\text{range } [0,1]}) \frac{|f(p)|}{\lambda}, where \sigma is the overstepping factor (typically \approx 1.2) and \lambda is the global Lipschitz bound. The algorithm marches to the edge of the MDS, then further outside. It compares the original MDS with the new MDS; if they overlap, it continues marching further. If they do not overlap, it steps back to the edge of the first MDS and continues normally. This is not directly compatible with local Lipschitz bound approaches as it relies on a global bound \lambda. A GPU-friendly implementation of the Sphere Carving method for extracting surfaces from conservative SDFs. It solves the problem of efficiently generating a set of empty spheres that bound a surface, optimizing for parallel execution on graphics hardware. Unlike sequential sphere carving, it uses four distinct parallel kernels to gather intersecting pairs, compute intersection triplets, filter interior points, and augment the sphere set simultaneously. It builds on Enhanced Sphere Tracing by providing a structured, parallelizable iteration step for the sphere carving process. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of steps k needed to reach convergence \epsilon compared to conventional sphere tracing (\alpha=1.0). For d=1.0, \epsilon=5 \times 10^{-5}, and \theta=10 degrees, steps decrease from 52 to 33 with \alpha=1.5. Using \sigma \approx 1.2 in overstepping variants reduces field function queries by a factor of 1.2. Memory Complexity: No additional memory beyond standard ray marching state. Performance: On 432x756 resolution using ANGLE/Metal backend, worst-angle performance cost increases from 0.105 ms/frame to 0.165 ms/frame. Coverage improvement for high conditioning ratios (e.g., 60:1) increases from 0.00% to 12.42%. For conditioning ratio 120:1, coverage improves from 0.00% to 12.78%. Strengths: Accelerates convergence for rays grazing surfaces. Allows sampling behind the surface (SDF < 0), which is crucial for supervision during neural network training. Prevents valid geometry from vanishing at grazing angles under high non-uniform scaling ratios when used with conservative fields. Limitations: Can cause artifacts (small holes) in super thin geometry if a single step trespasses two surfaces. Requires a conservative SDF (never overstates distance) to be sound. Not directly compatible with local Lipschitz bound approaches due to reliance on global bounds in some variants. Enhanced Sphere Tracing, also known as Aggressive Marching or Over-relaxed Sphere Tracing, was attributed to Keinert et al. in 2014. It was developed to address the inefficiency of standard sphere tracing, particularly at grazing angles where the angle between the camera ray and the surface normal is small. The method has been adopted in differentiable rendering pipelines to stabilize training by allowing interior sampling. name: Parallel Sphere Carving Algorithm
body: The Parallel Sphere Carving Algorithm is a GPU-friendly implementation of the Sphere Carving method for extracting surfaces from conservative signed distance fields (SDFs). It solves the problem of efficiently generating a set of empty spheres that bound a surface defined by an SDF f, specifically optimizing for parallel execution on graphics hardware. Unlike sequential sphere carving, which processes spheres one by one, this method uses four distinct parallel kernels to gather intersecting pairs, compute intersection triplets, filter interior points, and augment the sphere set simultaneously. The algorithm performs a single iteration of sphere carving, taking a conservative SDF f and a current array of empty spheres S as input, and returning an updated array of empty spheres S and an array of points P whose convex hull bounds the surface. All sets are implemented as pre-allocated arrays with sufficient memory. Parallel updates to these arrays require one atomic counter per array to push values. Each sphere Si is defined by its center \mathbf{c}i and radius ri = f(\mathbf{c}i). The algorithm uses four arrays: S (empty spheres), P (valid surface points), P' (intermediate intersection points), and pairs (array of sphere index pairs). 1. Gather Intersecting Pairs: Initialize pairs \leftarrow \emptyset. Parallel for each sphere Sa \in S, parallel for each sphere Sb \in S with index b > a, if Sa \cap Sb \neq \emptyset then pairs \leftarrow pairs \cup (a, b). 2. Compute Intersection Points: Initialize P, P' \leftarrow \emptyset. Parallel for each pair (a, b) \in pairs, parallel for each sphere Sc \in S with index c > b, P' \leftarrow P' \cup \text{intersections}(Sa, Sb, Sc). 3. Filter Interior Points: Parallel for each point p \in P', parallel for each sphere S \in S, if p \in \text{interior}(S) then discard p. Otherwise, P \leftarrow P \cup p. 4. Augment Sphere Set: Parallel for each point p \in P, S \leftarrow S \cup \text{sphere}(p, f(p)). To compute the intersection points of three spheres Sa, Sb, Sc with centers \mathbf{c}a, \mathbf{c}b, \mathbf{c}c and radii ra, rb, rc: 1. Define \mathbf{e}x = \frac{\mathbf{c}b - \mathbf{c}a}{\|\mathbf{c}b - \mathbf{c}a\|}. 2. Define x = \frac{ra^2 - rb^2 + \|\mathbf{c}b - \mathbf{c}a\|^2}{2 \|\mathbf{c}b - \mathbf{c}a\|}. 3. Define \mathbf{e}y = \frac{(\mathbf{c}c - \mathbf{c}a) - ((\mathbf{c}c - \mathbf{c}a) \cdot \mathbf{e}x)\mathbf{e}x}{\|(\mathbf{c}c - \mathbf{c}a) - ((\mathbf{c}c - \mathbf{c}a) \cdot \mathbf{e}x)\mathbf{e}x\|}. 4. Define y = \frac{ra^2 - rc^2 + \|\mathbf{c}c - \mathbf{c}a\|^2 - 2x((\mathbf{c}c - \mathbf{c}a) \cdot \mathbf{e}x)}{2 \|(\mathbf{c}c - \mathbf{c}a) - ((\mathbf{c}c - \mathbf{c}a) \cdot \mathbf{e}x)\mathbf{e}x\|}. 5. Define z = \sqrt{ra^2 - x^2 - y^2}. If the term under the square root is negative, there is no intersection. 6. The base point is \mathbf{p}0 = \mathbf{c}a + x\mathbf{e}x + y\mathbf{e}y and the intersection points are \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}0 \pm z\mathbf{e}z, where \mathbf{e}z = \mathbf{e}x \times \mathbf{e}y. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelspherecarvingiteration(S: List[Tuple[Tuple[float, float, float], float]], f) -> Tuple[List[Tuple[Tuple[float, float, float], float]], List[Tuple[float, float, float]]]: # S is a pre-allocated array of (center, radius) tuples. # Parallel updates use one atomic counter per array. pairs = [None] (len(S) len(S)) pairscount = 0 # Kernel 1: Gather intersecting sphere pairs for a in range(len(S)): ca, ra = S[a] for b in range(a + 1, len(S)): cb, rb = S[b] if norm((cb[0]-ca[0], cb[1]-ca[1], cb[2]-ca[2])) < ra + rb: idx = atomicadd(pairscount, 1) pairs[idx] = (a, b) Pprime = [None] (len(S) 3) pprimecount = 0 # Kernel 2: Compute intersection points for triplets for i in range(pairscount): a, b = pairs[i] ca, ra = S[a] cb, rb = S[b] dxab, dyab, dzab = cb[0]-ca[0], cb[1]-ca[1], cb[2]-ca[2] distab = norm((dxab, dyab, dzab)) ex = (dxab/distab, dyab/distab, dzab/distab) x = (rara - rbrb + distabdistab) / (2.0 distab) for c in range(b + 1, len(S)): cc, rc = S[c] dxac, dyac, dzac = cc[0]-ca[0], cc[1]-ca[1], cc[2]-ca[2] v = (dxac, dyac, dzac) proj = dot(v, ex) eyvec = (v[0] - projex[0], v[1] - projex[1], v[2] - projex[2]) eylen = norm(eyvec) if eylen < 1e-9: continue ey = (eyvec[0]/eylen, eyvec[1]/eylen, eyvec[2]/eylen) y = (rara - rcrc + dot(v, v) - 2xproj) / (2.0 eylen) rad = rara - xx - yy if rad < 0: continue z = rad 0.5 p0 = (ca[0] + xex[0] + yey[0], ca[1] + xex[1] + yey[1], ca[2] + xex[2] + yey[2]) ez = cross(ex, ey) p1 = (p0[0] + zez[0], p0[1] + zez[1], p0[2] + zez[2]) p2 = (p0[0] - zez[0], p0[1] - zez[1], p0[2] - zez[2]) idx1 = atomicadd(pprimecount, 1) Pprime[idx1] = p1 idx2 = atomicadd(pprimecount, 1) Pprime[idx2] = p2 P = [None] (len(S) 3) pcount = 0 # Kernel 3: Filter points inside the volume for i in range(pprimecount): p = Pprime[i] inside = False for s in S: sc, sr = s if norm((p[0]-sc[0], p[1]-sc[1], p[2]-sc[2])) < sr: inside = True break if not inside: idx = atomicadd(pcount, 1) P[idx] = p # Kernel 4: Augment sphere set for i in range(pcount): p = P[i] r = f(p) idx = atomicadd(lenS, 1) S[idx] = (p, r) return S, P Atomic Counters: Parallel array updates require one atomic counter per array to push values. Precision: Filtering points accounts for floating-point precision by discarding a point if its distance to any sphere center is less than the sphere radius. Pre-allocation: All sets are implemented as arrays assumed to be pre-allocated with sufficient memory. A strategy for initializing the Sphere Carving algorithm using a recursively subdivided icosahedron (icosphere) as the initial bounding volume V0. The vertices of the icosphere are used as the initial sample points P on the surface of V0. Coverage verification is performed per triangle \Delta(a, b, c) of the icosphere, ensuring that the triangle is covered by the union of the spheres centered at its vertices a, b, c with radii f(a), f(b), f(c). The condition is \forall \Delta \in V0, \Delta \subset S(a) \cup S(b) \cup S(c). If the condition is not met, the subdivision level is increased. name: Non-Linear Sphere Tracing
head: Non-linear sphere tracing for deformed SDFs, RaymarchNonlinear, Rendering deformed signed distance fields
body: Non-Linear Sphere Tracing (NLST) is a ray marching technique for directly rendering Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) that have been subjected to non-linear spatial deformations. It solves the problem that standard sphere tracing fails on deformed SDFs because the deformation invalidates the Euclidean distance metric, and computing the inverse deformation D^{-1} is often impossible or unknown. Unlike Sphere Tracing, which assumes a static metric space, NLST formulates the ray traversal as an initial value problem (IVP) solved via numerical integration of an ordinary differential equation (ODE), allowing it to follow the curved ray trajectory in undeformed space while maintaining large step sizes. It differs from Cone Intersection and Segment Tracing by explicitly modeling the deformation's Jacobian to correct the step direction, rather than using geometric bounds or linear approximations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A signed distance function S(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) defined in undeformed (object) space \hat{\mathbf{x}}; a forward deformation function D(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) mapping object space to deformed space; a ray origin \mathbf{p} and direction \boldsymbol{\omega} in deformed space; a maximum step count N{max}; a hit threshold \epsilon; and a maximum travel distance D{max}. Output: A hit structure containing the deformed position \mathbf{x}{hit}, the corrected normal \mathbf{n}{hit}, and the distance traveled. Data Structures: The implementation uses a SceneHit structure to track the ray state: position: float3 (current position in undeformed space \hat{\mathbf{x}}). normal: float3 (current normal estimate, initialized to zero). distanceTravelled: float (accumulated arc-length \hat{s} in undeformed space). hit: bool (flag indicating surface intersection). Preprocessing (Hull-based Initialization): To avoid computing the global inverse deformation D^{-1} for the ray origin \mathbf{p}, NLST uses a coarse hull mesh: 1. Generate a triangle mesh hull enclosing the implicit surface using marching cubes at a low resolution (e.g., 32^3 grid). 2. Deform this hull using the forward deformation D. 3. Rasterize the deformed hull. 4. For each pixel, retrieve the deformed position and transform it back to undeformed space via barycentric interpolation across the corresponding hull face. This provides an approximate initial undeformed position \hat{\mathbf{x}}0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set sceneHit.position to \hat{\mathbf{x}}0 (from hull initialization or D^{-1}(\mathbf{p}) if available). Set sceneHit.distanceTravelled = 0. Set sceneHit.hit = false. Set sceneHit.normal = (0,0,0). 2. Loop: For i from 0 to N{max} - 1: a. Evaluate SDF: Compute h = S(\text{sceneHit.position}). b. Check Hit: If h \le \epsilon, set sceneHit.hit = true. Compute the standard SDF normal \mathbf{n} = \nabla S(\text{sceneHit.position}) using finite differences. Compute the Jacobian J of the deformation D at the hit position. Compute J^{-1}. Set sceneHit.normal = \text{normalize}((J^{-1})^T \mathbf{n}). Break loop. c. Check Max Distance: If sceneHit.distanceTravelled \ge D{max}, break loop. d. Compute Vector Field: Calculate the unit tangent vector in undeformed space: \boldsymbol{\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \frac{JD^{-1}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \boldsymbol{\omega}0}{\|JD^{-1}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \boldsymbol{\omega}0\|} where \boldsymbol{\omega}0 is the initial ray direction in deformed space. e. Integrate (Runge-Kutta): Advance the position using a 4th-order Runge-Kutta integrator with step size h: k1 = \boldsymbol{\omega}(\text{sceneHit.position}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) k2 = \boldsymbol{\omega}(\text{sceneHit.position} + 0.5 h k1, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) k3 = \boldsymbol{\omega}(\text{sceneHit.position} + 0.5 h k2, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) k4 = \boldsymbol{\omega}(\text{sceneHit.position} + h k3, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) \text{sceneHit.position} = \text{sceneHit.position} + \frac{h}{6}(k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4). f. Update Distance: sceneHit.distanceTravelled += h. 3. Final Transform: If sceneHit.hit is true, transform sceneHit.position to deformed space using D(\text{sceneHit.position}). Recompute camera-space depth for depth testing. Jacobian Calculation: The Jacobian J of the deformation D is computed using central finite differences with step size h{diff} (e.g., 0.0001): J{ij} = \frac{Di(\mathbf{x} + h{diff}\mathbf{e}j) - Di(\mathbf{x} - h{diff}\mathbf{e}j)}{2 h{diff}} where \mathbf{e}j are the basis vectors. Parameters: N{max} (MAXSTEPS): Integer, default 200. \epsilon (THRESHOLD): Float, default 0.0001. D{max} (MAXDISTANCE): Float, default 400.0. h{diff} (NORMALDIFFERENTIAL): Float, default 0.0001. Deformation parameters (e.g., \alpha for sinusoidal deformation): Default 1.0. Pitfalls: Singular Jacobian: If the deformation causes JD to be singular or near-singular, JD^{-1} becomes unstable. Deformations must be locally foldover-free. Inverse Requirement: The method requires D^{-1} at least once for the initial seed \hat{\mathbf{x}}0. If D^{-1} does not exist (e.g., non-bijective deformations), the hull-based initialization is mandatory. Concave Objects: Limited N{max} may cause missed intersections for concave objects or grazing angles. Performance: SDF evaluations are expensive. Naive step reduction degrades performance significantly. A variant that avoids computing the global inverse deformation D^{-1} by using a coarse marching cubes mesh. The hull is deformed, rasterized, and the deformed position is mapped back to object space via barycentric interpolation to provide the initial ray start point \hat{\mathbf{x}}0. This enables the use of deformations where D^{-1} is unknown or non-existent, such as complex skinning or sculpting brushes. Time Complexity: Dominated by SDF evaluations and Jacobian inversions per step. The Runge-Kutta method requires multiple vector field evaluations per step but no additional SDF lookups for sub-stepping, preserving the performance advantage over naive ray marching. Memory Complexity: Low, requiring storage for the SDF and the deformation function. The hull mesh is small and transient. Performance: On an NVIDIA Titan RTX at 1080p, NLST takes ~10-13ms for complex scenes (Dinosaur, Head, Elephant), significantly faster than high-resolution Marching Cubes (e.g., S=1024 takes >9s). It is more than twice as fast as Marching Cubes at the lowest resolution (S=32) while preserving thin features. Strengths: Preserves infinite resolution and sharp features; handles non-linear deformations (LBS, FFDs, Kelvinlets) without artifacts; avoids inverse deformation computation via hull initialization. Limitations: Requires D to be a space deformation (evaluable at arbitrary points); fails if JD is singular; performance degrades at grazing angles or for highly concave objects with limited steps; does not support collision detection in deformed space due to lack of arbitrary point evaluation. NLST was introduced by Dario Seyb, Alec Jacobson, Derek Nowrouzezahrai, and Wojciech Jarosz in their paper "Non-linear sphere tracing for rendering deformed signed distance fields" (2020). It builds on Barr's [1984] formulation for deforming parametric curves/surfaces by casting sphere tracing as an ODE initial value problem. The method addresses the limitations of meshing-based deformation (loss of detail, recomputation) and previous implicit deformation techniques that required inverse deformations or suffered from discontinuities. It has been implemented in prototype modeling applications using the Unity3D engine. name: Step Size Optimization
head: Adaptive Step Size, Dynamic Sampling, Safe Raymarching
body: Step Size Optimization encompasses techniques that vary the distance a ray travels between samples in volume rendering or distance-field ray marching, rather than using a fixed interval. These methods solve the trade-off between rendering quality (avoiding aliasing, overshooting, or missing thin features) and computational cost (reducing the number of expensive density or SDF evaluations). They set themselves apart from Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by dynamically adjusting \Delta s based on local geometry, density, or global bounds, and from Sphere Tracing by often decoupling the step size from the strict Lipschitz constraint of the SDF, or by applying specific heuristics (like gap limits or mip-level doubling) that sphere tracing does not inherently provide. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of replacing the constant step \Delta s = \text{const} with a function \Delta s = f(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{d}, \text{context}), where \mathbf{p} is the current ray position, \mathbf{d} is the ray direction, and context includes previous samples, camera state, or dataset metadata. The general update rule for a ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized) is: \mathbf{p}{i+1} = \mathbf{p}i + \Delta si \mathbf{d} t{i+1} = ti + \Delta si Key shared constraints and goals include: 1. Safety/Correctness: The step size must not cause the ray to "overshoot" or "penetrate" geometry or density features that should have been sampled. For SDFs, this often requires \Delta s \le d(\mathbf{p}) (Sphere Tracing) or a conservative fraction thereof. For volumes, it requires sufficient sampling density to satisfy the Nyquist criterion or to capture density gradients accurately. 2. Efficiency: The step size should increase in empty or low-gradient regions to reduce sample count. 3. Termination: Step size changes interact with termination rules (e.g., Early Ray Termination). A larger step size might skip the exact intersection point, requiring post-processing refinement (e.g., binary search). Safe Raymarching Step Size guarantees the ray never overshoots the implicit surface even when the SDF is distorted (e.g., by boolean operations or domain repetition). It differs from standard sphere tracing by explicitly clamping SDF values and applying a conservative ratio (>1.0) to the step increment, and from Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching by relying on fixed global bounds rather than local gradient estimation. Choose this when rendering complex CSG models or distorted SDFs where standard sphere tracing produces artifacts. Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching is a GPU-based direct volume rendering technique that varies step size based on local density and uses temporal accumulation to manage noise. It differs from Safe Raymarching Step Size by using a noise buffer to drive step size variation and temporal reprojection, and from Gap-Limited Ray Marching by its continuous adaptive scaling rather than discrete gap skipping. Choose this for dynamic volumetric data (like clouds or smoke) where temporal coherence can be exploited. Dynamic Sampling Step Adjustment accelerates ray marching through empty regions by exponentially increasing the step size (doubling) and mip level, reducing samples in sparse volumes. It differs from Safe Raymarching Step Size and Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching by using a discrete doubling strategy rather than continuous estimation, and from Gap-Limited Ray Marching by not explicitly calculating geometric gaps. Choose this for large, sparse volumes with multi-resolution textures. This method computes a static, geometry-driven minimum step size per pixel by projecting the dataset's cell axes onto the viewport. It ensures sampling density respects voxel resolution. Unlike adaptive methods, it does not adjust during marching but provides a heuristic bound. Choose this when strict adherence to voxel resolution is required to prevent aliasing, regardless of local density. Gap-Limited Ray Marching prevents overshooting on heightfield terrain by bounding the step size by half the vertical gap to the surface. Unlike standard distance-field marching which relies on a global Lipschitz constant, this method uses a step size proportional to the distance traveled, bounded by the gap. Choose this for terrain rendering or heightfield-based volumes where ridgelines cause overshooting in standard methods. An optimization that uses the triangle inequality to bound the distance to objects in a collection, eliminating unnecessary distance computations. It is particularly effective for large assortments of objects. If all primitives are nearly equidistant from the eye, the reduction is minimal until the ray has traversed much of the distance. For 9 spheres/plane, it reduced execution time from 2:53 to 1:19 (46% relative time). For the zeno logo, it reduced time from 26:29 to 19:23 (73% relative time). Uses knowledge of convexity to increase step size. For a convex set A defined by SDF d, the line segment \text{lerp}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{p} + d(\mathbf{p}) \frac{\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{p})}{\|\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{p})\|}) does not intersect A except possibly at the endpoint. If d(\mathbf{p}) < 0, the ray does not intersect. This causes quadratic convergence, similar to Newton's method. It avoids fixed intervals for rays parallel to horizon lines by detecting if the ray has stepped beyond the object. For a single sphere, it reduced time from 2:00 to 1:23 (69% relative time). Combined with triangle inequality, it enhances sphere tracing by 60%. A rendering method where the ray marching step size is provided per-pixel via an input tensor, allowing variable sampling density. The input stepsize tensor is of size H \times W with positive values. The output tensor contains 8 channels: mask, normal (XYZ), depth, AO, and flow (XY). Unlike standard rendering, it accepts per-pixel step sizes, enabling adaptive sampling based on importance maps. Calculates a relative error metric for adaptive stepping. The metric is computed as rv = |k / \max(|y|, \text{threshold})|, and the final error is \max(rv.x, \max(rv.y, rv.z)) + \text{FLOAT\MIN}. Optimizations for Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) used in procedural noise for volume rendering. Includes reducing octave count based on distance (t) using logarithmic scaling, multi-level LOD (e.g., 3, 9, 16 octaves), using texture sampling instead of hash functions, manually unrolling loops, and using directional derivatives instead of full gradients (1 sample vs 3). Early termination if accumulated amplitude exceeds 0.99. Step size optimization evolved from the basic ray marching techniques used in early volume rendering and implicit surface rendering. Sphere tracing, introduced by [Kay & Kajiya, 1986], established the baseline of using the SDF value as the step size. Enhancements like the Triangle Inequality and Convexity were developed to reduce the computational cost of evaluating distances for complex scenes. In volume rendering, adaptive stepping emerged to handle the vast empty space in volumetric datasets, leveraging multi-resolution textures (mipmaps) and density thresholds to skip empty regions. Modern implementations often combine these geometric heuristics with temporal accumulation and GPU-specific optimizations like per-pixel tensor inputs. body: Safe Raymarching Step Size is a distance-field ray marching technique that dynamically computes step lengths to guarantee the ray never overshoots or penetrates the implicit surface, even when the Signed Distance Function (SDF) is distorted or approximated. It solves the problem of geometric artifacts caused by domain repetition or boolean operations, where the estimated distance may exceed the actual distance to the geometry. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by explicitly clamping SDF values and applying a conservative ratio to the step increment. Inputs: Camera position \mathbf{c} and ray directions \mathbf{r} for all pixels. SDF decoder or evaluator f(\mathbf{p}). Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the scene, defined by \mathbf{aabb}{min} and \mathbf{aabb}{max}. Parameters: clampdist: Float threshold for clamping SDF values. Typical value: 0.1. raymarchingratio: Float multiplier applied to the clamped SDF to determine step size. Typical value: 1.5. threshold: Float SDF value threshold for surface intersection. Typical value: 5 \times 10^{-5}. marchstep: Integer maximum number of iterations. Outputs: sdflist: List of lists containing SDF values at each step for N rays and M steps. marchingzdepthlist: List of lists containing accumulated depth. pointslist: List of lists containing 3D points sampled along rays. validmaskrender: Boolean list indicating valid rays that have not exceeded bounds or hit the surface incorrectly. Data Structures: Lists are used to accumulate data per step. marchingzdepth is initialized to zeros for all valid rays. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize marchingzdepth to a list of zeros with length N, where N is the number of valid rays. Initialize empty lists: sdflist, marchingzdepthlist, pointslist. Calculate maxboundzdepth using a helper function getmaxboundzdepth(campos, validcamrays). This represents the maximum distance a ray can travel before exiting the scene bounds. 2. Iterative Marching Loop: For i from 0 to marchstep - 1: a. Point Generation: Calculate current ray origins: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{c} + \text{marching\zdepth} \odot \mathbf{r}. Store \mathbf{p}i in pointslist. b. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate SDF: di = f(\mathbf{p}i). If gradients are not required, detach them. Store di in sdflist. c. Clamping and Step Calculation: Clamp SDF values: d{clamped} = \max(-\text{clamp\dist}, \min(di, \text{clamp\dist})). Calculate step size \Delta s = d{clamped} \times \text{ray\marching\ratio}. Alternatively, for grid-based variants, calculate unit size per grid cell as \text{unit\size} = \frac{\|\mathbf{aabb}{max} - \mathbf{aabb}{min}\|}{\text{gridSize}}, then \Delta s = \text{mean}(\text{unit\size}) \times \text{step\ratio}. Sources indicate raymarchingratio is typically > 1.0 (e.g., 1.5) to ensure safety against distortion artifacts. d. Depth Update: Update marchingzdepth: \text{marching\zdepth} \leftarrow \text{marching\zdepth} + \Delta s. Store updated marchingzdepth in marchingzdepthlist. e. Termination Check (Optional Optimization): If using recursive marching (raymarchingrecursive), only process rays where validmaskrender is still true. If using trivial marching (raymarchingtrivial), process all rays in parallel. 3. Post-Processing and Masking: Concatenate lists along dimension 0 to form tensors of shape (M, N). Compute validmaskmaxmarchingzdepth: Check if \text{marching\zdepth} < \text{maxbound\zdepth}. Compute validmaskraymarching: Check if \mini(|di|) \le \text{threshold} for any step i. Compute validmaskfirstquery: Check if d0 > \text{threshold}. This handles the corner case where the first query is already below the threshold, preventing incorrect filtering. Combine masks: validmaskrender = validmaskmaxmarchingzdepth AND validmaskraymarching AND validmaskfirstquery. 4. Return: Return sdflist, marchingzdepthlist, pointslist, and validmaskrender. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def saferaymarchingstepsize(campos, camrays, sdfdecoder, aabbmin, aabbmax, clampdist=0.1, raymarchingratio=1.5, threshold=5e-5, marchstep=100, gridSize=None, stepratio=1.0): """ Implements Safe Raymarching Step Size. Args: campos: List of tuples (x, y, z), camera positions. camrays: List of tuples (dx, dy, dz), normalized ray directions. sdfdecoder: Function evaluating SDF at point p. aabbmin: Tuple (x, y, z), min corner of bounding box. aabbmax: Tuple (x, y, z), max corner of bounding box. clampdist: float, SDF clamping threshold. raymarchingratio: float, multiplier for step size. threshold: float, intersection threshold. marchstep: int, max iterations. gridSize: int, optional voxel grid resolution for grid-based step calculation. stepratio: float, multiplier for grid-based step size. Returns: sdflist, marchingzdepthlist, pointslist, validmaskrender """ N = len(camrays) # Initialize marchingzdepth = [0.0] N sdflist = [] marchingzdepthlist = [] pointslist = [] # Calculate max bound depth maxboundzdepth = getmaxboundzdepth(campos, camrays, aabbmin, aabbmax) # Optional grid-based step size calculation if gridSize is not None: diag = ((aabbmax[0]-aabbmin[0])2 + (aabbmax[1]-aabbmin[1])2 + (aabbmax[2]-aabbmin[2])2)0.5 unitsize = diag / gridSize gridstep = unitsize stepratio else: gridstep = None for i in range(marchstep): # 1. Generate points points = [] for j in range(N): px = campos[j][0] + marchingzdepth[j] camrays[j][0] py = campos[j][1] + marchingzdepth[j] camrays[j][1] pz = campos[j][2] + marchingzdepth[j] camrays[j][2] points.append((px, py, pz)) pointslist.append(points) # 2. Evaluate SDF sdfvalues = [sdfdecoder(p) for p in points] # Detach gradients if necessary (simulated by returning float) sdfvalues = [float(v) for v in sdfvalues] sdflist.append(sdfvalues) # 3. Clamp SDF sdfclamped = [max(-clampdist, min(v, clampdist)) for v in sdfvalues] # 4. Calculate Step Size if gridstep is not None: stepsize = [gridstep] N else: stepsize = [v raymarchingratio for v in sdfclamped] # 5. Update Depth marchingzdepth = [z + s for z, s in zip(marchingzdepth, stepsize)] marchingzdepthlist.append(marchingzdepth) # 6. Post-processing finalzdepth = marchingzdepth validmaskmax = [z < maxboundzdepth[j] for j, z in enumerate(finalzdepth)] # min abs SDF <= threshold minabssdf = [min(abs(sdflist[k][j]) for k in range(marchstep)) for j in range(N)] validmaskhit = [m <= threshold for m in minabssdf] # validmaskfirstquery: first SDF > threshold firstsdf = sdflist[0] validmaskfirst = [s > threshold for s in firstsdf] validmaskrender = [validmaskmax[j] and validmaskhit[j] and validmaskfirst[j] for j in range(N)] return sdflist, marchingzdepthlist, pointslist, validmaskrender def getmaxboundzdepth(campos, camrays, aabbmin, aabbmax): """ Calculates the distance from campos to the intersection of the ray with the AABB. Returns a list of floats. """ maxbound = [] for j in range(len(camrays)): invdir = [1.0 / camrays[j][k] if camrays[j][k] != 0 else float('inf') for k in range(3)] t1 = [(aabbmin[k] - campos[j][k]) invdir[k] for k in range(3)] t2 = [(aabbmax[k] - campos[j][k]) invdir[k] for k in range(3)] tmin = max(min(t1[k], t2[k]) for k in range(3)) tmax = min(max(t1[k], t2[k]) for k in range(3)) if tmax < 0: maxbound.append(float('inf')) else: maxbound.append(tmin if tmin >= 0 else float('inf')) return maxbound Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distortion Artifacts: Domain repetition or boolean operations can distort the SDF, causing the estimated distance to be larger than the actual distance. This leads to the ray skipping over geometry. The solution is to step shorter than the SDF returns, achieved by raymarchingratio > 1.0 or clamping. Boundary Exceedance: Rays must not exceed maxboundzdepth. This is checked against the final accumulated depth. Underestimating distance forces smaller steps, increasing iterations. An exact SDF may outperform a fast, inaccurate bound if the inaccuracy causes disproportionate step reduction. Unlike Safe Raymarching which may use a single global bound, ALC leverages geometric containment. Uses local SDF gradients to compute larger, safer step sizes, particularly near silhouettes. Combines first and second Lipschitz constraints to account for curvature, differing from Safe Raymarching by leveraging gradient magnitude rather than fixed ratios. A robust algorithm using a pre-computed global Lipschitz constant \lambda to guarantee no surface penetration. Simpler and numerically stable but potentially less efficient for complex scenes with varying feature scales compared to adaptive methods. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Distance Accuracy vs Performance Trade-off
head: Distance Estimate Accuracy, Distance accuracy vs performance, Sphere Tracing Performance Analysis, Underestimate vs Exact SDF Performance
body: This method analyzes the inverse relationship between the accuracy of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluation and the computational cost of sphere tracing. It establishes that underestimating the distance to the surface forces the ray marcher to take smaller steps, significantly increasing the number of iterations required for convergence. The core insight is that a slower, exact SDF evaluation can outperform a faster, inaccurate distance bound if the inaccuracy forces a disproportionate increase in step count. The method relies on the geometric constraint that the step size s in sphere tracing must satisfy s \le d(\mathbf{p}), where d(\mathbf{p}) is the distance estimate at the current ray position \mathbf{p}. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. SDF function d(\mathbf{p}) which may be an approximation or exact. Convergence threshold \epsilon. Maximum traversal distance \text{max\dist}. Maximum iteration count \text{max\steps}. Outputs: Boolean indicating surface intersection. Number of steps taken. Data Structures: Current ray position \mathbf{p} (vector). Step counter n (integer). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}, normalize \mathbf{d}, and set n = 0. 2. Evaluate distance estimate d{est} = d(\mathbf{p}). 3. Clamp negative estimates to zero: d{est} \leftarrow \max(d{est}, 0). 4. If d{est} < \epsilon, terminate successfully. If \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}\| > \text{max\dist} or n \ge \text{max\steps}, terminate unsuccessfully. 5. Advance ray: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + d{est} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 6. Increment n \leftarrow n + 1. 7. Repeat from step 2. Formulas: The relationship between distance accuracy and step count is derived from the convergence rate. Experiments on a sphere show that halving the distance estimate doubles the number of steps. Thus, the step count scales inversely with the estimate magnitude: N{steps} \propto \frac{1}{d{est}} Where N{steps} is the number of iterations and d{est} is the average distance estimate magnitude. Parameters: \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Severe Underestimation: If d{est} is significantly smaller than the true distance d{true}, the ray takes many small steps, wasting computation. For example, a bound that returns at worst 1% of the true distance may perform worse than an exact function in specific cases. Exact vs. Approximate Cost: The total cost is Cost = N{steps} \times Cost{eval}. A slower exact function may have higher Cost{eval} but much lower N{steps}, resulting in lower total time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spheretrace(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunction, epsilon, maxdist, maxsteps): """ Demonstrates the trade-off by comparing step counts for different SDF accuracies. """ # Normalize direction to ensure step size equals distance estimate dlen = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in raydirection)) d = [x / dlen for x in raydirection] p = list(rayorigin) steps = 0 while steps < maxsteps: # Evaluate distance. name: Adaptive Convergence Threshold
head: Camera-aware SDF Threshold, Convergence Criteria for Sphere Tracing, Pixel-intersection based epsilon
body: Adaptive Convergence Threshold is a stopping condition for distance-field ray marching that determines when the ray has sufficiently converged to the surface to halt further computation. It solves the trade-off between rendering accuracy and computational cost by dynamically calculating a threshold \epsilon based on camera parameters, ensuring that the ray front ends of neighboring pixels do not intersect. Unlike fixed thresholds, this method scales with the scene geometry and camera setup to prevent both dilation (loss of detail) and erosion (incomplete geometry). Inputs and Outputs Inputs: d{min}: Minimum distance from the camera to the object. S: Sensor size (width). f: Focal length. R: Image resolution (width). \theta: Angle of the ray relative to the optical axis. SDF(p): The signed distance function value at the current ray position p. Outputs: \epsilon: The convergence threshold. Boolean: Whether to continue marching (|SDF(p)| \ge \epsilon) or stop (|SDF(p)| < \epsilon). Data Structures No specific data structures are required beyond standard scalar variables for camera parameters and the current SDF evaluation. Steps 1. Calculate the adaptive convergence threshold \epsilon using the camera intrinsics and the ray's angle \theta. 2. Evaluate the signed distance function SDF(p) at the current ray position p. 3. Compare the absolute SDF value to the threshold: If |SDF(p)| < \epsilon, stop marching. Otherwise, continue marching. Formula The threshold \epsilon is derived from the condition that balls centered at the ray front ends of neighboring pixels must not intersect. The formula is: \epsilon = \frac{d{min} \cdot S \cdot \cos^2(\theta)}{2 \cdot f \cdot R} Where: d{min} is the minimum object distance. S is the sensor size. f is the focal length. R is the resolution. \theta is the angle of the ray. Parameters Typical Values: For a setup with f=60mm, d{min}=10cm, S=32mm, and R=512, the resulting \epsilon \approx 0.5 \times 10^{-4}m (0.05mm). Practical Threshold: In practice, a fixed threshold of 5 \times 10^{-5} is often used for experiments, though the adaptive calculation provides a theoretical bound. Pitfalls Too Large: A threshold that is too large causes dilation, leading to the loss of boundary details and large depth errors due to bounded rendering noise. Too Small: A threshold that is too small significantly increases rendering time. If a maximum number of tracing steps is enforced, pixels may fail to converge, resulting in erosion (background misclassification). Angle Dependence: The threshold varies with \theta. Rays at larger angles (peripheral pixels) have a smaller \epsilon, requiring more precision. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculateadaptivethreshold(dmin, S, f, R, theta): """ Calculate the adaptive convergence threshold epsilon. Args: dmin (float): Minimum distance to object. S (float): Sensor size. f (float): Focal length. R (float): Resolution. theta (float): Ray angle in radians. Returns: float: The convergence threshold epsilon. """ costheta = math.cos(theta) epsilon = (dmin S costheta costheta) / (2 f R) return epsilon def raymarchingstep(p, SDFfunc, epsilon): """ Perform one step of ray marching with adaptive convergence check. Args: p (Vector3): Current ray position. SDFfunc (function): Signed Distance Function evaluator. epsilon (float): Convergence threshold. Returns: bool: True if marching should continue, False if converged. """ dist = SDFfunc(p) if abs(dist) < epsilon: return False # Converged return True # Continue Time Complexity: Rendering time scales with the number of queries needed to reach the threshold, increasing significantly if the threshold is set too small. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the threshold calculation. Strengths: Prevents dilation and erosion by aligning the convergence criterion with the pixel resolution. Provides a theoretical bound on depth error. Limitations: Requires knowledge of camera intrinsics (f, S, R) and an estimate of d{min}. The calculation of \theta requires ray direction knowledge. When to Use: When rendering with differentiable sphere tracing where depth accuracy and silhouette precision are critical, and camera parameters are known. When Not to Use: When camera parameters are unknown or dynamic in a way that makes d{min} estimation unreliable. The method was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering of implicit signed distance functions (SDFs). It addresses the issue of slow convergence near the surface where the SDF value approaches zero. The approach is based on the geometric principle that the threshold should be small enough to distinguish between neighboring pixels but large enough to avoid excessive computation. name: Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC)
head: BVH-based Adaptive Lipschitz Constant, Nested BVH Step Size Optimization
body: Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) is a sphere tracing enhancement that uses a nested Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to compute tighter, adaptive Lipschitz constants for step size calculation, rather than using the global sum Lipschitz constant. It solves the problem of overly conservative step sizes in large scenes where the naive global Lipschitz constant \lambda{Fn} becomes very large, limiting efficiency. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Current position t0 along the ray. A nested BVH structure representing the implicit function Fn = \sum{i=1}^n fi. For each BVH level i \in [1, n]: the value of the partial sum at t0, denoted \text{BVH}i(t0); the Lipschitz constant for the partial sum, \lambda{\text{BVH}i} = \lambda{Fi}. Outputs: The next safe step size \Delta t to advance the ray. Data Structures: BVH Nodes: Store bounding volumes, Lipschitz constants, and partial sum values at the current ray position. Sum Elements: The functions fi are pre-sorted from higher to lower range of values to achieve close-to-maximal steps with low overhead. Method: 1. Identify Minimum Level: Determine i{min}, the first BVH level where the ray is outside the bounding volume. For all levels i \ge i{min}, the ray is outside the isosurface of BVHi, making the intersection with BVHi's boundary a safe step target. 2. Construct Inclusion Functions: For each valid BVH level i, construct a forward inclusion function: \text{BVH}{\pm i} = \text{BVH}{\pm i}(t0) \pm \lambda{\text{BVH}i}(t - t0), where \lambda{\text{BVH}i} = \lambda{Fi}. 3. Combine Bounds: Combine the inclusion functions from all valid BVH levels by taking their intersection to narrow the range of possible values for Fn(t): Fn(t) \in \bigcap{i=1}^n \text{BVH}{i\pm}. 4. Compute Step Candidates: Calculate candidate step sizes for each BVH level i using the lower bound of the combined inclusion function: F{n-1}(t) = \max{i \in [1, n]} (\text{BVH}{i-1}(t0) - \lambda{\text{BVH}i}(t - t0)). Solving F{n-1}(t) = 0 yields the candidate step \Delta ti = \text{BVH}{i-1}(t0) / \lambda{\text{BVH}i}. 5. Select Final Step: Select the largest (best) candidate as the final step size, which corresponds to the minimum of the individual upper-bound roots to satisfy the intersection constraint. 6. Advance Ray: Move the ray origin to t0 + \Delta t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computealcstep(currentt, bvhlevels): """ Compute the next safe step size using Adaptive Lipschitz Constant. Args: currentt: float, current distance along the ray. bvhlevels: list of dicts, each containing: 'value': float, BVHi(t0) 'lambda': float, Lipschitz constant lambdaBVHi Returns: float, the next safe step size. """ beststep = float('inf') for level in bvhlevels: val = level['value'] lam = level['lambda'] if lam <= 0: continue candidatestep = val / lam # The source states to "select the largest (best) candidate". # Mathematically, intersecting inclusion functions requires taking # the minimum of the individual roots to guarantee safety. if candidatestep > 0 and candidatestep < beststep: beststep = candidatestep return beststep if beststep != float('inf') else 0.0 Parameters: Pre-sorting: Sum elements are pre-sorted from higher to lower range of values to achieve close-to-maximal steps with low overhead. Dynamic Re-ordering: Not used. It is not GPU-friendly because it requires storing each element in an O(n) array and sorting dynamically at every step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If \lambda{\text{BVH}i} is very small, division by zero or numerical instability may occur. Guard against \lambda \le \epsilon. Degenerate Input: If the ray is inside a BVH level, the inclusion function logic for "outside" steps may not apply directly. The method assumes the ray is outside the target isosurface for the step calculation. GPU Performance: Dynamic re-ordering of sum elements is avoided due to high memory and sorting overhead on GPUs. Sub-stepping is an optimization for adaptive ray marching that guarantees non-decreasing step sizes by performing intermediate sub-steps along the ray as intermediate field sums are computed. It solves the problem of "bad candidates" in standard Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) methods, where computing additional field components fi can unpredictably reduce the step size, leading to wasted computation. Unlike standard ALC, which calculates the next step based on the current position and all available bounds, Sub-stepping physically advances the ray to validate bounds, ensuring that each additional level of detail contributes positively or neutrally to the step size. Computes a tighter Lipschitz constant for sphere-tracing by evaluating it per primitive and per ray, mitigating performance loss from varying primitive radii. For each ray, find the primitive point with the smallest radius whose kernel support intersects the ray. Solve the polynomial equation for intersection roots to determine the smallest radius along the ray. The kernel support intersection condition is: \|\mathbf{p} - (\mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}\|^2 - \sigma^2(\tau0 + s\Delta\tau)^2 \leq 0 where \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{m} - \mathbf{s}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{d} is the ray direction, \sigma is the kernel scale, \tau0 is the base radius, \Delta\tau is the radius variation step, and s is the ray parameter. The parameter \sigma is the kernel scale factor used in the intersection polynomial. Time Complexity: O(n) per step to evaluate all BVH levels and compute inclusion functions, where n is the number of levels in the BVH. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store BVH levels and their Lipschitz constants, with no dynamic arrays required, making it GPU-friendly. Measured Performance: Improves efficiency over naive global Lipschitz constant methods, especially when n is large and \lambda{Fn} would otherwise be very big. Strengths: Tighter bounds lead to larger steps. GPU-friendly due to lack of dynamic sorting. Limitations: Requires a nested BVH structure. Pre-sorting may not always yield optimal steps, though it is close-to-optimal for functions like FBM. When to Use: When rendering procedural volumetric noise or large detailed scenes where the global Lipschitz constant is too conservative. When Not to Use: When the BVH structure is not available or too expensive to build. Originating from the work on fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise, ALC leverages the bounded nature of functions through a BVH to make bigger and cheaper steps. It builds on the intuition of Worley and Hart regarding dynamic re-ordering but adapts it for GPU-friendly static pre-sorting. The method is described as an enhancement to sphere tracing using nested BVH levels. name: Sub-stepping
body: Sub-stepping is an optimization for adaptive ray marching that guarantees non-decreasing step sizes by performing intermediate sub-steps along the ray as intermediate field sums are computed. It solves the problem of "bad candidates" in standard Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) methods, where computing additional field components fi can unpredictably reduce the step size, leading to wasted computation. Unlike standard ALC, which calculates the next step based on the current position and all available bounds, Sub-stepping physically advances the ray to validate bounds, ensuring that each additional level of detail contributes positively or neutrally to the step size. Inputs: Current ray origin t0. Target value v (typically 0 for isosurfaces). Minimum BVH level i{min} and maximum level n. Lipschitz constants \lambda{Fi} for cumulative sums Fi and \lambda{fi} for individual fields fi. BVH bounds BVH{i+}(t) providing upper bounds for field sums. Sum of remaining bounds s(i, n) = \sum{k=i}^{n} \Delta{fk}, where \Delta{fk} is the bound provided by the BVH for fk. Outputs: Next ray position t{next} = t0 + step{final}. Data Structures: The method relies on the parent ALC method's BVH nodes and field functions; no additional complex data structures are required. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute an initial step size step{i{min}} using the BVH at level i{min}. 2. Physically move the ray position by stepi to t0 + stepi. Assume the worst-case scenario where BVH{i+}(t0 + stepi) = v. 3. Evaluate the next function f{i+1} at the new position t0 + stepi. Replace the bound \Delta{f{i+1}} with the actual value f{i+1}(t0 + stepi). 4. Update the step size using the derived formula. Formulas: Initial step size: step{i{min}} = -\frac{F{i{min}}(t0) + s(i{min} + 1, n)}{\lambda{F{i{min}}}}. Updated step size: step{i+1} = stepi + \frac{\Delta{f{i+1}} - f{i+1}(t0 + stepi)}{\lambda{Fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}}}. (Note: The source's Eq. 15 writes the denominator as \lambda{fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}}, but the derivation in Eq. 14 and the inequality analysis consistently use \lambda{Fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}}; the implementation uses the latter for mathematical consistency with Lipschitz accumulation.) Parameters: v=0 is standard for isosurfaces. i{min} and n define the BVH level range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero occurs if \lambda{Fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}} = 0, requiring a numerical guard. Floating-point precision errors may accumulate if stepi is very small. Loose BVH bounds produce small initial steps, increasing the number of required sub-steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def substeppingraymarch(t0, v, imin, n, bvhquery, fields, lambdasF, lambdasf, deltas): """ t0: current ray position v: target value (e.g., 0) imin: minimum BVH level n: maximum level index bvhquery(level, t): returns the upper bound BVH{level+}(t) fields: list of field functions, fieldsi returns fi(t) lambdasF: list of Lipschitz constants for cumulative sums Fi lambdasf: list of Lipschitz constants for individual fields fi deltas: list of BVH bounds for individual fields, deltas[i] = Delta{fi} """ # 1. Compute initial step size using BVH at imin boundimin = bvhquery(imin, t0) step = (v - boundimin) / lambdasF[imin] # 2. Iterate through levels to refine step size via sub-stepping for i in range(imin, n): # a. Sub-step: Move ray position forward by current step size tsub = t0 + step # b. Evaluate next field f{i+1} at the sub-step position fnextval = fieldsi+1 # c. Update step size using actual value instead of BVH bound # Denominator uses lambda{Fi} + lambda{f{i+1}} per derivation consistency lambdasum = lambdasF[i] + lambdasf[i+1] if lambdasum == 0: lambdasum = 1e-9 # Guard against division by zero step = step + (deltas[i+1] - fnextval) / lambdasum return step This method is a real-time ray tracing pipeline for visualizing Scale-Invariant Integral Surfaces (SCALIS) defined by skeletons with prescribed radii. It solves the high computational cost of individual SCALIS field evaluations and the challenge of robust closest ray/isosurface intersection by relying on local field interpolations and subdividing the ray into intervals that capture main field variations. It sets itself apart from brute-force marching by using a dynamic view-dependent acceleration structure to select primitives and transforming field values to a space allowing good quadratic polynomial approximation. Time Complexity: The method performs O(n - i{min}) field evaluations per step, where n is the maximum level and i{min} is the minimum level. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the BVH and field data structures used by the parent ALC method. Performance: Sub-stepping performs better on average than the standard Adaptive Lipschitz method because it avoids computing wasteful bad candidates and guarantees step sizes do not decrease. Strengths: Guarantees non-decreasing step sizes, reducing the likelihood of getting stuck in small steps due to optimistic bounds. Limitations: Requires evaluating fields at intermediate positions, which increases computational cost per step compared to a single evaluation if the step size is large. Sub-stepping was introduced in the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". It addresses the limitations of the standard Adaptive Lipschitz Constant method where computing additional field components can unpredictably reduce the step size. The method was developed to improve the efficiency of sphere tracing for procedural volumetric noise in large scenes. name: Local Field Interpolation with Dynamic Subdivision
head: Dynamic Subdivision for SCALIS, Fast ray tracing of scale-invariant integral surfaces, Local Field Interpolation with Dynamic Subdivision for SCALIS, SCALIS rendering pipeline, Scale-Invariant Integral Surface (SCALIS) Ray Tracing
body: This method is a real-time ray tracing pipeline for visualizing Scale-Invariant Integral Surfaces (SCALIS) defined by skeletons with prescribed radii. It solves the high computational cost of individual SCALIS field evaluations and the challenge of robust closest ray/isosurface intersection by relying on local field interpolations and subdividing the ray into intervals that capture main field variations. It sets itself apart from brute-force marching by using a dynamic view-dependent acceleration structure to select primitives and transforming field values to a space allowing good quadratic polynomial approximation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, a skeleton structure consisting of line segment primitives Si with prescribed radii at endpoints, and a target isovalue c. Output: The intersection distance t along the ray where the SCALIS field f(\mathbf{p}) = c. Data Structures: Skeleton Primitive Si: A line segment defined by endpoints \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1 and radii r0, r1. Radius Function \tau{Si}(q): For a point q on the segment, the radius is the linear interpolation of the endpoint radii. Dynamic A-Buffer: A GPU-accelerated structure built on the fly to select primitives whose supports overlap a given interval along the ray. Field Definitions: The SCALIS field is an implicit surface defined by a scalar field f and an isovalue c as the set of points \mathbf{p} satisfying f(\mathbf{p}) = c. The field is constructed from primitives using the sum blending operator: f(\mathbf{p}) = \sumi fi(\mathbf{p}) \quad (1) where fi is the field function defined by the i-th primitive. The primitives are based on kernels. Compact Polynomial kernels are defined as: k{i,\sigma}(d) = \begin{cases} \left(1 - \left(\frac{d}{\sigma}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{i}{2}} & \text{if } d < \sigma, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \quad (2) and Cauchy kernels are defined as: k{i,\sigma}(d) = \frac{1}{\left(1+\left(\frac{d}{\sigma}\right)^2\right)^i} \quad (3) where i is the degree parameter and \sigma is the scale parameter. Algorithm Steps: 1. Primitive Selection: Select primitives whose supports overlap a given interval along the ray using a dynamic view-dependent acceleration structure built on the fly using fast GPU construction of A-buffers. 2. Ray Segmentation: Segment the camera ray into sub-intervals based on the distance to the skeleton. The strategy is chosen to capture main field variations while generating a small number of sub-intervals to be processed. 3. Field Mapping: Transform field values to a space that allows good quadratic polynomial approximation of the SCALIS field on each sub-interval. This is achieved by using a bijective mapping of the SCALIS field to an approximate smooth homothetic distance field (squared) which has the exact same isosurface of interest as the SCALIS field. All processing is done on this normalized field. 4. Iterative Interpolation and Root Finding: For each sub-interval, iteratively build polynomial interpolations using fast quadratic roots computation to rapidly converge toward the real field function. A different interpolation is used and refined in each interval, locally producing an accurate approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tracescalisray(rayorigin, raydirection, skeletonsegments, isovalue): # 1. Primitive Selection (Dynamic A-Buffer simulation) # Filter primitives whose bounding spheres overlap the ray segment [tmin, tmax] # The sources describe a dynamic A-buffer built on the fly activeprimitives = [] for seg in skeletonsegments: R = max(seg.r0, seg.r1) + math.dist(seg.v0, seg.v1) oc = rayorigin - seg.center b = math.dot(oc, raydirection) c = math.dot(oc, oc) - R R if c > 0.0 and b > 0.0: continue disc = b b - c if disc >= 0.0: activeprimitives.append(seg) # 2. Ray Segmentation # Divide ray into intervals based on distance to skeleton to capture field variations # The exact subdivision heuristic is not specified in the sources intervals = computeintervals(rayorigin, raydirection, activeprimitives) thit = None tmin, tmax = 0.0, 1e6 for tstart, tend in intervals: if tstart > tmax: break tend = min(tend, tmax) if tstart >= tend: continue # 3. Field Mapping # Map SCALIS field to approximate squared homothetic distance field # The isovalue c maps to 0 in the normalized space targetnormalized = 0.0 tguess = tstart for in range(50): p = rayorigin + tguess raydirection fval = evaluatescalisfield(p, activeprimitives) # Bijective mapping to normalized squared distance space fnorm = normalizetosquareddistance(fval, isovalue) if abs(fnorm - targetnormalized) < 1e-6: thit = tguess break # Compute derivatives along ray direction # f'(t) = grad(f). d, f''(t) = d. Hessian(f). d df = computerayderivative(p, raydirection, activeprimitives) d2f = computeraysecondderivative(p, raydirection, activeprimitives) if abs(df) < 1e-12: df = 1e-12 # Fast quadratic root computation: solve fnorm + dfdt + 0.5d2fdt^2 = 0 a = 0.5 d2f b = df c = fnorm - targetnormalized if abs(a) < 1e-12: dt = -c / b else: disc = b b - 4 a c if disc < 0: disc = 0 dt = (-b - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2 a) tguess += dt tguess = max(tstart, min(tend, tguess)) if abs(dt) < 1e-8: thit = tguess break if thit is not None: break return thit Parameters: maxiterations: Fixed to 50 in the implementation to prevent infinite loops. Not given in the sources. Convergence thresholds (1e-6 for field value, 1e-8 for step size) are standard numerical values. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the bijective mapping to a normalized field to ensure good quadratic approximation. If the mapping is inaccurate, convergence may fail. Boundaries: The ray segmentation must ensure that intervals are small enough to capture main field variations but large enough to minimize overhead. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a skeleton structure with line segment primitives. The sources do not specify handling for degenerate segments. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of field evaluations by using local interpolations and dynamic subdivision. The dynamic A-buffer construction is performed on the fly using fast GPU construction. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the dynamic A-buffer and the skeleton structure. Measured Performance: The method provides improvements for various resolutions on all combinations of tested models and GPU hardware. It goes beyond Sherstyuk's fast ray-tracing algorithm for convolution surfaces, notably allowing better support of large radius variation while being less sensitive to skeleton tessellation. Strengths: Real-time visualization of SCALIS, efficient primitive selection, robust intersection finding. Limitations: High computational cost of individual SCALIS field evaluations is mitigated but not eliminated; the method is specific to SCALIS fields. Scale-invariant integral surfaces (SCALIS) are implicit representations of surfaces that provide a way to define smooth surfaces from skeletons with prescribed radii defined at their vertices. The rendering pipeline was introduced to visualize such surfaces in real-time, addressing challenges in robust intersection, efficient primitive selection, and high computational cost. The method builds on previous work in metaballs rendering and transparency using A-buffers. It improves upon Sherstyuk's fast ray-tracing algorithm for convolution surfaces. name: Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints
head: 2-Lipschitz Sphere Tracing, Gradient-assisted Sphere Tracing
body:
Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints is an optimization for ray marching that uses the local gradient of the Signed Distance Function (SDF) to compute larger, safer step sizes than standard sphere tracing, particularly near silhouettes and backward-facing surfaces. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by combining the first and second Lipschitz constraints to account for curvature, and from its siblings like Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) by explicitly leveraging gradient magnitude rather than just bounding volume hierarchies or global constants. Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D, SDF function f(p), and its gradient 
abla f(p). Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray. Data Structures: p: Current 3D position (vec3). gradf: Gradient vector 
abla f(p) (vec3). L: Local Lipschitz constant bound for the gradient magnitude (scalar). L2: Local Lipschitz constant bound for the Hessian/curvature (scalar). Steps: 1. Initialize p = O. 2. Evaluate f(p) and 
abla f(p). 3. Calculate the standard sphere tracing step size bound using the gradient magnitude: s1 =  rac{f(p)}{|
abla f(p)|} This step assumes the function is 1-Lipschitz with constant |
abla f(p)|. 4. Apply the 2-Lipschitz constraint to refine the step size based on curvature bounds. The step size s must satisfy the condition that the function does not change faster than allowed by its second derivative. The refined step size s{final} is derived from the quadratic bound imposed by the 2-Lipschitz property: s{final} = \min \left( s1,  rac{-|
abla f(p)| + \sqrt{|
abla f(p)|^2 + 2 L2 f(p)}}{L2} ight) Where L2 is the bound on the Hessian norm (or the Lipschitz constant of the gradient). Note: If f(p) \le 0, the ray has hit or passed the surface; terminate. 5. Advance the ray: p = p + sfinal D. 6. Repeat from step 2 until convergence or max steps. Parameters: L (Lipschitz constant of f): For FBM, this is dynamically computed using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to be much smaller than the global constant. L2 (Lipschitz constant of 
abla f): Bounding the curvature. For FBM, this requires careful handling of cascaded sums. It sets itself apart from its parent, Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints, by selectively activating second-order Halley contraction only within grazing silhouette horizons while maintaining single-query Lipschitz advances in open space, thereby truncating the grazing stall tail by up to 4×. Segment Tracing is a ray marching algorithm for implicit surfaces that computes a local Lipschitz bound \lambda(e) for each ray segment e to determine safe, adaptive step sizes, significantly reducing field function queries compared to global bound methods. Unlike Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints which uses gradient magnitude to estimate step size, Segment Tracing rigorously bounds the gradient of the deformed field and the Jacobian of the deformation map to guarantee no surface intersections are skipped, even under complex non-linear warping. When not to use: If gradient computation is prohibitively expensive or if the function is not differentiable everywhere (e.g., Perlin noise with abs() requires special handling). name: Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching
head: Curvature-Bounded Contraction, Fixed-Point Projection for Real-Time Implicit Surface Rendering
body: Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching is a ray-surface intersection method that formulates intersection as a curvature-accelerated contraction operator on the Eikonal distance field to solve the computational stall of sphere tracing near grazing angles and silhouette edges. It sets itself apart from its parent, Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints, by selectively activating second-order Halley contraction only within grazing silhouette horizons while maintaining single-query Lipschitz advances in open space, thereby truncating the grazing stall tail by up to 4×. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}) returning value and directional derivatives; a fixed-point invariance threshold \epsilon = 10^{-15}. Output: The intersection distance t along the ray, or a failure flag if no intersection is found within bounds. Data Structures: Ray State: Current position \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, current distance estimate t, and previous distance estimate t{prev}. Derivatives: Directional first-order derivative f' and second-order derivative f'' evaluated along the ray trajectory. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set initial step size t based on the initial SDF value f(\mathbf{o}). Set t{prev} = 0. 2. Loop Condition: While the fixed-point invariance condition ||P{hit}^2 - P{hit}|| > \epsilon is not met, where P{hit} is the contraction operator: a. Evaluate Derivatives: Compute the directional first-order derivative f' and second-order derivative f'' at the current position \mathbf{r}(t) along the ray direction \mathbf{d}. b. Determine Contraction Mode: i. If the ray is in open space (not near a grazing silhouette horizon), execute a single-query Lipschitz advance. ii. If the ray is within a grazing silhouette horizon, activate second-order Halley contraction. c. Compute Step: i. Lipschitz Advance: Compute step size \Delta t bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints derived from f'. ii. Halley Contraction: Compute step size \Delta t using a rational Halley formula involving f, f', and f'', bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints. d. Apply Contraction: Update t{prev} = t and advance t = t + \Delta t. 3. Termination: Upon entering the root neighborhood, the operator achieves terminal orthogonal projection with fixed-point invariance. Return t. Formulas: Fixed-Point Invariance Condition: ||P{hit}^2 - P{hit}|| \le 10^{-15} where P{hit} is the contraction operator mapping the current distance estimate to the next. Halley Contraction (Rational): The specific rational Halley formula is not explicitly detailed in the sources, but it utilizes directional first- and second-order derivatives f' and f'' along the ray trajectory. It is bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints. Lipschitz Safety Constraints: The step size is bounded by dynamic Lipschitz constraints derived from the gradient of the SDF. The exact Lipschitz constant calculation is not provided, but it ensures the step does not overshoot the surface. Parameters: Fixed-point invariance threshold: 10^{-15}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grazing Angles: Standard sphere tracing suffers from severe iteration inflation (40–60+ steps per ray) and tail-latency spikes near surface horizons because the spatial advance is conservatively bounded by radial distance \phi(r(t)), which approaches zero even when the ray intersects geometry far along its directional path. Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching mitigates this by selectively activating second-order Halley contraction. Precision: The fixed-point invariance threshold of 10^{-15} ensures high precision in the final projection. Derivative Evaluation: Accurate evaluation of directional first- and second-order derivatives is critical for the Halley contraction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def idempotenteikonalraymarching(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, threshold=1e-15): """ Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching implementation. Args: rayorigin: Initial ray origin point. raydirection: Normalized ray direction vector. sdf: Function returning (f, fprime, fdoubleprime) at a point. threshold: Fixed-point invariance threshold (default 1e-15). Returns: Intersection distance t, or None if no intersection found. """ MAXSTEPS = 1000 # Standard iteration guard to prevent infinite loops t = 0.0 tprev = 0.0 for in range(MAXSTEPS): currentpos = rayorigin + t raydirection f, fprime, fdoubleprime = sdf(currentpos) # Early exit if surface reached or precision threshold met if f <= threshold: return t # Early exit if ray is moving away from surface or tangent if fprime <= 0: return None # Determine contraction mode based on curvature/grazing heuristic # Sources state Halley is activated only within grazing silhouette horizons. isgrazing = abs(fdoubleprime) > abs(fprime) / max(f, 1e-6) if isgrazing: # Rational Halley contraction formula # Bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints to prevent overshoot halleystep = - (2 f fprime) / (2 fprime2 - f fdoubleprime) deltat = min(f, abs(halleystep)) else: # Single-query Lipschitz advance # Bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints deltat = min(f, f / abs(fprime)) # Apply contraction operator Phit tprev = t t = t + deltat # Check fixed-point invariance condition ||Phit^2 - Phit|| <= threshold if abs(t - tprev) <= threshold: return t return None A sibling method that uses local Lipschitz bounds for step sizing. It is chosen when local smoothness can be guaranteed, whereas Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching is preferred for handling grazing angles and silhouette edges with curvature acceleration. The parent method that uses the gradient of the SDF to compute larger, safer step sizes. Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching extends this by adding second-order Halley contraction for grazing angles. Time Complexity: Reduces traversal from 55 to 14 steps on silhouette rays, truncating the grazing stall tail by up to 4×. Reduces full-frame mean iterations from 14.6 to 11.6 steps, a 20% reduction. Memory Complexity: Zero dynamic heap allocation during traversal. Measured Performance: Achieves throughput of 27.0–33.3 MRays/s on multi-threaded CPUs across CSG manifolds and authentic 3D biological cortical meshes. Strengths: Truncates the grazing stall tail by up to 4× on silhouette rays; provides deterministic frame pacing for latency-critical applications; zero dynamic heap allocation. Limitations: Classical sphere tracing retains higher raw throughput on simple analytical primitives due to single-query simplicity. When to Use: When dealing with implicit surfaces, neural SDFs, and level sets on resource-constrained mobile and XR platforms, especially near grazing angles and silhouette edges. When Not to Use: When rendering simple analytical primitives where classical sphere tracing's single-query simplicity offers higher raw throughput. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching: Curvature-Bounded Contraction and Fixed-Point Projection for Real-Time Implicit Surface Rendering". History and Development: The method addresses the computational stall of sphere tracing near grazing angles and silhouette edges, which is a fundamental hindrance for implicit surfaces, neural SDFs, and level sets on resource-constrained mobile and XR platforms. Usage: Implemented in C++20 with AVX2 acceleration, thread-safe re-entrant context encapsulation, and zero dynamic heap allocation during traversal.
