name: Segment Tracing with Local Lipschitz Bounds
head: Local Lipschitz Segment Tracing, Segment Tracing Using Local Lipschitz Bounds
body:
Segment Tracing is a ray marching algorithm for implicit surfaces that computes a local Lipschitz bound \lambda(e) for each ray segment e to determine safe, adaptive step sizes, significantly reducing field function queries compared to global bound methods. Unlike Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints which uses gradient magnitude to estimate step size, Segment Tracing rigorously bounds the gradient of the deformed field and the Jacobian of the deformation map to guarantee no surface intersections are skipped, even under complex non-linear warping. Inputs: A ray defined by origin o and direction d; a scalar field defined by a Blob Tree (sum of primitives, potentially with deformation operators); scene bounding box. Outputs: Intersection distance t, accumulated opacity \alpha, and accumulated color C. Blob Tree Node Hierarchy The scalar field is represented as a tree. Two primary node types are defined in the reference implementation: 1. BlobTreePoint (Primitive) Vector c: Center of the primitive. double r: Radius of the primitive. double e: Energy (intensity magnitude). Box box: Axis-aligned bounding box enclosing the primitive. double k: Precomputed global Lipschitz constant for this primitive. 2. BlobTreeBlend (Composite) BlobTreeNode e[2]: Pointers to left and right child nodes. Box box: Bounding box of the union of children. double k: Global Lipschitz constant (sum of children's k). Box Vector a: Minimum corner. Vector b: Maximum corner. Segment Defined by endpoints a and b (vectors). Used to compute local bounds. 1. Deformed Field Gradient For a warping function \omega: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R}^3 deforming space, the field function is fW = fN \circ \omega^{-1}. The gradient is: 
abla fW = 
abla(fN \circ \omega^{-1}) = 
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} where \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} is the Jacobian matrix of the inverse deformation. 2. Lipschitz Bound Estimation The local Lipschitz bound \lambda(e) for a segment e is estimated by bounding the gradient norm and the Jacobian norm: \|
abla(fN \circ \omega^{-1})\| \leq \|
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1}\| \cdot \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}\| Two bounds must be computed for segment e: the bound of the gradient norm \|
abla(fN \circ \omega^{-1})(e)\| and the bound of the Jacobian norm \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}(e)\|. 3. Gradient Bound via Bounding Sphere To bound the gradient over the deformed segment \omega^{-1}(e), a bounding sphere S is computed such that S \supset \omega^{-1}(e). Let \lambda be the global Lipschitz bound of \omega^{-1} and c be the segment center. The inclusion property is: \omega^{-1}(e) \subset \mathbf{S}(\omega^{-1}(c), \lambda \|e\|/2) The upper bound is then: \sup \|
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1}(e)\| \leq \sup \|
abla fN(S)\| This allows bounding the gradient by recursively querying the sub-tree for the sphere S, which is simpler than evaluating the curve \omega^{-1}(e) directly. 4. Jacobian Norm The Euclidean norm of the Jacobian is the square root of the spectral radius of \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}^: \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}\| = \sqrt{ho(\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}^)} In the general case where spectral norm computation is difficult, the Frobenius norm is used as a fallback: \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}\| \leq \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}\|F = \sqrt{\sum{i,j} (\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}){ij}^2} This is less accurate but easier to compute. 5. Intersection Rejection Criterion For a segment e=[a,b] with center c, the segment does not intersect the surface if:  rac{|f(c)|}{\lambda(e)} > \|e\| This allows early rejection in binary search bisection. 6. Optimized Bisection Instead of equal halves, the interval e=[a,b] is shrunk to [ea, eb] where: ea = a +  rac{|f(a)|}{\lambda(e)}, \quad eb = b -  rac{|f(b)|}{\lambda(e)} This discards parts of the interval guaranteed to be free of intersections. \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability, defined as 10^{-3}. e{overstep}: Overstep factor, range [1.0, 2.0]. Implementation uses 1.0. c{accel}: Acceleration factor for step size increase. Implementation uses 1.5. \lambda: Global Lipschitz bound of \omega^{-1}, used for bounding sphere radius. Intersect with scene bounding box tmin, tmax = boxmin.Intersect(rayo, rayd) if tmin is None: return False, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 t = tmin alpha = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] stepcount = 0 ts = tmax - tmin # initial max step size (full bbox depth) te = 0.0 # previous step size overstepe = 1.0 # e parameter ce = overstepe - 1.0 # = 0.0 per implementation accelc = 1.5 # c parameter epsilon = 1e-3 while t < tmax and alpha < 1.0: stepcount += 1 p = rayo + t rayd intensity = blobtree.Intensity(p) if intensity > 0.0: return True, t, alpha, color segstart = rayo + t rayd segend = rayo + (t + ts) rayd segment = Segment(segstart, segend) K = blobtree.K(segment) if K == 0.0: tk = ts else: tk = abs(intensity) / K tk = min(tk, ts) ts = tk if tk < ce te: t = t - ce te te = 0.0 continue te = max(tk overstepe, epsilon) t = t + te ts = tk accelc # Volume accumulation sigma = max(0.0, intensity - 0.5) # offset from intensity alphaseg = 1.0 - exp(-sigma te) color += alphaseg (1.0 - alpha) [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] alpha += alphaseg (1.0 - alpha) return False, t, alpha, color def Norm(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def SquaredNorm(v): return v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2 def Dot(u, v): return u[0]v[0] + u[1]v[1] + u[2]v[2] def Normalize(v): n = Norm(v) if n == 0.0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [x/n for x in v] class Segment: def init(self, start, end): self.start = start self.end = end def GetBox(self): return Box(Min(self.start, self.end), Max(self.start, self.end)) def Intersect(self, box): b = box.GetBox() for i in range(3): if self.start[i] > b.b[i] or self.end[i] < b.a[i]: return False return True class Box: def init(self, a, b): self.a = a self.b = b def GetBox(self): return self def Intersect(self, rayo, rayd): tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(rayd[i]) < 1e-6: if rayo[i] < self.a[i] or rayo[i] > self.b[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (self.a[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] t2 = (self.b[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax def Min(a, b): return [min(a[i], b[i]) for i in range(3)] def Max(a, b): return [max(a[i], b[i]) for i in range(3)] def BlobTreePointK(segment, c, r, e): a = segment.start b = segment.end if not segment.Intersect(Box([c[i]-r for i in range(3)], [c[i]+r for i in range(3)])): return 0.0 axis = Normalize(b - a) l = Dot(c - a, axis) kk = 0.0 if l < 0.0: kk = CubicFalloffK(SquaredNorm(c - a), SquaredNorm(c - b), r, e) elif Norm(b - a) < l: kk = CubicFalloffK(SquaredNorm(c - b), SquaredNorm(c - a), r, e) else: dd = SquaredNorm(c - a) - (l l) kk = CubicFalloffK(dd, max(SquaredNorm(c - b), SquaredNorm(c - a)), r, e) gradfactor = max(abs(Dot(axis, Normalize(c - a))), abs(Dot(axis, Normalize(c - b)))) return kk gradfactor def CubicFalloffK(asq, bsq, R, s): Rsq = R R if asq > Rsq: return 0.0 if bsq < (Rsq / 5.0): t = 1.0 - bsq / Rsq return abs(s) 6.0 (bsq0.5 / Rsq) (t t) elif asq > (Rsq / 5.0): t = 1.0 - asq / Rsq return abs(s) 6.0 (asq0.5 / Rsq) (t t) else: return 1.72 abs(s) / R 1. Spectral Norm Computation: Computing the exact spectral norm of the Jacobian is difficult. Use the Frobenius norm as a fallback. 2. Uniform Distribution: For objects with uniform primitive distribution and uniform Lipschitz bounds (e.g., Chess king, Amphora, Mechanic), the overhead of computing \lambda(e) makes Segment Tracing slower than Sphere Tracing. Use Ray or Sphere variations instead. 3. Degenerate BVH Partition: If std::partition places all elements on one side during BVH construction, adjust midIndex to (begin + end) / 2 to ensure recursion progresses. 4. Ray Parallel to Slab: In Box::Intersect, if a ray direction component d[i] is near zero (|d[i]| < \epsilon), the ray is parallel to the slab. If the origin is outside the slab, return no intersection. 5. Segment-BVH Culling: BlobTreeBlend::K checks if the segment's bounding box intersects the node's box. If not, return 0. Time: The algorithm reduces field function queries by one to two orders of magnitude for complex models compared to global Sphere Tracing. However, the computation of \lambda(e) adds overhead per step. Memory: Preserves the compact format of hierarchical implicit surface models (Blob Trees). Does not require additional memory structures like voxel grids. CPU: On Intel Core i7 3GHz, Segment Tracing reduced queries significantly for Chandelier and Temple models. GPU: On nVidia GeForce 2070, Segment Tracing achieved 67 Hz vs 6 Hz for standard Sphere Tracing, an acceleration factor close to an order of magnitude. Strengths: Significantly fewer field function queries for complex, non-linear deformations. Safe stepping guaranteed by local bounds. Limitations: Overhead of computing \lambda(e) can negate benefits for simple or uniformly distributed primitives. Computation of Jacobian norms can be costly if spectral norm is required. Use for complex implicit surfaces with non-linear deformations (warping) where global bounds are too conservative. Avoid for simple, uniformly distributed primitives where Ray or Sphere variations are faster. Segment Tracing was introduced by Eric Galin, Eric Guérin, Axel Paris, and Adrien Peytavie in 2020 in the paper "Segment Tracing Using Local Lipschitz Bounds" published in Computer Graphics Forum. The method builds upon Sphere Tracing and Lipschitz-constrained ray marching. It specifically addresses the inefficiency of global Lipschitz bounds in the presence of local variations in field complexity and deformation. The technique is particularly effective for blob trees with deformation operators (e.g., tapering). Rendering complex implicit surfaces defined by blob trees. Volume rendering using scalar fields defined by cubic falloff primitives. Global illumination secondary ray intersections where field function query cost is critical. name: Lipschitz Step Size Ray Marching
head: Hart's Sphere Tracing, Ray Marching with Lipschitz Step Size, Ray marching with Lipschitz bound, SDF ray marching with Lipschitz constant, Safe Raymarching with Lipschitz Bounds, Step-size ray marching
body: Lipschitz Step Size Ray Marching is a robust algorithm for finding the first intersection between a ray and an implicit surface defined by a signed distance field (SDF) f(\mathbf{p}) = 0. It guarantees that the ray never penetrates or overshoots the surface by computing the maximum safe step size using a global Lipschitz constant \lambda. Unlike adaptive methods that estimate local gradients, this method relies on a pre-computed global bound, making it simple to implement and numerically stable, though potentially less efficient for complex scenes with varying feature scales. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{u}. Ray domain bounds [t{min}, t{max}] (intersection with the scene bounding volume \Omega). Global Lipschitz constant \lambda for the field function f over \Omega. Hit threshold \mu (distance tolerance). Maximum iteration count N{max}. Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray, or a failure indicator if no intersection is found within bounds or iterations. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction \mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^3 with \|\mathbf{u}\| = 1. Field Function: f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, representing the signed distance to the implicit surface. Parameters: \lambda: Scalar, the global Lipschitz bound. Typical value: 1.0 for normalized SDFs. \mu: Scalar, the convergence threshold. Typical value: 0.01. N{max}: Integer, maximum steps. Typical value: 100. A function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} is Lipschitz continuous over a domain \Omega if there exists a constant \lambda \ge 0 such that for all \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q} \in \Omega: |f(\mathbf{p}) - f(\mathbf{q})| \leq \lambda \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\| The constant \lambda is the minimum bound satisfying this inequality. 1. Initialization: Compute the intersection of the ray with the domain \Omega to determine [t{min}, t{max}]. Set current distance t = t{min}. 2. Iteration Loop: While t < t{max} and iteration count < N{max}: 1. Evaluate the field function at the current point on the ray: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{u}, then d = f(\mathbf{p}). 2. Termination Check: If |d| < \mu, the ray has converged to the surface. Return t as the intersection distance. 3. Step Calculation: Compute the step size s using the Lipschitz bound: s = \frac{|d|}{\lambda} This step size guarantees that the next point is not closer to the surface than the current distance allows, preventing overshoot. 4. Advance: Update t \leftarrow t + s. 3. Failure: If the loop terminates without satisfying the hit condition, return failure (no intersection found within bounds or iterations). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lipschitzraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, fieldfunc, lambdaval, mu, maxiterations): """ Ray march using Lipschitz step size. Args: rayorigin: Vector3, origin of the ray. raydirection: Vector3, normalized direction of the ray. tmin: float, minimum distance along ray (start of domain). tmax: float, maximum distance along ray (end of domain). fieldfunc: function, f(p) -> float, returns signed distance. lambdaval: float, global Lipschitz constant. mu: float, hit threshold. maxiterations: int, maximum number of steps. Returns: float: Intersection distance t, or None if not found. """ t = tmin for i in range(maxiterations): # Check domain bounds before evaluation if t > tmax: return None # 1. Evaluate field at current position p = rayorigin + raydirection t d = fieldfunc(p) # 2. Check for intersection if abs(d) < mu: return t # 3. Compute step size step = abs(d) / lambdaval # 4. Advance along ray t = t + step return None Grazing Rays: The algorithm may require an arbitrarily large number of steps for rays that graze the surface, as the step size s becomes very small relative to the remaining distance. Large Radius Differences: When applied to primitives with significantly different radii (e.g., SCALIS primitives), the Lipschitz constant per primitive is inversely proportional to the prescribed radius, creating unnecessarily small steps globally. Density Fields: When used with density fields instead of distance fields, the algorithm suffers from null gradients near kernel support boundaries and difficulty in computing tight Lipschitz bounds for N-ary summation operators. Overestimation of \lambda: If \lambda is significantly larger than the true local Lipschitz constant, the step size s becomes smaller than necessary, increasing the number of iterations without improving accuracy. Discusses the balance between step size precision and computational cost. Extends this method by computing local Lipschitz bounds to improve efficiency. Uses gradient information to refine step sizes while maintaining safety guarantees. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of iterations required to converge. N depends on the scene complexity, ray angle, and the tightness of \lambda. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the storage for the field function. Strengths: Guaranteed no penetration of the surface. Simple implementation, no pre-processing required. Robust for direct content creation in shaders. Limitations: Inefficient for grazing rays. For SCALIS primitives with large radius differences, the Lipschitz constant per primitive is inversely proportional to the prescribed radius, creating unnecessarily small steps globally. Not suitable for density fields with complex kernel compositions without modification. When to Use: Ideal for simple SDFs and real-time shaders where simplicity and robustness are prioritized over maximum performance. When Not to Use: Scenes with large variations in feature scale, grazing ray scenarios, or density fields with complex kernel functions. The algorithm was introduced by Hart in 1996, often referred to as "Hart's Sphere Tracing", and formalized with the Lipschitz bound guarantee. It belongs to the ray-marching family and is widely used in real-time rendering, including games and shaders, due to its simplicity and robustness. Extensions such as Segment Tracing have been proposed to address its limitations by using local Lipschitz bounds. name: Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching
head: DDVR, DDVR Raymarching Shader, Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Size and Temporal Accumulation, Adaptive Step Size Volume Rendering
body: Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching is a GPU-based direct volume rendering technique that reduces computational cost by varying the ray marching step size based on local density and distance, combined with temporal accumulation to manage noise. Unlike linear sampling which uses a fixed interval, this method uses fine steps inside cloud density and coarse steps outside, optimizing the trade-off between performance and rendering quality. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Safe Raymarching Step Size by explicitly using a noise buffer to drive step size variation and temporal reprojection, and from Gap-Limited Ray Marching by its continuous adaptive scaling rather than discrete gap skipping. Inputs: Camera state: View matrix, projection matrix, eye position, and a flag indicating if the camera moved since the last frame. Volume data: 3D texture (volumeTexture) for static volumes, or two 3D textures (volumeTexture, volumeTexture4DNextFrame) for 4D time-varying volumes. Configuration: Bounding box (bbmin, bbmax), scalar range (scalarMinMax), base stepSize, and flags for accumulation, motionVectorCalc, and bVolume4D. Noise buffer: A 2D image (noiseImage) storing per-pixel noise offset and step size hints. Outputs: outputImage: Final rendered RGBA color. positionDepthBufferImage: World position and depth of the first hit. motionVectorImage: UV-space motion vectors for reprojection (if enabled). The method relies on the following GPU buffers and uniforms: 1. name: Dynamic Sampling Step Adjustment
head: Adaptive Step Doubling, Empty Space Step Doubling
body: Dynamic Sampling Step Adjustment accelerates ray marching through empty or low-density regions by exponentially increasing the step size, thereby reducing the number of samples required to traverse sparse volumes. It differs from Safe Raymarching Step Size and Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching by using a discrete doubling strategy rather than continuous estimation or gradient-based refinement, and from Gap-Limited Ray Marching by not explicitly calculating geometric gaps. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, initial step size s0, initial mip level offset m0, and a volume texture V with mipmaps. Outputs: Composed color and opacity for the ray. Data Structures: V: Multi-resolution volume texture. Access at mip level m requires scaling coordinates by 2^{-m}. s: Current step size. m: Current mip level offset. N{empty}: Counter for consecutive empty samples. Algorithm: 1. Initialize s = s0, m = m0, and N{empty} = 0. 2. March along the ray: a. Sample the volume at current position p using mip level m. Let density be \rho = V(p, m). b. If \rho < \epsilon (empty threshold): i. Increment N{empty}. ii. If N{empty} \ge 2 (consecutive empty samples), double the step size: s \leftarrow 2s. iii. Increase mip offset: m \leftarrow m + 1. c. If \rho \ge \epsilon (non-empty): i. Step back one step: p \leftarrow p - s{prev} (where s{prev} is the step size used in the previous iteration). ii. Restore step size: s \leftarrow s0. iii. Restore mip offset: m \leftarrow m0. iv. Reset N{empty} = 0. d. Advance position: p \leftarrow p + s. 3. Composite color using front-to-back blending with the sampled densities. Parameters: \epsilon: Empty density threshold. Not given in the sources. s0: Initial step size. Not given in the sources. m0: Initial mip level. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The optimization provides small performance gains and may cause artifacts in some cases. Stepping back one step upon encountering density requires storing the previous position and step size. Doubling the step size may skip thin features if the threshold \epsilon is too high or the initial step s0 is too large. A sampling strategy that refines step sizes according to the magnitude of the scalar field gradient |\nabla s|, which indicates local feature sharpness; smaller steps are taken near high-gradient regions resembling surfaces to capture transitions accurately. The step size is dynamically adjusted based on the gradient direction and a threshold, bounded by minimum and maximum distances to prevent under- or over-sampling. This method enhances detail preservation in boundary-heavy volumes, such as CT angiography data, while coarsening traversal in smooth interiors, achieving efficiency gains of 2-3x over uniform sampling without aliasing artifacts. Time Complexity: Reduces sample count in empty regions by a factor of 2 per doubling event. Overall speedup is modest. Memory Complexity: Requires storing previous step size and position. No additional memory for the volume itself. Performance: Provides small performance gains. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for sparse volumes. Limitations: May cause artifacts; small performance gains. When to use: Sparse volumes with large empty regions. When not to use: Dense volumes or when artifacts are unacceptable. This technique is used in real-time volume rendering, such as in cloud rendering pipelines. It is often combined with other optimizations like blue noise dithering and temporal upsampling to mitigate sampling artifacts. 体积云效果的实现，游戏世界的云合雾集, https://leihuo.163.com/institution/news/20230719/384231099592.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Volume ray casting — Grokipedia, https://grokipedia.com/page/Volumeraycasting, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Dynamic Texture Slice Resampling
head: Dynamic resampling
body: Dynamic Texture Slice Resampling is a step size optimization technique for distance-field ray marching that maintains a constant physical sampling step size along the ray by dynamically adjusting the texture coordinate increments based on the viewing direction. It solves the problem of striping artifacts caused by non-uniform sampling steps in hardware-accelerated volume rendering, particularly when using multitexturing or register combiners, while preserving high rendering performance. It sets itself apart from static step sizing by adapting to the ray's angle relative to the texture grid, ensuring consistent spatial resolution regardless of view orientation. Inputs and outputs: Input: Volume texture data, camera view matrix, ray origin, ray direction, target constant physical step size s{phys}. Output: Resampled texture coordinates or interpolated values for the current ray step. Data structures: Volume texture: 3D grid of scalar values. Ray state: Current position P, direction D. Method: 1. Calculate the intersection of the ray with the current voxel or texture boundary. 2. Determine the local scaling factors required to map the desired physical step size s{phys} to texture coordinate space. This involves the Jacobian of the transformation from world space to texture space, which depends on the viewing direction D and the texture grid dimensions. 3. Compute the dynamic texture step size \Delta u, \Delta v, \Delta w such that the Euclidean distance between consecutive samples equals s{phys}. 4. Advance the ray by s{phys} in world space. 5. Update texture coordinates using the dynamic steps. 6. Sample the volume texture at the new coordinates. 7. Accumulate the color and opacity (DVR) and repeat until termination. Formulas: Let s{phys} be the constant physical step size. Let D = (dx, dy, dz) be the ray direction in world space. Let Tx, Ty, Tz be the physical dimensions of the volume in world units. Let Nx, Ny, Nz be the number of texels in each dimension. The physical step size per texel in each dimension is \deltax = Tx / Nx, \deltay = Ty / Ny, \deltaz = Tz / Nz. The dynamic texture step size \Delta u (in normalized texture coordinates) for a ray step s{phys} is derived from the ray direction components. If the ray moves primarily along the x-axis, the texture step is larger than if it moves diagonally. The exact update depends on the specific hardware implementation (e.g., register combiners), but generally, the texture coordinate increment is scaled by the inverse of the ray direction's projection onto the texture axes to maintain constant physical spacing. For a ray direction D, the texture coordinate increment \Delta u is proportional to s{phys} / (|Dx| \cdot \deltax) (conceptually, ensuring the physical distance matches). In practice, this is often implemented by precomputing direction-dependent scaling factors or using hardware multitexturing units to interpolate texture coordinates at a rate that corresponds to s{phys}. Parameters: s{phys}: Constant physical step size. Typical value depends on volume resolution and view distance; often chosen to balance performance and aliasing. Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Degenerate rays: Rays parallel to texture axes may require special handling to avoid division by zero in direction-based scaling. Precision: Floating-point precision in texture coordinate updates can lead to drift over long rays. Boundaries: Ray termination at volume boundaries must be handled to prevent out-of-bounds texture access. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamictexturesliceresampling(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, sphys): # Initialize ray state t = 0.0 currentpos = rayorigin # Precompute texture grid dimensions and physical sizes Nx, Ny, Nz = volumetexture.dimensions Tx, Ty, Tz = volumetexture.physicaldimensions # Precompute physical step per texel deltax = Tx / Nx deltay = Ty / Ny deltaz = Tz / Nz # Precompute inverse direction components for dynamic step calculation # Avoid division by zero by clamping or handling parallel rays invdx = 1.0 / raydirection.x if abs(raydirection.x) > 1e-6 else float('inf') invdy = 1.0 / raydirection.y if abs(raydirection.y) > 1e-6 else float('inf') invdz = 1.0 / raydirection.z if abs(raydirection.z) > 1e-6 else float('inf') # Initial texture coordinates u, v, w = worldtotexture(currentpos, volumetexture) while t < raylength: # Calculate dynamic texture step size to maintain sphys # This is a simplified model; actual hardware implementation may vary # The goal is to ensure the physical distance between samples is sphys # Estimate texture step based on dominant direction # If ray is mostly along X, texture step is determined by dx if abs(raydirection.x) >= abs(raydirection.y) and abs(raydirection.x) >= abs(raydirection.z): texturestep = sphys invdx / deltax u += texturestep # v and w may also need adjustment if ray has components in those directions # For simplicity, assume primary axis update elif abs(raydirection.y) >= abs(raydirection.x) and abs(raydirection.y) >= abs(raydirection.z): texturestep = sphys invdy / deltay v += texturestep else: texturestep = sphys invdz / deltaz w += texturestep # Sample volume texture color, opacity = samplevolume(u, v, w, volumetexture) # Accumulate (DVR) #... # Advance ray in world space t += sphys currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Update texture coordinates for next step # In a full implementation, all u, v, w are updated based on ray direction u = worldtotexture(currentpos, volumetexture).u v = worldtotexture(currentpos, volumetexture).v w = worldtotexture(currentpos, volumetexture).w # Termination check if opacity >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor Time complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples along the ray. The dynamic step calculation adds a constant overhead per step. Memory complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray, plus the volume texture storage. Measured performance: Provides interactive frame rates for medium-sized datasets on commodity GPU hardware by leveraging multitexturing and register combiners. Strengths: Eliminates striping artifacts caused by non-uniform sampling; maintains high rendering performance; suitable for hardware acceleration. Limitations: Requires careful handling of ray directions; may introduce complexity in texture coordinate management. When to use: When visual quality (absence of striping) is critical and hardware supports dynamic texture coordinate updates. When not to use: When hardware does not support efficient dynamic texture coordinate updates or when performance is the sole priority and artifacts are acceptable. Dynamic Texture Slice Resampling was proposed by Zhang and colleagues as part of a hardware-accelerated volume rendering algorithm based on register combiners and multitexturing. It extends earlier concepts of dynamic sampling by integrating them with hierarchical wavelet representation for data compression. The method leverages the parallel architecture and stream computation capabilities of GPUs to achieve interactive frame rates for volume visualization. name: Compute Minimal Sample Distance Per Pixel
body: This method computes the minimal sample distance for each pixel by projecting the dataset's cell axes onto the viewport, accounting for camera and volume transformations. It serves as a geometric heuristic to determine the smallest viable step size for ray marching, ensuring that the sampling density respects the underlying voxel resolution. Unlike adaptive methods that adjust step size based on local density values during rendering, this approach calculates a static, geometry-driven minimum bound per pixel based on the current view. Inputs: renderer: A pointer to the rendering context, providing camera position, orientation, and viewport dimensions. volume: A pointer to the volume object, providing dataset geometry (extent, spacing) and transformation matrices. Outputs: A scalar value representing the minimal sample distance for the current pixel/camera configuration. Data Structures: The method relies on the internal state of the vtkRenderer and vtkVolume objects. Specifically, it accesses: Camera transformation matrix (model-view-projection). Volume transformation matrix. Dataset extent and spacing (voxel dimensions). Steps: 1. Retrieve the camera and viewport state from the renderer. 2. Retrieve the dataset geometry and transformation from the volume. 3. Project each axis of the dataset cell (voxel) onto the viewport plane. 4. Calculate the projected length of these axes in screen space. 5. Determine the minimal sample distance based on the smallest projected axis dimension. 6. Degeneracy Check: If any dataset axis is degenerate (i.e., aligned with the view direction, resulting in zero projected length), set the flag IgnoreSampleDistancePerPixel to true. This indicates that the geometric projection method cannot reliably determine a step size for this configuration. Parameters: IgnoreSampleDistancePerPixel: A boolean flag. When true, the renderer should fall back to a default or fixed step size, ignoring the computed minimal distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeminimalsampledistance(renderer, volume): # Get camera and viewport state camera = renderer.getcamera() viewport = renderer.getviewport() # Get volume geometry and transformation volumetransform = volume.gettransformationmatrix() datasetextent = volume.getextent() datasetspacing = volume.getspacing() # Project cell axes onto viewport # Axes are typically defined by the dataset spacing and orientation axes = [ datasetspacing[0] volumetransform.getcolumn(0), datasetspacing[1] volumetransform.getcolumn(1), datasetspacing[2] volumetransform.getcolumn(2) ] projectedlengths = [] for axis in axes: # Project axis vector onto the view plane # This involves transforming the axis by the view-projection matrix # and measuring its length in screen space projectedaxis = projecttoviewport(axis, camera, viewport) projectedlengths.append(length(projectedaxis)) # Find the minimal projected length if not projectedlengths: return 0.0 mindistance = min(projectedlengths) # Check for degeneracy (axis aligned with view direction) # If any projected length is effectively zero, the axis is parallel to view isdegenerate = any(length(axis) < epsilon for axis in axes) or \ any(projlen < epsilon for projlen in projectedlengths) if isdegenerate: # Set flag to ignore this calculation renderer.setignoresampledistanceperpixel(True) # Return a default or fallback value, or 0 to indicate invalidity return 0.0 return mindistance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Axes: If a dataset axis is aligned with the view direction, its projection onto the viewport is zero or near-zero. The method explicitly handles this by setting IgnoreSampleDistancePerPixel to true. Failure to handle this may result in division by zero or invalid step sizes. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when calculating projections for very small or very large datasets. Use a small epsilon threshold for degeneracy checks. This variant computes a scalar metric representing the projected size of a voxel relative to the camera, primarily used for Level of Detail (LOD) decisions and step size adaptation. It differs from the primary method by using a dot-product-based metric rather than direct axis projection lengths. Definition: Computes a scalar S representing the projected size of a voxel. Steps: 1. Compute vectors from the camera position to the lower-left (LL) and upper-right (UR) corners of the voxel's half-size box. 2. Normalize these vectors to obtain \mathbf{u}{LL} and \mathbf{u}{UR}. 3. Calculate the metric S = 1 - \mathbf{u}{LL} \cdot \mathbf{u}{UR}. Formula: S = 1 - \mathbf{u}{LL} \cdot \mathbf{u}{UR} where \mathbf{u}{LL} and \mathbf{u}{UR} are normalized vectors from the camera to the voxel corners. Pitfalls: The metric returns 0 when the camera is at the voxel center (dot product equals 1). It increases as the viewing angle widens. Lacks explicit clamping or fallback for degenerate near-plane cases, as noted in the source implementation. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per pixel, as it involves a fixed number of matrix-vector multiplications and projections. Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory, relying on existing renderer and volume data structures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of pixels, as the calculation is performed per pixel. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a geometrically accurate lower bound for step size based on voxel resolution. Simple to implement given access to camera and volume transforms. Limitations: Does not account for local density variations or opacity transfer functions. Fails for degenerate views (axes aligned with view direction). When to Use: Use when a static, geometry-based minimum step size is required for ray marching. Use when LOD or voxel visibility is determined by screen-space projection. When Not to Use: Do not use when adaptive sampling based on density is required. Do not use if the view direction may align with dataset axes without handling degeneracy. This method originates from the VTK (Visualization Toolkit) ecosystem, specifically within the vtkMultiVolumeRayCastMapper implementation. It is part of the volume rendering pipeline's step size optimization logic, ensuring that ray marching respects the underlying data resolution. name: Gap-Limited Ray Marching
head: Distance-Proportional Step with Gap Bound, Terrain Ray Marching with Gap Limiting
body: Gap-Limited Ray Marching is a step-size optimization for distance-field ray marching on heightfield terrain that prevents the ray from overshooting surface features like ridgelines. Unlike standard distance-field marching which relies on a global Lipschitz constant, this method uses a step size proportional to the distance traveled, bounded by half the vertical gap to the surface. This ensures the ray never steps through the surface, eliminating holes in terrain rendering while maintaining efficiency on flat areas. Inputs: Ray origin (ox, oy, oz) and direction (dx, dy, dz), where d is normalized. Heightfield function H(x, z) returning surface height at horizontal coordinates. Parameters: stepScale (dimensionless multiplier), minStep (minimum step size), maxSteps (iteration limit), tMax (maximum ray distance), refineSteps (bisection iterations). Outputs: Intersection distance t{hit} or -1 if no intersection is found within tMax. Data Structures: No complex structures required. Standard floating-point variables for ray parameters and height values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0. 2. Initialize prevT = 0. 3. Loop for i from 0 to maxSteps - 1: a. Calculate distance-proportional step: d{step} = t \times \text{stepScale}. b. Calculate current horizontal position: x = ox + dx \times t, z = oz + dz \times t. c. Calculate current ray height: y{ray} = oy + dy \times t. d. Sample heightfield: h{surf} = H(x, z). e. Calculate vertical gap: h = y{ray} - h{surf}. f. Calculate gap-limited step: g{step} = h \times 0.5. g. Determine step size: step = \min(d{step}, g{step}). h. Enforce minimum step: if step < \text{minStep}, set step = \text{minStep}. i. Update previous distance: prevT = t. j. Advance ray: t = t + step. k. Check termination: if t \ge \text{tMax}, return -1. l. Check surface crossing: if h \le 0 (ray is at or below surface): i. Perform binary search between prevT and t for refineSteps iterations: 1. mid = (\text{prevT} + t) \times 0.5. 2. Calculate ray height at mid: y{mid} = oy + dy \times mid. 3. Calculate horizontal position at mid: x{mid} = ox + dx \times mid, z{mid} = oz + dz \times mid. 4. Sample heightfield: h{mid} = H(x{mid}, z{mid}). 5. If y{mid} - h{mid} \le 0, set t = mid (surface crossed before mid). 6. Else, set prevT = mid (surface crossed after mid). ii. Return t as the intersection distance. 4. If loop completes without intersection, return -1. Pitfalls: Without the gap limiting term (h \times 0.5), the ray can step through the surface on steep ridgelines, causing holes in the rendered terrain. The stepScale parameter must be chosen carefully; if too large, the distance-proportional step may exceed the gap limit unnecessarily, though the gap limit acts as a hard cap. If too small, performance degrades on flat terrain. Precision issues on flat surfaces or at very small distances can cause infinite loops if minStep is not enforced. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps per ray, typically bounded by maxSteps. The binary search adds O(\log(\text{precision})) overhead per intersection. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Prevents overshooting on non-distance-field terrain (heightfields) where Lipschitz constants are not uniform or known. Efficient on flat terrain due to distance-proportional stepping. Limitations: Requires heightfield sampling at every step. Performance depends on terrain roughness; very rough terrain may require many small steps. When to use: Rendering heightfield-based terrain where surface continuity is critical and standard distance-field marching fails due to lack of a global Lipschitz bound. When not to use: When a true distance field is available and efficiently computable, as standard distance-field marching is generally more robust and simpler. This method is derived from techniques used in software-based terrain rendering, specifically in the theme1 project by mingderwang, which implements a no-GPU renderer for procedural terrain. It addresses the specific challenge of ray marching over heightfields without relying on a global distance bound, which is often unavailable or loose for complex terrain. mingderwang/theme1, https://github.com/mingderwang/theme1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Lambertian Shading with Gradient Normals
head: Gradient Normal Lambertian Shading, Lambertian Lighting with SDF, Diffuse Lighting with Gradient Normals, Lambertian Shading
body:
Lambertian Shading with Gradient Normals is a surface shading technique for ray-marched signed distance fields (SDFs) or scalar volumes that approximates the surface normal using the numerical gradient of the field, then applies the Lambertian reflectance model to compute diffuse illumination. It solves the problem of shading implicit surfaces that lack explicit mesh normals, allowing for realistic diffuse lighting without polygonization artifacts. Unlike sibling methods that may use analytic normals, tetrahedral interpolation, or regularization, this method relies exclusively on finite-difference gradient estimation of the scalar field f (or \phi) at the hit point. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{r} (normalized). Signed distance field function f(\mathbf{p}) returning the distance to the nearest surface. Light direction \mathbf{l} (normalized, pointing from surface to light). Default: (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) if not provided. Surface color \mathbf{c}{surf} (RGB, range [0, 1]). Default: (0.8, 0.5, 0.3). Ambient light intensity a (range [0, 1]). Default: 0.1. Background color \mathbf{c}{bg} (RGB, range [0, 1]). Default: (0.2, 0.2, 0.2). Hit threshold \epsilon (distance tolerance). Default: 0.001. Outputs: Shaded pixel color \mathbf{c}{out} (RGB). Data Structures: Point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Current ray position. Normal \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Estimated surface normal. Gradient 
abla f \in \mathbb{R}^3: Numerical gradient of the SDF. Steps: 1. Ray Marching: March along the ray \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{r} using the SDF f(\mathbf{p}) to find the first intersection where f(\mathbf{p}) < \epsilon. If no intersection is found within the maximum steps, return \mathbf{c}{bg}. 2. Gradient Estimation: Compute the gradient 
abla f at the hit point \mathbf{p} using central finite differences. For a step size h (typically the SDF's resolution or a small constant like 10^{-4}): 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) \approx \left(  rac{f(\mathbf{p} + h\mathbf{e}x) - f(\mathbf{p} - h\mathbf{e}x)}{2h},  rac{f(\mathbf{p} + h\mathbf{e}y) - f(\mathbf{p} - h\mathbf{e}y)}{2h},  rac{f(\mathbf{p} + h\mathbf{e}z) - f(\mathbf{p} - h\mathbf{e}z)}{2h} ight) where \mathbf{e}x, \mathbf{e}y, \mathbf{e}z are unit vectors along the axes. 3. Normal Normalization: Normalize the gradient to obtain the surface normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla f}{\|
abla f\|} If \|
abla f\| < 10^{-5}, the gradient is degenerate; return \mathbf{c}{surf} (or base color) without shading. 4. View Direction: Compute the view direction \mathbf{v} as the negative ray direction: \mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{r}. 5. Normal Orientation: Ensure the normal faces the viewer. If \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} < 0, flip the normal: 	ext{if } \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} < 0, \quad \mathbf{n} = -\mathbf{n}. 6. Lambertian Diffuse Calculation: Compute the dot product between the normal and the light direction: 	ext{ndotl} = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l} Clamp to [0, 1] to handle back-facing surfaces: 	ext{ndotl} = \max(0.0, 	ext{ndotl}). 7. Lighting Intensity: Combine ambient and diffuse lighting: I = a + (1.0 - a) 	imes 	ext{ndotl} Clip I to [0.0, 1.0]. 8. Final Color: Multiply the lighting intensity by the surface color: \mathbf{c}{out} = I 	imes \mathbf{c}{surf}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lambertianshadingwithgradientnormals(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunc, lightdir=None, surfacecolor=(0.8, 0.5, 0.3), ambient=0.1, background=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2), epsilon=0.001, maxsteps=64, stepsize=0.01, gradh=1e-4): """ Renders a single ray using Lambertian shading with gradient normals. Args: rayorigin: (float, float, float) Ray origin. raydirection: (float, float, float) Normalized ray direction. sdffunc: Callable returning float distance for a (float, float, float) point. lightdir: (float, float, float) Normalized light direction. Defaults to (1,1,1). surfacecolor: (float, float, float) Surface RGB color. ambient: float Ambient light intensity. background: (float, float, float) Background RGB color. epsilon: float Hit threshold. maxsteps: int Maximum ray march steps. stepsize: float Step size for ray marching. gradh: float Step size for gradient finite differences. Returns: (float, float, float) Shaded color. """ if lightdir is None: lightdir = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Normalize light direction llen = math.sqrt(lightdir[0]2 + lightdir[1]2 + lightdir[2]2) if llen > 0: lightdir = (lightdir[0]/llen, lightdir[1]/llen, lightdir[2]/llen) else: lightdir = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Fallback # Ray Marching t = 0.0 hitpoint = None for in range(maxsteps): p = (rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0] t, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1] t, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2] t) d = sdffunc(p) if d < epsilon: hitpoint = p break t += stepsize if hitpoint is None: return background # Gradient Estimation px, py, pz = hitpoint # Central differences for x fplusx = sdffunc((px + gradh, py, pz)) fminusx = sdffunc((px - gradh, py, pz)) gradx = (fplusx - fminusx) / (2.0 gradh) # Central differences for y fplusy = sdffunc((px, py + gradh, pz)) fminusy = sdffunc((px, py - gradh, pz)) grady = (fplusy - fminusy) / (2.0 gradh) # Central differences for z fplusz = sdffunc((px, py, pz + gradh)) fminusz = sdffunc((px, py, pz - gradh)) gradz = (fplusz - fminusz) / (2.0 gradh) gradnorm = math.sqrt(gradx2 + grady2 + gradz2) # Handle degenerate gradient if gradnorm < 1e-5: return surfacecolor # Normalize gradient to get normal nx = gradx / gradnorm ny = grady / gradnorm nz = gradz / gradnorm # View direction (negative ray direction) vx = -raydirection[0] vy = -raydirection[1] vz = -raydirection[2] # Flip normal if facing away from viewer dotnv = nx vx + ny vy + nz vz if dotnv < 0.0: nx = -nx ny = -ny nz = -nz # Lambertian Diffuse ndotl = nx lightdir[0] + ny lightdir[1] + nz lightdir[2] ndotl = max(0.0, ndotl) # Lighting Intensity intensity = ambient + (1.0 - ambient) ndotl intensity = max(0.0, min(1.0, intensity)) # Final Color r = intensity surfacecolor[0] g = intensity surfacecolor[1] b = intensity surfacecolor[2] return (r, g, b) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Gradients: If the gradient magnitude is near zero (e.g., at flat regions or singularities), normalization fails. Return base color or handle gracefully. Precision: Finite differences are sensitive to the step size h. Too large h causes aliasing; too small h causes floating-point noise. Back-Facing Normals: The gradient points in the direction of increasing distance. For the outside of an object, this is outward. However, if the ray hits the inside of a hollow object, the normal may face inward. Flipping based on view direction ensures consistent shading. Grid Artifacts: In volume rendering, low-resolution grids can cause jagged normals. Tricubic interpolation can mitigate this for liquid surfaces. Visualizes surface normals by taking the absolute value of each component and clamping to [0, 1]. It is used for debugging normal estimation rather than illumination. Generates smooth bevels on SDF primitives. It modifies the SDF function itself rather than the shading, resulting in geometrically smooth normals without gradient artifacts. A broader category of normal estimation techniques. This method is a specific instance using finite differences for Lambertian shading. Applies smoothing filters to estimated normals to reduce noise. It is used when gradient estimation is too noisy for stable shading. Estimates normals by interpolating within tetrahedral cells of a volume. It provides smoother normals than finite differences but is more computationally expensive. Computes normals from explicit polygonal faces. It is not applicable to pure SDF ray marching unless the SDF is converted to a mesh. Time Complexity: O(1) per hit point, but requires 6 additional SDF evaluations for the gradient (central differences). Total cost is proportional to the number of ray march steps plus 6 SDF calls per hit. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. No additional data structures are needed beyond the SDF function. Performance: Fast and simple to implement. The main cost is the extra SDF evaluations. On GPU, this can be optimized by batching gradient calculations if multiple rays hit the same region, but typically it is done per-pixel. Strengths: Simple, robust, works with any SDF, no preprocessing required. Limitations: Gradients can be noisy near sharp features or at low resolutions. Finite differences may not capture the true normal accurately if the SDF is not smooth. When to Use: When shading implicit surfaces without explicit normals is required, and performance is a concern. Suitable for real-time ray marching. When Not to Use: When high-quality normals are critical for complex lighting (e.g., specular highlights), or when the SDF is not smooth. In such cases, consider Tetrahedral Normal Estimation or Normal Regularization. Lambertian shading with gradient normals originates from the field of volume rendering and implicit surface rendering. Max (1995) described using the gradient of a scalar field to approximate contour surface normals for direct volume rendering, enabling shading without polygonization. This approach was later adopted in ray marching for SDFs, where the gradient of the distance field provides a natural normal estimate. It is widely used in real-time graphics, particularly in demoscene and procedural geometry rendering, due to its simplicity and efficiency. Raymarching Distance Fields (2013), http://9bitscience.blogspot.com/2013/07/raymarching-distance-fields14.html, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GitHub - narnia-ai-mason/iso-surface-rendering: Robust iso-surface..., https://github.com/narnia-ai-mason/iso-surface-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) [PDF] Optical Models for Direct Volume Rendering - Duke Computer Science, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/max95opticalModelsForDirectVolumeRendering.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Raymarching Distance Fields: Concepts and Implementation..., https://adrianb.io/2016/10/01/raymarching.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Loveof1ife7/cuVRender-A-CUDA-Accelerated-Volume-Rendering-Engine, https://github.com/Loveof1ife7/cuVRender-A-CUDA-Accelerated-Volume-Rendering-Engine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Normal Shading
head: Absolute Normal Visualization, Clamped Normal Visualization
body: Normal Shading is a visualization technique that maps surface normals to a color space by taking the absolute value of each normal component and clamping the result to the range [0, 1]. It serves as a diagnostic tool to inspect the orientation and continuity of surface normals derived from signed distance fields (SDFs) in ray marching algorithms. Unlike Lambertian shading, which computes lighting intensity, Normal Shading directly visualizes the geometric derivative information without applying a lighting model. Inputs: \mathbf{n}: The surface normal vector at the hit point, typically normalized such that |\mathbf{n}| = 1. Outputs: N{vis}: A color vector (RGB) where each channel corresponds to the clamped absolute value of the respective normal component. Data Structures: The normal \mathbf{n} is a 3D vector (nx, ny, nz). The output is a 3D vector (r, g, b) representing the color channels. Steps: 1. Compute the absolute value of each component of the normal vector \mathbf{n}: |ni| = |ni| \quad \text{for } i \in \{x, y, z\} 2. Clamp each absolute component to the range [0, 1]. Since \mathbf{n} is a unit vector, |ni| \in [0, 1], so the clamp operation is technically redundant for valid normals but ensures robustness against numerical errors or non-unit inputs. ci = \max(0, \min(1, |ni|)) 3. Assign the clamped components to the color channels: N{vis} = (cx, cy, cz) Formula: N{vis} = \max(0, \min(1, |\mathbf{n}|)) where |\mathbf{n}| denotes the element-wise absolute value of the vector \mathbf{n}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalshading(surfacenormals: Tensor) -> Tensor: """ Visualizes surface normals by taking the absolute value of each component and clamping to [0, 1]. Args: surfacenormals: A tensor of shape (..., 3) containing surface normal vectors. Returns: A tensor of shape (..., 3) containing the visualized normal colors. """ # Take absolute value of each component absnormals = surfacenormals.abs() # Clamp values to [0, 1] # Note: For unit vectors, abs() is already in [0, 1], but clamp ensures # robustness against numerical noise or non-normalized inputs. clampednormals = absnormals.clamp(0, 1) return clampednormals Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-unit normals: If the input normal is not normalized, the absolute values may exceed 1 before clamping, or the relative proportions may be distorted. The clamp operation handles values >1 by saturating them to 1, which can obscure the true magnitude if the normal was significantly unnormalized. Zero normals: If the normal is (0, 0, 0), the output is (0, 0, 0) (black). This may occur in degenerate geometry or at singularities. The Spin Shader visualizes surface geometry by mapping surface normals and camera orientation to a cyclic color field, mimicking spin-1/2 behavior where a 360-degree rotation reverses the texture orientation. It is chosen when one needs to visualize the spin orientation of objects relative to the camera, leveraging quaternion-based rotation tracking to maintain continuity across complex 3D rotations. The Normal Integrator renders the surface normal as a color by mapping the normal vector components from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] using a linear transformation (typically ci = \frac{ni + 1}{2}). It is chosen when the signed direction of the normal is important (e.g., distinguishing between front-facing and back-facing surfaces) rather than just the absolute orientation. Laplacian Shading visualizes the surface Laplacian by normalizing the Laplacian values to [-1, 1], flipping the sign, mapping to [0, 1], and applying gamma correction. It is used to inspect the curvature or smoothness of the SDF, as the Laplacian relates to the second derivative of the distance field. Formula: L{vis} = \left( \frac{-\frac{\Delta}{\max(|\Delta|)} + 1}{2} \right)^{1/2.33} where \Delta is the surface Laplacian, and the result is clamped to [0, 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def laplacianshading(surfacelaplacian: Tensor) -> Tensor: """ Visualizes the surface Laplacian with normalization, sign flip, and gamma correction. Args: surfacelaplacian: A tensor of shape (..., 1) or (..., 3) containing Laplacian values. Returns: A tensor of shape (..., 1) or (..., 3) containing the visualized Laplacian colors. """ # Normalize to [-1, 1] maxabs = surfacelaplacian.abs().max() if maxabs == 0: return surfacelaplacian # Avoid division by zero normalized = surfacelaplacian.div(maxabs) # Flip sign and map to [0, 1] # -normalized ranges from [-1, 1] to [1, -1] # Add 1: ranges from [0, 2] # Divide by 2: ranges from [0, 1] mapped = normalized.mul(-1).add(1).div(2) # Clamp to [0, 1] clamped = mapped.clamp(0, 1) # Apply gamma correction (gamma = 2.33) gammacorrected = clamped.pow(1 / 2.33) return gammacorrected Tangent Space Visualization projects the surface normal onto the sensor plane and visualizes the resulting 2D vector using domain coloring techniques. It is chosen when analyzing the tangential components of the normal relative to the camera view, which can reveal subtle geometric features or alignment issues. Steps: 1. Let e\alpha and e\beta be an orthonormal basis for the sensor plane, and vp be the unit vector from pixel p to the focal point. 2. Project the surface normal Np onto the sensor plane: Tp = Np - (Np \cdot vp)vp 3. Express Tp in the basis e\alpha, e\beta as Tp = \alpha e\alpha + \beta e\beta. The result is a vector (\alpha, \beta) where \alpha^2 + \beta^2 \leq 1. 4. Treat (\alpha, \beta) as a complex number \alpha + i\beta and apply domain coloring techniques to visualize the result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tangentspacevisualization( surfacenormals: Tensor, cameraorientationconj: Tensor, raydirections: Tensor, cycliccolourmap: Tensor, degree: int) -> Tensor: """ Visualizes the tangent space projection of surface normals using domain coloring. Args: surfacenormals: Tensor of shape (..., 3) containing surface normals. cameraorientationconj: Tensor of shape (..., 4) containing conjugate quaternions for camera orientation. raydirections: Tensor of shape (..., 3) containing ray directions from pixel to focal point. cycliccolourmap: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the cyclic color map. degree: int, the degree of the cyclic color map. Returns: Tensor of shape (..., 3) containing the visualized tangent space colors. """ # Normalize ray directions to get vp vp = raydirections / raydirections.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Project normal onto sensor plane: Tp = Np - (Np. vp) vp dotproduct = (surfacenormals vp).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) Tp = surfacenormals - dotproduct vp # Compute orthonormal basis ealpha, ebeta for the sensor plane # This requires constructing a basis from the camera orientation and ray direction. # For simplicity, we assume a standard basis construction or use the provided # cameraorientationconj to derive the basis. # Note: The exact construction of ealpha and ebeta depends on the camera model. # Here we assume a simplified approach where we project onto a plane perpendicular to vp. # To express Tp in the basis ealpha, ebeta, we need to define these vectors. # A common approach is to use the camera's up and right vectors, adjusted for the ray direction. # For this implementation, we will assume a simplified projection where we just # compute the components in a local coordinate system. # Let's assume we have a way to get the basis vectors ealpha and ebeta. # In a real implementation, these would be derived from the camera orientation. # For the sake of this pseudocode, we will assume ealpha and ebeta are available # or computed from the camera orientation. # Compute alpha and beta components # alpha = Tp. ealpha # beta = Tp. ebeta # This requires the basis vectors. We will assume they are computed elsewhere. # For a complete implementation, one would construct the basis from the camera's # orientation quaternion and the ray direction. # Placeholder for basis construction # ealpha, ebeta = computebasis(cameraorientationconj, vp) # For the purpose of this example, we will assume a simplified projection # where we just use the components of Tp in a local frame. # This is a simplification and may not be accurate for all camera models. # Let's assume we have a function to compute the basis ealpha, ebeta = computeorthonormalbasis(cameraorientationconj, vp) alpha = (Tp ealpha).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) beta = (Tp ebeta).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Apply domain coloring colors = domaincolouring(alpha, beta, cycliccolourmap, degree) return colors def computeorthonormalbasis(cameraorientationconj: Tensor, vp: Tensor) -> Tuple[Tensor, Tensor]: """ Computes an orthonormal basis (ealpha, ebeta) for the sensor plane given the camera orientation and ray direction. Args: cameraorientationconj: Tensor of shape (..., 4) containing conjugate quaternions. vp: Tensor of shape (..., 3) containing ray directions. Returns: Tuple of tensors ealpha and ebeta, each of shape (..., 3). """ # Convert quaternion to rotation matrix or use quaternion operations to get basis vectors # This is a simplified implementation. In practice, one would use the camera's # up and right vectors, transformed by the camera orientation. # Assume we have a function to get the camera's up and right vectors in world space # upworld, rightworld = getcameravectors(cameraorientationconj) # For this example, we will assume a simple basis construction # where ealpha is the right vector and ebeta is the up vector, # adjusted to be perpendicular to vp. # This is a placeholder and needs to be implemented based on the specific camera model. # For now, we will return a dummy basis. # In a real implementation, this would involve quaternion-to-matrix conversion # and vector transformations. # Dummy implementation for pseudocode completeness # ealpha = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # ebeta = torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # A more realistic approach would be: # 1. Get the camera's forward vector (negative of ray direction in camera space) # 2. Get the camera's up and right vectors in camera space # 3. Transform these vectors to world space using the camera orientation # 4. Project them onto the plane perpendicular to vp # For the sake of this example, we will assume a simplified basis # where ealpha and ebeta are orthogonal to vp and each other. # This is a complex operation and requires careful implementation. # We will leave this as a placeholder for the actual implementation. # Return dummy values to satisfy the type signature # In a real implementation, this function would be fully defined. raise NotImplementedError("Basis computation requires specific camera model details.") def domaincolouring( realpart: Tensor, imagpart: Tensor, cycliccolourmap: Tensor, degree: int) -> Tensor: """ Applies domain coloring to a complex number represented by real and imaginary parts. Args: realpart: Tensor of shape (..., 1) containing the real part. imagpart: Tensor of shape (..., 1) containing the imaginary part. cycliccolourmap: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the cyclic color map. degree: int, the degree of the cyclic color map. Returns: Tensor of shape (..., 3) containing the colored output. """ # Compute the angle of the complex number angle = torch.atan2(imagpart, realpart) # Normalize angle to [0, 1] normalizedangle = angle.div(math.tau).add(0.5) # Scale by degree and map to color map index cmapindex = normalizedangle.mul(degree).multiply(cycliccolourmap.shape[0]).floor().long().remainder(cycliccolourmap.shape[0]) # Get the color from the cyclic color map colours = cycliccolourmap[cmapindex,:] # Compute the brightness (magnitude of the complex number) brightness = torch.stack([realpart, imagpart], dim=-1).pow(2).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True).pow(1 / 2) # Multiply brightness by color return brightness.mul(colours) Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it involves only element-wise absolute value and clamp operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel, as it does not require storing intermediate data structures beyond the input normal. Strengths: Simple to implement, fast to compute, and effective for debugging normal continuity and orientation in SDF rendering. Limitations: Does not provide lighting information, so it is not suitable for final rendering. It only visualizes the absolute orientation, losing signed information about the normal direction. When to use: During development and debugging of SDF shaders to verify that normals are correctly computed and continuous across geometry boundaries. When not to use: For final image synthesis, where lighting models like Lambertian shading are required. Normal Shading is part of a collection of geometrically motivated shaders used in ray marching algorithms for rendering signed distance fields (SDFs). The technique is implemented in the kyle-rosa/raymarching repository, which provides a differentiable ray marching framework in PyTorch. The repository includes a constructive geometry system for building SDFs, ray marching operations, and various shaders for visualizing geometric properties. The use of PyTorch allows for differentiability, enabling gradient-based optimization of scene parameters based on rendered pixel values. kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Spin Shader
head: Spin Shading
body: The Spin Shader visualizes surface geometry by mapping surface normals and camera orientation to a cyclic color field, mimicking spin-1/2 behavior where a 360-degree rotation reverses the texture orientation. Inputs and Outputs: surfacenormals: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing unit surface normal vectors \mathbf{n} = (x, y, z). cameraorientationconj: A tensor of shape (N, 4) containing the conjugate of the camera orientation quaternion \overline{q}. cycliccolourmap: A lookup table or function mapping points on the unit circle \mathbb{S}^1 to RGB values. degree: An integer parameter (typically 1) passed to the domain colouring function. Output: color: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing RGB pixel values. Data Structures: Quaternions are represented as 4-element vectors (w, x, y, z). Surface normals are treated as pure-imaginary quaternions 0 + xi + yj + zk. Steps: 1. Embed Normal as Pure Quaternion: Convert the surface normal \mathbf{n} = (x, y, z) into a pure-imaginary quaternion Np by setting the real part to zero: Np = 0 + xi + yj + zk 2. Rotate by Camera Conjugate: Compute the product of the conjugate camera orientation quaternion \overline{q} and the normal quaternion Np to rotate the normal into the camera's local coordinate frame: q' = \overline{q} Np = a + bi + cj + dk \in \mathbb{S}^3 3. Map to \mathbb{S}^1: Transform the resulting quaternion q' into a point on the unit circle \mathbb{S}^1 by computing the real and imaginary parts of the squared quaternion mapping: \text{real} = a^2 - |\mathbf{v}|^2 \text{imag} = 2a|\mathbf{v}| where \mathbf{v} = (b, c, d) and |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{b^2 + c^2 + d^2}. The sequence of mappings is \mathbb{S}^3 \times \mathbb{S}^2 \to \mathbb{S}^3 \to \mathbb{S}^1 \to \mathbb{R}^3{\geq 0}. 4. Domain Colouring: Map the point (\text{imag}, \text{real}) from \mathbb{S}^1 to an RGB color using a cyclic colormap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Face Normal Computation
head: Face Normal Calculation, computeFaceNormal, getShadingFaceNormal
body: Face normal computation determines the geometric orientation of a polygonal face (typically a triangle) to provide a surface normal for shading or ray intersection handling. It solves the problem of defining a consistent surface orientation when explicit vertex normals are unavailable or when a flat, geometric normal is required for primary-ray shading in voxel or mesh-based rendering. It is distinguished from gradient-based SDF normal estimation by relying on discrete vertex positions rather than continuous distance field derivatives, and from vertex normal averaging by producing a single constant vector for the entire face rather than an interpolated value. The method computes the geometric normal of a triangle face from its three vertex positions. It involves extracting vertex indices, gathering positions, computing the cross product of two edge vectors, and normalizing the result. Inputs: f: Array of face indices, where each face is defined by three vertex indices [i0, i1, i2]. v: Array of vertex positions, where each vertex i has a 3D position vector \mathbf{p}i. Outputs: fn: Array of face normals, where each face j has a 3D normal vector \mathbf{n}j. Data Structures: v: float[N][3] or vec3[N], where N is the number of vertices. f: int[M][3] or ivec3[M], where M is the number of faces. fn: float[M][3] or vec3[M], where M is the number of faces. Steps: 1. Iterate over each face j from 0 to M-1. 2. Extract the vertex indices for face j: i0 = f[j][0], i1 = f[j][1], i2 = f[j][2]. 3. Gather the corresponding vertex positions: \mathbf{p}0 = v[i0], \mathbf{p}1 = v[i1], \mathbf{p}2 = v[i2]. 4. Compute two edge vectors: \mathbf{e}1 = \mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0 and \mathbf{e}2 = \mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0. 5. Compute the unnormalized face normal via the cross product: \mathbf{n}{raw} = \mathbf{e}1 \times \mathbf{e}2. 6. Check for degenerate faces. If the squared magnitude \|\mathbf{n}{raw}\|^2 < \epsilon (where \epsilon = 10^{-20}), substitute \mathbf{n}{raw} = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]. 7. Normalize the normal: \mathbf{n}j = \frac{\mathbf{n}{raw}}{\|\mathbf{n}{raw}\|}. 8. Store \mathbf{n}j in fn[j]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computefacenormals(v, f): """ Compute geometric face normals for a mesh. Args: v: List of vertex positions, each a tuple/list of 3 floats (x, y, z). f: List of face indices, each a tuple/list of 3 integers. Returns: List of face normals, each a tuple/list of 3 floats. """ epsilon = 1e-20 numfaces = len(f) facenormals = [] for j in range(numfaces): # Step 2: Extract vertex indices i0, i1, i2 = f[j] # Step 3: Gather vertex positions p0 = v[i0] p1 = v[i1] p2 = v[i2] # Step 4: Compute edge vectors e1 = [p1[0] - p0[0], p1[1] - p0[1], p1[2] - p0[2]] e2 = [p2[0] - p0[0], p2[1] - p0[1], p2[2] - p0[2]] # Step 5: Cross product nx = e1[1] e2[2] - e1[2] e2[1] ny = e1[2] e2[0] - e1[0] e2[2] nz = e1[0] e2[1] - e1[1] e2[0] # Step 6: Handle degenerate faces magsq = nxnx + nyny + nznz if magsq < epsilon: nx, ny, nz = 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 magsq = 1.0 # Step 7: Normalize mag = math.sqrt(magsq) facenormals.append([nx / mag, ny / mag, nz / mag]) return facenormals Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Faces: Triangles with zero area (collinear or identical vertices) produce zero-length normals. The method handles this by checking the squared magnitude against a threshold (10^{-20}) and substituting a default up vector [0, 0, 1] before normalization. Winding Order: The direction of the normal depends on the winding order of the vertices. Counter-clockwise (CCW) ordering typically yields a normal pointing outward, while clockwise (CW) yields an inward normal. Consistency in winding order is critical for correct shading. Precision: Using squared magnitude for the degeneracy check avoids expensive square root operations and potential division by zero. Computes a smooth shading normal by averaging vertex normals. Chose this when smooth shading is desired over flat geometric shading. Time Complexity: O(M), where M is the number of faces. Each face requires a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store the resulting face normals. Strengths: Simple, fast, and geometrically accurate for flat shading. Does not require pre-computed vertex normals or gradient information. Limitations: Produces faceted shading on curved surfaces. Sensitive to vertex winding order. Degenerate faces must be handled explicitly. When to use: Flat shading, collision detection, or when vertex normals are not available. When not to use: Smooth shading is required (use Vertex Normal Averaging or Gradient-Based Surface Normal Estimation). Face normal computation is a fundamental technique in computer graphics for determining surface orientation. It is widely used in rasterization and ray tracing for lighting calculations. The geometric approach using the cross product of edge vectors is a standard method described in introductory computer graphics literature. The specific handling of degenerate faces with a default up vector is noted in implementations such as DreamGaussian. The term "face normal" is often used in contrast to "vertex normal" or "shading normal". mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, https://github.com/leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) prateekchandan/Advanced-CG-High-Resolution-Sparse-Voxel-DAGs, https://github.com/prateekchandan/Advanced-CG-High-Resolution-Sparse-Voxel-DAGs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, https://github.com/dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Vertex Normal Averaging for Shading
head: Face Normal Computation (shading-based), Shading Normal Computation, Surface Normal Averaging for Shading
body: Vertex Normal Averaging for Shading computes a smooth shading normal for a polygonal face by averaging the pre-computed vertex normals of its three corners and normalizing the result. It serves as the shading-based alternative to geometric face normal computation. This approach reduces visible faceting on rendered isosurfaces compared to flat shading. Inputs: Three vertex normals \mathbf{n}0, \mathbf{n}1, \mathbf{n}2, each a 3D vector. These are typically pre-computed as renormalized averages of the surface normal vectors of the triangles that share the vertex. Outputs: A single normalized 3D vector \mathbf{n}{face} representing the shading normal for the face. Data Structures: Vertex normals are stored as 3D floating-point vectors. Bit-packing details are Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Retrieve the three vertex normals \mathbf{n}0, \mathbf{n}1, \mathbf{n}2 associated with the face's vertices. 2. Compute the component-wise arithmetic mean of the three vectors. 3. Normalize the resulting vector to ensure it is a unit vector. 4. Pass \mathbf{n}{face} to the underlying rendering function for use in shading the triangles. Formulas: Component-wise average: \mathbf{v}{avg} = \frac{\mathbf{n}0 + \mathbf{n}1 + \mathbf{n}2}{3.0} Normalization: \mathbf{n}{face} = \frac{\mathbf{v}{avg}}{\|\mathbf{v}{avg}\|} Where \mathbf{n}i = (xi, yi, zi) are the input vertex normals, \mathbf{v}{avg} is the intermediate average vector, and \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm. Parameters: Typical values are Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Geometry: If the three vertex normals sum to a zero vector (e.g., normals pointing in opposite directions that cancel out), normalization fails and requires a guard. Precision: The averaging process can slightly reduce the magnitude before normalization, but standard floating-point precision is sufficient for standard graphics applications. Boundary Conditions: This method relies entirely on the quality of the pre-computed vertex normals. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def truediv(self, scalar): return Vector3(self.x / scalar, self.y / scalar, self.z / scalar) def magnitude(self): return (self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2)0.5 def computeshadingnormal(n0, n1, n2): # Step 2: Compute component-wise average avg = (n0 + n1 + n2) / 3.0 # Step 3: Normalize the result mag = avg.magnitude() if mag < 1e-9: return Vector3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Default fallback for degenerate cancellation return avg / mag Time Complexity: O(1) per face. It involves three vector additions, one division, and one normalization (square root and division). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per face. Performance: Shading increases both computing time and memory usage compared to flat shading. The cost is low per triangle but adds up over large meshes. Strengths: Significantly reduces faceting artifacts on smooth surfaces or low-poly isosurfaces. It is computationally inexpensive compared to higher-order interpolation methods. Limitations: Not necessarily appropriate in all situations. It does not account for curvature within the face, only the average orientation of the vertices. This method is described in the context of the rgl package in R, specifically for rendering isosurfaces of density functions. The technique is used to smooth the visual appearance of multiple isosurfaces, such as those derived from tri-variate normal distributions. It is implemented by computing surface normal vectors at vertices as renormalized averages of the surface normal vectors of the triangles that share the vertex, which are then passed to the underlying rendering function triangles3d. name: Ray Marching with Single Scattering
head: Real-time Volumetric Rendering, Volumetric Cloud Rendering, Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Ray Marching
body: Ray marching with single scattering is a real-time technique for rendering volumetric clouds using OpenGL/WebGL ray marching, procedural noise for density, and physically-based single scattering illumination. It solves the problem of rendering translucent, animated volumetric media efficiently by approximating light transport with a single scattering event per sample, balancing visual fidelity against computational cost. It differs from SDF Cloud Rendering by using procedural noise instead of signed distance fields for density, and from Atmospheric Ray Marching by focusing on localized cloud volumes with explicit bounding boxes and wind animation rather than global atmospheric scattering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Eye position (e), screen position (s), camera rotation matrix (camRot), bounding box (bMin, bMax), sun position (uUserSunPos), sun color (uUserSunColor), time (uTime), resolution (uResolution), and various uniform parameters (step sizes, coefficients, noise settings). Output: Fragment color (fColor). Data Structures: Bounding Box: Defined by bMin and bMax. The effective bounds are adjusted by uUserSize: bMin.x -= uUserSize.x, bMax.x += uUserSize.x, etc.. Noise Texture (Optional): If using texture-based density, a FloatingPointTexture uses a Float32Array buffer of size textureWidth \times textureHeight \times 4. Pixels are stored in RGBA order, with index (x + y \times textureWidth) \times 4 for R, +1 for G, +2 for B, +3 for A. The texture is 2D, RGBA format, FLOAT type, NEAREST filtering, CLAMPTOEDGE wrapping. Procedural Noise: Uses Perlin or Simplex noise (cnoise or snoise) combined with Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm). Parameters: MAX\STEPS = 50. STEP\SIZE = 0.08. MAX\STEPS\LIGHT = 5. STEP\SIZE\LIGHT = 0.6. scatteringCoeff: 1.5 (sunset), 1.2 (day). absorptionCoeff: 0.4 (sunset), 0.2 (day). extinctionCoeff = scatteringCoeff + absorptionCoeff. WIND = vec3(0.7, 0.2, -0.5). SUN = normalize(vec3(1.5, 1.0, 1.0)). CAMERA = vec3(0.0, 0.0, -3.0). SUN\COLOUR\SUNSET = vec3(1.8, 1.1, 0.6). SUN\COLOUR\DAY = vec3(1.5, 1.3, 0.9). uUserSize, uUserSpeed, uUserSunPos, uUserSunColor, uUserDensity, uUserScale, uUserZoom, uUserControl, uRandomVector are user-defined uniforms. Formulas: Sky Color: screenRange = clamp(rayDir.y \times 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0); sky = mix(skyBottom, skyTop, screenRange). Sphere SDF: sdfSphere(p, r) = -length(p) + r. Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: henyeyGreenstien(cos\Theta) = mix(forward, backward, 0.4) \times 0.4 where forward = \frac{1 - g1^2}{(1 + g1^2 - 2g1 cos\Theta)^{1.5}}, \quad g1 = 0.7 backward = \frac{1 - g2^2}{(1 + g2^2 - 2g2 cos\Theta)^{1.5}}, \quad g2 = -0.2. Beer-Lambert Law: transmittance = exp(-density \times extinctionCoeff \times STEP\SIZE \times 1.5). Note: The source code applies an additional multiplier of 1.5 to the exponent. Single Scattering Approximation: scattering = (1. - localTransmittance) \times currentLightRayT. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
