Initialize Ray rayDir = normalize(s - e) # 2. Camera Setup CAM = vec3(0.0, 0.0, uUserZoom) if uUserControl == 1: camRot = createrotationmatrix(uMouse.x, uMouse.y) # Helper to create rotation matrix from mouse coords else: camRot = createrotationmatrix(mod(uTime 5.0, 350.0), 0.0) # Helper to create rotation matrix from time # 3. Sky Color sky = calculateskycolor(rayDir, sunset) # 4. Bounding Box Adjustment bMin = uBoundingBox.bMin - uUserSize bMax = uBoundingBox.bMax + uUserSize # 5. Main Loop Variables transmittance = 1.0 t = 0.0 colour = vec3(0.0) # 6. Main Ray Marching Loop for i in range(MAXSTEPS): p = e + t rayDir # Check if inside volume (using sphere SDF as example from S1, or bounding box from S2) # S1 uses sphere SDF: dist = sdfSphere(p, 2.0) # S2 uses rayMarch function with bounding box intersection # Merging logic: Check if p is within bMin and bMax if not (all(p >= bMin) and all(p <= bMax)): t += STEPSIZE continue # Calculate Density # S1: Procedural Noise # density = clamp(octaves(p + animationIndex WIND), 0.0, 1.0) smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, dist) # S2: Texture-based or procedural # density = volumetricDensityMap3d(marchPoint, textureOffset, uUserScale) / uUserDensity # Using procedural noise as primary method from S1 animationIndex = uTime # Assuming animationIndex is derived from time density = clamp(octaves(p + animationIndex WIND), 0.0, 1.0) # Apply soft boundary if using SDF # dist = sdfSphere(p, 2.0) # density = smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, dist) # Early exit for low density if density < 0.01: t += STEPSIZE continue # Light Marching Loop transmittanceLight = 1.0 tLight = 0.0 lightColor = vec3(0.0) for j in range(MAXSTEPSLIGHT): pLight = p + tLight SUN # Calculate Light Density # S1: Procedural densityLight = clamp(octaves(pLight + animationIndex WIND), 0.0, 1.0) # S2: Texture-based # lightDensity = volumetricDensityMap3d(lightMarchPoint, textureOffset, uUserScale) / uUserDensity # Early exit for light if densityLight < 0.05: tLight += STEPSIZELIGHT continue # Update Light Transmittance (Beer-Lambert) # Note: Source S1 uses extinctionCoeff 1.5 multiplier transmittanceLight = exp(-densityLight extinctionCoeff STEPSIZELIGHT 1.5) if transmittanceLight < 0.05: break tLight += STEPSIZELIGHT # Calculate Scattering # Phase Function cosTheta = dot(rayDir, SUN) phase = henyeygreenstein(cosTheta) # Ambient ambient = sky 0.7 # Scattered Light sunColour = uUserSunColor if not sunset else SUNCOLOURSUNSET # Select sun color based on mode scattered = ((sunColour transmittanceLight phase 6.0) + ambient) scatteringCoeff # Local Transmittance localTransmittance = exp(-density extinctionCoeff STEPSIZE 1.5) # Single Scattering Contribution # S2: scattering = (1. - localTransmittance) currentLightRayT # S1: colour += transmittance density scattered STEPSIZE # Merging: Use S1's accumulation with S2's scattering approximation if preferred, # but S1's code explicitly accumulates density scattered. # We follow S1's accumulation logic as it is more detailed in the shader. colour += transmittance density scattered STEPSIZE # Update Main Transmittance transmittance = localTransmittance # Early exit for main ray if transmittance < 0.01: break t += STEPSIZE # 7. Final Composition # Add sky contribution colour += transmittance sky # S2 adds cloudColor + col globalTransmittance, but S1 accumulates directly into colour. # We stick to S1's final output. fColor = vec4(colour, 1.0) return fColor def calculateskycolor(rayDir, sunset): screenRange = clamp(rayDir.y 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0) if sunset: skyTop = vec3(0.15, 0.30, 0.60) skyBottom = vec3(0.85, 0.45, 0.30) else: skyTop = vec3(0.2, 0.4, 0.8) skyBottom = vec3(0.7, 0.85, 1.0) return mix(skyBottom, skyTop, screenRange) def henyeygreenstein(cosTheta): g1 = 0.7 denom1 = 1.0 + g1 g1 - 2.0 g1 cosTheta forward = (1.0 - g1 g1) / pow(denom1, 1.5) g2 = -0.2 denom2 = 1.0 + g2 g2 - 2.0 g2 cosTheta backward = (1.0 - g2 g2) / pow(denom2, 1.5) return mix(forward, backward, 0.4) 0.4 def octaves(p): f = 0.0 amp = 0.5 freq = 2.0 for i in range(maxOctaves): noiseval = cnoise(p) # or snoise(p) f += amp noiseval p = freq freq += 0.20 amp = 0.5 return f Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Density Optimization: If density < 0.01, the step is skipped to save computation, but t is still incremented. Early Exit for Light: If light transmittance drops below 0.05, the light march stops. Early Exit for Main Ray: If main transmittance drops below 0.01, the main march stops. Max Distance Limit: The main march stops if t exceeds 20.0. WebGL 1 Limitation: Dynamic loop bounds are not supported, so STEP\SIZE and STEP\SIZE\LIGHT must be hardcoded constants. Precision: The Beer-Lambert law uses an additional multiplier of 1.5 in the exponent in the source implementation, which may deviate from standard physical definitions. Time Complexity: O(MAX\STEPS \times MAX\STEPS\LIGHT) per fragment. With MAX\STEPS=50 and MAX\STEPS\LIGHT=5, this is 250 noise evaluations and transmittance calculations per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1) for procedural noise. If using texture-based density, O(textureWidth \times textureHeight \times 4) for the texture buffer. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Quality can be increased by decreasing STEP\SIZE and STEP\SIZE\LIGHT, but this increases computational cost linearly. Strengths: Real-time performance on WebGL 1/2 hardware; physically-based single scattering approximation; procedural noise allows infinite resolution and easy animation. Limitations: Single scattering approximation is less physically accurate than multiple scattering; procedural noise may lack the detailed structure of texture-based volumes; WebGL 1 requires hardcoded step sizes. When to use: Real-time cloud rendering in games or interactive applications where performance is critical. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring high physical accuracy or complex multiple scattering effects. It was popularized by demos and open-source projects such as gmanishaa/volumetric-rendering and M4trixStrike/WebGL-Volumetric-clouds. The method combines classic ray marching with single scattering approximation, using procedural noise for density and Henyey-Greenstein phase function for light scattering. head: Signed Distance Field Clouds
body: SDF Cloud Rendering is a technique for rendering volumetric clouds using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) via ray marching in a fragment shader, utilizing warped sphere primitives and smooth unions to create complex shapes. It differs from Ray Marching with Single Scattering and Atmospheric Ray Marching by constructing the volume geometry explicitly through analytic distance functions rather than sampling a density field or solving the radiative transfer equation with phase functions. Inputs: Fragment coordinates (glFragCoord), screen resolution (screenSize), camera field of view (45.0 degrees), and a random seed (seed). Outputs: Final color in glFragColor. No complex data structures are used. The scene is defined by a single scalar field function sceneSDF composed of analytic primitives. MAXMARCHINGSTEPS: 100. MINDIST: 0.0. MAXDIST: 100.0. EPSILON: 0.0001. STEPSCALE: 0.67. EXPOSURE: 1.0. WHITE: 200.0. LIGHT: vec3(-10.0, 10.0, 3.0). LIGHTCOLOR: vec3(100.0, 100.0, 100.0). DARKCOLOR: vec3(5.0, 8.0, 20.0). Smooth Union: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 + 0.5 \frac{d2 - d1}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) \text{result} = \text{mix}(d2, d1, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) Where d1, d2 are distances and k is the blending factor. Hable Tone Mapping: \text{result} = \frac{x(Ax + CB) + DE}{x(Ax + B) + DF} - \frac{E}{F} Where A=0.15, B=0.50, C=0.10, D=0.20, E=0.02, F=0.30. Unverified code. origin) - radius def smoothunion(d1, d2, k): h = clamp(0.5 + 0.5 (d2 - d1) / k, 0.0, 1.0) return mix(d2, d1, h) - k h (1.0 - h) def scenesdf(samplepoint): warped = warp(samplepoint, 1.5) d1 = spheresdf(warped, vec3(0.5, 0.0, 0.0), 1.0) d2 = spheresdf(warped, vec3(-0.5, -0.4, 0.2), 0.5) smoothed = smoothunion(d1, d2, 0.4) d3 = spheresdf(warped, vec3(-0.8, 0.55, 0.2), 0.3) return min(smoothed, d3) def raydirection(fieldofview, size, fragcoord): xy = fragcoord - size / 2.0 z = size.y / tan(radians(fieldofview) / 2.0) return normalize(vec3(xy, -z)) def raymarchdistance(eye, marchingdirection, start, end): depth = start for i in range(MAXMARCHINGSTEPS): dist = scenesdf(eye + depth marchingdirection) if dist < EPSILON: return depth depth += dist STEPSCALE if depth >= end: return end return end def calculateshadow(origin, dir): k = 2.0 t = 100.0 EPSILON res = 1.0 for i in range(MAXMARCHINGSTEPS): h = scenesdf(origin + t dir) if h < EPSILON: return 0.0 t += h STEPSCALE res = min(res, k h / t) return res def tonemap(x): A = 0.15 B = 0.50 C = 0.10 D = 0.20 E = 0.02 F = 0.30 return (x (A x + C B) + D E) / (x (A x + B) + D F) - E / F def render(): dir = raydirection(45.0, screenSize, glFragCoord.xy) eye = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 8.0) dist = raymarchdistance(eye, dir, MINDIST, MAXDIST) if dist > MAXDIST - EPSILON: d = dot(dir, normalize(vec3(0.0, -1.0, 0.0))) d = 6.0 d = d / 2.0 + 0.5 d = max(0.0, min(1.0, d)) return mix(vec3(4.0, 40.0, 100.0), vec3(20.0, 100.0, 100.0), d) intersection = eye + dist dir tolight = normalize(vec3(-10.0, 10.0, 3.0) - intersection) shadowfactor = calculateshadow(intersection, tolight) return mix(vec3(5.0, 8.0, 20.0), vec3(100.0, 100.0, 100.0), shadowfactor) def main(): color = render() wscale = 1.0 / tonemap(EXPOSURE WHITE) glFragColor = vec4(tonemapvec(EXPOSURE color) wscale, 1.0) Precision: The jitter function uses sin and division by scale. If scale becomes too large or mixamount is extreme, precision loss may occur. Boundaries: The ray marcher returns end if dist >= end or if the loop completes. This handles rays that miss the cloud entirely. Degenerate Input: If screenSize is zero or invalid, raydirection will fail. Ensure screenSize is positive. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of pixels and M is MAXMARCHINGSTEPS (100). Each step involves a warp and SDF evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel. No buffers are allocated. Performance: Runs in real-time on modern GPUs as a single pass fragment shader. Strengths: Simple implementation, no texture lookups, analytic geometry. Limitations: Limited to specific shapes (warped spheres), no true volumetric scattering, single shadow ray per pixel. The method was created by Dave Pagurek as a small experiment in rendering with signed distance fields, presented at Graphics Interface 2019. It demonstrates the use of SDFs for organic shapes like clouds. davepagurek/sdf-clouds, https://github.com/davepagurek/sdf-clouds, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Beam Optimization
head: Beam Optimization for Primary Rays, Ray Batching, Ray Grouping Optimization
body: Beam Optimization is an acceleration technique for primary rays in distance-field ray marching that groups adjacent rays into beams to reduce redundant intersection tests. By marching a group of rays together along a central path, the method exploits spatial coherence: if the distance to the nearest geometry is large relative to the group's spatial extent, all rays in the group can advance simultaneously without individual checks. This reduces the number of scene queries for rays far from geometry, at the cost of potential over-stepping or splitting when rays diverge near surfaces. Inputs: A rectangular grid of primary rays (pixels), a Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluator, and a beam size parameter (typically 8 \times 8 pixels). Outputs: Hit distances or visibility flags for each pixel. Data Structures: Beam: A 2D block of pixels defined by top-left coordinate (x, y) and dimensions (w, h). Ray State: For each pixel, stores current position \mathbf{p}, direction \mathbf{d}, and accumulated distance t. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Divide the image into non-overlapping beams of size W \times H (default 8 \times 8). Initialize all rays with t=0 and \mathbf{p} = \text{origin} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. 2. Marching Loop: While there are active beams: a. Central March: For each active beam, compute the SDF value d{center} at the center pixel's current position. b. Step Size: Advance the center ray by t{step} = d{center}. Update the center ray's position \mathbf{p}{center} \leftarrow \mathbf{p}{center} + t{step} \cdot \mathbf{d}{center}. c. Collision Check: Calculate the maximum possible deviation of any ray in the beam from the center ray after the step. Let R{beam} be the radius of the beam's spatial extent (approx. \max(w, h) \cdot \text{pixel\pitch}). If d{center} > R{beam}, the beam is safe to advance without splitting because no ray in the group can have hit geometry yet. d. Splitting: If d{center} \le R{beam}, the beam might contain rays intersecting geometry. Split the beam into four sub-beams (quadrants). e. Discard: If a beam has stepped far enough into the scene such that its minimum possible distance to geometry exceeds the maximum ray length, discard it. f. Termination: If a sub-beam contains only one ray and that ray has hit an object (SDF value \le \epsilon), mark the pixel as hit and remove the beam from the active list. 3. Repeat: Process the new set of sub-beams. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def beamoptimization(rays, beamsize=8, maxsteps=100): # rays: list of Ray objects, each with position, direction, t, hit # Initialize beams beams = createbeams(rays, beamsize) while beams: nextbeams = [] for beam in beams: # Get center ray of the beam centerray = beam.getcenterray() # March center ray dist = sdf(centerray.position) if dist <= 0: # Hit detected for center, likely need split or individual trace # For simplicity, split if not already single if len(beam.rays) > 1: nextbeams.extend(splitbeam(beam)) else: centerray.hit = True centerray.t += dist continue # Calculate beam spatial radius # Assuming uniform pixel pitch and direction spread beamradius = calculatebeamradius(beam) if dist > beamradius: # Safe to advance all rays in beam by dist for ray in beam.rays: ray.position += ray.direction dist ray.t += dist # Beam remains intact, no split needed # Note: In a strict implementation, we might keep it in 'beams' # for next iteration if not finished, or mark as 'advanced' # Here we assume we re-evaluate in next loop or keep in queue # To avoid infinite loop, we process and remove if done if isbeamdone(beam): pass # Discard else: nextbeams.append(beam) else: # Potential collision, split if len(beam.rays) == 1: # Single ray, handle individually ray = beam.rays[0] ray.position += ray.direction dist ray.t += dist if ray.hit: pass # Done else: nextbeams.append(beam) else: nextbeams.extend(splitbeam(beam)) beams = nextbeams return rays def splitbeam(beam): # Split 2D beam into 4 quadrants w, h = beam.width, beam.height midx, midy = beam.x + w // 2, beam.y + h // 2 subbeams = [] subbeams.append(createbeam(beam.x, beam.y, w // 2, h // 2)) subbeams.append(createbeam(beam.x + w // 2, beam.y, w - w // 2, h // 2)) subbeams.append(createbeam(beam.x, beam.y + h // 2, w // 2, h - h // 2)) subbeams.append(createbeam(beam.x + w // 2, beam.y + h // 2, w - w // 2, h - h // 2)) return subbeams Parameters: Beam Size: 8 \times 8 pixels is a common default. Larger beams reduce overhead but increase split frequency near geometry. Edge Cases: Precision: Floating-point errors in SDF evaluation can cause rays to oscillate or miss intersections near the threshold. Boundaries: Rays near the edge of the image must be handled to avoid out-of-bounds beam creation. An extension of beam optimization applied to shadow ray tracing. Instead of primary rays, beams are shot from the view-sample position to the area light. Method: Shoot a beam of four rays per pixel from the view-sample to the light. Find the conservative furthest distance along these rays where no geometry is intersected. Shorten all shadow rays for that pixel by this distance. Trace the same beam rays in reverse (from light to view) to find a conservative interval where geometry may be intersected. Benefit: Improves traversal speed of shadow rays and allows discarding pixels whose entire beams have no intersection with geometry, requiring no additional shadow rays. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of SDF evaluations for rays far from geometry. Complexity is roughly O(N \cdot \frac{1}{k}) where k is the beam size factor, but degrades to O(N) near complex geometry due to frequent splitting. Memory Complexity: Low overhead, only requiring storage for beam metadata. Strengths: Significant speedup for primary rays in scenes with large empty spaces. Limitations: Inefficient for scenes with high-frequency geometry or where rays are frequently occluded, as splitting overhead dominates. When to Use: Best for primary rays in large, sparse scenes. Less effective for secondary rays (shadows, reflections) unless adapted as in the soft shadow variant. Beam optimization was introduced by Laine and Karras in 2010 for high-resolution sparse voxel DAGs. It builds on the concept of ray grouping to leverage the coherence of primary rays in rasterization-based rendering pipelines. The technique is particularly relevant in the context of distance-field ray marching, where sphere tracing is the standard traversal method. High resolution sparse voxel DAGs, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262367808HighresolutionsparsevoxelDAGs, fetched 2026-10-27 Sphere Tracing GPU An evaluation of the Sphere Tracing algorithm and a GPU designed to run it, https://odr.chalmers.se/items/37b0e53f-fc76-4b0e-96d8-8e864573ada9/full, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Performance Optimizations for SDF Ray Marching
head: Optimisations, SDF Ray Marching Optimizations
body: Performance Optimizations for SDF Ray Marching refers to a set of techniques designed to reduce the computational cost of rendering scenes defined by Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) while maintaining visual fidelity. It solves the primary bottleneck of ray marching: the high number of SDF evaluations and shader instructions required per pixel, particularly in complex or high-resolution scenes. What sets these optimizations apart from sibling methods like Beam Optimization is their focus on reducing the number of march steps or the cost of each step through geometric culling, resolution scaling, and parameter tuning, rather than changing the fundamental traversal structure or parallelism model. The method consists of several independent optimization strategies applied during the ray marching loop or the rendering pipeline setup. Inputs: Scene SDF functions, camera parameters, ray origin/direction, maximum step count (MAXSTEPS), epsilon threshold (EPSILON), and resolution settings. Outputs: Rendered image with reduced computational cost. No new data structures are strictly required for the core optimizations listed below, though they may utilize existing scene graphs or texture buffers (e.g., for baked shadows). 1. Early-Out Bounding Volumes Surround expensive sub-scenes or complex geometry with a fast, simple SDF (typically a sphere). Before evaluating the complex SDF, check the bounding SDF. If the distance returned by the bounding SDF is greater than the current ray marching step size, skip the detailed evaluation entirely. Let d{bound} be the distance from the current ray point P to the bounding volume. Let d{step} be the current step size (usually the SDF value of the active geometry). Condition: If d{bound} > d{step}, skip the complex SDF evaluation. 2. Level of Detail (LOD) Adjustment Adjust the marching parameters based on the distance to the camera or the object. For distant geometry, reduce the maximum number of steps and increase the epsilon threshold. The visual difference is imperceptible beyond a certain distance (e.g., 10 scene units). Let dist be the distance from the camera to the current ray point. If dist > 10, set MAX\STEPS{distant} < MAX\STEPS{near} and EPSILON{distant} > EPSILON{near}. 3. Resolution Scaling Render the scene at a lower resolution (e.g., half resolution) and upscale the result. This is cited as the most effective single optimization for real-time SDF rendering at larger resolutions. Let W, H be the target resolution. Render to buffer of size \lfloor W/2 \rfloor \times \lfloor H/2 \rfloor. Upscale using bilinear or nearest-neighbor filtering. 4. Over-Relaxation Multiply the step size d by a constant factor k where 1.1 \le k \le 1.6. This allows the ray to advance faster through empty space or open scenes. Update rule: t{new} = t{old} + d \times k. Pitfall: This risks artifacts near concave edges or thin geometry, as the ray may overshoot the surface if the step becomes too large relative to the local curvature. 5. Pre-marched Shadow and Ambient Occlusion Baking For static volumes (e.g., clouds), pre-calculate shadow and ambient occlusion data into a 3D texture. Baking Shadow: Pre-march a shadow ray through the volume. Due to low volume resolution (e.g., 4 shadow samples per cloud sample), this can be done in real-time or pre-computed. This allows dynamic time-of-day changes. Baking Ambient Occlusion: Pre-march ambient occlusion into the volume texture to add shading without runtime cost. Runtime Lookup: Use the baked texture to retrieve shadow/occlusion values with a single tex3D lookup, ensuring perfect alignment with cloud geometry. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizesdfraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, scenesdf, boundssdf, maxstepsnear, maxstepsfar, epsilonnear, epsilonfar, useoverrelaxation, overrelaxationfactor, bakedshadowtex, bakedaotex): """ Performs ray marching with performance optimizations. """ t = 0.0 steps = 0 # Determine initial LOD based on distance (simplified: assume near start) # In practice, this check happens inside the loop or per-object isdistant = False while steps < maxstepsnear: # Get current point p = rayorigin + raydirection t # 1. Early-Out Bounding Volumes # Check if we are inside a bounding volume that has a complex child # Simplified: Assume boundssdf returns distance to nearest complex object dbound = boundssdf(p) # If the bounding volume is further than our current step would allow, # we might skip, but typically this is used to skip the complex SDF call # if the point is far from the complex object. # Here, we assume boundssdf is a cheap sphere check. # If dbound is very large, we might skip detailed evaluation if we knew # we were outside the bounding box. For this generic implementation, # we proceed to the main SDF. # 2. Evaluate Main SDF d = scenesdf(p) # 3. Level of Detail disttocamera = length(p - rayorigin) if disttocamera > 10.0: isdistant = True currentmaxsteps = maxstepsfar currentepsilon = epsilonfar else: isdistant = False currentmaxsteps = maxstepsnear currentepsilon = epsilonnear if steps > currentmaxsteps: break # 4. Over-Relaxation if useoverrelaxation: stepsize = d overrelaxationfactor else: stepsize = d # Safety clamp to prevent infinite loops or negative steps if stepsize < 0.0001: stepsize = 0.0001 t += stepsize steps += 1 # Check for hit if d < currentepsilon: # 5. Pre-marched Shadow/AO Lookup (if applicable) shadow = 1.0 ao = 1.0 if bakedshadowtex is not None: shadow = tex3Dlookup(bakedshadowtex, p) if bakedaotex is not None: ao = tex3Dlookup(bakedaotex, p) return hit(p, shadow, ao) # Check for miss (max distance) if t > 100.0: # Arbitrary max distance break return miss() Approximates subsurface scattering by computing the local thickness of a surface along random inward hemispherical directions, then using the thickness to modulate a simplified SSS lighting term. It is chosen when full SSS simulation is too expensive but some translucency is desired. See Subsurface Scattering Approximation via Local Thickness. Uses SDF values to dynamically determine step sizes, allowing large skips in empty space and fine-grained sampling near surfaces. It is distinguished by its use of a configurable raymarchingratio to scale the SDF-derived step size and its integration with neural implicit representations and explicit termination masks. See Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF. A SDF raymarching algorithm designed to solve ray hit/miss in fewer iterations than sphere tracing by using a stack to manage coverage spans along the ray. It is chosen when exact hit/miss determination is prioritized over iterative approximation. See Coverage Search. Accelerates volumetric ray marching by using an SDF to skip large empty spaces. The SDF stores the distance to the nearest surface of the volume, allowing the ray to advance by that distance in empty space. See SDF-Accelerated Volumetric Ray Marching. Marches a ray through an SDF scene using an acceleration structure to skip empty space, adaptive step sizing, and sign-change detection for surface refinement. See Adaptive SDF Ray Marching with Cell Acceleration. Marches a ray through an SDF field while applying a correction factor to counteract distance elongation along non-cardinal directions caused by the Eikonal equation. See SDF Ray Marching with Eikonal Correction. Renders hair-thin strands (e.g., jellyfish tentacles) using SDFs combined with soft accumulation to anti-alias across frames. See Ray Marching with SDFs and Soft Accumulation. A technique to improve visual fidelity and performance by pre-calculating shadow and ambient occlusion data into the volume texture, leveraging the static nature of the volume. It involves pre-marching shadow and AO rays into a 3D texture, allowing runtime lookup with a single tex3D call. See Pre-marched Shadow and Ambient Occlusion Baking (Note: The source describes this under the context of SDF volumetric rendering, but the specific article link provided in the prompt for this variant is missing a dedicated URL. Based on the prompt's structure, this is a minor variant without its own article, so it is described here. However, the prompt lists specific children. I will treat this as a minor variant described in the notes but not having a dedicated child article link in the "Children" list, or it might be a sub-topic of one of the existing ones. The prompt says "Minor variants (they have no article of their own: write each one under Subtopics as a '### <Name>' entry carrying ALL of its details below, cited". So I will write it here.) Wait, the prompt lists specific children. "Pre-marched Shadow..." is listed under "Minor variants". It does not have a link in the "Children" list. I must write it under Subtopics. A technique to improve visual fidelity and performance by pre-calculating shadow and ambient occlusion data into the volume texture, leveraging the static nature of the cloud volume. It involves pre-marching a shadow ray through the volume (e.g., 4 shadow samples per cloud sample) and pre-marching ambient occlusion into the volume texture. This allows dynamic time-of-day changes and runtime shadow lookup with a single tex3D lookup, matching the cloud geometry perfectly. Time Complexity: Reduced by a factor proportional to the number of skipped steps (via early-outs and over-relaxation) and the reduction in pixel count (via resolution scaling). Memory Complexity: Minimal increase for LOD parameters. Baked shadow/AO textures increase memory usage proportional to the volume resolution. Measured Performance: Rendering at half resolution is cited as the "most effective single optimisation for real-time SDF rendering at larger resolutions". Strengths: Simple to implement; significant FPS gains in real-time applications; effective for static scenes (baking). Limitations: Over-relaxation can cause artifacts near concave edges. Baking requires static geometry. LOD adjustments may reduce visual quality for distant objects if not tuned correctly. When to use: Real-time rendering where frame rate is critical; static volumetric scenes; scenes with large empty spaces. When not to use: Dynamic scenes requiring high-fidelity shadows without pre-computation; scenes with very thin geometry where over-relaxation causes overshooting. The techniques described are derived from practical implementations of ray marching in real-time graphics, particularly in the context of SDF rendering and volumetric clouds. The concepts of early-out bounding volumes, LOD, and resolution scaling are common in production graphics. The specific application of pre-marching shadow and AO into volume textures for static clouds was detailed in a blog post by UHawkVR. The term "sphere tracing" was introduced by John C. Hart in 1996. name: Subsurface Scattering Approximation via Local Thickness
head: SSS thickness approximation, local thickness SSS
body: This method approximates subsurface scattering (SSS) by estimating the local thickness of a surface along random inward hemispherical directions, then using that thickness to modulate a simplified SSS lighting term. It differs from sibling methods like Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF or SDF-Accelerated Volumetric Ray Marching by focusing on a per-pixel thickness probe rather than global acceleration or volumetric integration, providing a cheap approximation of light transport through translucent materials. Inputs: Surface position pos, surface normal norm, SDF query function sceneSDF(p) which returns a signed distance (negative inside, positive outside). Outputs: A scalar thickness value in the range [0.0, 1.0] used to modulate lighting. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method relies on scalar accumulators and random number generation. Parameters: SSSSampleDepth (float): Maximum length of the random hemispherical sampling vector into the object. Default: 1.0. SSSThicknessSamples (int): Number of samples to perform when calculating local thickness. Default: 32. SSSThicknessSamplesI (float): Inverse of SSSThicknessSamples (1.0 / 32.0 = 0.03125), used to average the accumulated thickness. Default: 0.03125. Steps: 1. Initialize thickness accumulator to 0.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to SSSThicknessSamples - 1: a. Generate a random scalar sampleLength using a hash function: sampleLength = Hash11(i) SSSSampleDepth. b. Generate a random direction sampleDir in the hemisphere defined by the inward normal -norm using a hash function: sampleDir = GenerateSampleVector(-norm, i). c. Query the scene SDF at the probe endpoint: dist = sceneSDF(pos + sampleDir sampleLength).dist. d. Add the probe length and the SDF distance to the accumulator: thickness += sampleLength + dist. 3. Average the accumulated thickness by multiplying by SSSThicknessSamplesI. 4. Clamp the result to [0.0, 1.0] and return. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatelocalthickness(pos, norm, sceneSDF, SSSSampleDepth=1.0, SSSThicknessSamples=32): """ Approximates subsurface scattering thickness by sampling inward hemispherical directions. Args: pos: vec3, surface position. norm: vec3, surface normal (pointing outward). sceneSDF: function, returns a struct/object with a 'dist' field (signed distance). SSSSampleDepth: float, max probe length. SSSThicknessSamples: int, number of samples. Returns: float, clamped thickness value in [0.0, 1.0]. """ thickness = 0.0 invsamples = 1.0 / SSSThicknessSamples for i in range(SSSThicknessSamples): # Generate random length in [0, SSSSampleDepth] samplelength = hash11(i) SSSSampleDepth # Generate random direction in hemisphere defined by -norm sampledir = generatesamplevector(-norm, i) # Query SDF at probe endpoint # Note: sceneSDF returns a result object with a 'dist' attribute probepos = pos + (sampledir samplelength) sdfresult = sceneSDF(probepos) sdfdist = sdfresult.dist # Add length and SDF distance to thickness # Pitfall: SDF dist is negative inside. Adding samplelength ensures positive contribution. thickness += samplelength + sdfdist # Average and clamp result = thickness invsamples return clamp(result, 0.0, 1.0) def hash11(p): """ 1D hash function from Dave Hoskins. """ p3 = fract(vec3(p) 443.897) p3 += dot(p3, p3.yzx + 19.19) return fract((p3.x + p3.y) p3.z) def hash33(p3): """ 3D hash function from Dave Hoskins. """ p3 = fract(p3 vec3(443.897, 441.423, 437.195)) p3 += dot(p3, p3.yxz + 19.19) return fract((p3.xxy + p3.yxx) p3.zyx) def reflectvector(v, n): """ Reflect vector v along plane defined by normal n. """ return v - 2.0 n min(0.0, dot(v, n)) def generatesamplevector(norm, i): """ Generate random vector in hemisphere defined by normal 'norm' and random value 'i'. """ randdir = normalize(hash33(norm + i) - vec3(0.5)) return reflectvector(randdir, norm) def clamp(x, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(x, maxval)) def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def fract(v): return v - floor(v) def floor(v): return int(v) if isinstance(v, float) else [int(x) for x in v] # Simplified for pseudocode def normalize(v): length = sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def sqrt(x): return x 0.5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Internal SDF Values: The SDF returns negative values inside the surface. The formula sampleLength + dist is critical; if dist is negative, it reduces the contribution, but sampleLength ensures the total remains positive, preventing incorrect darkening. Boundary Conditions: If the probe exits the object, sceneSDF returns a positive distance. This increases the thickness value, which may not be physically accurate for thin surfaces but is handled by the clamping to [0.0, 1.0]. Precision: Using floating-point arithmetic for accumulation may introduce precision errors for very large scenes or many samples, though 32 samples is typically stable. The thickness value is typically used as a factor in a diffuse or subsurface scattering lighting equation (e.g., multiplying albedo or scattering color). This is not defined in the source but is the standard application. The quality of the hash functions (Hash11, Hash33) affects the visual noise of the approximation. The source uses Dave Hoskins' hash functions. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is SSSThicknessSamples. Each sample requires one SDF query and some arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. No buffers are allocated. Performance: With N=32, this is relatively expensive per pixel compared to simple diffuse shading, but cheaper than full volumetric ray marching. It is suitable for real-time rendering if optimized or reduced. Strengths: Simple to implement, works with any SDF, provides a plausible approximation of translucency. Limitations: Approximation quality depends on sample count; noisy with low samples; does not account for multiple scattering or wavelength-dependent effects. When to use: When a cheap approximation of subsurface scattering is needed for SDF-rendered objects and full volumetric methods are too expensive. When not to use: When high-fidelity SSS is required, or when the object is very thin (thickness may saturate). This method originates from real-time raymarching shaders, specifically shared in the context of ShaderToy and GitHub repositories focusing on SDF raymarching techniques. It is a practical adaptation of thickness-based subsurface scattering approximations for interactive graphics. cahekp/Raymarching, https://github.com/cahekp/Raymarching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF
head: Ray Marching with SDF, Ray Marching Ratio
body: Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF is a rendering technique that uses Signed Distance Field (SDF) values to dynamically determine step sizes along camera rays, allowing for large skips in empty space and fine-grained sampling near surfaces. It is distinguished from standard uniform ray marching by its use of a configurable raymarchingratio to scale the SDF-derived step size, and from pure SDF rendering by its integration with neural implicit representations (latent codes) and an explicit termination mask based on depth bounds and SDF thresholds. Inputs: Camera rays camraysnow (origin and direction). Initial depth offsets initzdepthnow derived from an unfinishedmask. A neural network decoder self.decoder and a latent code vector latent. Parameters: clampdist (default 0.1), stopthreshold, raymarchingratio, maxboundzdepth, marchstep, buffersize. Outputs: Tensors sdflist, marchingzdepthlist, and pointslist concatenated along dimension 0 to form shapes (self.marchstep, N), (self.marchstep, N), and (self.marchstep, N, 3) respectively. Data Structures: unfinishedmask: A boolean tensor indicating which rays are still active. marchingzdepth: Accumulated step distance along the ray. pointsnow: 3D coordinates of sample points. sdfnow: Raw SDF values from the decoder. sdfmarching: Clamped SDF values used for stepping. Algorithm: 1. Initialize initzdepthnow and marchingzdepthnow for all rays where unfinishedmask is true. 2. Generate sample points pointsnow along camraysnow starting at initzdepthnow + marchingzdepthnow. 3. Decode the SDF value sdfnow for pointsnow using self.decoder and latent. 4. Clamp sdfnow to the range [-clampdist, clampdist] to produce sdfmarching. 5. Update marchingzdepth by adding sdfmarching raymarchingratio. 6. Update unfinishedmask: Keep rays where marchingzdepth + initzdepth < maxboundzdepth. Keep rays where abs(sdfmarching) >= stopthreshold. Keep rays that were previously unfinished. 7. Terminate if torch.nonzero(unfinishedmask).shape[0] == 0. 8. Pad result lists to self.buffersize if necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aggressiveraymarching(camraysnow, initzdepthnow, unfinishedmask, decoder, latent, clampdist=0.1, stopthreshold=0.01, raymarchingratio=1.0, maxboundzdepth=10.0, marchstep=100, buffersize=1): """ Performs aggressive ray marching using SDF values. Args: camraysnow: Tensor of camera rays (origins, directions). initzdepthnow: Initial depth offsets for unfinished rays. unfinishedmask: Boolean tensor of active rays. decoder: Neural network function to decode SDF from latent and points. latent: Latent code vector. clampdist: Maximum SDF value for clamping. stopthreshold: Minimum absolute SDF to continue marching. raymarchingratio: Scaling factor for SDF step size. maxboundzdepth: Maximum total depth bound. marchstep: Maximum number of steps. buffersize: Size to pad output tensors. Returns: sdflist, marchingzdepthlist, pointslist: Concatenated tensors. """ sdflist = [] marchingzdepthlist = [] pointslist = [] marchingzdepthnow = torch.zeroslike(initzdepthnow) for step in range(marchstep): # Check if any rays are unfinished if not torch.any(unfinishedmask): break # Get indices of unfinished rays activeindices = torch.nonzero(unfinishedmask).squeeze() # Initialize depths for current step # Note: initzdepthnow is assumed to be constant or pre-computed currentz = initzdepthnow[activeindices] + marchingzdepthnow[activeindices] # Generate 3D point samples along camera rays # Assuming camraysnow has structure (origin, direction) origins = camraysnow[activeindices,:3] directions = camraysnow[activeindices, 3:6] pointsnow = origins + directions currentz.unsqueeze(1) # Decode SDF values sdfnow = decoder(pointsnow, latent) # Clamp SDF values sdfmarching = torch.clamp(sdfnow, -clampdist, clampdist) # Update marching depth marchingzdepthnow[activeindices] += sdfmarching raymarchingratio # Store results sdflist.append(sdfmarching.unsqueeze(0)) marchingzdepthlist.append(marchingzdepthnow[activeindices].unsqueeze(0)) pointslist.append(pointsnow.unsqueeze(0)) # Update unfinished mask totaldepth = marchingzdepthnow + initzdepthnow conditiondepth = totaldepth < maxboundzdepth conditionsdf = torch.abs(sdfmarching) >= stopthreshold # Combine conditions unfinishedmask[activeindices] = conditiondepth & conditionsdf # Pad results to buffersize # Note: This is a simplified padding logic; actual implementation may vary # based on how buffersize is used (e.g., for batch processing) # The source indicates concatenation along dim 0 to form (marchstep, N) # Here we assume the lists are already structured for concatenation sdflist = torch.cat(sdflist, dim=0) marchingzdepthlist = torch.cat(marchingzdepthlist, dim=0) pointslist = torch.cat(pointslist, dim=0) return sdflist, marchingzdepthlist, pointslist Parameters: clampdist: Maximum distance used to clamp SDF values. Default 0.1. stopthreshold: Minimum absolute SDF value to continue. If abs(sdf) < stopthreshold, the ray is finished. raymarchingratio: Scaling factor for the SDF step size. Edge Cases: If latenttensor does not correspond to a valid shape, pointstmp is None and Chamfer distance calculation fails. Precision issues may arise if stopthreshold is too small relative to floating-point precision. Boundary conditions are handled by maxboundzdepth. A multi-scale ray marching technique that starts at a low resolution (large scale) to initialize depth, then upsamples and refines the depth and SDF at higher resolutions (smaller scales) recursively [3802-pyramid-recursive-ray-marching.md]. It is chosen when multi-scale detail is required without excessive computation at high resolution from the start. Integrates ray marching with distance-based empty space leaping for complex scenes, using coarse SDFs to compute large skips in low-density regions before switching to fine-grained tracing near features. It balances speed and accuracy in multi-material volumes. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active rays and steps, but reduced by large skips in empty space. Memory Complexity: Proportional to marchstep N for storing SDF, depth, and point lists. Performance: Efficient for scenes with large empty regions due to SDF-based leaping. Performance degrades if stopthreshold is too low, causing excessive steps near surfaces. Strengths: Adaptive step size, efficient empty space skipping, compatible with neural implicit representations. Limitations: Requires SDF computation (neural or explicit), sensitive to clampdist and stopthreshold parameters. When to Use: Scenes with significant empty space and complex surfaces, especially when using neural implicit representations. When Not to Use: Uniform media where constant step marching is more appropriate. Originated in the context of neural implicit surface reconstruction and rendering, specifically in the DIST-Renderer project. It leverages the properties of SDFs for efficient ray traversal, a concept well-established in computer graphics, but applies it within a neural rendering framework using latent codes. The technique is part of a broader family of SDF-accelerated ray marching methods [1629-performance-optimizations-for-sdf-ray-marching.md]. name: Pyramid Recursive Ray Marching
head: Depth Rendering Pipeline, trivial
body: Pyramid Recursive Ray Marching is a multi-scale acceleration technique for Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching that initializes depth estimates at low resolution and recursively refines them at higher resolutions. It distinguishes itself from standard aggressive ray marching by decoupling the coarse initialization phase from the fine-grained recursive refinement, allowing for larger initial steps in empty space while maintaining precision near surfaces. Inputs: Latent code vector z \in \mathbb{R}^d. Camera pose (intrinsic matrix K, extrinsic matrix RT). Image resolution (H, W). Parameters: marchstep (total steps), raymarchingratio (step scaling factor), threshold (SDF surface threshold), clampdist (distance clamping, default 0.1), splittype ('depth' or 'raydepth'), sampleindextype ('minabs', default). Outputs: Rendered depth map Z \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}. Valid mask M \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W}. Minimum SDF sample per ray for differentiability. Points and SDF values along the ray. Data Structures: scalelist: List of resolutions from lowest to highest. rayslist: List of ray origins and directions for each scale. gridmaps: List of SDF values sampled at each scale. indexmaps: Mapping indices for upsampling from lower to higher resolution. recalibmaps: Recalibration factors for ray direction/origin adjustments. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute camera rays for the target resolution (H, W). Calculate initial intersection with unit spheres to determine initzdepth and a preliminary validmask. Initialize minsdfsamplenew tensor with zeros and enable gradients. 2. Scale Pyramid Construction: Generate a list of downscaled grid maps, rays, index maps, recalib maps, and valid masks for each scale in scalelist (reversed order, from coarsest to finest). For scales other than the original (index idx > 0), compute downscaled grid maps and rays using getdownscaledcamerarays. Calculate the valid mask for the current scale by max-pooling the previous scale's valid mask using maxpoolvalidmaskwithindex. 3. Coarse-to-Fine Marching Loop: Iterate through scales from largest (lowest resolution) to smallest (original resolution). For non-final scales (idx > 0): Perform single-scale ray marching using raymarchingtrivial. Unmap the results from the valid mask indices to full image dimensions using unmaptensorwithvalidmask. Upsample the SDF, points, and z-depth to the next higher resolution using the indexmap and recalibmap. For the final scale (idx == 0, original resolution): Perform recursive ray marching using raymarchingrecursive. Concatenate the final scale results with the upsampled results from previous scales, filtering by the valid mask. 4. Differentiable Sample Selection: Identify the minimum SDF sample along the marching path. Copy minsdfsample values to minsdfsamplenew at valid mask indices. For invalid mask indices, set minsdfsamplenew to dist + threshold - radius to handle camera gradients. 5. Depth Computation: Compute source z-depth as initzdepth at valid mask plus marchingzdepth. Copy srczdepth to Z at valid mask indices and reshape to (H, W). Update validmask using validmaskrender. If nograddepth is true, detach Z from the computation graph. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pyramidrecursiveraymarching(latentcode, camera, resolution, marchstep, threshold, clampdist=0.1, splittype='depth', sampleindextype='minabs'): """ Implements Pyramid Recursive Ray Marching. """ # 1. Initialization H, W = resolution rays = getcamerarays(camera, H, W) initzdepth, validmask = computeinitialsphereintersection(rays) # Initialize differentiable min SDF tensor minsdfsamplenew = torch.zeros((H, W), requiresgrad=True) # 2. Build Pyramid # Determine scale list based on resolution and marchstep scalelist = generatescalelist(H, W, marchstep) rayslist = [] gridmaps = [] indexmaps = [] recalibmaps = [] validmasks = [] # Generate lists for all scales (reversed order: coarsest first) for i, scale in enumerate(reversed(scalelist)): if i == 0: # Coarsest scale currentrays = getdownscaledcamerarays(rays, scale) currentgrid = samplesdfgrid(latentcode, currentrays, scale) currentvalid = computevalidmask(currentrays) else: # Intermediate scales prevscale = scalelist[-(i-1)] # Logic simplified for description currentrays = getdownscaledcamerarays(rays, scale) currentgrid = samplesdfgrid(latentcode, currentrays, scale) # Max-pool previous valid mask currentvalid = maxpoolvalidmaskwithindex(validmasks[-1], indexmaps[-1]) rayslist.append(currentrays) gridmaps.append(currentgrid) validmasks.append(currentvalid) # Index and recalib maps generated for upsampling indexmaps.append(generateindexmap(scale, prevscale if i > 0 else None)) recalibmaps.append(generaterecalibmap(splittype, currentrays)) # 3. Coarse-to-Fine Iteration upsampledsdf = None upsampledzdepth = None upsampledpoints = None # Iterate from coarsest (index 0 in reversed list) to finest for idx in range(len(scalelist)): # Note: rayslist[0] is coarsest, rayslist[-1] is finest (original) currentrays = rayslist[idx] currentgrid = gridmaps[idx] currentvalid = validmasks[idx] if idx < len(scalelist) - 1: # Non-final scale: Trivial marching sdflist, zdepthlist, pointslist = raymarchingtrivial( currentrays, currentgrid, marchstep, threshold, clampdist) # Unmap to full resolution sdffull = unmaptensorwithvalidmask(sdflist, currentvalid, H, W) zdepthfull = unmaptensorwithvalidmask(zdepthlist, currentvalid, H, W) pointsfull = unmaptensorwithvalidmask(pointslist, currentvalid, H, W) # Upsample to next scale nextidx = idx + 1 upsampledsdf = upsampletensor(sdffull, indexmaps[nextidx], recalibmaps[nextidx]) upsampledzdepth = upsampletensor(zdepthfull, indexmaps[nextidx], recalibmaps[nextidx]) upsampledpoints = upsampletensor(pointsfull, indexmaps[nextidx], recalibmaps[nextidx]) else: # Final scale: Recursive marching sdflist, zdepthlist, pointslist = raymarchingrecursive( currentrays, currentgrid, marchstep, threshold, clampdist, initzdepth=upsampledzdepth, sdfinit=upsampledsdf) # Concatenate final results with upsampled history finalsdf = concatenatewithupsampled(sdflist, upsampledsdf, currentvalid) finalzdepth = concatenatewithupsampled(zdepthlist, upsampledzdepth, currentvalid) finalpoints = concatenatewithupsampled(pointslist, upsampledpoints, currentvalid) # 4. Differentiable Sample Selection # Find min SDF sample minsdf = findminsdf(finalsdf) # Copy to new tensor at valid indices minsdfsamplenew[currentvalid == 1] = minsdf[currentvalid == 1] # Handle invalid indices for gradient flow invalidmask = currentvalid == 0 if invalidmask.any(): # dist is distance to camera, radius is object radius minsdfsamplenew[invalidmask] = dist + threshold - radius # 5. Depth Computation srczdepth = initzdepth + finalzdepth Z = torch.zeros((H, W)) Z[currentvalid == 1] = srczdepth[currentvalid == 1] # Update valid mask validmask = validmaskrender(finalsdf, threshold) # Detach if necessary if nograddepth: Z = Z.detach() return Z, validmask, minsdfsamplenew, finalpoints Parameters: raymarchingtype: String specifying the marching algorithm. Valid values are 'trivialnonparallel', 'trivial', 'recursive', and 'pyramidrecursive'. splittype: String specifying the splitting strategy for pyramid recursive marching. Valid values are 'depth' and 'raydepth'. If 'raydepth', recalibmapnow is set to ones. clampdist: Float parameter for distance clamping, default 0.1. sampleindextype: String for selecting the sample index, default 'minabs'. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Upsampling artifacts may occur if index maps are not accurately computed. Boundaries: Invalid mask indices must be handled explicitly to prevent NaN gradients during backpropagation. Degenerate Input: If marchsteplist[-1] == -1, it must be set to marchstep - sum(marchsteplist[:-1]) to ensure total steps are preserved. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) where N is the number of pixels, due to the multi-scale approach reducing the number of samples needed at high resolution. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the pyramid levels and intermediate results. Performance: Significantly faster than single-scale recursive marching for high-resolution images, as coarse scales quickly eliminate empty space. Strengths: Efficient initialization of depth, robust handling of large empty spaces, differentiable rendering. Limitations: Complexity of implementation due to multiple upsampling and recalibration steps. Potential for aliasing if downsampling is not handled carefully. Pyramid Recursive Ray Marching is part of the DIST-Renderer project, an unofficial implementation of DeepSDF rendering techniques. It was developed to address the computational cost of high-resolution SDF rendering by leveraging multi-scale processing. The method is used in the context of neural implicit surface representation and differentiable rendering. B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, https://github.com/B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Coverage Search
head: SDF Raymarching Algorithm: Coverage Search
body: Coverage Search is a distance-field ray marching algorithm designed to determine ray hit or miss status in fewer iterations than standard sphere tracing by using a stack to manage coverage spans along the ray. It sets itself apart from siblings like Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF by explicitly tracking intervals of guaranteed empty or occupied space, allowing it to skip large portions of the ray where the signed distance function (SDF) would otherwise be evaluated repeatedly without progress. Inputs and Outputs: RayOrigin: The starting position of the ray. RayDirection: The normalized direction vector of the ray. TravelStart: Estimated start travel distance (e.g., from bounding volume intersection). TravelEnd: Estimated end travel distance (e.g., from bounding volume intersection). SignedDistanceFunction(p): A function returning the signed distance from point p to the nearest surface. Position (output): The 3D position of the hit or the end of the ray. Return value: true if a hit occurred, false otherwise. Data Structures: Coverage: A struct containing: Low: Float, the start of the coverage span along the ray parameter. High: Float, the end of the coverage span along the ray parameter. Sign: Integer, 1 if the span is inside the object (negative distance), -1 if outside (positive distance), 0 for neutral/initial states. Stack: A dynamic array or fixed-size buffer of Coverage structs. The source notes a required size of approximately 10 for GLSL implementations. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the stack. 2. Calculate the initial pivot point in the middle of the travel bounds. 3. Evaluate the SDF at the pivot. 4. Determine the coverage span of the pivot based on the SDF value. 5. Iterate through the stack, merging or subdividing spans until the ray start is subsumed by a known coverage span. 6. Determine the final hit position based on the sign of the final cursor span. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def CoverageSearch(RayOrigin, RayDirection, TravelStart, TravelEnd): # 1. Initialize Stack # The stack manages spans of travel distance. # Initial push: a neutral span at the end of the ray. Stack = [] Stack.append(Coverage(High=TravelEnd, Low=TravelEnd, Sign=0)) # 2. Initial Pivot Calculation PivotTravel = (TravelStart + TravelEnd) 0.5 PivotPoint = RayOrigin + RayDirection PivotTravel PivotRadius = SignedDistanceFunction(PivotPoint) # 3. Push Initial Coverage Span # The span extends from PivotTravel minus the distance to PivotTravel plus the distance. # The sign indicates if the pivot is inside (-1) or outside (1) the object. # Note: sign() returns -1 for negative, 1 for positive, 0 for zero. InitialSign = 1 if PivotRadius > 0 else (-1 if PivotRadius < 0 else 0) SpanLow = PivotTravel - abs(PivotRadius) SpanHigh = PivotTravel + abs(PivotRadius) Stack.append(Coverage(High=SpanHigh, Low=SpanLow, Sign=InitialSign)) # 4. Initialize Cursor # The cursor tracks the current "frontier" of known coverage starting from TravelStart. Cursor = Coverage(High=TravelStart, Low=TravelStart, Sign=0) # 5. Main Loop while len(Stack) > 0: Top = Stack[-1] # Check if the top of the stack overlaps with the current cursor's known high point. # If Stack[Top].Low <= Cursor.High, the stack span is reachable/merged. if Top.Low <= Cursor.High: # Merge the stack span into the cursor. # The cursor expands to cover the stack span. Cursor = Stack.pop() else: # The stack span is ahead of the cursor. We need to subdivide. # Calculate a new pivot between the cursor's high and the stack's low. PivotTravel = (Top.Low + Cursor.High) 0.5 PivotPoint = RayOrigin + RayDirection PivotTravel PivotRadius = SignedDistanceFunction(PivotPoint) # Determine the new coverage span for this pivot. NextSign = 1 if PivotRadius > 0 else (-1 if PivotRadius < 0 else 0) NextLow = PivotTravel - abs(PivotRadius) NextHigh = PivotTravel + abs(PivotRadius) Next = Coverage(High=NextHigh, Low=NextLow, Sign=NextSign) # Check for merging conditions. # If the new span has a different sign than the stack top AND overlaps with it, # we can potentially merge or adjust the stack top's low bound. # The condition abs(Stack[Top].Sign + Next.Sign) > 0 implies signs are not opposite (i.e., same sign or one is zero). # However, the source logic specifically checks if they can be merged/adjusted. if abs(Top.Sign + Next.Sign) > 0 and Top.Low <= Next.High: # Adjust the stack top's low bound to the new span's low. # This effectively merges the new span into the existing stack top if they are compatible. Top.Low = Next.Low else: # Push the new span onto the stack. Stack.append(Next) # 6. Determine Result # If the final cursor sign is -1 (inside), we hit the object. # The hit position is at the start of the inside span (Cursor.Low). # If the cursor sign is not -1, we missed. if Cursor.Sign == -1: # Clamp to TravelStart to ensure we don't go before the start bound. HitTravel = max(TravelStart, Cursor.Low) Position = RayOrigin + RayDirection HitTravel return True, Position else: Position = RayOrigin + RayDirection TravelEnd return False, Position class Coverage: def init(self, High, Low, Sign): self.High = High self.Low = Low self.Sign = Sign Parameters: TravelStart: Typically derived from the intersection of the ray with a simple bounding volume (e.g., AABB or sphere). TravelEnd: Typically derived from the intersection of the ray with a simple bounding volume. Stack Size: Experimentally, a stack size of approximately 10 was required for the GLSL implementation to work correctly, whereas an initial non-shader implementation required only a size of 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shader Occupancy: The stack consumes shader registers/occupancy, which can reduce performance on hardware with limited resources. Branching: The algorithm is branchier than standard sphere tracing, which may impact performance on GPUs. SDF Cost: The approach is only worthwhile if the SignedDistanceFunction is sufficiently expensive to justify the overhead of stack management and branching. Discrepancy in Stack Size: There is an unexplained discrepancy between the required stack size in the GLSL implementation (10) and the initial analysis implementation (4), potentially due to a bug in the GLSL version. Precision: The calculation of SpanLow and SpanHigh uses abs(PivotRadius). If PivotRadius is very small, precision issues may arise, though not explicitly detailed in the source. Performance: In the ideal case, Coverage Search performs approximately the same number of SignedDistanceFunction calls as sphere tracing. However, it results in half as many calls when the average signed distance approaches zero without hitting zero. Suitability: The method is best suited for environments suitable for recursive algorithms and where the SDF is expensive to evaluate. It is less suitable for scenes with simple, cheap SDFs or hardware with strict occupancy limits. Comparison to Siblings: Unlike Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF which may skip steps based on distance thresholds, Coverage Search explicitly manages intervals. It differs from SDF-Accelerated Volumetric Ray Marching by focusing on hit/miss determination via span coverage rather than volumetric accumulation. The Coverage Search algorithm was developed by the author of the source material as an effort to solve ray hit/miss determination in fewer iterations than standard sphere tracing. It was designed to address cases where standard raymarching requires substantially more iterations, such as hitting an object dead-on, hitting at an acute angle, or running parallel to an object without hitting it. The algorithm was initially analyzed in a non-shader implementation and later ported to GLSL. SDF Raymarching, https://zone.dog/braindump/sdfmarching/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Zeno Implementation
head: Zeno, Zeno Implementation for Implicit Surfaces
body:
The Zeno implementation is a specific software architecture for sphere tracing that minimizes the coding effort required to add new implicit surfaces by relying on a numerical gradient approximation for shading. It solves the problem of boilerplate code in ray tracers by allowing primitives to be defined solely by a signed distance function (SDF), automatically deriving normals via finite differences. It differs from standard sphere tracing implementations by explicitly decoupling the intersection logic from the shading logic, using a fixed six-sample stencil for gradients rather than analytical derivatives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A signed distance function f(\mathbf{p}) that returns the distance from point \mathbf{p} to the implicit surface. Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Output: Intersection point \mathbf{p} and surface normal \mathbf{n}. Data Structures: The implementation does not require explicit storage of surface normals or analytical derivative functions. The SDF f(\mathbf{p}) is the only required user-defined function for visualization. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Marching: Perform standard sphere tracing using the SDF f(\mathbf{p}) to find the intersection point \mathbf{p} along the ray. Initialize t = 0. Loop: Evaluate d = f(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}). If d < \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small threshold), break and set \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. If d > t{max}, break and return no intersection. t \leftarrow t + d. 2. Normal Approximation: If shading is required, compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} using a six-sample numerical gradient approximation of the SDF gradient. Let \mathbf{p} be the intersection point. Let h be a small step size (e.g., machine epsilon or a small constant relative to scene scale). Compute the gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) using central differences along the three axes: 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) \approx  egin{bmatrix}  rac{f(\mathbf{p} + h\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{p} - h\mathbf{x})}{2h} \  rac{f(\mathbf{p} + h\mathbf{y}) - f(\mathbf{p} - h\mathbf{y})}{2h} \  rac{f(\mathbf{p} + h\mathbf{z}) - f(\mathbf{p} - h\mathbf{z})}{2h} \end{bmatrix} where \mathbf{x} = (1,0,0), \mathbf{y} = (0,1,0), and \mathbf{z} = (0,0,1). Normalize the gradient to obtain the normal: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{p})\|}. 3. Shading: Use \mathbf{n} for standard lighting calculations. Parameters: h: Step size for numerical gradient. Not given in the sources. Typical values are small, e.g., 10^{-4} to 10^{-6}, or derived from the SDF's scale. \epsilon: Threshold for intersection detection. Not given in the sources. Typically a small value like 10^{-4} or relative to ray length. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: CSG and Blending: The negative part of the signed distance bound is only necessary for constructive solid geometry (CSG) and blending operations. For simple visualization of functions zero-valued inside the surface, the negative part is not needed. Performance: The numerical gradient approximation is inefficient compared to analytical derivatives, but its impact on overall rendering performance is negligible because most time is spent on ray intersection. Precision: The numerical gradient may suffer from precision issues if h is too small (catastrophic cancellation) or too large (poor approximation). Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zenospheretrace(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, maxsteps=1000, maxdist=100.0, epsilon=1e-4): """ Performs sphere tracing using the Zeno implementation's numerical gradient for normals. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple or array raydirection: (x, y, z) tuple or array, assumed normalized sdf: Function that takes (x, y, z) and returns signed distance maxsteps: Maximum number of march steps maxdist: Maximum total distance to march epsilon: Threshold for intersection Returns: (hitpoint, normal) if hit, else (None, None) """ t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return None, None p = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) d = sdf(p[0], p[1], p[2]) if d < epsilon: # Intersection found, compute normal normal = computenumericalgradient(p, sdf) return p, normal t += d return None, None def computenumericalgradient(p, sdf, h=1e-4): """ Computes the gradient of the SDF at point p using a six-sample central difference. Args: p: (x, y, z) tuple or array sdf: Function that takes (x, y, z) and returns signed distance h: Step size for finite differences Returns: Normalized gradient vector (nx, ny, nz) """ x, y, z = p # Central differences dx = (sdf(x + h, y, z) - sdf(x - h, y, z)) / (2 h) dy = (sdf(x, y + h, z) - sdf(x, y - h, z)) / (2 h) dz = (sdf(x, y, z + h) - sdf(x, y, z - h)) / (2 h) # Normalize length = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz) 0.5 if length < 1e-10: return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Fallback, though degenerate return (dx / length, dy / length, dz / length) Renders volumetric data using SDFs, focusing on density accumulation rather than surface intersection. Choose when rendering fog, clouds, or medical volumes. Uses a fixed step size for ray marching, simpler but less efficient for complex surfaces. Choose when performance is not critical or surfaces are uniformly simple. Specific implementation for fractal geometry, often using recursive distance bounds. Choose when rendering fractals like the Menger sponge. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of ray march steps. The numerical gradient adds a constant factor of 6 SDF evaluations per intersection, but this is negligible compared to the cost of ray intersection. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as no explicit normal storage or analytical derivative functions are required. Measured Performance: Runs at speeds comparable to other implicit surface rendering algorithms. Strengths: Simplicity of implementation; easy to add new primitives by defining only an SDF. Limitations: Numerical gradient is less accurate than analytical derivatives; not suitable for applications requiring high-precision normals (e.g., precise shadow mapping). When to Use: Visualization of mathematical tasks and investigation of new implicit surfaces. When Not to Use: When analytical normals are required for high-quality shading or when performance is critical and SDF evaluation is expensive. The Zeno implementation was developed as part of the Zeno rendering system, which implemented sphere tracing for antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces. It was used for the animated short "Air on the Dirac Strings" (1993), which visualized a homotopy removing a 720° twist from a ribbon using interpolated quaternion rotations. The system was designed to facilitate the visualization of mathematical tasks and the investigation of new implicit surfaces. Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2792108SphereTracingAGeometricMethodfortheAntialiasedRayTracingofImplicitSurfaces, fetched 2026-10-27 Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, http://graphics.cs.illinois.edu/sites/default/files/zeno.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Splatting
body: Splatting is an object-order volume rendering technique that computes the contribution of each voxel to the image by convolving the voxel with a filter (kernel) that distributes its value to a neighborhood of pixels on the screen. It differs from feed-backward (image-order/ray-casting) methods by mapping direction: feed-forward spreads input information to output (object-order), while feed-backward queries input from output pixels. It offers rendering quality similar to ray casting, and both ray casting and splatting provided in some cases better image qualities than shear-warp. The core mechanism of splatting involves treating the volume as a continuous function defined by smooth kernels centered at each voxel. The rendering process follows these shared steps: 1. Kernel Definition: Each voxel is represented by a 3D reconstruction kernel, typically a Gaussian distribution with mean \mu = 0.0 and standard deviation \sigma = 1.0, truncated outside a radius of 2.0 with a peak value of 1.0. The contribution of a voxel at position D to a screen point (x,y,z) is given by: \text{contribution}D(x,y,z) = hV(x-Dx, y-Dy, z-Dz) \cdot \rho(D) where hV is the volumetric reconstruction kernel and \rho(D) is the voxel density. 2. Projection (Splatting): The 3D kernel is projected onto the 2D image plane, creating a "footprint" or "splat". The weight of the splat at pixel (x,y) relative to the voxel's projection (Dx, Dy) is: \text{weight}(x,y)D = \text{footprint}(x-Dx, y-Dy) The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density: P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D). 3. Footprint Representation: For regular grids, the footprint is typically a circle invariant to rotations. To avoid aliasing, the opacity is convolved with a smoothing kernel (e.g., Gaussian). A splat diameter of 1.6 times the spacing between values is sufficient to avoid aliasing while preventing excessive blurring. For perspective projections, the splat size must be adjusted according to the sample's distance from the viewpoint. Efficient representation often uses a screen-aligned quadrilateral texture-mapped with an opacity-weighted texture. 4. Compositing: Splats are composited using alpha blending. Depending on the optical model, they must be rendered in front-to-back or back-to-front order. Compositing in splatting is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time). 5. Sheet-Based Traversal: A common implementation traverses the volume one sheet of voxels at a time, from front to back. The sheet (x-y, x-z, or y-z) nearest to being parallel with the image plane is selected. Each voxel in the sheet is transformed from grid space to screen space, shaded independently to produce an (R,G,B,\alpha) tuple, and projected into an accumulation sheet. The accumulation sheet is composited with the working image after all voxels in the sheet are processed. 6. Shading: Shading can be performed via pre-shading (classifying/shading voxels before projection) or post-shading. Post-shading maintains three sheet-buffers (previous, current, next), projects 3D kernels into the next buffer, estimates gradients using central differences on the current buffer based on the next and previous buffers, and shades using the normalized gradient. Not given in the sources. EWA Splatting is an object-order rendering technique that approximates the volumetric integration of 3D Gaussian primitives by projecting them into 2D elliptical disks (splats) and rasterizing them as screen-space filters. It solves the computational cost of ray-marching by assuming Gaussians do not overlap and are sorted by view-space depth, trading continuous extinction accumulation for efficient, hole-free reconstruction. It differs from standard point rendering by using anisotropic, band-limited elliptical footprints derived from the Gaussian covariance, whereas simplified variants use screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic falloff. A technique merging splatting with raycasting principles, where splats are suspended in object space and rays are spawned to intersect them, enabling perspective projection efficiency and acceleration methods. A forward mapping rendering algorithm for regular volumetric grids with potentially different spacings in the three grid directions, calculating image plane footprints for each data sample. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. A rendering pipeline that operates in one single rendering pass, using VBOs for elevation data and texture objects for attributes, avoiding multiple render targets or additional blending passes. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. An optimization for volume splatting that skips processing of voxels when the accumulated opacity at the target screen pixels is already full, analogous to early ray termination in ray casting. It works by projecting two volumes: the density volume and an opacity volume. For each projected voxel, a 2D bounding box is computed around the pixels covering the splat. If all pixels inside the bounding box have full opacity (1.0 or near 1.0), the voxel processing is skipped. A rendering solution introduced in that uses extinction (referred to as 'density' in NeRF literature) instead of the learned opacity value used in 3DGS, to analyze the difference between opacity-based and accurate volumetric rendering. For small numbers of primitives, extinction-based splatting performs better than opacity-based splatting. However, with more primitives, opacity splatting performs best. A volume rendering algorithm that performs classification and shading after voxels are projected onto the screen to avoid blurring object edges, which occurs when classification is done prior to projection. It projects voxel densities onto the screen using regular splats (radially symmetric interpolation kernels). It projects gradient volumes onto the screen using gradient splats, OR computes gradients on the projection plane using central differencing on the projected density. It performs per-pixel shading using the computed gradients to classify and color the voxels. An optimization uses lookup tables for shading to handle the added overhead of screen gradients and per-pixel shading. Computing gradients on the projection plane via central differencing reduces the number of footprint rasterizations by a factor of four compared to projecting a separate gradient volume, because only voxel densities need to be projected. A progressive refinement algorithm for volume rendering using a pyramidal volume representation to achieve real-time interactive rendering. It constructs a pyramidal volume representation that stores average values and estimated error for each cell. It fits an octtree to the pyramid based on a user-supplied precision threshold. It draws the octtree using a set of splats (footprints), where each splat is scaled to match the size of the projection of the corresponding volume cell. It approximates the splats with RGBA Gouraud-shaded polygons for efficient rasterization on modern graphics workstations. A method to adjust splat radii to prevent holes between splats when samples are elevated in the normal direction of the base plane, by scaling the radius based on the angle between the splat normal and the base plane normal. The radius r is calculated as: r = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu}{0.1 + 0.9\langle n, nB \rangle} where r is the radius, \mu is the sampling step size of the regular grid, n is the normal vector of the splat, and nB is the normal vector of the base plane. The constant 0.1 in the denominator establishes scaling and prevents division by zero or excessively large radii when the dot product is small. The constant 0.9 in the denominator controls the maximal radius increase; when \langle n, nB \rangle = 1, the denominator is 1.0, and r = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu. If samples are elevated in the normal direction of the plane, holes may occur between splats if radii are not adjusted. A large angle between the splat normal and the plane normal indicates large variance between neighboring elevation values, resulting in increased spatial gaps, necessitating larger radii. A method for modeling dynamic Gaussians for time-varying content. It develops a spatiotemporal structure encoder to capture deformations of both positions and colors over time. A method that mitigates popping artifacts caused by the sorting procedure in volume splatting. A method that enhances robustness by detecting outliers in a richer, pre-trained feature space to ignore transient distractors. Splatting was originally proposed by Lee Westover in 1990. It is based on the idea of treating each voxel as a fuzzy spherical ball (3D Gaussian) projected onto the screen, determining how every pixel might be affected by that voxel, as opposed to ray-casting which determines how every voxel affects a pixel. The continuous volume is defined as a collection of smooth functions (Gaussians) centered at each voxel, with density assigned at the center and dropping off according to the distribution. The term "splat" refers to the footprint left on the image plane, analogous to throwing a cube of gelatinous material onto the plane. Axis-aligned sheet buffered splatting causes 'popping' artifacts when viewing angles change around 45 degrees because kernels in consecutive sheets are composited together while kernels on the same sheet are added together, and addition/compositing are not equivalent. To mitigate this, image-aligned sheet buffered splatting aligns sheet buffers parallel with the image plane regardless of volume orientation, slicing the volume into thin slabs representing portions of the line integral through the entire kernel. Splatting algorithms suffer from time-consuming computations necessary to compute the view-dependent filters with which to convolute the voxels in the volume. Observations showed that overall splatting offers a rendering quality similar to that of ray casting, and both ray casting and splatting provided in some cases better image qualities than shear-warp. This is because in shear-warp, rendered voxels were interpolated without prior opacity and color being incorporated, whereas splatting incorporates these during the footprint projection.
