name: Perspective Correct Splat Rasterization with EWA Approximation
head: Affine approximation to projective mapping, Approximate EWA splatting, EWA point splatting, Fast splat rasterization, Perspective Accurate Splatting with EWA Filter
body: This method is an improved splat rendering pipeline that combines a perspectively correct fast splat rasterization procedure with an approximation of the Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) filter. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts and visual holes in point-sampled geometry rendering, particularly when the model is viewed from flat angles or shifted from the viewing axis. Unlike its siblings, it uses an affine approximation to the projective mapping to ensure perspective-correct splat shapes without requiring per-point normals or complex anisotropic footprint calculations, trading exact band-limited footprints for a formulation that avoids holes and Moiré patterns. It builds on EWA Splatting by replacing the standard EWA covariance computation with a faster, perspective-correct affine approximation. The method operates in a multi-pass pipeline, typically involving a visibility pass, an attribute pass, and a normalization pass. It relies on an affine approximation of the projective mapping to compute the splat's screen-space shape. Inputs: Point-sampled geometry (positions, attributes), camera projection matrix, view matrix, window resolution. Outputs: Final composited image with alpha blending. Lookup Table (LUT): A 1D texture storing Gaussian filter weights. The index is determined by the squared distance r^2 from the splat center in screen space, normalized by the filter width. Conic Matrix: A 2 \times 2 matrix representing the inverse of the resampling filter's variance in screen space. 1. Vertex Processing (Visibility and Shape Approximation): For each splat k: a. Compute the projective mapping matrix Mk that maps the local Gaussian reconstruction kernel to screen space. b. Compute the inverse Mk^{-1} to derive the approximate variance matrix Q{000}. c. Numerical Stability Check: Calculate the condition number of Mk. If it exceeds a threshold (indicating the splat is degenerating into a line segment or is numerically ill-conditioned), discard the splat. d. Ellipse Check: Determine if the resulting conic Q{000} represents an ellipse using specific criteria (e.g., determinant sign and trace properties). If it is not an ellipse, discard the splat. e. Bounding Box: Compute the bounding box for the OpenGL point size based on the ellipse extent. f. Pass the 2 \times 2 conic matrix (Q{000} + H)^{-1} to the fragment program, where H is the Gaussian prefilter variance. 2. Fragment Processing (EWA Filtering): For every pixel x covered by the OpenGL point primitive: a. Evaluate the ellipse equation: r^2 = x (Q{000} + H)^{-1} x^T where x is the pixel coordinate vector relative to the splat center, available via the wpos input parameter. b. If r^2 < Fg^2 (where Fg is the Gaussian filter width threshold), use r^2 as an index into the 1D LUT to retrieve the Gaussian filter weight. c. Otherwise, discard the fragment. d. Output the weighted attribute value and alpha. 3. Normalization Pass: a. Copy the result of the attribute pass (weighted sum of attributes and alpha) to a texture. b. Render a window-sized rectangle using this texture. c. In the fragment program, perform the division by the accumulated alpha to normalize the color values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexprogram(splatposition, projectionmatrix, viewmatrix): # 1. Compute projective mapping matrix Mk Mk = computeprojectivemapping(splatposition, projectionmatrix, viewmatrix) # 2. Invert Mk to get Q000 Mkinv = invert2x2matrix(Mk) Q000 = computevariancefrominverse(Mkinv) # 3. Check condition number for numerical stability condnumber = conditionnumber(Mk) if condnumber > THRESHOLD: return discardsplat() # 4. Check if conic is an ellipse if not isellipse(Q000): return discardsplat() # 5. Compute bounding box for OpenGL point size pointsize = computeboundingboxsize(Q000) # 6. Compute final conic matrix for fragment shader # H is the Gaussian prefilter variance (constant or per-splat) H = getgaussianprefiltervariance() conicmatrix = invert2x2matrix(Q000 + H) return { 'pointsize': pointsize, 'conicmatrix': conicmatrix, 'splatcenter': projecttoscreen(splatposition) } def fragmentprogram(conicmatrix, splatcenter, wpos): # wpos is the pixel coordinate x = wpos - splatcenter # Evaluate ellipse equation r^2 = x (Q000 + H)^-1 x^T # Note: x is a row vector, so x^T is column rsquared = dotproduct(x, multiplymatrixvector(conicmatrix, transpose(x))) # Fg is the Gaussian filter width threshold if rsquared < Fgsquared: # Lookup Gaussian weight from 1D texture weight = texturelookup1d(gaussianlut, rsquared) return { 'color': splatcolor weight, 'alpha': splatalpha weight } else: return discardfragment() def normalizationpass(renderedtexture): # Render full-screen quad for each pixel: accumulatedcolor = texturelookup(renderedtexture, pixelcoord).color accumulatedalpha = texturelookup(renderedtexture, pixelcoord).alpha if accumulatedalpha > 0: finalcolor = accumulatedcolor / accumulatedalpha else: finalcolor = 0 return finalcolor Threshold for Condition Number: Not given in the sources. Gaussian Filter Width (Fg): Not given in the sources. Prefilter Variance (H): Not given in the sources. Numerical Ill-Conditioning: The inversion of Mk can be numerically unstable if the splat degenerates into a line segment. This is handled by checking the condition number and discarding the splat. Non-Elliptic Conics: The projective mapping can result in a conic that is not an ellipse. These must be detected and discarded to avoid incorrect rasterization. Splat Center Approximation: The splat centers are not mapped to the perspective-correct position (approximation in Section 4.4 of). However, no visual artifacts were observed due to this approximation. Clipping Overhead: Splat clipping adds overhead. The implementation switches between two fragment shaders (clipped and non-clipped) because typically only a few splats require clipping. Renders splats by first computing surface normals and then projecting them. It differs by explicitly handling surface orientation, whereas this method uses an affine approximation to projective mapping for perspective correctness without explicit normals. Link Applies Phong shading to splats. It differs by adding shading, while this method focuses on perspective-correct rasterization and EWA filtering. Link A general EWA splatting renderer for mesh-free data. It differs by being a general renderer, while this method specifically uses an affine approximation for perspective correctness. Link Uses k-NN for covariance estimation. It differs by using k-NN for covariance, whereas this method uses an affine approximation to the projective mapping. Link Time Complexity: The vertex program is relatively simple, while the fragment program is more complex due to the EWA filter evaluation. Compared to raycasting, the splatting approach requires simpler vertex programs but significantly more complex fragment programs. However, since the number of rasterized fragments is significantly larger than the number of splats (at least a factor of four in complete minification), the splatting approach is always more performant. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 1D LUT and intermediate textures for the normalization pass. Measured Performance: On Athlon64 3500+ / GeForce 7800 with Igea dataset at 1024x1024: 154k splats at 50 fps (7.7M splats/sec) vs 33 fps for raycasting; 460k splats at 40 fps (18.4M splats/sec) vs 26 fps; 1.4M splats at 22 fps (31M splats/sec) vs 13 fps; 2.5M splats at 15 fps (37.5M splats/sec) vs 9.2 fps; 5M splats at 6.5 fps (32.5M splats/sec) vs 5 fps. On GeForceFX 5950 GPU and Pentium IV 3.0 GHz CPU: Cg: 1 pass rendering achieved 2.9 million splats/sec at 512x512 and 2.8 million splats/sec at 1280x1024. The 3-pass algorithm achieved 1.4 million splats/sec at 512x512 and 1.2 million splats/sec at 1280x1024. Assembler: 1 pass rendering achieved 11.2 million splats/sec at 512x512 and 10.4 million splats/sec at 1280x1024. The 3-pass algorithm achieved 3.1 million splats/sec at 512x512 and 2.8 million splats/sec at 1280x1024. Strengths: Higher quality anti-aliasing filtering for splats in both minification and magnification cases compared to previous approximations. Avoids holes in the rendered image at flat viewing angles. Avoids Moiré patterns by using a Gaussian prefilter. Limitations: The fragment program is more complex than the vertex program. The approximation of splat centers may lead to minor inaccuracies, though no visual artifacts were observed. When to use: When high image quality and anti-aliasing are required for point-sampled geometry, especially with sharp features or CSG-generated objects. When perspective-correct splat shapes are needed to avoid holes at flat viewing angles. When not to use: When hardware does not support the required fragment program complexity or texture lookups. When real-time performance is critical and the overhead of the 3-pass algorithm is unacceptable. The method was presented in "Perspective Accurate Splatting" and "Splat/Mesh Blending, Perspective Rasterization and Transparency for Point-Based Rendering". It builds on the EWA splatting technique by Heckbert and improves upon previous approximations by Botsch et al. [BHZK05] and ZRB04. The approach was developed to address the limitations of earlier splatting methods, such as aliasing artifacts and holes at flat viewing angles. It is used in point-based rendering systems to render objects with sharp features created using CSG operations. name: Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting
head: Adaptive EWA Filtering, Adaptive EWA Splatting, Chen adaptive splatting, Distance-dependent Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting
body: Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting is a rendering technique that simplifies the computationally expensive Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) resampling filter by classifying volume particles into three cases based on their distance from the viewpoint. It solves the problem of high computational cost in full EWA splatting while maintaining aliasing-free quality. Unlike full EWA splatting, which always computes the combined covariance of the reconstruction and low-pass filters, this method uses only the reconstruction filter for close particles (magnification) and only the low-pass filter for far particles (minification), resorting to full EWA only in the transition zone. Inputs: Volume dataset (regular or rectilinear). Camera parameters (view angle fov, projection matrix). Reconstruction kernel cutoff radius rk and low-pass filter cutoff radius rh. Outputs: Rendered image with antialiasing. Data Structures: Packed Vertex Representation (32 bits): Used to store proxy geometry efficiently in GPU memory. tx: Volume texture coordinate X. Packed as mx \times 256 + ix. mx uses 7 bits, ix uses 8 bits. ty: Volume texture coordinate Y. Packed similarly (my 7 bits, iy 8 bits). fx, fy: Gaussian texture coordinates. Each uses 1 bit (values 0 or 1). Total: 7+8+7+8+1+1 = 32 bits. Lookup Table: Stored in constant registers, accessed via an address register in the vertex shader to decompress mx, my, fx, fy. Parameters: c{min}: Lower bound parameter for distance-dependent criteria. Typical value: 0.3. c{max}: Upper bound parameter for distance-dependent criteria. Typical value: 2.0 \times (1.0 + 2.0 \times \tan(fov/2)^2). Method Steps: 1. Patch Grouping: Group quads (voxels) of each slice into uniform rectangular patches. 2. Corner Computation: For each patch, compute the camera space coordinate u{k2} (depth) of each of the four corner voxels on-the-fly. 3. Classification: Evaluate the criteria from Equation 7 for the four vertices of the patch: Magnification (Close): If all four vertices satisfy u{k2} < \frac{rk}{rh} \times c{min}, use the reconstruction filter. Minification (Far): If all four vertices satisfy u{k2} > \frac{rk}{rh} \times c{max}, use the low-pass filter. Transition: Otherwise, use the full EWA resampling filter. 4. Filter Selection: Apply the appropriate vertex shader corresponding to the selected filter case. The filter function Hk(\mathbf{x}) is defined as: Hk(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x}^T \cdot \hat{\mathbf{V}}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{x}, & \text{if } u{k2} < \frac{rk}{rh} \times c{min} \\ \mathbf{x}^T \cdot \mathbf{V}h^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{x}, & \text{if } u{k2} > \frac{rk}{rh} \times c{max} \\ \mathbf{x} \cdot (\hat{\mathbf{V}}k + \mathbf{V}h)^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{x}, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \mathbf{x} is the screen-space offset vector. \hat{\mathbf{V}}k is the 2x2 variance matrix of the reconstruction filter, obtained by skipping the third row and column of the full 3x3 covariance matrix \mathbf{V}k. \mathbf{V}h is the 2x2 variance matrix of the Gaussian low-pass filter, usually the identity matrix. 5. Rasterization: Rasterize the proxy quads using the selected vertex shader to deform the unit Gaussian texture according to the footprint function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. CMIN = 0.3 def classifypatch(patchcornerscameraspace): """ Determines the filter type for a patch based on the depth of its four corners. patchcornerscameraspace: list of 4 tuples (uk0, uk1, uk2) Returns: 'MAGNIFICATION', 'MINIFICATION', or 'FULLEWA' """ allmagnification = True allminification = True for uk0, uk1, uk2 in patchcornerscameraspace: # Check Magnification Criterion if uk2 >= (RK / RH) CMIN: allmagnification = False # Check Minification Criterion if uk2 <= (RK / RH) CMAX: allminification = False # Early exit if neither extreme is possible for the whole patch if not allmagnification and not allminification: return 'FULLEWA' if allmagnification: return 'MAGNIFICATION' elif allminification: return 'MINIFICATION' else: return 'FULLEWA' def computefiltermatrix(filtertype, uk2, Vhatk, Vh): """ Computes the inverse covariance matrix used in the filter exponent. """ if filtertype == 'MAGNIFICATION': # Reconstruction filter only return Vhatk elif filtertype == 'MINIFICATION': # Low-pass filter only return Vh else: # Full EWA return Vhatk + Vh def renderpatch(patch): filtertype = classifypatch(patch.cornerscameraspace) filtermatrix = computefiltermatrix(filtertype, patch.avgdepth, patch.Vhatk, Vh) # Deform proxy quad geometry based on filtermatrix and rasterize # This part relies on specific vertex shader implementation details # not fully detailed in sources, but involves stretching unit Gaussian texture deformandrasterize(patch, filtermatrix) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transition Zone: In the transition between magnification and minification, neither approximation avoids aliasing artifacts without the full EWA computation. Memory Limits: A naive implementation of proxy geometry for a 256^3 volume requires 2240M bytes of memory, exceeding the 256M limit of commodity graphics hardware at the time of publication. Compression is necessary. Precision: The classification relies on conservative bounds derived from the maximum value of (u{k0}^2 + u{k1}^2 + u{k2}^2)/u{k2}^2, which is (1.0 + 2.0 \times \tan(fov/2)^2). Time Complexity: Reduces computation cost compared to full EWA splatting by using simpler filters (low-pass or reconstruction) in extreme cases, but adds classification overhead. Measured Performance: On a 512 \times 512 \times 3 checkerboard dataset: 6.88 fps vs 4.83 fps for full EWA. Engine dataset (256 \times 256 \times 110): 3.25 fps vs 2.90 fps (12% improvement). Bonsai dataset (256 \times 256 \times 128): 7.53 fps vs 6.90 fps (9% improvement). Lobster dataset (301 \times 324 \times 56): 10.60 fps vs 8.75 fps (21% improvement). UNC Head dataset (208 \times 256 \times 225): 3.00 fps vs 2.70 fps (11% improvement). Strengths: Achieves high image quality comparable to full EWA while reducing computational cost by 10% to 20%. Corrects aliasing artifacts and holes that occur with improper filters (reconstruction or low-pass only). Limitations: Adds classification overhead. The improvement is modest (10-20%). When to use: When interactive frame rates are required for large volume datasets and full EWA is too slow, but quality must be maintained. When not to use: When the scene is uniformly very close or very far, as the overhead of classification may not be justified if one filter could be used globally without quality loss (though full EWA is safer for mixed depths). Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting was introduced by Wei Chen et al. in 2004. It builds on the EWA Splatting method [1069-ewa-splatting.md] by observing that the EWA resampling filter computation is expensive and can be simplified adaptively based on depth. The method was implemented on GPU to gain additional performance for interactive frame rates. name: EWA Approximation with Tangent Vector Adjustment
head: Dynamic EWA Filtering, Minification-aware Splat Filtering
body: A high-quality filtering technique for point-based rendering that approximates the EWA resampling filter by dynamically adjusting the tangent vectors of isotropic splats during setup to prevent aliasing during minification, without requiring expensive per-fragment convolution. It sets itself apart from the original EWA framework by using projective mapping and tangent adjustment rather than affine mapping and Gaussians for both reconstruction and low-pass filters, and from Botsch et al. [BHZK05] by avoiding per-fragment filter evaluation, thus eliminating the fragment shader bottleneck. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of isotropic splats, each defined by a center position \mathbf{p}k, a surface normal \mathbf{n}k, and an initial radius (implicitly handled by the filter radius h). Output: Adjusted tangent vectors \mathbf{s}k and \mathbf{t}k for each splat, which define the orientation and extent of the reconstruction kernel for rasterization. Data Structures: Splat Data: For each splat k, store \mathbf{p}k = [px, py, pz]^T (position in camera space), \mathbf{n}k = [nx, ny, nz]^T (normalized normal). Tangent Vectors: \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k are 3D vectors. Parameters: h: Radius of the low-pass filter in the normalized image plane. Typical value: h = \sqrt{2} v{pw}, where v{pw} is the viewport width. Steps: 1. Compute Initial Tangents: For an isotropic splat with normal \mathbf{n}k, compute orthogonal initial tangent vectors \mathbf{s}k^0 and \mathbf{t}k^0 using cross products: \mathbf{s}k^0 = \mathbf{p}k \times \mathbf{n}k \mathbf{t}k^0 = \mathbf{n}k \times \mathbf{s}k^0 2. Project Tangent: For each tangent vector (e.g., \mathbf{t}k^0 = [tx, ty, tz]^T), compute its perspective projection \mathbf{t}k' onto the screen space: \mathbf{t}k' = \frac{1}{pz^2 - tz^2} \begin{bmatrix} tx pz - tz px \\ ty pz - tz py \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} 3. Check Minification: Calculate the length of the projected half-diameter \|\mathbf{t}k'\|. If \|\mathbf{t}k'\| \ge h, the splat is not significantly minified in this direction. Set the final tangent vector \mathbf{t}k = \mathbf{t}k^0. If \|\mathbf{t}k'\| < h, the splat is in minification. Adjust the tangent vector by projecting \mathbf{t}k^0 onto the image plane and scaling it so its projection size equals the filter radius: \mathbf{t}k = \frac{\mathbf{t}k'}{\|\mathbf{t}k'\|} pz h 4. Repeat for Second Tangent: Perform steps 2-3 for \mathbf{s}k^0 to obtain \mathbf{s}k. The vectors are adjusted independently. 5. Rasterize: Rasterize the reconstruction kernel using the adjusted tangent vectors \mathbf{s}k and \mathbf{t}k. The kernel is treated as an isotropic splat stretched by these vectors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adjusttangentvectors(pk, nk, h): """ Adjusts tangent vectors for a splat to handle minification. Args: pk: 3D position vector [px, py, pz] in camera space. nk: 3D normal vector [nx, ny, nz], assumed normalized. h: Filter radius in normalized image plane. Returns: sk, tk: Adjusted tangent vectors. """ # Step 1: Compute initial orthogonal tangents sk0 = cross(pk, nk) tk0 = cross(nk, sk0) # Step 2-4: Adjust each tangent independently sk = adjustsingletangent(pk, sk0, h) tk = adjustsingletangent(pk, tk0, h) return sk, tk def adjustsingletangent(pk, tk0, h): """ Adjusts a single tangent vector based on minification criteria. """ tx, ty, tz = tk0 px, py, pz = pk # Step 2: Project tangent to screen space # Denominator: pz^2 - tz^2 denom = pz2 - tz2 if abs(denom) < 1e-9: # Degenerate case: tangent parallel to view direction projection # Return original or handle as zero stretch? # Source implies this is handled by the heuristic or results in parallel vectors. # We return the projected vector scaled by h if length is small, # but strictly following formula: tkprime = [0, 0, 0] else: tkprime = [ (tx pz - tz px) / denom, (ty pz - tz py) / denom, 0 ] # Step 3: Check length normtprime = length(tkprime) if normtprime >= h: # No adjustment needed return tk0 else: # Adjust: scale projection to radius h, then scale back to object space magnitude # Formula: tk = (tk' / ||tk'||) pz h if normtprime < 1e-9: # Avoid division by zero if projection is zero # This implies the tangent is parallel to the view ray in a way that projects to a point. # The source states depth correction is lost and vectors become parallel to screen plane. # We return a vector parallel to screen plane with magnitude related to h. # A safe default is to return a vector in the direction of the original tangent's screen projection (zero) # or a default basis. However, the formula divides by norm. # If norm is 0, the direction is undefined. # Given the heuristic, this case is rare or handled by the orthogonality assumption. # We will return the original tangent to avoid NaNs, acknowledging potential artifact. return tk0 unittprime = [v / normtprime for v in tkprime] tk = [v pz h for v in unittprime] return tk Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Orthogonality Assumption: The heuristic for generating initial tangent vectors assumes orthogonality. For a 90-degree view frustum, the angle \alpha between screen-space projections of basis vectors ranges from 60 to 90 degrees (average 81.7). If \alpha \neq 90, the low-pass filter may be slightly truncated, but this is acceptable as the error is below output resolution. Depth Correction: Depth correction is lost for splats in minification because tangent vectors become parallel to the screen plane. This is intentional to prevent visibility artifacts caused by arbitrary depth values from infinite stretch values. Depth correction is not required for splats below a single pixel. Numerical Stability: Division by pz^2 - tz^2 can be unstable if tz \approx pz. This corresponds to the tangent vector being nearly parallel to the view direction in a way that projects to infinity or zero. The source notes that for minified splats, the vectors become parallel to the screen plane, implying tz behavior is managed by the scaling. A band-limiting technique that evaluates the reconstruction kernel in the surfel's tangent frame using object-space ray-splat intersection to eliminate perspective distortion of affine screen-space approximations. It maps a screen-space Gaussian pixel prefilter with covariance \sigmaf \mathbf{I} into the local coordinate system via the Jacobian \mathbf{J} = \partial(u, v)/\partial(x, y) of the ray-splat intersection mapping. The combined reconstruction-plus-prefilter kernel in object space has the modified covariance \Sigma{\text{mip}} = \mathbf{I} + \sigmaf \mathbf{J} \mathbf{J}^\top. The MIP-filtered Gaussian kernel is evaluated as G{\text{mip}}(\mathbf{u}) = nf \cdot \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{u}^T \Sigma{\text{mip}}^{-1} \mathbf{u}), where \mathbf{u} is the local coordinate vector and nf is the normalization factor. A pitfall is that per-pixel evaluation of \mathbf{J} can introduce numerical instability for highly tilted or thin surfels where the denominator of quotient-rule derivatives approaches zero. Time Complexity: Computations are done during splat setup, not rasterization. Unlike original EWA, no additional fragments are generated when not necessary (splats are extended only in directions of minification). Memory Complexity: Requires storing adjusted tangent vectors per splat. No per-fragment filter data needed. Performance: Avoids the fragment shader bottleneck associated with evaluating resampling and low-pass filters per fragment. Strengths: High-quality filtering, prevents aliasing during minification, efficient rasterization, handles hybrid splat/polygon rendering easily. Limitations: Approximation error due to non-orthogonal basis projections (though small), loss of depth correction for minified splats (intentional). When to Use: Point-based rendering requiring high-quality anti-aliasing without the cost of full EWA per-fragment computation, especially when splats are isotropic and preprocessing is acceptable. When Not to Use: When exact EWA filtering is required for extreme anisotropy or when depth precision is critical for minified splats (though artifacts are prevented). Originated in the context of point-based rendering and EWA filtering approximations. It was proposed as a new approximation between the optimal EWA resampling filter and the approximation of Botsch et al. [BHZK05] to dynamically adjust tangent vectors in object space. It addresses the issue where fine parts of a splat may fall between image samples during minification. name: Phong Splatting
head: Per-pixel lighting splatting, Phong Splat Generation, Splatting with linear normal fields
body: Phong Splatting is a surface splatting technique that assigns a linearly varying normal field to each elliptical splat, enabling per-pixel Phong shading without surface connectivity. It solves the piecewise constant shading artifacts of standard point-based rendering by providing smooth, Phong-like shading quality on modern GPUs. Unlike its sibling EWA Splatting, which uses a simplified isotropic kernel, Phong Splatting uses elliptical splats with projectively correct per-pixel parameterization, trading the simplicity of isotropic filtering for superior visual quality and exact depth values. Input: A dense set of surface sample points P = \{pi\} with associated normal vectors ni. Output: A set of elliptical surface splats Sj, each defined by a center cj, scaled orthogonal tangent vectors uj, vj, and linear normal field parameters. Each splat Sj requires 17 floating-point values: 1. Center: cj (3 floats: x, y, z in eye space). 2. Tangents: uj, vj (6 floats: 3 for each vector, scaled by ellipse radii). 3. Normal Field Parameters: \bar{n} (2 floats: \bar{x}, \bar{y} representing the center normal on the offset tangent plane). \alpha, \beta (2 floats: linear coefficients for the x and y components of the normal field). Note: The third component of the normal is implicitly 1 (homogeneous representation). 4. Clipping Data: Optional scalars (a, b, c) defining clip lines in tangent space (3 floats per line). 5. Precomputed Depth Factor: n \cdot (c^T n)^{-1} (1 float, computed in vertex shader). Comparison: Standard elliptical splatting requires only 12 floats per splat. However, Phong Splatting requires an order of magnitude fewer splats for comparable quality. Given input samples P and error tolerance \epsilon: 1. Selection: Generate an initial set of elliptical splats Sj covering P using a curvature-aware selection and global relaxation algorithm (e.g., [WK04]). 2. Association: For each splat Sj, identify the subset Pj \subset P of samples contained within the elliptical cylinder defined by Sj's tangents and offset by \pm \epsilon along the normal. 3. Frame Construction: Ensure uj and vj are aligned with principal curvature directions. If not, estimate them as eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of normals in Pj. 4. Normal Fitting: Represent each sample normal ni \in Pj in the local frame (uj, vj, uj \times vj). Set the third coordinate (normal direction) to 1. The normal is thus represented as a point (xi, yi) on an offset tangent plane. Solve for the linear field parameters \bar{n}=(\bar{x}, \bar{y}), \alpha, and \beta using least squares. The systems are uncoupled: \begin{pmatrix} |Pj| & \sum ui \\ \sum ui & \sum ui^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bar{x} \\ \alpha \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum xi \\ \sum xi ui \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} |Pj| & \sum vi \\ \sum vi & \sum vi^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bar{y} \\ \beta \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum yi \\ \sum yi vi \end{pmatrix} If |Pj| < 2 (underdetermined), compute the least-norm solution using the pseudo-inverse. Render each splat Sj as a single point primitive (vertex at cj). Vertex Shader: 1. Transform cj to window coordinates. 2. Transform uj, vj, nj to eye space. 3. Compute the rasterization square size size using the larger ellipse radius r = \max(\|uj\|, \|vj\|): size = 2r \cdot \frac{n}{z{eye}} \cdot \frac{h{vp}}{t-b} where n, t, b are frustum near, far, top, bottom parameters, h{vp} is viewport height, and z{eye} is the eye-space depth of cj. 4. Precompute the ray intersection factor: k = nj \cdot (cj^T nj)^{-1}. 5. Pass uj, vj, \bar{n}, \alpha, \beta as texture coordinates to the fragment shader. Fragment Shader: For each pixel in the size \times size square: 1. Ray Casting: Compute the point qn on the near plane corresponding to window pixel (x, y): qn = \begin{pmatrix} x \frac{wh}{w{vp}} - \frac{wh}{2} \\ y \frac{hn}{h{vp}} - \frac{hn}{2} \\ -n \end{pmatrix} where wh, hn are near plane width/height, and w{vp}, h{vp} are viewport dimensions. 2. Intersection: Compute the point q on the splat's supporting plane: q = qn \cdot k where k = \frac{cj^T nj}{qn^T nj}. 3. Local Parameters: Compute (u, v) by projecting q - cj onto the tangents: u = uj^T (q - cj), \quad v = vj^T (q - cj) 4. Inside Test: If u^2 + v^2 > 1, discard the fragment. 5. Clipping (Optional): If the splat has clip lines (a, b, c), discard if au + bv + c < 0. 6. Normal Interpolation: Compute the interpolated normal vector components on the offset plane: x{interp} = \bar{x} + \alpha u, \quad y{interp} = \bar{y} + \beta v The full normal in eye space is reconstructed from (x{interp}, y{interp}, 1) in the local frame (uj, vj, nj). 7. Lighting: Normalize the interpolated normal and use it to sample a precomputed cube map containing lighting terms (diffuse/specular intensities). 8. Depth: Compute the exact eye-space depth zq of fragment q for correct blending. To achieve high-quality antialiasing and correct transparency: 1. Pass 1 (Visibility Splatting): Render all splats with alpha blending. Assign a radially decreasing weight w(u,v) to each pixel (e.g., Gaussian falloff). Accumulate weighted color and weight sum. 2. Pass 2 (Normalization): Render a full-screen quad textured with the accumulated color and weight sum. Divide the color by the weight sum per pixel. Optimization: Render non-clipped splats first, then splats with one clip line, then two clip lines, to minimize shader state switches. Error Tolerance \epsilon: Controls the coverage of splats during generation. Not given in the sources. Frustum Parameters: n, t, b, h{vp} are standard camera settings. Underdetermined Systems: If a splat covers fewer than 2 samples, the normal fitting linear system is underdetermined. Use the pseudo-inverse to find the least-norm solution. Affine Approximation: Do not use an affine approximation for projection. It disables the exact per-pixel parameterization required for correct clipping and depth, and while it allows EWA filtering, the object-space filter alone is sufficient. Backface Culling: For closed models, perform a conservative backface test in the vertex shader using the transformed normal. Memory: 17 floats per splat (vs. 12 for standard elliptical splatting). However, because Phong Splatting achieves comparable visual quality with ~10x fewer splats than flat shading, total memory usage is lower. Speed: Achieves up to 4 million Phong-shaded, filtered, and blended splats per second on modern GPUs. Quality vs. Count: A torso model with 3,000 splats rendered with Phong Splatting achieves visual quality comparable to Phong-shaded triangle meshes. Flat shading requires 170,000 splats, and flat shading with Gaussian blending requires 33,000 splats for comparable quality. Strengths: Projectively correct per-pixel parameterization; exact depth values prevent blending artifacts; superior shading quality compared to flat or Gouraud-like splatting; efficient GPU implementation using cube maps for lighting. Limitations: Cannot use EWA filtering (combined object/image space Gaussian) because it relies on exact projective mapping rather than affine approximation. Requires preprocessing to generate splats and fit normal fields. Use when high visual quality (smooth shading) is required for point-based surfaces without connectivity. Use when rendering sharp features or clipped splats, as the method supports exact tangent-space clipping. Use EWA Splatting if isotropic filtering and simpler kernel implementation are preferred over per-pixel shading quality. Use Deferred Surface Splatting if deferred shading pipelines are already in place and per-pixel lighting overhead is a concern. Phong Splatting was introduced by in 2004. It builds on the concept of varying normal fields proposed by [KV01], but differs by using a dense input point cloud and a linear normal field fit over the splat area, rather than local Taylor expansions at the center. It addresses the limitations of earlier point-based rendering systems that used constant normals, resulting in flat shading artifacts. The method leverages the programmable pipeline of modern GPUs, specifically vertex and fragment shaders, to achieve real-time performance. name: EWA Splatting Renderer (Mesh-Free)
head: CamPoint splatting renderer, Point-cloud splatting renderer
body: A mesh-free rendering pipeline that projects raw point clouds directly to 2D camera views using EWA projection and Z-buffer occlusion, producing RGB images, label maps, and 2D-to-3D index maps without mesh reconstruction. It differs from its parent EWA Splatting by using simplified screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic linear falloff, trading anisotropic, correctly band-limited footprints for a formulation that requires no per-point normals or radii. Inputs: xyz: Point cloud coordinates, shape [N, 3], dtype float32 (world coordinates). rgb: Point colors, shape [N, 3], dtype uint8 (range 0–255) or float (range 0–1). label: Semantic labels, shape [N], dtype int64 (long). intr: Camera intrinsics, shape [M, 4] or [4], containing [fx, fy, cx, cy]. extr: Camera extrinsics, shape [M, 3, 4] or [3, 4] (rotation and translation). W, H: Output image width and height in pixels. splatradius: Pixel expansion radius r. extent: Frustum culling margin factor (e.g., 1.3 for 30% beyond viewport). cambatch: Number of cameras processed simultaneously on GPU. Outputs: colorcanvas: RGB image, shape [H, W, 3], dtype uint8. depthcanvas: Depth image, shape [H, W], dtype float32 (background set to inf). labelcanvas: Label map, shape [H, W], dtype int64 (background set to 0). indexcanvas: 2D-to-3D index map, shape [H, W], dtype int64 (background set to -1). Bucket Tensor: Used for Z-buffer occlusion. Size bucketsize M, where bucketsize = (mH + 1) (mW + 1). mW = int(extent W) + 1, mH = int(extent H) + 1. name: Ray-Driven Splatting
head: Hybrid Splatting/Ray Casting, Muller Yagel hybrid, Muller and Yagel hybrid, Ray-driven volume splatting
body: Ray-driven splatting is a hybrid volume rendering technique that combines the precomputation of voxel contributions via splatting with the pixel accumulation logic of ray casting. It solves the performance bottlenecks of traditional splatting under perspective projection by treating splats as suspended objects in object space and intersecting them with rays spawned from the camera. Unlike standard splatting, which projects footprints onto the screen plane, this method enables the use of ray-tracing optimizations such as early ray termination, space leaping, and spatial acceleration structures. The method operates in two distinct phases: precomputation of splat extents in object space and ray-based accumulation in screen space. Inputs: Volumetric dataset V with voxel positions and scalar values. Camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, viewport dimensions). Reconstruction kernel hV (typically Gaussian). Outputs: Final image buffer with color and opacity values. Data Structures: Splat List: A collection of splats, one per voxel. Each splat stores its 3D center position Ci and its precomputed footprint parameters (e.g., radius or covariance matrix) in object space. Ray Buffer: An array of rays, one per pixel, defined by origin O and direction D. Steps: 1. Precompute Splat Extents (Object Space): For each voxel i at position Pi with density \rhoi: Determine the 3D footprint of the reconstruction kernel centered at Pi. Project this 3D footprint onto the image plane to determine the 2D screen-space bounding box or extent. This step is similar to traditional splatting but the results are stored as metadata for the ray intersection phase rather than immediately composited. Store the splat Si = (Pi, \text{extent}i, \rhoi) in the Splat List. 2. Spawn Rays: For each pixel (x, y) in the viewport: Construct a ray R{x,y} originating from the camera eye position and passing through the pixel center in normalized device coordinates, transformed back to world space. 3. Ray-Splat Intersection: For each ray R: Traverse the Splat List to find all splats Si that intersect the ray. To optimize, use spatial acceleration structures (e.g., bounding volume hierarchies) or space-leaping techniques to skip empty regions or non-intersecting splats. For each intersecting splat Si, calculate the intersection point I and the distance t from the ray origin. Calculate the weight wi of the splat at the intersection point. This weight is derived from the reconstruction kernel hV evaluated at the distance between the ray intersection point and the splat center Pi. 4. Sort and Composite: Sort the intersecting splats for the ray by distance t (front-to-back or back-to-front, depending on the optical model). Accumulate the color and opacity using standard volume rendering integration (e.g., front-to-back alpha blending): C = \sum{i} ci \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) where ci is the color and \alphai is the opacity contribution of splat i, derived from \rhoi and the kernel weight wi. Parameters: Kernel width: Typically truncated at 2.0\sigma. Splat diameter: 1.6 times the spacing between values is sufficient to avoid aliasing. Edge Cases: Perspective Distortion: Unlike traditional splatting, ray-driven splatting is inherently insensitive to the complexity of the perspective viewing transform because the intersection is calculated in 3D space before projection. Aliasing: Incorrect visibility determination during back-to-front compositing can cause aliasing if kernels are assumed non-overlapping. Using EWA resampling filters can reduce these artifacts. Implements splat rasterization on GPUs by simulating a rasterization unit using standard graphics pipeline stages (vertex shaders for transformation, point primitives for fragment generation, fragment shaders for kernel evaluation). It is more efficient than previous GPU splatting implementations due to minimal instruction count in the fragment shader. Performance: In early implementations, rendered the MRbrain dataset (260^2 viewport) in 30 seconds on an SGI Indigo with a 200 MHz processor. Scalability: Offers competitive or superior performance for parallel projection and superior performance for perspective projection compared to traditional splatting. Strengths: Enables ray-tracing optimizations (early ray termination, spatial acceleration structures) which are not available in traditional voxel-driven splatting. Limitations: Requires efficient intersection testing between rays and splats, which can be computationally expensive if not optimized with acceleration structures. The method was proposed by Müller and Yagel as a hybrid approach to overcome the limitations of traditional splatting under perspective projection. Traditional splatting uses fast incremental schemes for orthographic projection but becomes slow and complex for perspective views due to the distortion of footprints. By merging splatting with raycasting principles, the method allows splats to be suspended in object space and intersected by rays, leveraging the efficiency of ray tracing for perspective views. name: Splat Rasterization via Raycasting
head: GPU-based raycasting of quadric surfaces
body: This method implements splat rasterization on GPUs by simulating a dedicated rasterization unit using standard graphics pipeline stages: vertex shaders for transformation and bounding box calculation, point primitives for fragment generation, and fragment shaders for kernel evaluation and depth computation. It solves the problem of efficiently projecting 3D splats onto the screen while maintaining accurate depth values and filtering weights, optimizing for minimal instruction count in the fragment shader. It is more efficient than previous GPU splatting implementations because the fragment shader requires only three computational instructions (two MADs and one texture fetch), whereas previous approaches were more expensive. Inputs: A set of 3D splats (quadric surfaces), camera parameters (projection and view matrices), and screen resolution. Outputs: A 2D image with accumulated color and depth values. Data Structures: Splat: Defined by a center position \mathbf{c}, a 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigma, and attributes (color, opacity). Point Primitive: A single vertex representing the splat center, drawn as a point primitive. Fragment Shader State: Screen-space coordinates (x, y), depth z, and the splat's transformed parameters. Steps: 1. Vertex Shader Processing: For each splat: a. Transform the splat center \mathbf{c} from world space to clip space using the model-view-projection matrix M{vp}. b. Perform view-frustum clipping on the bounding sphere of the splat in clip space using the Sutherland-Hodgman algorithm. If the bounding sphere does not intersect the view frustum, discard the splat. c. Perform perspective division to obtain normalized device coordinates (NDC) for the center. d. Calculate the screen-space bounding box or extent. This can be done using the exact raycasting method (see Subtopics: Weyrich et al. Splat Extent Calculation) or an approximate polygon bounding method. e. Determine the size of the point primitive (screen-space square) based on the calculated extent. 2. Rasterization: Draw the point primitive as a screen-space square covering the calculated extent. This generates fragments for every pixel within this square. 3. Fragment Shader Processing: For each fragment generated by the point primitive: a. Cast a ray from the camera origin through the fragment's screen-space position (x, y) into the scene. b. Test if the fragment's position lies within the splat's quadric surface in screen space. This involves evaluating the splat's equation at the fragment's coordinates. c. If the fragment is inside the splat, compute the contribution to the accumulated color and depth. The contribution is weighted by the splat's kernel function (e.g., Gaussian) evaluated at the fragment's distance from the splat center. d. The fragment shader performs this evaluation using minimal instructions: two MADs (Multiply-Add) and one texture fetch (for the splat's attributes or kernel lookup). e. Accumulate the result into the frame buffer, typically using alpha blending or depth-based sorting. Formulas: Splat Equation in Screen Space: Let the splat be defined by \mathbf{x}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x} \leq 1 in local space. After transformation to screen space, the equation becomes \mathbf{u}^T A \mathbf{u} \leq 1, where \mathbf{u} is the screen-space coordinate vector and A is the transformed covariance matrix. Raycasting Test: For a fragment at screen position \mathbf{u}, check if \mathbf{u}^T A \mathbf{u} \leq 1. Parameters: Point Primitive Size: Determined by the screen-space extent of the splat. Kernel Width: Typically 3-5 standard deviations for Gaussian splats. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise for very large or very small splats. Boundaries: Splats near the near plane may have underestimated extents if approximate methods are used. Degenerate Input: If the projected ellipse becomes a parabola or hyperbola, the exact raycasting method fails. A method to find screen-space position and extents by finding a plane in screen-space tangent to a quadric in parameter space (unit sphere), exploiting that normal vectors transform by the inverse transpose. It solves the problem of accurately determining the screen-space bounding box of a splat without using the inverse of the projective mapping. It is more accurate than Botsch et al.'s approximation, which can underestimate extents. When to choose it: When exact screen-space extents are required and the splat is not too close to the near plane or viewing frustum boundaries where degenerate projections might occur. Link: Weyrich et al. Splat Extent Calculation (Note: This is a variant of the parent method, not a separate article). Steps: 1. Exploit that normal vectors transform by the inverse transpose of a mapping. 2. Find a plane in screen-space tangent to the quadric in parameter space (unit sphere). 3. Solve a quadratic equation for each dimension to determine the tangent plane's coefficients. Pitfalls: Yields results in normalized device coordinates, preventing view-frustum clipping of the bounding box. Fails if the projected ellipse becomes a parabola or hyperbola. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of splats and K is the average number of fragments per splat (proportional to the screen-space area of the splat). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing splat data, plus frame buffer memory. Measured Performance: Optimized for NVIDIA hardware, requiring only three computational instructions in the fragment shader (two MADs and one texture fetch). Scaling: Scales well with the number of splats, but performance degrades with high splat density due to overdraw. Strengths: High performance on GPUs, accurate depth values, minimal instruction count in fragment shader. Limitations: Approximate methods can underestimate extents; exact methods fail for degenerate projections; requires careful handling of view-frustum clipping. When to use: Real-time volume rendering on GPUs where performance is critical and splats are well-behaved (not too close to near plane or viewing frustum boundaries). When not to use: When exact screen-space extents are required for splats near the near plane or viewing frustum boundaries, or when degenerate projections are likely. Origin: This method was developed in the context of GPU-based surface splatting, building on earlier work by Botsch et al. and Sigg et al.. It was adapted by Weyrich et al. for surface splatting. The implementation described in the source is from Sebastian Lipponer's "surfacesplatting" project. sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, https://github.com/sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: GPU Splat Rasterization via Vertex/Fragment Shaders
head: Point Primitive Splatting, Shader-based Splatting
body: This method implements splat rasterization on GPUs by simulating a dedicated rasterization unit using standard graphics pipeline stages: vertex shaders for transformation and bounding box calculation, point primitives for fragment generation, and fragment shaders for kernel evaluation and depth computation. It solves the problem of efficiently projecting 3D splats onto the screen while maintaining accurate depth values and filtering weights, optimizing for minimal instruction count in the fragment shader. It is more efficient than previous GPU splatting implementations because the fragment shader requires only three computational instructions (two MADs and one texture fetch), whereas previous approaches were more expensive. Inputs and Outputs: Splats are sent to the GPU using the standard point primitive. The output is a rasterized image with accumulated attributes and depth values, where each fragment corresponds to a pixel covered by a splat. Data Structures: Each splat k is represented by its inverse mapping matrix \mathbf{N}k and its center position. A 2D texture stores the precomputed 2D reconstruction kernel weights r0(x). Steps: 1. The vertex shader computes the inverse mapping matrix \mathbf{N}k for each splat. 2. The vertex shader computes a conservative 2D axis-aligned bounding box of the projected splat. 3. The position of the point primitive is set to the center of this bounding box. 4. The size of the point primitive is set to the largest dimension of the bounding box. 5. The fragment shader receives the matrix \mathbf{N}k transmitted as three column vectors. 6. The fragment shader performs the matrix multiplication to transform the fragment's screen-space coordinates into the splat's local space using only two MAD (Multiply-Add) instructions. 7. The weight r0(x) is retrieved from the 2D kernel texture via a single projective texture fetch. 8. The accurate window-space depth value is extracted from the fourth component of the matrix product result. 9. Fragments outside the splat are discarded using the alpha test unit. 10. Attributes are multiplied by the weight and accumulated using the blending unit. Formulas: Let \mathbf{N}k be the inverse mapping matrix for splat k. Let \mathbf{p} be the screen-space position of the fragment. The transformed local coordinate \mathbf{u} is computed as \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{N}k \mathbf{p}. The weight is w = r0(\mathbf{u}). The depth is z = (\mathbf{N}k \mathbf{p})4. Parameters: Kernel texture resolution: Not given in the sources. Alpha test threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: In cases of minification and high frequencies, resampling filters may miss pixels leading to aliasing artifacts. This is addressed by band-limiting reconstruction kernels via convolution with a screen-space pre-filter, as in the original EWA splatting framework. The conservative bounding box ensures all fragments are generated, which is necessary for correct coverage but may include fragments that are ultimately discarded by the alpha test. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mad(a, b, c): return a b + c def computeinversemappingmatrix(splat): # Computes the inverse mapping matrix Nk from splat parameters return [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]] def compute2daabb(Nk, center): # Computes conservative 2D axis-aligned bounding box of projected splat return type('Box', (), {'center': (0, 0), 'width': 1, 'height': 1})() def vertexshader(splat): Nk = computeinversemappingmatrix(splat) bbox = compute2daabb(Nk, splat.center) pointposition = bbox.center pointsize = max(bbox.width, bbox.height) return pointposition, pointsize, Nk def fragmentshader(pointposition, pointsize, Nk, fragmentscreenpos, kerneltexture, alphathreshold, fragmentattributes): # Nk is transmitted as three column vectors c1, c2, c3 = Nk[0], Nk[1], Nk[2] # Matrix multiplication using two MAD instructions for 2D coordinates ux = mad(c1[0], fragmentscreenpos[0], mad(c2[0], fragmentscreenpos[1], c3[0])) uy = mad(c1[1], fragmentscreenpos[0], mad(c2[1], fragmentscreenpos[1], c3[1])) # Depth is the fourth component of the matrix product depth = mad(c1[2], fragmentscreenpos[0], mad(c2[2], fragmentscreenpos[1], c3[2])) # Retrieve weight from precomputed 2D kernel texture weight = kerneltexture[ux, uy] # Discard fragments outside the splat using alpha test if weight < alphathreshold: return None # Multiply attributes by weight and accumulate via blending unit accumulated = fragmentattributes weight return accumulated, depth This variant focuses on voxelizing particle data by rendering screen-aligned bounding quads using an OpenGL geometry shader to project particle spheres onto the screen. For each generated fragment, the particle sphere is intersected with the corresponding camera ray, and all overlapped voxels in the corresponding column are marked using atomic bitwise operations. For particles with radius < 7 pixels on NVIDIA GTX Titan, a simple splatting CUDA kernel can be used for parallel processing, which projects particles onto the screen and loops over all pixels in an axis-aligned bounding quad sequentially. CUDA does not expose atomics on textures directly; they are accessible via the 'sured' instruction using inline PTX code. On GTX 970, pure OpenGL-based rendering is always faster than CUDA splatting. The fragment shader complexity is very low, requiring only three computational instructions (two MADs and one texture fetch). Memory usage depends on the number of splats and the kernel texture size. On NVIDIA GTX 970, splatting performance for 1024x1024 tile size is 76 ms, compression is 28 ms. On NVIDIA GTX 970, splatting performance for 512x512 tile size is 80 ms, compression is 28 ms. On NVIDIA GTX 970, splatting performance for 256x256 tile size is 182 ms, compression is 32 ms. On NVIDIA GTX 970, splatting performance for 128x128 tile size is 546 ms, compression is 47 ms. On NVIDIA GTX 970, splatting performance for 1024x512 tile size is 58 ms, compression is 28 ms. Performance scales with tile size and number of particles. SIMT efficiency is improved when particles are partially sorted by the simulation, grouping particles of approximately equal distance and size. The method offers high efficiency due to minimal fragment shader instructions and simple implementation using standard graphics pipeline stages. Aliasing artifacts may occur in minification without pre-filtering. CUDA-based splatting is slower than OpenGL-based rendering on GTX 970. This method was introduced in the paper "Splat/Mesh Blending, Perspective Rasterization and Transparency for Point-Based Rendering". It builds on previous GPU-based splatting implementations by optimizing the fragment shader to use only three computational instructions. The approach is part of the broader field of point-based rendering and splatting techniques. name: Footprint Evaluation
head: Footprint evaluation for volume rendering, Splatting (Westover), Westover 1990, Westover splatting, Westover's Footprint Evaluation
body: Footprint Evaluation is a forward-mapping object-order volume rendering algorithm that projects each voxel independently onto the 2D image plane, distributing its energy via a reconstruction kernel to form a "splat" or footprint. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering regular volumetric grids by avoiding the per-pixel ray traversal of image-order methods, instead building the image voxel-by-voxel. It sets itself apart from ray-casting by pre-computing the integration of the 3D kernel into a 2D footprint, reducing the per-voxel computational overhead from O(k^3) to O(k^2), where k is the filter dimension. Inputs: A regular 3D volume grid with voxel values \rho(s), a viewing transformation (orthographic or perspective), and a 3D reconstruction kernel h(x,y,z). Outputs: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity values. Data Structures: 1. Volume Grid: 3D array of voxel densities \rho(s) at positions (xs, ys, zs). 2. Footprint Table: A 2D lookup table storing the discrete integration of the footprint function F(x,y). For orthographic projection with symmetric kernels, one table suffices for the entire view. For perspective or asymmetric kernels, a view-transformed table or per-voxel table is required. 3. Sheet Buffer: A 2D accumulator buffer aligned with the volume axis most parallel to the image plane. It stores intermediate (R,G,B,\alpha) values for a slice of voxels. 4. Compositing Buffer: The final working image buffer where sheet buffers are composited. Formulas: The contribution of a data sample s to a point in space (x,y,z) is defined by the volume reconstruction kernel h and sample value \rho(s): Cs(x,y,z) = h(x-xs, y-ys, z-zs) \rho(s) The footprint function F(x,y) is the integral of the 3D reconstruction kernel along the ray direction (perpendicular to the screen, typically z): F(x,y) = \int h(x,y,w) dw The contribution of sample s to an image plane pixel p(x,y) is: Is(p) = \rho(s) F(x-xs, y-ys) The total intensity for pixel p is the sum over all samples: I(p) = \sums Is(p) = \sums \rho(s) F(x-xs, y-ys) For a Gaussian reconstruction kernel h(x,y,z) = \exp(-x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 - z^2/c^2), if a=b=c, the footprint is isotropic. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Select the reconstruction kernel w. A 3D Gaussian w(x,y,z) = d \exp(-x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 - z^2/c^2) is commonly used, ideally spherically symmetric to avoid directional bias. Pre-compute the 2D footprint function F(x,y) by integrating the 3D kernel along one axis. Store this as a finely sampled 2D lookup table. If using perspective projection or non-uniform scaling, calculate the view-transformed footprint extent and the mapping T^{-1} from the view-transformed footprint to the generic footprint. 2. Sheet Selection: Determine the stack of volume slices most parallel to the image plane based on the viewing angle (e.g., x-axis aligned for ~30 degrees, y-axis for ~70 degrees). 3. Voxel Processing (Per Sheet): Iterate through voxels in the selected sheet. Transform: Map each voxel from input grid space (i,j,k) to screen space (x,y,z). Shade: Classify and shade the voxel to produce attributes (R,G,B,A). This can be done pre-shading (before projection) or post-shading (after projection). Project (Splat): Determine the screen-space extent of the footprint centered at the projected voxel position (xs, ys). Identify all pixels within this extent. For each pixel in the extent, retrieve the weight from the footprint table. If using a view-transformed table, apply the reverse mapping T^{-1} to find the corresponding value in the generic footprint table. Accumulate the weighted contribution into the Sheet Buffer. 4. Compositing: Composite the Sheet Buffer into the Compositing Buffer using alpha blending. If using front-to-back compositing, the process can stop for a pixel when it becomes fully opaque. If using back-to-front compositing, correct visibility is guaranteed. 5. Finalization: Repeat steps 3-4 for all sheets in the selected stack. The Compositing Buffer becomes the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def footprintevaluation(volume, viewtransform, kernel, resolution): # 1. Precompute Footprint Table # Integrate 3D kernel along z-axis to get 2D footprint F(x,y) footprinttable = precomputefootprint(kernel) # 2. Determine Sheet Orientation # Select axis most parallel to image plane sheetaxis = determinesheetaxis(viewtransform) # 3. Initialize Buffers sheetbuffer = zeros(resolution) compositingbuffer = zeros(resolution) # 4. Process Sheets for sheet in getsheets(volume, sheetaxis): # Clear sheet buffer for this pass sheetbuffer = zeros(resolution) for voxel in sheet: # Transform voxel to screen space xs, ys, zs = transform(voxel.position, viewtransform) # Shade voxel color, alpha = shade(voxel.value) # Determine footprint extent # For orthographic: fixed radius. For perspective: distance-dependent. extent = getfootprintextent(voxel, viewtransform) # Splat onto sheet buffer for pixel in pixelsinextent(extent, xs, ys): # Get weight from footprint table # Apply view-transform mapping if necessary weight = getfootprintweight(footprinttable, pixel, xs, ys, viewtransform) # Accumulate into sheet buffer sheetbuffer[pixel] += weight color alpha sheetbufferalpha[pixel] += weight alpha # Composite sheet buffer into compositing buffer compositingbuffer = composite(compositingbuffer, sheetbuffer) return compositingbuffer def precomputefootprint(kernel): # Integrate 3D kernel h(x,y,z) along z to get F(x,y) # Return as 2D lookup table pass def getfootprintweight(table, pixel, xs, ys, viewtransform): # Calculate offset from center dx = pixel.x - xs dy = pixel.y - ys # If perspective/non-uniform, apply inverse transform T^-1 # to map (dx, dy) to generic footprint coordinates if viewtransform.isperspective or not viewtransform.isuniform: dx, dy = applyinversetransform(dx, dy, viewtransform) return table.sample(dx, dy) def composite(dest, src): # Alpha blending # dest.rgb = dest.rgb (1 - src.a) + src.rgb src.a # dest.a = dest.a + src.a (1 - dest.a) pass Parameters: Kernel Shape/Size: Critical for quality. Gaussian is common. Size must be tuned for pixel-to-voxel ratio; large footprints cause blurring, small ones cause gaps. Footprint Table Resolution: Finer sampling improves accuracy. Compositing Order: Front-to-back (faster, early exit) or back-to-front (correct visibility). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlapping Splats: Overlapping footprints lead to incorrect mixture of integration (3D to 2D) and compositing, causing aliasing. Perspective Distortion: Orthographic footprints are independent of viewpoint; perspective footprints are elliptical and require orientation computation. Anisotropic Grids: If volume spacings differ or viewing transform has non-uniform scaling, the footprint becomes elliptical, not circular. Blurring: Gaussian kernels cut high frequencies, resulting in blurry images for zoomed views. Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment is a forward-mapping volume rendering technique that prevents sample-rate aliasing in perspective views by dynamically scaling splat sizes and attenuating splat energy for voxels beyond a critical distance. It sets itself apart from standard splatting by varying the kernel size and energy as a function of depth to match the diverging integration grid rays, ensuring the integration grid sampling frequency remains above twice the maximum volume raster frequency. A projector model that accounts for the finite width of detector pixels and volume voxels, providing higher accuracy than methods that do not model finite widths (like Siddon or Joseph), though at higher computational cost. SF models finite detector/voxel widths, whereas Siddon and Joseph do not. SF is more accurate and avoids artifacts produced by Siddon/Joseph in some cases, but is more computationally expensive. A 2D reconstruction kernel used to implement the 3D spherically symmetric splat kernel by integrating it along one dimension, represented as a pre-computed 2D lookup table. The 2D footprint function is pre-computed by integrating the 3D spherically symmetric kernel along one axis and stored as a finely sampled 2D lookup table. The table is centered at the voxel's projected point on the image plane, and pixels within its extent sample the table to composite their values. The footprint table is recomputed once if volume grid spacing is regular, view projection is orthographic, and the splat kernel is radially symmetric; it must be recomputed per view for non-symmetric kernels and per voxel for perspective projections. Time Complexity: Splatting has a complexity of at most O(k^2 n^3), where k is the filter dimension and n^3 is the voxel count. This is faster than ray-casting, which has a complexity of at least O(k^3 n^3) because splatting precomputes the convolution and splats each voxel exactly once, requiring k^2 compositing operations per splat. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume grid, the footprint table (size depends on kernel support and resolution), and the sheet/compositing buffers. Performance: Splatting is inherently faster than ray-casting for large volumes. However, good splatting results may require as much CPU computing time as ray casting if high-quality kernels and large footprints are used. It supports perspective projection without excessive cost. Strengths: Inherently faster than ray-casting due to precomputed footprints. Supports perspective projection efficiently. Simple static parallel decomposition. Can handle scattered data (e.g., SPH) with sorting. Limitations: Poor quality in the original algorithm; requires tuning for quality. Blurry images for zoomed views due to Gaussian kernel properties. High fill-rate for zoomed splats. Overlapping splats cause aliasing. Sheet orientation changes can cause popping artifacts. When to Use: When rendering regular volumetric grids on CPU or GPU where speed is prioritized over perfect anti-aliasing. When perspective projection is needed. When adaptive resampling is required. When Not to Use: When high-frequency detail preservation is critical (Gaussian blurring). When exact visibility is required without sorting or careful compositing order (back-to-front is slow). Footprint Evaluation was introduced by Lee Westover in "Footprint evaluation for volume rendering," published in Computer Graphics, vol 24, no. 4, August 1990. It was the first described splatting algorithm, intended for rendering regular grids on a CPU. The method was later extended to improve quality and performance, including sheet-buffer methods by Mueller et al. and perspective splatting. It is applicable to scattered data such as SPH, requiring sorting of sample points. name: Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment
head: Antialiased splatting method, Perspective Anti-Aliased Splatting
body: Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment is a forward-mapping volume rendering technique that prevents sample-rate aliasing in perspective views by dynamically scaling splat sizes and attenuating splat energy for voxels beyond a critical distance. It sets itself apart from standard splatting by varying the kernel size and energy as a function of depth to match the diverging integration grid rays, ensuring the integration grid sampling frequency remains above twice the maximum volume raster frequency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset (typically stored as a subset of extracted voxels), camera parameters (eye position, view plane distance z{img}, pixel extent p, viewing frustum half-angle \phic), and a transfer function. Output: A 2D image with anti-aliased volume rendering. Data Structures: The volume subset is stored as a 2D array of splat rows. Each row is an array of voxels. Each voxel stores: Location (x, y, z) in eye space. Normal vector. Pre-computed transfer function value (e.g., color, opacity). Voxels in a row are not necessarily contiguous. The splat kernel is pre-computed and stored in a 256 \times 256 table, which is texture-mapped onto the polygon representing the splat. Critical Distance (zk or k): The distance zk along the z-axis where the volume raster sampling frequency p equals the integration grid sampling frequency \phi(z) divides eye space into two regions: Region 1 (z < zk): No aliasing; standard splatting is sufficient. Region 2 (z > zk): Aliasing possible; low-pass filtering (scaling/attenuation) is required. The critical distance is calculated from similar triangles: zk = \frac{p \cdot z{img}}{p - 1} where p is the extent of a pixel and z{img} is the distance from the eye point to the view plane. Note: uses k for this distance. Algorithm Steps: 1. Traverse the volume: Iterate through the voxels in back-to-front or front-to-back order. 2. Determine Distance: For each voxel, compute its distance zv (or d) from the eye point along the viewing axis. 3. Check Region: If zv < zk (or d < k): Draw the splat with its standard size in eye space. The polygon can be aligned parallel to the x-y plane or perpendicular to the ray. Use standard energy/alpha. If zv \ge zk (or d \ge k): Scale Radius: Scale the splat footprint radius to match the diverging rays. Using similar triangles: r2 = r1 \cdot \frac{zv}{zk} where r1 is the radius at zk and r2 is the radius at zv. expresses this as r2 = (k/d) \cdot r1 where r1 is the radius at distance k (this implies r1 in S1 is the scaled radius at k, effectively the base unit for scaling beyond k). The geometric intent is identical: radius grows linearly with distance beyond zk. Attenuate Energy: Attenuate the splat's energy (e.g., alpha channel) to preserve total projected energy and avoid brightness artifacts. The total attenuation factor is (zk / zv)^2. states E2 = (k^2 / d^2) \cdot E1. explicitly states: "We attenuate the alpha channel of the polygon according to the value of (zk/zv)". This implies the alpha is scaled by the square root of the energy attenuation factor, or that the energy attenuation is defined differently in their compositing model. Given says "total attenuation factor is (zk/zv)^2" and then says "attenuate alpha... according to (zk/zv)", we assume the alpha value itself is multiplied by (zk/zv). Footprint Alignment: Rotate the splat polygon so it is perpendicular to the ray passing from the eye point through the voxel position. Two alignment strategies exist: 1. Grid-aligned: Align stretched footprint with the y-axis of the grid. 2. Ray-perpendicular: Rotate stretched footprint to be perpendicular to the ray. Ray-perpendicular is more accurate near zk, while grid-aligned is better far from zk. 4. Render: Texture map the pre-computed kernel onto the polygon and composite into the screen buffer. Voxel Interpolation (Tri-Linear): For trilinear interpolation, the value is distributed to 8 surrounding voxels: 1. Offset voxel-space position by -0.5 to align with voxel centers: p = (x-0.5, y-0.5, z-0.5). 2. Find lower-left corner: corner = (\lfloor px \rfloor, \lfloor py \rfloor, \lfloor pz \rfloor). 3. Calculate fraction vector: f = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) - (\lfloor p \rfloor + 1 - p). 4. Loop over i, j, k \in \{0, 1\}: Invert fraction component for each axis at start of loop. Weight w = fx \cdot fy \cdot fz. Add value \cdot w to voxel at corner + (i, j, k) if in bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderantialiasedsplats(volumesubset, camera, kerneltable): """ volumesubset: List of rows, each row is a list of Voxel objects. camera: Object with eyepos, zimg, pixelextent p, frustumangle phic. kerneltable: 256x256 texture map of the splat kernel. """ # Calculate critical distance zk # p is pixel extent, zimg is distance to view plane zk = (camera.p camera.zimg) / (camera.p - 1) for row in volumesubset: for voxel in row: # 1. Calculate distance from eye # Assuming voxel.pos is in eye space and z-axis is viewing direction zv = voxel.pos.z # 2. Determine scaling and attenuation if zv < zk: # Region 1: Standard splat scalefactor = 1.0 alphascale = 1.0 # Alignment: Can be parallel to x-y plane or ray-perp # For simplicity, assume ray-perp for consistency with Region 2 logic # or use grid-aligned if zv is large isperp = True else: # Region 2: Anti-aliased splat scalefactor = zv / zk # Attenuate alpha by (zk / zv) as per alphascale = zk / zv isperp = True # Ray-perpendicular alignment recommended for accuracy near zk # 3. Create Polygon # Center at voxel position center = voxel.pos # If ray-perpendicular, rotate polygon normal to be parallel to eye-to-voxel ray if isperp: raydir = normalize(center - camera.eyepos) # Construct rotation matrix to align polygon normal with raydir # (Implementation detail: standard graphics pipeline rotation) polygon = createpolygon(center, radius=voxel.baseradius scalefactor, rotation=raydir) else: # Grid-aligned: parallel to x-y plane polygon = createpolygon(center, radius=voxel.baseradius scalefactor, rotation=Vector(0,0,1)) # 4. Texture Map and Composite # Apply kernel texture polygon.texture = kerneltable # Modulate alpha by attenuation factor polygon.alpha = alphascale # Composite into screen buffer compositepolygon(polygon) def trilinearinterpolate(value, pos, buffer): """ Distributes 'value' at 'pos' to 8 surrounding voxels in 'buffer' using tri-linear interpolation. """ # Offset by -0.5 to align with voxel centers p = Vector(pos.x - 0.5, pos.y - 0.5, pos.z - 0.5) # Lower-left corner corner = Vector(floor(p.x), floor(p.y), floor(p.z)) # Fraction vector # f = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) - (floor(p) + 1 - p) # Note: floor(p) is integer part. # Let's compute explicitly: frac = Vector(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) - (Vector(floor(p.x), floor(p.y), floor(p.z)) + Vector(1,1,1) - p) for k in range(2): frac.z = 1.0 - frac.z # Invert for next iteration? No, loop structure in inverts at start of loop # code: # for k in 0..1: # fraction[2] = 1.0 - fraction[2] # for j in 0..1: # fraction[1] = 1.0 - fraction[1] # for i in 0..1: # fraction[0] = 1.0 - fraction[0] # Resetting fraction for the loop structure in # Initial fraction calculation needs to be done before loops # But modifies fraction in place. pass # Re-writing loop exactly # Initial fraction vector f = Vector(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) - (Vector(floor(p.x), floor(p.y), floor(p.z)) + Vector(1,1,1) - p) for k in range(2): f[2] = 1.0 - f[2] for j in range(2): f[1] = 1.0 - f[1] for i in range(2): f[0] = 1.0 - f[0] weight = f[0] f[1] f[2] targetx = corner.x + i targety = corner.y + j targetz = corner.z + k if buffer.isinbounds(targetx, targety, targetz): buffer.add(targetx, targety, targetz, value weight) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Energy Attenuation: If splat energy is not attenuated when scaling size, the projected area changes incorrectly, leading to brightness artifacts. Alignment Errors: Footprint polygon not aligned perpendicularly with the sight ray causes errors in projected polygon extent, largest at the viewing frustum boundary. Sight rays from pixels other than the center traverse the footprint at an oblique angle. There is no known efficient solution outside of ray-driven splatting. Pre-integration: Pre-integrating a distorted kernel for one z-location and scaling it for another does not yield the correct footprint because relative kernel distortion varies with z. Grid Alignment: Aligning footprints with the grid causes indexed ray integrals to differ significantly from true ray integrals for rays maintaining a large angle with the viewing axis. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the subset. Per-voxel cost involves distance calculation, scaling factor computation, and polygon setup/compositing. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume subset size. Storing a 2D array of splat rows with non-contiguous voxels requires storing location and normal for each voxel. Kernel table is 256 \times 256. Performance: Achieved real-time performance on Silicon Graphics hardware for datasets like 512 \times 512 \times 103 (386K splats). Strengths: Prevents sample-rate aliasing in perspective views. Efficient compared to ray-driven splatting or computing unique footprints for every voxel with diverging rays. Can be implemented using standard rendering hardware (texture-mapped polygons). Limitations: Approximation errors in footprint alignment and projection. Grid-aligned alignment is less accurate for rays at large angles. Ray-perpendicular alignment is more accurate but requires rotation per voxel. Does not address aliasing from non-ideal reconstruction filters, only sample-rate aliasing. When to Use: Perspective volume rendering where aliasing artifacts are visible due to diverging rays or high volume resolution relative to image resolution. When Not to Use: Orthographic views with low resolution (aliasing is uniform and less severe, or handled by standard filtering). Origin: The method was introduced in the late 1990s. references "Perspective Splatting" (DTIC ADA363073) and "Splatting Errors and Antialiasing" (DTIC ADA606764, IEEE TVCG 1998). Development: Standard splatting (Westover) was designed for orthographic views. Perspective splatting introduced aliasing issues due to non-uniform sampling. This method extends splatting to perspective by scaling kernels and attenuating energy. Usage: Used in the "Tenderer" implementation on Silicon Graphics hardware. Applied to terrain datasets from satellite photographs and microtubule studies from confocal microscopy.
