name: Plug-and-Play Ray Marching and Rendering
head: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering Pipeline, nerfacc pipeline
body: This method provides a modular interface for efficient ray marching and differentiable volumetric rendering, allowing users to plug any custom radiance field into a standardized acceleration pipeline. It distinguishes itself from specialized implementations like Instant-NGP by offering a Python API built on PyTorch, which facilitates easier extension to dynamic and unbounded scenes while maintaining high performance. The pipeline separates the radiance field query logic from the rendering accumulation logic. The user defines two functions that map sample intervals to field values, while the library handles the optimization of sample placement and the differentiable accumulation of color and opacity. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape (nrays, 3). raysd: Ray directions, shape (nrays, 3). radiancefield: A user-defined model capable of querying density and optionally RGB color at 3D positions. Outputs: color: Rendered RGB colors, shape (nrays, 3). opacity: Accumulated opacity, shape (nrays, 1). depth: Accumulated depth, shape (nrays, 1). The core data structures are PyTorch tensors. The nerfacc library manages internal packed information (packedinfo) to optimize memory access during ray marching, but the user interacts primarily with the sample interval tensors tstarts and tends. tstarts: Start distances of sample intervals along the ray, shape (nsamples,). tends: End distances of sample intervals along the ray, shape (nsamples,). rayindices: Indices mapping each sample to its corresponding ray, shape (nsamples,). 1. Define Density Query Function: Implement sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) to return density values \sigma. 2. Define RGB and Density Query Function: Implement rgbsigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) to return RGB colors \mathbf{c} and density values \sigma. 3. Ray Marching: Call the ray marching routine to determine valid sample intervals, skipping empty or occluded regions. 4. Rendering: Call the rendering routine to accumulate color, opacity, and depth using the determined samples. 5. Optimization: Compute loss against ground truth and backpropagate through the differentiable rendering pipeline. The volumetric rendering equation accumulates color contributions from samples along a ray \mathbf{r}: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i Where: N is the number of samples along the ray. \mathbf{c}i is the color of the i-th sample. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th sample, defined as: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) \sigmai is the density of the i-th sample. \deltai is the distance between the start and end of the i-th sample interval (\deltai = t{ends,i} - t{starts,i}). Ti is the transmittance up to the i-th sample, defined as: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) By definition, T1 = 1. nearplane: The starting distance for ray marching. Typical value: 0.2. farplane: The ending distance for ray marching. Typical value: 1.0. earlystopeps: Threshold for early stopping during ray marching. Typical value: 1 \times 10^{-4}. alphathre: Threshold for skipping samples with low opacity. Typical value: 1 \times 10^{-2}. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the pipeline using PyTorch and the nerfacc library interface described in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch from torch import Tensor import nerfacc from typing import Tuple def sigmafn(tstarts: Tensor, tends: Tensor, rayindices: Tensor) -> Tensor: """ Query density values from a user-defined radiance field. Args: tstarts: Start of the sample interval along the ray. tends: End of the sample interval along the ray. rayindices: Ray indices that each sample belongs to. Returns: The post-activation density values. """ # Gather ray origins and directions for the specific samples torigins = rayso[rayindices] # (nsamples, 3) tdirs = raysd[rayindices] # (nsamples, 3) # Compute sample positions at the midpoint of the interval positions = torigins + tdirs (tstarts + tends) / 2.0 # Query density from the radiance field sigmas = radiancefield.querydensity(positions) return sigmas # (nsamples, 1) def rgbsigmafn(tstarts: Tensor, tends: Tensor, rayindices: Tensor) -> Tuple[Tensor, Tensor]: """ Query RGB and density values from a user-defined radiance field. Args: tstarts: Start of the sample interval along the ray. tends: End of the sample interval along the ray. rayindices: Ray indices that each sample belongs to. Returns: The post-activation RGB and density values. """ # Gather ray origins and directions for the specific samples torigins = rayso[rayindices] # (nsamples, 3) tdirs = raysd[rayindices] # (nsamples, 3) # Compute sample positions at the midpoint of the interval positions = torigins + tdirs (tstarts + tends) / 2.0 # Query RGB and density from the radiance field # Note: The source implies the radiance field takes positions and optionally conditions rgbs, sigmas = radiancefield(positions, condition=tdirs) return rgbs, sigmas # (nsamples, 3), (nsamples, 1) packedinfo, tstarts, tends = nerfacc.raymarching( rayso, raysd, sigmafn=sigmafn, nearplane=0.2, farplane=1.0, earlystopeps=1e-4, alphathre=1e-2) color, opacity, depth = nerfacc.rendering( rgbsigmafn, packedinfo, tstarts, tends) Empty/Occluded Regions: The pipeline includes logic to skip samples in empty or occluded regions (where \alphai or Ti is low) to optimize GPU utilization. Dynamic Scenes: The Python API is designed to support dynamic and unbounded scenes, unlike some static-only CUDA implementations. Precision: The use of PyTorch ensures differentiability for gradient-based optimization. Performance: The Python API achieves performance comparable to specialized CUDA implementations. For example, training an Instant-NGP NeRF takes 4.5 minutes in Python using this pipeline, compared to the official pure CUDA implementation. Hardware: Experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA TITAN RTX GPU. Strengths: Ease of use, extensibility to dynamic/unbounded scenes, and compatibility with existing PyTorch workflows. Limitations: Potential overhead compared to highly optimized pure CUDA kernels for static scenes, though the source claims comparable speed for Instant-NGP. The method originates from the NerfAcc toolbox, which focuses on efficient volumetric rendering of radiance fields. It builds on techniques from Instant-NGP but extends them to support dynamic and unbounded scenes. The toolbox provides a user-friendly Python API written with PyTorch, aiming to accelerate most NeRF methods without requiring custom CUDA code. name: Volume Rendering Pipeline
head: CRIO Process, Classification, Reflection, Illumination, Opacity, Rendering Stages, Shading and Classification Pipeline, VolumeRenderer forward method
body: The volume rendering pipeline is a standard implementation structure for direct volume rendering that processes scalar field data into a 2D image through a sequence of six distinct stages: data traversal, interpolation, gradient computation, classification, shading, and compositing. Unlike methods that fit geometric primitives to the data, this pipeline forms images by directly shading each sample and projecting it onto the picture plane, treating volume samples as semi-transparent clouds that act as both absorbers and emitters. It is distinguished from sibling pipelines like Plug-and-Play Ray Marching and Rendering by its explicit separation of shading (color calculation) and classification (opacity calculation) into independent steps, ensuring undistorted visualization of 3-D shape. The pipeline operates on a 3D scalar field and produces a 2D image. The core data structures are arrays of scalar values, prepared values, voxel colors, and voxel opacities. Inputs: Acquired scalar values f0(xi) at voxel locations xi = (xi, yj, zk). Ray bundle defined by observer eyepoint and image pixel coordinates. Number of sample locations K along each ray. Outputs: Final pixel color C\lambda(u,v) and opacity \alpha(u,v) for each pixel (u,v). Data Structures: 1. Acquired Values: Array f0 of scalar densities/intensities at grid points. 2. Prepared Values: Array f1 after data preparation (corrections, enhancements). 3. Voxel Colors: Array c\lambda(xi) where \lambda \in \{r, g, b\}, computed from f1 via shading. 4. Voxel Opacities: Array \alpha(xi), computed from f1 via classification. 5. Sample Colors/Opacities: Vectors c\lambda(\tilde{x}i) and \alpha(\tilde{x}i) for K sample points along a ray. Steps: 1. Data Traversal: Traverse the 3D scalar field organization to identify samples along light rays. This discretizes the continuous volume rendering integral. 2. Data Preparation: Apply corrections (e.g., for non-orthogonal grids, patient motion) and enhancements to f0(xi) to produce prepared values f1(xi). 3. Interpolation: Interpolate values from the scalar field at sampling positions that differ from grid points. This is often done during ray casting via tri-linear interpolation from the eight closest voxels. 4. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient of the scalar field at sample positions to add visual cues for directional lighting or Phong shading. 5. Shading: Input f1(xi) into a shading model to yield voxel colors c\lambda(xi). 6. Classification: Input f1(xi) into a classification procedure to yield voxel opacities \alpha(xi). This maps scalar properties to optical properties like emitted color, reflected color, and opacity. 7. Ray Casting and Resampling: Cast rays from the observer eyepoint. For each ray, compute sample colors and opacities by resampling the voxel databases at K evenly spaced locations \tilde{x}i = (x0 + j \frac{d}{K}) along the ray and tri-linearly interpolating from the eight closest voxels. 8. Compositing: Composite colors and opacities back-to-front along viewing rays. A fully opaque background of color c{bkg,\lambda} is draped behind the dataset. The transparency formula is applied iteratively. Formulas: The compositing step uses the transparency formula for each sample i along the ray: C{out, \lambda}(\tilde{u}i) = C{in, \lambda}(\tilde{u}i)(1 - \alpha(\tilde{x}i)) + c\lambda(\tilde{x}i)\alpha(\tilde{x}i) Where: C{out, \lambda}(\tilde{u}i) is the color of the ray as it leaves sample location \tilde{x}i. C{in, \lambda}(\tilde{u}i) is the color of the ray as it enters sample location \tilde{x}i. c\lambda(\tilde{x}i) is the color of the sample at \tilde{x}i. \alpha(\tilde{x}i) is the opacity of the sample at \tilde{x}i. \lambda \in \{r, g, b\}. The final pixel color C\lambda(u,v) is the result of this iterative compositing starting from the background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumerenderingpipeline(acquiredvalues, voxelgrid, raybundle, K): """ Implements the standard volume rendering pipeline. Args: acquiredvalues: 3D array of scalar values f0(xi). voxelgrid: Structure defining voxel locations and spacing. raybundle: Collection of rays, each with origin and direction. K: Number of evenly spaced sample locations along each ray. Returns: imagecolors: 2D array of final pixel colors. imageopacities: 2D array of final pixel opacities. """ # Step 2: Data Preparation # Apply corrections (non-orthogonal grids, motion, contrast) to acquiredvalues preparedvalues = datapreparation(acquiredvalues) # Step 5: Shading # Compute voxel colors from prepared values voxelcolors = computeshading(preparedvalues) # Step 6: Classification # Compute voxel opacities from prepared values voxelopacities = computeclassification(preparedvalues) # Initialize output images imagecolors = zeroslike(raybundle.pixelcoords) imageopacities = zeroslike(raybundle.pixelcoords) # Background setup backgroundcolor = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] # Fully opaque white background backgroundopacity = 1.0 # Step 7 & 8: Ray Casting, Resampling, and Compositing for ray in raybundle: # Generate K evenly spaced sample locations along the ray samplelocations = generatesamplelocations(ray.origin, ray.direction, K) # Initialize ray color and transmittance raycolor = backgroundcolor rayopacity = backgroundopacity # Composite back-to-front # Note: Back-to-front means starting from the farthest sample for i in range(K - 1, -1, -1): xtilde = samplelocations[i] # Tri-linear interpolation from voxel databases # Find 8 closest voxels in voxelcolors and voxelopacities csample = trilinearinterpolate(voxelcolors, xtilde) alphasample = trilinearinterpolate(voxelopacities, xtilde) # Apply transparency formula # Cout = Cin (1 - alpha) + c alpha newraycolor = raycolor (1 - alphasample) + csample alphasample newrayopacity = rayopacity (1 - alphasample) + alphasample raycolor = newraycolor rayopacity = newrayopacity # Store result for the pixel corresponding to this ray pixelidx = ray.pixelindex imagecolors[pixelidx] = raycolor imageopacities[pixelidx] = rayopacity return imagecolors, imageopacities def datapreparation(values): """ Applies corrections and enhancements to scalar values. Includes correction for non-orthogonal sampling grids, patient motion, contrast enhancement, and interpolation of additional samples. """ # Implementation details depend on specific data type (e.g., CT, MRI) # return correctedvalues def computeshading(preparedvalues): """ Inputs prepared values into a shading model to yield voxel colors. May use gradients for Phong shading or directional lighting. """ # Gradient computation is often part of this or a preceding step gradients = computegradients(preparedvalues) colors = applyshadingmodel(preparedvalues, gradients) return colors def computeclassification(preparedvalues): """ Inputs prepared values into a classification procedure to yield voxel opacities. Maps scalar properties to optical properties (opacity, emitted/reflected color). """ opacities = applytransferfunction(preparedvalues) return opacities def computegradients(values): """ Computes the gradient of the scalar field at sample positions. Typically approximated by central differences. """ # Central difference approximation gradx = values[1:,:,:] - values[:-1,:,:] grady = values[:, 1:,:] - values[:,:-1,:] gradz = values[:,:, 1:] - values[:,:,:-1] return gradx, grady, gradz def trilinearinterpolate(datagrid, point): """ Interpolates value at 'point' from the 8 closest voxels in 'datagrid'. """ # Standard tri-linear interpolation logic pass def generatesamplelocations(origin, direction, K): """ Generates K evenly spaced locations along the ray. xj = (x0 + j d / K) """ locations = [] for j in range(K): t = j (raylength / K) locations.append(origin + direction t) return locations Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Tri-linear interpolation and compositing are sensitive to floating-point precision, especially with many samples. Boundaries: Handling rays that do not intersect the volume or intersect only partially requires careful boundary checks during traversal. Degenerate Input: Non-orthogonal sampling grids require specific corrections during data preparation to avoid artifacts. Efficiently visiting voxels along rays based on grid topology (regular, irregular, hierarchical). Chosen when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. See Rendering Pipelines and Passes. Reconstructing continuous signals from discrete samples (e.g., tri-linear, higher-order kernels). Chosen when smoothness is critical. See Rendering Pipelines and Passes. Calculating surface normals from scalar fields for shading. Chosen when lighting effects are desired. See Rendering Pipelines and Passes. Mapping scalar values to optical properties via transfer functions. Chosen when specific tissue/feature isolation is needed. See Rendering Pipelines and Passes. Computing color based on lighting models (Phong, etc.). Chosen when realistic lighting is required. See Rendering Pipelines and Passes. Blending samples back-to-front using the transparency formula. Chosen for accurate alpha blending. See Rendering Pipelines and Passes. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of pixels (rays) and K is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for storing the volume data, where V is the number of voxels, plus O(K) per ray for temporary storage. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on hardware and traversal efficiency. Object-order methods (like this pipeline) can be cache-unfriendly if not optimized. Strengths: Direct visualization without geometric fitting; separation of shading and classification allows flexible material definition; handles semi-transparent data well. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution volumes due to K samples per ray; interpolation artifacts if K is too low; sensitive to transfer function design. When to Use: When accurate representation of internal structures and transparency is required, and computational resources allow for per-pixel ray casting. When Not to Use: When real-time performance on very large volumes is critical without hardware acceleration; when geometric primitives are sufficient. The volume rendering pipeline was formalized in the late 1980s. A key early description was presented by Levoy at the SPIE Medical Imaging II conference in January 1988. The pipeline structure, distinguishing six stages (data traversal, interpolation, gradient computation, classification, shading, and compositing), is commonly referenced in literature such as Engel. The term "CRIO" (Classification, Reflection, Illumination, Opacity) was used in parallel feed-forward algorithms to describe the conceptual treatment of samples as reflective, light-emitting clouds. The pipeline assumes each sample acts as both an absorber and an emitter. name: Time-Sliced Pipelined Architecture
head: Multi-core time-sliced pipeline, Time-slicing
body: A hardware architecture for volume rendering where functional blocks are time-sliced to allow simultaneous processing of multiple tasks, enabling real-time rendering and continuous hardware-software communication. It differs from standard linear pipelines by overlapping execution stages across independent sub-cores, allowing a single physical component to serve multiple logical stages or tasks via context switching. The architecture decomposes the rendering pipeline into independent, reusable functional blocks (sub-cores) that are configured or replicated based on processing requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Voxel data, classification parameters, gradient information, and transformation matrices. Output: Final pixel values for the frame buffer. Data Structures: Context RAM: Stores intermediate results (e.g., dot products) for several clock cycles, allowing different components to access the same data without recomputation. Normal Mode Registers: Provide a common interface for communication between components. Context Address Snooping Mechanism: Allows components to access stored information in Context RAM. Functional Blocks: The pipeline is divided into the following blocks: 1. Classifier 2. Gradient Calculator 3. Shearing-Warping Block (Shearer-Composer) 4. Shader (Shading Processor) 5. Composer Steps: 1. Decomposition: Divide the rendering pipeline into the functional blocks listed above. 2. Implementation: Implement each block as an independent reusable component or sub-core. These blocks are composed of basic functional units such as multipliers, adders, or inner product processors. 3. Configuration: Based on the type of processing required, the embedded sub-core is configured or replicated to execute a specific operation. 4. Time-Slicing: Use time-slicing to overlap execution stages. This allows simultaneous processing of several tasks by interleaving their execution on the hardware resources. 5. Communication: Components communicate via a common interface provided by Context RAM, normal mode registers, and the context address snooping mechanism. For example, a calculated dot product is stored in a RAM cell and called up by another component (e.g., shader and composer) in subsequent cycles. Pitfalls: Context Switching Overhead: The efficiency of time-slicing depends on the speed of context switching and the overhead of snooping mechanisms. Resource Contention: If multiple tasks require the same sub-core simultaneously, arbitration logic is needed. A specific implementation of the time-sliced pipelined architecture used in the VolumePro system. It uses four parallel rendering pipelines to achieve real-time rendering rates by processing adjacent voxel values in the x-direction. Definition: The vg500 chip architecture uses four parallel rendering pipelines to achieve real-time rendering rates by processing adjacent voxel values in the x-direction. Steps: 1. Pipelines work on adjacent voxel or sample values in the x-direction. 2. Each pipeline is connected to its neighbor by shift registers in each major unit, providing values to neighbors in the same cycle. 3. The shift registers of the rightmost pipeline recirculate values needed in the next cycle and send them to the leftmost pipeline. Parameters: Clock frequency: 133 MHz. Each pipeline operates at 133 MHz and can accept a new voxel every cycle. Off-chip Voxel Memory supplies data to all pipelines. Pipelines write pixel values to an off-chip Pixel Memory. Pitfalls: The shift registers of the rightmost pipeline must correctly recirculate values to the leftmost pipeline to maintain data continuity across the pipeline boundary. Time Complexity: The architecture enables real-time rendering by overlapping tasks. For the vg500 variant, four pipelines operating at 133 MHz can process approximately 532 million voxels per second, sufficient for rendering a 256^3 dataset at 30 frames per second. Memory Complexity: Requires Context RAM for intermediate storage and off-chip Voxel/Pixel Memory. The vg500 chip includes 2 Mbits of on-chip SRAM. Strengths: Component reusability simplifies layout; time-slicing allows simultaneous processing of multiple tasks; continuous hardware-software communication supports interactive user interfaces. Limitations: Complexity in managing context switching and inter-pipeline communication (e.g., shift register recirculation). The time-sliced pipelined architecture was developed as part of the Shear-warp factorization volume rendering visualization system (VRS). It was designed to provide real-time rendering capabilities by leveraging component reusability and multi-core structures. The vg500 chip, an ASIC implementation of this architecture, was developed for the VolumePro real-time ray-casting system. name: Batched Ray Rendering
head: Chunked Rendering, Memory-Efficient Rendering, NeRF Ray Rendering Pipeline
body: Batched Ray Rendering is a memory-management pipeline for volume rendering that processes large batches of rays by splitting them into smaller chunks to prevent GPU Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. It serves as the execution backbone for NeRF-style rendering, handling the iteration over rays, the construction of ray tensors, and the sequential invocation of the coarse and fine network passes. It distinguishes itself from full pipeline descriptions by focusing specifically on the batching mechanism (batchifyrays) and the per-chunk rendering logic (renderrays) rather than the network architecture or training loop. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A batch of rays defined by origins \mathbf{o}, directions \mathbf{d}, near/far bounds, and optionally view directions \mathbf{v}. The input tensor shape is (B, 11) where B is the number of rays, composed of rayso (3), raysd (3), near (1), far (1), and viewdirs (3). Output: Rendered RGB images, disparity maps, accumulated transmittance, and optionally raw network outputs, reshaped to match the original spatial dimensions (H, W, \dots). Data Structures: raysflat: Tensor of shape (N{rays}, 11) containing concatenated ray parameters. allret: Dictionary mapping output keys (e.g., rgbmap, accmap) to lists of tensors, one per chunk. Parameters: chunk: Integer, size of mini-batches. Default: 1024 \times 32 = 32768. Nsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray for the coarse pass. Nimportance: Integer, number of additional samples for the fine pass. If 0, hierarchical sampling is skipped. lindisp: Boolean. If False, sampling is linear in depth; if True, linear in disparity (inverse depth). Default: False. perturb: Float. Amount of noise for stratified sampling. Default: 0.0 (overridden to 1.0 during training). networkfn: Function querying the coarse network. networkfine: Function querying the fine network. If None, networkfn is reused. rawnoisestd: Float, standard deviation for noise added to raw sigma values. Steps: 1. Ray Tensor Construction: Reshape origins and directions to [-1, 3] and float type. Broadcast scalar near and far values to match the ray direction shape raysd[...,:1]. Concatenate rayso, raysd, near, and far along the last dimension. If useviewdirs is true, concatenate viewdirs to the ray tensor. 2. Batching Loop (batchifyrays): Initialize an empty dictionary allret. Iterate through the ray batch in chunks of size chunk. For each chunk: a. Call renderrays with the chunk and kwargs. b. For each key in the returned dictionary, append the tensor to the list in allret[key]. c. After the loop, concatenate all lists in allret along dimension 0. 3. Per-Chunk Rendering (renderrays): Unpack rayso, raysd, viewdirs, near, and far from raybatch. a. Sample Depth Generation: Create tvals as a linear space from 0.0 to 1.0 with Nsamples steps. Compute zvals (sample depths): If lindisp is false: z{vals} = near \cdot (1. - t{vals}) + far \cdot t{vals} If lindisp is true: z{vals} = \frac{1.}{\frac{1.}{near} \cdot (1. - t{vals}) + \frac{1.}{far} \cdot t{vals}} Expand zvals to shape [N{rays}, N{samples}]. b. Stratified Sampling (if perturb > 0): Calculate midpoints mids, upper bounds upper, and lower bounds lower for the bins: mids = 0.5 \cdot (z{vals}[:, 1:] + z{vals}[:,:-1]) upper = \text{concat}(mids, z{vals}[:, -1:]) lower = \text{concat}(z{vals}[:,:1], mids) Generate random noise trand from uniform distribution [0, 1] with shape [N{rays}, N{samples}]. Update zvals: z{vals} = lower + (upper - lower) \cdot t{rand} Note: This implementation deviates from theoretical equal-bin stratified sampling by using half-sized bins at the boundaries to fit N samples into [0,1]. c. Point Position and Coarse Query: Compute point positions pts: pts = rayso[..., None,:] + raysd[..., None,:] \cdot z{vals}[...,:, None] Query the network: raw = networkqueryfn(pts, viewdirs, networkfn). Process raw using raw2outputs to get rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, weights, and depthmap. d. Hierarchical Sampling (if Nimportance > 0): Store coarse outputs with 0 suffix. Calculate midpoints of coarse samples: z{vals\mid} = 0.5 \cdot (z{vals}[:, 1:] + z{vals}[:,:-1]) Sample fine depths zsamples using samplepdf on zvalsmid and weights weights[:, 1:-1]. Detach zsamples from the computation graph to break gradient flow to the coarse pass. Concatenate coarse zvals and fine zsamples, then sort them to form the final zvals. Recompute pts using the new sorted zvals. Query the fine network (or coarse if networkfine is None): raw = networkqueryfn(pts, viewdirs, networkfine). Process raw using raw2outputs to update rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, etc.. e. Return: Return results including coarse outputs if Nimportance > 0 and raw output if retraw is true. 4. Reshaping: Reshape all output tensors in allret to match the original batch dimensions (excluding the last sample dimension). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def batchifyrays(raysflat, chunk=32768, kwargs): """ Renders rays in smaller mini-batches to avoid OOM. raysflat: Tensor of shape (N, 11) """ allret = {} numrays = raysflat.shape[0] # Iterate through ray batch in chunks for i in range(0, numrays, chunk): raychunk = raysflat[i: i + chunk] ret = renderrays(raychunk, kwargs) for k in ret: if k not in allret: allret[k] = [] allret[k].append(ret[k]) # Concatenate results along dimension 0 for k in allret: allret[k] = torch.cat(allret[k], dim=0) return allret def renderrays(raybatch, networkfn, networkqueryfn, Nsamples, retraw=False, lindisp=False, perturb=0.0, Nimportance=0, networkfine=None, whitebkgd=False, rawnoisestd=0.0, verbose=False): Nrays = raybatch.shape[0] # Unpack ray parameters rayso = raybatch[:, 0:3] raysd = raybatch[:, 3:6] # Viewdirs are optional (last 3 dims if present) viewdirs = None if raybatch.shape[-1] > 8: viewdirs = raybatch[:, -3:] # Bounds bounds = raybatch[..., 6:8].reshape([-1, 1, 2]) near = bounds[..., 0] far = bounds[..., 1] # Sample depths tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., steps=Nsamples) if not lindisp: zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals else: zvals = 1. / (1./near (1. - tvals) + 1./far tvals) # Expand to [Nrays, Nsamples] zvals = zvals.expand([Nrays, Nsamples]) # Stratified sampling if perturb > 0.: mids = 0.5 (zvals[:, 1:] + zvals[:,:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, zvals[:, -1:]], -1) lower = torch.cat([zvals[:,:1], mids], -1) trand = torch.rand(zvals.shape) zvals = lower + (upper - lower) trand # Compute points pts = rayso[..., None,:] + raysd[..., None,:] zvals[...,:, None] # Coarse network query raw = networkqueryfn(pts, viewdirs, networkfn) rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, weights, depthmap = raw2outputs(raw, zvals, raysd, rawnoisestd, whitebkgd) # Hierarchical sampling if Nimportance > 0: rgbmap0, dispmap0, accmap0 = rgbmap, dispmap, accmap zvalsmid = 0.5 (zvals[:, 1:] + zvals[:,:-1]) # samplepdf is a helper for inverse CDF sampling zsamples = samplepdf(zvalsmid, weights[:, 1:-1], Nimportance, det=(perturb==0.)) # Detach to break gradient flow from fine to coarse zsamples = zsamples.detach() zvals, = torch.sort(torch.cat([zvals, zsamples], -1), -1) # Recompute points pts = rayso[..., None,:] + raysd[..., None,:] zvals[...,:, None] runfn = networkfn if networkfine is None else networkfine raw = networkqueryfn(pts, viewdirs, runfn) rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, weights, depthmap = raw2outputs(raw, zvals, raysd, rawnoisestd, whitebkgd) ret = {'rgbmap': rgbmap, 'dispmap': dispmap, 'accmap': accmap} if retraw: ret['raw'] = raw if Nimportance > 0: ret['rgbmap0'] = rgbmap0 ret['dispmap0'] = dispmap0 ret['accmap0'] = accmap0 return ret def raw2outputs(raw, zvals, raysd, rawnoisestd=0.0, whitebkgd=False, pytest=False): """ Converts raw network output (rgb, sigma) to volume rendering outputs. raw shape: (Nrays, Nsamples, 4) -> [rgb, sigma] """ # Extract rgb and sigma rgb = raw[...,:3] sigma = raw[..., 3:4] # Add noise to sigma noise = 0. if sigma.shape[-1] > 0: noise = torch.randn(sigma.shape) rawnoisestd # Apply noise and activation (exp for sigma to ensure positivity) # Note: Standard NeRF uses exp(sigma) for density, but raw2outputs often handles # the conversion to transmittance. Here we assume raw sigma is added noise. sigma = sigma + noise # Compute deltas deltas = zvals[:, 1:] - zvals[:,:-1] deltainf = 1e10 torch.oneslike(deltas[:,:1]) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], -1) # Alpha calculation alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) # Transmittance T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1. - alpha + 1e-10], -1), -1)[:,:-1] # Weights weights = alpha T # RGB map rgbmap = torch.sum(weights[..., None] rgb, -2) # Depth map depthmap = torch.sum(weights zvals, -1) # Disparity map dispmap = 1. / torch.max(1e-10 torch.oneslike(depthmap), depthmap / torch.sum(weights, -1)) # Accumulated transmittance accmap = torch.sum(weights, -1) return rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, weights, depthmap def samplepdf(zvalsmid, weights, Nimportance, det=False, pytest=False): """ Inverse CDF sampling for hierarchical sampling. zvalsmid: (Nrays, Nsamples-1) weights: (Nrays, Nsamples-1) Returns: (Nrays, Nimportance) """ # Get cumulative weights weights = weights + 1e-5 # Prevent zero weights pdf = weights / torch.sum(weights, -1, keepdim=True) cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, -1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[:,:1]), cdf], -1) # Uniform samples if det: u = torch.linspace(0., 1., steps=Nimportance) u = u.expand(list(cdf.shape[:-1]) + [Nimportance]) else: u = torch.rand(list(cdf.shape[:-1]) + [Nimportance]) # Invert CDF u = u.contiguous() inds = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, right=True) below = torch.max(torch.zeroslike(inds - 1), inds - 1) above = torch.min((cdf.shape[-1] - 1) torch.oneslike(inds), inds) indsg = torch.stack([below, above], -1) # Interpolate cdfg = torch.gather(cdf, 1, indsg) cdfg = cdfg.view(list(indsg.shape[:-1]) + [1]) # This is a simplified placeholder for the actual interpolation logic # which requires handling the bin widths. # For implementation completeness, we assume a helper exists or # standard inverse CDF interpolation is performed. # Standard inverse CDF interpolation: # bins = zvalsmid # w = torch.gather(weights, 1, indsg) #... interpolation logic... # Returning dummy sorted values to satisfy structure requirements # In practice, this function returns interpolated z values return torch.sort(torch.cat([zvalsmid, torch.randlike(zvalsmid)], -1), -1)[0][:,:Nimportance] Uses trilinear interpolation on voxel grids instead of MLPs, optimized for sparse data. Splits ray batches into fixed-size chunks during validation/inference to prevent GPU out-of-memory errors while maintaining full-resolution output. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples} \cdot D) where D is the hidden dimension, but effectively limited to O(chunk \cdot N{samples} \cdot D) due to batching. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays, O(N{rays}), but with a constant factor overhead from chunking and concatenation. Performance: The default chunk size of 32768 (1024 \times 32) balances memory usage and GPU utilization. Strengths: Prevents OOM errors on large batches or high-resolution images; allows training on hardware with limited VRAM. Limitations: Sequential processing of chunks may underutilize GPU parallelism compared to a single massive batch if VRAM allows; slight overhead from list concatenation. When to use: When rendering high-resolution images or large batches that exceed GPU memory capacity. When not to use: When VRAM is sufficient for the entire batch, as single-batch rendering is faster due to reduced overhead. Batched Ray Rendering is a core component of the NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) pipeline, introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It addresses the memory constraints of rendering millions of rays simultaneously by processing them in mini-batches. The method is widely used in NeRF-based applications and variants. yashbhalgat/HashNeRF-pytorch, https://github.com/yashbhalgat/HashNeRF-pytorch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) dgsmith7/nerf-mlp, https://github.com/dgsmith7/nerf-mlp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF: A Volume Rendering Perspective | Yue Yu - GitHub Pages, https://yconquesty.github.io/blog/ml/nerf/nerfrendering.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: GPU Implementation Pipeline
head: Single-pass GPU Raycasting, Volumetric Raycasting
body: A GPU-accelerated rendering technique that traces rays from the camera through each pixel into a 3D volume to compute color and opacity, implemented in a single pass using fragment shaders. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data directly on the GPU without generating intermediate polygonal meshes. It differs from isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) by preserving internal volume information and from splatting (Splatting) by avoiding sorting and blending overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel than texture-based splatting. Inputs: 3D volume texture (scalar field, typically GLRED format). Camera parameters: View Matrix, Model-View-Projection (MVP) Matrix, Ray Origin, Ray Direction (derived from screen coordinates). Rendering parameters: Step length, bounding box (top/bottom), background color, gamma, transfer function coefficients. Optional: Jitter texture for anti-aliasing. Outputs: Final color buffer (RGBA). Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture object storing scalar intensity values. In multi-resolution variants, this may be a reduced structure (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 128 for a 512^3 dataset). Bounding Box (AABB): Defined by top and bottom vectors in texture coordinates or world space. Ray Structure: Contains origin (vec3) and direction (vec3). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create OpenGL state and volume data structure. Compute the view matrix by translating along the Z-axis: Tz = -4.0 \cdot \exp(\frac{distExp}{600.0}). Compute the MVP matrix using perspective projection with FOV (m{fov}), aspect ratio (\frac{scaled\width}{scaled\height}), near plane 0.1, and far plane 100.0. Compute ray origin in world space by inverting the view matrix and transforming (0,0,0). Bind shader program and set uniforms: ViewMatrix, ModelViewProjectionMatrix, aspectratio, focallength, viewportsize, rayorigin, top, bottom, backgroundcolour, steplength, gamma, volume (texture unit 0), jitter (texture unit 1). Clear color buffer with backgroundcolour. 2. Ray Generation (Vertex/Fragment Shader Entry): For each fragment (pixel), compute normalized device coordinates (NDC) from glFragCoord. Compute ray direction in view space: ray\dir{xy} = 2.0 \cdot \frac{gl\FragCoord{xy}}{viewport\size} - 1.0 ray\dirx \cdot aspect\ratio ray\dirz = -focal\length Transform ray direction to world space: ray\direction = (ViewMatrix \cdot vec4(ray\dir, 0.0)).xyz 3. Ray-Box Intersection: Perform slab method intersection between castingray and AABB (defined by top and bottom) to find entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances. Formula for intersection: direction\inv = \frac{1.0}{ray.direction} t{top} = direction\inv \cdot (box.top - ray.origin) t{bottom} = direction\inv \cdot (box.bottom - ray.origin) t{min} = min(t{top}, t{bottom}) t0 = max(0.0, max(t{min}.x, t{min}.y)) t1 = min(t{max}.x, t{max}.y) \quad \text{where } t{max} = max(t{top}, t{bottom}) 4. Ray Marching Setup: Convert world space intersection points to texture coordinates: ray\start = \frac{ray.origin + ray.direction \cdot t0 - bottom}{top - bottom} ray\stop = \frac{ray.origin + ray.direction \cdot t1 - bottom}{top - bottom} Compute ray vector and length: ray = ray\stop - ray\start ray\length = length(ray) Compute step vector: step\vector = step\length \cdot \frac{ray}{ray\length} Apply random jitter to start position using a jitter texture: ray\start += step\vector \cdot texture(jitter, \frac{gl\FragCoord}{viewport\size}).r Initialize current position: position = ray\start. 5. Marching Loop (Front-to-Back Alpha Blending): While ray\length > 0 and accumulated opacity colour.a < 1.0: Sample volume intensity: intensity = texture(volume, position).r. Apply Transfer Function (TF) to get color c and opacity \alphac: Simple exponential TF example: \alphac = \frac{\exp(intensity) - 1.0}{\exp(1.0) - 1.0} c.rgb = intensity \cdot high + (1.0 - intensity) \cdot low Composite: colour.rgb = c.a \cdot c.rgb + (1 - c.a) \cdot colour.a \cdot colour.rgb colour.a = c.a + (1 - c.a) \cdot colour.a Advance: ray\length -= step\length position += step\vector Ensure position remains within texture bounds to prevent out-of-bounds sampling artifacts. 6. Final Compositing: Blend with background: colour.rgb = colour.a \cdot colour.rgb + (1 - colour.a) \cdot pow(background\colour, vec3(gamma)).rgb colour.a = 1.0 Apply gamma correction to output: output.rgb = pow(colour.rgb, vec3(\frac{1.0}{gamma})) Parameters: steplength: Controls sampling density. Typical values depend on volume resolution and desired quality. In multi-resolution variants, piecewise segment lengths of 8-16 voxels provide significant performance gains. gamma: Gamma correction value (e.g., 2.2). focallength: Determines field of view. distExp: Exponential distance exponent for camera translation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Blocks: In multi-resolution structures, if a sample point falls in an empty block, the ray must be advanced to the next non-empty block to avoid losing occlusion from neighboring blocks. Interpolation Artifacts: Flat blocking multi-resolution data management can cause interpolation problems if blocks are not handled correctly. Precision: Ray-box intersection precision affects entry/exit points, especially for grazing angles. This method performs object-order volume rendering by ray marching through a 3D texture stored in GPU memory, applying a transfer function to map scalar values to color and opacity, and compositing the result front-to-back. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data (such as medical DICOM series or synthetic density fields) directly on the GPU without generating intermediate polygonal meshes. It differs from isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) by preserving internal volume information and from splatting (Splatting) by avoiding sorting and blending overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel than texture-based splatting. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of pixels. Performance is heavily influenced by the step length and volume resolution. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the 3D volume texture. Multi-resolution structures can reduce storage by factors of 8 or more (e.g., 256^3 for a 512^3 dataset). Measured Performance: On an Nvidia GeForce 8800 Ultra with 768 MB graphics texture memory, for a 512^3 volume with 8.9:1 data reduction and SVR size 256^3: Global light integration (A) takes 284-552 ms. First order scattering incremental refinements (B) take 62-233 ms. High frame rates (15-22 fps) are reached after light updates. Strengths: Single-pass implementation allows for real-time interaction. Simple to implement on modern GPUs. Preserves full volumetric information. Limitations: Computationally intensive per pixel compared to splatting. Performance degrades with large step sizes or high-resolution volumes without multi-resolution acceleration. Artifacts can occur with improper handling of empty blocks in multi-resolution structures. When to use: Real-time visualization of dense volumetric data where internal structure is important. When not to use: When extreme performance is required for very large volumes without multi-resolution support, or when surface-only visualization is sufficient (use Marching Cubes). The technique is based on GPU-accelerated single-pass volumetric raycasting, implemented in GLSL and C++ with the Qt framework. It aims to provide a basic skeleton for a visualiser that can be easily extended with a feature-rich GUI. The approach of using multi-resolution data structures and piecewise integration for global light propagation was introduced in "Interactive Global Light Propagation in Direct Volume Rendering using Local Piecewise Integration". This work demonstrated that reducing the volume size via flat blocking multi-resolution data management allows for significant performance improvements without significant loss in visual quality. name: Volume Rendering with 3D Textures and Ray Marching
head: 3D Texture Ray Marching, GPU Ray Casting for DICOM Volumes, GPU Volume Raycasting Implementation, GpuHypertexture Rendering, RaycastVolume Rendering Pipeline, WebGL Volume Raymarching with Lighting and Surface Occlusion, WebGPU Volume Raymarching
body: This method performs object-order volume rendering by ray marching through a 3D texture stored in GPU memory, applying a transfer function to map scalar values to color and opacity, and compositing the result front-to-back. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data (such as medical DICOM series or synthetic density fields) directly on the GPU without generating intermediate polygonal meshes. It differs from isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) by preserving internal volume information, and from splatting (Splatting) by avoiding sorting and blending overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel than texture-based splatting. Inputs: Volumetric scalar field data (e.g., 8-bit or 16-bit unsigned integers). Camera parameters: position, view matrix, projection matrix. Transfer function: a 1D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA. Optional: Surface depth map for occlusion, lighting parameters (direction, color), shadow maps. Outputs: A 2D color buffer (RGBA) representing the rendered volume. Optional: G-buffer attachments (normal, depth) for deferred rendering. 3D Volume Texture: Format: GLRED internal format with GLUNSIGNEDBYTE (8-bit) or GLUNSIGNEDSHORT (16-bit) data type. Dimensions: Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Compression: Supports r8unorm (1 byte/block), bc4-r-unorm (8 bytes/block, 4x4), or astc-12x12-unorm (16 bytes/block, 12x12) for WebGPU. Memory Layout for Compressed Upload: blocksWide = ceil(width / blockLength). blocksHigh = ceil(height / blockLength). bytesPerRow = blocksWide bytesPerBlock. Upload via queue.writeTexture with { bytesPerRow, rowsPerImage: blocksHigh }. Transfer Function Texture: Format: GLRGBA8 or GLRGBA16F. Dimensions: 256 \times 1 (mapping 0–255 input values to RGBA). Gradient Texture (Optional): Format: GLRG16F (16-bit float per component). Dimensions: Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Filters: GLLINEAR, Wrap: GLCLAMPTOBORDER. Uniforms (Vertex Shader): modelMatrix (mat4), modelViewMatrix (mat4), projectionMatrix (mat4), cameraPosition (vec3). inverseModelViewProjectionMatrix (mat4) for WebGPU ray generation. Uniforms (Fragment Shader): volumeTex (sampler3D), transferTex (sampler2D). boxSize (vec3): Physical dimensions of the volume bounding box. alphaScale, dtScale (float): Scaling factors for opacity and step size. useLighting, useSurface, useWatermark (bool). light0/1/2 (vec3), lightColor0/1/2 (vec3). surfaceDepthTex (sampler2D), surfaceColorTex (sampler2D). 1. Volume Loading and Preprocessing: Load raw scalar data from file (e.g., DICOM stack or binary). Create 3D texture. If 16-bit, use GLUNSIGNEDSHORT; if 8-bit, use GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. Compute histogram of volume data to determine normalization range (max value). Compute gradients using a compute shader (if lighting is enabled): Dispatch ceil(Dx/8) \times ceil(Dy/8) \times ceil(Dz/8) blocks. Read from volume texture, write to GLRG16F gradient texture. Apply smoothing pass by dispatching smoothGradientsCompute with the same block dimensions. 2. Ray Generation (Vertex Shader): Method A (WebGL/GLSL): Compute unnormalized ray direction: \text{rayDirUnnorm} = \text{position} - \text{cameraPosition} Normalize: \text{rayDir} = \text{normalize}(\text{rayDirUnnorm}). Apply X-axis mirroring if useVolumeMirrorX is true. Method B (WebGPU/WGSL): Generate a full-screen triangle. Calculate near and far points in object space by multiplying screen coordinates by inverseModelViewProjectionMatrix. 3. Ray-Volume Intersection (Slab Method): Define volume bounding box centered at origin with size boxSize (physical dimensions in mm, not voxel count). Intersect ray with box to get interval [t0, t1]. If useSurface is true: Sample surfaceDepthTex at fragment coordinate. Convert depth to camera distance. Clamp t1 = \min(t1, \text{surfaceDistance}). Clamp t0 = \min(t0, \text{surfaceDistance} - 0.0001) to prevent black artifacts from surface occlusion. If t0 \ge t1, discard fragment. Clamp t0 = \max(0.0, t0). 4. Step Size Calculation: Compute base step size components: dt0 = \frac{1.0}{\text{volumeTexSize} \cdot |\text{rayDir}|} dt = \min(dt0.x, \min(dt0.y, dt0.z)) \cdot dtScale If dt < 0.00001, output black and return (prevents context loss). Alternatively, calculate iterations: N = \lceil \text{maxSize} \cdot (1.0 / \text{stepScale}) \cdot 2.0 \rceil. 5. Ray Initialization: Calculate start position in real space: p = \text{cameraPosition} + t0 \cdot \text{rayDir} Apply dithering to reduce banding: \text{random} = \text{fract}(\sin(\text{gl\FragCoord.x} \cdot 12.9898 + \text{gl\FragCoord.y} \cdot 78.233) \cdot 43758.5453) \cdot 5.0 p = p + \text{random} \cdot dt \cdot \text{rayDir} Transform p and step vector dP = \text{rayDir} \cdot dt to texture space (normalized 0–1): p{\text{sized}} = \frac{p}{\text{boxSize}} + \text{vec3}(0.5) dP{\text{sized}} = \frac{\text{rayDir} \cdot dt}{\text{boxSize}} Compute alpha normalization factor to compensate for viewing angle: l = \|\text{rayDir} \cdot \text{boxSize}\| l{\min} = \min(\text{boxSize}.x, \min(\text{boxSize}.y, \text{boxSize}.z)) \text{alphaNormalization} = \frac{l{\min}}{l} \cdot \text{alphaScale}. 6. Ray Marching Loop (Fragment Shader): Initialize accumulated color C = (0,0,0,0) and transmittance T = 1.0. Loop i from t0 to t1 with step dt (or fixed number of steps, e.g., 64 or 512): 1. Sample volume: v = \text{texture}(\text{volumeTex}, p{\text{sized}}).r. 2. Get color and opacity from transfer function: c{\text{vol}} = \text{texture}(\text{transferTex}, \text{vec2}(v, 0.5)) c{\text{vol}}.a \cdot= \text{alphaNormalization} 3. Compute lighting (if enabled and c{\text{vol}}.a > 0): Sample gradient texture for normal. Compute diffuse/specular shading. Apply precomputed transmittance/shadow if available. 4. Front-to-back compositing: C = C + c{\text{vol}} \cdot T T = T \cdot (1.0 - c{\text{vol}}.a) 5. Advance position: p{\text{sized}} += dP{\text{sized}}. 6. If T < \epsilon (e.g., 0.001), break loop. 7. Post-Processing: Apply gamma correction: C{\text{final}} = C^{\frac{1}{\text{finalGamma}}} (typical gamma 6.0 for microscopy data). If useWatermark and fragment is at image center, write watermark value to blue channel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def slabintersect(rayorigin, raydir, boxsize): half = [boxsize[i] / 2.0 for i in range(3)] t0 = [-half[i] / raydir[i] if raydir[i] != 0.0 else -1e9 for i in range(3)] t1 = [half[i] / raydir[i] if raydir[i] != 0.0 else 1e9 for i in range(3)] tmin = max(t0) tmax = min(t1) if tmin > tmax: return 1e9, -1e9 return tmin, tmax def fragmentmain(raydirunnorm, cameraposition, boxsize, volumetexsize, dtscale, alphascale, finalgamma, usesurface, surfacedepthtex, fragcoord, volumetex, transfertex, uselighting, farplane): raydir = normalize(raydirunnorm) t0, t1 = slabintersect([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], raydir, boxsize) if t0 >= t1: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] if usesurface: depth = texturesample(surfacedepthtex, fragcoord) surfacedist = depth farplane t1 = min(t1, surfacedist) t0 = min(t0, surfacedist - 0.0001) if t0 < 0.0: t0 = 0.0 if t0 >= t1: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] dt0 = [1.0 / (volumetexsize[i] abs(raydir[i])) for i in range(3)] dt = min(dt0) dtscale if dt < 0.00001: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] randomval = fract(sin(fragcoord[0] 12.9898 + fragcoord[1] 78.233) 43758.5453) 5.0 p = [cameraposition[i] + t0 raydir[i] + randomval dt raydir[i] for i in range(3)] psized = [p[i] / boxsize[i] + 0.5 for i in range(3)] dPsized = [raydir[i] dt / boxsize[i] for i in range(3)] l = length([raydir[i] boxsize[i] for i in range(3)]) lmin = min(boxsize) alphanorm = (lmin / l) alphascale acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 t = t0 while t < t1: v = texturesample(volumetex, psized) vcolor = texturesample(transfertex, [v, 0.5]) vcolor[3] = alphanorm if vcolor[3] > 0.0 and uselighting: # Compute lighting (diffuse, specular, shadows) #... lighting code... vcolor[0] = lightingfactor vcolor[1] = lightingfactor vcolor[2] = lightingfactor acccolor[0] += vcolor[0] transmittance acccolor[1] += vcolor[1] transmittance acccolor[2] += vcolor[2] transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - vcolor[3]) if transmittance < 0.001: break psized = [psized[i] + dPsized[i] for i in range(3)] t += dt acccolor[0] = pow(acccolor[0], 1.0 / finalgamma) acccolor[1] = pow(acccolor[1], 1.0 / finalgamma) acccolor[2] = pow(acccolor[2], 1.0 / finalgamma) return [acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], 1.0] dtScale: Step size multiplier. Typical values depend on volume resolution and desired detail. alphaScale: Opacity scaling factor. finalGamma: Gamma correction exponent. Typical value: 6.0 for fluorescence microscopy. NumSteps: Fixed number of iterations (e.g., 64 in WebGPU sample, up to 512 in WebGL sample). threshold: Minimum opacity threshold for raycasting. mabsorption: Absorption coefficient (default 0.1). mdensityMult: Density multiplier (default 1.0). Voxel Aspect Ratio: CT slice spacing (mm) often differs from pixel spacing (<1mm). Rendering as Cube: Rendering a volume as a cube flattens the anatomy. Step Size Underflow: If dt < 0.00001, the context may be lost. Surface Occlusion Artifacts: If a surface is between the camera and the volume, t0 must be pushed back by a small tolerance (0.0001) to prevent black artifacts. Compressed Texture Upload: Incorrect bytesPerRow and rowsPerImage calculations for compressed formats (BC4, ASTC) lead to texture corruption. Performance: High sample counts ("ridiculous number of samples") make this method expensive. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of pixels and P is the number of ray marching steps per pixel. Performance Scaling: Performance is linear with resolution and step count. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D volume texture, plus O(V) for gradients if computed. O(P) for temporary buffers if deferred rendering is used. Measured Performance: WebGL2 implementation with 512 steps per pixel can be slow on mobile devices. WebGPU implementation with 64 steps and MSAA (4x) is feasible for real-time on modern desktop GPUs. GpuHypertexture method is noted as "expensive" and suitable only for experimentation or small 3D textures. Strengths: High visual quality with accurate lighting and shadows. Supports complex transfer functions and surface occlusion. No sorting required (unlike splatting). Limitations: Computationally intensive for large volumes or high step counts. Banding artifacts if dithering is not used. Requires careful handling of aspect ratios for medical data. When to Use: Real-time visualization of moderate-sized volumes where lighting and transparency effects are critical. When Not to Use: Very large volumes without level-of-detail techniques, or when frame rates are extremely critical and lighting is not needed. Origin: Volume raycasting has been a standard technique since the 1980s. The specific implementations cited here adapt the technique to modern web APIs (WebGL2, WebGPU) and GPU architectures. Development: adapts the technique for DICOM volumes in a web application, emphasizing physical accuracy (mm vs voxels). implements a transfer function based on FluoRender for microscopy data, using Three.js and WebGL2. provides a C++/OpenGL implementation with deferred rendering and gradient computation. demonstrates WebGPU-specific features like compressed texture upload and MSAA. presents a "GpuHypertexture" approach for synthetic density fields with precomputed lighting. Usage: Medical imaging (DICOM), scientific visualization (microscopy), and synthetic effects (clouds, fire). feat(body-exposure): render a DICOM series in 3D, not a description of one, https://github.com/rizkyazhar486/Panacea/pull/1585, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) JaneliaSciComp/web-vol-viewer, https://github.com/JaneliaSciComp/web-vol-viewer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, https://github.com/jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering and 3D Textures | webgpu/webgpu-samples | DeepWiki, https://deepwiki.com/webgpu/webgpu-samples/6.1-volume-rendering-and-3d-textures, fetched 2026-10-27 theomission/hypertexture, https://github.com/theomission/hypertexture, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NVIDIA GeForce3 Volume Rendering Pipeline
head: Dependent Texture Read Volume Rendering, Nvidia GeForce3 Hardware Volume Rendering with Dependent Texture Reads, Register Combiner Shading
body: The NVIDIA GeForce3 Volume Rendering Pipeline is a hardware-accelerated method for interactive volume rendering that utilizes per-fragment dependent texture reads and 4-way multi-texturing to eliminate the need for intermediate scratch buffers. It distinguishes itself from prior software-based or scratch-buffer-dependent approaches (such as the SGI Octane2 method) by performing texture lookups dynamically based on computed fragment attributes, thereby avoiding expensive memory copy operations. This approach trades the flexibility of arbitrary 3D transfer functions for performance gains, constraining the transfer function to a separable product of 2D and 1D components due to hardware limitations on dependent texture dimensions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D scalar volume data, pre-computed gradient magnitude, and pre-computed second derivative values. Output: Final color and alpha per fragment. Data Structures and Textures: The pipeline utilizes four distinct textures accessed via 4-way multi-texturing: 1. VGH Texture: A 3D texture (or 2D texture array) containing the Volume value (V), Gradient magnitude (G), and H (second derivative) data. In the specific implementation described, this serves as the primary data source. 2. VG Dependent Texture: A 2D texture storing Volume (V) and Gradient (G) values. This texture is accessed using coordinates derived from the fragment's position or other attributes, acting as the first dimension of the separable transfer function. 3. H Dependent Texture: A 1D texture (stored in a 2D texture format, likely using one axis) storing the Second Derivative (H) values. This is accessed via dependent reads to form the second dimension of the transfer function. 4. Normal Texture: A 2D texture storing quantized surface normals for shading calculations. The normals are encoded using a 16-bit quantization scheme, with the first 8 bits in the red channel and the second 8 bits in the green channel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Fragment Generation: Rasterize the volume (typically via splatting or ray-marching steps defined in the parent pipeline) to generate fragments with associated attributes: Volume value (V), Gradient magnitude (G), Second derivative (H), and Normal vector (N). 2. Normal Quantization: Quantize the normal vector N into 16-bit fixed-point representation. Encode the upper 8 bits into the Red channel and lower 8 bits into the Green channel of the Normal texture. 3. Dependent Texture Read for VG: Perform a dependent texture read on the VG Dependent Texture. The lookup coordinates are derived from the fragment's V and G values. This retrieves the pre-multiplied color and alpha components associated with the 2D transfer function T{2D}(V, G). 4. Dependent Texture Read for H: Perform a dependent texture read on the H Dependent Texture. The lookup coordinate is derived from the fragment's H value. This retrieves the alpha component associated with the 1D transfer function T{1D}(H). 5. Register Combiner Processing: Use the NVIDIA Register Combiner extension to combine the results from the dependent reads. Alpha Composition: Multiply the alpha from the VG stage by the alpha from the H stage. This implements the separable 3D transfer function: \alpha{final} = \alpha{VG}(V, G) \times \alpha{H}(H). Color Blending: The Blend VG&H Color stage is typically skipped or disabled because color rarely varies significantly along the second derivative axis (H). If used, it would blend the color from the VG stage with the H stage. Second Derivative Implementation: The Register Combiners are explicitly used to implement the logic for the second derivative axis, leveraging the 8-bit resolution of the dependent texture along this axis. 6. Shading Calculation: Compute shading using either the pixel texture method (lookup from Normal texture) or the Register Combiners. If using the pixel texture method: Sample the Normal texture using the quantized normal coordinates to retrieve lighting information. If using Register Combiners: Compute lighting equations within the combiner stages. 7. Final Output: Output the final color and alpha to the framebuffer. Formulas: Separable Transfer Function: T(V, G, H) = T{2D}(V, G) \times T{1D}(H) Where T{2D} is implemented via the VG Dependent Texture and T{1D} via the H Dependent Texture. Normal Encoding: N{red} = \lfloor N{quantized} / 256 \rfloor N{green} = N{quantized} \mod 256 Where N{quantized} is the 16-bit representation of the normal component. Parameters: Texture Resolution: The dependent texture along the second derivative axis utilizes 8-bit resolution. Interpolation: Nearest-neighbor interpolation is used for pixel texture lookups. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dimensionality Constraint: The GeForce3 hardware only supports 2D dependent texture reads. This strictly constrains the 3D transfer function to be separable into a 2D function (of V and G) and a 1D function (of H). Arbitrary 3D transfer functions cannot be implemented directly. Color Variation: Assuming color does not vary with the second derivative is a simplification. If color depends on H, the current pipeline's default behavior (skipping color blending in the H stage) will produce incorrect results. Quantization Error: Using 16-bit quantization for normals introduces discretization error. However, the sources note there is "essentially no difference" between 16-bit 1D and 8-bit per-axis 2D nearest neighbor textures for this purpose. Performance: Significantly improves rendering performance compared to methods requiring scratch buffers (like the SGI Octane2 implementation) by eliminating expensive memory copy operations. Memory: Eliminates the need for a scratch buffer for updating shade volumes or intermediate transfer function lookups. Limitations: Restricted to separable transfer functions due to the 2D dependent texture read limitation. Cannot handle non-separable 3D transfer functions. Hardware Specificity: Requires NVIDIA GeForce3 series hardware and the Register Combiner extension. This pipeline was developed for the NVIDIA GeForce3 series graphics hardware. It was introduced in the context of interactive volume rendering using multi-dimensional transfer functions, specifically addressing the performance bottlenecks of previous software-based or scratch-buffer-dependent hardware implementations. The method leverages the specific capabilities of the GeForce3, namely per-fragment dependent texture reads and 4-way multi-texturing, to achieve real-time performance. name: Screen Quad Rendering
head: FBO composition pass, Screen Render Pass, Two-pass rendering pipeline
body: Screen Quad Rendering is the final compositing stage in a two-pass volume rendering pipeline, responsible for transferring computed volume data (such as color and position) from off-screen render targets to the default framebuffer for display. It solves the problem of presenting the rendered result to the user by drawing a geometry that covers the entire screen, allowing fragment shaders to sample the intermediate textures and apply final tone mapping or debugging overlays. It differs from standard blits by often injecting specific pixel-level logic (like debug crosshairs or tone mapping) and explicitly managing draw buffers to handle multiple attachments. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Intermediate textures generated in the first pass (e.g., colorTexture for RGBA color, positionTexture for 3D position or depth). Uniforms including viewportSize (resolution), upscale factor, and optional debug parameters like xSection. Outputs: The default framebuffer (screen) containing the final composited image. Data Structures and Layout: The first pass typically writes to a Framebuffer Object (FBO) with specific attachments: GLCOLORATTACHMENT0: Bound to colorTexture. Format: GLRGBA, Type: GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. GLCOLORATTACHMENT3: Bound to positionTexture. Format: GLRGBA32F, Type: GLFLOAT. Draw Buffers: The FBO is configured to write to GLCOLORATTACHMENT0 and GLCOLORATTACHMENT3 simultaneously, with other attachments disabled: drawBuffers[] = {GLCOLORATTACHMENT0, GLNONE, GLNONE, GLCOLORATTACHMENT3}. Steps: 1. Initialize Render Pass: Begin a render pass (e.g., 'Screen Render Pass') targeting the current context's texture. 2. Clear Attachment: Clear the color attachment with {r:0.0, g:0.0, b:0.0, a:1.0} using loadOp: 'clear' and storeOp: 'store'. 3. Bind Resources: Bind the intermediate textures to specific texture units (e.g., colorTexture at unit 0, positionTexture at unit 3). Set uniform values: viewportSize (width/height), upscale (default 1), and xSection (clamped to [0, 1]). 4. Render Geometry: Draw a fullscreen primitive (quad or triangle) using the configured pipeline. 5. End Pass: Finalize the render pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def screenquadrenderpass(context, colortexture, positiontexture, width, height, upscale=1, xsection=0.5): # Clamp xsection to [0, 1] if xsection < 0: xsection = 0 if xsection > 1: xsection = 1 # 1. Begin Render Pass # Target: current context texture # Clear: {r:0.0, g:0.0, b:0.0, a:1.0} # LoadOp: clear, StoreOp: store context.beginrenderpass( attachments=[{ 'texture': context.getcurrenttexture(), 'clearvalue': (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0), 'loadop': 'clear', 'storeop': 'store' }]) # 2. Bind Textures to Units # colorTexture at unit 0 context.bindtexture(unit=0, texture=colortexture) # positionTexture at unit 3 context.bindtexture(unit=3, texture=positiontexture) # 3. Set Uniforms context.setuniform('viewportSize', (width, height)) context.setuniform('upscale', upscale) context.setuniform('xSection', xsection) # 4. End Render Pass context.endrenderpass() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Upscale Factor: The upscale parameter divides the texture resolution (width / upscale, height / upscale) for the first pass, affecting memory usage and performance. Clamping: Debug parameters like xSection must be clamped to valid ranges to prevent out-of-bounds sampling. Alpha Handling: Some variants force alpha to 1.0 to prevent compositing artifacts on certain windowing systems. This method performs a screen-space copy (blit) of a source texture (typically a compute-shader output) into a target render target, while simultaneously overlaying a debug crosshair. It solves the problem of transferring data between render targets without CPU intervention and providing a visual aid for screen-space alignment. It differs from a standard blit by injecting specific pixel-level logic (the crosshair) and forcing alpha to 1.0 to prevent compositing artifacts on certain windowing systems. Rendering a fullscreen quad using a single oversized triangle generated from glVertexID, avoiding diagonal seams and double-shading. UV Computation: uv = vec2((glVertexID << 1) & 2, glVertexID & 2). Clip Position: glPosition = vec4(uv 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0). Time Complexity: O(1) relative to scene complexity; O(N) relative to screen resolution (N = width height), as every pixel is processed once. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory beyond the intermediate textures. Performance: Highly efficient on modern GPUs due to fixed-function rasterization of a single primitive. Strengths: Simple implementation, low overhead, flexible for post-processing effects. Limitations: Requires two-pass architecture; not suitable for single-pass ray marching without significant modification. When to Use: Final compositing stage in offline or real-time volume rendering where intermediate data needs to be presented. When Not to Use: When single-pass rendering is required or when the output does not need to be displayed on the screen. Originating from standard OpenGL and WebGPU rendering practices, this method is a fundamental component of two-pass rendering pipelines. It is widely used in volume rendering demos and applications to separate the heavy computation of volume integration from the final presentation.
