width) def GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(texel): # Extracts the bone index from a float4 texel return int(texel[0]) def ReconstructCovariance3x3(covA, covB): # Reconstructs symmetric 3x3 matrix from packed components return [ [covA[0], covA[1], covA[2]], [covA[1], covB[0], covB[1]], [covA[2], covB[1], covB[2]] ] def ExtractCovarianceComponents(matrix): # Packs symmetric 3x3 matrix back into covA and covB covA = [matrix[0][0], matrix[0][1], matrix[0][2]] covB = [matrix[1][1], matrix[1][2], matrix[2][2]] return covA, covB def GsplatLoadSkinWeight(sourceid): indexoffset = sourceid 4 boneindices = [ GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(GsplatSkinIndexTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(indexoffset, GsplatSkinIndexTextureWidth)]), GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(GsplatSkinIndexTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(indexoffset + 1, GsplatSkinIndexTextureWidth)]), GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(GsplatSkinIndexTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(indexoffset + 2, GsplatSkinIndexTextureWidth)]), GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(GsplatSkinIndexTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(indexoffset + 3, GsplatSkinIndexTextureWidth)]) ] boneweights = GsplatSkinWeightTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(sourceid, GsplatSkinWeightTextureWidth)] return {"boneIndices": boneindices, "boneWeights": boneweights} def GsplatLoadBoneMatrix(boneindex): matrixoffset = boneindex 4 row0 = GsplatSkinBoneTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(matrixoffset, GsplatSkinBoneTextureWidth)] row1 = GsplatSkinBoneTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(matrixoffset + 1, GsplatSkinBoneTextureWidth)] row2 = GsplatSkinBoneTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(matrixoffset + 2, GsplatSkinBoneTextureWidth)] row3 = GsplatSkinBoneTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(matrixoffset + 3, GsplatSkinBoneTextureWidth)] return [row0, row1, row2, row3] def GsplatLoadReferenceInverse(sourceid): matrixoffset = sourceid 3 row0 = GsplatSkinReferenceTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(matrixoffset, GsplatSkinReferenceTextureWidth)] row1 = GsplatSkinReferenceTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(matrixoffset + 1, GsplatSkinReferenceTextureWidth)] row2 = GsplatSkinReferenceTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(matrixoffset + 2, GsplatSkinReferenceTextureWidth)] row3 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] return [row0, row1, row2, row3] def GsplatSkinMatrix(sourceid): skindata = GsplatLoadSkinWeight(sourceid) currentmatrix = [[0.0]4 for in range(4)] for i in range(4): boneidx = skindata["boneIndices"][i] boneweight = skindata["boneWeights"][i] bonematrix = GsplatLoadBoneMatrix(boneidx) for r in range(4): for c in range(4): currentmatrix[r][c] += boneweight bonematrix[r][c] refinverse = GsplatLoadReferenceInverse(sourceid) # Matrix multiplication: refinverse @ currentmatrix skinmatrix = [[sum(refinverse[r][k] currentmatrix[k][c] for k in range(4)) for c in range(4)] for r in range(4)] return skinmatrix def GsplatTransformCovariance(covariance, transform3x3): covA, covB = covariance source = ReconstructCovariance3x3(covA, covB) # deformed = transform @ source @ transpose(transform) transposedtransform = [[transform3x3[r][c] for r in range(3)] for c in range(3)] temp = [[sum(transform3x3[r][k] source[k][c] for k in range(3)) for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] deformed = [[sum(temp[r][k] transposedtransform[k][c] for k in range(3)) for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] return ExtractCovarianceComponents(deformed) def ApplySkinning(modelcenter, covariance, modelnormal, sourceid): if GsplatSkinningEnabled == 0: return modelcenter, covariance, modelnormal skinmatrix = GsplatSkinMatrix(sourceid) # Transform Position poshomogeneous = [modelcenter[0], modelcenter[1], modelcenter[2], 1.0] transformedposhomogeneous = [sum(skinmatrix[r][c] poshomogeneous[c] for c in range(4)) for r in range(4)] transformedcenter = (transformedposhomogeneous[0], transformedposhomogeneous[1], transformedposhomogeneous[2]) # Transform Covariance deformationmatrix = [ [skinmatrix[0][0], skinmatrix[0][1], skinmatrix[0][2]], [skinmatrix[1][0], skinmatrix[1][1], skinmatrix[1][2]], [skinmatrix[2][0], skinmatrix[2][1], skinmatrix[2][2]] ] transformedcovariance = GsplatTransformCovariance(covariance, deformationmatrix) # Transform Normal transformednormal = deformationmatrix @ modelnormal # Vector-matrix multiplication transformednormal = tuple(v / ((sum(vv for v in transformednormal))0.5) for v in transformednormal) return transformedcenter, transformedcovariance, transformednormal GsplatSkinningEnabled: Integer flag (0 or 1). sourceId: Unique splat identifier. Bone weights: Typically sum to 1.0, but the algorithm sums weighted matrices regardless. Skinning Disabled: If GsplatSkinningEnabled is 0, all skinning functions return immediately without modifying inputs. Reference Matrix Construction: When using the Texture2D backend, the reference inverse matrix is stored with only 3 rows. The 4th row must be explicitly set to (0, 0, 0, 1) to form a valid 4 \times 4 matrix. Covariance Reconstruction: The source covariance matrix must be correctly reconstructed from covA and covB components before transformation. The result must be re-extracted into covA and covB. Precision: Matrix multiplications involve floating-point operations. Precision issues may arise with very small or very large bone weights, though standard float32 is implied. Time: Constant time O(1) per splat, involving a fixed number of texture/buffer loads (up to 13 texels for Texture2D backend: 4 indices, 1 weight, 4 bone rows, 3 reference rows) and matrix multiplications. Memory: Depends on the backend. Texture2D uses 4 textures where each bone index consumes 4 texels and each source consumes 1 texel for weights and 3 texels for reference inverse. StructuredBuffer allows direct indexing, potentially simpler but may have different memory layout requirements. Not given in the sources. Scales linearly with the number of splats. The cost per splat is constant regardless of scene complexity, as it depends only on the splat's local skin data. Strengths: Supports skeletal animation for Gaussian splats. Texture2D backend offers GPU portability. StructuredBuffer backend offers direct access. Limitations: Limited to 4 bones per splat. Requires pre-computed skin weights and bone matrices. Texture2D backend requires coordinate conversion. Use when skeletal animation of Gaussian splats is required. Choose Texture2D backend for maximum GPU compatibility. Choose StructuredBuffer backend for potentially simpler memory access patterns if the hardware supports it efficiently. This method is part of the UnitySplats project by ARLOOPA, specifically designed for Gaussian Splatting in Unity. It enables dynamic skinning of splats, allowing them to deform with skeletal animations. arloopa/UnitySplats, https://github.com/arloopa/UnitySplats, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Single-Pass Splat Rendering Pipeline
head: Single-Pass High-Quality Splatting
body: A real-time splat rendering pipeline that combines splat and mesh rendering components to enable high-quality shader effects (reflection, refraction) in a single rendering pass, avoiding multi-pass blending artifacts and reducing memory/workload compared to dense point sets. It differs from sibling methods like the Three-Pass GPU Point Rendering Pipeline by replacing screen-space blending with object-space attribute interpolation on regular grid patches, allowing for complex lighting in one pass. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point set representing a surface, pre-processed into patches. Each patch consists of a planar domain, a height field (elevation map), and optional attribute maps (color, normals). Output: A rendered image with continuous attributes and high-quality shading effects. Data Structures: The model is stored completely on graphics hardware. Connectivity is implicit. 1. Patch Data Structure: Plane Parameters: A 3D point (origin), a normal vector, and grid resolution (N \times M). Height Field: A rectangular array of height values (h{i,j}). Flags: A special height value indicates that the patch does not include a point above that grid point (allowing arbitrary support shapes). Attribute Maps: Optional texture maps (color, normal) of arbitrary resolution, stored as texture objects. Transformation: One 4 \times 4 transformation matrix per patch. 2. Vertex Buffer Object (VBO): Stores point positions and elevation data for each patch. Point positions on the patch plane are expressed by a single index value (combined row and column address in the sampling grid). 3. Index Buffer: A linear list 1, 2, \dots, n, where n is the number of points in the patch. No connectivity encoding is needed. 4. Texture Objects: Store additional attribute maps (color, normal) for each patch individually. Algorithm Steps: 1. Patch Construction (Pre-processing): Partition the input 3D point set into patches. Each patch is parameterized as an elevation map over a planar domain. Resample the surface patch on a regular grid using Moving Least Squares (MLS) surface reconstruction. Overlap Handling: To prevent gaps due to MLS reconstruction limitations, patches slightly overlap. An input point is included in a patch if its \epsilon-neighborhood intersects the point set of the region, where \epsilon > 0. Resample attribute fields (normals, textures) onto the regular grid. Normals can be computed as MLS surface normals or interpolated from input point normals using bilinear interpolation in a Delaunay triangulation of projected points. 2. Data Upload: Upload VBOs (elevation data) and Texture Objects (attributes) to GPU memory once before rendering. 3. Rendering Loop: Iterate over all patches. For each patch: 1. Address the respective texture objects. 2. Trigger the corresponding VBO for rendering. 4. Vertex Shader: Translation: Translate point positions according to their elevation values. The position P on the patch plane is offset along the plane normal N by the height h: P{translated} = P{grid} + h \cdot N where P{grid} is the base grid point on the support plane. Rotation: Rotate the translated points using the patch's 4 \times 4 transformation matrix to place them on the surface of the original model. Radius Calculation: Set the radius of each point sprite. The base radius is \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu, where \mu is the sampling step size. Adjust radii based on the angle between neighboring elevation values to prevent holes. The formula is: r = \max(r{min}, \min(r{max}, c1 \cdot \frac{1}{\cos(\theta)} + c2 \cdot \Delta h)) where \theta is the angle between normals, \Delta h is the variance between neighboring elevation values, and c1, c2 are scaling constants. r{min} and r{max} establish minimal and maximal radii. 5. Fragment Shader: Splat Simulation: Transform point-sprite fragments to simulate splatting, as point sprites are screen-aligned primitives. Attribute Interpolation: Determine per-fragment UV coordinates using continuous attribute interpolation. This involves projecting pixel shader fragments back onto the patches to interpolate attributes from nearby points, replacing disadvantageous splat blending. View rays are intersected with the splats for direct evaluation of UV coordinates. Intersecting the view ray with the plane through neighboring splat centers provides corrected interpolation of UV coordinates. Illumination: Perform final illumination by summing contributions from: Lighting (e.g., Phong shading) Texture mapping Reflectance mapping (using cube mapping) Refraction mapping. Parameters: \epsilon: Positive value for patch overlap during construction. Typical value: Not given in the sources. \mu: Sampling step size of the grid. c1, c2: Scaling constants for radius adjustment. Typical values: Not given in the sources. r{min}, r{max}: Minimal and maximal splat radii. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gaps between patches: MLS resampling cannot guarantee no gaps. Patches must overlap slightly using \epsilon to ensure continuous error-free rendering. Holes due to elevation variance: High variance between neighboring elevation values increases spatial gaps. Radii must be increased in these areas. Screen-aligned primitives: Point sprites are screen-aligned, so fragment shader transformation is mandatory to simulate splatting correctly. Time Complexity: Single rendering pass. This simplifies overall rendering complexity compared to current GPU-based splatting techniques which require at least three rendering passes. Memory Complexity: The resampled model is stored completely on graphics hardware. Connectivity information is implicit and does not require additional memory. Performance: Accelerates rendering and simplifies current splatting techniques. Avoids performance-hungry GPU functionality such as multiple render targets and additional blending passes. Strengths: Enables high-quality shader effects (reflection, refraction) without densely sampled models. Improves quality of reconstructed attributes (normals, texture coordinates) by interpolating in object space rather than blending in screen space. Continuous attributes on and between splats. Limitations: Requires pre-processing to construct patches and resample data. Relies on GPU vertex and fragment shader functionality and point-sprite extension. When to use: Real-time rendering of point-sampled surfaces where high-quality shading effects are required and performance is critical. When not to use: When dynamic topology changes require frequent re-meshing or when the input data is not available in a compressed/patched form. Origin: Introduced by Tilo Ochotta, Stefan Hiller, and Dietmar Saupe in September 2006. Publication: Published as Konstanzer Schriften in Mathematik und Informatik Nr. 219. Development: Builds on previous work on elevation map compression [16] and Moving Least Squares surface reconstruction [2, 1]. Usage: Used for real-time splat rendering with enhanced shader effects in entertainment applications. name: Three-Pass GPU Point Rendering Pipeline
head: Hardware Accelerated Point Splatting Pipeline
body: This method renders point clouds by decomposing the splatting process into three distinct rendering passes to achieve perspective-accurate results on modern GPUs. It solves the problem of correctly projecting and blending 3D points into a 2D image while handling depth occlusion and filter weight normalization. It differs from single-pass approaches by explicitly separating depth estimation, color accumulation, and normalization, allowing for more accurate handling of projective distortions and varying splat sizes. Inputs: A set of 3D points with associated attributes (color, position, orientation) and camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics). Outputs: A final color image. Data Structures: Framebuffers: DepthBuffer: Stores depth values. Initialized to infinity. ColorBuffer: Stores accumulated color values (RGB). Initialized to zero. WeightBuffer: Stores accumulated filter weights (scalar). Initialized to zero. (Implicit in normalization step). Steps: 1. Pass 1: Depth Offset Rendering Render a depth image of the scene. The depth values are slightly offset along the viewing rays to resolve depth conflicts during subsequent blending. This pass establishes the occlusion order. 2. Pass 2: Splat Accumulation Draw splats using OpenGL points (preferred over quads or triangles for performance and simplicity). Enable depth testing to ensure only the closest splat contributes to each pixel. Disable depth buffer updates (write-only depth test). Enable color blending. In the fragment shader, compute the splat's contribution. The fragment shader accumulates color values in the ColorBuffer and filter weights in the WeightBuffer. This effectively computes the weighted sum of the splat contributions. 3. Pass 3: Normalization Normalize the accumulated color values by dividing the color in ColorBuffer by the accumulated filter weights in WeightBuffer for each pixel. This corrects for the varying density and overlap of splats. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def threepasspointrendering(points, cameraparams): # Initialize framebuffers depthbuffer = createbuffer(inf) colorbuffer = createbuffer(0.0) weightbuffer = createbuffer(0.0) # Pass 1: Render depth offset renderdepthoffset(points, cameraparams, depthbuffer) # Pass 2: Accumulate splats enabledepthtest() disabledepthwrite() enablecolorblend() for point in points: # Compute splat projection and variance matrix # Note: Inversion of projective mapping may be ill-conditioned # if splat degenerates into a line segment splat = computesplat(point, cameraparams) # Rasterize splat # Fragment shader updates colorbuffer and weightbuffer rasterizesplat(splat, colorbuffer, weightbuffer) # Pass 3: Normalize for pixel in imageresolution: if weightbuffer[pixel] > epsilon: colorbuffer[pixel] /= weightbuffer[pixel] else: colorbuffer[pixel] = 0.0 return colorbuffer Parameters: Rendering Primitive: OpenGL points. Depth Offset: Small value along viewing ray. Epsilon: Small value to prevent division by zero in normalization. Edge Cases: Ill-conditioned Inversion: Computing the variance matrix requires inverting the projective mapping, which can be numerically ill-conditioned if the splat is about to degenerate into a line segment. Zero Weight: Pixels with no splat coverage have zero weight; normalization must handle this to avoid NaNs. This variant describes the core assembly step for standard point splatting, writing point colors to a canvas based on depth sorting and a fixed or implicit radius. It involves initializing canvases (depthcanvas with inf, colorcanvas and labelcanvas with zeros, indexcanvas with -1), sorting points by depth, and iteratively writing colors if the point's depth is less than the current depth at that pixel. A written mask is created where depthcanvas < inf, and unwritten pixels are set to default values. Time Complexity: O(N) for N points, assuming constant-time splat rasterization. The three-pass structure adds a small constant overhead compared to single-pass methods. Memory Complexity: O(WH) for the framebuffers (depth, color, weight), where W and H are image dimensions. Strengths: Perspective-accurate splatting, handles occlusion correctly via depth testing, leverages GPU hardware acceleration efficiently. Limitations: Requires multiple passes, potentially ill-conditioned matrix inversion for extreme view angles, requires careful handling of depth offsets. When to use: When perspective accuracy is critical and hardware acceleration is available. When not to use: For very simple orthographic projections where single-pass suffices, or on hardware with limited multi-pass support. Originated from research on perspective-accurate splatting using modern GPU vertex and fragment programs. It builds on previous methods for hardware-accelerated point splatting. The use of OpenGL points instead of quads/triangles is a key optimization noted in the source. name: Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline
head: 4-Stage Rendering Pipeline, Smoker Rendering Pipeline
body: A rendering pipeline that processes smoke volumes through four distinct stages (Clear, Construction, Insertion, Evaluation) using fragment lists to store and evaluate per-pixel data, chosen to maintain accuracy and avoid raytracing/self-intersection problems. It differs from raytracing-based methods by circumventing self-intersection and global intersection artifacts inherent in volumetric ray marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Smoke volume geometry (typically triangle meshes representing isosurfaces or volume boundaries), OpenGL buffer objects for state management. Output: Final rendered image on the screen buffer. Data Structures: OpenGL Buffer Objects: Used to store intermediate per-pixel data generated during the Insertion stage. Specific layouts depend on the visualization method (e.g., pixel counters, fragment lists) but must be compatible with the Evaluation stage. Fragment List: A storage structure (implied by the name) where fragments are inserted during the Insertion stage. The exact memory layout (e.g., linked lists, arrays with head pointers) is not specified in the general overview but is critical for performance. Steps: The pipeline consists of four stages executed by three shader programs: Clear, Render (combining Construction and Insertion), and Display (Evaluation). 1. Clear: Reset OpenGL buffer objects for the subsequent frame. Initiated by rendering a single screen-filling quad. Fragment shader threads are launched to zero out or clear the storage structures. 2. Construction: Vertex shader performs perspective transformation of vertices. Assigns additional vertex data (e.g., density, flow tangents). Geometry shader assembles primitives and processes triangle-related data (orientation, topology, volume information). Forwards results to the Insertion stage. 3. Insertion: Primitives are rasterized and forwarded to the fragment shader. Process incoming fragments according to the visualization method. This ranges from a simple pixel counter to insertion into a complicated storage data structure (fragment list). Fragment processing must be compatible with the Evaluation step. Note: Construction and Insertion belong to the same shader program (the Render stage). 4. Evaluation: Render a single screen-filling quad to initiate fragment evaluation. name: Custom Pass Rendering
head: DemoRenderer pipeline, Multi-pass Octree Rendering Pipeline, NanoVolume Custom Pass Rendering, SSVDAG rendering passes
body: Custom Pass Rendering is a multi-pass, object-order rendering pipeline designed for high-performance visualization of large-scale volumetric data (specifically NanoVDB) and implicit surfaces using GPU compute and fragment shaders. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering complex, high-resolution volumetric datasets by decoupling geometry reconstruction, shading, and post-processing effects into distinct render passes. Unlike monolithic ray-marching approaches, it separates the initial ray-casting/trace phase from lighting calculations, allowing for optimized memory access patterns and modular effect integration (SSAO, shadows). It is distinct from Plug-and-Play Ray Marching and Rendering by its explicit multi-pass FBO management and from Volume Rendering Pipeline by its specific use of NanoVDB structures and Unity's HDRenderPipeline integration. The pipeline executes a sequence of fullscreen passes, each writing to a specific Framebuffer Object (FBO) attachment. The core logic involves casting rays through the volume, reconstructing hit positions and normals, filtering normals, computing ambient occlusion, and finally shading with materials and shadows. Inputs: Camera matrices: View, Projection, and their inverses. Camera position (WorldSpaceCameraPos). Screen resolution (screenRes). Volumetric data: NanoVDB structure (accessed via usamplerBuffer or usampler3D depending on configuration). Optional Material Octree data (encoded in a GLTEXTUREBUFFER). Outputs: Final color buffer (RGBA32F or similar, depending on the final pass configuration). The pipeline uses a series of Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) to store intermediate results. Each FBO is bound to specific texture attachments with defined formats and filtering modes. FBO Layout: FBO[0] (Primary Rays/Depth): Attachment 0: glTexDepth (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGBA32F, screen resolution, GLLINEAR filtering). FBO[1] (Hit Position/Normal): Attachment 0: glTexHitPos (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGB32F, screen resolution, GLNEAREST filtering). Attachment 1: glTexHitNorm (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGB32F, screen resolution, GLNEAREST filtering). FBO[2] (Materials, if enabled): Attachment 0: glTexHitMaterial (GLTEXTURE2D, GLR8UI, screen resolution, GLNEAREST filtering). FBO[3] (Normal Filtering): Attachment 0: glTexHitNormFiltered (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGB32F, screen resolution, GLNEAREST filtering). FBO[4] (Shadows): Attachment 0: glTexShadows (GLTEXTURE2D, GLR32F, screen resolution, GLNEAREST filtering). FBO[5] (AO): Attachment 0: glTexAO (GLTEXTURE2D, GLR32F, screen resolution, GLNEAREST filtering). FBO[6] (AO Blurred): Attachment 0: glTexAOBlurred (GLTEXTURE2D, GLR32F, screen resolution, GLNEAREST filtering). Uniforms and Constants: screenRes: vec2 (screen width, height). depth: int (texture index for depth). projectionFactor: float (calculated from FOV and screen tolerance). matOctree: int (texture index for material octree). matOctreehalfSide, matOctreeCenter, matOctreeLevels: float/vec3/int (octree metadata). inputTex: int (source texture index for filtering/SSAO). hitPosTex, hitNormTex, hitNormTexFiltered, depthTex, noiseTex, shadowsTex, aoTex, aoTexBlurred, materialTex: int (texture indices). samples: vec3 array (SSAO sample positions). materials: vec3 array (material colors, if USEMATERIALS is defined). Parameters: sigma: 4.0f (Normal filtering/SSAO smoothing parameter). bsigma: 0.4f (Bilateral filtering/SSAO smoothing parameter). msize: 10 (Kernel size for normal filtering, defines MSIZE in shader). ssaoRadius: eo->getHalfSide(eo->getNLevels()) 100.0f (SSAO sample radius). ssaoNSamples: 32 (Number of SSAO samples). ssaoNoiseTexSide: 64 (Side length of SSAO noise texture). renderMode: 0 (Render mode selector). useDif: true (Enable diffuse shading). filterNormals: true (Enable normal filtering pass). doSSAO: true (Enable SSAO pass). doShadows: true (Enable shadow pass). useMaterials: false (Enable material lookup pass). 1. Initialization: Create NUMPASSES RendererMonitor instances and start them. Setup the shader as a FullScreenPass with #pragma target 5.0 and #pragma usedxc. Include common headers: CustomPassCommon.hlsl, PseudoRandom.hlsl, NanoVolumePass.hlsl. 2. Pass 1: Pos and Norm Computation: Compile and link the pass using vertex shader from sqr.getDefaultVertexProgram() and fragment shader from SHADERPOSNORMFILE. Set uniforms: screenRes, depth (TEXNUMDEPTH), projectionFactor. Fragment Shader Logic: Load camera depth at varyings.positionCS.xy using LoadCameraDepth. Get position inputs using GetPositionInput with screen size, depth, inverse view-projection matrix, and view matrix. Calculate normalized view direction using GetWorldSpaceNormalizeViewDir(posInput.positionWS). Call core volume rendering function NanoVolumePass with WorldSpaceCameraPos and negated view direction -viewDirection. Return resulting color with alpha blending: float4(color.rgb, color.a). Note: The GLSL source for demoposnormpass.frag.glsl shows an alternative implementation for ray casting: Compute screen coordinates: screenCoords = (glFragCoord.xy / screenRes) 2.0 - 1.0. Compute camera ray direction rd using projMatInv and viewMatInv. Fetch depth val.x from depthTex. Compute hit position: hitPosition = r.o + val.x r.d. Compute diffuse factor dif: If useDif, dif = max(0.001, 2.0(val.yprojectionFactor) / val.x). Apply smoothing: if dif > MINK (5.0), dif = mix(dif, 1.0, min(dif-MINK, MAXK-MINK)/(MAXK-MINK)) where MAXK=20.0. Compute normal hitNormal using calcNormal(r.d, dif). Handle back-face culling: if dot(n, camDir) > 0, n = -n. 3. Pass 2: Material Finding (Optional): If materialOctree is not NULL, compile and link the pass using SHADERMATERIALFILE. Set uniforms: matOctree (TEXNUMMATOCTREE), screenRes, depth, matOctreehalfSide, matOctreeCenter, matOctreeLevels. Create a GLTEXTUREBUFFER backed by a GL buffer containing the material octree's encoded data, bound to TEXNUMMATOCTREE. Shader Logic: The getMaterial function in demoshadingpass.frag.glsl traverses the octree to find the material ID for a given position p. 4. Pass 3: Normal Filtering: Compile and link the pass using SHADERNORMALFILTERFILE. Define MSIZE as msize (default 10). Set uniform: inputTex (TEXNUMHITNORM). Apply bilateral or Gaussian filtering to glTexHitNorm to produce glTexHitNormFiltered. 5. Pass 4: SSAO (Screen Space Ambient Occlusion): Compile and link the pass using SHADERSSAOFILE. Define NUMSAMPLES as ssaoNSamples (default 32) and SIDENOISETEX as ssaoNoiseTexSide (default 64). Set uniforms: hitPosTex (TEXNUMHITPOS), hitNormTex (TEXNUMHITNORMFILTERED), depthTex (TEXNUMDEPTH), noiseTex (TEXNUMAONOISE). Generate ssaoNSamples 3D samples via generateSSAOSamples and upload to samples uniform. Generate a noise texture of size ssaoNoiseTexSide x ssaoNoiseTexSide via generateNoiseTex and bind to TEXNUMAONOISE. Fragment Shader Logic (demossaopass.frag.glsl): Fetch hitPos, hitNorm, and hitDepthcellSize from textures. Offset hit position: hitPos += hitNorm hitDepthcellSize.y/5.0. Generate TBN matrix using noise vector rvec. Loop NUMSAMPLES: Transform sample samp to world space: samp = hitPos + (tbn samples[i]) radius. Project to clip space: offset = projMat viewMat vec4(samp, 1.0). Normalize to NDC: offset.xyz /= offset.w; offset.xyz = offset.xyz 0.5 + 0.5. Fetch sample depth sampleDepth from depthTex. Calculate range check: rangeCheck = smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, radius / abs(hitDepthcellSize.x - sampleDepth)) or binary check. Accumulate occlusion: occlusion += (sampleDepth < length(camPos - samp) ? 1.0: 0.0) rangeCheck. Output visibility: outVisibility = (count > 0.0) ? 1.0 - occlusion / count: 1.0. 6. Pass 5: Blur: Compile and link the pass using SHADERBLURFILE. Set uniform: inputTex (TEXNUMAO). Apply blur to glTexAO to produce glTexAOBlurred. 7. Pass 6: Shading: Compile and link the pass using SHADERSHADINGFILE. If materialOctree is not NULL, define USEMATERIALS and NUMMATERIALS. Set uniforms: screenRes, hitPosTex (TEXNUMHITPOS), hitNormTex (TEXNUMHITNORMFILTERED), shadowsTex (TEXNUMSHADOW), aoTex (TEXNUMAOBLURRED), depthTex (TEXNUMDEPTH), materialTex (TEXNUMMATERIAL). If materials are used, upload material colors to materials uniform. Fragment Shader Logic (demoshadingpass.frag.glsl): Fetch pos, norm, shadow, ao from textures. If pos == vec3(0,0,0), return sky color. If renderMode == 0: Determine diffuseColor: Default vec3(0.8, 0.8, 0.8). If useMaterials, fetch matID from materialTex and lookup materials[matID]. Handle special IDs (255: magenta, else: cyan). Apply lighting: color =... (diffuse, specular, ambient, shadow, AO). If renderMode == 4, output step count visualization. Else, discard. Projection Factor: \text{projectionFactor} = \frac{\text{inv\2tan\half\fovy}}{\text{screen\tolerance}} Where: \text{inv\2tan\half\fovy} = \frac{1.0}{2.0 \times \tan(0.5 \times \text{fovy})} \text{fovy} = 60^\circ = 60 \times \frac{\pi}{180} \text{ radians} \text{screen\tolerance} = \frac{1.0}{\text{screenRes}[1]} Diffuse Factor Smoothing: \text{dif} = \max(0.001, \frac{2.0 \times (\text{val.y} \times \text{projectionFactor})}{\text{val.x}}) If \text{dif} > \text{MINK} (5.0): \text{dif} = \text{mix}(\text{dif}, 1.0, \frac{\min(\text{dif}-\text{MINK}, \text{MAXK}-\text{MINK})}{\text{MAXK}-\text{MINK}}) Where \text{MAXK} = 20.0. SSAO Visibility: \text{outVisibility} = \begin{cases} 1.0 - \frac{\text{occlusion}}{\text{count}} & \text{if count} > 0.0 \\ 1.0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where \text{occlusion} = \sum (\text{sampleDepth} < \|\text{camPos} - \text{samp}\| ? 1.0: 0.0) \times \text{rangeCheck}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initpipeline(): # Create RendererMonitor instances monitors = [RendererMonitor() for in range(NUMPASSES)] for m in monitors: m.start() # Setup shader shader = FullScreenPass(target=5.0, usedxc=True) shader.include("CustomPassCommon.hlsl") shader.include("PseudoRandom.hlsl") shader.include("NanoVolumePass.hlsl") # Setup FBOs fbodepth = createfbo(attachment=GLRGBA32F, filter=GLLINEAR) fbohit = createfbo([ createattachment(GLRGB32F, GLNEAREST, "hitPos"), createattachment(GLRGB32F, GLNEAREST, "hitNorm") ]) fbomaterial = createfbo(attachment=GLR8UI, filter=GLNEAREST) if usematerials else None fbonormfiltered = createfbo(attachment=GLRGB32F, filter=GLNEAREST) fboshadow = createfbo(attachment=GLR32F, filter=GLNEAREST) fboao = createfbo(attachment=GLR32F, filter=GLNEAREST) fboaoblurred = createfbo(attachment=GLR32F, filter=GLNEAREST) # Setup textures and buffers texdepth = fbodepth.colorattachment texhitpos = fbohit.colorattachments[0] texhitnorm = fbohit.colorattachments[1] texnormfiltered = fbonormfiltered.colorattachment texshadow = fboshadow.colorattachment texao = fboao.colorattachment texaoblurred = fboaoblurred.colorattachment if usematerials: texmaterial = fbomaterial.colorattachment matoctreebuffer = createtexturebuffer(materialoctreedata) def passposnorm(): # Bind FBO[1] bindfbo(fbohit) # Set uniforms setuniform("screenRes", screenres) setuniform("depth", texdepth) setuniform("projectionFactor", calculateprojectionfactor()) # Execute shader executeshader("SHADERPOSNORMFILE") # Shader logic (simplified): # 1. Load depth at current pixel # 2. Compute camera ray # 3. Trace volume (NanoVolumePass) or compute hit via depth # 4. Write hitPos and hitNorm to attachments def passmaterial(): if not usematerials: return bindfbo(fbomaterial) setuniform("matOctree", matoctreebuffer) setuniform("screenRes", screenres) setuniform("depth", texdepth) setuniform("matOctreehalfSide", matoctreehalfside) setuniform("matOctreeCenter", matoctreecenter) setuniform("matOctreeLevels", matoctreelevels) executeshader("SHADERMATERIALFILE") def passnormalfilter(): bindfbo(fbonormfiltered) setuniform("inputTex", texhitnorm) setuniform("MSIZE", msize) executeshader("SHADERNORMALFILTERFILE") def passssao(): bindfbo(fboao) # Generate samples and noise samples = generatessaosamples(ssaoNSamples) noisetex = generatenoisetex(ssaoNoiseTexSide) setuniform("hitPosTex", texhitpos) setuniform("hitNormTex", texnormfiltered) setuniform("depthTex", texdepth) setuniform("noiseTex", noisetex) setuniform("samples", samples) setuniform("radius", ssaoRadius) setuniform("NUMSAMPLES", ssaoNSamples) setuniform("SIDENOISETEX", ssaoNoiseTexSide) executeshader("SHADERSSAOFILE") def passblur(): bindfbo(fboaoblurred) setuniform("inputTex", texao) executeshader("SHADERBLURFILE") def passshading(): bindfbo(fbodepth) # Or final output FBO setuniform("screenRes", screenres) setuniform("hitPosTex", texhitpos) setuniform("hitNormTex", texnormfiltered) setuniform("shadowsTex", texshadow) setuniform("aoTex", texaoblurred) setuniform("depthTex", texdepth) if usematerials: setuniform("materialTex", texmaterial) setuniform("materials", materialcolors) define("USEMATERIALS") define("NUMMATERIALS", len(materialcolors)) executeshader("SHADERSHADINGFILE") def calculateprojectionfactor(): fovyrad = 60.0 3.14159 / 180.0 inv2tanhalffovy = 1.0 / (2.0 tan(0.5 fovyrad)) screentolerance = 1.0 / screenres[1] return inv2tanhalffovy / screentolerance Precision: Depth values are stored in GLRGBA32F for FBO[0] and GLR32F for others. Ensure sufficient precision for large scenes to avoid z-fighting or incorrect ray intersections. Boundaries: The SSAO pass discards fragments where hitPos == vec3(0,0,0) (background). Ensure background pixels are handled correctly in subsequent passes. Degenerate Input: If materialOctree is NULL, the material pass is skipped, and USEMATERIALS should not be defined to avoid shader compilation errors. Stereo Rendering: The Unity implementation uses UNITYSETUPSTEREOEYEINDEXPOSTVERTEX to handle stereo eyes. Ensure the pipeline is compatible with the target rendering API's stereo support. Filtering: Normal filtering uses a kernel size MSIZE. Ensure MSIZE is odd and appropriate for the resolution to avoid excessive blurring or aliasing. The core volume rendering function that traces rays through the NanoVDB structure. It is responsible for computing the initial hit position and normal. It is distinct from other ray marching methods by its use of the NanoVDB format and optimized traversal. A specialized pass that looks up material IDs from a material octree. It is chosen when material-based shading is required. It differs from simple color lookup by using a hierarchical structure for efficient access. Computes screen-space ambient occlusion using a set of pre-generated samples and a noise texture. It is chosen for adding depth cues to flat-looking volumes. It differs from other AO methods by its reliance on screen-space depth and normal information. A bilateral or Gaussian filter applied to the computed normals to reduce noise. It is chosen when the raw normals from ray casting are too jagged. It differs from simple blurring by preserving edges. Time Complexity: The pipeline is O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of passes (typically 6-7). Each pass is a fullscreen pass, so the total time is proportional to the screen resolution multiplied by the number of passes. The ray tracing pass complexity depends on the volume traversal depth, which is generally logarithmic with respect to the volume size for tree-based structures. Memory Complexity: The pipeline requires memory for 7 FBOs. For a 1920 \times 1080 screen, this is approximately 7 \times 1920 \times 1080 \times 4 bytes (for 32F textures) \approx 64 MB, plus additional memory for the NanoVDB structure and material octree. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on the hardware and the complexity of the volume. The use of #pragma target 5.0 and #pragma usedxc suggests optimization for modern GPUs. The SSAO pass with 32 samples per pixel can be a bottleneck. Scaling: The pipeline scales linearly with screen resolution. The volume traversal complexity scales with the depth of the octree, which is typically shallow for well-structured data. Strengths: Modular design allows for easy addition/removal of effects (SSAO, shadows). Efficient memory access patterns due to FBO separation. Support for material-based shading. Limitations: High memory usage due to multiple FBOs. Latency introduced by multiple passes. Dependency on specific shader features (DXC, GLSL 440). When to Use: High-quality visualization of large volumetric datasets where post-processing effects are desired. When Not to Use: Real-time applications with strict memory constraints or low-end hardware. Simple volume rendering without complex lighting. Custom Pass Rendering originated from the SSVDAG (Sparse Sparse Volume Data Access Graph) project and was adapted for Unity via the NanoVolume Custom Pass Rendering implementation. The SSVDAG project, by ajaspe, focuses on efficient rendering of sparse volumetric data using DAG-based structures. The Unity implementation, by andersblomqvist, integrates NanoVDB (a compressed, GPU-friendly format for OpenVDB data) into Unity's High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRenderPipeline). The pipeline was developed to address the limitations of traditional ray marching in terms of performance and flexibility, allowing for complex lighting and material effects. It is used in scientific visualization and high-end rendering applications. ssvdag, https://github.com/ajaspe/ssvdag, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) unity-nanovdb-renderer, https://github.com/andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Stop-the-pop
body: Stop-the-pop is a technique to mitigate popping artifacts in volume splatting that are caused by the sorting procedure of Gaussians along the ray. It uses hierarchical or pixel-resorting to remove popping artifacts without sacrificing speed. It is distinct from methods that modify opacity compensation terms or use ray-tracing-style intersections for accurate depth. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, color, opacity) and a camera view. Outputs: A rendered image with reduced popping artifacts. Data Structures: Gaussian List: Array of Gaussian primitives. Pixel Bucket: For each pixel, a list of Gaussians sorted by depth. Hierarchical Structure: A tree or grid structure allowing fast re-sorting of Gaussians within a local region (pixel or tile). Steps: 1. Project all 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space to determine their footprint and depth. 2. For each pixel (or tile), identify the Gaussians whose footprints cover it. 3. Sort these Gaussians by depth (front-to-back). 4. Apply the Stop-the-pop algorithm: Detect potential popping events: These occur when the relative depth order of Gaussians changes significantly between frames or when a Gaussian enters/leaves the pixel's view, causing abrupt changes in the accumulated color/opacity. Hierarchical/Pixel-resorting: Instead of a global sort, perform a localized sort or use a hierarchical structure to maintain a consistent depth ordering for Gaussians contributing to the same pixel or small region. This ensures that the compositing order remains stable even if the exact depth values fluctuate slightly due to floating-point precision or camera movement. The specific implementation details of the hierarchical structure (e.g., k-d tree, grid) are not provided in the sources. The core idea is to prevent the "pop" caused by the discrete nature of the sorting process. 5. Composite the sorted Gaussians using alpha blending. Parameters: Sorting threshold: Not given in the sources. Hierarchical level: Not given in the sources. Edge cases: Degenerate input: If Gaussians have identical depths, the sort order may be unstable. The hierarchical approach helps mitigate this by maintaining a consistent local order. Precision: Floating-point errors in depth calculation can cause sorting instability. The method aims to reduce the visual impact of these errors. Time complexity: The hierarchical sorting reduces the complexity compared to a global sort, but the exact complexity is not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Additional memory is required for the hierarchical structure. Performance: It removes popping artifacts without sacrificing speed. Strengths: Reduces visual artifacts (popping) caused by sorting. Limitations: Adds complexity to the sorting step. Origin: Stop-the-pop (StopThePop) was introduced by Radl et al. at SIGGRAPH 2024. History: It addresses issues in 3D Gaussian Splatting where the sorting procedure can cause popping artifacts. Usage: It is used in 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines to improve visual quality. name: SpotlessSplats
body: SpotlessSplats is a robustness-enhancing variant of Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction designed to improve reconstruction quality in casual captures by ignoring transient distractors. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SWAG by detecting outliers in a richer, pre-trained feature space rather than relying solely on learned appearance embeddings or unsupervised transient Gaussian training. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and a collection of input images with known camera poses. Outputs: An optimized set of 3D Gaussians representing the static scene or avatar, excluding transient occluders. Data Structures: Gaussian i: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, Covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or quaternion/scale representation), Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for view-dependent color. Feature Vector \mathbf{f}i: A high-dimensional feature embedding for each Gaussian, extracted from a pre-trained network. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians using standard 3DGS densification or capture geometry. 2. Feature Extraction: For each Gaussian i, compute a feature vector \mathbf{f}i using a pre-trained feature extractor (e.g., DINO or similar self-supervised vision transformer) based on the Gaussian's projected image region or associated pixel features. 3. Outlier Detection: Identify transient distractors by detecting outliers in the feature space \{\mathbf{f}i\}. Gaussians whose feature vectors deviate significantly from the cluster of static scene features are marked as transient. 4. Optimization: Train the remaining Gaussians (static) using standard differentiable rendering loss (e.g., L1 + D-SSIM) while suppressing or removing the identified transient Gaussians. Parameters: Feature extractor: Not specified in sources. Outlier threshold: Not specified in sources. Edge cases: Precision: Feature space dimensionality affects outlier detection sensitivity. Boundaries: Transient objects that are persistent across many frames may not be detected as outliers. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Improves reconstruction quality in casual captures compared to standard Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction. Strengths: Enhanced robustness to transient distractors (e.g., moving people, shadows) in casual video captures. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained feature extractor, adding computational overhead during feature extraction. When to use: When capturing casual videos with transient occluders and high-quality static reconstruction is desired. When not: When real-time performance is critical and feature extraction overhead is prohibitive, or when the scene is static and clean. Origin: SpotlessSplats was introduced as an extension to Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction to address robustness issues in casual captures. It builds on the idea of using feature spaces for outlier detection, following SWAG's approach of handling transient occluders. History: The method is cited in recent surveys on 3D Gaussian Splatting applications (2025). Usage: Used for novel view synthesis and avatar reconstruction from casual video captures where transient distractors are common. name: Splatting for Anti-aliasing Small Cells
head: Anti-Aliased Ellipsoidal Splats, Anti-Aliasing for Small Cells via Splatting, Anti-aliased Splatting for Small Cells, Gaussian Splatting for Small Cells, Gaussian ellipsoid splatting, Small cell anti-aliasing, Splatting Anti-Aliasing
body: This method prevents the loss of important details in adaptive meshes by rendering small cells that would otherwise be missed between slice planes or by pixel samples during scan conversion. It replaces the complex rendering of filtered polygons with anti-aliased ellipsoidal splats, ensuring that small cells in regions of high gradients or complex geometry contribute to the final image. Unlike siblings that rely on pre-sampling filters or motion blur, this approach uses Gaussian ellipsoids to smoothly interpolate the scalar field while avoiding overlap with larger, fully opaque polygonal slices. Inputs: A set of polyhedral cells from an adaptive mesh or curvilinear grid. A volume threshold V{thresh} to distinguish "small" cells from "large" cells. A transfer function mapping cell properties (e.g., density, volume) to RGBA color and opacity. A set of parallel slice planes perpendicular to the viewing direction. Camera parameters (viewing direction, projection type). Outputs: A composited 2D image where small cells are rendered as anti-aliased splats and large cells as polygons. 1. Cell Data: Each cell Ci stores its geometric vertices, volume Vi, and center of gravity (centroid) Pi. 2. Splat Data: For each small cell, a Gaussian ellipsoid is defined. The ellipsoid is characterized by its center Pi and a shape matrix approximating the cell's geometry. 3. Texture Maps: Pre-computed textures containing the 2D circular Gaussian footprints for small cells, grouped by slicing direction and slice index. 4. Stencil Buffer: A buffer recording the presence of large cell polygons to prevent splat overlap. 1. Classification: For each cell Ci, calculate its volume Vi. If Vi < V{thresh}, classify Ci as a small cell; otherwise, classify it as a large cell. 2. Assignment: Assign each small cell to the closest slice plane. 3. Ellipsoid Fitting: Fit each small cell with a Gaussian ellipsoid that approximates its shape. In a curvilinear grid with a slowly varying Jacobian derivative matrix, these splats sum to near unity at any point, ensuring smooth interpolation of the scalar field. 4. Footprint Calculation: Project the 3D ellipsoid to the image plane to obtain an elliptical footprint. Convolve this footprint with a Gaussian pre-sampling filter in the image plane to create an enlarged 2D splat for anti-aliasing. 5. Rectangle Enclosure: Enclose the elliptical footprint of the enlarged splat in an axis-aligned rectangle. 6. Preprocessing (Sorting and Texturing): Sort small cells closest to each slice by the depth of their centers of gravity. Splat these sorted cells into an image in back-to-front order. Read back the image and determine a rectangle enclosing its non-zero values. Create texture maps per slicing direction. Each map contains as many textured rectangles (from consecutive slices) as would fit. The texture value is a 2D circular Gaussian multiplied by an RGBA color derived from the transfer function, cell volume, and enlarged footprint size. 7. Interactive Rendering: Load texture maps for the current slicing direction into texture objects. Render polygons for large cells in each slice. Record their presence in a stencil buffer. Position the rectangle representing the splats on the slice plane. Composite the splats using texture mapping. Apply a stencil test restricted to regions where polygons are absent, so splats do not contribute where full opacity is already accounted for by large cells. Unverified code. Step 1: Classification for cell in cells: if cell.volume < threshold: smallcells.append(cell) else: largecells.append(cell) # Step 2: Assignment and Step 3: Ellipsoid Fitting # For each small cell, find closest slice and fit ellipsoid splatdata = [] for cell in smallcells: closestplane = findclosestplane(cell.centroid, sliceplanes) # Fit Gaussian ellipsoid approximating cell shape ellipsoid = fitgaussianellipsoid(cell) splatdata.append({ 'cell': cell, 'plane': closestplane, 'ellipsoid': ellipsoid, 'centroid': cell.centroid }) # Step 4 & 5: Footprint and Rectangle # Preprocessing: Sort and create texture maps # Group splats by slice plane splatsbyplane = groupbyplane(splatdata, sliceplanes) texturemaps = {} for plane in sliceplanes: planesplats = splatsbyplane.get(plane, []) if not planesplats: continue # Step 6a: Sort by depth planesplats.sort(key=lambda s: depthof(s.centroid, plane)) # Step 6b: Splat into image to find bounds # Render splats back-to-front into a temporary buffer tempimage = rendersplatstoimage(planesplats, transferfunction) # Step 6c: Determine bounding rectangle of non-zero values bounds = findnonzerobounds(tempimage) # Step 6d: Create texture map # The texture contains the 2D circular Gaussian multiplied by RGBA # Color is determined by transfer function, cell volume, and footprint size texture = creategaussiantexture(bounds, transferfunction, planesplats) texturemaps[plane.id] = texture return texturemaps, largecells def renderframe(texturemaps, largecells, sliceplanes, stencilbuffer): """ Interactive rendering phase. """ clearstencilbuffer(stencilbuffer) # Render large cells first for plane in sliceplanes: planelargecells = [c for c in largecells if isclosetoplane(c, plane)] for cell in planelargecells: renderpolygon(cell) recordinstencil(stencilbuffer, cell) # Render small cells (splats) for plane in sliceplanes: if plane.id in texturemaps: texture = texturemaps[plane.id] # Position rectangle on slice plane rendersplatrectangle(texture, plane, stencilbuffer) Volume Threshold (V{thresh}): Determines the cutoff between small and large cells. Not given in the sources. Gaussian Filter Width: Controls the size of the anti-aliasing blur. Not given in the sources. Precision: The method relies on accurate calculation of cell volumes and centroids. Errors here may lead to incorrect classification or assignment. Boundary Conditions: The stencil test must correctly handle regions where polygons are absent. If the stencil test is not restricted, splats may overlap fully opaque polygon regions, causing visual artifacts. Degenerate Input: Cells with zero or near-zero volume may cause numerical instability in ellipsoid fitting. Not given in the sources. Renders cells with motion blur to handle temporal aliasing. Choose when objects are moving rapidly. Motion-Blurred Splats Uses thresholding on scalar values to determine slice visibility. Choose when scalar field discontinuities are important. Threshold Slicing and Anti-Aliasing Applies a filter to the data before rendering to reduce aliasing. Choose when pre-processing time is available and data is static. Interactive rendering is efficient as splats are rendered via texture mapping. Memory Complexity: Requires storing texture maps for all slicing directions. Memory usage scales with the number of small cells and the resolution of the texture maps. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Prevents loss of small details in adaptive meshes; efficient hardware rendering via texture mapping; smooth interpolation of scalar fields. Limitations: Requires preprocessing; may introduce blurring due to Gaussian filtering; complex implementation due to stencil testing and texture management. When to Use: When rendering adaptive meshes with small cells that are critical for visualization and are prone to being missed by standard slicing. When Not to Use: When small cells are not important or when preprocessing time is prohibitive. This method was developed for volume rendering of curvilinear and unstructured grids, particularly in the context of adaptive meshes. It builds on the work of Westover on splatting and Zwicker et al. on Gaussian splatting for anti-aliasing. name: Motion-Blurred Splats
head: Motion Blur in Volume Rendering, Temporal Antialiasing Technique for Splatting
body: Motion-blurred splats approximate temporal integration in volume rendering by stretching the spatial footprint of each voxel splat along its projected motion vector, thereby smoothing high-frequency temporal artifacts such as flickering and scintillation during rapid camera or object movement. Unlike standard splatting which suffers from aliasing in animation, or Threshold Slicing and Anti-Aliasing which addresses spatial frequency, this method specifically targets the time domain by distributing energy over the motion path, though it does not resolve visibility changes or popping artifacts caused by sorting order variations. The method extends object-order splatting by associating a linear motion vector with each voxel and modifying the splat's geometric footprint to represent the path traveled during a frame interval. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volume dataset defined on a raster grid; for each voxel, a linear motion vector \vec{v} (typically derived from camera velocity or object transformation); a static radial splat radius s; and a base opacity \alpha. Output: A rendered image where moving objects exhibit temporal blur proportional to their velocity. Data Structures Each voxel sample carries: Position (x, y, z) Value (opacity/density) Motion vector \vec{v}{world} in world space. Steps 1. Transform Motion Vector: For each voxel, transform its linear motion vector \vec{v}{world} into eye space. Project this vector onto the viewing plane to determine the 2D direction and length l of the motion blur. 2. Construct Footprint Geometry: For radially symmetric footprint functions, approximate the motion by stretching the footprint in the direction of the projected velocity vector. The motion-blurred splat is drawn between positions t{i-1} and ti. The original circular footprint is conceptually cut in half and stretched between these positions, resulting in a shape composed of: Two half-circles (A and B) at the endpoints, each with radius s. A rectangle (C) connecting the two half-circles, with length l (distance between t{i-1} and ti) and width 2s. 3. Rotate Footprint: For arbitrary projected velocity vector directions, rotate the constructed motion-blurred splat (the combination of half-circles and rectangle) to align with the velocity direction, using a rotation scheme similar to that of Crawfis and Max. 4. Adjust Opacity for Energy Conservation: To maintain constant energy contribution, the integrated intensity of the motion-blurred splat must equal that of a single stationary splat. Since the area increases, the opacity is scaled down. Let A1 be the area of the static circular footprint (\pi s^2). Let A2 be the area of the motion-blurred footprint. The area is calculated as: A2 = A1 + 2ls where l is the distance between t{i-1} and ti, and s is the radial splat radius. The new opacity \alpha' is scaled by the ratio of the static area to the blurred area: \alpha' = \alpha \cdot \frac{A1}{A2} = \alpha \cdot \frac{\pi s^2}{\pi s^2 + 2ls} 5. Rasterize: Draw the rotated, opacity-scaled motion-blurred splat onto the frame buffer. Parameters s: Radial splat radius. Typical values depend on the voxel size relative to the pixel size, often set to 1.0 or slightly larger to cover neighboring voxels. l: Projected motion length. Determined by the frame rate and velocity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Visibility/Popping: The algorithm does not address the visibility problem (changing hidden surfaces) or popping artifacts caused by voxel sorting changes; it only addresses integrated energy across the time domain. High Velocity: At very high velocities, the footprint becomes a long thin rectangle. The linear approximation assumes constant velocity within the frame. Precision: The opacity scaling factor approaches zero as l increases, potentially leading to underflow or very faint rendering for extremely fast-moving objects. A variant that distributes each sample's value evenly across the voxels it touches along its motion vector. It differs by folding the temporal domain into the spatial domain for efficient rasterization, but loses lighting detail and cannot cancel out camera motion relative to primitives. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels N, O(N), as each voxel requires a constant number of geometric transformations and a single rasterization pass of an elongated shape. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the motion vectors for each voxel. Measured Performance: Applied to a 512 x 512 x 76 nerve cell dataset from confocal microscopy, motion blur dominated the visual result, making the difference between antialiased and motion-blurred splats less visible for objects with high movement. Strengths: Effectively reduces flickering and scintillation artifacts in animations of spinning or rapidly moving volumes, such as terrain datasets from satellite data. Limitations: Does not solve visibility sorting issues; the approximation of smearing a circular footprint into a capsule shape is an approximation and may not perfectly integrate energy for non-radial kernels or complex motion paths. When to use: When temporal aliasing (flickering) is the primary artifact in animated volume rendering and performance constraints prevent full temporal integration or supersampling. When not to use: When accurate visibility sorting is critical or when the motion is non-linear/rotational in a way that the linear smearing approximation fails to capture accurately. The technique was introduced by Mueller et al. in their work on splatting errors and antialiasing, published in the IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (Vol. 4, No. 2, April-June 1998). It builds on earlier work by Max [7] and Crawfis et al. [2] regarding compositing order for X-ray-like or emission volume models, where compositing order is immaterial. The authors noted that motion blurring in volume rendering had not yet been addressed and presented this as initial work in that area. name: Motion Blur via Splat Smearing
head: Line Drawing Smear, Voxel Motion Blur
body: Motion Blur via Splat Smearing is a technique to approximate motion blur in voxel buffers by distributing each sample's value evenly across the voxels it touches along its motion vector, preserving the total sum of values. It differs from correct temporal integration by folding the temporal domain into the spatial domain, which allows for efficient rasterization but results in loss of lighting detail and inability to cancel out camera motion relative to primitives. Inputs: Start position (vsStart), end position (vsEnd), primitive value (value), voxel buffer, and optional sampling factor (samplingFactor). Outputs: Updated voxel buffer with smeared values. Data Structures: vsStart, vsEnd: 3D vectors representing the primitive's position at the start and end of the frame. value: The scalar or vector quantity associated with the primitive (e.g., density, color). buffer: The voxel grid storing accumulated values. Steps: 1. Calculate the motion vector: vsLine = vsEnd - vsStart. 2. Determine the number of samples: numSamples = \max(2, \lceil \|vsLine\| \rceil). If a sampling factor is used: numSamples = \max(2, \lceil samplingFactor \cdot \|vsLine\| \rceil). 3. Iterate i from 0 to numSamples - 1: a. Calculate the fraction: fraction = \frac{i}{numSamples - 1}. b. Calculate the sample position: vsP = \text{lerp}(vsStart, vsEnd, fraction). c. Write the antialiased point with value \frac{value}{numSamples} to the buffer at vsP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def writeline(vsstart, vsend, value, buffer, samplingfactor=1.0): # Calculate motion vector vsline = vsend - vsstart # Calculate number of samples numsamples = max(2, int(math.ceil(samplingfactor vsline.length()))) # Distribute value valuepersample = value / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): # Calculate fraction to avoid accumulation errors fraction = i / (numsamples - 1) # Interpolate position vsp = lerp(vsstart, vsend, fraction) # Write antialiased point writeantialiasedpoint(vsp, valuepersample, buffer) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + (b - a) t def writeantialiasedpoint(pos, val, buf): # Standard antialiased accumulation into the voxel buffer buf.accumulate(pos, val) Parameters: samplingFactor: A scaling factor to allow undersampling for speed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Error Accumulation: Using incremental position updates can cause accumulation of errors in splat positions. Calculating the fraction explicitly avoids this. Lighting Detail: Smearing before lighting is technically incorrect because it folds the temporal domain into the spatial domain, losing information about when a primitive occupies a position. This causes loss of lighting detail, making sharp features look artificially soft. Camera Motion Cancellation: If the camera moves at the same speed as primitives, motion should cancel out, but because motion blur is baked into the voxel buffer, this is not possible. Post-rasterization smearing is a technique to approximate motion blur in voxel buffers by deferring the blurring operation until after the rasterization/splatting phase is complete. Unlike methods that smear individual samples during rasterization, this approach accumulates velocity information in a separate buffer and applies a single, global smear pass. It is chosen when performance is prioritized over handling complex overlapping primitives with divergent motion vectors. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of primitives and the length of their motion vectors. Undersampling reduces this by a factor of samplingFactor. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel buffer size. Post-rasterization variants require an additional velocity buffer. Performance: Faster than correct temporal integration for large numbers of primitives. Post-rasterization smearing is often faster than per-sample smearing. Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient, preserves sum of values. Limitations: Loss of lighting detail, incorrect lighting for smeared primitives, inability to cancel camera motion, artifacts from undersampling if not randomized. When to Use: When performance is critical and approximate motion blur is acceptable. When Not to Use: When correct lighting interaction with moving primitives is required, or when camera and primitive motion should cancel out. Originated in the context of production volume rendering, specifically for handling motion blur in voxel buffers where correct temporal integration is computationally prohibitive for thousands or millions of volumetric primitives. The technique leverages standard line-drawing algorithms adapted for 3D voxel grids. name: Post-rasterization Smearing
head: Accumulated Motion Blur, Post-Rasterization Velocity Smearing, Velocity Buffer Smear, Velocity buffer smearing
body: Post-rasterization smearing approximates motion blur in voxel buffers by deferring the blurring operation until after the rasterization or splatting phase completes. Unlike methods that smear individual samples during rasterization, this approach accumulates velocity information in a separate buffer and applies a single global smear pass. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel buffer containing density/intensity values, and a separate velocity buffer storing accumulated motion vectors for each voxel. Output: A motion-blurred voxel buffer. Data Structures: 1. Density Buffer: Standard voxel grid storing scalar values (e.g., density, color). 2. Velocity Buffer: A voxel grid storing a 3D vector per voxel representing accumulated motion. Layout: Not given in the sources. Initialization: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Rasterization/Splatting with Velocity Accumulation: During rasterization or splatting, accumulate a velocity vector for each voxel in the separate velocity buffer. 2. Global Smear Pass: Once all rasterization and splatting is complete, use the accumulated velocity to smear the entire density buffer in a single step. 3. Variant (Average Motion): To resolve direction ambiguity when multiple primitives overlap, track the average motion vector per voxel, though this can cause visual artifacts. 4. Variant (Deferred Rendering): Retain both the density and velocity buffers and calculate the motion blur during rendering to avoid reduced shading detail in motion-blurred areas, though the overlapping primitive problem remains. 5. Variant (Post-Lighting): If the lit volume is voxelized, apply motion blur after lighting to solve the problem of lighting a voxel buffer with baked-in blur, though artifacts persist where overlapping primitives have different velocity vectors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def postrasterizationsmearing(densitybuffer, velocitybuffer, primitives): # Step 1: Accumulate velocities during rasterization/splatting for primitive in primitives: motionvec = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Standard retrieval of primitive motion vector # Standard rasterization of primitive into density buffer for voxelidx in primitive.getaffectedvoxelindices(): velocitybuffer[voxelidx] += motionvec # Step 2: Global smear pass blurredbuffer = [row[:] for row in densitybuffer] # Deep copy of input buffer for y in range(len(blurredbuffer)): for x in range(len(blurredbuffer[0])): for z in range(len(blurredbuffer[0][0])): v = velocitybuffer[y][x][z] if v[0] == 0 and v[1] == 0 and v[2] == 0: # Guard against zero motion continue # The exact interpolation kernel for distributing values along v is Not given in the sources. # Standard linear accumulation along the velocity direction: blurvalue = 0.0 for t in range(-5, 6): # Fixed kernel radius; sources do not specify tx, ty, tz = x + v[0] t, y + v[1] t, z + v[2] t if 0 <= tx < len(blurredbuffer[0]) and 0 <= ty < len(blurredbuffer) and 0 <= tz < len(blurredbuffer[0][0]): blurvalue += blurredbuffer[ty][tx][tz] blurredbuffer[y][x][z] = blurvalue / 11.0 # Normalization return blurredbuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlapping Primitives with Divergent Velocities: If input primitives overlap and have drastically different motion vectors, it becomes impossible to calculate a valid single direction to smear in. Visual Artifacts: Keeping track of the average motion vector in overlapping voxels can cause visual artifacts in the final render. Camera Motion Cancellation: If the camera moves at the same speed as the primitives, motion should cancel out, but because the motion blur is baked into the voxel buffer via accumulated velocity, this cancellation is not possible, leading to incorrect blur. Retains both density and velocity buffers and calculates motion blur during rendering. It sets itself apart by avoiding reduced shading detail in motion-blurred areas, though it still suffers from the overlapping primitive problem. Choose it for microvoxel-based volume renderers where shading fidelity is prioritized. See Motion Blur via Splat Smearing. Applies motion blur after lighting if the lit volume is voxelized. It sets itself apart by solving the problem of lighting a voxel buffer with motion blur baked in, though artifacts persist where overlapping primitives have different velocity vectors. Choose it when lighting accuracy must be preserved before blurring. See Motion Blur via Splat Smearing. Performance: Often faster than smearing each sample as it is written to the buffer, as it requires only a single global smear pass after rasterization. Memory: Requires an additional velocity buffer. Exact memory overhead is Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of primitives and the global smear pass resolution, but degrades in scenes with high primitive overlap and divergent velocities. Strengths: Reduced per-sample overhead; simplified pipeline by deferring blur to a single post-process step. Limitations: Poor handling of complex scenes with overlapping primitives having divergent motion vectors; cannot correctly handle camera motion cancellation. Use Cases: Suitable for simple scenes or when performance is critical and visual artifacts from overlapping divergent motions are acceptable. This method is described in the context of production volume rendering fundamentals, specifically as an alternative to per-sample smearing during rasterization. It is part of a broader discussion on motion blur techniques in voxel-based rendering pipelines. name: Threshold Slicing and Anti-Aliasing
head: Threshold-based hybrid slicing
body: Threshold Slicing and Anti-Aliasing is a hybrid volume rendering technique for curvilinear and unstructured grids that combines geometric slicing with splatting to handle data density variations. It solves the problem of visual artifacts in sparse or heterogeneous datasets by rendering high-value regions as precise polygons and low-value regions as smooth, anti-aliased splats. Unlike pure splatting methods like Splatting for Anti-aliasing Small Cells which approximate all geometry, or pure slicing methods which may miss inter-slice details, this method adapts the representation based on a scalar threshold. Inputs: A volume dataset defined on curvilinear or unstructured grids; a scalar threshold value T; a set of parallel slicing planes; camera parameters for orthogonal projection. Outputs: A 2D image with anti-aliased boundaries and filled interiors. Data Structures: 1. Grid Cells: Each cell is a convex polyhedron defined by its vertices and faces. 2. Slicing Planes: A collection of closely spaced parallel planes Pi. 3. Pixel Buffer: Accumulates color and opacity contributions. Steps: 1. Classification: For each cell in the dataset, determine its representative scalar value V (e.g., average or maximum). 2. Branching: If V \ge T: The cell is considered "high-density." It is sliced by the collection of parallel planes. The intersections form polygons. These polygons are projected onto the image plane. For orthogonal projection, the viewing ray segment length l within the cell is calculated for each pixel covered by the polygon. The cell is rendered as a solid polygon with appropriate opacity integration. If V < T: The cell is considered "low-density" or sparse. It is not sliced into polygons. Instead, it is rendered using an anti-aliased ellipsoidal splat, similar to the method by Zwicker et al.. This splat covers the area where the cell might lie between slice planes or pixel samples, preventing holes in the visualization. 3. Compositing: All rendered elements (polygons from high-value cells and splats from low-value cells) are composited using standard front-to-back or back-to-front alpha blending, depending on the desired visual effect and performance constraints. Formulas: Ray Segment Length: For orthogonal projection, the length l of the viewing ray segment within a convex polyhedral cell is determined by the intersection of the ray with the cell's front-facing and back-facing faces. Threshold Condition: V{cell} \ge T triggers polygonal slicing; V{cell} < T triggers splatting. Parameters: Threshold T: Determines the boundary between polygonal and splatted rendering. Typical values depend on the data's scalar range and the desired level of detail. Plane Spacing: The distance between parallel slicing planes. Closer spacing increases accuracy for polygonal rendering but increases computational cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when calculating intersections for polygonal slicing, especially for cells nearly parallel to the slicing planes. Boundary Artifacts: Discontinuities may appear at the threshold boundary if the transition between polygonal and splatted rendering is not handled smoothly. Degenerate Input: Cells with zero volume or degenerate geometry should be skipped or handled specially to avoid division by zero or invalid intersections. Time Complexity: Depends on the distribution of data relative to the threshold. High-density regions require polygon intersection calculations, which are more expensive than splatting but provide higher accuracy. Low-density regions use efficient splatting. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the grid data, slicing planes, and intermediate polygonal representations for high-density cells. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts in sparse regions while maintaining geometric accuracy in dense regions. Efficient for large datasets with varying density. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the threshold and plane spacing. May introduce visual discontinuities if not implemented carefully. When to Use: Ideal for visualizing curvilinear and unstructured grids with significant variations in data density, where both accuracy and performance are critical. When Not to Use: Not suitable for uniformly dense datasets where pure slicing or pure splatting would be more efficient. This method was proposed in the context of volume rendering for curvilinear and unstructured grids. It builds on earlier work by Yagel et al. for slicing cells into polygons and Zwicker et al. for anti-aliased ellipsoidal splats. The approach was developed to address the challenges of rendering large, heterogeneous datasets interactively, leveraging parallel processing for scalability. name: Opacity Compensation Methods
head: Opacity compensation terms, transparency modulation
body: Opacity compensation methods are techniques used in volume rendering to correct inaccuracies introduced by approximations in splatting or compositing, ensuring that the final image accurately represents the underlying data density and structure. These methods solve the problem of premature occlusion or incorrect surface appearance by adjusting the opacity contribution of individual samples based on specific criteria such as value proximity, depth, or statistical uncertainty. Unlike standard volume rendering which applies a fixed transfer function, these methods dynamically modulate opacity to preserve internal features or enhance surface clarity. Inputs: Sample values (v), sample depths (d), target values, allowable deviations, statistical moments (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma), and rendering parameters (max opacity, modulation factors). Outputs: Compensated opacity (\alpha), potentially compensated mean color (\mu{cond}) and covariance (\Sigma{cond}). No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard sample buffers containing position, value, and depth. For statistical methods (UBS), covariance matrices (\Sigma) and Cholesky factors (\hat{L}) are required. This formula calculates surface opacity based on the proximity of a sample's value to a target value, differing from Levy's thickness-based approach. \alpha = \alpha{max} \times \left( 1.0 - \frac{|v - v{target}|}{\delta{allow}} \right) \alpha{max}: Maximum surface opacity, range [0.0, 1.0]. 0.0 is transparent/colorless; 1.0 is completely opaque. v: Current sample value. v{target}: The center of the rendering window. \delta{allow}: Allowable deviation defining the "window" of values rendered. Samples near the center are more opaque than those near the edges. Logic: 1. Calculate the absolute difference |v - v{target}|. 2. If |v - v{target}| > \delta{allow}, assign \alpha = 0.0. 3. Otherwise, compute \alpha using the formula above. Comparison: Levy's formula uses surface thickness and local gradient: \alpha{Levy} = 1 - \frac{|v - v{target}|}{thickness \times local\gradient}. VIPER is computationally faster and produces brighter images. This method compensates for quick transparency accumulation in standard volume compositing by using depth values to calculate importance, assuming important features are further down the viewing ray. \beta = 1 - (di - d{i-1}) = 1 - \Delta{step} \beta: Modulation factor for accumulated transparency. di: Depth value of the incoming sample. d{i-1}: Depth value of the previous sample. \Delta{step}: Sample step (distance between samples). Logic: 1. Compute the depth difference between consecutive samples along the viewing ray. 2. Calculate \beta as 1 - \Delta{step}. 3. Apply \beta to modulate the transparency accumulation. Pitfall: Since \Delta{step} > 0, \beta < 1. Consequently, accumulated transparency can never reach full opacity, resulting in a transparent look where all samples contribute. This reveals underlying structures occluded in direct volume rendering. UBS evaluates modulation factors and computes covariance-derived slicing using tanh-capped values for opacity and diagonal coupling for mean/covariance. Parameters: \hat{L}q: Cholesky factor of \Sigma{qq} such that \hat{L}q \hat{L}q^\top = \Sigma{qq}. \betai: Modulation factor, often evaluated as 4 \exp(\beta^{raw}i). \Lambda\beta: Coupling factor, often \min(\beta/4, 1). Formulas: 1. Compute intermediate variable Z^{UBS} and depth term di: Z^{UBS} = \hat{L}q^{-1} \delta di = \tanh((zi^{UBS})^2) 2. Compute compensated opacity \alpha{cond}: \alpha{cond} = \alpha \prod{i=1}^C (1 - di)^{\betai} 3. Compute compensated mean \mu{cond}: \mu{cond} = \mup + \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} \text{diag}(\LambdaB) \delta 4. Compute compensated covariance \Sigma{cond}: \Sigma{cond} = \Sigma{pp} - \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} \text{diag}(\Lambda\beta) \Sigma{qp} Pitfall: Tanh values are capped below one for finite opacity evaluation. Unverified code.
