name: Gaussian Splatting
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting, 3DGS, 3DGS representation, EWA Volume Splatting, Elliptical Weighted Average splatting, Gaussian Splat, Volume Splatting, 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, 3D Gaussian Splat Representation & Band-0 SH Decoding
body: Gaussian Splatting is an object-order direct volume rendering algorithm that represents a scene as a collection of overlapping 3D Gaussian primitives, projecting them onto the image plane and alpha-compositing them to generate the final image. It serves as a fast, high-quality alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by leveraging volumetric rendering principles to preserve differentiability while employing point-based rasterization for efficient training and rendering. Unlike traditional opacity-based splatting, 3DGS assigns a single opacity value per primitive, allowing for constant transparency regardless of viewing direction and enabling the optimization of a well-behaved, bounded scalar. It builds on EWA Splatting but simplifies the formulation by ignoring self-attenuation and approximating perspective projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M 3D Gaussians \{gi\}{i=1}^M, where each gi is defined by center \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \sigmai, and color ci; a camera with intrinsics K and extrinsics W; and image dimensions H \times W. Output: A 2D image I of size H \times W. Data Structures: Each Gaussian splat stores the following fields: pos: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, center position in world space. scale: s \in \mathbb{R}^3, size along each local axis (stored in log space). rot: q \in \mathbb{R}^4, orientation as a unit quaternion. color: ci \in \mathbb{R}^3, RGB color. In the standard format, this is decoded from spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Band-0 SH coefficients f{dc} \in \mathbb{R}^3 are converted to RGB using C0 = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}} \approx 0.282: \text{color} = \text{clamp}(0.5 + C0 \cdot f{dc}, 0, 1) opacity: \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}, opacity in [0, 1] (stored as a logit). The 3D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i is parameterized via diagonalization \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i = V S V^T, where S = \text{diag}(e^{s1}, e^{s2}, e^{s3}) and V is the rotation matrix derived from the quaternion q. Rendering Pipeline: The rendering process follows these steps: 1. Projection: For each Gaussian i, compute the 2D screen-space covariance matrix \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i. First, transform the 3D covariance to camera coordinates: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i = W \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i W^T. Then, approximate the perspective projection PK around the Gaussian center \boldsymbol{\mu}i using its Jacobian \mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times3}: PK(\mathbf{x}) \approx PK(\boldsymbol{\mu}i) + \mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i) The projected 2D covariance is: \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i = \mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i \mathbf{J}^T The projected mean is \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i = PK(\boldsymbol{\mu}i). 2. Rasterization (Splatting): For each pixel p in the image, identify the set of K Gaussians whose projected footprints cover p. This is typically done using a tile-based rasterization strategy. For each covering Gaussian, evaluate the 2D Gaussian value at pixel p: \tilde{G}i(p) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(p - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i)^T \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i^{-1} (p - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i)\right) 3. Sorting: Sort the K Gaussians intersecting the view ray for pixel p by distance from their centers to the camera position (back-to-front order). Note: This sorting is based on centers, which is an approximation. 4. Alpha-Compositing: Compute the final pixel intensity If by alpha-compositing the sorted Gaussians: If = \sum{i=1}^N ci \tilde{\sigma}i \tilde{G}i(p) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \left(1 - \tilde{\sigma}j \tilde{G}j(p)\right) where N is the number of sorted Gaussians, \tilde{\sigma}i = \sigmai, and \tilde{G}i(p) is the Gaussian value at p. Training and Optimization: The scene parameters \theta (the set of Gaussians) are optimized by minimizing the photometric loss between the rendered image I{\theta,i} and the input view Ii: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \| I{\theta,i} - Ii \|^2 Gradients are backpropagated to update Gaussian parameters using Adam. During training, the number of Gaussians is dynamically adjusted: splitting large Gaussians, cloning those that underfit detail, and pruning those with low opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. alpha) if alphabuffer[y][x][0] < 1e-4: break return colorbuffer def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): x, y, z, w = q return [ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - zw), 2(xz + yw)], [2(xy + zw), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - xw)], [2(xz - yw), 2(yz + xw), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ] def decodeshband0(fdc): SHC0 = 0.28209479177387814 return [max(0.0, min(1.0, 0.5 + SHC0 c)) for c in fdc] def inverse2x2(M): det = M[0][0]M[1][1] - M[0][1]M[1][0] return [[M[1][1]/det, -M[0][1]/det], [-M[1][0]/det, M[0][0]/det]] def matmul(A, B): return [[sum(A[i][k]B[k][j] for k in range(len(B))) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] def transpose(M): return [[M[j][i] for j in range(len(M))] for i in range(len(M[0]))] def vec3add(a, b): return [a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]] A ray-marching algorithm implemented on 3D Gaussians to study the impact of approximations like spatial overlap and sorting in 3DGS. A rendering technique that treats each point as a Gaussian reconstruction kernel on the surface, projects it into screen space, and convolves it with a low-pass filter to produce a resampling filter actually rasterized. This implementation uses a simplified kernel: screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic linear falloff, rasterized as plain point sprites, trading anisotropic, correctly band-limited footprint for a formulation needing no per-point normals or radii. A rendering approach that correctly accounts for the attenuation of a Gaussian's own extinction along the ray path (self-attenuation), rather than ignoring it or using a first-order Taylor approximation. An optimization for the inner pixel loop of a Gaussian splatting rasterizer that hoists row-constant terms outside the inner (column) loop to minimize arithmetic operations per pixel. Computes the 2D screen-space covariance matrix and its inverse for a 3D Gaussian splat, ensuring numerical stability by adding a small epsilon to the diagonal to guarantee positive definiteness. A method that separates intrinsic and dynamic appearance attributes per Gaussian point to mitigate transient occlusions and photometric variations. It employs an adaptive sampling strategy, leverages 2D visibility maps, uses depth regularization, and aligns pixel appearance features from image triplanes directly to 3D Gaussians. A method for 'in-the-wild' settings that integrates robust DINO features and a lightweight appearance modeling module within the 3DGS framework. It handles unconstrained photo collections. A method for modeling dynamic Gaussians for time-varying content. It develops a spatiotemporal structure encoder to capture deformations of both positions and colors over time. An extension that introduces 2D and 3D Gaussian filters to improve robustness to aliasing caused by resolution changes. A method that employs an unscented transform for more precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane, improving the affine approximation of the projection operator. A method that extends 3DGS by conditioning Gaussians on learned appearance embeddings and training unsupervised transient Gaussians to ignore occluders. A method that uses a feed-forward network (FFN) for monocular reconstruction, generating 3DGS scenes by estimating depth from a single view. A method that tokenizes two to four images and their camera parameters, concatenates them, and passes them through a transformer block whose output tokens are decoded into Gaussian parameters. A method that incorporates an epipolar transformer to generalize features between two views, paired with a probabilistic prediction of Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays. A method that improves sparse-view reconstruction by defining two independent reconstructions and comparing them to discard inaccurate Gaussians. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Complex scenes require approximately 200,000–500,000 Gaussians, resulting in significant memory and storage demands. Each Gaussian stores position, scale, rotation, SH coefficients, and opacity. Time: Rendering is O(M \cdot A), where M is the number of Gaussians and A is the average number of splats per pixel. Training uses gradient descent to update Gaussian parameters, but the rasterization pipeline itself is highly optimized for real-time performance. Performance: 3DGS enables real-time rendering capabilities for novel view synthesis. It is significantly faster than NeRFs for rendering, as it avoids the need for volumetric ray marching and MLP evaluation. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High-quality view synthesis, real-time rendering, differentiable optimization. Limitations: High memory footprint. The emission-absorption model limits performance on highly reflective surfaces and prevents relighting. Standard 3DGS uses a dilation-based filter which fails to suppress high-frequency artifacts when varying focal length or camera distance. Approximations in visibility resolution (sorting by centers) can cause popping artifacts. Self-attenuation is not treated correctly. When to Use: Use for real-time novel view synthesis of static scenes with moderate complexity. Avoid for scenes with highly reflective surfaces or when relighting is required. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It builds on EWA Volume Splatting and other point-based rendering works. The method was developed to overcome the computational cost of evaluating the volume rendering equation via quadrature, which requires querying points outside Gaussian supports. It provides a fast, high-quality alternative to NeRF by using a hybrid, primitive-based rendering method. name: Unnormalized 3D Gaussian Function
head: 3D Gaussian amplitude, Unnormalized Gaussian
body: The Unnormalized 3D Gaussian Function is a Gaussian representation used in 3D Gaussian Splatting where the amplitude a at the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} equals the opacity, representing the peak capacity to block or emit light. It differs from the Normalized 3D Gaussian Function by parameterizing the function via its peak value rather than its integral, making a the intensity at the center rather than the total light capacity. Inputs: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The query point in 3D space. a \in \mathbb{R}: The amplitude (peak value) at the mean. \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The mean position (center) of the Gaussian. \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: The covariance matrix defining the shape and orientation. Outputs: g \in \mathbb{R}: The value of the unnormalized Gaussian function at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: The function requires the covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} and its inverse \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}. In implementation, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is often derived from a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} and a scaling vector \mathbf{s} such that \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}). Formulas: The unnormalized Gaussian function \mathcal{G}D^\mu is defined as: \mathcal{G}D^\mu(\mathbf{x}, a, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = a \mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \mathcal{N}D(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) Where \mathcal{N}D is the standard D-dimensional Gaussian probability density function (PDF): \mathcal{N}D(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{\mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} And \mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) is the unbounded integral of the exponential part, ensuring the PDF integrates to one: \mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \sqrt{(2\pi)^D \det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} Substituting the PDF into the unnormalized definition, the \mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) terms cancel out, yielding the practical computation formula: \mathcal{G}D^\mu(\mathbf{x}, a, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = a e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} Conversion to Normalized Weight: To convert between the unnormalized amplitude a and the normalized weight w (where w is the integral of the function over all space), the following relationship holds: a = \frac{w}{\mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def unnormalizedgaussian(x, a, mu, Sigmainv): """ Computes the value of the unnormalized 3D Gaussian function. Args: x: Query point (3,) a: Amplitude at the mean (scalar) mu: Mean position (3,) Sigmainv: Inverse covariance matrix (3, 3) Returns: Value of the Gaussian at x """ diff = [x[i] - mu[i] for i in range(3)] exponent = 0.0 for i in range(3): rowsum = 0.0 for j in range(3): rowsum += Sigmainv[i][j] diff[j] exponent += diff[i] rowsum return a math.exp(-0.5 exponent) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is singular (non-invertible), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} cannot be computed. In practice, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is constructed from a rotation and scaling, ensuring it remains positive semi-definite. Degenerate scaling (zero scale) leads to infinite amplitude for a fixed weight w, or zero width for a fixed amplitude a. Precision: For points far from \boldsymbol{\mu}, the exponent becomes large and negative, potentially causing underflow to zero. This is standard behavior for Gaussian splatting cutoffs. Uses weight w as the integral rather than peak amplitude. Choose when the total light capacity is the primary physical quantity of interest. Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation, dominated by the matrix-vector multiplication in the exponent. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary storage per Gaussian for the inverse covariance. Strengths: Directly parameterizes the peak intensity, which aligns with how opacity is often interpreted in rendering (peak blocking/emission). Limitations: The value at the mean depends on the spread of the Gaussian; a wider Gaussian with the same peak amplitude a contributes less total energy than a narrow one. This makes a less intuitive for conservation of energy compared to w. The unnormalized Gaussian function is defined in as a Gaussian representation used in 3D Gaussian Splatting where the amplitude at the mean equals the opacity. It serves as a standard mathematical primitive for spatial distribution modeling in splatting-based rendering pipelines. name: Normalized 3D Gaussian Function
head: Normal Distribution Helper, Normalized Gaussian, Probability Density Function Gaussian
body: The Normalized 3D Gaussian Function is a probability density function (PDF) scaled to integrate to unity, serving as the fundamental building block for extinction models in EWA splatting and Gaussian Splatting. It differs from its sibling, the Unnormalized 3D Gaussian Function, by explicitly including the normalization constant 1/\mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}), ensuring the total integral over space equals one, whereas the unnormalized variant sets the peak amplitude at the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} directly to the opacity parameter. Inputs: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The evaluation point in 3D space. \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The mean position (center) of the Gaussian. \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: The covariance matrix defining the shape and orientation. w \in \mathbb{R}: The weight parameter representing the total capacity to block or emit light (equivalent to the unbounded integral of the function). Outputs: g \in \mathbb{R}: The value of the weighted normalized Gaussian function at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}: A 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix representing covariance. \boldsymbol{\mu}: A 3-component vector. w: A scalar weight. Steps: 1. Compute the displacement vector: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}. 2. Compute the inverse covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}. 3. Compute the quadratic form: Q = \mathbf{d}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{d}. 4. Compute the normalization factor \mathcal{I}3(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \sqrt{(2\pi)^3 \det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}. 5. Compute the normalized Gaussian value: \mathcal{N}3(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{\mathcal{I}3(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} e^{-\frac{1}{2} Q}. 6. Scale by weight: g = w \cdot \mathcal{N}3(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}). Formulas: The normalized 3D Gaussian function is defined as: \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{\mathcal{I}{\mathcal{D}}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} where \mathcal{I}{\mathcal{D}}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) is the normalization factor: \mathcal{I}D(\mathbf{\Sigma}) = \sqrt{(2\pi)^D \det(\mathbf{\Sigma})} The weighted normalized Gaussian function \mathcal{G}{\mathcal{D}}^n is: \mathcal{G}{\mathcal{D}}^n(\mathbf{x}, w, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = w \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) This ensures that the integral over all space equals w: \int{\mathbb{R}^D} \mathcal{G}D^n(\mathbf{x}, w, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \, d\mathbf{x} = w Parameters: D: Dimensionality. For 3D Gaussians, D=3. \pi: The mathematical constant Pi. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is singular (determinant is zero), the normalization factor becomes zero, leading to division by zero. Precision: Computing \det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} directly can be numerically unstable if the Gaussian is highly anisotropic. It is often more stable to compute the Cholesky decomposition or use the inverse directly if the matrix is well-conditioned. Evaluation Point: The formula is valid for any \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. However, for rendering, points far from \boldsymbol{\mu} yield values close to zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It serves as the core evaluation kernel for determining the contribution of a projected 3D Gaussian splat to a pixel in Gaussian Splatting rendering. Unlike the unnormalized variant, this method includes the normalization constant 1/(2\pi\sqrt{\det(\Sigma)}), ensuring the integral over the entire plane equals one. It is distinct from the conic-based variant by explicitly computing the inverse covariance matrix rather than using a pre-computed conic matrix. Modeling the extinction function f(\mathbf{x}) as a mixture of normalized 3D Gaussians, each potentially having a view-dependent radiance ci(\mathcal{R}). The extinction function is defined as: \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^N \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathbf{x}, wi, \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) The radiance contribution is: c(\mathcal{R}, t) = \sum{i=0}^N ci(\mathcal{R}) \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathbf{x}, wi, \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) where ci(\mathcal{R}) is the radiance for ray \mathcal{R}. The normalization ensures that w has a direct physical interpretation as total integrated density or opacity capacity. Limitations: Requires computing the inverse and determinant of the covariance matrix, which can be computationally expensive compared to unnormalized variants where these terms cancel out. The normalized 3D Gaussian function originates from the mathematical theory of Gaussian distributions and is used as a building block for EWA (Elliptical Weighted Average) splatting. name: Gaussian Interpolation
head: Gaussian Filter, Gaussian Kernel Interpolation
body: Gaussian Interpolation uses a Gaussian function as an interpolation kernel to reconstruct signals from discrete samples. It builds on the Normalized 3D Gaussian Function and is distinguished from other filters by being the only filter that is both separable and rotationally symmetric. This unique property allows it to integrate one dimension out of the kernel, enabling 2D reconstruction instead of 3D, which is particularly advantageous in point-tossing approaches like splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Discrete sample values and their spatial coordinates. Output: The interpolated value at the target reconstruction point. Data Structures: Exact layouts are not given in the sources. The method operates on a list of sample values and their positions. The kernel itself is defined by a single scalar parameter. Numbered Steps: 1. For each sample contributing to the reconstruction point, calculate the distance z between the sample's position and the target position. 2. Compute the kernel weight w using the formula w = e^{-\frac{z^2}{2\sigma^2}}. 3. Multiply the sample's value by its corresponding weight w. 4. Sum the weighted values of all contributing samples. 5. Normalize the result by dividing by the sum of the weights if the truncated kernel does not integrate to unity. Formulas: The one-dimensional Gaussian interpolation kernel is defined as: f{\text{Gaussian}}(z) = e^{-\frac{z^2}{2\sigma^2}} where: z is the distance from the sample to the reconstruction point. \sigma is the standard deviation controlling the width. Parameters: \sigma (Sigma): Controls the width of the Gaussian kernel. Typical values are not given in the sources. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Infinite Extent: The Gaussian kernel has infinite extent in both spatial and frequency domains. In practice, it must be truncated. Because it asymptotically falls to zero quickly, truncation can be performed in the near-zero area without causing significant ringing artifacts. Blurring: The filter distorts the passband by attenuating high-frequency components of the main replica, which causes blurring in the output. This makes it less suitable for applications requiring sharp edge preservation compared to filters with sharper cutoffs. Truncation: While truncation is safe due to the rapid decay, the truncation radius must be chosen carefully to balance performance and accuracy. A common heuristic is to truncate at 3\sigma or 4\sigma, where the value is negligible. A specific application of Gaussian interpolation used in volumetric rendering, particularly in temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) for froxel-based rendering. It is applied to jittered sub-froxel samples to improve edge quality and stability compared to a box filter. The weight W(x) for a sample at distance x from the center of the froxel is given by: W(x) = e^{-2.29x^2} This specific form is a Gaussian fit to the Blackman-Harris 3.3 window function. It provides better edge quality and stability under motion than a spatiotemporal box filter, which suffers from poor edge quality and instability due to sharp edges. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method's separability allows decomposing N-dimensional interpolation into N one-dimensional passes, reducing computational cost compared to full 3D reconstruction. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Separability and rotational symmetry allow for efficient 2D reconstruction from 3D data in splatting methods. Smooth decay reduces ringing artifacts upon truncation. Limitations: Causes blurring due to high-frequency attenuation. Infinite extent requires truncation, which may introduce slight inaccuracies if the truncation radius is too small. When to Use: Suitable for applications where smoothness is preferred over sharpness, such as in splatting-based volume rendering or temporal anti-aliasing where stability is key. When Not to Use: Not ideal for applications requiring sharp edge preservation or high-frequency detail retention due to inherent blurring. Gaussian interpolation is notably used in point-tossing approaches like splatting [Westover 90] because of its separability and rotational symmetry, which allow for efficient 2D reconstruction. In the context of volumetric rendering, it has been applied in temporal anti-aliasing methods for froxel-based rendering to improve edge quality and stability. The specific Gaussian fit to Blackman-Harris 3.3 was introduced by Karis for use in TAA. name: 2D Gaussian Probability Density (Standard)
head: 2D Gaussian PDF
body: Computes the probability density function (PDF) value of a 2D Gaussian at point xy, given mean and covariance matrix. It serves as the core evaluation primitive for determining the contribution of a projected 3D Gaussian splat to a pixel in Gaussian Splatting rendering. Inputs: xy: A 2D point (vector) representing the location in screen space where the PDF is evaluated. gaussianmean: A 2D vector representing the mean (center) of the Gaussian. gaussiancovariance: A 2 \times 2 symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix \Sigma. Outputs: pdf: A scalar float representing the probability density at xy. Data Structures: xy: vec2 (float x, float y). gaussianmean: vec2 (float x, float y). gaussiancovariance: mat2x2 (float m00, m01, m10, m11). Note: m{01} = m{10} for symmetric covariance. Steps: 1. Compute mean difference: Calculate the vector from the Gaussian mean to the evaluation point. \Delta = xy - gaussian\mean 2. Compute determinant: Calculate the determinant of the covariance matrix. \det(\Sigma) = \Sigma{00}\Sigma{11} - \Sigma{01}\Sigma{10} 3. Compute inverse covariance: Calculate the inverse of the 2 \times 2 covariance matrix analytically. \Sigma^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det(\Sigma)} \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma{11} & -\Sigma{01} \\ -\Sigma{10} & \Sigma{00} \end{bmatrix} 4. Compute quadratic form: Calculate the Mahalanobis distance squared (quadratic form). q = \Delta^T \Sigma^{-1} \Delta This is computed as: \Delta^T \Sigma^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \Deltax & \Deltay \end{bmatrix} \Sigma^{-1} q = (\Delta^T \Sigma^{-1}) \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \Deltax \\ \Deltay \end{bmatrix} 5. Compute exponent: Multiply the quadratic form by -0.5. exponent = -0.5 \cdot q 6. Return PDF: Compute the final normalized probability density. PDF = \frac{\exp(exponent)}{2 \pi \sqrt{\det(\Sigma)}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compute2dgaussianpdfstandard(xy, gaussianmean, gaussiancovariance): # xy, gaussianmean: (x, y) tuples or arrays # gaussiancovariance: [[m00, m01], [m10, m11]] list of lists # Step 1: Compute mean difference xymean = (xy[0] - gaussianmean[0], xy[1] - gaussianmean[1]) # Step 2: Compute determinant detcov = gaussiancovariance[0][0] gaussiancovariance[1][1] - gaussiancovariance[0][1] gaussiancovariance[1][0] # Guard against singular covariance if detcov <= 0.0: return 0.0 # Step 3: Compute inverse covariance matrix analytically for 2x2 invm00 = gaussiancovariance[1][1] / detcov invm01 = -gaussiancovariance[0][1] / detcov invm10 = -gaussiancovariance[1][0] / detcov invm11 = gaussiancovariance[0][0] / detcov # Step 4: Compute quadratic form # xymean @ invcov tempx = xymean[0] invm00 + xymean[1] invm10 tempy = xymean[0] invm01 + xymean[1] invm11 # dot product with xymean quadraticform = tempx xymean[0] + tempy xymean[1] # Step 5: Compute exponent exponent = -0.5 quadraticform # Step 6: Return normalized PDF return math.exp(exponent) / (2.0 math.pi math.sqrt(detcov)) Parameters: \pi: Mathematical constant pi. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Covariance: If \det(\Sigma) = 0, the inverse is undefined. Precision: For very small covariances, \sqrt{\det(\Sigma)} may underflow. For very large covariances, the exponent may underflow to 0. Computes the probability density value p and its gradients with respect to the Gaussian mean (\frac{dp}{d\mean}) and covariance (\frac{dp}{d\cov}) for a 2D Gaussian. This method provides three variants: normalized (including the 1/(2\pi\sqrt{\det}) factor), unnormalized (excluding the factor), and conic-based (using the conic matrix representation). It builds on 2D Gaussian Probability Density (Standard) by providing the necessary derivatives for optimization, specifically for training Gaussian splats where gradients must flow back to mean and covariance parameters. Computes the alpha value for a single 3D Gaussian projected onto a 2D pixel by evaluating the 2D Gaussian probability density function (PDF) at the pixel center. It builds on 2D Gaussian Probability Density (Standard) by handling the full pipeline of transforming 3D Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale) into camera space, projecting the covariance to screen space, and combining the resulting PDF with the Gaussian's intrinsic opacity. It differs from its sibling Gradient of 2D Gaussian PDF (Conic) by returning a scalar alpha value rather than the gradient of the PDF. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance with hardware, resolution and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use it and when not: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of Gaussian Splatting for 3D Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction, specifically within implementations like taichi3dgaussiansplatting. It is a fundamental component of the EWA (Elliptical Weighted Average) splatting technique used to project 3D Gaussians onto the 2D image plane. The method relies on the standard definition of the multivariate Gaussian distribution. wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gradient of 2D Gaussian PDF (Conic)
head: Gradient of 2D Gaussian Probability Density (Normalized/Unnormalized Factor Only), Gradient of 2D Gaussian Probability Density from Conic and Rescale
body: Computes the probability density value p and its gradients with respect to the Gaussian mean (\frac{dp}{d\mean}) and covariance (\frac{dp}{d\cov}) for a 2D Gaussian. This method provides three variants: normalized (including the 1/(2\pi\sqrt{\det}) factor), unnormalized (excluding the factor), and conic-based (using the conic matrix representation). It builds on 2D Gaussian Probability Density (Standard) by providing the necessary derivatives for optimization, specifically for training Gaussian splats where gradients must flow back to mean and covariance parameters. Inputs: xy: 2D point coordinates, vector \mathbb{R}^2. gaussianmean: 2D mean vector, \mu \in \mathbb{R}^2. gaussiancovariance: 2×2 symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix, \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. conicandrescale: (For conic variant) A 4D vector or struct containing the conic matrix elements and a rescale factor. The conic matrix C is derived from the inverse covariance \Sigma^{-1}. The vector contains [C{00}, C{01}, C{11}, R] where R is the rescale factor. Outputs: p: Scalar probability density value. dpdmean: Gradient of p with respect to gaussianmean, vector \mathbb{R}^2. dpdcov: Gradient of p with respect to gaussiancovariance, matrix \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. Vector2: 2D vector with components x, y. Matrix2: 2×2 matrix with elements M{00}, M{01}, M{10}, M{11}. For symmetric covariance, M{01} = M{10}. ConicAndRescale: A structure or vector of 4 floats. Based on the source code, the layout is:.x: C{00}.y: C{01} (which equals C{10}).z: C{11}.w: Rescale factor R. Let \Delta = xy - gaussian\mean. 1. Normalized Variant: p = \frac{\exp(-0.5 \Delta^T \Sigma^{-1} \Delta)}{2\pi\sqrt{\det(\Sigma)}} \frac{dp}{d\mean} = p \cdot \Sigma^{-1} \Delta \frac{dp}{d\cov} = -0.5 p (\Sigma^{-1} - \Sigma^{-1} \Delta \Delta^T \Sigma^{-1}). 2. Unnormalized Variant: p = \exp(-0.5 \Delta^T \Sigma^{-1} \Delta) \frac{dp}{d\mean} = p \cdot \Sigma^{-1} \Delta \frac{dp}{d\cov} = 0.5 p (\Sigma^{-1} \Delta \Delta^T \Sigma^{-1}). 3. Conic Variant: Let C be the conic matrix (inverse covariance) and R be the rescale factor. p = \exp(-0.5 \Delta^T C \Delta) \cdot R \frac{dp}{d\mean} = p \cdot C \Delta \frac{dp}{d\cov} = 0.5 p (C \Delta \Delta^T C). Note: The gradient with respect to the rescale factor R is not computed. For Normalized and Unnormalized Variants: 1. Compute the displacement vector: \Delta = xy - gaussian\mean. 2. Compute the determinant of the covariance matrix: \det(\Sigma) = \Sigma{00}\Sigma{11} - \Sigma{01}\Sigma{10}. 3. Compute the inverse covariance matrix \Sigma^{-1}: \Sigma^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det(\Sigma)} \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma{11} & -\Sigma{01} \\ -\Sigma{10} & \Sigma{00} \end{bmatrix}. 4. Compute the term \Sigma^{-1} \Delta: v = \Sigma^{-1} \Delta. 5. Compute the exponent term: exponent = -0.5 (\Delta^T v) = -0.5 (\Deltax vx + \Deltay vy). 6. Compute the exponential: exp\val = \exp(exponent). 7. Compute p: Normalized: p = \frac{exp\val}{2\pi\sqrt{\det(\Sigma)}}. Unnormalized: p = exp\val. 8. Compute \frac{dp}{d\mean}: \frac{dp}{d\mean} = p \cdot v. 9. Compute the outer product \Delta \Delta^T: outer = \begin{bmatrix} \Deltax^2 & \Deltax \Deltay \\ \Deltay \Deltax & \Deltay^2 \end{bmatrix}. 10. Compute \frac{dp}{d\cov}: Normalized: \frac{dp}{d\cov} = -0.5 p (\Sigma^{-1} - \Sigma^{-1} outer \Sigma^{-1}). Unnormalized: \frac{dp}{d\cov} = 0.5 p (\Sigma^{-1} outer \Sigma^{-1}). For Conic Variant: 1. Compute the displacement vector: \Delta = xy - gaussian\mean. 2. Construct the conic matrix C from conicandrescale: C = \begin{bmatrix} conic\and\rescale.x & conic\and\rescale.y \\ conic\and\rescale.y & conic\and\rescale.z \end{bmatrix}. 3. Compute the term C \Delta: v = C \Delta. 4. Compute the exponent term: exponent = -0.5 (\Delta^T v) = -0.5 (\Deltax vx + \Deltay vy). 5. Compute the exponential: exp\val = \exp(exponent). 6. Compute p: p = exp\val \cdot conic\and\rescale.w. 7. Compute \frac{dp}{d\mean}: \frac{dp}{d\mean} = p \cdot v. 8. Compute the outer product \Delta \Delta^T: outer = \begin{bmatrix} \Deltax^2 & \Deltax \Deltay \\ \Deltay \Deltax & \Deltay^2 \end{bmatrix}. 9. Compute \frac{dp}{d\cov} (gradient w.r.t. conic matrix elements, interpreted as covariance gradient in the source context): \frac{dp}{d\cov} = 0.5 p (C outer C). Unverified code. Displacement delta = [xy[0] - gaussianmean[0], xy[1] - gaussianmean[1]] # 2. Determinant detcov = gaussiancovariance[0][0] gaussiancovariance[1][1] - gaussiancovariance[0][1] gaussiancovariance[1][0] # 3. Inverse Covariance invcov = [ [gaussiancovariance[1][1] / detcov, -gaussiancovariance[0][1] / detcov], [-gaussiancovariance[1][0] / detcov, gaussiancovariance[0][0] / detcov] ] # 4. invcov @ delta covinvdelta = [ invcov[0][0] delta[0] + invcov[0][1] delta[1], invcov[1][0] delta[0] + invcov[1][1] delta[1] ] # 5. Exponent exponent = -0.5 (delta[0] covinvdelta[0] + delta[1] covinvdelta[1]) # 6. Exponential expval = math.exp(exponent) # 7. p (Normalized) p = expval / (2.0 math.pi math.sqrt(detcov)) # 8. dp/dmean dpdmean = [p covinvdelta[0], p covinvdelta[1]] # 9. Outer Product delta delta^T outer = [ [delta[0]delta[0], delta[0]delta[1]], [delta[1]delta[0], delta[1]delta[1]] ] # 10. dp/dcov # Term: invcov @ outer @ invcov # First: invcov @ outer temp1 = [ [invcov[0][0]outer[0][0] + invcov[0][1]outer[1][0], invcov[0][0]outer[0][1] + invcov[0][1]outer[1][1]], [invcov[1][0]outer[0][0] + invcov[1][1]outer[1][0], invcov[1][0]outer[0][1] + invcov[1][1]outer[1][1]] ] # Second: temp1 @ invcov temp2 = [ [temp1[0][0]invcov[0][0] + temp1[0][1]invcov[1][0], temp1[0][0]invcov[0][1] + temp1[0][1]invcov[1][1]], [temp1[1][0]invcov[0][0] + temp1[1][1]invcov[1][0], temp1[1][0]invcov[0][1] + temp1[1][1]invcov[1][1]] ] # dp/dcov = -0.5 p (invcov - temp2) dpdcov = [ [-0.5 p (invcov[0][0] - temp2[0][0]), -0.5 p (invcov[0][1] - temp2[0][1])], [-0.5 p (invcov[1][0] - temp2[1][0]), -0.5 p (invcov[1][1] - temp2[1][1])] ] return p, dpdmean, dpdcov def gradient2dgaussianunnormalized(xy, gaussianmean, gaussiancovariance): """ Computes p, dp/dmean, dp/dcov for unnormalized 2D Gaussian. """ delta = [xy[0] - gaussianmean[0], xy[1] - gaussianmean[1]] detcov = gaussiancovariance[0][0] gaussiancovariance[1][1] - gaussiancovariance[0][1] gaussiancovariance[1][0] invcov = [ [gaussiancovariance[1][1] / detcov, -gaussiancovariance[0][1] / detcov], [-gaussiancovariance[1][0] / detcov, gaussiancovariance[0][0] / detcov] ] covinvdelta = [ invcov[0][0] delta[0] + invcov[0][1] delta[1], invcov[1][0] delta[0] + invcov[1][1] delta[1] ] exponent = -0.5 (delta[0] covinvdelta[0] + delta[1] covinvdelta[1]) expval = math.exp(exponent) p = expval dpdmean = [p covinvdelta[0], p covinvdelta[1]] outer = [ [delta[0]delta[0], delta[0]delta[1]], [delta[1]delta[0], delta[1]delta[1]] ] temp1 = [ [invcov[0][0]outer[0][0] + invcov[0][1]outer[1][0], invcov[0][0]outer[0][1] + invcov[0][1]outer[1][1]], [invcov[1][0]outer[0][0] + invcov[1][1]outer[1][0], invcov[1][0]outer[0][1] + invcov[1][1]outer[1][1]] ] temp2 = [ [temp1[0][0]invcov[0][0] + temp1[0][1]invcov[1][0], temp1[0][0]invcov[0][1] + temp1[0][1]invcov[1][1]], [temp1[1][0]invcov[0][0] + temp1[1][1]invcov[1][0], temp1[1][0]invcov[0][1] + temp1[1][1]invcov[1][1]] ] # dp/dcov = 0.5 p (invcov @ outer @ invcov) dpdcov = [ [0.5 p temp2[0][0], 0.5 p temp2[0][1]], [0.5 p temp2[1][0], 0.5 p temp2[1][1]] ] return p, dpdmean, dpdcov def gradient2dgaussianconic(xy, gaussianmean, conicandrescale): """ Computes p, dp/dmean, dp/dcov for conic 2D Gaussian. conicandrescale: [C00, C01, C11, R] """ delta = [xy[0] - The normalization factor is 2\pi\sqrt{\det(\Sigma)}. Rescale Factor Gradient: The gradient with respect to the rescale factor (conicandrescale.w) is not computed. Determinant Zero: If \det(\Sigma) = 0, the inverse covariance is undefined. In practice, a small epsilon should be added to the determinant to avoid division by zero. Precision: The computation involves exponentials and matrix inversions. For very large or small variances, numerical stability should be considered. Time: O(1) per Gaussian evaluation. The operations involve fixed-size matrix multiplications (2×2) and vector operations. Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory per evaluation. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides exact gradients for optimization. The conic variant avoids explicit matrix inversion, which can be more stable and efficient if the conic matrix is already available. Limitations: The conic variant does not provide gradients for the rescale factor. The normalized variant requires computing the determinant and its square root, which can be slightly more expensive than the unnormalized variant. Use the normalized variant when the absolute probability density value is required for loss functions or normalization. Use the unnormalized variant when the normalization constant is handled separately or is irrelevant for the optimization (e.g., if it cancels out in the gradient). Use the conic variant when the conic matrix is already computed (e.g., from a previous step in the rendering pipeline) to avoid redundant matrix inversion. The method is derived from the implementation in the unofficial Taichi-based 3D Gaussian Splatting repository. It is used in the context of training Gaussian point clouds for novel view synthesis. name: 2D Gaussian Probability Density (Conic)
head: 2D Gaussian Probability Density from Conic and Rescale
body: Computes the unnormalized probability density of a 2D Gaussian at a query point xy given its mean, conic matrix components, and a rescaling factor. The conic matrix represents the inverse covariance matrix. It differs from the Standard variant by operating directly on the conic components and an explicit rescaling factor rather than a full covariance matrix. Inputs: xy: A 2D point (x, y) representing the query location. gaussianmean: A 2D vector (\mux, \muy) representing the Gaussian center. conicandrescale: A 4-component vector containing the conic matrix elements and the rescaling factor. Outputs: p: The unnormalized probability density value at xy. Data Structures: The conicandrescale parameter layout maps to C{00}, C{01}, C{11}, and R respectively. Steps: 1. Compute the difference vector \Delta \mathbf{x} between the query point and the Gaussian mean: \Delta x = xy.x - gaussian\mean.x, \Delta y = xy.y - gaussian\mean.y. 2. Compute the exponent using the conic matrix components: E = -0.5 (\Delta x^2 C{00} + \Delta y^2 C{11}) - \Delta x \Delta y C{01}. 3. Apply the exponential and rescale: p = \exp(E) \cdot R. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compute2dgaussianpdfconic(xy, gaussianmean, conicandrescale): dx = xy[0] - gaussianmean[0] dy = xy[1] - gaussianmean[1] C00 = conicandrescale[0] C01 = conicandrescale[1] C11 = conicandrescale[2] R = conicandrescale[3] exponent = -0.5 (dx dx C00 + dy dy C11) - dx dy C01 return math.exp(exponent) R Parameters: R: The rescaling factor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision, boundaries, and degenerate input handling are not specified in the sources. Computes the exponent term of the 2D Gaussian probability density function at given 2D points for rasterization or shading. It operates on batches of points and means. Definition: Computes P = -\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x}m^T C{2D}^{-1} \mathbf{x}m), where \mathbf{x}m is the difference vector and C{2D}^{-1} is the inverse covariance matrix. Steps: 1. Compute difference vector: \mathbf{x}m = \text{points}{2D} - \text{means}{2D}. 2. Reshape for batched matrix multiplication: \mathbf{x}m^{\text{col}} = \mathbf{x}m.\text{unsqueeze}(-1), \mathbf{x}m^{\text{row}} = \mathbf{x}m.\text{unsqueeze}(-2). 3. Compute inverse covariance: C{2D}^{-1} = \text{cov}{2D}.\text{inverse}(), unsqueezed for broadcasting. 4. Compute quadratic form: P = -0.5 \cdot (\mathbf{x}m^{\text{row}} @ C{2D}^{-1} @ \mathbf{x}m^{\text{col}}).\text{squeeze}(-1).\text{squeeze}(-1). When to choose: Use this variant when working with batched tensor operations (e.g., in PyTorch) and when the covariance matrix is available directly rather than its inverse. wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fhz2346/3D-Gaussian-Splatting, https://github.com/Fhz2346/3D-Gaussian-Splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Single Point Alpha Forward
head: Gaussian Alpha Computation, Single Point Alpha
body: Computes the alpha value for a single 3D Gaussian projected onto a 2D pixel by evaluating the 2D Gaussian probability density function at the pixel center. It builds on 2D Gaussian Probability Density (Standard) by handling the full pipeline of transforming 3D Gaussian parameters into camera space, projecting the covariance to screen space, and combining the resulting PDF with the Gaussian's intrinsic opacity. It differs from its sibling Gradient of 2D Gaussian PDF (Conic) by returning a scalar alpha value rather than the gradient of the PDF. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters: mean position \mathbf{xyz} \in \mathbb{R}^3, pre-activation scale s \in \mathbb{R}^3, pre-activation quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (w, x, y, z), pre-activation opacity \sigma{pre} \in \mathbb{R}. Camera matrices: World-to-camera transformation T{camera} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, camera intrinsic matrix K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Pixel coordinates: \mathbf{uv}{center} \in \mathbb{R}^2 representing the pixel center in screen space. Outputs: Alpha value \alpha \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: No persistent data structures; the computation is stateless for a single Gaussian. Steps: 1. Homogenize Position: Construct the homogeneous coordinate vector \mathbf{xyz1} = [\mathbf{xyz}, 1]^T. 2. Transform to Camera Space: Compute \mathbf{xyz1}{camera} = T{camera} \cdot \mathbf{xyz1}. 3. Extract Camera Coordinates: Let \mathbf{xyz}{camera} be the first three components of \mathbf{xyz1}{camera}. 4. Project to Screen Space: Compute \mathbf{uv1} = K \cdot \mathbf{xyz}{camera}. The screen coordinates are \mathbf{uv} = \mathbf{uv1}{0:2} / \mathbf{uv1}2 via perspective division. 5. Compute Scale Matrix: Construct the diagonal scale matrix S = \text{diag}(\exp(s)). 6. Compute Rotation Matrix: Construct the rotation matrix R from the quaternion q. 7. Compute 3D Covariance: Compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma = R S S R^T. 8. Compute Projection Jacobian: Compute the Jacobian J of the projection transformation. 9. Compute 2D Covariance: Let W be the upper-left 3 \times 3 rotation part of T{camera}. Compute the 2D covariance matrix in screen space: cov = J W \Sigma W^T J^T. 10. Compute Probability Density: Evaluate the 2D Gaussian PDF at the pixel center. Let \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{uv}{center} - \mathbf{uv}. The exponent is p = \exp(-0.5 \mathbf{d}^T cov^{-1} \mathbf{d}). 11. Compute Alpha: Apply the sigmoid function to the pre-activation opacity \sigma{pre} to get the base opacity \sigma(\sigma{pre}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\sigma{pre}}}. The final alpha is \alpha = \sigma(\sigma{pre}) \cdot p. Parameters: Sigmoid activation for opacity: Standard logistic sigmoid. Exponential activation for scale: Standard exponential. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Zero: If Z=0 (camera plane), perspective division fails. Singular Covariance: If the Gaussian is degenerate (e.g., zero scale), cov may be singular. Numerical Stability: Very small or large exponents in the PDF evaluation can lead to underflow or overflow. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources for single-point evaluation. When to use: When precise alpha values at specific pixel centers are needed, or as a component in a larger rasterization pipeline. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def singlepointalphaforward(xyz, s, q, sigmapre, Tcamera, K, uvcenter): """ Computes alpha for a single 3D Gaussian projected to a 2D pixel. Args: xyz: (3,) array, 3D mean position. s: (3,) array, pre-activation scale (log scale). q: (4,) array, pre-activation quaternion (w, x, y, z). sigmapre: float, pre-activation opacity. Tcamera: (4, 4) array, world-to-camera transformation matrix. K: (3, 3) array, camera intrinsic matrix. uvcenter: (2,) array, pixel center coordinates (u, v). Returns: alpha: float, the computed alpha value. """ # 1. Homogenize position xyz1 = np.append(xyz, 1.0) # 2. Transform to camera space xyz1camera = Tcamera @ xyz1 # 3. Extract camera coordinates xyzcamera = xyz1camera[:3] X, Y, Z = xyzcamera # 4. Project to screen space uv1 = K @ xyzcamera uv = uv1[:2] / uv1[2] # 5. Compute scale matrix S S = np.diag(np.exp(s)) # 6. Compute rotation matrix R from quaternion q w, x, y, z = q R = np.array([ [1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x2 + y2)] ]) # 7. Compute 3D covariance Sigma Sigma = R @ S @ S @ R.T # 8. Compute Jacobian J of projection if abs(Z) < 1e-6: return 0.0 Jproj = np.array([ [1/Z, 0, -X/(Z2)], [0, 1/Z, -Y/(Z2)] ]) K2x3 = K[:2,:] J = K2x3 @ Jproj # 9. Compute 2D covariance cov W = Tcamera[:3,:3] cov = J @ W @ Sigma @ W.T @ J.T # 10. Compute probability density p d = uvcenter - uv # Regularize covariance for numerical stability cov += np.eye(2) 1e-6 covinv = np.linalg.inv(cov) exponent = -0.5 (d @ covinv @ d) p = np.exp(exponent) # 11. Compute alpha sigma = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-sigmapre)) alpha = sigma p return alpha Evaluates the alpha for all pixels in a frame for a set of Gaussians using batched tensor operations. It creates a meshgrid of pixel coordinates xs, ys from W, H, stacks and flattens them to points2D of shape (WH, 2), and expands dimensions so points2D becomes (1, WH, 2) and means2D becomes (N, 1, 2). It evaluates the 2D Gaussian function to produce power with shape (N, WH), computes the exponential term using torch.where(power > 0.0, 0.0, torch.exp(power)), multiplies by opacity to get alphas of shape (N, WH), and reshapes alphas to (N, H, W). It clamps alphas to a maximum of 0.99 for numerical stability and zeros out values below 1/255.0. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian per pixel. For batched evaluation over N Gaussians and P pixels, it is O(N \cdot P). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources for single-point evaluation. For batched evaluation, it stores (N, H, W) tensors. Strengths: Direct evaluation allows for precise alpha computation at specific points. The batched variant enables full-frame rendering via tensor operations. Limitations: Single-point evaluation only accounts for the pixel center, not the full coverage area. Requires careful handling of singular covariances and perspective division edge cases. When to use: When precise alpha values at specific pixel centers are needed, or as a component in a larger rasterization pipeline. The batched version is suitable for full-frame rendering. The method is part of the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, specifically the alpha computation step for projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D. It relies on the mathematical formulation of projecting 3D covariance matrices to 2D screen space using the Jacobian of the projection transformation. wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fhz2346/3D-Gaussian-Splatting, https://github.com/Fhz2346/3D-Gaussian-Splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 2D Gaussian Alpha Computation (Batched)
head: Alpha Computation, Batched Gaussian Alpha Forward
body: This method computes the alpha values for all N 2D Gaussians across all W \times H pixels in a single batched operation, serving as the core rasterization step in Gaussian Splatting. It builds on Single Point Alpha Forward by vectorizing the evaluation over the entire image grid, enabling efficient GPU execution. It differs from Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing by computing raw alpha contributions for all pixel-gaussian pairs rather than identifying explicit intersection pairs for compositing. Inputs: means2D: Tensor of shape (N, 2), the 2D means of the Gaussians in screen space. cov2D: Tensor of shape (N, 2, 2), the 2D covariance matrices for each Gaussian. opacities: Tensor of shape (N,), the opacity values for each Gaussian. W, H: Integer width and height of the image. Outputs: alphas: Tensor of shape (N, H, W), the alpha values for each Gaussian at each pixel. Data Structures: points2D: Tensor of shape (W \cdot H, 2), containing the coordinates of every pixel center. power: Tensor of shape (N, W \cdot H), containing the negative half-squared Mahalanobis distance for each Gaussian-pixel pair. exppower: Tensor of shape (N, W \cdot H), containing the exponential of the power term. Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Grid: Create a meshgrid of pixel coordinates (x, y) for x \in [0, W-1] and y \in [0, H-1], stack and flatten them into points2D of shape (W \cdot H, 2). 2. Broadcast Dimensions: Expand points2D to shape (1, W \cdot H, 2) and means2D to shape (N, 1, 2) to enable broadcasting during evaluation. 3. Evaluate 2D Gaussian: Compute the power term for all pairs using the standard 2D Gaussian exponent -\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^T \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}), resulting in power of shape (N, W \cdot H). 4. Compute Exponential: Calculate the exponential term, clamping positive power values to zero to prevent numerical overflow: \text{exp\power} = \exp(\min(0, \text{power})). 5. Apply Opacity: Multiply the exponential term by the opacity of each Gaussian, resulting in a tensor of shape (N, W \cdot H). 6. Reshape: Reshape the alpha tensor to (N, H, W) to match the image layout. 7. Clamp for Stability: Clamp all alpha values to a maximum of 0.99 to prevent numerical instability during subsequent compositing steps. 8. Threshold Small Values: Zero out alpha values smaller than 1/255.0 to reduce memory bandwidth and computation for negligible contributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computebatchedalphas(means2D, cov2D, opacities, W, H): # Step 1: Generate pixel grid points2D = [] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): points2D.append([float(x), float(y)]) # points2D shape: (WH, 2) # Step 2: Broadcast dimensions (conceptual for pure Python, handled by loops below) N = len(means2D) numpixels = W H # Step 3: Evaluate 2D Gaussian power power = [[0.0] numpixels for in range(N)] for i in range(N): covinv = inverse2x2(cov2D[i]) for j in range(numpixels): diff = [points2D[j][0] - means2D[i][0], points2D[j][1] - means2D[i][1]] leftprod = matmulvector2x2(diff, covinv) dot = leftprod[0] diff[0] + leftprod[1] diff[1] power[i][j] = -0.5 dot # Step 4: Compute exponential with overflow guard exppower = [[math.exp(power[i][j]) if power[i][j] <= 0.0 else 0.0 for j in range(numpixels)] for i in range(N)] # Step 5: Apply opacity alphasflat = [[opacities[i] exppower[i][j] for j in range(numpixels)] for i in range(N)] # Step 6: Reshape to (N, H, W) alphas = [[[alphasflat[i][r W + c] for c in range(W)] for r in range(H)] for i in range(N)] # Step 7: Clamp for stability alphas = [[[min(alphas[i][r][c], 0.99) for c in range(W)] for r in range(H)] for i in range(N)] # Step 8: Threshold small values alphas = [[[0.0 if alphas[i][r][c] < 1.0 / 255.0 else alphas[i][r][c]] for c in range(W)] for r in range(H)] for i in range(N)] return alphas def inverse2x2(M): det = M[0][0] M[1][1] - M[0][1] M[1][0] return [[M[1][1] / det, -M[0][1] / det], [-M[1][0] / det, M[0][0] / det]] def matmulvector2x2(v, M): return [M[0][0] v[0] + M[0][1] v[1], M[1][0] v[0] + M[1][1] v[1]] Parameters: Clamping threshold: 0.99. Zeroing threshold: 1/255.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Overflow: Positive power values due to precision errors cause \exp(\text{power}) to overflow, so the source clamps them to zero before exponentiation. Covariance Inversion: Degenerate covariances with zero determinants cause inversion failures, which is typically handled by ensuring valid covariance matrices in earlier pipeline stages. Memory Usage: The intermediate power tensor has shape (N, W \cdot H), creating a memory bottleneck for high-resolution images and many Gaussians. The final rasterization pass in the 2D Gaussian Splatting pipeline that combines pre-computed alpha values into a final RGB image and alpha mask using front-to-back compositing. It is distinguished by operating on explicit intersection pairs (gaussianid, pixelid, imageid) rather than iterating over pixels or Gaussians, allowing arbitrary intersection patterns and leveraging automatic differentiation for the backward pass. Choose it when explicit ray-splat intersection tracking and gradient flow are required. See Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing
head: accumulate
body: Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing is the final rasterization pass in the 2D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, responsible for combining the pre-computed 2D Gaussian alpha values into a final RGB image and an alpha mask. It solves the problem of correctly blending overlapping splats along each pixel's viewing ray using front-to-back compositing. It is distinguished from parent methods by operating on explicit intersection pairs (gaussianid, pixelid, imageid) rather than iterating over pixels or Gaussians, allowing arbitrary intersection patterns and leveraging automatic differentiation for the backward pass. Inputs: pixelidsx and pixelidsy (integer arrays of shape [M]), imageids (integer array of shape [M]), gaussianids (integer array of shape [M]), means2d (array of shape [N, 2]), conics (array of shape [N, 3]), opacities (array of shape [N]), colors (array of shape [N, C]), imageheight and imagewidth (integers), and MAXALPHA (scalar float). Outputs: renders (array of shape [H, W, C]) and alphasout (array of shape [H, W, 1]). Data Structures: The method relies on a flat list of intersections of size M. Each entry i represents one Gaussian splatting onto one pixel. The arrays pixelids, imageids, and gaussianids are parallel arrays indexing into the global Gaussian attributes. Steps: 1. Compute Pixel Coordinates: Convert flat or structured pixel IDs into 2D coordinates. \text{pixel\coords} = [\text{pixel\ids}x, \text{pixel\ids}y] + 0.5 Shape: [M, 2]. The +0.5 centers the coordinate within the pixel. 2. Gather Gaussian Parameters: Using imageids and gaussianids, gather the corresponding means2d, conics, opacities, and colors for each intersection. 3. Compute Gaussian Exponent (Sigma): Calculate the exponent of the 2D Gaussian function at the pixel center. Let \Delta = \text{pixel\coords} - \text{means}{sel} be the displacement vector [\Deltax, \Deltay]. \sigmai = 0.5 \cdot (\text{conics}{i,0} \Delta{i,x}^2 + \text{conics}{i,2} \Delta{i,y}^2) + \text{conics}{i,1} \Delta{i,x} \Delta{i,y} Shape: [M]. 4. Compute Per-Intersection Alpha: Calculate the alpha value for each intersection, clamped to MAXALPHA. \alphai = \min(\text{opacities}{sel, i} \cdot e^{-\sigmai}, \text{MAX\ALPHA}) Shape: [M]. 5. Compute Ray Indices: Map each intersection to a unique ray index for compositing. For a single image batch, this is simply the flattened pixel index. \text{ray\index}i = \text{image\ids}i \cdot (H \cdot W) + \text{pixel\ids}i Shape: [M]. 6. Compute Compositing Weights: Perform front-to-back alpha compositing to determine the weight of each splat. This involves computing transmittance T and weight w. For a ray with intersections sorted front-to-back: T0 = 1 wi = \alphai \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) T{i+1} = Ti (1 - \alphai) The function renderweightfromalpha returns weights (wi) and transmittances (unused in final output but used for gradients). 7. Accumulate Colors: Sum the weighted colors for each ray. \text{render}r = \sum{i \in \text{ray } r} wi \cdot \text{colors}{sel, i} 8. Accumulate Alpha: Sum the weights for each ray to get the final alpha (since \sum wi = 1 - T{final}). \alpha{out, r} = \sum{i \in \text{ray } r} wi 9. Reshape Outputs: Reshape the accumulated arrays from flat ray indices to image dimensions. \text{renders} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} \text{alphas\out} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 1} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def explicitintersectionalphacompositing( pixelidsx, pixelidsy, imageids, gaussianids, means2d, conics, opacities, colors, imageheight, imagewidth, MAXALPHA=1.0): M = len(pixelidsx) totalpixels = imageheight imagewidth C = len(colors[0]) # 1. Compute pixel coordinates pixelcoords = [(float(x) + 0.5, float(y) + 0.5) for x, y in zip(pixelidsx, pixelidsy)] # 2. Gather parameters means2dsel = [means2d[g] for g in gaussianids] conicssel = [conics[g] for g in gaussianids] opacitiessel = [opacities[g] for g in gaussianids] colorssel = [colors[g] for g in gaussianids] # 3. Compute sigma sigmas = [] for i in range(M): dx = pixelcoords[i][0] - means2dsel[i][0] dy = pixelcoords[i][1] - means2dsel[i][1] c0, c1, c2 = conicssel[i] sigmas.append(0.5 (c0 dx2 + c2 dy2) + c1 dx dy) # 4. Compute alpha alphasperisect = [min(o math.exp(-s), MAXALPHA) for o, s in zip(opacitiessel, sigmas)] # 5. Compute ray indices rayindices = [int(img) totalpixels + int(px) for img, px in zip(imageids, pixelidsx)] # 6. Compute weights (front-to-back compositing) # Assumes intersections are sorted front-to-back per ray raygroups = {} for i in range(M): raygroups.setdefault(rayindices[i], []).append(i) weights = [0.0] M for r, indices in raygroups.items(): T = 1.0 for i in indices: alpha = alphasperisect[i] weights[i] = alpha T T = (1.0 - alpha) # 7 & 8. Accumulate colors and alpha rendersflat = [0.0] (totalpixels C) alphasflat = [0.0] totalpixels for i in range(M): r = rayindices[i] w = weights[i] alphasflat[r] += w for c in range(C): rendersflat[r C + c] += w colorssel[i][c] # 9. Reshape outputs renders = [[rendersflat[r C + c] for c in range(C)] for r in range(totalpixels)] renders = [renders[r imagewidth:(r + 1) imagewidth] for r in range(imageheight)] alphasout = [[alphasflat[r imagewidth + c]] for r in range(totalpixels)] alphasout = [alphasout[r imagewidth:(r + 1) imagewidth] for r in range(imageheight)] return renders, alphasout Parameters: MAXALPHA: Clamping value for alpha to prevent 1 - \alpha from becoming zero, which causes division by zero or NaN in gradients. Typical value: 0.99 or 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential e^{-\sigma} can underflow for large \sigma. This is handled by the clamping of alpha. Sorting: The correctness of front-to-back compositing depends on the intersections being sorted by depth (Z-coordinate) within each ray. If the rasterization step does not provide sorted intersections, the compositing will be incorrect. Boundaries: Pixel coordinates must be within [0, H-1] \times [0, W-1]. Intersections outside the image bounds should be filtered out before this step. Time Complexity: O(M) where M is the number of intersections. The dominant cost is the gather operations and the compositing reduction, which is linear in the number of splats per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(M) for storing the intersection arrays and intermediate weights. Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPUs. The explicit intersection list allows for efficient memory access patterns compared to pixel-order rendering when the scene is sparse. Strengths: Supports arbitrary intersection patterns. Enables automatic differentiation for end-to-end training. Efficient for sparse scenes. Limitations: Requires sorting intersections per ray for correct compositing. Memory usage scales with the number of splats per pixel. This method is part of the 2D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, specifically the rendering stage. It builds on the 2D Gaussian Alpha Computation (Batched) method. The approach of explicit intersection compositing is common in differentiable rendering pipelines to allow gradients to flow through the compositing operation. name: Row-constant hoisting for Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
body: Row-constant hoisting is an optimization for the inner pixel loop of a Gaussian splatting rasterizer that hoists row-constant terms outside the inner (column) loop to minimize arithmetic operations per pixel. It reduces the computational cost of evaluating the 2D Gaussian exponent by precomputing terms dependent only on the row coordinate. Input: A projected Gaussian primitive p with screen-space center (sx, sy), bounding box [x0, y0, x1, y1], inverse covariance matrix elements a, b, d, opacity \alphap, and color Cp. Input: A framebuffer fb of width w, where each cell stores accumulated color and opacity. Input: Parameters saturation (maximum accumulated opacity) and alphathreshold (minimum alpha for contribution). Output: Updated framebuffer cells for pixels covered by the splat. Framebuffer Cell: A tuple (Vec3, f32) storing the accumulated color (3 floats) and accumulated opacity (1 float). Projected Gaussian: Contains screen coordinates, bounding box, inverse covariance matrix components, opacity, and color. 1. Extract inverse covariance elements a, b, d from the projected Gaussian's inverse covariance matrix. 2. Compute coefficients for the quadratic form: dx{coeff} = -0.5 \cdot a dy{coeff} = -0.5 \cdot d cross{coeff} = -b (derived from -0.5 \cdot 2 \cdot b) 3. Initialize saturation and alphathreshold from parameters. 4. Iterate over each row py from y0 to y1 inclusive: a. Compute dy = py - sy. b. Precompute row-constant terms: row{base} = dy{coeff} \cdot dy^2 row{slope} = cross{coeff} \cdot dy row{offset} = py \cdot w (for framebuffer indexing) c. Iterate over each column px from x0 to x1 inclusive: i. Calculate framebuffer index idx = row{offset} + px. ii. Check saturation: if fb[idx].opacity >= saturation, skip to next pixel. iii. Compute dx = px - sx. iv. Calculate the power term: power = dx{coeff} \cdot dx^2 + row{slope} \cdot dx + row{base}. v. If power > 0.0, skip the pixel (exponential would exceed 1 or be invalid). vi. Compute alpha: \alpha = (\alphap \cdot e^{power}).\min(0.999). vii. If \alpha < alpha{threshold}, skip the pixel. viii. Compute contribution: t = 1.0 - fb[idx].opacity, contrib = t \cdot \alpha. ix. Update framebuffer: fb[idx].color += contrib Cp, fb[idx].opacity += contrib. The Gaussian exponent power is calculated as: power = dx{coeff} \cdot dx^2 + row{slope} \cdot dx + row{base} where: dx{coeff} = -0.5 \cdot a row{slope} = -b \cdot dy row{base} = -0.5 \cdot d \cdot dy^2 a, b, d are elements of the inverse covariance matrix dx, dy are screen-space offsets from the Gaussian center saturation: The maximum accumulated opacity value in the framebuffer cell. If reached, further splats are skipped. alphathreshold: The minimum alpha value for a splat to contribute. Splats with alpha below this are skipped. If the computed power is positive, the exponential term would exceed 1 (or be invalid for the Gaussian model), so the pixel is skipped. Alpha is clamped to 0.999 to prevent numerical issues when blending. Unverified code.
