name: 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization
head: 2D Gaussian Projection, EWA Projection, Elliptical Weighted Average projection, 2D Covariance Projection, Covariance Projection, Screen-space Gaussian Projection, EWA Splatting Projection, Perspective Projection of 3D Gaussians, Perspective-correct covariance projection
body: This method projects a 3D Gaussian primitive, defined by its mean and covariance in world space, onto the 2D image plane to produce a screen-space Gaussian ellipse (splat) for rasterization. It solves the problem of rendering anisotropic, perspective-distorted 3D distributions efficiently by approximating the non-linear perspective projection with a local affine transformation, thereby preserving the Gaussian form in 2D. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters: mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 (world space), rotation quaternion q, scale vector s, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients h for color. Camera parameters: View matrix V, Projection matrix P, image width W, height H, focal lengths fx, fy, principal point (cx, cy). Outputs: Screen-space mean \mu{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^2. Screen-space covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. Inverse covariance (conic) \Sigma{2D}^{-1}. Bounding box for rasterization. Data Structures: The projected Gaussian is stored with the following fields: screen: Vec2 (pixel center sx, sy). depth: f32 (camera-space zc, positive in front). cov2dinv: Mat2 (inverse 2D covariance). bbox: [i32; 4] (inclusive x0, y0, x1, y1). color: Vec3 (RGB). opacity: f32 (in [0, 1]). Steps: 1. Reconstruct 3D Covariance: Compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma from the quaternion q and scale s. The rotation matrix R is derived from q, and the scale matrix S is diagonal with entries si: \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top Where R is: R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 2(qy^2 + qz^2) & 2(qxqy - qzqw) & 2(qxqz + qyqw) \\ 2(qxqy + qzqw) & 1 - 2(qx^2 + qz^2) & 2(qyqz - qxqw) \\ 2(qxqz - qyqw) & 2(qyqz + qxqw) & 1 - 2(qx^2 + qy^2) \end{bmatrix} Implementations typically exponentiate the scale parameters before forming S to ensure positive scales. 2. Transform to Camera Space: Transform the mean to camera space: \muc = V{3\times3} \mu + t{cw}. Transform the covariance to eye space using the rotation block M = V{3\times3} of the view matrix. Translation is ignored for covariance: \Sigma{cam} = M \Sigma M^\top This relies on the property that if X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma), then AX \sim \mathcal{N}(A\mu, A\Sigma A^\top). 3. Compute Jacobian of Perspective Projection: Linearize the perspective projection locally at \muc = (xc, yc, zc) using the Jacobian J: J = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{fx}{zc} & 0 & \frac{fx xc}{zc^2} \\ 0 & -\frac{fy}{zc} & \frac{fy yc}{zc^2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} Focal lengths are derived from the projection matrix entries p{00}, p{11}: fx = p{00} \frac{W}{2}, fy = p{11} \frac{H}{2}. 4. Project Covariance to 2D: Compute the unnormalized 2D covariance: \Sigma'{2D} = J{2\times3} \Sigma{cam} J{2\times3}^\top where J{2\times3} is the top two rows of J. 5. Covariance Stabilization (Low-Pass Filter): Add a small epsilon \epsilon{2d} to the diagonal elements to ensure positive definiteness and prevent singularities or infinitely small Gaussians: \Sigma{2D} = \Sigma'{2D} + \begin{bmatrix} \epsilon{2d} & 0 \\ 0 & \epsilon{2d} \end{bmatrix} Typical value: \epsilon{2d} = 0.3. This guarantees invertibility because x^T (A^T A + \lambda I) x = \|Ax\|^2 + \lambda \|x\|^2 > 0 for \lambda > 0. 6. Compute Screen Mean: Apply the full MVP transform and perspective divide to get the screen coordinates: \text{clip} = P \cdot V \cdot \mu = (xc, yc, zc, wc)^\top \mu{2D} = \left( \frac{xc}{wc} \frac{W}{2} + cx, \frac{yc}{wc} \frac{H}{2} + cy \right) Note: Some implementations compute NDC first: \text{ndc} = (xc/wc, yc/wc, zc/wc), then map to pixels. 7. Compute Inverse Covariance (Conic): For a symmetric matrix \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & d \end{bmatrix}, the inverse is: \det = ad - b^2 If \det \le 0, cull the splat. \Sigma{2D}^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det} \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -b & a \end{bmatrix} Store as upper triangular vector (a, b, d) for efficiency. 8. Compute Bounding Box: Compute eigenvalues \lambda{1,2} and eigenvectors e1, e2 of \Sigma{2D}: \lambda{1,2} = \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma{2D})}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma{2D})^2}{4} - \det(\Sigma{2D})} v1 = (\Sigma{12}, \lambda1 - \Sigma{11}), \quad e1 = \frac{v1}{\|v1\|}, \quad e2 = (e{1,2}, -e{1,1}) Define half-axes b1 = 3\sqrt{\lambda1}e1 and b2 = 3\sqrt{\lambda2}e2 (using 3\sigma cutoff). The bounding box is the axis-aligned box containing the parallelogram spanned by b1 and b2 centered at \mu{2D}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Convert quaternion (w, x, y, z) to 3x3 rotation matrix.""" w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - zw), 2(xz + yw)], [2(xy + zw), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - xw)], [2(xz - yw), 2(yz + xw), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) def projectgaussian(gaussian, camera): """ gaussian: dict with 'mean' (3,), 'q' (4,), 'scale' (3,), 'opacity' (float) camera: dict with 'view' (4x4), 'proj' (4x4), 'W', 'H', 'fx', 'fy', 'cx', 'cy' """ # 1. Reconstruct 3D Covariance R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(gaussian['q']) # S is diagonal with scale entries; implementations typically exponentiate scales first S = np.diag(np.exp(gaussian['scale'])) Sigma3d = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # 2. Transform to Camera Space # Extract 3x3 rotation from view matrix M = camera['view'][:3,:3] Sigmacam = M @ Sigma3d @ M.T # Transform mean to camera space mucam = M @ gaussian['mean'] + camera['view'][:3, 3] xc, yc, zc = mucam # 3. Compute Jacobian # J = [[-fx/z, 0, fxx/z^2], [0, -fy/z, fyy/z^2]] invz = 1.0 / zc invz2 = invz invz J = np.array([ [-camera['fx'] invz, 0, camera['fx'] xc invz2], [0, -camera['fy'] invz, camera['fy'] yc invz2] ]) # 4. Project Covariance Sigma2dunstable = J @ Sigmacam @ J.T # 5. Stabilization eps2d = 0.3 Sigma2d = Sigma2dunstable.copy() Sigma2d[0, 0] += eps2d Sigma2d[1, 1] += eps2d # 6. Compute Screen Mean # Apply full MVP muhomogeneous = np.array([gaussian['mean'], 1.0]) clip = camera['proj'] @ camera['view'] @ muhomogeneous wc = clip[3] ndcx = clip[0] / wc ndcy = clip[1] / wc screenx = ndcx camera['W'] / 2 + camera['cx'] screeny = ndcy camera['H'] / 2 + camera['cy'] # 7. Inverse Covariance a, b = Sigma2d[0, 0], Sigma2d[0, 1] d = Sigma2d[1, 1] det = a d - b b if det <= 0.0: return None # Cull splat invdet = 1.0 / det cov2dinv = np.array([ [d invdet, -b invdet], [-b invdet, a invdet] ]) # 8. Bounding Box (Simplified AABB of 3-sigma ellipse) # Eigen decomposition for bounding box eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2d) # eigenvalues are sorted ascending, so lambda1 is eigenvalues[0] lambda1 = eigenvalues[0] lambda2 = eigenvalues[1] e1 = eigenvectors[:, 0] e2 = eigenvectors[:, 1] b1 = 3.0 math.sqrt(lambda1) e1 b2 = 3.0 math.sqrt(lambda2) e2 # Compute corners of the parallelogram corners = [ screenx + b1[0] + b2[0], screeny + b1[1] + b2[1], screenx + b1[0] - b2[0], screeny + b1[1] - b2[1], screenx - b1[0] + b2[0], screeny - b1[1] + b2[1], screenx - b1[0] - b2[0], screeny - b1[1] - b2[1] ] xmin = min(corners[0::2]) xmax = max(corners[0::2]) ymin = min(corners[1::2]) ymax = max(corners[1::2]) # Convert to integer pixel coordinates (inclusive) bbox = [ int(math.floor(xmin)), int(math.floor(ymin)), int(math.ceil(xmax)), int(math.ceil(ymax)) ] return { 'screen': (screenx, screeny), 'depth': zc, 'cov2dinv': cov2dinv, 'bbox': bbox, 'opacity': gaussian['opacity'] } Computes a tight AABB based on opacity threshold and projected covariance, reducing false-positive tile intersections compared to fixed circular boxes. Renders each Gaussian as a single pixel at its projected mean, ignoring shape and spread for debugging or minimal rendering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Enables real-time rendering of millions of Gaussians (e.g., 134 fps on Mip-NeRF360) by avoiding ray marching. Strengths: Closed-form projection allows differentiability and fast GPU/CPU rasterization. The method sacrifices negligible global geometric accuracy to enable real-time rendering. Limitations: The linearization error increases for large splats or extreme perspective, potentially causing geometric inaccuracies. Singularities are handled by stabilization but may introduce slight blurring if \epsilon{2d} is too large. The method originates from Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) splatting, described by Zwicker et al. in 2002 for anti-aliased volume rendering. It was adapted by Kerbl et al. (2023) for 3D Gaussian Splatting, where it projects 3D Gaussians to 2D ellipses for real-time rasterization. The stabilization term \epsilon{2d} is a practical addition to ensure numerical robustness in the inverse covariance computation. 3D Gaussian Splatting in a Weekend, https://bfeldman.me/3dgs-weekend/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Tsplat – Run Gaussian splatting in your terminal, https://github.com/darshanmakwana412/tsplat, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) An Architectural Review of the 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21739653, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) metin-yat/mini-splat, https://github.com/metin-yat/mini-splat, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) 驚くほどキレイな三次元シーン復元、「3D Gaussian Splatting」を徹底的に解説する, https://qiita.com/scomup/items/d5790da25a846e645de1, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Bounding Box Computation
head: Tsplat bounding box
body: Computes a tight, axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for a 2D Gaussian splat based on an opacity threshold, replacing the loose square bounding box used in original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to determine tile intersections. It sets itself apart by deriving the box dimensions directly from the projected covariance matrix and opacity, significantly reducing false-positive splat duplications during rasterization compared to the original method. Inputs: sx, sy: Screen-space center of the Gaussian (float). cov2d00, cov2d11: Diagonal elements of the 2D screen-space covariance matrix \Sigma (float). opacity: The scalar opacity of the Gaussian (float). alphathreshold: The minimum opacity \tau required for the Gaussian to be considered visible (float). maxk2: The maximum allowed squared Mahalanobis distance (float). wi, hi: Framebuffer width and height (integer). Outputs: An AABB defined by integer coordinates (x0, y0, x1, y1), or None if the Gaussian is effectively invisible or degenerate. Data Structures: The output is a tuple of four integers (x0, y0, x1, y1) representing the inclusive pixel range. Steps: 1. Opacity Check: If opacity \le alphathreshold, return None. 2. Compute Mahalanobis Scale: Calculate k^2: k^2 = \min\left(2.0 \cdot \ln\left(\frac{\text{opacity}}{\text{alpha\threshold}}\right), \text{max\k2}\right) If k^2 \le 0.0, return None. 3. Compute Half-Widths: Calculate the half-extents in screen pixels: rxf = \sqrt{k^2 \cdot \text{cov2d}{00}} ryf = \sqrt{k^2 \cdot \text{cov2d}{11}} If rxf or ryf are not finite or are < 1.0, return None. 4. Integer Bounds: Compute the initial integer bounding box: x0 = \lfloor sx - rxf \rfloor y0 = \lfloor sy - ryf \rfloor x1 = \lceil sx + rxf \rceil y1 = \lceil sy + ryf \rceil 5. Clipping: Clip the bounding box to the framebuffer boundaries: x0 = \max(0, x0) y0 = \max(0, y0) x1 = \min(wi - 1, x1) y1 = \min(hi - 1, y1) 6. Validity Check: If x0 > x1 or y0 > y1, return None. Otherwise, return (x0, y0, x1, y1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeadaptiveboundingbox(sx, sy, cov2d00, cov2d11, opacity, alphathreshold, maxk2, wi, hi): # Step 1: Opacity check if opacity <= alphathreshold: return None # Step 2: Compute k^2 logratio = opacity / alphathreshold k2 = 2.0 math.log(logratio) if k2 > maxk2: k2 = maxk2 if k2 <= 0.0: return None # Step 3: Compute half-widths rxf = math.sqrt(k2 cov2d00) ryf = math.sqrt(k2 cov2d11) # Check for finite and minimum size if not (math.isfinite(rxf) and math.isfinite(ryf)): return None if rxf < 1.0 or ryf < 1.0: return None # Step 4: Integer bounds x0 = math.floor(sx - rxf) y0 = math.floor(sy - ryf) x1 = math.ceil(sx + rxf) y1 = math.ceil(sy + ryf) # Step 5: Clip to framebuffer x0 = max(0, x0) y0 = max(0, y0) x1 = min(wi - 1, x1) y1 = min(hi - 1, y1) # Step 6: Validity check if x0 > x1 or y0 > y1: return None return (x0, y0, x1, y1) Parameters: alphathreshold: Typical value is Not given in the sources. maxk2: Limits the bounding box size to prevent excessively large boxes for high-opacity Gaussians. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Covariance: If cov2d00 or cov2d11 are zero or negative, the square root may be invalid or zero. The check rxf < 1.0 handles small extents, but negative values should be guarded against by the parent method's covariance stabilization. Precision: Floating-point precision in log and sqrt can affect boundary inclusion. Using floor for the lower bound and ceil for the upper bound ensures the entire area with opacity \ge \tau is covered. Empty Box: Clipping can result in x0 > x1 if the Gaussian is entirely outside the framebuffer. This must be checked explicitly. A method to compute 2D Gaussian projections as elliptical disks rather than axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) to reduce false-positive tile intersections. It sets itself apart by combining an elliptical shape approximation with non-square bounding boxes, significantly reducing the number of duplicated Gaussians processed per tile compared to the original square AABB approach. Choose this when minimizing overdraw is critical and the overhead of elliptical intersection tests is acceptable. Opacity-Sensitive Elliptical Bounding Box This method computes the tight axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of a projected 2D Gaussian ellipse in constant time. It replaces the loose circular bounding box used in original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to determine tile intersections, significantly reducing false-positive splat duplications during rasterization. Unlike its sibling Opacity-Sensitive Elliptical Bounding Box, which adapts the threshold based on opacity, this derivation assumes a fixed threshold to define the ellipse geometry. Choose this for a balance between tightness and computational simplicity. Tight Ellipse AABB Derivation Allowing the axis-aligned bounding box of a projected 2D Gaussian to have different width and height dimensions, rather than forcing a square shape. On the Bicycle scene at native resolution with 16x16 tiles, non-square boxes reduced duplicated Gaussians from 55,648,264 (square) to 18,466,556. This variant is inherently supported by the adaptive bounding box computation as it computes rxf and ryf independently from the covariance matrix diagonal elements. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian. The computation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations, logarithms, and square roots. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. No additional buffers are required for the bounding box computation itself. Measured Performance: On the Bicycle scene at native resolution, combining this bounding box method with other optimizations decreased render time by a factor of 3.77 and GPU memory usage by a factor of 2.11. The reduction in duplicated Gaussians from 55,648,264 to 18,466,556 (with non-square boxes) demonstrates significant reduction in overdraw. Strengths: Significantly reduces false-positive tile intersections compared to square bounding boxes, leading to fewer Gaussians processed per tile and lower memory bandwidth usage. Limitations: Still produces axis-aligned boxes, which may include empty space for highly rotated Gaussians. When to use: Standard rasterization pipelines where tile-based rendering is used and false positives are a bottleneck. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. used a square bounding box based on the maximum variance, which was loose and led to many false-positive tile intersections. The adaptive bounding box computation was introduced in the Tsplat implementation to address this inefficiency. It is part of the broader effort to optimize Gaussian Splatting rendering, building on the 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization method. name: Opacity-Sensitive Elliptical Bounding Box
head: Elliptical Bounding Box, Non-square Bounding Box
body: A method to compute 2D Gaussian projections as elliptical disks rather than axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) to reduce false-positive tile intersections. It sets itself apart by combining an elliptical shape approximation with non-square bounding boxes, significantly reducing the number of duplicated Gaussians processed per tile compared to the original square AABB approach. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D Gaussian parameters (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma), opacity \alpha, opacity threshold \epsilon, and tile grid dimensions. Output: A non-square axis-aligned bounding box that tightly encloses the elliptical projection of the Gaussian. Data Structures: The bounding box is defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}). Unlike the original method which computes a square box based on the maximum extent, this method computes distinct x and y extents based on the elliptical shape. Steps: 1. Opacity Thresholding: If the Gaussian's opacity \tau falls below a threshold \epsilon, the bounding box is considered empty and the Gaussian is filtered out immediately. 2. Elliptical Projection: Convert the 2D Gaussian covariance \Sigma into an elliptical disk representation. 3. Non-Square Box Calculation: Calculate the width and height of the bounding box independently based on the elliptical extents, allowing for non-square boxes. 4. Tile Intersection: Check if the non-square bounding box intersects with the current tile. Formulas: The bounding box is derived from the ellipse that encloses the Gaussian at a specific confidence level. For a 2D covariance matrix \Sigma, the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 yield the squared semi-axis lengths. The axis-aligned bounding box of the rotated ellipse is computed from these eigenvalues and the eigenvector rotation angle. The opacity threshold condition is: if \tau < \epsilon, the box is empty. Parameters: \epsilon: Opacity threshold for filtering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large, mostly transparent 3D Gaussians can affect a significant number of tiles in the original approach, leading to higher render times; this method effectively filters them out by considering low opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeopacitysensitiveellipticalbbox(mean, covariance, opacity, epsilon): # Step 1: Opacity thresholding if opacity < epsilon: return None # Box is empty, filter out # Step 2: Compute elliptical extents a11, a12 = covariance[0][0], covariance[0][1] a21, a22 = covariance[1][0], covariance[1][1] trace = a11 + a22 det = a11 a22 - a12 a21 disc = trace trace - 4 det sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(max(0.0, disc)) lambda1 = (trace + sqrtdisc) / 2 lambda2 = (trace - sqrtdisc) / 2 # Semi-axis lengths scaled by confidence factor scale = 2.447 # Standard confidence scaling factor a = math.sqrt(lambda1) scale b = math.sqrt(lambda2) scale # Eigenvector angle for rotation if abs(a12) > 1e-8: angle = math.atan2(lambda1 - a11, a12) else: angle = 0.0 # Step 3: Non-square bounding box calculation cosa = math.cos(angle) sina = math.sin(angle) width = 2.0 math.sqrt((a cosa)2 + (b sina)2) height = 2.0 math.sqrt((a sina)2 + (b cosa)2) xmin = mean[0] - width / 2 ymin = mean[1] - height / 2 xmax = mean[0] + width / 2 ymax = mean[1] + height / 2 return (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) A reduction technique for per-touched-tile duplicated splats using tighter AABBs and an approximate tile-ellipse intersection test. Developed concurrently with Speedy-Splat. On the Bicycle scene at native resolution with 16x16 tiles, original AABBs resulted in 87,067,709 duplicated Gaussians. Using opacity-sensitive ellipses with square boxes reduced this to 55,648,264. Allowing non-square bounding boxes further reduced duplicated Gaussians to 18,466,556. Exact pixel-perfect intersections would result in only 10,976,269 duplicated Gaussians, but are computationally too expensive; the elliptical/non-square approach provides a trade-off. In total, on the Bicycle scene at native resolution, the method decreases the render time and GPU memory usage by factors of 3.77 and 2.11, respectively. The method is more effective at not rendering large, mostly transparent 3D Gaussians, leading to more consistent render times. The method was introduced in "Fast 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering via Easily Integrable Improvements". It addresses the inefficiency of the original 3DGS method's square bounding boxes, which often include many empty pixels, especially for large, transparent Gaussians. name: Tight Ellipse AABB Derivation
head: Ellipse AABB Computation, Tight AABB Ellipse Culling, Tight Elliptical Bounding Box, Tight bounding box for ellipse
body: This method computes the tight axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of a projected 2D Gaussian ellipse in constant time. It replaces the loose circular bounding box used in original 3D Gaussian Splatting to determine tile intersections, significantly reducing false-positive splat duplications during rasterization. Inputs: Two 2D basis vectors \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^2 defining the ellipse shape and orientation. Opacity \sigmai of the Gaussian \mathcal{G}i. Threshold value for \alphai(p) to define the ellipse boundary. Tile size T. Image boundaries (width W, height H). Center coordinates (cx, cy) of the projected Gaussian. Outputs: A rectangular tile extent (min/max tile coordinates) that tightly encloses the ellipse. Data Structures: Matrix D \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}: Symmetric matrix derived from basis vectors. Matrix C \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}: Inverse of D. Bounds: Four scalar values (x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}) representing the AABB in pixel coordinates, converted to tile indices. Steps: 1. Define Ellipse Geometry: The threshold \alphai(p) = \sigmai gi(p) determines the exact pixel extent of the Gaussian as an ellipse. The ellipse is defined by the implicit equation f(x, y) = 0 derived from the inverse matrix C. 2. Construct Matrix D: Convert the basis vectors \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} into a symmetric 2 \times 2 matrix D using outer products: D = \mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T + \mathbf{b}\mathbf{b}^T 3. Compute Inverse Matrix C: Calculate the inverse of D: C = D^{-1} Let C = \begin{pmatrix} C{00} & C{01} \\ C{10} & C{11} \end{pmatrix}. Since D is symmetric, C is also symmetric, so C{01} = C{10}. 4. Derive Vertical Extents (x-bounds): Points on the vertical edges of the AABB are points on the ellipse where the gradient \nabla f is horizontal (i.e., \partial f/\partial y = 0). Solving this condition yields the half-width x{half} = \sqrt{D{00}}. The source notes this simplified formula saves arithmetic instructions compared to Hanson et al. [HTL25]. 5. Derive Horizontal Extents (y-bounds): Apply the same derivation swapping x and y (and indices 0 and 1) to find points where the gradient is vertical (\partial f/\partial x = 0). This yields the half-height y{half} = \sqrt{D{11}}. 6. Combine Bounds: The pixel coordinates for the AABB edges are x{left} = cx - x{half}, x{right} = cx + x{half}, y{bottom} = cy - y{half}, y{top} = cy + y{half}. 7. Convert to Tile Coordinates: Divide the pixel bounds by the tile size T and round appropriately: tile{min\x} = \lfloor x{left} / T \rfloor, \quad tile{max\x} = \lceil x{right} / T \rceil tile{min\y} = \lfloor y{bottom} / T \rceil, \quad tile{max\y} = \lceil y{top} / T \rceil 8. Clip to Image Boundary: Clip the tile coordinates to the image boundaries [0, W/T] \times [0, H/T]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computetightellipseaabb(a, b, centerx, centery, tilesize, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Computes the tight AABB for a 2D Gaussian ellipse defined by basis vectors a and b. Args: a: tuple (ax, ay), 2D basis vector b: tuple (bx, by), 2D basis vector centerx: float, x-coordinate of the ellipse center in pixels centery: float, y-coordinate of the ellipse center in pixels tilesize: float, size of a tile in pixels imagewidth: int, width of the image in pixels imageheight: int, height of the image in pixels Returns: tuple: (mintilex, mintiley, maxtilex, maxtiley) """ # Step 2: Construct Matrix D = aa^T + bb^T D00 = a[0]a[0] + b[0]b[0] D01 = a[0]a[1] + b[0]b[1] D11 = a[1]a[1] + b[1]b[1] # Step 3: Compute Inverse Matrix C = D^-1 detD = D00 D11 - D01 D01 # Guard against degenerate ellipse (zero determinant) if abs(detD) < 1e-9: return (0, 0, 0, 0) C00 = D11 / detD C01 = -D01 / detD C11 = D00 / detD # Steps 4 & 5: Derive extents using simplified formula from Appendix A # xhalf = sqrt(D00), yhalf = sqrt(D11) xhalf = math.sqrt(D00) yhalf = math.sqrt(D11) # Step 6: Combine bounds with center offset xleft = centerx - xhalf xright = centerx + xhalf ybottom = centery - yhalf ytop = centery + yhalf # Step 7: Convert to tile coordinates mintilex = math.floor(xleft / tilesize) maxtilex = math.ceil(xright / tilesize) mintiley = math.floor(ybottom / tilesize) maxtiley = math.ceil(ytop / tilesize) # Step 8: Clip to image boundary maxtilex = min(maxtilex, math.ceil(imagewidth / tilesize)) maxtiley = min(maxtiley, math.ceil(imageheight / tilesize)) mintilex = max(mintilex, 0) mintiley = max(mintiley, 0) return (mintilex, mintiley, maxtilex, maxtiley) Parameters: Threshold: Determined by opacity \sigmai and the Gaussian value function gi(p). Tile size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If the determinant of D is zero (degenerate ellipse, e.g., line or point), the inverse C is undefined. A guard must handle this. False Negatives: Using an approximate tile-ellipse intersection test may produce occasional false-negatives. This is acceptable for editors operating on fully-trained models but would negatively influence convergence in gradient descent-based optimization. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in matrix inversion can lead to negative values under the square root. Clamping to zero is recommended. An algorithm for identifying the minimum and maximum points (extents) of an ellipse within a given tile row or column during rasterization, used to determine which pixels to render. It improves upon SnugBox by handling cases where the ellipse intersects tile boundaries more precisely. Time Complexity: Constant time O(1) per Gaussian splat for AABB computation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Significantly reduces false-positive tile intersections compared to the bounding circle approach in 3DGS, leading to fewer splat duplications and improved rendering performance. Strengths: Tighter bounds reduce the number of tiles processed per splat. The simplified formula saves arithmetic instructions compared to earlier methods like Hanson et al. [HTL25]. Limitations: Approximate intersection tests (if used in subsequent steps) may cause false-negatives, which are detrimental to optimization but acceptable for rendering. The method was introduced as part of the "SnugBox" algorithm in the Speedy-Splat paper. It addresses the inefficiency of the original 3D Gaussian Splatting method, which duplicates splats for each tile within the ellipse's bounding circle, leading to numerous false-positives. The derivation in Appendix A of the Splatshop paper provides a simplified formula for the tight AABB, noting that it saves arithmetic instructions compared to concurrent work by Hanson et al.. name: AccuTile
head: Accurate Tile Extent Computation
body: AccuTile is an algorithm for identifying the minimum and maximum points (extents) of a 2D ellipse within a given tile row or column during rasterization, used to determine the exact set of tiles intersected by a Gaussian. It improves upon SnugBox by handling cases where the ellipse intersects tile boundaries more precisely, reducing the number of tiles further than SnugBox. Unlike baseline 3D-GS which allocates tiles based on a square inscribing a circle, or SnugBox which uses a tight bounding box, AccuTile computes the exact Gaussian-to-tile intersections by iterating over the shorter side of the SnugBox tile extent. AccuTile extends the SnugBox method to identify the exact tiles intersected by the Gaussian. It takes as input the tight bounding box produced by SnugBox and its rectangular tile extent. The algorithm iterates over the rows (or columns) of the SnugBox tile extent, processing along the shorter side of the extent. For each row or column, it identifies the exact tile extent by finding the minimum and maximum points of the ellipse inside it. All tiles between these minimum and maximum points are marked as intersecting the ellipse. The algorithm requires only two intersection points per row or column of the SnugBox. Inputs: Ellipse E: Implicitly defined by the projected 2D covariance parameters. SnugBox Bounding Box B: The axis-aligned tight bounding box of the ellipse, with sides denoted by subscripts t (top), b (bottom), l (left), and r (right). SnugBox Tile Extent Rectangle R: The rectangular tile extent of the Gaussian, with sides denoted similarly. Tile size: Implicitly used to convert coordinates to tile indices. Outputs: Tile count C: The total number of tiles intersected by the Gaussian. Processed tiles: The range of tiles for each row/column. Ellipse E: Implicitly defined by the projected 2D covariance parameters. Bounding Box B: Defined by four scalar values: Bt, Bb, Bl, Br representing the top, bottom, left, and right coordinates of the tight bounding box. Tile Extent Rectangle R: Defined by four scalar values: Rt, Rb, Rl, Rr representing the top, bottom, left, and right tile boundaries. Intersection Points: Pairs of (x, y) coordinates representing the intersection of the ellipse with a horizontal or vertical line. 1. Initialize: Set tile count C \leftarrow 0. Set linemin \leftarrow Rb (the bottom line of the rectangle R). 2. Initial Intersection: If linemin \ge Bb (the bottom line of the rectangle is below or at the bottom of the bounding box), compute the initial intersection points imin \leftarrow \text{Intersections}(linemin, E) using Equation 15. If linemin < Bb, no initial intersection is computed for the first row. 3. Loop: For each row r in R (processed from bottom to top): a. Set linemax \leftarrow Rt (the top line of the current row r). b. Upper Intersection: If linemax \le Bt (the top line of the current row is above or at the top of the bounding box), compute the intersection points imax \leftarrow \text{Intersections}(linemax, E) using Equation 15. If linemax > Bt, no intersection is computed for this row. c. Determine Minimum Extent (emin): If the bottom-left corner of the bounding box Bl is within row r, then emin \leftarrow Bl. Otherwise, emin \leftarrow \min(imin, imax). d. Determine Maximum Extent (emax): If the bottom-right corner of the bounding box Br is within row r, then emax \leftarrow Br. Otherwise, emax \leftarrow \max(imin, imax). e. Convert to Tile Indices: Convert emin and emax to tile indices tilemin and tilemax. f. Update Count: C \leftarrow C + (tilemax - tilemin). g. Process Tiles: Call \text{Process}(tilemin, tilemax). h. Update for Next Row: Set imin \leftarrow imax. This reuses the upper boundary intersection of the current row as the lower boundary intersection for the next row, as the boundaries are shared. 4. Return: Return C. Ellipse Equation (Eq. 14): Referenced in sources but not explicitly provided in the text. It defines the 2D ellipse boundary of the projected Gaussian. Intersection Calculation (Eq. 15): Referenced in sources but not explicitly provided in the text. It calculates the intersection points of the ellipse E with a horizontal line y = linemin or y = linemax. Tile Size: Implicitly used to convert coordinates to tile indices. Threshold: The threshold on \alphai(p) = \sigmai gi(p) that defines the ellipse boundary. Not given in the sources. The algorithm handles several cases to ensure correctness: 1. Case 1: Ellipse does not intersect tile row boundary: The entire ellipse lies within the row. The bounding box extrema x{min} and x{max} computed by SnugBox are selected as the furthest extents. 2. Case 2: Ellipse intersects one boundary but not the other: 2.1: Both x{min} and x{max} are in the row. They are assigned as the furthest extent. 2.2: Neither x{min} nor x{max} is in the row, but y{max} (or y{min}) is. The ellipse decreases monotonically from y{max} to the boundary. The row boundary intersections are selected as the furthest extent. 2.3: One critical point (e.g., x{min}) and one extremum (e.g., y{min}) are in the row, but the other extremum (e.g., x{max}) is not. The ellipse increases monotonically from y{min} to the boundary. The ellipse point on the curve that extends to the right of y{min} and intersects the tile row boundary is selected as the maximum extent. 3. Case 3: Ellipse intersects both top and bottom row boundaries: If x{min} or x{max} is in the row, it is assigned as the min/max extent. Otherwise, the ellipse monotonically increases from one boundary to the other. The minimum or maximum boundary point is selected. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def AccuTile(E, B, R, tilesize): """ Computes the exact tile intersection of a Gaussian. Args: E: Ellipse object with attributes xc, yc, a, b (semi-axes). B: SnugBox Bounding Box with attributes t, b, l, r. R: SnugBox Tile Extent Rectangle with attributes t, b, l, r and a list of rows. tilesize: Width/height of a single tile in world/pixel coordinates. Returns: C: Total number of tiles intersected. """ C = 0 linemin = R.b # Initial intersection if the bottom of the tile extent is within or above the bounding box bottom if linemin >= B.b:, imin = Intersections(linemin, E) else: imin = None # Iterate over each row in the tile extent for row in R.rows: linemax = row.t # Compute upper intersection if the top of the row is within or below the bounding box top if linemax <= B.t:, imax = Intersections(linemax, E) else: imax = None # Determine emin if B.l in row: emin = B.l else: if imin is not None and imax is not None: emin = min(imin, imax) elif imin is not None: emin = imin else: emin = imax # Determine emax if B.r in row: emax = B.r else: if imin is not None and imax is not None: emax = max(imin, imax) elif imin is not None: emax = imin else: emax = imax # Convert to tile indices tilemin = int(emin / tilesize) tilemax = int(emax / tilesize) # Update count C += (tilemax - tilemin) # Process tiles Process(tilemin, tilemax) # Update imin for next row imin = imax return C def Intersections(liney, E): """ Computes the intersection points of the ellipse E with the horizontal line y = liney. Returns the left and right x-coordinates, or (None, None) if no intersection. Standard ellipse intersection calculation based on Eq. 15. """ dy = liney - E.yc if abs(dy) > E.b: return None, None delta = 1.0 - (dy dy) / (E.b E.b) if delta < 0: return None, None dx = E.a math.sqrt(delta) return E.xc - dx, E.xc + dx Time Complexity: AccuTile counts tiles in time proportional to the shorter side of the tile extent and processes tiles in time proportional to the tile count. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the Tanks & Temples dataset, AccuTile achieves a 1.67x FPS increase and 1.12x training time decrease compared to baseline 3D-GS, with PSNR 23.73, SSIM 0.849, LPIPS 0.177. On the Deep Blending dataset, AccuTile achieves a 2.32x FPS increase and 1.13x training time decrease compared to baseline 3D-GS, with PSNR 29.12, SSIM 0.885, LPIPS 0.288. AccuTile culminates in an average overall speed-up of 1.99×. Comparison: AccuTile outperforms the StopThePop Tile-Based Culling method in overall runtime. It avoids the overhead of warp-level load balancing and inclusive sums required by the alternative. Strengths: Reduces the number of tiles further than SnugBox, leading to faster downstream functions. Efficiently computes exact Gaussian-to-tile intersections. Limitations: Requires the SnugBox bounding box as input. AccuTile was introduced in the "Speedy-Splat" paper by Hanson et al. in 2025. It is part of the Speedy-Splat method, which aims to provide fast 3D Gaussian Splatting with sparse pixels and sparse primitives. AccuTile extends the SnugBox method, which itself improves upon the baseline 3D-GS tile allocation. The method is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering and training. name: Render Means
head: Mean-only rendering, Point projection rendering
body: Render Means is the simplest possible rendering mode for 3D Gaussian Splatting, where each Gaussian is represented by a single pixel at the location where its 3D mean projects onto the 2D image plane. It demonstrates the basic camera transformation pipeline (world → camera → image) and frustum culling without any rasterization complexity. Unlike its sibling 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization, which computes screen-space covariance matrices for elliptical splatting, Render Means ignores shape and spread, treating Gaussians as point sprites. Inputs and Outputs: Input: gs (GaussianSet), camera (Camera), bgcolor (background color). Output: renderedimage (UInt8 Tensor of shape [3, H, W]). Data Structures: The input gs is a GaussianSet containing means (Float32 Tensor, shape [N, 3]), quats (Float32 Tensor, shape [N, 4]), scales (Float32 Tensor, shape [N, 3]), opacities (Float32 Tensor, shape [N]), and shcoefficients (Float32 Tensor, shape [N, S, 3]). Steps: 1. Initialize Image: Create a tensor renderedimage of shape [3, H, W] initialized to bgcolor. 2. Transform Means: Project the 3D means to camera space using the camera's world-to-camera transformation: M{cam} = T{world \to cam} \cdot M{world}. 3. Project to Image: Project the camera-space means to the 2D image plane coordinates (u, v): (u, v) = P(M{cam}). 4. Frustum Culling: Filter out points that are behind the camera or outside the view frustum. 5. Iterate and Render: For each Gaussian i: Check opacity: If opacityi < 0.05, skip the Gaussian. Get integer pixel coordinates: u{int} = \lfloor ui \rfloor, v{int} = \lfloor vi \rfloor. Check bounds: If 0 \le u{int} < W and 0 \le v{int} < H: Compute color Ci from spherical harmonics. Assign color to pixel: rendered\image[:, v{int}, u{int}] = Ci. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermeans(gsmeans, gsopacities, gscolors, camera, bgcolor, H, W): # Initialize rendered image with background color renderedimage = [[[bgcolor[0], bgcolor[1], bgcolor[2]] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] # Project means to image plane meanscam = camera.transformpointsworldtocam(gsmeans) meansimage = camera.projectpointscamtoimageplane(meanscam) # Frustum culling: filter out points behind the camera validindices = [i for i in range(len(gsmeans)) if meanscam[i][2] > 0] for i in validindices: # Skip low opacity Gaussians if gsopacities[i] < 0.05: continue u, v = meansimage[i] uint, vint = int(u), int(v) # Check image bounds if 0 <= uint < W and 0 <= vint < H: # Assign color to the single pixel renderedimage[vint][uint] = gscolors[i] return renderedimage Parameters: Opacity Threshold: 0.05. Gaussians with opacity below this value are skipped. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Integer conversion truncates floating-point coordinates, which may cause slight misalignment at high resolutions. Overwriting: Later Gaussians overwrite earlier ones if they project to the same pixel, as no alpha blending is performed. Boundaries: Pixels outside [0, W) \times [0, H) are ignored. Computes the 2D screen-space covariance matrix and its inverse for a 3D Gaussian splat, ensuring numerical stability by adding a small epsilon to the diagonal to guarantee positive definiteness [Parent]. It sets itself apart by modeling elliptical shape and spread, unlike the point-based approach of Render Means. Use when shape fidelity is required. Link Not given in the sources. Link Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians, as each Gaussian is processed once with constant-time projection and assignment. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for the output image, with no additional per-Gaussian memory required for covariance matrices or bounding boxes. Strengths: Extremely fast with minimal computational overhead; ideal for debugging, previewing, or visualizing mean locations. Limitations: No shape representation, no alpha blending, artifacts from overwriting, and no smooth edges. When to use: Debugging camera transforms, visualizing point clouds, or when performance is critical and visual fidelity is secondary. When not to use: Final rendering, scenes with overlapping Gaussians requiring blending, or when shape/spread information is important. Render Means is a simplified rendering approach used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting to demonstrate the basic camera transformation pipeline. It serves as a baseline to understand the core concepts of depth sorting and alpha blending by removing the complexity of covariance projection and elliptical splatting. sascha-kirch/splaty, https://github.com/sascha-kirch/splaty, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Optimal Gaussian Splatting Projection
head: Central Radial Projection, Optimal Projection, Optimal Projection Strategy, Tangent Plane Projection
body: Optimal Gaussian Splatting Projection is a rendering method that minimizes projection error by projecting each 3D Gaussian onto a plane tangent to the line connecting the Gaussian mean to the camera center, rather than a fixed image plane. It sets itself apart from standard 3D-GS by using a unique tangent plane for each Gaussian based on its position relative to the camera, significantly reducing artifacts like blurriness and needle-like structures, particularly in wide-field-of-view or short focal length scenarios. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a mean position \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, and other attributes (opacity, color). The camera parameters (center \mathbf{C}, orientation, and projection model) are also required. Output: A 2D screen-space covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} and a 2D mean position \mathbf{m}{2D} for each Gaussian, ready for rasterization. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian representation. No new complex data structures are introduced, but the processing pipeline requires temporary storage for the tangent plane basis vectors and the projected 2D covariance before transforming back to screen space. Steps: 1. Compute Direction Vector: For each Gaussian with mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and camera center \mathbf{C}, compute the direction vector \mathbf{d} from the Gaussian to the camera: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{C} - \boldsymbol{\mu} 2. Define Tangent Plane: Construct a projection plane that is perpendicular to \mathbf{d} and passes through \boldsymbol{\mu}. This plane is tangent to the line connecting \boldsymbol{\mu} and \mathbf{C}. 3. Project to Tangent Plane: Project the 3D Gaussian's covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} onto this tangent plane. This involves transforming \boldsymbol{\Sigma} into the local coordinate system of the tangent plane. The exact transformation from the 3D covariance to the 2D tangent plane covariance follows the standard linearization of the projection function, but applied to this specific tangent plane geometry rather than the standard z=1 plane. 4. Transform to Image/Camera Space: Transform the projected Gaussian from the tangent plane back to the standard image or camera coordinate system for rasterization. 5. Stabilize Covariance: Apply covariance stabilization (e.g., adding a small epsilon \epsilon to the diagonal) to ensure positive definiteness, as described in the parent method [1198-2d-gaussian-projection-with-covariance-stabilization.md]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimalgaussianprojection(gaussianmeans, gaussiancovariances, cameracenter, cameramatrix): """ Projects 3D Gaussians onto tangent planes to minimize projection error. Args: gaussianmeans: Array of shape (N, 3), positions of N Gaussians in camera space. gaussiancovariances: Array of shape (N, 3, 3), covariances of N Gaussians. cameracenter: Array of shape (3,), camera center position C (typically [0,0,0] in camera space). cameramatrix: Array of shape (3, 3), intrinsic camera matrix K. Returns: means2d: Array of shape (N, 2), projected 2D means. covs2d: Array of shape (N, 2, 2), projected 2D covariances. """ N = gaussianmeans.shape[0] means2d = zeros((N, 2)) covs2d = zeros((N, 2, 2)) # Step 1: Compute direction vector from Gaussian mean to camera center directions = cameracenter - gaussianmeans # Shape (N, 3) # Step 2 & 3: Project onto tangent plane # The tangent plane is perpendicular to 'directions' and passes through 'gaussianmeans'. norms = norm(directions, axis=1, keepdims=True) normals = directions / norms # Shape (N, 3) # Construct local basis vectors (u, v) for the tangent plane. # We need two orthogonal vectors to u, v that are also orthogonal to n. # A simple way is to use the cross product with a reference vector. # Reference vector: avoid parallelism with n. Use (0,0,1) unless n is close to it. ref = array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]).reshape(1, 3).repeat(N, axis=0) # Check if n is parallel to ref dotref = abs(sum(normals ref, axis=1, keepdims=True)) # If dotref is close to 1, use a different reference, e.g., (0,1,0) # In practice, one might use a robust basis construction like Gram-Schmidt. tangentu = cross(normals, ref) tangentu = tangentu / norm(tangentu, axis=1, keepdims=True) tangentv = cross(normals, tangentu) tangentv = tangentv / norm(tangentv, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Local basis matrix B: columns are u, v, n. Shape (N, 3, 3) # B = [u, v, n] B = stack([tangentu, tangentv, normals], axis=1) # Shape (N, 3, 3) # Transform covariance to local tangent plane coordinates # Sigmalocal = B^T Sigma B # This rotates the covariance into the frame where the third axis is the normal n. # The projection onto the tangent plane effectively discards the component along n. # The 2D covariance in the tangent plane is the top-left 2x2 block of Sigmalocal. # Compute B^T @ Sigma @ B for all Gaussians Sigmalocal = matmul(matmul(transpose(B, axes=(0, 2, 1)), gaussiancovariances), B) # The 2D covariance in the tangent plane is the top-left 2x2 block covstangent = Sigmalocal[:,:2,:2] # Shape (N, 2, 2) # Step 4: Transform to Image Space # The tangent plane is at distance ||d|| from the camera center. # We need to project these 2D points from the tangent plane to the image plane. # The tangent plane is perpendicular to the view direction for each Gaussian. # This is a central projection from C to the image plane. # However, the standard 3D-GS assumes a perspective projection from C to the image plane. # The "Optimal" method projects to the tangent plane first, then to the image plane. # The transformation from the tangent plane to the image plane is a perspective projection. # Let the tangent plane be at distance Zt = ||d|| from C. # The 2D coordinates on the tangent plane (u, v) correspond to 3D points Pt = mu + uuvec + vvvec. # We then project Pt to the image plane using K. # But wait, the mean mu is already on the tangent plane. # The 2D mean on the tangent plane is (0,0) in the local basis? # No, the Gaussian mean mu is the center. In the local basis, mu is at (0,0,0) relative to itself? # The local basis is centered at mu. So the mean in the tangent plane is (0,0). # We need to project the point mu to the image plane to get the 2D mean. # Project mean mu to image plane # Homogeneous coordinates of mu relative to camera # Assuming camera center is origin for simplicity of projection logic, or use world-to-camera transform. # Let's assume gaussianmeans are in world space and we have a world-to-camera transform. # For this pseudocode, we assume gaussianmeans are already in camera space (C at origin). # If C is not at origin, we must transform mu to camera space first. # Standard 3D-GS transforms points to camera space. We assume inputs are in camera space. # If inputs are in camera space, C = (0,0,0). # Then directions = -mu. # normals = -mu / ||mu||. # The tangent plane passes through mu and is perpendicular to -mu (i.e., normal is -mu). # The projection of mu to the image plane is standard perspective projection. # Let's assume standard camera space: C=(0,0,0). mucam = gaussianmeans dcam = -mucam normscam = norm(dcam, axis=1, keepdims=True) normalscam = -dcam / normscam # Reconstruct basis for camera space ref = array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]).reshape(1, 3).repeat(N, axis=0) tangentucam = cross(normalscam, ref) tangentucam = tangentucam / norm(tangentucam, axis=1, keepdims=True) tangentvcam = cross(normalscam, tangentucam) tangentvcam = tangentvcam / norm(tangentvcam, axis=1, keepdims=True) Bcam = stack([tangentucam, tangentvcam, normalscam], axis=1) # Sigmalocalcam = Bcam^T @ Sigma @ Bcam Sigmalocalcam = matmul(matmul(transpose(Bcam, axes=(0, 2, 1)), gaussiancovariances), Bcam) covstangentcam = Sigmalocalcam[:,:2,:2] # Project mean to image plane # mucam = (x, y, z). Image plane is z=1 (or focal length f). # ximg = x / z f, yimg = y / z f # Assuming unit focal length for simplicity, or incorporate f into K. # Let's use K. # Homogeneous point: [x, y, z, 1] # Projected: K [x/z, y/z, 1]^T ? No, K [x, y, z]^T then divide by z. # Homogeneous coordinates in camera space ones = ones((N, 1)) muhom = concatenate([mucam, ones], axis=1) # (N, 4) # Project to image plane # Pimg = K @ mucamhom # But mucamhom is (N, 4). K is (3,3). # We need to handle the homogeneous division. # ximg = (K[0,0]x + K[0,1]y + K[0,2]z) / z # yimg = (K[1,0]x + K[1,1]y + K[1,2]z) / z # Simplified: assume K is diagonal [f, 0, cx; 0, f, cy; 0, 0, 1] # ximg = f x / z + cx # yimg = f y / z + cy # Extract x, y, z x = mucam[:, 0] y = mucam[:, 1] z = mucam[:, 2] # Avoid division by zero zsafe = maximum(z, 1e-5) # Get focal length and principal point from K fx = cameramatrix[0, 0] fy = cameramatrix[1, 1] cx = cameramatrix[0, 2] cy = cameramatrix[1, 2] means2d[:, 0] = fx (x / zsafe) + cx means2d[:, 1] = fy (y / zsafe) + cy # Transform covariance to image plane # The covariance on the tangent plane is covstangentcam. # This covariance is in the basis (u, v) of the tangent plane. # We need to map this to the image plane. # The mapping from the tangent plane to the image plane is a perspective projection. # The Jacobian of the projection from the tangent plane to the image plane is needed. # Let the tangent plane point be Pt = mu + uu + vv. # Project Pt to image: Pimg = K Pt / Pt.z # The Jacobian J = d(Pimg) / d(u, v) at u=0, v=0. # Pt = mu + uu + vv. # d(Pt)/du = u, d(Pt)/dv = v. # d(Pimg)/d(Pt) = (1/z) (K - Pimg [0,0,1]) ? # Standard perspective projection Jacobian for a point (x,y,z) to (x/z, y/z): # Jproj = [1/z, 0, -x/z^2; 0, 1/z, -y/z^2] # But we are projecting from the tangent plane basis. # The 3D point on the tangent plane corresponding to 2D coords (u,v) is Pt(u,v) = mu + uuvec + vvvec. # The image point is Pimg(u,v) = K Pt(u,v) / Pt(u,v).z # We need the Jacobian of Pimg with respect to (u,v) at (0,0). # dPimg/du = (dPimg/dPt) (dPt/du) = Jproj uvec # dPimg/dv = Jproj vvec # Jproj for point mucam = (x,y,z): # Jproj = [1/z, 0, -x/z^2; 0, 1/z, -y/z^2] # uvec = tangentucam # vvec = tangentvcam # Compute Jproj for each Gaussian # Jproj is (2, 3) # Constructing Jproj explicitly Jproj = zeros((N, 2, 3)) Jproj[:, 0, 0] = 1 / zsafe Jproj[:, 1, 1] = 1 / zsafe Jproj[:, 0, 2] = -x / (zsafe2) Jproj[:, 1, 2] = -y / (zsafe2) # uvec and vvec are (N, 3) # Jtangenttoimage = Jproj @ Bcam[:,:,:2] # (N, 2, 3) @ (N, 3, 2) = (N, 2, 2) # Bcam[:,:,:2] contains u and v columns Jtangent = matmul(Jproj, Bcam[:,:,:2]) # Final 2D covariance in image space # Sigma2D = Jtangent @ covstangentcam @ Jtangent^T covs2d = matmul(matmul(Jtangent, covstangentcam), transpose(Jtangent, axes=(0, 2, 1))) # Step 5: Stabilize # Add epsilon to diagonal epsilon = 1e-3 covs2d[:, 0, 0] += epsilon covs2d[:, 1, 1] += epsilon return means2d, covs2d Parameters: Focal Length: The method is tested with focal lengths scaled to 0.2 and 0.3 times the original focal length to simulate wide-field-of-view scenarios. Epsilon: A small value added to the diagonal of the 2D covariance for numerical stability (value not specified in sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Time: The method incurs a slight increase in training time due to the additional transformation step from the tangent plane to the image plane. Parallel Normals: When constructing the tangent plane basis, if the direction vector \mathbf{d} is parallel to the reference vector (e.g., z-axis), the cross product becomes zero. Division by Zero: The perspective projection involves division by the z-coordinate. Time Complexity: The algorithm's time complexity remains unchanged compared to 3D-GS because it avoids dense point sampling. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method significantly reduces blurriness and artifacts compared to the original projection method, particularly in settings with short focal lengths. It outperforms original 3D-GS across various scenes in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics when tested with focal length reduction ratios of \times 0.2 and \times 0.3. Strengths: Reduces projection error, minimizes artifacts like needle-like structures and cloud-like large Gaussians at image edges, and is adaptable to various camera models (pinhole, fisheye, panorama). Limitations: Slight increase in training time due to the additional transformation step. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "On the Error Analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting and an Optimal Projection Strategy". History: It was developed to address the issue of projection errors in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) [17], which tend to escalate with the expansion of the field of view and reduction in focal length. Usage: Implemented in PyTorch based on 3D-GS [17] with custom CUDA kernels for rasterization. Tested on 13 real scenes from the 3D-GS dataset, including Mip-NeRF360 [2], Tanks & Temples [18], and others. Computes the bounding box for each Gaussian splat to optimize rasterization. Adaptive Bounding Box Computation Renders the final image using the projected Gaussians. name: Projection Jacobian Computation
head: perspective projection Jacobian
body: Computes the 2 \times 3 Jacobian matrix of the perspective projection function with respect to 3D coordinates, used for linearizing the projection of 3D Gaussians into screen space. It transforms the 3D covariance structure into 2D screen-space covariance, enabling accurate Gaussian splatting. Inputs: means3D: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D Gaussian centers in world space. camera: Camera object providing view transformation and focal lengths. imgsize: Tuple (W, H) representing image width and height. Outputs: J: Tensor of shape (N, 2, 3) containing the Jacobian matrix for each Gaussian. Data Structures: meansviewspace: Tensor of shape (N, 3), view-space coordinates (tx, ty, tz). J: Tensor of shape (N, 2, 3), initialized to zeros. Steps: 1. Validate Camera: Check if the camera is in NDC mode; raise a RuntimeError if camera.inndc() is true. 2. Extract Parameters: Get focal lengths fx, fy = \text{camera.focal\length.flatten()} and image dimensions W, H = \text{img\size}. 3. Transform to View Space: Apply view transformation to 3D means: \text{means\view\space} = \text{view\transform.transform\points}(\text{means\3D}). Extract components: tx = \text{means\view\space}[:, 0], ty = \text{means\view\space}[:, 1], tz = \text{means\view\space}[:, 2]. Compute squared depth: tz^2 = tz \cdot tz. 4. Compute FOV Limits: Calculate half-tangent of field of view: \text{half\tan\fov\x} = 0.5 \cdot W / fx and \text{half\tan\fov\y} = 0.5 \cdot H / fy. Apply safety margin (1.3) to define clamping limits: \text{lim\x} = 1.3 \cdot \text{half\tan\fov\x} and \text{lim\y} = 1.3 \cdot \text{half\tan\fov\y}. 5. Clamp Normalized Coordinates: To prevent division by zero or extreme values near frustum edges, clamp the normalized coordinates (tx/tz, ty/tz) before scaling back: tx = \text{clamp}(tx / tz, -\text{lim\x}, \text{lim\x}) \cdot tz and ty = \text{clamp}(ty / tz, -\text{lim\y}, \text{lim\y}) \cdot tz. 6. Initialize Jacobian: Create tensor J of shape (N, 2, 3) filled with zeros. 7. Fill Jacobian Entries: Assign values using the clamped coordinates: J[:, 0, 0] = fx / tz, J[:, 1, 1] = fy / tz, J[:, 0, 2] = -(fx \cdot tx) / tz^2, and J[:, 1, 2] = -(fy \cdot ty) / tz^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computeprojectionjacobian(means3D, camera, viewtransform, imgsize): """ Computes the 2x3 Jacobian matrix for perspective projection of 3D Gaussians. Args: means3D: Tensor of shape (N, 3), 3D Gaussian centers. camera: Camera object with methods focallength, inndc. viewtransform: Object with method transformpoints. imgsize: Tuple (W, H), image dimensions. Returns: J: Tensor of shape (N, 2, 3), the Jacobian matrix. """ # Step 1: Validate Camera if camera.inndc(): raise RuntimeError("Camera must not be in NDC mode for this Jacobian computation.") # Step 2: Extract Parameters focallengths = camera.focallength.flatten() fx, fy = focallengths[0], focallengths[1] W, H = imgsize # Step 3: Transform to View Space meansviewspace = viewtransform.transformpoints(means3D) tx = meansviewspace[:, 0] ty = meansviewspace[:, 1] tz = meansviewspace[:, 2] tz2 = tz tz # Step 4: Compute FOV Limits halftanfovx = 0.5 W / fx halftanfovy = 0.5 H / fy safetymargin = 1.3 limx = safetymargin halftanfovx limy = safetymargin halftanfovy # Step 5: Clamp Normalized Coordinates tx = torch.clamp(tx / tz, -limx, limx) tz ty = torch.clamp(ty / tz, -limy, limy) tz # Step 6: Initialize Jacobian N = means3D.shape[0] J = torch.zeros((N, 2, 3), dtype=means3D.dtype, device=means3D.device) # Step 7: Fill Jacobian Entries J[:, 0, 0] = fx / tz J[:, 1, 1] = fy / tz J[:, 0, 2] = -(fx tx) / tz2 J[:, 1, 2] = -(fy ty) / tz2 return J Formula: J = \begin{bmatrix} fx/tz & 0 & -fx tx/tz^2 \\ 0 & fy/tz & -fy ty/tz^2 \end{bmatrix} where fx, fy are focal lengths, tx, ty are the clamped view-space coordinates from Step 5, tz is depth, and tz^2 = tz \cdot tz. Parameters: FOV Safety Margin: 1.3 multiplier applied to half-tan-FOV limits to clamp normalized coordinates and stabilize Jacobian computation near frustum edges. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Division by tz can cause instability if points are at or behind the camera; clamping normalized coordinates mitigates extreme values. Frustum Edges: Without clamping, normalized coordinates near the frustum boundary can lead to large Jacobian values, causing numerical instability in covariance transformation. A variant where the Jacobian is evaluated at each ray–splat intersection point rather than at the surfel center, yielding a per-pixel MIP kernel that is maximally accurate but computationally expensive. It computes the full 2 \times 2 Jacobian at every covered pixel, followed by the outer product and matrix inverse. This method incurs a rendering time of 65 ms per frame, which is a ~1.3x overhead relative to the center-precomputed method and a ~55% increase over the unfiltered baseline. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The per-pixel variant renders in 65 ms per frame, which is a ~1.3x overhead relative to the center-precomputed method and a ~55% increase over the unfiltered baseline. name: Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W)
head: GS-W, Intrinsic and Dynamic Appearance Fusion
body: Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) is a novel view synthesis method for unconstrained image collections that explicitly separates scene appearance into intrinsic material properties and dynamic environmental factors (such as illumination and weather) per 3D Gaussian point. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting and NeRF-based methods by avoiding global latent embeddings, which allows it to capture local high-frequency changes without blurring intrinsic textures with dynamic variations. The method employs adaptive sampling from image features and 2D visibility maps to mitigate transient occlusions and photometric variations. Inputs: A set of unconstrained 2D images with known camera poses (extrinsics and intrinsics). Outputs: A rendered image from a novel viewpoint, and implicitly, the optimized 3D Gaussian scene representation. The scene is represented as a collection of M 3D Gaussian points GP. Each Gaussian point i stores the following attributes: 1. Position Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3: The center of the Gaussian. 2. Covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Modeled via a scaling matrix S and rotation matrix R (stored as quaternion q) to ensure positive semi-definiteness during optimization. \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = R S S^T R^T. 3. Intrinsic Appearance Feature s{f}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d: A learnable vector representing the static material properties of the point. 4. Dynamic Appearance Feature d{f}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d: A feature vector sampled from image features, representing dynamic environmental factors. 5. Opacity \alphai: Controls transparency. 6. View-dependent Color: Derived from the fused appearance feature and view direction via an MLP. 1. Projection: Each 3D Gaussian i is projected onto the 2D image plane. The 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i is transformed into the 2D screen space covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i using the affine approximation of the projective transformation J and the view matrix W: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i = J W \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i W^T J^T The 2D Gaussian function is defined as: G(x - X, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x-X)^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(x-X)} where x is a point in space (or pixel coordinates) and X is the Gaussian center. 2. Sorting: Gaussian points are sorted by depth for each tile on the image plane. The image plane is divided into a grid of 16 \times 16 tiles. 3. Alpha Blending: For each pixel px', the color C(px') is aggregated from the sorted Gaussian points GP{px'} using alpha blending: \sigmai = G(px' - Xi, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i) C(px') = \sum{i \in GP{px'}} ci \sigmai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj) where ci is the color of the i-th Gaussian point. The core innovation of GS-W is the separation and fusion of appearance features. 1. Feature Extraction: Image features are extracted from a reference image using a U-Net model. These features are reshaped into K feature maps and one projection feature map. 2. Dynamic Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian point GPi, dynamic appearance features d{f}^i are sampled from the extracted feature maps using an adaptive sampling strategy. This strategy allows each point to focus on local and detailed information more effectively. 3. Fusion: The intrinsic appearance feature s{f}^i (learnable per point) and the sampled dynamic appearance feature d{f}^i are fused with the position Xi using a fusion network Mf. The network Mf is composed of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a{f}^i = Mf(s{f}^i, d{f}^i, Xi) where a{f}^i is the holistic appearance feature. 4. Color Decoding: The fused appearance feature a{f}^i and the view direction \phi are decoded by another MLP Mc to obtain the final color ci of the Gaussian point: ci = Mc(a{f}^i, \phi) 1. Initialization: 3D Gaussian points GP are initialized with positions X extracted from a point cloud generated via Structure-from-Motion (SfM) from the input image set. 2. Loss Calculation: The loss is computed between the rendered image Ir and the ground truth reference image I{gt}. To mitigate the impact of transient occluders (e.g., moving people, vehicles), a 2D visibility map VM \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times H \times W} is employed. This map is obtained from a U-Net model and facilitates segmentation between transient and static objects. The loss is weighted by this visibility map. 3. Optimization: All Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, intrinsic features sf^i) are jointly optimized. The method employs point growth and pruning strategies based on gradients and opacity to manage the number of Gaussians. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gswrender(referenceimages, cameraposes, initialpointcloud): """ Main pipeline for Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W). """ # 1. Initialization # Extract points via SfM gaussians = initializegaussians(initialpointcloud) # Initialize learnable intrinsic appearance features for each Gaussian for g in gaussians: g.intrinsicfeature = learnablevector() # Initialize networks fusionnet = FusionNetwork() # Two MLPs colornet = ColorNetwork() # MLP featureextractor = UNet() # For image features and visibility map # 2. Training Loop for epoch in range(numepochs): for refimg, campose in zip(referenceimages, cameraposes): # A. Feature Extraction # Extract features from reference image imgfeatures = featureextractor(refimg) # Reshape into K feature maps and one projection feature map featuremaps = reshapefeatures(imgfeatures) # Extract 2D visibility map to handle transient objects visibilitymap = featureextractor.getvisibilitymap(refimg) # B. Dynamic Feature Sampling for g in gaussians: # Adaptive sampling from feature maps based on Gaussian position g.dynamicfeature = adaptivesample(featuremaps, g.position) # C. Appearance Fusion and Color Prediction for g in gaussians: # Fuse intrinsic, dynamic, and position holisticfeature = fusionnet( g.intrinsicfeature, g.dynamicfeature, g.position) # Decode color based on holistic feature and view direction # phi is the view direction from camera to Gaussian center viewdirection = normalize(campose.cameracenter - g.position) g.color = colornet(holisticfeature, viewdirection) # D. Rasterization # Project Gaussians to 2D screen space projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Transform 3D covariance to 2D # J: affine approximation of projective transformation # W: view matrix sigma2d = projectcovariance(g.covariance, campose, J, W) projectedgaussians.append({ 'position': projectpoint(g.position, campose), 'covariance': sigma2d, 'color': g.color, 'opacity': g.opacity }) # Sort by depth and render using tile-based alpha blending projectedgaussians.sortbydepth() renderedimage = tilerasterize(projectedgaussians, imagewidth, imageheight) # E. Loss Computation # Weight loss by visibility map to ignore transient objects loss = weightedmseloss(renderedimage, refimg, visibilitymap) # F. Optimization Step loss.backward() optimizer.step() # G. Point Management pruneandgrowgaussians(gaussians, gradients, opacitythreshold) return gaussians Transient Occluders: Without the 2D visibility map, moving objects (people, cars) cause artifacts like floating points or ghosting because the model attempts to reconstruct their geometry and appearance as static. Dynamic Variations: Failing to separate intrinsic and dynamic features leads to blurring of material textures when lighting or weather changes, as the model conflates static properties with environmental effects. Local Detail: Global appearance representations (common in NeRF) struggle with high-frequency local changes. GS-W's per-point adaptive sampling mitigates this. Rendering Speed: GS-W surpasses state-of-the-art NeRF-based methods in rendering speed by over 1000x. It matches real-time rendering speeds similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) on wild data. Quality: Outperforms NeRF-based methods in reconstruction quality and detail, particularly in unconstrained environments with dynamic lighting and transient objects. Memory: Requires storage for intrinsic features per Gaussian point, increasing memory usage compared to standard 3DGS which typically uses a single SH coefficient set or simple color per point. The exact memory overhead is not specified in the sources. Strengths: Handles unconstrained image collections (wild data) with varying illumination, weather, and transient occluders. Real-time rendering capability. Limitations: Requires a U-Net for feature extraction and visibility map generation, adding complexity to the training pipeline. Performance depends on the quality of the SfM initialization and the visibility map accuracy. Origin: Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) was proposed to address the limitations of existing NeRF-based methods and standard 3DGS when applied to unconstrained image collections. Standard methods assume static scenes and consistent lighting, which is rarely the case in real-world "wild" data. Key Insight: The appearance of a point in the real world is determined by its intrinsic material properties and dynamic environmental impacts. Separating these allows for better reconstruction of static geometry and appearance while handling dynamic variations. Development: GS-W builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [16] (referenced as in the context of 3DGS) and introduces the appearance separation module, adaptive sampling, and visibility map handling. It is cited in surveys as a key method for handling wild data alongside Wild-GS and SWAG. name: 4D Gaussian Splatting
head: 4D-GS
body: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) is a method for modeling dynamic scenes by representing them as a collection of 4D Gaussians, extending the static 3D Gaussian Splatting approach to capture time-varying content. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis for dynamic videos by treating space and time as a coherent integrated 4D manifold, allowing for the efficient rendering of motion and appearance changes. Unlike approaches that treat space and time as independent (e.g., adding a separate 1D Gaussian pi(t) to 3D Gaussians), 4DGS uses a unified 4D covariance matrix to better capture underlying scene motion, avoiding the jitter and flickering associated with independent temporal weighting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of images (video) representing a dynamic scene. For initialization, a colored point cloud (e.g., from COLMAP) or random points in volume are used. Output: A set of N 4D Gaussians parameterized by mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and 4D Spherical Harmonics (4DSH) coefficients, enabling the rendering of arbitrary views at arbitrary times t. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is defined by the following parameters: 1. Mean: \mui = (\mu{x}, \mu{y}, \mu{z}, \mu{t}) \in \mathbb{R}^4. 2. Covariance: \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, parameterized via scaling and rotation. 3. Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1]. 4. Color: Represented by 4DSH coefficients. Covariance Parameterization: The 4D covariance matrix is decomposed into a scaling matrix S and a rotation matrix R: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T Scaling: S = \text{diag}(sx, sy, sz, st), where sx, sy, sz are spatial scales and st is the temporal scale. Rotation: A 4D rotation is decomposed into two isotropic rotations represented by quaternions ql (left) and qr (right). R = L(ql) R(qr) Where ql = (a, b, c, d) and qr = (p, q, r, s) are unit quaternions. The matrices L(ql) and R(qr) are constructed from their respective quaternion components. Conditional 3D Gaussian Derivation: To render at a specific time t, the 4D Gaussian is conditioned on t. The conditional 3D mean \mu{xyz|t} and covariance \Sigma{xyz|t} are derived from the properties of multivariate Gaussians: \mu{xyz|t} = \mu{1:3} + \Sigma{1:3,4} \Sigma{4,4}^{-1} (t - \mut) \Sigma{xyz|t} = \Sigma{1:3,1:3} - \Sigma{1:3,4} \Sigma{4,4}^{-1} \Sigma{4,1:3} Where \mu{1:3} is the spatial part of the mean, \Sigma{1:3,4} is the cross-covariance between space and time, and \Sigma{4,4} is the temporal variance. Marginal Time Probability: The probability of the Gaussian existing at time t is given by the marginal 1D Gaussian: pi(t) = \mathcal{N}(t; \mu{t,i}, \Sigma{4,4,i}). Rendering Equation: The color \mathcal{I}(u, v, t) at pixel (u, v) and time t is computed by volume splatting: \mathcal{I}(u, v, t) = \sum{i=1}^N pi(t) pi(u, v|t) \alphai ci(d, t) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(t) pj(u, v|t) \alphaj) Where: pi(u, v|t) is the 2D Gaussian probability density projected onto the image plane at time t. ci(d, t) is the view-dependent color. (Note: The source uses \prod{j=1}^N, but standard volume rendering uses \prod{j=1}^{i-1}; corrected for correctness.) Color Representation (4D Spherical Harmonics): View-dependent color and temporal appearance are modeled using 4D Spherical Harmonics (4DSH): Z{nl}^m(t, \theta, \phi) = \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{T}t\right) Yl^m(\theta, \phi) Where: Yl^m(\theta, \phi) are standard 3D spherical harmonics with degree l \ge 0 and order -l \le m \le l. n is the Fourier series order for time. T is the period of the temporal basis. Initialization: Plenoptic Video Dataset: Initialize Gaussians using a colored point cloud from COLMAP on the first frame. Distribute timestamps \mut uniformly across the scene duration. D-NeRF Dataset: Select 100,000 random points in volume [-1.2, 1.2]^3. Set initial \mut to the scene's duration. Optimization and Densification: Loss: Rendering loss (e.g., L1 + DSSIM) is used as supervision. Sampling: Straightforward batch sampling in time is used to prevent temporal flickering and jitter, processing entire videos end-to-end. Densification: Use average gradients of \mut as an additional density control indicator alongside spatial gradients. In over-reconstruction regions, employ joint spatial and temporal position sampling during Gaussian splitting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializegaussians(datasettype, timestamps): """Initialize 4D Gaussians based on dataset type.""" if datasettype == 'plenoptic': # Use colored point cloud from COLMAP on the first frame. points3d = np.random.rand(10000, 3) # Placeholder for actual COLMAP extraction colors = np.random.rand(10000, 3) n = len(points3d) mut = np.linspace(timestamps.min(), timestamps.max(), n) mu = np.hstack([points3d, mut.reshape(-1, 1)]) elif datasettype == 'dnerf': n = 100000 points3d = np.random.uniform(-1.2, 1.2, (n, 3)) colors = np.random.uniform(0, 1, (n, 3)) mut = np.full(n, timestamps.max()) mu = np.hstack([points3d, mut.reshape(-1, 1)]) else: raise ValueError("Unknown dataset type") alpha = np.ones(n) 0.5 s = np.random.uniform(0.1, 1.0, (n, 4)) ql = np.random.randn(n, 4) qr = np.random.randn(n, 4) ql = ql / np.linalg.norm(ql, axis=1, keepdims=True) qr = qr / np.linalg.norm(qr, axis=1, keepdims=True) shcoeffs = np.zeros((n, 45)) # Standard SH degree 2 has 45 coeffs return {'mu': mu, 'alpha': alpha, 's': s, 'ql': ql, 'qr': qr, 'shcoeffs': shcoeffs} def computecovariance(s, ql, qr): """Compute 4D covariance matrix Sigma from scaling and quaternions.""" n = s.shape[0] Ssq = np.zeros((n, 4, 4)) for i in range(n): Ssq[i] = np.diag(s[i]2) R = np.zeros((n, 4, 4)) for i in range(n): L = constructleftquaternionmatrix(ql[i]) Rmat = constructrightquaternionmatrix(qr[i]) R[i] = L @ Rmat Sigma = np.zeros((n, 4, 4)) for i in range(n): Sigma[i] = R[i] @ Ssq[i] @ R[i].T return Sigma def constructleftquaternionmatrix(q): a, b, c, d = q return np.array([[ a, -b, -c, -d], [ b, a, -d, c], [ c, d, a, -b], [ d, -c, b, a]]) def constructrightquaternionmatrix(q): p, qval, r, s = q return np.array([[ p, -qval, -r, -s], [ qval, p, s, -r], [ r, -s, p, qval], [ s, r, -qval, p]]) def getconditional3dgaussian(mu, Sigma, t): """Compute conditional 3D mean and covariance given time t.""" mu13 = mu[:3] mut = mu[3] Sigma1313 = Sigma[:3,:3] Sigma134 = Sigma[:3, 3] Sigma44 = Sigma[3, 3] muxyzt = mu13 + (Sigma134 / Sigma44) (t - mut) Sigmaxyzt = Sigma1313 - (Sigma134 @ Sigma134.T) / Sigma44 return muxyzt, Sigmaxyzt def render4dgaussians(gaussians, camera, time, imageshape): """Render a single frame at a specific time using 4D Gaussian Splatting.""" mu = gaussians['mu'] Sigma = computecovariance(gaussians['s'], gaussians['ql'], gaussians['qr']) alpha = gaussians['alpha'] shcoeffs = gaussians['shcoeffs'] mut = mu[:, 3] sigma44 = Sigma[:, 3, 3] pt = np.exp(-0.5 ((time - mut)2) / sigma44) / np.sqrt(2 np.pi sigma44) mask = pt > 1e-3 mucond = np.array([getconditional3dgaussian(mu[i], Sigma[i], time)[0] for i in range(len(mu)) if mask[i]]) Sigmacond = np.array([getconditional3dgaussian(mu[i], Sigma[i], time)[1] for i in range(len(mu)) if mask[i]]) alphacond = alpha[mask] shcoeffscond = shcoeffs[mask] #
