name: 3DGUT
head: 3D Gaussian Uncentred Transform
body: 3DGUT is a Gaussian projection technique that employs an unscented transform to improve the affine approximation of the projection operator, providing more precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane. It addresses the accuracy limitations of the standard linearization used in Gaussian Splatting by capturing higher-order statistical moments of the projection, thereby reducing approximation errors in the resulting 2D covariance. 3DGUT modifies the standard Gaussian Splatting projection pipeline by replacing the first-order Taylor expansion (affine approximation) of the projection function with an unscented transform. This allows for a more accurate estimation of the mean and covariance of the projected Gaussian. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters: Mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, Covariance \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite). Camera parameters: View matrix V, Projection matrix P, Intrinsics K. Outputs: 2D Gaussian parameters: Mean \mu{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^2, Covariance \Sigma{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. Data Structures: Sigma Points: A set of 2n+1 points (where n=3 for 3D Gaussians) derived from the mean and covariance. Weights: Scalar weights associated with each sigma point for mean and covariance calculation. Steps: 1. Generate Sigma Points: Calculate 2n+1 sigma points \chii from the 3D mean \mu and covariance \Sigma. Let L be the lower triangular Cholesky factor of \Sigma such that \Sigma = LL^T. The points are defined as: \chi0 = \mu \chii = \mu + (\sqrt{(n+\kappa)L})i \quad \text{for } i=1,\dots,n \chi{i+n} = \mu - (\sqrt{(n+\kappa)L})i \quad \text{for } i=1,\dots,n where \kappa is a scaling parameter (typically \kappa = 3-n for optimal performance in 3D) and (\sqrt{(n+\kappa)L})i denotes the i-th column of the matrix square root scaled by (n+\kappa). 2. Propagate Sigma Points: Apply the full non-linear projection function f(\cdot) to each sigma point \chii. This involves transforming the 3D point to camera coordinates, projecting to homogeneous coordinates, and dividing by depth to get 2D image coordinates. \tilde{\chi}i = f(\chii) 3. Calculate Weighted Mean: Compute the projected mean \mu{2D} using the weighted sum of the projected sigma points. \mu{2D} = \sum{i=0}^{2n} Wi^m \tilde{\chi}i where W0^m = \frac{\kappa}{n+\kappa} and Wi^m = \frac{1}{2(n+\kappa)} for i > 0. 4. Calculate Weighted Covariance: Compute the projected covariance \Sigma{2D} using the weighted outer products of the deviations from the mean. \Sigma{2D} = \sum{i=0}^{2n} Wi^c (\tilde{\chi}i - \mu{2D})(\tilde{\chi}i - \mu{2D})^T + Q where W0^c = \frac{\kappa}{n+\kappa} - 1 + \beta and Wi^c = \frac{1}{2(n+\kappa)} for i > 0. \beta is a parameter (typically \beta=2 for Gaussian distributions) and Q is a small regularization term to ensure positive definiteness if necessary. Parameters: \kappa: Scaling parameter. Typical value: 3-n (i.e., 0 for n=3). \beta: Incorporates prior knowledge of the distribution. Typical value: 2 for Gaussian distributions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Positive Definiteness: The resulting \Sigma{2D} must remain positive semi-definite. Numerical errors in the unscented transform can occasionally violate this. A small regularization term Q or a check to enforce positive definiteness is required. Depth Zero: If any sigma point projects to a depth of zero or negative (behind the camera), the projection is invalid. These points should be handled by clamping depth or excluding them, though this is rare for well-formed Gaussians. Computational Cost: Generating and propagating 2n+1 points is more expensive than a single affine approximation, though still efficient compared to full quadrature. Defines the base Gaussian density. 3DGUT operates on these functions but changes the projection step. Optimizes rasterization. 3DGUT is a pre-rasterization projection method. Another projection refinement. 3DGUT uses unscented transform; this method uses stabilization terms. Handles wild data. 3DGUT can be integrated into GS-W for better projection accuracy. Adds time. 3DGUT can be applied per-frame. Alternative reconstruction. 3DGUT is a rendering/projection technique. Alternative shape. 3DGUT is specific to Gaussians. Rendering backend. 3DGUT provides the projected Gaussians. Rendering backend. 3DGUT provides the projected Gaussians. Rasterization step. 3DGUT provides the 2D Gaussians. Time Complexity: O(n^3) for Cholesky decomposition and sigma point generation, plus O(n) projections. For n=3, this is constant and small. More expensive than standard affine projection (O(1)) but negligible compared to rasterization. Memory Complexity: O(n^2) to store sigma points and weights. Minimal overhead. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Strengths: More accurate projection than affine approximation, especially for large or highly anisotropic Gaussians. Reduces artifacts caused by projection errors. Limitations: Slightly higher computational cost than affine projection. Requires careful handling of numerical stability. When to use: When high fidelity is required and projection artifacts are visible. When not: When performance is critical and standard projection is sufficient. 3DGUT was introduced to address the limitations of the affine approximation in Gaussian Splatting projection. It leverages the unscented transform, a technique from state estimation, to provide a more precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane. The method is cited in recent surveys on 3D Gaussian Splatting as a way to improve rendering accuracy. name: Transformer-based Reconstruction
head: Feed-forward Gaussian Reconstruction, Direct Gaussian Prediction
body: Transformer-based Reconstruction refers to a family of feed-forward neural network methods that directly predict 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters from 2D image inputs, bypassing the iterative optimization required by standard 3DGS. Unlike iterative approaches that refine a scene representation over time, these models infer the scene geometry and appearance in a single forward pass, enabling real-time reconstruction from sparse or single views. The family is distinguished from sibling rasterization and rendering optimizations by its focus on the generative reconstruction pipeline rather than the rendering speed or mathematical stability of the Gaussian primitives themselves. All methods in this family share the following core mechanism: 1. Input Modality: The input consists of 2D images (monocular or multi-view) and, for multi-view methods, corresponding camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics). 2. Direct Parameter Prediction: The network outputs the full set of 3D Gaussian parameters directly: mean position (\mu), covariance matrix (\Sigma), color (c), and opacity (\alpha). 3. Transformer Architecture: The core processing unit is a transformer block (or sequence of blocks) that attends to relationships between image features and camera poses to infer 3D structure. 4. Feed-Forward Nature: The reconstruction is non-iterative; the output is generated in a single inference step without gradient descent or scene optimization loops. 5. Supervision: Training is supervised using photometric losses (e.g., LPIPS, SSIM) and potentially depth consistency losses, comparing rendered outputs against ground-truth input images. Flash3D is a feed-forward method for monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction. It addresses the challenge of generating 3DGS scenes from a single view by estimating depth and directly predicting Gaussian parameters. It is distinguished from sibling methods like PixelSplat and GS-LRM by its reliance on a single image input and depth estimation, whereas PixelSplat uses epipolar transformers for two views and GS-LRM tokenizes multiple images. When to choose: Use when only a single image is available and real-time reconstruction is required. Link: Flash3D GS-LRM is a feed-forward transformer-based method that reconstructs 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from a small set of input views (2–4 images). It solves the sparse-view reconstruction problem by directly predicting Gaussian parameters without iterative optimization. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as MVSplat and NoPoSplat, by its specific tokenization strategy of concatenating images with camera parameters before processing them through a transformer block. When to choose: Use when 2–4 views with known camera poses are available and iterative optimization is too slow. Link: GS-LRM PixelSplat incorporates an epipolar transformer to generalize features between two views, paired with a probabilistic prediction of Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays. When to choose: Use when exactly two views are available and epipolar geometry is leveraged for feature matching. Link: PixelSplat Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) is a feedforward model for single image to 3D reconstruction. When to choose: Use for general single-image 3D reconstruction tasks, potentially extending beyond Gaussian Splatting to other representations. Link: Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) The concept of feed-forward reconstruction for 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a solution to the computational bottleneck of iterative optimization in standard 3DGS. Traditional 3DGS requires thousands of optimization steps to converge, making it unsuitable for real-time applications from sparse inputs. Transformer-based methods leverage the attention mechanism's ability to model long-range dependencies and spatial relationships, allowing them to infer 3D structure from 2D projections directly. Flash3D pioneered the monocular approach by integrating depth estimation into the Gaussian prediction pipeline. GS-LRM extended this to sparse multi-view settings by explicitly incorporating camera parameters into the transformer's token sequence. These methods represent a shift from optimization-based reconstruction to learning-based direct prediction. Flash3D and GS-LRM notes, URL not provided, date fetched not provided. body: GS-LRM is a feed-forward transformer-based method that reconstructs 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from a small set of input views. It solves the sparse-view reconstruction problem by directly predicting Gaussian parameters without iterative optimization. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as MVSplat and NoPoSplat, by its specific tokenization strategy of concatenating images with camera parameters before processing them through a transformer block. Inputs: A set of 2 to 4 input images and their corresponding camera parameters (extrinsics and intrinsics). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, color, opacity) aligned along camera-to-3D pixel rays. Data Structures: The method processes tokens representing visual and geometric information. 1. Image Tokens: Features extracted from the input images. 2. Camera Tokens: Embeddings representing the camera pose and intrinsics. 3. Concatenated Sequence: The image and camera tokens are concatenated into a single sequence. Steps: 1. Tokenization: Extract features from the 2–4 input images. Generate embeddings for the associated camera parameters. 2. Concatenation: Concatenate the image features and camera parameter embeddings into a unified token sequence. 3. Transformer Processing: Pass the concatenated sequence through a transformer block. The transformer attends to the relationships between views and camera poses to infer 3D structure. 4. Decoding: Decode the output tokens from the transformer block into the final Gaussian parameters (mean, covariance, color, opacity). Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: 3D Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering
head: Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids, Gaussian Ellipsoid Ray Tracing, VoGE, VoGE Ray Tracing with Ellipsoidal Gaussians, VoGE Volume Density Ray Tracing, VoGE Volume Rendering, VoGE: A Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids for Analysis-by-Synthesis
body: 3D Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering (VoGE) is a differentiable volume rendering method that represents scenes as a sum of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids and computes image synthesis via ray tracing rather than rasterization. It solves the occlusion ambiguity inherent in distance-based blending by accumulating volume density distributions along viewing rays, enabling realistic interaction between overlapping objects. Unlike its sibling Gaussian Splatting, which approximates volume rendering through 2D rasterization of projected splats, VoGE replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture exact volume density distributions for blending. Inputs: A set of K Gaussian ellipsoids, each defined by a center location \mathbf{M}k \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a symmetric spatial variance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}; a camera configuration defining viewing rays \mathbf{r}(t); and per-kernel attributes (e.g., color \mathbf{c}k). Outputs: A synthesized 2D image where each pixel color is a weighted sum of kernel attributes. Data Structures: Each kernel k stores: \mathbf{M}k: Center coordinates (\mu{k,x}, \mu{k,y}, \mu{k,z}). \mathbf{\Sigma}k: 3 \times 3 symmetric covariance matrix. \mathbf{c}k: Attribute vector (e.g., RGB color). Precomputation per Kernel: For each kernel k, the method precomputes scalars to simplify ray integration: 1. \mathbf{V}k: Vector from the ray point of closest approach to the center. 2. lk: The distance along the ray where density is maximized. 3. qk: Log-density magnitude offset. 4. \sigmak^2: Variance of the 1D Gaussian projection along the ray direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, sample a viewing ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{D} t, where \mathbf{D} is the normalized direction vector and t is the distance from the camera origin. 2. Kernel Parameter Calculation: For each kernel k and ray direction \mathbf{D}, compute the following scalars: Calculate the length lk along the ray that maximizes the density \rhok(\mathbf{r}(t)): lk = \frac{\mathbf{M}k^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{M}k}{2 \cdot \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D}} Calculate the vector \mathbf{V}k from the point lk \mathbf{D} on the ray to the center \mathbf{M}k: \mathbf{V}k = \mathbf{M}k - lk \mathbf{D} Compute the precomputed scalar qk representing the peak density magnitude offset: qk = -0.5 \mathbf{V}k^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{V}k Compute the precomputed scalar \sigmak^2 representing the variance of the 1D Gaussian along the ray: \sigmak^2 = \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} Note: The condition \mathbf{V}k^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{V}k = 0 holds by definition of lk, simplifying the exponent. 3. Volume Density Definition: The volume density \rho(\mathbf{X}) at any location \mathbf{X} is the sum of ellipsoidal Gaussian kernels: \rho(\mathbf{X}) = \sum{k=1}^K \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi} \|\mathbf{\Sigma}k\|2} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{M}k)^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot (\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{M}k)\right) Along the ray \mathbf{r}(s) = s\mathbf{D}, the density of the k-th kernel reduces to a 1D Gaussian: \rhok(\mathbf{r}(s)) = \frac{e^{qk}}{\sqrt{2\pi} \|\mathbf{\Sigma}k\|2} \exp\left(-\frac{(s - lk)^2}{2 \sigmak^2}\right) 4. Occupancy Accumulation: Compute the occupancy T(t) along the ray, which represents the probability of not being occluded up to distance t. This is derived by integrating the total volume density: T(t) = \exp\left(-\tau \int{-\infty}^t \rho(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds\right) Substituting the 1D Gaussian form and using the error function \operatorname{erf}(x) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int0^x e^{-u^2} du, the closed-form solution is: T(t) = \exp\left(-\sum{k=1}^K e^{qk} \frac{\operatorname{erf}\left((t - lk)/\sigmak\right) + 1}{2}\right) Here, \tau is a scattering coefficient. The integral limits are effectively -\infty to t because the Gaussian support is infinite. 5. Kernel-to-Pixel Weight Computation: Compute the weight Wk for each kernel to determine its contribution to the final pixel color. The exact weight is the integral of the reweighted density: Wk(t) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} T(t) \rhok(\mathbf{r}(t)) dt Since the integral of T(t) involving \operatorname{erf} is analytically intractable, VoGE approximates T(t) as constant T(lk) over the kernel's support (centered at lk): Wk \approx T(lk) e^{qk} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi} \|\mathbf{\Sigma}k\|2} \exp\left(-\frac{(t - lk)^2}{\sigmak^2}\right) dt The integral of the normalized Gaussian part equals 1. Thus, the approximate closed-form weight is: Wk = T(lk) e^{qk} The error introduced by this approximation converges to a fixed value of 0.0256, which is negligible compared to the integral result W=1. 6. Image Synthesis: For each pixel, sum the contributions of all kernels weighted by their computed weights Wk and their attributes \mathbf{c}k: \mathbf{C}{pixel} = \sum{k=1}^K Wk \mathbf{c}k Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computekernelparams(Mk, Sigmak, D): """ Precompute scalars for a single kernel along a ray direction D. Mk: (3,) center vector Sigmak: (3,3) symmetric covariance matrix D: (3,) normalized ray direction vector Returns: lk, qk, sigmaksq """ Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigmak) term1 = np.dot(Mk, np.dot(Sigmainv, D)) term2 = np.dot(D, np.dot(Sigmainv, Mk)) denominator = 2.0 np.dot(D, np.dot(Sigmainv, D)) if denominator == 0: # Guard against degenerate covariance projection return 0.0, 0.0, 1e-8 lk = (term1 + term2) / denominator Vk = Mk - (lk D) qk = -0.5 np.dot(Vk, np.dot(Sigmainv, Vk)) sigmaksq = np.dot(D, np.dot(Sigmainv, D)) return lk, qk, sigmaksq def rendervoge(kernels, rayorigin, raydirection, tau=1.0): """ Render a single ray using VoGE. kernels: List of dicts with keys 'M', 'Sigma', 'color' rayorigin: (3,) camera origin raydirection: (3,) normalized direction tau: scattering coefficient Returns: pixelcolor (3,) """ # Step 1 & 2: Precompute kernel parameters for this ray kerneldata = [] for k in kernels: M = k['M'] Sigma = k['Sigma'] lk, qk, sigmaksq = computekernelparams(M, Sigma, raydirection) sigmak = math.sqrt(max(sigmaksq, 1e-8)) kerneldata.append({ 'lk': lk, 'qk': qk, 'sigmak': sigmak, 'color': k['color'] }) pixelcolor = np.zeros(3) # Step 4 & 5: Compute Occupancy T(lk) and Weight Wk for each kernel for kd in kerneldata: lk = kd['lk'] qk = kd['qk'] sigmak = kd['sigmak'] # Compute T(lk): Occupancy at the peak of kernel k # T(t) = exp(-tau sum{j} e^{qj} (erf((t - lj)/sigmaj) + 1)/2) densityintegralsum = 0.0 for otherkd in kerneldata: lother = otherkd['lk'] qother = otherkd['qk'] sigmaother = otherkd['sigmak'] arg = (lk - lother) / sigmaother erfval = math.erf(arg) term = math.exp(qother) (erfval + 1.0) / 2.0 densityintegralsum += term Tlk = math.exp(-tau densityintegralsum) # Step 5: Compute Weight Wk Wk = Tlk math.exp(qk) # Step 6: Accumulate Color pixelcolor += Wk kd['color'] return pixelcolor Parameters: \tau: Scattering coefficient. Typical value: 1.0. K: Total number of Gaussian kernels. Varies by scene complexity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distance-based blending ambiguity: Traditional splatting blends based on viewing distance, causing unrealistic color shifts when foreground objects move relative to background objects (e.g., purple blending). VoGE avoids this by using density-based blending. Integral infeasibility: The exact integral of T(t) involving the error function is analytically intractable. The approximation Wk \approx T(lk)e^{qk} is used. The error is bounded and negligible (0.0256). Degenerate Covariance: If \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} is zero or near-zero, lk is undefined. This occurs if the ray direction is orthogonal to the principal axes in a way that makes the projection singular. Guard against division by zero. The Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive replaces long-tailed Gaussian kernels with constant-density ellipsoidal shapes to reduce spatial overlap and memory usage. It addresses the non-differentiability of hard-boundary ellipsoids by employing a sigmoid-based formulation, allowing for stable gradient-based optimization against 3D intensity fields. Unlike its sibling Ever Rendering, which relies on ray-based accumulation to implicitly soften boundaries, this method ensures the primitive itself is fully differentiable, making it suitable for direct volumetric training. Ever Rendering is a real-time volumetric rendering method that represents a radiance field as a set of constant-density volumetric ellipsoids, avoiding the 2D billboard approximation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike its sibling Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive, it replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture volume density distributions for blending, enabling exact transmittance calculation without approximation errors. Each point is represented by a 3D Gaussian ellipsoid GV to facilitate general grids; it becomes a sphere for cubic grids. The volume-space Gaussian is defined as GV = \frac{1}{2\pi V} e^{-0.5(x - vj)^T V^{-1} (x - vj)}. This ellipsoid is transformed into view-space G{MVM} using the viewing matrix M. Time Complexity: VoGE provides real-time level rendering speed, competitive with PyTorch3D. The complexity is dominated by the per-ray, per-kernel evaluation of the error function and exponential terms. With N pixels and K kernels, the complexity is roughly O(N \cdot K). The use of closed-form approximations avoids expensive numerical integration. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of kernels K, storing \mathbf{M}k, \mathbf{\Sigma}k, and attributes for each. Strengths: Resolves occlusion ambiguities better than distance-based blending. Fully differentiable, suitable for analysis-by-synthesis tasks like pose estimation and texture fitting. Real-time performance achievable via CUDA implementation. Limitations: Approximation error in weight calculation (though negligible). When to use: When accurate occlusion reasoning and differentiability are required, such as in object pose estimation, shape/texture fitting, and scenes with significant overlapping objects. When not to use: When maximum frame rate is critical and occlusion accuracy is less important than speed, or when the scene can be well-approximated by 2D billboards (standard 3DGS). VoGE (Volume Gaussian Ellipsoid) was proposed as a differentiable volume renderer that utilizes volumetric Gaussian reconstruction kernels as geometric primitives. It was developed to address the limitations of current state-of-the-art differentiable renderers that use rasterization and distance-based blending, which suffer from ambiguity when objects overlap. The code is available at https://github.com/Angtian/VoGE. VoGE: A Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids for Analysis-by-Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2205.15401, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric Points - Stony Brook Computer Science, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/teaching/cse616/volPts.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive
head: Sigmoid-based ellipsoidal primitive
body: The Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive is a geometric representation used in volume rendering that replaces long-tailed Gaussian kernels with constant-density ellipsoidal shapes to reduce spatial overlap and memory usage. It addresses the non-differentiability of hard-boundary ellipsoids by employing a sigmoid-based formulation, allowing for stable gradient-based optimization against 3D intensity fields. Unlike its sibling Ever Rendering, which relies on ray-based accumulation to implicitly soften boundaries, this method ensures the primitive itself is fully differentiable, making it suitable for direct volumetric training. The method defines a primitive using a center intensity, a mean position, and a covariance matrix, modulated by a sharpness parameter. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Primitive parameters \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 (center), \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (covariance), I \in \mathbb{R} (center intensity), and k \in \mathbb{R} (sharpness). Query point x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Scalar intensity value \tilde{P}(x). Data Structures: Each primitive stores: 1. \mu: 3D vector. 2. \Sigma: 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix. 3. I: Scalar intensity. 4. k: Scalar sharpness (typically fixed). Formulas: Let d = x - \mu be the displacement vector from the center. The unnormalized primitive profile is defined as: P(x) = I \cdot \sigma(k \cdot (1 - d^T \Sigma^{-1} d)) where \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} is the sigmoid function. To decouple peak intensity from the sharpness parameter k, the primitive is normalized: \tilde{P}(x) = \frac{P(x)}{P(\mu)} = I \cdot \frac{\sigma(k \cdot (1 - d^T \Sigma^{-1} d))}{\sigma(k)} This normalization ensures that the peak intensity at the center (d=0) remains exactly I, regardless of k. Parameters: k: Controls boundary sharpness. A fixed hyperparameter is used in practice for efficiency. Typical values: Lower values cause peak intensity reduction in the unnormalized case; higher values increase boundary sharpness. Steps: 1. Compute displacement d = x - \mu. 2. Compute quadratic form q = d^T \Sigma^{-1} d. 3. Compute unnormalized sigmoid value s = \sigma(k \cdot (1 - q)). 4. Compute normalization factor n = \sigma(k). 5. Return \tilde{P}(x) = I \cdot (s / n). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Peak Intensity Deviation: If k is small and the primitive is not normalized, the peak intensity at the center decreases, deviating from the desired unit response. Truncation Artifacts: When using a fixed cutoff for rendering or voxelization, the spatial support varies with k. The cutoff region must be adjusted according to k to avoid truncation artifacts. Non-differentiability of Hard Boundaries: Using the indicator function form (as in EVER) results in vanishing gradients during optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(z): """Standard sigmoid function.""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-z)) def differentiableellipsoidprimitive(x, mu, Sigmainv, I, k): """ Computes the normalized intensity of a differentiable ellipsoid primitive at point x. Args: x: Query point (3,) mu: Primitive center (3,) Sigmainv: Inverse covariance matrix (3x3) I: Center intensity (scalar) k: Sharpness parameter (scalar) Returns: Normalized intensity value (scalar) """ # 1. Compute displacement d = x - mu # 2. Compute quadratic form d^T Sigma^{-1} d q = d @ Sigmainv @ d # 3. Compute unnormalized sigmoid argument arg = k (1.0 - q) # 4. Compute unnormalized value sunnorm = sigmoid(arg) # 5. Compute normalization factor sigma(k) normfactor = sigmoid(k) # 6. Return normalized intensity return I (sunnorm / normfactor) A training stage that optimizes ellipsoidal primitive parameters to fit a volumetric intensity field, storing center intensity I and geometric parameters (\mu, \Sigma). It differs from view-dependent color learning (e.g., 3DGS) by directly modeling the per-voxel scalar value of the original volume. Definition: Optimizes primitives to predict voxel intensity \hat{V}(x) by summing normalized primitive profiles. Formula: The predicted voxel intensity is \hat{V}(x) = \sum{i \in N} \tilde{P}i(x) = \sum{i \in N} Ii \frac{\sigma(k(1 - di^\top \Sigmai^{-1} di))}{\sigma(k)}, where N is the set of primitives contributing at x. Steps: 1. Subsample a ground truth subvolume V{gt} \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times s \times s} from the GT volume at each iteration. 2. Align primitive coordinates to the GT volume coordinates. 3. Voxelize only the overlapping region to obtain the prediction subvolume \hat{V}. 4. Compute loss L{\text{rec}} = \beta L1 + (1 - \beta) L{\text{D-SSIM}} with \beta \in [0, 1]. When to choose: Use when training against a known 3D intensity field (e.g., medical volumes, scientific data) rather than multi-view images. Time Complexity: Rendering/voxelization depends on the number of primitives N and the spatial support. The ellipsoidal shape reduces spatial footprint by up to 9\times compared to Gaussian 3\sigma support, reducing overlap and computational cost. Memory Complexity: Reduced memory usage due to smaller spatial overlap and constant-density representation. Performance: Using k as a fixed hyperparameter improves efficiency. Making k learnable per primitive improves quality but adds overhead and reduces speed. Strengths: Fully differentiable primitive enables stable training against 3D intensity fields; reduced spatial overlap compared to Gaussians. Limitations: Requires careful adjustment of cutoff regions to avoid truncation artifacts; fixed k may limit adaptability compared to learnable k. When to use: Scalable learning on volumes exceeding GPU memory; scenarios requiring direct volumetric optimization. When not to use: When ray-based accumulation is preferred (see Ever Rendering); when extreme adaptability of boundary sharpness is required and speed is not a concern. The method originates from the ESVR (3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering) framework. It was developed to address the excessive spatial overlap and high memory usage caused by long-tailed Gaussian primitives in volume rendering. The approach is inspired by EVER [29], which uses indicator functions for ellipsoidal boundaries, but adapts it for differentiable volumetric optimization by replacing the hard boundary with a sigmoid function. ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ever Rendering
head: Exact Volumetric Ellipsoid Rendering
body: Ever Rendering is a real-time volumetric rendering method that represents a radiance field as a set of constant-density volumetric ellipsoids, avoiding the 2D billboard approximation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike its sibling Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive, it replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture volume density distributions for blending, enabling exact transmittance calculation without approximation errors. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian ellipsoids, each defined by a center position \mathbf{t}k, a rotation matrix \mathbf{R}k, and a scaling vector \mathbf{s}k = [s{kx}, s{ky}, s{kz}]^T. An optimized scalar parameter \alphak \in [0, 1] representing the peak opacity along the shortest axis. Color \mathbf{c}k for each ellipsoid, stored as spherical harmonics coefficients for the first two degrees to model view-dependence. Camera parameters (position, orientation, intrinsics). Target images for optimization. Outputs: A rendered image with color and depth. Gradients for optimization via adjoint rendering, which recomputes function values during the backwards pass instead of storing them. The scene representation consists of a list of ellipsoids. Each ellipsoid k stores: \mathbf{t}k \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{R}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix (orthonormal). \mathbf{s}k \in \mathbb{R}^3: Axis scaling factors. \alphak \in \mathbb{R}: Optimized opacity parameter. \mathbf{c}k \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color. AABB: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box computed from \mathbf{t}k, \mathbf{R}k, \mathbf{s}k for BVH acceleration. The acceleration structure is a Binary Volume Hierarchy (BVH) built using NVIDIA OptiX, where each leaf node contains an ellipsoid's AABB and intersection logic. Density Calculation: To ensure non-zero gradients even when opacity approaches 1, the method optimizes \alphak and maps it to density \sigma(\alphak) using the minimum axis scale: \sigma(\alphak) = -\frac{\log(1 - 0.99 \cdot \alphak)}{\min(s{kx}, s{ky}, s{kz})} This ensures that a primitive viewed along its shortest axis has a peak opacity equal to \alphak. Transmittance: The volume rendering transmittance is calculated as: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \exp(-\sigmaj \Delta tj) This is identical to the quadrature rule derived by Max [30] using piecewise-constant approximation. In Ever Rendering, this is an intentional design decision with no approximation errors. Splitting Condition: A splitting condition detects vanished gradients when opacity is near 1 across the entire primitive along the major axis: 0.99 < 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\alphak) \cdot \max(s{kx}, s{ky}, s{kz})) If this inequality holds, the primitive is a candidate for splitting. Regularizer Loss: To discourage overly anisotropic primitives (which cause large AABBs and slow BVH traversal), a regularizer is applied only to visible primitives: \mathcal{L}{reg} = \text{stopgrad}(1 - \alpha) \cdot (\max(sx, sy, sz) - \min(sx, sy, sz)) where \alpha \in [0, 1] is the opacity and s \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the ellipsoid axis scaling vector. Splitting Threshold: 2.5 \times 10^{-7} (modified from 3DGS due to smaller spatial gradients). Cloning Threshold: 0.1. Density Division: When splitting, the density of the new primitives is divided in half. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def rayellipsoidintersect(rayo, rayd, ellt, ellR, ells): """ Computes near and far intersection distances along the ray. Transforms ray to ellipsoid local space and solves quadratic for unit sphere. """ invs = 1.0 / ells localo = (ellR.T @ (rayo - ellt)) invs locald = (ellR.T @ rayd) invs a = torch.dot(locald, locald) b = 2.0 torch.dot(localo, locald) c = torch.dot(localo, localo) - 1.0 disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return None, None sqrtdisc = torch.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 return t1, t2 def computedensity(alphak, sk): """Maps optimized opacity parameter alphak to density sigma.""" minscale = torch.min(sk) term = torch.clamp(1.0 - 0.99 alphak, min=1e-7) return -torch.log(term) / minscale def renderray(rayo, rayd, ellipsoids): """ Renders a single ray using Ever Rendering's front/back event decoupling. """ events = [] # List of (t, deltasigma, deltapremultipliedcolor) for ell in ellipsoids: tnear, tfar = rayellipsoidintersect(rayo, rayd, ell.t, ell.R, ell.s) if tnear is None: continue sigma = computedensity(ell.alpha, ell.s) # Front surface: add density and premultiplied color events.append((tnear, sigma, sigma ell.c)) # Back surface: subtract density and premultiplied color events.append((tfar, -sigma, -sigma ell.c)) # Sort events by distance along the ray events.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) runningsigma = 0.0 runningpremultc = torch.zeros(3) totaltransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = torch.zeros(3) prevt = events[0][0] if events else 0.0 for t, dsigma, dpremultc in events: deltat = t - prevt if deltat > 0 and runningsigma > 0: intervalcolor = runningpremultc / runningsigma intervalcontrib = intervalcolor (1.0 - torch.exp(-runningsigma deltat)) accumulatedcolor += totaltransmittance intervalcontrib totaltransmittance = torch.exp(-runningsigma deltat) if totaltransmittance < 1e-4: break prevt = t runningsigma += dsigma runningpremultc += dpremultc return accumulatedcolor def optimizestep(ellipsoids, images, targets, bvh): """ One step of optimization with adjoint rendering and ADC. """ renderedimages = [] for ray in rays: color = renderray(ray.origin, ray.direction, ellipsoids) renderedimages.append(color) loss = torch.mean((torch.stack(renderedimages) - targets) 2) # Add Regularizer Loss regloss = torch.tensor(0.0) for ell in visibleellipsoids: alphadetached = ell.alpha.detach() anisotropy = torch.max(ell.s) - torch.min(ell.s) regloss += (1.0 - alphadetached) anisotropy loss += regloss # Backward pass (adjoint rendering recomputes forward values) loss.backward() # Adaptive Density Control (ADC) for ell in ellipsoids: sigma = computedensity(ell.alpha, ell.s) maxscale = torch.max(ell.s) opacitymajor = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma maxscale) if opacitymajor > 0.99: splitellipsoid(ell) elif spatialgradient(ell) > 2.5e-7: splitellipsoid(ell) elif spatialgradient(ell) > 0.1: cloneellipsoid(ell) return loss def splitellipsoid(ell): """ Splits an ellipsoid: reduces size, perturbs position, halves density. """ newscale = ell.s 0.5 perturbation = torch.randn(3) 0.01 newt = ell.t + perturbation # Density is halved by adjusting alpha or scale; here we keep alpha and halve contribution newalpha = ell.alpha newc = ell.c / 2.0 # Create two new primitives with these parameters return [Ellipsoid(newt, ell.R, newscale, newalpha, newc), Ellipsoid(newt, ell.R, newscale, newalpha, newc)] def cloneellipsoid(ell): """ Clones an ellipsoid to add detail. """ perturbation = torch.randn(3) 0.01 newt = ell.t + perturbation return Ellipsoid(newt, ell.R, ell.s, ell.alpha, ell.c) def computespatialgradients(ellipsoids, renderedimages, targets): """ Accumulates xy gradients per primitive from the loss backward pass. Standard operation: maps per-pixel gradients to intersected primitives. """ for ell in ellipsoids: ell.grad = torch.zeros(3) # Placeholder for accumulated gradient magnitude return ell.grad Vanishing Gradients: If opacity approaches 1, gradients vanish. The mapping \sigma(\alphak) ensures non-zero gradients by anchoring \alphak to the shortest axis view. Anisotropy: Highly anisotropic primitives create large AABBs, slowing BVH traversal. The regularizer loss discourages this. Precision: The log term in density calculation must handle \alphak close to 1. The factor 0.99 prevents \log(0). BVH Rebuild: The BVH is rebuilt at every training step, taking tens of milliseconds. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved, with performance on Mip-NeRF360 reaching 36 FPS. Memory Complexity: 1134 MB on Mip-NeRF360. Performance: On Mip-NeRF360, EVER achieves PSNR 27.51, SSIM 0.825, LPIPS 0.194. Scaling: The method scales to larger scenes (Zip-NeRF) with improved sharpness. Strengths: Real-time performance, consistent 3D radiance field, no approximation errors in transmittance, improved blending and sharpness compared to 3DGS. Limitations: BVH rebuild overhead during training (tens of ms per step). Ever Rendering was introduced in the paper "EVER: Exact Volumetric Ellipsoid Rendering for Real-Time View Synthesis". It builds on the optimization framework of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) but replaces rasterization with ray tracing using NVIDIA OptiX and Slang for automatic differentiation. The method addresses the 2D billboard limitation of 3DGS by using 3D Gaussian ellipsoids that blend into a proper 3D radiance field. It is used for real-time 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis, specifically enabling effects like defocus blur and fish-eye camera distortion. EVER: Exact Volumetric Ellipsoid Rendering for Real-Time View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51701.2025.00469, fetched 2026-10-27

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced)
head: 3DGS Weekend Renderer, Depth-based Splat Sorting, Instanced Gaussian Splatting with Back-to-Front Sorting
body: This method renders trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by projecting 3D Gaussians into 2D screen-space quads, sorting them by camera-space depth on the CPU, and drawing them using instanced rendering with standard alpha blending. It solves the transparency ordering problem inherent in translucent splatting by ensuring fragments are blended from back to front. Unlike the official tile-based CUDA rasterizer which sorts fragments on the GPU, this approach prioritizes implementation simplicity and CPU-side control, making it suitable for display-only renderers or environments where GPU sorting is unavailable. Inputs: gs: A collection of M 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i has: means: 3D position (x, y, z) in world space. covariances: 3D covariance matrix \Sigma{3D} (or scale/rotation parameters). opacities: Scalar opacity \alphai. shcoefficients: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for view-dependent color. camera: View matrix V and projection matrix P. imagesize: Width W and Height H in pixels. Outputs: Rendered image buffer of size W \times H \times 3 (RGB). GpuGaussian Struct (uploaded to GPU for instancing): centroid: vec3 (12 bytes) opacity: float (4 bytes) scale: array<float, 3> (12 bytes) rotation: array<float, 4> (16 bytes) Total size: 44 bytes. SplatSortEntry Struct (used for CPU sorting): cameraZ: float (4 bytes) splatIndex: sizet (8 bytes) Depth Mix Buffer (alternative JS-based implementation): depthMix: A BigInt64Array of size vertexCount. Viewed as Float32Array (floatMix) and Uint32Array (indexMix). Each splat j occupies two consecutive floats: index at 2j, depth at 2j+1. Depth calculation: depth = 10000 + viewProj[2] x + viewProj[6] y + viewProj[10] z, where x, y, z are splat center coordinates. 1. Transform and Project Gaussians: Transform 3D means to camera space: \mathbf{p}{cam} = V \mathbf{p}{world}. Project to 2D image plane to get screen coordinates (u, v). Transform 3D covariances to camera space: \Sigma{cam} = R{view} \Sigma{world} R{view}^T. Project 3D covariance to 2D using the Jacobian of the perspective projection. Add a minimum epsilon (e.g., 0.3) to the diagonal to stabilize inversion. 2. Frustum Culling and Filtering: Remove Gaussians outside the camera frustum (image bounds and near/far planes). Skip Gaussians with opacity below a threshold (e.g., 0.01 or 0.05). 3. CPU Sorting: Sort the remaining Gaussians by their camera-space depth z{cam} in increasing order (far-to-near, since camera looks down negative Z). Create an array of SplatSortEntry containing cameraZ and original index. Sort using standard library sort (e.g., std::sort or JavaScript Array.sort). Reorder the GpuGaussian data and SH coefficients according to the sorted indices. 4. GPU Rendering Setup: Disable depth testing: glDisable(GLDEPTHTEST). Enable alpha blending: glEnable(GLBLEND) with glBlendFunc(GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). 5. Vertex Shader (Instanced): For each instance i and vertex v of the unit quad: Compute clip space position: \mathbf{c} = P V \mathbf{p}{centroid}, \mathbf{ndc} = \mathbf{c} / \mathbf{c}.w. Compute 2D covariance components with jitter (add 0.3 to diagonals): a = \Sigma{2D}[0][0] + 0.3, b = \Sigma{2D}[1][0], d = \Sigma{2D}[1][1] + 0.3. Eigen-decompose the 2 \times 2 covariance to get eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and eigenvectors \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2: \text{det} = ad - b^2, \text{mid} = 0.5(a+d), \text{rad} = \sqrt{\max(\text{mid}^2 - \text{det}, 0.0)}, \lambda1 = \max(\text{mid} + \text{rad}, 0.01), \lambda2 = \max(\text{mid} - \text{rad}, 0.01). \mathbf{e}1 = \text{normalize}(b, \lambda1 - a) if |b| > 10^{-5}, else (1,0) if a \ge d, else (0,1). \mathbf{e}2 = (-\mathbf{e}1.y, \mathbf{e}1.x). Compute 3-sigma half-axes in pixels: \mathbf{b}1 = 3\sqrt{\lambda1} \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{b}2 = 3\sqrt{\lambda2} \mathbf{e}2. Compute vertex offset in NDC: \Delta \mathbf{pixel} = v.x \mathbf{b}1 + v.y \mathbf{b}2, \Delta \mathbf{ndc} = \Delta \mathbf{pixel} / (0.5 \times \text{viewport\size}). Set final position: \mathbf{gl\Position} = (\mathbf{ndc}.xy + \Delta \mathbf{ndc}, \mathbf{ndc}.z, 1.0). Pass varyings: splatCoord (quad corner v), splatColor (evaluated SH color), splatOpacity (sigmoid of stored opacity). 6. Fragment Shader: For each fragment with local coordinates (px, py): Compute power term: \text{power} = -4.5 (px^2 + py^2). Discard if power < -9.0 (approx e^{-9} \approx 0). Compute alpha: \alpha = \min(0.99, \text{splatOpacity} \times e^{\text{power}}). Discard if alpha < 0.001. Output color: FragColor = vec4(splatColor, alpha). Closed-form eigen-decomposition of 2x2 covariance: \text{determinant} = a \cdot d - b^2, \text{mid} = 0.5(a + d), \text{radius} = \sqrt{\max(\text{mid}^2 - \text{determinant}, 0.0)}, \lambda1 = \max(\text{mid} + \text{radius}, 0.01), \lambda2 = \max(\text{mid} - \text{radius}, 0.01). Gaussian value at fragment position (px, py): G(px, py) = \exp(-4.5(px^2 + py^2)). Derived from substituting di = 3\sqrt{\lambdai}pi into \exp(-di^2 / (2\lambdai)). Depth packing (JS variant): \text{depth} = 10000 + \text{viewProj}[2] \cdot x + \text{viewProj}[6] \cdot y + \text{viewProj}[10] \cdot z, where x, y, z are splat center coordinates. Jitter added to 2D covariance diagonal elements: 0.3. Minimum eigenvalue clamp: 0.01. Alpha clamping maximum: 0.99. Alpha discard threshold: 0.001. Power discard threshold: -9.0. Quad corners: Unit quad with corners at (-1,-1), (1,-1), (-1,1), (1,1). Opacity threshold for culling: 0.01 or 0.05. Precision issues: Fragments with power < -9.0 are discarded to avoid precision issues and unnecessary computation at quad corners. Near-transparent edges: Fragments with alpha < 0.001 are discarded to handle soft Gaussian edges. Minor camera movements: Cause redundant sorting. Handled by computing dot product of viewProj components 2, 6, 10 against lastProj. If \text{Math.abs}(\text{dot} - 1) < 0.01, the function returns early without sorting. Pixel centering: 0.5 is added to pixel coordinates when computing distance to center the Gaussian within the pixel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x)) def cpusortandprepare(gsmeans, gsopacities, viewmatrix, shcoeffs): """ CPU-side sorting and data preparation for instanced rendering. gsmeans: (N, 3) world space means gsopacities: (N,) scalar opacities viewmatrix: (4, 4) view matrix shcoeffs: (N, K) spherical harmonic coefficients Returns sorted arrays ready for GPU upload. """ N = gsmeans.shape[0] # 1. Transform means to camera space ones = np.ones((N, 1)) meanshom = np.hstack([gsmeans, ones]) meanscamhom = (viewmatrix @ meanshom.T).T meanscam = meanscamhom[:,:3] # 2. Filter low-opacity Gaussians visiblemask = gsopacities >= 0.01 visibleindices = np.where(visiblemask)[0] meanscamvis = meanscam[visibleindices] opacitiesvis = gsopacities[visibleindices] shvis = shcoeffs[visibleindices] if len(visibleindices) == 0: return np.empty((0, 3)), np.empty((0,)), np.empty((0, 0)) # 3. CPU Sorting (Back-to-Front) # Sort by camera Z (increasing = far to near in OpenGL camera space) sortorder = np.argsort(meanscamvis[:, 2]) # 4. Reorder data for instanced drawing sortedmeanscam = meanscamvis[sortorder] sortedopacities = opacitiesvis[sortorder] sortedsh = shvis[sortorder] return sortedmeanscam, sortedopacities, sortedsh A GPU-parallel rasterization method that divides the image into tiles (default 32x32 pixels) to manage memory and processing load, assigning Gaussians to tiles based on their axis-aligned bounding boxes [2061-tiled-2d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization.md]. It differs from CPU-sorted instancing by performing sorting and blending within each tile on the GPU, allowing for early ray termination and better cache locality [2061-tiled-2d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization.md]. Choose this for high-performance real-time rendering on modern GPUs. Renders 3D Gaussian splats as screen-space quads using a pre-sorted order buffer and view-space projection data, handling transparency via alpha blending and discarding fragments behind the camera or with negligible alpha [2075-gaussian-splat-rendering-screen-space-quad.md]. It is a variant of the instanced approach that may use different sorting mechanisms or quad generation strategies [2075-gaussian-splat-rendering-screen-space-quad.md]. Sorts the list of staged splats by depth before creating per-tile fragments, unlike 3DGS which sorts fragments after splitting. This reduces sorting costs because the number of fragments is 1.5 to 4x higher than visible splats. It uses a 32-bit radix sort with depth as the key, whereas standard 3DGS uses a 48-bit key (tile ID + depth). Time Complexity: O(M \log M) for CPU sorting, where M is the number of Gaussians. Rendering is O(M \cdot A) where A is the average area of a splat in pixels, but effectively O(W \cdot H) due to fragment shader execution per pixel covered by splats. Memory Complexity: O(M) for storing Gaussian attributes and sorted indices. Performance: Significantly slower than tile-based GPU rasterization for large scenes due to CPU sorting overhead and lack of early ray termination. Suitable for scenes with < 10^6 Gaussians or for debugging/prototyping. Strengths: Simple implementation, no custom GPU kernels required, works on any OpenGL/Vulkan/DirectX renderer with instancing support. Limitations: Poor scaling with Gaussian count, no early termination, sorting latency on every frame. This method is based on the paper "3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering" by Kerbl et al. (2023). It was popularized by the "3D Gaussian Splatting in a Weekend" tutorial, which provided a complete, display-only renderer implementation using standard OpenGL and CPU sorting. It serves as an accessible entry point for understanding 3DGS rendering without the complexity of CUDA-based tile rasterization. 3D Gaussian Splatting in a Weekend, https://bfeldman.me/3dgs-weekend/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, https://github.com/akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) sascha-kirch/splaty, https://github.com/sascha-kirch/splaty, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
body: Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization is a GPU-parallel rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that divides the image into fixed-size tiles to manage memory and processing load, assigning Gaussians to tiles based on their axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs). It solves the performance bottleneck of sorting millions of splats per pixel by grouping work into tiles, enabling real-time rendering. Unlike non-tiled approaches that iterate over all Gaussians per pixel or use screen-space quads without tiling, this method restricts pixel iteration to relevant Gaussians within each tile, significantly reducing redundant computations. Inputs: gs: A collection of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by a mean position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, a 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, an opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. camera: A pinhole camera model with focal lengths fx, fy, principal point (cx, cy), image dimensions W \times H, and extrinsic parameters (rotation R \in SO(3), translation t \in \mathbb{R}^3). tilesize: Integer, default 32. sigmamultiplier: Float, default 3.0 (or 3.33 in some implementations). Controls the extent of the Gaussian's bounding box. Outputs: color: A tensor of shape [3, H, W] containing the final RGB image. alpha: A tensor of shape [H, W] containing the accumulated alpha values. Data Structures: tiledict: A mapping from tile index (u, v) to a list of Gaussian indices assigned to that tile. conics: A tensor of shape [N, 3] storing the inverse 2D covariance matrix elements a, b, c for each Gaussian. Steps: 1. Initialize background color tensor bg of shape [3, H, W] with black values (0.0) and clone it. 2. Transform Gaussian means to camera space using camera.transformpointsworldtocam and project to image plane using camera.projectpointscamtoimageplane. 3. Perform frustum culling with cullnearfarplanes=True, cullimagebounds=False, and fovmarginratio=0.3. 4. Sort Gaussians by depth of means back-to-front (backtofront=False). 5. Rotate 3D covariances to camera space using camera.rotatecovariancesworldtocam. 6. Approximate 2D covariances using approximate2dcovariances with eps2d=0.3. 7. Compute conics (inverse covariance matrices) using computeconics(covariancesimage). 8. Compute axis-aligned bounding boxes using computeaxisalignedboundingbox with usesimpleradius=True. 9. Assign Gaussians to tiles using assigngaussianstotiles based on bounding boxes and tilesize. 10. Evaluate spherical harmonics colors using evalsphericalharmonicscolor with degree=gs.shdegree. 11. Initialize output color tensor color of shape [3, H, W] and alpha tensor alpha of shape [H, W] to zeros. 12. Iterate over each tile (tileidxu, tileidxv) in tiledict. If no Gaussians are in the tile, continue. 13. Extract contiguous tensors for the tile: opacitiestile, shcolorstile, meansimagetile, conicstile indexed by idxgaussiansintile. 14. Calculate pixel bounds for the tile: u{start} = tile\idx\u \times tile\size, v{start} = tile\idx\v \times tile\size, u{end} = \min(u{start} + tile\size, W), v{end} = \min(v{start} + tile\size, H). 15. Iterate over pixels u{pix} from u{start} to u{end} and v{pix} from v{start} to v{end}. 16. For each pixel, iterate over Gaussians in the tile. If alpha[vpix, upix] >= 0.99, skip the Gaussian (early termination). 17. Retrieve Gaussian properties: opacitygaussian, shcolor, a, b, c from conicstile, and umean, vmean from meansimagetile. 18. Compute squared Mahalanobis distance: dist\sq = a \cdot du^2 + 2 \cdot b \cdot du \cdot dv + c \cdot dv^2, where du = u{pix} - u{mean} and dv = v{pix} - v{mean}. 19. Accumulate alpha and color: alpha[vpix, upix] += opacitygaussian exp(-0.5 distsq) and color[:, vpix, upix] += shcolor opacitygaussian exp(-0.5 distsq). 20. After processing all tiles, add background: color += bg (1 - alpha)[None,:,:]. 21. Clamp color to [0.0, 1.0] and convert to uint8 by multiplying by 255. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def tiled2dgaussiansplattingrasterization(gsmeans, gscovs, gsopacities, gsshcoeffs, camera, tilesize=32, sigmamultiplier=3.0): N = gsmeans.shape[0] H, W = camera.height, camera.width eps2d = 0.3 bg = torch.zeros((3, H, W)) # 1. Transform to Camera Space R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(camera.qworldtocam) meanscam = (R @ gsmeans.T).T + camera.tworldtocam # 2. Project to Image Plane zcam = meanscam[:, 2] u = camera.fx (meanscam[:, 0] / zcam) + camera.cx v = camera.fy (meanscam[:, 1] / zcam) + camera.cy # 3. Frustum Culling valid = (zcam > camera.nearplane) & (zcam < camera.farplane) meanscam = meanscam[valid] opacities = gsopacities[valid] covscam = [] for i in range(N): if valid[i]: covcam = R @ gscovs[i] @ R.T covscam.append(covcam) covscam = torch.stack(covscam) u = u[valid] v = v[valid] zcam = zcam[valid] # 4. Sort Gaussians by depth back-to-front, sortidx = torch.sort(zcam, descending=True) meanscam = meanscam[sortidx] opacities = opacities[sortidx] covscam = covscam[sortidx] u = u[sortidx] v = v[sortidx] zcam = zcam[sortidx] # 5. Approximate 2D Covariances & Compute Conics J = torch.zeros((len(valid), 2, 3)) J[:, 0, 0] = camera.fx / zcam J[:, 0, 2] = -camera.fx meanscam[:, 0] / (zcam 2) J[:, 1, 1] = camera.fy / zcam J[:, 1, 2] = -camera.fy meanscam[:, 1] / (zcam 2) L = R[:2,:2] Sigma2D = torch.zeros((len(valid), 2, 2)) for i in range(len(valid)): cov2dpart = L @ covscam[i][:2,:2] @ L.T Sigma2D[i] = J[i] @ cov2dpart @ J[i].T + eps2d torch.eye(2) det = Sigma2D[:, 0, 0] Sigma2D[:, 1, 1] - Sigma2D[:, 0, 1] Sigma2D[:, 1, 0] a = Sigma2D[:, 1, 1] / det b = -Sigma2D[:, 0, 1] / det c = Sigma2D[:, 0, 0] / det conics = torch.stack([a, b, c], dim=1) # 6. Compute Bounding Boxes & Assign to Tiles bboxes = computeboundingboxes(u, v, Sigma2D, sigmamultiplier) tiledict = {} numtilesu = math.ceil(W / tilesize) numtilesv = math.ceil(H / tilesize) for i in range(len(valid)): umin, vmin, umax, vmax = bboxes[i] tileumin = max(0, int(umin // tilesize)) tilevmin = max(0, int(vmin // tilesize)) tileumax = min(numtilesu - 1, int(umax // tilesize)) tilevmax = min(numtilesv - 1, int(vmax // tilesize)) for tu in range(tileumin, tileumax + 1): for tv in range(tilevmin, tilevmax + 1): key = (tu, tv) if key not in tiledict: tiledict[key] = [] tiledict[key].append(i) # 7. Initialize Output color = torch.zeros((3, H, W)) alpha = torch.zeros((H, W)) # 8. Rasterize Tiles for (tu, tv), indices in tiledict.items(): if not indices: continue idxtensor = torch.tensor(indices) opacitiestile = opacities[idxtensor] conicstile = conics[idxtensor] meanstile = torch.stack([u[idxtensor], v[idxtensor]], dim=1) # Evaluate spherical harmonics colors colorstile = torch.zeroslike(meanstile) ustart = tu tilesize vstart = tv tilesize uend = min(ustart + tilesize, W) vend = min(vstart + tilesize, H) for vpix in range(vstart, vend): for upix in range(ustart, uend): if alpha[vpix, upix] >= 0.99: continue currentalpha = alpha[vpix, upix] currentcolor = color[:, vpix, upix] for k in range(len(indices)): alphag = opacitiestile[k] ag, bg, cg = conicstile[k] ug, vg = meanstile[k] colorg = colorstile[k] du = upix - ug dv = vpix - vg distsq = ag du2 + 2 bg du dv + cg dv2 w = alphag torch.exp(-0.5 distsq) currentalpha += w currentcolor += colorg w alpha[vpix, upix] = currentalpha color[:, vpix, upix] = currentcolor # 9. Composite Background color = color + bg (1 - alpha)[None,:,:] color = torch.clamp(color, 0.0, 1.0) return color, alpha def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): # Standard quaternion-to-rotation conversion w, x, y, z = q[0], q[1], q[2], q[3] return torch.tensor([ [1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - zw), 2(xz + yw)], [2(xy + zw), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - xw)], [2(xz - yw), 2(yz + xw), 1 - 2(x2 + y2)] ]) def computeboundingboxes(u, v, Sigma2D, sigmamultiplier): # Simplified AABB from covariance trace scaled by sigmamultiplier trace = Sigma2D[:, 0, 0] + Sigma2D[:, 1, 1] radius = sigmamultiplier torch.sqrt(trace) umin = u - radius vmin = v - radius umax = u + radius vmax = v + radius return torch.stack([umin, vmin, umax, vmax], dim=1) A rasterization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that iterates over Gaussians rather than tiles, using axis-aligned bounding boxes to limit pixel iteration and transmittance-based early ray termination for performance optimization. It produces visually identical results to tiled rasterization in most cases but is significantly faster due to early stopping and better culling. Tile-Based Culling computes a precise Gaussian-to-Tile mapping to cull irrelevant tiles during 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. It improves upon standard conservative bounding box assignment by computing tight, opacity-aware bounding boxes and iteratively verifying tile intersections. It is distinguished from SnugBox by its iterative tile examination process, which results in higher runtime costs for the culling phase compared to AccuTile, though it may show marginal downstream performance gains due to undercounting artifacts. The Tile-based Rasteriser is the GPU-optimized sorting and compositing component of the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline that assigns projected 2D Gaussian splats to image tiles and sorts them by depth using a single global radix sort. It solves the performance bottleneck of per-pixel depth sorting for millions of splats by grouping work into tiles, enabling real-time rendering and efficient backpropagation. Unlike non-tiled approaches that sort per pixel or per tile independently, it uses a unified 64-bit key to bin and sort all (splat, tile) pairs in one pass. This method is a compute-shader stage that projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space, performs visibility and frustum culling, computes lighting, and prepares data for tile-based sorting. It bridges raw 3D Gaussian data and the tiled rasterization pipeline by ensuring only visible splats are processed and ordered by tile and depth. It differs from non-tiled approaches by explicitly preparing tile-boundary data and from tile-based culling by handling full projection and sorting key generation. Filters out Gaussians whose opacity \tau falls below the alpha-threshold \epsilon immediately during tile intersection, as their axis-aligned bounding box is considered empty. Combining all modifications decreased rendering time on the Bicycle scene at native resolution by a factor of 3.77 and GPU memory usage by a factor of 2.11 compared to the reference. Splits the rendering of Gaussians into batches. If gaussianspersplat is -1, splats all Gaussians in one call. If positive, splits into batches. Higher values increase speed but raise GPU memory usage. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Tiled rasterization enables real-time rendering of large scenes with millions of Gaussians. Performance gains from precomputation and opacity filtering are greatest at higher resolutions. Strengths: Efficient memory usage, parallelizable on GPU, supports real-time frame rates. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of tile size and sigma multiplier. Performance can degrade if tiles are too small (overhead) or too large (cache misses). Originated from the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline and detailed in. The tiled rasterization approach divides the image into tiles to manage memory and processing load, assigning Gaussians based on their bounding boxes. It is used in modern 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations to enable real-time rendering. sascha-kirch/splaty, https://github.com/sascha-kirch/splaty, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fast 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering via Easily Integrable Improvements, https://doi.org/10.1109/lsp.2024.3521379, fetched 2026-10-26 Fhz2346/3D-Gaussian-Splatting, https://github.com/Fhz2346/3D-Gaussian-Splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling
body: A rasterization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that iterates over Gaussians rather than tiles, using axis-aligned bounding boxes to limit pixel iteration and transmittance-based early ray termination for performance optimization. It produces visually identical results to tiled rasterization in most cases but is significantly faster due to early stopping and better culling. Inputs: gs: List of N Gaussians, each with 3D mean, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. camera: Camera object containing intrinsic parameters (fx, fy, cx, cy), image dimensions (W, H), and extrinsic rotation/translation. sigmamultiplier: Scaling factor for the 2D covariance approximation (default 3.33). Outputs: renderedimage: An H \times W \times 3 image tensor in uint8 format. Data Structures: umean, vmean: Projected 2D mean coordinates in pixel space. opacitygaussian: Scalar opacity value. shcolor: 3-channel color vector derived from SH evaluation. a, b, c: Elements of the inverse 2D covariance matrix (conics). umin, vmin, umax, vmax: Axis-aligned bounding box coordinates in pixel space. color, alpha: H \times W tensors initialized to zeros, accumulating final color and alpha per pixel. Steps: 1. Initialize color and alpha tensors to zeros. 2. Perform background initialization, projection, and sorting identical to rendersplats: transform means to camera space, project to image plane, frustum cull with fovmarginratio=0.3, sort Gaussians back-to-front, rotate covariances to camera space, approximate 2D covariances with eps2d=0.3, compute conics (a, b, c), evaluate SH colors, and compute AABBs. 3. Iterate over each Gaussian index i from 0 to len(gs). 4. Retrieve properties: umean, vmean, opacitygaussian, shcolor, a, b, c, umin, vmin, umax, vmax. 5. If opacitygaussian < 0.01, skip the Gaussian. 6. Iterate over pixels upix from umin to umax and vpix from vmin to vmax. 7. Check if pixel is within image bounds: if 0 <= upix < W and 0 <= vpix < H. 8. Read current pixel alpha. If alphapixel >= 0.99, skip the Gaussian for this pixel (early termination). 9. Compute squared Mahalanobis distance with half-pixel offset: du = u\pix + 0.5 - u\mean, dv = v\pix + 0.5 - v\mean, dist\sq = a \cdot du^2 + 2 \cdot b \cdot du \cdot dv + c \cdot dv^2. 10. Calculate Gaussian alpha \alphag = \exp(-0.5 \cdot dist\sq) \cdot opacity\gaussian and update pixel alpha and color using standard alpha blending. 11. After processing all Gaussians, add background and clamp/convert to uint8 as in rendersplats. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendersplatsfovculltransmittance(gs, camera, sigmamultiplier=3.33): W, H = camera.width, camera.height # Initialize color and alpha buffers color = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] alpha = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] # Preprocessing identical to rendersplats # Transform means, project, frustum cull (fovmarginratio=0.3), sort back-to-front # Rotate covariances, approximate 2D covariances (eps2d=0.3), compute conics # Evaluate SH colors, compute AABBs # (Assumed implemented in gs object or preprocessing step) for i in range(len(gs)): umean, vmean = gs[i].umean, gs[i].vmean opacitygaussian = gs[i].opacity shcolor = gs[i].shcolor a, b, c = gs[i].conics umin, vmin, umax, vmax = gs[i].aabb if opacitygaussian < 0.01: continue for upix in range(umin, umax + 1): for vpix in range(vmin, vmax + 1): if 0 <= upix < W and 0 <= vpix < H: if alpha[vpix][upix] >= 0.99: continue du = upix + 0.5 - umean dv = vpix + 0.5 - vmean distsq = a du2 + 2 b du dv + c dv2 alphag = math.exp(-0.5 distsq) opacitygaussian currentalpha = alpha[vpix][upix] alphanew = currentalpha + alphag (1.0 - currentalpha) colornew = [ color[vpix][upix][0] + shcolor[0] alphag (1.0 - currentalpha), color[vpix][upix][1] + shcolor[1] alphag (1.0 - currentalpha), color[vpix][upix][2] + shcolor[2] alphag (1.0 - currentalpha) ] alpha[vpix][upix] = alphanew color[vpix][upix] = colornew # Add background color and clamp/convert to uint8 for v in range(H): for u in range(W): for c in range(3): color[v][u][c] = max(0.0, min(1.0, color[v][u][c])) return [[int(c 255) for c in row] for row in color] Edge cases and pitfalls: Low-opacity Gaussians (opacitygaussian < 0.01) are skipped entirely to save computation. Fully opaque pixels (alphapixel >= 0.99) trigger early termination for subsequent Gaussians, preventing redundant blending. The half-pixel offset in the Mahalanobis distance calculation aligns the Gaussian center with pixel sampling coordinates. Bounding box iteration must be clamped to image dimensions to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Performance: Significantly faster than tiled rasterization due to early stopping and better culling, while producing visually identical results in most cases. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Tile-Based Culling
head: StopThePop Tile-Based Culling
body: Tile-Based Culling computes a precise Gaussian-to-Tile mapping to cull irrelevant tiles during 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. It improves upon standard conservative bounding box assignment by computing tight, opacity-aware bounding boxes and iteratively verifying tile intersections. It is distinguished from SnugBox by its iterative tile examination process, which results in higher runtime costs for the culling phase compared to AccuTile, though it may show marginal downstream performance gains due to undercounting artifacts. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color); image resolution; tile dimensions (typically 32x32 pixels, inherited from Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization). Outputs: A list of tile IDs for each Gaussian that require processing. Data Structures: Gaussian: Structure containing 3D position \mathbf{p}, 3x3 covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, and color. Tile: Identified by integer coordinates (tx, ty). Bounding Box: Axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in screen space, defined by min/max coordinates (x{min}, y{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}). Parameters: Padded Alpha Threshold: A value required to accurately compute bounding boxes and prevent undercounting of Gaussian-to-Tile mappings. The specific value is not provided in the source ablation study. In the cited implementation, this parameter was omitted, leading to loose bounding boxes and undercounting. Steps: 1. Compute Tight Bounding Box: For each Gaussian, compute a tight, opacity-aware axis-aligned bounding box in screen space. This involves projecting the Gaussian's 2D extent into screen space and determining the bounds based on opacity. Note: The source indicates that using thresholds in the original code prevents all bounding boxes from being tight. 2. Iterative Tile Examination: For each Gaussian, identify all tiles that intersect with the computed bounding box. Iteratively examine each candidate tile to determine if it should be included in the final mapping. 3. Warp-Level Load Balancing: Accelerate the tile examination process using warp-level load balancing techniques to handle the iterative checks efficiently on the GPU. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilebasedculling(gaussians, imagewidth, imageheight, tilesize): numtilesx = imagewidth // tilesize numtilesy = imageheight // tilesize gaussiantilemap = [] for gaussian in gaussians: # Step 1: Compute tight, opacity-aware bounding box bbox = computetightbbox(gaussian, tilesize) # Determine tile range covering the bounding box tileminx = max(0, bbox.xmin // tilesize) tileminy = max(0, bbox.ymin // tilesize) tilemaxx = min(numtilesx - 1, bbox.xmax // tilesize) tilemaxy = min(numtilesy - 1, bbox.ymax // tilesize) candidatetiles = [] # Step 2: Iteratively examine each tile touching the bounding box for ty in range(tileminy, tilemaxy + 1): for tx in range(tileminx, tilemaxx + 1): if istileintersectinggaussian(tx, ty, gaussian, tilesize): candidatetiles.append((tx, ty)) # Step 3: Warp-level load balancing accelerates this examination on GPU gaussiantilemap.append(candidatetiles) return gaussiantilemap def computetightbbox(gaussian, tilesize): # Project 3D position to screen space centerscreen = projecttoscreen(gaussian.position) # Compute 2D extent from covariance and opacity extent = compute2dextent(gaussian.covariance, gaussian.opacity) return BoundingBox(centerscreen[0] - name: SnugBox
body: SnugBox is a precise algorithm for computing Gaussian-to-tile bounding box intersections in 3D Gaussian Splatting, replacing the overly conservative tile assignment of standard 3D-GS to reduce the number of pixels processed per Gaussian. It computes an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) around each Gaussian using its elliptical extent in image space, allowing for tighter identification of intersected tiles compared to the standard method which inscribes a circle within a square. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters: mean \mui, scale si, rotation ri, opacity \sigmai. Camera parameters: viewing transform W, perspective projection Jacobian J. Image resolution and tile size. Outputs: Tile indices [x{min}, x{max}] \times [y{min}, y{max}] representing the tight AABB intersecting the Gaussian's elliptical extent. Data Structures: \Sigma{i{3D}}: 3x3 3D covariance matrix. \Sigma{i{2D}}: 2x2 2D projected covariance matrix. \Sigma{i{2D}}^{-1}: Inverse of the 2D covariance matrix, represented as \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{pmatrix}. t: Threshold value derived from opacity. Steps: 1. Project Covariance: Compute the 3D covariance \Sigma{i{3D}} = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T, where Si and Ri are diagonal scale and rotation matrices derived from si and ri. Project to 2D via \hat{\Sigma}{i{3D}} = J W \Sigma{i{3D}} W^T J^T, where J is the Jacobian of the first-order approximation of the perspective projection and W is the viewing transform. Drop the last row and column of \hat{\Sigma}{i{3D}} to obtain \Sigma{i{2D}}. 2. Compute Inverse and Threshold: Compute the inverse of the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{i{2D}}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{pmatrix}. Compute the threshold t = 2 \log(255 \sigmai). 3. Compute Extrema: The pixel extent satisfies the ellipse equation t = axd^2 + 2bxdyd + cyd^2, where xd = px - \mux and yd = py - \muy are coordinates relative to the 2D mean \mu{i{2D}}. Rearrange to solve for yd: yd = \frac{-bxd \pm \sqrt{(b^2 - ac)xd^2 + tc}}{c}. Find the xd values (x{d{args}}) where \partial yd / \partial xd = 0: x{d{args}} = \pm \sqrt{\frac{-b^2 t}{(b^2 - ac)a}}. Calculate y{min} and y{max} by substituting x{d{args}} into the rearranged equation and adding \muy. Calculate x{min} and x{max} by swapping yd and xd and constants a and c in the equations, solving for y{d{args}}, and adding \mux. 4. Map to Tiles: Convert bounding box edges to tile indices by dividing by tile size, rounding, and clipping to the image boundary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computesnugbox(mu2d, a, b, c, t, tilesize, imgw, imgh): """ Computes the tight AABB tile indices for a Gaussian using SnugBox. Args: mu2d: (2,) array, 2D mean [x, y] a, b, c: float, elements of inverse 2D covariance [[a, b], [b, c]] t: float, threshold 2 log(255 opacity) tilesize: int, pixels per tile imgw, imgh: int, image dimensions Returns: (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax): Tile indices """ # 1. Compute xd extrema locations denomyext = (b2 - ac) a if denomyext == 0: return (0, 0, 0, 0) # Guard against division by zero radicandx = (-b2 t) / denomyext if radicandx < 0: radicandx = 0 xdargs = math.sqrt(radicandx) # Evaluate yd at both + and - xdargs to find global min/max ycandidates = [] for xd in [xdargs, -xdargs]: rad = (b2 - ac) (xd2) + tc if rad < 0: rad = 0 sq = math.sqrt(rad) y1 = (-b xd + sq) / c y2 = (-b xd - sq) / c ycandidates.extend([y1, y2]) yminpx = mu2d[1] + min(ycandidates) ymaxpx = mu2d[1] + max(ycandidates) # 2. Compute yd extrema locations (swapped a/c) denomxext = (b2 - ca) c if denomxext == 0: return (0, 0, 0, 0) # Guard against division by zero radicandy = (-b2 t) / denomxext if radicandy < 0: radicandy = 0 ydargs = math.sqrt(radicandy) # Evaluate xd at both + and - ydargs xcandidates = [] for yd in [ydargs, -ydargs]: rad = (b2 - ca) (yd2) + ta if rad < 0: rad = 0 sq = math.sqrt(rad) x1 = (-b yd + sq) / a x2 = (-b yd - sq) / a xcandidates.extend([x1, x2]) xminpx = mu2d[0] + min(xcandidates) xmaxpx = mu2d[0] + max(xcandidates) # 3. Map to Tiles xmintile = int(math.floor(xminpx / tilesize)) xmaxtile = int(math.ceil(xmaxpx / tilesize)) ymintile = int(math.floor(yminpx / tilesize)) ymaxtile = int(math.ceil(ymaxpx / tilesize)) # Clip to image boundary maxxtile = imgw // tilesize maxytile = imgh // tilesize xmintile = max(0, min(xmintile, maxxtile)) xmaxtile = max(0, min(xmaxtile, maxxtile)) ymintile = max(0, min(ymintile, maxytile)) ymaxtile = max(0, min(ymaxtile, maxytile)) return (xmintile, xmaxtile, ymintile, ymaxtile) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Covariance: If the determinant of \Sigma{i{2D}} is zero (degenerate Gaussian), the inverse is undefined. A guard should handle this, potentially returning a minimal bounding box or skipping the Gaussian. Numerical Stability: The term under the square root in the extrema calculation and the coordinate solving must be non-negative. Numerical errors may cause slight negative values; these should be clamped to zero. Division by Zero: The denominators in the extrema formulas involve a and c. If these are zero, the formula breaks. This corresponds to axis-aligned ellipses with infinite extent in one direction, which is physically unlikely for a valid Gaussian but possible in degenerate cases. Time Complexity: Constant number of operations per Gaussian. It is called twice in the rendering pipeline: once during preprocessing to count Gaussians per tile, and once in duplicateWithKeys to populate the Gaussian-to-tile arrays. Memory Complexity: No additional significant memory overhead beyond the computed bounding box indices. Performance: Produces an average overall inference speed-up of 1.82× on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending datasets compared to baseline 3D-GS. Strengths: Significantly tighter bounding boxes than the standard 3D-GS method, reducing the number of tiles processed per Gaussian. Limitations: More complex than the standard square-inscribing-circle method, though the overhead is small. SnugBox was introduced in the "Speedy-Splat" paper (2025) as a plug-and-play optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the overly conservative tile assignment of the original 3D-GS algorithm, which assigns a Gaussian to any tile intersecting a square inscribing a circle. SnugBox replaces this with a tight AABB derived from the Gaussian's elliptical extent.
