name: Tile-based Rasteriser
head: 3DGS GPU Rasterization, Radix Sort Binning, Tile-Based Rasterization, Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort, Tile-based Rasterizer, Tile-based sorting rasterizer
body: The Tile-based Rasteriser is the GPU-optimized sorting and compositing component of the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline that assigns projected 2D Gaussian splats to image tiles and sorts them by depth using a single global radix sort. It solves the performance bottleneck of per-pixel depth sorting for millions of splats by grouping work into tiles, enabling real-time rendering and efficient backpropagation. Unlike non-tiled approaches that sort per pixel or per tile independently, it uses a unified 64-bit key to bin and sort all (splat, tile) pairs in one pass. Inputs: List of N projected 2D Gaussian splats, each defined by center (xi, yi), 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i, color ci, opacity \alphai, and depth Zc. Image resolution (W, H) and tile dimensions 16 \times 16 pixels. Outputs: A sorted list of (splat, tile) pairs, ordered by tile ID and then by depth Zc within each tile. The final rendered image and gradients for training. Data Structures: Splat List: Array of N splats. Each splat stores its projected 2D parameters: position (xi, yi), covariance \Sigma'i, color ci, opacity \alphai, and depth Zc. Tile Grid: Implicit grid of tiles covering the image, with tile dimensions Tw \times Th = 16 \times 16 pixels. Sort Key: A 64-bit integer key for each (splat, tile) pair, packing the tile ID into the high bits and the splat's depth Zc into the low bits. Sorted Pairs: Array of (splatindex, tileid, depth) tuples, ordered by the Sort Key. Steps: 1. Tile Assignment: Assign each Gaussian to every tile its projected 2D splat touches. If a splat straddles tile boundaries, it is duplicated into each relevant tile. 2. Key Packing: For each (splat, tile) pair, pack the tile ID into the high bits and the splat's depth Zc into the low bits of a 64-bit integer key. 3. Global Radix Sort: Perform one GPU radix sort over all (splat, tile) pairs. This simultaneously bins splats by tile ID (contiguity) and sorts them by depth within each tile. 4. Tile Processing: Each tile is processed by one GPU thread block that walks the sorted list. 5. Compositing: For each pixel in a tile, run the front-to-back compositing loop using the tile's sorted list of splats, evaluating per-pixel alpha \alphai(\mathbf{x}) and breaking early when transmittance T < \epsilon. 6. Backpropagation: Reuse the same sorted lists for training, allowing gradients to flow to position, shape, opacity, and color without additional sorting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tilebasedrasterization(splats, imagewidth, imageheight, tilewidth=16, tileheight=16, epsilon=1e-3): numtilesx = (imagewidth + tilewidth - 1) // tilewidth numtilesy = (imageheight + tileheight - 1) // tileheight # Step 1 & 2: Tile Assignment and Pair Generation pairs = [] for i, splat in enumerate(splats): # Determine tile coordinates overlapping the splat's 2D projection tileminx = max(0, int((splat['x'] - 2 splat['sigmax']) / tilewidth)) tilemaxx = min(numtilesx - 1, int((splat['x'] + 2 splat['sigmax']) / tilewidth)) tileminy = max(0, int((splat['y'] - 2 splat['sigmay']) / tileheight)) tilemaxy = min(numtilesy - 1, int((splat['y'] + 2 splat['sigmay']) / tileheight)) for ty in range(tileminy, tilemaxy + 1): for tx in range(tileminx, tilemaxx + 1): tileid = ty numtilesx + tx pairs.append((i, tileid, splat['Zc'])) # Step 3: Key Packing and Global Radix Sort # Pack tileid into high bits and depth into low bits keys = [(tileid << 32) | depth for i, tileid, depth in pairs] sortedindices = sorted(range(len(keys)), key=lambda k: keys[k]) sortedpairs = [pairs[i] for i in sortedindices] # Step 4 & 5: Tile Processing and Compositing image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] for tileid in range(numtilesx numtilesy): ty = tileid // numtilesx tx = tileid % numtilesx ystart, yend = ty tileheight, min((ty + 1) tileheight, imageheight) xstart, xend = tx tilewidth, min((tx + 1) tilewidth, imagewidth) # Extract contiguous segment for this tile from sorted list tilesegment = [] for idx, (splatidx, tid, depth) in enumerate(sortedpairs): if tid == tileid: tilesegment.append((splatidx, depth)) elif tid > tileid: break for y in range(ystart, yend): for x in range(xstart, xend): transmittance = 1.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for splatidx, in tilesegment: splat = splats[splatidx] alpha = computegaussianalpha(splat, x, y) if alpha > 0: color[0] += splat['color'][0] alpha transmittance color[1] += splat['color'][1] alpha transmittance color[2] += splat['color'][2] alpha transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < epsilon: break image[y][x] = color return image def computegaussianalpha(splat, x, y): # Standard 2D Gaussian evaluation at pixel coordinates dx = x - splat['x'] dy = y - splat['y'] invdet = 1.0 / (splat['sigmaxx'] splat['sigmayy'] - splat['sigmaxy']2) exponent = -0.5 invdet (splat['sigmayy'] dx2 - 2 splat['sigmaxy'] dx dy + splat['sigmaxx'] dy2) return splat['opacity'] max(0.0, math.exp(exponent)) Parameters: Tile size: 16 \times 16 pixels. Early termination threshold: \epsilon (implementation-defined, typically small). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sorting per pixel is too slow for millions of splats; tile-based sorting with a single global radix sort is required for real-time performance. A splat straddling tile boundaries must be duplicated into each relevant tile. Precision issues in depth sorting may affect compositing order; ensure depth values are packed correctly into the sort key. Time Complexity: One O(n) radix sort over all (splat, tile) pairs, where n is the number of (splat, tile) pairs. This replaces thousands of per-tile sorts. Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing the (splat, tile) pairs and sorted indices. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 benchmark, the method reaches 27.21 dB PSNR and 0.214 LPIPS at 134 fps, rendering roughly three orders of magnitude faster than previous quality leaders. Scaling: The method scales well with the number of splats due to the single global sort. Strengths: Real-time performance, efficient use of GPU parallelism, shared sorting for rendering and training. Limitations: Memory overhead for duplicating splats across tiles. When to Use: Real-time rendering and training of 3D Gaussian Splatting. When Not to Use: Scenes with very few splats where the overhead of tile management outweighs the benefits. The Tile-based Rasteriser was introduced as part of the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It was designed to address the performance bottleneck of sorting millions of splats for real-time rendering and training. The method leverages GPU-optimized radix sorting to achieve efficient per-tile depth ordering. It is used in the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline for novel-view synthesis. name: Gaussian Splat Projection and Sorting
body: This method is a compute-shader stage that projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space, performs visibility and frustum culling, computes lighting, and prepares data for tile-based sorting. It bridges raw 3D Gaussian data and the tiled rasterization pipeline by ensuring only visible splats are processed and ordered by tile and depth. It differs from non-tiled approaches by explicitly preparing tile-boundary data and from tile-based culling by handling full projection and sorting key generation. Inputs: SplatsBuffer: std430 buffer of Splat structs. InstanceTransformsBuffer: std430 buffer of mat4 instance model matrices. SplatInstanceIdsBuffer: std430 buffer of uvec2 where x is the unique instance ID and y is the index into SplatsBuffer. Uniforms: std140 uniform block containing camerapos, time, dims (image resolution), pointcount, and lightcount. LightRigBuffer: std430 buffer of vec4 light data. SplatLightingBuffer: std430 buffer of uint packed lighting data. InstanceRelightBuffer: std430 buffer of vec4 per-instance relighting data. GridDimensionsBuffer: std430 buffer storing grid dimensions. projectionmatrix, viewmatrix: Standard camera matrices. Outputs: CulledBuffer: std430 buffer of RasterizeData structs for visible splats. SortKeysBuffer: std430 buffer of uint keys for sorting. SortValuesBuffer: std430 buffer of uint values (splat indices) for sorting. Histograms: std430 buffer containing sortbuffersize and histogram data. Data Structures: Unverified code. Used to partition the screen into tiles for sorting. SHC0 to SHC36: Spherical harmonic constants. SHC0=0.28209479177387814, SHC1=0.4886025119029199, SHC20=1.0925484305920792, SHC21=1.0925484305920792, SHC22=0.31539156525252005, SHC23=1.0925484305920792, SHC24=0.5462742152960396, SHC30=0.5900435899266435, SHC31=2.890611442640554, SHC32=0.4570457994644658, SHC33=0.3731763325901154, SHC34=0.4570457994644658, SHC35=1.445305721320277, SHC36=0.5900435899266435. If id >= pointcount, return. 2. Barrier: Synchronize workgroup. 3. Retrieve Instance Data: instanceid = splatinstancedata[id].x, uniquesplatindex = splatinstancedata[id].y. 4. Load Data: Load splat from splatbuffer[uniquesplatindex] and modelmatrix from instancemodelmatrices[instanceid]. 5. Visibility Check: If modelmatrix[0][3] < 0.5, return. Set modelmatrix[0][3] = 0.0. 6. Frustum Culling: Compute objectlinear from modelmatrix. Compute worldcovariance = objectlinear DECODECOVARIANCE(splat.covariance) transpose(objectlinear). Compute worldpos = modelmatrix vec4(splat.position, 1.0). Compute viewpos = viewmatrix worldpos. Compute clippos = projectionmatrix viewpos. Check bounds: If any component of clippos.xyz is less than vec3(-viewbounds, 0.0) or greater than vec3(viewbounds, clippos.w), return. viewbounds = clippos.w 1.2. 7. Time Animation: splattime = time - splat.time. timefactor = easeoutcubic(clamp(splattime, 0, 1)). timefactorlate = easeoutcubic(clamp(splattime - 0.35, 0, 1)). splatopacity = splat.opacity timefactorlate timefactorlate. splatscale = mix(2.0, 1.0, timefactorlate). easeoutcubic(x) = 1.0 - (1.0-x)^3. 8. Project Covariance: Call projectcovariance(worldcovariance, splatscale, viewpos.xyz, dims). Return vec3(cov2d[0][0]+0.3, cov2d[0][1], cov2d[1][1]+0.3). 9. Check Determinant: det = covariance.xcovariance.z - covariance.ycovariance.y. If det == 0.0, return. 10. Compute View Direction: viewdir = normalize(inverse(objectlinear) (worldpos.xyz - camerapos)). 17. Compute Base Color: basecolor = getcolor(viewdir, splat.shcoefficients). getcolor evaluates SH up to degree 3 using constants SHC0..SHC36 and coefficients from splat.shcoefficients. 18. Relighting: relight = instancerelight[instanceid 2]. If relight.w > 0.5: If relight.z > 0.5, basecolor = max(0.0, 0.5 + splat.shcoefficients[0..2] SHC0). Else, basecolor = relightfactor(uniquesplatindex, worldpos.xyz, objectlinear, relight.x, relight.y, instancerelight[instanceid2+1].rgb). 19. Fill RasterizeData: data.imagepos = imagepos. data.conic = vec3(covariance.z, -covariance.y, covariance.x) / det. data.color = vec4(basecolor, splatopacity). data.posxy = worldpos.xy. data.posz = worldpos.z. data.depthdata = vec4(-viewpos.z, 0, 0, 0). Loop y from rectbounds.y to rectbounds.w, x from rectbounds.x to rectbounds.z: tileid = ygridsize.x + x. key = (tileid << 16) | depth. sortkeys[sortbufferoffset] = key. sortvalues[sortbufferoffset] = id. sortbufferoffset++. body: This method renders 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by projecting 3D Gaussian distributions into 2D screen-space quads, utilizing a pre-sorted order buffer and view-space projection data to handle transparency via alpha blending. Unlike its parent 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced), which uses instanced drawing with standard alpha blending, this method explicitly constructs screen-space quads in the vertex shader to allow for precise frustum culling and selection highlighting, and it differs from the sibling Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by not using tiled memory optimizations or screen-space depth sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-sorted order buffer (OrderBuffer) mapping instance IDs to splat indices, and view-space projection data (SplatViewData) containing camera-space positions, axes, and colors for each splat. Output: A framebuffer with composited colors and alpha values, where splats are drawn as screen-space quads. Data Structures: OrderBuffer: An array of integers where the index corresponds to the draw call instance ID, and the value is the index into the splat data buffer. SplatViewData: A structure containing pre-computed view-space data for each splat. Fields include centerClipPos (clip-space position for depth and behind-camera checks), axis1 and axis2 (2D vectors for projected Gaussian axes), color (packed color and opacity, often stored as half-floats), and pos (normalized screen-space position for falloff calculation). Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Shader: Instance Mapping and Validation Map instance ID to splat index: instID = OrderBuffer[instanceID]. Load view data: view = SplatViewData[instID]. Check if behind camera: if view.centerClipPos.w <= 0. If behind, output a NaN vertex to discard the primitive. 2. Vertex Shader: Quad Position Calculation Decompress color from view.color (half-floats) into o.col.rgba. Calculate quad position in clip space: quadPos = float2(instanceID & 1, (instanceID >> 1) & 1) 2.0 - 1.0. Scale quad position: quadPos = 2.0. Calculate screen delta: deltaScreenPos = (quadPos.x view.axis1 + quadPos.y view.axis2) 2.0 / ScreenParams.xy. Apply delta: o.vertex.xy += deltaScreenPos view.centerClipPos.w. 3. Vertex Shader: Selection Highlighting (Optional) If SplatBitsValid is true, calculate wordIdx = instID // 32 and bitIdx = instID & 31. Load selection word: selVal = SplatSelectedBits.Load(wordIdx 4). If bit set, set o.col.a = -1 to mark as selected. 4. Fragment Shader: Gaussian Evaluation and Compositing Calculate falloff: power = -dot(i.pos, i.pos). Compute alpha: alpha = exp(power). If not selected (i.col.a >= 0), saturate alpha: alpha = saturate(alpha i.col.a). If selected (i.col.a < 0), apply magenta outline: if alpha > 7.0/255.0, set alpha = 1 and i.col.rgb = selectedColor if alpha < 10.0/255.0; otherwise alpha = saturate(alpha + 0.3) and tint i.col.rgb = lerp(i.col.rgb, selectedColor, 0.5). Discard if alpha < 1.0/255.0. Output final color: res = half4(i.col.rgb alpha, alpha). Formulas: Screen Delta Calculation: \text{deltaScreenPos} = \frac{(\text{quadPos}x \cdot \text{axis1} + \text{quadPos}y \cdot \text{axis2}) \cdot 2}{\text{ScreenResolution}} Where quadPos is the normalized quad corner (-1 to 1), axis1 and axis2 are the projected Gaussian axes in screen space, and ScreenResolution is the pixel dimensions. Gaussian Alpha: \alpha = e^{-\|\mathbf{p}\|^2} Where \mathbf{p} is the normalized screen-space position relative to the splat center. Parameters: ScreenParams.xy: Screen resolution in pixels. selectedColor: Magenta color vector for highlighting selected splats. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Behind Camera: Splats with clip-space w \le 0 must be discarded to prevent rendering artifacts, handled by outputting a NaN vertex. Precision: Half-float decompression must be handled correctly to avoid color banding or incorrect alpha values. Selection Logic: The selection bit logic relies on a 32-bit word array, so instance IDs must be correctly mapped to word and bit indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. a) t def decompresshalffloat(halfval): return halfval # Conceptual decompression DISCARDPRIMITIVE = object() DISCARDFRAGMENT = object() SELECTEDCOLOR = Vec3(1.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Magenta def vertexshader(instanceid, orderbuffer, splatviewdata, screenparams, splatbitsvalid, splatselectedbits): instid = orderbuffer[instanceid] view = splatviewdata[instid] if view.centerclippos.w <= 0: return DISCARDPRIMITIVE ocol = decompresshalffloat(view.color) quadx = instanceid & 1 quady = (instanceid >> 1) & 1 quadpos = Vec2(quadx, quady) 2.0 - 1.0 quadpos = Vec2(quadpos.x 2.0, quadpos.y 2.0) delta = Vec2((quadpos.x view.axis1.x + quadpos.y view.axis2.x) 2.0 / screenparams.x, (quadpos.x view.axis1.y + quadpos.y view.axis2.y) 2.0 / screenparams.y) overtex = Vec2(view.centerclippos.x + delta.x view.centerclippos.w, view.centerclippos.y + delta.y view.centerclippos.w) if splatbitsvalid: wordidx = instid // 32 bitidx = instid & 31 selval = splatselectedbits.Load(wordidx 4) if (selval & (1 << bitidx)): ocol.a = -1.0 return {'vertex': overtex, 'color': ocol, 'pos': view.pos} def fragmentshader(inputdata): power = -dot(inputdata['pos'], inputdata['pos']) alpha = math.exp(power) if inputdata['color'].a >= 0: alpha = saturate(alpha inputdata['color'].a) else: if alpha > 7.0 / 255.0: if alpha < 10.0 / 255.0: alpha = 1.0 rgb = SELECTEDCOLOR else: alpha = saturate(alpha + 0.3) rgb = lerp(inputdata['color'].rgb, SELECTEDCOLOR, 0.5) else: rgb = inputdata['color'].rgb if alpha < 1.0 / 255.0: raise DISCARDFRAGMENT return Vec4(rgb.r alpha, rgb.g alpha, rgb.b alpha, alpha) WebGL Gaussian Splatting is a real-time rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes in web browsers, typically implemented using WebGL 1.0 and libraries like Three.js. It solves the problem of displaying large-scale, photorealistic radiance field reconstructions on standard client hardware without requiring neural network inference or heavy server-side processing. Unlike parent method Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad), which relies on a pre-sorted order buffer and view-space projection data, this method performs depth sorting in a JavaScript Web Worker and projects 3D Gaussians into screen-space quads using custom vertex and fragment shaders. It sets itself apart from sibling Gaussian Splat Fragment Shader by providing the complete pipeline, including data parsing, instance matrix construction, and CPU-side sorting, rather than just the shading logic. The Gaussian Splat Fragment Shader evaluates the 2D Gaussian alpha value at each fragment to determine splat coverage and modulates the fragment color accordingly. It composites the new splat over the existing framebuffer color using pre-multiplied alpha blending. It is distinguished from its parent method by handling the per-pixel transparency logic, alpha cutoffs, and framebuffer packing directly in the fragment stage, rather than relying on CPU-side sorting or generic quad rasterization. Debug Splat Point Rendering renders small quads at the center of each splat for debugging, optionally displaying the splat index as color. The vertex shader loads splat data, transforms the center to world and clip space, and applies a small offset in screen space based on SplatSize and ScreenParams.xy. If DisplayIndex is true, the splat index is encoded into the RGB color channels for visualization. Gaussian Splat Shader Property Configuration configures the material property block with splat count, SH degree, brightness, scale, antialiasing, transform matrix, and optional skinning/volume lighting data for the GPU render pass. Key parameters include shDegree (capped by the asset's SHBands property), brightness (default 1.0f), and scaleFactor (default 1.0f). A pitfall is that portable shader variants require valid sampled resources even when skinning is disabled; binding null or uninitialized buffers causes shader compilation/runtime errors. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of splats, as each splat is processed once in the vertex shader and potentially once in the fragment shader. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the order buffer and view-space projection data. Measured Performance: Performance is highly dependent on the number of splats and the efficiency of the pre-sorted order buffer. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of splats. Strengths: Simple implementation, efficient use of standard rasterization pipelines, effective frustum culling, and support for selection highlighting. Limitations: Requires CPU-side sorting, which can be a bottleneck for very large scenes. When to Use: Ideal for real-time visualization of 3DGS scenes in desktop and mobile applications where simplicity and compatibility are prioritized. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes requiring dynamic, per-frame sorting or complex lighting effects that cannot be captured by the simple Gaussian falloff model. The method originates from the broader field of 3D Gaussian Splatting, introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The specific implementation of screen-space quad rendering with pre-sorted order buffers was popularized by open-source projects such as UnityGaussianSplatting and svorenderer. It is widely used in web-based viewers (e.g., WebGL Gaussian Splatting) and desktop applications (e.g., UnitySplats) for real-time visualization of photorealistic 3D reconstructions. mmalesadev/svorenderer, https://github.com/mmalesadev/svorenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) aras-p/UnityGaussianSplatting, https://github.com/aras-p/UnityGaussianSplatting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) arloopa/UnitySplats, https://github.com/arloopa/UnitySplats, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

body: WebGL Gaussian Splatting is a real-time rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes in web browsers, typically implemented using WebGL 1.0 and libraries like Three.js. It solves the problem of displaying large-scale, photorealistic radiance field reconstructions on standard client hardware without requiring neural network inference or heavy server-side processing. Unlike parent method Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad), which relies on a pre-sorted order buffer and view-space projection data, this method performs depth sorting in a JavaScript Web Worker and projects 3D Gaussians into screen-space quads using custom vertex and fragment shaders. It sets itself apart from sibling Gaussian Splat Fragment Shader by providing the complete pipeline, including data parsing, instance matrix construction, and CPU-side sorting, rather than just the shading logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary.splat file containing Gaussian parameters (position, scale, quaternion, color, opacity). Output: A rendered image of the Gaussian splats composited via alpha blending. Data Structures: The implementation uses InstancedBufferGeometry with the following attributes: 1. position: A Float32Array of size 18 (6 vertices 3 components) defining a hardcoded quad with vertices at (2,2,0), (-2,2,0), (-2,-2,0), (2,-2,0) and their duplicates for triangle indexing. 2. splatColor: A Float32Array of size 4 \times N, where N is the vertex count. Stores RGBA values normalized to [0,1]. 3. splatCenterCovariance: A Float32Array of size 9 \times N. Stores the upper-triangular 3x3 covariance matrix components. Layout per splat: [centerx, centery, centerz, M11, M12, M13, M22, M23, M33]. Binary File Layout (.splat): Each vertex occupies 32 bytes: Offset 0-11: Float32 center (3 floats). Offset 12-23: Float32 scale (3 floats). Offset 24-27: Uint8 color (R, G, B, A). Offset 28-31: Uint8 quaternion (x, y, z, w). The quaternion is stored as integers 0-255 and must be normalized by subtracting 128 and dividing by 128.0, with the z-component negated. Numbered Steps: 1. Data Parsing: Read the binary file into a Uint8Array. Calculate N = \lfloor \text{byteLength} / 32 \rfloor. For each vertex i: Extract center from fbuffer[8i + 0..2]. Extract scale from fbuffer[8i + 3..5]. Extract quaternion bytes from ubuffer[32i + 28..31]. Normalize: q = (\text{byte} - 128) / 128.0. Negate qz. Extract color bytes from ubuffer[32i + 24..27]. Normalize to [0,1]. Construct a 4x4 instance matrix Mi: Create rotation matrix R from quaternion q. Create scale matrix S from scale vector. Mi = R \cdot S \cdot R^T (transposes and premultiplication form the transformation matrix). Set position components of Mi to center. Set color/alpha components of Mi (elements 3, 7, 11, 15) to normalized RGBA. 2. Depth Sorting (Web Worker): Pass the array of N instance matrices and the camera view vector (from camera.matrixWorld elements 2, 6, 10) to a sorting function. Calculate depth for each splat i: di = \text{view}x \cdot Mi[12] + \text{view}y \cdot Mi[13] + \text{view}z \cdot Mi[14]. The notes describe a 16-bit single-pass counting sort, but the provided implementation uses JavaScript's native.sort() method, yielding O(N \log N) complexity. Reorder matrices: M{sorted}[j] = M{original}[depthIndex[j]]. Transfer sorted matrices back to the main thread via postMessage with transferable objects to avoid blocking. 3. Vertex Shader Execution (Per Instance): Projection: Extract splat center C and instance matrix M. Compute camera-space position: C{cam} = V \cdot C, where V is the view matrix. Compute focal length: f = \frac{h}{2 \tan(\frac{fov \cdot \pi}{360})}, where h is viewport height and fov is vertical FOV in degrees. Compute Jacobian J of the projection: J = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{fx}{z} & 0 & -\frac{fx x}{z^2} \\ 0 & \frac{fy}{z} & -\frac{fy y}{z^2} \end{bmatrix} where (x,y,z) = C{cam} and fx, fy are focal lengths. Compute transformation matrix T = W \cdot J, where W is the rotation part of the view matrix (transpose of view matrix rotation). Compute 2D covariance: \mathbf{cov}{2D} = T^T \mathbf{M}{instance} T. Regularize: Add 0.3 to \mathbf{cov}{2D}[0][0] and \mathbf{cov}{2D}[1][1] to prevent singularities. Eigen Decomposition: d1 = \mathbf{cov}{2D}[0][0], d2 = \mathbf{cov}{2D}[1][1], o = \mathbf{cov}{2D}[0][1]. mid = 0.5(d1 + d2). radius = \sqrt{(\frac{d1 - d2}{2})^2 + o^2}. \lambda1 = mid + radius. \lambda2 = \max(mid - radius, 0.1). Basis Vectors: d = \text{normalize}(o, \lambda1 - d1). v1 = \min(\sqrt{2\lambda1}, 1024.0) \cdot d. v2 = \min(\sqrt{2\lambda2}, 1024.0) \cdot d^\perp (where d^\perp = (dy, -dx)). Positioning and Culling: Compute screen center: v{Center} = \frac{pos{2d}}{w}, where pos{2d} is the projected center. Compute final position for quad vertex (x,y): p{screen} = v{Center} + \frac{x \cdot v2 + y \cdot v1}{viewport} \cdot 2.0 Set gl\Position = (p{screen}, 0.0, 1.0). Frustum Culling: bounds = 1.2 \cdot w. If pos{2d}.z < -pos{2d}.w or |pos{2d}.x| > bounds or |pos{2d}.y| > bounds, set gl\Position = (0,0,2,1) and return. 4. Fragment Shader Execution: Compute squared distance from pixel to splat center: A = -\mathbf{v}{Position} \cdot \mathbf{v}{Position}. If A < -4.0 (i.e., distance squared > 4.0), discard fragment. Compute alpha: B = e^A \cdot v{Color}.a. Output color: gl\FragColor = (B \cdot v{Color}.rgb, B). 5. Blending: Use custom blending: blendSrc = OneMinusDstAlphaFactor, blendDst = OneFactor, blendSrcAlpha = OneMinusDstAlphaFactor, blendDstAlpha = OneFactor. Disable depth test and depth write. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vertexshader(instancematrix, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, viewport, fov, quadvertex): # 1. Extract center and compute camera space center = instancematrix.position centercam = viewmatrix vec4(center, 1.0) x, y, z = centercam.xyz # 2. Compute Jacobian fx = viewport.y / (2.0 math.tan(fov math.pi / 360.0)) fy = fx # Assuming square pixels or similar scaling J = mat3( fx / z, 0, -(fx x) / (z z), 0, fy / z, -(fy y) / (z z), 0, 0, 0) # 3. Compute 2D Covariance # Extract 3x3 rotation matrix from viewmatrix W = mat3(viewmatrix[0][0], viewmatrix[0][1], viewmatrix[0][2], viewmatrix[1][0], viewmatrix[1][1], viewmatrix[1][2], viewmatrix[2][0], viewmatrix[2][1], viewmatrix[2][2]) T = transpose(W) J cov2d = transpose(T) instancematrix.covariance3x3 T # 4. Regularize cov2d[0][0] += 0.3 cov2d[1][1] += 0.3 # 5. Eigen Decomposition d1 = cov2d[0][0] d2 = cov2d[1][1] off = cov2d[0][1] mid = 0.5 (d1 + d2) radius = math.sqrt(((d1 - d2) / 2.0)2 + off2) lambda1 = mid + radius lambda2 = max(mid - radius, 0.1) # 6. Basis Vectors diagvec = normalize(vec2(off, lambda1 - d1)) v1 = min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda1), 1024.0) diagvec v2 = min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda2), 1024.0) vec2(diagvec.y, -diagvec.x) # 7. Project Center pos2d = projectionmatrix vec4(center, 1.0) vcenter = pos2d.xy / pos2d.w # 8. Final Position projectedcov = vcenter + (quadvertex.x v2 + quadvertex.y v1) / viewport 2.0 glPosition = vec4(projectedcov, 0.0, 1.0) # 9. Culling bounds = 1.2 pos2d.w if pos2d.z < -pos2d.w or abs(pos2d.x) > bounds or abs(pos2d.y) > bounds: glPosition = vec4(0, 0, 2, 1) return def fragmentshader(vposition, vcolor): A = -dot(vposition, vposition) if A < -4.0: return # Discard fragment B = math.exp(A) vcolor.a return vec4(B vcolor.rgb, B) Time Complexity: Sorting is O(N \log N) using JavaScript's native.sort() method, performed in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread. Rendering is O(N \cdot P) where P is the number of pixels covered by quads. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing splat data and instance matrices. Performance: Real-time on ordinary graphics hardware, significantly faster than NeRFs for inference. Performance depends on vertex count and viewport resolution. Limitations: Does not support view-dependent shading (spherical harmonics) in this basic implementation to reduce file size. name: Depth-First Splat Sorting
head: Pre-fragment depth sort, Sorting visible splats by depth
body: Depth-First Splat Sorting is a preprocessing step for 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering that sorts visible Gaussian splats by camera-space depth before they are expanded into per-tile fragments. It solves the problem of high sorting overhead inherent in the original 3DGS pipeline, where fragments (one per tile a splat touches) are sorted using a combined 48-bit key. By sorting the smaller set of visible splats first, this method reduces the number of items to sort by a factor of 1.5 to 4, significantly lowering computational cost while maintaining correct depth ordering for subsequent rasterization. The method operates on a list of "staged splats" (visible 3D Gaussians projected into screen space). The goal is to produce a list of tile fragments that preserves the depth order of the original splats, allowing for efficient grouping by tile ID later. Inputs: splatlist: An array of N visible splats. Each splat i contains: depth: Camera-space depth value (zi). tileids: A list of tile IDs touched by the splat. tilecounts: The number of tiles touched (ki = \text{len}(tile\ids)). index: The original index in the unsorted list (used as the sort value). Outputs: fragmentlist: An array of tile fragments. The total size is \sum{i=0}^{N-1} ki. Fragments are stored such that fragments from splat i occupy a contiguous block in the array, and these blocks are ordered by the depth of splat i. Data Structures: Splat Item: Contains depth (float), tileids (array of integers), tilecount (integer). Fragment Item: Contains tileid (integer), splatindex (integer, referencing the original splat), and potentially other attributes copied from the splat (position, covariance, color). The exact layout depends on the downstream rasterizer but must include tileid for grouping. Steps: 1. Sort Splats by Depth: Perform a stable radix sort on the splatlist using depth as the key and index as the value. Key: 32-bit depth value. Value: 32-bit splat index. This produces a permutation of splats ordered from nearest to farthest. 2. Compute Exclusive Prefix Sum: Calculate the exclusive prefix sum of the tilecounts from the sorted splats to determine storage offsets for fragments. Let ki be the number of tiles touched by the i-th splat in the sorted list. Let Oi be the offset for the i-th splat's fragments. O0 = 0 Oi = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} kj \quad \text{for } i > 0 This can be computed in a single pass: python offsets = [] currentoffset = 0 for splat in sortedsplatlist: offsets.append(currentoffset) currentoffset += splat.tilecount 3. Create Fragments: Iterate through the sorted splats and their corresponding offsets. For each splat i: Let Oi be the computed offset. For each tile ID t in splat.tileids: Create a fragment object. Set fragment.tileid = t. Set fragment.splatindex = splat.index. Copy necessary attributes from the splat to the fragment. Store the fragment at fragmentlist[Oi + j], where j is the index of the tile ID in splat.tileids. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Depth values must be compared consistently. Using 32-bit floats is standard, but ensure the radix sort handles the bit representation correctly for depth comparison. Empty Splats: If a splat touches no tiles (e.g., outside the screen), it should be filtered out before sorting or handled with a tile count of 0. Stability: The sort must be stable to preserve the relative order of splats with identical depths, although this is rare in practice. The prefix sum approach relies on the sorted order being preserved during fragment creation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthfirstsplatsort(splatlist): """ Sorts splats by depth and creates depth-ordered tile fragments. Args: splatlist: List of dicts with keys 'depth', 'tileids', 'index'. Returns: fragmentlist: List of fragment dicts. """ # Step 1: Sort splats by depth # Using a stable sort to preserve original order for equal depths sortedsplats = sorted(splatlist, key=lambda s: s['depth']) # Step 2: Compute exclusive prefix sum of tile counts offsets = [] currentoffset = 0 for splat in sortedsplats: offsets.append(currentoffset) currentoffset += len(splat['tileids']) totalfragments = currentoffset fragmentlist = [None] totalfragments # Step 3: Create fragments for i, splat in enumerate(sortedsplats): offset = offsets[i] tileids = splat['tileids'] splatindex = splat['index'] for j, tileid in enumerate(tileids): fragindex = offset + j fragmentlist[fragindex] = { 'tileid': tileid, 'splatindex': splatindex, # Copy other necessary attributes from splat here 'depth': splat['depth'] } return fragmentlist This variant emphasizes the use of an exclusive prefix sum to determine fragment storage offsets. It ensures that fragments from each splat are stored contiguously in the output array, inheriting the depth-sorted order of the splats. This allows for a subsequent stable sort by tile ID to group fragments per tile without breaking the depth order within each tile. The key advantage is that the initial depth sort is performed on N splats rather than M fragments (M > N), reducing sorting complexity. Time Complexity: Sorting N splats takes O(N \log N) or O(N) with radix sort. Prefix sum and fragment creation take O(M), where M is the total number of fragments. Since M \approx 1.5-4N, the dominant cost is the initial sort on N items, which is significantly cheaper than sorting M fragments. Memory Complexity: Requires O(N) for the sorted splats and O(M) for the fragment list. The prefix sum array requires O(N). Performance: Reduces sorting overhead by a factor of 1.5 to 4 compared to the original 3DGS approach. This is particularly beneficial for scenes with high overlap where splats touch many tiles. Strengths: Lower sorting cost, simpler key generation (32-bit vs 48-bit), easier to implement on CPU. Limitations: Requires two passes (sort splats, then create fragments) compared to the original single sort of fragments. The fragment list is not yet grouped by tile, requiring a subsequent stable sort by tile ID. This method was introduced in the Splatshop paper as an optimization for editing large Gaussian Splat models. It addresses the inefficiency of the original 3DGS rendering pipeline, which sorts fragments after splitting splats into tiles. By sorting splats first, it reduces the number of items to sort, leveraging the fact that the number of fragments is typically 1.5 to 4 times the number of visible splats. head: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) Projection, Gaussian Splatting Rendering (Software), GaussianSplatPipeline01, GaussianSplatPipeline02, Local Affine Approximation, Standard 3D-GS Projection
body: This method renders a scene represented as a collection of 3D Gaussians to a 2D image buffer by projecting each Gaussian onto the image plane (z=1) using a local affine approximation of the projective transformation. It computes a 2D covariance matrix for each Gaussian and rasterizes the resulting ellipses. Unlike production renderers that use tile-based CUDA rasterization, spherical harmonics, or adaptive density control, this software implementation serves as a foundational reference for the underlying mathematical projection and rasterization pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of N 3D Gaussians defined by their parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients) and a camera model (view and projection matrices). Output: A 2D image buffer containing the accumulated color and opacity values for each pixel. Data Structures: The Gaussian data is stored in a struct GaussianData with the following fields: xyz: np.ndarray, float32, shape [N, 3] — World space positions. rot: np.ndarray, float32, shape [N, 4] — Quaternions representing rotation. scale: np.ndarray, float32, shape [N, 3] — Log-space scales (exponentiated during preprocessing). opacity: np.ndarray, float32, shape [N, 1] — Log-space opacities (sigmoided during preprocessing). sh: np.ndarray, float32, shape [N, SHdim] — Concatenated spherical harmonic coefficients. The vertex shader output for each Gaussian consists of a tuple: glposition: Vector4<f32> — Clip-space position. conic: Vector3<f32> — Packed inverse 2D covariance matrix containing cov2dinv[(0,0)], cov2dinv[(0,1)], and cov2dinv[(1,1)]. coordxy: Vector2<f32> — Screen-space center coordinates. Preprocessing: Before rendering, the Gaussian parameters must be normalized from their stored format: 1. Normalize Rotations: rots = rots / \|rots\|{axis=-1, keepdims=True}. 2. Exponentiate Scales: scales = \exp(scales). 3. Sigmoid Opacities: opacities = 1 / (1 + \exp(-opacities)). 4. Concatenate SH Coefficients: shs = \text{concat}([features\dc.reshape(-1, 3), features\extra.reshape(len(features\dc), -1)], axis=-1). Projection and Rasterization Steps: For each Gaussian i in the list: 1. Compute 3D Covariance: Construct the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma{3D} from the rotation quaternion q and scale vector s. The rotation matrix R is derived from q, and \Sigma{3D} = R \cdot \text{diag}(s^2) \cdot R^T. 2. Transform to Camera Space: Apply the viewing transformation matrix W to transform the Gaussian mean \mu and covariance \Sigma{3D} to camera space: \mu' = W\mu \Sigma' = W\Sigma{3D}W^T 3. Local Affine Approximation: Project the Gaussian from camera space to the image plane (z=1) using the projection function \phi(\mathbf{x}') = \mathbf{x}' (\mathbf{x}0^\top \mathbf{x}')^{-1}, where \mathbf{x}0 = [0, 0, 1]^\top. Since Gaussians are not closed under projective transformations, 3D-GS uses a local affine approximation via the Jacobian J = \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial \mathbf{x}'} evaluated at \mu'. 4. Compute 2D Covariance: Calculate the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} in the image space: \Sigma{2D} = J\Sigma'J^T Note: The matrix J has rank 2. The inverse of \Sigma{2D} is effectively the inverse of the 2 \times 2 covariance matrix obtained by skipping the third row and column of the full projected covariance. 5. Compute Screen Position: The 2D mean is \mu{2D} = \phi(\mu'). Convert \mu{2D} to screen coordinates (u, v). 6. Compute Conic Matrix: Invert the 2 \times 2 \Sigma{2D} to get \Sigma{2D}^{-1}. Pack the upper triangle into the conic vector: \text{conic} = [\Sigma{2D}^{-1}[0,0], \Sigma{2D}^{-1}[0,1], \Sigma{2D}^{-1}[1,1]] 7. Determine Bounding Box: Calculate the bounding box size for the Gaussian in screen space. The multiplier is 3.0, representing the 3-sigma extent: \text{bboxsize\cam} = [3.0 \sqrt{\Sigma{2D}[0,0]}, 3.0 \sqrt{\Sigma{2D}[1,1]}] Convert to NDC and then to pixel coordinates using the camera width w and height h: \text{bboxsize\ndc} = \frac{\text{bboxsize\cam}}{[w, h]} \times 2.0 The bounding box in pixels is centered at (u, v) with dimensions derived from bboxsizendc. 8. Rasterization: For each pixel (u, v) within the bounding box, evaluate the 2D Gaussian value: G{2D}(x{2D}) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (x{2D} - \mu{2D})^\top \Sigma{2D}^{-1} (x{2D} - \mu{2D}) \right) where x{2D} = [u, v]^\top. Perform alpha blending with the existing pixel color and opacity using the Gaussian's opacity and the computed G{2D} value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rendergaussians(gaussians, camera): """ Render a list of 3D Gaussians to a 2D image buffer. Args: gaussians: List of dicts with keys 'xyz', 'rot', 'scale', 'opacity', 'sh'. camera: Object with methods getviewmatrix(), and attributes w, h. Returns: image: np.ndarray of shape (H, W, 3) alpha: np.ndarray of shape (H, W) """ H, W = camera.h, camera.w image = np.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) alpha = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float32) viewmat = camera.getviewmatrix() Wlinear = viewmat[:3,:3] N = len(gaussians) xyz = np.array([g['xyz'] for g in gaussians], dtype=np.float32) rot = np.array([g['rot'] for g in gaussians], dtype=np.float32) scale = np.array([g['scale'] for g in gaussians], dtype=np.float32) opacity = np.array([g['opacity'] for g in gaussians], dtype=np.float32) sh = np.array([g['sh'] for g in gaussians], dtype=np.float32) # Preprocessing rot = rot / np.linalg.norm(rot, axis=-1, keepdims=True) scale = np.exp(scale) opacity = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-opacity)) # Compute 3D Covariance def quattorot(q): w, x, y, z = q[:, 0], q[:, 1], q[:, 2], q[:, 3] R = np.zeros((N, 3, 3)) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2(y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2(xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2(xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2(xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2(x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2(yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2(xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2(yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2(x2 + y2) return R Rmat = quattorot(rot) cov3d = np.zeros((N, 3, 3)) for i in range(N): cov3d[i] = Rmat[i] @ np.diag(scale[i]2) @ Rmat[i].T # Transform to Camera Space xyzh = np.hstack([xyz, np.ones((N, 1))]) xyzcam = (viewmat @ xyzh.T).T[:,:3] cov3dcam = np.zeros((N, 3, 3)) for i in range(N): cov3dcam[i] = Wlinear @ cov3d[i] @ Wlinear.T # Project to 2D zcam = xyzcam[:, 2] xcam = xyzcam[:, 0] ycam = xyzcam[:, 1] zsafe = np.maximum(zcam, 1e-6) J = np.zeros((N, 2, 3)) J[:, 0, 0] = 1.0 / zsafe J[:, 0, 2] = -xcam / (zsafe2) J[:, 1, 1] = 1.0 / zsafe J[:, 1, 2] = -ycam / (zsafe2) cov2d = np.zeros((N, 2, 2)) for i in range(N): cov2d[i] = J[i] @ cov3dcam[i] @ J[i].T # Invert 2D Covariance det = cov2d[:, 0, 0] cov2d[:, 1, 1] - cov2d[:, 0, 1] cov2d[:, 1, 0] safedet = np.where(np.abs(det) > 1e-6, det, 1e-6) cov2dinv = np.zeros((N, 2, 2)) cov2dinv[:, 0, 0] = cov2d[:, 1, 1] / safedet cov2dinv[:, 0, 1] = -cov2d[:, 0, 1] / safedet cov2dinv[:, 1, 0] = -cov2d[:, 1, 0] / safedet cov2dinv[:, 1, 1] = cov2d[:, 0, 0] / safedet # Screen Coordinates undc = xcam / zsafe vndc = ycam / zsafe upix = (undc + 1.0) 0.5 W vpix = (1.0 - vndc) 0.5 H # Bounding Box bboxsizecam = np.stack([3.0 np.sqrt(np.abs(cov2d[:, 0, 0])), 3.0 np.sqrt(np.abs(cov2d[:, 1, 1]))], axis=-1) bboxsizendc = bboxsizecam / np.array([W, H]) 2.0 bboxsizepix = (bboxsizendc + 1.0) 0.5 np.array([W, H]) bboxx = bboxsizepix[:, 0] bboxy = bboxsizepix[:, 1] # Rasterization for i in range(N): cx, cy = upix[i], vpix[i] covinv = cov2dinv[i] op = opacity[i, 0] color = sh[i,:3] minx = max(0, int(cx - bboxx[i])) maxx = min(W, int(cx + bboxx[i])) miny = max(0, int(cy - bboxy[i])) maxy = min(H, int(cy + bboxy[i])) for y in range(miny, maxy): for x in range(minx, maxx): dx = x - cx dy = y - cy exponent = -0.5 np.dot([dx, dy], covinv @ [dx, dy]) val = np.exp(exponent) alphaval = op val currentalpha = alpha[y, x] currentcolor = image[y, x] newalpha = currentalpha + alphaval (1.0 - currentalpha) if newalpha > 1e-6: image[y, x] = (currentcolor currentalpha + color alphaval (1.0 - currentalpha)) / newalpha alpha[y, x] = newalpha return image, alpha 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP is a self-contained, pure-PyTorch implementation of the core 3D Gaussian Splatting algorithm. It renders a list of 3D Gaussians to a 2D buffer by projecting them to screen space, computing a 2D covariance matrix, and rasterizing the resulting ellipses. Unlike production renderers, it intentionally skips tile-based CUDA rasterization, spherical harmonics, and adaptive density control, serving instead as a teaching reference for the underlying mathematics. A differentiable method for evaluating 3D Gaussians along per-pixel viewing rays that avoids matrix inversion, ensuring numerical stability and eliminating special handling for degenerate splats. It performs evaluation without matrix inversions to ensure stability. Unlike the affine approximation used in standard 3D-GS, which causes perspective distortion artifacts at close distances, this method provides fully perspective-correct rendering. Unlike ray-tracing frameworks which calculate intersection points with per-pixel viewing rays but have significantly lower rendering speeds, this method is implemented within a rasterization-based pipeline for real-time performance. Time and Memory Complexity: The projection step is O(N) for N Gaussians. The rasterization step is O(N \cdot B) where B is the average bounding box area in pixels. Memory complexity is O(N) to store Gaussian parameters and O(W \cdot H) for the image buffer. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on the rasterization backend. The software implementation described here is significantly slower than GPU-accelerated versions due to the lack of parallelization and tile-based optimization. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement and understand; serves as a good reference for the mathematical projection steps; no external dependencies beyond basic linear algebra. Limitations: Slow performance due to software rasterization; uses local affine approximation which introduces perspective distortion artifacts, especially at close distances or wide angles; requires special handling for degenerate splats if matrix inversion fails (though the software renderer assumes invertibility). When to Use: Use this method for educational purposes, prototyping, or when a GPU-accelerated solution is not available. It is not suitable for production real-time rendering due to performance limitations. 3D Gaussian Splatting represents scenes with 3D Gaussians and projects them onto the image plane (z=1) using a local affine approximation of the projective transformation to achieve real-time rasterization. Given a set of images with the camera parameters calibrated by SfM, the method optimizes a set of 3D Gaussians as graphical primitives to explicitly represent the scene. thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) On the Error Analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting and an Optimal Projection Strategy, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72643-915, fetched 2026-10-29 Efficient Perspective‐Correct 3D Gaussian Splatting Using Hybrid Transparency, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70014, fetched 2026-10-30

body: 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP is a self-contained, pure-PyTorch implementation of the core 3D Gaussian Splatting algorithm. It renders a list of 3D Gaussians to a 2D buffer by projecting them to screen space, computing a 2D covariance matrix, and rasterizing the resulting ellipses. Unlike production renderers, it intentionally skips tile-based CUDA rasterization, spherical harmonics, and adaptive density control, serving instead as a teaching reference for the underlying mathematics. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians defined by parameters; a pinhole camera model (view and projection matrices); image dimensions (H, W). Outputs: A rendered RGB image of size (H, W, 3) and an alpha mask of size (H, W, 1). Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is parameterized by: mean: 3D position vector \mathbf{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. scale: 3D scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (stored in log-space). rotation: Unit quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4. color: RGB color vector \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. opacity: Scalar \alphai \in [0, 1]. The 3D covariance matrix \Sigmai is constructed from scale and rotation to ensure it is symmetric positive semi-definite (PSD): \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T where Ri is the rotation matrix derived from \mathbf{q}i, and Si = \text{diag}(\exp(\mathbf{s}i)) is the scale matrix. Algorithm Steps: 1. World-to-Camera Transform: Transform the mean \mathbf{\mu}i and the 3D covariance \Sigmai from world space to camera space using the view transformation matrix W. \mathbf{\mu}'i = W \mathbf{\mu}i \Sigma'i = W \Sigmai W^T 2. 2D Projection: Project the 3D covariance into the 2D screen space using the EWA / Zwicker-style projection Jacobian J: \Sigma{2d, i} = J W \Sigmai W^T J^T A small isotropic dilation (blur) is added to \Sigma{2d, i} for numerical stability. 3. Depth Sort: Sort the Gaussians by their depth (z-coordinate in camera space) using argsort. Note that argsort is non-differentiable across order changes; gradients flow through the values given the fixed ordering. 4. Rasterization: Iterate over each Gaussian in sorted order using a Python loop rather than vectorizing over all (H, W, N) at once for readability. 5. Alpha Compositing: Perform per-pixel front-to-back alpha compositing using the volume-rendering equation with anisotropic 2D Gaussian weights: C{u,v} = \sum{i \in \text{sorted}} ci \cdot \alphai \cdot w{i, u, v} \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj \cdot w{j, u, v}) \alpha{u,v} = \sum{i \in \text{sorted}} \alphai \cdot w{i, u, v} \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj \cdot w{j, u, v}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def rendergaussiansmvp(gaussians, camera, H, W): """ gaussians: dict with keys 'mean', 'scale', 'rotation', 'color', 'opacity' camera: object with 'viewmatrix', 'fx', 'fy', 'cx', 'cy' H, W: image height and width """ N = gaussians['mean'].shape[0] means = gaussians['mean'] scales = gaussians['scale'] quats = gaussians['rotation'] colors = gaussians['color'] opacities = gaussians['opacity'] # 1. World to Camera Transform Wview = camera.viewmatrix # (4, 4) # Transform means meanshomogeneous = torch.cat([means, torch.ones(N, 1)], dim=1) # (N, 4) meanscam = (Wview @ meanshomogeneous.T).T[:,:3] # (N, 3) # Transform Covariance: Sigma3d = R S S^T R^T S = torch.exp(scales) # (N, 3) R = quattorotmatrix(quats) # (N, 3, 3) Sigma3d = R @ (S.unsqueeze(2) S.unsqueeze(1)) @ R.transpose(1, 2) # (N, 3, 3) Sigmacam = Wview[:3,:3] @ Sigma3d @ Wview[:3,:3].transpose(1, 2) # (N, 3, 3) # 2. Project to 2D fx, fy = camera.fx, camera.fy cx, cy = camera.cx, camera.cy X, Y, Z = meanscam[:, 0], meanscam[:, 1], meanscam[:, 2] J = torch.zeros(N, 2, 3) J[:, 0, 0] = fx / Z J[:, 0, 2] = -fx X / (Z2) J[:, 1, 1] = fy / Z J[:, 1, 2] = -fy Y / (Z2) # Sigma2d = J Sigmacam J^T Sigma2d = torch.bmm(torch.bmm(J, Sigmacam), J.transpose(1, 2)) # (N, 2, 2) # Add isotropic dilation for stability Sigma2d[:, 0, 0] += 0.3 Sigma2d[:, 1, 1] += 0.3 # 3. Depth Sort depths = meanscam[:, 2] sortindices = torch.argsort(depths, dim=0) meanscamsorted = meanscam[sortindices] Sigma2dsorted = Sigma2d[sortindices] colorssorted = colors[sortindices] opacitiessorted = opacities[sortindices] # 4. Rasterization outcolor = torch.zeros(H, W, 3) outalpha = torch.zeros(H, W, 1) for i in range(N): # Project mean to 2D screen space xproj = fx meanscamsorted[i, 0] / meanscamsorted[i, 2] + cx yproj = fy meanscamsorted[i, 1] / meanscamsorted[i, 2] + cy mu2d = torch.tensor([xproj, yproj]) cov2d = Sigma2dsorted[i] color = colorssorted[i] alpha = opacitiessorted[i] # Compute bounding box (3-sigma radius) eigenvalues = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(cov2d) radius = torch.ceil(torch.sqrt(torch.max(eigenvalues) 3.0)) xmin = max(0, int(xproj - radius)) xmax = min(W, int(xproj + radius)) ymin = max(0, int(yproj - radius)) ymax = min(H, int(yproj + radius)) # Create pixel grid for this bounding box ys, xs = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(ymin, ymax), torch.arange(xmin, xmax), indexing='ij') pixelcoords = torch.stack([xs.float(), ys.float()], dim=-1) # (H', W', 2) # Compute weights diff = pixelcoords - mu2d # (H', W', 2) invcov = torch.inverse(cov2d) # (2, 2) temp = torch.einsum('...k,kl->...l', diff, invcov) # (H', W', 2) dist = torch.sum(temp diff, dim=-1) # (H', W') weights = torch.exp(-0.5 dist) # (H', W') # Alpha compositing (front-to-back) currentalpha = outalpha[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax] # (H', W', 1) currentcolor = outcolor[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax] # (H', W', 3) alphaexpanded = (alpha weights).unsqueeze(-1) # (H', W', 1) newalpha = currentalpha + alphaexpanded (1 - currentalpha) newcolor = currentcolor (1 - alphaexpanded) + color.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) alphaexpanded outalpha[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax] = newalpha outcolor[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax] = newcolor return outcolor, outalpha def quattorotmatrix(quats): # Converts [w, x, y, z] quaternions to rotation matrices w, x, y, z = quats[:, 0], quats[:, 1], quats[:, 2], quats[:, 3] R = torch.zeros(quats.shape[0], 3, 3) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2(y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2(xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2(xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2(xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2(x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2(yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2(xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2(yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2(x2 + y2) return R Parameters: Camera Model: Pinhole camera with lookat function using OpenCV/COLMAP convention. Isotropic Dilation: Added to \Sigma{2d} for stability. Value not specified in sources, but a small constant (e.g., 0.3) is used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Sort: Uses argsort which is non-differentiable across order changes. Gradients flow through values given the ordering. This is accepted for the fit-from-scratch demo. Performance: The rasterizer uses a Python loop over Gaussians rather than vectorizing over all (H, W, N) at once for readability. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: End-to-end run takes ~30 seconds on CPU for a 64×64 image. Strengths: Pure PyTorch implementation, no custom CUDA kernels, easy to read and modify, suitable for teaching and debugging. Limitations: Slow due to Python loops, lacks optimizations like tile-based rasterization, spherical harmonics, and adaptive density control. When to Use: For educational purposes, prototyping, or when CUDA is unavailable. When Not to Use: For production rendering, large scenes, or real-time applications. 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP is based on the core algorithm described in "3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering" by Kerbl et al. (SIGGRAPH 2023). The MVP implementation is a self-contained Jupyter notebook intended as a teaching reference to allow users to implement the math without the complexity of custom CUDA kernels. It is distributed as a standalone tutorial material within a larger experiment repository. body:
3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization is the core rendering engine that projects 3D Gaussian primitives to 2D screen space and accumulates color per pixel using alpha compositing, enabling gradients to flow back to Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color). It differs from naive point-sampling approaches by explicitly handling the 2D covariance transformation and alpha blending order, and from production CUDA implementations by providing a Python/PyTorch-based reference implementation that prioritizes gradient correctness and pedagogical clarity over raw throughput. It builds on Gaussian Splatting by implementing the specific differentiable accumulation logic required for gradient-based optimization. Inputs: means3D: [N, 3] tensor of 3D Gaussian centers. quats: [N, 4] tensor of unit quaternions (w, x, y, z) representing rotation. scales: [N, 3] tensor of Gaussian scales. opacities: [N] tensor of scalar opacities. colors: [N, 3] or [N, D] tensor of direct colors (or SH coefficients if shdegree is set). viewmats: [C, 4, 4] camera-to-world matrices. Ks: [C, 3, 3] camera intrinsic matrices. width, height: Image dimensions. backgrounds: [C, 3] background colors. tilesize: Integer, default 16. nearplane, farplane: Floats, defaults 0.01, 1e10. rendermode: String, e.g., "RGB", "D", "ED". rasterizemode: String, "classic" or "antialiased". cameramodel: String, "pinhole", "ortho", "fisheye". shdegree: Integer or None. persplat: Integer, optional batch size for memory management. Outputs: rendercolors: [C, H, W, D] tensor. renderalphas: [C, H, W, 1] tensor. info: Dictionary containing radii, means2D, depths, conics, compensations. Data Structures: cov3D: [N, 3, 3] symmetric positive-definite matrix. means2D: [C, N, 2] projected centers. cov2D: [C, N, 2, 2] projected 2D covariance. conics: [C, N, 3] upper triangular inverse covariance (packed as [b{00}, b{01}, b{11}]). radii: [C, N, 2] bounding box radii in pixels. alphas: [C, N, H, W] per-pixel alpha values. transmittance: [C, N, H, W] accumulated transmittance. weights: [C, N, H, W] contribution weights. Steps: 1. Input Validation: Verify rendermode \in \{"RGB", "D", "ED", "RGB+D", "RGB+ED", "d", "Ed", "RGB+d", "RGB+Ed"\}, rasterizemode \in \{"classic", "antialiased"\}, and cameramodel \in \{"pinhole", "ortho", "fisheye"\}. 2. 3D Covariance Construction: Compute the 3D covariance matrix from quaternions and scales: \mathbf{C}{3D} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S}^2 \mathbf{R}^T where \mathbf{R} is the rotation matrix derived from quats and \mathbf{S} is the diagonal scale matrix from scales. Result shape: [N, 3, 3]. 3. 2D Projection: Linearize the projection of 3D means and 3D covariance to 2D screen space using camera intrinsics/extrinsics and image size. Transform means3D to camera space. Project means3D to 2D screen coordinates. Transform cov3D to 2D using the Jacobian of the projection transformation. Output: means2D [C, N, 2] and cov2D [C, N, 2, 2]. 4. Bounding Box and Conic Calculation: Compute radii radii [C, N, 2] in pixels to define the bounding box for each Gaussian. Compute conics [C, N, 3] as the upper triangular part of the inverse 2D covariance matrix \mathbf{C}{2D}^{-1}. If rasterizemode is "antialiased", compute compensations to correct for aliasing. 5. Tile Intersection: Compute tile dimensions: tilewidth = \lceil 	ext{width} / 	ext{tile\size} ceil, tileheight = \lceil 	ext{height} / 	ext{tile\size} ceil. Identify which tiles each Gaussian intersects using radii and means2D. Generate isectids and flattenids to map Gaussians to tiles and pixels efficiently. 6. Color Computation (Spherical Harmonics): If shdegree is not None, compute view directions \mathbf{d} = 	ext{means}{3D} - 	ext{campos}, normalize \mathbf{d}, and evaluate spherical harmonics to get RGB colors. Clamp colors: 	ext{rgb} = \max(	ext{rgb} + 0.5, 0.0). If shdegree is None, use direct colors. 7. Alpha and Transmittance Calculation: Broadcast opacities to [C, N]. If compensations exist, multiply opacities by them. Compute alpha for each Gaussian at each pixel: \alpha{i,p} = 	ext{opacity}i \cdot \exp\left(- rac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x}p -  oldsymbol{\mu}i)^T \mathbf{C}{2D,i}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}p -  oldsymbol{\mu}i)ight) where \mathbf{x}p is the pixel coordinate and  oldsymbol{\mu}i is the 2D mean. Compute transmittance: T{i,p} = \prod{j < i} (1 - \alpha{j,p}). 8. Sorting and Depth Handling: Filter Gaussians behind the camera (z < 0). Sort remaining Gaussians by depth (camera-space Z). If persplat is set, split Gaussians into mini-batches to manage memory, passing starttransmittance between batches. 9. Alpha Compositing: Compute weights: w{i,p} = \alpha{i,p} \cdot T{i,p}. Composite color: Cp = \sumi w{i,p} \cdot 	ext{color}i. Composite mask (alpha): \alphap = \sumi w{i,p}. Composite depth (if requested): Dp = \sumi w{i,p} \cdot zi. Normalize depth by alpha: Dp = Dp / \max(\alphap, 10^{-10}). 10. Background Blending: Blend with background color: C{final} = \alphap Cp + (1 - \alphap) C{bg}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quattorotmat(quats): w, x, y, z = quats[:, 0], quats[:, 1], quats[:, 2], quats[:, 3] R = np.zeros((quats.shape[0], 3, 3)) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2(y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2(xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2(xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2(xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2(x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2(yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2(xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2(yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2(x2 + y2) return R def computecov3D(quats, scales): R = quattorotmat(quats) cov3D = R @ (scales[:,:, None] scales[:, None,:]) @ R.T return cov3D def projectto2d(means3D, cov3D, viewmats, Ks, width, height): C = viewmats.shape[0] N = means3D.shape[0] means2D = np.zeros((C, N, 2)) cov2D = np.zeros((C, N, 2, 2)) for c in range(C): V = viewmats[c] K = Ks[c] meansc = (V[:3,:3] @ means3D.T + V[:3, 3:4]).T depthsc = meansc[:, 2:3] means2D[c] = (K @ meansc.T).T[:,:2] / depthsc J = np.zeros((2, 3)) J[0, 0] = K[0, 0] / depthsc[:, 0] J[0, 2] = -K[0, 0] meansc[:, 0] / (depthsc[:, 0]2) J[1, 1] = K[1, 1] / depthsc[:, 0] J[1, 2] = -K[1, 1] meansc[:, 1] / (depthsc[:, 0]2) cov2D[c] = J @ cov3D @ J.T return means2D, cov2D def computeconics(cov2D): C, N,, = cov2D.shape conics = np.zeros((C, N, 3)) for c in range(C): for n in range(N): M = cov2D[c, n] det = M[0, 0]M[1, 1] - M[0, 1]M[1, 0] det = max(det, 1e-6) conics[c, n, 0] = M[1, 1] / det conics[c, n, 1] = -M[0, 1] / det conics[c, n, 2] = M[0, 0] / det return conics def computeradii(cov2D, width, height): C, N,, = cov2D.shape radii = np.zeros((C, N, 2)) for c in range(C): for n in range(N): M = cov2D[c, n] trace = M[0, 0] + M[1, 1] det = M[0, 0]M[1, 1] - M[0, 1]M[1, 0] disc = np.sqrt(max(trace2 - 4det, 0)) lambda1 = (trace + disc) / 2 lambda2 = (trace - disc) / 2 rx = 3.0 np.sqrt(max(lambda1, 0)) ry = 3.0 np.sqrt(max(lambda2, 0)) radii[c, n, 0] = min(rx, width) radii[c, n, 1] = min(ry, height) return radii def tileintersection(means2d, radii, depths, tilesize, tilewidth, tileheight): C, N, = means2d.shape isectids = [] flattenids = [] for c in range(C): for n in range(N): if depths[c, n] < 0: continue x, y = means2d[c, n] r = radii[c, n] minx, maxx = int(x - r), int(x + r) miny, maxy = int(y - r), int(y + r) for ty in range(max(0, miny), min(tileheight, maxy + 1)): for tx in range(max(0, minx), min(tilewidth, maxx + 1)): isectids.append((c, n, ty, tx)) flattenids.append(n) return np.array(isectids), np.array(flattenids) def computealphas(opacitiescn, means2d, conics, width, height): C, N, = means2d.shape alphas = np.zeros((C, N, height, width)) for c in range(C): for n in range(N): b00, b01, b11 = conics[c, n] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): dx = x - means2d[c, n, 0] dy = y - means2d[c, n, 1] val = 0.5 (b00dxdx + 2b01dxdy + b11dydy) alphas[c, n, y, x] = opacitiescn[c, n] np.exp(-val) return alphas def rasterization(means3D, quats, scales, opacities, colors, viewmats, Ks, width, height, backgrounds, tilesize=16, nearplane=0.01, farplane=1e10, rendermode="RGB", rasterizemode="classic", cameramodel="pinhole", shdegree=None, persplat=0): assert rendermode in {"RGB", "D", "ED", "RGB+D", "RGB+ED", "d", "Ed", "RGB+d", "RGB+Ed"} assert rasterizemode in {"classic", "antialiased"} assert cameramodel in {"pinhole", "ortho", "fisheye"} C = viewmats.shape[0] N = means3D.shape[0] H, W = height, width cov3D = computecov3D(quats, scales) means2D, cov2D = projectto2d(means3D, cov3D, viewmats, Ks, width, height) radii = computeradii(cov2D, width, height) conics = computeconics(cov2D) depths = np.zeros((C, N)) for c in range(C): V = viewmats[c] meansc = (V[:3,:3] @ means3D.T + V[:3, 3:4]).T depths[c] = meansc[:, 2] tilewidth = int(np.ceil(W / tilesize)) tileheight = int(np.ceil(H / tilesize)) isectids, flattenids = tileintersection(means2D, radii, depths, tilesize, tilewidth, tileheight) if shdegree is not None: campos = viewmats[:,:3, 3] dirs = means3D[None,:,:] - campos[:, None,:] dirsnorm = np.maximum(np.linalg.norm(dirs, axis=-1, keepdims=True), 1e-8) dirs = dirs / dirsnorm colorsforraster = colors[None,:,:] else: colorsforraster = colors[None,:,:] opacitiescn = np.broadcastto(np.expanddims(opacities, 0), (C, N)) alphas = computealphas(opacitiescn, means2D, conics, width, height) sortedindices = np.argsort(depths, axis=1) means2dsorted = np.takealongaxis(means2D, sortedindices[:,:, None], axis=1) alphassorted = np.takealongaxis(alphas, sortedindices[:,:, None, None], axis=1) colorssorted = np.takealongaxis(colorsforraster[:,:, None, None,:], sortedindices[:,:, None, None, None], axis=1) transmittance = np.ones((C, 1, H, W)) rendercolors = np.zeros((C, H, W, colorssorted.shape[-1])) renderalphas = np.zeros((C, H, W, 1)) for i in range(alphassorted.shape[1]): alphai = alphassorted[:, i,:,:] colori = colorssorted[:, i,:,:,:] weight = alphai transmittance rendercolors += weight[..., None] colori renderalphas += weight[..., None] transmittance = (1 - alphai) rendercolors = rendercolors + transmittance[..., None] backgrounds[:, None, None,:] return rendercolors, renderalphas, {"radii": radii, "means2D": means2D, "depths": depths, "conics": conics} The 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer is the core rendering engine that projects 3D Gaussian primitives to 2D screen space and accumulates color per pixel using alpha compositing, enabling gradients to flow back to Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color). It differs from naive point-sampling approaches by explicitly handling the 2D covariance transformation and alpha blending order, and from production CUDA implementations by providing a Python/PyTorch-based reference implementation that prioritizes gradient correctness and pedagogical clarity over raw throughput. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by implementing the specific differentiable accumulation logic required for gradient-based optimization. Optimal Gaussian Splatting is a rendering method that reduces projection error by radially projecting each 3D Gaussian onto a unique tangent plane perpendicular to the line connecting the Gaussian mean to the camera center, rather than projecting all Gaussians onto a single plane z=1. Unlike the original 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization which uses a fixed perspective plane, this method treats the projection as a radial mapping onto a unit sphere, ensuring the projection of the Gaussian mean coincides with the ray direction from the camera center. It differs from NeRF by avoiding extensive ray sampling, instead determining which tangent-plane Gaussians intersect the ray on the unit sphere. Hybrid Transparency is a blending formulation that combines depth-ordered alpha blending for the first K fragments (the 'core') with order-independent accumulation for the remaining fragments (the 'tail') to mitigate popping artifacts while maintaining real-time performance. It solves the inconsistency of splat shapes and popping artifacts across viewpoints in VR and motion by avoiding the performance cost of hierarchical sorting or ray tracing. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which uses approximate per-primitive sorting, Hybrid Transparency guarantees correct depth ordering for the front-most contributions and uses fast, unsorted blending for the rest. This method computes the value of a 3D Gaussian primitive for a given viewing ray in screen space without performing matrix inversion, utilizing Plücker coordinates to represent the ray and calculate the distance to the Gaussian's center. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization by providing a closed-form, numerically stable solution for perspective-correct splat evaluation that handles degenerate ellipsoids and avoids the computational cost of matrix inversions. This method renders X-ray projections from a 3D Gaussian representation by integrating the 3D Gaussian density along cone-beam ray paths, resulting in a sum of 2D Gaussians rather than the alpha-compositing used in standard visible-light rendering. It solves the problem of simulating X-ray CT projections from learned 3D Gaussian fields by adapting the rasterization pipeline to a pinhole camera model, enabling analytical integration of radiative density. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which composites opacities, this method sums projected 2D densities, fundamentally addressing integration bias issues where learning integrated density in 2D leads to inconsistencies in 3D density retrieval. Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading computes the color contribution of 3D Gaussians to a pixel by analytically integrating the Gaussian probability density function over the pixel area, rather than sampling the center. It solves the aliasing artifacts inherent in point-sampling approaches by approximating the pixel area integral using a conditioned logistic function. It sets itself apart from vanilla 3DGS by providing anti-aliased results and from Mip-Splatting by using a different analytical approximation that maintains higher detail fidelity, albeit with a slight computational overhead. The Speedy-Splat Rendering Pipeline is a GPU-accelerated rasterization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that optimizes the rendering loop by replacing coarse bounding-box tile intersection tests with precise Gaussian-tile intersection checks and sorting-based depth ordering. It addresses the inefficiency of standard 3D-GS rasterization, which overestimates Gaussian extents and processes non-intersecting pixels, by generating a sparse set of Gaussian-tile pairs and sorting them for efficient pixel-wise compositing. Ghost Ellipsoids for Chunked Training resolves boundary artifacts in chunked volume training by including ellipsoids from neighboring chunks in the loss computation without updating their parameters, providing boundary context without requiring a global volume or merged model. Unlike chunk-based 3DGS methods that resolve boundary inconsistencies by merging chunks into a global coarse model or through post-training stages, this method requires boundary support during training itself without access to a global volume. Analytic Transmittance 3DGS is a rasterization-based rendering method that replaces the approximate alpha computation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytic integration of the volume rendering equation along the camera ray. It computes physically accurate transmittance and alpha values without projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D splats, thereby avoiding the linearization of the exponential transmittance and the assumption of non-self-occlusion inherent in splatting. Unlike its sibling 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer which relies on 2D Gaussian projection, this method integrates 3D Gaussians directly in ray-space to better represent opaque surfaces and improve view synthesis quality. Ref-Gaussian Deferred Surfel Rendering with Split-Sum IBL is a real-time deferred shading method for relighting 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models on mobile hardware (specifically iOS/Metal). It solves the problem of dynamic environment lighting in Gaussian splats by decomposing splats into physically-based rendering (PBR) materials (albedo, normal, roughness, reflectance) and computing lighting via a deferred pipeline with split-sum environment map integration. Unlike forward-shading Gaussian splatters that bake lighting into spherical harmonics or use analytic approximations, this method separates the material definition from the lighting environment, allowing the environment map to be swapped or rotated in real-time without retraining or re-rasterizing the splats. It differs from standard PBR deferred renderers by adapting the splat-based rasterization and surfel accumulation to the deferred G-buffer workflow. Calculates the self-shadowing transmittance T{light} for each Gaussian along the sun direction. It represents the 'front occlusion transmittance' to model self-shadowing effects in volume rendering. Light Space Rasterization computes T{light}, the front-facing occlusion transmittance for each 3D Gaussian along a directional sun direction, enabling physically plausible self-shadowing in volume cloud rendering. It differs from voxel-based fallbacks by providing full continuous gradients and zero parameter expansion, allowing for differentiable relighting without requiring specific training hyperparameters. 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization renders a scene represented by 2D Gaussian surfels by projecting them to screen space and performing ray-surfel intersection per pixel, accumulating colour, alpha, and normal maps via front-to-back alpha compositing. It differs from the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization.md] by treating primitives as planar surfels with 2D covariance structures rather than 3D ellipsoids, which simplifies the intersection geometry but requires specific handling of the surfel plane orientation relative to the view ray. A method to adapt the rasterization projection for panoramic images by mapping pixel coordinates to the unit sphere. Compute the marginal probability pi(t) for each 4D Gaussian i at the current frame's timestamp t, then discard Gaussians with negligible pi(t) before executing standard frustum culling. Unlike methods where Gaussian count scales with video length, this filtering keeps active Gaussians constant, making the approach friendly to long videos in terms of rendering speed. u-dependent critical value interpolation to handle fat-tailed Student's t-distributions. For t-distributions with thin tails (high 
u), apply the standard three-sigma rule directly. For fat-tailed distributions (low 
u), obtain critical values for different 
u degrees from reference [9] and interpolate between them to compute the appropriate truncation threshold. Using a fixed three-sigma threshold on fat-tailed t-distributions causes excessive truncation or leakage; interpolation across 
u degrees resolves this. Uses ray-tracing-style intersection for accurate depth and derives a level-set surface from accumulated opacity. Uses progressive propagation along normals to fill texture-less regions. Uses zero-thickness oriented surfels. Combines NeuS-style SDF with a GS rasterizer.
