name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer
head: 2D Gaussian Rasterization, 3DGS rasterization pipeline, Gaussian Rasterization (Python/C++ Autograd Wrapper), diff-gaussian-rasterization wrapper
body: The 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer is the core rendering engine that projects 3D Gaussian primitives to 2D screen space and accumulates color per pixel using alpha compositing, enabling gradients to flow back to Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color). It differs from naive point-sampling approaches by explicitly handling the 2D covariance transformation and alpha blending order, and from production CUDA implementations by providing a Python/PyTorch-based reference implementation that prioritizes gradient correctness and pedagogical clarity over raw throughput. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by implementing the specific differentiable accumulation logic required for gradient-based optimization. The method consists of a forward rasterization pass that computes pixel colors and a backward pass that computes gradients with respect to the input Gaussian parameters. The implementation described here is a Python/PyTorch reference that iterates over Gaussians, serving as a baseline before transitioning to CUDA kernels. Inputs: means3D: Tensor of shape (N, 3), 3D camera-space centers of N Gaussians. opacity: Tensor of shape (N, 1) or (N), per-Gaussian opacity values. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3), per-Gaussian scaling factors. rotations: Tensor of shape (N, 4), per-Gaussian quaternions. colorsprecomp: Tensor of shape (N, 3), precomputed RGB colors (if SH degree is 0). shs: Tensor of shape (N, K, 3), Spherical Harmonics coefficients (if colorsprecomp is not used). features: Tensor of shape (N, D), auxiliary features (e.g., normals). rastersettings: Object containing camera and rendering configuration (see Layout below). Outputs: renderedimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), the composited RGB image. renderedopacity: Tensor of shape (H, W, 1), the accumulated opacity. rendereddepth: Tensor of shape (H, W, 1), the accumulated depth. renderedfeature: Tensor of shape (H, W, D), accumulated features. radii: Tensor of shape (N), the maximum screen-space radius of each Gaussian (used for culling). numrendered: Count of Gaussians contributing to at least one pixel. The GaussianRasterizationSettings object holds camera and rendering parameters. Its layout is: | Field | Type | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | imageheight | int | Height of the output image in pixels. | | imagewidth | int | Width of the output image in pixels. | | tanfovx | float | Tangent of half horizontal field of view. | | tanfovy | float | Tangent of half vertical field of view. | | cx | float | Principal point x-coordinate in pixels. | | cy | float | Principal point y-coordinate in pixels. | | bg | torch.Tensor | Background color tensor (shape (3)). | | scalemodifier | float | Multiplicative scalar applied to Gaussian scales. Default 1.0. | | viewmatrix | torch.Tensor | 4 \times 4 view transformation matrix. | | projmatrix | torch.Tensor | 4 \times 4 projection matrix. | | shdegree | int | Degree of Spherical Harmonics. | | campos | torch.Tensor | Camera position in world space. | | prefiltered | bool | Flag indicating if colors are prefiltered. | | backwardgeometry | bool | Flag to enable geometry gradient computation. | | computerpseudonormal | bool | Flag to enable pseudo-normal computation. | | debug | bool | Debug mode flag. | 1. Input Validation: Ensure exactly one of shs or colorsprecomp is provided. Ensure exactly one of (scales, rotations) or cov3Dprecomp is provided. Replace missing tensors with empty tensors of appropriate shape. If features is None, initialize as empty tensor matching means3D feature dimension. 2. Projection: Project 3D camera-space centers xyzcam to 2D pixel coordinates means2D using the perspective projection formula: \text{means2D}x = \frac{\text{xyz\cam}x \cdot f}{\text{xyz\cam}z} + \text{camera}.cx \text{means2D}y = \frac{\text{xyz\cam}y \cdot f}{\text{xyz\cam}z} + \text{camera}.cy where f is derived from the focal length and image dimensions, and camera.cx, camera.cy are the principal points. 3. Sorting: Sort Gaussians by depth (xyzcam[:, 2]) in descending order (back-to-front) to ensure correct alpha compositing order. 4. Initialization: Initialize a canvas of zeros with shape (H, W, 3) and a transmittance buffer T of ones with shape (H, W, 1). 5. Rasterization Loop: Iterate through each Gaussian i in the sorted list: a. Covariance Inverse: Compute the inverse of the 2D covariance matrix cov2d[i] for the current Gaussian: invcov = torch.inverse(cov2d[i]). b. Displacement: For each pixel, compute the displacement vector d from the pixel center to the Gaussian mean. c. Power Calculation: Calculate the exponent for the 2D Gaussian density: \text{power} = -0.5 \cdot (dx^2 \cdot \text{inv\cov}{0,0} + dy^2 \cdot \text{inv\cov}{1,1} + 2 \cdot dx \cdot dy \cdot \text{inv\cov}{0,1}) where d = [dx, dy] is the 2D displacement vector and invcov is the 2 \times 2 inverse covariance matrix. d. Alpha Computation: Compute the per-pixel alpha value by exponentiating the power, multiplying by the Gaussian's opacity, and clamping the result to a maximum of 0.99: \alpha = \text{clamp}(\exp(\text{power}) \cdot \text{opacities}[i], \max=0.99) e. Color Update: Update the canvas color by adding the Gaussian's color weighted by its alpha and the current transmittance: \text{canvas} = \text{canvas} + \text{colors}[i] \cdot \alpha \cdot T f. Transmittance Update: Update the transmittance buffer by multiplying it by (1 - \alpha): T = T \cdot (1 - \alpha) 6. Final Composition: Add the background color weighted by the final transmittance T to the canvas. The backward pass computes gradients with respect to input Gaussian parameters. It is implemented via a custom autograd wrapper that restores context tensors and invokes a C++ backward kernel or equivalent PyTorch gradient logic. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def gaussianrasterizerforward(means3D, opacity, scales, rotations, colorsprecomp, shs, features, rastersettings): """ Forward pass of the 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer. Implements projection, sorting, and alpha compositing loop. """ H, W = rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth bg = rastersettings.bg cx, cy = rastersettings.cx, rastersettings.cy tanfovx = rastersettings.tanfovx # 1. Projection: Project 3D camera-space centers to 2D pixel coordinates # f is derived from focal length and image dimensions f = (W / 2) / tanfovx # Standard pinhole camera focal length from tan(FOV/2) xyzcam = means3D # Assume already in camera space means2Dx = (xyzcam[:, 0] f / xyzcam[:, 2]) + cx means2Dy = (xyzcam[:, 1] f / xyzcam[:, 2]) + cy means2D = torch.stack([means2Dx, means2Dy], dim=-1) # (N, 2) # 2. Covariance Computation: Compute 2D covariance matrices # cov2d shape: (N, 2, 2) # cov2d = compute2dcovariance(means3D, scales, rotations, rastersettings) # cov2d = torch.zeros((means3D.shape[0], 2, 2), device=means3D.device) # Placeholder for covariance projection logic # 3. Color Assembly: Select colors from precomputed or SH coefficients if colorsprecomp is not None: colors = colorsprecomp else: # colors = evaluatesh(shs, rastersettings.shdegree) # colors = torch.zeroslike(means3D[:,:3]) # Placeholder for SH evaluation logic # 4. Sorting: Sort Gaussians by depth (z) in descending order depths = xyzcam[:, 2] sortedindices = torch.argsort(depths, descending=True) means2D = means2D[sortedindices] cov2d = cov2d[sortedindices] colors = colors[sortedindices] opacity = opacity[sortedindices] # 5. Initialization: Canvas and transmittance buffer canvas = torch.zeros((H, W, 3), device=means3D.device) T = torch.ones((H, W, 1), device=means3D.device) N = means2D.shape[0] # 6. Rasterization Loop: Iterate through sorted Gaussians for i in range(N): # Covariance Inverse invcov = torch.inverse(cov2d[i]) # (2, 2) # Displacement vector d from pixel center to Gaussian mean pixelcenters = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid( torch.arange(W, device=means3D.device) + 0.5, torch.arange(H, device=means3D.device) + 0.5, indexing='ij'), dim=-1).float() d = pixelcenters - means2D[i] # (H, W, 2) # Power Calculation power = -0.5 ( d[:,:, 0]2 invcov[0, 0] + d[:,:, 1]2 invcov[1, 1] + 2 d[:,:, 0] d[:,:, 1] invcov[0, 1]) # (H, W) # Alpha Computation alpha = torch.clamp(torch.exp(power).unsqueeze(-1) opacity[i], max=0.99) # (H, W, 1) # Color Update canvas = canvas + colors[i] alpha T # Transmittance Update T = T (1 - alpha) # 7. Final Composition: Add background weighted by final transmittance renderedimage = canvas + bg T return renderedimage, T lambdadssim: Weight for SSIM term in loss function. Typical value not specified in text. lambdaopacity: Weight for opacity mask loss. Enabled when > 0. lambdanormalrenderdepth: Weight for normal consistency loss. Typical value 0.01. Memory Constraints: The Python/PyTorch loop implementation is slow and memory-intensive for large N. The roadmap indicates a transition to CUDA kernels for real-time performance. Covariance Singularity: If the 2D covariance matrix is singular, torch.inverse will fail. A small epsilon should be added to the diagonal. Alpha Clamping: Alpha values are clamped to a maximum of 0.99 to prevent division by zero in transmittance updates and ensure numerical stability. Sorting Order: Incorrect sorting (e.g., front-to-back) will result in incorrect alpha compositing and visual artifacts. Performance: Not suitable for real-time rendering or large-scale scenes without CUDA optimization. Analytic-Splatting is a differentiable rasterization method that replaces the point-sampling of 2D Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytical approximation of the integral of the Gaussian signal over the pixel window area. It solves the aliasing artifacts (blurring or jaggies) caused by treating pixels as isolated points when the camera zooms or resolution changes. Unlike Mip-Splatting which uses a hybrid low-pass filter that suppresses high-frequency components and causes over-smoothing, Analytic-Splatting preserves high-quality details by calculating the integral analytically using a conditioned logistic function approximation of the Gaussian CDF. LinPrim Gradient Computation computes the gradients of intersection depths \mathbf{i} with respect to the ray-space triangle corners \mathbf{v}^{\text{ray}} to enable differentiable rendering of linear primitives. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by backpropagating gradients through a linear primitive rasterizer (MTIA) rather than a Gaussian splatting kernel, requiring specific handling of ray-space to world-space transformations and quaternion-based rotation updates. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer by replacing the Gaussian alpha-blending gradient flow with opacity calculations based on intersection depths. This method implements the vertex shader stage of a GPU-based rasterizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting, transforming 3D Gaussian primitives into 2D screen-space ellipses for instanced rendering. It differs from fragment-based or compute-shader approaches by performing all geometric projection, covariance transformation, and ellipse basis computation within the vertex shader, passing only the final vertex positions and attributes to the rasterizer. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer by handling the specific data unpacking and frustum culling required for efficient vertex-driven splatting. The Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline orchestrates camera setup, spherical harmonic (SH) evaluation, feature assembly, and Gaussian rasterization for a single view. It projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space, rasterizes them into tiles, and composites them front-to-back using alpha blending to produce novel views. It sets apart from its siblings by managing the pre-computation of covariances, colors, and lighting models, and assembling auxiliary features before invoking the differentiable rasterizer. This method is a parallelization scheme for the backward pass of 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization that maps CUDA threads to 2D splats rather than pixels to eliminate atomic contention on gradient accumulation. It differs from the original 3DGS approach, which maps threads to pixels and suffers from serialized atomic operations when multiple threads contend for the same Gaussian's gradient, by having threads maintain per-splat state and exchange smaller per-pixel states (transmittance T and accumulated color RGB) via intra-warp shuffling. Validates mutually exclusive input tensors for color representation and 3D covariance before invoking the CUDA rasterization backend. It checks if exactly one of shs or colorsprecomp is provided, and if exactly one of the scale/rotation pair or cov3Dprecomp is provided. If both are None or both are not None, it raises an exception. It replaces any missing shs, colorsprecomp, scales, rotations, or cov3Dprecomp tensors with empty tensors of appropriate shape. If features is None, it initializes it as an empty tensor matching the feature dimension of means3D (slice [...,:0]). It then calls the CUDA rasterization routine rasterizegaussians with all prepared tensors and rastersettings. Holds camera and rendering parameters. tanfovx/tanfovy are the tangent of half horizontal/vertical field of view, computed as math.tan(camera.FoVx 0.5) and math.tan(camera.FoVy 0.5). cx/cy are principal point coordinates in pixels, extracted from intrinsic[0, 2] and intrinsic[1, 2]. scalemodifier is a multiplicative scalar applied to Gaussian scales during rasterization, with a default value of 1.0 in renderview. backwardgeometry is a boolean flag passed to the CUDA backend to enable geometry gradient computation. computerpseudonormal is a boolean flag (note source typo) to enable pseudo-normal computation in the rasterizer. It is a NamedTuple with fields: imageheight (int), imagewidth (int), tanfovx (float), tanfovy (float), cx (float), cy (float), bg (torch.Tensor), scalemodifier (float), viewmatrix (torch.Tensor), projmatrix (torch.Tensor), shdegree (int), campos (torch.Tensor), prefiltered (bool), backwardgeometry (bool), computerpseudonormal (bool), debug (bool). Time Complexity: The Python/PyTorch reference implementation is O(N \cdot H \cdot W) due to the nested loop over Gaussians and pixels, making it interpreter-bound and slow. Production CUDA implementations reduce this to near-linear time with respect to the number of pixels and Gaussians by using tile-based rasterization and parallel processing. Memory Complexity: O(N + H \cdot W) for storing Gaussian parameters and intermediate buffers (canvas, transmittance). The Python loop is memory-intensive for large N. Measured Performance: The reference implementation is capped by consumer-grade VRAM limits and the interpreter-bound nature of the custom rendering loop, preventing dense point-cloud representation typical of production-level 3DGS. Strengths: Provides a clear, differentiable reference implementation for understanding the 3DGS pipeline. Easy to debug and modify. Limitations: Slow due to Python loops. Not suitable for real-time rendering or large-scale scenes without CUDA optimization. When to Use: For educational purposes, debugging, or as a baseline for developing optimized CUDA kernels. When Not to Use: For production applications requiring real-time performance or large-scale scene rendering. The 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer is part of the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework, which was introduced for novel view synthesis of static scenes. The method projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and accumulates color per pixel using alpha compositing, allowing gradients to flow back to Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color). The Python/PyTorch reference implementation serves as a pedagogical deep-dive into the mechanics of radiance fields, moving beyond high-level abstractions to implement the differentiable rendering pipeline and volumetric accumulation from first principles. The roadmap indicates a transition to CUDA kernels for real-time performance and efficient memory management. ldyken53/VEG, https://github.com/ldyken53/VEG, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) metin-yat/mini-splat, https://github.com/metin-yat/mini-splat, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

head: Analytic Integration for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Analytic-Splatting is a differentiable rasterization method that replaces the point-sampling of 2D Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytical approximation of the integral of the Gaussian signal over the pixel window area. It solves the aliasing artifacts (blurring or jaggies) caused by treating pixels as isolated points when the camera zooms or resolution changes. Unlike Mip-Splatting which uses a hybrid low-pass filter that suppresses high-frequency components and causes over-smoothing, Analytic-Splatting preserves high-quality details by calculating the integral analytically using a conditioned logistic function approximation of the Gaussian CDF. Inputs: Set of N projected 2D Gaussians, each defined by mean \hat{\bm{\mu}}i \in \mathbb{R}^2, covariance \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}i \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2}, opacity \alphai \in [0,1], and color \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Pixel center coordinates \mathbf{u} = [ux, uy]^\top. Outputs: Final color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u}) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}g^{2D}}{\partial \hat{\bm{\mu}}}, \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}g^{2D}}{\partial \lambda}, \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}g^{2D}}{\partial \mathbf{v}} for backpropagation. Data Structures: \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}: 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix. \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{-1}: Inverse covariance matrix, decomposed into coefficients a, b, c. \lambda1, \lambda2: Eigenvalues of \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}. \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2: Eigenvectors of \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}, forming matrix V = [\mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2]. \sigma1 = \sqrt{\lambda1}, \sigma2 = \sqrt{\lambda2}. Parameters: Logistic approximation coefficients: linear term 1.6, cubic term 0.07. Derivative coefficient: 0.21 (derived from the derivative of -0.07 \cdot x^3). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Compute Inverse Covariance Coefficients: Calculate the determinant |\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}| = \hat{\Sigma}{11}\hat{\Sigma}{22} - \hat{\Sigma}{12}^2. Compute coefficients for \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}: a = \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{22}}{|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}|}, \quad b = -\frac{\hat{\Sigma}{12}}{|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}|}, \quad c = \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{11}}{|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}|} 2. Eigenvalue Decomposition: Perform eigenvalue decomposition on \hat{\bm{\Sigma}} to obtain eigenvalues \{\lambda1, \lambda2\} and corresponding eigenvectors \{\mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2\}. Define standard deviations \sigma1 = \sqrt{\lambda1} and \sigma2 = \sqrt{\lambda2}. 3. Transform Pixel Center: Transform the pixel center \mathbf{u} into the diagonalized coordinate system defined by the eigenvectors. Let \tilde{\mathbf{u}} = [\tilde{u}x, \tilde{u}y]^\top. \tilde{\mathbf{u}} = V^\top (\mathbf{u} - \hat{\bm{\mu}}) Component-wise: \tilde{u}x = v{1x}(ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{1y}(uy - \hat{\mu}y) \tilde{u}y = v{2x}(ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{2y}(uy - \hat{\mu}y) 4. Compute 1D Logistic Approximations: Define the conditioned logistic function S(x) for the standard Gaussian CDF (\sigma=1): S(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-1.6 \cdot x - 0.07 \cdot x^3)} Define the scaled logistic function for standard deviation \sigma: S\sigma(x) = S\left(\frac{x}{\sigma}\right) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-1.6 \cdot \frac{x}{\sigma} - 0.07 \cdot \left(\frac{x}{\sigma}\right)^3\right)} 5. Compute 2D Intensity Integral: Approximate the integral of the 2D Gaussian signal over the 1x1 pixel window centered at \mathbf{u}. The 2D integral \mathcal{I}g^{2D}(\mathbf{u}) is decomposed into the product of two independent 1D integrals along the eigenvectors: \mathcal{I}g^{2D}(\mathbf{u}) = 2\pi \sigma1 \sigma2 \left[ S{\sigma1}\left(\tilde{u}x + \frac{1}{2}\right) - S{\sigma1}\left(\tilde{u}x - \frac{1}{2}\right) \right] \left[ S{\sigma2}\left(\tilde{u}y + \frac{1}{2}\right) - S{\sigma2}\left(\tilde{u}y - \frac{1}{2}\right) \right] Let \mathcal{I}{\sigma1} = \sigma1 \left[ S{\sigma1}(\tilde{u}x + \frac{1}{2}) - S{\sigma1}(\tilde{u}x - \frac{1}{2}) \right] and \mathcal{I}{\sigma2} = \sigma2 \left[ S{\sigma2}(\tilde{u}y + \frac{1}{2}) - S{\sigma2}(\tilde{u}y - \frac{1}{2}) \right]. Then: \mathcal{I}g^{2D}(\mathbf{u}) = 2\pi \mathcal{I}{\sigma1} \mathcal{I}{\sigma2} 6. Volume Rendering: Compute the final color using alpha blending, replacing the point sample g^{2D} with the integral \mathcal{I}g^{2D}: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u}) = \sum{i \in N} Ti \mathcal{I}{g-i}^{2D}(\mathbf{u} | \hat{\bm{\mu}}i, \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}i) \alphai \mathbf{c}i Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \left( 1 - \mathcal{I}{g-j}^{2D}(\mathbf{u} | \hat{\bm{\mu}}j, \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}j) \alphaj \right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. ds1minusdx) diffux dIdv1y = 2.0 math.pi isigma2 (ds1plusdx - ds1minusdx) diffuy dIdv2x = 2.0 math.pi isigma1 (ds2plusdy - ds2minusdy) diffux dIdv2y = 2.0 math.pi isigma1 (ds2plusdy - ds2minusdy) diffuy return { 'dIdmu': [dIdmux, dIdmuy], 'dIdlambda1': dIdlambda1, 'dIdlambda2': dIdlambda2, 'dIdv1': [dIdv1x, dIdv1y], 'dIdv2': [dIdv2x, dIdv2y] } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Correlation Term: The 2D integral with the correlation term b(x-\hat{\mu}x)(y-\hat{\mu}y) is intractable analytically. The method resolves this by diagonalizing the covariance matrix and rotating the integration domain to align with eigenvectors, approximating the 2D integral as a product of two independent 1D integrals. Small Standard Deviation: Unlike Mip-Splatting which convolves with a Gaussian kernel and suppresses high-frequency components causing over-smoothing, Analytic-Splatting calculates the integral analytically to preserve details. Super Sampling: Unlike Monte Carlo super sampling, this method uses a closed-form approximation, avoiding the computation burden of increasing sample counts. Time Complexity: The method replaces the exponential evaluation of the 2D Gaussian with a few logistic function evaluations and arithmetic operations. It is comparable in speed to standard 3DGS point sampling but more expensive than simple point sampling due to the eigen-decomposition and logistic calculations. It is significantly faster than super-sampling methods. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the standard Gaussian parameters. The logistic function uses fixed constants. Strengths: Removes aliasing artifacts (blurring/jaggies) during zooming or resolution changes. Preserves high-frequency details better than Mip-Splatting. Limitations: Requires eigenvalue decomposition per Gaussian, which can be computationally intensive if not optimized. The approximation error depends on the validity of the logistic approximation for the specific range of \sigma values encountered. When to use: When anti-aliasing is critical and high-frequency detail preservation is desired, especially for dynamic camera movements or varying resolutions. When not to use: If computational resources are extremely limited and aliasing is acceptable. Analytic-Splatting was introduced by Zhihao Liang, Qi Zhang, Wenbo Hu, Lei Zhu, Ying Feng, and Kui Jia in the paper "Analytic-Splatting: Anti-Aliased 3D Gaussian Splatting via Analytic Integration" (arXiv:2403.11056, 2024). It addresses the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which treats pixels as isolated points and suffers from aliasing when the pixel footprint changes due to focal length or camera distance adjustments. The method builds on the 3DGS framework but replaces the point-sampling shading with an analytical integration of the Gaussian signal over the pixel window area. name: Analytic-Splatting Gradient Computation
head: Gradient of 2D Gaussian integral w.r.t covariance matrix, Gradient of Analytic 2D Gaussian Splat
body: This method computes the exact gradient of the analytically integrated 2D Gaussian splat intensity with respect to the elements of the 2D covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma}. It enables differentiable training of Gaussian splat parameters by providing the necessary backpropagation signals for the covariance, which is critical for optimizing the shape and orientation of the Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on Analytic-Splatting by extending the analytical integration to include the derivative terms required for gradient-based optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The analytically integrated 2D Gaussian intensity \mathcal{I}^{2D}g, the 2D covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma} (symmetric, 2 \times 2), and the pixel center coordinates (ux, uy) relative to the Gaussian center (\hat{\mu}x, \hat{\mu}y). Output: The gradient matrix \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}} with respect to the independent elements \hat{\Sigma}{11}, \hat{\Sigma}{12}, \hat{\Sigma}{22}. Data Structures: The covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma} is represented by its eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and corresponding eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. \lambda1, \lambda2 \in \mathbb{R}: Eigenvalues. \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2 \in \mathbb{R}^2: Eigenvectors, normalized such that \|\mathbf{v}i\|=1. Method Steps: The gradient is computed using the chain rule over the eigenvalues and eigenvectors. For each element \hat{\Sigma}{ij} where (i,j) \in \{(1,1), (1,2), (2,2)\}: 1. Decompose Covariance: Compute the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2 of \hat{\Sigma}. 2. Compute Intensity Gradients w.r.t Eigenvalues: Calculate \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \lambda1} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \lambda2}. These are derived from the analytical intensity formula provided in Analytic-Splatting. 3. Compute Eigenvalue Gradients w.r.t Covariance: Calculate \frac{\partial \lambda1}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} and \frac{\partial \lambda2}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}}. The source notes refer to external literature [26] for these specific derivatives. 4. Compute Intensity Gradients w.r.t Eigenvectors: Calculate \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \mathbf{v}1} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \mathbf{v}2}. 5. Compute Eigenvector Gradients w.r.t Covariance: Calculate \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}1}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} and \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}2}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}}. The source provides a specific closed-form expression for \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}2}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}}: \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}2}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} = 2\pi \mathcal{I}{\sigma 1} \left( \frac{\partial S{\sigma2}(\tilde{u}y + 1/2)}{\partial \tilde{u}y} - \frac{\partial S{\sigma2}(\tilde{u}y - 1/2)}{\partial \tilde{u}y} \right) \begin{bmatrix} ux - \hat{\mu}x \\ uy - \hat{\mu}y \end{bmatrix} where: \mathcal{I}{\sigma 1} is the intensity component associated with the first principal axis (derived from \lambda1). S{\sigma2}(\cdot) is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a 1D Gaussian with standard deviation \sigma2 = \sqrt{\lambda2}. \tilde{u}y is the projected coordinate along the second eigenvector \mathbf{v}2. The term \frac{\partial S{\sigma2}(z)}{\partial z} is the probability density function (PDF) of the 1D Gaussian: \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma2} e^{-z^2 / (2\sigma2^2)}. The gradient for \mathbf{v}1 is computed similarly, swapping indices 1 and 2. 6. Assemble Final Gradient: Combine the terms using the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \lambda1} \frac{\partial \lambda1}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} + \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \lambda2} \frac{\partial \lambda2}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} + \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \mathbf{v}1}\right)^\top \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}1}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} + \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \mathbf{v}2}\right)^\top \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}2}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def analyticsplattinggradient(I2Dg, sigma, mu, ux, uy): """ Computes gradient of analytic 2D Gaussian intensity w.r.t covariance matrix elements. Args: I2Dg: Analytic intensity value (scalar). sigma: 2D covariance matrix Sigmahat (2x2 symmetric). mu: Gaussian center (2,). ux, uy: Pixel coordinates (scalars). Returns: gradsigma: Gradient w.r.t Sigmahat elements (2x2 symmetric, stored as [d11, d12, d22]). """ # 1. Eigen decomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(sigma) lambda1, lambda2 = eigenvalues[0], eigenvalues[1] v1, v2 = eigenvectors[:, 0], eigenvectors[:, 1] # 2. Compute intensity gradients w.r.t eigenvalues # Note: Exact formulas for dI/dlambda depend on the specific analytic integral definition # from the parent article. Here we assume helper functions are available. dIdlambda1 = getdIdlambda1(I2Dg, lambda1, lambda2, ux, uy, mu) dIdlambda2 = getdIdlambda2(I2Dg, lambda1, lambda2, ux, uy, mu) # 3. Compute eigenvalue gradients w.r.t covariance elements # Refer to external literature [26] for exact formulas. # dlambda/dSigmaij dlambda1dSigma = getdlambdadSigma(lambda1, lambda2, v1, v2) dlambda2dSigma = getdlambdadSigma(lambda2, lambda1, v2, v1) # Symmetry handling # 4. Compute intensity gradients w.r.t eigenvectors # dI/dvk is a vector in R^2 dIdv1 = getdIdv1(I2Dg, lambda1, lambda2, v1, v2, ux, uy, mu) dIdv2 = getdIdv2(I2Dg, lambda1, lambda2, v1, v2, ux, uy, mu) # 5. Compute eigenvector gradients w.r.t covariance elements # Using the specific formula from for dv2/dSigma sigma2 = np.sqrt(lambda2) sigma1 = np.sqrt(lambda1) # Project pixel offset onto eigenvectors offset = np.array([ux - mu[0], uy - mu[1]]) utilde1 = np.dot(offset, v1) utilde2 = np.dot(offset, v2) # PDF of 1D Gaussian def gaussianpdf(z, sigma): return (1.0 / (np.sqrt(2 np.pi) sigma)) np.exp(-0.5 (z / sigma)2) # Boundary terms for eigenvector gradient # Ssigma2 is CDF, derivative is PDF termyplus = gaussianpdf(utilde2 + 0.5, sigma2) termyminus = gaussianpdf(utilde2 - 0.5, sigma2) # Pre-factor for dv2/dSigma # Isigma1 is the intensity component along axis 1 Isigma1 = getIsigma1component(lambda1, sigma1, utilde1) prefactor = 2 np.pi Isigma1 (termyplus - termyminus) directionvector = offset # [ux - mux, uy - muy] # dv2/dSigmaij is a vector in R^2 scaled by the scalar derivative dSigmaij/dSigmaij (which is 1 or 2 for symmetric) # The formula in gives the vector part. We need to map this to specific matrix elements. # For a symmetric matrix, dSigma12 is shared. # Construct gradients for each element # This is a simplified representation; exact mapping requires careful handling of symmetric matrix derivatives grad11 = np.zeros(2) grad12 = np.zeros(2) grad22 = np.zeros(2) # Example calculation for dv2/dSigma11, dv2/dSigma12, dv2/dSigma22 # These depend on the specific derivative of eigenvectors w.r.t matrix elements. # The source Eq 32 gives the vector result of the derivative operation. # We assume helper functions compute the scalar coefficients for each matrix element. dv2dSigma11 = getdvdSigmaelement(v2, 1, 1) prefactor directionvector dv2dSigma12 = getdvdSigmaelement(v2, 1, 2) prefactor directionvector dv2dSigma22 = getdvdSigmaelement(v2, 2, 2) prefactor directionvector # Similarly for v1 #... (symmetric logic for v1) # 6. Assemble final gradient # gradSigmaij = dI/dlambda1 dlambda1/dSigmaij + dI/dlambda2 dlambda2/dSigmaij + (dI/dv1)^T dv1/dSigmaij + (dI/dv2)^T dv2/dSigmaij # Return gradients for Sigma11, Sigma12, Sigma22 return [grad11, grad12, grad22] Parameters: \sigma1, \sigma2: Standard deviations derived from eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2. \tilde{u}y: Projected coordinate along the second eigenvector. Typical values: None specified; depends on scene geometry and Gaussian scale. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Eigenvalues: If \lambda1 \approx \lambda2, the eigenvectors are not unique, leading to numerical instability in the gradient computation. A small regularization term may be needed. Precision: The calculation involves exponentials and square roots. Care must be taken to avoid underflow/overflow for very small or large Gaussians. Symmetric Matrix Handling: The covariance matrix is symmetric. The gradient w.r.t \hat{\Sigma}{12} must account for the fact that changing \hat{\Sigma}{12} affects both the (1,2) and (2,1) entries. The source formula assumes standard matrix calculus conventions. Time Complexity: Dominated by eigen decomposition (O(1) for 2 \times 2 matrix) and evaluation of Gaussian PDFs/CDFs. Constant time per splat per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per splat. Strengths: Provides exact gradients for the analytic integration, enabling stable training of Gaussian shapes and reducing aliasing artifacts compared to point-sampling gradients. Limitations: More complex to implement than standard rasterization gradients due to the need for eigen-decomposition and specific eigenvector derivative formulas. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models with analytic integration to improve visual quality and reduce aliasing. The method originates from the "Analytic-Splatting" paper, which proposes anti-aliased 3D Gaussian Splatting via analytic integration. The gradient computation is a crucial component for the differentiable rendering pipeline, allowing the optimization of Gaussian parameters (including covariance) via gradient descent. The specific eigenvector gradient formula is derived in the context of this paper. name: LinPrim Gradient Computation
head: Backpropagation through ray space intersection, Gradient propagation for LinPrim
body: LinPrim Gradient Computation computes the gradients of intersection depths \mathbf{i} with respect to the ray-space triangle corners \mathbf{v}^{\text{ray}} to enable differentiable rendering of linear primitives. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by backpropagating gradients through a linear primitive rasterizer (MTIA) rather than a Gaussian splatting kernel, requiring specific handling of ray-space to world-space transformations and quaternion-based rotation updates. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer by replacing the Gaussian alpha-blending gradient flow with opacity calculations based on intersection depths. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gradients of the loss with respect to the final pixel color \frac{\partial L}{\partial C}, the intersection depths \mathbf{i}1, \mathbf{i}2 for the primitive, the ray-space triangle corners \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}, \mathbf{v}1^{\text{ray}}, \mathbf{v}2^{\text{ray}}, and the barycentric coordinates u, v of the intersection point. Output: Gradients of the loss with respect to the ray-space corners \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}}}, which are subsequently transformed to world space and propagated to primitive parameters (distance, rotation). Data Structures: Ray-space corners: \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for k \in \{0, 1, 2\}. Intersection depths: \mathbf{i}1, \mathbf{i}2 \in \mathbb{R}, representing the entry and exit depths of the ray through the primitive along the view ray. Barycentric coordinates: u, v \in [0, 1] such that u+v \le 1. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Opacity Gradient Calculation: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the intersection depths \mathbf{i}1 and \mathbf{i}2 using the opacity function: o(\mathbf{i}1, \mathbf{i}2) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\alpha) \cdot (\mathbf{i}2 - \mathbf{i}1)) where \sigma(\alpha) is a scaling factor for opacity \alpha. The gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{i}k} is derived from \frac{\partial L}{\partial C} and \frac{\partial o}{\partial \mathbf{i}k}. 2. Barycentric Coordinate Derivatives: Compute the partial derivatives of the barycentric coordinates u and v with respect to the ray-space corners. The barycentric coordinates are invariant to depth, so they have only two non-zero components (x and y). Let \mathbf{r} be the pixel ray coordinates and d be the determinant of the triangle projection in ray space. For corner \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}: \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}} = \frac{1}{d} \left( \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{r}y \\ \mathbf{r}x - \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}} \end{pmatrix} - u \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}} \\ \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}} \end{pmatrix} \right) \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}} = \frac{1}{d} \left( \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{r}y - \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}} \\ \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{r}x \end{pmatrix} - v \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}} \\ \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}} \end{pmatrix} \right) Analogous formulas apply for \mathbf{v}1^{\text{ray}} and \mathbf{v}2^{\text{ray}}. 3. Intersection Depth Gradient w.r.t. Corners: Compute the gradient of the intersection depth \mathbf{i} with respect to each corner \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}}. The source provides specific formulas for \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}: \frac{\partial \mathbf{i}}{\partial \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}} = \begin{pmatrix} -\left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,x}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ - \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ 1 - u - v \end{pmatrix} The source text contains typos in indices for \mathbf{v}1^{\text{ray}} and \mathbf{v}2^{\text{ray}} (e.g., \partial u / \partial \mathbf{v}{1,x} appearing twice). Implementers should derive analogous formulas based on symmetry. Corrected symmetric formulas for \mathbf{v}1^{\text{ray}} and \mathbf{v}2^{\text{ray}} are: \frac{\partial \mathbf{i}}{\partial \mathbf{v}1^{\text{ray}}} = \begin{pmatrix} -\left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ - \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ -v \end{pmatrix} \frac{\partial \mathbf{i}}{\partial \mathbf{v}2^{\text{ray}}} = \begin{pmatrix} -\left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ - \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ -u \end{pmatrix} 4. Ray-Space Center Gradient: Compute the gradient with respect to the ray-space center. The process follows the same procedure as for the corners. 5. Transformation to World Space: Undo the ray-space and view-space transformations. Since these are matrix multiplications, the gradients are propagated by multiplying with the transpose of the transformation matrices. 6. Propagation to Primitive Parameters: Map the world-space corner gradients to the primitive's distance and rotation parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computelinprimgradients(lossgradcolor, i1, i2, v0ray, v1ray, v2ray, r, sigmaalpha): """ Computes gradients for LinPrim intersection depths. Args: lossgradcolor: Gradient of loss w.r.t. pixel color. i1, i2: Intersection depths (entry, exit). v0ray, v1ray, v2ray: Ray-space triangle corners (3D vectors). r: Pixel ray coordinates (2D vector). sigmaalpha: Scaling factor for opacity. Returns: gradv0, gradv1, gradv2: Gradients w.r.t. ray-space corners. """ # Step 1: Opacity Gradient expterm = np.exp(-sigmaalpha (i2 - i1)) gradi2 = lossgradcolor sigmaalpha expterm gradi1 = -lossgradcolor sigmaalpha expterm # Step 2: Barycentric Derivatives dx1 = v1ray[0] - v0ray[0] dy1 = v1ray[1] - v0ray[1] dx2 = v2ray[0] - v0ray[0] dy2 = v2ray[1] - v0ray[1] d = dx1 dy2 - dy1 dx2 # Compute barycentric coordinates u, v for intersection point r u = ((v2ray[1] - r[1]) (v0ray[0] - r[0]) + (r[1] - v0ray[1]) (v2ray[0] - r[0])) / d v = ((v0ray[1] - r[1]) (v1ray[0] - r[0]) + (r[1] - v0ray[1]) (v0ray[0] - r[0])) / d # Helper to compute 2D barycentric derivatives for a corner def barycentricderivs(vk, vnext, vprev): # vk is the corner being differentiated, vnext is the next corner in CCW order, vprev is previous # Derivatives w.r.t vk.x and vk.y dudk = np.array([vprev[1] - r[1], r[0] - vprev[0]]) / d - u np.array([vprev[1] - vnext[1], vnext[0] - vprev[0]]) / d dvdk = np.array([r[1] - vnext[1], vnext[0] - r[0]]) / d - v np.array([vprev[1] - vnext[1], vnext[0] - vprev[0]]) / d return dudk, dvdk duv0, dvv0 = barycentricderivs(v0ray, v1ray, v2ray) duv1, dvv1 = barycentricderivs(v1ray, v2ray, v0ray) duv2, dvv2 = barycentricderivs(v2ray, v0ray, v1ray) # Step 3: Intersection Depth Gradient w.r.t. Corners def computeintersectiongrad(duk, dvk, vk, vnext, vprev, uval, vval): # 2D components gradx = -((duk[1] + dvk[0]) vk[2] + duk[0] vprev[2] + dvk[0] vnext[2]) grady = -((duk[1] + dvk[1]) vk[2] + duk[1] vprev[2] + dvk[1] vnext[2]) # 3D component (barycentric coordinate derivative) gradz = 1.0 - uval - vval return np.array([gradx, grady, gradz]) gradiv0 = computeintersectiongrad(duv0, dvv0, v0ray, v1ray, v2ray, u, v) gradiv1 = computeintersectiongrad(duv1, dvv1, v1ray, v2ray, v0ray, u, v) gradiv1[2] = -vval # Corrected z-component for v1 gradiv2 = computeintersectiongrad(duv2, dvv2, v2ray, v0ray, v1ray, u, v) gradiv2[2] = -uval # Corrected z-component for v2 # Step 4 & 5: Backpropagate through opacity and transform to world space gradv0ray = gradiv0 (gradi1 - gradi2) gradv1ray = gradiv1 (gradi1 - gradi2) gradv2ray = gradiv2 (gradi1 - gradi2) # World space transformation (transpose of view/ray matrices) # gradv0world = Tview.T @ Tray.T @ gradv0ray # gradv1world = Tview.T @ Tray.T @ gradv1ray # gradv2world = Tview.T @ Tray.T @ gradv2ray return gradv0ray, gradv1ray, gradv2ray Parameters: Color learning rate: 2.5 \times 10^{-3}. SH Coefficients learning rate: 1.25 \times 10^{-4}. Opacity learning rate: 2.5 \times 10^{-2}. Rotation learning rate: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Distance learning rate: 2.6 \times 10^{-4}, scaled by the maximum distance between a known camera pose and the mean camera pose. 2D filter kernel size: 0.1. For octahedra, the ray space vector is moved by half that amount (0.05). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Octahedra Negation: For octahedra, vertices are in positive or negative directions from the center. The gradient onto the actual ray-space feature can be negated. This negation is omitted in the provided formulas for readability. Density Normalization: Do not propagate gradients through the density normalization factor. Source Typos: The source text contains typos in indices for \mathbf{v}1 and \mathbf{v}2 gradients (e.g., \partial u / \partial \mathbf{v}{1,x} appearing twice). Implementers must correct these based on symmetry. name: LinPrim Optimization
head: LinPrim Differentiable Optimization
body: LinPrim Optimization is the parameter update phase of the LinPrim rendering pipeline, which adjusts the geometric and appearance features of linear primitives (triangles) to minimize a differentiable loss function. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) optimization by backpropagating gradients through a linear primitive rasterizer (MTIA) rather than a Gaussian splatting kernel, requiring specific handling of ray-space to world-space transformations and quaternion-based rotation updates. It builds on LinPrim Gradient Computation to compute the necessary gradients for intersection depths. The optimization process minimizes a loss function using the ADAM optimizer, backpropagating gradients through the entire differentiable rendering pipeline. Inputs: Current primitive parameters: position \mathbf{p}, quaternion \mathbf{q}, scale/distance features \mathbf{s}, view-dependent color coefficients, and opacity \alpha. Training views: camera poses and intrinsics. Target images: ground truth RGB images. Loss weights: \lambda{\text{L1}} and \lambda{\text{SSIM}} following the 3DGS formulation. Outputs: Updated primitive parameters for the next optimization step. Data Structures: Primitives are stored as a list of objects containing: center: 3D position vector. quaternion: 4D unit quaternion for rotation. distances: 3D vector representing scale/extent features. color: View-dependent color coefficients. opacity: Scalar alpha value. Steps: 1. Forward Pass: Render the scene using the LinPrim rasterizer to produce an image I{\text{rendered}}. 2. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of L1 loss and SSIM loss between I{\text{rendered}} and the target image I{\text{target}}, following the 3DGS formulation. 3. Rasterization Backpropagation: Compute gradients of the loss with respect to the output alpha \alpha and color C of each primitive. The gradient \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alpha} indicates the desired transparency change. If \alpha needs to increase, intersections should move closer; if decrease, farther apart. Propagate gradients from \alpha to the intersection depths d along the ray. Compute gradients of intersection depths with respect to the triangle corner positions in ray space, \frac{\partial d}{\partial \mathbf{v}^{\text{ray}}}, using the results from LinPrim Gradient Computation. Aggregate gradients over all corners and both intersections (entry and exit) to obtain gradients with respect to the ray-space center and corner offsets. 4. Preprocessing Backpropagation (Ray Space to World Space): Reverse the view and projection transformations to convert ray-space gradients to world-space gradients. Compute the final gradient with respect to the primitive center \mathbf{p}. This combines the propagated ray-space center gradients with the gradient arising from the impact of position on the ray-space approximation and view-dependent color. Split the gradient flow with respect to the corners when undoing the rotation. The gradients are distributed to the quaternion \mathbf{q} and the distance features \mathbf{s}. 5. Learning Rate Adjustment: Calculate the maximum distance D{\text{max}} between any two training cameras to approximate scene size. Adjust learning rates for position and distance features based on D{\text{max}} to handle scale ambiguity. 6. Parameter Update: Apply the ADAM optimizer to update \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{s}, color, and opacity using the computed gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizelinprimstep(primitives, trainingviews, targetimages, optimizer, lambdal1, lambdassim): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 for view, target in zip(trainingviews, targetimages): renderedimg = forwardrasterize(primitives, view) l1loss = lambdal1 meanabsoluteerror(renderedimg, target) ssimloss = lambdassim computessim(renderedimg, target) totalloss += l1loss + ssimloss totalloss /= len(trainingviews) totalloss.backward() maxcamdist = 0.0 for i, v1 in enumerate(trainingviews): for v2 in trainingviews[i+1:]: d = vectornorm(v1.position - v2.position) if d > maxcamdist: maxcamdist = d # Scale gradients for position and distance features based on maxcamdist # The sources state learning rates are adjusted based on maxcamdist, but do not specify the exact scaling formula. for prim in primitives: prim.gradposition /= maxcamdist prim.graddistances /= maxcamdist optimizer.step() def forwardrasterize(primitives, view): # Standard differentiable rasterization forward pass return renderimage(primitives, view) def meanabsoluteerror(img1, img2): return sum(abs(img1[i][j][k] - img2[i][j][k]) for i in range(H) for j in range(W) for k in range(3)) / (H W 3) def computessim(img1, img2): # Standard SSIM computation return ssimmetric(img1, img2) def vectornorm(v): return sqrt(sum(v[j]2 for j in range(3))) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Ambiguity: Scenes are scale-ambiguous, requiring careful adjustment of learning rates for position and distance features based on scene size. Quaternion Normalization: When updating quaternions, normalization must be applied to maintain unit length. Degenerate Triangles: If primitives collapse to lines or points, gradient computation may become unstable. The forward pass that renders linear primitives. It computes intersection depths and blends colors. LinPrim Rasterization Computes gradients of intersection depths with respect to ray space triangle corners. LinPrim Gradient Computation The baseline optimization method using Gaussian primitives, which LinPrim adapts. 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Empirically mirrors the behavior of 2D Mip filters, reducing visible aliasing. Strengths: Differentiable rendering allows end-to-end optimization of linear primitives. The use of L1 and SSIM losses provides robust convergence. Limitations: Requires careful handling of scale ambiguity and quaternion updates. Population control (adding/removing primitives) is not part of this optimization step and requires separate mechanisms. When to Use: When optimizing linear primitives for differentiable volumetric rendering where aliasing reduction is important. When Not to Use: When Gaussian primitives are sufficient or when computational resources are extremely limited, as linear primitives may have higher overhead. LinPrim Optimization was introduced in the paper "LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering". It extends the differentiable rendering framework of 3D Gaussian Splatting to linear primitives (triangles). The method uses the ADAM optimizer and backpropagates through the entire rendering pipeline, including a custom rasterizer (MTIA) and preprocessing steps. The approach addresses visible aliasing by incorporating filtering mechanisms that mimic 2D Mip filters. name: Gaussian Splat Rasterization (Vertex Shader)
head: GSplat Vert, Splat Vertex Shader
body: This method implements the vertex shader stage of a GPU-based rasterizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting, transforming 3D Gaussian primitives into 2D screen-space ellipses for instanced rendering. It differs from fragment-based or compute-shader approaches by performing all geometric projection, covariance transformation, and ellipse basis computation within the vertex shader, passing only the final vertex positions and attributes to the rasterizer. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer by handling the specific data unpacking and frustum culling required for efficient vertex-driven splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: utexture: A usampler2D containing packed Gaussian data (position and covariance). projection: A 4 \times 4 projection matrix. view: A 4 \times 4 view matrix. focal: A vec2 containing the focal lengths (fx, fy). viewport: A vec2 containing the viewport dimensions (w, h). position: A vec2 instance attribute representing the local basis of the quad (typically [-2, -2] to [2, 2]). index: A uint instance attribute identifying the Gaussian splat. Outputs: glPosition: The clip-space position of the four vertices of the ellipse quad. Data Structures and Layout: The input texture utexture stores Gaussian data in a 2D grid layout optimized for batched access. Each Gaussian splat i occupies two texels (columns) in the texture. The texture width is fixed at 2048 pixels (1024 Gaussians per row). The row index is calculated as row = i >> 10 (integer division by 1024). The column index for the center data is col = (i & 0x3ff) << 1. The column index for the covariance data is col = ((i & 0x3ff) << 1) | 1. Each texel is a uvec4 (four 32-bit unsigned integers). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Fetch Center Data: Retrieve the packed center position from the texture using the instance index: glsl uvec4 cen = texelFetch(utexture, ivec2((uint(index) & 0x3ffu) << 1, uint(index) >> 10), 0); 2. Transform to Camera Space: Convert the packed integer center to a float vector and transform it into camera space: glsl vec4 cam = view vec4(uintBitsToFloat(cen.xyz), 1.0); 3. Project to Clip Space: Compute the clip-space position: glsl vec4 pos2d = projection cam; 4. Frustum Culling: Perform early-out culling with a 1.2x margin to ensure splats near the edge are not clipped incorrectly by the rasterizer. If the splat is outside the frustum, discard it by setting glPosition to a post-depth value: glsl float clip = 1.2 pos2d.w; if (pos2d.z < -pos2d.w || pos2d.z > pos2d.w || pos2d.x < -clip || pos2d.x > clip || pos2d.y < -clip || pos2d.y > clip) { glPosition = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0); return; } 5. Fetch Covariance Data: Retrieve the packed covariance and color data: glsl uvec4 cov = texelFetch(utexture, ivec2(((uint(index) & 0x3ffu) << 1) | 1u, uint(index) >> 10), 0); 6. Unpack Covariance Components: Unpack the half-precision floating-point components from cov.x, cov.y, and cov.z into vec2 pairs u1, u2, and u3 using unpackHalf2x16. 7. Reconstruct 3D Covariance Matrix: Reconstruct the symmetric 3 \times 3 covariance matrix V{rk} in 3D space from the unpacked components: glsl mat3 Vrk = mat3( u1.x, u1.y, u2.x, u1.y, u2.y, u3.x, u2.x, u3.x, u3.y); 8. Compute Projection Jacobian: Calculate the Jacobian J of the perspective projection transformation: glsl mat3 J = mat3( focal.x / cam.z, 0.0, -(focal.x cam.x) / (cam.z cam.z), 0.0, focal.y / cam.z, -(focal.y cam.y) / (cam.z cam.z), 0.0, 0.0, 0.0); 9. Transform Covariance to Camera Space: Compute the transformation matrix T and the resulting 2D covariance matrix cov{2d}: glsl mat3 T = transpose(mat3(view)) J; mat3 cov2d = transpose(T) Vrk T; 10. Apply Low-Pass Filter: Add a small constant to the diagonal elements to prevent numerical instability and ensure positive definiteness: glsl cov2d[0][0] += 0.1; cov2d[1][1] += 0.1; 11. Compute Eigenvalues: Calculate the eigenvalues \lambda1 and \lambda2 of the upper-left 2 \times 2 submatrix of cov{2d}: glsl float mid = (cov2d[0][0] + cov2d[1][1]) / 2.0; float radius = length(vec2((cov2d[0][0] - cov2d[1][1]) / 2.0, cov2d[0][1])); float lambda1 = mid + radius; float lambda2 = mid - radius; 12. Check Validity: If \lambda2 < 0.0, the covariance is invalid (negative variance). Discard the splat: glsl if (lambda2 < 0.0) { glPosition = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0); return; } 13. Compute Axis Vectors: Determine the major and minor axis directions and magnitudes. The scale factor is 2.5, and the maximum axis length is capped at 1024.0: glsl vec2 diagonalVector = normalize(vec2(cov2d[0][1], lambda1 - cov2d[0][0])); vec2 majorAxis = 2.5 vec2(min(sqrt(2.0 lambda1), 1024.0)) diagonalVector; vec2 minorAxis = 2.5 vec2(min(sqrt(2.0 lambda2), 1024.0)) vec2(diagonalVector.y, -diagonalVector.x); 14. Unpack Color: Extract the RGBA color from the w component of the covariance texel: glsl vec4 color = vec4( float((cov.w) & 0xffu), float((cov.w >> 8) & 0xffu), float((cov.w >> 16) & 0xffu), float((cov.w >> 24) & 0xffu)) / 255.0; 15. Compute Final Vertex Positions: Transform the local quad positions into screen space using the computed axes and viewport dimensions: glsl vec2 vCenter = vec2(pos2d) / pos2d.w; glPosition = vec4( vCenter + (position.x majorAxis + position.y minorAxis) / viewport, pos2d.z / pos2d.w, 1.0); Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def uintbitstofloat(u): import struct return struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', u))[0] def unpackhalf2x16(u): lo = u & 0xFFFF hi = (u >> 16) & 0xFFFF def halftofloat(h): sign = (h >> 15) & 0x1 exp = (h >> 10) & 0x1F frac = h & 0x3FF if exp == 0: return (-1)sign (frac / 1024.0) 2-14 elif exp == 31: return (-1)sign float('inf') if frac else (-1)sign float('inf') else: return (-1)sign (1.0 + frac / 1024.0) (2(exp - 15)) return [halftofloat(lo), halftofloat(hi)] def texelfetch(texture, col, row): return texture[row][col] def splatvertexshader(index, position, view, projection, focal, viewport, utexture): # 1. Fetch Center row = index >> 10 colcenter = (index & 0x3ff) << 1 cen = texelfetch(utexture, colcenter, row) # 2. Transform to Camera Space camxyz = [uintbitstofloat(cen[0]), uintbitstofloat(cen[1]), uintbitstofloat(cen[2])] cam = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] for i in range(4): for j in range(4): cam[i] += view[i][j] (camxyz[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) # 3. Project to Clip Space pos2d = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(4): for j in range(4): pos2d[i] += projection[i][j] cam[j] # 4. Frustum Culling clipmargin = 1.2 pos2d[3] if (pos2d[2] < -pos2d[3] or pos2d[2] > pos2d[3] or pos2d[0] < -clipmargin or pos2d[0] > clipmargin or pos2d[1] < -clipmargin or pos2d[1] > clipmargin): return [0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0] # 5. Fetch Covariance colcov = ((index & 0x3ff) << 1) | 1 cov = texelfetch(utexture, colcov, row) # 6. Unpack Covariance u1 = unpackhalf2x16(cov[0]) u2 = unpackhalf2x16(cov[1]) u3 = unpackhalf2x16(cov[2]) # 7. Reconstruct 3D Covariance Vrk = [[u1[0], u1[1], u2[0]], [u1[1], u2[1], u3[0]], [u2[0], u3[0], u3[1]]] # 8. Compute Jacobian J = [[focal[0] / cam[2], 0.0, -(focal[0] cam[0]) / (cam[2] cam[2])], [0.0, focal[1] / cam[2], -(focal[1] cam[1]) / (cam[2] cam[2])], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]] # 9. Transform Covariance view3x3 = [[view[0][0], view[0][1], view[0][2]], [view[1][0], view[1][1], view[1][2]], [view[2][0], view[2][1], view[2][2]]] T = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): for k in range(3): T[i][j] += view3x3[k][i] J[k][j] cov2d = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): for k in range(3): for m in range(3): cov2d[i][j] += T[k][i] Vrk[k][m] T[m][j] # 10. Low-Pass Filter cov2d[0][0] += 0.1 cov2d[1][1] += 0.1 # 11. Eigenvalues mid = (cov2d[0][0] + cov2d[1][1]) / 2.0 radius = math.sqrt(((cov2d[0][0] - cov2d[1][1]) / 2.0)2 + cov2d[0][1]2) lambda1 = mid + radius lambda2 = mid - radius # 12. Validity Check if lambda2 < 0.0: return [0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0] # 13. Axis Vectors diaglen = math.sqrt(cov2d[0][1]2 + (lambda1 - cov2d[0][0])2) diagonalvector = [cov2d[0][1] / diaglen, (lambda1 - cov2d[0][0]) / diaglen] scale = 2.5 majoraxis = [scale min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda1), 1024.0) diagonalvector[0], scale min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda1), 1024.0) diagonalvector[1]] minoraxis = [scale min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda2), 1024.0) diagonalvector[1], scale min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda2), 1024.0) -diagonalvector[0]] # 14. Unpack Color color = [ float(cov[3] & 0xff) / 255.0, float((cov[3] >> 8) & 0xff) / 255.0, float((cov[3] >> 16) & 0xff) / 255.0, float((cov[3] >> 24) & 0xff) / 255.0 ] # 15. Final Position vcenter = [pos2d[0] / pos2d[3], pos2d[1] / pos2d[3]] finalx = vcenter[0] + (position[0] majoraxis[0] + position[1] minoraxis[0]) / viewport[0] finaly = vcenter[1] + (position[0] majoraxis[1] + position[1] minoraxis[1]) / viewport[1] return [finalx, finaly, pos2d[2] / pos2d[3], 1.0] Time Complexity: O(1) per splat vertex. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the Gaussian data in the texture, where N is the number of splats, requiring 2 \times N texels. Strengths: Early frustum culling reduces the number of splats processed in later stages. The use of half-precision packing reduces memory bandwidth. Limitations: The fixed texture width of 2048 pixels limits the number of splats per row, potentially requiring multiple rows for large scenes. The method assumes a specific data layout and may require adaptation for different hardware or API constraints. This method is derived from the gsplat-opengl implementation by liaozhangsheng, which provides an unofficial OpenGL-based rasterizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It adapts the differentiable rasterization principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting to a vertex-shader-driven pipeline, optimizing for performance by moving geometric computations to the vertex stage. liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline, Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, Tile-based Gaussian Rasterization, render_view pipeline
body: The Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline orchestrates camera setup, spherical harmonic (SH) evaluation, feature assembly, and Gaussian rasterization for a single view. It projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space, rasterizes them into tiles, and composites them front-to-back using alpha blending to produce novel views. It sets apart from its siblings by managing the pre-computation of covariances, colors, and lighting models, and assembling auxiliary features before invoking the differentiable rasterizer. The pipeline processes a single camera view to produce a rendered image and associated auxiliary features. It assumes the existence of a GaussianModel object (pc) containing the 3D Gaussians and a pipeline configuration object (pipe) controlling computation modes. Inputs: pc: The Gaussian model containing means3D (N, 3), scales (N, 3), rotations (N, 4), opacities (N), shs (N, K, 3), and covariance data. camera: Object with imagewidth, imageheight, fovx, fovy, cx, cy, worldviewtransform, fullprojtransform, cameracenter. pipe: Configuration object with flags computecov3Dpython, computeSHspython, and integer shdegree. background: Tensor (3,) representing the background color. overridecolor: Optional tensor for direct color override. lighttransform: Optional object providing light direction; if absent, headlights are used. Outputs: renderedimage: Tensor (H, W, 3) of the final RGB image. renderedopacity: Tensor (H, W, 1) of accumulated opacity. rendereddepth: Tensor (H, W, 1) of depth. renderedfeature: Tensor containing concatenated auxiliary features. radii: Tensor (N,) of screen-space radii for each Gaussian. numrendered: Count of Gaussians contributing to at least one pixel. numcontrib: Count of Gaussians contributing to each pixel. GaussianRasterizationSettings: A configuration object passed to the rasterizer. Fields include imagewidth, imageheight, tanfovx, tanfovy, cx, cy, background, scalemodifier, viewMatrix, projMatrix, shdegree, cameraPosition. screenspacepoints: Tensor (N, 2) initialized to zeros on CUDA with requiresgrad=True to capture 2D mean gradients. 1. Initialize Gradient Tracking: Create screenspacepoints as a zero tensor on CUDA with requiresgrad=True. Attempt to retain gradients via retaingrad() for debugging purposes. 2. Compute Camera Intrinsics: Calculate tangent field-of-view values: \text{tanfovx} = \tan(\text{fov}x / 2) \text{tanfovy} = \tan(\text{fov}y / 2) Extract principal points cx and cy from the camera intrinsics. 3. Construct Rasterization Settings: Assemble GaussianRasterizationSettings with: Image dimensions from camera. tanfovx, tanfovy, cx, cy. background color. scalemodifier (default 1.0). viewMatrix and projMatrix from camera.worldviewtransform and camera.fullprojtransform. shdegree from pipe. cameraPosition from camera.cameracenter. 4. Select Covariance Representation: If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true: Compute cov3Dprecomp by calling pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier). Otherwise: Retrieve scales and rotations directly from pc.getscaling() and pc.getrotation() to be processed by the CUDA kernel. 5. Select Color Representation: If overridecolor is None and pipe.computeSHspython is true: Normalize view directions. Extract SH coefficients from pc.shs. Evaluate SH functions to compute colors. Apply RGB conversion and clamp to [0.0, 1.0] using: \text{colors\precomp} = \max(\text{sh2rgb} + 0.5, 0.0) (Note: The source specifies clampmin(sh2rgb + 0.5, 0.0), implying a specific SH basis or offset handling). Otherwise: Pass shs directly to the rasterizer, allowing the CUDA kernel to handle SH evaluation. 6. Compute Lighting and Features: Determine view directions and incident light directions. If lighttransform exists and provides a light direction, use it; otherwise, default to view directions (headlights). Evaluate Blinn-Phong shading using renderingequationBlinnPhongpython to produce brdfcolor and extraresults. Concatenate features for rasterization: Training: Concatenate [brdfcolor, normal, offsetcolor, diffusefactor, shininess, ambientfactor, specularfactor, extraresults['offsetcolornorm']]. Inference: Replace the last element with mean diffuse, specular, and ambient renders. 7. Invoke Rasterizer: Call the rasterizer with the following arguments: means3D: 3D positions. means2D: Initial 2D positions (often zeros or projected means). shs: Spherical harmonic coefficients. colorsprecomp: Pre-computed colors (if applicable). opacities: Opacity values. scales: Scale values. rotations: Rotation quaternions. cov3Dprecomp: Pre-computed covariances (if applicable). features: Concatenated feature tensor. Unpack the outputs: numrendered, numcontrib, renderedimage, renderedopacity, rendereddepth, renderedfeature, renderedpseudonormal, renderedsurfacexyz, radii. 8. Split Rendered Features: Split renderedfeature into components based on channel widths [3, 3, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] corresponding to: renderedphong (3 channels) renderednormal (3 channels) renderedoffsetcolor (3 channels) rendereddiffusefactor (1 channel). renderedshininess (1 channel). renderedamibentfactor (1 channel). renderedspecularfactor (1 channel). renderedoffsetcolornorm (1 channel). Step 1: Initialize gradient tracking screenspacepoints = torch.zeros((pc.getxyz().shape[0], 2), device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) try: screenspacepoints.retaingrad() except Exception: pass # Step 2: Compute Camera Intrinsics tanfovx = math.tan(camera.fovx / 2) tanfovy = math.tan(camera.fovy / 2) cx = camera.cx cy = camera.cy # Step 3: Construct Rasterization Settings rastersettings = GaussianRasterizationSettings( imagewidth=camera.imagewidth, imageheight=camera.imageheight, tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, cx=cx, cy=cy, background=background, scalemodifier=1.0, viewMatrix=camera.worldviewtransform, projMatrix=camera.fullprojtransform, shdegree=pipe.shdegree, cameraPosition=camera.cameracenter) # Step 4: Select Covariance Representation if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(1.0) else: scales = pc.getscaling() rotations = pc.getrotation() cov3Dprecomp = None # Step 5: Select Color Representation if overridecolor is None and pipe.computeSHspython: viewdirs = normalize(camera.viewdirection) shcoeffs = pc.shs sh2rgb = evaluatesh(shcoeffs, viewdirs) colorsprecomp = torch.clamp(sh2rgb + 0.5, min=0.0) else: colorsprecomp = None shs = pc.shs # Step 6: Compute Lighting and Features if lighttransform is not None and lighttransform.haslightdirection(): lightdir = lighttransform.getlightdirection() else: lightdir = camera.viewdirection brdfcolor, extraresults = renderingequationBlinnPhongpython(pc, lightdir, camera.viewdirection) # Concatenate features if pipe.trainingmode: features = torch.cat([ brdfcolor, pc.normals, pc.offsetcolor, pc.diffusefactor, pc.shininess, pc.ambientfactor, pc.specularfactor, extraresults['offsetcolornorm'] ], dim=-1) else: meandiffuse = torch.mean(pc.diffusefactor) meanspecular = torch.mean(pc.specularfactor) meanambient = torch.mean(pc.ambientfactor) features = torch.cat([ brdfcolor, pc.normals, pc.offsetcolor, pc.diffusefactor, pc.shininess, pc.ambientfactor, pc.specularfactor, meandiffuse ], dim=-1) # Step 7: Invoke Rasterizer rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer(rastersettings) means3D = pc.getxyz() means2D = screenspacepoints numrendered, numcontrib, renderedimage, renderedopacity, rendereddepth, renderedfeature, renderedpseudonormal, renderedsurfacexyz, radii = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=colorsprecomp, opacities=pc.getopacity(), scales=scales if not pipe.computecov3Dpython else None, rotations=rotations if not pipe.computecov3Dpython else None, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp, features=features) # Step 8: Split Rendered Features channelwidths = [3, 3, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] startidx = 0 renderedphong = renderedfeature[..., startidx:startidx+3] startidx += 3 renderednormal = renderedfeature[..., startidx:startidx+3] startidx += 3 renderedoffsetcolor = renderedfeature[..., startidx:startidx+3] startidx += 3 rendereddiffusefactor = renderedfeature[..., startidx:startidx+1] startidx += 1 renderedshininess = renderedfeature[..., startidx:startidx+1] startidx += 1 renderedamibentfactor = renderedfeature[..., startidx:startidx+1] startidx += 1 renderedspecularfactor = renderedfeature[..., startidx:startidx+1] startidx += 1 renderedoffsetcolornorm = renderedfeature[..., startidx:startidx+1] return { 'renderedimage': renderedimage, 'renderedopacity': renderedopacity, 'rendereddepth': rendereddepth, 'renderedfeature': renderedfeature, 'radii': radii, 'numrendered': numrendered, 'numcontrib': numcontrib, 'features': { 'phong': renderedphong, 'normal': renderednormal, 'offsetcolor': renderedoffsetcolor, 'diffusefactor': rendereddiffusefactor, 'shininess': renderedshininess, 'ambientfactor': renderedamibentfactor, 'specularfactor': renderedspecularfactor, 'offsetcolornorm': renderedoffsetcolornorm } } Parameters: near: Depth clipping plane near distance. Default: 2e-3. far: Depth clipping plane far distance. Default: 100. pixguard: Pixel guard band width for culling. Default: 64. T: Tile size for rasterization (number of pixels per tile dimension). name: Backpropagation with Per-Splat Parallelization
head: Per-splat backward, Splat-parallel backprop
body: This method is a parallelization scheme for the backward pass of 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization that maps CUDA threads to 2D splats rather than pixels to eliminate atomic contention on gradient accumulation. It differs from the original 3DGS approach, which maps threads to pixels and suffers from serialized atomic operations when multiple threads contend for the same Gaussian's gradient, by having threads maintain per-splat state and exchange smaller per-pixel states (transmittance T and accumulated color RGB) via intra-warp shuffling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Depth-sorted list of splats per tile, forward pass intermediate states (per-pixel states stored at intervals), tile dimensions, and bucket size N=32. Output: Gradients for Gaussian parameters accumulated per splat. Data Structures: Autodiff Context: Stores per-pixel state snapshots (T, RGB) every N splats. Per-Splat State: Maintained by each thread, containing the gradient contributions for the specific splat assigned to that thread. Per-Pixel State: Contains transmittance T and accumulated color RGB. Parameters: Bucket Size (N): Splats are divided into buckets of size 32, each scheduled to a single CUDA warp. Threads per Tile: Typically equal to the number of pixels in the tile, but the logic assumes a simplified setting where \#threads = \#pixels = \#splats = N for explanation. Steps: 1. Forward Pass Storage: During the forward pass, for each tile, store the per-pixel state (T, RGB) for all pixels j after blending every N-th splat (e.g., splats 0, N, 2N, \dots). This creates available starting states (0, j), (N, j), \dots for all pixels j in the autodiff context. 2. Backward Pass Initialization: Each thread i in a tile initializes its local per-pixel state for pixel j by reconstructing the state (i, j) from the stored starting states. 3. State Exchange: Threads within a warp exchange their current per-pixel states (T, RGB) using fast intra-warp shuffling operations. 4. Gradient Computation: For each splat i in the bucket, thread i receives the per-pixel state (i, j), applies the default alpha blending logic to compute the state (i+1, j) from (i, j) and the properties of splat i, and incorporates this information into the gradient. 5. Optimization - Last Contributor Tracking: Track the last contributing splat for each pixel across the tile during the forward pass. In the backward pass, skip entire groups of splat-tile pairings where the pixel is already saturated, exploiting occlusion observed in the forward pass. 6. Optimization - Tighter Culling: Apply tighter culling techniques (as proposed by Radl et al. [2024]) to minimize redundant splats in both forward and backward passes. Formulas: Alpha Blending: T{new} = T{old} \cdot (1 - \alpha), C{new} = C{old} + C{splat} \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - T{old}), where \alpha is splat opacity, C is color, and T is transmittance. Gradient Accumulation: \nabla{splat} = \sum{j} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial C{new}} \cdot \frac{\partial C{new}}{\partial \text{splat params}}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backwardpersplat(tilesplats, forwardsnapshots, tiledims, lastcontributor): """ tilesplats: List of splat objects sorted by depth for the tile. forwardsnapshots: Dict mapping snapshotindex -> list of (T, RGB) for each pixel. Only stores states for snapshotindex % 32 == 0. tiledims: Tuple (width, height) of the tile. lastcontributor: Array of last contributing splat index per pixel. """ N = 32 numpixels = tiledims[0] tiledims[1] splatgrads = [None] len(tilesplats) for bucketstart in range(0, len(tilesplats), N): bucketend = min(bucketstart + N, len(tilesplats)) # Initialize per-pixel states for this bucket pixelstates = [] for j in range(numpixels): # Find nearest stored snapshot index <= current splat index snapidx = (bucketstart // N) N if snapidx in forwardsnapshots: state = forwardsnapshots[snapidx][j] else: state = (1.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) # Default: fully transparent, black # Reconstruct forward from snapshot to bucketstart for k in range(snapidx, bucketstart): state = alphablend(state, tilesplats[k], j) pixelstates.append(state) # Process each splat in the bucket for i in range(bucketstart, bucketend): splat = tilesplats[i] # In CUDA, threads would shuffle pixelstates via shflsync. # Here we simulate gathering all pixel states for thread i. currentstates = list(pixelstates) # Skip if pixel saturated (optimization) for j in range(numpixels): if currentstates[j][0] < 1e-6: continue # Apply alpha blending to get state after splat i nextstate = alphablend(currentstates[j], splat, j) # Compute gradient contribution grad = computegradient(currentstates[j], nextstate, splat) if splatgrads[i] is None: splatgrads[i] = grad else: splatgrads[i] += grad # Update state for next splat pixelstates[j] = nextstate return splatgrads def alphablend(state, splat, pixelidx): """Standard alpha compositing for transmittance and color.""" T, C = state alpha = splat.opacity color = splat.color Tnew = T (1.0 - alpha) Cnew = C + color alpha (1.0 - T) return (Tnew, Cnew) def computegradient(prevstate, nextstate, splat): """Accumulates gradient based on color change.""" dC = nextstate[1] - prevstate[1] return dC Uses analytic derivatives for splatting, differing in how gradients are computed but sharing the goal of differentiable rendering. Analytic-Splatting Focuses on linear primitive gradients, offering an alternative to Gaussian splats. LinPrim Gradient Computation Implements splatting in the vertex shader, differing in the execution model (GPU shader vs. CUDA kernel). Gaussian Splat Rasterization (Vertex Shader) Describes the overall pipeline, of which this method is a part. Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline Time Complexity: Reduces the time complexity of the backward pass by eliminating atomic contention. The original 3DGS has O(P \cdot S) with high constant factors due to atomics, where P is pixels and S is splats. This method maintains O(P \cdot S) but with much lower constant factors due to warp-level parallelism and shuffling. Memory Complexity: Requires storing per-pixel states at intervals of N=32 splats, increasing memory usage slightly compared to storing no intermediate states, but less than storing all states. Measured Performance: Significantly faster backward pass compared to original 3DGS and DISTWAR. Strengths: Eliminates atomic contention, leverages fast intra-warp communication, exploits occlusion. Limitations: Requires careful state management and reconstruction. When to Use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models and backward pass performance is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method was introduced in "Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources" (2024) to address the performance bottleneck in the backward pass of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the original 3DGS rasterization method by Kerbl et al. [2023] and addresses the atomic contention issues identified in concurrent work like DISTWAR [Durvasula et al. 2023].
