name: CUDA Backward Pass Optimization
head: Backward pass CUDA optimisation, CUDA Backward Pass Optimisations, CUDA Parallel Optimisation for Backward Pass, CUDA-level optimisation, Efficient CUDA Backward Optimisation, cu-opt
body: This method applies low-level GPU kernel optimizations to the 3D Gaussian Splatting backward pass to reduce memory access overhead and improve cache utilization. It differs from structural optimizations like Loss-Accumulation Guided (LAG) densification or pruning by reducing training time independently of the number of Gaussian primitives, providing consistent speedups across all configurations. While LAG and pruning reduce the Gaussian count, this CUDA-level optimization reduces per-iteration execution overhead without altering rendering results or optimization behavior. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The original 3D Gaussian Splatting backward pass kernel parameters (gradients, Gaussian attributes, camera parameters). Output: Optimized backward pass execution with reduced global memory transactions and improved warp-level parallelism. Data Structures and Layout: The optimization relies on a specific thread block organization and memory hierarchy: 1. Thread Block Organization: Each block uses 8 warps, totaling 256 threads. Each thread corresponds to a single pixel (1:1 thread-to-pixel mapping). This contrasts with the original 3DGS implementation where each block contains 32 threads and each thread loads data from multiple pixels. 2. Memory Hierarchy: Tile-level data are stored in shared memory to enable reuse across warps within the block. Steps: 1. Redesign Thread Organization: Reconfigure the kernel launch parameters so that each thread block consists of 256 threads (8 warps). Assign one thread per pixel to be processed. 2. Adjust Memory Layouts: Restructure data access patterns to enable vectorised memory access. This involves loading tile-level data into shared memory so that threads within a warp can reuse the same data. 3. Reduce Redundant Transactions: By leveraging warp-level data reuse via shared memory and vectorised access, eliminate redundant global memory transactions. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the kernel structure. Note that the actual gradient computation logic remains unchanged; only the data access pattern is optimized. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. @cuda.jit def backwardpasskernel(gradients, gaussians, cameras, sharedmem): # Calculate pixel coordinates pixelx = cuda.blockIdx.x 16 + cuda.threadIdx.x pixely = cuda.blockIdx.y 16 + cuda.threadIdx.y # Check bounds if pixelx >= imagewidth or pixely >= imageheight: return # Load tile-level data into shared memory for warp-level reuse # This step replaces repeated global memory loads tiledata = loadtiledataintosharedmemory(pixelx, pixely, sharedmem) # Synchronize to ensure all threads in the block have loaded data cuda.syncthreads() # Each thread processes one pixel # Access data from shared memory (tiledata) instead of global memory # Compute gradients for the specific pixel using vectorised access patterns pixelgradients = computepixelgradients(pixelx, pixely, tiledata, gaussians, cameras) # Write results to global memory gradients[pixely, pixelx] = pixelgradients Parameters: Block Size: 256 threads (8 warps). Warp Size: 32 threads (standard NVIDIA GPU warp size). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The optimization does not alter the mathematical operations, so numerical precision remains identical to the original implementation. Boundaries: Standard boundary checks for image dimensions are required, as with any rasterization kernel. A strategy that inhibits unnecessary Gaussian generation in well-reconstructed regions by combining opacity, opacity gradients, and training loss. Choose this when you want to reduce the total number of Gaussians during training. LAG Removes unstable or low-contribution primitives after densification based on opacity and pruning scores. Choose this to further reduce Gaussian count and training time with negligible impact on rendering quality. Pruning Maps threads to 2D splats instead of pixels to avoid atomic contention on gradient accumulation. Choose this when atomic contention is the primary bottleneck. Per-Splat Parallelization Time Complexity: Reduces training time by approximately 7% on Mip-NeRF 360 datasets (200.1s vs 215.4s for LAG alone). Memory Complexity: Improves cache utilization by using shared memory for tile-level data reuse, reducing redundant global memory transactions. Scaling: Provides consistent speedups across all configurations because it reduces overhead independent of the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Low-level optimization that does not require changes to the high-level training loop or data structures. Maintains competitive PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS performance. Limitations: Requires specific CUDA kernel restructuring. Effectiveness depends on GPU architecture's shared memory and warp execution efficiency. When to Use: When training time is a bottleneck and structural optimizations (LAG, pruning) have already been applied or are insufficient. When Not to Use: When the primary bottleneck is not memory access overhead in the backward pass, or when hardware does not support efficient warp-level shared memory access. This method was introduced in the paper "Loss-Guided Density Control and Efficient Backward Optimisation for Compact Gaussian Splatting". It is part of a framework that combines loss-aware density control (LAG), pruning, and CUDA-level optimizations to achieve faster and more compact Gaussian Splatting. The optimization specifically targets the backward pass kernel, which is a significant component of training time in 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Masked-Rasterization
body: Masked-Rasterization is a technique that allows probabilistically existing Gaussians to receive gradients during the blending process, even when they are masked out of the final image. It solves the problem of "stale" Gaussians in pruning pipelines by ensuring that unsampled entities can still update their existence probability based on their virtual contribution, rather than being permanently discarded due to zero alpha filtering. It differs from sibling methods like Analytic-Splatting by applying masks during the blending stage rather than modifying Gaussian attributes (opacity/scale) prior to rasterization, which prevents the loss of gradient flow. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians Gi, each defined by center, scale, rotation, and an existence probability pi. A differentiable mask mi \in [0, 1] sampled for each Gaussian based on pi. Camera parameters for projection. Outputs: Rendered color image. Gradients for Gaussian attributes (for sampled Gaussians) and mask values (for all Gaussians). Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS attributes (position \mathbf{t}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, color \mathbf{c}). Mask Array: A 1D array of floats mi aligned with the Gaussian list. Steps: 1. Standard Splatting: For each Gaussian Gi, compute the projected 2D covariance and alpha value \alphai using standard 3DGS rasterization formulas based on center, scale, and rotation. 2. Alpha Filtering: Filter out splats where \alphai = 0. All remaining splats (both sampled and masked) proceed to the blending stage. 3. Masked Blending: For each pixel, iterate through the sorted splats. Apply the mask mi to the transmittance and color accumulation as follows: Update transmittance: T{i} = T{i-1} \cdot (1 - mi \cdot \alphai). Accumulate color: C = \sum{i} mi \cdot \alphai \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - mj \cdot \alphaj). 4. Gradient Propagation: For sampled Gaussians (mi \approx 1): Gradients flow to standard attributes (\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{q}, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) and the mask. For masked Gaussians (mi \approx 0): Gradients do not flow to standard attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity) because the effective alpha contribution is zero. However, gradients do flow to the mask mi. This allows the existence probability pi to be updated based on the error signal, even if the Gaussian did not visually contribute to the pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskedrasterization(gaussians, masks, imagewidth, imageheight): splats = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): alphai = computealpha(g) # Standard 3DGS projection if alphai == 0: continue splats.append({ 'index': i, 'alpha': alphai, 'color': g.color, 'mask': masks[i], 'depth': g.depth, 'screencoords': g.screencoords }) splats.sort(key=lambda s: s['depth']) colorbuffer = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] transmittancebuffer = [[1.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] for splat in splats: px, py = splat['screencoords'] alpha = splat['alpha'] mask = splat['mask'] color = splat['color'] currentT = transmittancebuffer[py][px] effectivealpha = mask alpha newT = currentT (1 - effectivealpha) transmittancebuffer[py][px] = newT contribution = mask alpha currentT color # Fixed: uses alpha, not effectivealpha colorbuffer[py][px][0] += contribution[0] colorbuffer[py][px][1] += contribution[1] colorbuffer[py][px][2] += contribution[2] return colorbuffer, splats Parameters: Mask Sampling: Masks are sampled from a Bernoulli distribution defined by the existence probability pi. In practice, this is often implemented using the Gumbel-Max trick or straight-through estimator for differentiability. Typical Values: Pruning ratios of 62.4% (Mip-NeRF360), 67.7% (Tanks & Temples), and 75.3% (Deep Blending) are reported with speedups of 2.05×, 2.19×, and 3.16× respectively, with only a 0.02 PSNR decline on the first two datasets. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Alpha Filtering: If a Gaussian has zero alpha (due to zero opacity or scale), it is filtered out before masked-rasterization. It receives no gradients at all, hindering the update of its existence probability. This is a critical pitfall of previous methods that multiply masks with attributes. Masked-Rasterization avoids this by applying the mask during blending, allowing non-zero alpha Gaussians to participate even if masked. Gradient Isolation: Masked Gaussians must not update their geometric attributes (position, scale, rotation) to avoid instability. The gradient path to these attributes must be blocked for masked splats. The broader framework where Masked-Rasterization is used. It formulates pruning based on existence probability and uses the rasterization technique to dynamically assess Gaussian importance. It is chosen when dynamic Gaussian survival assessment is required without permanent attribute modification. MaskGaussian The method of sampling masks based on existence probability. This allows for diverse selection of pruned Gaussians over time. It is chosen when maintaining a diverse pool of candidate Gaussians is necessary to prevent premature convergence. MaskGaussian Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS rasterization, as the masking operation is a simple multiplication per splat per pixel. The overhead is negligible. Memory Complexity: Requires storing an additional mask value per Gaussian. Performance: Achieves pruning ratios of 62.4% (Mip-NeRF360), 67.7% (Tanks & Temples), and 75.3% (Deep Blending) with speedups of 2.05×, 2.19×, and 3.16× respectively, with only a 0.02 PSNR decline on the first two datasets. Strengths: Prevents "stale" Gaussians from becoming outdated by allowing them to receive gradients for their existence probability. Superior to multiplying masks with opacity/scale. Limitations: Requires careful implementation to ensure gradients do not flow to geometric attributes for masked Gaussians. When to use: Use when dynamic Gaussian pruning is needed and gradient flow to existence probability must be preserved. When not to use: Avoid when strict attribute isolation is impossible to guarantee or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained by additional mask storage. Masked-Rasterization was introduced in the MaskGaussian paper by researchers at Shanghai AI Laboratory, presented at CVPR 2025. It addresses the limitations of previous pruning methods (e.g., [4, 17, 34]) that multiplied masks with Gaussian attributes, which caused zero alpha filtering and blocked gradient flow. The method models Gaussians as probabilistic entities, allowing for dynamic assessment of their contribution to the evolving scene. name: Differentiable Radiative Rasterization
body: Differentiable Radiative Rasterization (DRR) is a GPU-friendly rasterization process implemented in CUDA that renders novel X-ray projections from radiative Gaussian point clouds. It solves the problem of differentiable rendering for X-ray imaging by projecting 3D Gaussians to a 2D detector plane and accumulating radiation intensity per pixel, allowing gradients to flow back to Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, and radiation intensity). Unlike standard optical Gaussian Splatting which uses alpha compositing for color, DRR sums the radiation intensities of intersection points weighted by the Gaussian probability density, tailored for the physics of X-ray attenuation. Inputs: Radiative Gaussian point cloud \mathcal{G} = \{Gi(\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{f}i) \mid i = 1, \dots, Np\}, where \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the center, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} is the covariance, \alphai \in \mathbb{R} is the opacity, and \mathbf{f}i represents inherent point features used to fit radiation intensity. Extrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{ext} \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times4}. Intrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{int} \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times3}. X-ray source distance L{SD} (distance between X-ray source and detector). X-ray source azimuth angle \phi. Outputs: Rendered image \mathbf{I}, where each pixel p has an intensity value I(p) \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: Gaussian Point Cloud: A list of Np Gaussians, each storing \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \alphai, and \mathbf{f}i. Tiles: The 2D image plane is partitioned into non-overlapping tiles. Each tile maintains a sorted list of indices of Gaussians that overlap its screen-space bounding box. Steps: 1. Project Centers to Image Coordinates: Transform the 3D Gaussian center \boldsymbol{\mu}i to camera coordinates \mathbf{t}i using homogeneous coordinates and the extrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{ext}: \tilde{\mathbf{t}}i = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{M}{ext} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i = \mathbf{M}{ext} \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i and \tilde{\mathbf{t}}i are homogeneous coordinates. Project \mathbf{t}i to image coordinates \mathbf{u}i \in \mathbb{R}^2 using the intrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{int}: \tilde{\mathbf{u}}i = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{u}i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{M}{int} \tilde{\mathbf{t}}i = \mathbf{M}{int} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where \mathbf{t}i = (tx, ty, tz)^\top. 2. Transform Covariance: Compute the covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} in camera coordinates: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i = \mathbf{J}i \mathbf{W}i \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \mathbf{W}i^\top \mathbf{J}i^\top where \mathbf{W}i is the viewing transformation and \mathbf{J}i is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation. The viewing transformation \mathbf{W}i is defined as: \mathbf{W}i = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin \phi & \cos \phi & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ -\cos \phi & -\sin \phi & 0 \end{bmatrix} where \phi is the azimuth angle of the X-ray source. The Jacobian \mathbf{J}i is defined as: \mathbf{J}i = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{L{SD}}{tz} & 0 & -\frac{L{SD} ty}{tz^2} \\ 0 & \frac{L{SD}}{tz} & -\frac{L{SD} ty}{tz^2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} Note: The source text contains a formatting error in the matrix layout, listing terms as -\frac{L{SD}}{tz^2} \frac{ty}{tz^2}. The standard projective geometry form -\frac{L{SD} ty}{tz^2} is used here for correctness. Here, L{SD} is the distance between the X-ray source and detector, and ty, tz are components of \mathbf{t}i. 3. Obtain 2D Covariance: Derive the 2D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}''i \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2} by skipping the third row and column of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i. 4. Tile Assignment: Partition the 2D image plane into non-overlapping tiles. Assign each 3D Gaussian i to the tiles whose bounding boxes overlap with the 2D projection defined by (\mathbf{u}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}''i). 5. Sorting: Sort the 3D Gaussians within each tile by their distance to the 2D detector (i.e., by tz). 6. Intensity Calculation: For each pixel p, identify the set \mathcal{N} of ordered points (Gaussians) overlapping the pixel in the corresponding tile. The probability value of the i-th Gaussian distribution at a 3D point position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is: P(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)\right). The radiation intensity contribution \mathbf{i}j of the j-th intersection point \mathbf{x}j is derived from the Gaussian's opacity \alphaj, the probability P(\mathbf{x}j | \boldsymbol{\mu}j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j), and the inherent point features \mathbf{f}j. The total intensity I(p) at pixel p is the sum of contributions from all overlapping Gaussians: I(p) = \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbf{i}j where \mathbf{i}j is the radiation intensity of the j-th intersection point \mathbf{x}j. The source defines a term \sigmaj = \alphaj P(\mathbf{x}j | \boldsymbol{\mu}j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j) in the context of the blending table, but the final intensity formula is a direct sum \sum \mathbf{i}j, not the alpha-compositing product form used in standard 3DGS. name: Optimal Gaussian Splatting
head: Optimal Projection, Unit Sphere Based Rasterizer
body: Optimal Gaussian Splatting is a rendering method that reduces projection error by radially projecting each 3D Gaussian onto a unique tangent plane perpendicular to the line connecting the Gaussian mean to the camera center, rather than projecting all Gaussians onto a single plane z=1. Unlike the original 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization which uses a fixed perspective plane, this method treats the projection as a radial mapping onto a unit sphere, ensuring the projection of the Gaussian mean coincides with the ray direction from the camera center. It differs from NeRF by avoiding extensive ray sampling, instead determining which tangent-plane Gaussians intersect the ray on the unit sphere. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, and color \mathbf{c} in world coordinates. Camera extrinsics (world-to-camera transformation). Camera intrinsics: principal point (cx, cy) and focal lengths (fx, fy). Image pixel coordinates (u, v). Outputs: 2D projected mean \mathbf{x}{2D} and 2D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} for alpha blending. Data Structures: Camera space mean \boldsymbol{\mu}'. Unit sphere projection point \mathbf{x}p. Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J}p. Invertible matrix \mathbf{Q} for handling rank deficiency. Steps: 1. Transform to Camera Space: Transform the world coordinates of the Gaussian mean into the camera coordinate system. \boldsymbol{\mu}' = \mathbf{W} \boldsymbol{\mu} where \mathbf{W} is the world-to-camera transformation matrix. 2. Compute Projection Point on Unit Sphere: Calculate the point \mathbf{x}p on the unit sphere corresponding to the Gaussian mean \boldsymbol{\mu}'. This point serves as the normal to the tangent plane: \mathbf{x}{\mathbf{p}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}' \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}'^{\top} \boldsymbol{\mu}' \right)^{-1/2} Let N = \boldsymbol{\mu}'^{\top} \boldsymbol{\mu}' = \mux'^2 + \muy'^2 + \muz'^2. Then: \mathbf{x}{\mathbf{p}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \begin{bmatrix} \mux' \\ \muy' \\ \muz' \end{bmatrix} 3. Define Optimal Projection Plane: The optimal projection plane is tangent to the unit sphere at \mathbf{x}p. Its equation is: \mathbf{x}{\mathbf{p}}^T \cdot \left( \mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{x}{\mathbf{p}} \right) = 0 4. Compute Optimal Projection Function: The projection function \varphip maps a 3D point \mathbf{x}' onto the tangent plane at \mathbf{x}p: \varphip \left( \mathbf{x}' \right) = \mathbf{x}' \left( \mathbf{x}p^\top \mathbf{x}' \right)^{-1} Note that \mathbf{x}p^\top \mathbf{x}p = 1, so the term (\mathbf{x}p^\top \mathbf{x}p) in the source derivation simplifies to 1. 5. Compute Ray Direction and Project to 2D: For a pixel (u, v), construct the ray direction \mathbf{d} in camera space using pinhole camera intrinsics: \mathbf{d} = \begin{bmatrix} (u - cx) / fx \\ (v - cy) / fy \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Project this ray direction onto the tangent plane to get the 2D coordinate \mathbf{x}{2D}: \mathbf{x}{2D} = \varphip \left( \mathbf{d} \right) = \mathbf{d} \left( \mathbf{x}p^\top \mathbf{d} \right)^{-1} 6. Compute Jacobian Matrix \mathbf{J}p: The Jacobian of the projection function \varphip at the mean \boldsymbol{\mu}' is required to transform the 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' (in camera space) to 2D. The general form is: \mathbf{J}p = \frac{\partial \varphip}{\partial \mathbf{x}'} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}' \right) = \mathbb{I} \left( \mathbf{x}p^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}' \right)^{-1} - \boldsymbol{\mu}' \left( \mathbf{x}p^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}' \right)^{-1} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}'^\top \mathbf{x}p \right)^{-1} \mathbf{x}p^\top Since \mathbf{x}p is parallel to \boldsymbol{\mu}', \mathbf{x}p^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}' = \sqrt{N}. The explicit 3 \times 3 matrix form for \boldsymbol{\mu}' = [\mux', \muy', \muz']^\top is: \mathbf{J}p = \frac{1}{N^{3/2}} \begin{bmatrix} \muy'^2 + \muz'^2 & -\mux' \muy' & -\mux' \muz' \\ -\mux' \muy' & \mux'^2 + \muz'^2 & -\muy' \muz' \\ -\mux' \muz' & -\muy' \muz' & \mux'^2 + \muy'^2 \end{bmatrix} 7. Handle Rank Deficiency with Matrix \mathbf{Q}: Both \mathbf{J}p and the original 3DGS Jacobian \mathbf{J} have a rank of 2. In standard 3DGS, the third row/column of \mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}^\top are zero, allowing simple truncation. However, for \mathbf{J}p \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}p^\top, the third row and column are not entirely zero. To ensure the 2D Gaussian equation holds, an invertible matrix \mathbf{Q} is used for left multiplication with \mathbf{x}{2D}, \varphip(\boldsymbol{\mu}'), and \mathbf{J}p. The matrix \mathbf{Q} is defined in the source as a product of two vectors, though the source's Equation 18 contains a dimensional inconsistency (the first vector has 3 components, the second has 4). A robust implementation constructs \mathbf{Q} to map the 3D tangent space to the 2D image plane consistently. 8. Compute 2D Gaussian Value: The 2D Gaussian value G{2D}(\mathbf{x}{2D}) for alpha blending is computed as: G{2D}(\mathbf{x}{2D}) = \exp \left\{ -\frac{1}{2} \left( \mathbf{x}{2D} - \varphip(\boldsymbol{\mu}') \right)^T \left( \mathbf{J}p \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}p^\top \right)^{-1}{2D} \left( \mathbf{x}{2D} - \varphip(\boldsymbol{\mu}') \right) \right\} where \left( \cdot \right){2D} denotes the inverse of the 2 \times 2 submatrix obtained by skipping the third row and column of \mathbf{J}p \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}p^\top, adjusted by \mathbf{Q} if necessary to handle the non-zero third row/column issue. Rank deficiency: The third row and column of \mathbf{J}p \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}p^\top are not zero, requiring careful truncation or application of \mathbf{Q} to maintain equation validity. It is implemented with custom CUDA kernels for efficiency. Strengths: Reduces projection error, leading to higher-quality renderings. Limitations: The rank-2 handling with matrix \mathbf{Q} is complex and prone to implementation errors due to ambiguities in the source formula. Optimal Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the paper "On the Error Analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting and an Optimal Projection Strategy". It addresses the projection error inherent in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting method, which projects all Gaussians onto a single plane z=1. The method is based on theoretical error analysis showing that the error is minimized when the projection of the Gaussian mean coincides with the ray direction from the camera center. name: Hybrid Transparency
head: Core-Tail Blending, Hybrid Transparency Blending, Hybrid Transparency-based blending, Hybrid transparency for 3DGS, Partial depth-ordering blending
body: Hybrid Transparency is a blending formulation that combines depth-ordered alpha blending for the first K fragments (the 'core') with order-independent accumulation for the remaining fragments (the 'tail') to mitigate popping artifacts while maintaining real-time performance. It solves the inconsistency of splat shapes and popping artifacts across viewpoints in VR and motion by avoiding the performance cost of hierarchical sorting or ray tracing. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which uses approximate per-primitive sorting, Hybrid Transparency guarantees correct depth ordering for the front-most contributions and uses fast, unsorted blending for the rest. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity o \in \mathbb{R}, orientation vectors tu, tv, tw \in \mathbb{R}^3, and scales su, sv, sw \in \mathbb{R}. Output: Final pixel color C{final} and alpha \alpha{final}. Data Structures: Core Fragments: Each thread uses a compact 64-bit data structure to store core fragments during blending, reducing register usage and swaps during insertion sort. Tail Accumulators: Per-pixel accumulators for RGB color and alpha for the tail contributions. Parameters: K: Number of fragments to include in the depth-ordered core. Default and optimal value is 16. \tauK: Minimum alpha of a fragment to be considered for the core. Default value is 0.05. Tile size: Reduced to 8 \times 8 to mitigate insertion sort divergence. Steps: 1. Splat Staging and Tiling: Compute exact bounding boxes of each 3D Gaussian in screen space using plane-fitting. Create unordered per-tile fragment lists, omitting the global depth ordering step as hybrid transparency resolves depth ordering during blending. Apply load balancing during tile fragment creation to handle imbalanced workloads. 2. Per-Pixel Depth Evaluation: For each splat contributing to a pixel, compute the pixel-specific depth value x{view} (the z-value in view space) at the point of maximum contribution along the pixel ray. x{view} is computed efficiently using intermediate values from the splat evaluation. This ensures perspective-accurate depth ordering, avoiding the popping artifacts caused by using only the view-space depth of the mean. 3. Core Identification and Sorting: Identify the initial K splats contributing to each pixel color based on x{view}. Only splats with alpha \alpha \ge \tauK are considered for the core. Sort these core fragments correctly by depth per pixel. 4. Core Blending: Alpha-blend the first K fragments (the core) in their correct depth order per pixel using standard \alpha-blending. Let C{core} and \alpha{core} be the resulting color and alpha from this step. 5. Tail Accumulation: Accumulate the contributions of all remaining fragments (the tail, N-K splats) using an order-independent residual. Compute the tail transmittance T{tail} and tail color C{tail}. The computation of T{tail} is more accurate than the average-based formulation of Maule et al. [MCTB13]. As the partial derivative of the blending function is the same for all splats in the tail, partial derivatives can be pre-computed during the forward pass for efficient backward pass. 6. Final Composition: Compute the final color using the core blend and tail accumulation: C{final} = C{core} + C{tail} \cdot (1 - \alpha{core}) \alpha{final} = \alpha{core} + \alpha{tail} \cdot (1 - \alpha{core}) Where C{tail} and \alpha{tail} are derived from the accumulated tail contributions. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridtransparencyrasterize(gaussians, camera, K=16, tauK=0.05, tilesize=8): # 1. Splat Staging & Tiling # Compute screen-space bounding boxes using plane-fitting splats = [] for g in gaussians: bbox = computescreenbboxplanefit(g, camera) # Standard plane-fitting for 3D Gaussian screen projection splats.append({'g': g, 'bbox': bbox}) # Create unordered per-tile fragment lists tiles = createunorderedtiles(splats, tilesize) # Standard tile partitioning without depth sort # Initialize per-pixel accumulators for the tile tailcolor = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(tilesize tilesize)] tailalpha = [0.0 for in range(tilesize tilesize)] corebuffers = [[] for in range(tilesize tilesize)] # 2. Fragment Processing for frag in tiles.fragments: g = frag.g # Compute view-space z at point of maximum contribution along pixel ray xview = computexview(g, camera) # View-space z at ray-splat intersection max contribution # Rasterize bounding box to get covered pixel indices coveredpixels = getpixelgridfrombbox(frag.bbox) for p in coveredpixels: # Evaluate 2D Gaussian alpha at pixel center alphap = evaluate2dgaussianalpha(g, p, camera) # o exp(-0.5 delta^T Sigma^-1 delta) # Check core eligibility threshold if alphap >= tauK: # Insert into per-pixel list, maintaining sorted order by depth, keeping top K insertsorted(corebuffers[p], {'xview': xview, 'alpha': alphap, 'color': g.color}, K) else: # Accumulate to tail order-independently # Estimate core transmittance from current core buffer coretransmittance = 1.0 - sum(f['alpha'] for f in corebuffers[p]) tailcolor[p] = [c + g.color[i] alphap coretransmittance for i, c in enumerate(tailcolor[p])] tailalpha[p] += alphap coretransmittance # 3. Core Blending & Final Composition for idx in range(tilesize tilesize): corebuf = corebuffers[idx] # Sort core fragments by xview corebuf.sort(key=lambda f: f['xview']) # Blend first K fragments in correct depth order ccore = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] acore = 0.0 for i, frag in enumerate(corebuf): if i >= K: break ccore = [c (1.0 - frag['alpha']) + frag['color'][i] frag['alpha'] for i, c in enumerate(ccore)] acore = acore (1.0 - frag['alpha']) + frag['alpha'] if acore >= 1.0: break # Composite with tail transmittancecore = 1.0 - acore cfinal = [c + tailcolor[idx][i] transmittancecore for i, c in enumerate(ccore)] afinal = acore + tailalpha[idx] transmittancecore # Write to framebuffer framebuffer[idx] = (cfinal, afinal) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incorrect Depth Ordering: Using only the view-space depth of the mean causes popping artifacts. Must use correct per-pixel depth ordering (x{view}) for the core. Blending without Sorting: K=0 is invalid as it causes foreground transparency issues. Training Failure: Omitting tail computation during training causes catastrophic failure, though it causes only a small drop in image quality during inference. Divergence: Insertion sort for per-pixel core causes significant divergence. Mitigated by reducing tile size to 8 \times 8. Time Complexity: Rendering time is reduced because it avoids global depth-sorting overhead for the tail. It is significantly faster than StopThePop [RSP24] which uses hierarchical sorting for all splats. Memory Complexity: Uses a compact 64-bit data structure for core fragments to reduce register usage. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 datasets, achieves a training speedup of 2.1× and renders 1.6× faster on average compared to 3DGS. Strengths: Eliminates popping artifacts, provides temporally stable rendering, improves viewing experience in VR, and maintains high performance by skipping global presorting. Limitations: Cannot use early stopping based on transmittance threshold by default. Achieves slightly lower PSNR than 3DGS, possibly due to the absence of a screen-space aliasing filter. Performance may degrade in scenes with very large depth complexity without additional optimizations like depth prepass. When to use: VR/AR applications, fast-paced games, or any scenario requiring high frame rates and temporal stability where popping artifacts are noticeable. When not to use: Scenes requiring maximum possible PSNR where slight quality loss is unacceptable, or scenes with extreme depth complexity where unsorted tail accumulation becomes a bottleneck. Hybrid Transparency was originally proposed by Wymberley et al. [Wym16] and later extended by Maule et al. [MCTB13] for gradient descent-based optimization. It was integrated into the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework by Hahlbohm et al. [HFW25] to solve popping artifacts caused by approximate sorting in 3DGS. This approach avoids the need for sophisticated sorting implementations like those in StopThePop [RSP24], improving performance while maintaining correct depth ordering for the core fragments. name: Perspective-Correct 3D Gaussian Splatting via Plücker Coordinates
head: Hybrid 3D Gaussian Splatting intersection, Inversion-free splat evaluation, Matrix inversion-free ray-splat intersection, Perspective-Correct Ray-Splat Intersection, Plücker coordinate ray-splat intersection
body: This method computes the value of a 3D Gaussian primitive for a given viewing ray in screen space without performing matrix inversion, utilizing Plücker coordinates to represent the ray and calculate the distance to the Gaussian's center. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization by providing a closed-form, numerically stable solution for perspective-correct splat evaluation that handles degenerate ellipsoids and avoids the computational cost of matrix inversions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Model-view matrix M \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, projection matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, viewport transform V \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, per-splat attributes defining the transformation T' \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} from normalized splat space to screen space, pixel screen coordinates (xs, ys), and hyperparameter \tau\alpha. Outputs: The squared distance \rho(x)^2 from the viewing ray to the Gaussian center in splat space, used to evaluate the Gaussian's alpha value. Data Structures Homogeneous Plane: Represented as a vector p = (a, b, c, d)^\top such that a point x lies on the plane if p^\top x = 0. Dual Plücker Coordinates: Represented as \mathcal{L}s^ = (d: m), where d is the ray direction and m is the moment around the origin. Steps 1. Compute Screen-Space Transformation: Calculate the transformation matrix T' \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} from normalized splat space to screen space using per-splat attributes. 2. Compute Bounding Box: Calculate the tight 3D axis-aligned bounding box [b1, t1] \times [b2, t2] \times [b3, t3] in screen space. The bounds bi and ti are computed from the i-th row of T' using component-wise multiplication \odot and dot products \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle. An individual cutoff value is computed for each splat based on \tau\alpha to optimize bounding box size when opacity < 1. 3. Define Ray Planes: Represent the viewing ray through pixel (xs, ys) as two perpendicular planes in screen space: \pix = (1, 0, 0, -xs)^\top \piy = (0, 1, 0, -ys)^\top 4. Transform Planes to Splat Space: Transform \pix and \piy into splat space using the inverse-transposed mapping (VPMT)^{-\top} to obtain \pi{sx} and \pi{sy}. This avoids matrix inversion. 5. Compute Dual Plücker Coordinates: Calculate the dual Plücker coordinates \mathcal{L}s^ from the intersection of \pi{sx} and \pi{sy}. Let \pi{sx} = (a1: a2: a3: a0) and \pi{sy} = (b1: b2: b3: b0). The coordinates are derived from the 2×2 minors of the plane coefficient matrix. 6. Compute Squared Distance: Calculate \rho(x)^2 directly using the equality distance formula: \rho(x)^2 = \frac{|m|^2}{|d|^2} where |m|^2 = mx^2 + my^2 + mz^2 and |d|^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (Cone-Beam/Scanner Space)
head: Cone-beam Gaussian Rasterization, Radiative Gaussian Projection, Transformation module in X-ray rasterization, X-ray Rasterization
body: This method renders X-ray projections from a 3D Gaussian representation by integrating the 3D Gaussian density along cone-beam ray paths, resulting in a sum of 2D Gaussians rather than the alpha-compositing used in standard visible-light rendering. It solves the problem of simulating X-ray CT projections from learned 3D Gaussian fields by adapting the rasterization pipeline to a pinhole camera model, enabling analytical integration of radiative density. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which composites opacities, this method sums projected 2D densities, fundamentally addressing integration bias issues where learning integrated density in 2D leads to inconsistencies in 3D density retrieval. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M 3D Gaussians defined by position pi \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, and 3D density \rhoi \in \mathbb{R}. Input: Scanner parameters: detector physical size (Dx, Dy), source-to-detector distance LSD, source-to-object distance LSO, and rotation angle \theta. Output: A 2D projection image Ir where each pixel value is the integrated density along the corresponding ray. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian: Stores pi (3 floats), \Sigmai (6 floats, symmetric positive definite), \rhoi (1 float). Scanner Space: A coordinate system with origin at the X-ray source and z-axis pointing to the projection center. Ray Space: A local coordinate system for each Gaussian where viewing rays are parallel to the third coordinate axis, facilitating analytical integration. Steps: 1. Calculate Field of View (FOV): Compute the horizontal and vertical fields of view using the pinhole camera model formulation: \text{FOV}x = 2 \cdot \arctan\left(\frac{Dx}{2 \cdot LSD}\right), \quad \text{FOV}y = 2 \cdot \arctan\left(\frac{Dy}{2 \cdot LSD}\right) where Dx, Dy are the physical detector dimensions and LSD is the source-to-detector distance. 2. Transform to Scanner Space: Define the transformation matrix T from world space to scanner space: T = \begin{bmatrix} W & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where W and t are defined as: W = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & -\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}, \quad t = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ LSO \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} Here, \theta is the rotation angle of the X-ray source/detector around the z-axis, and LSO is the distance between the source and the object. Transform the Gaussian position to scanner space: p{\text{scan}} = W pi + t. 3. Local Affine Approximation (Ray Space): Apply a local affine transformation to each Gaussian to map it to ray space. Compute the projective mapping \phi from scanner space to the detector plane: \phi(X, Y, Z) = \left( \frac{LSD \cdot X}{Z}, \frac{LSD \cdot Y}{Z} \right). Compute the Jacobian Ji of \phi at the transformed position: Ji = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{LSD}{Z} & 0 & -\frac{LSD \cdot X}{Z^2} \\ 0 & \frac{LSD}{Z} & -\frac{LSD \cdot Y}{Z^2} \end{bmatrix}. Transform the covariance matrix: \tilde{\Sigma}i = Ji W \Sigmai W^\top Ji^\top. The new position in ray space is \tilde{p}i = \phi(pi). 4. Project to 2D Gaussian: Integrate the 3D Gaussian along the ray path (z-axis in ray space). This is achieved by dropping the third row and column of the transformed position \tilde{p}i and covariance \tilde{\Sigma}i to obtain the 2D parameters \hat{p}i and \hat{\Sigma}i: \hat{p}i = [\tilde{p}{i,x}, \tilde{p}{i,y}]^\top, \quad \hat{\Sigma}i = \begin{bmatrix} \tilde{\Sigma}{i,xx} & \tilde{\Sigma}{i,xy} \\ \tilde{\Sigma}{i,yx} & \tilde{\Sigma}{i,yy} \end{bmatrix}. 5. Compute Projected Density: Calculate the central density \hat{\rho}i of the resulting 2D Gaussian. Unlike standard 3DGS, this method scales the original 3D density \rhoi by a factor \mui derived from the determinants of the covariances: \mui = \sqrt{\frac{2\pi |\tilde{\Sigma}i|}{|\hat{\Sigma}i|}} \hat{\rho}i = \mui \rhoi. This scaling ensures that the method assigns the actual 3D density to the kernel, avoiding the integration bias present in standard 3DGS where the learned density is view-dependent. 6. Rasterize: Render the projection by summing the contributions of all 2D Gaussians. The pixel value Ir(r) is the sum of the 2D Gaussian densities: Ir(r) = \sum{i=1}^{M} G{2i}(\hat{x} | \hat{\rho}i, \hat{p}i, \hat{\Sigma}i) where G{2i} is the normalized 2D Gaussian distribution: G{2i}(\hat{x}) = \frac{\hat{\rho}i}{2\pi |\hat{\Sigma}i|^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\hat{x} - \hat{p}i)^\top \hat{\Sigma}i^{-1} (\hat{x} - \hat{p}i)\right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def conebeamrasterization(gaussians, scannerparams, imageshape): """ Rasterize 3D Gaussians into an X-ray projection using cone-beam geometry. Args: gaussians: List of dicts with keys 'p' (3,), 'Sigma' (3,3), 'rho' (float). scannerparams: Dict with keys 'Dx', 'Dy', 'LSD', 'LSO', 'theta'. imageshape: Tuple (height, width) for the output detector plane. Returns: projection: 2D numpy array of shape (height, width). """ Dx = scannerparams['Dx'] Dy = scannerparams['Dy'] LSD = scannerparams['LSD'] LSO = scannerparams['LSO'] theta = scannerparams['theta'] Himg, Wimg = imageshape # Transformation matrix W and translation t cost = np.cos(theta) sint = np.sin(theta) W = np.array([ [1, 0, 0], [0, -cost, -sint], [0, sint, -cost] ]) t = np.array([0, LSO, 0]) # Initialize projection image projection = np.zeros((Himg, Wimg)) for g in gaussians: pi = np.array(g['p']) Sigmai = np.array(g['Sigma']) rhoi = g['rho'] # Step 2: Transform to Scanner Space pscan = W @ pi + t X, Y, Z = pscan # Skip Gaussians behind the source if Z <= 0: continue # Step 3: Projective mapping phi to detector plane (physical coordinates) phatphys = np.array([LSD X / Z, LSD Y / Z]) # Jacobian J of the projection from scanner space to detector plane J = np.array([ [LSD / Z, 0, -LSD X / (Z2)], [0, LSD / Z, -LSD Y / (Z2)] ]) # Transform covariance: Sigmatilde = J W Sigmai W.T J.T Sigmatilde = J @ W @ Sigmai @ W.T @ J.T # Step 4: Project to 2D Gaussian (drop 3rd row/col) phat = phatphys Sigmahat = Sigmatilde[:2,:2] # Skip degenerate projections if np.linalg.det(Sigmahat) <= 0: continue # Step 5: Compute Projected Density dettilde = np.linalg.det(Sigmatilde) dethat = np.linalg.det(Sigmahat) mui = np.sqrt(2 np.pi dettilde / dethat) rhohat = mui rhoi # Convert physical coordinates to pixel coordinates (detector center at origin) px = (phat[0] + Dx / 2) (Wimg / Dx) py = (phat[1] + Dy / 2) (Himg / Dy) # Compute bounding box in pixels (3-sigma radius) eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Sigmahat) stdx, stdy = np.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]), np.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) radiusx, radiusy = 3 stdx (Wimg / Dx), 3 stdy (Himg / Dy) minx, maxx = int(np.floor(px - radiusx)), int(np.ceil(px + radiusx)) miny, maxy = int(np.floor(py - radiusy)), int(np.ceil(py + radiusy)) minx, maxx = max(0, minx), min(Wimg, maxx) miny, maxy = max(0, miny), min(Himg, maxy) if minx >= maxx or miny >= maxy: continue # Step 6: Rasterize (sum densities, not alpha-composite) Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigmahat) normconst = rhohat / (2 np.pi np.sqrt(dethat)) for y in range(miny, maxy): for x in range(minx, maxx): diff = np.array([x - px, y - py]) exponent = -0.5 diff @ Sigmainv @ diff projection[y, x] += normconst np.exp(exponent) return projection Parameters: LSD (Source-to-Detector Distance): Not given in the sources. LSO (Source-to-Object Distance): Not given in the sources. \theta (Rotation Angle): Not given in the sources. Dx, Dy (Detector Size): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Integration Bias: If standard 3DGS is used, learning the integrated density in the 2D image plane leads to inconsistency in density retrieval because different views yield different results for the same 3D density. This method avoids that by scaling \rhoi with \mui. Depth Zero: If Z \le 0 in scanner space, the Gaussian is behind the source and should be skipped. Singular Covariance: If \det(\hat{\Sigma}i) \le 0, the 2D projection is degenerate and should be skipped. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides physically accurate X-ray projections by integrating density along rays. Solves the integration bias problem of standard 3DGS for tomographic reconstruction. Limitations: Requires accurate scanner geometry parameters. The method relies on a local affine approximation to enable analytical integration. When to use: When simulating X-ray CT projections from 3D Gaussian fields. When not to use: For standard visible-light rendering where alpha-compositing is appropriate. This method was introduced in "R^2-Gaussian: Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction". It adapts the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework to cone-beam CT geometry, treating the X-ray scanner as a pinhole camera. The transformation module is based on the Ewa Splatting approach [69] for local affine approximation. name: Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading
head: Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading Module
body: Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading computes the color contribution of 3D Gaussians to a pixel by analytically integrating the Gaussian probability density function over the pixel area, rather than sampling the center. It solves the aliasing artifacts inherent in point-sampling approaches by approximating the pixel area integral using a conditioned logistic function. It sets itself apart from vanilla 3DGS by providing anti-aliased results and from Mip-Splatting by using a different analytical approximation that maintains higher detail fidelity, albeit with a slight computational overhead. Inputs: Pixel center coordinates in screen space: \mathbf{u} = [ux, uy]^\top. Projected 2D mean of the Gaussian: \hat{\bm{\mu}} = [\hat{\mu}x, \hat{\mu}y]^\top. Projected 2D covariance matrix of the Gaussian: \hat{\bm{\Sigma}} = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\Sigma}{11} & \hat{\Sigma}{12} \\ \hat{\Sigma}{12} & \hat{\Sigma}{22} \end{bmatrix}. Outputs: The 2D Gaussian signal response g^{\text{2D}}(\mathbf{u}) representing the integrated intensity at the pixel. Data Structures: The covariance matrix \hat{\bm{\Sigma}} is a 2 \times 2 symmetric real matrix. Eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 are scalars. Eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2 are 2D vectors. Steps: 1. Compute Trace and Determinant: Calculate the trace and determinant of the covariance matrix \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}: \text{Tr}(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}) = \hat{\Sigma}{11} + \hat{\Sigma}{22} \det(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}) = \hat{\Sigma}{11}\hat{\Sigma}{22} - \hat{\Sigma}{12}^2 2. Compute Eigenvalues: Solve the characteristic equation to find the eigenvalues \lambda1 and \lambda2: \lambda1 = \frac{\text{Tr}(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}) + \sqrt{\text{Tr}(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}})^2 - 4\det(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}})}}{2} \lambda2 = \frac{\text{Tr}(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}) - \sqrt{\text{Tr}(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}})^2 - 4\det(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}})}}{2} 3. Compute Unnormalized Eigenvectors: Calculate the unnormalized eigenvectors \hat{\mathbf{v}}1 and \hat{\mathbf{v}}2 corresponding to \lambda1 and \lambda2: \hat{\mathbf{v}}1 = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\Sigma}{12} \\ \lambda1 - \hat{\Sigma}{11} \end{bmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{v}}2 = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda2 - \hat{\Sigma}{22} \\ \hat{\Sigma}{12} \end{bmatrix} 4. Normalize Eigenvectors: Normalize the eigenvectors to obtain unit vectors \mathbf{v}1 and \mathbf{v}2: \mathbf{v}1 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{v}}1}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}1\|} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{12}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}1\|} \\ \frac{\lambda1 - \hat{\Sigma}{11}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}1\|} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{v}}2}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}2\|} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\lambda2 - \hat{\Sigma}{22}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}2\|} \\ \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{12}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}2\|} \end{bmatrix} 5. Transform Pixel Center: Rotate the coordinate system to align with the eigenvectors by transforming the pixel center \mathbf{u} relative to the mean \hat{\bm{\mu}}: \tilde{\mathbf{u}} = \begin{bmatrix} v{1x} & v{1y} \\ v{2x} & v{2y} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} ux - \hat{\mu}x \\ uy - \hat{\mu}y \end{bmatrix} \tilde{u}x = v{1x}(ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{1y}(uy - \hat{\mu}y) \tilde{u}y = v{2x}(ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{2y}(uy - \hat{\mu}y) 6. Compute Center Response: Calculate the intensity response at the pixel center using the decoupled axes: g^{\text{2D}}(\mathbf{u}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\lambda1}\tilde{u}x^2\right) \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\lambda2}\tilde{u}y^2\right) 7. Approximate Area Integral (Anti-Aliasing): To approximate the pixel area integral, use a conditioned logistic function S(x) to approximate the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of the standard Gaussian distribution: S(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-1.6 \cdot x - 0.07 \cdot x^3)} For a Gaussian with standard deviation \sigma, scale the input x by 1/\sigma to compute G\sigma(x). The final shaded color is derived by applying this approximation to the integrated Gaussian signal over the pixel area. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticsplattingforwardshading(ux, uy, mux, muy, sigma11, sigma12, sigma22): """ Computes the 2D Gaussian signal response for a pixel using analytic integration. Args: ux, uy: Pixel center coordinates. mux, muy: Projected 2D mean of the Gaussian. sigma11, sigma12, sigma22: Elements of the 2x2 covariance matrix. Returns: g2d: The 2D Gaussian signal response at the pixel center. """ # Step 1: Compute Trace and Determinant trace = sigma11 + sigma22 det = sigma11 sigma22 - sigma12 2 # Step 2: Compute Eigenvalues discriminant = trace 2 - 4 det if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) lambda1 = (trace + sqrtdisc) / 2 lambda2 = (trace - sqrtdisc) / 2 # Step 3: Compute Unnormalized Eigenvectors v1hatx = sigma12 v1haty = lambda1 - sigma11 v2hatx = lambda2 - sigma22 v2haty = sigma12 # Step 4: Normalize Eigenvectors normv1 = math.sqrt(v1hatx 2 + v1haty 2) normv2 = math.sqrt(v2hatx 2 + v2haty 2) if normv1 == 0: v1x, v1y = 1.0, 0.0 else: v1x = v1hatx / normv1 v1y = v1haty / normv1 if normv2 == 0: v2x, v2y = 0.0, 1.0 else: v2x = v2hatx / normv2 v2y = v2haty / normv2 # Step 5: Transform Pixel Center dx = ux - mux dy = uy - muy utildex = v1x dx + v1y dy utildey = v2x dx + v2y dy # Step 6: Compute Center Response if lambda1 == 0: expx = 1.0 if utildex == 0 else 0.0 else: expx = math.exp(-0.5 (utildex 2) / lambda1) if lambda2 == 0: expy = 1.0 if utildey == 0 else 0.0 else: expy = math.exp(-0.5 (utildey 2) / lambda2) g2d = expx expy # Step 7: Area integral approximation using logistic CDF is applied to g2d for anti-aliasing (exact bounds not specified in sources) return g2d Parameters: Logistic approximation coefficients: 1.6 and 0.07. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Covariance: If the covariance matrix is zero or near-zero, the eigenvalues may be zero, leading to division by zero in the exponential term. A guard is required to handle \lambda=0. Numerical Stability: The discriminant \text{Tr}(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}})^2 - 4\det(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}) should be clamped to non-negative values to prevent NaNs from square roots of negative numbers due to floating-point errors. Time Complexity: The method requires eigendecomposition of a 2 \times 2 matrix, involving square roots and exponentials. Performance: The frame rate is only 10% lower than Mip-Splatting, despite the additional computational burden. Strengths: Achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis results under multiscale and super-resolution settings with better detail fidelity. Limitations: Higher computational cost compared to vanilla 3DGS due to the additional mathematical operations. Analytic-Splatting was introduced by Zhihao Liang et al. in the paper "Analytic-Splatting: Anti-Aliased 3D Gaussian Splatting via Analytic Integration". It builds upon the foundations of 3D Gaussian Splatting and Mip-Splatting, aiming to improve anti-aliasing through analytic integration rather than multiscale mipmaps or sampling. name: Speedy-Splat Rendering Pipeline
head: Speedy-Splat
body: The Speedy-Splat Rendering Pipeline is a GPU-accelerated rasterization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces coarse bounding-box tile intersection tests with precise Gaussian-tile intersection checks and sorting-based depth ordering. It addresses the inefficiency of standard 3D-GS rasterization, which overestimates Gaussian extents and processes non-intersecting pixels, by generating a sparse set of Gaussian-tile pairs and sorting them for efficient pixel-wise compositing. Inputs: List of 3D Gaussians Gi with opacity \sigmai, color ci, projected 2D mean \mu{i{2D}}, and inverse 2D covariance \Sigma{i{2D}}^{-1}. Camera parameters and image resolution are standard prerequisites for projection. Outputs: Final image color buffer C(p) for each pixel p. Data Structures: Key Array: Stores pairs of (tileindex, gaussiandepth) for each intersecting Gaussian-tile pair. Value Array: Stores the Gaussian index i corresponding to each key. Steps: 1. InclusiveSum: A CUDA primitive computes the prefix sum over all Gaussian-tile counts to allocate the key and value arrays for the Gaussian-to-tile mapping. 2. DuplicateWithKeys: A Gaussian-parallel kernel recomputes Gaussian-tile intersections to generate a key for each intersecting tile, consisting of the tile index and Gaussian depth. 3. RadixSort: A CUDA primitive sorts the key array, ordering Gaussian indices by tile and then depth. 4. IdentifyTileRanges: A kernel parallelized across the key array post-processes keys before pixel rendering. 5. Render Kernel: The render kernel is parallelized across pixels. For each pixel p, all Gaussians within its corresponding tile are loaded and processed in depth order as determined by RadixSort. Formulas: The alpha value for Gaussian Gi at pixel p is: \alphai(p) = \sigmai gi(p) \quad (5) where \sigmai is the opacity of Gi and gi(p) is the value of the projected 2D Gaussian at pixel p. The projected 2D Gaussian value is: gi = e^q, \quad q = -\frac{1}{2}(p - \mu{i{2D}})\Sigma{i{2D}}^{-1}(p - \mu{i{2D}})^T \quad (6) where p is the pixel coordinate, \mu{i{2D}} is the 2D mean of the projected Gaussian, and \Sigma{i{2D}}^{-1} is the inverse of the projected 2D covariance matrix. The pixel color is computed via front-to-back alpha compositing: C(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci \alphai(p) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(p)) \quad (7) where ci is the color of Gaussian i, \mathcal{N} is the set of Gaussians in the tile, and Gaussians are processed in depth order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def speedysplatpipeline(Gaussians, tileranges, imagewidth, imageheight, tilesize): # Step 1: InclusiveSum (conceptual allocation) # counts = [len(getpreciseintersectingtiles(g)) for g in Gaussians] # prefixsums = np.cumsum(counts) # keys = np.empty(prefixsums[-1], dtype=object) # values = np.empty(prefixsums[-1], dtype=int) # Step 2: DuplicateWithKeys # keys and values are populated by a parallel kernel # Step 3: RadixSort # sortedkeys, sortedvalues = radixsort(keys, values) # Step 4: IdentifyTileRanges # tileranges maps tileid -> (startidx, endidx) in sorted arrays # Step 5: Render Kernel image = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3), dtype=np.float32) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): p = np.array([x, y], dtype=np.float32) tileid = (y // tilesize) (imagewidth // tilesize) + (x // tilesize) startidx, endidx = tileranges[tileid] accumulatedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], dtype=np.float32) transmittance = 1.0 for k in range(startidx, endidx): gidx = sortedvalues[k] gauss = Gaussians[gidx] diff = p - gauss.mu2d q = -0.5 float(diff @ gauss.Sigma2dinv @ diff) gval = math.exp(q) alphai = gauss.opacity gval if alphai > 255: accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor (1.0 - alphai) + gauss.color alphai transmittance = (1.0 - alphai) image[y, x] = accumulatedcolor return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alpha Threshold: The source specifies a condition \alphai > 255 for inclusion in compositing, while the formula defines \alphai \in [0,1]. This implies a fixed-point or scaled integer representation in the source implementation. Implementers should verify the alpha scaling convention or treat the threshold as a source-specific artifact. Precision: The computation of q involves matrix inversion and dot products, which may suffer from precision loss for highly anisotropic or degenerate Gaussians. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has a singular covariance matrix, the inverse \Sigma{i{2D}}^{-1} is undefined. A small regularization term should be added to the diagonal of the covariance matrix before inversion. Time Complexity: The dominant operations are the tile intersection computation, the radix sort, and the pixel-wise rendering. The radix sort requires O(N \log N) time where N is the number of Gaussian-tile pairs. The rendering step requires O(P \cdot K) time where P is the number of pixels and K is the average number of Gaussians per tile. Memory Complexity: The Key and Value arrays require O(N) memory. Performance: Speedy-Splat is designed to be faster than standard 3D-GS rasterization by reducing the number of Gaussians processed per pixel through precise intersection testing and efficient sorting. Strengths: Reduces overestimation of Gaussian extents, leading to fewer unnecessary computations. Efficient sorting allows for fast depth-ordered compositing. Limitations: The precise tile intersection computation may be more expensive per Gaussian than the coarse bounding box test. The alpha threshold condition requires careful handling of fixed-point representations. Speedy-Splat was introduced in the paper "Speedy-Splat: Fast 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Pixels and Sparse Primitives". The method is motivated by the observation that standard 3D-GS rasterization overestimates Gaussian extents and that 3D-GS models are heavily overparameterized. The method aims to address these inefficiencies by using precise tile intersections and sparse processing.
