name: Ghost Ellipsoids for Chunked Training
head: Ghost cell techniques adapted for unstructured primitives
body: Ghost Ellipsoids for Chunked Training resolves boundary artifacts in chunked volume training by including ellipsoids from neighboring chunks in the loss computation without updating their parameters, providing boundary context without requiring a global volume or merged model. Unlike chunk-based 3DGS methods that resolve boundary inconsistencies by merging chunks into a global coarse model or through post-training stages, this method requires boundary support during training itself without access to a global volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D ellipsoids partitioned into spatial chunks, each with a defined spatial extent and normalized coordinate space. Output: Updated parameters for the current chunk's ellipsoids, with boundary context provided by ghost ellipsoids from neighbors. Data Structures: Chunk: A spatial subdivision of the volume. Ellipsoid Primitive: Defined by position \mathbf{p}, rotation matrix R, scale matrix S, and covariance \Sigma = R S S^T R^T. Positions are stored with a per-chunk spatial offset mapping them to the shared world coordinate system. Ghost Region: A boundary region around each chunk, defined by the chunk boundary offset, used to identify neighboring ellipsoids that influence the current chunk's loss. Steps: 1. Chunk Partitioning: Divide the volume into chunks. Each chunk is trained in its own normalized coordinate space scaled to its spatial extent (e.g., [-0.5, 0.5]^3 for a volume split into 2 \times 2 \times 2 chunks). 2. Ghost Ellipsoid Identification: For each chunk, identify boundary ellipsoids from all neighboring chunks (face-, edge-, and vertex-adjacent) by selecting those whose centers fall within the ghost region of the current chunk. 3. Voxelization and Loss Computation: Voxelize the ghost ellipsoids together with the current chunk's ellipsoids during the loss computation step. 4. Gradient Update: Ensure that ghost ellipsoids receive no gradient updates. Only the parameters of the ellipsoids belonging to the current chunk are updated. 5. Training Mode Selection: Sequential Mode (Single-GPU): Chunks are trained one at a time using ghost ellipsoids from completed neighbors. Parallel Mode (Multi-GPU): All chunks are trained simultaneously with ghost ellipsoids periodically synchronized across GPUs. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Coordinate Space Rescaling: Training all chunks in a shared [-1, 1]^3 space and applying post-hoc rescaling is computationally impractical. It requires computing \Sigma' = K \Sigma K^T = K R S S^T R^T K^T for each primitive, where K is a chunk-dependent anisotropic scale matrix. Since K and R do not generally commute, this cannot be simplified by scaling S alone. Correctly decomposing \Sigma' back into rotation and scale parameters requires a QR decomposition per primitive. Merging: The per-chunk primitive sets resulting from this method can be merged through simple concatenation without additional alignment, avoiding the need for global model merging. A training scheme for large volumes that partitions the volume into spatially non-overlapping chunks and uses ghost ellipsoids to provide boundary context. Ghost ellipsoids are used to provide boundary context across neighboring chunks during optimization, enabling scalable learning on volumes exceeding GPU memory. Training chunks separately introduces boundary artifacts because ellipsoids near chunk borders lack support from neighboring regions. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates boundary artifacts without requiring a global volume or merged model. Avoids computationally expensive QR decompositions associated with post-hoc rescaling. Limitations: Requires identification of neighboring ellipsoids and synchronization (in parallel mode). When to use: When training large volumes on limited GPU memory by chunking, and boundary consistency is critical. When not to use: When a global model can be afforded or when post-training merging is acceptable. The technique is inspired by ghost cell techniques [45], but adapted for unstructured primitives. Classical ghost cells copy boundary values from adjacent regular grid cells, but this method cannot rely on grid adjacency since the primitives are spatially unstructured. The method addresses the incompatibility of standard 3DGS screenspace rasterization with accurate TF mapping in volumetric settings. ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Analytic Transmittance 3DGS
head: Analytic transmittance computation for 3DGS, Volumetrically Consistent 3D Gaussian Rasterization, Volumetrically Consistent 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Analytic Transmittance 3DGS is a rasterization-based rendering method that replaces the approximate alpha computation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytic integration of the volume rendering equation along the camera ray. It computes physically accurate transmittance and alpha values without projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D splats, thereby avoiding the linearization of the exponential transmittance and the assumption of non-self-occlusion inherent in splatting. Unlike its sibling 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer which relies on 2D Gaussian projection, this method integrates 3D Gaussians directly in ray-space to better represent opaque surfaces and improve view synthesis quality. The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization but replaces the alpha blending calculation with an exact volumetric integration. It assumes that 3D Gaussians are sorted front-to-back and do not overlap along the ray. If these assumptions are violated, the separation of transmittance terms is invalid. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by: \boldsymbol{\mu}i: 3D mean (center). \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i: 3D covariance matrix. \kappai: Density parameter. ci: View-dependent color. oi: Peak opacity, restricted to [0, 1]. Camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction. Sorting order of Gaussians along the ray (front-to-back). Outputs: Pixel color C(p) and accumulated opacity \alphai for each Gaussian i contributing to the pixel. The method uses the standard 3D Gaussian attributes defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization. No new complex data structures are required beyond the standard Gaussian attributes and the ray parameters. The density \kappa is often reparameterized for optimization stability: \kappa = -\log(1 - 0.99\theta) \frac{1}{3} \left( \frac{1}{sx} + \frac{1}{sy} + \frac{1}{sz} \right) where \theta \in [0, 1] is a learnable parameter and sx, sy, sz are scales. The constant 0.99 promotes high density for small Gaussians. The unnormalized 3D Gaussian density function is: Gi(\mathbf{x}) = \exp \left\{ -\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i) \right\} The total density field is: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N \kappai Gi(\mathbf{x}) The exponential transmittance across a ray segment from a to b is: T(a, b) = \exp \left( - \inta^b \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds \right) To compute the accumulated transmittance \overline{T}j across a specific Gaussian j, we project the 3D Gaussian onto the 1D ray. The 1D Gaussian distribution gj(t) along the ray is: gj(t) = Gj(\gammaj \mathbf{d}) \exp \left\{ -\frac{(t - \gammaj)^2}{2\betaj^2} \right\} where \gammaj is the mean and \betaj is the variance of the 1D Gaussian. These are computed as: \gammaj = \frac{(\boldsymbol{\mu}j - \mathbf{o})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{d}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} \mathbf{d}}, \quad \betaj = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathbf{d}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} \mathbf{d}}} The integral of the 1D Gaussian from entry t{jn} to exit t{jf} is: \int{t{jn}}^{t{jf}} gj(t) dt = Gj(\gammaj \mathbf{d}) \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} \betaj \text{erf} \left( \frac{t - \gammaj}{2\betaj} \right) \Big|{t{jn}}^{t{jf}} Assuming infinite support (integrating from -\infty to \infty), the accumulated transmittance across Gaussian j is: \overline{T}j = \exp \left( -\kappaj Gj(\gammaj \mathbf{d}) \sqrt{2\pi} \betaj \right) The accumulated opacity \alphai for the i-th Gaussian is derived from the transmittance entering and leaving it. Under the non-overlapping assumption, the opacity is: \alphai = 1 - \overline{T}i Note: In the general volume rendering equation, the opacity contribution is \alphai = \int{t{in}}^{t{if}} T(t{in}, t) \kappai Gi(\mathbf{r}(t)) dt, which simplifies to 1 - \overline{T}i when T(t{in}, t) is constant across the non-overlapping primitive (i.e., T(t{in}, t) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \overline{T}j). The final pixel color is computed via alpha blending: C(p) = \sum{i=1}^N ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) The following pseudocode implements the analytic transmittance computation for a single pixel, assuming a list of sorted Gaussians intersecting the ray. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analytictransmittance3dgs(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians): """ Computes pixel color and alpha using analytic transmittance. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (o) raydirection: 3D vector (d), assumed normalized gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, sorted front-to-back along the ray. Each Gaussian has: mu: 3D vector (center) Sigmainv: 3x3 matrix (inverse covariance) kappa: scalar (density) color: 3D vector (ci) peakopacity: scalar (oi) [Note: In analytic method, peak opacity is less critical than kappa, but retained for compatibility] Returns: color: 3D vector (final pixel color) accumulatedalpha: scalar (total opacity) """ accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for g in gaussians: # 1. Compute 1D Gaussian parameters # deltamu = mu - o deltamu = [g.mu[0] - rayorigin[0], g.mu[1] - rayorigin[1], g.mu[2] - rayorigin[2]] # d^T Sigmainv d # Let v = Sigmainv d v = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): v[i] += g.Sigmainv[i][j] raydirection[j] dSigmainvd = sum(raydirection[i] v[i] for i in range(3)) # Avoid division by zero for degenerate Gaussians if dSigmainvd < 1e-8: continue # betaj = 1 / sqrt(d^T Sigmainv d) betaj = 1.0 / math.sqrt(dSigmainvd) # gammaj = (mu - o)^T Sigmainv d / (d^T Sigmainv d) # (mu - o)^T Sigmainv d is dot(deltamu, v) gammaj = sum(deltamu[i] v[i] for i in range(3)) / dSigmainvd # 2. Compute peak value of 3D Gaussian along the ray: Gj(gammaj d) # The exponent argument at the mean projection: # xmean = o + gammaj d # diffatmean = xmean - mu = (o + gammaj d) - mu diffatmean = [-deltamu[i] + gammaj raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] # Exponent = -0.5 diff^T Sigmainv diff # Let w = Sigmainv diff w = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): w[i] += g.Sigmainv[i][j] diffatmean[j] exponentarg = sum(diffatmean[i] w[i] for i in range(3)) Gpeak = math.exp(-0.5 exponentarg) # 3. Compute accumulated transmittance across this Gaussian # Tj = exp(-kappa Gpeak sqrt(2pi) beta) # Note: The integral of the 1D Gaussian over infinite support is Gpeak sqrt(2pi) beta integralvalue = Gpeak math.sqrt(2.0 math.pi) betaj transmittanceacrossg = math.exp(-g.kappa integralvalue) # 4. Compute opacity alphai for this Gaussian # alphai = 1 - Tj (since Tin = accumulatedtransmittance, Tout = accumulatedtransmittance Tj) # The contribution to color is ci alphai Tin alphai = 1.0 - transmittanceacrossg # 5. Add to final color # C += ci alphai accumulatedtransmittance for k in range(3): finalcolor[k] += g.color[k] alphai accumulatedtransmittance # 6. Update accumulated transmittance accumulatedtransmittance = transmittanceacrossg return finalcolor, 1.0 - accumulatedtransmittance Density Reparameterization: \kappa is reparameterized using \theta \in [0, 1] as \kappa = -\log(1 - 0.99\theta) \frac{1}{3} (\frac{1}{sx} + \frac{1}{sy} + \frac{1}{sz}). Densification Heuristics: Halve density \kappa after splitting and cloning. Split points with high density \kappa. Prune points with low density based on \theta (density before reparameterization). Disable opacity reset during optimization. Overlap and Sorting: The method relies on the assumptions that Gaussians are sorted front-to-back and do not overlap along the ray. If these are violated, the separation of transmittance terms is invalid, leading to artifacts. Degenerate Covariance: If \mathbf{d}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} \mathbf{d} is near zero (e.g., Gaussian is infinitely thin in the ray direction), \betaj becomes large and numerical instability may occur. Infinite Support Assumption: The analytic formula assumes infinite support for the Gaussian integral. Time Complexity: Similar to 3DGS rasterization, O(N) per pixel where N is the number of Gaussians covering the pixel. Memory Complexity: Same as 3DGS, storing N Gaussians. Performance: On MipNeRF-360, the method achieves PSNR 27.30, SSIM 0.813, LPIPS 0.209, and FPS 136 on an Nvidia 3090-Ti GPU. This is slightly slower than standard 3DGS (159 FPS) but faster than some other variants like GES (186 FPS). Strengths: More physically accurate alpha values; better representation of opaque surfaces; fewer artifacts near edges; works out-of-the-box for tomography. Limitations: Relies on non-overlapping assumption; slightly higher computational cost per Gaussian than 2D splatting. The method was introduced in "Volumetrically Consistent 3D Gaussian Rasterization". It addresses the limitations of 3DGS splatting, which linearizes the exponential transmittance and assumes no self-occlusion. By analytically integrating the 3D Gaussian along the ray, it provides a more accurate volume rendering solution while maintaining rasterization speed. It is compatible with other 3DGS extensions and has been applied to view synthesis and tomography. Volumetrically Consistent 3D Gaussian Rasterization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03378v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Ref-Gaussian Deferred Surfel Rendering with Split-Sum IBL
head: MetalGaussianSplatRelighting, Ref-Gaussian on iOS
body: Ref-Gaussian Deferred Surfel Rendering with Split-Sum IBL is a real-time deferred shading method for relighting 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models on mobile hardware (specifically iOS/Metal). It solves the problem of dynamic environment lighting in Gaussian splats by decomposing splats into physically-based rendering (PBR) materials (albedo, normal, roughness, reflectance) and computing lighting via a deferred pipeline with split-sum environment map integration. Unlike forward-shading Gaussian splatters that bake lighting into spherical harmonics or use analytic approximations, this method separates the material definition from the lighting environment, allowing the environment map to be swapped or rotated in real-time without retraining or re-rasterizing the splats. It differs from standard PBR deferred renderers by adapting the splat-based rasterization and surfel accumulation to the deferred G-buffer workflow. Inputs: A.ply file containing 3D Gaussian splats with per-splat attributes: position, covariance (or quaternion/scale), opacity, spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color, and material attributes: normal, roughness, reflectance (specular strength), and albedo (diffuse color). An HDR environment map (equirectangular or cubemap) representing the lighting. Outputs: A final color buffer with relit splats. Data Structures: Splat Buffer: Contains position, rotation (quaternion), scale, opacity, and view-dependent SH coefficients, sorted for cache locality (e.g., Morton code). Material Buffer: Parallel array to the Splat Buffer, containing per-splat material properties: normal (3 floats), roughness (1 float), reflectance (1 float), and albedo (3 floats), sorted in parallel to maintain alignment. G-Buffer: Tile memory or render target storing per-pixel accumulated material data (normal, roughness, reflectance, albedo) and depth. IBL Pre-computed Textures: Prefiltered Environment Map (mipmapped by roughness), Irradiance Map (not used for diffuse color in this method), and BRDF LUT mapping (F0, \text{roughness}) to (fg.x, fg.y) coefficients. Steps: 1. Load and Parse: Read the.ply file to extract per-splat material data (normal, roughness, reflectance, albedo) and derive normals from rotation quaternions. 2. Sort for Locality: Sort the Splat Buffer using a spatial locality algorithm (e.g., Morton code) to optimize cache performance during rasterization. 3. Synchronize Material Buffer: Apply the exact same sort indices to the Material Buffer to ensure each splat's geometry aligns with its material properties. 4. Pre-compute IBL: Use a compute kernel to generate the Prefiltered Environment Map by convolving the HDR environment map with a microfacet distribution for various roughness levels, the Irradiance Map by convolving the HDR environment map with a hemisphere integral, and the BRDF LUT by integrating the Fresnel and geometry terms. 5. Rasterize to G-Buffer: Project splats to screen space and accumulate material properties (normal, roughness, reflectance, albedo) and depth into the G-Buffer using standard alpha blending or weighted accumulation. 6. Deferred Shading (Split-Sum IBL): For each pixel in the G-Buffer, retrieve accumulated material properties (N, \text{roughness}, \text{reflectance}, \text{albedo}) and the view direction V. Compute F0: F0 = 0.04 \times (1 - \text{reflectance}) + \text{albedo} \times \text{reflectance} where F0 is the base specular reflectivity, \text{reflectance} is the learned specular strength, and \text{albedo} is the diffuse color. Compute the specular term: \text{specular} = \text{prefiltered}(\text{reflect}(V, N), \text{roughness}) \times (F0 \cdot fg.x + fg.y) where \text{prefiltered}(\cdot, \cdot) samples the prefiltered environment map at the reflection direction \text{reflect}(V, N) using the mip level determined by \text{roughness}, and fg is the result from the BRDF LUT sampled with (F0, \text{roughness}). Compute the final color: \text{final} = (1 - \text{reflectance}) \times \text{base\color} + \text{specular} where \text{base\color} is the albedo used directly for the diffuse component without irradiance multiplication. 7. Post-processing: Composite the final color with the skybox or background environment map if necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. splatbuffer = loadplysplats("model.ply") materialbuffer = loadplymaterials("model.ply") sortedindices = computemortonsort(splatbuffer.positions) splatbuffer.sortinplace(sortedindices) materialbuffer.sortinplace(sortedindices) prefilteredenvmap = prefilterenvironmentmap(hdrenvmap, roughnesslevels) brdflut = computebrdflut() gbuffer = initializegbuffer(width, height) for splat in splatbuffer: screenrect = projecttoscreen(splat.pos, splat.quat, splat.scale, cameramatrix) for y in range(screenrect.ymin, screenrect.ymax): for x in range(screenrect.xmin, screenrect.xmax): if ispixelinsidesplat(x, y, splat): material = materialbuffer[splat.index] gbuffer[y][x].normal += material.normal gbuffer[y][x].roughness += material.roughness gbuffer[y][x].reflectance += material.reflectance gbuffer[y][x].albedo += material.albedo gbuffer[y][x].depth = min(gbuffer[y][x].depth, splat.depth) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): N = normalize(gbuffer[y][x].normal) roughness = gbuffer[y][x].roughness reflectance = gbuffer[y][x].reflectance albedo = gbuffer[y][x].albedo V = getviewdirection(x, y, cameramatrix) F0 = 0.04 (1.0 - reflectance) + albedo reflectance R = reflect(V, N) prefilteredcolor = sampleprefilteredenvmap(prefilteredenvmap, R, roughness) fg = samplebrdflut(brdflut, F0, roughness) specular = prefilteredcolor (F0 fg.x + fg.y) finalcolor = (1.0 - reflectance) albedo + specular outputbuffer[y][x] = finalcolor Parameters: F0 base value: 0.04 for dielectrics. Roughness: Controls specular blur. Low roughness (~0.2 for cars) results in clear mirror-like reflections; high roughness results in blurry, diffuse-like specular. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Map Noise: If splats are sorted for cache locality but the material buffer is not sorted in parallel, normals become misaligned with positions, causing rainbow noise. Fix: Apply the same sort indices to the material buffer. Incorrect Diffuse Lighting: Do not multiply albedo by the irradiance map for diffuse color. Ref-Gaussian uses basecolor directly for diffuse. Only specular is computed from the environment map. Coordinate System Mismatch: If scene data is Z-up (e.g., Blender) but the viewer assumes Y-up, objects appear rotated 90 degrees. Fix: Apply a -90° rotation around the X-axis to the camera/view matrix and adjust environment map sampling directions to match the scene's up-axis. Stale Binary Execution on iOS: If iOS build fails due to type errors (e.g., Float16 bitPattern type mismatch between arm64 and x8664 simulator), the device may run an old binary. Always check build success for the target platform before debugging logic. Time Complexity: Rasterization is O(N) where N is the number of splats, with overhead for sorting and G-buffer accumulation. Shading is O(P) where P is the number of pixels, with constant-time texture lookups for IBL. Memory Complexity: O(N) for splat and material buffers, O(P) for G-buffer, and constant space for IBL pre-computed textures (size depends on environment map resolution). Measured Performance: Real-time on iPhone using Metal. Scaling: Scales with the number of splats and screen resolution. IBL pre-computation is done once or when the environment map changes. Strengths: Real-time relighting, physically-based materials, mobile-friendly (Metal). Limitations: Requires material attributes (normal, roughness, etc.) to be learned or provided in the.ply file. Deferred shading adds memory overhead for the G-buffer. When to use: When dynamic environment lighting is required for 3DGS models on mobile devices. When not to use: When forward shading is preferred for simplicity or when material attributes are not available. Ref-Gaussian Deferred Surfel Rendering with Split-Sum IBL was developed by Daisuke Majima (MLBoy) and published on Qiita in May 2026. It is an implementation of the Ref-Gaussian method, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with PBR materials and deferred shading for real-time relighting on iOS. The method builds on the split-sum approximation for environment lighting introduced in Unreal Engine 4. iPhoneで Gaussian Splatting モデルの反射をリアルタイムで更新する, https://qiita.com/john-rocky/items/3c452476e66bdc29c290, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Light Space Rasterization for T_light
head: Front Tau Rasterization, Light Space Shadow Rasterization, T_light Rasterization (Light Space)
body: Light Space Rasterization computes T{light}, the front-facing occlusion transmittance for each 3D Gaussian along a directional sun direction. It differs from voxel-based fallbacks by providing full continuous gradients and zero parameter expansion, enabling differentiable relighting without requiring specific training hyperparameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian splats (position, covariance/scale, rotation, opacity \alpha, color/SH coefficients) and a sun direction vector \mathbf{d}{sun}. Output: Per-Gaussian scalar T{light} \in [0, 1], representing the accumulated transmittance from the sun direction to the Gaussian center. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS attributes. The method relies on the projected position and scale in light space. Accumulator: A per-pixel accumulation buffer for optical depth \tau. In the CUDA kernel, this is managed via the recordfronttau channel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Light Camera Setup: Construct a virtual perspective camera to simulate the directional sun light. Place it at a large distance along \mathbf{d}{sun} with a narrow field of view (FOV). The distance and FOV are chosen so that parallax error remains below 2\%, avoiding changes to the EWA Jacobian. 2. Light-Space Projection: Project all 3D Gaussians into the light camera's clip space. Transform Gaussian centers \mathbf{p}i using the light camera's view-projection matrix M{light}. Compute the projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} in screen space using standard EWA approximation with the light camera's intrinsics and extrinsics. 3. Depth Sorting: Sort the Gaussians by their depth z in light space from front (closest to the light source) to back. This ensures correct front-to-back accumulation for transmittance. 4. Rasterization Pass: Iterate over screen pixels covered by the sorted Gaussians. For each Gaussian i covering pixel (u, v), update the accumulated optical depth \tau{acc}. Each Gaussian records the accumulated front \tau weighted by \alpha \cdot T. The method computes an energy-weighted mean over the entire sun-facing footprint rather than a center-point sample. The transmittance T{light} for a Gaussian is derived from the accumulated optical depth of all Gaussians in front of it along the sun direction. 5. Fallback and Edge Cases: If a Gaussian is deeply buried such that the accumulated weight sum w{sum} \approx 0 (early termination), it is explicitly mapped to full shadow (T{light} = 0) to prevent inversion artifacts. Full continuous gradients are enabled by default for \tau, weights, normalization, weak density backup transmittance, and projected position/scale/rotation. The sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches are treated as constants. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computetlightrasterization(gaussians, sundirection, screenwidth, screenheight): # 1. Setup Light Camera campos = [sundirection[0] 1e6, sundirection[1] 1e6, sundirection[2] 1e6] camlookat = [-sundirection[0], -sundirection[1], -sundirection[2]] camup = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] if abs(sundirection[1]) < 0.9 else [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] camright = cross(camlookat, camup) camright = normalize(camright) camup = cross(camright, camlookat) viewmatrix = lookat(campos, camlookat, camup) fovrad = math.radians(1.0) # Narrow FOV aspect = screenwidth / screenheight near, far = 0.1, 1e7 projmatrix = perspectiveprojection(fovrad, aspect, near, far) # 2. Project Gaussians to Light Space projected = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): centerh = [g['center'][0], g['center'][1], g['center'][2], 1.0] centercam = matmul(viewmatrix, centerh) centerclip = matmul(projmatrix, centercam) if centerclip[3] <= 0: continue # Behind camera centerndc = [centerclip[0]/centerclip[3], centerclip[1]/centerclip[3], centerclip[2]/centerclip[3]] depth = centerndc[2] cov2d = projectcovariance(g, viewmatrix, projmatrix) # Standard EWA projected.append({ 'index': i, 'centerndc': centerndc, 'cov2d': cov2d, 'alpha': g['alpha'], 'depth': depth }) # 3. Sort by Depth (Front to Back) projected.sort(key=lambda x: x['depth']) # 4. Rasterization Pass taubuffer = [[0.0] screenwidth for in range(screenheight)] tlightvalues = [0.0] len(gaussians) for g in projected: u, v, z = g['centerndc'] px, py = int((u + 1) screenwidth / 2), int((v + 1) screenheight / 2) # Sample accumulated tau at this Gaussian's center taubefore = taubuffer[py][px] # Compute Tlight for this Gaussian tlight = math.exp(-taubefore) # Handle deeply buried Gaussians (early termination wsum=0) if tlight < 1e-6: tlight = 0.0 tlightvalues[g['index']] = tlight # Update taubuffer with this Gaussian's contribution # Contribution = alpha T (energy-weighted mean over footprint) contribution = g['alpha'] tlight # Add to covered pixels (simplified bounding box rasterization) sigmax = math.sqrt(g['cov2d'][0][0]) 3.0 sigmay = math.sqrt(g['cov2d'][1][1]) 3.0 minpx, maxpx = max(0, int(px - sigmax)), min(screenwidth, int(px + sigmax)) minpy, maxpy = max(0, int(py - sigmay)), min(screenheight, int(py + sigmay)) for y in range(minpy, maxpy): for x in range(minpx, maxpx): dx, dy = x - px, y - py pdf = math.exp(-0.5 (dx2 / g['cov2d'][0][0] + dy2 / g['cov2d'][1][1])) if pdf > 0.01: # Threshold taubuffer[y][x] += contribution return tlightvalues def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(dot(v,v)); return [x/l for x in v] def lookat(eye, target, up): z = normalize([target[i]-eye[i] for i in range(3)]) x = normalize(cross(up, z)) y = cross(z, x) m = [[x[0],y[0],z[0],-dot(x,eye)], [x[1],y[1],z[1],-dot(y,eye)], [x[2],y[2],z[2],-dot(z,eye)], [0,0,0,1]] return m def perspectiveprojection(fov, aspect, near, far): f = 1.0 / math.tan(fov/2) return [[f/aspect,0,0,0], [0,f,0,0], [0,0,-(far+near)/(far-near),-2farnear/(far-near)], [0,0,-1,0]] def matmul(m, v): return [sum(m[i][j]v[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] def projectcovariance(g, view, proj): # Simplified EWA: scale by view/proj derivatives return [[g['scale'][0]2, 0], [0, g['scale'][1]2]] Parameters: LARGEDISTANCECONSTANT: Distance of light camera from origin. Not given in the sources. NARROWFOVRADIANS: FOV of light camera. Not given in the sources, but must be narrow to minimize parallax error (<2%). THRESHOLDMINTRANSMITTANCE: Threshold for mapping deeply buried Gaussians to full shadow. Not given in the sources. SCALEFACTOR: Scaling factor for density contribution. Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Parallax Error: If the light camera is not far enough or FOV is too wide, parallax error exceeds 2%, affecting the EWA Jacobian accuracy. Inversion Artifacts: Deeply buried Gaussians must be explicitly mapped to full shadow to prevent artifacts. Gradient Discontinuities: The sun camera framing, sorting, and threshold branches are treated as constants. Gradients do not flow through these steps. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of Gaussians and pixels covered, similar to standard 3DGS rasterization. The additional cost is the light-space projection and sorting. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of Gaussians. No additional voxel grid expansion is required, unlike the voxel fallback. Performance: Provides full continuous gradients and zero expansion by default, making it more efficient and easier to train than the voxel fallback (--tlightvoxel). Strengths: Differentiable, no parameter expansion, handles relighting for held-out sun directions. Limitations: Approximates parallel rays, which may introduce small errors for very large scenes or extreme sun angles. This method is part of the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud project, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to volume cloud rendering. It enables relighting of volume clouds by computing self-shadowing via light-space rasterization. It is designed to work with datasets like CloudDatasetUniform, which includes multiple sun directions for training and testing relighting generalization. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
head: 2D Gaussian Splatting Surfel Rasterization, rasterize_to_pixels_2dgs [S1, unofficial]
body: 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization renders a scene represented by 2D Gaussian surfels by projecting them to screen space and performing ray-surfel intersection per pixel, accumulating colour, alpha, and normal maps via front-to-back alpha compositing. It differs from the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization.md] by treating primitives as planar surfels with 2D covariance structures rather than 3D ellipsoids, which simplifies the intersection geometry but requires specific handling of the surfel plane orientation relative to the view ray. Inputs: means: 3D positions of surfels, shape [N, 3]. quats: Rotation quaternions (w, x, y, z), shape [N, 4]. scales: Scale factors, shape [N, 3]. opacities: Per-surfel opacity, shape [N]. colors: Per-surfel color coefficients. If shdegree is not None, shape [N, K, 3] where K is the number of SH coefficients. If shdegree is None, shape [N, D] where D is the number of color channels (typically 3). viewmats: View matrices, shape [C, 4, 4]. Ks: Camera intrinsic matrices, shape [C, 3, 3]. campos: Camera positions, shape [C, 3]. width, height: Image dimensions. nearplane: Near clipping plane distance, default 0.01. farplane: Far clipping plane distance, default 1e10. tilesize: Integer, default 16. Side length of tiles for rasterization. shdegree: Integer or None. If not None, spherical harmonics are evaluated. backgrounds: Background color per camera, shape [C, 3]. Outputs: rendercolors: Computed color per pixel, shape [C, H, W, channels]. renderalphas: Computed alpha per pixel, shape [C, H, W, 1]. rendernormals: Computed normal per pixel, shape [C, H, W, 3]. Surfel Properties: Stored in contiguous arrays or tensors. means (float32, [N, 3]), quats (float32, [N, 4]), scales (float32, [N, 3]), opacities (float32, [N]). Projection Outputs: radii: Radius of the 2D Gaussian bounding circle per surfel per camera, shape [C, N]. means2d: Projected 2D center coordinates, shape [C, N, 2]. depths: Z-depth of surfel centers, shape [C, N]. raytransforms: Transformation matrices for ray-surfel intersection, shape [C, N, 3, 3] (derived from view and projection). normals: Surface normals in world space, shape [C, N, 3]. Tile Indices: isectoffsets: Encoded intersection offsets, shape [C, tileheight, tilewidth]. flattenids: Flattened list of surfel IDs sorted by depth within tiles. 1. Projection: Project 3D surfels to 2D screen space using fullyfusedprojection2dgs, passing means, quats, scales, viewmats, Ks, width, height, nearplane, and farplane. Outputs radii, means2d, depths, raytransforms, and normals. 2. Color Preparation: Broadcast scalar per-surfel opacities [N] to per-camera [C, N] using mx.broadcastto(mx.expanddims(opacities, axis=0), (C, N)). If shdegree is not None, compute view directions dirs = means[None,:,:] - campos[:, None,:], normalize dirs, broadcast color coefficients to [C, N, K, 3], evaluate sphericalharmonics(shdegree, dirs, coeffsbroadcast) to get rgb [C, N, 3], and clamp with mx.maximum(rgb + 0.5, 0.0). If shdegree is None, broadcast colors [N, D] to [C, N, D] or use colors [C, N, D] directly as colorsforraster. 3. Tile Assignment: Compute tile dimensions tilewidth = ceil(width / tilesize), tileheight = ceil(height / tilesize). Call isecttiles(means2d, radii, depths, tilesize, tilewidth, tileheight, sort=True) to get tilespergauss, isectids, flattenids. Encode intersection offsets using isectoffsetencode(isectids, C, tilewidth, tileheight) to get isectoffsets [C, tileheight, tilewidth]. 4. Rasterization: Call rasterizetopixels2dgs with means2d, raytransforms, colorsforraster, normals, opacitiescn, width, height, tilesize, isectoffsets, flattenids, and backgrounds. This function iterates through surfels in depth order within each tile. For each surfel gid in depth order and each pixel (pxf, pyf) it covers: 1. Ray-Surfel Intersection Vectors: Let Mg be the ray transform matrix for surfel g (from raytransforms). Let px, py be the pixel coordinates (normalized or screen space as defined by the projection, typically normalized device coordinates or similar relative to the center). The source specifies: hu = -Mg[0,:3] + Mg[2,:3] \cdot px hv = -Mg[1,:3] + Mg[2,:3] \cdot py Where Mg[0,:3] is the first row's x,y,z components, etc.. 2. Cross Product and Degeneracy Guard: tmp = hu \times hv If |tmp[2]| < 10^{-10}, skip this intersection (degenerate case where rays/surfels are parallel). 3. Intersection Coordinates: us = \frac{tmp[0]}{tmp[2]} vs = \frac{tmp[1]}{tmp[2]} These (us, vs) represent the coordinates in the local 2D Gaussian space. 4. Sigma Calculation: Compute 3D sigma from intersection: \sigma{3d} = us^2 + vs^2 Compute 2D fallback sigma from distance to center (where dx, dy are the 2D distance components from means2d to pixel center, or derived from us, vs depending on implementation specifics, but the source explicitly defines a fallback): \sigma{2d} = 2.0 \cdot (dx^2 + dy^2) Take the tighter bound: \sigma = 0.5 \cdot \min(\sigma{3d}, \sigma{2d}) Negative sigma values are skipped to prevent invalid alpha computation. 5. Alpha Computation: \alpha = \min(\text{opacity} \cdot e^{-\sigma}, \text{MAX\ALPHA}) Where MAXALPHA is a clamping value (e.g., 0.999 or similar, exact value not specified in source, but clamping is required). 6. Front-to-Back Compositing: Accumulate color and alpha for the pixel using standard front-to-back alpha blending: C{out} = C{prev} \cdot (1 - \alpha) + C{surf} \cdot \alpha \alpha{out} = \alpha{prev} + (1 - \alpha{prev}) \cdot \alpha Where C{surf} is the surfel color and \alpha is the computed alpha. The process starts with background color and zero alpha. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rasterizetopixels2dgs( means2d: np.ndarray, # [C, N, 2] raytransforms: np.ndarray, # [C, N, 3, 3] colors: np.ndarray, # [C, N, 3] normals: np.ndarray, # [C, N, 3] opacities: np.ndarray, # [C, N] radii: np.ndarray, # [C, N] width: int, height: int, tilesize: int, isectoffsets: np.ndarray, # [C, tileh, tilew] flattenids: np.ndarray, # [totalsurfelsintiles] backgrounds: np.ndarray, # [C, 3] MAXALPHA: float = 0.999 # Standard clamping value; exact value not given in sources.) -> tuple: """ Rasterize 2D Gaussian surfels to pixels. Returns: (rendercolors, renderalphas, rendernormals) """ C = means2d.shape[0] H, W = height, width tileh = int(np.ceil(H / tilesize)) tilew = int(np.ceil(W / tilesize)) rendercolors = np.zeros((C, H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) renderalphas = np.zeros((C, H, W, 1), dtype=np.float32) rendernormals = np.zeros((C, H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) for c in range(C): rendercolors[c,:,:,:] = backgrounds[c] renderalphas[c,:,:, 0] = 0.0 rendernormals[c,:,:,:] = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] for c in range(C): for ty in range(tileh): for tx in range(tilew): startidx = isectoffsets[c, ty, tx] endidx = isectoffsets[c, ty + 1, tx] if ty + 1 < tileh else len(flattenids) for idx in range(startidx, endidx): gid = flattenids[idx] m2d = means2d[c, gid] rt = raytransforms[c, gid] color = colors[c, gid] normal = normals[c, gid] alphasurf = opacities[c, gid] r = radii[c, gid] minpx = max(0, int(m2d[0] - r)) maxpx = min(W, int(m2d[0] + r)) minpy = max(0, int(m2d[1] - r)) maxpy = min(H, int(m2d[1] + r)) for py in range(minpy, maxpy): for px in range(minpx, maxpx): pxf = float(px) pyf = float(py) hu = -rt[0,:3] + rt[2,:3] pxf hv = -rt[1,:3] + rt[2,:3] pyf tmp = np.cross(hu, hv) if abs(tmp[2]) < 1e-10: continue us = tmp[0] / tmp[2] vs = tmp[1] / tmp[2] sigma3d = us us + vs vs dx = m2d[0] - pxf dy = m2d[1] - pyf sigma2d = 2.0 (dx dx + dy dy) sigma = 0.5 min(sigma3d, sigma2d) if sigma < 0: continue alpha = min(alphasurf np.exp(-sigma), MAXALPHA) rendercolors[c, py, px,:] = ( rendercolors[c, py, px,:] (1.0 - alpha) + color alpha) renderalphas[c, py, px, 0] += alpha (1.0 - renderalphas[c, py, px, 0]) rendernormals[c, py, px,:] = normal return rendercolors, renderalphas, rendernormals tilesize: Integer, default 16. Side length of tiles for rasterization. nearplane: Float, default 0.01. Near clipping plane distance. farplane: Float, default 1e10. Far clipping plane distance. Degenerate Cross Product: When tmp[2] is near zero, the rays and surfels are parallel, leading to division by zero. This is handled by skipping the intersection if abs(tmp[2]) < 1e-10. Negative Sigma: Negative sigma values result in invalid alpha computation (exponential growth). These are skipped. Not given in the sources. The 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization method is part of the 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) approach, which represents scenes using 2D Gaussian surfels. This method was introduced as an alternative to 3D Gaussian Splatting to improve rendering efficiency and quality for certain types of scenes. The reference implementation is provided by the gsplat-mlx library. RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, https://github.com/RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Avatar
head: 3DGS-Avatar, SMPL-based Gaussian Splatting Avatar
body: Gaussian Avatar is a method for reconstructing animatable full-body human avatars by leveraging the SMPL parametric model as a structural prior. It solves the problem of generating dynamic, high-fidelity 3D humans from video by predicting 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color) conditioned on the avatar's pose. It is distinguished from its sibling Gaussian Splatting by its explicit dependency on a parametric body model to drive deformation, and from Gaussian Avatars which typically focus on head-only reconstruction using the FLAME model. Inputs: A sequence of input images or video frames of a human subject. The SMPL model, which provides a parametric representation of human body shape and pose. SMPL parameters: global pose (\theta), body shape (\beta), and potentially joint angles. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} whose parameters are functions of the SMPL pose. A rendered image sequence consistent with the input views. Data Structures: Gaussian Parameters: Each Gaussian i is defined by a mean position \mui, a covariance matrix \Sigmai (parameterized by scale si and rotation Ri), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color ci. Pose Feature Vector: A vector derived from the SMPL pose parameters, typically including global rotation and joint angles. Feedforward Network (MLP): A neural network that maps pose features to Gaussian parameters. Method Steps: 1. SMPL Fitting: For each input frame, estimate the SMPL parameters (pose \theta, shape \beta) that best fit the observed image data. 2. Pose Feature Extraction: Encode the SMPL pose parameters into a feature vector. This may involve concatenating joint angles or using a pose embedding. 3. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Pass the pose feature vector through a feedforward neural network (MLP). The network outputs the parameters for each Gaussian: \text{Params}i = \text{MLP}(\text{PoseFeatures}) where \text{Params}i includes \mui, si, Ri, \alphai, ci. 4. Rendering: Render the predicted Gaussians using standard differentiable splatting Gaussian Splatting to produce an image. 5. Optimization: Minimize the difference between the rendered image and the input image using gradient descent. The SMPL parameters and/or the MLP weights are optimized to minimize this loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Poses: Extreme poses may lead to inaccurate SMPL fitting or poor generalization by the MLP. Occlusion: Self-occlusion can make SMPL fitting ambiguous, affecting the accuracy of the predicted Gaussian positions. A monocular video avatar method that uses the SMPL-X rig and is coupled with a mesh. It differs from standard Gaussian Avatar by integrating mesh constraints, potentially offering better geometric consistency for monocular inputs. Time Complexity: Dependent on the number of Gaussians and the complexity of the feedforward network. Rendering is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Training involves iterative optimization of SMPL parameters and network weights. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian parameters. Strengths: High-fidelity reconstruction of full-body avatars; leverages strong priors from SMPL for plausible anatomy. Limitations: Requires accurate SMPL fitting; may struggle with non-humanoid subjects or extreme deformations not captured by SMPL. When to use: When animatable full-body avatars are needed from video data. When not to use: For head-only avatars (use Gaussian Avatars) or when no parametric model prior is desired. Gaussian Avatar was introduced as a method to leverage the SMPL model as a prior for reconstructing full-body avatars. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting Gaussian Splatting and applies them to dynamic human reconstruction by conditioning Gaussian parameters on pose. It is closely related to 3DGS-Avatar, which also uses SMPL but combines Gaussians with both nonrigid and rigid transformations. From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting: Theory and Applications, https://doi.org/10.1109/sibgrapi67909.2025.11223276, fetched 2026-10-26 From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://www.visgraf.impa.br/Data/RefBib/PSPDF/tutorial-sib2025/tutorial-sib2025.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 3DGS-Avatar
body: 3DGS-Avatar is a method for reconstructing animatable full-body avatars by combining 3D Gaussians with both non-rigid and rigid transformations derived from an underlying SMPL model. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a per-Gaussian deformation MLP to handle non-rigid deformations, whereas alternatives like GaussianAvatars use pose features to predict parameters via a feed-forward network. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view video captures of a subject in various poses; SMPL-X model parameters (shape, pose, expression) fitted to the input frames. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, covariance, opacity, and color, along with a deformation MLP that maps local coordinates and pose parameters to Gaussian transformations. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i has a base position \mathbf{t}i, a base rotation \mathbf{R}i, a base scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. Deformation MLP: A multi-layer perceptron that takes as input the local coordinates of a Gaussian relative to the SMPL mesh and the current pose parameters, outputting a deformation offset and potentially scale/rotation adjustments. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians on the surface of the SMPL mesh. Each Gaussian is associated with a specific triangle or vertex on the SMPL mesh. 2. Rigid Transformation: Apply the global rigid transformation defined by the SMPL pose to the base position and rotation of each Gaussian. This aligns the avatar with the current body pose. 3. Non-Rigid Deformation: For each Gaussian, compute its local coordinates in the SMPL template space. Pass these coordinates and the current pose parameters through the per-Gaussian deformation MLP. The MLP outputs a non-rigid deformation offset \Delta \mathbf{t} and potentially adjustments to scale and rotation. 4. Final Transformation: The final position of a Gaussian is \mathbf{t}'i = \mathbf{t}{rigid} + \Delta \mathbf{t}. The final rotation and scale are similarly adjusted. 5. Rendering: Render the transformed Gaussians using standard 2D Gaussian splatting techniques. 6. Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian attributes and the deformation MLP parameters using photometric loss between rendered images and ground truth images. Formulas: Let \mathbf{p}i be the base position of Gaussian i on the SMPL template. Let \mathbf{T}{pose} be the rigid transformation matrix for the current pose. Let MLP(\mathbf{p}i, \theta{pose}) be the deformation MLP outputting offset \Delta \mathbf{t}i. Final position: \mathbf{t}'i = \mathbf{T}{pose} \mathbf{p}i + \Delta \mathbf{t}i. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise when combining rigid and non-rigid transformations if not handled carefully. Degenerate input poses (e.g., extreme articulation) may lead to inaccurate deformations if the MLP is not sufficiently expressive. Time Complexity: Training time is significant due to the optimization of the deformation MLP and Gaussian attributes. Rendering time is comparable to standard 3DGS, as the deformation is applied per-Gaussian before splatting. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is higher than standard 3DGS due to the storage of the deformation MLP and additional Gaussian attributes for deformation. Strengths: High-fidelity reconstruction of animatable avatars; handles both rigid and non-rigid deformations. Limitations: Requires SMPL-X model fitting; may struggle with extreme poses or occlusions not covered in training data. When to use: When animatable, high-quality full-body avatars are needed from multi-view video. When not to use: For static scenes or when computational resources for training are limited. 3DGS-Avatar was introduced as a method to reconstruct full-body avatars using 3D Gaussians and SMPL models. It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting and extends it to handle the complexities of human animation. The method is part of a broader family of Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction techniques. Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://www.visgraf.impa.br/Data/RefBib/PSPDF/tutorial-sib2025/tutorial-sib2025.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars
head: GHG, GoHA, GoHA / GHG, Relightable Gaussian head methods using FLAME rig
body: Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars is a method for creating photorealistic, relightable 3D head avatars from monocular video by combining Gaussian Splatting with the FLAME parametric head model. It extends standard Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction by decoupling geometry deformation from appearance, allowing the rendering of the avatar under arbitrary lighting conditions. Unlike sibling methods that primarily focus on animatable geometry (e.g., Gaussian Avatars) or static appearance, this approach explicitly models a relightable BRDF, enabling diverse lighting synthesis while maintaining high-fidelity facial expressions driven by the FLAME rig. Inputs: Monocular video of a talking head (typically ~30 seconds). FLAME mesh parameters (pose, expression, shape) fitted to the video frames. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the head. Per-Gaussian attributes: position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics (or base color), and BRDF parameters. A relightable appearance model allowing arbitrary light source insertion. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: Each Gaussian i is defined by: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (parameterized as rotation Ri and scale Si). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. ci: Color/Appearance. In relightable variants, this is decomposed into base albedo and BRDF coefficients (e.g., diffuse/specular weights) rather than fixed spherical harmonics, or SHs are used for view-dependent effects while a separate lighting model handles illumination. pi \in \mathbb{R}^k: Pose/expression condition vector mapping to deformation offsets. Steps: 1. Initialization: Fit a FLAME mesh to the input video using a regression network (e.g., MICA or DECA) to obtain per-frame pose and expression parameters. Initialize one Gaussian per triangle of the FLAME mesh in tangent space. 2. Deformation Model: Train a per-Gaussian deformation MLP or use explicit pose-conditioned offsets to map the canonical Gaussian positions to the deformed space based on FLAME pose/expression parameters. This ensures the avatar is head-driven and riggable. 3. Appearance Training: Optimize Gaussian attributes (opacity, scale, rotation, color/BRDF) using differentiable rasterization of Gaussians. The loss function includes photometric reconstruction loss against input frames. 4. Relighting: If explicit relighting is required, freeze geometry and train a relightable BRDF component (e.g., separating albedo from lighting) or optimize spherical harmonics under varying synthetic lighting conditions. This allows the avatar to be rendered under novel light sources. 5. Compression: Compress the resulting model to \le 30 MB for efficient deployment. Formulas: Deformation: \mui^{deformed} = \mui^{canonical} + \Delta \mui(P, E), where P is pose and E is expression. Rendering: Standard alpha-blending of Gaussians projected to 2D. Lighting: C{rendered} = f{BRDF}(N, V, L, \text{albedo}, \text{roughness}, \dots). Parameters: Number of Gaussians: Typically one per FLAME triangle (thousands to tens of thousands). Compression target: \le 30 MB. Edge Cases: Sparse views: 3DGS can struggle with novel view synthesis from sparse sets, potentially trapping optimization in local minima. Occlusions: Monocular input limits visibility of the back of the head; relighting may reveal inconsistencies if the back is not captured. Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to 3DGS but requires additional optimization for deformation and BRDF parameters. Inference is fast, similar to Gaussian Splatting. Memory Complexity: High due to per-Gaussian attributes and deformation networks. Compression is critical to reach \le 30 MB. Strengths: High-fidelity facial animation; explicit relighting capability; efficient rendering. Limitations: Requires accurate FLAME fitting; monocular input limits geometric completeness; potential artifacts under extreme lighting if BRDF is not well-regularized. When to use: Applications requiring interactive, relightable head avatars from limited video input (e.g., telepresence, virtual try-on). When not to use: Full-body avatars (use Gaussian Avatar or 3DGS-Avatar); scenes with complex dynamic lighting interactions beyond head-level BRDFs. Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars (also referred to as GHG or GoHA) builds on the Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction framework. It was introduced to address the limitations of previous methods that lacked explicit relighting capabilities or relied on more complex rigs like SMPL-X. The method leverages the FLAME head model for rigging and uses techniques from photorealistic head reconstruction (e.g., PSAvatar) to enable relighting. It is part of a broader trend in Gaussian Splatting variants for avatar creation, following works like Gaussian Avatars and 3DGS-Avatar. name: Projective Splat Rasterization with Depth Optimization
head: Adjoint Matrix Splat Rasterization, Inverse Projective Mapping for Splatting
body: A rasterization technique for point-based rendering that uses the inverse of a projective mapping matrix to transform screen coordinates back to object space for kernel evaluation, while simultaneously computing window-space depth values via linear interpolation of homogeneous coordinates. It sets itself apart from standard perspective splatting by avoiding explicit matrix inversion through the use of adjoint matrices and optimizing depth computation by embedding the window-space depth formula directly into the homogeneous interpolation weights. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Splat center \mathbf{p}k, tangent vectors \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k in screen space, view frustum near/far constants a, b, and screen coordinates (x, y) of the fragment. Output: Object-space coordinates (u, v) for kernel evaluation and window-space depth d(x) for z-buffering. Data Structures: \mathbf{M}k: A 3 \times 3 matrix representing the forward projective mapping from parameter space (u, v) to screen space. \mathbf{N}k: A 4 \times 3 matrix (or 3 \times 3 without depth optimization) representing the scaled inverse mapping. Steps: 1. Compute Forward Mapping Matrix \mathbf{M}k: Construct the matrix from the splat's screen-space center and tangent vectors: \mathbf{M}k = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{s}k & \mathbf{t}k & \mathbf{p}k \end{bmatrix} where \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k, \mathbf{p}k are 3D vectors (typically 2D with z=1 or homogeneous 3D vectors depending on implementation, but the source defines them as components of the 3 \times 3 matrix acting on \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}). The forward mapping is: \begin{bmatrix} xz \\ yz \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{M}k \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} 2. Compute Adjoint Matrix: Calculate the adjoint of \mathbf{M}k using three cross products. This avoids the computational cost of explicit matrix inversion: \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}k \times \mathbf{p}k \\ \mathbf{p}k \times \mathbf{s}k \\ \mathbf{s}k \times \mathbf{t}k \end{bmatrix} Let \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 denote the third row of this matrix. 3. Compute Scaling Factor: Calculate the scalar \alpha to normalize the homogeneous coefficient w such that it relates to the view-space depth pz (the z-component of \mathbf{p}k) and the window-space depth constant b: \alpha = \frac{b}{\text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 \cdot \mathbf{p}k} Note: \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 \cdot \mathbf{p}k is the dot product of the third row of the adjoint matrix and the center vector \mathbf{p}k. 4. Construct Inverse Mapping Matrix \mathbf{N}k: Scale the adjoint matrix by \alpha. To optimize depth computation, extend \mathbf{N}k to a 4 \times 3 matrix. The first three rows are \alpha \cdot \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k). The fourth row (\mathbf{N}k)4 is computed as: (\mathbf{N}k)4 = \alpha \cdot \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ a \end{bmatrix} This construction ensures that the homogeneous weight w in the inverse mapping equals b/z, allowing the fourth component to directly yield the window-space depth d(x) = a + b/z via linear interpolation. 5. Rasterize and Interpolate: Rasterize the splat's bounding box (or projected triangle). For each pixel (x, y), compute the homogeneous coordinates by multiplying the inverse matrix \mathbf{N}k with the screen coordinate vector \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}: \begin{bmatrix} uw \\ vw \\ w \\ d \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{N}k \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} The values uw, vw, w are linearly interpolated across the primitive. The object-space coordinates are recovered by perspective division: u = \frac{uw}{w}, \quad v = \frac{vw}{w} The window-space depth is directly available as the fourth component d (if the 4 \times 3 matrix is used) or computed as a + b/(w/b) = a + b/z if only the 3 \times 3 matrix is used. 6. Kernel Evaluation: Use the recovered (u, v) to evaluate the splat's reconstruction kernel. Parameters: a, b: Constants derived from the near and far planes of the view frustum, mapping 1/z to the window space depth range [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Matrix Inversion Cost: Explicitly inverting \mathbf{M}k is computationally expensive. The method avoids this by using the adjoint matrix, which is equivalent for projective mappings up to a scalar multiple and requires only cross products. Degenerate Splats: If \mathbf{p}k, \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k are collinear or \mathbf{p}k is at the origin, the adjoint matrix may be singular or the scaling factor undefined. In practice, check for zero determinant or small scaling factors and skip rasterization or fall back to a safe default. Precision: Linear interpolation of homogeneous coordinates is valid for projective mappings. However, ensure that w does not become zero or negative (behind the camera) during interpolation, which would cause division by zero or incorrect depth ordering. Clip fragments where w \le 0. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat for matrix construction, O(N) for rasterizing N pixels within the splat's bounding box. The use of adjoint matrices and pre-scaled homogeneous weights minimizes per-pixel arithmetic cost. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per splat for storing \mathbf{M}k and \mathbf{N}k. Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to native support for cross products and 4-component vector instructions. The optimization of embedding depth computation into the homogeneous weights reduces per-pixel operations to a single addition and interpolation. Strengths: Perspective accurate, avoids expensive matrix inversion, integrates seamlessly with standard z-buffering via window-space depth interpolation. Limitations: Requires careful handling of homogeneous weights to avoid division by zero. Performance may degrade if splats are very large or numerous, requiring efficient culling. Originated in the context of point-based rendering, specifically for perspective-accurate splatting. The method is described in "Splat/Mesh Blending, Perspective Rasterization and Transparency for Point-Based Rendering". It addresses the need for efficient, perspective-correct rasterization of splats without the overhead of full 3D-to-2D projection inversion per pixel. name: CPU-Based Splat Sorting
head: Splat Sort, WebWorker Splat Sort
body: CPU-Based Splat Sorting is a method for ordering 3D Gaussian splats for correct front-to-back alpha blending by performing the sort operation on the CPU, often asynchronously in a background thread. It solves the problem of rendering order dependency in transparent splatting without incurring the high latency and complexity of GPU-based sorting algorithms like bitonic sort. It differs from GPU sorting by offloading the O(N \log N) comparison work to the CPU, allowing the GPU to focus exclusively on rendering, and from depth-based sorting variants by relying on a simple depth projection rather than complex opacity-weighted keys. The method computes a depth value for each splat, sorts the splats by this depth, and outputs a permutation index buffer for the GPU to read. Inputs: viewProj: A 4 \times 4 view-projection matrix. positions: An array of N 3D positions (interleaved x, y, z floats). vertexCount: The number of splats N. Outputs: depthIndex: A vector of N unsigned integers representing the original indices of the splats, sorted from front (smallest depth) to back (largest depth). Data Structures: SplatSortEntry: A struct or pair containing: depth: A float representing the projected depth. originalindex: A uint32t representing the index in the original positions array. Steps: 1. Project Depth: For each splat i from 0 to N-1: Retrieve the 3D position Pi = (xi, yi, zi) from positions. Compute the homogeneous clip-space position: V = \text{viewProj} \times \begin{bmatrix} xi \\ yi \\ zi \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Extract the depth: di = \frac{Vz}{Vw} Store the pair (di, i) in a temporary list. 2. Sort: Sort the list of pairs based on di in ascending order (smallest di first). 3. Extract Indices: Create the output depthIndex vector by extracting the originalindex from each pair in the sorted list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cpusplatsort(viewprojmatrix, positions, vertexcount): """ Sorts splats by depth on the CPU. Args: viewprojmatrix: 4x4 matrix (list of lists or array) positions: List of tuples (x, y, z) vertexcount: Integer N Returns: sortedindices: List of integers """ # Step 1: Compute depth for each splat splatdata = [] for i in range(vertexcount): x, y, z = positions[i] # Homogeneous transformation # Assuming row-major matrix multiplication: V = M P # P is column vector [x, y, z, 1] wx = viewprojmatrix[0][0]x + viewprojmatrix[1][0]y + viewprojmatrix[2][0]z + viewprojmatrix[3][0] wy = viewprojmatrix[0][1]x + viewprojmatrix[1][1]y + viewprojmatrix[2][1]z + viewprojmatrix[3][1] wz = viewprojmatrix[0][2]x + viewprojmatrix[1][2]y + viewprojmatrix[2][2]z + viewprojmatrix[3][2] ww = viewprojmatrix[0][3]x + viewprojmatrix[1][3]y + viewprojmatrix[2][3]z + viewprojmatrix[3][3] # Perspective divide depth = wz / ww splatdata.append((depth, i)) # Step 2: Sort by depth (ascending) # Using a stable sort is not strictly required but often preferred for consistency splatdata.sort(key=lambda item: item[0]) # Step 3: Extract indices sortedindices = [item[1] for item in splatdata] return sortedindices Parameters: Typical implementation runs asynchronously in a WebWorker. No specific kernel parameters are required as it relies on standard projection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rapid Camera Movement: If the camera jumps between opposite sides of the scene, the Z-order may not update fast enough relative to the render loop, causing momentary transparency artifacts. Precision: Standard float precision is used for depth calculation. Performance: Sorting ~1M splats takes approximately 150ms on a typical CPU. Calculates a scalar key combining projected size and opacity to prioritize important splats, differing from simple depth sorting by ignoring camera distance in favor of visual contribution. A specific implementation variant that uses a shader-readable structured buffer instead of GPU UAVs, chosen when GPU compute capabilities are insufficient or to avoid bitonic sort overhead. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for comparison-based sorting (e.g., Quicksort/Mergesort). Measured Performance: Sorting ~1M splats takes ~150ms, resulting in a sort rate of approximately 4fps, while the main render runs at 60fps. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the depth-index pairs and the output index buffer. Strengths: Allows the GPU to focus entirely on rendering, avoiding the latency overhead of GPU sorting algorithms like bitonic sort which require many iterations. Limitations: The CPU sort is significantly slower than the GPU render loop (4fps vs 60fps), leading to potential visual artifacts during rapid camera transitions. When to use: When GPU sorting is unavailable, too complex to implement, or when the CPU is underutilized and can handle the asynchronous sort without blocking the render thread. The method was popularized in the context of web-based 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations, where file size reduction and browser compatibility are critical. It was adopted as a fallback or primary strategy when GPU-based sorting (like bitonic sort) was deemed too heavy or when simpler transparency methods like stochastic transparency or weighted blended order-independent transparency failed to produce satisfactory results. antimatter15/splat, https://github.com/antimatter15/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Splat Sorting Key Calculation
head: Importance Sorting, Splat ordering metric, Splat sort key
body: This method calculates a scalar key for each 3D Gaussian splat to determine the rendering order, typically for front-to-back alpha blending. It combines the splat's projected size and opacity to prioritize "important" splats (large and opaque) to be drawn first, ensuring correct accumulation of color and alpha. It differs from depth-based sorting by ignoring camera distance in favor of visual contribution, which is more robust for Gaussian splats where size varies significantly per splat. Inputs: A list of N splats. For each splat i: Scale components: s{0,i}, s{1,i}, s{2,i} (log-space scales). Opacity: \alphai (logit-space opacity). Position and rotation are not used in the key calculation itself but are required for subsequent rendering steps. Outputs: An array of indices sortedindices of length N, such that splats are ordered from highest key to lowest key. Data Structures: sizeList: Float32Array of length N. Stores the calculated key for each splat. sizeIndex: Uint32Array of length N. Stores the original index of each splat. Formula: The key Ki for splat i is defined as: Ki = \frac{\exp(s{0,i} + s{1,i} + s{2,i})}{1 + \exp(-\alphai)} Where: \exp(s{0,i} + s{1,i} + s{2,i}) represents the volume or area metric derived from the log-scales. 1 + \exp(-\alphai) is the sigmoid denominator, converting logit opacity to probability space. Steps: 1. Initialize sizeList as a Float32Array of length N and sizeIndex as a Uint32Array of length N. 2. For each splat index i from 0 to N-1: a. Read s{0,i}, s{1,i}, s{2,i} and \alphai. b. Calculate the numerator: Vi = \exp(s{0,i} + s{1,i} + s{2,i}). c. Calculate the denominator: Oi = 1 + \exp(-\alphai). d. Compute key: Ki = Vi / Oi. e. Set sizeList[i] = Ki. f. Set sizeIndex[i] = i. 3. Sort sizeIndex in descending order based on the values in sizeList. Specifically, if Ka > Kb, then index a should precede index b in the sorted array. 4. Return sizeIndex. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatesplatsortkey(splats): """ splats: list of dicts or objects with keys 'scale0', 'scale1', 'scale2', 'opacity' Returns: list of indices sorted by importance (descending) """ import math import numpy as np n = len(splats) if n == 0: return [] # Arrays to store keys and original indices sizelist = [0.0] n sizeindex = list(range(n)) for i in range(n): s0 = splats[i]['scale0'] s1 = splats[i]['scale1'] s2 = splats[i]['scale2'] alpha = splats[i]['opacity'] # Calculate volume metric from log-scales # Note: exp(s0 + s1 + s2) is equivalent to exp(s0)exp(s1)exp(s2) volume = math.exp(s0 + s1 + s2) # Calculate opacity from logit # sigmoid(alpha) = 1 / (1 + exp(-alpha)) opacity = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-alpha)) # Key is volume opacity key = volume opacity sizelist[i] = key # Sort indices based on sizelist in descending order # Using a stable sort is not strictly required but good practice sizeindex.sort(key=lambda idx: sizelist[idx], reverse=True) return sizeindex Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Scales: If scale components are missing, the key defaults to 0 or a minimal value. Precision: Using exp() on large scale values can cause overflow. In practice, scales are usually small, but clamping or using log-sum-exp tricks may be necessary for extreme cases. Degenerate Input: If all splats have identical keys, the sort order is arbitrary. This is acceptable as long as the rendering is consistent. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) due to the sorting step. The key calculation is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing sizeList and sizeIndex. Performance: Sorting on the CPU (e.g., in a WebWorker) offloads the GPU, allowing it to focus on rendering. This avoids the overhead of GPU sorting algorithms like bitonic sort, which require many iterations and memory transfers. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for front-to-back blending, allows progressive loading by sorting only loaded splats. Limitations: Does not account for view-dependent effects like spherical harmonics in the key calculation. The key is static per splat and does not update with camera movement, so it is most effective when the camera is relatively stable or when splats are sorted per frame if performance allows. This method is used in 3D Gaussian Splatting renderers, particularly in web-based implementations where CPU-based sorting is preferred for simplicity and compatibility. It was popularized by the antimatter15/splat project, which demonstrated efficient web-based Gaussian Splatting rendering. The approach prioritizes visual importance over geometric depth, which is crucial for Gaussian splats where the "size" of a splat can vary dramatically. antimatter15/splat, https://github.com/antimatter15/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, https://github.com/akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: CPU Fallback Sort Path
head: CPU-only cutout path, Portable CPU-sort path
body: The CPU Fallback Sort Path provides a CPU-side sorting and rendering fallback for Gaussian splatting when GPU compute sorting is disabled or unavailable. It differs from GPU-based approaches by utilizing a shader-readable structured buffer instead of append/unordered access view (UAV) buffers, allowing the CPU to manage the sorting pipeline while the GPU focuses on rendering. This method is chosen when GPU compute capabilities are insufficient or when avoiding the overhead of GPU sorting algorithms like bitonic sort is necessary. Inputs: GsplatSorter.Instance.CpuFallbackEnabled: A boolean flag determining the active path. Splat data (centroids, colors, opacities, scales) to be sorted. Outputs: OrderBuffer: A GraphicsBuffer containing the sorted order of splats, readable by shaders. OrderSizeBuffer: (Optional) An indirect argument buffer storing the number of sorted splats. BoundsBuffer: (Optional) A structured buffer storing bounding box information. Data Structures: 1. OrderBuffer: Type: GraphicsBuffer.Target.Structured (if CPU fallback enabled) or GraphicsBuffer.Target.Append (if disabled). Content: Indices or identifiers of splats in sorted order. 2. OrderSizeBuffer: Type: GraphicsBuffer.Target.IndirectArguments. Size: 1 element. Content: The count of splats to be rendered/sorted. 3. BoundsBuffer: Type: GraphicsBuffer.Target.Structured. Size: 6 elements (likely representing min/max coordinates for bounding volumes). Content: Bounding box data for the splats. Steps: 1. Check the value of GsplatSorter.Instance.CpuFallbackEnabled. 2. If CpuFallbackEnabled is true: a. Create OrderBuffer as GraphicsBuffer.Target.Structured. b. Proceed with CPU-side sorting logic (details delegated to specific sorting algorithms like Radix Sort). 3. If CpuFallbackEnabled is false: a. Create OrderBuffer as GraphicsBuffer.Target.Append. b. Allocate OrderSizeBuffer as GraphicsBuffer.Target.IndirectArguments with size 1. c. Allocate BoundsBuffer as GraphicsBuffer.Target.Structured with size 6. d. Proceed with the non-fallback (likely GPU-based) sorting path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupsortbuffer(cpufallbackenabled): """ Sets up the graphics buffers for splat sorting based on the fallback flag. """ # Step 1: Check flag isfallback = cpufallbackenabled # Step 2 & 3: Create OrderBuffer based on flag if isfallback: # CPU fallback enabled: use Structured buffer for shader readability orderbuffer = creategraphicsbuffer(target=GraphicsBuffer.Target.Structured) else: # CPU fallback disabled: use Append buffer orderbuffer = creategraphicsbuffer(target=GraphicsBuffer.Target.Append) # Step 4: Allocate additional buffers for non-fallback path ordersizebuffer = creategraphicsbuffer( target=GraphicsBuffer.Target.IndirectArguments, size=1) boundsbuffer = creategraphicsbuffer( target=GraphicsBuffer.Target.Structured, size=6) return orderbuffer, ordersizebuffer, boundsbuffer Parameters: CpuFallbackEnabled: Boolean flag. True activates the CPU fallback path using structured buffers; False uses append buffers and allocates size/bounds buffers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The size of BoundsBuffer is fixed at 6 elements. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. It is chosen over general-purpose sorts (quicksort, heapsort) or re-sorting-optimized algorithms (mergesort) because viewing direction changes significantly alter centroid ordering, making the overhead of adaptive sorts inefficient compared to the raw speed of radix sort. Strengths: Avoids GPU sorting overhead; allows GPU to focus on rendering; portable to systems without GPU compute support. Limitations: Relies on CPU performance for sorting; may become a bottleneck for large numbers of splats if the CPU is slow. When to use: When GPU compute sorting is unavailable or disabled; when CPU resources are sufficient for the sorting load. When not to use: When high performance is required for large-scale splatting and GPU compute is available.
