name: Multi-Texture Performance Enhancement
head: Multi-Texture Speedup, Multi-Texture Optimization
body: Multi-Texture Performance Enhancement is a technique to accelerate 2D texture-based volume rendering by reducing the number of draw calls and frame buffer reads. It achieves this by mapping the texture images of n consecutive volume slices onto a single polygon using n independent multi-texture units, combining them in one clock cycle. Unlike standard multi-texturing which may apply textures sequentially or without specific blending logic for transparency, this method explicitly compensates for perspective displacement to maintain visual correctness while theoretically reducing rendering time and frame buffer access by a factor of 1/n. It builds on Multi-Texture Interpolation by addressing the performance bottleneck of fixed slice counts, but differs from Multi-Texture Pipeline Rendering by focusing on simultaneous combination on a single geometry rather than pipelined stages. Inputs and Outputs: Input: n texture images representing consecutive volume slices (where n is the number of available independent multi-texture units); camera position \tilde{c}; slice spacing d; base polygon width w and height h. Output: A single rendered polygon with fragments containing the combined color and alpha of n slices, blended into the frame buffer. Data Structures: Polygon: A single quad with modified dimensions to accommodate perspective displacement. Width: W = w + 2 \cdot d \cdot (n-1) Height: H = h + 2 \cdot d \cdot (n-1) Textures: n textures, each containing one slice image. Border: Initialized to zero values to handle out-of-bounds coordinates. Texture Coordinates: 2D coordinates (s, t) for each texture unit, calculated per vertex. Steps: 1. Polygon Scaling: Increase the width w and height h of the slice polygon by 2 \cdot d \cdot (n-1) to create a bounding area that covers the maximum possible perspective displacement of the n slices. 2. Texture Coordinate Calculation: For each texture unit k (representing slice i+k), calculate the texture coordinates for the four vertices of the polygon. Identify the corner \tilde{b} of the slice image that corresponds to the polygon vertex. Calculate the view vector \tilde{v} = (vx, vy, vz)^T = \tilde{c} - \tilde{b}, where \tilde{c} is the camera position. Calculate the projected width w' and height h' of the slice at the polygon's depth. Compute the displacement in s and t directions: \Delta s = d \frac{vx}{vz} \Delta t = d \frac{vy}{vz} The texture coordinates (s, t) at the vertex are given by: s = \frac{w'}{W} \left( 1 + \frac{h'}{d} + \frac{h' vy}{d vz} \right) t = \frac{h'}{H} \left( 1 + \frac{w'}{d} + \frac{w' vx}{d vz} \right) (Note: The source formula (2) is garbled, but the description implies adjusting coordinates based on projected dimensions and view vector components to account for perspective shift.) 3. Hardware Combination: Configure the multi-texture hardware combiners to combine the n textures in a single clock cycle. The specific combiner setup depends on the desired blending behavior (see Multi-Texture Correct Blending for the correct alpha blending setup). 4. Rendering: Draw the single polygon. The hardware samples the n textures, combines them, and blends the resulting fragment into the frame buffer. 5. Edge Handling: Ensure that texture coordinates outside the range [0, 1] result in zero texel values. Since hardware-specific extensions like SGIStextureedgeclamp may not be supported, use standard OpenGL clamping and initialize the texture borders with zero values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermultitextureslices(camerapos, slicespacing, basewidth, baseheight, numslices, textures): """ Renders n slices onto a single polygon using multi-texturing. Args: camerapos: (cx, cy, cz) tuple, camera position in world space. slicespacing: float, distance between slices (d). basewidth: float, original width of a slice polygon (w). baseheight: float, original height of a slice polygon (h). numslices: int, number of slices to combine (n). textures: list of n texture objects, each containing slice data and border. Returns: None (renders directly to frame buffer). """ # Step 1: Scale polygon dimensions # Increase width and height by 2 d (n-1) to cover perspective displacement polygonwidth = basewidth + 2 slicespacing (numslices - 1) polygonheight = baseheight + 2 slicespacing (numslices - 1) # Define the four vertices of the scaled polygon in world space # Assuming the polygon is centered at origin for simplicity, # actual positions depend on the specific volume rendering setup. # Let's assume the polygon lies in a plane perpendicular to the view direction. # For simplicity, we define vertices relative to the polygon center. # In practice, these vertices are transformed by the model-view matrix. verticesworld = [ (-polygonwidth/2, -polygonheight/2, 0), (polygonwidth/2, -polygonheight/2, 0), (polygonwidth/2, polygonheight/2, 0), (-polygonwidth/2, polygonheight/2, 0) ] # Step 2: Calculate texture coordinates for each texture unit # Note: The exact mapping of slice index to texture unit and vertex corner # depends on the specific implementation. The source describes adjusting # coordinates based on the view vector to the corner of the slice. texturecoords = [] # List of n arrays, each containing 4 (s, t) pairs for k in range(numslices): # Assume slice k is mapped to texture unit k # The source describes calculating coordinates for the slice in the same plane # and adjusting for subsequent slices. # For a single polygon, all textures are sampled at the same vertex positions. # The texture coordinates must be adjusted so that the correct part of the # texture image is sampled at each vertex, accounting for perspective. coordsfortexture = [] for vertex in verticesworld: # Vertex is in world space. The source provides a formula, # but implementing it requires precise knowledge of the geometry. # We will use a placeholder value. s = 0.5 t = 0.5 coordsfortexture.append((s, t)) texturecoords.append(coordsfortexture) # Step 3: Configure multi-texture hardware # This step is hardware-specific. The source mentions using n independent # multi-texture units. # The combiner setup should be configured to combine the textures correctly. # See Multi-Texture Correct Blending for details. # Step 4: Render the polygon # Bind the textures to the multi-texture units. # Set the texture coordinates for each unit. # Draw the polygon. # Step 5: Handle edge cases # Ensure texture borders are zero. # Use standard OpenGL clamping. Parameters: n: Number of multi-texture units. Typical values depend on hardware (e.g., 2, 4). Not given in the sources. d: Slice spacing. Not given in the sources. w, h: Base polygon dimensions. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Coordinates > 1: Perspective displacement can cause texture coordinates to exceed [0, 1]. Texel values outside this range must be zero. Clamping: Hardware-specific extensions like SGIStextureedgeclamp may not be supported (e.g., on GeForce 256). Use standard OpenGL clamping and initialize texture borders with zero values. Perspective Displacement: If not compensated, slices will appear shifted. The polygon width and height must be increased by 2 \cdot d \cdot (n-1). Uses register combiners to combine n texture images on a single polygon such that the resulting fragment blends into the frame buffer with the exact same result as rendering n separate polygons with single textures. It solves the problem of incorrect alpha blending when multiple volume slices are rendered simultaneously on a single geometry, ensuring mathematical equivalence to the standard back-to-front polygon rendering order. It sets itself apart from standard multi-texturing by explicitly computing the composite alpha term (1 - A{t0})(1 - A{t1}) to preserve the correct transparency accumulation, whereas standard multi-texturing often fails to account for the multiplicative nature of alpha subtraction in sequential blending. Choose this when correct alpha blending is required for transparency. Time Complexity: Theoretically reduces rendering time by a factor of 1/n compared to rendering n separate polygons, assuming the combination of n texture images can be computed in one clock cycle. Memory Complexity: Reduces frame buffer reads for back-to-front alpha blending by a factor of 1/n. Performance: The actual speedup depends on the hardware's ability to combine n textures in one clock cycle. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant reduction in draw calls and frame buffer accesses. Limitations: Requires n independent multi-texture units. Perspective displacement compensation adds complexity. Clamping limitations on some hardware. When to Use: When n multi-texture units are available and performance is critical. When Not to Use: When correct alpha blending is required and the hardware does not support the necessary combiner setup (use Multi-Texture Correct Blending instead). This technique was described in the context of interactive volume rendering on standard PC graphics hardware, specifically addressing the limitations of early 2D texture-based rendering methods. It was developed to leverage the multi-texturing capabilities of graphics hardware (such as the GeForce 256) to improve performance. name: Multi-Texture Correct Blending
body: Multi-Texture Correct Blending is a technique that uses register combiners to combine n texture images on a single polygon such that the resulting fragment blends into the frame buffer with the exact same result as rendering n separate polygons with single textures. It solves the problem of incorrect alpha blending when multiple volume slices are rendered simultaneously on a single geometry, ensuring mathematical equivalence to the standard back-to-front polygon rendering order. It sets itself apart from standard multi-texturing by explicitly computing the composite alpha term (1 - A{t0})(1 - A{t1}) to preserve the correct transparency accumulation, whereas standard multi-texturing often fails to account for the multiplicative nature of alpha subtraction in sequential blending. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two texture images (Texture 0 and Texture 1), each providing RGB color values (C{t0}, C{t1}) and Alpha values (A{t0}, A{t1}). The current frame buffer color (Cd). Outputs: A single fragment with final color Cs and final alpha As, which is then blended into the frame buffer. Data Structures and Layout: The method relies on the OpenGL Register Combiner architecture (specifically NVregistercombiner or similar extensions). It utilizes two combiner stages: 1. General Combiner 0: RGB Portion: Calculates the intermediate terms C{t0} A{t0} and C{t1} A{t1}. Alpha Portion: Calculates the term (1 - A{t0})(1 - A{t1}). 2. Final Combiner: Takes the RGB output from Combiner 0 and the Alpha output from Combiner 0. Computes the final color Cs and passes the alpha As directly. Numbered Steps: 1. Setup Blending Function: Configure the OpenGL blending function to glBlendFunc(GLONE, GLSRCALPHA). This ensures the fragment color is added to the destination buffer weighted by its alpha, and the destination buffer is weighted by (1 - As). 2. Configure Combiner 0 RGB: Program the RGB portion of General Combiner 0 to compute the products of texture color and alpha for both textures. Specifically, it calculates C{t0} A{t0} and C{t1} A{t1}. 3. Configure Combiner 0 Alpha: Program the Alpha portion of General Combiner 0 to compute the product of the inverted alphas: (1 - A{t0})(1 - A{t1}). 4. Configure Final Combiner RGB: Route the RGB outputs from Combiner 0 to the Final Combiner. Program it to calculate the final color Cs using the formula: Cs = C{t0} A{t0} (1 - A{t1}) + C{t1} A{t1} This effectively combines the contribution of the first texture (modulated by the transparency of the second) and the second texture. 5. Configure Final Combiner Alpha: Route the Alpha output from Combiner 0 directly to the output register of the Final Combiner, setting the fragment alpha to: As = (1 - A{t0}) (1 - A{t1}) 6. Render: Draw the single polygon with both textures bound. The hardware executes the combiner operations, producing the fragment (Cs, As). 7. Blend: The fragment is blended into the frame buffer using the setup blending function: C{d00} = Cs \cdot 1 + Cd \cdot As Substituting the values: C{d00} = C{t1} A{t1} + C{t0} A{t0} (1 - A{t1}) + Cd (1 - A{t0}) (1 - A{t1}) This matches the result of rendering two separate polygons back-to-front. Formulas: Standard Sequential Blending (Reference): Blending first polygon: C{d0} = C{t0} A{t0} + Cd (1 - A{t0}). Blending second polygon: C{d00} = C{t1} A{t1} + C{d0} (1 - A{t1}). Expanded: C{d00} = C{t1} A{t1} + C{t0} A{t0} (1 - A{t1}) + Cd (1 - A{t0}) (1 - A{t1}). Multi-Texture Correct Blending Output: Final Color: Cs = C{t0} A{t0} (1 - A{t1}) + C{t1} A{t1}. Final Alpha: As = (1 - A{t0}) (1 - A{t1}). Parameters: Blending Function: GLONE for source, GLSRCALPHA for destination. Texture Environment: GLREPLACE is assumed for the base texture sampling before combiner processing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The calculation involves multiple multiplications and additions. Fixed-point hardware or limited precision in register combiners may introduce artifacts, particularly when alpha values are very small or very close to 1. Number of Textures: The provided source details the setup for two textures (n=2). Extending this to n > 2 requires additional combiner stages to compute the product (1 - A{t0})(1 - A{t1})...(1 - A{t(n-1)}) and the weighted sum of colors. The source does not provide the specific layout for n > 2. Hardware Support: This method requires support for the Register Combiner extension (e.g., GLNVregistercombiners). It is not available on modern programmable shader pipelines without emulation or equivalent logic in fragment shaders. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Constant time per fragment for the combiner operations, independent of the number of slices if n is fixed and small. However, the complexity of the combiner setup grows with n. Memory: Requires storage for the combiner state and the texture images. No additional frame buffer memory is used compared to standard rendering. Measured Performance: The source does not provide specific performance metrics (FPS, memory usage) for this specific technique. Scaling: Scaling to more than two textures requires additional combiner stages. The source only describes the two-texture case. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides mathematically exact equivalence to sequential polygon rendering, avoiding the visual artifacts of standard multi-texturing alpha blending. Limitations: Limited to the number of available combiner stages and texture units. Requires specific hardware extensions (Register Combiners) that are obsolete in modern graphics APIs. When to Use: Use when exact alpha blending equivalence is required and the hardware supports Register Combiners. Not suitable for modern GPU architectures without shader-based equivalents. Origin: The technique was introduced in the context of interactive volume rendering on standard PC graphics hardware, specifically to leverage rasterization hardware for efficient volume visualization. History and Development: It was presented in the paper "Interactive Volume Rendering on Standard PC Graphics Hardware". The method exploits the capabilities of the OpenGL Register Combiner extension to perform complex blending operations in hardware, avoiding the need for multiple draw calls and depth sorting for every slice. Where it is used: It is used in volume rendering applications that require high-quality alpha blending on older hardware supporting the Register Combiner extension. name: Multi-Texture Pipeline Rendering
head: 2D Multi-Texture, 2D-Multi-Texture Based Methods, Multi-Texture Volume Rendering
body: Multi-Texture Pipeline Rendering is a method that supplements 2D-texture based volume rendering by using multiple 2D texture units in a pipeline to enhance accuracy and image quality while preserving efficient memory management. It addresses the limitations of single-texture approaches by allowing separate updates for different components (e.g., color, light map, fog map) at different resolutions, whereas single texture maps all components together. It builds on Multi-Texture Interpolation by utilizing the hardware's ability to chain texture operations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of 2D texture slices representing the volume data, and an incoming fragment color C{in}. Output: The final fragment color C{out}. Data Structures: The method relies on the hardware's multi-texture unit architecture. Each texture unit i holds a texture sample T^{(i)}{in}. The units are arranged in a strict sequence (pipeline). Steps: 1. Initialize the fragment color C{in} (typically from the vertex shader or previous pipeline stage). 2. For each texture unit i from 0 to n-1 in the pipeline: a. Sample the texture T^{(i)} at the current coordinate. b. Multiply the current color by the sampled texture value. 3. The final result is the output of the last unit. Formulas: The single texture application is defined as: C{out} = C{in} \times T{in} where C{in} is the incoming fragment color, C{out} is the output color, and T{in} is the interpolated texture sample color. This is calculated component-wise for each color channel. The multi-texture pipeline application, connecting n units in series, is defined as: C{out} = T^{(n-1)}{in} \times (T^{(n-2)}{in} \times (\dots \times (T^{(0)}{in} \times C{in}))) where T^{(i)}{in} is the texture sample from unit i. The input for each individual texturing unit is determined by the output value of the previous unit. Parameters: n: The number of texture units in the pipeline. Not given in the sources. Resolution of textures: Can vary per unit (e.g., high resolution for color, low for fog). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The strict pipeline provided by the OpenGL specification is limiting for effects requiring more flexible texture combination (e.g., per-pixel illumination, normal maps). Precision issues may arise from multiple multiplications, though not explicitly detailed in sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multitexturepipelinerendering(Cin, texturesamples): """ Cin: vec3 or vec4, incoming fragment color texturesamples: list of vec3 or vec4, samples from texture units 0 to n-1 Returns: vec3 or vec4, final color """ currentcolor = Cin # Iterate through texture units in strict pipeline order for i in range(len(texturesamples)): Tin = texturesamples[i] # Component-wise multiplication currentcolor = currentcolor Tin return currentcolor A hardware-accelerated Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) algorithm based on register combiners and multitexturing. It proposes a viewing-direction-based dynamic texture slice resampling scheme. The slicing steps are dynamically updated according to viewing directions, maintaining a constant step size during the DVR process to avoid striping artifacts caused by nonuniform sampling step while maintaining high-rendering performance. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Lower memory requirements compared to 3D-texture approaches by removing the necessity to duplicate the volume data in memory. Performance: Maintains high-rendering performance. Strengths: Enhances accuracy and image quality of 2D-texture based rendering; allows separate updates for different components at different resolutions; avoids striping artifacts in DVR variants. Limitations: The strict pipeline is too limiting for many desired texturing effects like per-pixel illumination or normal maps, which require programmable rasterization (pixel shaders). When to use: When 3D-texture hardware is not available or restricted, and higher accuracy than fixed-slice 2D rendering is needed. When not to use: When complex per-pixel lighting or normal mapping is required, as the strict pipeline lacks flexibility. The approach was developed as an alternative to 3D-texture based rendering, which was restricted to a very limited number of hardware implementations on the consumer market at the time. It leverages flexible rasterization and texturing units with a high degree of programmability available on numerous graphics boards. The concept of connecting texture units in series is a standard feature in OpenGL. The DVR variant was developed by Zhang and colleagues. name: GPU-based Cut-off Slice Generation
head: Rezk-Salama method, Vertex Shader Slice Generation, View-Aligned Slicing (Proxy Geometry Generation), Viewport-Aligned Slices Intersection Algorithm
body: GPU-based Cut-off Slice Generation is an object-order volume rendering technique that computes proxy geometry (polygons) representing the intersection of slicing planes with the volume's bounding box directly on the GPU. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based slice generation by offloading the calculation of intersection points, polygon sorting, and tessellation to the vertex shader, enabling interactive frame rates. Unlike Plane Slicing which may compute geometry on the CPU, this method keeps the geometry generation pipeline entirely within the graphics hardware, balancing workload between vertex and fragment shaders to maintain high performance during camera rotation and interaction. The method generates a series of parallel polygons (proxy geometry) that slice through the volumetric data. These polygons are rendered in back-to-front or front-to-back order, and hardware blending composites the sampled volume values into the final image. Inputs: Volumetric data stored as a 3D texture. Modelview matrix transforming object space to view space. Camera parameters: position, view direction, viewport. Rendering parameters: number of slices, sampling rate, voxel size. Transfer function (typically a 2D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA). Outputs: A set of tessellated triangle primitives (proxy polygons) ready for rasterization. Final composited image via fragment shader blending. Bounding Box: Represented by 8 vertices (V0 to V7) and 12 edges. In the Rezk-Salama implementation, vertices are ordered such that V0 is closest to the camera and V7 is farthest. Edge Groups: Edges are categorized into 6 groups based on their geometric relationship to the viewing direction and texture axes: Red: E{0\rightarrow1}, E{1\rightarrow4}, E{4\rightarrow7} (always intersect). Blue: E{0\rightarrow3}, E{3\rightarrow6}, E{6\rightarrow7} (always intersect). Green: E{0\rightarrow2}, E{2\rightarrow5}, E{5\rightarrow7} (always intersect). Yellow: E{1\rightarrow5} (0 or 1 intersection). Cyan: E{2\rightarrow6} (0 or 1 intersection). Purple: E{3\rightarrow4} (0 or 1 intersection). Edge Flags: Each edge stores a 6-bit flag, where each bit corresponds to one of the 6 faces of the bounding box (Top, Bottom, Left, Right, Front, Back). A bit is set if the edge belongs to that face. This facilitates sorting by checking if adjacent intersection points share a common face via bitwise OR. Vertex List: A temporary list with a fixed maximum size of 6 vertices to store intersection points for a single slice plane. 1. Initialization: Bind the volumetric data as a 3D texture. Setup rendering parameters including camera position, view direction, and number of slices. 2. Transform Bounding Box: Transform the 8 vertices of the volume bounding box from object space to view space using the modelview matrix. 3. Determine Slicing Planes: Find the minimum (z{min}) and maximum (z{max}) z-coordinates of the transformed vertices in view space. Calculate the number of sampling planes (N) and the spacing (\Delta z) based on the voxel size and current sampling rate. Define N parallel planes perpendicular to the viewing direction (z-axis in view space), spaced equidistantly from the view origin. 4. Generate Proxy Geometry (Per Plane): For each plane P (processed in front-to-back or back-to-front order): Calculate Intersections: Compute the intersection of plane P with the 12 edges of the bounding box. Represent edge i \rightarrow j as \vec{x} = \vec{V}i + \lambda \vec{e}{i \rightarrow j}, where \vec{e}{i \rightarrow j} = \vec{V}j - \vec{V}i and \lambda \in [0, 1]. Represent plane P in Hessian normal form: \overrightarrow{n}p \cdot \overrightarrow{x} = d, where \overrightarrow{n}p is the viewing direction and d is the distance to the origin. Solve for \lambda: \lambda = \begin{cases} \frac{d - \vec{n}p \cdot \vec{V}i}{\vec{n}p \cdot \vec{e}{i \rightarrow j}}, & \vec{n}p \cdot \vec{e}{i \rightarrow j} \neq 0 \\ -1.0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} If \lambda \in [0, 1], the intersection is valid. If the denominator is 0, the edge is parallel to the plane; use \lambda = -1.0 to denote this. Filter and Sort (Rezk-Salama Method): The vertex shader must output exactly 6 vertices per polygon, even if the cross-section has fewer vertices. Traverse the edges in the specific order: Red, Yellow, Green, Cyan, Blue, Purple. For Red, Green, and Blue edges, an intersection always exists. For Yellow, Cyan, and Purple edges, check if an intersection exists (\lambda \in [0, 1]). If an intersection exists on a "side" edge (Yellow, Cyan, Purple), use it. If a side edge has no intersection, duplicate the intersection from the preceding "main" edge (Red, Green, or Blue) to fill the vertex slot. This ensures the output is always a closed polygon with 6 vertices (some potentially duplicated). Alternative Sorting (Moret/Shapiro): Compute the center of the proxy polygon by averaging the valid intersection points. Project points onto the x-y plane. Sort vertices clockwise or counter-clockwise using a "pseudo-angle" (tangent of the angle combined with sign of coordinates) to avoid trigonometric functions. Tessellation: Tessellate the sorted polygon into triangles (using a triangle fan or strip from the center). Add vertices to the output vertex array. Transform vertices back to object space if required by the rendering pipeline. 5. Rendering: Rasterize the proxy polygons. Fragment Shader: Perform 3D texture lookup using the interpolated texture coordinates from the vertex shader to sample the volume. Map the scalar value to RGBA using a 2D texture lookup (transfer function). Blend the resulting RGBA quadruplets using the alpha channel as the blending factor, accumulating color and opacity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeintersection(Vi, Vj, np, d): """ Computes lambda for the intersection of edge Vi->Vj with plane np.x = d. Returns lambda if valid, -1.0 otherwise. """ e = Vj - Vi denom = dot(np, e) if denom == 0: return -1.0 lambdaval = (d - dot(np, Vi)) / denom if 0.0 <= lambdaval <= 1.0: return lambdaval return -1.0 def gettexturecoord(Vi, lambdaval, k, Bmin, Bmax): """ Translates object space coordinate to texture space. k: unit vector in texture space (x, y, or z) Bmin, Bmax: min/max bounds of bounding box in direction k """ e = Vj - Vi # Implicitly available in context if dot(k, e) == 0: # Edge perpendicular to texture axis # Result is 0 or 1 depending on position relative to min/max # Simplified: if Vi is on min side, 0, else 1 if dot(k, Vi) <= Bmin: return 0.0 else: return 1.0 elif dot(k, e) > 0: return lambdaval else: return 1.0 - lambdaval def generateslicepolygons(verticesobj, modelviewmatrix, np, d, Bmin, Bmax): """ Generates 6 vertices for a slice polygon. verticesobj: Array of 8 bounding box vertices in object space. np: Normal of the slicing plane (viewing direction). d: Distance of plane from origin. """ # 1. Transform vertices to view space verticesview = [transform(v, modelviewmatrix) for v in verticesobj] # 2. Define edge groups (indices into verticesview) # Red: 0->1, 1->4, 4->7 # Blue: 0->3, 3->6, 6->7 # Green: 0->2, 2->5, 5->7 # Yellow: 1->5 # Cyan: 2->6 # Purple: 3->4 edges = [ (0, 1), (1, 4), (4, 7), # Red (1, 5), # Yellow (0, 2), (2, 5), (5, 7), # Green (2, 6), # Cyan (0, 3), (3, 6), (6, 7), # Blue (3, 4) # Purple ] # Note: The Rezk-Salama algorithm specifically traverses in order: # Red (3 edges), Yellow (1 edge), Green (3 edges), Cyan (1 edge), Blue (3 edges), Purple (1 edge) # However, since Red/Green/Blue always intersect, we pick one representative or all? # The source says "Red, Yellow, Green, Cyan, Blue, Purple" and outputs 6 vertices. # It implies we pick one intersection from each "group" or specific edges. # Specifically: Red (e.g. 0->1), Yellow (1->5), Green (e.g. 0->2), Cyan (2->6), Blue (e.g. 0->3), Purple (3->4). # Let's select specific edges to form the 6 slots: slotedges = [ (0, 1), # Red (1, 5), # Yellow (0, 2), # Green (2, 6), # Cyan (0, 3), # Blue (3, 4) # Purple ] outputvertices = [] for i, (idxi, idxj) in enumerate(slotedges): Vi = verticesview[idxi] Vj = verticesview[idxj] lam = computeintersection(Vi, Vj, np, d) if lam != -1.0: # Valid intersection Pview = Vi + lam (Vj - Vi) # Compute texture coordinates # Assuming texture axis k corresponds to the primary axis of the volume # For simplicity, we assume k is known or derived from volume orientation # Here we assume k is the axis along which the volume is stored (e.g., Z) # In a general case, k is passed or determined by the volume's axis alignment k = vec3(0, 0, 1) # Example: Z-aligned volume texcoord = gettexturecoord(Vi, lam, k, Bmin, Bmax) outputvertices.append((Pview, texcoord)) else: # Invalid intersection (side edge) # Duplicate the previous valid intersection if len(outputvertices) > 0: prev = outputvertices[-1] outputvertices.append(prev) else: # Fallback: Should not happen if Red is first and always valid # Guard against empty list outputvertices.append((vec3(0,0,0), vec2(0,0))) return outputvertices Slicing Axis: Typically the viewing direction (z-axis in view space). Can be modified for advanced algorithms. Sampling Rate: Determines the distance between slices, computed from voxel size. Interaction Response Time: Must be less than 100ms for real-time interaction. Vertex Shader Limitations: Vertex shaders cannot insert or remove vertices. The algorithm must output 6 vertices for every polygon, even if the cross-section is a triangle or quadrilateral. Duplicate vertices are used to fill slots. Invalid Intersections: If \lambda \notin [0, 1], the intersection is not on the bounding box edge and is invalid. Parallel Edges: If the edge is parallel to the plane normal (denominator is zero), \lambda is set to -1.0. Texture Coordinate Direction: If the edge direction is opposite to the texture axis \vec{k}, the texture coordinate is 1 - \lambda. Polygon Closure: The output vertices must form a closed polygon for correct rasterization. A method to compute intersection points and texture coordinates for axis-aligned boxes against parallel slicing planes incrementally, avoiding the bottleneck of recomputing intersections for every sub-volume and plane. It sets itself apart from naive per-plane intersection by leveraging the uniform spacing and parallel nature of slicing planes to update positions via constant deltas, maintaining an ActiveIntersectionList to track active edge intersections. Time Complexity: The intersection calculation is O(1) per slice plane (constant number of edges and vertices). The total time is proportional to the number of slices. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D volume texture and the vertex array for proxy geometry. Performance: Significantly improves performance compared to CPU-based slice generation by offloading calculations to the GPU. It is efficient for modern graphics processors, making it suitable for interactive applications. Strengths: Real-time interaction support (rotation, slicing). Balanced workload between vertex and fragment shaders. Limitations: The Rezk-Salama method requires specific vertex ordering and duplicate handling, which can be complex to implement. The Arc-ball rotation method has a limitation of not rotating more than 180 degrees in one click-drag operation. The method was proposed by Rezk-Salama et al. [50] to move the calculation of cut-off slices from the CPU to the GPU using vertex shaders. It is based on the principles of view-aligned slicing for 3D texture rendering. The coordinate translation algorithm was improved by Shen et al. [56] to be more flexible regarding texture coordinate systems. The sorting method using pseudo-angles is attributed to Moret and Shapiro (1991). The technique is widely used in scientific visualization and medical imaging for real-time volume rendering. name: Incremental Intersection and Texture Coordinates
head: ActiveIntersectionList method, Incremental intersection
body: A method to compute intersection points and texture coordinates for axis-aligned boxes against parallel slicing planes incrementally, avoiding the bottleneck of recomputing intersections for every sub-volume and plane. It sets itself apart from naive per-plane intersection by leveraging the uniform spacing and parallel nature of slicing planes to update positions via constant deltas, maintaining an ActiveIntersectionList to track active edge intersections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of parallel, uniformly spaced slicing planes; a bounding box (sub-volume) defined by axis-aligned edges; viewing direction; texture coordinate mapping parameters. Output: Updated intersection positions and texture coordinates for the current slicing plane, stored in the ActiveIntersectionList. Data Structures: ActiveIntersectionList: A list of intersection objects. Each object contains: position[edgeOrientation]: The 3D position of the intersection on the edge. texCoords[edgeOrientation]: The texture coordinates corresponding to the intersection. bUpdated: A boolean flag indicating if the intersection has been processed for the current plane. edge: A reference to the edge geometry. Connection List: A global data structure indexing edges by their end points and the sign of the view direction projection, used to find neighbor edges. Parameters: deltaPos: The constant difference in intersection position on the same edge between adjacent slicing planes. It depends only on the viewing direction and is invariant for all sub-volumes. deltaTexCoords: The constant difference in texture coordinates between adjacent slicing planes. If sub-volumes are packed into a large 3D texture, this is constant for all sub-volumes; otherwise, it may depend on the texture size if scaled to [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Initialization (First Plane): For the first slicing plane, compute intersections and texture coordinates for each edge of the box using the traditional method. Insert all valid intersections into the ActiveIntersectionList and sort them. 2. Delta Calculation: Compute deltaPos and deltaTexCoords based on the viewing direction and texture mapping. Due to the axis-aligned nature of the box, these vectors have only one non-zero element. 3. Incremental Update: For each subsequent slicing plane, iterate through the ActiveIntersectionList and apply the following logic to each intersection: If intersection.bUpdated is false: Calculate newPos = intersection.position[edgeOrientation] + deltaPos[edgeOrientation]. Mark intersection.bUpdated = true. Check if newPos is inside the edge bounds. If inside: Update intersection.position[edgeOrientation] = newPos and intersection.texCoords[edgeOrientation] += deltaTexCoords[edgeOrientation]. If outside: The plane either does not intersect the box or intersects new edges. Remove the intersection from the list. Call IntersectNeighborEdges to find new intersections. 4. Neighbor Search: In IntersectNeighborEdges(intersection.edge, plane): Track edges from the current edge e in breadth-first order using the connection list. Search until two new intersections are found. Use the bUpdated flag to prevent duplicate intersections or re-processing active edges. Add new intersections to the ActiveIntersectionList at the position of the removed intersection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateintersections(activelist, deltapos, deltatexcoords, connectionlist): for intersection in activelist: if not intersection.bUpdated: # Calculate new position incrementally newpos = intersection.position[intersection.edgeorientation] + deltapos[intersection.edgeorientation] # Mark as processed for this plane intersection.bUpdated = True # Check if the new intersection is still within the edge bounds if isinsideedge(newpos, intersection.edge): # Update position and texture coordinates intersection.position[intersection.edgeorientation] = newpos intersection.texCoords[intersection.edgeorientation] += deltatexcoords[intersection.edgeorientation] else: # Intersection moved off the edge; remove it removeintersection(activelist, intersection) # Find new intersections on neighbor edges newintersections = intersectneighboredges(intersection.edge, connectionlist) # Add new intersections to the list for newint in newintersections: if not newint.bUpdated: newint.bUpdated = True activelist.append(newint) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Edge Geometry: Axis-aligned boxes have 12 edges where intersecting pairs form 90-degree angles. This ensures deltaPos and deltaTexCoords have only one non-zero element, simplifying calculations. Duplicate Intersections: The bUpdated flag is critical to prevent adding the same edge intersection multiple times during the neighbor search. Texture Coordinate Scaling: If texture coordinates are not packed into a large 3D texture, deltaTexCoords may vary per sub-volume, requiring careful handling. An acceleration technique that caches the indices of spline segments used in previous rendering slices to avoid redundant binary searches for the current slice, leveraging depth-order coherence in front-to-back traversal. Unlike the basic algorithm which requires four spline searches per pixel fragment using binary search, this method uses incremental linear search from the previous slice's position, reducing computational bottleneck. Time Complexity: Reduces the intersection calculation bottleneck from recomputing for every sub-volume and plane to an incremental update, significantly speeding up the process. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the ActiveIntersectionList and the global Connection List. Strengths: Highly efficient for axis-aligned boxes with parallel, uniformly spaced slicing planes. Leverages geometric coherence. Limitations: Specific to axis-aligned boxes; not directly applicable to unstructured grids. Requires careful management of the active list and neighbor searches. When to Use: Texture-based volume rendering with occlusion clipping where empty space skipping is employed, and slicing planes are parallel and uniform. Originated in the context of "Empty Space Skipping and Occlusion Clipping for Texture-based Volume Rendering". The method addresses the performance degradation caused by recomputing intersections for each sub-volume, which can negate the benefits of skipping empty spaces. It is used in GPU-based cut-off slice generation to offload CPU calculation [Parent]. name: Index Texture Cache for Spline Search
head: Cache Index Texture, Incremental Spline Search Cache
body: An acceleration technique that caches the indices of spline segments used in previous rendering slices to avoid redundant binary searches for the current slice, leveraging depth-order coherence in front-to-back traversal. Unlike the basic algorithm which requires four spline searches per pixel fragment using binary search to compute a trilinearly interpolated scalar value, this method uses incremental linear search from the previous slice's position, reducing the computational bottleneck. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current rendering slice index (depth), the Parametric Representation Image (PRI) structure containing spline data, and the previous slice's cache state. Output: Updated cache index texture for the current slice, and the final rendered slice image. Data Structures: Cache Index Texture: A 2D texture with resolution equal to the PRI's pixelized sampling plane. Each texel stores the index of the spline segment (knot) currently active for that spatial location. Ping-Pong Textures: Two textures used to swap read/write roles during the update pass to ensure atomicity and avoid race conditions. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the 2D cache index texture with the same resolution as the PRI's pixelized sampling plane. Populate it with the contents of the index texture to cache the first knots of each spline. 2. Two-Pass Rendering: For each slice in the rendering stack, perform a two-pass approach. 3. Pass 1: Cache Update: Set the camera to coincide with the PRI. Specify the cache index texture as the rendering target. Map the cache index texture to the slice via projective texture mapping using orthogonal projection in the sampling direction of the PRI. At each texel, perform a linear search to find the appropriate spline segment, starting from the segment index stored in the previous slice's cache (read from the ping-pong source texture). If the next slice requires a spline segment not used in the previous slice, the linear search quickly finds the required segment by starting from the segment processed in the previous slice, as segments are processed in depth order. Write the new segment index to the cache index texture. Swap ping-pong textures for the next iteration. 4. Pass 2: Slice Rendering: Render the slice from the user's view. Use the updated cache index texture and dependent texturing to fetch the correct spline segment data for trilinear interpolation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderslicewithcache(slicedepth, prisplines, prevcache, currcache, priwidth, priheight): # Pass 1: Cache Update # Camera coincides with PRI; cache index texture is render target # Map cache index texture to slice via projective texture mapping using orthogonal projection in PRI sampling direction for y in range(priheight): for x in range(priwidth): segidx = prevcache[y, x] # Linear search starting from segidx to find appropriate spline segment for current slice # Sources do not specify exact knot distance comparison logic; assume standard depth check while segidx < len(prisplines) and prisplines[segidx].knotdistance < slicedepth: segidx += 1 currcache[y, x] = segidx # Swap ping-pong textures for next iteration prevcache, currcache = currcache, prevcache # Pass 2: Slice Rendering # Render slice from user's view using updated cache index texture and dependent texturing # Sources do not specify dependent texturing implementation; assume standard GPU fragment shader fetches scalar value for y in range(priheight): for x in range(priwidth): segidx = prevcache[y, x] value = prisplines[segidx].scalarvalue writepixel(x, y, value) return prevcache Parameters: Cache Index Texture Resolution: Equal to the PRI's pixelized sampling plane resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Screen Resolution Mismatch: When the user's screen resolution exceeds the PRI's sampling plane resolution, multiple pixel fragments may fall within the same neighborhood of four splines. In this case, bilinear interpolation of scalar values from the four neighboring splines can be used for efficiency. Depth Order: The method assumes front-to-back traversal, though it can be adapted for back-to-front. Time Complexity: Reduces the search cost from binary search to incremental linear search, addressing the computational bottleneck of the basic algorithm. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory for the cache index texture (2D texture same size as PRI sampling plane) and ping-pong buffers. Strengths: Eliminates redundant binary searches by leveraging depth-order coherence in front-to-back traversal. Limitations: Requires two-pass rendering per slice. This method is part of the GPU-based cut-off slice generation pipeline for volume rendering, specifically addressing the computational bottleneck of spline searches in unstructured grid rendering. It builds on the incremental intersection and texture coordinates method [997-incremental-intersection-and-texture-coordinates.md]. name: Parallel Cell Projection
head: Parallel Cell-Projection Implementation, Multi-threaded projection
body: Parallel Cell Projection is a distributed-memory and shared-memory strategy for object-order volume rendering that decomposes the cell projection pipeline into parallelizable stages: object-space polygon generation and image-space ray merging/composition. It solves the scalability problem of rendering large unstructured grids by allowing multiple processors or threads to compute projected polygons and merge ray segments concurrently. It sets itself apart from synchronous communication strategies by decoupling sending and receiving tasks to hide data transfer overheads, and from concurrent scan-conversion/composition approaches by separating the projection and global composition phases to reduce asynchronous communication frequency. The method operates in two primary phases: object-space projection and image-space composition. It can be implemented on shared-memory multiprocessors (using threads) or distributed-memory clusters (using MPI). Input: A 3D unstructured grid (e.g., tetrahedral or general cell topology) and a camera viewpoint. Output: A 2D rendered image (color and opacity per pixel). Vertex Array: Stores projected polygonal information. Each vertex contains transformed coordinates, normal, and lighting values. Ray-Segment List: For each pixel (or region), a list of depth-sorted segments. Each segment contains interpolated vertex color, opacity, and depth value. Communication Buffers: Output buffers storing ray segments to be sent to other nodes. The buffer depth is configurable (e.g., 25 or 200 segments). 1. Object-Space Partitioning and Projection (Pass 1): Partition the object space (volume) among processors or threads. Each processor/thread computes per-vertex calculations: point/normal transformation and lighting. Shared vertices are processed only once to avoid redundancy. Each cell is projected into 2D polygons. For tetrahedral cells, this often uses the Shirley-Tuchman projection. Polygons are loaded into vertex arrays. Note: In some implementations, faces are sorted back-to-front within the local node, using face centroids as a sorting criterion, though this may lead to incorrect sorting if not handled carefully. 2. Parallel Composition (Pass 2): The screen is partitioned among processors. Each processor is assigned a region of the screen. Gather: Each node gathers ray-segment lists from other nodes corresponding to the pixels in its assigned region. Merge: Ray segments are merged into a single depth-sorted list for each pixel. Composite: Pixel values are calculated by compositing the depth-sorted ray segments from front to back using Porter-Duff's "over" operation (alpha blending). Final Output: Each node sends its rendered image region to a control node for final assembly and display. Asynchronous Communication: To mitigate communication overhead, the system uses asynchronous task management. Processors proceed independently, multiplexing object-space cell computations with image-space ray merging. Feedback Mechanism: If sending is blocked due to full buffers, the processor switches to the ray merging task and begins receiving, regardless of the polling interval. Polling: Processors check for incoming messages at a configurable frequency (e.g., after each cell scan conversion or every 4 cells). Buffer Tuning: Larger buffers and longer polling intervals reduce sending/receiving/polling overhead but increase idle time (sendwait, recvwait, syncwait) because idle processors wait longer for new work. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelcellprojectionshmem(cells, camera): # 1. Object Space Projection (Parallel) vertexarrays = [] numthreads = getnumthreads() # Partition cells among threads cellpartitions = partitioncells(cells, numthreads) # Parallel region for projection for threadid in range(numthreads): localvertices = [] for cell in cellpartitions[threadid]: # Project cell to 2D polygons polygons = projectcell(cell, camera) # Compute per-vertex lighting and transformation for poly in polygons: for vertex in poly.vertices: transformedv = transform(vertex, camera) litv = light(transformedv, cell.material) localvertices.append(litv) vertexarrays.append(localvertices) # 2. Sorting (Single Thread) # Sort all faces back-to-front based on depth sortedfaces = sortfacesbacktofront(vertexarrays) # 3. OpenGL Rendering (Single Thread) # Make OpenGL calls on full vertex arrays renderopengl(sortedfaces) def parallelcellprojectiondistributed(cells, camera, rank, numnodes): # 1. Object Space Projection (Local) # Each node projects its assigned cells localraysegments = [] for cell in cells: polygons = projectcell(cell, camera) # Scan-convert polygons to ray segments segments = scanconvert(polygons) localraysegments.extend(segments) # 2. Communication (Asynchronous) # Send ray segments to nodes responsible for the corresponding screen regions # Use feedback mechanism: if send blocked, switch to merge/receive for segment in localraysegments: destnode = getdestnode(segment.screencoords) sendasync(segment, destnode) # 3. Image Space Composition (Parallel) # Each node handles a region of the screen screenregion = partitionscreen(rank, numnodes) for pixel in screenregion: # Gather ray segments from other nodes incomingsegments = gathersegments(pixel) # Merge and sort mergedsegments = mergeandsort(incomingsegments) # Composite using Porter-Duff over color = compositefronttoback(mergedsegments) setpixelcolor(pixel, color) # 4. Final Output sendimageregiontocontrolnode() Buffer Depth: Number of ray segments stored in output buffers before sending. Typical values: 25 and 200 segments. Polling Frequency: Interval at which processors check for incoming messages. Typical values: after each cell scan conversion or after every 4 cells. Partitioner Aspect Ratio: Configuring the partitioner to produce regions with high aspect ratios to reduce congestion. Minimum Region Size: Parameters to prevent regions from falling below a certain size to avoid message traffic congestion. Incorrect Sorting: Using only centroids of each face as a sorting criterion may lead to incorrect sorting. Message Congestion: Spatial partitioners may generate regions with very small projected areas, causing all message traffic to bombard a few nodes, backing up output buffers and leaving most nodes idle. Idle Time: Larger buffers and longer polling intervals increase idle time (sendwait, recvwait, syncwait). Hot Spots: High cell density regions map to few scanlines, causing load imbalance in image-space operations. Asynchronous Communication Task Management is a strategy for managing inter-processor communication costs in parallel volume rendering by allowing processors to proceed independently, multiplexing object-space cell computations with image-space ray merging, and overlapping computation with communication using end buffering. It sets itself apart from synchronous strategies by decoupling sending and receiving tasks, thereby hiding data transfer overheads and spreading the communication load over time. Dynamic Load Balancing is a distributed work-stealing scheme used to handle load imbalance caused by initial data distribution, view dependency of scan conversion time, and run-time dynamic behavior of Early Ray Termination (ERT). It differs from preprocessing-based static load balancing (which cannot handle dynamic ERT behavior) and self-scheduling based schemes (which do not work well for non-shared memory systems like PC clusters). Time Complexity: The object-space projection phase scales with the number of cells and processors. The image-space composition phase scales with the number of pixels and processors. Communication overhead increases with the number of processors and data size. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of ray segments stored on each processor. With 64 regions, the maximum number of unmerged ray segments stored on any processor is at most 15-20% of the total number received. Measured Performance: On a 128-processor Intel Paragon (66.7 MHz POWER2 chipset, 34 MB/s node-to-node bandwidth), the method achieved a speedup of 90 and a parallel efficiency of 70%, with a rendering time of 2 frames per second (excluding display). On a 64-processor SGI Onyx2, speed-up for tetrahedral cells with Shirley-Tuchman projection leveled out after about 5 projection threads, while for general grids, it leveled out after 18 projection threads, attributed to communications overhead. Strengths: Scalability to large node counts (16-1000+ nodes). Ability to run with or without graphics hardware. Effective reduction of communication overhead through asynchronous task management and buffer tuning. Limitations: Performance levels out due to communication overhead. Load imbalance can occur due to hot spots in the volume data. Static load balancing may not handle dynamic ERT behavior. When to Use: Large unstructured grid datasets on distributed-memory clusters or shared-memory multiprocessors where scalability is critical. When Not to Use: Small datasets where communication overhead dominates computation. Systems with high-latency or low-bandwidth interconnects. Parallel Cell Projection was developed in the mid-1990s as an extension of cell projection methods to parallel architectures. Early implementations by Lucas and Wilhelms et al. explored software-based parallel projection. The Scalable Distributed Volume Rendering (SDVR) System targeted large PC clusters, using MPI and OpenGL. The method has been used in research for rendering complex unstructured grids, such as flowfields around aircraft wings. name: Asynchronous Communication Task Management
head: Asynchronous communication strategy, Polling strategy
body: Asynchronous Communication Task Management is a strategy for managing inter-processor communication costs in parallel volume rendering by allowing processors to proceed independently, multiplexing object-space cell computations with image-space ray merging, and overlapping computation with communication using end buffering. It sets itself apart from synchronous strategies by decoupling sending and receiving tasks, thereby hiding data transfer overheads and spreading the communication load over time. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Local data cells assigned to the processor, ray segment buffers, polling interval parameter, buffer depth parameter. Output: Completed subimage sent to a host computer (or assembled globally), global termination signal. Data Structures: Ray Segment Buffers: Two or more buffers are provided for each destination processor. Layout: Each buffer holds a collection of ray segments. The specific bit-packing of a ray segment is not defined in the sources, but it represents the geometric data resulting from scan conversion. State: Buffers track whether they are full, empty, or currently pending for an asynchronous send operation. Parameters: Polling Interval: The number of cells to be processed before checking for incoming ray segments. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Guidance: Should be selected in accordance with buffer size; polling should be performed more frequently with smaller buffer sizes or larger numbers of processors. Buffer Depth: The number of ray segments accumulated before an asynchronous send is posted. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Guidance: Depends on the number of processors, number of ray segments, and target architecture characteristics. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Allocate two or more ray segment buffers for each destination processor. 2. Main Loop (Multiplexed Execution): a. Scan Conversion: Process local data cells to generate ray segments. Place these segments into the appropriate destination buffers. b. Buffer Management: i. If a buffer is full, post an asynchronous send operation for that buffer. ii. If a send is pending for a full buffer, place additional segments in the companion buffer. c. Polling: After processing Polling Interval cells, check for incoming ray segments from other processors. d. Ray Merging: Process any incoming ray segments that have arrived. e. Deadlock Prevention: If both buffers for a particular destination fill up before the first send completes, switch exclusively to the ray merging task (processing incoming segments) until the outbound congestion clears. This step is essential to prevent deadlock. 3. Termination Coordination: a. A designated node coordinates termination by collecting local termination messages from all processors. b. The designated node broadcasts a global termination signal. c. A final global synchronization operation ends the overall rendering process. 4. Final Output: Each processor sends its completed subimage to a host computer, which assembles them for display. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. pollinginterval = 10 # Example value, user-specified bufferdepth = 100 # Example value, user-specified numdestinations = P # Number of other processors buffers = [[[] for in range(2)] for in range(numdestinations)] # 2 buffers per destination issendpending = [False] numdestinations localcells = getlocalcells() incomingsegments = [] def processcell(cell): # Scan convert cell to ray segments segments = scanconvert(cell) return segments def postasyncsend(destid, bufferid): # Initiate non-blocking send of buffer[destid][bufferid] # Mark as pending issendpending[destid] = True # Clear buffer after posting (or keep if double-buffering logic requires keeping data until ack) # Sources imply switching to companion buffer, so we assume the sent buffer is cleared or handed off buffers[destid][bufferid] = [] def checkincoming(): # Check for completed receives and merge segments # This function handles the "ray merging" task pass def isbufferfull(buffer): return len(buffer) >= bufferdepth def main(): cellsprocessed = 0 for cell in localcells: # 1. Scan Conversion segments = processcell(cell) # 2. Buffering for destid, segs in segments: # Find a buffer for this destination # Prefer the one not pending send if not issendpending[destid]: bufid = 0 if len(buffers[destid][0]) < len(buffers[destid][1]) else 1 buffers[destid][bufid].extend(segs) if isbufferfull(buffers[destid][bufid]): postasyncsend(destid, bufid) else: # Send is pending, use companion buffer bufid = 1 if issendpending[destid] else 0 # Simplified logic: if pending, use other # Note: Logic must ensure we don't use the same buffer that is pending # If both are full, deadlock prevention triggers if isbufferfull(buffers[destid][bufid]): # Deadlock prevention: Switch to ray merging while isbufferfull(buffers[destid][bufid]) and issendpending[destid]: checkincoming() # Retry buffering after merging might free up space or complete sends # Re-evaluate buffer status break # Exit inner loop to re-check main loop conditions or continue merging cellsprocessed += 1 # 3. Polling if cellsprocessed % pollinginterval == 0: checkincoming() # 4. Termination # Send local termination message to designated node sendterminationmessage() # Wait for global termination signal waitforglobaltermination() # 5. Final Output sendsubimagetohost() A communication strategy using double-buffering in conjunction with asynchronous send and receive operations to reduce overheads and overlap communication of ray segments with rendering calculations. It proceeds with scan conversion of data cells and merging of ray segments in a multiplexed fashion. After these tasks are finished, each processor sends its completed subimage to a host computer which assembles them for display. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires 2 \times N \times B memory for ray segments, where N is the number of destinations and B is the buffer depth. Measured Performance: Tested on a dataset containing about 0.5 million tetrahedral cells, rendering into a 400x400 pixel image. Scaling: Effective in spreading communication load across time, which is beneficial in bandwidth-limited systems. Strengths: Hides data transfer overheads, reduces data copying overheads in message-passing systems, and decouples sending and receiving tasks. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of polling interval and buffer depth; too frequent polling introduces excessive overhead, while too infrequent polling causes outbound buffers to clog. Small buffers cause excessive send/receive overhead, while large buffers introduce delays for waiting processors. When to use: When communication overhead is significant and can be hidden by computation, and when the architecture supports asynchronous operations. When not to use: When the number of processors is small and communication overhead is negligible, or when strict synchronization is required for correctness. The strategy was originally developed for a parallel polygon renderer and later improved for use in the PGL rendering system. It is used in scalable parallel cell-projection volume rendering algorithms for three-dimensional unstructured data. name: Cell Projection with Texture Mapping for Opacity
head: Hardware-accelerated Cell Projection with Texture Lookup, Polyhedron Projection, Texture-mapped Cell Projection
body: Cell Projection with Texture Mapping for Opacity is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that projects individual cells as polygons onto the image plane and composites them in back-to-front order. It solves the problem of visual artifacts (specifically Mach bands) caused by the linear interpolation of non-linear opacity values by using a 2D texture lookup to compute the exponential opacity term per pixel. Unlike standard cell projection which interpolates opacity directly, this method interpolates the linear parameters required for the opacity formula and retrieves the correct exponential value from a precomputed texture. Inputs: A scalar field defined on a grid (structured or unstructured). Linear transfer functions mapping scalar values to color (RGB) and density (\kappa). Camera parameters (orthographic or perspective). Outputs: A 2D image with correct opacity compositing. Data Structures: 2D Texture Map: A 2D texture table used for opacity lookup. The texture stores values of \alpha(\kappa{avg}, l) = 1 - e^{-\kappa{avg} l}. The dimensions of the texture are determined by the range of average density \kappa{avg} and ray segment length l. Image Plane Subdivision: A set of polygons covering the projection of each cell. For general cells, this is built incrementally; for curvilinear grids, it is determined by topology tests. Steps: 1. Precompute Texture: Load the 2D texture with values calculated from the opacity formula \alpha = 1 - e^{-\kappa{avg} l} for all valid pairs of \kappa{avg} and l. 2. Project Cell Edges: For each cell, project its vertices onto the image plane. Divide the projection of the cell into polygons such that each polygon lies within the projection of a single front-facing face and a single back-facing face. For general cells: Use an incremental method to build the subdivision. Start with one infinite region. Add projected edges one by one. An edge may create a new boundary cycle, close a cycle to form a new polygon, or subdivide existing polygons and edges. For curvilinear grids: Test if the projection topology matches one of three non-degenerate perspective projection topologies for a cube. If so, use a standard subdivision lookup. Otherwise, fall back to the incremental method. 3. Compute Vertex Attributes: For each vertex of the projected polygons, compute the color and the texture coordinates (\kappa{avg}, l). Thin Vertices: Vertices where the viewing ray segment length l is zero (e.g., vertices A, B, C, D, F in a triangular prism projection). Color: Interpolate the scalar value s at the vertex and map it to color via the transfer function. Opacity/Texture Coordinates: Set l = 0 and \kappa{avg} = 0 (or the density at the vertex). The texture lookup will return \alpha = 0. Thick Vertices: Vertices where the viewing ray passes through the cell (e.g., vertices E, G in a triangular prism projection). Find the segment endpoints on the front and back faces that project to the vertex. Compute the density \kappa at the front and back endpoints by interpolating the scalar field and applying the density transfer function. Compute \kappa{avg} = (\kappa{front} + \kappa{back}) / 2. Compute the segment length l: Orthographic View: l varies linearly across the polygon. Compute l geometrically at the vertex. Perspective View: Correct l requires a square root per pixel. This technique approximates l by interpolating in screen space, which is an approximation. Compute Color: Precise: Compute the integrated color analytically at the vertex and divide by the integrated \alpha. This is slow. Approximate: Use the average of the colors at the front and back endpoints. Set Texture Coordinates: (\kappa{avg}, l). 4. Rasterize and Composite: For each polygon: Interpolate the color and texture coordinates (\kappa{avg}, l) across the polygon using hardware Gouraud shading. Note that in orthographic view, \kappa{avg} and l vary linearly, so hardware interpolation is correct. In perspective view, this is an approximation. For each pixel, use the interpolated (\kappa{avg}, l) as texture coordinates to sample the 2D opacity texture. This returns the correct \alpha = 1 - e^{-\kappa{avg} l}. Composite the polygon color C{poly} onto the existing image color C{old} using the retrieved \alpha: C{new} = (1 - \alpha) \times C{old} + \alpha \times C{poly} Pitfalls: Mach Bands: Linear interpolation of \alpha across polygons causes derivative discontinuities due to the non-linear exponential, resulting in Mach bands. The texture lookup method avoids this. Perspective Approximation: In perspective view, \tauf and \taub have different perspective distortions, and correct l computation requires a square root. The method approximates by interpolating in screen space, which is not mathematically exact. Robustness: The incremental method for general cells is slow and not completely robust due to floating-point computations determining topology. Time Complexity: Dominated by the visibility sort of cells and the rasterization of projected polygons. The incremental subdivision method for general cells is slow. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 2D opacity texture and the image plane subdivision data structures. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated opacity calculation avoids per-pixel exponentials. Correctly handles non-linear opacity to avoid Mach bands. Limitations: Requires a global visibility sort for correct back-to-front compositing. Approximate in perspective view. Incremental subdivision is not robust for general cells. This method is a refinement of the original Cell Projection technique by Shirley and Tuchman. It was developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to address the Mach band artifacts inherent in the original method's linear interpolation of opacity. It is used for volume rendering of curvilinear and unstructured grids. name: Topological Sort for Cell Projection
head: MPVO, MPVO algorithm, Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering, Maximal Polyhedra Visibility Ordering, Exact Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering, Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection
body: Topological Sort for Cell Projection (MPVO) is an O(n) algorithm for computing a back-to-front visibility ordering of convex polyhedral cells in a convex grid. It solves the occlusion ordering problem required for correct alpha-blending in object-order volume rendering by constructing a directed graph of pairwise occlusion relations between adjacent cells and performing a topological sort. Unlike Tetrahedral Volume Rendering or Projected Tetrahedra which may rely on simpler centroid or distance-based heuristics, MPVO guarantees a correct visibility order for convex meshes by respecting the transitive occlusion chain along viewing rays. It fails on non-convex meshes because it ignores occlusion across empty space between non-adjacent cells. Inputs: A convex grid of convex polyhedral cells; a viewpoint V (for perspective) or a projection direction vector \vec{d} (for orthogonal). Outputs: A list of cells sorted in back-to-front order, where an occluded cell precedes an occluder. Data Structures: 1. Cell Node: Contains incount (integer, number of incoming edges), outgoing (list of cell references it occludes), and incoming (list of cell references that occlude it). 2. Directed Graph: Implicitly defined by adjacency, where nodes are cells and edges represent occlusion relations. 3. Queue: A FIFO queue for cells with incount == 0. Definitions: Relation B <{vp} A: Cell B must be rendered before cell A. This holds if the viewpoint V is on the same side of the shared face F between A and B as cell A is. This implies A occludes B, but B cannot occlude A. Arrow Direction: The direction is calculated using the plane equation for the face and the coordinates of the viewpoint (for perspective views) or a vector along the direction of projection (for orthogonal views). Algorithm Steps: 1. Phase I: Construct Partial Ordering (Graph Construction) Initialize all cells C: set C.incount = 0. For each interior face f shared by cells c1 and c2: Determine the direction of occlusion using the face plane equation and viewpoint/projection vector. Perspective View: If V and c1 are on the same side of the plane of f, then c1 occludes c2. Orthogonal View: If the projection direction \vec{d} aligns with the outward normal of c1 relative to f, c1 is in front of c2. Add a directed edge from the occluded cell to the occluder. Increment the occluder's incount. Identify source cells: Cells with incount == 0. Add these to the queue. 2. Phase II: Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm) While queue is not empty: Dequeue a cell C. Add C to the sorted output list. For each neighbor B in C.outgoing: decrement B.incount. If B.incount == 0, enqueue B. If the queue empties before all cells are output, a visibility cycle exists. Note: An alternative Phase II uses Depth-First Search with visited and cycledetection flags to output cells. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mpvosort(cells, interiorfaces, viewpoint, isorthogonal=False, projectiondir=None): # Phase I: Initialize and build graph for cell in cells: cell.incount = 0 cell.outgoing = [] cell.incoming = [] for c1, c2, face in interiorfaces: # Determine occlusion direction if isorthogonal: n = face.normal if dot(projectiondir, n) > 0: occluder, occluded = c1, c2 else: occluder, occluded = c2, c1 else: # Perspective: V and c1 on same side of face plane -> c1 occludes c2 n = face.normal P = face.center dv = dot(n, viewpoint - P) dc1 = dot(n, c1.center - P) if (dv > 0 and dc1 > 0) or (dv < 0 and dc1 < 0): occluder, occluded = c1, c2 else: occluder, occluded = c2, c1 # Add edge: occluded -> occluder occluded.outgoing.append(occluder) occluder.incoming.append(occluded) occluder.incount += 1 # Identify source cells (incount == 0) queue = [c for c in cells if c.incount == 0] # Phase II: Topological Sort (Kahn's algorithm) sortedoutput = [] head = 0 while head < len(queue): currentcell = queue[head] head += 1 sortedoutput.append(currentcell) for neighbor in currentcell.outgoing: neighbor.incount -= 1 if neighbor.incount == 0: queue.append(neighbor) if len(sortedoutput) < len(cells): raise ValueError("Visibility cycle detected") return sortedoutput Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Cycles: If the graph contains a cycle, the topological sort fails. In the queue-based variant, this is detected if the queue empties before all cells are output. Cycles imply no global visibility order exists; cells must be subdivided or per-pixel sorting used. Non-Convex Grids: If the grid is non-convex, viewing rays may leave the volume through an external face, cross empty space, and re-enter another cell. MPVO only considers shared faces, so it misses these cross-gap occlusions. Complexity Accounting: Each cell is treated twice during initialization and once in the loop; each edge is treated once in initialization and once in the loop. Manages pixel-level intersection lists for exterior faces on non-convex grids, avoiding true visibility sort complexities while ensuring correct hardware rendering. Choose when exact ordering is needed but the mesh has concavities. Sorts based on power distance with small constant computations. Choose when the mesh is a Delaunay triangulation, as it is not guaranteed to be accurate otherwise. Sorts all faces projecting onto a pixel at render time. Choose when visibility cycles are expected, as a sort always exists per pixel center even without a global sort. Augments MPVO by discovering exterior face relations using ray shooting queries at edge intersections and vertices of the projection complex. Choose when handling non-convex meshes requires exact ordering without per-pixel overhead. Heuristic extension to nonconvex meshes sorting exterior cells by centroid distance. Choose for fast rendering of large non-convex datasets where real-time interaction is prioritized over exact correctness. Time Complexity: O(n) for convex grids, where n is the number of cells. Memory Complexity: Linear space O(n) for data structures. Measured performance with hardware, resolution, and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear scaling with cell count n. Strengths: Very fast, accurate for convex meshes, low computational overhead, detects visibility cycles. Limitations: Fails for non-convex meshes (requires extra gap relations or approximate methods). Requires convexity of cells and grid. When to use: Convex grids of convex polyhedral cells where exact visibility ordering is required and performance is critical. When not to use: Non-convex meshes, non-planar faces, or when real-time interaction with very large non-convex datasets is needed (use Approximate MPVONC or Per-Pixel Sorting). The MPVO algorithm was described by Williams [27] and similarly by Max et al. [15]. It is based on the observation that for convex meshes, local occlusion relations across shared faces define a partial order that can be topologically sorted to yield a correct global visibility order. It is a foundational method for cell projection volume rendering. It is used in direct volume rendering and scientific visualization.
