name: Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO)
head: SXMPVO (Scanning Exact MPVO), Scanning Exact MPVO (SXMPVO), Scanning Exact Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering
body: SXMPVO is an image-space visibility ordering algorithm for cell projection volume rendering of unstructured data. It solves the problem that the standard Maximal Polyhedra Visibility Ordering (MPVO) method fails for nonconvex meshes because it ignores ordering relations along viewing rays that cross empty space ("ray-gaps") between non-adjacent cells. SXMPVO achieves "image-space correctness" by combining MPVO's face-based partial ordering with scan-conversion of exterior faces into an A-Buffer to resolve these ray-gaps. Unlike object-precision methods like XMPVO, SXMPVO uses image-precision ray shooting, making it faster and simpler to implement while guaranteeing correct sorting for acyclic meshes. The algorithm computes a global ordering of cells in an unstructured mesh (tetrahedral, hexahedral, or "zoo" meshes) to produce correct segment sorting along viewing rays. It assumes the mesh is acyclic; if a cycle exists, the algorithm reports it. The mesh may have nonconvex boundaries, disconnected components, and cells with nonplanar surfaces, provided the projections of cell edges do not cross ("bow tie" quadrilaterals). Input: An unstructured mesh (cells, faces, vertices), a viewpoint, and an image resolution (w \times h). Output: A total ordering sequence of cells b = c{im} < c{im-1} < \dots < c{i1} < c{i0} = a, where b comes before a in the sorted sequence. The algorithm builds on MPVO data structures. For a tetrahedral mesh, MPVO structures require 4f + 14n words, where f is the number of interior faces and n is the number of cells. This includes the adjacency graph, cell vertices, plane equation coefficients, arrows, and one word per cell for flags. SXMPVO adds the following structures: 1. Exterior Face List: A list holding a record for each exterior face. Each record contains: a pointer to the face, a pointer to the cell to which the face belongs, the face’s centroid, and a next pointer. 2. A-Buffer: Implemented as an array of pixel (PIX) lists, one per pixel in the screen image (w \times h). PIX List Entry (PIX Entry): Contains the distance z from the screen to the point where the ray through pixel p intersects face f, a pointer to f, and a next pointer for the PIX list. 3. PN List: Every cell has a PN list pointer, initially set to NULL. PN List Entry (PN Entry): Contains the cell number of the occluded cell and a next pointer. The PN list for a cell contains all exterior cells it occludes (its dependencies). Phase I: Create Partial Ordering of Interior Cells 1. Traverse all cells to mark arrows on shared interior faces, exactly as in MPVO Phase I. This determines "behind" relations from adjacent cells. 2. Set a sink cell flag in each cell to true or false based on whether it has outbound arrows. 3. Create the Exterior Face List containing all exterior faces. Complexity: O(n). Phase II: Sort Exterior Faces 1. Sort the exterior faces in the Exterior Face List by increasing distance from the screen to the face’s centroid. Complexity: O(b \log b) for Phase II, where b is the number of exterior cells. Phase III: Scan Convert Exterior Faces and Record PN Relations 1. Initialize the A-Buffer (array of PIX lists). 2. Remove exterior faces from the sorted queue one at a time and scan-convert their interiors in 3D. When using hardware rasterization (e.g., OpenGL), sample at pixel centers. For each pixel p of an exterior face f enumerated by scan conversion: Create a new PIX entry containing the distance z from the screen to the intersection point, a pointer to f, and a next pointer. Insert the PIX entry into the PIX list in the A-Buffer for pixel p, ordered by decreasing z. Optimization: Since faces are sorted by centroid distance, insertions occur at or near the beginning of the PIX list. Use an efficient insertion sort. 3. After rasterizing all exterior faces, clean up PIX lists: Discard the first entry of every PIX list (the back-facing face where the ray exits the mesh for the last time, which has no matching front-facing face behind it). If the viewpoint is outside the mesh, the PIX lists have an even number of entries, so also discard the last entry (the face through which the ray enters the mesh for the first time). 4. Traverse each PIX list in the A-Buffer to discover dependencies: For each pair of consecutive entries on a PIX list (after cleanup), identify a Pseudoneighbor (PN) relation. A PN pair consists of a front-facing face of cell c{ij} and a back-facing face of cell c{ij-1}. The cell contributing the back-facing face (c{ij-1}) is the occluding PN. The cell contributing the front-facing face (c{ij}) is the occluded PN. Add a PN entry to the PN list of the occluding PN, containing the cell number of the occluded cell. Set the sink cell flag of the occluded PN to false. Duplicate Handling: Check if the PN relation is already in the occluding PN's PN list. If not, add it to the head of the list. If found, move it to the head if not already there (to exploit coherence). Complexity: O(wh + a) for most data sets, where a is the total area of all exterior faces (pixels scanned). Phase IV: Depth First Search (DFS) for Total Ordering 1. Traverse all cells to find sink cells (those whose sink cell flag is still true). 2. Perform a Depth First Search (DFS) on the directed graph to generate the total ordering of the cells. Traverse each edge in the graph twice. Modification: Occluded neighbors (cells on the PN list of cell c) are now eligible neighbors of c in the DFS. Complexity: O(n + a). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sxmpvo(mesh, viewpoint, imagewidth, imageheight, viewpointoutside): n = mesh.numcells b = mesh.numexteriorfaces w, h = imagewidth, imageheight # Phase I: Create Partial Ordering of Interior Cells exteriorfaces = [] for cell in mesh.cells: cell.sinkflag = True for face in cell.faces: if face.isinterior(): face.arrow = True # Mark arrow for MPVO behind relation else: exteriorfaces.append({'face': face, 'cell': cell, 'centroid': face.centroid, 'next': None}) # Phase II: Sort Exterior Faces exteriorfaces.sort(key=lambda f: distance(viewpoint, f['centroid'])) # Phase III: Scan Convert Exterior Faces and Record PN Relations # A-Buffer: array of head pointers for PIX linked lists abuffer = [None] (w h) pnlists = [None] n # PN list head pointers, initially NULL def insertpixentry(head, entry): # Insertion sort by decreasing z if head is None or entry['z'] >= head['z']: entry['next'] = head return entry curr = head while curr['next'] and curr['next']['z'] > entry['z']: curr = curr['next'] entry['next'] = curr['next'] curr['next'] = entry return head for frecord in exteriorfaces: face = frecord['face'] # Scan-convert face, sampling at pixel centers pixelscovered = scanconvertface(face, viewpoint) for pidx, pcenter in pixelscovered: z = computezdistance(viewpoint, pcenter, face) pixentry = {'z': z, 'face': face, 'next': None} abuffer[pidx] = insertpixentry(abuffer[pidx], pixentry) # Clean up PIX lists for pidx in range(w h): head = abuffer[pidx] if head is None: continue # Discard first entry (back-facing face where ray exits mesh last time) head = head['next'] abuffer[pidx] = head # Discard last entry if viewpoint outside mesh if viewpointoutside: if head is None: continue curr = head while curr['next'] is not None: curr = curr['next'] curr['next'] = None # Traverse PIX list to discover PN dependencies curr = head while curr is not None and curr['next'] is not None: frontentry = curr['next'] backentry = curr occludedcell = frontentry['face'].cell occludingcell = backentry['face'].cell # Add PN relation to occluding PN's list addpnrelation(pnlists, occludingcell.index, occludedcell.index) occludedcell.sinkflag = False # Update sink flag curr = curr['next'] # Phase IV: Depth First Search (DFS) for Total Ordering sinkcells = [c for c in mesh.cells if c.sinkflag] ordering = [] visited = set() def dfs(cell): if cell.index in visited: return visited.add(cell.index) for pnidx in getpnlist(pnlists, cell.index): neighbor = mesh.cells[pnidx] dfs(neighbor) ordering.append(cell) for sink in sinkcells: dfs(sink) return ordering def addpnrelation(pnlists, occludingidx, occludedidx): # Check for duplicates and move to head if found head = pnlists[occludingidx] curr = head while curr is not None: if curr['cellidx'] == occludedidx: # Move to head if not already there if curr != head: pnlists[occludingidx] = curr['next'] curr['next'] = head head = curr pnlists[occludingidx] = head return curr = curr['next'] # Add new entry to head pnlists[occludingidx] = {'cellidx': occludedidx, 'next': head} def getpnlist(pnlists, cellidx): # Standard linked list traversal result = [] curr = pnlists[cellidx] while curr is not None: result.append(curr['cellidx']) curr = curr['next'] return result def scanconvertface(face, viewpoint): # Standard rasterization returning list of (pixelindex, pixelcenter) return [] def computezdistance(viewpoint, pixelcenter, face): # Compute distance from viewpoint to intersection along ray return 0.0 def distance(point1, point2): # Euclidean distance return 0.0 Image Resolution: The visibility ordering is correct if the image resolution used for volume rendering is the same as the one used for computing the visibility ordering relations. Mesh Constraint: The mesh must be acyclic. Geometry Constraint: Cells may have nonplanar surfaces, provided their edges do not have projections that cross each other ("bow tie" quadrilateral projections). Tiny Cells: Tiny cells (those not projecting onto any screen pixels) may be output out of order if they are exterior cells, because the relationship a <{vp} b is only guaranteed if there is a continuous sequence of adjacent intervening cells. Sorting sink cells by increasing distance of their centroid to the viewpoint reduces sorting errors for tiny exterior cells. Splatting: If splatting is used for antialiasing, sorting errors may occur for tiny cells because the relationship a <{vp} b is not guaranteed across regions where ray-gaps may occur. Non-strict Ordering: The sort may not be a strict visibility ordering if overlapping faces are not sampled at points in the region of overlap, though the image space ordering remains correct. An algorithm that improves XMPVO results by building a view-independent BSP tree of the exterior faces to reduce the number of ray shooting queries needed. It augments MPVO ordering using binary space partitions on boundary elements. Runtime is O(n + bp), where p is the size of a small subset of exterior cells. However, building the BSP structure is very slow, and the tree can become deep and unbalanced, leading to O(b) cost per search and O(b^2) overall flavor. Results are orders of magnitude better than previous exact methods, but SXMPVO is faster and easier to implement than BSP-XMPVO. Time Complexity: O(wh + a + n) for most data sets, where w, h are image dimensions, a is the projected area (pixels scanned), and n is the number of cells. Expected cost is O(wh(\hat{d}e + 1) + n), where \hat{d}e is the average depth complexity of exterior faces. Memory Complexity: O(wh + a) for A-Buffer, O(a) for PN lists, O(n) for PN list head pointers, and O(b) for exterior face list. Performance: On an SGI Power Onyx (R10000 250 MHz), for helix3.5 (3.57M cells, 375x450 image), SXMPVO uses 367 MB total vs MPVONC's 347.4 MB. Sorting time for a tetrahedral mesh with 1.5 million cells and 550,000 exterior faces was measured as a linear function of projected exterior face area. On a 2.53 GHz Pentium 4, throughput is 500K-600K tetrahedra per second for a 1,050,000 pixel image. Strengths: Faster than all published exact visibility ordering algorithms in object or image space. Handles nonconvex boundaries, disconnected meshes, and mixed cell types. No extra preprocessing compared to MPVO. Limitations: Slower than MPVONC because it must determine and respect every relationship MPVONC does, plus exterior face relations. Requires acyclic meshes. Tiny exterior cells may be out of order. SXMPVO was introduced by Cook, Max, Williams, and Silva in a manuscript received in 2003 and accepted in 2004. It builds on MPVO and XMPVO. ZSWEEP is a related algorithm by Mitchell, Silva, and Farias (2000) that uses a sweep plane approach. SXMPVO is used for volume rendering systems based on cell projection of unstructured data, specifically tetrahedral and zoo meshes. name: BSP-XMPVO
head: Binary Space Partition MPVO
body: BSP-XMPVO is a technique for fast polyhedral cell sorting for the interactive rendering of unstructured grids. It computes a correct global visibility ordering for cell projection volume rendering by augmenting the approximate ordering produced by Maximal Polyhedra Visibility Ordering (MPVO) with a view-independent Binary Space Partition (BSP) tree of the mesh's exterior faces. Unlike MPVO, which only computes an approximate ordering in general datasets resulting in visual artifacts, BSP-XMPVO provides exact sorting. It differs from its parent method, SXMPVO, by using a view-independent BSP tree of exterior faces for preprocessing, whereas SXMPVO relies on image-precision ray shooting via scan conversion [Parent]. Inputs and outputs: Input: An unstructured mesh composed of polyhedral cells. The mesh must be acyclic to guarantee a valid topological sort [Parent]. Output: A global visibility ordering of the cells suitable for back-to-front compositing in volume rendering. Data structures: 1. BSP Tree: A binary space partition tree constructed from the exterior faces of the mesh. Node Layout: Each node contains a splitting plane, two children pointers (left and right), and optionally a list of faces or cells contained in the node's region. Construction: Built once during preprocessing. 2. MPVO Ordering: An initial approximate ordering of cells generated by the MPVO algorithm. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (View-Independent): Build a BSP tree using the exterior faces of the mesh as splitting planes. This step is performed once and is view-independent. 2. Initial Ordering: Compute an initial cell ordering using the MPVO algorithm. MPVO assumes the mesh is “well-behaved” (acyclic and convex) for exactness, but provides a fast baseline for general meshes. 3. Augmentation via BSP Tree: Use the BSP tree to resolve visibility conflicts that MPVO could not handle due to non-convex boundaries or complex topology. The algorithm effectively shoots query rays through pixel centers, using polygon scan conversion of the exterior faces to add exterior face relations only at the precision necessary for the current image. The BSP structure augments the MPVO ordering by providing exact visibility relationships between cells separated by exterior faces. Formulas and Parameters: n: Number of cells in the mesh. b: Number of exterior faces in the mesh. p: Size of a small subset of exterior cells. Time complexity: O(n + bp). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class BSPNode: def init(self, plane, left=None, right=None, faces=None): self.plane = plane self.left = left self.right = right self.faces = faces def buildbsptree(exteriorfaces): """ Builds a view-independent BSP tree from exterior faces. """ if not exteriorfaces: return None pivot = exteriorfaces[0] plane = pivot.plane front = [f for f in exteriorfaces[1:] if f.distancetoplane(plane) > 0] back = [f for f in exteriorfaces[1:] if f.distancetoplane(plane) <= 0] return BSPNode(plane=plane, left=buildbsptree(front), right=buildbsptree(back), faces=exteriorfaces) def augmentmpvo(cells, mpvoordering, bsproot): """ Augments MPVO ordering using the BSP tree to resolve visibility conflicts. """ ordered = list(mpvoordering) # Rays are shot through pixel centers; exterior faces are scan-converted # to establish exact occlusion relations at image precision for cell in ordered: constraints = traversebsp(bsproot, cell) ordered = applytopologicalconstraints(ordered, constraints) return ordered def traversebsp(node, cell): """ Traverses the BSP tree to collect exterior face visibility constraints for a cell. """ if node is None: return [] if cell.isinfront(node.plane): return traversebsp(node.left, cell) + [node.plane.face] else: return traversebsp(node.right, cell) def applytopologicalconstraints(ordering, constraints): """ Reorders cells to satisfy BSP-derived occlusion constraints. """ # Standard topological sort constrained by the collected face relations return sorted(ordering, key=lambda c: c.visibilityrank) Edge cases and pitfalls: BSP Tree Depth: The BSP tree can become deep and unbalanced, leading to increased processing overhead. Preprocessing Cost: Building the BSP structure is a very slow step. Runtime Overhead: If the tree is unbalanced, searches can take O(b) time, leading to an O(b^2) flavor in the worst case. Time and memory complexity: The time complexity is O(n + bp), where n is the number of cells, b is the number of exterior faces, and p is the size of a small subset of exterior cells. Memory complexity is dominated by the storage of the BSP tree, which is proportional to the number of exterior faces b. Measured performance: BSP-XMPVO results are orders of magnitude better than previous exact methods of sorting cells. It leads to an order of magnitude improvement in sorting times over XMPVO. Scaling: The performance depends on the number of exterior faces b. If the BSP tree becomes deep and unbalanced, the cost per search can degrade to O(b), leading to an overall O(b^2) flavor in practical cases. Strengths and limitations: Strengths: Provides exact visibility ordering for general unstructured meshes, significantly faster than previous exact methods. Limitations: The preprocessing step (building the BSP tree) is very slow and can add considerable processing overhead. The algorithm can become sluggish if the BSP tree becomes deep and unbalanced. When to use it and when not: Not given in the sources. BSP-XMPVO was proposed by João Luiz Dihl Comba, James T. Klosowski, Nelson Max, and Peter L. Williams in 1999. It was introduced as an improvement on the XMPVO method by Silva et al., which itself was an extension of MPVO by Williams. The method was published in the journal Computers & Graphics (or Computer Graphics Forum, as indicated by the source title) in September 1999. It addresses the limitations of MPVO, which only provides approximate ordering for general datasets, and XMPVO, which, while exact, can be slower due to dynamic ray shooting. name: A-buffer visibility sort for non-convex grids
head: Visibility sorting for non-convex grids, Topological Sort with A-Buffer for Non-Convex Grids
body: This method extends the Topological Sort for Cell Projection to handle non-convex grids by using a software A-buffer to detect and resolve visibility relations between boundary cells that are separated by gaps in the grid volume. While the parent method assumes convexity and shared faces, this variant handles cases where viewing rays exit the grid through an exterior face, traverse empty space, and re-enter a different cell. It differs from siblings like Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) by avoiding expensive pairwise occlusion tests or BSP-tree preprocessing, instead relying on per-pixel fragment lists to extract ordering constraints. Inputs: A non-convex curvilinear grid consisting of n cells. A set of exterior (boundary) faces, with count b. Image dimensions w \times h. A viewing direction and camera setup defining pixel sample rays. Outputs: A topologically sorted list of cells suitable for back-to-front volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. Exterior Face List: A list of all exterior faces. Each face contains its geometric definition (vertices) and its centroid depth zc along the viewing direction. 2. Software A-Buffer: An array of size w \times h. Each pixel entry contains a pointer to a linked list of fragments. 3. Fragment: A structure stored in the A-buffer linked lists, containing: faceid: Identifier of the exterior face intersecting the ray. z: The depth of the intersection point along the viewing ray. next: Pointer to the next fragment in the sorted list. 4. Relation Graph: The directed acyclic graph (DAG) used by the topological sort, containing edges for shared faces and edges extracted from the A-buffer. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sort Exterior Faces: Sort the list of b exterior faces in descending order of their centroid depth zc. This ensures that when scan-converting, new intersections are likely to be added to the head of the A-buffer lists, minimizing list maintenance cost. 2. Initialize A-Buffer: Allocate the w \times h A-buffer array. Initialize all pixel entries to null pointers. This step incurs a cost proportional to the number of pixels wh. 3. Scan-Convert and Populate A-Buffer: For each exterior face f in the sorted list: a. Determine the pixel coverage of face f in the image plane. b. For each covered pixel (x, y): i. Compute the intersection point P of the pixel's viewing ray with the face f. ii. Calculate the depth z = P \cdot \vec{v}, where \vec{v} is the normalized viewing direction. iii. Insert a new fragment {faceid: f.id, z: z} into the linked list at A-Buffer[x, y]. iv. Maintain the linked list in ascending order of z (front-to-back). Since faces are processed back-to-front, the new fragment will typically be inserted at the head or near the head of the list. 4. Extract Gap Relations: Iterate through every pixel (x, y) in the A-buffer: a. If the linked list at A-Buffer[x, y] contains more than one fragment, iterate through the list from front to back. b. For every consecutive pair of fragments (Fi, F{i+1}) in the list: i. Let f{front} = Fi.face\id and f{back} = F{i+1}.face\id. ii. Add a directed edge f{back} \to f{front} to the Relation Graph. This edge signifies that f{front} is visible in front of f{back} along this specific ray segment crossing a gap. 5. Process Shared Face Relations: Add the standard topological edges derived from shared faces between adjacent cells in the grid. For two cells Ci and Cj sharing a face, if the viewpoint is in Ci, add edge Cj \to Ci. 6. Topological Sort: Perform a topological sort on the combined Relation Graph (containing both shared-face edges and gap-extracted edges) to produce the final cell ordering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def abuffervisibilitysort(grid, imagewidth, imageheight, viewdirection): # 1. Identify exterior faces and compute centroid depths exteriorfaces = grid.getexteriorfaces() for face in exteriorfaces: face.centroiddepth = dot(face.centroid, viewdirection) # Sort faces back-to-front by centroid depth exteriorfaces.sort(key=lambda f: f.centroiddepth, reverse=True) # 2. Initialize A-Buffer # Each pixel holds a linked list of fragments sorted by z (ascending) abuffer = [None] (imagewidth imageheight) # 3. Scan-convert exterior faces into A-Buffer for face in exteriorfaces: # Determine bounding box of face projection in pixel coordinates pixelcoords = getprojectedpixels(face, imagewidth, imageheight) for (x, y) in pixelcoords: # Compute ray intersection with face rayorigin, raydirection = getpixelray(x, y, viewdirection) intersectionpoint = intersectrayface(rayorigin, raydirection, face) if intersectionpoint is not None: z = dot(intersectionpoint, viewdirection) # Create fragment fragment = { 'faceid': face.id, 'z': z, 'next': None } # Insert into sorted linked list at abuffer[y width + x] head = abuffer[y imagewidth + x] if head is None or z < head['z']: fragment['next'] = head abuffer[y imagewidth + x] = fragment else: current = head while current['next'] is not None and current['next']['z'] < z: current = current['next'] fragment['next'] = current['next'] current['next'] = fragment # 4. Extract relations from A-Buffer relationgraph = RelationGraph() for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): head = abuffer[y imagewidth + x] current = head while current is not None: nextfrag = current['next'] if nextfrag is not None: # Extract relation: nextfrag is behind current # Edge from back cell to front cell backfaceid = nextfrag['faceid'] frontfaceid = current['faceid'] relationgraph.addedge(backfaceid, frontfaceid) current = nextfrag # 5. Add shared face relations sharedfacerelations = grid.getsharedfacerelations(viewdirection) relationgraph.addedges(sharedfacerelations) # 6. Topological Sort sortedcells = relationgraph.topologicalsort() return sortedcells Parameters and Typical Values: w, h: Image resolution. Typical values depend on the target display or output size. b: Number of exterior faces. Depends on grid complexity. a: Projected area of external faces in pixels. Proportional to the number of pixels covered by exterior faces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Planar Faces: In curvilinear grids, quadrilateral faces may not be planar. A viewing ray can leave a cell and re-enter it across the same face, making a strict visibility sort impossible for that face. The algorithm handles this by treating the face as a single intersection event in the A-buffer, but correctness of the topological sort for such cells is not guaranteed in a geometric sense, though image correctness is maintained. Occlusion Outside Pixel Centers: The algorithm does not produce a true global visibility sort because cells may occlude each other along rays that do not pass through pixel centers. However, since the A-buffer rays match the pixel sample rays used in final hardware rendering, the final image is correct. Memory Overhead: The A-buffer stores a linked list per pixel. In scenes with high overlap of exterior faces, lists can become long, increasing memory usage and traversal time. An A-Buffer technique by Farias et al. that optimizes for sorting and memory usage. k-Buffer Analysis is a software-based diagnostic method used to determine the optimal fixed buffer size k for the k-buffer visibility sorting algorithm in hardware-assisted volume rendering. It solves the problem of selecting a k value that balances rendering precision against memory and computational efficiency by analyzing the depth-ordering requirements of a specific dataset. Unlike the unbounded A-buffer, which stores all fragments, or conservative sorting schemes like ZSWEEP, the k-buffer limits storage to k entries per pixel, requiring an analysis of how "nearly sorted" the fragment stream is to ensure correct compositing. Time Complexity: The algorithm typically takes time O(b \log b + wh + a + n). b \log b: Sorting the exterior faces by centroid depth. wh: Overhead for setting up and checking the A-buffer lists for all pixels. a: Cost of scan-converting exterior faces, extracting relations from A-buffer lists, and processing them during the topological sort. This is proportional to the projected area a of the external faces in pixels. n: Processing relations across shared faces, same as in the convex case. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the A-buffer, which requires storage for wh linked lists. The total number of fragments stored is proportional to the total number of intersections between viewing rays and exterior faces, which is bounded by a \times k{max}, where k{max} is the maximum number of overlapping exterior faces projected onto a single pixel. Performance and Scaling: The method is faster than pairwise occlusion tests (O(b^2)) or BSP-tree based approaches for general non-convex grids. It scales linearly with the number of pixels and the projected area of exterior faces. However, it may degrade if the number of overlapping exterior faces per pixel is very large, leading to long linked lists. Strengths: Avoids complex geometric preprocessing like BSP trees. Handles non-convex grids with gaps between boundary cells. Ensures image correctness by aligning visibility checks with pixel sample rays. Limitations: Not a true geometric visibility sort; relies on pixel-level sampling. Memory intensive for high-resolution images or highly overlapping exterior faces. Performance depends on the projected area a; large exterior faces increase cost. The A-buffer was introduced by Loren Carpenter in 1984 as a method to resolve visibility and aliasing problems by maintaining multiple fragments per pixel. The application of the A-buffer to visibility sorting for non-convex grids in volume rendering was proposed by Comba, Silva, and others in the early 2000s. This approach was developed to address the limitations of topological sorting methods that assumed convexity, allowing for efficient rendering of complex curvilinear and unstructured grids without the overhead of BSP-tree construction. name: ZSWEEP
head: ZSweep, ZSweep Algorithm
body: ZSWEEP is an exact, object-order cell projection algorithm for volume rendering on unstructured grids that optimizes for sorting efficiency and memory usage. It solves the problem of correctly ordering cell segments for front-to-back compositing without the high memory overhead of ray-casting or the complexity of true global visibility sorts. It sets itself apart from its parent A-buffer visibility sort for non-convex grids by using a sweep-plane approach that exploits the implicit global ordering induced by vertex z-coordinates, rather than maintaining full A-buffer lists for all pixels simultaneously. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unstructured mesh containing tetrahedral and/or hexahedral cells. Output: A rendered image with correct front-to-back compositing of cell contributions. Data Structures: Sweep Plane State: A set of active cells and faces currently intersected by the sweep plane. Pixel Lists: For each pixel, a short list of ordered face intersections. This list is maintained to be correct and complete at the instant each stage of computation is completed. Auxiliary Structures: Stores partial information taken from a small number of "slices" of the dataset, rather than the entire dataset in memory. Steps: 1. Sort Vertices: Order all vertices of the mesh by their z-coordinate (depth) relative to the viewing plane. 2. Initialize Sweep: Initialize the sweep plane at the minimum z-coordinate of the mesh. 3. Sweep and Project: Advance the sweep plane to the next vertex in the sorted z-order. Identify all cells incident to the current vertex. Project the faces of these cells onto the image plane. Avoid Double Projection: Apply logic to ensure internal faces are not projected twice (once for each adjacent cell). Update Pixel Lists: Update the ordered face intersection lists for the affected pixels. The z-ordering of vertices induces an approximate global ordering on the cells, which helps maintain the correct front-to-back order in the pixel lists. 4. Compute Contribution: For each pixel, use the current short list of ordered face intersections to compute the color and opacity contribution. Ensure the list is correct and complete before computing the contribution for that stage. Composite the contribution into the frame buffer using standard front-to-back alpha compositing equations. 5. Sparsification (Optional): Apply a data sparsification technique to reduce the number of cells processed, if applicable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zsweep(mesh, viewdirection): # 1. Sort vertices by z-coordinate vertices = mesh.getvertices() sortedvertices = sortbyz(vertices, viewdirection) # 2. Initialize data structures # pixellists: dict mapping pixelid -> list of (face, zdepth) pixellists = {} # activecells: set of cells currently intersected by sweep plane activecells = set() # 3. Sweep through vertices for vertex in sortedvertices: # Get cells incident to this vertex incidentcells = mesh.getincidentcells(vertex) # Update active cells for cell in incidentcells: if cell not in activecells: activecells.add(cell) # Project faces of the cell faces = cell.getfaces() for face in faces: # Check if face is internal to avoid double projection if not isinternalface(face, activecells): projectedface = projectface(face, viewdirection) # Update pixel lists for the pixels covered by this face updatepixellists(pixellists, projectedface, vertex.z) # 4. Compute contributions for affected pixels affectedpixels = getaffectedpixels(activecells) for pixelid in affectedpixels: if pixelid in pixellists: # Ensure list is sorted and complete sortpixellist(pixellists[pixelid]) # Compute and composite contribution compositepixel(pixelid, pixellists[pixelid]) return framebuffer def isinternalface(face, activecells): # A face is internal if it is shared by two cells in the active set # This is a simplified check; actual implementation requires adjacency info neighbors = face.getneighbors() inactive = [n for n in neighbors if n in activecells] return len(inactive) > 1 def updatepixellists(pixellists, projectedface, zdepth): for pixelid in projectedface.getcoveredpixels(): if pixelid not in pixellists: pixellists[pixelid] = [] # Insert face into list maintaining z-order insertinorder(pixellists[pixelid], (projectedface, zdepth)) Parameters: Cell Types: Handles tetrahedral and/or hexahedral cells. Sparsification: A simple technique may be applied to reduce dataset size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double Projection: Internal faces must be carefully handled to avoid double counting. Ordering Correctness: The implicit ordering induced by vertex z-coordinates is approximate; care must be taken to assure correctness in the projection order. Hardware Mapping: There is no simple way to map this algorithm into currently available graphics hardware. Out-of-Core ZSWEEP is a direct volume rendering technique for large unstructured grids that extends the in-core ZSWEEP algorithm to handle datasets exceeding available RAM by processing data in tiles and loading meta-cells from disk only when needed. It differs from its sibling MIR by being substantially faster and leveraging the ZSWEEP optimization of front-to-back sorting, at the cost of more complex preprocessing and higher main-memory requirements. Time Complexity: Up to 5 times faster than the best previously-known exact algorithms that use comparable amounts of memory. Memory Complexity: Memory efficient, using much less memory than ray-casting. Auxiliary structures store only partial information from a small number of dataset slices. Strengths: Simple, fast, and memory-efficient for exact rendering of unstructured datasets. Adaptable to general non-tetrahedral cell formats. Limitations: No simple way to map into currently available graphics hardware. Requires careful handling of internal faces and ordering correctness. When to Use: When exact rendering of unstructured grids is required, and memory is a constraint, and hardware acceleration is not a primary requirement. When Not to Use: When hardware acceleration is needed or when approximate rendering is acceptable. ZSWEEP was introduced by Ricardo Farias, Joseph S. B. Mitchell, and Claudio Silva in 2000. It is an A-Buffer technique that optimizes for sorting and memory usage. The algorithm is hardware-independent and handles datasets containing tetrahedral and/or hexahedral cells. name: Out-of-Core ZSWEEP
head: OOC-ZSWEEP
body: Out-of-Core ZSWEEP is a direct volume rendering technique for large unstructured grids that extends the in-core ZSWEEP algorithm to handle datasets exceeding available RAM by processing data in tiles and loading meta-cells from disk only when needed. It differs from its sibling MIR by being substantially faster and leveraging the ZSWEEP optimization of front-to-back sorting, at the cost of more complex preprocessing and higher main-memory requirements. The algorithm is divided into two distinct phases: a view-independent preprocessing phase performed once to generate disk files, and a view-dependent rendering phase. Input: An unstructured volumetric grid defined by vertices and cells. Output: A rendered image (pixel colors/compositing results). The preprocessing generates two primary files on disk: 1. Meta-cell File: A small file containing a high-level description for each meta-cell. Each entry includes: Bounding box. Number of vertices. Number of cells. Pointer to the start of the meta-cell's data in the main data file. 2. Meta-cell Data File: A larger file containing the actual list of vertices and cells for each meta-cell. Vertices and cells may appear repeated across different meta-cells because each meta-cell is a self-contained unit. During rendering, the following in-memory structures are used: Pixel Intersection Lists: For each pixel in the current tile, a sorted list of intersections storing z-values and auxiliary information. Vertex Queue: A queue used for sweeping vertices. Vertices are tagged as either 'bounding-box' or 'dataset' vertices. Meta-cell Memory Buffer: Holds the vertices and cells of the currently active meta-cell(s) loaded from disk. 1. Chunk Creation (Meta-cell Generation): Let v be the total number of vertices and m be the target number of vertices per meta-cell. Externally sort all vertices by their x-values. Partition the sorted vertices into \lceil v/m \rceil consecutive parts. For each part, externally sort its vertices by y-values. Partition each part into \lceil v/m \rceil sub-parts. For each refined part, externally sort its vertices by z-values. Take the final parts as chunks (meta-cells). These chunks have roughly the same number of vertices but may differ in volume. 2. Meta-cell Association: Compute which cells spatially intersect each meta-cell and identify the vertices belonging to those cells. This is performed in external memory. The output is the two files described above. Note: Unlike the meta-cells in Chiang et al. [2], a cell in this variant can belong to as many meta-cells as it spatially intersects. The rendering is performed tile by tile. 1. Tile Division: Subdivide the screen into tiles. 2. Tile Processing: For each tile: 1. Compute the set of meta-cells that project into (intersect) the current tile. 2. Sort these meta-cells in a front-to-back order based on their depth relative to the camera. 3. Initialize the vertex queue and pixel intersection lists for the tile. 4. Sweep Loop: While the queue is not empty: Dequeue the next vertex v. If v is a bounding-box vertex: If the meta-cell m associated with this bounding box has not been loaded: Retrieve all vertices and cells of m from the disk files. Transform the vertices to view space. Insert these vertices into the queue, tagging them as dataset vertices. Increment the counter of bounding-box vertices seen for meta-cell m. If the counter for m reaches 8: Deallocate the memory for meta-cell m (free memory from disk). If v is a dataset vertex: Project the faces incident to v. For each pixel covered by the face, compute the intersection of the ray emanating from the pixel with the face. Store the z-value and auxiliary information in the pixel's intersection list in sorted order. Compositing: As the sweep plane reaches the "target Z" plane for each pixel, perform compositing using the accumulated intersection list for that pixel. Target vertices per meta-cell (m): Determines the size of the chunks. The number of meta-cells should be small enough to fit in memory. Tile Size: Determines the granularity of screen subdivision. Smaller tiles reduce peak memory usage for pixel intersection lists but increase overhead. Memory Usage: Main memory usage is dominated by pixel intersection lists and the "use set" of each vertex (cells incident to each vertex) for the currently loaded meta-cells. Cell Overlap: A single cell may be stored in multiple meta-cells if it spatially intersects multiple meta-cells. This increases disk space but simplifies the rendering logic by making meta-cells self-contained. Bounding Box Count: The algorithm assumes 8 bounding-box vertices per meta-cell (likely corresponding to a hexahedral bounding box). If the meta-cell geometry differs, the deallocation condition must be adjusted. Memory Complexity: Constant memory usage with respect to dataset size. For a large 2048-by-2048 image of the Delta dataset, in-core ZSWEEP requires over 380 MB, while OOC-ZSWEEP requires about 24 MB. Time Complexity: Rendering times depend on the number of cells and resolution. For the SPX3 dataset at 2048^2 resolution, OOC-ZSWEEP took 1157 seconds to generate the image, with a cost of 174 µs per cell. Comparison with MIR: OOC-ZSWEEP is usually more efficient than MIR (Memory Insensitive Rendering), sometimes by a factor of 10 or more. However, it requires preprocessing and uses more memory than MIR. MIR is simpler to implement and may be preferred for rendering the same viewpoint with different transfer functions, as lighting calculations are deferred. Strengths: Enables rendering of datasets larger than RAM; faster than purely disk-based methods like MIR; leverages ZSWEEP's early compositing and sorting optimizations. Limitations: Complex preprocessing; higher memory usage than MIR; implementation complexity due to lazy loading and queue management. Out-of-Core ZSWEEP was introduced by Farias et al. as an extension of the ZSWEEP algorithm [4] to handle unstructured grids that do not fit in main memory. It builds on the meta-cell concept from Chiang et al. [2], adapting it for the specific needs of the ZSWEEP sweep process. The method was designed to address the limitations of in-core algorithms when dealing with large scientific datasets, providing a balance between the speed of in-core rendering and the capacity of out-of-core techniques. name: k*-Buffer Analysis
head: k*-Buffer, k-value Analysis
body: k-Buffer Analysis is a software-based diagnostic method used to determine the optimal fixed buffer size k for the k-buffer visibility sorting algorithm in hardware-assisted volume rendering. It solves the problem of selecting a k value that balances rendering precision against memory and computational efficiency by analyzing the depth-ordering requirements of a specific dataset. Unlike the unbounded A-buffer, which stores all fragments, or conservative sorting schemes like ZSWEEP, the k-buffer limits storage to k entries per pixel, requiring an analysis of how "nearly sorted" the fragment stream is to ensure correct compositing. The method consists of two phases: the operational logic of the k-buffer itself and the analytical procedure to derive the required k. Inputs: A set of 3D primitives (e.g., tetrahedra or triangles) from a volume dataset. A camera viewpoint and projection parameters. A target resolution (e.g., 512 \times 512). Outputs: The maximum required k (k{max}) for the dataset. The distribution of pixels requiring specific k values (e.g., count of pixels where k > 2 or k > 6). Identification of geometric degeneracies (e.g., sliver cells) causing high k requirements. A-Buffer (for Analysis): A 2D array of lists, one per pixel. Each list stores fragments sorted by depth (distance from viewpoint). Fragment entry: {depth: float, color: vec3, opacity: float}. k-buffer (for Operational Logic): A fixed-size array of k entries per pixel. Entry: {depth: float, color: vec3, opacity: float}. In hardware implementations, entries are often kept unsorted to simplify logic, relying on the property that the input sequence is k-nearly sorted. This phase simulates an ideal A-buffer to measure the true sorting distance of fragments. 1. Initialize an A-buffer for the target resolution. Each pixel contains an empty sorted list. 2. Rasterize the dataset from the viewpoint, generating a stream of fragments. 3. For each fragment f{new} with depth d{new}: a. Find the correct insertion position in the pixel's sorted A-buffer list such that depths are in increasing order (for front-to-back compositing). b. Let i be the index of the insertion position (0-based). c. Record the insertion depth metric: k{pixel} = \max(k{pixel}, i). Note: The definition of k in the analysis is "the number of positions any fragment had to move to its correct position in the sorted order minus one for compositing". Effectively, if a fragment must be inserted at index i, it implies that up to i closer fragments exist. For compositing, we need access to the closest and second closest, so the buffer size requirement relates to this displacement. The analysis reports k as the maximum index i observed across all fragments for that pixel. 4. Aggregate results: a. k{max} = \max{\text{pixels}} (k{pixel}). b. Count pixels where k{pixel} > 2. c. Count pixels where k{pixel} > 6. 5. Visualize (optional) the spatial distribution of k requirements to identify problematic regions (e.g., sliver cells). This phase describes how the determined k is used during rendering. 1. Initialize a k-buffer of size k for each pixel. 2. For each fragment f{new} arriving at a pixel: a. If the k-buffer is not full: i. Insert f{new} into the buffer. ii. If maintaining sorted order: shift elements to maintain depth order. iii. If unsorted (hardware simplification): append f{new} to the end. b. If the k-buffer is full: i. Determine if f{new} should replace an existing fragment. ii. For front-to-back compositing, the fragment furthest from the viewer (largest depth) is the least relevant for early ray termination and compositing accuracy of the front surface. iii. Discard the fragment with the largest depth (or the first entry f1 if sorted front-to-back, where f1 is closest? Correction: The source states "dislodges the first entry (f1)" for front-to-back. In a front-to-back sorted list, f1 is the closest. However, standard k-buffer logic for streaming usually discards the furthest to keep the closest k. Note that... f{new} may be inserted at the beginning... if it is closer... or at the end if further." This implies the buffer maintains the k closest fragments. Safe Implementation Description: The k-buffer maintains the k fragments with the smallest depth values (closest to viewer). 1. If buffer size < k, insert f{new}. 2. If buffer size == k: a. If depth(f{new}) < depth(f{max}) (where f{max} is the fragment with largest depth in buffer): i. Insert f{new}. ii. Remove f{max}. b. Else: i. Discard f{new}. This ensures the k closest are kept. The source's mention of "dislodging f1" likely refers to a specific implementation detail or a typo where f1 denotes the last element in a 0-indexed array or the element being evicted. I will note the source's specific text but provide the logically correct implementation for volume rendering. 3. Compositing: a. Retrieve the k fragments from the buffer. b. Sort them by depth (if not kept sorted). c. Perform front-to-back compositing using the pre-integrated table lookup. Note that k+1 entries are required for correct compositing of a k-nearly sorted sequence because the closest and second closest must be available for the lookup. k: The number of fragment entries stored per pixel. Typical Value: 6 is the standard value in existing HAVS implementations. Experimental Values: 6, 8, 10, 12. Trade-off: Larger k yields more precise results but lower efficiency (higher memory and processing time). Highly Out-of-Order Input: If the incoming fragment sequence is not k-nearly sorted, the output will be incorrect and artifacts may be visible. Sliver Cells: Large, thin cells with bad aspect ratios cause high k requirements. Solution 1: Subdivide degenerate cells into smaller, more symmetric cells using Delaunay tetrahedralization properties (empty circumsphere). Solution 2: Mesh smoothing operations to eliminate bad cells without creating additional tetrahedra. Artifact Visibility: Artifacts from limited k are often hard to notice, especially with transparent transfer functions. In worst-case scenarios (e.g., Torso dataset), only a small percentage of pixels (0.6%) were truly incorrect. Unverified code. """ # Initialize A-buffer: list of lists, one per pixel # Each inner list stores fragments sorted by depth (ascending) abuffer = [[[] for in range(resolution[1])] for in range(resolution[0])] # Track max k per pixel kperpixel = [[0 for in range(resolution[1])] for in range(resolution[0])] # Generate fragments from dataset fragments = rasterize(dataset, viewpoint, resolution) for frag in fragments: u, v = frag.screencoords depth = frag.depth # Find insertion index in sorted A-buffer pixellist = abuffer[u][v] insertidx = 0 for i, existingfrag in enumerate(pixellist): if depth < existingfrag.depth: insertidx = i break else: insertidx = i + 1 # Insert fragment pixellist.insert(insertidx, frag) # Record k requirement for this pixel # k is defined as the number of positions the fragment had to move # (or its index in the sorted list) minus one for compositing logic? # Source says: "number of positions any fragment had to move to its correct position # in the sorted order minus one for compositing" # And "Max k" is the max index observed. # We use the index as the metric for k requirement. kperpixel[u][v] = max(kperpixel[u][v], insertidx) # Aggregate results maxk = 0 countkgt2 = 0 countkgt6 = 0 for u in range(resolution[0]): for v in range(resolution[1]): kval = kperpixel[u][v] if kval > maxk: maxk = kval if kval > 2: countkgt2 += 1 if kval > 6: countkgt6 += 1 return { "maxk": maxk, "pixelskgt2": countkgt2, "pixelskgt6": countkgt6, "distribution": kperpixel } def kbufferinsert(buffer, frag, k): """ Inserts a fragment into a k-buffer of size k. Maintains the k closest fragments. """ # If buffer is not full, insert and sort if len(buffer) < k: buffer.append(frag) buffer.sort(key=lambda x: x.depth) return # Buffer is full # Find the fragment with the largest depth (furthest) furthestidx = -1 maxdepth = -1 for i, f in enumerate(buffer): if f.depth > maxdepth: maxdepth = f.depth furthestidx = i # If new fragment is closer than the furthest in buffer, replace it if frag.depth < maxdepth: buffer[furthestidx] = frag buffer.sort(key=lambda x: x.depth) # Else, discard the new fragment A sibling method that uses a conservative technique for compositing samples to avoid memory space explosion in the A-buffer. The k-buffer offers a less conservative sorting scheme but requires analysis to ensure k is sufficient. The parent method that uses an unbounded buffer. k-buffer analysis determines the fixed size k needed to approximate the A-buffer's behavior efficiently. Time Complexity: Analysis: O(N \log K) or O(N \cdot K) depending on implementation, where N is the number of fragments. The source notes that sorting n fragments with a k-nearly sorted property can be done in O(n) time. Rendering: O(1) per fragment insertion if k is fixed and small. Memory Complexity: O(k \cdot W \cdot H), where W, H are image dimensions. This is significantly less than the unbounded A-buffer O(N \cdot W \cdot H) in worst cases. Origin: The k-buffer was introduced as part of the Hardware-Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS) algorithm for unstructured grid volume rendering. History: Developed by Steve Callahan and colleagues, as detailed in the MS thesis "The k-Buffer and Its Applications to Volume Rendering". name: Power Distance Sort
head: Power Distance Sorting, Power Sorting, Radical axis sorting, Visibility sorting via circumcircles
body: Power Distance Sort is a visibility sorting method that orders primitives (triangles or tetrahedra) front-to-back relative to a camera origin by comparing the power of the viewpoint with respect to the circumcircles or circumspheres of the primitives. It serves as a fast, constant-time sorting criterion for Delaunay triangulations, distinguishing itself from general-purpose sorts by leveraging geometric properties of the mesh topology. Unlike exact visibility algorithms, it is not guaranteed to produce correct ordering for non-Delaunay meshes. Inputs: A set of primitives Ti (triangles in 2D or tetrahedra in 3D) forming a Delaunay triangulation/tetrahedralization. A camera origin \mathbf{o}. Outputs: A sorted list of primitives in back-to-front order relative to \mathbf{o}. Data Structures: Each primitive T stores its circumcenter \mathbb{O}(T) and circumradius \mathbb{R}(T). These are precomputed based on the vertices of T. Steps: 1. For each primitive T, compute the power of the viewpoint \mathbf{o} relative to the circumcircle/circumsphere of T. 2. Sort all primitives in ascending order of this power value. Formula: The power P(T) of the viewpoint \mathbf{o} with respect to the circumsphere of primitive T is defined as: P(T) = \|\mathbb{O}(T) - \mathbf{o}\|2^2 - \mathbb{R}(T)^2 Where: \mathbb{O}(T) is the center of the circumsphere of T. \mathbb{R}(T) is the radius of the circumsphere of T. \mathbf{o} is the camera origin. \|\cdot\|2 denotes the Euclidean norm. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computepowerdistancesort(primitives, cameraorigin): """ Sorts primitives by power distance relative to cameraorigin. Assumes primitives form a Delaunay triangulation/tetrahedralization. Args: primitives: List of primitive objects, each having attributes: circumcenter: tuple (x, y, z) or (x, y) circumradius: float cameraorigin: tuple (x, y, z) or (x, y) Returns: List of primitives sorted from back to front (ascending power distance). """ # Step 1: Compute power distance for each primitive scoredprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: # Calculate squared Euclidean distance between circumcenter and camera origin dx = prim.circumcenter[0] - cameraorigin[0] dy = prim.circumcenter[1] - cameraorigin[1] # Add z-component if 3D if len(prim.circumcenter) == 3: dz = prim.circumcenter[2] - cameraorigin[2] distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz else: distsq = dxdx + dydy # Power distance formula: ||O - o||^2 - R^2 power = distsq - (prim.circumradius 2) scoredprimitives.append((power, prim)) # Step 2: Sort by power distance ascending # Ascending order corresponds to back-to-front for Delaunay meshes relative to origin scoredprimitives.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Return just the primitives in sorted order return [prim for, prim in scoredprimitives] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Delaunay Meshes: The method is not guaranteed to produce an accurate visibility ordering unless the mesh is a Delaunay triangulation. There is no way to tell in advance whether a given non-Delaunay mesh will be correctly sorted. Viewpoint Position: The sort order is relative to the ray origin, making it valid for fisheye lenses and distorted projections. However, simple schemes like power distance sorts may fail from certain viewpoints or viewing directions even for Delaunay meshes if the geometric assumptions are violated (e.g., degenerate configurations). Precision: Computing circumcenters and radii can be numerically unstable for nearly cospherical points, which may lead to incorrect sorting if precision is insufficient. Time Complexity: O(n \log n) due to sorting, where n is the number of primitives. The computation of power distance per primitive is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(n) to store the power values and primitive references. Performance: Fast with very small constant computations and straightforward implementation for Delaunay meshes. Strengths: Works with distorted projections (e.g., fisheye) because it is based on the camera origin rather than a view direction. Limitations: Not applicable to general non-Delaunay meshes without guarantees of correctness. Accuracy is not predictable for arbitrary meshes. Power Distance Sort was described by Cignoni et al. and Wittenbrink. It leverages the geometric property that for two adjacent triangles in a Delaunay triangulation, the shared edge lies along the radical axis of their circumcircles. The radical axis divides the plane into two regions where the viewpoint has a lower power distance to one circumcircle or the other. Since the relative depth order of the two triangles flips only when the viewpoint crosses this axis, sorting by power distance yields the correct visibility order. This property generalizes to 3D, where the shared face of two tetrahedra lies on the radical plane. name: Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant)
head: Wilhelms et al. Per-Pixel Sort, Wilhelms et al. Sorting
body: Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant) is an image-space visibility ordering method that sorts all cell faces projecting onto a specific pixel at render time, just prior to compositing. Unlike Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO), which sorts only exterior faces, this variant processes the entire set of projected faces. It handles visibility cycles gracefully because a local visibility sort always exists for each pixel center, even if no global cell sort exists. It differs from Power Distance Sort and Newell-based Visibility Sorting by relying on explicit per-pixel sorting structures (buckets and lists) rather than distance metrics or normal-based approximations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of convex polyhedral cells (or meshes) with their geometric definitions (vertices, faces) and the viewing parameters (camera position, projection matrix, screen resolution). Output: A list of fragments (face segments) sorted back-to-front for each pixel, ready for alpha compositing. Data Structures: The method adapts scan-line visible surface algorithm techniques using the following structures: 1. Y-Buckets: A list of lists indexed by scan line y. Each bucket contains faces that intersect that scan line. 2. Active List: A list of faces currently intersecting the current scan line y. 3. X-Buckets: A list of lists indexed by pixel column x within the current scan line. Each bucket contains faces covering that pixel. 4. Z-Sorted List: A list of fragments (or face segments) at the current pixel (x, y), sorted by depth z. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create empty Y-Buckets for all scan lines y in the image height. 2. Scan Line Processing: Iterate through each scan line y from top to bottom (or bottom to top, consistent with coordinate system): a. Update Active List: Add faces from the Y-Bucket at y to the Active List. Remove faces from the Active List that no longer intersect y (i.e., their y-range has ended). b. Pixel Processing: Iterate through each pixel x in the scan line: i. Update X-Buckets: For each face in the Active List, determine if it covers pixel x. If so, add the face segment to the X-Bucket at x. (Note: Sources describe using X-Buckets for the first pixel a face covers, implying a sweep or incremental update). ii. Sort Z-List: Collect all face segments in the X-Bucket at x. Sort these segments by their depth z at the pixel center (or average depth) in back-to-front order. If multiple overlapping meshes are handled, z-values must be updated and the sort rechecked or resorted at each new pixel. iii. Composite: Perform alpha compositing on the sorted Z-List to produce the final pixel color. iv. Cleanup: Clear the X-Bucket at x for the next pixel. 3. Termination: After all scan lines and pixels are processed, the image is complete. Formulas: Depth z for a face at pixel (x, y) is typically computed via perspective division of the transformed vertex coordinates or interpolated across the face. The sort order is determined by z{back} > z{front} (assuming back-to-front compositing). Parameters: k: Not applicable directly, but related to Nearly-Sorted Object-Space Visibility Ordering which relaxes this strict sort. Resolution: Screen width and height determine the number of pixels and scan lines. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Cycles: The method handles cycles gracefully per pixel, as a local sort always exists. Coherence: The method takes partial advantage of coherence in x (via X-Buckets/Active List updates) but not in y (since Y-Buckets are accessed sequentially but Active List updates are not fully coherent across scan lines in the same way). Performance: Since exterior faces are a small fraction of total faces in most meshes, this method spends far greater effort on per-pixel sorting compared to exterior-face-only methods. Hardware Status: Hardware implementations (e.g., R-Buffer) do not exist; software versions repeat sorts from scratch independently at each pixel, doing more work than incremental updates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perpixelsortgeneralvariant(cells, screenwidth, screenheight): # Initialize Y-Buckets: list of lists, one per scan line ybuckets = [[] for in range(screenheight)] # Populate Y-Buckets with faces for face in cells: ymin, ymax = face.getyrange() if ymin < screenheight and ymax >= 0: ymin = max(0, ymin) ymax = min(screenheight - 1, ymax) for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): ybuckets[y].append(face) image = [[None for in range(screenwidth)] for in range(screenheight)] for y in range(screenheight): activelist = [] # Add faces starting at this scan line for face in ybuckets[y]: activelist.append(face) # Remove faces that end before this scan line (if not handled by bucket logic) # Note: The source implies Y-Buckets store faces for the first scan line they cross. # We need to manage the active list based on face y-ranges. # Simplified: Assume ybuckets[y] contains faces that start at y. # We need a separate mechanism to remove faces that end. # For completeness, we assume a standard scan-line algorithm structure. # Re-initialize active list properly based on face extents activelist = [face for face in allfaces if face.ymin <= y <= face.ymax] for x in range(screenwidth): # Identify faces covering pixel (x, y) # This requires checking face bounding boxes or rasterization coveringfaces = [] for face in activelist: if face.coverspixel(x, y): coveringfaces.append(face) # Sort faces by depth z at (x, y) # Depth calculation depends on projection sortedfaces = sortbydepth(coveringfaces, x, y) # Composite color = compositebacktofront(sortedfaces) image[y][x] = color return image def sortbydepth(faces, x, y): # Calculate depth z for each face at pixel (x, y) # This is a placeholder for the specific depth calculation (e.g., plane equation) facedepths = [] for face in faces: z = face.getdepthatpixel(x, y) facedepths.append((z, face)) # Sort back-to-front (descending z if z increases away from camera) # Assuming standard view where larger z is further facedepths.sort(key=lambda item: item[0], reverse=True) return [item[1] for item in facedepths] Note: The pseudocode above is a high-level representation. The source notes emphasize the use of Y-Buckets, Active Lists, X-Buckets, and Z-Sorted Lists. The exact implementation of "X-Buckets" in the source suggests an incremental update where faces are added to the current pixel's bucket as they are encountered, rather than re-scanning the active list for every pixel. A more efficient implementation would update the active list and x-buckets incrementally. Revised Pseudocode (closer to source description): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perpixelsortgeneralvariantoptimized(cells, screenwidth, screenheight): # Y-Buckets: list of lists, one per scan line ybuckets = [[] for in range(screenheight)] # Populate Y-Buckets for face in cells: ymin, ymax = face.getyrange() if ymin < screenheight and ymax >= 0: ymin = max(0, ymin) ymax = min(screenheight - 1, ymax) # Store face in the bucket of its first scan line ybuckets[ymin].append(face) image = [[None for in range(screenwidth)] for in range(screenheight)] for y in range(screenheight): activelist = [] # Add faces starting at this scan line for face in ybuckets[y]: activelist.append(face) # X-Buckets: list of lists, one per pixel in the current scan line xbuckets = [[] for in range(screenwidth)] for x in range(screenwidth): # Update X-Buckets: Add faces from active list that cover this pixel # This is the "incremental" part, taking advantage of x-coherence for face in activelist: if face.coverspixel(x, y): xbuckets[x].append(face) # Remove faces from active list that no longer cover the current scan line # This requires checking face ymax activelist = [face for face in activelist if face.ymax >= y] # Sort Z-List: Sort faces in xbuckets[x] by depth sortedfaces = sortbydepth(xbuckets[x], x, y) # Composite color = compositebacktofront(sortedfaces) image[y][x] = color return image Mammen's Technique is a software algorithm designed to sort transparent fragments per pixel, specifically positioning them in front of the front-most opaque fragment. It addresses the visibility ordering problem in object-order rendering where transparent surfaces must be composited from back to front. Unlike incremental methods that exploit spatial coherence between adjacent pixels, Mammen's Technique performs independent, complete sorts for each pixel, which distinguishes it from its sibling Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant) by prioritizing simplicity of logic over computational efficiency. A relaxation of exact sorting where fragments are allowed to be up to k positions out of order in object-space, allowing for faster sorting algorithms while requiring exact sorting during fragment processing. It generates nearly-sorted sequences using hierarchical spatial data structures like BSP-trees or simple centroid sorting. The k-buffer can sort a k-nearly sorted sequence of n fragments in O(n) time. Time Complexity: The method spends significant effort on per-pixel sorting. Since it sorts all faces (not just exterior), the complexity is higher than exterior-face-only methods. The source notes that software versions repeat sorts from scratch independently at each pixel, which is less efficient than incremental updates. Memory Complexity: Requires substantial amounts of memory proportional to the projected area of all faces in pixels. This contrasts with methods that only handle boundary faces, which require memory proportional to the projected area of the mesh boundary. Strengths: Handles visibility cycles gracefully. Simple logic. Limitations: High memory usage. No hardware implementation exists. Does not take advantage of coherence in y. When to Use: Situations where visibility cycles are common and a global sort is not feasible. Rendering glass helmets or windshields in games (as suggested for R-Buffer hardware). When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or when exterior faces dominate the visual complexity (use SXMPVO instead). The method was proposed by Wilhelms et al.. It is based on scan-line visible surface algorithm techniques. The R-Buffer hardware proposal by Wittenbrink aimed to implement a similar method for tetrahedral primitives, but the hardware does not exist. The method is used in contexts where exact visibility ordering is difficult due to non-convexity or cycles. name: Mammen's Technique
head: Per-pixel transparent fragment sorting
body: Mammen's Technique is a software algorithm to sort per-pixel transparent fragments in front of the front-most opaque one. It addresses the visibility ordering problem in object-order rendering where transparent surfaces must be composited from back to front. Unlike incremental methods that exploit spatial coherence between adjacent pixels, Mammen's Technique performs independent, complete sorts for each pixel from scratch. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of polygonal fragments projected onto a specific pixel, each containing a depth value (z) and an opacity attribute. Output: A sorted list of transparent fragments ordered from back to front, followed by the front-most opaque fragment. Data Structures: A list of fragments projecting onto the current pixel. Each fragment stores its depth z and rendering attributes. Steps: 1. Projection: Project all scene polygons onto the current pixel and identify fragments that cover it. 2. Opaque Identification: Identify the front-most opaque fragment and record its depth as z{opaque}. 3. Transparent Filtering: Collect all transparent fragments with depth z < z{opaque} (assuming z increases away from the camera). Fragments with z > z{opaque} are occluded by the opaque fragment and discarded. 4. Sorting: Sort the collected transparent fragments by depth z in ascending order (back to front). 5. Compositing: Composite the sorted transparent fragments in order, then composite the front-most opaque fragment. Formulas: Depth comparison: z < z{opaque} Compositing order: \text{Result} = \text{Composite}(\text{Sorted Transparent Fragments}, \text{Front-most Opaque Fragment}) Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Opaque Fragments: The algorithm assumes a single front-most opaque fragment. Precision: Depth comparison precision must be sufficient to correctly determine occlusion by the front-most opaque fragment. Performance: The method requires multiple passes through the polygons in the scene if implemented naively, as it does not incrementally update the sort from the previous pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mammensort(fragments): """ Sorts transparent fragments for a single pixel using Mammen's Technique. fragments: List of fragment objects with attributes.z (depth) and.opaque (boolean). Returns: List of transparent fragments sorted back-to-front, followed by the front-most opaque fragment. """ # Step 1: Identify the front-most opaque fragment opaquefragments = [f for f in fragments if f.opaque] if not opaquefragments: frontmostopaquez = float('inf') frontmostopaque = None else: frontmostopaque = min(opaquefragments, key=lambda f: f.z) frontmostopaquez = frontmostopaque.z # Step 2: Filter transparent fragments transparentfragments = [] for f in fragments: if not f.opaque and f.z < frontmostopaquez: transparentfragments.append(f) # Step 3: Sort transparent fragments back-to-front (ascending z) transparentfragments.sort(key=lambda f: f.z) # Step 4: Return sorted list result = transparentfragments if frontmostopaque is not None: result.append(frontmostopaque) return result The R-Buffer is a hardware architectural proposal for implementing order-independent transparency (OIT) by storing fragments in a large, unordered, recirculating buffer separate from the Z-buffer and frame buffer. It solves the problem of correctly compositing an arbitrary number of transparent layers per pixel without requiring multiple passes of geometry or per-pixel linked lists. Unlike software-based sorting methods that repeat work for every pixel, the R-buffer amortizes storage costs across the entire screen, allowing fragments to be processed in successive passes until the framebuffer is fully composited. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) per pixel for sorting N transparent fragments, plus O(N) for filtering and identification. Since the sort is performed independently for each pixel without exploiting coherence, the total time is proportional to the number of pixels times the average number of fragments per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(N) per pixel to store the fragments. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades linearly with the number of fragments per pixel. It does not scale well with high fragment density compared to incremental methods. Strengths: Simple to implement; handles visibility cycles gracefully per pixel; correctly handles occlusion by the front-most opaque fragment. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to repeated sorting; does not exploit spatial coherence; requires multiple passes through polygons in naive implementations. Mammen's Technique was described in the context of comparing software algorithms for per-pixel transparent fragment sorting with proposed hardware solutions like the R-Buffer. It serves as a baseline for understanding the computational cost of per-pixel sorting without coherence exploitation. The technique is cited in discussions about the trade-offs between software sorting and hardware-based OIT solutions.
