name: R-Buffer
head: Wittenbrink's R-Buffer, Recirculating Fragment Buffer
body: The R-Buffer is a hardware architectural proposal for implementing order-independent transparency (OIT) by storing fragments in a large, unordered, recirculating buffer separate from the Z-buffer and frame buffer. It solves the problem of correctly compositing an arbitrary number of transparent layers per pixel without requiring multiple passes of geometry or per-pixel linked lists. Unlike software-based sorting methods that repeat work for every pixel, the R-buffer amortizes storage costs across the entire screen, allowing fragments to be processed in successive passes until the framebuffer is fully composited. The R-Buffer implements a fragment-level sorting and compositing mechanism. While originally proposed as dedicated hardware, it is often simulated or approximated in software using Multiple Render Targets (MRT) to store k-buffer entries. The method replaces per-primitive sorting with per-pixel sorting to handle high depth complexity. Input: A stream of fragments generated by rasterizing primitives (e.g., tetrahedra split into triangles). Each fragment carries position (X, Y, Z), color (RGBA), and scalar data value (v). Output: A final composited image in the framebuffer with correct order-independent transparency. 1. Framebuffer Stores the accumulated color and opacity of fragments that have already been composited and removed from the sorting process. Typically stores associated color and opacity. 2. R-Buffer (Recirculating Fragment Buffer) A circular First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue shared for the entire screen. Stores fragments that are neither the closest opaque fragment nor the furthest transparent fragment in the current framebuffer state. Layout: Each entry stores X, Y, Z (depth), and RGBA values. Memory Overhead: Experiments show required memory is 2.1 to 3.6 times higher than a traditional Z-buffer for detailed CAD models. 3. K-Buffer (Hardware Implementation Variant) In GPU implementations (e.g., using ATI MRT extensions), the R-buffer logic is approximated using a fixed-size "k-buffer" per pixel. Layout: Each entry consists of a scalar data value v and distance d from the eye. Capacity: Stores k entries. In the cited implementation, k=3, allowing the sorting of up to seven fragments in a single pass (six entries from the k-buffer plus the incoming fragment). Tags: Holes (concavities) can be handled by storing tags as the signs of v and d (internal/external classification). The process involves a single geometry pass followed by multiple recirculation passes until all fragments are composited or discarded. 1. Rasterization: Scan-convert all polygons only once. Fragments are generated with their view-space depth d (calculated in the vertex program and passed to the fragment shader). 2. Initial Classification: If a fragment is opaque and closer than the current framebuffer depth, it replaces the framebuffer content. If a fragment is transparent, it is compared against the framebuffer. Fragments not stored in the framebuffer are sent to the R-buffer. 3. Recirculation Pass (Per Pixel): Fetch current entries from the R-buffer (or k-buffer). Find the two closest fragments to the eye by sorting entries based on stored distance d. Compute the ray segment defined by these two entries. Look up color and opacity from a 3D pre-integrated texture using the scalar values (v1, v2) and distance difference (\Delta d = d2 - d1) of the two closest entries. Composite the resulting color and opacity with the color and opacity from the framebuffer (Porter and Duff compositing). Discard the closest fragment (it has been composited). Write the remaining entries back into the R-buffer (or k-buffer) for the next pass. 4. Termination: The process repeats in successive passes. Termination occurs when the framebuffer opacity exceeds a threshold (early ray termination) or when the R-buffer is empty. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kbufferpass(fnew, kbuffer, framebuffer): # Stage 1: Read Framebuffer c1 = framebuffer.color if c1.isopaque: return framebuffer # Early termination, opaque fragment occludes all others # Stage 2: Fetch K-Buffer Entries f1, f2, f3 = kbuffer allfragments = [fnew, f1, f2, f3] # Find the closest fragment to the eye (minimum depth) n1 = min(allfragments, key=lambda f: f.depth) remaining = [f for f in allfragments if f is not n1] # Find the second closest fragment from the remaining n2 = min(remaining, key=lambda f: f.depth) r1, r2, r3 = remaining # The rest are written back # Stage 3: Lookup and Composite d1 = n1.depth d2 = n2.depth v1 = n1.scalar v2 = n2.scalar deltad = d2 - d1 # Look up color/opacity for the segment between n1 and n2 # from a pre-integrated 3D texture c2 = readpreintegratedtexture(v1, v2, deltad) # Composite the segment color c2 with the accumulated framebuffer color c1 # Standard front-to-back compositing for unassociated color: alpha2 = c2.alpha c1out = c1.color (1.0 - alpha2) + c2.color alpha2 alpha1out = c1.alpha + alpha2 (1.0 - c1.alpha) framebuffer.color = c1out framebuffer.alpha = alpha1out # Stage 4: Write Back kbuffer = (r1, r2, r3) return framebuffer k (K-Buffer size): In the cited implementation, k=3. Framebuffer Resolution: 512x512 pixels in experimental simulations. Memory Factor: 2.1 to 3.6 times the Z-buffer size for CAD models; supports average depth complexity of 10 fragments per pixel with 5x framebuffer storage. Holes/Concavities: Properly handling holes requires dynamic tagging of vertices as boundary/internal and k-buffer entries as internal/external. Ray segments with both vertices on the boundary should have zero color/opacity. However, the logic to update these tags dynamically exceeds current hardware instruction limits in the cited implementation. Consequently, the implementation uses only a single tag for initialization and does not handle holes properly. Hardware Status: The original R-buffer hardware does not exist; implementations are software simulations or GPU shader approximations. Performance: The software version does more work than incremental sorting algorithms (like Wilhelms et al.) because sorts are repeated from scratch independently at each pixel. Precision: View-space depth d must be accurately calculated in the vertex program and passed to the fragment stage to ensure correct sorting. Time Complexity: Run time complexity depends on the average depth complexity squared (O(D^2)). Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the projected area of all faces in the mesh, unlike methods proportional only to the boundary. The R-buffer amortizes this over the screen, requiring 2.1 to 3.6 times the Z-buffer memory for detailed models. Measured Performance: Phoenix Dataset: 1022k pixels, average depth complexity 27.6, 66 passes, tot/Z bandwidth ratio 17.4. Head Full Dataset: 9287k pixels, average depth complexity 201.6, 475 passes, tot/Z bandwidth ratio 135.1. Strengths: Handles arbitrary depth complexity without fixed limits on transparent layers. Single geometry pass required; no repeated rasterization of primitives. Amortizes storage costs across the entire screen, efficient for irregular grids with varying fragment counts. Unassociated color storage with associated compositing reduces triangle artifacts at model edges. Limitations: High memory overhead compared to Z-buffering. Performance degrades significantly with high depth complexity due to quadratic pass count. Current hardware implementations struggle with dynamic hole handling (concavities). Not suitable for volume rendering where the number of fragments is proportional to the entire mesh surface area rather than just the boundary. The R-Buffer was proposed by Wittenbrink as a hardware component for rendering tetrahedral primitives. It is similar in spirit to Carpenter’s software A-buffer but implements the sorting in hardware to avoid the inefficiencies of Z-buffering (which is a read-modify-write operation and does not perform an actual sort). The concept was further explored in the context of GPU implementations via the "k-buffer" technique by Callahan et al., which uses Multiple Render Targets to simulate the recirculating buffer behavior. It is primarily associated with unstructured tetrahedral volume rendering and order-independent transparency. name: Newell-based Visibility Sorting
head: Visibility Sorting (Newell-based)
body: Newell-based Visibility Sorting is an algorithm to sort cells into a back-to-front ordered list for correct hardware compositing. It extends the Newell, Newell, and Sancha polygon sorting method to the case of polyhedra. By definition, if cell A partially occludes cell B from a particular viewpoint V, cell B must come before cell A in the list. It differs from its siblings by using a general iterative occlusion testing strategy rather than topological graph traversal (as in Topological Sort for Cell Projection) or per-pixel depth buffers (as in Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant)). Inputs and outputs: Input: A list of n cells, each defined by its vertices and geometry. Output: A sorted list of cells in back-to-front order. Data structures: cells: List of cell objects. initiallist: List of cell indices, initially sorted by rear-most depth. outputlist: List of cell indices, built incrementally. movedflag: Boolean array of size n, initialized to false. Steps: 1. Initial Sort: Sort cells from back to front by the depth coordinate (z) of their rear-most vertex. Let this ordered list be initiallist. 2. Iterative Testing: While initiallist is not empty: a. Take the rearmost cell A from initiallist. b. Test cell A against all other cells B in initiallist (excluding A). c. If cell A does not occlude any other cell B: i. Remove A from initiallist. ii. Append A to outputlist. d. If cell A occludes a cell B: i. Move B to the rearmost position on initiallist. ii. Mark B as having been moved (set movedflag[B] = true). iii. Continue testing with B as the new current cell A (i.e., do not remove B yet, but re-evaluate it against the remaining cells in initiallist). iv. If B is moved a second time (i.e., movedflag[B] was already true), it indicates a visibility cycle. In this case, no visibility sort is possible unless one of the cells in the cycle is subdivided. Occlusion Test: Testing pairs of cells for mutual occlusion is the most expensive part. A sequence of tests of increasing difficulty is used to eliminate the possibility of occlusion early. The specific geometric tests are not detailed in the provided sources, but the hierarchy implies simple bounds checks first, followed by more complex intersection tests. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Visibility Cycles: Occur when cells mutually occlude each other. No visibility sort is possible unless one of the cells in the cycle is subdivided. Complexity: The algorithm performs O(n^2) pair-wise occlusion tests for a data volume of n cells. name: XMPVO
head: Extended Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering
body: XMPVO is an algorithm that improves the runtime of the Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering (MPVO) method by using ray shooting queries to discover exterior face relations for nonconvex meshes. It addresses the problem of determining the correct back-to-front rendering order for convex volumes filled with convex polyhedral cells when the standard topological sort is insufficient due to occlusions between exterior faces. It sets itself apart from its parent Topological Sort for Cell Projection by augmenting the graph with geometric visibility checks, and from its sibling Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) by performing these checks in object-space precision rather than image-space. Inputs: A set of n convex polyhedral cells forming a mesh. A viewpoint position. The projection complex of the mesh (the arrangement of projected cell edges and vertices on the image plane). Outputs: A topologically sorted list of cells suitable for back-to-front volume rendering. Data Structures: Visibility Graph: A directed graph where nodes represent cells. Edges represent visibility relations. Edges from the parent MPVO algorithm (based on shared faces and viewpoint containment). Additional edges representing exterior face occlusions discovered via ray shooting. Projection Complex: A data structure storing the 2D intersections of projected cell edges and the projected vertices. Steps: 1. Construct Projection Complex: Project the 3D cell edges and vertices onto the image plane. Compute the intersections of these projected edges to form the projection complex. 2. Identify Query Points: Identify all edge intersections and vertices within the projection complex. 3. Ray Shooting Queries: For each point identified in Step 2, perform a ray shooting query from the viewpoint through that point into the scene. The purpose is to discover which exterior faces occlude other exterior faces. If face A occludes face B at a query point, add a directed edge from cell containing A to cell containing B in the visibility graph. 4. Topological Sort: Perform a topological sort on the augmented visibility graph (containing both MPVO relations and discovered exterior face relations) to determine the final rendering order. Formulas: Time Complexity: O(n + b^2), where n is the number of cells and b is the number of exterior faces. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The ray shooting queries are performed in object-precision (3D space), which is expensive and makes it hard to avoid redundant queries. Robustness: Robustly computing the intersections of the projections of cell edges is difficult and may require exact arithmetic packages, which slows down performance. Redundancy: Due to the object-precision nature, redundant queries are hard to avoid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Limitations: Performs ray shooting queries in object-precision, which is expensive. Hard to avoid redundant queries due to object-precision. name: Kraus and Ertl Method
body: The Kraus and Ertl method handles visibility cycles in convex meshes during cell projection volume rendering. It addresses cases where a global topological sort of cells is impossible due to cyclic visibility dependencies, while a local sort still exists for each pixel center. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projected images of convex, non-overlapping cells on the screen. Output: A correctly sorted and composited image that resolves visibility cycles. Data Structures: The method relies on the output of the basic MPVO sorting algorithm to identify cycle pixels. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Apply the basic MPVO sorting algorithm to detect pixels where the cell ordering forms a cycle. 2. Isolate these pixels and their associated cells. 3. Use special hardware compositing methods to scan-convert each isolated cycle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def krausandertlmethod(mpvosortresults): outputbuffer = {} cyclepixels = [] # Step 1 & 2: Detect and isolate cycles using MPVO output for pixel, sortdata in mpvosortresults.items(): if sortdata.hascycle: cyclepixels.append(pixel) # Step 3: Hardware compositing for each cycle for pixel in cyclepixels: cyclecells = sortdata.cyclecells # The source does not specify the exact hardware compositing # or scan-conversion algorithm used to resolve the cycle. outputbuffer[pixel] = cyclecells return outputbuffer Parameters: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Rendering costs per cycle increase quadratically in the number of cells involved in the cycle. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles visibility cycles gracefully for convex non-overlapping cells. For convex non-overlapping cells, there is always a visibility sort for each pixel center even if there is no global visibility sort of the cells. Limitations: Quadratic cost per cycle. When not to use: When rendering non-convex meshes without extension. The method was introduced by Kraus and Ertl. The method could be extended to nonconvex meshes using the SXMPVO algorithm. name: MPVONC
head: MPVO Non-Convex
body: MPVONC is a heuristic visibility sorting algorithm for cell projection volume rendering that extends the MPVO method to non-convex meshes. It solves the problem of ordering non-convex cells back-to-front by augmenting the partial ordering of MPVO with a centroid-based sort of exterior front-facing cells, followed by a depth-first search (DFS). Unlike exact methods such as SXMPVO or A-buffer sorting, MPVONC is significantly faster but is approximate; it may produce visual artifacts due to sorting errors when occlusion relationships are not captured by the topological graph. Inputs: A set of polyhedral cells forming a non-convex mesh. A viewpoint position V. The directed graph G of "behind" relationships derived from MPVO (edges point from occluded to occluding cells across shared faces). Outputs: A total ordering of cells suitable for back-to-front volume rendering. Data Structures: Graph G=(C, E): Nodes C are cells. Edges E represent the MPVO partial ordering. Exterior Front-Facing Set S{ext}: A subset of cells c \in C that have at least one face visible from the viewpoint (exterior front-facing). Centroid Distance: For each cell c, the Euclidean distance d(c, V) between its centroid Cc and the viewpoint V. Steps: 1. Identify Exterior Front-Facing Cells: Determine the set S{ext} of all cells that have at least one face that is front-facing with respect to the viewpoint. 2. Sort Exterior Cells: Sort the cells in S{ext} in decreasing order of their centroid distance to the viewpoint: d(ci, V) \ge d(cj, V) \implies ci \text{ precedes } cj Let the sorted list be L = [c1, c2, \dots, ck]. 3. Depth-First Search (DFS): Initialize an empty list OrderedCells. Iterate through each cell c in L: If c has not been visited in the current traversal or globally: Perform a DFS starting from c in the graph G. Append visited nodes to OrderedCells in post-order (or as they are finalized by the DFS) to ensure back-to-front order relative to the graph edges. Mark visited nodes to avoid re-processing. 4. Result: The OrderedCells list constitutes the total visibility ordering. Pitfalls: Sorting Errors: MPVONC may fail to produce a correct ordering if one cell occludes another across a region where ray-gaps are possible. This occurs specifically when the occluding cell has a centroid farther from the viewpoint than the occluded cell's centroid. In such cases, the heuristic sort places the occluded cell before the occluding one, leading to visual artifacts. Non-Convexity: The method assumes the underlying MPVO graph is valid. If the mesh is highly non-convex or contains complex topological features not captured by face-sharing relationships, the heuristic may not resolve all occlusions. A variant that removes the assumption that the mesh is convex by combining a sweep algorithm with the MPVO method. It is substantially faster than previous exact methods for general meshes. Time Complexity: Very fast, comparable to MPVO. The sorting step is O(N \log N) for exterior cells, and DFS is O(N+E). Accuracy: Approximate. It usually generates a correct visibility ordering but is not guaranteed to be exact. Strengths: Simple to implement, very fast, handles non-convex meshes better than standard MPVO. Limitations: Prone to sorting errors and visual artifacts in specific non-convex configurations where centroid distance does not correlate with occlusion. Not suitable when artifact-free rendering is required. MPVONC was described by Williams in [27] as a heuristic to extend the MPVO algorithm to non-convex meshes. It was developed to address the limitations of MPVO, which only computes an approximate ordering for general (non-convex) datasets, resulting in visual artifacts. The method augments the MPVO partial ordering with a centroid-based sort and DFS. It is cited in works discussing image-space visibility ordering for cell projection volume rendering of unstructured data. name: Convex Grid Topological Visibility Sorting
head: Convex Grid Topological, Visibility Sorting (Convex Grid Topological)
body: Convex Grid Topological Visibility Sorting is an O(n) algorithm for determining the back-to-front rendering order of cells in a convex grid composed of convex polyhedral cells. It solves the visibility sorting problem by constructing a directed graph of pairwise occlusion relations between adjacent cells and performing a topological sort. Unlike Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) which may require more complex geometric checks, this method relies solely on the convexity of the grid volume and the cells to guarantee that local face-sharing relations imply global visibility order. It is a specific instance of Topological Sort for Cell Projection optimized for convex topologies. Inputs: 1. A set of n convex cells forming a convex grid volume. 2. The 3D position of the viewpoint V. 3. The geometric definition of each cell, specifically its faces and neighbors. For each cell C, the set of adjacent cells sharing a common face is known. Outputs: 1. A list of cells sorted in back-to-front order (from farthest to nearest relative to V). Cell Object: Represents a single cell. Contains: id: Unique identifier. incount: Integer, initialized to 0. Counts the number of direct predecessors in the occlusion graph (cells that must be rendered before this cell). neighbors: List of cell IDs sharing a face with this cell. facenormals: List of outward-pointing normal vectors for each face, or a method to determine the side of a point relative to a face. Queue: A FIFO queue (or stack, as any valid topological order is acceptable) containing cell IDs with incount equal to 0. Output List: A list to store the final sorted cell IDs. The core relation is B <{vp} A, meaning cell B must precede cell A in the visibility sort. Definition: Let A and B be two cells sharing a common face F. Let V be the viewpoint. The relation B <{vp} A holds if and only if the viewpoint V and cell A lie on the same side of the plane defined by face F. Geometric Test: Let N be the outward-pointing normal vector of face F (pointing away from cell A and into cell B, or vice versa; consistency is key). Let PA be any point inside cell A and PV be the viewpoint. If the normal N points from A to B: 1. Calculate dA = (PA - P{face}) \cdot N. By definition, dA < 0 (or >0 depending on normal direction convention, but A is on the "negative" side if N points out). 2. Calculate dV = (PV - P{face}) \cdot N. 3. If dV has the same sign as dA (i.e., V is on the same side of the face as A), then A occludes B from the perspective of V. Thus, B <{vp} A. Note: The sources state "If the viewpoint V is on the same side of the face F between cells A and B as cell A is, then cell A occludes cell B". This implies that the ray from V to B must pass through A's volume or the shared face is oriented such that A is "in front" of B relative to V. 1. Initialize Counts: For each cell C in the grid: Set C.incount = 0. 2. Build Occlusion Graph: For each cell A in the grid: For each neighbor B of A (sharing a face F): Determine if B <{vp} A using the geometric test above. If B <{vp} A: Increment A.incount by 1. (Implicitly, add a directed edge from B to A in the graph). 3. Initialize Queue: For each cell C in the grid: If C.incount == 0: Add C to the Queue. 4. Topological Sort: While the Queue is not empty: Remove a cell C from the Queue. Append C to the Output List. For each neighbor B of C: Check if there is an occlusion relation C <{vp} B (i.e., C must precede B). Note: The sources describe iterating over "directed edges from C to a cell B". In the graph construction, an edge B \to A exists if B <{vp} A. Therefore, if we process C, we look for cells B such that C <{vp} B. This is equivalent to checking neighbors B where the relation C <{vp} B holds. If C <{vp} B: Decrement B.incount by 1. If B.incount == 0: Add B to the Queue. 5. Cycle Detection: If the Queue becomes empty and the Output List contains fewer than n cells, a visibility cycle exists. This indicates the algorithm cannot produce a valid linear order for the current configuration (though for convex grids, this should not happen if the grid is truly convex and the viewpoint is outside or properly handled). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convexgridtopologicalsort(cells, viewpoint): """ Sorts convex cells in a convex grid back-to-front. Args: cells: List of Cell objects. Each Cell has: id: int neighbors: List of Cell objects sharing a face getfacenormal(faceindex): Returns outward normal vector getcenter(): Returns centroid point viewpoint: Point3D representing the camera position. Returns: List of Cell objects sorted back-to-front. """ n = len(cells) outputlist = [] queue = [] # Step 1: Initialize incounts for cell in cells: cell.incount = 0 # Step 2: Build graph and compute incounts # We iterate over all directed edges. An edge B->A exists if B <vp A. # B <vp A means B must be rendered before A. # This happens if V and A are on the same side of the shared face F. for cellA in cells: for neighborB in cellA.neighbors: # Check if neighborB <vp cellA # Find the shared face between cellA and neighborB # Note: Implementation detail: finding the shared face geometry # is assumed to be available or computable. face = getsharedface(cellA, neighborB) if face is None: continue # Determine if B <vp A # Condition: Viewpoint V and Cell A are on the same side of Face F. # Let N be the normal of F pointing OUT of A (into B). # Point Acenter is inside A. Point V is viewpoint. # Vector from Face to Acenter is roughly opposite to N. # Vector from Face to V is V - FacePoint. # Let's define the test precisely based on sources: # "If the viewpoint V is on the same side of the face F between cells A and B as cell A is" # Get a point on the face facepoint = face.center # Get normal pointing out of A normal = face.normaloutofA # Vector from face to A's center vecA = cellA.center - facepoint # Vector from face to Viewpoint vecV = viewpoint - facepoint # Dot products to determine side # If normal points out of A, vecA. normal should be negative (or positive depending on convention) # Let's assume standard outward normal: vecA. normal < 0 sideA = dot(vecA, normal) sideV = dot(vecV, normal) # Check if they are on the same side # Same side means (sideA > 0 and sideV > 0) or (sideA < 0 and sideV < 0) if (sideA > 0 and sideV > 0) or (sideA < 0 and sideV < 0): # V and A are on the same side. # Source: "cell A occludes cell B... B must come before A" # So B <vp A. # Edge in graph: B -> A. # Increment incount of A. cellA.incount += 1 # Step 3: Initialize Queue for cell in cells: if cell.incount == 0: queue.append(cell) # Step 4: Process Queue while queue: cellC = queue.pop(0) # Remove from front outputlist.append(cellC) # For all directed edges from C to a cell B # Edge C -> B exists if C <vp B for neighborB in cellC.neighbors: # Check if C <vp B face = getsharedface(cellC, neighborB) if face is None: continue facepoint = face.center # Normal pointing out of C normal = face.normaloutofC vecC = cellC.center - facepoint vecV = viewpoint - facepoint sideC = dot(vecC, normal) sideV = dot(vecV, normal) if (sideC > 0 and sideV > 0) or (sideC < 0 and sideV < 0): # C and V are on the same side of the face. # C occludes B. C <vp B. # Edge C -> B. # Decrement incount of B. neighborB.incount -= 1 if neighborB.incount == 0: queue.append(neighborB) # Step 5: Check for cycles if len(outputlist) < n: raise Exception("Visibility cycle detected. Grid may not be convex or viewpoint handling is incorrect.") return outputlist Convexity: The algorithm assumes the entire grid volume is convex. If the grid is non-convex, the algorithm may fail or produce incorrect results because a viewing ray might exit the grid and re-enter it. Boundary Cells: Cells with external faces (boundary cells) are handled, but the simple topological sort does not account for rays crossing external gaps. For non-convex grids, additional O(b^2) tests between boundary cells are required. Visibility Cycles: If the queue empties before all cells are processed, a cycle exists. In a strictly convex grid with a valid viewpoint, this should not occur. Precision: Geometric tests involving dot products and point-in-halfspace checks are sensitive to floating-point precision. Degenerate cases (viewpoint exactly on a face plane) require careful handling. Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of cells. The initialization and graph building steps process each cell and each edge (face sharing) a constant number of times. Since each cell has a maximum of 6 faces (in a hexahedral grid), the number of edges is proportional to n. Space Complexity: O(n) to store the graph (incounts) and the queue/output list. Strengths: Extremely fast for convex grids. No complex geometric intersection tests are needed during the sort phase, only local face tests. Limitations: Only applicable to convex grids of convex cells. Fails or requires augmentation for non-convex grids. Does not handle self-occlusion or complex internal structures that break convexity. When to Use: Ideal for structured grids (e.g., regular hexahedral meshes) where the domain is convex and the viewpoint is external or the grid is treated as a convex hull. When Not to Use: Non-convex domains, unstructured grids with non-convex cells, or when high precision is required for complex occlusion scenarios not covered by local face relations. Origin: The algorithm is described in the paper "Volume rendering for curvilinear and unstructured grids" by Comba et al.. History: It was developed as a faster alternative to O(n^2) pairwise occlusion tests for volume rendering on curvilinear and unstructured grids. The method leverages the topological properties of convex grids to reduce the sorting problem to a graph topological sort. Usage: Used in volume rendering pipelines for scientific visualization where the data domain is convex and structured or curvilinear grids are used. name: Parallelized Accurate Sorting for Projected Tetrahedra
head: Logical partition sorting, Quick and accurate sorting algorithm of tetrahedral datasets
body: Parallelized Accurate Sorting is a view-dependent sorting algorithm for tetrahedral datasets that uses logical partitioning to enable parallel processing, solving the dependency and sequence limitations of neighboring tetrahedra in parallel performance. It sets itself apart from other cell projection sorting methods by dividing the dataset into spatial blocks along the viewing direction and peeling unobstructed layers in parallel, thereby enhancing topological sorting parallelization and reducing sorting time. The method sorts tetrahedra for projected tetrahedra rendering in four sequential steps: spatial partitioning, parallel layer peeling, logical boundary partitioning, and optical accumulation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A tetrahedral dataset T and a viewing direction vector \vec{v}. Output: A back-to-front sorted list of tetrahedra ordered along \vec{v}, ready for hardware rendering. Data Structures Blocks: A list of spatial blocks covering the dataset volume, where each block contains a subset of tetrahedra. Layers: Within each block, tetrahedra are organized into unobstructed layers for parallel processing. Steps 1. Spatial Partitioning: Divide the space containing the tetrahedral datasets into a list of blocks along the viewing direction, with every block containing a subset of tetrahedra. 2. Parallel Sorting (Layer Peeling): Sort tetrahedra accurately by peeling tetrahedral subsets into unobstructed layers in parallel. 3. Logical Boundary Partitioning: Partition tetrahedra on the boundary logically. 4. Optical Accumulation: Compute the optical contribution of each subset with segment integration and accumulate the optical contribution of each subset along the viewing direction. Pseudocode The following pseudocode implements the four-step process using standard vector operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelizedaccuratesorting(tetrahedra, viewdirection): # Step 1: Spatial Partitioning # Divide the space containing tetrahedral datasets into a list of blocks along the viewing direction. # Exact block sizing and assignment algorithm not given in sources. blocks = {} for t in tetrahedra: depth = sum(c d for c, d in zip(t.centroid, viewdirection)) blockidx = int(depth) # Block size not given blocks.setdefault(blockidx, []).append(t) sortedtetrahedra = [] # Step 2: Parallel Sorting (Layer Peeling) # Sort accurately by peeling tetrahedral subsets into unobstructed layers in parallel. # Exact peeling logic and dependency resolution not given in sources. for blockidx in sorted(blocks.keys()): remaining = list(blocks[blockidx]) while remaining: layer = [] for t in remaining: # Check if t has no unrendered predecessors in the current block # Dependency check logic not given in sources. ishead = True # Topological dependency resolution not given if ishead: layer.append(t) sortedtetrahedra.extend(layer) remaining = [t for t in remaining if t not in layer] # Step 3: Logical Boundary Partitioning # Partition tetrahedra on the boundary logically. # Exact boundary handling algorithm not given in sources. # Tetrahedra are already ordered by block index and layer peeling. # Step 4: Optical Accumulation # Compute the optical contribution of each subset with segment integration. # Accumulate the optical contribution of each subset along the viewing direction. # This step belongs to the rendering phase, not the sorting phase. return sortedtetrahedra Parameters Block Size: Not given in the sources. Early Termination: An early tetrahedron termination scheme can be applied during accumulation to gain more than 10% rendering performance for datasets with more than a million tetrahedra. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Tetrahedra: Tetrahedra crossing block boundaries require logical partitioning to ensure correct ordering. Dependency Resolution: The method addresses the sequence and dependency limitations of neighboring tetrahedra, which are common pitfalls in parallel sorting. Multi-segment and Multi-stage Projected Tetrahedra is a technique designed to solve the time-consuming sorting problem inherent in Projected Tetrahedra rendering by partitioning datasets into multiple spatial segments and dividing the visualization procedure into multiple temporal stages. It sets itself apart from standard Projected Tetrahedra by introducing spatial partitioning to enable parallel sorting without write access violations, and temporal staging to satisfy varying user requirements and increase cognition. It builds on Parallelized Accurate Sorting for Projected Tetrahedra by addressing the scalability limits of sorting large datasets through distributed or cloud-based architectures. A volume rendering technique for tetrahedral datasets that enhances parallelization by dividing space into blocks along the viewing direction, sorting tetrahedra by peeling unobstructed layers in parallel, partitioning boundary tetrahedra logically, and accumulating optical contributions via segment integration. The algorithm reduces sorting time largely and improves rendering performance greatly compared to previous methods. Performance: GPU implementation of the parallelized accurate sorting scheme achieves 91% acceleration compared with the CPU implementation. Scalability: The early tetrahedron termination scheme has a gain of more than 10% in terms of rendering performance for datasets with more than a million tetrahedra. Strengths: Enhances the parallelization of topological sorting, reduces sorting time largely, and improves rendering performance greatly. Limitations: The method is view-dependent, requiring sorting for each frame. The method was proposed by Xin Li, W. Chen, X. Wu, and W. Zuo in August 2013 in the paper "Fast projected tetrahedra volume rendering based on parallelized accurate sorting". It addresses the limitations of parallel performance in projected tetrahedra rendering caused by the sequence and dependency of neighboring tetrahedra. It builds on Parallelized Accurate Sorting for Projected Tetrahedra by addressing the scalability limits of sorting large datasets through distributed or cloud-based architectures. The method addresses the view-dependent nature of Projected Tetrahedra, which requires sorting tetrahedra before rendering to correctly display interior features. The core innovation is the decomposition of the problem into spatial and temporal dimensions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Large-scale tetrahedral datasets (e.g., geographic data). name: GPU-based Cell Projection for Structured Data
head: Cell projection algorithm for large volumetric data sets, GPU-based PT for structured grids
body: This method provides an interactive rendering technique for large, regular (structured) volumetric data sets on GPUs by exploiting data regularity to eliminate redundant projection and sorting computations. It differs from general Projective Tetrahedra (PT) algorithms by avoiding the computationally expensive visibility sorting of cells, as the traversal order for a regular grid is determined in constant time. Unlike Hardware-Based Ray Casting (HARC), it consumes significantly less memory. Inputs: A structured (regular) 3D grid of voxels (e.g., 256^3 to 512^3). Outputs: A 2D image composited in back-to-front order. Data Structures: 1. Vertex Array: Stores volume information. Each entry corresponds to a grid vertex but is rendered multiple times (once per incident tetrahedron). Position: 3D coordinates derived from lattice indices. Normal: Encoded with auxiliary data: x-coordinate: tetid (integer, 0–4), identifying which of the five tetrahedra in the volunit is being rendered. y-coordinate: vertid (integer, 0–3), identifying the specific vertex of that tetrahedron. 2. Basis Hexahedron Parameters (Uniforms): Precomputed once on the CPU for a single reference hexahedron. Stored values for each of the five basis tetrahedra include: basisprojectionclass: Determined by four cross-product tests. basisprojectedvertices: Screen coordinates of the projected vertices. basisthickvertex: Coordinates of the thick vertex. basisintersectionparameters: Used to compute front (sf) and back (sb) scalar values. basisrenderingorder: The order in which the five tetrahedra must be rendered. basisthickness: The thickness l for the thick vertex. 3. Transfer Function: A 1D texture with 256 positions mapping scalar values to RGBA (chromaticity and opacity/extinction coefficient \tau). Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (CPU): Subdivide each hexahedron in the volume into five tetrahedra. This set is termed a "volunit". 2. Basis Projection (CPU): Compute projection parameters for a single "basis hexahedron" using orthographic projection. Determine the projection class for each of the five basis tetrahedra using four cross-product tests. Compute the thick vertex coordinates, basis projected vertices coordinates, basis intersection parameters (for sf, sb), and basis rendering order. Store these values as global uniforms for the GPU. 3. Traversal Order (CPU): Determine a traversal order for the whole volume in constant time. This avoids the sorting step required by general PT algorithms. 4. Data Allocation (CPU): Allocate volume information into the Vertex Array structure. 5. Rendering Loop (GPU): Iterate through the volume according to the traversal order. For each volunit: Render each of the five tetrahedra as a triangle fan. The first vertex of the fan (central node) is the basis thick vertex. The number of triangles in the fan depends on the basis projection class. Triangles are drawn in the basis rendering order (back-to-front). 6. Vertex Shader Execution: For each vertex in the lattice: Compute vertex coordinates on the fly using the 3 integer lattice indices and the basis hexahedron uniform variables to displace the vertex. Encode tetid in the normal's x and vertid in the normal's y. Compute scalar values (sf, sb) and thickness (l): If the vertex is not the thick vertex: sf = sb = \text{original scalar}, and l = 0. If the vertex is the thick vertex: Calculate sf and sb using the basis intersection parameters, and set l to the precomputed basis thickness. 7. Fragment Shader Execution: Receive trilinearly interpolated (sf, sb, l) values for the fragment. Compute the average scalar value s{avg} = (sf + sb) / 2. Lookup the extinction coefficient \tau and color C{new} from the 1D transfer function texture using s{avg}. Compute opacity \alpha using the formula: \alpha = 1 - e^{-\tau \cdot l} Compose the fragment with the frame buffer color C{fb}: C{fb} = \alpha \cdot C{new} + (1 - \alpha) C{fb} This composition occurs in back-to-front order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolume(volumedata, griddims, transferfunctiontexture): # Step 1-3: CPU Preprocessing # Subdivide hexahedra into volunits (5 tetrahedra each) # Compute basis hexahedron projection parameters # Determine constant-time traversal order # Step 4: CPU Data Allocation vertexarray = allocatevertexarray(volumedata, griddims) # Step 5-7: GPU Rendering for volunit in volumearraytraversedinorder: for tetid in range(5): # Get basis parameters for this tetrahedron params = basisparams[tetid] # Determine triangle fan structure based on projection class triangles = gettrianglesforclass(params.class) # Render triangle fan # First vertex is the thick vertex # Subsequent vertices are the projected basis vertices for triangle in triangles: # Vertex Shader Logic (per vertex in triangle) # Vertex coordinates are displaced from basis using lattice indices # Normal.x = tetid # Normal.y = vertid # Compute scalar/thickness per vertex if vertex is thickvertex: sf, sb = computescalarsfromintersection(params.intersectionparams) l = params.thickness else: sf = volumedata[vertex.latticeindex] sb = sf l = 0.0 # Fragment Shader Logic # Interpolate sf, sb, l across the triangle sffrag, sbfrag, lfrag = interpolate(sf, sb, l) # Lookup transfer function savg = (sffrag + sbfrag) / 2.0 tau, cnew = transferfunctiontexture.sample(savg) # Compute opacity alpha = 1.0 - exp(-tau lfrag) # Composite cfb = framebuffer.read() cfb = alpha cnew + (1.0 - alpha) cfb framebuffer.write(cfb) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundant Computation: Computing projection for every voxel individually is inefficient. This method solves this by computing parameters only once for the basis hexahedron. Precision: The method relies on orthographic projection to ensure all volunits project identically. Perspective projection would break the basis reuse assumption. Performance: Achieves rendering speeds of over 5.0 M Tet/s on current graphics hardware. Time Distribution: More than 60% of the processing time is dedicated solely to the rendering pipeline, as projection and sorting costs are virtually eliminated. Memory: Consumes less memory than HARC (Hardware-Based Ray Casting). Strengths: High performance for large structured datasets; avoids expensive sorting; efficient GPU utilization. Limitations: Restricted to structured (regular) grids; not suitable for unstructured grids without significant modification. This method is an implementation of the Projective Tetrahedra (PT) algorithm proposed by Shirley and Tuchman (1990). It was specifically adapted for GPU implementation to address the challenges of interactive visualization of large 3D data sets in medical and scientific visualization, where data sets are typically regular grids ranging between 256^3 and 512^3 voxels. The approach builds on the observation that for regular grids, visibility sorting is straightforward, allowing the elimination of the most computationally expensive part of general PT algorithms. name: Cell Projection with Scan-line Conversion
head: Irregular grid cell projection, Parallel Software Scan Conversion / Cell Projection, Wilhelms et al. Cell Projection with Scan-line Conversion, Y-bucket scan conversion
body: Cell Projection with Scan-line Conversion is a software-based direct volume rendering method for irregular and multiple grids that uses Y-bucket sorting and scanline generation to leverage spatial coherence, avoiding expensive graphics hardware while handling unstructured tetrahedral and curvilinear grids. It sets itself apart from its siblings by producing image quality equivalent to ray casting but faster due to coherence, yielding noticeably clearer images with fewer artifacts than hardware Gouraud shading methods, though it is slower. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data defined on irregular grids (e.g., unstructured tetrahedral, curvilinear, or hexahedral grids). Output: A 2D image with accumulated color, opacity, and depth values for each pixel. Data Structures: Triangle List: Volumetric primitives are decomposed into triangles. For example, a hexahedron is decomposed into twelve triangles. Y-Bucket Lists: A list of triangles that first appear on a specific scan-line (Y-coordinate). X-Bucket Lists: Used in conjunction with Y-buckets to manage triangles along the scan-line. Pixel Frame Buffer: Stores accumulated color, opacity, and depth for each pixel. KD-Tree: A hierarchical structure used for culling invisible regions and merging polygons for distant views. Steps: 1. Decomposition: Decompose volumetric primitives into triangles depending on the grid type (e.g., twelve triangles for a hexahedron). 2. Bucket Sorting: Use scan-line conversion with Y- and X-bucket lists consisting of triangles first appearing on the scan-line. This allows the use of coherence between adjacent pixels and scan-lines. 3. Traversal/Hierarchy: For close views, traverse the original data. For distant views, use a hierarchical scheme based on KD-trees to merge polygons based on a user-defined threshold. Use the KD-tree to cull invisible regions from the current viewpoint. 4. Scan-line Conversion: Process triangles within the buckets. For each pixel covered by a triangle, calculate the intersection and depth. 5. Accumulation: Accumulate color and opacity front-to-back for each pixel. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: User-defined threshold: Used in the KD-tree hierarchical scheme to merge polygons for distant views. Viewport size: Example given is 512 \times 512. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opaque Data: The method is not optimized for opaque data sets. Ray casting can be competitive or faster on opaque datasets (e.g., head) because it can halt early when a pixel becomes opaque. Performance: Rendering images with a 512 \times 512 viewport takes up to one minute and more on the SGI Onyx with four processors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cellprojectionscanline(primitives, viewparams, threshold): # 1. Decompose primitives into triangles triangles = [] for primitive in primitives: triangles.extend(decomposeintotriangles(primitive)) # 2. Build Y-bucket lists # Y-buckets contain triangles that first appear on a specific scan-line ybuckets = buildybuckets(triangles, viewparams.imageheight) # 3. Build KD-tree for culling and merging kdtree = buildkdtree(triangles) # 4. Initialize frame buffer framebuffer = initializeframebuffer(viewparams.width, viewparams.height) # 5. Process each scan-line for y in range(viewparams.imageheight): currenttriangles = ybuckets[y] # 5a. Cull invisible regions using KD-tree if necessary visibletriangles = cullwithkdtree(currenttriangles, kdtree, viewparams) # 5b. Sort triangles by depth for front-to-back accumulation # Note: Perfect depth sorting is difficult; approximate sorting may be used visibletriangles = sorttrianglesbydepth(visibletriangles, viewparams) # 5c. Scan-convert triangles for triangle in visibletriangles: scanconverttriangle(triangle, y, framebuffer, viewparams) return framebuffer def decomposeintotriangles(primitive): # Example: Hexahedron decomposed into 12 triangles if primitive.type == 'hexahedron': return decomposehexahedron(primitive.vertices) elif primitive.type == 'tetrahedron': return decomposetetrahedron(primitive.vertices) else: raise ValueError("Unsupported primitive type") def buildybuckets(triangles, imageheight): ybuckets = [[] for in range(imageheight)] for triangle in triangles: miny = int(min(triangle.vertices, key=lambda v: v.y).y) maxy = int(max(triangle.vertices, key=lambda v: v.y).y) # Add triangle to buckets from miny to maxy for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): ybuckets[y].append(triangle) return ybuckets def cullwithkdtree(triangles, kdtree, viewparams): # Cull triangles that are not visible from the current viewpoint visible = [] for triangle in triangles: if isvisible(triangle, kdtree, viewparams): visible.append(triangle) return visible def scanconverttriangle(triangle, y, framebuffer, viewparams): # For each pixel in the triangle's bounding box on scan-line y for x in range(triangle.minx, triangle.maxx + 1): if isinsidetriangle(x, y, triangle): # Calculate depth and color at (x, y) depth, color, opacity = calculateintersection(x, y, triangle, viewparams) # Accumulate front-to-back accumulatepixel(framebuffer, x, y, depth, color, opacity) def accumulatepixel(framebuffer, x, y, depth, color, opacity): # Standard front-to-back compositing currentopacity = framebuffer[x, y].opacity currentcolor = framebuffer[x, y].color # Update frame buffer with new contribution framebuffer[x, y].color = currentcolor (1 - opacity) + color opacity framebuffer[x, y].opacity = currentopacity + opacity (1 - currentopacity) framebuffer[x, y].depth = depth # Update depth if needed A sorting scheme to process scan conversion in depth-sorted order to reduce ray-segment list length and manipulation cost, using the depth order of cell centers of gravity. Perfect depth order is impossible because cell depth order may change pixel-by-pixel, and sorting must be recalculated when the viewpoint changes. This approximation does not cause any quality error in the final image. It differs from octree search by being simpler and less costly, avoiding the computational cost of sorting and list manipulation required for near-perfect order. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Rendering images with a 512 \times 512 viewport takes up to one minute and more on the SGI Onyx with four processors. Scaling: Vertex transforming and bucket sorting can both be parallelized. Strengths: Produces image quality equivalent to ray casting but faster due to coherence. Produces noticeably clearer images with fewer artifacts than hardware Gouraud shading methods. Limitations: Noticeably slower than hardware methods. Not optimized for opaque data sets; ray casting can be competitive or faster on opaque datasets. When to use: When high image quality is required and hardware acceleration is not available or insufficient. When not to use: When rendering opaque datasets where early ray termination can provide significant speedups. The method was developed by Wilhelms et al.. It is a software-based approach to direct volume rendering on irregular and multiple grids. The technique leverages spatial coherence to avoid expensive graphics hardware. name: Row-difference projection for AMR cells
head: exact row-difference projection, in-place row-difference accumulation
body: Row-difference projection is an exact rendering method for rotated Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) cells that projects them along pixel rows using row-difference accumulation, replacing a separate per-pixel exact path. It handles cells truncated by depth ranges and unit cubes used for interpolation tables by treating them as large cells within the row-difference framework. It sets itself apart from its siblings by eliminating the need for general clipped-polytope volume calculations and separate exact paths, relying instead on the divergence theorem for efficient volume integration within quadrants. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A rotated AMR cell (or unit cube), a z-range [z{min}, z{max}] defining the projection depth limits, and the image grid geometry. Output: Accumulated row-difference values for the affected pixels, which are later summed to produce the final image contribution. Data Structures: Second-difference buffer: A floating-point buffer (float64) storing the second differences of the projected values per pixel. This buffer must remain in double precision to maintain accuracy. Quadrant limits: Clamped coordinates defining the extent of the cell within the image grid. Steps: 1. Clamp Quadrant Limits: Before processing, clamp the quadrant limits to the cube's geometric extent. This avoids numerical cancellation errors when the projection is called with effectively infinite z-limits. 2. Determine Projection Path: If the rotated cell covers a size threshold and lies entirely within the z-range, use the precomputed interpolation table. Otherwise, project the cell exactly using the row-difference method. This replaces the previous logic where cells truncated by depth ranges or unit cubes used a separate per-pixel exact path. 3. Row Projection with Z-Range: The row projection accepts the z-range [z{min}, z{max}]. Identify the cross-sections of the cube at z{min} and z{max}. These cross-sections introduce up to 12 additional lines along which the column's gradient changes. Limit the integration chords to the specified z-range. 4. Volume Calculation via Divergence Theorem: Calculate the volume of the cube within a specific quadrant and the z-range using the divergence theorem. Apply the theorem about a point located on three of the four clipping planes. This approach ensures that only the clipped cube faces and one cross-section contribute to the integral, replacing the general clipped-polytope calculation which is now removed. 5. In-Place Accumulation: Perform cumulative sums, clamping, and addition on the second-difference buffer in place. This reduces memory usage from 28 bytes per pixel (per thread) to 12 bytes per pixel, consisting of the float32 result and the float64 buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectrotatedcellamr(cell, zmin, zmax, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Projects a rotated AMR cell using row-difference accumulation. Args: cell: Rotated AMR cell geometry. zmin: Minimum z-depth for projection. zmax: Maximum z-depth for projection. imagewidth: Width of the output image in pixels. imageheight: Height of the output image in pixels. Returns: Updated second-difference buffer (float64) and final values (float32). """ # Initialize buffers # seconddiffbuffer: float64, shape (imageheight, imagewidth) # finalvalues: float32, shape (imageheight, imagewidth) seconddiffbuffer = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth), dtype=float64) finalvalues = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth), dtype=float32) # Step 1: Clamp quadrant limits to cube extent # This avoids numerical cancellation with infinite limits quadrantlimits = clamptocubeextent(cell.quadrantlimits, cell.geometry) # Step 2: Determine if table lookup is applicable # If cell covers size threshold and is within z-range, use table if cell.coverssizethreshold() and zmin <= cell.zmin and cell.zmax <= zmax: # Use interpolation table for efficiency tablevalues = lookupinterpolationtable(cell, quadrantlimits) # Accumulate table values into seconddiffbuffer accumulateintoseconddiff(seconddiffbuffer, tablevalues) else: # Step 3: Exact row-difference projection # Identify gradient change lines from cross-sections at zmin and zmax # Up to 12 lines are added where column gradient changes gradientlines = getcrosssectionlines(cell, zmin, zmax) # Step 4: Calculate volume contribution using Divergence Theorem for quadrant in cell.quadrants: # Apply divergence theorem about a point on three clipping planes # Only clipped faces and one cross-section contribute volumecontribution = computevolumedivergencetheorem( cell, quadrant, zmin, zmax) # Accumulate volume contribution into seconddiffbuffer # based on the projected pixel coverage accumulatevolumeintobuffer(seconddiffbuffer, quadrant, volumecontribution) # Step 5: In-place cumulative sums, clamping, and addition # Perform sums, clamping, and addition in place to save memory # This reduces peak memory from 28 bytes/pixel to 12 bytes/pixel cumulativesum = zeroslike(seconddiffbuffer, dtype=float64) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Compute cumulative sum if y > 0: cumulativesum[y, x] = cumulativesum[y-1, x] + seconddiffbuffer[y, x] else: cumulativesum[y, x] = seconddiffbuffer[y, x] # Clamp and add to final values clampedvalue = clamp(cumulativesum[y, x]) finalvalues[y, x] += float32(clampedvalue) return finalvalues, seconddiffbuffer def clamptocubeextent(limits, cubegeometry): """Clamps quadrant limits to the cube's geometric extent.""" # Implementation details for clamping logic return max(limits.min, cubegeometry.min), min(limits.max, cubegeometry.max) def getcrosssectionlines(cell, zmin, zmax): """Identifies lines where column gradient changes due to z-range cross-sections.""" # Returns up to 12 lines based on intersection of cube faces with z planes lines = [] # Logic to intersect cube faces with zmin and zmax planes return lines def computevolumedivergencetheorem(cell, quadrant, zmin, zmax): """Calculates volume using divergence theorem about a point on three clipping planes.""" # Select a reference point on three of the four clipping planes # Integrate over clipped cube faces and one cross-section # This replaces general clipped-polytope calculation pass # Detailed vector calculus implementation def accumulateintoseconddiff(buffer, values): """Accumulates table lookup values into the second-difference buffer.""" # Update buffer based on table values pass def accumulatevolumeintobuffer(buffer, quadrant, volume): """Accumulates volume contribution into the buffer based on pixel coverage.""" # Map volume contribution to relevant pixels in the quadrant pass def clamp(value): """Clamps the cumulative sum value.""" # Apply necessary clamping to prevent overflow or invalid values return max(0.0, min(value, MAXVALUE)) Parameters: rowthreshold: This parameter was removed. Rotated cells now use a table if they cover their size and lie within the z range; otherwise, they are projected exactly. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Cancellation: Quadrant limits must be clamped to the cube's extent before use to avoid numerical cancellation when called with effectively infinite limits. Memory Usage: The final cumulative sums over the second-difference buffer previously created three image-sized temporaries, peaking at 28 bytes per pixel per thread. This is reduced to 12 bytes per pixel by performing sums, clamping, and addition in place, keeping the float64 buffer in double precision. Time Complexity: Depth-limited projections are 2-20x faster than the previous method. Other projections are unchanged within timing noise. Memory Complexity: Peak memory usage is reduced to 12 bytes per pixel (per thread) for the second-difference buffer and final values, down from 28 bytes per pixel. Measured Performance: Tested on synthetic lattices and Ramses test data. Strengths: Eliminates the need for general clipped-polytope calculations and separate per-pixel exact paths, simplifying the codebase and improving performance for depth-limited projections. Limitations: Requires careful handling of numerical precision, necessitating double precision for the second-difference buffer. When to Use: Use for rendering rotated AMR cells, especially when depth-limited projections are required or when cells are truncated by depth ranges. When Not to Use: Not applicable for non-rotated cells or when table lookup is sufficient and performance is not critical. This method was introduced in the context of the pynbody library, specifically within the pynbody.imaging package, to handle AMR rendering more efficiently. It was developed to replace a separate per-pixel exact path for cells truncated by depth ranges and unit cubes used for interpolation tables. The change was part of a broader effort to move rendering from pynbody.sph to a new pynbody.imaging package, reflecting the handling of both AMR and SPH simulations.
