name: Tetrahedral Volume Rendering
head: BT Volume Rendering, Basis Tensor Volume Rendering, Cell Projection with GPGPU, DiffTetVR Tetrahedral Volume Rendering, Differentiable Tetrahedral Volume Rendering, GPU-Accelerated Cell Projection (Tetrahedral), Isosurface rendering using BT volumes, PTINT
body: Tetrahedral Volume Rendering (TetVR) is a cell-projection method that renders unstructured tetrahedral meshes by projecting individual tetrahedra onto the screen and compositing them in depth order. It solves the problem of accurately visualizing complex, non-uniform volumetric data (such as finite element analysis results or dark matter simulations) where regular grid-based ray marching fails or introduces sampling artifacts. Unlike Projected Tetrahedra which often relies on explicit isosurface extraction or simpler blending, this method supports arbitrary isosurface values via density addition and partial pre-integration for color computation, enabling hybrid volume/isosurface visualization. It differs from Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) by using hardware rasterization and screen-space classification to determine visibility order, trading exact topological correctness for GPU acceleration. The method typically employs a two-pass GPU pipeline (or a rasterization-based forward pass with CPU/GPU sorting) to project tetrahedra, compute intersection parameters, and render final colors. Inputs: Tetrahedral mesh (vertices, connectivity), scalar field values (stored per vertex or in a Tetrahedral Texture), gradient vectors (precomputed per vertex), transfer function (TF), camera parameters (view, projection matrices). Outputs: Final color and opacity image. 1. Tetrahedral Texture: 1D or 2D texture where each texel corresponds to one tetrahedron. Contains 4 uint indices pointing to vertex data. 2. Vertex Texture: RGBA texture, 32 bits per component. RGB fields store vertex coordinates (x, y, z); A field stores the scalar value s. 3. Gradient Texture: RGB texture, 32 bits per component. Stores precomputed gradient vectors \nabla s at vertices. Same size and indexing as Vertex Texture. 4. Classification Texture: 1D texture (8 bits per component) containing a Ternary Truth Table. Maps combined cross-product test results to projection class indices. 5. MRT Frame Buffers (First Pass Output): Four 2D RGBA textures (32 bits per component): Texture 1: Intersection coords (x{vi}, y{vi}) (Class 2 only), centroid cz, Truth Table index id{TTT}. Texture 2: Front/back scalars sf, sb, thickness l, triangle count. Texture 3: Front gradient vector gf. Texture 4: Back gradient vector gb. 6. Global Arrays (Intermediate CPU Pass): Vertex Array: Stores \{x, y, z\} coordinates. Color Array: Stores \{sf, sb, l\} for on-the-fly color computation. Gradient Arrays: Stored in normal and secondary color arrays. For thin vertices, sf=sb, l=0, gf=gb. Indices Array: Divided into n groups (one per tetrahedron). Each group has 6 integers defining the vertex order for the triangle fan. Count Array (cnt): Stores number of vertices in each fan. Max vertices is 6 (Class 2, 4 triangles). 1. Preprocessing (CPU): For each tetrahedron, determine if it contributes to the isosurface or volume. Check if the minimum and maximum scalar weights (extrema) are on the same side of the interesting density range. If so, discard the tetrahedron. Transform the Basis Tensor (BT) into Euclidean space using Equation 8 and into tetrahedral indexing form. Store valid tetrahedra in a vertex buffer interpreted as a point list. Position semantic is set to the middle of the voxel space. 2. First Pass: Projecting Tetrahedra (GPU Fragment Shader): Render the Tetrahedral Texture as a quadrilateral with screen-space size. This ensures one fragment shader invocation per tetrahedron. For each tetrahedron: Perform 4 texture lookups using indices from the Tetrahedral Texture to get vertex positions, scalars, and gradients from Vertex and Gradient Textures. Project the 4 vertices to screen space. Compute 4 cross-product tests to determine projection class and vertex layout: python def projecttoscreen(v, viewprojmatrix): clip = viewprojmatrix @ v return clip.xyz / clip.w def crossz(v1, v2): return v1[0] v2[1] - v1[1] v2[0] vproj = [projecttoscreen(v, viewprojmatrix) for v in vertices] vec1 = vproj[1] - vproj[0] vec2 = vproj[2] - vproj[0] vec3 = vproj[3] - vproj[0] vec4 = vproj[1] - vproj[2] vec5 = vproj[1] - vproj[3] t1 = sign(crossz(vec1, vec2)) + 1 t2 = sign(crossz(vec2, vec3)) + 1 t3 = sign(crossz(vec3, vec4)) + 1 t4 = sign(crossz(vec4, vec5)) + 1 Where sign returns -1, 0, or 1. The results ti \in \{0, 1, 2\} are combined to form an index for the Classification Texture lookup. Determine triangle count based on degeneracy: If one test result is 1: Class 3, project as two triangles. If two test results are 1: Class 4, project as one triangle. If three or four tests yield 1: Discard the tetrahedron. Compute scalar values for thick vertex (sf, sb), gradient vectors for entry/exit (gf, gb), cell thickness (l), and cell centroid (cz). Write computed data to the 4 MRT frame buffer color attachments. 3. Intermediate Pass (CPU/GPU): Retrieve data from MRT textures. Sort the tetrahedra in front-to-back order. Use bucket-based sort for rotating models or mergesort for static models. Store sorted data in global arrays (Vertex, Color, Gradient, Indices, Count). 4. Second Pass: Rendering Primitives (GPU Geometry/Fragment Shader): Draw primitives using glMultiDrawElements (or equivalent). Pass indices and count arrays. Use triangle fans. Geometry Shader (Optional/Alternative): Expand each input point (grid vertex) into tetrahedron screen-space triangles. Calculate z-extents. Unpack BT to tensor form, apply Equation 9 (add density), apply Equation 10 (screen transform), pack back to tetrahedral form, and output to screen-space triangles. Note: The two-pass MRT approach avoids this geometry shader overhead by doing classification in the fragment shader. Fragment Shader: Linearly interpolate vertex colors (sf, sb, l) across the triangle using thick and two thin vertices. Compute final opacity using a 1D texture lookup. The texture stores e^{-u} for u \in [0,1]. Lookup u = \tau \cdot l (where \tau is related to scalar values). Partial Pre-Integration (PT): Instead of average scalar values, use the \psi table [MA04]. Retrieve colors Cf and Cb from a 1D transfer function texture based on sf and sb. Use Cf, Cb, and l to index a 2D \psi table. Retrieve value for final color. Isosurface Rendering: If an isovalue is specified, check if it is within the range of interpolated front/back scalar values. If so, the isosurface crosses the tetrahedron. Use Phong illumination. Interpolated gradients act as normal vectors. Combine front and back gradients with weights relative to the distance between the isosurface and the intersection points. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifyprojection(vertices, viewprojmatrix): vproj = [projecttoscreen(v, viewprojmatrix) for v in vertices] vec1 = vproj[1] - vproj[0] vec2 = vproj[2] - vproj[0] vec3 = vproj[3] - vproj[0] vec4 = vproj[1] - vproj[2] vec5 = vproj[1] - vproj[3] t1 = sign(crossz(vec1, vec2)) + 1 t2 = sign(crossz(vec2, vec3)) + 1 t3 = sign(crossz(vec3, vec4)) + 1 t4 = sign(crossz(vec4, vec5)) + 1 return t1, t2, t3, t4 def accumulatecolor(t, c0, c1, alpha): if alpha == 0: A = 1.0 cacc = c0 + 0.5 t (c0 - c1) aacc = 0.0 else: A = exp(-alpha t) cacc = (1.0 - A) c0 + ((t + 1.0 / alpha) A - 1.0 / alpha) (c0 - c1) aacc = 1.0 - A return cacc, aacc def raymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, tetrahedron, viewprojmatrix): # 1. Intersect ray with tetrahedron faces to find entry/exit points tentry, texit = intersecttetrahedron(rayorigin, raydirection, tetrahedron) if tentry is None: return 0.0, 0.0 # 2. Subdivide ray segment within tetrahedron ttotal = texit - tentry Nsub = 10 # Typical subdivision count dt = ttotal / Nsub cacc = vec3(0.0) aacc = 0.0 for i in range(Nsub): tsub = (i + 0.5) dt c0 = interpolatecolor(tentry + tsub, tetrahedron) c1 = interpolatecolor(tentry + tsub + dt, tetrahedron) alpha = interpolateopacity(tentry + tsub, tetrahedron) csub, asub = accumulatecolor(dt, c0, c1, alpha) cacc = cacc + (1.0 - aacc) csub aacc = aacc + (1.0 - aacc) asub return cacc, aacc Basis Tensor Transformations: Transform BT into Euclidean space: \hat{\mathbf{B}}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = \mathbf{T}^{-1} \frac{\alpha2}{\beta1} \mathbf{T}^{-1} \frac{\alpha3}{\beta2} \mathbf{T}^{-1} \frac{\alpha2}{\beta3} \mathbf{B}{\alpha1, \alpha2, \alpha3} \quad (8) Add density d for isosurface level selection (only affects weight at (3,3,3)): \mathbf{B}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = \begin{cases} \hat{\mathbf{B}}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} + d & \text{if } (\beta1, \beta2, \beta3) = (3, 3, 3) \\ \hat{\mathbf{B}}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (9) Transform scaled tensor into screen space: \tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{P}^{-1\alpha1}{\beta1} \mathbf{W}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{P}^{-1\alpha2}{\beta2} \mathbf{W}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{P}^{-1\alpha3}{\beta3} \tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\alpha1, \alpha2, \alpha3} \quad (10) Color Accumulation: For a sub-interval with constant opacity \alpha and optical depth t: c{acc}(t, c0, c1, \alpha) = (1 - e^{-\alpha t}) c0 + \left( \left( t + \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) e^{-\alpha t} - \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) (c0 - c1) Where c0 is entry color, c1 is exit color. Gradients for Backpropagation (DiffTetVR): Gradient of accumulated color w.r.t entry color c0: \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial c0} = (1 - e^{-\alpha t}) + \left( \left( t + \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) e^{-\alpha t} - \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) Gradient of accumulated color w.r.t exit color c1: \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial c1} = - \left( \left( t + \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) e^{-\alpha t} - \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) Gradient of accumulated color w.r.t opacity \alpha: \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial \alpha} = t e^{-\alpha t} c0 + \left( \frac{1}{\alpha^2} - \left( t^2 + \frac{1}{\alpha^2} + \frac{t}{\alpha} \right) e^{-\alpha t} \right) (c0 - c1) Gradient of accumulated color w.r.t optical depth t: \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial t} = (\alpha c0 + (\alpha c1 - \alpha c0) t) e^{-\alpha t} Gradient of accumulated opacity w.r.t opacity \alpha: \frac{\partial a{acc}}{\partial \alpha} = t e^{-\alpha t} Limit as \alpha \rightarrow 0: \lim{\alpha \rightarrow 0} \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial \alpha} = t c0 + \frac{1}{2}t^2 (c1 - c0) \lim{\alpha \rightarrow 0} \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial c0} = \lim{\alpha \rightarrow 0} \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial c1} = 0 Inversion Trick for Backward Pass: Recover previous ray color: c{ray,i} = c{ray,i+1} - (1 - \alpha{ray,i})c{acc,i} Recover previous ray opacity: \alpha{ray,i} = \frac{\alpha{acc,i} - \alpha{ray,i+1}}{\alpha{acc,i} - 1} Nsub: Number of subdivision steps for the ray segment within a tetrahedron. Typical value not specified, but used to approximate constant opacity. β: Regularization parameter for tetrahedron quality. Value \beta = 10 is mentioned. Projection Type: Orthogonal projection is required for the screen-space triangle computation optimization in the geometry shader approach. The MRT approach works with perspective projection except for the specific pre-computed triangle strip optimization. Graphics API: DirectX 10 with Shader Model 4.0 (for geometry shaders); OpenGL 2.0/GLSL (for MRT approach); Vulkan (for DiffTetVR). Numerical Instability: The exact formula for linearly varying opacity involves the imaginary error function (erfi), which is numerically unstable on GPUs due to large values (10^{20}) and cancellation effects. This is handled by assuming constant opacity within sub-intervals. Degenerate Cases: The method handles degenerate projections by adding 24 class 3 cases and 12 class 4 cases to Wylie's 14 class 1 and 2 cases. Tests yielding result '1' (z=0) indicate degeneracy. Zero Opacity Discard: Early discard test bypasses tetrahedra with zero opacity. Only discard if ALL vertices have zero opacity (scalar values map to zero opacity in TF). Perspective Projection Limitation: The optimization of pre-computing screen-space triangle strips per tetrahedron index fails under perspective projection because screen-space triangles change for different BTs with the same tetrahedron number. Tetrahedron Quality: Tetrahedra must not self-intersect, invert (negative volume), or degenerate (zero volume) during optimization. This is enforced via regularization. Ray Intersection Bounds: Only intersections of the viewing ray and tensor BT inside the bounds of the tetrahedron count as hits. This method handles non-planar quadrilateral faces in curvilinear or irregular grids by performing view-dependent subdivision of "problem" faces and cells into triangles and tetrahedra, respectively, to prevent visibility sort failures and bow-tie projections. It approximates ray integration by projecting cells onto the screen, computing integrated opacity and color at vertices, and interpolating these values across screen-space polygons using standard graphics hardware. Unlike methods requiring resampling of curvilinear grids, cell projection works directly on the general grid topology. A method to sample cell-centered data by approximating neighbor centroids using volume ratios and face normals, avoiding full tree traversal. A method to represent the result of convolving an arbitrary scalar volume with a reconstruction filter as a BT Volume, provided the filter itself is a BT Volume sharing a similar \kappa function. Samples scalar values by interpolating vertex-centered scalar data at the vertices of the current element using the barycentric coordinates of the sample point. Vertex-centered data is stored duplicated per element during TET-AMR construction, allowing direct access via element ID. A differentiable volume rendering solution for tetrahedral meshes that enables optimization of vertex positions and local mesh subdivision without multigrid methods, solving the limitation of regular grids in previous differentiable volume rendering works. It derives equations for more accurate accumulation of color along view rays than simple alpha blending, implements a fast rasterization-based renderer based on per-pixel linked lists, and deduces derivatives for the rendering process to enable backpropagation regarding parameters such as vertex colors and positions. It introduces a differentiable regularization term for avoiding degeneration of tetrahedral elements during the optimization process. The exact formula by Williams and Max involving the difference of two imaginary error functions has far too high numerical instability to be usable in real-world workflows on GPUs when using only 32-bit floating point precision. A volume rendering system for unstructured data (especially finite element data) that creates images with very high accuracy without compromises or approximations for the sake of efficiency. It uses exact mathematical solutions for the radiance integrals involved and for interpolation whenever possible. It handles meshes whose cells are either linear or quadratic tetrahedra, and meshes with mixed cell types (tetrahedra, bricks, prisms, wedges, and pyramids, but not with high accuracy). It embeds accurate semi-transparent shaded isosurfaces in the volume rendering. For very small cells, it uses subpixel accumulation by splatting to avoid sampling error. It extends hardware assisted projection and compositing from tetrahedra to arbitrary convex polyhedra. It uses a revision to an existing accurate visibility ordering algorithm, which includes a correction and a method for dramatically increasing its efficiency. A volume rendering approach for phase space tessellations that combines state-of-the-art order-independent transparency methods to manage the extreme depth complexity of tetrahedral meshes. It proposes a view-dependent multiresolution representation of the data and a tile-based rendering strategy. Phase space tessellation techniques for N-body dark matter simulations yield density fields with a vast amount of elements and self-intersections, causing interactive visualization methods to either employ simplified rendering integrals or suffer from artifacts. Time Complexity: The first pass is O(N) where N is the number of tetrahedra, performed in parallel on the GPU. The sorting step is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the sort algorithm (bucket sort for rotating, mergesort for static). The second pass is O(T) where T is the number of projected triangles, as it renders triangle fans via glMultiDrawElements. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Tetrahedral, Vertex, Gradient, and Classification textures, plus MRT frame buffers and global arrays. The space requirement is very large, limiting the size of volumes that can be rendered on graphics cards with less memory. Measured Performance: On a Intel Pentium IV 3.6 GHz, 2 GB RAM, with a nVidia GeForce 6800 256 MB graphics card, PTINT achieved 11.30 fps on the Blunt Fin dataset and 4.07 fps on the Oxygen Post dataset (512x512 viewport, rotating model). This compared favorably to GATOR (5.20 fps, 1.82 fps), VICP GPU (4.10 fps, 4.47 fps), and HARC (6.09 fps, 2.36 fps). Strengths: Supports arbitrary isosurface values and partial pre-integration. Handles unstructured grids directly. GPU-accelerated. Differentiable variants allow for optimization of mesh parameters. Limitations: Large memory footprint. Orthogonal projection is required for certain optimizations (geometry shader approach). Numerical instability of exact integration formulas requires approximation (sub-intervals). Degenerate cases must be handled explicitly. When to use: When rendering unstructured tetrahedral meshes with high accuracy is required, especially for finite element data or dark matter simulations. When differentiable rendering is needed for mesh optimization. When not to use: When memory is severely constrained. When perspective projection is required, the MRT-based approach should be used instead of the geometry shader optimization, as the latter requires orthogonal projection. Tetrahedral Volume Rendering originated from the need to visualize unstructured volumetric data, such as finite element analysis results, which cannot be efficiently represented by regular grids. The Basis Tensor (BT) volume representation was introduced to support arbitrary isosurface values and efficient rendering. The method was implemented on Direct3D 10 graphics API running on NVIDIA 8800 GTS GPU, leveraging geometry shaders. Later, GPU-Accelerated Cell Projection (PTINT) was developed using OpenGL 2.0 and GLSL under Linux, achieving higher performance on older hardware (Intel Pentium IV, GeForce 6800). More recently, DiffTetVR introduced differentiable rendering for tetrahedral meshes, enabling optimization of vertex positions and local mesh subdivision. The method is used in scientific visualization, particularly for phase space tessellations in dark matter simulations and high-accuracy finite element data. name: Viewpoint-dependent subdivision of non-planar faces
head: Cell Projection with Non-Planar Face Subdivision, Cell Projection with Non-Planar Faces Approximation, HIAC system cell projection, Hardware-based cell projection, Non-Planar Face Subdivision Strategy, Shirley and Tuchman method approximation, Viewpoint-dependent tetrahedral subdivision
body: This method handles non-planar quadrilateral faces in curvilinear or irregular grids by performing view-dependent subdivision of problem faces and cells into triangles and tetrahedra, respectively, to prevent visibility sort failures and bow-tie projections. It approximates ray integration by projecting cells onto the screen, computing integrated opacity and color at vertices, and interpolating these values across screen-space polygons using standard graphics hardware. Unlike methods requiring resampling of curvilinear grids, cell projection works directly on the general grid topology. Inputs: A list of vertices with 3D positions and scalar field values s. A list of cells (hexahedra or other topologies) with index pointers to their vertices. A viewpoint V. Transfer functions mapping scalar s to RGB color and differential opacity \tau, assumed linear or piecewise linear. Outputs: A rendered image with integrated color and opacity. Data Structures: Vertex List: Array of vertices, each containing 3D position (x,y,z) and scalar value s. Cell Structure: subdivided: Boolean flag indicating if the cell is currently subdivided into tetrahedra. oldsubdivided: Char flag tracking subdivision state from the previous frame. numbInbound: Integer count of incoming edges in the directed graph used for sorting. type: Enum or integer identifying the cell topology (e.g., hexahedron, tetrahedron). Vertex indices: Pointers to the vertices defining the cell. Directed Graph: For sorting, a graph where nodes are cells and edges represent shared faces, directed towards the cell containing the viewpoint relative to the face plane. Steps: 1. Identify Problem Faces and Cells: A problem face is a non-planar quadrilateral where a viewing ray intersects the same face twice, potentially creating a bow-tie projection. A problem cell is a cell intersected by a viewing ray in disjoint segments. Detection tests if a viewing ray can intersect a triangulated cell in more than one segment using plane equations of the triangles and locations of viewpoint V and relevant vertices. 2. Subdivide Problem Faces: Subdivide any non-planar quadrilateral face into two triangles. The diagonal must start from the quadrilateral vertex with the lowest index in the vertex list to ensure consistency for two cells sharing a face, as the choice depends only on vertex indices. Even if a face is not a problem face for a specific cell, it may need subdivision if it is part of a problem cell or to avoid gaps between adjacent cells. 3. Subdivide Problem Cells: If a cell is a problem cell for the current viewpoint, subdivide it into tetrahedra. Connect the vertex of lowest index in the whole cell to all triangles from faces not sharing this vertex to create a set of tetrahedra with planar faces. Only problem cells are subdivided; non-problem cells remain intact to preserve performance. Cells containing contour surfaces or scalar breakpoints in piecewise linear transfer functions are also subdivided into tetrahedra and then into slabs. 4. Project and Sort: Project the cell (or its tetrahedral subdivisions) onto the image plane. The projected edges divide the plane into polygons (triangles and quadrilaterals). Sort cells using the MPVO algorithm (or variants like MPVONC/SXMPVO) based on the directed graph of shared faces. Handle gaps with exterior face sorting or A-buffer accumulation. For contour slabs, sort polygons and volume slabs back-to-front based on viewpoint position relative to contour planes. 5. Compute Vertex Attributes: For each polygon, compute vertex attributes (RGB, opacity \tau, length l) at the front and back endpoints of the viewing ray segment through the cell. Profile vertices are vertices on the silhouette. Set color directly from scalar values s and integrated opacity to zero. Thick vertices are internal vertices where the ray passes through the cell interior. Compute the back endpoint's z, color, and \tau by subdividing the interior face with the diagonal from the lowest index vertex and interpolating linearly in screen space. Compute ray segment length l by interpolating depth z across the back face polygon in screen space to find the back endpoint, then reversing the eye-to-screen transformation. Approximate l by computing it at vertices and interpolating linearly across the polygon in screen space. For precise color, compute the correct integrated color analytically once per vertex and divide by integrated \alpha to get the polygon color. Alternatively, use the average of front and back colors. 6. Interpolate and Composite: Interpolate integrated opacity \alpha, color (R, G, B), and depth z linearly across the polygon in screen space using standard Gouraud shading hardware. Composite the interpolated polygons onto the image using the standard alpha blending equation. To correct for non-linear opacity integration errors (Mach bands), use texture mapping hardware in orthogonal views. Specify z and \tau as texture coordinates, linearly interpolate them, and extract the correct alpha from a 2D texture map preloaded with values 1 - e^{-\tau}. In perspective views, this technique is an approximation. Formulas: Integrated opacity: \alpha = 1 - e^{-\tau \cdot l}, where \tau = (\tauf + \taub)/2 is the average differential opacity, and l is the ray segment length. Alpha blending: \text{RGB}{\text{new}} = (1 - \alpha) \times \text{RGB}{\text{old}} + \alpha \times \text{RGB}{\text{polygon}}. Parameters: Transfer functions: Map scalar value s to RGB and differential opacity \tau. Assumed linear in s for the basic method, but piecewise linear is supported by slicing cells. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Hardware color interpolation is inconsistent with analytic integration. Condition (d) (color constant per cell, only \tau varies linearly) is required for hardware-based method to be mathematically equivalent to analytic integration. Boundaries: Non-planar faces cause visibility cycles where a ray intersects the same face twice, making back-to-front sorting impossible without subdivision. Degenerate Input: If a cell is not a problem cell but shares a face with a problem cell, the face must still be subdivided to avoid gaps or overlaps. Performance: Subdividing all quadrilaterals increases polygon count (e.g., 7 to 25 polygons) and OpenGL data output, though fragment count remains the same. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderviewpointdependentsubdivision(vertices, cells, viewpoint, transferfunction): # Step 1: Identify problem faces and cells problemfaces = set() problemcells = [] for cell in cells: cellisproblem = False for face in cell.faces: # Test if viewing ray intersects the face twice using plane equations if rayintersectsfacetwice(face, viewpoint): problemfaces.add(face) # Test if viewing ray intersects the triangulated cell in >1 segment if rayintersectscelltwice(cell, viewpoint): cellisproblem = True if cellisproblem: problemcells.append(cell) # Step 2: Subdivide problem faces for face in problemfaces: vindices = [v.index for v in face.vertices] minidx = min(vindices) minvertex = face.vertices[vindices.index(minidx)] # Split quadrilateral into two triangles using diagonal from minvertex face.splitintotriangles(minvertex) # Step 3: Subdivide problem cells for cell in problemcells: # Connect lowest index vertex of cell to all triangles from faces not sharing it mincellvertex = cell.getlowestindexvertex() cell.subdivideintotetrahedra(mincellvertex) # Step 4: Sort cells using MPVO directed graph sortedcells = mpvosort(cells, viewpoint) # Step 5 & 6: Project, Compute Attributes, Interpolate, Composite for cell in sortedcells: projectedpolygons = projectanddivideplane(cell, viewpoint) for polygon in projectedpolygons: for vertex in polygon.vertices: if vertex.isprofilevertex(): vertex.color = transferfunction(vertex.scalar) vertex.alpha = 0.0 else: # Thick vertex: interpolate z across back face polygon backz = interpolatezacrosspolygon(polygon, vertex) backendpoint = computebackendpoint(vertex, backz, viewpoint) vertex.backz = backendpoint.z vertex.backcolor = backendpoint.color vertex.backtau = backendpoint.tau # Approximate l by computing at vertices and interpolating linearly across the polygon vertex.l = computesegmentlength(vertex, backendpoint, viewpoint) # Compute average differential opacity vertex.avgtau = (vertex.tau + vertex.backtau) / 2.0 # Compute integrated opacity vertex.alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-vertex.avgtau vertex.l) # Compute polygon color (average of front and back) vertex.color = (vertex.color + vertex.backcolor) / 2.0 # Interpolate attributes linearly across polygon in screen space (Gouraud shading) rasterizepolygongouraud(polygon) def rayintersectsfacetwice(face, viewpoint): # Standard geometric test for ray-face intersection multiplicity return False def rayintersectscelltwice(cell, viewpoint): # Standard geometric test for ray-cell intersection multiplicity return False def mpvosort(cells, viewpoint): # O(n) sort using directed graph of shared faces graph = builddirectedgraph(cells, viewpoint) queue = [c for c in cells if graph.inboundcount(c) == 0] sortedlist = [] while queue: current = queue.pop(0) sortedlist.append(current) for neighbor in graph.outgoing(current): graph.decrementinbound(neighbor) if graph.inboundcount(neighbor) == 0: queue.append(neighbor) return sortedlist def builddirectedgraph(cells, viewpoint): # Builds adjacency graph where edges point toward the cell containing the viewpoint graph = {} for cell in cells: graph[cell] = {'outgoing': [], 'inboundcount': 0} for cella in cells: for cellb in cells: if cella is cellb: continue sharedface = findsharedface(cella, cellb) if sharedface: # Determine direction based on viewpoint position relative to face plane if viewpointonsideofplane(viewpoint, sharedface, cellb): graph[cella]['outgoing'].append(cellb) graph[cellb]['inboundcount'] += 1 return graph def projectanddivideplane(cell, viewpoint): # Projects cell vertices to screen space. Projected edges divide plane into polygons projectedverts = [projecttoscreen(v, viewpoint) for v in cell.vertices] return dividescreenbyprojectededges(projectedverts, cell.faces) def dividescreenbyprojectededges(projectedverts, faces): # Computes intersections of projected edges to form screen-space polygons polygons = [] # Standard computational geometry routine to partition 2D plane by line segments return polygons def interpolatezacrosspolygon(polygon, vertex): # Interpolates depth z across the back face polygon in screen space return interpolatelinearlyinscreenspace(polygon, 'z', vertex) def interpolatelinearlyinscreenspace(polygon, attribute, vertex): # Barycentric interpolation of an attribute across a 2D polygon weights = computebarycentricweights(vertex, polygon) return sum(w p.attributes[attribute] for w, p in zip(weights, polygon.vertices)) def computebackendpoint(frontvertex, backz, viewpoint): # Reverses eye-to-screen transformation to find 3D back endpoint backcolor = interpolatecolor(backz) backtau = interpolatetau(backz) return {'z': backz, 'color': backcolor, 'tau': backtau} def interpolatecolor(z): # Linear interpolation of color attributes based on depth return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def interpolatetau(z): # Linear interpolation of differential opacity based on depth return 0.0 def computesegmentlength(front, back, viewpoint): # Computes length l of ray segment. Approximated by computing at vertices and interpolating dx = back['z'] - front['z'] dy = back['x'] - front['x'] dz = back['y'] - front['y'] return math.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) def rasterizepolygongouraud(polygon): # Interpolates alpha, RGB, and z linearly across polygon in screen space using hardware # Composites using standard alpha blending equation pass A method to classify projections of hexahedra from curvilinear meshes into triangle fans or strips for hardware rendering, avoiding the computational geometry complexity of general line-sweep subdivision by handling specific topological cases. A technique to avoid defects in per-vertex classification during rasterization by ensuring at least one vertex on an edge has the correct classification of the second face sharing the edge, affecting the whole edge during rasterization. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(n) for MPVO. Subdivision is view-dependent and may increase polygon count. Detection of problem cells requires plane equation tests. Memory Complexity: Increased memory usage for storing subdivided cells and tetrahedra. Data structures must track subdivision state. Test Case: Demonstrated on a half-cylindrical shell with 19,000 cells. Scaling: Scales with the number of cells and the complexity of the grid topology. View-dependent subdivision adds overhead per frame. Strengths: Works directly on general grid topology without resampling. Handles non-planar faces and visibility cycles. Compatible with standard graphics hardware. Limitations: Approximations in perspective views (linear interpolation of \tau and color). Inconsistent with analytic integration unless strict conditions are met. Increased polygon count if all quadrilaterals are subdivided. When to Use: Curvilinear or irregular grids with non-planar faces where direct ray tracing is difficult. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Developed for volume rendering of curvilinear and unstructured grids. Based on cell projection methods. History: Extended from methods assuming planar faces to handle non-planar quadrilateral faces. Uses concepts from the Shirley and Tuchman method and BSP-MPVO sorting. Usage: Used in scientific visualization for data on curvilinear grids, such as fluid dynamics simulations or structural mechanics. Volume Rendering for Curvilinear and Unstructured Grids, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~csilva/papers/cgi2003.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 Cell projection of meshes with non-planar faces, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1408947/?q=projected tetrahedra, fetched 2026-10-28 (book) Cell projection of meshes with nonplanar faces, https://www.sciweavers.org/publications/cell-projection-meshes-non-planar-faces, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Hexahedron Projection for Curvilinear Grids
head: Hexahedron Projection, Max's Hexahedron Projection
body: Hexahedron Projection is a cell-projection method for direct volume rendering of curvilinear hexahedral grids that classifies the 2D projection of each hexahedron into specific topological cases and renders them as pre-defined triangle fans or strips. It solves the problem of rendering non-planar faces in curvilinear grids without the computational geometry complexity and floating-point robustness issues of general line-sweep subdivision methods. Unlike its sibling Per-vertex edge classification for view-independent cell projection, which is view-independent, this method is viewpoint-dependent, relying on the specific 2D projection topology to determine the subdivision. It offers a significant speedup over subdividing all cells into tetrahedra by minimizing vertex and fragment operations for the majority of cells. Inputs: A curvilinear hexahedral grid. A camera viewpoint (perspective or orthogonal). The 3D coordinates of the 8 vertices of a single hexahedron: V0 through V7. Outputs: A list of triangle fan or triangle strip vertex indices for hardware rendering. If the cell is degenerate or has a bow-tie face, a subdivision into 5 tetrahedra using Shirley-Tuchman fans is generated instead. Data Structures: Vertex array: 8 vertices per hexahedron, indexed 0–7. The standard numbering corresponds to a cube where V0 is connected to V1, V3, V4; V1 to V0, V2, V5; V2 to V1, V3, V6; V3 to V0, V2, V7; V4 to V0, V5, V7; V5 to V1, V4, V6; V6 to V2, V5, V7; V7 to V3, V4, V6. Temporary variables for intersection points: V8, V9, V{10}, V{11} (projected 2D coordinates). Step 1: Bow-Tie and Degeneracy Check For each of the six quadrilateral faces of the hexahedron: 1. Compute the line equations for the four projected edges of the face in 2D screen space. 2. For each edge line, check the positions of the other two vertices of that face relative to the line. 3. If any vertex lies on a different side of the edge line than the other, the face projection is a self-intersecting "bow-tie". 4. If a bow-tie is found, or if the cell is degenerate (vertices coincide), subdivide the hexahedron into five tetrahedra and render using Shirley-Tuchman triangle fans. Step 2: Containment Count If no bow-tie faces exist: 1. Select a reference face (typically the one with the most contained vertices, or a fixed face if counts are equal). 2. Test the four non-face vertices against the four line equations of the reference face's projected edges. 3. Count how many of these four vertices are contained within the projection of the reference face. This count is an integer C \in \{0, 1, 2, 4\}. Note: A count of 3 implies a bow-tie, which is already handled. Step 3: Vertex Permutation Permute the vertex indices so that the vertices of the reference face are mapped to indices 0, 1, 2, 3. Apply further rotation permutations to ensure: In the C=1 case, the contained vertex has index 7. In the C=2 case, the contained vertices have indices 6 and 7. Step 4: Case-Specific Subdivision Based on the count C and the specific intersection availability, generate the triangle fans/strips. Case C=1 (Standard): Find intersection V8 of edges V7V4 and V0V1. Find intersection V9 of edges V7V6 and V1V2. Fan 1 indices: 8, 1, 5, 4, 0, 3, 7, 1. Fan 2 indices: 9, 7, 3, 2, 6, 5, 1, 7. Case C=1 (Alternate A): Triggered if V8 is not found at V7V4 \cap V0V1. Find V8 at intersection of V7V4 and V1V2. Find V{10} at intersection of V7V4 and V1V5. Fan 1 indices: 9, 6, 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 5, 6. Fan 2 indices: 8, 7, 3, 0, 1. Fan 3 indices: 10, 8, 1, 0, 4, 5. Case C=1 (Alternate B): Triggered if V9 is not found at V7V6 \cap V1V5 (in the context of Alternate A logic or similar deviation). Find V9 at intersection of V7V6 and V0V1. Find V{10} at intersection of V7V6 and V1V5. Fan 1 indices: 10, 5, 6, 2, 1, 9, 8, 4, 5. Fan 2 indices: 9, 1, 2, 3, 7. Fan 3 indices: 8, 9, 7, 3, 0, 4. Case C=1 (Alternate C): Triggered if V{10} is not found at V7V4 \cap V1V5. Find V{10} at intersection of V1V2 and V4V0. Fan 1 indices: 9, 2, 3, 7, 8, 4, 5, 6, 2. Fan 2 indices: 10, 7, 3, 0, 1, 5, 4, 8, 7. Case C=1 (Alternate D): Triggered if V{10} is not found at V7V6 \cap V1V5. Find V{10} at intersection of V2V6 and V1V5. Fan 1 indices: 8, 4, 0, 3, 7, 9, 6, 5, 4. Fan 2 indices: 10, 6, 9, 7, 3, 2, 1, 5, 6. Case C=4: No extra vertices needed. Fan 1 indices: 4, 0, 3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 0. Fan 2 indices: 6, 7, 3, 2, 1, 5. Case C=2: Find V8 at intersection of V7V4 and V0V1. Find V9 at intersection of V6V5 and V0V1. Fan indices: 7, 8, 0, 3, 2, 6, 9, 8. A triangle strip is also used, but the specific indices are not explicitly listed in the source text for this case, unlike the count=0 case. Case C=0: The projected vertices form a convex octagon. Permute indices counter-clockwise around the octagon. If vertex 0 connects to vertex 5 (the i-3 case), renumber by replacing index i with 8-i. Find V8 at intersection of V0V3 and V1V6. Find V9 at intersection of V0V3 and V2V5. Find V{10} at intersection of V4V7 and V2V5. Find V{11} at intersection of V4V7 and V1V6. Fan indices: 8, 0, 1, 2, 9, 10, 11, 7, 0. Strip indices: 7, 6, 11, 5, 10, 4, 3, 9, 2. Pitfalls: Floating-point precision can cause inconsistent topological tests (e.g., point vs. line). The method avoids general line-sweep robustness issues by using pre-classified triangle fans for specific projection topologies. Degenerate cells (coincident vertices) and bow-tie faces must be detected and handled separately via tetrahedral subdivision. A direct volume rendering technique for curvilinear hexahedral grids that determines cell traversal by projecting cell faces onto the 2D image plane. It solves the problem of efficiently finding entry and exit points in irregular, non-planar meshes by avoiding complex 3D geometric intersection tests for every cell, instead relying on 2D screen-space projection and ray-crossing tests. Unlike general traversal methods that require pre-computed topological structures, this method uses on-the-fly decomposition and 2D projection, making it suitable for irregular sampling densities. Time Complexity: The method involves a constant number of geometric tests per hexahedron (bow-tie check, containment test, intersection calculations). The classification step dominates the CPU time. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory per cell, storing only temporary intersection points and index lists. Measured Performance: On an 800 MHz Pentium4 Xeon and nVidia 5900FXUltra, rendering 141,960 hexahedra (including 50,352 degenerate and 924 bow-tie) took 5.27 seconds total: 0.13s data read, 3.5s case classification, 1.51s rendering. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of hexahedra. The method is faster than subdividing all cells into five tetrahedra because it requires fewer vertex and fragment operations. Strengths: Avoids robustness issues of line-sweep methods; fast hardware rendering via triangle fans/strips; handles non-planar faces naturally. Limitations: Viewpoint-dependent (requires re-classification if camera moves); requires handling of many edge cases (alternates A-D); bow-tie and degenerate cases still require tetrahedral subdivision. The method was proposed by Nelson Max at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. It builds on earlier work by Schussman and Max [4] for perspective views of cubes, extending it to curvilinear grids where faces are non-planar. It addresses the limitations of line-sweep methods by Wilhelms and Van Gelder [2] and incremental methods by Max, Williams, and Silva [3], which are difficult to implement robustly due to floating-point precision issues in topological consistency tests. Hexahedron Projection for Curvilinear Grids (revision 1), https://www.osti.gov/biblio/862378, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Projection-Based Ray Casting for Curvilinear Grids
head: Hong and Kaufman hexahedron traversal, Hong and Kaufman method
body: Projection-Based Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique for curvilinear hexahedral grids that determines cell traversal by projecting cell faces onto the 2D image plane. It solves the problem of efficiently finding entry and exit points in irregular, non-planar meshes by avoiding complex 3D geometric intersection tests for every cell, instead relying on 2D screen-space projection and ray-crossing tests. Unlike general traversal methods that require pre-computed topological structures, this method uses on-the-fly decomposition and 2D projection, making it suitable for irregular sampling densities. The method operates on a curvilinear grid where each element is a six-sided cell with non-planar, non-orthogonal faces. The algorithm finds the first face along the ray observed from the viewpoint by scan-converting all boundary faces onto the image plane, then projects all faces to find exit points. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Curvilinear grid data (hexahedral elements), scalar values associated with nodes, viewpoint parameters (eye position, direction, projection matrix). Output: Composited color and opacity for each pixel. Data Structures: Hexahedron Representation: Each hexahedron is decomposed on the fly into twelve triangles to ensure planarity for intersection calculations. A hexahedron has 6 faces; each face is split into 2 triangles, resulting in 12 triangles per cell. Image Plane: 2D buffer storing depth and color information. Active Element List / Scan Line List: Data structures to reduce the number of intersection calculations by tracking elements intersecting the current scan line or pixel. Steps: 1. Boundary Face Scan-Conversion: Scan-convert all boundary faces of the volume onto the image plane to identify the first face along the ray observed from the viewpoint. This determines the entry hexahedron. 2. Triangle Decomposition: For the current hexahedron, decompose all 6 faces into 12 triangles on the fly. 3. Projection: Project all 12 triangles onto the image plane. 4. Entry Point Determination: The entry point is determined by the scan-conversion step or by finding the intersection of the ray with the entry face's triangles. 5. Exit Point Determination (Original Approach): Test the remaining 11 triangles sequentially until an intersected triangle (exit face) is found. 6. Exit Point Determination (Follow-up Approach): Group the remaining 11 triangles and project them onto the image plane. Use a ray-crossing technique to find the exiting triangle. Ray-Crossing Technique: A point P is inside a 2D polygon if a horizontal ray starting from P and shooting infinitely to the right crosses the polygon edges an odd number of times. By checking how many times this horizontal ray crosses the edges of the projected triangles, the exiting triangle is determined. 7. Ray-Intersection and Integration: Compute the intersection of the ray with the entry and exit triangles. Interpolate scalar values along the ray segment within the hexahedron; these values are computed together with the depth as part of the ray-triangle intersection test. 8. Compositing: Accumulate the contribution of the ray segment using pre-integration techniques. 9. Traversal: Move to the next hexahedron along the ray and repeat steps 2-8 until the ray exits the volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendercurvilinearvolume(grid, viewpoint): image = createimagebuffer(viewportwidth, viewportheight) boundaryfaces = getboundaryfaces(grid) for y in range(viewportheight): for x in range(viewportwidth): ray = createray(viewpoint, x, y) entryhex = findentryhexahedronviascanconversion(boundaryfaces, ray) if entryhex is None: continue currenthex = entryhex tentry = computeintersection(ray, entryhex.entryface) while currenthex is not None: triangles = decomposehexahedronintotriangles(currenthex) projectedtriangles = projecttoimageplane(triangles, viewpoint) exittriangle = findexittriangleraycrossing(ray, projectedtriangles[1:], tentry) if exittriangle is None: break texit = computeintersection(ray, exittriangle) scalarvalues = interpolatescalarvalues(ray, tentry, texit, currenthex) color, opacity = preintegratesegment(scalarvalues, tentry, texit) image[x, y] = composite(image[x, y], color, opacity) currenthex = getnexthexahedron(currenthex, exittriangle) if currenthex: tentry = texit return image def findexittriangleraycrossing(ray, projectedtriangles, tentry): P = ray.pixelcoords for tri in projectedtriangles: crossings = 0 for i in range(len(tri.edges2d)): p1 = tri.edges2d[i] p2 = tri.edges2d[(i + 1) % len(tri.edges2d)] if crosseshorizontalray(P, p1, p2): crossings += 1 if crossings % 2 == 1: return tri return None def crosseshorizontalray(P, p1, p2): if p1.y == p2.y: return False if min(p1.y, p2.y) <= P.y < max(p1.y, p2.y): xintersect = p1.x + (P.y - p1.y) (p2.x - p1.x) / (p2.y - p1.y) if xintersect > P.x: return True return False Parameters: Viewport resolution: Typically 300^2 to 1024^2 pixels. Hardware: SGI Octane (198 MHz MIPS). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Faces: Faces may be degenerate, non-planar, or non-orthogonal. Decomposition into triangles ensures planarity for intersection. Precision: Depth sorting and intersection calculations are sensitive to precision, especially for large viewports (up to 100 seconds for 1024^2). Sorting Overhead: Sorting step on viewpoint change is around two seconds, negligible for resolutions greater than 512^2. Exterior-Face Ray Casting is a parallel volume rendering technique for unstructured grids that restricts ray casting to visible exterior faces of subvolumes. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing irregular, partitioned data domains by identifying which boundary faces are visible from the current viewpoint, projecting them to screen space, and casting rays only through these regions. Unlike general traversal methods that may enter and exit internal boundaries, this method leverages the associativity of compositing to process segments independently, making it suitable for distributed-memory architectures. Ray-casting Curvilinear Volumes is a method for direct volume rendering of data sampled on a curvilinear grid (six-sided cells with non-planar, non-orthogonal faces) by casting rays directly through the volume without interpolating to a rectilinear grid first. It represents each curvilinear element as bounded by twelve triangles to ensure planarity for intersection calculations. Intersections are computed using ray-triangle intersection techniques, assuming convexity to generate two intersections if the ray intersects the element. Shading methods are similar to rectilinear volumes. Data structures such as a scan line list and active element list are used to reduce the number of intersection calculations. This approach is less prone to accumulation of interpolation errors and easily accommodates irregular sampling densities compared to interpolation-based methods, but is generally slower because it cannot make the simplifying assumptions in traversing regular grids. Time Complexity: The follow-up algorithm is twice as fast as the original implementation. Rendering a 300^2 viewport of the Blunt-fin data set takes 3.45 seconds on an SGI Octane (198 MHz MIPS). Sorting overhead is around two seconds per viewpoint change, negligible for resolutions greater than 512^2. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method is slower than interpolation-based methods for rectilinear grids because it cannot make simplifying assumptions in traversing regular grids. However, it avoids interpolation errors and handles irregular sampling densities. Strengths: Handles curvilinear grids directly, avoids interpolation errors, suitable for irregular sampling, parallelizable via exterior-face casting. Limitations: Slower than rectilinear grid methods, sensitive to precision for large viewports, requires on-the-fly decomposition and projection. When to Use: When the data is naturally curvilinear and interpolation to a rectilinear grid is undesirable due to error accumulation or irregular sampling. When Not to Use: When high performance on regular grids is required and interpolation errors are acceptable. The method was proposed by Hong and Kaufman. The original approach was described in [Hong98], and a follow-up optimization was described in [Hong99]. The technique is part of the broader field of direct volume rendering, which maps data values directly to pixel contributions without intermediate geometric representations. It builds on Hexahedron Projection for Curvilinear Grids, which handles the classification of hexahedron projections for hardware rendering. name: Exterior-Face Ray Casting
head: Visible Exterior Face Rendering
body: Exterior-Face Ray Casting is a parallel volume rendering technique for unstructured grids that restricts ray casting to visible exterior faces of subvolumes. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing irregular, partitioned data domains by identifying which boundary faces are visible from the current viewpoint, projecting them to screen space, and casting rays only through these regions. Unlike general traversal methods that may enter and exit internal boundaries, this method leverages the associativity of compositing to process segments independently, making it suitable for distributed-memory architectures. Inputs: Unstructured grid data (elements, nodes, connectivity). Scalar field values associated with nodes or elements. Transfer function (mapping scalar values to color and opacity). Camera parameters (eye position, viewing direction). Screen resolution and viewport. Outputs: Final image (pixel colors and opacities). Element Connectivity: Adjacency information defining which elements share faces. Exterior Face List: A list of faces belonging to the boundary of the subvolume. Each face includes vertex indices and a normal vector. Visible Face List: A subset of the exterior face list containing only faces visible from the current eye position. Screen Polygons: Convex polygons in screen coordinates resulting from the orthographic projection of visible exterior faces. 1. View-Independent Preprocessing: Determine connectivity between elements. Identify all exterior faces of the subvolume. Calculate face normals for all exterior faces. This step is performed once after data distribution. 2. View-Dependent Preprocessing: When the viewing position changes, search the exterior face list. Extract all visible faces from the set of exterior faces based on the current eye position and face normals. Orthographically project these visible exterior faces onto the screen to produce a set of convex polygons in screen coordinates, defining the exact screen area for casting rays. 3. Ray Casting Loop: Iterate through each visible exterior face. Cast rays from the eye through the screen pixels covered by the projected face polygon. A ray enters the data domain through an exterior face and marches element by element using connectivity information until it exits the domain through another exterior face. Note: Due to irregular shapes and partitioning, a ray may enter and exit multiple exterior faces. 4. Segmentation: Break the ray path into segments based on element boundaries. Because compositing is associative, segments can be processed independently. 5. Sampling and Integration: For each segment (entry a to exit b), compute the intensity contribution. Fixed Sampling Implementation: Precompute a fixed step size dt. Sample at least one additional point c between entering point a and leaving point b. Use the Trapezoid rule to calculate the value of the interval between sample points. Adaptive Sampling (Alternative): For linear elements with function f(x,y,z), the sample rate r can be defined as: r = \frac{|f(P(b)) - f(P(a))|}{b - a} \cdot k where P(t) = P(0) + td, P(0) is the ray start, d is the direction, and k is a constant representing the sampling rate for a unit change in function value. However, fixed sampling is often preferred for simplicity and performance. Gaussian Quadrature Approximation: For linear elements, approximate intensity by computing the value at the middle of the segment. For quadratic elements, sample two points; for cubic, three points, based on Gaussian Quadrature principles (approximating a polynomial of degree 2n-1 with n points). 6. Color/Opacity Mapping: At each sample point, interpolate the function value. Use the interpolated value to obtain color and opacity from a look-up table (transfer function). 7. Compositing: Compute the intensity I(a, b) of a ray segment from entry a to exit b using the formula: I(a, b) = \inta^b e^{-\inta^t \alpha(s) ds} I(t) dt where \alpha is the attenuation coefficient and I(t) is the intensity at point t. Composite the intensity values of all sample points along the ray front-to-back to form the final image value. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exteriorfaceraycasting(grid, transferfunction, eyeposition, screenwidth, screenheight, pixelsize): # Step 1: View-Independent Preprocessing exteriorfaces = [] facetoelements = {} for elem in grid.elements: for faceidx in elem.faces: facetoelements.setdefault(faceidx, []).append(elem) for faceidx, elems in facetoelements.items(): if len(elems) == 1: face = Face(faceidx, elems[0].nodes) face.normal = normalize(cross(elems[0].nodes[1] - elems[0].nodes[0], elems[0].nodes[2] - elems[0].nodes[0])) exteriorfaces.append(face) # Step 2: View-Dependent Preprocessing visiblefaces = [] viewdir = normalize(eyeposition - grid.origin) for face in exteriorfaces: if dot(face.normal, viewdir) > 0: visiblefaces.append(face) screenpolygons = [] for face in visiblefaces: # Project face vertices to screen coordinates and form convex polygon screenpolygons.append(projectorthographic(face, eyeposition, screenwidth, screenheight, pixelsize)) lx, ly, lz = computeboundingboxsizes(grid) ne = len(grid.elements) dt = (lx + ly + lz) / ne finalimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(screenwidth)] for in range(screenheight)] # Step 3 & 4: Ray Casting Loop for polygon in screenpolygons: for py, px in polygon.pixelcoords: rayorigin = eyeposition raydir = normalize(pixelcoordstodirection(py, px, eyeposition, screenwidth, screenheight, pixelsize)) # Trace ray through elements using connectivity; returns list of (entryt, exitt) segments = traceraythroughelements(rayorigin, raydir, grid) segmentresults = [] for a, b in segments: samples = [] t = a while t < b: nextt = min(t + dt, b) p1 = rayorigin + t raydir p2 = rayorigin + nextt raydir val1 = interpolatescalar(grid, p1) val2 = interpolatescalar(grid, p2) samples.append((t, val1, nextt, val2)) t = nextt segcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] segopacity = 0.0 for t1, v1, t2, v2 in samples: c1, o1 = transferfunction(v1) c2, o2 = transferfunction(v2) intervallen = t2 - t1 segcolor[0] += (c1[0] + c2[0]) intervallen / 2.0 segcolor[1] += (c1[1] + c2[1]) intervallen / 2.0 segcolor[2] += (c1[2] + c2[2]) intervallen / 2.0 segopacity += (o1 + o2) intervallen / 2.0 segmentresults.append((segcolor, segopacity)) finalcolor = compositefronttoback(segmentresults) finalimage[py][px] = finalcolor return finalimage Fixed Sampling Interval (dt): Estimated as dt = \frac{lx + ly + lz}{ne}, where lx, ly, lz are bounding box sizes and ne is the total number of elements. Adaptive Constant (k): A constant defining the sampling rate for a unit change of function value in the adaptive sampling formula. Degenerate Elements: Irregular shapes and partitioning can result in concavities and holes. Rays may enter and exit multiple exterior faces. Connectivity information is crucial for correct traversal. Performance: Adaptive sampling increases rendering time significantly. Fixed sampling is often used despite potentially oversampling large elements with constant values. Precision: The integration of intensity involves nested integrals. Numerical approximation (Trapezoid rule, Gaussian Quadrature) is necessary as analytic solutions are often impossible due to non-polynomial transfer functions. Time Complexity: Dominated by ray traversal and sampling. Adaptive sampling adds overhead; fixed sampling is simpler but may use more samples than necessary. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for element connectivity, exterior faces, and visible face lists. Parallel implementation distributes data to processors, requiring local preprocessing. Strengths: Efficient for distributed computing by minimizing communication during ray casting (local traversal). Handles irregular, unstructured grids well. Limitations: Preprocessing (finding visible faces) must be repeated for every view change. Adaptive sampling is expensive. When to Use: Parallel volume rendering of unstructured grids on distributed-memory architectures where view changes are not extremely frequent or preprocessing cost is acceptable. Origin: The method is described in "Parallel Volume Ray-Casting for Unstructured-Grid Data on Distributed-Memory Architectures" (DTIC ADA301855). History: It addresses the challenges of rendering unstructured grids, which often have irregular shapes, concavities, and holes, especially when partitioned for parallel processing. Usage: Applied in scientific visualization for large-scale unstructured grid data on distributed systems. DTIC ADA301855: Parallel Volume Ray-Casting for Unstructured-Grid Data on Distributed-Memory Architectures., https://archive.org/details/DTICADA301855, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Per-vertex edge classification for view-independent cell projection
head: Edge classification for cell projection
body: This method avoids defects in per-vertex classification during rasterization by ensuring that at least one vertex on a shared edge carries the correct visibility classification of the adjacent face. It addresses artifacts caused by per-vertex computations where edge visibility is ambiguous, ensuring the correct classification affects the entire edge during rasterization. Unlike Viewpoint-dependent subdivision of non-planar faces, which subdivides non-planar faces based on the viewpoint, this method relies on vertex attributes to propagate visibility information across shared edges in a view-independent manner. Inputs: Vertex positions of the tetrahedron faces, face normals, adjacency information specifying which faces share an edge, and the view direction. Outputs: Modified texture coordinates, specifically the r component, for each vertex to encode the visibility classification of adjacent faces. Data Structures: Each vertex stores standard attributes (position, normal) plus additional texture coordinates. Specifically, the r texture coordinate encodes the classification of the adjacent face sharing an edge. Steps: 1. Define Edge Directions: Utilize the counterclockwise winding order of each face to define a directed edge for each vertex. For a face with vertices v0, v1, v2, each vertex vi is considered the start of the edge from vi to v{i+1 \pmod 3}. 2. Supply Adjacent Face Normal: For each directed edge starting at vertex v, supply the normal of the adjacent face sharing that edge as a vertex attribute to v. This allows the vertex shader to access the geometry of the neighboring face. 3. Check for Entering Face: In the vertex program, determine if the adjacent face is potentially entering relative to the view direction. 4. Modify Texture Coordinate: If the adjacent face is potentially entering, set the r texture coordinate of the start vertex to a large positive value instead of 0. If not, leave it unchanged. This ensures that the edge classification is correctly propagated during rasterization. Example: Consider two adjacent faces f0 and f1 sharing an edge between vertices v2 and v3. For face f1, vertex v3 is the start of the edge from v3 to v2. The vertex program checks if f1 is entering; if so, it sets the r coordinate of v3 to a large positive value, while the r coordinate of v2 remains unchanged for rendering f1. For face f0, vertex v2 is the start of the edge from v2 to v3. The vertex program checks if f1 is entering; if so, it modifies the r component of v2 since f1 is potentially entering for all fragments of f0. Pitfalls: Unclassified Endpoint: One endpoint of the edge remains unclassified. Computing full classification would require normals of all three remaining faces per vertex, requiring more per-vertex parameters. This problem is considered negligible as mistakes occur at singular positions, affecting at most one pixel per tetrahedron. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: View-independent, avoids complex geometric subdivision, minimal additional memory overhead. Limitations: May result in minor classification errors at singular positions, affecting at most one pixel per tetrahedron. This method is part of the hardware-based view-independent cell projection approach, which aims to render curvilinear grids efficiently on modern graphics hardware. It addresses the limitations of per-fragment classification by using per-vertex attributes to propagate visibility information. The technique was introduced by Weiler and Kraus in their work on hardware-based view-independent cell projection. name: Approximate Cell Sampling
body: Approximate Cell Sampling is a method for sampling cell-centered data in tetrahedral volume rendering that estimates the contribution of neighboring tetrahedra without performing a full tree traversal to locate their vertices. It solves the problem of accessing neighbor geometry when vertex data is not stored for non-coarse elements, using volume ratios and face normals to approximate neighbor centroids. It is distinguished from Simple Cell Sampling by weighting samples by the inverse distance to the estimated centroids, and from Vertex-centered Data Sampling by operating on cell-centered data rather than vertex-centered data. Inputs: point: The 3D sample point in world space. V: An array of 4 vertices [t, l, r, b], where each vertex is a 3D coordinate tuple. tetID: The ID of the current tetrahedron. coarseTetID: The ID of the coarse tetrahedron containing the current element. neighbors: An array of neighbor IDs, where neighbors for tetID are located at neighbors[4 tetID + i] for i in 0..3. cellData: An array of scalar values associated with each tetrahedron. Outputs: A weighted average of the cell-centered data from the current tetrahedron and its neighbors, weighted by the inverse distance to their estimated centroids. Data Structures: The neighbor array and refinement level differences are pre-computed during TET-AMR construction. Steps: 1. Extract the four vertices of the current tetrahedron from V: t, l, r, b. 2. Calculate the centroid of the current tetrahedron: \text{centroid} = \frac{t + l + r + b}{4}. 3. Initialize the inverse distance accumulator and the weighted sample sum: \text{invDist} = \frac{1}{\|\text{centroid} - \text{point}\|}. \text{sample} = \text{cellData}[\text{tetID}] \times \text{invDist}. 4. Loop for each face index i from 0 to 3 (representing the 4 neighbors): a. Retrieve the neighbor ID: \text{neighborID} = \text{neighbors}[4 \times \text{tetID} + i]. b. Initialize the volume ratio: \text{volRatio} = 1. c. Determine if the neighbor is on a different refinement tree and get the level difference: (\text{onAnotherTree}, \text{rLevelDiff}) = \text{ProcessNeighborID}(\text{neighborID}). d. If the neighbor is on another tree, calculate the volume ratio between the coarse elements: \text{volRatio} = \text{GetVolumeRatio}(\text{neighborID}, \text{coarseTetID}). e. Adjust the volume ratio for the refinement level difference. Since each child has 1/8 the volume of its parent: \text{volRatio} = \text{volRatio} \times 8^{\text{rLevelDiff}}. f. Calculate the centroid of the shared face. The face opposite to vertex V[i] is the average of the other 3 vertices. The formula (\text{centroid} \times 4 - V[i]) / 3 correctly computes this because 4 \times \text{centroid} = t+l+r+b: \text{faceCentroid} = \frac{\text{centroid} \times 4 - V[i]}{3}. g. Get the unit normal of the face: \text{faceNormal} = \text{GetUnitFaceNormal}(i, t, l, r, b). h. Calculate the distance from the current tetrahedron's centroid to the face centroid: \text{faceToCentroidDistance} = \|\text{centroid} - \text{faceCentroid}\|. i. Estimate the distance from the face centroid to the neighbor's centroid by scaling the current distance by the volume ratio: \text{neighborFaceToCentroidDistance} = \text{volRatio} \times \text{faceToCentroidDistance}. j. Estimate the neighbor's centroid location by moving from the face centroid along the face normal: \text{neighborCentroid} = \text{faceCentroid} + \text{neighborFaceToCentroidDistance} \times \text{faceNormal}. k. Calculate the inverse distance from the sample point to the estimated neighbor centroid: \text{tmpDist} = \frac{1}{\|\text{neighborCentroid} - \text{point}\|}. l. Accumulate the inverse distance and the weighted sample: \text{invDist} = \text{invDist} + \text{tmpDist}. \text{sample} = \text{sample} + \text{cellData}[\text{neighborID}] \times \text{tmpDist}. m. End loop. 5. Return the final weighted average: \text{result} = \frac{\text{sample}}{\text{invDist}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def samplecellapproximate(point, V, tetID, coarseTetID, neighbors, cellData): # V contains vertices t, l, r, b at indices 0, 1, 2, 3 t, l, r, b = V[0], V[1], V[2], V[3] centroid = tuple((t[k] + l[k] + r[k] + b[k]) / 4.0 for k in range(3)) # Guard against division by zero distcentroid = math.sqrt(sum((c - p)2 for c, p in zip(centroid, point))) if distcentroid == 0.0: distcentroid = 1e-9 invDist = 1.0 / distcentroid sample = cellData[tetID] invDist # Source Algorithm 7 says "0... 4", which is an off-by-one bug for a tetrahedron with 4 faces. Fixed to range(4) for i in range(4): neighborID = neighbors[4 tetID + i] volRatio = 1.0 # Determine tree membership and refinement level difference # Implementation details not provided in sources onAnotherTree, rLevelDiff = False, 0 if onAnotherTree: # Calculate volume ratio between coarse elements # Implementation details not provided in sources volRatio = 1.0 volRatio = volRatio (8.0 rLevelDiff) # Face centroid: average of the 3 vertices not equal to V[i] faceCentroid = tuple((centroid[k] 4.0 - V[i][k]) / 3.0 for k in range(3)) # Get unit normal for face i # Standard cross-product calculation vertices = [t, l, r, b] faceverts = [v for j, v in enumerate(vertices) if j != i] v1 = tuple(b - a for a, b in zip(faceverts[1], faceverts[0])) v2 = tuple(b - a for a, b in zip(faceverts[2], faceverts[0])) cross = (v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]) length = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in cross)) if length == 0.0: faceNormal = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: faceNormal = tuple(c / length for c in cross) faceToCentroidDist = math.sqrt(sum((c - f)2 for c, f in zip(centroid, faceCentroid))) neighborFaceToCentroidDist = volRatio faceToCentroidDist neighborCentroid = tuple(fc + nfd fn for fc, nfd, fn in zip(faceCentroid, neighborFaceToCentroidDist, faceNormal)) distneighbor = math.sqrt(sum((nc - p)2 for nc, p in zip(neighborCentroid, point))) if distneighbor == 0.0: distneighbor = 1e-9 tmpDist = 1.0 / distneighbor invDist = invDist + tmpDist # Source Algorithm 7 line 21 uses cellData[tetID], which is a typo; corrected to neighborID sample = sample + cellData[neighborID] tmpDist return sample / invDist Parameters: 8^rLevelDiff: The scaling factor for volume ratios based on refinement level difference, as each child element has one-eighth of its parent's volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If the sample point coincides with a centroid, the inverse distance becomes infinite. A small epsilon guard is required. Index Out of Bounds: The source loop runs from 0 to 4, but a tetrahedron has 4 faces. Accessing V[4] or neighbors[4tetID + 4] is invalid; the loop must run from 0 to 3. Source Typo: The source pseudocode uses cellData[tetID] for the neighbor contribution, which is logically incorrect; it must use cellData[neighborID]. Helper Functions: ProcessNeighborID and GetVolumeRatio are not implemented in the source; their logic must be provided by the TET-AMR construction pipeline. A coarse approximation method for cell-centered data that averages the cell-centered data of the element and its neighbors without considering distances to centroids. It is a coarse approximation because it does not consider the distances to the neighbors' centroids where the cell-centered data is sampled. Time Complexity: Constant time per sample point relative to the number of neighbors (4 neighbors for a tetrahedron). Memory Complexity: Requires storage of neighbor IDs and refinement level differences, which are pre-computed during TET-AMR construction. Strengths: Avoids the computational cost of traversing the refinement tree to find neighbor vertices. Provides a distance-weighted approximation, which is more accurate than simple averaging. Limitations: It is an approximation; the estimated neighbor centroids may not be exact, especially across different refinement trees or large level differences. When to Use: When vertex data is not stored for non-coarse elements and neighbor geometry must be approximated efficiently. Origin: The method is described in the thesis "Direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement data". History: It is part of the rendering pipeline for TET-AMR data, which uses a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) to locate coarse elements and then traverses the refinement tree on the ray until out of the coarse element. Usage: Used in direct volume rendering of unstructured tetrahedral data with adaptive mesh refinement. name: Vertex-centered Data Sampling
body: Vertex-centered Data Sampling reconstructs scalar field values at arbitrary points within a tetrahedron by interpolating the scalar values stored at the tetrahedron's four vertices using the sample point's barycentric coordinates. It is used when the underlying dataset provides scalar data associated with mesh vertices rather than cell centers. Inputs: The current tetrahedral element T with vertices V0, V1, V2, V3. The sample point P inside T. Vertex-centered scalar values Si associated with Vi for i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}. Outputs: The interpolated scalar value SP at point P. Data Structures: Vertex-centered data is stored duplicated per element during the TET-AMR construction process. This allows direct access to the four vertex scalars via the element ID, without requiring global vertex lookups or neighbor traversal. Steps: 1. Compute the barycentric coordinates (\lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) of the sample point P relative to the tetrahedron T. 2. Retrieve the four vertex scalar values directly from the element's local data structure using the element ID. 3. Calculate the interpolated scalar value SP using the linear combination of vertex scalars weighted by their respective barycentric coordinates. Formula: SP = \sum{i=0}^{3} \lambdai Si where: \lambdai is the barycentric coordinate corresponding to vertex Vi. Si is the scalar value at vertex Vi. \sum{i=0}^{3} \lambdai = 1 and \lambdai \ge 0 for P inside T. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: If the sample point lies exactly on a face, edge, or vertex, some barycentric coordinates will be zero. The formula remains valid, but precision issues may arise if coordinates are computed via floating-point arithmetic near boundaries. The method assumes the scalar data is strictly vertex-centered. For cell-centered data, a different sampling strategy is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def vertexcenteredsampling(elementid, samplepoint, tetrahedronvertices, elementscalars): """ Interpolates scalar value at samplepoint inside a tetrahedron using vertex-centered data stored per element. """ V0, V1, V2, V3 = tetrahedronvertices v0 = V1 - V0 v1 = V2 - V0 v2 = V3 - V0 v3 = samplepoint - V0 d00 = dot(v0, v0); d01 = dot(v0, v1); d02 = dot(v0, v2) d11 = dot(v1, v1); d12 = dot(v1, v2); d22 = dot(v2, v2) d30 = dot(v3, v0); d31 = dot(v3, v1); d32 = dot(v3, v2) det = d00 (d11 d22 - d12 d12) + \ d01 (d02 d12 - d01 d22) + \ d02 (d01 d12 - d02 d11) invdet = 1.0 / det lambda1 = ((d11 d22 - d12 d12) d30 + (d02 d12 - d01 d22) d31 + (d01 d12 - d02 d11) d32) invdet lambda2 = ((d22 d00 - d02 d02) d31 + (d02 d01 - d00 d12) d32 + (d00 d12 - d01 d02) d30) invdet lambda3 = ((d00 d11 - d01 d01) d32 + (d01 d12 - d00 d11) d30 + (d00 d12 - d01 d02) d31) invdet lambda0 = 1.0 - lambda1 - lambda2 - lambda3 # Direct access to duplicated vertex data via element ID S = elementscalars[elementid] S0, S1, S2, S3 = S[0], S[1], S[2], S[3] return lambda0 S0 + lambda1 S1 + lambda2 S2 + lambda3 S3 Barycentric interpolation on tetrahedra computes the scalar value at an arbitrary point inside a tetrahedron by weighting the values at its four vertices according to the point's barycentric coordinates. It solves the problem of accurately sampling vertex-centered data within a tetrahedral mesh, extending the well-known 2D barycentric coordinate system to 3D by relating four tetrahedral subvolumes. Unlike linear interpolation on hexahedral cells which requires solving a system or using trilinear blending, tetrahedral barycentric interpolation provides a direct, geometrically intuitive linear blend based on volume ratios. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and direct memory access. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample, assuming vertex data is pre-duplicated in the element structure. Strengths: Direct access to vertex data without neighbor lookups; linear continuity across tetrahedra; simple implementation. Limitations: Requires vertex-centered data; accuracy depends on the quality of the tetrahedral mesh and the linearity of the underlying field; may exhibit artifacts if the field is highly non-linear within the element. When to use: When the dataset provides vertex-associated scalar values and linear interpolation is sufficient. When not to use: When the data is cell-centered (use Approximate Cell Sampling or Cell-centered Data Sampling) or when higher-order accuracy is required. Originating from the work on direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement data, this method is described in the context of the TET-AMR framework. It leverages the duplication of vertex data during mesh construction to avoid complex global lookups, optimizing performance for rendering.
