name: Volumetric Spot Noise Rendering
head: Hybrid Rendering Pipeline, Shell Spot Noise, Shell noise, Volumetric Shell Spot Noise, Volumetric Spot Noise Rendering Pipeline, Volumetric Spot Noise for Procedural 3D Shell Texture Synthesis, Volumetric fuzzy details synthesis
body: Volumetric Spot Noise Rendering is an interactive method for synthesizing procedural 3D shell textures (volumetric surface details like hair, grass, or fur) by projecting random impulse distributions onto arbitrary surfaces and rendering them as sums of anisotropic Gaussian kernels. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering millions of semi-transparent, oriented primitives without the performance penalty of per-frame depth sorting or the aliasing artifacts of simple geometry instancing. It sets itself apart from its parent 3D Gaussian Splatting via Instancing by using a hybrid pipeline that combines geometry instancing for depth/opacity with EWA splatting and Order Independent Transparency (OIT) for color, specifically addressing the "popping" and "halo" artifacts common in pure OIT or sorting-based approaches. Inputs: A 3D mesh surface. A set of impulses, each defined by position \mathbf{M}, orientation \mathbf{R} (rotation matrix), scale \mathbf{S}, and color \mathbf{C}. Kernel parameters: number of Gaussian components per kernel (typically up to 3). Outputs: A final color buffer with anti-aliased, depth-corrected volumetric appearance. Impulse Texture: A 2D texture of size 4046 \times 4046 texels. Each impulse occupies 6 consecutive texels. Texel 0: Position \mathbf{M} (vec3, 0 padding). Texel 1: Rotation Column 0 \mathbf{R}0 (vec3, 0 padding). Texel 2: Rotation Column 1 \mathbf{R}1 (vec3, 0 padding). Texel 3: Rotation Column 2 \mathbf{R}2 (vec3, 0 padding). Texel 4: Scale \mathbf{S} (vec3, 0 padding). Texel 5: Color \mathbf{C} (vec4). Accumulation Framebuffer: Attachment 0 (Color): GLRGBA32F. Attachment 1 (Count/Alpha): GLR8. Depth: GLDEPTHCOMPONENT32. Resolution: 1024 \times 1024 (or target screen resolution). 1. Impulse Generation: If impulses are not pre-generated, they are placed on the surface. An octree partitions the space around the mesh. For each leaf node (voxel) colliding with the mesh, 15 impulses are generated at the collision point with slight displacements. The position is projected onto a plane approximating the surface using the nearest face normal. Orientation is derived from the normal and random vectors. Scale and color are sampled randomly. 2. Geometry Instancing Pass (Depth/Opacity): Render the impulse primitives using geometry instancing to populate the depth buffer. This pass determines the closest kernel for each pixel, which is used later for the "Improved OIT" calculation. Enable depth writing. Disable color writing. Draw instanced primitives. 3. EWA Splatting Pass (Color Accumulation): Render the impulses again, but this time accumulating color and coverage using EWA splatting and OIT. Disable depth writing. Enable blending. Attachment 0 (Color): Blend function GLONE + GLONE (additive). Attachment 1 (Count): Blend function GLZERO + GLONEMINUSSRCCOLOR (subtractive from 1.0, effectively counting hits/alpha). Clear Attachment 0 to black and Attachment 1 to white (1.0). Draw instanced primitives using the 'accum' shader. 4. Compositing Pass: Bind the default framebuffer. Clear color and depth. Draw the solid mesh (black) to occlude volume behind it. Disable depth testing. Enable blending GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA. Draw a full-screen quad using the 'composite' shader, sampling accumulated color from Attachment 0 and count/alpha from Attachment 1. 3D Gaussian Kernel: The kernel for an impulse is defined as: K(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{x}0) = \frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}0)^T \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}0)\right)}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^3 |\Sigma|}} where \mathbf{x}0 is the center, and \Sigma = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T is the covariance matrix, with \mathbf{R} being the orientation matrix and \mathbf{S} the scale matrix (diagonal). Perspective Divide Approximation: To handle the non-linearity of the perspective divide, an affine approximation using the Jacobian J is used: J = \frac{\partial m}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/x3 & 0 & -x1/x3^2 \\ 0 & 1/x3 & -x2/x3^2 \\ x1/|\mathbf{x}| & x2/|\mathbf{x}| & x3/|\mathbf{x}| \end{bmatrix} where m maps camera space to screen space. Transformed Covariance: The covariance in screen space is approximated by: \Sigma' = J \mathbf{W}{3\times 3} \Sigma \mathbf{W}{3\times 3}^T J^T where \mathbf{W}{3\times 3} is the rotational component of the world-to-camera transformation. Screen-Space Variance and Filter: The 2D variance matrix \Sigma'{2\times 2} is the top-left 2\times 2 partition of \Sigma'. To avoid aliasing, a low-pass filter (identity matrix scaled by \lambda) is added: Q = (\Sigma'{2\times 2} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1} The scale factor for the Gaussian is: \text{scalefactor} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \det(Q)}}. Per-Pixel Weight and Accumulation: The distance d in screen space is computed as d = \mathbf{disp}^T Q \mathbf{disp}, where \mathbf{disp} is the displacement from the kernel center in NDC space scaled by 1024.0. The alpha contribution is: ai = \min(1.0, \text{scalefactor} \cdot e^{-0.5 \cdot d}). The final weight w for OIT combines color, alpha, and depth: w = \max(\min(1.0, \max(cr, cg, cb) \cdot ai \cdot ca), ai \cdot ca) \cdot \text{clamp}\left(\frac{0.03}{10^{-5} + (Uz/200.0)^4}, 10^{-2}, 3 \times 10^3\right) where c is the spot color, Uz is the camera-space depth, and \alpha is implicitly handled by ai and ca. Improved OIT Final Color: To fix artifacts with opaque kernels, the closest kernel's contribution is maximized using the depth buffer from Step 2: L \approx \tilde{K}(\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{p}f) \alphaf + \left( \frac{\sum{i=0}^{N-1} L{\mathcal{C}i}}{\sum{i=0}^{N-1} \sum{\mathbf{p}j \in \mathcal{C}i^} T(\mathbf{p}j)} \right) (1 - \alphaf) where \mathbf{p}f is the closest impulse and \alphaf its transparency. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def diag(vals): """Create a diagonal matrix from a list of values.""" n = len(vals) return [[vals[i] if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)] def mat3fromcols(c0, c1, c2): """Construct a 3x3 matrix from three column vectors.""" return [[c0[0], c1[0], c2[0]], [c0[1], c1[1], c2[1]], [c0[2], c1[2], c2[2]]] def matmul(A, B): """Multiply two 3x3 matrices.""" return [[sum(A[i][k]B[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def matmulvec(M, v): """Multiply a 3x3 matrix by a 3D vector.""" return [sum(M[i][j]v[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] def inverse2x2(m): """Invert a 2x2 matrix.""" det = m[0][0]m[1][1] - m[0][1]m[1][0] return [[m[1][1]/det, -m[0][1]/det], [-m[1][0]/det, m[0][0]/det]] def vertexshaderaccumulation(instanceid, mvpmatrix, impulsestexture): idoffset = instanceid 6 texx = idoffset % 4046 texy = idoffset // 4046 M = impulsestexture[texx, texy][:3] R0 = impulsestexture[texx+1, texy][:3] R1 = impulsestexture[texx+2, texy][:3] R2 = impulsestexture[texx+3, texy][:3] S = impulsestexture[texx+4, texy][:3] C = impulsestexture[texx+5, texy] R = mat3fromcols(R0, R1, R2) Sdiag = diag(S) Sigma = matmul(matmul(R, Sdiag), matmul(R, Sdiag)) # Simplified: R diag(S) R^T diag(S) is not standard. # Correct covariance: Sigma = R diag(S.x^2, S.y^2, S.z^2) R^T Ssqdiag = diag([ss for s in S]) Sigma = matmul(matmul(R, Ssqdiag), matmul(R, Ssqdiag)) # Wait, R Ssq R^T. Transpose of R is R.T. # Let's fix to standard: Sigma = R @ Ssq @ R.T RT = [[R[j][i] for i in range(3)] for j in range(3)] Sigma = matmul(matmul(R, Ssqdiag), RT) Mcam = matmulvec(mvpmatrix, M) # Simplified MVP application x1, x2, x3 = Mcam normU = (x1x1 + x2x2 + x3x3)0.5 J = [[1.0/x3, 0.0, -x1/(x3x3)], [0.0, 1.0/x3, -x2/(x3x3)], [x1/normU, x2/normU, x3/normU]] W3x3 = mvpmatrix[:3] # Extract 3x3 rotation/scale from MVP Sigmaprime = matmul(matmul(matmul(J, W3x3), Sigma), matmul(W3x3, J)) # J W Sigma W^T J^T Sigma2x2 = [row[:2] for row in Sigmaprime[:2]] Q = inverse2x2([[Sigma2x2[0][0]+1.0, Sigma2x2[0][1]], [Sigma2x2[1][0], Sigma2x2[1][1]+1.0]]) detQ = Q[0][0]Q[1][1] - Q[0][1]Q[1][0] scalefactor = 1.0 / (2.0 3.14159265 detQ)0.5 ndcx = x1 / x3 ndcy = x2 / x3 return Q, scalefactor, ndcx, ndcy, x3, C def fragmentshaderaccumulation(Q, scalefactor, ndcx, ndcy, Uz, color, screenpos): dispx = screenpos[0] - ndcx 1024.0 dispy = screenpos[1] - ndcy 1024.0 disp = [dispx, dispy] Qdisp = [Q[0][0]disp[0] + Q[0][1]disp[1], Q[1][0]disp[0] + Q[1][1]disp[1]] d = disp[0]Qdisp[0] + disp[1]Qdisp[1] ai = min(1.0, scalefactor (-0.5 d)0.5) # exp(-0.5d) # Correct exp: import math ai = min(1.0, scalefactor math.exp(-0.5 d)) maxc = max(color[0], max(color[1], color[2])) depthfactor = 0.03 / (1e-5 + (Uz/200.0)4) depthfactor = max(0.01, min(3000.0, depthfactor)) w = max(min(1.0, maxc ai color[3]), ai color[3]) depthfactor accumout = [color[0]w, color[1]w, color[2]w, w] countout = 1.0 - w return accumout, countout Impulse Texture Resolution: 4046 \times 4046. Texels per Impulse: 6. Octree Radius Threshold: 0.2 (for impulse generation). Impulses per Collision: 15. Viewport Scaling Factor: 1024.0 (for NDC conversion). Depth Falloff Clamp: [10^{-2}, 3 \times 10^3]. Lighting Multiplier: 0.06. Slices (Ns): Controls precision of kernel evaluation for semi-transparent kernels (5-60+ fps depending on density). Aliasing: The perspective divide is non-linear. Using the Jacobian approximation prevents the kernel from losing its Gaussian shape. Popping Artifacts: Avoided by using depth-weighted OIT instead of per-frame sorting. Halos: Lighter bands around objects due to excessive blending in OIT. Mitigated by adjusting the weight function. Z-Fighting: Geometry instancing alone causes z-fighting for small kernels. The hybrid approach mitigates this by using EWA splatting for color. Triangle Sampling: Barycentric coordinates must be clamped to keep points within triangles during impulse generation. Texture Wrapping: Instance IDs must be correctly mapped to texture coordinates using modulo 4046. Exceeding texture capacity causes incorrect wrapping. Division by Zero: Jacobian calculation requires Uz > 0 (camera-space depth). Time Complexity: Interactive. Performance depends on kernel density and viewpoint. Flat kernels: 5-60+ fps. Semi-transparent volumetric kernels: 55 fps (2.5k kernels) to 1.5 fps (300k kernels). Memory Complexity: Extremely low. Memory footprint depends on kernel definition (few kilobytes), not the number of impulses. Strengths: Handles millions of kernels interactively; parameterization-free surface projection; avoids sorting overhead; reduces aliasing compared to instancing. Limitations: OIT can introduce halos; complex semi-transparent structures require more slices (Ns), reducing FPS; depth precision issues with very small kernels. When to Use: Procedural hair, grass, fur, and fuzzy surface details where performance and visual quality (anti-aliasing) are critical. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring exact depth peeling or where simple opaque instancing suffices. Volumetric Spot Noise Rendering was introduced by Nicolas Pavie et al. in the paper "Volumetric Spot Noise for Procedural 3D Shell Texture Synthesis". It extends Locally Controlled Spot Noise (LCSN) to model volumetric surface details using 3D kernels. The method builds on EWA volume splatting [ZPvBG01] and Depth Weighted Order Independent Transparency by McGuire and Bavoil. It is used for rendering hair and grass textures. name: Procedural Instancing for Voxel Blocks
head: Cubic Grid Voxel Rendering with Instance Buffers, Feature/center instancing, GalensUnified Cubic Grid Renderer, Procedural Instancing, center instancing, voxel object generator
body: Procedural instancing for voxel blocks replaces baked mesh geometry with a compact instance record per voxel, resolving position, color, and occlusion in the vertex shader using a shared cube template. It differs from surface-based instancing by operating on the full cubic grid occupancy rather than extracted surfaces, and from 3D Gaussian splatting by using hard-edged geometric primitives rather than soft volumetric blobs. Inputs: Occupancy data: A list of occupied voxel coordinates. Texture atlas: A 2D texture array containing block face textures. Shared geometry: A static vertex buffer containing a 24-vertex cube template (6 faces × 4 vertices). Outputs: Rasterized image of the voxel scene. Data Structures: 1. Instance Record (Per Voxel): The instance data is stored in a structured buffer (e.g., StructuredBuffer in HLSL or std430 buffer in GLSL). The layout varies slightly by implementation but generally contains: Position: vec3 or float3 (x, y, z coordinates). Texture Index: int or uint identifying the texture in the atlas. Shape/Rotation: uint or packed ushort fields. In, this is a 32-bit uint where the lower 16 bits represent the shape index and the upper 16 bits represent the rotation index. The rotation is calculated as (int)up 4 + forward. Tint: vec3 or float3 (r, g, b). Clip Parameter: In some implementations (e.g., Unity), a float4 position is used where the w component stores a clip distance. GLSL std430 Layout Example (32 bytes): posX: float (4 bytes) posY: float (4 bytes) posZ: float (4 bytes) textureIndex: int (4 bytes) shapeRotation: uint (4 bytes) tintR: float (4 bytes) tintG: float (4 bytes) tintB: float (4 bytes) Compact Layout Example (6 bytes per voxel): Flat grid index (integer) Six-bit surviving-face mask (uint8) Orbit byte (uint8). 2. Vertex Buffer (Shared): Contains the vertices of a unit cube centered at the origin or (0,0,0) to (1,1,1). Total vertices: 24 (4 vertices per face × 6 faces). Each vertex includes position and UV coordinates. Algorithm Steps: 1. Instance Buffer Population: For each occupied voxel, generate an instance record containing its world position, texture ID, rotation/orientation, and tint color. Store these records in a GPU-accessible buffer. 2. Draw Call: Issue a single instanced draw call (e.g., DrawInstanced or glDrawArraysInstanced) using the shared 24-vertex cube template. The number of instances equals the number of occupied voxels. 3. Vertex Shader Execution (Per Vertex per Instance): The vertex shader transforms the shared cube vertices into world/screen space for each instance. Step 3.1: Vertex Selection Determine which vertex of the shared cube is being processed. v{index} = gl\VertexID + (shapeRotation \ \& \ 0xFFFF) \times verticesPerShape Where shapeRotation & 0xFFFF extracts the lower 16 bits (shape index). Step 3.2: Rotation Matrix Retrieval Retrieve the precomputed rotation matrix corresponding to the instance's orientation. R = \text{RotationMatrixArray}[shapeRotation \gg 16] Where shapeRotation >> 16 extracts the upper 16 bits (rotation index). Step 3.3: Position Transformation Transform the local vertex position v{local} to world space: v{centered} = v{local} - 0.5 v{rotated} = R \times v{centered} v{translated} = v{rotated} + 0.5 + P{instance} + P{chunk} Where P{instance} is the voxel position from the instance buffer, and P{chunk} is an optional chunk offset. Step 3.4: Clip Space Conversion Convert to homogeneous clip space: v{clip} = Projection \times View \times v{translated} If a clip parameter C is present in the instance data (e.g., Unity's Clip), adjust the w-component: v{clip}.w = v{clip}.w + C Or set a clip distance to discard hidden faces by moving corners outside the clip volume. Step 3.5: Output Attributes Pass the texture index and tint color to the fragment shader. 4. Fragment Shader Execution: Sample the texture atlas using the interpolated UV coordinates and the texture index from the vertex shader. Apply the tint color to the sampled albedo. Parameters: verticesPerShape: Uniform integer specifying the number of vertices per shape (typically 24 for a cube). chunkPos: Uniform vec3 for chunk-based positioning. view, projection: Uniform matrices for camera transformation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hidden Faces: Instancing submits whole cubes. Hidden faces are culled by moving their vertices outside the clip volume in the vertex shader rather than omitting them from the draw call. This increases vertex processing load by 2.0× to 3.3× for zero-gap layouts but avoids the overhead of multiple draw calls or buffer rebuilds. Precision Drift: GPU float32 arithmetic can cause drift. The drift is bounded to under 10^{-7} of the unit box, which is less than half a step of an 8-bit channel, ensuring visual correctness. Matrix Multiplication Order: Care must be taken with row-major vs. column-major matrix storage. A workaround (e.g., spvWorkaroundRowMajor) may be needed to ensure correct transformation. CPU/GPU Precision Mismatch: Axis center tables should be kept as Float64Array on the CPU to prevent precision drift, converting to f32 only for GPU copy. Memory Usage: Significantly reduced compared to baked meshes. Memory per voxel is approximately 6 bytes (vs. over 1 kilobyte for six baked quads). At resolution R=64, specimen memory reduced from 42.0 MB to 649 KB. Performance: Geometry build speed is 1.9–4.6× faster than pre-branch core methods. Whole build speed is 1.3–1.8× faster. Maintains interactive frame rates (~60 FPS) at high voxel densities. Cache Efficiency: Cache capacity increases from 6 specimens to ~394 specimens at R=64 before exhausting memory limits. Limitations: Increased vertex work for dense, zero-gap layouts due to submitting whole cubes and culling in the shader. This technique is used in projects such as the block-showroom by lardratboy and the GalensUnified Cubic Grid Renderer. It leverages GPU instancing capabilities to render large numbers of voxel blocks efficiently by minimizing data transfer and draw calls. name: GPU Instancing with Indirect Draw Calls
head: DrawMeshInstancedIndirect, GPU Instanced Voxel Rendering via DrawMeshInstancedIndirect, Graphics.RenderMeshIndirect, Indirect GPU Instancing, Indirect Voxel Rendering, Instanced Voxel Debug Visualization, Instanced Voxel Mesh Rendering
body: GPU Instancing with Indirect Draw Calls is a rendering technique that efficiently draws millions of identical meshes (voxels) by issuing a single draw command that reads instance counts and parameters from a GPU-accessible buffer, allowing the GPU to generate draw commands itself. Unlike standard GPU instancing which requires CPU-side iteration to set up per-instance data or multiple draw calls, this method batches the rendering of all instances into one or few calls, significantly reducing CPU-GPU synchronization overhead. It sets itself apart from Surface-based Instancing with Noise Modulation by rasterizing explicit geometry rather than evaluating implicit surfaces, and from 3D Gaussian Splatting via Instancing by using discrete cube primitives rather than splatted ellipsoids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single voxel mesh (typically a cube), a buffer of instance positions/attributes (e.g., StructuredBuffer or ComputeBuffer), and an indirect argument buffer containing draw command parameters. Output: Rasterized voxels on the screen, with empty voxels clipped based on occupancy data. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Mesh: A cube mesh with 24 vertices (4 per face) and 36 indices (2 triangles per face, 6 faces) to ensure flat shading via unique normals per face. 2. Indirect Argument Buffer (GraphicsBuffer): Target: GraphicsBuffer.Target.IndirectArguments. Layout: Array of GraphicsBuffer.IndirectDrawIndexedArgs structs. Struct Fields: indexCountPerInstance (uint): Number of indices per instance (e.g., 36). instanceCount (uint): Number of instances to draw. Note: Standard indirect args often include 5 integers. specifies the array passed to SetData as [vertex count per instance, instance count, starting vertex index, starting index index, reserved value]. uses IndirectDrawIndexedArgs which maps to indexCountPerInstance and instanceCount. 3. Instance Data Buffer: Type: StructuredBuffer<float4> (Shader) or ComputeBuffer (CPU). Layout: Each element represents a voxel. The x, y, z components store position. The w-component stores occupancy (1.0 for solid, 0.0 for empty). Size: xGridSize yGridSize zGridSize elements, stride 16 bytes. Numbered Steps: 1. Generate Voxel Mesh: Create a cube mesh with 24 vertices and 36 indices to support flat shading. Vertices: 4 per face, duplicated to ensure unique normals. Indices: 6 triangles per face (2 triangles), 6 faces total. 2. Initialize Buffers: Create the Indirect Argument Buffer with size commandCount (e.g., 1 or 2). Create the Instance Data Buffer with size equal to the total number of potential voxel slots. Populate the Instance Data Buffer with voxel positions and occupancy flags. 3. Configure Indirect Arguments: Set indexCountPerInstance to the mesh's index count (36). Set instanceCount to the number of active voxels (or total grid size if clipping is handled in shader). Set other fields (start vertex/index) to 0. Upload this data to the GPU using commandBuf.SetData(commandData). 4. Shader Setup (Procedural Instancing): Define a setup() function to retrieve per-instance data from the position buffer using unityInstanceID. Construct a translation matrix Matrix from the position (x, y, z). Calculate a clip value Clip based on the w-component: Clip = -1.0 + position.w. If w=0 (empty), Clip=-1.0; if w=1 (solid), Clip=0.0. Enable procedural instancing via #pragma instancingoptions procedural:setup. 5. Vertex Shader Processing: Retrieve instance ID and command ID using GetIndirectInstanceID(svInstanceID) and GetCommandID(0). Alternative Grid Calculation: If not using a position buffer but a grid, calculate 2D/3D coordinates from instance ID: x = instanceID % GridWidth, z = instanceID / GridWidth. Transform vertex: v.vertex = mul(Matrix, v.vertex) or wpos = mul(ObjectToWorld, v.vertex + float4(gridPosition, 0)). Output position: o.pos = mul(UNITYMATRIXVP, wpos). 6. Fragment Shader Processing: Discard fragments where Clip < 0 using clip(Clip). Assign color (e.g., deterministic hash based on instance ID or grid position). 7. Execute Draw Call: Call Graphics.DrawMeshInstancedIndirect(mesh, 0, material, bounds, argsBuffer) or Graphics.RenderMeshIndirect(rp, mesh, commandBuf, commandCount). Pseudocode (C# / Unity API): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. // 1. Initialization (Start) void Start() { // Generate voxel mesh (24 verts, 36 indices) Mesh voxelMesh = GenerateVoxelMesh(voxelSize); // Initialize indirect argument buffer int commandCount = 1; commandBuf = new GraphicsBuffer(GraphicsBuffer.Target.IndirectArguments, commandCount, GraphicsBuffer.IndirectDrawIndexedArgs.size); // Initialize instance data buffer (e.g., 1000x1000x1000 grid) int totalVoxels = xGridSize yGridSize zGridSize; ComputeBuffer voxelPointsBuffer = new ComputeBuffer(totalVoxels, sizeof(float) 4); // Populate voxelPointsBuffer with positions and occupancy (w=1 for solid, w=0 for empty) //... (CPU-side population logic)... } // 2. Update / Render void RenderVoxels() { // Configure indirect arguments // Args: [indexCountPerInstance, instanceCount, startVertex, startIndex, reserved] int[] args = new int[] { voxelMesh.GetIndexCount(0), // 36 totalActiveVoxels, // Number of instances to draw 0, // Start vertex 0, // Start index 0 // Reserved }; commandBuf.SetData(args); // Set shader buffers material.SetBuffer("Positions", voxelPointsBuffer); // Execute indirect draw Graphics.DrawMeshInstancedIndirect( voxelMesh, 0, // Submesh index material, bounds, commandBuf); } // 3. Cleanup void OnDestroy() { commandBuf?.Release(); voxelPointsBuffer?.Release(); } Pseudocode (HLSL Shader): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. #ifdef UNITYPROCEDURALINSTANCINGENABLED StructuredBuffer<float4> Positions; float4x4 Matrix; half Clip; void setup() { float4 position = Positions[unityInstanceID]; Matrix = float4x4( 1, 0, 0, position.x, 0, 1, 0, position.y, 0, 0, 1, position.z, 0, 0, 0, 1); // Clip empty voxels (w=0 -> Clip=-1 -> discard) Clip = -1.0 + position.w; } #endif void vert(inout appdatafull v, out Input data) { UNITYINITIALIZEOUTPUT(Input, data); #ifdef UNITYPROCEDURALINSTANCINGENABLED v.vertex = mul(Matrix, v.vertex); #endif } void surf (Input IN, inout SurfaceOutputStandard o) { clip(Clip); // Discard if Clip < 0 o.Albedo = Color.rgb; } Formulas: Grid Position (if not using position buffer): x = \text{instanceID} \pmod{\text{GridWidth}} z = \lfloor \text{instanceID} / \text{GridWidth} \rfloor \text{gridPosition} = (x \cdot \text{Spacing}, 0, z \cdot \text{Spacing}) Clip Value: \text{Clip} = -1.0 + \text{position}.w Deterministic Color Hash: n = (n \ll 13U) \oplus n n = n \cdot (n \cdot n \cdot 15731U + 0x789221U) + 0x1376312589U \text{color} = \frac{n \ \& \ 0x7fffffffU}{0x7fffffff} Parameters: commandCount: Number of indirect draw commands (typically 1). gridWidth, gridHeight, gridDepth: Dimensions of the voxel grid. spacing: Distance between instances (if using grid calculation). voxelSize: Size of the cube mesh. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Leaks: Failing to release GraphicsBuffer and ComputeBuffer in OnDestroy causes memory leaks. Use null-conditional operators (?.) for safety. Empty Voxels: If the w-component of the position buffer is 0, the fragment is discarded. If not handled, empty voxels render as solid blocks. Precision: Using uint for instance IDs is necessary for large grids (e.g., 1 million instances). Null References: Ensure buffers are not null before calling Release() or SetData(). Batches chunk rendering using glMultiDrawElementsIndirect to reduce draw call overhead, storing chunk geometry in a large shared VBO. Choose this when rendering large, static voxel worlds with chunk-based culling. A general-purpose instanced renderer. Choose this for simpler setups where full indirect argument complexity is not required. Uses geometry shaders to generate cubes from points. Choose this when vertex shader instancing is insufficient for dynamic topology changes. Time Complexity: O(1) draw calls regardless of the number of instances, reducing CPU overhead from O(N) to O(1). Memory Complexity: O(N) for instance data buffers, where N is the number of potential voxel slots. Performance: Capable of rendering 1 million voxels simultaneously on integrated GPUs (e.g., Intel XE Graphics). Strengths: Minimal CPU overhead, scalable to millions of instances, simple implementation via standard APIs. Limitations: Requires GPU support for indirect drawing (DirectX 11 / OpenGL 4.3+). Clipping empty voxels in the shader can cause overdraw if not carefully managed. When to Use: Debugging voxel occupancy, rendering large static voxel sets, or when CPU-side instancing setup is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When dynamic per-vertex data is required that cannot be stored in buffers, or on very old hardware lacking indirect draw support. This technique was popularized in the context of high-performance voxel engines in Unity, specifically demonstrated in "Building a High-Performance Voxel Engine in Unity: A Step-by-Step Guide Part 7: 'One Million Voxels'" by CodeComplex (2024). It leverages the DrawMeshInstancedIndirect API introduced in Unity to batch draw calls, contrasting with earlier optimization techniques like sparse voxel DAGs. The method is also used in GPU mesh voxelizers to render voxelized meshes efficiently. Building a High-Performance Voxel Engine in Unity: A Step-by... - Medium, https://medium.com/@adamy1558/building-a-high-performance-voxel-engine-in-unity-a-step-by-step-guide-part-7-one-million-ed987e894b71, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Schokolasbotter/volumetric-smoke-raymarching, https://github.com/Schokolasbotter/volumetric-smoke-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) GPU Mesh Voxelizer Part 3: Render tons of voxels with..., https://bronsonzgeb.com/index.php/2021/06/05/gpu-mesh-voxelizer-part-3-render-tons-of-voxels-with-drawmeshinstancedindirect/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Chunk Rendering with Multidraw Indirect
head: GPU Instanced Voxel Rendering via DrawMeshInstancedIndirect, Indirect Voxel Rendering
body: Chunk Rendering with Multidraw Indirect is a technique for rendering voxel worlds that batches chunk geometry using OpenGL's glMultiDrawElementsIndirect to reduce draw call overhead. It stores chunk geometry in a large shared Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) and uses indirect commands to specify per-chunk offsets and counts. It is distinguished from its parent GPU Instancing with Indirect Draw Calls by its specific application to voxel chunks, where geometry is aggregated into a single massive buffer rather than relying on per-instance vertex attributes for position, instead using a separate vertex attribute for chunk offsets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of "remeshed chunks" containing visible voxel geometry (quads). Each chunk has a world position (chunkPos) and a mesh with a quad count. Output: A single GPU draw call rendering all visible chunks. Data Structures: 1. blocksIbo (Index Buffer): Size: maxIndices elements. Layout: Pre-generated indices for a single quad mesh repeated for each potential chunk. Content: For each chunk index i from 0 to maxIndices / 6, the buffer contains 6 indices: {0, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2} offset by i 4. Total Indices: CHUNKSIZE 6 6. 2. hugeVbo (Vertex Buffer): Capacity: std::pow(GetSettings()->GetRenderDistance(), 3ULL) CHUNKSIZE / 2 elements of type BlockQuad. Layout: Concatenated vertex data for all active chunks. 3. multidrawCommands (Indirect Command Buffer): Layout: Array of DrawElementsIndirectCommand structures. Fields per command: count (indices to draw), instanceCount (1), firstIndex (0), baseVertex (offset into hugeVbo), baseInstance (chunk index i). 4. multidrawChunkOffsets (Vertex Buffer): Layout: Array of glm::vec3 (3 floats). Content: Chunk location offsets relative to the player. 5. ChunkDrawCall Structure: Fields: Chunk pointer, number of indices to draw, chunk's shader position offset. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Index Buffer: Create blocksIbo with size maxIndices. Loop i from 0 to maxIndices / 6. For each i, write 6 indices to the buffer: indices[0] + (i 4), indices[1] + (i 4),..., indices[5] + (i 4). 2. Copy Remeshed Chunks: Iterate through each chunk in remeshedChunks. If mesh->GetQuadCount() == 0, skip the chunk. Ensure GL buffers exist. Reserve VBO/IBO capacity at 1.5 meshcount. Copy mesh data to mapped buffers via memcpy. Write to hugeVbo range via WriteToRange. Swap next buffers. 3. Prepare Multidraw Commands: Create darray for chunkOffsets and commands. Loop i from 0 to chunksToDraw. For each chunk, create a DrawElementsIndirectCommand: count: Number of indices to draw for this chunk. instanceCount: 1. firstIndex: 0. baseVertex: chunkVboRange->GetOffset() 4. baseInstance: i. Add chunk offset to chunkOffsets. 4. Execute Multidraw: Bind blockMultidrawShader. Bind blocksIbo and hugeVbo. Bind multidrawChunkOffsets as vertex buffer at binding point 4. Bind multidrawCommands as indirect buffer. Call glMultiDrawElementsIndirect(GLTRIANGLES, GLUNSIGNEDINT, (const void)0, chunksToDraw, 0). Formulas: Shader Position Offset: The position offset for a chunk in the shader is calculated as: \text{vec3}(\text{chunkLocation} - \text{playerPos}) Where: \text{chunkLocation} = \text{vec3}(\text{chunkPos}.x \times \text{CHUNK\LENGTH}, \text{chunkPos}.y \times \text{CHUNK\LENGTH}, \text{chunkPos}.z \times \text{CHUNK\LENGTH}) Parameters: Huge VBO Reserve Capacity: std::pow(GetSettings()->GetRenderDistance(), 3ULL) CHUNKSIZE / 2 elements of type BlockQuad. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Chunks: Chunks with 0 quads are skipped during buffer copy to avoid wasting buffer space and draw commands. Base Vertex Calculation: The baseVertex in the indirect command must be multiplied by 4 (assuming 4 bytes per vertex component or similar stride logic) to correctly offset into the hugeVbo. Buffer Swapping: Buffers must be swapped after copying to ensure the GPU does not read from a buffer currently being written to by the CPU. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderchunkswithmultidrawindirect(remeshedchunks, playerpos, chunklength, hugevbocapacity): # Step 1: Initialize Index Buffer maxindices = hugevbocapacity 6 # Assuming 6 indices per quad, but source says CHUNKSIZE 6 6 # Note: Source specifies total indices as CHUNKSIZE 6 6. # We will assume maxindices is pre-calculated based on render distance. blocksibo = createbuffer(maxindices) indicesbase = [0, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2] for i in range(maxindices // 6): for j in range(6): blocksibo[i 6 + j] = indicesbase[j] + (i 4) # Step 2: Copy Remeshed Chunks hugevbo = createbuffer(hugevbocapacity) chunkoffsets = [] commands = [] currentvbooffset = 0 for chunk in remeshedchunks: mesh = chunk.mesh if mesh.getquadcount() == 0: continue # Reserve capacity (source mentions 1.5 meshcount, but we are appending) # Copy mesh data to hugevbo meshdata = mesh.getvertexdata() hugevbo.writerange(currentvbooffset, meshdata) # Step 3: Prepare Multidraw Commands # baseVertex is offset in bytes? Source says chunkVboRange->GetOffset() 4 # Assuming GetOffset() returns index count, and we multiply by 4 for bytes (vec3? or vec4?) # Source says baseVertex = chunkVboRange->GetOffset() 4 basevertex = currentvbooffset 4 command = { 'count': mesh.getindexcount(), 'instanceCount': 1, 'firstIndex': 0, 'baseVertex': basevertex, 'baseInstance': len(commands) } commands.append(command) # Calculate chunk offset chunkpos = chunk.pos chunklocation = vec3(chunkpos.x chunklength, chunkpos.y chunklength, chunkpos.z chunklength) offset = chunklocation - playerpos chunkoffsets.append(offset) currentvbooffset += mesh.getvertexcount() # Step 4: Execute Multidraw multidrawcommandsbuf = createbuffer(commands) multidrawchunkoffsetsbuf = createbuffer(chunkoffsets) bindshader(blockmultidrawshader) bindindexbuffer(blocksibo) bindvertexbuffer(0, hugevbo) # Attributes 0-3 bindvertexbuffer(4, multidrawchunkoffsetsbuf) # Attribute 4 # Bind indirect buffer # Note: glMultiDrawElementsIndirect takes the indirect buffer as an array of commands # The source binds multidrawCommands as indirect buffer. glmultidrawelementsindirect( primitivetype=GLTRIANGLES, indextype=GLUNSIGNEDINT, indirect=(const void)0, # Points to multidrawcommandsbuf drawcount=len(commands), stride=0 # Assuming tightly packed commands) A variant step where the ChunkDrawCall structure is initialized with the chunk pointer, the number of indices to draw, and the chunk's shader position offset. This structure is used to aggregate data before creating the final indirect commands. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of visible chunks, as each chunk is processed once to build the command buffer. The draw call itself is O(1) relative to the number of chunks, though the GPU work is proportional to the total number of vertices and indices. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the hugeVbo and command buffers, where N is the number of chunks. The VBO size is pre-allocated based on render distance. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of chunks because it reduces the CPU overhead of issuing many draw calls. The bottleneck shifts to the GPU's ability to process the large vertex buffer and the bandwidth of the VBO. Strengths: Significantly reduces draw call overhead compared to individual draw calls or instanced drawing with base vertex. Limitations: Requires a large contiguous VBO, which may be difficult to allocate for very large render distances. The source disables individual draw calls and instanced drawing with glDrawElementsInstancedBaseVertexBaseInstance via #if false, suggesting this method is preferred for this specific implementation. When to Use: When rendering a large number of similar geometry chunks (voxels) where draw call overhead is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When the number of chunks is small, or when memory constraints prevent allocating a large VBO. This technique is implemented in the gabkhanfig/Cube repository, an unofficial project. It uses OpenGL's glMultiDrawElementsIndirect to batch chunk rendering. The source code explicitly disables alternative methods like individual draw calls and glDrawElementsInstancedBaseVertexBaseInstance, indicating a design choice to favor multidraw indirect for this voxel engine. gabkhanfig/Cube, https://github.com/gabkhanfig/Cube, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cube Rasterization via SSBO
head: GL_DRAW_ELEMENTS instancing, Instanced voxel rendering, Voxel Instance Rendering
body: Cube Rasterization via SSBO is a voxel rendering technique that explicitly rasterizes the visible faces of each voxel as triangle geometry rather than using point sprites or ray-marching. It solves the problem of rendering large voxel fields with exact geometric boundaries and explicit face culling by packing voxel data into a Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO) and using a single large index buffer to draw 3 faces per voxel instance. It differs from Surface-based Instancing with Noise Modulation by using explicit triangle primitives instead of implicit surface definitions, and from Instancing with Procedural/Shader Generation by relying on a pre-computed index buffer for face selection rather than procedural generation in the vertex shader. Input: A list of voxel instances, each defined by a position and material properties. Output: Rasterized triangles representing the visible faces of the voxels. 1. Index Buffer: A single static buffer containing indices for 3 faces of a cube. Each instance requires 18 indices (6 triangles). The total size is N{instances} \times 18. 2. SSBO (Shader Storage Buffer Object): Bound at binding point 0. Contains one uvec2 per voxel instance. data.x: Packed position. Bits 0-10: X coordinate (11 bits). Bits 11-20: Y coordinate (10 bits). Bits 21-31: Z coordinate (11 bits). data.y: Packed material properties. Bits 0-15: ALBEDO (16 bits, R5G6B5 format). Bits 16-19: METAL (4 bits). Bits 20-23: ROUGH (4 bits). Bits 24-27: INTENSITY (4 bits). Bits 28-31: TYPE (4 bits). 1. Initialization: Create a static index buffer defining 3 faces of a cube. The indices correspond to 6 triangles (18 indices total per instance). Create an SSBO large enough to hold numinstances uvec2 elements. Populate the SSBO with voxel data, packing position and material properties as defined above. 2. Rendering Loop: Bind the SSBO at binding point 0. Bind the static index buffer. Issue a draw call using GLDRAWELEMENTS with instancing. The vertex count is 18 per instance. 3. Vertex Shader Processing: Determine the instance index from glVertexID: instance = \lfloor gl\VertexID / 8 \rfloor Note: The source code uses bit shift glVertexID >> 3, which is equivalent to integer division by 8. Retrieve voxel data from the SSBO using the instance index. Unpack position from data.x and albedo from data.y. Compute world position from the packed bits. Determine the local camera position: local\camera\pos = camera\origin - world\position Determine the cube face orientation based on the sign of localcamerapos. The vertex shader uses glVertexID to identify the local vertex within the cube (0-7). The face selection logic flips the vertex coordinates based on the camera direction to ensure only the 3 visible faces are rendered correctly. xyz = uvec3(gl\VertexID \& 0x1, (gl\VertexID \& 0x2) >> 1, (gl\VertexID \& 0x4) >> 2) For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: if (local\camera\pos.i > 0.0) \quad xyz.i = 1 - xyz.i Transform the local vertex: uvw = vec3(xyz) position = view\projection\matrix \times vec4(uvw \times 2.0 - 1.0, 1.0) The source code scales by 0.05 before adding world position. The formula in the source is: gl\Position = view\projection\matrix \times vec4(uvw \times 2.0 - 1.0, 1.0) \times 0.05 + world\position Wait, the source code says: position = viewprojectionmatrix vec4(position.xyz 0.05 + worldposition, 1.0);. This implies the scaling and translation happen in world space before projection. Correct interpretation: local\vertex = uvw \times 2.0 - 1.0 world\vertex = local\vertex \times 0.05 + world\position gl\Position = view\projection\matrix \times vec4(world\vertex, 1.0) Output color and position. numcubeindices: Total number of indices in the index buffer. num\cube\indices = num\instances \times 3 \times 2 \times 3 (3 faces, 2 triangles per face, 3 vertices per triangle). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. uniform uvec2 voxeldata[MAXINSTANCES]; uniform mat4 viewprojectionmatrix; uniform vec3 cameraorigin; out vec3 color; out vec3 worldpos; out vec3 clippos; const float CUBESCALE = 0.05; void main() { # Determine instance index uint instanceid = glVertexID >> 3; # Retrieve voxel data uvec2 data = voxeldata[instanceid]; # Unpack position uint x = data.x & 0x7FF; # 11 bits uint y = (data.x >> 11) & 0x3FF; # 10 bits uint z = (data.x >> 21) & 0x7FF; # 11 bits # Convert to world position (assuming normalized 0-1 range scaled by CUBESCALE) # Note: Exact mapping from bits to world coordinates depends on the specific implementation. # The source code implies a direct mapping, likely assuming a fixed grid or normalized coordinates. # For the purpose of this article, we assume the bits represent normalized coordinates [0, 1]. vec3 worldposition = vec3(float(x) / 2048.0, float(y) / 1024.0, float(z) / 2048.0); # Unpack albedo uint albedo = data.y & 0xFFFF; uint ured = (albedo & 0x7C00) >> 11; # R5 uint ugreen = (albedo & 0x03E0) >> 5; # G6 uint ublue = albedo & 0x001F; # B5 vec3 albedocolor = vec3(float(ured) / 31.0, float(ugreen) / 63.0, float(ublue) / 31.0); # Determine face orientation vec3 localcamerapos = cameraorigin - worldposition; uint vertexlocalid = glVertexID & 0x7; # 3 bits for 8 vertices uvec3 xyz = uvec3(vertexlocalid & 0x1, (vertexlocalid & 0x2) >> 1, (vertexlocalid & 0x4) >> 2); if (localcamerapos.x > 0.0) { xyz.x = 1 - xyz.x; } if (localcamerapos.y > 0.0) { xyz.y = 1 - xyz.y; } if (localcamerapos.z > 0.0) { xyz.z = 1 - xyz.z; } vec3 uvw = vec3(xyz); # Transform vertex vec3 localvertex = uvw 2.0 - 1.0; vec3 worldvertex = localvertex CUBESCALE + worldposition; glPosition = viewprojectionmatrix vec4(worldvertex, 1.0); color = albedocolor; worldpos = worldposition; clippos = glPosition.xyz; } Precision: The position packing uses 11+10+11 bits. Ensure the world space coordinates fit within this range. If the voxel grid is larger, the precision may be insufficient, leading to visible artifacts. Face Culling: The face selection logic relies on the camera position relative to the voxel. If the camera is exactly aligned with a voxel face, the sign check may be ambiguous. However, the strict inequality > 0.0 ensures a consistent choice. Index Buffer Size: The index buffer size grows linearly with the number of instances. For very large voxel counts, this may exceed GPU memory limits. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels. Each voxel requires a constant amount of work in the vertex shader. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the SSBO and index buffer. Each voxel uses 8 bytes in the SSBO and 18 indices in the index buffer. Performance: On dedicated graphics cards, this method is approximately twice as slow as Surface-based Instancing with Noise Modulation (MODEQUAD). On Intel Integrated graphics, performance is similar. Strengths: Exact cube geometry, explicit face culling, no ray-marching overhead in the fragment shader. Limitations: Higher memory bandwidth usage due to explicit triangle geometry. Slower on dedicated GPUs compared to point-sprite based methods. This method was described by Sebastian Aaltonen in a tweet. It is implemented in the voxel-renderer project by Clay John. The technique is part of a series of voxel rendering experiments exploring different rasterization strategies. name: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Geometry
head: AABB Geometry, RenderClippedBoundingBox, Volume Extent Bounding Box
body: Renders the clipped bounding box geometry of a volume extent to the framebuffer, optionally including texture coordinates. It defines the wireframe or solid outline of the volume using a fixed set of vertices representing the 6 faces of the box. Unlike sibling methods that may draw arbitrary debug lines or dynamic bounds, this method specifically targets the static volume extent defined by minimum and maximum corners. Inputs: currentBlock: sizet index of the current rendering block. numberOfBlocks: sizet total number of blocks to process. tcoordFlag: Boolean/int flag indicating whether to render texture coordinates. renWin: Pointer to the render window context. minB: Minimum corner of the bounding box, typically (-1.0, -1.0, -0.42578125). maxB: Maximum corner of the bounding box, typically (1.0, 1.0, 0.42578125). Outputs: Framebuffer with the bounding box geometry rendered. Boolean return value: true if rendering should abort, false otherwise. Data Structures: Vertices Array: A flat array of 36 floats (12 triangles \times 3 vertices \times 3 components) defining the 6 faces of the box. The vertices are hardcoded to represent the AABB defined by minB and maxB. VAO (Vertex Array Object): Stores the vertex attribute configuration. VBO (Vertex Buffer Object): Stores the vertex data in GPU memory. Steps: 1. Validate that currentBlock is within the range [0, numberOfBlocks). If invalid, abort rendering. 2. Generate a Vertex Array Object (VAO) and a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) using standard OpenGL calls. 3. Upload the hardcoded vertex data (36 floats) to the VBO using GLSTATICDRAW. 4. Set the vertex attribute pointer for position (attribute index 0) to read 3 floats per vertex, with no stride and no offset. 5. Enable the vertex attribute array. 6. Render the geometry (typically as lines or triangles) to the framebuffer. 7. Return true if rendering should abort, false otherwise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderaabbgeometry(currentblock, numberofblocks, tcoordflag, renwin, minb, maxb): # Step 1: Validate block index if currentblock >= numberofblocks: return True # Abort rendering # Step 2: Generate VAO and VBO vao = glGenvertexarrays(1) vbo = glGenbuffers(1) # Step 3: Define vertices for AABB # 6 faces, 2 triangles per face, 3 vertices per triangle = 36 vertices # Coordinates are derived from minb and maxb # Example for minb=(-1,-1,-0.42578125), maxb=(1,1,0.42578125) vertices = [ # Front face (z = maxb.z) minb.x, minb.y, maxb.z, maxb.x, minb.y, maxb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, minb.x, minb.y, maxb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, minb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, # Back face (z = minb.z) minb.x, minb.y, minb.z, minb.x, maxb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, minb.z, minb.x, minb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, minb.y, minb.z, # Left face (x = minb.x) minb.x, minb.y, minb.z, minb.x, maxb.y, minb.z, minb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, minb.x, minb.y, minb.z, minb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, minb.x, minb.y, maxb.z, # Right face (x = maxb.x) maxb.x, minb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, maxb.x, minb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, maxb.x, minb.y, maxb.z, # Bottom face (y = minb.y) minb.x, minb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, minb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, minb.y, maxb.z, minb.x, minb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, minb.y, maxb.z, minb.x, minb.y, maxb.z, # Top face (y = maxb.y) minb.x, maxb.y, minb.z, minb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, minb.x, maxb.y, minb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, maxb.z, maxb.x, maxb.y, minb.z ] # Step 4: Upload vertex data glBindbuffer(GLARRAYBUFFER, vbo) glbufferdata(GLARRAYBUFFER, len(vertices) 4, vertices, GLSTATICDRAW) # Step 5: Set vertex attribute pointer glBindvertexarray(vao) glVertexAttribPointer(0, 3, GLFLOAT, GLFALSE, 3 4, None) glEnableVertexAttribArray(0) # Step 6: Render # Note: Texture coordinates are not explicitly generated in the source notes, # but tcoordFlag suggests they might be used if available. # Assuming rendering as triangles or lines based on the 36-vertex structure. gldrawarrays(GLTRIANGLES, 0, 36) # Step 7: Cleanup (optional, depending on context) # gldeletebuffers(1, vbo) # gldeletevertexarrays(1, vao) return False # Continue rendering Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The z-coordinate 0.42578125 is a specific value from the source. Using floating-point comparisons for bounds validation should account for epsilon if dynamic bounds are used. Boundaries: The method assumes a fixed AABB. If the volume extent changes, the vertex data must be regenerated. Degenerate Input: If minb equals maxb, the box has zero volume and will not render visibly. Draws arbitrary bounding boxes for debugging. Choose when you need to visualize dynamic or non-axis-aligned bounds. Time Complexity: O(1) for geometry generation and upload, as the vertex count is fixed at 36 floats. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring storage for 36 floats and one VAO/VBO pair. Strengths: Simple, fast, and deterministic. Ideal for visualizing the static extent of a volume block. Limitations: Does not adapt to dynamic volume changes without regeneration. Only renders axis-aligned boxes. When to use: Debugging volume rendering by visualizing the extent of individual blocks or the entire volume. When not to use: When dynamic, non-axis-aligned, or complex bounding volumes are required. This method is derived from implementations in VTK-based volume ray casters and custom ray tracing engines. name: Ray-Box Intersection via Quad Rasterization
body: A voxel rendering technique where each voxel is represented by a single point in a vertex array, sized to cover the voxel's projected area, with the actual voxel geometry (cube) intersected with a ray in the fragment shader using an optimized ray-box intersection test. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sparse Voxel Octree Rendering via Square Splats and Voxel Point Sprite Rendering by deferring the geometric intersection logic entirely to the fragment shader, allowing for a single draw call per voxel set rather than rasterizing explicit cube faces or traversing tree structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of voxel positions encoded as 32-bit integers in a vertex buffer, camera parameters (position, projection matrix), and screen resolution. Output: A depth-buffered image where voxels are rendered as solid cubes. Data Structures: The vertex buffer stores one entry per voxel. Each entry consists of two 32-bit unsigned integers: 1. pos: A packed 32-bit integer representing the voxel's (x, y, z) coordinates. Bits 0-10: x coordinate (11 bits). Bits 11-16: y coordinate (6 bits, shifted left by 11). Bits 17-31: z coordinate (15 bits, shifted left by 21). 2. albedo: A packed 32-bit integer representing color. Bits 0-4: Red (5 bits). Bits 5-10: Green (6 bits, shifted left by 5). Bits 11-15: Blue (5 bits, shifted left by 11). Bits 16-31: Alpha (16 bits, unused in the provided snippet but part of the 32-bit word). In the fragment shader, the following structures are used for intersection: Box: Contains vec3 center, vec3 radius, vec3 invRadius, and mat3 rotation. Ray: Contains vec3 origin and vec3 direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Setup: Create a vertex buffer containing one vertex per voxel. The vertex position is typically (0,0,0) in local space, but the point size is set to cover the projected area of the voxel cube. Enable GLPROGRAMPOINTSIZE to allow the vertex shader to define the point size dynamically. 2. Draw Call: Render all voxels using a single glDrawArrays call with the GLPOINTS primitive. 3. Fragment Shader - Ray Reconstruction: Reconstruct the eye-space position from glFragCoord. Compute the ray direction as the normalized vector from the reconstructed eye-space position to the camera origin: ray.direction = -\frac{camera\origin - eyePos}{||camera\origin - eyePos||} Set ray.origin to cameraorigin. 4. Fragment Shader - Intersection Test: Define the voxel box. The voxel center is derived from the vertex data (unpacked from pos). The radius is hardcoded to 0.05 in the fragment shader. Call the intersection function ourIntersectBoxCommon with the voxel center, radius, and ray. Pass false for rayCanStartInBox and false for oriented to optimize for axis-aligned boxes where the ray starts outside. 5. Fragment Shader - Depth Writing: If the intersection test fails, discard the fragment. If it succeeds, compute the fragment depth using the intersection distance and write it to glFragDepth to ensure correct depth testing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. void main() { // Unpack position from vertex buffer if necessary, # but typically points are rendered at (0,0,0) and transformed by model/view/projection. # The key is setting the point size to cover the voxel. glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix modelmatrix vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); glPointSize = pointsizecoveringvoxel; # Set to cover projected cube area } struct Ray { vec3 origin; vec3 direction; }; struct Box { vec3 center; vec3 radius; vec3 invRadius; mat3 rotation; }; // Optimized ray-box intersection for axis-aligned, ray outside box bool ourIntersectBoxCommon(Ray ray, Box box, out float tmin, out float tmax) { // Precompute invRayDirection to avoid division by zero in shader vec3 invRayDir = 1.0 / ray.direction; vec3 t0 = (box.center - box.radius - ray.origin) invRayDir; vec3 t1 = (box.center + box.radius - ray.origin) invRayDir; vec3 tminvec = min(t0, t1); vec3 tmaxvec = max(t0, t1); tmin = max(max(tminvec.x, tminvec.y), tminvec.z); tmax = min(min(tmaxvec.x, tmaxvec.y), tmaxvec.z); return tmax >= tmin; } void main() { // Reconstruct eye-space position vec4 clippos = vec4(glFragCoord.xy, 0.0, 1.0); // z=0 for near plane approximation or use inverse projection // More accurate reconstruction: vec4 ndc = vec4(glFragCoord.x / viewportwidth 2.0 - 1.0, glFragCoord.y / viewportheight 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0); vec4 eyepos = inverseprojectionmatrix ndc; eyepos /= eyepos.w; vec3 rayorigin = cameraposition; vec3 raydirection = normalize(eyepos.xyz - cameraposition); // Unpack voxel center from vertex attribute uint pos = vertexpos; uint x = pos & 0x7FF; uint y = (pos >> 11) & 0x3F; uint z = (pos >> 17) & 0x7FFF; vec3 voxelcenter = vec3(float(x), float(y), float(z)); Box box; box.center = voxelcenter; box.radius = vec3(0.05); // Hardcoded radius box.invRadius = 1.0 / box.radius; box.rotation = mat3(1.0); // Axis-aligned Ray ray; ray.origin = rayorigin; ray.direction = raydirection; float tmin, tmax; if (!ourIntersectBoxCommon(ray, box, tmin, tmax)) { discard; } // Compute depth float depth = length(ray.origin + ray.direction tmin - cameraposition); glFragDepth = depth; // Output color glFragColor = vec4(vertexalbedo / 255.0, 1.0); } Parameters: Voxel radius: 0.05 (hardcoded in the fragment shader). Point size: Sized to cover the voxel's projected area. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: When computing distance to plane, if the ray direction component is zero, division by zero occurs. The code precomputes invRayDirection (1.0 / ray.direction) and passes it to avoid runtime division, assuming finite values. Ray Origin Inside Box: The intersection function is called with rayCanStartInBox = false, which is an optimization for axis-aligned boxes where the ray starts outside. If the ray starts inside, this may lead to incorrect intersection results. Renders voxels as square splats but traverses a sparse voxel octree structure. Choose when memory efficiency is critical and the scene is sparse. Renders voxels as point sprites with depth peeling or similar techniques for transparency. Choose when handling transparent voxels is required. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as each voxel is processed in a single draw call. The fragment shader performs a constant-time ray-box intersection. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the vertex buffer storing voxel positions and attributes. Measured Performance: On dedicated graphics cards, MODEQUAD is approximately twice as fast as MODECUBE. On Intel Integrated graphics, performance is similar between the two techniques. Strengths: Single draw call for all voxels, efficient use of fragment shader for intersection, reduced overdraw compared to MODECUBE. Limitations: Requires fragment shader support for ray-box intersection, potential precision issues with ray reconstruction, not suitable for highly transparent scenes without additional techniques. When to Use: Dense voxel scenes on dedicated GPUs where performance is critical. When Not to Use: Scenes with high transparency requiring depth peeling, or on integrated graphics where the performance gain is negligible. Originated from a short test project in efficient voxel rendering by Clay John, demonstrating two modes: MODEQUAD and MODECUBE. MODEQUAD uses the ray-box intersection method described in the Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques (JCGT) paper "Ray-Box Intersection for 3D Grids" (https://jcgt.org/published/0007/03/04/). The technique was developed as an experiment in high-performance voxel rendering, leveraging modern GPU capabilities for fragment shader-based ray tracing. name: 3-axis rasterization voxelization
head: 6-separating voxelization of 2D input, CNS*11 method, FBP09 method
body: This method produces a 6-separating voxelization of 2D input geometry by rasterizing primitives along three axis-aligned projection directions in three separate passes. It is designed to generate a sparser voxel set than 26-separating methods, which is sufficient and preferable when ray marching algorithms utilize 6-connected paths. It differs from its siblings by relying on simple point-depth evaluations at pixel centers rather than complex geometric intersection tests against volumetric targets. Inputs: A set of 2D input primitives (e.g., triangles or curves) defined in 3D space. Outputs: A set of occupied voxels Sd that form a 6-separating boundary. Data Structures: The output is a sparse set of voxel coordinates. No specific bit-packing is mandated by the core definition, though implementations typically use hash maps or sparse grids. The internal state for each pass involves a 2D rasterization buffer (depth buffer) aligned with the projection plane. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty set Sd for the output voxels. 2. Define the three axis-aligned projection directions: x, y, and z. 3. For each direction d \in \{x, y, z\}: a. Project the input primitives onto the 2D plane perpendicular to d. b. Rasterize the projected primitives into a 2D grid (pixel buffer). c. For each pixel (u, v) covered by the rasterization: i. Evaluate the depth z{prim} of the primitive at the center of the pixel. The "center" corresponds to the voxel face center in the projection plane. ii. Determine the voxel index k along the projection axis d such that the voxel center is closest in depth to z{prim}. iii. Add the voxel at position (u, v, k) (mapped to global coordinates) to Sd. 4. Return Sd. Formulas: Let the voxel grid have unit spacing. For a projection along axis d, let the pixel coordinates be (u, v). The voxel center in the projection plane is (u + 0.5, v + 0.5). Let P(u, v) be the point on the primitive surface directly above/below this center. The depth value is z{prim} = P(u, v) \cdot \hat{d}. The voxel index k is: k = \text{round}(z{prim}) The voxel is added to the set if it is the closest voxel center to the primitive surface along the projection ray. Parameters: Voxel Resolution: Not specified in the sources. Passes: Exactly 3 (one per axis). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Curved Primitives: The method produces 6-separating results even for curved primitives, relying only on point depth evaluations. Precision: The method requires accurate point evaluations of depth at pixel centers. Separation Guarantee: The 6-separation property holds because the effective intersection target is the "crosshairs" shape (connecting voxel face centers), which allows continuous paths between 6-neighbors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelize3axis(primitives, voxelsize=1.0): occupiedvoxels = set() # Define projection axes and their corresponding 2D planes # Axis 0 (X): Project onto YZ plane # Axis 1 (Y): Project onto XZ plane # Axis 2 (Z): Project onto XY plane axes = [ {'axis': 0, 'plane': (1, 2), 'depthaxis': 0}, {'axis': 1, 'plane': (0, 2), 'depthaxis': 1}, {'axis': 2, 'plane': (0, 1), 'depthaxis': 2} ] for proj in axes: axisidx = proj['axis'] planeindices = proj['plane'] depthidx = proj['depthaxis'] # 1. Rasterize along this axis # We iterate over the bounding box of the primitives in the 2D plane # For each pixel in the 2D plane: for u, v in getrasterizedpixels(primitives, planeindices): # 2. Evaluate depth at pixel center # Pixel center in 3D space relative to voxel grid # Assuming voxel grid origin at 0,0,0 and unit spacing # The 'u' and 'v' here are integer grid coordinates center2d = [0, 0, 0] center2d[planeindices[0]] = u + 0.5 center2d[planeindices[1]] = v + 0.5 # Find the point on the primitive closest to this 2D center along the depth axis # This requires solving for the primitive intersection or evaluation # For a triangle, this is a standard barycentric evaluation # For a curve, this is a root finding or parameter evaluation depthval = evaluateprimitivedepth(primitives, center2d, depthidx) # 3. Determine closest voxel # The voxel index along the depth axis is the rounded depth value k = round(depthval) # Construct the 3D voxel coordinate voxelcoord = [0, 0, 0] voxelcoord[planeindices[0]] = u voxelcoord[planeindices[1]] = v voxelcoord[depthidx] = k occupiedvoxels.add(tuple(voxelcoord)) return occupiedvoxels The geometric interpretation of this method. It uses line segments connecting voxel face centers. It is minimal for 6-separation, unlike octahedral targets which are supersets. GPU Implementations (FBP09, CNS11): Specific GPU-based realizations of this method. They are equivalent to the crosshairs target and are 6-separating for curved primitives. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of primitives and R is the number of pixels in the rasterization buffer. Three passes are required. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of occupied voxels. Performance: The method is efficient on GPUs due to the simplicity of rasterization and depth evaluation. Strengths: Produces a sparse, 6-separating voxel set. Works with curved primitives using only point evaluations. Limitations: Only 6-separating, not 26-separating. Requires three full rasterization passes. The method was analyzed in the context of topological voxelization by Laine et al.. It is equivalent to the GPU-based voxelization methods used by Forest et al. [FBP09] and Crassin et al. [CNS11]. The theoretical basis for 6-separation relies on the work of Cohen-Or and Kaufman [COK97] regarding connected ray paths. A Topological Approach to Voxelization, https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/pubs/2013-06A-Topological-Approach/laine2013egsrpaper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Chunked UV Rasterization with Face ID Storage
head: UV Space Rasterization for Voxelization
body: This method converts a triangle mesh into a voxelized representation by rasterizing triangles into a 2D texture buffer in UV space, storing the face ID in the alpha channel to enable per-texel face identification and subsequent 3D position interpolation. It builds on Rasterization-based Voxelization by decoupling the rasterization step from the 3D grid storage, allowing for memory-friendly chunked processing of large meshes. Unlike 3D Grid Rasterization which operates directly in 3D, this approach projects the mesh onto a 2D plane, leveraging standard 2D rasterization hardware or libraries to determine coverage and face identity before mapping results back to 3D voxel coordinates. Inputs: outvertices: Tensor of vertex positions, shape (Nv, 3). outfaces: Tensor of face indices, shape (Nf, 3). outuvs: Tensor of UV coordinates for vertices, shape (Nv, 2). texturesize: Resolution of the 2D rasterization buffer (e.g., 1024). chunksize: Number of faces to process per rasterization call (default 100,000). Outputs: rast: A 4D tensor of shape (1, \text{texture\size}, \text{texture\size}, 4) representing the rasterization buffer. The RGB channels store interpolated UV or depth information (implementation dependent), and the Alpha channel stores the face ID. pos: Interpolated 3D positions for each valid texel, shape (\text{texture\size}, \text{texture\size}, 3). Data Structures: rast: Float32 tensor. The alpha channel is used to store the global face index i. mask: Boolean tensor indicating valid texels where alpha > 0. Steps: 1. Prepare UV Coordinates: Convert vertex UVs to clip space coordinates for rasterization. The UVs are scaled to [-1, 1] and extended to homogeneous coordinates (u, v, 0, 1). \text{uvs\rast} = \text{cat}([\text{out\uvs} \times 2 - 1, \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}], \text{dim}=-1) Shape: (Nv, 4). 2. Initialize Rasterization Buffer: Create a zero-initialized tensor for the 2D buffer. \text{rast} = \text{zeros}((1, \text{texture\size}, \text{texture\size}, 4), \text{device}=\text{'cuda'}, \text{dtype}=\text{float32}) 3. Chunked Rasterization Loop: Iterate over faces in chunks of size chunksize (default 100,000). For each chunk starting at index i: a. Rasterize Chunk: Call the rasterization function dr.rasterize with the UV coordinates and the current face chunk. The function returns a rasterization result rastchunk and auxiliary data. \text{rast\chunk}, \ = \text{dr.rasterize}(\text{ctx}, \text{uvs\rast}, \text{out\faces}[i:i+\text{chunk\size}], \text{resolution}=[\text{texture\size}, \text{texture\size}]) b. Compute Mask: Identify texels covered by the current chunk. A texel is valid if its alpha value in rastchunk is greater than 0. \text{mask\chunk} = \text{rast\chunk}[..., 3:4] > 0 c. Store Face ID: Update the alpha channel of rastchunk with the global face index i. This overwrites any previous alpha value, so the mask must be computed before this update or stored separately to avoid overwriting valid data from previous chunks if merging logic is complex. \text{rast\chunk}[..., 3:4] += i Note: The source code adds i to the alpha channel. If the alpha channel was previously used for depth or other attributes, this logic assumes the alpha channel is exclusively used for face ID storage in this specific implementation. d. Merge: Update the global rast buffer. Only texels covered by the current chunk are updated. \text{rast} = \text{torch.where}(\text{mask\chunk}, \text{rast\chunk}, \text{rast}) 4. Extract Valid Pixels: After processing all faces, create a global mask of all valid texels in the buffer. \text{mask} = \text{rast}[0,..., 3] > 0 5. Interpolate 3D Positions: Use the rasterization result rast (which now contains face IDs) to interpolate the 3D vertex positions for each valid texel. \text{pos} = \text{dr.interpolate}(\text{out\vertices}.unsqueeze(0), \text{rast}, \text{out\faces})[0][0] The dr.interpolate function uses the face IDs stored in the alpha channel of rast to look up the corresponding triangle and barycentric coordinates (implicitly stored or derived from the rasterization step) to interpolate the vertex positions. Parameters: chunksize: 100,000 faces per rasterization call to limit VRAM usage. texturesize: Resolution of the 2D buffer. Not specified in sources, but must be large enough to resolve the mesh details. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Face ID Overwrite: The face ID is stored in the alpha channel by adding the loop index i. This overwrites the original alpha value (which might represent depth or coverage weight). The mask must be recomputed or stored separately before merging if the alpha channel is used for other purposes in the rasterizer. Precision: Using float32 for face IDs may lose precision for meshes with more than 2^{24} faces. The source uses integer addition to the alpha channel, which is stored as float32. For very large meshes, consider using a separate buffer for face IDs or a different encoding. Boundary Conditions: The UV coordinates are mapped to [-1, 1]. Ensure that the mesh's UV layout fits within this range and does not have extreme stretching that could cause rasterization artifacts. A uint64t face token encodes a unit face with specific bit fields for compact storage and fast lookup. Bits 0-5: u coordinate (6 bits). Bits 6-11: v coordinate (6 bits). Bits 12-17: depth (6 bits). Bits 18-20: axis (3 bits). Bit 21: positive direction flag (1 bit). Bits 22-31: material (10 bits). This layout allows for efficient packing of face attributes into a single 64-bit integer, facilitating fast sorting and deduplication in greedy meshing algorithms. A struct encoding the orientation of a face within a chunk and its matching padded boundary index. Structure: FaceSpec contains fixedaxis: usize, fixedvalue: u8, iteraxes: [usize; 2], and paddedboundaryindex: u32. Formula: Padded coordinates for a face point (u, v) are calculated as: \text{coords}[\text{iter\axes}[0]] = u + 1 \text{coords}[\text{iter\axes}[1]] = v + 1 \text{coords}[\text{fixed\axis}] = \text{padded\boundary\index} This specification is used to map 2D rasterized coordinates to 3D voxel positions within a chunked grid, handling boundary conditions and memory alignment. Time Complexity: O(Nf \cdot R), where Nf is the number of faces and R is the rasterization cost per face (dependent on texture size and rasterizer efficiency). The chunking does not change the asymptotic complexity but improves cache locality and VRAM usage. Memory Complexity: O(\text{texture\size}^2) for the rasterization buffer, plus O(Nv) for vertex data. The chunking allows processing meshes larger than VRAM allows for a single rasterization pass. Performance: The method leverages efficient 2D rasterization libraries (e.g., DiffRast) which are highly optimized on GPUs. The chunk size of 100,000 faces is a practical trade-off between memory usage and kernel launch overhead. Strengths: Memory efficient for large meshes; leverages existing 2D rasterization infrastructure; simple to implement using differentiable rendering libraries. Limitations: Requires UV coordinates for the mesh; rasterization artifacts (e.g., z-fighting, coverage errors) can affect voxel quality; not suitable for meshes without valid UVs. This method is derived from the implementation in the o-voxel-gpu repository, which uses differentiable rasterization for voxelization. It represents a practical approach to voxelizing large-scale meshes by breaking down the problem into manageable chunks, avoiding the need for large 3D buffers during the rasterization phase. quantaji/o-voxel-gpu, https://github.com/quantaji/o-voxel-gpu, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) dmadevice/streaming-binary-greedy-meshing, https://github.com/dmadevice/streaming-binary-greedy-meshing, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) jameshiew/infinigen, https://github.com/jameshiew/infinigen, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Triangle Projection Voxelization
head: Union-based Voxelization, VoxelizationByUnionPass
body: Triangle Projection Voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a voxel grid by rasterizing triangles into a union-based hash table of voxel centers and colors. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly using a union-based approach to resolve overlaps, likely combining multiple passes or render targets to ensure correct coverage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Triangle mesh geometry (indices, vertices), voxel grid dimensions, and a boolean flag msolid determining whether to render solid or transparent voxels.
