name: Axis-Aligned Projection via Face Normal
head: Face Normal Axis Selection, Optimal Axis Projection
body: This method is a geometry shader technique used in rasterization-based voxelization to project 3D mesh triangles onto a 2D plane aligned with the axis most perpendicular to the triangle's face normal. By selecting the optimal viewing axis (X, Y, or Z) for each triangle, it minimizes projection overlap and distortion, ensuring that the triangle's area is preserved as much as possible in the chosen projection plane. This approach is distinct from fixed-axis projection methods by adapting the projection direction per primitive, which is particularly useful for reducing artifacts in voxel grids where triangles might otherwise be foreshortened or occluded incorrectly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle strip consisting of vertices, each with a world-space position, a normal vector, and texture UV coordinates. Output: A geometry stream containing transformed clip-space positions, world-space positions, and texture UVs, ready for rasterization into a voxel texture or buffer. Data Structures: Vertex Input: Contains vertex.xyz (world position), normal (world normal), and uv (texture coordinates). Geometry Output: Contains positionCS (clip space position), positionWS (world space position), and uv (texture coordinates). Steps: 1. Calculate Face Normal: Compute the average of the three input vertex normals and normalize the result to obtain the triangle's face normal. \mathbf{n}{face} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{n}0 + \mathbf{n}1 + \mathbf{n}2) 2. Determine Optimal Axis: Calculate the absolute dot product of the face normal with the three world-space axes (\mathbf{x}=(1,0,0), \mathbf{y}=(0,1,0), \mathbf{z}=(0,0,1)). Select the axis with the maximum dot product. dx = |\mathbf{n}{face} \cdot \mathbf{x}|, \quad dy = |\mathbf{n}{face} \cdot \mathbf{y}|, \quad dz = |\mathbf{n}{face} \cdot \mathbf{z}| The axis index is determined as follows: If dx is maximum, select the X-axis (projection onto the ZY plane). If dy is maximum, select the Y-axis (projection onto the XZ plane). If dz is maximum, select the Z-axis (projection onto the XY plane). 3. Transform to Clip Space: For each vertex, transform its world-space position to clip space. \mathbf{p}{clip} = \text{TransformWorldToHClip}(\mathbf{p}{world}) 4. Normalize to NDC: Divide the clip space position by its w-component to normalize to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC). \mathbf{p}{ndc} = \frac{\mathbf{p}{clip}}{w} 5. Adjust Z Range (Platform Specific): If the platform uses a 0-1 Z range for clip space (e.g., DirectX), convert the Z coordinate from 0-1 to -1-1 range. This is typically checked using a platform-specific constant like UNITYNEARCLIPVALUE. \text{if } \text{UNITY\NEAR\CLIP\VALUE} \ge 0: \quad z{ndc} = z{ndc} \times 2.0 - 1.0 6. Permute Coordinates: Swap the XYZ coordinates of the NDC position to align the selected projection axis with the depth (Z) axis for rasterization. If X-axis is dominant (Index 0): Swap to ZY. \mathbf{p}{permuted} = (z, y, x)? No, the source says positionCS.xyz = positionCS.zyx. This maps original X to Z, Y to Y, Z to X? Let's re-read carefully. Source: if (axisIdx == 0)... positionCS.xyz = positionCS.zyx; Axis 0 is X-axis dominant. The projection plane is ZY. The depth axis for rasterization should be the one we are projecting onto? No, we are projecting along the X axis. So the depth buffer should represent X. But the source permutes to zyx. Let's trace: Original (x, y, z). Permute to (z, y, x). The new Z is the old X. This makes the old X the depth axis. This aligns with projecting along the X axis (where X is the depth). If Y-axis is dominant (Index 1): Swap to XZ. positionCS.xyz = positionCS.xzy. Original (x, y, z) \to (x, z, y). New Z is old Y. Depth is Y. If Z-axis is dominant (Index 2): No swap. Original (x, y, z) \to (x, y, z). New Z is old Z. Depth is Z. This permutation ensures that the axis of projection (the one with the highest normal alignment) becomes the depth axis (Z) in the clip space, allowing standard rasterization to accumulate coverage along that axis. 7. Restore Z Range (Platform Specific): If the platform uses a 0-1 Z range, convert the Z coordinate back from -1-1 to 0-1. \text{if } \text{UNITY\NEAR\CLIP\VALUE} \ge 0: \quad z{permuted} = z{permuted} \times 0.5 + 0.5 8. De-normalize: Multiply the permuted position by w to restore the clip space scale. \mathbf{p}{final} = \mathbf{p}{permuted} \times w 9. Output: Output the final clip space position, the original world space position, and the texture UV to the geometry stream. Restart the triangle strip. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processtriangle(inputvertices): # Step 1: Calculate Face Normal n0 = inputvertices[0].normal n1 = inputvertices[1].normal n2 = inputvertices[2].normal facenormal = normalize(n0 + n1 + n2) # Step 2: Determine Optimal Axis axisx = float3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) axisy = float3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) axisz = float3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) dotx = abs(dot(facenormal, axisx)) doty = abs(dot(facenormal, axisy)) dotz = abs(dot(facenormal, axisz)) # Select axis index: 0 for X, 1 for Y, 2 for Z if dotx >= doty and dotx >= dotz: axisidx = 0 elif doty >= dotx and doty >= dotz: axisidx = 1 else: axisidx = 2 outputstream = [] for i in range(3): vertex = inputvertices[i] # Step 3: Transform to Clip Space positioncs = transformworldtohclip(vertex.vertex.xyz) # Step 4: Normalize to NDC w = positioncs.w positionndc = positioncs.xyz / w # Step 5: Adjust Z Range (Platform Specific) # UNITYNEARCLIPVALUE >= 0 implies 0-1 Z range (e.g., DirectX) if UNITYNEARCLIPVALUE >= 0: positionndc.z = positionndc.z 2.0 - 1.0 # Step 6: Permute Coordinates if axisidx == 0: # X-axis dominant -> Project onto ZY, Depth is X # Swap to ZY: x->z, y->y, z->x? No, source says zyx # Original: (x, y, z) -> New: (z, y, x) # New Z is old X. positionpermuted = float3(positionndc.z, positionndc.y, positionndc.x) elif axisidx == 1: # Y-axis dominant -> Project onto XZ, Depth is Y # Swap to XZ: x->x, y->z, z->y? Source says xzy # Original: (x, y, z) -> New: (x, z, y) # New Z is old Y. positionpermuted = float3(positionndc.x, positionndc.z, positionndc.y) else: # Z-axis dominant -> Project onto XY, Depth is Z # No swap positionpermuted = positionndc # Step 7: Restore Z Range (Platform Specific) if UNITYNEARCLIPVALUE >= 0: positionpermuted.z = positionpermuted.z 0.5 + 0.5 # Step 8: De-normalize positionfinal = positionpermuted w # Step 9: Output outputvertex = { 'positionCS': positionfinal, 'positionWS': vertex.vertex.xyz, 'uv': transformtex(vertex.uv, BaseMap) } outputstream.append(outputvertex) outputstream.restartstrip() return outputstream Parameters: UNITYNEARCLIPVALUE: A platform-specific constant. If \ge 0, the platform uses a 0-1 Z range for clip space (e.g., DirectX), requiring conversion to/from -1-1. If < 0, it uses a -1-1 range (e.g., OpenGL/Vulkan). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visual Incorrectness: The geometry shader output is visually incorrect if rendered directly to a standard screen because the coordinate permutation is intended for rasterization into a specific texture layout (voxel grid), not for standard screen projection. The technique relies on the pixel shader running on the permuted data, not on the visual correctness of the geometry shader output. Degenerate Triangles: Triangles with zero area or collinear vertices may produce undefined normals. The source does not specify handling for this, but standard geometry shader practices should include a check for degenerate triangles to avoid artifacts. Precision: The normalization and dot product calculations are sensitive to floating-point precision. Ensure that the normal calculation is robust for nearly coplanar or degenerate triangles. Time Complexity: The method adds a constant amount of computation per triangle in the geometry shader. The complexity is O(N) where N is the number of triangles, as each triangle is processed independently to determine its projection axis. Memory Complexity: The method requires storing the transformed positions and attributes for the output stream. The memory usage is proportional to the number of vertices in the output stream, which is 3 \times N for N triangles. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the efficiency of the geometry shader and the rasterization stage. The source does not provide specific performance metrics, but the method is designed to be efficient by avoiding complex ray-casting or marching cubes algorithms. Strengths: Reduces projection distortion and overlap by adapting to the triangle's orientation. Simple to implement within a geometry shader pipeline. Limitations: Relies on rasterization, which may have limitations in handling complex overlaps or transparency. The visual output is not directly interpretable as a standard 3D view. When to Use: Suitable for real-time voxelization of meshes where projection quality is important and the target is a voxel grid rather than a standard screen image. When Not to Use: Not suitable for offline rendering or when a standard 3D view is required directly from the geometry shader output. This technique is described in a Unity-focused blog post by "seyakara". It is part of a broader effort to perform real-time GPU-based voxelization of 3D models using Unity's Universal Render Pipeline (URP). The method builds on the concept of triangle projection voxelization, where triangles are rendered into a voxel grid [5432-triangle-projection-voxelization.md]. The specific approach of choosing the projection axis based on the face normal is a heuristic to optimize the rasterization process for voxel coverage. 【Unity】GPUで3Dモデルをリアルタイムにボクセル化する, https://qiita.com/seyakara/items/b635939f6c6106a15d40, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering
head: Fourier projection rendering, Fourier approach to volume rendering, Attenuation-only rendering via Fourier projection-slice theorem, Frequency Domain Volume Rendering
body: Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering is a method for generating attenuation-only images (X-ray-like projections) by exploiting the Fourier projection-slice theorem to compute projections in O(N^2 \log N) time per view, avoiding the O(N^3) cost of digital compositing. Unlike conventional volume rendering or ray-casting, this method does not exhibit occlusion or hidden surface removal; it computes an order-independent linear projection where voxels on a viewing ray contribute equally regardless of distance. It is distinguished from its sibling Domain-transform methods by its specific reliance on frequency-domain slicing to achieve computational efficiency for parallel projections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume f(\mathbf{x}) sampled on a 3D integer lattice of size N \times N \times N. Output: A 2D projection image I for a given viewing direction. Data Structures: 3D Spectrum: An array of N^3 complex coefficients (or real coefficients if using a Hartley transform). Requires 32-bit floating point precision for accuracy, increasing memory by a factor of 4 compared to 8-bit input volume. If using standard complex arithmetic, it requires 16 bytes per voxel (pair of 64-bit doubles). 2D Slice: An array of N^2 coefficients extracted from the 3D spectrum. Parameters: N: Side length of the cubical volume. Assumed to be an integer power of two for FFT efficiency. V: Normalized viewing direction vector. Defines the orientation of the slice in frequency space. Note: V points away from the eye. W: Nonzero width of the interpolating filter used during slice extraction. Typical value: 4 (a 4^3 tap filter). k2: Factor by which volume width is increased via zero-padding. Typical value: k2 = 4/3 (16% margin). M: Resolution of the projection slice (M \times M). Must be high enough to prevent aliasing. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Frequency Domain Transformation): Compute the 3D discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of the scalar volume f(\mathbf{x}). For real volumes, a Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) may be substituted to halve memory and time. Vignetting Correction: To cope with vignetting (attenuation of the periphery due to non-ideal filter response), premultiply the volume data f(\mathbf{x}) by the reciprocal of the filter response Pm(\mathbf{x}) = 1/h(\mathbf{x}) before the forward transformation. Here H(\mathbf{s}) is the interpolation filter in frequency space, and h(\mathbf{x}) is its spatial response. Zero Padding: Surround the data with a margin of zeros to avoid ghosting artifacts. A typical margin is 16% (k2=4/3). 2. Slice Extraction (Per View): For each view defined by direction V: Define an extraction plane passing through the origin of the frequency domain and perpendicular to V. Interpolate the discrete spectrum F(\mathbf{s}) along this plane using a filter H(\mathbf{s}). Since the plane does not typically pass through integer lattice points, interpolation from nearby samples is required. Resample the interpolated spectrum to obtain a 2D spectrum. 3. Inverse Transform: Compute the inverse 2D Fourier transform (or inverse FHT) of the extracted 2D slice to generate the final projection image I. Formulas: The Fourier projection-slice theorem states that the 2D image obtained by taking line integrals of the volume along rays perpendicular to the image plane is a Fourier transform pair with the 2D spectrum obtained by extracting a slice from the Fourier transform of the volume along a plane which includes the origin and is parallel to the image plane. Mathematically, the projection operator \PiV is defined as: I = \PiV(f) = \mathcal{F}2^{-1} \{ \mathcal{F}3 \{ f \} \deltaV \} where \mathcal{F}3 is the 3D Fourier transform, \mathcal{F}2^{-1} is the 2D inverse Fourier transform, and \deltaV restricts the spectrum to a plane passing through the origin and perpendicular to viewing direction V. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fourierprojectionslicerendering(volume, viewingdirection): """ volume: 3D list of lists of lists of floats, shape (N, N, N). viewingdirection: list of 3 floats, normalized vector V pointing away from eye. Returns: 2D list of lists of floats, shape (M, M), the projection image. """ N = len(volume) k2 = 4.0 / 3.0 margin = int(N (k2 - 1) / 2) paddedsize = int(N k2) M = N # 1. Preprocessing: Zero Padding paddedvolume = [[[0.0] paddedsize for in range(paddedsize)] for in range(paddedsize)] for i in range(N): for j in range(N): for k in range(N): paddedvolume[i + margin][j + margin][k + margin] = volume[i][j][k] # 2. Vignetting Correction # Premultiply by reciprocal of filter spatial response h(x) correctedvolume = [[[0.0] paddedsize for in range(paddedsize)] for in range(paddedsize)] for i in range(paddedsize): for j in range(paddedsize): for k in range(paddedsize): x, y, z = i - margin, j - margin, k - margin hval = spatialfilterresponse(x, y, z) correctedvolume[i][j][k] = paddedvolume[i][j][k] / max(hval, 1e-8) # 3. Forward 3D FFT spectrum = fft3d(correctedvolume) # 4. Slice Extraction # Generate orthonormal basis (U, T) for the plane perpendicular to V U, T = generateorthonormalbasis(viewingdirection) center = paddedsize // 2 slice2d = [[[0.0] M for in range(M)] for in range(2)] for i in range(M): for j in range(M): # Map 2D pixel indices to 3D frequency coordinates sx = center + U[0] (i - M / 2) + T[0] (j - M / 2) sy = center + U[1] (i - M / 2) + T[1] (j - M / 2) sz = center + U[2] (i - M / 2) + T[2] (j - M / 2) # Interpolate complex spectrum at (sx, sy, sz) slice2d[0][i][j], slice2d[1][i][j] = interpolate3dcomplex(spectrum, sx, sy, sz) # 5. Inverse 2D FFT projection = ifft2d(slice2d) return projection def spatialfilterresponse(x, y, z): # Returns the spatial response h(x) of the interpolation filter. # Typically a separable kernel (e.g., 4^3 tap tricubic spline). return 1.0 def generateorthonormalbasis(V): # Standard vector math to find two vectors orthogonal to V arbitrary = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] if abs(V[0]) < 0.9 else [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] u = cross(V, arbitrary) u = normalize(u) t = cross(V, u) t = normalize(t) return u, t def interpolate3dcomplex(grid, x, y, z): # Standard 3D grid interpolation (e.g., tricubic spline) for complex values. return 0.0, 0.0 def fft3d(data): # Standard radix-2 3D FFT algorithm pass def ifft2d(data): # Standard radix-2 2D IFFT algorithm pass This variant focuses on practical optimizations for the base algorithm. Slices are extracted using a tricubic interpolating spline. A key optimization is replacing the FFT with a Fast Hartley Transform (FHT), which halves per-view rendering time and memory requirements for real-valued data. Further speedups can be achieved by optimizing the filter and trimming zero padding. A shading model that approximates exponential attenuation with locally varying coefficients by linear attenuation with a constant coefficient, allowing the integrand to be expressed as a Fourier projection. This restores depth perception to the otherwise occlusion-free X-ray projections. Time Complexity: Preprocessing: O(N^3 \log N) operations to compute the 3D spectrum. Per-View Rendering: O(N^2 \log N) operations for the inverse transform, plus O(W^3 N^2) for slice extraction where W is the filter width. The overall cost is dominated by the 2D inverse FFT, O(n^2 \log n). Interpolation Cost: High interpolation cost is a bottleneck. Interpolation is O(n^2) with large constant factors, often taking more time than the FFT for practical data sizes (128^3 or 256^3). Memory Complexity: Requires 16 bytes per voxel (pair of 64-bit doubles) for complex arithmetic, compared to 1 byte in spatial domain algorithms. Zero padding increases memory by a factor of k2^3. Performance: For N=256, digital compositing requires 16M operations, while FVR requires 512K operations (speedup >10x) theoretically. In practice, interpolation overhead reduces this gain. GPU acceleration can achieve highly interactive framerates (factor of 17 speedup reported). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fast generation of X-ray-like projections; suitable for MR angiography and attenuation-only renderings where speed is prioritized. Limitations: No occlusion or depth cues (unless added via shading models); vignetting artifacts; ghosting artifacts from interpolation; high memory usage; only supports parallel projection. The method is based on the Fourier projection-slice theorem, which states that the inverse transform of a slice extracted from the frequency domain representation of a volume yields a projection of the volume in a direction perpendicular to the slice. It was independently proposed for image synthesis by Dunne and Malzbender. Marc Levoy published the foundational paper "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem" in 1992. Takashi Totsuka and Marc Levoy extended this in 1993 with "Frequency Domain Volume Rendering," introducing shading models in the frequency domain. Later, Viola et al. accelerated the method using GPU-based pipelines. name: Implementation Details for Fourier Volume Rendering
head: Fourier Volume Rendering Implementation, Fourier Volume Rendering with Zero Padding and Tricubic Interpolation, Implementation Details for Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering
body: This article details the specific algorithmic steps, data structures, and parameter choices required to implement the Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering method Parent. It solves the problem of efficiently generating attenuation-only images (X-ray-like projections) and shaded volume renderings by exploiting the Fourier projection-slice theorem. What sets this implementation apart from standard digital compositing is the use of frequency-domain slicing and inverse transformation, reducing the per-view complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^2 \log N). Input: A 3D voxel volume V of size N \times N \times N (typically 128^3). Output: A 2D image I of size 128 \times 128. 1. Preprocessed Volume (V{pad}): A 3D array of size N{pad} \times N{pad} \times N{pad}, where N{pad} = \lceil 1.16 N \rceil. The original data occupies the center, surrounded by a 16% zero-margin. 2. 3D Spectrum (\hat{V}): The result of the 3D FFT of V{pad}. 3. Slices: 2D arrays extracted from \hat{V} corresponding to specific viewing angles. 1. Edge Enhancement: Apply an edge sharpening operator to the input volume V. 2. Nonlinear Windowing: Apply a nonlinear density range windowing operator to the edge-enhanced data. This step may be skipped for specific attenuation-only visualizations (e.g., X-ray projections). 3. Zero Padding: Surround the processed volume with a margin of zeros equal to 16% of the volume width. The padded dimension is N{pad} = \lceil 1.16 N \rceil. This margin prevents "ghosting" artifacts caused by spectral leakage. 1. Weighting: Apply the desired shading or attenuation weighting function W to the preprocessed volume V{pad} to create a weighted volume Vw. 2. 3D FFT: Compute the 3D Fast Fourier Transform of Vw to obtain the spectrum \hat{V}. \hat{V} = \text{FFT3D}(Vw) For each viewing direction defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n}: 1. Slice Extraction: Extract a 2D slice from the 3D spectrum \hat{V} that corresponds to the projection plane orthogonal to \mathbf{n}. The slice width equals the spectral width of the volume. Use a tricubic interpolating spline to extract the slice values from the discrete 3D spectrum grid. 2. 2D Inverse FFT: Compute the 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transform of the extracted slice to obtain a 2D projection in the spatial domain. P = \text{IFFT2D}(\text{Slice}(\hat{V}, \mathbf{n})) 3. Weighting: Apply viewing or lighting direction weights to the projection P. 4. Summation: Sum the weighted projections from all necessary angles (or a single projection for attenuation-only) to produce the final 128 \times 128 image I. I = \sum Pi Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def edgeenhance(volume): # Standard edge enhancement applies a spatial filter (e.g., Laplacian) # The exact operator is not specified in the sources. return volume # Placeholder for spatial convolution def nonlinearwindow(volume, alpha=2.0): # Nonlinear windowing remaps intensity (e.g., power law or sigmoid) # The exact function is not specified in the sources. return np.power(volume, alpha) # Placeholder for intensity remapping def applyweighting(volume, weights): # Weights depend on the shading model (attenuation, diffuse, etc.) return volume weights def getslicecoordinates(viewdirection, Npad): # Maps viewdirection to 2D plane coordinates in the frequency grid. # Standard approach computes orthonormal basis vectors u, v orthogonal to viewdirection. # The exact geometric mapping is not detailed in the sources. return np.zeros((Npad, Npad)) # Placeholder for coordinate mapping def tricubicinterpolate(spectrum, coords): # Standard tricubic spline interpolation samples the 3D spectrum at coords. # The exact implementation is not detailed in the sources. return np.zeroslike(coords) # Placeholder for spline interpolation def applyviewweights(projection, viewdirection): # Applies lighting/attenuation weights based on view direction. # Model-specific weighting is not detailed in the sources. return projection 0.5 # Placeholder for directional weighting def fouriervolumerendering(V, views, weights3d, imagesize=128): N = V.shape[0] margin = int(0.16 N) Npad = N + 2 margin # Initialize padded volume with zeros Vpad = np.zeros((Npad, Npad, Npad), dtype=V.dtype) # Place original data in the center start, end = margin, N + margin Vpad[start:end, start:end, start:end] = V # Preprocessing Vpad = edgeenhance(Vpad) Vpad = nonlinearwindow(Vpad) # Precomputation Vweighted = applyweighting(Vpad, weights3d) spectrum = np.fft.fftn(Vweighted) # Per-View Rendering finalimage = np.zeros((imagesize, imagesize)) for view in views: coords = getslicecoordinates(view, Npad) slice2d = tricubicinterpolate(spectrum, coords) projection = np.fft.ifftn(slice2d) projection = applyviewweights(projection, view) finalimage += np.real(projection) return finalimage Zero Padding Margin: 16% of the volume width. Interpolation Method: Tricubic interpolating spline. Input Volume Size: Typically 128^3 voxels. Output Image Size: Typically 128 \times 128 pixels. Ghosting: Failing to add the 16% zero-padding margin results in ghosting artifacts due to spectral leakage. Interactive Segmentation: Preprocessing steps (edge sharpening, nonlinear windowing) are applied before the 3D FFT. Changing these operators requires recomputing the entire 3D spectrum, which hinders interactive data segmentation. Mitigation: If segmentation is linear, it can be handled by precomputing spectra for basis materials (e.g., fat, muscle, bone) and weighting them at image generation time. An optimization technique for frequency domain volume rendering that selects between a large and a small interpolation filter based on the local spectral energy of the 3D spectrum, reducing interpolation cost while maintaining image quality. This variant highlights the preprocessing stage where edge sharpening and nonlinear density range windowing operators are applied directly to the input volume data before computing the forward 3D Fourier transform. The key pitfall is that modifying these operators requires recomputing the entire 3D Fourier spectra, which hinders interactive data segmentation if hardwired into the preprocessing pipeline. Time Complexity: O(N^2 \log N) per view, avoiding the O(N^3) cost of digital compositing. Memory Complexity: Varies by shading model. 48 MB for simple attenuation models (equation 3.1.4) to 256 MB for complex shading models (equation 3.3.2) for a 128^3 volume. Performance: On a 36 MHz Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX with a sequential C implementation: Simple model: ~6 seconds per view (~1.5 seconds per slice). Complex model: >1 minute per view (due to paging). Optimizations: Replacing FFT with Fast Hartley Transform (FHT) halves per-view rendering time and memory requirements. Optimizing the filter and trimming zero padding can provide another factor of two speedup. Parallelization is possible at fine grain (within FFT) or coarse grain (between slices). Hardware acceleration using video coprocessors or DSPs is amenable, especially with fixed-point frequency spectra. Strengths: Asymptotically faster than conventional volume rendering for very large volumes. Limitations: High constant factor makes it slower than conventional methods for small volumes. Preprocessing changes require full spectrum recomputation. Origin: The method is based on the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, as described by Marc Levoy in "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem". History: The implementation was tested on early 1990s hardware (Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX). The approach was developed to address the high computational cost of traditional volume rendering. Usage: Used for generating attenuation-only projections (X-rays) and shaded volume renderings. name: Adaptive Frequency Domain Filtering
head: Adaptive Filtering in Frequency Domain, Adaptive Slice Extraction Filtering, Adaptive filtering scheme
body: Adaptive Frequency Domain Filtering is an optimization technique for frequency domain volume rendering that reduces interpolation cost by selectively applying larger or smaller interpolation filters based on local spectral properties. It solves the performance bottleneck of slice extraction in Fourier-based rendering by identifying regions of the 3D spectrum where the signal magnitude is sufficiently low to permit coarser approximation without visible quality loss. It sets itself apart from standard frequency domain methods by introducing a preprocessing step that marks voxels, allowing the extraction phase to skip expensive multi-voxel support checks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume data V. Output: 2D projection image. Intermediate: 3D spectrum S (computed via Hartley or Fourier transform). Data Structures: Spectrum (S): A 3D grid of complex (or real-valued Hartley) values. The sources note that due to the wide dynamic range, a floating-point format (e.g., 64-bit double) is necessary. Mark Array (M): A boolean grid of the same dimensions as S. M[i,j,k] = \text{true} indicates the voxel is "marked" and eligible for the smaller filter. Parameters: Larger Filter Size: 3 \times 3 \times 3. Smaller Filter Size: 1 \times 1 \times 1 (point sampling). Threshold (\epsilon): The maximum difference in response allowed. The sources specify a value of 0.3. This threshold determines the boundary for switching filters. Marking Condition: A voxel is marked if its magnitude satisfies a specific equation (referred to as Equation 16 in or 1G in). The exact formula for Equation 16/1G is not provided in the source text, but it is defined as "magnitude is small enough". Steps: 1. Transform: Compute the 3D spectrum S of the volume data V using the Hartley transform or Fourier transform. 2. Preprocess (Marking): Iterate through every voxel in S. Check if the voxel's magnitude satisfies the threshold condition (Equation 16/1G). Optimized Marking: To avoid testing all neighbors during extraction, mark a voxel v only if: 1. v satisfies the threshold condition. 2. All neighboring voxels within a distance equal to one-half of the support of the larger filter (3 \times 3 \times 3) also satisfy the threshold condition. Store the result in M. This process is done only once after transformation. 3. Slice Extraction: For each sample point on the slice plane: Identify the spectrum voxel v closest to the sample position. Check if M[v] is true. If true, use the smaller filter (1 \times 1 \times 1). If false, use the larger filter (3 \times 3 \times 3). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivefrequencydomainfiltering(volumedata): # Step 1: Transform to frequency domain # Using Hartley transform as suggested for memory efficiency spectrum = hartleytransform(volumedata) # Step 2: Preprocess - Mark voxels # Dimensions of spectrum dimx, dimy, dimz = spectrum.shape # Initialize mark array marked = np.zeros((dimx, dimy, dimz), dtype=bool) # Define larger filter support radius # Larger filter is 3x3x3, so radius is 1 (distance <= 1 covers neighbors) # "distance equal to one-half of the support" -> support size 3, half is 1.5? # The text says "neighboring voxels lying within a distance... equal to one-half of the support". # For a 3x3x3 filter, the support extends 1 voxel in each direction. # Half of support (3) is 1.5. Distance <= 1.5 includes immediate neighbors (dist 1). # We assume integer grid distance. supportradius = 1 for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): # Check if current voxel satisfies threshold condition # Equation 16/1G is not explicitly defined, but implies magnitude check if issmallenough(spectrum[x, y, z], threshold=0.3): # Check all neighbors within supportradius allneighborsok = True for dx in range(-supportradius, supportradius + 1): for dy in range(-supportradius, supportradius + 1): for dz in range(-supportradius, supportradius + 1): if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz # Boundary check if 0 <= nx < dimx and 0 <= ny < dimy and 0 <= nz < dimz: if not issmallenough(spectrum[nx, ny, nz], threshold=0.3): allneighborsok = False break if not allneighborsok: break if not allneighborsok: break if allneighborsok: marked[x, y, z] = True # Step 3: Slice Extraction projection = [] for samplepoint in sliceplanesamples: # Find closest spectrum voxel voxelcoords = getclosestvoxelcoords(samplepoint, spectrum) x, y, z = voxelcoords if marked[x, y, z]: # Use smaller filter (1x1x1) value = spectrum[x, y, z] else: # Use larger filter (3x3x3) # Interpolation logic for 3x3x3 filter would go here # Standard trilinear or box filtering over 3x3x3 neighborhood value = interpolatelargefilter(spectrum, x, y, z) projection.append(value) # Inverse transform to get spatial domain image image = inversehartleytransform(projection) return image def issmallenough(value, threshold): # Placeholder for Equation 16/1G # Based on context, this checks if magnitude is below threshold return abs(value) <= threshold Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The spectrum requires floating-point representation due to wide dynamic range. Using integer formats will cause significant error. Boundary Conditions: The marking step requires checking neighbors. Boundary voxels must be handled carefully to avoid out-of-bounds access. Threshold Selection: The threshold of 0.3 is specific to the implementation described. Changing it affects the trade-off between speed and accuracy. Time Complexity: The preprocessing step is O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the spectrum, with a constant factor depending on the filter support size (3 \times 3 \times 3). The extraction step is O(M) where M is the number of slice samples, with O(1) cost for marked voxels and O(K) for unmarked voxels (K is filter support size). Memory Complexity: The spectrum requires floating-point storage. The sources note that a double-precision format consumes 16 times more memory than a spatial domain algorithm using 1-byte voxels. Using the Hartley transform and shorter number representations can control this explosion. Performance: The scheme reduced the cost of interpolation to about 15% of the non-adaptive case. Accuracy: Relative error was always below 40dB, a level at which image differences are not visible. Strengths: Significant reduction in interpolation cost; maintains high image quality. Limitations: Requires additional preprocessing step; high memory usage for spectrum storage. Origin: The method was introduced by Takashi Totsuka and Marc Levoy in their 1993 paper "Frequency Domain Volume Rendering". History: It was developed as part of the broader research into Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering. The technique leverages the properties of the Hartley transform to reduce memory costs compared to the standard Fourier transform. Usage: It is used in frequency domain volume rendering systems to optimize the slice extraction phase. name: FDK Pre-Filtering (Ramp Filter + Cone Weighting)
head: CPU FDK Pre-Filter, Ramp Filter Kernel Mapping, applyFDKPreFilter
body: This method implements the pre-filtering stage of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm on the CPU, preparing 2D projection data for subsequent backprojection. It solves the problem of correcting for the cone-beam geometry and high-frequency attenuation inherent in filtered backprojection by applying a ramp filter and cone weighting to each projection slice. It is distinguished from its sibling Adaptive Frequency Domain Filtering by its fixed, global ramp filter kernel and explicit geometric cone weighting, rather than adaptive frequency-domain adjustments. The method processes P projections, each of size W \times H pixels. It operates by iterating over each projection, applying geometric cone weighting based on the source-to-detector distance and pixel coordinates, and then applying a 1D ramp filter along the detector rows (horizontal axis) using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). Inputs: projections: A flat std::vector<float> of size P \times W \times H, containing the raw projection data. P: Integer, number of projections (angles). W: Integer, detector width in pixels. H: Integer, detector height in pixels. voxelSize: Float, physical size of a voxel in the reconstruction volume (mm). sdd: Float, Source-to-Detector Distance (mm). pixelSize: Float, physical size of a detector pixel (mm). Outputs: filteredprojections: A std::vector<float> of size P \times W \times H, containing the cone-weighted and ramp-filtered projections. std::vector<float> projections: Input data layout is row-major: projections[p W H + u H + v] corresponds to projection p, column u, row v. std::vector<std::complex<double>>: Used internally for FFT operations. std::vector<double> rampfilter: Pre-computed frequency domain ramp filter kernel. MPI: 3.14159265358979323846. padN: The smallest power of 2 greater than or equal to W (computed via nextPow2). Typical values: P=360, W=512, H=512 (example dimensions). 1. Initialization: Calculate projSize = W \times H. Calculate padN = nextPow2(W). Build the ramp filter kernel for size padN using buildRampFilter(padN). Copy input projections to output buffer out. 2. Iterate Projections: For each projection p from 0 to P-1: Get pointer proj to the start of the current projection in out. 3. Cone Weighting: For each column u from 0 to W-1: Calculate horizontal coordinate a = -((u - 0.5 \times (W-1)) \times \text{pixelSize}). For each row v from 0 to H-1: Calculate vertical coordinate b = ((v - 0.5 \times (H-1)) \times \text{pixelSize}). Calculate cone weight cw = \frac{\text{sdd}}{\sqrt{\text{sdd}^2 + a^2 + b^2}}. Update value: proj[u H + v] = (proj[u H + v] / voxelSize) cw. 4. Ramp Filtering (Row-wise): For each row v from 0 to H-1: Extract the row data from proj into a temporary vector row of size padN. Copy proj[u H + v] for u=0 \dots W-1 into row[0 \dots W-1]. Zero-pad row[W \dots padN-1] with zeros. Perform 1D In-place FFT on row with sign -1 (forward transform). Multiply each element row[u] by the corresponding rampfilter[u]. Perform 1D In-place FFT on row with sign +1 (inverse transform). Calculate normalization factor norm = 1.0 / (padN 2.0). Update proj[u H + v] with staticcast<float>(row[u].real() norm) for u=0 \dots W-1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import cmath def nextpow2(n): """Returns the smallest power of 2 greater than or equal to n.""" if n <= 0: return 1 p = 1 while p < n: p = 2 return p def fftinplace(a, sign): """ Performs an in-place FFT on a list of complex numbers. sign: -1 for forward, +1 for inverse. """ N = len(a) # Bit-reversal permutation j = 0 for i in range(1, N): bit = N >> 1 while j & bit: j ^= bit bit >>= 1 j ^= bit if i < j: a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i] length = 2 while length <= N: wlen = cmath.exp(complex(0, sign 2.0 math.pi / length)) for i in range(0, N, length): w = complex(1, 0) halflen = length // 2 for j in range(halflen): u = a[i + j] v = a[i + j + halflen] w a[i + j] = u + v a[i + j + halflen] = u - v w = wlen length = 2 def buildrampfilter(size): """ Creates a ramp filter kernel in the frequency domain. Returns a list of real numbers representing the filter. """ f = [0.0] size f[0] = 0.25 # Collect odd indices nodd = [] for i in range(1, size // 2 + 1, 2): nodd.append(i) for i in range(size // 2 - 1, 0, -2): nodd.append(i) for i, idx in enumerate(nodd): f[1 + i 2] = -1.0 / (math.pi idx math.pi idx) # Convert to complex and FFT fc = [complex(x, 0) for x in f] fftinplace(fc, -1) # Multiply by 2 real part for i in range(len(fc)): fc[i] = complex(2.0 fc[i].real, 0) return [x.real for x in fc] def applyfdkprefilter(projections, P, W, H, voxelsize, sdd, pixelsize): """ Applies cone weighting and ramp filtering to projections. """ padn = nextpow2(W) rampfilter = buildrampfilter(padn) # Output buffer out = list(projections) for p in range(P): # Pointer offset for current projection baseidx = p W H # Cone Weighting for u in range(W): a = -((u - 0.5 (W - 1)) pixelsize) for v in range(H): b = ((v - 0.5 (H - 1)) pixelsize) cw = sdd / math.sqrt(sdd2 + a2 + b2) idx = baseidx + u H + v out[idx] = (out[idx] / voxelsize) cw # Ramp Filtering (Row-wise) for v in range(H): # Extract row and pad row = [complex(0, 0)] padn for u in range(W): idx = baseidx + u H + v row[u] = complex(out[idx], 0) # Remaining elements are already 0 # Forward FFT fftinplace(row, -1) # Apply Ramp Filter for u in range(padn): row[u] = row[u] complex(rampfilter[u], 0) # Inverse FFT fftinplace(row, 1) # Normalize and write back norm = 1.0 / (padn 2.0) for u in range(W): idx = baseidx + u H + v out[idx] = row[u].real norm return out Precision: The implementation uses double for FFT intermediate calculations to maintain precision, casting back to float for the output. Boundary Conditions: The ramp filter is applied only to the first W elements after inverse FFT; the zero-padded portion is discarded. Degenerate Input: If W is already a power of 2, padN equals W, and no zero-padding occurs. Adjusts the filter kernel dynamically based on local frequency content or geometry, unlike the fixed global ramp filter here. Choose this when non-uniform resolution or specific artifact reduction is required. Adaptive Frequency Domain Filtering Time Complexity: O(P \cdot H \cdot W \log W) due to the 1D FFT of size W applied to each of the H rows in each of the P projections. Memory Complexity: O(P \cdot W \cdot H) for storing projections, plus O(W) for temporary row buffers and filter kernel. Performance: The method is designed for CPU execution, processing all rows in parallel across projections. In the reference implementation, it handles 360 \times 128 work-items (projections \times rows) efficiently. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and easy to implement on CPU. Provides a baseline for GPU acceleration. Limitations: Fixed filter may not optimally handle all cone angles or noise characteristics compared to adaptive methods. CPU-bound for large datasets. This method is part of the CPU-side implementation of the FDK algorithm, specifically mapping the ramp filter kernel strategy used in the Full GPU path. It serves as a reference implementation for validating GPU-based reconstructions. The approach is derived from standard FDK theory, adapted for efficient CPU processing using in-place FFTs. hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gamma-Corrected Hemispherical Shading
head: Cubic Shading in Fourier Domain, Fourier Domain Gamma-Corrected Shading, GCHS, Gamma-Corrected Shading
body:
Gamma-Corrected Hemispherical Shading (GCHS) is a method for computing diffuse illumination in Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) that approximates the non-linear max(0, N·L) operator with a cubic polynomial of the gradient and light direction, enabling efficient evaluation in the frequency domain. It improves upon standard hemispherical shading by raising the term to the power of three, which effectively culls back-lit surfaces and preserves visual contrast without requiring non-linear operations that break Fourier linearity. Input: Volume data f(x,y,z), light direction vector L = (l1, l2, l3) (normalized). Output: Shaded volume intensity image. Frequency Domain Data: F(\omegax, \omegay, \omegaz), the 3D Fourier transform of f. Frequency Coordinates: \Omega = (\omegax, \omegay, \omegaz). Storage Optimization: To reduce memory usage for the expanded polynomial terms, the method can utilize twenty 8-bit sample basis images for the geometric terms Vi and a 20 	imes 20 matrix derived from corresponding lighting directions for the coefficients ai. The goal is to approximate the diffuse shading term. The base hemispherical shading operator is defined as: E =  rac{1}{2}(1 + N \cdot L) where N is the normalized normal vector and L is the normalized light vector. Ignoring visibility in this linear form results in negative intensity values and reduced contrast, resembling overcast lighting. To improve contrast and cull back-lit surfaces, GCHS raises the hemispherical term to a gamma power g. The gamma-corrected shading operator is: E = \left(  rac{1 + N \cdot L}{2} ight)^g The exponent g is typically set to 3. This value is chosen because it is the lowest integer power that produces an inflection point, allowing the curve to pass through both 0 and 1, thereby minimizing error in both zero and non-zero portions of the shading curve. In the context of volume rendering, the normal N is approximated by the gradient 
abla f. The term (1 + N \cdot L)^3 is expanded into a polynomial of dot products between the gradient and the light direction, normalized by the gradient magnitude \|
abla f\|: (1 + N \cdot L)^3 = \left(1 + 3  rac{
abla f \cdot L}{\|
abla f\|} + 3  rac{(
abla f \cdot L)^2}{\|
abla f\|^2} +  rac{(
abla f \cdot L)^3}{\|
abla f\|^3}ight) This expansion results in twenty (20) lighting and geometry terms when fully expanded. The shading is computed by implementing each term of the expanded polynomial separately as convolutions in the Fourier domain. The implementation proceeds by computing the linear, quadratic, and cubic components of 
abla f \cdot L in the Fourier domain. 1. Compute the Linear Term: The linear term is 
abla f \cdot L. Differentiation in the spatial domain corresponds to multiplication by a linear ramp in the Fourier domain. Let F be the Fourier transform of f. The Fourier transform of the linear term is: T\{
abla f \cdot L\} = (\Omega \cdot L) F Explicitly, if \Omega = (\omegax, \omegay, \omegaz), then: T\{
abla f \cdot L\} = (\omegax l1 + \omegay l2 + \omegaz l3) F 2. Compute the Quadratic Term: The quadratic term is (
abla f \cdot L)^2. This requires computing products of derivatives. Using the identity for the product of two functions in the frequency domain: fa fb =  rac{1}{2}(\mathcal{F}^2){ab} - f f{ab} where (\mathcal{F}^2){ab} represents the convolution of the Fourier transforms of the derivatives, and f{ab} is the second derivative. The Fourier transform of the quadratic term is: T\{(
abla f \cdot L)^2\} =  rac{1}{2}(\Omega \cdot L)^2(F \otimes F) - (F \otimes ((\Omega \cdot L)^2 F)) Here, \otimes denotes convolution. 3. Compute the Cubic Term: The cubic term is (
abla f \cdot L)^3. Using the identity for the product of three functions: fa fb fc =  rac{1}{6}(f^3){abc} -  rac{1}{2}f(f^2){abc} +  rac{1}{2}f^2 f{abc} The Fourier transform of the cubic term is: T\{(
abla f \cdot L)^3\} =  rac{1}{6}(\Omega \cdot L)^3(F \otimes F \otimes F) -  rac{1}{2}(F \otimes ((\Omega \cdot L)^3(F \otimes F))) +  rac{1}{2}(F \otimes F \otimes ((\Omega \cdot L)^3 F)) 4. Normalization: The terms derived above assume unnormalized gradients. The original expansion includes normalization by \|
abla f\|. The sources note that normalization with  rac{1}{\|
abla f\|} can be precomputed. However, the exact Fourier-domain implementation of the division by \|
abla f\| is not explicitly detailed in the provided equations, which focus on the polynomial expansion of the dot products. In practice, this normalization is often handled by precomputing the basis images or approximating the gradient magnitude. 5. Assembly: Combine the linear, quadratic, and cubic components according to the expansion coefficients (1, 3, 3, 1) and scale by the hemispherical bias factor  rac{1}{2} and gamma power if not already integrated into the polynomial coefficients. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gammacorrectedhemisphericalshading(F, Omega, L): """ Compute GCHS shading in the Fourier domain. Args: F: Complex array, Fourier transform of volume f. Omega: Tuple of arrays (wx, wy, wz), frequency coordinates. L: Tuple of floats (l1, l2, l3), normalized light direction. Returns: Shaded intensity in Fourier domain (before inverse transform). """ l1, l2, l3 = L wx, wy, wz = Omega # 1. Linear Term: T{grad f. L} # T{grad f. L} = (Omega. L) F linearterm = (wx l1 + wy l2 + wz l3) F # 2. Quadratic Term: T{(grad f. L)^2} # Identity: fa fb = 0.5 (Fa Fb) - F Fab # Here, Fa corresponds to derivative in direction L. # Let DLF = (Omega. L) F (Fourier transform of grad f. L) DLF = linearterm # Convolution of DLF with itself # Note: Convolution in frequency domain corresponds to multiplication in spatial, # but the formula uses convolution in frequency domain for product of derivatives? # Wait, the source says: T{fa fb} = 0.5 (Fa Fb) - F Fab. # Fa is FT of fa. Fa Fb is convolution in frequency domain. # So we need convolution of DLF with DLF. convDLDL = convolve3d(DLF, DLF) # Second derivative term: Fab corresponds to derivative of (grad f. L) in direction L? # The source formula: T{(grad f. L)^2} = 0.5 (Omega. L)^2 (F conv F) - F conv ((Omega. L)^2 F) # Let's follow the source formula directly. # Term A: 0.5 (Omega. L)^2 (F conv F) # F conv F is convolution of F with itself convFF = convolve3d(F, F) termA = 0.5 ((wx l1 + wy l2 + wz l3)2) convFF # Term B: F conv ((Omega. L)^2 F) # (Omega. L)^2 F is the Fourier transform of the second derivative in direction L? # Actually, (Omega. L)^2 F is the FT of (d/dL)^2 f. secondderivF = ((wx l1 + wy l2 + wz l3)2) F termB = convolve3d(F, secondderivF) quadraticterm = termA - termB # 3. Cubic Term: T{(grad f. L)^3} # Formula: 1/6 (Omega. L)^3 (F conv F conv F) # - 1/2 F conv ((Omega. L)^3 (F conv F)) # + 1/2 F conv F conv ((Omega. L)^3 F) # Precompute powers of (Omega. L) omegadotL = wx l1 + wy l2 + wz l3 omegadotL3 = omegadotL3 # Convolution of F with itself twice convFFF = convolve3d(convFF, F) # Term C: 1/6 (Omega. L)^3 (F conv F conv F) termC = (1.0/6.0) omegadotL3 convFFF # Term D: 1/2 F conv ((Omega. L)^3 (F conv F)) # (Omega. L)^3 (F conv F) termDinner = omegadotL3 convFF termD = 0.5 convolve3d(F, termDinner) # Term E: 1/2 F conv F conv ((Omega. L)^3 F) # (Omega. L)^3 F thirdderivF = omegadotL3 F termEinner = convolve3d(F, thirdderivF) termE = 0.5 convolve3d(F, termEinner) # Note: Source says F conv F conv... # Re-reading source Eq 11: # 1/2 (F conv F conv ((Omega. L)^3 F)) # This implies convolving F, F, and the third derivative term. # My termEinner is F conv thirdderivF. # So termE should be convolve3d(F, termEinner) ? # Source: 1/2 (F \otimes F \otimes ((\Omega \cdot L)^3 F)) # Yes, that is F conv (F conv thirdderivF). cubicterm = termC - termD + termE # 4. Combine # Expansion: 1 + 3(grad.L)/|grad| + 3(grad.L)^2/|grad|^2 + (grad.L)^3/|grad|^3 # The source formulas for T{...} compute the transforms of the dot product terms. # The normalization by |grad| is noted as precomputable basis images. # For the purpose of this implementation, we assume the basis images handle the normalization. # If not, the raw polynomial terms are: # Raw polynomial in frequency domain (ignoring normalization for now as per source focus on dot products) # Eraw = T{1} + 3 T{grad.L} + 3 T{(grad.L)^2} + T{(grad.L)^3} # T{1} is a delta function at origin, usually handled by bias. # The source states: "The above computation can be implemented... by considering each of the terms separately" # And "Equation 6, 9, and 11 show how the components... can be implemented". # Final Shaded Signal (unnormalized) shadedsignal = linearterm + 3 quadraticterm + cubicterm # Note: The hemispherical bias (1/2) and the constant term 1 are part of the (1 + N.L) base. # The source expands (1 + N.L)^3. # T{1} is not computed via convolution. It is a DC offset. # In the frequency domain, the constant 1 corresponds to a spike at the origin. # However, the source focuses on the variable parts. return shadedsignal def convolve3d(A, B): """ 3D Convolution in the frequency domain. Note: Convolution in frequency domain is computationally expensive (O(N^3 log N) or O(N^4) naive). In practice, this might be approximated or precomputed for constant light. """ # Inverse FFT to spatial domain aspatial = ifft3d(A) bspatial = ifft3d(B) # Multiply in spatial domain cspatial = aspatial bspatial # Forward FFT back to frequency domain C = fft3d(cspatial) return C Light Direction Changes: The equations require convolution with a full volume. This can only be precomputed for a constant light source. If the light direction changes, the terms in the quadratic and cubic equations must be recomputed. Normalization: The expansion includes normalization by \|
abla f\|. The sources note this can be precomputed as basis images, but the exact Fourier-domain division is not explicitly defined in the core convolution formulas. Negative Intensity: Ignoring visibility (using simple hemispherical shading without gamma correction) results in negative image intensity values and reduced contrast. Time Complexity: The method involves convolutions in the Fourier domain, which are computationally expensive. The source notes that rendering speed for a 128^3 synthetic sphere is 32fps (no depth cueing) and 25fps (with depth cueing) for cubic illumination, compared to 36fps (no depth cueing) and 27fps (with depth cueing) for traditional FVR. Memory Complexity: The method can be optimized using twenty 8-bit sample basis images and a 20 	imes 20 matrix, reducing the memory required for surface normal data. Strengths: Higher accuracy than linear shading by better approximating the max function, reducing erroneous energy on back-facing surfaces. Limitations: Lower frame rates than linear shading due to additional calculations (convolutions). Not suitable for dynamic light directions without recomputation. Gamma-Corrected Hemispherical Shading was introduced by Scoggins et al. as an improvement over the hemispherical shading method by Totsuka and Levoy. The method was adapted for Fourier Volume Rendering by Entezari, Scoggins, Möller, and Machiraju. The key insight was that culling back-lit surfaces is equivalent to using the maximum operator, and raising the hemispherical term to the cube approximates this behavior while remaining expandable into a polynomial suitable for Fourier domain processing. name: Depth Cueing via Linear Attenuation
head: Approximate exponential attenuation, Linear attenuation shading model, X-rays with depth cueing
body: This method approximates the perceptual depth cues of exponential attenuation in volume rendering by replacing the variable absorption coefficient with a linear function of position, enabling the integrand to be evaluated as a Fourier projection. It sets itself apart from standard exponential attenuation models by allowing efficient computation via the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, producing X-ray-like images where occlusion is absent but depth perception is enhanced through linear shading. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume density function \rho(x,y,z), volume color function C(x,y,z), constant opacity/absorption coefficient \tau, viewing direction vector \mathbf{V}, and ray segment bounds a, b. Output: Total energy IP arriving at the end of the viewing ray. Data Structures: \rho: Scalar field representing density. C: Vector field representing color/emission. \mathbf{V}: Normalized 3D vector pointing away from the eye. \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}): Linear position function \mathbf{D} = m\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{b}, where m and \mathbf{b} are constants defining the depth cueing geometry. Steps: 1. Define the viewing ray \mathbf{P}(t) parameterized by length t. 2. Construct the linear depth function \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)) = m\mathbf{P}(t) + \mathbf{b}. 3. Compute the dot product \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{V} to determine the local attenuation weight. 4. Evaluate the integrand: \rho(\mathbf{P}(t)) C(\mathbf{P}(t)) [\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} (\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{V})]. 5. Integrate the result from t=a to t=b. Formula: The total energy IP arriving at point \mathbf{P}(b) is given by: IP = \int{a}^{b} \rho(\mathbf{P}(t)) C(\mathbf{P}(t)) \left[ \frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} (\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{V}) \right] dt Where: \rho(\mathbf{P}(t)): Density at position \mathbf{P}(t). C(\mathbf{P}(t)): Color/emission at position \mathbf{P}(t). \tau: Constant opacity/absorption coefficient. \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)): Linear function of position, \mathbf{D} = m\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{b}. \mathbf{V}: Normalized viewing direction vector (points away from the eye). a, b: Start and end parameters of the ray segment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelinearattenuationenergy(rho, color, tau, m, bvec, v, tstart, tend, numsamples): """ Computes the integrated energy for linear depth cueing. Args: rho: Function returning density at (x,y,z). color: Function returning color vector at (x,y,z). tau: Constant opacity coefficient. m: Scalar constant for linear depth function. bvec: 3D vector constant for linear depth function. v: Normalized 3D viewing direction vector (away from eye). tstart: Start parameter 'a'. tend: End parameter 'b'. numsamples: Number of integration steps. Returns: Total energy IP. """ dt = (tend - tstart) / numsamples totalenergy = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tstart + i dt # Position along ray P(t) pt = getrayposition(t) # Implementation depends on ray origin/direction # Linear depth function D = mP + b dt = m pt + bvec # Attenuation weight: tau/2 + tau/2 (D. V) dotproduct = dot(dt, v) weight = (tau / 2.0) + (tau / 2.0) dotproduct # Integrand: rho C weight density = rho(pt) c = color(pt) # Accumulate energy (scalar product for monochromatic or component-wise for color) # Assuming scalar energy for simplicity or per-channel accumulation energysample = density c weight totalenergy += energysample dt return totalenergy Edge Cases: If \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{V} results in negative weights, the physical interpretation of attenuation may break down, though the formula remains mathematically valid. Precision issues may arise if \tau is very large or very small relative to the integration step size. A shading model that enhances depth perception in X-ray projections by weighting volume points based on their distance from the viewer, without introducing occlusion. It replaces per-voxel shading followed by projection with projection followed by per-pixel shading, allowing depth cueing (linear attenuation) to be computed efficiently by factoring the viewing direction out of the integral. Unlike opaque volume renderings, this method produces X-ray-like projections with no occlusion, but the linear shading provides sufficient shape cues for spatial understanding, especially in motion. Time Complexity: O(N^2 \log N) per view when implemented via the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, avoiding the O(N^3) cost of digital compositing [Parent]. Memory Complexity: Requires storage of the 3D frequency domain representation of the volume. Strengths: Efficient rendering of depth-cued X-ray images; leverages fast Fourier transforms. Limitations: Approximates exponential attenuation; does not model occlusion; accuracy depends on the linearity assumption of the depth cue. When to use: When real-time or near-real-time X-ray-like visualization with depth cues is required and occlusion is not a primary concern. When not to use: When physically accurate exponential attenuation with variable coefficients is necessary. The method was introduced by Marc Levoy in his work on volume rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. It addresses the computational cost of exponential attenuation by linearizing the absorption term, allowing the use of frequency domain methods for shading. The approach is based on the observation that linear attenuation with a constant coefficient can be expressed as a Fourier projection, enabling efficient rendering. name: Linear Depth Cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem
head: Fourier Projection-Slice Depth Cueing, Linear Attenuation via Fourier Projection-Slice, Linear Depth Cueing
body: A shading model that enhances depth perception in X-ray projections by weighting volume points based on their distance from the viewer, without introducing occlusion. It replaces per-voxel shading followed by projection with projection followed by per-pixel shading, allowing depth cueing (linear attenuation) to be computed efficiently by factoring the viewing direction out of the integral. Unlike opaque volume renderings, this method produces X-ray-like projections with no occlusion, but the linear shading provides sufficient shape cues for spatial understanding, especially in motion. Inputs: Volume density \rho(x,y,z) and emission coefficient C(x,y,z), combined as f(x,y,z) = \rho(x,y,z)C(x,y,z). Normalized viewing direction vector \mathbf{V} = (Vx, Vy, Vz), pointing away from the eye. Constant linear attenuation coefficient \tau. Linear depth function \mathbf{D}(P) = mP + b, where P is position along the ray. Outputs: 2D projection image I. Data Structures: Four 3D spectra (frequency domain representations) of the volume, each of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz (complex values). Two-dimensional slices extracted from these spectra for inverse transformation. Steps: 1. Precomputation: Create four copies of the volume data f(x,y,z). Multiply the first copy by 1. Multiply the second copy by Dx(x,y,z), the x-component of the depth function. Multiply the third copy by Dy(x,y,z), the y-component of the depth function. Multiply the fourth copy by Dz(x,y,z), the z-component of the depth function. Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of each of the four modified volumes to yield four 3D spectra: \mathcal{F}\{f\}, \mathcal{F}\{Dx f\}, \mathcal{F}\{Dy f\}, and \mathcal{F}\{Dz f\}. 2. Per-view Rendering: For the current viewing direction \mathbf{V}, extract 2D slices from each of the four 3D spectra corresponding to the projection plane defined by \mathbf{V}. Compute the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform of each extracted slice to obtain spatial domain images. Weight the inverse-transformed images by the components of \mathbf{V} and the constant terms derived from the attenuation model: Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{Dx f\} by Vx. Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{Dy f\} by Vy. Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{Dz f\} by Vz. Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{f\} by the constant c1 = \tau/2 - \tau/2 (Vx + Vy + Vz). Sum the four weighted images to produce the final output image I. Formula: The intensity I at a pixel is given by: I = Vx \Pi{\mathbf{V}} \left[ \left(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} Dx \right) \rho C \right] + Vy \Pi{\mathbf{V}} \left[ \left(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} Dy \right) \rho C \right] + Vz \Pi{\mathbf{V}} \left[ \left(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} Dz \right) \rho C \right] + c1 \Pi{\mathbf{V}} [\rho C] where \Pi{\mathbf{V}} is the projection operator, Dx, Dy, Dz are components of \mathbf{D}, and c1 = \tau/2 - \tau/2 (Vx + Vy + Vz). The underlying integral being approximated is: IP = \inta^b \rho(P(t)) C(P(t)) \left[ \frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} (\mathbf{D}(P(t)) \cdot \mathbf{V}) \right] dt where \mathbf{D} = mP + b is a linear function of position. Parameters: \tau: Constant linear attenuation coefficient. \mathbf{V}: Normalized viewing direction vector. m, b: Constants defining the linear depth function \mathbf{D}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ghosting: To avoid ghosting artifacts caused by spectral leakage, the input volume must be surrounded by a margin of zeros. The margin width is N(k2-1)/2 on each side, where k2 is the factor by which the volume width is increased. Viewing Direction Convention: \mathbf{V} must point away from the eye, not towards it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputespectra(rho, C, Dx, Dy, Dz): """ Precomputes the four 3D spectra required for linear depth cueing. Args: rho: 3D array of density values. C: 3D array of emission coefficients. Dx, Dy, Dz: 3D arrays of depth function components. Returns: spectra: List of four 3D complex arrays [Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz]. """ f = rho C # Standard 3D FFT implementation Sf = fft3d(f) SDx = fft3d(f Dx) SDy = fft3d(f Dy) SDz = fft3d(f Dz) return [Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz] def renderlineardepthcueing(spectra, V, tau): """ Renders a single view using linear depth cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. Args: spectra: List of four 3D complex arrays [Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz]. V: Tuple (Vx, Vy, Vz) normalized vector pointing away from eye. tau: Constant linear attenuation coefficient. Returns: image: 2D array representing the rendered projection. """ Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz = spectra Vx, Vy, Vz = V c1 = tau / 2.0 - (tau / 2.0) (Vx + Vy + Vz) # Extracts a 2D slice from the 3D spectrum along the plane orthogonal to V, per the Fourier slice theorem slicef = extractslice(Sf, V) sliceDx = extractslice(SDx, V) sliceDy = extractslice(SDy, V) sliceDz = extractslice(SDz, V) # Standard 2D IFFT implementation imgf = ifft2d(slicef) imgDx = ifft2d(sliceDx) imgDy = ifft2d(sliceDy) imgDz = ifft2d(sliceDz) # Weight and sum according to the projection formula # The tau/2 factor is applied here to match the exact mathematical formulation termbase = c1 imgf termDx = Vx (tau / 2.0) imgDx termDy = Vy (tau / 2.0) imgDy termDz = Vz (tau / 2.0) imgDz image = termbase + termDx + termDy + termDz return image.real Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading is a frequency-domain rendering technique that simultaneously applies linear depth cueing (attenuation) and hemispherical directional shading to volume data. It solves the problem of efficiently computing both effects within the Fourier Projection-Slice framework, where naive spatial-domain computation would be prohibitively expensive. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Linear Depth Cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, by combining the attenuation model with a hemispherical illumination model that avoids the nonlinear absolute value operator, allowing the lighting direction to be factored out of the integral. This requires 16 precomputed spectra and is slower than individual models due to a high constant factor, though asymptotically less expensive than conventional rendering. Memory: 48 megabytes for the 128^3 voxel cube implementation described. Performance: Rendering time was approximately 6 seconds per view on a 36 MHz Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX for the linear depth cueing equation (approx. 1.5 seconds per extracted slice). Scaling: Per-view processing time increases by a factor of k2^2 if the volume width is increased by a factor of k2 due to zero padding. Memory requirements increase by a factor of k2^3. Strengths: Efficient computation of depth cueing in the frequency domain; produces X-ray-like projections with shape cues. Limitations: No occlusion; requires zero-padding to avoid ghosting artifacts. Originated in the work of Marc Levoy, described in "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem". The method is part of a family of algorithms for generating realistically shaded renderings of volume data using the Fourier projection-slice theorem. Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/fourier/fourier.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem in Volume Rendering, https://www.scribd.com/document/796298963/Marc-Levoy-Volume-rendering-using-the-Fourier-projection-slice-theorem, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading
head: Composite Shading Model, Hemispherical Illumination Shading
body: Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading is a frequency-domain rendering technique that simultaneously applies linear depth cueing (attenuation) and hemispherical directional shading to volume data. It solves the problem of efficiently computing both effects within the Fourier Projection-Slice framework, where naive spatial-domain computation would be prohibitively expensive. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Linear Depth Cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, by combining the attenuation model with a hemispherical illumination model that avoids the nonlinear absolute value operator, allowing the lighting direction to be factored out of the integral. This requires 16 precomputed spectra and is slower than individual models due to a high constant factor, though asymptotically less expensive than conventional rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume of albedo \Omega(x,y,z), orientation field N(x,y,z), depth vector field D(x,y,z), viewing direction V, lighting direction L, attenuation parameter \tau, and light intensity Is. Output: Rendered image intensity I. Data Structures: The method relies on 16 precomputed 3D spectra derived from the albedo volume \Omega and the geometric fields N and D. VL Vector: A tuple of 13 elements representing products of viewing direction components V and lighting direction components L. Layout: (Vx Lx, Vx Ly, Vx Lz, Vy Lx, Vy Ly, Vy Lz, Vz Lx, Vz Ly, Vz Lz, Vx, Vy, Vz, Lx, Ly, Lz). Note: The source text refers to it as a 12-element vector, but explicitly lists 13 components in the formula. DN Vector: A tuple of 13 elements representing products of depth vector components D and orientation components N. Layout: (Dx Nx, Dx Ny, Dx Nz, Dy Nx, Dy Ny, Dy Nz, Dz Nx, Dz Ny, Dz Nz, Dx, Dy, Dz, Nx, Ny, Nz). Formulas: The rendered intensity I is calculated as: I = \frac{\tau \pi}{2} VL \cdot \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} DN(x,y,z)\right) Is \Omega(x,y,z) \right] + \frac{\tau \pi}{2} c3 \PiV [Is \Omega(x,y,z)] Where: Is: Intensity of the light source. \tau: Attenuation coefficient parameter. \PiV: Fourier projection operator along viewing direction V. c3: Constant term defined as c3 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \sumi VLi. VL \cdot \PiV [\dots] denotes the dot product between the VL vector and the corresponding vector of projected spectra. Steps: 1. Precomputation (Offline): 1. Expand the integrand product (\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} N \cdot L)(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} D \cdot V) into 16 basis terms: 1, Ni (3 terms), Dj (3 terms), and Ni Dj (9 terms). 2. Create 16 basis volumes by multiplying Is \Omega(x,y,z) by each basis term. 3. Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of each basis volume to yield 16 precomputed spectra. 2. Per-View Rendering (Online): 1. For the current viewing direction V and lighting direction L, extract 2D slices from each of the 16 precomputed 3D spectra along V. 2. Compute the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform of each extracted slice to obtain spatial domain images. 3. Weight each image by coefficients derived from L and V, and sum them according to the expanded formula. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def fft3d(vol): # Standard 3D Fast Fourier Transform return np.fft.fftn(vol) def ifft2d(slice2d): # Standard 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transform return np.fft.ifft2(slice2d) def slicespectrum(spec3d, dirv): # Extract 2D slice from 3D spectrum along direction dirv # Standard operation in Fourier projection-slice rendering return extractslicealongvector(spec3d, dirv) def compositedepthcueingshading(volume, orientation, depthfield, viewingdir, lightingdir, tau, lightintensity): """ Renders a volume using composite depth cueing and directional shading. Args: volume: 3D array of albedo Omega(x,y,z) orientation: 3D array of orientation field N(x,y,z) depthfield: 3D array of depth vector field D(x,y,z) viewingdir: 3D vector V lightingdir: 3D vector L tau: float, attenuation parameter lightintensity: float, Is Returns: 2D array, rendered image """ # Precomputation (Assumed to be done once or cached) # Basis functions for the 16 spectra based on expansion of (1/2 + 1/2 N.L) (tau/2 + tau/2 D.V) # Terms: 1, Ni (3), Dj (3), NiDj (9) basisvolumes = [] # Base albedo (1) basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume) # N components (3) basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume orientation[:,:,0]) # Nx basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume orientation[:,:,1]) # Ny basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume orientation[:,:,2]) # Nz # D components (3) basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume depthfield[:,:,0]) # Dx basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume depthfield[:,:,1]) # Dy basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume depthfield[:,:,2]) # Dz # Cross terms Ni Dj (9) for i in range(3): for j in range(3): basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume orientation[:,:,i] depthfield[:,:,j]) # Compute 3D FFT for each basis volume spectra = [fft3d(bv) for bv in basisvolumes] # Per-view rendering V = viewingdir L = lightingdir # Extract slices from spectra along V slices = [slicespectrum(spec, V) for spec in spectra] # Inverse FFT to get spatial images images = [ifft2d(s) for s in slices] # Coefficients from expanded integrand: Is Omega (pitau/4) [1 + sum(Li Ni) + sum(Vj Dj) + sum(Li Vj Ni Dj)] coeffbase = (tau np.pi) / 4 coeffn = [(tau np.pi) / 4 L[i] for i in range(3)] coeffd = [(tau np.pi) / 4 V[i] for i in range(3)] coeffnd = [[(tau np.pi) / 4 L[i] V[j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] # Map images to coefficients and sum # Image 0: Base # Image 1-3: Ni # Image 4-6: Dj # Image 7-15: Ni Dj imagesum = images[0] coeffbase for i in range(3): imagesum += images[1+i] coeffn[i] for i in range(3): imagesum += images[4+i] coeffd[i] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): imagesum += images[7 + i3 + j] coeffnd[i][j] return imagesum Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Emission: The composite model ignores emission \rho C from the depth cueing equation. In this context, emission can be interpreted as ambient illumination. Memory: The requirement for 16 spectra can lead to significant memory usage, potentially causing paging on older systems. This method combines linear depth cueing and directional shading within the frequency domain to replace O(n^3) spatial domain computations with O(n^2) frequency domain operations. It solves the problem of efficiently applying both attenuation and illumination in Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering [Parent]. It sets itself apart from naive frequency domain combinations by reversing the standard order of operations (applying depth cueing and interpolation first, then shading) to utilize a single composite filter, thereby avoiding the computational cost of multiple convolutions. Time Complexity: Asymptotically less expensive than conventional volume rendering (O(n^2) vs O(n^3)), but with a high constant factor due to the 16 spectra and 16 inverse FFTs per view. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 16 3D spectra. For a 128^3 voxel cube, this amounts to 256 megabytes. Measured Performance: On a 36 MHz Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX, rendering time was over a minute per view for a 128^2 image, mostly due to paging. Strengths: Efficiently combines two shading effects; avoids nonlinear operators; plausible shading for diffuse objects resembling a cloudy day appearance. Limitations: High constant factor makes it slower than conventional rendering for small volumes; sensitive to memory constraints; ignores emission/ambient light. When to Use: Large volumes where asymptotic efficiency outweighs constant overhead; scenes requiring both depth cueing and directional shading. When Not to Use: Small volumes; hardware with limited memory; scenes requiring accurate ambient lighting or emission. The method was developed by Marc Levoy as part of his work on Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering. It appears in the paper "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem". The technique was demonstrated on a CT scan of a human skull. The approach was implemented in C on a Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX. The paper suggests that replacing the FFT with an FHT (Fast Hartley Transform) could halve the rendering time and memory requirements. PDF Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/fourier/fourier.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem in Volume Rendering, https://www.scribd.com/document/796298963/Marc-Levoy-Volume-rendering-using-the-Fourier-projection-slice-theorem, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
