name: Isosurface extraction
body: Isosurface extraction generates an explicit polygonal mesh representing the surface where a scalar field equals a specific threshold (isovalue) from volumetric data. It solves the problem of visualizing internal structures or boundaries within volumetric data by approximating the implicit surface f(x,y,z) = I. What sets this family apart from direct volume rendering is that it produces an explicit geometric representation (mesh) rather than a rasterized image. Unlike Blocky meshing, which produces voxel-aligned stair-step surfaces, isosurface methods typically interpolate between grid points to create smooth, curved surfaces. All isosurface extraction algorithms operate on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values at its vertices. The core mechanism involves traversing the grid cells and evaluating the scalar field at cell vertices or edges. For cubic grids, vertex values are compared against the isovalue to determine a topological configuration (e.g., a 256-case index). For tetrahedral or hybrid grids, the method identifies edges where the scalar field changes sign. Intersection points are computed using inverse linear interpolation for the parameter and linear interpolation for 3D coordinates: t = (I - fa) / (fb - fa) and P = Va + t(Vb - Va). The intersection points are then connected to form primitives (triangles, quads, or polygons). Adjacent cell primitives are merged into a coherent mesh, often requiring vertex merging to avoid duplicates. Generates a triangular mesh from a 3D scalar field by processing each voxel independently. It determines the topology of the isosurface intersection with cube boundaries based on vertex values relative to an isolevel. Uses a fixed lookup table to resolve intersections, making it straightforward but complicated to implement due to fifteen distinct special cases. Choose it for general-purpose cubic grid extraction. Places a single vertex inside each grid cell intersected by the surface, optimizing its position by minimizing a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) derived from Hermite data. Unlike Marching Cubes, which places vertices on cell edges, it preserves sharp features and produces manifold, watertight meshes. Choose it when feature preservation and watertightness are critical. Begins with a seed point and grows a triangulation across an implicit surface by advancing the front boundary. Choose it for incremental surface generation or when starting from a known point on the surface. Projects a query point onto a surface defined by input points and normals by fitting a local quadratic function. Choose it for refining vertex positions or projecting points onto implicit surfaces. Provides a standardized interface for invoking various extraction algorithms. Choose it to abstract algorithm selection and manage multiple extraction methods uniformly. Extracts isosurfaces from 3D voxel data by constructing a wire frame of N-cycles (closed loops of voxel faces) enclosing active voxels, which are then triangulated. Choose it for volume-enclosing surfaces from voxel data without topological ambiguities. Constructs a mesh by placing a single vertex per active voxel at the weighted average of grid points on intersected edges. Unlike Marching Cubes, it generates exactly one vertex per voxel, resulting in a sparser mesh. Choose it for performance-critical applications where exact vertex placement is less important than speed and sparsity. Reconstructs a Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane in Volume of Fluid (VOF) simulations on arbitrary polyhedral grids. Choose it for fluid dynamics simulations requiring accurate interface reconstruction. Generates a 3D mesh from a trained DVR model by querying an implicit occupancy field using adaptive resolution. Choose it for neural implicit surface reconstruction. Precomputed data structures mapping voxel corner signs to intersected edges and triangle indices. Solves topology determination without runtime branching. Choose it for CPU/GPU implementations prioritizing simplicity and topological consistency over geometric optimality. Produces topologically consistent surfaces with a local convexity property, where the polygonal contour inside each cell encloses a convex negative space. Choose it when topological robustness and convexity guarantees are required. GPU-accelerated technique processing a 3D scalar volume grid using a compute shader. Adapts classic Marching Cubes for parallel execution with fixed-size buffers and atomic counters. Choose it for real-time or high-throughput implicit function to mesh conversion on GPUs. Data structure to obtain active cells for a particular isosurface with optimal query complexity O(\log(n) + k). Choose it for accelerating cell extraction in large volumes. Uses an octree as a spatial discretization structure instead of a Cartesian grid. Allows for adaptive resolution but may cause cracks if not adapted to the surface. Choose it for multi-resolution data where adaptive sampling is beneficial. Approximates the isosurface position between two sample points by iteratively halving the interval based on scalar field values. Choose it for high-precision interpolation in sparse or expensive-to-evaluate fields. Generates triangulation tables for isosurface extraction in n-dimensional hypercubes. Choose it for extracting surfaces from higher-dimensional data or hypercubic grids. Smooths a 2D or 3D binary embedding array by assigning negative/positive values to preserve fine details and thin structures. Choose it for post-processing binary embeddings to retain thin features. Extracts intersection-free isosurfaces using intersections with a tetrahedral grid's edges, guaranteeing freedom from self-intersections. Choose it when topological correctness and intersection-free output are mandatory. Triangulates non-convex or complex polygons resulting from extraction into triangles, minimizing total area to reduce visual artifacts. Choose it for post-processing extracted polygons to improve mesh quality. Maps one of the 256 possible cube configurations to one of 23 canonical base cases using precomputed rotation and base case mappings to simplify triangle generation logic. Choose it to reduce lookup table size and simplify implementation. Converts isosurfaces to point clouds by evaluating chunks of voxels and extracting vertices at the center of intersected edges, without generating face data. Choose it for point-based rendering or when surface reconstruction is deferred to the GPU. Detects patch boundaries as groups of rings of linear contours on cell faces for automatic construction of look-up tables. Choose it for automated table generation in custom contouring methods. Sequentially visits all cells in the volume to identify active cells containing the isosurface by checking if the isovalue is contained in the half-open interval [v{min}, v{max}). Requires only storage for the original volume data and yields linear time complexity O(n). Choose it for simple, memory-efficient extraction when acceleration structures are unnecessary. name: Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces
head: Continuation, Surface Tracking
body:
The Advancing Front Framework is an isosurface extraction method that constructs a triangulated mesh by growing a front across the implicit surface, starting from a seed point and extending it edge-by-edge. Unlike grid-based methods such as Marching Cubes or Marching Tetrahedra which traverse a discretized domain to determine topology locally, this method operates without a pre-defined volume description, requiring the algorithm to discover and chart the surface geometry dynamically. It is distinguished by its ability to generate high-quality, well-shaped triangles directly, avoiding the post-processing often required by topological grid methods, though it is computationally more intensive [S1, 947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An implicit surface defined by a scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) = 0, where the gradient 
abla f and Hessian Hf are non-zero everywhere. A seed point \mathbf{p}0 on the surface. Output: A manifold triangular mesh representing the isosurface. Data Structures: Front: A list of edges forming the boundary of the generated mesh. Each edge is defined by two vertices \mathbf{v}i, \mathbf{v}j. Mesh: A collection of triangles, each defined by three vertices. Intersection Check: A spatial data structure (e.g., bounding volume hierarchy or grid) to detect collisions between the proposed new triangle and existing front edges or mesh triangles. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Place the seed point \mathbf{p}0 on the surface. Compute the normal \mathbf{n}0 = 
abla f(\mathbf{p}0) / \|
abla f(\mathbf{p}0)\|. Create an initial triangle or edge set to start the front. The initial front must be a closed loop or a set of edges that can be advanced. 2. Front Selection: Select an edge e = (\mathbf{v}a, \mathbf{v}b) from the current front. The selection criterion (e.g., shortest edge, longest edge) determines the growth strategy. 3. Triangle Construction: Determine the third vertex \mathbf{v}c to form a new triangle T = (\mathbf{v}a, \mathbf{v}b, \mathbf{v}c). The position of \mathbf{v}c is determined by the surface geometry and desired element size. The target position \mathbf{p}{target} is projected onto the surface: f(\mathbf{p}{target}) = 0. The normal at \mathbf{v}c is computed to ensure smoothness. 4. Collision Detection: Check if the new triangle T intersects with any existing edge in the front or any triangle in the already generated mesh. Self-Intersection: If T intersects the same front it was created from, the front is split into two separate fronts at the intersection point. The algorithm continues advancing both new fronts. Front Merging: If T intersects a different front, the two fronts are merged. The shared boundary is removed, and the new edges are added to the unified front. Valid Advance: If no intersection occurs, the triangle T is added to the mesh, and the front is updated by removing edge e and adding the new edges (\mathbf{v}b, \mathbf{v}c) and (\mathbf{v}c, \mathbf{v}a). 5. Termination: The process repeats until the front is empty or the surface is fully enclosed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def advancingfrontimplicitsurface(f, seedpoint): # f is the implicit function f(x) = 0 # seedpoint is a point on the surface # Initialize front with a small loop around seedpoint # Requires computing tangent plane and sampling points on f(x)=0 front = createinitialfront(seedpoint, f) mesh = [] while front is not empty: # Select edge from front edge = selectedge(front) va, vb = edge.vertices # Compute candidate third vertex # This step involves projecting a point onto the surface # and ensuring element size constraints are met. vc = computethirdvertex(va, vb, f, front) newtriangle = Triangle(va, vb, vc) # Check for intersections intersection = checkintersection(newtriangle, front, mesh) if intersection is None: # No intersection: advance front mesh.add(newtriangle) front.remove(edge) front.addedge(vb, vc) front.addedge(vc, va) elif intersection.isselfintersection: # Split front front = splitfront(front, intersection.point) elif intersection.isfrontmerge: # Merge fronts front = mergefronts(front, intersection.otherfront) return mesh Parameters and Edge Cases: Element Size: The length of the new triangle edges is critical. Heuristic sizing can lead to poor quality or interference. Gradient/Hessian Non-Zero: The method assumes 
abla f 
eq 0 and Hf 
eq 0 everywhere to ensure the surface is well-defined and smooth. Front Interference: A major pitfall is the front intersecting itself or other fronts incorrectly. Robust intersection detection is required. Uses a scalar guidance field g(\mathbf{x}) to constrain edge lengths based on curvature, ensuring robust front interference detection and well-shaped triangles. It replaces heuristic sizing with a theoretically grounded approach. Time Complexity: Generally higher than grid-based methods due to the need for continuous surface evaluation and complex front management (splitting/merging) [S1, 947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md]. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of triangles generated. The front data structure can become complex with many splits and merges. Strengths: Produces high-quality, well-shaped meshes directly without the need for downstream smoothing or remeshing often required by Marching Cubes [S1, 947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md]. Limitations: Computationally slower; sensitive to the choice of seed points and initial front; requires robust intersection detection [S1, 947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md]. When to Use: When high-quality mesh topology is critical and computational resources allow for more expensive generation. The advancing front technique originated in the mesh generation community for numerical simulation, where it was used to create high-quality meshes for well-defined domains. The application to implicit surfaces, where no pre-defined volume description exists, was a significant extension. Key references include work by Borouchaki et al. on gradation control and other early works on implicit surface triangulation. High-Quality Extraction of Isosurfaces from Regular and Irregular Grids, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2006.149, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field
head: Guidance Field Advancing Front, Schreiner et al. method
body:
This method extracts isosurfaces from implicit functions using an advancing front algorithm guided by a scalar field g(\mathbf{x}) that constrains edge lengths based on surface curvature and user parameters. It builds on the Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces by replacing heuristic edge sizing with a theoretically grounded guidance field that ensures robust front interference detection and well-shaped triangles. Unlike Marching Cubes or Marching Tetrahedra, which produce meshes requiring downstream processing, this method generates high-quality meshes directly, though it is computationally slower [S1, 963-multi-threaded-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md]. The algorithm constructs a guidance field from initial surface samples to determine ideal edge lengths, culls redundant samples for efficiency, seeds the front, and iteratively advances the front by adding triangles or merging/splitting fronts based on interference checks. Inputs: Implicit function f(\mathbf{x}), its gradient 
abla f, its Hessian H(f), isovalue k, accuracy parameter ho, and well-shapedness parameter \eta. Outputs: A triangular mesh approximating the isosurface f(\mathbf{x}) = k. Sample Set S: A set of points \mathbf{s} on the surface, each associated with a maximum curvature \kappa{\max}(\mathbf{s}) and ideal edge length \iota(\mathbf{s}). Guidance Field g: A scalar field defined as the lower envelope of cone functions 	ilde{g}s for all s \in S. Active Fronts: A collection of front objects, where each front represents a boundary edge or sequence of edges on the mesh. KD-Tree: A 4-dimensional KD-tree used to store samples for culling, where each node stores coordinates [sx, sy, sz, sr], with [sx, sy, sz] being the sample location and sr being the height of the cone function 	ilde{g}s at that location. 1. Ideal Edge Length: \iota(s) =  rac{2 \sin(ho/2)}{\kappa{\max}(s)} where \iota(s) is the ideal edge length at sample s, ho is the accuracy parameter, and \kappa{\max}(s) is the maximum absolute curvature at s. 2. Cone Function: 	ilde{g}s(x) = (1 - \eta^{-1}) \cdot |x - s| + \eta^{-1} \cdot \iota(s) where 	ilde{g}s is the cone function induced by sample s, x is a point in embedding space, s is a sample point on the surface, and \iota(s) is the ideal edge length at s. 3. Guidance Field: g(x) = \min{s \in S} 	ilde{g}s(x) where g(x) is the guidance field, S is the set of sampled points, and 	ilde{g}s is the cone function for sample s. 4. Projection Matrix: P = I - n n^T H where P is the projection matrix onto the tangent plane, I is the identity matrix, n = 
abla f / |
abla f| is the normalized gradient, and H is the Hessian matrix of f. Note: The source text contains typos in the Hessian matrix entries (e.g., \partial^2 f / \partial x \partial x in off-diagonals), but the structure is I - n n^T multiplied by the Hessian. 5. Curvature Bound: \kappa{\max} \leq \|P\| \cdot \|H\| \cdot \|P\| \cdot \|I/|
abla f|\| where \kappa{\max} is the maximum curvature, P is the projection matrix, H is the Hessian, and \|\cdot\| denotes the matrix norm (specifically Frobenius norm \|M\|2 = \sqrt{\sum m{ij}^2}). ho: User-defined parameter controlling reconstruction accuracy. It determines the angle subtended by edges on the minimum osculating circle. Typical values: 0.2, 0.3, 0.5. \eta: User-defined parameter controlling the rate of triangle expansion (well-shapedness). It bounds the ratio of adjacent edge lengths: |e1|/|e2| \leq \eta if |e1| > |e2|. Typical values: 2, 3, 5. 1. Generate Samples: Create a jittered random set of points inside cells neighboring the surface and project them onto the surface via gradient descent to form set S. 2. Compute Guidance Field: Evaluate the lower envelope of cone functions 	ilde{g}s for all s \in S to form g(x). 3. Cull Guidance Field: Remove unnecessary samples from S to minimize memory and computation time while preserving the properties of g(x). 4. Seed Fronts: Compute seed points (e.g., using efficient algorithms like [6]) and project them onto the surface using gradient descent to initialize the Active front set. 5. Advance Front: While Active is not empty: a. Get a front from Active. b. Check if it is OK to add a triangle using parameters ho and \eta. c. If OK, add the triangle to the front. d. If not OK, get the interfering front. e. If the interfering front is the same as the current front, split the front into two new fronts (f1, f2), remove the old front, and add the two new fronts to Active. f. If the interfering front is different, merge the current front and the interfering front into a new front, remove both from Active, and add the new front to Active. 6. Create Triangles: Determine the correct edge size from the guidance field g. Project the new point onto the surface using the dihedral angle of the edge as a free parameter and searching for the isovalue. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def TRIANGULATE(f, gradf, hessf, k, rho, eta): # Step 1: Generate initial samples S = [] # Create jittered random points in cells neighboring the surface f(x) = k # Project each point onto the surface using gradient descent # Append projected points to S pass # See Section 4.1 of for sampling condition # Step 2: Compute guidance field # For each s in S, compute kappamax(s) using P and H # Compute iota(s) = (2 sin(rho/2)) / kappamax(s) # Define cone function gtildes(x) = (1 - 1/eta) |x - s| + (1/eta) iota(s) # g(x) is the lower envelope of all gtildes pass # Step 3: Cull guidance field CULL(g, rho, eta) # Step 4: Seed the front Active = SEEDFRONTS(S) # See Section 3.2 of # Step 5: Advance front while len(Active) > 0: front = GETANYFRONT(Active) if OKTOADDTRIANGLE(front, rho, eta): ADDTRIANGLETOFRONT(front, rho, eta) else: other = GETINTERFERINGFRONT(front) if other == front: f1, f2 = SPLIT(front) REMOVEFRONTS(Active, {front}) ADDFRONTS(Active, {f1, f2}) else: newfront = MERGE(front, other) REMOVEFRONTS(Active, {front, other}) ADDFRONTS(Active, {newfront}) def CULL(g, rho, eta): # Insert all points in the guidance field into a 4-dimensional kd-tree # Coordinates for each sample s are [sx, sy, sz, sr], where [sx, sy, sz] is location # and sr is the height of gtildes at s tree = KDTREE(g.samples) # Sort samples by maximum curvature (kappamax) in descending order sortedsamples = SORT(g.samples, key=lambda s: s.kappamax, reverse=True) for si in sortedsamples: if not si.marked: # Construct a cone c defined by si, rho, eta # Apex: [sx, sy, sz, sr], Axis: [0, 0, 0, 1], Angle: atan(eta / (eta - 1)) c = CONE(si, rho, eta) # Query kd-tree for points inside cone c and mark them MarkIfInside(tree, c) # If all children of a kd-tree node are marked, mark the node pass # Pruning logic for KD-Tree # Discard all marked samples from g(x) g.samples = [s for s in g.samples if not s.marked] Front Interference: If the test fails to detect front interference, two or more sheets of triangles may form over portions of the surface. The algorithm uses a robust front intersection test procedure proven by the guidance field properties. Insufficient Sampling: If the guidance field is not sufficiently sampled, features smaller than the sampling density can be missed, and g(x) may not bound \iota(x), leading to triangles larger than allowed by curvature. Sharp Curvature Changes: Standard adaptive advancing front algorithms fail when sharp changes in curvature lead to sharp changes in triangle size and poorly shaped triangles. The guidance field prevents this by bounding the gradient magnitude of g. Critical Points: The method assumes the isosurface does not pass through critical points of f. This method parallelizes the Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field [947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md] by distributing the work of projecting points onto the advancing fronts across a set of worker threads. Compared to Marching Cubes Marching Cubes or Marching Tetrahedra Marching Tetrahedra, the algorithm is slower but generates meshes requiring negligible or no downstream processing, unlike MC/MT results. A technique to reduce the number of samples in a guidance field by removing samples that are 'dominated' by others, where a sample s1 dominates s2 if the edge length required for curvature at s1 is always smaller than that of s2, ensuring the guidance field remains sufficient and Lipschitz-continuous. It inserts all points into a 4-dimensional kd-tree, sorts samples by maximum curvature in descending order, and iteratively marks samples inside cones defined by dominant samples, pruning branches when all children are marked. Time Complexity: The culling step typically removes a large percentage of sample points, resulting in significantly faster guidance field queries and total running time, despite the additional processing overhead. For example, culling can reduce running time from 27m05s to 7m27s for the Silicium dataset with ho=0.2. Memory Complexity: Culling significantly reduces memory usage by discarding unnecessary samples. Performance: The method is slower than Marching Cubes or Marching Tetrahedra but produces high-quality meshes with negligible downstream processing needs [S1, 963-multi-threaded-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md]. Strengths: Robust front interference detection, well-shaped triangles, and guaranteed feature capture with sufficient sampling. Limitations: Requires sufficient sampling to avoid missing features; assumes smooth surfaces and no critical points on the isosurface. When to Use: When high-quality, well-shaped meshes are required without downstream processing, and computational resources allow for the higher cost of the advancing front algorithm. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical, or when the surface has sharp features that cannot be adequately captured by the sampling density. The method is based on the work of Schreiner et al. [45], who introduced a solid theoretical foundation for advancing front algorithms using a guidance field. It addresses issues such as sharp changes in curvature and robust front interference detection that hindered previous advancing front algorithms. The enhancements described in (sampling condition and culling procedure) were presented to guarantee correct reproduction of features and reduce memory usage. name: Multi-threaded Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction
head: Parallel Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction
body:
This method parallelizes the Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field [947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md] by distributing the work of projecting points onto the advancing fronts across a set of worker threads. Compared to Marching Cubes Marching Cubes or Marching Tetrahedra Marching Tetrahedra, the algorithm is slower but generates meshes requiring negligible or no downstream processing, unlike MC/MT results. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An implicit function f(\mathbf{x}) defined over a domain, a target isovalue k, and a guidance field g(\mathbf{x}) computed from parameters ho and \eta. The function must admit well-defined gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) and Hessian Hf(\mathbf{x}). Output: A triangular mesh approximating the isosurface f(\mathbf{x}) = k with bounded distance error and bounded normal error. Data Structures: Front: A shared set of vertices and edges defining the extracted surface boundary. It requires thread-safe access for concurrent updates. Task Queue: A shared collection of candidate points awaiting projection onto the front. Thread Pool: A fixed set of N worker threads that independently pop tasks, project points, and update the front. Parameters: Thread Count (N): The number of worker threads. Experiments use N=4. ho, \eta: Guidance field parameters controlling edge length constraints based on surface curvature. Numbered Steps: 1. Parallel Guidance Field and Culling: Compute the guidance field g(\mathbf{x}) for the domain and perform culling entirely in parallel. 2. Task Distribution: Distribute the work of projecting points onto the advancing fronts across the worker threads. 3. Parallel Advancement: Each worker thread evaluates f(\mathbf{x}), 
abla f(\mathbf{x}), and Hf(\mathbf{x}) at candidate points, uses g(\mathbf{x}) to determine appropriate edge lengths and projection steps, and projects points to satisfy f(\mathbf{x}) \approx k. 4. Synchronization: Threads synchronize when modifying the shared front structure; advancing front algorithms are mostly local, allowing independent decisions for distant surface parts. 5. Termination: The process repeats until the front is closed or no valid points remain in the queue. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import threading import queue def multithreadedadvancingfrontextraction(f, k, gfunc, Nthreads, domainbounds, gridspacing): # 1. Parallel guidance field computation and culling # Sample domain on a uniform grid candidates = [] for x in range(domainbounds[0][0], domainbounds[0][1], gridspacing): for y in range(domainbounds[1][0], domainbounds[1][1], gridspacing): for z in range(domainbounds[2][0], domainbounds[2][1], gridspacing): point = (x, y, z) if gfunc(point) < 2.0: # Threshold not specified in sources candidates.append(point) # 2. Initialize front and task queue front = [] taskqueue = queue.Queue() for p in candidates: taskqueue.put(p) frontlock = threading.Lock() def worker(): while not taskqueue.empty(): try: point = taskqueue.getnowait() except queue.Empty: break # 3. Parallel Advancement: Project point to isosurface f(x) = k x = list(point) for in range(20): fx = f(x) if abs(fx - k) < 1e-5: break # Central difference gradient eps = 1e-6 grad = [ (f([x[0]+eps, x[1], x[2]]) - f([x[0]-eps, x[1], x[2]])) / (2eps), (f([x[0], x[1]+eps, x[2]]) - f([x[0], x[1]-eps, x[2]])) / (2eps), (f([x[0], x[1], x[2]+eps]) - f([x[0], x[1], x[2]-eps])) / (2eps) ] gradnormsq = sum(gg for g in grad) + 1e-12 stepsize = gfunc(x) # Guidance field scales step size dx = [-fx g / gradnormsq stepsize for g in grad] x = [x[i] + dx[i] for i in range(3)] # Update front and distribute new tasks with frontlock: front.append(tuple(x)) # Neighbor generation strategy not specified in sources # 4. Distribute work across worker threads threads = [] for in range(Nthreads): t = threading.Thread(target=worker) threads.append(t) t.start() for t in threads: t.join() return front Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Regular Surfaces: The method requires the implicit function to admit a well-defined gradient and Hessian. Sharp corners do not admit a regular isosurface representation (where f(\mathbf{x}) = k and 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) 
eq 0). Thread Safety: The front structure must be protected during concurrent updates. Precision: High-order meshes (degree ~10) may have high-frequency features. The method is oblivious to the underlying mesh but relies on accurate gradient/Hessian computation. Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field [947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md]: The single-threaded parent method. Marching Cubes Marching Cubes: A grid-based method. Marching Tetrahedra Marching Tetrahedra: Similar to Marching Cubes but avoids ambiguity. Time Complexity: The algorithm is slower than Marching Cubes (MC) or Marching Tetrahedra (MT) implementations. Running times are typically several minutes for larger datasets. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experiments were conducted on a PC with two dual-core AMD Opteron processors at 2.25GHz, 4GB RAM, SuSE Linux 10.0. Four threads were used for all experiments. Scaling: The method scales with the number of threads by distributing the projection work. The source notes that advancing front algorithms are "mostly local," which facilitates parallelization. Strengths: Generates high-quality meshes with bounded distance and normal error. 99% of triangles have quality at least half of optimal, and the median quality is within 3% of optimal across different models, ho, \eta, and surface definitions. Triangle counts are often less than MC. The meshes require negligible or no downstream processing. Limitations: Slower than MC/MT. Requires well-defined gradient and Hessian. Not suitable for sharp corners. When to Use: When high-quality, high-fidelity triangulation is required, and the implicit function is smooth (band-limited). When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical, or when the input data contains sharp corners or non-smooth features that violate the regular isosurface assumption. The method is described in "High-Quality Extraction of Isosurfaces from Regular and Irregular Grids". It builds on the Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces and specifically the guidance-field-based approach. The authors implemented the algorithm in C++ and tested it on various models including Catmull-Rom splines and B-splines, as well as unstructured meshes like Nielson interpolation and MLS approximation. The technique is generalizable to any surface formulation that admits gradient and Hessian computation, making it applicable to high-order meshes (typically degree ~10). name: MLS Projection
head: MLS projection via Hermite Point Set Surfaces, Moving Least Squares Surface, Parabolic Case Triangulation
body:
MLS Projection is an iterative algorithm that projects a query point onto a surface defined by a set of input points and their associated normals using Moving Least Squares (MLS) approximation. It solves the problem of reconstructing smooth, noise-resistant implicit surfaces from unorganized point clouds by fitting local quadratic functions to the Hermite data (positions and normals). It sets itself apart from standard isosurface extraction methods like Marching Cubes by operating directly on point sets rather than grid samples, and from Dual Contouring by explicitly computing a projected point and normal via iterative tangent plane averaging rather than optimizing a vertex position via a Quadratic Error Function (QEF). Inputs: inputPositions: Array of 3D points Pi. inputNormals: Array of unit normal vectors Ni corresponding to each point. inputPointsetKdTree: A spatial index (e.g., KD-Tree) built from inputPositions for nearest neighbor search. queryPoint: The 3D point to be projected onto the surface. knn: Number of nearest neighbors to consider (default: 20). radius: Radius parameter for the kernel function. kerneltype: Selector for the weighting kernel (0=Gaussian, 1=Wendland, 2=Singular). numberOfIterations: Number of iterations for the projection loop. Outputs: outputPoint: The projected point on the surface. outputNormal: The normal vector at the projected point. Data Structures: Vectors are 3D floats (x, y, z). Accumulators are initialized to zero vectors or scalars as appropriate. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set currentPoint = queryPoint. 2. Iteration Loop: For iter from 0 to numberOfIterations - 1: a. Neighbor Search: Find the knn nearest neighbors of currentPoint using inputPointsetKdTree. Retrieve their indices idnearestneighbors and squared distances squaredistancestoneighbors. b. Accumulator Initialization: Initialize accumulators: sumweight = 0.0 sumweightedneighbors = (0, 0, 0) sumweightednormals = (0, 0, 0) Note: Some implementations use a polynomial fitting approach with accumulators sum1, sum2, sum3, sum4, u123, u0, u4. The following pseudocode describes the simpler Hermite projection variant described in, which is the primary definition of "MLS Projection" in the context of HPSS. c. Weighted Accumulation: Loop over neighbor index i from 0 to knn - 1: i. Get neighbor position: neighbor = inputPositions[idnearestneighbors[i]]. ii. Get neighbor normal: neighborNormal = inputNormals[idnearestneighbors[i]]. iii. Project onto Tangent Plane: Compute the projection of currentPoint onto the tangent plane of the neighbor: 	ext{ProjOnTang} = 	ext{currentPoint} - 	ext{dot}(	ext{currentPoint} - 	ext{neighbor}, 	ext{neighborNormal}) 	imes 	ext{neighborNormal} iv. Compute Weight: Calculate weight using the kernel function: 	ext{weight} = K(\sqrt{	ext{square\distances	o
eighbors}[i]}) Where K(r) depends on kerneltype (see Subtopics). v. Update Accumulators: 	ext{sum\weighted
eighbors} \ += \ 	ext{weight} 	imes 	ext{ProjOnTang} 	ext{sum\weight} \ += \ 	ext{weight} 	ext{sum\weighted
ormals} \ += \ 	ext{weight} 	imes 	ext{neighborNormal} d. Compute New Center and Normal: i. New center point: c =  rac{	ext{sum\weighted
eighbors}}{	ext{sum\weight}} ii. New normal: n = 	ext{normalize}(	ext{sum\weighted
ormals}) e. Update State: 	ext{outputPoint} = c 	ext{outputNormal} = n 	ext{currentPoint} = 	ext{outputPoint} 3. Return: Return outputPoint and outputNormal. Alternative Polynomial Fitting Variant: Some sources describe a variant where the MLS surface is defined by a quadratic polynomial f(x) = u4 x^T x + u{123}^T x + u0. In this variant, the accumulators track terms to solve for coefficients u4, u{123}, u0: u4 = 0.5 	imes  rac{	ext{sum\1} - 	ext{dot}(	ext{sum\2}, 	ext{sum\3})/	ext{sum\weight}}{	ext{sum\4} - 	ext{dot}(	ext{sum\2}, 	ext{sum\2})/	ext{sum\weight}} u{123} =  rac{	ext{sum\3} - 2 u4 	ext{sum\2}}{	ext{sum\weight}} u0 = - rac{	ext{dot}(	ext{sum\2}, u{123}) + u4 	ext{sum\4}}{	ext{sum\weight}} The update step becomes: 	ext{diff} = (u0 + 	ext{dot}(u{123}, 	ext{outputPoint}) + u4 	ext{dot}(	ext{outputPoint}, 	ext{outputPoint})) 	imes 	ext{outputNormal} and 	ext{outputPoint} = 	ext{outputPoint} - 	ext{diff}. This variant is cited in but the tangent-plane averaging variant is the direct definition of "MLS Projection" for HPSS. The tangent-plane method is preferred for its simplicity in defining the projection operator. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Neighbors: If neighbors are collinear or coplanar, the normal estimation may be unstable. A guard should check if sumweight is near zero or if the normal vector has near-zero magnitude, falling back to the average normal of the neighbors or the input normal if available. Precision: Squared distances should be used to avoid square roots in the loop, but the kernel function may require the actual distance r. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes the query point is reasonably close to the surface. If the query point is far, the local approximation may not converge to the correct surface branch. APSS is an iterative method to project a query point onto a surface defined by a point set with normals, using Moving Least Squares (MLS). It builds on MLS Projection by computing a local coordinate system and higher-order approximations via weighted accumulators, distinguishing it from standard MLS by explicitly tracking cross-product and dot-product terms for refined surface fitting. Choose APSS when higher-order surface continuity or accuracy is required beyond the quadratic approximation of standard MLS. Link: APSS. Moving Least Squares (MLS) Implicit Surface Reconstruction is a technique for reconstructing a surface from an unordered 3D point cloud by creating an implicit function field using Moving Least Squares, from which isosurfaces are extracted. It differs from its parent MLS Projection by constructing a global implicit field defined by local quadratic fits rather than iteratively projecting query points, and from its sibling APSS by relying on a standard MLS approximation of the signed distance function rather than approximate projected point set surfaces. Choose this when a global implicit representation is needed for rendering or ray tracing rather than a mesh. Link: Moving Least Squares Implicit Surface Reconstruction. A set of kernel functions used to weight neighbors in MLS surface reconstruction based on distance r and scale h. The choice of kernel affects the smoothness and support of the local approximation. Gaussian kernel (kerneltype=0): K(r) = e^{-r^2/h^2}. Wendland kernel (kerneltype=1): K(r) = (1 - r/h)^4 (1 + 4r/h). Singular kernel (kerneltype=2): K(r) = (r/h)^{-w}. Parameter kerneltype is an integer selector (0, 1, or 2). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K \cdot I) per query point, where N is the number of neighbors considered (knn), K is the cost of the KD-tree nearest neighbor search (typically O(\log N{total})), and I is the number of iterations. Memory Complexity: O(N{total}) to store the point cloud and KD-tree. Performance: The method is local and can be parallelized across query points. However, the iterative nature and KD-tree lookups make it slower than grid-based methods like Marching Cubes for dense data. Strengths: Handles unstructured point clouds with normals; robust to noise due to smoothing effect of MLS; produces smooth surfaces. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large datasets; requires normals as input; sensitive to the choice of radius and kernel parameters. When to use: When input data is a point cloud with normals and high smoothness is required. When not to use: When input is a scalar grid (use Marching Cubes) or when real-time performance on massive datasets is critical without GPU acceleration. MLS Projection was introduced as part of the Hermite Point Set Surfaces (HPSS) method by Boubekeur and Sillion. It is based on the Moving Least Squares approximation technique originally developed for surface fitting. The method has been extended to APSS for higher-order continuity and is often used in conjunction with dual contouring for implicit surface reconstruction. name: APSS (Approximate Projected Point Set Surfaces)
head: MLS projection via Approximate Projected Point Set Surfaces
body: APSS is an iterative method to project a query point onto a surface defined by a point set with normals, using Moving Least Squares (MLS). It builds on MLS Projection by computing a local coordinate system and higher-order approximations via weighted accumulators, distinguishing it from standard MLS by explicitly tracking cross-product and dot-product terms for refined surface fitting. Inputs: inputPositions: Array of 3D points defining the surface. inputNormals: Array of 3D normals corresponding to inputPositions. inputPointsetKdTree: A KD-tree structure built from inputPositions for efficient nearest neighbor search. queryPoint: The 3D point to project onto the surface. knn: Number of nearest neighbors to consider. Default value is 20. radius: The radius parameter for the kernel function used to weight neighbors in the MLS computation. numberOfIterations: The number of iterations for the MLS algorithm loop. Outputs: outputPoint: The projected point on the surface. outputNormal: The normal at the projected point. Data Structures: idnearestneighbors: Array of knn indices into inputPositions. squaredistancestoneighbors: Array of knn squared distances from the current query point to the neighbors. Accumulators (scalars or 3D vectors, initialized to zero): u123, u4, u0, sum1, sum4, sum2, sum3, sumweight. Steps: 1. Initialize outputPoint to queryPoint. 2. Initialize outputNormal to a default vector (e.g., (0,0,1)). 3. Loop iter from 0 to numberOfIterations - 1: a. Find the knn nearest neighbors to outputPoint using inputPointsetKdTree.knearest, retrieving idnearestneighbors and squaredistancestoneighbors. b. Initialize accumulators to zero: u123=(0,0,0), u4=0.0, u0=0.0, sum1=0.0, sum4=0.0, sum2=(0,0,0), sum3=(0,0,0), sumweight=0.0. c. Loop i from 0 to knn - 1: i. Retrieve neighbor position p from inputPositions using idnearestneighbors[i]. ii. Retrieve neighbor normal n from inputNormals using idnearestneighbors[i]. iii. Compute weight w from squaredistancestoneighbors[i] and radius. iv. Update accumulators: sumweight += w, sum1 += w, sum2 += w p, sum3 += w (p - outputPoint), sum4 += w |p - outputPoint|^2, u0 += w (n · (p - outputPoint)), u4 += w |n|^2, u123 += w (n × (p - outputPoint)). d. [Comment: The provided text ends abruptly inside the APSS neighbor loop. The final calculation of outputPoint and outputNormal from the accumulators is not present in this document part.] Formulas: Weight computation: w = \max(0, 1 - d^2/r^2)^2, where d^2 is the squared distance and r is the radius. name: Moving Least Squares Implicit Surface Reconstruction
head: MLS implicit method
body: Moving Least Squares (MLS) Implicit Surface Reconstruction is a technique for reconstructing a surface from an unordered 3D point cloud by creating an implicit function field using Moving Least Squares, from which isosurfaces are extracted. It differs from its parent MLS Projection by constructing a global implicit field defined by local quadratic fits rather than iteratively projecting query points, and from its sibling APSS by relying on a standard MLS approximation of the signed distance function rather than approximate projected point set surfaces. Inputs: An unordered 3D point cloud V (vertices) and a neighbor count k for normal estimation. Outputs: A triangular mesh representing the isosurface. Data Structures: V: Matrix of size N \times 3, where N is the number of input points. N{norm}: Matrix of size N \times 3, storing per-vertex normals. C: Constraint points matrix. Size (3N) \times 3. D: Constraint values vector. Size 3N. k: Number of nearest neighbors for PCA. \epsilon: Small offset distance for constraint generation. nn\dist: Average distance to nearest neighbors (used for scaling \epsilon). Steps: 1. Normal Estimation: For each vertex vi \in V, compute the normal ni using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on its k-nearest neighbors. Find k nearest neighbors of vi. Compute the centroid m of these neighbors. Center the neighbor points: P{centered} = P{neighbors} - m. Compute the covariance matrix S = P{centered}^T P{centered}. Perform eigenvalue decomposition on S. Select the eigenvector corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue as the normal ni. 2. Constraint Generation: Generate constraints for the implicit function. For each vertex vi with normal ni: Constraint 1 (Vertex): Point c1 = vi, Value d1 = 0. Constraint 2 (Outside): Point c2 = vi + \epsilon ni, Value d2 = \epsilon. Constraint 3 (Inside): Point c3 = vi - \epsilon ni, Value d3 = -\epsilon. Note: The source code uses eps and nndist to compute the offset, suggesting \epsilon may be scaled by local density. 3. Implicit Function Evaluation: Evaluate the MLS implicit function f(x) at grid vertices. The function is defined by minimizing the weighted least squares error of the constraints C and D. For a query point x, the value f(x) is derived from the local quadratic fit that best approximates the signed distance function defined by the constraints. The specific MLS formulation involves weighting constraints by distance to x and solving a local linear system to determine the function value and gradient. 4. Isosurface Extraction: Extract the zero-level set of the implicit function field using Marching Tetrahedra. This method divides the grid into tetrahedra and determines intersections with the isosurface within each tetrahedron, offering fewer configurations and no ambiguity compared to Marching Cubes. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mlsimplicitreconstruction(V, k, epsilonscalefactor): """ V: Nx3 array of input points k: number of neighbors for normal estimation epsilonscalefactor: factor to scale epsilon relative to neighbor distance Returns: Mesh (list of triangles) """ N = V.shape[0] normals = np.zeroslike(V) # Step 1: Normal Estimation via PCA for i in range(N): p = V[i] # Find k nearest neighbors nnindices, nndists = findknearestneighbors(V, p, k) nnpoints = V[nnindices] # Compute centroid m = np.mean(nnpoints, axis=0) # Center points Pcentered = nnpoints - m # Covariance matrix S = Pcentered.T @ Pcentered # Eigen decomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(S) # Normal is eigenvector with smallest eigenvalue minidx = np.argmin(eigenvalues) normals[i] = eigenvectors[:, minidx] # Handle orientation consistency if needed (not specified in source) # Step 2: Constraint Generation # Calculate average neighbor distance for scaling epsilon nndistsall = [] for i in range(N): p = V[i], nndists = findknearestneighbors(V, p, k) nndistsall.append(np.mean(nndists)) avgnndist = np.mean(nndistsall) epsilon = epsilonscalefactor avgnndist C = np.zeros((3 N, 3)) D = np.zeros(3 N) for i in range(N): p = V[i] n = normals[i] # Constraint 1: Vertex itself C[i] = p D[i] = 0.0 # Constraint 2: Outside along normal C[N + i] = p + epsilon n D[N + i] = epsilon # Constraint 3: Inside along negative normal C[2 N + i] = p - epsilon n D[2 N + i] = -epsilon # Step 3: Evaluate Implicit Function on Grid # Define grid bounds and resolution gridbounds = computeboundingbox(V) gridresolution =... # Not given in sources gridpoints = generategridpoints(gridbounds, gridresolution) fvalues = np.zeros(gridpoints.shape[0]) for idx, x in enumerate(gridpoints): # MLS Evaluation # For each constraint point cj with value dj, compute weight wj based on distance to x # Solve local system to find f(x) # The source implies a standard MLS formulation where f(x) minimizes sum(wj (f(x) - dj)^2) # However, MLS for implicit surfaces typically fits a quadratic function q(x) such that q(cj) approx dj # and f(x) is the root of q(x) or the value of q(x) if it represents signed distance directly. # Given the constraints are signed distances, f(x) is likely the MLS approximation of the signed distance field. weights = computemlsweights(x, C, kmls) # kmls not specified, assume same as k or fixed # Solve weighted least squares for quadratic coefficients # A coeffs = b # A involves basis functions evaluated at constraint points weighted by distance to x # b involves constraint values D weighted by distance to x # f(x) is then derived from coeffs and x fvalues[idx] = evaluatemlsfunction(x, C, D, weights) # Implementation detail not in source # Step 4: Marching Tetrahedra mesh = marchingtetrahedra(gridpoints, fvalues, gridbounds, gridresolution) return mesh def findknearestneighbors(V, p, k): # Placeholder for actual KNN search (e.g., using KDTree) # Returns indices and distances pass def computemlsweights(x, C, k): # Compute weights based on distance from x to constraint points C # Common weight: wj = 1 / (dist(x, C[j])^2 + epsilon^2) pass def evaluatemlsfunction(x, C, D, weights): # Solve local system to approximate signed distance at x # This step requires the specific MLS formulation for implicit surfaces # which is not fully detailed in the source code excerpt. # Typically, this involves fitting a quadratic function q(y) = a^T y + y^T B y # such that q(C[j]) approx D[j], and then finding the root or value at x. # Given the constraints are signed distances, f(x) is often the value of the # approximated signed distance function at x. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Orientation: The PCA step yields normals without guaranteed consistent orientation across the surface. The source code does not show an orientation propagation step, which may lead to incorrect inside/outside constraints if the input normals are not already oriented or if the point cloud is not manifold. Boundary Effects: Points near the boundary of the point cloud may have biased normals if the neighbor search is not handled carefully (e.g., using a half-space PCA). Precision: The use of floating-point arithmetic in eigenvalue decomposition and least squares solving may introduce small errors in the implicit function values, affecting the accuracy of the extracted isosurface. Time Complexity: Normal estimation requires O(N \cdot k \log N) or O(N \cdot k) with a KD-tree. Constraint generation is O(N). Implicit function evaluation requires O(M \cdot 3N \cdot k) or O(M \cdot 3N) where M is the number of grid points, assuming a fixed number of constraints per point. Marching Tetrahedra is O(M). Overall, it is dominated by the implicit function evaluation on the grid. Memory Complexity: O(N + M), where N is the number of points and M is the number of grid points. The constraints matrix C and values D take O(N) space. Strengths: Produces smooth surfaces. Marching Tetrahedra avoids the ambiguity issues of Marching Cubes. Limitations: Requires a dense point cloud for accurate normal estimation. The quality of the reconstruction depends heavily on the choice of k and \epsilon. The method is computationally expensive for high-resolution grids. When to use: When a smooth, implicit representation is desired from a noisy or unordered point cloud, and computational resources allow for grid-based evaluation. When not to use: For real-time applications or very large datasets where memory and time constraints are tight. The method is described in the context of a minimal dependency implementation for 3D reconstruction using accelerated Moving Least Squares and Marching Tetrahedra. The implementation uses Eigen for linear algebra and a custom KD-tree for neighbor search. It is presented as an alternative to more complex surface reconstruction techniques, emphasizing simplicity and the use of Marching Tetrahedra for unambiguous isosurface extraction. mwrazam/marchingtets-reconstruction, https://github.com/mwrazam/marchingtets-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Isosurface Extraction API
head: Marching Cubes Function Interface
body: The Isosurface Extraction API provides a high-level interface for extracting a manifold triangular mesh from a continuous implicit scalar field defined by a user-supplied function, rather than a pre-computed discrete grid. It solves the problem of converting mathematical implicit surfaces into polygonal meshes by internally managing an adaptive octree traversal and calling a Rust-based core extraction routine. It sets itself apart from standard grid-based methods like Marching Cubes by accepting a callable function func(x,y,z) directly, handling gradient estimation via finite differences if not provided, and supporting adaptive refinement through octree depth parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: func: A vectorized implicit function. It accepts an (N, 3) array of float64 positions and returns an (N,) array of float64 scalar values. It may optionally return an (N, 3) array of float64 gradients. bboxmin, bboxmax: 3-element tuples defining the axis-aligned bounding box of the extraction domain. isovalue: The scalar isovalue for extraction (default 0.0). mindepth, maxdepth: Integers defining the octree depth range. The number of cells per axis is 2^{\text{depth}}. mindepth must be \ge 1 and maxdepth must be \le 12. anglethreshold: Float in degrees (0, 180). Normals differing by more than this value trigger sharp-feature handling. fdstep: Float for finite difference gradient estimation when func does not return gradients (default 10^{-5}). Outputs: vertices: A (V, 3) float64 array of mesh vertices. faces: A (F, 3) int64 array of triangle indices. Empty cases return arrays with shape (0, 3). Data Structures: The API uses a callback adapter evalbatch to bridge Python and the Rust core. This adapter ensures that the output of func is converted to numpy arrays of correct dtype (float64) and shape. The Rust core extractmesh handles the octree traversal and mesh generation. Steps: 1. Validate Inputs: Check that bboxmin and bboxmax are 3-element tuples and bboxmin < bboxmax in all dimensions. Raise ValueError if not. Check that mindepth and maxdepth are integers, 1 \le \text{min\depth} \le \text{max\depth} \le 12. Raise ValueError if not. Check that anglethreshold is in (0, 180). Raise ValueError if not. 2. Normalize Bounding Box: If the bounding box is non-cubic, expand it to the smallest enclosing cube centered on the original bounding box center. Issue a warning during this expansion. 3. Create Callback Adapter: Define evalbatch(points) which calls func(points). If func returns a tuple (values, gradients), validate that values has shape (N,) and gradients has shape (N, 3). If gradients is None, the core will use finite differences with step fdstep. If func returns only values, ensure shape is (N,). 4. Call Core Extraction: Invoke the Rust function extractmesh with the callback, the normalized bounding box, mindepth, maxdepth, anglethreshold, isovalue, and an adaptive flag. 5. Post-process Output: Ensure the returned vertices are float64 with shape (V, 3) and faces are int64 with shape (F, 3). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def isosurfaceextractionapi( func, bboxmin: tuple, bboxmax: tuple, isovalue: float = 0.0, mindepth: int = 1, maxdepth: int = 12, anglethreshold: float = 10.0, fdstep: float = 1e-5) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: """ Extract isosurface from implicit function using adaptive octree. """ # 1. Validate Inputs bboxminarr = np.asarray(bboxmin, dtype=np.float64) bboxmaxarr = np.asarray(bboxmax, dtype=np.float64) if bboxminarr.shape != (3,) or bboxmaxarr.shape != (3,): raise ValueError("Bounding boxes must be 3-element tuples.") if not np.all(bboxminarr < bboxmaxarr): raise ValueError("bboxmin must be strictly less than bboxmax.") if not (1 <= mindepth <= maxdepth <= 12): raise ValueError("Depth must be in [1, 12] and min <= max.") if not (0.0 < anglethreshold < 180.0): raise ValueError("Angle threshold must be in (0, 180).") # 2. Normalize Bounding Box to Cubic center = (bboxminarr + bboxmaxarr) / 2.0 extents = (bboxmaxarr - bboxminarr) / 2.0 maxextent = np.max(extents) # Expand to cubic bboxmincubic = center - maxextent bboxmaxcubic = center + maxextent # Warning issued here in implementation # 3. Define Callback Adapter def evalbatch(points: np.ndarray) -> tuple: """ Wrapper for func to ensure correct output format for Rust core. """ result = func(points) if isinstance(result, tuple): values, gradients = result values = np.asarray(values, dtype=np.float64) if values.shape[0] != points.shape[0]: raise ValueError("Value count mismatch.") if gradients is not None: gradients = np.asarray(gradients, dtype=np.float64) if gradients.shape != (points.shape[0], 3): raise ValueError("Gradient shape mismatch.") return values, gradients else: # Core will handle finite differences if gradients is None return values, None else: values = np.asarray(result, dtype=np.float64) if values.shape[0] != points.shape[0]: raise ValueError("Value count mismatch.") return values, None # 4. Call Rust Core # Note: This is a conceptual call to the underlying Rust implementation. # The actual implementation uses a compiled binary. vertices, faces = extractmeshrustcore( callback=evalbatch, bboxmin=bboxmincubic, bboxmax=bboxmaxcubic, mindepth=mindepth, maxdepth=maxdepth, anglethreshold=anglethreshold, isovalue=isovalue, fdstep=fdstep, adaptive=True) # 5. Ensure Output Types vertices = np.asarray(vertices, dtype=np.float64) faces = np.asarray(faces, dtype=np.int64) # Handle empty cases if vertices.ndim != 2 or vertices.shape[1] != 3: vertices = np.empty((0, 3), dtype=np.float64) if faces.ndim != 2 or faces.shape[1] != 3: faces = np.empty((0, 3), dtype=np.int64) return vertices, faces Separates a polygonal isosurface mesh into connected components (shells) to handle disjoint surfaces or allow user selection of specific regions. Time Complexity: Determined by the octree traversal and the number of leaf cells evaluated. The adaptive nature means complexity scales with the surface area and detail, not just the volume. The Rust core provides efficient memory management and parallelization. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of leaf cells in the octree and the resulting mesh size. The adaptive approach minimizes memory usage for smooth regions by using larger cells. Performance: Produces identical results to marchingcubes on a pre-computed grid for the same domain and resolution, as verified by assertallclose. Strengths: No need to pre-compute a dense grid; supports arbitrary implicit functions; adaptive resolution captures detail efficiently; sharp feature handling via angle threshold. Limitations: Requires a callable function; gradient estimation via finite differences adds computational overhead if not provided; non-cubic bounding boxes are expanded, potentially wasting computation on empty space. When to Use: When the scalar field is defined by a complex mathematical function or simulation output that is expensive to sample on a full grid, or when adaptive resolution is desired. When Not to Use: When a pre-computed grid is already available and fixed resolution is sufficient (use Marching Cubes directly for potentially lower overhead). The Isosurface Extraction API is part of the isomesh library, which provides a Python interface to a Rust-based isosurface extraction engine. It builds upon the principles of adaptive isosurface extraction, specifically leveraging Manifold Dual Contouring techniques for sharp feature preservation and manifold guarantee. The API abstracts the complexity of octree traversal and cell processing, providing a simple function-call interface similar to scipy.ndimage.marchingcubes but for implicit functions. pmneila/PyMCubes, https://github.com/pmneila/PyMCubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, https://github.com/narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Manual Shell Extraction
head: Connected Component Separation, Disjoint Mesh Isolation, Shell Extraction via Manual Traversal, findShell, Shell Extraction via Connectivity Filter, vtkPolyDataConnectivityFilter
body: Manual Shell Extraction separates a polygonal isosurface mesh into its connected components (shells) to handle disjoint surfaces or allow user selection of specific regions. It differs from automated connectivity filters by explicitly traversing the mesh graph from a starting triangle ID to identify all connected triangles belonging to the same shell, allowing for interactive selection of disjoint parts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An isosurface mesh (isosurfacePolydata) containing triangles, and optionally a starting triangle ID for manual traversal. Output: A subset of the mesh corresponding to the selected shell, or the complete mesh if no selection is required. Data Structures: triangleIndex: A mapping from vtkIdType (triangle ID) to int. Values are 0 (unvisited) or 1 (visited). foundMeshes: A vector of sets, std::vector<std::set<vtkIdType>>, storing the IDs of triangles belonging to each identified shell. shellTriangles: A vtkCellArray used to construct the final output mesh. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize allVisited = false, numShells = 0, and foundMeshes as an empty vector of triangle ID sets. 2. If manual traversal is selected: a. Initialize a queue with a starting triangle ID and an empty set for shell triangles. b. While the queue is not empty: i. Dequeue the current triangle ID. ii. Get the point IDs of the current triangle. iii. For each point in the triangle, find neighbor triangles sharing that point. iv. For each neighbor, if it has not been visited (i.e., triangleIndex does not contain it or its value is not 1): Mark it visited by setting triangleIndex[neighborID] = 1. Push the neighbor ID to the queue. Add the neighbor ID to the current shell's set in foundMeshes. c. Repeat the traversal process for any remaining unvisited triangles to identify all disjoint shells, incrementing numShells for each new shell found. 3. If numShells > 1, prompt the user for a selectedShell index. 4. If selectedShell == 0, render the complete isosurfacePolydata. 5. Otherwise, decrement selectedShell and retrieve the shellTriangleIds from foundMeshes[selectedShell]. 6. Iterate through shellTriangleIds to construct vtkTriangle objects using vertex indices from triangleV0Index, triangleV1Index, and triangleV2Index. 7. Insert the constructed triangles into shellTriangles (vtkCellArray) and assign this cell array to the output isosurfacePolydata. 8. Map the resulting mesh to the renderer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def manualshellextraction(isosurfacepolydata, starttriangleid=None): # Data structures triangleindex = {} # Maps vtkIdType to int (0=unvisited, 1=visited) foundmeshes = [] # std::vector<std::set<vtkIdType>> numshells = 0 allvisited = False # Initialize triangleindex for all triangles in isosurfacepolydata for triangleid in range(isosurfacepolydata.getnumberofcells()): triangleindex[triangleid] = 0 # Helper function for manual traversal def findshell(startid): queue = [startid] shelltriangles = set() triangleindex[startid] = 1 shelltriangles.add(startid) while queue: currentid = queue.pop(0) # Get point IDs of the current triangle pointids = isosurfacepolydata.gettrianglepoints(currentid) for pointid in pointids: # Find neighbor triangles sharing this point neighborids = isosurfacepolydata.gettrianglessharingpoint(pointid) for neighborid in neighborids: if triangleindex.get(neighborid, 0) != 1: triangleindex[neighborid] = 1 queue.append(neighborid) shelltriangles.add(neighborid) return shelltriangles # Extract all shells if starttriangleid is not None: # Manual selection from a specific start shelltriangles = findshell(starttriangleid) foundmeshes.append(shelltriangles) numshells = 1 # Note: The source implies a loop for all shells if not manually seeded, # but here we assume the user selects one shell via starttriangleid or # the system extracts all if numShells > 1 is checked later. # Based on, if numShells > 1, user selects. If we start with one, # we might need to find others if the user wants to see all. # However, the source says "Initialize... numShells=0... After extraction, if numShells > 1". # This implies the extraction step finds ALL shells. # Re-evaluating based on: "Initialize... numShells=0... After extraction..." # This suggests a loop that finds all shells. # Correct interpretation of: Find ALL shells first foundmeshes = [] numshells = 0 for triangleid in range(isosurfacepolydata.getnumberofcells()): if triangleindex[triangleid] == 0: shelltriangles = findshell(triangleid) foundmeshes.append(shelltriangles) numshells += 1 # User Selection if numshells > 1: selectedshell = promptuserforshellindex(numshells) else: selectedshell = 0 # Only one shell exists if selectedshell == 0: return isosurfacepolydata # Render complete mesh # Construct selected shell shelltriangleids = foundmeshes[selectedshell - 1] # Decrement index as per shellcellarray = vtkcellarray() for triangleid in shelltriangleids: v0idx = isosurfacepolydata.gettrianglev0(triangleid) v1idx = isosurfacepolydata.gettrianglev1(triangleid) v2idx = isosurfacepolydata.gettrianglev2(triangleid) # Construct vtkTriangle triangle = vtktriangle() triangle.setpointids([v0idx, v1idx, v2idx]) shellcellarray.insertnextcell(triangle.gettype(), triangle.getpointids()) # Assign to output polydata outputpolydata = vtkpolydata() outputpolydata.setpolys(shellcellarray) outputpolydata.copypointsfrom(isosurfacepolydata) # Copy points if not already referenced return outputpolydata Parameters: starttriangleid: Optional. If provided, extraction starts from this triangle. If not, all shells are found. selectedshell: User-provided index (1-based) of the shell to extract. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If findShell fails to update triangleIndex, the traversal loop becomes infinite. Degenerate triangles (NULL triangles) should be filtered out during mesh construction. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles in the mesh, O(N), where N is the number of triangles, as each triangle is visited at most once. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles, O(N), for storing triangleIndex and foundMeshes. Strengths: Allows interactive selection of disjoint shells; avoids custom graph traversal code if using VTK's vtkPolyDataConnectivityFilter as an alternative. Limitations: Requires manual user input if multiple shells exist; manual traversal implementation is prone to infinite loops if visited flags are not updated correctly. When to use: When the isosurface contains disjoint components and the user needs to select specific regions for rendering or further processing. When not to use: When all shells are required simultaneously or when automated processing without user interaction is needed (use vtkPolyDataConnectivityFilter with SetExtractionModeToAllRegions() instead). Manual Shell Extraction is part of the isosurface extraction pipeline, often implemented using VTK's vtkPolyDataConnectivityFilter or custom traversal logic. It is used in volume rendering applications where disjoint surfaces need to be handled separately, such as in medical imaging or scientific visualization. The method is described in the context of the Marching Tetrahedra algorithm implementation. andresbejarano/MarchingTetrahedra, https://github.com/andresbejarano/MarchingTetrahedra, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Minimal Area Triangulation for Polygons
head: Minimal Area Triangulation, Minimal Area Triangulation of Isopolygons, Polygon Triangulation
body: Minimal Area Triangulation is a method for converting complex, non-convex 3D polygons (isopolygons) resulting from isosurface extraction into a set of triangles by minimizing the total surface area of the resulting mesh. It solves the problem of generating a high-quality, artifact-free mesh from the closed loops formed by intersecting an implicit field with octree nodes. Unlike standard triangulation methods that may produce self-intersecting or visually noisy surfaces, this method leverages the geometric property that isopolygons lie on the boundary of convex bodies (octree nodes) to guarantee a homeomorphic-to-disk triangulation that is minimal in area. It is distinct from sibling methods like Dual Contouring which optimize vertex positions via QEF, and Surface Nets which use cell centers, by strictly optimizing the connectivity of existing intersection vertices to minimize geometric error. Inputs: A simple closed 3D polygon P defined by an ordered list of n vertices \{p1, p2, \dots, pn\}, where each pi is a 3D point. The polygon lies on the boundary of a convex octree node. Outputs: A list of triangles \{t1, t2, \dots, tm\} that triangulate P with minimal total area. Data Structures: 1. Vertices: Array of n 3D points. 2. DP Table M: A 2D array of size n \times n storing the minimal area M(i, j) for sub-polygons. 3. Split Table K: A 2D array of size n \times n storing the index k that minimizes the recurrence relation for each sub-polygon. Definitions: A(i, j, k): The area of the triangle formed by vertices pi, pj, pk. P{i,j}: The sub-polygon defined by the sequence of vertices from pi to pj along the polygon boundary. M(i, j): The minimal area of the triangulation of sub-polygon P{i,j}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Check for Cofacial Vertices: Determine if all vertices of the polygon lie on the same cube face (are cofacial). This is detected using an IsoVertex::CoFacial check. If true: Perform a fan triangulation from the centroid to avoid introducing edges on the cube face, which can cause artifacts. 1. Calculate the centroid C = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} pi. 2. Create triangles (pi, p{i+1}, C) for i=1 \dots n-1 and (pn, p1, C). 3. Return these triangles and terminate. If false: Proceed to Dynamic Programming. 2. Initialize DP Tables: Initialize M and K with zeros or undefined values. 3. Compute Minimal Areas (Dynamic Programming): Iterate over the length of the sub-polygon chain len from 2 to n-1. For each starting vertex i from 1 to n: Let j be the ending vertex, calculated as (i + len - 1) % n. Base Cases: If i == j or i == (j + 1) % n (sub-polygon has 0 or 1 edge), set M(i, j) = 0. Recursive Step: Initialize minarea to infinity and bestk to -1. Iterate over all possible split vertices k strictly between j and i along the polygon boundary (i.e., k \in (j, i)). Calculate the cost: \text{cost} = M(i, k) + M(k, j) + A(i, j, k) If cost < minarea: minarea = cost bestk = k Set M(i, j) = \text{min\area} Set K(i, j) = \text{best\k} Note on Area Calculation: A(i, j, k) is the area of triangle \{pi, pj, pk\}. For 3D points, this is half the magnitude of the cross product of two edge vectors: A(i, j, k) = \frac{1}{2} \| (pj - pi) \times (pk - pi) \|. 4. Reconstruct Triangles: Start with the full polygon range (1, 2). Use a recursive function ExtractTriangles(i, j): If i == j or i == (j + 1) % n, return (no triangle). Let k = K(i, j). Add triangle \{pi, pj, pk\} to the output list. Recursively call ExtractTriangles(i, k). Recursively call ExtractTriangles(k, j). Call ExtractTriangles(1, 2) to populate the final triangle list. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minimalareatriangulation(vertices): """ vertices: List of 3D points [p1, p2,..., pn] Returns: List of triangles, each triangle is a tuple of 3 vertex indices """ n = len(vertices) if n < 3: return [] # Check for cofacial vertices (implementation detail depends on source geometry) # If all vertices lie on the same cube face, use fan triangulation from centroid if iscofacial(vertices): centroid = sum(vertices) / n triangles = [] for i in range(n): p1 = vertices[i] p2 = vertices[(i + 1) % n] # Triangle indices: i, (i+1)%n, centroidindex # Note: Centroid is a new point, but typically mapped to existing structure or handled as special case # Based on, we create triangles connecting edges to centroid index cIdx triangles.append((i, (i + 1) % n, -1)) # -1 represents centroid placeholder return triangles # Initialize DP tables # M[i][j] stores minimal area for sub-polygon from i to j # K[i][j] stores the optimal split vertex k M = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] K = [[-1] n for in range(n)] # Helper to calculate triangle area def trianglearea(i, j, k): p1 = vertices[i] p2 = vertices[j] p3 = vertices[k] # Vector cross product magnitude / 2 v1 = [p2[x] - p1[x] for x in range(3)] v2 = [p3[x] - p1[x] for x in range(3)] cross = [ v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0] ] mag = (cross[0]2 + cross[1]2 + cross[2]2)0.5 return 0.5 mag # Fill DP table # Length of the chain of vertices in the sub-polygon (number of edges) # A sub-polygon from i to j has (j - i + 1) % n vertices? In the context of the recurrence M(i,j), if M(1,2) is a base case (0 area), it cannot be the start of reconstruction. It is highly likely the source meant starting the computation at small lengths, or the reconstruction starts at the full polygon M(1,n). However, looking at, it says "Start at entry M(1, 2)... to obtain the final set of triangles." This is contradictory to the DP structure where M(1,2) is a leaf. It is possible the source uses a different indexing where M(i,j) represents the triangle fan or a different sub-problem. Given the ambiguity, the standard implementation of "Minimal Area Triangulation" (which is equivalent to the optimal polygon triangulation problem) starts reconstruction from the full polygon range. I will note this discrepancy. Self-Correction: The source might be referring to the specific order of processing or a specific data structure traversal. However, for a generic implementation, one must start with the full polygon. I will add a comment regarding the start index. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cofacial Vertices: If vertices lie on the same cube face, standard DP may create edges on the face, causing artifacts. Detect this and use fan triangulation from the centroid. Self-Intersections: The method finds the minimal area triangulation, not necessarily the minimal area surface. While differential geometry guarantees that the minimal area surface bounded by a simple closed curve on a convex body is not self-intersecting, the triangulation itself is not guaranteed to be free of self-intersections, though none are observed in practice. Precision: Floating-point errors in area calculations can affect the choice of k. Use double precision for area accumulation. Merging Triangulations is the final assembly step in hierarchical surface reconstruction methods that use adaptive clustering and piecewise polynomial approximation. It combines individual optimal triangulations generated for separate cluster regions into a single, watertight mesh by filling the gaps along cluster boundaries defined by a BSP tree hierarchy. Unlike methods that operate directly on raw data points, this approach exploits the connectivity of the clustering hierarchy to stitch pre-computed triangulations, ensuring that the resulting mesh approximates the underlying data within a prescribed error bound. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a reverse-order subdivision process and its specific handling of boundary polygons to maintain geometric consistency across cluster interfaces. The Fuchs-Kedem-Uselton Contour Method is a volume rendering coercion technique that generates minimum-area surfaces from isosurfaces by solving for minimum-cost cycles in a directed-toroidal graph. It preprocesses data to generate contours within single slices (intra-slice) and then forms inter-slice triangles between these contours. The method bounds the maximum cost of finding the optimal solution for contours with m points in one contour and n points in the other as \tau(m, n) < (\lceil \log2 m \rceil + 2) \times (2mn + m) for m < n. It is used to generate the minimum-area surface as the optimal solution for rendering. Time Complexity: O(n^3), where n is the number of vertices in the polygon. This is due to the three nested loops in the dynamic programming table filling (length, start vertex, split vertex). Space Complexity: O(n^2), required to store the M (minimal area) and K (split vertex) tables. Measured Performance: The method is efficient for polygons with a moderate number of vertices, typical of octree-based isosurface extraction where each isopolygon is a simple closed curve on a convex node boundary. It is significantly faster than methods requiring global optimization or mesh refinement. Strengths: Produces a minimal area triangulation, reducing visual artifacts and noise. Guarantees a homeomorphic-to-disk triangulation for well-behaved isopolygons. Does not require refinement of the octree or modification of vertex values. Limitations: Does not guarantee a minimal area surface (only triangulation). Self-intersections are not theoretically guaranteed to be absent, though rare in practice. Cofacial vertices require special handling (fan triangulation). When to Use: Use when extracting isosurfaces from octrees and high-quality, minimal-area triangulation of the resulting isopolygons is required, and the polygons are simple closed curves on convex boundaries. When Not to Use: Avoid if the polygons are not simple closed curves or do not lie on convex boundaries, as the theoretical guarantees do not hold. Also avoid if real-time performance is critical and O(n^3) per polygon is too slow for large n. The method originates from the work on unconstrained isosurface extraction on arbitrary octrees. It leverages results from differential geometry [MY80, MY82] regarding minimal area surfaces bounded by simple closed curves on convex bodies. The specific algorithm for computing the minimal area triangulation is attributed to [BS95]. It is used in the context of mesh simplification and high-quality isosurface extraction from adaptive octrees. The Fuchs-Kedem-Uselton variant is a historical method from 1977 for volume rendering coercion.
