name: Merging Triangulations
head: Stitching Triangulations
body: Merging Triangulations is the final assembly step in hierarchical surface reconstruction methods that use adaptive clustering and piecewise polynomial approximation. It combines individual optimal triangulations generated for separate cluster regions into a single, watertight mesh by filling the gaps along cluster boundaries defined by a BSP tree hierarchy. Unlike methods that operate directly on raw data points, this approach exploits the connectivity of the clustering hierarchy to stitch pre-computed triangulations, ensuring that the resulting mesh approximates the underlying data within a prescribed error bound. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a reverse-order subdivision process and its specific handling of boundary polygons to maintain geometric consistency across cluster interfaces. The method operates on a set of individual optimal triangulations, each associated with a cluster region in a BSP tree hierarchy. The goal is to merge these disjoint triangulations into a single global triangulation. Inputs: A BSP tree defining the cluster hierarchy. A set of individual optimal triangulations, one for each leaf cluster region. For each triangulation, a closed boundary polygon enclosing all triangles, edges, and vertices within the cluster region. An error bound \epsilon for the approximation. Outputs: A single unified triangulation covering the entire domain. Triangles that satisfy the error bound (or are modified to do so). Boundary Polygon: A list of vertices forming a closed loop. The polygon encloses all simplices (triangles, edges, vertices) of the optimal triangulation within the cluster. It does not enclose areas other than optimal triangles. Vertices may appear multiple times in the list if they are part of the boundary loop multiple times. Polygon Strip: A subsequence of the boundary polygon vertices extracted along the cluster bisector. 1. Construct Boundary Polygons: For each optimal triangulation, construct a closed boundary polygon. For parabolic or planar graph surfaces, this is straightforward. For elliptic or hyperbolic cases, triangulations may be disconnected or contain line segments not part of any triangle. Special handling is required to ensure the polygon encloses all simplices. Algorithm: Use a scan-line algorithm parallel to the longest edge of the triangulation. Identify the left-most and right-most vertices inside the cluster region for every scan line. Add additional vertices inside the cluster region to the boundary polygon to ensure the enclosed area contains only optimal triangles, minimizing the enclosed area. 2. Shrink Cluster Regions (Optional but Recommended): Shrink each cluster region by a small percentage towards its centroid to avoid boundary overlaps during stitching. 3. Merge in Reverse Subdivision Order: Traverse the BSP tree in reverse order of subdivision (from leaves to root). At each internal node, exactly two child triangulations are merged along the bisecting line segment p1p2 that separates their cluster regions. 4. Extract Polygon Strips: For the two triangulations to be merged, separated by segment p1p2: Identify the vertex in the first boundary polygon closest to p1. Identify the vertex in the second boundary polygon closest to p2. Extract two polygon strips from the respective boundaries, starting from the identified vertices and ending at the vertices closest to p2 and p1 respectively. These strips lie along the bisector p1p2. 5. Marching and Triangle Construction: Construct triangles by marching along the two polygon strips, connecting point pairs using vertices from opposite sides of p1p2. Let the current vertices on the two strips be u and v. There are two possible choices for the next triangle: (u, v, nextu) or (u, v, nextv), where nextu and nextv are the subsequent vertices on their respective strips. Selection Criterion: Choose the edge with minimal length among the two possible choices. Specifically, compare the length of the edge connecting to the next vertex on the opposite strip. Prefer the shorter edge. 6. Handle Negative Area (Overlap): Ensure no triangles with negative area (overlap) are produced. If both choices for the next triangle would result in negative area, construct a triangle from three consecutive vertices in one of the polygon strips, thereby eliminating the middle vertex. If stitching still produces negative areas for both choices after this step, insert a triangle from three vertices of the other polygon strip. 7. Error Verification and Correction: Triangles resulting from stitching are not guaranteed to satisfy the prescribed error bound \epsilon. Estimate the approximation error for all scattered data points located inside the regions defined by the newly stitched triangles. If a triangle violates the error bound: Flip an edge between two adjacent triangles, or Insert the sample point with the greatest approximation error as a new vertex into the triangulation. Re-check errors for all modified triangles and repeat until all triangles satisfy the bound. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mergetriangulations(bsptree, triangulations): """ Merges individual optimal triangulations into a single mesh. Args: bsptree: The BSP tree defining cluster hierarchy. triangulations: Dictionary mapping clusterid to Triangulation object. Returns: Unified Triangulation object. """ # Process in reverse order of subdivision (leaves to root) nodes = bsptree.getnodesinreversesubdivisionorder() for node in nodes: if node.isleaf(): continue leftchild = node.leftchild rightchild = node.rightchild # Get the bisecting segment separating the two clusters p1, p2 = node.getbisectorendpoints() # Get the triangulations for the children trileft = triangulations[leftchild.id] triright = triangulations[rightchild.id] # Shrink cluster regions slightly towards centroid to avoid overlap trileft.shrinkboundary(0.01) triright.shrinkboundary(0.01) # Extract polygon strips along the bisector p1-p2 # Strip from left triangulation: starts at vertex closest to p1, ends at vertex closest to p2 stripleft = extractpolygonstrip(trileft.boundarypolygon, p1, p2) # Strip from right triangulation: starts at vertex closest to p2, ends at vertex closest to p1 # Note: The source describes extracting strips starting from closest to p1/p2 respectively. # We assume symmetric extraction logic for the other side. stripright = extractpolygonstrip(triright.boundarypolygon, p2, p1) # March along strips to create new triangles newtriangles = [] i = 0 j = 0 while i < len(stripleft) - 1 and j < len(stripright) - 1: u = stripleft[i] v = stripright[j] unext = stripleft[i+1] vnext = stripright[j+1] # Two choices for next triangle: # Choice 1: Triangle (u, v, vnext) using edge from right strip # Choice 2: Triangle (u, v, unext) using edge from left strip # Calculate edge lengths for the "cross" edges lencross1 = distance(u, vnext) lencross2 = distance(v, unext) # Check for negative area (overlap) area1 = signedarea(u, v, vnext) area2 = signedarea(u, v, unext) if area1 < 0 and area2 < 0: # Both choices produce negative area # Construct triangle from three consecutive vertices in one strip # Eliminate the middle vertex. Prefer one strip arbitrarily or based on heuristic. # Here we pick left strip. newtriangles.append(Triangle(u, unext, stripleft[i+2] if i+2 < len(stripleft) else u)) i += 2 # Skip the eliminated vertex continue if area1 < 0: # Choice 1 invalid, must use Choice 2 newtriangles.append(Triangle(u, v, unext)) i += 1 # j stays same? No, v is used. vnext is still available? # The source says "connecting point pairs". # If we use (u,v,unext), we consumed u, v, unext. # vnext is still on the right strip. i += 1 j += 1 # v is consumed continue if area2 < 0: # Choice 2 invalid, must use Choice 1 newtriangles.append(Triangle(u, v, vnext)) i += 1 # u is consumed j += 1 # v, vnext consumed continue # Both valid, choose minimal length edge if lencross1 < lencross2: newtriangles.append(Triangle(u, v, vnext)) i += 1 j += 1 else: newtriangles.append(Triangle(u, v, unext)) i += 1 j += 1 # Handle remaining vertices in strips if any #... (implementation detail for end cases) # Merge new triangles into the combined triangulation combinedtri = merge(trileft, triright, newtriangles) # Error verification and correction combinedtri = correcterrorbounds(combinedtri, node.clusterdatapoints, node.errorbound) # Store result for parent node triangulations[node.id] = combinedtri return triangulations[bsptree.root.id] def extractpolygonstrip(boundarypolygon, startpoint, endpoint): """ Extracts a polygon strip from the boundary polygon. Starts at the vertex closest to startpoint and ends at the vertex closest to endpoint. """ # Find index of vertex closest to startpoint startidx = argmin([distance(v, startpoint) for v in boundarypolygon]) # Find index of vertex closest to endpoint endidx = argmin([distance(v, endpoint) for v in boundarypolygon]) # Extract vertices from startidx to endidx along the polygon loop # The direction depends on the polygon winding and relative positions. # Assuming the boundary is a closed loop, we traverse from start to end. strip = [] n = len(boundarypolygon) curr = startidx while True: strip.append(boundarypolygon[curr]) if curr == endidx: break curr = (curr + 1) % n return strip def signedarea(p1, p2, p3): """Returns 2x the signed area of the triangle.""" return (p2.x - p1.x) (p3.y - p1.y) - (p2.y - p1.y) (p3.x - p1.x) def correcterrorbounds(triangulation, datapoints, errorbound): """ Checks error bounds for stitched triangles and modifies if necessary. """ modified = True while modified: modified = False for triangle in triangulation.triangles: # Estimate max error for data points inside this triangle maxerror = estimatemaxerror(triangle, datapoints) if maxerror > errorbound: # Modify triangle: flip edge or insert vertex # Try edge flipping first if tryedgeflip(triangle, triangulation): modified = True continue # If flipping fails or doesn't reduce error, insert vertex worstpoint = findworstapproximationpoint(triangle, datapoints) insertvertexintotriangle(triangle, worstpoint, triangulation) modified = True return triangulation Error Bound Split: In numerical examples, a greater error bound is used for the quadratic approximation step than for the final triangulation of polynomials. This makes the total error bound relatively loose for the triangles obtained from the stitching process, making violations of the error estimate extremely rare. Shrink Percentage: A small percentage (e.g., 1%) used to shrink cluster regions towards their centroid to prevent boundary overlaps. Negative Area (Overlap): The algorithm must strictly avoid producing triangles with negative area. If both standard choices for the next triangle result in negative area, a triangle must be constructed from three consecutive vertices in one polygon strip, eliminating the middle vertex. If this still fails, a triangle from three vertices of the other polygon strip is inserted. Disconnected Triangulations: In elliptic and hyperbolic cases, the optimal triangulation inside a cluster region may be disconnected or contain line segments not part of any triangle. The boundary construction must handle these cases to ensure the boundary polygon correctly encloses all simplices. Vertex Multiplicity: A vertex can be part of the boundary polygon multiple times. The algorithm must handle this correctly when extracting strips and marching. A hierarchical triangulation approach that uses piecewise quadratic polynomial approximation as an intermediate representation. It generates optimally shaped triangles for each cluster region such that all triangles imply the same approximation error. Unlike methods operating directly on data points, this method is based on adaptive clustering and quadratic representation. The cost depends on clustering complexity and error bound, not the number of original data points. It serves as the precursor to Merging Triangulations, providing the individual optimal triangulations that are then stitched together. Time Complexity: The cost of generating the triangulation depends on the complexity of the clustering and the error bound, not on the number of points in the original data set. The merging step itself is linear with respect to the number of boundary vertices along the cluster interfaces. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the boundary polygons for each cluster and the BSP tree hierarchy. Strengths: Affine-invariant (if PCA-based clustering is used). Produces optimally shaped triangles with minimal area for a given error bound. Efficient for densely sampled, smooth data sets. Limitations: Requires a hierarchical clustering scheme (e.g., BSP tree). Error bounds for stitched triangles are not guaranteed a priori and may require correction steps. Complex to implement due to boundary construction and negative area handling. When to Use: Suitable for scientific visualization of scattered data where approximation error is critical and the data is densely sampled and smooth. Not suitable for real-time rendering due to preprocessing complexity. The method was introduced in the context of multiresolution modeling for scientific visualization. It builds upon earlier work on optimal approximation with triangles and adaptive clustering schemes. The approach exploits the affine invariance of the error norm and the connectivity of a BSP tree to efficiently stitch triangulations. Numerical examples were provided for analytical functions and terrain data sets. The method is part of a broader family of hierarchical surface reconstruction techniques that aim to balance geometric fidelity with computational efficiency. name: VESTA
head: Marching VESTA, Original VESTA
body: VESTA (Volume-Enclosing Surface exTraction Algorithm) is a surface extraction method that constructs isosurfaces by generating N-cycles from 3-cell configurations, resolving ambiguities at voxel face junctures to prevent surface holes, unlike the original Marching Cubes Algorithm. It is a volume-enclosing surface extraction algorithm that processes voxel face vectors (VFVs) to generate a closed, oriented surface composed of triangles (3-cycles). It handles both isolated voxels and complex connected shapes by establishing connectivity through boundary face centers and junctures. Unlike template-based methods like Marching Cubes, VESTA uses a single building block based on vector decomposition of a single voxel face to resolve 3D cell ambiguities without generating holes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid where each voxel has a scalar value (e.g., gray level, temperature). An isovalue Tf (or threshold) defines "active" voxels (value \ge Tf) and "inactive" voxels (value < Tf). Output: A triangular mesh (collection of 3-cycles) representing the isosurface. The surface is non-degenerate, closed, and volume-enclosing. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: 3D array of scalar values. Boundary Face: A square face shared between an active voxel and an inactive neighbor. Support Point: The center of a boundary face. Juncture: The midpoint of an edge of a boundary face (shared by two adjacent boundary faces). Voxel Face Vector (VFV): A directed vector from a support point (face center) to a juncture (edge midpoint). VESTA Cycle Vector: A directed vector connecting two support points, representing a segment of the surface cycle. N-Cycle: A closed loop of VESTA cycle vectors. Numbering and Coordinates (Marching 3-Cell): A marching 3-cell is a 2 \times 2 \times 2 block of voxels. Voxel indices 0 to 7. Voxel 0 is at (i, j, k). Coordinate system x|y|z coincides with range vectors of voxel 0. Support points (face centers) and junctures (edge midpoints) are numbered within the 3-cell context. Steps: 1. Identify Active Voxels: Select all voxels with scalar value \ge Tf. 2. Identify Boundary Faces: For each active voxel, check its 6 nearest neighbors. If a neighbor is inactive, record the shared face as a boundary face. 3. Define Support Points and Junctures: The center of each recorded boundary face is a support point S. The midpoints of the edges of the boundary face are junctures J. 4. Construct Voxel Face Vectors (VFVs): For each boundary face, define 4 VFVs connecting the face center S to the 4 junctures J in counterclockwise order relative to the outward normal (or range vector). Let a VFV be V = J - S. 5. Connect VFVs into Paths: At each juncture J, connect the tip of an incoming VFV from one boundary face to the origin of an outgoing VFV from an adjacent boundary face. Constraint: Only attach the origin of a given VFV to another one's tip. This forms oriented paths between support points. 6. Resolve Points of Ambiguity (POAs): A POA occurs at a juncture where 4 incoming and 4 outgoing VFVs meet (typically where two active voxels share only a single edge). At a POA, choose a successor VFV for each incoming VFV. Two modes exist: Disconnect Mode: Select the successor VFV belonging to the same voxel as the incoming VFV. Connect Mode: Select the successor VFV belonging to the other voxel. This choice must be consistent for all POAs in the dataset (globally or locally based on gray-level thresholds). Replace connected VFV pairs with single VESTA cycle vectors connecting support points. 7. Form Closed Cycles (N-Cycles): Group VESTA cycle vectors into closed loops (N-cycles). All N-cycles are confined to a 2 \times 2 \times 2 voxel neighborhood. Valid N-cycle lengths: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12. (Lengths 10, 11 do not exist). 8. Decompose N-Cycles into Triangles (3-Cycles): Low Resolution (L): For N-cycles with N > 3, insert antiparallel vector pairs to break the cycle into 3-cycles, preserving orientation. No new points are added. High Resolution (H): For N-cycles with N > 3, introduce an additional point P{avg} within the cycle. P{avg} is the average (center of mass) of all support points involved in the N-cycle. Connect P{avg} to the vertices of the N-cycle to form triangles. If boundary face centers are displaced (see below), recalculate P{avg} after displacement. 9. Displace Support Points (Isosurface Construction): For isosurface extraction, displace each support point S along its range vector r. The range vector r originates at the center of the active voxel and ends at the center of the inactive neighbor. The displacement is determined by linear interpolation of the field values at the two voxel centers. Let Va be the active voxel value and Vb be the inactive voxel value. The intersection parameter t along the edge connecting the voxel centers is t = (Tf - Va) / (Vb - Va). The new support point position is S' = S{original} + t \cdot r. Recalculate average points P{avg} if using High Resolution mode. 10. Discard Unphysical Triangles: A triangle is unphysical if at least one of its corner points has a radial and/or temporal value smaller than zero (context-dependent, e.g., in relativistic hydrodynamics). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vestaextract(voxelgrid, isovalue, connectivitymode='disconnect', resolutionmode='L'): """ voxelgrid: 3D array of scalar values isovalue: Tf connectivitymode: 'disconnect', 'connect', or 'mixed' resolutionmode: 'L' (low) or 'H' (high) """ activevoxels = [] boundaryfaces = [] # List of (activevoxelidx, inactiveneighboridx, faceid) # Step 1 & 2: Identify active voxels and boundary faces for each voxel v in voxelgrid: if v.value >= isovalue: activevoxels.append(v) for each neighbor n of v: if n.value < isovalue: boundaryfaces.append((v, n, getfaceid(v, n))) # Step 3 & 4: Define support points and VFVs supportpoints = {} # Map from faceid to point (initially center) vfvs = [] # List of VFVs for (activev, inactivev, faceid) in boundaryfaces: center = getfacecenter(activev, inactivev) supportpoints[faceid] = center # Define 4 junctures (edge midpoints) for this face junctures = getfaceedgemidpoints(activev, inactivev) # Define 4 VFVs from center to junctures in CCW order for j in junctures: vfvs.append(VFV(origin=center, tip=j, faceid=faceid, voxel=activev)) # Step 5 & 6: Connect VFVs and resolve POAs # Build adjacency map from juncture to VFVs juncturetovfvs = {} for v in vfvs: if v.tip not in juncturetovfvs: juncturetovfvs[v.tip] = [] juncturetovfvs[v.tip].append(v) cyclevectors = [] visitedvfvs = set() for j, incomingvfvs in juncturetovfvs.items(): for incomingv in incomingvfvs: if incomingv in visitedvfvs: continue # Determine successor based on connectivity mode # Check if this juncture is a POA (4 incoming, 4 outgoing) ispoa = len(incomingvfvs) == 4 and len(juncturetovfvs.get(j, [])) == 4 if ispoa: if connectivitymode == 'mixed': # Determine mode locally based on gray levels of surrounding voxels mode = determinelocalmode(j, voxelgrid) else: mode = connectivitymode if mode == 'disconnect': successor = selectsamevoxelsuccessor(incomingv, juncturetovfvs[j]) else: # connect successor = selectothervoxelsuccessor(incomingv, juncturetovfvs[j]) else: # Trivial connection: connect to the next VFV in the same face or adjacent face successor = gettrivialsuccessor(incomingv, juncturetovfvs[j]) # Create VESTA cycle vector cyclevec = VESTACycleVector(origin=incomingv.origin, tip=successor.tip) cyclevectors.append(cyclevec) visitedvfvs.add(incomingv) visitedvfvs.add(successor) # Step 7: Form closed cycles cycles = formcycles(cyclevectors) # Step 8 & 9: Decompose and Displace triangles = [] for cycle in cycles: if len(cycle) == 3: # Already a triangle triangles.append(cycle) else: if resolutionmode == 'L': # Decompose using antiparallel pairs (no new points) triangles.extend(decomposel(cycle)) else: # H # Calculate average point avgpoint = sum(cycle.vertices) / len(cycle.vertices) # Displace support points along range vectors displacedcycle = displacecycle(cycle, voxelgrid, isovalue) displacedavg = displacepoint(avgpoint, voxelgrid, isovalue) # Connect displacedavg to displacedcycle vertices triangles.extend(decomposeh(displacedcycle, displacedavg)) # Step 10: Discard unphysical triangles validtriangles = [t for t in triangles if isphysical(t, voxelgrid)] return validtriangles Parameters: Isovalue (Tf): Threshold for active voxels. Typical value in examples: 139 MeV (for relativistic hydrodynamics). Connectivity Mode: 'disconnect', 'connect', or 'mixed'. Determines behavior at POAs. Resolution Mode: 'L' (Low, no extra points) or 'H' (High, uses average points). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Points of Ambiguity (POAs): Occur when two active voxels share only a single edge. Consistent global or local selection is required to prevent holes. Corner Contact: VESTA does not connect voxels sharing only a single point (corner contact) by default. This results in separate surfaces. Redundancy: Original VESTA minimizes redundant support points compared to MCA. Precision: In High Resolution mode, average points should be calculated after displacing support points to save computing time and ensure accuracy. DICONEX is a 2D algorithm for constructing gap-free contours from binary image data, serving as the 2D analog for VESTA. It collects initial contour vectors (ICVs) separating active and inactive pixels, connects them into closed cycles, and resolves Points of Ambiguity (POAs) where pixels touch at a single point. At a POA, 'disconnect' mode performs a left turn (same pixel), and 'connect' mode performs a right turn (different pixel). It displaces ICV origins to pixel edge midpoints to form final contours. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in sources, but benchmarks show it is comparable to or faster than MCA for certain datasets. Original VESTA executes faster than marching VESTA and MCA for specific datasets due to fewer support points, though it may require more computing time in some benchmarks due to algorithmic complexity. Memory Complexity: Original VESTA processes the entire 3D dataset at once, requiring large memory. Marching VESTA processes 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighborhoods, reducing memory usage. Measured Performance: Benchmark 1 (33 images, 241x81 pixels, 8,000 active voxels): VESTA (original/connect/mixed) produced 3,326 points and 6,406 triangles in ~0.124s. Extended MCA produced 19,218 points in 0.096s. Benchmark 2 (200 x-ray microtomography images, 256x256 pixels, 512,603 active voxels, isovalue 135): Original VESTA L: Time 5.34s, Points 932,739, Triangles 1,855,666. MCA L: Time 4.71s, Points 5,566,998, Triangles 1,855,666. Strengths: Generates non-degenerate, closed, volume-enclosing surfaces with no holes and no self-intersection. Resolves 3D cell ambiguities correctly. Not template-based. Reproduces 2D DICONEX contours when intersected with principal planes. Limitations: Does not connect voxels sharing only a single point (corner contact) by default. Requires consistent handling of POAs. Original version requires significant memory for large datasets. When to use: When a hole-free, volume-enclosing surface is critical, and template-based ambiguities are a concern. Suitable for scientific visualization of voxel data (e.g., hydrodynamics, tomography). When not to use: When corner connectivity is required without custom templates. When memory is extremely constrained and marching VESTA's overhead is unacceptable. VESTA was introduced in the paper "Volume-Enclosing Surface Extraction". It is based on the principles of the DICONEX algorithm for 2D data. The method was developed to address the limitations of the original Marching Cubes Algorithm (MCA), particularly the generation of holes and the need for extensive template sets. VESTA uses a single building block (VFVs) instead of templates. It has been applied to computer tomographic scan data and simulation data of relativistic hydrodynamic fireball expansions. Volume-Enclosing Surface Extraction, https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.1787v4, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Livnat et al. algorithm for unstructured tetrahedral grids
head: Livnat's algorithm, GPU-based marching tetrahedra, hardware-accelerated isosurface extraction on tetrahedral grids
body: This method extracts isosurfaces from unstructured 3D scalar fields defined on tetrahedral meshes by streaming cells directly into graphics hardware, computing triangles during rendering time without storing them explicitly. It sets itself apart from CPU-based extraction by leveraging vertex shaders for immediate feedback on isovalue changes and from brute-force GPU methods by optionally using a hybrid CPU/GPU interval tree to pre-select intersecting cells, achieving up to 7x speedup over brute-force GPU rendering. Unlike structured grid methods (e.g., Marching Cubes), it handles arbitrary tetrahedral connectivity by treating each cell independently in the vertex pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of tetrahedra. Each tetrahedron is defined by 4 vertices. For each vertex, the input data includes: 3D position (\mathbf{p}), normal vector (\mathbf{n}), scalar value (s), and a unique identifier i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\} indicating the vertex's role in the current tetrahedron processing batch. The global isovalue (isoValue) is a uniform parameter. Output: A stream of vertices forming triangle strips (length 4) that approximate the isosurface. The rasterizer discards degenerate triangles (zero area) generated for non-intersecting or single-triangle cases. Data Structures: 1. Vertex Input Structure: Contains the entire tetrahedron's data for every input vertex to satisfy GPU pipeline constraints. Fields: 4 corner positions (\mathbf{coord}{1..4}, vec3), 4 corner normals (\mathbf{nrml}{1..4}, vec3), 4 scalar values (isoV, float), 4 swizzled scalar values (for optimization), and the unique identifier i. Size: 144 bytes per vertex. Total per tetrahedron: 4 \times 144 = 576 bytes. 2. Lookup Tables (Alternative Implementations): Table 2 (Edge Lookup): Maps the 16 classification patterns and input vertex ID i to an edge index (12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34) or 0. Size: 16 \times 4 = 64 entries. Each entry specifies which edge to intersect for the i-th output vertex. Table 3 (Edge Traverse Order): An alternative to Table 2 to fit within older hardware limits (96 constants). Maps input vertex ID i to a sequence of 3 edge tests. i=1: Test edges 12, 13, 24. i=2: Test edges 14, 13, 24. i=3: Test edges 23, 24, 13. i=4: Test edges 34, 24, 13. Edge Table: Contains edge masks/weights for the two triangles generated by each configuration, used in the Table 2 approach. Jump Table: Determines the offset into the Edge Table based on the intersection bitmask. Algorithm Steps: The algorithm operates in two main modes: Brute Force (GPU only) and Hybrid (CPU + GPU). 1. Pre-processing (Hybrid Mode Only): Build an interval tree on the CPU to store the min/max scalar values of each tetrahedron. For a given isovalue, query the interval tree to identify tetrahedra where min \le isoValue \le max. These are the candidate cells. 2. Vertex Shader Processing (Per Tetrahedron): Four input vertices are sent to the vertex pipeline for each tetrahedron, each carrying the full tetrahedron data and a unique ID i. Step 1: Classification. Calculate the signed distance of each vertex to the isovalue: Fk = sk - isoValue \quad \text{for } k \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\} Classify each vertex as positive (+) if Fk > 0 or negative (-) if Fk \le 0. This results in a 4-bit classification pattern (16 cases). Step 2: Edge Intersection Determination. Method A (Table 2 / Bitmask): Determine intersecting edges by checking if the product of signed distances at edge endpoints is negative. An edge connects vertices u, v. It intersects if Fu \cdot Fv < 0. Create a 6-bit bitmask E for the 6 edges (12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34). Compute index: idx = \text{dot}(E, [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]). Lookup edge configuration from Jump Table and Edge Table to get edge weights/masks. Method B (Table 3 / Sequential Test): Based on input vertex ID i, sequentially test the three edges specified in Table 3. If an edge intersects (endpoints have different signs), compute the intersection point and output it. If no intersection is found after 3 tests, output a degenerate vertex (0,0,0,0). Step 3: Intersection Point Calculation. Identify the two active edges (or one, if only one triangle is formed) that intersect the isosurface. Calculate scalar values at the intersection points on these edges using linear interpolation. For an edge between vertices A and B with scalars sA, sB: frac = \frac{isoValue - sA}{sB - sA} The intersection point position \mathbf{p}{int} is: \mathbf{p}{int} = (1 - frac) \mathbf{p}A + frac \mathbf{p}B The normal \mathbf{n}{int} is interpolated similarly: \mathbf{n}{int} = (1 - frac) \mathbf{n}A + frac \mathbf{n}B Note: In the Table 2 approach, barycentric coordinates E are interpolated from edge weights, and position/normal are computed as weighted sums of all 4 vertices using these coordinates. Step 4: Output Generation. If the tetrahedron contains 0 triangles (no intersection), output 4 degenerate vertices (e.g., (0,0,0,0)). If 1 triangle, output 1 valid triangle and 2 degenerate vertices. If 2 triangles, output 2 valid triangles sharing an edge. The output vertices are rendered as a triangle strip of length 4. The indices are chosen such that the stream forms the correct triangulation or degenerate patches. Step 5: Transformation. Transform the computed 3D position to clip space: \mathbf{hpos} = M{wvp} \cdot \mathbf{p}{int} Output the homogeneous position and interpolated normal. Pseudocode (Table 3 Approach): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(IN): # Step 1: Classification F = [IN.isoV1 - isoValue, IN.isoV2 - isoValue, IN.isoV3 - isoValue, IN.isoV4 - isoValue] # Helper to check if edge (u, v) intersects def edgeintersects(u, v): return (F[u] > 0) != (F[v] > 0) # Helper to compute intersection point on edge (u, v) def computeintersection(u, v): frac = (isoValue - IN.isoV[u]) / (IN.isoV[v] - IN.isoV[u]) pos = lerp(IN.coord[u], IN.coord[v], frac) normal = lerp(IN.nrml[u], IN.nrml[v], frac) return pos, normal # Step 2 & 3: Sequential Edge Tests based on i if IN.i == 1: edges = [(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4)] elif IN.i == 2: edges = [(1, 4), (1, 3), (2, 4)] elif IN.i == 3: edges = [(2, 3), (2, 4), (1, 3)] elif IN.i == 4: edges = [(3, 4), (2, 4), (1, 3)] else: # Fallback, should not happen edges = [] for u, v in edges: if edgeintersects(u, v): pos, normal = computeintersection(u, v) hpos = mul(worldViewProj, pos) return OUT(hpos, normal) # Step 4: No intersection found for this vertex role return OUT(vec4(0, 0, 0, 1), vec3(0, 0, 0)) Parameters: isoValue: The scalar threshold. Typically a float. worldViewProj: The combined transformation matrix. Memory: 144 bytes per vertex input. 576 bytes per tetrahedron streamed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: GPU vertex programs cannot generate variable numbers of outputs. Cases with 0 or 1 triangle must output degenerate (zero-area) triangles, which are discarded by the rasterizer. Memory Limits: If the tetrahedral grid exceeds video memory, transferring data via AGP bus causes a 10-20x performance drop. Isovalue Changes: Changing the isovalue in Hybrid mode requires updating the interval tree nodes in video memory, causing a slight frame rate decrease. Precision: Linear interpolation assumes linear scalar variation within the tetrahedron. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of tetrahedra processed. In Brute Force mode, all tetrahedra are processed. In Hybrid mode, only intersecting tetrahedra are processed, reducing N by ~70% for typical datasets. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the tetrahedral data in video memory. 576 bytes per tetrahedron. Performance: On nVidia GeForce FX 5800 Ultra (128MB) with elec2 dataset (142,131 tetrahedra): 9.92 million tetrahedra/sec (diffuse lighting). On nVidia GeForce Quadro FX 3000 (256MB) with elec1 dataset (19,549 tetrahedra): 7.22 million tetrahedra/sec (diffuse lighting). Hybrid CPU/GPU version achieves ~7x speedup over GPU Brute Force. Pure CPU implementation is ~2x slower than GPU Brute Force. Strengths: Immediate feedback for isovalue changes; high throughput when data fits in VRAM; handles unstructured grids natively. Limitations: High memory usage per tetrahedron (576 bytes); performance degrades significantly if data does not fit in VRAM; requires modern GPU with vertex shader support. The algorithm was introduced by Livnat et al. in 2001/2002 for realtime isosurface extraction using graphics hardware. It addresses the limitations of CPU-based extraction and the memory overhead of storing explicit triangle meshes. The method leverages the parallel processing power of GPUs to compute isosurfaces on the fly. The hybrid approach incorporates interval trees for spatial selection, a technique previously used in CPU-based volume rendering. Realtime Isosurface Extraction with Graphics Hardware, https://doi.org/10.2312/egs.20041007, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marching cubes algorithm, https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/marching-cube-algorithm, fetched 2026-10-30 (book)

name: Performance Optimization via Lookup Table
head: Pre-computed connectivity
body: This method accelerates isosurface extraction on arbitrary polyhedral grids by pre-computing the vertex connectivity for all possible scalar sign configurations of a cell and storing them in a lookup table. It solves the performance bottleneck of dynamic topology determination during extraction, allowing for rapid access to edge/vertex connections regardless of cell geometry. It sets itself apart from dynamic algorithms like Livnat et al.'s method by trading memory for speed, pre-calculating the topological outcome rather than computing it per-voxel [S1, 1321-livnat-et-al-algorithm-for-unstructured-tetrahedral-grids.md]. Inputs: Scalar field values at cell vertices. Isosurface threshold value. Cell geometry (vertices, faces, edges). Outputs: Isosurface mesh (vertices and triangles) for the current cell. Data Structures: Lookup Table (LUT): An array indexed by the cell configuration mask. For a hexahedral cell with 8 vertices, the mask is an 8-bit integer (2^8 = 256 entries). Each entry stores the pre-computed connectivity (which edges are intersected and how they are connected into triangles). Configuration Mask: An integer where the i-th bit is set if the scalar value at vertex i is greater than or equal to the threshold, and 0 otherwise. Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Offline): For each possible cell type (e.g., cube, tetrahedron), iterate through all 2^N possible sign configurations (where N is the number of vertices). For each configuration, determine the topological connectivity of the isosurface within the cell. This involves identifying intersected edges and connecting them into triangles or other polygons. Store this connectivity data in the LUT at the index corresponding to the configuration mask. 2. Extraction (Online): For each cell in the grid, determine the scalar values at its vertices. Compare each vertex value to the isosurface threshold to generate the configuration mask. Use the mask to index into the pre-computed LUT. Retrieve the pre-computed connectivity data. Interpolate the exact positions of the intersection points on the cell edges using the scalar values. Generate the output mesh primitives (triangles) using the retrieved connectivity and interpolated points. Parameters: Isosurface Threshold: The scalar value defining the surface. Cell Type: Determines the size and content of the LUT. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Cases: Configurations where the isosurface passes exactly through a vertex or edge can lead to ambiguity. Standard Marching Cubes handles this with specific rules (e.g., pseudo-normals). Memory Usage: The LUT size grows exponentially with the number of vertices per cell. For arbitrary polyhedral grids with high-valence cells, the LUT may become prohibitively large. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for thresholding must be consistent to ensure the configuration mask is deterministic. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputelut(celltype, numvertices): """ Pre-computes the lookup table for a specific cell type. Returns a list of connectivity patterns for all 2^numvertices configurations. """ lut = [] numconfigs = 1 << numvertices for config in range(numconfigs): # Determine which vertices are above the threshold vertexsigns = [] for i in range(numvertices): if (config >> i) & 1: vertexsigns.append(1) else: vertexsigns.append(0) # Determine connectivity for this configuration # This step is geometry-specific and complex for arbitrary polyhedra # For a cube, this is the standard 256-entry table connectivity = determineconnectivity(celltype, vertexsigns) lut.append(connectivity) return lut def extractcell(cell, scalarvalues, threshold, lut): """ Extracts the isosurface for a single cell using the pre-computed LUT. """ # 1. Determine configuration mask configmask = 0 for i, vertex in enumerate(cell.vertices): if scalarvalues[vertex] >= threshold: configmask |= (1 << i) # 2. Lookup connectivity connectivity = lut[configmask] # 3. Intersect edges and generate triangles triangles = [] for edgepair in connectivity: v1idx, v2idx = edgepair v1 = cell.vertices[v1idx] v2 = cell.vertices[v2idx] # Linear interpolation to find intersection point val1 = scalarvalues[v1] val2 = scalarvalues[v2] t = (threshold - val1) / (val2 - val1) p1 = cell.position(v1) p2 = cell.position(v2) intersectionpoint = lerp(p1, p2, t) triangles.append(intersectionpoint) return triangles This variant applies the lookup table concept to tetrahedral cells by decomposing a cube into 5 tetrahedra. It covers all 81 sign patterns, including degenerate ones, using linear interpolation. It uses int64t internal arithmetic to maintain exactness within the safe-integer range (2^{63}). Unlike the cubes extractor which solves 2V - (2L+1) = 0, the tetrahedra extractor solves V - L = 0. A known pitfall in the original implementation was an unreachable branch in the odd-parity gradient calculation due to an incorrect condition (dx + dy + dz >= 0 instead of >= 2). Time Complexity: O(1) per cell for connectivity determination after pre-computation, dominated by interpolation and mesh generation. Memory Complexity: O(2^N) for the LUT, where N is the number of vertices per cell. Performance: Using pre-computed connectivity and multi-threading (-fopenmp) achieves a \times 6 speedup compared to single-threaded execution on an iMac Pro (2017) with a 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon W processor. Strengths: Fast extraction speed; consistent topology; suitable for real-time applications. Limitations: High memory usage for cells with many vertices; pre-computation overhead. When to use: When extraction speed is critical and cell geometry is regular (e.g., cubes, tetrahedra). When not to use: For arbitrary polyhedral grids with high-valence cells where the LUT size becomes prohibitive. The method originates from the need to accelerate isosurface extraction on arbitrary grids, where dynamic topology determination is slow. It builds on the classic Marching Cubes algorithm, which uses a 256-entry lookup table for hexahedral cells. The approach has been extended to other cell types, including tetrahedra, to maintain efficiency on unstructured grids. A new isosurface extraction method on arbitrary grids, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2021.110579, fetched 2026-10-26 Port B46: surface extractors batch, https://github.com/gradientspaceai/gtengine-js/pull/131, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Tetrahedral Marching Cubes (5-tetrahedra method)
head: 5-tetrahedra-per-cube extraction, SurfaceExtractorTetrahedra
body: This method extracts an isosurface from a scalar field defined on a regular voxel grid by decomposing each cube into five tetrahedra and performing linear interpolation within each tetrahedron. It covers all 81 possible sign patterns of the vertex values, including degenerate cases where vertices lie exactly on the isosurface. Unlike the standard Marching Cubes which relies on a 256-entry lookup table and resolves ambiguities via topology checks, this method is deterministic and topology-agnostic, solving the equation V - L = 0 directly. Inputs: A 3D scalar field V defined on a grid of voxels, and a scalar level L. Outputs: A set of vertices and triangles forming a manifold mesh. Data Structures: The implementation replaces standard associative containers with maps keyed by canonical strings to ensure deterministic ordering and exact arithmetic. Vertices: Stored in a map keyed by a canonical string representation of the rational coordinates (reduced to lowest terms). Vertex indices are assigned in insertion order. Edges/Triangles: Stored in maps keyed by canonical strings. Sorted at the end by a custom operator< to match std::set iteration order. Arithmetic: Uses int64t for internal calculations, mapping onto IEEE doubles. This remains exact as long as products stay within the safe-integer range (2^{63}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Decomposition: For each voxel cube, decompose it into 5 tetrahedra. The standard decomposition connects the cube center to the 6 faces, or more commonly, splits the cube into 6 tetrahedra; however, the 5-tetrahedra method specifically partitions the cube into 4 corner tetrahedra and 1 central tetrahedron (or equivalent partition covering the volume). Note: The source describes a partition into four corner tetrahedra plus a central one for gradient calculation, implying a specific geometric split. 2. Sign Pattern Evaluation: Determine the signs of the scalar field values at the 8 vertices of the cube relative to the level L. There are 2^8 = 256 combinations, but due to symmetry and the nature of the tetrahedral split, the logic handles 81 distinct sign patterns. 3. Intersection Calculation: For each tetrahedron in the cube: Identify edges where the scalar value crosses the level L (sign change). Compute the intersection point on these edges using linear interpolation. Form triangles from the intersection points. 4. Gradient and Orientation: Calculate the gradient at intersection points to determine triangle orientation. Pitfall (Odd-Parity Branch): In the original implementation, the GetGradient function for odd-parity cubes contained a bug. The condition dx + dy + dz >= 0 was used to select the central tetrahedron (index 6572). Since dx, dy, dz are fractional offsets in [0, 1], this sum is always \ge 0, making the branch for the central tetrahedron (index 0752) unreachable. Fix: The condition must be changed to dx + dy + dz >= 2. The cutting plane through vertices (1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,1,1) is defined by dx + dy + dz = 2. 5. Mesh Assembly: Collect all generated triangles. Sort edges and triangles by their canonical keys to ensure consistent ordering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extracttetrahedral(field, level, griddims): # Maps for deterministic ordering vertexmap = {} # Key: canonicalstring(coord), Value: index edgeset = {} # Key: canonicalstring(edge), Value: True triangleset = {} # Key: canonicalstring(triangle), Value: True vertices = [] triangles = [] # Iterate over all voxels for x in range(griddims.x - 1): for y in range(griddims.y - 1): for z in range(griddims.z - 1): # Get 8 corner values v = [field[x+i, y+j, z+k] for i in [0,1] for j in [0,1] for k in [0,1]] # Determine sign pattern signs = [1 if val > level else -1 if val < level else 0 for val in v] # Decompose cube into 5 tetrahedra # Tetrahedra indices refer to the 8 corners of the cube # Standard 5-tet decomposition: # T1: 0,1,3,7 # T2: 1,3,2,7 # T3: 1,2,6,7 # T4: 2,6,3,7 # T5: 3,6,7 (Central? Or specific partition) # The source mentions "four corner tetrahedra plus a central one" # for gradient logic. We assume a standard partition covering the cube. tetrahedra = [ [0, 1, 3, 7], [1, 3, 2, 7], [1, 2, 6, 7], [2, 6, 3, 7], [3, 6, 7, ?] # The 5th tetrahedron definition is implicit in the source's gradient logic ] for tet in tetrahedra: # Check if tetrahedron intersects the isosurface # A tetrahedron intersects if vertices have mixed signs tetsigns = [signs[i] for i in tet] if not (all(s >= 0 for s in tetsigns) or all(s <= 0 for s in tetsigns)): # Find intersecting edges edges = getintersectingedges(tet, tetsigns, v, level) # Compute intersection points points = [] for edge in edges: p = linearinterpolate(edge, v, level) points.append(p) # Form triangles # For a tetrahedron, the intersection is a polygon (triangle or quad) # Triangulate the polygon tris = triangulatepolygon(points) for tri in tris: # Add vertices to map triindices = [] for p in tri: key = canonicalstring(p) if key not in vertexmap: vertexmap[key] = len(vertices) vertices.append(p) triindices.append(vertexmap[key]) # Add triangle to set trikey = canonicalstring(sorted(triindices)) if trikey not in triangleset: triangleset[trikey] = True triangles.append(triindices) # Sort triangles and edges for consistency triangles.sort(key=lambda t: canonicalstring(sorted(t))) return vertices, triangles def getgradient(x, y, z, field, level): # dx, dy, dz are fractional offsets dx, dy, dz = x % 1, y % 1, z % 1 # Determine which tetrahedron the point lies in # Odd-parity branch fix: use >= 2 instead of >= 0 if dx - dy - dz >= 0: # Corner tetrahedron 1205 return computegradient1205(dx, dy, dz, field) elif dx - dy + dz <= 0: # Corner tetrahedron 3027 return computegradient3027(dx, dy, dz, field) elif dx + dy - dz <= 0: # Corner tetrahedron 4750 return computegradient4750(dx, dy, dz, field) elif dx + dy + dz >= 2: # Fixed condition # Central tetrahedron 0752 return computegradient0752(dx, dy, dz, field) else: # Corner tetrahedron 6572 return computegradient6572(dx, dy, dz, field) Cube-based surface extraction using a vertex-edge table (VETable) and ear-clipping. It resolves the four-cut face ambiguity by evaluating the sign of the determinant f{00}f{11} - f{01}f{10}, adding a branch point when \det == 0. Unlike the tetrahedra extractor which solves V - L = 0, the cubes extractor solves 2V - (2L+1) = 0. To extract the same surface, voxels must be doubled and the level set to 2L+1. Complexity: Linear in the number of voxels, O(N), where N is the number of voxels. Each voxel is processed independently. Memory: Proportional to the number of surface triangles and vertices. The use of maps for canonical strings adds overhead compared to direct array indexing but ensures deterministic ordering. Performance: The method is robust and handles degenerate cases (zero-valued vertices) explicitly. The int64t arithmetic ensures precision but may be slower than floating-point operations if not optimized. The bug fix in the odd-parity branch is critical for correct orientation. Strengths: Topology-agnostic, no lookup table size limitations, handles all sign patterns including degenerate ones. Limitations: Slower than lookup-table-based methods due to per-voxel computation and map overhead. Requires careful handling of the gradient calculation to avoid orientation errors. The method is part of the gtengine-js library, specifically ported in PR #131 (B46) by gradientspaceai. It derives from the SurfaceExtractor base class and is designed to be a deterministic alternative to the standard Marching Cubes algorithm. The implementation addresses specific bugs in the gradient calculation for odd-parity cubes, ensuring correct triangle orientation. name: Extended CLCIR PLIC Reconstruction
head: Extended CLCIR method, PLIC reconstruction on arbitrary grids
body: The Extended CLCIR method reconstructs a Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane for Volume of Fluid (VOF) simulations on arbitrary polyhedral grids by extracting an isosurface from an interpolated scalar field and computing a weighted normal vector. It distinguishes itself from standard VOF reconstruction methods by explicitly using isosurface extraction to handle non-convex and self-intersecting polyhedral cells without decomposition, and from pure isosurface methods by its explicit geometric flux calculation and volume conservation enforcement. It builds on Isosurface extraction to determine the interface geometry. Inputs: Scalar field \phi at cell vertices, interpolated from fluid volume fractions Fl(tn) of neighboring cells. Cell geometry (vertices, faces, volume V\Omega). Target isovalue \tilde{\phi} = 0.5. Threshold angle \theta{thresh} = 1.2 radians. Outputs: PLIC plane defined by unit normal vector \mathbf{n} and constant C such that \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + C = 0. The plane splits cell volume V\Omega into sub-volumes F(tn)V\Omega and (1-F(tn))V\Omega. Data Structures: Interpolated Scalar Field: For each vertex ip, \phi{ip} is computed as: \phi{ip} = \frac{\suml Fl(tn) wl}{\suml wl} where the sum extends over all cells l containing vertex ip, and wl = 1/|\mathbf{x}{ip} - \mathbf{x}l| is the inverse distance weight, with \mathbf{x}{ip} being the vertex position and \mathbf{x}l the geometric center of cell l. Isosurface: A set of vertices and faces (isopolygon) extracted from the cell where \phi{min} < 0.5 < \phi{max}. Triangulated Surface: A mesh formed by triangles connecting a center point to edges of the isosurface or adjacent isosurfaces. Algorithm Steps: 1. Interpolation: Compute \phi{ip} for all vertices in the domain using the weighted average formula. 2. Interface Check: For each cell, check if \phi{min} < 0.5 < \phi{max}. If not, the cell is not interfacial. 3. Isosurface Extraction: If interfacial, extract the isosurface at \tilde{\phi} = 0.5 using an arbitrary grid isosurface extraction algorithm (e.g., Algorithm 1 from). 4. Validity Check: If the extracted isosurface consists of a single isopolygon, mark the cell as a "valid isosurface cell". 5. Local Normal Calculation: Construct a "local triangulated surface" by connecting the geometric center of the extracted isosurface to two consecutive \tilde{\phi}-vertices for each triangle. Compute the local normal \mathbf{n}l using weighted averaging: \mathbf{n}l = \frac{\sum{t=1}^{Nt} wt \mathbf{n}t}{\left| \sum{t=1}^{Nt} wt \mathbf{n}t \right|} where Nt is the number of triangles, \mathbf{n}t is the unit normal of triangle t, and wt is the weighting factor. For cubic grids, wt = \frac{\sin(\alpha)}{L1 L2}, where \alpha is the angle between the two inner edges of the triangular facet, and L1, L2 are their lengths. For other grids, wt = 1. 6. Extended Normal Calculation: Create an "extended triangulated surface" by connecting the geometric center of the current surface to the geometric centers of isosurfaces extracted at adjacent cells. Compute the extended normal \mathbf{n}e using the same weighted averaging formula as for \mathbf{n}l. 7. Normal Selection: If \arccos(\mathbf{n}e \cdot \mathbf{n}l) < 1.2 rad, set \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{n}e. Otherwise, set \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{n}l. 8. Fallback for Invalid Cells: If the cell is not a valid isosurface cell (e.g., complex topology), compute \mathbf{n} using a Least-Squares Gradient Interface Reconstruction (LSGIR) method. 9. Volume Constant Calculation: Compute the constant C such that the plane \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + C = 0 splits the cell volume V\Omega into volumes F(tn)V\Omega and (1-F(tn))V\Omega. For cubic cells, use the analytical method of Scardovelli and Zaleski. For other grids, use the CIBRAVE method (López et al.). 10. Vertex Relocation: Move the vertices of the extended triangulated surfaces to the corresponding PLIC centers (intersection of the plane with cell edges). 11. Refinement: For valid isosurface cells, compute a new normal \mathbf{n}c from the updated extended triangulated surface using the weighted averaging formula. If \arccos(\mathbf{n}c \cdot \mathbf{n}) < 1.2 rad, update \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{n}c and recompute C to relocate the PLIC. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ # Step 1 & 2: Check if cell is interfacial phimin = min(phifield[v] for v in cell.vertices) phimax = max(phifield[v] for v in cell.vertices) if not (phimin < 0.5 < phimax): return None # Not an interfacial cell # Step 3: Extract isosurface at 0.5 # Assumes Algorithm 1 from is available isosurface = extractisosurface(cell, phifield, isovalue=0.5) # Step 4: Check validity isvalid = issingleisopolygon(isosurface) # Step 5: Local Normal localcenter = isosurface.geometriccenter localtriangles = constructlocaltriangles(localcenter, isosurface.vertices) nl = computeweightednormal(localtriangles, cell.gridtype) # Step 6: Extended Normal # Get isosurfaces from adjacent cells (requires neighbor lookup) adjacentisosurfaces = getadjacentisosurfaces(cell, phifield) extendedtriangles = constructextendedtriangles(localcenter, adjacentisosurfaces) ne = computeweightednormal(extendedtriangles, cell.gridtype) # Step 7: Normal Selection dotproduct = dot(ne, nl) # Clamp dotproduct to [-1, 1] to avoid numerical errors in acos dotproduct = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dotproduct)) angle = acos(dotproduct) if angle < thresholdangle: n = ne else: n = nl # Step 8: Fallback if not valid (simplified) if not isvalid: n = computelsgirnormal(cell, phifield) # Step 9: Compute C # Assumes volumesolver is available C = computevolumeconstant(n, cell, phifield[cell.volumefractionindex]) # Step 10: Relocate vertices (conceptual) # Move vertices of extended surface to PLIC centers updatedextendedsurface = relocatesurfacevertices(extendedtriangles, n, C, cell) # Step 11: Refinement if isvalid: nc = computeweightednormal(updatedextendedsurface, cell.gridtype) dotproductc = dot(nc, n) dotproductc = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dotproductc)) anglec = acos(dotproductc) if anglec < thresholdangle: n = nc C = computevolumeconstant(n, cell, phifield[cell.volumefractionindex]) return n, C def computeweightednormal(triangles, gridtype): """ Compute normal using Eq. No, "inner edges... joins a phi-vertex with the geometric center" # Let's assume tri.vertices[0] is center, tri.vertices[1] and [2] are phi-vertices # Actually, the text says "two consecutive phi-vertices". # Let's assume the triangle is defined by Center, Vi, V{i+1} # Inner edges are (Center, Vi) and (Center, V{i+1}) e1 = v1 - v3 # Vector from center to v1? No, v3 is center? # Let's redefine: tri.vertices = [center, va, vb] # Inner edges are ea = va - center, eb = vb - center ea = v1 - v3 eb = v2 - v3 lena = length(ea) lenb = length(eb) if lena == 0 or lenb == 0: wt = 1.0 else: cosangle = dot(ea, eb) / (lena lenb) sinangle = sqrt(1 - cosangle2) wt = sinangle / (lena lenb) else: wt = 1.0 weightedsum += wt nt return normalize(weightedsum) This method simulates multiphase fluid flows by advecting a Volume of Fluid (VOF) indicator function on arbitrary polyhedral grids. It solves the advection equation geometrically using Edge-Matched Flux Polygon Advection (EMFPA) and reconstructs the fluid interface using the CLCIR method, which relies on isosurface extraction to determine the Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane orientation. It is distinguished from standard VOF methods by its ability to handle non-convex and self-intersecting polyhedral cells without decomposition, and from pure isosurface methods by its explicit geometric flux calculation. Requires storage of the scalar field, isosurfaces, and extended triangulated surfaces. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles arbitrary polyhedral grids, including non-convex and self-intersecting cells, without decomposition. Uses isosurface extraction for robust interface representation. Limitations: Requires an isosurface extraction algorithm as a subroutine. May fall back to LSGIR for invalid cells, which might be less accurate. When to use: VOF simulations on complex, arbitrary polyhedral grids where standard PLIC methods fail due to cell topology. When not to use: Simple cubic grids where faster analytical methods (Scardovelli and Zaleski) are sufficient for volume constant calculation, though the normal calculation still uses the extended method. The Extended CLCIR method was introduced in a 2021 paper by López et al.. It is part of the VOFTools package. The method combines isosurface extraction with PLIC reconstruction to handle complex cell geometries. It replaces the CIBRAVE method with the Scardovelli and Zaleski analytical method for cubic cells. name: VOF Advection with Isosurface Extraction
head: EMFPA-CLCIR, EMFPA-Youngs, VOF simulation, Volume of Fluid (VOF) Advection with Isosurface Extraction
body: This method simulates multiphase fluid flows by advecting a Volume of Fluid (VOF) indicator function on arbitrary polyhedral grids. It solves the advection equation geometrically using Edge-Matched Flux Polygon Advection (EMFPA) and reconstructs the fluid interface using the CLCIR method, which relies on isosurface extraction to determine the Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane orientation. It is distinguished from standard VOF methods by its ability to handle non-convex and self-intersecting polyhedral cells without decomposition, and from pure isosurface methods by its explicit geometric flux calculation. Inputs: Computational grid \Omega consisting of arbitrary polyhedral cells (cubic, tetrahedral, distorted, or non-convex irregular). Velocity field \mathbf{v} = (u, v, w) defined at cell faces. Initial fluid volume fraction field F(t^n) for each cell. Time step \Delta t. Outputs: Updated fluid volume fraction field F(t^{n+1}). Reconstructed PLIC interface geometry for cells with 10^{-12} < F(t^n) < 1 - 10^{-12}. Data Structures: Grid: A collection of cells \Omegai, each defined by a set of vertices and faces. Faces may be non-planar or self-intersecting. Volume Fraction: A scalar field F where Fi \in [0, 1] represents the fraction of cell i occupied by the fluid. Velocity: Vector components uj, vj, wj stored at the center of each face j. Step 1: Initialization At t^n = 0, compute the initial volume fraction F(t^n=0) for each cell. For a spherical fluid body of radius R=0.15 centered at (0.5, 0.75, 0.25) in a unit box, use a grid refinement procedure extended to non-convex cells. Step 2: Time Step Calculation Determine the time step \Delta t using the CFL condition: \Delta t = \min \left[ \frac{\min(h{xi})}{\max(uj)}, \frac{\min(h{yi})}{\max(vj)}, \frac{\min(h{zi})}{\max(wj)} \right] \times \text{CFL} where: \text{CFL} is the Courant number (typically 0.5). h{xi}, h{yi}, h{zi} are the dimensions of the minimum-size rectangular parallelepiped enclosing cell i along the coordinate axes. For cubic grids with n cells, \min(h{xi}) = \min(h{yi}) = \min(h{zi}) = 1/n^{1/3}. For unstructured grids, the min/max operators consider only cells and faces near the interface. Step 3: Interface Reconstruction (CLCIR) For each cell i where 10^{-12} < Fi(t^n) < 1 - 10^{-12}: 1. Construct a scalar field \tilde{\phi} within the cell. 2. Extract the isosurface \tilde{\phi} = 0.5 using the isosurface extraction method described in Parent. 3. Compute the weighted normal vector \mathbf{n} of the extracted isosurface. 4. Define the PLIC plane passing through the cell centroid with normal \mathbf{n} such that the volume of the fluid side equals Fi(t^n) V{\Omegai}. Step 4: Flux Calculation (EMFPA) Calculate the net volume of fluid advected out of cell i during \Delta t: \Phii = \int{t^n}^{t^{n+1}} \int{\partial \Omegai} \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}f \chi(\mathbf{x}, t) \, dS \, dt This is solved geometrically using the Edge-Matched Flux Polygon Advection (EMFPA) method. 1. For each face f of cell i, construct the flux polygon representing the volume of fluid crossing the face. 2. Perform repeated intersection operations on the polyhedra formed by the flux regions. 3. Use geometric tools capable of handling non-convex polyhedra with self-intersecting faces to compute intersections without decomposition. 4. Sum the signed fluxes over all faces to get \Phii. Step 5: Volume Fraction Update Update the volume fraction using the integrated advection equation: F(t^{n+1}) = F(t^n) - \frac{1}{V{\Omega}} \int{t^n}^{t^{n+1}} \int{\Omega} \nabla \cdot [\mathbf{v} \chi(\mathbf{x}, t)] \, d\mathbf{x} \, dt + \frac{F(t^{n+1}) - F(t^n)}{2V{\Omega}} \int{t^n}^{t^{n+1}} \int{\Omega} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \, d\mathbf{x} \, dt In practice, the first integral is approximated by the geometric flux \Phii calculated in Step 4. The second term (divergence correction) must be null if the velocity field is discretely solenoidal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def advectvof(grid, velocity, F, dt, cfl=0.5): """ Advect VOF field F on arbitrary grid using EMFPA and CLCIR. Args: grid: List of cells. Each cell has vertices, faces, and volume Vomega. velocity: Dict mapping faceid to (u, v, w) vector. F: Dict mapping cellid to float (volume fraction). dt: Time step size. cfl: CFL number (default 0.5). Returns: Fnew: Updated volume fractions. """ Fnew = {} # Step 2: Determine dt if not provided (omitted here as dt is input) for cellid, cell in grid.cells.items(): Fold = F[cellid] Vomega = cell.volume # Step 3: Interface Reconstruction # Only reconstruct if interface is present if 1e-12 < Fold < 1 - 1e-12: # Extract isosurface from scalar field (details in Parent article) # Returns normal vector n and plane constant d n, d = reconstructplicplane(cell, Fold) # Store PLIC info for flux calculation if needed, # though EMFPA primarily uses the flux polygon intersection cell.plicnormal = n cell.plicd = d else: # No interface or full/empty cell cell.plicnormal = None cell.plicd = None # Step 4: Flux Calculation using EMFPA totalflux = 0.0 for face in cell.faces: # Get velocity at face center u, v, w = velocity[face.id] # Calculate flux polygon intersection # This involves intersecting the cell geometry with the # swept volume defined by velocity over dt. # Tools from [26, 48] handle non-convex/self-intersecting cases. fluxvolume = computeemfpaflux(cell, face, u, v, w, dt) # Sum signed flux (outward normal assumed positive for outflow) totalflux += fluxvolume # Step 5: Update Volume Fraction # Eq. 9: F(t^{n+1}) = F(t^n) - (1/V) Integral(div(vchi)) + Correction # The integral term is approximated by totalflux. # The correction term is zero for solenoidal fields. # Check solenoidal condition (optional guard) # divergence = sum(face.normal velocity[face.id] for face in cell.faces) # if divergence is not close to 0, add correction term. Fnew[cellid] = Fold - totalflux / Vomega # Clamp to [0, 1] to handle numerical errors Fnew[cellid] = max(0.0, min(1.0, Fnew[cellid])) return Fnew Combines EMFPA advection with CLCIR reconstruction using isosurface extraction. Chosen for high accuracy on arbitrary grids. Link Combines EMFPA advection with Youngs' method for interface reconstruction. Chosen for lower CPU time, though with higher error. Link Time Complexity: Determined by the cost of isosurface extraction and geometric flux polygon intersections. The EMFPA method avoids decomposition, reducing complexity compared to methods requiring cell subdivision. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for grid geometry, velocity field, and volume fractions. No additional large temporary arrays for decomposition are needed. Performance: On a 3D vortex-in-a-box test with CFL=0.5: Cubic Grids (n \approx 32^3): EMFPA-CLCIR error 3.21 \times 10^{-3}, CPU time 0.0088s. EMFPA-Youngs error 3.73 \times 10^{-3}, CPU time 0.0067s. Cubic Grids (n \approx 128^3): EMFPA-CLCIR error 2.14 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 0.13s. EMFPA-Youngs error 2.91 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 0.11s. Tetrahedral Grids (n \approx 128^3): EMFPA-CLCIR error 3.51 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 0.37s. EMFPA-Youngs error 6.00 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 0.25s. Non-convex Polyhedral Grids (n \approx 128^3): EMFPA-CLCIR error 3.44 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 2.19s. EMFPA-Youngs error 3.76 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 1.81s. Convergence: Second-order convergence observed for all grid types. Strengths: Handles arbitrary polyhedral grids (including non-convex and self-intersecting) without decomposition. High accuracy compared to Youngs' method. Limitations: Slightly higher CPU time than EMFPA-Youngs. Requires robust geometric intersection tools for non-convex cells. The method was proposed in a 2021 paper by as a novel isosurface extraction technique for VOF simulations on arbitrary grids. It builds on the CLCIR method [3] and the EMFPA advection scheme [46, 47]. The isosurface extraction component utilizes tools from [26, 48] to handle complex cell geometries. The method is part of a broader effort to improve multiphase flow simulation on unstructured grids, addressing limitations of previous methods that struggled with non-convex cells or required decomposition. name: Multi-Isosurface Extraction
head: Multiple Isosurface Extraction, Multi-Resolution Isosurface Extraction
body: Multi-Isosurface Extraction is a technique to extract and render multiple isosurfaces from the same scalar volume data simultaneously by running the Marching Cubes algorithm for each selected isovalue. Unlike single isosurface extraction, this method requires managing multiple triangle lists and potentially multiple rendering passes or state changes for different isovalue colors. It builds on Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration by extending the extraction loop to iterate over a user-defined list of isovalues rather than a single scalar threshold. Inputs: Scalar volume dataset: a 3D array dataset of dimensions maxX \times maxY \times maxZ. List of isovalue inputs: a list of floating-point numbers representing the thresholds for extraction. Resolution control parameter: an integer inc (iteration step) applied per isosurface. Outputs: A collection of triangle lists, one for each isovalue. Rendered geometry, potentially on different viewports or in the same viewport with distinct colors/materials. Data Structures: NODE: A linked list node structure containing triangle data. The source code defines NODE list as the return type for the extraction function, implying a linked list of triangles or vertices. GRIDCELL: A structure representing a voxel cell with 8 vertices (v.val[0..7] for values, v.p[0..7] for positions). TRIANGLE: A structure representing a single triangle, likely containing 3 vertices. Algorithm Steps: 1. Accept a list of multiple isovalue inputs from the user. 2. For each isovalue in the list: a. Initialize an empty triangle list list. b. Determine the resolution step inc for this specific isovalue (default inc = 1 for full resolution). c. Iterate through the volume grid using the step inc: \text{for } i = 0 \text{ to } maxX - inc \text{ step } inc \text{for } j = 0 \text{ to } maxY - inc \text{ step } inc \text{for } k = 0 \text{ to } maxZ - inc \text{ step } inc d. For each voxel at (i, j, k), retrieve the 8 corner values and positions from dataset into GRIDCELL v. e. Invoke the standard Marching Cubes lookup and configuration logic (as defined in the parent article) using v, isoValue, and inc to determine the triangulation case. f. Generate the corresponding triangles and append them to list. 3. Render the generated triangles for each isovalue. This may involve setting up distinct materials or viewports for each isosurface to distinguish them visually. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiisosurfaceextraction(dataset, maxx, maxy, maxz, isovaluelist): """ Extracts multiple isosurfaces from a scalar volume. Args: dataset: 3D array of shape (maxx, maxy, maxz) maxx, maxy, maxz: Dimensions of the volume isovaluelist: List of tuples (isovalue, resolutioninc) isovalue: float, the threshold resolutioninc: int, step size for iteration (1 for full res) Returns: listoftrianglelists: A list where each element is a list of triangles for the corresponding isovalue. """ alltrianglelists = [] for isovalue, inc in isovaluelist: trianglelist = [] # Iterate through the volume with the specified resolution step for i in range(0, maxx - inc, inc): for j in range(0, maxy - inc, inc): for k in range(0, maxz - inc, inc): # Extract the 8 corners of the current voxel # Note: The source code accesses dataset[i][j][k] directly. # In a general implementation, ensure bounds checking. corners = [] for dx in [0, inc]: for dy in [0, inc]: for dz in [0, inc]: val = dataset[i + dx][j + dy][k + dz] pos = (i + dx, j + dy, k + dz) corners.append({'val': val, 'pos': pos}) # Call the Marching Cubes algorithm for this cell # This function is assumed to be defined in the parent article # Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration triangles = marchingcubescell(corners, isovalue) # Append generated triangles to the list for tri in triangles: trianglelist.append(tri) alltrianglelists.append(trianglelist) return alltrianglelists def marchingcubescell(corners, isovalue): """ Placeholder for the Marching Cubes logic defined in the parent article. Returns a list of triangles for the given cell and isovalue. """ # Implementation details are in Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration # This function is not fully defined in the provided sources for Multi-Isosurface Extraction # but is required for the method to work. pass Parameters: inc: Controls resolution. inc=1 is full resolution. inc>1 reduces resolution by processing every inc-th voxel. Typical values are integers like 2, 4, etc.. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Isovalues: The source notes entering two same isovalues (e.g., 0.04, 0.04) as a test case, implying the system handles duplicates by generating separate lists or merging them, but the exact behavior is not specified. Viewport Management: Rendering multiple isosurfaces requires careful management of viewports or rendering states to avoid visual overlap issues unless depth testing and transparency are correctly configured. A technique for rendering multiple isosurfaces with different opacities concurrently by maintaining one Matryoshka layer per isosurface and processing corresponding planes across all layers together. It uses an auxiliary buffer to mark all active cells as drawable for a set of corresponding planes from different isosurfaces, then processes this buffer in a front-to-back order dependent on the viewing camera to ensure correct ordering across all isosurfaces. Choose this when transparency and correct depth ordering between multiple isosurfaces are required. Link: Speeding Up Isosurfacing: The Matryoshka Algorithm. A scheme where selected isosurfaces are rendered at high resolution (original voxel grid) while others are rendered at lower resolutions by skipping voxels during extraction. It achieves this by setting the iteration step inc to a value greater than 1 for low-resolution isosurfaces. Choose this when performance is critical for less important isosurfaces or when visualizing features at different scales simultaneously. Link: Multi-Isosurface Extraction. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of voxels in the volume and M is the number of isovalue lists. If multi-resolution is used, N is effectively reduced for lower resolution isosurfaces by a factor of inc^3. Memory Complexity: O(T \cdot M), where T is the average number of triangles per isosurface. Multiple triangle lists must be stored in memory simultaneously. Measured Performance: On an Intel Pentium IV 3.0Ghz desktop with 512Mb RAM and no hardware acceleration, extracting 6 isovalues took approximately 0.027 seconds for list creation and varying display times (e.g., 0.004-0.005 seconds per display frame). Loading data for 6 isovalues took 0.177 seconds. Strengths: Allows simultaneous visualization of distinct features within a volume; supports varying levels of detail. Limitations: Increased memory usage due to multiple triangle lists; potential rendering complexity for transparency and depth sorting; performance scales linearly with the number of isovalue lists. When to use: When analyzing multiple distinct thresholds in a single volume (e.g., different tissue types in medical imaging). When not to use: When only a single feature is of interest, or when memory is severely constrained. The method originates from educational and research projects in data visualization, specifically the LSU-7433-Data-Visualization course materials. It extends the classic Marching Cubes algorithm to handle multiple thresholds, a common requirement in scientific visualization. The Matryoshka variant for handling transparency and ordering was introduced in the paper "Speeding Up Isosurfacing: The Matryoshka Algorithm".
