name: Convex Contouring with Decision Trees
head: Convex Contouring, Convex contouring of volumetric data
body: Convex Contouring with Decision Trees is a table-driven isosurface extraction technique that generates topologically consistent surfaces where the negative space inside each cell is convex. Unlike Marching Cubes, which may produce disconnected or non-convex negative space, this method ensures that the polygonal contour inside each cell encloses a convex hull of negative corners and edge intersections. This convexity property enables fast collision detection on the triangulated isosurface. The method distinguishes itself by using pre-computed decision trees to dynamically select the correct triangulation from a set of candidates based on the exact positions of edge intersections, rather than relying solely on vertex signs. The algorithm assumes the underlying implicit function is trilinear within each cell. The core mechanism involves identifying the convex hull of the negative space (defined by negative cell corners and edge intersections) and extracting the portion of this hull that lies interior to the cell. Input: A regular grid of volumetric data with scalar values at vertices; an isovalue I. Output: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface. 1. Composite Look-up Table: Maps each sign configuration (the signs of the 8 cell corners relative to the isovalue) to a compact decision tree. 2. Decision Tree: A binary tree structure where each node represents a "4-point test". Node: Contains indices for four distinct edge intersections (V1, V2, V3, V4). Children: Left child (test false), Right child (test true). Leaf: Contains the final triangulation (a set of triangles) for the patch. 3. Patch Data: A connected component of the convex contour, which may contain holes. 1. Cell Traversal: Iterate through all cells in the grid. 2. Sign Configuration: Determine the sign of each of the 8 cell corners relative to the isovalue I. Let si \in \{-1, 1\} be the sign of corner i. 3. Edge Intersection Calculation: For each edge of the cell where the sign changes, calculate the intersection point P using linear interpolation: t = \frac{I - fa}{fb - fa} P = Va + t(Vb - Va) where fa, fb are scalar values at endpoints Va, Vb. 4. Patch Identification: Identify the linear convex contours on the faces of the cell. These contours connect edge intersections and are uniquely determined by the corner signs. Group these contours into connected components called "patches". 5. Pre-triangulation (Filtering): Construct the set S of all possible triangulations for the patch. The vertices of these triangles are restricted to the fixed cell edge intersections. Eliminate triangulations containing "ineligible" triangles. A triangle is ineligible if it lies completely to the back of all non-degenerate border triangles formed by the patch boundary edges. This reduces the size of S. 6. Decision Tree Lookup: Retrieve the pre-computed decision tree from the look-up table corresponding to the current sign configuration. 7. Triangulation Selection: Walk down the decision tree using 4-point tests to identify the correct triangulation from the reduced set S. 8. Mesh Generation: Output the triangles from the selected triangulation. Fill the negative regions on the cell faces with triangles to complete the convex hull of the negative space. The decision tree nodes perform a geometric predicate to eliminate incorrect triangulations. Given four distinct edge intersections V1, V2, V3, V4: 1. Form the triangle T = (V1, V2, V3). 2. Determine if V4 lies on the "front-facing" side of T. This is typically determined by the sign of the dot product between the triangle normal \mathbf{n} = (V2 - V1) \times (V3 - V1) and the vector (V4 - V1). If V4 is on the front-facing side (i.e., \mathbf{n} \cdot (V4 - V1) > 0): The inverted triangle (V1, V3, V2) does not belong to the convex contour. Triangles (V1, V2, V4), (V2, V3, V4), and (V3, V1, V4) do not satisfy the convex hull property. If V4 is NOT on the front-facing side (i.e., \mathbf{n} \cdot (V4 - V1) \le 0): Triangles (V1, V2, V3), (V1, V4, V2), (V2, V4, V3), and (V1, V3, V4) do not lie on the convex contour. If all vertices are coplanar, either choice can be made. Each test eliminates triangulations in S that contain any of the ruled-out triangles. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def convexcontouring(grid, isovalue): """ Main entry point for Convex Contouring. grid: 3D array of scalar values. isovalue: The threshold for surface extraction. Returns: List of triangles (each triangle is a tuple of 3 vertices). """ triangles = [] # Pre-computed lookup table mapping signconfig -> decisiontree # decisiontree is a Node object or None lookuptable = buildlookuptable() # Iterate over all cells (assuming 0-indexed, dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz) for x in range(grid.shape[0] - 1): for y in range(grid.shape[1] - 1): for z in range(grid.shape[2] - 1): celltriangles = processcell(grid, x, y, z, isovalue, lookuptable) triangles.extend(celltriangles) return triangles def processcell(grid, x, y, z, isovalue, lookuptable): # 1. The method relies on the assumption that triangles on the convex contour face inside the convex hull of the negative space. The test determines the orientation of V4 relative to the triangle formed by V1, V2, V3. Data Structures: Points Vi are 3D coordinates (xi, yi, zi). Calculate N and D as defined above. 2. Check the sign of D: If D > 0 (or D \ge 0 depending on convention, but strictly "front-facing" implies a specific side), V4 lies on the front-facing side of (V1, V2, V3). If D < 0, V4 does not lie on the front-facing side. 3. Rule out triangles based on the result: Case A (V4 is front-facing): Rule out the inverted triangle (V1, V3, V2) and the triangles (V1, V2, V4), (V2, V3, V4), and (V3, V1, V4). name: Pre-triangulation of Convex Contour
body: Pre-triangulation of Convex Contour is a process to identify triangles that will not appear on the convex contour during lookup table construction based on sign configuration, reducing the set of possible triangulations. It solves the combinatorial explosion of possible surface configurations by applying geometric constraints derived from the convex hull property. Unlike the 4-point test, which selects among remaining candidates at runtime, this method statically prunes the search space during table generation based solely on the sign configuration of the cell corners. The method identifies triangles that are geometrically impossible to lie on the convex hull of the negative space. It relies on the observation that for a triangle on the convex contour, the half-space on its front-facing side must contain (or partially contain) every other cell edge exhibiting a sign change. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A cell sign configuration (binary mask of 8 corners) and a candidate triangle defined by vertices on three distinct cell edges. Output: A boolean flag indicating whether the candidate triangle is ruled out from the convex contour. Data Structures: Cell Corners (Ci): The 8 vertices of the voxel, indexed i=1 \dots 8. Cell Edges: Defined by pairs of corners. A sign change occurs on an edge if the scalar values at its endpoints have different signs relative to the isovalue. Border Triangles: Triangles formed by selecting one endpoint from each of three distinct cell edges in order. Steps: 1. Identify Intersecting Edges: Determine all cell edges that exhibit a sign change. 2. Select Candidate Triangles: Consider a triangle T formed by three vertices v1, v2, v3, where each vj lies on a distinct intersecting edge E{a}, E{b}, E{c}. 3. Construct Border Triangles: For the three edges Ea=(C1, C2), Eb=(C3, C4), and Ec=(C5, C6), construct the border triangle by taking the endpoints of these edges in order, such as (C1, C3, C5). 4. Check Back-Facing Condition: Check if any other intersecting edge E{other} (distinct from the three defining T) lies completely to the back of the border triangle. 5. Prune: If such an edge E{other} exists, then any triangle T whose vertices belong to the three defining edges is ruled out from the convex contour. If the edge lies partially to the front of at least one border triangle, the triangle may exist in the triangulation and is not ruled out. Formulas: Let P be the plane defined by a border triangle with vertices A, B, C. The plane equation is: \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{A}) = 0 where \mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A}) \times (\mathbf{C} - \mathbf{A}). An edge defined by endpoints \mathbf{U} and \mathbf{V} lies completely to the back of P if: \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{U} - \mathbf{A}) < 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{A}) < 0. (Note: Strict inequality assumes non-degenerate triangles and general position.) Parameters: Isovalue: Implicitly handled by the sign configuration. Convex Hull Property: The fundamental constraint ensuring the front-facing half-space contains other sign-changing edges. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Border Triangles: If three selected endpoints are collinear or coplanar in a way that forms a zero-area triangle, the border triangle is degenerate and ignored in the back-facing check. Partial Front-Facing: If an intersecting edge lies partially to the front of at least one border triangle, the triangle is not ruled out. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for "back" vs "front" must handle near-zero values carefully to avoid incorrect pruning due to numerical noise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Returns: True if the triangle is ruled out, False otherwise. """ # Identify the three edges that the triangle vertices lie on triedgeindices = [] for v in trianglevertices: edgeidx = None for i, edge in enumerate(edgeintersections): if v in edge: edgeidx = i break if edgeidx is None: return False # Vertex not on an intersecting edge, invalid input triedgeindices.append(edgeidx) # Get the three edges e1 = edgeintersections[triedgeindices[0]] e2 = edgeintersections[triedgeindices[1]] e3 = edgeintersections[triedgeindices[2]] # Construct the border triangle by taking one endpoint of each edge in order c1, c2, c3 = e1[0], e2[0], e3[0] # Check if any other intersecting edge lies completely to the back of the border triangle for otheredgeidx, otheredge in enumerate(edgeintersections): if otheredgeidx in triedgeindices: continue # Skip the edges defining the triangle # Calculate normal of the border triangle v1 = cellcorners[c2] - cellcorners[c1] v2 = cellcorners[c3] - cellcorners[c1] normal = cross(v1, v2) # Check both endpoints of the other edge u = cellcorners[otheredge[0]] v = cellcorners[otheredge[1]] # Check if both are strictly on the back side if dot(normal, u - cellcorners[c1]) >= 0 or dot(normal, v - cellcorners[c1]) >= 0: continue # Edge is not completely to the back # If we reach here, the edge is completely to the back return True # Triangle is ruled out return False A pre-computed structure used to distinguish the correct triangulation from all possible triangulations in set S by performing a minimal set of 4-point tests. body: A pre-computed structure used to distinguish the correct triangulation from all possible triangulations in set S by performing a minimal set of 4-point tests. It builds on Pre-triangulation of Convex Contour by resolving the remaining ambiguity in the convex contour patches. Unlike Marching Cubes, which relies on a static lookup table for all cases, this method uses a dynamic traversal of a decision tree to select the triangulation that ensures the resulting surface is manifold and crack-less. Inputs: A set of candidate triangulations S for a specific convex contour patch. Edge intersection points on the edges of the cubic cell. A pre-computed decision tree structure for the specific patch type and sign configuration. Outputs: A single unique triangulation from set S. Data Structures: The decision tree is a binary tree where each node represents a 4-point test. Node: Contains indices of four vertices (v1, v2, v3, v4). The first three vertices define a triangle, and the fourth is the test point. Leaf: Contains the indices of the edges forming the selected triangulation. Algorithm: 1. Start at the root of the decision tree corresponding to the current patch. 2. Perform a 4-point test using the vertices (v1, v2, v3, v4) specified at the current node. 3. Determine the position of v4 relative to the triangle formed by v1, v2, v3. If v4 lies on the front-facing side of the triangle (defined by the order v1 \to v2 \to v3), traverse to the left child. Otherwise, traverse to the right child. 4. Repeat steps 2-3 until a leaf node is reached. 5. Return the triangulation stored at the leaf node. Formula: The 4-point test determines the orientation of point v4 with respect to the plane defined by v1, v2, v3. Let \mathbf{n} be the normal vector of the triangle (v1, v2, v3): \mathbf{n} = (v2 - v1) \times (v3 - v1) The test checks the sign of the dot product: d = \mathbf{n} \cdot (v4 - v1) If d > 0, the point is on the front-facing side. Parameters: Maximum depth of decision trees: 5. Average tree depth: 1.88. Maximum number of point-face trials: 5. Average number of point-face trials: \le 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision errors in floating-point calculations may affect the sign of d when v4 is nearly coplanar with the triangle. A small epsilon threshold or robust geometric predicates should be used to handle degenerate cases. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversedecisiontree(node, edgeintersections): """ Traverses a decision tree to find the correct triangulation. Args: node: A DecisionTreeNode instance. Leaf nodes have attribute triangulationedges (list of edge indices). Internal nodes have attribute testvertices (tuple of 4 edge indices). Internal nodes also have leftchild and rightchild. edgeintersections: List of 12 3D points, one for each edge of the cubic cell. Returns: A list of edge indices representing the triangulation. """ # Check if current node is a leaf if hasattr(node, 'triangulationedges'): return node.triangulationedges # Internal node: perform 4-point test v1idx, v2idx, v3idx, v4idx = node.testvertices # Map edge indices to intersection points p1 = edgeintersections[v1idx] p2 = edgeintersections[v2idx] p3 = edgeintersections[v3idx] p4 = edgeintersections[v4idx] # Calculate normal of triangle (p1, p2, p3) explicitly nx = (p2[0] - p1[0]) (p3[1] - p1[1]) - (p2[1] - p1[1]) (p3[0] - p1[0]) ny = (p2[1] - p1[1]) (p3[2] - p1[2]) - (p2[2] - p1[2]) (p3[1] - p1[1]) nz = (p2[2] - p1[2]) (p3[0] - p1[0]) - (p2[0] - p1[0]) (p3[2] - p1[2]) # Check if p4 is on the front-facing side dot = nx (p4[0] - p1[0]) + ny (p4[1] - p1[1]) + nz (p4[2] - p1[2]) if dot > 0: return traversedecisiontree(node.leftchild, edgeintersections) else: return traversedecisiontree(node.rightchild, edgeintersections) A table containing 256 entries, one for each sign configuration of a cubic cell, storing pre-computed decision trees for each patch. It allows for fast retrieval of the decision trees by the signs at the cell corners. Each entry is a list of triangulations and 4-point tests traversed from the decision tree in pre-order. Each non-leaf node contains a 4-point test (represented by indices of the four vertices). Each leaf node stores a triangulation (represented by indices of the edges on which intersections lie). This structure enables the contouring process to be performed in two steps: look up the decision trees by sign configuration, then perform 4-point tests on specified edge intersections until arriving at a single triangulation. Each entry contains the decision tree structure for the patches in that sign configuration. Performance: The method ensures manifold and crack-less contours. It is suitable for real-time navigation applications, as demonstrated in the source. Strengths: Guarantees topological correctness (manifoldness) by distinguishing the correct triangulation from all others in set S. Pre-computation allows for efficient runtime performance. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of decision trees for all patch types and sign configurations. head: Multi-resolution Convex Contouring with Decision Trees
body: Multi-resolution Convex Contouring is a view-dependent surface extraction method that accelerates rendering by contouring volumetric data at varying grid resolutions based on the viewer's distance. It extends Convex Contouring with Decision Trees by introducing transition cells to maintain topological consistency across resolution boundaries, significantly reducing triangle count and processing time while preserving visual detail. Unlike uniform contouring, it trades off some implementation complexity for performance gains, though its speed is still largely dominated by the processing of regular cells. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric scalar field defined on a nested grid structure consisting of regular cells at multiple resolutions and transition cells at the boundaries between resolutions. The viewer position determines the resolution of each cell. Output: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface, with topological consistency preserved across all resolution boundaries. Data Structures: The method relies on pre-computed look-up tables (LUTs) for transition cells. The layout is defined by the cell geometry and sign configurations at corners. 1. 2D Transition Cell: Geometry: 5 corners, 5 edges. LUT Size: Not explicitly defined as a power of 2 in the text for 2D, but treated similarly to regular cells for consistency. 2. 3D Transition Cells: 9-Corner Cell: Adjacent to two fine cells on an edge. Geometry: 9 corners, 6 faces. LUT Size: 2^9 = 512 entries. Each entry corresponds to a unique sign configuration at the 9 corners. 13-Corner Cell: Adjacent to four fine cells on a face. Geometry: 13 corners, 9 faces. LUT Size: 2^{13} = 8192 entries. Each entry corresponds to a unique sign configuration at the 13 corners. LUT Content: Each entry stores compact decision trees for patch triangulation. The decision trees determine the triangulation via successive 4-point tests on edge intersections. Algorithm Steps: 1. Grid Construction: Create a series of nested bounding boxes centered at the viewer. Assign grid resolutions to cells such that resolution decreases by a factor of 2 with increasing distance from the viewer. 2. Cell Classification: Classify each cell in the grid as either a regular cell or a transition cell. Transition cells are coarse cells adjacent to cells at a finer resolution. 3. Regular Cell Contouring: Apply standard Convex Contouring with Decision Trees to all regular cells. 4. Transition Cell Contouring: a. Face Tracing: For each transition cell, compute the linear convex contour on each face. Since the linear convex contour is unique for a given sign configuration, the boundary of patches on the convex contour can be pre-computed using the face-tracing algorithm described in the parent method. b. LUT Lookup: Determine the sign configuration at the cell's corners. Use this configuration to index into the appropriate LUT (9-corner or 13-corner) to retrieve the pre-computed decision trees for each patch. c. Perturbation (13-Corner Only): If the cell is a 13-corner cell and the convex hull of the negative space degenerates onto a plane due to four co-planar faces, apply a small outward perturbation perpendicular to the plane containing those faces. This ensures the convex hull is non-degenerate for the decision tree tests. d. Triangulation: Apply the decision trees to determine the triangulation. The 4-point tests are performed on edge intersections computed from the (perturbed, if necessary) cell corners. The final triangulation is mapped back to the unperturbed geometry to preserve topological consistency with adjacent fine cells. 5. Assembly: Combine the triangles from all regular and transition cells. The shared edges between coarse and fine cells will have identical contours, ensuring a crack-free surface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degeneracy in 13-Corner Cells: Four co-planar faces in a 13-corner cell can cause the convex hull of the negative space to degenerate onto a plane. This requires perturbation of the cell corners to perform the 4-point tests correctly. The perturbation must be small and perpendicular to the plane to ensure the convex hull structure is preserved, and the final triangulation must be mapped back to the unperturbed geometry to maintain topological consistency. Time Complexity: The performance is dominated by the processing of regular cells, as the majority of cells in a multi-resolution grid are regular. Transition cells add overhead due to larger LUTs and more complex topology, but their count is relatively small. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for LUTs for 9-corner (2^9 entries) and 13-corner (2^{13} entries) cells. The size of these LUTs is larger than those for regular cells, but they are pre-computed and static. Measured Performance: On a Dragon model at 256^3 resolution: Uniform grid: 219ms, 269,392 triangles. 2-level grid: 109ms, 137,558 triangles. 3-level grid: 47ms, 50,792 triangles. Strengths: Significantly reduces triangle count and rendering time compared to uniform contouring while preserving visual details. It allows for interactive navigation if contours on uniform grids are pre-computed and only transition cells are processed in real-time. Limitations: Performance is still dominated by uniform contouring, limiting the speedup for very high-resolution data. The implementation is more complex due to the need to handle transition cells and perturbations. When to Use: When interactive rendering of large volumetric datasets is required and the viewer position changes frequently. It is suitable when visual detail can be sacrificed at a distance without noticeable quality loss. When Not to Use: When the viewer is always close to the object (where uniform resolution is needed) or when the overhead of managing transition cells outweighs the benefits (e.g., very small datasets). Multi-resolution Convex Contouring was introduced by Jutao et al. in the paper "Convex contouring of volumetric data". It builds upon the Convex Contouring with Decision Trees method to address the computational cost of rendering high-resolution volumetric data. The method leverages the view-dependent nature of rendering to adapt the grid resolution, providing a balance between performance and visual fidelity. name: Octree-based Isosurfacing
head: Contouring using Octrees, Isosurfacing with Octree discretization
body: Octree-based isosurfacing replaces the uniform Cartesian grid of standard isosurface extraction algorithms (such as Marching Cubes or Dual Contouring) with an adaptive octree spatial discretization. This approach allows for variable resolution, refining the mesh only where the scalar field exhibits high complexity, thereby reducing memory usage and computation time for sparse or heterogeneous data. Unlike uniform grid methods, it lacks inherent topological guarantees; specifically, if the octree depth varies discontinuously around the isosurface, standard algorithms like Marching Cubes may produce topological cracks in the resulting mesh. The method operates by constructing a hierarchical spatial partition of the domain and evaluating the scalar field on this structure. The implementation typically follows a domain-object pattern where the octree, value function, and gradient function are encapsulated to decouple traversal logic from the specific surface extraction algorithm. Inputs: bbox: A 3D bounding box defined by minimum and maximum corner points. splitpredicate: A function or criterion determining whether an octree node should be subdivided. valuefunction: A function V(P) returning the scalar value at any point P in space. gradientfunction: (Optional, required for Dual Contouring) A function G(P) returning the gradient vector at any point P. isovalue: The scalar threshold t defining the isosurface. Outputs: points: A collection of 3D vertices forming the mesh. triangles: A collection of triangle indices (or polygons) forming the mesh surface. Octree Node: Represents a cubic region of space. Each node maintains a bounding box and a list of children (up to 8). Leaf nodes represent the finest resolution cells where the scalar field is sampled or interpolated. Domain Object: A generic interface that binds the octree structure with the value and gradient functions. It provides methods to query values at specific locations and traverse the tree structure. 1. Initialize Octree: Create an octree rooted at the bounding box defined by bboxmin and bboxmax. 2. Refine Octree: Recursively subdivide nodes based on the splitpredicate. The predicate typically checks if the range of scalar values within the node's bounding box contains the isovalue or if the geometric complexity exceeds a threshold. 3. Traverse to Leaves: Collect all leaf nodes of the refined octree. These leaves define the active cells for surface extraction. 4. Construct Domain: Instantiate a domain object that associates the octree with the valuefunction and gradientfunction. This allows the extraction algorithm to query scalar values at arbitrary points within the octree's spatial hierarchy. 5. Execute Extraction Algorithm: Run the chosen isosurfacing algorithm (e.g., Marching Cubes or Dual Contouring) on the domain object. For Marching Cubes: The algorithm traverses the octree leaves, identifies edges crossing the isovalue, and generates triangles. Note that mismatched depths between adjacent leaves can lead to cracks. For Dual Contouring: The algorithm computes vertices inside cells and projects them onto the isosurface using gradients. It may skip face triangulation if specified. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def octreeisosurfacing(bboxmin, bboxmax, splitpredicate, valuefunc, gradientfunc, isovalue, algorithm="dualcontouring"): # 1. Initialize Octree octree = Octree() octree.initialize(bboxmin, bboxmax) # 2. Refine Octree # The splitpredicate determines if a node should be subdivided. # It typically evaluates the range of values in the node's bounding box. octree.refine(splitpredicate) # 3. Traverse to Leaves # Collect all leaf nodes to define the active domain leaves = octree.traverseleaves() # 4. Construct Domain Object # Bind the octree structure with the value and gradient functions values = ValueFunction(valuefunc, octree) gradients = GradientFunction(gradientfunc, octree) domain = Domain(octree, values, gradients) # 5. Execute Extraction points = [] triangles = [] if algorithm == "dualcontouring": # Run Dual Contouring # Parameters: donottriangulatefaces=True, constraintocell=False dualcontouring(domain, isovalue, points, triangles, donottriangulatefaces=True, constraintocell=False) elif algorithm == "marchingcubes": # Run Marching Cubes # Note: Cracks may appear if octree is not adapted to surface marchingcubes(domain, isovalue, points, triangles) return points, triangles donottriangulatefaces: Boolean flag for Dual Contouring. If true, skips the triangulation of polygonal faces, outputting polylines or polygons instead of triangles. constraintocell: Boolean flag for Dual Contouring. If false, allows vertices to be placed anywhere within the cell, not just constrained to the cell boundaries. Cracks: In Marching Cubes, if adjacent octree leaves have different depths (i.e., one leaf is a child of a coarse node while its neighbor is a coarse node itself), the shared face may not be triangulated consistently, leading to topological holes or cracks. Lack of Guarantees: Unlike uniform grid methods, octree-based extraction does not guarantee a watertight mesh unless specific constraints or post-processing (like crack-fixing algorithms) are applied. Predicate Design: The splitpredicate must be robust. If it fails to subdivide a node containing the isosurface, the surface will be missed. If it over-subdivides, performance degrades. The Standard Interval Tree is a spatial indexing structure used to efficiently identify active cells (cells intersected by an isosurface) in volumetric data, serving as a pre-processing step for surface extraction algorithms like Marching Cubes or Marching Tetrahedra. It solves the problem of O(N) traversal cost by providing optimal output-sensitive query complexity O(\log n + k), where n is the number of cells and k is the number of active cells. It sets itself apart from its parent Octree-based Isosurfacing by operating on a fixed logical grid structure rather than an adaptive octree, and from siblings like IsoOctree by using a binary tree of value intervals rather than a spatial hierarchy of cell groups. Marching Cubes with Octree extracts a triangle mesh from an implicit scalar field defined over an adaptive octree structure, replacing the uniform Cartesian grid of standard Marching Cubes. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on a generic domain interface (MCDomain) that decouples the traversal logic from the specific octree implementation, allowing for parallel execution and arbitrary split predicates. Unlike uniform grid methods, it adapts resolution to the field's complexity, but it lacks inherent guarantees against topological cracks if the octree depth varies discontinuously around the isosurface. IsoOctree is an unconstrained isosurface extraction method that operates on arbitrary octrees by computing the Euclidean Distance Transform (EDT) of an input mesh and adapting the octree to sample this transform. It solves the problem of generating simplified, adaptive polygonal representations of meshes by refining the octree resolution near the surface and in high-curvature regions. It sets itself apart from constrained octree methods by allowing arbitrary octree structures (non-conforming) and by operating on the distance field rather than raw scalar voxel data, enabling direct mesh simplification. A hierarchical spatial subdivision method using an octree to accelerate isosurface extraction by pruning branches that cannot contain the isosurface. It differs from uniform grid methods by adapting resolution to data density and from sibling octree methods by relying on strict value-range bounding intervals for early termination during traversal. Ashida and Badla Octree Contouring is an isosurface extraction method that operates directly on adaptive octrees, avoiding the need for a uniform grid or dual hexahedral mesh. It identifies cycles of contour faces intersecting each octree cell and generates one vertex per cycle. Unlike Wilhelms and Van Gelder Octree which may require complex crack-fixing, this method aims for manifold output through cycle identification, though it is computationally expensive and prone to non-manifold artifacts between neighboring cells. This method extracts a provably watertight isosurface directly from an arbitrary octree without requiring tree refinement or modification of vertex values. Unlike dual marching cubes, which can generate topological holes in flat regions, this primal approach guarantees that the isosurface separates samples on opposite sides of the isovalue by introducing an isovertex along every isovalue-crossing edge. It sets itself apart by using binary edge-trees to resolve inconsistencies at face boundaries between leaf nodes of different depths, ensuring watertightness even when the octree topology is unconstrained. This method defines the position of an isovertex on an octree edge consistently by traversing an "edge-tree" to a unique leaf node with value 1, ensuring watertightness in isosurface extraction. It solves the problem of ambiguous isovertex positions when a coarse edge contains multiple sign changes, which causes standard polygonization methods like [Blo88] to fail. Unlike methods that refine the tree or modify vertex values, this approach uses the existing edge-tree structure to resolve ambiguity, ensuring that the extracted isopolylines are closed loops and each edge is shared by exactly two isopolygons. It differs from the minimal edge definition in [JLSW02] only when there is more than one isovalue-crossing along an edge. This method generates an adaptive octree for isosurface extraction by recursively refining nodes based on the geometric flatness of the surface intersection, assigning vertex values via Euclidean distance transform sampling. It differs from sibling methods like IsoOctree and Wilhelms and Van Gelder Octree by using a curvature-based flatness metric rather than simple field uniformity or depth constraints to determine refinement, allowing for coarser representation of planar surface regions. Sampled DMC is a mesh generation technique that adapts the Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) algorithm to hashed octrees using Morton keys. It constructs a dual grid where vertices are located at the center of each octree leaf node, allowing for adaptive resolution isosurfacing without requiring a uniform grid. Unlike standard Marching Cubes implementations that expect Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) as direct input, Sampled DMC takes the data octree itself, making it suitable for storing and extracting meshes from sampled points, complex SDFs, or destructible environments. Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration is a recursive octree traversal algorithm designed to extract isosurface meshes from volumetric data discretized by an octree. It solves the problem of adapting standard Marching Cubes to non-uniform spatial structures by explicitly enumerating voxel faces, edges, and vertices across potentially mismatched tree depths, delegating the actual mesh generation to a standard Marching Cubes routine only at leaf nodes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by its explicit separation of traversal logic (face, edge, vertex enumeration) from the surface extraction logic, allowing for robust handling of arbitrary octree configurations without requiring a globally consistent grid. The elementary method for cell extraction that sequentially visits all cells in the volume to identify active cells containing the isosurface. For each cell C{i,j,k}, it checks if the isovalue t is contained in the half-open interval [v{min}, v{max}), where v{min} = \min(V{i,j,k}) and v{max} = \max(V{i,j,k}). The range of the interpolation function \hat{f} in a cell is defined as \hat{f}(C{i,j,k}) = [v{min}, v{max}]. This method requires only storage for the original volume data and a small constant amount for variables, with a time complexity of O(n), where n is the size of the volume data. Time Complexity: The time complexity depends on the extraction algorithm and the octree structure. For canonical enumeration on the octree leaves, it is linear in the number of leaves n. However, the refinement phase adds overhead. The primary benefit is that the number of active cells (leaves) is often much smaller than the total number of cells in a uniform grid of equivalent maximum resolution, leading to faster extraction for sparse data. Memory Complexity: The octree structure requires additional memory for node pointers and metadata compared to a flat array. However, it significantly reduces memory usage compared to a uniform grid of the same maximum resolution, as only relevant regions are stored. Strengths: Adaptive resolution allows for high-fidelity representation of complex surfaces with fewer polygons. Efficient pruning of empty space. Limitations: Lack of topological guarantees (cracks) in standard algorithms like Marching Cubes. Increased implementation complexity due to tree traversal and domain abstraction. Performance can degrade if the split predicate causes excessive refinement. When to Use: Suitable for large, sparse, or heterogeneous volumetric data where uniform grid resolution is prohibitive. Ideal for applications requiring variable detail levels. When Not to Use: When topological correctness (watertightness) is critical and cannot be ensured by post-processing or specific algorithm variants (like Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction). When the data is dense and uniform, a simple Cartesian grid may be faster and simpler. Octree-based isosurfacing emerged as a solution to the memory and computational limitations of uniform grid methods for large-scale volumetric data. Wilhelms and Van Gelder proposed using octrees for isosurface extraction to accelerate the cell identification phase by pruning branches that cannot contain the isosurface. This approach was later integrated with standard algorithms like Marching Cubes and Dual Contouring, as demonstrated in libraries such as CGAL. The method addresses the need for adaptive resolution in scientific visualization and computer graphics, allowing for detailed surface representation where needed while ignoring empty space. 3D Isosurfacing, https://doc.cgal.org/latest/Isosurfacing3/index.html, fetched 2026-10-29 Optimal hybrid memory constrained isosurface extraction, http://nbn-resolving.de/urn:nbn:de:bsz:352-130091, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction
head: Cignoni et al. Interval Tree, Interval Tree, Interval-Tree Based Isosurface Extraction, Normal Interval Tree
body: The Standard Interval Tree is a spatial indexing structure used to efficiently identify active cells (cells intersected by an isosurface) in volumetric data, serving as a pre-processing step for surface extraction algorithms like Marching Cubes or Marching Tetrahedra. It solves the problem of O(N) traversal cost by providing optimal output-sensitive query complexity O(\log n + k), where n is the number of cells and k is the number of active cells. It sets itself apart from its parent Octree-based Isosurfacing by operating on a fixed logical grid structure rather than an adaptive octree, and from siblings like IsoOctree by using a binary tree of value intervals rather than a spatial hierarchy of cell groups. Inputs: A structured volume grid of dimensions \Delta x \times \Delta y \times \Delta z, containing m = (\Delta x - 1)(\Delta y - 1)(\Delta z - 1) cells. Each cell i has a scalar value range [v{min}^i, v{max}^i]. A target isovalue t. Outputs: A list of active cells C{active} such that v{min}^i \le t \le v{max}^i for all i \in C{active}. Data Structures: The structure is a binary tree. Each node stores: 1. A threshold value t0. 2. Two doubly-linked lists (or arrays) of cell indices: min-list: Cells sorted by increasing v{min}. max-list: Cells sorted by decreasing v{max}. 3. Pointers to left and right children. Memory Layout: For each cell stored in a node, the storage consists of: v{min} (2 bytes, typically) v{max} (2 bytes, typically) Pointer to cell in min-list (4 bytes) Pointer to cell in max-list (4 bytes) Total per cell: 12 bytes. The total memory overhead for the general representation is 3h + 2m words, where h is the number of distinct extremes of intervals and m is the number of cells. In 8-bit volumes, the total space usage including the volume data is approximately 9 times the size of the raw volume data. Construction Algorithm: 1. Collect all cell intervals [v{min}^i, v{max}^i] for i = 1 \dots m. 2. Call BuildTree(intervals): a. If intervals is empty, return null. b. Choose a threshold t0 from the set of interval endpoints. (Optimal choice minimizes tree height; a common heuristic is the median of the endpoints). c. Partition intervals into three sets: S{contain}: Intervals where v{min} \le t0 \le v{max}. S{below}: Intervals where v{max} < t0. S{above}: Intervals where v{min} > t0. d. Create a new node with threshold t0. e. For each cell in S{contain}: i. Add cell to the node's min-list and max-list. ii. Insert into min-list maintaining sort order of v{min}. iii. Insert into max-list maintaining sort order of v{max}. f. Set node.left = BuildTree(Sbelow). g. Set node.right = BuildTree(Sabove). h. Return node. Query Algorithm: 1. Start at root. 2. If root is null, return empty list. 3. Let t be the target isovalue. 4. If t < root.t0: a. Iterate through root.min-list from the beginning. b. For each cell c in the list: i. If c.v{min} > t, stop iteration (list is sorted by increasing v{min}, so no subsequent cells can contain t). ii. Else, add c to C{active}. c. Recurse: C{active} \leftarrow C{active} \cup \text{Query}(root.left, t). 5. Else If t > root.t0: a. Iterate through root.max-list from the beginning. b. For each cell c in the list: i. If c.v{max} \le t, stop iteration (list is sorted by decreasing v{max}, so no subsequent cells can contain t). ii. Else, add c to C{active}. c. Recurse: C{active} \leftarrow C{active} \cup \text{Query}(root.right, t). 6. Else (t = root.t0): a. Add all cells in root.min-list (or root.max-list) to C{active}. b. Return C{active} (terminate search, as all containing intervals are stored here). Parameters: Pointer size: 4 bytes. Value type size: 2 bytes (commonly used for 16-bit scalars). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Space Inefficiency: The memory overhead is significant. For 8-bit volumes, total space is ~9x the volume size. This can be prohibitive for large datasets. Threshold Selection: Poor choice of t0 leads to unbalanced trees, degrading query performance from O(\log n) to O(n). Duplicate Reporting: The algorithm ensures each active cell is reported exactly once because intervals are partitioned into disjoint sets (S{contain}, S{below}, S{above}) at each step. Fixed-Sized Buckets is an output-optimal algorithm for accelerated isosurface extraction from volumetric data sets. It identifies active cells (cells intersected by the isosurface) with work proportional to the output size rather than the input size, using a logical 2D array data structure to sort cells by intensity ranges. It sets itself apart from its parent Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction by using a simpler array-based structure that avoids tree traversal overhead, and from siblings like Interval Table for Isosurface Extraction by relying on two-pass sorting rather than interval merging. The Interval Tree with Cell Grouping is a memory-optimized variant of the Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction. It reduces the memory overhead of the auxiliary lists by having each pointer reference a group of eight adjacent cells rather than a single cell, resulting in a tree size approximately 1/8th that of a regular interval tree. This reduction comes at the cost of increased query time, as intersecting groups require checking all eight constituent cells individually. Span Space Isosurface Extraction is a method for rapidly locating cells intersecting an isosurface in large scalar datasets by mapping cell extrema to a 2D "span space" and indexing them with a kd-tree. It solves the problem of efficient interval search by reducing the dimensionality of the query from interval containment to point location relative to the diagonal y=x. Unlike the Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction, which achieves O(\log n + k) query complexity, this method achieves a worst-case search complexity of O(\sqrt{n} + k). It is chosen when a simpler, pointerless kd-tree implementation is preferred over complex interval tree structures, accepting a slightly higher worst-case asymptotic bound for potentially better constant factors and memory locality. Out-of-core Interval Tree Extraction is a method for isosurface extraction that stores the interval tree and associated min/max lists on disk in blocks, loading only the necessary blocks based on isovalue intervals. It builds on Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction by partitioning the tree structure to fit within fixed-size disk blocks, enabling the processing of datasets larger than available main memory. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly models the I/O cost of reading tree nodes and min/max lists as a function of isovalue probability distributions. The Interval Table is a pre-processing data structure that maps scalar value intervals to tetrahedron IDs, allowing the extraction algorithm to skip tetrahedra whose function span does not contain the isovalue. It differs from the Standard Interval Tree by using a fixed-size array of buckets (intervals) rather than a dynamic tree structure, offering a simpler implementation with comparable performance for uniform scalar distributions. Matryoshka Layer Insertion is a data structure construction technique where cells are inserted into layers defined by six planes (X=x0, X=x1, Y=y0, Y=y1, Z=z0, Z=z1) based on coordinate minima, allowing O(1) insertion and O(k) total construction time for k cells. Steps: 1. Calculate min^1 as the minimum of the values cellx, celly, cellz. 2. Calculate min^2 as the minimum of the values (\Delta x - 1) - cellx, (\Delta y - 1) - celly, (\Delta z - 1) - cellz. 3. Determine the layer index by taking the minimum of min^1 and min^2. 4. Inside the selected layer, insert the cell into the appropriate plane list by checking if cellx equals x0 or x1; if not, check celly against y0/y1, then cellz against z0/z1. Pitfall: To avoid a second processing round, the insertion of a cell in the layers is merged into the query process of the interval tree. Complexity: Construction complexity is O(k) where k is the number of cells; memory overhead is directly proportional to k. Edge-Covering Space Reduction is a space reduction technique for interval/kd-trees by restricting the data structure to a subset of cells that covers all edges, reducing storage by a factor of 4. Steps: 1. Select a subset of cells such that every edge in the volume grid is covered by at least one selected cell. Since an edge is shared by four cells, only one out of four neighboring cells needs to be considered. 2. After extraction from the data structure, propagate the isosurface from the reported active cells onto neighboring cells that were not covered in the data structure. Time Complexity: Query: O(\log n + k), where n is the number of cells and k is the number of active cells. Search Complexity: Specifically O(k + \log h), where h is the number of nodes in the tree. For scalar data volumes, k (active cells) usually dominates \log n, as k is often in the hundreds of thousands or millions. Memory Complexity: General representation: O(n) space. Specifically 3h + 2m words, where h is the number of distinct extremes and m is the number of cells. Pointer overhead: For 8-bit volumes, the interval tree holds pointers to cells in two auxiliary lists, with each cell referenced by two pointers. With 4-byte pointers, the space overhead is 8(\Delta x - 1)(\Delta y - 1)(\Delta z - 1) bytes. Total space usage including volume data is approximately 9 times the size of the volume. Performance and Scaling: The method considerably improves the performance of the traversal phase with respect to standard marching tetrahedra and marching cubes algorithms. Memory overhead becomes a critical factor in high-resolution datasets. Strategies to reduce space occupancy include optimized representations for unstructured datasets (reducing overhead to 3h + m, <25%) and chess-board approaches for structured datasets. Strengths: Optimal output-sensitive time complexity for active cell extraction. Effective speedup for isosurface extraction traversal. Limitations: High memory consumption (up to 9x volume size) can be prohibitive. Not adaptive to memory constraints without hybrid approaches. When to use: When fast extraction of active cells is required and sufficient memory is available. When the number of active cells is large relative to the total cells, making O(\log n + k) significantly better than O(n). When not to use: When memory is severely constrained and O(n) overhead is unacceptable. When the dataset is extremely large and out-of-core processing is required (use Out-of-core Interval Tree Extraction). The Standard Interval Tree for isosurface extraction was proposed by Cignoni, Marino, Montani, and Puppo. It is based on the general properties of interval trees [BvKOS00, Ede80] and was introduced as an alternative to kd-trees for spatial indexing in visualization. The method was tested on various structured and unstructured datasets, demonstrating significant speedups over standard marching algorithms. It is cited in the Visualization Handbook and various research papers on optimal hybrid memory constrained isosurface extraction. name: Fixed-Sized Buckets for Isosurface Extraction
head: Fixed-Sized Buckets, Isosurface Extraction Using Fixed-Sized Buckets, SpanQuad, SpanQuad method, Waters-Co-Joy Method
body: Fixed-Sized Buckets is an output-optimal algorithm for accelerated isosurface extraction from volumetric data sets. It identifies active cells (cells intersected by the isosurface) with work proportional to the output size rather than the input size, using a logical 2D array data structure to sort cells by intensity ranges. It sets itself apart from its parent Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction by using a simpler array-based structure that avoids tree traversal overhead, and from siblings like Interval Table for Isosurface Extraction by relying on two-pass sorting rather than interval merging. Inputs: An array R of N cell records, where each record contains a handle to the cell, its minimum intensity value (min), and its maximum intensity value (max). A user-defined bucket size B. An isovalue q. Outputs: A list of active cells intersected by the isosurface defined by q. Data Structures: The method maintains a logical 2D array implemented as a 1D array mcells of Record structs. struct Record: Contains CellHandle cell, Type min, and Type max. Type depends on the data precision (e.g., float, int). mcells: Stores all N records. The array is divided into buckets of size B. mmindict: An array of size numbuckets storing the min value of the last cell in each bucket. This acts as a lookup table to quickly identify active buckets. mlastbkt: The index of the last bucket. mlastbktlen: The number of cells in the last bucket (which may be smaller than B). Construction: 1. Sort by Min: Sort all N records in mcells by their min value in ascending order. 2. Calculate Buckets: Compute numbuckets = N / B + 1. Set mlastbkt = numbuckets - 1 and mlastbktlen = N - mlastbkt B. 3. Build Min-Dictionary: For each bucket i from 0 to mlastbkt - 1, set mmindict[i] to the min value of the last cell in that bucket (index (i+1)B - 1). Set mmindict[mlastbkt] to the min value of the last cell in the entire array (index N-1). 4. Sort by Max: Within each bucket, resort the records by their max value in descending order. For full buckets (i < m\last\bkt), sort B cells starting at mcells[iB]. For the last bucket, sort mlastbktlen cells starting at mcells[mlastbktB]. Full Extraction: Given isovalue q: 1. Outer Loop (Active Buckets): Iterate through buckets c0, c1, \dots using mmindict. A bucket ci trivially satisfies the min-criterion if mmindict[i] >= q. Let ca be the final active bucket where mmindict[a] < q. All buckets c0 \dots c{a-1} satisfy the min-criterion trivially. 2. Inner Loop (Normal Buckets): For each bucket ci where i < a, traverse its records. Since records are sorted by max descending, collect cells as active as long as record.max >= q. Stop when record.max < q or the end of the bucket is reached. These active cells form a contiguous block at the start of the bucket. 3. Special Case (Last Active Bucket ca): For bucket ca, the min-criterion is not trivially satisfied. Iterate through all records in this bucket (up to lim records, where lim is B or mlastbktlen). For each record, check both record.max >= q AND q >= record.min. If both hold, the cell is active. Active cells in this bucket may be non-contiguous. Incremental Extraction (Increasing Isovalue q' > q): Maintain markers for each bucket tracking the last visited cell during the previous extraction. 1. Identify Bucket Categories: Buckets c0 \dots c{a-1} remain active but may contain cells that become inactive (deactivation needed). Bucket ca remains active but may have interleaved active/inactive cells (activation/deactivation needed). New buckets c{a+1} \dots c{a'} become active (activation needed). 2. Process: Use markers to skip cells known to be unchanged. For deactivation, check cells from the marker to the end of the active block. For activation, check new buckets and the split region in ca. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class SpanQuad: def init(self, B): self.B = B self.mcells = None self.mmindict = None self.mlastbkt = 0 self.mlastbktlen = 0 def construct(self, R, N): # Step 1: Sort all cells by min # Assuming R is a list of objects with.min,.max,.cell R.sort(key=lambda x: x.min) self.mcells = R # Step 2: Calculate bucket parameters numbuckets = N // self.B + 1 self.mlastbkt = numbuckets - 1 self.mlastbktlen = N - self.mlastbkt self.B # Step 3: Create min-dictionary self.mmindict = [0] numbuckets for i in range(self.mlastbkt): # Last cell in bucket i is at index (i+1)B - 1 self.mmindict[i] = self.mcells[(i + 1) self.B - 1].min # Last bucket's min-dict entry is the last cell in the entire array self.mmindict[self.mlastbkt] = self.mcells[N - 1].min # Step 4: Sort each bucket by max (descending) for i in range(self.mlastbkt): # Sort B cells starting at iB startidx = i self.B endidx = startidx + self.B self.mcells[startidx:endidx].sort(key=lambda x: x.max, reverse=True) # Sort the last bucket startidx = self.mlastbkt self.B endidx = startidx + self.mlastbktlen self.mcells[startidx:endidx].sort(key=lambda x: x.max, reverse=True) def search(self, q, addcellcallback): cb = 0 # Normal active buckets: trivially satisfy min-criterion while cb < self.mlastbkt and q >= self.mmindict[cb]: rec = 0 startidx = cb self.B # Traverse records in this bucket for i in range(startidx, startidx + self.B): record = self.mcells[i] if record.max >= q: addcellcallback(record.cell) rec += 1 else: # Since sorted by max descending, remaining cells fail max-criterion break # Last active bucket ca lim = self.mlastbktlen if cb == self.mlastbkt else self.B startidx = cb self.B for i in range(startidx, startidx + lim): record = self.mcells[i] if record.max >= q and q >= record.min: addcellcallback(record.cell) An optimization that reuses state from a previous query to accelerate new queries by tracking active/inactive cell boundaries via markers, avoiding full re-scanning. It builds on Fixed-Sized Buckets by maintaining boundary markers that allow the algorithm to skip over cells whose active status is known to be unchanged. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N \log N), dominated by the first sorting pass. The second pass is O((N/B) \cdot B \log B) = O(N \log B), which is subsumed if B is constant. Initial extraction and average-case runtime complexity is O(K), where K is the number of active cells, making it output optimal. Worst-case performance is O(N). Memory Complexity: The method incurs a 3 + 1/B factor increase in memory consumption relative to the input data, or 3 + 2/B if incremental search is desired. For large B, this factor is effectively 3. Strengths: Simple implementation, output optimal average-case performance, works with floating-point and quantized data, small memory footprint. Limitations: Worst-case O(N) performance. The last active bucket requires checking all B cells, which can be a bottleneck if B is large and the isosurface is sparse in that region. When to use: When output optimality is critical and the data distribution allows for efficient bucketing. Suitable for large-scale visualization systems where incremental extraction is beneficial. The method was introduced by Kenneth W. Waters, Christopher S. Co, and Kenneth I. Joy at the University of California, Davis. It is used in the SpanQuad class implementation for isosurface extraction, demonstrated with Engine and Kyle unstructured flow simulation data sets. The method is amenable to out-of-core implementation using out-of-core sorting algorithms. name: Incremental Isosurface Extraction
head: Incremental extraction, Incremental search
body: Incremental isosurface extraction is an optimization for isosurface extraction that reuses the state from a previous query (with isovalue q) to accelerate a new query (with isovalue q'), avoiding full re-scanning of the data structure by tracking active/inactive cell boundaries via markers. It builds on Fixed-Sized Buckets for Isosurface Extraction by maintaining boundary markers that allow the algorithm to skip over cells whose active status is known to be unchanged, rather than re-evaluating every cell in the active range. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The fixed-sized bucket data structure (min-dictionary, cell records, and optional marker cells), the previous isovalue q, the new isovalue q', and the previous set of active buckets/cells. Output: The set of active cells for isovalue q'. Data Structures: The method relies on the data structure from Fixed-Sized Buckets, extended with markers for incremental operation: Cell Records: N records, one for each cell in the dataset. Min-Dictionary: N/B + 1 values, storing the minimum intensity value for each bucket. Marker Cells: N/B + 1 additional cells (one per bucket) used to track the boundary between active and inactive cells within a bucket. These are only required if incremental extraction is used. Memory Complexity: O(N + 2 \cdot N/B + 2) = O(N). Parameters: B: Bucket size (number of cells per bucket). Typical value is 4096. Empirical results show average active cell lookup time decreases toward 4096 and increases past 8192. The optimal choice is not related to input data size. Algorithm Steps: The algorithm distinguishes between increasing isovalue (q' > q) and decreasing isovalue (q' < q). Let c^0, \dots, c^a be the set of active buckets for the previous isovalue q, and c^0, \dots, c^{a'} be the set for the new isovalue q'. The buckets to visit fall into three categories: 1. Buckets c^0 \dots c^{a-1} remain active: These buckets were active in the previous query and remain active. Markers are pushed upward to deactivate cells that are no longer active. Only the max-criterion is checked when updating markers because the bucket satisfies the min-criterion (it is already known to be active). 2. The former last active bucket c^a: This bucket now has a single contiguous block of active cells and a single contiguous block of inactive cells. Cells are traversed one by one to determine activation/deactivation status. 3. Buckets c^{a+1} \dots c^{a'} have just become active: These buckets were inactive in the previous query but are now active. The full extraction method is applied starting at bucket c^{a+1} rather than c^0. The buckets to visit fall into three categories: 1. Buckets c^0 \dots c^{a'-1} remain active: These buckets were active in the previous query and remain active. Markers are pushed downward to activate cells that are newly active. Only the max-criterion is checked in updating markers. 2. The new last active bucket c^{a'}: This bucket contains non-contiguous blocks of cells that must be activated and deactivated. Cells are traversed to determine status. 3. Buckets c^{a'+1} \dots c^a have become inactive: These buckets were active in the previous query but are now inactive. The full extraction method is applied starting at bucket c^{a'+1}, but instead of activating cells, the visited cells are deactivated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalextraction(mindict, cellvalues, prevactivebuckets, prevmarkers, q, qprime, B): """ Incremental isosurface extraction using fixed-sized buckets. Args: mindict: List of minimum intensity values per bucket. cellvalues: List of intensity values for all N cells. prevactivebuckets: List of bucket indices active for isovalue q. prevmarkers: List of marker indices per bucket from previous query. q: Previous isovalue. qprime: New isovalue. B: Bucket size (cells per bucket). Returns: activecells: List of cell indices active for qprime. newmarkers: Updated marker indices per bucket. """ # Determine new active buckets: bucket is active if its minimum value <= isovalue newactivebuckets = [b for b in range(len(mindict)) if mindict[b] <= qprime] activecells = [] newmarkers = list(prevmarkers) if qprime > q: # === Increasing Isovalue === # 1. Buckets c0...ca-1 remain active for i in range(len(prevactivebuckets) - 1): b = prevactivebuckets[i] marker = prevmarkers[b] start = b B # Push marker upward to deactivate cells passed along the way. # Only max-criterion (cellvalue <= qprime) is checked. for idx in range(marker, start - 1, -1): if cellvalues[idx] > qprime: marker -= 1 else: break newmarkers[b] = marker activecells.extend(range(start, marker + 1)) # 2. Former last active bucket ca if prevactivebuckets: b = prevactivebuckets[-1] start = b B end = min(start + B, len(cellvalues)) # Traverse cells one by one to determine activation/deactivation for idx in range(start, end): if cellvalues[idx] <= qprime: activecells.append(idx) # 3. Buckets ca+1...ca' have just become active startidx = len(prevactivebuckets) for i in range(startidx, len(newactivebuckets)): b = newactivebuckets[i] start = b B end = min(start + B, len(cellvalues)) # Full extraction method applied starting at this bucket # (see Fixed-Sized Buckets for Isosurface Extraction) for idx in range(start, end): if cellvalues[idx] <= qprime: activecells.append(idx) else: # === Decreasing Isovalue === # 1. Buckets c0...ca'-1 remain active for i in range(len(newactivebuckets) - 1): b = newactivebuckets[i] marker = prevmarkers[b] start = b B end = min(start + B, len(cellvalues)) # Push marker downward to activate cells passed along the way. # Only max-criterion is checked. for idx in range(marker, end): if cellvalues[idx] <= qprime: marker += 1 else: break newmarkers[b] = marker activecells.extend(range(start, marker + 1)) # 2. New last active bucket ca' if newactivebuckets: b = newactivebuckets[-1] start = b B end = min(start + B, len(cellvalues)) # Traverse cells to determine status (handles non-contiguous blocks) for idx in range(start, end): if cellvalues[idx] <= qprime: activecells.append(idx) # 3. Buckets ca'+1...ca have become inactive startidx = len(newactivebuckets) for i in range(startidx, len(prevactivebuckets)): # Cells are deactivated by not being added to activecells pass return activecells, newmarkers Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pathological Worst-Case: If only one cell is active and located at the bottom of the last bucket, the algorithm traverses N/B buckets and B inactive cells. This is extremely rare in real application data. Time Complexity: Average-Case: O(K + B), where K is the number of active cells and B is the bucket size. This is derived from at most three comparisons per cell in a normal bucket (one max-criterion per active cell, one min-dictionary check, one failed max-criterion check per bucket) and at most two comparisons per cell in the last active bucket (bounded by B). Total: O(3K + 2B) = O(K + B). Worst-Case: O(N/B + B) = O(N), if only one cell is active and located at the bottom of the last bucket, traversing N/B buckets and B inactive cells. If B = \sqrt{N}, the average and worst case extraction is upper-bounded to O(K + \sqrt{N}). Memory Complexity: O(N), with a constant factor increase of 3 + 1/B without incremental extraction markers and 3 + 2/B with incremental extraction markers. Measured Performance: RockerArm Dataset: Full extraction average search time 0.967 ms; Incremental extraction 0.444 ms; Coherence 63%. Engine Dataset: Full extraction average search time 2.285 ms; Incremental extraction 0.432 ms; Coherence 88%. Strengths: Competitive with the interval tree method, an optimal technique. Achieves O(K) performance on average for real datasets. Limitations: Performance depends on the coherence of the data. Pathological worst-case is rare but possible. Incremental isosurface extraction was proposed in the paper "Isosurface Extraction Using Fixed-Sized Buckets" (2005) as an optimization for the fixed-sized bucket method. It was designed to improve performance in scenarios where isovalue changes are frequent and coherent, such as in interactive visualization or animation. The method is competitive with the interval tree method, which is considered an optimal technique for isosurface extraction. name: Interval Tree with Cell Grouping
head: Grouped Interval Tree
body: The Interval Tree with Cell Grouping is a memory-optimized variant of the Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction. It reduces the memory overhead of the auxiliary lists by having each pointer reference a group of eight adjacent cells rather than a single cell, resulting in a tree size approximately 1/8th that of a regular interval tree. This reduction comes at the cost of increased query time, as intersecting groups require checking all eight constituent cells individually. Inputs: A 3D scalar volume grid; an isovalue q. Outputs: A list of active cells (or groups of cells) intersecting the isovalue q. Data Structures: The tree structure mirrors the Standard Interval Tree but with grouped pointers. Node: Contains a splitting value qx and two auxiliary lists: I-Left and I-Right. Pointer: Each entry in I-Left and I-Right is a pointer to a group of eight adjacent cells. Group Definition: The volume is partitioned into disjoint groups of eight adjacent cells. The group with the lowest coordinates (x, y, z) serves as the representative for the set. The group's bounding box is defined by the global minimum and maximum values of all eight constituent cells. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construction: 1. Partition the volume into disjoint groups of eight adjacent cells. 2. For each group, compute the global minimum value v{min} and global maximum value v{max} across all eight cells. 3. Insert the group into the interval tree using v{min} and v{max} as the interval bounds, treating the group as a single entity. 4. Store the pointer to the group in the appropriate auxiliary lists (I-Left for cells with v{max} < qx, I-Right for cells with v{min} > qx). 2. Query: 1. Traverse the tree to find nodes where the interval [v{min}, v{max}] intersects the query isovalue q. 2. For each intersecting node, iterate through the I-Left and I-Right lists. 3. Stop Condition: Terminate iteration through a specific list as soon as a group is encountered whose interval does not intersect q. 4. Verification: For every group identified as intersecting q, iterate through all eight constituent cells. 5. Check each of the eight cells individually to determine if the isovalue q lies within their specific scalar range. 6. Add all cells that satisfy the condition to the output list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def querygroupedintervaltree(root, q): activecells = [] traverse(root, q, activecells) return activecells def traverse(node, q, activecells): if node is None: return # Check if the node's interval intersects q if node.maxval < q or node.minval > q: return # Check auxiliary lists # I-Left: sorted by maxval ascending. Stop when maxval < q. for group in node.ileft: if group.maxval < q: break verifygroupcells(group, q, activecells) # I-Right: sorted by minval descending. Stop when minval > q. for group in node.iright: if group.minval > q: break verifygroupcells(group, q, activecells) # Recurse if node.leftchild: traverse(node.leftchild, q, activecells) if node.rightchild: traverse(node.rightchild, q, activecells) def verifygroupcells(group, q, activecells): # Iterate through the 8 constituent cells of the group for cell in group.cells: if cell.minval <= q <= cell.maxval: activecells.append(cell) Parameters: Group Size: 8 cells per pointer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Worst-Case Query Performance: The complexity degrades to O(\log(n) + 8k) if the isosurface intersects exactly one cell from each group of eight. This scenario is rare in practical data volumes but represents the theoretical upper bound. Precision: The method relies on exact comparisons of scalar values. Floating-point precision issues may affect boundary conditions where q equals a cell's min or max value. An extension that combines cell grouping with sorting information to accelerate queries. Definition: Stores pointers to groups of eight cells in two lists, sorted by the group's minimum value (ascending) and maximum value (descending). Layout: Each group includes an order vector of eight numbers (1–8), indicating the permutation of cells within the group. This vector requires 3 bits per number, totaling 24 bits (3 bytes) per group. Complexity: Space overhead is 1.75 bytes per cell (calculated as 2 \times (4 \text{ bytes pointer} + 3 \text{ bytes order}) / 8 \text{ cells}). Query times are intermediate between the standard interval tree and the unsorted grouped tree. Usage: Choose when memory is constrained but query speed of the basic grouped tree is insufficient. Time Complexity: Query complexity is O(\log(n) + 8k), where k is the number of active cells in the original (un-grouped) tree. The factor of 8 arises from the worst-case need to check all sub-cells in intersecting groups. Memory Complexity: The total size of the interval tree is approximately 1/8th of a regular interval tree. The height of the tree is also reduced because it effectively manages 1/8th the number of nodes. Performance: Tests on an 8-bit volume show significant size reduction compared to the standard tree. Query times are slower than the standard interval tree but faster than the unsorted grouped variant when ordering is applied. Strengths: Drastic reduction in memory footprint, enabling larger volumes to fit in cache or main memory. Limitations: Increased query time due to per-cell verification within groups; worst-case performance is significantly worse than the standard tree. The Interval Tree with Cell Grouping was introduced as a method to address the prohibitive memory requirements of standard interval trees for isosurface extraction, which can require up to nine times the size of the volume data. It was proposed in the context of the Matryoshka Algorithm for speeding up isosurfacing. name: Span Space Isosurface Extraction
head: Span Space Algorithm, Livat, Shen, and Johnson method
body: Span Space Isosurface Extraction is a method for rapidly locating cells intersecting an isosurface in large scalar datasets by mapping cell extrema to a 2D "span space" and indexing them with a kd-tree. It solves the problem of efficient interval search by reducing the dimensionality of the query from interval containment to point location relative to the diagonal y=x. Unlike the Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction, which achieves O(\log n + k) query complexity, this method achieves a worst-case search complexity of O(\sqrt{n} + k). It is chosen when a simpler, pointerless kd-tree implementation is preferred over complex interval tree structures, accepting a slightly higher worst-case asymptotic bound for potentially better constant factors and memory locality. Inputs: A scalar volume dataset consisting of n cells. For each cell i, the minimum vertex value ai and maximum vertex value bi. An isovalue v (or t). Outputs: A list of all cells i such that ai < v < bi (active cells). Span Space Point: Each cell i is represented as a point pi = (ai, bi) in 2D span space, where ai = \minj \{vj\}i and bi = \maxj \{vj\}i. By definition, ai \le bi, so all points lie on or above the line y=x. Kd-Tree Node (Pointerless Layout): The kd-tree is stored as a 1D array to save pointer overhead. Structure: A completely balanced binary tree. Root: Placed at the middle index of the array. Children: For a node at index m in a subtree of size N, the left child occupies the first N/2 nodes of the remaining space, and the right child occupies the last (N-1)/2 nodes. Fields per Node: 1. min: The minimum value ai of the cell (stored at odd levels of recursion, alternating with max). 2. max: The maximum value bi of the cell. 3. cellptr: A pointer/reference to the original cell data. Memory: 2 real numbers + 1 pointer per node. If values are 2 bytes and pointer is 4 bytes, this totals 8 bytes per cell plus tree structure overhead. 1. Compute Extrema: For every cell i in the dataset, calculate ai = \min(\text{vertex values}) and bi = \max(\text{vertex values}). 2. Build Kd-Tree: Recursively partition the set of span points P = \{pi\} into a kd-tree. At each level, alternate the splitting dimension between the minimum coordinate (x) and maximum coordinate (y). Select the median value of the current dimension using a Quicksort-based selection algorithm. Note: While worst-case is O(n^2), average case is O(n), requiring no additional memory. Partition points into left subtree (values < median) and right subtree (values > median). Store the median value in the current node. Repeat recursively until leaf nodes are reached. 3. Flatten: Store the resulting balanced kd-tree in a 1D array using the pointerless layout described above. Given an isovalue v, the goal is to find all points (ai, bi) such that ai < v < bi. Geometrically, this corresponds to points strictly to the left of the vertical line x=v and strictly above the horizontal line y=v (upper-left of (v,v)). Search Routines: Two recursive routines are defined based on the current splitting dimension: 1. SearchMinMax(isovalue, node): Used when the current node splits on the minimum dimension (x). 2. SearchMaxMin(isovalue, node): Used when the current node splits on the maximum dimension (y). Logic: If the region corresponding to a node is entirely contained in the area upper-left of (v,v), report all cells in that subtree as active. If the region is disjoint from that area, report them as empty. Otherwise, traverse children. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def searchminmax(isovalue, node): """ Called when 'node' splits on the minimum dimension (x). We check if node.min < isovalue. """ if node.min < isovalue: # The minimum condition is satisfied for this node and potentially its left subtree. if node.max > isovalue: # This specific cell intersects the isosurface. constructpolygonfromcell(node.cellptr) # Since node.min < isovalue, the left subtree (all values < node.min) # also satisfies the min condition. We can skip checking min for them. # We switch to SearchMaxMin for the left subtree. searchmaxmin(isovalue, node.left) # For the right subtree, node.min > isovalue is NOT guaranteed. # We must check min again. searchminmax(isovalue, node.right) else: # node.min >= isovalue. # The left subtree (values < node.min) might still have min < isovalue? # No, left subtree values are < node.min. If node.min >= isovalue, # left subtree values could be < isovalue. # However, standard kd-tree logic for range queries: # If we are splitting on X, and node.val >= isovalue, # the left child (vals < node.val) MUST be checked. # The right child (vals > node.val) CANNOT satisfy min < isovalue. # Correction based on standard kd-tree search: # If splitting on X: # Left child: vals < node.val. If node.val >= isovalue, left child might contain valid points. # Right child: vals > node.val. If node.val >= isovalue, right child min >= isovalue. Invalid. searchminmax(isovalue, node.left) # Right subtree is skipped because its min values are >= node.min >= isovalue def searchmaxmin(isovalue, node): """ Called when 'node' splits on the maximum dimension (y). We check if node.max > isovalue. """ if node.max > isovalue: # The maximum condition is satisfied. if node.min < isovalue: constructpolygonfromcell(node.cellptr) # Splitting on Y. # Left child: vals < node.val (max). Left child max < node.max. # If node.max > isovalue, left child max might still be > isovalue. # Right child: vals > node.val. Right child max > node.max > isovalue. # Right child definitely satisfies max condition. # Optimization from source: "skip odd levels for the left subtree" # This implies switching to searchmin for subtrees where one condition is met. searchmaxmin(isovalue, node.left) searchmaxmin(isovalue, node.right) else: # node.max <= isovalue. # Right child (vals > node.val) has max > node.max. Might be > isovalue. # Left child (vals < node.val) has max < node.max <= isovalue. Invalid. searchmaxmin(isovalue, node.right) Note: The source provides a simplified pseudocode for SearchMinMax. The full implementation requires alternating between SearchMinMax and SearchMaxMin based on the tree depth/dimension, and utilizing the "skip" optimization where one condition is already known to be true. Median Selection: Quicksort-based selection is recommended for its average O(n) performance and low memory overhead. Isovalue Perturbation: To handle degenerate cells, the isovalue may be perturbed by a small amount. Degenerate Cells: Cells with multiple vertices sharing the minimum or maximum value. If the isovalue equals the extremum, the surface touches but does not intersect the cell interior. Pitfall: Ignoring face-touching cases causes holes in the isosurface; ignoring edge/vertex cases is safe. Solution: Perturb the isovalue slightly to force intersection with only one side, or perform expensive equality checks on both sides of the kd-tree. Precision: Floating-point comparisons must be strict (< and >) to exclude points on the boundary lines x=v and y=v unless degenerate handling is implemented. Time Complexity: Construction: O(n \log n). Query (Worst-case): O(\sqrt{n} + k), where n is the number of cells and k is the number of active cells. This bound was established by Lee and Wong. Query (Average-case): O(k) for typical applications where k \sim n^{2/3}, making the algorithm optimal \theta(k). Memory Complexity: O(n). Using a pointerless kd-tree, the overhead is approximately 8 bytes per cell (2 bytes min, 2 bytes max, 4 bytes pointer). Strengths: Simple data structure (kd-tree) compared to interval trees. Pointerless layout improves cache locality and reduces memory overhead. Near-optimal performance for large datasets. Limitations: Worst-case complexity O(\sqrt{n} + k) is asymptotically worse than the Standard Interval Tree's O(\log n + k). Degenerate cells require special handling to avoid topological errors. When to use: Large-scale datasets where implementation simplicity and memory locality are prioritized over worst-case query guarantees. When not to use: When strict worst-case query time bounds are required, or when the dataset has many degenerate cells and perturbation is not acceptable. The Span Space Isosurface Extraction method, also known as the NOISE (Near Optimal Isosurface Extraction) algorithm, was developed by Livat, Shen, and Johnson. It addresses the limitations of earlier interval-based methods that required maintaining separate sorted lists for minimum and maximum values. By introducing the "span space" representation and utilizing kd-trees, the method allows for simultaneous ordering of cells by both extrema. The worst-case complexity analysis was provided by Lee and Wong. It is primarily used in medical imaging and large-scale scientific visualization where near-interactive rates for high-resolution datasets are required.
