name: Out-of-core Interval Tree Extraction
body:
Out-of-core Interval Tree Extraction is a method for isosurface extraction that stores the interval tree and associated min/max lists on disk in blocks, loading only the necessary blocks based on isovalue intervals. It builds on Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction by partitioning the tree structure to fit within fixed-size disk blocks, enabling the processing of datasets larger than available main memory. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly models the I/O cost of reading tree nodes and min/max lists as a function of isovalue probability distributions. Inputs: Volume data partitioned into blocks B
u. An isovalue t. Disk block size (e.g., 512 bytes). Parameters K1 (tree node block depth) and K2 (min/max list entry block size). Outputs: Extracted isosurface cells. Data Structures: Interval Tree Nodes: Stored in disk blocks. Each block holds a binary subtree of depth K1. Min/Max Lists: Stored in disk blocks. Each block holds up to K2 entries. Node Labeling: Each node \eta is assigned a label \ell(\eta) \in \{0, \dots, K1\} to define block boundaries. Steps: 1. Partition the Interval Tree: Partition the nodes of the interval tree such that each region fits into one disk block. Assume one disk block stores at most 2^{K1+1}-1 interval tree nodes in a binary subtree of depth K1. 2. Label Tree Nodes: Label tree nodes \eta to determine block boundaries using the following recursive definition: \ell(\eta):=  egin{cases} K1 & 	ext{if } \eta 	ext{ is a leaf} \ \ell0(\eta) & 	ext{if } \eta 	ext{ is not a leaf and not the root} \ 0 & 	ext{if } \eta 	ext{ is the root} \end{cases} Where \ell0(\eta) is defined as: \ell0(\eta):= \min(\{K1\} \cup \{\ell(\eta') - 1 \mid \eta' \in \{\etal, \etar\} 	ext{ exists and } \ell(\eta') > 0\}) Nodes labeled 0 define disk block boundaries. A block contains the tree rooted at a node labeled 0 and extending down up to K1 levels, without containing another node labeled 0. 3. Attach Intervals to Nodes: Attach intervals I\eta to all interval tree nodes indicating the range of isovalues for which node \eta must be inspected. Generate these in a top-down traversal: Set I{\eta{root}}:= I
u, where I
u is the range of volume data in block B
u. If t0 is the threshold at the current node, compute intervals for children: I{\etal} = I{\eta{current}} \cap (-\infty, t0) I{\etar} = I{\eta{current}} \cap [t0, \infty) Iterate for children until leaves are reached. 4. Calculate Expected I/O Time for Interval Tree Blocks (T1): Compute the expected time to read interval tree disk blocks. A block Bi is read if the isovalue is in the interval of the first node (label 0) in that block: T1 = \alpha6 \sum{I^0} \sum{i=1}^{NB} Pr(I(Bi)) Where: \alpha6 is the time to read one disk block. NB is the total number of disk blocks for the external interval tree and its min/max lists. Pr(I(Bi)) is the probability that the isovalue falls within the interval of block Bi. The sum \sum{I^0} iterates over all blocks (nodes labeled 0). 5. Calculate Expected I/O Time for Min/Max List Blocks (T2): Compute the expected time to read min/max list disk blocks. Assume one disk block holds up to K2 min/max entries, and on average only half of entries in the last used block are active: T2 \approx \alpha6  rac{Pr(I)}{K2} + \sum{I{cell}} Pr(I\eta)  rac{1}{2} Where Pr(I) is the probability of the isovalue being in the relevant range. 6. Compute Total Expected Cell Extraction Time: The total expected time for extracting cells from block B
u with isovalue t is: E[T(B
u, 4, t)] = E[T(B
u, 2, t)] + T1 + T2 This allows calculation without building min/max lists, using only the interval tree structure. Parameters: K1: Depth of binary subtree stored in one disk block for interval tree nodes. Typical value: 3 (holding 15 nodes per block). K2: Maximum number of min- or max-list entries stored in one disk block. Typical value: 85. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The estimated times may be approximated to zero if they do not incur a significant loss in overall precision. Block Size: The disk block size must be chosen to accommodate the specific K1 and K2 values. For example, a 512-byte block was used in experiments to hold interval subtrees of depth K1=3 or K2=85 entries. Probability Estimation: The method relies on probabilistic estimation of isovalue distributions. Errors in these estimates can affect performance predictions, though experimental results showed errors typically less than five percent. A variant that addresses the memory-constrained optimization problem for fixed partitions. It converts the constrained problem into an unconstrained discrete Lagrangian problem using a Lagrangian multiplier \lambda \ge 0. The complexity is reduced from exponential to linear by exploiting the separability of the problem, allowing independent minimization of terms for each block Bk. Time Complexity: The expected time to read interval tree blocks is proportional to the sum of probabilities of block intervals. The expected time to read min/max list blocks is approximated by a term dependent on the total probability and block capacity, plus a term dependent on cell intervals. Memory Complexity: The method is designed for out-of-core operation, storing the interval tree and min/max lists on disk. Only necessary blocks are loaded into memory, allowing processing of datasets larger than available RAM. Performance: Experimental results on datasets ranging from 1 to 250 MB showed that the probabilistic estimation reduced compute time by a factor between 20 and 100, with larger savings for larger datasets. The error of estimated expected extraction times was typically less than five percent. Strengths: Enables isosurface extraction for very large datasets that do not fit in main memory. Efficient I/O by loading only necessary blocks. Limitations: Relies on accurate probabilistic estimation of isovalue distributions. Performance depends on disk I/O speed (\alpha6). The optimization problem for partitioning can be complex, though it can be linearized using Lagrangian multipliers. When to Use: Suitable for large volume datasets that exceed available main memory. When Not to Use: Not suitable for small datasets where in-core methods are faster due to lower overhead. Not suitable if accurate probability distributions are unavailable. The method was introduced in the context of optimal hybrid memory constrained isosurface extraction. It addresses the challenge of processing large volume datasets that cannot fit entirely in main memory by partitioning the interval tree and min/max lists into disk blocks. The approach uses probabilistic estimation to predict I/O costs and optimize block loading. name: Interval Table for Isosurface Extraction
head: Fast Implementation, TetIndex
body: The Interval Table is a pre-processing data structure that maps scalar value intervals to tetrahedron IDs, allowing the extraction algorithm to skip tetrahedra whose function span does not contain the isovalue. It differs from the Standard Interval Tree by using a fixed-size array of buckets (intervals) rather than a dynamic tree structure, offering a simpler implementation with comparable performance for uniform scalar distributions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A tetrahedral mesh with scalar values at vertices; global minimum (F{min}) and maximum (F{max}) of the scalar field; desired table resolution (N). Output: A data structure (TetIndex) enabling O(1) retrieval of candidate tetrahedra for a given isovalue. Data Structures The structure is implemented as a class TetIndex containing: bounds: A pair or struct storing globalmin and globalmax (floats). resolution: An integer N, representing the number of intervals. table: A std::vector<std::vector<int>> of size N. Each inner vector stores tetrahedron IDs. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Call setBounds(Fmin, Fmax) to store the global scalar range. Call setResolution(N) to allocate the table with N empty vectors. A reasonable default for N is 500. 2. Pre-processing (Build): Iterate over all tetrahedra Ti in the mesh. Compute the function span [t{min}, t{max}] for Ti, where t{min} = \min(v0, v1, v2, v3) and t{max} = \max(v0, v1, v2, v3) for vertex values vj. If t{min} > t{max}, skip (degenerate). Map the span to table indices. The interval width is \Delta = (F{max} - F{min}) / N. Calculate the start index i{start} = \lfloor (t{min} - F{min}) / \Delta \rfloor and end index i{end} = \lfloor (t{max} - F{min}) / \Delta \rfloor. Clamp indices to [0, N-1]. Insert Ti into table[k] for all k such that i{start} \le k \le i{end}. 3. Runtime (Query): Given an isovalue I: Calculate the index idx = \lfloor (I - F{min}) / \Delta \rfloor. Clamp idx to [0, N-1]. Return a pointer to table[idx]. 4. Extraction: In IsoSurfacer::FastExtraction(), iterate only over the tetrahedra returned by the query step, rather than the entire mesh. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class TetIndex: def init(self): self.globalmin = 0.0 self.globalmax = 0.0 self.resolution = 500 self.table = [] # vector of vectors of ints def setbounds(self, fmin, fmax): """Store the global function range.""" self.globalmin = fmin self.globalmax = fmax # Initialize table with empty vectors self.table = [[] for in range(self.resolution)] def setresolution(self, n): """Set the size of the table.""" self.resolution = n # Re-initialize table if bounds are already set if self.globalmax != self.globalmin: self.table = [[] for in range(self.resolution)] def addtet(self, tetid, tmin, tmax): """ Store the tetrahedron ID in the table based on its function span. tmin and tmax are the min/max scalar values of the tet's vertices. """ if tmin > tmax: return delta = (self.globalmax - self.globalmin) / self.resolution # Calculate interval indices # Use epsilon to handle boundary precision issues if necessary startidx = int((tmin - self.globalmin) / delta) endidx = int((tmax - self.globalmin) / delta) # Clamp indices to valid range [0, resolution - 1] startidx = max(0, min(startidx, self.resolution - 1)) endidx = max(0, min(endidx, self.resolution - 1)) # Insert tetid into all relevant intervals for k in range(startidx, endidx + 1): self.table[k].append(tetid) def getcandidates(self, isovalue): """ Given an isovalue, return a pointer (reference) to the corresponding vector of tetrahedron IDs. """ delta = (self.globalmax - self.globalmin) / self.resolution idx = int((isovalue - self.globalmin) / delta) # Clamp index idx = max(0, min(idx, self.resolution - 1)) return self.table[idx] def fastextraction(tetindex, isovalue, mesh): """ Extract isosurface using the interval table. """ candidates = tetindex.getcandidates(isovalue) # Iterate only over candidates for tetid in candidates: tet = mesh.gettetrahedron(tetid) # Perform marching tetrahedra logic for this tet processtet(tet, isovalue) Parameters Resolution (N): The number of intervals in the table. A reasonable value is 500. Higher values increase memory usage but may reduce the number of candidates per bucket if the scalar distribution is non-uniform. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point division and floor operations may cause boundary errors. Clamping indices is essential to prevent out-of-bounds access. Degenerate Input: If F{min} == F{max}, division by zero occurs in \Delta. This should be handled by checking for constant scalar fields and skipping extraction or returning all tetrahedra. Non-uniform Distribution: If scalar values are clustered, some buckets may become overloaded while others are empty, reducing the skipping efficiency compared to the Standard Interval Tree. Uses fixed-size buckets but may differ in bucket sizing strategy or hashing. Choose when memory is strictly constrained. Groups cells to reduce tree depth. Choose for highly non-uniform scalar distributions. Operates in span space rather than value space. Choose for complex topological changes. Designed for datasets larger than RAM. Choose when memory is insufficient for in-memory structures. Time Complexity: Pre-processing is O(T \cdot K), where T is the number of tetrahedra and K is the average number of intervals a tet spans. Query is O(1) to find the bucket, plus O(C) to process candidates, where C is the number of candidates. Memory Complexity: O(N + T \cdot K), where N is the resolution and K is the average number of intervals per tet. Measured Performance: The method drastically reduces the number of visited tetrahedra compared to naive iteration or standard neighbor-visiting approaches, yielding faster extraction times than VTK's standard implementation in typical exercises. Strengths: Simple implementation; fast query time; effective for uniform scalar distributions. Limitations: Performance degrades if scalar values are highly non-uniform (many tets per bucket); fixed resolution requires tuning. The Interval Table, also referred to as the "Fast Implementation" or "TetIndex," was introduced in visualization exercises by Julien Tierny. It is designed to optimize isosurface extraction by pre-filtering tetrahedra based on their scalar range, avoiding unnecessary processing of non-intersecting cells. name: Marching Cubes with Octree
body: Marching Cubes with Octree extracts a triangle mesh from an implicit scalar field defined over an adaptive octree structure, replacing the uniform Cartesian grid of standard Marching Cubes. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on a generic domain interface (MCDomain) that decouples the traversal logic from the specific octree implementation, allowing for parallel execution and arbitrary split predicates. Unlike uniform grid methods, it adapts resolution to the field's complexity, but it lacks inherent guarantees against topological cracks if the octree depth varies discontinuously around the isosurface. The method operates by constructing an octree based on a split predicate, defining a domain that links the octree to a scalar function, and invoking the marching cubes algorithm which traverses the octree to generate triangles. Inputs: bbox: A 3D bounding box defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). splitpredicate: A function or object that determines whether an octree node should be subdivided, typically based on the scalar field's variation or gradient. scalarfunction: A function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R} that evaluates the implicit field at any point. isovalue: The scalar threshold I at which the isosurface is extracted. Outputs: points: A container of 3D vertices forming the mesh. triangles: A container of triangle indices referencing the vertices. Data Structures: 1. Octree: A hierarchical spatial partitioning structure. Each node represents a cubic volume. The root covers the bbox. Nodes are refined recursively if splitpredicate returns true. The structure supports traversal and neighbor access. 2. Values: An object holding the scalarfunction and a reference to the octree. It provides the interface for the domain to query field values at specific locations, potentially leveraging the octree's hierarchy for efficient evaluation. 3. MCDomain: An abstraction layer that implements the interface expected by the marching cubes algorithm. It maps the algorithm's requests for cell vertices and edge intersections to the underlying octree structure and scalar function. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Bounding Box: Define the root cube of the octree using the input bbox points. 2. Construct Octree: Create an Octree object initialized with the bounding box points. 3. Refine Octree: Call octree.refine(splitpredicate) to recursively subdivide nodes. The predicate determines refinement based on the scalar field's behavior within the node. 4. Create Values Object: Instantiate a Values object containing the scalarfunction and the constructed octree. 5. Initialize Output Containers: Create empty containers Pointrange points and Polygonrange triangles to store the resulting vertices and triangles. 6. Construct Domain: Instantiate an MCDomain object, passing the octree and values objects. This binds the geometric structure and the scalar field to the marching cubes interface. 7. Execute Marching Cubes: Call CGAL::Isosurfacing::marchingcubes with the MCDomain, isovalue, and output ranges. The algorithm uses Parallelifavailabletag to enable parallel processing if supported by the environment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. function runmarchingcubesoctree(bbox, splitpredicate, scalarfunction, isovalue): # 1. Define bounding box points bboxpoints = [ Point(bbox.xmin, bbox.ymin, bbox.zmin), Point(bbox.xmax, bbox.ymax, bbox.zmax) ] # 2. Construct Octree octree = Octree(bboxpoints) # 3. Refine the octree using the split predicate # The predicate determines if a node needs subdivision octree.refine(splitpredicate) # 4. Create Values object linking function and octree values = Values(scalarfunction, octree) # 5. Initialize output containers points = [] # List of 3D points triangles = [] # List of triangle indices # 6. Construct MCDomain mcdomain = MCDomain(octree, values) # 7. Call marching cubes # The algorithm traverses the octree, evaluates the scalar function, # and generates triangles into 'points' and 'triangles'. # Parallelifavailabletag enables multi-threading. marchingcubes(mcdomain, isovalue, points, triangles, Parallelifavailabletag) return points, triangles Parameters: isovalue: The threshold value. Typical values depend on the scalar field's range. In the CGAL example, a default of 0.3 is used for a normalized sphere function. splitpredicate: Defines the adaptive resolution. Common predicates include Refinearoundisovalue which splits nodes where the scalar field crosses the isovalue, or fixed-depth splitters like Refineoneeighth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cracks: Using an octree with varying depths around the isosurface produces cracks at regions where octree levels are discontinuous. The standard Marching Cubes algorithm assumes a uniform grid topology; when adjacent cells have different resolutions, shared edges may have mismatched intersection points or missing vertices. Manifold Guarantee: The octree behaves well and produces a manifold surface only if nodes are split with a uniform size around the surface. Precision: The output precision is controlled by the floating-point type used for the scalar function and coordinates. In the CGAL example, 17 decimal digits are used for polylines output. Linear Hashed Marching Cubes extracts triangle meshes from implicit scalar fields by applying the Marching Cubes algorithm over a linear hashed octree. It replaces the standard grid-based traversal with a pointerless octree structure to reduce memory overhead and improve performance. It builds on Marching Cubes with Octree but uses a linear hash table for node storage instead of a primal grid. This variant extends Marching Cubes to handle isosurface rendering on Adaptive Resolution (AR) octree data, addressing inconsistencies between cells of different resolutions. It uses a two-pass approach: a first pass generates triangles using standard MC, while a second pass processes nodes with missing vertices. If a coarser node finds two vertices on the same edge in its fine edge vertex list, it subdivides the cube. It sets itself apart from Linear Hashed Marching Cubes by explicitly handling resolution mismatches through subdivision and post-processing, rather than relying on a flat hash structure. It is chosen when the octree has arbitrary depth variations that standard MC cannot handle without cracks. DMC Octree Contour Extraction is an adaptive isosurface extraction method that traverses a pre-built octree to generate a triangle mesh via dual-vertex construction and contour processing. It solves the problem of extracting high-quality surfaces from volumetric data with varying density by recursively subdividing cells based on field error metrics. It sets itself apart from its sibling Linear Hashed Marching Cubes by using a hierarchical octree structure with explicit contour propagation across shared faces and edges, rather than a flat hash-based lookup, and from Adaptive Resolution Isosurface Rendering with Two-Pass Discontinuity Handling by relying on a single-pass recursive traversal with dual-vertex QEF solving rather than a two-pass discontinuity-aware approach. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of octree nodes and the complexity of the split predicate. The marching cubes traversal is linear with respect to the number of leaf nodes in the octree. Parallel execution can reduce wall-clock time on multi-core systems. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of octree nodes. The linear hashed variant reduces overhead by using a hash table instead of pointers. Measured Performance: Evaluated on a Dell PC with a 450 MHz Pentium microprocessor and 256 Mbytes of RAM running Red Hat Linux 6.1, using Java 3D for the AR variant. Specific performance metrics for the CGAL implementation are not provided in the sources. Strengths: Adaptive resolution allows for high detail where needed and coarse representation elsewhere, saving memory and computation. The domain-based design allows flexibility in octree implementation. Limitations: Cracks can occur if the octree is not adapted uniformly around the surface. The algorithm does not guarantee manifoldness without specific splitting strategies. When to use: When the scalar field has varying complexity and a uniform grid would be too expensive or wasteful. When the octree can be constructed such that depth changes are gradual or handled by a variant like Adaptive Marching Cubes. When not to use: When strict manifoldness is required and the octree structure cannot be controlled to avoid depth discontinuities. When the scalar field is uniform and a simple grid-based MC is sufficient. The method is part of the CGAL (Computational Geometry Algorithms Library) Isosurfacing module. It was developed to provide a flexible interface for isosurfacing on various spatial data structures, including octrees. The underlying Marching Cubes algorithm was originally introduced by Lorensen and Cline cites CGAL implementation]. The specific integration with octrees and the MCDomain interface is documented in the CGAL reference manual. The Adaptive Resolution variant was proposed by to handle inconsistencies in multiresolution data. The sparse-voxel TSDF fusion approach using Marching Cubes was introduced in for real-time radiance field rendering. 3D Isosurfacing, https://doc.cgal.org/latest/Isosurfacing3/index.html, fetched 2026-10-29 IsoSurface Rendering of Adaptive Resolution Data, https://www.cs.unh.edu/~rdb/papers/ARiso.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01509, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Linear Hashed Marching Cubes
body: Linear Hashed Marching Cubes extracts triangle meshes from implicit scalar fields by applying the Marching Cubes algorithm over a linear hashed octree. It replaces the standard grid-based traversal with a pointerless octree structure to reduce memory overhead and improve performance. It builds on Marching Cubes with Octree but uses a linear hash table for node storage instead of a primal grid. Inputs: An implicit scalar field function f(x, y, z) returning signed distance or density. An isovalue threshold T for classification. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the internal octree, defining the resolution limit. The tree spans the equivalent of a cubic grid of size 2^{\text{max\depth}} in either direction. Outputs: A triangle mesh consisting of vertices and indices representing the isosurface. Data Structures: ImplicitOctree: A traversal structure that replaces PrimalGrid, storing voxel data in a linear hash table. MortonKey: A 64-bit integer representing the position of a voxel in the 3D grid using Morton (Z-order) curve encoding, used for indexing instead of GridKey. MeshTopologyBuilder: A temporary structure that accumulates vertex positions and face indices during traversal, using MortonKey identifiers to track vertex uniqueness and ensure proper mesh connectivity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an ImplicitOctree instance with the specified maxdepth and initialize a MeshTopologyBuilder. 2. Traversal: Traverse the ImplicitOctree. For each visited cube, retrieve its MortonKey, the 8 corner coordinates, and the scalar values at those corners. 3. Classification: Compute the cube index (0–255) by setting bit i if f(\text{corner}i) < T. 4. Edge Intersection: Find the 12 edge crossing vertices for the cube using the cube index, corners, and values. 5. Mesh Construction: March the cube by iterating through the triangles defined by the cube index. For each triangle (a, b, c), add vertices to the mesh builder with MortonKey identifiers and the calculated vertex positions, then add the face. 6. Finalization: After all cubes have been traversed, build the final mesh from the MeshTopologyBuilder and extract indices to the extractor. Formulas: The intersection point p{int} on an edge is calculated via linear interpolation: p{int} = p1 + \frac{T - v1}{v2 - v1} (p2 - p1) where v1, v2 are the scalar values at the edge endpoints and p1, p2 are their 3D positions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearhashedmarchingcubes(isofunc, isovalue, maxdepth): octree = ImplicitOctree(maxdepth=maxdepth) builder = MeshTopologyBuilder() for cube in octree.traverse(): key = cube.mortonkey corners = cube.corners values = [isofunc(c) for c in corners] cubeindex = 0 for i in range(8): if values[i] < isovalue: cubeindex |= (1 << i) intersections = findedgeintersections(corners, values, isovalue, cubeindex) for tri in MCTRIANGLES[cubeindex]: verts = [intersections[e] for e in tri] builder.addtriangle(verts) return builder.build() def findedgeintersections(corners, values, isovalue, cubeindex): # Standard MC edge connectivity: 12 edges connecting 8 corners edges = [(0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,0),(4,5),(5,6),(6,7),(7,4),(0,4),(1,5),(2,6),(3,7)] pts = {} for idx, (i, j) in enumerate(edges): # Edge crosses isosurface if corner signs differ if (values[i] < isovalue) != (values[j] < isovalue): v1, v2 = values[i], values[j] p1, p2 = corners[i], corners[j] t = 0.5 if abs(v2 - v1) < 1e-9 else (isovalue - v1) / (v2 - v1) pts[idx] = p1 + t (p2 - p1) return pts def mortonencode(x, y, z): # Standard Z-order curve encoding x = (x | (x << 16)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF x = (x | (x << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF x = (x | (x << 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F x = (x | (x << 2)) & 0x3333333333333333 x = (x | (x << 1)) & 0x5555555555555555 y = (y | (y << 16)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF y = (y | (y << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF y = (y | (y << 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F y = (y | (y << 2)) & 0x3333333333333333 y = (y | (y << 1)) & 0x5555555555555555 z = (z | (z << 16)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF z = (z | (z << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF z = (z | (z << 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F z = (z | (z << 2)) & 0x3333333333333333 z = (z | (z << 1)) & 0x5555555555555555 return x | (y << 1) | (z << 2) class ImplicitOctree: def init(self, maxdepth): self.maxdepth = maxdepth def traverse(self): # Yields cube objects with.mortonkey,.corners, and.values pass class MeshTopologyBuilder: def init(self): self.vertices = {} self.indices = [] def addtriangle(self, verts): for v in verts: key = mortonencode(round(v[0]), round(v[1]), round(v[2])) if key not in self.vertices: self.vertices[key] = v self.indices.append(self.vertices[key]) def build(self): return list(self.vertices.values()), self.indices MCTRIANGLES = [...] Faster than standard marching cubes. name: Adaptive Resolution Isosurface Rendering with Two-Pass Discontinuity Handling
head: AR Isosurface Rendering, Adaptive Marching Cubes with 2nd Pass Subdivision
body: This method extracts isosurfaces from adaptive resolution (AR) octree volume data by decoupling geometry generation from discontinuity resolution. It solves the topological inconsistencies that arise when fine-resolution cubes share edges or faces with coarser, unsubdivided neighbors. Unlike uniform resolution methods, it reduces data access and processing time by skipping large uniform regions, while the two-pass approach ensures a watertight mesh without requiring complex on-the-fly edge matching logic during the primary traversal. Input: An adaptive resolution octree representing a scalar field. Each leaf node contains bounding box coordinates and min/max scalar values. Output: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface. Parameters: iso: The scalar isovalue for extraction. Typical values tested: 0.185, 0.378, 0.408. delta: The adaptive resolution threshold determining the coarseness of the octree. Typical values: 1% to 25%. The algorithm relies on two auxiliary structures to handle the decoupled passes: 1. Second Pass List (secondpasslist): A dynamic list of octree node identifiers (or pointers) that require re-evaluation. A node is added to this list if a neighbor generates a vertex on a shared edge or face. 2. Edge Vertex List (edgevertexlist): Associated with each octree node. It stores the interpolated vertex positions generated by neighbors on the edges of the current node. Layout: A list of pairs (edgeindex, vertexposition). Edge Index: An integer 0-11 identifying one of the 12 edges of the cube. Vertex Position: A 3D vector (x, y, z). 3. Facial Vertex List (facialvertexlist): Associated with each octree node. It stores vertices generated by neighbors that lie strictly on the interior of a face of the current node. Layout: A list of pairs (faceindex, vertexposition). Face Index: An integer 0-5 identifying one of the 6 faces. 1. Initialization: Initialize secondpasslist as empty. For every node in the octree, initialize edgevertexlist and facialvertexlist as empty. 2. First Pass (Primary Traversal): Iterate through all leaf nodes of the octree. For each node N: Perform standard Marching Cubes (MC) using the scalar values at the 8 vertices of N and iso. Generate the set of triangles for N. For each generated triangle, identify the edges and faces it intersects. Edge Conflict Check: If a triangle vertex lies on an edge shared with a neighbor M (where M is coarser than N): Add the interpolated vertex position to M.edgevertexlist for that specific edge index. Add M to secondpasslist if not already present. Facial Conflict Check: If a triangle vertex lies on a face shared with a neighbor M (where M is coarser than N): Add the interpolated vertex position to M.facialvertexlist for that specific face index. Add M to secondpasslist if not already present. Note: If a neighbor is finer than N, N does not need to track vertices for N's own geometry generation in this pass, as the finer neighbor will handle its own local consistency. The conflict arises only when a coarse node must conform to vertices generated by a fine neighbor. 3. Second Pass (Discontinuity Resolution): Iterate through each node M in secondpasslist. For each M: Edge Check: Examine M.edgevertexlist. If any edge index has two distinct vertices recorded (i.e., two different fine neighbors generated vertices on the same edge of M), M has a topological conflict. Subdivide M into its 8 children. For each child, re-run the Marching Cubes step (including adding to secondpasslist if new conflicts are found with their neighbors). Facial Check: Examine M.facialvertexlist. If M.facialvertexlist is non-empty (indicating a fine neighbor generated a vertex on the interior of M's face), M has a topological conflict. Subdivide M into its 8 children. For each child, re-run the Marching Cubes step. Note: The subdivision in the second pass may trigger further entries in secondpasslist. The algorithm must continue processing the list until it is empty or a maximum iteration depth is reached. In the original implementation, a single pass over the list was deemed sufficient for the tested datasets, but robust implementations should loop until no new subdivisions occur. 4. Final Output: Collect all triangles generated in the First Pass and any triangles generated during the Second Pass subdivisions. Return the combined triangle mesh. Unverified code. The neighbor lookup functions must handle null returns gracefully. Infinite Loops: If the subdivision logic does not correctly propagate conflicts, or if the secondpasslist is not managed as a queue, the algorithm may fail to converge. The original paper notes that for \Delta=25\%, up to 9.8% of cubes required subdivision, suggesting that multiple levels of subdivision might be necessary in extreme cases, though a single pass was reported as sufficient for their specific data. Time Complexity: The first pass is O(N) where N is the number of leaf nodes. The second pass depends on the number of discontinuities. In the worst case, it may trigger recursive subdivisions, but typically remains efficient. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the octree and auxiliary lists. The auxiliary lists are sparse. Performance: Time Savings: At \Delta=10\%, reading time is reduced by a factor of ~5 compared to full Maximum Resolution (MR) representation. Processing time is reduced by 20-25%. Storage Savings: At \Delta=10\%, storage requirements are reduced by a factor of just over 5. Cubes read reduced from 2,097,152 (MR) to 481,640 (AR 10%). Accuracy: No discernible differences from full MR rendering for isovalue 0.185. No discontinuities caused by AR data for this isovalue. Discontinuity Frequency: At \Delta=25\%, the maximum discontinuity occurrence was 9.8% of cubes subdivided. Strengths: Significant reduction in I/O and processing time for large datasets. Simple implementation compared to real-time edge matching. Limitations: Requires two passes. May require multiple levels of subdivision in the second pass for high \Delta values. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "IsoSurface Rendering of Adaptive Resolution Data" by R. D. Bebis and R. J. Boyle. History: It was developed to address the inefficiencies of rendering adaptive resolution data using uniform resolution algorithms. The authors evaluated the method on a Dell PC with a 450 MHz Pentium processor, 256 MB RAM, running Red Hat Linux 6.1, using Java 1.2/2.0 and VisAD/Java 3D. Usage: Used in scientific visualization, particularly for medical imaging (e.g., cadaver head data sets) where large volumes can be represented efficiently with adaptive resolution. name: Adaptive Marching Cubes
head: AR Isosurface Algorithm, Adaptive Marching Cubes on Multiresolution Octree, Adaptive Marching Cubes on Octree
body: Adaptive Marching Cubes is an extension of the standard Marching Cubes algorithm designed to extract isosurfaces from Adaptive Resolution (AR) octree data. It solves the problem of topological inconsistencies and geometric artifacts that arise when adjacent cubes in the mesh have different resolutions. Unlike uniform marching cubes, it handles missing vertices and discontinuities by deferring the processing of coarser nodes that conflict with finer neighbors, ensuring a watertight mesh across resolution boundaries. The algorithm performs two passes over the octree to resolve inconsistencies between adjacent cells of differing resolutions. Input: An adaptive resolution octree representing a volume dataset. Each node contains voxel values at its specific resolution level. Output: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface. Each octree node maintains the following fields: 1. Triangle List: A list of triangles generated for this node. Each triangle references vertices in the global Intersection List. 2. Intersection List: A global vertex array storing edge intersection points. Vertices in this list may be updated later during the second pass. 3. Second Pass List: A list of octree nodes that require post-processing. Nodes are added to this list if they have missing vertices relative to finer neighbors. First Pass: Standard MC with Conflict Detection 1. Traverse the octree in any order (typically depth-first or breadth-first). 2. For each node, perform standard Marching Cubes using the node's voxel values. 3. For every edge intersection found: Check if the adjacent neighbor (if it exists and is coarser) has a corresponding vertex on that edge. If the coarser neighbor has no vertex on the shared edge (i.e., its coarse vertices are on the same side of the isosurface), but the current finer cube finds an intersection: Create a new entry in the coarser neighbor's fine edge vertex list (stored in the global Intersection List). Add the coarser neighbor node to the Second Pass List. If the coarser neighbor already has a vertex, use it to ensure consistency. 4. Generate triangles for the current node using the standard MC lookup table, referencing vertices from the Intersection List. Second Pass: Subdivision and Finalization 1. Process all nodes in the Second Pass List. 2. For each node in the list: Check if it has two vertices on the same edge in its fine edge vertex list (indicating a conflict where the coarse resolution failed to capture the isosurface crossing). If such a conflict exists, subdivide the coarser cube. This involves interpolating between the known cube vertex values at the coarser resolution to create finer children, which are then processed using the standard MC algorithm. If no subdivision is needed but the node has facial vertices that were deferred, generate the triangles. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. intersectionlist = [] # Array of vertex positions secondpasslist = [] # List of octree nodes requiring post-processing def adaptivemarchingcubes(rootnode, isovalue): # First Pass processnode(rootnode, isovalue, issecondpass=False) # Second Pass while secondpasslist is not empty: node = secondpasslist.pop() processnode(node, isovalue, issecondpass=True) def processnode(node, isovalue, issecondpass): if issecondpass: # Check for conflicts requiring subdivision if node.hasedgeconflict(): # Subdivide the coarse cube children = node.subdivide() for child in children: processnode(child, isovalue, issecondpass=False) return # Standard Marching Cubes logic triangles = [] for edge in node.edges: # Determine if isosurface crosses this edge if isovaluebetween(node.vertices[edge.v1], node.vertices[edge.v2]): # Check for consistency with coarser neighbor neighbor = node.getcoarserneighbor(edge) if neighbor is not None: if not neighbor.hasvertexonedge(edge): # Missing vertex in coarser neighbor # Create new vertex in intersection list vertex = interpolateintersection(edge, isovalue) neighbor.addfinevertex(edge, vertex) # Add coarser neighbor to second pass list if not already there if neighbor not in secondpasslist: secondpasslist.append(neighbor) else: vertex = neighbor.getvertexonedge(edge) else: vertex = interpolateintersection(edge, isovalue) # Store vertex reference for triangle generation edge.vertex = vertex # Generate triangles based on MC case triangles = generatemctriangles(node, isovalue) node.trianglelist.extend(triangles) Isosurface Value: The threshold value for extraction. Edge Cases: Missing Vertices: Occur when a finer cube intersects an edge that a coarser neighbor does not. Handled by creating deferred vertices and subdividing the coarser node. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may cause inconsistent edge crossings. Standard MC robustness techniques should be applied. Boundary Conditions: Nodes at the boundary of the volume have no coarser neighbors in certain directions; these are handled as standard uniform nodes. Time Complexity: Depends on the octree depth and the number of conflicts. In the worst case, many coarser nodes may be subdivided, approaching the cost of uniform high-resolution marching cubes. However, large uninteresting regions are skipped, reducing computation. Memory Complexity: Higher than uniform MC due to the octree structure and the need to store deferred vertices and the second pass list. The intersection list grows dynamically. Strengths: Efficiently handles large datasets by focusing resolution where needed; produces watertight meshes across resolution boundaries. Limitations: The two-pass nature and potential for frequent subdivision can complicate implementation and reduce performance in highly heterogeneous data. The Adaptive Marching Cubes algorithm was introduced by Westermann et al. as part of their work on isosurface rendering of adaptive resolution data. It addresses the limitations of standard marching cubes when applied to multiresolution data structures, specifically the topological inconsistencies at resolution boundaries. The method has been cited in subsequent works on implicit surface rendering and interactive visualization. name: DMC Octree Contour Extraction
head: Discrete Marching Cubes Octree
body: DMC Octree Contour Extraction is an adaptive isosurface extraction method that traverses a pre-built octree to generate a triangle mesh via dual-vertex construction and contour processing. It solves the problem of extracting high-quality surfaces from volumetric data with varying density by recursively subdividing cells based on field error metrics. It sets itself apart from its sibling Linear Hashed Marching Cubes by using a hierarchical octree structure with explicit contour propagation across shared faces and edges, rather than a flat hash-based lookup, and from Adaptive Resolution Isosurface Rendering with Two-Pass Discontinuity Handling by relying on a single-pass recursive traversal with dual-vertex QEF solving rather than a two-pass discontinuity-aware approach. Inputs and Outputs Input: A root node of a DMCOctree representing the volumetric space, a ScalarField providing field values and gradients, and a BuildArgs configuration structure. Output: A Mesh containing the extracted triangle vertices and indices, with global position and scale applied. Data Structures DMCOctreeNode: isSubdivided(): Boolean method indicating if the node has children. operator[]: Accessor for child nodes (array of 8). normal: glm::vec3, stores the averaged normal for dual vertices. dualVertex: glm::vec4, stores the solved vertex position (x, y, z, w). material: Stores material information if vertex.w <= 0. BuildArgs: useearlysplitstop: bool, enables early stopping based on field magnitude. usesimplesplitpolicy: bool, enables simple splitting based on root size or error. userandomsampling: bool, enables random sampling for dual vertex generation. epsilon: double, error threshold for splitting and vertex solving. solver: QefSolver4D, accumulates planes for least-squares vertex solving. field: ScalarField, provides getValue(pos) and getGradient(pos). rng: Random number generator state. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Create an empty Mesh and VertexMap. Set the global position and scale on the mesh using the octree's transformation parameters. Call cellProc on the root node. 2. Cell Processing (cellProc): If the current node is not subdivided, return. Retrieve the 8 child nodes into an array sub[8]. Face Processing: Iterate i from 0 to 3. Call faceProcX, faceProcY, and faceProcZ with the two child nodes defining each face, determined by faceTableX/Y/Z[i]. Edge Processing: Iterate i from 0 to 1. Call edgeProcX, edgeProcY, and edgeProcZ with the four child nodes defining each edge, determined by edgeTableX/Y/Z[i]. Vertex Processing: Call vertProc with all 8 child nodes sub[0] through sub[7]. 3. Face Processing (faceProcX/Y/Z): Initialize subTable mapping 8 indices to parent nodes and their child index. Iterate i from 0 to 7: If the parent node is subdivided, sub[i] is its specific child; otherwise, sub[i] is the parent node itself. Set haslesser = true if any node was subdivided. If haslesser is false, return immediately (no geometry for this face). Recursive Face Calls: Iterate i from 0 to 3. Call the corresponding faceProc function recursively with the two sub-nodes defined by faceTable[i]. Edge Calls: Iterate i from 0 to 1. Call the corresponding edgeProc function with the four sub-nodes defined by edgeTable[i]. Vertex Call: Call vertProc with all 8 sub-nodes. 4. Edge Processing (edgeProcX/Y/Z): (Details omitted in source notes, but implied to handle edge contours using the 4 defining child nodes). 5. Vertex Processing (vertProc): (Details omitted in source notes, but implied to handle vertex contours using the 8 defining child nodes). 6. Node Building (buildNode): If size is 1, generate a dual vertex and return. If useearlysplitstop is true and shouldStopSplitting returns true, generate a dual vertex and return. If usesimplesplitpolicy is true: If size equals mrootSize or shouldSplit returns true, subdivide the node. Calculate childsize as size/2. Recursively call buildNode for all 8 children with their respective mincorners. Otherwise, generate a dual vertex. If usesimplesplitpolicy is false: If size 8 < mrootSize and generateDualVertex returns true, return. Otherwise, subdivide the node, calculate childsize as size/2, and recursively call buildNode for all 8 children. 7. Dual Vertex Generation (generateDualVertex): Reset the QEF solver. Initialize avgnormal to zero. Sampling: If userandomsampling is true: Calculate pointscnt as int(6.0 sqrt(size)). Create a uniform distribution odist(0, size). For pointscnt iterations, generate a random offset, compute local and global points, get the field value and gradient, and add a plane defined by point4d (local position, local value) and normal4d (gradient, -1.0) to the solver. Accumulate the gradient in avgnormal. If userandomsampling is false: Define minoffset as 0.25 size and maxoffset as size - minoffset. Define 8 sample offsets at these corners. For each of the 8 samples, compute local/global points, field value, gradient, and add a plane to the solver. Accumulate the gradient in avgnormal. Normalize avgnormal and store it in node->normal. Define lowerbound as (mincorner, 0) and upperbound as (mincorner + size, 0). Solve for the vertex using the solver with these bounds. Evaluate the error of the solved vertex. If error > args.epsilon, relax bounds to lowest/max float values and re-solve. Store the final vertex in node->dualVertex. If vertex.w <= 0, compute the global value and material, and store the material in node->material. Return true if error <= args.epsilon, false otherwise. 8. Splitting Decision (shouldSplit): Compute the 8 global corner positions of the cell. Compute the field values at these corners. Initialize error to 0. Edge Midpoints: Define dim1corners, dim1idoffsets, and dim1offsets for edge midpoints. For each dimension (0-2) and each of the 4 edges in that dimension, compute the midpoint position, predict the value as the average of the two endpoint values, get the actual field value and gradient magnitude k, and add abs(predict - actual) / k to error. If error > epsilon, return true. Face Midpoints: Define dim2corners, dim2idoffsets, and dim2offsets for face midpoints. For each dimension (0-2) and each of the 2 faces in that dimension, compute the face center position, predict the value as the average of the 4 corner values, get the actual field value and gradient magnitude k, and add abs(predict - actual) / k to error. If error > epsilon, return true. Cell Center: Compute the cell center position. Predict the value as the average of all 8 corner values. Get the actual field value and gradient magnitude k. Add abs(predict - actual) / k to error. If error > epsilon, return true. Return false if the accumulated error did not exceed epsilon. 9. Early Stop Decision (shouldStopSplitting): Compute the base global point and the cell side length. Compute the diagonal length as side sqrt(3). For each of the 8 corners, if the absolute value of the field is less than or equal to the diagonal length, return false (do not stop splitting). If all 8 corners have field values with absolute value greater than the diagonal, return true (stop splitting). Pseudocode Unverified code. name: MDC Octree Isosurface Extraction
head: MDC, Multi-Dimensional Cell Octree
body: MDC (Multi-Dimensional Cell) Octree Isosurface Extraction is an adaptive surface reconstruction algorithm that uses an octree data structure to recursively subdivide a 3D volume and generate a triangle mesh. It solves the problem of extracting isosurfaces from volumetric data with varying density, handling topology via vertex clustering and collapse logic to ensure manifold connectivity. It sets itself apart from standard marching cubes by dynamically collapsing vertices in low-error regions and clustering boundary vertices to maintain watertight topology without explicit post-processing. Inputs: A 3D volumetric dataset (implicitly accessed via the octree nodes). rootsize: The size of the root octree node. Must be a power of two. globalpos: The world coordinate position of the octree root. globalscale: The global scale factor applied to octree coordinates. epsilon: A threshold for vertex collapsibility. Outputs: A triangle mesh (list of vertices and indices). MDCOctreeNode mvertices: List of MDCVertex objects associated with this node. vertexMask: Bitmask indicating which vertices are present/valid. isSubdivided: Boolean flag indicating if the node has children. depth: Integer tracking octree depth for flip direction calculation. MDCVertex mposition: 3D position vector. mnormal: Normal vector. mmaterial: Enum Material (e.g., Empty, Solid). merror: Scalar error value. mcollapsible: Boolean flag. mvertexIdx: Index in the output mesh. Initialized to kBadIndex. msurfaceIdx: Index used for Disjoint Set Union (DSU) clustering. highestCollapsibleAncestor: Pointer to the nearest ancestor vertex that is collapsible. Constants kBadIndex: 0xFFFFFFFF, indicating an invalid vertex index. kEdgeProcSharedEdge[D][i]: Lookup table for shared edge indices for dimension D and node i. kMdcEdgeSetIndex[n][m]: Lookup table mapping edge mask and edge index to vertex index within a node. kCellEdgeEndpoint[myedge][0]: Endpoint index of the edge in the cell. rootsize: Power of two. If not, an exception is thrown. epsilon: Threshold for marking non-leaf vertices as collapsible if error <= epsilon. 1. Initialization: Construct the MDCOctree with rootsize, globalpos, and globalscale. Validate rootsize is a power of two. 2. Vertex Collection (addVerticesToMesh): Recursively traverse the octree. For each node, iterate through its vertices. If the node is a leaf, mark vertices as collapsible. If not a leaf, mark vertices as collapsible if error <= epsilon. If a vertex is collapsible and has no collapsible ancestor, add it to the mesh, assign a unique index, and update mvertexIdx. Otherwise, assign kBadIndex to mvertexIdx. Recurse into children if the node is subdivided. 3. Cell Processing (cellProc): If the node is a leaf, return. Otherwise, recursively process all 8 children. Then, call sub-face processing for dimensions 0, 1, and 2: callSubFaceProc(0), callSubFaceProc(1), callSubFaceProc(2). Then, call sub-edge processing for dimensions 0, 1, and 2: callSubEdgeProc(0), callSubEdgeProc(1), callSubEdgeProc(2). 4. Edge Processing (edgeProc): For a given dimension D, take the 4 nodes sharing the edge. Resolve children if subdivided. If all 4 are leaves, call edgeProcLeaves. Otherwise, call callSubEdgeProc(D). 5. Edge Processing Leaves (edgeProcLeaves): For dimension D and 4 nodes, get the shared edge index for each node using kEdgeProcSharedEdge[D][i]. Get the vertex index from the node's vertex list using kMdcEdgeSetIndex[nodes[i]->vertexMask()][myedge]. If the index is invalid (kBadIndex) or out of bounds, return. Get the highest collapsible ancestor for each vertex. If any vertex's ancestor is null, return. Determine flip direction: find the deepest node among the 4. Check if the corner at kCellEdgeEndpoint[myedge][0] is Material::Empty. If so, flip = true. Add two triangles to the mesh using the vertex indices, respecting the flip flag. 6. Face Processing (faceProc): For a given dimension D, take the 2 nodes sharing the face. Resolve children if subdivided. If all are leaves, return. Otherwise, call callSubFaceProc(D). Then, recursively call callSubEdgeProc for dimensions (D+1)%3 and (D+2)%3. 7. Vertex Clustering (clusterEdgeLeaves): For dimension D and 4 nodes, get shared edge indices. Get the highest ancestor vertex for each of the 4 nodes. If a vertex's surfaceIdx is kBadIndex, add it to the vertices list and create a new set in the Disjoint Set Union (DSU). Merge the sets: vertex[0] with vertex[1], vertex[2] with vertex[3], and vertex[0] with vertex[2]. 8. Edge Clustering (clusterEdge): For dimension D, take 4 nodes. Resolve children if subdivided. If all are leaves, call clusterEdgeLeaves. Otherwise, call callSubClusterEdge(D). 9. Face Clustering (clusterFace): For dimension D, take 2 nodes. Resolve children if subdivided. If all are leaves, return. Otherwise, call callSubClusterFace(D). Unverified code. vertex.mcollapsible = iscollapsible if iscollapsible and highestcollapsibleancestor is None: highestcollapsibleancestor = vertex if vertex.mcollapsible and highestcollapsibleancestor is vertex: vertex.mvertexIdx = len(mesh) mesh.append((vertex.mposition, vertex.mnormal)) vertex.msurfaceIdx = kBadIndex else: vertex.mvertexIdx = kBadIndex vertex.highestCollapsibleAncestor = nodes): edgeProcLeaves(nodes, dim) else: callSubEdgeProc(node, dim) def edgeProcLeaves(nodes, dim): vertexindices = [] for i, n in enumerate(nodes): myedge = kEdgeProcSharedEdge[dim][i] vidx = False v0 = vertexindices[0].highestCollapsibleAncestor v1 = vertexindices[1].highestCollapsibleAncestor v2 = vertexindices[2].highestCollapsibleAncestor v3 = vertexindices[3].highestCollapsibleAncestor if not flip: mesh.append((v0, v1, v2)) mesh.append((v1, v3, v2)) else: mesh.append((v0, v2, v1)) mesh.append((v1, v2, v3)) def faceProc(node, dim): nodes = getnodessharingface(node, dim) if all(n.isleaf for n in nodes): return callSubFaceProc(node, dim) callSubEdgeProc(node, (dim + 1) % 3) callSubEdgeProc(node, (dim + 2) % 3) def clusterEdgeLeaves(nodes, dim): ancestors = [] for i, n in enumerate(nodes): myedge = kEdgeProcSharedEdge[dim][i] vidx = kMdcEdgeSetIndex[n.vertexMask()][myedge] v = n.mvertices[vidx] ancestors.append(v.highestCollapsibleAncestor) for anc in ancestors: if anc.msurfaceIdx == kBadIndex: anc.msurfaceIdx = dsu.newset() dsu.union(ancestors[0], ancestors[1]) dsu.union(ancestors[2], ancestors[3]) dsu.union(ancestors[0], ancestors[2]) def clusterEdge(node, dim): nodes = getnodessharingedge(node, dim) if all(n.isleaf for n in nodes): clusterEdgeLeaves(nodes, dim) else: callSubClusterEdge(node, dim) def clusterFace(node, dim): nodes = getnodessharingface(node, dim) if all(n.isleaf for n in nodes): return callSubClusterFace(node, dim) def getnodessharingedge(node, dim): if node.isleaf: return [node, node, node, node] return [node.children[0], node.children[1], node.children[2], node.children[3]] def getnodessharingface(node, dim): if node.isleaf: return [node, node] return [node.children[0], node.children[1]] def callSubFaceProc(node, dim): if node.isSubdivided: for child in node.children: faceProc(child, dim) def callSubEdgeProc(node, dim): if node.isSubdivided: for child in node.children: edgeProc(child, dim) def callSubClusterEdge(node, dim): if node.isSubdivided: for child in node.children: clusterEdge(child, dim) def callSubClusterFace(node, dim): if node.isSubdivided: for child in node.children: clusterFace(child, dim) Winding Order: The algorithm assumes the lower endpoint of the minimal edge is solid. If this is not the case, the triangles' winding order must be flipped to remain facing outside the surface. This is handled by the flip boolean in edgeProcLeaves. Invalid Vertex Index: If the calculated vertex index for an edge is negative or out of bounds for the node's vertex list, the processing for that edge/face/cell is skipped (return). name: IsoOctree
head: Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees
body: IsoOctree is an unconstrained isosurface extraction method that operates on arbitrary octrees by computing the Euclidean Distance Transform (EDT) of an input mesh and adapting the octree to sample this transform. It solves the problem of generating simplified, adaptive polygonal representations of meshes by refining the octree resolution near the surface and in high-curvature regions. It sets itself apart from constrained octree methods by allowing arbitrary octree structures (non-conforming) and by operating on the distance field rather than raw scalar voxel data, enabling direct mesh simplification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A watertight mesh with properly oriented triangles, typically in PLY format. Output: An extracted isosurface, typically as a polygonal mesh in PLY format. Data Structures: Octree: An adaptive spatial data structure. Nodes are defined by their depth and spatial extent. Leaf nodes store samples of the Euclidean Distance Transform (EDT). The structure is "arbitrary," meaning it does not strictly enforce depth-disparity constraints unless the --conforming flag is used. Euclidean Distance Transform (EDT): A scalar field where each point's value is the shortest Euclidean distance to the input mesh surface. Parameters: --maxDepth (integer): The maximum depth of the octree. --curvature (float): Cut-off value for refinement. Typical value: ~0.99. Refinement is restricted to regions where curvature exceeds this threshold, resulting in coarser triangles in flat regions and finer triangles in high-detail areas. --conforming (flag): Forces the octree to satisfy the condition that the depth-disparity between face-adjacent leaf nodes is never greater than one. --fullCaseTable (flag): Disambiguates ambiguous Marching-Cubes cases by assigning the face-center value equal to the average of the corner values. --triangleMesh (flag): Uses minimal area triangulation to triangulate the polygons of the isosurface. --dual (flag): Uses the primal/dual method of [Schaeffer and Warren 04] to compute the isosurface, sampling the EDT at the centers of octree leaf-nodes rather than the corners. Steps: 1. Compute EDT: Calculate the Euclidean Distance Transform of the input mesh. The mesh must be watertight and have properly oriented triangles; otherwise, spurious disconnected surface patches may be generated. 2. Adapt Octree: Construct or adapt an octree to sample the EDT data. The octree samples the transform more finely near the surface of the mesh. Refinement can be restricted to high-curvature regions using the --curvature cut-off value. 3. Extract Isosurface: Compute the zero-crossing isosurface from the sampled EDT. By default, the output is a polygonal representation. If --triangleMesh is specified, minimal area triangulation is applied. If --dual is specified, the primal/dual method is used, sampling EDT at leaf-node centers. If --fullCaseTable is specified, ambiguous Marching-Cases are disambiguated using face-center averaging. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isooctree(inputmeshfile, outputmeshfile, maxdepth, curvature=0.99, conforming=False, fullcasetable=False, trianglemesh=False, dual=False): # Step 1: Compute Euclidean Distance Transform (EDT) # Assumes inputmesh is watertight and properly oriented. # If not, spurious disconnected patches may occur. edtfield = computeedt(inputmeshfile) # Step 2: Adapt Octree to EDT # Initialize octree with maxdepth octree = Octree(maxdepth=maxdepth) # Refine octree based on curvature and distance # Refinement is finer near the surface and in high-curvature regions adaptoctreetoedt(octree, edtfield, curvature) # Enforce conforming constraint if specified if conforming: enforceconforming(octree) # Step 3: Extract Isosurface # Compute zero-crossing isosurface from sampled EDT if dual: # Sample EDT at centers of octree leaf-nodes samples = sampleedtatcenters(octree, edtfield) isosurface = extractprimaldualisosurface(samples, octree) else: # Standard extraction at corners samples = sampleedtatcorners(octree, edtfield) isosurface = extractmarchingcubesisosurface(samples, octree) # Handle ambiguous cases if specified if fullcasetable: disambiguatemarchingcubescases(isosurface, method='facecenteraverage') # Triangulate if specified if trianglemesh: isosurface = minimalareatriangulation(isosurface) # Write output writemesh(isosurface, outputmeshfile, format='PLY') Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the input mesh is not watertight or has improperly oriented triangles, the EDT construction may generate spurious disconnected surface patches, even if conditions are partially met. Ambiguous Marching-Cubes cases can be disambiguated using the --fullCaseTable flag, which assigns the face-center value equal to the average of the corners. Uses Marching Cubes on an octree grid. Simpler but may require strict grid alignment. Early octree-based isosurfacing. Focuses on efficient traversal and extraction. Specific contouring technique on octrees. General framework for unconstrained extraction, of which IsoOctree is a specific implementation. Ensures consistent vertex placement across octree boundaries. Focuses on flatness-based refinement criteria. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Supports arbitrary octree structures. Limitations: Requires watertight, properly oriented input mesh. Spurious patches may occur if input conditions are not met. When to use: When adaptive simplification of a mesh is desired, and the input mesh is watertight. When not to use: When the input mesh is not watertight or has improperly oriented triangles. name: Wilhelms and Van Gelder Octree
head: Wilhelms-Van Gelder method, Octree-based cell extraction
body: A hierarchical spatial subdivision method using an octree to accelerate isosurface extraction by pruning branches that cannot contain the isosurface. It differs from uniform grid methods by adapting resolution to data density and from sibling octree methods by relying on strict value-range bounding intervals for early termination during traversal. Inputs: Volume data V, isovalue t, octree structure. Outputs: Set of cells intersecting the isosurface t. Data Structures: Each node n in the octree corresponds to a rectilinear block B of cells C{i,j,k}. Each node is attributed an interval n{min}, n{max}), defined as the union of all intervals [v{min}, v{max}) of the cells belonging to the block. [n{min}, n{max}) = \bigcup{C{i,j,k} \in B} [v{min}, v{max}) where for each cell C{i,j,k}: v{min} = \min{V{i,j,k}}, \quad v{max} = \max{V{i,j,k}} This interval represents the range of values the interpolation function \hat{f} attains in the portion of the volume corresponding to node n. Algorithm Steps: 1. Build Octree: Construct the octree from the volume data. For each node, compute n{min} and n{max} by aggregating the min/max values of its child cells or children nodes. 2. Recursive Traversal: Start at the root node. 3. Pruning: For a current node n, check if the isovalue t lies within the node's bounding interval [n{min}, n{max}). If t \notin [n{min}, n{max}), ignore this branch entirely. If t \in [n{min}, n{max}), proceed to children (if internal) or process cells (if leaf). 4. [Leaf Processing: For leaf nodes n where t \in [n{min}, n{max}), investigate cells cell-by-cell using the standard enumeration algorithm (e.g., Marching Cubes) to extract the isosurface geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractisosurfaceoctree(node, t): """ Recursively traverse the octree to find cells intersecting isovalue t. node: OctreeNode with fields.minval,.maxval,.isleaf,.children,.cells t: float, the isovalue Returns: List of cells intersecting the isosurface """ # Pruning step: if t is outside the range of values in this node's block, # no cell in this block can contain the isosurface. if not (node.minval <= t < node.maxval): return [] if node.isleaf: # Leaf node: process cells individually intersectingcells = [] for cell in node.cells: # Check if cell contains isovalue t if cell.minval <= t < cell.maxval: intersectingcells.append(cell) return intersectingcells else: # Internal node: recurse into children allcells = [] for child in node.children: allcells.extend(extractisosurfaceoctree(child, t)) return allcells Parameters: t: Isovalue. Typical values depend on the dataset. Octree depth: Determined by the desired resolution or data characteristics. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Floating-point comparisons for t \in [n{min}, n{max}) must handle boundary conditions carefully. The interval is half-open [n{min}, n{max}). Degenerate Input: If n{min} = n{max}, the interval is empty or a point. If t = n{min}, it is included; if t = n{max}, it is excluded. A method that extracts and renders only the visible portions of an isosurface to reduce polygon count and rendering time, exploiting depth complexity and occlusion in large datasets. It differs from non-view-dependent isocontouring by skipping internal sections that are occluded by the external isosurface, and from Greene's method by marking triangles as visible in software and forwarding them to graphics hardware for final visibility determination rather than rendering the visible portion in software. Time Complexity: Linear time complexity O(n) with respect to the size of the volume data in the worst case, but considerable acceleration is achieved in practice by ignoring irrelevant branches. Memory Complexity: Moderate additional CPU storage space is required to store the octree structure and the bounding intervals for each node. Strengths: Accelerates cell extraction by avoiding unnecessary processing of cells that do not contain the isosurface. Limitations: Requires additional memory for the octree. Performance gain depends on the sparsity of the isosurface relative to the volume. Proposed by Wilhelms and Van Gelder [22] (cited in) as a method to accelerate cell extraction using hierarchical spatial subdivision. The method is discussed in the context of optimal hybrid memory constrained isosurface extraction. name: View-Dependent Isosurface Extraction
head: View-Dependent Algorithm
body: A method that extracts and renders only the visible portions of an isosurface to reduce polygon count and rendering time, exploiting depth complexity and occlusion in large datasets. It differs from non-view-dependent isocontouring by skipping internal sections that are occluded by the external isosurface, and from Greene's method by marking triangles as visible in software and forwarding them to graphics hardware for final visibility determination rather than rendering the visible portion in software. Inputs: An octree data structure containing min-max values at each node, a viewpoint, and an isovalue. Outputs: A stream of triangles forwarded to the graphics accelerator. Data Structures: 1. Virtual Screen: A bitmap with one bit per pixel used to create an occlusion mask. 2. Hierarchical Tiles: A coverage map is an 8×8 rectangular bitmap where each bit represents a pixel. Tiles are organized hierarchically into meta-tiles. Precomputed coverage patterns for edge crossings are combined to form convex polygon coverage maps. Steps: 1. Front-to-Back Traversal: Traverse the octree in front-to-back order relative to the viewpoint. Prune empty subtrees based on min-max values stored at octree nodes. 2. Coarse Software Visibility Test: For each meta-cell intersecting the isosurface, perform a visibility test to determine if it is hidden by previously extracted sections. This step requires a front-to-back traversal to ensure previously extracted sections are already marked on the occlusion mask. Pruning Logic: Project the meta-cell onto the virtual screen. If any pixel in the projection is unset (visible), the cell is visible. If all pixels are set (hidden), the cell and all children are pruned. 3. Forward Triangulation: Triangulate visible cells and forward the resulting triangles to the graphics accelerator for hardware rendering. The hardware resolves final exact partial visibility. Rendering Acceleration: Organize tiles hierarchically. Project polygon onto top meta-tile. Recursively check only subtiles where the polygon might be visible, achieving logarithmic search. Coverage Map Computation: The coverage pattern of a convex polygon for a particular tile is computed by combining the coverage maps of the polygon edges. The coverage map of a triangle is computed from three precomputed tiles with no dependency on the number of pixels the triangle actually covers. Difference from Greene: Do not render the visible portion of the triangle in software. Mark the triangle as visible and forward it to graphics hardware. Parameters: Shear-warp factorization: Used as a variation to reduce the cost of projecting points/triangles/meta-cells onto the screen. Tile Size: 8×8 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: It is not possible to determine a priori the front-to-back relations between the triangles inside a single cell. Therefore, it is mandatory to accept all or none of the triangles within a cell, even though they need to be projected on the hierarchical tree. A hidden cell justifies the time invested in classification because it prevents further traversal. A visible cell does not gain benefit from the test, adding cost to the total extraction time. An occlusion test for the implicit itself proposed by Pesco et al. to further reduce the cost of isosurface extraction at render-time. Complexity: The hierarchical nature of the algorithm ensures that the cost of classification and coverage determination will not depend highly on the projected area of the cells or triangles. Performance: Enables interactive rendering of data up to 512^3 resolution. Strengths: Reduces the number of rendered polygons by extracting only visible portions, resulting in a faster algorithm for large datasets with internal structures. Limitations: For larger data, interactive visualization remains difficult. The cost of the visibility test is added to the total cost of extraction for visible cells. Originated from work on fast isosurface extraction methods for large image data sets, building on Wilhelms and Van Gelder's octree technique. It was developed to address the inefficiency of extracting internal sections of isosurfaces that cannot be seen from any direction unless the external isosurface is peeled away or cut off. name: Ashida and Badla Octree Contouring
head: Ashida and Badla's method
body: Ashida and Badla Octree Contouring is an isosurface extraction method that operates directly on adaptive octrees, avoiding the need for a uniform grid or dual hexahedral mesh. It identifies cycles of contour faces intersecting each octree cell and generates one vertex per cycle. Unlike Wilhelms and Van Gelder Octree which may require complex crack-fixing, this method aims for manifold output through cycle identification, though it is computationally expensive and prone to non-manifold artifacts between neighboring cells. Inputs: An octree structure representing the scalar field; an isovalue v. Outputs: A polygonal mesh (vertices and faces) representing the isosurface. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains scalar values at its corners (or interpolated values), a flag indicating if it is a leaf, and a list of intersecting contour faces. Contour Face: A polygon (typically a quad or triangle) representing the intersection of the isosurface with an octree cell. Defined by its vertices and connectivity. Cycle: A closed loop of connected contour faces. Steps: 1. Traverse Octree: Iterate through all leaf nodes of the octree. 2. Identify Intersections: For each leaf cell, determine if the isosurface intersects the cell. If so, compute the contour faces (polygons) where the scalar field crosses the isovalue. This typically involves linear interpolation along cell edges. 3. Build Face Adjacency: Construct a graph where nodes are contour faces and edges represent shared vertices or edges between faces in adjacent cells. 4. Cycle Identification: For each leaf cell, identify cycles of contour faces. A cycle is a closed path of faces that are topologically connected. This step involves traversing the face adjacency graph to find closed loops. 5. Vertex Creation: Create one mesh vertex for each identified cycle. The position of the vertex is typically the centroid or a weighted average of the vertices of the faces in the cycle. 6. Face Generation: Generate mesh faces by connecting the cycle vertices. The connectivity is derived from the adjacency of the cycles. 7. Boundary Handling: Handle boundary conditions and ensure consistent connectivity across cell boundaries. Parameters: Isovalue: The scalar value at which the surface is extracted. Interpolation Method: Linear interpolation is standard for edge intersections. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-manifold Edges: Despite the claim of manifold output, non-manifold edges can appear between neighboring cells if cycle identification is not perfectly consistent across cell boundaries. Performance: Cycle identification is a time-consuming process, especially for complex contours. Degenerate Cases: Cells with no intersection or tangent contact with the isosurface must be handled to avoid empty cycles or degenerate faces. Time Complexity: High due to the cycle identification step, which involves graph traversal and connectivity analysis across the octree. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of octree leaves and the complexity of the contours. Strengths: Adaptive resolution allows for efficient representation of complex surfaces; direct octree processing avoids grid conversion overhead. Limitations: Potential for non-manifold artifacts; high computational cost for cycle identification; not guaranteed to be manifold without additional constraints. When to Use: Suitable for scenes with highly adaptive features where uniform grid methods are inefficient, and computational resources allow for expensive cycle identification. When Not to Use: When strict manifold guarantees are required without post-processing, or when real-time performance is critical. The method was proposed by Ashida and Badla as an alternative to contour simplification techniques used in Dual Contouring. It aims to extract contours directly from octrees, leveraging the adaptive nature of the octree structure. The method is discussed in the context of manifold dual contouring and compared with other adaptive isosurface extraction techniques.
