name: Manifold Vertex Clustering
head: Manifold Vertex Clustering Criterion, Topology criterion for collapsible vertices, Topology-Constrained Clustering
body: Manifold Vertex Clustering is a topological constraint applied to vertex clustering in adaptive isosurface extraction to ensure the resulting mesh is a closed 2-manifold. It solves the problem of non-manifold artifacts (edges shared by more than two polygons or vertices with non-disk-like neighborhoods) that arise when collapsing multiple fine-resolution vertices into a single coarse vertex. It sets itself apart from standard vertex clustering by adding a sufficient topological check based on the Euler characteristic and edge intersection counts, rather than relying solely on geometric error metrics like the Quadratic Error Function (QEF). Inputs: A vertex v on the simplified contour. Cv: The octree cell in which v was created by clustering. Sv: The set of all polygons on the unsimplified surface (extracted at the finest level of the octree) incident on vertices that are clustered to v. Outputs: A boolean indicating whether v is valid for clustering (i.e., satisfies the manifold criterion). Precomputed values for each vertex v: \chi(Sv) and ei(Sv) for i=1,\dots,12. For each vertex v, store 13 numbers: 1. \chi(Sv): The Euler characteristic of the surface portion Sv. 2. ei(Sv): The number of intersections of Sv with the i-th edge of the octree cell Cv, for i=1,\dots,12. 1. Base Case (Leaf Cell): For a vertex v in a leaf cell: Sv consists of a single vertex v connected to polygons dual to the edges associated with v. Set ei(Sv) = 1 for each edge associated with v, and 0 otherwise. Set \chi(Sv) = 1. 2. Recursive Intersection Count: For a clustered vertex v formed by clustering child vertices vk from the child cells of Cv: Compute ei(Sv) by summing the intersections of each child surface S{vk} along the edges of Cv. Specifically, for each edge i of Cv: ei(Sv) = \sumk ei(S{vk}) where ei(S{vk}) is the precomputed intersection count of S{vk} on edge i. 3. Recursive Euler Characteristic: Compute \chi(Sv) using the inductive formula: \chi(Sv) = \sumk \chi(S{vk}) - \frac{\sumk e(S{vk})}{4} where: vk are the vertices clustered to form v. e(S{vk}) is the sum of intersections of S{vk} along the internal edges of Cv. The internal edges of Cv are the edges shared between child cells within Cv. 4. Manifold Criterion Check: A vertex v is valid for clustering (generates a closed 2-manifold) if: 1. \chi(Sv) = 1. 2. For each of the 6 faces of Cv, the number of intersections of Sv with the 4 edges of that face is either 0 or 2. Euler Characteristic Definition: \chi(Sv) = V(Sv) - E(Sv) + F(Sv) where V(Sv), E(Sv), and F(Sv) are the numbers of vertices, edges, and faces of Sv. Recursive Euler Characteristic Update: \chi(Sv) = \sumk \chi(S{vk}) - \frac{\sumk e(S{vk})}{4} where e(S{vk}) = \sum{j \in \text{internal edges of } Cv} ej(S{vk}). Cv: The octree cell containing vertex v. Sv: The set of polygons from the finest level incident on vertices clustered to v. \chi(Sv) \neq 1: Clustering may remove a surface component or result in a non-manifold vertex. For example, if Sv is a sphere (\chi=2) or cylinder (\chi=0), clustering is invalid. Violation of Intersection Condition: If the number of intersections of Sv with the edges of a face of Cv is not 0 or 2 (e.g., 4 intersections), clustering may introduce a non-manifold edge shared by four polygons. Sufficiency: The two conditions are sufficient but not necessary. Genus Preservation: Since \chi(Sv)=1 implies the genus of Sv is zero, vertex clustering preserves the genus of the unsimplified surface. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemanifoldproperties(childvertices): """ Computes chi(Sv) and ei(Sv) for vertex v in octree cell Cv. childvertices: list of (vk, ek) tuples from recursive bottom-up calls. Returns (chiv, ev) where ev is a list of 12 intersection counts. """ chisum = 0 etotal = [0] 12 einternalsum = 0 for vk, ek in childvertices: chisum += vk.chi for i in range(12): etotal[i] += ek[i] # Each child cell in an octree subdivision has exactly 4 internal edges. # Sum intersections on these edges to correct for overcounting in the Euler formula. for internaledgeidx in vk.internaledges: einternalsum += ek[internaledgeidx] chiv = chisum - (einternalsum / 4) return VertexProperties(chi=chiv, e=etotal) def checkmanifoldcriterion(ev): """ Checks if vertex v satisfies the manifold criterion. ev: VertexProperties object with chi and e (list of 12 ints). """ # Condition 1: Euler characteristic must be 1 if ev.chi != 1: return False # Condition 2: For each of the 6 faces of Cv, # the number of intersections of Sv with the 4 edges of that face is 0 or 2. for faceidx in range(6): faceedges = getfaceedges(faceidx) intersectioncount = sum(ev.e[i] for i in faceedges) if intersectioncount not in (0, 2): return False return True def getfaceedges(faceidx): """ Returns the 4 edge indices belonging to a given face of the octree cell. Standard octree face-edge mapping. Indices 0-11 represent the 12 edges. """ # Mapping depends on octree layout; returns 4 indices per face. faceedgemap = { 0: [0, 1, 2, 3], 1: [4, 5, 6, 7], 2: [8, 9, 10, 11], 3: [0, 4, 8, 12], 4: [1, 5, 9, 13], 5: [2, 6, 10, 14] } # Adjusted to 12 edges total: standard layout uses 0-11. # Simplified standard mapping for 6 faces, 4 edges each: return [0, 1, 2, 3] if faceidx == 0 else [4, 5, 6, 7] if faceidx == 1 else [8, 9, 10, 11] if faceidx == 2 else [0, 4, 8, 1] if faceidx == 3 else [2, 6, 10, 3] if faceidx == 4 else [1, 5, 9, 2] def VertexProperties(chi, e): class VP: def init(self): self.chi = chi self.e = e return VP() The base method that extracts contours directly from octrees. Manifold Vertex Clustering is a constraint applied on top of this method to ensure manifoldness. The general technique of collapsing multiple vertices into one. Manifold Vertex Clustering adds topological checks to this general technique. Time Complexity: The computation of \chi(Sv) and ei(Sv) is done recursively during the bottom-up octree collapse. Each vertex requires constant time operations (summing 13 values) relative to its children, making the overhead linear in the number of vertices. Memory Complexity: Each vertex stores 13 integers (or floats), which is a small constant overhead. Strengths: Ensures the output mesh is a closed 2-manifold, preserving genus and avoiding non-manifold edges. Efficiently verifiable during clustering. Limitations: The conditions are sufficient but not necessary, potentially rejecting valid collapses. Requires tracking the finest-level surface polygons for each clustered vertex, which may increase memory usage if not managed carefully. When to Use: When a manifold mesh is required, such as for simulation or rendering, and adaptive resolution is used. When Not to Use: When non-manifold geometry is acceptable or when performance is critical and the topological overhead is prohibitive. Manifold Vertex Clustering is a topological constraint developed for adaptive dual contouring to address non-manifold artifacts that occur when vertices are clustered. The method builds on the recursive nature of octree-based contouring to efficiently compute topological invariants during the bottom-up collapse. name: Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees
head: Primal Isosurface Extraction on Octrees, Unconstrained Octree Isosurface Extraction
body: This method extracts a provably watertight isosurface directly from an arbitrary octree without requiring tree refinement or modification of vertex values. Unlike dual marching cubes, which can generate topological holes in flat regions, this primal approach guarantees that the isosurface separates samples on opposite sides of the isovalue by introducing an isovertex along every isovalue-crossing edge. It sets itself apart by using binary edge-trees to resolve inconsistencies at face boundaries between leaf nodes of different depths, ensuring watertightness even when the octree topology is unconstrained. Inputs: An arbitrary octree structure where nodes may have varying depths and no depth-disparity constraints are enforced. Scalar values associated with the vertices of the octree. A target isovalue (scalar threshold) for extraction. Outputs: A triangulated polygon mesh representing the watertight isosurface. Octree Node: children: Array of 8 child nodes (or null if leaf). vertices: Array of 8 scalar values associated with the node's corners. geometry: Spatial bounds (min/max coordinates) of the node. Edge-Tree Node: value: Binary integer (0 or 1). children: Array of 2 child nodes (since an octree edge is shared by two sibling nodes, the edge-tree is a binary tree). associatededge: Reference to the specific octree edge in the parent octree node. Isovertex: position: 3D coordinate along the octree edge. edgeref: Reference to the octree edge where the isovertex resides. 1. Construct Edge-Trees: For each edge in the octree, construct a binary edge-tree. The root of the edge-tree corresponds to the coarsest octree edge. If an octree edge is subdivided, its children in the octree define the children in the edge-tree. The topology of the edge-tree is inherited from the octree's subdivision history. 2. Compute Edge-Tree Values: For each edge-tree node, compute its binary value based on the scalar values at the endpoints of the associated octree edge and the isovalue. Let v{start} and v{end} be the scalar values at the two endpoints of the octree edge. Let I be the isovalue. The binary value v{node} is defined as: v{node} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } (v{start} < I \land v{end} \ge I) \lor (v{start} \ge I \land v{end} < I) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This indicates whether the edge crosses the isovalue. Note that multiple crossings along a single edge result in a value of 0 if both endpoints are on the same side. 3. Propagate Edge-Tree Values: For interior nodes in the edge-tree, the value is determined by the sum modulo 2 of its children's values. This ensures consistency across different levels of the octree. v{parent} = \left( \sum{i=1}^{2} v{childi} \right) \mod 2 This property guarantees that if an edge has value 1 (crossing), it has a unique child with value 1, allowing for a consistent definition of the isovertex position. 4. Define Isovertices: For each octree edge with value 1, traverse down the edge-tree to find the unique leaf node with value 1. The isovertex is defined at the position corresponding to this leaf edge. If the edge has value 0, no isovertex is defined for that edge. 5. Extract Isopolygons per Leaf Node: For each leaf node in the octree: Iterate over the 6 faces of the node. On each face, identify the iso-edges (edges of the face that have value 1). Use a marching-squares-like algorithm to link iso-edges sharing common isovertices to form closed loops (isopolygons) on the face. If a face has no iso-edges, no polygon is generated for that face. 6. Resolve Depth-Disparity Inconsistencies: When face-adjacent leaf nodes have different resolutions (depths), the iso-edges computed independently may not match. Identify coarser nodes that are adjacent to finer nodes. Copy the iso-edges from the finer neighbors to the coarser node. Flip the orientation of the copied iso-edges to maintain consistent winding order. This step ensures that the boundary between nodes of different resolutions is watertight. 7. Triangulate Isopolygons: The extracted isopolygons are 3D polygons that may be non-planar. Use a minimum area triangulation algorithm for 3D polygons to convert each isopolygon into a set of triangles. The algorithm minimizes the sum of the areas of the resulting triangles to ensure a smooth and accurate representation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractisosurface(octree, isovalue): """ Extracts a watertight isosurface from an arbitrary octree. Args: octree: Root node of the octree. isovalue: Scalar threshold for extraction. Returns: List of triangles representing the isosurface. """ # Step 1 & 2: Construct Edge-Trees and Compute Values edgetrees = buildedgetrees(octree) computeedgetreevalues(edgetrees, isovalue) # Step 3: Propagate Values (Mod 2 Sum) propagateedgetreevalues(edgetrees) # Step 4: Define Isovertices isovertices = defineisovertices(edgetrees) # Step 5: Extract Isopolygons isopolygons = [] for leaf in octree.leaves(): facepolygons = extractfacepolygons(leaf, isovertices) isopolygons.extend(facepolygons) # Step 6: Resolve Depth-Disparity resolvedepthdisparity(isopolygons, octree) # Step 7: Triangulate triangles = [] for polygon in isopolygons: triangles.extend(minareatriangulate(polygon)) return triangles def buildedgetrees(octree): """ Builds binary edge-trees for all edges in the octree. """ edgetrees = {} for node in octree.allnodes(): for edge in node.edges: if edge not in edgetrees: edgetrees[edge] = EdgeTreeNode(edge) return edgetrees def computeedgetreevalues(edgetrees, isovalue): """ Computes initial binary values for edge-tree nodes based on endpoint values. """ for edge, tree in edgetrees.items(): vstart = edge.startvertex.value vend = edge.endvertex.value if (vstart < isovalue and vend >= isovalue) or (vstart >= isovalue and vend < isovalue): tree.value = 1 else: tree.value = 0 def propagateedgetreevalues(edgetrees): """ Propagates values up the edge-tree using mod 2 sum. """ # Process from leaves to root for tree in edgetrees.values(): if tree.isinterior(): tree.value = (tree.children[0].value + tree.children[1].value) % 2 def defineisovertices(edgetrees): """ Defines isovertices by traversing edge-trees. """ isovertices = {} for edge, tree in edgetrees.items(): if tree.value == 1: # Traverse down to find unique leaf with value 1 current = tree while not current.isleaf(): # Find child with value 1 for child in current.children: if child.value == 1: current = child break # Define isovertex at the leaf edge isovertices[edge] = current.leafedge.position return isovertices def extractfacepolygons(leaf, isovertices): """ Extracts isopolygons from a leaf node's faces. """ polygons = [] for face in leaf.faces: isoedges = [edge for edge in face.edges if edge in isovertices] if len(isoedges) >= 3: polygon = linkisoedges(isoedges) if polygon.isclosed(): polygons.append(polygon) return polygons def resolvedepthdisparity(isopolygons, octree): """ Resolves inconsistencies between nodes of different depths. """ for coarsenode in octree.leaves(): for neighbor in coarsenode.faceadjacentleaves(): if neighbor.depth > coarsenode.depth: # Copy iso-edges from finer neighbor to coarser node for edge in neighbor.edges: if edge in isovertices: # Add to coarse node's polygon list with flipped orientation addisoedgetocoarse(coarsenode, edge, flipped=True) def minareatriangulate(polygon): """ Triangulates a 3D polygon using minimum area algorithm. """ # Implementation of minimum area triangulation for 3D polygons # This is a complex geometric algorithm, typically dynamic programming based # on minimizing the sum of triangle areas. # For brevity, we assume a standard implementation exists. return triangulatepolygon(polygon) Isovalue: The scalar threshold for extraction. Not given in the sources as a specific value, but it is a required input. Flatness Measure: Used in the context of generating the adaptive octree, defined as the ratio of the length of the mean curvature vector of the intersected surface to its area. This is not part of the extraction algorithm itself but is used to generate the input octree. Multiple Isovalue-Crossings: If an edge has multiple crossings, the edge-tree assigns a value of 0 if both endpoints are on the same side. This ensures a consistent binary representation and prevents ambiguity in isovertex definition. Depth-Disparity: Without resolving depth-disparity, the extracted mesh may not be watertight. The method handles this by copying iso-edges from finer neighbors to coarser nodes. Topological Holes: Dual marching cubes can generate topological holes if the adaptive octree is much coarser than the model thickness. This primal method avoids this by guaranteeing that the isosurface separates samples on opposite sides of the isovalue. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The algorithm involves traversing the octree and edge-trees, which is linear in the number of nodes and edges. The triangulation step is more complex but depends on the number of polygons. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method requires storing edge-trees, which adds memory overhead compared to methods that do not use them. Not given in the sources. The paper evaluates the method in the context of mesh simplification and compares it to dual marching cubes, but specific performance metrics (e.g., FPS, memory usage) are not provided. The method scales with the size of the octree. Since it does not require refinement, it can handle large, arbitrary octrees efficiently. Strengths: Guarantees watertightness for arbitrary octrees. Does not require tree refinement or modification of vertex values. Avoids topological holes common in dual marching cubes. Limitations: Requires additional memory for edge-trees. The triangulation step for non-planar polygons can be computationally expensive. Use this method when extracting isosurfaces from arbitrary, unconstrained octrees where watertightness is critical and tree refinement is not desirable. Do not use if the octree is already constrained (e.g., depth-disparity limited) and a simpler method like Marching Cubes with Octree is sufficient. Do not use if computational efficiency is the primary concern and watertightness can be approximated. The method was introduced by Michael Kazhdan, Allison Klein, Ketan Dalal, and Hugues Hoppe in their paper "Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees". The paper builds on previous work in isosurface extraction from octrees, such as the work by Wilhelms and Van Gelder [WG92] and Bloomenthal [Blo88]. The key innovation is the use of edge-trees to resolve inconsistencies in arbitrary octrees. The method is used in mesh simplification and surface reconstruction, particularly in scenarios where adaptive octrees are generated based on surface flatness or other criteria. It is also used in computer graphics for generating watertight meshes from volumetric data. name: Consistent Isovertex Definition via Edge-Trees
head: Edge-Tree Isovertex Definition, Edge-Tree Traversal for Isovertex
body: This method defines the position of an isovertex on an octree edge consistently by traversing an "edge-tree" to a unique leaf node with value 1, ensuring watertightness in isosurface extraction. It solves the problem of ambiguous isovertex positions when a coarse edge contains multiple sign changes, which causes standard polygonization methods like [Blo88] to fail. Unlike methods that refine the tree or modify vertex values, this approach uses the existing edge-tree structure to resolve ambiguity, ensuring that the extracted isopolylines are closed loops and each edge is shared by exactly two isopolygons. It differs from the minimal edge definition in [JLSW02] only when there is more than one isovalue-crossing along an edge. Inputs: An octree representing the scalar field. An edge-tree structure associated with the octree edges. A scalar isovalue. Outputs: A set of isovertices, each associated with an octree edge. Data Structures: Edge-Tree Node: Represents an octree edge or a sub-segment of it. value: Binary integer (0 or 1). 1 indicates an isovalue crossing (sign change) exists in the segment represented by this node. 0 indicates no crossing. children: List of child nodes (for interior nodes). Leaf nodes have no children. geometry: Geometric representation of the edge segment (start point, end point, or center/length for interpolation). Algorithm: 1. Identify Crossing Edges: For every edge e in the octree, determine if it crosses the isovalue. If the scalar values at the endpoints of e have different signs relative to the isovalue, set the root of the corresponding edge-tree node to value = 1. Otherwise, value = 0. 2. Compute Edge-Tree Values: For every interior node in the edge-tree, compute its value based on its children. The binary value of an interior node is the sum modulo 2 of its children's values: \text{value}(\text{parent}) = (\text{value}(\text{child}1) + \text{value}(\text{child}2)) \pmod 2 This property guarantees that if an edge e has value = 1, it must have a unique child that also has value = 1. 3. Traverse to Leaf: For each edge e with value = 1: Start at the root node of the edge-tree corresponding to e. Recursively traverse down the unique child that has value = 1. Continue until a leaf node \tilde{e} is reached. The path e \supseteq \dots \supseteq \tilde{e} consists entirely of nodes with value = 1. 4. Define Isovertex Position: Assign the isovertex position p to be the position defined by the leaf node \tilde{e}. Denote this assignment as p \in e. The position p is typically interpolated within the segment represented by \tilde{e} based on the scalar values at the endpoints of \tilde{e}. Note: p \in e and e' \supseteq e does not imply p \in e'. The isovertex is tied to the specific leaf \tilde{e}, not the coarse edge e. 5. Handle Multiple Crossings: If an edge has multiple sign changes, the edge-tree structure ensures that the value = 1 property propagates down to a unique leaf that represents one of the crossings. The isovertex is assigned to the finest leaf node in the edge-tree that still indicates a crossing. This resolves ambiguity compared to standard methods. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeedgetreevalues(node): """ Recursively computes the binary value of an edge-tree node based on its children. """ if node.isleaf(): # Value is already set based on scalar field sign change return node.value # Compute value from children childvalues = [computeedgetreevalues(child) for child in node.children] node.value = sum(childvalues) % 2 return node.value def findisovertex(edgeroot): """ Traverses the edge-tree to find the leaf node defining the isovertex. Assumes edgeroot.value == 1. """ if edgeroot.isleaf(): return edgeroot # Find the unique child with value 1 for child in edgeroot.children: if child.value == 1: return findisovertex(child) # This should not happen if the tree is correctly constructed raise ValueError("No child with value 1 found") def defineisovertices(octreeedges): """ Defines isovertices for all edges in the octree. """ isovertices = {} # Step 1 & 2: Compute edge-tree values for edge in octreeedges: if edge.hassignchange(): edge.edgetreeroot.value = 1 computeedgetreevalues(edge.edgetreeroot) # Step 3 & 4: Traverse and define positions for edge in octreeedges: if edge.edgetreeroot.value == 1: leafnode = findisovertex(edge.edgetreeroot) # Interpolate position within the leaf segment p = interpolateposition(leafnode) isovertices[edge] = p return isovertices Parameters: Isovalue: The scalar value at which the isosurface is extracted. Typical values depend on the scalar field. Interpolation Method: Linear interpolation is typically used within the leaf segment. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Sign Changes: Standard polygonization fails if an edge has multiple sign changes. This method handles it by assigning the isovertex to the finest leaf node in the edge-tree that still indicates a crossing. Notation Ambiguity: The notation p \in e does not imply p \in e' for an ancestor edge e' \supseteq e. The isovertex is tied to the specific leaf \tilde{e} in the edge-tree, not the coarse edge e itself. Precision: Interpolation within the leaf segment may introduce precision errors if the leaf segment is very small or if the scalar field values are close to the isovalue. Twin Isovertex Pairing is a post-processing step in octree-based isosurface extraction that closes open isopolylines into closed isopolygons by identifying and connecting "twin" isovertices. It solves the problem of watertightness in meshes extracted from arbitrary octrees where a single edge may contain multiple sign changes, resulting in isovertices with valence one that cannot be paired within the local leaf node. Unlike methods that refine the tree or modify vertex values, this method uses the existing edge-tree structure to pair vertices, ensuring the resulting mesh is watertight without altering the underlying scalar field representation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of edges in the octree, as each edge is traversed once to find its leaf node. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of edges in the octree, to store the edge-tree structure. Strengths: Ensures watertightness and closed isopolylines without modifying the scalar field or refining the tree unnecessarily. Handles multiple sign changes on a single edge. Limitations: Requires the construction and maintenance of the edge-tree structure. The position of the isovertex is tied to the finest leaf, which may not be the "true" crossing point if multiple crossings exist. When to Use: When watertightness is critical and the octree may have arbitrary refinement levels, including cases with multiple sign changes on coarse edges. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the edge-tree construction overhead is prohibitive, or when the scalar field is guaranteed to have at most one sign change per edge. This method was introduced in the paper "Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees". It addresses the challenges of isosurface extraction on arbitrary octrees, where traditional methods like Marching Cubes may produce cracks or non-watertight meshes due to inconsistent isovertex definitions. The method builds on the properties of edge-trees to ensure consistency. name: Twin Isovertex Pairing for Isopolyline Closure
head: Isopolyline Closure, Isovertex Pairing
body: Twin Isovertex Pairing is a post-processing step in octree-based isosurface extraction that closes open isopolylines into closed isopolygons by identifying and connecting "twin" isovertices. It solves the problem of watertightness in meshes extracted from arbitrary octrees where a single edge may contain multiple sign changes, resulting in isovertices with valence one that cannot be paired within the local leaf node. Unlike methods that refine the tree or modify vertex values, this method uses the existing edge-tree structure to pair vertices, ensuring the resulting mesh is watertight without altering the underlying scalar field representation. Input: An octree where each edge e has an associated binary value (0 or 1) derived from the sign changes of the scalar field along that edge. An isovertex p is defined on an edge e with valence one (an endpoint of an open isopolyline). Output: A twin isovertex p' and an iso-edge (p, p') added to the set of iso-edges for the leaf node N, reducing the count of valence-one isovertices. The method relies on the Edge-Tree structure established in Consistent Isovertex Definition via Edge-Trees. Edge Node: Represents an octree edge at a specific level of refinement. Fields: value: Binary integer (0 or 1). Indicates the parity of sign changes on the edge. 1 implies an odd number of sign changes (isovertex exists); 0 implies an even number (no net isovertex or paired isovertices at this scale). parent: Reference to the parent edge node. children: References to child edge nodes (if not a leaf). Isovertex: Defined by a leaf edge node e' in the edge-tree. The position is interpolated on the geometric edge corresponding to e'. The procedure finds the twin p' for an isovertex p located on edge e. 1. Check for Restricted Octree Special Case: If the octree is a restricted octree [WKE99], there can be at most two valence-one isovertices per edge. In this case, the twin p' is simply the other valence-one isovertex on the same edge e. Connect p and p' directly. Terminate. 2. Traverse Up to Find Ancestor with Value 0: Starting from edge e, traverse up the parent pointers until finding the first ancestor edge \tilde{e} such that \tilde{e}.value == 0. Guarantee: Such an edge \tilde{e} always exists because the root of the octree has value 0 (assuming the domain boundary or root scalar values do not exhibit a net sign change, or by convention). Property: Since \tilde{e} has value 0, and e is a descendant with value 1, the parity of sign changes implies that both children of \tilde{e} must have value 1. 3. Select the Sibling Branch: Identify the two children of \tilde{e}. One child is an ancestor of the original edge e (let's call it e{anc}). The other child is not an ancestor of e (let's call it e{sib}). Select e{sib} as the starting point for the downward traversal. 4. Traverse Down to Leaf: Starting from e{sib}, traverse down the edge-tree following only nodes with value == 1 until reaching a leaf node e'. Note: The path is deterministic because at each step, we follow the child that maintains the value 1 property required to reach the twin isovertex. 5. Define Twin and Close Edge: The isovertex p' is defined by the leaf node e'. Add the iso-edge (p, p') to the set of iso-edges for the leaf node N associated with the original isovertex p. This connects the open isopolyline endpoint p to p', closing the loop locally. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findtwinisovertex(pedge, octreeroot): """ Finds the twin isovertex for an isovertex p located on edge pedge. Args: pedge: The leaf edge node in the edge-tree defining the position of isovertex p. octreeroot: The root of the octree's edge-tree structure. Returns: twinedge: The leaf edge node defining the position of the twin isovertex p'. """ # Step 1: Check for restricted octree case # Note: Detecting if the octree is 'restricted' is implementation-specific. # If restricted, there are at most 2 valence-one isovertices per edge. if isrestrictedoctree(octreeroot): # Find the other valence-one isovertex on the same geometric edge. # This requires scanning the edge-tree for pedge's geometric edge # and finding the other leaf with value 1. twinedge = findothervalenceoneonsameedge(pedge) return twinedge # Step 2: Traverse up to find the first ancestor with value 0 currentedge = pedge while currentedge.value != 0: if currentedge.parent is None: raise Error("Root edge must have value 0. No twin found.") currentedge = currentedge.parent ancestorzero = currentedge # This is ~e (tilde e) # Step 3: Identify the sibling branch # Find the child of ancestorzero that is NOT an ancestor of pedge siblingedge = None for child in ancestorzero.children: if not isancestorof(child, pedge): siblingedge = child break if siblingedge is None: raise Error("Could not find sibling branch. Structure invariant violated.") # Step 4: Traverse down through nodes with value 1 to a leaf currentedge = siblingedge while currentedge.children is not None: # We must follow a child with value 1. # In a valid edge-tree for this method, the path to the twin # consists of nodes with value 1. foundchild = False for child in currentedge.children: if child.value == 1: currentedge = child foundchild = True break if not foundchild: # This case should theoretically not happen if the tree is consistent # and the twin exists. raise Error("Path to twin broken: no child with value 1 found.") twinedge = currentedge return twinedge def isancestorof(ancestor, descendant): """ Checks if 'ancestor' is an ancestor of 'descendant' in the edge-tree. """ current = descendant while current is not None: if current is ancestor: return True current = current.parent return False Restricted Octrees: In restricted octrees [WKE99], the algorithm simplifies significantly. The twin is the other valence-one isovertex on the same edge. This is because the number of isovertices on an edge with valence one must always be even, and restricted octrees limit this to at most two. Precision: The position of the twin isovertex p' is determined by the leaf node e' in the edge-tree. The interpolation precision depends on the resolution of the leaf node. Valence: This method specifically handles isovertices with valence one. Isovertices with higher valence are handled by the standard local polygonization logic. Time Complexity: The upward traversal takes O(h) where h is the height of the octree. The downward traversal also takes O(h). Thus, finding a twin is O(h). Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the existing edge-tree structure. Strengths: Ensures watertightness without modifying the scalar field or refining the tree. Leverages the hierarchical structure of the octree for efficient pairing. Deterministic and robust for arbitrary octrees. Limitations: Requires the edge-tree structure to be fully built and consistent. Performance depends on the depth of the octree. When to Use: Use this method as the final step in isosurface extraction from arbitrary octrees to close isopolylines. It is particularly useful when the octree is not restricted and multiple sign changes can occur on a single edge. Twin Isovertex Pairing was introduced in the context of unconstrained isosurface extraction on arbitrary octrees. The method addresses the limitations of earlier polygonization methods (such as [Blo88]) which struggled with edges exhibiting multiple sign changes. By defining isovertices consistently via edge-trees and then pairing them using the tree's hierarchy, the method guarantees that the extracted isopolylines form closed loops, satisfying the requirements for a watertight polygonal mesh. The approach was detailed in the paper "Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees". name: Adaptive Octree Generation with Flatness Criterion
head: Adaptive Octree Generation
body: This method generates an adaptive octree for isosurface extraction by recursively refining nodes based on the geometric flatness of the surface intersection, assigning vertex values via Euclidean distance transform sampling. It differs from sibling methods like IsoOctree and Wilhelms and Van Gelder Octree by using a curvature-based flatness metric rather than simple field uniformity or depth constraints to determine refinement, allowing for coarser representation of planar surface regions. Inputs: Root node bounding box. Scalar field function F(\mathbf{p}) and threshold T. Base sampling size S{base}. Dropoff D, HorizontalScale Hs, VerticalScale Vs (used in field evaluation). Outputs: An adaptive octree where leaf nodes contain surface intersections. Vertex values assigned via Euclidean distance transform sampling. Data Structures: OctreeNode: Bounds: Axis-aligned bounding box (min, max vectors). Depth: Integer depth level (root is 0). Children: Array of 8 child nodes (null if leaf). Children are ordered in fixed binary index order: 0) (-X, -Y, -Z), 1) (+X, -Y, -Z), 2) (-X, +Y, -Z), 3) (+X, +Y, -Z), 4) (-X, -Y, +Z), 5) (+X, -Y, +Z), 6) (-X, +Y, +Z), 7) (+X, +Y, +Z). Flatness Metric: The flatness of a surface intersection is defined as the ratio of the length of the mean curvature vector to the area of the intersection: \text{flatness} = \frac{\|\vec{H}\|}{\text{Area}} where \vec{H} is the mean curvature vector and Area is the surface area. Nodes are refined if they intersect the surface and the intersection is not "too flat". The specific threshold for "too flat" is not given in the sources. Vertex Value Assignment: Vertex values are assigned by sampling the Euclidean distance transform. The exact implementation of this sampling is not detailed in the provided sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Start with the root node. 2. For each node, calculate the sampling interval: S = S{base} \cdot \ln(\text{Depth} + 2) 3. Calculate the number of samples per axis: nx = 1 + \lceil \frac{\text{size}x}{S} \rceil, \quad ny = 1 + \lceil \frac{\text{size}y}{S} \rceil, \quad nz = 1 + \lceil \frac{\text{size}z}{S} \rceil 4. If nx < 3 or ny < 3 or nz < 3, do not split the node. 5. Iterate over interior sample points only: z from 1 to nz - 2 y from 1 to ny - 2 x from 1 to nx - 2 6. Compute sample position using linear interpolation: xf = \text{Lerp}(\text{min}x, \text{max}x, \frac{x}{nx}) yf = \text{Lerp}(\text{min}y, \text{max}y, \frac{y}{ny}) zf = \text{Lerp}(\text{min}z, \text{max}z, \frac{z}{nz}) 7. Evaluate the field at (xf, yf, zf). Track if any sample is below threshold (isBelow) and any is above threshold (isAbove). 8. If both isBelow and isAbove are true, split the node into 8 children. Child bounds: \text{newSize} = \text{size} \cdot 0.5 \text{halfNewSize} = \text{newSize} \cdot 0.5 \text{childMin} = \text{nodeMin} + \text{halfNewSize} \text{childMax} = \text{nodeMax} - \text{halfNewSize} Create children in fixed order using min/max offsets. 9. Recursively apply steps 2-8 to children. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateoctree(rootbounds, depth, samplingsizebase, threshold, dropoff, hscale, vscale): """ Recursively generates an adaptive octree based on flatness criterion. Note: The flatness calculation itself is not implemented as the source does not provide the algorithm for computing mean curvature vector H or Area. This implementation follows the sampling and splitting logic from. """ node = OctreeNode(bounds=rootbounds, depth=depth) # Calculate sampling interval samplingsize = samplingsizebase math.log(depth + 2) # Calculate number of samples nsamples = countsamples(node.bounds, samplingsize) # Check minimum sample requirement if nsamples.x < 3 or nsamples.y < 3 or nsamples.z < 3: return node # Sample interior points isbelow = False isabove = False for z in range(1, nsamples.z - 1): for y in range(1, nsamples.y - 1): for x in range(1, nsamples.x - 1): # Linear interpolation xf = lerp(node.bounds.min.x, node.bounds.max.x, x / nsamples.x) yf = lerp(node.bounds.min.y, node.bounds.max.y, y / nsamples.y) zf = lerp(node.bounds.min.z, node.bounds.max.z, z / nsamples.z) # Evaluate field val = samplefield(Vector3(xf, yf, zf), threshold, dropoff, hscale, vscale) if val > threshold: isabove = True else: isbelow = True # Early exit if both states found if isbelow and isabove: break if isbelow and isabove: break if isbelow and isabove: break # Split if surface intersects if isbelow and isabove: newsize = node.bounds.size 0.5 halfnewsize = newsize 0.5 nodemin = node.bounds.min nodemax = node.bounds.max node.children = [] for i in range(8): # Determine child min/max based on binary index # 0: -X -Y -Z, 1: +X -Y -Z, 2: -X +Y -Z, 3: +X +Y -Z # 4: -X -Y +Z, 5: +X -Y +Z, 6: -X +Y +Z, 7: +X +Y +Z cxmin = nodemin.x if (i & 1) == 0 else nodemin.x + newsize.x cxmax = nodemin.x + newsize.x if (i & 1) == 0 else nodemax.x cymin = nodemin.y if (i & 2) == 0 else nodemin.y + newsize.y cymax = nodemin.y + newsize.y if (i & 2) == 0 else nodemax.y czmin = nodemin.z if (i & 4) == 0 else nodemin.z + newsize.z czmax = nodemin.z + newsize.z if (i & 4) == 0 else nodemax.z childbounds = Bounds(Vector3(cxmin, cymin, czmin), Vector3(cxmax, cymax, czmax)) childnode = generateoctree(childbounds, depth + 1, samplingsizebase, threshold, dropoff, hscale, vscale) node.children.append(childnode) else: node.children = None return node def countsamples(bounds, sampleinterval): x = 1 + math.ceil(bounds.size.x / sampleinterval) y = 1 + math.ceil(bounds.size.y / sampleinterval) z = 1 + math.ceil(bounds.size.z / sampleinterval) return Vector3Int(x, y, z) def samplefield(point, threshold, dropoff, hscale, vscale): # Placeholder for field evaluation logic # The source uses Dropoff, HorizontalScale, VerticalScale # but does not provide the exact formula for SampleField. # Assuming a simple signed distance or noise function scaled by these parameters. # This is a gap filler for implementers; the core method definition relies on for flatness. return 0.0 # Not given in the sources. Parameters: SamplingSize: Base physical spacing between samples. Default: 1.0f. Threshold: Field value threshold for surface extraction. Default: 0.5f. Dropoff: Controls vertical falloff of the field. Default: 100.0f. HorizontalScale, VerticalScale: Scale factors for field sampling coordinates. Default: 0.01f, 0.05f. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The flatness metric requires computing the mean curvature vector and area, which is not detailed in the sources. Implementers must define how to approximate these from the sampled field or mesh. The sampling interval formula uses Mathf.Log(node.Depth + 2), which grows slowly with depth, potentially leading to insufficient sampling in deep nodes if SamplingSize is not adjusted. The child ordering is fixed and specific to the implementation in; deviations may cause cracks if not consistent with downstream rendering. OcMesher is a method for extracting memory-efficient, highly detailed triangle meshes from unbounded scenes represented by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It uses a view-dependent adaptive octree structure driven by a given set of camera views to refine geometry only where visible. Unlike parent methods that generate octrees based on surface flatness alone, OcMesher incorporates camera projection metrics to prioritize resolution based on projected pixel density. This method constructs an octree leaf node representing a voxel containing an isosurface by solving a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) to determine the precise surface position and normal from edge intersections. It differs from its parent, Adaptive Octree Generation with Flatness Criterion, which assigns vertex values via Euclidean distance transform sampling, by using a least-squares geometric fit to refine the surface location within the leaf. It is distinct from OcMesher by relying on a global QEF solver over all edge crossings rather than local marching cubes-style triangulation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the cost of flatness calculation and field sampling. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the number of refined nodes. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows for coarser representation of planar regions, potentially reducing mesh complexity compared to uniform refinement. Limitations: The flatness metric calculation is complex and not fully specified. The method may produce cracks if depth disparity is not managed, as noted in the parent article. When to use: When surface flatness is a good indicator of refinement need and computational cost of curvature calculation is acceptable. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and curvature calculation is too expensive, or when the field does not have a well-defined curvature. The method was introduced in the context of mesh simplification, comparing octree refinement to dual marching cubes. It was developed to ensure that the octree is restricted so that the depth-disparity between adjacent nodes is never greater than one, following the approach of Wilhelms and Van Gelder. The flatness criterion was defined as the ratio of the mean curvature vector length to the area. name: OcMesher
head: OcMesher Octree Construction and Mesh Extraction, View-Dependent Octree-based Mesh Extraction
body: OcMesher is a method for extracting memory-efficient, highly detailed triangle meshes from unbounded scenes represented by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It uses a view-dependent adaptive octree structure driven by a given set of camera views to refine geometry only where visible. Unlike parent methods that generate octrees based on surface flatness alone, OcMesher incorporates camera projection metrics to prioritize resolution based on projected pixel density. Inputs: cameras: A tuple (camposes, Ks, Hs, Ws) where camposes are N \times 4 \times 4 world-to-camera matrices, Ks are N \times 3 \times 3 intrinsic matrices, and Hs, Ws are heights and widths. bounds: Axis-aligned bounding box limits [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz]. kernels: A list of callable functions Ki(\mathbf{p}) that return the SDF value at point \mathbf{p}. Parameters: pixelspercube (default 8), invscale (default 10), mindist (default 1), memorylimitmb (default 1000), bisectioniters (default 15), enclosed (default True), simplifyoccluded (default True), visiblerelaxiter (default 2), coarsecount (default 500000). Outputs: A list of trimesh.Trimesh objects containing vertices, faces, and visibility tags. Data Structures: struct node: Contains cube c and int nxts[8]. nxts[i] is the index of the i-th child in the nodes vector, or -1 if absent. Leaf nodes have nxts[0] = -2. struct cube: Contains int coords[3] and int L. L is the level. Special values: L >= 0 (regular), L == -1 (boundary), L == -2 (exterior). struct computedvertex: Contains T c[3] (coordinates), l, r (SDF values). Camera data is flattened into a numpy array of shape (23 ncameras). Each camera entry stores: inverse pose (first 12 values, 3 \times 4), intrinsic matrix K (9 values), height H (1 value), width W (1 value). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute scene center \mathbf{c}{center} as the midpoint of bounds. Compute size S = 1.1 \times \max(\text{bounds dimensions}). Flatten camera data into the cameras array. 2. Coarse Visibility: Call runcoarse with center, size, camera count, camera data, pixelspercube, invscale, mindist, coarsecount, memorylimitmb, and number of SDF kernels. Initialize root node at coords=[0,0,0], L=0. Push root to priority queue ordered by projectedsize. While queue not empty and node count < coarsecount: Pop node with highest projectedsize. If projectedsize < invscale, break. Expand node fully using expandoctree. Push 8 children to queue. Mark remaining nodes as grid nodes and return nblocks. 3. Coarse Refinement (SDF-aware): Loop while finegroup() returns inc > 0: finegroup() batches nodes into memory-limited chunks. Call fineiteration() with SDF pointer. While n > 0: Get positions via fineiterationoutput(). Compute SDFs: \text{sdf} = \min{k} Kk(\text{positions}). Pass SDFs to fineiteration(). fineiteration identifies bipolar edges (SDF sign changes) and expands nodes containing them. 4. Visibility Filtering: Call visfilter(simplifyoccluded, visiblerelaxiter) to return nvisblock. This removes blocks occluded by the mesh geometry. 5. Fine Mesh Construction: Initialize nv array. Visible Blocks: While finaliteration() returns n > 0: Get positions via finaliteration2(). Compute SDFs using kernelcaller. Call finaliteration3() with SDFs. Occluded Blocks: Call finaliterationoccluded(). If n != 0, get positions, compute SDFs, call finaliteration3occluded(). Remaining: Reset nv to zeros. Call finalremaining(). 6. Per-Element Mesh Extraction: For each element e: Get vertex centers via getvertscenter(e, centers). Compute center SDFs: centersdf = kernelcaller(kernels[e], centers). Initialize cubes array. Call updateverts(e, emptysdf, emptysdf, cubes). Bisection Refinement: Repeat bisectioniters times: Compute SDFs for cubes: sdf = kernelcaller(kernels[e], cubes). Call updateverts(e, sdf, centersdf, cubes). Get left/right vertices via getlrverts(e, cubes, cubesr). Compute SDFs for left/right: sdfl, sdfr. Call finalizeverts(e, sdfl, sdfr, vertices). Construct faces via constructfaces(e, vertices, cnts) returning nve, nvf, nf. 7. Edge and Face Vertex Refinement: Get extra vertex centers: edgeverticesc, faceverticesc via getextravertscenter. Compute their SDFs: ecentersdf, fcentersdf. Initialize left/right extra vertices arrays. Call updateextraverts with empty SDFs. Bisection Refinement: Repeat bisectioniters times: Compute SDFs for left/right edge/face vertices. Call updateextraverts with computed SDFs. Get refined left/right extra vertices via getlrextraverts. Compute SDFs for refined vertices. Call finalizeextraverts to produce final edgevertices and facevertices. 8. Final Assembly: Concatenate vertices, edgevertices, facevertices. Get visibility tags via getinviewtag. Create trimesh.Trimesh objects. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def ocmesher(cameras, bounds, kernels, pixelspercube=8, invscale=10, mindist=1, memorylimitmb=1000, bisectioniters=15, enclosed=True, simplifyoccluded=True, visiblerelaxiter=2, coarsecount=500000): # 1. Initialization camposes, Ks, Hs, Ws = cameras ncameras = len(camposes) # Flatten cameras: [invpose(12), K(9), H(1), W(1)] per camera camerasflat = np.zeros(23 ncameras, dtype=np.float64) for i in range(ncameras): invpose = np.linalg.inv(camposes[i])[:3,:4].reshape(-1) K = Ks[i].reshape(-1) camerasflat[23i: 23(i+1)] = np.concatenate([invpose, K, [Hs[i]], [Ws[i]]]) center = (bounds[0::2] + bounds[1::2]) / 2.0 size = 1.1 np.max(bounds[1::2] - bounds[0::2]) # 2. Coarse Visibility # Note: runcoarse is a C++ function call in implementation nblocks = runcoarse( center, size, ncameras, camerasflat, pixelspercube, invscale, mindist, coarsecount, memorylimitmb, len(kernels)) # 3. Coarse Refinement while True: inc = finegroup() if inc == 0: break n = fineiteration(np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32)) while n > 0: positions = np.zeros((n, 3), dtype=np.float64) fineiterationoutput(positions) # Compute min SDF across all kernels sdfbatch = kernelcaller(kernels, positions) sdfmin = np.min(sdfbatch, axis=-1) n = fineiteration(sdfmin.astype(np.float32)) # 4. Visibility Filtering nvisblock = visfilter(simplifyoccluded, visiblerelaxiter) # 5. Fine Mesh Construction nv = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32) # Visible while True: n = finaliteration(nv) if n == 0: break positions = np.zeros((n, 3), dtype=np.float64) finaliteration2(positions) sdf = kernelcaller(kernels, positions) inc = finaliteration3(sdf.astype(np.float32)) # Occluded n = finaliterationoccluded(nv) if n != 0: positions = np.zeros((n, 3), dtype=np.float64) finaliteration2(positions) sdf = kernelcaller(kernels, positions) finaliteration3occluded(sdf.astype(np.float32)) # Remaining nv = np.zeros(len(kernels), dtype=np.int32) finalremaining(nv) # 6. Per-Element Mesh Extraction meshes = [] inviewtags = [] for e in range(len(kernels)): ke = [kernels[e]] centers = np.zeros((nv[e], 3), dtype=np.float64) getvertscenter(e, centers) centersdf = kernelcaller(ke, centers) cubes = np.zeros((nv[e] 8, 3), dtype=np.float64) updateverts(e, np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), cubes) for in range(bisectioniters): sdf = kernelcaller(ke, cubes) updateverts(e, sdf.astype(np.float32), centersdf.astype(np.float32), cubes) cubesr = np.zeroslike(cubes) getlrverts(e, cubes, cubesr) sdfl = kernelcaller(ke, cubes) sdfr = kernelcaller(ke, cubesr) vertices = np.zeros((0, 3), dtype=np.float64) finalizeverts(e, sdfl.astype(np.float32), sdfr.astype(np.float32), vertices) faces = np.zeros((0, 3), dtype=np.int32) nve, nvf, nf = constructfaces(e, vertices, faces) # 7. Edge/Face Refinement edgeverticesc = np.zeros((nve, 3), dtype=np.float64) faceverticesc = np.zeros((nvf, 3), dtype=np.float64) getextravertscenter(edgeverticesc, faceverticesc) ecentersdf = kernelcaller(ke, edgeverticesc) fcentersdf = kernelcaller(ke, faceverticesc) edgeverticeslr = np.zeros((nve 2, 3), dtype=np.float64) faceverticeslr = np.zeros((nvf 4, 3), dtype=np.float64) updateextraverts( np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), edgeverticeslr, faceverticeslr) for in range(bisectioniters): esdf = kernelcaller(ke, edgeverticeslr) fsdf = kernelcaller(ke, faceverticeslr) updateextraverts( esdf.astype(np.float32), fsdf.astype(np.float32), ecentersdf.astype(np.float32), fcentersdf.astype(np.float32), edgeverticeslr, faceverticeslr) edgeverticesr = np.zeros((nve 2, 3), dtype=np.float64) faceverticesr = np.zeros((nvf 4, 3), dtype=np.float64) getlrextraverts(edgeverticeslr, edgeverticesr, faceverticeslr, faceverticesr) esdfl = kernelcaller(ke, edgeverticeslr) esdfr = kernelcaller(ke, edgeverticesr) fsdfl = kernelcaller(ke, faceverticeslr) fsdfr = kernelcaller(ke, faceverticesr) finaledgevertices = np.zeros((nve, 3), dtype=np.float64) finalfacevertices = np.zeros((nvf, 3), dtype=np.float64) finalizeextraverts( esdfl.astype(np.float32), esdfr.astype(np.float32), finaledgevertices, fsdfl.astype(np.float32), fsdfr.astype(np.float32), finalfacevertices) # 8. Assembly allvertices = np.concatenate([vertices, finaledgevertices, finalfacevertices]) inviewtag = np.zeros(allvertices.shape[0], dtype=bool) getinviewtag(e, inviewtag) inviewtags.append(inviewtag) meshes.append(trimesh.Trimesh(vertices=allvertices, faces=faces, process=False)) return meshes, inviewtags def kernelcaller(kernels, XYZall, enclosed=True, bounds=None): if len(XYZall) == 0: return np.zeros((0, len(kernels)), dtype=np.float32) step = 10000000 sdfs = [] for i in range(0, len(XYZall), step): XYZ = XYZall[i:i+step] sdfsi = [] outbound = np.zeros(len(XYZ), dtype=bool) if enclosed: for c in range(3): outbound |= XYZ[:, c] <= bounds[c2] outbound |= XYZ[:, c] >= bounds[c2+1] for kernel in kernels: sdf = kernel(XYZ) if enclosed: sdf[outbound] = 1.0 sdfsi.append(sdf) sdfs.append(np.stack(sdfsi, axis=-1).astype(np.float32)) return np.concatenate(sdfs, axis=0) Subtopics: Octree Leaf Construction with QEF Surface Fitting: Uses Quadratic Error Functions to fit surfaces at octree leaves. Choose when higher geometric accuracy per vertex is needed at the cost of increased computation per leaf. Time Complexity: Dominated by SDF evaluations. The coarse step is O(N \log N) where N is the number of octree nodes, prioritized by projected size. The fine step is proportional to the number of visible blocks and bisection iterations. Memory Complexity: Controlled by memorylimitmb during coarse refinement and coarsecount for the initial octree size. Performance: Used in Infinigen for procedural synthetic data generation. It is memory-efficient for unbounded scenes because it only generates geometry in view-dependent regions. Strengths: Handles unbounded scenes; view-dependent refinement reduces mesh size; handles multiple SDF kernels. Limitations: Requires camera poses and intrinsics; SDF evaluation can be slow for complex kernels; enclosed mode clamps out-of-bounds values which may affect boundary accuracy. OcMesher was developed by Zeyu Ma at Princeton University. It is used by default in the Infinigen project to speed up video generation and export terrain meshes. The method was presented in the paper "View-Dependent Octree-based Mesh Extraction in Unbounded Scenes for Procedural Synthetic Data" (arXiv:2312.08364). princeton-vl/OcMesher, https://github.com/princeton-vl/OcMesher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Octree Leaf Construction with QEF Surface Fitting
head: QEF-based Octree Leaf Construction, Quadratic Error Function Surface Fitting for Octree Leaves
body: This method constructs an octree leaf node representing a voxel containing an isosurface by solving a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) to determine the precise surface position and normal from edge intersections. It differs from its parent, Adaptive Octree Generation with Flatness Criterion, which assigns vertex values via Euclidean distance transform sampling, by using a least-squares geometric fit to refine the surface location within the leaf. It is distinct from OcMesher by relying on a global QEF solver over all edge crossings rather than local marching cubes-style triangulation. Inputs: globalPos: The 3D world position of the voxel corner (vec3). resolution: The side length of the voxel (float). msampleCache: A cache for volume sampling (Sampler object). msize: The size parameter for the sampler (int). Outputs: Octree leaf node containing: mdrawPos: The fitted surface position (vec3). mqef: The QEF data structure (QEF object). maverageNormal: The averaged surface normal (vec3). mcorners: The bitmask of occupied corners (uint8t). Data Structures: Octree: Represents a node in the octree. If it is a leaf, it stores mdrawPos, mqef, maverageNormal, and mcorners. If it is an internal node, it stores a field (bitmask) and an array of 8 child pointers. QEF: A solver for the Quadratic Error Function. add(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz): Adds a point-normal constraint. solve(position, error, sweeps, error): Solves for the optimal position. getData(): Returns the QEF data. getMassPoint(): Returns the centroid of the added points. Parameters: QEFERROR: Convergence tolerance for the QEF solver. Value: 10^{-6}. QEFSWEEPS: Number of sweeps for the QEF solver. Value: 4. MATERIALAIR: Integer constant for air. Value: 0. MATERIALSOLID: Integer constant for solid. Value: 1. MAXCROSSINGS: Maximum number of edge crossings to process per voxel. Value: 6. CHILDMINOFFSETS: An array of 8 vec3 offsets defining the corners of the child voxel relative to the local position. Steps: 1. Corner Bitmask Initialization: Initialize corners bitmask to 0. Loop i from 0 to 7: Calculate cornerPos = localPos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[i]. Sample the volume at cornerPos using Sampler::SampleCache(msampleCache, msize+1, cornerPos). If sample > 0, set bit i in corners: corners |= (1 << i). 2. Leaf Initialization: Create a new Octree leaf: leaf = new Octree(resolution, globalPos). Initialize edgeCount = 0. Initialize averageNormal = vec3(0.0f). Initialize a qef solver instance. 3. Edge Crossing Detection and QEF Assembly: Loop i from 0 to 11 (representing the 12 edges of the voxel) while edgeCount < MAXCROSSINGS: Get edge vertices indices: c1 = edgevmap[i][0], c2 = edgevmap[i][1]. Get material states: m1 = (corners >> c1) & 1, m2 = (corners >> c2) & 1. If m1 == m2, continue (no crossing). Calculate edge endpoints: p1 = globalPos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c1], p2 = globalPos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c2]. Determine zero-crossing position p: If m1 > m2, p = ApproximateZeroCrossingPositionBinarySearch(p1, p2). Else, p = ApproximateZeroCrossingPositionBinarySearch(p2, p1). Calculate surface normal n = CalculateSurfaceNormal(p). Add point p and normal n to QEF solver: qef.add(p.x, p.y, p.z, n.x, n.y, n.z). Accumulate normal: averageNormal += n. Increment edgeCount. 4. QEF Solution and Leaf Finalization: Solve QEF: qef.solve(qefPosition, QEFERROR, QEFSWEEPS, QEFERROR). Store result in leaf: leaf->mdrawPos = vec3(qefPosition.x, qefPosition.y, qefPosition.z). Store QEF data: leaf->mqef = qef.getData(). Calculate average normal: leaf->maverageNormal = glm::normalize(averageNormal / (float)edgeCount). Store corner bitmask: leaf->mcorners = corners. Return leaf. Pitfalls: If corners == 0 (voxel fully outside) or corners == 255 (voxel fully inside), return nullptr (no leaf node created). Boundary check: If leaf->mdrawPos is outside the voxel bounds [globalPos, globalPos + leaf->msize] in any axis, fallback to QEF mass point: leaf->mdrawPos = vec3(qef.getMassPoint().x, qef.getMassPoint().y, qef.getMassPoint().z). This check is performed twice. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructleaf(globalpos, resolution, samplecache, size): # Step 1: Corner Bitmask Initialization corners = 0 for i in range(8): cornerpos = globalpos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[i] sample = samplersamplecache(samplecache, size + 1, cornerpos) if sample > 0: corners |= (1 << i) # Pitfall: Check for fully inside or outside if corners == 0 or corners == 255: return None # Step 2: Leaf Initialization leaf = Octree(resolution, globalpos) edgecount = 0 averagenormal = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) qef = QEF() # Step 3: Edge Crossing Detection and QEF Assembly for i in range(12): if edgecount >= MAXCROSSINGS: break c1 = edgevmap[i][0] c2 = edgevmap[i][1] m1 = (corners >> c1) & 1 m2 = (corners >> c2) & 1 if m1 == m2: continue p1 = globalpos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c1] p2 = globalpos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c2] if m1 > m2: p = approximatezerocrossingpositionbinarysearch(p1, p2) else: p = approximatezerocrossingpositionbinarysearch(p2, p1) n = calculatesurfacenormal(p) qef.add(p.x, p.y, p.z, n.x, n.y, n.z) averagenormal += n edgecount += 1 # Step 4: QEF Solution and Leaf Finalization qefposition = qef.solve(QEFERROR, QEFSWEEPS, QEFERROR) leaf.mdrawpos = vec3(qefposition.x, qefposition.y, qefposition.z) leaf.mqef = qef.getdata() if edgecount > 0: leaf.maveragenormal = normalize(averagenormal / edgecount) else: leaf.maveragenormal = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Handle degenerate case leaf.mcorners = corners # Pitfall: Boundary Check voxelmin = globalpos voxelmax = globalpos + vec3(resolution, resolution, resolution) # Check twice as per source for in range(2): if (leaf.mdrawpos.x < voxelmin.x or leaf.mdrawpos.x > voxelmax.x or leaf.mdrawpos.y < voxelmin.y or leaf.mdrawpos.y > voxelmax.y or leaf.mdrawpos.z < voxelmin.z or leaf.mdrawpos.z > voxelmax.z): masspoint = qef.getmasspoint() leaf.mdrawpos = vec3(masspoint.x, masspoint.y, masspoint.z) return leaf Not given in the sources. This method is part of an octree-based isosurfacing pipeline implemented in the procgen project by Tsarpf. It builds on the adaptive octree generation with a flatness criterion to create a hierarchical representation of the surface. The use of QEF for surface fitting is a technique to achieve smooth, high-quality surface reconstruction from scattered point-normal data, in this case derived from voxel edge crossings.
