name: Sampled DMC
head: Linear Hashed Marching Cubes
body: Sampled DMC is a mesh generation technique that adapts the Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) algorithm to hashed octrees using Morton keys. It constructs a dual grid where vertices are located at the center of each octree leaf node, allowing for adaptive resolution isosurfacing without requiring a uniform grid. Unlike standard Marching Cubes implementations that expect Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) as direct input, Sampled DMC takes the data octree itself, making it suitable for storing and extracting meshes from sampled points, complex SDFs, or destructible environments. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A HashedOctree<T> where T implements the McNode trait, providing density() (distance from node center to contour) and normal() (normalized gradient of the SDF) for each node. A scale parameter (f32) applied to vertex positions. Output: A Mesh struct containing a Vec<Vertex> and Vec<u32> indices. Vertices are in counter-clockwise order. Data Structures: McNode: Trait requiring density(&self) -> f32 and normal(&self) -> Vector3<f32>. NodeData: Struct with density: f32 and normal: Vector3<f32>. Vertex: Struct with position: Point3<f32> and normal: Vector3<f32>. Normals are normalized. DualGrid: Constructed from the octree. Contains volumes, where each volume is an array of 8 MortonKeys representing the corners of a dual cell. CellVertexData: Struct with positions: [Point3<f32>; 12] and normals: [Vector3<f32>; 12]. Numbered Steps: 1. Construct Dual Grid: Call DualGrid::fromoctree(octree). Get all leaf nodes of the octree. For each leaf, determine its vertex keys. For each vertex key, find neighboring leaves at the same level. Filter neighbors to ensure they match the current leaf's level and are not the source vertex itself. 2. Process Volumes in Parallel: Iterate over dual.volumes using a parallel iterator (e.g., rayon). 3. Fetch Volume Data: For each volume, call fetchvolumedata(volume, octree). Initialize cubeindex = 0 and an array of 8 NodeData. Map volume vertex indices to Marching Cubes vertex indices using VOLUMETOMCVERTEX: [3, 2, 7, 6, 0, 1, 4, 5]. If any vertex key is MortonKey::none(), return immediately (boundary handling). Retrieve density and normal from the octree for each vertex. If density > 0.0, set the corresponding bit in cubeindex. Store density and normal in the nodes array. 4. Filter Visibility: Call iscellvisible(cubeindex). If cubeindex is 0 (all negative) or 0xFF (all positive), skip the volume. 5. Calculate Interpolated Data: For visible volumes, call calculatemcvertexdata(volume, nodes, cubeindex, scale). Get the edge mask from tables::EDGETABLE[cubeindex]. For each of the 12 edges, if the edge is active (bit set in mask): Get the two volume vertex indices from MCCUBEEDGES. Calculate the interpolation factor R using the densities of the two vertices. Interpolate the position and normal using R. Scale the position by vertexpositionscale. 6. Obtain Vertices: Call obtainmcvertices(celldata, cubeindex). Get triangle indices from tables::TRITABLE[cubeindex]. Chunk the table into groups of 3. For each valid chunk, create Vertex structs using the interpolated positions and normals. 7. Collect Results: Collect all vertices into a Vec. Generate indices as (0..vertices.len() as u32).collect(). Formulas: Interpolation Factor: R = \frac{0 - p1}{p2 - p1} Where p1 and p2 are the densities at the two endpoints of the edge. This estimates the relative value R such that p1 + (p2 - p1) \cdot R == 0. Special cases: If |p1| < 0.00001, return p1. If |p2| < 0.00001, return p2. If |p1 - p2| < 0.00001, return p1. Position Interpolation: \text{pos} = (\text{pos}1 \oplus \text{pos}2, R) \cdot \text{scale} Where \oplus denotes linear interpolation. Normal Interpolation: \text{norm} = \text{norm}1 \oplus \text{norm}2, R (Note: The source code does not explicitly normalize the interpolated normal, but the McNode trait requires normalized normals, and the Vertex struct stores normalized normals. The implementation relies on the input normals being normalized.) Parameters: scale: f32. A scaling factor applied to vertex positions. Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: If any vertex in a volume is MortonKey::none(), the volume is on the edge of the octree. The function returns immediately, skipping that volume. This may result in missing mesh parts at the boundary. Cell Visibility: Cells with cubeindex == 0 or cubeindex == 0xFF are filtered out. This is correct for isosurfacing but must be understood to avoid expecting triangles in uniform regions. Vertex Merging: The algorithm does not merge vertices. Indices are simply incremental integers. This can lead to higher vertex counts and potential visual artifacts at shared edges if normals are not consistent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshfromoctree(octree: HashedOctree, scale: f32) -> Mesh: dual = DualGrid.fromoctree(octree) vertices = [] for volume in dual.volumes.pariter(): nodes, cubeindex = fetchvolumedata(volume, octree) if not iscellvisible(cubeindex): continue celldata = calculatemcvertexdata(volume, nodes, cubeindex, scale) vertices.extend(obtainmcvertices(celldata, cubeindex)) indices = list(range(len(vertices))) return Mesh(vertices, indices) def fetchvolumedata(volume: [MortonKey; 8], octree: HashedOctree) -> (VolumeData): VOLUMETOMCVERTEX = [3, 2, 7, 6, 0, 1, 4, 5] nodes = [None] 8 cubeindex = 0 for volumei, key in enumerate(volume): mci = VOLUMETOMCVERTEX[volumei] if key == MortonKey.none(): return VolumeData(nodes, 0) # Skip boundary nodedata = octree.value(key) density = nodedata.density() normal = nodedata.normal() if density > 0.0: cubeindex |= (1 << mci) nodes[volumei] = NodeData(density, normal) return VolumeData(nodes, cubeindex) def calculatemcvertexdata(volume: [MortonKey; 8], nodes: [NodeData; 8], cubeindex: u8, scale: f32) -> CellVertexData: MCCUBEEDGES = [ (4, 5), (1, 5), (0, 1), (0, 4), (6, 7), (3, 7), (2, 3), (2, 6), (4, 6), (5, 7), (1, 3), (0, 2) ] positions = [None] 12 normals = [None] 12 edges = tables.EDGETABLE[cubeindex] for i in range(12): if (edges & (1 << i)) > 0: v1i, v2i = MCCUBEEDGES[i] factor = interpolationfactor(nodes[v1i].density, nodes[v2i].density) pos1 = volume[v1i].position() pos2 = volume[v2i].position() positions[i] = (pos1.interpolate(pos2, factor) scale) norm1 = nodes[v1i].normal norm2 = nodes[v2i].normal normals[i] = norm1.interpolate(norm2, factor) return CellVertexData(positions, normals) def obtainmcvertices(celldata: CellVertexData, cubeindex: u8) -> [Vertex]: tritable = tables.TRITABLE[cubeindex] vertices = [] for chunk in tritable.chunks(3): if chunk[0] == -1: break v1 = celldata.positions[chunk[0]] v2 = celldata.positions[chunk[1]] v3 = celldata.positions[chunk[2]] n1 = celldata.normals[chunk[0]] n2 = celldata.normals[chunk[1]] n3 = celldata.normals[chunk[2]] vertices.append(Vertex(v1, n1)) vertices.append(Vertex(v2, n2)) vertices.append(Vertex(v3, n3)) return vertices def interpolationfactor(p1: f32, p2: f32) -> f32: if abs(p1) < 0.00001: return p1 if abs(p2) < 0.00001: return p2 if abs(p1 - p2) < 0.00001: return p1 return (0.0 - p1) / (p2 - p1) Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of dual volumes (leaf nodes in the octree). Parallel processing is used via rayon. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of dual volumes. Each volume is processed independently, and vertices are collected into a single vector. Performance: Fast due to parallel processing and efficient data structures. The use of Morton keys allows for efficient spatial locality. Strengths: Adaptive resolution via octree; no need for uniform grid; suitable for dynamic/destructible environments; parallelizable. Limitations: No vertex merging (higher vertex count); boundary handling skips cells; requires McNode implementation; not suitable for non-octree data. When to use: When working with octree-based data structures, adaptive resolution is needed, or the environment is dynamic. When not to use: When vertex merging is critical for performance or visual quality, or when working with uniform grid data. Sampled DMC is an implementation of the Dual Marching Cubes technique, also known as Linear Hashed Marching Cubes. It was developed as part of the dmc crate, available on crates.io. The method adapts the original Marching Cubes algorithm, which uses a uniform grid, to hashed octrees using Morton keys. This allows for adaptive resolution isosurfacing, which is particularly useful for complex SDFs, destructible environments, or objects with different levels of detail (LODs). The crate uses cgmath for vector math and rayon for parallel processing. aleokdev/dmc, https://github.com/aleokdev/dmc, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration
head: Dual Marching Cubes Tree Traversal
body: Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration is a recursive octree traversal algorithm designed to extract isosurface meshes from volumetric data discretized by an octree. It solves the problem of adapting standard Marching Cubes to non-uniform spatial structures by explicitly enumerating voxel faces, edges, and vertices across potentially mismatched tree depths, delegating the actual mesh generation to a standard Marching Cubes routine only at leaf nodes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by its explicit separation of traversal logic (face, edge, vertex enumeration) from the surface extraction logic, allowing for robust handling of arbitrary octree configurations without requiring a globally consistent grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree root node, a scalar field function (or sampled values), and configuration parameters. Output: A mesh (list of vertices and triangles) representing the isosurface. Data Structures: The tree node structure contains the following fields: vectortype minimum: The minimum coordinate of the voxel. configtype config: Configuration flags. std::sizet gridsize: Size of the grid within the voxel. scalartype gridwidth: Physical width of the grid. vector<std::sizet, 3> size: Dimensions of the voxel in grid units. std::vector<nodetype> children: Pointers to child nodes (if branch). std::vector<boost::objectpool<branchnodetype>> branchpool: Memory pool for branch nodes. std::vector<boost::objectpool<leafnodetype>> leafpool: Memory pool for leaf nodes. Parameters: gridwidth: Default 1.0. tolerance: Default 0.1. maximumdepth: Default max(std::sizet). nominalweight: Default 0.1. Algorithm Steps: The algorithm uses three specialized recursive functions: fx, fy, fz for faces; exy, eyz, exz for edges; and v for vertices. These functions traverse the octree to gather the necessary geometric context for Marching Cubes. 1. Face Enumeration (fx, fy, fz): Takes two nodes (representing adjacent voxels sharing a face) and a receiver. Checks if either node is a branch. If so, it recurses by mapping child indices to traverse the adjacent voxels. For fx (face perpendicular to X-axis), the recursion maps children as follows: Child 2 with Child 0 Child 3 with Child 1 Child 6 with Child 4 Child 7 with Child 5 Similar mappings apply for fy and fz based on the face orientation. If both nodes are leaves, it calls the Marching Cubes routine for the face. 2. Edge Enumeration (exy, eyz, exz): Takes four nodes (representing voxels sharing an edge) and a receiver. Recurses on specific child index pairs to traverse the edge. Eventually calls enumerateimplv with eight nodes. 3. Vertex Enumeration (v): Takes eight nodes (representing the 8 voxels sharing a vertex) and a receiver. If any node is a branch, it recurses with child indices [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0]. If all eight nodes are leaves, it extracts vertex pointers and calls the standard Marching Cubes routine. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseface(node1, node2, facetype, receiver): """ Enumerates a face shared by two voxels. facetype: 'x', 'y', or 'z' """ # Handle mismatched depths or boundary conditions # If a child does not exist, fall back to the current node if node1 is branch: # Map child indices based on facetype # Example for facetype 'x': # children[2] with children[0], children[3] with children[1], etc. traverseface(node1.children[2], node2.children[0], facetype, receiver) traverseface(node1.children[3], node2.children[1], facetype, receiver) traverseface(node1.children[6], node2.children[4], facetype, receiver) traverseface(node1.children[7], node2.children[5], facetype, receiver) elif node2 is branch: # Similar recursion for node2 pass else: # Both are leaves, call Marching Cubes receiver.processface(node1, node2, facetype) def traverseedge(node1, node2, node3, node4, edgetype, receiver): """ Enumerates an edge shared by four voxels. """ if any(node is branch for node in [node1, node2, node3, node4]): # Recurse with specific child index pairs # Eventually calls traversevertex pass else: # All leaves, call traversevertex traversevertex(node1, node2, node3, node4, receiver) def traversevertex(node1, node2, node3, node4, node5, node6, node7, node8, receiver): """ Enumerates a vertex shared by eight voxels. """ if any(node is branch for node in [node1,..., node8]): # Recurse with child indices [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0] # This ensures consistent ordering for the Marching Cubes lookup pass else: # All leaves, extract vertex pointers and call Marching Cubes receiver.processvertex(node1, node2, node3, node4, node5, node6, node7, node8) def main(octreeroot, receiver): # Initial calls to traverse faces, edges, and vertices # The exact initial calls depend on the octree structure and boundary conditions pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mismatched Tree Depths: The algorithm handles this by using the ternary operator b1 ? b1->children()[i]: n1 to fall back to the current node n1 when a child does not exist. Boundary Conditions: Care must be taken to handle voxels at the boundary of the domain, ensuring that missing neighbors are handled gracefully. A simpler approach that applies Marching Cubes directly on an octree, potentially leading to cracks if not adapted. Uses an octree specifically designed for isosurface extraction, with different traversal and data structures. An early octree-based isosurfacing method, focusing on efficient traversal and memory usage. A method for contouring on octrees, with specific handling for edge cases. A method that allows for arbitrary octree structures without strict constraints. Uses edge-trees to ensure consistent vertex definitions across the isosurface. Focuses on adaptive octree generation based on a flatness criterion. A sampled version of the Dual Marching Cubes method, with different sampling strategies. Time Complexity: Depends on the octree depth and the number of leaves. In the worst case, it is proportional to the number of voxels in the octree. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of nodes in the octree. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with adaptive octrees, as it only processes relevant regions. Strengths: Robust handling of arbitrary octree structures, explicit separation of traversal and extraction logic. Limitations: Complexity of implementation, potential for cracks if not carefully handled. When to use: When working with adaptive octrees and needing robust isosurface extraction. When not to use: When a uniform grid is sufficient, or when performance is critical and the overhead of traversal is unacceptable. The method originates from the "planaria/dmc" repository, an unofficial implementation of the Dual Marching Cubes algorithm. It is part of a broader family of octree-based isosurfacing methods, building on the principles of hierarchical traversal and adaptive resolution. planaria/dmc, https://github.com/planaria/dmc, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: High-Dimensional Triangulation Tables
head: Bhaniramka et al. triangulation algorithm
body: High-Dimensional Triangulation Tables is a method for generating precomputed triangulation tables for isosurface extraction in n-dimensional hypercubes. It addresses the excessive simplex count produced by recursive contour-meshing, which requires subdividing 4-cells into 4-simplices before contouring. Unlike recursive contour-meshing, which creates more triangles than the Marching Cubes algorithm, this method uses a lookup table similar to Marching Cubes but generalized for any n-dimensional hypercube. Inputs: Scalar field values at the vertices of an n-dimensional hypercube cell. An isovalue I. Outputs: A set of triangles (simplices) representing the isosurface intersection within the cell. A triangulation table mapping vertex configurations to edge intersections/triangles. Data Structures: Vertex Labels: A bit mask of length 2^n, where each bit corresponds to a vertex of the hypercube. Bit k is 1 if the scalar value at vertex k is greater than the isovalue, and 0 otherwise. Triangulation Table: A lookup structure indexed by the vertex label bit mask. For an n-dimensional hypercube, the table size is 2^{(2^n)} entries. Each entry contains the list of edges intersecting the isosurface or the resulting triangulation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Label Vertices: Assign a positive label to each vertex vi if its scalar value f(vi) > I. Assign a negative label if f(vi) < I. 2. Identify Intersecting Edges: Collect the midpoints of all edges of the hypercube where one endpoint has a positive label and the other has a negative label. 3. Construct Convex Hull: Create the convex hull of the collected midpoints together with the vertices of the hypercube that share the same label (positive or negative, used consistently). This forms an n-polytope lying within the hypercube. 4. Remove Boundary Faces: Remove any faces of the resulting polytope that lie on the boundary of the hypercube. A face is on the boundary if it shares any vertices with the hypercube. 5. Extract Isosurface Faces: The remaining faces of the polytope comprise the isosurface within the cell. 6. Triangulate: If the remaining faces are not simplices (triangles in 3D, triangles in 2D, etc.), perform triangulation. Ensure consistent triangulation between adjacent faces of the hypercube to maintain mesh continuity. 7. Table Lookup (Runtime): For a given cell, compute the vertex label bit mask. Use this mask to index the precomputed triangulation table to determine which edges intersect the isosurface and retrieve the corresponding triangulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetriangulationtable(n): """ Precomputes the triangulation table for an n-dimensional hypercube. Returns a dictionary mapping vertex masks to triangulation results. """ numvertices = 2 n table = {} # Iterate through all possible vertex configurations (2^(2^n) cases) # Note: This is computationally expensive for n >= 4 for mask in range(1 << numvertices): # Skip trivial cases where all vertices are on one side if mask == 0 or mask == (1 << numvertices) - 1: table[mask] = [] continue # Step 1 & 2: Identify intersecting edges and midpoints midpoints = [] intersectingedges = [] for edgeidx in range(numvertices n // 2): # Approximate edge count logic # Determine vertices of the edge v1idx, v2idx = getedgevertices(edgeidx, n) # Check if edge intersects isosurface v1bit = (mask >> v1idx) & 1 v2bit = (mask >> v2idx) & 1 if v1bit != v2bit: intersectingedges.append((v1idx, v2idx)) # Midpoint in hypercube coordinates (0 to 1) mid = [(getvertexcoord(v1idx, n) + getvertexcoord(v2idx, n)) / 2.0 for in range(n)] midpoints.append(mid) if not midpoints: table[mask] = [] continue # Step 3: Create convex hull of midpoints and same-label vertices # Include vertices with positive label (bit 1) positivevertices = [] for vidx in range(numvertices): if (mask >> vidx) & 1: positivevertices.append(getvertexcoord(vidx, n)) # Convex hull computation (conceptual) polytopefaces = computeconvexhullfaces(midpoints + positivevertices) # Step 4: Remove boundary faces interiorfaces = [] for face in polytopefaces: # Check if face shares any vertex with the hypercube boundary isboundary = False for vidx in face: if ishypercubevertex(vidx, n): isboundary = True break if not isboundary: interiorfaces.append(face) # Step 5 & 6: Triangulate remaining faces triangulation = [] for face in interiorfaces: # Triangulate non-simplex face triangles = triangulateface(face, n) triangulation.extend(triangles) table[mask] = triangulation return table def extractisosurfacecell(cellvertices, isovalue, triangulationtable, n): """ Extracts isosurface for a single n-dimensional cell using the table. """ # Step 1: Label vertices mask = 0 for i, val in enumerate(cellvertices): if val > isovalue: mask |= (1 << i) # Step 7: Lookup return triangulationtable.get(mask, []) Parameters: Dimension n: The dimension of the hypercube. Typical values are n=3 for standard 3D volume rendering. Table Size: The number of entries in the triangulation table is 2^{(2^n)}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exponential Growth: The table size grows doubly exponentially with dimension. For n=3, there are 256 cases. For n=4, there are 65,536 cases. For n=5, there are over four billion cases (2^{32}). This makes precomputation and storage impractical for n \ge 5. Degenerate Cases: If the isovalue equals a vertex value, the label assignment is ambiguous. Standard practice is to treat equality as one side (e.g., \ge) to ensure consistency, though the sources do not specify the exact tie-breaking rule. Non-Simplex Faces: The convex hull faces may not be simplices, requiring additional triangulation steps. Consistency between adjacent cells must be enforced during this triangulation to avoid gaps or overlaps. Time Complexity: Precomputation of the table is O(2^{(2^n)} \cdot \text{poly}(n)), which is infeasible for n \ge 5. Runtime lookup is O(1) per cell after table construction, assuming the table fits in memory. Memory Complexity: The table requires O(2^{(2^n)}) entries. For n=3, this is manageable (256 entries). For n=4, it is large but potentially feasible (65,536 entries). For n=5, it is prohibitive (over 4 billion entries). Strengths: Provides a consistent, precomputed triangulation for any n-dimensional hypercube, avoiding the overhead of on-the-fly convex hull computation during rendering. Limitations: The exponential growth of the table size limits practical application to low dimensions (n \le 4). Compared to Marching Cubes, it does not reduce triangle count for n=3 but generalizes the concept. When to Use: When isosurface extraction is required in dimensions higher than 3, and the dimension is low enough (n \le 4) to allow table precomputation. Not suitable for n \ge 5 due to memory constraints. The method was proposed by Bhaniramka et al. [14] to address the excessive simplex count produced by recursive contour-meshing in n-dimensional spaces. Recursive contour-meshing requires subdividing 4-cells into 4-simplices before contouring, analogous to breaking a cube into five or six tetrahedra in 3D, which creates more triangles than the Marching Cubes algorithm. Bhaniramka et al. generalized the Marching Cubes lookup table approach to any n-dimensional hypercube. The method is described in the Visualization Handbook (2005). Han-Wei Shen, "Time-Dependent Isosurface Extraction," in Visualization Handbook, 2005, Chapter 3.2.2. URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B978012387582250006X, fetched 2026-10-30. (book)

name: Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra
head: Subgrid MT, single-tet reconstruction
body: Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra (Subgrid MT) is an isosurface extraction algorithm that reconstructs an intersection-free triangulation by decomposing a regular cubic grid into tetrahedra and resolving the scalar field crossings within each tetrahedron. Unlike its sibling Marching Cubes, which suffers from topological ambiguities in specific configurations, this method guarantees a manifold, self-intersection-free surface by enforcing a consistent local construction policy based on edge intersection counts. It produces a mesh that matches voxel data more accurately than Marching Cubes, at the cost of a higher vertex count. Subgrid MT operates in two phases: global grid traversal to determine edge intersections, and local tetrahedral reconstruction to generate triangles. The method accepts three input types: a triangle mesh remeshed on a grid, an analytical Signed Distance Function (SDF), or precomputed edge intersections in.npz format. Edge Coordinates (Single Tet): An array of six non-negative integers representing the number of times the isosurface crosses each edge of a single tetrahedron. The order is fixed as: \text{edge\coords} = [e{01}, e{02}, e{03}, e{23}, e{13}, e{12}] where e{ij} is the intersection count on the edge between vertex i and vertex j. Result Structures: 1. sgmtresult (C Library): triangles: int32t array, 3 indices per triangle. numtriangles: Count of triangles. numedgepoints: Count of intersection points on edges. numsteiner: Count of Steiner points. steinerbary: Array of 4 barycentric coordinates per Steiner point. 2. PrimalResult (Python): vertices: (N, 3) float64 array. faces: List of index arrays (one per face, potentially n-gons). 3. DualResult (Python): Contains dual polygon mesh data via Quadric Error Function (QEF) solve. 1. Grid Construction and Intersection Detection: If input is a mesh, weld vertices, triangulate, center/scale to [-1, 1]^3, and apply a rigid translation offset (magnitude 0.01, seed-dependent) to break axis-alignment. Construct an n^3 cubic grid, which decomposes into 5n^3 tetrahedra. Compute edge intersections. For mesh input, use ray intersection or CGAL exact queries. For SDF, evaluate at grid vertices and interpolate. Store intersection counts and parameters (t-values) for all grid edges. Validate the "even-sum" condition: For each tetrahedron, the sum of intersections on its faces must be even. A non-zero count of "non-even tets" indicates potential non-watertightness or numerical artifacts. 2. Local Tetrahedral Reconstruction: For each tetrahedron in the grid, invoke the reconstruction routine with its six edge intersection counts. Input Validation: Ensure exactly six non-negative integers are provided. If validation fails, abort. Simplicial Embedding: By default, use simplicial embedding (flag simplicial=1). This places Steiner points inside the tetrahedron to resolve ambiguities. Curve Classification: Identify boundary curves on the tetrahedron faces. Curves are classified as: Open: Curves that do not close within the tetrahedron. Scoop: Curves that wrap around a vertex. Normal: Standard intersection curves. Triangulation: Construct the local surface using one of three policies: Primal: Standard triangulation interpolating edge crossings. Dual: Solve a QEF for dual vertices to create a dual polygon mesh. Greedy: Fan triangulation from boundary curves. Steiner Points: If simplicial embedding is active, compute barycentric coordinates for internal Steiner points. 3. Vertex Merging and Output: Combinatorial Merge (Default): Merge vertices based on edge identity to ensure manifold connectivity. Numerical Merge: If mergeEPS >= 0, merge vertices within a positional epsilon. No Merge: If noMerge is set, output a raw triangle soup. Iterate over the result triangles array in strides of three, outputting vertex indices. Unverified code. Args: inputtype: 'mesh', 'sdf', or 'npz' inputdata: Path to mesh/SDF name or.npz file resolution: Grid resolution n (creates n^3 grid) simplicial: Use simplicial embedding for ambiguity resolution mergeeps: Positional merge epsilon. -1 for combinatorial merge. usecgal: Use CGAL for exact intersection queries (mesh input only) Returns: Result object containing vertices and faces """ # 1. Preprocessing if inputtype == 'mesh': mesh = loadandweldmesh(inputdata) mesh = centerandscaletounitcube(mesh) mesh = applyseedoffset(mesh, seed=1) # 2. Grid Intersection gridedges, edgeintersections = computegridintersections( mesh, resolution, usecgal=usecgal) elif inputtype == 'sdf': gridedges, edgeintersections = computesdfintersections( inputdata, resolution) elif inputtype == 'npz': gridedges, edgeintersections = loadprecomputedintersections(inputdata) else: raise ValueError("Invalid input type") # 3. Local Reconstruction alltriangles = [] allvertices = [] steinerpoints = [] noneventets = 0 for tetidx, tetvertices in enumerate(gridedges.tetrahedra): # Get edge intersection counts for this tet edgecounts = [edgeintersections[edge].count for edge in tetedges] # Validate even-sum condition if not isevensum(edgecounts): noneventets += 1 # Reconstruct local surface localresult = reconstructtet( edgecounts=edgecounts, tetvertices=tetvertices, simplicial=simplicial) # Merge local vertices with global indices mergedtriangles, newvertices = mergevertices( localresult.triangles, localresult.vertices, allvertices, mergeeps=mergeeps) alltriangles.extend(mergedtriangles) allvertices.extend(newvertices) steinerpoints.extend(localresult.steinerbary) # 4. Output return PrimalResult( vertices=allvertices, faces=alltriangles, noneventets=noneventets, steinerpoints=steinerpoints) def reconstructtet(edgecounts, tetvertices, simplicial=True): """ Reconstructs a single tetrahedron's surface from edge coordinates. Args: edgecounts: List of 6 integers [e01, e02, e03, e23, e13, e12] tetvertices: Array of 4 vertices (x, y, z) simplicial: Boolean flag for simplicial embedding Returns: sgmtresult with triangles, edge points, and steiner points """ # Validate input if len(edgecounts) != 6 or any(c < 0 for c in edgecounts): raise ValueError("Invalid edge coordinates") # Classify curves opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves = classifyboundarycurves( edgecounts, tetvertices) # Check for non-even tets if not isevensum(edgecounts): # Output may have holes or be non-orientable pass # Construct local surface if simplicial: # Place Steiner points and resolve ambiguities steinerbary = computesteinerbarycentric(edgecounts) triangles = buildsimplicialtriangulation( edgecounts, tetvertices, steinerbary) else: triangles = buildstandardtriangulation( edgecounts, tetvertices) # Compute intersection points edgepoints = computeedgeintersections(edgecounts, tetvertices) return sgmtresult( triangles=triangles, numtriangles=len(triangles), numedgepoints=len(edgepoints), numsteiner=len(steinerbary), steinerbary=steinerbary) def computeedgeintersections(edgecounts, tetvertices): """ Computes 3D coordinates of intersection points on edges. Args: edgecounts: List of 6 integers tetvertices: Array of 4 vertices Returns: List of 3D points """ points = [] edgepairs = [(0,1), (0,2), (0,3), (2,3), (1,3), (1,2)] for i, count in enumerate(edgecounts): v1, v2 = tetvertices[edgepairs[i]] for in range(count): # Interpolate t-value (simplified: uniform distribution for demo) # In practice, t is computed from scalar field values t = computetvalue(v1, v2) point = lerp(v1, v2, t) points.append(point) return points def lerp(v1, v2, t): """Linear interpolation between two 3D vectors.""" return [v1[i] + t (v2[i] - v1[i]) for i in range(3)] def computetvalue(v1, v2): """ Computes the parameter t for intersection. Assumes scalar values f1, f2 are available from context. Formula: t = (I - f1) / (f2 - f1) where I is isovalue. """ # Placeholder for actual scalar field evaluation # In a real implementation, f1 and f2 are passed or looked up f1 = 0.0 # Placeholder f2 = 1.0 # Placeholder isovalue = 0.5 # Placeholder if abs(f2 - f1) < 1e-9: return 0.5 return (isovalue - f1) / (f2 - f1) edgecoords[6]: Array of six non-negative integers. Order: (e{01}, e{02}, e{03}, e{23}, e{13}, e{12}). simplicial: Boolean flag. Default 1 (on). Enables simplicial embedding. mergeEPS: Positional merge epsilon. Default -1 (combinatorial merge). Values \ge 0 switch to numerical merge. noMerge: Disables vertex merging, outputting a raw triangle soup. mod2: Uses mod2 intersection reduction before subgrid construction. greedy: Uses greedy construction (fan triangulation from boundary curves). cgal: Uses exact CGAL (EPECK) intersection queries. Requires build with -DSUBGRIDWITHCGAL=ON. Only applies to mesh input. USEROBUSTQUERIES: Static constexpr bool. Default false. Enables FCPW watertight test + iterative all-hits ray intersection. Disabled by default due to ~2x slowdown. scoopbulge: Controls bulging parameter for scoop curves. Default 1e-3. Affects intersection-free property. scoopmidvertices: Controls mid-vertex placement for scoop curves. resolution: Integer n for n^3 grid. Typical values: 32, 64, 128. Non-Even Tets: If the even-sum condition is not satisfied (noneventets > 0), the output mesh may not be orientable and may contain open holes. This typically indicates a non-watertight input or a grid edge-intersection issue. Input Validation: The program requires exactly one input type (--input mesh, --inputSDF, or --npz). Passing a.npz file to --input triggers an error. CGAL Usage: The --cgal flag applies only to mesh input (-i). Using it with SDF or NPZ inputs triggers an error. Self-Intersections: The output is mathematically guaranteed to be free of self-intersections. Numerical tests may flag near-overlapping triangles as false positives. Marching Tetrahedrons is an isosurface extraction algorithm that decomposes each voxel of a 3D grid into tetrahedra to determine the intersection of a scalar field with a target isovalue. Unlike its sibling Marching Cubes, which suffers from topological ambiguities in specific configurations, this method guarantees a manifold, intersection-free surface by resolving these ambiguities through tetrahedral decomposition. It produces a mesh that matches voxel data more accurately than Marching Cubes, at the cost of a higher vertex count. Choose this when topological correctness is critical and vertex count is not a primary constraint. Optimal Extraction via Partition Index is a method for extracting isosurfaces from a tetrahedral grid that guarantees visiting only the tetrahedra actually intersected by the level set, thereby achieving optimal runtime complexity for the extraction phase. It distinguishes itself from standard marching tetrahedra by pre-processing the mesh into partitions separated by saddle contours, allowing the algorithm to jump directly to connected components of the isosurface via a partition index. Choose this for large sparse datasets where most of the grid is empty. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra in the grid, O(n^3) for an n^3 grid. The local reconstruction per tetrahedron is constant time. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra and the resulting mesh size. Storage for edge intersections and vertex merging structures is required. Measured Performance: Benchmarking shows that enabling robust queries (USEROBUSTQUERIES) results in a ~2x slowdown with negligible effect on robustness. Strengths: Guarantees intersection-free, manifold surfaces. Resolves topological ambiguities inherent in Marching Cubes. Supports multiple input types (mesh, SDF, precomputed intersections). Limitations: Higher vertex count than Marching Cubes. Sensitive to non-watertight inputs (results in non-even tets). Numerical precision issues can arise at low resolutions or with degenerate inputs. When to Use: When topological correctness and intersection-free guarantees are required. Suitable for medical imaging, scientific visualization, and CAD data. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and approximate surfaces are acceptable. Not ideal for highly sparse datasets where partition-based methods are more efficient. Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra was introduced by H. Baktash et al. as a method for extracting intersection-free isosurfaces. The algorithm addresses the topological ambiguities of Marching Cubes by using a tetrahedral decomposition and a consistent local reconstruction policy. The method has been implemented in both C and Python, with support for various input types and reconstruction policies. The official implementation is available on GitHub, and an unofficial reference implementation is also available. body: Marching Tetrahedrons is an isosurface extraction algorithm that decomposes each voxel of a 3D grid into tetrahedra to determine the intersection of a scalar field with a target isovalue. Unlike its sibling Marching Cubes, which suffers from topological ambiguities in specific configurations, this method guarantees a manifold, intersection-free surface by resolving these ambiguities through tetrahedral decomposition. It produces a mesh that matches voxel data more accurately than Marching Cubes, at the cost of a higher vertex count. Inputs: A scalar field defined on a grid (structured or unstructured). An isovalue (threshold) iso. Outputs: A list of triangles representing the isosurface. Data Structures: Tetrahedron: A struct containing four vertices. Each vertex has 3D coordinates (X, Y, Z) and a scalar field value F. Fields: X[4], Y[4], Z[4] (float), F[4] (float). Lookup Table (lup): A 16x6 integer array mapping case indices to edge pairs. lup[icase][e] stores the index of the e-th edge pair for case icase. Edge indices are defined as: 0=(0,1), 1=(1,2), 2=(0,2), 3=(1,3), 4=(2,3), 5=(0,3). If no segment exists, the value is -1. Segment Count Table (numSegments): An array of size 16 mapping case indices to the number of segments (triangles or quads) to generate. Edge Definition: The tetrahedron has 6 edges connecting its 4 vertices (indices 0-3): Edge 0: Vertex 0 to Vertex 1 Edge 1: Vertex 1 to Vertex 2 Edge 2: Vertex 0 to Vertex 2 Edge 3: Vertex 1 to Vertex 3 Edge 4: Vertex 2 to Vertex 3 Edge 5: Vertex 0 to Vertex 3 Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate Cells: For each cell in the input grid, if it is a tetrahedron (4 vertices), extract its coordinates and scalar values into a Tetrahedron struct. 2. Compute Case Index: Determine the binary case index icase (0-15) based on the scalar values F[i] relative to the isovalue iso. If F[i] < iso, the i-th bit is 0. If F[i] \ge iso, the i-th bit is 1. icase = \sum{i=0}^{3} biti \cdot 2^i. Note: Some implementations classify vertices as "inside" (v \le iso) or "outside". The bit logic must be consistent with the lookup table. The provided source uses F[i] < iso for bit 0. 3. Lookup Configuration: Retrieve the number of segments: n = numSegments[icase]. If n=0, no surface intersects this tetrahedron. Continue to next cell. 4. Compute Intersections: Retrieve the edge indices from lup[icase]. For each edge index e in the lookup table (until -1 is reached), compute the intersection point on the corresponding edge using linear interpolation. Let the edge connect vertex v0 (scalar F0, position P0) and vertex v1 (scalar F1, position P1). Calculate the interpolation factor t: t = \frac{iso - F0}{F1 - F0} Handle division by zero: If |F1 - F0| < \epsilon (where \epsilon = 10^{-6}), set t = 0.5 or clamp based on context. Clamp t to [0, 1] to prevent extrapolation outside the edge segment. Calculate the intersection point P{int}: P{int} = P0 + t \cdot (P1 - P0) Store the resulting points in temporary arrays (e.g., x[], y[], z[] for 1 triangle; x1[], y1[], z1[] for 2 triangles). 5. Generate Triangles: Case n=1 (Triangle): The lookup table specifies 3 edges. The 3 intersection points form a single triangle. Add it to the output list. Case n=2 (Quad): The lookup table specifies 4 edges. The 4 intersection points form a quadrilateral. Triangulate the quad into two triangles. The connectivity depends on icase: If icase \in \{5, 10\}: Connect vertices 0-2-3 and 0-1-2 (or equivalent diagonal). Specifically, the source code adds triangles (0,1,2) and (0,2,3)? No, the source says: "for icase 5 or 10, connect vertices 0-2-3". Let's look at the code: python tl.AddTriangle(x1[0], y1[0], z1[0], x1[1], y1[1], z1[1], x1[2], y1[2], z1[2]) if (icase == 5) or (icase == 10): tl.AddTriangle(x1[0], y1[0], z1[0], x1[2], y1[2], z1[2], x1[3], y1[3], z1[3]) else: # icase 3, 12, 6, 9 tl.AddTriangle(x1[1], y1[1], z1[1], x1[2], y1[2], z1[2], x1[3], y1[3], z1[3]) This implies two different diagonals are used to maintain manifold connectivity across shared faces in the grid. For icase \in \{5, 10\}: Triangles are (0,1,2) and (0,2,3). For icase \in \{3, 12, 6, 9\}: Triangles are (0,1,2) and (1,2,3). Note: The exact vertex ordering in the lookup table determines the indices 0-3. The source code assumes the points are stored in the order they appear in lup. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marchingtetrahedrons(tetrahedron, isovalue, lup, numsegments): """ Extracts isosurface triangles from a single tetrahedron. Args: tetrahedron: Object with attributes X[4], Y[4], Z[4], F[4] (floats). isovalue: Scalar threshold. lup: 16x6 integer array mapping case index to edge pairs. numsegments: Array of size 16 mapping case index to segment count. Returns: List of triangles, where each triangle is a tuple of 3 (x, y, z) points. """ EPS = 1e-6 triangles = [] # 1. Compute Case Index icase = 0 for i in range(4): if tetrahedron.F[i] >= isovalue: icase |= (1 << i) # 2. Lookup Segment Count nsegments = numsegments[icase] if nsegments == 0: return triangles # 3. Compute Intersection Points # Edge mapping: 0:(0,1), 1:(1,2), 2:(0,2), 3:(1,3), 4:(2,3), 5:(0,3) edgemap = [ (0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (0, 3) ] points = [] for eidx in lup[icase]: if eidx == -1: break v0idx, v1idx = edgemap[eidx] v0 = (tetrahedron.X[v0idx], tetrahedron.Y[v0idx], tetrahedron.Z[v0idx]) v1 = (tetrahedron.X[v1idx], tetrahedron.Y[v1idx], tetrahedron.Z[v1idx]) f0 = tetrahedron.F[v0idx] f1 = tetrahedron.F[v1idx] # Linear Interpolation denom = f1 - f0 if abs(denom) < EPS: t = 0.5 else: t = (isovalue - f0) / denom t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # Clamp to [0, 1] px = v0[0] + t (v1[0] - v0[0]) py = v0[1] + t (v1[1] - v0[1]) pz = v0[2] + t (v1[2] - v0[2]) points.append((px, py, pz)) # 4. Generate Triangles if nsegments == 1: # 3 points form 1 triangle triangles.append((points[0], points[1], points[2])) elif nsegments == 2: # 4 points form 2 triangles (quad) p0, p1, p2, p3 = points[0], points[1], points[2], points[3] # Determine diagonal based on case index if icase in [5, 10]: # Diagonal 0-2: Triangles (0,1,2) and (0,2,3) triangles.append((p0, p1, p2)) triangles.append((p0, p2, p3)) else: # Diagonal 1-3: Triangles (0,1,2) and (1,2,3) # Note: Source code for else branch: AddTriangle(1,2,3) after adding (0,1,2) # Wait, source code: # tl.AddTriangle(x1[0]...x1[2]) -> (0,1,2) # else: tl.AddTriangle(x1[1]...x1[3]) -> (1,2,3) triangles.append((p0, p1, p2)) triangles.append((p1, p2, p3)) return triangles Uses an adaptive octree to subdivide the volume, applying Marching Tetrahedrons only at leaf nodes where the isovalue is present. Reduces computation in empty regions compared to uniform grid traversal. Processes each tetrahedron independently without vertex sharing, resulting in non-manifold surfaces with cracks. Serves as a baseline for understanding the core decomposition logic. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra in the grid. Each tetrahedron is processed independently in O(1) time. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles generated. The output mesh size is typically larger than Marching Cubes for the same geometry due to the finer decomposition. Performance: Produces a mesh that matches voxel data better than Marching Cubes but creates significantly more vertices, making it slower and more memory-intensive. Strengths: Resolves topological ambiguities inherent in Marching Cubes (e.g., cases 6 and 7) by ensuring a consistent manifold surface through tetrahedral decomposition. Limitations: Higher vertex count leads to larger file sizes and increased rendering cost. Requires the input grid to be decomposable into tetrahedra (or an existing unstructured tetrahedral mesh). When to use: When topological correctness is critical and the ambiguity of Marching Cubes is unacceptable, or when working with unstructured tetrahedral grids. When not to use: When performance and memory efficiency are paramount and the visual difference from Marching Cubes is negligible. The method was developed as part of undergraduate science visualization coursework, utilizing C++, CMake, and VTK data files. It is an alternative to Marching Cubes, designed to address the "tetrahedron ambiguity" where a single cube can be split in two topologically distinct ways. By decomposing the cube into tetrahedra, the algorithm ensures a unique, consistent surface for each configuration. It is often implemented in graphics engines and visualization tools that require robust isosurface extraction from volumetric data. adrian-sierra/Marching-Tetrahedrons, https://github.com/adrian-sierra/Marching-Tetrahedrons, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Scrawk/Marching-Cubes, https://github.com/Scrawk/Marching-Cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Torbenhjl/Marching-Tetrahedra-on-CT-headscan, https://github.com/Torbenhjl/Marching-Tetrahedra-on-CT-headscan, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Octree Marching Tetrahedra
body: An isosurface extraction method that uses an adaptive octree to subdivide a 3D volume only where the scalar field contains the target isovalue, applying the Marching Tetrahedra algorithm at leaf nodes to generate the mesh. It differs from its parent Marching Tetrahedrons by introducing spatial adaptivity via octree subdivision, reducing computation in empty regions, and from Naive Isosurface Extraction by avoiding uniform grid traversal. Inputs: A 3D scalar field stored in a 1D array teapotColour of size X \times Y \times Z (source assumes fixed 256^3). Target isovalue iso. Volume bounds defined by topLeftFront and bottomRightBack points. Outputs: A list of vertices (newvert) representing the isosurface mesh. Data Structures: Point: Struct with fields int x, int y, int z. Default constructor initializes to (-1, -1, -1). Octree Node: Point topLeftFront: Minimum corner of the node's bounding box. Point bottomRightBack: Maximum corner of the node's bounding box. Point point: If NULL, the node is internal; if (-1, -1, -1), the node is empty. vector<Octree> children: Array of 8 child pointers. Algorithm Steps: 1. Build Octree (make function): Calculate midpoints: midx = (topLeftFront->x + bottomRightBack->x) / 2, midy = (topLeftFront->y + bottomRightBack->y) / 2, midz = (topLeftFront->z + bottomRightBack->z) / 2. Iterate through all voxels in the node's bounds to find miniso and maxiso from teapotColour using index z 256 256 + y 256 + x. If node dimensions are greater than 1 (checked by (midx - topLeftFront->x) > 1 || (midy - topLeftFront->y) > 1 || (bottomRightBack->z - midz) > 1), create 8 child octants. Child indices (0-7) are defined by their bounding boxes relative to midpoints: Child 0: (x1,y1,z1) to (midx,midy,midz) Child 1: (midx,y1,z1) to (x2,midy,midz) Child 2: (x1,midy,z1) to (midx,y2,midz) Child 3: (midx,midy,z1) to (x2,y2,midz) Child 4: (x1,y1,midz) to (midx,midy,z2) Child 5: (midx,y1,midz) to (x2,midy,z2) Child 6: (x1,midy,midz) to (midx,y2,z2) Child 7: (midx,midy,midz) to (x2,y2,z2). Recursively call make() on children if their dimensions > 1. 2. Leaf Processing (explore function): When a leaf node is reached (dimensions equal 1, i.e., (-topLeftFront->x + bottomRightBack->x) == 1 &&...), identify the 8 vertices of the cube. Indices into teapotColour (assuming 256^3 grid): a (BottomLeftFront): topLeftFront->z256256 + topLeftFront->y256 + topLeftFront->x b (BottomRightFront): a + 1 c (TopLeftFront): a + 257 d (BottomLeftBack): a + 256 e (TopLeftBack): 256256 + a f (TopRightFront): e + 1 g (TopRightBack): e + 257 h (TopLeftBack? Note: Source labels h as TopLeftBack in comment but uses it in specific tetrahedra): e + 256. Decompose the cube into 5 tetrahedra. For each tetrahedron, pass the scalar values of its 4 vertices to the tetra function. Tet 1: Vertices h, g, c, f Tet 2: Vertices h, c, d, b Tet 3: Vertices d, a, e, b Tet 4: Vertices h, d, e, b Tet 5: Vertices h, c, f, b. 3. Marching Tetrahedra Logic (tetra function): Determine the case index based on which vertices are inside the isosurface (val > isolevel). For each case, compute intersection points on the edges using linear interpolation: \text{interpolate}(v1, v2, \text{isolevel}, col1, col2) = v1 + \frac{\text{isolevel} - col1}{col2 - col1} (v2 - v1) Store resulting Vector3f in newvert array. Example Case 0x0C (vertices d, b, a, c inside? Source code implies specific mapping): Intersect edge d-b: interpolate(Vertices[d], Vertices[b], isolevel, col[3], col[1]) Intersect edge a-d: interpolate(Vertices[a], Vertices[d], isolevel, col[0], col[3]) Intersect edge a-c: interpolate(Vertices[a], Vertices[c], isolevel, col[0], col[2]). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interpolate(v1, v2, isolevel, col1, col2): """Linear interpolation of vertex v1 and v2 based on scalar values col1 and col2.""" if col2 == col1: return v1 # Avoid division by zero t = (isolevel - col1) / (col2 - col1) return v1 + t (v2 - v1) def getindex(x, y, z, width=256): """Get 1D index from 3D coordinates.""" return z width width + y width + x def makeoctree(topleft, bottomright, teapotcolor): """Recursively build the adaptive octree.""" midx = (topleft.x + bottomright.x) // 2 midy = (topleft.y + bottomright.y) // 2 midz = (topleft.z + bottomright.z) // 2 # Check if subdivision is needed if (midx - topleft.x > 1 or midy - topleft.y > 1 or bottomright.z - midz > 1): # Define 8 children bounds childrenbounds = [ (topleft, (midx, midy, midz)), ((midx, topleft.y, topleft.z), (bottomright.x, midy, midz)), ((topleft.x, midy, topleft.z), (midx, bottomright.y, midz)), ((midx, midy, topleft.z), (bottomright.x, bottomright.y, midz)), ((topleft.x, topleft.y, midz), (midx, midy, bottomright.z)), ((midx, topleft.y, midz), (bottomright.x, midy, bottomright.z)), ((topleft.x, midy, midz), (midx, bottomright.y, bottomright.z)), ((midx, midy, midz), bottomright) ] for bounds in childrenbounds: child = OctreeNode(bounds[0], bounds[1]) makeoctree(bounds[0], bounds[1], teapotcolor) # Add child to parent else: # Leaf node exploreleaf(topleft, bottomright, teapotcolor) def exploreleaf(topleft, bottomright, teapotcolor): """Process a leaf node (1x1x1 cube) using Marching Tetrahedra.""" # Calculate indices for the 8 vertices # Note: Source assumes fixed width 256 aidx = getindex(topleft.x, topleft.y, topleft.z) bidx = aidx + 1 cidx = aidx + 257 didx = aidx + 256 eidx = 256256 + aidx fidx = eidx + 1 gidx = eidx + 257 hidx = eidx + 256 # Get scalar values col = [ teapotcolor[hidx], teapotcolor[gidx], teapotcolor[cidx], teapotcolor[fidx], teapotcolor[didx], teapotcolor[bidx], teapotcolor[aidx], teapotcolor[eidx] ] # Define vertices coordinates # Assuming integer coordinates for simplicity based on source verts = [ Point(topleft.x, topleft.y, topleft.z), # a Point(topleft.x+1, topleft.y, topleft.z), # b Point(topleft.x, topleft.y+1, topleft.z), # c Point(topleft.x, topleft.y, topleft.z+1), # d Point(topleft.x, topleft.y+1, topleft.z+1), # e Point(topleft.x+1, topleft.y+1, topleft.z), # f Point(topleft.x+1, topleft.y+1, topleft.z+1), # g Point(topleft.x, topleft.y, topleft.z+1) # h (Note: Source h is TopLeftBack, same as d? Source code ambiguity) ] # Decompose cube into 5 tetrahedra # Tet 1: h, g, c, f tetra([col[hidx], col[gidx], col[cidx], col[fidx]], [verts[hidx], verts[gidx], verts[cidx], verts[fidx]]) # Tet 2: h, c, d, b tetra([col[hidx], col[cidx], col[didx], col[bidx]], [verts[hidx], verts[cidx], verts[didx], verts[bidx]]) # Tet 3: d, a, e, b tetra([col[didx], col[aidx], col[eidx], col[bidx]], [verts[didx], verts[aidx], verts[eidx], verts[bidx]]) # Tet 4: h, d, e, b tetra([col[hidx], col[didx], col[eidx], col[bidx]], [verts[hidx], verts[didx], verts[eidx], verts[bidx]]) # Tet 5: h, c, f, b tetra([col[hidx], col[cidx], col[fidx], col[bidx]], [verts[hidx], verts[cidx], verts[fidx], verts[bidx]]) def tetra(scalars, vertices): """Apply Marching Tetrahedra to a single tetrahedron.""" # Determine case index case = 0 for i in range(4): if scalars[i] > isolevel: case |= (1 << i) # Handle cases if case == 0x0C: # Example case from source # Intersect edges d-b, a-d, a-c # Note: Source mapping is ambiguous, using generic edge intersection logic p1 = interpolate(vertices[3], vertices[1], isolevel, scalars[3], scalars[1]) p2 = interpolate(vertices[0], vertices[3], isolevel, scalars[0], scalars[3]) p3 = interpolate(vertices[0], vertices[2], isolevel, scalars[0], scalars[2]) newverts.append(p1) newverts.append(p2) newverts.append(p3) Parameters: iso: Target isovalue. Grid dimensions: xaxis, yaxis, zaxis (source uses fixed 256). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grid indexing assumes a fixed width of 256 for index calculation (z 256 256 + y 256 + x), which fails for volumes with different Y-axis dimensions. name: Naive Isosurface Extraction
head: Simple Isosurface Extraction, Naive Tetrahedral Isosurface Extraction
body: Naive Isosurface Extraction is a surface extraction algorithm that processes each tetrahedron in a tetrahedral mesh independently to generate a collection of individual, unconnected polygons. It solves the problem of identifying the intersection between a scalar field and a specific isovalue within a volumetric representation. Unlike optimized variants that ensure manifold connectivity through vertex reuse, this method creates new vertices for every intersection point, resulting in non-manifold surfaces with cracks at shared edges. It serves as the foundational, unoptimized baseline for understanding tetrahedral isosurface generation, building on the decomposition logic of Marching Tetrahedrons. Inputs: A tetrahedral mesh (tet-mesh) consisting of a list of tetrahedra. A scalar field defined at the vertices of the mesh. A target isovalue (level set value). Outputs: An output surface representation (e.g., a polygonal mesh) containing the intersection polygons. Data Structures: Input Tetrahedron: Defined by 4 vertex indices. Each vertex has an associated scalar value from the input field. Output Points: A list of 3D coordinates where new vertices are inserted. Output Cells: A list of polygons, each defined by a list of vertex indices pointing to the Output Points. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize empty lists for output points and output cells. 2. Loop over Tetrahedra: Iterate through every tetrahedron T in the input mesh. 3. Check Intersection: For each tetrahedron T, determine if it is intersected by the isovalue. Retrieve the scalar values s0, s1, s2, s3 at the four vertices of T. Check if the isovalue v lies between the minimum and maximum scalar values of the tetrahedron. If \min(si) \le v \le \max(si), the tetrahedron is intersected. 4. Compute Intersection Polygon: If intersected, compute the intersection polygon using ComputeSimpleIntersection(): Initialize an empty list pointIds to store vertex indices. Loop over Edges: Iterate through the 6 edges of the tetrahedron. Each edge connects two vertices with scalar values sa and sb. Check Edge Intersection: For each edge, determine if it is intersected by the isovalue. An edge is intersected if (sa - v) and (sb - v) have opposite signs (or one is zero). Compute Intersection Point: If the edge is intersected, calculate the intersection point P using linear interpolation: P = Va + \frac{v - sa}{sb - sa} (Vb - Va) where Va and Vb are the 3D coordinates of the edge endpoints. Create Vertex: Insert point P into the output points list. Let the returned index be id. Store ID: Append id to pointIds. Reorder Vertices: Reorder the vertex IDs in pointIds to ensure a consistent winding order around the tetrahedron to prevent visual artifacts like cracks. Insert Cell: Insert a new polygon cell into the output using pointIds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def naiveisosurfaceextraction(tetmesh, scalarfield, isovalue): """ Extracts isosurface from a tetrahedral mesh using the naive approach. Args: tetmesh: List of tetrahedra, where each tetrahedron is a list of 4 vertex indices. scalarfield: Array of scalar values corresponding to mesh vertices. isovalue: The target scalar value for the isosurface. Returns: outputpoints: List of 3D coordinates for the surface vertices. outputcells: List of polygons, where each polygon is a list of vertex indices. """ outputpoints = [] outputcells = [] # Helper function to check if a cell (edge or tet) is on the level set def iscellonlevelset(vertexindices): """ Returns True if the cell defined by vertexindices is intersected by the isovalue. Works for both edges (2 vertices) and tetrahedra (4 vertices). """ scalars = [scalarfield[i] for i in vertexindices] mins = min(scalars) maxs = max(scalars) return mins <= isovalue <= maxs # Helper function to compute intersection point on an edge def computeedgeintersection(v1idx, v2idx): """ Computes the intersection point of the edge connecting v1 and v2 with the isovalue. """ p1 = tetmesh.getvertexposition(v1idx) # Assumes access to vertex positions p2 = tetmesh.getvertexposition(v2idx) s1 = scalarfield[v1idx] s2 = scalarfield[v2idx] # Linear interpolation # t = (isovalue - s1) / (s2 - s1) # point = p1 + t (p2 - p1) # Handle division by zero if s1 == s2 (though iscellonlevelset should handle degenerate cases) if abs(s2 - s1) < 1e-9: return p1 # Fallback, though geometrically ambiguous t = (isovalue - s1) / (s2 - s1) return p1 + t (p2 - p1) # Helper function to reorder edge vertices for consistent winding def reordertetedges(edgeindices): """ Reorders the list of edge intersection points to form a consistent polygon winding. This is a placeholder for the specific reordering logic required to fix cracks. In the reference exercise, this function ensures the vertices are ordered around the tetrahedron. """ # Note: The exact reordering algorithm depends on the specific topology of the # intersection polygon (triangle or quad) within the tetrahedron. # A robust implementation would map the edges to the tetrahedron's geometry # and sort them angularly or by connectivity. # For the purpose of this naive implementation, we assume a standard reordering # exists that resolves the crack artifacts mentioned in the source. return edgeindices # Placeholder: Actual reordering logic required to fix cracks # Main extraction loop for tetidx, tetvertices in enumerate(tetmesh): # Step 1: Check if tetrahedron is intersected if iscellonlevelset(tetvertices): pointids = [] # Step 2: Iterate over all 6 edges of the tetrahedron # Edges are defined by pairs of vertex indices in the tetrahedron edges = [ (tetvertices[0], tetvertices[1]), (tetvertices[0], tetvertices[2]), (tetvertices[0], tetvertices[3]), (tetvertices[1], tetvertices[2]), (tetvertices[1], tetvertices[3]), (tetvertices[2], tetvertices[3]) ] intersectionpoints = [] for v1, v2 in edges: # Check if edge is intersected if iscellonlevelset([v1, v2]): # Compute intersection point point = computeedgeintersection(v1, v2) intersectionpoints.append(point) # Step 3: Reorder points for consistent winding # The naive approach often produces inconsistent winding without this step orderedpoints = reordertetedges(intersectionpoints) # Step 4: Create vertices and insert polygon for point in orderedpoints: # InsertNextPoint returns the ID of the newly created vertex vertexid = outputpoints.append(point) pointids.append(vertexid) # InsertNextCell creates the polygon outputcells.append(pointids) return outputpoints, outputcells Parameters: Isovalue: The scalar threshold. Typical values depend on the dataset (e.g., 0.5 for normalized density). Tolerance: Not explicitly defined in the naive source, but floating-point comparisons for iscellonlevelset should use a small epsilon to handle precision issues. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Manifold Surfaces: The naive approach creates duplicate vertices at shared edges because each tetrahedron generates its own intersection points independently. This leads to cracks and non-manifold geometry. Inconsistent Winding: The order of vertices in the generated polygon may be inconsistent across adjacent tetrahedra, causing visual artifacts like cracks. This requires a specific reordering function (ReOrderTetEdges) to fix. Performance: The algorithm is slow compared to optimized implementations because it does not reuse vertices or use spatial indexing. An isosurface extraction algorithm that reuses intersection vertices created by neighboring tetrahedra to ensure manifold connectivity and avoid duplicate vertices. Unlike the naive approach, which has quadratic complexity if vertex merging is attempted without spatial indexing, this approach avoids quadratic complexity by reusing vertices directly via neighbor lookup. It requires pre-computing neighbor tetrahedra for each tetrahedron during mesh loading and storing vertex IDs within each tetrahedron's data structure to enable efficient reuse. It is chosen when manifold connectivity and performance are required, whereas the naive approach is used for simplicity or debugging. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra for the basic loop, but the lack of vertex reuse means the output size is proportional to the number of intersected tetrahedra times the average number of intersection points per tetrahedron (typically 3 or 4). The naive approach is described as "slow" compared to optimized implementations. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of intersected tetrahedra. Since vertices are not shared, memory usage is higher than necessary for manifold surfaces. Strengths: Simple to implement; no need for complex data structures like spatial indices or vertex hash maps; serves as a clear pedagogical baseline. Limitations: Produces non-manifold surfaces with cracks; inconsistent vertex winding causes visual artifacts; inefficient memory usage due to duplicate vertices; slow performance due to lack of optimization. When to Use: Educational purposes, debugging, or when the output is only used for visualization where cracks are tolerable or fixed by post-processing. When Not to Use: When manifold connectivity is required (e.g., for simulation, 3D printing, or accurate rendering); when performance is critical. The naive isosurface extraction method is presented as a foundational exercise in isosurface generation, specifically within the context of tetrahedral meshes. It originates from a visualization exercise by Julien Tierny, designed to teach the principles of surface extraction before introducing optimizations like vertex reuse. The exercise highlights the common pitfalls of naive implementations, such as non-manifold geometry and inconsistent winding, to motivate the development of more robust algorithms like the "Appropriate Isosurface Extraction" variant. name: Optimal Extraction via Partition Index
head: OptimalExtraction, Saddle-based Partitioning
body: Optimal Extraction via Partition Index is a method for extracting isosurfaces from a tetrahedral grid that guarantees visiting only the tetrahedra actually intersected by the level set, thereby achieving optimal runtime complexity for the extraction phase. It distinguishes itself from standard marching tetrahedra by pre-processing the mesh into partitions separated by saddle contours, allowing the algorithm to jump directly to connected components of the isosurface via a partition index. Inputs and Outputs Input: A tetrahedral mesh with a scalar field defined on vertices; an isovalue (v{iso}). Output: A set of triangles forming the isosurface, guaranteed to be connected components without self-intersections. Data Structures 1. Partition: A collection of vertices belonging to a region where the isosurface is a single connected component. Layout: std::set<std::pair<VertexID, ScalarValue>>. Ordering: Ordered by ScalarValue (ascending). 2. PartitionIndex: An interval table mapping scalar value ranges to the partitions intersecting those ranges. Layout: Similar to TetIndex but maps intervals to Partition objects instead of tetrahedra. Definitions Regular Vertex: A vertex where the set of neighbors with function values lower than the vertex forms a single connected component AND the set of neighbors with function values higher than the vertex forms a single connected component. Saddle Vertex: Any vertex that is not regular. This includes minima, maxima, and vertices where the lower/higher neighbor groups are disconnected. Saddle Contour: The boundary separating regions of regular vertices, passing through saddle vertices. Algorithm Steps 1. Identify Saddles: Iterate over all vertices in the mesh. For each vertex, check the connectivity of its neighbors with values strictly lower and strictly higher than the vertex's value. If either group is not a single connected component, mark the vertex as a saddle. 2. Partition the Mesh: Initialize an empty list of partitions and a visited set for vertices. Iterate through all regular vertices. If a vertex is not visited: Create a new Partition. Perform a flood fill (BFS/DFS) starting from this vertex. Add a neighbor to the current partition if and only if the edge connecting the current vertex and the neighbor does not cross a saddle contour. An edge crosses a saddle contour if one endpoint is a saddle and the other is not, or if the edge connects two saddles in a way that separates regions (specifically, the partition grows only through edges between regular vertices that do not cross the "saddle barrier"). Note: The source specifies growing from regular vertices and adding neighbors if the edge crosses no saddle contour. Mark all added vertices as visited and add them to the partition. Repeat until all regular vertices are assigned to a partition. Saddle vertices themselves are typically not included in the partition sets or handled as boundaries. 3. Build PartitionIndex: For each partition, determine the minimum and maximum scalar values among its vertices. Insert an entry into the PartitionIndex interval table mapping the interval [min\val, max\val] to the partition. 4. Query Intersected Partitions: Given v{iso}, query the PartitionIndex to retrieve all partitions whose scalar range contains v{iso}. 5. Find Seed Vertices and Tetrahedra: For each intersected partition: Use std::set::lowerbound() on the partition's vertex set to find the vertex with the smallest function value \ge v{iso}. This is the seed vertex. Identify all tetrahedra containing the seed vertex. Check each tetrahedron using IsCellOnLevelSet() (i.e., does the tetrahedron's min/max scalar range bracket v{iso}?). Select one such tetrahedron as the seed tetrahedron. 6. Extract Contour: Call ExtractContour(seedtetrahedron) for each seed tetrahedron found. ExtractContour implementation: Initialize a queue Q with the seed tetrahedron ID. Maintain a visitedtetrahedra set. While Q is not empty: Pop tetrahedron T from Q. If T is in visitedtetrahedra, continue. Mark T as visited. Compute the intersection of T with the isosurface (e.g., using ComputePartialIntersection()). For each neighbor T' of T: If T' is not in visitedtetrahedra AND T''s scalar range intersects v{iso} (checked via IsCellOnLevelSet() or similar span check): Push T' to Q. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def OptimalExtraction(mesh, scalarfield, isovalue): # Step 1: Identify Saddles saddles = set() for vertex in mesh.vertices: lowerneighbors = [n for n in vertex.neighbors if scalarfield[n] < scalarfield[vertex]] higherneighbors = [n for n in vertex.neighbors if scalarfield[n] > scalarfield[vertex]] # Check connectivity of lower neighbors lowerconnected = isconnected(lowerneighbors, mesh.edges) # Check connectivity of higher neighbors higherconnected = isconnected(higherneighbors, mesh.edges) if not (lowerconnected and higherconnected): saddles.add(vertex) # Step 2: Partition Mesh partitions = [] visitedvertices = set() for vertex in mesh.vertices: if vertex in saddles: continue if vertex in visitedvertices: continue currentpartition = set() queue = [vertex] visitedvertices.add(vertex) while queue: curr = queue.pop(0) currentpartition.add(curr) for neighbor in curr.neighbors: if neighbor in visitedvertices: continue if neighbor in saddles: continue # Check if edge crosses saddle contour # An edge (u, v) crosses a saddle contour if one is saddle and other is not, # or if it separates regions. Based on source: "add neighbor if edge crosses no saddle contour" # Implementation detail: The source implies growing through regular vertices. # We assume the partition grows only between regular vertices not separated by saddles. # A simple heuristic for "crosses saddle contour" in this context: # If the edge connects two regular vertices, it is part of the partition. # If it connects to a saddle, it is a boundary. # The source says "add neighbor... if edge crosses no saddle contour". # Since we only iterate regular vertices and skip saddles in the loop, # we only consider edges between regular vertices. # Re-reading source: "grow a region starting from a regular vertex and add each of its neighbors # to the partition if the corresponding edge crosses no saddle contour." # This implies we might check neighbors that are saddles? No, saddles are boundaries. # Let's assume we only add regular neighbors. # To be precise: The partition is a set of regular vertices. # The boundary is defined by saddles. if isedgecrossingsaddlecontour(curr, neighbor, saddles): continue visitedvertices.add(neighbor) queue.append(neighbor) partitions.append(currentpartition) # Step 3: Build PartitionIndex partitionindex = IntervalTable() for partition in partitions: minval = min(scalarfield[v] for v in partition) maxval = max(scalarfield[v] for v in partition) partitionindex.insert(minval, maxval, partition) # Step 4 & 5: Query and Find Seeds intersectedpartitions = partitionindex.query(isovalue) seedtetrahedra = [] for partition in intersectedpartitions: # Find seed vertex using lowerbound # partition is a set of (vertexid, value) or just vertices ordered by value # Assuming partition is a list/set of vertices sorted by value seedvertex = None for v in partition: if scalarfield[v] >= isovalue: seedvertex = v break if seedvertex is None: seedvertex = partition[0] # Fallback, though logic suggests >= exists # Find seed tetrahedron tetrahedracontainingseed = mesh.gettetrahedracontainingvertex(seedvertex) for tet in tetrahedracontainingseed: if iscellonlevelset(tet, scalarfield, isovalue): seedtetrahedra.append(tet) break # Pick one arbitrarily # Step 6: Extract Contours alltriangles = [] visitedtets = set() for seedtet in seedtetrahedra: triangles = extractcontour(seedtet, scalarfield, isovalue, visitedtets) alltriangles.extend(triangles) return alltriangles def extractcontour(seedtet, scalarfield, isovalue, visitedtets): queue = [seedtet] triangles = [] while queue: tet = queue.pop(0) if tet in visitedtets: continue visitedtets.add(tet) # Compute intersection tri = computepartialintersection(tet, scalarfield, isovalue) if tri: triangles.append(tri) for neighbor in tet.neighbors: if neighbor not in visitedtets: if iscellonlevelset(neighbor, scalarfield, isovalue): queue.append(neighbor) return triangles def isconnected(vertices, edges): if not vertices: return True start = next(iter(vertices)) visited = set() queue = [start] visited.add(start) while queue: curr = queue.pop(0) for neighbor in curr.neighbors: if neighbor in vertices and neighbor not in visited: visited.add(neighbor) queue.append(neighbor) return len(visited) == len(vertices) def isedgecrossingsaddlecontour(u, v, saddles): # If either endpoint is a saddle, the edge is on the boundary if u in saddles or v in saddles: return True return False Parameters and Edge Cases Isovalue: Must be within the range of the scalar field. Degenerate Input: If the scalar field has no regular vertices (all saddles), the partitioning step yields no partitions. The algorithm may fail to extract anything unless saddle vertices are handled separately (not specified in source). Precision: Floating point comparisons for scalarfield[v] >= isovalue should use a small epsilon if necessary, though the source uses exact comparisons. Time Complexity: The extraction phase is optimal, visiting only intersected tetrahedra. The pre-processing (partitioning) is O(V+E) where V is vertices and E is edges, due to flood fill. Memory Complexity: Requires storing partitions and the partition index. The partition index is an interval table, typically O(P) where P is the number of partitions. Strengths: Avoids visiting non-intersected tetrahedra, which is a significant speedup for sparse isosurfaces or high-resolution grids where most cells do not intersect the level set. Limitations: Requires pre-processing the mesh to identify saddles and build partitions. This adds overhead for single-frame extraction or dynamic scalar fields that change frequently. This method originates from visualization exercises and educational materials on isosurface extraction, specifically associated with Julien Tierny. It is presented as a "simplest to implement" optimal algorithm compared to more complex adaptive methods, leveraging the topological properties of saddle points to decompose the mesh.
