name: Discrete k-d tree isosurface extraction
head: KD-tree contour edge traversal
body: Extracts an isosurface from a scalar field by traversing a discrete k-d tree hierarchy along contour edges, refining nodes until contouring leaves are found, then generating quads. It differs from standard marching cubes by operating directly on the hierarchical k-d tree structure, allowing for adaptive resolution and handling of complex topologies through recursive contour edge traversal. Inputs: A discrete k-d tree representing a scalar field. A threshold value defining the isosurface level. An error threshold for precision checks. Outputs: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface. Data Structures: Kdtree::EdgeKd: An array of 4 Kdtree::Node pointers, indexed 0..3. Accessed as nodes[i2] and nodes[i2+1] for pairs. AALine: A struct containing a point (of type PositionCode) and a dir (integer). PositionCode: A vector-like type with integer components accessible via [dir], representing grid coordinates. Vertex: Represents a point in space, often with Hermite interpolation data (hermiteP). Parameters: threshold (float): Scalar value defining the isosurface level, used in isContouringLeaf checks. error (float): Command-line argument for error threshold, defaults to 10^{-7}. Steps: 1. Initialize an EdgeKd array of 4 nodes. 2. Call detectQuad to traverse down the tree for each pair of nodes until nodes are contouring leaves or hit boundaries. 3. Compute quadDir2 = 3 - quadDir1 - line.dir. Check minimal edge validity via checkMinialEdge. 4. Convert min/max codes to positions. If minEnd[dir] >= maxEnd[dir], the edge is degenerate and the quad is skipped. 5. Traverse each node while not a contouring leaf and planeDir != line.dir, updating via nextQuadIndex. If a node becomes null, return immediately to prevent segfaults. 6. If all 4 nodes are contouring leaves, call generateQuad. 7. Otherwise, for each node that is not a contouring leaf and planeDir == line.dir, split into two recursive contourEdge calls with children[0] and children[1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractisosurface(tree, threshold, error=1e-7): mesh = Mesh() # Assuming tree has a root and methods for traversal # The core logic is encapsulated in contouredge traversal contouredge(tree.root, AALine(PositionCode(0,0,0), 0), threshold, error, mesh) return mesh def contouredge(node, line, threshold, error, mesh): # Initialize EdgeKd array of 4 nodes edgekd = [None] 4 # detectQuad traverses down the tree for each pair # until nodes are contouring leaves or hit boundaries detectquad(node, line, threshold, edgekd) # Check if all 4 nodes are contouring leaves if all(iscontouringleaf(n, threshold) for n in edgekd if n is not None): generatequad(edgekd, line, mesh) else: # For each node that is not a contouring leaf and planeDir == line.dir for i in range(4): if edgekd[i] is not None and not iscontouringleaf(edgekd[i], threshold): # Split into two recursive contourEdge calls # Note: planeDir logic is implicit in line.dir comparison if planedir(edgekd[i]) == line.dir: contouredge(edgekd[i].children[0], line, threshold, error, mesh) contouredge(edgekd[i].children[1], line, threshold, error, mesh) def detectquad(node, line, threshold, edgekd): # Traverse down the tree # Update edgekd nodes based on traversal # If node becomes null, return immediately if node is None: return # Logic to update edgekd based on line.dir and threshold # This involves checking isContouringLeaf and updating via nextQuadIndex # Pseudocode simplified based on notes for i in range(4): # Access nodes[i2] and nodes[i2+1] for pairs # This part is complex and relies on specific tree structure # Assuming edgekd is populated by traversal logic pass def generatequad(edgekd, line, mesh): # Compute quadDir2 = 3 - quadDir1 - line.dir quaddir1 = line.dir quaddir2 = 3 - quaddir1 - line.dir # Check minimal edge validity if not checkminimaledge(edgekd, line.dir): return # Convert min/max codes to positions minend, maxend = getminmaxcodes(edgekd, line.dir) # Generate quads from the 4 nodes # This involves creating vertices and triangles # Based on S1, this may involve concave/convex handling vertices = [] for node in edgekd: if node is not None: vertices.append(getvertex(node)) # Create triangles from vertices # Specific triangulation logic depends on topology # S1 mentions handling of concave faces and intersection-free conditions createtriangles(vertices, mesh) def checkminimaledge(edgekd, linedir): # Compute minEnd and maxEnd by intersecting min/max codes # If minEnd[dir] >= maxEnd[dir], the edge is degenerate minend = getmincode(edgekd, linedir) maxend = getmaxcode(edgekd, linedir) if minend[linedir] >= maxend[linedir]: return False return True def iscontouringleaf(node, threshold): # Check if node is a leaf and meets threshold criteria return node.isleaf and abs(node.value - threshold) < 1e-7 # Placeholder for exact logic Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Null Pointers: During traversal, if a node pointer becomes null (e.g., boundary of tree), the function returns immediately to prevent segfaults. Degenerate Edges: checkMinialEdge computes minEnd and maxEnd by intersecting min/max codes of the 4 nodes along line.dir. If minEnd[dir] >= maxEnd[dir], the edge is degenerate and the quad is skipped. Precision: The error parameter (default 10^{-7}) is used for precision checks, though its exact application in comparisons is not fully detailed in the notes. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Depends on the depth of the k-d tree and the number of contouring leaves. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Depends on the size of the k-d tree and the number of vertices/triangles generated. Performance: Implemented in Danielhu/KdtreeISO example viewer for extracting iso-surfaces from volume data (tiff files) using oct/kd trees. Strengths: Adaptive resolution, handles complex topologies. Limitations: Complexity of implementation, potential for degenerate edges. Origin: Implemented in Danielhu/KdtreeISO example viewer. History: Not explicitly given. Usage: Extracting iso-surfaces from volume data (tiff files) using oct/kd trees. Danielmelody/KdtreeISO, https://github.com/Danielmelody/KdtreeISO, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Isomesh Octree Build and Clustering
head: Isomesh
body:
Isomesh is a hierarchical mesh generation method that constructs an octree over a uniform grid to extract a surface mesh while preserving material properties and minimizing reconstruction error. It differs from standard dual contouring by recursively clustering vertices at every node level (leaves, edges, faces, and cells) using Disjoint Set Union (DSU) and Quadratic Error Function (QEF) solvers, ensuring topological consistency across the hierarchy. Inputs: A scalar field function f(\mathbf{p}) and its gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{p}). A grid size N (must be a power of two, 2 \le N \le 1024). A global scale factor S{global}. Outputs: A Mesh object containing vertices, normals, materials, and triangle indices. UniformGrid: msize: Integer grid dimension N. mhalfSize: N / 2. mgridStep: Physical size of one voxel. mmat: Raw array of Material of size (N+1)^3. values: Temporary array of floats of size (N+1)^3 storing scalar field values. Indexing is Z-major: idx = ((y + mhalfSize) (N + 1) + (x + mhalfSize)) (N + 1) + (z + mhalfSize). Octree Node: mvertices: List of vertex structures. misLeaf: Boolean flag. mchild[8]: Pointers to child nodes (if not leaf). mcorners: Array of 8 Material values for the cell corners. mvertexMask: 8-bit integer, bit i set if mcorners[i] != Material::Empty. Vertex Structure: mposition: glm::vec3 position. mnormal: glm::vec3 normal. mmaterial: Material enum. merror: Float QEF error value. mqef: QEF state object. msurfaceIdx: Index into the storage structure (used during clustering). mparent: Pointer to the parent node's vertex (used during upward clustering). Edge Storage: Three separate storage structures (medgeX, medgeY, medgeZ) for edges aligned with X, Y, and Z axes respectively. Each stores surfacePoint(), surfaceNormal(), solidEndpointMaterial(), isLesserEndpointSolid(), and geometric coordinates. kCellCornerOffset[8]: Offsets for the 8 corners of a cube. kCellEdgeDirection[12]: Direction vectors for the 12 edges. kCellEdgeEndpoint[12][2]: Indices of the two endpoints for each edge. kMdcEdgeSetIndex[256][12]: Lookup table mapping a vertex mask and edge index to a solver index (or -1 if the edge is not intersected). kEdgeProcChildTable[3][4] and kFaceProcChildTable[3][4]: Tables defining which children of a node are involved in edge/face processing for dimensions D=0,1,2. kBadIndex: Sentinel value for invalid indices. Populate the UniformGrid with scalar field values and materials. 1. Iterate y, x, z from -m\halfSize to m\halfSize. 2. Compute global position \mathbf{p} = 	ext{localToGlobal}(x, y, z). 3. Compute v = f(\mathbf{p}). 4. Store v in values[idx]. 5. If v > 0, set mmat[idx] = Material::Empty. 6. Else, set mmat[idx] = f.material(\mathbf{p}, v). Detect isosurface intersections on grid edges and store them in edge storage structures. X-Axis Edges: 1. Iterate y from -m\halfSize to m\halfSize, z from -m\halfSize to m\halfSize, x from -m\halfSize to m\halfSize - 1. 2. Get indices idx1 for (x, y, z) and idx2 for (x+1, y, z). 3. Compute signs s1 = (values[idx1] \le 0.0) and s2 = (values[idx2] \le 0.0). 4. If s1 
eq s2: Compute global position \mathbf{p}0 = 	ext{localToGlobal}(x, y, z). Solve for intersection px along the X-axis using linear interpolation: px = x0 +  rac{0 - v1}{v2 - v1} (x1 - x0) where x0, x1 are global coordinates of the edge endpoints, and v1, v2 are the scalar values. Compute intersection point \mathbf{p}{int} = (px, \mathbf{p}0.y, \mathbf{p}0.z). Compute gradient \mathbf{g} = 
abla f(\mathbf{p}{int}). Compute offset o = (px - x0) / m\gridStep. Determine material from the solid endpoint. Call medgeX.addEdge(x, y, z, \mathbf{g}, o, 0, s1, mat). Y and Z-Axis Edges: Repeat similar logic for Y and Z axes, iterating appropriate ranges (x < m\halfSize for X, y < m\halfSize for Y, z < m\halfSize for Z) and using findAlongY/findAlongZ and respective edge storages. Recursively build the octree and process leaves. buildNode(node, mincorner, size): 1. If size == 1: Call buildLeaf(node, mincorner). 2. Else: Call node->subdivide(). Compute childsize = size / 2. For i from 0 to 7: Compute childmincorner = mincorner + childsize kCellCornerOffset[i]. Recursively call buildNode(node->child(i), childmincorner, childsize). buildLeaf(node, mincorner): 1. Get corners = args.grid.materialsOfCell(args.grid.pointToIndex(mincorner)). 2. Compute vertexmask: set bit i if corners[i] != Material::Empty. 3. Call node->setCorners(corners) and node->setVertexMask(vertexmask). 4. Initialize solver[4], filter[4], avgnormal[4]. 5. Initialize cornerused[8] to false. 6. Leaf Edge Processing: For i from 0 to 11 (12 edges): Get idx = kMdcEdgeSetIndex[vertexmask][i]. If idx < 0, continue. Get storage from storages[kCellEdgeDirection[i]]. Calculate edgepos = mincorner + kCellCornerOffset[kCellEdgeEndpoint[i][0]]. Find edge iterator iter = storage.findEdge(edgepos.x, edgepos.y, edgepos.z). Get point = iter->surfacePoint() and normal = iter->surfaceNormal(). Call solver[idx].addPlane(point, normal). Add normal to avgnormal[idx]. Determine mat = iter->solidEndpointMaterial(). Determine corneridx: if iter->isLesserEndpointSolid() is true, corneridx = kCellEdgeEndpoint[i][0], else corneridx = kCellEdgeEndpoint[i][1]. If !cornerused[corneridx]: Call filter[idx].add(mat). Set cornerused[corneridx] = true. 7. Leaf Vertex Solving: Determine surfacecnt (max idx + 1 from the loop). Resize node->mvertices to surfacecnt. Define lowerbound = mincorner and upperbound = mincorner + size. For i from 0 to surfacecnt - 1: Solve point = solver[i].solve(lowerbound, upperbound). Set node->mvertices[i].mposition = point. Set mnormal = glm::normalize(avgnormal[i]). Set mmaterial = filter[i].select(). Set merror = solver[i].eval(point). Set mqef = solver[i].state(). Merge vertices from children into parents to ensure topological consistency. clusterCell(node, mincorner, size): 1. If node->isLeaf(), return. 2. Compute subsize = size / 2. 3. For i from 0 to 7: Compute subpos = mincorner + subsize kCellCornerOffset[i]. Recursively call clusterCell(node->child(i), subpos, subsize). 4. Initialize DSU dsu and VertexArray vertices. 5. Call callSubClusterFace(0), callSubClusterFace(1), callSubClusterFace(2). 6. Call callSubClusterEdge(0), callSubClusterEdge(1), callSubClusterEdge(2). callSubClusterFace(D) and callSubClusterEdge(D): 1. Iterate children using kFaceProcChildTable[D] or kEdgeProcChildTable[D]. 2. For each child node n: If n is subdivided, get specific child sub[i] = n->child(k...[i][1]) and set allleaves = false. Else sub[i] = n. 3. If allleaves is true: Call clusterFaceLeaves<D>(nodes, dsu, vertices) or clusterEdgeLeaves<D>(nodes, dsu, vertices). Return. 4. Otherwise, recursively call callSubClusterFace(D) or callSubClusterEdge(D) on the children. Vertex Merging in Cell (Post-Clustering): 1. Map DSU sets to new indices. 2. Initialize setidx vector of size dsu.size() with kBadIndex. 3. For i from 0 to dsu.size()-1: Get leader = dsu.getSetLeader(i). If setidx[leader] == kBadIndex: Set setidx[leader] = newcnt. Increment newcnt. Set setidx[i] = setidx[leader]. 4. Resize node->mvertices to newcnt. Solving Clustered Vertices: 1. Initialize solver vector of size newcnt with copies of origsolver. 2. Initialize filter and avgnormal vectors of size newcnt. 3. For each vertex v in vertices: Get idx = setidx[v->msurfaceIdx]. Set v->msurfaceIdx = kBadIndex. Call solver[idx].merge(v->mqef). Add v->mnormal to avgnormal[idx]. Call filter[idx].add(v->mmaterial). Set v->mparent = &node->mvertices[idx]. Final Vertex Assignment: 1. For i from 0 to newcnt - 1: Solve point = solver[i].solve(lowerbound, upperbound). Set node->mvertices[i].mposition = point. Set mnormal = glm::normalize(avgnormal[i]). Set mmaterial = filter[i].select(). Set merror = solver[i].eval(point). Set mqef = solver[i].state(). 1. Scale epsilon by 1 / (S{global} 	imes S{global}) to get scaledepsilon. 2. Create Mesh mesh. 3. Call addVerticesToMesh(&mroot, mesh, scaledepsilon). 4. Call cellProc(&mroot, mesh) to generate triangles. 5. Set global position and scale on mesh. 6. Return mesh. Time Complexity: The octree build is O(N^3) where N is the grid size. Clustering involves traversing the tree and merging vertices, which is generally efficient due to the DSU structure, but depends on the number of intersected edges/faces. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the uniform grid storage (N+1)^3 and the octree nodes. The edge storage structures also consume memory proportional to the number of intersected edges. Strengths: Preserves material properties at vertices; minimizes reconstruction error via QEF; handles complex topology through hierarchical clustering. Limitations: Grid size is constrained to powers of two up to 1024; requires significant memory for large grids; implementation complexity is high due to the hierarchical clustering logic. Isomesh is an open-source project by Svenny, hosted on GitHub. It implements a dual contouring approach on an octree structure, focusing on material-aware mesh generation. The method was developed as an alternative to traditional marching cubes or standard dual contouring, aiming to provide better material handling and topological consistency in volumetric data. Svenny/isomesh, https://github.com/Svenny/isomesh, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Intersection-Free Dual Contouring
head: DC No Inter, Dual Contouring Intersection-Free Algorithm, Ju et al. 2006, genContourNoInter2
body: Intersection-Free Dual Contouring is a variant of Dual Contouring that ensures the resulting mesh is manifold and free of self-intersections by detecting intersecting triangles and performing local tessellation or vertex splitting. It solves the problem of self-intersecting triangles produced by the original Dual Contouring algorithm, which may occur when the linearized constraints are insufficient to guarantee manifoldness. It sets itself apart from siblings like Manifold Dual Contouring by using explicit pairwise intersection tests and post-processing tessellation rather than modifying the underlying optimization or constraint formulation to inherently prevent intersections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree structure representing the volume data, constructed with a simplifythreshold parameter (default -1, not set). Output: A triangle mesh (IndexedTriangleList or TriangleList) that is free of self-intersections. Data Structures: HashMap / HashMap2: Used to track unique vertices and triangles during mesh generation to avoid duplicates and facilitate intersection checks. IndexedTriangleList: The container for the final output mesh. Steps: 1. Check Flag: Determine if the nointer flag is present in the execution arguments. 2. Generate Contour: If nointer is present, call genContourNoInter2. If nointer is not present, call the standard genContour. 3. Intersection-Free Generation (genContourNoInter2): Initialize hash maps for vertex and triangle tracking. Iterate through the octree leaves to generate dual vertices and constraints (as per parent method Dual Contouring with Octree). Solve the least-squares system for each dual vertex to find the minimizer. Generate triangles connecting the dual vertices. Intersection Testing: Perform pairwise intersection tests on the generated triangles using Intersection::testIntersection. Resolution: If intersections are detected, perform local tessellation or vertex splitting to resolve them. Store non-intersecting triangles in the output list. 4. Output: Return the cleaned triangle list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def genContourNoInter2(argv): # Initialize data structures vertexmap = HashMap() trianglelist = TriangleList() # Iterate through octree leaves (inherited from parent method) for leaf in octree.leaves: # 1. Collect constraints and normals from leaf neighbors constraints = collectconstraints(leaf) normals = collectnormals(leaf) # 2. Solve least-squares system to find dual vertex position # This minimizes the distance to the hyperplanes defined by constraints # Using QR decomposition or similar solver as per Ju et al. 2002/2006 dualvertex = solveleastsquares(constraints, normals) # 3. Generate triangles for this leaf # Connect dual vertices of adjacent leaves triangles = generatetrianglesforleaf(leaf, dualvertex) # 4. Check for intersections with existing triangles for tri in triangles: isintersecting = False for existingtri in trianglelist: if Intersection.testIntersection(tri, existingtri): isintersecting = True break if isintersecting: # 5. Resolve intersection via local tessellation or vertex splitting # This step is implementation-specific but aims to remove self-intersection resolvedtriangles = resolveintersection(tri, trianglelist) trianglelist.extend(resolvedtriangles) else: trianglelist.add(tri) return trianglelist Parameters: simplifythreshold: Controls the simplification threshold for octree construction. Default value is -1 (not set). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Intersection testing is computationally expensive, especially for high-resolution meshes, as it involves pairwise comparisons. Precision: Numerical precision issues in intersection testing may lead to false positives or negatives, potentially leaving small self-intersections or removing valid geometry. Ensures manifoldness by modifying the constraint system or topology during extraction, avoiding the need for post-processing intersection tests. Choose when computational cost of intersection testing is prohibitive or when a strictly manifold output is required without post-processing [2138-manifold-dual-contouring.md]. Uses vertex clustering on an octree to adaptively refine the mesh, potentially reducing the number of triangles and thus intersection tests. Choose when adaptive resolution is needed [2142-adaptive-contouring-via-octree-vertex-clustering.md]. Extends Dual Contouring with adaptive refinement based on error metrics. Choose when high-fidelity detail is needed in specific regions [3664-adaptive-dual-contouring.md]. Uses a k-d tree for efficient spatial queries, which may speed up intersection testing or neighbor lookups. Choose when spatial indexing performance is critical [3816-kdtree-based-iso-surface-extraction.md]. Time Complexity: The core Dual Contouring step is linear with respect to the number of octree leaves. However, the intersection testing step is potentially quadratic with respect to the number of triangles in the worst case (pairwise comparison), though spatial hashing or bounding volume hierarchies can reduce this. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of octree leaves and output triangles, plus overhead for hash maps. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guarantees a mesh free of self-intersections, which is crucial for downstream applications like simulation or 3D printing. Limitations: High computational cost for intersection testing, especially on dense meshes. When to Use: When self-intersections are unacceptable and the mesh resolution is moderate enough for pairwise intersection testing to be feasible. When Not to Use: For very high-resolution meshes where intersection testing becomes prohibitively slow. Intersection-Free Dual Contouring was introduced by Tao Ju in 2006, referenced as [Ju et al. 2006]. It builds upon the original Dual Contouring algorithm by Ju et al. 2002. The method was developed to address the limitation of the original algorithm, which could produce self-intersecting triangles due to the linearization of constraints. It is implemented in open-source repositories such as aewallin/dualcontouring and ChessQian/DualContouring. aewallin/dualcontouring, https://github.com/aewallin/dualcontouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChessQian/DualContouring, https://github.com/ChessQian/DualContouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Octree Construction for Dual Contouring
head: Recursive Octree Construction for Dual Contouring
body: This method constructs the spatial hierarchy required for Dual Contouring by recursively subdividing a volume into an octree, pruning branches that do not intersect the isosurface. It differs from sibling methods like Mesh Extraction from K-D Tree by using a fixed-depth hierarchical grid structure rather than a binary spatial partition, and from Isomesh Octree Build and Clustering by focusing on single-vertex-per-leaf extraction logic rather than clustering. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which voxels contain surface geometry to minimize memory usage and processing time for sparse volumes. Inputs: A root OctreeNode representing the entire volume bounding box. A scalar field function DensityFunc(p) returning the density at position p. Constants: MATERIALSOLID (density < 0), MATERIALAIR (density >= 0), MAXCROSSINGS (6), H (0.001f), steps (8). Outputs: A pruned octree where leaf nodes (NodeLeaf) contain OctreeDrawInfo with vertex position, normal, and QEF data. Internal nodes (NodeInternal) contain pointers to children. Nodes with no surface intersection are deleted (nullptr). OctreeNode type (enum): NodeNone, NodeInternal, NodePsuedo, NodeLeaf. min (ivec3): Minimum corner of the node's bounding box in voxel coordinates. size (int): Side length of the cube in voxels. children (OctreeNode [8]): Pointers to 8 child nodes. drawInfo (OctreeDrawInfo): Pointer to drawing data; nullptr for internal nodes. OctreeDrawInfo index (int): Vertex buffer index. corners (int): Bitmask of corner states (bit i is 1 if solid, 0 if air). position (vec3): Calculated vertex position. averageNormal (vec3): Normalized sum of edge normals. qef (QEF): Quadric Error Function solver state. Constants CHILDMINOFFSETS (ivec3 [8]): Offsets for child bounding box minimums relative to parent. Indices 0-7 map to (0,0,0) through (1,1,1). 1. Recursive Construction: Call ConstructOctreeNodes on the root. 2. Leaf Evaluation: If node->size == 1, call ConstructLeaf. 3. Child Creation: If node->size > 1, create 8 children. For child i: child->size = node->size / 2 child->min = node->min + (CHILDMINOFFSETS[i] child->size) child->type = NodeInternal Recursively call ConstructOctreeNodes(child). 4. Pruning: If all 8 children return nullptr, delete the current node and return nullptr. Otherwise, return the node. 5. Corner Sampling: In ConstructLeaf, sample DensityFunc at 8 corners. Corner i position is leaf->min + CHILDMINOFFSETS[i]. Set bit i of corners to 1 if density < 0, else 0. 6. Discard Check: If corners == 0 (all air) or corners == 255 (all solid), delete leaf and return nullptr. 7. Edge Intersection: Iterate 12 edges defined by edgevmap[i][0] and edgevmap[i][1] (corner indices). Check material states m1 and m2 from corners. If m1 == m2, skip edge. Otherwise, calculate zero crossing position p and normal n for the edge. Store p and n in positions[edgeCount] and normals[edgeCount]. Increment edgeCount. Stop if edgeCount == MAXCROSSINGS. 8. Zero Crossing Approximation: For edge endpoints p0 and p1: Sample 8 points along the segment. t ranges from 0 to 1 in steps of 1/8. p = p0 + (p1 - p0) t Find t minimizing abs(DensityFunc(p)). Return p0 + (p1 - p0) t. 9. Normal Calculation: For intersection point p: dx = DensityFunc(p + (H,0,0)) - DensityFunc(p - (H,0,0)) dy = DensityFunc(p + (0,H,0)) - DensityFunc(p - (0,H,0)) dz = DensityFunc(p + (0,0,H)) - DensityFunc(p - (0,0,H)) n = normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) 10. QEF Solve: Initialize QEF with edgeCount, normals, and positions. Solve for position. 11. Clamping: If position is outside leaf's bounding box (min to min + size), clamp position to qef.masspoint (average of input positions). 12. Finalize: Sum normals, normalize to get averageNormal. Set leaf->type = NodeLeaf. Assign drawInfo. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MATERIALSOLID = -1 MATERIALAIR = 0 MAXCROSSINGS = 6 H = 0.001 STEPS = 8 def calculatesurfacenormal(p, densityfunc): dx = densityfunc(p + vec3(H, 0, 0)) - densityfunc(p - vec3(H, 0, 0)) dy = densityfunc(p + vec3(0, H, 0)) - densityfunc(p - vec3(0, H, 0)) dz = densityfunc(p + vec3(0, 0, H)) - densityfunc(p - vec3(0, 0, H)) return normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) def approximatezerocrossingposition(p0, p1, densityfunc): minval = 100000.0 bestt = 0.0 increment = 1.0 / STEPS currentt = 0.0 while currentt <= 1.0: p = p0 + (p1 - p0) currentt density = abs(densityfunc(p)) if density < minval: minval = density bestt = currentt currentt += increment return p0 + (p1 - p0) bestt def constructoctreenodes(node): if node is None: return None if node.size == 1: return constructleaf(node) childsize = node.size // 2 haschildren = False for i in range(8): child = OctreeNode() child.size = childsize child.min = node.min + (CHILDMINOFFSETS[i] childsize) child.type = NodeInternal childnode = constructoctreenodes(child) node.children[i] = childnode haschildren = haschildren or (childnode is not None) if not haschildren: delete node return None return node def constructleaf(leaf): corners = 0 # Sample 8 corners for i in range(8): cornerpos = leaf.min + CHILDMINOFFSETS[i] density = densityfunc(cornerpos) if density < 0: corners |= (1 << i) # Discard if no surface intersection if corners == 0 or corners == 255: delete leaf return None positions = [vec3() for in range(MAXCROSSINGS)] normals = [vec3() for in range(MAXCROSSINGS)] edgecount = 0 # Iterate 12 edges for i in range(12): c1 = edgevmap[i][0] c2 = edgevmap[i][1] m1 = (corners >> c1) & 1 m2 = (corners >> c2) & 1 # Skip if both endpoints are same material if m1 == m2: continue if edgecount >= MAXCROSSINGS: break p1 = leaf.min + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c1] p2 = leaf.min + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c2] # Find intersection point p = approximatezerocrossingposition(p1, p2, densityfunc) # Calculate normal at intersection n = calculatesurfacenormal(p, densityfunc) positions[edgecount] = p normals[edgecount] = n edgecount += 1 # Solve QEF drawinfo = OctreeDrawInfo() drawinfo.qef.initialize(edgecount, normals, positions) drawinfo.position = drawinfo.qef.solve() # Clamp position to bounding box minv = vec3(leaf.min) maxv = vec3(leaf.min + ivec3(leaf.size)) if (drawinfo.position.x < minv.x or drawinfo.position.x > maxv.x or drawinfo.position.y < minv.y or drawinfo.position.y > maxv.y or drawinfo.position.z < minv.z or drawinfo.position.z > maxv.z): drawinfo.position = drawinfo.qef.masspoint # Calculate average normal avgnormal = vec3(0, 0, 0) for i in range(edgecount): avgnormal += normals[i] drawinfo.averagenormal = normalize(avgnormal) drawinfo.corners = corners leaf.type = NodeLeaf leaf.drawinfo = drawinfo return leaf Precision: The zero-crossing approximation uses only 8 samples. This may miss narrow features or introduce positional error. QEF Solution Outside Box: The QEF solver may produce a vertex outside the leaf's bounding box. This must be clamped to the masspoint to maintain topological consistency. Memory: The algorithm constructs all internal nodes before pruning leaves, leading to wasted memory for empty branches. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of nodes in the full octree up to the leaf level, as every node is visited. Pruning reduces the number of leaf evaluations. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of nodes in the pruned octree. Internal nodes consume memory even if they contain no surface data until the bottom-up pruning step. Strengths: Simple to implement; hierarchical structure allows for efficient culling of empty space. Limitations: Inefficient memory usage due to pre-construction of internal nodes; fixed sampling rate for zero-crossing may lack accuracy for complex surfaces. This method is described in an unofficial blog post by Nigel Gildea, which provides a simple implementation of Dual Contouring. It diverges from the reference implementation's class hierarchy by using a single OctreeNode class with a type enum. The approach is designed for simplicity rather than optimal performance, explicitly acknowledging the wastefulness of constructing parent nodes before evaluating leaves. Implementing Dual Contouring, http://ngildea.blogspot.com.br/2014/11/implementing-dual-contouring.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Surface Nets
head: Naive Surface Nets
body: Surface Nets is an isosurface extraction algorithm that constructs a mesh by placing a single vertex per active voxel (cube) at the weighted average of the grid points on the cube's edges that cross the isosurface. Unlike Marching Cubes, which interpolates along every intersected edge and can produce multiple vertices per cell, Surface Nets generates exactly one vertex per voxel where the surface passes through, resulting in a sparser mesh with fewer vertices and triangles. Compared to Dual Contouring, it requires no normals or linear solves but yields less accurate vertex placement. Inputs: A 3D scalar field grid data of dimensions dims[0] x dims[1] x dims[2], an isovalue level, and a boolean storeFlag indicating whether to store geometry or count it. Outputs: A mesh structure containing a list of vertices p (float3) and a list of triangle indices t (int3). Data Structures: edgetable[256]: A lookup table mapping the 8-bit vertex configuration mask of a voxel to a 12-bit mask indicating which of the 12 cube edges are intersected by the isosurface. cubeedges[24]: An array storing the indices of the two vertices defining each of the 12 edges of a unit cube, used to unpack edge geometry. buffer: A temporary storage mapping voxel coordinates to vertex indices, used to facilitate triangle generation without global vertex merging. Preprocessing: 1. Call initsurfacenets() to populate cubeedges and edgetable. cubeedges is populated by iterating all 8 vertices i and finding neighbors p that differ by exactly one bit (Hamming distance 1), storing pairs (i, p). edgetable is computed by iterating all 256 masks. For each mask, it checks all 12 edges defined in cubeedges. An edge is marked as intersected if the signs of the two corner vertices differ (i.e., !(i & (1<<e0)) != !(i & (1<<e1))). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize verticeslength = 0, faceslength = 0, and bufno = 1. 2. Define stride arrays R for the grid: R[0] = 1, R[1] = dims[0] + 1, R[2] = (dims[0] + 1) (dims[1] + 1). 3. Iterate through each voxel cube in the grid with coordinates x from 0 to dims[0]-2, y from 0 to dims[1]-2, and z from 0 to dims[2]-2. 4. For each voxel, sample the 8 corner values into a local grid array and compute a binary mask where bit g is set if data[idx] - level < 0. 5. If mask is 0 or 0xff (all corners on the same side of the isosurface), skip the voxel. 6. Retrieve the intersected edges for the current mask: edgemask = edgetable[mask]. 7. Initialize a vertex accumulator v to (0,0,0) and an edge counter ecount to 0. 8. Iterate through the 12 edges of the cube (index i from 0 to 11): If the i-th bit of edgemask is not set, skip the edge. Increment ecount. Unpack the two corner indices e0 and e1 from cubeedges[i2] and cubeedges[i2+1]. Retrieve their grid values g0 and g1. Compute the interpolation parameter t. If |g0 - g1| > 1e-6, set t = g0 / (g0 - g1); otherwise, skip this edge's contribution to avoid division by zero. Accumulate the interpolated point into v. For each dimension j (0 to 2): Check if the edge spans dimension j by comparing bits of e0 and e1 at position j. If they differ, add 1.0 - t if e0 has the bit set, else add t. If they do not differ, add 1.0 if e0 has the bit set, else add 0. 9. Compute the final vertex position: v[j] = x[j] + (1.0 / ecount) v[j] for each dimension j. 10. Store the vertex index in buffer at position m (where m tracks the voxel's position in the flattened grid structure) and increment verticeslength. If storeFlag is true, store the coordinates in vertices[verticeslength-1]. 11. Generate triangles for the voxel. Iterate through the first 3 edges (indices 0, 1, 2) of the cube: If the edge is not intersected (!(edgemask & (1<<i))), skip. Determine two adjacent edges iu = (i+1)%3 and iv = (i+2)%3. If either adjacent edge lies on a boundary (coordinate 0 in that dimension), skip triangle generation for this combination to avoid out-of-bounds access. Compute relative strides du = R[iu] and dv = R[iv]. Create two triangles using the current vertex index buffer[m] and the buffered indices of the adjacent voxels: If mask & 1 is true (corner 0 is below isosurface): Triangle 1: (buffer[m], buffer[m-du-dv], buffer[m-du]). Triangle 2: (buffer[m], buffer[m-dv], buffer[m-du-dv]). Else: Triangle 1: (buffer[m], buffer[m-du], buffer[m-du-dv]). Triangle 2: (buffer[m], buffer[m-du-dv], buffer[m-dv]). Increment faceslength by 2 for each pair. 12. After processing all voxels, set mesh->np = verticeslength and mesh->nt = faceslength. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initsurfacenets(): cubeedges = [] for i in range(8): for j in [1, 2, 4]: p = i ^ j if i <= p: cubeedges.append(i) cubeedges.append(p) edgetable = [0] 256 for i in range(256): em = 0 for j in range(0, 24, 2): e0 = cubeedges[j] e1 = cubeedges[j+1] # Check if edge crosses surface: signs of vertices differ # Assuming mask bit g is 1 if data < level val0 = (i & (1 << e0)) == 0 val1 = (i & (1 << e1)) == 0 if val0 != val1: em |= (1 << (j >> 1)) edgetable[i] = em return cubeedges, edgetable def surfacenets(data, dims, level, storeflag): cubeedges, edgetable = initsurfacenets() vertices = [] triangles = [] buffer = {} # Map from voxel coordinate tuple to vertex index # Strides for 3D grid indexing R = [1, dims[0] + 1, (dims[0] + 1) (dims[1] + 1)] for x in range(dims[0] - 1): for y in range(dims[1] - 1): for z in range(dims[2] - 1): # Sample 8 corners grid = [] mask = 0 for k in range(2): for j in range(2): for i in range(2): idx = x + i + dims[0] (y + j + dims[1] (z + k)) val = data[idx] - level grid.append(val) if val < 0: mask |= (1 << (k 4 + j 2 + i)) if mask == 0 or mask == 0xFF: continue edgemask = edgetable[mask] vaccum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] ecount = 0 for i in range(12): if not (edgemask & (1 << i)): continue ecount += 1 e0 = cubeedges[i 2] e1 = cubeedges[i 2 + 1] g0 = grid[e0] g1 = grid[e1] diff = g0 - g1 if abs(diff) > 1e-6: t = g0 / diff else: continue # Accumulate weighted position # Check which dimensions the edge spans for dim in range(3): bit = 1 << dim hase0 = (e0 & bit) != 0 hase1 = (e1 & bit) != 0 if hase0 != hase1: # Edge spans this dimension if hase0: vaccum[dim] += 1.0 - t else: vaccum[dim] += t else: # Edge does not span this dimension if hase0: vaccum[dim] += 1.0 else: vaccum[dim] += 0.0 # Average and offset by voxel position if ecount > 0: invcount = 1.0 / ecount vertexpos = [ x + invcount vaccum[0], y + invcount vaccum[1], z + invcount vaccum[2] ] else: vertexpos = [x + 0.5, y + 0.5, z + 0.5] # Fallback vertexidx = len(vertices) buffer[(x, y, z)] = vertexidx if storeflag: vertices.append(vertexpos) # Generate triangles for i in range(3): if not (edgemask & (1 << i)): continue iu = (i + 1) % 3 iv = (i + 2) % 3 # Check boundary: if coordinate in dimension iu or iv is 0, skip coordiu = [x, y, z][iu] coordiv = [x, y, z][iv] if coordiu == 0 or coordiv == 0: continue # Neighbor coordinates (subtract 1 in respective dimensions) nx1 = x - (1 if iu == 0 else 0) ny1 = y - (1 if iu == 1 else 0) nz1 = z - (1 if iu == 2 else 0) nx2 = x - (1 if iv == 0 else 0) ny2 = y - (1 if iv == 1 else 0) nz2 = z - (1 if iv == 2 else 0) nx3 = x - (1 if iu == 0 else 0) - (1 if iv == 0 else 0) ny3 = y - (1 if iu == 1 else 0) - (1 if iv == 1 else 0) nz3 = z - (1 if iu == 2 else 0) - (1 if iv == 2 else 0) idx1 = buffer[(nx1, ny1, nz1)] idx2 = buffer[(nx2, ny2, nz2)] idx3 = buffer[(nx3, ny3, nz3)] if mask & 1: triangles.append((vertexidx, idx3, idx2)) triangles.append((vertexidx, idx2, idx1)) else: triangles.append((vertexidx, idx2, idx3)) triangles.append((vertexidx, idx3, idx1)) return vertices, triangles An isosurface extraction algorithm that generates a quad-mesh by placing vertices at the average of edge-crossing points on the grid cells, serving as a substitute for Marching Cubes. It differs from the standard triangle-based Surface Nets by outputting quads. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as it iterates through each voxel a constant number of times (12 edge checks, 3 triangle checks). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the vertex and triangle buffers. Performance: The method is generally faster and uses less memory than Marching Cubes due to the reduced number of vertices and triangles. Strengths: Simplicity of implementation; no need for normals or linear solvers. Limitations: Less accurate vertex placement compared to Dual Contouring or Marching Cubes; can produce artifacts if the isosurface is not well-sampled within the voxel. When to use: When vertex count reduction is prioritized over geometric accuracy, or when normals/solvers are unavailable. When not to use: When high geometric accuracy or smooth shading is required. Surface Nets was introduced by Mikola Lysenko in 2012 for smooth voxel terrain generation. It was later translated to C by Roberto Toro. The method is based on the principle of placing dual vertices at the centroid of intersection points, a concept related to dual contouring but without the optimization step. r03ert0/surface-nets, https://github.com/r03ert0/surface-nets, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GuangyanCai/isoext, https://github.com/GuangyanCai/isoext, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) JohnnyMalmberg/IsosurfaceExtraction, https://github.com/JohnnyMalmberg/IsosurfaceExtraction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: JSurfaceNets
head: Constrained Elastic Surface Nets, SurfaceNets (JSurfaceNets variant)
body: JSurfaceNets is an isosurface extraction algorithm that generates a quad-mesh by placing vertices at the average of edge-crossing points within grid cells, serving as a computationally efficient substitute for Marching Cubes. It differs from the original Gibson method by using this averaged vertex position for quad-mesh generation, resulting in a topology that is generally simpler and faster to compute while maintaining geometric fidelity for many scalar fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: data, a 1D array of doubles representing the scalar field values at grid vertices; dims, an integer array [width, height, depth] specifying the grid dimensions. Output: A Mesh object containing two lists: vertices (list of 3D coordinate arrays) and faces (list of 4-element integer arrays representing quad indices). Data Structures: cubeedges: A static integer array of size 24. It stores pairs of vertex indices (0-7) for the 12 edges of a cube. Initialized by iterating i from 0 to 7 and j as powers of 2 (1, 2, 4), adding the pair (i, i \oplus j) if i \le i \oplus j. edgetable: A static integer array of size 256. For each possible 8-bit mask i, it computes a 12-bit bitmask em where bit k is set if the k-th edge of the cube is crossed (i.e., the signs of the two vertices defining that edge differ). vertexBuffer: A dynamically resized integer array used to store vertex indices for the current and previous slices. It is indexed using a layout array R. R: A layout array [1, dims[0]+1, \pm(dims[0]+1)(dims[1]+1)]. R[0] is the x-stride, R[1] is the y-stride, and R[2] is the z-stride, which toggles sign to handle buffer wrapping. location: An integer array [x, y, z] tracking the current cell coordinates. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize location to [0, 0, 0]. Initialize bufno = 1 (buffer slice selector). Initialize R[2] = (dims[0] + 1) (dims[1] + 1). Resize vertexBuffer to at least R[2] 2 if necessary. Initialize empty lists vertices and faces. Initialize counter n = 0 (linear index into data). 2. Voxel Traversal: Loop z from 0 to dims[2] - 2: Toggle bufno (bufno ^= 1). Negate R[2] (R[2] = -R[2]). Initialize buffer pointer m = 1 + (dims[0] + 1) (1 + bufno (dims[1] + 1)). Loop y from 0 to dims[1] - 2: Increment n and m by 2 (n += 1, m += 2). Loop x from 0 to dims[0] - 2: Increment n and m by 1 (n += 1, m += 1). Set location[0] = x, location[1] = y, location[2] = z. 3. Cell Processing: Read the 8 scalar values surrounding the current cell into grid[0..7]. The index into data is computed based on n and the grid strides. Compute mask: an 8-bit integer where bit g is set if grid[g] < 0. Edge Case: If mask == 0 or mask == 0xff, the cell does not intersect the isosurface. Skip to the next cell. Compute edgemask = edgetable[mask]. Initialize sum vector v = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0} and counter ecount = 0. 4. Vertex Position Calculation: Iterate over the 12 edges of the cube (index i from 0 to 11): If (edgemask & (1 << i)) is false, the edge is not crossed. Continue. Increment ecount. Retrieve the two vertex indices of the edge from cubeedges: e0 = cubeedges[2i], e1 = cubeedges[2i+1]. Retrieve the scalar values: g0 = grid[e0], g1 = grid[e1]. Compute interpolation parameter t: t = \frac{g0}{g0 - g1} If |g0 - g1| \le 10^{-6}, skip this edge (precision guard). Accumulate the intersection point into v. For each axis j \in \{0, 1, 2\}: Check if the edge vertices differ on bit j of their index (i.e., if the edge is parallel to another axis). If they differ on bit j, the intersection lies along axis j. Add t or 1-t to v[j] depending on which vertex is 0 and which is 1. Specifically, if vertex e0 has bit j as 0, add t; else add 1-t. If they do not differ on bit j (edge is parallel to axis j), the coordinate is constant. Add the coordinate value of the vertex (0 or 1) to v[j]. Compute the final vertex position relative to the cell origin: v{final}[j] = \frac{v[j]}{e\count} Store the new vertex index in vertexBuffer[m]. Append the absolute coordinate location + vfinal to the vertices list. 5. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels N = W \times H \times D. Each cell is processed once with a constant number of operations (12 edges, 3 axes). Memory Complexity: Linear. Requires storage for the vertex buffer (proportional to grid size) and the output mesh. Performance: Generally faster than Marching Cubes due to simpler topology (quads vs triangles) and fewer geometric calculations per cell. Strengths: Produces a quad-dominant mesh which is often desirable for subdivision surfaces or CAD operations. Efficient implementation using 1D arrays and bitwise operations. Limitations: The quad topology can be irregular if the isosurface is complex. It may produce non-manifold geometries or artifacts if the scalar field is not well-behaved. The "average point" heuristic may not always yield the most accurate geometric representation compared to linear interpolation on individual edges. When to use: When a quad-mesh is required and performance is critical, and the scalar field is relatively smooth. When not to use: When high geometric accuracy is paramount (use Marching Cubes or Tetrahedral Marching Cubes), or when the input is multi-material with sharp boundaries (use Multi-Material Surface Nets). JSurfaceNets is based on the "Constrained Elastic Surface Nets" algorithm by S.F. Gibson, published in a 1998 MERL Tech Report. The specific implementation described here is a compact JavaScript port by Mikola Lysenko, later adapted into Java by Michael Hoffer for the Mihosoft VRL library. It serves as a lightweight alternative to Marching Cubes for isosurface extraction and supports basic Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) operations. miho/JSurfaceNets, https://github.com/miho/JSurfaceNets, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Material Surface Nets
head: MMCellMap, Surface Nets for multi-label segmentations
body: Multi-Material Surface Nets is an isosurface extraction algorithm that constructs closed, watertight quad-meshes from multi-label volumetric segmentations while preserving sharp boundaries between different materials. It extends JSurfaceNets by storing material labels at cell corners and associating labels with the top and bottom faces of generated quads, allowing distinct materials to share geometric boundaries without blending. Unlike standard surface extraction methods that assume a single scalar field, this method operates directly on discrete label volumes, ensuring that interfaces between adjacent materials remain sharp and topologically consistent. Inputs: A 3D volumetric grid of integer labels (material IDs) with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz, and a voxel size vx, vy, vz. Outputs: A set of vertices, a quad-mesh (list of quads), and per-quad material labels. The core data structure is MMCellMap, which manages the grid and extracted geometry. MMCellMap Layout: marraySize[3]: Integer array storing the dimensions of the interior grid (Nx, Ny, Nz). mvoxelSize[3]: Float array storing (vx, vy, vz). mcellArray: Pointer to an array of Cell structures. The array size is (Nx+2) \times (Ny+2) \times (Nz+2) to accommodate padding. mnumVertices: Integer count of extracted vertices. mvertices: Pointer to an array of Vertex structures. Cell Layout (stored in mcellArray): label (unsigned short): The material label of the cell's bottom-left-back corner. flag (MMCellFlag): A bitmask or struct indicating vertex type and face crossing types. vertexIndex (int): Index into mvertices if this cell contains a vertex, or -1 otherwise. vertexOffset[3] (float): The local position of the vertex within the cell, relative to the cell's bottom-left-back corner. Values are in [0, 1]. Vertex Layout (stored in mvertices): cellIndex[3]: The global integer index of the cell containing this vertex. position[3]: The absolute world position of the vertex. Quad Output Layout: quadCorners[12]: Float array storing the 4 corner positions of the quad (x0, y0, z0, \dots, x3, y3, z3). quadLabels[2]: Integer array storing [labelTopFaceOfQuad, labelBottomFaceOfQuad]. 1. Initialization and Padding: Allocate mcellArray with dimensions (Nx+2) \times (Ny+2) \times (Nz+2). Iterate over all cells. For interior cells (1 \le i \le Nx, 1 \le j \le Ny, 1 \le k \le Nz), set cell.label to the input label at (i-1, j-1, k-1). Set cell.vertexOffset to (0, 0, 0). For boundary cells (indices 0 or N+2 in any dimension), set cell.label to a reserved padding label (e.g., ReservedLabel::Padding) and initialize offsets to (0,0,0). 2. Vertex Classification and Counting: Iterate over all interior cells. Determine the vertexType for each cell based on edge crossings. A cell has a vertex if it contains an edge crossing between two different material labels. Count the total number of vertices mnumVertices. Allocate mvertices array of size mnumVertices. Second pass: Assign a unique vertexIndex to each cell containing a vertex and store the cell's global index in the corresponding Vertex struct. 3. Relaxation (Fairing): Perform numRelaxIterations iterations. In each iteration, update the position of each vertex to smooth the surface while preserving sharp features. For each vertex idxVtx: a. Retrieve the containing cell pCell and its global index cellIdx[3]. b. Initialize avgP[3] = {0, 0, 0} and numNeighbors = 0. c. If pCell.flag.vertexType() == SurfaceVertex: Iterate over the 6 faces of the cell (Left, Right, Bottom, Top, Front, Back). If pCell.flag.faceCrossingType(face) != NoFaceCrossing: Get the neighbor cell nbrCell and its global index nbrIdx[3]. Accumulate the neighbor's relative position: avgPx += nbrCell.vertexOffsetx + nbrIdxx - cellIdxx avgPy += nbrCell.vertexOffsety + nbrIdxy - cellIdxy avgPz += nbrCell.vertexOffsetz + nbrIdxz - cellIdxz Increment numNeighbors. d. Else (if vertexType is not SurfaceVertex, implying a junction): Iterate over the 6 faces. If pCell.flag.faceCrossingType(face) == JunctionFaceCrossing: Get neighbor nbrCell and nbrIdx. Accumulate: avgPx += nbrCell.vertexOffsetx + nbrIdxx - cellIdxx avgPy += nbrCell.vertexOffsety + nbrIdxy - cellIdxy avgPz += nbrCell.vertexOffsetz + nbrIdxz - cellIdxz Increment numNeighbors. e. If numNeighbors > 0: Average the accumulated positions: avgPx /= numNeighbors, \quad avgPy /= numNeighbors, \quad avgPz /= numNeighbors Update the vertex offset p (pointing to pCell.vertexOffset) using relaxation factor \alpha: px = (1 - \alpha) px + \alpha \cdot avgPx py = (1 - \alpha) py + \alpha \cdot avgPy pz = (1 - \alpha) pz + \alpha \cdot avgPz Constrain the position to the range [0.5 - maxDist, 0.5 + maxDist] for each axis. If a coordinate is outside this range, clamp it to the nearest bound. 4. Quad Generation: Iterate over all interior cells. For each edge of the cell that crosses between two different materials (isEdgeCrossing is true): a. Identify the two cells sharing this edge. Let them be pCellFirst and pCellSecond. b. Retrieve their labels: pCellFirstLabel = pCellFirst.label, pCellSecondLabel = pCellSecond.label. c. Identify the 4 cells surrounding this edge. These are the cells that share the edge or are adjacent to it in the plane perpendicular to the edge. d. Retrieve the vertices located in these 4 cells. e. Order the 4 vertices clockwise around the edge. The edge orientation convention is: Left-to-Right, Back-to-Front, Bottom-to-Top. f. Store the 4 vertex positions in quadCorners[12]. g. Store the material labels in quadLabels[2]: quadLabels[0] = pCellFirstLabel quadLabels[1] = pCellSecondLabel This assigns the label of the "first" cell to the top face of the quad and the "second" cell to the bottom face, preserving the material boundary. name: Reducing Surface Self-Intersections
head: Partitioning optimization for Surface Nets, Self-intersection avoidance in Surface Nets
body: This method prevents local self-intersections in triangle meshes generated by Surface Nets by selecting the optimal triangulation for each non-planar quadrilateral. While standard Surface Nets places vertices at voxel centers to produce smoother surfaces than edge-based methods, the resulting quadrilaterals are generally non-planar. This non-planarity, particularly near sharp boundaries or edges, can lead to intersecting triangles if the diagonal partitioning is chosen arbitrarily. This technique resolves that ambiguity by minimizing local surface area. Inputs: A mesh of non-planar quadrilaterals generated by the Surface Nets algorithm. Outputs: A triangle mesh where each quadrilateral is partitioned into two triangles without local self-intersections. Data Structures: Quadrilateral: Defined by four vertices v0, v1, v2, v3 in counter-clockwise order. Triangle: Defined by three vertices. Steps: 1. For each quadrilateral Q in the mesh: 2. Define the two possible triangulation patterns: Pattern A: Triangles (v0, v1, v2) and (v0, v2, v3). Diagonal connects v0 and v2. Pattern B: Triangles (v0, v1, v3) and (v1, v2, v3). Diagonal connects v1 and v3. 3. Calculate the total surface area for Pattern A (AA) and Pattern B (AB). The area of a triangle with vertices a, b, c is: Area(a,b,c) = \frac{1}{2} \| (b-a) \times (c-a) \| AA = Area(v0, v1, v2) + Area(v0, v2, v3) AB = Area(v0, v1, v3) + Area(v1, v2, v3) 4. Select the pattern with the smaller area: If AA < AB, output triangles from Pattern A. Otherwise, output triangles from Pattern B. 5. Repeat for all quadrilaterals. Parameters: None. The decision is deterministic based on geometry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-planarity: Surface Nets quadrilaterals are rarely planar. The choice of diagonal affects the local surface shape significantly. Neighboring Intersections: When a quadrilateral is highly non-planar (e.g., near an edge), the choice of partitioning for neighboring quadrilaterals can cause triangles to intersect each other. This local minimization helps but does not guarantee global non-intersection. Performance: This approach is slightly slower than fixed-diagonal partitioning due to the extra area calculations. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of quadrilaterals. Each quadrilateral requires constant-time area calculations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per quadrilateral. Strengths: Reduces local self-intersections, which is critical for applications like tetrahedralization and 3D printing. Produces a smoother output surface compared to edge-based vertex placement methods. Limitations: Does not guarantee global non-intersection. Slightly higher computational cost than naive triangulation. When to use: When exporting Surface Nets geometry to formats requiring watertight or non-intersecting meshes (e.g., OBJ for 3D printing). When not to use: When performance is critical and self-intersections are tolerable or handled by downstream processes. Surface Nets was developed as an extension to Marching Cubes to solve ambiguities and create higher quality output surfaces by placing intersecting vertices in the middle of volume voxels rather than at the edges. Dual Contouring was later developed as an extension to both Surface Nets and Marching Cubes, retaining a dual vertex within the voxel but interpolating its position using edge crossings and normals to retain sharp features. The self-intersection reduction technique is applied during the export of Surface Nets geometry, particularly for OBJ file generation. name: Parallel SurfaceNets
body: Parallel SurfaceNets (PSN) is a high-performance, parallel discrete isocontouring algorithm that extracts a surface mesh from volumetric scalar fields, specifically segmented label maps. It addresses the limitations of sequential algorithms like Marching Cubes (MC) and the memory bottlenecks of incremental allocation by using a four-pass parallel approach with computational edge trimming and pre-allocated output arrays. Unlike MC, which produces duplicated polygons between adjacent labeled regions, PSN produces a mesh where boundaries between extracted objects are fully shared, and it extracts multiple segmented objects in a single execution rather than requiring separate passes per label. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A structured volumetric scalar field with scalar values s{i,j,k} associated with lattice points. The field contains a set of labeled regions L and a background label B (any scalar value not in L). Output: A triangular mesh representing the isosurfaces for all labels in L, with points and triangles fully shared between neighboring objects. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Triad (t{i,j,k}): An 8-bit unsigned char associated with each voxel cell v{i,j,k}. It stores 5 bits of classification information: 1 bit: Scalar classification (inside labeled region L or background B). 3 bits: Whether the x, y, and z voxel edges emanating from the cell origin intersect the isosurface. 1 bit: Whether the voxel cell produces an output point (PRODUCE POINT bit). The volume of triads is padded by one triad in each \pm x, \pm y, \pm z direction, resulting in dimensions (M+2) \times (N+2) \times (O+2) for a volume of size M \times N \times O. 2. Volume X-Edge Metadata: A 2D array of size (N+2) \times (O+2) allocated for each padded volume x-edge E{j,k}. It stores five values: Number of output points. Number of quadrilaterals. Number of smoothing stencil edges. IDs controlling output write positions (after prefix sum). Edge trim (starting and ending voxels along the row). Algorithm Steps: Pass 1: Process Volume X-Edges For each volume x-edge E{j,k}, process independently and in parallel: 1. Visit all voxel x-edges e{i,j,k} composing E{j,k}. 2. Mark edges where the interval intersects the isosurface Qi. 3. Determine the left and right trim positions x{L{j,k}} and x{R{j,k}}, and the number of x-intersections along E{j,k}. 4. Gather classification information for each triad (whether s{i,j,k} \in L or s{i,j,k} \in B). Pass 2: Process Y- and Z-Voxel-Cell Edges For each volume cell row V{j,k}, process independently and in parallel: 1. Visit triads between the trim interval [x{L{j,k}}, x{R{j,k}}). 2. Intersect y- and z-triad edges against Qi. 3. Adjust the trim interval to produce a final trim interval [\bar{x}{L{j,k}}, \bar{x}{R{j,k}}) based on classification. 4. Use classification from Pass 1 to accelerate checks: if voxel edge endpoints s0, s1 are both in background B, no edge intersection exists. Edge Case: If the initial x-edge trim is empty but contours intersect only y- and/or z-cell edges, Pass 2 adjusts the trim to include these intersections. Pass 3: Configure Output For each voxel row V{j,k}, process independently and in parallel: 1. Compute the voxel edge case number c{e{i,j,k}} by combining eight voxel triads forming the voxel cell v{i,j,k}. 2. If c{e{i,j,k}} = 0, no point is generated. Otherwise, a point and smoothing stencil are produced. If any triad edges are intersected, a quadrilateral polygon is produced. 3. Record the number of output points, quadrilaterals, and smoothing stencil edges as per-edge metadata. 4. Race Condition Avoidance: Process voxel cell rows V{j,k} in a 2x2 checkerboard pattern. Group edges E{j,k} into bundles of four neighbors numbered 0-3. Process all edges numbered n in order using four total threaded processing loops. This ensures no t{i,j,k} is modified (specifically the PRODUCE POINT bit) during the processing of that specific number, avoiding data races. 5. Update metadata via a prefix sum operation to produce an indexing mapping input data to output primitives. 6. Precisely allocate memory for output based on the prefix sum results. Pass 4: Generate Output For each V{j,k}, process in parallel: 1. Initialize a voxel row edge iterator with point IDs from the prefix sum operation. 2. Advance point IDs along V{j,k} and immediate neighbors in \pm j and \pm k directions using a 3x3 iteration kernel. 3. Query the PRODUCE POINT bit in t{i,j,k} for each of the nine voxel triads in the kernel; if set, increment the point ID. 4. Use these IDs to define voxel center points, up to three quadrilaterals, and smoothing stencil edges. 5. Write directly into pre-allocated output arrays without mutexes or locks. Smoothing Step: 1. Implement constrained Laplacian smoothing in parallel using double-buffering to avoid data races. 2. Create two arrays of points P0 and P1. Initialize P0 with output points from surface extraction. 3. Compute P1 from P0 using the smoothing stencil. The position update is: pi = pi + \lambda \Delta pj where \Delta pj = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j=0}^N (pj - pi) Here, pi is the current point position, \lambda is the convergence factor, N is the number of connected points in the stencil, and pj are the positions of the connected points. 4. The total motion of pi is constrained relative to its generating voxel cell (e.g., via a constraint sphere centered at the voxel center). 5. Swap P0 and P1 and repeat. Typically 25 iterations are used. Triangulation Step: 1. Triangulate the mesh quadrilaterals in parallel by generating two triangles from each quadrilateral. 2. Select the tessellating diagonal using methods such as greedy, shortest diagonal, minimum area, or most co-planar. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelsurfacenets(volume, labels, isovalue): # volume: 3D array of scalars # labels: set of scalar values representing labeled regions L # isovalue: scalar value for isosurface extraction (subset of L) M, N, O = volume.shape # Pad dimensions for triads and metadata paddedM, paddedN, paddedO = M + 2, N + 2, O + 2 # Initialize data structures # Triads: (M+2)x(N+2)x(O+2) uint8 triads = np.zeros((paddedM, paddedN, paddedO), dtype=np.uint8) # X-Edge Metadata: (N+2)x(O+2) array of 5 integers # Fields: [numpoints, numquads, numstencils, writeid, trimstart, trimend] # Note: trimstart/end are part of the 5 values mentioned in source, # source says "five values... IDs... and edge trim". # We assume metadata stores counts initially, then IDs after prefix sum. metadata = np.zeros((paddedN, paddedO, 5), dtype=np.int64) # Pass 1: Process Volume X-Edges # Parallel loop over j, k for j, k in paralleledges(): # Process x-edges along Ej,k trimstart, trimend, xintersections = processxedges(volume, j, k, labels) metadata[j, k, 4] = trimstart metadata[j, k, 5] = trimend # Assuming index 4,5 for trim if 5 fields are counts+ids # Note: Source says 5 values. Let's map: # 0: numpoints, 1: numquads, 2: numstencils, 3: writeid (post-prefix), 4: trimstart, 5: trimend? # Source: "five values: number of points, number of quadrilaterals, number of smoothing stencil edges (initially), # IDs controlling output write positions in Pass 4 (after prefix sum), and edge trim (starting and ending voxels)" # This implies 6 slots or combined trim. We'll store trim as two ints or a tuple. # For simplicity in pseudocode, we store trim indices. metadata[j, k, 4] = trimstart metadata[j, k, 5] = trimend # Adjusting array size to 6 if needed, or packing trim. # Let's assume metadata is (N+2, O+2, 6) to be safe, or source implies 5 total fields including trim as one? # "five values... and edge trim". It lists 4 specific counts/IDs and then "edge trim". # We will assume metadata[j,k] has 6 elements: [pts, quads, stencils, id, triml, trimr] # Pass 2: Process Y- and Z-Voxel-Cell Edges for j, k in parallelrows(): triml = metadata[j, k, 4] trimr = metadata[j, k, 5] # Adjust trim interval based on y/z intersections newtriml, newtrimr = processyzedges(volume, j, k, labels, triml, trimr, triads) metadata[j, k, 4] = newtriml metadata[j, k, 5] = newtrimr # Pass 3: Configure Output # Checkerboard pattern to avoid races for parity in [0, 1]: for j, k in parallelrowsparity(parity): # Combine 8 triads to form edge case edgecase = computeedgecase(volume, j, k, triads) # Determine if point is produced if edgecase != 0: # Set PRODUCE POINT bit in relevant triads # This is safe due to checkerboard processing setproducepointbit(triads, j, k) # Count primitives metadata[j, k, 0] += 1 # Point metadata[j, k, 1] += numquads(edgecase) metadata[j, k, 2] += numstencils(edgecase) # Prefix Sum to allocate memory and compute write IDs # Apply prefix sum along the x-dimension for each row/col for j, k in parallelrows(): prefixsum(metadata[j, k,:3]) # Store write IDs in metadata[j, k, 3] computewriteids(metadata[j, k]) # Allocate output arrays based on prefix sums totalpoints = sum(metadata[:,:, 0]) totalquads = sum(metadata[:,:, 1]) outputpoints = np.zeros((totalpoints, 3)) outputquads = np.zeros((totalquads, 4), dtype=np.int64) outputstencils = [] # List of lists or flattened array # Pass 4: Generate Output for j, k in parallelrows(): triml = metadata[j, k, 4] trimr = metadata[j, k, 5] writeptr = metadata[j, k, 3] # 3x3 kernel iteration for di in range(-1, 2): for dj in range(-1, 2): for dk in range(-1, 2): # Iterate over triads in the kernel # Use iterator to advance point IDs # Generate points, quads, stencils generateoutput(volume, j, k, di, dj, dk, triml, trimr, writeptr, outputpoints, outputquads, outputstencils) # Smoothing P0 = outputpoints.copy() P1 = np.zeroslike(P0) for iteration in range(25): computesmoothingstep(P0, P1, outputstencils) # Double buffer swap P0, P1 = P1, P0 # Triangulation triangles = triangulatequads(outputquads) return triangles Parameters: Smoothing Iterations: Typically 25. Lambda (\lambda): Convergence factor controlling motion amount. Threads: Performance evaluated with 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 threads. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pathological Trims: Initial x-edge trim may be empty if contours intersect only y- and/or z-cell edges. Pass 2 adjusts the trim interval to handle this. Data Races: Setting the PRODUCE POINT bit in t{i,j,k} during threaded processing of neighboring voxel rows causes race conditions. Solved by 2x2 checkerboarding and processing edges by number (0-3) in separate loops. Memory Limits: Large volumes (e.g., 2048^3) can exceed main memory (e.g., 64 GB) due to billions of points/quads/stencils. PSN allows extraction of subsets of labeled regions to mitigate this. Memory Bus Saturation: Parallel efficiency falls rapidly from 8 to 16 threads on 10-core CPUs due to high generation rates of output primitives impacting the memory bus. Time Complexity: Scalar classification is O(1) for a single label (N=1) using cache, O(N) for intermediate labels, and O(\log(N)) for large N using a set. The overall algorithm is parallelized over volume edges. Memory Complexity: Requires pre-allocation of output arrays based on prefix sums. Memory usage scales with the number of output primitives. Large volumes may require significant RAM. Performance: PSN is typically one to two orders of magnitude faster than sequential algorithms like MC on commodity CPU hardware. On the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas, PSN achieved a 312x speedup over MC. On the Connectome dataset (240 labels), PSN (16 threads) achieved a 37.95x speedup over MC (9.98s vs 378.60s). On the Torso dataset, PSN (16 threads) achieved a 125.81x speedup over MC (0.405s vs 51.000s). Strengths: Fully shared boundaries between neighboring objects (no duplicate points/triangles). Single execution for multiple labels. No incremental memory allocation or mutexes. Scalable via task stealing (e.g., TBB). Limitations: Assumes non-manifold surfaces (multiple materials can join in a single voxel). Memory bus saturation at high thread counts on limited core hardware. Performance is sensitive to the number of labels and output density. When to Use: Ideal for parallel extraction of discrete, segmented label maps where shared boundaries and high performance are required, especially on multi-core CPUs. When Not to Use: When manifold surfaces are strictly required and the number of labels is small (FE may be faster). When memory is severely constrained for very large volumes without subsetting. Parallel SurfaceNets was developed by Will Schroeder, Spiros Tsalikis, and others at Kitware and Brigham and Women's Hospital, building on the original SurfaceNets algorithm by Frisken (Multi-Material workflow) and concepts from the Flying Edges algorithm. It was designed to address the inefficiencies of sequential discrete isocontouring methods like Marching Cubes when applied to large-scale medical and biological data, such as connectomics and anatomical atlases. The algorithm is implemented in the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) as vtkSurfaceNets3D and used in software like 3D Slicer. name: MISE (Meshing Isosurfaces by Extracting)
head: DVR Mesh Generation via MISE, Meshing Isosurfaces by Extracting
body: MISE generates a 3D mesh from a trained Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) model by querying an implicit occupancy field using an adaptive resolution strategy. It sets itself apart from static grid-based siblings like Surface Nets or Marching Cubes by iteratively refining the mesh geometry only where necessary, rather than evaluating a uniform grid at a fixed resolution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained DVR model (implicit occupancy field f: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}), a bounding box, and parameters resolution0, upsamplingsteps, threshold, padding, and pointsbatchsize. Output: A triangular mesh representing the isosurface at the specified threshold. Data Structures: MISE object: Maintains the current set of query points and their occupancy values. It manages the hierarchical refinement logic. points: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the 3D coordinates of the current query points. values: A tensor of shape (N, 1) containing the raw model outputs (logits or probabilities) corresponding to the points. Parameters: threshold: The occupancy threshold for the isosurface. Default: 0.5. resolution0: The initial grid resolution for the first query. Default: 16. upsamplingsteps: The number of adaptive refinement iterations. Default: 3. padding: Padding added to the bounding box size. Default: 0.1. pointsbatchsize: Batch size for model inference. Default: 100,000. Steps: 1. Threshold Conversion: Convert the float occupancy threshold to log-odds space to match the model's output distribution. \text{log\threshold} = \ln(\text{threshold}) - \ln(1 - \text{threshold}) 2. Initialization: If upsamplingsteps is 0, generate a uniform grid of points using make3dgrid with resolution nx = resolution0. Evaluate the model on these points and reshape to a 3D grid. If upsamplingsteps > 0, initialize the MISE structure with resolution0, upsamplingsteps, and the logthreshold. 3. Iterative Refinement Loop: Query points from the MISE structure using meshextractor.query(). Let the returned points be P. While points.shape[0] is not 0: a. Normalize points P to the bounding box coordinates. b. Evaluate the DVR model on P in batches of size pointsbatchsize to get occupancy values V. c. Update the MISE structure with P and V. The MISE structure identifies regions where the occupancy crosses the logthreshold and generates new query points for the next iteration (typically by subdividing cells or adding points near the boundary). d. Query the next set of points from MISE. 4. Mesh Generation: Convert the final MISE structure to a dense 3D grid using meshextractor.todense(). Apply a standard isosurface extraction algorithm (e.g., Marching Cubes) on this dense grid to generate the final mesh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch def misemeshing(model, boundingbox, resolution0=16, upsamplingsteps=3, threshold=0.5, padding=0.1, pointsbatchsize=100000): """ Generate mesh using MISE algorithm. """ # Step 1: Convert threshold to log-odds logthreshold = np.log(threshold) - np.log(1.0 - threshold) # Step 2: Initialize MISE if upsamplingsteps == 0: # Uniform grid evaluation points = make3dgrid(resolution=resolution0, bbox=boundingbox, padding=padding) values = evaluatemodel(model, points, batchsize=pointsbatchsize) gridvalues = reshapeto3d(values, resolution=resolution0) # Direct meshing from grid (e.g., Marching Cubes) return extractmeshfromgrid(gridvalues, boundingbox) # Initialize MISE structure mise = MISE(resolution0=resolution0, upsamplingsteps=upsamplingsteps, threshold=logthreshold, bbox=boundingbox, padding=padding) # Step 3: Iterative refinement points = mise.query() while points.shape[0] != 0: # Normalize points to bounding box normalizedpoints = normalizetobbox(points, boundingbox) # Evaluate model values = evaluatemodel(model, normalizedpoints, batchsize=pointsbatchsize) # Update MISE with new samples mise.update(points, values) # Query next set of points points = mise.query() # Step 4: Convert to dense grid and extract mesh densegrid = mise.todense() return extractmeshfromgrid(densegrid, boundingbox) def evaluatemodel(model, points, batchsize): """ Evaluate the DVR model on points in batches. """ allvalues = [] for i in range(0, len(points), batchsize): batchpoints = points[i:i+batchsize] # Model returns logits or probabilities; ensure format matches logthreshold expectation batchvalues = model(batchpoints) allvalues.append(batchvalues) return torch.cat(allvalues, dim=0) def make3dgrid(resolution, bbox, padding): """ Generate a uniform 3D grid of points within the bounding box with padding. """ # Implementation details for grid generation # Returns tensor of shape (N, 3) pass def normalizetobbox(points, bbox): """ Normalize points from world coordinates to [0, 1] or [-1, 1] range of the bbox. """ # Implementation details for normalization pass def extractmeshfromgrid(gridvalues, bbox): """ Extract mesh from 3D grid using Marching Cubes or similar. """ # Implementation details for mesh extraction pass The MISE class implementation is not provided in the source. The query() method returns points where the occupancy is likely to cross the threshold, and update() incorporates new samples to refine the boundary estimate. The todense() method aggregates these samples into a regular grid suitable for standard isosurface extraction. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations (upsamplingsteps) and the number of points queried per iteration. Adaptive refinement reduces the total number of points compared to a uniform grid of the final resolution, but each iteration requires a full model evaluation pass. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of points stored in the MISE structure and the final dense grid. The dense grid size is determined by the final resolution after upsampling. Strengths: Achieves high-quality meshes at lower computational cost than uniform high-resolution grids by focusing queries near the surface. Limitations: Requires a trained DVR model. Performance depends on the model's ability to provide smooth occupancy gradients. When to use: When generating meshes from neural implicit representations where uniform sampling is too expensive. When not to use: For static scalar fields where a single uniform grid evaluation is sufficient and faster. MISE was introduced in the context of Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) to efficiently extract meshes from learned implicit occupancy fields. It addresses the inefficiency of uniform grid sampling for isosurface extraction by adaptively refining the query points around the estimated surface. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Boolean Voxel Meshing
head: VoxelGrid to Mesh
body:
Boolean Voxel Meshing converts a discrete boolean voxel occupancy grid into a triangular mesh by detecting faces and vertices at voxel boundaries. It differs from interpolation-based methods like Marching Cubes by outputting axis-aligned cube meshes directly from the grid, resulting in simpler but blocky geometry unless voxel resolution is high. It builds on Blocky meshing by explicitly generating the vertex and face connectivity required for rendering, rather than just culling or merging blocks. Inputs: occ: A 3D boolean numpy array of shape (nx, ny, nz) representing the voxel occupancy grid. True indicates an occupied voxel, False indicates empty space. loc: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the world-space origin of the voxel grid. scale: A scalar representing the world-space size of one voxel unit. Outputs: vertices: A numpy array of shape (N, 3) containing the 3D coordinates of the mesh vertices in world space. faces: A numpy array of shape (M, 4) containing the indices of the vertices forming each quad face. Data Structures: occ: Boolean grid. v: A boolean grid of shape (nx+1, ny+1, nz+1) indicating which vertices are part of the surface. vidx: An integer grid of shape (nx+1, ny+1, nz+1) mapping vertex grid coordinates to unique vertex indices. Initialized to -1. Steps: 1.
