name: Poisson Meshlet-Based (PMB) Extraction
head: Meshlet-Based Isosurface Extraction, Real-Time Meshlet Extraction from Scalar Volumes
body: Poisson Meshlet-Based (PMB) Extraction is a real-time isosurface extraction method that partitions scalar volumes into larger blocks and extracts non-trivial persistent meshlets compatible with mesh shader pipelines, improving rendering efficiency over trivial small-voxel approaches. It differs from its parent method, Mesh Shader: Transient Isosurface Extraction, by introducing a hierarchical partitioning of extraction blocks into subblocks of varying sizes (8×8×4, 4×4×4, 2×2×2) to respect meshlet size constraints while minimizing overhead. Unlike Direct Isosurface Rasterization, which rasterizes directly, PMB generates persistent geometry buffers for subsequent rendering. The method uses a two-stage GPU pipeline: a region analysis task shader stage followed by a meshlet extraction mesh shader stage. Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset, an isovalue threshold, and rendering parameters (viewing frustum for culling). Output: Global vertex and index buffers containing meshlet geometry, and a dense array of meshlet descriptors containing offsets to buffer segments. Extraction Block: A 3D grid of cells with dimensions 8 \times 8 \times 4 (256 cells total). Subblocks: Hierarchical partitions of the extraction block: 8 \times 8 \times 4, 4 \times 4 \times 4, and 2 \times 2 \times 2. Memory Interface: On-chip memory passed from task shader to mesh shader. It encodes: All occupied cell indices within a subblock. Offset to the first occupied cell. Number of occupied cells for each subblock. Meshlet Descriptor: Stored in a dense global array. Contains: Index of the first meshlet extracted from the block. Number of meshlets the block contains. Global Buffers: Vertex buffer: Stores unique vertex positions and attributes. Index buffer: Stores triangle indices. Descriptor array: Aligned with occupied block indices. T: Workgroup size (number of threads). Typical value: 32 (standard subgroup size on NVIDIA GPUs). R: Number of cells analyzed by each thread. Typical value: 8. \beta: Number of cells in an extraction block. Calculated as T \times R. Value: 256. Block dimensions: 8 \times 8 \times 4 cells. C: Maximum number of occupied cells permitted within a subblock. Typical value: 128. Limits memory interface size and work per thread. 1. Region Analysis (Task Shader): 1. The task shader workgroup processes the extraction block. Each thread analyzes R=8 cells. 2. For each cell, determine if it is a core or padding cell for each possible subblock size (8 \times 8 \times 4, 4 \times 4 \times 4, 2 \times 2 \times 2) using modulo operations based on the cell's position within the block. 3. Characterize isosurface geometry at the subblock level to derive subregions whose meshlets approach optimal vertex and index counts while satisfying strict meshlet size constraints. 4. Calculate the number of vertices and indices created by the block. 5. Hierarchically partition the block into subblocks (8 \times 8, 4 \times 4, 2 \times 2 in 2D projection, corresponding to 3D volumes) whose extracted geometry respects meshlet size limits while avoiding arbitrarily small meshlets. 6. Reserve space in dense global memory buffers for meshlet descriptors, indices, and vertex attributes. 7. Store the index of the first meshlet extracted from the block and the number of meshlets the block contains in a dense array aligned with occupied block indices. 8. Encode all occupied cell indices in the on-chip memory interface passed to mesh shaders, along with an offset to the first occupied cell and number of occupied cells for each subblock. 2. Meshlet Extraction (Mesh Shader): 1. Each mesh shader workgroup extracts exactly one meshlet from its assigned subblock. 2. Read data from the task and mesh memory interface to determine which parent block cells to use. 3. Extend the Parallel Marching Blocks (PMB) technique [LCDW16] by separating vertex extraction and index extraction stages: First, extract vertices and vertex indices from all occupied cells. Allow each thread to process multiple cells (up to C=128 occupied cells per subblock) to reduce the number of mesh shader workgroups. Then, derive triangle indices from the extracted vertices. 4. Write vertex and index data to global vertex and index buffers. 5. Store a meshlet descriptor containing offsets to the relevant buffer segments. 6. Culling (Optional): Extract bounding volume representations (implicit AABBs, explicit AABBs, bounding spheres, normal cones) during meshlet extraction for rendering culling. 3. Rendering (Task Shader - Optional Culling): 1. If culling is active, launch task shader workgroups so each thread checks if one meshlet should be culled with respect to the viewing frustum. 2. Store global indices of potentially visible meshlets in the on-chip memory interface. 3. Launch a mesh shader workgroup for each potentially visible meshlet. 4. Rendering (Mesh Shader): 1. Retrieve geometry buffer offsets and counts based on local meshlet descriptors. 2. Read, project, and write meshlet vertex information to a local vertex buffer. 3. Transfer index data to a local index buffer. 4. Rasterize and fragment shade. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. T = 32 # Workgroup size (threads) R = 8 # Cells analyzed per thread C = 128 # Max occupied cells per subblock BLOCKDIMS = (8, 8, 4) def iscorecell(cellpos, subblockdims): """Determine if a cell is a core or padding cell for a given subblock size.""" x, y, z = cellpos dx, dy, dz = subblockdims return (x % dx != 0 and x % dx != dx - 1) and \ (y % dy != 0 and y % dy != dy - 1) and \ (z % dz != 0 and z % dz != dz - 1) def taskshaderregionanalysis(blockid, volumedata, isovalue): """Region analysis task shader: partitions block and prepares memory interface.""" occupiedcells = [] subblockconfigs = [(8, 8, 4), (4, 4, 4), (2, 2, 2)] subblockpartitions = [] vertexcounts = {dims: 0 for dims in subblockconfigs} indexcounts = {dims: 0 for dims in subblockconfigs} # Each thread analyzes R cells for threadidx in range(T): for celloffset in range(R): cellpos = getcellposition(blockid, threadidx, celloffset) if volumedata[cellpos] > isovalue: occupiedcells.append(cellpos) # Determine core/padding status for each partitioning for dims in subblockconfigs: if iscorecell(cellpos, dims): vertexcounts[dims] += 1 indexcounts[dims] += 1 # Hierarchical partitioning based on counts and C limit for dims in subblockconfigs: if vertexcounts[dims] > 0: subblockpartitions.append({'dims': dims, 'cells': occupiedcells}) # Reserve space in global buffers descriptoroffset = sum(len(p['cells']) for p in subblockpartitions) vertexbuffersize = descriptoroffset 128 indexbuffersize = descriptoroffset 254 # Encode occupied cells and offsets for mesh shader memoryinterface = [] currentoffset = 0 for i, part in enumerate(subblockpartitions): memoryinterface.append({ 'subblockid': i, 'dims': part['dims'], 'offset': currentoffset, 'count': len(part['cells']) }) currentoffset += len(part['cells']) # Store descriptor info descriptor = { 'blockid': blockid, 'firstmeshletidx': blockid len(subblockpartitions), 'meshletcount': len(subblockpartitions), 'vertexbufferoffset': 0, 'indexbufferoffset': 0 } return memoryinterface, descriptor, vertexbuffersize, indexbuffersize def meshshaderextraction(subblockid, memoryinterface, volumedata, isovalue): """Mesh shader: extracts meshlet geometry and writes to global buffers.""" subblockinfo = memoryinterface[subblockid] occupiedcells = subblockinfo.get('cells', []) # Stage 1: Vertex Extraction (PMB-style to avoid duplicates) vertices = [] vertexindices = [] vertexmap = {} for cell in occupiedcells: if cell not in vertexmap: vpos = computevertexposition(cell, volumedata, isovalue) vnorm = computevertexnormal(cell, volumedata) vertexmap[cell] = len(vertices) vertices.append({'pos': vpos, 'norm': vnorm}) # Stage 2: Index Extraction indices = [] for i in range(len(occupiedcells) - 2): indices.extend([vertexmap[occupiedcells[i]], vertexmap[occupiedcells[i+1]], vertexmap[occupiedcells[i+2]]]) # Write to global buffers globalvertexbuffer.extend(vertices) globalindexbuffer.extend(indices) # Store descriptor descriptor = { 'vertexoffset': len(globalvertexbuffer) - len(vertices), 'indexoffset': len(globalindexbuffer) - len(indices), 'vertexcount': len(vertices), 'indexcount': len(indices) } return descriptor def computevertexposition(cellpos, volumedata, isovalue): """Compute vertex position via trilinear interpolation.""" return cellpos def computevertexnormal(cellpos, volumedata): """Compute vertex normal via gradient approximation.""" return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Workgroup Size: Increasing workgroup size beyond a single subgroup (T > 32) causes performance degradation due to overhead of communicating between subgroups (shared memory and explicit barriers). Vulkan implementations exhibit performance degradations when employing workgroups consisting of more than one warp (T > 32). Culling Overhead: Computing normal cones for culling imposes high extraction overhead and is unsuitable because geometry within a meshlet can exhibit arbitrary normal spread. Implicit AABBs and explicit AABBs provide the best tradeoff. Meshlet Size Limits: The smallest subblock size (2 \times 2 \times 2) results in a maximum of 54 vertices and 40 primitives, which does not exceed typical size limits. Total vertices per subblock are limited to 128 (addressable with 8-bit indices), and total triangles are limited to 254. A real-time isosurface extraction method that uses coupled task and mesh shaders to partition scalar volumes into size-constrained meshlets, addressing the lack of control over meshlet size constraints in its parent method, Poisson Meshlet-Based (PMB) Extraction. It replaces PMB's single compute shader with a task/mesh shader pair to reduce thread-level divergence, enable hierarchical partitioning via task shader tree-expansion, and allow asynchronous execution for pipeline overlap. Parallel Marching Blocks (PMB) is a block-based isosurface extraction algorithm that generates indexed triangle meshes from 3D scalar volumes on the GPU. It solves the problem of redundant vertex data in traditional marching cubes by ensuring vertices are shared between simplices within a processing block, producing compact meshlets suitable for mesh shader pipelines. Unlike standard marching cubes which output a triangle soup, PMB avoids internal duplication within a block, though vertices on block boundaries are duplicated and must be welded by the consumer for a fully connected mesh. Time Complexity: Extraction performance is optimized when each thread analyzes R=8 cells and workgroup size is T=32. Memory Complexity: Memory interface size is limited by C=128 occupied cells per subblock. Measured Performance: Outperforms the state-of-the-art Parallel Marching Blocks extraction approach by 12% to 27% for a variety of models and isovalue ranges. The extracted meshlet representation results in a rendering time that is only 20% higher on average for large volumes than an offline-optimized meshlet representation, despite performing meshlet creation three orders of magnitude faster. Hardware: Evaluated on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU and Intel Core i9-13900K CPU running at 3.00 GHz. Strengths: Improves rendering efficiency by extracting from larger blocks, increasing primitives per meshlet. Reduces thread-level divergence by focusing extraction on occupied cells. Limitations: Performance degrades with workgroup sizes >32 threads. Normal cone culling is unsuitable due to high overhead and arbitrary normal spread. When to Use: Dynamic isosurface exploration scenarios requiring real-time extraction and rendering. When Not to Use: When normal cone culling is required, or when hardware does not support mesh shader pipelines with efficient subgroup communication. The method was proposed in "Real-Time Meshlet Extraction from Scalar Volumes". It builds on the Parallel Marching Blocks (PMB) technique [LCDW16] and addresses limitations in previous approaches like Nishidate and Fujishiro [NF24] by hierarchically assigning subblocks of varying size without producing meshlets that exceed size constraints. The implementation was tested in modern OpenGL 4.6 using the GLNVmeshshader extension and experimented with Vulkan. name: Meshlet Extraction using Mesh Shader Pipelines
head: Mesh Shader Meshlet Extraction
body: A real-time isosurface extraction method that uses coupled task and mesh shaders to partition scalar volumes into size-constrained meshlets, addressing the lack of control over meshlet size constraints in its parent method, Poisson Meshlet-Based (PMB) Extraction. It replaces PMB's single compute shader with a task/mesh shader pair to reduce thread-level divergence, enable hierarchical partitioning via task shader tree-expansion, and allow asynchronous execution for pipeline overlap. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar volume V, isovalue, block size parameters (Bx, By, Bz), meshlet vertex and index count constraints. Output: A list of meshlets, each containing a descriptor, an index buffer, and vertex attribute buffers (positions, normals). Data Structures: Min-Max Volume: Precomputed volume storing min/max scalar values for each block, used to cull empty blocks. Global Memory Buffers: Dense arrays for meshlet descriptors, index buffers, and vertex attribute buffers (positions, normals). Occupied Block Indices: A dense array aligned with occupied block indices, storing the index of the first meshlet and the count of meshlets per block. Parameters: Block Size: 8 \times 8 \times 4 cells. Subblock Sizes: Hierarchical levels of 4 \times 4 \times 4 and 2 \times 2 \times 2 cells. Threads per Workgroup (T): 32 (one per warp). Total Cells per Block (\beta): Bx \times By \times Bz = 256. Cells per Thread (R): R = \beta / T = 8. Convex Subblocks: The block size combines 32 convex subblocks of size 2 \times 2 \times 2. Steps: 1. Preliminaries: Implicitly divide the scalar volume V into 3D blocks where block size along each axis is a power of two. Calculate a min-max volume from V. Index cells in Morton order to ensure compact regions for subgroup communication. 2. Occupied Block Filtering: Use the same approach as PMB to locate occupied blocks where isosurfaces should be extracted. 3. Task Shader Workgroup Analysis: Execute a single task shader workgroup per occupied block. The workgroup has T=32 threads. Each thread Ti analyzes the i-th subregion of R cells (where R=8). Cells are indexed in Morton order. Each thread counts the number of vertices and primitives (triangles) produced by the isosurface within its assigned R cells. Threads store indices of cells contributing to the isosurface and indices of padding cells contributing to the isosurface for each possible partitioning (8\times8\times4, 4\times4\times4, 2\times2\times2). A cell's status as a core or padding cell for each partitioning is determined using modulo operations based on the cell's position and subblock size. Use efficient subgroup communication to analyze and summarize block and subblock regions (vertex/primitive counts). 4. Hierarchical Partitioning (Region Analysis): Determine if all isosurface geometry in the block can be represented by a single meshlet. If yes, mark the block for single meshlet extraction. If not, determine if the isosurface in each 4 \times 4 \times 4 subblock can be represented by a single meshlet. If a 4 \times 4 \times 4 subblock cannot be represented by one meshlet, partition it into 2 \times 2 \times 2 subblocks. Subblocks must be convex to allow implicit identification of core and padding cells. 5. Meshlet Extraction: Spawn mesh shader workgroups for each resulting partition (subblock) that contains isosurface geometry. Empty subblocks are skipped. Each mesh shader workgroup extracts a meshlet from its assigned subblock using the PMB extraction kernel. 6. Buffer Reservation and Metadata: Reserve space in dense global memory buffers for meshlet descriptors, indices, and vertex attributes based on calculated counts. Store the index of the first meshlet extracted from the block and the number of meshlets the block contains in a dense array aligned with the occupied block indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. T = 32 threads, R = 8 cells per thread, beta = 256 cells per block T = 32 R = 8 beta = 256 # Shared memory for subgroup communication sharedcounts = [[0, 0] for in range(3)] # [level, (vcount, tcount)] # Each thread analyzes R cells in Morton order threadid = getthreadid() # standard hardware intrinsic startcell = threadid R endcell = startcell + R localvcount = 0 localtcount = 0 localcoreindices = [] localpaddingindices = {0: [], 1: [], 2: []} for i in range(startcell, endcell): cellidx = blockcells[i] # Check occupancy using min-max volume or scalar value if isoccupied(cellidx, isovalue, minmaxvolume): # Count vertices and triangles for this cell v, t = countgeometry(cellidx) localvcount += v localtcount += t # Store cell index localcoreindices.append(cellidx) # Determine padding status for each partition level using modulo for level in range(3): if ispaddingcell(cellidx, level, R): localpaddingindices[level].append(cellidx) # Subgroup reduction to sum counts across threads totalv = sum(localvcount for in range(T)) # simplified subgroup sum totalt = sum(localtcount for in range(T)) # Determine partitioning strategy # Check if whole block fits in one meshlet if fitsinmeshlet(totalv, totalt, vertexlimit, indexlimit): partition = [0] # Level 0: whole block else: # Check 4x4x4 subblocks (4 subblocks) subblockpartitions = [] for subblockid in range(4): # Aggregate counts for this 4x4x4 subblock using subgroup communication subv, subt = aggregatesubblockcounts(subblockid, localvcount, localtcount, sharedcounts) if fitsinmeshlet(subv, subt, vertexlimit, indexlimit): subblockpartitions.append(1) # Level 1 else: # Partition into 2x2x2 subblocks (8 per 4x4x4) for innersubblockid in range(8): innerv, innert = aggregateinnersubblockcounts(subblockid, innersubblockid, localvcount, localtcount, sharedcounts) if fitsinmeshlet(innerv, innert, vertexlimit, indexlimit): subblockpartitions.append(2) # Level 2 else: # Should not happen given block size constraints pass partition = subblockpartitions # Reserve space in global buffers nummeshlets = len(partition) offset = reserveglobalbuffers(nummeshlets) # Store metadata occupiedblockmetadata[blockid].firstmeshletindex = offset occupiedblockmetadata[blockid].nummeshlets = nummeshlets # Launch mesh shader workgroups for meshletid, subblocktype in enumerate(partition): if subblocktype != -1: # -1 represents empty launchmeshshaderworkgroup( blockid=blockid, meshletid=meshletid, subblocktype=subblocktype, globalbufferoffset=offset + meshletid) def meshshaderworkgroup(blockid, meshletid, subblocktype, globalbufferoffset, blockcells): # Extract meshlet from the assigned subblock using PMB kernel meshlet = pmbextractmeshlet(subblocktype, blockcells) # Write to global buffers writemeshletdescriptor(globalbufferoffset, meshlet) writeindexbuffer(globalbufferoffset, meshlet.indices) writevertexbuffers(globalbufferoffset, meshlet.vertices) def getthreadid(): return 0 # standard hardware intrinsic def isoccupied(cellidx, isovalue, minmaxvolume): return minmaxvolume[cellidx].max > isovalue # standard occupancy test def countgeometry(cellidx): return 1, 1 # placeholder for PMB kernel geometry count logic def ispaddingcell(cellidx, level, R): return cellidx % (R (2 level)) != 0 # simplified modulo check per evidence def aggregatesubblockcounts(subblockid, localv, localt, shared): return localv, localt # placeholder for subgroup reduction logic def aggregateinnersubblockcounts(subblockid, innerid, localv, localt, shared): return localv, localt # placeholder for subgroup reduction logic def fitsinmeshlet(v, t, vlimit, ilimit): return v <= vlimit and t <= ilimit # standard constraint check def reserveglobalbuffers(count): return 0 # placeholder for buffer offset tracking def launchmeshshaderworkgroup(blockid, meshletid, subblocktype, globalbufferoffset): pass # standard shader launch mechanism def pmbextractmeshlet(subblocktype, blockcells): return type('Meshlet', (), {'indices': [], 'vertices': []})() # placeholder for PMB kernel output def writemeshletdescriptor(offset, meshlet): pass # standard buffer write def writeindexbuffer(offset, indices): pass # standard buffer write def writevertexbuffers(offset, vertices): pass # standard buffer write A hierarchical partitioning approach that subdivides blocks into convex subblocks to ensure meshlets do not exceed vertex/index constraints. It checks if the whole block fits in one meshlet; if not, it checks 4 \times 4 \times 4 subblocks; if those fail, it partitions into 2 \times 2 \times 2 subblocks. Unlike Kreskowski et al. [KRF22] which groups cells arbitrarily, this method divides blocks into convex subblocks to maintain compatibility with the PMB extraction kernel, allowing implicit identification of core and padding cells. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces thread-level divergence (TLD) in geometry extraction compared to PMB's single compute shader; allows hierarchical partitioning via task shader tree-expansion; enables asynchronous execution for pipeline overlap without complex multi-queue orchestration; extracts unique vertices within meshlets to maximize primitive count per meshlet. Limitations: Requires hardware support for task and mesh shaders; relies on convex subblocks for efficient core/padding cell identification. When to use: When real-time isosurface extraction is required and hardware supports mesh shader pipelines, especially when PMB's lack of size constraint control is a bottleneck. When not: When hardware lacks task/mesh shader support or when scene complexity does not benefit from reduced TLD. Originated in the paper "Real-Time Meshlet Extraction from Scalar Volumes". It is the first approach to real-time extraction of isosurfaces as meshlets from scalar volumes using task and mesh shaders. It builds on Poisson Meshlet-Based (PMB) Extraction. name: Parallel Marching Blocks
body: Parallel Marching Blocks (PMB) is a block-based isosurface extraction algorithm that generates indexed triangle meshes from 3D scalar volumes on the GPU. It solves the problem of redundant vertex data in traditional marching cubes by ensuring vertices are shared between simplices within a processing block, producing compact meshlets suitable for mesh shader pipelines. Unlike standard marching cubes which output a triangle soup, PMB avoids internal duplication within a block, though vertices on block boundaries are duplicated and must be welded by the consumer for a fully connected mesh. PMB operates in two main phases: an offline preprocessing stage and a runtime extraction stage. The runtime stage consists of occupied block filtering and isosurface extraction. Inputs: Scalar field V: Defined either as an analytic CUDA device function or a sampled array. Domain bounds: Axis-aligned bounding box defined by origin x0 and size L. Grid resolution N: Integer dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz). Block dimensions: Bx \times By \times Bz cells per block. Isosurface value: Typically 0 (zero level set). Data types: Floating-point type ftype (e.g., np.float32) for coordinates and scalars; integer type itype (e.g., uint32) for indices. Outputs: Vertices buffer V: Array of shape (nv, 3) with ftype components. Indices buffer I: Array of shape (nt, 3) with itype components. If the zero level set is empty, both buffers are None. 1. Min-Max Volume: An auxiliary volume storing the minimum and maximum scalar values for each block, used to determine if a block contains the isosurface. 2. Active Block List: A dense global memory array storing indices of occupied blocks, generated via stream compaction. 3. Shared Memory Array: Within each workgroup, a shared memory array stores the location (offset) of each cell's vertices in the block's dense vertex array. 4. Output Buffers: Device-side buffers for vertices and indices. These can be standard CUDA buffers or mapped OpenGL buffers. 1. Preprocessing: Compute the min-max volume from the input scalar volume V. This is done offline or once before runtime. 2. Occupied Block Filtering: Access the min-max volume to determine which blocks of size Bx \times By \times Bz contain the isosurface. Optionally, use analytic block predicates (computed via interval or affine arithmetic) to discard blocks that cannot contain the surface. This allows performance to scale with surface area rather than volume. Store the indices of occupied blocks in a dense global memory array using stream compaction. 3. Isosurface Extraction (Per Occupied Block): Launch a compute shader workgroup for each occupied block. Workgroup Size: Launch a workgroup of size (Bx + 1) \times (By + 1) \times (Bz + 1). This includes "core" cells (within the block) and "padding" cells (neighboring cells outside the block) to ensure vertices required for edge triangles are available. Thread Mapping: Map each thread to one cell. Vertex Extraction: Threads extract vertices lying on the three edges of their assigned cell for which only that thread is responsible. Threads calculate the location of their cell's vertices in the block's dense vertex array using prefix sum operations. Store these locations in the shared-memory array. Triangle Generation: Retrieve indices from the shared-memory array when creating triangles. This generates an index buffer for the block without duplicated vertices within the block. Ensure consistent orientation: Normals point from negative to positive scalar values. Triangles are counterclockwise when viewed from the positive side. Buffer Management: Kernels read active block, vertex, and simplex counts from device counters. If counts exceed buffer capacity, reallocate buffers and relaunch kernels step-by-step. Once buffers are large enough, perform a single device-to-host copy. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelmarchingblocks(scalarfield, domainorigin, domainsize, gridresolution, blocksize, isosurfacevalue=0.0): """ Extracts isosurface using Parallel Marching Blocks. Args: scalarfield: Function or array defining the scalar field. domainorigin: Tuple (x0, y0, z0) defining the start of the domain. domainsize: Tuple (Lx, Ly, Lz) defining the size of the domain. gridresolution: Tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz) defining the grid dimensions. blocksize: Tuple (Bx, By, Bz) defining the block dimensions. isosurfacevalue: The scalar value to extract (default 0). Returns: vertices: Array of shape (nv, 3) or None. indices: Array of shape (nt, 3) or None. """ # 1. Preprocessing: Create min-max volume # Note: In practice, this is often done offline or cached. minmaxvolume = computeminmaxvolume(scalarfield, domainorigin, domainsize, gridresolution, blocksize) # 2. Occupied Block Filtering # Identify blocks containing the isosurface occupiedblocks = [] for blockidx in range(totalblocks): blockmin, blockmax = getblockminmax(minmaxvolume, blockidx) # Check if isosurface is within the block's scalar range if blockmin <= isosurfacevalue <= blockmax: # Optional: Use analytic block predicates for finer culling if checkblockpredicate(scalarfield, blockidx, domainorigin, domainsize, gridresolution, blocksize): occupiedblocks.append(blockidx) if not occupiedblocks: return None, None # Stream compaction to create dense array of occupied block indices activeblockindices = streamcompact(occupiedblocks) # 3. Isosurface Extraction vertices = [] indices = [] # Allocate initial buffers maxvertices = estimatemaxvertices(activeblockindices, blocksize) maxindices = estimatemaxindices(activeblockindices, blocksize) vertexbuffer = allocatebuffer(maxvertices, 3, dtype=float32) indexbuffer = allocatebuffer(maxindices, 3, dtype=uint32) for blockidx in activeblockindices: # Launch workgroup for this block # Workgroup size: (Bx+1) x (By+1) x (Bz+1) wgsize = (blocksize[0] + 1, blocksize[1] + 1, blocksize[2] + 1) # Shared memory for vertex locations sharedvertexlocations = allocatesharedmemory(wgsize, dtype=int32) # Execute kernel # Each thread handles one cell (core or padding) executemarchingkernel( scalarfield=scalarfield, blockidx=blockidx, domainorigin=domainorigin, domainsize=domainsize, gridresolution=gridresolution, blocksize=blocksize, isosurfacevalue=isosurfacevalue, sharedvertexlocations=sharedvertexlocations, vertexbuffer=vertexbuffer, indexbuffer=indexbuffer) # 4. Buffer Management and Copy # Read counts from device counters numvertices = getdevicecounter("vertexcount") numindices = getdevicecounter("indexcount") # If counts exceed capacity, reallocate and relaunch if numvertices > len(vertexbuffer) or numindices > len(indexbuffer): vertexbuffer = reallocatebuffer(vertexbuffer, numvertices) indexbuffer = reallocatebuffer(indexbuffer, numindices) # Relaunch kernels step-by-step for blockidx in activeblockindices: executemarchingkernel(...) # Same as above # Single device-to-host copy vertices = copytohost(vertexbuffer, numvertices) indices = copytohost(indexbuffer, numindices) return vertices, indices def executemarchingkernel(scalarfield, blockidx, domainorigin, domainsize, gridresolution, blocksize, isosurfacevalue, sharedvertexlocations, vertexbuffer, indexbuffer): """ Kernel executed by each workgroup. """ # Thread indices tid = getthreadid() cellcoords = getcellcoordinates(tid, blocksize) # Includes padding # Determine if this thread is responsible for a core cell or padding cell iscore = iswithinblock(cellcoords, blocksize) # Extract vertices for edges assigned to this thread # Only core threads contribute to the final vertex array to avoid duplication if iscore: vertexindices = extractverticesforcell( scalarfield, cellcoords, domainorigin, domainsize, gridresolution, isosurfacevalue) # Calculate location in dense vertex array using prefix sum # This requires synchronization and atomic operations or shared memory prefix sum localoffset = computeprefixsum(vertexindices, sharedvertexlocations) # Store vertex locations in shared memory storevertexlocations(cellcoords, localoffset, sharedvertexlocations) # Write vertices to global buffer writeverticestobuffer(vertexindices, localoffset, vertexbuffer) # Generate triangles using indices from shared memory triangleindices = generatetriangles(cellcoords, sharedvertexlocations) writeindicestobuffer(triangleindices, indexbuffer) N: Grid size, passed as a kernel argument, not a template parameter. scalar function: Analytic CUDA device function or sampled array. Signature: template <typename T, typename I, I dim> device forceinline T scalar(const trove::array<T,dim>& p, const trove::array<I,dim>& i). ftype: Floating-point type for coordinates and scalar values (e.g., np.float32). itype: Integer type for indices (e.g., uint32). x0: Domain origin. L: Domain size. Padding Cells: Triangles from cells on the edge of the block require vertices from cells not in the block. This is handled by including padding cells in the workgroup. Empty Zero Level Set: If the zero level set is empty, output buffers V and I are None. Boundary Duplication: Vertices lying on faces shared by two blocks are duplicated. Users must weld them by position for a fully connected mesh. Cache Invalidation: Headers included from other directories via extrabuildoptions are not part of the cache key. The cache must be cleared when these headers change. Precision: Supports single (float32) or double (float64) precision for vertices. Time Complexity: Performance scales with the surface area when block predicates are used, rather than the full volume. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of vertices and indices in the extracted meshlets. Buffer reallocation may occur if initial estimates are insufficient. Strengths: Avoids redundant vertex/index data within a block. Generates indexed meshes compatible with mesh shader pipelines. Supports dynamic domains and kernel parameters. Can use OpenGL buffers for zero-copy rendering. Limitations: Provides little control over the maximum number of vertices and indices extracted, potentially producing meshlets that do not conform to size constraints. Requires post-processing (welding) for fully connected meshes across block boundaries. When to Use: Real-time isosurface extraction where meshlet-based rendering is beneficial and block boundaries can be handled by the renderer or post-processing. When Not to Use: When strict meshlet size constraints are required or when a fully connected mesh without boundary welding is needed. Parallel Marching Blocks (PMB) was introduced by Liu et al. in the paper "Parallel Marching Blocks: A Practical Isosurfacing Algorithm for Large Data on Many-Core Architectures" (CGF 2022). It is implemented in the cupmb library (Cuda Parallel Marching Blocks) by Jean-Baptiste Keck. The method builds on the principles of block-based isosurfacing to improve efficiency over trivial small-voxel approaches [Parent]. name: Direct Isosurface Rasterization
head: Direct Isosurface Rasterization via Task and Mesh Shaders, Direct isosurface visualization, Transient isosurface extraction
body: Direct Isosurface Rasterization is a rasterization-based approach for rendering isosurfaces that avoids intermediate explicit mesh storage by leveraging task and mesh shaders to identify subvolumes containing isosurface geometry and extract primitives on the fly for direct consumption by the rasterizer. It solves the problem of high memory bandwidth and storage requirements associated with indirect methods (like standard Marching Cubes) and the resolution-dependent performance costs of ray-marching. Unlike its siblings, it generates transient indexed triangles directly from volume data without precomputing or storing a persistent mesh structure. The method operates in two main stages: occlusion culling to determine the Potentially Visible Set (PVS) of blocks, and transient extraction to render the isosurface. Both stages utilize the task and mesh shader pipeline. Input: A scalar volume dataset V. Precomputed min-max grid storing the minimum and maximum data values for each block. Output: Rasterized pixels representing the isosurface at a specified isovalue. Block Definition A block is a virtual subvolume comprised of U \times V \times W cells. Dimensions: U=8, V=8, W=4. Total cells per block: 256. Indexing: Cells within a block are indexed using 8-bit integers (0 to 255). Note: Blocks are a virtual subdivision; the underlying volume data does not require rearrangement. Min-Max Grid Format: 2-channel volume texture. Resolution: Matches the block grid resolution of the volume. Content: Stores (min, max) values for each block. Purpose: Allows occupancy determination with a single texture lookup. Memory Interface Block Purpose: Shared memory interface between a task shader workgroup and its emitted mesh shader workgroups. Content: Provides mesh shader workgroups with a compact list of occupied cells to process. Benefit: Increases the chance of high warp occupancy by grouping related cell processing. The pipeline processes mutually exclusive sets of blocks depending on their visibility state in the current and previous frame. This stage identifies which blocks contain visible isosurface geometry. 1. Task Shader (Block Classification): Each task shader workgroup processes one block. It performs a texture lookup on the min-max grid for the block. If the isovalue lies within [min, max], the block is considered potentially occupied. The task shader emits mesh shader workgroups for these potentially occupied blocks. 2. Mesh Shader (Proxy Generation): Mesh shader instances generate proxy geometry (e.g., bounding boxes or simplified representations) for the blocks identified by the task shader. This proxy geometry is rasterized to perform conservative occlusion culling. The result determines the final Potentially Visible Set (PVS) of blocks for the current frame. This stage extracts and renders the actual isosurface geometry for the PVS blocks. 1. Task Shader (Cell Classification): Each task shader workgroup processes one block from the PVS. It iterates through all U \times V \times W cells in the block. For each cell, it applies the Marching Cubes cell classification [LC87] to determine if the isosurface intersects the cell. Cells that produce geometry are marked as "occupied". The task shader creates a compact list of these occupied cells. It emits mesh shader workgroups, assigning them subsets of the occupied cells to process. 2. Mesh Shader (Primitive Extraction): Each mesh shader instance receives a list of occupied cells. For each occupied cell, it performs the Marching Cubes algorithm to extract the specific triangle indices. It generates indexed triangles representing the isosurface segment for that cell. The extracted primitives are passed directly to the rasterization units. 3. Rasterization: The rasterizer consumes the primitives directly. No intermediate mesh storage is used. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. U, V, W = 8, 8, 4 CELLSPERBLOCK = U V W # 256 class MemoryInterfaceBlock: occupiedcellindices: list[int] # List of 8-bit indices (0-255) count: int def taskshaderworkgroup(blockid: int): # 1. Check Block Occupancy (for Culling or Extraction) minval, maxval = loadminmax(blockid) # From min-max grid texture if not isovalueinrange(minval, maxval): return # Block is empty or fully outside isovalue # 2. Identify Occupied Cells within the Block occupiedcells = [] for cellidx in range(CELLSPERBLOCK): # Get voxel values for the 8 vertices of the cell # Note: cellidx maps to specific (x,y,z) coordinates in the block vertexvalues = getcellvertices(blockid, cellidx) # Apply Marching Cubes classification # Returns true if the isosurface intersects this cell if marchingcubesclassify(vertexvalues, isovalue): occupiedcells.append(cellidx) if len(occupiedcells) == 0: return # 3. Emit Mesh Shader Workgroups # Distribute occupied cells to mesh shader workgroups # The exact distribution strategy (e.g., round-robin or chunking) # is implementation-specific but aims to balance load. interface = MemoryInterfaceBlock() interface.occupiedcellindices = occupiedcells interface.count = len(occupiedcells) # Emit mesh shader workgroups, passing 'interface' as shared memory emitmeshshaderworkgroups(interface) def meshshaderworkgroup(interface: MemoryInterfaceBlock): # 1. Process Assigned Cells for cellidx in interface.occupiedcellindices: # Get voxel values for the 8 vertices of the cell vertexvalues = getcellvertices(interface.blockid, cellidx) # 2. Extract Geometry using Marching Cubes # Returns a list of triangle indices (vertex indices in the output buffer) triangles = marchingcubesextract(vertexvalues, isovalue) # 3. Output Triangles for tri in triangles: writetriangletooutputbuffer(tri) Block Dimensions: U=8, V=8, W=4. Isovalue: User-defined scalar threshold. Typical Use Case: Interactive analysis scenarios requiring frequent isovalue adjustment. Visibility State: The pipeline works on mutually exclusive sets of blocks depending on their visibility state in the current and previous frame. Conservative Culling: The occlusion culling must be conservative rather than probabilistic to avoid missing visible geometry. Precision: Standard Marching Cubes precision applies; no special handling is noted for floating-point precision issues in the sources. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in Big-O notation, but performance is competitive with ray-marching and significantly better at high resolutions. Memory Complexity: Negligible additional memory compared to indirect methods, as no explicit mesh is stored. Requires storage for the min-max grid. Measured Performance: At 3840x2160 resolution, average draw times were: CT Head: 0.19ms (vs 1.54ms for min-max octree ray marching). Vertebra: 0.26ms (vs 1.95ms). Chameleon: 1.26ms (vs 2.59ms). Timeseries Supernova: 0.29ms (vs 1.41ms). Scaling: Performance is less dependent on display resolution than ray-marching because rasterization units are highly optimized, whereas ray-marching performance has a linear dependence on resolution. Strengths: Low memory bandwidth and storage overhead. High performance at high resolutions. Suitable for interactive analysis with frequent isovalue changes. Straightforward integration into existing rasterization pipelines. Limitations: Requires preprocessing to compute min-max grids. Relies on modern graphics hardware features (task/mesh shaders). When to Use: Applications where isosurface geometry is highly variable, requiring frequent isovalue adjustment, and high resolution is desired. When Not to Use: Legacy hardware without task/mesh shader support, or scenes where preprocessing min-max grids is prohibitive. Origin: First published on 20 March 2023. Paper: "Efficient Direct Isosurface Rasterization of Scalar Volumes". History: Builds on the concept of direct isosurface visualization (ray marching) and indirect visualization (Marching Cubes). It leverages modern graphics hardware features like task and mesh shading pipelines, which were introduced to address the inefficiencies of traditional geometry shaders. The method adapts techniques from raster occlusion culling [KT14, LJSL21] to volume rendering. Usage: Suitable for interactive analysis of static and dynamic data sets, including time-varying data streams. It supports modern graphics features like multi-view stereo. name: Cuberille Method
head: Cuberille Model, Herman-Liu method, Meagher's method, Octree Cuberille
body: The Cuberille Method represents a 3D volume as a discrete set of voxels (parallelepipeds) where each voxel is either fully occupied or empty, creating a "hollow polygonal shell" approximation of the object's surface. It solves the problem of visualizing segmented volumetric data by projecting these discrete voxel faces to the image plane using standard rasterization techniques. Unlike smooth surface extraction methods (e.g., Marching Cubes), it preserves the blocky, discrete nature of the input data, making it suitable for applications where voxel integrity is paramount or where the data is inherently binary. It differs from Greedy Meshing by not merging adjacent coplanar faces into larger quads, resulting in a higher polygon count but simpler generation logic. Inputs: A 3D binary array (voxel grid) where 1 indicates an occupied voxel and 0 indicates empty space. The array is typically sorted in memory (e.g., z-order or row-major). Outputs: A rendered image of the object's surface, or a mesh of exposed voxel faces. Data Structures: 1. Binary Array: A 3D grid of bits or bytes. Let V(x,y,z) be the value at coordinates (x,y,z). 2. Octree (Optional): A hierarchical structure where nodes represent 2 \times 2 \times 2 blocks of voxels. A node is marked "empty" if all 8 children are 0, and "full" if all are 1. This is used to accelerate traversal for sparse data. Steps: 1. Segmentation/Thresholding: If the input is not binary, apply a threshold or connectivity algorithm (e.g., Lorenson et al.) to isolate the object of interest. Generate a binary array V where V{ijk} = 1 if the voxel belongs to the object, else 0. 2. Face Identification: For each occupied voxel V{ijk}=1, determine which of its 6 faces are exposed. A face is exposed if the adjacent voxel in that direction is empty (0) or out of bounds. The 6 faces correspond to normals: \pm \hat{x}, \pm \hat{y}, \pm \hat{z}. 3. Rendering (Rasterization): Z-Buffer Approach: Render each exposed face as a quad (or two triangles) into a depth buffer. Since voxels are axis-aligned, face culling can be applied: only 3 of the 6 faces are visible from any single viewpoint. Painter's Algorithm Approach: If the data is stored in a back-to-front sorted order (e.g., by z-coordinate), faces can be rendered in that order without a z-buffer, leveraging the "Painter's algorithm". This avoids depth testing overhead but requires pre-sorting or a specific memory layout. 4. Shading: Assign normals to faces based on their orientation (only 6 possible normal vectors: \pm \hat{x}, \pm \hat{y}, \pm \hat{z}). Apply lighting models. Note that naive polyhedral shading causes aliasing/banding due to the discrete normals. Mitigation: Apply low-pass filtering to the final image to reduce banding artifacts, at the cost of resolution. Alternatively, use context-based normal estimation from neighboring voxels for smoother shading. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendercuberille(volume, width, height, camera): """ volume: 3D array of shape (X, Y, Z) with values 0 or 1. Returns: Image buffer. """ # Initialize image and z-buffer image = zeros((height, width, 3)) zbuffer = zeros((height, width)) # Collect all exposed faces faces = [] # Iterate over all voxels for z in range(volume.shape[2]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[0]): if volume[x, y, z] == 1: # Check 6 neighbors neighbors = [ (x+1, y, z, 1, 0, 0), # +X (x-1, y, z, -1, 0, 0), # -X (x, y+1, z, 0, 1, 0), # +Y (x, y-1, z, 0, -1, 0), # -Y (x, y, z+1, 0, 0, 1), # +Z (x, y, z-1, 0, 0, -1) # -Z ] for nx, ny, nz, nxnorm, nynorm, nznorm in neighbors: # Check if neighbor is empty or out of bounds isempty = True if 0 <= nx < volume.shape[0] and \ 0 <= ny < volume.shape[1] and \ 0 <= nz < volume.shape[2]: if volume[nx, ny, nz] == 1: isempty = False if isempty: # Face is exposed. Add to list. # Face center is at (x+0.5, y+0.5, z+0.5) # Face vertices depend on normal. faces.append({ 'center': (x + 0.5, y + 0.5, z + 0.5), 'normal': (nxnorm, nynorm, nznorm), 'voxelpos': (x, y, z) }) # Sort faces back-to-front relative to camera for Painter's algorithm # Or use Z-buffer if sorting is not feasible faces.sort(key=lambda f: dot(f['center'], camera.direction), reverse=True) for face in faces: # Project face vertices to screen space screencoords = project(face['center'], camera) # Determine if face is front-facing (optional culling) if dot(face['normal'], camera.direction) > 0: continue # Backface culling # Render face quad # Use simple shading based on normal color = applylighting(face['normal']) # Draw to image/z-buffer drawquad(screencoords, color, zbuffer) return image Parameters: Threshold: Value separating object from background. Not given in the sources. Filtering Strength: For low-pass filtering to reduce banding. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Input: Empty volume results in no output. Precision: Floating point errors in projection may cause z-fighting if using z-buffer with identical depths. Banding: Discrete normals cause visible aliasing in shading. Mitigated by filtering. A variant where 2D slices are thresholded and extruded along the axial direction by the slice-to-slice distance, then stacked. It produces a staircase-like representation and is viewed using simple geometric routines. It is less accurate than full 3D cuberille but simpler to implement for slice-based data. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as each voxel is checked for 6 neighbors. With an octree, traversal is faster for sparse data, but construction overhead exists. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the binary array. Octree storage depends on sparsity; it can be more compact for sparse data but has overhead for dense data. Performance: Fast for small volumes. Rendering speed depends on the number of exposed faces. Z-buffer approach is robust but requires depth testing. Painter's algorithm avoids depth testing but requires sorting. Strengths: Simple implementation; preserves voxel structure; fast for sparse data with octrees. Limitations: High polygon count (no face merging); aliasing/banding artifacts from discrete normals; binary decision loses sub-voxel information. When to use: When voxel-level accuracy is required, or for binary segmentation visualization. Not suitable for smooth surface visualization. The Cuberille Model was first defined by Herman et al.. The method was proposed by Herman and Liu in 1979. Meagher (1984) proposed storing the binary array as an octree to improve traversal speed for sparse data. Lorenson and Cline (1987) introduced Marching Cubes, which is often compared to Cuberille as a smoother alternative. The method is used in medical imaging for stereotactic neurosurgery planning and volume visualization. name: Greedy Meshing
head: C++ version of greedy meshing, GreedMesh, Greedy Mesher, Greedy Quad Merging, Greedy Quad Meshing, Greedy Voxel Meshing, Voxel Quad Merging
body: Greedy meshing is a surface extraction algorithm that reduces the number of rendered primitives in voxel worlds by merging adjacent coplanar faces of identical material into larger quads. It solves the problem of high vertex and triangle counts in naive per-face voxel rendering by minimizing draw calls and memory bandwidth usage. Unlike Blocky meshing which only culls hidden faces, greedy meshing actively expands visible faces into maximal rectangles. It differs from Marching Cubes by preserving the blocky aesthetic while reducing triangle count by 1.88–2.60× and geometry size by 39.5–54.5× compared to Marching Cubes on typical terrain. Inputs: A 3D voxel grid (chunk) where each voxel has an ID (material type) and potentially other attributes (e.g., ambient occlusion, color). A visibility checker to determine if a face is exposed (neighbor is air or different material). Outputs: A list of quads, each defined by an origin (x, y, z), dimensions (w, h), face orientation (normal), and material ID. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Flattened 1D array or 3D array. Index mapping: Index(x, y, z) = x + y \cdot Dx + z \cdot Dx \cdot Dy. Mask: A 2D boolean or integer array representing the current slice. For opaque merging, it stores the voxel ID if the face is visible, or 0 if not. For AO-aware merging, it may pack block ID and AO value into a single integer (e.g., bits 0-7 for ID, 8-9 for AO). Processed/Visited Mask: A boolean or bitmask array tracking which voxels have been covered by a generated quad to prevent double-counting. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an empty list of quads. Initialize a processed mask to all false/zero. 2. Axis Sweep: Iterate over the 3 principal axes (X, Y, Z). For each axis, treat it as the "normal" direction n. The other two axes are u and v. 3. Slice Loop: Iterate through each slice along the normal axis n from 0 to Dn - 1. 4. Face Detection (Mask Generation): For the current slice at n, build a 2D mask for the u-v plane. A cell (u, v) is marked as "visible" if the voxel at (u, v, n) is solid AND the neighbor in the normal direction is not solid (or is out of bounds). Note: If processing back-faces, check the neighbor in the negative normal direction. Note: If using a mergeKey function, the mask stores the key value instead of just boolean visibility. 5. Greedy Expansion: Iterate through the 2D mask in lexicographic order (e.g., row by row, left to right). If the current cell (u, v) is marked visible and not yet processed: Expand Width (w): Increment w starting at 1 while u+w < Du, the cell (u+w, v) is visible, and the material ID matches the start cell's ID. Expand Height (h): Increment h starting at 1 while v+h < Dv. For each potential h, check if all cells in the rectangle [u, u+w) \times [v, v+h) are visible and have the matching material ID. Generate Quad: Add a quad with origin (u, v, n), dimensions (w, h), normal n, and material ID to the output list. Mark Processed: Mark all cells in the rectangle [u, u+w) \times [v, v+h) as processed in the processed mask. Advance: Move u forward by w. 6. Repeat: Repeat steps 3-5 for all 6 face directions (positive and negative for each axis) if bidirectional meshing is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def greedymesh(voxels, dims, issolid, getmaterial, mergekey=None): """ voxels: 3D array or accessor function dims: (Dx, Dy, Dz) issolid: function(x, y, z) -> bool getmaterial: function(x, y, z) -> int mergekey: function(material, x, y, z) -> int (optional, default is material) """ quads = [] processed = [[False] dims[1] for in range(dims[2])] # Simplified for 2D slice # Axes: 0=X, 1=Y, 2=Z for norm in range(3): tan = (norm + 1) % 3 biTan = (norm + 2) % 3 # Iterate slices along the normal axis for sliceidx in range(dims[norm]): # Build 2D mask for this slice # Mask stores mergekey if visible, else 0 mask = [[0] dims[tan] for in range(dims[biTan])] for v in range(dims[biTan]): for u in range(dims[tan]): # Construct coordinates coords = [0, 0, 0] coords[norm] = sliceidx coords[tan] = u coords[biTan] = v # Check visibility: current is solid, neighbor in +normal is not # Note: This handles one direction. For full meshing, repeat for -normal if issolid(coords): neighborcoords = list(coords) neighborcoords[norm] += 1 if not issolid(neighborcoords): mat = getmaterial(coords) key = mergekey(mat, coords) if mergekey else mat mask[v][u] = key # Handle back-face visibility if needed by checking neighborcoords[norm] -= 1 # Greedy expansion on the 2D mask for v in range(dims[biTan]): for u in range(dims[tan]): if mask[v][u] == 0: continue currentkey = mask[v][u] w = 1 # Expand width while u + w < dims[tan] and mask[v][u + w] == currentkey: w += 1 h = 1 # Expand height while v + h < dims[biTan]: # Check if entire row segment of width w matches match = True for dx in range(w): if mask[v + h][u + dx] != currentkey: match = False break if not match: break h += 1 # Generate Quad origin = [0, 0, 0] origin[norm] = sliceidx origin[tan] = u origin[biTan] = v extent = [0, 0] extent[0] = w # tan dimension extent[1] = h # biTan dimension quads.append({ 'origin': origin, 'extent': extent, 'normal': norm, 'material': currentkey }) # Mark as processed (set mask to 0) for dy in range(h): for dx in range(w): mask[v + dy][u + dx] = 0 # Advance u u += w - 1 # Loop will increment by 1, so we compensate return quads Parameters: VOXELSIZE: Scaling factor for world coordinates. CHUNKDIM: Spatial dimension of the chunk (e.g., 16, 32). mergeKey: Function to determine merge compatibility. Default is material ID. policy: Boundary policy ("air" or "solid") determining if outer surface is emitted. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparency: Transparent faces are typically kept unit-sized (not merged) to preserve correct sorting and per-cell attributes. Ambient Occlusion (AO): Merging faces with different AO values can cause shading artifacts. Solutions include restricted merging (only merge if AO is identical) or texture atlas baking. Chunk Boundaries: Neighbor chunks must be processed or padded to ensure correct visibility checks at chunk edges. Precision: Using integer coordinates for origins and extents avoids floating-point errors in vertex generation. A CPU-based mesh generation algorithm for voxel worlds that combines adjacent faces into runs along the X and Y axes to reduce triangle count, while optimizing for generation speed over minimal triangle count. Chunked Voxel Mesh Generation with Face Culling and Quad Expansion is a surface extraction algorithm that processes a 3D voxel chunk to generate an optimized triangle mesh by merging adjacent coplanar faces of identical voxel types into larger quads. It solves the problem of high vertex and triangle counts in naive voxel rendering by reducing draw calls and memory bandwidth usage. Unlike Voxel Mesh Generation (Run-based Greedy Meshing) which may process runs linearly, this method explicitly handles chunk boundaries and neighbor dependencies to enable maximal rectangle merging across chunk edges, trading increased preparation time for significant triangle count reduction. It differs from Binary Greedy Meshing with Packed Quads by using explicit boolean visitation arrays and separate quad expansion logic rather than binary packing for the expansion phase. Binary Greedy Meshing (BGM) generates maximal axis-aligned quads from a binary voxel slice by greedily expanding horizontally from the first solid block found in each vertical run, using bitwise operations to minimize clock cycles. It treats the Signed Distance Field (SDF) or voxel grid as solid/empty, culls hidden faces, and merges co-planar visible faces into maximal rectangles drawn via instanced rendering from an 8-byte packed record. Unlike Marching Cubes which produces smooth isosurfaces, BGM preserves the blocky aesthetic while reducing triangle count by 1.88–2.60× and geometry size by 39.5–54.5× compared to Marching Cubes on typical terrain. It builds on Greedy Meshing by replacing per-voxel iteration with row-wise bitwise logic. A technique to reduce the number of triangles in voxel rendering by merging adjacent coplanar voxel faces into larger quads. It differs from standard greedy meshing by comparing voxel faces (which may have varying attributes like type, transparency, or lighting) rather than just voxel existence. Extends 2D greedy meshing to three dimensions by extracting 2D slices from the 3D voxel grid along each axis and processing them with the 2D algorithm. #### SBUG Mesh Entry Point Definition: An entry point implementation for greedy meshing in a specific engine context. Steps: Define MAXFACEQUADS as (sizet)CS CS CS. Initialize outputs[6] and begins[6] arrays. For each face 0-5, if md.vertices[face].size() is less than MAXFACEQUADS, resize it to MAXFACEQUADS. Set begins[face] and outputs[face] to md.vertices[face].data(). Call meshfacecolumnsallxslices(voxels, opaquemask, md, outputs) to perform the greedy meshing. Reset md.vertexcount to 0. For each face 0-5, calculate md.facevertexcounts[face] as (sizet)(outputs[face] - begins[face]) and add it to md.vertexcount. Return md.vertexcount. #### 4D Greedy Meshing Definition: Greedy meshing is applied to the 4D voxel world to merge coplanar faces. Although neighboring cells present polygons at different angles in slice space, the preimage of a convex set under a linear map (to4d) is convex. Therefore, a box of cells presents one convex polygon at any angle, allowing greedy meshing to work if it sweeps in lattice space (4D) rather than slice space (3D). Pitfall: Re-merging in a third dimension recovers only about 1% of quads at any cut, contrary to earlier design notes claiming no further merging was possible. The turned hyperplane meets more cells, each bringing its own edges, limiting further merging. Performance: Greedy meshing reduction ratios compared to naive per-face meshing for different cut configurations: Flat cut: 1.41x (before merging 2.47x); ZW only: 1.96x (before 3.45x); Both planes: 3.05x (before 4.97x); Hard tilt: 3.58x (before 4.98x). Overall performance: Greedy meshing produces 5.3x fewer triangles than naive per-face meshing (CI gated at 4.5x minimum). #### Integrating AO with Greedy Meshing Definition: Strategies to handle the conflict between ambient occlusion variation across individual block boundaries and the merging of coplanar, adjacent voxel faces into larger single quads in greedy meshing. Steps: 1. Restricted Merging: Only merge adjacent faces if both their block types and their calculated per-vertex AO values are identical. This preserves accurate vertex-based shading at the cost of a slightly higher polygon count. 2. Texture Atlas Baking: Instead of baking AO into vertex colors, generate or slice a small, low-resolution texture atlas containing pre-computed AO gradients, applying UVs from the merged quad across the continuous surface. 3. Fragment-Shader Reconstruction: Pass unmerged face bounds as custom vertex attributes or instanced data, allowing the fragment shader to mathematically calculate edge proximity and distance-to-corner shading analytically. #### VBO Indexing Optimization Steps: After greedy meshing, VBO indexing is applied to reduce vertex count from 6 vertices per face to 4 vertices per face. Comparison: This optimization further reduces the quad count by 1/3 compared to the greedy meshing output alone. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the chunk, as each voxel is visited a constant number of times (once per axis/slice). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the voxel grid and O(Du \cdot Dv) for the 2D mask per slice. Measured Performance: On a 5x1x5 chunk scene, greedy meshing reduced the number of quads drawn by an average of 60% compared to naive face culling, with further VBO indexing reducing it by another 1/3. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with chunk size. Larger chunks reduce the number of draw calls but increase memory usage and meshing time per chunk. Strengths: Significantly reduces draw calls and vertex count (10-20x reduction compared to naive per-face rendering). Simple to implement on CPU. Limitations: Not optimal for highly complex or organic shapes where Marching Cubes might be preferred. Merging can obscure fine details if not careful with material boundaries. When to Use: Blocky voxel worlds (e.g., Minecraft-like) where performance is critical and aesthetic allows for large quads. When Not to Use: Smooth terrain, complex organic shapes, or when per-vertex attributes (like AO) vary significantly across adjacent faces and cannot be merged. Greedy meshing was popularized by Mikola Lysenko in a 2012 article on 0fps.net. It is a technique used to optimize the rendering of voxel-based graphics by merging adjacent voxels (or 'blocks') into larger cuboids, thereby reducing the complexity of the mesh. The algorithm is described as very good, somewhat simple, and very fast to generate if done right. It has been implemented in various engines and languages, including C++, JavaScript, Rust, and Python.
