name: Frequency Domain Directional Shading
head: Frequency domain shading, Gradient moment shading, Gradient-based frequency shading, Hemispherical light source shading, Nusselt's analog shading
body:
Frequency Domain Directional Shading is a local illumination technique for volume rendering that computes diffuse shading entirely in the frequency domain, avoiding spatial domain differentiation. It solves the problem of applying directional lighting cues to volume data without the computational cost or nonlinearity issues of spatial domain methods. Unlike Simplified Phong Lighting Model and Lambert Shading with Shadow Rays, which operate in the spatial domain or require shadow rays, this method leverages the property that spatial differentiation corresponds to multiplication by a linear ramp in the frequency domain. It differs from Gradient-based Shading with Phase Functions by using a hemispherical light source model to maintain linearity, enabling efficient frequency domain computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Premultiplied volume data f(x) m(x), where f(x) is the density and m(x) is the opacity mask. Input: Light direction vector L (unit vector). Input: Interpolation filter H(s). Output: Shaded projection slice I(x). Data Structures: Volume data: 3D array of complex numbers representing the Fourier transform of the premultiplied volume. Gradient magnitude spectrum: Fourier transform of |
abla f(x)| m(x). Frequency coordinates: 3D grid of frequency vectors s = [sx, sy, sz]. Steps: 1. Compute Gradient Magnitude Spectrum: Compute the gradient magnitude |
abla f(x)| in the spatial domain from the volume data f(x). Multiply by the opacity mask m(x) to get |
abla f(x)| m(x). Compute the 3D Fourier Transform to obtain F\{|
abla f(x)| m(x)\}. Note: There is no simple frequency domain representation for gradient magnitude, so this requires a separate volume extraction. 2. Reconstruct Pure Spectrum: Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of the premultiplied volume f(x) m(x) to get F\{f(x) m(x)\}. Apply the interpolation filter H(s) to reconstruct the pure spectrum of f(x). This step compensates for the filter response during slice extraction. 3. Compute First Moment for Directional Shading: The directional shading term involves the gradient 
abla f(x). By the derivative theorem, the gradient in the spatial domain corresponds to the first moment in the frequency domain. Multiply the pure spectrum F\{f(x)\} by i \pi s (where s is the frequency vector) to obtain the spectrum of the gradient 
abla f(x). Specifically, the term 
abla f(x) \cdot L is computed by multiplying the spectrum by i \pi (s \cdot L). 4. Combine Shading Terms: The hemispherical light source model provides a linear diffuse term: Ei = L{dif}  rac{1}{2} (1 + N \cdot L). For volumes, the normal N is approximated by the normalized gradient direction, but the model uses the gradient magnitude |
abla f(x)| and the gradient vector 
abla f(x) directly. The shaded contribution is computed as: C{dif} L{dif}  rac{1}{2} \left( |
abla f(x)| + (
abla f(x) \cdot L) ight) In the frequency domain, this corresponds to combining the spectrum of |
abla f(x)| m(x) and the moment term of F\{f(x)\}. The ambient term C{amb} L{amb} f(x) is added separately. 5. Slice Extraction: Perform slice extraction (inverse Fourier transform) on the combined frequency domain shading terms to obtain the spatial slice. The method operates entirely in the frequency domain and requires computations only on the plane of the slice being extracted. Formulas: Hemispherical irradiance: Ei = L{dif}  rac{1}{2} (1 + N \cdot L). Volume diffuse term: C{dif} L{dif}  rac{1}{2} (|
abla f(x)| + (
abla f(x) \cdot L)). Frequency domain differentiation: Multiplication by i \pi s in frequency domain equals differentiation in spatial domain. Parameters: Light direction L: Usually set perpendicular to the view vector V to maximize shading effect and eliminate the adjustment term in combined depth cueing/shading. C{dif}: Diffuse color constant. L{dif}: Directional light intensity constant. C{amb}: Ambient color constant. L{amb}: Ambient light intensity constant. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Magnitude Computation: The gradient magnitude |
abla f(x)| cannot be computed simply in the frequency domain, requiring a second spectrum F\{|
abla f(x)| m(x)\} and thus two slice extractions from two volumes. Negative Values: A linear shading equation such as C{amb} L{amb} f(x) + C{dif} L{dif} 
abla f(x) can be derived but requires restricting the upper bound of C{dif} to avoid negative values, which restricts the shading effect. Sine Wave Depth Cueing: If depth cueing is implemented as a sine wave, the filter H' requires shifting H and adding three copies with complex weights, increasing filter kernel size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def frequencydomaindirectionalshading(volumedata, lightdirection, viewdirection, interpolationfilter): """ Compute directional shading in the frequency domain. Args: volumedata: 3D array of complex numbers representing F{f(x) m(x)} lightdirection: Unit vector L viewdirection: Unit vector V interpolationfilter: Function H(s) returning filter value at frequency s Returns: shadedslice: 2D array of real numbers for the extracted slice """ # Step 1: Compute gradient magnitude spectrum # Gradient magnitude cannot be computed simply in frequency domain, requiring a second spectrum spatialvolume = inversefouriertransform(volumedata) gradientmagnitudespatial = computegradientmagnitude(spatialvolume) gradientmagnitudespectrum = fouriertransform(gradientmagnitudespatial) # Step 2: Reconstruct pure spectrum # Apply interpolation filter H(s) to reconstruct pure spectrum of f(x) freqgrid = generatefrequencygrid(volumedata.shape) purespectrum = volumedata interpolationfilter(freqgrid) # Step 3: Compute first moment for directional shading # Multiply spectrum by i pi s to apply directional shading # The term (grad f. L) corresponds to multiplying the spectrum by i pi (s. L) directionalcomponentspectrum = purespectrum (1j np.pi np.dot(freqgrid, lightdirection)) # Step 4: Combine shading terms # Combine gradient magnitude spectrum and directional component spectrum shadedspectrum = gradientmagnitudespectrum + directionalcomponentspectrum # Step 5: Slice extraction # Perform slice extraction (inverse Fourier transform) on the combined frequency domain terms shadedspatial = inversefouriertransform(shadedspectrum) # Add ambient term (simplified, assuming ambient is just f(x)) ambientspatial = inversefouriertransform(volumedata) finalslice = ambientspatial + shadedspatial return finalslice def fouriertransform(data): """Compute 3D discrete Fourier transform.""" return np.fft.fftn(data) def inversefouriertransform(data): """Compute 3D inverse discrete Fourier transform.""" return np.fft.ifftn(data).real def computegradientmagnitude(spatialdata): """Compute gradient magnitude |∇f(x)| in spatial domain.""" # Compute partial derivatives along each axis dx = np.gradient(spatialdata, axis=0) dy = np.gradient(spatialdata, axis=1) dz = np.gradient(spatialdata, axis=2) # Return magnitude return np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) def generatefrequencygrid(shape): """Generate 3D frequency coordinate grid s = [sx, sy, sz].""" sx = np.fft.fftfreq(shape[0]) sy = np.fft.fftfreq(shape[1]) sz = np.fft.fftfreq(shape[2]) return np.meshgrid(sx, sy, sz, indexing='ij') A local shading model that simulates diffuse reflection from a virtual hemisphere light source to provide directional illumination cues. It enhances shape perception by weighting volume points based on orientation relative to a light direction. Unlike standard volume rendering, it uses a hemisphere light source for directional illumination, though it remains a local approximation. It builds on Frequency Domain Directional Shading by computing directional shading in the frequency domain using an orientation field. Time Complexity: The method operates entirely in the frequency domain and requires computations only on the plane of the slice being extracted. Computing a moment incurs a few additional floating-point operations per sample on the slice, which is small relative to the convolution operations. Memory Complexity: Requires a pair of floating-point numbers for each voxel due to the wide dynamic range and complex arithmetic of Fourier transforms. Additionally, it requires a second spectrum for the gradient magnitude, effectively doubling the memory requirement for the volume data during processing. Measured Performance: The additional expense of computing the moment is small relative to the convolution operations. However, the need for two slice extractions (one for the volume and one for the gradient magnitude) increases the overall computational cost. Strengths: Avoids the nonlinearity of the MAX function used in Lambertian reflection, allowing computation entirely in the frequency domain. Efficient for large datasets as it leverages FFTs. Limitations: Requires two slice extractions due to the lack of a simple frequency domain representation for gradient magnitude. The shading effect is restricted if a linear shading equation is used to avoid negative values. When to Use: Suitable for volume rendering where directional shading cues are important and computational efficiency in the frequency domain is desired. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or when the overhead of two slice extractions is prohibitive. Origin: Developed by Takashi Totsuka and Marc Levoy. History: Presented in the paper "Frequency Domain Volume Rendering" at SIGGRAPH 1993. Development: The method builds on previous work in frequency domain volume rendering, extending it to include directional shading using a hemispherical light source model. Usage: Used in volume rendering applications where efficient directional shading is required, particularly in medical imaging and scientific visualization. name: Hemisphere Illumination
head: Directional Shading (Hemisphere Illumination), Directional Shading via Hemispherical Illumination, Frequency Domain Directional Shading (Hemisphere Illumination)
body: Hemisphere Illumination is a local shading model for volume rendering that simulates diffuse reflection from a virtual hemisphere light source to provide directional illumination cues in volume projections. It enhances the perception of shape and spatial relationships by weighting volume points based on their orientation relative to a light direction, effectively treating the volume as a collection of diffusely reflecting surfaces. Unlike standard volume rendering which often lacks explicit shading cues, this method uses a hemisphere light source to provide directional illumination, though it remains a local approximation without global occlusion. It builds on Frequency Domain Directional Shading by computing directional shading in the frequency domain using an orientation field. Inputs: Volume data \Omega(x,y,z) (albedo/density). Orientation field N(x,y,z) = (Nx, Ny, Nz), typically derived from the gradient of the volume data. Lighting direction L = (Lx, Ly, Lz), a unit vector. Source intensity Is (constant). Viewing direction V (normalized, pointing away from the eye). Outputs: Rendered image intensity I. Data Structures: The volume \Omega and orientation field N are represented in the frequency domain. Four 3D spectra are computed during precomputation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precompute(volumeomega, orientationN, sourceintensity): # Create four copies of Is Omega specx = fft3d(sourceintensity volumeomega orientationN.x) specy = fft3d(sourceintensity volumeomega orientationN.y) specz = fft3d(sourceintensity volumeomega orientationN.z) specc = fft3d(sourceintensity volumeomega) return specx, specy, specz, specc def render(specx, specy, specz, specc, viewingdirectionV, lightingdirectionL): # Extract slices along viewing direction V slicex = extractslice(specx, V) slicey = extractslice(specy, V) slicez = extractslice(specz, V) slicec = extractslice(specc, V) # Compute constant c2 c2 = pi/2 - pi/2 (L.x + L.y + L.z) # Combine slices intensity = L.x slicex + L.y slicey + L.z slicez + c2 slicec return intensity Steps: 1. Precomputation: Create four copies of the product Is \Omega(x,y,z). Multiply the first copy by Nx(x,y,z), the second by Ny(x,y,z), the third by Nz(x,y,z), and leave the fourth copy as Is \Omega(x,y,z). Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of each of the four copies to yield four 3D spectra. 2. Rendering (for a given view and light direction): Extract the relevant slices from the four 3D spectra corresponding to the viewing direction V. Compute the image intensity I using the linear combination of the extracted slices: I = Lx \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} Nx\right) Is \Omega \right] + Ly \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} Ny\right) Is \Omega \right] + Lz \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} Nz\right) Is \Omega \right] + c2 \PiV \left[ Is \Omega \right] Where: \PiV denotes the projection-slice operation along viewing direction V. c2 = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{2} (Lx + Ly + Lz). Formula Derivation Context: The weighting assigned to each point P(t) along a ray is based on the integral of the source intensity modulated by the diffuse reflection model: IP = \inta^b Is \Omega(P(t)) \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} (N(P(t)) \cdot L) \right] dt This integral is decomposed into the linear combination shown above to allow efficient computation via the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. Parameters: Light Hemisphere Direction: Typically placed on the right side of the picture, shining leftwards. This corresponds to a lighting direction L with a negative x-component in a standard right-handed coordinate system where the viewer looks down the negative z-axis or similar convention. Viewing Direction: V points away from the eye. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Padding: To avoid aliasing in the frequency domain, the input volume may need to be zero-padded. Increasing the volume width by a factor of k^2 (surrounding data with a margin of zeros of width N(k^2-1)/2) increases per-view processing time by a factor of k^2, memory by k^3, and preprocessing time by a factor of k^2. Orientation Field: The accuracy of the shading depends on the quality of the orientation field N. No Occlusion: The method does not account for occlusion between volume elements. A global illumination solution that models single-bounce light contribution from the sky by creating a virtual skybox of infinite directional lights and sampling it over the hemisphere directed away from the surface normal. Unlike typical raster renderers that model the sky as one or more directional lights (causing inaccurate shadowing and dark scenes), this method provides accurate shadowing and illumination by integrating radiance over the hemisphere. Time Complexity: Preprocessing time is proportional to the size of the zero-padded volume. Per-view processing time increases with the amount of zero padding. Memory Complexity: Memory requirements increase with the size of the zero-padded volume. Strengths: Provides strong directional shading cues that enhance shape perception and spatial relationships in volume data. Computed efficiently in the frequency domain via 3D Fourier transforms. Limitations: Does not model occlusion or global illumination effects like inter-reflections. Accuracy depends on the quality of the orientation field. When to Use: When directional shading cues are needed to improve shape perception in volume renderings, and computational efficiency is important. When Not to Use: When accurate shadows, occlusion, or global illumination effects are required. The method was described in the context of volume rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. It was developed to generate realistically shaded renderings of volume data by simulating diffuse reflection from a hemisphere light source. The approach leverages the efficiency of frequency domain computations to apply complex shading models to volume data. name: Global Illumination via Hemisphere Sampling
head: Diffuse GI, Sky GI
body: A global illumination solution that models single-bounce light contribution from the sky by creating a virtual skybox of infinite directional lights and sampling it over the hemisphere directed away from the surface normal. Unlike typical raster renderers that model the sky as one or more directional lights (causing inaccurate shadowing and dark scenes), this method provides accurate shadowing and illumination by integrating radiance over the hemisphere. Inputs: Surface position p, surface normal n, surface roughness \alpha (for specular variant), temporal samples temporal\x, temporal\y \in [0, 1], sky radiance function s{sky}(\omegai), shadow hardness parameter k. Outputs: Diffuse Global Illumination color contribution GI{diffuse} and/or Specular Global Illumination color contribution GI{specular}. Data Structures: temporalx: Float, temporal sample X coordinate. temporaly: Float, temporal sample Y coordinate. n: Normalized 3D vector, surface normal. T: 3D vector, tangent basis vector. B: 3D vector, bitangent basis vector. H: 3D vector, hemisphere sample direction in local space. omegai: 3D vector, world-space sample direction. Parameters: Shadow hardness k=3 for diffuse GI. Shadow hardness k = 3 + 1/\alpha for specular GI. Steps: 1. Construct Tangent Basis: Calculate the tangent vector T to avoid degeneracy when the normal is aligned with the Z-axis: T = \begin{cases} \{0, 0, 1\} \times n & \text{if } |nz| < 0.999 \\ \{1, 0, 0\} \times n & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Calculate the bitangent B: B = n \times T 2. Sample Direction: Depending on the variant (Diffuse or Specular), compute the sample direction \omegai using the respective sampling function. For Diffuse GI (Uniform Hemisphere Sampling): Compute local hemisphere coordinates H: \phi = 2\pi \cdot temporal\x \theta = 0.5\pi \cdot temporal\y H = \{\cos\phi \sin\theta, \sin\phi \sin\theta, \cos\theta\} Transform to world space: \omegai = \{T, B, n\} \cdot H For Specular GI (GGX Importance Sampling): Compute \cos\theta based on roughness \alpha: \cos\theta = \frac{1 - temporal\x}{1 + (\alpha^2 - 1) temporal\y} Derive \sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta}. Compute \phi = 2\pi \cdot temporal\x. Compute local hemisphere coordinates H: H = \{\cos\phi \sin\theta, \sin\phi \sin\theta, \cos\theta\} Transform to world space: \omegai = \{T, B, n\} \cdot H 3. Calculate Soft Shadow: Compute the soft shadow term SoftMarch(p, \omegai, k). 4. Compute Radiance Contribution: Diffuse GI: GI{diffuse} = \frac{kd c}{\pi} \int{\Omega} s{sky}(\omegai) SoftMarch(p, \omegai, 3) (n \cdot \omegai) d\omegai In practice, this is approximated by the single sample: GI{diffuse} \approx \frac{kd c}{\pi} s{sky}(\omegai) SoftMarch(p, \omegai, 3) (n \cdot \omegai) where kd is the diffuse coefficient and c is a scaling constant. Specular GI: GI{specular} = ks \int{\Omega} \frac{D F G}{4 (\omegao \cdot n) (\omegai \cdot n)} s{sky}(\omegai) SoftMarch(p, \omegai, 3 + \frac{1}{\alpha}) (n \cdot \omegai) d\omegai In practice, approximated by the single sample: GI{specular} \approx ks \frac{D F G}{4 (\omegao \cdot n) (\omegai \cdot n)} s{sky}(\omegai) SoftMarch(p, \omegai, 3 + \frac{1}{\alpha}) (n \cdot \omegai) where ks is the specular coefficient, D, F, G are Cook-Torrance BRDF terms, and \omegao is the view direction. 5. Accumulate: Add GI{diffuse} to the pixel color from the first shading pass. Add GI{specular} to the pixel color computed from the first shading pass and diffuse GI pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehemispheregi(p, n, alpha, temporalx, temporaly, ssky, k, kd, c, ks, D, F, G, wo): # 1. Construct Tangent Basis if abs(n[2]) < 0.999: T = cross([0, 0, 1], n) else: T = cross([1, 0, 0], n) B = cross(n, T) # 2. Sample Direction (Diffuse variant shown; swap logic for Specular) phi = 2 math.pi temporalx theta = 0.5 math.pi temporaly costheta = math.cos(theta) sintheta = math.sin(theta) H = [math.cos(phi) sintheta, math.sin(phi) sintheta, costheta] omegai = [dot(T, H), dot(B, H), dot(n, H)] # 3. Calculate Soft Shadow # SoftMarch(p, w, k): Shadow ray march. Not given in the sources. shadow = SoftMarch(p, omegai, k) # 4. Compute Radiance Contribution ndotw = dot(n, omegai) diffuseterm = (kd c / math.pi) ssky(omegai) shadow ndotw # Specular variant uses different k and Cook-Torrance terms specularterm = ks (D F G) / (4 dot(wo, n) dot(omegai, n)) ssky(omegai) shadow ndotw return diffuseterm, specularterm Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If |nz| \ge 0.999, the standard cross product for T might be degenerate or unstable; the code switches to using the X-axis vector \{1, 0, 0\} for the cross product. Using only one sample per frame produces a checkerboard pattern without Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA). Relies on TAA for accurate results because it uses Monte Carlo integration over time with limited samples. A reflection technique that samples the skybox using a specular lobe distribution based on the Cook-Torrance specular term and surface roughness \alpha, instead of uniform hemisphere sampling. It differs from diffuse GI by using a specular lobe distribution (GGX) dependent on roughness \alpha rather than uniform hemisphere sampling. It relies on Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) for accurate results because it uses Monte Carlo integration over time with limited samples. Complexity: Computationally expensive to integrate fully over the hemisphere, so it relies on single-sample Monte Carlo integration per frame. Performance: Requires Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) to converge to an accurate image within a few frames; without TAA, the result is noisy (checkerboard pattern). Strengths: Provides accurate shadowing and illumination from the sky, avoiding the dark scenes and inaccurate shadows caused by modeling the sky as simple directional lights in typical raster renderers. Limitations: Single-sample approach introduces noise without temporal accumulation; dependent on TAA stability. This method was implemented in a real-time renderer using CUDA, aiming to achieve visual fidelity comparable to offline high-fidelity techniques like ray tracing, while surpassing typical real-time raster renderers in quality. It addresses the limitation of engines like the Source Engine, which model the sky as directional lights (sun and sky lights) that fail to contribute accurate shadowing. The approach was evaluated at 1280 × 720 on an RTX 2080 Super, comparing against Blender Cycles and UE4. name: Simplified Phong Lighting Model
head: Phong Illumination, Phong Lighting Model, Phong Reflection Model, Phong Illumination Model
body:
The Simplified Phong Lighting Model is a local illumination technique adapted for volume rendering to enhance the perception of 3D structure by simulating surface-like shading on scalar field data. It solves the problem of flat, unlit volume visualization by calculating diffuse and specular contributions based on the gradient of the volume data, which serves as an approximation of the surface normal. Unlike physically based light transport methods, it is a heuristic shading model that modulates the existing pixel color or volume samples to create highlights and shadows, distinguishing itself from its siblings by typically relying on a single light source and explicit vector math rather than precomputed spectral expansions or complex phase functions. The method operates by iterating along rays cast through the volume data. For each ray, it identifies the first significant voxel where the volume value exceeds a threshold, computes the local surface normal from the gradient of the scalar field, and applies the Phong reflection model to calculate the final color contribution. Inputs: volume: A 3D scalar field (voxel grid) containing density or intensity values. viewmatrix: A 4x4 matrix defining the camera orientation and projection, used to derive view vectors. lightposition: The 3D position of the light source in world or texture space. lightintensity: The color and intensity of the light source. ambientlight: The global ambient light color/intensity. materialproperties: Reflectance coefficients for ambient (ka), diffuse (kd), and specular (ks) lighting, and the shininess exponent (n or \alpha). Outputs: color: The final RGB color value for the pixel, combining ambient, diffuse, and specular components. Voxel: A single element in the volume grid, accessed via integer coordinates (x, y, z). Vector: 3D floating-point vectors for normals (N), light direction (L), view direction (V or r), and reflection direction (R or v). Material: A structure or set of parameters holding ka, kd, ks, and shininess. 1. Initialization: Initialize the output color to the ambient component: C = ka \cdot Ia. Initialize a flag surfacefound to False. Initialize the normal vector N to zero. 2. Ray Casting and Surface Detection: Iterate along the ray from the camera plane into the volume. The iteration step size k can be fixed (e.g., 50) for performance or 1 for accuracy. For each step, calculate the voxel coordinates (x, y, z) using the view vector and pixel base position. Sample the voxel value v at (x, y, z). If v > 1 (or a defined threshold) and surfacefound is False: Set surfacefound to True. Compute the gradient 
abla f = ( rac{\partial f}{\partial x},  rac{\partial f}{\partial y},  rac{\partial f}{\partial z}) at the current coordinates. Calculate the magnitude |
abla f|. Normalize the gradient to obtain the surface normal: N =  rac{
abla f}{|
abla f|}. Break the loop or continue for compositing, depending on the specific implementation (e.g., ray marching vs. first-hit). 3. Vector Calculation: Calculate the normalized light direction vector L: L = 	ext{normalize}(	ext{light\position} - 	ext{point}). Calculate the normalized view direction vector V (from point to eye): V = 	ext{normalize}(	ext{eye\position} - 	ext{point}). Note: Some implementations use the variable name r for the view vector and v for the reflection vector, which is non-standard but functionally equivalent if consistent. 4. Diffuse Calculation: Compute the dot product between the normal and light direction: dot{LN} = N \cdot L. Apply the facing parameter: If dot{LN} < 0, the surface is facing away from the light. Otherwise, calculate the diffuse factor: diffuse actor = \max(dot{LN}, 0.0). Calculate the diffuse color contribution: C{diffuse} = kd \cdot Il \cdot diffuse actor. 5. Specular Calculation: Calculate the reflection vector R of the light direction around the normal: R = 	ext{reflect}(-L, N). Compute the dot product between the view direction and the reflection vector: dot{RV} = V \cdot R. Apply the facing check for specular: If dot{RV} < 0, the reflection is not visible to the viewer. Otherwise, calculate the specular factor using the shininess exponent n (or \alpha): specular actor = \max(dot{RV}, 0.0)^n. Calculate the specular color contribution: C{specular} = ks \cdot Il \cdot specular actor. 6. Final Color Composition: Sum the components: C{final} = C{ambient} + C{diffuse} + C{specular}. If using a simplified shadowing approach based on the angle between normal and view (as in), multiply the existing pixel color by a shadow factor derived from N \cdot V mapped to [0, 1]. However, standard Phong models do not include self-shadowing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simplifiedphonglighting(volume, viewmatrix, lightposition, lightintensity, ambientlight, material, eyeposition): """ Computes the color for a single ray/sample point using the Simplified Phong Lighting Model. """ # 1. Ambient Component color = material['ka'] ambientlight # 2. Find Surface and Compute Normal surfacefound = False normal = None point = None imagesize = viewmatrix.shape[0] imagecenter = imagesize / 2.0 uvector = viewmatrix[0:3] vvector = viewmatrix[4:7] volumecenter = [volume.dimx / 2, volume.dimy / 2, volume.dimz / 2] # Ray casting loop with step size 50 for performance for k in range(0, imagesize, 50): voxelcoordinatex = uvector[0] (k - imagecenter) + vvector[0] (k - imagecenter) + volumecenter[0] voxelcoordinatey = uvector[1] (k - imagecenter) + vvector[1] (k - imagecenter) + volumecenter[1] voxelcoordinatez = uvector[2] (k - imagecenter) + vvector[2] (k - imagecenter) + volumecenter[2] value = volume[voxelcoordinatex, voxelcoordinatey, voxelcoordinatez] if value > 1.0 and not surfacefound: surfacefound = True point = (voxelcoordinatex, voxelcoordinatey, voxelcoordinatez) deltaf = computegradient(volume, point) magnitudef = math.sqrt(deltaf[0]2 + deltaf[1]2 + deltaf[2]2) normal = (deltaf[0] / magnitudef, deltaf[1] / magnitudef, deltaf[2] / magnitudef) break if not surfacefound or normal is None: return color # 3. Vector Calculations L = normalize(lightposition - point) V = normalize(eyeposition - point) # 4. Diffuse Component dotLN = dot(normal, L) if dotLN < 0.0: diffuse = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: diffusefactor = dotLN diffuse = material['kd'] lightintensity diffusefactor # 5. Specular Component R = reflect(-L, normal) dotRV = dot(V, R) if dotRV < 0.0: specular = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: specularfactor = pow(max(dotRV, 0.0), material['shininess']) specular = material['ks'] lightintensity specularfactor # 6. Final Color color += diffuse + specular return color Shininess (n or \alpha): Controls the size of the specular highlight. Higher values produce smaller, sharper highlights. Typical values range from 1 to 1000, depending on the desired material appearance. Light Position: Often set to a fixed world coordinate, e.g., (8, 20, 8) or (0, 20, 0). Ambient Light: Often a dim white or gray, e.g., 0.5 \cdot (1,1,1) or 0.025 \cdot (0.8, 0.8, 0.8). Light Intensity: Often set to (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) or (0.2, 0.4, 0.4). Step Size: In interactive modes, the ray marching step can be increased (e.g., 50) for performance, while production renders use 1. Self-Shadowing: Volume self-shadowing is computationally expensive and is typically ignored in this simplified model to maintain performance and clarity. Gradient Noise: The normal vector derived from the gradient can be noisy in low-resolution or noisy volume data, leading to flickering specular highlights. Facing Direction: The model correctly handles back-facing surfaces by returning zero diffuse/specular contribution when N \cdot L < 0. Reflection Visibility: Specular highlights are only visible if the reflection vector points towards the viewer (V \cdot R > 0). Extends the Fourier Projection-Slice technique to support Phong specular reflections by expanding the specular term into a polynomial, allowing evaluation via precomputed Fourier spectra without per-voxel shading. Applies the Phong model to volume data projected onto 2D/3D textures, leveraging hardware-accelerated texture lookups and blending for interactive performance on older hardware. The standard local illumination model applied to volume samples, using the gradient as the normal vector and explicit vector math for reflection and view directions. Uses the half-vector between light and view directions for specular calculation, avoiding the expensive reflection vector calculation and providing smoother lobes. Combines Blinn-Phong shading with depth cueing to enhance depth perception and simulate atmospheric perspective by fading distant voxels. This variant integrates the Simplified Phong Lighting Model with texture mapping and environment mapping. It utilizes built-in trilinear texture interpolation to smoothly reconstruct normal vectors from attribute maps, ensuring continuous per-fragment normals. These normals are then used for Phong shading, as well as for implementing reflection and refraction via cube mapping. The final fragment color is computed by summing contributions from lighting, texture mapping, reflectance mapping, and refraction mapping in a single rendering pass, avoiding multiple render targets or additional blending passes. Performance: Fast and suitable for real-time or interactive visualization, especially when using larger step sizes or hardware-accelerated texture lookups. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally efficient, enhances visual perception of 3D structure, and works well with scalar field data. Limitations: Occlusion shadows are typically ignored to maintain performance and clarity. Gradient-derived normals can be noisy in low-resolution data. When to Use: Interactive visualization and non-photorealistic rendering where conveying information is prioritized over photographic realism. When Not to Use: Scientific visualization requiring quantitative accuracy, or scenes with complex lighting interactions like shadows and reflections. The Phong Lighting Model was originally developed by Bui Tuong Phong for polygonal surfaces. Its application to volume rendering emerged as a heuristic to enhance the visual quality of scalar field data, which otherwise appears flat and unstructured. The simplified version for volumes typically involves computing the gradient of the scalar field to approximate surface normals and applying the standard Phong reflection model to these normals. This approach has been widely adopted in non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) and interactive volume visualization systems due to its simplicity and effectiveness. name: Specular Reflections via Polynomial Expansion
head: Fourier Projection-Slice Phong, Polynomial Phong Shading, Specular Reflections via Polynomial Approximation
body: This method extends the Fourier Projection-Slice volume rendering framework to handle specular highlights by analytically expanding the Phong specular term |N \cdot H|^n into a polynomial. It solves the problem of rendering shiny surfaces in participating media without the recursive overhead of ray tracing or the approximation errors of numerical integration. Unlike Simple Reflections, which uses iterative raymarching, this approach relies on precomputed spectra and a linear combination of Fourier projections. It builds on Simplified Phong Lighting Model by adapting its local illumination term to the frequency domain. Inputs: Volume data I\Omega(x,y,z). Surface normals N(x,y,z) (or derived from volume gradients). Light direction L and view direction V. Specular exponent n (integer). Outputs: Rendered image intensity I. Data Structures: Precomputed Spectra: A set of 3D Fourier transforms of the volume data filtered by specific polynomial basis functions. The count K is determined by the multinomial theorem. Spectral Slices: 2D slices extracted from the 3D Fourier volume along the viewing direction V for per-view rendering. Steps: 1. Polynomial Expansion: Expand the term (N \cdot H)^n into a sum of monomials using the multinomial theorem. Define vectors Hn and Nn containing the directional factors and coefficients from the expansion. 2. Integral Formulation: The specular contribution along a viewing ray P(t) from t=a to t=b is given by: IP = \inta^b I\Omega(P(t)) \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} (N(P(t)) \cdot H)^n \right] dt The \frac{\pi}{2} constants implement hemispherical illumination to avoid the absolute value operator in |N \cdot H|^n. 3. Fourier Projection: Apply the Fourier projection-slice theorem to convert the integral into a linear combination of projections. The output image is: I = Hn \cdot \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} Nn(x,y,z)\right) I\Omega(x,y,z) \right] + c4 \PiV [I\Omega(x,y,z)] where \PiV denotes the projection operator along view direction V, and c4 is a suitable constant accounting for the polynomial's constant term. 4. Per-View Rendering: Extract the required 2D slices from the precomputed 3D spectra corresponding to the current view direction V. Compute the inverse Fourier transform on each slice to obtain spatial domain projections. Weight the projections by the components of Hn and sum them to produce the final image intensity. Parameters: n: Specular exponent. Typical value is n=10. H: Halfway vector, H = \frac{L+V}{\|L+V\|}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and Memory: The number of spectra grows rapidly with n. For n=10, 286 spectra are required. This leads to significant memory usage and slower rendering compared to conventional volume rendering. Degenerate Input: If N or H are undefined at boundaries or in homogeneous regions, the polynomial expansion may fail. Ensure normals are normalized and handle zero-length vectors by clamping or using a default normal. Hemispherical Illumination: The \frac{\pi}{2} constants assume a specific hemispherical illumination model. Deviations from this assumption require adjustment of the constant terms. Polynomial Depth Cueing is an adaptation of the specular reflection method to provide non-linear depth cueing (e.g., inverse square law falloff) by replacing the normal N and halfway vector H with the depth vector D and view vector V in the polynomial expansion. It is chosen when linear attenuation is insufficient to disambiguate depth in scenes with high depth complexity. For an inverse square law falloff, the term (D \cdot V)^2 is used, requiring 10 slices from 10 precomputed spectra. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of precomputed spectra, which is determined by the multinomial theorem for the exponent n. For n=10, 286 spectra are needed. Memory Complexity: Requires storing K 3D Fourier volumes, where K is the number of spectra. Measured Performance: The method is slower than conventional volume rendering due to the large number of spectra required, even for very large volumes. Strengths: Analytical evaluation of specular highlights; no recursive ray tracing; compatible with the Fourier projection-slice framework. Limitations: High memory and computational cost for large n; limited to polynomial approximations of the specular term. When to use: When analytical specular highlights are needed in a Fourier-based volume rendering pipeline and memory is not a constraint. When not to use: For real-time applications or when n is very large, due to the exponential growth in required spectra. The method originates from the work on Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, specifically in the context of extending the technique to handle complex lighting models like Phong shading. It was developed to allow for the integration of local illumination effects, such as specular reflections, into the frequency-domain volume rendering framework. The approach leverages the linearity of the Fourier transform to decompose the non-linear Phong term into a sum of linear terms. name: Simple Reflections
head: Iterative Specular Reflections
body: Simple Reflections is a local illumination technique that approximates specular highlights by raymarching along the geometric reflection vector at a surface hit point and blending the resulting color with the base surface color. It calculates a simple reflection by raymarching off the surface normal and blending the result with the surface color. Unlike Specular Reflections via Polynomial Expansion, which uses polynomial expansion of the Phong term for analytical evaluation, Simple Reflections relies on iterative numerical raymarching. Inputs: color: The base surface color (RGB) at the hit point. point: The 3D coordinates of the surface hit point. direction: The incoming view direction vector (normalized). scene: The signed distance field or scene representation providing normal and raymarching queries. light: The light source definition. reflection-count: Integer, maximum number of bounces allowed (default 3). DRAW-DISTANCE: Float, maximum raymarch distance for a valid hit. Outputs: finalcolor: The blended RGB color including reflections. Data Structures: Vectors are 3-component floats (\mathbf{v} = [x, y, z]). Colors are 3-component floats in range [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Initialize state variables: p \leftarrow \text{point} d \leftarrow \text{direction} n \leftarrow \text{get-normal}(p, \text{scene}) i \leftarrow 0 \text{not-done?} \leftarrow \text{true} C{\text{out}} \leftarrow \text{color} 2. Loop while i < \text{reflection-count} AND \text{not-done?}: 1. Compute the reflection vector \mathbf{r} using the surface normal \mathbf{n} and incoming direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{d} - 2(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} 2. Raymarch from a point slightly above the surface to avoid self-intersection. Start position p{\text{start}} = p + \mathbf{n} \cdot \epsilon (implemented as above-surface-point in the source). 3. March ray in direction \mathbf{r} through the scene. Let the hit distance be distance and the hit color be hitcolor. 4. If distance < DRAW-DISTANCE: 1. Update position: p \leftarrow p + \mathbf{r} \cdot \text{distance}. 2. Update normal: n \leftarrow \text{get-normal}(p, \text{scene}). 3. Update direction: d \leftarrow \mathbf{r}. 4. Compute lightness L{\text{hit}} at the new point p. 5. Attenuate lightness by factor 0.5: l \leftarrow L{\text{hit}} / 2. 6. Blend colors. For each channel c \in \{R, G, B\}: c{\text{new}} = (c{\text{old}} + c{\text{hit}} \cdot l) \cdot 0.66 Update C{\text{out}} with these new channel values. 7. Increment bounce counter: i \leftarrow i + 1. 5. Else (ray did not hit within distance): 1. Set \text{not-done?} \leftarrow \text{false}. 3. Return C{\text{out}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simplereflections(color, point, direction, scene, light, reflectioncount=3, drawdistance=100.0): """ Computes simple iterative specular reflections. Args: color: tuple (r, g, b) base surface color. point: vec3 hit point. direction: vec3 incoming view direction. scene: object with getnormal(p) and marchray(p, d) methods. light: object with pointlightness(p, scene) method. reflectioncount: int max bounces. drawdistance: float max raymarch distance. Returns: tuple (r, g, b) final color. """ # Initialize state p = list(point) d = list(direction) n = scene.getnormal(p) i = 0 notdone = True outcolor = list(color) while i < reflectioncount and notdone: # 1. Compute reflection vector r = d - 2(d. n)n dotdn = sum(d[j] n[j] for j in range(3)) r = [d[j] - 2 dotdn n[j] for j in range(3)] # 2. Raymarch from above surface point epsilon = 1e-4 startpoint = [p[j] + n[j] epsilon for j in range(3)] # 3. March ray distance, hitcolor = scene.marchray(startpoint, r) if distance < drawdistance: # 4. Hit found p = [p[j] + r[j] distance for j in range(3)] n = scene.getnormal(p) d = r # Compute lightness and attenuate lightness = light.pointlightness(p, scene) l = lightness / 2.0 # Blend colors newcolor = [] for j in range(3): cold = outcolor[j] chit = hitcolor[j] cnew = (cold + chit l) 0.66 newcolor.append(cnew) outcolor = newcolor i += 1 else: notdone = False return tuple(outcolor) Parameters: reflection-count: Maximum number of reflection bounces allowed. Default value in code is 3. 0.66: Color blending factor applied after adding hit color to prevent overflow and maintain brightness across bounces. 0.5: Light attenuation factor applied to reflection bounces to make them appear darker. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Recursion: Prevented by checking i < reflection-count and not-done?. Self-Intersection: The raymarch starts from above-surface-point (offset by normal) to prevent the ray from immediately hitting the surface it just reflected off. Language Limitations: In languages without a break statement (e.g., Fennel), the loop counter must be incremented manually at the end of each iteration, and not-done? must be used to exit early. Color Overflow: The multiplication by 0.66 ensures that the sum of base and reflected colors does not exceed 1.0, preventing clipping artifacts. Maps reflected directions to cube map texture coordinates following OpenGL specifications. It computes reflected directions using reflecteddirections = 2 surfacenormals sum(viewdirections surfacenormals, dim=-1, keepdim=True) - viewdirections. It finds the max absolute component index and value to determine the cube face, then computes texture coordinates by dividing the reflected direction by the max absolute value. Linear mapping is used for the third coordinate, and grid coordinates are constructed for each face based on the max index and sign, stacking (u, v, faceindex) where faceindex is mapped from 0-5 to -1 to 1. The cube map is sampled using nn.functional.gridsample and the output is permuted. This variant is chosen when environment mapping is preferred over iterative raymarching for reflections. Time Complexity: O(k \cdot m), where k is the number of reflection bounces (default 3) and m is the number of steps per raymarch. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it only stores current state variables. Performance: Fast for low bounce counts. Performance degrades linearly with increased reflection-count. Strengths: Simple to implement, avoids environment maps by computing reflections via direct raymarching. Limitations: Approximate, limited by DRAW-DISTANCE. Not suitable for complex inter-reflections beyond the fixed bounce count. When to use: Real-time raymarched scenes with mirror-like surfaces. When not to use: High-fidelity rendering requiring accurate global illumination or infinite bounces. Originated in the context of raymarching signed distance fields (SDFs) for real-time graphics. The technique was popularized in blog posts and tutorials demonstrating SDF rendering with simple lighting models. It is a foundational technique for adding specular highlights to raymarched scenes without resorting to recursive ray tracing. name: Phong Shading Model for Volume Data
head: Direct Volume Rendering using Textures, Engel, Kraus & Ertl technique, Gradient-based Phong Shading, Texture Mapping Based Volume Rendering with Phong Illumination
body: This method renders 3D volume data by mapping it to 2D or 3D textures and projecting polygonal planes (oriented to the object or view) onto the screen, where a fragment shader computes Phong illumination (ambient, diffuse, specular) and alpha blending. It differs from ray-marching approaches by leveraging hardware-accelerated texture lookups and fixed-function or early programmable pipeline blending, trading physical light transport accuracy for interactive performance on older hardware. It builds on Simplified Phong Lighting Model by applying the Phong reflection model directly to volume samples accessed via texture coordinates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset stored in a sampler3D texture unit bound to TEXUNIT0. Input: Texture coordinates (texPos0) for the polygon vertices from TEXCOORD0. Input: Lighting parameters: light position, eye position, light color, and reflection coefficients. Output: A 4D color value (OUT) representing the final fragment color and alpha. Data Structures: sampler3D samplerTex0: Bound to TEXUNIT0, holding the volume data. float4 texPos0: Input texture coordinate from TEXCOORD0. float4 OUT: Output color, initialized to white with alpha 1.0. Parameters: globalAmbient: Uniform float3 for global ambient light color. lightColor: Uniform float3 for the light source color. lightPosition: Uniform float3 for the light source position. eyePosition: Uniform float3 for the camera/eye position. Ka: Uniform float3 for the ambient reflection coefficient. Kd: Uniform float3 for the diffuse reflection coefficient. Ks: Uniform float3 for the specular reflection coefficient. shininess: Uniform float for the specular exponent. Steps: 1. Initialize Output: Set OUT to (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0). 2. Sample Volume: Sample the 3D texture at texPos0 using samplerTex0 to obtain texvalue. 3. Extract Alpha: Set OUT.a to the alpha component of texvalue. 4. Compute Normal: Compute the surface normal by expanding the RGB components of texvalue using expand(v) = (v - 0.5) 2, which maps the [0, 1] range to [-1, 1]. This assumes the volume data's RGB channels store pre-computed surface normals or a representation that can be linearly mapped to normal space. 5. Lighting Calculation (Conditional): If OUT.a > 0: a. Ambient: Compute ambient lighting: ambient = lightColor Ka. b. Halfway Vector: Compute the normalized halfway vector between the light and the eye: H = normalize(lightPosition - eyePosition). c. Diffuse: Compute diffuse lighting using diffuse = max(dot(lightPosition, normal), 0) Kd lightColor. d. Specular: Compute specular lighting using the Blinn-Phong approximation: specular = pow(dot(H, normal), shininess) Ks. e. Combine: Set OUT.rgb to the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular components. 6. Return: Return OUT. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def expand(v: Vector3) -> Vector3: """Maps [0,1] range to [-1,1] range for normal extraction.""" return (v - 0.5) 2.0 def main(texPos0: Vector4, globalAmbient: Vector3, lightColor: Vector3, lightPosition: Vector3, eyePosition: Vector3, Ka: Vector3, Kd: Vector3, Ks: Vector3, shininess: float, samplerTex0: Texture3D) -> Vector4: # 1. Initialize output OUT = Vector4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # 2. Sample volume data # Standard 3D texture fetch with trilinear interpolation texvalue = samplerTex0.fetch(texPos0.xyz) # 3. Extract alpha OUT.a = texvalue.a # 4. Compute normal from RGB components normal = expand(texvalue.rgb) # 5. Lighting calculation if alpha is non-zero if OUT.a > 0: # Ambient component ambient = lightColor Ka # Halfway vector halfway = normalize(lightPosition - eyePosition) # Diffuse component # Note: Source code uses lightPosition directly in dot product, # which is a specific implementation detail deviating from standard Phong. diffuse = max(dot(lightPosition, normal), 0.0) Kd lightColor # Specular component (Blinn-Phong) specular = pow(dot(halfway, normal), shininess) Ks # Combine OUT.rgb = ambient + diffuse + specular return OUT Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Alpha: If OUT.a is 0, the lighting calculation is skipped, and OUT remains white (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) with alpha 0. If alpha blending is used without proper alpha testing or if the background is not black, this results in white fragments being blended into the image. Normal Interpretation: The method assumes the RGB components of the volume data represent surface normals. If the volume data represents scalar density, this approach will produce incorrect lighting unless the RGB channels are explicitly pre-computed as normals. Light Position Usage: The diffuse term uses lightPosition directly in the dot product instead of the normalized light direction vector \mathbf{L}. This is a specific implementation detail of the cited source and deviates from the standard Phong model definition. Ray Marching Incompatibility: This method projects polygonal planes and computes lighting per-fragment via texture sampling; it does not traverse rays through volume cells. Test cases expecting ray-marching behavior (e.g., step-based traversal, front-to-back compositing) will fail because the algorithm operates on a fundamentally different rendering primitive. Volume Shading Modes are a set of three shading strategies applied during volume ray marching to compute lighting and shadows for each sample along a ray. They extend the Phong Shading Model for Volume Data by providing specific heuristics for handling illumination in participating media, distinguishing themselves through their approach to gradient estimation and shadow accumulation. A shading technique that modulates intensity by the strength of the local gradient raised to a power, similar to Phong shading in polygon rendering. It calculates the absolute value of the derivative (1D gradient) of the input signal, raises the gradient magnitude to a power to accentuate regions of rapid change, and multiplies the original input signal by the raised gradient result to select regions of rapid change. The exponent controls highlight width, where higher powers narrow the highlight and introduce more high frequencies. The gradient operator acts as a high-pass filter (Fourier transform j\omega) that enhances high frequencies, which can cause aliasing during resampling if not filtered. Performance: The technique using fragment shaders (Cg) results in lower performance compared to using the fixed-function pipeline of OpenGL. Texture Orientation: 3D textures oriented to the view plane have substantially lower performance than those oriented to the object plane. Texture Access: 3D texture accesses are slower than 2D texture accesses due to irregular memory access patterns. Alpha Testing: Enabling alpha test generates more frames per second compared to disabling it. Zoom Effect: The performance of polygons oriented to the projection plane improves when the zoom increases. Measured Performance: For a "Fat" volume at zoom 1.0 in motion: OpenGL 2D Object Textures: 32-34 FPS (Alpha Test On), 23-24 FPS (Alpha Test Off). OpenGL 3D Object Textures: 15 FPS (Alpha Test On), 12-13 FPS (Alpha Test Off). OpenGL+Cg 3D View Textures: 4 FPS (Alpha Test On), 3 FPS (Alpha Test Off). Strengths: Leverages hardware texture interpolation and blending; suitable for real-time visualization on older hardware. Limitations: Does not account for light transport within the volume (scattering/absorption); performance degrades with 3D textures and view-oriented planes; requires pre-computed normals in RGB channels or specific data layout. The technique is used in the implementation described by Engel, Kraus & Ertl. It applies the Phong reflection model to volume data rendered via texture mapping, aiming to provide visual cues for shape and depth in volume rendering. The Phong model components (ambient, diffuse, specular) are adapted from polygon shading to volume samples. name: Volume Shading Modes
body: Volume Shading Modes are a set of three shading strategies applied during volume ray marching to compute lighting and shadows for each sample along a ray. They extend the Phong Shading Model for Volume Data by providing specific heuristics for handling illumination in participating media, distinguishing themselves through their approach to gradient estimation and shadow accumulation. The method operates within a ray-marching loop, transforming rays to object space, sampling the volume, computing gradients, and applying shading based on the selected mode. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin and direction in world space, volume data, transformation matrices (world-to-object, object-to-world), shading parameters (shadingScale, gradientStep), and light parameters (ambient color, directional light color and direction). Output: Shaded color and accumulated alpha for the ray segment. Data Structures RadiancePayload: Contains rng (pointer to RandomTEA), alpha (float), and color (vec3f). Packaged via packPointer(&payload, u0, u1) for OptiX trace. Numbered Steps 1. Transform Ray: Transform ray origin and direction to object space: cpp const vec3f org = xfmPoint(wto, org); const vec3f dir = xfmVector(wto, dir); 2. Initialize Tracking (Single Shade Heuristic): If using SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC, initialize tracking variables: cpp vec3f highestContributionOrg = 0.f; vec3f highestContributionColor = 0.f; float highestContributionAlpha = 0.f; 3. March Ray: Iterate along the ray using raymarchingiterator(self, org, dir, tMin, tMax, self.step, & {... }). 4. Sample Position: Compute sample position with jitter: cpp const auto p = org + lerp(jitter, t.x, t.y) dir; 5. Compute Gradient: Compute gradient in object space. Negate it because opacity correlates to the scalar field, and the gradient points toward increasing values (outside), requiring a flip for correct lighting: cpp const vec3f No = -sampleGradient(self.volume, p, sampleValue, gradientStep); 6. Transform Normal: Transform gradient to world space: cpp const vec3f Nw = xfmNormal(otw, No); 7. Apply Shading: GRADIENTSHADING: Compute shaded color and blend: cpp const vec3f shadingColor = shadescivislight(dir, Nw, sampleColor, params.matgradientshading, params.lightambient, params.lightdirectionalrgb, params.lightdirectionaldir); sampleColor = lerp(shadingScale, sampleColor, shadingColor); SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Track the point with the highest contribution: cpp if (highestContributionAlpha < (1.f - payload.alpha) sampleAlpha) { highestContributionOrg = p; highestContributionColor = sampleColor; highestContributionAlpha = (1.f - payload.alpha) sampleAlpha; } 8. Continue Marching: Return payload.alpha < nearlyone to continue marching while alpha is below threshold. Parameters shadingScale: Controls the interpolation weight between base color and shaded color in lerp(shadingScale, base, shaded). gradientStep: Step size used for finite-difference gradient estimation in sampleGradient. Pitfalls Gradient Direction: The gradient direction must be negated (-sampleGradient) because the implementation assumes opacity directly correlates to the volume scalar field, meaning the gradient naturally points toward higher values (outside), requiring a flip for correct lighting. name: Blinn-Phong Lighting Model
head: Blinn-Phong Lighting on Isosurface, Blinn-Phong Shading, Blinn-Phong Shading for Volume Data, Isosurface Shading, Volumetric Shading
body:
The Blinn-Phong Lighting Model applies the Blinn-Phong shading approximation to volume rendering data, typically by computing surface normals from the scalar field gradient to simulate isosurface shading. It enhances the perception of depth and shape structure in volumetric data by combining ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting components, offering a computationally cheap alternative to full ray-traced shadows while providing stronger visual cues than unshaded volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar volume data V, light direction vector \mathbf{l}, view direction vector \mathbf{v}, lighting coefficients (ka, kd, ks), and light intensity IL. Output: Shaded color I for each sample point or voxel. Data Structures: Scalar Volume: 3D texture or array storing scalar values s(x,y,z). Gradient Data (Optional): If precomputed, a 3D texture storing the gradient vector 
abla s or its components. If not precomputed, gradients are derived on-the-fly from the scalar volume. Steps: 1. Compute Surface Normal: Calculate the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the current sample point by computing the gradient of the scalar field. The sources specify using central differences between neighboring voxels. Let x be the voxel spacing (or distance between sample points). The gradient 
abla I is computed as: 
abla I = \left(  rac{I{right} - I{left}}{2x},  rac{I{top} - I{bottom}}{2x},  rac{I{front} - I{back}}{2x} ight) Normalize the result to obtain the unit normal vector \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla I}{\|
abla I\|} 2. Calculate Diffuse Component: Compute the diffuse lighting contribution based on the angle between the light direction and the surface normal. The light direction \mathbf{l} (or \mathbf{lightDir}) must be normalized. 	ext{diffuseStrength} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0.0) 3. Calculate Specular Component: Compute the specular highlight. The sources describe two variations for the reflection vector. One approach uses the reflection of the light vector about the normal: \mathbf{r} = 	ext{reflect}(-\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{n}) 	ext{specularStrength} = \max(0.0, \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{r})^{	ext{shininess}} where \mathbf{v} is the normalized view direction (ray origin direction) and the exponent is typically 64.0. Note: The standard Blinn-Phong model uses the half-vector \mathbf{h} =  rac{\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}\|} and computes \max(0.0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})^{	ext{shininess}}. The source presents the general Blinn-Phong formula using \mathbf{h}, while implements the reflection vector variant. Both are cited as Blinn-Phong shading in the context of volume rendering. 4. Combine Lighting: Composite the shaded colors using the Blinn-Phong illumination model equation: I = ka + IL kd (\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{n}) + IL ks (\mathbf{h} \cdot \mathbf{n}) Or, using the specific implementation details from which scales the base color: 	ext{color.rgb} = (	ext{diffuseStrength} + 	ext{specularStrength}) 	imes 	ext{val\color.rgb} where 	ext{val\color} is the base color of the volume at that point, potentially modulated by alpha/transparency. The ambient term ka is often added as a constant or base color if not included in the scaling factor. Parameters: ka, kd, ks: Ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients. User-set. IL: Light intensity. Shininess: Exponent for specular term. Source uses 64.0. x: Voxel spacing/distance between neighbors for gradient calculation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Noise: Computing normals on-the-fly requires 6 texture fetches per calculation (3 pairs of neighbors). This can be noisy if the volume data is sparse or low-resolution. Memory Trade-off: Precalculating normals on the host and storing them in voxel data requires 4x texture memory (3 components for normal + 1 for value, or separate gradient textures). Boundary Conditions: Gradient calculation at the volume boundaries requires handling missing neighbors (e.g., clamping or zero-padding). View Direction: The view direction \mathbf{v} must be normalized. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blinnphongshading(volume, samplepoint, lightdir, viewdir, ka, kd, ks, IL, shininess, voxelspacing): """ Computes Blinn-Phong shading for a volume sample. Args: volume: 3D array or texture of scalar values. samplepoint: (x, y, z) coordinates of the current sample. lightdir: Normalized light direction vector. viewdir: Normalized view direction vector. ka: Ambient coefficient. kd: Diffuse coefficient. ks: Specular coefficient. IL: Light intensity. shininess: Specular exponent. voxelspacing: Distance between voxel centers. Returns: Shaded color value. """ # 1. Compute Normal via Central Differences # Get neighboring voxel values # Note: Boundary checks required in implementation valleft = volume.get(samplepoint.x - voxelspacing, samplepoint.y, samplepoint.z) valright = volume.get(samplepoint.x + voxelspacing, samplepoint.y, samplepoint.z) valbottom = volume.get(samplepoint.x, samplepoint.y - voxelspacing, samplepoint.z) valtop = volume.get(samplepoint.x, samplepoint.y + voxelspacing, samplepoint.z) valback = volume.get(samplepoint.x, samplepoint.y, samplepoint.z - voxelspacing) valfront = volume.get(samplepoint.x, samplepoint.y, samplepoint.z + voxelspacing) gradx = (valright - valleft) / (2 voxelspacing) grady = (valtop - valbottom) / (2 voxelspacing) gradz = (valfront - valback) / (2 voxelspacing) normal = normalize(vec3(gradx, grady, gradz)) # 2. Calculate Diffuse Component diffusestrength = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) # 3. Calculate Specular Component # Using reflection vector as per # reflect(-lightdir, normal) computes the reflection of the light vector reflectdir = reflect(-lightdir, normal) specularstrength = pow(max(dot(viewdir, reflectdir), 0.0), shininess) # 4. Combine Lighting # Base color from volume (simplified as 1.0 for scalar, or fetched from color map) basecolor = vec3(1.0) # Placeholder for actual color mapping # Ambient term ambient = ka # Diffuse and Specular terms scaled by light intensity and coefficients # Note: formula includes IL in diffuse and specular terms diffuseterm = IL kd diffusestrength specularterm = IL ks specularstrength finalcolor = ambient + diffuseterm + specularterm # Apply to base color if needed (as per scaling approach) # finalcolor = (diffusestrength + specularstrength) basecolor # This depends on specific implementation choice between and return finalcolor Time Complexity: O(1) per sample for shading calculation. On-the-fly normal computation adds 6 texture fetches per sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) extra memory if normals are computed on-the-fly. O(N) extra memory (4x volume size) if normals are precomputed and stored. Performance: Described as "quite cheap and simple to compute". Strengths: Provides strong depth and shape cues; simple to implement; works well with composite ray functions. Limitations: Approximates surface shading on volumetric data; does not account for volumetric shadows or subsurface scattering unless extended (e.g., via second raymarch). When to use: When visual clarity of internal structures is needed and performance is a concern. When not to use: When physically accurate light transport (shadows, scattering) is required. The Blinn-Phong model is a modification of the Phong reflection model, introduced by Jim Blinn. In the context of volume rendering, it is applied to scalar fields to simulate isosurface lighting, enhancing the visual interpretation of 3D data. It is commonly used in scientific visualization tools and real-time volume rendering engines. name: Phong Shading
head: Phong Shading Model, Phong Illumination Model, Phong Lighting Model, Phong Reflection Model, Phong model, Phong Illumination
body: Phong Shading is a local illumination model that calculates the color of a surface point by summing ambient, diffuse, and specular components. It approximates direct lighting by combining a constant ambient term with a diffuse term proportional to the surface normal and light direction, and a specular term based on the alignment between the view direction and the surface reflection vector. Unlike physically based models, it is an empirical approximation that does not account for occlusion or interreflection. It is distinguished from its sibling Blinn-Phong Shading Model by using the explicit reflection vector R rather than the halfway vector H for the specular calculation. Inputs: Surface position x (world space). Surface normal N (unit vector, world space). View direction V (unit vector, from x to camera). Light direction L (unit vector, from x to light source). Material parameters: ambient coefficient ka, diffuse coefficient kd, specular coefficient ks, shininess exponent \alpha (or n). Light parameters: ambient intensity Ia, diffuse intensity I{d}, specular intensity I{s} (often represented as light colors). Material colors: ambient color Oa, diffuse color Od, specular color Os. Outputs: Fragment color C (RGB). Data Structures: Material: A structure containing floats for ka, kd, ks, \alpha and RGB vectors for Oa, Od, Os. Light: A structure containing RGB vectors for ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities. Steps: 1. Transform Vectors: Ensure N, L, and V are normalized unit vectors in the same coordinate space (typically world space or view space). If using a graphics pipeline, transform vertex positions and normals using the model matrix M and view-projection matrices. World position: p{world} = M \cdot p{local}. World normal: n{world} = (M^{-1})^T \cdot n{local} (using the upper-left 3x3 submatrix of M). 2. Compute Reflection Vector: Calculate the direction of perfect reflection R for the light source. R = 2(N \cdot L)N - L where N \cdot L is the dot product. 3. Compute Ambient Component: Calculate the ambient contribution, which is constant regardless of geometry. C{ambient} = ka Oa Ia. Note: Some implementations assume Oa = Od or simplify Ia. 4. Compute Diffuse Component: Calculate the Lambertian reflection. C{diffuse} = kd Od Id \max(N \cdot L, 0). The \max function ensures back-facing surfaces receive no diffuse light. 5. Compute Specular Component: Calculate the specular highlight based on the angle between the reflection vector R and the view vector V. C{specular} = ks Os Is \max(R \cdot V, 0)^\alpha. Here \alpha is the shininess exponent. Higher values produce smaller, sharper highlights. 6. Combine: Sum the components. C = C{ambient} + C{diffuse} + C{specular}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phongshading(position, normal, viewdirection, lightdirection, material, light): """ Calculate Phong shading for a single light source. Args: position: vec3, world space position of the fragment. normal: vec3, normalized world space surface normal. viewdirection: vec3, normalized direction from position to camera. lightdirection: vec3, normalized direction from position to light. material: dict or object with keys: ka, kd, ks, shininess, colorambient, colordiffuse, colorspecular. light: dict or object with keys: ambient, diffuse, specular (RGB vectors). Returns: vec3, final fragment color. """ # 1. Normalize inputs (ensure unit vectors) N = normalize(normal) L = normalize(lightdirection) V = normalize(viewdirection) # 2. Ambient Component # Cambient = ka Oa Ia ambient = material['ka'] material['colorambient'] light['ambient'] # 3. Diffuse Component # Cdiffuse = kd Od Id max(N. L, 0) difffactor = max(dot(N, L), 0.0) diffuse = material['kd'] material['colordiffuse'] light['diffuse'] difffactor # 4. Specular Component # R = 2 (N. L) N - L # Cspecular = ks Os Is max(R. V, 0)^shininess R = 2.0 dot(N, L) N - L specfactor = max(dot(R, V), 0.0) specular = material['ks'] material['colorspecular'] light['specular'] (specfactor material['shininess']) # 5. Combine color = ambient + diffuse + specular return color (Note: normalize, dot, max are standard vector/math operations.) Parameters: Shininess (\alpha or n): Controls the size of the specular highlight. Default values in implementations often range from 10 to 64. For a perfect reflector, the exponent is infinite. Coefficients (ka, kd, ks): Typically in the range [0, 1]. Some implementations use values > 1 for specular to simulate energy gain (non-physical). Colors (Oa, Od, Os): RGB vectors. Simplified implementations may assume Oa = Od and Os is a blend of Od and white. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Back-facing surfaces: The diffuse term must be clamped to 0 when N \cdot L < 0 to prevent light from shining through the back of the object. Non-physical results: The model does not conserve energy; the sum of reflected light can exceed incident light if coefficients are not carefully tuned. Vector normalization: Failure to normalize N, L, V before dot products results in incorrect shading intensity. Coordinate spaces: Vectors must be in the same space. Uses the halfway vector H = \frac{L+V}{|L+V|} instead of the reflection vector R. It is computationally cheaper (no reflection vector calculation) and produces slightly different highlight shapes. Choose when performance is critical or the specific highlight shape of Blinn-Phong is desired [2239-blinn-phong-shading-model.md]. Extends Blinn-Phong with depth-based fading to simulate atmospheric effects. Choose for scenes requiring depth-based visibility cues [2448-blinn-phong-lighting-with-depth-cueing.md]. Adapts the Phong model for volume rendering by using gradient vectors as normals and lookup tables for illumination. Choose for ray-casted volume visualization [1353-phong-shading-model-for-volume-data.md]. Approximates the specular term using polynomial expansions for faster computation. Choose when hardware does not support efficient power functions or for specific optimization constraints [1172-specular-reflections-via-polynomial-expansion.md]. Time Complexity: O(1) per light source per fragment. The cost is dominated by a few dot products, a power function, and vector arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(1) for material and light parameters. No large tables are required for the standard model. Performance: Suitable for real-time rendering on CPUs and GPUs, as it is an inexpensive method for shader-based rendering. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, visually pleasing for many materials. Limitations: Not physically based (does not account for occlusion or interreflection), specular highlights are view-dependent in a way that can look unrealistic for rough surfaces, no shadowing or ambient occlusion included. When to use: Real-time applications where performance is critical and physical accuracy is not required. Good for stylized rendering or as a baseline lighting model. When not to use: Physically based rendering (PBR) pipelines, scenes requiring accurate energy conservation, or when realistic shadowing and global illumination are needed. The Phong shading model was developed by Bui Tuong Phong in 1975. It was introduced as an empirical model to approximate the way light reflects off surfaces, specifically focusing on the specular highlight. It became a standard in computer graphics due to its simplicity and visual effectiveness. It is widely used in real-time rendering engines, educational contexts, and as a component in more complex lighting pipelines. The model is often implemented in fragment shaders in OpenGL pipelines. head: Fragment Shader Lighting, Standard Lighting
body: A fragment shading model that combines ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting components with exponential distance fog to blend the computed surface color with a fog color based on the fragment's distance from the camera. It uses an exponential decay function for fog attenuation instead of linear fog, as linear fog is commented out in the reference implementation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Vertex attributes Normal (vec3), Position (vec4), viewSpace (vec4); light properties color (vec3), ambientIntensity (float), diffuseIntensity (float), direction (vec3); camera property eyePosition (vec3); material properties shininess (float), specularIntensity (float); fog parameters FogDensity (float), fogColor (vec3). Outputs: Final fragment color (finalColor). Data Structures: The vertex shader passes Normal, Position, and viewSpace to the fragment shader. Parameters: FogDensity: Exponential fog density constant, value 0.01f. fogColor: Fog color, value vec3(0.0f, 0.3f, 0.6f). material.shininess: Exponent for specular highlight. material.specularIntensity: Multiplier for specular color. Steps: 1. Calculate Ambient Component: Multiply the light's color by its ambient intensity, setting alpha to 1.0: ambientColor = vec4(light.color, 1.0f) light.ambientIntensity. 2. Calculate Diffuse Component: Compute the diffuse factor using the dot product of the normalized surface normal and normalized light direction: diffuseFactor = max(dot(normalize(Normal), normalize(direction)), 0.0f). Compute the diffuse color: diffuseColor = vec4(light.color light.diffuseIntensity diffuseFactor, 1.0f). 3. Calculate Specular Component: If diffuseFactor > 0.0f, compute the vector from the fragment to the eye: fragToEye = normalize(eyePosition - Position.xyz). Compute the reflection vector: reflectedVertex = normalize(reflect(direction, normalize(Normal))). Compute the specular factor: specularFactor = dot(fragToEye, reflectedVertex). If specularFactor > 0.0f, raise it to the material's shininess: specularFactor = pow(specularFactor, material.shininess). Compute specular color: specularColor = vec4(light.color material.specularIntensity specularFactor, 1.0f). 4. Combine Lighting: Sum the components: finalColor = ambientColor + diffuseColor + specularColor. 5. Calculate Fog Factor: Compute the distance from the camera in view space: dist = length(viewSpace). Compute the exponential fog factor: fogFactor = 1.0 / exp(dist FogDensity). Clamp fogFactor to [0.0, 1.0]. 6. Apply Fog: Mix the lit color with the fog color using the source's specific mixing formula: color = mix(color 1.5f, vec4(fogColor, 1.0f), (1.0f - fogFactor)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phongshadingwithexponentialfog(Normal, Position, viewSpace, lightcolor, lightambientintensity, lightdiffuseintensity, lightdirection, eyeposition, materialshininess, materialspecularintensity, fogdensity, fogcolor): # 1. Ambient ambientcolor = vec4(lightcolor, 1.0) lightambientintensity # 2. Diffuse N = normalize(Normal) L = normalize(lightdirection) diffusefactor = max(dot(N, L), 0.0) diffusecolor = vec4(lightcolor lightdiffuseintensity diffusefactor, 1.0) # 3. Specular specularcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) if diffusefactor > 0.0: V = normalize(eyeposition - Position.xyz) R = normalize(reflect(lightdirection, N)) specfactor = dot(V, R) if specfactor > 0.0: specfactor = pow(specfactor, materialshininess) specularcolor = vec4(lightcolor materialspecularintensity specfactor, 1.0) # 4. Combine finalcolor = ambientcolor + diffusecolor + specularcolor # 5. Fog dist = length(viewSpace) fogfactor = 1.0 / exp(dist fogdensity) fogfactor = clamp(fogfactor, 0.0, 1.0) # 6. Apply Fog # Source mixes finalcolor 1.5 with fogcolor foggedcolor = mix(finalcolor 1.5, vec4(fogcolor, 1.0), 1.0 - fogfactor) return foggedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The source multiplies the final lit color by 1.5 before fog mixing, which is an implementation detail that may cause over-brightening in scenes without fog or with low fog density. The source calls reflect(direction, normalize(Normal)) directly on the light direction vector without negation, implying the implementation assumes direction represents the incident vector or follows a specific non-standard convention. With FogDensity = 0.01, fog becomes significant at distances around 100 units (1/e \approx 0.37). Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the Proccraft project by Fredrik Erik Johansson. Proccraft, https://github.com/FredrikErikJohansson/Proccraft, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
