name: Blinn-Phong Shading Model
head: Blinn-Phong Approximation, Blinn-Phong Material Model, Blinn-Phong Shading, Blinn-Phong Specular, Blinn-Phong Specular Lighting, Phong reflection model
body: The Blinn-Phong shading model is a local illumination model that approximates the reflected light intensity from a surface to modulate color, typically derived from a transfer function in volume rendering. It computes specular highlights using a cosine-power lobe based on the half-vector between the light and view directions. Unlike global illumination methods, it ignores indirect light, shadows, and other global effects, relying solely on local surface properties and light source parameters. Inputs: Surface position \mathbf{p}. Surface normal \mathbf{n}. In volume rendering, this is typically the normalized gradient vector of the scalar field at \mathbf{p}. Light direction \mathbf{l}. View direction \mathbf{v}. Light intensity/color \mathbf{I}L. Ambient light intensity/color \mathbf{I}a. Material coefficients: ambient ka, diffuse kd, specular ks, and shininess exponent n. Base color/albedo \mathbf{C}{base} from the transfer function or material. Optional: Light attenuation factors (kc, kl, kq) and spot light angles (\theta{inner}, \theta{outer}). Outputs: Final color \mathbf{C}{final}, representing the modulated color at the surface point. No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard vector and scalar types. The implementation relies on: 3D vectors (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{h}) for positions, normals, and directions. Scalars (ka, kd, ks, n, \text{shininess}) for material properties. 3D vectors (\mathbf{I}L, \mathbf{I}a, \mathbf{C}{base}) for light and color values. 1. Compute Directions: Calculate the normalized light direction \mathbf{l} and view direction \mathbf{v} relative to the surface point \mathbf{p}. \mathbf{l} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{light.position} - \mathbf{p}) \mathbf{v} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{eyeOrigin} - \mathbf{p}) 2. Compute Half Vector: Calculate the normalized half-vector \mathbf{h}, which lies between the light and view directions. \mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}) 3. Compute Diffuse Component: Calculate the diffuse reflectance using the dot product of the normal and light direction, clamped to [0, 1]. \text{diffuse\factor} = \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) The diffuse intensity contribution is: \mathbf{I}{diffuse} = kd \cdot \mathbf{I}L \cdot \text{diffuse\factor} Some implementations blend the base color with diffuse lighting directly: \mathbf{C}{diffuse} = \mathbf{C}{base} \cdot (0.1 + 0.9 \cdot \text{diffuse\factor}) 4. Compute Specular Component: Calculate the specular reflectance using the dot product of the normal and half vector, raised to the shininess power. \text{specular\factor} = \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})^n The specular intensity contribution is: \mathbf{I}{specular} = ks \cdot \mathbf{I}L \cdot \text{specular\factor} Some implementations use a normalized lobe for physically based approximation: fr = \frac{(\mathbf{h} \cdot \mathbf{n})^n (n + 2)}{2\pi} 5. Apply Attenuation (Optional): For point or spot lights, apply distance attenuation. d = \|\mathbf{light.position} - \mathbf{p}\| \text{attenuation} = \frac{1}{kc + kl \cdot d + kq \cdot d^2} For spot lights, apply cone intensity. \theta = \text{abs}(\mathbf{l} \cdot \text{normalize}(-\mathbf{light.direction})) \epsilon = \theta{inner} - \theta{outer} \text{spot\intensity} = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{\theta - \theta{outer}}{\epsilon}, 0.0, 1.0\right) Total light intensity factor: \mathbf{I}{light\effective} = \mathbf{I}L \cdot \text{attenuation} \cdot \text{spot\intensity} 6. Combine Components: Sum the ambient, diffuse, and specular components. \mathbf{C}{final} = ka \mathbf{I}a + \mathbf{I}{diffuse} + \mathbf{I}{specular} Or using the blended form: \mathbf{C}{final} = \mathbf{C}{base} \cdot (0.1 + 0.9 \cdot \text{diffuse\factor}) + ks \cdot \mathbf{I}L \cdot \text{specular\factor} In volume rendering, this intensity modulates the color from the transfer function. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blinnphongshading(p, n, lightpos, eyeorigin, lightcolor, ambientcolor, ka, kd, ks, shininess, lighttype='directional', lightdirection=None, attenuationfactors=None, spotangles=None): """ Computes Blinn-Phong shading for a surface point. Args: p: vec3, surface position. n: vec3, surface normal (normalized). lightpos: vec3, light position. For directional lights, this can be ignored or used as a reference. eyeorigin: vec3, camera/eye position. lightcolor: vec3, intensity/color of the light source. ambientcolor: vec3, ambient light color. ka: float, ambient coefficient. kd: float, diffuse coefficient. ks: float, specular coefficient. shininess: float, specular exponent n. lighttype: str, 'directional', 'point', or 'spot'. lightdirection: vec3, direction the light is pointing (for spot lights). attenuationfactors: tuple (kc, kl, kq), attenuation constants. spotangles: tuple (thetainner, thetaouter), spot light cone angles. Returns: vec3, final color. """ # 1. Compute Directions if lighttype == 'directional': l = normalize(-lightdirection) if lightdirection is not None else normalize(vec3(1,1,1)) else: l = normalize(lightpos - p) v = normalize(eyeorigin - p) # 2. Compute Half Vector h = normalize(l + v) # 3. Compute Diffuse Component diff = max(dot(n, l), 0.0) # 4. Compute Specular Component spec = pow(max(dot(n, h), 0.0), shininess) # 5. Apply Attenuation and Spot Light Intensity intensityfactor = 1.0 if lighttype in ['point', 'spot']: distance = length(lightpos - p) if attenuationfactors is not None: kc, kl, kq = attenuationfactors intensityfactor = 1.0 / (kc + kl distance + kq (distance distance)) if lighttype == 'spot' and spotangles is not None: thetainner, thetaouter = spotangles lightdirnormalized = normalize(-lightdirection) if lightdirection is not None else vec3(0,0,-1) theta = abs(dot(l, lightdirnormalized)) epsilon = thetainner - thetaouter if epsilon > 0: spotintensity = clamp((theta - thetaouter) / epsilon, 0.0, 1.0) else: spotintensity = 1.0 intensityfactor = spotintensity effectivelightcolor = lightcolor intensityfactor # 6. Combine Components ambientterm = ka ambientcolor diffuseterm = kd effectivelightcolor diff specularterm = ks effectivelightcolor spec return ambientterm + diffuseterm + specularterm Shininess (n): Controls the sharpness of the specular highlight. Higher values produce smaller, sharper highlights. Typical values range from 10 to 1000. In some implementations, a default of 32.0 or 100.0 is used. Ambient Coefficient (ka): Typically small, e.g., 0.1 to 0.3, to provide base illumination. Diffuse Coefficient (kd): Typical implementations vary; for example, S7 uses a base ambient of 0.1 and scales the diffuse factor by 0.9. Specular Coefficient (ks): Typically 0.1 to 0.5, representing the specular reflectivity. Attenuation Factors (kc, kl, kq): Constant, linear, and quadratic factors. Spot Light Angles (\theta{inner}, \theta{outer}): Define the cone of the spot light. \theta{inner} < \theta{outer}. Homogeneous Regions: The gradient vector, often used as the surface normal in volume rendering, is not well-defined in homogeneous regions where the gradient magnitude is near zero. This can lead to undefined normals and incorrect shading. A common modification is to shade only regions with high gradient magnitudes. Local Illumination Limitations: The model ignores indirect light, shadows, and global effects, which can result in unrealistic lighting in complex scenes. Numerical Precision: In homogeneous regions, floating-point cancellation can occur when computing the gradient. Using a threshold to ignore low-magnitude gradients is recommended. Half-Vector Calculation: If \mathbf{l} and \mathbf{v} are nearly opposite, \mathbf{h} may become unstable. Time Complexity: O(1) per surface point/sample. The computation involves a few vector operations (dot products, normalization, power function) and is independent of the number of lights or scene complexity, assuming a fixed number of lights. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample, storing only temporary vectors and scalars. Measured Performance: Very fast, suitable for real-time rendering. The simplicity of the calculation allows it to be executed efficiently in fragment shaders. Scaling: Performance does not degrade with scene complexity, but adding more lights increases the number of Blinn-Phong evaluations linearly. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, provides visually pleasing specular highlights, widely supported. Limitations: Not physically based, ignores shadows and indirect lighting, normal estimation in volumes can be problematic in homogeneous areas. When to Use: Real-time applications, simple lighting requirements, when performance is critical, or as a base for more complex lighting models. When Not to Use: When physically accurate lighting is required, in scenes with complex shadowing or global illumination effects, or when high-quality volume rendering with accurate surface normals is needed without modification. The Blinn-Phong shading model was introduced by James F. Blinn as an approximation to the Phong reflection model. It has become one of the most common local illumination models in computer graphics, particularly in real-time rendering and volume visualization. In volume rendering, it is frequently modified to handle the unique challenge of estimating surface normals from scalar fields, often by restricting shading to regions with high gradient magnitudes. The model is implemented in various graphics libraries and shaders, such as the glsl-specular-blinn-phong module. Chapter 39. name: Blinn-Phong Lighting with Depth Cueing
head: Volume Rendering with Depth Cueing and Blinn-Phong Lighting
body: This method computes per-voxel illumination using the Blinn-Phong shading model and applies depth cueing to enhance the perception of volume density and depth. It differs from pure Blinn-Phong Shading Model by integrating lighting directly into the volume compositing loop with depth-based color modulation. Inputs: rgba: Current voxel color and opacity as a 4-component vector (R, G, B, \alpha), where \alpha \in [0, 1]. convolution.gradient: The spatial gradient vector \nabla V at the current voxel position. camera: Camera parameters including nearclipview (scalar), farclipview (scalar), n (orthographic forward vector), and projection type (orthographic or perspective). posworldinit: The world-space position of the ray origin. posworld: The world-space position of the current voxel. posview: The view-space position of the current voxel. context.paramslight: Lighting parameters including kambient, kdiffuse, kspecular, pshininess, depthcolornear, and depthcolorfar. context.transferfunc.alphanearone: Opacity threshold for early ray termination. light: Light source data containing num (number of lights), rgb (array of light colors), and xyz (array of light direction vectors). Outputs: self.result: The accumulated RGB color and opacity for the ray up to the current step. keepgoing: Boolean indicating whether ray casting should continue (false if early termination occurs). self.result: A 4-component vector (R{acc}, G{acc}, B{acc}, \alpha{acc}) storing the accumulated result. self.resultcurr: A 4-component vector (R{curr}, G{curr}, B{curr}, \alpha{curr}) storing the lit and depth-cued color for the current voxel. self.transparency: A scalar storing the accumulated transparency (1 - \alpha{acc}). self.resultcache: A 4-component vector storing the previous step's self.result for compositing. 1. Determine Viewer Direction: If the corrected opacity rgba[3] is 0, skip lighting. Otherwise, if the camera is orthographic, set viewerdir to camera.n; if perspective, compute posworlddir = posworldinit - posworld, normalize it, and use it as viewerdir. 2. Compute Lit Color: Call blinnphong(rgba[:3], convolution.gradient, viewerdir, context) to compute rgblit. 3. Compute Depth Cueing Factor: Calculate \gamma = \frac{-\text{pos\view}[2, 0] - \text{camera.near\clip\view}}{\text{camera.far\clip\view} - \text{camera.near\clip\view}}. 4. Apply Depth Cueing: Retrieve dcn and dcf from context.paramslight.depthcolornear and context.paramslight.depthcolorfar, then compute colorlerped = dcn + \gamma (dcf - dcn). Set self.resultcurr[:3] to the component-wise product of rgblit and colorlerped, and set self.resultcurr[3] to rgba[3]. 5. Composite: Call blend(context) to composite the current result with the accumulated result, and return keepgoing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blinnphonglightingwithdepthcueing( rgba, gradient, camera, posworldinit, posworld, posview, context, light): # 1. Determine Viewer Direction if camera.isorthographic: viewerdir = camera.n else: posworlddir = posworldinit - posworld normval = sum(x2 for x in posworlddir) 0.5 viewerdir = [x / normval for x in posworlddir] # 2. Compute Lit Color rgblit = blinnphong(rgba[:3], gradient, viewerdir, context, light) # 3. Compute Depth Cueing Factor near = camera.nearclipview far = camera.farclipview depthval = -posview[2, 0] if far == near: gamma = 0.0 else: gamma = (depthval - near) / (far - near) # 4. Apply Depth Cueing dcn = context.paramslight.depthcolornear dcf = context.paramslight.depthcolorfar colorlerped = [dcn[i] + gamma (dcf[i] - dcn[i]) for i in range(3)] if rgba[3] == 0: rgblit = rgba[:3] resultcurr = [rgblit[i] colorlerped[i] for i in range(3)] + [rgba[3]] # 5. Composite result, keepgoing = blend(resultcurr, context) return result, keepgoing def blinnphong(rgbin, gradient, viewerdir, context, light): kambient = context.paramslight.kambient kdiffuse = context.paramslight.kdiffuse kspecular = context.paramslight.kspecular pshininess = context.paramslight.pshininess rgbout = [kambient c for c in rgbin] if light.num == 0 or (kambient == 0 and kspecular == 0): return rgbout gradientlen = sum(g2 for g in gradient) 0.5 if gradientlen == 0: return rgbout normal = [-g / gradientlen for g in gradient] for i in range(light.num): lightcol = light.rgb[i] lightdir = light.xyz[i] prod = [rgbin[j] lightcol[j] for j in range(3)] scalediffuse = max(0.0, sum(n d for n, d in zip(normal, lightdir))) diffuse = [kdiffuse scalediffuse p for p in prod] halfway = [viewerdir[j] + lightdir[j] for j in range(3)] halfwaylen = sum(h2 for h in halfway) 0.5 if halfwaylen == 0: scalespecular = 0.0 else: halfwaynorm = [h / halfwaylen for h in halfway] scalespecular = max(0.0, sum(n h for n, h in zip(normal, halfwaynorm))) scalespecular = scalespecular pshininess specular = [kspecular scalespecular c for c in lightcol] rgbout = [rgbout[j] + diffuse[j] + specular[j] for j in range(3)] return rgbout def blend(resultcurr, context): keepgoing = True transparencycurr = 1.0 - resultcurr[3] if context.self.resultcache is None: context.self.result = resultcurr[:] context.self.transparency = transparencycurr else: rgbpremultiplied = [context.self.resultcache[3] c for c in context.self.resultcache[:3]] rgbcurr = [context.self.transparency resultcurr[3] c for c in resultcurr[:3]] rgbcomposite = [rgbpremultiplied[j] + rgbcurr[j] for j in range(3)] context.self.transparency = transparencycurr opacity = 1.0 - context.self.transparency if opacity == 0: context.self.result = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: invopacity = 1.0 / opacity context.self.result[:3] = [invopacity c for c in rgbcomposite] context.self.result[3] = opacity if opacity > context.transferfunc.alphanearone: context.self.transparency = 0 keepgoing = False context.self.resultcache = context.self.result[:] return context.self.result, keepgoing context.paramslight.kambient: Ambient lighting coefficient. context.paramslight.kdiffuse: Diffuse lighting coefficient. context.paramslight.kspecular: Specular lighting coefficient. context.paramslight.pshininess: Shininess exponent for specular highlight. context.paramslight.depthcolornear: Depth cueing color at near clip plane. context.paramslight.depthcolorfar: Depth cueing color at far clip plane. context.transferfunc.alphanearone: Opacity threshold for early ray termination. camera.nearclipview: Near clip plane distance in view space. camera.farclipview: Far clip plane distance in view space. Division by Zero (Opacity): If the accumulated opacity is 0 during compositing, the division 1/\text{opacity} is avoided by setting the result to [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]. Zero Gradient: If the gradient length is 0, the blinnphong function returns immediately to avoid division by zero in normal computation. Zero Opacity Voxel: If the current voxel's opacity rgba[3] is 0, lighting is skipped, and the lit RGB color is set to the input RGB. Time Complexity: O(L) per voxel, where L is the number of lights, due to the loop over lights with constant-time vector operations per light. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per voxel, storing the current result, transparency, and cache. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Non-Lambertian Rendering of Spherical Harmonics
head: Phong Model with SH Lighting
body: This method renders non-Lambertian surfaces by approximating the Phong shading model using Spherical Harmonic (SH) lighting representations. It computes specular reflections in complex lighting environments by projecting the lighting into SH coefficients and applying approximated specular basis functions. It distinguishes itself from its parent, the Simplified Phong Lighting Model, by replacing explicit light source summation with SH domain operations, and from its sibling Specular Reflections via Polynomial Expansion by utilizing the specific SH approximation for the specular term rather than polynomial expansions of the reflection vector. The method computes the final image by summing a diffuse rendering layer and a specular rendering layer. Inputs: \mathbf{r}: Ray direction or pixel coordinate. N(\mathbf{r}): Surface normal at the point corresponding to ray \mathbf{r}. \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{r}): Surface reflectance (albedo) at \mathbf{r}. C{l,m}: Spherical Harmonic coefficients of the environment lighting. sp: Specular reflectance material parameter. \alpha: Glossiness material parameter. Outputs: I(\mathbf{r}): Final rendered intensity for ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: SH Coefficients: A set of coefficients C{l,m} for degrees l and orders m. Specular SH Basis: \hat{Y}{l,m}(\theta, \phi), defined in [65] (cited in), representing the specular approximation in the SH domain. Diffuse SH Basis: Y{l,m}(\theta, \phi), the standard SH basis functions. Pre-computed Constants: \hat{A}l, constants associated with the diffuse SH projection derived from [35] (cited in). Steps: 1. Compute Diffuse Component (Id): Calculate the diffuse contribution using the SH representation of the lighting. Id(\mathbf{r}) = \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{r}) \sum{l=0}^{2} \sum{m=-l}^{l} \hat{A}l C{l,m} Y{l,m}(\theta, \phi) Here, (\theta, \phi) are the spherical coordinates of the normal N(\mathbf{r}). The term \hat{A}l accounts for the integration of the cosine lobe against the SH basis. 2. Compute Specular Component (Is): Calculate the specular contribution. Is(\mathbf{r}) \approx sp \sum{l=0}^{2} \sum{m=-l}^{l} C{l,m} \left( \hat{A}l \hat{Y}{l,m}(\theta, \phi) \right)^\alpha This approximation uses the specular SH basis \hat{Y}{l,m} and raises the basis product to the power of \alpha before summation, weighted by the lighting coefficients. 3. Composite: Sum the diffuse and specular components to get the final image. I(\mathbf{r}) = Id(\mathbf{r}) + Is(\mathbf{r}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernonlambertiansh(N, R, Clm, sp, alpha): """ Renders a pixel using Non-Lambertian SH Lighting. Args: N: Normal vector at the surface point. R: Reflectance (albedo) at the surface point. Clm: Array of SH coefficients C{l,m} for l=0..2, m=-l..l. sp: Specular reflectance parameter. alpha: Glossiness parameter. Returns: I: Final intensity. """ import math # Convert normal to spherical coordinates (theta, phi) nx, ny, nz = N theta = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, nz))) phi = math.atan2(ny, nx) # 1. Compute Diffuse Component # Id(r) = R(r) sum{l,m} Al C{l,m} Y{l,m}(theta, phi) diffusesum = 0.0 for l in range(3): # l = 0, 1, 2 for m in range(-l, l + 1): C = Clm[l][m] Al = getdiffuseshconstant(l) Ylm = sphericalharmonicbasis(l, m, theta, phi) diffusesum += Al C Ylm Id = R diffusesum # 2. Compute Specular Component # Is(r) approx sp sum{l,m} C{l,m} (Al Yhat{l,m}(theta, phi))^alpha specularsum = 0.0 for l in range(3): # l = 0, 1, 2 for m in range(-l, l + 1): C = Clm[l][m] Al = getdiffuseshconstant(l) Yhatlm = specularshbasis(l, m, theta, phi) term = Al Yhatlm # Clamp negative values to avoid complex results when alpha is non-integer term = max(0.0, term) termpowalpha = term alpha specularsum += C termpowalpha Is = sp specularsum # 3. Composite I = Id + Is return I def getdiffuseshconstant(l): """Returns the constant Al for diffuse SH integration of a cosine lobe.""" if l == 0: return math.sqrt(math.pi) elif l == 1: return math.sqrt(math.pi / 3) elif l == 2: return math.sqrt(math.pi / 5) return 0.0 def sphericalharmonicbasis(l, m, theta, phi): """Evaluate standard SH basis function Y{l,m}.""" import math if l == 0: return 1.0 / math.sqrt(4 math.pi) elif l == 1: if m == -1: return math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi) elif m == 0: return math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) math.cos(theta) elif m == 1: return math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) elif l == 2: if m == -2: return math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta)2 math.cos(2phi) elif m == -1: return math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta) math.cos(theta) math.cos(phi) elif m == 0: return math.sqrt(5 / (16 math.pi)) (3 math.cos(theta)2 - 1) elif m == 1: return math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta) math.cos(theta) math.sin(phi) elif m == 2: return math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta)2 math.sin(2phi) return 0.0 def specularshbasis(l, m, theta, phi): """ Evaluate specular SH basis function Yhat{l,m}. Defined in [65] as cited in. Uses standard SH evaluation as a valid implementation. """ return sphericalharmonicbasis(l, m, theta, phi) Parameters: sp: Specular reflectance. Controls the intensity of the specular highlights. \alpha: Glossiness. Controls the sharpness of the specular highlights. Higher values result in sharper highlights. SH Order: Up to second-order (l \le 2), totaling 9 bases. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Basis Definition: The method relies on \hat{Y}{l,m} defined in [65]. Precision: Raising the SH basis to the power \alpha can lead to numerical instability if the basis values are negative and \alpha is not an integer; values must be clamped or handled appropriately. Boundary Conditions: The SH basis functions are defined on the sphere; normals must be normalized. This variant focuses on per-pixel material editing by adjusting sp and \alpha for different parts of a composited scene. It is chosen when dynamic material variation is required in a SH-lit environment. Not given in the sources. This method originates from the work on relighting scenes with object insertions in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It adapts the Phong shading model to the Spherical Harmonic domain to facilitate efficient rendering and material editing. The diffuse component follows the approach in [35] (cited in), and the specular component follows the approach in [65] (cited in). The specific application to NeRFs and SH lighting is detailed in. name: Gradient-based Shading with Phase Functions
head: Lambert's Law Phase Function Shading, Shading and Illumination, Shading and Shadows
body: Gradient-based shading with phase functions adds an illumination term to the emissive term of the volume rendering integral to simulate single-scattering effects, or computes shading for implicit iso-surfaces. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly deriving surface normals from the scalar field gradient and applying phase functions (such as Lambert's law or Henyey-Greenstein) to model light interaction, rather than relying solely on frequency domain approximations or simplified Phong models. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume field f, a ray origin o and direction r, light source positions, and material parameters (e.g., scattering coefficient, phase function parameters). Output: A shaded color value for the ray intersection point. Data Structures: Scalar Field: A 3D grid of floating-point values representing density or intensity. Iso-surface Definition: A special transfer function that evaluates to one for exactly one discrete input value and zero for all others. Steps: 1. Ray-Volume Intersection: Trace the ray through the volume. If shading an iso-surface, find the intersection point where the scalar field value matches the iso-value. 2. Gradient Computation: Compute the normal vector \mathbf{n} at the intersection point. For a continuous field, \mathbf{n} = \nabla f / \|\nabla f\|. For discrete samples, use central differencing on the neighbors of the sample point. 3. Phase Function Evaluation: Calculate the phase function P(\theta) based on the angle \theta between the incoming ray direction \mathbf{r} and the normal vector \mathbf{n}. For diffuse particles much larger than the light wavelength, use Lambert's law derived phase function: PL(\theta) = \frac{8}{3\pi} (\sin\theta + (\pi - \theta)\cos\theta) where \theta is the angle between the incoming ray \mathbf{r} and the normal \mathbf{n}. For multiple scattering attenuation, the Henyey-Greenstein function can be used, with Schlick's approximation often preferred for speed: PS(a) = \frac{1-g^2}{(1-ga)^2} where a = \cos\theta and g is a scattering parameter. 4. Shading Application: Combine the phase function with lighting models. This can include Phong shading with multiple light sources or global illumination techniques. For shadows, a two-pass approach may be used: first render the volume from the light source using the absorption model to store light contribution, then apply this to the view pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class ScalarField: def init(self, data, spacing=1.0): self.data = data self.spacing = spacing self.shape = (len(data), len(data[0]), len(data[0][0])) def getvalue(self, x, y, z): ix, iy, iz = int(x / self.spacing), int(y / self.spacing), int(z / self.spacing) ix = max(0, min(ix, self.shape[0] - 1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, self.shape[1] - 1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, self.shape[2] - 1)) return self.data[ix][iy][iz] def computegradientshading(grid, rayorigin, raydir, lightpositions, isovalue, maxdist=100.0, step=0.01): # 1. Ray marching to find iso-surface intersection t = 0.0 point = None while t < maxdist: x, y, z = rayorigin[0] + t raydir[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydir[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydir[2] val = grid.getvalue(x, y, z) if abs(val - isovalue) < 1e-4: point = (x, y, z) break t += step if point is None: return None # 2. Gradient computation via central differencing eps = 0.01 dx = grid.getvalue(point[0]+eps, point[1], point[2]) - grid.getvalue(point[0]-eps, point[1], point[2]) dy = grid.getvalue(point[0], point[1]+eps, point[2]) - grid.getvalue(point[0], point[1]-eps, point[2]) dz = grid.getvalue(point[0], point[1], point[2]+eps) - grid.getvalue(point[0], point[1], point[2]-eps) gradlen = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if gradlen < 1e-6: normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) else: normal = (dx/gradlen, dy/gradlen, dz/gradlen) # 3. Phase function evaluation costheta = raydir[0]normal[0] + raydir[1]normal[1] + raydir[2]normal[2] costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) theta = math.acos(costheta) phase = (8.0 / (3.0 math.pi)) (math.sin(theta) + (math.pi - theta) math.cos(theta)) # 4. Shading application color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for lightpos in lightpositions: lightvec = (lightpos[0]-point[0], lightpos[1]-point[1], lightpos[2]-point[2]) lightlen = math.sqrt(lightvec[0]2 + lightvec[1]2 + lightvec[2]2) if lightlen < 1e-6: continue lightdir = (lightvec[0]/lightlen, lightvec[1]/lightlen, lightvec[2]/lightlen) diff = max(0.0, normal[0]lightdir[0] + normal[1]lightdir[1] + normal[2]lightdir[2]) color = (color[0] + diff phase, color[1] + diff phase, color[2] + diff phase) return color Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides intuitive depth cues; computationally efficient compared to full multiple scattering solutions; allows for standard surface shading techniques (Phong) to be applied to volumes. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that the volume can be approximated by an iso-surface or that local gradients are meaningful; may produce artifacts if the volume is noisy or has low resolution. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This technique originates from the need to enhance the visual quality of direct volume rendering by incorporating lighting models traditionally used for surfaces. The use of gradients for normal estimation in discrete volumes was established by Höhne and Bernstein. The application of Lambert's law derived phase functions for diffuse particles larger than the wavelength was described by Blinn. The integration of these concepts into volume rendering pipelines allows for the simulation of single-scattering effects and shadows, significantly improving the perceptibility of depth. name: Point Light Shading with Shadow Offset
body: This method computes direct illumination from a point light at a surface intersection point, incorporating shadow testing with a geometric offset to prevent self-shadowing artifacts such as shadow acne. It extends basic Lambert shading by introducing a bias term to the shadow ray origin to ensure robust occlusion detection. Inputs: Intersection point P on the surface. Surface normal N (normalized). Incoming camera ray direction V (normalized, pointing towards the surface). Light position L{pos} (world space). Light radiance L. Material reflectance fr. Shadow offset bias \epsilon. Outputs: Reflected radiance Lr at point P. Data Structures: Ray: Struct containing origin O and direction D. Intersection: Struct containing point P, normal N, and distance t. Parameters: \epsilon: Geometric bias for shadow ray origin. Typical value: 10^{-9}. fr: Diffuse material reflectance. Typical value: 1/\pi for ideal diffuse. Steps: 1. Compute intersection point P and surface normal N. 2. Compute light direction \vec{L}{dir} = L{pos} - P and squared distance d^2 = \|\vec{L}{dir}\|^2. 3. Apply a small offset to the shadow ray origin along the normal direction based on the sign of the dot product between the camera ray direction V and the normal N. 4. Trace a shadow ray to the light. 5. If the shadow ray hits an object closer than the light, mark as in shadow (\text{inShadow} = \text{true}). 6. Compute cosine term \cos\theta. 7. Calculate radiance using the point light formula. 8. Multiply by material reflectance. Formula: Lr = \text{clamp}\left( \frac{L \cdot fr \cdot \cos\theta \cdot (1 - \text{inShadow})}{d^2 \cdot 4\pi} \right) where L is light radiance, fr is material reflectance, \cos\theta is the clamped dot product of light direction and normal, \text{inShadow} is a boolean, and d is distance to light. Pitfalls: Shadow acne occurs when the shadow ray originates exactly on the surface. It is handled by shifting the origin along the normal by \epsilon, with direction determined by the sign of V \cdot N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointlightshadingwithshadowoffset(P, N, V, Lpos, L, fr, epsilon): # 1. Compute light direction and squared distance Ldir = Lpos - P dsq = dot(Ldir, Ldir) if dsq < 1e-12: return 0.0 d = sqrt(dsq) Ldirnorm = Ldir / d # 2. Determine shadow ray origin with offset # Direction determined by sign of dot product between camera ray (V) and normal (N) sign = 1.0 if dot(V, N) > 0.0 else -1.0 Oshadow = P + epsilon sign N # 3. Trace shadow ray # A step the sources do not give is a comment saying so. # hit = tracescene(shadowray, mint=epsilon, maxt=d) inshadow = False # Default state per standard ray tracing logic # 4. Compute cosine term costheta = max(0.0, dot(N, Ldirnorm)) # 5. Calculate radiance # Formula: Lr = clamp(L fr cosθ (1 - inShadow) / (d² 4π)) numerator = L fr costheta (1.0 if not inshadow else 0.0) denominator = dsq 4.0 3.14159265358979323846 if denominator == 0.0: return 0.0 Lr = numerator / denominator return max(0.0, min(1.0, Lr)) Time Complexity: O(1) shading calculation plus the cost of one shadow ray trace per point light. The shadow ray trace complexity depends on the scene acceleration structure (e.g., O(\log N) for BVH). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for local variables. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively reduces shadow acne artifacts common in basic shadow ray implementations. Limitations: The fixed offset \epsilon may cause "Peter Panning" (shadow detachment) if too large, or fail to prevent acne if too small. It does not account for soft shadows or penumbrae. When to use: Real-time rendering or offline rendering where point lights are used and shadow acne is a visible artifact. When not to use: When soft shadows are required, or when the offset causes noticeable visual artifacts due to large surface curvature or small feature sizes. This method is a practical extension of basic shadow ray shading, commonly found in ray tracing implementations to handle the numerical precision issues of floating-point arithmetic when testing for self-intersection. The specific implementation details, including the formula and offset logic, are documented in the VolumeSingleScattering repository by WangYue. wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Shading for Semi-Transparent Volumes
head: Local diffuse illumination for semi-transparent volumes, Semi-transparent volume shading with local diffuse illumination, Shaded semi-transparent volume rendering
body: Shading for Semi-Transparent Volumes is a technique that enables local diffuse illumination for semi-transparent volume rendering using multi-stage rasterization hardware, specifically leveraging register combiners. It solves the problem of computing per-voxel lighting without requiring a frame buffer copy or multi-pass rendering, allowing for interactive frame rates on early PC hardware. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by sacrificing real trilinear interpolation to fit gradient and color data into separate 2D textures, whereas alternatives like the method in [9] likely use 3D textures or multi-pass techniques to preserve interpolation quality. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset containing gradient vectors and scalar values (mapped to color/opacity). A light direction vector \mathbf{L}. Output: A shaded 2D image with alpha blending, where each fragment color includes ambient and diffuse components based on the local gradient. Data Structures The method requires two separate 2D textures to store volume data, as hardware limits input textures to two at a time, preventing real trilinear interpolation. 1. Texture 0 (Gradient Texture): Format: RGB. Content: Stores the gradient vector (\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}) for each voxel. Mapping: Gradient components are typically mapped to the range [0, 1] for RGB storage, as hardware combiners often expect unsigned normalized inputs. Note: Signed vector components are supported by hardware via specific combiner operations, avoiding large-scale workarounds. 2. Texture 1 (Color/Opacity Texture): Format: RGBA or Paletted (RGB indices + Alpha). Content: Stores the ambient color and opacity for each voxel. Mapping: The RGB channels store the ambient color C{ambient}. The Alpha channel stores the opacity \alpha. Constraint: The hardware does not provide a component-wise color lookup table. Therefore, it is not possible to use the alpha component as a color index to specify ambient color for each voxel independently if using a paletted texture for gradients. However, Texture 1 can be a paletted texture of color indices to save memory, with the same memory requirements as the isosurface algorithm (excluding the color table). Register Combiner Setup The shading is computed in a single pass using two combiner stages: General Combiner 0 and the Final Combiner. General Combiner 0: Input A: Texture 0 (Gradient vector \mathbf{G}). Input B: Light direction vector \mathbf{L} (passed as a constant or varying). Input C: ZERO. Operation: Computes the dot product \mathbf{G} \cdot \mathbf{L}. Output: A{comb0} = \mathbf{G} \cdot \mathbf{L}. Final Combiner: Input A: Output from General Combiner 0 (A{comb0}). Input B: Primary Color (Diffuse Color C{diffuse}). This is typically a constant color representing the light's diffuse intensity. Input C: ZERO. Input D: Texture 1 (Ambient Color C{ambient}). Operation: Sums the ambient color and the product of the diffuse color and the dot product. Output: C{final} = C{diffuse} \cdot (\mathbf{G} \cdot \mathbf{L}) + C{ambient}. Note on Formula: The source diagram shows the final combiner output as AB + (1-A)C + D. With C=ZERO, this simplifies to AB + D. Here, A is the dot product, B is the diffuse color, and D is the ambient color from Texture 1. Pseudocode The following pseudocode describes the configuration of the register combiners and the rendering loop. It assumes a fixed-function pipeline with multi-texturing support. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupshadingforsemitransparentvolumes(): """ Configures the register combiners for shaded semi-transparent volume rendering. Assumes hardware supports 2D multi-texturing and register combiners. """ # 1. Texture Setup # Texture 0: Gradient information (RGB) # Texture 1: Ambient color (RGB) and Opacity (Alpha) # Note: Real trilinear interpolation is not possible because hardware # only supports two input textures at a time. bindtexture(0, gradienttexture) # RGB: Gradient vector G bindtexture(1, coloropacitytexture) # RGBA: Ambient color Cambient, Alpha alpha # 2. General Combiner 0 Setup # Computes dot product of Light Vector (B) and Gradient from Texture 0 (A) setcombinerstage(0, inputa=TEXTURE0, inputb=LIGHTDIRECTION, inputc=ZERO, inputd=ZERO, operation=DOTPRODUCT) # Output of Stage 0: Adot = G. L # 3. Final Combiner Setup # Sums Ambient Color (D from Texture 1) and Diffuse Color (B) Dot Product (A from Stage 0) # Formula: Cfinal = Cdiffuse (G. L) + Cambient setcombinerstage(FINAL, inputa=COMBINER0OUTPUT, # The dot product inputb=DIFUSECOLOR, # Constant diffuse light color inputc=ZERO, inputd=TEXTURE1, # Ambient color from Texture 1 operation=COMBINEADD) # Final Output: RGB = Cdiffuse (G. L) + Cambient # Alpha is handled by standard alpha blending from Texture 1 # 4. Additional Light Support (Optional) # Variables C and D of the first combiner stage can be used to compute # diffuse illumination for a second colored light source, since the input # registers for secondary color and constant color 1 are unused. # This requires sacrificing either trilinear interpolation or separate # ambient/diffuse color specification if not using the two-texture approach. def rendervolumeslices(): """ Renders the volume using slice-based rendering with the configured shading. """ enablealphablending() enablemultitexturing() # For each slice in the volume: for slice in volumeslices: # Calculate cross-section of slicing plane with bounding box # Cut polygon into stripes # Specify alpha values for the slice # Apply multi-texture rendering # The fragment shader/combiner pipeline automatically computes shading # based on the gradient and light direction drawpolygonstripes(slice) Parameters and Typical Values Light Direction (\mathbf{L}): Typically normalized. Diffuse Color (C{diffuse}): Constant color, e.g., white (1, 1, 1) for neutral lighting. Ambient Color (C{ambient}): Per-voxel, stored in Texture 1. Gradient Mapping: Gradient components must be mapped to [0, 1] if the hardware combiner expects unsigned inputs, or handled via signed extensions if supported. Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Real Trilinear Interpolation: Because the hardware limits input textures to two, and both gradient and color/opacity must be stored separately, real trilinear interpolation of the volume data is not possible. This is the main drawback, leading to limited image quality compared to methods using 3D textures or multi-pass techniques. No Per-Voxel Ambient Color via Alpha Index: The hardware does not provide a component-wise color lookup table. It is not possible to use the alpha component as a color index to specify ambient color for each voxel independently if using a paletted texture for gradients. Signed Vector Components: While early workarounds were needed, modern (for the time) hardware supports signed vector components directly, avoiding large-scale workarounds. Limited Lighting: Adding a second colored diffuse light source requires sacrificing either trilinear interpolation or the specification of separate colors for ambient and diffuse light if not using the two-texture approach. Time and Memory Complexity Time Complexity: Single-pass rendering. The dot product is computed directly by hardware, avoiding multi-pass overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires two 2D textures. Memory requirements are similar to the isosurface algorithm, disregarding the memory allocated for the color table if a paletted texture is used for Texture 1. Measured Performance Performance on a GeForce 256 with a viewport size of 600 \times 600 pixels: 128 \times 128 \times 64: 22.5 fps 256 \times 256 \times 128: 4.1 fps 256 \times 256 \times 256: 2.0 fps Scaling Performance scales with resolution and viewport size. The method achieves interactive frame rates for moderate resolutions but degrades significantly for larger volumes due to the single-pass nature and texture bandwidth limitations. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Interactive frame rates via single-pass rendering; hardware-supported dot products; no large-scale workarounds for signed vector components. Limitations: Limited image quality due to missing real trilinear interpolation; inability to assign ambient color for every data value independently using RGB channels for gradient and alpha for opacity. When to Use Use this method when interactive frame rates are required on hardware with limited texturing units (e.g., early PC graphics cards) and when the loss of trilinear interpolation is acceptable. It is suitable for applications where local diffuse illumination is desired without the overhead of multi-pass rendering. When Not to Use Do not use this method when high image quality is critical, particularly if smooth interpolation is required. Alternatives using 3D textures or multi-pass techniques (like the method in [9]) should be considered if hardware supports them. Origin The technique was introduced in the context of interactive volume rendering on standard PC graphics hardware. It builds on the fast algorithm for displaying isosurfaces, adapting it for semi-transparent volume rendering by using alpha blending instead of alpha testing. History and Development The method was developed to leverage multi-stage rasterization hardware (register combiners) available on early PC GPUs (e.g., GeForce 256). It addresses the limitations of previous methods that required large-scale workarounds for signed vector components or multi-pass rendering. The authors note that future hardware would likely provide a higher number of texturing units or 3D-texturing capabilities, which would resolve the trilinear interpolation limitation. Applications The technique is used in medical imaging and scientific visualization, where interactive volume rendering is essential for multi-planar reformatting (MPR) and real-time exploration of 3D datasets. Interactive Volume Rendering On PC Hardware, http://gd.tuwien.ac.at/visual/OpenQVis/Publ.2000.5.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Interactive Volume Rendering on Standard PC Graphics..., https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/VolVisforPCHardware.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Cook-Torrance BRDF
head: GGX Cook-Torrance, Microfacet BRDF, PBR Lighting Model
body: The Cook-Torrance BRDF is a physically based rendering (PBR) lighting model for fully opaque materials that determines how light is reflected by a surface given its microgeometry and material type (metal or dielectric). It distinguishes between metals and dielectrics, conserves energy, and accurately represents real-world reflectance compared to older models like Phong. It sets itself apart from siblings like Shading models by explicitly modeling surface roughness via microfacets rather than empirical exponents, and from Whitted-Style Shading with Diffuse/Glossy Materials by providing a continuous, physically grounded specular lobe rather than discrete reflection rays. The model computes the outgoing radiance Lo as the sum of emitted light Le and reflected light, where reflected light is the integral of incoming light Li multiplied by the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) fr and the cosine of the incident angle: Lo = Le + \int{\Omega} fr Li (\omegai \cdot n) d\omegai where \Omega is the unit hemisphere aligned with the surface normal n, \omegai is the incoming light direction, and \omegao is the outgoing (view) direction. The BRDF fr is a weighted sum of a diffuse term and a specular term: fr = kd f{Lambert} + ks f{CookTorrance} where kd and ks are the weights for diffuse and specular components, respectively, constrained by kd + ks = 1 to ensure energy conservation. The diffuse term is the surface albedo c normalized for integration over the hemisphere: f{Lambert} = \frac{c}{\pi} The specular term f{CookTorrance} is defined as the product of three functions—Normal Distribution Function (D), Fresnel Function (F), and Geometry Function (G)—divided by four times the dot products of the normal with the outgoing and incoming directions: f{CookTorrance} = \frac{D F G}{4 (\omegao \cdot n) (\omegai \cdot n)} Inputs: Surface normal n (unit vector). Incoming light direction \omegai (unit vector, pointing towards the surface). Outgoing view direction \omegao (unit vector, pointing towards the camera). Roughness parameter \alpha (scalar, typically 0 \le \alpha \le 1). Base reflectivity F0 (vector, typically RGB). Surface albedo c (vector, typically RGB). Light radiance Li (vector). Emitted light Le (vector). Outputs: Outgoing radiance Lo (vector). No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard vector types (vec3, vec4) and scalar floats. The light attenuation model uses coefficients A{Constant}, A{Linear}, A{Quadratic} and light radius r. 1. Calculate Halfway Vector: Compute the normalized halfway vector h between the light direction l (equivalent to -\omegai in some conventions, but here defined as incoming light vector) and view vector v (equivalent to \omegao): h = \frac{l + v}{\|l + v\|} 2. Compute Normal Distribution Function (D): Use the Trowbridge-Reitz GGX approximation. The roughness parameter \alpha is often remapped from a user-facing roughness value r{user} as \alpha = r{user}^2. The formula is: D{GGX{TR}}(n, h, \alpha) = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi ((n \cdot h)^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1)^2} Note: Source provides the denominator as \pi (n \cdot h)^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1 without the square on the outer parenthesis, but standard GGX/Trowbridge-Reitz formulation implies the squared term in the denominator's main bracket or the square of the whole denominator term. Source explicitly writes: D{GGX{TR}}(n, h, \alpha) = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi (n \cdot h)^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1}. However, standard GGX is \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi ((n \cdot h)^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1)^2}. Source formula (22) is written as: D{GGX{TR}}(n, h, \alpha) = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi (n \cdot h)^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1}. This appears to be a typo in the source text missing the square on the denominator's main term or the parenthesis. Standard implementation uses the squared denominator. We follow the standard GGX form for correctness, noting the source discrepancy. 3. Compute Geometry Function (G): Use Schlick-GGX with Smith's method. First, compute the roughness parameter k from \alpha: k = \frac{(\alpha + 1)^2}{8} Then compute the geometry attenuation for a vector i (where i is either v or l): G{Schlick}(n, i, k) = \frac{n \cdot i}{(n \cdot i)(1 - k) + k} The total geometry function is the product of the view and light terms: G(n, v, l, \alpha) = G{Schlick}(n, v, k) G{Schlick}(n, l, k) 4. Compute Fresnel Function (F): Use the Fresnel-Schlick approximation. F0 is the base reflectivity (0.04 for non-metals, albedo for metals): F(h, v, F0) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - h \cdot v)^5 5. Combine Terms: Calculate the specular BRDF component: f{specular} = \frac{D F G}{4 (\omegao \cdot n) (\omegai \cdot n)} Calculate the diffuse BRDF component: f{diffuse} = \frac{c}{\pi} Determine weights. The diffuse weight kd is often derived from energy conservation as 1 - F (or 1 - F{average}), and ks = F. Specifically, kd = 1 - F and ks = F ensures conservation. fr = (1 - F) \frac{c}{\pi} + \frac{D F G}{4 (\omegao \cdot n) (\omegai \cdot n)} 6. Calculate Light Radiance Li: If using a point light with polynomial attenuation, calculate Li using light color l{dehomogenized}, distance d, light radius r, and attenuation coefficients A{Constant}, A{Linear}, A{Quadratic}: Li = l{dehomogenized} \frac{A{Constant} + d A{Linear} + d^2 A{Quadratic}}{r - d} where l{dehomogenized} is the light color vector (lr, lg, lb, lw) dehomogenized to RGB. 7. Calculate Outgoing Light: Integrate over the hemisphere (or sum for discrete lights): Lo = Le + \sum{lights} fr Li (\omegai \cdot n) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cooktorrancebrdf(n, l, v, roughness, F0, albedo, Le, lights): """ Compute outgoing radiance using Cook-Torrance BRDF. Args: n: Surface normal (vec3) l: Light direction vector (vec3, pointing TO surface) v: View direction vector (vec3, pointing TO camera) roughness: Scalar roughness parameter (0.0 to 1.0) F0: Base reflectivity (vec3) albedo: Surface color/albedo (vec3) Le: Emitted light (vec3) lights: List of light objects with pos, color, radius, attenuationcoeffs Returns: Lo: Outgoing radiance (vec3) """ # Normalize vectors n = normalize(n) l = normalize(l) v = normalize(v) # Halfway vector h = normalize(l + v) # Dot products ndotl = dot(n, l) ndotv = dot(n, v) ndoth = dot(n, h) hdotv = dot(h, v) # Cull backfacing surfaces if ndotl <= 0 or ndotv <= 0: return Le # Roughness remapping: alpha = roughness^2 alpha = roughness roughness # 1. Normal Distribution Function (GGX/Trowbridge-Reitz) # Standard GGX formula: alpha^2 / (pi ((n.h)^2 (alpha^2 - 1) + 1)^2) denom = (ndoth ndoth) (alpha alpha - 1.0) + 1.0 D = (alpha alpha) / (3.141592653589793 denom denom) # 2. Geometry Function (Schlick-GGX) k = (roughness + 1.0) (roughness + 1.0) / 8.0 G1v = ndotv / (ndotv (1.0 - k) + k) G1l = ndotl / (ndotl (1.0 - k) + k) G = G1v G1l # 3. Fresnel Function (Schlick) F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) pow(1.0 - hdotv, 5.0) # 4. Specular BRDF # Denominator: 4 (n.o) (n.i) # Here n.o is ndotv, n.i is ndotl speculardenom = 4.0 ndotv ndotl Fspecular = (D F G) / speculardenom # 5. Diffuse BRDF # Energy conservation: kd = 1 - F, ks = F # Diffuse term: (1 - F) albedo / pi diffuseterm = (1.0 - F) albedo / 3.141592653589793 # Total BRDF fr = diffuseterm + Fspecular # 6. Light Contribution Lo = Le for light in lights: # Calculate light radiance Li # Distance from surface to light # Assuming light.pos is the position of the light source # l is direction TO light, so light.pos = surface.pos + l dist # We need distance d. If l is normalized direction, we need d. # For point lights, l is usually (lightpos - surfacepos) / dist # Here we assume l is provided as normalized direction, so we need d from context. # If not provided, we assume d is available or light is directional (d=infinity). # For this implementation, we assume d is passed or calculated. # Let's assume d is available in light object or calculated. d = light.distancetosurface # Placeholder for actual distance calculation # Attenuation # Li = ldehomogenized (Aconst + dAlin + d^2Aquad) / (r - d) # Note: Source formula (28) has r - d in denominator. # This implies r > d. If d >= r, light is 0. if d >= light.radius: Li = vec3(0.0) else: # ldehomogenized is light.color (RGB) # Aconst, Alin, Aquad are light.attenuationcoeffs att = light.Aconstant + d light.Alinear + (d d) light.Aquadratic Li = light.color (att / (light.radius - d)) # Add contribution: fr Li (n. l) Lo += fr Li ndotl return Lo F0: Base reflectivity. Default value is 0.04 for non-metals. Equal to albedo for metallic surfaces (metalness=1). \alpha: Roughness parameter. Often remapped from user input roughness r as \alpha = r^2. A{Constant}, A{Linear}, A{Quadratic}: Polynomial attenuation model coefficients. r: Light radius. Backfacing: If n \cdot l < 0 or n \cdot v < 0, the surface is not visible to the light or camera. Return 0 or emitted light only. Light Radius: If distance d \ge r, the light contribution is zero to avoid division by zero or negative radiance. Precision: At grazing angles (h \cdot v \to 0), the Fresnel term approaches 1. Numerical stability in D calculation should handle small n \cdot h values. Metallic vs Dielectric: F0 must be set correctly. For metals, F0 is the albedo. For dielectrics, F0 is typically 0.04. A physically based rendering BRDF combining Cook-Torrance specular with Lambertian diffuse, featuring anisotropic GGX normal distribution function, Smith height-correlated geometry term, and Schlick Fresnel approximation. It calculates the specular component using anisotropic GGX NDF, geometry term using Smith height-correlated model, and Fresnel term using Schlick approximation. The diffuse component uses Lambertian model with energy-conserving division by \pi. It applies Fresnel-weighted energy conservation between the diffuse and specular lobes and uses roughness-aware Fresnel for environment map reflections. Time Complexity: O(1) per light per pixel, assuming a fixed number of lights. The cost is dominated by the evaluation of D, F, G functions. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for shading variables. Performance: More computationally expensive than Phong due to the evaluation of multiple transcendental functions (pow, sqrt, dot products). Strengths: Physically accurate, energy-conserving, handles a wide range of materials (metals, dielectrics, rough, smooth). Limitations: Does not account for subsurface scattering or complex inter-reflections within the material (requires additional models). Computationally heavier than empirical models. When to use: When physically accurate shading is required, especially for metallic and rough surfaces. When not to use: For stylized rendering where physical accuracy is not desired, or in real-time applications with extremely limited compute budget where Phong might suffice. The Cook-Torrance BRDF is based on the microfacet surface model. It was introduced by Cook and Torrance in 1982. It is a foundational model in Physically Based Rendering (PBR). It is widely used in modern real-time and offline renderers to simulate realistic lighting. name: Direct Lighting and Shading
head: Direct Lighting, Lambertian Diffuse with GGX Specular, Lighting and Shading
body: This method computes the direct illumination contribution for a surface or volume element by combining Lambertian diffuse reflection, an ambient floor, emissive terms, and a non-standard GGX-like specular highlight. It is distinguished from standard PBR implementations by its specific half-vector definition (H = \text{normalize}(L - V)) and its integration into voxel-based or splat-based rendering pipelines where immediate shading precedes rasterization or splatting. It serves as the local illumination component in broader light transport simulations, building on Lighting Models. Inputs: Surface normal N (unit vector). Light direction L (unit vector, pointing from surface to light). View direction V (unit vector, pointing from surface to camera). Light color/intensity C{light}. Material albedo \rho (diffuse reflectance). Material roughness \alpha (or similar parameter for specular width). Block type flag (e.g., BLOCKEMISSIVE). Emissive intensity C{emissive} (if applicable). Outputs: Final shaded color C{final} (linear HDR). Data Structures: No complex data structures required for the core shading calculation. Requires access to environment maps (for IBL variants) or light sources. Steps: 1. Compute Diffuse Term: Calculate the Lambertian diffuse contribution using the dot product of the normal and light direction. C{diffuse} = \max(N \cdot L, 0) \cdot C{light} 2. Compute Specular Term (Non-Standard GGX-like): Half-Vector: Compute the half-vector H using the non-standard definition: H = \text{normalize}(L - V) Note: Standard GGX uses H = \text{normalize}(L + V). This deviation may produce incorrect specular highlights relative to physical models. Fresnel Approximation: Apply Schlick's Fresnel approximation to determine reflectivity F. Let F0 be the base reflectivity (often 0.04 for dielectrics or derived from albedo for metals). F = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - H \cdot V)^5 Specular Intensity: Compute the specular term. While the exact GGX distribution term (D) and geometry term (G) are not fully specified in the primary source, the method implies a standard GGX-like structure scaled by F. C{specular} = F \cdot C{light} \cdot D(H, \alpha) \cdot G(...) 3. Add Emissive Contribution: If the surface block is marked as emissive (determined by hash functions hash13 and hash12 in voxel contexts), add the emissive intensity. C{emissive\term} = \begin{cases} C{emissive} & \text{if is\emissive} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 4. Combine and Tone Map: Sum the contributions and apply exponential tone mapping. C{lit} = C{diffuse} + C{specular} + C{emissive\term} + C{ambient} C{final} = 1 - \exp(-2 \cdot C{lit}) Parameters: Tone mapping constant: 2.0 Ambient floor: Not specified in sources. (Typically a small constant or sky color). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Half-Vector Definition: The use of L - V instead of L + V is a known deviation from standard GGX. Implementers must be aware this will not conserve energy or reflect light correctly according to standard microfacet theory unless specifically intended for a stylized look. Degenerate Normals: If N is zero or undefined, the diffuse term becomes 0. Voxel Interior Origins: If the ray origin is inside a voxel, the initial normal fallback is (0, 1, 0), which may be inaccurate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directlightingshading(N, L, V, Clight, rho, alpha, isemissive, Cemissive, Cambient): # 1. Diffuse Term ndotl = max(dot(N, L), 0.0) Cdiffuse = ndotl Clight # 2. Specular Term (Non-Standard GGX-like) # Note: H = normalize(L - V) is non-standard H = normalize(L - V) # Base reflectivity F0 # For dielectrics, F0 is typically 0.04. For metals, F0 = rho. # Assuming dielectric default if not specified F0 = 0.04 # Schlick Fresnel Approximation vdotH = dot(V, H) F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) pow(1.0 - vdotH, 5.0) # GGX-like specular intensity # D and G terms are not fully specified in, assuming standard GGX D and Schlick-G # This is a placeholder for the missing microfacet distribution details # In a full implementation, D(H, alpha) and G(N, L, V, alpha) would be calculated here. # For the purpose of this method description, we assume a simplified specular term # proportional to F Clight. # Standard GGX D term: alphasq = alpha alpha # denom = 4.0 pow(dot(N, H), 2.0) - 3.0 alphasq + 1.0 # D = alphasq / (3.14159 denom denom) if denom > 0 else 0 # Schlick-G geometry term # chi = max(dot(N, L), 0.0) # GL = chi / (chi (1.0 - alpha) + alpha) # chi = max(dot(N, V), 0.0) # GV = chi / (chi (1.0 - alpha) + alpha) # G = GL GV # Cspecular = F D G Clight # Simplified specular for direct implementation based on emphasis on F # Since D and G are not explicitly defined in, we cannot provide exact code. # We will assume a basic specular highlight for demonstration, noting the missing details. # [Comment: Exact D and G terms not provided in source. Implementation requires standard GGX D/G or stylized approximation.] Cspecular = F Clight 0.5 # Placeholder factor for missing D/G # 3. Emissive Term Cemissiveterm = Cemissive if isemissive else vec3(0.0) # 4. Combine Clit = Cdiffuse + Cspecular + Cemissiveterm + Cambient # 5. Tone Mapping Cfinal = 1.0 - exp(-2.0 Clit) return Cfinal A forward shading strategy where each surfel is shaded independently before rasterization using split-sum Image-Based Lighting (IBL), producing a linear HDR color value that enters the splatting pipeline. It separates the rendering equation into diffuse and specular components, allowing precomputed environment maps and BRDF LUTs to be used efficiently. Choose this when rendering large numbers of surfels with complex environment lighting in a splatting context. Formula: ck = kd \rho Ld(\mathbf{n}) + Ls(\mathbf{r}, r) (F0 \beta1 + \beta2) Where: ck: Outgoing radiance kd: Diffuse weight, kd = (1 - F0)(1 - \rho) \rho: Albedo Ld(\mathbf{n}): Diffuse irradiance from pre-convolved environment map along normal \mathbf{n} Ls(\mathbf{r}, r): Prefiltered specular radiance along reflection direction \mathbf{r} = 2(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{v} at MIP level determined by roughness F0: Base reflectivity, F0 = 0.04(1 - \rho) + \rho^2 \beta1, \beta2: Scale and bias from BRDF LUT indexed by (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}, \text{roughness}) A method for generating anisotropic specular highlights using the Disney roughness-to-alpha convention. It is used when stylized, anisotropic surface reflections are desired in voxel or ray-traced scenes. Time Complexity: O(1) per surface/volume element for the core shading calculation. Split-Sum IBL adds O(1) texture lookups (environment map + BRDF LUT). Memory Complexity: O(1) for local shading. Split-Sum IBL requires storage for environment maps and BRDF LUTs. Strengths: Simple to implement; Split-Sum IBL allows for efficient pre-filtering and avoids complex normal filtering issues in splatting. Limitations: The non-standard half-vector definition in the base method may lead to physically inaccurate specular highlights. Atmosphere and lighting approximations (e.g., single-step integration) may lack fidelity in complex scenes. When to use: Real-time voxel rendering, stylized graphics, or when integrating with splat-based forward rendering pipelines. When not to use: Physically accurate offline rendering requiring strict energy conservation and standard microfacet theory. The base method originates from a GLSL voxel-world shader implementation, utilizing a non-standard GGX-like specular term and exponential tone mapping. The Split-Sum IBL variant is derived from 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering (3DSS), which adopts the split-sum approximation for efficient forward shading of surfels. The Anisotropic Specular Highlights variant is associated with the Disney roughness-to-alpha convention in voxel raytracing contexts. name: Whitted-Style Shading with Diffuse/Glossy Materials
head: Diffuse Reflection, Lambertian reflection, Whitted-Style Shading
body: Whitted-style shading with diffuse/glossy materials computes the color of a ray intersection by combining ambient lighting with direct illumination from light sources, using a simplified reflectance model for surfaces. It differs from full path tracing by limiting recursion to a single bounce (or fixed depth) and using analytical approximations for specular/glossy reflections rather than stochastic sampling, and it differs from pure local illumination models by explicitly casting shadow rays to determine visibility. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray \vec{r} (origin \vec{o}, direction \vec{d}), a scene containing a list of objects (objList) and light sources (LightSourceList), and material properties for each object. Output: A color value (RGB) representing the radiance at the intersection point. Data Structures: Ray: Contains origin \vec{o}, direction \vec{d}, minimum distance minT, maximum distance maxT, and recursion depth. Shape: Represents an object in the scene, providing intersection methods and material properties. Material: Contains diffuse coefficient, emissive status, and methods to compute reflectance. LightSource: Represents a light emitter in the scene. Steps: 1. Intersection: Find the closest intersection between the input ray and any object in objList. If no intersection is found, return the background color. 2. Emissive Check: If the intersected object's material is emissive, return its emissive radiance. 3. Ambient Contribution: Initialize the color to zero. Add an ambient term calculated as ambientconstant diffusecoefficient. The default ambientconstant is (0.25, 0.25, 0.25). 4. Direct Illumination: For each light source in LightSourceList: a. Calculate the vector from the intersection point to the light source. b. Compute the reflectance using the material's getReflectance method, passing the surface normal, view direction, and light direction. c. Cast a shadow ray from the intersection point to the light source. Set the shadow ray's maxT to the distance to the light source. d. If the shadow ray does not intersect any object (i.e., the light is visible), add the reflected radiance to the total color. 5. Glossy Reflection (Optional): If the material has a glossy component, compute the reflection direction \vec{R} based on the surface normal and view direction. Distribute outgoing rays around \vec{R} using a shininess exponent \alpha to model rough surface reflections. Formulas: Lambertian Diffuse Reflection: The reflected radiance Lr(\vec{\omega}r) is given by: Lr(\vec{\omega}r) = \frac{\rho}{\pi} \int{\Omegai} Li(\vec{\omega}i) \cos \thetai d\omegai where \rho is the material reflectance fraction, Li(\vec{\omega}i) is the incident radiance, \thetai is the angle between the incident direction and the surface normal, and the integral is over the hemisphere \Omegai. The BRDF fr is constant and related to \rho by \rho = \pi fr. Glossy Reflection: The contribution is approximated by: Lr(\vec{\omega}r) = Lr d\omegar (\max(\vec{R} \cdot \vec{\omega}r), 0)^\alpha where \vec{R} is the perfect mirror reflection vector, \vec{\omega}r is the view direction, and \alpha is the shininess exponent. Parameters: ambientconstant: Default (0.25, 0.25, 0.25). \alpha (shininess): Controls the narrowness of glossy highlights; higher values yield sharper highlights. Epsilon: 10^{-4}, used to offset shadow ray origins to prevent self-intersection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Shadowing: Shadow rays must be offset from the surface point by a small epsilon to avoid intersecting the surface they originated from. Negative Dot Products: In glossy reflection, dot products between \vec{R} and \vec{\omega}r must be clamped to 0, \infty) to handle cases where the reflection direction is behind the surface. Emissive Objects: Emissive objects should return their radiance directly without further shading calculations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def whittedshading(ray, scene): # 1. Find closest intersection hit = getclosestintersection(ray, scene.objectsList) # 2. No intersection: return background if hit is None: return scene.backgroundcolor # 3. Emissive material: return emissive radiance if hit.material.isemissive: return hit.material.emissiveradiance # 4. Initialize color with ambient contribution color = Vector3D(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) ambientconstant = Vector3D(0.25, 0.25, 0.25) color += ambientconstant hit.material.diffusecoefficient # 5. Direct illumination from lights for light in scene.lightSourceList: # Calculate vector to light lightdir = light.position - hit.point distance = lightdir.length() lightdir = lightdir.normalize() # Get reflectance reflectance = hit.material.getreflectance( hit.normal, ray.direction, lightdir) # Cast shadow ray shadoworigin = hit.point + hit.normal Epsilon shadowray = Ray(shadoworigin, lightdir, ray.depth + 1, Epsilon, distance) shadowhit = getclosestintersection(shadowray, scene.objectsList) # If light is visible, add contribution if shadowhit is None: color += reflectance light.intensity / (distance 2) return color A simplified variant that returns emissive radiance or diffuse reflectance based on material properties, using shadow rays to determine direct light visibility. It finds the closest intersection, checks for emissive materials, and if no intersection is found, returns the background color. Models reflections on rough surfaces by distributing outgoing rays around the perfect mirror reflection direction, controlled by a shininess exponent \alpha. It computes the dot product between the reflection vector \vec{R} and view direction \vec{\omega}r, clamps it to [0, \infty), and raises it to the power of \alpha to determine the intensity of the glossy highlight. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of light sources and objects in the scene for each ray, due to intersection tests and shadow ray casts. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of objects and lights stored in the scene. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides visually plausible results for scenes with few light sources; efficient for real-time rendering. Limitations: Does not account for indirect lighting (global illumination) beyond direct shadows; glossy reflections are approximated and may not be physically accurate for complex rough surfaces. When to Use: Suitable for real-time applications or scenes where [direct lighting and shadows are the primary visual concerns. When Not to Use: Unsuitable for scenes requiring accurate global illumination, such as those with significant color bleeding or complex inter-reflections. The concept of Lambertian diffuse reflection, where apparent brightness is independent of observer and light source positions, has been a fundamental model in computer graphics since the early days of rendering. Whitted-style shading, named after Turner Whitted's 1980 paper "An Improved Illumination Model for Shaded Display," introduced recursive ray tracing for specular reflections and shadows. The specific implementation with diffuse/glossy materials and ambient lighting as described here is commonly found in educational ray tracers and early real-time rendering systems.
