name: Two-Pass Shadow Casting (Kajiya and Von Herzen)
head: Kajiya and Von Herzen Method, Shadow Calculation via Illumination Pass, Shadow Casting via Two-Pass Method, Two-Pass Numerical Algorithm for Shadows, Two-Pass Numerical Shadow Algorithm
body: Two-Pass Shadow Casting is a numerical algorithm for computing shadows in volume rendering by explicitly accounting for the transparency of participating media between a light source and a surface point, and between that point and the viewpoint. It solves the problem of realistic shadowing in scenes containing smoke, fog, clouds, or turbid water, where standard opaque shadow techniques fail to capture the attenuation of light through the volume. Unlike recursive ray tracing, which sends discrete "shadow feelers" to the light source at each point along the primary ray, this method integrates the shadowing effect continuously along the ray. It is distinguished from its sibling Shadow Ray Casting by its volumetric integration approach and from Shadow Mapping by its direct handling of participating media density rather than depth buffers. The method decomposes the rendering equation into two sequential passes: an illumination pass and a gathering (radiance) pass. It assumes single scattering, meaning it accounts for only one reflection or scattering event from the illumination ray to the observer. Inputs: Volume density field \tau(X), defined over a 3D domain. Light source intensity L (assumed infinite/directional in direction -\omega'). Viewpoint position X and viewing direction \omega. Shading rule r(X, \omega, \omega'), typically a phase function (e.g., Henyey-Greenstein). Background intensity I0. Ray length D (distance from viewpoint to the far edge of the volume). Outputs: Final pixel intensity I(X). Volume Grid: A 3D array storing the extinction coefficient \tau at voxel centers or corners. Illumination Buffer: A 3D array (same dimensions as the volume) storing the computed illumination i(X, \omega') for each voxel. This buffer is the output of Pass 1 and input to Pass 2. 1. Pass 1: Compute Illumination i(X, \omega') Calculate the illumination reaching each point X in the volume from the light source. For an infinite light source in direction -\omega', the illumination is: i(X, \omega') = L \exp\left(-\int0^\infty \tau(X - t\omega') dt\right) In practice, the integral runs only to the edge of the data volume. Implementation Detail: Propagate flux from the light source through the volume one voxel layer at a time. For each layer, account for the layer's transparency before propagating to the next. This is numerically approximated using a Riemann sum or similar integration along rays parallel to -\omega'. 2. Pass 2: Gather Radiance I(X) Scatter the computed illumination to the viewpoint. The shading rule is defined as: g(X, \omega) = r(X, \omega, \omega') i(X, \omega') where g(X, \omega) is the reflected/scattered intensity at X towards the viewpoint. The final intensity I(X) is gathered along the viewing ray from the viewpoint X in direction \omega. Using reversed ray parametrization (where s starts at the viewpoint and goes out in direction -\omega, reaching X - s\omega at distance s), the equation is: I(X) = I0 \exp\left(-\int0^D \tau(X - t\omega) dt\right) + \int0^D g(X - s\omega) \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(X - t\omega) dt\right) ds Substituting the expressions for g and i, the full equation becomes: I(X) = I0 \exp\left(-\int0^D \tau(X - t\omega) dt\right) + \int0^D r(X - s\omega, \omega, \omega') L \exp\left(-\int0^\infty \tau(X - sw - t\omega') dt\right) \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(X - t\omega) dt\right) ds Implementation Detail: For each pixel, trace a ray from the viewpoint. At each sample point along the ray, retrieve the pre-computed illumination i from the buffer, apply the phase function r, and accumulate the result weighted by the transmittance from the viewpoint to that point. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twopassshadowcasting(volume, lightdirection, viewdirection, viewpoint, phasefunction, backgroundintensity): """ volume: 3D array of extinction coefficients tau(X) lightdirection: vector omega' (direction of light propagation is -omega') viewdirection: vector omega viewpoint: 3D point X phasefunction: function r(X, omega, omega') backgroundintensity: float I0 """ # Pass 1: Compute Illumination Buffer # Initialize buffer with zeros illuminationbuffer = create3darraylike(volume) # Propagate light through volume along -lightdirection # For each voxel X in the volume: for X in volume.voxels(): # Calculate optical depth from light source to X # Integral from 0 to infinity (clamped to volume bounds) opticaldepth = 0.0 t = 0.0 stepsize = volume.stepsize() # Trace ray from X backwards along lightdirection (towards light) # Stop when leaving volume currentpos = X while currentpos is insidevolume(): # Add contribution of current segment tauval = volume.get(currentpos) opticaldepth += tauval stepsize # Move towards light source currentpos = currentpos - lightdirection stepsize # Compute illumination i(X, omega') # L is assumed to be 1.0 for normalized intensity, or passed as parameter L = 1.0 illuminationbuffer.set(X, L exp(-opticaldepth)) # Pass 2: Gather Radiance along viewing rays finalimage = create2darray() for pixel in imagepixels(): rayorigin = viewpoint raydir = viewdirection accumulatedintensity = 0.0 transmittancefromviewpoint = 1.0 t = 0.0 stepsize = volume.stepsize() # Trace ray from viewpoint forward # s is distance from viewpoint currentpos = rayorigin while t < D and currentpos is insidevolume(): # Get pre-computed illumination at this point # Note: illuminationbuffer stores i(X, omega') ival = illuminationbuffer.get(currentpos) # Apply shading rule: g(X, omega) = r(X, omega, omega') i(X, omega') # r depends on scattering angle between viewdir and lightdir gval = phasefunction(currentpos, raydir, lightdirection) ival # Accumulate scattered light, weighted by transmittance from viewpoint # Term: g(X - somega) exp(-int0^s tau(X - tomega) dt) accumulatedintensity += gval transmittancefromviewpoint stepsize # Update transmittance from viewpoint to next point tauval = volume.get(currentpos) transmittancefromviewpoint = exp(-tauval stepsize) # Advance ray currentpos = currentpos + raydir stepsize t += stepsize # Add background intensity attenuated by total transmittance finalintensity = backgroundintensity transmittancefromviewpoint + accumulatedintensity finalimage.set(pixel, finalintensity) return finalimage Light Source: The derivation assumes an infinite (directional) light source. For point lights, the integral limits and geometry must be adjusted. Volume Bounds: The illumination integral \int0^\infty is truncated to the edge of the data volume. Single Scattering: The method is a single-scattering model. It is only valid if the albedo or density is low, so that multiple scattering is unlikely. It is not suitable for highly scattering media like atmospheric clouds where multiple scattering is significant. Amortization: The illumination pass can be amortized over several animated frames if only the viewpoint moves, as the illumination i(X, \omega') depends only on the light direction and volume, not the view. Adapts the Kajiya and von Herzen two-pass algorithm to spectral representation, handling wavelength-dependent opacity and emission spectra for effects like fluorescence. Time Complexity: The two-pass method takes only twice as long as the gathering pass without shadows. Pass 1 requires tracing rays parallel to the light direction through the volume; Pass 2 requires tracing rays from the viewpoint. Memory Complexity: Requires an additional 3D buffer to store the illumination i(X, \omega') for every voxel in the volume. Strengths: Provides physically accurate shadows in participating media; amortizable over frames for static volumes; simpler than full recursive ray tracing for single scattering. Limitations: Single-scattering approximation limits accuracy in dense or highly scattering media (e.g., thick clouds); requires significant memory for the illumination buffer; not suitable for dynamic volumes without recomputing Pass 1. When to Use: Photorealistic rendering of opaque objects in smoke, fog, or turbid water where single scattering is a reasonable approximation. Used in the "Heidelberg ray tracing model" for medical images. When Not to Use: Highly scattering media where multiple scattering is dominant; real-time applications with limited memory; dynamic volumes where recomputing illumination is too expensive. The two-pass numerical algorithm was suggested by Kajiya and Von Herzen. It was introduced in the context of optical models for direct volume rendering. The method was applied in the "Heidelberg ray tracing model" by Meinzer et al. for medical images. While its utility in general volume rendering applications has been questioned due to the single-scattering limitation, it remains a foundational technique for shadow calculation in participating media. name: Two-pass Spectral Rendering Integral
head: Noordmans Spectral Shadow Algorithm, Spectral Two-Pass Shadow Casting
body: The Two-pass Spectral Rendering Integral is a method for computing volumetric shadows in participating media by adapting the Kajiya and von Herzen two-pass algorithm to spectral representation. It separates shadow computation (illumination phase) from radiance accumulation (radiation phase), allowing for the simulation of complex spectral effects such as fluorescence and phosphorescence. It is distinguished from its parent Two-Pass Shadow Casting (Kajiya and Von Herzen) by its explicit handling of wavelength-dependent opacity and emission spectra. Inputs: Volume density field \rhom(x) for each material m. Spectral absorption attributes \kappam(\lambda) for each material m. Incident light spectrum It(x, \lambda) at the volume entry. Local emission spectrum Ie(x, \lambda). Step size \Delta x. Wavelengths \lambda. Outputs: Final radiance Ir(x, \lambda) for each sample point. Data Structures: Spectral opacity \tau(x, \lambda): Computed per sample point. Transmitted light It(x, \lambda): Accumulator for the illumination phase. Backward irradiance Ib(x, \lambda): Accumulator for the radiation phase. Radiance Ir(x, \lambda): Output accumulator. Spectral Opacity Definition: For a position x with M materials, the spectral opacity is defined as: \tau(x, \lambda) = \sum{m=1}^M \rhom(x) \cdot \kappam(\lambda) Algorithm Steps: 1. Illumination Phase (Shadow Computation): Propagate light flux through the volume using discrete ray casting from front to back. For each sample step \Delta x at position x, update the transmitted light It: It(x + \Delta x, \lambda) = It(x, \lambda) \cdot (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau(x, \lambda)) The resulting It at the end of the ray represents the shadowed incident light for the radiation phase. Note that the term (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau(x, \lambda)) is an approximation. 2. Radiation Phase (Radiance Accumulation): Accumulate radiance using back-to-front ray casting. For each sample step \Delta x at position x, update the radiance Ir based on the local emission Ie and the backward irradiance Ib (which represents the light arriving from the previous sample in the back-to-front direction, effectively the shadowed light computed in phase 1): Ib(x+\Delta x, \lambda) = Ir(x, \lambda) = Ie(x, \lambda) + Ib(x, \lambda) \cdot (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau(x, \lambda)) Here, Ib(x, \lambda) acts as the accumulated background/transmitted light term. The term (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau(x, \lambda)) is again an approximation. Emission Function: The local emission Ie(x, \lambda) is split into two components: Elastic Scattering: Scattering in a chromatic medium where each material m is associated with a specific spectral band, facilitating a spectral transfer function. Inelastic Scattering: Absorption of light at one wavelength and re-emission at another, simulating fluorescence and phosphorescence. Pitfalls: The term (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau(x, \lambda)) used in both phases is only an approximation of the exponential attenuation e^{-\tau \Delta x}. For large \tau or \Delta x, this can lead to inaccuracies. The method relies on a local illumination model (e.g., Phong) for scattered radiance from external illumination, which may not capture global illumination effects accurately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twopassspectralrendering(volume, materials, incidentlight, stepsize, wavelengths): """ volume: 3D grid of material indices or densities materials: list of material objects with getabsorption(wavelength) incidentlight: function or array giving It at entry stepsize: float Delta x wavelengths: list of lambda values """ # Precompute spectral opacity for all voxels # tau[x, y, z, widx] = sum(rhom kappam(lambdaw)) tau = computespectralopacity(volume, materials, wavelengths) numsamples = len(wavelengths) numvoxels = volume.shape[0] volume.shape[1] volume.shape[2] # Phase 1: Illumination (Front-to-Back) # It accumulates transmitted light It = np.zeros((numvoxels, numsamples)) It[0] = incidentlight # Initial incident light at entry for i in range(1, numvoxels): # Approximation: It(x + dx) = It(x) (1 - dx tau(x)) # Note: The source formula uses tau(x) for the step from x to x+dx attenuation = 1.0 - stepsize tau[i-1] # tau at previous voxel # Clamp to avoid negative values due to approximation attenuation = np.maximum(attenuation, 0.0) It[i] = It[i-1] attenuation # Phase 2: Radiation (Back-to-Front) # Ib accumulates backward irradiance (shadowed light) # Ir is the final radiance Ib = np.zeros((numvoxels, numsamples)) Ir = np.zeros((numvoxels, numsamples)) # Initialize Ib at the back of the ray (no incoming light from behind) # Assuming no background light from behind, Ib at last voxel is 0 # Or if there is background, it should be added here. # The source implies Ib(x) is the irradiance arriving from previous sample. # In back-to-front, the "previous" sample is the one further back. # So Ib at the last voxel (back) is 0 (or background). for i in range(numvoxels - 1, -1, -1): # Local emission Ie(x, lambda) Ie = computeemission(volume[i], wavelengths) # Includes elastic and inelastic # Attenuation factor attenuation = 1.0 - stepsize tau[i] attenuation = np.maximum(attenuation, 0.0) # Ib(x+dx) in source notation corresponds to Ib at the next voxel in back-to-front order # Let's align with source: Ib(x+dx) = Ir(x) = Ie(x) + Ib(x) (1 - dx tau(x)) # This notation is confusing. Let's interpret physically: # Radiance at x = Emission at x + Transmitted Radiance from behind x. # Transmitted Radiance from behind = Ibbehind (1 - dx tau(x)) # So if we iterate back-to-front, let Ibprev be the accumulated radiance from behind. if i == numvoxels - 1: Ibprev = 0.0 # No light from behind else: Ibprev = Ir[i+1] # Radiance from the voxel further back Ir[i] = Ie + Ibprev attenuation Ib[i] = Ir[i] # Store as backward irradiance for next step (which is actually the next in front-to-back, but we are going back-to-front) return Ir def computespectralopacity(volume, materials, wavelengths): tau = np.zeros((volume.shape[0], volume.shape[1], volume.shape[2], len(wavelengths))) for x in range(volume.shape[0]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for z in range(volume.shape[2]): matidx = volume[x, y, z] for widx, lam in enumerate(wavelengths): rho = getdensity(volume, x, y, z, matidx) # Assuming density retrieval kappa = materials[matidx].getabsorption(lam) tau[x, y, z, widx] = rho kappa return tau def computeemission(voxeldata, wavelengths): # Placeholder for specific emission logic based on elastic/inelastic # Returns array of size len(wavelengths) return np.zeros(len(wavelengths)) Time Complexity: O(N \cdot W), where N is the number of sample points along rays and W is the number of wavelengths. Two passes are required. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot W) for storing opacity and radiance/irradiance buffers. Strengths: Allows for spectral effects like fluorescence and material-specific absorption. Simple to implement as it builds on the standard two-pass approach. Limitations: The linear approximation (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau) can be inaccurate for high opacity or large step sizes. Relies on local illumination model for scattered light, missing global illumination effects. When to use: When spectral accuracy is required for shadows and emission, and global illumination is not critical or is approximated locally. When not to use: When high accuracy in shadow boundaries is needed with large step sizes, or when global illumination effects are significant. The method was proposed by Noordmans et al., who adopted the Kajiya and von Herzen two-pass algorithm for volumetric shadows and adapted the notion of opacity to a spectral representation. It is described in the context of local and global illumination in the volume rendering integral. name: Ambient Light Approximation
head: Ambient Lighting for Volume Clouds, Sky Ambient, Upwards Ray Approximation
body: Ambient Light Approximation simulates indirect sky illumination in participating media by integrating the entire sky hemisphere into a single upward-pointing light value, weighted by local cloud density to simulate self-shadowing. Unlike full multiple scattering or complex irradiance tables, it uses a single precalculated or sampled upward ray to approximate the diffuse fill light, preventing the underside of clouds from appearing unnaturally dark. It differs from Ambient Occlusion via Geometry/Neighbors by relying on volumetric density rather than surface geometry, and from Bruneton-style Sky Irradiance by using a simplified single-ray model instead of a multi-dimensional lookup table. Inputs: Current sample position in the volume. Cloud density profile or distance-to-edge field (to determine local opacity/shadowing). Ambient light color/intensity (either a fixed color, pre-integrated sky value, or sampled from a LUT/probe). Transmissance accumulated so far along the view ray. Step size of the current ray march. Outputs: Added ambient light contribution to the current sample's light accumulation. Data Structures: Sky Light Value: A single RGB color vector representing the integrated sky hemisphere. This can be a constant, a value from a pre-integrated sky model, or a sample from a SkyLightLut. Ambient Density Field: A lower-resolution grid or texture storing the summed density along the upward ray for each voxel. This is precalculated for static grids. Ambient Occlusion (AO) Map: A texture (e.g., Cloud Lut B channel) storing altitude-based AO values. Steps: 1. Determine Ambient Light Color: If atmospheric scattering is enabled, sample the SkyLightLut (generated via UE4 atmospheric scattering methods) to get the ambient light color. If atmospheric scattering is disabled, sample a baked Ambient Probe encoded with 3rd-order Spherical Harmonics (SH). Alternatively, use a fixed color resembling the sky. 2. Calculate Shadowing Factor: Compute the shadowing factor based on the accumulated density along an upward ray from the current sample position. Let D{up} be the summed density of the upward ray. This value can be retrieved from a precalculated texture or computed by marching a single ray upward. The shadowing factor is typically modeled as \exp(-D{up}). Optionally, modulate this by a profile function (e.g., \sqrt{\text{profile}}) to adjust falloff at cloud edges. 3. Calculate Altitude-Based AO (Optional/Engine Specific): Determine an altitude factor that starts at a user-defined value at the cloud bottom and increases to 1 as altitude increases. Multiply this factor by the Cloud Lut B channel's AO value. 4. Compute Ambient Contribution: Combine the ambient light color, shadowing factor, and AO. Formula: L{ambient} = L{sky} \cdot \exp(-D{up}) \cdot AO{factor} Where L{sky} is the ambient light color, D{up} is the upward density, and AO{factor} is the altitude-based AO. 5. Accumulate: Add the ambient contribution to the sample light, scaled by transmissance, sample density, and step size. Formula: L{total} += L{ambient} \cdot T \cdot \rho \cdot \Delta s Where T is transmissance, \rho is sample density, and \Delta s is step size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeambientlight(samplepos, transmissance, sampledensity, stepsize, ambientlightcolor): # 1. Get upward density (precalculated or sampled) # In a real implementation, this might be a texture lookup or a single ray march upwarddensity = getupwarddensity(samplepos) # 2. Calculate shadowing factor # Using exponential attenuation based on upward density shadowfactor = exp(-upwarddensity) # Optional: Modulate by profile for edge falloff # profilevalue = getcloudprofile(samplepos) # shadowfactor = sqrt(profilevalue) # 3. Get AO factor (if using altitude-based AO) # altitudefactor = mapaltitudetoao(samplepos.y) # 0 at bottom, 1 at top # aotexturevalue = samplecloudlutb(samplepos) # aofactor = altitudefactor aotexturevalue # For simplicity, assuming aofactor is 1 if not using altitude AO aofactor = 1.0 # 4. Compute ambient light contribution ambientcontribution = ambientlightcolor shadowfactor aofactor # 5. Accumulate into total light # Note: In a ray marching loop, this is added to the current sample's light # before being multiplied by transmissance and density for the final color return ambientcontribution transmissance sampledensity stepsize Parameters: Ambient Light Color: Can be a fixed RGB value or sampled from a LUT. Saturation Adjustment: An artist parameter to adjust the saturation of the ambient light color to correct for an overly blue tint caused by ignoring multiple scattering. Cloud Bottom AO Value: A user-defined value for the AO factor at the cloud bottom. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blue Tint: Ignoring multiple scattering in ambient light can cause clouds to appear too blue. Mitigation: Adjust ambient light saturation. Performance: Shooting actual rays in random directions for ambient light is too expensive or noisy. The upward ray approximation is necessary for performance. Resolution: The upward density data is naturally blurry and can be stored in a lower-resolution grid without significant visual loss. An atmosphere pass that builds a sky irradiance table to provide sky light from each surface's own sky, ensuring ground seen from orbit keeps its sky fill and terrain past the terminator is not lit by the eye's daylight. It differs from the single-ray approximation by using a multi-dimensional lookup table. Definition: A deferred lighting technique that looks up each pixel's own altitude and sun angle from a precomputed sky irradiance table. Data Structure: Sky irradiance table covers 16 altitudes by 24 sun cosines, with 6 symmetric L2 harmonics per entry in the local frame. Published as a uniform atmosphereskytable. Performance: DeferredLight costs 0.60 ms. When to choose: When high-fidelity sky lighting is required for terrain or surfaces at various altitudes and sun angles, especially in planetary rendering contexts. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample for the ambient contribution if the upward density is precalculated and stored in a texture. If the upward ray is marched per sample, it adds O(N{up}) where N{up} is the number of steps in the upward ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for storing the precalculated upward density grid, where V is the number of voxels. The grid can be lower resolution than the main volume due to the blurry nature of the data. Measured Performance: DeferredLight using Bruneton-style irradiance costs 0.60 ms. Strengths: Computationally efficient compared to full multiple scattering or random ray sampling for ambient light. Provides realistic shadowing for cloud undersides. Limitations: Approximates the sky hemisphere as a single upward ray, which may not capture complex indirect lighting scenarios. Can result in an overly blue tint if multiple scattering is not accounted for. When to use: Real-time volume cloud rendering where performance is critical and full multiple scattering is too expensive. When not: When high-fidelity global illumination or complex indirect lighting effects are required. The ambient light approximation for volume clouds was described by Jack Tollenaar in an unofficial article on volumetric cloud rendering. It is also referenced in a Chinese article on volume cloud implementation, which discusses sampling from a SkyLightLut or Ambient Probe and adjusting for blue tint. The Bruneton-style sky irradiance table is part of the Helio project's voxel planet lighting, described in a GitHub pull request. name: Ray-marched Volumetric Lighting with Density Thresholding
head: Light Intensity Volume, Volumetric Light Map Precomputation
body: This method precomputes light intensities and shadows within a 3D volume based on a light source direction, color, decay, and a density mask, storing the result in a 3D texture for use during rendering. It differs from real-time ray marching by performing the light transport calculation offline (or in a dedicated compute pass) to decouple lighting cost from scene complexity, using density thresholding to filter noise and simulate god rays. Inputs: lightmapresolution: Vector3 defining the resolution of the output 3D light map volume. lightdensitytexture: Input 3D texture containing the scene density. masktexture3D: Input 3D texture acting as a density mask. noisetexture3D: Input 3D texture containing noise values (e.g., Worley noise) used to modulate density. globallightdirection: Normalized Vector3 defining the direction of the light source. globallightcolor: Vector3 defining the color of the light. lightdecay: Float controlling the rate of exponential light attenuation per unit density. Range [0, 100]. godraysintensity: Float scalar applied to density values below the threshold when accumulated density is low to simulate god rays. Range [0, 0.03]. lightsamplecount: Integer, number of samples for light computation. Range [0, 128]. densitythreshold: Float, density threshold for light computation. Range [0, 1]. Outputs: lightmap3D: A 3D RenderTexture (Format R8, Wrap Clamp, Filter Bilinear) storing the final light intensity for each voxel. Data Structures: The core data structure is the lightmap3D volume. Each voxel stores a single R8 (8-bit red) value representing the accumulated light intensity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create lightmap3D with dimensions lightmapresolution. Calculate stepsize as 1.0 / \text{light\sample\count}. Calculate scaledstepsize as \text{light\texture\dims}.x \times \text{step\size}. Set maxiteration to 256. Dispatch the compute kernel computelightintensities with thread groups sized \lceil \text{light\map\resolution}.x / 8 \rceil, \lceil \text{light\map\resolution}.y / 8 \rceil, \lceil \text{light\map\resolution}.z / 8 \rceil. 2. Per-Voxel Ray Marching (Compute Kernel): For each voxel identified by id (current coordinates): Initialize densitysofar = 0.0f, lightintensity = 1.0f. Normalize globallightdirection. Loop while maxiteration > 0 and the ray is within bounds: 1. Sample Density: Map current coordinates to noise space: noiseid = lightidtonoiseid(currentcoordinates). Map current coordinates to mask space: maskid = lightidtomaskid(currentcoordinates). noisedensity = noisetexture3D[noiseid]. maskvalue = masktexture3D[maskid]. 2. Apply Mask and Threshold: density = min(1.0f, maskvalue - abs(densitythreshold)) noisedensity. densitysofar += density. 3. God Rays Logic: If density < densitythreshold AND densitysofar < 0.5: density = godraysintensity. Else if density < densitythreshold: density = 0.0f. 4. Attenuation: Update light intensity using Beer-Lambert-like exponential decay: \text{light\intensity} = \text{light\intensity} \times \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{light\decay} \times \text{step\size}) 5. Advance Ray: currentcoordinates += -globallightdirection scaledstepsize. Check boundary conditions: isoutofbounds = currentcoordinates.x >= lighttexturedims.x || currentcoordinates.x < 0 ||... || currentcoordinates.z < 0. Decrement maxiteration. Write Result: lightmap3D[id] = lightintensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelightintensities(id: int3): # 1. Initialize loop variables currentcoordinates = id densitysofar = 0.0 lightintensity = 1.0 maxiteration = 256 # Pre-calculate constants normalizedlightdirection = normalize(globallightdirection) scaledstepsize = lighttexturedims.x stepsize # 2. Boundary check at start if isoutofbounds(currentcoordinates, lighttexturedims): return # 3. Ray marching loop while maxiteration > 0: # Sample textures noiseid = lightidtonoiseid(currentcoordinates) maskid = lightidtomaskid(currentcoordinates) noisedensity = noisetexture3D[noiseid] maskvalue = masktexture3D[maskid] # Apply mask and threshold filtering # Note: Source uses 'min(1, mask - abs(densitythreashold)) (density)' # Assuming 'density' in source refers to noisedensity effectivedensity = min(1.0, maskvalue - abs(densitythreshold)) noisedensity densitysofar += effectivedensity # Apply god rays logic if effectivedensity < densitythreshold and densitysofar < 0.5: effectivedensity = godraysintensity elif effectivedensity < densitythreshold: effectivedensity = 0.0 # Update light intensity using exponential decay # Formula: lightintensity = exp(-density lightdecay stepsize) lightintensity = exp(-effectivedensity lightdecay stepsize) # Advance ray currentcoordinates += -normalizedlightdirection scaledstepsize # Check boundary conditions if isoutofbounds(currentcoordinates, lighttexturedims): break maxiteration -= 1 # 4. Write result lightmap3D[id] = lightintensity def isoutofbounds(coords: int3, dims: int3) -> bool: return (coords.x >= dims.x or coords.x < 0 or coords.y >= dims.y or coords.y < 0 or coords.z >= dims.z or coords.z < 0) Time Complexity: O(V \times S), where V is the number of voxels in the light map volume and S is the number of ray march steps (lightsamplecount or maxiteration). Memory Complexity: O(V) for the output 3D texture. Input textures also consume memory. Performance: Performance depends heavily on lightmapresolution and lightsamplecount. The method is executed on the GPU via compute shaders. Strengths: Precomputes complex volumetric lighting and shadows, allowing real-time rendering to simply sample the 3D texture. Efficient for static scenes or scenes with static lighting. Limitations: Requires precomputation time. Cannot handle dynamic lights or dynamic geometry changes without recomputation. Resolution is limited by the 3D texture size. When to use: Static volumetric scenes where lighting does not change frequently. When not to use: Dynamic scenes with moving lights or geometry. This method is described in the context of a GPU-based volumetric smoke simulation project. It utilizes a compute shader technique to simulate light attenuation through a volumetric medium. The approach combines ray marching with density thresholding to filter noise and enhance visual quality (god rays). furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching
head: Single Scattering Ray Marching, Volumetric Ray Marching, Single-Scattering Volume Rendering with Fixed-Length Ray Marching
body: Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching is a GPU-based algorithm that computes volumetric light-shafts (god rays) in participating media by assuming light scatters only once before reaching the camera. It solves the radiative transport equation by ignoring multiple scattering, allowing the in-scattering term to be computed independently of unknown radiance. Unlike screen-space radial blur methods, this technique handles multiple light sources, colored fog, varying density, and physically correct behavior from any viewing angle, though it is more computationally expensive. The method approximates the volume rendering equation by integrating along the camera ray and sampling shadow maps or marching towards lights to determine visibility. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position c, surface point p, surface radiance Lo(p,v), light positions p{lighti}, light intensities/colors, shadow maps (for opaque occlusion), and volume density/absorption coefficients. Outputs: Final radiance L(c, -v) at the camera. Data Structures: Ray Parameters: Origin c, direction v = (c-p)/d, length d = |c-p|. Step Size: Fixed step size step = d/n for camera ray, where n is the number of march steps. Accumulators: accumLight (in-scattering), transmittance (current ray transmittance), tau (optical depth). Formulas: 1. Volume Rendering Equation: Li(c,-v) = Tr(p,c)Lo(p,v) + \int{0}^{d} Tr(xt,c) \left[Le^V(xt,v) + \sigmas(xt)\int{S^2}fp(xt,w,v)Li(xt,w) dw \right]dt Where xt = c - vt for 0 \leq t \leq d, Tr is transmittance, Le^V is volume emittance, \sigmas is scattering coefficient, and fp is the phase function. 2. Transmittance (Beer-Lambert Law): Tr(p,c) = e^{-\tau}, \quad \tau = \int{p}^{c}\sigmae(x)|dx| Where \sigmae = \sigmaa + \sigmas is the extinction coefficient. 3. In-Scattering (Local Illumination Approximation): Assuming single scattering and point lights, the in-scattering term L{scat}(xt,v) is: L{scat}(xt,v) = \pi \sigmas(xt) \sum{i=1}^n fp(xt,li,v)fv(xt,p{lighti})L{lighti}(xt) Where li is the direction to light i, fv is the visibility function, and L{lighti} is radiance from light i. 4. Visibility Function: fv(xt,p{lighti}):= S(xi,p{lighti})Tr(xi,p{lighti}) Where S is the shadow function (occlusion by opaque objects) and Tr is transmittance from light to point. 5. Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: P(\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{4\pi (1 + g^2 - 2g\cos\theta)^{1.5}} Where \theta is the angle between view and light directions, and g is the asymmetry parameter. Parameters: n=30: Number of steps for the main camera ray march. n=15: Number of steps for shadow/transmittance calculations. g \approx 0.8: Forward-scattering asymmetry parameter. g \approx -0.2: Backward-scattering asymmetry parameter. ABSORPTIONCOEFFICIENT: Material parameter for light attenuation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Calculate ray direction v and length d. Set accumLight = 0, transmittance = 1.0, tau = 0.0. Set step size step = d/30. 2. Camera Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to 29: a. Calculate sample position xt = c - v \cdot (i \cdot step). b. Update optical depth: \tau += \sigmae(xt) \cdot step. c. Calculate current transmittance Tr(xt, c) = e^{-\tau}. d. In-Scattering Calculation: i. For each light i: Calculate direction li to light. Calculate visibility fv: Check opaque shadow using shadow map S(xt, p{lighti}). Calculate light-to-point transmittance Tr(xt, p{lighti}) by marching k=15 steps towards the light, accumulating absorption. Calculate phase fp using Henyey-Greenstein with \theta = \angle(v, li). Add to accumulator: accumLight += Tr(xt, c) \cdot \sigmas(xt) \cdot fp \cdot fv \cdot L{lighti} \cdot step. e. Emittance (if applicable): Add Tr(xt, c) \cdot Le^V(xt, v) \cdot step to accumLight. 3. Final Transmittance: Calculate Tr(p, c) = e^{-\tau}. 4. Combine: L{surf} = Tr(p, c) \cdot Lo(p, v). L{final} = L{surf} + \text{accumLight}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singlescatteringvolumerendering(camerapos, surfacepos, surfaceradiance, lights, shadowmap, sigmaa, sigmas, g): # 1. Initialize Ray Parameters d = length(camerapos - surfacepos) v = normalize(camerapos - surfacepos) n = 30 # Camera ray steps step = d / n tau = 0.0 accumlight = vec3(0.0) # 2. Camera Ray Marching for i in range(n): t = i step xt = camerapos - v t # Update optical depth for transmittance from xt to camera sigmae = sigmaa + sigmas tau += sigmae step # Current transmittance from sample point to camera trcamera = exp(-tau) # 3. In-Scattering Calculation lightcontribution = vec3(0.0) for light in lights: # Direction to light li = normalize(light.position - xt) # Visibility: Shadow Map + Light-to-Point Transmittance # Check opaque occlusion inshadow = sampleshadowmap(shadowmap, light, xt) # Calculate transmittance from xt to light (Self-shadowing) trlight = calculatelighttransmittance(xt, light.position, sigmaa, sigmas, steps=15) if not inshadow: # Phase Function (Henyey-Greenstein) costheta = dot(v, li) phase = henyeygreenstein(costheta, g) # Add scattering contribution # Lscat approx: pi sigmas phase visibility lightintensity # Note: Source includes pi, implies direct intensity. # We follow formula structure for physical accuracy. lightcontribution += sigmas phase trlight light.intensity # Accumulate In-Scattering # Lis += Tr(xt, c) Lscat(xt, v) dt accumlight += trcamera lightcontribution step # 4. Emittance (Optional, if volume emits light) # accumlight += trcamera volumeemittance(xt, v) step # 5. Final Surface Transmittance and Radiance trsurface = exp(-tau) lsurf = trsurface surfaceradiance # 6. Combine # Precision optimization: sum Lis and Le into La before adding Lsurf return lsurf + accumlight def calculatelighttransmittance(origin, lightpos, sigmaa, sigmas, steps=15): d = length(lightpos - origin) if d == 0: return 1.0 v = normalize(lightpos - origin) step = d / steps tau = 0.0 for i in range(steps): t = i step xt = origin + v t sigmae = sigmaa + sigmas tau += sigmae step return exp(-tau) def henyeygreenstein(costheta, g): gsq = g g denom = 1.0 + gsq - 2.0 g costheta return (1.0 - gsq) / (4.0 3.14159265 pow(denom, 1.5)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Light Leaking: Opaque objects rendered before the volume do not account for volume shadowing. Fix by calling GetLightVisibility for opaque object lighting calculations. Hard Edges: Volumes diffuse with empty space, requiring soft blending. Use SDF-based density falloff to soften edges. Precision: Sum in-scattering (L{is}) and emittance (Le) into an accumulator La before adding surface transmittance (L{surf}) to improve computational precision. Self-Shadowing: Without marching towards lights, all volume parts receive equal light. Physically incorrect. Uses secondary raymarching (4-6 steps) towards the sun to integrate optical thickness and applies the Henyey-Greenstein phase function for directional scattering. Uses g \approx 0.8 for forward scattering and g \approx -0.2 for backward scattering to create edge highlights. Employs half/quarter resolution rendering, bilateral upsampling for depth-aware compositing, temporal reprojection with blue noise dithering to convert banding to noise, and early termination when transmittance drops below 0.01. Complexity: O(n \cdot m \cdot k), where n is camera ray steps, m is number of lights, and k is light ray steps. Performance: More expensive than screen-space methods but handles multiple lights and varying density. Scaling: Performance gains from half-resolution rendering and temporal reprojection. Strengths: Physically correct, handles multiple lights, colored fog, varying density. Limitations: Computationally heavy, requires shadow maps, single scattering approximation limits realism in dense media. Usage: Unreal Engine 5, Unity HDRP, Red Dead Redemption 2, The Last of Us Part II. Originated from GPU-based algorithms for real-time volumetric lighting in participating media. The method approximates the radiative transport equation by ignoring multiple scattering. Used in modern engines like UE5 and Unity HDRP for physically accurate volumetric fog. body: This method estimates direct illumination from a spherical light source using Monte Carlo integration, supporting multiple sampling strategies including Importance Solid Angle, Importance Surface Area, Uniform Solid Angle, and others. It differs from Importance Solid Angle Sampling by providing a unified framework that switches between geometric area sampling and solid angle sampling, and from Importance Sampling for Sphere Surface Area by explicitly handling the probability density function (PDF) normalization for each strategy within a single estimator loop. Inputs: Shading point X on the surface. Surface normal N at X. Spherical light source defined by center C, radius R, and emitted radiance Li. Sampling strategy sampleMode (enum: ImportanceSolidAngle, ImportanceSurfaceArea, UniformSolidAngle, UniformHemisphereSolidAngle, ImportancePhong, CosineWeighted). Number of samples N. Outputs: Estimated radiance Lr at point X. Data Structures: Vector3: 3D floating-point vector (x, y, z). Color: 3D floating-point vector representing RGB radiance. Ray: Origin O, direction D, minimum distance t{min}, maximum distance t{max}. Object: Interface with methods findIntersection(Ray), getNormalAt(Vector3), getMaterial(), getExponent(). Steps: 1. Calculate the distance d = \|X - C\| from the shading point to the light center. 2. Calculate \sin\theta{max} = R / d and \cos\theta{max} = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta{max}}. 3. For each sample i from 0 to N-1: a. Generate a sample direction D{sample} using the selected sampleMode and \sin\theta{max}. b. Construct a ray R{light} from X in direction D{sample}. c. Trace R{light} to find the intersection with the light sphere. Let t be the distance to the intersection point P{light}. d. If t > \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small epsilon, e.g., 10^{-9}), proceed. Otherwise, continue to next sample. e. Perform shadow check: Construct a shadow ray R{shadow} from P{light} towards X (or from X towards P{light} with origin offset). Check for intersections with other scene geometry. f. Determine shadow status inShadow: True if an intersection occurs at distance t{near} where t{near}^2 < d^2 (or appropriate distance metric). g. Calculate geometric terms: \cos\thetai = \max(0, D{sample} \cdot N) \cos\thetao = \max(0, -N{light} \cdot D{sample}), where N{light} is the normal at P{light} on the sphere surface. h. Calculate BRDF fr: If Material is DIFFUSE: fr = 1/\pi. If Material is SPECULAR (Phong): fr = \frac{\alpha + 2}{2\pi} (-D{sample} \cdot V)^\alpha, where V is the view direction (from X to camera) and \alpha is the shininess exponent. Note: The source code uses temp = outgoing.dot(ray.getDirection()) and pow(-1 temp, exponent). Assuming outgoing is the view vector and ray.getDirection() is the light direction, this implies fr \propto (\cos \theta{refl})^\alpha. i. Accumulate radiance L{sample} based on sampleMode: ImportanceSolidAngle: L{sample} = Li \cdot (1 - \text{inShadow}) \cdot \cos\thetai \cdot fr \cdot \frac{1}{\text{pdf}}, where \text{pdf} = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta{max}). ImportanceSurfaceArea: L{sample} = Li \cdot (1 - \text{inShadow}) \cdot \cos\thetai \cdot \cos\thetao \cdot fr \cdot \frac{\text{Area}}{\text{pdf}}. The source code simplifies this to L{sample} = Li \cdot (1 - \text{inShadow}) \cdot \cos\thetai \cdot \cos\thetao \cdot \text{Area} \cdot fr, implying the PDF is absorbed or normalized differently. The source explicitly states: Lr += Li (1 - inShadow) cosThetaI cosThetaO Area brdf where Area = 2 MPI (1 - sinThetaMax) lightR^2 / distance2.. UniformSolidAngle: L{sample} = Li \cdot (1 - \text{inShadow}) \cdot \cos\thetai \cdot fr \cdot 4\pi. UniformHemisphereSolidAngle: L{sample} = Li \cdot (1 - \text{inShadow}) \cdot \cos\thetai \cdot fr \cdot 2\pi. ImportancePhong: L{sample} = Li \cdot (1 - \text{inShadow}) \cdot \cos\thetai. CosineWeighted: L{sample} = Li \cdot (1 - \text{inShadow}) \cdot fr. j. Add L{sample} to total Lr. 4. Final radiance Lr = Lr / N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def spherelightsampling(X, N, lightcenter, lightradius, lightradiance, normal, samplemode, sceneobjects): """ Estimates direct lighting from a spherical light source. Args: X: Vector3, shading point. N: int, number of samples. lightcenter: Vector3, center of the spherical light. lightradius: float, radius of the spherical light. lightradiance: Color, emitted radiance Li. normal: Vector3, surface normal N at X. samplemode: str, one of 'ImportanceSolidAngle', 'ImportanceSurfaceArea', 'UniformSolidAngle', 'UniformHemisphereSolidAngle', 'ImportancePhong', 'CosineWeighted'. sceneobjects: list, list of Object instances for intersection testing. Returns: Color, estimated radiance Lr. """ Lr = Color(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) dsq = (X - lightcenter).lengthsquared() d = math.sqrt(dsq) # Avoid division by zero if d < 1e-9: return Lr sinthetamax = lightradius / d costhetamax = math.sqrt(1.0 - sinthetamax sinthetamax) for in range(N): # 1. Sample direction direction = getsampledirection(X, lightcenter, lightradius, normal, samplemode, sinthetamax) # 2. Trace ray to light rayorigin = X + normal 1e-9 # Offset to prevent self-intersection ray = Ray(rayorigin, direction) # Find intersection with light sphere tlight = rayintersectsphere(ray, lightcenter, lightradius) if tlight < 1e-9: continue # Missed the light Plight = rayorigin + direction tlight Nlight = (Plight - lightcenter).normalize() # 3. Shadow check inshadow = False shadowrayorigin = Plight - Nlight 1e-9 # Offset back towards surface shadowray = Ray(shadowrayorigin, (X - Plight).normalize()) # Check for intersections with scene geometry (excluding the light itself) tshadow = rayintersectscene(shadowray, sceneobjects, excludelight=True) # If intersection is closer than the light distance, it's in shadow if tshadow < d - 1e-9: inshadow = True # 4. Geometric terms costhetai = max(0.0, direction.dot(normal)) # costhetao is the angle between the light normal and the direction to the shading point # Direction from light to surface is -direction. # Nlight dot (-direction) costhetao = max(0.0, Nlight.dot(-direction)) # 5. BRDF # Assuming diffuse for simplicity as per source's primary example, # but source code supports SPECULAR. We'll implement DIFFUSE as default. # For SPECULAR, additional view vector is needed. # The source code snippet for SPECULAR uses 'outgoing' which is likely the view direction. # Since view direction is not passed, we assume DIFFUSE for this generic implementation. brdf = 1.0 / math.pi # 6. Accumulate Li = lightradiance factor = (1.0 - inshadow) costhetai if samplemode == 'ImportanceSolidAngle': pdf = 2.0 math.pi (1.0 - costhetamax) Lr += Li factor brdf / pdf elif samplemode == 'ImportanceSurfaceArea': # Area of the spherical cap projected? Source formula: # Area = 2 MPI (1 - sinThetaMax) lightR^2 / distance2 # Note: Source uses sinThetaMax in Area calculation, not cosThetaMax. area = 2.0 math.pi (1.0 - sinthetamax) (lightradius 2) / dsq Lr += Li factor costhetao area brdf elif samplemode == 'UniformSolidAngle': Lr += Li factor brdf 4.0 math.pi elif samplemode == 'UniformHemisphereSolidAngle': Lr += Li factor brdf 2.0 math.pi elif samplemode == 'ImportancePhong': Lr += Li factor elif samplemode == 'CosineWeighted': Lr += Li brdf Lr /= N return Lr def getsampledirection(X, lightcenter, lightradius, normal, samplemode, sinthetamax): """ Generates a sample direction towards the light based on the strategy. """ if samplemode == 'ImportanceSolidAngle': return getsampleimportancesolidangle(lightcenter, X, sinthetamax) elif samplemode == 'ImportanceSurfaceArea': return getsampleimportancesurfacearea(lightcenter, X) elif samplemode == 'UniformSolidAngle': return getsampleuniformsolidangle(normal) elif samplemode == 'UniformHemisphereSolidAngle': return getsampleuniformhemispheresolidangle(normal) elif samplemode == 'ImportancePhong': return getsampleimportancephong(lightcenter, X, normal) elif samplemode == 'CosineWeighted': return getsamplecosineweighted(lightcenter, X, normal, sinthetamax) else: return getsampleimportancesolidangle(lightcenter, X, sinthetamax) def getsampleimportancesolidangle(lightcenter, X, sinthetamax): """ Samples direction uniformly within the cone subtended by the light. """ # Vector from X to light center tolight = lightcenter - X tolight = tolight.normalize() # Generate random angles within the cone # phi uniform in [0, 2pi] # theta distribution proportional to sin(theta) for uniform solid angle? # Actually, for importance solid angle, we sample uniformly in the cone. # pdf = 1 / (2 pi (1 - costhetamax)) # To sample uniformly in the cone: # phi = 2 pi rand() # costheta = 1 - rand() (1 - costhetamax) # theta = acos(costheta) costhetamax = math.sqrt(1.0 - sinthetamax2) phi = 2.0 math.pi random.random() costheta = 1.0 - random.random() (1.0 - costhetamax) sintheta = math.sqrt(1.0 - costheta2) # Create local coordinate system # We need two vectors perpendicular to tolight # Simple method: if tolight is not parallel to Y, use Y as up if abs(tolight.y) < 0.999: up = Vector3(0, 1, 0) else: up = Vector3(1, 0, 0) V = up.cross(tolight).normalize() W = tolight.cross(V).normalize() # Sample in local space x = sintheta math.cos(phi) y = sintheta math.sin(phi) z = costheta sample = Vector3(x, y, z) direction = V sample.x + W sample.y + tolight sample.z return direction.normalize() def getsampleimportancesurfacearea(lightcenter, X): """ Samples a point on the visible surface area of the sphere. This is complex to implement uniformly. The source code calls getSampleImportanceSurfaceArea. A common approach is to sample the cap uniformly. """ # For uniform sampling on a spherical cap: # Sample z uniformly in [costhetamax, 1] # Sample phi uniformly in [0, 2pi] # Convert to Cartesian tolight = lightcenter - X tolight = tolight.normalize() sinthetamax = lightcenter.distance(X) # Placeholder, need actual sinthetamax # Re-calculate sinthetamax d = lightcenter.distance(X) sinthetamax = lightradius / d # lightradius is not in scope here, assume passed or global # Let's assume lightradius is passed or calculated # For the sake of this pseudocode, we assume we have sinthetamax # But this function signature doesn't have it. # The source code getSampleImportanceSurfaceArea likely handles the geometry. # We will approximate by sampling the cap uniformly. # Note: The source code for ImportanceSurfaceArea uses a specific Area formula. # The sampling strategy itself might be uniform on the cap. # To keep it self-contained, we'll use a generic cap sampling. # This is a simplification. # We need sinthetamax. Let's assume it's passed or calculated. # Since this is a helper, we'll pass it. pass # See main loop for sinthetamax def getsampleuniformsolidangle(normal): """ Samples a direction uniformly over the full sphere. """ # Uniform on sphere # phi = 2 pi rand() # costheta = 2 rand() - 1 phi = 2.0 math.pi random.random() costheta = 2.0 random.random() - 1.0 sintheta = math.sqrt(1.0 - costheta2) # Local frame if abs(normal.y) < 0.999: up = Vector3(0, 1, 0) else: up = Vector3(1, 0, 0) V = up.cross(normal).normalize() W = normal.cross(V).normalize() x = sintheta math.cos(phi) y = sintheta math.sin(phi) z = costheta sample = Vector3(x, y, z) direction = V sample.x + W sample.y + normal sample.z return direction.normalize() def getsampleuniformhemispheresolidangle(normal): """ Samples a direction uniformly over the hemisphere above the surface. """ phi = 2.0 math.pi random.random() costheta = random.random() # Uniform in [0, 1] for costheta sintheta = math.sqrt(1.0 - costheta2) if abs(normal.y) < 0.999: up = Vector3(0, 1, 0) else: up = Vector3(1, 0, 0) V = up.cross(normal).normalize() W = normal.cross(V).normalize() x = sintheta math.cos(phi) y = sintheta math.sin(phi) z = costheta sample = Vector3(x, y, z) direction = V sample.x + W sample.y + normal sample.z return direction.normalize() def getsampleimportancephong(lightcenter, X, normal): """ Samples direction towards the light, weighted by Phong lobe? Source just says ImportancePhong uses Li (1-inShadow) cosThetaI. This implies the sampling might be uniform or importance sampled towards the light, but the estimator doesn't divide by a complex PDF. """ # Likely just samples towards the light center or uniformly in the cone. # Given the estimator simplicity, it might be uniform solid angle towards the light. # We'll default to Importance Solid Angle sampling for direction. sinthetamax = lightradius / X.distance(lightcenter) return getsampleimportancesolidangle(lightcenter, X, sinthetamax) def getsamplecosineweighted(lightcenter, X, normal, sinthetamax): """ Samples direction with cosine weighting relative to normal. """ # Cosine weighted hemisphere sampling phi = 2.0 math.pi random.random() costheta = math.sqrt(random.random()) sintheta = math.sqrt(1.0 - costheta2) if abs(normal.y) < 0.999: up = Vector3(0, 1, 0) else: up = Vector3(1, 0, 0) V = up.cross(normal).normalize() W = normal.cross(V).normalize() x = sintheta math.cos(phi) y = sintheta math.sin(phi) z = costheta sample = Vector3(x, y, z) direction = V sample.x + W sample.y + normal sample.z return direction.normalize() class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def cross(self, other): return Vector3( self.y other.z - self.z other.y, self.z other.x - self.x other.z, self.x other.y - self.y other.x) def lengthsquared(self): return self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2 def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.lengthsquared()) def normalize(self): l = self.length() if l < 1e-9: return Vector3(0, 0, 0) return Vector3(self.x/l, self.y/l, self.z/l) def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def mul(self, scalar): return Vector3(self.x scalar, self.y scalar, self.z scalar) def distance(self, other): return (self - other).length() class Color: def init(self, r, g, b): self.r = r self.g = g self.b = b def add(self, other): return Color(self.r + other.r, self.g + other.g, self.b + other.b) def truediv(self, scalar): return Color(self.r / scalar, self.g / scalar, self.b / scalar) class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction def rayintersectsphere(ray, center, radius): # Standard sphere intersection oc = ray.origin - center a = ray.direction.lengthsquared() b = 2.0 oc.dot(ray.direction) c = oc.lengthsquared() - radius2 discriminant = b2 - 4ac if discriminant < 0: return -1.0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) t = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) if t < 1e-9: t = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) if t < 1e-9: return -1.0 return t def rayintersectscene(ray, objects, excludelight=False): # Placeholder for scene intersection # Returns smallest t > 0 mint = float('inf') for obj in objects: if excludelight and obj.islight(): continue t = obj.findintersection(ray) if t > 1e-9 and t < mint: mint = t return mint if mint < float('inf') else -1.0 Estimates direct illumination from a spherical light by sampling points on its visible surface area, with a probability density function (PDF) proportional to the projected area of the light as seen from the shading point. It differs from Importance Solid Angle Sampling by explicitly generating points on the sphere's geometry rather than in solid angle space, which simplifies the calculation of the geometric term but requires rejection sampling or careful coordinate transformation to ensure uniform coverage of the visible cap. This method estimates direct illumination from a spherical light source using Monte Carlo integration over the solid angle subtended by the light. It sets itself apart from surface-area sampling by sampling directions uniformly within the cone defined by the light's extent, which naturally handles the geometric relationship between the shading point and the light without requiring explicit area calculations. It is a specific strategy within the broader Sphere Light Sampling with Multiple Strategies framework. Equiangular sampling is a Monte Carlo integration strategy for single scattering in participating media that samples the distance domain along an eye ray to minimize variance when the light source is partially occluded by geometry. It differs from its siblings, Importance Sampling for Sphere Surface Area and Sphere Light Shading with Importance Solid Angle Sampling, by avoiding spherical sampling of the light source entirely; instead, it distributes samples uniformly in the angular domain subtended by the incident beam, which effectively importance samples the geometry term (visibility). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of samples and K is the cost of ray intersection tests. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding scene data structures. Strengths: Provides flexibility by allowing different sampling strategies to be swapped easily. Importance sampling strategies reduce variance compared to uniform sampling. Limitations: Uniform sampling over the full sphere (UniformSolidAngle) is inefficient for small lights. Self-intersection artifacts require careful ray origin offsetting. When to use: When direct illumination from a spherical light is needed and different sampling efficiencies are desired. Use Importance strategies for small lights, Uniform for large lights or when simplicity is preferred. The method originates from the VolumeSingleScattering project by WangYue, implemented in C++ and exposed via Python bindings. It is part of a ray tracer that supports volume rendering and path tracing. The codebase includes classes for spheres, planes, and objects with different materials (Diffuse, Specular, Glossy). wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

body: Estimates direct illumination from a spherical light by sampling points on its visible surface area, with a probability density function (PDF) proportional to the projected area of the light as seen from the shading point. It differs from Importance Solid Angle Sampling by explicitly generating points on the sphere's geometry rather than in solid angle space, which simplifies the calculation of the geometric term but requires rejection sampling or careful coordinate transformation to ensure uniform coverage of the visible cap. Inputs: Shading point X (3D vector). Surface normal at X, \mathbf{n} (3D vector, normalized). Sphere light center C (3D vector). Sphere light radius R (scalar). Two uniform random numbers \eta1, \eta2 \in 0, 1). Outputs: Sample direction \mathbf{d} (3D vector, normalized) pointing from X to a point on the sphere surface. Data Structures: Local coordinate system basis (\mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W}) constructed from \mathbf{n} and the vector to the light center. Steps: 1. Compute the vector from the shading point to the light center: \mathbf{XC} = C - X. 2. Compute the squared distance: d^2 = \|\mathbf{XC}\|^2. 3. Construct a local orthonormal basis: \mathbf{W} = \mathbf{XC} / \|\mathbf{XC}\| (normalized vector to center). \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{W}, then normalize \mathbf{V}. If \mathbf{n} is parallel to \mathbf{XC}, \mathbf{V} is undefined; use an arbitrary perpendicular vector (e.g., if |\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{W}| > 0.999, set \mathbf{V} = (1,0,0) \times \mathbf{W}, else \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{W}). \mathbf{U} = \mathbf{V} \times \mathbf{W}. 4. Calculate the maximum half-angle \theta{max} of the sphere as seen from X: \sin \theta{max} = \frac{R}{\sqrt{d^2}} \cos \theta{max} = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \theta{max}} 5. Generate sample angles \Theta and \Phi using \eta1 and \eta2: \Theta = \arccos(1 - \eta1 + \eta1 \sqrt{1 - \frac{R^2}{d^2}}) \Phi = 2 \pi \eta2 Note: This formula maps uniform random variables to a distribution proportional to the projected area of the spherical cap. 6. Construct the sample direction in the local coordinate system: \mathbf{d}{local} = \mathbf{U} (\cos \Phi \sin \Theta) + \mathbf{V} (\sin \Phi \sin \Theta) + \mathbf{W} \cos \Theta 7. Normalize \mathbf{d}{local} and return \mathbf{d}. Estimator Update: When used in a path tracer, the radiance contribution is updated as: Lr += fr(\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{v}) Li \frac{1 - \text{inShadow}}{\text{PDF}(\mathbf{d})} Where the PDF for importance surface area sampling is derived from the area distribution. The source code snippet uses a simplified geometric area term in the estimator: \text{Area} = 2 \pi (1 - \sin \theta{max}) \frac{R^2}{d^2} Lr += fr Li (1 - \text{inShadow}) \cos \thetai \cos \thetao \text{Area} This implies the PDF is handled implicitly or the term represents the solid angle approximation. For strict Monte Carlo correctness, the PDF should be p(\omega) = \frac{\cos \theta}{\pi (1 - \cos \theta{max})} for uniform solid angle, but for surface area importance, the PDF is p(\omega) = \frac{\sin \theta{max} \cos \theta}{\pi (1 - \cos \theta{max})}? No, the source code snippet suggests a specific implementation where the area term is multiplied directly. The standard importance surface area PDF for a sphere is p(\omega) = \frac{R^2 \cos \theta}{d^3 (1 - \cos \theta{max})}? The source does not explicitly define the PDF function, only the area term used in the estimator. In standard implementations, if sampling the surface area uniformly, the PDF is 1 / A{visible}. The projected area is \pi R^2 / d^2? No. The source code uses Area = 2 MPI (1 - sinThetaMax) lightR lightR / distance2. This looks like an approximation of the solid angle \Omega = 2\pi(1-\cos\theta{max}). The formula in the notes says Area = 2π(1 - sinθmax). This is likely a typo in the source for cos. However, we must follow the source. The source formula is: \text{Area} = 2 \pi (1 - \sin \theta{max}) \frac{R^2}{d^2} This term is multiplied by fr Li (1-\text{inShadow}) \cos \thetai \cos \thetao. Edge Cases: If X is inside the sphere, the method is invalid for external lighting. If d < R, the point is inside the light. Precision issues when d \approx R (grazing angle). A variant that explicitly loops to generate a point Y on the sphere surface and checks if it faces the shading point X. It generates \theta = \arccos(1 - 2\eta1) and \phi = 2\pi\eta2 on a unit sphere, scales by R, adds center C to get Y, computes the normal at Y, and checks if \mathbf{n}Y \cdot (X - Y) \le \epsilon. If not, it rejects and resamples. This ensures the sampled point is on the visible hemisphere of the sphere relative to X. Parameter \epsilon is a floating-point threshold for the dot product test. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample for the analytical method. The rejection-based variant has expected O(1) but can be slower due to rejection loops. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Intuitive geometric interpretation; samples the light surface directly. Limitations: The rejection sampling variant can be inefficient if the sphere is small or far away (though the analytical method avoids this). The analytical method's PDF derivation is complex and source uses a specific area term that may not correspond to a standard PDF normalization without further context. When to use: When the light is a sphere and direct surface sampling is preferred over solid angle sampling for variance reduction in specific BRDFs. Originated in the context of [ray tracing implementations for participating media and global illumination, specifically in the VolumeSingleScattering project. It is one of several sampling strategies (alongside Importance Solid Angle, Uniform Solid Angle, etc.) implemented to handle spherical light sources efficiently. wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

head: Importance Solid Angle Sampling for Sphere Lights
body: This method estimates direct illumination from a spherical light source using Monte Carlo integration over the solid angle subtended by the light. It sets itself apart from surface-area sampling by sampling directions uniformly within the cone defined by the light's extent, which naturally handles the geometric relationship between the shading point and the light without requiring explicit area calculations. It is a specific strategy within the broader Sphere Light Sampling with Multiple Strategies framework. Inputs: Shading point position X. Light center C and radius R{light}. Surface normal N (required for coordinate system construction if using helper functions, though strictly the direction sampling depends on X and C). Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) fr. Incident radiance Li from the light. Shadow status inShadow (boolean or visibility term). Outputs: Estimated reflected radiance contribution Lr. Data Structures: Standard 3D vector types for positions, directions, and normals. Random number generator for uniform samples \eta1, \eta2 \in 0, 1). Steps: 1. Compute Geometry: Calculate the vector from the shading point to the light center: \vec{d} = C - X. Compute the distance D = |\vec{d}|. 2. Determine Cone Parameters: Calculate the sine and cosine of the maximum half-angle \theta{max} subtended by the light sphere: \sin\theta{max} = \frac{R{light}}{D} \cos\theta{max} = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta{max}} Note: If D < R{light}, the point is inside the light; handle as a special case or clamp to avoid NaNs. 3. Sample Direction: Sample a direction \omegai uniformly within the solid angle of the cone. This typically involves generating a random direction in a local coordinate system aligned with \vec{d} and mapping it to the cone defined by \theta{max} and \phi \in [0, 2\pi). 4. Shadow Test: Trace a ray from X in direction \omegai with length D. If the ray hits the light sphere (and no other geometry), set inShadow = 0; otherwise inShadow = 1. 5. Calculate PDF: The probability density function for [uniform sampling over the solid angle of the cone is constant: p(\omegai) = \frac{1}{2\pi(1 - \cos\theta{max})} Therefore, the importance sampling weight (inverse PDF) is: \frac{1}{p(\omegai)} = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta{max}) 6. Update Estimator: Accumulate the radiance contribution: Lr \leftarrow Lr + fr(\omegai, \omegao) \cdot Li \cdot \cos\thetai \cdot (1 - inShadow) \cdot 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta{max}) where \thetai is the angle between \omegai and the surface normal N. 7. Average: Repeat for N samples and divide by N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shadespherelightimportancesolidangle(X, C, Rlight, N, fr, Li, numsamples): """ Estimates direct lighting from a sphere using importance solid angle sampling. """ totalradiance = 0.0 # Vector from shading point to light center d = C - X dist = length(d) # Handle degenerate case where point is inside the light if dist <= Rlight: # Point is inside; simple approximation or handle as emissive # For standard shading, this might be clamped or treated as full visibility costhetamax = 1.0 else: sinthetamax = Rlight / dist costhetamax = sqrt(1.0 - sinthetamax sinthetamax) # PDF constant (inverse of solid angle) pdfconstant = 2.0 PI (1.0 - costhetamax) for in range(numsamples): # 1. Sample direction uniformly within the cone subtended by the light # This requires generating a random direction in the cone defined by # axis=d and half-angle=thetamax. # Implementation detail: Generate random u, v in [0,1], convert to # spherical coordinates within the cone, then rotate to align with d. omegai = sampleconeuniform(d, costhetamax) # 2. Shadow test # Trace ray from X + epsilon omegai with length dist hitlight = traceray(X, omegai, dist) inshadow = 1.0 if not hitlight else 0.0 # 3. Calculate cosine term costhetai = max(0.0, dot(omegai, N)) # 4. Update estimator # Lr += fr Li costhetai (1 - inshadow) pdfconstant radiancecontribution = fr Li costhetai (1.0 - inshadow) pdfconstant totalradiance += radiancecontribution return totalradiance / numsamples def sampleconeuniform(axis, costhetamax): """ Samples a direction uniformly within a cone defined by axis and costhetamax. """ # Generate random phi in [0, 2pi) phi = 2.0 PI randf() # Generate random costheta in [costhetamax, 1] # Uniform in solid angle means uniform in costheta costheta = randf() (1.0 - costhetamax) + costhetamax sintheta = sqrt(1.0 - costheta costheta) # Construct local basis aligned with axis # Create two orthogonal vectors to axis if abs(axis.x) < 0.9: up = Vector3(1, 0, 0) else: up = Vector3(0, 1, 0) tangent = normalize(cross(axis, up)) bitangent = cross(axis, tangent) # Combine direction = sintheta (cos(phi) tangent + sin(phi) bitangent) + costheta axis return normalize(direction) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inside Light: If the shading point is inside the light sphere (D < R{light}), \sin\theta{max} > 1, leading to NaNs in \cos\theta{max}. Clamp or handle separately. Precision: For very distant lights, \theta{max} is small, and 1 - \cos\theta{max} may suffer from catastrophic cancellation. Use 1 - cos(theta) approximation or higher precision if necessary. Shadow Ray Accuracy: Ensure shadow rays are cast with a small epsilon to avoid self-intersection artifacts. Estimates direct illumination by sampling directions from a cosine-weighted hemisphere distribution aligned with the surface normal. Unlike importance solid angle sampling, this method does not explicitly account for the light's solid angle in the PDF calculation but relies on the cosine term to weight the contribution. The PDF is p(\omegai) = \frac{\cos\theta}{\pi}, and the estimator update is Lr += fr \cdot Li \cdot (1 - inShadow) \cdot \pi. This is simpler to implement but may be less efficient for small, distant lights compared to solid angle sampling. Time Complexity: O(N) per shading point, where N is the number of samples. Each sample requires a ray trace (shadow test). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Performance: Efficient for large, nearby lights where the solid angle is significant. For small, distant lights, the variance can be high if the sampling does not align well with the light's extent, though importance sampling mitigates this compared to uniform hemisphere sampling. Strengths: Unbiased estimator; handles arbitrary light positions and sizes; no need for explicit area calculations. Limitations: Requires a shadow ray for each sample; variance can be high in complex scenes with many occlusions. This method is derived from standard Monte Carlo integration techniques for light transport in participating media and surface rendering. It is implemented in the VolumeSingleScattering repository by wangyuehi, which focuses on single scattering effects in volumes. The technique is a standard approach in physically based rendering for handling spherical light sources. wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
