name: Neural Photon Field Rendering
head: Neural Path Tracer, Neural Photon Field Rendering Pipeline, PFF, Photon Field Network, Wavefront Path Tracing with Neural Fields
body: Neural Photon Field Rendering is a GPU-based path tracing method that estimates direct illumination via standard ray-marching techniques and approximates indirect global illumination by querying a pre-trained neural field. Unlike traditional path tracers that recursively trace secondary rays for global illumination, this method computes only the first volume interaction and uses the neural network to predict the incoming radiance Li from the rest of the scene. It is distinguished from its sibling Emissive Volume Rendering by its explicit handling of indirect scattering via a learned photon field, whereas emissive rendering typically focuses on self-emission without complex global illumination approximation. The method operates as a wavefront path tracer. It replaces the expensive secondary ray tracing required for global illumination with a neural network inference step, significantly reducing stochastic noise and computational cost at low sample counts. Inputs: Camera parameters, volume density field, phase function coefficients (g), pre-trained neural photon field network, number of samples per pixel (SPP). Outputs: Final radiance L per pixel. 1. Rays Buffer: Stores ray origins, directions, and intersection status for rays that hit the volume bounding box. 2. Samples Buffer: A fixed-size buffer of size |samples|{max} = SPP \times |rays|. Each entry stores the 3D position, the phase coefficient g used for that sample, and validity flags. Invalid interactions (where delta tracking failed or the ray escaped) are left blank. 3. Neural Network Input: A 6-dimensional vector consisting of the 3D position (x, y, z) and the phase coefficient g. The position is encoded using hashgrid encoding. SPP: Samples per pixel. Typically 1 for performance measurement, but supports accumulation. Maximum Path Length: Set to 16 for all rendering evaluations. Phase Coefficients (G): The network is trained on a discrete subset G \subset [-1, 1]. It generalizes to unseen g \notin G. Photon Map Size: The underlying data is generated from photon maps consisting of 12M total photons, distributed as 4M photons per phase. 1. Ray Generation: Spawn view rays based on camera parameters. Perform basic intersection testing against the volume bounding box. Store intersecting rays in the Rays Buffer. 2. Volume Sampling: For each ray in the buffer, use delta tracking to estimate the depth of the first interaction with the volume. Generate SPP samples per ray. Store the interaction positions and the corresponding phase coefficient g in the Samples Buffer. Invalid interactions are marked as blank. 3. Photon Field Prediction: Batch all valid samples from the Samples Buffer into a single neural network inference step. The network takes the 6D input (position + g) and outputs the predicted incoming radiance Li^{pred}. This is decoded using the network's output layer (Equation 7 in) to obtain the final radiance value. 4. Compaction: Compact the Samples Buffer by discarding samples where delta tracking did not generate a valid interaction, removing 'holes' to optimize subsequent memory access. 5. Direct Illumination: Use Next-Event Estimation (NEE) and delta tracking to sample light sources directly from the generated sample points. This computes the direct illumination term Ld. 6. Composition: Compute the scattering probability \sigmas at each sample point. Determine Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) weights wd (for NEE) and wi (for the neural network prediction). Compose the total illumination using the formula below. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neuralphotonfieldrendering(camera, neuralfield, spp): # 1. Ray Generation rays = raygeneration(camera) # 2. Volume Sampling # Generate spp interactions per ray using delta tracking samples = volumesampling(rays, spp) # 3. Photon Field Prediction # Batch all samples for single inference step # Input: 6D vector (position, phasecoefficient) # Output: Predicted incoming radiance Lipred lipred = neuralfield.decode(samples) # 4. Compaction (Implicit in efficient implementation, # but logically removes invalid samples before composition) validsamples = compact(samples) validlipred = lipred[validsamples] # 5. Direct Illumination # Use NEE and delta tracking from sample points ld = directillumination(validsamples) # 6. name: Ambient Occlusion via Shadow Rays
head: Ambient Occlusion Approximation, Hardware Ray Traced AO, RTAO (Ray-Traced Ambient Occlusion), Ray-traced AO, Shadow Ray Ambient Occlusion, getPixelColorAmbientOcclusion
body: Ambient Occlusion via Shadow Rays estimates the local visibility of a surface point by casting shadow rays into the hemisphere above the surface normal to determine how much of the environment is obscured by neighboring geometry. It differs from Direct Illumination with Shadow Rays by integrating over the hemisphere to approximate indirect lighting rather than evaluating specific light sources, and from Variance Shadow Mapping for NeRFs by using explicit ray casting rather than probabilistic depth distributions. It provides a view-independent occlusion factor that can be combined with arbitrary direct illumination, offering a computationally efficient alternative to full global illumination. Inputs: Surface point position p, surface normal n, scene geometry (accessible via ray tracing acceleration structure), number of shadow rays NR, number of samples per ray NS (optional, depending on variant), and a maximum occlusion distance d{max}. Outputs: Ambient occlusion factor A(p) \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: Ray: Origin o, direction d, minimum hit distance t{min} (typically epsilon to avoid self-intersection), maximum hit distance t{max} (typically d{max}). Hit Record: Intersection distance t, hit point p{hit}, normal n{hit}. Formulas: The theoretical definition of ambient occlusion is the integral of visibility over the hemisphere: A(p) = \frac{1}{\pi} \int{\Omega} V(p, \omega) \cos \theta \, d\omega where: \Omega is the hemisphere oriented by the surface normal n at p. V(p, \omega) is the binary visibility function: 1 if the ray from p in direction \omega hits no geometry within d{max}, and 0 otherwise. \theta is the angle between n and \omega. In practice, this integral is approximated by Monte Carlo sampling. The occlusion factor is computed as the average visibility of sampled directions: A(p) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} V(p, \omegai) where N is the total number of samples. Sampling Strategies: Two common sampling strategies are cited: 1. Uniform Solid Angle (Default): Directions are sampled uniformly over the hemisphere. The contribution of each sample is weighted by \cos \theta and the solid angle factor 2/\pi. 2. Cosine-Weighted Sampling: Directions are sampled according to the cosine distribution. The contribution is weighted by 1/\pi. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize occlusionsum = 0.0 and samplecount = 0. 2. For each shadow ray i from 0 to NR - 1: a. Sample a direction \omegai from the hemisphere defined by normal n at p using the chosen sampling strategy. b. Construct a ray with origin o = p + \epsilon n (where \epsilon is a small epsilon to prevent self-intersection) and direction d = \omegai. c. Trace the ray against the scene geometry. d. If the ray hits geometry at distance t < d{max}, set visibility = 0.0. Else, set visibility = 1.0. e. Calculate the weight wi based on the sampling strategy: If Uniform Solid Angle: wi = \cos \thetai \cdot \frac{2}{\pi}. If Cosine-Weighted: wi = \frac{1}{\pi}. f. Add visibility wi to occlusionsum. g. Increment samplecount. 3. Compute final occlusion factor: A(p) = \text{clamp}(\text{occlusion\sum}, 0.0, 1.0). 4. Multiply the surface color by A(p) to obtain the final shaded color. Parameters: NR (Number of rays): Typically 1 to 2 samples per pixel/surface in hardware-accelerated implementations due to performance constraints. Some implementations use higher counts (e.g., 64 rays per pixel) for offline or high-quality rendering. d{max} (Maximum distance): Defines the neighborhood radius. Zhukov's distance function is often used, which bounds the influence to a maximum distance to reduce computational cost. \epsilon (Epsilon): Small offset to prevent self-intersection. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise: Low sample counts (1-2 samples) lead to very noisy images. Denoising algorithms (spatial and temporal convolutional denoisers) are commonly applied to mitigate this. Performance: Computational complexity scales with scene complexity, leading to variable performance across different scenes. Precision: Ray tracing precision issues may cause self-intersection artifacts if \epsilon is not chosen correctly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeambientocclusion(p: Vector3, n: Vector3, scene: RayTracingScene, numrays: int, maxdist: float) -> float: """ Computes ambient occlusion at point p with normal n by casting shadow rays. """ occlusionsum = 0.0 samplecount = 0 for i in range(numrays): # Sample direction from hemisphere # Implementation detail: sampleUniformHemisphere(n) returns a direction omega omega = sampleuniformhemisphere(n) # Calculate theta for weighting (angle between normal and direction) costheta = dot(n, omega) # Construct ray # Epsilon is a small value to prevent self-intersection rayorigin = p + n EPSILON raydirection = omega ray = Ray(rayorigin, raydirection) # Trace ray hit = scene.trace(ray, maxt=maxdist) # Determine visibility # If hit is None or hit.distance > maxdist, visibility is 1 (open) # Otherwise, visibility is 0 (occluded) if hit is None or hit.distance > maxdist: visibility = 1.0 else: visibility = 0.0 # Weighting based on sampling strategy # Using Uniform Solid Angle strategy as default per weight = costheta (2.0 / PI) occlusionsum += visibility weight samplecount += 1 # Average the result if samplecount > 0: aofactor = occlusionsum / samplecount else: aofactor = 1.0 return clamp(aofactor, 0.0, 1.0) def sampleuniformhemisphere(n: Vector3) -> Vector3: """ Samples a direction uniformly over the hemisphere defined by normal n. Returns a unit vector. """ # Generate random direction in local space where n is (0,0,1) # Using standard rejection sampling or spherical coordinate transformation u1 = randomfloat() u2 = randomfloat() # Convert to spherical coordinates theta = 2.0 PI u1 phi = acos(1.0 - u2) # Uniform distribution on hemisphere # Local direction localdir = Vector3( sin(phi) cos(theta), sin(phi) sin(theta), cos(phi)) # Transform to world space # Construct orthonormal basis from n # This is a simplified implementation; robust basis construction is recommended if abs(n.z) < 0.999: up = Vector3(0, 0, 1) else: up = Vector3(1, 0, 0) tangent = normalize(cross(up, n)) bitangent = cross(n, tangent) worlddir = tangent localdir.x + bitangent localdir.y + n localdir.z return worlddir Measures sky visibility by comparing sampled distance along the normal to the distance field value. Choose when distance fields are available. Updates one ray direction per frame using OpenGL blend operations for interactive computation. Choose when user interaction during AO computation is required. Accelerates traversal in sparse voxel structures by stopping when a node subtends a small solid angle. Choose for sparse voxel grids to reduce ray traversal cost. Empirical model attenuating the ambient term of Phong lighting. Choose for computationally cheaper, aesthetically driven results similar to radiosity. Stores accumulated AO values in spatial hashmap cells to avoid reprojection for static geometry. Choose for static or slowly moving scenes to reduce redundant ray tracing. A storage and reconstruction method where the reciprocal of a quadratic polynomial encodes how ambient occlusion changes with distance. Coefficients are stored in a cube map. Requires reconstructing the ambient occlusion factor at runtime, which incurs a performance penalty. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of shadow rays NR and the complexity of the scene traversal. Memory Complexity: Low, primarily storing the scene acceleration structure and the resulting AO texture/volume. Measured Performance: With hardware-accelerated ray tracing (DXR, Vulkan RT), 1-2 samples per pixel are feasible, but result in noisy images requiring denoising. Higher sample counts (e.g., 64 rays) provide better quality but are significantly more expensive. Strengths: View-independent, combines easily with direct illumination, physically plausible approximation of indirect lighting. Limitations: Noisy at low sample counts, performance scales with scene complexity, requires ray tracing hardware or software rasterization for efficient implementation. When to use: Real-time rendering with hardware ray tracing, offline rendering where quality is prioritized over speed, scenes with complex geometry where screen-space methods fail. When not to use: Scenes with highly dynamic geometry where caching is ineffective, hardware without ray tracing support (unless using approximations), real-time applications with strict performance budgets and no denoising. Ambient occlusion was introduced by Zhukov et al. [Zhukov 1998] and Iones [2003] as "obscurances," an efficient technique for perceptually similar results to global illumination with lower cost. It was detailed by Landis [2002] for adding realism to models and extended to ray tracing by Méndez et al. [2003b]. The method is a property of geometry, independent of lighting conditions and viewpoint, allowing combination with arbitrary direct illumination. It differs from its siblings Incremental Local Ambient Occlusion and Zhukov Ambient Occlusion by relying on a global distance field texture rather than local geometric primitives or hemisphere sampling, making it suitable for dynamic or deforming scenes where explicit geometry is unavailable or expensive to query. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{p}) representing the scene, a surface point \mathbf{x}, the surface normal \mathbf{n} at \mathbf{x}, a maximum sample count i{max}, and a contrast parameter \tau. Output: A scalar occlusion value C. Data Structures: SDF: A function or volume texture mapping 3D coordinates to a scalar distance value. Evans uses a convention where the distance is positive inside the surface and negative outside. This is the inverse of the standard convention (negative inside, positive outside) often used in modern ray marching. Parameters: i{max}: The number of samples taken along the normal. Not given in the sources. \tau: A parameter defining the overall contrast of the occlusion effect. Not given in the sources. di: The distance of the i-th sample from the surface point \mathbf{x}. The distances are strictly increasing (di < d{i+1}) with d0 = 0. Not given in the sources. Method: The method estimates occlusion by comparing the actual distance traveled along the normal against the distance reported by the SDF at each sample point. In an unoccluded region, the SDF value at a point \mathbf{x} + di \mathbf{n} should equal the distance di from the origin \mathbf{x}, because the closest surface is the one at \mathbf{x} itself. If another surface is closer, the SDF value will differ from di. 1. Initialize an accumulator for the occlusion difference to zero. 2. Iterate from i = 0 to i{max}. 3. Calculate the sample position: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{x} + di \mathbf{n}. 4. Query the SDF at \mathbf{p}i to get f(\mathbf{p}i). 5. Calculate the difference: \Deltai = di - f(\mathbf{p}i). Note: Due to Evans' sign convention (positive inside, negative outside), if the ray moves into empty space (outside), f(\mathbf{p}i) is negative. If it hits another surface, f(\mathbf{p}i) is the distance to that surface. The difference di - f(\mathbf{p}i) accumulates the "missing" distance caused by occlusion. 6. Sum the differences: S = \sum{i=0}^{i{max}} \Deltai. 7. The source writes e^\tau. If \tau is negative, it acts as a decay. If \tau is positive, it amplifies. Given "contrast", it likely scales the sum. I will implement it exactly as: C = \exp(\tau) \times \sum{i=0}^{i{max}} (di - f(\mathbf{x} + di \mathbf{n})). Wait, if di - f is positive (occlusion), and \tau is positive, C grows. If \tau is negative, C shrinks. I will provide the pseudocode using the formula from the source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Evans' Normal Modification
head: Ambient Occlusion with Normal Modification, Evans Normal Modification AO, Normal perturbation AO
body: Evans' Normal Modification is a variant of ambient occlusion that perturbs the surface normal at each sample step to better approximate sky visibility effects. It differs from its sibling Quilez Ambient Occlusion by modifying the ray direction per step and changing the accumulation base from 2 to 1.1. It builds on Evans Ambient Occlusion by tilting the marching direction toward the sky dome. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface point x, initial normal n, scene distance field function f(r), upward unit vector u, maximum steps k{max}, step size \Delta t, scale parameter s, and normal modification parameter \alpha. Output: Final occlusion value in [0, 1]. Data Structures: k: Integer loop counter. d: Float distance query result. occlusion: Float accumulator. r: Float3 sample position. n: Float3 current normal vector. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize k = 1, d = 0, occlusion = 0. 2. Loop while k < k{max}: a. Calculate sample position: r = x + \Delta t \cdot k \cdot n. b. Query distance: d = f(r). c. Update occlusion: occlusion = 1.1^k \cdot (k \cdot \|n\| \cdot \Delta tk - d). d. Modify normal: n = n + \alpha u. e. Increment counter: k = k + 1. 3. Return 1 - \text{clamp}(s \cdot occlusion, 0, 1). Formulas: r = x + \Delta t \cdot k \cdot n: Sample position along the current normal, scaled by step index k and step size \Delta t. occlusion = 1.1^k \cdot (k \cdot \|n\| \cdot \Delta tk - d): Occlusion estimate per step using base 1.1 instead of 2, where \Delta tk is the step size at iteration k (typically constant \Delta t) and \|n\| is the Euclidean length of the current normal. n = n + \alpha u: Normal perturbation formula, where u is the upward unit vector and \alpha scales the tilt. 1 - \text{clamp}(s \cdot occlusion, 0, 1): Final occlusion mapping to [0, 1] using scale s. Parameters: \alpha: Normal modification strength. Evans used 0.5. u: Upward pointing unit vector of the scene (e.g., (0, 1, 0)). k{max}: Maximum number of sample steps. \Delta t: Step size for ray marching. s: Scale variable determining darkening intensity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Robustness: The method is not robust; parameters lack obvious defaults and require scene-specific tuning. Exaggerated Occlusion: Applying the algorithm globally can cause exaggerated occlusion or incorrect highlighting (e.g., a box appearing highlighted near its top) when shapes are near each other, requiring different parameters than those for isolated shapes like spheres. Hybrid Usage: The method may need to be combined with the standard Evans AO algorithm; for instance, Algorithm 3.4 handles ground points while Algorithm 3.7 handles sphere points to avoid incorrect shading interactions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def evansnormalmodificationao(x, n, f, u, kmax, deltat, s, alpha): k = 1 occlusion = 0.0 currentn = n # Work on a copy to avoid mutating the original if needed while k < kmax: # Calculate sample point position along the current normal r = x + deltat k currentn # Query distance field d = f(r) # Update occlusion using the modified base 1.1 # deltatk is the step size at iteration k (constant deltat here) normn = math.sqrt(currentn[0]2 + currentn[1]2 + currentn[2]2) term = k normn deltat - d occlusion = (1.1 k) term # Modify the normal vector to tilt towards the sky currentn = currentn + alpha u k = k + 1 # Final result result = 1.0 - max(0.0, min(1.0, s occlusion)) return result Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample steps k{max}, as each step performs a distance field query and vector arithmetic. Memory Complexity: Constant O(1) auxiliary memory, maintaining only scalar and vector variables. Strengths: Better approximates sky visibility effects for curved surfaces, making sphere-traced images resemble reference images more closely than standard ray marching AO. Limitations: Not robust across different geometries; requires manual tuning of parameters (\alpha, s, k{max}) for different scene types. When to use: When rendering isolated curved surfaces (e.g., spheres) where sky visibility is prioritized. When not to use: For ground planes or box-like structures where standard AO performs better, or when a robust, parameter-free solution is required. Origin: Based on work by Evans [Eva06a], who suggested influencing the surface point normal to better approximate sky effects. History: Presented as Algorithm 3.7 in the source material, modifying Algorithm 3.4 by adding the normal modification step, changing the accumulation base from 2 to 1.1, and explicitly showing the ray equation. Usage: Used in GPU ray marching of distance fields for ambient occlusion, particularly where visual fidelity for curved surfaces is prioritized over cross-geometry robustness. name: Quilez Ambient Occlusion
head: Ambient Occlusion Approximation, Cheap Ambient Occlusion, Constant step ray marching AO, Quilez approach
body: Quilez Ambient Occlusion is a fast approximation for ambient occlusion in Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering that estimates surface visibility by ray marching along the surface normal. Unlike Evans Ambient Occlusion, which measures the difference between the sampled distance and the distance field value at a single point, Quilez's method accumulates occlusion contributions from multiple samples along the normal, weighting closer geometry more heavily. It differs from standard ray marching by using no explicit intersection checks and marching along the normal instead of a hemisphere. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface point \mathbf{x}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, Signed Distance Field function f(\mathbf{p}), maximum step count k{max}, step size \Delta t, and scale factor s. Output: Ambient occlusion value AO \in [0, 1], where 0 is full occlusion and 1 is no occlusion. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method relies on scalar accumulators and the SDF query function. Steps: 1. Initialize k = 1, d = 0, and occlusion = 0. 2. While k < k{max}: a. Calculate ray position: r = \mathbf{x} + k \Delta t \mathbf{n}. b. Sample SDF: d = f(r). c. Accumulate occlusion: occlusion = occlusion + \frac{1}{2^k} (k \Delta t - d). d. Increment k = k + 1. 3. Return 1 - \text{clamp}(s \cdot occlusion, 0, 1). Formulas: The ray position at sample k is defined as: rn(k) = \mathbf{x} + k \Delta t \mathbf{n} where k \in \{1, 2, \dots, k{max}\}. Note that k=0 is omitted because measuring the distance to the surface point itself yields no useful computation for occlusion. In the absence of occlusion, the sum of distance field values equals the sum of ideal distances: \sum{k=1}^{k{max}} f(rn(k)) = \sum{k=1}^{k{max}} \Delta t \cdot k. With occlusion, the sum of distance field values is strictly less than the sum of ideal distances: \sum{k=1}^{k{max}} f(rn(k)) < \sum{k=1}^{k{max}} \Delta t \cdot k. The ambient occlusion value is calculated as: AO = 1 - s \sum{k=1}^{k{max}} \frac{1}{2^k} (k \Delta t - f(rn(k))) The final ambient term applied to shading is ambient = Ia ka(\mathbf{x}) AO. The result is clamped to [0, 1]. Parameters: k{max}: Maximum number of samples. Typically 5. \Delta t: Step size for ray marching. Typical value: 0.01. s: Scale variable determining the darkening effect. Not given in the sources. lim: Maximum distance to march. Value: 0.1. (Used in recursive variants.) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Banding effect: The occlusion does not change uniformly in color, resulting in visible "rings" of different shades of gray, attributed to taking steps of finite length along the ray. Boundary handling: The result is clamped to [0, 1] to prevent out-of-range values. Degenerate input: If the SDF returns negative values (inside geometry), the term (k \Delta t - d) increases, correctly increasing occlusion, but extreme values may require clamping or normalization in practice. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def quilezao(x, n, sdf, kmax, deltat, s): """ Calculate Quilez Ambient Occlusion. Args: x (vec3): Surface point. n (vec3): Surface normal. sdf (function): Signed Distance Field function. kmax (int): Maximum number of samples (typically 5). deltat (float): Step size (typically 0.01). s (float): Scale factor for darkening. Returns: float: Ambient occlusion value in [0, 1]. """ occlusion = 0.0 k = 1 while k < kmax: # Ray position at sample k r = x + (k deltat) n # Sample SDF d = sdf(r) # Accumulate weighted occlusion # Weight is 1/2^k, term is (idealdistance - actualdistance) weight = 1.0 / (2 k) occlusion += weight (k deltat - d) k += 1 # Clamp and scale result ao = 1.0 - s occlusion return max(0.0, min(1.0, ao)) Alternative Implementation (Fixed Steps): Some implementations use fixed distances rather than a loop with k: 1. Initialize occ = 0.0, scale = 1.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to 4: a. dist = 0.02 + 0.12 \times i. b. h = sdf(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{n} \times dist). c. occ += (dist - h) \times scale. d. scale = 0.6. 3. Return \text{clamp}(1.0 - occ, 0.0, 1.0). Time Complexity: O(k{max}), where k{max} is the number of samples. Typically constant (~5 steps). Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a few scalar variables. Performance: Very fast due to low sample count and no intersection checks. Strengths: Simple to implement, low computational cost, suitable for real-time SDF rendering. Limitations: Can produce banding effects (rings of different shades) due to finite step sizes. When to use: Real-time rendering with SDFs where performance is critical and high-quality hemisphere sampling is too expensive. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Quilez Ambient Occlusion is a modification of Evans' approach, using ray marching along the surface normal to estimate ambient occlusion. It was presented by Inigo Quilez. The method is based on the concept of constant step ray marching. It is used in sphere tracing for implicit surfaces to approximate ambient occlusion. sungiant/sdf, https://github.com/sungiant/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) MohammadHossinzehi/sdf-raymarcher, https://github.com/MohammadHossinzehi/sdf-raymarcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GPU Ray Marching of Distance Fields, https://www2.compute.dtu.dk/pubdb/edoc/imm6392.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU Ray Marching for Ambient Occlusion, https://www.scribd.com/document/520755804/imm6392, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Incremental Local Ambient Occlusion
head: LAO, LAO-I
body: Incremental Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO) is a shading model for direct volume rendering that enhances ambient lighting by computing incident light from a local spherical neighborhood around each voxel, rather than using a constant ambient factor or global shadows. It solves the problem of missing local shadowing and context in volume rendering while avoiding global shadows that obscure relevant internal structures. Unlike traditional "all-or-nothing" ambient occlusion methods that treat voxels as opaque blockers, LAO incorporates semitransparency by integrating opacity along rays, and it uses an incremental update scheme to allow interactive frame rates during computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, a transfer function (TF) mapping density to opacity \alpha and color, and a set of ray directions distributed over a sphere. Output: An ambient light intensity texture (3D texture) storing the accumulated occlusion values A(x) for each voxel, which is combined with the emissive color during the final rendering pass. Data Structures: 1. Packed Volume Texture: The regular linear volume is divided into blocks (typically 16^3 voxels). Each block is encoded with multiple levels of detail (LOD): 8^3, 4^3, 2^3, 1^3 voxels. These are packed into a single 3D texture. 2. Forward Mapping Index Texture: Maps packed texture coordinates to original volume coordinates. 3. Reverse Mapping Index Texture: Maps original volume coordinates back to packed texture coordinates. To reduce size, the minimum LOD for non-empty blocks is often restricted to 4^3 voxels, making this texture 64 times smaller than the packed volume. 4. Ambient Light Texture: Stores the accumulated intensity A(x). It has the same dimensions and multiresolution layout as the packed volume texture. 5. Direction Texture: Stores the ray directions and their associated weights wk. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Divide the volume into blocks of size 16^3 voxels. Generate LOD representations (8^3, 4^3, 2^3, 1^3) for each block. Pack the volume data into the Packed Volume Texture. Create the Forward and Reverse Mapping Index Textures. Generate ray directions by subdividing a tetrahedron, icosahedron, or octahedron to achieve the desired number of rays K. Store these directions and weights wk in the Direction Texture. 2. Incremental Update Loop: Initialize the Ambient Light Texture to zero (A0 = 0). For each ray direction k from 1 to K: Render a quad covering the entire framebuffer, where each pixel maps to one voxel in the mapped 3D slice of the Packed Volume Texture. In the fragment shader, for each voxel x: Determine the current LOD block containing x. Calculate the number of samples M based on the block's resolution. For the highest resolution, M=15 is typical. Compute the light contribution Ak(x) for direction k using the discretized integral: Ak(x) = \sum{m=1}^{M} gm \prod{i=1}^{m-1} (1 - di) where gm = 1 (due to scaling), and di is the opacity at sample position i derived from the transfer function. The sample positions are determined by the ray direction and the neighborhood radius Rb. The integration range is from a small offset a (to avoid self-occlusion) to Rb. Update the accumulated intensity in the Ambient Light Texture using the OpenGL blend operation: Ak = \frac{1}{k} A{k-1} + \left(1 - \frac{1}{k}\right) A{k-1} Note: The source text contains a garbled formula Ak¼1 kAkþ11 k  Ak1;ð9Þ. The standard incremental average formula implied by the text description "adds a fraction of the intensity" and the context of averaging k directions is: A{new} = \frac{1}{k} A{old} + \frac{k-1}{k} A{prev\accumulated} However, the text explicitly states Ak is the accumulated intensity after k directions and A0=0. The blend operation adds a fraction. A common incremental mean update is: Ak = \frac{1}{k} A{k\current} + \frac{k-1}{k} A{k-1} Where A{k\current} is the result of the ray trace for direction k (which is Ak(x) in the notation of Eq 7, but here Ak in Eq 9 refers to the contribution of the k-th ray). Let Ck be the contribution of ray k. Then: Ak = \frac{1}{k} Ck + \frac{k-1}{k} A{k-1} The source text's Eq 9 is garbled. Based on Eq 7 A(x) = \frac{1}{K} \sum wk Ak(x), if weights are uniform, the incremental update is an average. We assume the blend operation implements this averaging. Interleave rendering with intensity texture updates to allow user interaction. 3. Final Rendering: After processing all K directions, the final ambient light intensity volume is used in the standard volume rendering pass. The final color is computed by combining the emissive color and the accumulated ambient occlusion. Formulas: Light Contribution Integral: Ak(x) = \int{a}^{Rb} gA(s) \cdot e^{-\int{a}^{s} \alpha(t) dt} ds where Ak(x) is the light contribution for direction k at voxel x, Rb is the radius of the spherical neighborhood, a is a small offset to avoid self-occlusion, gA(s) is the light contribution function, and \alpha(t) is the extinction coefficient (opacity). Volumetric Light Contribution Function: gA(s) = \frac{1}{Rb} \cdot \alpha(s) + cE(s) where cE(s) is an emissive color component derived from a separate transfer function or TF primitive. This formulation avoids sharp shadow boundaries associated with boundary-only light sources. Discretized Light Contribution: Ak(x) = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^{M} gm \prod{i=1}^{m-1} (1 - di) where M is the number of samples, gm is the discretized light contribution (equal to 1 due to scaling), and di is the opacity at sample position i according to the transfer function. Combined Local Ambient Occlusion: A(x) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} wk Ak(x) where A(x) is the combined local ambient occlusion, K is the number of ray directions, and wk is the weight for direction k. Parameters: Rb: Radius of the surrounding LAO sphere. Typical values: 16 voxels, 32 voxels. M: Number of samples for the highest resolution fixed sampling rate. Value: 15. K: Number of ray directions. Baseline for quality: 128 directions. Too few directions decrease the ambient effect. Block Size: Typically 16^3 voxels. LOD Levels: 8^3, 4^3, 2^3, 1^3 voxels per block. Minimum LOD: Often restricted to 4^3 voxels for non-empty blocks to reduce reverse index texture size. Offset a: Small offset to avoid self-occlusion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Shadow Boundaries: Using boundary light contribution (gA(s) = \delta(s-Rb)) causes hard shadows if any occluder intersects the sphere. Solution: Use volumetric light contribution (gA(s) = \frac{1}{Rb}\alpha(s)) to smooth shadows. Insufficient Directions: Using too few ray directions decreases the ambient effect. 128 directions are recommended as a baseline. Loss of High-Frequency Details: LAO alone may lose high-frequency surface details. Combining LAO with diffuse shading can help explore fine structures. Clip Plane Boundaries: Boundaries of active volumes (clip planes) have poorly defined gradients, making gradient-based illumination inappropriate. LAO improves cross-section visibility in these areas. Absorption TF: Improved context from separate absorption TF in LAO is only noticeable when the absorption of the tissue used in the rendering pass is lower than the LAO absorption. Interblock Interpolation: Not considered in LAO computations to avoid excessive texture lookups, leading to minor artifacts at block boundaries. A method to improve LAO performance by adjusting sampling density along rays for voxels in lower resolution blocks. It uses adaptive step lengths based on the sampled block's resolution to avoid missing occluding features. For a ray originating in a block of scale \epsilon, the step length is adjusted with \epsilon{max}/\epsilon for all samples along that ray, where \epsilon{max} is the maximum resolution. This reduces artifacts but increases execution time due to processing different numbers of samples for neighboring voxels and decreased parallelism. Time Complexity: The performance gain from multiresolution is significant. Data reduction via LOD selection directly implies performance gain because processing is driven by the multiresolution layout. The number of voxels is decreased, and low-resolution blocks permit longer sample steps, reducing the average time per occlusion calculation. The LAO computation time per ray is slightly superlinear with respect to data reduction. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Packed Volume Texture, Forward/Reverse Mapping Index Textures, and the Ambient Light Texture. The reverse mapping index texture is optimized to be 64 times smaller than the packed volume by restricting minimum LOD. Measured Performance: Tested on a volume with native resolution 512^3 voxels. Performance is measured in frames per second (FPS) for LAO map creation. Adaptive sampling has slightly reduced performance compared to fixed sampling due to higher quality and decreased parallelism. Strengths: Interactive frame rates; incorporates semitransparency; less sensitive to noisy data sets compared to gradient-based methods (e.g., diffuse shading); improves visibility at clip planes; allows user interaction during computation. Limitations: Loses high-frequency surface details if used alone; requires recomputation when transfer functions change; does not support color bleeding; interblock interpolation is not supported. When to Use: Medical DVR for diagnosis and surgical planning, specifically for MRI data sets, virtual autopsies, and clip plane rendering. Useful when local shape and density context is more important than global shadows or fine high-frequency details. When Not to Use: When color bleeding is required; when fine high-frequency surface details are the primary focus and noise levels are low (diffuse shading may be better); when global shadows are necessary. Local Ambient Occlusion was proposed by Hernell et al. in 2010. It builds on earlier ambient occlusion techniques such as Landis [Landis 2002] and Zhukov [Zhukov 1998], and volumetric versions like Vicinity Shading by Stewart [Stewart 2003] and Ropinski et al. [Ropinski 2008]. The incremental approach allows for interactive refinement, addressing the computational cost of global shadowing in participating media. It is primarily used in medical imaging for MRI data sets. Advanced illumination and view-selection techniques for volume rendering and its application to medical imaging, http://hdl.handle.net/10803/371154, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Local Ambient Occlusion in Direct Volume Rendering, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/44596498LocalAmbientOcclusioninDirectVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Solid Angle Early Termination for Ambient Occlusion
head: Solid Angle Culling for AO, Solid Angle Thresholding for AO
body: Solid Angle Early Termination for Ambient Occlusion accelerates shadow ray traversal in sparse voxel structures by stopping traversal when a node subtends a solid angle below a specified threshold, effectively using a lower level-of-detail representation for distant points. It differs from Evans Ambient Occlusion and Zhukov Ambient Occlusion by relying on geometric projection thresholds rather than hemisphere sampling or precomputed angular distributions, and from Incremental Local Ambient Occlusion by using a static threshold rather than an adaptive accumulation scheme. Inputs: A sparse voxel structure (e.g., Sparse Voxel Octree or DAG); a shading point P; a cone angle threshold \theta{thresh}. Outputs: A traversal decision indicating whether to continue or terminate traversal for the current branch. Data Structures: The method operates on nodes of the sparse voxel hierarchy. Steps: 1. Project Node: Project the node onto the unit hemisphere centered at P. 2. Calculate Solid Angle: Compute the solid angle \Omega subtended by the node. 3. Compare Threshold: If \Omega < \Omega{thresh}, terminate traversal for this branch. 4. Continue: If \Omega \ge \Omega{thresh}, continue traversal to children or process the node. Formulas: The threshold is defined by a cone angle \theta{thresh}, where \Omega{thresh} = 2\pi(1 - \cos(\theta{thresh})). Parameters: Cone angle threshold: 9^\circ (corresponding to 0.07 sr). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Darkening: The method results in images that are darker than ground-truth because distant contributions are ignored. Quality: Despite the darkening, it maintains high quality for near-contact occlusion. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shouldtraverse(nodeC, pointP, thetathreshrad): # Vector from shading point to node center u = nodeC.center - pointP distsq = dot(u, u) if distsq == 0: return True # Point inside node, always traverse dist = sqrt(distsq) # Project node onto unit hemisphere and calculate solid angle solidangle = computesolidangleaabb(nodeC, pointP) # Threshold in steradians omegathresh = 0.07 if solidangle < omegathresh: return False return True def computesolidangleaabb(box, point): # Standard geometric calculation for solid angle of an AABB from a point # Implementation projects the 8 corners to the unit sphere and computes # the area of the resulting spherical polygon using the spherical excess formula. corners = [] hx, hy, hz = box.dimensions.x / 2, box.dimensions.y / 2, box.dimensions.z / 2 for dx in [-hx, hx]: for dy in [-hy, hy]: for dz in [-hz, hz]: corners.append(vec3(box.center.x + dx, box.center.y + dy, box.center.z + dz)) # Project to unit sphere unitcorners = [normalize(c - point) for c in corners] # Compute spherical polygon area (solid angle) by decomposing faces into triangles solidangle = 0.0 faces = [ (0, 1, 3, 2), (4, 5, 7, 6), (0, 1, 5, 4), (2, 3, 7, 6), (0, 2, 6, 4), (1, 3, 7, 5) ] for f in faces: v1, v2, v3, v4 = unitcorners[f[0]], unitcorners[f[1]], unitcorners[f[2]], unitcorners[f[3]] solidangle += solidangletriangle(v1, v2, v3) solidangle += solidangletriangle(v1, v3, v4) return abs(solidangle) def solidangletriangle(v1, v2, v3): # Oosterom and Strackee formula for solid angle of a triangle from origin u1, u2, u3 = normalize(v1), normalize(v2), normalize(v3) numerator = dot(u1, cross(u2, u3)) denominator = 1.0 + dot(u1, u2) + dot(u2, u3) + dot(u3, u1) return 2.0 atan2(numerator, denominator) Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: The method reduces traversal time by skipping distant nodes. The memory consumption is determined by the sparse voxel structure (e.g., DAG). Measured Performance: In the SANMIGUEL scene, the method provides faster traversal speed for AO rays compared to full traversal. Scaling: The method scales with the density of the scene and the chosen threshold. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster than standard traversal; maintains high quality for near-contact occlusion. Limitations: Results in images that are darker than ground-truth. When to Use: Use when performance is critical and slight darkening in distant areas is acceptable. The method was introduced in the context of high-resolution sparse voxel DAGs. It leverages the properties of the SVO and DAG scene representations to optimize shadow ray casting. High resolution sparse voxel DAGs, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262367808HighresolutionsparsevoxelDAGs, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Octree Subdivision for Multiple Scattering
body: This method computes multiple scattering contributions in participating media by traversing an octree of volume samples to identify a "tree cut" of nodes that significantly influence a camera sample point. It addresses the computational cost of evaluating light transport from distant or less relevant volume samples by combining solid angle thresholds with phase function checks. It builds on Solid Angle Early Termination for Ambient Occlusion by extending early termination logic to higher-order scattering events. Inputs: Camera sample position Pk. Camera ray direction \hat{o}. Octree cell C with center C.r and incoming light direction C.d. Volume sample positions vi associated with nodes in the hierarchy. Scattering coefficient \sigmas. Extinction coefficient \sigmai for each sample i. Phase function p(\cdot, \cdot). Precomputed multiple scattering table. Thresholds \epsilon1 and \epsilon2. Outputs: Multiple scattering contribution to the radiance at Pk in direction \hat{o}. Data Structures: Octree Cell: Contains center position C.r, incoming light direction C.d, references to child cells, and a reference to the volume sample vi stored at the leaf. Volume Sample: Contains position vi, intensity I{vi}, and extinction coefficient \sigmai. Steps: 1. Initialize traversal at the root of the octree. 2. For the current cell C and sample point Pk, compute the vector \mathbf{u} = Pk - C.r and its unit vector \hat{u}. 3. Calculate the solid angle \Omega(Pk, C) subtended by cell C at Pk. 4. Apply subdivision criteria: if \Omega(Pk, C) > \epsilon1, subdivide and process children. Else if \Omega(Pk, C) > \epsilon2 and (p(\hat{o}, \hat{u}) > \pi/4 or p(\hat{u}, C.d) > \pi/4), subdivide. Else, add C to the tree cut. 5. For each node vi in the tree cut, compute double scattering using the formula: \text{double}(Pk) = \sigmas^2 \sum{vi} \frac{e^{-\sigmai ri} I{vi}}{ri^2} p(\hat{\alpha}, \hat{r}i) p(\hat{r}i, \hat{\alpha}{vi}) where \mathbf{r}i = Pk - vi, ri = \|\mathbf{r}i\|, \hat{r}i = \mathbf{r}i/ri, \hat{\alpha} = \hat{o}, and \hat{\alpha}{vi} = C.d. 6. Handle weak singularities caused by 1/ri^2 by clamping the distance squared. 7. Use the same tree cut to compute higher-order multiple scattering via a precomputed table generated by Monte Carlo simulation of photon propagation in an infinite medium. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemultiplescattering(Pk, ohat, octreeroot, epsilon1, epsilon2, sigmas, phasefunction, precomputedtable): treecut = [] def traverse(node): uvec = Pk - node.center uhat = uvec / length(uvec) omega = solidangle(node, Pk) # if omega > epsilon1: for child in node.children: traverse(child) elif omega > epsilon2: cond1 = phasefunction(ohat, uhat) > math.pi / 4 cond2 = phasefunction(uhat, node.incominglightdir) > math.pi / 4 if cond1 or cond2: for child in node.children: traverse(child) else: treecut.append(node.sample) else: treecut.append(node.sample) traverse(octreeroot) doublescattering = 0.0 for sample in treecut: rvec = Pk - sample.position rdist = length(rvec) rhat = rvec / rdist rdistsq = max(rdist 2, 1e-6) # term = (sigmas 2) (exp(-sample.extinction rdist) sample.intensity / rdistsq) term = phasefunction(ohat, rhat) term = phasefunction(rhat, sample.incominglightdir) doublescattering += term # Higher-order scattering uses a precomputed table from Monte Carlo simulation of photon propagation in an infinite medium. return doublescattering Parameters: \epsilon1: Threshold for solid angle to force subdivision. \epsilon2: Secondary threshold for solid angle combined with phase function check. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. \sigmai: Extinction coefficient for sample i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Weak Singularities: The 1/ri^2 term in the double scattering formula can cause numerical instability when ri is very small. This is handled by clamping the distance squared. Degenerate Input: If Pk coincides with a sample position, ri = 0. Clamping prevents division by zero. This variant focuses specifically on the double scattering component, computing only the first two scattering events (sample to Pk to camera) using the tree cut mechanism. It explicitly evaluates the 1/r^2 attenuation and phase functions for each node in the cut. The stopping criterion uses the solid angle sustained by the node from Pk and the phase function between the outgoing direction \hat{o} and the direction from Pk to the node center vi. The double scattering contribution is calculated as \text{double}(Pk) = \sigmas^2 \sum{vi} \frac{e^{-\sigmai ri} I{vi}}{ri^2} p(\hat{\alpha}, \hat{r}i) p(\hat{r}i, \hat{\alpha}{vi}). Weak singularities from 1/r^2 are handled by clamping. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the octree and the number of nodes in the tree cut; worst case traverses the entire tree, but solid angle and phase checks prune it significantly. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of volume samples stored in the octree. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently approximates multiple scattering by ignoring distant or poorly oriented samples and reduces the number of expensive phase function and attenuation calculations. Limitations: Accuracy depends on the thresholds \epsilon1 and \epsilon2; poorly chosen thresholds can lead to over-subdivision or under-subdivision artifacts; assumes homogeneous media or precomputed per-sample properties. When to Use: When simulating participating media with significant multiple scattering and performance is a concern. When Not to Use: When high accuracy is required for near-field scattering or when the media is highly heterogeneous and cannot be well-represented by the octree samples. The method originates from point-based rendering for homogeneous participating media with refractive boundaries. It extends the PBGI (Point-Based Global Illumination) approach to multiple scattering events. The tree cut mechanism is inspired by solid angle-based early termination techniques used in ambient occlusion. The precomputed table for higher-order scattering is generated via Monte Carlo simulation of photon propagation in an infinite medium. Point-Based Rendering for Homogeneous Participating Media with Refractive Boundaries, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2017.2768525, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Zhukov Ambient Occlusion
head: Ambient Occlusion (Empirical Model), Geometric Obscurance, Obscurance
body: Zhukov Ambient Occlusion is an empirical illumination model that simulates indirect lighting by computing the geometric obscurance of a surface point, representing how open it is to the environment. Unlike radiosity, which measures secondary reflection intensity, it attenuates the constant ambient term of the Phong model based on local geometric occlusion, prioritizing computational speed and aesthetic appeal over physical accuracy. It builds on Ambient Occlusion via Shadow Rays by incorporating a cosine-weighted hemisphere integration directly into the sampling scheme. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface point x, surface normal n, scene geometry (for ray intersection tests). Output: Ambient Occlusion factor OA(x, n), a value in [0, 1]. Data Structures: The source does not specify scene acceleration structures, assuming standard ray-scene intersection routines. Steps: 1. Define a hemisphere \Omega oriented with normal n centered at surface point x. 2. Sample directions \omega uniformly over the hemisphere \Omega. 3. For each direction \omega, cast a ray from x in direction \omega. 4. Evaluate the visibility function V(x, \omega): set V(x, \omega) = 1 if an occluding surface is found, and 0 otherwise. 5. Compute the integrand term V(x, \omega) |\omega \cdot n|. 6. Approximate the integral over \Omega to compute OA(x, n). 7. Multiply the constant ambient term of the Phong model by (1 - OA(x, n)) to approximate global illumination effects. Formula: The ambient occlusion factor is defined as: OA(x, n) = \frac{1}{\pi} \int{\Omega} V(x, \omega) |\omega \cdot n| d\omega Where: x: Surface point. n: Surface normal. \Omega: Hemisphere oriented with n centered at x. V(x, \omega): Visibility function (1 if occluder found, 0 otherwise). |\omega \cdot n|: Absolute value of the dot product between direction \omega and normal n. Parameters: OA(x, n): Range [0, 1]. Value 1 denotes full occlusion (repressed), value 0 denotes no occluding geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def sampleuniformhemisphere(n): u1 = random.uniform(0, 1) u2 = random.uniform(0, 1) z = u1 r = math.sqrt(1.0 - z z) theta = 2.0 math.pi u2 if abs(n[2]) < 0.999: u = normalize(cross(n, (0.0, 0.0, 1.0))) else: u = normalize(cross(n, (1.0, 0.0, 0.0))) v = normalize(cross(n, u)) return normalize((u[0]rmath.cos(theta) + v[0]rmath.sin(theta) + n[0]z, u[1]rmath.cos(theta) + v[1]rmath.sin(theta) + n[1]z, u[2]rmath.cos(theta) + v[2]rmath.sin(theta) + n[2]z)) def computezhukovao(x, n, scene, numsamples): """Computes Zhukov Ambient Occlusion for point x with normal n.""" totalocclusion = 0.0 for in range(numsamples): omega = sampleuniformhemisphere(n) hitdistance = scene.rayintersect(x, omega) v = 1.0 if hitdistance is not None else 0.0 dotproduct = abs(dot(omega, n)) totalocclusion += v dotproduct # The source formula is OA = (1/pi) integral. # Monte Carlo approximation over hemisphere (area 2pi) with uniform PDF (1/2pi) yields: # OA approx (1/pi) (2pi / N) sum(V |w.n|) = (2 / N) sum(...) # The source formula is an integral, not an estimator, and does not specify the PDF return (2.0 / numsamples) totalocclusion Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Small errors in ray origin (self-intersection) can cause incorrect occlusion. Boundaries: The integration is strictly over the hemisphere defined by the normal. Degenerate Input: The source assumes standard exterior surface points; behavior inside geometry is not specified. Zhukov Obscurance is a generalization of ambient occlusion where the binary visibility function is replaced by a distance suitability function \rho(d(x, \omega)). It measures ambient light magnitude based on the distance to the first intersection, rather than just presence/absence. Definition: It computes an obscurance value W(x, n) that maps distance to ambient light contribution. Formula: W(x, n) = \frac{1}{\pi} \int{\Omega} \rho(d(x, \omega)) |\omega \cdot n| d\omega Where: W: Obscurance value (0 \le W \le 1). d(x, \omega): Distance to the first intersection in direction \omega. \rho: Distance suitability mapping function. The reflected intensity is calculated as: I(x) = Ia ka(x) W(x) Where: Ia: Ambient light intensity. ka(x): Diffuse reflectance for ambient light. Distance Suitability Function: The function \rho(d) is defined by the following properties: 1. \rho(0) = 0 (fully occluded). 2. \rho(+\infty) = 1 (fully open). 3. \rho'(d) > 0 (monotonically increasing). 4. \rho''(d) < 0 (monotonically decreasing derivative/smoothness). A suggested family of functions is: \rho(d) = 1 - e^{-\tau d} Where \tau is a positive parameter defining the decay rate. When to choose: Choose Zhukov Obscurance when a smooth falloff based on distance is preferred over binary occlusion, allowing for more nuanced ambient light attenuation. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to the number of samples and the cost of ray intersection tests; it is generally faster than full radiosity because it computes only local geometric obscurance. Memory complexity is low, typically storing the result as vertex attributes or texture maps for later use. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Computationally cheaper than radiosity; aesthetically pleasing; simulates indirect illumination effects effectively. Limitations: Not physically correct; relies on empirical parameters; does not account for light source directionality in the basic AO model (only ambient). When to use it and when not: Use for static scenes where precomputed ambient occlusion maps are beneficial, or for real-time approximations of indirect lighting where physical accuracy is secondary to performance and aesthetics. Do not use when physically accurate global illumination is required. Zhukov Ambient Occlusion was introduced by Zhukov et al. in 1998. The method was designed to achieve illumination effects of occlusion similar to those acquired from radiosity but in a shorter time period. It has become a basis for many other techniques, including those by Iones et al. [IKSZ03] and Kontkanen et al. [KL05]. The technique has become quite popular in the movie industry and has undergone refinement since its introduction. GPU Ray Marching for Ambient Occlusion, https://www.scribd.com/document/520755804/imm6392, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Spatially Cached Raytraced Ambient Occlusion
head: Spatial Hashing for Raytraced Ambient Occlusion
body:
Spatially Cached Raytraced Ambient Occlusion (SC-RTAO) is an optimization for raytraced ambient occlusion that stores accumulated occlusion values in spatial cells within a hashmap. Since ambient occlusion is view-independent, these values can be accumulated into a cell without reprojection when the camera moves, reducing redundant ray tracing for static geometry across frames. It sets itself apart from naive RTAO by trading memory bandwidth and atomic overhead for significant performance gains in static or slowly moving scenes, distinguishing it from sibling methods like Evans AO or Zhukov AO which rely on different sampling or approximation strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Face position (facepos), face normal (normal), pixel coordinate (pixel), frame index (uniforms.frameindex), cell size, hash map parameters. Outputs: Updated hash map payloads (occlusion count and sample count); final AO value derived from the hash map in a separate shading pass. Data Structures: 1. spatialhashkey: A struct containing two 32-bit unsigned integers: hash: The spatial hash key derived from position and normal. checksum: A checksum for collision verification. 2. hashpayloads: An array of 32-bit unsigned integers. The layout packs two 16-bit values: Upper 16 bits: occlusioncount (number of rays that hit geometry). Lower 16 bits: raycount (total number of rays cast for this cell, typically VXAORAYSPERPIXEL). Layout formula: (occlusioncount << 16u) | raycount. 3. hashchecksums: An array of 32-bit unsigned integers storing the checksum for each hash slot. 4. hashframes: An array of 32-bit unsigned integers storing the last frame index in which each hash slot was accessed. Parameters: VXAOHASHMASK: Mask for the hash map size (e.g., for 16 million elements, this is 0xFFFFFF if power-of-two, or specific mask for the chosen size). VXAOMAXCELLAGE: Maximum age (in frames) before a cell is considered expired. VXAOSAMPLELIMIT: Maximum number of samples allowed per hash cell before stopping accumulation. VXAORAYSPERPIXEL: Number of rays cast per pixel for the AO calculation. cellsize: Size of the spatial cell for hashing. Hash map size: 16 million elements (recommended to prevent running out of space during rapid camera movement at 4k resolutions). Steps: 1. Generate Key: Compute the spatial hash key from the face position and normal: key = makespatialhashkey(facepos, normal, cellsize). 2. Lookup/Insert: Call spatialhashfindorinsert(key) to find the index in the hash map. 3. Check Validity: If the returned index is 0xFFFFFFFFu (not found/failed) or the current sample count in the payload exceeds VXAOSAMPLELIMIT, return immediately without casting rays. 4. Offset Ray Origin: Calculate the ray origin by offsetting the face position along the normal: pos = offsetray(facepos, normal). 5. Generate Frame Seed: Create a seed based on the current frame index to vary the sampling pattern across frames: 	ext{frame\seed} = (	ext{frame\index} 	imes 0x9E3779B9u, 	ext{pcg}(	ext{frame\index} \oplus 0xA511E9B3u)) 6. Generate Pixel Noise: Compute a 2D noise vector based on the pixel coordinate and frame seed: 	ext{pixel
oise} = 	ext{as
ormalized loat}(	ext{pcg2d}(	ext{pixel} \oplus 	ext{frame\seed})) 7. Initialize Count: Set occlusioncount = 0. 8. Cast Rays: Loop i from 0 to VXAORAYSPERPIXEL - 1: a. Calculate sample direction u: u = 	ext{frac}(	ext{pixel
oise} + 	ext{r2\sequence}(i)) b. Sample hemisphere: v = 	ext{sample\cosine\weighted\hemisphere}(u) c. Orient direction: 	ext{dir} = 	ext{orient\sample\direction}(v, 	ext{normal}) d. Perform DDA (Digital Differential Analyzer) ray march against the voxel grid for uniforms.rtaoradius. e. If a hit is detected, increment occlusioncount. 9. Atomic Update: Atomically add the results to the hash map payload at the found index: 	ext{InterlockedAdd}(	ext{hash\payloads}[index], (	ext{occlusion\count} \ll 16u) | 	ext{VX\AO\RAYS\PER\PIXEL}, 	ext{ex}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computespatiallycachedrtao(facepos, normal, pixel, uniforms): # 1. Generate Key key = makespatialhashkey(facepos, normal, uniforms.cellsize) # 2. Lookup/Insert index = spatialhashfindorinsert(key) # 3. Check Validity # Extract current ray count from lower 16 bits currentraycount = hashpayloads[index] & 0xFFFFu if index == 0xFFFFFFFFu or currentraycount >= VXAOSAMPLELIMIT: return # 4. Offset Ray Origin pos = offsetray(facepos, normal) # 5. Generate Frame Seed frameseedx = uniforms.frameindex 0x9E3779B9u frameseedy = pcg(uniforms.frameindex ^ 0xA511E9B3u) frameseed = uint2(frameseedx, frameseedy) # 6. Generate Pixel Noise pixelnoise = asnormalizedfloat(pcg2d(pixel ^ frameseed)) # 7. Initialize Count occlusioncount = 0u # 8. Cast Rays for i in range(VXAORAYSPERPIXEL): # a. Calculate sample direction u u = frac(pixelnoise + r2sequence(float(i))) # b. Sample hemisphere v = samplecosineweightedhemisphere(u) # c. Orient direction dir = orientsampledirection(v, normal) # d. Perform DDA if dda(pos, dir, uniforms.rtaoradius): occlusioncount += 1u # 9. Atomic Update # Pack occlusion count (upper 16) and rays cast (lower 16) updatevalue = (occlusioncount << 16u) | VXAORAYSPERPIXEL InterlockedAdd(hashpayloads[index], updatevalue) def spatialhashfindorinsert(key): frame = uniforms.frameindex index = key.hash & VXAOHASHMASK for probe in range(VXAOHASHPROBECOUNT): exchecksum = 0 InterlockedCompareExchange(hashchecksums[index], 0, key.checksum, exchecksum) if exchecksum == 0 or exchecksum == key.checksum: exframe = 0 InterlockedExchange(hashframes[index], frame, exframe) return index exframe = hashframes[index] # Check age if frame - exframe > VXAOMAXCELLAGE: InterlockedExchange(hashchecksums[index], key.checksum) InterlockedExchange(hashpayloads[index], 0) InterlockedExchange(hashframes[index], frame) return index # Linear probe index = (index + 1u) & VXAOHASHMASK return 0xFFFFFFFFu Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Map Saturation: At 4k resolutions, the algorithm may fail to find a free slot older than 20 frames if the hash map is too small. A size of 16 million elements is recommended to mitigate this. Atomic Overhead: The hashmap lookup involves multiple atomic operations (InterlockedCompareExchange, InterlockedExchange, InterlockedAdd), which add overhead compared to regular buffer reads. Register Allocation: Maintaining many float3 variables during the computation can bloat register allocation, reducing shader occupancy (e.g., from ~40% to ~20% in some implementations). Time Complexity: O(1) average case for hash map lookup, but with a high constant factor due to atomic operations and potential linear probing. Ray casting is O(N) where N is the number of rays per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(M) where M is the hash map size (e.g., 16 million elements). Requires storage for hashpayloads, hashchecksums, and hashframes. Measured Performance: On a Macbook Air (M2) with the Sponza scene at 4k resolution: Baseline RTAO: 39.04 FPS (46.16 ms). With SC-RTAO (Cell size 5->10): 71.73 FPS (23.50 ms), a ~83.72% improvement. Further optimizations (checkerboard update, rasterized brick coordinates) pushed FPS to ~72.00 (19.33 ms). Strengths: Significant performance improvement in static or slowly moving scenes by avoiding redundant ray tracing. View-independent accumulation allows for smooth camera movement without reprojection artifacts. Limitations: High memory usage for the hash map. Atomic operations can become a bottleneck. Performance degrades if the camera moves rapidly, causing frequent cache misses and overwrites. Precision issues with float3 can impact shader occupancy. When to Use: Scenes with significant static geometry where AO is a major performance bottleneck. When Not to Use: Highly dynamic scenes with rapid camera movement or frequent geometry changes, as the cache invalidation overhead may negate benefits. Spatially Cached Raytraced Ambient Occlusion was developed as an optimization for voxel raytracers, specifically documented in the "Voxel Raytracer Devlog" by the author of the nelari.us blog. The method was introduced around August 2026 (commit 4a6c4b7) to address performance issues in the RTAO hashmap update pass. It builds on the concept of spatial hashing for raytraced ambient occlusion, leveraging the view-independence of AO to cache results across frames. Voxel Raytracer Devlog // My thought repository, https://nelari.us/post/voxel-ray-tracing/, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Shadow Receiving for Volumes
head: Hard shadows, Receiving shadows, Soft shadows, Volume shadow receiving
body: Shadow Receiving for Volumes is a technique that allows volumetric data to receive shadows cast by polygonal geometry, enhancing depth perception and realism without requiring the volume to be rendered twice. Unlike standard shadow pipelines that render shadow-casting objects separately, this method integrates shadow occlusion checks directly into the volume ray traversal process, significantly reducing computational overhead. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Variance Shadow Mapping for NeRFs by relying on standard shadow maps applied to the volume's ray-marched samples rather than probabilistic variance techniques or neural field approximations. The method operates within a GPU-based volume ray casting pipeline, specifically utilizing the vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper2 architecture. It avoids the performance penalty of double rendering by checking shadow occlusion against a pre-computed shadow map during the traversal of each view ray. Inputs: Volume dataset (scalar field). Polygonal geometry acting as shadow casters. Light source position and direction. Shadow map texture (depth buffer) generated from the light's perspective. Volume transfer function (opacity and color). Outputs: Final color buffer with shadows cast by polygons onto the volume. The implementation relies on the VTK rendering pipeline objects: vtkShadowMapPass: Manages the shadow map generation and application. vtkShadowMapBakerPass: Bakes shadow information and handles receiver flags. vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper2: The mapper performing the ray casting and shadow checks. vtkVolume: The actor representing the volume data. vtkInformation: Used to store property keys, specifically the RECEIVER flag. SoftShadows (Boolean): When true, activates soft shadow rendering. Default is false (hard shadows). SoftShadowsOffset (Float): Controls the offset of the soft shadow in pixels. Linear interpolation is used for the shadow texture, so this value does not need to be an integer. A typical value is 1.0. 1. Initialize Pipeline: Create a rendering pipeline including vtkShadowMapPass and vtkShadowMapBakerPass. 2. Configure Casters: Set up polygonal objects as shadow casters using standard VTK shadow mechanisms. 3. Configure Receiver: Create a vtkInformation object. Set the key vtkShadowMapBakerPass::RECEIVER() to 0 or 1 (the specific value is not strictly differentiated in the source, but the presence of the key enables the feature). Apply this information to the volume actor using volume->SetPropertyKeys(info). 4. Enable Soft Shadows (Optional): If soft shadows are desired, call mapper->SetSoftShadows(true) on the volume mapper. Set mapper->SetSoftShadowsOffset(offset) where offset is the pixel offset for the soft shadow blur. 5. Ray Traversal with Shadow Check: For each pixel, cast a view ray through the volume. During the ray marching steps, for each sample point P in the volume: Transform P into the light's clip space to obtain shadow map coordinates. Sample the shadow map at these coordinates. Determine if the sample point is occluded by comparing the depth of P against the depth stored in the shadow map. If occluded, attenuate the light contribution for that sample. Accumulate the color and opacity using the standard volume ray casting integration equation, modified by the shadow factor. The following pseudocode illustrates the integration of shadow receiving into the volume ray casting loop, based on the VTK implementation described in. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. mapper = vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper2.New() volume = vtkVolume.New() volume.SetMapper(mapper) info = vtkInformation.New() info.Set(vtkShadowMapBakerPass.RECEIVER(), 0) # 0 or 1 enables receiving volume.SetPropertyKeys(info) mapper.SetSoftShadows(True) mapper.SetSoftShadowsOffset(1.0) def RenderVolumeRay(viewRayOrigin, viewRayDirection, lightTransform, shadowMap): accumulatedColor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentAlpha = 0.0 rayPos = viewRayOrigin # Step through the volume while InsideVolume(rayPos): # Get volume value and color at current position value = GetVolumeValue(rayPos) color, opacity = TransferFunction(value) # Shadow Check # Transform rayPos to light space lightPos = lightTransform.TransformPoint(rayPos) shadowCoords = lightPos.ToShadowMapCoords() # Sample shadow map shadowDepth = shadowMap.Sample(shadowCoords) # Determine if occluded # Note: Exact comparison logic depends on depth buffer format (linear/non-linear) isOccluded = rayPos.ZinLightSpace > shadowDepth + epsilon # Attenuate light contribution lightFactor = 1.0 if not isOccluded else 0.0 # Standard Volume Ray Casting Integration # dT = opacity lightFactor dT = opacity lightFactor accumulatedColor += color dT (1.0 - currentAlpha) currentAlpha += dT (1.0 - currentAlpha) if currentAlpha >= 1.0: break rayPos += viewRayDirection stepSize return accumulatedColor Performance Loss: Using the standard shadow pipeline (rendering shadows separately) would require rendering the volume twice, causing significant performance loss. This method avoids that by integrating the check into the traversal. Soft Shadow Offset: The SoftShadowsOffset parameter controls the blur radius. While it represents pixels, it can be a float because linear interpolation is used for the shadow texture. Blend Mode: If BlendModeIsosurface is set to true, the blending mode is forced to isosurface rendering, and other blending modes have no effect. To use other blending modes, BlendModeIsosurface must be set to false. A technique for efficient self-shadowing in volume rendering that uses an opacity shadow map to determine occlusion by the volume itself. It solves the problem of expensive per-view-ray light sampling by precomputing transmittance values from the light's perspective. Unlike Shadow Receiving for Volumes, which handles shadows from external polygons, this method focuses on self-shadowing. Explicitly constructs a volumetric shadow buffer. This differs from Shadow Receiving for Volumes, which uses 2D shadow maps applied during ray traversal. Time Complexity: The additional cost is proportional to the number of volume samples per ray multiplied by the cost of shadow map lookups. Since the volume is not rendered twice, the complexity is dominated by the single pass of ray casting with shadow checks. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the shadow map (depth texture) and the volume data. No additional volumetric buffers are needed for shadow receiving. Strengths: Avoids double rendering of the volume, preserving performance. Provides realistic depth cues by allowing polygons to cast shadows onto the volume. Supports soft shadows via configurable offset and linear interpolation. Limitations: Shadows are only cast from polygonal geometry onto the volume. Self-shadowing of the volume requires additional techniques (e.g., Ray Marching with Shadow Mapping). Shadow map resolution limits the accuracy of shadow boundaries on the volume. When to Use: When realistic depth perception is needed for volumes interacting with polygonal objects, and performance constraints prevent double rendering. When Not to Use: When self-shadowing is the primary requirement, or when high-precision soft shadows are needed without the overhead of additional shadow map passes. This technique was introduced in the context of the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) to enhance realism in volume rendering applications, particularly in simulators where depth perception is critical. The method was developed to address the performance bottleneck of rendering volumes twice in a standard shadow mapping pipeline. It was implemented in vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper2 and documented in research on refined isosurface rendering and shadow mapping. Adding Refined Isosurface Rendering and Shadow Mapping to vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper, https://insight-journal.org/pdfs/880.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27
