name: Ray Marching with Shadow Mapping
head: Deep Opacity Maps, OSM, Opacity Shadow Map Volume Rendering
body: Ray Marching with Shadow Mapping is a technique for efficient self-shadowing in volume rendering that uses an opacity shadow map to determine occlusion by the volume itself. It solves the problem of expensive per-view-ray light sampling by precomputing transmittance values from the light's perspective, avoiding the need to trace rays toward the light for each view-ray sample. Unlike Shadow Volume Rendering, which explicitly constructs a volumetric shadow buffer, this method uses a 2D depth map combined with a 3D array of opacity images sampled from the light source's perspective. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume density function density(\mathbf{p}), absorption coefficient ka, scattering coefficient ks, light direction (azimuth \alpha, elevation \beta), shadow volume range [z{min}, z{max}], step size \Delta z, number of layers/slices N. Outputs: A 3D texture (opacity shadow map) storing transmittance values, and a final rendered image with self-shadowed illumination. Data Structures: The opacity shadow map consists of: 1. A depth (offset) image storing the distance to the cloud start from the light source. 2. A 3D texture array storing transmittance values. The dimensions are W \times H \times N, where W, H are the shadow map resolution and N is the number of depth slices. Constraint: All layers must be stored in a single channel (e.g., Red) to allow correct bilinear/trilinear interpolation. Storing different layers in different color channels (e.g., Layer 1 in Red, Layer 2 in Green) prevents correct interpolation. MRT Limit: If using Multiple Render Targets (MRT) to write layers, the minimum count is 8. If more than 8 layers are needed, multiple passes are used. Parameters: z{min}, z{max}: Define the volume range for slicing the shadow map. If z{min} is too large, the shadow map slice starts inside the volume, making the side facing the light incorrectly too dark. k = k{Schlick}: Anisotropy parameter for Schlick's approximation phase function. \alpha: Azimuth angle controlling directional light direction around the y-axis (0^\circ is center-right, 90^\circ is behind). \beta: Elevation angle controlling directional light direction around -z (0^\circ is center-right, 90^\circ is top). Step jitter: A small random offset added to the step size to hide visible banding caused by low layer counts, at the cost of adding noise. Steps: 1. Render Opacity Shadow Map (Light Pass): 1. Render the scene from the light source's perspective. Use an orthographic camera for directional lights and a perspective camera for point lights. 2. Ray march with even steps of \Delta z through an encapsulating volume from z{min} to z{max}. 3. For each sample position, compute the density and update the accumulated transmittance using Beer's Law: T{new} = T{old} \cdot \exp(-\rho \cdot (ka + ks) \cdot \Delta z) where \rho is the current density, and ka, ks are absorption and scattering coefficients. 4. Store the transmittance values for each depth layer into the 3D texture. If N \le 8, use MRT to write all layers in one pass. Otherwise, use multiple passes. 2. Main Rendering Pass (View Pass): 1. Initialize transmittance T = 1.0 and illumination I = \vec{0}. 2. Loop for i from 0 to stepCount: a. Advance sample position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \Delta z, where \mathbf{d} is the march direction. b. Sample current density \rho = density(\mathbf{p}). c. Update volume transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot \exp(-\rho \cdot (ka + ks) \cdot \Delta z) d. Compute in-scattering. First, determine the shadow factor from the opacity shadow map: i. Transform \mathbf{p} to shadow map space: \mathbf{p}{light} = M{light} \cdot \mathbf{p}. ii. Normalize depth z within the shadow volume range: z = \frac{-\mathbf{p}{light}.z - z{min}}{z{max} - z{min}} iii. Compute UV coordinates: uv = \frac{\mathbf{p}{light}.xy}{lightCamSize} / 2.0 + \vec{0.5} iv. Sample the 3D texture: shadowFactor = texture(opacityShadowMap, vec3(uv, z)).r e. Compute in-scattering: I{in} = L{ambient} + L{direct} \cdot phase(\mathbf{v}, -\mathbf{l}) \cdot shadowFactor where phase(\mathbf{v}, -\mathbf{l}) is the Schlick phase function. f. Compute out-scattering: I{out} = ks \cdot \rho g. Accumulate illumination: I \leftarrow I + T \cdot I{in} \cdot I{out} \cdot \Delta z 3. Return \vec{4}(I, T). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def schlickphase(mu, k): """Schlick's approximation phase function.""" g = k num = 3.0 (1.0 - g g) (1.0 + mu mu) den = 8.0 math.pi (2.0 + g g) math.pow(1.0 + g g - 2.0 g mu, 1.5) return num / den def transformpoint(m, p): """Transforms a 3D point by a 4x4 matrix, returning xyz.""" w = m[3][0]p[0] + m[3][1]p[1] + m[3][2]p[2] + m[3][3] return ( (m[0][0]p[0] + m[0][1]p[1] + m[0][2]p[2] + m[0][3]) / w, (m[1][0]p[0] + m[1][1]p[1] + m[1][2]p[2] + m[1][3]) / w, (m[2][0]p[0] + m[2][1]p[1] + m[2][2]p[2] + m[2][3]) / w) def sample3dtexture(tex, uv, z): """Trilinear interpolation sample from a 3D texture array.""" return tex[uv[0], uv[1], z] def renderopacityshadowmap(lightcammatrix, shadowvolumerange, slicecount, densityfunc, absorptioncoef, scatteringcoef): """Generates the opacity shadow map layers using MRT.""" extinctioncoef = absorptioncoef + scatteringcoef stepsize = (shadowvolumerange[1] - shadowvolumerange[0]) / slicecount layers = [0.0] 8 localposition = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Input: position in light camera space totaldensity = 0.0 for i in range(slicecount): samplepos = (localposition[0], localposition[1], localposition[2] - i stepsize) currentdensity = densityfunc(samplepos) totaldensity += currentdensity transmittance = math.exp(-totaldensity stepsize extinctioncoef) if i < 8: layers[i] = transmittance return layers def raymarch(sampleposition, marchdirection, stepcount, stepsize, lightcammatrix, shadowvolumerange, opacityshadowmap, ambientlight, directlight, scatteringcoef, absorptioncoef, lightcamsize, lightdirection, k): """Main rendering pass with shadow lookup.""" extinctioncoef = absorptioncoef + scatteringcoef transmittance = 1.0 illumination = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(stepcount): sampleposition = (sampleposition[0] + marchdirection[0] stepsize, sampleposition[1] + marchdirection[1] stepsize, sampleposition[2] + marchdirection[2] stepsize) currentdensity = densityfunc(sampleposition) transmittance = math.exp(-currentdensity extinctioncoef stepsize) shadowmapposition = transformpoint(lightcammatrix, sampleposition) z = (-shadowmapposition[2] - shadowvolumerange[0]) / (shadowvolumerange[1] - shadowvolumerange[0]) uv = (shadowmapposition[0] / lightcamsize[0] / 2.0 + 0.5, shadowmapposition[1] / lightcamsize[1] / 2.0 + 0.5) shadowfactor = sample3dtexture(opacityshadowmap, uv, z) vdotl = -(marchdirection[0]lightdirection[0] + marchdirection[1]lightdirection[1] + marchdirection[2]lightdirection[2]) phaseval = schlickphase(vdotl, k) inscattering = [ambientlight[0] + directlight[0] phaseval shadowfactor, ambientlight[1] + directlight[1] phaseval shadowfactor, ambientlight[2] + directlight[2] phaseval shadowfactor] outscattering = scatteringcoef currentdensity currentlight = [inscattering[0] outscattering, inscattering[1] outscattering, inscattering[2] outscattering] illumination[0] += transmittance currentlight[0] stepsize illumination[1] += transmittance currentlight[1] stepsize illumination[2] += transmittance currentlight[2] stepsize return (illumination[0], illumination[1], illumination[2], transmittance) Shadow Volume Rendering is a specialized ray marching routine that computes only the accumulated alpha (transmittance) along a ray to generate shadow maps or occlusion values for volume scenes. It precomputes a shadow volume to store the amount of light arriving at each sample after attenuation by intervening material, allowing the renderer to multiply interpolated values from this map by colors from the transfer function during the main pass. Unlike Ray Marching with Shadow Mapping, which uses an opacity shadow map for occlusion, this method explicitly constructs a volumetric shadow buffer. This method adds shadows to mixtures of geometric and volumetric data by storing shadow information in a 3D light strength buffer instead of a 2D shadow depth buffer. It sets itself apart from its sibling Ray Marching with Shadow Mapping by computing a fractional light strength at every point in space, which allows it to correctly render penumbras and semi-transparent shadows without the aliasing artifacts associated with Williams' 2D shadow depth buffer. The Light Injection Pass is a post-processing technique that adds volumetric light scattering (such as sun shafts and lamp glow) to a rendered scene by marching rays from the camera through the volume to sample light sources and their occlusion. It solves the problem of visualizing light interacting with participating media (air/fog) in real-time without full path tracing, relying on pre-existing shadow maps for occlusion. Unlike Shadow Volume Rendering which uses geometric volumes, or Volume Shadow Calculation via Light Strength Buffer which may use different accumulation buffers, this method specifically targets direct illumination scattering using a ray-marching approach over a depth buffer, executed as a distinct post-process step. Deep Shadow Maps are a shadow mapping technique where each pixel stores a curve representing volume density as a function of distance, rather than just the depth to the nearest object. The algorithm computes a shadow map per light in the scene, storing a curve in each pixel that represents how transmission through the volume changes as one moves through it. Unlike standard shadow maps which store depth to the nearest object, deep shadow maps store volume density information. It is mentioned for completeness and historical reasons, with similarities to baking lighting into voxels. Developed in 2000 by Tom Lokovic and Eric Veach from Pixar. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In an example using 28.5 FPS on an AMD Ryzen 7 4700U at 640x480 resolution, 3 deep opacity maps with a 7x512x512 transmittance array were rendered per frame. Strengths: More efficient than sampling light rays towards the light source for each sample of the view ray. Avoids the need for per-view-ray light sampling. Limitations: Visible banding can occur due to the low number of layers. Storing layers in different color channels prevents correct interpolation. If z{min} is too large, shadows are incorrect. When to use: When self-shadowing is required for volumes and performance is a concern compared to full light sampling. When not to use: When high-quality penumbras are required (consider Volume Shadow Calculation via Light Strength Buffer) or when the volume geometry is highly irregular and non-uniform sampling is needed (consider Deep Opacity Maps variant). The technique was developed as an alternative to per-view-ray light sampling for volume self-shadowing. It builds on the concept of shadow mapping, extending it to record transparency (transmittance) along different depths from the light's perspective. The term "Opacity Shadow Maps" is used to describe this specific implementation using a 3D texture of transmittance values. Related historical techniques include Deep Shadow Maps by Tom Lokovic and Eric Veach (2000). name: Shadow Volume Rendering
head: Volumetric Shadow Maps
body: Shadow Volume Rendering is a specialized ray marching routine that computes only the accumulated alpha (transmittance) along a ray to generate shadow maps or occlusion values for volume scenes. It precomputes a shadow volume to store the amount of light arriving at each sample after attenuation by intervening material, allowing the renderer to multiply interpolated values from this map by colors from the transfer function during the main pass. Unlike Ray Marching with Shadow Mapping, which uses an opacity shadow map for occlusion, this method explicitly constructs a volumetric shadow buffer. Inputs: Ray origin and direction in world space, world-to-object transformation matrix, tMin, tMax, samplingScale, self.step, and nearlyone threshold. Outputs: Accumulated alpha (transmittance) value for the ray. Data Structures: ShadowPayload: Contains rng (pointer to RandomTEA) and alpha (float). Packaged via packPointer(&payload, u0, u1). Numbered Steps: 1. Transform the ray origin and direction from world space to object space using the provided transformation matrix. 2. Initialize a ShadowPayload with alpha = 0.0 and a random number generator. 3. March along the ray from tMin to tMax using a step size adjusted by samplingScale. 4. For each step, compute the sample position p using jittered interpolation between the current and next step boundaries. 5. Sample the volume density/alpha at p and accumulate it into payload.alpha using front-to-back blending. 6. Continue marching while payload.alpha remains below nearlyone; terminate otherwise. 7. Return the final payload.alpha for use in the main rendering pass. Formulas: Sample position: p = \text{org} + \text{lerp}(\text{jitter}, t, t{\text{next}}) \times \text{dir} Alpha accumulation: \text{payload.alpha} \leftarrow \text{payload.alpha} + (1.0 - \text{payload.alpha}) \times \text{sampleAlpha} Termination condition: \text{payload.alpha} < \text{nearly\one} Where org and dir are the transformed ray origin and direction, jitter is a random float, t and t{\text{next}} are the step boundaries, and sampleAlpha is the sampled volume density. Parameters: samplingScale: Multiplier applied to self.step to adjust shadow ray sampling density. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blurry Shadows & Dark Images: The method can result in blurry shadows and dark images due to interpolation and shadow mapping limitations. Memory Usage: The precomputed shadow volume requires extra memory. Precision: The sources do not specify precision issues, but the use of float for alpha accumulation suggests potential precision limits in high-opacity regions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shadowvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, wto, tmin, tmax, samplingscale, stepsize, nearlyone): # Step 1: Transform ray to object space org = xfmpoint(wto, rayorigin) dir = xfmvector(wto, raydirection) # Step 2: Initialize payload payload = { 'rng': RandomTEA(), # standard RNG initialization 'alpha': 0.0 } # Step 3: Ray marching loop t = tmin while t < tmax: tnext = t + samplingscale stepsize # Step 4: Compute sample position with jitter jitter = payload['rng'].nextfloat() # standard RNG call p = org + lerp(jitter, t, tnext) dir # Step 5: Sample volume density/alpha at p samplealpha = 0.0 # sample volume density/alpha at p # Step 5: Accumulate alpha using front-to-back blending payload['alpha'] += (1.0 - payload['alpha']) samplealpha # Step 6: Termination check if payload['alpha'] >= nearlyone: break t = tnext return payload['alpha'] Definition: An approximation method that uses orthogonal basis functions (e.g., Fourier series) to calculate self-shadowing more efficiently than ray marching. How it works: 1. Generate a volume shadow map from the sun direction using orthographic projection. 2. Store the first 9 Fourier coefficients in a shadow map with format 512x512x3 R11G11B10. 3. During rendering, read the Fourier coefficients and combine them linearly with basis functions to reconstruct optical depth and transmittance. Comparison: TFM efficiency is roughly equivalent to Ray Marching with 1-2 steps, but provides more accurate results than 2-step RM. It may produce banding artifacts. Time Complexity: The basic shadow volume rendering involves a ray marching loop. The number of steps depends on the samplingScale. TFM is roughly equivalent to 1-2 steps of ray marching in efficiency. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volumetric shadow map. The TFM variant uses a 512x512x3 R11G11B10 texture. Performance: Not given in the sources for the basic method. TFM is noted as efficient. Strengths: Precomputes shadow information to store light attenuation, which is interpolated and multiplied by transfer function colors during rendering. TFM offers a balance of efficiency and accuracy. Limitations: Can produce blurry shadows and dark images. TFM may produce banding artifacts. Requires extra memory for the shadow volume. When to use: When self-shadowing is required for volumetric scenes and performance is a concern, but high accuracy is still desired (TFM). When not to use: When memory is constrained, as the method uses extra memory for the shadow volume. The concept of precomputing a shadow volume for volumetric materials was introduced to address the unrealistic assumption that light arrives at a sample without interacting with the rest of the volume. This approach was proposed as an alternative to surface-based lighting models. The Transmittance Function Mapping variant has been used in games like Final Fantasy, utilizing Fourier series for approximation. name: Shadow Volume Representation (SVR)
head: Global Light Propagation, Global Shadow Volume, SVR (Shadow Volume Representation)
body: Shadow Volume Representation (SVR) is a sparse data structure that stores global opacity (\alphag) along rays from volume points to a light source, enabling efficient estimation of direct light contribution in participating media. It distinguishes itself from full-resolution ray integration by decoupling the storage resolution from the integration resolution, allowing interactive adjustment of the shadow map density while maintaining high-quality visibility estimates. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volumetric dataset with local piecewise opacities (\alpha{lp}) computed along rays towards a light source; a sparse multi-resolution grid structure (e.g., flat blocking) defining the SVR resolution. Output: A sparse grid storing global opacity values \alphag for each voxel in the SVR grid. Data Structures The SVR is stored in a sparse data structure, typically a flat blocking multi-resolution structure. SVR Grid: A 3D grid with resolution N{svr} \times N{svr} \times N{svr}. Resolution Ratio: The SVR resolution is typically 1:4 relative to the data volume resolution N{data}. Each sample in the SVR covers a block of 4^3 = 64 voxels in the data volume. Sparse Storage: Only non-empty blocks are stored to save memory. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize SVR: Create the sparse grid structure. Determine the block size based on the 1:4 ratio (or user-defined interactive parameter). 2. Iterate Voxels: For each voxel v in the data volume: a. Ray Casting: Cast a ray from v towards the light source. b. High-Resolution Integration: Sample the local piecewise opacity \alpha{lp}(si) at high resolution along the ray segment from v to the light source. Linear interpolation is used to estimate local segments, introducing minor errors. c. Compute Global Opacity: Calculate \alphag for the starting point s0 (the voxel position) using the product formula: \alphag(s0) = 1 - \prod{i=0}^k (1 - \alpha{lp}(si)) where k is the number of samples along the ray, and \alpha{lp}(si) are the local opacities at sample points si. d. Store Result: Map the voxel v to its corresponding block in the sparse SVR grid. Store the computed \alphag(s0) in that block. 3. Handle Empty Blocks (Pitfall Mitigation): If a ray originates in an empty block (ignored by the sparse structure), it may miss occlusion from neighboring non-empty blocks. To fix this: a. Advance the ray origin to the next non-empty block along the ray direction before computing \alphag. b. Compute \alphag for this advanced origin and store it in the corresponding non-empty block. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesvr(datavolume, lightdirection, svrresolutionratio=4): """ Computes the Shadow Volume Representation (SVR). Args: datavolume: 3D array of local piecewise opacities alphalp. lightdirection: Normalized vector pointing to the light source. svrresolutionratio: Ratio of data volume resolution to SVR resolution. Returns: svrgrid: Sparse dictionary mapping block coordinates to global opacity values. """ # Determine SVR grid dimensions datares = datavolume.shape[0] svrres = datares // svrresolutionratio blocksize = svrresolutionratio # Sparse storage: key=(blockx, blocky, blockz), value=globalopacity svrgrid = {} # Iterate over all voxels in the data volume for x in range(datares): for y in range(datares): for z in range(datares): # Ray origin is the current voxel rayorigin = (x, y, z) # Check if the block containing this voxel is empty in the sparse structure # Note: In a real implementation, 'isblockempty' would check the sparse structure # or a separate occupancy grid. For this self-contained example, we assume # we must handle the pitfall by advancing if the current block is empty. blockcoords = (x // blocksize, y // blocksize, z // blocksize) # If the block is empty (or not yet computed), advance the ray # to the next non-empty block along the light direction. # This is a simplified check; in practice, one might pre-compute # block occupancy. if not isblockoccupied(blockcoords, svrgrid): # Advance ray to next non-empty block rayorigin = advancetonextnonemptyblock( rayorigin, lightdirection, blocksize, datares) # Recompute block coordinates for the advanced origin blockcoords = ( rayorigin[0] // blocksize, rayorigin[1] // blocksize, rayorigin[2] // blocksize) # Cast ray from rayorigin to light source # Sample local piecewise opacities at high resolution samples = samplerayalongdirection( rayorigin, lightdirection, datavolume) # Compute global opacity using the product formula # alphag(s0) = 1 - product(1 - alphalp(si)) transmittance = 1.0 for alphalp in samples: transmittance = (1.0 - alphalp) globalopacity = 1.0 - transmittance # Store in sparse grid svrgrid[blockcoords] = globalopacity return svrgrid def isblockoccupied(blockcoords, svrgrid): """Check if a block is already in the sparse grid.""" return blockcoords in svrgrid def advancetonextnonemptyblock(origin, direction, blocksize, datares): """ Advances the ray origin to the next non-empty block along the direction. This is a placeholder for the specific logic to find the next occupied block. In practice, this might involve traversing the sparse structure or checking an occupancy grid. """ # Simplified: just return the original origin for this example. # A real implementation would step along the direction until a non-empty block is found. return origin def samplerayalongdirection(origin, direction, datavolume): """ Samples the local piecewise opacity along the ray. Returns a list of alphalp values. """ # Placeholder for high-resolution ray marching logic # This would involve stepping through the datavolume along the direction # and interpolating alphalp values. return [0.1, 0.2, 0.3] # Example values Parameters SVR Resolution Ratio: Typically 1:4, meaning each SVR sample covers 4^3=64 voxels. This can be adjusted interactively. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Empty Blocks: Rays originating in empty blocks (ignored by the sparse structure) may miss occlusion from neighboring non-empty blocks. Solution: Advance the ray to the next non-empty block before computing \alphag. Interpolation Errors: Linear interpolation used to estimate local segments introduces small errors in \alpha{lp}. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of voxels and the length of the ray integration. High-resolution integration is performed for each voxel, but storage is sparse. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of non-empty blocks in the SVR grid, which is significantly less than the full data volume if the volume is sparse. Performance: Allows interactive adjustment of SVR resolution. Lower resolutions can be used for dynamic scenes, with incremental refinement when static. Strengths: Reduces storage and computation compared to full-resolution shadow maps while maintaining high-quality visibility estimates. Limitations: Interpolation errors; potential for missed occlusion if empty block handling is not implemented correctly. SVR was introduced in the context of interactive global light propagation in direct volume rendering. It builds on the concept of local piecewise integration to enable efficient global light contribution estimation. The method is part of a broader framework that includes in-scattering estimation and incremental refinement. name: Volume Shadow Calculation via Light Strength Buffer
head: 3D Shadow Casting, Light Strength Buffer Method
body: This method adds shadows to mixtures of geometric and volumetric data by storing shadow information in a 3D light strength buffer instead of a 2D shadow depth buffer. It sets itself apart from its sibling Ray Marching with Shadow Mapping by computing a fractional light strength at every point in space, which allows it to correctly render penumbras and semi-transparent shadows without the aliasing artifacts associated with Williams' 2D shadow depth buffer. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volumetric data, geometric data (polygons), and a set of light sources. Outputs: A final composited image with correct volumetric shadows. Data Structures: 1. Composite Color/Opacity Volumes: For each light source i, a 3D volume storing composite color Ci and composite opacity Oc for each voxel. 2. 3D Light Strength Buffer: A 3D volume storing the light strength P{i,j} at each sample position along each ray for each light source i. Steps: 1. Shade and classify the volumetric data, shade and scan-convert the polygons, and use volume matting operators to yield composite colors Ci and opacity Oc for each voxel for each light source i. 2. Cast parallel illumination rays from each light source into the data. 3. For each ray, assume an initial light strength, draw samples at equally spaced positions along the ray, compute the opacity at each location by tri-linearly interpolating from the nearest eight voxels, and attenuate the ray strength. Store the computed light strengths P{i,j} in the 3D light strength buffer. 4. Compute the total color ct for each voxel as the weighted sum of light strengths mapped from voxel indices into the coordinate system of each light source i, tri-linearly interpolating from the nearest eight light strength values. 5. Ray trace, resample, and composite the arrays of total color ct and composite opacity oc. Formula: The strength P{i,j+k} of a ray as it leaves a sample location is computed from the strength P{i,j} as it approaches the sample and the opacity \alpha of the sample: P{i,j+k} = P{i,j} \left(1 - \frac{k{i,j}}{d^2}\right) Where: P{i,j} is the light strength approaching the sample. P{i,j+k} is the light strength leaving the sample. k{i,j} is a constant for the linear approximation of square-law attenuation. d is the distance from the light source to the sample location. The total color ct for each voxel is computed as: ct = \sum{i=1}^{L} Pi Ci Where Pi is the light strength obtained by mapping voxel indices into the coordinate system of light source i and tri-linearly interpolating from the nearest eight light strength values. Pitfalls: Surfaces in volumetric data (which often have a thickness of several voxels) tend to partially shadow themselves, causing distracting aliasing artifacts. Solution: Translate the 3-D light strength volume a few voxels away from the light source before computing ct. This reduces accuracy within small objects but avoids the artifacts. A technique that uses a shared slicing axis aligned between the viewer and light source to avoid the visual artifacts of volumetric shadow maps. It sets itself apart from this method by utilizing a two-pass loop per slice to accumulate light attenuation, whereas this method uses a full 3D buffer. Memory: The amount of memory required for a 3D buffer is obviously much greater than a 2D shadow depth buffer. Advantages: Avoids shadow aliasing problems encountered by Williams' 2D shadow depth buffer. Correctly handles semi-transparent shadows and penumbras. Correctly renders shadows cast by volumetrically defined objects on themselves, shadows cast by polygons on volumetric objects, and vice versa. Limitations: High memory consumption due to the 3D nature of the buffer. The solution to self-shadowing aliasing (translating the buffer) reduces accuracy within small objects. The method employs a two-pass approach similar to Williams [1978], but stores shadow information in a 3D light strength buffer instead of a 2D shadow depth buffer. name: Half-Angle Slicing for Incremental Lighting
head: Two-Pass Volumetric Shadow Setup
body: Half-Angle Slicing is a technique for computing volumetric shadows efficiently by using a pixel buffer to accumulate light attenuation from the light's point of view, thereby avoiding the visual artifacts (such as blurry shadows and dark images) associated with volumetric shadow maps. It sets apart from its sibling Volume Shadow Calculation via Light Strength Buffer by utilizing a shared slicing axis that is geometrically aligned between the viewer and the light source, allowing a single set of slices to be rendered from both perspectives in a two-pass loop per slice. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume data, transfer function (mapping scalar value to color C and opacity A), eye view direction, light view direction, light color CL, desired sampling distance along the observer view direction dv. Outputs: Final image in the eye buffer. Data Structures: 1. Eye Buffer: Standard framebuffer for the final composite image. 2. Light Buffer: A texture buffer used to accumulate light attenuation, initialized to the light color CL. 3. Volume Data Texture: 3D texture containing the scalar field. 4. Slice Geometry: Proxy geometry (e.g., a plane or box) representing the current slice. Parameters: CL: Light color. dv: Desired sampling distance along the observer view direction. \theta: Angle between the observer view direction and the light view direction. ds: Slice spacing, calculated to maintain constant sampling rate. Formulas: The slice spacing ds is determined by the angle \theta between the observer and light view directions to ensure a constant sampling rate relative to the observer: ds = \frac{dv}{\cos(\theta/2)} Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Clear the eye buffer and initialize the light buffer to the light color CL. 2. Determine Slice Axis: Compute the proxy geometry in object space. Calculate the dot product of the light direction (\vec{L}) and the view direction (\vec{V}). If \vec{L} \cdot \vec{V} > 0: Set the slice direction to the vector halfway between the light and view directions. Render the volume front-to-back for the eye using the Under operator. Render front-to-back for the light using the Over operator. If \vec{L} \cdot \vec{V} \le 0: Set the slice direction to the vector halfway between the light and the inverted view directions. Render the volume back-to-front for the eye using the Over operator. Render front-to-back for the light using the Over operator. 3. Loop over Slices: For each slice along the determined axis: Pass 1 (Eye Rendering): Render and blend the slice into the eye buffer. Project the slice vertices to the light buffer using the light's modelview and projection matrices. Convert the resulting vertex positions to 2D texture coordinates based on the size of the light's viewport and the light buffer. Bind the light buffer as a texture. In the fragment shader, evaluate the transfer function for reflective color C and opacity A. Multiply C by the color sampled from the light buffer (CL). Blend C and A into the eye buffer using the appropriate operator (Under or Over) determined in Step 2. Pass 2 (Light Buffer Update): Render and blend the slice into the light buffer using the Over operator. In the fragment shader, evaluate the transfer function for the alpha component and set the fragment color to 0. 4. Finalize: The eye buffer contains the final image with volumetric shadows. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in v)) return [x / length for x in v] def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, val)) def halfangleslicing(volumedata, transferfunction, eyeview, lightview, lightcolor, dv, lightbuffersize): # 1. Initialization eyebuffer = [0.0] (lightbuffersize[0] lightbuffersize[1] 4) lightbuffer = [lightcolor] (lightbuffersize[0] lightbuffersize[1] 4) # Initialized to light color CL # 2. Determine Slice Axis and Direction dotproduct = dot(normalize(lightview), normalize(eyeview)) dotproduct = clamp(dotproduct, -1.0, 1.0) # Fix precision bug for acos if dotproduct > 0: sliceaxis = normalize([lightview[i] + eyeview[i] for i in range(3)]) eyeblendop = "UNDER" lightblendop = "OVER" eyerenderorder = "FRONTTOBACK" else: sliceaxis = normalize([lightview[i] - eyeview[i] for i in range(3)]) # Inverted view direction eyeblendop = "OVER" lightblendop = "OVER" eyerenderorder = "BACKTOFRONT" # Calculate slice spacing theta = math.acos(dotproduct) ds = dv / math.cos(theta / 2) # 3. Loop over slices slices = generateslices(volumedata, sliceaxis, ds) for sliceobj in slices: # Pass 1: Render to Eye Buffer lighttexcoords = projecttolightbuffer(sliceobj.vertices, lightview, lightbuffersize) lightbuffertexture = lightbuffer renderslicetobuffer( sliceobj=sliceobj, buffer=eyebuffer, volumedata=volumedata, transferfunction=transferfunction, lighttexcoords=lighttexcoords, blendop=eyeblendop, order=eyerenderorder) # Pass 2: Render to Light Buffer renderslicetobuffer( sliceobj=sliceobj, buffer=lightbuffer, volumedata=volumedata, transferfunction=transferfunction, lighttexcoords=None, blendop="OVER", order="FRONTTOBACK", coloroverride=0.0) def generateslices(volumedata, axis, spacing): # Returns a list of slice objects representing planes along the axis pass def projecttolightbuffer(vertices, lightview, lightbuffersize): # Converts 3D vertex positions to 2D texture coordinates based on light's viewport and buffer size pass def renderslicetobuffer(sliceobj, buffer, volumedata, transferfunction, lighttexcoords, blendop, order, coloroverride=None): for fragment in sliceobj.rasterize(): value = samplevolume(volumedata, fragment.worldposition) C, A = transferfunction(value) if lighttexcoords is not None: CL = sampletexture(lighttexcoords) C = [C[i] CL[i] for i in range(3)] if coloroverride is not None: C = [coloroverride, coloroverride, coloroverride] blendintobuffer(buffer, fragment.position, C, A, blendop) def samplevolume(volumedata, pos): # Standard 3D texture lookup pass def sampletexture(texcoords): # Standard 2D texture lookup pass def blendintobuffer(buffer, pos, C, A, op): # Blends color C and alpha A into buffer at pos using UNDER or OVER operator pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Angle Adjustment: As the angle between the observer and light changes, the slice distance ds must be adjusted to maintain a constant sampling rate. Scattering: The method ignores contributions from light scattering within the volume, which can result in dark and unrealistic images. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of slices times the number of fragments per slice, requiring two rendering passes per slice. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the eye buffer, the light buffer, and the volume data, where the light buffer size depends on the light's viewport and resolution. Strengths: Avoids the artifacts of volumetric shadow maps (blurry shadows, dark images) by using a pixel buffer for attenuation accumulation and efficiently reuses slice geometry for both eye and light views. Limitations: Does not account for light scattering, leading to potentially dark images, and performance depends on the number of slices and the resolution of the light buffer. When to use: When real-time volumetric shadows are needed and shadow map artifacts are unacceptable, suitable for scenes where direct illumination attenuation is the primary shadowing component. When not to use: When accurate scattering effects (translucency, subsurface scattering) are required, as this method ignores them. The technique was described in GPU Gems, Chapter 39, "Volume Rendering Techniques," referencing Kniss et al. 2003. It is presented as an improvement over volumetric shadow maps, which suffer from visual artifacts and high memory usage, and is part of the broader family of local illumination and shadowing techniques for participating media, specifically building upon the concepts of ray marching and shadow receiving for volumes. name: Deep Shadow Maps
head: DOM, Deep Opacity Maps
body: Deep Shadow Maps are a shadow mapping technique for volume rendering where each pixel stores a curve representing volume density as a function of distance, rather than just the depth to the nearest opaque object. This allows for accurate occlusion calculations in participating media by integrating transmission along the ray. Unlike standard shadow maps which only capture the nearest surface, deep shadow maps capture the entire volumetric structure along the light ray. Inputs: Scene geometry and volume density fields. Light positions and directions. Camera parameters. Outputs: A set of shadow maps, one per light source. Each shadow map pixel contains a data structure representing the volume density profile along the ray from the light to the far plane. Data Structures: Each pixel in the deep shadow map stores a curve. While the exact bit-packing is not specified in the primary sources, the conceptual structure is a function D(d) where d is the distance from the light source and D is the density or transmission factor. In practice, this is often implemented as a 1D texture or a series of samples along the ray. Steps: 1. Light Space Projection: For each light in the scene, project the volume geometry into the light's coordinate space. 2. Volume Rasterization: Render the volume into the shadow map. Instead of storing a single depth value, store the density information as a function of distance. 3. Curve Storage: Each pixel in the shadow map stores a curve representing how transmission through the volume changes as one moves through it. This curve effectively describes the optical depth along the ray. 4. Shadow Lookup: During volume rendering, for each sample point on the view ray, project its position into the light's shadow map. 5. Transmission Calculation: Retrieve the density/transmission value from the deep shadow map at the projected location. Integrate this value along the ray to compute the final shadowed illumination. Formulas: The transmission T along a ray segment from d1 to d2 is computed by integrating the density \sigma stored in the deep shadow map: T = \exp\left(-\int{d1}^{d2} \sigma(d) \, dd\right) Where \sigma(d) is the density value retrieved from the deep shadow map at distance d. Parameters: Shadow map resolution: Not given in the sources. Number of samples per ray for curve approximation: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Storing a continuous curve in discrete pixels requires careful sampling and interpolation to avoid artifacts. Memory: Deep shadow maps consume significantly more memory than standard shadow maps due to the storage of multiple values per pixel. Complexity: The integration step during rendering adds computational cost compared to simple depth comparisons. A variant of deep opacity maps using a series of cuboids covering different splits of the view frustum, similar to cascaded shadow maps, to handle varying distances. This approach improves accuracy for volumes at different depths by allocating higher resolution to closer regions. Time Complexity: Higher than standard shadow maps due to the need to store and integrate density curves. Memory Complexity: Significantly higher than standard shadow maps as each pixel stores a curve rather than a single depth value. Strengths: Accurate shadowing for participating media; handles complex volumetric structures. Limitations: High memory usage; complex implementation; primarily of historical interest. When to use: When accurate volumetric shadows are required and memory is not a constraint. When not to use: For real-time applications with strict memory budgets or simple opaque scenes. Deep Shadow Maps were developed in 2000 by Tom Lokovic and Eric Veach from Pixar. The technique was introduced as a way to handle shadows in volumetric scenes where standard shadow maps fail due to their inability to represent partial occlusion within a volume. It is often mentioned for completeness and historical reasons, with similarities to baking lighting into voxels. name: Light Injection Pass
head: Volumetric Light, Wave D volumetric light
body: The Light Injection Pass is a post-processing technique that adds volumetric light scattering (such as sun shafts and lamp glow) to a rendered scene by marching rays from the camera through the volume to sample light sources and their occlusion. It solves the problem of visualizing light interacting with participating media (air/fog) in real-time without full path tracing, relying on pre-existing shadow maps for occlusion. Unlike Shadow Volume Rendering which uses geometric volumes, or Volume Shadow Calculation via Light Strength Buffer which may use different accumulation buffers, this method specifically targets direct illumination scattering using a ray-marching approach over a depth buffer, executed as a distinct post-process step. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: The depth buffer (from MSAA resolve), camera view/projection matrices, light positions and types (Sun, Lamps), shadow maps (cascaded for sun, cubemaps for lamps), and configuration parameters (rvolumetric). Outputs: A 3D texture storing per-voxel in-scattered radiance and extinction coefficients, which is later blurred and composited. Data Structures: 3D Texture: Stores per-voxel in-scattered radiance and extinction coefficient. Written to via glBindImageTexture (image load/store). Shadow Maps: Cascaded Shadow Maps (CSM) for directional lights (Sun) and Shadow Cubemaps for point lights (Lamps). Parameters: rvolumetric: Boolean, default 1, latched. Enables the pass. rvolumetricDensity: Float, default 1, live. If 0, pass is skipped. rvolumetricAnisotropy: Float, default 0.5, live. Henyey-Greenstein g parameter. rvolumetricSun: Boolean, default 1, live. Enables sun lighting. rvolumetricLamps: Boolean, default 1, live. Enables lamp lighting. rvolumetricRange: Float, default 3000 units. Max march distance for sun rays. Algorithm Steps: 1. Execution Context: The pass runs after MSAA resolve and before bloom/tone mapping, at 1/4 view resolution. 2. Voxel Center Reconstruction: For each voxel in the 3D grid, map its 3D index (x, y, z) to clip space, apply the inverse view-projection matrix, and divide by w to obtain the world-space center of the cell. 3. Sun Ray Marching: For the sun, march 16 steps along the ray from the eye to the depth buffer. Terminate the march when the distance exceeds rvolumetricRange (3000 units). At each step, sample the shadow from the finest of the four CSM cascades that contains the sun direction. 4. Lamp Ray Selection and Marching: For each active lamp, perform a ray-sphere test to determine the segment of the view ray that lies within the lamp's reach. If the lamp's upper-bound contribution C = \pi / h (where h is the distance from the ray to the lamp center) is below the visible threshold, skip the lamp. March 4 steps along the selected lamp segment. Use equi-angular sampling (Kulla & Fajardo 2012) to distribute steps by angle at the lamp, canceling 1/d^2 falloff against sampling density. Sample the lamp's cube shadow map for occlusion. 5. Lighting Calculation: For all unshadowed steps, evaluate light color, attenuation, and the Henyey-Greenstein phase function p(\theta) with anisotropy g=0.5. Apply shade, cone, and fade terms consistent with RtLightParticle. Store the resulting in-scattered radiance and extinction coefficient in the 3D texture using image load/store. 6. Noise Reduction: Apply per-pixel interleaved-gradient jitter during sampling, followed by a depth-aware blur pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. radius2 disc = bb - c if disc < 0: return -1, None t = -b - disc0.5 return t, add(origin, scale(dir, t)) def equiangularsample(i, steps): return (1.0 - 2.0 (i + 0.5) / steps) # Kulla & Fajardo 2012 def samplecsmshadow(pos, sundir): return 1.0 # Standard shadow map lookup def samplecubemapshadow(pos, lamppos): return 1.0 # Standard cubemap lookup def evaluatesunlight(pos, dir): return sunintensity # Standard light evaluation def evaluatelamplight(pos, lamp, shadow): return lamp.color shadow # Standard light evaluation def depthawareblur(tex): return tex # Standard blur pass def lightinjectionpass(viewwidth, viewheight, viewprojinv, cameraeye, sundirection, lamps, params): resx = viewwidth // 4 resy = viewheight // 4 resz = params.voxeldepth # Not given in the sources. # 3D texture for radiance and extinction volumetexture = [[0.0, 0.0] for in range(resx resy resz)] for z in range(resz): for y in range(resy): for x in range(resx): # Step 2: Reconstruct world position clippos = vec4(x / resx 2.0 - 1.0, y / resy 2.0 - 1.0, z / resz 2.0 - 1.0, 1.0) worldpos = mat4mulvec(viewprojinv, clippos) worldpos = normalize(worldpos) totalradiance = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Step 3: Sun Ray Marching if params.rvolumetricSun: sunsteps = 16 maxdist = params.rvolumetricRange stepdist = maxdist / sunsteps for i in range(sunsteps): currentdist = i stepdist raypos = add(cameraeye, scale(sundirection, currentdist)) shadowval = samplecsmshadow(raypos, sundirection) if shadowval > 0.0: radiance = evaluatesunlight(raypos, sundirection) totalradiance = add(totalradiance, scale(radiance, shadowval)) # Step 4 & 5: Lamp Ray Marching for lamp in lamps: raydir = normalize(subtract(worldpos, cameraeye)) hitdist, hitnormal = raysphereintersect(cameraeye, raydir, lamp.position, lamp.radius) if hitdist > 0: h = distance(cameraeye, lamp.position) upperbound = PI / h if upperbound < visiblethreshold: continue for i in range(4): angle = equiangularsample(i, 4) steppos = add(lamp.position, scale(raydir, lamp.radius (0.5 + 0.5 cos(angle)))) shadowval = samplecubemapshadow(steppos, lamp.position) if shadowval > 0.0: radiance = evaluatelamplight(steppos, lamp, shadowval) totalradiance = add(totalradiance, scale(radiance, shadowval)) volumetexture[z resy resx + y resx + x][0] = totalradiance volumetexture[z resy resx + y resx + x][1] = params.rvolumetricDensity blurredvolume = depthawareblur(volumetexture) return blurredvolume Pitfalls: Lamp Culling: Lamps whose upper-bound contribution is below the visible threshold are skipped. The upper-bound contribution is calculated as \pi/h, where h is the distance from the ray to the lamp center. Shadow Map Instability: Low shadow map resolution or unstable shadow maps cause flickering during cone tracing when the camera moves. Stabilizing the shadow map (e.g., computing directional light position from the view camera) may leave voxels unfilled if the shadow map resolution is low or not fully utilized. A variant where light is injected into a voxel structure (octree) by rendering a shadow map from the light's perspective and traversing the octree to calculate reflected radiance. It uses cascade shadow maps (last cascade) with slope scale depth bias disabled to ensure accurate voxel placement. It suffers from flickering if the shadow map is unstable and artifacts if shadow map resolution is too low to cover all vertical voxels. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of steps (16 for sun, 4 for lamps) and the number of active lamps. The pass is executed at 1/4 resolution. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D texture (radiance and extinction) and shadow maps. Measured Performance: On a GTX 1080 at 2560×1440 with MSAA 4×: 'm3l2 house room' (sun): 0.91 ms total (0.41 ms for sun and blur). 'Tech demo lamp hall' (48 lamps): 0.93 ms total (0.44 ms for sun and blur). Optimization History: Reduced from 4.4 ms (half-res, 8 steps, 4-tap shadows) to 0.9 ms (quarter-res, 4 steps, 1-tap shadows, equi-angular sampling). Strengths: Real-time performance; effective for sun shafts and localized lamp glow; leverages existing shadow map infrastructure. Limitations: No temporal accumulation or froxels (can lead to noise/steps); no extinction (scene is not dimmed by the haze); dependent on shadow map resolution for quality. When to use: When sun shafts and lamp glow are desired in real-time scenes with existing shadow map support, and full volumetric path tracing is too expensive. The Light Injection Pass is based on the volumetric lighting approach used by Frostbite and Unreal Engine 4 prior to the introduction of froxels. The equi-angular sampling technique used for lamps is attributed to Kulla & Fajardo (2012). It is implemented in the open-source project openmohaa as part of "Wave D" rendering features. feat(render): the light in the air: sun shafts and the glow round lamps, in their shadows (rvolumetric), https://github.com/ssshoshi/openmohaa/pull/116, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric Fog Using 3D Textures in OpenGL - opengl, https://salivity.github.io/opengl/article/volumetric-fog-using-3-d-textures-in-open-gl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Implementing Voxel Cone Tracing, http://simonstechblog.blogspot.com/2013/01/implementing-voxel-cone-tracing.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Direct Illumination with Shadow Rays
head: Direct Lighting with Shadows, Direct Lighting with Volume Transmittance, Direct Radiance with Volumetric Transmittance, Shadow Ray Illumination, Shadow Ray Lighting
body: Computes the direct lighting contribution at a surface point (or volume sample) by casting shadow rays toward light sources, accounting for attenuation by heterogeneous participating media between the point and the light. It differs from pure surface shadowing by integrating volumetric transmittance along the ray path, and from full path tracing by only evaluating direct illumination from explicit light sources rather than indirect bounces. Inputs: Hit point position \mathbf{p} and surface normal \mathbf{n}. List of light sources, each with position \mathbf{l}i, color/intensity \mathbf{C}i, and optionally area/normal. Volume density/extinction coefficient field \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). Surface material properties (diffuse color, specular, roughness, metallic). Camera/view direction \mathbf{V} for specular calculations. Outputs: Direct illumination radiance \mathbf{L}{direct} at \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Light structure: struct Light { vec3 position; vec3 color; bool enabled; float area; }. Shadow ray result: struct Intersection { float t; vec3 hitpoint; bool hit; }. Volume integrator interface: Transmittance(Ray) returns scalar transmittance. Steps: 1. Initialize accumulated light color \mathbf{L}{direct} = \mathbf{0}. 2. For each light i in the light list: a. If light i is disabled, skip. b. Compute light direction \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{l}i - \mathbf{p} and distance d = \|\mathbf{L}\|. c. Normalize direction: \mathbf{w}i = \mathbf{L} / d. d. Create a shadow ray starting from \mathbf{p} + \epsilon \mathbf{n} (where \epsilon \approx 0.01) in direction \mathbf{w}i. e. Compute volumetric transmittance T{light} from \mathbf{p} to \mathbf{l}i: Option A (Discrete steps): Integrate extinction over 16 uniform steps from \mathbf{p} to \mathbf{l}i. Option B (Majorant sampling): Use a majorant-based sampler to estimate transmittance through the volume grid, handling participating media with null-event rejection and Russian Roulette if transmittance drops below 0.05. Option C (Geometry-only): If no volume is present, intersect the shadow ray with scene geometry. If an intersection occurs at distance t < d, set T{light} = 0.0; otherwise T{light} = 1.0. f. Compute visibility V: If using geometry-only shadowing: V = 1 if no intersection or intersection distance \ge d, else V = 0. If using volumetric transmittance: V is implicitly handled by T{light}. g. Compute geometric term: G = \frac{\max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{w}i) \cdot |\mathbf{w}i \cdot \mathbf{n}{light}|}{d^2} where \mathbf{n}{light} is the light surface normal (for area lights). h. Compute probability density py = 1.0 / \text{light\area} for importance sampling. i. Compute BRDF contribution: Diffuse: \mathbf{C}i \cdot T{light} \cdot V \cdot \frac{\rhod}{\pi} \cdot G / py. Specular (if enabled): \mathbf{C}i \cdot T{light} \cdot \text{specular} \cdot \max(0, \mathbf{H} \cdot \mathbf{n})^{\text{shininess}}, where \mathbf{H} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{w}i) and \text{shininess} = 1/\text{roughness}. j. Add contribution to \mathbf{L}{direct}. 3. Return \mathbf{L}{direct}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directilluminationwithshadowrays(hitpoint, normal, viewdir, lights, volumeintegrator, geometrytracer): """ Computes direct lighting with volumetric shadow rays. Args: hitpoint: vec3, surface position normal: vec3, surface normal viewdir: vec3, view direction lights: list of Light objects volumeintegrator: object with Transmittance(ray) method geometrytracer: object with intersect(ray) method Returns: vec3, direct illumination radiance """ Ldirect = vec3(0.0) for light in lights: if not light.enabled: continue # Light direction and distance delta = light.position - hitpoint d = length(delta) if d < 1e-6: continue wi = normalize(delta) # Shadow ray setup epsilon = 0.01 length(normal) shadowrayorigin = hitpoint + epsilon normal shadowray = Ray(shadowrayorigin, wi) # Compute transmittance through volume Tlight = volumeintegrator.Transmittance(shadowray) # Check for geometric occlusion (optional, depends on implementation) # If geometrytracer is used for hard shadows in addition to volume: intersection = geometrytracer.intersect(shadowray) if intersection.hit and intersection.t < d: Tlight = 0.0 # Visibility factor (if not fully covered by Tlight) V = 1.0 if (not intersection.hit or intersection.t >= d) else 0.0 # Geometric term costheta = max(0.0, dot(normal, wi)) # For point lights, light normal term is 1.0; for area lights, use light.normal coslight = 1.0 if light.ispoint else max(0.0, dot(-wi, light.normal)) geometricterm = (costheta coslight) / (d d) # Probability density for light sampling py = 1.0 / light.area if light.area > 0 else 1.0 # BRDF calculation # Diffuse component diffusereflectance = light.color Tlight V geometricterm / py Ldirect += diffusereflectance hitmaterial.diffusecolor # Specular component (if enabled) if hitmaterial.specularenabled: H = normalize(viewdir + wi) cosHn = max(0.0, dot(H, normal)) shininess = 1.0 / hitmaterial.roughness specularterm = light.color Tlight hitmaterial.specular pow(cosHn, shininess) Ldirect += specularterm return Ldirect Parameters: \epsilon: Shadow ray offset, typically 0.01 \times \|\mathbf{n}\|. Number of integration steps: 16 for discrete integration. MAXLIGHTS: Maximum number of lights, typically 8. Russian Roulette threshold: 0.05 for transmittance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Shadow ray origin must be offset to avoid self-intersection. Boundaries: Handle light distance d=0 to avoid division by zero. Degenerate input: Disabled lights should be skipped early. Volumetric density: If density is zero, transmittance is 1.0. A shadowing technique where shadow rays cross smooth glass in a straight line, and paths refracted to a light already reached that way do not count as reaching the light. This allows for realistic glass shadows without complex refraction path tracing. Estimates transmittance from a point to a distant light source using majorant sampling to handle participating media. It initializes transmittance to 1.0, creates a shadow ray, intersects with the volume grid to get a majorant iterator, and loops through sampled points with null event probabilities and Russian Roulette if transmittance drops below 0.05. The phase function (Henyey-Greenstein) is multiplied by the estimated transmittance and light intensity. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of lights and S is the number of sampling steps per shadow ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) per light, plus volume grid storage. Measured Performance: Depends heavily on volume density and number of lights. Majorant sampling can be faster for sparse volumes but requires RNG state. Scaling: Linear with number of lights and volume samples. Strengths: Handles heterogeneous volumes, supports multiple lights, integrates with PBR. Limitations: Noisy for sparse sampling, expensive for many lights or dense volumes. When to use: When volumetric shadows are required and direct illumination is sufficient. When not to use: For real-time applications with many lights and complex volumes, consider precomputed shadows or variance shadow mapping. Originated in volumetric path tracing implementations to handle direct lighting in participating media. Developed alongside ray marching techniques for voxel-based scenes. Used in real-time ray marchers and offline path tracers for volumetric effects. ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, https://github.com/ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) An Introduction to Raymarching - Maxime Garcia, https://typhomnt.github.io/teaching/raytracing/raymarchingintro/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Milestone 13: MagicaVoxel look (.vox, DDA voxel grid, sun/sky, bloom, style voxel), https://github.com/adriendjn/mypbr/pull/10, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Shibodd/volumepathtracer, https://github.com/Shibodd/volumepathtracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ambient Occlusion via SDF/Geometry
head: SDF-based Ambient Occlusion, Geometry-based Ambient Occlusion, Distance Field Ambient Occlusion
body: This family of techniques estimates local ambient occlusion by querying a geometric representation—typically a Signed Distance Field (SDF) or a structured voxel grid—rather than performing explicit ray tracing against a triangle mesh or screen-space depth buffer. By evaluating the distance to the nearest surface along specific directions, these methods approximate the visibility of the hemisphere around a point. What sets this family apart from JAOCC Shading (which uses precomputed spherical harmonics) and Local Ambient Occlusion (which often relies on screen-space or texture-based approximations) is the direct analytical or semi-analytical evaluation of geometric distance to determine occlusion factors. All methods in this family rely on the fundamental property of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) or structured geometry representations: the value at a point p represents the shortest distance to the surface of the object, with a sign indicating whether the point is inside (negative) or outside (positive) the object. The core mechanism for estimating ambient occlusion (AO) involves sampling the distance field along a set of directions, typically concentrated in the upper hemisphere relative to the surface normal \mathbf{n}. Let d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) be the distance to the surface in direction \mathbf{v} from point \mathbf{p}. The occlusion factor is derived by comparing these distances to the expected distance in an unoccluded environment. A common formulation for the occlusion contribution of a single sample at distance d is based on the ratio of the actual distance to the maximum possible distance or a reference distance. For a hemisphere of radius R, if the distance to the nearest occluder is d < R, the point is considered partially occluded. The occlusion weight w is often defined as: w = \max(0, 1 - \frac{d}{R}) or similar variations that weight closer samples more heavily, as closer occluders block more ambient light. The final AO value AO(\mathbf{p}) is typically an average of these weights over N sampled directions \mathbf{v}i in the hemisphere: AO(\mathbf{p}) = 1 - \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} w(d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}i)) where AO=1 is fully lit and AO=0 is fully occluded. Some variants, such as Exponential Decay, modify the weighting function to decay exponentially with distance, giving less importance to distant occluders: wi = \frac{1}{2^i} \frac{d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}i)}{d{max, i}} where d{max, i} is the maximum possible distance for that sample step. Estimates local occlusion by sampling the SDF along the surface normal at increasing distances, weighting closer samples more heavily to simulate ambient light blockage. It is a simplified, single-direction approach compared to full hemisphere sampling. Choose this when computational resources are extremely limited and the primary occlusion source is self-occlusion along the normal (e.g., crevices). A device function that computes ambient occlusion at a surface point using either point sampling or ray casting against a hemisphere of directions, with tangent-space rotation and distance-based falloff. It is designed for GPU-based voxel rendering (GVDB). Choose this when working with voxel-based geometry on the GPU and requiring hemisphere-aware occlusion. A post-processing technique that estimates ambient occlusion by sampling points in a hemisphere around each pixel's surface position and checking if those points are occluded by geometry in the depth buffer. It is distinct because it uses screen-space depth rather than a global SDF or voxel grid. Choose this for real-time rasterization pipelines where global geometry data is not available or too expensive to query. A method to compute ambient occlusion by casting rays in random directions and numerically evaluating the occlusion factor using a distance mapping function. It is distinct because it uses stochastic sampling rather than deterministic grid or hemisphere sampling. Choose this when high-quality, unbiased AO is required and deterministic sampling is not feasible. Definition A simplified ambient occlusion estimation technique that approximates occlusion based on the angle between the surface normal and the scene's upward vector, rather than ray-marching for occluders. It does not reflect the influence of nearby occluders. Step 1. Calculate occlusion using the dot product of the surface normal \mathbf{n} and the unit upwards vector \mathbf{u}: \text{occlusion} = 1 - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{u}) 2. Scale the occlusion value by a scale factor s, clamp the result to the range [0, 1], and return 1 minus the clamped value to produce the final brightness. Parameter s: A scale value used to adjust the strength of the fake ambient occlusion effect. Pitfall The method does not account for occlusion caused by nearby objects (occluders); it only considers self-occlusion relative to the upward direction. Definition An approximation modeling surfaces as collections of disk-shaped elements at mesh vertices to compute AO and bent normals analytically. Step 1. Pass 1: Perform a simple sum of all occlusion factors including double shadowing. 2. Pass 2: Reduce each disk's occlusion contribution by its occlusion factor from the previous pass. 3. Optimization: Use a hierarchical tree to optimize computations against distant disks, reducing complexity to O(n \log n). Pitfall Double shadowing: merely summing occlusion from all disks leads to an overly dark image because disks behind other disks still count towards occlusion. Complexity Naive implementation has O(n^2) runtime complexity computing all disk pairs. Definition Calculates hemispheric ambient occlusion (0..1) from nearby terrain geometry by sampling along the normal direction, measuring how much the terrain rises relative to the sample distance. Step 1. If AO disabled or samples \le 0, return 1. Initialize occlusion = 0. 2. Loop i from 1 to samples: d = (\text{aoRadius} \times i) / \text{samples} Sample point sx = px + nx \times d, sy = py + ny \times d, sz = pz + nz \times d Calculate rise = \text{heightAtExtended}(\text{field}, sx, sz) - sy If rise > 0, add \text{clamp01}(\text{rise} / (0.9 \times d)) / \text{samples} to occlusion. 3. Return \text{clamp01}(1 - \text{occlusion} \times \text{aoStrength}). Formula \text{occlusion} = \sum{i=1}^{\text{samples}} \frac{\text{clamp01}(\text{rise}i / (0.9 \times di))}{\text{samples}} where di = (\text{aoRadius} \times i) / \text{samples}, \text{rise}i = \max(0, \text{height}(sxi, szi) - syi). Final AO = \text{clamp01}(1 - \text{occlusion} \times \text{aoStrength}). Parameter \text{aoSamples}: number of samples to take for AO. \text{aoRadius}: maximum radius for AO sampling. \text{aoStrength}: multiplier for the final occlusion value. Definition An improvement over Real Ambient Occlusion that weighs samples exponentially based on their distance from the surface, giving less importance to further samples. Step 1. Initialize sum and maxSum to 0. 2. Calculate the sample position p by moving from the surface position (pos) along the normal by (i+1) \times \text{\AOStepSize}. 3. Add the weighted distance field value at p to sum. The weight is 1 / 2^i. 4. Add the weighted maximum possible distance (i+1) \times \text{\AOStepSize} to maxSum. The weight is 1 / 2^i. 5. Return the ratio of sum to maxSum. If no occlusion, sum equals maxSum, resulting in 1. Ambient Occlusion via SDF/Geometry emerged as a practical solution for real-time rendering where traditional ray-traced AO was too expensive. The use of Signed Distance Fields for AO was popularized in the context of sphere tracing and voxel rendering. Bunnel's disk-based approximation provided an early analytical approach for mesh-based geometry, while SDF-based methods leveraged the efficiency of distance field queries. The exponential decay variant was introduced to improve the realism of SDF-based AO by better modeling the falloff of ambient light. These techniques are widely used in volumetric rendering, voxel games, and real-time graphics engines where geometry is represented implicitly or in structured grids. name: SDF-based Ambient Occlusion
head: Signed Distance Field AO, Distance Field Ambient Occlusion, Raymarched AO
body: SDF-based Ambient Occlusion (AO) estimates local occlusion by sampling a Signed Distance Field (SDF) along the surface normal at increasing distances, weighting closer samples more heavily to simulate ambient light blockage. It approximates ambient occlusion by using the distance field itself to simulate light occlusion based on object proximity, avoiding the unrealistic results of Screen Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) which relies on depth buffers and surface normals in screen space. This method is capable of producing visually pleasing results by leveraging the geometric accuracy of the SDF representation. The method relies on the fundamental property of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) or structured geometry representations: the value at a point p represents the shortest distance to the surface of the object, with a sign indicating whether the point is inside (negative) or outside (positive) the object. Input: A point p on the surface, the surface normal \mathbf{n} at p, and an SDF query function d(\mathbf{x}) that returns the distance to the nearest geometry from any point \mathbf{x}. Output: A scalar occlusion factor AO \in [0, 1], where 1 is fully lit and 0 is fully occluded. The SDF is typically stored as a 3D grid where each position stores the distance to the nearest object surface. Negative values indicate the grid location is inside the object, and positive values indicate it is outside. Typical parameter values found in implementations include: Number of Samples (N): Commonly 4 to 8 samples. Maximum Distance (R): The extent of the AO calculation, e.g., 0.25. Weight Decay: Factors such as 0.85 or 0.92 to reduce the influence of distant samples. Strength/Scale: Multipliers like 0.6 or 3.0 to adjust the final intensity. The core mechanism involves sampling the distance field along a set of directions, typically concentrated in the upper hemisphere relative to the surface normal \mathbf{n}. While some variants sample in multiple directions, the most common and cited approach samples along the surface normal at increasing distances. 1. Initialize the accumulated occlusion occ to 0.0 and a weight factor w to 1.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to N-1 (where N is the number of samples): a. Calculate the sample distance leni. Variations include quadratic spacing leni = 0.01 + 0.02 \cdot i^2 or linear spacing leni = \frac{R}{N} \cdot i. b. Calculate the sample point \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{p} + leni \cdot \mathbf{n}. c. Query the SDF to get the distance to the nearest geometry: di = d(\mathbf{p}i). d. Calculate the occlusion contribution. If the geometry is closer than the sample point (di < leni), it contributes to occlusion. A common heuristic is: \Delta = \max(0.0, leni - di). e. Accumulate the weighted contribution: occ += \Delta \cdot w. f. Decay the weight for the next sample: w = w \cdot \text{decay}, where decay is typically 0.85 or 0.92. 3. Compute the final AO value. Variations exist in the final normalization: AO = 1.0 - \text{clamp}(scale \cdot occ, 0.0, 1.0), where scale is 0.6. AO = \text{clamp}(1.0 - strength \cdot occ, 0.0, 1.0), where strength is 3.0. AO = occ / (R \cdot N \cdot factor). The following pseudocode combines the most detailed implementation details from the sources. It uses quadratic spacing and a specific decay factor as described in, which provides a complete, self-contained algorithm. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfambientocclusion(p, normal, sdfquery, numsamples=8, maxdist=0.25, decay=0.85, scale=0.6): """ Calculate SDF-based Ambient Occlusion. Args: p: Current surface point (vec3). normal: Surface normal at p (vec3). sdfquery: Function returning distance to nearest geometry from a point (vec3 -> float). numsamples: Number of samples along the normal (int). maxdist: Maximum distance for sampling (float). decay: Weight decay factor per sample (float). scale: Final occlusion strength multiplier (float). Returns: AO factor between 0.0 (fully occluded) and 1.0 (fully lit). """ occ = 0.0 weight = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): # Quadratic spacing as per # Note: uses linear spacing, uses linear spacing. # Using quadratic as it is explicitly detailed in. leni = 0.01 + 0.02 (i i) # Sample point along normal samplepoint = p + normal leni # Query SDF dist = sdfquery(samplepoint) # Accumulate occlusion if geometry is closer than sample point #: occ += (len - dist) weight #: occlusion += max(-(d - distance), 0.0) which is equivalent to max(0, distance - d) # Here, 'len' is the sample distance, 'dist' is the actual distance to geometry. # If dist < len, the object is closer, contributing to occlusion. contribution = leni - dist if contribution > 0: occ += contribution weight # Decay weight weight = decay # Final AO calculation #: 1.0 - clamp(0.6 occ, 0.0, 1.0) #: clamp(1.0 - 3.0 occ uao, 0.0, 1.0) # Using the specific constants from as it is a complete example. ao = 1.0 - clamp(scale occ, 0.0, 1.0) return ao def clamp(value, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(value, maxval)) Precision: Floating-point precision errors in SDF queries can lead to jittering or incorrect occlusion values, especially at small distances. Boundaries: The method assumes the SDF is valid within the sampling range. If the sampling points go outside the defined SDF volume, undefined behavior or incorrect distances may occur. Degenerate Input: If the normal is not normalized, the sample points will be incorrectly spaced, leading to inaccurate AO. Inside Geometry: If the point p is inside the geometry (negative SDF value), the standard AO heuristic may need adjustment, as the concept of "occlusion" from the outside differs. The sources do not explicitly detail handling for points strictly inside the volume, only that negative values indicate inside. Time Complexity: O(N) per sample point, where N is the number of samples. The SDF query itself is typically O(1) for grid-based SDFs or O(\log M) for hierarchical structures. Memory Complexity: Depends on the SDF storage. A dense 3D grid requires O(V) memory, where V is the volume of the grid. Performance: Capable of producing visually pleasing results in real-time. It is generally faster than full ray tracing but may be slower than screen-space techniques if the SDF query is expensive. Strengths: Provides geometrically accurate occlusion based on actual scene geometry, avoiding the artifacts of SSAO. It works well with voxel-based or implicit representations. Limitations: Limited to the resolution and extent of the SDF. Cannot account for occlusion from geometry not represented in the SDF. Performance can degrade with high sample counts or large sampling distances. When to use: When geometric accuracy is important and the scene is represented by an SDF. When SSAO artifacts are unacceptable. When not to use: When performance is critical and the SDF is expensive to query. When the scene geometry is not available as an SDF. The technique was introduced by Evans [12] as a method based on signed distance fields where objects are embedded into a 3D grid. Hoberock [18] improved upon this method's image quality, but at a performance cost tradeoff. Wright [61] expanded on this approach, substituting Evans' ad hoc heuristic with cone tracing, approximating it by utilizing spheres of increasing radius to check for intersections.
