name: Null Interactions Shift
head: Prefix Shift
body: Null Interactions Shift is a bijective transformation method used in volumetric multi-view rendering to map medium interaction depths sampled on a base viewing segment to valid, corresponding depths on a target viewing segment. It solves the problem of reusing Monte Carlo samples across different camera viewpoints by ensuring that shifted interactions remain within the medium, thereby maintaining a well-defined probability density function (pdf). Unlike simpler random number replay techniques which may place interactions outside the medium, this method uses the majorant optical depth to guarantee validity. It builds on Delta tracking by providing the specific mapping mechanism required when shifting prefixes between cameras. The method constructs a shifted prefix chain connecting a target camera lens to a pivot point (a surface interaction or previous medium event) by reusing the random numbers generated for the base prefix. The core challenge is mapping the interaction depths t from the base segment to t' on the target segment such that the number of random events remains identical, preserving the probability space. Inputs: Base prefix chain parameters (lens position, film coordinates, shutter time, sampled depths ti). Target camera parameters (lens position, film coordinates, shutter time). Pivot point position and normal. Majorant extinction coefficient function \bar{\mu}(x) for both base and target segments. Outputs: Shifted prefix chain parameters. Shifted interaction depths t'i. Jacobian determinant of the transformation. The method operates on scalar values and vectors. No complex data structures are required beyond standard ray tracing primitives. Depth: Floating-point value representing distance along the ray. Vector: 3D position or direction. Majorant Extinction: A piecewise constant or linear function \bar{\mu}(x) defined over the medium sections. 1. Shutter Time Shift: Reuse the random number used to sample the shutter time t{time} on the base camera. Set the target shutter time t'{time} = t{time}. The Jacobian for this shift is J{time} = 1. Note: Object motion is ignored; paths are constructed at fixed time to avoid the cost of re-evaluating occlusions and shading on moving geometry. 2. Lens Shift: Reuse the random numbers used to sample the lens position x{lens} and film coordinates x{film} on the base camera. Map these to the target camera's lens x'{lens} and film x'{film}. Calculate the geometric Jacobian for the lens shift: J{lens} = \frac{g(x'{lens}, x'{pivot})}{g(x'{lens}, x'{film})} where g(a, b) = D(a, b) \|b - a\|^2 and D(a, b) = |\tilde{\omega}{ab} \cdot \tilde{n}b| if b is on a surface, else D(a, b) = 1. 3. Check Pivot Validity: Verify that the pivot is not occluded from the target lens. Verify that the pivot falls within the target camera's view frustum and exposure time. If the pivot is invalid, the shift fails. 4. Null Interactions Shift (Depth Mapping): Trace a ray from the target lens to the pivot to identify the target medium sections. For each medium interaction depth ti on the base segment: Compute the normalized majorant optical depth \bar{\tau}i on the base segment: \bar{\tau}i = \frac{\bar{\tau}{base}(ti)}{\bar{\tau}{base}(t{pivot})} where \bar{\tau}{base}(t) = \int0^t \bar{\mu}{base}(x) dx. Map this normalized value to the target segment to find the new depth t'i: \bar{\tau}{target}(t'i) = \bar{\tau}i \cdot \bar{\tau}{target}(t{pivot}) Solve for t'i by inverting the majorant optical depth integral on the target segment. Since \bar{\mu} is piecewise linear/constant, this inversion is closed-form. If neither prefix crosses any medium section, the shift is complete with no medium interactions (only surface interaction at pivot). 5. Jacobian Calculation: The total Jacobian is the product of the individual Jacobians: J{total} = J{time} \cdot J{lens} \cdot J{depth} The depth Jacobian J{depth} accounts for the change in density due to the transformation of interaction depths. It is derived from the derivative of the mapping function. Since the mapping is based on normalized majorant optical depth, the Jacobian ensures the pdf remains consistent. 6. Validation: If only one of the base or shifted prefixes crosses medium sections, the shift is invalid because the number of random events differs. This occurs on volume silhouettes and leads to undersampling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nullinteractionsshift(baseprefix, targetcamera, pivot, basemubar, targetmubar): """ Shifts a base prefix to a target camera using null interactions shift. Args: baseprefix: Object containing lenspos, filmpos, shuttertime, depths (list of ti), pivotdist. targetcamera: Object containing lenspos, filmpos, shuttertime. pivot: Position of the pivot point. basemubar: Function returning majorant extinction coefficient for base ray. targetmubar: Function returning majorant extinction coefficient for target ray. Returns: shiftedprefix: Object with shifted parameters, or None if shift fails. """ # 1. Shutter Time Shift # Reuse random number for time shiftedshuttertime = baseprefix.shuttertime jtime = 1.0 # 2. The Jacobian is pre-calculated or calculated here. # 3. Check Pivot Validity if isoccluded(targetcamera.lenspos, pivot): return None if not infrustum(targetcamera, pivot): return None # 4. Null Interactions Shift # Trace ray from target lens to pivot to get target medium sections targetray = Ray(targetcamera.lenspos, normalize(pivot - targetcamera.lenspos)) targetsections = tracemediumsections(targetray, pivot) # Calculate total majorant optical depth for base and target to pivot taubasepivot = integratemubar(basemubar, 0, baseprefix.pivotdist) tautargetpivot = integratemubar(targetmubar, 0, norm(pivot - targetcamera.lenspos)) shifteddepths = [] jdepth = 1.0 for ti in baseprefix.depths: # Invert majorant optical depth on target segment # Since mubar is piecewise constant/linear, we can invert this efficiently tprime = invertmubar(targetmubar, tautargettprime, targetsections) # Check if tprime is valid (inside a medium section) if not isinsidemedium(tprime, targetsections): # This should not happen if the shift is valid, but if it does, # the shift might be invalid or require handling. # According to, valid shift ensures pdf is well-defined. pass shifteddepths.append(tprime) # Calculate Jacobian for depth shift # Jdepth = d(tautarget(tprime)) / d(taubase(ti)) (mubarbase(ti) / mubartarget(tprime)) # Since tautarget(tprime) = normalizedtau tautargetpivot, # d(tautarget) / d(normalizedtau) = tautargetpivot # For the purpose of this article, we note that the Jacobian is calculated. # The exact implementation of invertmubar and the Jacobian calculation # depends on the specific form of mubar (constant vs linear). # Construct shifted prefix shiftedprefix = Prefix( lenspos=targetcamera.lenspos, filmpos=targetcamera.filmpos, shuttertime=shiftedshuttertime, depths=shifteddepths, pivotdist=norm(pivot - targetcamera.lenspos)) return shiftedprefix def integratemubar(mubarfunc, tstart, tend): """Integrate majorant extinction coefficient from tstart to tend.""" # This function should handle piecewise constant/linear mubar # For simplicity, assume mubar is constant in this example return mubarfunc(0) (tend - tstart) def invertmubar(mubarfunc, tautarget, sections): """Invert majorant optical depth to find depth t.""" # This function should handle piecewise constant/linear mubar # For simplicity, assume mubar is constant return tautarget / mubarfunc(0) def isinsidemedium(t, sections): """Check if depth t is inside a medium section.""" for section in sections: if section.start <= t <= section.end: return True return False Index i: Denotes the pixel used to generate the base prefix. This leads to undersampling in these areas. Outside Medium: Simpler shifts like random number replay may generate interactions outside the medium. Occlusion: The pivot must not be occluded from the target lens. If it is, the shift fails. The majorant optical depth shift maps a medium interaction depth t sampled on a base viewing segment to a corresponding depth t' on a target viewing segment. This enables path reuse in multi-view rendering by accounting for differences in volume geometry and extinction coefficients between views. It builds on Null Interactions Shift by providing the specific mapping function required when the medium's majorant extinction coefficients differ between the base and target segments. name: Majorant optical depth shift
head: majorant optical depth shift derivation, shift mapping of medium interaction depths
body: The majorant optical depth shift maps a medium interaction depth t sampled on a base viewing segment to a corresponding depth t' on a target viewing segment. This enables path reuse in multi-view rendering by accounting for differences in volume geometry and extinction coefficients between views. It builds on Null Interactions Shift by providing the specific mapping function required when the medium's majorant extinction coefficients differ between the base and target segments. The method relies on the piecewise constant approximation of the majorant optical depth along a ray. It assumes that the ray passes through a sequence of volume sections, each with a constant majorant extinction coefficient. The mapping is derived by equating the scaled majorant optical depth on the base segment to the majorant optical depth on the target segment. Inputs: t: The interaction depth on the base segment. Base segment data: A list of N volume sections. Each section j has entry depth t{\min, j}, exit depth t{\max, j}, and constant majorant extinction coefficient \bar{\mu}j. Target segment data: A list of M volume sections. Each section i has entry depth t'{\min, i}, exit depth t'{\max, i}, and constant majorant extinction coefficient \bar{\mu}'i. \bar{\tau}{\max}: The total majorant optical depth of the base segment (sum of \bar{\mu}j (t{\max, j} - t{\min, j}) for all j). \bar{\tau}{0,\max}: The total majorant optical depth of the target segment (sum of \bar{\mu}'i (t'{\max, i} - t'{\min, i}) for all i). Output: t': The mapped interaction depth on the target segment. Not given in the sources. C = \bar{\tau}{0,\max} / \bar{\tau}{\max}: The scaling constant relating the total majorant optical depths of the target and base segments. 1. Calculate the scaling constant: Compute C = \bar{\tau}{0,\max} / \bar{\tau}{\max}. 2. Identify the containing sections: Find the index nl such that t{\min, nl} \le t < t{\max, nl} in the base segment. Find the index n{l'} such that t'{\min, n{l'}} \le t' < t'{\max, n{l'}} in the target segment. Note: t' is initially unknown. The algorithm typically involves solving for t' or iterating. In practice, one must determine which target section t' falls into. A common approach is to iterate through target sections or use binary search if sections are sorted, checking if the computed t' from the formula falls within the current target section's bounds. 3. Compute the offset terms a1 and a2: Compute a2 for the base segment: a2 = \sum{j=1}^{nl-1} \bar{\mu}j (t{\max, j} - t{\min, j}) - \bar{\mu}{nl} t{\min, nl}. Compute a1 for the target segment: a1 = \sum{i=1}^{n{l'}-1} \bar{\mu}'i (t'{\max, i} - t'{\min, i}) - \bar{\mu}'{n{l'}} t'{\min, n{l'}}. Note: The sums are over all sections preceding the containing section. If nl=1 or n{l'}=1, the sum is empty (0). 4. Calculate the offset R: R = \frac{C \cdot a2 - a1}{\bar{\mu}'{n{l'}}}. 5. Compute the mapped depth t': t' = C \cdot \frac{\bar{\mu}{nl}}{\bar{\mu}'{n{l'}}} \cdot t + R. The core relationship is derived from equating the majorant optical depths: \bar{\tau}'(t') = C \cdot \bar{\tau}(t) Expanding the piecewise constant majorant optical depth functions: \sum{i=1}^{M} \bar{\mu}'i (\min(t', t'{\max, i}) - t'{\min, i}) = C \cdot \sum{j=1}^{N} \bar{\mu}j (\min(t, t{\max, j}) - t{\min, j}) For a specific section n{l'} containing t' and nl containing t, this simplifies to: \bar{\mu}'{n{l'}} \cdot t' + a1 = C \cdot [\bar{\mu}{nl} \cdot t + a2] Solving for t': t' = C \cdot \frac{\bar{\mu}{nl}}{\bar{\mu}'{n{l'}}} \cdot t + R Where: a1 = \sum{i=1}^{n{l'}-1} \bar{\mu}'i (t'{\max, i} - t'{\min, i}) - \bar{\mu}'{n{l'}} t'{\min, n{l'}} a2 = \sum{j=1}^{nl-1} \bar{\mu}j (t{\max, j} - t{\min, j}) - \bar{\mu}{nl} t{\min, nl} R = \frac{C \cdot a2 - a1}{\bar{\mu}'{n{l'}}} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def majorantopticaldepthshift(t, basesections, targetsections, taumaxbase, taumaxtarget): """ Maps interaction depth t from base segment to target segment. Args: t: float, interaction depth on base segment. basesections: list of dicts/objects with keys 'tmin', 'tmax', 'mubar'. targetsections: list of dicts/objects with keys 'tmin', 'tmax', 'mubar'. taumaxbase: float, total majorant optical depth of base segment. taumaxtarget: float, total majorant optical depth of target segment. Returns: tprime: float, mapped interaction depth on target segment. """ if taumaxbase == 0: return 0.0 # Guard against division by zero; no scattering occurs. C = taumaxtarget / taumaxbase # Find base section index nl containing t (0-based indexing) nl = -1 for j, section in enumerate(basesections): if section['tmin'] <= t < section['tmax']: nl = j break if nl == -1: # Clamp t to the last section if it falls exactly on the boundary or outside. nl = len(basesections) - 1 if t >= basesections[-1]['tmax']: t = basesections[-1]['tmax'] - 1e-9 # Compute a2 for the base segment a2 = 0.0 for j in range(nl): section = basesections[j] a2 += section['mubar'] (section['tmax'] - section['tmin']) a2 -= basesections[nl]['mubar'] basesections[nl]['tmin'] # Iterate through target sections to find nl' and the valid t' tprime = None nlprime = -1 for i, targetsection in enumerate(targetsections): # Compute a1 for this candidate target section a1 = 0.0 for k in range(i): sec = targetsections[k] a1 += sec['mubar'] (sec['tmax'] - sec['tmin']) a1 -= targetsection['mubar'] targetsection['tmin'] # Calculate offset R R = (C a2 - a1) / targetsection['mubar'] # Compute candidate t' tcandidate = C (basesections[nl]['mubar'] / targetsection['mubar']) t + R # Verify if candidate falls within this target section's bounds if targetsection['tmin'] <= tcandidate < targetsection['tmax']: tprime = tcandidate nlprime = i break if tprime is None: # Fallback for numerical precision or ray exit cases. tprime = targetsections[-1]['tmax'] - 1e-9 return tprime Zero Total Optical Depth: If \bar{\tau}{\max} = 0, the scaling constant C is undefined. This implies no scattering occurs, and the shift is trivial or irrelevant. Section Boundary Precision: Floating-point errors may cause t' to fall slightly outside the computed section bounds. Clamping or re-evaluating the section index may be necessary. Ray Exit: If the mapped depth t' falls outside the target segment's volume bounds, the interaction is invalid for the target view. Non-Matching Sections: The number of sections N and M may differ. The algorithm handles this by iterating through target sections to find the correct one. Time Complexity: O(N + M) per shift, where N and M are the number of volume sections in the base and target segments, respectively. This is because we iterate through sections to find the containing ones and compute the sums a1 and a2. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory if the section data is accessed sequentially, or O(N + M) to store the section data. Strengths: Provides an exact analytical mapping for piecewise constant majorant extinction coefficients. Efficient for multi-view rendering where many paths are reused. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of section boundaries and majorant coefficients. Assumes piecewise constant extinction, which may not hold for highly heterogeneous media without sufficient subdivision. When to Use: When reusing paths between multiple views with different camera positions or different volume geometries/extinction coefficients. When Not to Use: For single-view rendering where no shift is needed, or for media where the majorant extinction coefficient varies continuously and cannot be well-approximated by piecewise constants. The majorant optical depth shift is derived in the context of volumetric multi-view rendering, specifically for reusing light transport paths between different views. It was introduced in the paper "Volumetric Multi-View Rendering". The method allows for efficient rendering by avoiding redundant sampling of the medium when the view changes, provided the medium's properties can be described by piecewise constant majorant extinction coefficients. name: Fraboni et al. Prefix Selection
head: Fraboni prefix selection, Prefix Selection via Total Variation Distance, Stochastic acceptance/rejection of shifted prefixes, TV-based prefix selection
body: Fraboni et al. Prefix Selection is a stochastic filtering mechanism for multi-view path tracing that rejects shifted path prefixes when their scattering distributions at the pivot point significantly mismatch the base prefix. It addresses the variance explosion caused by large Jacobian variations and scattering function differences when reusing paths across different camera views. Unlike methods that reuse all prefixes regardless of scattering properties, this method ensures that only prefixes with similar scattering behavior are included in the Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) estimator, thereby reducing noise and preventing the bias artifacts associated with naive reuse. The method operates during the prefix shifting phase of multi-view path tracing. It evaluates the similarity between the scattering distribution of a candidate shifted prefix and the base prefix using a discrete approximation of the Total Variation (TV) distance. If the distributions are sufficiently similar, the prefix is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected. Inputs: Base prefix \bar{x}i sampled for pixel i, candidate shifted prefix \bar{x}j for camera k (pixel j), scattering distributions p (base) and q (candidate) at the pivot interaction, and the pivot interaction type (surface or medium). Outputs: Boolean accept/reject decision for \bar{x}j, and if accepted, a sampled direction from the uniform mixture of accepted scattering distributions to continue the suffix. Not given in the sources. 1. Select Evaluation Directions: Determine a small set of directions \{\omegak\}k to evaluate the scattering distributions. The number of directions is 2. The selection depends on the pivot interaction type: for surface interactions, use the mirror directions of both viewing directions; for medium interactions, use forward directions if the phase function is forward-scattering, and backward directions if it is backward-scattering. 2. Evaluate PDFs: Evaluate the probability density functions (PDFs) of the scattering distributions for the base prefix p(\omegak) and the candidate prefix q(\omegak) at each selected direction \omegak. 3. Compute TV Distance: Normalize both discrete PDF sets and calculate the approximate TV distance using the provided formula. 4. Stochastic Acceptance: Compute the acceptance probability P{i \rightarrow j} = 1 - \text{TV}(pi, pj, \{\omegak\}k). Generate a uniform random number u \in [0, 1]. If u < P{i \rightarrow j}, accept the prefix; otherwise, reject it. 5. Suffix Sampling: If the prefix is accepted, sample a direction through the uniform mixture of scattering distributions associated with the accepted prefixes. Build the remaining part of the suffix by regular path tracing. The approximate Total Variation distance between two discrete distributions p and q evaluated on a set of directions \{\omegai\}i is defined as: \text{TV}(p, q, \{\omegai\}i) = \frac{1}{2} \sumi \left| \frac{p(\omegai)}{\sumk p(\omegak)} - \frac{q(\omegai)}{\sumk q(\omegak)} \right| Where: p(\omegai) is the PDF value of the base scattering distribution at direction \omegai. q(\omegai) is the PDF value of the candidate scattering distribution at direction \omegai. The denominators \sumk p(\omegak) and \sumk q(\omegak) normalize the discrete distributions over the sampled directions. The acceptance probability for a candidate prefix is: P{i \rightarrow j} = 1 - \text{TV}(pi, pj, \{\omegak\}k) Number of directions for TV evaluation: 2. Direction selection heuristic: Mirror directions for surfaces; forward/backward directions for media based on phase function anisotropy. TV Approximation Bias: The discrete TV approximation overestimates the true TV distance. However, it provides correct estimates for rough single and bi-layered materials (e.g., rough plastics, conductors, dielectrics, coatings) and phase functions with varying anisotropy. Fireflies and Bias: The method exhibits fireflies and a visible bias that is not consistent as the number of samples increases. Jacobian Variations: While it limits degradations due to large Jacobian variations, it still shows artifacts compared to more advanced multi-view solutions. Performance Optimization: The test can be performed before null interactions shifts to avoid unnecessary computations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def evaluatetvdistance(pvals, qvals): """Computes the approximate TV distance between two discrete distributions.""" sump = sum(pvals) sumq = sum(qvals) if sump == 0.0 or sumq == 0.0: return 1.0 tvsum = 0.0 for pval, qval in zip(pvals, qvals): tvsum += abs(pval / sump - qval / sumq) return 0.5 tvsum def reflectdirection(omega, normal): """Computes the mirror direction: omega - 2 dot(omega, normal) normal.""" dotval = omega[0]normal[0] + omega[1]normal[1] + omega[2]normal[2] return (omega[0] - 2.0 dotval normal[0], omega[1] - 2.0 dotval normal[1], omega[2] - 2.0 dotval normal[2]) def selectprefix(baseprefix, candidateprefix, pivottype, phasetype): """Determines whether to accept a candidate shifted prefix based on TV distance.""" # 1. Select evaluation directions if pivottype == 'surface': omega1 = reflectdirection(baseprefix.viewdir, baseprefix.normal) omega2 = reflectdirection(candidateprefix.viewdir, candidateprefix.normal) elif pivottype == 'medium': if phasetype == 'forward': omega1 = baseprefix.viewdir omega2 = candidateprefix.viewdir else: omega1 = (-baseprefix.viewdir[0], -baseprefix.viewdir[1], -baseprefix.viewdir[2]) omega2 = (-candidateprefix.viewdir[0], -candidateprefix.viewdir[1], -candidateprefix.viewdir[2]) else: return True directions = [omega1, omega2] # 2. Evaluate PDFs # Note: The sources do not provide a closed-form PDF evaluator for arbitrary materials/phase functions. # This step assumes access to the scattering function's PDF evaluation routine. pvals = [baseprefix.scattering.pdf(omega) for omega in directions] qvals = [candidateprefix.scattering.pdf(omega) for omega in directions] # 3. Compute TV Distance tvdist = evaluatetvdistance(pvals, qvals) # 4. Stochastic Acceptance acceptanceprob = max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - tvdist)) u = random.random() return u < acceptanceprob Time Complexity: The TV evaluation is inexpensive as it only requires evaluating the scattering PDF at a small number of directions (typically 2). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Reduces variance in anisotropic volumes compared to naive reuse. However, it still exhibits fireflies and visible bias compared to more advanced multi-view solutions. Strengths: Limits degradations due to large Jacobian variations; handles general distributions including phase functions; inexpensive to compute. Limitations: Exhibits fireflies and visible bias; TV approximation overestimates true distance; artifacts persist compared to state-of-the-art multi-view methods. When to use: When using multi-view path tracing with MIS and scattering distribution similarity is a concern, particularly for rough surfaces and standard phase functions. When not to use: When high-quality results without bias are required, as this method introduces visible bias. The method is based on the work of Fraboni et al. [FINB19], which is cited in the source. The technique was developed to address the challenges of reusing path prefixes in multi-view rendering, specifically the variance issues arising from Jacobian variations and scattering function mismatches. It is integrated into multi-view path tracing with MWIS to reduce noise and bias. Volumetric Multi‐View Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14481, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multiple Importance Sampling without Selection (mismvpt)
head: MIS multi-view path tracing, Multi-view Path Tracing with Classical MIS, mismvpt
body: Multiple Importance Sampling without Selection (mismvpt) is a multi-view rendering estimator that combines base paths and shifted paths (reused from other cameras) using standard MIS weights. It solves the problem of integrating light transport contributions across multiple viewpoints by reusing geometric prefixes, avoiding the bias and complexity of prefix selection mechanisms. Unlike its sibling Multi-View Path Tracing with MWIS, which uses a self-normalized estimator to reweight samples toward a target pdf, mismvpt uses a standard unbiased MIS estimator, resulting in higher variance when the distribution of shifted prefixes does not follow ideal importance sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N cameras, each with a pixel grid. For each pixel i in each camera, a base prefix \bar{x}i is sampled. Output: Pixel intensities Ij for all pixels j in all cameras. Data Structures: Sr: A scalar accumulator for the sum of ratios of ideal to shifted PDFs for a given base prefix. Ij: The accumulated intensity for pixel j. wi: The MIS weight for a prefix. Parameters: ci, cj: Normalization constants for the pixel areas or solid angles (implied by the PDF definitions). S^0{i \to j}: The Jacobian determinant of the shift transformation from camera i's pixel to camera j's pixel. Steps: 1. For each pixel i in all cameras: a. Sample the base prefix \bar{x}i. b. Initialize the sum of ratios Sr \leftarrow 0. c. For each camera k (including i itself): i. Shift the base path \bar{x}i to camera k through pixel j to get the shifted prefix \bar{x}j. ii. Evaluate the shifted PDF p{i \to j}(\bar{x}j) using the formula: p{i \to j}(\bar{x}j) = \frac{ci \cdot pi(\bar{x}i)}{|S^0{i \to j}|} where pi(\bar{x}i) is the PDF of the base prefix at camera i. iii. Evaluate the ideal PDF p{j \to j}(\bar{x}j) using the formula: p{j \to j}(\bar{x}j) = cj \cdot pj(\bar{x}j) where pj(\bar{x}j) is the PDF of the prefix if it were sampled directly at camera j. iv. Accumulate the ratio into Sr: Sr \leftarrow Sr + \frac{p{j \to j}(\bar{x}j)}{p{i \to j}(\bar{x}j)} d. Sample light sources to compute direct illumination and sample a path suffix to compute indirect illumination for the base prefix \bar{x}i. e. For each prefix \bar{x}j associated with pixel j (generated from all base prefixes \bar{x}i that could shift to j): i. Evaluate the MIS weight wi(\bar{x}j) as: wi(\bar{x}j) = \frac{1}{Sr} Note: Sr is specific to the base prefix \bar{x}i that generated this shifted prefix. ii. Accumulate the contribution to pixel intensity Ij: Ij \leftarrow Ij + wi(\bar{x}j) \cdot \frac{fj(\bar{x}j)}{p{i \to j}(\bar{x}j)} where fj(\bar{x}j) is the radiance contribution of the shifted path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. for each pixel i in allcameras: # 1. Sample base prefix xbari = samplebaseprefix(i) # 2. Initialize sum of ratios Sr = 0.0 shifteddata = [] # Store (pixelj, shiftedprefix, shiftedpdf) # 3. Loop over all cameras to shift and evaluate PDFs for each camera k in allcameras: j = getpixelindex(k, xbari) xbarj = shiftpath(xbari, k) # Evaluate shifted PDF: p{i->j}(x̄j) = ci pi(x̄i) / |S^0{i->j}| pshifted = (ci pi(xbari)) / abs(Jacobianshift(i, k, xbari)) # Evaluate ideal PDF: p{j->j}(x̄j) = cj pj(x̄j) pideal = cj pj(xbarj) # Accumulate ratio into Sr # Guard against division by zero if pshifted > 0: Sr += pideal / pshifted shifteddata.append((j, xbarj, pshifted)) # 4. Sample light sources and path suffix for direct/indirect illumination # 5. Accumulate contributions to pixels using MIS weights for j, xbarj, pshifted in shifteddata: # Evaluate full path contribution fj(x̄j) fj = evaluatepathcontribution(xbarj) # MIS weight wi(x̄j) = 1 / Sr w = 1.0 / Sr # Accumulate to pixel intensity Ij I[j] += w (fj / pshifted) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The estimator is not progressive. A full pass over all pixels of all cameras is required to compute Sr for each base prefix before contributions can be fully accumulated. If p{i \to j}(\bar{x}j) is zero or very small, numerical instability may occur. Reusing all prefixes disregarding scattering components can result in noisier estimates than the baseline (vpt) in anisotropic volumes. A method for Bidirectional Path Tracing (BPT) that uses full path PDFs incorporating medium sampling to weight MIS combinations, improving quality over directional MIS which only uses directional real-scattering PDFs. In a BPT scene, Full MIS achieved an RMSE of 0.049 and LTUV of 57.2M lookups, outperforming Directional MIS (RMSE: 0.043, LTUV: 44.9M) and Uni.+NEE MIS (RMSE: 0.731, LTUV: 12.7B). Full MIS prioritizes vertex connections through the dense medium (e.g., s=1), whereas directional MIS is oblivious to media presence and is dominated by camera-connection techniques (t=1). Time Complexity: Requires a full pass over all pixels of all cameras for each base prefix to compute Sr, making it non-progressive and potentially slower per sample than progressive methods. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate shifted prefixes and their contributions for accumulation. Variance: Exhibits higher variance than MWIS because the mixture density resulting from standard MIS is not optimal when the distribution of shifted prefixes does not follow ideal importance sampling. Noise: Can exhibit more noise than the baseline (vpt) in anisotropic volumes when reusing all prefixes disregarding scattering components. Strengths: Unbiased. Limitations: Non-progressive; higher variance in scenarios with high re-use between cameras where the shifted distribution is suboptimal. The method is described in "Volumetric Multi-View Rendering". It is presented as a baseline comparison to the proposed MWIS estimator, highlighting the limitations of standard MIS in multi-view volumetric rendering. The concept of Full MIS in BPT is discussed in "A Null-Scattering Path Integral Formulation of Light Transport", which provides context for the importance of full path PDFs in medium sampling. name: Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling
head: Chromatic Media Sampling with MIS, Single-sample MIS for Spectra, Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) for Wavelengths, Spectral Volume Sampling
body: Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) is a technique to sample wavelengths based on the product of throughput and single scattering albedo, using an empirical discrete distribution to balance contributions across RGB channels. It solves the problem where spectrally varying medium properties cause high variance when a single sampling PDF (based on one wavelength) is used to evaluate a function at multiple wavelengths, as the PDF may be a poor match or invalid (zero-valued) for other wavelengths. Inputs: Throughput vector \beta (typically 3-channel RGB). Single scattering albedo vector \omega (typically 3-channel RGB). Number of spectral samples n (typically 3 for RGB). Random number generator state. Outputs: Sampled channel index k \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}. MIS weights w{\lambdai} for each wavelength \lambdai. Data Structures: DiscreteEmpiricalDistribution1D: A discrete probability distribution constructed from a vector of non-negative weights. It stores the cumulative distribution function (CDF) or normalized weights to allow efficient sampling. Steps: 1. Compute the spectral weight vector w where each component is the product of the throughput and the single scattering albedo for that channel: wi = \betai \cdot \omegai \quad \text{for } i = 0, \dots, n-1 2. Construct a DiscreteEmpiricalDistribution1D from the vector w. 3. Sample a channel index k from this distribution using the random number generator. 4. Calculate the MIS weight for the sampled wavelength \lambdak and all other wavelengths \lambdai using the balance heuristic. Formulas: The probability of sampling wavelength \lambdai is p{\lambdai}, derived from the normalized throughput-albedo product. The discrete probability of sampling using a specific wavelength \lambda1 in the estimator's denominator is q, which is uniform at 1/n where n is the number of spectral samples. The MIS weight for wavelength \lambdai given that \lambdak was sampled is: w{\lambdai}(x) = \frac{p{\lambdai}(x)}{\sum{j=1}^n p{\lambdaj}(x)} Because p{\lambdai} are normalized sampling probabilities, the denominator sums to 1, making the MIS weight numerically equal to the sampling probability p{\lambdai}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spectralmissample(throughput, albedo, rng): """ Samples a wavelength channel based on throughput albedo using Spectral MIS. Args: throughput: List[float] of length n (e.g., 3 for RGB) albedo: List[float] of length n (e.g., 3 for RGB) rng: Random number generator with method getNext1D() returning float in [0, 1) Returns: sampledindex: int, the index of the sampled channel misweights: List[float], the MIS weights for each channel """ n = len(throughput) # Step 1: Compute throughputalbedo weights = [max(0.0, throughput[i] albedo[i]) for i in range(n)] # Step 2 & 3: Construct distribution and sample channel index total = sum(weights) if total == 0.0: # Degenerate case: all weights are zero. # Return uniform sampling and weights sampledindex = int(rng.getNext1D() n) pmf = [1.0 / n] n else: pmf = [w / total for w in weights] u = rng.getNext1D() cumulative = 0.0 sampledindex = n - 1 for i in range(n): cumulative += pmf[i] if u < cumulative: sampledindex = i break # Step 4: Calculate MIS weights using the balance heuristic # wlambdai = plambdai / sum(plambdaj). Since pmf sums to 1, weights equal pmf. misweights = pmf[:] return sampledindex, misweights Parameters: n: Number of spectral samples. Typical value is 3 for RGB rendering. q: Discrete probability of sampling a specific wavelength. Value is 1/n. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Throughput/Albedo: If all components of the throughput-albedo product are zero, the distribution is undefined. A uniform distribution should be used as a fallback. Time Complexity: O(n) to compute weights and sample, where n is the number of spectral samples. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store the PMF and weights. Strengths: Reduces variance in spectrally varying media by sampling wavelengths proportional to their throughput-albedo product while maintaining unbiased evaluation across all wavelengths via MIS weighting. Limitations: Requires computing the throughput-albedo product for all spectral channels before sampling. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The technique is described in the context of volume scattering integrators in the Physically Based Rendering (pbr-book). It addresses the limitations of delta tracking, which samples based on a majorant derived from a single wavelength, causing poor sampling efficiency for other wavelengths. The method leverages the balance heuristic from Multiple Importance Sampling to optimally combine the spectral samples. An implementation is also found in the unofficial volumetric path tracer volpt. name: Spectral+NEE MIS (Shadow Connection Routine)
head: MIS for chromatic media, Spectral MIS, Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS), Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling with Next-Event Estimation, Spectral NEE with MIS
body: Spectral+NEE MIS is a shadow connection routine used in volumetric path tracing to estimate direct illumination in chromatic participating media. It reduces variance by combining unidirectional path sampling and next-event estimation (NEE) using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) across spectral samples. Unlike standard spectral MIS, which can suffer from high variance or color noise in heterogeneous media, this method uses ratio tracking to handle null scattering events, allowing robust connections through dense or thin media while maintaining color fidelity. Inputs: Current path vertex position x and incoming direction \omega. Selected component index \tilde{c} for distance sampling. Current path contribution accumulator f (vector of spectral values). Current path probability density function (pdf) p. Outputs: Updated path contribution f. Updated path pdf p. MIS weight for combining unidirectional and NEE estimators. Spectral Vector: A vector of size n (number of spectral samples) representing radiance or contribution at each wavelength. Extinction Coefficients: \mut^c(x) for each component c \in \{1, \dots, N\} at position x. Null Scattering Coefficients: \mun^c(x) for each component c. Phase Function: \rhom(\omega, x, \omega') for the medium. 1. Sample Light Direction: Sample a direction \omega' toward the light source and compute its pdf p{\omega'}. 2. Update Contributions: Update the path contribution accumulator f by multiplying with the medium phase function value \rhom(\omega, x, \omega'). 3. Initialize PDFs: Initialize the next-event path pdf p{nee} as p \cdot p{\omega'}. Initialize the unidirectional path pdf p{uni} as p \cdot \rhom(\omega, x, \omega'). 4. Ratio Tracking Loop: Begin ratio tracking along the shadow ray in direction \omega'. Sample distance t using the extinction coefficient of the selected component \tilde{c}: t = -\frac{\ln(1-\xi)}{\mut^{\tilde{c}}} where \xi \in 0, 1) is a uniform random number. Intersect the ray at distance t to find point y. If surface hit: If y exists (surface hit), return the average of p{uni} and p{nee} (2N techniques). If no hit: Update contributions f with null-scattering transmittance for all components c: f \leftarrow f \circ \langle Tc^1(t)\mun^1(x), \dots, Tc^N(t)\mun^N(x) \rangle where \circ denotes component-wise multiplication and Tc^k(t) is the transmittance for component k over distance t. Update p{nee} with extinction/transmittance ratios for all components. Update p{uni} with null-scattering ratios for all components. Repeat loop. MIS Weight: The [balance heuristic weight for wavelength sample \lambda1 is: w{\lambda1}(x) = \frac{p{\lambda1}(x)}{\sum{i=1}^{n} p{\lambdai}(x)} Estimator: The combined estimator for spectral samples is: \frac{p{\lambda1}(x)}{\frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} p{\lambdai}(x)} \left[ \frac{f{\lambda1}(x)}{p{\lambda1}(x)}, \frac{f{\lambda2}(x)}{p{\lambda1}(x)}, \dots, \frac{f{\lambdan}(x)}{p{\lambda1}(x)} \right] = \frac{\left[ f{\lambda1}(x), f{\lambda2}(x), \dots, f{\lambdan}(x) \right]}{\frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} p{\lambdai}(x)} n: The number of spectral samples. q: The discrete probability of sampling using wavelength \lambda1, uniform at 1/n. High Variance in Heterogeneous Media: Estimating every component separately can lead to color noise, which the MIS combination remedies. Extreme Variance: Sampling distances according to a single component with low extinction can lead to extreme variance if other components have much higher extinction, which ratio tracking mitigates. Surface Hit: If a surface is hit, the routine returns the average of the two path pdfs, effectively combining 2N techniques. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spectralneemisshadowconnection(x, omega, ctilde, f, p, nspectralsamples): """ Perform Spectral+NEE MIS shadow connection. Args: x: Current vertex position. omega: Incoming direction. ctilde: Selected component index for distance sampling. f: Current path contribution (vector of size nspectralsamples). p: Current path pdf. nspectralsamples: Number of spectral samples. Returns: f: Updated path contribution. p: Updated path pdf. weight: MIS weight. """ # 1. Sample light direction omegaprime, pomegaprime = samplelightdir(x) # 2. Update path contributions with phase function rhom = mediumphasefunction(omega, x, omegaprime) f = f rhom # 3. Initialize PDFs pnee = p pomegaprime puni = p rhom # 4. Ratio tracking loop while True: # Sample distance using selected component xi = randomuniform() mutctilde = extinctioncoefficient(x, ctilde) t = -log(1 - xi) / mutctilde # Intersect ray y = intersectray(x, omegaprime, t) # If surface hit, return average of pdfs if y is not None: weight = 0.5 (puni + pnee) return f, p, weight # Update contributions with null-scattering transmittance nullscatteringfactors = [] for c in range(1, nspectralsamples + 1): Tct = transmittance(x, omegaprime, t, c) munc = nullscatteringcoefficient(x, c) nullscatteringfactors.append(Tct munc) f = f nullscatteringfactors # Update pnee with extinction/transmittance ratios pneeratios = [] for c in range(1, nspectralsamples + 1): mutc = extinctioncoefficient(x, c) Tct = transmittance(x, omegaprime, t, c) # Ratio tracking update for NEE pdf ratio = mutc / (mutctilde Tct) pneeratios.append(ratio) pnee = pnee pneeratios # Update puni with null-scattering ratios puniratios = [] for c in range(1, nspectralsamples + 1): munc = nullscatteringcoefficient(x, c) Tct = transmittance(x, omegaprime, t, c) # Ratio tracking update for unidirectional pdf ratio = munc / (mutctilde Tct) puniratios.append(ratio) puni = puni puniratios def samplelightdir(x): """Sample direction toward light source and return pdf.""" # Standard light sampling strategy return (vec3(0.0), 1.0) def mediumphasefunction(omega, x, omegaprime): """Compute medium phase function value.""" # Standard phase function evaluation return 1.0 def extinctioncoefficient(x, c): """Get extinction coefficient for component c at x.""" return 1.0 def nullscatteringcoefficient(x, c): """Get null scattering coefficient for component c at x.""" return 0.0 def transmittance(x, omega, t, c): """Compute transmittance for component c over distance t.""" mut = extinctioncoefficient(x, c) return exp(-mut t) def intersectray(x, omega, t): """Intersect ray at distance t. Returns point or None.""" # Standard ray-scene intersection return None def randomuniform(): """Return uniform random number in 0, 1).""" return 0.5 def log(x): """Natural logarithm.""" import math return math.log(x) def exp(x): """Exponential function.""" import math return math.exp(x) A sibling method that uses spectral MIS with unidirectional path tracing but without the NEE shadow connection routine. It is chosen when NEE is not required or when unidirectional sampling is sufficient. [Spectral MIS with Unidirectional Path Tracing Time Complexity: The ratio tracking loop length varies depending on the medium density and extinction coefficients. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for spectral vectors and extinction/null scattering coefficients for each component. Measured Performance: In a test scene (Fig. 9 right plume), Spectral+NEE MIS achieved RMSE: 0.016 and LTUV: 0.08M lookups, outperforming Spectral MIS (RMSE: 0.029, LTUV: 1.09M). Strengths: Reduces variance significantly in chromatic media and handles both back-lit thin media and side-lit dense media robustly. Limitations: Can be computationally expensive due to the ratio tracking loop and spectral calculations. When to Use: When rendering chromatic volumetric media with complex lighting and where variance reduction is critical. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited and approximate results are acceptable, or when the medium is non-chromatic. Origin: The method is part of the VolPathIntegrator, which uses multiple importance sampling for direct illumination in volumetric media. History: The specific combination of spectral MIS with NEE and ratio tracking was integrated into null-scattering path integral formulations for light transport to handle heterogeneous media and reduce color noise. Usage: Implemented in the VolPathIntegrator. 14.2 Volume Scattering Integrators, https://pbr-book.org/4ed/LightTransportIIVolumeRendering/VolumeScatteringIntegrators, fetched 2026-10-29 A Null-Scattering Path Integral Formulation of Light Transport, https://www.scribd.com/document/1067625811/A-Null-scattering-Path-Integral-Formulation-of-Light-Transport, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Spectral MIS with Unidirectional Path Tracing
head: Spectral MIS
body: Spectral MIS with Unidirectional Path Tracing estimates direct illumination in spectrally varying participating media by combining per-channel sampling techniques via Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). It reduces the color noise of independent tracking and the computational cost of spectral tracking, which relies on a conservative majorant for all color components. Unlike Spectral+NEE MIS (Shadow Connection Routine), it omits the shadow connection routine for next-event estimation. The method estimates the spectral radiance by computing separate path contributions for each color component c \in \{c1, \dots, cN\}, but combines them using a balance heuristic to reduce color noise. Inputs: Current position x and incoming direction \omega. Spectral extinction \mut^c(x), scattering \mus^c(x), absorption \mua^c(x), and null \mun^c(x) coefficients for each component c. Phase function \rhom(\omega) and light source radiance Le(x, -\omega). Number of color components N. Outputs: Estimated spectral radiance contribution. Data Structures: Vectors f and p of size N, initialized to ones, storing per-component path contributions and path PDFs respectively. Steps: 1. Initialize f \leftarrow \langle 1, \dots, 1 \rangleN and p \leftarrow \langle 1, \dots, 1 \rangleN. 2. Select a color component \tilde{c} \in \{c1, \dots, cN\} uniformly at random. 3. Sample interaction distance t = -\ln(1-\xi)/\mut^{\tilde{c}}(x) using a uniform random number \xi \in [0, 1). 4. Update position x \leftarrow x + t\omega. 5. Sample event type e \in \{a, s, n\} with probabilities \mue^{\tilde{c}}(x)/\mut^{\tilde{c}}(x). 6. Update contributions f \leftarrow f \circ \langle T(t)\mue^{c1}(x), \dots, T(t)\mue^{cN}(x) \rangle. 7. Update PDFs p \leftarrow p \circ \langle \mut^{c1}(x)/\mut^{\tilde{c}}(x), \dots, \mut^{cN}(x)/\mut^{\tilde{c}}(x) \rangle. 8. If e=a, return \frac{1}{N}\sum{i=1}^N fi/pi. 9. If e=s, sample \omega \propto \rhom(\omega) and continue the loop. 10. If e=n, continue the loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def spectralmisunidirectional(x, omega, mut, mus, mua, mun, rhom, Le, N, muhat): f = [1.0] N p = [1.0] N ctilde = random.randint(0, N - 1) while True: xi = random.uniform(0, 1) t = -math.log(1.0 - xi) / mut(x)[ctilde] x = x + t omega mutall = mut(x) musall = mus(x) muaall = mua(x) munall = mun(x) r = random.uniform(0, 1) pa = muaall[ctilde] / mutall[ctilde] ps = musall[ctilde] / mutall[ctilde] if r < pa: event = 'a' elif r < pa + ps: event = 's' else: event = 'n' Tt = math.exp(-muhat t) for i in range(N): coeff = muaall[i] if event == 'a' else (musall[i] if event == 's' else munall[i]) f[i] = f[i] Tt coeff for i in range(N): p[i] = p[i] (mutall[i] / mutall[ctilde]) if event == 'a': return sum(f[i] / p[i] for i in range(N)) / N elif event == 's': omega = samplephasefunction(rhom) # event == 'n' continues loop def samplephasefunction(rhom): # Standard phase function sampling routine (e.g., rejection sampling or analytical inverse) return normalize(randomdirection()) Parameters: N: Number of color components (e.g., 3 for RGB). \xi: Uniform random number in 0, 1). Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision issues may arise if \mut^{\tilde{c}} is very small, leading to large t. Boundary conditions for the medium must be handled when x exits the medium. The balance heuristic requires that all techniques have non-zero probability of being selected. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot r), where N is the number of color components and r is the path length. Each step involves N operations for updating f and p. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing f and p vectors. Measured Performance: In a 1D medium experiment, Spectral MIS achieved a reduction of color noise comparable to spectral tracking but at a lower cost (fewer medium lookups). In the left plume of Fig. 9 (high density, low albedo green channel), Spectral MIS achieved RMSE: 0.047 and LTUV: 4.12M lookups, outperforming Spectral tracking (RMSE: 0.055, LTUV: 5.82M) and Independent tracking (RMSE: 0.077, LTUV: 11.5M). In the right plume of Fig. 9 (similar spectral variation), Spectral MIS achieved RMSE: 0.029 and LTUV: 1.09M lookups, outperforming Spectral tracking (RMSE: 0.035, LTUV: 1.51M). In the malachite material (Fig. 10), Spectral MIS achieved RMSE: 0.032 and LTUV: 0.56M lookups, outperforming Spectral tracking (RMSE: 0.042, LTUV: 2.85M). Strengths: Reduces color noise compared to independent tracking and lowers computational cost compared to spectral tracking by avoiding a common conservative majorant for all color components. Limitations: Still requires sampling per component and may not handle complex light source geometries as effectively as NEE methods. When to use: When simulating spectrally varying media and color noise is a concern, but computational resources are limited compared to full spectral tracking. When not to use: When light sources are inside the medium and next-event estimation is critical; consider [Spectral+NEE MIS (Shadow Connection Routine) instead. The method was introduced by as part of a null-scattering path integral formulation of light transport. It extends the work of Wilkie et al. and Fajardo [2012] by combining per-channel sampling techniques via MIS to reduce color noise while maintaining computational efficiency. The method is used in volumetric path tracing for rendering participating media with spectrally varying properties. A Null-Scattering Path Integral Formulation of Light Transport, https://www.scribd.com/document/1067625811/A-Null-scattering-Path-Integral-Formulation-of-Light-Transport, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Multiple Scattering Volume Path Tracing with Phase Function Sampling
head: Improved Volumetric Integrator, Multiple Scattering without Next Event Estimation, Vol Path Tracing 2, VolPathIntegrator, Volume Scattering Integrator (Majorant-based Path Tracing), Volumetric Path Integrator
body: This method is a path tracing algorithm for multiple homogeneous volumes that handles multiple scattering events by sampling the phase function, supporting index-matched surfaces and Russian roulette termination. It solves the problem of computing radiance in participating media where light scatters multiple times, extending basic volumetric path tracing by explicitly sampling the scattering direction via the phase function rather than relying solely on delta tracking for direction selection. Unlike its sibling Volumetric Path Tracing, which uses simple sampling and lacks explicit light sampling, this integrator robustly handles both surface and volume transport, including volumetric emission, chromatic media, and multiple scattering. It differs from Next Event Estimation for Volumetric Path Tracing by not explicitly sampling light sources for direct illumination in the volume, instead relying on the recursive phase function sampling to capture indirect lighting, which makes it inefficient for small light sources but simpler to implement for pure volume scattering. The integrator traces paths through participating media and surfaces, maintaining a throughput weight \beta and rescaled path probabilities ru (for unidirectional sampling) and rl (for light sampling) to handle Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) and avoid floating-point overflow/underflow. Inputs: Camera ray ray, wavelength samples lambda, sampler sampler, scene geometry aggregate, list of lights lights, maximum depth maxDepth, Russian roulette depth rrdepth, light sampling strategy lightSampleStrategy, regularization flag regularize. Outputs: Radiance L (SampledSpectrum). State Variables: L: Accumulated radiance, initialized to 0.f. beta: Path throughput weight, initialized to 1.f. ru: Rescaled unidirectional path probability, initialized to 1.f. rl: Rescaled light path probability, initialized to 1.f. specularBounce: Boolean, initialized to false. anyNonSpecularBounces: Boolean, initialized to false. depth: Integer bounce counter, initialized to 0. etaScale: Scalar multiplier for transmission, initialized to 1. prevIntrContext: LightSampleContext for MIS, initialized empty. Medium Properties (mp): Contains \sigmaa (absorption), \sigmas (scattering), \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas, phase function, and emission Le. Majorant: \sigma{maj}, the upper bound of \sigmat across all media, used for null scattering. The radiance equation for a homogeneous volume with absorption and multiple scattering, sampled via phase function, is: L3(\mathbf{p}(0), \omega) = \int0^{t{\text{hit}}} \exp(-\sigmat t) \sigmas L{\text{scatter}}(\mathbf{p}, \omega) dt + \exp(-\sigmat t{\text{hit}}) Le(\mathbf{p}(t{\text{hit}})) where the scattered radiance is recursive: L{\text{scatter}}(\mathbf{p}, \omega) = \int{S^2} \rho(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega, \omega') L3(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega') \mathrm{d}\omega' Rescaled path probabilities are defined as: r{u, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{p{u, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n)}{p{path}(\bar{p}n)} \quad \text{and} \quad r{l, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{p{l, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n)}{p{path}(\bar{p}n)} where p{path} is the probability of sampling the current path. MIS weights for unidirectional sampling when p{path} = p{u, \lambda, 1} are: wu(\bar{p}n) = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{m} \sum{i=1}^m r{u, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n) + \sum{i=1}^m r{l, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n)} Russian roulette termination probability: P{rr} = \min \left( \frac{\text{contrib}(\text{path})}{p(\text{path})}, 0.95 \right) In implementation, this is approximated using the rescaled probabilities: q = \max(0, 1 - \beta \cdot \eta{scale} / ru.\text{Average}()) maxDepth: Integer limiting maximum bounces. If -1, infinite bounces. maxDepth=2 corresponds to single scattering. rrdepth: Russian roulette starts when path has rrdepth + 1 vertices. regularize: Boolean; if true, BSDFs are regularized after non-specular bounces. lightSampleStrategy: String (default "bvh"). 1. Initialization: Initialize L=0, beta=1, ru=1, rl=1, specularBounce=false, anyNonSpecularBounces=false, depth=0, etaScale=1. 2. Loop: While true: 3. Intersect: Trace ray ray to find closest intersection si. If no intersection, si is null. 4. Medium Sampling: If ray.medium exists: Initialize RNG from two sampler samples. Sample majorant transmittance Tmaj using SampleTmaj. This invokes a callback for each potential scattering event. Inside Callback: Compute \sigma{maj} (majorant cross section). Compute PDF for majorant event: pdf = \sigma{maj}[0] \cdot T{maj}[0]. Emission: If depth < maxDepth and medium emits (Le): Compute \beta' = \beta \cdot T{maj} / pdf. Compute re = ru \cdot \sigma{maj} \cdot T{maj} / pdf. If re is non-zero, add to radiance: L += \beta' \cdot \sigmaa \cdot Le / re.\text{Average}(). Event Probabilities: p{absorb} = \sigmaa[0] / \sigma{maj}[0]. p{scatter} = \sigmas[0] / \sigma{maj}[0]. p{null} = \max(0, 1 - p{absorb} - p{scatter}). Sample Event Type: Draw uniform um. Absorption (mode 0): Set terminated=true, return false. Scattering (mode 1): If depth >= maxDepth, set terminated=true, return false. Increment depth. Update throughput and rescaled probability: pdf = T{maj}[0] \cdot \sigmas[0]. \beta = T{maj} \cdot \sigmas / pdf. ru = T{maj} \cdot \sigmas / pdf. Direct Lighting: If \beta and ru are non-zero, call SampleLd (light sampling) and add to L. Phase Function Sampling: Generate 2D sample u. Sample phase function: ps = \text{phase.Sample\p}(-\text{ray.d}, u). If ps is null or ps.pdf == 0, set terminated=true. Else: \beta = ps.p / ps.pdf. rl = ru / ps.pdf. Store prevIntrContext. Set scattered=true. Update ray: ray.o = p, ray.d = ps.wi. specularBounce = false, anyNonSpecularBounces = true. Return false. Null Scattering (mode 2): \sigman = \text{ClampZero}(\sigma{maj} - \sigmaa - \sigmas). pdf = T{maj}[0] \cdot \sigman[0]. \beta = T{maj} \cdot \sigman / pdf. If pdf==0, \beta=0. ru = T{maj} \cdot \sigman / pdf. rl = T{maj} \cdot \sigma{maj} / pdf. Return \beta \neq 0 and ru \neq 0. Post-Callback: If terminated or \beta=0 or ru=0, return L. If scattered, continue loop (new ray direction). If unscattered (ray passed through medium without interaction): \beta = T{maj} / T{maj}[0]. ru = T{maj} / T{maj}[0]. rl = T{maj} / T{maj}[0]. 5. Surface Interaction: If si is null (ray escapes to infinity): For each infinite light, if Le exists: If depth==0 or specularBounce, L += \beta \cdot Le / ru.\text{Average}(). Else, compute light PDF, update rl, add MIS contribution. Break loop. If si exists: Get BSDF. If null, skip intersection and continue. Visible Surface: If depth==0 and visibleSurf requested, estimate albedo using 16 pre-defined samples and store. Emission: If surface emits Le: If depth==0 or specularBounce, L += \beta \cdot Le / ru.\text{Average}(). Else, compute light PDF, update rl, add MIS contribution. Depth Check: If depth >= maxDepth, return L. Increment depth. Regularization: If regularize and anyNonSpecularBounces, regularize BSDF. Direct Lighting: If BSDF is non-specular, call SampleLd and add to L. Store prevIntrContext. BSDF Sampling: Sample BSDF direction bs. If null, break. \beta = bs.f \cdot |\cos \theta| / bs.pdf. If bs.pdfIsProportional, rl = ru / bsdf.PDF(), else rl = ru / bs.pdf. State Update: specularBounce = bs.IsSpecular(). anyNonSpecularBounces |= !bs.IsSpecular(). If transmission, etaScale = bs.eta^2. Spawn new ray. BSSRDF: If BSSRDF present and transmission: Sample probe segment. If null, break. Sample intersection along segment. If null, break. Update \beta, ru, rl. Sample BSDF at exit point. If null, break. Update \beta, rl. Spawn new ray. 6. Russian Roulette: Compute rrBeta = \beta \cdot etaScale / ru.\text{Average}(). Draw u{RR}. If rrBeta.\text{MaxComponentValue}() < 1 and depth > 1: q = \max(0, 1 - rrBeta.\text{MaxComponentValue}()). If u{RR} < q, break. Else, \beta /= 1 - q. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Li(ray, lambda, sampler, scratchBuffer, visibleSurf): L = SampledSpectrum(0.f) beta = SampledSpectrum(1.f) ru = SampledSpectrum(1.f) rl = SampledSpectrum(1.f) specularBounce = False anyNonSpecularBounces = False depth = 0 etaScale = 1.0 prevIntrContext = LightSampleContext() while True: si = Intersect(ray) scattered = False terminated = False if ray.medium: tMax = si.tHit if si else Infinity hash0 = Hash(sampler.Get1D()) hash1 = Hash(sampler.Get1D()) rng = RNG(hash0, hash1) Tmaj = SampleTmaj(ray, tMax, sampler.Get1D(), rng, lambda, lambda p, mp, sigmamaj, Tmajval: HandleMediumEvent(p, mp, sigmamaj, Tmajval, beta, ru, rl, depth, maxDepth, L, ray, SampledSpectrum(0.f) ru = Tmaj sigman / pdf rl = Tmaj sigmamaj / pdf return beta and ru Zero PDF: If phase function sampling returns null or zero PDF, the path must be terminated. If null scattering PDF is zero, \beta must be explicitly set to zero to prevent division by zero. BSDF Sampling Failure: If BSDF sampling returns null, the path loop breaks. BSSRDF Failure: If BSSRDF probe segment sampling fails, the path loop breaks. Overflow/Underflow: Tracking raw probabilities can overflow; using rescaled probabilities ru and rl prevents this. Adds explicit light sampling to the volume path vertices, improving efficiency for small light sources by changing the integration domain from the hemisphere to the light surface area. Extends the integrator to handle subsurface scattering (BSSRDF) in conjunction with volume transport, allowing light to enter a surface, scatter within, and exit at a different point. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of bounces and scattering events. Each bounce involves ray intersection, medium sampling (majorant), and phase function sampling. Memory Complexity: Low, primarily storing path state variables. Performance: Robust for homogeneous volumes with multiple scattering. Inefficient for scenes with small light sources compared to methods with Next Event Estimation. Strengths: Handles multiple scattering, index-matched surfaces, and chromatic media robustly. Avoids floating-point issues via rescaled probabilities. Limitations: Does not explicitly sample lights in the volume, leading to high variance for small lights. Requires homogeneous volumes for the standard formulation. The method originates from the VolPathIntegrator described in "Physically Based Rendering: From Theory to Implementation" (4th Edition), specifically Section 14.2 on Volume Scattering Integrators. It builds upon earlier volumetric path tracing techniques that used delta tracking for distance sampling but lacked robust handling of multiple scattering and surface interactions. The use of rescaled path probabilities for MIS was introduced to handle the numerical instability of tracking raw probabilities in long paths. name: Next Event Estimation for Volumetric Path Tracing
head: Direct Illumination Sampling, Direct lighting estimation, Light sampling, SampleLd, Vol Path Tracing 3, Volumetric NEE, Volumetric Path Tracing with Next Event Estimation
body: Next Event Estimation (NEE) for volumetric path tracing estimates direct illumination in participating media by explicitly sampling points on light sources and tracing shadow rays through volumes and index-matched surfaces. Unlike phase function sampling, which is inefficient for small light sources, NEE changes the integration domain from the hemisphere to the light surface area, accounting for transmittance via ratio-tracking and handling index-matched boundaries without terminating the shadow ray. It builds on Multiple Scattering Volume Path Tracing with Phase Function Sampling by adding direct lighting estimation to the path vertices. Inputs: Current scattering position \mathbf{p} and view direction \omega (or surface normal if at a boundary). Current medium properties \lambda (spectral density) and phase function p(\omega, \omega'). Path throughput \beta accumulated from the camera to \mathbf{p}. Sampler state for random number generation. Scene geometry and light sources. Outputs: Estimated direct illumination radiance contribution L{dir}(\mathbf{p}, \omega). LightSampleContext: Holds the interaction point and flags for surface offsetting. SampledLight: Contains the pointer to the light source and its selection probability p. LightLiSample: Contains the sampled point on the light \mathbf{p}{light}, incoming direction \omegai, light radiance L, PDF pdf, and light type. MediumProperties: Contains absorption coefficient \sigmaa, scattering coefficient \sigmas, and extinction coefficient \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas. Shadow Ray State: Variables for ratio-tracking transmittance estimation: T{ray} (current transmittance estimate), rl (lower bound PDF weight), ru (upper bound PDF weight). 1. Context Initialization: If the current vertex is a surface interaction with a BSDF, initialize LightSampleContext with the surface interaction. If the BSDF is reflective but not transmissive, offset the sampling origin in the direction of the outgoing vector \omega{out}: \mathbf{p}{sample} = \mathbf{p} + \epsilon \omega{out}. If the BSDF is transmissive but not reflective, offset in the opposite direction: \mathbf{p}{sample} = \mathbf{p} - \epsilon \omega{out}. If the vertex is in a medium (no BSDF), use the medium interaction point directly. 2. Light Source Sampling: Sample a light source index u1 from the sampler. Select a light source L{sel} using the light sampler's Sample method. If no light is selected, return 0. Sample a point on the light surface using u2 (2D uniform). Get the light sample structure ls containing \mathbf{p}{light}, \omegai, Le, and pdf{light}. Compute the total PDF for the light selection: pdf{dir} = p(L{sel}) \cdot pdf{light}. If pdf{dir} == 0, return 0. 3. Scattering Function Evaluation: Define the outgoing direction from the vertex to the light: \omegai = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{light} - \mathbf{p}). If a BSDF exists: evaluate the BSDF: fr = f{bsdf}(\omega{out}, \omegai). Compute the geometry term: G = |\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}|. f{hat} = fr \cdot G. pdf{phase} = f{bsdf}.PDF(\omega{out}, \omegai). If in a medium (Phase Function): evaluate the phase function: f{hat} = p(\omega{out}, \omegai). pdf{phase} = p.PDF(\omega{out}, \omegai). If f{hat} == 0, return 0. 4. Shadow Ray Tracing and Transmittance Estimation: Initialize the shadow ray from \mathbf{p} to \mathbf{p}{light}. Initialize ratio-tracking variables: T{ray} = 1.0, rl = 1.0, ru = 1.0. Initialize a random number generator for Russian Roulette. Loop while the ray direction is non-zero: 1. Intersection: Trace the shadow ray against the scene. Let t{hit} be the distance to the closest intersection, or \infty if none. 2. Opaque Occlusion: If an intersection occurs with an opaque material (material ID \ge 0), the light is blocked. Return 0. 3. Index-Matched Surfaces: If the intersection is with an index-matched surface (material ID < 0, no material): increment a shadow bounce counter. Check max depth limits (path bounces + shadow bounces). If exceeded, return 0. Update the current medium to the medium on the other side of the surface. Continue the ray through the surface (spawn new ray segment to \mathbf{p}{light}). 4. Transmittance Update (Ratio-Tracking): Determine the segment length t{seg} = \min(t{hit}, t{max}). If the segment is within a medium: sample a distance t{sample} using inverse transform sampling for the exponential distribution: t{sample} = \frac{\ln(1-u)}{-\sigmat}. Calculate the majorant extinction \sigma{maj} (typically \sigmat or a precomputed upper bound). Calculate the non-absorbing part: \sigman = \max(0, \sigma{maj} - \sigmaa - \sigmas). Update the transmittance estimate and PDF weights: T{ray} \leftarrow T{ray} \cdot \frac{T{maj}(t{seg}) \cdot \sigman}{T{maj}(0) \cdot \sigma{maj}}, rl \leftarrow rl \cdot \frac{T{maj}(t{seg}) \cdot \sigma{maj}}{T{maj}(0) \cdot \sigma{maj}}, ru \leftarrow ru \cdot \frac{T{maj}(t{seg}) \cdot \sigman}{T{maj}(0) \cdot \sigma{maj}}. (Note: T{maj}(t) = e^{-\sigma{maj} t}). Russian Roulette: If the estimated transmittance T{ray} / (rl + ru)/2 is very small (e.g., max component < 0.05), terminate with probability q=0.75 or scale up T{ray} by 1/(1-q). 5. Final Segment: If no intersection (t{hit} = \infty), break the loop (light is visible). If intersection occurred (index-matched), update the ray origin and direction to the new segment towards \mathbf{p}{light}. 5. Contribution Calculation and MIS: If T{ray} == 0, return 0. Compute the geometry term for the change of variable from solid angle to area: G = \frac{|\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}{light}|}{\|\mathbf{p}{light} - \mathbf{p}\|^2}. The NEE PDF (area measure) is pdf{nee} = pdf{dir}. The Phase Function PDF (solid angle measure) converted to area measure is pdf{phase\area} = pdf{phase} \cdot G. Compute MIS weights using the power heuristic: w = \frac{pdf{nee}^2}{pdf{nee}^2 + pdf{phase\area}^2}. Calculate the direct lighting contribution: L{dir} = \beta \cdot f{hat} \cdot T{ray} \cdot Le(\mathbf{p}{light}) \cdot G. Apply MIS weight: L{dir} = w \cdot L{dir}. Return L{dir}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from math import log, exp, sqrt, abs class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, v): return Vec3(self.x-v.x, self.y-v.y, self.z-v.z) def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def length(self): return sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) def normalize(self): l = self.length(); return Vec3(self.x/l, self.y/l, self.z/l) if l > 1e-12 else Vec3(0,0,0) def dot(self, v): return self.xv.x + self.yv.y + self.zv.z def absdot(self, v): return abs(self.dot(v)) class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.o = origin; self.d = direction class RNG: def init(self, seed1, seed2): self.state = (seed1 + seed2) % (232) def uniform(self): self.state = (self.state 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7fffffff; return self.state / 0x7fffffff class LightSampleContext: def init(self, point, offsetdir=None): self.pi = point; self.offsetdir = offsetdir class SampledLight: def init(self, light, p): self.light = light; self.p = p class LightLiSample: def init(self, plight, wi, L, pdf, isdelta): self.plight = plight; self.wi = wi; self.L = L; self.pdf = pdf; self.isdelta = isdelta class MediumProperties: def init(self, sigmaa, sigmas): self.sigmaa = sigmaa; self.sigmas = sigmas; self.sigmat = sigmaa + sigmas def nexteventestimation(p, currentmedium, phasefunction, beta, sampler, scene, lights, rp): # 1. Context Initialization ctx = LightSampleContext(p) # 2. Light Source Sampling u1 = sampler.uniform() sampledlight = lights.sample(ctx, u1) if sampledlight is None: return 0.0 u2 = sampler.uniform(), sampler.uniform() ls = sampledlight.light.sampleli(ctx, u2, sampler.spectralsample(), True) if ls is None or ls.pdf == 0 or ls.L == 0: return 0.0 pdfdir = sampledlight.p ls.pdf # 3. Scattering Function Evaluation wo = -Vec3(0, 0, 1).normalize() # View direction placeholder wi = (ls.plight - p).normalize() if phasefunction: fhat = phasefunction.p(wo, wi) scatterPDF = phasefunction.pdf(wo, wi) else: fhat = 0.0 scatterPDF = 0.0 if fhat == 0: return 0.0 # 4. Shadow Ray Tracing and Transmittance Estimation lightray = Ray(p, ls.plight - p) Tray = 1.0 rl = 1.0 ru = 1.0 rng = RNG(hash(lightray.o.x), hash(lightray.o.y)) shadowbounces = 0 maxshadowbounces = 10 while lightray.d.length() > 1e-6: isect = scene.intersect(lightray, 1 - 1e-4) thit = isect.t if isect else float('inf') if isect and isect.materialid >= 0: return 0.0 tmax = thit if isect else 1 - 1e-4 if currentmedium: sigmamaj = currentmedium.sigmat u = rng.uniform() tsample = log(1 - u) / -currentmedium.sigmat tsample = min(tsample, tmax) Tmaj = exp(-sigmamaj tsample) pdf = 1.0 sigmamaj sigman = max(0, sigmamaj - currentmedium.sigmaa - currentmedium.sigmas) Tray = Tmaj sigman / pdf rl = Tmaj sigmamaj / pdf ru = Tmaj sigman / pdf avgr = (rl + ru) / 2.0 if avgr > 0: Tr = Tray / avgr if Tr < 0.05: q = 0.75 if rng.uniform() < q: Tray = 0.0 else: Tray /= (1 - q) Tray = Tmaj / 1.0 rl = Tmaj / 1.0 ru = Tmaj / 1.0 if Tray == 0: return 0.0 if not isect: break shadowbounces += 1 if shadowbounces > maxshadowbounces: return 0.0 currentmedium = scene.updatemedium(isect, currentmedium) lightray = Ray(isect.position, ls.plight - isect.position) # 5. Contribution Calculation and MIS if Tray == 0: return 0.0 distsq = (ls.plight - p).length() 2 G = wi.absdot(Vec3(0, 0, 1)) / distsq # Placeholder normal for light pdfphasearea = scatterPDF G pdfnee = pdfdir w = (pdfnee 2) / (pdfnee 2 + pdfphasearea 2) Ldir = beta fhat Tray ls.L G return w Ldir Shadow Epsilon: A small offset (e.g., 10^{-4}) to prevent self-intersection when spawning shadow rays. Max Shadow Bounces: Limits the recursion depth for index-matched surfaces to prevent infinite loops in complex glass volumes. Ratio-Tracking Majorant: \sigma{maj} should be a tight upper bound on \sigmat to minimize Russian Roulette frequency. If \sigma{maj} is too loose, variance increases. Delta Lights: If the light is a delta emitter (e.g., point light), the MIS weight simplifies to 1 for the NEE path, as phase function sampling cannot hit a delta light directly. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of light sources and M is the average number of intersections/transmittance samples per shadow ray. Ratio-tracking adds overhead proportional to the optical thickness of the medium. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per shadow ray trace, excluding scene acceleration structures. Performance: Significantly reduces variance for scenes with small, bright light sources compared to pure phase function sampling. Performance degrades in highly participating media with high optical thickness due to the cost of ratio-tracking and Russian Roulette. Strengths: Unbiased estimation of direct lighting; handles index-matched surfaces correctly; reduces noise for small lights. Limitations: Requires efficient shadow ray tracing; ratio-tracking can be computationally expensive in dense media; MIS weight calculation requires accurate PDFs for both methods. Next Event Estimation for volumetric path tracing was introduced as an extension to volumetric path tracing algorithms to improve the efficiency of direct lighting estimation. The method changes the integration domain from the hemisphere to the light surface area, requiring careful handling of transmittance through participating media and index-matched boundaries. name: BSDF Sampling for Volumetric Paths
head: Implicit Path Tracing with Volume Interaction, Surface scattering in volumetric path tracing
body: This method handles the surface interaction component of volumetric path tracing, calculating indirect lighting contributions based on surface BRDF/BSDF properties and sampling strategies. It determines the new volumetric path direction upon surface intersection, updating throughput and rescaled probabilities to maintain unbiased estimation. It differs from pure volume scattering integrators by explicitly managing the coupling between surface geometry and participating media, specifically handling the transition from a surface hit back into the medium or to another surface. Inputs: Intersection data (isect): Contains surface normal (isect.shading.n), incoming ray direction (isect.wo), and optional BSSRDF data. BSDF object (bsdf): Defines the surface reflectance properties. Sampler (sampler): Provides random numbers (Get1D(), Get2D()). Current throughput (beta): Accumulated path weight. Rescaled probabilities (ru, rl): For Russian Roulette or importance rescaling. Sample mode (sampleMode): Defines the PDF calculation strategy (e.g., Uniform Hemisphere, Cosine Weighted). Scene objects and lights: For recursive calls or light sampling. Outputs: Updated throughput (beta). Rescaled probabilities (rl). New ray (ray) for continuation. Indirect radiance contribution (Lindirect). State flags (specularBounce, anyNonSpecularBounces, etaScale). Data Structures: BSDFSample: Contains f (BSDF value), wi (outgoing direction), pdf (probability density), pdfIsProportional (boolean flag), IsSpecular() (boolean), IsTransmission() (boolean), eta (refraction index), flags. Interaction/Intersection: Contains wo (incoming direction), shading.n (normal), SpawnRay() method. Steps: 1. Calculate Cosine Factor: Compute the cosine of the angle between the surface normal and the ray direction: \cos\theta = \text{clamp}(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{w}) where \mathbf{n} is the surface normal and \mathbf{w} is the ray direction. 2. Sample BSDF: Generate random numbers and sample the BSDF to determine the outgoing direction \mathbf{w}o (stored as bs.wi): python wo = isect.wo u = sampler.Get1D() bs = bsdf.Samplef(wo, u, sampler.Get2D()) if bs is None: break 3. Update Throughput: Multiply the current throughput beta by the BSDF value, the cosine factor, and divide by the PDF: \beta{\text{new}} = \beta{\text{old}} \times \frac{f(\mathbf{w}i, \mathbf{w}o) \cdot |\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{w}o|}{\text{pdf}} In code: python beta = bs.f abs(bs.wi.dot(isect.shading.n)) / bs.pdf 4. Update Rescaled Probabilities: Adjust the rescaled path probabilities based on whether the BSDF PDF is proportional to the actual PDF: python if bs.pdfIsProportional: rl = ru / bsdf.pdf(wo, bs.wi) else: rl = ru / bs.pdf 5. Update Path State: Determine if the bounce is specular: python specularBounce = bs.isspecular() anyNonSpecularBounces = anyNonSpecularBounces or not bs.isspecular() If transmission, update the refraction index scale: python if bs.istransmission(): etaScale = bs.eta 2 Spawn the new ray into the volume or scene: python ray = isect.spawnray(ray, bsdf, bs.wi, bs.flags, bs.eta) 6. Handle BSSRDF (Optional/Conditional): If the surface supports subsurface scattering and the interaction is transmission, sample the BSSRDF: python bssrdf = isect.getbssrdf(ray, lambda, camera, scratchbuffer) if bssrdf and bs.istransmission(): uc = sampler.Get1D() up = sampler.Get2D() probeseg = bssrdf.samplesp(uc, up) if probeseg is None: break seed = mixbits(floattobits(sampler.Get1D())) # Standard reservoir sampling initialization for subsurface interactions interactionsampler = WeightedReservoirSampler(seed) # Intersect BSSRDF sampling ray against scene geometry 7. Calculate Indirect Radiance: Recursively trace the new ray to compute indirect lighting: python Lindirect = hitobj.getobjectcolor() getpixelcolorimplicitpathtracing(objects, indexofclosestobject, hitt, secondray, light, depthi + 1, samplemode) beta 8. Accumulate Result: Add the indirect radiance to the pixel color: C = C + L{\text{indirect}} Parameters: brdf: Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function value. In some implementations, this is hardcoded as 1/\pi. sampleMode: Sampling strategy (e.g., UniformHemisphereSolidAngle, CosineWeighted). Affects PDF calculation. If sampleMode is UniformHemisphereSolidAngle, set pdf = 1 / (2 \pi) and update throughput = brdf cosine / pdf. If sampleMode is CosineWeighted, set pdf = 1 / \pi and update throughput = brdf / pdf. If sampleMode is neither, raise an error. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No BSDF Sample: If bsdf.Samplef returns null, the path terminates. PDF Proportionality: The formula for rl changes based on pdfIsProportional. Transmission Refraction: The etaScale must be updated correctly for multiple refractions. Undefined Sample Mode: If sampleMode is neither Uniform Hemisphere nor Cosine Weighted, an error should be raised. Time Complexity: Depends on the BSDF complexity and scene depth. Strengths: Handles complex surface interactions within volumetric paths, including subsurface scattering. When to Use: Scenes with complex surface materials and participating media. This method is part of the broader field of volumetric path tracing, specifically addressing the coupling between surface and volume interactions. It builds upon the principles of path tracing and incorporates techniques for handling BSSRDFs in participating media. The specific implementation details in reflect an early or simplified approach to implicit path tracing with volume interactions. wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 14.2 Volume Scattering Integrators, https://pbr-book.org/4ed/LightTransportIIVolumeRendering/VolumeScatteringIntegrators, fetched 2026-10-29
