head: Beam Query, Point Data, 2D Blur, Jarosz et al. estimate, VK method, Varying Kernel method, Volumetric Photon Mapping (Reformulated), Volumetric Photon Mapping with Beam Estimate, Volumetric Photon Mapping with Ray Query
body: The Beam Radiance Estimate (BRE) is a photon-based technique for estimating accumulated in-scattered radiance along an entire camera ray in participating media, serving as the core gathering step for Volumetric Photon Mapping. Unlike conventional volumetric photon mapping, which estimates incident radiance at discrete points along a ray via spherical neighborhood queries, BRE queries all photons intersecting the ray line simultaneously, replacing Dirac delta and Heaviside functions with a 2D smoothing kernel perpendicular to the ray. This approach eliminates redundant photon gathering and noise associated with large step sizes in ray marching, concentrating computational effort only where photons intersect the viewing path. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A photon map (set of photons with position \mathbf{x}i, direction \vec{\omega}i, and weight \alphai), a camera ray defined by origin \mathbf{x}, direction \vec{\omega}, and length s, and scattering properties (\sigmas, \sigmaa). Outputs: The accumulated in-scattered radiance Lb along the ray segment [0, s]. Data Structures: 1. Photon Map: Traditionally stores 20 bytes per photon. For BRE with Variable Kernel (VK) radii, each photon stores an additional 7 floating-point values (radius and bounding box coordinates), increasing size to 46 bytes per photon. 2. Bounding-Box Hierarchy (BBH): A hierarchy constructed over "photon discs" (the 2D blur area of each photon perpendicular to the ray). It reuses the balanced kd-tree structure of the photon map. Each node stores a bounding box enclosing its photon's radius and the bounding boxes of its children. Algorithm Steps: 1. Shoot Photons: Shoot photons from light sources into the scene, recording interactions. 2. Construct kd-Tree: Build a balanced kd-tree for the photon positions. 3. Assign Photon Radius: For fixed-width kernels, use a constant radius r. For Variable Kernel (VK) method, estimate local density to assign a per-photon radius ri. Compute the distance d{i,m} to the m-th nearest neighbor in the kd-tree. Estimate the radius for n neighbors assuming uniform density: ri = d{i,m} \sqrt[3]{\frac{n}{m}} where m \ll n is a search parameter (default m = \sqrt{n}) and n controls blur amount. 4. Construct BBH: Traverse the kd-tree from leaves to root. For each node p, compute its bounding box B as the union of the bounding box of its photon disc and the bounding boxes of its children. Store B in p.bbox. The kd-tree can be freed after BBH construction. 5. Render (Gathering): For each camera ray, traverse the BBH to find all photons whose bounding spheres intersect the ray. For each intersecting photon i, compute its contribution using the radiance estimate equation. Formulas: The beam radiance estimate for a ray \mathbf{x} with direction \vec{\omega} and length s is: Lb(\mathbf{x} \leftarrow \vec{\omega}, s) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N Ki(\mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, s, \mathbf{x}i, ri) Tr(\mathbf{x} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}'i) \sigmas(\mathbf{x}'i) p(\mathbf{x}i, \vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}i) \alphai Where: N is the total number of photons (normalization factor for the Monte Carlo estimator). Ki is the per-photon smoothing kernel. Tr(\mathbf{x} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}'i) is the transmittance between the ray origin and the photon's projection. \sigmas(\mathbf{x}'i) is the scattering coefficient at the projection point. p(\mathbf{x}i, \vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}i) is the phase function. \alphai is the photon weight. Cylindrical Coordinates: Photons are evaluated in cylindrical coordinates (ti, \thetai, ri) about the ray: ti = (\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}) \cdot \vec{\omega}: Projected distance along the ray. \mathbf{x}'i = \mathbf{x} + ti \vec{\omega}: Projection of photon position onto the ray. di = \|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}'i\|: Shortest distance from photon to ray. Kernel Function: The 2D biweight kernel is used: K(\mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, s, \mathbf{x}i, ri) = \begin{cases} ri^{-2} K2\left(\frac{di}{ri}\right) & \text{if } di \in [0, ri] \text{ and } 0 \le ti \le s \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} K2(u) = \frac{3}{\pi}(1-u^2)^2 This kernel is normalized for 2D because the integration along the ray is handled explicitly, blurring only perpendicular to the ray. Heterogeneous Media Transmittance: For heterogeneous media, precompute transmission terms Tr(x \leftrightarrow x'i) by marching along the ray and storing values in a 1D lookup table. Interpolate within this table during gathering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computetransmittancetable(rayorigin, raydir, raylength, sigmatfunc, numsamples=100): """Marches along the ray to compute transmittance T(t) = exp(-int0^t sigmat dt).""" table = [] dt = raylength / numsamples currentt = 0.0 opticaldepth = 0.0 table.append((0.0, 1.0)) for i in range(1, numsamples + 1): currentt = i dt pos = (rayorigin[0]+raydir[0]currentt, rayorigin[1]+raydir[1]currentt, rayorigin[2]+raydir[2]currentt) opticaldepth += sigmatfunc(pos) dt table.append((currentt, math.exp(-opticaldepth))) return table def interpolatetransmittance(table, t): """Linear interpolation of transmittance from the lookup table.""" if t <= table[0][0]: return table[0][1] if t >= table[-1][0]: return table[-1][1] for i in range(len(table) - uu)2 (3.0 / math.pi) / (photon.radius2) tr = interpolatetransmittance(transmittancetable, ti) phase = evaluatephase(raydir, photon.direction) contribution = kernelval tr photon.sigmas phase photon.weight totalradiance += contribution return totalradiance / N Adaptive Beam Width is a technique for estimating radiance in participating media that uses photon differentials to dynamically adjust the smoothing kernel width of photon beams. It solves the problem of over-blurring and banding artifacts inherent in fixed-width beam estimates, particularly in regions with sharp lighting features like volume caustics. Unlike fixed-width methods, it allows for small beam widths in focused regions and larger widths in sparse regions, enabling crisp reconstruction of sharp details with significantly fewer photons. Time Complexity: BBH construction is linear in the number of photons. Adaptive kernel width computation is inexpensive, typically <1–2% of total render time. Memory Complexity: Increases photon storage from 20 bytes to 46 bytes per photon due to BBH and radius data. Performance: More efficient than conventional volumetric photon mapping for scenes with concentrated lighting (e.g., caustics) because it avoids redundant gathering and large step-size noise. Strengths: Eliminates ray marching noise; handles heterogeneous media via lookup tables; adaptive kernels improve quality in focused regions. Limitations: Biased due to kernel blurring; requires preprocessing for radii and BBH; small m values in radius computation can cause noisy radii. Developed by Henrik Wann Jensen and colleagues, building on the theory of volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams. It reformulates Volumetric Photon Mapping by treating photon contributions as 2D discs perpendicular to the query ray, derived from the measurement equation in ray space. name: Adaptive Beam Width
head: Adaptive Beam Blur, Photon Beam Rendering with Adaptive Width, Photon Beams, Varying Kernel Beam Estimate, beam tracing for participating media, photon point beams
body: Adaptive Beam Width is a radiance estimation technique for participating media that uses photon differentials to dynamically adjust the smoothing kernel width of photon beams. It solves the over-blurring and banding artifacts inherent in fixed-width beam estimates, particularly around sharp lighting features like volume caustics. Unlike fixed-width methods, it assigns small beam widths in focused regions and larger widths in sparse regions, enabling crisp reconstruction with significantly fewer photons. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Photon beams generated during the photon tracing stage, including photon differentials (Jacobian matrices of the photon path) at each beam's start point. Output: Radiance estimate at a query point or along a camera ray. Data Structures: Photon Beam: Extends the standard photon point representation. For heterogeneous media, it stores a 1D transmittance function along the beam's length, analogous to deep shadow maps, which can be significantly compressed for efficient storage. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Photon Differentials: Stored at the start of each beam, representing the local mapping from the light source parameter space to spatial position, enabling local cross-section and width calculation. Parameters: Beam Width: Determined adaptively by the photon differentials rather than a fixed scalar. Typical values are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Photon Tracing: Trace photons through the scene and store the resulting beams. Compute and store the photon differentials at each beam's start point. 2. Heterogeneous Transmittance (Optional): If the medium is heterogeneous, compute and store a 1D transmittance function along each beam during the tracing stage. This enables accurate visibility calculations during rendering without ray marching. 3. Radiance Estimation (Beam x Beam Query): For a query point or along a camera ray, identify all photon beams that contribute to the estimate. 4. Adaptive Width Calculation: For each contributing beam, calculate its effective width using the photon differentials. The differentials define the local density and spread of the photon flux. 5. Cross-Section Calculation: For secondary scattering events, compute the cross-section at the start of the child beam using the photon differentials' footprint. This induces a conical frustum shape and avoids division by zero. 6. Kernel Evaluation: Use the adaptive width to define the smoothing kernel. The kernel width is small in focused regions (high density) and large in sparse regions. 7. Aggregation: Sum the contributions of all contributing beams, weighted by their respective kernels and the stored transmittance if applicable. Formulas: The radiance estimate at a query point x is computed as: L(x) = \sum{i} \frac{Pi \cdot Ti(x) \cdot K(\|x - ci\|, wi)}{Ai} where L(x) is the estimated radiance, Pi is the power of beam i, Ti(x) is the transmittance along beam i to point x, K is the smoothing kernel, \|x - ci\| is the perpendicular distance from x to the beam axis, wi is the adaptive beam width, and Ai is the cross-section at the beam start. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def mul(self, scalar): return Vec3(self.x scalar, self.y scalar, self.z scalar) def dot(self, other): return self.xother.x + self.yother.y + self.zother.z def norm(self): return math.sqrt(self.dot(self)) EPSILON = 1e-6 def estimateradianceadaptive(querypoint, photonbeams, heterogeneous=False): """Estimate radiance at querypoint using adaptive beam widths.""" radiance = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for beam in photonbeams: # Sources do not give the exact beam intersection test. Typically checks if query point lies within the beam's conical frustum bounds. if not beamcontainspoint(beam, querypoint): continue width = calculateadaptivewidth(beam.differentials) crosssection = calculatecrosssection(beam.differentials) if crosssection < EPSILON: crosssection = EPSILON distancetoaxis = distancetoaxis(beam, querypoint) kernelweight = kernelfunction(distancetoaxis, width) beamenergy = beam.power transmittance = gettransmittance(beam, querypoint) if heterogeneous else 1.0 contribution = (beamenergy transmittance kernelweight) / crosssection radiance = radiance + contribution return radiance def beamcontainspoint(beam, point): # Sources do not give the exact beam intersection test. Typically checks if query point lies within the beam's conical frustum bounds. return point.norm() <= beam.maxlength def calculateadaptivewidth(differentials): # Sources do not give the exact formula for width from differentials. Typically derived from the Jacobian determinant or norm. return math.sqrt(abs(differentials.determinant())) def calculatecrosssection(differentials): # Sources do not give the exact formula for cross-section from differentials. Corresponds to the area element defined by the differential mapping at the beam start. return abs(differentials.determinant()) def distancetoaxis(beam, point): # Sources do not give the exact distance projection formula. Projects query point onto beam axis and computes perpendicular distance. return (point - beam.origin).norm() def kernelfunction(distance, width): # Standard isotropic smoothing kernel (uniform disk) if distance <= width: return 1.0 / (math.pi width width) return 0.0 def gettransmittance(beam, point): # Sources do not give the exact transmittance lookup. Interpolates the stored 1D transmittance function along the beam's depth. depth = (point - beam.origin).dot(beam.direction) return beam.transmittancefunction.interpolate(depth) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Fixed-width beams or beams with zero cross-section at the start can lead to division by zero. Using photon differentials to induce a conical frustum shape with a non-zero starting cross-section avoids this. Banding Artifacts: Fixed-width beams result in over-blurring and banding artifacts, especially in focused regions of volume caustics. Adaptive widths mitigate this. Multiple Scattering: While adaptive widths work well for single scattering and caustics, they were not as successful for multiple scattering in the reported implementation. Heterogeneous Media: Handling heterogeneous transmittance along photon beams is more costly than homogeneous media. It requires storing and querying 1D transmittance functions. Time Complexity: The current implementation uses a BVH over all beams to accelerate Beam x Beam queries, though room for improvement exists via tailored data structures. Memory Complexity: Storing photon beams with 1D transmittance functions for heterogeneous media increases memory usage compared to simple photon points, though these functions can be significantly compressed. Measured Performance: In a volume caustic scene, photon beams converged to a crisp solution using 32k beams in 43 seconds, whereas 512k photons took almost twice the time and resulted in an over-blurred and noisy caustic. In the bumpy sphere scene, 90k photon beams reconstructed sharp features in about 100 seconds, whereas the same number of photon points suffered from over-blurring. Strengths: Reduces bias and variance compared to photon points. Eliminates shadow rays by reusing visibility information from the photon tracing stage. Avoids VPL singularities by using finite cross-sections instead of clamping inverse-squared distance terms. Renders extremely sharp details with tens of thousands of beams, whereas previous methods required millions or billions of photons. Limitations: Adaptive widths were not as successful for multiple scattering. Current BVH acceleration structure may not be optimal. Handling heterogeneous media adds computational and memory overhead. When to Use: Use when rendering scenes with sharp lighting features like volume caustics, especially with area lights or multiple bounces, and when computational resources are limited compared to the requirements of photon point methods. When Not to Use: Avoid for multiple scattering if the adaptive width implementation does not perform well, or if heterogeneous media handling is too costly for the application. Origin: Introduced by as part of a comprehensive theory of volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams. History: The method generalizes photon points to beams, allowing for area light sources and multiple specular and diffuse bounces. It builds on the concept of photon mapping and beam tracing. Usage: Used in volumetric photon mapping for rendering participating media, particularly for efficient estimation of in-scattered radiance. A comprehensive theory of volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams, https://doi.org/10.1145/1899404.1899409, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multiple Scattering Approximation via Light Volume Lookup
head: Light Volume Lookup, Precomputed Light Volume for Multiple Scattering
body: This method approximates multiple scattering in participating media by precomputing light attenuation into a volumetric data structure (the "light volume") and treating the multiple scattering contribution as a lookup operation based on accumulated optical thickness and a derived blurring width. It solves the problem of expensive numerical integration of the radiative transfer equation for multiple scattering orders by replacing it with a spatially varying blur lookup, allowing for real-time or near-real-time rendering of complex volumetric effects like smoke and clouds. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Voxel Cone Tracing by explicitly modeling the spatial spreading of light beams through the medium using a derived width parameter, rather than relying on cone tracing or spherical harmonics for visibility approximation. Inputs: Density volume grid \rho(x) storing medium density at voxel centers. Optical properties: Absorption cross-section C{abs} and Scattering cross-section C{sca} (assumed constant or spatially varying). Light source positions and intensities. Camera ray parameters (origin, direction). Outputs: Final radiance L{total} for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Density Volume: A 3D grid of size N^3 (e.g., 128^3) storing \rho(x). Each voxel stores a single floating-point value for density. 2. Light Volume Pyramid: A mip-map structure storing precomputed attenuated radiance. Each level stores the result of light propagation through the medium, blurred by the estimated multiple scattering width. 3. Optical Thickness Squared Volume: An auxiliary volume storing \tau^2 for the light path, used to handle inhomogeneous media without runtime integration. Formulas: Scattering coefficient: a(x) = C{abs} \cdot \rho(x). Scattering coefficient: b(x) = C{sca} \cdot \rho(x). Optical thickness (light path): \tau = \int{0}^{s0} b(x{start} + s \cdot \hat{\omega}) ds. Blurring width w: Derived from path integral analysis, approximating the spatial spread of the light beam. It is a function of optical thickness and scattering properties. Multiple scattering phase function: P{MS}(\theta, \tau). Path curvature: C = \alpha \cdot \theta^2 / \tau. Weight for multiple scattering contribution: weight = \exp(-(c/b)\tau) \cdot \exp(-C) \cdot P{MS}(\theta, \tau). Parameters: w: Blurring level, used as an index or parameter for the light volume lookup. C{abs}: Absorption cross-section. C{sca}: Scattering cross-section. \rho(x): Density of the medium at point x. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Light Volume Construction): 1. For each light source, compute the optical thickness \tau from the light to every voxel in the density volume. 2. For inhomogeneous media, compute and store \tau^2 in the auxiliary volume to avoid expensive runtime integration. 3. Propagate light through the medium, applying attenuation based on a(x) and b(x). 4. Apply spatial blurring to the propagated light using the derived blurring width w to simulate multiple scattering spread. 5. Store the attenuated and blurred radiance in the Light Volume Pyramid at appropriate mip-map levels corresponding to different blur widths. 2. Rendering (Ray Marching): 1. For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera. 2. March along the ray. For single scattering, use small step sizes to resolve fine features. 3. For multiple scattering, march with progressively larger step sizes as the distance from the camera increases, because the blur width w is monotonically increasing with distance. 4. Track the camera path optical thickness \tau1 as the ray steps further into the volume. 5. At each sample point xi: a. Compute the scattering angle \theta = \arccos(\hat{\omega}{light} \cdot \hat{\omega}{view}). b. Determine the blurring width w based on the accumulated optical thickness and medium properties. c. Perform lookup: L = \text{Lookup}(xi, LV, w), where LV is the Light Volume. This returns the precomputed attenuated radiance. d. Compute the multiple scattering phase function P = P{MS}(\theta, \tau). e. Compute path curvature C = \alpha \cdot \theta^2 / \tau. f. Compute weight: weight = \exp(-(c/b)\tau) \cdot \exp(-C) \cdot P. g. Add contribution: L{total} = L{total} + L \cdot weight. 6. Return L{total} for the pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: ray: Ray origin and direction. densityvolume: 3D array of density values rho(x). lightvolumepyramid: Mip-map structure for precomputed attenuated radiance. opticalthicknesssqvolume: 3D array of precomputed tau^2 for light paths. Cabs: Absorption cross-section. Csca: Scattering cross-section. Returns: Ltotal: Final radiance for the ray. """ Ltotal = 0.0 # Step size for single scattering (small) and multiple scattering (progressively larger) stepsizesingle = 0.01 stepsizemultistart = 0.1 stepsizemultigrowth = 1.5 currentpos = ray.origin distance = 0.0 taucamera = 0.0 # Optical thickness for camera path while distance < ray.maxdistance: # Determine step size based on component # Single scattering uses fixed small step # Multiple scattering uses increasing step size step = stepsizesingle # Get density at current position rho = densityvolume.sample(currentpos) # Compute coefficients a = Cabs rho b = Csca rho # Update camera path optical thickness taucamera += b step # For multiple scattering, we need the light path optical thickness tau # In inhomogeneous media, this is precomputed as tau^2 # Assume we have a function to get tau from the precomputed volume taulight = gettaufromvolume(currentpos, opticalthicknesssqvolume) # Compute blurring width w based on tau and medium properties # This is a simplified representation; the exact formula for w is derived in the source w = computeblurringwidth(taulight, b, Csca) # Lookup precomputed radiance from light volume Lprecomputed = lightvolumepyramid.lookup(currentpos, w) # Compute scattering angle # Assume light direction is known or averaged omegalight = getlightdirection(currentpos) omegaview = ray.direction theta = acos(dot(normalize(omegalight), normalize(omegaview))) # Compute multiple scattering phase function Pms = computephasefunctionmultiplescattering(theta, taulight) # Compute path curvature # alpha is a constant parameter, assumed to be 1 for simplicity if not specified alpha = 1.0 Ccurvature = alpha (theta 2) / taulight if taulight > 0 else 0.0 # Compute weight # Note: The formula in the source uses 'c' which is likely a typo for 'Ccurvature' or similar # Based on the source: weight = exp(-(c/b)tau) exp(-C) P # Assuming 'c' in the source refers to Ccurvature or a related term. # However, the source explicitly writes 'c/b'. Let's assume c is a constant or typo. # Given the context, it's likely exp(-Ccurvature) is the main term. # Let's stick to the source formula as closely as possible, assuming c is a parameter. # If c is not defined, we might assume it's 0 or related to Ccurvature. # The source says: weight = exp( -(c/b)) exp( -C) P # The backtick likely represents tau. # So: weight = exp( -(c/b) tau) exp( -C) P # If c is not defined, we cannot implement this exactly. # However, looking at the source, it might be a typo for Ccurvature. # Let's assume c is a constant parameter for now, or 0 if not given. # Given the ambiguity, we will use Ccurvature for the first exp term if c is not defined. # But the source explicitly distinguishes C and c. # Let's assume c is a constant parameter provided by the user or 0. cparam = 0.0 # Not given in sources, assuming 0 for safety or placeholder weight = exp(-(cparam / b) taulight) exp(-Ccurvature) Pms # Add contribution Ltotal += Lprecomputed weight # Increment position currentpos += ray.direction step distance += step # Increase step size for multiple scattering component as we move further # This is a simplification; in practice, the step size might be managed differently if distance > stepsizemultistart: stepsizemultistart = stepsizemultigrowth return Ltotal def computeblurringwidth(tau, b, Csca): """ Computes the blurring width w based on optical thickness and scattering properties. The exact formula is derived from path integral analysis and is not explicitly given in the notes. """ # Placeholder for the actual formula derived in the source # The source mentions w is used as an index or parameter for lookup # and is monotonically increasing with distance. return tau Csca # Simplified assumption def gettaufromvolume(pos, opttausqvol): """ Retrieves the optical thickness tau from the precomputed volume. """ tausq = opttausqvol.sample(pos) return sqrt(tausq) if tausq > 0 else 0.0 def computephasefunctionmultiplescattering(theta, tau): """ Computes the multiple scattering phase function. """ # Placeholder for the actual phase function return 1.0 / (4.0 pi) # Isotropic approximation as a default def getlightdirection(pos): """ Returns the direction to the light source from the given position. """ # Placeholder return vector(0, 1, 0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: For inhomogeneous media, the optical thickness \tau varies spatially. Computing \tau along the path during rendering is expensive, hence the precomputation of \tau^2. Precomputing the light attenuation volume for each light source becomes expensive for a large number of light sources. The method considers only the overall statistics of the phase function, not its particular shape, leading to quantitative differences with Monte Carlo simulations. The computation of multiply scattered light attenuation is not straightforward and relies on the approximation of spatial spreading. Precision issues may arise when computing \tau from \tau^2 if \tau^2 is very small or negative due to numerical errors. The Beam Spreading Width Model provides a closed-form expression for the spatial width w of a collimated light beam as it propagates through a participating medium, approximating the spatial blurring effects caused by multiple scattering. It distinguishes itself from rigorous methods that lack general closed-form solutions by offering an easy-to-evaluate formula that explicitly accounts for absorption, scattering coefficients, and the mean square scattering angle. PSF-based Multiple Scattering Rendering is a practical method for rendering volumetric multiple scattering effects by treating the participating medium as a point spread function (PSF) that blurs incident radiance, thereby avoiding the costly direct numerical simulation of the radiative transfer equation. Unlike diffusion approximation, which is valid only for optically dense homogeneous media and assumes uniform angular distribution, this method handles spatially varying general materials and highly directional effects. Unlike the method by Narasimhan and Nayar, which is restricted to homogeneous isotropic media, this rendering algorithm allows for spatially varying participating media and accounts for anisotropic sources and visibility effects. In-scattering approximation is a technique for estimating the light scattered into a viewing ray from surrounding volume elements, treating the scattered portion of direct global light as an emittance source to capture short-range scattering effects. It sets itself apart from its siblings by offering a computationally cheap, non-iterative approximation that accounts for phase function and depth into the medium using remapped exponential decay, thereby avoiding the expensive integration required by exact multiple scattering methods. Unlike Beam Spreading Width Model which models spatial spread, or Precomputed Multiple Scattering Table which relies on precomputed data, this method computes the effect analytically per sample based on accumulated density and light direction. Multiple scattering corresponds to light that has reached vi, is scattered several times before reaching Pk and is scattered one last time into direction \hat{o}. Bergner et al. [7, 8] developed a spectral volume rendering integral based on a simplified multiple scattering model. It removes global illumination elements to facilitate ray casting with local illumination and post-illumination with different light sources. Time Complexity: The preprocessing step is O(N^3 \cdot L) where N is the grid resolution and L is the number of light sources. The rendering step is O(R \cdot S) where R is the number of rays and S is the number of samples per ray. However, the use of progressively larger step sizes for multiple scattering reduces the effective S for that component. Memory Complexity: Storage for the density volume grid (128^3 voxels) is 8 Mb. The light volume pyramid requires 32 Mb. The precomputed \tau^2 volume requires an additional 8 Mb. Total precomputed storage is approximately 48 Mb for the example scene. Measured Performance: For a rising smoke image, the algorithm took approximately 10 minutes, compared to 3 hours for a traditional Monte Carlo ray marching solution. For an inhomogeneous scene (800x800 resolution, 9 samples per pixel), rendering took about 30 minutes on a 1 GHz Powerbook G4 with 512 Mb of RAM. Monte Carlo methods with standard variance reduction techniques took almost 12 hours for the same inhomogeneous scene. Scaling: The method scales well with resolution due to the precomputed light volume, but the preprocessing cost increases with the number of light sources. Strengths: Captures qualitative features of multiple scattering, such as spatial blurring, more efficiently than previous methods. Simple to implement once the precomputation is done. Handles inhomogeneous media. Limitations: Quantitative differences with Monte Carlo simulations due to phase function approximation. Expensive preprocessing for many light sources. Single scattering computation can dominate rendering time for inhomogeneous media because it requires small step sizes. When to use: Suitable for real-time or near-real-time rendering of volumetric effects where qualitative accuracy is sufficient, and performance is critical. When not to use: When high quantitative accuracy is required, or when the number of light sources is very large, making preprocessing prohibitive. The method was presented in the paper "Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in Participating Media" by Raviraj et al.. It was developed to address the computational cost of simulating multiple scattering in participating media, which is typically done using Monte Carlo methods that are slow to converge. The key insight is to use spatial spreading and precomputed light volumes to approximate the multiple scattering contribution, allowing for faster rendering. The method has been used in the rendering of rising smoke and inhomogeneous participating media in a Cornell box. name: Beam Spreading Width Model
head: Spatial beam spread width
body: The Beam Spreading Width Model provides a closed-form expression for the spatial width w of a collimated light beam as it propagates through a participating medium, approximating the spatial blurring effects caused by multiple scattering. It distinguishes itself from rigorous methods that lack general closed-form solutions by offering an easy-to-evaluate formula that explicitly accounts for absorption, scattering coefficients, and the mean square scattering angle. Inputs: S: Distance along the beam path from the source. a: Absorption coefficient of the medium. b: Scattering coefficient of the medium. \langle \theta^2 \rangle: Mean square scattering angle, derived from the phase function P. Outputs: w(S): The spatial width (radius) of the beam at distance S. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the model is a direct mathematical evaluation. Parameters: \langle \theta^2 \rangle: Typical value in simulation is 0.24 (corresponding to Henyey-Greenstein asymmetry factor g=0.9). a: Typical value in simulation is 0.0003 mm⁻¹. b: Variable parameter determining the number of scattering events. Formulas: The core equation for the squared beam width is: w^2(S) = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{2a}{3S} + \frac{16\alpha}{bS^2} \right)^{-1} Where \alpha is defined as: \alpha = \frac{1}{2\langle \theta^2 \rangle} Alternatively, using the diffusive path length l, the formula is: w^2(S) = \frac{\langle \theta^2 \rangle b S^3}{16(1 + S^2/12l^2)} Where the diffusive path length l is defined as: l^2 = \frac{1}{ab\langle \theta^2 \rangle} Limiting Cases: 1. Long paths (S \gg l): The width grows linearly with distance: w^2 = \frac{3}{4} \langle \theta^2 \rangle b S l^2 2. No absorption (l = \infty): w^2 = \frac{b \langle \theta^2 \rangle S^3}{16} Pitfalls: The beam spread width expression has no upper bound. This is mitigated because attenuation increases at an even faster rate than the spread. The model assumes a Gaussian profile for the beam core; a wider non-Gaussian component exists in reality but is not captured by this model. The formula differs from Tessendorf [Tes87] by a constant factor of 3/2. To align with Tessendorf's rigorous derivation for specific limiting cases, multiply the result by 2/3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def beamspreadingwidth(S, a, b, thetasqmean): """ Calculate the squared beam width w^2(S) using the Beam Spreading Width Model. Args: S (float): Distance along the beam path. a (float): Absorption coefficient. b (float): Scattering coefficient. thetasqmean (float): Mean square scattering angle <theta^2>. Returns: float: The squared beam width w^2. """ if thetasqmean <= 0: raise ValueError("Mean square scattering angle must be positive.") if b <= 0: raise ValueError("Scattering coefficient must be positive.") if S <= 0: return 0.0 # Calculate alpha alpha = 1.0 / (2.0 thetasqmean) # Calculate diffusive path length squared # l^2 = 1 / (a b <theta^2>) lsq = 1.0 / (a b thetasqmean) # Calculate w^2 using the form involving l # w^2 = (<theta^2> b S^3) / (16 (1 + S^2 / (12 l^2))) numerator = thetasqmean b (S 3) denominator = 16.0 (1.0 + (S 2) / (12.0 lsq)) wsq = numerator / denominator return wsq Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation. The model is a closed-form expression requiring only basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No precomputed tables or volumes are required. Strengths: Easy to evaluate; provides a general closed-form solution unlike rigorous methods; explicitly includes absorption effects which narrow the beam compared to scattering-only models. Limitations: Lacks an upper bound on width (though mitigated by attenuation); does not capture the wider non-Gaussian component of the beam profile; differs from rigorous derivations (e.g., Tessendorf) by a constant factor. When to use: When an efficient, approximate spatial blurring model is needed for real-time or interactive applications where rigorous solutions are too slow or unavailable. The model was derived using a path integration framework and presented in the paper "Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in Participating Media". It builds upon earlier work on beam spread in scattering media, such as McLean et al. [MFW98] and Tessendorf [Tes87], adapting them for computer graphics applications where computational efficiency is critical. The derivation is detailed in a companion document [APRN04]. name: PSF-based Multiple Scattering Rendering
head: PSF convolution method, Point Spread Function method
body: PSF-based Multiple Scattering Rendering is a practical method for rendering volumetric multiple scattering effects by treating the participating medium as a point spread function (PSF) that blurs incident radiance, thereby avoiding the costly direct numerical simulation of the radiative transfer equation. Unlike diffusion approximation, which is valid only for optically dense homogeneous media and assumes uniform angular distribution, this method handles spatially varying general materials and highly directional effects. Unlike the method by Narasimhan and Nayar, which is restricted to homogeneous isotropic media, this rendering algorithm allows for spatially varying participating media and accounts for anisotropic sources and visibility effects. The core principle is that light transport in volumes can be formalized as a convolution of incident illumination and the PSF of the medium, where the PSF measures the spreading of incident radiance due to scattering events. The method relies on the mathematical path integration framework introduced by Tesfa [Tes87] and Perez et al. [PAS03] to describe multiple scattering effects in terms of spatial and angular blurring. Inputs: Incident illumination field (light volume). Medium optical properties: scattering coefficients and phase function. Medium geometry and spatial variation data. Outputs: Rendered image or volume radiance field including multiple scattering contributions. The method utilizes a multi-level light volume representation. Light Volume: A 3D grid or texture storing incident radiance. Blurred Levels: A set of pre-computed blurred versions of the light volume, each corresponding to a different kernel size (level of detail) representing different degrees of scattering spreading. Scattering Coefficients: Basic optical properties of the medium used to express the PSF. Phase Function: Basic optical property of the medium used to express the PSF. Kernel Sizes: Different sizes of blurring kernels applied to the light volume. 1. Compute Reduced Intensity: Calculate the amount of light available for redistribution due to multiple scattering by computing the simple attenuation of the incident illumination. 2. Pre-compute Blurred Light Volume: Apply the point spread function to the light volume by blurring it with kernels of different sizes. Store the light volume at various levels of detail corresponding to these blurs. 3. Rendering Lookup: During rendering, at every point in the volume, compute the amount of spreading (blurring) occurring due to multiple scattering. Look up the result from the pre-computed blurred representation of the light volume based on the computed spreading. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputelightvolume(incidentlightvolume, scatteringcoefficients, phasefunction): """ Step 1: Compute reduced intensity. Step 2: Apply PSF by blurring with different kernel sizes. """ # Compute reduced intensity due to simple attenuation # Note: Exact attenuation formula depends on specific optical properties # Assuming standard Beer-Lambert law for attenuation reducedintensity = incidentlightvolume exp(-scatteringcoefficients distance) # Generate blurred levels of detail blurredlevels = [] kernelsizes = [size1, size2, size3] # Defined by scattering properties for size in kernelsizes: # Blur the reduced intensity with a kernel of specific size # Convolution operation blurred = convolve(reducedintensity, getkernel(size, phasefunction)) blurredlevels.append(blurred) return blurredlevels def rendervolume(viewpoint, cameraray, blurredlevels, scatteringcoefficients, phasefunction): """ Step 3: Look up result from pre-computed blurred representation. """ # For each sample point along the ray in the volume: for point in volumesamples: # Compute the amount of spreading (blurring) occurring due to multiple scattering # at this specific point based on local optical properties spreadingwidth = computespreadingwidth(point, scatteringcoefficients, phasefunction) # Select the appropriate blurred level based on spreadingwidth # Interpolation between levels if necessary blurredlevel = selectblurredlevel(blurredlevels, spreadingwidth) # Look up the radiance from the blurred light volume # Trilinear or higher-order interpolation in the blurred volume multiplescatteringradiance = samplevolume(blurredlevel, point) # Accumulate radiance accumulateradiance(multiplescatteringradiance) Computational Cost of Alternatives: Volumetric Monte Carlo and finite element techniques are computationally expensive, with solution times ranging from a few hours to a few days, making them impractical for usual computer graphics imagery. This method aims to avoid such costs. Homogeneous vs. Inhomogeneous: The method is designed to handle inhomogeneous media, unlike diffusion approximation which is limited to homogeneous media. Directional Effects: The method accounts for highly directional effects and visibility, which are not easily handled by simpler analytic models restricted to homogeneous media. Time Complexity: The pre-computation phase involves blurring the light volume with multiple kernels, which is generally faster than full radiative transfer simulation. The rendering phase involves lookups and interpolations, which are efficient. Memory Complexity: Requires storing multiple levels of blurred light volumes, increasing memory usage compared to a single light volume. Strengths: Handles spatially varying participating media, anisotropic sources, and visibility effects. More practical than Monte Carlo methods for real-time or near-real-time applications. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the PSF approximation. May not capture all complex scattering phenomena as accurately as full simulation. When to Use: When realistic multiple scattering effects are needed in spatially varying volumes, and full simulation is too slow. When Not to Use: When extreme accuracy is required and computational resources are sufficient for Monte Carlo methods, or when the medium is optically dense and homogeneous (diffusion approximation might be simpler). The mathematical path integration framework used to describe multiple scattering effects was introduced by Tesfa [Tes87] and Perez et al. [PAS03]. The method was presented as a practical approach to computing lighting and volumetric effects in spatially varying inhomogeneous scattering media, taking directionally-varying lighting effects into account. It addresses the limitation of previous analytic models that were restricted to homogeneous and/or optically dense media. name: In-Scattering Approximation
head: Local Approximation of In-scattering
body: In-scattering approximation is a technique for estimating the light scattered into a viewing ray from surrounding volume elements, treating the scattered portion of direct global light as an emittance source to capture short-range scattering effects. It sets itself apart from its siblings by offering a computationally cheap, non-iterative approximation that accounts for phase function and depth into the medium using remapped exponential decay, thereby avoiding the expensive integration required by exact multiple scattering methods. Unlike Beam Spreading Width Model which models spatial spread, or Precomputed Multiple Scattering Table which relies on precomputed data, this method computes the effect analytically per sample based on accumulated density and light direction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Accumulated density along the view ray (\rho{accum} or \tau{acc}), the dot product between the view direction and the light source direction (\mu{sun} or \cos\theta), and a base dimensional profile parameter (P) representing the local cloud structure or distance from the cloud boundary. Outputs: An in-scattering factor (S or Ie) that modulates the direct light contribution to simulate the brightening of inner cloud volumes. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar variables for density, direction, and profile. The method operates on per-sample values during ray marching. Steps: 1. Accumulate Density: During the volume ray march, accumulate the optical depth or density (\tau{acc} or \rho{accum}) from the camera to the current sample point. 2. Compute Light Direction Dot Product: Calculate the dot product between the ray direction and the light source direction (\mu{sun}). 3. Remap Parameters: Apply a remapping function to the sun dot product and the base dimensional profile to control the exponent's sensitivity. The remapping function maps an input range [a, b] to an output range [c, d]. 4. Calculate In-Scattering Factor: Compute the in-scattering factor using the exponential decay formula involving the accumulated density and the remapped parameters. 5. Modulate Light: Multiply the direct light contribution by this in-scattering factor to approximate the multiple scattering effect. Formulas: The core approximation for the in-scattering factor S is given by: S = \exp(-\rho{accum} \cdot R(\mu{sun}, P)) Where R(\mu{sun}, P) is a remapped value derived from the sun dot product and the base dimensional profile: R(\mu{sun}, P) = \text{Remap}(\mu{sun}, 0.0, 0.9, 0.25, \text{Remap}(P, 1.0, 0.0, 0.05, 0.25)) The \text{Remap}(x, a, b, c, d) function linearly maps x from the interval [a, b] to [c, d]: \text{Remap}(x, a, b, c, d) = c + \frac{(x - a)(d - c)}{b - a} Alternatively, for a more rigorous first-order scattering approximation treating scattered direct light as emittance, the intensity Ie(s0) is calculated as: Ie(s0) = \int{s0}^{R\Omega} q(s) e^{-\int{s0}^s \tau(t) dt} d\tau Where q(s) is the direct global light distribution, R\Omega is the scattering sphere radius, and \tau(t) is the optical depth. This integral is discretized as: Is = \sum{j=0}^J \Phij \sum{m=0}^M Id(sm) \prod{i=0}^{m-1} (1 - \alpha(si)) Where J is the number of ray directions, M is the number of sampling steps, \Phij is the normalized light contribution from direction j, Id(sm) is the direct light at sample m, and \alpha(si) is the opacity. Parameters: Scattering Sphere Radius (R\Omega): Defines the range over which in-scattering is integrated. Short-range effects are dominant, so a limited radius is sufficient. Phase Function: Weights incoming light from different directions. An isotropic phase function is often used for simplicity, weighting light equally in all directions. Ray Directions (J): The number of directions discretizing the scattering sphere, found by subdividing a tetrahedron, icosahedron, or octahedron. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def remap(value, inmin, inmax, outmin, outmax): """Linearly remaps value from [inmin, inmax] to [outmin, outmax].""" if inmax == inmin: return outmin t = (value - inmin) / (inmax - inmin) return outmin + t (outmax - outmin) def inscatteringapprox(basedimensionalprofile, sundot, accumulateddensity): """ Computes the in-scattering factor using remapped exponential decay. Args: basedimensionalprofile (float): Profile parameter representing cloud structure/distance. sundot (float): Dot product between view direction and light direction. accumulateddensity (float): Accumulated density/optical depth from camera to current sample. Returns: float: In-scattering factor. """ # Remap base dimensional profile from [1.0, 0.0] to [0.05, 0.25] # Note: The source uses Remap(P, 1.0, 0.0, 0.05, 0.25), implying P is in [0,1] but mapped inversely or the range is specified as [1.0, 0.0]. # Assuming standard remap where input range is [inmin, inmax]. # If P is in [0, 1], and we want to map 1.0->0.05 and 0.0->0.25, the range is [0.0, 1.0]. # The source code snippet: Remap(baseDimensionalProfile, 1.0, 0.0, 0.05, 0.25) # This implies the input range is [1.0, 0.0] (descending) or the arguments are (value, min, max, outmin, outmax). # Standard remap usually assumes min < max. Let's implement the logic as described: # Map P from [0.0, 1.0] to [0.25, 0.05] if P=0->0.25, P=1->0.05? # Source says: Remap(P, 1.0, 0.0, 0.05, 0.25). # If input is 1.0, output is 0.05. If input is 0.0, output is 0.25. pmapped = remap(basedimensionalprofile, 0.0, 1.0, 0.25, 0.05) # Remap sundot from [0.0, 0.9] to [0.25,...] ? # Source: Remap(sundot, 0.0, 0.9, 0.25,...) # The second remap output is the input to the first remap's output range? # Actually, the formula is: Remap(sundot, 0.0, 0.9, 0.25, Remap(P, 1.0, 0.0, 0.05, 0.25)) # This syntax is ambiguous. Let's look at the code: # exp(-accumulatedDensity Remap(sundot, 0.0, 0.9, 0.25, Remap(baseDimensionalProfile, 1.0, 0.0, 0.05, 0.25))) # It seems the 4th argument to the outer Remap is the result of the inner Remap. # So: innerval = Remap(P, 1.0, 0.0, 0.05, 0.25) # outerval = Remap(sundot, 0.0, 0.9, 0.25, innerval) innerval = remap(basedimensionalprofile, 0.0, 1.0, 0.25, 0.05) # Mapping 0->0.25, 1->0.05 based on source order 1.0->0.05, 0.0->0.25 # Outer remap: sundot in [0.0, 0.9] maps to [0.25, innerval] # If sundot is 0.0, result is 0.25. If sundot is 0.9, result is innerval. exponentfactor = remap(sundot, 0.0, 0.9, 0.25, innerval) return exp(-accumulateddensity exponentfactor) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential function can underflow to zero for large accumulated densities, which is physically correct (opaque regions) but may cause numerical issues if not handled. Boundaries: The approximation assumes a certain depth into the cloud. At the very edge, the profile parameter P should be handled carefully to avoid discontinuities. Degenerate Input: If the sun dot product is outside the assumed range [0.0, 0.9], the remapping may produce unexpected results. Clamping or extending the remapping range may be necessary. A neural network-based module that estimates primary transmission and depth-dependent scatter contributions, primarily for X-ray imaging. It uses a learned convolutional architecture to refine scatter estimation based on depth context, unlike the analytical remapped exponential decay of the parent method. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, as it involves only basic arithmetic operations and a single exponential evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring no additional storage beyond the current sample's density and direction. Measured Performance: The method is described as "very cheap" and "not too bad" since direct lighting is significantly stronger, making the approximation effective for real-time rendering. Strengths: Computationally efficient, easy to implement, and provides a visually plausible brightening of inner cloud volumes. Limitations: Not perfectly accurate; cannot produce "Dark Edge" effects without additional techniques like Beer's-Powder attenuation. It is an approximation that may fail in scenes with very high multiple scattering contributions relative to direct light. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering where performance is critical and direct lighting dominates, such as in cloud rendering. When Not to Use: When high physical accuracy is required, or when specific effects like dark edges are crucial and cannot be achieved by combining with other techniques. The concept of approximating in-scattering by treating scattered direct light as emittance originates from early volume rendering research, such as the work by Max [Max95] and later refined in the context of Local Approximation of In-scattering (LAO) [HLY07]. The specific remapped exponential decay formulation for cloud rendering was popularized in real-time graphics, as seen in Jack Tollenaar's volumetric cloud rendering tutorials. The technique is widely used in game engines and real-time renderers to simulate multiple scattering effects efficiently. name: Depth-Aware Scatter Estimator
body: The Depth-Aware Scatter Estimator is a neural network-based module designed to estimate primary transmission and depth-dependent scatter contributions along rays, primarily in the context of X-ray imaging simulations. It computes Beer-Lambert primary transmission, accumulates a scatter source, mixes it with an ASPP-conditioned gate, and adds a bounded scatter contribution to the primary image. It is a child of In-Scattering Approximation, which provides a cheap approximation for in-scattering using remapped exponential decay, whereas this method uses a learned convolutional architecture to refine scatter estimation based on depth context. The method implements a neural network that takes ray-based volumetric data as input and outputs a corrected image with primary transmission and estimated scatter. Input: Volumetric data along rays, typically represented as a tensor of shape [B, C, D, H, W] or similar, where B is batch size, C is channels (e.g., attenuation coefficient \mu), D is depth samples, H is height, and W is width. The specific input channels are not fully detailed beyond \mu and dz (step size) being used for transmission calculation. Output: A tensor of shape [B, 1, H, W] representing the final pixel intensity I{out}. The module consists of several initialized convolutional layers and modules: 1. Depth Convolution (depthconv): A causal 1D convolution with kernel size 5, padding 4, and dilation 2. 2. Encoder Convolution (enc): A 1x1 convolution mapping 2 \cdot in\ch channels to base\ch channels. 3. ASPP Module: Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling module with base\ch input and output channels. 4. Alpha Head (alphahead): A convolution mapping base\ch to 1 channel, initialized with a bias of -3.0 to keep alpha near 0 at initialization. 5. Scatter Convolution (scatterconv): A convolution mapping in\ch + base\ch channels to 1 channel with kernel size 3. 6. Parameter alphamax: Upper bound on the learned scatter gating weight. Default is 0.4. The algorithm proceeds as follows: 1. Compute Cumulative Attenuation: Calculate the cumulative attenuation \tauz along the ray dimension D using the cumulative sum of the product of the attenuation coefficient \mu and the step size dz: \tauz = \text{cumsum}(\mu \cdot dz) 2. Compute Per-Sample Transmission: Calculate the transmission Iz for each sample: Iz = \exp(-\tauz) 3. Extract Primary Transmission: Extract the primary transmission I{primary} as the transmission at the last sample along the ray (index -1): I{primary} = Iz[-1] 4. Compute Scatter Source: Calculate the scatter source Sz per depth: Sz = \mu \cdot dz \cdot Iz 5. Apply Depth-Aware Weighting: Permute Sz to shape [B \cdot H \cdot W, C, D]. Apply depthconv (causal 1D convolution). Reshape back to [B, C, D, H, W] to get weighted scatter source Sw. 6. Sum Scatter Source: Sum Sw along the depth dimension D to get total scatter S: S = \sum{d=0}^{D-1} Sw[:,:, d,:,:] 7. Extract Exit Attenuation: Extract \tau{exit} from the last sample of \tauz: \tau{exit} = \tauz[-1] 8. Encode Conditioning Features: Concatenate I{primary} and \tau{exit} along the channel dimension. Apply ReLU activation. Apply enc convolution to get encoded features F{enc}. 9. Compute Context Features: Apply the ASPP module to F{enc} to get context features F{aspp}: F{aspp} = \text{ASPP}(F{enc}) 10. Compute Scatter Map: Concatenate scatter S and ASPP features F{aspp} along the channel dimension. Apply ReLU activation. Apply scatterconv to get the scatter map M{scatter}. 11. Compute Alpha Gating Weight: Apply sigmoid to the output of alphahead (applied to F{aspp}). Scale by alphamax to get the gating weight \alpha: \alpha = \text{alpha\max} \cdot \sigma(\text{alpha\head}(F{aspp})) 12. Compute Final Output: Add the primary transmission to the product of alpha and the scatter map: I{out} = I{primary} + \alpha \cdot M{scatter} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class DepthAwareScatterEstimator(nn.Module): def init(self, inch, basech, alphamax=0.4): super().init() # Initialize depthconv: causal 1D conv, kernel=5, padding=4, dilation=2 self.depthconv = nn.Conv1d(inch, inch, kernelsize=5, padding=4, dilation=2, groups=inch) # Initialize enc: 1x1 conv, 2inch -> basech self.enc = nn.Conv2d(2 inch, basech, kernelsize=1) # Initialize ASPP module (placeholder for actual ASPP implementation) self.aspp = ASPPModule(basech) # Initialize alphahead: basech -> 1, bias=-3.0 self.alphahead = nn.Conv2d(basech, 1, kernelsize=1, bias=True) self.alphahead.bias.data.fill(-3.0) # Initialize scatterconv: inch + basech -> 1, kernel=3 self.scatterconv = nn.Conv2d(inch + basech, 1, kernelsize=3) self.alphamax = alphamax def forward(self, mu, dz): # mu: [B, C, D, H, W], dz: [B, 1, D, H, W] or broadcastable # Step 1: Compute cumulative attenuation tauz # cumsum along depth dimension D (dim=2) mudz = mu dz tauz = torch.cumsum(mudz, dim=2) # Step 2: Compute per-sample transmission Iz Iz = torch.exp(-tauz) # Step 3: Extract primary transmission Iprimary Iprimary = Iz[:,:, -1,:,:] # [B, C, H, W] # Step 4: Compute scatter source Sz Sz = mu dz Iz # Step 5: Apply depth-aware weighting # Permute to [BHW, C, D] B, C, D, H, W = Sz.shape Szperm = Sz.permute(0, 3, 4, 1, 2).reshape(B H W, C, D) # Apply depthconv Swperm = self.depthconv(Szperm) # Reshape back to [B, C, D, H, W] Sw = Swperm.reshape(B, H, W, C, D).permute(0, 3, 4, 1, 2) # Step 6: Sum along depth dimension D S = Sw.sum(dim=2) # [B, C, H, W] # Step 7: Extract exit attenuation tauexit tauexit = tauz[:,:, -1,:,:] # [B, C, H, W] # Step 8: Encode conditioning features # Concatenate Iprimary and tauexit along channel dim condfeatures = torch.cat([Iprimary, tauexit], dim=1) # [B, 2C, H, W] condfeatures = F.relu(condfeatures) Fenc = self.enc(condfeatures) # [B, basech, H, W] # Step 9: Compute context features Faspp = self.aspp(Fenc) # [B, basech, H, W] # Step 10: Compute scatter map scatterinput = torch.cat([S, Faspp], dim=1) # [B, C + basech, H, W] scatterinput = F.relu(scatterinput) Mscatter = self.scatterconv(scatterinput) # [B, 1, H, W] # Step 11: Compute alpha gating weight alphaheadout = self.alphahead(Faspp) # [B, 1, H, W] alpha = self.alphamax torch.sigmoid(alphaheadout) # [B, 1, H, W] # Step 12: Compute final output Iout = Iprimary + alpha Mscatter return Iout class ASPPModule(nn.Module): def init(self, inch): super().init() # Placeholder for actual ASPP implementation # Typically involves convolutions with different dilations self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inch, inch, kernelsize=1) self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(inch, inch, kernelsize=3, padding=1, dilation=1) self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(inch, inch, kernelsize=3, padding=1, dilation=2) self.conv4 = nn.Conv2d(inch, inch, kernelsize=3, padding=1, dilation=4) self.conv5 = nn.Conv2d(inch, inch, kernelsize=1) def forward(self, x): # Simplified ASPP: sum of convolutions out = self.conv1(x) + self.conv2(x) + self.conv3(x) + self.conv4(x) + self.conv5(x) return out Initialization: The alpha head is initialized with a bias of -3.0 to ensure that the initial scatter contribution is near zero, preventing early training instability. Causality: The depthconv is causal, meaning it only uses information from previous depth samples, which is critical for physically plausible scatter estimation along the ray. Precision: The use of cumsum for attenuation can accumulate floating-point errors for very long rays or high attenuation coefficients. Using exp(-cumsum) directly is standard but may suffer from underflow for large \tauz. Boundary Conditions: The causal convolution with padding 4 and kernel 5 requires careful handling of the first few depth samples, which are influenced by the padding (assumed to be zero or reflected values depending on implementation). Time Complexity: The method involves several convolutions and element-wise operations. The complexity is dominated by the convolutions, which are O(B \cdot H \cdot W \cdot D \cdot k) for the depth convolution and O(B \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C{in} \cdot C{out}) for the 2D convolutions, where k is the kernel size. Memory Complexity: The method requires storing intermediate tensors for Iz, Sz, Sw, and feature maps. The memory usage is proportional to B \cdot H \cdot W \cdot D \cdot C. Performance: Specific performance metrics are not provided in the sources. Strengths: The method learns to estimate scatter based on depth context, potentially providing more accurate results than simple exponential decay approximations. The causal convolution ensures physical plausibility. Limitations: The method requires training data and a neural network inference step, which may be slower than analytical approximations. The performance depends on the quality of the training data and the architecture choices. When to Use: Use when a learned, depth-aware scatter estimation is needed and training data is available. When Not to Use: Use when real-time performance is critical and training data is not available, or when a simpler analytical approximation is sufficient. The Depth-Aware Scatter Estimator is part of the FlashDRR project, which focuses on fast digital radiograph generation. It was developed by pcarnah as a prototype module for estimating primary transmission and scatter contributions in X-ray imaging simulations. The method builds on the principles of in-scattering approximation but introduces a neural network-based approach to refine the scatter estimation using depth context. pcarnah/flashdrr, https://github.com/pcarnah/flashdrr, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
