name: Precomputed Lighting (Baking)
head: Baking Lighting, Baking the lighting, Direct Lighting Caching, Precomputed Light Transmissivity, Precomputed Transfer Function
body: Precomputed Lighting (Baking) is a technique to accelerate volumetric rendering by pre-computing the lighting term (Li) and storing it in the grid's voxels, allowing the renderer to skip evaluating Li at each raymarching step on the camera ray. It approximates volumetric shadows by precalculating illumination for each voxel center, enabling trilinear interpolation at render time. Unlike Voxel Cone Tracing which computes lighting dynamically during traversal, this method is view-independent but scene and light source dependent. It is primarily mentioned for reference and historical reasons rather than current practical utility. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing the participating medium (density field), light source positions, and light intensities. Output: A 3D voxel grid (or texture) storing the pre-computed direct lighting term (Li) for each voxel. Data Structures: Lighting Cache: A 3D texture or grid with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Resolution: The cache resolution can be lower than the actual voxel resolution because light is inherently blurry. Memory Layout: Data is typically stored in memory such that iterating over x first, then y, then z ensures sequential access, minimizing cache misses. Steps: 1. Pre-pass (Baking Pass): Iterate through every voxel in the grid. For each voxel center, calculate the direct lighting contribution (Li) from all light sources. This involves determining visibility (shadowing) from the voxel center to the light sources. Store the calculated Li value in the corresponding voxel of the lighting cache. 2. Main Pass (Rendering): Perform standard volumetric raymarching. For each sample point along the camera ray, retrieve the pre-computed Li value from the lighting cache via trilinear interpolation. Use this interpolated Li value in the rendering equation instead of evaluating the lighting term directly. Note: Some implementations may perform a few real light sample steps before sampling the cache to handle high-frequency lighting details, though the core definition relies on full pre-computation. Formulas: The rendering equation for a sample point x along a ray is modified to use the pre-computed term: Lo(x, \omegao) = \int{\Omega} fr(x, \omegai, \omegao) Li(x, \omegai) d\omegai Where Li(x, \omegai) is retrieved from the cache rather than computed via ray tracing or shadow maps. Parameters: Cache Resolution: Can be lower than the actual voxel resolution. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Re-baking: The technique requires re-baking whenever the lighting or the simulation changes. Performance: The baking pass still takes significant time, offsetting some rendering gains. Blurriness: Since light is blurry, lower resolution caches are acceptable, but excessive downsampling may lose shadow detail. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakelighting(grid, lights): # grid: 3D array of density values # lights: list of light source definitions (position, intensity) # lightingcache: 3D array to store Li for z in range(grid.resolutionz): for y in range(grid.resolutiony): for x in range(grid.resolutionx): voxelcenter = grid.getposition(x, y, z) # Calculate direct lighting for this voxel li = 0.0 for light in lights: # Check visibility from voxelcenter to light # This typically involves a secondary raymarch or shadow map lookup isvisible = checkshadow(voxelcenter, light.position) if isvisible: # Compute direct illumination contribution # Distance attenuation and cosine factor would be applied here contribution = computedirectlight(voxelcenter, light) li += contribution lightingcache.setvalue(x, y, z, li) def rendervolumetric(grid, lightingcache, camera): for each pixel in screen: ray = camera.generateray(pixel) color = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 while transmittance > 0.01 and ray.t < maxdistance: samplepos = ray.getposition() # Retrieve pre-computed lighting via trilinear interpolation li = lightingcache.interpolate(samplepos) # Get density at sample point density = grid.sample(samplepos) # Accumulate color # Note: Standard volume rendering equation uses Li here scattering = density stepsize li color += transmittance scattering transmittance = exp(-density stepsize) ray.t += stepsize setpixelcolor(pixel, color) Hybrid Preshading with Postclassification is a real-time volume rendering optimization that decouples classification from shading to balance visual fidelity and performance. Unlike pure preclassification/preshading which risks artifacts without opacity-weighted interpolation, or pure postclassification/postshading which is computationally expensive, this method performs classification after interpolation (postclassification) but shading before interpolation (preshading). It builds on Precomputed Lighting (Baking) by precomputing lighting contributions for a discrete set of surface normals, allowing the renderer to apply shading via texture lookup during the raymarching step while retaining the visual benefits of post-classification. Pre-computation is a technique used in volume rendering to accelerate the evaluation of light transport in participating media by calculating and storing intermediate radiance variables as voxel data. It solves the problem of redundant per-voxel integration during ray marching by pre-calculating terms such as direct radiance (L{ri}), diffusion radiance (L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d}), and their density derivatives, allowing the renderer to reuse these values instead of recomputing them for every camera ray. Unlike Hybrid Preshading with Postclassification, which may handle post-classification differently, this method explicitly pre-computes the diffusion components via a solver to enable efficient derivative-based shading. Time Complexity: The baking pass is O(N \cdot L) where N is the number of voxels and L is the number of light sources. The rendering pass is O(R) where R is the number of ray samples, with a constant-time texture lookup for lighting. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the lighting cache. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significantly speeds up the rendering pass by eliminating per-sample lighting calculations. Limitations: Requires re-baking for any change in lighting or geometry. The baking pass itself is expensive. View-independent, so it cannot handle dynamic view-dependent effects like specular highlights from the camera perspective if they depend on the view vector in the lighting calculation (though direct lighting is generally view-independent). When to use: Static scenes with static lighting where rendering performance is critical and baking time is acceptable. When not to use: Dynamic scenes with moving lights or geometry. Origin: Mentioned in various volume rendering tutorials and academic lectures as a historical optimization technique. It is often compared to deep shadow maps, which store density as a function of distance rather than just depth. Volume Rendering Based On 3D Voxel Grids, https://scratchapixel.com/lessons/3d-basic-rendering/volume-rendering-for-developers/volume-rendering-voxel-grids.html, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) PDF CS 519: Scientific Visualization - University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs519/fa2017/Lecture%2012%20-%20Volume%20Visualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volumetric Cloud Rendering - Jack Tollenaar, https://www.jacktollenaar.top/articles/clouds.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid Preshading with Postclassification
head: Hybrid Classification and Shading
body:
Hybrid Preshading with Postclassification is a real-time volume rendering optimization that decouples classification from shading to balance visual fidelity and performance. Unlike pure preclassification/preshading which risks artifacts without opacity-weighted interpolation, or pure postclassification/postshading which is computationally expensive, this method performs classification after interpolation (postclassification) but shading before interpolation (preshading). It builds on Precomputed Lighting (Baking) by precomputing lighting contributions for a discrete set of surface normals, allowing the renderer to apply shading via texture lookup during the raymarching step while retaining the visual benefits of post-classification. Inputs: Volume dataset (scalar field). Transfer function (mapping scalar values to color and opacity). Lighting model (e.g., Phong) with light positions and material properties. Number of quantized space directions (N{dir}), typically 8192. Outputs: Rendered image with shaded volume data. Data Structures: 1. Volume Grid: Standard 3D array of scalar values. 2. Gradient Grid: 3D array of 3D vectors (
abla V), precomputed from the volume grid. 3. Preshaded Reflectance Map (PRM): A 3D texture or lookup table indexed by: Quantized direction index (d \in [0, N{dir}-1]). Scalar value (or classification result). Stores the precomputed color contribution (reflectance) for that direction and value. 4. Direction Index Grid: 3D array storing an integer index (0 \dots N{dir}-1) for each voxel, corresponding to the quantized space direction of the precomputed gradient at that location. Steps: 1. Precompute Gradients: Calculate the volume gradient 
abla V(x,y,z) for every voxel in the volume grid using finite differences or central differences. 2. Quantize Directions: Define a set of N{dir} unit vectors representing space directions. A common choice is N{dir} = 8192. Map each precomputed gradient vector to the nearest index in this set. Store this index in the Direction Index Grid for each voxel. 3. Generate Preshaded Reflectance Map: For each quantized direction di in the set: a. Iterate through all possible scalar values (or classification bins) v. b. Compute the shading color C{shade} for direction di and value v using the chosen lighting model (e.g., Phong) and transfer function. c. Store C{shade} in the PRM at index (di, v). Note: This step is performed once before rendering. 4. Raymarching with Hybrid Shading: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. For each sampling step along the ray: a. Interpolation: Trilinearly interpolate the scalar value v and the Direction Index idx from the 8 surrounding voxels of the current sampling location. b. Classification: Use the interpolated scalar value v to determine the optical properties (opacity \alpha, base color C{base}) via the transfer function. This is the "postclassification" step. c. Shading Lookup: Use the interpolated Direction Index idx to look up the precomputed shading color C{shade} from the PRM, indexed by idx and v (or the classification result). d. Composite: Combine C{base} and C{shade} to get the final sample color C{sample}. e. Accumulate: Perform standard volume compositing (e.g., front-to-back) using C{sample} and the interpolated opacity \alpha. Formulas: Gradient: 
abla V = \left[  rac{\partial V}{\partial x},  rac{\partial V}{\partial y},  rac{\partial V}{\partial z} ight]. Direction Index: idx = \arg \min{j} \|  rac{
abla V}{\|
abla V\|} - \vec{d}j \| where \vec{d}j is the j-th quantized direction. Shading Lookup: C{shade} = 	ext{PRM}[idx, v]. Sample Color: C{sample} = 	ext{Combine}(C{base}(v), C{shade}). Parameters: N{dir} = 8192. Sampling rate \Delta s = 0.5 (distance between interpolations), allowing 2-4 samplings per cell. Image resolution: 512 	imes 512 pixels. Pixel subdivisions and precomputed rays: 16 	imes 16. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Zero: If 
abla V = 0, the direction index is undefined. Assign a default direction (e.g., (0,0,1)) or handle as a special case in the quantization step. Quantization Artifacts: Discrete directions may cause directional aliasing. The large number of directions (8192) mitigates this. Artifact Claim: Contrary to Mueller et al. [24] who reported artifacts with preshading/postclassification, this implementation shows no visible artifacts. Decouples classification/illumination from geometric filtering via a P-buffer, improving performance by 5-10%. Integrates shading directly into the projection pipeline using local gradients, combining geometric and contextual shading. Replaces per-voxel Phong calculations with a pre-computed color lookup table indexed by quantized normals. Time Complexity: Precomputation is O(N{voxels} + N{dir} \cdot N{values}). Rendering is O(N{pixels} \cdot N{steps}) with constant-time shading lookup. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for Volume Grid, Gradient Grid, Direction Index Grid, and PRM. PRM size is N{dir} 	imes N{values} 	imes 3 floats. Performance: High efficiency for interactive rendering. Benchmarks performed on MMX/SSE/3DNow! SIMD processors. Strengths: Avoids artifacts associated with pure preclassification/preshading (without opacity-weighted interpolation) and is faster than pure postclassification/postshading. Limitations: Requires precomputation of gradients and PRM. Directional aliasing possible if N{dir} is too small. This method is described in "A new object-order ray-casting algorithm". It addresses the trade-off between the speed of preclassification/preshading and the visual quality of postclassification/postshading. The authors argue against the artifact claims of Mueller et al. [24] for this specific implementation. A new object-order ray-casting algorithm, https://doi.org/10.5555/602099.602130, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Fast Two-Pass Shading
head: P-buffer shading, Two-pass shading
body: Fast Two-Pass Shading is a rendering optimization that avoids redundant per-fragment computations—specifically volume texture access, classification, and lighting—by sharing intermediate results between pixels covered by the same splat. It improves rendering performance by 5%–10% on typical hardware, distinguishing itself from sibling methods like Congradient Shading by explicitly decoupling the classification/illumination step from the geometric filtering step via a P-buffer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A slice of voxels to be rendered as splats. Output: A composited image of the slice. Intermediate Data: A P-buffer (render target) storing intermediate results for each splat. Data Structures: The P-buffer stores one entry per splat. The exact layout is not specified in the sources, but it must contain the results of: 1. Volume texture access. 2. Voxel classification (via lookup table). 3. Illumination computation. Numbered Steps: 1. First Pass (P-buffer Generation): Project each voxel of the current slice as a single-pixel point. For each point splat, compute: Volume texture access. Voxel classification. Illumination. Store these intermediate results in the P-buffer (render target). 2. Second Pass (Splat Rendering): Project the full splat geometry (covering multiple pixels, e.g., 2×2 up to 40×40 pixels depending on viewpoint). For each fragment covered by the splat: Perform per-fragment lighting. Apply EWA (Elliptical Weighted Average) filtering. Reuse the intermediate results from the P-buffer via lookup. 3. Final Composition: Composite all splats from the slice into the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fasttwopassshading(sliceofvoxels): # Initialize P-buffer render target pbuffer = createrendertarget() # Pass 1: Compute intermediate results for each splat for voxel in sliceofvoxels: # Project as single-pixel point pointsplat = projectaspoint(voxel) # Compute intermediate results texturesample = accessvolumetexture(voxel) classification = classifyvoxel(texturesample) illumination = computeillumination(classification, voxel) # Store in P-buffer storeinpbuffer(pbuffer, pointsplat, { 'texturesample': texturesample, 'classification': classification, 'illumination': illumination }) # Pass 2: Render full splats with filtering for voxel in sliceofvoxels: # Project full splat geometry fullsplat = projectfullsplat(voxel) # Render fragments for fragment in fullsplat.fragments: # Lookup intermediate results from P-buffer intermediate = lookuppbuffer(pbuffer, fragment.position) # Apply per-fragment lighting and EWA filtering # Note: The sources state "per-fragment lighting" is reused, # but also mention "EWA filtering". The exact combination # of lighting vs filtering in pass 2 is described as # "per-fragment lighting and EWA filtering". finalcolor = applyewafiltering(intermediate, fragment) # Composite compositeintoimage(finalcolor, fragment) # Final composition of all splats from each slice is handled by the # standard alpha blending/compositing of the fragments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Context Switches: The additional rendering pass increases the number of context switches, which can offset some performance gains. Splat Size: Splat sizes vary from 2×2 to as many as 40×40 pixels depending on the viewpoint. Performance Improvement: 5%–10%. Hardware: Measured on a 2.4 GHz P4 system with 2 GB memory and an ATI 9800 Pro video card (256 MB local memory) using DirectX 9.0 SDK. Strengths: Reduces redundant computation for pixels covered by the same splat. Limitations: Increased context switches due to the extra pass. When to Use: When rendering large splats (up to 40×40 pixels) where redundant texture access and classification are significant. When Not to Use: When splats are very small (e.g., 1×1 pixel) or when context switch overhead dominates. Origin: Proposed in "Hardware-Accelerated Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting" by Wei Chen et al.. History: Implemented with DirectX 9.0 SDK under Windows XP. Usage: Used in volume rendering for scientific visualization, specifically for EWA volume splatting. Hardwareaccelerated adaptive ewa volume splatting, https://core.ac.uk/works/16783031, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Hardware-Accelerated Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting, https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pubfiles/pub4/chenwei20041/chenwei20041.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Congradient Shading
head: Gradient-based Table-driven Shading
body: Congradient shading is a real-time volume rendering technique that defines the surface orientation of a voxel using a finite set of local gradients, enabling a fast, table-driven shading mechanism. It distinguishes itself by integrating shading directly into the projection pipeline as an integral part of the rendering process, rather than performing it in a separate post-processing stage. This approach combines the geometric accuracy of gradient shading with the contextual robustness of contextual shading. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (voxel grid), light source parameters (position, intensity), and a finite set of predefined local gradient directions. Output: A shaded 2D image (frame buffer). Data Structures: Congradient Value: A data structure holding concatenated values of the voxel's color and its local gradient index. The exact bit-packing is not specified, but it serves as a composite index. Look-Up Table (LUT): A 2D array mapping congradient values to shaded colors based on light source parameters. Steps: 1. Projection and Congradient Generation: For each pixel in the projection plane, a ray is cast through the volume. The system identifies the first opaque voxel along the ray (or the relevant voxel for shading). 2. Gradient Computation: The local gradient for the selected voxel is computed. Two implementations are described: Unidirectional Shading: The gradient is computed using only the depth values of horizontal neighbors. Bidirectional Shading: The gradient is computed using both horizontal and vertical neighbors. 3. Congradient Formation: The color of the voxel and the computed local gradient index are concatenated to form a single congradient value. 4. Pipelining: The production of the congradient value for one pixel is interleaved with the projection time of the next pixel. 5. Shading via LUT: The congradient value is used as an index into a look-up table. 6. Color Retrieval: The LUT translates the congradient value into a final shaded color based on the current light source parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelocalgradientbidirectional(voxel, neighbors): """ Computes local gradient using horizontal and vertical neighbors. neighbors: dict with keys 'left', 'right', 'up', 'down' containing depth values. """ # Gradient calculation logic is not explicitly detailed in sources, # but it relies on depth differences of neighbors. # Standard finite difference approximation for gradient vector. dx = neighbors['right'] - neighbors['left'] dy = neighbors['down'] - neighbors['up'] # Quantize gradient to a finite set of directions gradientindex = quantizegradient(dx, dy) return gradientindex def computelocalgradientunidirectional(voxel, neighbors): """ Computes local gradient using only horizontal neighbors. """ dx = neighbors['right'] - neighbors['left'] gradientindex = quantizegradient(dx, 0) return gradientindex def quantizegradient(dx, dy): """ Maps continuous gradient components to a finite set of indices. Implementation detail: Typically involves normalizing (dx, dy) and mapping to a predefined set of normal vectors (e.g., 8 or 16 directions). """ # Placeholder for specific quantization scheme not provided in sources return 0 # Not given in the sources. def congradientshading(volume, lightsource, framebuffer): """ Main shading loop. """ # Precompute LUT based on light source parameters lut = buildlut(volume, lightsource) for each pixel in framebuffer: # 1. Ray casting / Projection voxel = castrayandfindfirstopaque(volume, pixel) if voxel is None: continue # 2. Get neighbors for gradient computation neighbors = getvoxelneighbors(volume, voxel) # 3. Compute gradient (choose approach) # Using bidirectional as example gradientidx = computelocalgradientbidirectional(voxel, neighbors) # 4. Form congradient value (concatenate color and gradient) color = voxel.color congradientvalue = concatenate(color, gradientidx) # 5. Lookup shaded color shadedcolor = lut[congradientvalue] # 6. Write to frame buffer framebuffer[pixel] = shadedcolor def buildlut(volume, lightsource): """ Builds the look-up table mapping congradient values to shaded colors. """ lut = {} # Iterate over all possible congradient values (color + gradient index combinations) for color in volume.uniquecolors: for gradientidx in range(numgradientdirections): congradientvalue = concatenate(color, gradientidx) # Lighting model calculation (e.g., Phong) using lightsource # and the normal corresponding to gradientidx. shadedcolor = calculatelighting(color, gradientidx, lightsource) lut[congradientvalue] = shadedcolor return lut Parameters: Light Source Location: Can be arbitrarily changed, providing motion parallax. Gradient Set: A finite set of local gradients. The size is not specified, but the approach allows for hardware realization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Neighbor access for gradient computation must handle volume boundaries. Standard clamping or reflection is assumed. Precision: The method relies on quantization of gradients. The specific quantization error is not discussed, but the finite set size impacts shading quality. Computes gradients using only horizontal neighbors. Simpler hardware implementation, suitable for basic shading needs. Link Computes gradients using both horizontal and vertical neighbors. Slightly more complex but potentially more accurate surface orientation estimation. Link Time Complexity: The total time for an arbitrary projection is O(n^2 \log n), where n is the resolution dimension, allowing real-time arbitrary projection. The shading itself adds no additional time because the congradient calculation time for each pixel is much less than its projection time. Memory Complexity: Uses a single 2D array (e.g., a frame buffer) for the projection stage. The LUT size depends on the number of unique colors and gradient directions. Performance: Faster than alternative techniques that use separate post-processors. Strengths: Real-time performance, hardware-friendly, supports dynamic light sources for motion parallax. Limitations: Quality depends on the finite set of gradients; may lack smooth shading compared to continuous gradient methods. Congradient shading was developed for the Cube architecture, emphasizing real-time performance. It capitalizes on the advantages of both gradient shading and contextual shading. The technique was implemented and tested on various workstations including Sun-S, Sun-4, Silicon Graphics IRIS, and HP Turbo SRX, using resolutions such as 128^3, 256^3, and 512^3. name: Fake Phong Illumination via Normal Quantization
head: Color map Phong approximation, Normal Vector Quantization Lighting, Pre-computed Phong Lighting, Pre-computed Phong illumination
body: Fake Phong Illumination via Normal Quantization is a real-time approximation technique for volume rendering that replaces per-voxel Phong lighting calculations with a pre-computed color lookup table indexed by quantized surface normals. It solves the performance bottleneck of interactive volumetric rendering by moving the computational cost of the Phong equation to a pre-processing stage, allowing rendering to proceed via simple texture mapping. Unlike real-time Phong illumination which calculates lighting dynamically for every sample, this method sacrifices image fidelity to achieve speed, specifically introducing directional aliasing artifacts due to the discrete nature of the normal vector quantization. The method relies on the "infinite viewer and light" approximation, where the light direction (\mathbf{lightDir}) and view direction (\mathbf{viewDir}) are assumed constant for all points in the volume. Under this assumption, the Phong illumination equation depends only on the normal vector (\mathbf{normal}) at the point being lit (p). Input: Volumetric scalar field data; a static set of N pre-defined normal vector directions; Phong lighting parameters (ambient, diffuse, specular coefficients, shininess). Output: A rendered image where each voxel's color is determined by a lookup into a pre-computed color map based on the quantized normal index stored in the voxel data. 1. Normal Vector Table A static table containing N pre-defined normal vector directions. Size: N entries. Typical value is N=240. Content: Each entry is a 3D unit vector (x, y, z). Generation: In standard implementations, the unit sphere is tessellated by subdividing a regular dodecahedron into 60 triangles, and each triangle is further subdivided into 4 smaller triangles, yielding 240 almost equal-sized triangles. Each normal vector is quantized to the center of gravity of the respective triangle. 2. Voxel Data The volume data structure used for rendering. Layout: Instead of storing the full gradient vector or normal vector, each voxel stores a single integer index. Size: 1 integer per voxel. Content: The index points to an entry in the Normal Vector Table. 3. Color Map (Lookup Table) A pre-computed table mapping normal indices to colors. Size: N entries (typically 240). Constraint: Hardware typically supports color maps with 256 entries. Content: Each entry contains the RGB color result of the Phong equation evaluated for the corresponding normal vector in the Normal Vector Table. 1. Pre-processing: Gradient Calculation Calculate the gradient vector \nabla f for each voxel in the volume data. This gradient serves as the surface normal approximation. 2. Quantization Quantize each calculated gradient vector to one of the N pre-defined normal vector directions from the Normal Vector Table. For each gradient \mathbf{g}, find the index i in the Normal Vector Table such that the vector \mathbf{n}i minimizes the angular distance (or maximizes the dot product) with \mathbf{g}. Store the index i in the Voxel Data structure for that voxel, replacing the full vector. 3. Pre-rendering: Phong Evaluation Evaluate the Phong illumination equation for every normal vector \mathbf{n}i in the Normal Vector Table. The Phong equation factors are: position p, normal vector \mathbf{normal}, light direction \mathbf{lightDir}, and view direction \mathbf{viewDir}. Under the infinite viewer/light approximation, \mathbf{lightDir} and \mathbf{viewDir} are constant. Thus, the result depends only on \mathbf{n}i. Compute the color Ci for each \mathbf{n}i. 4. Color Map Construction Create the Color Map by storing the computed colors Ci at index i. 5. Rendering For each voxel during texture-mapping: Retrieve the stored index i from the Voxel Data. Look up the pre-computed Phong color Ci from the Color Map. Use this color for the voxel's contribution to the final image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fakephongnormalquantization(volumedata, phongparams): """ Implements Fake Phong Illumination via Normal Quantization. Args: volumedata: 3D array of scalar values. phongparams: Object containing ambient, diffuse, specular coefficients, shininess, lightDir, viewDir. Returns: renderedimage: 2D array of colors. """ # Step 1: Define Normal Vector Table # Standard implementation: 240 normals from subdivided dodecahedron N = 240 normaltable = generatedodecahedronnormals(N) # Step 2: Pre-processing - Calculate Gradients and Quantize # Create a new volume data structure storing indices instead of vectors quantizedvoxeldata = createemptyvolume(volumedata.shape, dtype=int) for each voxel (x, y, z) in volumedata: # Calculate gradient vector (normal approximation) gradient = calculategradient(volumedata, x, y, z) # Quantize gradient to nearest normal in table # Find index i that maximizes dot product with gradient bestindex = 0 maxdot = -infinity for i in range(N): dotproduct = dot(gradient, normaltable[i]) if dotproduct > maxdot: maxdot = dotproduct bestindex = i # Store index instead of full vector quantizedvoxeldata[x, y, z] = bestindex # Step 3: Pre-rendering - Evaluate Phong for all normals # Create Color Map colormap = createemptyarray(N, dtype=float) for i in range(N): normal = normaltable[i] # Evaluate Phong equation # Note: lightDir and viewDir are constant per infinite approximation color = evaluatephongequation( normal=normal, lightDir=phongparams.lightDir, viewDir=phongparams.viewDir, ambient=phongparams.ambient, diffuse=phongparams.diffuse, specular=phongparams.specular, shininess=phongparams.shininess) colormap[i] = color # Step 4: Rendering - Lookup colors # Assuming a ray-casting or texture-mapping renderer that iterates voxels renderedimage = rendervolumewithlookup( quantizedvoxeldata, colormap, phongparams) return renderedimage def generatedodecahedronnormals(N): """ Generates N normals by subdividing a regular dodecahedron. 1. Start with regular dodecahedron (60 faces). 2. Subdivide each face into 4 smaller triangles. 3. Total triangles = 60 4 = 240. 4. Return center of gravity for each triangle. """ if N != 240: raise ValueError("Standard implementation assumes N=240") # Implementation detail: Generate dodecahedron vertices # Generate 60 triangular faces # Subdivide each face into 4 # Compute centroid of each sub-triangle # Normalize centroids to unit sphere normals = [] #... (Specific geometric generation omitted as per source focus on method)... return normals def evaluatephongequation(normal, lightDir, viewDir, ambient, diffuse, specular, shininess): """ Standard Phong illumination model. """ # Normalize inputs if necessary n = normalize(normal) l = normalize(lightDir) v = normalize(viewDir) # Diffuse component diff = max(dot(n, l), 0.0) # Specular component r = reflect(-l, n) spec = pow(max(dot(r, v), 0.0), shininess) # Combine color = ambient + diffuse diff + specular spec return color N: The number of pre-defined normal vector directions. Typical value is 240. Quantizer Type: Static (dodecahedron subdivision) is standard; data-dependent (Simulated Annealing) is mentioned as future work. Directional Aliasing: The major problem is image quality. Because gradients are quantized to a discrete set of directions (usually 240), the resulting image exhibits strong "directional aliasing" artifacts. Hardware Limits: Hardware typically supports color maps with 256 entries. If N exceeds this, the method may require extension or reduction of N. Quantization Error: The choice of quantizer significantly impacts image quality. A poor quantizer will exacerbate aliasing. Time Complexity: Rendering time is reduced to O(1) per voxel lookup, as the expensive Phong calculation is moved to pre-processing. Pre-processing is O(V \cdot N) where V is the number of voxels and N is the number of normals. Memory Complexity: Requires storing an index per voxel (1 integer) plus the Color Map (N colors) and Normal Table (N vectors). Performance: Evaluating the Phong equation for 240 vectors can be done in real-time without problems. Using a color map for texture-mapping is supported by current graphics hardware. Strengths: Enables interactive frame rates for volumetric data that would otherwise be too slow for per-voxel Phong lighting. Limitations: Significant loss of image quality due to directional aliasing. The approximation is only valid under the "infinite viewer and light" assumption. When to use: When interactive performance is required and the lighting setup allows for the infinite viewer/light approximation. When not to use: When high-fidelity lighting is required, or when light/view directions vary significantly across the volume. Origin: The technique is described in the context of interactive volume rendering using 3D texture mapping. History: Current implementations use a static quantizer based on subdividing a regular dodecahedron. Future work involves data-dependent quantizers using Simulated Annealing to improve the distribution of normal vectors and allow for different numbers of vectors. Usage: Used in real-time volume rendering systems where Phong illumination is desired but per-voxel calculation is prohibitive. name: Pre-computation
body: Pre-computation is a technique used in volume rendering to accelerate the evaluation of light transport in participating media by calculating and storing intermediate radiance variables as voxel data. It solves the problem of redundant per-voxel integration during ray marching by pre-calculating terms such as direct radiance (L{ri}), diffusion radiance (L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d}), and their density derivatives, allowing the renderer to reuse these values instead of recomputing them for every camera ray. Unlike Hybrid Preshading with Postclassification, which may handle post-classification differently, this method explicitly pre-computes the diffusion components via a solver to enable efficient derivative-based shading. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial diffusion radiance estimates L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d} and their derivatives; scattering coefficient \kappa; absorption coefficient \kappaa; total extinction coefficient \kappat; source term S. Outputs: Pre-computed radiance fields L{ri}, L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d} and their density derivatives \partial\pi L{ri}, \partial\pi L{0d}, \partial\pi \vec{L}{1d} stored as voxels. Data Structures: The method stores fields as 3D grids (voxels). Each voxel at position v{xu} holds scalar or vector values for the radiance terms and their derivatives. The exact bit-packing or memory layout is not specified in the sources. Steps: The pre-computation is performed in parallel for all voxel positions v{xu} in the volume. 1. Compute Radiance and Derivatives (L{ri}): Calculate L{ri}(v{xu}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') and its density derivative \partial\pi L{ri}(v{xu}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') using the source equations. The source cites Equation 31 and 41 for this step. The text notes that L{ri} involves estimating the integral of solid angle over the unit sphere S^2 using the Monte Carlo Method. 2. Compute Intermediate Variable Q{0ri}: Calculate Q{0ri}(v{xu}) and \partial\pi Q{0ri}(v{xu}) using Equations 37 and 15. 3. Compute Intermediate Variable \vec{Q}{1ri}: Calculate \vec{Q}{1ri}(v{xu}) and \partial\pi \vec{Q}{1ri}(v{xu}) using Equations 38 and 16. 4. Compute Extinction Coefficient \kappa: Calculate \kappa(v{xu}) and \partial\pi \kappa(v{xu}) using Equations 35 and 12. 5. Compute Source Term S: Calculate S(v{xu}) and \partial\pi S(v{xu}) using Equations 36 and 14. 6. Solve Diffusion Radiance: Call DiffusionSolver to compute the final diffusion radiance L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d} and their derivatives \partial\pi L{0d}, \partial\pi \vec{L}{1d} using the pre-computed S, \kappa, \kappaa. The solver uses a Jacobi iterative method to solve the differential diffusion equation. 7. Return Results: Return the fields L{ri}, L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d} and their derivatives. L0d, L1d: Initial diffusion radiance estimates (scalar and vector) S: Source term field kappa: Extinction coefficient field kappaa: Absorption coefficient field kappat: Total extinction coefficient field """ # Numerical stability during the Jacobi iteration for diffusion radiance is critical. Boundaries: Boundary conditions for the diffusion solver are not specified in the provided text. It involves parallel iteration over all voxels and a global diffusion solver. The exact complexity is not given, but it is O(N) for the voxel loop where N is the number of voxels, plus the cost of the diffusion solver. Memory Complexity: Requires storing multiple fields (L{ri}, L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d} and their derivatives) for every voxel. The exact memory footprint is not given. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates redundant calculations during ray marching by reusing pre-computed voxel data. Enables efficient computation of radiance derivatives for density-based shading. Limitations: Requires significant memory to store the pre-computed fields. The diffusion solver may be computationally expensive if not optimized. When to Use: When rendering participating media with density-dependent shading effects where ray marching is performed frequently. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or the volume changes dynamically every frame without pre-computation updates. Origin: The method is described in "A Differential Diffusion Theory for Participating Media". History: The technique is part of a broader effort to apply differential diffusion theory to real-time volume rendering. name: Local Piecewise Integration for Light Propagation
head: Local Piecewise Integration
body: Local Piecewise Integration is a precomputation technique used in direct volume rendering to efficiently calculate high-resolution global shadows and light propagation from a distant light source through a participating medium. It solves the problem of expensive per-voxel absorption integration by approximating the opacity integral using short, reusable local segments, enabling interactive frame rates for large-scale volumes. Unlike object-order light propagation methods, it allows the light source to be positioned anywhere in the scene, including within the volume, and handles large scales via multi-resolution data management. Compared to simple blur-based approximations like Kniss et al. [KPH03], it provides nearly physically correct scattering effects. Inputs: Volumetric dataset with extinction/opacity field. Light source direction and intensity I0. Transfer Function (TF) mapping scalar values to opacity \alpha. Parameters: N: Number of samples per local segment (Not given in the sources). \Delta s: Step length for global integration, equal to the local piecewise segment length (Typically 8-16 voxels). I{bias}: Minimum lighting bias to prevent completely dark regions. R\Omega: Scattering sphere radius (Not given in the sources). SVR Resolution: Resolution of the Shadow Volume Representation storage (Not given in the sources). Outputs: Precomputed local piecewise transparency values T{lp}(sn) stored in the Shadow Volume Representation (SVR). Global light intensity I(s) for each voxel during rendering. Data Structures: Shadow Volume Representation (SVR): A 3D grid storing precomputed light information. The resolution can differ from the volume dataset to balance performance and quality. Local Piecewise Segments: For each voxel, a sequence of transparency values T{lp}(sn) corresponding to segments of length \Delta s extending towards the light source. Algorithm Steps: 1. Local Segment Opacity Calculation: For each voxel location s0 in the volume, cast a ray in the direction of the light source. Divide the ray into segments of length \Delta s. For the n-th segment starting at sn = n \Delta s: a. Sample N points ni along the segment [sn, s{n+1}] using the current Transfer Function to get point opacities \alpha(ni). b. Compute the segment opacity \alpha{lp}(sn) using the product of individual sample transparencies: \alpha{lp}(sn) = 1 - \prod{i=0}^{N} (1 - \alpha(ni)) c. Compute the segment transparency T{lp}(sn): T{lp}(sn) = 1 - \alpha{lp}(sn) (Note: The source defines T{lp}(sn) = e^{-\int{sn}^{sn+1} \tau(t) dt} and relates it to opacity via \alpha{lp} = 1 - T{lp}). d. Store T{lp}(sn) in the SVR for the voxel at sn. 2. Global Light Integration (Precomputation/Update): Using the precomputed local segments, calculate the global light intensity reaching each voxel. The intensity I(s) at position s is: I(s) = I0 \times \prod{n=0}^{k} T{lp}(sn) where k is the number of segments from the light source to s. This integration is updated at a lower frequency than the rendering frame rate. An bias term I{bias} may be applied to ensure no region is completely dark. 3. Rendering: During ray marching for image generation: a. For each sample along the view ray, perform one additional texture look-up in the SVR to retrieve the pre-computed light intensity/transparency. b. Composite the volume color using the retrieved lighting information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelocalpiecewisesegments(volumedata, lightdirection, deltas, numsamplespersegment): """ Precomputes local piecewise transparency segments for all voxels. Args: volumedata: 3D array of scalar values. lightdirection: Normalized vector pointing from volume to light. deltas: Length of each piecewise segment in voxels. numsamplespersegment: Number of samples N to take within each segment. Returns: svr: 3D array storing Tlp(sn) for each voxel and segment index. """ # Determine grid dimensions dims = volumedata.shape svr = np.zeros(dims) # For each voxel, compute the local segment transparency towards the light for x in range(dims[0]): for y in range(dims[1]): for z in range(dims[2]): # Current voxel position currentpos = np.array([x, y, z]) # Cast ray in light direction # We need to compute Tlp for segments starting at s0, s1,... # s0 is currentpos. sn = currentpos + n deltas lightdirection n = 0 while True: sn = currentpos + n deltas lightdirection # Check if segment start is within volume bounds if not iswithinbounds(sn, dims): break # Sample N points along the segment [sn, sn + deltas lightdirection] segmentopacities = [] for i in range(numsamplespersegment + 1): # i from 0 to N # Interpolate position within segment t = i / numsamplespersegment samplepos = sn + t deltas lightdirection # Get scalar value from volume val = interpolatevolume(volumedata, samplepos) # Get opacity from Transfer Function alphani = transferfunction(val) segmentopacities.append(alphani) # Compute segment transparency Tlp(sn) # alphalp = 1 - product(1 - alpha(ni)) # Tlp = 1 - alphalp = product(1 - alpha(ni)) producttransparency = 1.0 for alpha in segmentopacities: producttransparency = (1.0 - alpha) Tlp = producttransparency # Store in SVR # Note: SVR might have different resolution, but for simplicity assuming 1:1 mapping here svr[int(sn[0]), int(sn[1]), int(sn[2])] = Tlp n += 1 return svr def renderwithlocalpiecewise(volumedata, svr, lightintensity, viewraysamples): """ Renders volume using precomputed local piecewise segments. Args: volumedata: 3D array of scalar values. svr: Precomputed transparency segments. lightintensity: I0, intensity of the light source. viewraysamples: List of sample positions along the view ray. Returns: imagecolor: Rendered color for the ray. """ accumulatedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for samplepos in viewraysamples: # Retrieve precomputed light intensity/transparency from SVR # This requires mapping samplepos to SVR coordinates and segment index # For simplicity, assume we retrieve the global light intensity I(s) directly # or the relevant Tlp values to compute it. # In the source, only one additional texture look-up is performed. # Let's assume SVR stores the final global light intensity I(s) for simplicity # or we compute it from Tlp values. # If SVR stores Tlp, we need to accumulate them from light source to samplepos. # However, the source says "global light integration is updated... using piecewise segments". # And "only one additional texture look-up... to apply pre-computed light intensities". # This implies SVR might store the accumulated global light intensity I(s). # Let's assume SVR stores I(s) directly for the rendering step. Is = lookupsvrlightintensity(svr, samplepos) # Standard volume rendering compositing val = interpolatevolume(volumedata, samplepos) alpha = transferfunction(val) color = transferfunctioncolor(val) # Weighted contribution weight = alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor += weight color Is accumulatedalpha += weight if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break return accumulatedcolor A variant or related step where the multiple scattering source term q{ri}(x) for external directional light Ll is computed as q{ri}(x) = Ll \cdot \sigmas(x) \cdot T(x), where \sigmas is the scattering coefficient and T(x) is transmittance. This term is computed via raymarching and stored at the full resolution of the dataset extinction field. A propagation scheme using radial grids (topologically equivalent to rectilinear grids but cyclic in two angular dimensions) for local point lights. It allows approximate treatment of space as locally Euclidean and extends Principal-Ordinates Propagation (POP) to local light sources by using spherical grids aligned with the initial principal directions of the point source. VPLs are prefiltered based on importance and anisotropy. Time Complexity: Integration of light intensities without the local piecewise approximation is approximately 10 times slower. Performance: Global light integration updates in 284-552 ms (for 8 voxel segments) depending on SVR size; first order scattering incremental refinements take 62-233 ms. High frame rates (15-22 fps) are reached during rendering since only one additional texture look-up is performed per sample. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Shadow Volume Representation (SVR). The SVR size can be reduced for performance, but this may introduce artifacts. Accuracy: Root Mean Square (RMS) error of 0.19 for \Delta E (CIE 1976 Luv color space), with 6% of pixels having \Delta E above 6. Strengths: Nearly physically correct scattering effects compared to blur-based methods; light source can be positioned anywhere, even within the volume; handles large scale volumes via multi-resolution data management. Limitations: Block artifacts (jagged edges) appear on sharp edges if SVR resolution is too low; banding effects appear due to interpolation between shadowed and un-shadowed regions when SVR size is reduced. When to use: When interactive global shadowing and light propagation in large volumetric datasets is required, and the light source is distant or directional. When not to use: When local point lights are the primary source (requires radial grids variant) or when multiple scattering is the dominant effect (requires diffusion-based methods). Local Piecewise Integration was introduced in the paper "Interactive Global Light Propagation in Direct Volume Rendering using Local Piecewise Integration". It builds on the concept of piecewise integration for opacity [Max95] and opacity correction [PH89]. The method was developed to address the computational cost of global light propagation in volume rendering, offering an interactive alternative to object-order methods and more accurate results than simple blur approximations. name: Style Transfer Function (1D)
head: 1D Style Transfer Function, 1D Transfer Function with Cubic Spline Interpolation, Lit Sphere Maps, STF, Style Transfer Function lookup, Style-based Volume Rendering
body: A Style Transfer Function (STF) is a data-driven illumination technique that extends the traditional 1D transfer function by incorporating surface normal direction into the domain, allowing color and shading style to be defined as a function of both scalar data value and eye-space normal direction. Unlike standard transfer functions that map data values directly to RGBA tuples, STFs use a lit sphere map to provide flexible, non-photorealistic shading based on data values and normals. This method avoids the prohibitively high storage requirements of a single 3D/4D texture by storing discrete styles separately and using references in the lookup table. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Continuous volumetric scalar field f(P), where P is the sample point. Output: Final color (r, g, b) and directional opacity \alphad for the sample. Data Structures: The implementation relies on three textures: 1. Transfer Function Texture (tft): A 1D texture mapping data values to style indices and uniform opacity. Layout: Width corresponds to the data value range (typically 256 units). Fields: Stores a pair (i, \alphau) for each data value. i: Index value ranging from 0 to N-1, where N is the number of style nodes specified in the transfer function. Fractional values indicate interpolation between styles. \alphau: Uniform opacity value in range [0, 1], controlling overall opacity independent of normal direction. 2. Index Function Texture (ift): A 1D texture mapping style indices to distinct style identifiers. Layout: Width equals N (number of style nodes). Fields: Stores integer style indices j ranging from 0 to M-1, where M is the number of distinct styles. Note: This mapping is discrete; no interpolation is performed. If no style is used multiple times, this texture can be skipped. 3. Style Function Texture (sft): Contains the discrete set of M distinct styles. Layout: Each style is a 2D image (lit sphere map). Stored as a 2D texture (preferred), 3D texture (with mipmapping disabled), or texture array. Fields: Stores (r, g, b, \alphad) tuples indexed by eye-space normal direction. \alphad: Directional opacity, varying based on normal direction. Algorithm Steps: At each sample point P in the volume: 1. Compute Scalar and Normal: Compute scalar value s = f(P). Compute gradient g = \nabla f(P). Compute normalized eye-space normal n = g / |g|. Let n = (nx, ny, nz). 2. Lookup Uniform Properties: Retrieve index i and uniform opacity \alphau from tft using sample value s: (i, \alphau) = \text{tft}(s) 3. Compute Interpolation Weights: Compute integer indices for the index function texture: i0 = \lfloor i \rfloor i1 = i0 + 1 Compute interpolation weight: w = i - i0 4. Retrieve Style Indices: Perform two lookups into ift to get style indices j0 and j1: j0 = \text{ift}(i0) j1 = \text{ift}(i1) Pitfall: If no style is used multiple times in the transfer function, j0 = j1 and these lookups can be skipped. 5. Interpolate Style and Opacity: Perform two lookups into sft using the eye-space normal components (nx, ny) and the style indices j0, j1. Linearly interpolate between the results: (r, g, b, \alphad) = \text{sft}(nx, ny, j0) \cdot (1 - w) + \text{sft}(nx, ny, j1) \cdot w 6. Final Composition: The final sample color is (r, g, b). The final opacity is the product of uniform and directional opacity: \alpha = \alphau \cdot \alphad. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def styletransferfunctionlookup(s, nx, ny, tft, ift, sft): """ s: scalar data value (float) nx, ny: eye-space normal components (float) tft: 1D texture storing (index, alphau) ift: 1D texture storing style index j sft: 3D/2D texture storing (r, g, b, alphad) indexed by (nx, ny, styleindex) """ # Step 2: Lookup uniform properties i, alphau = tft.sample1d(s) # Step 3: Compute weights i0 = floor(i) i1 = i0 + 1 w = i - i0 # Step 4: Retrieve style indices # Note: ift lookup is discrete, no interpolation j0 = ift.sample1d(i0) j1 = ift.sample1d(i1) # Step 5: Interpolate style # sft lookup uses nx, ny and style index style0 = sft.sample2dstyle(nx, ny, j0) style1 = sft.sample2dstyle(nx, ny, j1) # Linear interpolation of style tuples r = style0.r (1 - w) + style1.r w g = style0.g (1 - w) + style1.g w b = style0.b (1 - w) + style1.b w alphad = style0.a (1 - w) + style1.a w # Step 6: Final opacity alpha = alphau alphad return (r, g, b, alpha) Parameters: T: User-defined thickness value for contour control. Used in curvature threshold calculations. Typical value not specified. Texture Width: The resulting 1D transfer function texture typically has a fixed width of 256. \alphau: Uniform opacity range [0, 1]. N: Number of styles specified in the style transfer function. Index values in tft range from 0 to N-1. M: Number of distinct styles in the style transfer function. Style indices in sft range from 0 to M-1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory: A naive implementation using a single 3D texture for all data values and normal directions is impractical due to high storage requirements. Interpolation Constraint: Interpolation between styles must be uniform for all normal directions (transitions only between whole styles) unless intermediate styles are added. Gradient Magnitude: When gradient magnitude approaches zero, the normal direction becomes unreliable. This affects the validity of the lit sphere map lookup. Mip-mapping for style functions is a technique to avoid aliasing in style lookups while preventing mixing between styles at higher mip-map levels. It builds on Style Transfer Function (1D) by adding anti-aliasing capabilities to the discrete style selection process. Unlike standard hardware mip-mapping which may blend distinct styles, this method ensures temporal coherence and spatial anti-aliasing without corrupting style boundaries. An extension of the style transfer function to two-dimensional domains (e.g., data value and gradient magnitude, or data value and object identifier) using bilinear interpolation across four styles. Definition: Extends the 1D concept to 2D textures for both the transfer function and index function. Step: 1. Compute indices: ix0 = \lfloor ix \rfloor, iy0 = \lfloor iy \rfloor, ix1 = ix0 + 1, iy1 = iy0 + 1. 2. Compute weights: wx = ix - ix0, wy = iy - iy0. 3. Perform four lookups into ift: j{00} = \text{ift}(ix0, iy0), j{10} = \text{ift}(ix1, iy0), j{01} = \text{ift}(ix0, iy1), j{11} = \text{ift}(ix1, iy1). 4. Perform four lookups into sft using (nx, ny) and j{00}, j{10}, j{01}, j{11}. 5. Compute final color via bilinear interpolation: (r,g,b,\alphad) = (\text{sft}(nx,ny,j{00}) \cdot (1-wx) + \text{sft}(nx,ny,j{10}) \cdot wx) \cdot (1-wy) + (\text{sft}(nx,ny,j{01}) \cdot (1-wx) + \text{sft}(nx,ny,j{11}) \cdot wx) \cdot wy Layout: Transfer function texture: 2D texture storing two indices ix and iy. ix increases along horizontal axis, iy along vertical. Index function texture: 2D texture. Width = max horizontal style nodes, Height = max vertical nodes. Time Complexity: The lookup requires a maximum of four additional texture fetches compared to a regular 1D transfer function (two for ift, two for sft). Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to a full 3D/4D lookup table by storing discrete styles separately. Measured Performance: On GeForce 8 series hardware, the additional fetches incur overhead, but the cost of evaluating the illumination model is saved. The index function texture benefits heavily from texture caching. Strengths: Allows flexible combination of different shading styles (e.g., unshaded, tone shading, cartoon, metallic) in a single rendering. Enables inconsistent lighting of different structures to accentuate features. Lit sphere maps provide an intuitive preview image for the style. Limitations: Requires Shader Model 3.0 GPUs for conditional loops and dynamic branching. Interpolation is limited to whole styles unless intermediate styles are added. When to use: When non-photorealistic, stylized volume rendering is desired, and the user wants to switch or blend between distinct artistic styles based on data values. When not to use: When photorealistic, physically-based lighting is required, or when memory bandwidth is extremely constrained and the overhead of multiple texture fetches is prohibitive. Origin: Introduced by Stefan Bruckner and Michael E. Gröller in the paper "Style Transfer Functions for Illustrative Volume Rendering". History: The method was developed to address the difficulty of integrating multiple non-photorealistic rendering approaches into a single framework. It extends the concept of data-dependent lighting by allowing the user to specify styles captured from existing artwork directly in the transfer function. Usage: Implemented in C++ and OpenGL/GLSL for GPU-based ray casting. Used in illustrative volume rendering to generate high-quality volumetric illustrations with controlled contours and transparency. name: Mip-Mapping for Style Functions
head: Mip-mapped Style Transfer Function
body: Mip-mapping for style functions is a technique to avoid aliasing in style lookups while preventing mixing between styles at higher mip-map levels. It builds on Style Transfer Function (1D) by adding anti-aliasing capabilities to the discrete style selection process. Unlike standard hardware mip-mapping, it manually computes mip-map levels to avoid undefined derivatives in raycasting loops and prevents style boundary corruption. Input: Raycasting sample points, data values, surface normals, style transfer function (SFT) texture, index function texture. Output: Mip-map level index for the SFT lookup. Style Transfer Function (SFT): Can be stored as a 3D texture, a texture array, or a 2D texture. 3D Texture: Styles stored as slices. Texture Array: Collection of 2D images in layers (e.g., EXTtexturearray). 2D Texture: Styles arranged in a single 2D texture. 1. Determine Base Mip-map Level: Manually compute the projected voxel size at each sample point. Calculate the screen-space derivative of the texture coordinates. Since raycasting involves loops/conditionals, hardware derivatives are undefined. Compute the size of the projected voxel in texture space. Determine the base mip-map level L based on the ratio of the projected voxel size to the texture resolution. 2. Bias Mip-map Level: Calculate curvature and gradient magnitude from the data and normals. Apply a bias function B to the base level L: L{final} = L + B(\text{curvature}, \|\nabla f\|) The bias accounts for areas of high curvature where gradient direction varies quickly, which can lead to artifacts. Handle zero-magnitude gradient vectors, which are unreliable for normal prediction. 3. Lookup: Use L{final} to select the appropriate mip-map level for the SFT lookup. Perform the texture fetch using the biased level. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemiplevel(datavalue, normal, voxelsize, textureresolution): # 1. Manual projection size calculation projectedsize = voxelsize textureresolution # 2. Base level determination maxlevel = int(log2(textureresolution)) baselevel = clamp(log2(projectedsize / textureresolution), 0, maxlevel) # 3. Bias calculation # Compute gradient magnitude and curvature from normals/data gradientmagnitude = length(normal) curvature = divergence(normal) # Sources do not specify the exact bias formula safegradient = max(gradientmagnitude, 1e-6) bias = curvature / safegradient finallevel = clamp(baselevel + bias, 0, maxlevel) return finallevel 3D Texture Mixing: If the SFT is a 3D texture, standard mipmapping causes undesired mixing between styles at higher levels. Solution: Disable mipmapping for 3D SFT or use texture arrays/2D textures. Undefined Derivatives: Standard hardware mip-map level determination using screen-space derivatives is undefined in conditionals or loops (e.g., raycasting). High Curvature: High curvature areas cause rapid gradient direction variation, leading to artifacts. Zero Gradient: Zero-magnitude gradient vectors are unreliable for normal prediction. Mipmapped Smooth Transitions is a technique that applies mipmapping to style transfer functions to ensure temporal coherence and anti-aliasing during interactive volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard mipmapping by specifically targeting the visual artifacts caused by rapid changes in style parameters, allowing for smooth interpolation between different visual representations (such as DVR and MIP) without the mixing of distinct styles at higher mip levels[782-mip-mapping-for-style-functions.md]. Performance: Requires a maximum of four additional texture fetches (two for index function, two for style function) compared to a regular 1D transfer function. Caching: The index function texture is small and does not require filtering, benefiting heavily from texture caching. Hardware: On GeForce 8 series, the index function can be implemented as a buffer texture using EXTtexturebufferobject for additional performance gains. Measured Performance: In tests with a 256 \times 256 \times 230 volume and 512 \times 512 viewport, style transfer functions achieved comparable or slightly lower frame rates than regular transfer functions (e.g., 11.7 fps vs 11.9 fps for Figure 7(a)). Originated in the context of illustrative volume rendering to handle discrete style mappings efficiently. The technique was developed to address the limitations of standard hardware mip-mapping when applied to multi-style textures, ensuring that style boundaries remain sharp while providing anti-aliasing benefits. It is used in real-time volume rendering applications, particularly for medical imaging and scientific visualization. name: Mipmapped Smooth Transitions
head: Smooth mipmapping transitions, Mipmapped style transitions
body: Mipmapped Smooth Transitions is a technique that applies mipmapping to style transfer functions to ensure temporal coherence and anti-aliasing during interactive volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard mipmapping by specifically targeting the visual artifacts caused by rapid changes in style parameters, allowing for smooth interpolation between different visual representations (such as DVR and MIP) without the mixing of distinct styles at higher mip levels [782-mip-mapping-for-style-functions.md]. The method integrates mipmapping into the lookup of style functions (such as opacity or color transfer functions) to handle high-frequency variations in input parameters or view direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data, style function parameters (e.g., user interaction state), current mip level index. Output: Smoothed style function value (opacity/color) for the current ray step. Data Structures: Mipmap chain for style functions: A set of precomputed or on-the-fly generated style function samples at decreasing resolutions. Each level i contains N/2^i samples. Standard 1D texture or array structure for storing style values. Steps: 1. Determine Mip Level: Calculate the appropriate mip level based on the rate of change of the style parameter or view direction. If the derivative of the style parameter with respect to screen space or time exceeds a threshold, select a higher mip level (lower resolution) to average out high-frequency noise. 2. Sample Mipmap: Retrieve the style function value from the selected mip level. This involves interpolating between the samples available at that resolution. 3. Apply Style Function: Use the sampled value to determine the final opacity or color contribution for the current voxel/ray step. Formula: Let S(t) be the style function value at parameter t. When using mipmapping, the effective style value S{eff}(t) is derived from the mipmapped lookup: S{eff}(t) = \text{MipmapLookup}(t, \text{mip\level}) where \text{mip\level} is determined by the local frequency of change in t. Parameters: Mip level selection threshold: Not given in the sources. Number of mip levels: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Low mip levels may lose fine detail in the style function. Boundaries: Ensure mip levels are precomputed or generated correctly to avoid artifacts at boundaries. Degenerate Input: If the style parameter does not change, the lowest mip level (highest resolution) should be used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getmipmappedstyle(styleparam, viewdirection, miplevels): # Calculate the rate of change of the style parameter # This is a placeholder for the specific derivative calculation # based on the rendering context (e.g., screen-space derivative) rateofchange = calculaterateofchange(styleparam, viewdirection) # Determine the mip level based on the rate of change # Higher rate of change -> higher mip level (lower resolution) miplevel = determinemiplevel(rateofchange, miplevels) # Sample the style function from the selected mip level # This involves interpolating between samples at the chosen resolution stylevalue = samplemiplevel(styleparam, miplevel, miplevels) return stylevalue A visual representation technique that transitions between Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) and Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) to reveal inner details during interaction. It uses a parameter C changing from -1 to 1, where -1 corresponds to DVR, 0 to Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA), and 1 to MIP. The style function S(t) is mapped to this domain using the formula S(t) = \frac{C(t) + 1}{2}. This differs from standard DVR/MIP by interpolating between them based on user interaction, allowing dynamic revelation of inner details. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of mip levels and the cost of determining the mip level. Precomputed mipmaps reduce runtime cost. Memory Complexity: Additional memory required for storing mipmaps of the style function. Measured Performance: In a test with a 1024^3 trabecular bone volume, using smooth mipmapping achieved 2040 Hz, compared to 60 fps without it. Strengths: Provides temporal coherence and anti-aliasing, improving visual quality during interaction. Limitations: Requires additional memory for mipmaps and computation for mip level selection. When to Use: Interactive volume rendering where smooth transitions between styles are needed. When Not to Use: Static rendering or when high-frequency detail in the style function is critical and cannot be averaged out. The concept of smooth transitions based on mipmapping for temporal coherence and anti-aliasing was introduced in the context of real-time volume rendering. The specific application to DVR-MIP interpolation was proposed by Bruckner and Gröller [BG09] and further detailed in research on dynamic focus+context for volume rendering. name: Multi-dimensional Style Transfer Function (2D)
head: 2D Style Transfer Function, 2D Transfer Function
body: This method extends the Style Transfer Function (1D) approach to map two input attributes, such as data value and gradient magnitude, to visual styles using a two-dimensional domain. It allows for finer control and more sophisticated visualization by leveraging the joint distribution of attributes, distinguishing it from the single-attribute mapping of its parent. Unlike standard 2D transfer functions that map directly to color/opacity, this method interpolates between discrete styles defined in a style function texture. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two normalized input attributes (u, v) (e.g., data value and gradient magnitude), and the eye-space normal components (nx, ny). Outputs: Final color (r, g, b) and opacity \alphad. Data Structures: 1. Transfer Function Texture (tfTex): A 2D texture storing two indices (ix, iy) instead of a single index i. ix increases along the horizontal axis. iy increases along the vertical axis. Layout: Each texel contains the pair (ix, iy) corresponding to the input coordinates (u, v). 2. Index Function Texture (ift): A 2D texture mapping style indices. Width: Maximum number of horizontal style nodes in the 2D transfer function. Height: Maximum number of vertical style nodes. Layout: Each texel stores a single integer style index j. 3. Style Function Texture (sft): A 3D texture (or 2D texture with index dimension) storing the visual styles. Dimensions: (nx, ny, j), where nx, ny are normal components and j is the style index. Layout: Each texel stores a color (r, g, b) and opacity \alphad. Steps: 1. Map Inputs to Indices: Convert the input attributes (u, v) into continuous texture coordinates (ix, iy) for the transfer function texture. The specific mapping depends on the domain of the attributes (e.g., normalized to [0, 1]). 2. Compute Grid Indices: Calculate the integer grid coordinates for bilinear interpolation: i{x0} = \lfloor ix \rfloor, \quad i{y0} = \lfloor iy \rfloor i{x1} = i{x0} + 1, \quad i{y1} = i{y0} + 1 3. Compute Interpolation Weights: wx = ix - i{x0} wy = iy - i{y0} 4. Lookup Style Indices: Perform four lookups into the index function texture ift to retrieve the style indices at the corners of the grid cell: j{00} = \text{ift}(i{x0}, i{y0}) j{10} = \text{ift}(i{x1}, i{y0}) j{01} = \text{ift}(i{x0}, i{y1}) j{11} = \text{ift}(i{x1}, i{y1}) 5. Lookup Styles: Perform four lookups into the style function texture sft using the eye-space normal components (nx, ny) and the retrieved style indices: C{00} = \text{sft}(nx, ny, j{00}) C{10} = \text{sft}(nx, ny, j{10}) C{01} = \text{sft}(nx, ny, j{01}) C{11} = \text{sft}(nx, ny, j{11}) Where each C is a vector (r, g, b, \alphad). 6. Bilinear Interpolation: Compute the final color and opacity by bilinearly interpolating the four style vectors: C{final} = \left( C{00} \cdot (1 - wx) + C{10} \cdot wx \right) \cdot (1 - wy) + \left( C{01} \cdot (1 - wx) + C{11} \cdot wx \right) \cdot wy Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def styletransfer2d(u, v, nx, ny, tfTex, ift, sft): # 1. Map input attributes to transfer function texture coordinates # Note: The exact mapping from (u, v) to (ix, iy) depends on the # specific attribute domains and normalization. # Assuming u, v are already normalized to [0, 1] relative to the # transfer function texture dimensions. ix = u tfTex.width iy = v tfTex.height # 2. Compute grid indices ix0 = floor(ix) iy0 = floor(iy) ix1 = ix0 + 1 iy1 = iy0 + 1 # 3. Compute interpolation weights wx = ix - ix0 wy = iy - iy0 # 4. Lookup style indices from index function texture j00 = ift[ix0, iy0] j10 = ift[ix1, iy0] j01 = ift[ix0, iy1] j11 = ift[ix1, iy1] # 5. Lookup styles from style function texture c00 = sft[nx, ny, j00] c10 = sft[nx, ny, j10] c01 = sft[nx, ny, j01] c11 = sft[nx, ny, j11] # 6. Bilinear interpolation # Interpolate along x-axis cx0 = c00 (1 - wx) + c10 wx cx1 = c01 (1 - wx) + c11 wx # Interpolate along y-axis cfinal = cx0 (1 - wy) + cx1 wy return cfinal Parameters: Input Attributes: Common choices are data value and gradient magnitude. Other attributes include object identifier, distance, saliency, or importance. Axis Mapping: Horizontal axis typically maps to data values; vertical axis typically maps to gradient magnitudes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If ix or iy exceed the texture bounds, clamping or wrapping must be applied. The sources do not specify the default behavior. Opacity Correction: When using fewer slices or changing the sampling rate s from a reference rate s0, the opacity must be scaled to maintain overall intensity. The formula is provided in but not explicitly detailed in the notes for the 2D case. [G: Typically, opacity is scaled by s/s0 or similar factor depending on the integration method]. Normal Components: The method requires eye-space normal components (nx, ny). These must be computed from the volume gradient and transformed to eye space before lookup. Optimizes the lookup of the style function texture by using mipmaps to reduce aliasing and improve performance. Mip-Mapping for Style Functions Details the efficient implementation of the lookup process on the GPU, leveraging texture units and fragment shaders. GPU Implementation of Style Transfer Function Lookup Time Complexity: The lookup involves a constant number of texture accesses (4 for ift, 4 for sft) and simple arithmetic operations. It is independent of the number of style nodes. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 2D transfer function texture, the 2D index function texture, and the 3D style function texture. The size of the index function texture is determined by the number of style nodes. Performance: Measured on an AMD Athlon 64 X2 Dual 4600+ CPU and NVidia GeForce 7900 GTX GPU, style transfer functions showed comparable or slightly better performance than regular transfer functions (e.g., 11.9 fps vs 11.7 fps in one test case). Strengths: Allows for intuitive direct manipulation via brushes to paint into the 2D transfer function texture. Provides finer control over feature classification by incorporating gradient magnitude. Limitations: Requires computation of gradients and normals. The complexity of the transfer function design increases with the number of dimensions. The method was introduced by Stefan Bruckner and Michael E. Gröller in their paper "Style Transfer Functions for Illustrative Volume Rendering". It extends the 1D style transfer function approach to multi-dimensional domains, specifically 2D, to handle attributes like data value and gradient magnitude. The concept of using 2D transfer functions for data value and gradient magnitude was previously explored by Kindlmann and Durkin. The method is used in illustrative volume rendering to achieve artistic styles while maintaining data fidelity.
