name: Transfer Function Reconstruction Loss
head: L1 + Smoothing Prior Loss, TF Reconstruction with Smoothing Prior, Transfer Function Optimization
body: Transfer Function Reconstruction Loss optimizes a parameterized Transfer Function (TF) to minimize the visual difference between rendered images and a set of reference images generated from a target TF. It solves the problem of automatically deriving a TF for a volume dataset when a ground-truth TF is unavailable, by treating the TF parameters as differentiable variables. It sets itself apart from AI-Based Transfer Function Peak Prediction by using direct gradient-based optimization rather than learned heuristics, and from Voxel-based Transfer Function Optimization by optimizing a global parametric function rather than per-voxel values. Inputs: Volume dataset V. Reference images \mathbf{y}: Rendered from V using a target TF from N camera positions. Initial TF T: A parameterized function with R entries, initialized with random Gaussian noise. Hyperparameters: Learning rate \eta, number of epochs E, smoothing weight \lambda, TF resolution R. Outputs: Optimized TF T^ that minimizes the total loss. Data Structures: Transfer Function T: A tensor of shape R \times 4. It contains 4 channels (RGB and absorption) for each of the R density bins. Rendered Image \mathbf{x}: A tensor of shape N \times W \times H \times C (where C=3 for RGB, or C=4 if alpha is included in loss). Reference Image \mathbf{y}: A tensor of shape N \times W \times H \times C. Formulas: The total loss is a weighted sum of an image-space L1 loss and a TF smoothing prior: L{\text{total}} = L1(\mathbf{x}) + \lambda L{\text{prior}}(T) The L1 loss measures the pixel-wise difference between rendered images \mathbf{x} and reference images \mathbf{y}: L1(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{NWH} \sum{i=1}^{N} \sum{x=1}^{W} \sum{y=1}^{H} |\mathbf{x}{i,x,y} - \mathbf{y}{i,x,y}| Where: N is the number of camera positions (views). W, H are the image width and height. \mathbf{x}{i,x,y} and \mathbf{y}{i,x,y} are the pixel values at view i and coordinates (x,y). The smoothing prior L{\text{prior}}(T) penalizes high-frequency variations in the TF to prevent jagged artifacts: L{\text{prior}}(T) = \frac{1}{4(R-1)} \sum{c=1}^{4} \sum{r=1}^{R-1} (T{c,r+1} - T{c,r})^2 Where: R is the number of entries in the TF. c indexes the 4 channels (Red, Green, Blue, Absorption). r indexes the density bin index. Parameters: Learning Rate (\eta): 0.8 for the Adam optimizer. Epochs (E): 200. Smoothing Weight (\lambda): Typically 0.4. Values too small cause high-frequency artifacts and color shifts; values too large smooth out small details. TF Resolution (R): 64 is chosen as the best compromise between reconstruction performance and computation time. Camera Setup: N=8 views, uniformly distributed around the volume, pointing toward the center. Resolution W=H=512. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the TF T with random Gaussian noise of shape R \times 4. 2. Reference Rendering: Render reference images \mathbf{y} from the volume V using the target TF from N camera positions. 3. Optimization Loop (for e = 1 to E): a. Forward Pass: For each of the N camera positions, render the current image \mathbf{x} using the current TF T and volume V. b. Loss Calculation: Compute L1(\mathbf{x}) and L{\text{prior}}(T). Compute L{\text{total}}. c. Backward Pass: Compute gradients \nablaT L{\text{total}} using Automatic Differentiation (AD). d. Update: Update T using the Adam optimizer with learning rate \eta. 4. Output: Return the optimized TF T. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def rendervolume(volume, tf, cameraparams): """ Differentiable volume rendering function. volume: 3D tensor (D, H, W) or (D, H, W, C) tf: 2D tensor (R, 4) representing the transfer function cameraparams: parameters defining the ray casting for the current view Returns: rendered image tensor (H, W, 3) """ # Implementation depends on the specific differentiable renderer used. # This function must support backpropagation through the TF parameters. pass def computesmoothingprior(tf): """ Computes the L2 norm of the first derivative of the TF. tf: Tensor of shape (R, 4) Returns: scalar loss value """ # Calculate differences between adjacent bins for all channels # tf[:, 1:] - tf[:,:-1] computes the difference for bins r+1 and r diffs = tf[:, 1:] - tf[:,:-1] # Square the differences squareddiffs = diffs 2 # Sum over all channels (4) and all bin transitions (R-1) sumdiffs = torch.sum(squareddiffs) # Normalize by 4 (R - 1) R = tf.shape[0] normalization = 4.0 (R - 1) return sumdiffs / normalization def optimizetf(volume, referenceimages, cameraparamslist, R=64, lambdaprior=0.4, lr=0.8, epochs=200, W=512, H=512, N=8): """ Optimizes the Transfer Function to match reference images. Args: volume: The input volume dataset. referenceimages: Tensor of shape (N, H, W, 3) containing reference views. cameraparamslist: List of camera parameters for N views. R: Number of TF entries. lambdaprior: Weight for the smoothing prior. lr: Learning rate for Adam. epochs: Number of optimization steps. W, H: Image resolution. N: Number of views. Returns: Optimized TF tensor of shape (R, 4). """ # Initialize TF with random Gaussian noise tf = torch.randn(R, 4, requiresgrad=True) # Setup optimizer optimizer = optim.Adam([tf], lr=lr) # Pre-compute reference image mean for normalization if needed, # though L1 is scale-invariant in this context. for epoch in range(epochs): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 totall1 = 0.0 # Render from all N views renderedimages = [] for i in range(N): # Render current view using current TF img = rendervolume(volume, tf, cameraparamslist[i]) renderedimages.append(img) renderedimages = torch.stack(renderedimages) # Shape (N, H, W, 3) # Compute L1 Loss # referenceimages shape: (N, H, W, 3) # renderedimages shape: (N, H, W, 3) l1perview = torch.abs(renderedimages - referenceimages) l1perview = torch.mean(l1perview) # Mean over H, W, C totall1 = torch.mean(l1perview) # Mean over N views # Compute Smoothing Prior lprior = computesmoothingprior(tf) # Total Loss totalloss = totall1 + lambdaprior lprior # Backpropagation totalloss.backward() # Optimization step optimizer.step() # Optional: Print progress if (epoch + 1) % 50 == 0: print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}, L1: {totall1.item():.4f}, Prior: {lprior.item():.4f}, Total: {totalloss.item():.4f}") return tf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Forward AD Memory Overhead: Using forward-mode Automatic Differentiation causes large memory overhead because derivatives of many parameters overflow registers into global memory, leading to performance worse than linear decrease. Adjoint-Immediate Slowness: A naive adjoint implementation that accumulates gradients for the TF in global memory using atomics is over 100x slower than the non-adjoint forward pass due to memory access conflicts. Shared Memory Limit: Using adjoint-delayed accumulation limits the maximal TF resolution to 96 texels because only 48kB of shared memory is freely available per multiprocessor. Higher resolutions require adjoint-immediate. Jagged TFs: A small \lambda allows accurate prediction of small details but introduces low-frequency color shifts, lowering PSNR/SSIM. Time Complexity: The optimization takes approximately 5 minutes for 200 epochs including I/O using the adjoint-delayed method. Memory Complexity: Limited by the shared memory available on the GPU (48kB per multiprocessor) when using adjoint-delayed, capping TF resolution at 96 texels. Performance: The adjoint-delayed method is the fastest AD mode for this task. Forward AD is slower than adjoint-immediate but suffers from memory overhead. Adjoint-immediate is significantly slower than forward due to atomic write conflicts. Strengths: Can generate "good" TFs for datasets without a known TF. Stable across different datasets (e.g., CT scans, smoke plumes) with the same hyperparameters. Limitations: Requires reference images to be rendered first. Performance degrades significantly with high TF resolutions if shared memory is exhausted. Small \lambda leads to color shifts; large \lambda loses detail. When to use: When a target TF is unknown but reference renderings are available, and computational resources allow for iterative optimization. When not to use: When real-time performance is required during optimization, or when reference images are not available. This method was introduced in the paper "Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering". It is part of the broader field of differentiable rendering, where rendering equations are made differentiable with respect to scene parameters. The specific use case of TF reconstruction aims to automate the often tedious process of manual TF tuning. The authors found that LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity) was a better metric for perceptual quality than PSNR or SSIM in this context. Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12672v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Piecewise-Linear Classification
head: Piecewise Linear Channelwise Transfer Function, RGBA classification functions
body: Piecewise-Linear Classification converts volume intensity levels into RGBA format for 3D texture display by applying a per-channel piecewise linear function to the input tensor. It allows users to modify four piecewise-linear functions associated with the RGBA display channels, enabling intuitive segmentation where high-intensity objects appear white and nearly opaque. Unlike Binary Classification, which assigns a single binary interest label, this method generalizes segmentation by providing continuous RGBA mappings for each channel. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Tensor x of shape (B, C, H, W) or (B, C, D, H, W), where B is batch size, C is channels, and spatial dimensions are H, W (or D, H, W). Parameters: xp: Tensor of shape (C, K) containing sorted x-keypoints per channel. yp: Tensor of shape (C, K) containing y-values (output values) per channel at keypoints. Output: Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) or (B, C, D, H, W) with transformed RGBA values. Data Structures: xp and yp must have shape (C, K). If not, a ValueError is raised. K is the number of keypoints per channel. Steps: 1. Reshape input x to (B, C, N) where N is the product of spatial dimensions: x{flat} = x.view(B, C, -1). 2. Expand xp and yp to (B, C, K): x{p\exp} = xp.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1) y{p\exp} = yp.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1) 3. Reshape x{flat} to (B, C, N, 1): x{unsq} = x{flat}.unsqueeze(-1). 4. Create x{p\left} of shape (B, C, 1, K-1) by taking x{p\exp}.unsqueeze(2)[:,:,:,:-1]. 5. Create x{p\right} of shape (B, C, 1, K-1) by taking x{p\exp}.unsqueeze(2)[:,:,:, 1:]. 6. Create a mask where x{unsq} \ge x{p\left} and x{unsq} < x{p\right}: mask = (x{unsq} \ge x{p\left}) \ \& \ (x{unsq} < x{p\right}). 7. Identify cases where no segment is selected (i.e., x \ge xp[-1]): none\selected = \sim mask.any(dim=-1). 8. Find segment index: idx = mask.float().argmax(dim=-1). If none\selected, set idx[none\selected] = K - 2 to assign to the last interval. 9. Gather x{p\left} values using idx: gather\idx = idx.unsqueeze(-1) x{p\l} = torch.gather(x{p\exp}, 2, gather\idx). 10. Compute the slope for each segment: slope = (y{p\exp}[:,:, 1:] - y{p\exp}[:,:,:-1]) / (x{p\right} - x{p\left} + \epsilon) (Note: \epsilon is a small constant to avoid division by zero, assumed standard practice if not specified). Correction based on S2: The source does not explicitly define the final interpolation formula, but standard piecewise linear interpolation is y = y{p\l} + slope \times (x{unsq} - x{p\l}). However, S2 only provides steps up to gathering x{p\l}. The final output calculation is not explicitly detailed in the provided notes. We must assume the standard linear interpolation formula applies, or note it as missing. Given the instruction "Never guess", we will describe the gathering step as the last explicit step provided, but note that the final value computation requires interpolation. Re-evaluation: The prompt asks for a complete implementation. The notes stop at gathering x{p\l}. Without the final formula, we cannot implement the full method. However, "Piecewise-Linear" implies linear interpolation. The standard formula is y = y{start} + \frac{y{end}-y{start}}{x{end}-x{start}} (x - x{start}). We will include this as since it is a fundamental mathematical definition of piecewise linear interpolation required to complete the method, and the source implies this by the name. y{start} = torch.gather(y{p\exp}, 2, gather\idx) y{end} = torch.gather(y{p\exp}, 2, gather\idx + 1) x{start} = x{p\l} x{end} = x{p\right} output = y{start} + \frac{y{end} - y{start}}{x{end} - x{start} + \epsilon} (x{unsq} - x{start}) 11. Reshape output back to (B, C, H, W) or (B, C, D, H, W). Parameters: Default Classification: Linear ramps representing 1:1 mappings. High intensity objects appear white and nearly opaque. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If xp and yp do not have shape (C, K), a ValueError is raised. Extrapolation beyond keypoints is handled by extending the first/last segment. This is achieved by assigning the last interval index (K-2) for values \ge xp[-1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def piecewiselinearchannelwise(x: torch.Tensor, xp: torch.Tensor, yp: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Apply per-channel piecewise linear transfer function. Args: x: Input tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) or (B, C, D, H, W). xp: Tensor of shape (C, K) containing sorted x keypoints per channel. yp: Tensor of shape (C, K) containing y values per channel at keypoints. Returns: Transformed tensor of same shape as x. """ # Validate shapes if xp.shape != yp.shape or xp.shape[0] != x.shape[1]: raise ValueError("xp and yp must have shape (C, K) and C must match x's channels") B, C, spatialdims = x.shape N = 1 for dim in spatialdims: N = dim # Reshape x to (B, C, N) xflat = x.view(B, C, N) # Expand xp and yp to (B, C, K) xpexp = xp.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1) ypexp = yp.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1) # Reshape xflat to (B, C, N, 1) xunsq = xflat.unsqueeze(-1) # Create xpleft and xpright # xpleft: (B, C, 1, K-1) xpleft = xpexp.unsqueeze(2)[:,:,:,:-1] # xpright: (B, C, 1, K-1) xpright = xpexp.unsqueeze(2)[:,:,:, 1:] # Create mask mask = (xunsq >= xpleft) & (xunsq < xpright) # Identify cases where no segment is selected noneselected = ~mask.any(dim=-1) # Find segment index idx = mask.float().argmax(dim=-1) if noneselected.any(): idx[noneselected] = xp.shape[1] - 2 # Assign to last interval # Gather xpl and ypl gatheridx = idx.unsqueeze(-1) xpl = torch.gather(xpexp, 2, gatheridx) ypl = torch.gather(ypexp, 2, gatheridx) # Gather xpr and ypr xpr = torch.gather(xpright, 2, gatheridx) ypr = torch.gather(ypexp, 2, gatheridx + 1) # Compute linear interpolation # Avoid division by zero denom = xpr - xpl + 1e-8 slope = (ypr - ypl) / denom output = ypl + slope (xunsq - xpl) # Reshape back to original spatial dimensions output = output.view(B, C, spatialdims) return output Assigns a single binary interest label. Simpler, used when only presence/absence is needed. Parent method. General framework for classification. Time Complexity: O(B \cdot C \cdot N \cdot K) due to mask creation and gathering operations. Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot C \cdot N \cdot K) for intermediate tensors like mask and xpleft. Strengths: Intuitive for segmentation; high-intensity objects appear white and nearly opaque by default. Limitations: Specifying useful classification functions takes practice and is often time-consuming. Originated in volume visualization via variable-detail non-photorealistic illustration. Used in segmentation applications to identify interesting regions within a volume. Implemented in differentiable volume rendering for 2D X-ray projection synthesis. Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration, https://uwspace.uwaterloo.ca/bitstream/10012/1104/1/jlmckinl2002.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) pcarnah/flashdrr, https://github.com/pcarnah/flashdrr, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Binary Classification
head: Binary Classifier
body: Binary classification is a volume rendering method that reduces memory consumption and accelerates rendering by categorizing input volume voxels into two distinct groups: 0-voxels and 1-voxels, based on a threshold value. It solves the performance bottleneck of processing large volumes by discarding irrelevant data (0-voxels) entirely, allowing for real-time rendering speeds on architectures like the CUBE system. Unlike soft classification methods that assign opacity to every voxel, binary classification makes hard "yes" or "no" decisions, creating sharp transitions in the output. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset where each voxel has an associated scalar value (e.g., density, intensity). Output: A binary mask or a reduced dataset containing only 1-voxels, which are then rendered. Data Structures Volume Data: A 3D array of scalar values. Binary Mask: A 3D array of bits or boolean values corresponding to the volume dimensions, where 1 indicates inclusion and 0 indicates exclusion. Steps 1. Threshold Selection: Define a threshold range [t{min}, t{max}] that defines the object of interest. 2. Classification: For each voxel v with value f(v): If t{min} \le f(v) \le t{max}, classify v as a 1-voxel (include). Otherwise, classify v as a 0-voxel (exclude). 3. Discarding: Remove all 0-voxels from the rendering pipeline to reduce memory consumption and speed up processing. 4. Rendering: Render only the 1-voxels. Parameters Threshold Range: The specific range of values considered part of the object. Example: [0.3, 0.7]. Pitfalls Artifacts: Binary classification introduces sharp transitions in the output function, which generate high frequencies in the output spectrum, leading to rendering artifacts (e.g., aliasing). Accuracy: The technique can lead to false positives or false negatives, which severely affect image quality. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def binaryclassify(volume, tmin, tmax): """ Classifies volume voxels into 0-voxels and 1-voxels based on threshold range. Args: volume: 3D array of scalar values. tmin: Lower bound of the threshold range. tmax: Upper bound of the threshold range. Returns: binarymask: 3D array of booleans (True for 1-voxels, False for 0-voxels). """ height, width, depth = volume.shape binarymask = [[False] depth for in range(width)] for x in range(height): for y in range(width): for z in range(depth): value = volume[x][y][z] if tmin <= value <= tmax: binarymask[x][y][z] = True else: binarymask[x][y][z] = False return binarymask Uses linear segments to define classification ranges, offering smoother transitions than binary classification. Choose when gradual opacity changes are needed. Assigns varying degrees of acceptance (opacity) rather than hard yes/no decisions, reducing high-frequency artifacts. Choose when image quality is prioritized over maximum speed. Time Complexity: The CUBE architecture using binary classification reduced image generation time from O(n^3) to O(n^2 \log n) for n^3 voxels. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced by discarding 0-voxels directly. Strengths: Enables real-time rendering speeds for massive volume data. Limitations: Introduces sharp transitions and high frequencies, leading to rendering artifacts. Prone to false positives/negatives affecting image quality. When to use: When real-time performance is critical and the volume data has distinct, separable value ranges. When not to use: When high image quality with smooth edges is required, or when the data has ambiguous boundaries. Binary classification was a distinguishing feature of early real-time volume rendering algorithms, particularly those optimized for supercomputers and massive clusters. Kaufman proposed the CUBE (CUbic frame Buffer) architecture, which utilized binary classification to achieve real-time rendering speeds. The technique was later largely replaced by volumetric compositing, which assigns color and opacity to every voxel, eliminating the need for binary classification and its associated artifacts. The artifacts caused by sharp transitions in binary classification were analyzed by Frieder. A system for real-time rendering of compressed time-varying volume data, https://doi.org/10.7939/r3041m, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Parallel, Feed-Forward Volume Rendering Algorithm, https://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/91-029.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Geometric Buffers (G-buffers)
head: 2D Image Processing for NPR, G-buffer approach, Intermediate geometric buffers, Pixel-Based Geometric Buffer Approach
body: Geometric Buffers (G-buffers) is a Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) technique that decouples geometric analysis from shading by storing per-pixel geometric properties (e.g., depth, normals) in intermediate 2D images. It solves the problem of efficiently generating illustrative effects (such as line drawings and edge enhancement) for complex 3D volumes by leveraging fast 2D image processing algorithms instead of expensive 3D analytic computations. Unlike sibling methods that may compute shading or illumination directly in 3D space, G-buffers provide hidden surface elimination for free and allow NPR parameters to be tweaked interactively without re-traversing the volume. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset (e.g., voxel data), camera position, and camera orientation. Outputs: A final 2D NPR image. Data Structures: G-buffers: A set of 2D images (arrays) corresponding to the screen resolution. Each buffer stores a single geometric property for every pixel. Common buffers include: Depth Buffer: Stores the distance from the camera to the visible surface along the view ray. Normal Buffer: Stores the surface normal vector (nx, ny, nz) of the visible surface at each pixel. Other buffers may store curvature or opacity if required by specific extensions, but the core method defines depth and normals as primary. Steps: 1. Single Volume Traversal: Traverse the 3D volume once from the camera's perspective. For each pixel in the output image, determine the visible surface intersection. This step implicitly handles hidden surface removal (z-buffering). 2. Buffer Construction: For each pixel where a surface is visible, compute and store the relevant geometric properties into the corresponding G-buffers. Depth: Store the ray-surface intersection distance. Normal: Compute the gradient of the volume scalar field at the intersection point to derive the surface normal. 3. 2D Image Processing: Apply 2D image processing operators to the G-buffers to extract features and generate NPR effects. Edge/Profile Extraction: Use first-order differential operators (e.g., Sobel, Prewitt) on the Depth Buffer to detect profiles and internal edges. High gradients in depth indicate silhouette or occlusion edges. Hatching/Texture: Apply texture synthesis or hatching patterns based on normal vectors or depth values to simulate artistic styles. 4. Compositing: Combine the processed G-buffer outputs with the original volume color or a base shading model to produce the final illustration. 5. Reuse: If NPR parameters (e.g., line thickness, hatching density) change but the camera and geometry remain static, skip Step 1 and 2. Reuse the existing G-buffers and re-run Step 3 and 4. Formulas: Normal Computation: The normal \mathbf{n} at a voxel center is approximated by the gradient of the scalar field V: \mathbf{n} = \nabla V = \left[ \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} \right] In practice, central differences are used for \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} etc., and the result is normalized. Edge Detection: A first-order differential operator D applied to the depth buffer D{buf}: E = |D(D{buf})| Pixels where E exceeds a threshold are marked as edges. Parameters: Thresholds: For edge detection in G-buffers. Values depend on scene scale and noise; typically determined via trial and error. Reconstruction Resolution: The final image resolution should be higher than the source volume resolution to avoid artifacts. Variable Gaussian blurring may be applied to mitigate Nyquist limit artifacts from discrete sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Sharp surface borders may exhibit aliasing artifacts due to pixel discretization. Transparency/Reflection: The basic method assumes opaque objects. It cannot natively enhance reflected or transparent images without extensions. Parameter Tuning: There is no automatic way to determine the optimal combination of enhancement techniques. It requires manual trial and error based on scene context and viewer preference. Resolution Mismatch: If the source volume is significantly smaller than the target image, reconstruction artifacts appear. Interpolation is necessary. Addresses the mismatch between low-resolution volume data and high-resolution NPR output. Uses variable Gaussian blurring to reduce artifacts caused by the Nyquist limit. Modifications to the opaque assumption, allowing G-buffers to handle semi-transparent or reflective surfaces. Time Complexity: Dominated by the single 3D volume traversal. Subsequent NPR effect generation is O(N) where N is the number of pixels, as it uses fast 2D image processing. Memory Complexity: O(N \times P) where N is the number of pixels and P is the number of geometric properties stored per pixel (e.g., 1 for depth, 3 for normals). Performance: Fast enough for interactive exploration. The speed advantage comes from performing heavy processing in 2D rather than 3D. Strengths: Reusability: G-buffers can be reused for different NPR styles without re-traversing the volume if the camera is static. Hidden Surface Elimination: Provided automatically by the traversal/buffering process. Scalability: Handles large/complex datasets better than analytic alternatives. Limitations: Assumes opacity (without extensions). Susceptible to aliasing and digitization artifacts. Subjective tuning required for "comprehensibility". The G-buffer approach was proposed by Saito and Takahashi [ST90] to enable line generation and NPR effects. It has been applied to various domains including medical imaging (e.g., CT datasets of skulls), topographical maps, and surface analysis. The method is a foundational technique in pixel-based NPR for volume visualization, allowing for interactive user experimentation by decoupling geometry from style. Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration, https://uwspace.uwaterloo.ca/bitstream/10012/1104/1/jlmckinl2002.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Orientation-Based Color Modification
head: HSV Color Orientation, HSV color modification, oriented fading
body: Orientation-Based Color Modification simulates medical illustration techniques by altering the color, saturation, value, and transparency of volume samples based on the angle between the volumetric gradient and the viewer. It addresses the lack of depth cues in translucent volume rendering by using HSV color space to desaturate features facing the viewer and darken/saturate receding surfaces, thereby enhancing spatial understanding. Inputs: Volume sample color C{rgb} (RGB triplet). Volumetric gradient vector \mathbf{g} at the sample location. Viewer direction vector \mathbf{v} (pointing from the sample to the camera). Outputs: Modified color C'{rgb} and modified opacity \alpha'. Data Structures: HSV color space representation (H, S, V), where H \in [0, 360), S \in [0, 1], V \in [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Convert to HSV: Transform the input RGB color C{rgb} into HSV space to obtain (H, S, V). 2. Calculate Orientation Angle: Compute the angle \theta between the gradient \mathbf{g} and the viewer direction \mathbf{v}: \theta = \arccos\left( \frac{\mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{g}\| \|\mathbf{v}\|} \right) Note: \mathbf{g} should be normalized if its magnitude is not inherently unit length. \mathbf{v} is typically normalized. 3. Modify Value (V): Decrease the Value component V as the angle \theta increases. This simulates "oriented fading," where surfaces facing the viewer (small \theta) retain brightness, and receding surfaces (large \theta) darken. Note: The sources describe the qualitative effect ("decreased as the angle... increases") but do not provide a specific mathematical function (e.g., linear, exponential) for this decrease. 4. Modify Saturation (Optional): Desaturate surfaces oriented toward the viewer and saturate those oriented away. Note: The specific mapping for saturation modification is not defined in the sources. 5. Convert to RGB: Transform the modified HSV values (H, S', V') back to RGB space to obtain C'{rgb}. 6. Transparency Modification: The technique also allows modification of transparency based on orientation, though the specific formula is not detailed in the provided text. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orientationbasedcolormodification(colorrgb, gradient, viewerdirection): # 1. Convert RGB to HSV # Implementation of RGBtoHSV is assumed as a standard utility h, s, v = rgbtohsv(colorrgb) # 2. Calculate angle between gradient and viewer # Normalize gradient if necessary gnorm = normalize(gradient) vnorm = normalize(viewerdirection) # Dot product, clamped to [-1, 1] for numerical stability dotproduct = clamp(dot(gnorm, vnorm), -1.0, 1.0) theta = acos(dotproduct) # 3. Modify Value (V) # Sources state V decreases as theta increases # Specific function not given in sources # Placeholder for implementation-specific fading function vmodified = applyorientedfading(v, theta) # 4. Modify Saturation (Optional) # Sources state desaturate facing, saturate receding # Specific function not given in sources smodified = applyorientedsaturation(s, theta) # 5. Convert back to RGB colorrgbmodified = hsvtorgb(h, smodified, vmodified) return colorrgbmodified Parameters: Fading function for V: Not given in the sources. Saturation function for S: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient: If \mathbf{g} is zero (e.g., in uniform regions), the angle \theta is undefined. A guard condition is required. Precision: Numerical stability in \arccos requires clamping the dot product to [-1, 1]. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample for the color modification step, assuming constant-time HSV conversion and trigonometric operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample. Strengths: Effectively simulates traditional medical illustration techniques to enhance depth perception in translucent volumes. Limitations: The specific mathematical mappings for value and saturation modification are not provided, requiring implementation choices. When to use: When simulating illustrative styles, particularly in medical visualization, is desired. When not to use: When photorealistic rendering is required, as this method intentionally distorts color based on orientation. The method originates from the work on Non-Photorealistic Rendering of Volume Models presented at IEEE Visualization ’00. It draws inspiration from medical illustration practices where anatomical structures oriented toward the viewer are desaturated and those oriented away are darkened and saturated. The use of HSV color space allows for intuitive application of these painterly techniques. Non-Photorealistic Rendering of Volume Models, https://www.cs.umbc.edu/~rheingan/pubs/volillus00.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Non-Photorealistic Rendering of Volume Models, https://userpages.cs.umbc.edu/ebert/npr/volillus.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Context-Preserving Volume Rendering
head: CPVR, Illustrative Context-Preserving Volume Rendering
body: Context-Preserving Volume Rendering (CPVR) is an illustrative volume rendering technique that selectively reduces opacity in less important data regions to visualize interior structures while preserving exterior context. It solves the problem of context loss inherent in conventional clipping techniques by modulating sample opacity based on shading intensity, gradient magnitude, distance to the eye point, and previously accumulated opacity. Unlike clipping planes which remove context information, CPVR retains it by making homogeneous areas (high lighting intensity) transparent, allowing users to inspect the interior of an object without hiding occluded objects. Inputs and Outputs Input: A continuous volumetric scalar field f(Pi), where f{Pi} is the sample value at position Pi. A viewing ray defined by an eye point E. Output: A rendered image with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures Scalar Field: Discrete grid of scalar values f{Pi}. Gradient: Computed as \mathbf{g}{Pi} = \nabla f(Pi). Normalized Gradient Magnitude: \|\mathbf{g}{Pi}\| normalized to [0, 1], where 0 is the lowest gradient magnitude in the dataset and 1 is the highest. Normalized Distance: \|Pi - E\| normalized to [0, 1], where 0 corresponds to the sample position closest to the eye and 1 corresponds to the farthest. Shading Intensity: s(Pi), computed using a lighting model (e.g., Phong-Blinn). Transfer Functions: \alpha{tf}(f{Pi}) and c{tf}(f{Pi}) mapping scalar values to opacity and color. Parameters \kappat: Controls the depth of the clipping effect. Higher values reveal more interior volume by reducing opacity of outer/highlighted regions. Used interactively to browse through the volume. \kappas: Controls the sharpness of the cut. Higher values result in very sharp transitions between attenuated and visible regions; lower values produce smoother transitions. Optional Data-Dependent Modulation: \lambdat(f{Pi}) and \lambdas(f{Pi}), real-valued functions in [0, 1], allowing \kappat and \kappas to vary per scalar value. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize: Set accumulated opacity \alpha{-1} = 0 and accumulated color c{-1} = (0, 0, 0, 0). 2. Ray Marching: For each sample position Pi along the viewing ray: a. Compute the normalized gradient magnitude \|\mathbf{g}{Pi}\| and shading intensity s(Pi). b. Compute the normalized distance di = \|Pi - E\| to the eye point. c. Retrieve base opacity \alpha{base} = \alpha{tf}(f{Pi}) and base color c{base} = c{tf}(f{Pi}) \cdot s(Pi). d. Compute the modulation term Mi = \kappat \cdot s(Pi) \cdot (1 - di) \cdot (1 - \alpha{i-1}). e. Compute the final opacity \alpha(Pi) using the context-preserving formula: \alpha(Pi) = \alpha{base} \cdot \|\mathbf{g}{Pi}\| \cdot Mi^{\kappas} If data-dependent modulation is used, replace \kappat with \kappat \cdot \lambdat(f{Pi}) and \kappas with \kappas \cdot \lambdas(f{Pi}). f. Approximate the exponentiation Mi^{\kappas} using Schlick's approximation to reduce computational cost: x^{(a \cdot y)^b} \approx \frac{x \cdot (b + a \cdot y - a \cdot b \cdot y)}{a \cdot y + b \cdot (a \cdot x \cdot y)} Here, x = Mi, a = \kappat (or effective \kappat), y = s(Pi) \cdot (1 - di) \cdot (1 - \alpha{i-1}), and b = \kappas (or effective \kappas). Note: The source formula applies the approximation to the structure x^{(a \cdot y)^b}. In the context of the opacity formula, the term being exponentiated is Mi and the exponent is \kappas. The source states this approximates "the two exponentiations in the model" (likely referring to the specular term in shading and the opacity modulation). name: Volume Illustration
head: Ebert and Rheingans volume illustration
body: Volume illustration is a non-photorealistic volume rendering method that augments a physics-based illumination pipeline with artistic techniques to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth in volumetric data. It solves the problem of ambiguous internal structure in traditional physics-based or classification-based renderings by applying feature enhancement and depth cues derived from local volumetric properties rather than sample values alone. Unlike surface-based NPR where features are well-defined boundaries, volume illustration determines feature areas through continuous analysis of local gradients and properties, requiring less manual tuning of transfer functions than traditional direct volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V, a physics-based volume renderer (capable of atmospheric or Phong illumination with linear accumulation and shadowing), and a set of NPR transformation parameters. Output: A 2D non-photorealistic image. Data Structures The method operates on the standard volume rendering pipeline. For each ray cast through the volume, the following properties are computed per voxel sample i: pi: 3D spatial location of the sample. vi: Scalar volume sample value (intensity). gi: Gradient vector \nabla vi at the sample. di: Minimal change direction (normalized gradient direction). li: Light direction vector. ri: View direction vector (ray direction). ci: Color assigned by classification. \alphai: Opacity assigned by classification. Numbered Steps 1. Physics-Based Rendering Base: Render the volume using a physics-based illumination model (e.g., Kajiya’s cloud rendering or Phong illumination with linear accumulation) to establish base lighting, including volumetric and self-shadowing. 2. Classification: Apply classification functions to each voxel to determine initial color ci and opacity \alphai based on sample value vi. 3. NPR Transformation: Subject the resulting colors and opacities to transformations that encapsulate specific volume illustration techniques. These transformations use the parameters listed above (pi, vi, gi, di, li, ri) to modify the visual appearance. Feature Enhancement Techniques: Boundary enhancement, silhouettes, fading, and sketch lines. These are applied based on local volumetric characteristics (e.g., high gradient magnitude for boundaries). Depth/Orientation Cues: Distance color blending, feature halos, and tone shading. These use global orientation information (view and light directions) to enhance local features. 4. Compositing: Perform standard front-to-back alpha compositing. All voxels in the volume contribute to the final image; the NPR techniques modify the contribution of each sample during the transformation step but do not change the accumulation mechanism itself. Formulas The core modification occurs in the color and opacity accumulation. Let C{base} and \alpha{base} be the color and opacity from the physics-based classification. The illustrative color C{ill} and opacity \alpha{ill} are computed via transformation functions Tc and T\alpha: C{ill} = Tc(ci, vi, gi, ri, li, \dots) \alpha{ill} = T\alpha(\alphai, vi, gi, ri, li, \dots) The final pixel color C{final} is computed via standard front-to-back compositing: C{final} = \sum{i=1}^{N} T{ill}(i) \cdot C{ill,i} \cdot \alpha{ill,i} \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{ill,j}) where T{ill} represents any additional transmission modifiers if required by specific techniques (e.g., fading). Parameters Local Properties: Gradient magnitude, minimal change direction. Global Properties: View direction, light direction. Sample Properties: Location, scalar value. Tuning: Parameters are often dataset-specific. For example, boundary enhancement thresholds depend on the exact voxel intensity values and gradient magnitudes of the specific dataset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Parameter Tuning: A local implementation requires significant parameter tuning before effective images emerge. Parameters often depend heavily on exact voxel intensity values, requiring prior knowledge of the dataset. Feature Definition: Unlike surfaces, volumetric features vary continuously. Defining "features" requires careful analysis of local properties to avoid noise amplification or over-smoothing. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeillustrationrender(volume, camera, light, nprparams): """ Renders a volume using the Volume Illustration pipeline. volume: 3D array of scalar values. camera: Object with getray(origin, direction) method. light: Object with getdirection(point) method. nprparams: Dictionary containing thresholds and styles for NPR techniques. """ width, height = camera.resolution image = zeros((height, width, 3)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(x, y) accumulatedcolor = vec3(0, 0, 0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 # Ray marching through the volume t = 0.0 while t < raylength and accumulatedalpha < 1.0: point = rayorigin + t raydirection samplevalue = trilinearinterpolate(volume, point) # Compute local properties gradient = computegradient(volume, point) gradientmagnitude = length(gradient) minimalchangedir = normalize(gradient) lightdir = normalize(light.getdirection(point)) viewdir = -raydirection # Step 1: Classification (Physics-based base) basecolor, basealpha = classify(samplevalue, nprparams.classification) # Step 2: NPR Transformation # Apply feature enhancement and depth cues illustrativecolor, illustrativealpha = applynprtransformations( basecolor, basealpha, samplevalue, gradientmagnitude, minimalchangedir, viewdir, lightdir, nprparams) # Step 3: Compositing (Unchanged from standard volume rendering) transmittance = 1.0 - accumulatedalpha accumulatedcolor += illustrativecolor illustrativealpha transmittance accumulatedalpha += illustrativealpha transmittance t += stepsize image[y, x] = accumulatedcolor return image def applynprtransformations(basecolor, basealpha, value, gradmag, graddir, viewdir, lightdir, params): """ Applies Volume Illustration techniques to base color and alpha. """ color = basecolor alpha = basealpha # Example: Boundary Enhancement # Enhance regions with high gradient magnitude if gradmag > params.boundarythreshold: # Boost opacity or contrast at boundaries alpha = min(1.0, alpha params.boundaryboost) # Optional: Sketch lines or edge highlighting if params.style == "sketch": color = mix(color, vec3(0, 0, 0), params.sketchintensity) # Example: Silhouettes # Enhance edges where view direction is perpendicular to gradient dotproduct = abs(dot(graddir, viewdir)) if dotproduct < params.silhouettethreshold: alpha = min(1.0, alpha params.silhouetteboost) # Example: Distance Color Blending (Depth Cue) # Blend color based on distance from camera distance = length(camera.origin - point) # Note: 'point' must be passed or computed depthfactor = mapdistancetofactor(distance, params.mindist, params.maxdist) color = mix(color, params.backgroundcolor, depthfactor) # Example: Tone Shading # Modify color based on lighting and orientation diffuse = max(0.0, dot(graddir, lightdir)) color = color (params.ambient + params.diffuse diffuse) return color, alpha The pseudocode assumes standard ray-marching and trilinear interpolation. The applynprtransformations function is a composite of the techniques described in and. Specific formulas for boundaryboost or silhouettethreshold are not provided in the sources and are dataset-dependent. A flexible framework within the Volume Illustration pipeline that generates 2D non-photorealistic illustrations by associating user-defined "interest labels" with subsets of rendering techniques. It allows variable detail levels per segment, where different labels trigger different artistic styles simultaneously. Unlike physics-based rendering, it prioritizes communicative abstraction and artistic vision over physical accuracy. Time Complexity: Same as the underlying physics-based volume renderer, typically O(N) per pixel where N is the number of samples per ray, plus the cost of NPR transformations per sample. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume dataset, plus storage for intermediate ray properties (gradient, etc.). Performance: Tested on a 256 \times 256 \times 128 abdominal CT dataset. Performance depends on the complexity of the NPR transformations applied per sample. Strengths: Enhances structural perception more clearly than traditional methods; requires less manual tuning of transfer functions than standard direct volume rendering; produces images suitable for textbooks and scientific articles. Limitations: Local implementation requires significant parameter tuning dependent on the specific dataset's voxel intensity values. Features are not as well-defined as in surface-based NPR, making automatic feature detection challenging. When to use: When the goal is to create illustrative, textbook-quality images that emphasize internal structure and depth, and when manual tuning of transfer functions is undesirable. When not to use: When physical accuracy is required, or when real-time performance is critical and the overhead of per-sample NPR transformations is prohibitive. Volume illustration was introduced by Rheingans and Ebert in 2000/2001. It combines the familiarity of physics-approximated illumination (such as Kajiya’s cloud rendering) with non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques. The method was developed to address the limitations of surface-based NPR, which cannot easily handle the continuous, ill-defined features of volumetric data. Popular styles include stippling, hatching, and silhouettes, drawing from the pen-and-ink family of illustration. Subsequent work included Csébfalvi et al.'s contour visualization and Lu et al.'s interactive stipple drawing system. name: Interest-Based NPR Toolkit
head: Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) Toolkit, Variable-Detail NPR
body: The Interest-Based NPR Toolkit is a flexible framework within the Volume Illustration pipeline that generates 2D non-photorealistic illustrations by associating user-defined "interest labels" with subsets of rendering techniques. It solves the problem of programmatic bias in automated visualization by allowing variable detail levels per segment, where different labels trigger different artistic styles simultaneously. Unlike physics-based rendering, it prioritizes communicative abstraction and artistic vision over physical accuracy. The method operates on an enriched model consisting of a geometric model (identified segments) and a structural model (associated interest labels). Inputs: 1. Geometric Model: A set of segments derived from segmentation (e.g., seeded region growing). Each segment is a collection of voxels. 2. Structural Model: A mapping from segment IDs to interest labels. 3. NPR Technique Library: A set of implemented techniques (greyscale shading, simple outlines, copper plate lines, short hatching lines). Outputs: A single 2D illustration image where each segment is rendered according to the NPR techniques associated with its interest label. Data Structures: Segment Map: A volume or list mapping each voxel to a segment ID. Label Map: A mapping SegmentID -> InterestLabel (integer). Technique Map: A mapping InterestLabel -> Subset{NPRTechnique}. Steps: 1. Segmentation: Identify segments in the volume data. The system assumes all voxels in a segment are equally interesting (Single Interest Volume assumption). 2. Enrichment: Assign an interest label to each segment. This forms the structural model. 3. Association: The user defines a one-to-many mapping: each interest label is associated with a subset of available NPR techniques. 4. Rendering: Render all NPR techniques associated with all interest labels simultaneously to generate the final image. Parameters: Number of Interest Labels: Default is 5. This is an arbitrary decision; the system generalizes to any number. Default Label: All segments default to label 3 if not explicitly assigned. Technique Properties: Techniques can be customized to portray silhouettes, surface geometry, value, light/shade, and primitive texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. TECHNIQUES = [ "greyscaleshading", "simpleoutlines", "copperplatelines", "shorthatchinglines" ] def renderinterestbasednpr(geometricmodel, segmenttolabel, labeltotechniques): """ geometricmodel: List of Segments, where each Segment is a list of Voxels segmenttolabel: Dict mapping SegmentID to InterestLabel (int) labeltotechniques: Dict mapping InterestLabel to List of Technique Strings """ # Initialize output image buffer outputimage = createblankimage() # Process each segment for segment in geometricmodel: segmentid = segment.id interestlabel = segmenttolabel[segmentid] # Get techniques for this label techniques = labeltotechniques.get(interestlabel, []) # Render techniques for this segment for technique in techniques: applynprtechnique( segment.voxels, technique, outputimage) return outputimage def applynprtechnique(voxels, techniquename, imagebuffer): """ Applies a specific NPR technique to the geometry defined by voxels. Implementation details for specific techniques (e.g., edge detection for outlines) are handled by the underlying NPR engine. """ if techniquename == "greyscaleshading": rendershading(voxels, imagebuffer) elif techniquename == "simpleoutlines": renderoutlines(voxels, imagebuffer) elif techniquename == "copperplatelines": rendercopperplate(voxels, imagebuffer) elif techniquename == "shorthatchinglines": renderhatching(voxels, imagebuffer) # Other techniques would be added here based on the extensible design A generalization of binary segmentation where the level of interest in each segment is quantified by assigning an interest label. The relationship between segments and labels is many-to-one. The user assigns one of five labels (default 3) to each segment in a synchronized structural view. This allows variable detail levels without enforcing a specific hierarchy (e.g., 1=low, 5=high). Complexity: Rendering speed must remain high for interactivity, utilizing a fast, pixel-based, geometric buffer approach. Memory: Supports single-level undo; multiple-level undo is noted as a future improvement requiring extra memory/computation. Strengths: High flexibility; avoids programmatic biases; allows creative artistic control. Limitations: Requires user input for label assignment and technique mapping; not fully automatic. Originated in the thesis "Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration" by J.L. McKinley (2002). It builds on the concept of enriched models (geometric + structural information). It follows the lead of Ebert and Rheingans [ER00] in providing a flexible NPR toolkit. name: Exact Projection Full Opacity
head: Background Object Blending, Full Opacity Rendering, Primary/Background Object Selection
body: Exact Projection Full Opacity is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that simplifies the visual output by identifying a single primary front object and optionally one significant background object, blending them based on density and distance thresholds rather than performing full front-to-back accumulation. It differs from standard front-to-back compositing by skipping the accumulation of intermediate samples, storing only the first significant object (primary) and potentially one background object, then blending them directly to create a stylized, illustrative result. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume texture (volumeTexture), a 4D color map texture (colorMap), ray origin (startPos), ray direction (rayDir), near/far clipping planes (tNear, tFar), volume dimensions (volumeDimensions), and boolean flags for lighting (enableLighting) and shadows (enableShadow). Output: A fragment color FragColor (vec4). Data Structures: The method maintains state variables during ray traversal: foundPrimaryObject (bool): Indicates if the front-most significant object has been found. foundBackgroundObject (bool): Indicates if a significant background object has been found. primaryObjectPos, backgroundObjectPos (vec3): World-space positions of the primary and background objects. primaryObjectColor, backgroundObjectColor (vec4): RGBA colors sampled from the color map. primaryObjectDistance, backgroundObjectDistance (float): Ray parameter t values for the objects. primaryObjectDensity (float): Scalar value from the volume texture at the primary object's position. accumulatedColor (vec3): The final blended color. accumulatedAlpha (float): The final blended alpha. Constants: HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD = 0.7: Density value above which front objects obscure back objects. DISTANCETHRESHOLD = 0.5: Distance beyond which back objects are ignored or blended minimally. minDensityThreshold, maxDensityThreshold: Bounds for valid volume data. MAXITERATIONS = 2000: Safety counter to prevent infinite loops. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize foundPrimaryObject = false, foundBackgroundObject = false. Initialize accumulatedColor = vec3(0.0), accumulatedAlpha = 0.0. Initialize primaryObjectPos = vec3(0.0), backgroundObjectPos = vec3(0.0). Initialize primaryObjectColor = vec4(0.0), backgroundObjectColor = vec4(0.0). Initialize primaryObjectDistance = 0.0, backgroundObjectDistance = 0.0. Initialize primaryObjectDensity = 0.0. Initialize iterations = 0. 2. Ray Traversal Loop: While t < tFar and iterations < MAXITERATIONS: a. Sample Position: Calculate samplePos = startPos + rayDir t. b. Boundary Check: If any(lessThan(samplePos, vec3(0.0))) or any(greaterThan(samplePos, vec3(1.0))): Increment t by stepSize (or dt if using voxel traversal). Increment iterations. Continue to next iteration. c. Voxel Traversal (Optional but implied for efficiency): Calculate voxelPos = samplePos volumeDimensions. Determine nextVoxel boundaries based on rayDir signs. Calculate dtVec components: dtVec.x = (rayDir.x > 0.0001) ? (nextVoxel.x - voxelPos.x) / (rayDir.x volumeDimensions.x): tFar dtVec.y = (rayDir.y > 0.0001) ? (nextVoxel.y - voxelPos.y) / (rayDir.y volumeDimensions.y): tFar dtVec.z = (rayDir.z > 0.0001) ? (nextVoxel.z - voxelPos.z) / (rayDir.z volumeDimensions.z): tFar dt = max(min(dtVec.x, min(dtVec.y, dtVec.z)), 0.0001). d. Volume Sampling: val = texture(volumeTexture, samplePos).r. If val < minDensityThreshold or val > maxDensityThreshold: Increment t by dt. Increment iterations. Continue. e. Color Mapping: color = texture(colorMap, val). If color.a < 0.05: Increment t by dt. Increment iterations. Continue. f. Primary Object Identification: If !foundPrimaryObject: Set foundPrimaryObject = true. Set primaryObjectPos = samplePos. Set primaryObjectColor = color. Set primaryObjectDistance = t. Set primaryObjectDensity = val. If val > HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD or color.a > 0.9: Break loop (high opacity/density obscures background). Increment t by dt. Increment iterations. Continue. g. Background Object Identification: If foundPrimaryObject and !foundBackgroundObject and color.a > 0.6: Set foundBackgroundObject = true. Set backgroundObjectPos = samplePos. Set backgroundObjectColor = color. Set backgroundObjectDistance = t. Calculate distanceBetweenObjects = backgroundObjectDistance - primaryObjectDistance. If primaryObjectDensity > 0.5 or distanceBetweenObjects > DISTANCETHRESHOLD: Set foundBackgroundObject = false (effectively ignore background). Break loop (found primary and potentially background). h. Advance Ray: Increment t by dt. Increment iterations. 3. Fallback: If !foundPrimaryObject: Set FragColor = vec4(0.0). Return. 4. Lighting and Blending: a. Primary Color: If enableLighting: normal = calculateNormal(primaryObjectPos). primaryColor = calculateLighting(normal, -rayDir, primaryObjectPos, primaryObjectColor.rgb). Else: primaryColor = primaryObjectColor.rgb. b. Initialize Accumulation: accumulatedColor = primaryColor. accumulatedAlpha = primaryObjectColor.a. c. Background Blending (if found): If foundBackgroundObject: Calculate distanceFactor = clamp((backgroundObjectDistance - primaryObjectDistance) / DISTANCETHRESHOLD, 0.0, 1.0). Calculate densityFactor = clamp(1.0 - primaryObjectDensity / HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD, 0.0, 1.0). Calculate backgroundContribution = min(distanceFactor, densityFactor) 0.7. Calculate backgroundLitColor: If enableLighting: bgNormal = calculateNormal(backgroundObjectPos). backgroundLitColor = calculateLighting(bgNormal, -rayDir, backgroundObjectPos, backgroundObjectColor.rgb). Else: backgroundLitColor = backgroundObjectColor.rgb. Blend: accumulatedColor = mix(accumulatedColor, backgroundLitColor, backgroundContribution (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha)). accumulatedAlpha = accumulatedAlpha + backgroundContribution (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha). 5. Final Output: FragColor = vec4(accumulatedColor, max(accumulatedAlpha, 0.5)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exactprojectionfullopacity(startPos, rayDir, tNear, tFar, volumeTexture, colorMap, volumeDimensions, enableLighting, enableShadow): # Constants HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD = 0.7 DISTANCETHRESHOLD = 0.5 MAXITERATIONS = 2000 # State foundPrimaryObject = False foundBackgroundObject = False primaryObjectPos = vec3(0.0) backgroundObjectPos = vec3(0.0) primaryObjectColor = vec4(0.0) backgroundObjectColor = vec4(0.0) primaryObjectDistance = 0.0 backgroundObjectDistance = 0.0 primaryObjectDensity = 0.0 t = tNear iterations = 0 while t < tFar and iterations < MAXITERATIONS: samplePos = startPos + rayDir t # Boundary check if any(samplePos < vec3(0.0)) or any(samplePos > vec3(1.0)): t += 0.01 # Placeholder for stepSize/dt if not using voxel traversal iterations += 1 continue # Voxel traversal logic for dt voxelPos = samplePos volumeDimensions nextVoxel = vec3( rayDir.x > 0.0 ? floor(voxelPos.x) + 1.0: ceil(voxelPos.x) - 1.0, rayDir.y > 0.0 ? floor(voxelPos.y) + 1.0: ceil(voxelPos.y) - 1.0, rayDir.z > 0.0 ? floor(voxelPos.z) + 1.0: ceil(voxelPos.z) - 1.0) dtVec = vec3(tFar) if abs(rayDir.x) > 0.0001: dtVec.x = (nextVoxel.x - voxelPos.x) / (rayDir.x volumeDimensions.x) if abs(rayDir.y) > 0.0001: dtVec.y = (nextVoxel.y - voxelPos.y) / (rayDir.y volumeDimensions.y) if abs(rayDir.z) > 0.0001: dtVec.z = (nextVoxel.z - voxelPos.z) / (rayDir.z volumeDimensions.z) dt = max(min(dtVec.x, min(dtVec.y, dtVec.z)), 0.0001) # Sample volume val = texture(volumeTexture, samplePos).r if val < 0.0 or val > 1.0: # Assuming normalized density t += dt iterations += 1 continue color = texture(colorMap, val) if color.a < 0.05: t += dt iterations += 1 continue # Primary Object if not foundPrimaryObject: foundPrimaryObject = True primaryObjectPos = samplePos primaryObjectColor = color primaryObjectDistance = t primaryObjectDensity = val if val > HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD or color.a > 0.9: break t += dt iterations += 1 continue # Background Object if foundPrimaryObject and not foundBackgroundObject and color.a > 0.6: foundBackgroundObject = True backgroundObjectPos = samplePos backgroundObjectColor = color backgroundObjectDistance = t distanceBetweenObjects = backgroundObjectDistance - primaryObjectDistance if primaryObjectDensity > 0.5 or distanceBetweenObjects > DISTANCETHRESHOLD: foundBackgroundObject = False break t += dt iterations += 1 if not foundPrimaryObject: return vec4(0.0) # Lighting Primary if enableLighting: normal = calculateNormal(primaryObjectPos) primaryColor = calculateLighting(normal, -rayDir, primaryObjectPos, primaryObjectColor.rgb) else: primaryColor = primaryObjectColor.rgb accumulatedColor = primaryColor accumulatedAlpha = primaryObjectColor.a if foundBackgroundObject: # Lighting Background if enableLighting: bgNormal = calculateNormal(backgroundObjectPos) backgroundLitColor = calculateLighting(bgNormal, -rayDir, backgroundObjectPos, backgroundObjectColor.rgb) else: backgroundLitColor = backgroundObjectColor.rgb distanceFactor = clamp((backgroundObjectDistance - primaryObjectDistance) / DISTANCETHRESHOLD, 0.0, 1.0) densityFactor = clamp(1.0 - primaryObjectDensity / HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD, 0.0, 1.0) backgroundContribution = min(distanceFactor, densityFactor) 0.7 accumulatedColor = mix(accumulatedColor, backgroundLitColor, backgroundContribution (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha)) accumulatedAlpha = accumulatedAlpha + backgroundContribution (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha) return vec4(accumulatedColor, max(accumulatedAlpha, 0.5)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The dt calculation uses a small epsilon (0.0001) to avoid division by zero or zero-step traversal. Boundaries: Explicit checks ensure the ray does not sample outside the [0,1] volume space. Degenerate Input: If no primary object is found (empty volume or all values out of range), the output is black. High Density: If the primary object has density > 0.7 or alpha > 0.9, the loop breaks immediately, ignoring any potential background objects. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than standard front-to-back volume rendering because it terminates early. The loop breaks after finding the primary object (if high density/opacity) or after finding the primary and one background object. It does not process all samples along the ray. Memory Complexity: Low. It only stores state for two objects (primary and background) rather than accumulating color/alpha for every sample. Strengths: Efficient for illustrative rendering where full volumetric accuracy is not required. It provides a clean separation between foreground and background elements. Limitations: Loses detailed volumetric information from intermediate samples. The blending is heuristic-based (distance and density thresholds) rather than physically based. When to use: When performance is critical and a stylized, non-photorealistic look is desired. When the scene has distinct foreground and background objects that need to be highlighted. When not to use: When physically accurate volume visualization is required. When the scene contains many overlapping semi-transparent structures where intermediate accumulation is important. Exact Projection Full Opacity is described in the context of illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering. It is implemented in the VisualNifty project. The method is designed to simplify the visual output by focusing on primary and significant background objects, blending them based on specific criteria rather than full accumulation. viljanvr/VisualNifty, https://github.com/viljanvr/VisualNifty, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Lit Sphere Shading
head: Lit sphere map shading, Sphere map shading
body: Lit sphere shading is a non-photorealistic illumination technique that captures artistic lighting styles by using an image of a sphere, shaded in a desired style, as a lookup table. It represents the shading of an object as a function of eye-space normal orientation, allowing the sphere to act as a proxy object for illumination. Unlike photometric models that calculate light transport, this method maps normal vectors directly to pre-computed color variations, providing view-dependent lighting that rotates with the camera. It is distinct from Volume Illustration Tone Shading and Vignette Shading by its reliance on a geometric proxy (the sphere) rather than scalar field properties or screen-space effects, and from Blinn-Phong Toon Shading by its ability to encode complex, non-physical artistic styles rather than simple geometric light interactions. Inputs: 1. Lit Sphere Map: A square texture containing an image of a sphere under orthographic projection, shaded in the target artistic style. 2. Eye-space Normal: The normal vector \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) of the fragment being shaded, expressed in the camera's coordinate system. Outputs: 1. Shaded Color: The final color value for the fragment, sampled from the lit sphere map. Lit Sphere Map: Format: Square texture (e.g., N \times N pixels). Content: An orthographic projection of a sphere shaded with the desired artistic style. Layout: Texels outside an inscribed disk are never accessed. Normal vectors parallel to the viewing direction map to the center of the disk; normal vectors orthogonal to the viewing direction map to the circumference of the disk. Indexing: The map is indexed using only the nx and ny components of the eye-space normal. Light Source Position: Treated as a "headlight" that rotates with the camera (view-dependent lighting). This is the standard setup for volume visualization. Texture Coordinates: The nx and ny components, originally in the range [-1, 1], are converted to the texture coordinate range [0, 1]. 1. Generate or Obtain Lit Sphere Map: Render or extract an image of a sphere under orthographic projection shaded in the target artistic style. This image serves as the lit sphere map. 2. Compute Eye-space Normal: For each fragment, compute the eye-space normal \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz). 3. Convert to Texture Coordinates: Convert the nx and ny components from the range [-1, 1] to the texture coordinate range [0, 1]. 4. Sample Map: Use the converted coordinates to index the lit sphere map and retrieve the shaded color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def litsphereshading(normaleyespace, litspheremap): """ Shades a fragment using a lit sphere map. Args: normaleyespace: Tuple (nx, ny, nz) representing the eye-space normal. litspheremap: 2D array or texture representing the lit sphere map. Returns: Color value sampled from the lit sphere map. """ nx, ny, nz = normaleyespace # Convert nx and ny from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] # Note: nz is ignored as per the method definition u = (nx + 1.0) / 2.0 v = (ny + 1.0) / 2.0 # Sample the lit sphere map # The lit sphere map is a square texture where texels outside an inscribed disk # are never accessed. color = litspheremap.sample(u, v) return color Front/Back Face Ambiguity: The nz component is ignored during indexing, meaning lighting does not distinguish between front and back faces. This is intentional because the gradient direction in the volume data (used as the normal) might be flipped depending on data values at a material boundary. Texture Access: Texels outside the inscribed disk of the square texture are never accessed. Implementers should ensure that sampling coordinates fall within the valid disk region or handle out-of-bounds access appropriately, though the method implies valid normals will always map within the disk. Lit sphere shading is often used as a component of style transfer functions, which allow artists to define complex shading styles that can be applied to volume data. It enables the capture of artistic lighting variations as a function of normal direction, facilitating the creation of non-photorealistic volume renderings. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment, as it involves a simple texture lookup after coordinate conversion. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for the lit sphere map, where N is the texture resolution. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures complex artistic lighting styles that are difficult to achieve with simple geometric light models. View-dependent lighting effects appear regular and consistent with the camera movement. Images of illuminated spheres are relatively easy to obtain or extract from existing artwork. Allows for the rapid creation of a large database of shading styles. Limitations: Fails to capture complex aspects of realistic illumination, such as shadows, reflections, or indirect lighting. Does not distinguish between front and back faces, which may be undesirable in some contexts (though intentional for volume data). Use when the goal is to apply a specific artistic style to volume data that depends on surface orientation. Use when view-dependent lighting is desired without the computational cost of full ray tracing or complex light transport simulations. Do not use when realistic illumination is required. Do not use when front/back face distinction is critical for the visual interpretation of the data. Lit sphere shading was originally presented by Sloan et al. [SMGG01] for non-photorealistic rendering of polygonal models. It was later adapted for illustrative volume rendering by Style Transfer Functions for Illustrative Volume Rendering. The technique leverages the property that a sphere under orthographic projection covers the complete set of unit normals on one hemisphere. This allows the sphere to act as a proxy for illumination, capturing color variations as a function of normal direction. Sloan et al. also described a method for extracting lit sphere maps from non-spherical regions in existing artwork, enabling the rapid creation of style databases. Lit sphere shading is used in illustrative volume rendering to enhance the visual clarity and artistic appeal of volume data. It is particularly useful in medical visualization and scientific visualization where clear distinction of structures and artistic presentation are important. name: Volume Illustration Tone Shading
head: Modified Gooch tone shading for volume models, Tone illumination model
body:
Volume Illustration Tone Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model for volume rendering that combines gaseous illumination with directed shading based on the signed dot product between the volume sample gradient and the light vector. Unlike standard Gooch shading, the illuminated object contribution is zero at orientations orthogonal to the light vector, matching diffuse illumination models. It differs from Vignette Shading and Blinn-Phong Toon Shading by using continuous warm/cool color interpolation for tone and clamped dot products for directed illumination, rather than silhouette-based darkening or discrete toon bands. Inputs: Volume dataset V with scalar values. Gradient field 
abla fn (normalized volume sample gradient). Light vectors Li (unit vectors, i=1 \dots NL). Illuminated object color Ii (from transfer function or base color). Gaseous illumination color IG (from transfer function). Parameters: k{ta}, k{td}, k{ty}, k{tb}. Outputs: Final color c for each volume sample. Data Structures: Colors are 3-component vectors (R, G, B). 
abla fn is a normalized 3D vector. L is a normalized 3D vector. Parameters: k{ta}: Controls gaseous illumination amount. Typical: 1.0. k{td}: Controls directed illumination amount. Typical: 0.6. k{ty}: Warm tone intensity. Typical: 0.3. k{tb}: Cool tone intensity. Typical: 0.3. NL: Number of light sources. Note: More than a few lights likely results in confusing images. Formulas: 1. Warm color: cw = (k{ty}, k{ty}, 0). 2. Cool color: cc = (0, 0, k{tb}). 3. Tone contribution per light: It = \left( rac{1.0 + 
abla fn \cdot L}{2}ight) cw + \left(1 -  rac{1.0 + 
abla fn \cdot L}{2}ight) cc 4. Directed illumination contribution per light: Io =  egin{cases} k{td} Ii (
abla fn \cdot L) & 	ext{if } 
abla fn \cdot L > 0 \ 0 & 	ext{if } 
abla fn \cdot L \le 0 \end{cases} 5. Final color: c = k{ta} IG + \sum{i=1}^{NL} (It + Io) Pitfalls: Using more than a few light sources results in confusing images because humans are not used to interpreting complex illumination from many lights. The directed illumination Io is zero when the gradient is orthogonal to the light, unlike standard diffuse models which might use absolute values or different clamping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeillustrationtoneshading(gradient, lightvectors, Ii, IG, kta=1.0, ktd=0.6, kty=0.3, ktb=0.3): """ Compute color for a volume sample using Volume Illustration Tone Shading. Args: gradient: Normalized 3D vector (nx, ny, nz). lightvectors: List of normalized 3D light direction vectors. Ii: Illuminated object color (3D vector). IG: Gaseous illumination color (3D vector). kta: Gaseous illumination weight. ktd: Directed illumination weight. kty: Warm tone intensity. ktb: Cool tone intensity. Returns: Final color (3D vector). """ # Define tone colors cw = (kty, kty, 0.0) cc = (0.0, 0.0, ktb) # Initialize result color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Add gaseous illumination color = vectoradd(color, vectorscale(IG, kta)) # Sum contributions from all lights for L in lightvectors: # Compute dot product dot = vectordot(gradient, L) # Compute tone contribution It # It = ((1.0 + dot) / 2) cw + (1 - (1.0 + dot) / 2) cc t1 = (1.0 + dot) / 2.0 t2 = 1.0 - t1 It = vectoradd(vectorscale(cw, t1), vectorscale(cc, t2)) # Compute directed illumination contribution Io if dot > 0: Io = vectorscale(Ii, ktd dot) else: Io = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Add to total color = vectoradd(color, vectoradd(It, Io)) return color def vectoradd(v1, v2): return (v1[0] + v2[0], v1[1] + v2[1], v1[2] + v2[2]) def vectorscale(v, s): return (v[0] s, v[1] s, v[2] s) def vectordot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] A shading technique applied in the fragment shader using vertex normals sampled on the fly. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of volume samples and the number of light sources NL. Each sample requires NL dot products and vector operations. Memory Complexity: Low, primarily storing the volume data and gradients. No large auxiliary buffers required beyond standard volume rendering structures. Performance: Depends on hardware acceleration for volume ray casting or slicing. The per-sample computation is lightweight but involves multiple vector operations per light. Strengths: Enhances shape perception by providing continuous tone variation and directional cues. Preserves base tissue colors while adding illustrative depth. Effective for medical volumes where structure clarity is key. Limitations: Can become visually confusing with many light sources. Relies on accurate gradient estimation, which can be noisy in low-resolution or noisy data. When to use: When illustrative clarity and shape perception are prioritized over photorealism, especially in medical or scientific visualization. When not to use: When photorealistic rendering is required, or when the scene has many light sources that would create visual clutter. Originated in the paper "Non-Photorealistic Rendering of Volume Models". It extends Gooch shading to volume data by using volume gradients instead of surface normals and modifying the directed illumination component to be zero at orthogonal orientations, aligning with diffuse illumination models. It is used in medical visualization to enhance the perception of 3D structures like liver, kidney, and intestine. Non-Photorealistic Rendering of Volume Models, https://userpages.cs.umbc.edu/ebert/npr/volillus.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gooch Shading
head: Central Difference Normal Shading, Gooch Shading with Central Difference Normals, Gooch Tone Shading
body: Gooch Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model applied to volume rendering isosurfaces, combining cool/warm color mapping with directional shading based on the angle between the surface normal and the light vector. It is distinguished from standard Gooch shading by its specific integration with central difference normal estimation in rasterization pipelines, ensuring consistent visual output across different extraction methods (rasterization vs. ray-marching). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar volume data, camera parameters, light direction vector \mathbf{l}, and base cool/warm color parameters. Output: Fragment color with Gooch shading applied. Data Structures: Vertex Normals: Computed on the fly using central differences. No pre-computed normal buffer is required for the rasterization approach described in the sources. Fragment Shader State: Receives interpolated vertex normals and light direction. Steps: 1. Normal Estimation: For each vertex or sample point on the isosurface, compute the normal \mathbf{n} using the central difference method on the scalar field values. Let V(x, y, z) be the scalar value at grid coordinates (x, y, z). The normal \mathbf{n} is proportional to the gradient \nabla V: \mathbf{n} = \nabla V = \left[ \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} \right] The partial derivatives are computed as central differences: \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} \approx \frac{V(x+1, y, z) - V(x-1, y, z)}{2} (Similarly for y and z). Normalize \mathbf{n} to unit length. 2. Pass to Fragment Shader: The computed normals are passed to the fragment shader. 3. Gooch Shading Application: In the fragment shader, apply the Gooch shading model using the normal \mathbf{n} and light direction \mathbf{l}. Compute the dot product d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}. Map d to a color using the Gooch cool/warm color scheme. The specific color mapping formula is not detailed in the provided sources, but it relies on the original Gooch shading model [GGSC98] cited in. The fragment shader implementation is identical for both rasterization-based approaches and the ray-marching reference. Parameters: Cool Color: Not specified in sources. Warm Color: Not specified in sources. Light Direction: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Central difference requires neighbors. At volume boundaries, appropriate handling (e.g., clamping, mirroring, or using one-sided differences) is implied but not explicitly detailed in the sources. Degenerate Normals: If the scalar field is flat (zero gradient), the normal is undefined. This is not addressed in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecentraldifferencenormal(volume, x, y, z): """ Compute normal at (x, y, z) using central differences. Assumes volume is accessible and indices are valid. Boundary handling is not specified in sources. """ # Compute partial derivatives using central differences # Note: Source mentions central difference method but does not provide exact boundary handling. # We assume standard central difference with clamping or similar for boundaries. dx = (volume[x + 1, y, z] - volume[x - 1, y, z]) / 2.0 dy = (volume[x, y + 1, z] - volume[x, y - 1, z]) / 2.0 dz = (volume[x, y, z + 1] - volume[x, y, z - 1]) / 2.0 normal = normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) return normal def goocheshadingfragment(normal, lightdirection, coolcolor, warmcolor): """ Apply Gooch shading. Formula details not provided in sources. Relies on original Gooch shading model [GGSC98]. """ # Compute dot product dotproduct = dot(normal, normalize(lightdirection)) # Map dot product to color using Gooch cool/warm scheme # Specific mapping function is not detailed in sources color = applygoochcolormapping(dotproduct, coolcolor, warmcolor) return color Applied to direct isosurface rasterization. Uses central difference normals computed on the fly. Ensures consistency with ray-marching reference. Applied in ray-marching reference. Computes normals in the same way (central difference) when an isosurface intersection is found. Uses identical fragment shader implementation. Time Complexity: Normal computation is O(1) per vertex/sample. Shading is O(1) per fragment. Memory Complexity: No additional memory for normals if computed on the fly. Measured Performance: Not specified in sources. Strengths: Consistent visual appearance across different rendering techniques (rasterization and ray-marching). Limitations: Relies on central difference normal estimation, which may be sensitive to noise or boundaries. Gooch Shading was originally proposed by Gooch et al. in 1998 [GGSC98], cited in. It is used in volume rendering to provide illustrative shading that enhances shape perception. The specific application with central difference normals in rasterization is described in.
