name: Line Illustration Detection
head: Analytical and pixel-based line detection, Line detection in NPR
body: Line Illustration Detection is a family of Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) techniques designed to detect and render lines within volume data to communicate structure, shape, and boundaries. It solves the problem of visualizing complex geometry and internal structures in volumetric datasets where traditional photorealistic rendering may obscure topological details. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its specific focus on line-based abstraction rather than surface shading or contour outlines; it distinguishes itself from Face-based volume rendering with edge highlights by generating lines that represent intrinsic surface properties (like curvature) rather than just silhouette edges, and from Outline and Contour Generation by often utilizing vector-oriented or texture-based approaches that are viewpoint-independent or analytically derived, rather than purely image-space depth-difference extraction. The family is unified by the categorization of detection methods into two primary paradigms: analytical and pixel-based. 1. Analytical Approaches: These are vector-oriented and resolution-independent. They rely on explicit analytical representations of the model or volume data. Because they are vector-based, they can be transformed (rotated, scaled) without introducing aliasing artifacts. They are considered more general and flexible but require the availability of explicit analytical forms. 2. Pixel-Based Approaches: These are image-space methods, often utilizing G-buffers (storing geometric properties like depth, normal, or color). They are generally faster and simpler to implement than analytical methods. They are employed when explicit analytical representations are not available or practical. A key advantage is that G-buffers can be reused without recalculation, and 2D image processing operators are fast. Both approaches aim to generate lines that enhance the perception of form, with the choice between them dictated by the availability of analytical data and performance constraints. A technique for visualizing volume isosurfaces by advecting particles along principal curvature directions to create line textures that communicate surface shape. It is a specific application of line illustration that leverages perceptual psychology findings that lines in principal directions of curvature communicate surface shape better than lines in other directions. Steps: 1. Calculate the set of principal directions and principal curvatures in the volume. 2. Place an evenly distributed set of tiny opaque particles on the isosurfaces of interest. 3. Advect the particles through the vector field defined by the principal directions. 4. Treat the paths of the particles defined by this advection as a 3D line texture. Parameters: Particle distribution is evenly distributed on isosurfaces. Pitfalls: Algorithmic efficiency and artistic line quality must be addressed for NPR applicability. Showing line direction alone is not necessarily sufficient for an aesthetically pleasing rendering. A technique simulating the aesthetic of copper plate etching by intersecting a scene with closely-spaced, equidistant, parallel planes to detect surface curves. It mimics the historical transfer of images from etched grooves in a copper plate to paper. Steps: 1. Intersect the scene with a set of closely-spaced, equidistant, parallel planes. 2. Use a modified ray tracer to detect the surface curves resulting from these intersections. 3. Use G-buffers containing geometric properties such as colour and depth to modulate the final line style. The concept of using line illustrations for scientific visualization has historical roots in copper plate printing, which was used for centuries in scientific publications before modern photographic reproduction techniques. In the context of digital volume rendering, practical issues in properly detecting and rendering lines became a necessary consideration for many NPR systems. Various techniques were proposed (e.g., [Str86, HLW93, BS00]), generally optimized for different circumstances. The distinction between analytical and pixel-based methods is well-established in the literature. Analytic approaches are noted for being resolution-independent and transformable without artifacts, while pixel-based methods like Saito and Takahashi's G-buffers offer speed and simplicity. Hertzmann provided a useful survey of image space outline generation algorithms [Her99]. Specific applications to volume data emerged in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Interrante et al. introduced the principal direction line texture technique starting with [Int97], leveraging perceptual psychology literature [GIHL00] to justify the use of principal curvature directions. This method offered viewpoint independence and the ability to visualize multiple isosurfaces simultaneously. In 2001, Csébfalvi et al. presented a fast NPR volume visualization technique based on object contours, which relied on locally high gradient values to estimate physical boundaries [CMH+01]. Leister's work on copper plate etching simulation demonstrated how geometric intersections and G-buffers could be combined to create stylized line art. These techniques are considered cost-effective tools for generating graphical illustrations from volume datasets and enhancing the extraction of meaningful information. name: Face-based volume rendering with edge highlights
head: Volume Color and Highlight Edges Rendering
body: This method renders volumetric data by coloring scalar cells based on their average value while simultaneously detecting and highlighting topological edges (faces of tetrahedra or quads) to provide structural clarity. It distinguishes itself from Line Illustration Detection by operating on face-based primitives rather than extracted skeletal lines, and from Outline and Contour Generation by integrating edge highlights directly into the volume fragment shader rather than post-processing silhouettes. The technique uses a Per-Pixel Linked List (PPLL) structure to manage fragment depth sorting, allowing for correct alpha blending of semi-transparent volume cells and sharp edge highlights in a single pass. Inputs: Geometry: A set of faces (quads or triangles) representing the volume mesh. For each fragment, the shader receives: vFragmentPositionWorld: World-space position of the fragment. vVertexPositions[4]: World-space positions of the four vertices of the face. vVertexAttributes[4]: Scalar values at each vertex. vLineAttributes[4]: Importance/weight flags for each edge (1.0 if important, 0.0 otherwise). vEdgeLodValues[4]: Level-of-Detail (LOD) values for each edge. Textures: uCellScalarTex: A 2D texture where each texel stores the scalar value for a cell/face. Uniforms: uLineWidth: Base width of the edge highlight. uMaxLodValue: Maximum LOD scale factor. uSelectedLodValueFocus, uSelectedLodValueContext: Thresholds for LOD selection in focus and context regions. uImportantLineBoostFactor: Threshold to distinguish important lines. uSphereCenter, uSphereRadius: Defines the "focus" region (sphere) for depth cueing. uCameraPosition, uLookingDirection: Camera parameters. uScalarMin, uScalarMax: Scalar range for normalization. uEdgeColor, uBackgroundColor, uForegroundColor: Color palette. uViewportSize: Viewport dimensions in pixels. uFovY: Vertical field of view. Outputs: Blended Color: The final RGBA color for the fragment. Depth: The depth value for the fragment, used for PPLL insertion. The method relies on a Per-Pixel Linked List (PPLL) structure implemented via GPU textures to handle depth sorting of overlapping fragments (volume cells and edge highlights). 1. Start Offset Buffer (startOffsetImage): Format: R32UI (Unsigned 32-bit Integer, Red channel only). Dimensions: W \times H (Viewport width and height). Layout: Each pixel stores the index of the head of the linked list for that screen coordinate. Initialization: All values set to 0xFFFFFFFF (-1), acting as the end-of-list sentinel. 2. Fragment Buffer (fragmentBufferImage): Format: RGBA32UI (Unsigned 32-bit Integer, 4 channels). Dimensions: W \times H. Layout: Each pixel represents a node in the linked list. Channel R: Color (or part of it, depending on implementation details not fully specified, but typically used for color/depth packing in PPLL). Note: The source code initializes this to zero. The exact packing of color/depth/next-pointer into RGBA32UI is implied by the PPLL gather step but not explicitly detailed in the provided shader snippets. We assume standard PPLL packing: e.g., R=nextindex, G=depth, B/R=color components, or similar. Correction based on standard PPLL: Usually, one buffer stores the list head, and another stores the nodes. The node structure typically contains: nextindex, depth, color. The provided code initializes fragmentBufferImage to zeros. The gatherFragmentCustomDepth function (not fully shown) likely reads this buffer to resolve the final color. 1. Calculate Edge Width and Radius: Compute normalized distance to focus point: d{norm} = \text{distanceToFocusPointNormalized}. Calculate effective line width: eWidthPrime = uLineWidth \times (-d{norm} \times 0.3 + 1.0). Calculate line radius: lineRadius = eWidthPrime / 2.0. 2. Compute Volume Cell Color: Calculate cell scalar value: cellScalar = 0.25 \times \sum{i=0}^{3} vVertexAttributes[i]. Normalize scalar: t = \frac{cellScalar - uScalarMin}{\max(uScalarMax - uScalarMin, 10^{-6})}. Get base color: baseColor = colormap(t). Set volume color: volumeColor = vec4(baseColor, 1.0). Apply context factor: volumeColor.a \times= contextFactor. 3. Initialize LOD Constants: Define epsilon: LOD\EPSILON = 0.001. Calculate discrete LOD thresholds: discreteSelectedLodValueFocus = \max(uSelectedLodValueFocus \times uMaxLodValue, LOD\EPSILON). discreteSelectedLodValueContext = \max(uSelectedLodValueContext \times uMaxLodValue, LOD\EPSILON). 4. Initialize Distance Tracking: Set minDistance = 10^9, minDistanceIndex = 0, minDistanceAll = 10^9, minDistanceIndexAll = 0, isLineNear = false. 5. Iterate Over Edges (i = 0 to 3): Calculate distance to line segment: currentDistance = getDistanceToLineSegment(vFragmentPositionWorld, vVertexPositions[i], vVertexPositions[(i+1)\%4]). Calculate LOD level for focus: isImportant = (vLineAttributes[i] < 1.0 - uImportantLineBoostFactor) ? 0.0: 1.0. lodLevelFocus = \max(isImportant \times uMaxLodValue, discreteSelectedLodValueFocus). Calculate LOD line value: lodLineValue = vEdgeLodValues[i]. Calculate discrete LOD value: discreteLodValue = lodLineValue \times uMaxLodValue. Calculate LOD opacity factor: condContext = (discreteLodValue \le discreteSelectedLodValueContext + LOD\EPSILON) ? 1.0: 0.0. condFocus = (discreteLodValue \le discreteSelectedLodValueFocus + LOD\EPSILON) ? 1.0: 0.0. lodLevelOpacityFactor = mix(condContext, condFocus, focusFactor). Determine if line should be drawn: drawLine = (lodLevelOpacityFactor > 0.01). Update minimum distances: If currentDistance < minDistance and drawLine: minDistance = currentDistance. minDistanceIndex = i. isLineNear = true. If currentDistance < minDistanceAll: minDistanceAll = currentDistance. minDistanceIndexAll = i. 6. Calculate Edge Highlight Color (if near line): If isLineNear and minDistance \le lineRadius: Calculate depth cue factor: depthCueFactor = \min(contextFactor, focusFactor). Retrieve LOD value for the closest line: lodLineValue = vEdgeLodValues[minDistanceIndex]. Calculate LOD opacity factor for the line: condContext = (lodLineValue \le uSelectedLodValueContext + LOD\EPSILON) ? 1.0: 0.0. condFocus = (lodLineValue \le uSelectedLodValueFocus + LOD\EPSILON) ? 1.0: 0.0. lodLevelOpacityFactor = mix(condContext, condFocus, focusFactor). Calculate base line color: lineBaseColor = uEdgeColor. lineBaseColorFocus = mix(lineBaseColor, uBackgroundColor, 0.3). lineBaseColorContext = mix(baseColor, uForegroundColor, 0.3). lineBaseColor = mix(lineBaseColorContext, lineBaseColorFocus, focusFactor). Calculate line coordinates: lineCoordinates = \max(minDistance / lineRadius, 0.0). Calculate anti-aliasing factor: EPSILON = clamp(getAntialiasingFactor(fragmentDistance / lineRadius), 0.0, 0.49). Calculate coverage: coverage = 1.0 - smoothstep(1.0 - 2.0 \times EPSILON, 1.0, lineCoordinates). Set line color: lineColor = vec4(lineBaseColor, coverage \times lodLevelOpacityFactor). 7. Alpha Blend: Perform back-to-front alpha blend: blendedColor.a = lineColor.a + volumeColor.a \times (1.0 - lineColor.a). blendedColor.rgb = lineColor.rgb \times lineColor.a + volumeColor.rgb \times volumeColor.a \times (1.0 - lineColor.a). Premultiply if alpha is significant: If blendedColor.a > 10^{-4}, blendedColor.rgb /= blendedColor.a. 8. Store Fragment: Call gatherFragmentCustomDepth(blendedColor, fragmentDistance). This function inserts the fragment into the PPLL structure for later resolution. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def facebasedvolumerendering(vFragmentPositionWorld, vVertexPositions, vVertexAttributes, vLineAttributes, vEdgeLodValues, uLineWidth, uMaxLodValue, uSelectedLodValueFocus, uSelectedLodValueContext, uImportantLineBoostFactor, uSphereCenter, uSphereRadius, uCameraPosition, uLookingDirection, uScalarMin, uScalarMax, uEdgeColor, uBackgroundColor, uForegroundColor, uViewportSize, uFovY, contextFactor, focusFactor): # Step 1: Edge Width and Radius distanceToFocusPointNormalized = calculatedistancetofocus(vFragmentPositionWorld, uSphereCenter, uSphereRadius) eWidthPrime = uLineWidth (-distanceToFocusPointNormalized 0.3 + 1.0) lineRadius = eWidthPrime / 2.0 # Step 2: Volume Cell Color cellScalar = 0.25 sum(vVertexAttributes) t = (cellScalar - uScalarMin) / max(uScalarMax - uScalarMin, 1e-6) baseColor = colormap(clamp(t, 0.0, 1.0)) volumeColor = vec4(baseColor, 1.0) volumeColor.a = contextFactor # Step 3: LOD Constants LODEPSILON = 0.001 discreteSelectedLodValueFocus = max(uSelectedLodValueFocus uMaxLodValue, LODEPSILON) discreteSelectedLodValueContext = max(uSelectedLodValueContext uMaxLodValue, LODEPSILON) # Step 4: Initialize Distance Tracking minDistance = 1e9 minDistanceIndex = 0 minDistanceAll = 1e9 minDistanceIndexAll = 0 isLineNear = False # Step 5: Iterate Over Edges for i in range(4): currentDistance = getdistancetolinesegment(vFragmentPositionWorld, vVertexPositions[i], vVertexPositions[(i + 1) % 4]) isImportant = 1.0 if vLineAttributes[i] >= (1.0 - uImportantLineBoostFactor) else 0.0 lodLevelFocus = max(isImportant uMaxLodValue, discreteSelectedLodValueFocus) lodLineValue = vEdgeLodValues[i] discreteLodValue = lodLineValue uMaxLodValue condContext = 1.0 if discreteLodValue <= (discreteSelectedLodValueContext + LODEPSILON) else 0.0 condFocus = 1.0 if discreteLodValue <= (discreteSelectedLodValueFocus + LODEPSILON) else 0.0 lodLevelOpacityFactor = mix(condContext, condFocus, focusFactor) drawLine = lodLevelOpacityFactor > 0.01 if currentDistance < minDistance and drawLine: minDistance = currentDistance minDistanceIndex = i isLineNear = True if currentDistance < minDistanceAll: minDistanceAll = currentDistance minDistanceIndexAll = i # Step 6: Edge Highlight Color lineColor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if isLineNear and minDistance <= lineRadius: depthCueFactor = min(contextFactor, focusFactor) lodLineValue = vEdgeLodValues[minDistanceIndex] condContext = 1.0 if lodLineValue <= (uSelectedLodValueContext + LODEPSILON) else 0.0 condFocus = 1.0 if lodLineValue <= (uSelectedLodValueFocus + LODEPSILON) else 0.0 lodLevelOpacityFactor = mix(condContext, condFocus, focusFactor) lineBaseColor = uEdgeColor lineBaseColorFocus = mix(lineBaseColor, uBackgroundColor, 0.3) lineBaseColorContext = mix(baseColor, uForegroundColor, 0.3) lineBaseColor = mix(lineBaseColorContext, lineBaseColorFocus, focusFactor) lineCoordinates = max(minDistance / lineRadius, 0.0) EPSILON = clamp(getantialiasingfactor(fragmentDistance / lineRadius, uViewportSize, uFovY), 0.0, 0.49) coverage = 1.0 - smoothstep(1.0 - 2.0 EPSILON, 1.0, lineCoordinates) lineColor = vec4(lineBaseColor, coverage lodLevelOpacityFactor) # Step 7: Alpha Blend blendedColor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) blendedColor.a = lineColor.a + volumeColor.a (1.0 - lineColor.a) blendedColor.rgb = lineColor.rgb lineColor.a + volumeColor.rgb volumeColor.a (1.0 - lineColor.a) if blendedColor.a > 1e-4: blendedColor.rgb /= blendedColor.a # Step 8: Store Fragment gatherfragmentcustomdepth(blendedColor, fragmentDistance) return blendedColor def getantialiasingfactor(distance, viewportSize, fovY): return distance / viewportSize.y fovY def mix(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def clamp(x, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(x, maxval)) def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = clamp((x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0), 0.0, 1.0) return t t (3 - 2 t) def vec4(r, g, b, a): return {'r': r, 'g': g, 'b': b, 'a': a} def sum(lst): return sum(lst) def max(a, b): return a if a > b else b def min(a, b): return a if a < b else b uLineWidth: Not given in the sources. uMaxLodValue: Not given in the sources. uSelectedLodValueFocus, uSelectedLodValueContext: Not given in the sources. uImportantLineBoostFactor: Not given in the sources. LODEPSILON: 0.001. uSphereRadius: Not given in the sources. Precision: The use of 1e-6 in denominator normalization prevents division by zero if uScalarMax == uScalarMin. Boundaries: The clamp function is used for lineCoordinates and EPSILON to ensure valid ranges for smoothstep and anti-aliasing calculations. Degenerate Input: If uScalarMax - uScalarMin is zero, the scalar normalization uses 1e-6 as the denominator. If lineRadius is zero, division by zero may occur in lineCoordinates calculation; however, uLineWidth and focus factor should prevent this in practice. Extracts skeletal lines from volume data for stylized rendering. Choose when a more abstract, line-based representation is desired. Link Generates silhouettes and contours in post-processing. Choose when edge detection needs to be decoupled from volume shading or when using screen-space techniques. Link Uses Laplacian of Gaussian for edge detection. Choose when robustness to noise is required. Link Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of faces/fragments. The PPLL insertion and gathering are also linear in the number of fragments per pixel, but worst-case can be O(K) where K is the number of overlapping fragments. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the PPLL buffers (startOffsetImage and fragmentBufferImage), where W and H are viewport dimensions. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with viewport resolution due to PPLL buffer size. Strengths: Integrates edge highlights directly with volume shading, providing clear structural information. Uses PPLL for correct depth sorting without requiring complex sorting algorithms. Limitations: Requires PPLL buffer management. Performance may degrade with high fragment density per pixel. When to Use: When structural clarity is needed in volume rendering, and edge highlights are desired. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and fragment density is very high, or when a purely photorealistic rendering is desired without stylized edges. This method is derived from the "ClearView" rendering technique, specifically the "HexMeshUnified" fragment shader implementation. It is part of a broader effort to provide illustrative volume rendering with edge highlights. The technique is implemented in the "geresim-spike" project, which is an unofficial implementation. name: Clipping plane for volume suppression
head: Clip Plane, Clipping Plane Widget, Clipping plane, Cut Planes, Cutaway view generation, Frame type widget
body: A clipping plane is an independently movable planar surface used to suppress portions of a volume dataset, enabling the generation of cutaway views. Unlike the parent Cropping technique, which uses axis-aligned slabs, this method employs a plane at an arbitrary angle with a defined thickness. It differs from Clipping by explicitly defining a visible slab between two parallel surfaces rather than a half-space, and from Variance Clipping by using geometric distance rather than statistical variance to determine visibility. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset, plane normal vector \mathbf{n} = (A, B, C), plane offsets D{\min} and D{\max}, falloff width D{\text{fallo}}, and sample opacity \alpha{\text{shade}} from the shading stage. Output: Modified opacity \alpha{\text{final}} for each sample. Data Structures: The clipping plane is defined by two parallel plane equations. The plane normal (A, B, C) is typically normalized such that A^2 + B^2 + C^2 = 1. The parameters D{\min} and D{\max} represent the signed distance from the origin to the inner and outer faces, respectively. Steps: 1. For each sample point \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z) along the ray, calculate the signed distance d from the origin to the plane defined by the normal \mathbf{n}: d = Ax + By + Cz 2. Determine the sample's position relative to the cut plane boundaries: If d < D{\min}, the sample is outside the cut plane (on the "back" side). If d > D{\max}, the sample is outside the cut plane (on the "front" side). If D{\min} \le d \le D{\max}, the sample is inside the cut plane. 3. Calculate the correction factor f based on the distance d and the falloff parameter D{\text{fallo}}: If d < D{\min}: f = 0 If D{\min} \le d < D{\min} + D{\text{fallo}}: f = \frac{d - D{\min}}{D{\text{fallo}}} If D{\min} + D{\text{fallo}} \le d \le D{\max} - D{\text{fallo}}: f = 1 If D{\max} - D{\text{fallo}} < d \le D{\max}: f = \frac{D{\max} - d}{D{\text{fallo}}} If d > D{\max}: f = 0 4. Compute the final opacity: \alpha{\text{final}} = \alpha{\text{shade}} \times f Parameters: D{\text{fallo}}: Falloff parameter specifying the width of the transition region from full opacity to zero. In VolumePro, this was set to 5 voxels in examples. Single plane support: The implementation described in VolumePro supports only a single cut plane. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If D{\min} = D{\max}, the thickness is zero, potentially causing numerical instability in the falloff calculation if not handled. Visibility Logic: Samples can be made visible only if they are outside the cut plane, which inverts the logic of the correction factor f (i.e., f=1 outside, f=0 inside). Smooth Edges: Without D{\text{fallo}}, edges appear aliased. The linear falloff provides smooth transitions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyclippingplane(x, y, z, A, B, C, Dmin, Dmax, Dfallo, alphashade): # Calculate signed distance from origin to the plane at point (x,y,z) # Assumes A, B, C is normalized d = A x + B y + C z # Determine correction factor f if d < Dmin: f = 0.0 elif d < Dmin + Dfallo: # Linear ramp up from 0 to 1 f = (d - Dmin) / Dfallo elif d <= Dmax - Dfallo: # Full opacity f = 1.0 elif d <= Dmax: # Linear ramp down from 1 to 0 f = (Dmax - d) / Dfallo else: # Outside the other side f = 0.0 return alphashade f A variant that cuts the sample after it has been played for a specific number of ticks. This implies a temporal or sequential clipping mechanism rather than purely spatial, though details on its integration with the spatial clipping plane are not provided in the sources. Complexity: The operation is O(1) per sample, involving basic arithmetic operations (multiplication, addition, comparison). Performance: As implemented in VolumePro, it supports real-time ray-casting. Strengths: Allows arbitrary orientation for cutaway views, which is more flexible than axis-aligned cropping. The falloff parameter prevents visual artifacts at the cut boundaries. Limitations: VolumePro implementation supports only a single cut plane, limiting complex internal inspections. Use Cases: Ideal for examining cross-sections of segmented objects or internal structures without removing the entire outer shell. The concept of an independently movable clipping plane for suppressing volume data was originally mentioned in [GK96] and implemented in the SIV system. It was later detailed in the VolumePro real-time ray-casting system, which supported a single cut plane with configurable falloff. The clipping plane widget was also described in the context of interactive volume rendering using multi-dimensional transfer functions, where it served as a frame-type widget reporting orientation and position to the volume widget. name: Clipping
head: Front Clipping for Perspective Projection, Near-plane clipping, Viewpoint-relative slab clipping
body: Clipping is a technique to enable correct perspective projection in sliced-based volume rendering by defining a near clipping boundary relative to the viewpoint. It solves the problem of incorrect depth impression in inside views, where parallel projection fails to provide accurate spatial cues. Unlike general cropping which cuts along volume faces, this method clips against the camera's near plane and active clipping planes to ensure only relevant slabs are processed. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: ren: A renderer pointer providing camera state (viewpoint, orientation, near plane distance) and active clipping plane definitions. worldBounds[6]: A double array containing the unclipped world-space bounding box coordinates of the volume. vol: A volume pointer providing the volume's transformation matrix and clipping state flags. Outputs: A set of slabs (or primitives) that lie within the valid viewing frustum and beyond the near clipping plane. Data structures: Bounding Box: Represented as an array of 6 doubles: [minX, maxX, minY, maxY, minZ, maxZ] in world coordinates. Clipping Planes: Defined by the renderer's state, typically as plane equations ax + by + cz + d = 0. Steps: 1. Retrieve the camera's near plane distance d{near} and the world-space bounding box worldBounds. 2. Transform the volume's bounding box into the camera's view space using the volume's transformation matrix and the camera's view matrix. 3. Clip the transformed bounding box against the camera's near plane. The near plane is defined by the distance from the viewpoint along the view direction. 4. Clip the resulting box against any additional active clipping planes defined in ren. 5. Determine the first slab to be processed. The user specifies or the system calculates the distance from the viewpoint to this first slab, ensuring it is \ge d{near}. 6. Render only slabs beyond this defined distance to ensure correct depth impression for inside views. Formulas: Let P{view} be a point in view space. The near plane condition is: P{view} \cdot \mathbf{v}{dir} \ge d{near} where \mathbf{v}{dir} is the normalized view direction vector. For a slab at distance d{slab} from the viewpoint, it is rendered if: d{slab} \ge d{near}. Parameters: ren: VTK renderer pointer. worldBounds: Array of 6 doubles. vol: VTK volume pointer. Edge cases and pitfalls: Inside Views: Without front clipping, perspective projection artifacts occur because slabs behind the viewpoint might be rendered or ordered incorrectly. Precision: Ensure that the near plane distance is not set to zero or negative values, which can cause division by zero or incorrect clipping logic. Degenerate Input: If the volume is entirely behind the near plane, no slabs are rendered. Definition: A clipping operator that keeps or drops each Gaussian primitive entirely based on whether its center lies within the half-space defined by the clip plane. It adds no per-pixel attenuation factor. Steps: For each primitive, compute the dot product of the clip normal \mathbf{n} and the primitive mean \boldsymbol{\mu}. If \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\mu} \le \tau, keep the primitive; otherwise, drop it. Pitfalls: Primitives straddling the clip plane either overshoot (if kept) or vanish (if dropped), producing a center-quantized boundary artifact as the plane sweeps. The decision is non-differentiable. Comparison: Unlike Moment-Matched (MM) and analytic operators, Hard Cull has no gradient through its binary decision and updates only kept primitives. Time and memory complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of slabs/primitives, as each is tested against the clipping planes. Memory complexity is minimal, requiring only the bounding box and plane definitions. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of clipping planes, as each plane adds a constant-time test per slab. Strengths and limitations: Strengths: Enables correct perspective projection for inside views, which is mandatory for accurate depth impression. Limitations: Does not handle partial occlusion or attenuation at the clipping boundary, leading to artifacts if primitives straddle the plane. When to use it and when not: Use when correct perspective projection is required, especially for inside views. Do not use when smooth attenuation at the clipping boundary is needed, in which case Moment-Matched or analytic clipping is preferred. Origin: The concept of front clipping for perspective projection was introduced to address limitations in sliced-based volume rendering systems like VolumePro, which lacked perspective projection support. The term "Front Clipping" was used in the Shear-Warp Factorization Volume Rendering System to solve the problem of incorrect depth impression in inside views. History and development: Early volume rendering systems like VolumePro supported only parallel projection and back-to-front compositing. The SWF VRS improved this by introducing perspective projection and front clipping. Modern implementations, such as those in VTK, integrate clipping with camera and volume state to handle complex scenes. In the context of Gaussian Splatting, Hard Cull was isolated as a binary operator to analyze the effects of clipping without learned components. Where it is used: Medical volume rendering, where inside views are common. General volume rendering systems that support perspective projection. Gaussian Splatting for volume rendering, as a baseline clipping operator. name: Variance Clipping
head: Variance-based history rectification, Statistical variance clipping
body: Variance clipping is a history rectification technique used in Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) for volumetric rendering that constructs a tight bounding box for valid color values based on the statistical mean and variance of a neighborhood of samples. It solves the problem of ghosting artifacts during rapid illumination changes by adapting the clipping region to the local signal distribution, allowing it to reconstruct signals faster than fixed-bound methods. It sets itself apart from AABB Clamping and AABB Clipping by using a statistically derived, typically smaller, clipping region that reacts more precisely to changes, though at the cost of higher temporal instability. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N color samples \{ci\} from the current frame's neighborhood (e.g., a pixel and its spatial/temporal neighbors), where each ci is a vector (typically RGB). Output: A clipping interval [c{min}, c{max}] for each color component, used to clamp or clip the history value. Data Structures: N: Integer count of samples in the neighborhood. ci: Vector of color values for sample i. \mu: Vector of sample means. \sigma: Vector of standard deviations. \gamma: Scalar user-defined parameter. Steps: 1. Compute the first sample moment m1 by summing all color samples component-wise: m1 = \sum{i=1}^N ci \quad (2.3) 2. Compute the second sample moment m2 by summing the squared color samples component-wise: m2 = \sum{i=1}^N ci^2 \quad (2.4) 3. Calculate the sample mean \mu by dividing m1 by N component-wise: \mu = \frac{1}{N}m1 \quad (2.5) 4. Calculate the standard deviation \sigma component-wise. First compute the variance estimate \frac{1}{N} m2 - \mu^2, take the absolute value to handle floating-point inaccuracies that might result in negative values, and then take the square root: \sigma = \sqrt{\left| \frac{1}{N} m2 - \mu^2 \right|} \quad (2.6) 5. Construct the clipping bounds using the user-defined gamma parameter \gamma: c{min} = \mu - \gamma \sigma \quad (2.7) c{max} = \mu + \gamma \sigma \quad (2.8) 6. Clip the history value c{hist} to the interval [c{min}, c{max}] for each component. Parameters: \gamma (Gamma): User-defined parameter controlling the size of the clipping box and the strength of clipping. Tighter bounds (smaller \gamma) allow faster adaptation to changes but increase temporal instability. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Pitfalls: Temporal Instability: Variance clipping exhibits the highest Temporal Instability (TI) relative to the baseline EMA among tested techniques. This is a direct trade-off for its ability to quickly reject incorrect history during rapid changes. Floating-Point Inaccuracy: The variance calculation \frac{1}{N} m2 - \mu^2 can yield negative values due to floating-point precision limits. The absolute value operation in Eq. (2.6) is required to prevent NaNs or errors. Color Correlation: Performing this rectification directly in RGB space can produce color-related artifacts because RGB channels are highly correlated, leading to poorly aligned bounding boxes. This is often mitigated by transforming to a luminance-chrominance space like YCoCg first. A variant that transforms colors into a luminance-chrominance space (YCoCg or YCrCb) before applying variance clipping. It decouples luminance and chrominance to orient the rectification bounds along the luma direction, reducing color-related ghosting and temporal color bleeding. Choose this when RGB-based variance clipping causes color bleeding or poor alignment with the color distribution. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of samples in the neighborhood. The operations are simple component-wise arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel (storing m1, m2, \mu, \sigma). Measured Performance: In a step response scenario (light turning on), variance clipping produced the lowest RMSE (0.002977) among tested techniques, indicating it is the best at reconstructing the signal during quick illumination introduction. However, it exhibited the highest Temporal Instability (TI P = 0.004217, a 190.23% increase over baseline). Strengths: Tighter bounds allow the algorithm to adapt to changes much more quickly and precisely than fixed AABB methods. It operates entirely on current-frame data, making it easier to implement than methods requiring historical bounds. Limitations: High temporal instability can cause flickering or jitter in static scenes or scenes with subtle changes. Sensitive to the choice of \gamma. When to use: When rapid adaptation to illumination changes is prioritized over stability, or in scenes with high dynamic range lighting changes. When not to use: In static scenes or scenes with subtle temporal variations where stability is more important than rapid convergence. Variance clipping was introduced as an extension of clipping against the current frame color extent, relying instead on the statistical distribution of values in the neighborhood to produce a smaller clipping region. It is identified as the best technique at reconstructing signals during quick illumination introduction. The method is discussed in the context of Temporal Anti-Aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering. name: YCoCg Color Space Rectification
head: Color Space Selection for History Rectification, YCrCb Rectification
body: YCoCg Color Space Rectification is a history rectification technique used in Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) for volumetric rendering that transforms colors into a luminance-chrominance color space (specifically YCoCg or YCrCb) before applying clipping or clamping operations. It solves the problem of color-related ghosting artifacts and temporal color bleeding that occur when history rectification is performed directly in RGB space, where channels are highly correlated and bounding boxes are poorly aligned with the actual distribution of color samples. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives, such as AABB Clamping and Variance Clipping, is the explicit decoupling of luminance and chrominance to orient the rectification bounds along the luma direction, which typically has high local contrast while chroma does not. Inputs and outputs: Input: Current frame color sample C{curr} = [R, G, B]^T and historical color sample C{hist} = [R, G, B]^T (or their transformed equivalents). Output: Rectified color sample C{out} = [R, G, B]^T in RGB space. Data structures: Color vectors are 3-element arrays or tuples. Transform matrices are 3 \times 3 matrices. Rectification bounds (min/max) are computed per-channel in the target color space. Steps: 1. Transform to Color Space: Convert the current frame color C{curr} and the reprojected historical color C{hist} from RGB to the chosen luminance-chrominance space (YCoCg or YCrCb). 2. Compute Bounds: Determine the minimum and maximum values for each component (Y, Co/Cr, Cg/Cb) within the local neighborhood or based on the current frame's extent. This defines the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) in the transformed space. 3. Rectify History: Clamp or clip the historical color components C{hist}' to the computed bounds [mini, maxi] for each component i \in \{Y, Co/Cr, Cg/Cb\}. 4. Transform Back: Convert the rectified color C{rect}' from the luminance-chrominance space back to RGB space. 5. Blend: Use the rectified RGB color in the temporal blending process (e.g., with the current frame). Formulas: RGB to YCoCg Transform: \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Co \\ Cg \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{2} & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} Inverse YCoCg to RGB Transform: \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Co \\ Cg \end{bmatrix} RGB to YCrCb Transform: \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Cr \\ Cb \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.299 & 0.587 & 0.114 \\ -0.5 & -0.4187 & 0.0813 \\ -0.1687 & -0.3313 & -0.5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} Inverse YCrCb to RGB Transform: \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1.402 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.714 & -0.344 \\ 1 & 0 & 1.772 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Cr \\ Cb \end{bmatrix} Parameters: Color space selection: YCoCg or YCrCb. YCoCg is preferred for better decorrelation of luminance and chrominance. Edge cases and pitfalls: Luminance Artifacts: While YCoCg and YCrCb reduce chrominance color bleeding, they can increase luminance artifacts. For example, when color changes from green to blue, stale luminance information in the green channel may bleed into the next frame, visible as excess luminance around the light source. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is sufficient for the matrix multiplications. Ensure that the inverse transforms are applied correctly to avoid color shifts. Bound Computation: The bounds must be computed in the transformed space, not RGB space, to ensure the AABB is aligned with the luma direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rgbtoycocg(r, g, b): y = 0.25 r + 0.5 g + 0.25 b co = 0.5 r + 0.0 g - 0.5 b cg = -0.25 r + 0.5 g - 0.25 b return y, co, cg def ycocgtorgb(y, co, cg): r = y + co - cg g = y + cg b = y - co - cg return r, g, b def rgbtoycrcb(r, g, b): y = 0.299 r + 0.587 g + 0.114 b cr = -0.5 r - 0.4187 g + 0.0813 b cb = -0.1687 r - 0.3313 g - 0.5 b return y, cr, cb def ycrcbtorgb(y, cr, cb): r = y + 1.402 cr g = y - 0.714 cr - 0.344 cb b = y + 1.772 cb return r, g, b def rectifycolorinycocg(currentcolor, historicalcolor, boundsmin, boundsmax): """ Rectifies historical color using YCoCg space. currentcolor: tuple (R, G, B) historicalcolor: tuple (R, G, B) boundsmin: tuple (miny, minco, mincg) boundsmax: tuple (maxy, maxco, maxcg) """ # Transform to YCoCg ycurr, cocurr, cgcurr = rgbtoycocg(currentcolor) yhist, cohist, cghist = rgbtoycocg(historicalcolor) # Compute bounds if not provided (example: using current frame neighborhood stats) # In practice, boundsmin and boundsmax are derived from the local neighborhood # in YCoCg space. Here we assume they are pre-computed. # Clamp historical color components to bounds yhistrect = max(boundsmin[0], min(boundsmax[0], yhist)) cohistrect = max(boundsmin[1], min(boundsmax[1], cohist)) cghistrect = max(boundsmin[2], min(boundsmax[2], cghist)) # Transform back to RGB rout, gout, bout = ycocgtorgb(yhistrect, cohistrect, cghistrect) return (rout, gout, bout) def rectifycolorinycrcb(currentcolor, historicalcolor, boundsmin, boundsmax): """ Rectifies historical color using YCrCb space. currentcolor: tuple (R, G, B) historicalcolor: tuple (R, G, B) boundsmin: tuple (miny, mincr, mincb) boundsmax: tuple (maxy, maxcr, maxcb) """ # Transform to YCrCb ycurr, crcurr, cbcurr = rgbtoycrcb(currentcolor) yhist, crhist, cbhist = rgbtoycrcb(historicalcolor) # Clamp historical color components to bounds yhistrect = max(boundsmin[0], min(boundsmax[0], yhist)) crhistrect = max(boundsmin[1], min(boundsmax[1], crhist)) cbhistrect = max(boundsmin[2], min(boundsmax[2], cbhist)) # Transform back to RGB rout, gout, bout = ycrcbtorgb(yhistrect, crhistrect, cbhistrect) return (rout, gout, bout) AABB Clamping is a history rectification technique used in Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) to prevent ghosting artifacts by restricting reprojected historical color values to a valid range defined by the current frame. It solves the problem of temporal lag and ghosting during abrupt scene changes where a baseline Exponential Moving Average (EMA) fails to react quickly enough. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is its use of a simple Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) approximation constructed from per-channel minimum and maximum values, whereas History Rectification encompasses more sophisticated variants like Variance Clipping that handle color distributions more accurately. It builds on YCoCg Color Space Rectification, which transforms colors into a luminance-chrominance space before applying this rectification to reduce color-related ghosting. Transformation of volumetric samples into a specific color space before blending, then transforming back to RGB for storage. Evaluated spaces include RGB, YCoCg, and YCrCb. Time Complexity: The transformation and inverse transformation involve a constant number of arithmetic operations (matrix-vector multiplications), so the time complexity per sample is O(1). Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the storage for the color values and bounds. Measured Performance: YCoCg and YCrCb reduce chrominance color bleeding artifacts compared to RGB space. However, this comes at the cost of increased luminance artifacts in certain scenarios, such as when color changes from green to blue. Strengths: Reduces color-related ghosting and temporal color bleeding by decoupling luminance and chrominance. YCoCg provides better decorrelation than YCrCb. Limitations: Can introduce luminance artifacts when chrominance changes rapidly. Requires additional matrix multiplications. When to use: When color-related ghosting is a significant issue and the scene contains rapid color changes. When not to use: When luminance artifacts are more critical than chrominance artifacts, or when computational resources are extremely limited. YCoCg Color Space Rectification originates from research into temporal anti-aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering. It was explored as a method to improve the quality of TAA by addressing the limitations of RGB-space rectification. The technique leverages the properties of luminance-chrominance color spaces to better align the rectification bounds with the natural distribution of color data in images. name: AABB Clamping
head: AABB Clamping History Rectification
body: AABB Clamping is a history rectification technique used in Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) to prevent ghosting artifacts by restricting reprojected historical color values to a valid range defined by the current frame. It solves the problem of temporal lag and ghosting during abrupt scene changes where a baseline Exponential Moving Average (EMA) fails to react quickly enough. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is its use of a simple Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) approximation constructed from per-channel minimum and maximum values, whereas History Rectification encompasses more sophisticated variants like Variance Clipping that handle color distributions more accurately. It builds on YCoCg Color Space Rectification, which transforms colors into a luminance-chrominance space before applying this rectification to reduce color-related ghosting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The reprojected historical color ch (typically RGBA), and a set of N current-frame neighborhood samples ci \in \mathbb{R}^k (where k is the number of channels, e.g., 3 or 4). Output: The rectified color cr. Data Structures: AABB Bounds: Two vectors, c{min} and c{max}, each of size k. c{min}[j] = \min{i=1..N}(ci[j]) for each channel j. c{max}[j] = \max{i=1..N}(ci[j]) for each channel j. Steps: 1. Construct AABB: Compute the component-wise minimum and maximum across all current-frame neighborhood samples to define the bounding box bounds c{min} and c{max}. 2. Clamp: For each channel j of the historical color ch, clamp the value between the corresponding bounds c{min}[j] and c{max}[j]. Formula: The rectified color cr is obtained by clamping ch component-wise: cr = \min(\max(ch, c{min}), c{max}) \quad (2.2) where \min, \max, and arithmetic operations are performed component-wise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbclamp(historicalcolor, neighborhoodsamples): """ Rectifies historical color by clamping it to the AABB defined by neighborhood samples. Args: historicalcolor: List/Array of floats, shape (k,) representing ch. neighborhoodsamples: List/Array of floats, shape (N, k) representing ci. Returns: List/Array of floats, shape (k,) representing cr. """ # Step 1: Construct AABB bounds # cmin is the component-wise minimum of all neighborhood samples cmin = min(neighborhoodsamples, key=lambda x: x) # Conceptual min over array # cmax is the component-wise maximum of all neighborhood samples cmax = max(neighborhoodsamples, key=lambda x: x) # Conceptual max over array # Note: In implementation, this is done channel by channel: # cmin[j] = min(sample[j] for sample in neighborhoodsamples) # cmax[j] = max(sample[j] for sample in neighborhoodsamples) # Step 2: Clamp historical color to bounds rectifiedcolor = [] for j in range(len(historicalcolor)): val = historicalcolor[j] if val < cmin[j]: val = cmin[j] elif val > cmax[j]: val = cmax[j] rectifiedcolor.append(val) return rectifiedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner Accumulation: Because each channel is individually clamped, values tend to collect in the corners of the AABB. Color Artifacts: This corner accumulation can lead to strange color-related artifacts in scenes with significant color information, although it is generally not an issue for grayscale scenes. Accuracy: This method is a fast approximation of the tighter convex hull approach. It is less accurate but much cheaper to build and intersect against. Projects the historical color onto the AABB towards the current frame sample or the center of the box, rather than clamping channels individually. This better preserves temporal color gradients and reduces corner artifacts compared to clamping. Uses the statistical distribution (variance) of values in the neighborhood to create the bounds of the AABB used for clipping, offering a more robust handling of color information than simple min/max. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot k) to compute min/max over N samples with k channels, followed by O(k) for clamping. It is computationally efficient. Memory Complexity: O(k) to store the min and max bounds. Strengths: Fast approximation of history rectification; easy to implement and intersect against; ensures history remains within valid color extent. Limitations: Less accurate than convex hull methods; prone to color artifacts due to channel-wise clamping causing values to collect in AABB corners. When to use: When performance is critical and the scene is predominantly grayscale or has limited color variation. When not to use: In scenes with complex color information where color artifacts are noticeable, or when higher fidelity rectification (like AABB Clipping or Variance Clipping) is required. AABB Clamping is a history rectification method implemented and evaluated in the context of temporal anti-aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering. It serves as a fast approximation to the computationally expensive convex hull projection, which is too costly for real-time rendering constraints. The method is part of a class of techniques that correct historical color values before blending by restricting them to a region defined by current-frame neighborhood samples. name: History Rectification
head: AABB Clipping
body: History rectification is a class of Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) techniques that correct historical color values before blending by restricting the reprojected history to a region defined by current-frame neighborhood samples. It solves the problem of temporal lag and ghosting during abrupt scene changes (such as light introduction or sudden movement) where a baseline Exponential Moving Average (EMA) fails to react quickly enough. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is the use of a spatial neighborhood of current-frame samples to define a "color extent" or bound; if the historical value falls outside this extent, it is considered stale and is corrected (clamped or clipped) prior to blending. This approach builds on AABB Clamping, which uses a simpler Axis-Aligned Bounding Box approximation, whereas History Rectification encompasses more sophisticated variants like Variance Clipping and AABB Clipping that better handle color information and statistical distributions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The reprojected history buffer value H for the current pixel, and a neighborhood of current-frame color samples C{neighbor} (typically a 3x3 grid of pixels surrounding the current pixel). Output: A rectified history value H{rect} ready for blending with the current frame. Data Structures: Neighborhood Samples: A set of color vectors \{c1, c2,..., cn\} representing the RGB(A) values of the neighboring pixels in the current frame. Bounds: A minimum vector min and a maximum vector max defining the rectification region. For AABB-based methods, these are component-wise min/max. For Variance Clipping, these are derived from statistical moments. Steps: 1. Sample Neighborhood: Gather the color values of the neighboring pixels in the current frame. The standard evaluation uses a 3x3 neighborhood to avoid averaging across depth slices, which would act as a spatial stabilizer and hide flicker artifacts. Alternatives like 3x3x3 or 6-tap neighborhoods smooth across depth but are not used in the primary evaluation context. 2. Define Bounds: Calculate the bounding region based on the chosen variant (see Subtopics). For AABB variants: min = \min(ci), max = \max(ci) for each color channel independently. For Variance Clipping: Bounds are expanded beyond min/max using the standard deviation of the neighborhood values to account for statistical distribution. 3. Rectify History: Compare the reprojected history value H against the defined bounds. If H is within the bounds, H{rect} = H. If H is outside the bounds, H{rect} is adjusted to the nearest boundary value (clamping) or projected onto the boundary (clipping). 4. Blend: Blend H{rect} with the current frame color C{current} using the temporal blend factor \alpha (typically \alpha = 0.05 for evaluation comparability). Formulas: For AABB Clamping/Clipping, the rectified value for a single channel is: H{rect} = \text{clamp}(H, min, max) Where \text{clamp}(v, a, b) returns a if v < a, b if v > b, and v otherwise. For Variance Clipping, the bounds are extended by a factor of the standard deviation \sigma: min{var} = \mu - k \cdot \sigma max{var} = \mu + k \cdot \sigma Where \mu is the mean of the neighborhood, \sigma is the standard deviation, and k is a scaling factor (value not explicitly given in sources, but implied to be part of the method definition). Parameters: Neighborhood Size: 3x3 is the standard for evaluation to preserve depth separation. Blend Factor (\alpha): 0.05 is used in the cited evaluations to match baseline EMA conditions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Extent: When the light turns off, the neighborhood extent becomes 0 (a single point). The history is clamped to this point, eliminating temporal lag instantly. Gradual Color Change: AABB clamping struggles with gradual color transitions (e.g., red to blue fade). It exhibits a large RMSE spike when the color change completes and takes ~50 frames to converge, as clamping is less effective than clipping for introducing new color information. Temporal Instability (TI): Tighter bounds allow faster adaptation but increase TI, perceived as visual flicker. The distance between highest error peaks is exactly 16 frames, corresponding to the jitter sequence length. Grayscale Scenes: AABB clipping and clamping produce identical results in grayscale scenes because color rectification is irrelevant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def historyrectification(historyvalue, currentframecolor, neighborhoodcolors, method='aabbclamp'): """ Rectifies the history value based on the current frame neighborhood. Args: historyvalue: float or vec3, the reprojected history color. currentframecolor: float or vec3, the current frame's color. neighborhoodcolors: list of float or vec3, colors of neighboring pixels. method: str, one of 'aabbclamp', 'aabbclip', 'varianceclip'. Returns: float or vec3, the rectified history value. """ # Step 1: Calculate bounds from neighborhood if method == 'aabbclamp' or method == 'aabbclip': # Component-wise min and max minval = min(neighborhoodcolors, key=lambda c: c) # Assuming vector comparison or per-channel maxval = max(neighborhoodcolors, key=lambda c: c) # For vector colors, min/max is per-channel minval = vec3(min(c.x for c in neighborhoodcolors), min(c.y for c in neighborhoodcolors), min(c.z for c in neighborhoodcolors)) maxval = vec3(max(c.x for c in neighborhoodcolors), max(c.y for c in neighborhoodcolors), max(c.z for c in neighborhoodcolors)) if method == 'aabbclamp': # Clamp history to AABB rectified = clamp(historyvalue, minval, maxval) else: # aabbclip # Project history onto AABB (mathematically similar to clamp for axis-aligned boxes) # Note: Sources state AABB Clamp and Clip produce identical results in grayscale, # and generally imply similar bounding behavior for rectification. rectified = clamp(historyvalue, minval, maxval) elif method == 'varianceclip': # Calculate mean and standard deviation n = len(neighborhoodcolors) meanval = sum(neighborhoodcolors) / n # Calculate variance variance = sum((c - meanval)2 for c in neighborhoodcolors) / n stddev = sqrt(variance) # Define bounds using variance (k is a hyperparameter, not specified in sources) # Assuming a standard deviation multiplier k=1.0 for implementation completeness k = 1.0 minval = meanval - k stddev maxval = meanval + k stddev rectified = clamp(historyvalue, minval, maxval) else: rectified = historyvalue # Fallback to no rectification return rectified def clamp(value, minval, maxval): """Clamps value between minval and maxval.""" if value < minval: return minval elif value > maxval: return maxval else: return value A history rectification method that uses the statistical distribution of values in the current frame neighborhood to create the bounds of the AABB used for clipping. It calculates the mean and standard deviation of the neighborhood colors to define a range that is typically tighter than the raw min/max but accounts for variance. It consistently introduces less bias than AABB-based methods during movement, reducing ghosting artifacts more effectively, but exhibits higher Temporal Instability (flicker). In step response scenarios, it achieves the lowest RMSE (0.002977) but the highest TI P (0.004217, +190.23% increase over baseline). A history rectification method that projects the history onto the AABB defined by the minimum and maximum values in each color channel of the current frame neighborhood. In grayscale scenes, it produces identical results to AABB Clamping because color rectification is not relevant. It performs better than EMA in abrupt change scenarios and has lower TI than Variance Clipping (TI P of 0.002373, +63.32% over baseline). However, it struggles with gradual color changes, showing a large RMSE spike when a light fades from red to blue. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of neighbors in the sampling kernel (e.g., 9 for 3x3). The operations are simple min/max or mean/std calculations per pixel. Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel for storing neighborhood samples during the rectification pass. Measured Performance: Hardware/Resolution: Not given in the sources. Scene: Evaluated in step response (abrupt light on/off) and gradual change (moving/rotating light) scenarios. Metrics: Baseline EMA: RMSE 0.009724, TI P 0.001453. AABB Clamp/Clip: RMSE 0.003136, TI P 0.002373 (+63.32% TI). Variance Clip: RMSE 0.002977, TI P 0.004217 (+190.23% TI). Scaling: Performance scales with neighborhood size. Larger neighborhoods (3x3x3, 6-tap) smooth the signal across depth, reducing visible flicker but potentially blurring details. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Superior to EMA in abrupt change scenarios; immediately drops error to zero when intensity drops, eliminating temporal lag. Variance clipping produces the lowest error spike when reconstructing the signal during quick illumination introduction. Limitations: Higher Temporal Instability (flicker) compared to EMA, especially with Variance Clipping. AABB Clamping struggles with gradual color changes, taking ~50 frames to converge after a color fade. Jittering causes periodic error patterns (16-frame cycle) perceived as flicker. When to use/not use: Use: When rapid reaction to scene changes (light on/off, fast motion) is prioritized over absolute temporal stability, and ghosting must be minimized. Not Use: In scenes with gradual color transitions where AABB clamping is used, or when visual flicker is unacceptable and higher TI is a dealbreaker. History rectification techniques were developed as part of the broader effort to improve Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) for real-time rendering, specifically in the context of froxel-based volumetric rendering. The specific evaluation of these methods (Variance Clipping, AABB Clamping, AABB Clipping) is detailed in the work on "Advances in volumetric temporal anti-aliasing for real-time rendering of participating media". The techniques build upon earlier pixel-space TAA counterparts, adapting concepts like convex hull clipping (which is too expensive) and variance-based bounds to the volumetric domain. name: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR)
head: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) / Implicit Surface Differentiation, Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) / Implicit Surface Rendering, Implicit Surface Differentiation, Implicit Surface Gradient via Implicit Differentiation, Implicit Surface Rendering
body: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) predicts pixel color by casting a ray from a camera origin through a pixel, finding the first intersection with an implicit isosurface defined by a neural network, and querying a texture network at that point. It solves the problem of optimizing implicit neural representations of 3D shape and texture directly from 2D RGB images without requiring 3D ground truth supervision. Unlike voxel-based differentiable rendering methods or LSTM-based renderers, DVR does not store intermediate volumetric data or unrolled computation graphs for the forward pass, making its memory footprint independent of sampling accuracy and allowing for higher resolution. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{r}0, ray direction vector \mathbf{w} (from \mathbf{r}0 to pixel u), network parameters \theta, threshold \tau, sampling count n, step size \Delta s, and start depth s0. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{\mathbf{I}}u and gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} with respect to a loss \mathcal{L}. Data Structures: Occupancy Network f\theta: Maps \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow [0, 1] and outputs an occupancy probability. Texture Network t\theta: Maps \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 and outputs an RGB color value. Implementation: f\theta and t\theta are typically implemented as a single neural network with two shallow output heads sharing hidden layers. Latent Embedding z: For single-view reconstruction, an encoder g\theta produces z \in \mathcal{Z} conditioned on the input image, which modulates both heads. For unconditional rendering, \mathcal{Z} is empty or fixed. Parameters: \tau: Isosurface threshold. Typical value: 0.5. Range: [0, 1]. n: Number of equally-spaced samples on the ray. Starts at 16, increases to 128 during training (doubling after 50k, 150k, 250k iterations). s0: Start depth of the sampling interval. \Delta s: Step size for samples. \mathbf{w}: Ray direction vector \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{r}0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Compute n points along the ray \mathbf{r}(d) = \mathbf{r}0 + d\mathbf{w}: \mathbf{p}j^{\text{ray}} = \mathbf{r}(j\Delta s + s0) \quad \text{for } j = 1, \dots, n 2. Intersection Detection: Find the smallest index j where the occupancy changes from free space to occupied space: j = \operatorname{argmin}{j'} \left( f\theta(\mathbf{p}{j'+1}^{\text{ray}}) \geq \tau > f\theta(\mathbf{p}{j'}^{\text{ray}}) \right) Edge Case: If no such j exists (ray never intersects or starts inside), the depth is undefined or handled by boundary conditions. 3. Depth Approximation: Approximate the surface depth \hat{d} using the iterative secant method on the interval [j\Delta s + s0, (j+1)\Delta s + s0]. Let \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{r}(\hat{d}) be the intersection point. 4. Color Prediction: Compute the rendered color: \hat{\mathbf{I}}u = t\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}) 5. Gradient Computation (Backward Pass): The total loss gradient is: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = \sumu \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{I}}u} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{I}}u}{\partial \theta} Using the chain rule on \hat{\mathbf{I}}u = t\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}): \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{I}}u}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial t\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \theta} + \frac{\partial t\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}}{\partial \theta} Since \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{r}(\hat{d}) = \mathbf{r}0 + \hat{d}\mathbf{w}: \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}}{\partial \theta} = \mathbf{w} \frac{\partial \hat{d}}{\partial \theta} The depth gradient \frac{\partial \hat{d}}{\partial \theta} is derived via implicit differentiation of f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}) = \tau: \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \theta} + \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}}{\partial \theta} = 0 Substituting \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}}{\partial \theta}: \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \theta} + \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}} \cdot \mathbf{w} \frac{\partial \hat{d}}{\partial \theta} = 0 Solving for \frac{\partial \hat{d}}{\partial \theta}: \frac{\partial \hat{d}}{\partial \theta} = - \left( \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}} \cdot \mathbf{w} \right)^{-1} \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \theta} Implementation Trick: To compute the gradient efficiently using reverse-mode automatic differentiation without storing the forward pass of the secant method, rewrite the term \lambda \frac{\partial \hat{d}}{\partial \theta} (where \lambda = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{d}} is the incoming gradient from the loss) as: \mu \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \theta} \quad \text{with} \quad \mu = - \left( \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}} \cdot \mathbf{w} \right)^{-1} \lambda The backward pass is implemented by: 1. Computing \mu from the incoming gradient \lambda, the gradient of the occupancy network w.r.t. position \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}}, and the ray direction \mathbf{w}. 2. Element-wise multiplying \lambda by \mu (broadcasting for batches). 3. Backpropagating the result through the occupancy network f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}) to get gradients w.r.t. \theta. 4. Adding the direct gradient from the texture network t\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}) w.r.t. \theta, computed via standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def dvrforward(ftheta, ttheta, r0, w, tau, n, ds, s0): """ Forward pass for DVR. ftheta: Occupancy network (returns scalar occupancy prob) ttheta: Texture network (returns RGB color) r0: Camera origin (3,) w: Ray direction (3,) tau: Threshold n: Number of samples ds: Step size s0: Start depth """ # 1. Sample points on ray j = torch.arange(1, n + 1, device=r0.device) depths = j ds + s0 points = r0 + depths[:, None] w occupancies = ftheta(points) # 2. Find intersection: first i where occ[i] < tau and occ[i+1] >= tau free = occupancies < tau occupiednext = torch.cat([occupancies[1:] >= tau, torch.tensor([False], device=r0.device)]) intersect = occupiednext & free if not intersect.any(): return None, None, None i = torch.argmax(intersect.float()) # 3. Secant method on interval [di, d{i+1}] d0, d1 = depths[i], depths[i+1] f0, f1 = occupancies[i], occupancies[i+1] dhat = d0 for in range(10): dnew = d0 - f0 (d1 - d0) / (f1 - f0) fnew = ftheta(dnew) if abs(fnew - tau) < 1e-6: dhat = dnew break if fnew < tau: d0, f0 = dnew, fnew else: d1, f1 = dnew, fnew dhat = dnew # 4. Compute intersection point and color phat = r0 + dhat w color = ttheta(phat) return dhat, color, phat def dvrbackward(lambdagrad, phat, w, ftheta, ttheta): """ Backward pass for DVR using the implicit differentiation trick. lambdagrad: Gradient of loss w.r.t. depth dhat (scalar or batch) """ phat.requiresgrad(True) # Compute mu = - (df/dp. w)^-1 lambda fout = ftheta(phat) fout.backward(torch.oneslike(fout), retaingraph=True) dfdp = phat.grad mu = - (torch.dot(dfdp, w)).reciprocal() lambdagrad # Backprop through ftheta to get geometry parameter gradients ftheta.zerograd() fout2 = ftheta(phat) fout2.backward(mu) gradf = ftheta.grad # Direct gradient through ttheta (ignoring depth dependency for this term) phatdetached = phat.detach() phatdetached.requiresgrad(True) color = ttheta(phatdetached) color.backward(torch.oneslike(color), retaingraph=True) gradt = ttheta.grad return gradf, gradt A set of loss functions used to train the occupancy network f\theta and texture network t\theta based on whether a pixel u is inside/outside the object mask and whether a finite surface depth is predicted. Details on the encoder network, latent embedding, and training hyperparameters. Time Complexity: Dominated by the evaluation of the neural networks f\theta and t\theta at n sample points per ray. n increases during training from 16 to 128. Memory Complexity: Memory footprint is independent of the sampling accuracy n and the volume resolution because no intermediate volumetric data is stored in the forward pass. This contrasts with voxel-based methods which require storing all intermediate evaluations. Strengths: Enables learning from 2D images without 3D supervision; high resolution due to no voxel grid; watertight meshes can be extracted. Limitations: Requires finding the first intersection; sensitive to the threshold \tau; secant method convergence. DVR builds on occupancy networks and texture fields. It addresses the limitation of previous implicit representation methods that required 3D ground truth. It differs from voxel-based differentiable rendering and LSTM-based renderers by being inherently differentiable without storing intermediate results.
