name: DVR Training Losses
head: DVR Loss Functions, Multi-Loss Training for DVR, Occupancy Network Losses
body: DVR Training Losses constitute a multi-component objective function used to train the occupancy network f\theta and texture network t\theta in Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR). The method solves the problem of optimizing implicit neural representations from 2D image supervision by distinguishing pixels into three disjoint sets (P0, P1, P2) based on object mask membership and predicted surface depth finiteness. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly decoupling photometric consistency, freespace regularization, and occupancy induction into separate loss terms applied to specific pixel subsets, rather than relying on a single global rendering loss. Inputs: A batch of training images Ik with corresponding camera intrinsics, extrinsics, and binary object masks Mk. Optional ground truth depth maps Dk. The current parameters \theta of the occupancy network f\theta and texture network t\theta. A sampling count Np, the number of pixels to sample from the image plane per batch. Outputs: A scalar total loss value \mathcal{L}(\theta) used for backpropagation. The method operates on sets of pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} on the image plane. These pixels are classified into three mutually exclusive sets: P0: Pixels inside the object mask Mk where the occupancy network predicts a finite surface depth \hat{d}. P1: Pixels outside the object mask Mk. P2: Pixels inside the object mask Mk where the occupancy network predicts an infinite surface depth (no intersection). 1. Sampling: Randomly sample an image Ik from the training set and select Np points \mathbf{u} on the image plane. 2. Classification: For each sampled point \mathbf{u}, determine its membership in P0, P1, or P2 based on the mask Mk and the predicted depth \hat{d} from the occupancy network. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the relevant loss terms for each set: For \mathbf{u} \in P0: Compute \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} and optionally \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}. For \mathbf{u} \in P1: Compute \mathcal{L}{\text{freespace}}. For \mathbf{u} \in P2: Compute \mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}. 4. Aggregation: Sum the losses to form the total objective. 5. Optimization: Update parameters \theta using gradient descent. RGB Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}}) Applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P0. It enforces photo-consistency between the ground truth image features and the rendered image features. \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P0} \|\xi(\mathbf{I}){\mathbf{u}} - \xi(\hat{\mathbf{I}}){\mathbf{u}}\| Where: \xi(\cdot) is a feature extractor computing RGB values and optionally image gradients. \|\cdot\| is a robust error metric, typically the L1-norm. \hat{\mathbf{I}} is the rendered image. Depth Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}) Applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P0 when ground truth depth d is available. \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P0} |d - \hat{d}|1 Where: d is the ground truth depth value for pixel \mathbf{u}. \hat{d} is the predicted surface depth for pixel \mathbf{u}. Freespace Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{freespace}}) Applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P1. It penalizes finite predicted depth outside the object mask, encouraging the network to predict free space (f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}) \approx 0). \mathcal{L}{\text{freespace}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P1} \text{BCE}(f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}), 0) Where: \text{BCE}(p, y) = -[y \log(p) + (1-y) \log(1-p)] is the Binary Cross Entropy. \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{r}(\hat{d}) is the predicted surface point on the ray \mathbf{r}. Edge Case: If no finite surface depth is predicted for \mathbf{u} \in P1, apply the BCE loss to a randomly sampled point on the ray with target 0. Occupancy Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}) Applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P2. It encourages the network to predict occupied space (f\theta \approx 1) along rays where a surface is expected but not found. \mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P2} \text{BCE}(f\theta(\mathbf{r}(d{\text{random}})), 1) Where: d{\text{random}} are uniformly sampled depth values along the ray. Single-View Exception: In single-view reconstruction experiments, d{\text{random}} is replaced by the depth of the visual hull (first point on the ray inside all object masks) or ground truth depth if available. Normal Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}) Optional smoothness prior applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P0. It regularizes surface normals by minimizing the distance between the normal at the predicted surface point and a randomly sampled neighbor. \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P0} \|\mathbf{n}(\hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}}) - \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{q}{\mathbf{u}})\|2 Where: \mathbf{n}(\cdot) denotes the normal vector computed via gradients of f\theta. \hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}} is the predicted surface point for pixel \mathbf{u}. \mathbf{q}{\mathbf{u}} is a randomly sampled neighbor of \hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedvrlosses( image: Tensor, mask: Tensor, depthgt: Optional[Tensor], camerarayfn: Callable, occupancynet: Module, texturenet: Module, Np: int) -> Tuple[Tensor, Dict[str, Tensor]]: """ Computes the DVR training losses for a single image. Args: image: Ground truth image tensor (H, W, 3). mask: Binary object mask tensor (H, W). 1 if inside object, 0 otherwise. depthgt: Optional ground truth depth tensor (H, W). camerarayfn: Function that returns ray origin and direction for pixel coordinates. occupancynet: Neural network ftheta predicting occupancy probability. texturenet: Neural network ttheta predicting texture/color. Np: Number of pixels to sample. Returns: totalloss: Scalar tensor. losses: Dictionary containing individual loss components. """ H, W = mask.shape device = mask.device # Step 1: Sample Np random pixel coordinates uindices = torch.randint(0, H W, (Np,), device=device) uy = uindices // W ux = uindices % W # Get ray origins and directions for sampled pixels origins, directions = camerarayfn(uy, ux) # Predict surface depth and points for all sampled pixels # This requires finding the root of ftheta(r(d)) = 0 along each ray # Implementation detail: This is typically done via binary search or Newton's method # as described in the parent article Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) predicteddepths, predictedpoints = findsurfacedepth(origins, directions, occupancynet) # Step 2: Classify pixels into P0, P1, P2 # P0: Inside mask AND finite depth # P1: Outside mask # P2: Inside mask AND infinite depth (no intersection found) insidemask = (mask[uy, ux] == 1) finitedepth = predicteddepths < INFTHRESHOLD # INFTHRESHOLD is a large number p0mask = insidemask & finitedepth p1mask = ~insidemask p2mask = insidemask & ~finitedepth losses = {} totalloss = torch.tensor(0.0, device=device) # Step 3: Compute Losses for P0 if p0mask.any(): # RGB Loss # Render image at predicted points for P0 pixels # Note: In practice, this might involve rendering the full image or just querying texture # Here we assume we can get rendered features for the sampled points renderedfeatures = getrenderedfeatures(ux[p0mask], uy[p0mask], predictedpoints[p0mask], texturenet) gtfeatures = getimagefeatures(image, ux[p0mask], uy[p0mask]) # L1 loss on features rgbloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(gtfeatures - renderedfeatures)) losses['rgb'] = rgbloss totalloss += rgbloss # Depth Loss (if available) if depthgt is not None: gtdepth = depthgt[uy[p0mask], ux[p0mask]] preddepth = predicteddepths[p0mask] depthloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(gtdepth - preddepth)) losses['depth'] = depthloss totalloss += depthloss # Normal Loss (Optional) # Compute normals at predicted points normalspred = computenormals(predictedpoints[p0mask], occupancynet) # Sample random neighbors neighbors = sampleneighbors(predictedpoints[p0mask]) normalsneighbor = computenormals(neighbors, occupancynet) normalloss = torch.mean(torch.norm(normalspred - normalsneighbor, dim=1)) losses['normal'] = normalloss totalloss += normalloss # Step 3: Compute Losses for P1 if p1mask.any(): # Freespace Loss # If finite depth was predicted, use that point # If not, sample a random point on the ray pointsforloss = [] for i in range(len(ux[p1mask])): if finitedepth[p1mask][i]: pointsforloss.append(predictedpoints[p1mask][i]) else: # Random point on ray randomd = torch.rand(1, device=device) MAXDEPTH pointsforloss.append(origins[p1mask][i] + directions[p1mask][i] randomd) pointsforloss = torch.stack(pointsforloss) occupancyvals = occupancynet(pointsforloss) # Target is 0 (free space) freespaceloss = torch.mean(binarycrossentropy(occupancyvals, torch.zeroslike(occupancyvals))) losses['freespace'] = freespaceloss totalloss += freespaceloss # Step 3: Compute Losses for P2 if p2mask.any(): # Occupancy Loss # Encourage occupancy (target 1) pointsforloss = [] for i in range(len(ux[p2mask])): # Single-view exception logic would go here if applicable # For general case, sample random depths randomd = torch.rand(1, device=device) MAXDEPTH rayorigin = origins[p2mask][i] raydir = directions[p2mask][i] pointsforloss.append(rayorigin + raydir randomd) pointsforloss = torch.stack(pointsforloss) occupancyvals = occupancynet(pointsforloss) # Target is 1 (occupied) occupancyloss = torch.mean(binarycrossentropy(occupancyvals, torch.oneslike(occupancyvals))) losses['occupancy'] = occupancyloss totalloss += occupancyloss return totalloss, losses def binarycrossentropy(predictions, targets): # Standard BCE implementation eps = 1e-7 predictions = torch.clamp(predictions, eps, 1 - eps) return -(targets torch.log(predictions) + (1 - targets) torch.log(1 - predictions)) def findsurfacedepth(origins, directions, occupancynet): """ Finds the surface depth for each ray by solving ftheta(r(d)) = 0. This is a placeholder for the root-finding algorithm described in the parent article. """ # Implementation depends on the specific root-finding method (e.g., binary search) # Returns predicteddepths and predictedpoints pass def getrenderedfeatures(ux, uy, points, texturenet): """ Retrieves texture values at the predicted points. """ # Implementation depends on texture network query pass def getimagefeatures(image, ux, uy): """ Computes features (RGB + optional gradients) from the ground truth image. """ # Extract RGB values features = image[uy, ux] # Optionally add gradients return features def computenormals(points, occupancynet): """ Computes surface normals by taking the gradient of the occupancy network output. """ points.requiresgrad(True) occupancy = occupancynet(points) gradoutputs = torch.oneslike(occupancy) gradients = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=occupancy, inputs=points, gradoutputs=gradoutputs, creategraph=True)[0] normals = torch.nn.functional.normalize(gradients, dim=1) return normals def sampleneighbors(points, numneighbors=1): """ Samples random neighbors for normal loss. """ # Add small random noise to points noise = torch.randnlike(points) 0.01 return points + noise \xi(\cdot): Feature extractor. Typically uses RGB values and optionally image gradients. \|\cdot\|: Robust error metric. Typically L1-loss. P0: Set of pixels inside object mask with finite predicted surface depth. P1: Set of pixels outside object mask. P2: Set of pixels inside object mask but with infinite predicted surface depth. Np: Number of random pixels sampled from the image plane per batch. N: Number of images in the training set. Single-View Reconstruction: For the Occupancy Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}), random depth sampling is replaced by the visual hull depth (first point on the ray inside all object masks) or ground truth depth if available. Freespace Loss with No Depth: If a pixel in P1 has no predicted finite depth, the Freespace Loss must be applied to a randomly sampled point on the ray rather than the predicted surface point. Gradient Flow: The gradient from the RGB loss flows through the texture network and the surface point prediction, which depends on the occupancy network. The Freespace and Occupancy losses provide direct gradients to the occupancy network. Time: The complexity is dominated by the root-finding operation for surface depth for each sampled pixel Np. This typically involves multiple queries to the occupancy network f\theta. The number of queries depends on the precision of the root-finding algorithm (e.g., binary search iterations). The loss computation itself is O(Np). Memory: Memory usage is proportional to Np for storing sampled points, depths, and intermediate gradients. The network parameters are stored separately. The method works with as little as one image per object. It can incorporate depth information if available, improving performance. The Normal Loss is particularly useful for real-world data to enforce natural shapes in unconstrained areas. The method scales linearly with the number of sampled pixels Np. It scales with the number of training images N. Strengths: Explicitly handles different pixel types (inside/outside mask, finite/infinite depth), allowing for targeted supervision. Works with minimal supervision (2D masks). Limitations: Relies on accurate object masks. The quality of the Freespace and Occupancy losses depends on the correct classification of pixels into P1 and P2, which in turn depends on the current state of the occupancy network. Use when training DVR networks from 2D image supervision with object masks. Use when depth information is available to incorporate \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}. Use when real-world data requires smoothness priors, enabling \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}. Do not use if only 3D ground truth (e.g., point clouds or meshes) is available without 2D images; consider Training Losses for Implicit Surface Learning instead. Do not use if object masks are not available, as the classification into P0, P1, P2 is not possible. The DVR Training Losses were introduced by Niemeyer et al. in the paper "Differentiable Volumetric Rendering: Learning Implicit 3D Representations Without 3D Supervision". The method was developed to enable the training of implicit neural representations using only 2D image supervision. It builds on the Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) framework, which allows gradients to flow from the rendered image back to the implicit surface representation. The method is used in single-view and multi-view 3D reconstruction from images, particularly in scenarios where 3D supervision is unavailable or expensive. It is a core component of the Occupancy Networks framework. name: DVR Network Architecture and Training Setup
head: DVR, DVR Implementation Details, DepthFunction, DepthModule, Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (Depth Estimation via Implicit Surface), Network Architecture and Training Configuration, Volume Rendering Integration
body: This article specifies the neural network architecture and training configuration for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR). It defines the implicit function network mapping 3D coordinates to occupancy logits and texture values, and details the hyperparameters, optimization strategy, and ray-sampling schedules required to train the model from single-view or multi-view inputs. The method builds on Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) and relates to DVR Training Losses and Training Losses for Implicit Surface Learning. Inputs: Ray Origin (\mathbf{r}0): 3D camera origin for each pixel. Ray Direction (\mathbf{d}): Normalized direction vector from camera origin through the pixel. Decoder Network (f\theta): The implicit neural representation parameters \theta. Context (c): Latent code or conditioning vector (e.g., from an encoder network for single-view reconstruction). Threshold (\tau): Occupancy logit threshold for surface intersection (default 0.5). Depth Range: Interval [s0, n\Delta s + s0] covering the volume of interest. Outputs: Surface Depth (\hat{d}): The distance along the ray to the first intersection with the isosurface f\theta(\mathbf{p}) = \tau. Texture/Color: RGB values sampled at the surface point \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{r}0 + \hat{d}\mathbf{d}. Combined Network (Implicit Representation): Architecture: 5 fully-connected ResNet blocks with ReLU activation. Input: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) concatenated with context c (if applicable). Output Layer: Dimension 4. Index 0: Occupancy probability/logit. Indices 1-3: Texture (RGB) values. Encoder Network (Single-View Reconstruction): Architecture: ResNet-18. Input: Single RGB image. Output: 256-dimensional latent code z. DepthModule Parameters: tau (float): Threshold for occupancy logits. Default: 0.5. nsteps (tuple): Number of evaluation steps for initial ray sampling. If nsteps is None, use self.nsteps. Default: [128, 129]. nsecantsteps (int): Number of refinement steps for root-finding. Default: 8. depthrange (tuple): Range of possible depth values. Not relevant when unit cube intersection is used. Default: [0., 2.4]. method (string): Refinement method. Options: 'secant' (default). checkcubeintersection (bool): Whether to intersect rays with the unit cube. Default: True. maxpoints (int): Maximum number of points loaded to GPU memory. Default: 3,700,000. scheduleraysampling (bool): Whether to schedule ray sampling accuracy. Default: True. schedulemilestones (list): Training iterations after which sampling accuracy doubles. Default: [50000, 100000, 250000]. initresolution (int): Initial resolution for ray sampling. Default: 16. 1. Initialization: Initialize DepthModule with parameters listed above. 2. Determine Sampling Steps: If nsteps is None, use self.nsteps. If scheduleraysampling is True and current iteration it is provided, call getsamplingaccuracy(it) to determine the effective number of steps. 3. Ray Sampling: Calculate step size \Delta s based on the depth range and number of steps n. Generate n equally-spaced sample points along the ray: \mathbf{p}j^{\text{ray}} = \mathbf{r}0 + (j\Delta s + s0)\mathbf{d}, \quad j = 0, \dots, n-1 where s0 determines the closest possible surface point. 4. Surface Detection: Evaluate the decoder f\theta(\mathbf{p}j^{\text{ray}}, c) for all samples. Find the smallest index j such that the occupancy logit crosses the threshold \tau: j = \operatorname{argmin}{j'} \left( f\theta(\mathbf{p}{j'+1}^{\text{ray}}) \geq \tau > f\theta(\mathbf{p}{j'}^{\text{ray}}) \right) This identifies the interval [j\Delta s + s0, (j+1)\Delta s + s0] containing the surface. 5. Refinement (Bisection Method): Apply the bisection method within the identified interval to find the precise depth \hat{d}. Iterate n{\text{secant\steps}} times to refine the depth estimate. 6. Texture Sampling: Compute surface point \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{r}0 + \hat{d}\mathbf{d}. Query the decoder at \hat{\mathbf{p}} to retrieve RGB values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch class DepthFunction(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, nsteps, nsecantsteps, tau, depthrange, checkcubeintersection, maxpoints): # 1. Determine number of steps if isinstance(nsteps, tuple) and len(nsteps) > 1: n = nsteps[0] else: n = nsteps s0, s1 = depthrange deltas = (s1 - s0) / n # 2. Generate sample points jindices = torch.arange(n, device=ray0.device).float() offsets = jindices deltas + s0 # offsets shape: (n,) # ray0 shape: (B, 3), raydirection shape: (B, 3) points = ray0.unsqueeze(1) + offsets.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2) raydirection.unsqueeze(1) # 3. Evaluate decoder pointsflat = points.view(-1, 3) B = ray0.size(0) # Handle context broadcasting if c.dim() == 2 and c.size(0) == 1: cflat = c.expand(B, -1).repeatinterleave(n, dim=0) else: cflat = c.repeatinterleave(n, dim=0) with torch.nograd(): outputs = decoder(pointsflat, cflat) outputs = outputs.view(B, n, -1) occupancy = outputs[..., 0] # 4. Find crossing interval # Condition: f(p{j+1}) >= tau > f(pj) crossing = (occupancy[:, 1:] >= tau) & (occupancy[:,:-1] < tau) if not torch.any(crossing): return torch.full((B,), float('inf')) jcrossing = torch.argmax(crossing.float(), dim=1) # 5. Bisection Refinement dlow = offsets[jcrossing] dhigh = offsets[jcrossing + 1] dpred = (dlow + dhigh) / 2.0 for in range(nsecantsteps): pmid = ray0 + dpred.unsqueeze(1) raydirection if c.dim() == 2 and c.size(0) == 1: cmid = c.expand(B, -1) else: cmid = c with torch.nograd(): fmid = decoder(pmid, cmid)[..., 0] - tau indlow = fmid < 0 dlow[indlow] = dpred[indlow] dhigh[~indlow] = dpred[~indlow] dpred = 0.5 (dlow + dhigh) return dpred @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradoutput): # The sources specify that gradients are computed analytically via implicit differentiation # without unrolling the forward pass. This requires computing the normal vector n = gradp ftheta(p) # and applying the chain rule. This step is omitted from the pseudocode as it is framework-dependent. return None, None, None, None, None, None, None, None, None, None, None def getsamplingaccuracy(it, schedulemilestones, initresolution): if not schedulemilestones: return [128, 129] res = initresolution for milestone in schedulemilestones: if it < milestone: return [res, res + 1] res = res 2 return [res, res + 1] Batch Size: 64 images. Pixels per Image: 1024 random pixels. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate \gamma = 10^{-4}. Learning Rate Schedule: Decrease by factor of 5 after 750 and 1000 epochs. Hardware: Single NVIDIA V100 GPU. Ray Sampling Schedule: Start with n=16. Double n after 50,000, 150,000, and 250,000 iterations, reaching n=128. No Surface Intersection: If no crossing is found along the ray, the depth is set to infinity. Precision: The bisection method refines the depth estimate, but precision depends on the number of refinement steps (default 8) and the initial sampling density. Memory Management: The maxpoints parameter caps the number of points evaluated per batch to manage GPU memory allocation. Time Complexity: The forward pass involves N \times n evaluations of the decoder for initial sampling, where N is the number of pixels and n is the number of samples per ray. The bisection refinement adds N \times n{\text{secant\steps}} evaluations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is constrained by the maxpoints parameter, which limits the number of points loaded to GPU memory per batch. Performance: Trained on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU with a batch size of 64 images and 1024 pixels each. Strengths: Differentiable rendering allows for end-to-end training from single-view images without explicit 3D supervision. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Origin: The DVR method was introduced by Mescheder et al. in "Occupancy Networks: Learning 3D Reconstruction in Function Space" (CVPR 2019) and extended by Niemeyer et al. in "Differentiable Volumetric Rendering: Learning Implicit 3D Representations without 3D Supervision" (CVPR 2020). History: The method builds on the concept of occupancy networks, which represent 3D shapes as implicit functions. The differentiable rendering component allows these implicit representations to be trained from 2D images. Usage: DVR is used for 3D shape and texture reconstruction from single-view or multi-view images, particularly in scenarios where 3D supervision is unavailable. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Differentiable Volumetric Rendering: Learning Implicit 3D Representations without 3D Supervision, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lcub1KH-mmk, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Differentiable Volumetric Rendering - CVF Open Access, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/contentCVPR2020/html/NiemeyerDifferentiableVolumetricRenderingLearningImplicit3DRepresentationsWithout3DSupervisionCVPR2020paper.html, fetched 2026-10-30

name: NeRF Model Initialization
head: NeRF MLP Setup, NeRF Network Initialization
body: NeRF Model Initialization configures the multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and positional encoders required for differentiable volumetric rendering of a scene. It establishes the coordinate encoding scheme, the network topology for density and color prediction, and the sampling parameters for coarse and fine ray marching. Inputs: Scene data (poses, images) loaded via loaddata. Hyperparameters: netdepth, netwidth, multires, multiresviews, Nsamples, Nimportance, perturb, rawnoisestd, useviewdirs. Outputs: model: Coarse MLP instance. modelfine: Fine MLP instance (optional). renderkwargstrain: Dictionary of rendering parameters for training. renderkwargstest: Dictionary of rendering parameters for evaluation. Data Structures: Positional Encoder (embedfn): Maps 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to a higher-dimensional space using sinusoidal embeddings up to frequency 2^{\text{multires}-1}. Directional Encoder (embeddirsfn): Maps 2D view directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^2 to a higher-dimensional space using sinusoidal embeddings up to frequency 2^{\text{multires\views}-1}. Coarse MLP (model): A fully connected network with netdepth layers, netwidth hidden units, and skip connections from input to layers 4, 8, \dots. Input dimension is determined by embedfn output size. If useviewdirs is true, view directions are encoded and concatenated to hidden layer representations before the final output layer. Output dimension is 4 (RGB + volume density \sigma). Fine MLP (modelfine): Same architecture as model but with potentially different netdepthfine and netwidthfine. Steps: 1. Instantiate Positional Encoders: Create embedfn for 3D coordinates using getembedder(multires, iembed). If useviewdirs is true, create embeddirsfn for 2D view directions using getembedder(multiresviews, iembed). 2. Create Coarse MLP: Initialize model using initnerfmodel with: Depth: netdepth (default 8). Width: netwidth (default 256). Input channels: Determined by embedfn output size. Output channels: 4 (RGB + \sigma). Skip connections: Added at layer indices 4, 8, \dots (every 4 layers). View direction input: If useviewdirs, encode view directions and concatenate to hidden layer representations before the final output layer. 3. Create Fine MLP (Optional): If Nimportance > 0, initialize modelfine with netdepthfine and netwidthfine. Add modelfine parameters to the gradient variables list gradvars. 4. Define Network Query Function: Create networkqueryfn that wraps runnetwork. This function takes ray origins, directions, and the encoders, applies the positional encoding, passes data through the MLP, and returns raw RGB and \sigma values. 5. Configure Training Render Kwargs: Create renderkwargstrain dictionary with: perturb: args.perturb (default 1.0, jitter for sampling). Nimportance: args.Nimportance (default 0). Nsamples: args.Nsamples (default 64). networkfn: networkqueryfn. networkfine: networkqueryfn for modelfine if Nimportance > 0. useviewdirs: args.useviewdirs. whitebkgd: Boolean flag for background. rawnoisestd: args.rawnoisestd (default 1e0, noise added to \sigma for regularization). 6. Configure Test Render Kwargs: Create renderkwargstest as a copy of renderkwargstrain with: perturb: False. rawnoisestd: 0.. 7. Load Checkpoints (Optional): If a checkpoint directory ckpts exists, sort files containing 'model' but not 'fine' or 'optimizer'. Load weights into model using model.setweights(np.load(ftweights, allowpickle=True)). If modelfine exists, load corresponding weights using the filename pattern '{}fine{}'.format(ftweights[:-11], ftweights[-10:]). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import os import numpy as np def linear(x, W, b): # Standard fully connected layer: y = xW + b return np.dot(x, W) + b def relu(x): # Standard ReLU activation return np.maximum(0, x) def concat(a, b, axis=-1): # Standard tensor concatenation return np.concatenate([a, b], axis=axis) def getembedder(multires, iembed): # Standard positional encoding: concatenates input with sin/cos of frequencies 2^0 to 2^(multires-1) def embedfn(x): out = [x] for freq in range(multires): freqval = 2.0 freq out.append(math.sin(x freqval)) out.append(math.cos(x freqval)) return np.concatenate(out, axis=-1) embedfn.outdim = x.shape[-1] (1 + 2 multires) return embedfn def initnerfmodel(netdepth, netwidth, inputch, outputch, useviewdirs, embedfn, embeddirsfn): # Standard MLP with skip connections at layers 4, 8,... class MLP: def init(self): self.layers = [] self.useviewdirs = useviewdirs self.inputch = inputch self.netwidth = netwidth self.outputch = outputch self.embedfn = embedfn self.embeddirsfn = embeddirsfn self.layers.append({'in': inputch, 'out': netwidth}) for i in range(netdepth - 1): if i % 4 == 0 and i > 0: self.layers.append({'in': inputch + netwidth, 'out': netwidth}) else: self.layers.append({'in': netwidth, 'out': netwidth}) if useviewdirs: self.dirlayer = {'in': netwidth, 'out': netwidth} self.outputlayer = {'in': netwidth + embeddirsfn.outdim, 'out': outputch} else: self.outputlayer = {'in': netwidth, 'out': outputch} def forward(self, xyz, dirs=None): x = self.embedfn(xyz) h = x for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): h = linear(h, np.random.randn(layer['in'], layer['out']), np.zeros(layer['out'])) if i > 0: h = relu(h) if i % 4 == 0 and i > 0: h = concat([h, x], axis=-1) if self.useviewdirs: dirh = linear(h, np.random.randn(self.dirlayer['in'], self.dirlayer['out']), np.zeros(self.dirlayer['out'])) dirh = relu(dirh) dirsembedded = self.embeddirsfn(dirs) h = concat([dirh, dirsembedded], axis=-1) raw = linear(h, np.random.randn(self.outputlayer['in'], self.outputlayer['out']), np.zeros(self.outputlayer['out'])) return raw return MLP() def runnetwork(xyz, dirs, networkfn, netchunk): # Chunked forward pass to manage memory Nrays = xyz.shape[0] rawlist = [] for i in range(0, Nrays, netchunk): chunkxyz = xyz[i:i+netchunk] chunkdirs = dirs[i:i+netchunk] if dirs is not None else None rawlist.append(networkfn(chunkxyz, chunkdirs)) return concat(rawlist, axis=0) def setupneRF(args, basedir): # 1. Instantiate encoders embedfn = getembedder(args.multires, args.iembed) embeddirsfn = None if args.useviewdirs: embeddirsfn = getembedder(args.multiresviews, args.iembed) # 2. Create coarse MLP model = initnerfmodel( netdepth=args.netdepth, netwidth=args.netwidth, inputch=embedfn.outdim, outputch=4, useviewdirs=args.useviewdirs, embedfn=embedfn, embeddirsfn=embeddirsfn) gradvars = list(model.parameters()) # 3. Create fine MLP (optional) modelfine = None if args.Nimportance > 0: modelfine = initnerfmodel( netdepth=args.netdepthfine, netwidth=args.netwidthfine, inputch=embedfn.outdim, outputch=4, useviewdirs=args.useviewdirs, embedfn=embedfn, embeddirsfn=embeddirsfn) gradvars.extend(modelfine.parameters()) # 4. Define network query function def networkqueryfn(inputs): xyz = inputs[...,:3] dirs = inputs[..., 3:] if args.useviewdirs else None raw = runnetwork(xyz, dirs, model, netchunk=102464) rawfine = runnetwork(xyz, dirs, modelfine, netchunk=102464) if modelfine is not None else None return raw, rawfine # 5. Configure render kwargs renderkwargstrain = { 'perturb': args.perturb, 'Nimportance': args.Nimportance, 'Nsamples': args.Nsamples, 'networkfn': networkqueryfn, 'networkfine': networkqueryfn if args.Nimportance > 0 else None, 'useviewdirs': args.useviewdirs, 'whitebkgd': args.whitebkgd, 'rawnoisestd': args.rawnoisestd } renderkwargstest = {renderkwargstrain, 'perturb': False, 'rawnoisestd': 0.0} # 6. Load checkpoints ckpts = sorted([f for f in os.listdir(args.ckpts) if 'model' in f and 'fine' not in f and 'optimizer' not in f]) if ckpts: ftweights = ckpts[-1] model.setweights(np.load(os.path.join(args.ckpts, ftweights), allowpickle=True)) if modelfine is not None: fineweightsname = '{}fine{}'.format(ftweights[:-11], ftweights[-10:]) fineweightspath = os.path.join(args.ckpts, fineweightsname) if os.path.exists(fineweightspath): modelfine.setweights(np.load(fineweightspath, allowpickle=True)) return model, modelfine, renderkwargstrain, renderkwargstest, gradvars Parameters: netdepth: Number of layers in the MLP. Default: 8. netwidth: Number of channels (hidden units) per layer. Default: 256. multires: Log2 of the maximum frequency for positional encoding of 3D coordinates. Default: 10. multiresviews: Log2 of the maximum frequency for positional encoding of 2D view directions. Default: 4. Nsamples: Number of coarse samples per ray. Default: 64. Nimportance: Number of additional fine samples per ray. Default: 0. perturb: Jitter factor for sampling. Default: 1.0. Set to 0. for no jitter. rawnoisestd: Standard deviation of noise added to the regularized \sigma output. Default: 1e0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. What it is: A method that uses explicit 3D voxel grids to store density and color, optimized via differentiable rendering. What sets it apart: Uses explicit memory structures (voxels) instead of implicit neural networks (MLPs), leading to different memory and compute characteristics. When to choose: When memory constraints are tight or when faster training convergence is needed for specific scene types compared to MLPs. Link: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. bmild/nerf, https://github.com/bmild/nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO)
head: SimpleDVGO
body: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) is a differentiable volume rendering method that combines ray sampling, coordinate rescaling, voxel grid interpolation for density and color, and volume rendering into a single forward pass. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF by replacing the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with direct lookup and interpolation in learned voxel grids, significantly reducing memory usage and training time while maintaining competitive rendering quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: rays tensor of shape (N, 6), where the first 3 components are ray origins and the last 3 are ray directions. Output: Rendered color image tensor of shape (N, 3). Data Structures: tvalues: 1D tensor of shape (num\samples), storing the midpoints between sampled depths. min, max: Buffers storing the minimum and maximum corners of the scene bounding box in scene coordinates. shape: Buffer storing the dimensions of the voxel grid. rgbvoxelgrid: A voxel grid data structure with shape config.shape and dimension 3, storing RGB color values. densityvoxelgrid: A voxel grid data structure with shape config.shape and dimension 1, storing density values. Parameters: near: Float, near plane distance for ray sampling. Default: 1.5. far: Float, far plane distance for ray sampling. Default: 3.5. numsamples: Integer, number of sample points along each ray. Default: 64. mincorner: Tuple of floats, minimum corner of the scene bounding box. Default: (-1.0, -1.0, 0.0). maxcorner: Tuple of floats, maximum corner of the scene bounding box. Default: (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). shape: Tuple of ints, dimensions of the voxel grid. Default: (128, 128, 128). background: Color value used for background in volume rendering. Default: WHITE. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute depths as linearly spaced values from near to far with numsamples + 1 points. Compute tvalues as the midpoints between adjacent depths: ti = \frac{depths{i+1} + depthsi}{2}. Initialize rgbvoxelgrid with shape config.shape, dimension 3, filled with BLUE. Initialize densityvoxelgrid with shape config.shape, dimension 1, filled with 0.001. Register background color. 2. Forward Pass: Sample points along rays using samplerays with tvalues and input rays. Rescale sampled points from scene coordinates to grid coordinates: rescaled = shape \times \frac{samples - min}{max - min}. Query density grid: density = \text{ReLU}(\text{squeeze}(\text{density\voxel\grid}(rescaled))). Query RGB grid: rgb = \text{clamp}(\text{rgb\voxel\grid}(rescaled), 0.0, 1.0). Render using renderalongray with density, rgb, and background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F BLUE = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0], dtype=torch.float32) WHITE = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], dtype=torch.float32) class Config: near: float = 1.5 far: float = 3.5 numsamples: int = 64 mincorner: tuple = (-1.0, -1.0, 0.0) maxcorner: tuple = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) shape: tuple = (128, 128, 128) background = WHITE class VoxelGrid(nn.Module): def init(self, shape, d, fill): super().init() filltensor = fill if isinstance(fill, torch.Tensor) else torch.full((1, d) + shape, fill, dtype=torch.float32) self.registerbuffer('data', filltensor) self.shape = shape def forward(self, coords): # coords: (N, numsamples, 3) in grid coordinates [0, shape-1] # Normalize to [-1, 1] for gridsample shapetensor = torch.tensor(self.shape, dtype=torch.float32, device=coords.device) coordsnorm = 2.0 (coords / (shapetensor - 1.0)) - 1.0 coordsnorm = coordsnorm.unsqueeze(2).unsqueeze(3) return F.gridsample(self.data, coordsnorm, mode='trilinear', aligncorners=False) def samplealongray(ts, origins, directions): # ts: (N, numsamples), origins: (N, 3), directions: (N, 3) return origins.unsqueeze(1) + directions.unsqueeze(1) ts.unsqueeze(2) def renderalongray(density, rgb, background, tvalues): # density: (N, numsamples), rgb: (N, numsamples, 3) # Compute sample spacing deltas = torch.cat([tvalues[1:] - tvalues[:-1], torch.tensor([1e-10], device=tvalues.device)]) # Compute alpha and transmittance alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-density deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha[:,:-1]], dim=1), dim=1) weights = alpha T[:,:-1] # Composite color color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(2) rgb, dim=1) + T[:, -1].unsqueeze(1) background return color class SimpleDVGO(nn.Module): def init(self, config=None): super().init() if config is None: config = Config() # Initialize sampler parameters self.depths = torch.linspace(config.near, config.far, config.numsamples + 1, dtype=torch.float32) self.registerbuffer('tvalues', 0.5 (self.depths[1:] + self.depths[:-1])) # Set up conversion from scene coordinates to grid coordinates self.registerbuffer('min', torch.tensor(config.mincorner, dtype=torch.float32)) self.registerbuffer('max', torch.tensor(config.maxcorner, dtype=torch.float32)) self.registerbuffer('shape', torch.tensor(config.shape, dtype=torch.float32)) # Initialize color grid to blue self.rgbvoxelgrid = VoxelGrid(config.shape, d=3, fill=BLUE) # Initialize density grid with very low density self.densityvoxelgrid = VoxelGrid(config.shape, d=1, fill=torch.full((), 0.001, dtype=torch.float32)) # Record background color for rendering self.registerbuffer('background', config.background) def forward(self, rays, training=True): # Sample points along rays samples = samplerays(self.tvalues, rays, training=training) # Rescale to fit within the grid rescaled = self.shape (samples - self.min) / (self.max - self.min) # Query Density Voxel Grid density = torch.squeeze(self.densityvoxelgrid(rescaled), dim=2) density = F.relu(density) # Query RGB Voxel Grid rgb = torch.squeeze(self.rgbvoxelgrid(rescaled), dim=2) rgb = torch.clamp(rgb, 0.0, 1.0) # Render return renderalongray(density, rgb, self.background, self.tvalues) def samplerays(tvalues, rays, training=True): """Sample points along the rays.""" origins = rays[...,:3].to(dtype=torch.float32) directions = rays[..., 3:].to(dtype=torch.float32) if training: with torch.nograd(): n = rays.size(0) randomscalar = (torch.rand(n, device=rays.device) - 0.5) / n actualts = tvalues.clone() + randomscalar else: actualts = tvalues.clone() return samplealongray(actualts, origins, directions) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Density values must be non-negative; achieved by applying ReLU nonlinearity after querying the density grid. RGB values must be in [0, 1]; achieved by clamping after querying the RGB grid. Training a NeRF can take a long time, so float32 is used everywhere to reduce GPU resources compared to float64. This method adapts the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) architecture by replacing its standard volume rendering integral with a reparameterized estimate based on differentiable ray point sampling. It solves the problem of high computational cost in standard ray marching by allowing the number of radiance samples to be explicitly controlled and minimized, particularly during the coarse training stage. It sets itself apart from standard DVGO by trading off rendering quality (PSNR) for significant training speed improvements in the coarse stage, while maintaining competitive performance in the fine stage only when sample counts are kept low. DVGO uses float32 everywhere to reduce GPU resources compared to float64, acknowledging that NeRF training takes a long time. The default configuration uses a 128^3 voxel grid and 64 samples per ray. DVGO (Direct Voxel Grid Optimization) was introduced by Sun et al. [2022]. It is a differentiable volume rendering method that combines ray sampling, coordinate rescaling, voxel grid interpolation for density and color, and volume rendering into a single forward pass. 7.6. name: DVGO with Reparameterized Rendering
head: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization with proposed reparameterized estimates
body: This method adapts the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) architecture by replacing its standard volume rendering integral with a reparameterized estimate based on differentiable ray point sampling. It solves the problem of high computational cost in standard ray marching by allowing the number of radiance samples to be explicitly controlled and minimized, particularly during the coarse training stage. It sets itself apart from standard DVGO by trading off rendering quality (PSNR) for significant training speed improvements in the coarse stage, while maintaining competitive performance in the fine stage only when sample counts are kept low. The method retains the DVGO data structures and training pipeline but modifies the forward rendering pass. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin o, ray direction d, density grid \sigma, radiance grid C, and an optional view-dependent MLP C{mlp}. Outputs: Rendered color C{render}. Data Structures: The method uses the same grids as DVGO: 1. Density Grid: A 3D tensor storing volume density \sigma. 2. Radiance Grid: A 3D tensor storing view-independent color C. 3. View-Dependent Radiance (Fine Stage): A combination of the radiance grid and a small MLP. 4. Auxiliary Mask: A binary mask identifying empty space regions to skip optimization. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Instead of fixed-step ray marching, sample k points along the ray segment within the bounding box. The points are sampled according to a stratified distribution. 2. Grid Interpolation: For each sampled point, interpolate the density and color from the respective 3D grids using the same scheme as the parent DVGO architecture. 3. Reparameterized Estimate Calculation: Compute the transmittance and color contribution using the reparameterized estimate formula (Equation 4 in). The standard volume rendering integral is approximated by the sum over the k samples: C{render} = \sum{i=1}^{k} Ti \alphai Ci where \alphai is the opacity derived from \sigmai and the distance between samples, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i. 4. Differentiable Backpropagation: Compute gradients with respect to the grid values using the chain rule through the sampling and interpolation steps. Parameters: Number of radiance samples (k): Varies during evaluation and training. Tested values: 1, 8, 32, 64. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderreparameterized(rayo, rayd, densitygrid, radiancegrid, k, bboxmin, bboxmax): # 1. Ray-box intersection (slab method) tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for d in range(3): if abs(rayd[d]) < 1e-8: if rayo[d] < bboxmin[d] or rayo[d] > bboxmax[d]: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: t1 = (bboxmin[d] - rayo[d]) / rayd[d] t2 = (bboxmax[d] - rayo[d]) / rayd[d] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 2. Stratified sampling of k points along the valid ray segment tvalues = [tmin + i (tmax - tmin) / k for i in range(k + 1)] tmid = [(tvalues[i] + tvalues[i+1]) / 2.0 for i in range(k)] # 3. Sample points along ray points = [[rayo[j] + rayd[j] tmid[i] for j in range(3)] for i in range(k)] # 4. Trilinear interpolation from grids sigma = [trilinearinterpolate(densitygrid, p) for p in points] color = [[trilinearinterpolate(radiancegrid, p, c) for c in range(3)] for p in points] # 5. Compute opacity and transmittance deltat = [tvalues[i+1] - tvalues[i] for i in range(k)] alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[i] deltat[i]) for i in range(k)] # Accumulate transmittance Ti = product{j<i} (1 - alphaj) T = [1.0] k prod = 1.0 for i in range(1, k): prod = (1.0 - alpha[i-1]) T[i] = prod # 6. Compute final color colorrender = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(k): for c in range(3): colorrender[c] += T[i] alpha[i] color[i][c] return colorrender def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point, channel=None): # Standard trilinear interpolation ix, iy, iz = int(math.floor(point[0])), int(math.floor(point[1])), int(math.floor(point[2])) fx, fy, fz = point[0] - ix, point[1] - iy, point[2] - iz # Handle boundary clamping ix = max(0, min(ix, grid.shape[0] - 2)) iy = max(0, min(iy, grid.shape[1] - 2)) iz = max(0, min(iz, grid.shape[2] - 2)) if channel is None: # Interpolate scalar density v00 = grid[ix][iy][iz] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy][iz] fx v10 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz] fx v01 = grid[ix][iy][iz+1] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy][iz+1] fx v11 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz+1] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz+1] fx return v00 (1-fy) (1-fz) + v10 fx (1-fy) (1-fz) + v01 (1-fy) fz + v11 fx (1-fy) fz else: # Interpolate color channel v00 = grid[ix][iy][iz][channel] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy][iz][channel] fx v10 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz][channel] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz][channel] fx v01 = grid[ix][iy][iz+1][channel] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy][iz+1][channel] fx v11 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz+1][channel] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz+1][channel] fx return v00 (1-fy) (1-fz) + v10 fx (1-fy) (1-fz) + v01 (1-fy) fz + v11 fx (1-fy) fz Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance: Lower PSNR in the proposed method is caused by estimate variance during training, not just inference sampling. Sample Count Sensitivity: Noise artifacts are visible for k=1 but disappear for k=8. Training vs. Inference Robustness: A model trained with 64 samples can achieve PSNR 34.33 even if only 16 samples are used during evaluation, indicating robustness to inference sample count if training was sufficient. Training Speed (Coarse Stage): Improves training time by 20-30% compared to standard DVGO due to fewer radiance samples. Training Speed (Fine Stage): Improves training speed only when the number of samples is lower than DVGO's average radiance calls (13.4 in the tested scenario). Rendering Quality (PSNR): Generally lower than standard DVGO. On the Lego scene, DVGO achieved 34.60 PSNR. The proposed method achieved 34.15 (64 samples), 33.95 (32 samples), 33.29 (8 samples), and 29.84 (1 sample). Memory Usage: Memory usage is comparable to DVGO, as the grid structures remain the same. Implementation Note: To achieve performance competitive with DVGO's custom CUDA kernels, the method requires optimization using PyTorch's just-in-time (JIT) compilation module. This method was proposed in the paper "Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling". It builds upon the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) architecture, which was known for its fast training times due to lightning-fast architecture, progressive scaling, and custom CUDA kernels. The authors tested their rendering algorithm on the official DVGO implementation, replacing only the rendering algorithm based on Equation 4 of their paper. name: Training Losses for Implicit Surface Learning
head: Photometric and Occupancy Losses
body: This method defines a set of loss functions to train the occupancy network f\theta and texture network t\theta using 2D image supervision. It categorizes sampled pixels into three sets—P0 (inside mask, finite depth), P1 (outside mask), and P2 (inside mask, infinite depth)—to enforce photometric consistency, remove spurious geometry, and encourage surface presence where expected. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly handling the ambiguity of empty space (P1) and missing surfaces (P2) through targeted binary cross-entropy penalties, rather than relying solely on photometric error. Inputs: Training image Ik and corresponding camera intrinsics/extrinsics. Object mask Mk indicating the silhouette of the object in Ik. Optional ground truth depth map Dk. Occupancy network f\theta(\mathbf{p}) and texture network t\theta(\mathbf{p}). Number of random pixels to sample Np. Outputs: Gradients for \theta to update f\theta and t\theta. Pixel Set P0: Set of pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} such that \mathbf{u} \in Mk AND the predicted depth \hat{d} is finite. Pixel Set P1: Set of pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} such that \mathbf{u} \notin Mk. Pixel Set P2: Set of pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} such that \mathbf{u} \in Mk AND the predicted depth \hat{d} is infinite (no surface found). Ray \mathbf{r}(d): Function mapping a depth value d to a 3D point in camera space. Feature Extractor \xi(\cdot): Computes features from an image. Uses RGB values and optionally image gradients. 1. Randomly sample Np points \mathbf{u} on the image plane of image Ik. 2. For each \mathbf{u}, predict the surface depth \hat{d} using the current network parameters. 3. Classify each \mathbf{u} into one of the three sets: If \mathbf{u} \in Mk and \hat{d} is finite, add \mathbf{u} to P0. If \mathbf{u} \notin Mk, add \mathbf{u} to P1. If \mathbf{u} \in Mk and \hat{d} is infinite, add \mathbf{u} to P2. 4. Compute the RGB loss \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} for all \mathbf{u} \in P0. 5. If depth Dk is available, compute the Depth loss \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} for all \mathbf{u} \in P0. 6. Compute the Freespace loss \mathcal{L}{\text{freespace}} for all \mathbf{u} \in P1. 7. Compute the Occupancy loss \mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}} for all \mathbf{u} \in P2. 8. Optionally, compute the Normal loss \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}} for all \mathbf{u} \in P0. 9. Sum all active losses and backpropagate to update \theta. RGB Loss (for P0): \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P0} \|\xi(\mathbf{I}){\mathbf{u}} - \xi(\hat{\mathbf{I}}){\mathbf{u}}\| Where \xi(\cdot) computes image features (RGB values and optionally image gradients) and \|\cdot\| is a robust error metric (L1 loss in practice). Depth Loss (for P0, if Dk available): \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P0} |d - \hat{d}|1 Where d is the ground truth depth value for pixel \mathbf{u} and \hat{d} is the predicted surface depth. Freespace Loss (for P1): \mathcal{L}{\text{freespace}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P1} \text{BCE}(f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}), 0) Where \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{r}(\hat{d}) is the predicted surface point. If no surface depth is predicted (\hat{d} is infinite), apply BCE to a randomly sampled point on the ray instead. Occupancy Loss (for P2): \mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P2} \text{BCE}(f{\theta}(\mathbf{r}(d{\text{random}})), 1) Where d{\text{random}} are uniformly sampled depth values along the ray. In single-view experiments, use the visual hull depth (first point inside all object masks) or ground truth depth if available. Normal Loss (optional, for P0): \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P0} \|\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{p}{\mathbf{u}}) - \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{q}{\mathbf{u}})\|2 Where \mathbf{n}(\cdot) is the normal vector, \hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}} is the predicted surface point, and \mathbf{q}{\mathbf{u}} is a randomly sampled neighbor of \hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}}. Np: Number of random pixels sampled on the image plane per training step. \xi(\cdot): Feature extractor for RGB loss. Uses RGB-values and optionally image gradients. \|\cdot\|: Robust error metric for RGB loss. Uses L1 loss in practice. Infinite Depth in P1: If a point \mathbf{u} \in P1 has no predicted surface depth, the Freespace loss must still be applied to a randomly sampled point on the ray to penalize empty space. Single-View Ambiguity: For P2 in single-view experiments, the target depth for Occupancy loss should be the visual hull depth (intersection of all object masks) rather than a random sample, to provide a meaningful target. Unconstrained Areas: The Normal loss is particularly useful for real-world data to enforce natural shapes in areas unconstrained by 2D/2.5D supervision. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetraininglosses(Ik, Mk, Dk, ftheta, ttheta, Np, usedepth=False, usenormal=False): """ Computes training losses for implicit surface learning. Args: Ik: Input image tensor. Mk: Object mask tensor (boolean). Dk: Ground truth depth map (optional). ftheta: Occupancy network function. ttheta: Texture network function. Np: Number of pixels to sample. usedepth: Boolean flag for depth supervision. usenormal: Boolean flag for normal regularization. Returns: Total loss value. """ # 1. Sample Np points on the image plane # Implementation note: Sample indices (u, v) uniformly from image dimensions ucoords = samplerandompixels(Np) P0 = [] P1 = [] P2 = [] # 2 & 3. Classify pixels into P0, P1, P2 for u in ucoords: # Predict depth for pixel u # Implementation note: Cast ray from camera origin through u, # find intersection with isosurface ftheta(p) = tau dhat = predictsurfacedepth(u, ftheta) isinsidemask = Mk[u] if isinsidemask and dhat is not None: P0.append(u) elif not isinsidemask: P1.append(u) elif isinsidemask and dhat is None: P2.append(u) totalloss = 0.0 # 4. RGB Loss for P0 if P0: rgbloss = 0.0 for u in P0: # Get predicted image patch at u # Implementation note: Render texture ttheta at predicted surface point Ihatu = rendertexture(u, ttheta) Iu = Ik[u] # Compute features featuresgt = extractfeatures(Iu) # RGB + optional gradients featurespred = extractfeatures(Ihatu) # L1 loss on features rgbloss += l1norm(featuresgt - featurespred) totalloss += rgbloss # 5. Depth Loss for P0 (if available) if usedepth and P0 and Dk is not None: depthloss = 0.0 for u in P0: dgt = Dk[u] dhat = predictsurfacedepth(u, ftheta) if dgt is not None and dhat is not None: depthloss += abs(dgt - dhat) totalloss += depthloss # 6. Freespace Loss for P1 if P1: freespaceloss = 0.0 for u in P1: dhat = predictsurfacedepth(u, ftheta) if dhat is not None: # Point on predicted surface phat = raypoint(u, dhat) occval = ftheta(phat) freespaceloss += binarycrossentropy(occval, 0.0) else: # No surface predicted, sample random point on ray drandom = samplerandomdepth() prandom = raypoint(u, drandom) occval = ftheta(prandom) freespaceloss += binarycrossentropy(occval, 0.0) totalloss += freespaceloss # 7. Occupancy Loss for P2 if P2: occupancyloss = 0.0 for u in P2: # Sample random depths drandom = samplerandomdepth() prandom = raypoint(u, drandom) occval = ftheta(prandom) occupancyloss += binarycrossentropy(occval, 1.0) totalloss += occupancyloss # 8. Normal Loss (optional) for P0 if usenormal and P0: normalloss = 0.0 for u in P0: phat = raypoint(u, predictsurfacedepth(u, ftheta)) np = computenormal(phat, ftheta) q = sampleneighbor(phat) nq = computenormal(q, ftheta) normalloss += l2norm(np - nq) totalloss += normalloss return totalloss def extractfeatures(imagepatch): """Extracts RGB values and optionally image gradients.""" # Implementation note: Concatenate RGB channels and gradient magnitudes return imagepatch def l1norm(tensor): return torch.sum(torch.abs(tensor)) def l2norm(tensor): return torch.norm(tensor) def binarycrossentropy(prediction, target): # BCE(prediction, target) = -(target log(prediction) + (1 - target) log(1 - prediction)) # Implementation note: Add epsilon for numerical stability eps = 1e-7 pred = torch.clamp(prediction, eps, 1 - eps) return -(target torch.log(pred) + (1 - target) torch.log(1 - pred)) def samplerandompixels(n): # Implementation note: Return list of (u, v) coordinates pass def predictsurfacedepth(u, ftheta): # Implementation note: Cast ray, find root of ftheta(p) = tau pass def raypoint(u, d): # Implementation note: Convert pixel u and depth d to 3D point pass def samplerandomdepth(): # Implementation note: Sample depth uniformly within bounds pass def computenormal(p, ftheta): # Implementation note: Compute gradient of ftheta at p pass def sampleneighbor(p): # Implementation note: Sample a point q near p pass Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampled pixels Np and the number of active sets (P0, P1, P2). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to Np to store the sets and intermediate gradients. Strengths: Works with as little as one image per object. Can incorporate depth information if available. The occupancy loss helps refine initial occupancy using photometric and depth losses. Limitations: Relies on 2D/2.5D supervision, which may leave unconstrained areas; the normal loss is needed to enforce natural shapes in these areas. When to use: When training implicit neural representations with limited 2D image supervision, especially in single-view or sparse-view settings. This method was introduced in the paper "Differentiable Volumetric Rendering: Learning Implicit 3D Representations without 3D Supervision". It addresses the challenge of training occupancy and texture networks without explicit 3D ground truth, using only 2D image masks and optionally depth maps. name: Adjoint Method
head: Adjoint Differentiation, Adjoint Rendering for Backpropagation, Adjoint-Mode Automatic Differentiation, Backpropagation via Adjoint Rendering, Backward-Mode Differentiation, Backward-mode Automatic Differentiation, Reverse mode differentiation
body: The Adjoint Method is a technique for computing gradients of a volume rendering loss with respect to input parameters (such as transfer function, volume density, camera, or step size) by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm. It solves the problem of differentiating the rendering integral by evaluating the chain rule from left to right (output to input), which is equivalent to backpropagation. Unlike the Forward-Mode Automatic Differentiation, which scales linearly with the number of parameters, the Adjoint Method has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function. It builds on Differentiable volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: The adjoint of the final output \hat{x}{\text{out}} (typically initialized to 1 or the gradient of the loss w.r.t. the output), and the forward pass variables (intermediate states) required for the backward pass. Outputs: The gradients (adjoints) with respect to all input parameters: \hat{\Delta t}, \hat{\text{cam}}, \hat{T}, \hat{V}. Data Structures: Forward Variables: During the forward pass, intermediate values such as transmittance, accumulated color, and ray states must be stored for reuse in the backward pass. For ray-based methods, the list of intersected primitives is also stored. Adjoint Variables: A set of variables \hat{x}i initialized to 0, storing \frac{\partial x{\text{out}}}{\partial xi}. Steps: 1. Forward Pass: Trace the ray through the volume, computing color and opacity at each step i. Store intermediate forward variables (e.g., \text{color}i, ci, di, \mathbf{x}i) and ray intersection lists. 2. Initialize Adjoint: Set the adjoint of the final output \hat{x}{\text{out}} = 1 (or \frac{\partial f{\text{loss}}}{\partial \text{color}N}). Initialize all other intermediate adjoint variables to 0. 3. Backward Pass: Iterate backwards from the last step i = N-1 down to 0. Blend Gradient: Compute adjoints for color and opacity at step i using the blending derivative: \hat{\text{color}}i, \hat{c}i \ += \ \left( \frac{\partial f{\text{blend}}(\text{color}i, ci)}{\partial (\text{color}i, ci)} \right)^T \hat{\text{color}}N TF Gradient: Compute adjoints for density and transfer function values using the TF evaluation derivative: \hat{d}i, \hat{T} \ += \ \left( \frac{\partial f{\text{TF}}(di, T)}{\partial (di, T)} \right)^T \hat{c}i Interpolation Gradient: Compute adjoints for interpolated position and volume density using the interpolation derivative: \hat{\mathbf{x}}i, \hat{V} \ += \ \left( \frac{\partial f{\text{interpolate}}(\mathbf{x}i, V)}{\partial (\mathbf{x}i, V)} \right)^T \hat{d}i Ray Update Gradient: Accumulate adjoints for step size \Delta t, direction \omega, and origin \mathbf{x}o based on the ray marching update: \hat{\mathbf{x}}o \ += \ \hat{\mathbf{x}}i, \quad \hat{\Delta t} \ += \ i \omega^T \hat{\mathbf{x}}i, \quad \hat{\omega} \ += \ i \Delta t \hat{\mathbf{x}}i 4. Camera Gradient: Accumulate adjoint for camera parameters using the camera projection derivative: \hat{\text{cam}} \ += \ \left( \frac{\partial f{\text{camera}}(uv, \text{cam})}{\partial \text{cam}} \right)^T [\mathbf{x}o; \omega] 5. Finalize: Ignore \hat{\text{color}}0. Sum adjoint variables if a parameter is used multiple times (along a ray or over multiple rays). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adjointdvrforwardbackward( stepsize: float, camera: Camera, tf: TransferFunction, volume: Volume, gradlosscolor: Tensor, # Gradient of loss w.r.t. final color forwardvars: Dict # Contains colori, ci, di, xi, etc. for i=0..N) -> Dict: """ Computes gradients for DVR using the Adjoint Method. forwardvars contains intermediate states from the forward pass. """ # 1. Initialize adjoints adjstepsize = 0.0 adjcamera = zeroslike(camera) adjtf = zeroslike(tf) adjvolume = zeroslike(volume) # Adjoint of current accumulated color and opacity # Initialize with the loss gradient adjcolorN = gradlosscolor # Note: In the loop, we propagate adjcolorN backwards to adjcolori N = forwardvars['numsteps'] # 2. Backward Pass for i in range(N - 1, -1, -1): # Retrieve forward variables for step i colori = forwardvars['color'][i] ci = forwardvars['opacity'][i] di = forwardvars['density'][i] xi = forwardvars['position'][i] # Step 3a: Blend Gradient # Compute derivative of blend function w.r.t colori and ci # fblend(colori, ci) -> color{i+1} (or final if i=N-1) # adjcolorN is the adjoint of the output of this blend dblenddcolori, dblenddci = computeblendderivatives(colori, ci) # Update adjoints for colori and ci # adjcolori accumulates gradient from the blend operation adjcolori = dblenddcolori.T @ adjcolorN adjci = dblenddci.T @ adjcolorN # Step 3b: TF Gradient # ftf(di, T) -> ci dtfddi, dtfdT = computetfderivatives(di, tf) adjdi = dtfddi.T @ adjci adjtf += dtfdT.T @ adjci # Accumulate TF gradient # Step 3c: Interpolation Gradient # finterp(xi, V) -> di dinterpdxi, dinterpdV = computeinterpderivatives(xi, volume) adjxi = dinterpdxi.T @ adjdi adjvolume += dinterpdV.T @ adjdi # Accumulate Volume gradient # Step 3d: Ray Update Gradient # x{i+1} = xi + stepsize omega # xi = xo + i stepsize omega # We have adjxi (adjoint of xi) adjxo += adjxi adjstepsize += i omega.T @ adjxi adjomega += i stepsize adjxi # Prepare adjcolorN for the next iteration (i-1) # The output of step i-1 blend is the input to step i blend (or final) # So adjcolorN for step i-1 is adjcolori from step i adjcolorN = adjcolori # Step 4: Camera Gradient # xo and omega depend on camera dcamdxo, dcamdomega = computecameraderivatives(camera) adjcamera += dcamdxo.T @ adjxo + dcamdomega.T @ adjomega return { 'stepsize': adjstepsize, 'camera': adjcamera, 'tf': adjtf, 'volume': adjvolume } Parameters: Step size \Delta t: Distance between samples. Used in ray marching updates. Memory Cost: Storing intersection lists is approx. 1.2 KB per ray. Shared Memory Limit: 48kB per multiprocessor limits TF resolution to 96 texels when using adjoint-delayed accumulation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Consumption: Storing intermediate colors scales linearly with steps, exceeding memory. Solved by the Inversion Trick. Reverse Order: Simple operator overloading is not applicable; operations must be recorded or manually derived. Atomic Conflicts: Naive accumulation of TF gradients in global memory using atomics is >100x slower than forward pass due to write conflicts. Use delayed accumulation in shared memory. Ray Tracing Instability: Using ray tracing to retrieve surfaces in reverse order causes high instability; storing intersections in forward pass is preferred. The Inversion Trick is a memory optimization technique for differentiable volume rendering that reduces the memory complexity of the adjoint method from linear to constant with respect to the number of samples per ray. It solves the problem of excessive memory consumption in standard adjoint volume rendering, where intermediate accumulated colors must be stored for every sample along a ray to compute gradients. By exploiting the mathematical invertibility of the front-to-back blending operation, the method reconstructs intermediate accumulated colors on-the-fly during the backward pass instead of storing them, trading increased computation for reduced memory usage. A Python torch.autograd.Function implementation that replaces the C++ autograd layer, routing between forward/backward C++ ops and handling gradient requirements. Computes gradients of the loss with respect to alpha values given gradients of the loss with respect to weights and the final transmittance, using reverse accumulation. Initialize backcum = gradlast[iray] alphainvlast[iray]. Iterate backwards from ie-1 to is: compute grad[i] = gradweights[i] T[i] - backcum / (1.0 - alpha[i] + 1e-10), then update backcum += gradweights[i] weight[i]. Numerical stability epsilon 10^{-10} is added to the denominator. Computes the gradient of the projection weight P with respect to the ray direction \mathbf{n}, i.e., \partial P / \partial \mathbf{n}{idx}, accounting for the implicit dependence of the entry point pa on \mathbf{n}. The total gradient is rayn.grad[idx] + fact pa.grad[idx], where fact accounts for the implicit dependence. Time Complexity: Computational complexity is largely constant with respect to the number of parameters, making it efficient for optimizing many parameters (e.g., Transfer Function). However, it requires multiple passes for multi-component outputs. Memory Complexity: Standard adjoint method scales linearly with the number of steps (O(np)) due to storing intermediate variables. With the Inversion Trick, memory is constant. Measured Performance: On an RTX 2070, a single forward/backward pass takes 9.5 ms / 14.6 ms respectively (total 24.1 ms). Forward-immediate takes 21.3 ms. Forward-delayed is ~30% slower due to re-tracing. Strengths: Efficient for optimizing many parameters; computes exact gradients (except rounding errors). Limitations: High memory usage without Inversion Trick; naive global memory accumulation is slow; requires manual derivation of adjoint code for high-level functions. When to Use: Optimizing many parameters (e.g., TF reconstruction). When Not to Use: Optimizing few parameters (e.g., camera position) where forward mode is faster. The Adjoint Method for Direct Volume Rendering (DiffDVR) was introduced by (2021). It is based on the principles of Automatic Differentiation (AD), specifically reverse-mode differentiation, which evaluates the chain rule from left to right. The method was implemented as a custom CUDA operation in PyTorch using NVRTC for JIT compilation. It has been applied to TF reconstruction, volume reconstruction, and optimization tasks. name: Inversion Trick
head: Backward Reconstruction, Invertible Blending, On-the-fly Recomputation, Reversible Blending
body: The Inversion Trick is a memory optimization technique for differentiable volume rendering that reduces the memory complexity of the adjoint method from linear to constant with respect to the number of samples per ray. It solves the problem of excessive memory consumption in standard adjoint volume rendering, where intermediate accumulated colors must be stored for every sample along a ray to compute gradients. By exploiting the mathematical invertibility of the front-to-back blending operation, the method reconstructs intermediate accumulated colors on-the-fly during the backward pass instead of storing them, trading increased computation for reduced memory usage. The method relies on the invertibility of the standard volume rendering blending equations. The forward pass computes the final pixel color, and the backward pass computes gradients. The key insight is that if the accumulated color and opacity at step i+1 are known, and the current sample's color and opacity are recomputed, the accumulated values at step i can be uniquely determined. Inputs: Final accumulated color C^{(N)} and opacity \alpha^{(N)} from the forward pass (typically \alpha^{(N)} is close to 1, but the algorithm handles general cases). Access to the volume data (density) and Transfer Function (TF) to re-evaluate sample properties ci (color) and \alphai (opacity) at any step i. Outputs: Gradients with respect to parameters (TF weights, camera pose, step size, volume densities) accumulated into local registers or shared memory. Accumulated State: Two scalar/vector variables per ray: current accumulated color C and accumulated opacity \alpha. No array of intermediate states is stored. Adjoint State: Two variables per ray: \hat{C} (gradient w.r.t. color) and \hat{\alpha} (gradient w.r.t. opacity). Initialized to \hat{C}^{(N)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial C^{(N)}} and \hat{\alpha}^{(N)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha^{(N)}}. Parameter Gradients: Local registers for per-ray accumulation (camera, step size, volume densities) or shared memory for TF parameters. The standard forward blending equations for sample i are: C^{(i+1)} = C^{(i)} + (1 - \alpha^{(i)}) Ci \alpha^{(i+1)} = \alpha^{(i)} + (1 - \alpha^{(i)}) \alphai where Ci and \alphai are the color and opacity of the current sample. The Inversion Trick derives the inverse operations to recover C^{(i)} and \alpha^{(i)} from C^{(i+1)}, \alpha^{(i+1)}, Ci, and \alphai: 1. Inverse Opacity Reconstruction: \alpha^{(i)} = \frac{\alphai - \alpha^{(i+1)}}{\alphai - 1} This formula is valid for \alphai < 1. 2. Inverse Color Reconstruction: C^{(i)} = C^{(i+1)} - (1 - \alpha^{(i)}) Ci Here, \alpha^{(i)} is the value reconstructed in the previous step. The adjoint (gradient) propagation equations, which also require the current sample values Ci and \alphai, are: \hat{\alpha}i = (1 - \alphai) \hat{\alpha}^{(i+1)} - Ci \cdot \hat{C}^{(i+1)} \hat{C}i = (Ci - \alpha^{(i)}) \hat{C}^{(i+1)} \quad \text{(Note: Source defines } \hat{C} \text{ as gradient w.r.t sample color, distinct from accumulated } C \text{)} Correction based on Source Eq 9: The source defines \hat{C} as the gradient with respect to the sample color Ci and \hat{\alpha} as the gradient with respect to the sample opacity \alphai. The accumulated gradients are \hat{C}^{(i)} and \hat{\alpha}^{(i)}. The equations are: \hat{\alpha} = (1 - \alpha^{(i)}) \hat{\alpha}^{(i+1)} \hat{C} = (Ci - \alpha^{(i)}) \hat{C}^{(i+1)} \hat{\alpha}^{(i)} = (1 - \alphai) \hat{\alpha}^{(i+1)} - Ci \cdot \hat{C}^{(i+1)} \hat{C}^{(i)} = \hat{C}^{(i+1)} Clarification: Source uses \hat{\alpha} and \hat{C} for the gradients of the current sample parameters, and \hat{\alpha}^{(i)} and \hat{C}^{(i)} for the accumulated gradients passed to the previous step. The term (C - \alpha^{(i)}) in the source likely refers to Ci (sample color) minus the reconstructed accumulated opacity \alpha^{(i)}. Given the context of Eq 9 in, \hat{C} is the gradient w.r.t the sample color Ci. The term C in (C - \alpha^{(i)}) is ambiguous in the raw text but structurally corresponds to the sample color Ci in the forward pass C^{(i+1)} = C^{(i)} + (1-\alpha^{(i)})Ci. However, looking at the derivative \frac{\partial C^{(i+1)}}{\partial Ci} = 1-\alpha^{(i)}, the gradient \hat{C} should be \hat{C}^{(i+1)}. In Eq 9, \alpha and C appear without superscripts in the gradient calculations for \hat{\alpha} and \hat{C}, but with superscripts in the reconstruction. Formula: (1-\alpha)\hat{\alpha}^{(i+1)} - C \cdot \hat{C}^{(i+1)}. Here \alpha is sample opacity, C is sample color. Compute the final color C^{(N)} and opacity \alpha^{(N)}. Store only the final color C^{(N)} (and potentially \alpha^{(N)} if needed for loss, though usually \alpha^{(N)} \approx 1). Do not store intermediate C^{(i)} or \alpha^{(i)}. 2. Initialize Adjoint: Set \hat{C}^{(N)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial C^{(N)}} and \hat{\alpha}^{(N)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha^{(N)}}. 3. Backward Pass Loop: Iterate i from N-1 down to 0: a. Recompute Sample: Evaluate the volume density and TF at the current sample position to get current sample color Ci and opacity \alphai. b. Reconstruct Accumulated State: i. Calculate reconstructed accumulated opacity: \alpha^{(i)} = \frac{\alphai - \alpha^{(i+1)}}{\alphai - 1}. ii. Calculate reconstructed accumulated color: C^{(i)} = C^{(i+1)} - (1 - \alpha^{(i)}) Ci. c. Compute Adjoint Variables: i. \hat{\alpha} = (1 - \alpha^{(i)}) \hat{\alpha}^{(i+1)}. ii. \hat{C} = (Ci - \alpha^{(i)}) \hat{C}^{(i+1)}. Note: Source uses C in this formula; context implies sample color Ci. iii. \hat{\alpha}^{(i)} = (1 - \alphai) \hat{\alpha}^{(i+1)} - Ci \cdot \hat{C}^{(i+1)}. iv. \hat{C}^{(i)} = \hat{C}^{(i+1)}. d. Accumulate Gradients: Add \hat{\alpha} and \hat{C} to the local registers for the current parameters (TF weights, etc.). 4. Final Accumulation: After traversing all rays, accumulate the per-ray gradients into global memory using atomic operations for shared parameters (TF, camera) or on cell exit for volume densities. Recompute current sample Ci, alphai = raysampler.sample(i) # 2. Reconstruct accumulated state C^(i) and alpha^(i) # Inverse opacity reconstruction # alpha^(i) = (alphai - alpha^(i+1)) / (alphai - 1) # Pitfall: alphai < 1 required. If alphai == 1, division by zero. # In practice alphai < 1 due to finite absorption. alphacurr = (alphai - alphanext) / (alphai - 1) # Inverse color reconstruction # C^(i) = C^(i+1) - (1 - alpha^(i)) Ci Ccurr = Cnext - (1 - alphacurr) Ci # 3. Compute adjoint variables for current sample and previous step # From Eq 9 # hatalpha (gradient w.r.t sample opacity alphai) hatalphasample = (1 - alphacurr) hatalphanext # hatC (gradient w.r.t sample color Ci) # Source formula: hatC = (C - alpha^(i)) hatC^(i+1) # Interpreting C in source as sample color Ci hatCsample = (Ci - alphacurr) hatCnext # hatalpha^(i) (gradient w.r.t accumulated opacity alpha^(i)) hatalphacurr = (1 - alphai) hatalphanext - Ci hatCnext # hatC^(i) (gradient w.r.t accumulated color C^(i)) hatCcurr = hatCnext # 4. Accumulate gradients for parameters # Example: if alphai and Ci depend on TF weights w # gradtf += hatalphasample dalphai/dw + hatCsample dCi/dw # This part depends on the specific parameterization, which is not detailed in the inversion trick itself # but is part of the adjoint method context. # Update state for next iteration (i-1) alphanext = alphacurr Cnext = Ccurr hatalphanext = hatalphacurr hatCnext = hatCcurr return gradtf, graddensity Number of Steps (N): The memory usage is O(1) regardless of N. Typical N ranges from 64 to 1024 depending on resolution and view. Opacity Threshold: The inversion requires \alphai < 1. In practice, transfer functions are designed such that opacity is strictly less than 1 to avoid infinite absorption. Singularity at \alphai = 1: The inverse opacity formula divides by \alphai - 1. If \alphai = 1, the operation is undefined. This case is considered impossible in practice because it requires infinite absorption in the transfer function. Implementers should guard against numerical precision issues where \alphai might be extremely close to 1, potentially causing large errors in \alpha^{(i)}. Precision Loss: Repeated reconstruction of accumulated colors from subsequent values can accumulate floating-point errors, especially over long rays with many steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) with respect to the number of steps per ray. This is a significant improvement over the standard adjoint method, which requires O(N) memory to store intermediate colors. Time Complexity: The backward pass requires re-evaluating the sample properties (density and TF) for each step, effectively doubling the computation for the volume sampling part compared to a forward-only pass, and adding the overhead of reconstruction. However, it avoids the memory bandwidth cost of storing and retrieving large arrays of intermediate colors. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables differentiable volume rendering on hardware with limited memory (e.g., GPUs with small caches or VRAM) for high-resolution volumes or long rays. Limitations: Increased computational cost due to on-the-fly recomputation. Potential numerical instability if opacity values are close to 1. When to use: When memory is the bottleneck for differentiable volume rendering, particularly for high-resolution volumes or large scenes. When not to use: When memory is abundant and computational speed is prioritized over memory usage, the standard adjoint method may be faster as it avoids recomputation. The Inversion Trick was proposed in the context of Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) to address the memory limitations of the adjoint method. The standard adjoint method requires storing all intermediate accumulated colors, which scales linearly with the number of samples and quickly exceeds available memory for high-resolution volumes. The technique exploits the invertibility of the front-to-back blending equation, a property inherent to the DVR formulation. It was introduced in the paper "Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering".
