name: Plenoxels regularization ablation
head: Plenoxels TV and sparsity regularization
body: This article documents the regularization strategies used in the Plenoxels framework to stabilize the optimization of sparse voxel-based radiance fields. It addresses the problem of visual artifacts (floaters, holes) and memory inefficiency inherent in high-dimensional, non-convex optimization of explicit representations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining Total Variation (TV) regularization on both voxel opacities and spherical harmonic coefficients with scene-specific sparsity and beta losses, rather than relying solely on geometric constraints or tomographic projections [S1, 3265-space-time-tomographic-projection-stp-regularizer.md, 3273-anisotropic-total-variation.md]. The core mechanism involves adding penalty terms to the reconstruction loss to enforce smoothness and sparsity. The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{recon} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV} + \mathcal{L}{aux} where \mathcal{L}{recon} is the reconstruction loss computed over sampled rays [1132-plenoxel-optimization-with-tv-regularization.md]. The primary regularization term \mathcal{L}{TV} is the isotropic Total Variation computed over sampled voxels and SH dimensions: \mathcal{L}{TV} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum{\substack{\mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{V} \\ d \in [D]}} \sqrt{\Deltax^2(\mathbf{v}, d) + \Deltay^2(\mathbf{v}, d) + \Deltaz^2(\mathbf{v}, d)} Here, D is the dimensionality of the SH coefficients, \mathcal{V} is a stochastic batch of active voxels, and \Delta^2x(\mathbf{v}, d) is the squared difference between the d-th value in voxel \mathbf{v}=(i,j,k) and its neighbor (i+1,j,k), normalized by the voxel resolution. The terms \Delta^2y and \Delta^2z are computed analogously for the y and z directions. The TV weight \lambda{TV} is fixed per scene type (bounded, forward-facing, 360°) and differs for SH coefficients and \sigma. Auxiliary losses \mathcal{L}{aux} include sparsity and beta regularizers applied to specific scene types. This method trains sparse voxel-based radiance fields by combining MSE reconstruction loss with TV regularization on voxel opacities (\sigma) and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients [1132-plenoxel-optimization-with-tv-regularization.md]. It explicitly penalizes high-frequency spatial variations in the voxel grid to prevent visual artifacts and ill-conditioning [1132-plenoxel-optimization-with-tv-regularization.md]. It builds on Plenoxels and Plenoxels regularization ablation. These are auxiliary regularizers used in addition to TV regularization. Sparsity Loss is applied to forward-facing and 360° scenes to encourage voxels to be empty, reducing memory footprint and quality loss during upsampling. It is evaluated at each sample on each active ray in each minibatch. The formula is: \mathcal{L}s = \lambdas \sum{i,k} \log \left( 1 + 2\sigma(\mathbf{r}i(tk))^2 \right) where \sigma(\mathbf{r}i(tk)) is the opacity of sample k along training ray i. Beta Loss is applied to 360° scenes to promote clear foreground-background decomposition by encouraging foreground transmittance to be either fully opaque or empty. The formula is: \mathcal{L}\beta = \lambda\beta \sum{\mathbf{r}} (\log(T{FG}(\mathbf{r})) + \log(1 - T{FG}(\mathbf{r}))) where T{FG}(\mathbf{r}) is the accumulated foreground transmittance of ray \mathbf{r}. Comparison and Ablation Results: On 8 forward-facing NeRF scenes, applying TV on both SH and \sigma yields PSNR 26.29, SSIM 0.839, LPIPS 0.210. Removing TV drops PSNR to 25.25 (TV \sigma only) or 25.80 (TV SH only). Sparsity alone yields PSNR 26.31. TV regularization on \sigma has a quantitatively larger effect than on SH, but both are essential for avoiding visual artifacts on forward-facing scenes with few training views. Without TV regularization on either, 3 out of 8 scenes run out of memory. The sparsity regularizer is not strictly necessary for image quality but is retained to reduce memory footprint. The Plenoxels framework utilizes sparse voxel grids and spherical harmonics to represent radiance fields without neural networks, enabling fast rendering and optimization. The regularization strategies described herein were developed to address the instability and memory issues associated with optimizing high-dimensional SH coefficients in sparse voxel structures. The implementation relies on custom CUDA extensions for differentiable volume rendering due to limited support in standard autodiff libraries. name: Plenoxel Optimization with TV Regularization
head: Chambolle-Pock TV, Plenoxels TV and sparsity regularization, TV regularization, Total Variation Reconstruction
body: Plenoxel Optimization with TV Regularization trains sparse voxel-based radiance fields by combining mean squared error (MSE) reconstruction loss with Total Variation (TV) regularization on voxel opacities (\sigma) and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. It addresses visual artifacts and ill-conditioning in high-dimensional, non-convex optimization by explicitly penalizing high-frequency spatial variations in the voxel grid. It builds on Plenoxels and Plenoxels regularization ablation. Inputs: Ground truth images and corresponding camera poses. A sparse voxel grid structure containing opacity (\sigma) and SH coefficients for each active voxel. Optimization hyperparameters: \lambda{TV} (TV weight), learning rates for \sigma and SH coefficients, and batch sizes for rays \mathcal{R} and voxels \mathcal{V}. Outputs: Optimized voxel opacities and SH coefficients. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A sparse 3D grid where each active voxel stores a scalar opacity \sigma and a vector of SH coefficients. Ray Sample \mathcal{R}: A stochastic subset of training rays used for the reconstruction loss. Voxel Sample \mathcal{V}: A stochastic subset of active voxels used for the TV loss. Formulas: The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{recon} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV} The reconstruction loss is the MSE between rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and ground truth C(\mathbf{r}): \mathcal{L}{recon} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|C(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 The TV regularization loss is the sum of isotropic gradients over sampled voxels and SH dimensions: \mathcal{L}{TV} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum{\substack{\mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{V} \\ d \in [D]}} \sqrt{\Deltax^2(\mathbf{v}, d) + \Deltay^2(\mathbf{v}, d) + \Deltaz^2(\mathbf{v}, d)} where D is the dimensionality of the SH coefficients, and \Delta^2x(\mathbf{v}, d) is the squared difference between the d-th value in voxel \mathbf{v}=(i,j,k) and its neighbor (i+1,j,k), normalized by the voxel resolution. Analogous definitions apply for \Delta^2y and \Delta^2z. Parameters: \lambda{TV}: Fixed per scene type (bounded, forward-facing, 360°). Different weights are used for SH coefficients and \sigma. Optimizer: RMSProp, chosen to handle ill-conditioning without the cost of second-order methods. Learning Rate: Fixed for all scenes in main experiments, but tuned separately for opacity and harmonic coefficients. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sample Rays and Voxels: For each optimization step, draw a stochastic batch of rays \mathcal{R} for reconstruction and a stochastic batch of voxels \mathcal{V} for TV regularization. 2. Render: Compute rendered colors \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for all \mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R} using differentiable volume rendering. 3. Compute Reconstruction Loss: Calculate \mathcal{L}{recon} using the formula above. 4. Compute TV Loss: For each voxel \mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{V} and each SH dimension d \in [D], compute the finite differences in x, y, and z directions. Normalize by resolution, square them, sum them, and take the square root to get the isotropic gradient magnitude. Sum over all sampled voxels and dimensions to get \mathcal{L}{TV}. 5. Combine Losses: Compute \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{recon} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV}. 6. Backpropagate: Compute gradients of \mathcal{L} with respect to voxel opacities and SH coefficients. 7. Update: Update parameters using RMSProp. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def optimizeplenoxelstv(voxelgrid, gtimages, cameras, lambdatv, lrsigma, lrsh, niters, batchsizerays, batchsizevoxels): # Initialize RMSProp optimizers for opacity and SH coefficients optsigma = RMSProp(voxelgrid.opacities, lr=lrsigma) optsh = RMSProp(voxelgrid.shcoeffs, lr=lrsh) for step in range(niters): # 1. Stochastic sampling of rays and voxels rays = samplerays(cameras, batchsizerays) voxels = samplevoxels(voxelgrid, batchsizevoxels) # 2. Differentiable volume rendering renderedcolors = renderrays(voxelgrid, rays) gtcolors = getgtcolors(rays, gtimages) # 3. Reconstruction loss lrecon = meansquarederror(renderedcolors, gtcolors) # 4. TV regularization loss ltvsigma = computetvloss(voxelgrid, voxels, voxelgrid.opacities, isscalar=True) ltvsh = computetvloss(voxelgrid, voxels, voxelgrid.shcoeffs, isscalar=False) ltv = ltvsigma + ltvsh # 5. Combine losses loss = lrecon + lambdatv ltv # 6. Backpropagation and parameter update loss.backward() optsigma.step() optsh.step() optsigma.zerograd() optsh.zerograd() def computetvloss(voxelgrid, voxels, field, isscalar): """Computes the isotropic TV loss per voxel and dimension as defined in.""" tvsum = 0.0 count = 0 res = voxelgrid.resolution for v in voxels: if isscalar: valv = field[v] gradsqsum = 0.0 for direction in ['x', 'y', 'z']: neighbor = voxelgrid.getneighbor(v, direction) if neighbor is not None: diff = (valv - field[neighbor]) / res gradsqsum += diff 2 tvsum += math.sqrt(gradsqsum) else: for d in range(field.shape[1]): valv = field[v, d] gradsqsum = 0.0 for direction in ['x', 'y', 'z']: neighbor = voxelgrid.getneighbor(v, direction) if neighbor is not None: diff = (valv - field[neighbor, d]) / res gradsqsum += diff 2 tvsum += math.sqrt(gradsqsum) count += 1 return tvsum / count if count > 0 else 0.0 def samplerays(cameras, n): return [cameras[i] for i in range(n)] def samplevoxels(grid, n): return list(grid.activevoxels)[:n] def renderrays(grid, rays): return [grid.renderray(r) for r in rays] def getgtcolors(rays, images): return [images[r.imageid] for r in rays] def meansquarederror(pred, target): return sum((p - t)2 for p, t in zip(pred, target)) / len(pred) This variant leverages the observation that during the first 1-2 minutes of optimization (or first 12,800 batches for synthetic scenes), fewer than 10% of voxels have non-zero gradients, with as few as 1% updating per batch in synthetic cases. This sparsity allows for significant computational savings by only updating active voxels. Implementation requires a custom PyTorch CUDA extension for fast differentiable volume rendering to exploit this sparsity efficiently. Time Complexity: The method uses stochastic sampling for both rays and voxels, making each iteration faster than full-batch methods. The use of RMSProp avoids the high cost of second-order methods. Performance: Achieves high-quality results after less than 1.5 minutes (first epoch) on synthetic scenes. Dramatic speedup in training compared to prior methods. Strengths: Prevents visual artifacts, handles ill-conditioning, and enables fast training. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \lambda{TV} and learning rates for different parameters. The non-convex nature of the rendering formula makes optimization challenging. When to use: When training sparse voxel radiance fields and needing to prevent artifacts and control memory. The method originates from the Plenoxels paper, which introduced radiance fields without neural networks using sparse voxel grids and SH coefficients. TV regularization is applied to the loss function to mitigate visual artifacts observed in ablation studies. Implementation details for the optimization framework are documented in an unofficial repository. name: Sparse Gradient Optimization
head: Gradient Sparsity
body: Sparse Gradient Optimization leverages the observation that during the early stages of Plenoxel training, the gradient of the density field is highly sparse, with fewer than 10% of voxels having non-zero gradients. This method enables efficient training by focusing computational resources only on active voxels, avoiding the overhead of updating the entire voxel grid. It distinguishes itself from dense gradient-based methods by exploiting this sparsity for significant speedups in optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of training rays, current Plenoxel density values, and gradient information. Output: Updated Plenoxel density values for active voxels. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D grid storing density values (\sigma) for each voxel. The grid is sparse, meaning many voxels may be inactive or zero. Gradient Map: A structure tracking which voxels have non-zero gradients. This is implicitly handled by the custom CUDA extension. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting and Rendering: For each training ray, compute the accumulated color and transmittance using differentiable volume rendering. This step is implemented via a custom PyTorch CUDA extension to handle sparse voxel structures efficiently. 2. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradients of the loss function with respect to the density values of the voxels along the ray. Due to the nature of the rendering equation and the sparsity of the scene, most voxels will have zero gradients. 3. Sparsity Identification: Identify the subset of voxels with non-zero gradients. In the first 1-2 minutes of optimization (or first 12,800 batches for synthetic scenes), fewer than 10% of voxels have non-zero gradients, and as few as 1% update per batch in synthetic cases. 4. Parameter Update: Update only the density values of the voxels with non-zero gradients using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Voxels with zero gradients are skipped, saving computation. Formulas: The core rendering equation for a ray \mathbf{r} is: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance, \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, and \mathbf{c}i is the color at step i. The gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigmai} are computed via backpropagation. Voxels with \frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigmai} = 0 are not updated. Parameters: Optimization Steps: The sparsity effect is most pronounced in the first 1-2 minutes of optimization. Batch Size: Synthetic scenes may see as few as 1% of voxels updating per batch. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The custom CUDA implementation must handle sparse data structures correctly to avoid missing updates or accessing invalid memory. Boundaries: Voxels at the boundary of the active region may have non-zero gradients due to ray intersections, even if their density is zero. These must be handled correctly. Degenerate Input: If the scene is entirely empty or fully opaque, the gradient sparsity may not hold, potentially leading to inefficiencies or incorrect updates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsegradientoptimizationstep(voxelgrid, rays, optimizer, sparsitythreshold=0.0): """ Performs one step of sparse gradient optimization for Plenoxels. Args: voxelgrid: Sparse 3D grid of density values. rays: List of rays to render. optimizer: PyTorch optimizer instance. sparsitythreshold: Not used directly; sparsity is implicit in the CUDA kernel. Returns: Updated voxelgrid. """ # 1. Forward pass: Render rays using custom CUDA kernel # The kernel computes colors and transmittances, and accumulates gradients # only for voxels with non-zero gradients. # This is implemented in a custom PyTorch CUDA extension. renderedcolors, transmittances = customcudarender(voxelgrid, rays) # 2. Compute loss # Assuming ground truth colors are available loss = computeloss(renderedcolors, groundtruthcolors) # 3. Backward pass: Compute gradients # The custom CUDA kernel handles sparse gradient accumulation loss.backward() # 4. Update only active voxels # The optimizer step is applied only to voxels with non-zero gradients # This is handled by the sparse data structure in the CUDA extension optimizer.step() # 5. Clear gradients for next step optimizer.zerograd() return voxelgrid A regularization term added to the density gradient to encourage sparsity, using a Cauchy-like function. The formula for the Cauchy sparsity gradient contribution is sparsityloss (4 sigma / (1 + 2 (sigma sigma))). An alternative implementation in Alphs version is commented out: currgradsigma += sparsityloss EXP(-pcnt) ray.worldstep;. The parameter sparsityloss is a scalar weight for the sparsity loss term; if 0, the term is skipped. Time Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to dense methods due to sparse gradient updates. Memory Complexity: Lower memory usage as only active voxels are stored and updated. Measured Performance: Dramatic speedup in training compared to prior methods, alongside real-time rendering. Quality results are achieved after the first epoch, less than 1.5 minutes. Scaling: Scales well with scene complexity due to sparsity. Strengths: Fast training, efficient memory usage, real-time rendering capability. Limitations: Requires custom CUDA implementation for optimal performance. When to Use: Ideal for large-scale scenes where training speed is critical. When Not to Use: If custom CUDA implementation is not feasible, or for very small scenes where overhead is negligible. Plenoxels was introduced by as a method for radiance field representation without neural networks. The observation of gradient sparsity was a key insight that enabled efficient optimization. The method builds on earlier work in volume rendering and neural radiance fields. name: Efficient O(N) Distortion Loss
head: Distortion Regularizer, Linear-time Distortion Loss, MipNeRF360 Distortion Loss, O(N) Distortion Loss
body: The Efficient O(N) Distortion Loss is a regularization term for differentiable volume rendering that prevents "floaters" (small, disconnected regions of volumetrically dense space) and "background collapse" (distant surfaces incorrectly modeled as semi-transparent clouds close to the camera). It minimizes the integral of distances between all pairs of points along the 1D step function parameterized by ray distances and weights. It sets itself apart from naive implementations by reducing computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N), enabling the handling of point-based queries with large numbers of sampled points (e.g., >256) without excessive GPU memory consumption. Unlike NeRF's noise injection regularizer, it more effectively eliminates artifacts without reducing reconstruction quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \mathbf{s}: Array of normalized ray distances for N samples per ray, shape (N,) or (B, N) for batched rays. Values are non-linearly normalized from near-far clipping distances to [0, 1]. \mathbf{w}: Array of weights for N samples per ray, shape (N,) or (B, N). wi is the transmittance-weighted contribution of the i-th sample. \lambda: Hyperparameter balancing the data term and the regularizer. Typical value: 0.01. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}: Scalar distortion loss value. \nabla{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}: Gradient of the loss with respect to weights, shape (N,) or (B, N). Data Structures: Intervals: Defined by endpoints si and s{i+1} for i \in [0, N-1]. Midpoints: mi = \frac{si + s{i+1}}{2}. Prefix/Suffix Sums: Precomputed arrays to allow O(1) lookup during the outer summation and gradient computation. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Midpoints: Calculate the midpoint mi for each interval i: mi = \frac{si + s{i+1}}{2} Ensure mi < m{i+1}. 2. Compute Prefix Sums: Compute prefix sums for weights w and weighted midpoints w \odot m. Let Pw[k] = \sum{j=0}^{k-1} wj and P{wm}[k] = \sum{j=0}^{k-1} wj mj for k \in [1, N], with Pw[0] = 0, P{wm}[0] = 0. 3. Compute Suffix Sums: Compute suffix sums for weights w and weighted midpoints w \odot m. Let Sw[k] = \sum{j=k+1}^{N-1} wj and S{wm}[k] = \sum{j=k+1}^{N-1} wj mj for k \in [0, N-2], with Sw[N-1] = 0, S{wm}[N-1] = 0. 4. Compute First Term (\mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}^{\text{1st}}): Calculate the sum of weighted distances between all pairs of interval midpoints using prefix sums to achieve O(N) complexity: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}^{\text{1st}} = 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi mi Pw[i] - 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi P{wm}[i] This formulation eliminates the diagonal term (i=j) and avoids the O(N^2) pairwise comparison. 5. Compute Second Term: Calculate the sum of weighted interval sizes: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}^{\text{2nd}} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} wi^2 (s{i+1} - si) This term minimizes the weighted size of each individual interval. 6. Combine Terms: Add the first and second terms to get the total distortion loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}^{\text{1st}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}^{\text{2nd}}. 7. Compute Gradients: Calculate the gradient with respect to each weight wk using prefix and suffix sums: \frac{\partial}{\partial wk} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}^{\text{1st}} = 2mk Pw[k] - 2 P{wm}[k] + 2 S{wm}[k] - 2mk Sw[k] The gradient for the second term is: \frac{\partial}{\partial wk} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}^{\text{2nd}} = \frac{2}{3} wk (s{k+1} - sk) Total gradient: \frac{\partial}{\partial wk} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial wk} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}^{\text{1st}} + \frac{\partial}{\partial wk} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}^{\text{2nd}}. 8. Scale Loss: Multiply the total distortion loss by \lambda and add it to the total loss. Pseudocode: import torch def efficientdistortionloss(s, w, lambdadist=0.01): """ Computes the Efficient O(N) Distortion Loss and its gradient. Args: s (Tensor): Normalized ray distances, shape (N,) or (B, N). w (Tensor): Weights, shape (N,) or (B, N). lambdadist (float): Hyperparameter balancing data term and regularizer. Returns: loss (Tensor): Scalar distortion loss. gradw (Tensor): Gradient of loss w.r.t. w, shape (N,) or (B, N). """ # Ensure inputs are on the same device device = s.device # Handle batch dimension if present if s.dim() == 1: s = s.unsqueeze(0) w = w.unsqueeze(0) batchsize = 1 else: batchsize, N = s.shape # Compute midpoints mi = (si + s{i+1}) / 2 # s has shape (B, N), so s[:, 1:] are s{i+1} and s[:,:-1] are si m = (s[:,:-1] + s[:, 1:]) / 2.0 # Shape (B, N-1) # Compute interval lengths lengths = s[:, 1:] - s[:,:-1] # Shape (B, N-1) # Compute prefix sums for w and wm # Pad w and wm with zeros at the beginning for easier indexing wpadded = torch.cat([torch.zeros(batchsize, 1, device=device), w[:,:-1]], dim=1) wmpadded = torch.cat([torch.zeros(batchsize, 1, device=device), w[:,:-1] m], dim=1) Pw = torch.cumsum(wpadded, dim=1) # Shape (B, N) Pwm = torch.cumsum(wmpadded, dim=1) # Shape (B, N) # Compute suffix sums for w and wm # Reverse, cumsum, reverse back wrev = torch.flip(wpadded, [1]) wmrev = torch.flip(wmpadded, [1]) Swrev = torch.cumsum(wrev, dim=1) Swmrev = torch.cumsum(wmrev, dim=1) Sw = torch.flip(Swrev, [1]) # Shape (B, N) Swm = torch.flip(Swmrev, [1]) # Shape (B, N) # Compute first term: 2 sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi mi Pw[i] - 2 sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi Pwm[i] # Note: indices in formula are 1-based for i, corresponding to 0-based index i in code for i in [1, N-1] # w[:, 1:-1] corresponds to wi for i in [1, N-2] if we consider N samples. # However, the formula sums over intervals i=0 to N-1. # Let's align with the paper's notation: N samples, N-1 intervals. # The paper uses N samples, so indices i=0..N-1 for intervals. # But s has N+1 points for N intervals? No, s has N samples, so N-1 intervals between them? # Wait, the paper says "N sampled points", and intervals are defined by si and s{i+1}. # If there are N samples, there are N-1 intervals between them? # Or are si the boundaries? # In NeRF, s usually denotes the sample positions. # The paper says: "si is the non-linearly normalized distance of the i-th sample". # And intervals are [si, s{i+1}). # If there are N samples, there are N-1 intervals? # Let's check the formula: sum{i=0}^{N-1}. name: MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion
head: Masked MSE and PSNR Computation, Masked Volume MSE/PSNR Computation, Mean Squared Error (MSE) Calculation, Mean Squared Error Loss, Photometric Loss Computation, img2mse
body: MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion computes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and target RGB values (or volume voxels) to serve as the primary photometric loss for training neural volume rendering models, and converts this error into Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for logging and evaluation. It is distinguished from structural metrics like SSIM by treating all pixel errors equally and from geometric losses like Normal-L2 by operating directly on color intensity rather than surface normals. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Predicted RGB tensor (shape [N, 3] or volume voxels), Target RGB tensor (ground truth, same shape), and optionally a binary mask indicating valid regions. Outputs: Scalar MSE loss value, PSNR value (float or infinity), and optionally masked voxel counts. Data Structures: Predicted/Target Tensors: Floating-point arrays (typically float32) normalized to [0, 1] or [0, 255] depending on implementation. For masked volume metrics, inputs are 3D voxel grids. Mask: Boolean array of same spatial dimensions as the volume/image, where True indicates valid pixels/voxels for loss computation. Parameters: maskthresholdrel: Relative threshold applied to the normalized mask volume to create the boolean mask. Default value is 0.01. batchsize: Number of random pixels sampled per iteration for training. lr: Adam learning rate used in the optimization loop. Steps: 1. Sample Rays/Pixels: For training, sample random pixel coordinates (x, y) from the image plane. Generate a ray bundle from these coordinates using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. 2. Forward Pass: Render the scene using the current model state to obtain predicted RGB values (x) at the sampled ray origins/directions. Retrieve ground truth RGB values (y) at the same coordinates. 3. Compute Raw MSE: Calculate the mean squared error between predicted and target values. For unmasked images: MSE = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (xi - yi)^2 where N is the number of pixels/voxels, xi is the predicted value, and yi is the target value. 4. Masking (Optional): If a mask is provided: Calculate the absolute mask threshold: threshold = mask\threshold\rel \cdot \max(mask\volume). Create a boolean mask where maskvolume > threshold. Compute masked MSE only over voxels/pixels where the mask is true: MSE{masked} = \frac{1}{N{mask}} \sum{i \in mask} (v{ref, i} - v{comp, i})^2 where N{mask} is the number of voxels in the mask. If the mask has no true values, raise a RuntimeError. 5. Compute PSNR: Convert MSE to PSNR for logging. If MSE > 0: PSNR = 20 \cdot \log{10}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{MSE}}\right) = -10 \cdot \log{10}(MSE) If MSE = 0, set PSNR = \infty to avoid division by zero in the logarithm. 6. Optimization Step: Use the computed MSE as the loss function. Backpropagate through the model and update weights using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch def computemseandpsnr(predictedrgb, targetrgb, mask=None): """ Computes MSE and PSNR between predicted and target RGB values. Args: predictedrgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3) or (H, W, 3) with predicted colors. targetrgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3) or (H, W, 3) with ground truth colors. mask: Optional boolean tensor of shape (N,) or (H, W) indicating valid pixels. Returns: mse: Float, the Mean Squared Error. psnr: Float, the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (or inf). maskedvoxelcount: Int, number of valid pixels/voxels. """ # Flatten to (N, 3) if necessary predflat = predictedrgb.view(-1, 3) targetflat = targetrgb.view(-1, 3) # Compute squared error sqerror = (predflat - targetflat) 2 if mask is not None: # Ensure mask is flattened maskflat = mask.view(-1) # Check for empty mask if not maskflat.any(): raise RuntimeError("Mask has no true values; cannot compute masked MSE.") # Apply mask maskedsqerror = sqerror[maskflat] maskedvoxelcount = int(maskflat.sum().item()) # Compute masked MSE mse = float(maskedsqerror.mean().item()) else: # Compute unmasked MSE mse = float(sqerror.mean().item()) maskedvoxelcount = int(predflat.shape[0]) # Compute PSNR if mse > 0.0: psnr = 20.0 math.log10(1.0 / math.sqrt(mse)) else: psnr = math.inf return mse, psnr, maskedvoxelcount def trainstep(model, raybundle, targetrgb, optimizer, mask=None): """ Single training step for neural volume rendering using MSE loss. """ # Forward pass optimizer.zerograd() predictedrgb = model(raybundle) # Compute loss mse, psnr, = computemseandpsnr(predictedrgb, targetrgb, mask) loss = mse # Backpropagation loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss, psnr Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero MSE: If the prediction perfectly matches the target, MSE is 0. The PSNR formula involves \log{10}(0), which is undefined. The implementation must explicitly handle this by returning infinity. Empty Mask: If the boolean mask contains no True values, the denominator in the masked MSE calculation becomes zero. This should raise an error rather than returning NaN or infinity. Precision: Use float32 or float64 consistently. In C++ implementations, cast inputs to double before squaring differences to prevent overflow for large intensity values. Normalization: Ensure predicted and target values are in the same range (e.g., both [0, 1] or both [0, 255]). Mismatched ranges will result in incorrect MSE values. Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is a standard benchmark metric used to evaluate the quality of reconstructed images in novel view synthesis and volume rendering by comparing rendered output against ground-truth reference images. It quantifies the logarithmic ratio between the maximum possible pixel intensity and the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the two images, providing a single scalar value where higher indicates better fidelity. Unlike structural metrics such as SSIM, PSNR measures pixel-level photometric error averaged over the entire frame, making it sensitive to large smooth regions but less responsive to small, high-frequency details like specular highlights. The Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) measures the perceived distortion between a rendered image and a ground truth image by comparing local patterns of pixel intensities, assuming the human visual system is highly adapted to structured natural scene information. It serves as a standard benchmark for image quality in radiance-field optimization, complementing pixel-wise metrics like MSE and PSNR. Unlike MSE, which treats all errors equally, SSIM accounts for luminance, contrast, and structural correlations, providing a value between -1 and 1 where 1 indicates identical images. The Normal-L2 score quantifies the geometric fidelity of a predicted surface by measuring the L2 distance between predicted surface normals and reference normals. It serves as a shape-aware alternative to RGB-based metrics like MSE, focusing on shading cues rather than color accuracy. It is distinct from PSNR and SSIM, which evaluate pixel intensity and structural similarity respectively, by operating on vector fields derived from surface geometry. A method to exclude empty froxels from evaluation metrics by including only froxels affected by radiance. A froxel is included if any of its RGB channels contain a non-zero value at any point during the test scenario. The Region of Interest (ROI) is computed separately for each tested algorithm; the union of the scenario's ROI and the ground truth's ROI is used to create ROI{effective} = ROI{scenario} \cup ROI{truth}, ensuring only relevant froxels are included while excluding completely empty regions. Treating the TAA (Temporal Anti-Aliasing) algorithm as a biased estimator to analyze correctness using Mean Squared Error (MSE), decomposed into variance and bias squared. The formula is MSE[F] = \mathbb{E}[(F - G)^2] = V[F] + \beta[F]^2, where F is the output of the estimator, G is the true value (ground truth), V[F] is the variance of the estimator, and \beta[F] is its bias. A mathematical metric that treats an image as a 2D signal and calculates the dissimilarities between a reference image and a test image. The formula is E{\gamma} = \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N |xi - yi|^{\gamma} \right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma}} where N is the number of samples in the image, xi and yi are the i-th samples of image x and y, and \gamma is a value in the range between 1, \infty. When \gamma = 2, this reduces to the square root of MSE. A variant that uses Huber loss instead of MSE for robustness to outliers, combined with masking. It renders predicted RGB and depth values, splits the tensor, blends ground truth RGB with background, and computes per-ray Huber loss for RGB with \delta=0.1, masked by rayisvalid, and averaged over valid rays. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of pixels or voxels being compared. The operation is element-wise and parallelizable on GPUs. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the squared error tensor before reduction, though this can be optimized to O(1) with streaming reduction. Performance: Computationally inexpensive compared to structural metrics like SSIM or perceptual losses. It is the standard loss function for training NeRF and similar neural radiance fields due to its simplicity and differentiability. Strengths: Simple to implement, differentiable everywhere, widely used as a baseline for comparison. Limitations: Does not account for structural similarity or perceptual quality, often leading to blurry results in optimization. Sensitive to outliers and noise. When to Use: As a primary loss for initial training, or when computational efficiency is critical. When Not to Use: When perceptual quality is more important than pixel-wise accuracy, or when dealing with noisy data where Huber or L1 loss might be more robust. The Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss is a fundamental concept in statistics and machine learning, widely adopted in neural volume rendering (e.g., NeRF) as the primary photometric loss function. The conversion from MSE to PSNR is a standard practice in image processing for logging and evaluation. Variants like masked MSE are used in volume rendering to exclude empty regions from evaluation. The use of MSE in the context of temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) for volumetric rendering highlights its role in decomposing error into bias and variance components. bmild/nerf, https://github.com/bmild/nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, https://github.com/Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ValentinKraft/vgs, https://github.com/ValentinKraft/vgs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Temporal Anti-Aliasing for Real-Time Froxel-Based Volumetric Rendering - Advances in volumetric temporal anti-aliasing for real-time ren dering of participating media, https://openalex.org/W7218067689, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial) Real-Time Ray Traced Voxel Global Illumination, https://doi.org/10.34626/0vdq-7m27, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) blurgyy/jaxngp, https://github.com/blurgyy/jaxngp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: PSNR Metric Calculation
head: PSNR Calculation, PSNR Metric, Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio
body: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) evaluates the quality of reconstructed images in novel view synthesis and volume rendering by comparing rendered output against ground-truth reference images. It quantifies the logarithmic ratio between the maximum possible pixel intensity and the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the two images, providing a single scalar value where higher indicates better fidelity. Unlike structural metrics such as SSIM, PSNR measures pixel-level photometric error averaged over the entire frame, making it sensitive to large smooth regions but less responsive to small, high-frequency details like specular highlights. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two images (or volumes) of identical dimensions: the ground-truth image I{gt} and the reconstructed/predicted image I{pred}. Both must have the same width W and height H (or voxel grid dimensions for 3D volumes). Output: A single floating-point value representing the PSNR in decibels (dB). Data Structures: Images are treated as arrays of pixel values. For RGB images, each pixel has 3 channels (R, G, B). For grayscale or volumetric data, the channel count may vary, but the MSE calculation sums squared differences across all channels per spatial location. Values are typically normalized to the range [0, 1] or scaled to an integer range (e.g., [0, 255]). The parameter \text{MAX} depends on this normalization. Steps: 1. Validation: Verify that I{gt} and I{pred} have identical spatial dimensions (W \times H). If dimensions mismatch, the metric is undefined or returns an error/infinity. 2. MSE Calculation: Compute the Mean Squared Error between the two images. For each pixel i from 0 to N-1 (where N = W \times H), compute the squared difference for each channel c. Sum these squared differences. Divide by the total number of pixels N to get MSE. The standard definition in and uses the mean over all pixels, summing channel differences within the pixel. Formula for MSE: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \sum{c \in \{R,G,B\}} (I{gt,i,c} - I{pred,i,c})^2 3. PSNR Calculation: Apply the logarithmic formula. To prevent division by zero or \log(0) when MSE is zero (perfect prediction), a small epsilon \epsilon is added to the denominator or MSE. Formula: \text{PSNR} = 10 \log{10} \left( \frac{\text{MAX}^2}{\text{MSE} + \epsilon} \right) Alternatively, using the property \log(a/b) = \log(a) - \log(b): \text{PSNR} = 20 \log{10}(\text{MAX}) - 10 \log{10}(\text{MSE} + \epsilon) If \text{MSE} = 0, PSNR is theoretically infinite. In practice, it is capped or logged as a special value. Parameters: MAX: The maximum possible pixel value. For images normalized to [0, 1], \text{MAX} = 1.0. For 8-bit images, \text{MAX} = 255. eps: A small constant to prevent numerical instability. Commonly 10^{-10}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatepsnr(imagegt, imagepred, maxval=1.0, eps=1e-10): """ Calculate Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio between two images. Args: imagegt: Array-like of ground truth pixel values. Shape (H, W, C) or (H, W). imagepred: Array-like of predicted pixel values. Same shape as imagegt. maxval: Maximum possible pixel value (e.g., 1.0 for [0,1] normalized). eps: Small constant to prevent log(0). Returns: float: PSNR in dB. """ # 1. Validate dimensions if len(imagegt) != len(imagepred) or len(imagegt[0]) != len(imagepred[0]): raise ValueError("Images must have identical dimensions.") # 2. Compute MSE totalsquareddiff = 0.0 totalelements = 0 for rowgt, rowpred in zip(imagegt, imagepred): for valgt, valpred in zip(rowgt, rowpred): totalsquareddiff += (valgt - valpred) 2 totalelements += 1 mse = totalsquareddiff / totalelements # 3. Compute PSNR if mse == 0: return float('inf') psnr = 10 math.log10((maxval 2) / (mse + eps)) return psnr Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero MSE: If the prediction is identical to the ground truth, MSE is 0, leading to infinite PSNR. Dimension Mismatch: If input images have different sizes, the metric is invalid. Weighting Bias: PSNR averages over all pixels. Large smooth regions dominate the error score, while small bright features (specular highlights, thin structures) have negligible impact on the final score. Interpretation: A difference of 3 dB corresponds to a halving of the squared error; 6 dB corresponds to a quartering. 3D Evaluation Metrics assess the fidelity of reconstructed volumetric or radiance-field representations against ground-truth data. The method computes statistical similarity metrics on voxel grids and surface geometries to evaluate both visual appearance and spatial accuracy. Unlike PSNR which measures pixel-level photometric error in 2D projections, this method aggregates errors across 3D volume dimensions (axial, coronal, sagittal) and surface normals. It complements Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation, which focuses strictly on triangular mesh topology and spatial accuracy rather than volumetric or photometric appearance. Noise Floor Estimation via MAD uses Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) estimators to determine the noise standard deviation \sigma in a volume, allowing for the calculation of a "noise floor" PSNR. Laplacian MAD: Compute the D-dimensional discrete Laplacian response. Scale the MAD of the response by 1/(0.6745 \cdot \sqrt{2D(2D+1)}) to estimate \sigma. Haar Finite-Difference MAD: Compute diagonal second differences d = I(y,x) - I(y,x+1) - I(y+1,x) + I(y+1,x+1). Estimate \sigma = \text{median}(|d|) / (0.6745 \cdot \sqrt{2}). Noise Floor PSNR: Calculated as 10 \log{10}(1/\sigma^2). Pitfall: MAD estimators may return exactly zero for some volumes (e.g., Mouse heart nuclei), indicating the model is signal-limited, not noise-limited, and thus the noise floor is not estimable. Benchmark numbers provide context for typical PSNR values in modern radiance-field optimization methods on standard datasets like Mip-NeRF 360 (room scale). Vanilla 3DGS: ~27.4 PSNR. Mip-Splatting: ~27.7 PSNR. Scaffold-GS: ~27.9 PSNR. 2DGS: ~27.0 PSNR (with better geometry). GES: Comparable PSNR to baselines with ~30% fewer primitives. Hierarchical 3DGS: Comparable performance with Level of Detail (LoD) streaming. Target: For NeRF paper Blender scenes, target PSNR is 31–33 dB. This metric isolates the error ratio independent of the bit depth (MAX), as MAX cancels out in the logarithmic difference. The difference \Delta between a configuration and the full method is: \Delta = \text{PSNR}{\text{config}} - \text{PSNR}{\text{full}} = 10 \log{10} \frac{\text{MSE}{\text{full}}}{\text{MSE}{\text{config}}}. The MSE ratio can be recovered from the PSNR difference: \frac{\text{MSE}{\text{config}}}{\text{MSE}{\text{full}}} = 10^{-\Delta/10}. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of pixels (or voxels) in the image/volume. The calculation involves a single pass to compute squared differences and a logarithmic operation. Memory Complexity: O(N) if images are not in-place, or O(1) auxiliary space if computing MSE incrementally. Strengths: Simple to compute, widely understood, and provides a single scalar for easy comparison. Limitations: It is heavily biased towards large, smooth areas. When to Use: When a quick, standard photometric error metric is required for logging during training or for comparing against historical baselines. When Not to Use: When perceptual quality is more important than pixel-wise accuracy, or when evaluating structural fidelity. PSNR has been adopted as a standard benchmark in computer graphics, particularly for novel view synthesis and volume rendering, to evaluate the reconstruction quality of radiance fields and neural radiance fields (NeRFs). The metric is frequently reported alongside SSIM and LPIPS to provide a more comprehensive evaluation. name: 3D Evaluation Metrics
body: 3D Evaluation Metrics assess the fidelity of reconstructed volumetric or radiance-field representations against ground-truth data. The method computes statistical similarity metrics on voxel grids and surface geometries to evaluate both visual appearance and spatial accuracy. Unlike PSNR Metric Calculation which measures pixel-level photometric error in 2D projections, this method aggregates errors across 3D volume dimensions (axial, coronal, sagittal) and surface normals. It complements Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation, which focuses strictly on triangular mesh topology and spatial accuracy rather than volumetric or photometric appearance. Inputs: Reconstructed volume V{rec} and ground-truth volume V{gt}, normalized to [0, 1]. Reconstructed mesh/point cloud and ground-truth mesh/point cloud for geometric metrics. Rendered images or crops for standard rendering metrics. Outputs: Mean PSNR and SSIM for axial, coronal, and sagittal views. Normal Consistency (NC) score. Standard rendering metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID/KID). Data Structures: Volumes are stored as 3D arrays with shape (D, H, W) or (X, Y, Z). Meshes are represented as sets of vertices and faces or point clouds. Steps: 1. Volume Normalization: Ensure V{rec} and V{gt} are scaled to [0, 1]. If not, apply V' = \frac{V - V{min}}{V{max} - V{min}}. 2. Axial/Coronal/Sagittal Slicing: Iterate over the three principal axes. For each axis k \in \{x, y, z\}, extract 2D slices by fixing the coordinate along k. 3. Slice-wise PSNR and SSIM: Compute PSNR and SSIM for each slice pair (S{rec}, S{gt}). Let SSIM{slice} be the score for a single slice. 4. Volume PSNR Calculation: Compute Mean Squared Error (MSE) averaged over all voxels, including background: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (V{rec,i} - V{gt,i})^2 where N is the total number of voxels. Compute PSNR: \text{PSNR} = 10 \log{10}\left(\frac{1}{\text{MSE}}\right) This is equivalent to 10 \log{10}(\text{MAX}^2 / \text{MSE}) with \text{MAX}=1. 5. Aggregation: Print the mean PSNR and SSIM for each view (axial, coronal, sagittal). 6. Normal Consistency (NC) Calculation: For surface reconstruction, compute the angular difference between estimated normals Ni and ground-truth normals Ni^ for N points: \text{NC} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (1 - \cos(Ni, Ni^)) \times 100\% where \cos(Ni, Ni^) is the cosine similarity. 7. Standard Rendering Metrics: Compute PSNR, SSIM/MS-SSIM, LPIPS, and FID/KID on rendered images or crops as defined in standard rendering literature. Parameters: SSIM Window Size: 11. SSIM Sigma: 1.5. Splat Counts: Geometrically spaced doubling from 1K to 512K, extended to 1M and 2M for specific light-sheet volumes. Fitting Settings (Contextual): Conservative culling (99.9% amplitude retention), 20,000 max iterations, early stopping patience 500 iterations, L1 loss, dynamic operations enabled. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Background Inclusion: MSE must be averaged over all voxels, including background, to avoid artificially inflated scores. Normalization: Volumes must be normalized to [0, 1] before PSNR calculation to ensure the \text{MAX}=1 assumption holds. Held-out Voxels: In benchmarking, 5% of voxels may be randomly selected and replaced with the median of their 26 neighbors in a 3×3×3 donut (excluding center) to simulate missing data or compression artifacts. Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation quantifies the geometric fidelity of a reconstructed triangular mesh against a ground-truth reference mesh. It solves the problem of assessing how well a surface reconstruction method captures the true shape, topology, and detail of the underlying scene. Unlike radiance-field metrics that evaluate visual appearance, this method focuses strictly on spatial accuracy, distinguishing it from PSNR Metric Calculation which measures pixel-level photometric error. Normal Consistency is a metric for 3D surface reconstruction measuring consistency between estimated and ground truth surface normals. It quantifies the angular deviation between the predicted surface orientation and the true geometry. The metric is defined as \text{NC} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (1 - \cos(Ni, Ni^)) \times 100\%, where Ni and Ni^ are the estimated and ground truth surface normals for the i-th point, \cos(Ni, Ni^) is the cosine similarity, and N is the number of points. A lower NC indicates better geometric alignment. Standard Rendering Metrics include PSNR, SSIM, MS-SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and KID. PSNR is cheap to compute but insensitive to perceptual quality. SSIM and MS-SSIM are structural metrics used as standard companions to PSNR. LPIPS is a learned perceptual metric that correlates better with human judgment. FID and KID are computed on rendered crops versus training images, primarily used for evaluating generative models. Time Complexity: PSNR and SSIM computation scales linearly with the number of voxels N for PSNR and N \times W^2 for SSIM (where W is window size). Normal Consistency scales linearly with the number of surface points N. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the full volume or mesh. For SSIM, temporary buffers for local means and variances are needed per window. Performance: PSNR is very fast to compute. SSIM is slower due to local window operations. LPIPS and FID are slower due to learned model inference. Strengths: Provides a comprehensive view of reconstruction quality by separating visual (PSNR/SSIM) and geometric (NC) errors. Limitations: PSNR is insensitive to perceptual quality. SSIM parameters (window size, sigma) can affect results. NC requires accurate ground-truth normals, which are often unavailable in real-world scenarios. 3D evaluation metrics have evolved alongside volume rendering and 3D reconstruction techniques. Early metrics focused on simple error measures like MSE. With the rise of differentiable rendering and Gaussian Splatting, more sophisticated metrics like SSIM and perceptual metrics (LPIPS) became standard. The specific formulation of PSNR on normalized volumes including background is highlighted in microscopy applications. Normal Consistency is a standard metric in computer vision for surface reconstruction. The categorization of metrics into rendering and geometry types is common in recent 3D Gaussian Splatting literature. name: Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation
body: Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation quantifies the geometric fidelity of a reconstructed triangular mesh against a ground-truth reference mesh. It solves the problem of assessing how well a surface reconstruction method captures the true shape, topology, and detail of the underlying scene. Unlike radiance-field metrics that evaluate visual appearance, this method focuses strictly on spatial accuracy, distinguishing it from PSNR Metric Calculation which measures pixel-level photometric error. The evaluation computes statistical distances between the vertices of the reconstructed mesh and the ground-truth surface. The primary metrics are Chamfer Distance and F-Score. Inputs: Reconstructed mesh \mathcal{M}{rec} and ground-truth mesh \mathcal{M}{gt}, typically represented as sets of vertices and faces. Outputs: Scalar scores for Chamfer Distance and F-Score. Data Structures: Point clouds or vertex sets for distance queries; KD-trees or spatial hashing for efficient nearest-neighbor search. Steps: 1. Sample points uniformly from the surface of \mathcal{M}{rec} and \mathcal{M}{gt} to obtain point sets P{rec} and P{gt}. 2. Compute the Chamfer Distance (CD) as the sum of squared nearest-neighbor distances in both directions: CD(P{rec}, P{gt}) = \frac{1}{|P{rec}|} \sum{p \in P{rec}} \min{q \in P{gt}} \|p - q\|^2 + \frac{1}{|P{gt}|} \sum{q \in P{gt}} \min{p \in P{rec}} \|p - q\|^2. 3. Compute the F-Score at a threshold distance \tau by calculating precision (fraction of P{rec} within \tau of P{gt}) and recall (fraction of P{gt} within \tau of P{rec}), then taking the harmonic mean: F(\tau) = \frac{2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}. Parameters: Threshold \tau for F-Score, typically 0.01 to 0.02 of the bounding box diagonal. Number of sampled points per mesh, typically 10^4 to 10^5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-explanation: The method focuses heavily on geometric details, which can cause over-explanation of texture on flat surfaces with complex geometry, leading to visible artifacts. Metric Discrepancy: Quantitative mesh metrics (F-score, Chamfer distance) are good, but visualizations show apparent artifacts compared to ground truth. Evaluators should always inspect visual results alongside metrics. A mesh regularization term that encourages geometric flatness by minimizing the smallest eigenvalue of the vertex normal covariance matrix, weighted by vertex area. It distinguishes itself from smoothness-based regularizers like Laplacian smoothing by explicitly penalizing curvature to promote planar patches. Choose it when differentiable surface reconstruction requires explicit flatness constraints. It builds on Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation. name: Developability Regularizer
head: Stein et al. regularizer
body:
The Developability Regularizer is a mesh regularization term that encourages geometric flatness (developability) by minimizing the smallest eigenvalue of the vertex normal covariance matrix, weighted by vertex area. It builds on Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation. The method computes a per-vertex contribution to the loss based on the local geometry of incident triangles. It aggregates normal covariances and areas, then computes the minimum eigenvalue as a measure of non-developability. Inputs: tripos: Tensor of shape (T, 3, 3), containing the 3D positions of the three vertices for each of the T triangles. tris: Tensor of shape (T, 3), containing the vertex indices for each triangle. V: Number of unique vertices in the mesh. Outputs: loss: Scalar tensor representing the total developability loss. Data Structures: vertnormalcovariancesum: Tensor of shape (V, 9), initialized to zeros. Stores the flattened 3 	imes 3 normal covariance matrix for each vertex. vertarea: Tensor of shape (V), initialized to zeros. Stores the weighted area contribution for each vertex. vertdegree: Tensor of shape (V), initialized to zeros (int32). Stores the number of triangles incident to each vertex. Parameters: RELEPS: 1 	imes 10^{-6}. Added to the covariance matrix to ensure numerical stability during eigenvalue decomposition. POSEPS: 1 	imes 10^{-6}. Used in normalization denominators to prevent division by zero. Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulators: Set vertnormalcovariancesum, vertarea, and vertdegree to zero tensors of the specified shapes. 2. Iterate Over Triangle Corners: For each triangle t in the mesh, and for each corner index iC \in \{0, 1, 2\}: a. Gather Vertices: Let p{Root} = 	ext{tri\pos}[t, iC], pA = 	ext{tri\pos}[t, (iC + 1) \pmod 3], and pB = 	ext{tri\pos}[t, (iC + 2) \pmod 3]. b. Compute Edge Vectors: vA = pA - p{Root}, vB = pB - p{Root}, and normalize them to v{An} and v{Bn}. c. Compute Face Geometry: area
ormal = vA 	imes vB, face\area = 0.5 	imes \|area
ormal\|, and normal =  rac{area
ormal}{\|area
ormal\| + 	ext{POS\EPS}}. d. Compute Corner Angle: corner\angle = \arccos(	ext{clamp}(	ext{dot}(v{An}, v{Bn}), -1, 1)). e. Compute Normal Outer Product: outer = normal \otimes normal (Resulting in a 3 	imes 3 matrix), then flatten to a vector of length 9. f. Scatter Updates: Let idx = 	ext{tris}[t, iC]. Accumulate outer to 	ext{vert
ormal\covariance\sum}[idx], add  rac{face\area}{3} to 	ext{vert\area}[idx], and add 1 to 	ext{vert\degree}[idx]. 3. Process Covariance Matrices: Reshape vertnormalcovariancesum to (V, 3, 3) and add 	ext{REL\EPS} 	imes I to each matrix, where I is the identity matrix. 4. Compute Minimum Eigenvalues: Compute the eigenvalues for each vertex's covariance matrix and take the minimum absolute value: 	ext{min\eigvals}[v] = \min(|\lambda1|, |\lambda2|, |\lambda3|). 5. Mask Degree-3 Vertices: Set 	ext{vert\area}[v] = 0 where 	ext{vert\degree}[v] == 3. 6. Normalize Area: Normalize 	ext{vert\area} by scaling it: 	ext{vert\area} \leftarrow 	ext{vert\area} 	imes  rac{V}{\sum 	ext{vert\area}}. 7. Compute Loss: Return the element-wise product 	ext{vert\area} 	imes 	ext{min\eigvals}, summed to a scalar. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computedevelopabilityregularizer(tripos, tris, V, releps=1e-6, poseps=1e-6): """ Compute the Developability Regularizer loss. Args: tripos: Tensor (T, 3, 3) - Vertex positions for each triangle. tris: Tensor (T, 3) - Vertex indices for each triangle. V: int - Number of vertices. releps: float - Regularization epsilon for eigenvalues. poseps: float - Epsilon for normalization. Returns: loss: Tensor (1,) - Scalar loss value. """ T = tripos.shape[0] # Initialize accumulators vertnormalcovariancesum = torch.zeros((V, 9), device=tripos.device) vertarea = torch.zeros((V), device=tripos.device) vertdegree = torch.zeros((V), dtype=torch.int32, device=tripos.device) # Loop over triangles and corners for iC in range(3): # Gather vertices proot = tripos[:, iC] pa = tripos[:, (iC + 1) % 3] pb = tripos[:, (iC + 2) % 3] # Edge vectors va = pa - proot vb = pb - proot # Normalize edges normva = torch.norm(va, dim=1, keepdim=True) normvb = torch.norm(vb, dim=1, keepdim=True) van = va / (normva + poseps) vbn = vb / (normvb + poseps) # Face area and normal areanormal = torch.cross(va, vb, dim=1) facearea = 0.5 torch.norm(areanormal, dim=1) normareanormal = torch.norm(areanormal, dim=1, keepdim=True) normal = areanormal / (normareanormal + poseps) # Compute corner angle (computed per source, but unused in final loss) cornerangle = torch.acos(torch.clamp(torch.sum(van vbn, dim=1), -1.0, 1.0)) # Outer product of normal (3x3 matrix) outer = torch.einsum('ti,tj->tij', normal, normal) outerflat = outer.reshape(T, 9) # Scatter updates indices = tris[:, iC] vertnormalcovariancesum.scatteradd(0, indices.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, 9), outerflat) vertarea.scatteradd(0, indices, facearea / 3.0) vertdegree.scatteradd(0, indices, torch.ones(T, dtype=torch.int32, device=tripos.device)) # Reshape covariance to (V, 3, 3) covmatrix = vertnormalcovariancesum.reshape(V, 3, 3) # Add regularization identity = torch.eye(3, device=tripos.device) covmatrix = covmatrix + releps identity # Compute eigenvalues eigvals = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(covmatrix) # Minimum absolute eigenvalue mineigvals = torch.min(torch.abs(eigvals), dim=1).values # Mask out degree-3 vertices maskdegree3 = (vertdegree == 3) vertarea = vertarea.clone() vertarea[maskdegree3] = 0.0 # Normalize area totalarea = vertarea.sum() vertarea = vertarea (V / (totalarea + poseps)) # Final loss loss = torch.sum(vertarea mineigvals) return loss Not given in the sources. The Developability Regularizer originates from the FlexiCubes framework. It is used as a regularization term in differentiable surface reconstruction to encourage mesh flatness. name: Standard Rendering Metrics
head: PSNR, PSNR computation, Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio
body: Standard rendering metrics quantify pixel-wise reconstruction error and perceptual fidelity to evaluate radiance-field optimizations. PSNR provides a cheap, decibel-based error measurement, while SSIM and MS-SSIM serve as structural companions, LPIPS offers learned perceptual similarity, and FID and KID evaluate generative distributional quality on rendered crops. These metrics focus on image-space fidelity, distinct from geometry metrics like Chamfer distance. Inputs: Rendered image tensor \hat{I} and target image tensor I, both of shape [H, W, 3] in the same color space and range. Outputs: Scalar PSNR value in decibels. Data Structures: Images are stored as dense arrays or tensors. Direct pixel access is required for PSNR and SSIM. Steps: 1. Reshape the rendered RGB tensor to [H, W, 3] and convert to a standard numerical format (e.g., NumPy). 2. Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) as the mean of squared differences between the normalized render and ground-truth tensors. 3. Clamp the MSE to a minimum of 10^{-12} to prevent \log(0). 4. Calculate PSNR as -10 \times \log{10}(\text{clamped\MSE}). 5. Return the scalar float. 6. Compute SSIM using a separate function computessim(rgb, target). Formulas: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum (\hat{I} - I)^2 \text{PSNR} = -10 \log{10}(\max(\text{MSE}, 10^{-12})) where N is the total number of elements. Parameters: mseclampmin = 1e-12 (numerical stability floor for MSE before logarithm). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-finite PSNR values (NaN/Inf) trigger a ValueError with the offending filename. PSNR is cheap to compute but insensitive to perceptual quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import math def computepsnr(rendered: np.ndarray, target: np.ndarray) -> float: # 1. Reshape to [H, W, 3] and convert to numpy rendered = np.asarray(rendered).reshape(-1, 3) if rendered.ndim == 3 else rendered target = np.asarray(target).reshape(-1, 3) if target.ndim == 3 else target # 2. Compute MSE as mean of squared differences mse = np.mean((rendered - target) 2) # 3. Clamp MSE to minimum 1e-12 mseclamped = max(mse, 1e-12) # 4. Calculate PSNR psnr = -10.0 math.log10(mseclamped) # 5. Check for non-finite values and raise error if not math.isfinite(psnr): raise ValueError(f"Non-finite PSNR value: {psnr}") # 6. Return scalar float return float(psnr) Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance with hardware, resolution and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: PSNR is cheap to compute. SSIM and MS-SSIM provide structural comparisons. LPIPS correlates better with human judgment than PSNR. Limitations: PSNR is insensitive to perceptual quality. FID and KID are computed on rendered crops versus training images and are primarily used for evaluating generative models. When to use: Use PSNR for standard pixel-wise reconstruction error evaluation. Use LPIPS when perceptual quality assessment is required. Use FID and KID for generative model evaluation. Origin, history and development: Not given in the sources. Where it is used: Standard rendering metrics are used in 3D Gaussian Splatting and NeRFs to evaluate novel view synthesis quality. They are listed alongside geometry metrics (Chamfer distance, F-score, depth error, normal error) and standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending, NeRF Synthetic, DTU) in evaluation suites. damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, https://github.com/3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SSIM Metric Calculation
head: SSIM Metric, SSIM computation, Structural Similarity Index
body: The Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) measures the perceived distortion between a rendered image and a ground truth image by comparing local patterns of pixel intensities, assuming the human visual system is highly adapted to structured natural scene information. It serves as a standard benchmark for image quality in radiance-field optimization, complementing pixel-wise metrics like MSE and PSNR. It provides a value between -1 and 1, where 1 indicates identical images. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two images, x (prediction/rendered) and y (target/ground truth), typically 4D tensors of shape (N, C, H, W) or (1, 3, H, W). Output: A scalar SSIM score representing the mean structural similarity across the image. Data Structures: Gaussian Kernel: A 2D separable window generated from a 1D Gaussian kernel. Local Statistics: Tensors for local means (\mu), squared means (\mu^2), variances (\sigma^2), and covariance (\sigma{xy}) computed via convolution. Parameters: windowsize: Size of the Gaussian window. Default is 11. sigma: Standard deviation for the Gaussian kernel. Default is 1.5. c1: Stability constant for the mean difference denominator. Default is 0.01^2. c2: Stability constant for the variance/covariance denominator. Default is 0.03^2. Steps: 1. Kernel Generation: Create a 1D Gaussian kernel of size windowsize with standard deviation sigma. Construct a 2D separable window by taking the outer product of the 1D kernel with itself. Expand the window to match the number of image channels (e.g., if channels=3, the kernel is applied per-channel or grouped). 2. Local Means: Compute local means \mux and \muy for the prediction and target images by performing 2D convolution with the Gaussian kernel. Use padding equal to windowsize // 2 to preserve spatial dimensions. To handle multi-channel images efficiently, use grouped convolution where the group size equals the number of channels. \mux = \text{conv2d}(x, \text{window}, \text{padding}=\text{window\size}//2, \text{groups}=C) \muy = \text{conv2d}(y, \text{window}, \text{padding}=\text{window\size}//2, \text{groups}=C) 3. Squared Means and Cross-Mean: Compute \mux^2, \muy^2, and \mu{xy} (the product of means) element-wise. \mu{x\sq} = \mux^2 \mu{y\sq} = \muy^2 \mu{xy} = \mux \cdot \muy 4. Variances and Covariance: Compute local variances \sigmax^2, \sigmay^2 and covariance \sigma{xy} by convolving the squared images and the product of images, then subtracting the squared means. \sigma{x\sq} = \text{conv2d}(x^2, \text{window}, \text{padding}=\text{window\size}//2, \text{groups}=C) - \mu{x\sq} \sigma{y\sq} = \text{conv2d}(y^2, \text{window}, \text{padding}=\text{window\size}//2, \text{groups}=C) - \mu{y\sq} \sigma{xy} = \text{conv2d}(x \cdot y, \text{window}, \text{padding}=\text{window\size}//2, \text{groups}=C) - \mu{xy} 5. SSIM Map Calculation: Calculate the per-pixel SSIM value using the formula: \text{SSIM}(x, y) = \frac{(2\mu{xy} + c1)(2\sigma{xy} + c2)}{(\mu{x\sq} + \mu{y\sq} + c1)(\sigma{x\sq} + \sigma{y\sq} + c2)} 6. Aggregation: Return the mean of all pixel values in the SSIM map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def gaussiankernel(windowsize: int, sigma: float) -> torch.Tensor: """Create a 1D Gaussian kernel.""" coords = torch.arange(windowsize, dtype=torch.float32) coords -= windowsize // 2 g = torch.exp(-(coords 2) / (2 sigma 2)) g /= g.sum() return g def ssimmetric(pred: torch.Tensor, target: torch.Tensor, windowsize: int = 11, sigma: float = 1.5, c1: float = 0.012, c2: float = 0.032) -> torch.Tensor: """ Compute SSIM between prediction and target. Inputs: pred, target of shape (N, C, H, W) or (1, C, H, W). """ # Validate input shapes if pred.shape != target.shape: raise ValueError(f"Image shape mismatch: pred {pred.shape} vs target {target.shape}") # Ensure 4D input if pred.dim() == 3: pred = pred.unsqueeze(0) target = target.unsqueeze(0) N, C, H, W = pred.shape # 1. Generate 2D Gaussian Window # Create 1D kernel kernel1d = gaussiankernel(windowsize, sigma) # Create 2D separable kernel via outer product kernel2d = torch.outer(kernel1d, kernel1d) # Reshape for convolution: (1, 1, Hk, Wk) kernel2d = kernel2d.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # Expand kernel to match channels for grouped convolution # We repeat the same kernel for each channel group kernel = kernel2d.repeat(C, 1, 1, 1) padding = windowsize // 2 # 2. Compute Local Means mupred = F.conv2d(pred, kernel, padding=padding, groups=C) mutarget = F.conv2d(target, kernel, padding=padding, groups=C) # 3. Compute Squared Means and Cross Mean mupredsq = mupred 2 mutargetsq = mutarget 2 mupredtarget = mupred mutarget # 4. Compute Variances and Covariance # Convolve squared inputs predsq = pred 2 targetsq = target 2 predtarget = pred target convpredsq = F.conv2d(predsq, kernel, padding=padding, groups=C) convtargetsq = F.conv2d(targetsq, kernel, padding=padding, groups=C) convpredtarget = F.conv2d(predtarget, kernel, padding=padding, groups=C) sigmapredsq = convpredsq - mupredsq sigmatargetsq = convtargetsq - mutargetsq sigmapredtarget = convpredtarget - mupredtarget # 5. Calculate SSIM Map # Numerator: (2 mupredtarget + c1) (2 sigmapredtarget + c2) num = (2 mupredtarget + c1) (2 sigmapredtarget + c2) # Denominator: (mupredsq + mutargetsq + c1) (sigmapredsq + sigmatargetsq + c2) den = (mupredsq + mutargetsq + c1) (sigmapredsq + sigmatargetsq + c2) ssimmap = num / den # 6. Return Mean SSIM return ssimmap.mean() Creates and caches a 2D Gaussian window for SSIM loss computation to avoid recomputing the kernel in every iteration. The window size is fixed at 11x11 with a sigma of 1.5. Optimizations for Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficient updates and SSIM loss computation to reduce training time, specifically targeting the Adam optimizer bottleneck. SH Update Schedule: Switches all SH bands beyond the first (0th band) to a batched update schedule, performing only one step of Adam optimization every 16 iterations. The SH learning rate is increased four times to 0.001, while the opacity learning rate is reduced by half to 0.025. SH Data Layout: Extends the differential rasterizer to load Gaussian SH coefficients from separate tensors, avoiding combining the 0th SH band and higher bands into a single tensor before rasterization. SSIM Loss Optimization: Performs differentiable 2D convolution via two consecutive 1D convolutions using optimized CUDA kernels, leveraging the separability of Gaussian kernels. Uses a fused kernel for the evaluation of the SSIM metric from the convolved results. Time Complexity: The standard implementation involves multiple 2D convolutions. Optimized implementations use separable 1D convolutions to reduce computation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate tensors for means, variances, and covariance, proportional to the image size H \times W. Performance: Target SSIM scores for high-quality reconstructions are typically 0.95+. Strengths: Captures structural information and perceived quality better than pixel-wise metrics. Limitations: The main downside is its complexity and the nonlinearity of the human visual system. When to use: Used as a loss term in differentiable rendering frameworks like 3D Gaussian Splatting to encourage structural fidelity. The Structural Similarity Index was proposed by Wang et al. in 2004. It was designed to address the limitations of traditional metrics like MSE and PSNR by modeling image distortion as a change in structural information, based on the assumption that the human visual system is highly adapted to structured natural scene information. It has since become a standard benchmark for image quality assessment in computer vision and graphics. name: Normal-L2 Score Computation
head: Masked Normal L2, Normal Error Metric
body: The Normal-L2 score quantifies the geometric fidelity of a predicted surface by measuring the L2 distance between predicted surface normals and reference normals. It serves as a shape-aware alternative to RGB-based metrics like MSE, focusing on shading cues rather than color accuracy. It is distinct from PSNR and SSIM, which evaluate pixel intensity and structural similarity respectively, by operating on vector fields derived from surface geometry. Inputs: Predicted surface normals N{pred}: A tensor of shape (H, W, 3) containing normalized normal vectors for each pixel. Reference surface normals N{ref}: A tensor of shape (H, W, 3) containing interpolated normal vectors from a ground-truth mesh. Predicted mask M{pred}: A binary tensor of shape (H, W) indicating pixels belonging to the predicted surface. Ground-truth mask M{gt}: A binary tensor of shape (H, W) indicating pixels belonging to the ground-truth surface. Outputs: Normal-L2 score: A scalar value representing the mean squared error of the normal vectors over the valid region. Data Structures: Masks are typically boolean or float tensors where 1 indicates surface presence and 0 indicates background. Normals are 3D unit vectors. Steps: 1. Compute Intersection Mask: Calculate the intersection of the predicted and ground-truth masks to ensure normals are only compared where both surfaces exist. M{valid} = M{pred} \land M{gt} In implementation, this is often done via logical AND or element-wise multiplication followed by a threshold check. 2. Extract Valid Normals: Select normal vectors from N{pred} and N{ref} where M{valid} is true. N{pred}^{valid} = \{ n \in N{pred} \mid M{valid}(u,v) = 1 \} N{ref}^{valid} = \{ n \in N{ref} \mid M{valid}(u,v) = 1 \} 3. Compute Squared Differences: Calculate the squared Euclidean distance between corresponding valid normal vectors. D{uv} = \| N{pred}^{valid}(u,v) - N{ref}^{valid}(u,v) \|^2 D{uv} = (n{pred,x} - n{ref,x})^2 + (n{pred,y} - n{ref,y})^2 + (n{pred,z} - n{ref,z})^2 4. Average: Compute the mean of D{uv} over all valid pixels. \text{Normal-L2} = \frac{1}{|M{valid}|} \sum{(u,v) \in M{valid}} D{uv} Parameters: Camera positions: 32 evenly distributed fixed positions using a spherical Fibonacci sequence with radius 4. Render resolution: 512x512. Samples per pixel: 4. Renderer: Mitsuba 2 is used for mesh rendering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mask Misalignment: If masks do not overlap, the denominator becomes zero. The metric is only evaluated on the intersection. Normal Orientation: Normals must be consistently oriented (e.g., outward-facing) to avoid large errors due to sign flips. Interpolation: Reference normals are interpolated from the reference mesh, which may introduce artifacts at low resolutions or sharp edges. Numerical Stability: Normals should be normalized before comparison to ensure unit length. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computenormall2score(npred, nref, maskpred, maskgt): """ Compute Normal-L2 score. Args: npred: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), predicted normals. nref: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), reference normals. maskpred: Tensor of shape (H, W), predicted mask (1.0 for surface, 0.0 otherwise). maskgt: Tensor of shape (H, W), ground-truth mask (1.0 for surface, 0.0 otherwise). Returns: float: Normal-L2 score. """ # Step 1: Compute intersection mask # Ensure masks are boolean or float 0/1 validmask = (maskpred > 0.5) & (maskgt > 0.5) # Step 2: Extract valid normals # Use boolean indexing to get valid normals validnpred = npred[validmask] validnref = nref[validmask] # Check if any valid pixels exist if validnpred.numel() == 0: return 0.0 # Or raise an error, depending on convention # Step 3: Compute squared differences # Difference vector diff = validnpred - validnref # Squared L2 norm per pixel squareddiff = torch.sum(diff 2, dim=-1) # Step 4: Average normall2 = torch.mean(squareddiff) return normall2.item() Computes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between a standard normal distribution and a diagonal Gaussian parameterized by the mean and variance of an output embedding tensor. It is used to regularize the latent space of implicit surface models. Definition: Measures the divergence of the distribution of latent embeddings from a standard normal prior. Steps: 1. Compute mean \mud and standard deviation \sigmad along dimension 0 for each dimension d of the output embedding tensor. 2. Compute variance \sigmad^2 = \sigmad^2. 3. Compute KL per dimension: kld = 0.5 (\mud^2 + \sigmad^2 - \ln(\sigmad^2 + \epsilon) - 1). 4. Sum over all dimensions: KL = \sumd kld. Formula: KL = \sum{d} 0.5 \left( \mud^2 + \sigmad^2 - \ln(\sigmad^2 + \epsilon) - 1 \right) where \mud is the mean along dimension 0 for dimension d, \sigmad^2 is the variance, and \epsilon = 1e-8 for numerical stability. When to choose: Use when regularizing latent embeddings in generative models (e.g., VAEs) rather than evaluating surface geometry. Link: KL Normal Loss (Note: No separate article exists, so this is a subtopic entry). Time Complexity: O(H \times W) for mask intersection and normal comparison, where H and W are image dimensions. Rendering normals takes additional time depending on the renderer (e.g., Mitsuba 2). Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) to store normal tensors and masks. Measured Performance: Evaluated at 512x512 resolution with 4 samples per pixel. Strengths: Sensitive to surface orientation errors, which are perceptually important for shading. Complements RGB metrics by focusing on geometry. Limitations: Requires ground-truth mesh normals for comparison, which may not always be available. Sensitive to mask alignment errors. When to use: When evaluating geometric accuracy of implicit surface reconstructions, especially when shading quality is important. When not to use: When only RGB fidelity is of interest, or when ground-truth normals are unavailable. The Normal-L2 score was introduced in the context of Neural Geometric Level of Detail (NGLOD) for real-time rendering with implicit 3D shapes. It was used alongside intersection over union (iIoU) to evaluate shape silhouettes and surface normals, as these drive shading and are perceptually important. The metric is implemented using Mitsuba 2 for mesh rendering.
