name: Minkowski's Metric
head: Lgamma Loss, Lp Norm Loss
body: Minkowski's Metric is a full-reference mathematical distance measure that treats images as 2D signals to quantify dissimilarity between a reference image x and a test image y. It generalizes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) by allowing the exponent \gamma to vary, thereby controlling the sensitivity to large errors versus small errors. Unlike its sibling PSNR Metric Calculation which is a logarithmic transformation of MSE, or SSIM Metric Calculation which models structural information, Minkowski's Metric operates directly on pixel-wise intensity differences. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Reference image x (tensor of shape H \times W \times C or flattened), Test image y (same shape), Exponent \gamma \in [1, \infty). Output: Scalar distance E{\gamma}. Data Structures: Images are treated as sets of N samples. N is the total number of pixels across all channels (H \times W \times C). Samples xi, yi are the scalar intensity values at index i. Formula: E{\gamma} = \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N |xi - yi|^{\gamma} \right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma}} Where: N: Total number of samples in the image. xi: Intensity of the i-th sample in the reference image. yi: Intensity of the i-th sample in the test image. \gamma: The Minkowski order parameter. Parameters: \gamma: Typically \gamma=2 for MSE-like behavior. The source specifies the range \gamma \in [1, \infty). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minkowskimetric(reference: list[float], test: list[float], gamma: float) -> float: """ Computes the Minkowski distance between two image representations. Args: reference: Flattened list of pixel values for the reference image. test: Flattened list of pixel values for the test image. gamma: The exponent parameter (>= 1). Returns: The Minkowski distance Egamma. """ if len(reference) != len(test): raise ValueError("Reference and test images must have the same number of samples.") if gamma < 1: raise ValueError("Gamma must be >= 1.") n = len(reference) sumdiffgamma = 0.0 for i in range(n): diff = reference[i] - test[i] # Use absolute value to handle negative differences before exponentiation sumdiffgamma += abs(diff) gamma # Calculate the mean of the powered differences meandiffgamma = sumdiffgamma / n # Raise to the power of 1/gamma distance = meandiffgamma (1.0 / gamma) return distance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gamma = 1: Corresponds to the Mean Absolute Error (MAE). Gamma = 2: Corresponds to the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE). Note that standard MSE ignores the final root; see Subtopics for clarification. Large Gamma: As \gamma \to \infty, the metric approaches the maximum absolute difference (Chebyshev distance), becoming highly sensitive to outliers. Precision: For very large \gamma, intermediate values |xi - yi|^\gamma may overflow if not normalized or if pixel values are large. MSE is a specific case of Minkowski's metric where \gamma=2, but with a critical distinction in the final step. While Minkowski's metric with \gamma=2 yields the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), the standard MSE definition ignores the square root. Formula: E2 = \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N |xi - yi|^2 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{MSE} Here, E2 is the Minkowski distance (RMSE), and MSE is the standard Mean Squared Error. The source notes that MSE is the most commonly used metric among mathematical distortion measures, though it correlates poorly with human perception. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N), where N is the number of pixels. Requires a single pass over the image data. Memory: O(1) auxiliary space if computed in a streaming fashion, or O(N) if storing the full difference tensor. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement and compute. Provides a direct, differentiable measure of pixel-wise error. Limitations: As noted in the source, mathematical metrics like Minkowski's correlate very poorly with human visual perception because they do not account for the Human Visual System's (HVS) characteristics. They are highly objective but perceptually inadequate compared to structural metrics like SSIM. When to Use: When a simple, differentiable loss function is needed for optimization (e.g., in differentiable rendering). When computational efficiency is prioritized over perceptual accuracy. When Not to Use: When perceptual quality is the primary evaluation criterion. When structural integrity or texture preservation is more important than raw pixel accuracy. Minkowski's metric is a generalization of the Minkowski distance from mathematics, applied here to image processing as a full-reference metric. It is part of a family of mathematical distortion measures that includes Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Laplacian Mean Square Error. The source cites Eskicioglu for a list of other distortion measures and Girod for the demonstration of poor correlation with human perception. The specific formulation provided is from a thesis on Real-Time Ray Traced Voxel Global Illumination. name: Perceptual Loss Training
head: PIPS Loss, Perceptual Loss for 3DGS
body: Perceptual Loss Training is an optimization strategy that incorporates a perceptual loss term into the training objective to improve the perceptual quality of rendered images, addressing the inherent smoothness and blurriness issues associated with standard pixel-wise reconstruction losses. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Total Variation Regularization and L1+SSIM Loss by leveraging high-level feature representations from Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) rather than relying solely on low-level pixel statistics or structural similarity metrics. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered image I{render}, ground-truth image I{gt}, and a pre-trained feature extractor network (typically VGG or similar). Outputs: A scalar perceptual loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} used for gradient backpropagation. Data Structures: Feature Maps: The CNN extracts feature maps at multiple intermediate layers. Let \Phil(I) denote the feature map at layer l for image I. The layout is a tensor of shape (Cl, Hl, Wl), where Cl is the number of channels, and Hl, Wl are the spatial dimensions specific to layer l. Formulas: The total training loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted combination of L1 loss, Structural Similarity (SSIM) loss, and Perceptual Loss: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda1 - \lambda2)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda1\mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} + \lambda2\mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} Where: \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 reconstruction loss: \mathcal{L}1 = \| I{render} - I{gt} \|1. \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} is the structural similarity loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} is the perceptual loss, computed as the Euclidean distance between the feature representations of the rendered and ground-truth images. \lambda1 is the weight for the SSIM loss term. Value not explicitly given in sources. \lambda2 is the weight for the perceptual loss term. Value not explicitly given in sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Render the image I{render} from the current model state (e.g., Gaussian Splatting parameters). 2. Pass both I{render} and I{gt} through the pre-trained CNN feature extractor to obtain feature maps \Phi(I{render}) and \Phi(I{gt}). 3. Compute the perceptual loss \mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} as the sum of squared differences between feature maps across selected layers. 4. Compute \mathcal{L}1 and \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}}. 5. Combine losses using the formula above to get \mathcal{L}. 6. Backpropagate gradients through \mathcal{L} to update model parameters. Computational Optimization: Because CNN-based computation increases training time, the perceptual loss \mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} is computed only every 20 training iterations. In iterations where it is not computed, its gradient contribution is effectively zero or carried over from the last computation, substantially alleviating computational overhead without noticeably increasing overall training time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeperceptuallosstraining(renderfn, gtimage, cnnextractor, lambda1, lambda2, iteration): """ Computes the total loss including perceptual loss, updating every 20 iterations. """ # 1. Render the current view renderedimage = renderfn() # 2. Compute standard losses l1loss = computel1loss(renderedimage, gtimage) ssimloss = computessimloss(renderedimage, gtimage) # 3. Compute perceptual loss only every 20 iterations if iteration % 20 == 0: # Extract features from CNN renderedfeatures = cnnextractor(renderedimage) gtfeatures = cnnextractor(gtimage) # Compute perceptual loss (e.g., L2 distance between feature maps) # Note: Specific layer selection and weighting within PIPS is not detailed in pipsloss = computepipsloss(renderedfeatures, gtfeatures) else: # Use cached value or zero gradient contribution # Implementation detail: typically one would cache the last computed pipsloss # and use its value for the loss sum, but gradients would be stale. # The source states it alleviates overhead, implying the term is skipped in backprop # or the gradient is not computed for this term. pipsloss = 0.0 # 4. Combine losses # Ensure weights sum to <= 1 to keep L1 weight positive l1weight = 1.0 - lambda1 - lambda2 totalloss = (l1weight l1loss) + (lambda1 ssimloss) + (lambda2 pipsloss) return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Overhead: The primary pitfall is the significant increase in training time due to CNN inference. Mitigated by computing it every 20 iterations. Metric Reliability: Perceptual metrics like LPIPS (closely related to PIPS) may be unreliable signals in certain settings, such as scenes with blurry backgrounds where lower LPIPS scores might correspond to perceptually inferior outputs. Proxy Geometry Dependency (Variant): In variants relying on proxy geometry (e.g., Stable View Synthesis), incorrect proxy geometry (especially for distant/unobserved content like trees) can cause the perceptual loss to fail or produce poor results. A view synthesis method that blends training images together, relying on proxy geometry from an external system. It is trained with a perceptual loss. It requires multiple large CNNs and access to all training images to render novel views. It may fail when the external proxy geometry is incorrect, particularly struggling with distant/unobserved content like trees. It is better suited to large piecewise planar objects (vehicles) due to reliance on piecewise planar mesh proxy geometry, whereas the proposed model handles natural content better. Time Complexity: Increases training time significantly due to CNN-based computation. Mitigated by computing the perceptual loss every 20 iterations. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the pre-trained CNN and intermediate feature maps. Strengths: Improves perceptual quality of rendered images, addressing the smoothness issues of pixel-wise losses. Limitations: Computationally expensive; relies on external CNNs; may be less effective or fail if dependent on incorrect proxy geometry (in variant contexts). When to use: When perceptual quality is prioritized over raw PSNR and computational resources allow for periodic CNN inference. When not to use: When real-time training speed is critical and the overhead of CNNs is prohibitive, or when the scene contains natural content that does not align well with piecewise planar proxy geometry (in SVS context). Perceptual loss training in the context of Gaussian Splatting and radiance fields was introduced to address the limitations of pixel-wise reconstruction errors, which often result in solutions with high signal-to-noise ratios that are perceptually smooth and less convincing. The approach builds on GAN-based models where perceptual losses have been proven effective. The specific formulation using \mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} in the context of Duplex-GS was presented in. The comparison with Stable View Synthesis (SVS), which also uses perceptual loss, highlights the trade-offs between proxy-geometry-dependent methods and direct optimization methods. name: Second-Order Chamfer Distance
head: Second-Order CD
body: Second-Order Chamfer Distance is a supervised geometric loss function that measures the discrepancy between a predicted mesh vertex and a ground truth surface by incorporating local surface curvature. Unlike standard Chamfer Distance, which uses a simple quadratic point-to-point distance, this method approximates the distance function quadratically to account for the local geometry of the reference surface. It serves as a baseline for meshing implicit functions where ground truth meshes are available. Inputs and Outputs Input: A predicted mesh vertex \mathbf{x} (output of network h\phi) and a ground truth mesh. Output: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}. Derived Data: For the closest point \mathbf{y} on the ground truth mesh corresponding to \mathbf{x}, the surface normal \vec{n}, principal curvature directions \vec{e}1, \vec{e}2, and principal curvature magnitudes \hat{\delta}1, \hat{\delta}2 are required. Data Structures \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Query point coordinates. \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Closest point on the reference surface. \vec{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Unit normal vector at \mathbf{y}. \vec{e}1, \vec{e}2 \in \mathbb{R}^3: Orthonormal principal curvature directions at \mathbf{y}. \hat{\delta}1, \hat{\delta}2 \in \mathbb{R}: Principal curvature magnitudes at \mathbf{y}. Steps 1. Identify the query point \mathbf{x} as the mesh vertex predicted by the network h\phi. 2. Find the closest point \mathbf{y} on the ground truth mesh to \mathbf{x}. 3. Compute the surface normal \vec{n} at \mathbf{y}. 4. Compute the principal curvature directions \vec{e}1 and \vec{e}2 at \mathbf{y}. 5. Compute the principal curvature magnitudes \hat{\delta}1 and \hat{\delta}2 at \mathbf{y}. 6. Calculate the displacement vector \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}. 7. Compute the loss using the quadratic approximation formula: \mathcal{L} = \hat{\delta}1 (\vec{e}1 \cdot \mathbf{d})^2 + \hat{\delta}2 (\vec{e}2 \cdot \mathbf{d})^2 + (\vec{n} \cdot \mathbf{d})^2 Parameters \mathbf{x}: Predicted vertex. \mathbf{y}: Closest point on ground truth mesh (e.g., from ABC dataset). \hat{\delta}1, \hat{\delta}2: Principal curvatures at \mathbf{y}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls The method requires explicit access to the ground truth mesh to compute normals and curvatures, making it a supervised baseline. Curvature computation may be unstable on noisy or degenerate mesh geometries. The closest point search must be robust to ensure \mathbf{y} is geometrically relevant to \mathbf{x}. Time and Memory Complexity Not given in the sources. Measured Performance In an ablation study for meshing implicit functions, Second-Order Chamfer Distance (labeled "Order CD" under "Vert Supervision") achieved the following metrics compared to standard Chamfer Distance ("CD") and other variants: CD: 3.52 (metric 1), 91.70 (metric 2), 72.70 (metric 3), 3.54 (metric 4), 11.9 (metric 5) Order CD: 3.47, 91.00, 14.55, 3.49, 11.8 W/o Implicit NC: 3.40, 93.80, 11.64, 3.40, 11.3 Ours Supervision: 3.30, 94.90, 9.67, 3.20, 11.3 Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Incorporates local surface curvature information for a more accurate distance measure than first-order methods. Limitations: Requires ground truth mesh data (supervised). When to Use Use when a supervised baseline is needed for meshing implicit functions and ground truth meshes are available. The method is based on the quadratic approximation of point-point distance proposed in [51] (cited in). It is used as a supervised baseline for training networks to predict mesh vertices from implicit functions, using the ABC dataset as ground truth. name: Approximate Level Set Discrepancy
head: LSD-A
body: Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A) is a metric used to quantify the geometric discrepancy between a generated mesh and a ground truth mesh, specifically designed for scenarios where the ground truth is non-watertight or an analytic Signed Distance Field (SDF) is ill-defined. Unlike the Precise Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-P), which evaluates distance errors on a fixed grid near the surface, LSD-A measures the point-to-face distance from points sampled directly on the ground truth mesh to the generated mesh. It serves as a robust alternative to standard Chamfer Distance when strict watertightness cannot be guaranteed. Inputs: \mathcal{M}^: The ground truth mesh. \mathcal{M}: The generated (reconstructed) mesh. N: The number of points to sample on \mathcal{M}^. Outputs: A scalar value representing the average point-to-face distance. Data Structures: Points q: A set of N points sampled on the surface of \mathcal{M}^. Mesh \mathcal{M}: Represented as a collection of vertices and faces supporting point-to-face distance queries. Steps: 1. Sample N points q distributed over the surface of the ground truth mesh \mathcal{M}^. 2. For each point q \in \mathcal{M}^, compute the Euclidean distance to the closest point on the generated mesh \mathcal{M}. This distance is denoted as d^p(q, \mathcal{M}). 3. Sum these distances and divide by N to obtain the mean. Formula: \text{LSD-A} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{q \in \mathcal{M}^} d^p(q, \mathcal{M}) Where: \mathcal{M}^ is the ground truth mesh. \mathcal{M} is the generated mesh. q are points sampled on \mathcal{M}^. d^p(q, \mathcal{M}) is the point-to-face distance from point q to the generated mesh \mathcal{M}. N is the number of sampled points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def approximatelevelsetdiscrepancy(groundtruthmesh, generatedmesh, numsamples): """ Computes the Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A). Args: groundtruthmesh: Mesh object representing M. generatedmesh: Mesh object representing M. numsamples: Integer N, number of points to sample on M. Returns: float: The LSD-A score. """ # Step 1: Sample points on the ground truth mesh sampledpoints = samplepointsuniformly(groundtruthmesh, numsamples) totaldistance = 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Compute point-to-face distance and average for q in sampledpoints: dist = pointtofacedistance(q, generatedmesh) totaldistance += dist return totaldistance / numsamples def samplepointsuniformly(mesh, numsamples): # Standard area-weighted uniform sampling on a triangle mesh faces = mesh.faces areas = [trianglearea(f.v0, f.v1, f.v2) for f in faces] totalarea = sum(areas) cumareas = [] acc = 0.0 for a in areas: acc += a cumareas.append(acc) points = [] for in range(numsamples): r = random.uniform(0, totalarea) idx = 0 for i, ca in enumerate(cumareas): if r <= ca: idx = i break v0, v1, v2 = faces[idx].v0, faces[idx].v1, faces[idx].v2 s, t = random.random(), random.random() if s + t > 1: s, t = 1 - s, 1 - t points.append(vectoradd(v0, vectoradd(vectormul(s, vectorsub(v1, v0)), vectormul(t, vectorsub(v2, v0))))) return points def trianglearea(v0, v1, v2): return 0.5 vectornorm(vectorcross(vectorsub(v1, v0), vectorsub(v2, v0))) def pointtofacedistance(point, mesh): mindist = float('inf') for face in mesh.faces: dist = distancepointtotriangle(point, face.v0, face.v1, face.v2) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist return mindist def distancepointtotriangle(point, v0, v1, v2): # Standard point-to-triangle distance closest = computeclosestpointontriangle(point, v0, v1, v2) return vectornorm(vectorsub(point, closest)) def computeclosestpointontriangle(point, v0, v1, v2): # Standard barycentric projection v0v1 = vectorsub(v1, v0) v0v2 = vectorsub(v2, v0) v0p = vectorsub(point, v0) d1 = vectordot(v0v1, v0v1) d2 = vectordot(v0v2, v0v2) d3 = vectordot(v0v1, v0v2) d = d1 d2 - d3 d3 u = (d2 vectordot(v0v1, v0p) - d3 vectordot(v0v2, v0p)) / d v = (d1 vectordot(v0v2, v0p) - d3 vectordot(v0v1, v0p)) / d if u <= 0 and v <= 0: return v0 if u > 1 and v <= 0: return v1 if v > 1 and u <= 0: return v2 if u + v > 1: e = vectorsub(v2, v1) w = vectorsub(point, v1) denom = vectordot(e, e) t = max(0, min(1, vectordot(w, e) / denom)) return vectoradd(v1, vectormul(t, e)) return vectoradd(v0, vectoradd(vectormul(u, v0v1), vectormul(v, v0v2))) Parameters: N: The number of points sampled on the ground truth mesh \mathcal{M}^. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-watertight Ground Truth: LSD-A is specifically intended for cases where the ground truth mesh is non-watertight, making analytic SDF computation ill-defined. Distance Definition: The metric uses point-to-face distance, not point-to-vertex distance, ensuring that the entire surface area contributes to the error measurement. Precision: Floating-point comparisons in barycentric projection require epsilon guards to avoid degenerate edge cases. Precise Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-P) gauges the discrepancy in signed distance values between a reconstructed mesh and the ground truth mesh at fixed points sampled on a regular grid close to the ground truth surface. It is defined as \text{LSD-P} = \sum{g \in \tilde{\mathcal{G}}} \|\text{abs}(\mathbf{d}^p(\mathcal{M}^, g)) - \text{abs}(\mathbf{d}^p(\mathcal{M}, g))\|2, where \tilde{\mathcal{G}} is the grid of points and \mathbf{d}^p is the distance from a query point to its closest point on the surface. LSD-P is chosen when a fixed spatial grid is preferred over surface sampling, whereas LSD-A is preferred for non-watertight meshes where surface sampling is more robust. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Robust to non-watertight ground truth meshes; does not require an analytic SDF; directly measures surface proximity. Limitations: Requires sampling on the ground truth mesh; sensitive to the number of samples N; does not account for signed distance errors in the same way LSD-P does. When to Use: Use LSD-A when evaluating generated meshes against non-watertight ground truth meshes (e.g., ShapeNet dataset) where analytic SDF is ill-defined. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A) was introduced in the context of self-supervised dual contouring for 3D mesh reconstruction. It was specifically designed to handle the challenges posed by datasets like ShapeNet, which contain non-watertight meshes, making traditional SDF-based metrics unreliable. The metric was used in experiments to evaluate the quality of reconstructed meshes against ground truth in these challenging scenarios. name: Color-Corrected Error Metrics
head: Per-image quadratic color correction, Photometric variation mitigation metrics
body: Color-Corrected Error Metrics are an evaluation procedure designed to mitigate photometric variations—such as autoexposure, white balance shifts, and RGB clipping—in "in the wild" datasets like Tanks and Temples. By solving a per-image least squares problem to fit a quadratic polynomial expansion of rendered RGB values to ground truth, the method neutralizes global brightness and color shifts, making view synthesis models quantitatively comparable despite uncontrolled camera settings. Inputs: Rendered image I{render} (RGB), Ground truth image I{true} (RGB), and a mask M{valid} identifying non-saturated pixels. Outputs: Corrected error metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) computed on the color-adjusted render. Data Structures: I{render}, I{true}: 2D arrays of shape (H, W, 3), values in [0, 1]. M{valid}: Boolean mask of shape (H, W), true where pixel is not saturated/clipped. Steps: 1. Mask Saturated Pixels: Identify pixels where any channel in I{true} or I{render} is clipped (e.g., \ge 1.0 or \le 0.0). These are excluded from the fitting process. 2. Construct Design Matrix: For each valid pixel p, construct a feature vector xp representing the quadratic expansion of the rendered RGB values. For a pixel with rendered color r = [R, G, B], the expansion includes terms for linear components, squared components, and cross-products: xp = [1, R, G, B, R^2, G^2, B^2, RG, RB, GB]^T The constant term 1 accounts for bias/offset. 3. Solve Least Squares: Solve for the coefficient vector c that minimizes the squared error between the transformed render and the ground truth for all valid pixels: \minc \sum{p \in M{valid}} \| I{true}[p] - Xp c \|^2 where Xp is the row vector xp^T. This is solved via the normal equation: c = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T Y where X is the matrix of all xp and Y is the vector of all I{true}[p] for valid pixels. 4. Apply Correction: Compute the corrected rendered image I{corrected} by applying the fitted polynomial to every pixel in I{render}: I{corrected}[p] = Xp c 5. Compute Metrics: Calculate standard error metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) between I{corrected} and I{true}. Parameters: Polynomial degree: Quadratic (order 2). Saturated pixel threshold: Typically 0.0 or 1.0, depending on data normalization. Edge Cases: No Valid Pixels: If all pixels are saturated, the least squares problem is ill-posed. The sources do not specify a fallback, but logically, metrics cannot be computed. Precision: Inverting X^T X may be numerically unstable if the rendered colors are highly correlated or degenerate. Standard numerical linear algebra routines should be used. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def colorcorrectedmetrics(render, true, saturatedthreshold=0.99): """ render: (H, W, 3) array, values in [0, 1] true: (H, W, 3) array, values in [0, 1] saturatedthreshold: float, pixels with any channel >= this are ignored """ # 1. Mask saturated pixels # Assuming saturation is defined as values close to 1.0 or 0.0. # The source mentions "ignoring saturated pixels" and "clipped RGB". # We define valid pixels as those not near the boundaries. validmask = (render < saturatedthreshold).all(axis=-1) & \ (render > 1.0 - saturatedthreshold).all(axis=-1) & \ (true < saturatedthreshold).all(axis=-1) & \ (true > 1.0 - saturatedthreshold).all(axis=-1) # Flatten valid pixels renderflat = render[validmask] # (N, 3) trueflat = true[validmask] # (N, 3) if renderflat.shape[0] == 0: raise ValueError("No valid non-saturated pixels found.") # 2. Construct Design Matrix for quadratic expansion # Terms: 1, R, G, B, R^2, G^2, B^2, RG, RB, GB R, G, B = renderflat[:, 0], renderflat[:, 1], renderflat[:, 2] X = np.columnstack([ np.oneslike(R), R, G, B, R2, G2, B2, RG, RB, GB ]) # 3. Solve Least Squares: min || Xc - Y ||^2 # Using numpy's least squares solver for numerical stability # Y is trueflat (N, 3) c, residuals, rank, s = np.linalg.lstsq(X, trueflat, rcond=None) # 4. Apply Correction rendercorrectedflat = X @ c # (N, 3) # 5. Compute Metrics (Placeholder for actual metric implementation) # In practice, one would compute PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS between # rendercorrectedflat and trueflat, then reshape or average. # Here we just return the corrected image for metric calculation. return rendercorrectedflat A post-processing white balance technique that uses the Bradford chromatic adaptation transform to map colors from a Planck/CIE-daylight illuminant to D65. Unlike simple gray-world or white-patch algorithms, it explicitly models the chromatic adaptation process, providing a more physically grounded correction for white balance in rendering pipelines. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of valid pixels, dominated by the matrix construction and the least squares solve. The least squares solve is typically O(N \cdot D^2) or O(N \cdot D^3) where D=10 is the number of polynomial terms, which is constant and small. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the design matrix and intermediate vectors. Strengths: Effectively neutralizes global brightness and color shifts caused by autoexposure and white balance variations in "in the wild" datasets, allowing for fair comparison between models. Limitations: Does not correct for local photometric variations or non-linear tone mapping curves. It assumes a global quadratic relationship between the render and the ground truth, which may not hold for all scenes or camera responses. When to use: Evaluating view synthesis on datasets with uncontrolled camera settings (e.g., Tanks and Temples) where autoexposure/white balance varies between images. When not to use: When the dataset has fixed, calibrated camera settings, or when local color accuracy is more important than global color consistency. The method was introduced in the context of evaluating Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) on the Tanks and Temples dataset, where photometric variation (autoexposure, white balance, clipping) makes standard evaluation metrics ill-posed. It builds on earlier work by Martin-Brualla et al. who investigated specialized training and evaluation procedures for such datasets. The approach was used to compare the Mip-NeRF 360 model with Stable View Synthesis (SVS). name: L1+SSIM Loss
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training Loss, Photometric Loss, Training Loss
body: L1+SSIM Loss is a composite photometric objective used to optimize radiance fields (specifically 3D Gaussian Splatting) by minimizing the difference between rendered images and ground-truth photographs. It combines a pixel-wise L1 error term with a structural similarity (SSIM) term to balance color accuracy with perceptual sharpness. It differs from pure MSE-based losses by being less sensitive to outliers and from pure SSIM losses by retaining strict pixel-level fidelity, addressing the blurring artifacts common in differentiable volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A batch of camera poses \pi, viewing presets T (e.g., material parameters or lighting conditions), and reference RGB images \mathbf{I}. The model parameters \mathcal{G} (Gaussian positions, covariances, colors, opacities, and conditioning factors) are optimized. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L} and gradients with respect to \mathcal{G}, \pi, and T. Data Structures: Reference Image \mathbf{I}: A 2D tensor of shape (H, W, 3) containing normalized RGB values. Rendered Image \hat{\mathbf{I}}: A 2D tensor of shape (H, W, 3) produced by the differentiable renderer \mathcal{R}. SSIM Window: A local neighborhood window of size K \times K (typically 11 \times 11) used for structural similarity calculation. Parameters: \lambdas (or \lambda): Weight for the SSIM term. Default value is 0.2. \mathcal{L}1: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between rendered and reference images. \text{SSIM}(\cdot, \cdot): Structural Similarity Index Measure. Formulas: The rendered image is computed as: \hat{\mathbf{I}} = \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}; \pi, T) The total loss is a weighted sum: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambdas) \mathcal{L}1(\hat{\mathbf{I}}, \mathbf{I}) + \lambdas (1 - \text{SSIM}(\hat{\mathbf{I}}, \mathbf{I})) Where: \mathcal{L}1(\hat{\mathbf{I}}, \mathbf{I}) = \frac{1}{HW} \sum{h,w} \sum{c \in \{R,G,B\}} | \hat{\mathbf{I}}{h,w,c} - \mathbf{I}{h,w,c} | \text{SSIM}(\hat{\mathbf{I}}, \mathbf{I}) is the mean SSIM over the image, computed by sliding a window across both images and averaging the local SSIM scores. Steps: 1. Render: For each camera pose \pi and preset T in the batch, render the image \hat{\mathbf{I}} using the current Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} via the tile rasterizer \mathcal{R}. 2. Compute L1: Calculate the mean absolute RGB error between \hat{\mathbf{I}} and the reference \mathbf{I}. 3. Compute SSIM: Calculate the Structural Similarity Index between \hat{\mathbf{I}} and \mathbf{I}. 4. Combine: Compute the weighted loss using \lambdas = 0.2. 5. Backpropagate: Compute gradients of \mathcal{L} with respect to \mathcal{G}, \pi, and T using automatic differentiation through the compositing process. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def l1ssimloss(renderedimage, referenceimage, lambdas=0.2): """ Compute the L1+SSIM loss for volume rendering optimization. Args: renderedimage (Tensor): Shape (H, W, 3), normalized RGB. referenceimage (Tensor): Shape (H, W, 3), normalized RGB. lambdas (float): Weight for SSIM term. Default 0.2. Returns: Tensor: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Compute L1 Loss (Mean Absolute Error) # L1 = mean(|rendered - reference|) l1loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedimage - referenceimage)) # 2. Compute SSIM Loss # SSIM is typically computed using a sliding window (e.g., 11x11) # We use the standard implementation from torchvision or similar # Note: SSIM returns a value between -1 and 1, where 1 is perfect match. # We want to minimize (1 - SSIM), so higher SSIM means lower loss. ssimvalue = computessim(renderedimage, referenceimage) ssimloss = 1.0 - ssimvalue # 3. Combine Losses # L = (1 - lambdas) L1 + lambdas (1 - SSIM) totalloss = (1.0 - lambdas) l1loss + lambdas ssimloss return totalloss def computessim(img1, img2, windowsize=11, sizeaverage=True): """ Compute Structural Similarity Index. Simplified implementation for clarity. """ # Constants for stability C1 = 0.01 2 C2 = 0.03 2 # Convert to float if necessary img1 = img1.float() img2 = img2.float() # Apply Gaussian window window = creategaussianwindow(windowsize, channels=3) # Compute local means mu1 = F.conv2d(img1, window, padding=windowsize//2) mu2 = F.conv2d(img2, window, padding=windowsize//2) # Compute local variances and covariance mu1sq = mu1.pow(2) mu2sq = mu2.pow(2) mu1mu2 = mu1 mu2 sigma1sq = F.conv2d(img1 img1, window, padding=windowsize//2) - mu1sq sigma2sq = F.conv2d(img2 img2, window, padding=windowsize//2) - mu2sq sigma12 = F.conv2d(img1 img2, window, padding=windowsize//2) - mu1mu2 # Compute SSIM index ssimmap = ((2 mu1mu2 + C1) (2 sigma12 + C2)) / \ ((mu1sq + mu2sq + C1) (sigma1sq + sigma2sq + C2)) if sizeaverage: return ssimmap.mean() else: return ssimmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure images are normalized to [0, 1] or [-1, 1] consistently before computing L1 and SSIM to avoid scale mismatches. Boundaries: SSIM computation near image borders requires padding or window truncation to avoid artifacts. Degenerate Input: If the rendered image is completely black or white, SSIM may become unstable; add small constants (C1, C2) for numerical stability. Adds spatial smoothness constraints to reduce noise. Choose when the scene has large uniform regions. Optimizes ray sampling to reduce artifacts. Choose when ray marching is the bottleneck. Standard pixel-wise loss. Choose when PSNR is the primary metric and sharpness is less critical. Uses deep features for perceptual quality. Choose for high-level texture fidelity. Geometric loss for point clouds. Choose when geometry alignment is prioritized over photometry. Adjusts for color space differences. Choose when lighting or color calibration varies. General regularization techniques. Choose to prevent overfitting. Masks out occluded regions. Choose when visibility estimation is available. Incorporates uncertainty estimates. Choose for robust optimization. Ensures consistency across views. Choose for multi-view consistency. Regularizes Gaussian parameters. Choose for stability in Gaussian Splatting. Combines multiple losses. Choose for comprehensive optimization. Optimizes multiple parameters simultaneously. Choose for complex scenes. Specific to Forplane representations. Choose for Forplane-based rendering. Aligns geometry and normals. Choose when geometric accuracy is critical. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rendering step \mathcal{R} and the SSIM computation. SSIM is O(H \cdot W \cdot K^2) where K is the window size. L1 is O(H \cdot W). Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for storing intermediate images and gradients. Measured Performance: With \lambdas = 0.2, it typically yields higher perceptual quality (SSIM) than pure L1, while maintaining better pixel accuracy than pure SSIM. Scaling: Scales linearly with image resolution and number of Gaussians. Strengths: Balances color accuracy and sharpness; robust to outliers; widely adopted in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Limitations: SSIM computation can be slow; sensitive to \lambdas choice; may not preserve fine high-frequency details as well as perceptual losses. When to Use: Standard photometric optimization for Gaussian Splatting and radiance fields. When Not to Use: When geometric accuracy is more important than photometry; when real-time performance is critical and SSIM is too slow. The L1+SSIM loss was introduced in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting to address the blurring artifacts associated with MSE losses. It was further adopted in appearance-controllable Gaussian proxies for medical volume rendering, where it optimizes standard photometric loss through a conditioned renderer. The SSIM component is based on the work by Wang et al. (2004). name: Model Regularization
head: Zero Regularization Loss
body: Model regularization in radiance-field optimization refers to auxiliary loss terms applied directly to the neural network's internal predictions to stabilize training and prevent pathological behaviors, such as uncertainty values exploding or overfitting to noise. Unlike photometric losses that compare rendered images to ground truth, model regularization constrains the latent space or intermediate outputs (e.g., uncertainty, density) based on prior assumptions about the scene or network stability. This article focuses on the specific implementation of uncertainty regularization and the general framework for aggregating these losses, distinguishing it from geometric or perceptual sibling losses. The method operates by extracting specific internal variables from the radiance field model after forward propagation and computing penalty terms. These terms are weighted by hyperparameters and added to the total optimization objective. Inputs: The trained radiance field model (e.g., NeRF), a batch of rays \mathcal{R}, and configuration parameters including regularization weights \lambda. Outputs: A scalar regularization loss value \mathcal{L}{model} added to the total loss. The implementation typically uses a dictionary or object to store intermediate model outputs. out: A dictionary or object containing model predictions. Key fields include: uncertainty: A tensor of shape (N,) or (B, N) containing predicted uncertainty values \delta{ci} for each sample point i along rays in batch B. lossesmodelreg: A dictionary mapping regularization loss names (strings) to their computed scalar values. 1. Forward Pass: Compute model predictions for the input rays. 2. Extract Regularization Terms: Call the model's regularization method to compute specific loss components. For uncertainty regularization, compute \mathcal{L}0 using the predicted uncertainty \delta{ci}. 3. Aggregate Losses: Iterate through the computed regularization losses. 4. Weight and Sum: Multiply each loss by its corresponding lambda weight from the configuration and sum them to get the total model regularization loss. The primary model regularization loss cited is the Zero Regularization Loss (\mathcal{L}0), designed to prevent predicted uncertainty \deltai from blowing up to large values. \mathcal{L}0 = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \sum{i=1}^N \max(\delta{ci}, 0) Where: \mathcal{R} is the set of rays. N is the number of sample points per ray. ci is the query coordinate of the i-th sample point on ray r. \delta{ci} is the predicted uncertainty for query coordinate ci. \max(\delta{ci}, 0) ensures only positive uncertainty values contribute to the penalty, encouraging \deltai to be close to zero. The total uncertainty loss \mathcal{L}{unct} combines this with a standard uncertainty loss \mathcal{L}{SE} (not detailed here) as: \mathcal{L}{unct} = \alpha1 \mathcal{L}{SE} + \alpha2 \mathcal{L}0 Typical weights are \alpha1 = 1.0 and \alpha2 = 0.01. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemodelregularization(model, rays, config): """ Computes model regularization losses. Args: model: The radiance field model instance. rays: Input rays for the current batch. config: Configuration object containing loss weights. Returns: totalregloss: Scalar tensor of the total regularization loss. """ # Step 1: Forward pass and extraction of regularization terms # The model returns a dictionary/object 'out' containing internal predictions out = model(rays) # Step 2: Obtain regularization losses from the model # This extracts specific terms like uncertainty regularization lossesdict = model.regularizations(out) totalregloss = 0.0 # Step 3 & 4: Iterate, weight, and sum for name, lossvalue in lossesdict.items(): # Get the lambda weight for this specific regularization term lambdakey = f"lambda{name}" lambdaval = config.system.loss[lambdakey] # Add weighted loss to total weightedloss = lambdaval lossvalue totalregloss += weightedloss # Logging (optional, for debugging/tracking) # logloss(name, weightedloss) return totalregloss Uncertainty Explosion: If \delta{ci} becomes very large, \mathcal{L}0 provides a linear penalty. Without this, uncertainty predictions might diverge, especially in shallow networks where predicting exact error E(r) is difficult. Positive Only: The use of \max(\delta{ci}, 0) means negative uncertainty predictions (if allowed by the network) do not penalize the loss. This assumes uncertainty should be non-negative. Weight Sensitivity: The weight \alpha2 (or \lambda{\mathcal{L}0}) is typically small (e.g., 0.01) relative to the primary loss. Too high a weight may suppress useful uncertainty estimates. A specific regularization term \mathcal{L}0 that penalizes positive predicted uncertainty values to prevent them from growing excessively large during training. It is used in conjunction with other uncertainty losses to stabilize training of neural radiance fields, particularly when the network architecture makes direct error prediction difficult. It is chosen when uncertainty prediction is part of the model's output and stability is a concern. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot B), where N is samples per ray and B is batch size, as it iterates over all sample points to compute the max operation. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot B) to store intermediate uncertainty values before reduction. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally cheap, effectively prevents uncertainty blow-up. Limitations: Only addresses uncertainty magnitude, not spatial smoothness or geometric consistency. Does not replace photometric or geometric losses. When to use: When the model predicts uncertainty or other internal variables that can diverge. When not to use: When the model does not output such variables, or when other regularization (e.g., Total Variation) is more appropriate for the artifact being addressed. The concept of model regularization in this context originates from efforts to stabilize the training of neural radiance fields, particularly those predicting uncertainty. The specific \mathcal{L}0 loss was introduced in the context of Recursive-NeRF to handle the difficulty of predicting error E(r) in shallow networks. The general framework of aggregating model regularization losses via a dictionary and lambda weights is commonly found in modern NeRF implementations like Instant-NSR-PL. bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, https://github.com/bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Recursive-NeRF: An Efficient and Dynamically Growing NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2022.3204608, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Visibility-Based Photometric Loss
head: Visibility Masking for Photometric Loss
body: Visibility-Based Photometric Loss restricts the photometric error computation to pixels that are geometrically consistent across views, thereby excluding occluded regions and transient objects from the optimization signal. It differs from standard photometric losses by explicitly filtering out pixels where reprojection depth disagrees with rendered depth, preventing the model from fitting to non-static geometry or occlusion boundaries. The method computes a photometric error (typically L1) only on pixels identified as "visible" in both the source and target views. Visibility is determined by comparing the depth of a pixel reprojected from a source view into the target view against the directly rendered depth of that target view. Inputs: Source view color image Is and depth map Ds. Target view color image It and rendered depth map Dt. Camera poses for source and target views. Intrinsic camera parameters. Outputs: Scalar loss value L{photo}. Visibility Mask (Mv): A 2D tensor of shape (H, W) with values in \{0, 1\} (or continuous weights in variants). 1 indicates a visible pixel, 0 indicates occluded or transient. Reprojected Depth (D{reproj}): A 2D tensor of shape (H, W) containing the depth of the source view pixel projected into the target view coordinate system. 1. Reproject Depth: For each pixel (u, v) in the target view, project the corresponding 3D point from the source view using the source camera intrinsics, the source-to-target transformation, and the target camera intrinsics. Retrieve the depth value D{reproj}(u, v) from the source depth map Ds at the projected coordinates. 2. Retrieve Rendered Depth: Obtain the directly rendered depth Dt(u, v) for the target view at pixel (u, v). 3. Compute Depth Difference: Calculate the squared difference \Delta d^2 = (D{reproj}(u, v) - Dt(u, v))^2. 4. Determine Visibility: Mark pixel (u, v) as visible if \Delta d^2 < \tau, where \tau is a threshold. The sources specify \tau = 0.001. 5. Compute Photometric Loss: Calculate the L1 loss between the source color Is (warped to target view) and target color It only for pixels where the visibility mask is true. The visibility mask Mv(u, v) is defined as: Mv(u, v) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } (D{reproj}(u, v) - Dt(u, v))^2 < \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \tau = 0.001. The photometric loss L{photo} is: L{photo} = \frac{1}{\sum Mv} \sum{u,v} Mv(u, v) \cdot |Is^{warped}(u, v) - It(u, v)| where |\cdot| denotes the L1 norm. Threshold (\tau): 0.001. This value determines the tolerance for depth inconsistency. Precision: Depth values must be in consistent units. Small numerical errors in reprojection can lead to false occlusions if \tau is too small. Boundaries: Pixels near object boundaries may have ambiguous depth due to anti-aliasing or discretization, potentially causing flickering visibility masks. Degenerate Input: If depth maps are missing or invalid, reprojection fails. The method assumes valid depth inputs. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def visibilitybasedphotometricloss(Is, Ds, It, Dt, poses, poset, intrinsics, tau=0.001): """ Compute photometric loss only on visible pixels. Args: Is: Source view color image (H, W, 3) Ds: Source view depth map (H, W) It: Target view color image (H, W, 3) Dt: Target view rendered depth map (H, W) poses: Source camera pose (4, 4) poset: Target camera pose (4, 4) intrinsics: Camera intrinsics matrix (3, 3) tau: Depth difference threshold (float) Returns: Lphoto: Scalar photometric loss """ H, W = It.shape[:2] # Create grid of pixel coordinates u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='ij') # Convert pixel coordinates to homogeneous coordinates in target view # Assuming intrinsics are known, we can back-project to 3D in target view # However, the standard method reprojects FROM source TO target. # Step 1: Get 3D points from Source View # Back-project source pixels to 3D using Ds xs = (u - intrinsics[0,2]) / intrinsics[0,0] ys = (v - intrinsics[1,2]) / intrinsics[1,1] zs = Ds # 3D points in source camera frame ptsscam = torch.stack([xs zs, ys zs, zs], dim=-1) # (H, W, 3) # Transform to world frame ptssworld = transformpoints(ptsscam, poses) # (H, W, 3) # Transform to target camera frame ptstcam = transformpoints(ptssworld, inverse(poset)) # (H, W, 3) # Project to target image plane ureproj = (ptstcam[..., 0] / ptstcam[..., 2]) intrinsics[0,0] + intrinsics[0,2] vreproj = (ptstcam[..., 1] / ptstcam[..., 2]) intrinsics[1,1] + intrinsics[1,2] # Sample depth from source depth map at reprojected coordinates # Note: In practice, bilinear interpolation is used for sampling Dreproj = sampledepth(Ds, ureproj, vreproj) # (H, W) # Step 3: Compute depth difference deltadsq = (Dreproj - Dt) 2 # Step 4: Determine visibility Mv = (deltadsq < tau).float() # (H, W) # Warp source image to target view Iswarped = warpimage(Is, ureproj, vreproj) # (H, W, 3) # Step 5: Compute L1 loss on visible pixels diff = torch.abs(Iswarped - It) # (H, W, 3) lossperpixel = torch.mean(diff, dim=-1) # (H, W) # Masked mean visiblesum = torch.sum(Mv) if visiblesum > 0: Lphoto = torch.sum(Mv lossperpixel) / visiblesum else: Lphoto = torch.tensor(0.0) return Lphoto This variant uses a learned 2D visibility map VM \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times H \times W} generated by a U-Net model to segment transient objects (e.g., moving people) from static geometry. Unlike the geometric reprojection method, this approach relies on appearance-based segmentation. The loss between the rendered image Ir and reference image I{gt} is weighted by VM via Hadamard product (\odot). To prevent the network from suppressing all pixels to minimize loss, a regularization loss L{vm} = L2(VM, 1) is applied, encouraging the visibility map to remain close to ones. This method is chosen when transient objects are prevalent and geometric consistency alone is insufficient to exclude them. Time Complexity: O(HW) per view pair for reprojection and masking. The U-Net variant adds inference time for the segmentation network. Memory Complexity: O(HW) for storing depth maps and visibility masks. Strengths: Effectively removes artifacts from occlusions and transient objects. Improves reconstruction quality in dynamic scenes. Limitations: Requires accurate depth maps for the geometric variant. The threshold \tau is sensitive to noise. The U-Net variant requires additional training and memory. When to use: Multi-view reconstruction with occlusions or dynamic scenes. When not to use: Static scenes with no occlusions where simple photometric loss suffices. The geometric visibility-based photometric loss was introduced in the context of differentiable volume rendering and signed distance function (SDF) optimization. It addresses the issue of photometric errors being computed on occluded pixels, which leads to incorrect gradient updates. The transient object handling variant was proposed for 3D Gaussian Splatting in unconstrained image collections, where moving objects cause artifacts in the reconstructed scene. name: Uncertainty Prediction Loss
head: Uncertainty Loss
body: Uncertainty Prediction Loss is a regularization technique used in differentiable volume rendering and neural radiance field optimization to predict and penalize the aleatoric uncertainty of rendered outputs or geometric fields. It differs from standard photometric losses by explicitly modeling the confidence of the prediction, allowing the optimizer to down-weight noisy or ambiguous data points. Unlike Uniform and Gaussian Noise Models, which visualize uncertainty distributions, this method directly incorporates uncertainty parameters into the training objective to improve geometry and color reconstruction. The method predicts a scalar uncertainty value for each query point and incorporates it into the loss function via a weighted sum of a squared error term and a zero-regularization term. In point cloud SDF contexts, it models the SDF value as a Gaussian distribution with learnable mean and variance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query coordinates ci (for volume rendering) or point positions xP (for SDF). Output: Predicted uncertainty \deltai or \bar{\sigma}^2(xP), and the updated network weights. Data Structures: Network Output: The network F{\Phi} (or MLP{sdf}) outputs a feature vector y{pi} (or fea) and an uncertainty parameter. For Volume Rendering: A Linear layer follows the output feature y{pi} to predict \delta{ci}. For SDF: The MLP outputs f(xP), \sigma^2(xP), and fea. Steps: 1. Predict Uncertainty Parameter: For Volume Rendering: Compute \delta{ci} from the feature y{pi} using a Linear layer. For SDF: Compute raw variance \sigma^2(xP) and mean f(xP) via MLP{sdf}(xP). 2. Compute Valid Variance (SDF only): Apply softplus to the raw variance and add a minimum variance constraint \sigma0^2 to prevent collapse: \bar{\sigma}^2(xP) = \sigma0^2 + \log(1 + \exp(\sigma^2(xP))) 3. Compute Uncertainty Loss Components: Squared Error Loss (\mathcal{L}{SE} or \mathcal{L}{MSE}): Measures the error between the predicted value and the target. In the context of the general uncertainty loss formulation, this is the standard regression loss. Zero Regularization Loss (\mathcal{L}0): Encourages uncertainty to be close to zero for reliable points: \mathcal{L}0 = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \sum{i=1}^N \max(\delta{ci}, 0) Negative Log-Likelihood Loss (\mathcal{L}{usdf}): Used in SDF contexts, assuming ideal SDF values f\varepsilon(xP) are 0: \mathcal{L}{usdf} = \frac{1}{DP} \sum{xP \in P} \left[ \frac{\|f\varepsilon(xP) - f(xP)\|2^2}{2\bar{\sigma}^2(xP)} + \frac{\log \bar{\sigma}^2(xP)}{2} \right] 4. Combine Losses: Volume Rendering: The total uncertainty loss is a weighted sum: \mathcal{L}{unct} = \alpha1 \mathcal{L}{SE} + \alpha2 \mathcal{L}0 SDF: The loss is \mathcal{L}{usdf} directly. Parameters: \alpha1 = 1.0: Weight for the squared error component. \alpha2 = 0.01: Weight for the zero regularization component. \sigma0^2: Minimum variance constraint to prevent trivial solutions. DP: Number of points in the set P. f\varepsilon(xP): Ideal SDF value, set to 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeuncertaintylossvolumerendering(predictions, targets, features, alpha1=1.0, alpha2=0.01): """ Computes Uncertainty Prediction Loss for Volume Rendering (NeRF-like). predictions: Tensor of predicted colors/values. targets: Tensor of ground truth colors/values. features: Tensor of output features from the network. """ # Step 1: Predict uncertainty delta from features # Assuming a linear layer is applied to features to get delta # delta = Linear(features) # Note: The exact linear layer weights are part of the model, # but the loss computation uses the output delta. delta = predictuncertainty(features) # Step 2: Compute Squared Error Loss (LSE) # LSE is typically the standard MSE or L1 between prediction and target # The source refers to LSE as the error term penalized by uncertainty logic # However, the formula Lunct = a1 LSE + a2 L0 implies LSE is the base regression loss lse = meansquarederror(predictions, targets) # Step 3: Compute Zero Regularization Loss (L0) # Encourages delta to be close to zero l0 = sum(max(delta, 0)) # Step 4: Combine lunct = alpha1 lse + alpha2 l0 return lunct def computeuncertaintylosssdf(points, mlpsdf, sigma0sq=1e-6): """ Computes Uncertainty Estimation Loss for Point Cloud SDF. points: Tensor of point coordinates xP. mlpsdf: Neural network returning mean, rawvar, feature. """ # Step 1: Get predictions fx, rawvar, = mlpsdf(points) # Step 2: Compute valid variance # softplus(rawvar) + sigma0sq validvar = sigma0sq + softplus(rawvar) # Step 3: Compute Negative Log-Likelihood Loss # Ideal SDF value is 0 targetsdf = 0.0 errorsq = (targetsdf - fx) 2 # Term 1: Weighted squared error term1 = errorsq / (2 validvar) # Term 2: Log variance regularization term2 = log(validvar) / 2 # Average over points lusdf = mean(term1 + term2) return lusdf Uniform and Gaussian Noise Models are parametric statistical methods used to visualize uncertainty in differentiable volume rendering by approximating the distribution of ensemble samples with a uniform or Gaussian distribution. They differ from their parent method, Uncertainty Prediction Loss, by explicitly modeling the shape of the noise distribution rather than just penalizing its magnitude, and they differ from Nonparametric Uncertainty Modeling for DVR by assuming a specific parametric form (uniform or Gaussian) rather than using empirical quantiles. In the context of the Uncertainty Prediction Loss for volume rendering, the weights are set to \alpha1 = 1.0 and \alpha2 = 0.01. These weights balance the squared error loss against the zero regularization loss. In multi-stage or dynamically growing networks (e.g., Recursive-NeRF), the uncertainty loss is combined with MSE loss across all stages. The total loss is: \mathcal{L} = \sum{i=1}^D \beta1 \mathcal{L}{MSE}^i + \beta2 \mathcal{L}{unct}^i where D is the current number of stages, and \beta1 = 1.0, \beta2 = 0.1. All query coordinates are output through all outlets during training. This variant models the Signed Distance Function (SDF) value of each point in a point cloud as a Gaussian distribution with learnable mean and variance to capture aleatoric uncertainty (noise) in the input data. It uses a negative log-likelihood loss to optimize the model, assuming ideal SDF values are 0. Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead as it requires only an additional linear layer or MLP head for uncertainty prediction and simple arithmetic operations for the loss. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the predicted uncertainty values (\deltai or \bar{\sigma}^2) for each query point during training. Strengths: Helps the model ignore noisy or ambiguous data points by assigning them higher uncertainty, leading to more robust geometry and color reconstruction. Prevents the network from overfitting to noise. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization weights (\alpha2, \sigma0^2) to prevent uncertainty from blowing up or collapsing. The assumption that ideal SDF values are 0 may not hold for all datasets. When to use: When the input data contains significant noise or outliers, or when robustness to ambiguous regions is required. The Uncertainty Prediction Loss was introduced in the context of Recursive-NeRF, an efficient and dynamically growing NeRF architecture. It was designed to guide the dynamic growth of the network by identifying uncertain query points. A related formulation for point cloud SDF reconstruction was proposed in Point-NeuS, which uses uncertainty to handle noise in observed point clouds. name: Uniform and Gaussian Noise Models
head: Parametric statistical models for uncertainty visualization
body: Uniform and Gaussian Noise Models are parametric statistical methods used to visualize uncertainty in differentiable volume rendering by approximating the distribution of ensemble samples with a uniform or Gaussian distribution. They differ from their parent method, Uncertainty Prediction Loss, by explicitly modeling the shape of the noise distribution rather than just penalizing its magnitude, and they differ from Nonparametric Uncertainty Modeling for DVR by assuming a specific parametric form (uniform or Gaussian) rather than using empirical quantiles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of noise samples (ensemble predictions) for each voxel or pixel. Output: Visualized uncertainty using parametric distributions (Uniform or Gaussian) characterized by mean and width/variance. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Collect noise samples for the target region. 2. Estimate the mean (\mu) and width (for Uniform) or variance (\sigma^2, for Gaussian) directly from these noise samples. 3. Construct the parametric distribution using the estimated parameters. 4. Visualize the uncertainty based on this distribution. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The sources state that mean and width/variance are estimated from noise samples but do not provide the specific mathematical formulas for the estimation or the rendering integration. Parameters: For Gaussian models, the variance estimated from noise samples is a critical parameter. Adjusting this variance can significantly improve classification results. For Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs, a related parametric approach mentioned in the same context), four Gaussians per mixture are used, consuming memory comparable to eight quantiles in nonparametric models. Edge cases and pitfalls: The RMSE of the visualization is sensitive to the choice of parameter values for these parametric models. In the Osirix OBELIX dataset, visualizations using uniform and Gaussian noise models resulted in thicker bone rendering and failed to localize the right-kidney classification compared to the quantile mean technique. The mean-field approach loses significant information near kidneys, which parametric models also struggle with if parameters are not tuned. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimateuniformparams(samples): """ Estimates mean and width for a uniform distribution from samples. """ mean = sum(samples) / len(samples) # Width estimation formula not given in sources width = Not given in the sources return mean, width def estimategaussianparams(samples): """ Estimates mean and variance for a Gaussian distribution from samples. """ mean = sum(samples) / len(samples) # Variance estimation formula not given in sources variance = Not given in the sources return mean, variance def visualizeuncertainty(samples, modeltype='gaussian'): """ Visualizes uncertainty using parametric models. """ if modeltype == 'uniform': mu, w = estimateuniformparams(samples) # Visualization logic using Uniform(mu, w) not given in sources elif modeltype == 'gaussian': mu, sigma2 = estimategaussianparams(samples) # Visualization logic using Gaussian(mu, sigma2) not given in sources # Note: Adjusting sigma2 can significantly improve classification Nonparametric Uncertainty Modeling for DVR is a technique that represents volumetric uncertainty using empirical quantiles rather than parametric distributions (such as Gaussian or Uniform models), enabling accurate visualization of asymmetric or multimodal noise distributions. It differs from its parent method, Uniform and Gaussian Noise Models, by avoiding distributional assumptions, thereby capturing complex statistical structures in ensemble data that parametric models fail to represent. Strengths: Simple parametric assumption; adjusting Gaussian variance can significantly improve classification results. Limitations: Can result in thicker bone rendering and fail to localize specific structures (e.g., right-kidney) compared to nonparametric quantile techniques. RMSE is sensitive to parameter choice. Memory: Not given in the sources for pure Uniform/Gaussian models. GMMs (related) consume memory equal to three times the number of Gaussians. When to use: When a simple parametric approximation is sufficient and parameter tuning is feasible. When not: When the noise distribution is asymmetric or multimodal, or when precise localization is required. Originated in the context of Direct Volume Rendering with Nonparametric Models of Uncertainty, where parametric models (Uniform and Gaussian) were used as baselines or alternatives to nonparametric quantile-based approaches. The method was evaluated on the Osirix OBELIX dataset for bone and kidney classification.
