name: Plenoxels Training with Progressive Growing
head: Progressive Growing for Plenoxels
body: A training procedure for Plenoxels that uses progressive growing of the receptive field size to optimize a 3D voxel grid from multi-view images, incorporating TV loss and beta loss for regularization. It differs from static grid optimization by starting with a coarse, downsampled representation and refining it, which reduces training time and improves convergence stability. Inputs: Multi-view images (imgs), camera parameters (transformmatrices, cameraanglex), grid dimensions (gridsize), and hyperparameters (lr, tv, beta, steps, numberofrays, numsamples, deltastep, pointsdistance, progressivegrowing). Outputs: Optimized voxel grid gridcellsfull containing RGB and opacity values. Data Structures: gridcellsfull: Tensor of shape (X, Y, Z, 4). The last dimension stores cell information (RGB + Alpha). Initialized with requiresgrad=True. gridcoords: Tensor of shape (X \cdot Y \cdot Z, 3) storing the 3D coordinates of each voxel center. pointsdistance: Scalar defining the physical distance between grid points (default 0.0125). receptivefieldssizes: List of odd integers from 93 down to 3 (inclusive). Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Create gridcellsfull of shape gridsize + (4) on the target device. Initialize gridcellsfullgrad (accumulator for absolute gradients) to zeros of the same shape. Set receptivefieldssizes = [93, 91, \dots, 3]. Set stepsperfield = 5. 2. Training Loop: Iterate i from 0 to steps - 1. 3. Receptive Field Configuration: Calculate fieldindex = \lfloor i / \text{steps\per\field} \rfloor. If fieldindex < length(receptivefieldssizes), set receptivefieldsize = receptivefieldssizes[fieldindex]. Else, set receptivefieldsize = 1. 4. Grid Sub-sampling (Progressive Growing): If receptivefieldsize > 1 AND progressivegrowing is True: Calculate stride = \max(1, \lfloor \text{receptive\field\size} / 4 \rfloor). Calculate startindex = \lfloor \text{receptive\field\size} / 2 \rfloor. Extract sub-grid gridgrid from gridcellsfull using slice [startindex::stride, startindex::stride, startindex::stride]. Reshape gridgrid to gridindices (flattened spatial indices). Update pointsdistance = pointsdistanceoriginal stride. Compute gridcells by averaging gridcellsfull over the receptive field using averagepool3dgrid (implemented via 3D convolution with a uniform kernel). Else (static or final refinement): Set gridcells = gridcellsfull. Set gridindices = gridcellsfull.reshape(-1, 3) (or equivalent coordinate mapping). Set pointsdistance = pointsdistanceoriginal. 5. Ray Sampling: Call samplecameraraysbatched with transformmatrices, cameraanglex, imgs, numberofrays, numsamples, deltastep, evenspread, cameraray=False, and device. Returns samplesinterval (ray samples), pixelstorays (ground truth colors), camerapositions, raydirections. 6. Normalization and Voxel Assignment: Normalize samples: Call normalizesamplesforindecies with gridindices and samplesinterval using pointsdistance to get normalizedsamplesforindecies (coordinates in voxel index space). Clip gridcells to [0, 1]. Get nearest voxels: Call getnearestvoxels with normalizedsamplesforindecies and clipped gridcells. Inside getnearestvoxels: Round normalizedsamplesforindecies to nearest integer indices. Check bounds using findoutofbound. Fix out-of-bounds indices using periodic boundary conditions (fixoutofbounds) or mask them. Returns nearest (voxel values) and mask (boolean tensor indicating valid samples). Zero out invalid samples: nearest = nearest mask.unsqueeze(-1). 7. Rendering: Reshape nearest to (B, \text{number\of\rays}, \text{num\samples}, 4). Compute pixel colors: Call computealphaweightedpixels(nearest) to perform volume rendering (alpha compositing). Reshape pixelscolor to (B \cdot \text{number\of\rays}, \text{num\samples}). 8. Loss Computation: MSE Loss: mseloss = \text{MSE}(\text{pixels\color}, \text{pixels\to\rays}). loss = mseloss. TV Loss: If tv > 0 AND receptivefieldsize < 19: tvloss = tv tvloss(gridcells). loss = loss + tvloss. Beta Loss (Entropy Regularization): If beta > 0: Extract alpha channel: \alpha = \text{nearest}[:,:,:, -1]. betaloss = beta \text{mean}(\log(\alpha + 0.0001) - \log(1 - \alpha + 0.0001)). loss = loss + betaloss. 9. Optimization: optimizer.zerograd(). loss.backward(). optimizer.step(). 10. Gradient Accumulation: gridcellsfullgrad += \text{abs}(\text{grid\cells\full.grad}). 11. Checkpointing: Detach gridcellsfull to CPU. Save dictionary containing grid (gridcellsfull), gridgrad (gridcellsfullgrad), and param (device, numberofrays, numsamples, deltastep, evenspread, cameraray, pointsdistance, gridsize) to savepath. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F import torch.nn as nn def trilinearinterpolation(normalizedsamplesforindecies, selectedpoints, gridcells): """ Trilinear interpolation of grid values at sample points.:param normalizedsamplesforindecies: Tensor (N, 3):param selectedpoints: Tensor (N, 8, 3) indices of 8 corners:param gridcells: Tensor (X, Y, Z, 4):returns: Tensor (N, 4) """ inteplationfrac = torch.frac(normalizedsamplesforindecies) # Selection based on corner indices provided in selectedpoints # Indices 4-7 are ceil corners, 0-3 are floor corners (based on doc comment) selection0 = gridcells[selectedpoints[:, 4:, 0], selectedpoints[:, 4:, 1], selectedpoints[:, 4:, 2]] selection1 = gridcells[selectedpoints[:,:4, 0], selectedpoints[:,:4, 1], selectedpoints[:,:4, 2]] # Interpolate along X inteplationfracstep = inteplationfrac[:, 0].unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) newstep = (selection1 inteplationfracstep) + (selection0 (1 - inteplationfracstep)) del selection0, selection1 # Interpolate along Y inteplationfracstep = inteplationfrac[:, 1].unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) newstep = (newstep[:,:2] inteplationfracstep) + (newstep[:, 2:] (1 - inteplationfracstep)) # Interpolate along Z inteplationfracstep = inteplationfrac[:, 2].unsqueeze(-1) newstep = (newstep[:, 0] inteplationfracstep) + (newstep[:, 1] (1 - inteplationfracstep)) return newstep def findoutofbound(indecies, grid): """ Checks if indices are within grid bounds [0, X), [0, Y), [0, Z).:param indecies: Tensor (N, 3):param grid: Tensor (X, Y, Z,...):returns: Boolean Tensor (N,) True if inside bounds """ idx1, idx2, idx3 = indecies[:, 0], indecies[:, 1], indecies[:, 2] X, Y, Z, = grid.shape idx1ok = (idx1 >= 0) & (idx1 < X) idx2ok = (idx2 >= 0) & (idx2 < Y) idx3ok = (idx3 >= 0) & (idx3 < Z) return idx1ok & idx2ok & idx3ok def fixoutofbounds(indices, grid): """ Fixes out of bounds indices using periodic boundary conditions.:param indices: Tensor (N, 3):param grid: Tensor (X, Y, Z,...):returns: Tuple of Tensors (idx1, idx2, idx3) fixed indices """ idx1, idx2, idx3 = indices[:, 0], indices[:, 1], indices[:, 2] X, Y, Z, = grid.shape idx1 = idx1 % X idx2 = idx2 % Y idx3 = idx3 % Z return idx1, idx2, idx3 def getnearestvoxels(normalizedsamplesforindices, grid): """ Gets nearest voxel values for normalized sample indices.:param normalizedsamplesforindices: Tensor (N, 3):param grid: Tensor (X, Y, Z, 4):returns: Tuple (values Tensor (N, 4), mask Tensor (N,)) """ indices = torch.round(normalizedsamplesforindices).to(torch.long) outofbounds = findoutofbound(indices, grid) # Fix out of bounds for indexing idx1, idx2, idx3 = fixoutofbounds(indices, grid) values = grid[idx1, idx2, idx3] return values, outofbounds def averagepool3dgrid(gridcellsfull, receptivefieldsize): """ Averages grid cells over a receptive field using 3D convolution.:param gridcellsfull: Tensor (X, Y, Z, 4):param receptivefieldsize: int (odd):returns: Tensor (X, Y, Z, 4) """ # Permute to (1, 4, X, Y, Z) for conv3d tensor = gridcellsfull.permute(3, 0, 1, 2).unsqueeze(0).float() # Create uniform kernel kernelvalue = 1.0 / (receptivefieldsize 3) kernel = torch.full((1, 1, receptivefieldsize, receptivefieldsize, receptivefieldsize), kernelvalue, device=tensor.device) kernel = kernel.repeat(4, 1, 1, 1, 1) # Repeat for 4 channels # Convolve with padding to maintain size result = F.conv3d(tensor, kernel, padding=receptivefieldsize // 2, groups=4) # Permute back to (X, Y, Z, 4) result = result.squeeze(0).permute(1, 2, 3, 0) return result def trainplenoxelsprogressive(gridcellsfull, gridcoords, optimizer, imgs, transformmatrices, cameraanglex, steps, numberofrays, numsamples, deltastep, pointsdistanceoriginal, tv, beta, progressivegrowing, device): """ Main training loop for Plenoxels with progressive growing. """ receptivefieldssizes = list(range(93, 2, -2)) # 93 down to 3 stepsperfield = 5 gridcellsfullgrad = torch.zeroslike(gridcellsfull) for i in range(steps): # 1. Determine receptive field fieldindex = i // stepsperfield if fieldindex < len(receptivefieldssizes): receptivefieldsize = receptivefieldssizes[fieldindex] else: receptivefieldsize = 1 # 2. Configure Grid and Sampling if receptivefieldsize > 1 and progressivegrowing: stride = max(1, receptivefieldsize // 4) startindex = int(receptivefieldsize / 2) # Extract sub-grid gridgrid = gridcellsfull[startindex::stride, startindex::stride, startindex::stride] gridindices = gridgrid.reshape(-1, 3) # Placeholder for coordinate mapping logic pointsdistance = pointsdistanceoriginal stride # Average pool to get current representation gridcells = averagepool3dgrid(gridcellsfull, receptivefieldsize) else: gridcells = gridcellsfull gridindices = gridcoords # Placeholder pointsdistance = pointsdistanceoriginal # 3. Sample Rays (Placeholder for external function) # samplesinterval, pixelstorays, camerapositions, raydirections = samplecameraraysbatched(...) # For implementation completeness, we assume these are available samplesinterval = torch.rand((imgs.shape[0], numberofrays, numsamples, 3), device=device) # pixelstorays = torch.rand((imgs.shape[0], numberofrays, 3), device=device) # # 4. Normalize Samples # normalizedsamplesforindecies = normalizesamplesforindecies(gridindices, samplesinterval, pointsdistance) # Assuming simple scaling for demonstration if gridindices are coordinates normalizedsamplesforindecies = samplesinterval / pointsdistance # 5. Get Nearest Voxels clippedgrid = torch.clamp(gridcells, 0, 1) nearest, mask = getnearestvoxels(normalizedsamplesforindecies, clippedgrid) # Zero out invalid samples nearest = nearest mask.unsqueeze(-1).float() # 6. Render # Reshape for rendering: (B, rays, samples, 4) nearestreshaped = nearest.reshape(imgs.shape[0], numberofrays, numsamples, 4) # Compute Alpha Weighted Pixels (Placeholder for volume rendering logic) # pixelscolor = computealphaweightedpixels(nearestreshaped) # Simple sum for demonstration if alpha is not used, or standard compositing alphas = torch.sigmoid(nearestreshaped[..., 3:]) # Assuming last channel is logit alpha rgbs = nearestreshaped[...,:3] # Standard volume rendering: C = sum(Ti ci (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai))) # Simplified for placeholder: weighted sum weights = alphas (1 - alphas) # Placeholder weights pixelscolor = torch.sum(rgbs weights, dim=2) pixelscolor = pixelscolor.reshape(imgs.shape[0] numberofrays, numsamples) # Shape mismatch fix for loss calc # 7. Optimize optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # 9. Accumulate Gradients if gridcellsfull.grad is not None: gridcellsfullgrad += torch.abs(gridcellsfull.grad) return gridcellsfull, gridcellsfullgrad Parameters: lr: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Default: 0.0075. tv: Strength of Total Variation loss. Default: 10^{-5}. Set to 0 to disable. beta: Strength of Beta loss (entropy regularization on alpha). Default: 5 \times 10^{-3}. Set to 0 to disable. steps: Total training steps. Default: 500. numberofrays: Rays per camera. Default: 128. numsamples: Samples per ray. Default: 600. deltastep: Distance between samples. Default: 0.0125. pointsdistance: Grid spacing. Default: 0.0125. gridsize: Grid dimensions. Default: [256, 256, 256] if not specified. name: Joint Finetuning for Vector-Quantized Radiance Fields
head: VQ-DVGO, VQ-Plenoxels, VQ-TensoRF finetuning
body: Joint finetuning is a post-compression optimization procedure applied to vector-quantized radiance fields to recover rendering quality lost during voxel pruning and codebook initialization. It adapts gradient-based optimization to the constraints of vector-quantized structures, building on Plenoxels Optimization Configuration. The method recovers rendering quality in compressed radiance field representations through a sequence of pruning, initialization, and joint optimization. Inputs: A pre-trained radiance field model (DVGO, Plenoxels, or TensoRF), training images, camera poses, and a pruning quantile for cumulative score rates. Outputs: A vector-quantized radiance field model with recovered rendering quality and up to 100× lower storage cost compared to uncompressed models. The data structures depend on the specific variant being finetuned: 1. DVGO Model: Density grid, feature grid, and a shallow MLP for color estimation. 2. Plenoxels Model: Density grid and a feature grid filled with spherical harmonic coefficients. 3. TensoRF Model: Virtual grid for importance scoring, with points projected onto density and feature tri-planes by aggregating along each axis. 1. Pruning: Prune less important voxels according to the quantile of the cumulative score rate. 2. Codebook Initialization: Use only the pruned voxels for codebook initialization. 3. Joint Finetuning: Begin joint finetuning with method-specific learning rates and exponential decay schedules. The specific parameters for each variant are as follows: DVGO (VQ-DVGO) Density grid learning rate: 8 \times 10^{-2}. Feature grid and shallow MLP learning rate: 1.6 \times 10^{-3}. Decay schedule: Exponential decay, scaling learning rates by 0.3 every 10,000 iterations. Duration: 10,000 iterations. Batch size: 8,192 rays per iteration. Plenoxels (VQ-Plenoxels) Duration: 25,600 iterations, equivalent to two epochs in the original Plenoxels training. Scheduler reset: Reset to the sixth epoch of the original setting. TensoRF (VQ-TensoRF) Learning rate: 5 \times 10^{-3} for all density tri-planes, feature tri-planes, and the shallow MLP. Decay schedule: Exponential decay, scaling learning rate by 0.3 every 30,000 iterations. Duration: 10,000 iterations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jointfinetune(model, trainingdata, config): # 1. Pruning scores = computevoxelimportance(model) threshold = sorted(scores)[int(config['pruningquantile'] len(scores))] model.prunevoxelsbelow(threshold) # 2. Codebook Initialization model.initializecodebookfromprunedvoxels() # 3. Joint Finetuning numiterations = config['numiterations'] lrdensity = config['lrdensity'] lrfeature = config['lrfeature'] lrmlp = config['lrmlp'] decayfactor = config['decayfactor'] decayinterval = config['decayinterval'] raysperiter = config['raysperiter'] currentlrs = {'density': lrdensity, 'feature': lrfeature, 'mlp': lrmlp} for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample rays rays = sampleraysfromdataset(trainingdata, raysperiter) # Forward pass rendered = model.forward(rays) groundtruth = rays.gtimages # Compute loss loss = sum((r - g) 2 for r, g in zip(rendered, groundtruth)) / len(rendered) # Backward pass gradients = computegradients(loss, model.parameters()) # Update parameters for name, param in model.parameters().items(): param -= currentlrs[name] gradients[name] # Learning rate decay if config['variant'] == 'plenoxels': # Scheduler reset to sixth epoch is handled by external configuration pass else: if (iteration + 1) % decayinterval == 0: for name in currentlrs: currentlrs[name] = decayfactor return model Pruning Threshold: The quantile of the cumulative score rate must be chosen carefully to balance compression ratio and quality recovery. [Not given in the sources.] Scheduler Reset: For Plenoxels, the learning rate scheduler is reset to the sixth epoch of the original setting. Precision and Boundaries: Standard differentiable rendering precision limits apply during gradient computation through the quantized grids. A post-baking optimization step that refines only texel colors for 3,000 iterations while freezing geometry and view-dependent color parameters. It distinguishes itself from continuing neural teacher training by eliminating hash collisions inherent in the original hash grid and leveraging a larger parameter count (5–29× more) to exceed the teacher's performance. Choose this when recovering rendering quality after compression into a texture atlas is required. Storage Cost: Achieves up to 100× lower storage cost compared to uncompressed models while preserving rendering quality. Performance: Effectively preserves rendering quality, including fine details, compared to the uncompressed model. Computational Cost: Finetuning duration varies by variant: 10,000 iterations for DVGO and TensoRF, and 25,600 iterations for Plenoxels. Scalability: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant compression with minimal quality loss; recovers quality lost during quantization. Limitations: Performance depends on the underlying grid structure (e.g., hash grids for DVGO) and the chosen pruning quantile. Joint finetuning for vector-quantized radiance fields was introduced in "Compressing Volumetric Radiance Fields to 1 MB". The method addresses the challenge of compressing neural radiance fields while maintaining high rendering quality by applying targeted gradient-based optimization after quantization and pruning. name: Atlas Finetuning with Sparse Adam
head: Atlas Finetune Procedure, Atlas Finetuning, Atlas Optimization, Sparse Adam Finetuning, Baked + finetune, Texel finetune
body: Atlas Finetuning with Sparse Adam is a post-baking optimization step that recovers rendering quality lost during the quantization, pruning, and compression of a neural radiance field into a texture atlas. It treats the baked atlas as an initialization and refines only the texel colors for 3,000 iterations, freezing geometry and view-dependent color parameters. This method distinguishes itself from continuing neural teacher training by eliminating hash collisions inherent in the original hash grid and leveraging a larger parameter count (5–29× more parameters) to exceed the teacher's performance. Inputs and Outputs Input: A baked, BC7-compressed texture atlas (dequantized to FP16), frozen geometry (surfel positions/scales), frozen view-dependent color coefficients, and training images. Output: An optimized atlas texture where only the texel RGB values have been updated. Data Structures Atlas Texture: A 2D texture storing FP16 values. The layout is determined by the bake and texel allocation stage, which assigns specific tile sizes to surfels based on rate-distortion trade-offs. Optimizer State: Lazy sparse Adam state maintained only for texel rows that receive gradients, storing first and second moment estimates in BF16 precision to reduce memory usage. Parameters Iterations: 3,000. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Optimizer Hyperparameters: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999. Loss Weights: L1 loss weight 1.0, D-SSIM loss weight 0.2. Loss Function: L = L1 + 0.2(1 - SSIM). Algorithm Steps 1. Dequantization: Convert the baked BC7-compressed atlas into a trainable FP16 texture. 2. Freeze Non-Texel Parameters: Explicitly freeze the geometry (surfel positions and scales) and view-dependent color coefficients. 3. Differentiable Rasterization Setup: Configure the renderer to use the exact inference atlas fetch logic: Forward pass performs rect transform, coordinate clamping, and bilinear interpolation to fetch texel colors. Backward pass scatters the residual gradient from the bilinear read into the four contributing texels. 4. Sparse Optimization Loop: For each iteration from 1 to 3,000: Render the scene using the current atlas and frozen parameters to generate a predicted image. Compute the loss L = L1 + 0.2(1 - SSIM) against the ground truth training image. Compute gradients with respect to the atlas texels. Identify the set of texel rows touched by the current view (gradient sparsity is typically 5–7% of rows). Update only the touched texels using the Sparse Adam optimizer with BF16 moment storage. Continue the learning rate schedule from the teacher training phase; do not restart. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def atlasfinetune(atlastexture, frozengeometry, frozenviewcolor, trainingdataset, iterations=3000, lr=1e-3, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): optimizerstate = {} for step in range(iterations): gtimage, camera = next(trainingdataset) predictedimage = bilinearatlasfetch(atlastexture, frozengeometry, frozenviewcolor, camera) loss = meanabsoluteerror(predictedimage, gtimage) + 0.2 (1.0 - structuralsimilarity(predictedimage, gtimage)) gradients = computegradients(loss, atlastexture) touchedrows = [r for r in range(atlastexture.shape[0]) if any(gradients[r] != 0)] for rowidx in touchedrows: if rowidx not in optimizerstate: optimizerstate[rowidx] = {'mean': zeroslike(atlastexture[rowidx], dtype='bf16'), 'var': zeroslike(atlastexture[rowidx], dtype='bf16')} state = optimizerstate[rowidx] gradrow = gradients[rowidx] state['mean'] = bf16(beta1 state['mean'] + (1 - beta1) gradrow) state['var'] = bf16(beta2 state['var'] + (1 - beta2) (gradrow 2)) meanhat = state['mean'] / (1 - beta1 (step + 1)) varhat = state['var'] / (1 - beta2 (step + 1)) atlastexture[rowidx] = atlastexture[rowidx] - lr meanhat / (sqrt(varhat) + eps) return atlastexture def bilinearatlasfetch(texture, geometry, viewcolor, camera): uvcoords = maptouv(geometry, camera) uvcoords = clamp(uvcoords, 0.0, 1.0) return bilinearinterpolate(texture, uvcoords) def computegradients(loss, texture): return scatterbilineargradients(loss, texture) def meanabsoluteerror(pred, gt): return sum(abs(pred - gt)) / len(pred) def structuralsimilarity(pred, gt): return 1.0 - sum(abs(pred - gt)) / (len(pred) 3) def zeroslike(tensor, dtype): return tensor 0 def bf16(tensor): return tensor.to('bf16') def sqrt(tensor): return tensor 0.5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls Unfreezing Geometry: Unfreezing geometry during finetuning degrades quality, costing 0.18 dB PSNR and 0.009 LPIPS, even at 0.1× the learning rate. This is because moving surfels invalidates the binding between texels and scene positions established at bake time. Unfreezing View-Dependent Color: Jointly training view-dependent color with the atlas costs 2.7 dB PSNR. Unfreezing view-dependent color alone is neutral (0.01 dB tie), but joint training is ill-posed because the view-dependent term can cancel against the residual. Precision: Optimizer moments are stored in BF16 to halve memory usage. Time Complexity: The finetuning stage costs a few minutes per scene. The sparse update ensures that only 5–7% of texel rows are processed per iteration, reducing computational load compared to dense updates. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by half compared to dense Adam due to BF16 moment storage and lazy allocation for touched rows only. Performance: The finetuned atlas surpasses the neural teacher model by +0.24 to +0.47 dB PSNR and improves LPIPS by 0.025–0.026 on all benchmarks. It also improves SSIM on two of three datasets. Scaling: The method scales with the number of surfels and the sparsity of the gradient. The sparse update avoids the "slow random walk" that degrades the atlas when untouched texels are updated by dense optimizers. Strengths: Eliminates hash collisions present in the original hash grid; leverages higher parameter count (13× average) for better representation; low memory overhead; fast convergence. Limitations: Requires a prior bake step; only refines color, not geometry or view-dependence; sensitive to learning rate if geometry is accidentally unfrozen. Atlas Finetuning with Sparse Adam was introduced in the paper "Bake It Till You Make It: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting". It addresses the quality loss inherent in baking neural radiance fields into texture atlases due to quantization, Nyquist clamping, and pruning. The method was developed to allow real-time rendering of high-quality radiance fields by offloading the heavy neural network evaluation to a texture lookup, while recovering the lost fidelity through targeted optimization. name: PlenOctree Optimization
head: Structure Refinement (Octree Optimization)
body: PlenOctree Optimization is a post-training refinement stage that finetunes a converted PlenOctree on original training images to improve image quality. It solves the problem of residual artifacts and suboptimal density/color allocation in the initial sparse octree by applying gradient-based optimization. Unlike its siblings, which focus on configuration or pruning strategies during training, PlenOctree Optimization operates on a fixed tree structure using standard NeRF loss without sparsity regularization, leveraging the fact that the octree is already sparse. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A converted PlenOctree (density \sigma and SH coefficients \mathbf{c} at leaves) and a set of training images with camera poses. Output: An optimized PlenOctree with refined \sigma and \mathbf{c} values. Data Structures: The PlenOctree is a sparse octree. Each leaf node stores: Density \sigma (scalar). Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for RGB channels (vectors). The tree structure (parent-child pointers, leaf status) remains fixed during this optimization phase. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start with the converted PlenOctree. Ensure parameters are in float32 for stability. 2. Loss Calculation: For each training ray r, render the color \hat{C}(r) using the current PlenOctree. Compute the RGB loss: L{RGB} = \sum{r \in R} ||C(r) - \hat{C}(r)||2^2 where C(r) is the ground truth color. 3. Gradient Update: Use SGD to update the density and SH coefficients of the leaf nodes. Analytic derivatives of the rendering equation with respect to \sigma and \mathbf{c} are used. 4. Iteration: Repeat for a fixed number of epochs or until early stopping criteria are met. 5. Storage: After optimization, convert parameters to float16 to reduce model size. Parameters: Learning Rate: NeRF-synthetic dataset: 1 \times 10^{-7}. Tanks&Temples dataset: 1.5 \times 10^{-6}. Epochs: NeRF-synthetic: Maximum 80 epochs. Tanks&Temples: Maximum 40 epochs. Validation: For Tanks&Temples, hold out 10% of the training set as a validation set. Early Stopping: Monitor PSNR on the validation set; stop if no improvement. Precision: Float32 during optimization, Float16 for storage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def plenoptreeoptimization(plenoctree, trainingdata, config): """ Optimizes a PlenOctree using SGD on the NeRF loss. Args: plenoctree: The sparse octree with density and SH coefficients. trainingdata: List of (image, camerapose) pairs. config: Dictionary with learningrate, maxepochs, and validationsplit. Returns: Optimized plenoctree. """ # Initialize parameters in float32 for stability plenoctree.setprecision('float32') # Split data if validation is needed if config.get('usevalidation'): trainset, valset = splitdata(trainingdata, config['validationsplit']) else: trainset = trainingdata valset = None optimizer = SGD(parameters=plenoctree.getleafparams(), lr=config['learningrate']) bestpsnr = -1 patiencecounter = 0 for epoch in range(config['maxepochs']): # Training step for image, pose in trainset: # Render ray colors using current PlenOctree renderedcolors = renderplenoctree(plenoctree, pose) groundtruthcolors = image # Compute LRGB loss loss = sum((gt - pred)2 for gt, pred in zip(groundtruthcolors, renderedcolors)) # Compute analytic gradients and update parameters gradients = computeanalyticgradients(loss, plenoctree) optimizer.step(gradients) # Validation step if valset is not None: currentpsnr = computepsnr(plenoctree, valset) # Early stopping check if currentpsnr > bestpsnr: bestpsnr = currentpsnr savebestmodel(plenoctree) patiencecounter = 0 else: patiencecounter += 1 # Note: Specific patience value not given in sources if patiencecounter > 5: break # Convert to float16 for storage plenoctree.setprecision('float16') return plenoctree A pipeline to convert a trained NeRF-SH model into a sparse octree representation (PlenOctree) for real-time rendering. The octree stores density and SH coefficients at leaves. It involves rendering alpha maps to identify visible voxels, thresholding, and sampling points within remaining voxels to initialize leaf values. This method provides the closed-form gradients of the NeRF piecewise constant volume rendering equation with respect to the density (\sigma) and color (\mathbf{c}) parameters. It enables direct optimization of PlenOctree attributes using gradient-based methods (e.g., SGD) to refine image quality. Time Complexity: Optimization is significantly faster than NeRF training. It operates at about 3 million rays per second, compared to about 9,000 for NeRF training. Memory Complexity: The octree is sparse, reducing memory usage compared to dense grids. Storage is optimized by using float16 after optimization. Performance: Takes around 10 minutes to finish PlenOctree optimization for each scene on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. Strengths: Accelerates NeRF-based rendering by 5 orders of magnitude without loss in image quality. No sparsity loss is needed as the octree is already sparse. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained NeRF-SH model. The tree structure is fixed during optimization, so it cannot adapt to new geometric complexities that would require structural changes. PlenOctree Optimization was introduced in the context of PlenOctrees for Real-time Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). The method was developed to address the slow training times of original NeRFs by converting them into a sparse, explicit octree representation that can be optimized and rendered much faster. The approach demonstrates state-of-the-level performance for image quality and rendering speed on standard benchmarks. name: PlenOctree Conversion
head: NeRF-SH to PlenOctree conversion, PlenOctree extraction
body: PlenOctree Conversion is a pipeline that transforms a trained NeRF-SH (Neural Radiance Field with Spherical Harmonics) model into a sparse octree representation called a PlenOctree, enabling real-time volume rendering. It solves the performance bottleneck of conventional NeRFs, which require dense sampling and neural network inference for every ray sample dependent on viewing direction. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Analytic Derivatives of PlenOctree Rendering, is that it focuses on the construction and tabulation of the view-dependent volume from a pre-trained neural network, rather than the differentiable optimization of the octree structure itself. Inputs: A trained NeRF-SH model (a neural network that outputs density \sigma and Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for a given 3D position \mathbf{x}, eliminating the need for view-direction input to the network). Outputs: A sparse octree where each leaf node stores a density value \sigma and a set of SH coefficients representing view-dependent radiance. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains a density value \sigma and SH coefficients. The SH coefficients encode the view-dependent appearance. Voxel Grid: A uniformly spaced 3D grid used during the initial evaluation phase. Parameters: \tauw: Threshold for voxel weight (maximum ray weight) to determine which voxels are retained. Typical value not explicitly given, but used to eliminate non-visible voxels. \taua: Threshold for density to determine the bounding box of the scene content (used to scale the grid). N{samples}: Number of random points sampled per voxel to reduce aliasing. Value: 256. \gamma: Early-stopping transmittance threshold during rendering. Value: 0.01. Steps: 1. Evaluation: Evaluate the NeRF-SH model to obtain density values \sigma on a uniformly spaced 3D grid. The grid is automatically scaled to tightly fit the scene content by pre-evaluating \sigma on a larger grid and finding the bounding box of all points with \sigma \ge \taua. 2. Filtering: Render alpha maps for all training views using the voxel grid. Track the maximum ray weight 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) at each voxel, where \deltai is the segment length. Eliminate voxels whose weights are lower than the threshold \tauw. This filtering by maximum ray weight is superior to naively thresholding by \sigma at each point because it eliminates non-visible voxels. 3. Sampling: For each remaining voxel in the filtered grid, sample N{samples} = 256 random points within the voxel volume. Set the associated leaf of the octree to the mean of these sampled values (density and SH coefficients) to reduce aliasing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convertnerftoplenoctree(nerfshmodel, trainingviews, tauw, taua): # Step 1: Evaluation # Determine bounding box based on density threshold taua # This is done by pre-evaluating sigma on a larger grid boundingbox = findboundingbox(nerfshmodel, threshold=taua) # Create a uniformly spaced 3D grid within the bounding box grid = createuniform3dgrid(boundingbox) # Evaluate NeRF-SH model on grid points to get sigma # Note: NeRF-SH outputs SH coefficients, but for grid evaluation, # we primarily need sigma for the initial filtering. # The grid stores sigma values initially. gridsigma = evaluatenerfsigma(nerfshmodel, grid.points) # Step 2: Filtering # Render alpha maps for all training views to compute voxel weights voxelweights = computemaxrayweights(grid, trainingviews, gridsigma) # Retain only voxels with weight >= tauw retainedvoxels = [v for v in grid.voxels if voxelweights[v] >= tauw] # Step 3: Sampling # Build the octree from retained voxels plenoctree = Octree() for voxel in retainedvoxels: # Sample 256 random points within the voxel samples = samplerandompointsinvoxel(voxel, n=256) # Evaluate NeRF-SH model at these sample points # NeRF-SH returns (sigma, shcoeffs) sampleresults = [nerfshmodel(sample.position) for sample in samples] # Compute mean of sigma and SH coefficients meansigma = mean([r.sigma for r in sampleresults]) meanshcoeffs = mean([r.shcoeffs for r in sampleresults]) # Add leaf to octree plenoctree.addleaf(voxel.center, meansigma, meanshcoeffs) return plenoctree Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The conversion process takes about 15 minutes, indicating computational intensity. Boundaries: The grid scaling must tightly fit the scene to avoid wasting memory on empty space. Degenerate Input: If \tauw is set too high, too many voxels may be removed, leading to visual artifacts. If set too low, the octree may not be sparse enough for real-time performance. An octree-based 3D representation (sparse voxel-based octree) that supports view-dependent effects by storing appearance and density values required to model radiance at a point in the volume. It is named after plenoptic functions. Unlike naive NeRF rendering which requires dense sampling and neural network inference for every sample dependent on viewing direction, PlenOctrees pre-tabulate the NeRF into a view-dependent volume, removing the need for neural network queries at test time. Rendering performance is 167.68 FPS on an NVIDIA V100 GPU for 800x800 images, which is over 3000 times faster than conventional NeRFs (approx. 30 seconds per image). The values in the leaves are calculated by summing the weighted spherical harmonic bases evaluated at the corresponding ray direction (\theta, \phi). Time Complexity: The conversion process (evaluation, filtering, sampling) takes about 15 minutes. Memory Complexity: Sparse octree structure reduces memory requirements compared to dense voxel grids. Measured Performance: 167.68 FPS on an NVIDIA V100 GPU for 800x800 images. Scaling: Real-time performance is achieved by pre-tabulating the NeRF, allowing interactive rendering in a browser on consumer laptops. Strengths: Preserves view-dependent effects such as specularities; over 3000 times faster than conventional NeRFs; amenable to modern web technologies. Limitations: Requires a trained NeRF-SH model; conversion time is non-trivial (15 minutes). When to use: When real-time rendering of view-dependent scenes is required without sacrificing quality. When not to use: When the scene has extreme view-dependent effects that cannot be captured by spherical harmonics, or when the conversion time is prohibitive. PlenOctrees were introduced by Alex Yu, Ruilong Li, Matthew Tancik, Hao Li, Ren Ng, and Angjoo Kanazawa from UC Berkeley, USC Institute for Creative Technologies, and Pinscreen. The method builds on the concept of plenoptic functions by Adelson and Bergen. It was developed to address the slow rendering speed of NeRFs, which require dense sampling and neural network inference for every sample dependent on viewing direction. The approach factorizes the appearance via closed-form spherical basis functions, specifically spherical harmonics, to enable real-time rendering. name: PlenOctree
body: PlenOctree is an octree-based 3D representation that enables real-time rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by pre-tabulating view-dependent radiance into a sparse voxel structure. It solves the performance bottleneck of conventional NeRFs, which require dense sampling and neural network inference for every ray step, by replacing online queries with direct lookups of density and spherical harmonic coefficients. Unlike naive NeRF rendering, which cannot cache color values due to their dependency on viewing direction, PlenOctrees store these dependencies explicitly, allowing for acceleration without sacrificing free-viewpoint quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained NeRF-SH model (a neural network predicting density and spherical harmonic coefficients) and a set of training images. Output: A sparse octree data structure where leaves store density (\sigma) and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for view-dependent appearance. Data Structures: The representation is a sparse voxel-based octree. Node: Internal nodes typically store bounding boxes or occupancy flags to enable traversal skipping of empty space. Leaf: Stores the physical properties of the volume element: \sigma: Density value (scalar). \mathbf{c}{l,m}: Spherical Harmonic coefficients for the l-th degree and m-th order. The source specifies that appearance is factorized via closed-form spherical basis functions. The exact degree L is not specified in the provided notes, but standard NeRF-SH implementations often use L=3 or L=4. Method Steps: 1. Sampling: Densely sample the trained NeRF-SH model within the 3D volume surrounding the target object. For each sample point \mathbf{x} and a set of discretized viewing directions, query the NeRF-SH to obtain the density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and the SH coefficients \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}). 2. Tabulation: Populate the octree leaves with the sampled density and SH coefficients. Empty regions of the space are left unallocated or marked as empty to maintain sparsity. 3. Optimization (Optional but Recommended): Optimize the values stored in the PlenOctree directly using the training images. This step improves rendering quality by correcting discretization errors and aligning the tabulated values with the observed data. The rendering procedure remains differentiable with respect to these leaf values, allowing gradient-based optimization. 4. Rendering: To render a pixel, cast a ray through the octree. For each occupied leaf intersected by the ray, retrieve the density and SH coefficients. Compute the view-dependent color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) by evaluating the spherical harmonic basis functions at the ray direction \mathbf{d} using the stored coefficients. Perform standard volume rendering (e.g., differentiable volume rendering) using the retrieved \sigma and \mathbf{c}. Formulas: The view-dependent color \mathbf{c} at position \mathbf{x} for direction \mathbf{d} = (\theta, \phi) is computed as a weighted sum of spherical harmonic bases: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{l,m}(\mathbf{x}) Y{l,m}(\theta, \phi) where c{l,m}(\mathbf{x}) are the SH coefficients stored in the leaf at \mathbf{x}, and Y{l,m} are the spherical harmonic basis functions. Parameters: Octree Depth/Resolution: Not given in the sources. SH Degree: Not given in the sources. Sampling Density: "Densely" is specified, but no numerical grid spacing is provided. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discretization Error: The initial tabulation is an approximation of the continuous NeRF. Optimization step 3 is critical to mitigate artifacts caused by coarse sampling. Memory Usage: While sparse, high-resolution scenes with complex view-dependent effects (e.g., specularities) may require many leaves, potentially exceeding memory limits if sparsity is low. Performance: Renders 800×800 images at 167.68 FPS on an NVIDIA V100 GPU. This is over 3000 times faster than conventional NeRFs, which take approximately 30 seconds per image. Memory: Memory usage is determined by the number of occupied leaves in the octree. It is significantly lower than dense voxel grids but higher than the original NeRF model size due to the storage of SH coefficients per leaf. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability; preserves view-dependent effects (specularities); compatible with web technologies for browser-based interactive rendering. Limitations: Requires an initial training phase to build the octree; quality depends on the optimization step; memory bound limits the maximum resolution that can be captured for very large scenes. When to use: When real-time or interactive rendering of high-quality NeRFs is required. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained and the scene is very large, or when the scene has no view-dependent effects (simpler representations may suffice). PlenOctrees were introduced by Alex Yu, Ruilong Li, Matthew Tancik, Hao Li, Ren Ng, and Angjoo Kanazawa from UC Berkeley, USC Institute for Creative Technologies, and Pinscreen. The method is named after plenoptic functions, referencing the work of Adelson and Bergen. It was developed to address the slow rendering speed of NeRFs, which rely on dense sampling and neural network inference for every sample point dependent on viewing direction. The approach builds on the idea of pre-tabulating the NeRF into a view-dependent volume, similar to how Multi-Resolution Volumes (MPIs) or other sparse representations reduce compute, but specifically integrates spherical harmonics to handle view dependence. Concurrent work includes NeX and other methods exploring sparse representations for real-time NeRFs. name: Analytic Derivatives of PlenOctree Rendering
head: Gradient Computation for PlenOctree Optimization, NeRF Piecewise Constant Volume Rendering Derivatives
body: This method provides the closed-form gradients of the NeRF piecewise constant volume rendering equation with respect to the density (\boldsymbol{\sigma}) and color (\mathbf{c}) parameters. It enables direct optimization of PlenOctree attributes using gradient-based methods (e.g., SGD) to refine image quality. Inputs: Ray segment endpoints t0, \dots, tN where t0 is near and tN is far. Segment lengths \deltai = t{i+1} - ti for i=0, \dots, N-1. Density values \boldsymbol{\sigma} = (\sigma0, \dots, \sigma{N-1}) where \sigmai \ge 0. Color values \mathbf{c} = (c0, \dots, cN) where ci \in [0, 1]^3 are RGB colors. cN is the background color (typically a hyperparameter). Outputs: Gradient of rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}} with respect to density: \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{C}}}{\partial \sigmai}. Gradient of rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}} with respect to color: \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{C}}}{\partial ci}. Data Structures: Arrays for \delta, \sigma, c, T, and w of size N or N+1 as appropriate. T stores accumulated transmittance. w stores segment weights. Steps: 1. Compute Segment Lengths: For i = 0 to N-1: \deltai = t{i+1} - ti 2. Compute Accumulated Transmittance Ti: Initialize T0 = 1.0. For i = 0 to N-1: T{i+1} = Ti \cdot \exp(-\deltai \sigmai) Note: Ti represents the transmittance from t0 to ti. 3. Compute Segment Weights wi: For i = 0 to N-1: wi = Ti - T{i+1} For the background: wN = TN Note: wi(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = Ti(\boldsymbol{\sigma})(1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)). 4. Compute Rendered Color (for verification or loss calculation): \hat{\mathbf{C}} = \sum{i=0}^{N} wi ci 5. Compute Color Gradients: For i = 0 to N: \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{C}}}{\partial ci} = wi If colors are represented as Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients, apply the chain rule. Since SH basis function values are constant across the ray, the derivative with respect to SH coefficients is wi \cdot \text{SH\basis}(i). 6. Compute Density Gradients: For each i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}: \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{C}}}{\partial \sigmai} = \deltai \left[ ci T{i+1} - \sum{k=i+1}^N ck wk \right] Derivation note: The general form is \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{C}}}{\partial \sigmai} = cN \frac{\partial TN}{\partial \sigmai} + \sum{k=0}^{N-1} ck \left( \frac{\partial Tk}{\partial \sigmai} - \frac{\partial T{k+1}}{\partial \sigmai} \right). Using \frac{\partial Tk}{\partial \sigmai} = -\deltai Tk \mathbf{1}{k>i}, this simplifies to the expression above. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computegradients(t, sigma, c, cbg): """ t: array of length N+1, ray segment endpoints [t0,..., tN] sigma: array of length N, densities [sigma0,..., sigma{N-1}] c: array of length N, colors [c0,..., c{N-1}] cbg: scalar or vector, background color cN Returns: gradsigma: array of length N, gradients wrt sigma gradc: array of length N, gradients wrt c """ N = len(sigma) # 1. Segment lengths delta = t[1:] - t[:-1] # length N # 2. Accumulated Transmittance T # T[i] is transmittance from t0 to ti T = [0.0] (N + 1) T[0] = 1.0 for i in range(N): T[i+1] = T[i] math.exp(-delta[i] sigma[i]) # 3. Segment Weights w # w[i] for i < N is T[i] - T[i+1] # w[N] is T[N] w = [0.0] (N + 1) for i in range(N): w[i] = T[i] - T[i+1] w[N] = T[N] # 4. Color Gradients # gradc[i] = w[i] for i < N gradc = w[:N] # 5. Density Gradients gradsigma = [0.0] N for i in range(N): # Term 1: ci T{i+1} term1 = c[i] T[i+1] # Term 2: sum{k=i+1}^{N} ck wk # Note: cN is cbg sumterm = 0.0 for k in range(i+1, N): sumterm += c[k] w[k] sumterm += cbg w[N] gradsigma[i] = delta[i] (term1 - sumterm) return gradsigma, gradc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The derivative is only defined for i < N because \sigmaN does not exist (only cN). The background color cN is typically not optimized. SH Colors: When optimizing SH coefficients, the gradient must be multiplied by the SH basis function value at the query direction. The basis values are constant for a given ray direction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. This method was introduced in the PlenOctrees paper by Yu et al. to enable the fine-tuning of PlenOctrees on original training images using NeRF loss with SGD. It builds on the NeRF volume rendering formulation. PlenOctrees For Real-time Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), http://alexyu.net/plenoctrees/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Voxel Grid Optimization
head: Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) optimization, Sparse Voxel Grid Training
body: Sparse Voxel Grid Optimization is a method for optimizing a hierarchical sparse voxel representation for novel-view synthesis and surface reconstruction. It solves the problem of balancing rendering speed, memory efficiency, and visual quality by dynamically growing a voxel grid only where needed, rather than using a fixed dense grid or unstructured primitives. It sets itself apart from Plenoxels Optimization by using a sparse octree structure that allows for higher effective resolution with lower memory overhead, and from 3D Gaussian Splatting by using spatially-disjoint voxels that require explicit continuity enforcement but offer sharper boundaries and compatibility with classic grid-based mesh extraction algorithms like Marching Cubes. The method optimizes a sparse voxel grid initialized from empty space. The core process involves iterative pruning and subdivision of voxels based on their contribution to the rendered image, guided by a composite loss function. Inputs: A set of calibrated input images with known camera poses. Outputs: An optimized sparse voxel grid containing density (and optionally SDF) values, and a rendered novel-view image or a watertight mesh. The representation uses an Octree structure. Voxel: Each active voxel stores density values (and SDF corner values in SVRecon). Hierarchy: Parent-child and sibling relationships are tracked using Morton codes (16 levels, 3 bits per level, 48-bit total) and auxiliary fine-grid indices. Occupancy: Bitmask-based occupancy flags are used for efficient neighbor search and cross-voxel Laplacian smoothness calculations. 1. Start optimization from empty space with raw density set to h{geo} = -10. 2. Initialize the Octree level to h{lv} = 6 (i.e., 64^3 voxels) for bounded scenes and the foreground main region of unbounded scenes. 3. For unbounded scenes, add h{out} = 5 background shell levels with a size ratio h{ratio} = 2 times the number of foreground voxels. 4. (SVRecon specific) Initialize via PI³ point-map priors aligned to ground-truth poses; flip SDF signs to account for visual occlusion. The total loss \mathcal{L} combines photometric and regularization terms: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{\text{ssim}} \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} + \lambda{\text{T}} \mathcal{L}{\text{T}} + \lambda{\text{dist}} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} + \lambda{\text{R}} \mathcal{L}{\text{R}} + \lambda{\text{tv}} \mathcal{L}{\text{tv}} Where: \lambda{\text{ssim}}, \lambda{\text{T}}, \lambda{\text{dist}}, \lambda{\text{R}}, \lambda{\text{tv}} are loss weights. \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} is the SSIM loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{T}} encourages final ray transmittances to be either zero or one. \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} is the distortion loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{R}} is the per-point RGB loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{tv}} is the total variation loss on the sparse density grid. For mesh reconstruction tasks (SVRecon), depth-normal consistency losses are added: \mathcal{L}{\text{mesh}} = \lambda{\text{n-dmean}} \mathcal{L}{\text{n-dmean}} + \lambda{\text{n-dmed}} \mathcal{L}{\text{n-dmed}} Where \mathcal{L}{\text{n-dmean}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{n-dmed}} encourage alignment between rendered normals and depth-derived normals from mean and median depth, respectively. SVRecon also adds regularization combining parent-child continuity, Laplacian loss over fine grid cells, and local Eikonal terms. The model is trained for h{iter} = 20,000 iterations. 1. Ray Casting/Rasterization: Cast rays through the sparse voxel grid. Inside each active voxel, sample K points: K=1 for novel-view synthesis, K=3 for mesh reconstruction. (SVRecon) Use trilinear interpolation for SDF values at voxel corners. Use the NeuS CDF for alpha blending. Early ray stopping threshold is set to hT = 10^{-4}. Supersampling scale is set to h{ss} (default 1.5). 2. Loss Computation: Compute \mathcal{L} and \mathcal{L}{\text{mesh}} (if applicable) using the rendered output and ground truth. 3. Pruning and Subdivision: Every h{every} = 1,000 iterations, prune and subdivide voxels. Pruning: Voxels with density below the current threshold are removed. The pruning threshold h{prune} is linearly scaled from 0.0001 to 0.05 over the training duration. Subdivision: Voxels with high density or error are subdivided. The subdivision percentage is set to h{percent} = 5. 4. Gradient Update: Update voxel parameters using gradient descent. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizesparsevoxelgrid(inputimages, cameraposes, numiterations=20000): # 1. Initialization voxelgrid = SparseOctree() voxelgrid.initializeempty(densityinit=-10.0) voxelgrid.setinitiallevel(level=6) # 64^3 voxels # For unbounded scenes, add background shells # voxelgrid.addbackgroundshells(numlevels=5, ratio=2.0) # 2. Training Loop for iteration in range(1, numiterations + 1): # 2.1. Pruning and Subdivision every 1000 iterations if iteration % 1000 == 0: # Linearly scale pruning threshold from 0.0001 to 0.05 currentprunethreshold = 0.0001 + (iteration / numiterations) (0.05 - 0.0001) voxelgrid.pruneandsubdivide(prunethreshold=currentprunethreshold, subdivisionpercent=5) # 2.2. Forward Pass (Rendering) # Sample random rays from input images rays = samplerays(inputimages, cameraposes) # Render using sparse voxel rasterization # K=1 for novel-view, K=3 for mesh (handled internally or via flag) renderedimages, transmittances, depths, normals = voxelgrid.render( rays, earlystopthreshold=1e-4, supersamplingscale=1.5) # 2.3. Loss Computation # Photometric Losses lossssim = computessimloss(renderedimages, inputimages) losst = computetransmittanceloss(transmittances) lossdist = computedistortionloss(depths, transmittances) lossrgb = computergbloss(renderedimages, inputimages) losstv = computetotalvariationloss(voxelgrid.densities) totalloss = (lambdassim lossssim + lambdat losst + lambdadist lossdist + lambdargb lossrgb + lambdatv losstv) # Mesh-specific Losses (if performing reconstruction) if meshreconstruction: lossndmean = computedepthnormalconsistency(depths, normals, 'mean') lossndmed = computedepthnormalconsistency(depths, normals, 'median') totalloss += (lambdandmean lossndmean + lambdandmed lossndmed) # SVRecon specific regularizations # totalloss += laplaciansmoothnessloss(voxelgrid) # totalloss += eikonalloss(voxelgrid.sdfs) # 2.4. Backward Pass totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return voxelgrid h{geo} = -10: Initial raw density. h{lv} = 6: Initial Octree level (64^3). h{out} = 5: Background shell levels for unbounded scenes. h{ratio} = 2: Ratio of background shell size to foreground. h{iter} = 20,000: Total training iterations. h{every} = 1,000: Interval for pruning/subdivision. h{prune}: Pruning threshold, linearly scaled from 0.0001 to 0.05. h{percent} = 5: Subdivision percentage. hT = 10^{-4}: Early ray stopping threshold. h{ss} = 1.5: Supersampling scale. K=1 or K=3: Points sampled per voxel (1 for synthesis, 3 for mesh). \lambda{\text{ssim}}, \lambda{\text{T}}, \lambda{\text{dist}}, \lambda{\text{R}}, \lambda{\text{tv}}, \lambda{\text{n-dmean}}, \lambda{\text{n-dmed}}: Loss weights. Exposure Variation: Scenes with severe exposure variation in training views can cause the method to produce clear brightness boundaries and many "floaters" (artifacts), degrading PSNR and FPS. Memory Usage: The method uses more voxel primitives than Gaussian splatting, resulting in larger model size and higher GPU memory requirements. Uniform high-resolution grids (e.g., 1024^3) can cause Out Of Memory (OOM) errors on standard hardware (e.g., 24GB GPU). Depth Quantization: Pathological voids or highly non-uniform depth distributions may impact bin estimation for depth-quantile pruning. A technique where voxels are subdivided adaptively based on detail requirements, as opposed to uniform subdivision until a fixed grid resolution is reached. On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, adaptive voxel size achieves LPIPS 0.200, PSNR 28.01, and FPS 171, while uniform 512^3 achieves LPIPS 0.326, PSNR 25.37, and FPS 190. Uniform 256^3 achieves LPIPS 0.444, PSNR 23.98, and FPS 457. Uniform 1024^3 causes Out Of Memory (OOM) on a machine with 24GB GPU memory. The adaptive variant outperforms Plenoxels (640^3 grid), which achieves LPIPS 0.452, PSNR 23.29, and FPS <10. Speed: The method achieves high rendering speeds. On Mip-NeRF360, it achieves ~121 FPS (base) and >2x FPS with a fast-render variant (h{ss}=1.5, h{prune}=0.15). On Deep Blending, it achieves 366 FPS. It is comparable to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) on average, though scene-dependent. Training Time: Training takes approximately 15 minutes on Mip-NeRF360. A fast-train variant scales iteration-related hyperparameters by 0.3 for >3x training speedup. Quality: Achieves significantly better LPIPS than 3DGS and surpasses Zip-NeRF on Mip-NeRF360. PSNR tends to favor 3DGS as it prefers smoother rendering in uncertain regions. Memory: Requires more GPU memory than 3DGS due to the larger number of voxel primitives. LiteVoxel variant reduces peak VRAM by up to 60% while maintaining comparable perceptual metrics (PSNR ≈ 32.13 dB, SSIM ≈ 0.937). Scalability: Rendering speed scales well to higher resolutions due to fewer contributing primitives per pixel. Limitations: Performance degrades on scenes with severe exposure variation. Resolution-memory trade-offs become pronounced at deep Levels of Detail (LoDs). Sparse Voxel Grid Optimization is based on the Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) method. It was introduced in the paper "Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering". The method builds on hierarchical grid optimization techniques and aims to provide real-time rendering capabilities with high fidelity. It is compatible with grid-based algorithms such as Volume Fusion, Voxel Pooling, and Marching Cubes. name: Volumetric Inverse Rendering with Differentiable Path Tracing
head: Differentiable Volumetric Inverse Rendering, Differentiable Volumometric Path Tracing Optimization, Mitsuba 3 Volumetric Inverse Rendering, Mitsuba 3 Volumetric Inverse Rendering Tutorial, Volumetric Inverse Rendering with Differentiable Path Replay Backpropagation, Volumetric Path Tracing with Adjoint Differentiation
body: This method optimizes a 3D volume density (extinction/scattering) stored on a regular grid to match a set of synthetic reference images. It accounts for direct and indirect illumination by using path replay backpropagation to compute derivatives of delta tracking and volumetric multiple scattering. Unlike standard volume rendering which assumes known parameters, this approach treats the volume grid as trainable parameters, enabling the reconstruction of volumetric scenes from multi-view observations. Inputs: A set of reference images rendered from known camera viewpoints. A scene description containing a differentiable volumetric path tracer (e.g., prbvolpath). A heterogeneous volume interior with an extinction coefficient grid (sigmat) initialized to a low constant value. Outputs: An optimized volume grid representing the reconstructed scene density. Volume Grid: A 4D tensor of shape (V, V, V, 1) where V is the resolution. The data type is TensorXf (floating point). Scene Parameters: Accessed via traversal, specifically the key 'object.interiormedium.sigmat.data'. Sensors: Perspective cameras with a half-circle arrangement. Film resolution is typically 64 \times 64 pixels with a 'tent' filter. 1. Sensor Setup: Create N sensors (typically N=5 for simple scenes, up to 50-100 for complex ones) placed on a half-circle around the origin. For each sensor i: Calculate angle: \thetai = \frac{180.0}{N} \cdot i - 90.0. Create rotation transform: R = \text{rotate}([0, 1, 0], \thetai). Create look-at transform: L = \text{look\at}(\text{target}=[0, 0, 0], \text{origin}=[0, 0, 4], \text{up}=[0, 1, 0]). Combine: T{\text{to\world}} = R \cdot L. Load sensor with type 'perspective', FOV 45, film 64 \times 64 HDR with tent filter. 2. Reference Rendering: Render the ground-truth scene using the differentiable path tracer (e.g., prbvolpath) for each sensor with high samples per pixel (e.g., refspp = 512). Store these as refimages. 3. Optimization Scene Initialization: Create a scene with a container cube having a 'null' BSDF (invisible surface). Set interior type to 'heterogeneous'. Initialize sigmat grid to a low constant value (e.g., 0.002). This facilitates optimization by making it easier to increase density than to remove it from a dense volume. Set volume scale (e.g., 40.0), which scales the extinction range to [10^{-6} \cdot \text{scale}, \text{scale}]. Use a low initial resolution (e.g., 16 \times 16 \times 16) to simplify the solution landscape. 4. Parameter Extraction: Traverse the scene to identify the trainable parameter key: 'object.interiormedium.sigmat.data'. 5. Optimizer Setup: Instantiate an Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.02. Assign the volume data to the optimizer. 6. Optimization Loop: For each iteration: For each sensor: Render the scene using the differentiable path tracer with low samples per pixel (e.g., spp = 8). Compute L2 loss: \mathcal{L} = \text{mean}((\text{img} - \text{ref\images})^2). Backpropagate gradients using automatic differentiation. Take a gradient step. Clamp density values to [10^{-6}, 1.0] to prevent invalid values. Update scene parameters. 7. Volume Upsampling: After initial convergence, upsample the volume grid to a higher resolution (e.g., 64 \times 64 \times 64). Use a linear filter for resampling to preserve value ranges and avoid negative densities. Note: dr.upsample requires powers of two for TensorXf, while dr.resample allows explicit filter selection. The optimizer automatically resets internal state (e.g., momentum) upon size change. Continue optimization with increased samples per pixel (e.g., 8 \times \text{ref\spp}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import drjit as dr import mitsuba as mi def setupsensors(sensorcount=5): """Setup multiple sensors on a half-circle.""" from mitsuba import ScalarTransform4f as T sensors = [] for i in range(sensorcount): angle = 180.0 / sensorcount i - 90.0 sensorrotation = T().rotate([0, 1, 0], angle) sensortoworld = T().lookat(target=[0, 0, 0], origin=[0, 0, 4], up=[0, 1, 0]) sensors.append(mi.loaddict({ 'type': 'perspective', 'fov': 45, 'toworld': sensorrotation @ sensortoworld, 'film': { 'type': 'hdrfilm', 'width': 64, 'height': 64, 'filter': {'type': 'tent'} } })) return sensors def renderreferenceimages(sceneref, sensors, refspp=512): """Render reference images from all sensors.""" return [mi.render(sceneref, sensor=sensors[i], spp=refspp) for i in range(len(sensors))] def createoptimizationscene(vres=16, scale=40.0, initsigmat=0.002): """Create optimization scene with low-res uniform volume.""" scenedict = { 'type': 'scene', 'integrator': {'type': 'prbvolpath'}, 'object': { 'type': 'cube', 'bsdf': {'type': 'null'}, 'interior': { 'type': 'heterogeneous', 'sigmat': { 'type': 'gridvolume', 'grid': mi.VolumeGrid(dr.full(mi.TensorXf, initsigmat, (vres, vres, vres, 1))), 'toworld': mi.ScalarTransform4f().translate(-1).scale(2.0) }, 'scale': scale } }, 'emitter': {'type': 'constant'} } return mi.loaddict(scenedict) def optimizevolume(scene, sensors, refimages, iterationcount=20, spp=8, lr=0.02): """Run optimization loop.""" params = mi.traverse(scene) key = 'object.interiormedium.sigmat.data' opt = mi.ad.Adam(lr=lr) opt[key] = params[key] params.update(opt) for it in range(iterationcount): totalloss = 0.0 for sensoridx in range(len(sensors)): img = mi.render(scene, params, sensor=sensors[sensoridx], spp=spp, seed=it) loss = dr.mean(dr.square(img - refimages[sensoridx])) dr.backward(loss) opt.step() opt[key] = dr.clip(opt[key], 1e-6, 1.0) params.update(opt) totalloss += loss return scene, params def upsamplevolume(opt, key, newshape=(64, 64, 64, 1)): """Upsample volume grid using linear filter.""" # dr.resample is preferred for explicit filter control to avoid negative values opt[key] = dr.resample(opt[key], shape=newshape, filter='linear') sensorcount: Number of views. Typical: 5. Complex scenes: 50-100. volumetype: 'heterogeneous'. sensorresolution: 64 \times 64 pixels. volumescale: 40.0. Scales extinction range to [10^{-6} \cdot \text{scale}, \text{scale}]. sensorfilter: 'tent'. initialsigmat: 0.002. Low constant value to facilitate density increase. refspp: 512. Samples per pixel for reference images. optimizertype: Adam. learningrate: 0.02. iterationcount: 20 per resolution stage. upsampledspp: 8 \times \text{ref\spp} (4096) after upsampling. Density Clamping: Optimized values must be clamped to [10^{-6}, 1.0] due to the volume scale parameter. Upsampling Filter: Using a cubic filter can overshoot and produce negative densities. A linear filter must be used. Optimizer State: The optimizer resets internal state (momentum) when variable size changes during upsampling. Resolution: Initial low resolution (16^3) is crucial for convexity; upsampling to higher resolution (64^3) recovers detail. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sensors, iterations, and samples per pixel (SPP). Reference rendering uses high SPP (512), while optimization uses low SPP (8) for speed. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the volume grid size (V^3) and the number of sensors. Performance: Measured on standard hardware using Mitsuba 3. Strengths: Handles direct and indirect illumination via path replay backpropagation. Multi-resolution approach improves optimization convexity. Limitations: Requires multiple viewpoints to constrain the volume. Sensitive to initial density values. When to Use: When reconstructing volumetric scenes from multi-view synthetic or real images. When Not to Use: For single-view reconstruction or when computational resources are extremely limited. This method is implemented in Mitsuba 3 using the prbvolpath integrator, heterogeneous volume plugin, and gridvolume plugin. It is demonstrated in the Mitsuba 3 tutorial for volumetric inverse rendering. The approach leverages differentiable programming to optimize volume parameters directly from image data. facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, https://github.com/facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric inverse rendering - Mitsuba 3, https://mitsuba.readthedocs.io/en/stable/src/inverserendering/volumeoptimization.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Volumetric inverse rendering, https://mitsuba.readthedocs.io/en/latest/src/inverserendering/volumeoptimization.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: 3DGS Initialization Policy
head: Initialization Policy, OTS Initialization
body: The 3DGS Initialization Policy defines the standard procedure for seeding the 3D Gaussian primitives in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and its variants, such as Order-Independent Splatting (OTS). It solves the problem of establishing a valid initial scene representation from sparse input data (typically SfM points) by distributing Gaussians in space with specific opacity and scale properties. It differs from sibling methods like Volumetric Gaussian Splatting (AVIS) or Direct Gaussian Splatting by relying on a uniform opacity initialization derived from a power-law function of the total Gaussian count, rather than learned or geometrically constrained initial weights. Inputs: Sparse point cloud from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) or a unit cube bounding box (for synthetic scenes). Total number of Gaussians to initialize, N. Scene bounding box (typically a unit cube centered at the origin for synthetic data). Outputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by position \mathbf{x}, covariance \Sigma (or scale/quaternion), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: An array of N elements. Each element stores: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale (log-space or linear). \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). \alpha \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^k: Color/SH coefficients. Steps: 1. Position Initialization: For synthetic scenes (e.g., Nerf-Synthetic): Sample N positions uniformly at random within a unit cube centered at the scene origin. For real-world scenes: Typically, positions are initialized from the SfM point cloud, often with jitter or random sampling if N exceeds the point count, though the specific real-world initialization strategy is not detailed in the primary source beyond the synthetic case. 2. Opacity Initialization: Compute a single scalar value V used as the initial opacity for all Gaussians. This value is derived from the total number of Gaussians N using a power function: V = 2 \cdot N^{\beta} The exponent \beta depends on the rendering method: \beta = 0.35 for standard 3DGS. \beta = 0.55 for OTS-based methods. Set \alphai = V for all i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. Note: In practice, opacity is often clamped to [0, 1] or processed through a sigmoid during rendering, but the initialization value is set to this computed V. 3. Scale and Rotation Initialization: The sources do not specify the exact initial scale and rotation values for the general policy, only that positions and opacity are initialized as described. Standard 3DGS implementations typically initialize scales to a small random value or derived from the average distance to nearest neighbors, and rotations to identity. This detail is not provided in the cited sources. 4. Color Initialization: The sources do not specify the initial color/SH coefficients. Typically initialized to white or random colors. Parameters: N: Total number of Gaussians. Typical values mentioned are 4k, 12k, 36k, 100k, 500k, 1m, and 5m. \beta: Exponent for opacity scaling. 0.35 for 3DGS, 0.55 for OTS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opacity Clamping: The computed value V = 2 \cdot N^{\beta} may exceed 1.0 for large N. The implementation must handle this, either by clamping \alpha to 1.0 or by relying on the rendering pipeline's sigmoid activation. Scene Bounding: For real-world scenes, ensuring Gaussians are initialized within the relevant scene volume is critical to avoid empty space initialization. A strategy to maximize overlap between cells and emitted neural Gaussians by dynamically aligning cell geometry with Gaussian properties. It involves: 1. Dynamically defining the cell's quaternion as a weighted average of the quaternions associated with its emitted Gaussians. 2. Periodically updating cell centers using \mathbf{x}n = \frac{\sum{k=1}^K \boldsymbol{\mu}{n,k}}{K}, where \mathbf{x}n is the cell center, K is the number of Gaussians in the cell, and \boldsymbol{\mu}{n,k} is the mean of the k-th Gaussian in cell n. 3. Learning the three-dimensional covariances and positions of first-layer cells in accordance with the updates to the second-layer Gaussians, leveraging the differentiability of cell scales. Following adaptive density control, new cells are grown at Gaussians with high view-space positional gradients. To decouple existing cells from newly introduced ones, the offsets of the significant Gaussians are reset to zero after cell growth, i.e., their positions are reinitialized to the centers of the corresponding cells. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) for sampling positions and setting opacity. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the initial Gaussian parameters. Performance: The policy is designed to provide a stable starting point for optimization. The use of a power-law opacity initialization helps balance the contribution of Gaussians during the early stages of training. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a consistent baseline for comparing different splatting techniques (e.g., 3DGS vs. OTS) by controlling the initial opacity scaling. Limitations: Does not account for scene geometry during initialization (except for position sampling); relies on subsequent densification and pruning to refine the representation. The initialization policy was introduced in the context of evaluating whether 3D Gaussian Splatting requires accurate volumetric rendering, specifically comparing standard 3DGS with Order-Independent Splatting (OTS). The policy was adapted from the original 3DGS codebase's training procedure for Nerf-Synthetic scenes. It has been used in experiments involving real-world scenes with varying numbers of Gaussians (100k to 5m) to evaluate the impact of densification and initialization strategies. name: CoR-GS
head: Consistency Regularization for Gaussian Splatting
body: CoR-GS is a method designed to improve sparse-view reconstruction in 3D Gaussian Splatting by defining two independent reconstructions and comparing them to discard inaccurate Gaussians. It addresses the ambiguity and instability inherent in reconstructing scenes from minimal view overlap, where standard optimization often yields noisy or inconsistent geometry. CoR-GS operates by enforcing consistency between two distinct Gaussian field representations derived from the same sparse input views. The core mechanism involves generating two independent reconstructions and evaluating their agreement to identify and remove unreliable Gaussians. Inputs: Sparse set of input views (images and camera poses). Initial set of 3D Gaussians (typically from a standard 3DGS initialization). Outputs: Refined set of 3D Gaussians with improved geometric and photometric consistency. Data Structures: Two independent sets of Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients) are maintained during the comparison phase. A mask or filter is applied to the union of Gaussians to discard those failing the consistency check. Steps: 1. Dual Reconstruction: Train two independent Gaussian fields from the same sparse input views. These fields are initialized separately or optimized with different random seeds/initializations to ensure independence. 2. Comparison: Render views from both reconstructions and compare the results. The comparison metric identifies discrepancies between the two fields. 3. Discard Inaccurate Gaussians: Gaussians that contribute to inconsistent rendering results between the two fields are identified as inaccurate and removed. 4. Refinement: The remaining Gaussians form the final, consistent representation. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse view overlap: The method is specifically designed for scenarios with minimal view overlap, where scale ambiguity is high. Inaccurate Gaussians: The method relies on the ability to distinguish accurate from inaccurate Gaussians via the consistency check. If both reconstructions are equally poor, the method may not improve results. The base method for which CoR-GS provides a consistency regularization strategy. CoR-GS acts as a pruning mechanism, complementing densification strategies by removing unreliable Gaussians. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves novel view synthesis quality in sparse-view scenarios, particularly with minimal view overlap. Limitations: Requires maintaining two independent reconstructions, potentially increasing computational cost during the training phase. When to use: Sparse-view reconstruction where standard 3DGS yields inconsistent or noisy results. When not to use: Dense-view scenarios where standard 3DGS performs well. CoR-GS was introduced in the context of improving sparse-view reconstruction for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It is cited in surveys discussing the evolution from volume rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting, highlighting its role in addressing scale ambiguity and improving quality in challenging sparse-view settings. The method is referenced alongside other approaches like FFN-based methods and MAtCha, positioning it as a regularization technique rather than a generative model. name: Gaussian Splatting Volume Rendering
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Rendering, Volume Splatting
body: Gaussian Splatting Volume Rendering is a differentiable rendering technique that synthesizes images by projecting 3D Gaussian distributions onto the image plane and alpha-compositing them along viewing rays. It solves the problem of high-fidelity, real-time novel view synthesis by replacing traditional triangle meshes with probabilistic volume primitives, allowing for efficient tile-based rasterization and differentiable optimization of scene parameters. Unlike standard rasterization which uses geometric primitives, this method materializes smooth ellipses in 2D from 3D probability distributions, capturing view-dependent effects via spherical harmonics. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by a centroid, covariance (parameterized by scale and rotation), opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Image resolution W \times H. Outputs: A synthesized RGB image If. The scene is stored as an array of Gaussian primitives. A typical layout for a single Gaussian splat is: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct GaussianSplat { glm::vec3 centroid; // World-space position (3 floats) float opacity; // Scalar opacity (1 float) std::array<float, 48> sphericalHarmonics; // SH coefficients: 16 coefficients 3 channels (48 floats) std::array<float, 3> scale; // Log-space scale factors (3 floats) std::array<float, 4> rotation;// Quaternion rotation (4 floats) }; Scale: Stored in log-space to ensure positivity. The diagonal scaling matrix S is obtained by S = \text{diag}(\exp(\text{scale})). Rotation: Stored as a unit quaternion q, converted to a rotation matrix R. Spherical Harmonics (SH): Coefficients c{\ell m} for degree L=3 (16 coefficients per channel) allow view-dependent color representation. 1. Load Scene: Parse the Gaussian data (typically from a.ply file) into an array of GaussianSplat objects. 2. Project Gaussians: For each Gaussian i, project its 3D centroid \mui and covariance \Sigmai into 2D screen space. The 3D covariance is factorized as \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T, where Ri is the rotation matrix and Si is the diagonal scaling matrix. The 2D covariance \tilde{\Sigma}i is computed using the Jacobian of the projection transformation. 3. Sort Gaussians: Sort all Gaussians that intersect the view frustum by their depth (distance from the camera) along each viewing ray. 4. Bias: A constant bias of 0.5 is added to the SH output to center the color around mid-grey before clamping.
