head: 3D Gaussian Representation, Gaussian Set
body: The GaussianSet is a container class representing a collection of 3D Gaussian primitives, storing their parameters (means, orientations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients) and providing methods to compute their world-space covariance matrices. It solves the problem of organizing learnable parameters into a structured format suitable for differentiable volume rendering pipelines. It differs from its parent 3D Gaussian Splatting by focusing on the data container logic rather than the rendering algorithm, and from GaussianList Data Structure and Initialization by not explicitly managing contiguous memory layout or initialization routines. The GaussianSet stores raw learnable parameters and computes derived geometric properties on demand. It does not store the covariance matrix directly in its primary storage but computes it from rotation and scale parameters. Inputs: Raw learnable parameters for N Gaussians. Outputs: World-space covariance matrices for each Gaussian. The GaussianSet class contains the following fields, typically stored as PyTorch tensors or similar GPU-compatible structures: | Field | Type | Shape | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | means | Float32 Tensor | (N, 3) | 3D positions of the Gaussian centers. | | quats | Float32 Tensor | (N, 4) | Unit quaternions representing rotation. | | scales | Float32 Tensor | (N, 3) | Log-space scales (exponentiated at load/render). | | opacities | Float32 Tensor | (N,) | Log-space opacities (sigmoided at load/render). | | shcoefficients | Float32 Tensor | (N, S, 3) | Spherical Harmonics coefficients for color. | | covariances | Float32 Tensor | (N, 3, 3) | Computed world-space covariance matrices. | Note: The covariances field is often computed on-the-fly or cached, but the primary stored parameters are means, quats, scales, opacities, and shcoefficients. 1. Load/Initialize Parameters: Load raw parameters from a checkpoint or file. Normalize quaternions: q{norm} = \frac{q}{\|q\|2}. Exponentiate scales: s{actual} = \exp(s{raw}). Sigmoid opacities: \alpha{actual} = \sigma(\alpha{raw}). Concatenate SH coefficients if stored in separate levels. 2. Compute Covariance Matrix: Construct the local diagonal covariance matrix S from the exponentiated scales: S = \text{diag}(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) where sx, sy, sz are the components of the scale vector. Convert the normalized quaternion q to a rotation matrix R. Compute the world-space covariance matrix: Cov = R S R^T where R is the rotation matrix derived from the quaternion and S is the diagonal local covariance matrix. Covariance in World Coordinates: Cov = R S R^T where: R is the 3 \times 3 rotation matrix derived from the quaternion. S is the 3 \times 3 diagonal matrix of variances in local coordinates. Cov is the 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix in world coordinates. Local Covariance Matrix: S = \begin{bmatrix} sx^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz^2 \end{bmatrix} where sx, sy, sz are the scale parameters. N: Number of Gaussians. Not given in the sources. S: Degree of spherical harmonics. Not given in the sources. radiuspx: Base radius in pixels for rendering (used in simplified circle rendering, not core to GaussianSet structure). Not given in the sources. Quaternion Normalization: Quaternions must be normalized to ensure valid rotation matrices. Failure to normalize leads to incorrect covariance shapes. Scale Exponentiation: Scales are stored in log-space to ensure positivity. Exponentiation is required before computing variances. Opacity Sigmoid: Opacities are stored in log-space. Sigmoid is required to map to [0, 1]. Covariance Symmetry: The resulting covariance matrix Cov must be symmetric. Numerical errors in quaternion-to-matrix conversion can break symmetry; symmetrization (Cov = \frac{1}{2}(Cov + Cov^T)) may be needed. Unverified code. 2 (y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2 (xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2 (xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2 (xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2 (x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2 (yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2 (xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2 (yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2 (x2 + y2) return R def computecovariances(means, quats, scales): """Compute world-space covariance matrices from Gaussian parameters.""" # Normalize quaternions quats = F.normalize(quats, p=2, dim=-1) # Exponentiate scales scales = torch.exp(scales) # Construct local covariance matrix S (diagonal) # S = diag(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) S = torch.zeroslike(scales).unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, 3) S[:, 0, 0] = scales[:, 0]2 S[:, 1, 1] = scales[:, 1]2 S[:, 2, 2] = scales[:, 2]2 # Convert quaternions to rotation matrices R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(quats) # Compute world-space covariance: Cov = R S R^T # R is (N, 3, 3), S is (N, 3, 3) Cov = torch.bmm(torch.bmm(R, S), R.transpose(1, 2)) return Cov class GaussianSet: def init(self, means, quats, scales, opacities, shcoefficients): self.means = means self.quats = quats self.scales = scales self.opacities = opacities self.shcoefficients = shcoefficients self.covariances = None def computecovariances(self): """Compute and store covariance matrices.""" self.covariances = computecovariances(self.means, self.quats, self.scales) return self.covariances def loadfromcheckpoint(self, ckpt): """Load parameters from a checkpoint, applying necessary transformations.""" self.means = ckpt["means"] # Normalize quaternions self.quats = F.normalize(ckpt["quats"], p=2, dim=-1) # Exponentiate scales self.scales = torch.exp(ckpt["scales"]) # Sigmoid opacities self.opacities = torch.sigmoid(ckpt["opacities"]) # Concatenate SH coefficients self.shcoefficients = torch.cat([ckpt["sh0"], ckpt["shN"]], dim=-2) # Compute covariances self.computecovariances() ECoNGS (Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats) is a scene representation method that transforms time-consuming volume rendering into an efficient process by optimizing neural editable Gaussians and compressing their attributes via neural entropy coding. It solves the problem of large storage and computational costs in volume visualization by extracting multi-view images and point clouds, grouping geometrically similar scenes for joint learning, and compressing anchor attributes to exploit inter-scene redundancy. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which stores all attributes explicitly, ECoNGS uses a two-stage optimization process involving anchor attribute optimization and joint context model training, achieving compression with minimal distortion. The GaussianList is a column-major data structure that stores a batch of 3D Gaussian primitives for efficient differentiable volume rendering. It solves the problem of organizing learnable parameters (means, covariances, opacities, and spherical harmonics) into a format suitable for batched linear algebra operations during optimization. It differs from its parent GaussianSet by explicitly managing the contiguous memory layout and providing the initialization routines that convert raw geometric data into valid, differentiable parameters ready for gradient descent. Gaussian Property Loading parses 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics) from a PLY file into a structured data container suitable for differentiable rendering. It solves the problem of converting raw file data into a format suitable for GPU consumption by applying necessary inverse transformations (e.g., exponentiation for scale, sigmoid for opacity) and handling coordinate system inconsistencies. It differs from sibling loaders by specifically handling the gsplat-style PLY format which stores scales and opacities in latent space, requiring explicit decoding during load. Computes the 3D covariance matrix of a Gaussian from its scale and rotation parameters. It solves the problem of representing the spatial extent and orientation of a 3D Gaussian in world coordinates by transforming local axis-aligned variances into a full symmetric positive-definite matrix. What sets it apart from direct covariance optimization is that it derives the covariance from unconstrained rotation (quaternion) and scale parameters, ensuring the resulting matrix is always valid without requiring projection steps. The 3D Gaussian Data Layout defines the memory organization and field definitions for a single 3D Gaussian primitive within differentiable volume rendering pipelines. It serves as the fundamental unit of storage for position, scale, orientation, opacity, and color (spherical harmonics) data, enabling efficient GPU access and optimization. It differs from the higher-level GaussianSet Data Structure by focusing on the raw parameter representation rather than the container logic, and from Gaussian Data Packing by retaining floating-point precision for optimization rather than compacting into fixed-size integer buffers for rendering. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a differentiable, point-based scene representation that replaces the implicit multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and ray-marched volume integration of NeRF with an explicit collection of 3D anisotropic Gaussians. It enables real-time synthesis of high-fidelity novel views via a GPU-friendly tile-based rasterizer that depth-sorts and alpha-composites 2D projections of these Gaussians. Unlike NeRF, which infers density and color at arbitrary points, 3DGS optimizes the parameters of a fixed set of Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients) to minimize photometric loss, using adaptive density control to adjust the number of primitives during training. N-DGS (N-Dimensional Gaussian Splatting) is a parameterization method for the joint covariance matrix of 3D Gaussians in differentiable volume rendering. It solves the problem of optimizing the cross-covariance between spatial and query dimensions while maintaining positive-definiteness and numerical stability. Unlike sibling methods that may use direct regression or unbounded factorizations, N-DGS uses a bounded Cholesky factorization where coefficients are scaled by query diagonal scales, ensuring that the resulting cross-covariance and spatial extent remain within controlled bounds. It builds on GaussianSet Data Structure by defining how the covariance matrix components are stored and optimized. Time Complexity: Computing covariance matrices is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, involving matrix multiplications of fixed size (3 \times 3). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot (3 + 4 + 3 + 1 + S \cdot 3 + 9)) for storing means, quats, scales, opacities, SH coefficients, and covariances. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Explicit representation allows for efficient GPU-based rendering. Covariance computation is differentiable and efficient. Limitations: Requires storing all parameters explicitly, which can be memory-intensive for large scenes. Not given in the sources. When to Use: When differentiable optimization of Gaussian parameters is required. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained and compression is needed (use ECoNGS Optimization and Coding). The GaussianSet data structure is part of the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipeline, which was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It serves as the core data container for the learnable parameters of the Gaussian primitives. The structure has been adapted in various implementations, such as gsplat and splaty, to support efficient differentiable rendering. sascha-kirch/splaty, https://github.com/sascha-kirch/splaty, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: ECoNGS Optimization and Coding
head: ECoNGS (Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats), Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats
body: ECoNGS (Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats) is a scene representation method that transforms time-consuming volume rendering into an efficient process by optimizing neural editable Gaussians and compressing their attributes via neural entropy coding. It solves the problem of large storage and computational costs in volume visualization by extracting multi-view images and point clouds, grouping geometrically similar scenes for joint learning, and compressing anchor attributes to exploit inter-scene redundancy. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which stores all attributes explicitly, ECoNGS uses a two-stage optimization process involving anchor attribute optimization and joint context model training, achieving compression with minimal distortion. ECoNGS operates on a set of basic scenes, each represented by a collection of 3D Gaussian primitives. The method involves data extraction, two-stage optimization, and entropy coding. Inputs: Multi-view images and corresponding point clouds for each basic scene. Hyperparameters: \lambdas = 0.001 (scaling regularization weight), K=10 (number of neural editable Gaussians per anchor), learning rates (0.01 for anchor feature, opacity, scaling, rotation, TF embeddings; 1\times 10^{-4} for palette color), training iterations (10,000 per stage), and \lambdae (trade-off hyperparameter for compression losses). Outputs: A compressed binary bitstream of anchor attributes encoded via arithmetic coding. MLP parameters stored as 32-bit floating-point values. A complete VolVis scene representation formed by compositing trained basic scenes. The method relies on the GaussianSet Data Structure [Parent], which stores means, orientations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. ECoNGS introduces: Anchor Points: A subset of Gaussians whose attributes are optimized and compressed. Neural Editable Gaussians: Derived from anchor points; K=10 editable Gaussians are generated per anchor. Context Model: A lightweight MLP used to estimate probabilities for entropy coding. Hash Grids: Used for inter-scene redundancy; M+ and M- denote the total numbers of +1 and -1 values in the hash grids. The 3D Gaussian function is defined as: C(\mathbf{x}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^s)^\top \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^s)} where \mathbf{x} is an arbitrary 3D position, \mathbf{x}^s is the position attribute of the Gaussian point, and \mathbf{\Sigma} is the covariance matrix. The covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} is parameterized by a scaling factor s and a quaternion rotation vector q to ensure positive semi-definiteness. Rendering uses EWA volume splatting to transform 3D Gaussians G(\mathbf{x}) to 2D Gaussians G'(\mathbf{x}') on the image plane. Pixel color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}') is determined by \alpha-blending: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}') = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), \quad \alphai = oi Gi(\mathbf{x}') where c is modeled by spherical harmonics (SH) parameters, oi is opacity, and N is the number of depth-sorted layered 2D Gaussians. Loss Functions: Stage 1 loss: L{\text{stage1}} = L{\text{rec}} + \lambdas \sum{j=1}^{N^s} \text{prod}(\mathbf{s}j) where L{\text{rec}} is the image reconstruction loss (L1 + SSIM), N^s is the number of predicted editable Gaussians, \text{prod}(\cdot) is the vector product of scaling factors, and \lambdas = 0.001. Stage 2 loss: L{\text{stage2}} = L{\text{stage1}} + \lambdae \frac{L{\text{entropy}} + L{\text{hash}}}{N^a \times dA} where N^a is the number of anchors, dA is the sum of all anchor attribute dimensions, and \lambdae is the trade-off hyperparameter. L{\text{entropy}} and L{\text{hash}} encourage distribution of values within anchor attributes and a more concentrated hash grid, reducing bit consumption. 1. Data Extraction: Extract multi-view images and corresponding point clouds from different basic scenes. 2. Scene Grouping: Group geometrically similar scenes for joint learning. 3. Stage 1 Optimization: Optimize only anchor point attributes and lightweight MLPs for 10,000 iterations using L{\text{stage1}}. Turn off uniform noise for the first 3,000 iterations to stabilize optimization. 4. Stage 2 Optimization: Update all parameters, including the context model, for the remaining 10,000 iterations using L{\text{stage2}}. Enable uniform noise after 3,000 iterations. 5. Encoding: Encode the context model first. Then, encode anchor attributes into a binary bitstream using an arithmetic encoder based on probabilities estimated by the context model. 6. Storage: Store MLP parameters as 32-bit floating-point values. 7. Compositing: Composite all trained basic scenes to form a complete VolVis scene representation. Unverified code. """ # Step 1: Extract and Group # Extract multi-view images and point clouds (handled by data loader) # Group geometrically similar scenes for joint learning groupedscenes = groupsimilarscenes(scenes) # Initialize anchor attributes and lightweight MLPs anchors = initializeanchors(groupedscenes) contextmodel = initializelightweightmlp() # Step 2: Stage 1 Optimization optimizerstage1 = Adam(anchors.parameters() + contextmodel.parameters(), lr=hyperparams['learningrates']['anchor']) for iteration in range(hyperparams['iterationsperstage']): # Turn off uniform noise for first 3,000 iterations usenoise = iteration > 3000 # Forward pass: Render scenes using current anchors and context model renderedimages = renderscenes(anchors, contextmodel, usenoise) # Compute Lrec (L1 + SSIM) lossrec = computel1ssimloss(renderedimages, groundtruthimages) # Compute scaling regularization term scalingreg = sum(product(sj) for sj in anchors.scales) # Compute Lstage1 lossstage1 = lossrec + hyperparams['lambdas'] scalingreg # Backward pass optimizerstage1.zerograd() lossstage1.backward() optimizerstage1.step() # Decay learning rate for anchor feature, opacity, scaling, rotation, and TF embeddings decaylearningrates(optimizerstage1) # Step 3: Stage 2 Optimization optimizerstage2 = Adam(anchors.parameters() + contextmodel.parameters(), lr=hyperparams['learningrates']['anchor']) for iteration in range(hyperparams['iterationsperstage']): # Forward pass with noise enabled renderedimages = renderscenes(anchors, contextmodel, usenoise=True) # Compute Lstage1 lossrec = computel1ssimloss(renderedimages, groundtruthimages) scalingreg = sum(product(sj) for sj in anchors.scales) lossstage1 = lossrec + hyperparams['lambdas'] scalingreg # Compute Lentropy and Lhash lossentropy = computeentropyloss(anchors.attributes) losshash = computehashloss(anchors.hashgrids) # Compute Lstage2 lossstage2 = lossstage1 + hyperparams['lambdae'] (lossentropy + losshash) / (len(anchors) anchors.attributedimension) # Backward pass optimizerstage2.zerograd() lossstage2.backward() optimizerstage2.step() # Decay learning rates decaylearningrates(optimizerstage2) # Step 4: Encoding # Encode context model contextmodelbitstream = encodecontextmodel(contextmodel) # Encode anchor attributes using arithmetic encoder anchorbitstream = encodeanchorattributes(anchors, contextmodel) # Store MLP parameters as 32-bit floats mlpparameters = anchors.mlpparameters.astype(np.float32) return contextmodelbitstream, anchorbitstream, mlpparameters Early Optimization Instability: Uniform noise in quantization can cause instability. This is handled by turning off noise for the first 3,000 iterations. Model Capacity Loss: Too many overlapping primitives can cause model capacity loss. The scaling regularization term \lambdas \sum \text{prod}(\mathbf{s}j) encourages primitives to be small. Precision: MLP parameters are stored as 32-bit floats, which may limit precision compared to higher-precision formats, but is sufficient for the method's goals. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The method involves two stages of optimization, each with 10,000 iterations, and entropy coding. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The method compresses anchor attributes, reducing storage requirements compared to explicit storage of all Gaussian attributes. Measured Performance: Tested on volume datasets such as Argon, Bubble, Combustion, Ionization, and Tangaroa. For example, the Combustion dataset (multivariate) has 41 basic scenes, 1,920 × 2,880 × 480 resolution, and requires 24.3 GB CPU / 12.4 GB GPU memory. Strengths: Efficient rendering via tile-based rasterization, compression of anchor attributes, joint learning of similar scenes. Limitations: Requires multi-view images and point clouds for initialization, may have reconstruction fidelity trade-offs due to compression. When to Use: Suitable for large-scale volume visualization where storage and computational efficiency are critical. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with high geometric complexity that cannot be grouped effectively, or where high-fidelity reconstruction is paramount over compression. ECoNGS was introduced in the paper "ECoNGS: Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats for Volume Visualization". It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Parent] and extends it to volume visualization by incorporating neural entropy coding and joint learning of similar scenes. The method aims to address the limitations of traditional volume rendering, which is computationally intensive, by leveraging the efficiency of Gaussian splatting and the compression capabilities of neural entropy coding. body: The GaussianList is a column-major data structure that stores a batch of 3D Gaussian primitives for efficient differentiable volume rendering. It solves the problem of organizing learnable parameters (means, covariances, opacities, and spherical harmonics) into a format suitable for batched linear algebra operations during optimization. It differs from its parent GaussianSet by explicitly managing the contiguous memory layout and providing the initialization routines that convert raw geometric data into valid, differentiable parameters ready for gradient descent. Input: A vector of Gaussian objects (containing raw position, scale, opacity, rotation quaternion, and spherical harmonic coefficients). Output: A populated GaussianList instance with pre-computed 3D covariance matrices. The GaussianList struct stores attributes in column-major matrices to facilitate batch processing. The fields are: 1. positions: na::Matrix4xX<f32> (4 rows \times N columns). Stores 4D homogeneous coordinates. 2. scales: na::Matrix3xX<f32> (3 rows \times N columns). Stores scale components. 3. opacities: na::DVector<f32> (1D vector of size N). Stores opacity values. 4. rotations: na::Matrix4xX<f32> (4 rows \times N columns). Stores quaternion components. 5. sh: Matrix48xX<f32> (48 rows \times N columns). Stores spherical harmonic coefficients. 6. numgaussians: usize. The count of Gaussians N. 7. cov3d: na::Matrix3xX<f32> (3 rows \times N columns). Pre-allocated zeros, filled by computecov3d(). Spherical Harmonics Layout: Within each column of the sh matrix, coefficients are stored in the order: C{0,R}, C{0,B}, C{0,G}, C{1,R}, C{1,B}, C{1,G}, \dots, corresponding to RGB channels for each SH degree/order. 1. Set Count: Set numgaussians to the length of the input Gaussian vector. 2. Construct Positions: Iterate over the input Gaussians. Clone the position components (x, y, z) and append 1.0 to create 4D homogeneous coordinates. Store in positions. 3. Construct Scales: Clone the scale components (sx, sy, sz) into scales. 4. Construct Opacities: Clone opacity values into opacities. 5. Construct Rotations: Clone quaternion components (qx, qy, qz, qw) into rotations. 6. Construct SH Coefficients: Clone spherical harmonic coefficients into sh. 7. Initialize Covariance Buffer: Initialize cov3d with zeros of size 3 \times N. 8. Compute Covariances: Call computecov3d() to calculate the 3D covariance matrices based on rotations and scales. 9. Center Positions: Center the Gaussian positions around their mean (see below). To ensure numerical stability, the positions are centered around their centroid: 1. Initialize avgpos as a zero Vector3. 2. Iterate over all N Gaussians, adding each position \mathbf{p}i to avgpos. 3. Compute the mean: \mathbf{\mu} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \mathbf{p}i. 4. Iterate over all N Gaussians again, updating each position: \mathbf{p}i \leftarrow \mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{\mu}. For each Gaussian i from 0 to N-1: 1. Extract the rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i from rotations column i. 2. Convert \mathbf{q}i to a UnitQuaternion, then to a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix \mathbf{R}i. 3. Create a diagonal scale matrix \mathbf{S}i: \mathbf{S}i = \begin{bmatrix} s{x,i}^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s{y,i}^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & s{z,i}^2 \end{bmatrix} where s{x,i}, s{y,i}, s{z,i} are from scales column i. 4. Compute the covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i: \mathbf{\Sigma}i = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{R}i^\top 5. Copy the resulting 3 \times 3 matrix into cov3d at offset i \times 3 (column-major storage). This function computes the 2D covariance matrix for a single Gaussian given a camera view. Inputs: cov3d: The 3 \times 3 3D covariance matrix for the Gaussian. posw: The 3D position of the Gaussian in world space. viewmatrix: The 4 \times 4 view matrix. focalx, focaly: Focal lengths in pixels. htanfovxy: Tangent of half the horizontal and vertical FOV. Steps: 1. Convert posw to homogeneous vector: \mathbf{p}h = [x, y, z, 1.0]^\top. 2. Transform to camera space: \mathbf{p}{cam} = \text{viewmatrix} \times \mathbf{p}h. 3. Compute tangents of the Gaussian center: tx = \frac{p{cam,x}}{p{cam,z}}, \quad ty = \frac{p{cam,y}}{p{cam,z}} 4. Clamp tangents to limits defined by 1.3 \times \tan(\text{FOV}): tx = \text{clamp}(tx, -1.3 \cdot \tan(\text{FOV}x), 1.3 \cdot \tan(\text{FOV}x)) ty = \text{clamp}(ty, -1.3 \cdot \tan(\text{FOV}y), 1.3 \cdot \tan(\text{FOV}y)) Multiply back by p{cam,z} to get screen-space tangents t.x and t.y. 5. Compute the Jacobian J (3 \times 3 matrix) using focalx, focaly, t.x, t.y, t.z (where t.z = p{cam,z}). 6. Compute W as the transpose of the top-left 3 \times 3 submatrix of the view matrix. 7. Compute T = W \times J. 8. Compute the projected 2D covariance: \mathbf{\Sigma}{2D} = T^\top \mathbf{\Sigma}{3D}^\top T 9. Extract the top-left 2 \times 2 submatrix as cov2d. 10. Apply low-pass filter by adding 0.3 to the diagonal elements: \mathbf{\Sigma}{2D}[0,0] \leftarrow \mathbf{\Sigma}{2D}[0,0] + 0.3 \mathbf{\Sigma}{2D}[1,1] \leftarrow \mathbf{\Sigma}{2D}[1,1] + 0.3 11. Return cov2d. 1. Pass the SH coefficients column for the given index, the SH dimension, and the viewing direction to evalsphericalharmonics. 2. Return the resulting color vector and the Gaussian's opacity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializegaussianlist(inputgaussians): """ Initialize a GaussianList from a vector of Gaussian objects. inputgaussians: List of objects with attributes: position (3,), scale (3,), opacity (1,), rotation (4,), sh (48,). Returns: GaussianList struct/dict. """ N = len(inputgaussians) # 1. Set numgaussians numgaussians = N # 2. Construct positions (4xN) positions = np.zeros((4, N)) for i in range(N): pos = inputgaussians[i].position positions[0, i] = pos[0] positions[1, i] = pos[1] positions[2, i] = pos[2] positions[3, i] = 1.0 # 3. Construct scales (3xN) scales = np.zeros((3, N)) for i in range(N): scales[0, i] = inputgaussians[i].scale[0] scales[1, i] = inputgaussians[i].scale[1] scales[2, i] = inputgaussians[i].scale[2] # 4. Construct opacities (N,) opacities = np.zeros(N) for i in range(N): opacities[i] = inputgaussians[i].opacity # 5. Construct rotations (4xN) rotations = np.zeros((4, N)) for i in range(N): rot = inputgaussians[i].rotation rotations[0, i] = rot[0] rotations[1, i] = rot[1] rotations[2, i] = rot[2] rotations[3, i] = rot[3] # 6. Construct SH coefficients (48xN) sh = np.zeros((48, N)) for i in range(N): sh[:, i] = inputgaussians[i].sh # 7. Initialize cov3d (3xN) with zeros cov3d = np.zeros((3, N)) # 8. Compute cov3d cov3d = computecov3d(scales, rotations, N) # 9. Center positions positions = centerpositions(positions, N) return { 'positions': positions, 'scales': scales, 'opacities': opacities, 'rotations': rotations, 'sh': sh, 'numgaussians': numgaussians, 'cov3d': cov3d } def computecov3d(scales, rotations, N): """ Compute 3D covariance matrices for all Gaussians. scales: 3xN matrix rotations: 4xN matrix (quaternions) Returns: 3xN matrix (covariances stored column-wise) """ cov3d = np.zeros((3, N)) for i in range(N): # Extract quaternion q = rotations[:, i] # Convert quaternion to rotation matrix R (3x3) R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) # Create diagonal scale matrix S (3x3) sx = scales[0, i] sy = scales[1, i] sz = scales[2, i] S = np.diag([sx2, sy2, sz2]) # Compute covariance: R S R^T cov = R @ S @ R.T # Store in cov3d (column-major) cov3d[:, i] = cov.flatten() return cov3d def centerpositions(positions, N): """ Center Gaussian positions around their mean. positions: 4xN matrix Returns: 4xN matrix with centered positions """ # Extract 3D positions (first 3 rows) pos3d = positions[:3,:] # Compute mean avgpos = np.mean(pos3d, axis=1) # Subtract mean from each position pos3dcentered = pos3d - avgpos.reshape(3, 1) # Update positions matrix positions[:3,:] = pos3dcentered return positions def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """ Convert a quaternion (x, y, z, w) to a 3x3 rotation matrix. q: array of 4 floats Returns: 3x3 numpy array """ x, y, z, w = q # Normalize quaternion norm = np.sqrt(x2 + y2 + z2 + w2) x, y, z, w = x/norm, y/norm, z/norm, w/norm # Compute rotation matrix elements xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, yz = xy, xz, yz wx, wy, wz = wx, wy, wz R = np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) return R def projectcov3dtoscreen(cov3dcol, posw, viewmatrix, focalx, focaly, htanfovxy): """ Project a single 3D covariance matrix to 2D screen space. cov3dcol: 3x1 numpy array (covariance matrix flattened) posw: 3D position vector viewmatrix: 4x4 numpy array focalx, focaly: floats htanfovxy: tuple (htanfovx, htanfovy) Returns: 2x2 numpy array (cov2d) """ # 1. Convert position to homogeneous posh = np.array([posw[0], posw[1], posw[2], 1.0]) # 2. Transform to camera space poscam = viewmatrix @ posh # 3. Compute tangents tz = poscam[2] if tz == 0: tz = 1e-6 # Guard against division by zero tx = poscam[0] / tz ty = poscam[1] / tz # 4. Clamp tangents htanfovx, htanfovy = htanfovxy limitx = 1.3 htanfovx limity = 1.3 htanfovy tx = np.clip(tx, -limitx, limitx) ty = np.clip(ty, -limity, limity) # Multiply back by poscam.z tx = tz ty = tz # 5. Compute Jacobian J (3x3) # Note: Exact formula for J depends on projection model. # Assuming standard perspective projection Jacobian derivation. # J = d(xscreen, yscreen, zscreen) / d(xcam, ycam, zcam) # Simplified for this context based on source description: J = np.array([ [focalx / tz, 0, -focalx tx / (tz2)], [0, focaly / tz, -focaly ty / (tz2)], [0, 0, 1] ]) # 6. Compute W (transpose of top-left 3x3 of view matrix) W = viewmatrix[:3,:3].T # 7. Compute T = W J T = W @ J # 8. Compute cov2d = T^T cov3d^T T # Note: cov3dcol is flattened, reshape to 3x3 cov3dmat = cov3dcol.reshape(3, 3) cov2d = T.T @ cov3dmat.T @ T # 9. Extract top-left 2x2 cov2d = cov2d[:2,:2] # 10. Apply low-pass filter cov2d[0, 0] += 0.3 cov2d[1, 1] += 0.3 return cov2d Division by Zero: In projectcov3dtoscreen, if z{cam} = 0, the tangent calculation fails. A guard value (e.g., 10^{-6}) should be used. FOV Clamping: The limit 1.3 \times \tan(\text{FOV}) prevents extreme tangents that could cause numerical instability or incorrect projection for Gaussians near the frustum boundaries. Low-Pass Filter: The constant 0.3 ensures the Gaussian is at least one pixel wide/high, preventing aliasing and numerical issues with very small covariances. Quaternion Normalization: Quaternions must be normalized before converting to rotation matrices to ensure valid rotation matrices. Manages density of linear primitives during optimization by pruning, cloning, and splitting. Adapts techniques from this initialization method to non-spherical kernels. Focuses on the creation and parameterization of the initial set from raw geometric data, building on this data structure. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) for copying attributes and O(N) for covariance computation. Projection is O(1) per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing attributes. The column-major layout optimizes for batched matrix operations. Strengths: Efficient batch processing, clear separation of attributes, pre-computed covariances for rendering. Limitations: Fixed-size matrices may require resizing if N changes dynamically. When to Use: When optimizing a set of 3D Gaussians for differentiable rendering. When Not to Use: For static scenes with no optimization, or when memory is extremely constrained and N is very large (consider sparse representations). The GaussianList data structure originates from the implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting for differentiable volume rendering. It was developed to efficiently manage the learnable parameters of 3D Gaussians during optimization. The method builds on the foundational work of 3D Gaussian Splatting. thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: LinPrim Population Control
head: Adaptive Population Control, LinPrim-MMC, LinPrim-MCMC
body: LinPrim Population Control manages the density of linear primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra) during differentiable volume rendering optimization by pruning, cloning, and splitting primitives to adapt to scene complexity. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by redefining primitive size metrics to accommodate non-spherical kernels and adjusting sampling distributions to respect the anisotropic geometry of linear primitives. It builds on GaussianList Data Structure and Initialization and adapts techniques from Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization. Inputs: Current set of primitives \mathcal{P}, each with position \mathbf{p}, color \mathbf{c}, distances to corners \mathbf{d}, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}, and view-space positional gradient \nabla{\mathbf{p}}. Camera parameters for known views. Scene extent bounds. Outputs: Updated set of primitives \mathcal{P}' with modified count, positions, and sizes. Each primitive stores: position: 3D vector \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. color: 3D vector \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or SH coefficients). distances: Array of distances to corner vertices. For octahedra, 3 values (along axes); for tetrahedra, 4 values (to vertices). rotation: Quaternion \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4. gradientmomentum: 3D vector for Adam optimizer state. type: Enum (OCTAHEDRON, TETRAHEDRON). Remove primitives that fail fidelity or efficiency criteria. Size Definition: For Octahedra: Size S{oct} = 2 \cdot \max(\mathbf{d}), where \mathbf{d} are the distances along the principal axes. For Tetrahedra: Size S{tet} \approx \sqrt{2} \cdot d{max}, where d{max} is the distance to the furthest corner vertex. Criteria: A primitive is pruned if: 1. Opacity \alpha < \tau{opacity} (threshold, e.g., 0.005). 2. S > \tau{scene\scale} \cdot \text{SceneExtent}. 3. Screen-space area A{screen} > \tau{screen\space}. Initialize primitives from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points: 1. For each SfM point \mathbf{p}i with color \mathbf{c}i: Find closest SfM neighbor distance d{min}. Set initial distances \mathbf{d} = d{min} for all corners. Set rotation \mathbf{q} to a uniformly random quaternion. Set position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}i. Select primitives with large view-space positional gradients \|\nabla{\mathbf{p}}\| > \tau{grad}. Cloning (for small primitives): 1. Create new primitive \mathbf{p}{new} with identical features: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{c}{new} = \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d}{new} = \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{q}{new} = \mathbf{q}. 2. Reset gradient momentum: \mathbf{m}{new} = \mathbf{0}. Splitting (for large primitives): 1. Create two new primitives \mathbf{p}{a}, \mathbf{p}{b} with smaller sizes. 2. Sample positions from a PDF based on the original primitive's geometry. Sampling Logic: Octahedra: Standard deviations \sigmai = di (corresponding distance for each axis). Sample \Delta \mathbf{p} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \text{diag}(\sigma^2)). Apply rotation: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{q}) \Delta \mathbf{p}. This spreads primitives along longer dimensions. Tetrahedra: Set \sigma = \frac{1}{2} \max(\mathbf{d}) for all dimensions. Sample \Delta \mathbf{p} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}). Apply rotation: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{q}) \Delta \mathbf{p}. Adapt GS-MCMC population control by treating primitives as equivalent Gaussians. 1. Scale octahedron distances: \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{d} / 2.6. 2. Use \mathbf{d}' as Gaussian standard deviations for MCMC sampling. 3. Perform MCMC steps to draw samples from the scene distribution, allowing precise control over final population size. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def pruneprimitives(primitives, camera, sceneextent, opacitythresh=0.005, screenthresh=100.0): """Remove primitives based on opacity, size, and screen space.""" toremove = [] for i, prim in enumerate(primitives): # Check opacity if prim.opacity < opacitythresh: toremove.append(i) continue # Calculate size if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': size = 2.0 np.max(prim.distances) elif prim.type == 'TETRAHEDRON': size = np.sqrt(2.0) np.max(prim.distances) else: size = 0.0 # Check scene extent size if size > 0.1 sceneextent: # Threshold relative to scene toremove.append(i) continue # Check screen space area (simplified) screenarea = calculatescreenarea(prim, camera) if screenarea > screenthresh: toremove.append(i) # Remove in reverse order to maintain indices for i in reversed(toremove): primitives.pop(i) return primitives def cloneandsplit(primitives, gradthresh=0.001): """Clone small primitives with high gradients, split large ones.""" newprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(prim.gradient) if gradnorm > gradthresh: # Determine if clone or split based on size if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': size = 2.0 np.max(prim.distances) else: size = np.sqrt(2.0) np.max(prim.distances) if size < 0.05: # Arbitrary threshold for "small" # Clone newprim = copy(prim) newprim.gradientmomentum = np.zeros(3) # Reset momentum newprimitives.append(newprim) else: # Split # Sample two new positions posa, posb = samplesplitpositions(prim) newprima = copy(prim) newprima.position = posa newprima.gradientmomentum = np.zeros(3) newprimb = copy(prim) newprimb.position = posb newprimb.gradientmomentum = np.zeros(3) # Reduce size for children newprima.distances = [d 0.5 for d in prim.distances] newprimb.distances = [d 0.5 for d in prim.distances] newprimitives.append(newprima) newprimitives.append(newprimb) return newprimitives def samplesplitpositions(prim): """Sample positions for splitting based on primitive type.""" q = prim.rotation # Quaternion R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': # Standard deviations correspond to distances sigma = np.array(prim.distances) # Ensure symmetry for octahedron (distances are along axes) # Sample from diagonal covariance delta = np.random.normal(0, sigma) posoffset = R @ delta elif prim.type == 'TETRAHEDRON': # All standard deviations set to half the largest distance maxd = np.max(prim.distances) sigma = 0.5 maxd delta = np.random.normal(0, sigma, 3) posoffset = R @ delta else: posoffset = np.zeros(3) posa = prim.position + posoffset posb = prim.position - posoffset # Symmetric split return posa, posb def linprimmcmcstep(primitives, scalefactor=2.6): """Apply LinPrim-MCMC adjustments.""" for prim in primitives: if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': # Scale distances to mimic Gaussian std devs prim.distancesscaled = [d / scalefactor for d in prim.distances] # Perform MCMC sampling using scaled distances as Gaussian parameters # [Implementation of specific MCMC kernel omitted, relies on GS-MCMC logic] pass opacitythresh: Default 0.005. gradthresh: Threshold for view-space positional gradient norm. scalefactor (LinPrim-MCMC): 2.6. sceneextent: Bounding box diagonal or max dimension of the scene. Tetrahedron Splitting: Non-trivial to sample along principal axes due to lack of symmetry; use isotropic scaling with \sigma = \frac{1}{2} \max(\mathbf{d}). Octahedron Anisotropy: Must sample along local axes before rotating to spread along longer dimensions. Momentum Reset: Cloned primitives must reset gradient momentum to avoid biased updates. Magnitude Mismatch: Direct use of octahedron distances as Gaussian std devs is invalid; scaling by 2.6 is required for MCMC compatibility. Time Complexity: O(N) per frame for pruning and selection, where N is the number of primitives. Cloning/splitting increases N dynamically. Memory Complexity: O(N), growing as primitives are added. Performance: Efficiently adapts to scene detail; prevents over-rendering in uniform regions and under-rendering in complex areas. Strengths: Compatible with 3DGS advancements (e.g., MCMC); handles non-spherical primitives correctly. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of size thresholds; tetrahedron splitting is less geometrically precise than octahedron splitting. When to Use: When optimizing linear primitives for novel views or high-fidelity reconstruction where fixed initialization is insufficient. LinPrim Population Control originates from the LinPrim paper (2025), which adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting techniques to linear primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra). It addresses the need for dynamic population management in differentiable volumetric rendering with non-Gaussian kernels. The method incorporates insights from GS-MCMC and Distribution Alignment to handle magnitude differences between linear primitive distances and Gaussian standard deviations. LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16312, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization
head: 3D Gaussian Initialization, 3D Gaussian Splatting Training Initialization, Gaussian Initialization, Gaussian Parameter Initialization, Gaussians class init, Model Setup, pre-activation parameter setup
body: This method establishes the initial state of the learnable 3D Gaussian point cloud for differentiable rendering training. It solves the problem of converting raw geometric data (typically from Structure-from-Motion pipelines like COLMAP) or random noise into a set of valid, differentiable parameters (means, covariances, opacities, and spherical harmonics) that can be optimized via gradient descent. It is distinguished from sibling methods like LinPrim Population Control by focusing exclusively on the creation and parameterization of the initial set, rather than the dynamic modification of that set during training. Inputs: Source point cloud data: Typically a COLMAP.ply or.bin file containing N points with coordinates \mathbf{xyz} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and RGB colors \mathbf{c} \in [0, 1]^3. Alternatively, a random distribution if no source data is provided. Configuration flags: isotropic (boolean, default false), loadpath (string). Outputs: A Gaussian object containing the following learnable parameters: \mathbf{\mu} (means): Shape (N, 3). \mathbf{s} (pre-activation scales): Shape (N, 3) or (N, 1) if isotropic. \mathbf{q} (pre-activation rotations): Shape (N, 4), stored as quaternions [w, x, y, z]. \alpha{logit} (pre-activation opacity): Shape (N,). \mathbf{f}{dc} (DC spherical harmonics coefficients): Shape (N, 1, 3). \mathbf{f}{rest} (rest spherical harmonics coefficients): Shape (N, D, 3), initialized to zero. The parameters are stored as dense tensors on the CUDA device. Means: Shape (N, 3). Scaling: Shape (N, 3). Rotation: Shape (N, 4). Opacity: Shape (N, 1) or (N,). Features DC: Shape (N, 1, 3). Features Rest: Shape (N, \text{numcoeffs}, 3). 1. Initialize Means (\mathbf{\mu}) Copy the XYZ coordinates from the input point cloud directly to the GPU tensor. For random initialization, means are sampled from a random distribution. 2. Initialize Rotations (\mathbf{q}) Initialize all quaternions to the identity rotation [1, 0, 0, 0]. Some implementations use random uniform quaternions generated via the Shoemake method. 3. Initialize Scales (\mathbf{s}) Scales are stored as pre-activation values (log-space) to allow exponential activation during rendering. Method A (KNN-based): Compute the mean distance to k=50 nearest neighbors for each point. Clamp to a minimum of 10^{-7}. Set si = \log(\sqrt{di}). Replicate across 3 dimensions or keep separate. Method B (Fixed Base): Use a fixed base distance d{base} = 0.1. Set si = \log(\sqrt{d{base}}) repeated 3 times. Method C (Random): For random initialization, si = \log((\text{rand}() + 10^{-6}) \times 0.01). 4. Initialize Opacity (\alpha{logit}) Opacity is stored as a logit so that \alpha = \sigma(\alpha{logit}). Choose a target initial opacity \alpha{target} \in \{0.1, 0.5\}. Clamp to [10^{-4}, 0.99] to prevent extreme logit values. Compute \alpha{logit} = \ln(\alpha{target} / (1 - \alpha{target})). Alternatively, initialize to a constant high value like 8.0, yielding \sigma(8.0) \approx 0.9997. 5. Initialize Spherical Harmonics (\mathbf{f}{dc}, \mathbf{f}{rest}) Normalize input RGB colors to the range [-0.5, 0.5]. Compute the DC coefficient (degree 0) by dividing the normalized RGB by the SH basis constant C0 = 0.28209479177387814. Initialize all higher-order coefficients (\mathbf{f}{rest}) to zero. 6. Construct Covariance Matrices (Runtime/Forward Pass) While not stored directly, the covariance is derived from \mathbf{s} and \mathbf{q} for rendering. Create diagonal scaling matrix \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(\exp(\mathbf{s})). Normalize quaternion \mathbf{q} to unit length. Convert \mathbf{q} to rotation matrix \mathbf{R} (shape N \times 3 \times 3). Compute 3D covariance \Sigma = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T. 3D covariance: \Sigma = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{R} is the rotation matrix derived from quaternions and \mathbf{S} is the diagonal scaling matrix. 2D projection covariance: \Sigma' = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \Sigma \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T, where \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian of the perspective projection, \mathbf{W} is the world-to-camera rotation matrix, and \Sigma is the 3D covariance. Opacity activation: \alpha = \sigma(\alpha{logit}). Scale activation: \mathbf{s}{actual} = \exp(\mathbf{s}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def initializegaussians(pointsxyz, pointsrgb, isotropic=False): """ Initialize 3D Gaussian parameters from a point cloud. Args: pointsxyz: (N, 3) array of XYZ coordinates. pointsrgb: (N, 3) array of RGB colors in [0, 1]. isotropic: If True, scales are shared across x, y, z. Returns: A dictionary of initialized learnable parameters. """ N = pointsxyz.shape[0] device = torch.device("cuda") # 1. Means means = torch.tensor(pointsxyz, dtype=torch.float32, device=device, requiresgrad=True) # 2. Rotations (Identity) # Quaternion format: [w, x, y, z] rotations = torch.zeros((N, 4), dtype=torch.float32, device=device, requiresgrad=True) rotations[:, 0] = 1.0 # w = 1 # 3. Scales (Pre-activation) # Fixed base distance method basedist = 0.1 scalespre = torch.full((N, 3), torch.log(torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(basedist))), dtype=torch.float32, device=device, requiresgrad=True) # 4. Opacity (Pre-activation logit) alphatarget = 0.1 alphatarget = torch.clamp(torch.tensor(alphatarget), min=1e-4, max=0.99) opacitylogit = torch.logit(alphatarget).expand(N).to(device, requiresgrad=True) # 5. Spherical Harmonics rgbnorm = (torch.tensor(pointsrgb, dtype=torch.float32, device=device) - 0.5) C0 = 0.28209479177387814 featuresdc = (rgbnorm / C0).unsqueeze(1) featuresdc.requiresgrad = True featuresrest = torch.zeros((N, 0, 3), dtype=torch.float32, device=device, requiresgrad=True) return { "means": means, "scales": scalespre, "rotations": rotations, "opacitylogit": opacitylogit, "featuresdc": featuresdc, "featuresrest": featuresrest } def computecovariance(scales, rotations): """ Compute 3D covariance matrix from pre-activation scales and quaternions. Args: scales: (N, 3) pre-activation scales. rotations: (N, 4) quaternions [w, x, y, z]. Returns: cov3d: (N, 3, 3) covariance matrices. """ # Exponential activation for scales S = torch.exp(scales) # (N, 3) # Diagonal scaling matrix Sdiag = torch.zeros((scales.shape[0], 3, 3), device=scales.device) Sdiag[:, 0, 0] = S[:, 0] Sdiag[:, 1, 1] = S[:, 1] Sdiag[:, 2, 2] = S[:, 2] # Normalize quaternions qnorm = torch.nn.functional.normalize(rotations, p=2, dim=1) w, x, y, z = qnorm[:, 0], qnorm[:, 1], qnorm[:, 2], qnorm[:, 3] # Convert quaternion to rotation matrix R = torch.zeros((rotations.shape[0], 3, 3), device=rotations.device) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2 (y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2 (xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2 (xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2 (xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2 (x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2 (yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2 (xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2 (yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2 (x2 + y2) # Covariance: Sigma = R S S^T R^T cov3d = R @ Sdiag @ R.transpose(1, 2) return cov3d C0: 0.28209479177387814. Base Distance: 0.1. Initial Opacity Target: 0.1 or 0.5. Opacity Pre-activation Constant: 8.0 (yields \approx 0.9997). Numerical Stability Bias: 0.3 added to the diagonal of the 2D projected covariance matrix to prevent singularity. Max Scale: 10.0. Applied via torch.clamp(torch.exp(scales), max=10.0) to prevent excessively large Gaussians. Adam Learning Rates: Means: 0.00016. Scales: 0.005. Quaternions: 0.001. Features DC: 0.0025. Features Rest: 0.000125. Opacities: 0.05. Division by Zero: In the Jacobian computation for perspective projection, depth z is clamped with 10^{-7} to prevent division by zero. Singular Covariance: Adding 0.3 to the diagonal of the 2D covariance matrix ensures numerical stability. Quaternion Normalization: Quaternions must be normalized to unit length before converting to rotation matrices. Extreme Logits: Clamping the target opacity to [10^{-4}, 0.99] prevents extreme logit values that could cause gradient explosion. Focuses on the broader model setup, including camera parameters and scene graph initialization, rather than just the Gaussian point cloud. Choose it when configuring the full training environment alongside the splat parameters. Deals with the dynamic addition and removal of Gaussians during training, which occurs after the initial parameterization. Choose it when managing adaptive density control and refinement. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) for copying means and features. KNN distance computation is O(N \log N) or O(N^2) depending on implementation. Memory Complexity: Linear in N for the stored parameters. Strengths: Provides a stable starting point for optimization. Pre-activation parameterization ensures valid ranges for non-linear activations. Limitations: KNN computation can be slow for very large point clouds. Fixed base distance initialization may not capture local geometry variations as well as KNN-based methods. When to Use: Always used at the start of training. KNN-based is preferred for dense point clouds; fixed base is simpler and faster for sparse clouds or random initialization. The method originates from implementations of 3D Gaussian Splatting training pipelines. The specific parameterization using pre-activation values (logits for opacity, logs for scale) is a common technique in differentiable rendering to handle bounded parameters. The KNN-based scale initialization is a heuristic to ensure Gaussians are sized appropriately relative to the input point cloud density. name: Gaussian Model Initialization
body: Gaussian Model Initialization establishes the initial state of a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene by populating learnable parameters (position, features, scaling, rotation, and opacity) from input data, typically a Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud. It solves the problem of converting discrete, static geometric samples into a continuous, differentiable radiance field representation ready for optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Spherical Harmonics Initialization by handling the full geometric and attribute seeding rather than just color parameterization, and from Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) by relying on sparse reconstruction data rather than uniform volumetric sampling. The standard initialization process, often implemented via createfrompcd, converts a point cloud (xyz, rgb) into a GaussianModel instance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud with N points, where each point has a 3D position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and an RGB color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A GaussianModel object containing tensors for \mathbf{xyz}, \mathbf{features\dc}, \mathbf{scaling}, \mathbf{rotation}, and \mathbf{opacity}. Data Structures: The model stores parameters in PyTorch tensors on the target device (CPU or CUDA). xyz: Shape (N, 3), float32. featuresdc: Shape (N, 1, 3), float32. Stores the zeroth-order spherical harmonic coefficients (DC color). scaling: Shape (N, 3), float32. Stores the log-scale of the Gaussian axes. rotation: Shape (N, 4), float32. Stores quaternions (w, x, y, z). opacity: Shape (N, 1), float32. Stores initial opacity values. Numbered Steps: 1. Model Instantiation: Create the GaussianModel object and move it to the target device (CPU or GPU). 2. Point Cloud Population: Call createfrompcd(xyz, rgb) to populate the model parameters. Position: Initialize xyz directly from the input point cloud coordinates. Color: Initialize featuresdc with the input RGB colors. The higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients are set to zero [S1, 3163-spherical-harmonics-initialization.md, unofficial]. Opacity: Initialize opacity to a default value (typically uniform, e.g., 0.1 or derived from density). Scaling: Initialize scaling based on the nearest neighbor distance of the point cloud to ensure appropriate initial Gaussian size. Specifically, for each point, compute the distance to its nearest neighbor and use this as the scale factor. Rotation: Initialize rotation to identity quaternions (1, 0, 0, 0), implying no initial rotation. 3. Covariance Verification: Ensure the computed covariance matrix \Sigma is symmetric. The covariance is derived from scaling and rotation as \Sigma = R S S^T R^T. A test check verifies torch.allclose(cov0, cov0.T, atol=1e-6). Parameters: Learning rate for xyz: 1.6 \times 10^{-4}. Learning rate for featuresdc: 2.5 \times 10^{-3}. Sampling step: If the point cloud is dense, a sampling step may be applied to reduce N before initialization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def initializegaussianmodel(xyz: np.ndarray, rgb: np.ndarray, device: str = 'cuda'): """ Initialize a GaussianModel from a point cloud. Args: xyz: numpy array of shape (N, 3) with float32 coordinates. rgb: numpy array of shape (N, 3) with float32 RGB values in [0, 1]. device: 'cpu' or 'cuda'. Returns: model: A GaussianModel instance with initialized parameters. """ # 1. Instantiate model and move to device model = GaussianModel() model.to(device) N = xyz.shape[0] # 2. Populate Position # Directly copy xyz to xyz tensor model.xyz = torch.tensor(xyz, dtype=torch.float32, device=device) # 3. Populate Color (DC Spherical Harmonics) # Shape (N, 1, 3) for SH0 model.featuresdc = torch.tensor(rgb, dtype=torch.float32, device=device).unsqueeze(1) # 4. Populate Opacity # Initialize to a small constant value model.opacity = torch.ones((N, 1), dtype=torch.float32, device=device) 0.1 # 5. Populate Scaling # Compute nearest neighbor distances to set initial scales # Using a simple brute-force or KD-tree approach for nearest neighbor # For implementation simplicity, we assume a helper function nndistances exists # or compute it via broadcasting if N is small. # Here we use a placeholder logic for nearest neighbor distance calculation. # In practice, use scipy.spatial.cKDTree or similar. dists = np.linalg.norm(xyz[:, np.newaxis,:] - xyz[np.newaxis,:,:], axis=2) # Exclude self (distance 0) np.filldiagonal(dists, np.inf) nndistances = np.min(dists, axis=1) # Convert distances to log-scale for scaling # Add a small epsilon to avoid log(0) epsilon = 1e-6 logscales = np.log(nndistances + epsilon) # Repeat for 3 dimensions (isotropic scaling initially) scalinginit = np.tile(logscales, (3, 1)).T model.scaling = torch.tensor(scalinginit, dtype=torch.float32, device=device) # 6. Populate Rotation # Initialize to identity quaternion (1, 0, 0, 0) model.rotation = torch.zeros((N, 4), dtype=torch.float32, device=device) model.rotation[:, 0] = 1.0 # 7. Verify Covariance Symmetry # Compute covariance from scaling and rotation # R is constructed from quaternions, S is diagonal from exp(scaling) # Sigma = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # Check if Sigma is symmetric covariances = model.getcovariance() # Assumes model has this method if N > 0: cov0 = covariances[0] if not torch.allclose(cov0, cov0.T, atol=1e-6): raise ValueError("Covariance matrix is not symmetric after initialization.") return model Sets the initial view-dependent color representation by populating only the zeroth-order (DC) spherical harmonic coefficients with the input RGB colors, while leaving higher-order coefficients at zero. It solves the problem of providing a valid, differentiable starting point for view-dependent color optimization without introducing high-frequency artifacts. It sets itself apart from Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) by focusing exclusively on color parameterization rather than geometric pose and scale distribution. An initialization strategy for X-ray Gaussian Splatting that computes camera parameters from scanner specifications and uniformly samples Gaussian centers within a bounding cuboid, replacing Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Uses the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm to reconstruct a low-quality volume in less than 1 second. Excludes empty spaces using a density threshold \tau and randomly samples M points as kernel positions. Sets the scales of Gaussians as the nearest neighbor distances and assumes no rotation. Queries central densities from the FDK volume and scales them down with k to compensate for overlay between kernels. Parameters: M = 50,000 (number of initial Gaussians), \tau = 0.05 (density threshold), k = 0.15 (scaling term). Initializes K learnable sampling coordinates per Gaussian point to enable adaptive feature sampling on K feature maps. Steps: 1. Assign each Gaussian point i K sampling coordinates (sc1^i, sc2^i, \dots, scK^i) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 2}. 2. Randomly generate K matrices (M^1, M^2, \dots, M^K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 2 \times 3}. 3. Constrain each matrix such that the sum of its rows equals 1. 4. Multiply each matrix M^k with the Gaussian point's 3D position Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3 to compute the initial sampling coordinates. Formula: (sc1^1, sc2^2, \dots, scK^K){init} = (M^1 Xi, M^2 Xi, \dots, M^K Xi). Parameter: K = 3 (number of feature maps). Attaches samples (m{ik}, b{ik}) with weights based on initial Gaussian support at sampled voxels, keeping identifiers and weights fixed during optimization. Steps: 1. Compute weight: w{ik} \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}{ik} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^\top \Sigmai^{-1}(\mathbf{x}{ik} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)\right), normalized such that \sumk w{ik} = 1. 2. Keep identifiers and weights fixed as geometry is optimized. 3. Clone and split children inherit descriptors and factor rows from the nearest pre-existing primitive. 4. Pruning applies one mask to all attributes. Pitfall: Equation 12 makes the descriptor scale-aware: sub-voxel primitives concentrate on their own material, while larger primitives integrate over their footprint. TF changes use persistent material support rather than reassigning regions from optimized centers. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) for copying positions and colors, but O(N^2) or O(N \log N) if nearest neighbor distances are computed for scaling. FDK reconstruction for R2-Gaussian is O(V) where V is volume size, but typically fast (<1s). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D) where D is the dimensionality of parameters (position, color, scale, rotation, opacity). Strengths: Provides a geometrically grounded starting point for optimization. Simple and fast for standard SfM data. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the input point cloud. Poor reconstruction leads to poor initialization. Does not handle volumetric data natively without variants like R2-Gaussian. When to use: Standard 3DGS training on image collections with SfM data. When not to use: Volumetric tomography without modification (use R2-Gaussian), or unconstrained image collections requiring adaptive feature sampling (use GS-W). Originated with the introduction of 3D Gaussian Splatting. The createfrompcd method is a standard utility in implementations like mini-splat to bridge the gap between sparse SfM point clouds and the dense Gaussian representation. Variants like R2-Gaussian extend this to X-ray tomography, while GS-W and FactorSplat introduce specialized initializations for feature maps and material descriptors, respectively. metin-yat/mini-splat, https://github.com/metin-yat/mini-splat, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) R^2-Gaussian: Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20693v2, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian in the Wild: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unconstrained Image Collections, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73116-720, fetched 2026-10-27 FactorSplat: Appearance-Controllable Gaussian Proxies for Medical Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.02382, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Harmonics Initialization
body: Spherical Harmonics Initialization sets the initial view-dependent color representation for 3D Gaussians by populating only the zeroth-order (DC) spherical harmonic coefficients with the input RGB colors, while leaving higher-order coefficients at zero. It solves the problem of providing a valid, differentiable starting point for view-dependent color optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting without introducing high-frequency artifacts or unnecessary complexity during the early stages of training. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) by focusing exclusively on the color parameterization rather than the geometric pose and scale distribution. Inputs: N: Number of 3D Gaussians. \text{RGB}i \in [0, 1]^3: The initial RGB color for each Gaussian i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}. Outputs: \mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 27}: A tensor containing the initialized spherical harmonic coefficients for all Gaussians. The shape corresponds to N Gaussians, 3 RGB channels, and 9 coefficients per channel (for degree 2, which is standard for the DC-only initialization in many implementations, though the tensor size is fixed at 27). Data Structures: The SH coefficients are stored in a contiguous tensor. For each Gaussian, the coefficients for the three color channels (Red, Green, Blue) are interleaved or grouped. The standard layout in the source implies a shape of (N, 3, 9) before flattening, resulting in (N, 27). The first 9 elements correspond to the Red channel, the next 9 to Green, and the last 9 to Blue. Within each channel, index 0 is the DC term, and indices 1–8 are higher-order terms. Steps: 1. Allocation: Create a zero-filled tensor \mathbf{C} of shape (N, 3, 9). This initializes all SH coefficients to zero. 2. DC Coefficient Calculation: For each Gaussian i and each color channel c \in \{R, G, B\}: Let v be the input color value for channel c of Gaussian i. Compute the DC coefficient c{0,i,c} using the formula: c{0,i,c} = \frac{v}{k} where k = 0.28209479177387814 is the normalization constant for the zeroth-order spherical harmonic basis function. Assign c{0,i,c} to the coefficient at index 0 for channel c in \mathbf{C}. 3. Flattening: Flatten the last two dimensions of \mathbf{C} from (N, 3, 9) to (N, 27) to produce the final output tensor. Parameters: k = 0.28209479177387814: The normalization constant for the zeroth-order SH basis function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Higher-Order Coefficients: All coefficients with index >0 remain zero. This is intentional, as higher-order terms are optimized during training. Initializing them to non-zero values can cause instability or artifacts. Color Range: The input RGB values are assumed to be in the range [0, 1]. If inputs are in a different range (e.g., [0, 255]), they must be normalized before applying the formula. Precision: The division by k is a simple scaling operation. Standard floating-point precision is sufficient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializesh(rgbcolors: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Initialize spherical harmonic coefficients for 3D Gaussian splatting. Args: rgbcolors: Array of shape (N, 3) containing RGB values in [0, 1]. Returns: Array of shape (N, 27) containing SH coefficients. """ N = rgbcolors.shape[0] # Allocate zero tensor of shape (N, 3, 9) shcoeffs = np.zeros((N, 3, 9)) # Normalization constant for zeroth-order SH basis function k = 0.28209479177387814 # Assign scaled RGB values to the DC coefficient index (0) for all channels # rgbcolors has shape (N, 3), we need to assign to shcoeffs[:,:, 0] # shcoeffs[:, 0, 0] = R / k # shcoeffs[:, 1, 0] = G / k # shcoeffs[:, 2, 0] = B / k shcoeffs[:,:, 0] = rgbcolors / k # Flatten the last two dimensions to produce a tensor of shape (N, 27) shcoeffsflat = shcoeffs.reshape(N, 27) return shcoeffsflat This variant initializes a single splat object with specific geometric and color properties based on normalized coordinates. It is used in the JSplat library. SH Degree: The splat is created with spherical harmonic degree 3 using Splats.create(3). Position: Position coordinates are set by scaling normalized inputs (npx, npy, npz) with a constant size: splat.setPositionX(npx size), etc.. Scale: Uniform scale is set using a constant baseScale for all axes. Rotation: Identity rotation quaternion is set: (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0). Opacity: Opacity is set by converting a fixed alpha value of 1.0 using Splats.alphaToOpacity(1.0f). SH Coefficients: Degree-0 SH coefficients are set based on normalized coordinates. A special case exists for the exact point (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5), which uses 0.1 instead of the coordinate offset. Otherwise, the coefficient is colorToDirectCurrent(npx + 0.5) for Red, npy + 0.5 for Green, and npz + 0.5 for Blue. Append: The configured splat is appended to the target list. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians. The operation involves a single pass over all Gaussians to compute the DC coefficient. Memory Complexity: O(N), storing 27 coefficients per Gaussian. Performance: The initialization is extremely fast and negligible compared to the training time. It is performed once at the start of the optimization process. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and provides a stable starting point for color optimization. It avoids the need for complex color estimation from sparse point clouds. Limitations: Does not account for view-dependent effects initially, as only the DC term is set. Higher-order terms must be learned during training. When to use: Standard initialization for 3D Gaussian Splatting when no prior color information is available or when a simple baseline is desired. When not to use: If high-fidelity view-dependent effects are critical from the start, other methods might be preferred, though SH initialization is still the standard starting point. Spherical Harmonics Initialization is a core component of the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper. It leverages the mathematical properties of spherical harmonics to represent view-dependent colors in a compact and differentiable manner. The zeroth-order term corresponds to the average color (DC component), which is sufficient for initial setup. The method has become a standard practice in the field due to its simplicity and effectiveness. 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation, https://github.com/WangFeng18/3d-gaussian-splatting, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) JSplat, https://github.com/javagl/JSplat, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Harmonics Evaluation
head: SH Evaluation, Spherical Harmonics Color Computation, harmonic
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Evaluation computes the view-dependent RGB color of a 3D Gaussian splat by projecting its stored SH coefficients onto a viewing direction vector. It solves the problem of representing directional lighting and material properties in a differentiable, compact basis for real-time rendering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using hardcoded polynomial approximations of the SH basis functions to avoid expensive trigonometric calculations, enabling efficient GPU evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: sphericalharmonics: A tensor of shape (N, 48) containing the SH coefficients for N Gaussians. The coefficients are stored in order of increasing degree l and order m. Input: dir: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing normalized viewing direction vectors (x, y, z) for each Gaussian. Output: color: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the computed RGB color values. Data Structures: The SH coefficients are stored in a flat array per Gaussian. The layout follows the standard ordering: Degree 0 (l=0): 1 coefficient (3 channels: R, G, B). Indices 0-2. Degree 1 (l=1): 3 coefficients (9 channels). Indices 3-11. Degree 2 (l=2): 5 coefficients (15 channels). Indices 12-26. Degree 3 (l=3): 7 coefficients (21 channels). Indices 27-47. Total coefficients per Gaussian: 48. Constants: The evaluation uses pre-computed constants derived from the normalization factors of the real spherical harmonics. The specific constants used in the reference implementations are: Degree 0: SH\C0 = 0.28209479177387814 Degree 1: SH\C1 = 0.48860251190291987 Degree 2: SH\C2\0 = 1.0925484305920792 SH\C2\1 = -1.0925484305920792 SH\C2\2 = 0.94617469575755997 SH\C2\3 = -1.0925484305920792 SH\C2\4 = 0.54627421529603959 Degree 3: SH\C3\0 = 0.59004358992664352 SH\C3\1 = 2.8906114426405538 SH\C3\2 = 0.45704579946446572 SH\C3\3 = 0.3731763325901154 SH\C3\4 = 0.45704579946446572 SH\C3\5 = 1.4453057213202769 SH\C3\6 = 0.59004358992664352 Steps: 1. Normalize Direction: Ensure the input direction vector \mathbf{v} = (x, y, z) is normalized. If not, normalize it: \mathbf{v} \leftarrow \mathbf{v} / \|\mathbf{v}\|. 2. Initialize Color: Extract the Degree 0 coefficients (c0, c1, c2) from indices 0-2. Initialize the color vector \mathbf{C} as: \mathbf{C} = SH\C0 \cdot [c0, c1, c2]^T 3. Degree 1 Contribution: Extract coefficients c3 \dots c5 (indices 3-5). Compute the contribution using the direction components: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} - SH\C1 \cdot [y \cdot c3, -z \cdot c4, x \cdot c5]^T Note: The signs and axis mapping depend on the specific SH convention. The reference code uses: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} - SH\C1 \cdot y \cdot c3 + SH\C1 \cdot z \cdot c4 - SH\C1 \cdot x \cdot c5 (Wait, let's look at S1/S3 code carefully. S1: l1m1 = -... y, l1m0 =... z, l1p1 = -... x. S3: color = color - SHC1 y c1 + SHC1 z c2 - SHC1 x c3. Here c1, c2, c3 correspond to indices 3,4,5. So:) \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + SH\C1 \cdot [-y \cdot c3, z \cdot c4, -x \cdot c5]^T 4. Degree 2 Contribution: Extract coefficients c6 \dots c{10} (indices 6-10). Compute squared and mixed terms: xx=x^2, yy=y^2, zz=z^2, xy=xy, yz=yz, xz=xz. Update color: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + SH\C2\0 \cdot xy \cdot c6 + SH\C2\1 \cdot yz \cdot c7 + SH\C2\2 \cdot (2zz - xx - yy) \cdot c8 + SH\C2\3 \cdot xz \cdot c9 + SH\C2\4 \cdot (xx - yy) \cdot c{10} Mapping to RGB channels: The coefficients c6 \dots c{10} are vectors of size 3 (RGB). The scalar basis functions are multiplied by each channel. \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + \begin{bmatrix} SH\C2\0 \cdot xy \\ SH\C2\1 \cdot yz \\ SH\C2\2 \cdot (2zz - xx - yy) \\ SH\C2\3 \cdot xz \\ SH\C2\4 \cdot (xx - yy) \end{bmatrix} \otimes \begin{bmatrix} c6 \\ c7 \\ c8 \\ c9 \\ c{10} \end{bmatrix} Correction based on S2/S3 code structure: The code applies the scalar basis function to the entire RGB vector for that coefficient index. \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + SH\C2\0 \cdot xy \cdot c6 + SH\C2\1 \cdot yz \cdot c7 + SH\C2\2 \cdot (2zz - xx - yy) \cdot c8 + SH\C2\3 \cdot xz \cdot c9 + SH\C2\4 \cdot (xx - yy) \cdot c{10} 5. Degree 3 Contribution (Optional): If the SH dimension is greater than 27 (i.e., Degree 3 is used), extract coefficients c{11} \dots c{17} (indices 11-17). Update color: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + SH\C3\0 \cdot y(3xx - yy) \cdot c{11} + SH\C3\1 \cdot xyz \cdot c{12} + SH\C3\2 \cdot y(4zz - xx - yy) \cdot c{13} + SH\C3\3 \cdot z(2zz - 3xx - 3yy) \cdot c{14} + SH\C3\4 \cdot x(4zz - xx - yy) \cdot c{15} + SH\C3\5 \cdot z(xx - yy) \cdot c{16} + SH\C3\6 \cdot x(xx - 3yy) \cdot c{17} Note on S1/S3 code: S1: l3m3 =... y (-3.0 x x + y y) -> y(3xx - yy) with sign flip? No, -3x^2+y^2 = -(3x^2-y^2). S3: SHC30 y (3.0 xx - yy) c9. Let's stick to the explicit formulas from S3 which are clearer: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + SH\C3\0 \cdot y(3xx - yy) \cdot c{11} + SH\C3\1 \cdot xyz \cdot c{12} + SH\C3\2 \cdot y(4zz - xx - yy) \cdot c{13} + SH\C3\3 \cdot z(2zz - 3xx - 3yy) \cdot c{14} + SH\C3\4 \cdot x(4zz - xx - yy) \cdot c{15} + SH\C3\5 \cdot z(xx - yy) \cdot c{16} + SH\C3\6 \cdot x(xx - 3yy) \cdot c{17} 6. Bias and Clamping: Add a bias of 0.5 to the color vector to shift the range from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] (or similar, depending on coefficient storage range). Clip the result to [0.0, 1.0]. \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \text{clip}(\mathbf{C} + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0) Pseudocode: Unverified code.
