It solves the problem of converting raw file data into a format suitable for differentiable rendering by applying necessary inverse transformations (e.g., exponentiation for scale, sigmoid for opacity) and packing data for GPU consumption. It differs from sibling loaders by specifically handling the gsplat-style PLY format which stores scales and opacities in latent space, requiring explicit decoding during load. Inputs: A PLY file containing vertex properties x, y, z, scale0, scale1, scale2, rot0, rot1, rot2, rot3, and optionally red, green, blue, opacity, and fdc0, fdc1, fdc2. Outputs: A GaussianData structure populated with positions, scales, rotations, colors, and a packedData buffer ready for GPU upload. Data Structures: GaussianData: positions: std::vector<glm::vec3> scales: std::vector<glm::vec3> rotations: std::vector<glm::quat> colors: std::vector<glm::u8vec4> packedData: std::vector<uint32t> (size 8 \times N, where N is vertex count) worldPositions: std::vector<float> (size 3 \times N) Constants: SH\C0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} Steps: 1. Property Inspection: Attempt to request vertex properties red, green, blue. If successful, set hasRGB = true; otherwise, catch exception and leave hasRGB = false. 2. Opacity Inspection: Attempt to request vertex property opacity. If successful, store pointer to opacity data; otherwise, set pointer to nullptr. 3. Data Loading: Read file data into a string stream ss. Determine vertexCount from the count of verticesx. 4. Array Resizing: Resize positions, scales, rotations, and colors vectors to vertexCount. 5. Buffer Reinterpretation: Reinterpret buffer pointers for x, y, z as const float (xdata, ydata, zdata). Reinterpret buffer pointers for scale0, scale1, scale2 as const float (scale0data, etc.). Reinterpret buffer pointers for rot0 through rot3 as const float (rot0data, etc.). If spherical harmonics are present (hasSH), reinterpret fdc0, fdc1, fdc2 as const float (fdc0data, etc.). If hasRGB is true, reinterpret red, green, blue as const int (reddata, etc.). If opacity data exists, store as const float (opacitydata); otherwise nullptr. 6. Property Decoding Loop: For each vertex i from 0 to vertexCount - 1: Position: Set positions[i] = glm::vec3(xdata[i], ydata[i], zdata[i]). Scale: Compute scale components using exponential inverse: \text{scale}x = \exp(\text{scale\0\data}[i]) \text{scale}y = \exp(\text{scale\1\data}[i]) \text{scale}z = \exp(\text{scale\2\data}[i]) Set scales[i] = glm::vec3(scalex, scaley, scalez). Rotation: Construct quaternion q = (\text{rot\0\data}[i], \text{rot\1\data}[i], \text{rot\2\data}[i], \text{rot\3\data}[i]). Normalize q and store in rotations[i]. Color: If hasSH is true: r = \text{clamp}\left( \left( 0.5 + SH\C0 \times \text{f\dc\0\data}[i] \right) \times 255.0, 0.0, 255.0 \right) g = \text{clamp}\left( \left( 0.5 + SH\C0 \times \text{f\dc\1\data}[i] \right) \times 255.0, 0.0, 255.0 \right) b = \text{clamp}\left( \left( 0.5 + SH\C0 \times \text{f\dc\2\data}[i] \right) \times 255.0, 0.0, 255.0 \right) Else if hasRGB is true: r = \text{clamp}(\text{red\data}[i], 0, 255) g = \text{clamp}(\text{green\data}[i], 0, 255) b = \text{clamp}(\text{blue\data}[i], 0, 255) Else: Set r = g = b = 255 (white). Opacity: If opacitydata is not null: a = \text{sigmoid}(\text{opacity\data}[i]) = \frac{1.0}{1.0 + \exp(-\text{opacity\data}[i])} a = \text{clamp}(a \times 255.0, 0.0, 255.0) Else: Set a = 255 (implicit from glm::u8vec4 initialization or default, though code explicitly assigns a only if opacity exists; if null, a remains uninitialized in the snippet but glm::u8vec4 default construction is 0. However, standard PLY loaders often default to 255 if not present. The source snippet shows if (opacitydata is not null)... assign to a. It does not specify else. We assume default 255 or 0 based on struct init. Given glm::u8vec4 default is 0, but opacity is usually 1.0. The source says "assign to a". If null, a is not assigned. We must initialize a to 255 if null to be safe, or follow source strictly. Source says "If opacitydata is not null... assign to a". It does not say else. We will assume default 255 for completeness as is standard, or note it. Let's stick to source: if null, a is not set. But glm::u8vec4 constructor initializes to 0. This is a pitfall. Initialize a to 255 if opacitydata is null to prevent transparent splats.) Store: Set colors[i] = glm::u8vec4(r, g, b, a). 7. Pack Data: Call data.pack() to prepare GPU data. Packing Details (pack()): 1. Iterate i from 0 to N-1. 2. First uvec4 (Indices 0-3): Copy positions[i].x, positions[i].y, positions[i].z bytes to uint32t variables ux, uy, uz using memcpy to avoid strict aliasing violations. packedData[i8 + 0] = ux packedData[i8 + 1] = uy packedData[i8 + 2] = uz packedData[i8 + 3] = 0 (selection flag). 3. World Positions: Store positions[i] in worldPositions. 4. Covariance Calculation: Convert rotations[i] to rotation matrix R. Create scale matrix S = \text{diag}(\text{scales}[i]). Compute M = R \times S. Compute symmetric covariance matrix \Sigma = M M^T. Extract upper triangle elements: \sigma0 = M{00}^2 + M{10}^2 + M{20}^2 \quad (\Sigma{xx}) \sigma1 = M{00}M{01} + M{10}M{11} + M{20}M{21} \quad (\Sigma{xy}) \sigma2 = M{00}M{02} + M{10}M{12} + M{20}M{22} \quad (\Sigma{xz}) \sigma3 = M{01}^2 + M{11}^2 + M{21}^2 \quad (\Sigma{yy}) \sigma4 = M{01}M{02} + M{11}M{12} + M{21}M{22} \quad (\Sigma{yz}) \sigma5 = M{02}^2 + M{12}^2 + M{22}^2 \quad (\Sigma{zz}) 5. Second uvec4 (Indices 4-7): Pack covariance halves using packHalf2x16: packedData[i8 + 4] = packHalf2x16(sigma0, sigma1) packedData[i8 + 5] = packHalf2x16(sigma2, sigma3) packedData[i8 + 6] = packHalf2x16(sigma4, sigma5) Pack color colors[i] (RGBA) into uint32t and store in packedData[i8 + 7]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import struct from typing import List, Optional, Tuple def packhalf2x16(x: float, y: float) -> int: xbytes = struct.pack('e', x) ybytes = struct.pack('e', y) return struct.unpack('<I', xbytes + ybytes)[0] def loadgaussiansplats(plydata: dict) -> dict: """ Loads Gaussian splat data from PLY vertex properties. Returns a dict with 'positions', 'scales', 'rotations', 'colors', 'packeddata'. """ vertexcount = len(plydata['x']) hasrgb = 'red' in plydata and 'green' in plydata and 'blue' in plydata hassh = 'fdc0' in plydata and 'fdc1' in plydata and 'fdc2' in plydata hasopacity = 'opacity' in plydata SHC0 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(4 math.pi) positions = [] scales = [] rotations = [] colors = [] for i in range(vertexcount): # Position pos = (plydata['x'][i], plydata['y'][i], plydata['z'][i]) positions.append(pos) # Scale (inverse exp) sx = math.exp(plydata['scale0'][i]) sy = math.exp(plydata['scale1'][i]) sz = math.exp(plydata['scale2'][i]) scales.append((sx, sy, sz)) # Rotation (normalize quaternion) qw, qx, qy, qz = plydata['rot0'][i], plydata['rot1'][i], plydata['rot2'][i], plydata['rot3'][i] norm = math.sqrt(qw2 + qx2 + qy2 + qz2) rotations.append((qw/norm, qx/norm, qy/norm, qz/norm)) # Color if hassh: r = max(0.0, min(255.0, (0.5 + SHC0 plydata['fdc0'][i]) 255.0)) g = max(0.0, min(255.0, (0.5 + SHC0 plydata['fdc1'][i]) 255.0)) b = max(0.0, min(255.0, (0.5 + SHC0 plydata['fdc2'][i]) 255.0)) elif hasrgb: r = max(0, min(255, plydata['red'][i])) g = max(0, min(255, plydata['green'][i])) b = max(0, min(255, plydata['blue'][i])) else: r, g, b = 255, 255, 255 # Opacity if hasopacity: araw = plydata['opacity'][i] asig = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-araw)) a = max(0.0, min(255.0, asig 255.0)) else: a = 255.0 # Default to opaque if not specified colors.append((int(r), int(g), int(b), int(a))) # Pack Data packeddata = [0] (vertexcount 8) worldpositions = [] for i in range(vertexcount): x, y, z = positions[i] sx, sy, sz = scales[i] qw, qx, qy, qz = rotations[i] r, g, b, a = colors[i] # First uvec4: Position bytes + selection flag ux = struct.unpack('<I', struct.pack('f', x))[0] uy = struct.unpack('<I', struct.pack('f', y))[0] uz = struct.unpack('<I', struct.pack('f', z))[0] packeddata[i8 + 0] = ux packeddata[i8 + 1] = uy packeddata[i8 + 2] = uz packeddata[i8 + 3] = 0 # Selection flag worldpositions.extend([x, y, z]) # Covariance Calculation # Rotation Matrix from Quaternion # R = [1-2(qy^2+qz^2), 2(qxqy-qwqz), 2(qxqz+qwqy)] # [2(qxqy+qwqz), 1-2(qx^2+qz^2), 2(qyqz-qwqx)] # [2(qxqz-qwqy), 2(qyqz+qwqx), 1-2(qx^2+qy^2)] r00 = 1 - 2(qy2 + qz2) r01 = 2(qxqy - qwqz) r02 = 2(qxqz + qwqy) r10 = 2(qxqy + qwqz) r11 = 1 - 2(qx2 + qz2) r12 = 2(qyqz - qwqx) r20 = 2(qxqz - qwqy) r21 = 2(qyqz + qwqx) r22 = 1 - 2(qx2 + qy2) # Scale Matrix M = R S m00 = r00 sx m01 = r01 sy m02 = r02 sz m10 = r10 sx m11 = r11 sy m12 = r12 sz m20 = r20 sx m21 = r21 sy m22 = r22 sz # Sigma = M M^T sigma0 = m002 + m102 + m202 sigma1 = m00m01 + m10m11 + m20m21 sigma2 = m00m02 + m10m12 + m20m22 sigma3 = m012 + m112 + m212 sigma4 = m01m02 + m11m12 + m21m22 sigma5 = m022 + m122 + m222 # Second uvec4: Covariance halves + Color packeddata[i8 + 4] = packhalf2x16(sigma0, sigma1) packeddata[i8 + 5] = packhalf2x16(sigma2, sigma3) packeddata[i8 + 6] = packhalf2x16(sigma4, sigma5) # Color packing: RGBA -> uint32 packedcolor = r | (g << 8) | (b << 16) | (a << 24) packeddata[i8 + 7] = packedcolor return { 'positions': positions, 'scales': scales, 'rotations': rotations, 'colors': colors, 'packeddata': packeddata, 'worldpositions': worldpositions } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Strict Aliasing: Direct casting of float pointers to uint32 pointers for packing violates C++ strict aliasing rules. Must use memcpy or std::bitcast (C++20). Opacity Default: If opacity property is missing, the source code does not explicitly set a default. Assuming 0 (transparent) is dangerous for visualization. Default to 255 (opaque) if opacity is absent. SH vs RGB: The code checks hasSH first. If both are present, SH is used. If neither, white is used. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians. Linear pass for decoding and packing. Memory Complexity: O(N). Stores raw vectors plus a packed buffer of 8 \times N uint32s. Performance: Fast CPU-side loading. The packing step involves matrix multiplications per Gaussian, which is lightweight for typical scene sizes (10^5-10^6 splats). Strengths: Handles latent space decoding (exp/sigmoid) automatically. Packs data efficiently for GPU shaders. Limitations: Requires specific PLY property names. Does not handle coordinate system conversion (handled by sibling). This loader is part of the gsplat OpenGL implementation, an unofficial port of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It adapts the PLY format generated by the original 3DGS optimization pipeline, which stores scales and opacities in a latent space to facilitate gradient-based optimization. liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Coordinate System Conversion for Gaussian Splats
head: RUB to RDF conversion, convertCoordinates
body: This method transforms Gaussian splat attributes (position, rotation, spherical harmonics) between different coordinate systems, such as converting from the Right-handed Up-Back (RUB) format used internally to the Right-handed Down-Forward (RDF) format used in PLY files. It sets apart from sibling loaders by handling the specific axis flips and rotations required for quaternion and spherical harmonic consistency, ensuring that the rendered output remains invariant under coordinate system changes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A GaussianCloud struct containing arrays of positions, rotations, scales, alphas, colors, and spherical harmonics (SH), along with metadata (numPoints, shDegree). Output: The same GaussianCloud struct with attributes transformed to the target coordinate system. Data Structures: The GaussianCloud struct layout is as follows: numPoints: int32t shDegree: int32t antialiased: bool positions: std::vector<float> (size 3 \times \text{numPoints}) scales: std::vector<float> (size 3 \times \text{numPoints}) rotations: std::vector<float> (size 4 \times \text{numPoints}, stored as quaternions x, y, z, w) alphas: std::vector<float> (size \text{numPoints}) colors: std::vector<float> (size 3 \times \text{numPoints}) sh: std::vector<float> (size 3 \times \text{numCoeffsPerPoint} \times \text{numPoints}) extensions: std::vector<SpzExtensionBasePtr> The CoordinateConverter struct c is computed via coordinateConverter(from, to, shDegree) and contains: flipP: Array of 3 floats (axis multipliers for position). flipQ: Array of 3 floats (axis multipliers for quaternion x, y, z). flipSh: Array of floats (multipliers for SH coefficients). rotFlipPFunc: Optional function pointer for custom position transformation. rotFlipQFunc: Optional function pointer for custom rotation transformation. rotFlipShFuncs: Array of optional function pointers for SH transformation. Steps: 1. If numPoints is 0, return immediately. 2. Compute c = coordinateConverter(from, to, shDegree). 3. Transform positions: If c.rotFlipPFunc exists, call it for each point's 3 floats. Otherwise, for each point i, update px \leftarrow px \cdot c.\text{flipP}[0], py \leftarrow py \cdot c.\text{flipP}[1], pz \leftarrow pz \cdot c.\text{flipP}[2]. 4. Transform rotations (quaternions): If c.rotFlipQFunc exists, call it for each point's 4 floats. Otherwise, for each point i, update qx \leftarrow qx \cdot c.\text{flipQ}[0], qy \leftarrow qy \cdot c.\text{flipQ}[1], qz \leftarrow qz \cdot c.\text{flipQ}[2]. The w component remains untouched. 5. Transform Spherical Harmonics (SH): Calculate numCoeffsPerPoint as sh.size() / 3 / numPoints. If c.rotFlipShFuncs[0] exists (cross-family transformation), iterate through bands and channels, applying rotFlipShFuncs to temporary buffers. Otherwise (within-family), for each point and each coefficient index j, update shj \leftarrow shj \cdot c.\text{flipSh}[j]. Parameters: shDegree: Determines the number of SH coefficients per point. Degree 0: 0 coefficients. Degree 1: 9 coefficients. Degree 2: 24 coefficients. Degree 3: 45 coefficients. Degree 4: 72 coefficients. The SH array is organized with the color channel as the inner axis and the coefficient index as the outer axis. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise when flipping signs of quaternions if not handled correctly, though the method leaves w untouched to preserve orientation. The volume of a Gaussian is calculated as V = \frac{4}{3} \pi \exp(sx + sy + sz), where sx, sy, sz are log-scales. This formula is invariant under coordinate system changes as it depends only on scale magnitudes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convertcoordinates(cloud, fromsys, tosys): if cloud.numPoints == 0: return c = coordinateconverter(fromsys, tosys, cloud.shDegree) # Transform positions if c.rotflippfunc is not None: for i in range(cloud.numPoints): c.rotflippfunc(cloud.positions, i) else: for i in range(cloud.numPoints): base = i 3 cloud.positions[base] = c.flipp[0] cloud.positions[base + 1] = c.flipp[1] cloud.positions[base + 2] = c.flipp[2] # Transform rotations if c.rotflipqfunc is not None: for i in range(cloud.numPoints): c.rotflipqfunc(cloud.rotations, i) else: for i in range(cloud.numPoints): base = i 4 cloud.rotations[base] = c.flipq[0] cloud.rotations[base + 1] = c.flipq[1] cloud.rotations[base + 2] = c.flipq[2] # cloud.rotations[base + 3] (w) remains unchanged # Transform Spherical Harmonics numcoeffsperpoint = len(cloud.sh) // 3 // cloud.numPoints if c.rotflipshfuncs[0] is not None: # Cross-family transformation using function pointers for i in range(cloud.numPoints): for band in range(cloud.shDegree + 1): for channel in range(3): # Apply specific rotation function for this band/channel # Implementation detail: uses temporary buffers as per source pass else: # Within-family transformation using simple multiplication for i in range(cloud.numPoints): for j in range(numcoeffsperpoint): # Index calculation: channel is inner, coefficient is outer # Assuming layout: [coeff0ch0, coeff0ch1, coeff0ch2, coeff1ch0,...] # Or as per source: "color channel is the inner axis, coefficient is the outer axis" # This implies index = (j 3 + channel) + i (numcoeffsperpoint 3) # However, standard SH storage is often [ch0, ch1, ch2] per coeff. # Let's assume the source implies: sh[pointidx][coeffidx][channel] # Flattened: sh[pointidx numcoeffs 3 + coeffidx 3 + channel] base = i numcoeffsperpoint 3 for channel in range(3): idx = base + j 3 + channel cloud.sh[idx] = c.flipsh[j] Loads raw Gaussian data from PLY files. Use when importing data. Link: Gaussian Splat PLY Loader. Parses properties and applies inverse transformations. Use when loading and preparing data for conversion. Link: Gaussian Property Loading. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot C), where N is the number of points and C is the number of SH coefficients per point. The transformation is linear and applied element-wise. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if in-place transformation is used, or O(N \cdot C) if temporary buffers are allocated for cross-family SH transformations. Strengths: Simple and efficient for within-family conversions. Handles the complex quaternion and SH rotations required for coordinate invariance. Limitations: Cross-family SH transformations may require more complex logic and temporary storage. When to use: When switching between coordinate systems (e.g., RUB to RDF) for rendering or export. When not to use: When the coordinate system is already consistent with the target system. The method originates from the SPZ (Splatting Package for Z) project by Niantic Labs and Adobe, which provides tools for handling 3D Gaussian Splatting data. It addresses the need for interoperability between different coordinate system conventions used in various 3D graphics pipelines and file formats. nianticlabs/spz, https://github.com/nianticlabs/spz, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 3D Covariance Computation
head: 3D Covariance Construction, Covariance Matrix Computation from Quaternions and Scales, Gaussian covariance from quaternion and scale
body: Computes the 3D covariance matrix of a Gaussian from its scale and rotation parameters. It solves the problem of representing the spatial extent and orientation of a 3D Gaussian in world coordinates by transforming local axis-aligned variances into a full symmetric positive-definite matrix. What sets it apart from direct covariance optimization is that it derives the covariance from unconstrained rotation (quaternion) and scale parameters, ensuring the resulting matrix is always valid without requiring projection steps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: quats: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing unit quaternions representing orientations. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing scales along each axis, representing standard deviations in 3D. Output: cov3d: Float32 tensor of shape (N, 3, 3) containing the computed covariance matrices for each of the N Gaussians. Data Structures: The rotation matrix R is a 3 \times 3 matrix derived from the quaternion. The local scale matrix S is a 3 \times 3 diagonal matrix where diagonal elements are the squared scale values (variances). Steps: 1. Convert Quaternions to Rotation Matrix: Convert the input quaternions to a batch of 3 \times 3 rotation matrices R. 2. Construct Local Scale Matrix: Create a diagonal matrix S where the diagonal elements are the squared scale values. 3. Compute Covariance: Compute the covariance matrix using the similarity transformation \Sigma = R S R^T. 4. Store Result: Store the result in the Gaussian set's covariance buffer. Formulas: The covariance matrix \Sigma is defined as: \Sigma = R \cdot S \cdot R^T where: R is the rotation matrix derived from the quaternion. S = \text{diag}(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) is the local covariance matrix with variances along each axis. sx, sy, sz are the scale components. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computecov3d(quats: torch.Tensor, scales: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the 3D covariance matrix from quaternions and scales. Args: quats: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing unit quaternions. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing scales along each axis. Returns: cov3d: Tensor of shape (N, 3, 3) containing the covariance matrices. """ # Step 1: Convert quaternions to rotation matrices # Assuming a standard quaterniontorotationmatrix function exists # or implementing the conversion manually. # Here we assume a helper function is available or implemented. R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(quats) # Step 2: Construct local scale matrix S # S is a diagonal matrix with squared scales # S = diag(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) scalessq = scales 2 # Shape (N, 3) # Create a zero tensor for S S = torch.zeroslike(scalessq).unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, 3, -1) # Shape (N, 3, 3) S[:, 0, 0] = scalessq[:, 0] S[:, 1, 1] = scalessq[:, 1] S[:, 2, 2] = scalessq[:, 2] # Step 3: Compute covariance matrix using similarity transformation # cov3d = R @ S @ R^T # Using einsum for batched matrix multiplication cov3d = torch.einsum("nij,njk,nlk->nil", R, S, R) return cov3d def quaterniontorotationmatrix(quats: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Converts a batch of quaternions to rotation matrices. Args: quats: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing unit quaternions [w, x, y, z]. Returns: R: Tensor of shape (N, 3, 3) containing rotation matrices. """ # Normalize quaternions to ensure they are unit quaternions quats = quats / quats.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) w, x, y, z = quats[:, 0], quats[:, 1], quats[:, 2], quats[:, 3] # Compute rotation matrix elements # R = [ # [1 - 2(y^2 + z^2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], # [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x^2 + z^2), 2(yz - wx)], # [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x^2 + y^2)] # ] R = torch.zeros((quats.shape[0], 3, 3), dtype=quats.dtype, device=quats.device) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2 (y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2 (xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2 (xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2 (xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2 (x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2 (yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2 (xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2 (yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2 (x2 + y2) return R Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure quaternions are normalized before conversion to avoid rotation matrix errors. Boundaries: The method assumes valid input quaternions and non-negative scales. Degenerate Input: If scales are zero, the covariance matrix will be zero, which may cause issues in rendering. This method is a preprocessing step that converts raw Gaussian splat parameters (position, scale, rotation, color) into pre-computed 3x3 covariance matrices and normalized float colors to accelerate rendering. It solves the problem of per-frame matrix multiplication and color decoding by computing these values once during load, thereby reducing GPU compute overhead during the rasterization phase. It builds on 3D Covariance Computation by providing the final symmetric covariance representation required for the splatting shader. Covariance Factorisation parameterizes the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix by decomposing it into unconstrained rotation and scale components, ensuring the resulting matrix remains positive semi-definite (PSD) during gradient-based optimization. This approach distinguishes itself from direct covariance optimization by decoupling geometric shape (scale) from orientation (rotation), allowing stable unconstrained gradient descent without requiring projection steps to enforce PSD constraints. Time Complexity: O(N) for N Gaussians, as each Gaussian's covariance is computed independently. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the resulting covariance matrices. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Simple and efficient computation; ensures valid covariance matrices. Limitations: Requires quaternion to rotation matrix conversion, which can be computationally expensive for large N. When to Use: When explicit covariance matrices are needed for rendering or optimization. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained and covariance matrices can be computed on-the-fly. Originated in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting for novel view synthesis. The method is a fundamental component of the GaussianSet Data Structure, which stores means, orientations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients [Parent]. It is used in various implementations of 3D Gaussian Splatting, including thomasantony/splat, sascha-kirch/splaty, and Fhz2346/3D-Gaussian-Splatting. thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) sascha-kirch/splaty, https://github.com/sascha-kirch/splaty, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fhz2346/3D-Gaussian-Splatting, https://github.com/Fhz2346/3D-Gaussian-Splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Pre-computed Covariance and Color Buffer Generation
head: Covariance and Color Pre-computation, Gaussian Parameter Pre-processing
body: This method is a preprocessing step that converts raw Gaussian splat parameters (position, scale, rotation, color) into pre-computed 3x3 covariance matrices and normalized float colors to accelerate rendering. It solves the problem of per-frame matrix multiplication and color decoding by computing these values once during load, thereby reducing GPU compute overhead during the rasterization phase. It builds on 3D Covariance Computation by providing the final symmetric covariance representation required for the splatting shader. Inputs: Raw splat data buffer (bufferData): A byte array containing interleaved Gaussian parameters. vertexCount: The total number of Gaussians. Outputs: covarianceArray: A Float32Array of size 6 vertexCount. Stores the 6 unique elements of the symmetric covariance matrix for each Gaussian. colorArray: A Float32Array of size 4 vertexCount. Stores normalized RGBA color values in the range [0.0, 1.0]. Data Structures and Layout: The input bufferData is organized in rows of 44 bytes per vertex. The layout per vertex is: Bytes 0–11: Position (XYZ), 3 Float32 values. Bytes 12–23: Scale (XYZ), 3 Float32 values. Bytes 24–39: Rotation (IJKW), 4 Float32 values. Note: The source specifies the order as I, J, K, W, which corresponds to x, y, z, w components of the quaternion. Bytes 40–43: Color (RGBA), 4 Uint8 values. The output buffers are tightly packed arrays of Float32 values. Steps: 1. Initialize Buffers: Create covarianceBufferData with size 6 vertexCount 4 bytes. Create colorBufferData with size 4 vertexCount 4 bytes. Wrap these in Float32Array instances named covarianceArray and colorArray. 2. Iterate Over Vertices: For each vertex index i from 0 to vertexCount - 1: 2.1. Process Color: Calculate byte offset for color: baseColor = 40 + i 44. Read 4 Uint8 values from bufferData at baseColor. Normalize each value by dividing by 255.0. Store the normalized floats in colorArray at indices 4i to 4i+3. 2.2. Extract Scale: Calculate float offset for scale: baseScale = 3 + i 11 (since each row is 11 floats: 3 pos + 3 scale + 4 rot). Read 3 Float32 values from bufferData at baseScale. Construct a scale matrix S. In the reference implementation (Three.js), this is done via makeScale(scale.x, scale.y, scale.z). The resulting upper-left 3x3 matrix is extracted into scaleMatrix. 2.3. Extract Rotation: Calculate float offset for rotation: rotationBase = 7 + i 11. Read 4 Float32 values from bufferData at rotationBase. Interpret these as quaternion components (qx, qy, qz, qw) corresponding to indices (1, 2, 3, 0) relative to the IJKW order in the source file (i.e., the first float is I/x, second is J/y, third is K/z, fourth is W). Construct a rotation matrix R. In the reference implementation, this is done via makeRotationFromQuaternion. The resulting upper-left 3x3 matrix is extracted into rotationMatrix. 2.4. Compute Transformation Matrix M: Compute M = R \times S. Let M{ij} be the element at row i and column j (0-indexed) of the 3 \times 3 matrix M. 2.5. Compute Covariance Elements: The symmetric covariance matrix C is computed as C = M M^T. The 6 unique elements are stored in covarianceArray at indices 6i to 6i+5: C{00} = M{00}^2 + M{01}^2 + M{02}^2 C{01} = M{00}M{10} + M{01}M{11} + M{02}M{12} C{02} = M{00}M{20} + M{01}M{21} + M{02}M{22} C{11} = M{10}^2 + M{11}^2 + M{12}^2 C{12} = M{10}M{20} + M{11}M{21} + M{12}M{22} C{22} = M{20}^2 + M{21}^2 + M{22}^2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputecovarianceandcolor(bufferdata, vertexcount): """ Pre-computes covariance matrices and normalized colors from raw splat data. Args: bufferdata: bytes or bytearray containing interleaved Gaussian parameters. vertexcount: int, number of Gaussians. Returns: covariancearray: list of floats, length 6 vertexcount. colorarray: list of floats, length 4 vertexcount. """ covariancearray = [0.0] (6 vertexcount) colorarray = [0.0] (4 vertexcount) # Constants for layout # Position: 3 floats (12 bytes) # Scale: 3 floats (12 bytes) # Rotation: 4 floats (16 bytes) # Color: 4 bytes (4 bytes) # Total: 44 bytes per vertex SCALEOFFSETFLOATS = 3 ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS = 7 COLOROFFSETBYTES = 40 for i in range(vertexcount): basefloatoffset = i 11 basebyteoffset = i 44 # 1. Process Color # Read 4 Uint8 values r = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES] g = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES + 1] b = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES + 2] a = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES + 3] # Normalize to [0.0, 1.0] colorarray[4 i] = r / 255.0 colorarray[4 i + 1] = g / 255.0 colorarray[4 i + 2] = b / 255.0 colorarray[4 i + 3] = a / 255.0 # 2. Extract Scale sx = bufferdata[basefloatoffset + SCALEOFFSETFLOATS] sy = bufferdata[basefloatoffset + SCALEOFFSETFLOATS + 1] sz = bufferdata[basefloatoffset + SCALEOFFSETFLOATS + 2] # Scale Matrix S (diagonal) # S = [[sx, 0, 0], # [0, sy, 0], # [0, 0, sz]] # 3. Extract Rotation # Rotation is stored as IJKW (x,y,z,w) qx = bufferdata[basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS] qy = bufferdata[basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS + 1] qz = bufferdata[basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS + 2] qw = bufferdata[basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS + 3] # Compute Rotation Matrix R from Quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw) # Standard conversion from quaternion to rotation matrix # R = [[1 - 2(qy^2 + qz^2), 2(qxqy - qwqz), 2(qxqz + qwqy)], # [2(qxqy + qwqz), 1 - 2(qx^2 + qz^2), 2(qyqz - qwqx)], # [2(qxqz - qwqy), 2(qyqz + qwqx), 1 - 2(qx^2 + qy^2)]] qx2 = qx qx qy2 = qy qy qz2 = qz qz qw2 = qw qw r00 = 1 - 2 (qy2 + qz2) r01 = 2 (qx qy - qw qz) r02 = 2 (qx qz + qw qy) r10 = 2 (qx qy + qw qz) r11 = 1 - 2 (qx2 + qz2) r12 = 2 (qy qz - qw qx) r20 = 2 (qx qz - qw qy) r21 = 2 (qy qz + qw qx) r22 = 1 - 2 (qx2 + qy2) # 4. Compute M = R S # Since S is diagonal, Mij = Rij Sjj m00 = r00 sx m01 = r01 sy m02 = r02 sz m10 = r10 sx m11 = r11 sy m12 = r12 sz m20 = r20 sx m21 = r21 sy m22 = r22 sz # 5. Compute Covariance C = M M^T # C is symmetric, store upper triangle c00 = m00 m00 + m01 m01 + m02 m02 c01 = m00 m10 + m01 m11 + m02 m12 c02 = m00 m20 + m01 m21 + m02 m22 c11 = m10 m10 + m11 m11 + m12 m12 c12 = m10 m20 + m11 m21 + m12 m22 c22 = m20 m20 + m21 m21 + m22 m22 covariancearray[6 i] = c00 covariancearray[6 i + 1] = c01 covariancearray[6 i + 2] = c02 covariancearray[6 i + 3] = c11 covariancearray[6 i + 4] = c12 covariancearray[6 i + 5] = c22 return covariancearray, colorarray Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quaternion Order: The source explicitly notes that the rotation data is stored as IJKW (x, y, z, w). Standard libraries often expect WXYZ or XYZW. Misinterpreting this order will result in incorrect rotation matrices and thus incorrect covariance shapes. Matrix Multiplication Order: The covariance is derived from M = R \times S. Since S is diagonal, this scales the columns of R. If S were applied as S \times R, the rows would be scaled, which is incorrect for transforming a sphere into an ellipsoid defined by scale axes aligned with the rotation basis. Precision: The input color is Uint8. Normalization by 255.0 introduces floating-point representation errors, but this is standard for color data. The covariance elements are Float32, which may lose precision for very small or very large scales, potentially affecting rendering stability at extreme zoom levels. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians. The computation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N). The output buffers require 10 \times N \times 4 bytes (6 floats for covariance + 4 floats for color). Performance: This preprocessing moves computation from the GPU fragment/vertex shader to the CPU (or a compute shader) during asset loading. This reduces the per-frame cost of rendering, as the shader only needs to sample the pre-computed covariance and color values. Strengths: Eliminates per-pixel or per-vertex matrix multiplication and quaternion-to-matrix conversion during rendering. Simplifies the shader logic. Limitations: Requires storing additional data (covariance matrix) in memory. If the Gaussians are dynamic (e.g., animated), this pre-computation must be repeated every frame or whenever parameters change, negating the benefit. This method is part of the implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time web rendering, specifically within the context of Three.js and A-Frame viewers. It is based on the work of Mark Kellogg (GaussianSplats3D) and Kevin Kwok (WebGL implementation of Gaussian Splatting). The technique leverages the fact that the covariance matrix for a Gaussian splat is constant for a given set of scale and rotation parameters, allowing it to be pre-computed. akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, https://github.com/akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Covariance Factorisation
head: RQ Decomposition for Covariance, Rotation and Scale Parameterization
body: Covariance Factorisation parameterizes the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix by decomposing it into unconstrained rotation and scale components, ensuring the resulting matrix remains positive semi-definite (PSD) during gradient-based optimization. This approach distinguishes itself from direct covariance optimization by decoupling geometric shape (scale) from orientation (rotation), allowing stable unconstrained gradient descent without requiring projection steps to enforce PSD constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unconstrained optimization variables representing rotation and scale. Output: A 3 \times 3 symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix \Sigma. Data Structures: The method relies on two primary parameter sets per Gaussian primitive: 1. Scale (s): A vector of 3 values representing the standard deviations along the principal axes. 2. Rotation (R): A representation of orientation, typically derived from a quaternion or rotation matrix parameters. Steps: 1. Parameterize Scale: The scale parameters are optimized directly. To ensure physical plausibility and numerical stability, the diagonal elements of the resulting covariance are often constrained. Specifically, the standard deviation \sigma is parameterized as \sigma{min} + \text{softplus}(x), where x is the unconstrained optimization variable and \sigma{min} is a floor value. 2. Parameterize Rotation: The rotation parameters are optimized unconstrained. These are converted into a rotation matrix R (or quaternion) representing the orientation of the Gaussian ellipsoid. 3. Reconstruct Covariance: The covariance matrix \Sigma is reconstructed from the scale and rotation parameters. The standard reconstruction formula is: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T where S is a diagonal matrix containing the scale values. This factorization guarantees that \Sigma is positive semi-definite by construction, as it is formed by the product of a matrix and its transpose scaled by positive values. Formulas: Covariance Reconstruction: \Sigma = R \cdot \text{diag}(s)^2 \cdot R^T. Scale Floor: \sigmai = \sigma{min} + \text{softplus}(si). \sigma{min} = 1/\sqrt{12} voxels. \text{softplus}(x) = \ln(1 + e^x). Parameters: \sigma{min}: Minimum standard deviation, set to 1/\sqrt{12} voxels. This value represents the standard deviation of a uniform voxel, ensuring no splat is narrower than a voxel’s own spread. a{max}: A configurable maximum amplitude bound. Amplitudes are made non-negative by a softplus activation and upper-bounded by a{max}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Scales: If scale parameters approach zero, the Gaussian becomes singular. The \sigma{min} floor prevents this. Rotation Singularities: Standard Euler angle parameterizations can suffer from gimbal lock. Quaternions or RQ decomposition are preferred for stable optimization. Precision: The reconstruction R S S^T R^T must be computed with sufficient precision to maintain symmetry. Numerical noise may break exact symmetry, requiring a symmetrization step (\Sigma = (\Sigma + \Sigma^T)/2) before use in rendering. A method to parameterize the covariance matrix using Cholesky decomposition to guarantee positive-definiteness by construction. It stores D(D+1)/2 elements per splat (6 for 3D). The diagonal of the covariance is parameterised as \sigma{min} + \text{softplus}(\cdot), where \sigma{min} = 1/\sqrt{12} voxels, ensuring no splat is narrower than a voxel’s own spread. Amplitudes are made non-negative by a softplus activation and upper-bounded by a configurable maximum a{max}. This variant is chosen when strict positive-definiteness is required without relying on rotation-scale factorization, potentially offering a more compact representation for certain optimization landscapes. Time Complexity: The reconstruction of \Sigma from R and S is O(1) per Gaussian (constant time for fixed dimension 3). Memory Complexity: Stores 3 scale values and 3 rotation parameters (e.g., quaternion) per Gaussian, totaling 6 values, compared to 6 values for the full symmetric covariance matrix. However, the rotation parameters may require more bits for precision. Strengths: Ensures PSD property automatically, simplifying optimization by removing constraints. Compatible with standard unconstrained optimizers like Adam. Limitations: The separation of rotation and scale can lead to non-intuitive gradients if the scale is very small or rotation is near singularities. The Cholesky variant requires careful handling of the diagonal floor. When to use: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines where stable optimization is critical. When not to use: If memory is extremely tight and the overhead of rotation parameterization is prohibitive, or if the scene has extreme anisotropy that makes rotation-scale decoupling unstable. Originating from the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework, this method was introduced to enable fast, high-quality rendering of radiance fields. The factorization of the covariance into rotation and scale was identified as one of the four key components making 3DGS viable, alongside spherical-harmonic colour, EWA projection, and tile-based rasterization. The Cholesky parameterization variant has been explored in specialized applications such as microscopy and scientific data visualization (e.g., Luxar) to handle multidimensional data with strict positivity constraints. name: 3D Gaussian Data Layout
head: 3DGS Parameter Storage, Gaussian Struct Definition, GaussianModel, GaussianModel PyTorch Module
body: The 3D Gaussian Data Layout defines the memory organization and field definitions for a single 3D Gaussian primitive within differentiable volume rendering pipelines. It serves as the fundamental unit of storage for position, scale, orientation, opacity, and color (spherical harmonics) data, enabling efficient GPU access and optimization. It differs from the higher-level GaussianSet Data Structure by focusing on the raw parameter representation rather than the container logic, and from Gaussian Data Packing by retaining floating-point precision for optimization rather than compacting into fixed-size integer buffers for rendering. The layout stores per-primitive attributes in contiguous arrays to facilitate batched processing and differentiable updates. Two primary implementations exist: a Rust-based struct for rendering pipelines and a PyTorch module for optimization. Input: None for the static layout definition. For initialization, inputs may include a point cloud (XYZ, RGB). Output: A data structure instance containing raw parameters ready for covariance computation or rendering. Defined in, the Gaussian struct uses nalgebra types. It stores precomputed 3D covariance to avoid recomputation during rasterization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. #[derive(Clone, Debug)] pub struct Gaussian { pub position: na::Vector3<f32>, // x, y, z pub scale: na::Vector3<f32>, // scale0, scale1, scale2 pub opacity: f32, // Linear opacity [0, 1] pub rotation: na::Quaternion<f32>, // w, x, y, z pub sh: na::SVector<f32, 48>, // Spherical Harmonics coefficients pub cov3d: na::Matrix3<f32>, // 3x3 symmetric covariance matrix } position: na::Vector3<f32> (x, y, z). scale: na::Vector3<f32> (scale0, scale1, scale2). Represents linear scale factors. opacity: f32. Linear opacity value. rotation: na::Quaternion<f32> (w, x, y, z). Unit quaternion. sh: na::SVector<f32, 48>. Stores up to degree 3 spherical harmonics. shdim: The number of coefficients depends on the degree. DC (degree 0) uses 3 coefficients. Degree 1 uses 12. Degree 2 uses 27. Degree 3 uses 48. cov3d: na::Matrix3<f32>. Precomputed 3D covariance matrix. Defined in, the GaussianModel class stores parameters in log-space or raw tensors to ensure valid ranges during gradient descent. xyz: torch.Tensor of shape (N, 3). Float tensor for positions. featuresdc: torch.Tensor of shape (N, 1, 3). Float tensor for 0th degree spherical harmonics (base colors). scaling: torch.Tensor of shape (N, 3). Float tensor for log-scales. rotation: torch.Tensor of shape (N, 4). Float tensor for quaternions. opacity: torch.Tensor of shape (N, 1). Float tensor for log-odds opacity. When accessing parameters from the PyTorch optimization layout: 1. Get Scaling: Compute linear scale from log-space. \text{scale} = \text{clamp}(\exp(\text{self.scaling}), \text{max}=10.0) This converts log-space scaling to linear space with an upper bound of 10.0. 2. Get Rotation: Normalize the quaternion. \text{rotation} = \text{normalize}(\text{self.rotation}) This ensures quaternions are unit-length. 3. Get Opacity: Convert log-odds to probability. \text{opacity} = \sigma(\text{self.opacity}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\text{self.opacity}}} This converts log-odds to probability space [0, 1]. To create a GaussianModel from a COLMAP point cloud: 1. Input xyz: (N, 3) numpy array of 3D points. 2. Input rgb: (N, 3) numpy array of colors, values between 0 and 1. 3. Initialize xyz with xyz. 4. Initialize featuresdc with rgb. 5. Initialize scaling, rotation, and opacity with default zeros or small random values (implementation details for initialization body are not fully specified in the source, but gradients are applied to these tensors). Quaternion Normalization: Quaternions must be normalized after every update step to remain valid rotations. Scale Clamping: Exponential scaling can explode; an upper bound (e.g., 10.0) is applied to prevent numerical instability. Opacity Range: Log-odds initialization should avoid extreme values that saturate the sigmoid function immediately. SH Dimension: The size of the sh vector must match the active spherical harmonics degree. Using degree 3 requires 48 coefficients, while degree 0 requires only 3. The Gaussian Data Structure is the primary in-memory container for 3D Gaussian primitives in differentiable volume rendering pipelines, organizing per-primitive attributes into contiguous arrays for efficient GPU access and optimization. It differs from the raw 3D Gaussian Data Layout by providing a flat, list-based abstraction that facilitates dynamic resizing and batched processing, distinct from the tightly packed bit-level formats of Gaussian Data Packing. Gaussian Data Packing is a method for compacting 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives into a dense, GPU-friendly binary buffer for efficient rendering and sorting. It solves the problem of memory alignment and bandwidth efficiency by interleaving position, covariance, and color data into a fixed-size uint32t array, while storing raw floating-point positions in a separate parallel buffer. It is distinguished from its sibling Gaussian Data Structure by its specific bit-packing strategy for covariance matrices and its separation of position data into integer-reinterpreted and raw float formats. GeometryState contains contiguous memory blocks for P Gaussians, used during the rasterization phase. The layout includes: depths: float, size P. clamped: float, size P3. internalradii: float, size P. means2D: float, size P. cov3D: float, size P6 (symmetric 3x3 matrix stored as 6 elements). conicopacity: float, size P. rgb: float, size P3. tilestouched: uint32t, size P. scanningspace: Variable size, allocated via cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum. pointoffsets: uint32t, size P. Memory: The Rust struct uses approximately 3 \times 4 + 3 \times 4 + 4 + 4 \times 4 + 48 \times 4 + 9 \times 4 = 12 + 12 + 4 + 16 + 192 + 36 = 272 bytes per Gaussian (assuming Quaternion is 4 floats and Matrix3 is 9 floats, though nalgebra may have alignment padding). The PyTorch layout stores parameters in separate tensors, which may incur overhead due to tensor metadata and potential fragmentation if not managed carefully. Performance: Contiguous memory layout (as in Rust struct) facilitates efficient GPU access and vectorized operations. The PyTorch layout is optimized for gradient computation and dynamic resizing during training. Scalability: The layout supports N Gaussians. The scanningspace in GeometryState scales with P, requiring dynamic allocation. Strengths: Simple, direct mapping to mathematical parameters. Precomputed covariance (Rust) saves computation during rendering. Log-space parameters (PyTorch) stabilize optimization. Limitations: High memory usage for high-degree spherical harmonics (48 floats per Gaussian). Not optimized for bandwidth during rendering compared to packed formats. The 3D Gaussian Data Layout originates from the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework for differentiable volume rendering. The Rust implementation is part of an unofficial repository (thomasantony/splat) demonstrating efficient rendering pipelines. The PyTorch implementation is part of metin-yat/mini-splat, providing a minimal optimization setup. The GeometryState layout is from NorahCadeJS/GAI-GS, integrating CUDA-specific optimizations. These implementations adapt the core 3DGS primitives for specific hardware and software constraints. thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) metin-yat/mini-splat, https://github.com/metin-yat/mini-splat, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) NorahCadeJS/GAI-GS, https://github.com/NorahCadeJS/GAI-GS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Data Structure
head: GaussianList
body: The Gaussian Data Structure is the primary in-memory container for 3D Gaussian primitives in differentiable volume rendering pipelines, organizing per-primitive attributes into contiguous arrays for efficient GPU access and optimization. It differs from the raw 3D Gaussian Data Layout by providing a flat, list-based abstraction that facilitates dynamic resizing and batched processing, distinct from the tightly packed bit-level formats of Gaussian Data Packing. Inputs: A collection of N 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. Outputs: A structured data object containing contiguous buffers for all primitive attributes, ready for rendering or gradient-based optimization. Data Structures: The structure consists of two main views: the logical Gaussian struct and the physical GaussianList container. 1. Gaussian Struct (Logical Primitive): position: Vector3<f32> (3 floats: x, y, z) scale: Vector3<f32> (3 floats: sx, sy, sz) opacity: f32 (1 float) rotation: Quaternion<f32> (4 floats: w, x, y, z) sh: SVector<f32, 48> (48 floats, max for degree 3) cov3d: Matrix3<f32> (9 floats, symmetric positive definite covariance matrix) 2. GaussianList Struct (Physical Container): positions: Matrix4xX<f32> (Size 4 \times N). Stores x, y, z in rows 0-2; row 3 is unused/padding. scales: Matrix3xX<f32> (Size 3 \times N). Stores sx, sy, sz in rows 0-2. opacities: DVector<f32> (Size N). rotations: Matrix4xX<f32> (Size 4 \times N). Stores quaternion components w, x, y, z in rows 0-3. sh: Matrix48xX<f32> (Size 48 \times N). Flat array of SH coefficients. numgaussians: usize (Count N). cov3d: Matrix3xX<f32> (Size 3 \times N). Stores the 9 elements of the symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix. SH Coefficient Layout: The SH coefficients are stored in a flat array of size 48 (for maximum degree 3). The layout interleaves color channels per degree: C0R, C0B, C0G, C1R, C1B, C1G, \dots. Steps to Construct GaussianList from Primitives: 1. Initialize N primitives. 2. Allocate buffers in GaussianList based on N. 3. Iterate through each primitive i from 0 to N-1: a. Write position[i] to positions at indices i, i+N, i+2N. b. Write scale[i] to scales at indices i, i+N, i+2N. c. Write opacity[i] to opacities at index i. d. Write rotation[i] (quaternion) to rotations at indices i, i+N, i+2N, i+3N. e. Write sh[i] (48 floats) to sh at indices i to i+47N (strided by N). f. Compute cov3d[i] from scale and rotation if not precomputed, and write to cov3d buffer. 4. Set numgaussians = N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def creategaussianlist(primitives: List[Gaussian]) -> GaussianList: N = len(primitives) if N == 0: return GaussianList(numgaussians=0) # Allocate buffers # positions: 4xN, scales: 3xN, rotations: 4xN, sh: 48xN, cov3d: 3xN positions = zeros((4, N)) scales = zeros((3, N)) opacities = zeros(N) rotations = zeros((4, N)) sh = zeros((48, N)) cov3d = zeros((3, N)) for i in range(N): p = primitives[i] # Position positions[0, i] = p.position.x positions[1, i] = p.position.y positions[2, i] = p.position.z # Scale scales[0, i] = p.scale.x scales[1, i] = p.scale.y scales[2, i] = p.scale.z # Opacity opacities[i] = p.opacity # Rotation (Quaternion w, x, y, z) rotations[0, i] = p.rotation.w rotations[1, i] = p.rotation.x rotations[2, i] = p.rotation.y rotations[3, i] = p.rotation.z # SH Coefficients (48 floats) sh[:, i] = p.sh # Assuming p.sh is array of 48 floats # Cov3d (3x3 matrix flattened to 3 rows) # Note: cov3d is symmetric, so only 6 unique values, but stored as 9 in 3xN matrix cov = computecov3d(p.scale, p.rotation) cov3d[0, i] = cov[0, 0] cov3d[1, i] = cov[0, 1] cov3d[2, i] = cov[0, 2] # Rows 1 and 2 would store the rest, but standard layout often stores full 3x3 # Based on Matrix3xX<f32>, it implies 3 rows of N columns. # A 3x3 matrix has 9 elements. If stored as 3xN, it likely stores the 3 rows of the matrix # for each Gaussian? No, Matrix3xX usually means 3 rows, X columns. # If X=N, then each column is a Gaussian. But a Gaussian has a 3x3 matrix. # This implies the buffer stores the 3x3 matrix elements. # Common layout: 3 rows, N columns. Row 0: M00, Row 1: M01, Row 2: M02? # Or Row 0: M00, M10, M20? # Given "Matrix3xX", it is 3 rows. If it holds the full 3x3, it needs 9 rows or a different structure. # However, the source says "cov3d (Matrix3xX<f32>)". # In many implementations, cov3d is computed on the fly or stored as 6 values. # If strictly 3xN, it might store only the upper triangle or specific components. # Let's assume standard 3x3 storage requires 9 rows or the source implies a specific packing. # Given the ambiguity, we store the 3 rows of the 3x3 matrix for each Gaussian? # Actually, if it's 3xN, and N is the number of gaussians, we can't fit 9 values per gaussian in 3 rows. # It is likely that cov3d is not stored as a full 3x3 in this specific list structure, # or it is stored as 3 rows of N, where each row corresponds to a specific component of the covariance? # Let's stick to the source definition: cov3d is Matrix3xX. # We will assume it stores the 3 diagonal elements or a specific subset if space is constrained, # but typically cov3d is 9 floats. # Correction: In the source, cov3d is listed as Matrix3xX. # This might be a typo for Matrix9xX or it stores only the 3x3 upper triangle in a specific way. # For implementation, if cov3d is needed, it is often recomputed from scale and rotation. # If stored, it is likely 9 floats. # We will note that the exact packing of the 9 elements into 3 rows is not specified beyond the type name. # Assuming standard row-major storage of the 3x3 matrix, 9 rows would be needed. # If restricted to 3 rows, it might store only the 3 diagonal elements or the source implies a different layout. # Given the constraint to implement from text, and the ambiguity, we mark it as not fully specified for the 9 elements. pass return GaussianList( positions=positions, scales=scales, opacities=opacities, rotations=rotations, sh=sh, numgaussians=N, cov3d=cov3d) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SH Degree: The buffer size for SH is fixed at 48 (degree 3). If lower degrees are used, the remaining coefficients are zero-padded. Covariance Storage: The exact mapping of the 9 elements of the 3 \times 3 covariance matrix into the Matrix3xX buffer is not explicitly detailed in the sources beyond the type name. Implementers should verify if this stores the full matrix (requiring 9 rows) or a compressed form. Precision: All attributes are stored as f32 (32-bit float). A density control mechanism that uses a frequency-aware mask and photometric loss to compute densification and pruning scores for Gaussian primitives, reducing redundancy and improving fidelity compared to vanilla 3DGS [3396-composite-error-map-and-densification-pruning-scoring.md]. Dynamic Buffer Management handles the lifecycle of 3D Gaussian splat data structures during training by automatically resizing memory buffers when the number of active Gaussians exceeds current capacity. It solves the problem of frequent reallocation and data copying overhead by using a fixed over-allocation factor, differing from static allocation by adapting to scene complexity and from CUDA Virtual Memory management by relying on standard buffer reallocation rather than virtual memory mapping. A method that leverages neural signed distance functions (SDFs) for surface reconstruction to recover more detailed mesh structures. A method that leverages neural signed distance functions (SDFs) for surface reconstruction to recover more detailed mesh structures. A technique that introduces a learnable per-Gaussian scalar factor to reparameterize effective Gaussian scales, providing an optimization pathway for adapting primitive extent while retaining existing tile-culling rules. Step: Initialize a learnable scalar \betai \in \mathbb{R} to zero for each Gaussian primitive. Optimize \betai jointly with other Gaussian attributes using the Adam optimizer. Formula: The effective 2D covariance is modulated: \tilde{\Sigma}i^{2D} = \gammai^2 \Sigmai^{2D}, where \gammai = \text{sigmoid}(\betai). The gradient of the scale factor is \frac{\partial \gammai}{\partial \betai} = 2 \cdot \text{sigmoid}(\betai) \cdot (1 - \text{sigmoid}(\betai)). Comparison: Unlike vanilla 3DGS where covariance is fixed by base scales Si and rotation Ri, this method scales the covariance by \gammai^2, changing the overall extent while keeping anisotropic axis ratios governed by the base scales. Step: fromSplats iterates over a collection of Splat objects, extracts each parameter via getters, and writes them into the corresponding FloatBuffer at indices i \times \text{stride} + \text{component}. Layout: SplatData stores splat parameters in separate contiguous FloatBuffers: positions (size N \times 3), scales (size N \times 3), rotations (size N \times 4), opacities (size N), and spherical harmonics (size N \times \text{shDimensions} \times 3). Step: Scales are stored internally in log-space. When writing to buffers, linear values are converted to log-space via \log(). When reading for rendering or optimization, log-space values are converted to linear via \exp(). Formula: Linear scale is recovered from stored log-scale: s{\text{linear}} = \exp(s{\text{log}}). Step: Nested loops iterate over splat index i and coefficient index d. For each coefficient, the x, y, z components are written to buffer indices ((i \times \text{shDimensions}) + d) \times 3 + 0, +1, +2. Parameter: \text{shDimensions}: Total number of SH coefficients for a given degree, calculated via Splats.dimensionsForDegree(shDegree). Layout: SH coefficients are stored in a FloatBuffer of size N \times \text{shDimensions} \times 3. The memory order is grouped by splat, then by coefficient index, then by spatial dimension (x, y, z). A robust monocular RGB 3DGS-SLAM for dynamic in-the-wild scenes. Uses a shallow MLP over DINOv2 features to predict an uncertainty map that guides dynamic-object removal during tracking and mapping, feeding uncertainty-aware dense bundle adjustment and Gaussian-map optimization. Parameter: Input: DINOv2 features. History: Marked as 2026 SOTA update. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Access is O(1) per attribute due to contiguous memory layout. Memory Complexity: O(N \times C) where C is the constant size of attributes per Gaussian (approx. 60-70 floats for degree 3 SH). Performance: Contiguous buffers enable efficient vectorized memory access on GPUs, critical for the high-throughput rendering of millions of Gaussians. Strengths: Simple to implement, compatible with standard GPU memory allocators, easy to resize dynamically. Limitations: Fixed SH size (48) may waste memory for lower degrees. Covariance storage layout ambiguity may require implementation-specific decisions. When to Use: General-purpose 3DGS training and rendering where dynamic primitive counts are expected. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth is extremely constrained and bit-packing (see Gaussian Data Packing) is required. name: GSPull
head: GSDF / GSPull

name: Composite Error Map and Densification/Pruning Scoring
head: EffGS density control, Frequency-aware mask scoring
body: This method provides a density control mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a frequency-aware mask and photometric loss to compute densification and pruning scores for Gaussian primitives. It reduces redundancy and improves fidelity compared to vanilla 3DGS by replacing the original PUP 3D-GS pruning method, which requires storing a large Hessian matrix for every Gaussian, with a sensitivity-based metric that depends on the scalar projected Gaussian value. This reparameterization reduces storage requirements by 36×, enabling pruning to occur directly within the training pipeline. Inputs: Set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}t at update step t. K distinct training views sampled uniformly without replacement. Rendered images I{\text{rend}}^j and ground-truth images I{\text{gt}}^j for each sampled view j. Frequency-aware mask M{\text{freq}}^j for each view j. Parameters: \tau \in (0, 1) (error threshold), \taup \in [0, 1) (pruning score threshold), \taud \ge 0 (densification score threshold), \taus > 0 (scale threshold), \rho \in [0, 1] (pruning sampling ratio), \lambda{\text{dssim}} (SSIM weight), \omega(t) (densification schedule). Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}{t+1}. Removal set \mathcal{R}t and Densification set \mathcal{D}t. Data Structures: For each Gaussian i, store: opacity oi, scale-modulation factor \gammai, unconstrained modulation parameter \betai (where \gammai = 2 \text{sigmoid}(\betai)), position, covariance, spherical harmonics coefficients. For each view j, store: pixel grid \mathcal{P}j, frequency-aware mask M{\text{freq}}^j, rendered image I{\text{rend}}^j, ground-truth image I{\text{gt}}^j. For each Gaussian i and view j, compute: projected radius ri^j, set of contributing pixels \Omegai^j. Steps: 1. Compute Active Primitives: For each Gaussian i \in \mathcal{G}t: Determine projected radius ri^j for each sampled view j \in \{1, \dots, K\}. Define \mathcal{V}i = \{j: ri^j > 0\}. Let |\mathcal{V}i| = \sum{j=1}^K \mathbb{I}[ri^j > 0]. Define active set \mathcal{A}t = \{i \in \mathcal{G}t: |\mathcal{V}i| > 0\}. If \mathcal{A}t = \emptyset, skip density control. 2. Compute Composite Error Map: For each sampled view j: Compute raw per-pixel RGB reconstruction error: e^j(\mathbf{u}) = \frac{1}{3} \sum{c=1}^3 \left| I{\text{rend},c}^j(\mathbf{u}) - I{\text{gt},c}^j(\mathbf{u}) \right| Normalize error over pixel grid \mathcal{P}j: \bar{e}^j = \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{P}j}[e^j] where \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{P}j} is min-max normalization over \mathcal{P}j, mapping constant inputs to zero. Compute composite error mask: M{\text{err}}^j(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbb{I} \left[ \bar{e}^j(\mathbf{u}) > \tau \vee \left( M{\text{freq}}^j(\mathbf{u}) = 1 \wedge \bar{e}^j(\mathbf{u}) > 0.5\tau \right) \right] 3. Compute Weighted Pixel Counts: For each Gaussian i \in \mathcal{A}t and view j \in \mathcal{V}i: Compute weighted pixel count: ni^j = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \Omegai^j} M{\text{err}}^j(\mathbf{u}) where \Omegai^j is the set of pixels where Gaussian i contributes during compositing in view j. 4. Compute Photometric Loss: For each sampled view j: Compute mean L1 error: \mathcal{L}1^j = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}j|} \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{P}j} e^j(\mathbf{u}) Compute image-level photometric loss: E{\text{photo}}^j = (1 - \lambda{\text{dssim}}) \mathcal{L}1^j + \lambda{\text{dssim}} \left( 1 - \text{SSIM}(I{\text{rend}}^j, I{\text{gt}}^j) \right) 5. Compute Pruning Scores: For each Gaussian i \in \mathcal{A}t: Compute summed, loss-weighted count: Qi = \sum{j \in \mathcal{V}i} ni^j E{\text{photo}}^j Normalize pruning score over active set: sp^i = \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{A}t}Q 6. Compute Densification Scores: For each Gaussian i \in \mathcal{A}t: Compute valid-view average count: Ci = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}i|} \sum{j \in \mathcal{V}i} ni^j Compute densification score: sd^i(t) = \omega(t) Ci where \omega(t) is a positive, nondecreasing clipped-linear schedule over the densification interval. 7. Pruning: Identify mandatory removals: \mathcal{H}t = \{i \in \mathcal{A}t: oi < 0.1 \vee \gammai < 0.01\} Identify candidates: \mathcal{P}t = \{i \in \mathcal{A}t \setminus \mathcal{H}t: sp^i > \taup\} Sample bt = \lfloor \rho |\mathcal{P}t| \rfloor candidates without replacement using weights proportional to sp^i. Removal set: \mathcal{R}t = \mathcal{H}t \cup \text{sampled candidates}. 8. Densification: Select surviving active primitives with sd^i(t) > \taud. For each selected primitive i: If largest base-scale component < \taus: clone and shift along positional gradient. Otherwise: replace with two smaller Gaussians. New primitives inherit parent's unconstrained modulation parameter \betai \in \mathbb{R}, with \gammai = 2 \text{sigmoid}(\betai) \in (0, 2). Remaining attributes follow clone/split updates. 9. Execution: Apply pruning first if both pruning and densification coincide. New primitives are scored only at the next density update. Primitives outside \mathcal{A}t are unaffected. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositeerrormapanddensitycontrol(Gt, K, views, tau, taup, taud, taus, rho, lambdadssim, omegat): """ Gt: list of Gaussian primitives K: number of sampled views views: list of view objects with attributes: id, pixelgrid, freqmask, renderedimg, gtimg tau: error threshold taup: pruning score threshold taud: densification score threshold taus: scale threshold rho: pruning sampling ratio lambdadssim: SSIM weight omegat: densification schedule value at step t """ # Step 1: Compute Active Primitives At = [] Vimap = {} # Map Gaussian index to set of view indices rijmap = {} # Map (Gaussian index, view index) to projected radius for i, gauss in enumerate(Gt): validviews = [] for j, view in enumerate(views): rij = getprojectedradius(gauss, view) rijmap[(i, j)] = rij if rij > 0: validviews.append(j) Vimap[i] = validviews if len(validviews) > 0: At.append(i) if not At: return Gt, [], [] # Step 2: Compute Composite Error Map Merrmap = {} # Map view index to error mask for j, view in enumerate(views): ej = computerawerror(view.renderedimg, view.gtimg) ejnorm = minmaxnormalize(ej, view.pixelgrid) Merr = indicatorfunction(ejnorm > tau | (view.freqmask == 1 & ejnorm > 0.5 tau)) Merrmap[j] = Merr # Step 3: Compute Weighted Pixel Counts nijmap = {} # Map (Gaussian index, view index) to weighted count for i in At: for j in Vimap[i]: Omegaij = getcontributingpixels(Gt[i], views[j]) nij = sum(Merrmap[j][u] for u in Omegaij) nijmap[(i, j)] = nij # Step 4: Compute Photometric Loss Ephotomap = {} # Map view index to photometric loss for j, view in enumerate(views): L1j = meanl1error(view.renderedimg, view.gtimg) SSIMj = computessim(view.renderedimg, view.gtimg) Ephoto = (1 - lambdadssim) L1j + lambdadssim (1 - SSIMj) Ephotomap[j] = Ephoto # Step 5: Compute Pruning Scores Qimap = {} # Map Gaussian index to Qi for i in At: Qi = sum(nijmap[(i, j)] Ephotomap[j] for j in Vimap[i]) Qimap[i] = Qi Qvalues = [Qimap[i] for i in At] Qnorm = minmaxnormalize(Qvalues, At) spmap = {i: Qnorm[idx] for idx, i in enumerate(At)} # Step 6: Compute Densification Scores Cimap = {} # Map Gaussian index to Ci for i in At: Ci = sum(nijmap[(i, j)] for j in Vimap[i]) / len(Vimap[i]) Cimap[i] = Ci sdmap = {i: omegat Cimap[i] for i in At} # Step 7: Pruning Ht = [i for i in At if Gt[i].opacity < 0.1 or Gt[i].gamma < 0.01] Pt = [i for i in At if i not in Ht and spmap[i] > taup] bt = floor(rho len(Pt)) if bt > 0: sampledcandidates = samplewithoutreplacement(Pt, bt, weights=[spmap[i] for i in Pt]) else: sampledcandidates = [] Rt = Ht + sampledcandidates # Step 8: Densification Dt = [i for i in At if i not in Rt and sdmap[i] > taud] newgaussians = [] for i in Dt: if maxbasescale(Gt[i]) < taus: newg = cloneandshift(Gt[i]) else: newg1, newg2 = split(Gt[i]) newgaussians.append(newg1) newgaussians.append(newg2) continue newgaussians.append(newg) # Step 9: Execution # Remove primitives in Rt Gnew = [g for idx, g in enumerate(Gt) if idx not in Rt] # Add new primitives Gnew.extend(newgaussians) return Gnew, Rt, Dt def getprojectedradius(gauss, view): # Placeholder for rasterizer call pass def getcontributingpixels(gauss, view): # Placeholder for compositing logic pass def computerawerror(renderedimg, gtimg): return (1/3) sum(abs(renderedimg[u, c] - gtimg[u, c]) for u in renderedimg.shape for c in range(3)) def minmaxnormalize(data, indices): minval = min(data[i] for i in indices) maxval = max(data[i] for i in indices) if maxval == minval: return {i: 0 for i in indices} return {i: (data[i] - minval) / (maxval - minval) for i in indices} def indicatorfunction(condition): return 1 if condition else 0 def meanl1error(renderedimg, gtimg): return sum(computerawerror(renderedimg, gtimg)[u] for u in renderedimg.shape) / len(renderedimg.shape) def computessim(renderedimg, gtimg): # Placeholder for SSIM computation pass def samplewithoutreplacement(population, k, weights): # Placeholder for weighted sampling pass def cloneandshift(gauss): # Placeholder for cloning logic pass def split(gauss): # Placeholder for splitting logic pass def maxbasescale(gauss): # Placeholder for scale extraction pass The Efficient Pruning Score is a sensitivity-based metric used to identify and remove redundant 3D Gaussian primitives during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and inefficient gradient flow associated with the original PUP 3D-GS pruning method, which requires storing a large Hessian matrix for every Gaussian. By reparameterizing the sensitivity score to depend on the scalar projected Gaussian value rather than the full 3D spatial parameters, it reduces storage requirements by 36×, enabling pruning to occur directly within the training pipeline. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sampled views K, the number of primitives |\mathcal{G}t|, and the resolution of the views. Computing the error map and masks is O(K \cdot |\mathcal{P}j|). Computing scores is O(|\mathcal{A}t| \cdot K). Pruning and densification are O(|\mathcal{A}t|). Memory Complexity: Reduced by 36× compared to PUP 3D-GS due to the scalar projected Gaussian value dependency. No Hessian matrix storage required. Performance: Improves fidelity compared to vanilla 3DGS by reducing redundancy. Strengths: Efficient memory usage, direct integration into training pipeline, improved fidelity. Limitations: Requires sampling views and computing error maps, which adds computational overhead. When to use: When memory is a constraint and high fidelity is required. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and memory is not a bottleneck. Originated in EffGS: Efficient and High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting. It builds on Gaussian Data Structure and is related to Dynamic Buffer Management. name: Efficient Pruning Score
head: Speedy-Splat Pruning Score
body:
The Efficient Pruning Score is a sensitivity-based metric used to identify and remove redundant 3D Gaussian primitives during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and inefficient gradient flow associated with the original PUP 3D-GS pruning method, which requires storing a large Hessian matrix for every Gaussian. By reparameterizing the sensitivity score to depend on the scalar projected Gaussian value rather than the full 3D spatial parameters, it reduces storage requirements by 36×, enabling pruning to occur directly within the training pipeline. Inputs: The set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{G1, \dots, GN\}. The set of training camera poses \mathcal{P}{gt}. The rendered image gradients with respect to the projected Gaussian values, 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi), computed during the standard backward pass of the differentiable renderer. Outputs: A scalar pruning score 	ilde{U}i for each Gaussian Gi. A binary mask or list of Gaussians to be removed based on a threshold. Pruning Score Buffer: An array of size N (number of Gaussians) storing the accumulated score 	ilde{U}i for each Gaussian. This replaces the N 	imes 36 matrix required by the original PUP 3D-GS method. Gradient Accumulator: During the backward pass, the gradient 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) is squared and added to the corresponding entry in the Pruning Score Buffer. The original PUP 3D-GS sensitivity score Ui is defined as the log determinant of the second-order approximation of the L2 reconstruction error with respect to the mean \mui and scaling si parameters: Ui = \log \left| 
abla{\mui,si}^2 L2 ight| = \log \left| \sum{\phi \in \mathcal{P}{gt}} 
abla{\mui,si} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) 
abla{\mui,si} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi)^T ight| where 
abla{\mui,si} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) is a vector of gradients with respect to the 3D parameters. The Efficient Pruning Score 	ilde{U}i reparameterizes this by computing the Hessian approximation with respect to the 2D projected value gi of the Gaussian at pixel p: 	ilde{U}i = \log \left| \sum{\phi \in \mathcal{P}{gt}} 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi)^T ight| Since gi is a scalar at each pixel, the term inside the determinant is a 1 	imes 1 matrix (a scalar squared). Furthermore, because the logarithm is monotonically increasing, the log determinant simplifies to a sum of squared gradients: 	ilde{U}i = \sum{\phi \in \mathcal{P}{gt}} 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi)^2 Pruning Threshold: Not explicitly defined in the sources as a fixed constant. It is determined empirically to remove up to 90% of Gaussians while retaining high visual quality. Iteration Split: Soft Pruning: Applied during densification in the first 15,000 iterations. Hard Pruning: Applied after densification is completed, after iteration 15,000. The following pseudocode illustrates the integration of the Efficient Pruning Score into the training loop. It assumes access to the standard 3DGS backward pass which computes 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def efficientpruningbackwardpass(renderedimage, gtimage, gaussians, cameraposes): """ Standard differentiable rendering backward pass, modified to accumulate pruning scores. """ # 1. Compute image loss (e.g., L1 or L2) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, gtimage) # 2. Backward pass through the renderer # This computes gradients with respect to the projected Gaussian values gi # for each Gaussian contributing to each pixel. # gradientg: Dictionary or array mapping Gaussian index i to gradient value gradientg = backwardpassrenderer(renderedimage, gtimage, gaussians, cameraposes) # 3. Accumulate pruning scores # For each Gaussian i that contributed to the render for i, gradval in gradientg.items(): # Squared gradient is added to the score buffer # This corresponds to summing (gradgi)^2 over all pixels and views pruningscores[i] += gradval 2 return loss def prunegaussians(gaussians, pruningscores, currentiteration): """ Removes Gaussians based on the accumulated pruning score. """ # Determine pruning modality based on iteration if currentiteration < 15000: # Soft Pruning: During densification phase # Note: Implementation details for soft pruning thresholding are not specified # in the sources, but it uses the same score metric. pass else: # Hard Pruning: After densification phase # Identify Gaussians with high scores (high sensitivity/redundancy) # The sources state up to 90% can be pruned. threshold = determinethreshold(pruningscores, targetpruneratio=0.9) gaussianstoremove = [] for i, score in enumerate(pruningscores): if score > threshold: gaussianstoremove.append(i) # Remove Gaussians from the data structure removegaussians(gaussians, gaussianstoremove) # Reset scores for remaining Gaussians if necessary for future iterations # (Not explicitly stated, but implied by "accumulated" nature) Gradient Flow: The original PUP 3D-GS method requires back-propagating through the render kernel per pixel and then per Gaussian, which breaks the efficient gradient flow of 3DGS. The Efficient Pruning Score avoids this by using 
abla{gi} IG, which is already computed in the standard backward pass. Precision: The score relies on squared gradients. If gradients are very small, numerical precision issues may arise, though this is not explicitly detailed in the sources. Timing: Pruning must be carefully timed. Soft pruning occurs during densification (first 15,000 iterations), while hard pruning occurs after. Pruning too early or too late may affect convergence or final quality. Time Complexity: The score computation is O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels/views, but it is integrated into the existing backward pass, adding minimal overhead. Memory Complexity: Storage is proportional to N (one scalar per Gaussian), compared to N 	imes 36 for the original PUP 3D-GS method. This represents a 36× reduction in storage. Performance: The method allows pruning to be performed during training, reducing the final number of Gaussians by approximately 90% while maintaining high visual fidelity. This leads to increased rendering and training speeds. Strengths: Low memory overhead, compatible with standard 3DGS training pipeline, effective at removing redundant Gaussians. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of pruning thresholds and timing (soft vs. hard pruning). The Efficient Pruning Score was introduced in the "Speedy-Splat" paper, which builds upon the PUP 3D-GS method. PUP 3D-GS demonstrated that up to 90% of Gaussians could be pruned post-hoc, but its Hessian-based score was too memory-intensive for training-time use. Speedy-Splat addressed this by reparameterizing the score to use projected values, enabling efficient in-training pruning.
