name: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Preliminaries
head: Kerbl et al. 3DGS, Standard 3DGS representation, Vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting
body:
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a differentiable, point-based scene representation that replaces the implicit multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and ray-marched volume integration of NeRF with an explicit collection of 3D anisotropic Gaussians. It enables real-time synthesis of high-fidelity novel views via a GPU-friendly tile-based rasterizer that depth-sorts and alpha-composites 2D projections of these Gaussians. Unlike NeRF, which infers density and color at arbitrary points, 3DGS optimizes the parameters of a fixed set of Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients) to minimize photometric loss, using adaptive density control to adjust the number of primitives during training. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by a mean  oldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3	imes3}, an opacity scalar \alpha, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. A camera view defined by world-to-camera matrix W and projection parameters. Training images Iv for photometric supervision. Outputs: Rendered image \hat{I}v for a given camera view. Optimized Gaussian parameters after training. Each Gaussian primitive i stores the following parameters, which are optimized via gradient descent: Mean:  oldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (3D position). Rotation: A unit quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 representing orientation, normalized after each optimization step. Scale: A vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing scale along principal axes, stored in logarithmic space to ensure positivity. Opacity: A raw logit \alphai \in \mathbb{R}, mapped to [0,1] via a Sigmoid activation during rendering. Color: Spherical Harmonic coefficients up to degree \ell=3, resulting in 16 coefficients per channel (48 floats total per Gaussian). The covariance matrix \Sigmai is constructed from the rotation and scale parameters: \Sigmai = Ri \, \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{s}i)^2 \, Ri^	op where Ri is the rotation matrix derived from the unit quaternion qi. 1. Culling: Gaussians outside the view frustum or behind the camera are discarded. 2. Projection: Each Gaussian is projected into screen space. The 3D covariance \Sigma is transformed to a 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} using the Jacobian J of the perspective projection at the projected center  oldsymbol{\mu}c = W oldsymbol{\mu}: \Sigma{2D} = J \, W \, \Sigma \, W^	op J^	op \in \mathbb{R}^{2	imes2} This is an affine approximation (EWA splatting). 3. Bounding Box: A 2D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) is computed for each Gaussian based on \Sigma{2D}, typically expanded to cover the 3\sigma influence region (d^	op \Sigma^{-1} d \leq 9). 4. Tiling: The image is divided into tiles (default 16	imes16 pixels). Gaussians are binned into tile lists based on their AABB overlap. 5. Sorting: Within each tile, Gaussians are sorted front-to-back by their depth (center depth). 6. Rasterization and Compositing: For each pixel, the 2D Gaussian value is computed and alpha-composited with previously accumulated color. 3D Gaussian Function: The unnormalized Gaussian function at position \mathbf{x} is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\!\left(-	frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}- oldsymbol{\mu})^	op \Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}- oldsymbol{\mu})ight) 2D Gaussian Evaluation: For a pixel \mathbf{p}, the 2D Gaussian footprint Gi^{2D}(\mathbf{p}) is evaluated using the projected covariance \Sigma{2D} and the 2D displacement from the projected center. Alpha Compositing: The color C(\mathbf{p}) at pixel \mathbf{p} is computed by front-to-back alpha compositing of the sorted Gaussians N contributing to that pixel: C(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i\in N} \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{d}) \, \alphai \, Gi^{2D}(\mathbf{p}) \prod{j<i}\!\left(1 - \alphaj \, Gj^{2D}(\mathbf{p})ight) where \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{d}) is the view-dependent color evaluated from the SH coefficients for viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Loss Function: Training minimizes a combination of L1 loss and SSIM loss: \mathcal{L} = (1-\lambda)\,\|\hat{I}v - Iv\|1 + \lambda\,(1 - \mathrm{SSIM}(\hat{I}v, Iv)) with \lambda = 0.2. 1. Initialization: Start from a Structure-from-Motion (SfM) sparse point cloud (e.g., COLMAP). If no SfM is available, use random uniform points in the scene bound. 2. Optimization: Each iteration, pick a random training view, render \hat{I}v, compute loss, and backpropagate through the rasterizer to update parameters \{ oldsymbol{\mu}, q, s, \alpha, \mathrm{SH}\} using Adam. 3. Adaptive Density Control (ADC): Applied every K iterations (typically every 100 iterations within a window of 500–15,000): Densification: Where the 2D position gradient magnitude \|
abla{ oldsymbol{\mu}{2D}} L\| exceeds a threshold 	au
abla \sim 2	imes10^{-4}: Clone: For small Gaussians (under-reconstructed), duplicate and perturb position. Split: For large Gaussians (over-reconstructed), replace with two smaller Gaussians. Pruning: Remove Gaussians with opacity below \epsilon\alpha \sim 0.005, or those that are off-screen or have huge projections. Opacity Reset: Every 3000 iterations, reset opacity to 0.01 to escape local minima. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rendergaussians(gaussians, cameramatrix, imageshape, tilesize=16): """ Renders a set of 3D Gaussians to an image using tile-based rasterization. """ H, W = imageshape numtilesh = (H + tilesize - 1) // tilesize numtilesw = (W + tilesize - 1) // tilesize # Initialize output buffers C = np.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) T = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float32) # Precompute 2D projections and bounding boxes projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: mucam = cameramatrix[:3,:3] @ g.mu + cameramatrix[:3, 3] if mucam[2] <= 0.1: continue R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(g.q) S = np.diag(np.exp(g.s)) Sigma3D = R @ (S @ S.T) @ R.T z = mucam[2] fx, fy = 1.0, 1.0 cx, cy = W / 2.0, H / 2.0 J = np.array([ [fx/z, 0, -fxmucam[0]/(zz)], [0, fy/z, -fymucam[1]/(zz)], [0, 0, 0] ]) Wrot = cameramatrix[:3,:3] Sigma2D = J @ Wrot @ Sigma3D @ Wrot.T @ J.T eigenvalues, = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2D) maxextent = 3.0 np.sqrt(np.maximum(eigenvalues, 1e-6)) x2d = fx mucam[0] / mucam[2] + cx y2d = fy mucam[1] / mucam[2] + cy minx = int(max(0, x2d - maxextent[0])) maxx = int(min(W, x2d + maxextent[0])) miny = int(max(0, y2d - maxextent[1])) maxy = int(min(H, y2d + maxextent[1])) if minx >= maxx or miny >= maxy: continue projectedgaussians.append({ 'mu2d': np.array([x2d, y2d]), 'Sigma2D': Sigma2D, 'alpha': 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-g.alpha)), 'shcoeffs': g.shcoeffs, 'depth': mucam[2], 'bbox': (minx, maxx, miny, maxy) }) # Bin into tiles tiles = {} for i, pg in enumerate(projectedgaussians): minx, maxx, miny, maxy = pg['bbox'] tileminx = minx // tilesize tilemaxx = (maxx - 1) // tilesize tileminy = miny // tilesize tilemaxy = (maxy - 1) // tilesize for ty in range(tileminy, tilemaxy + 1): for tx in range(tileminx, tilemaxx + 1): key = (ty, tx) if key not in tiles: tiles[key] = [] tiles[key].append((i, pg['depth'])) # Sort and Composite per tile for (ty, tx), tiledata in tiles.items(): tiledata.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) ystart = ty tilesize xstart = tx tilesize for idx, depth in tiledata: pg = projectedgaussians[idx] mu2d = pg['mu2d'] Sigma2D = pg['Sigma2D'] alpha = pg['alpha'] shcoeffs = pg['shcoeffs'] minx, maxx, miny, maxy = pg['bbox'] minx = max(minx, xstart) maxx = min(maxx, xstart + tilesize) miny = max(miny, ystart) maxy = min(maxy, ystart + tilesize) ys, xs = np.meshgrid(np.arange(miny, maxy), np.arange(minx, maxx), indexing='ij') pixelcoords = np.stack([xs.flatten(), ys.flatten()], axis=-1).astype(np.float32) diff = pixelcoords - mu2d det = Sigma2D[0,0]Sigma2D[1,1] - Sigma2D[0,1]Sigma2D[1,0] if abs(det) < 1e-6: continue invSigma2D = np.array([ [Sigma2D[1,1], -Sigma2D[0,1]], [-Sigma2D[1,0], Sigma2D[0,0]] ]) / det exponents = -0.5 np.sum((diff @ invSigma2D) diff, axis=1) g2dvalues = np.exp(exponents) d = np.array([0, 0, 1]) color = evaluatesh(shcoeffs, d) flatg2d = g2dvalues.reshape(-1) flatcolor = np.tile(color, (len(flatg2d), 1)) pixelindices = np.arange(len(flatg2d)) imgy = miny + (pixelindices // (maxx - minx)) imgx = minx + (pixelindices % (maxx - minx)) for k in range(len(flatg2d)): y, x = imgy[k], imgx[k] a = alpha flatg2d[k] if a < 1e-4: continue tprev = T[y, x] if tprev > 0.9999: continue C[y, x] += flatcolor[k] a (1 - tprev) T[y, x] += a (1 - tprev) return C def evaluatesh(coeffs, direction): """Evaluate spherical harmonics for a given direction.""" return coeffs[:3] def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Convert unit quaternion to 3x3 rotation matrix.""" w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2yy - 2zz, 2xy - 2zw, 2xz + 2yw], [2xy + 2zw, 1 - 2xx - 2zz, 2yz - 2xw], [2xz - 2yw, 2yz + 2xw, 1 - 2xx - 2yy] ]) Iterations: 30,000 (7k–15k for fast preview). Learning Rates: Position: 1.6	imes10^{-4} (scaled by scene extent, exponential decay). Opacity: 5	imes10^{-2} (sigmoid raw). Scale: 5	imes10^{-3} (exp raw). Rotation: 10^{-3} (quaternion, normalized after step). SH: 2.5	imes10^{-3} for DC, /20 for higher bands. Densification: Gradient threshold 	au
abla \sim 2	imes10^{-4}, applied every 100 iterations within a window of 500–15,000. Opacity Reset: Every 3000 iterations, set \alpha \leftarrow 0.01. Tile Size: 16	imes16. SSIM Weight: \lambda = 0.2. SH Warm-up: Start with degree 0, add 1 band every 1000 iterations up to degree 3. Popping Artifacts: The per-tile depth sort uses the Gaussian center depth, not per-pixel depth. In distant tiles with strong overlap, the sort order can flip across views, causing popping. Pre-classification Limitation: Color is assigned prior to compositing (pre-classification), which is not aligned with transfer function mapping in alpha-blended ray casting, leading to inaccurate TF evaluation and artifacts in overlapping regions. Heuristic Densification: Adaptive density control based on 2D projections may fail to capture local structural characteristics, generating excessive overlapping Gaussians. 3σ Support: The 3\sigma cutoff (d^	op \Sigma^{-1} d \leq 9) often overestimates the primitive footprint, leading to redundant primitives and increased memory cost. Details the specific learning rates, decay schedules, and hyperparameters used in the Adam optimizer for 3DGS. A variant focusing on efficient coding and optimization strategies for 3DGS. Describes the data structure for storing and initializing the list of Gaussians. Methods for loading Gaussian properties from various sources. Algorithms for computing the 3D covariance matrix from rotation and scale parameters. Memory layout optimizations for 3D Gaussian data. An alternative parameterization for covariance matrices using bounded Cholesky decomposition. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) per pixel where N is the number of Gaussians contributing to the pixel, but accelerated by tiling and culling. Training is dominated by the rasterization and backpropagation steps, scaling with the number of Gaussians and image resolution. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Each Gaussian stores  oldsymbol{\mu} (12 bytes), q (16 bytes), s (12 bytes), \alpha (4 bytes), and SH coefficients (192 bytes for degree 3), totaling ~236 bytes per Gaussian. Performance: Real-time rendering (100–300 FPS at 1080p) is achievable on modern GPUs due to the tile-based rasterizer. Strengths: High-fidelity rendering, real-time performance, explicit representation allows for easy editing and manipulation. Limitations: Popping artifacts due to depth sorting, pre-classification artifacts, and heuristic densification can lead to redundancy. Not inherently designed for volumetric media, leading to inaccuracies in TF evaluation. When to Use: Ideal for static scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis where real-time performance and high visual quality are required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with complex volumetric effects (e.g., smoke, fire) without modifications, as it does not model volumetric ray integration. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 as a state-of-the-art reconstruction approach. It represents scenes using 3D Gaussians, serving as a baseline for many subsequent methods despite not being specifically designed for volumetric media. The method leverages hardware rasterization for efficient rendering, replacing the implicit MLPs of NeRF with explicit Gaussian primitives. It has become a foundational technique in computer graphics, inspiring numerous variants for dynamic scenes, compression, and volumetric rendering. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization Parameters
head: 3DGS Training Hyperparameters, Densification and Opacity Reset Settings
body:
This method defines the hyperparameters and procedural rules for optimizing a set of 3D Gaussians to reconstruct a scene from images. It solves the problem of initializing and maintaining an appropriate density of Gaussian primitives during training, ensuring the representation is neither too sparse (underfitting) nor too dense (overfitting/noise). It sets apart from static rendering by introducing adaptive density control (clone, split, prune) and periodic opacity resets, which are critical for converging to a high-fidelity radiance field. Inputs: Initial set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N. Training images with known camera poses. Optimization hyperparameters (see below). Outputs: Optimized set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with updated parameters ( oldsymbol{\mu}, q, s, \alpha, \mathrm{SH}). Each Gaussian gi stores:  oldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. qi \in \mathbb{R}^4: Orientation (quaternion, normalized). si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale (log-space or linear, depending on implementation; typically log-space for stability). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathrm{SH}i: Spherical Harmonics coefficients (typically degree 3, 48 coefficients). The covariance matrix \Sigmai is reconstructed from qi and si as: \Sigmai = Ri \, \mathrm{diag}(si)^2 \, Ri^	op where Ri is the rotation matrix derived from qi. The training process alternates between rendering, loss computation, and density control. 1. Initialization: Place initial Gaussians using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Set initial scales si based on the distance to nearest neighbors. Initialize opacities \alphai to a small value (e.g., 0.1) or 1.0 depending on the variant. Note: Original 3DGS initializes opacity to 0.1 to allow gradual growth. 2. Rendering: Project each Gaussian to 2D using EWA splatting. The 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} is obtained by linearizing the perspective projection at the Gaussian center  oldsymbol{\mu}c. Render image via alpha compositing of 2D Gaussian footprints. 3. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM) between rendered and ground-truth images. 4. Gradient Accumulation: Accumulate gradients for  oldsymbol{\mu}i and other parameters. Specifically, track the magnitude of the gradient of the loss with respect to the position  oldsymbol{\mu}i, denoted \|
abla{ oldsymbol{\mu}i} \mathcal{L}\|. 5. Adaptive Density Control (Every K iterations): Clone: For Gaussians with high gradient magnitude \|
abla{ oldsymbol{\mu}i} \mathcal{L}\| > 	au{clone} and low opacity \alphai < \alpha{thresh}, clone the Gaussian. The clone is placed at  oldsymbol{\mu}i with a small perturbation. Split: For Gaussians with high gradient magnitude \|
abla{ oldsymbol{\mu}i} \mathcal{L}\| > 	au{split} and scale si larger than a threshold, split the Gaussian into two. The new scales are reduced (e.g., by a factor of 1.6). Prune: Remove Gaussians with opacity \alphai < \alpha{prune} (e.g., 0.005) or scale si too small. Opacity Reset: Every K{reset} iterations, reset the opacity of all Gaussians to a small value (e.g., 0.01) and re-normalize or adjust scales to maintain visual consistency. This prevents opacities from saturating and allows further densification. Densification Gradient Threshold (	au{clone}, 	au{split}): Approximately 2 	imes 10^{-4}. Opacity Reset Interval (K{reset}): Every 3000 iterations. Pruning Threshold (\alpha{prune}): Typically 0.005 Note: Common value in original implementation. Clone/Scale Thresholds: Specific scale thresholds are not explicitly given in the sources; they are typically relative to the initial scale or a global average. "Not given in the sources." Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizegaussians(gaussians, images, poses, numiterations, gradthresholdclone=2e-4, gradthresholdsplit=2e-4, opacityresetinterval=3000, alphaprune=0.005): for iter in range(numiterations): # 1. Render renderedimage = render(gaussians, poses) # 2. Compute Loss loss = computeloss(renderedimage, images[iter % len(images)]) # 3. Backpropagate gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians) # 4. Update Parameters (SGD/Adam) updateparameters(gaussians, gradients) # 5. Adaptive Density Control if iter % 100 == 0: # Check every 100 iterations for g in gaussians: gradmag = norm(gradients[g].mu) # Clone condition if gradmag > gradthresholdclone and g.alpha < 0.01: clonegaussian(g) # Split condition if gradmag > gradthresholdsplit and g.scale > thresholdscale: splitgaussian(g) # Prune condition if g.alpha < alphaprune: prunegaussian(g) # 6. Opacity Reset if iter % opacityresetinterval == 0: resetopacities(gaussians) Precision: Using log-space for scales is recommended to prevent negative scales and improve optimization stability. Boundaries: Cloning and splitting can lead to explosion in the number of Gaussians if thresholds are too low. Monitor memory usage. Degenerate Input: If the scene has low texture, gradients may be small, leading to insufficient densification. Consider adjusting thresholds or using additional priors. Fixes scale-aliasing via 3D smoothing + 2D Mip filter. Use when high-frequency details cause aliasing artifacts. Replaces 3D ellipsoids with oriented disks for better surface reconstruction. Use when geometry/mesh extraction is the primary goal. Uses voxel anchors + tiny MLP for compression and far-view extrapolation. Use when model size is a constraint. Provides Level-of-Detail (LoD) from city-scale to centimeter close-ups. Use for large-scale scenes. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Densification adds overhead but is sparse. Memory Complexity: O(N) per Gaussian. Vanilla 3DGS uses 1–3 M Gaussians for room-scale scenes, occupying 200–800 MB on disk. Performance: Real-time rendering is achievable with tile-based rasterization. Optimization speed depends on the number of Gaussians and iterations. Strengths: High-quality novel view synthesis, real-time rendering, explicit representation. Limitations: Large model size, potential for popping artifacts due to per-tile center-depth sort (mitigated by StopThePop, GOF, exact pixel sort). When to Use: Photorealistic novel view synthesis, room-scale scenes with plenty of views. When Not to Use: When surface mesh quality is critical (use 2DGS), or when model size is extremely constrained (use compression techniques like LightGaussian, SOG, EAGLES, RDO-Gaussian). 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was introduced as a replacement for NeRF's MLP+ray-march approach, using explicit anisotropic Gaussians and tile rasterization for real-time rendering. The optimization parameters described here are based on the original 3DGS implementation and its subsequent refinements. The method has become a standard for radiance-field optimization, with numerous variants addressing specific challenges like compression, dynamic scenes, and geometry extraction. name: N-DGS Bounded Cholesky Parameterization
head: N-DGS
body: N-DGS (N-Dimensional Gaussian Splatting) is a parameterization method for the joint covariance matrix of 3D Gaussians in differentiable volume rendering. It solves the problem of optimizing the cross-covariance between spatial and query dimensions while maintaining positive-definiteness and numerical stability. Unlike sibling methods that may use direct regression or unbounded factorizations, N-DGS uses a bounded Cholesky factorization where coefficients are scaled by query diagonal scales, ensuring that the resulting cross-covariance and spatial extent remain within controlled bounds. It builds on GaussianSet Data Structure by defining how the covariance matrix components are stored and optimized. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The method parameterizes the joint covariance matrix \Sigma for a Gaussian primitive. It takes as parameters the bounded Cholesky coefficients and query diagonal scales. Output: The full joint covariance matrix \Sigma, from which the spatial covariance \Sigma{pp}, cross-covariance \Sigma{pq}, and query covariance \Sigma{qq} are derived. Data Structures: The joint covariance \Sigma is partitioned into blocks: \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{pp} & \Sigma{pq} \\ \Sigma{qp} & \Sigma{qq} \end{pmatrix} where \Sigma{pp} is the spatial covariance (p \times p), \Sigma{qq} is the query covariance (q \times q), and \Sigma{pq} is the cross-covariance (p \times q). The parameterization relies on a Cholesky factor A of the joint covariance. The off-diagonal entries of A contribute to both \Sigma{pq} and the spatial extent (\Sigma{pp}){ii}. Formulas: 1. Bounded Cholesky Factor: The cross-covariance block is derived from a bounded Cholesky factor B. Let sq be the diagonal scales of the query covariance. The factor B is defined as: B = \text{diag}(sq) Be where |B{e,jk}| \leq 1. This ensures: \|B\|2 \leq \|B\|F \leq \sqrt{p} \|sq\|2 Consequently, the cross-covariance block satisfies: \|(\Sigma{pq}){i,:}\|2 \leq \sqrt{p} \|sq\|2 \sqrt{(\Sigma{pp}){ii}} \quad 2. Regression Operator: The rendered spatial shift (conditional mean) is given by: \Delta \mu{\text{N-DGS}} = \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} \delta = M{\text{N-DGS}} \delta \quad where \delta is the query deviation. 3. Invariant Gaussian Bound: To analyze the shift independently of basis, define the normalized cross-covariance: K = \Sigma{pp}^{-1/2} \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1/2} Positive-definiteness implies \|K\|2 < 1. With the whitened query deviation h = \Sigma{qq}^{-1/2} \delta, the shift is: \Delta \mu{\text{N-DGS}} = \Sigma{pp}^{1/2} K h This yields the bound: \|\Sigma{pp}^{-1/2} \Delta \mu{\text{N-DGS}}\|2 \leq \|\Sigma{qq}^{-1/2} \delta\|2 \quad Parameters: sq: Diagonal scales of the query covariance. Be: Bounded Cholesky coefficients with entries in [-1, 1]. Typical values are not explicitly given, but the bounds rely on the magnitude of sq and the spatial scale \bar{s}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpretation of Off-Diagonals: The off-diagonal entries of the Cholesky factor A contribute to both \Sigma{pq} and the spatial extent (\Sigma{pp}){ii}. They should not be interpreted as producing cross-covariance independently of spatial scale. Ill-Conditioning: A bound on \Sigma{pq} alone does not bound the shift \Delta \mu. The inverse query covariance \Sigma{qq}^{-1} and the query deviation \delta also enter the regression. A narrow or ill-conditioned query covariance can amplify the regression operator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computendgscovariance(Achol, sq): """ Compute joint covariance blocks from bounded Cholesky factor and query scales. Args: Achol: Cholesky factor A of the joint covariance. sq: Diagonal scales of the query covariance. Returns: Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq: Blocks of the joint covariance. """ # Extract blocks from Cholesky factor A # A is structured such that its off-diagonals influence both Sigmapp and Sigmapq # The exact mapping from A to Sigma blocks depends on the specific Cholesky ordering # and is assumed to be handled by the underlying GaussianSet structure. # Compute B = diag(sq) Be # Be is derived from Achol, with entries bounded by 1 Be = extractboundedcholesky(Achol) B = diag(sq) @ Be # Compute Sigmapq from B # Sigmapq is related to B via the spatial covariance structure # For simplicity, assume Sigmapq is directly derived from B in the context of the joint factorization Sigmapq = computecrosscovariancefromB(B, Achol) # Compute Sigmapp from Achol Sigmapp = computespatialcovariance(Achol) # Compute Sigmaqq from sq Sigmaqq = diag(sq) @ diag(sq) return Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq def computeshift(Sigmapq, Sigmaqq, delta): """ Compute the rendered spatial shift. Args: Sigmapq: Cross-covariance block. Sigmaqq: Query covariance block. delta: Query deviation. Returns: Deltamu: Spatial shift. """ # Invert Sigmaqq Sigmaqqinv = invert(Sigmaqq) # Compute shift Deltamu = Sigmapq @ Sigmaqqinv @ delta return Deltamu dGS is a direct parameterization method for radiance-field optimization that replaces the covariance-derived conditioning steps of N-DGS with three explicit per-primitive parameters to compute opacity and position directly. It solves the problem of query-block inversion and covariance correction required by sibling methods like N-DGS and UBS, exposing rendered quantities instead. Unlike N-DGS, which parameterizes the joint covariance and derives regression via inversion, dGS explicitly stores the precision matrix and spatial coupling, avoiding intermediate tensor construction during slicing. Conditional-coordinate parameterization provides a non-redundant, smooth bijection between the space of joint Gaussian covariances and a set of operational quantities: conditional spatial covariance, query-space precision, and a regression operator. It solves the problem of efficiently representing and optimizing the cross-covariance between spatial and query dimensions in differentiable Gaussian splatting by avoiding the computational cost and instability of inverting the query covariance block during rendering. Unlike N-DGS, which derives the regression operator from a joint Cholesky factor, this method directly optimizes the regression operator and precision, treating the coupling as a block shear. Time and Memory Complexity: N-DGS requires the inversion of the query covariance block \Sigma{qq} to compute the regression operator M{\text{N-DGS}} = \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1}. This inversion is computationally expensive, especially for high-dimensional query spaces. The bounded Cholesky parameterization ensures numerical stability but does not reduce the complexity of the inversion step. Measured Performance: On two trained MCMC scenes with six views each, the opacity-weighted \|\Delta \mu\|/\bar{s} has a median of 0.29–0.30 and a 99th percentile of 4.8–7.0 for N-DGS. This is compared to dGS, which has a 99th percentile of 2.9–4.8. The ordering reverses when normalized by the smallest principal axis, supporting \bar{s} as an isotropic prior rather than a per-axis optimum. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: The bounded Cholesky factorization ensures that the cross-covariance and spatial extent remain within controlled bounds, improving numerical stability during optimization. The invariant Gaussian bound provides a basis-independent guarantee on the shift magnitude. Limitations: The method requires the inversion of the query covariance block, which can be computationally expensive and unstable if the query covariance is ill-conditioned. The interpretation of the Cholesky coefficients is complex, as off-diagonal entries contribute to both cross-covariance and spatial extent. When to Use: N-DGS is suitable when numerical stability is a primary concern and the query covariance is well-conditioned. It is less suitable for high-dimensional query spaces where the inversion cost is prohibitive, or when the query covariance is likely to be ill-conditioned. N-DGS was introduced in the context of differentiable Gaussian splatting to address the challenges of optimizing the joint covariance matrix. The method builds on the bounded Cholesky factorization to ensure positive-definiteness and stability. It is part of the broader family of N-Dimensional Gaussian Splatting methods, which extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to higher dimensions. Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22778, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: dGS Direct Regression Parameterization
head: Direct Conditional Parameterization for Gaussian Splatting, dGS
body: dGS is a direct parameterization method for radiance-field optimization that replaces the covariance-derived conditioning steps of N-DGS with three explicit per-primitive parameters to compute opacity and position directly. It solves the problem of query-block inversion and covariance correction required by sibling methods like N-DGS and UBS, exposing rendered quantities instead. Unlike N-DGS, which parameterizes the joint covariance and derives regression via inversion, dGS explicitly stores the precision matrix and spatial coupling, avoiding intermediate tensor construction during slicing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Base position \mup, base opacity \alpha, base scales sx, sy, sz, query deviation \delta = q - \muq (where q is the canonical view/time coordinate and \muq is its mean), and the learned parameters L, V{pq}, \Lambda. Outputs: Conditional opacity \alpha{\text{cond}} and conditional position \mu{\text{cond}}. The conditional covariance \Sigma{\text{cond}} remains query-independent and unchanged from standard 3DGS. Data Structures: Each primitive stores the following learned parameters: 1. L: A lower-triangular Cholesky factor in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}, where C is the dimensionality of the query (typically 3 for view or 4 for view+time). Layout: C(C+1)/2 elements. For C=4, all 10 lower-triangular entries are learned. Activation: Diagonal elements use an exponential activation to ensure V{qq} = LL^\top is symmetric positive-definite (SPD) by construction. 2. V{pq}: A spatial coupling factor in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C}. Layout: Defined as V{pq} = \bar{s} \Theta{pq}. \bar{s}: The average spatial scale, \text{mean}(sx, sy, sz). This is a fixed prior derived from the primitive's geometry, not a learned parameter. \Theta{pq}: A learnable direction tensor with unit Frobenius norm (\|\Theta{pq}\|F = 1). Constraints: \|V{pq}\|F = \bar{s} and \|V{pq}^{(i)}\|2 \leq \bar{s} for each row i. 3. \Lambda: A per-dimension coupling vector in [0, 1]^C. Layout: C elements. Activation: Stored as logits; channels of the same type (e.g., the three view dimensions) share a logit. Role: Weights the precision-transformed query channels. At \Lambda=0, position decouples (\mu{\text{cond}} = \mup); at \Lambda=1, it couples through the full opacity precision. Parameters: \lambdao: Opacity scaling factor, a fixed constant with value 0.35, inherited from N-DGS. Formulas: The conditional opacity and position are computed as follows: \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \exp(-\lambdao \| \mathbf{L}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta} \|2^2) \quad (5) \mu{\text{cond}} = \mup + \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \boldsymbol{\delta} \quad (6) Where: \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top is the precision matrix. \| \cdot \|2 denotes the Euclidean norm. \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) creates a diagonal matrix from \Lambda. Expanded Opacity for C=4 (View + Time): For the 4-dimensional case, the opacity formula expands to: \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \exp(-\lambdao (\deltav^\top \mathbf{V}{vv} \deltav + 2\deltat \deltav^\top \mathbf{v}{vt} + \deltat^2 vt)) Where \mathbf{V}{vv}, \mathbf{v}{vt}, and vt are the view, cross, and time blocks of \mathbf{V}{qq} respectively. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements the forward pass for a single primitive. It assumes L is lower-triangular, Vpq is 3 \times C, Lambda is length C, and delta is length C. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dgsforward(mup, alpha, L, Vpq, Lambda, delta): """ Computes conditional opacity and position for dGS. Args: mup: Base position (3,) alpha: Base opacity (scalar) L: Lower-triangular Cholesky factor (C, C) Vpq: Spatial coupling factor (3, C) Lambda: Coupling vector (C,) in [0, 1] delta: Query deviation (C,) Returns: alphacond: Conditional opacity (scalar) mucond: Conditional position (3,) """ C = L.shape[0] # 1. Compute Opacity # L^T delta # Since L is lower-triangular, L^T is upper-triangular. # We compute the vector product explicitly. Ltdelta = [0.0] C for i in range(C): sumval = 0.0 for j in range(i, C): # L^T[i, j] = L[j, i] sumval += L[j, i] delta[j] Ltdelta[i] = sumval # Squared norm || L^T delta ||2^2 normsq = sum(x x for x in Ltdelta) # alphacond = alpha exp(-lambdao normsq) lambdao = 0.35 alphacond = alpha math.exp(-lambdao normsq) # 2. Compute Position # Vqq = L L^T # We can compute Vqq delta directly or compute MdGS = Vpq diag(Lambda) Vqq # To avoid full matrix multiplication, we compute step-by-step: # Step A: Vqq delta Vqqdelta = [0.0] C for i in range(C): sumval = 0.0 for j in range(C): # Vqq[i, j] = sumk L[i, k] L[j, k] # Optimization: Since we only need Vqq delta, we can do: # Vqq delta = L (L^T delta) pass # Reuse Ltdelta from opacity step: Ltdelta = L^T delta # Now compute L Ltdelta Vqqdelta = [0.0] C for i in range(C): sumval = 0.0 for j in range(i, C): # L is lower triangular, so L[i, j] is 0 if j < i? No, L[i,j] is non-zero if j <= i. # Wait, L is lower triangular. L[i, j] != 0 only if j <= i. # So for row i, we sum over j from 0 to i. sumval += L[i, j] Ltdelta[j] Vqqdelta[i] = sumval # Step B: diag(Lambda) Vqqdelta LambdaVqqdelta = [Lambda[i] Vqqdelta[i] for i in range(C)] # Step C: Vpq (LambdaVqqdelta) # Vpq is (3, C). Result is (3,) shift = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): sumval = 0.0 for j in range(C): sumval += Vpq[i, j] LambdaVqqdelta[j] shift[i] = sumval # mucond = mup + shift mucond = [mup[i] + shift[i] for i in range(3)] return alphacond, mucond Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spatial Scale Prior: Removing the spatial factor \bar{s} from V{pq} degrades PSNR by 2.65 dB on NeRF Synthetic and 2.97 dB on 6DGS-PBR. Coupling Bounds: The coupling \Lambda is bounded in [0, 1]. Values outside this range are not supported by the standard formulation. Precision: The use of exponential activation on L's diagonal ensures SPD, avoiding numerical instability from non-SPD precision matrices. The parent method that dGS replaces. It uses bounded Cholesky coefficients multiplied by query diagonal scales. It requires query-block inversion. Link A sibling method that uses conditional coordinates. It differs from dGS in how it parameterizes the regression and conditioning. Link Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The kernel uses compile-time loop unrolling for C (3 or 4). Each thread processes one primitive. Computing L^\top \delta uses C(C+1)/2 multiplications followed by a dot product, all in per-thread registers. There is no intermediate tensor construction or shared-memory traffic. Memory: dGS stores L (C^2 elements, though only lower triangle is learned), V{pq} (3C elements), and \Lambda (C elements). For C=4, this is 10 + 12 + 4 = 26 parameters per primitive, plus the base 3DGS parameters. N-DGS uses 15/16 parameters for C=3/4. Measured Performance: On an A100 GPU with 1M primitives: For C=3: Slicing time is 0.67ms for dGS, compared to 0.71ms for N-DGS (7.1x faster than the optimized on-the-fly N-DGS baseline of 5.0ms implied by the ratio, though the table lists N-DGS as 0.71ms which seems to be a specific optimized variant; the text states dGS is 7.1x faster than N-DGS, implying N-DGS is ~4.76ms in the unoptimized case, but the table lists 0.71ms for N-DGS and 0.67ms for dGS, which is a slight speedup, not 7x. Re-reading: "Slicing time, C=3 (ms) 0.71 | 0.67 0.10 (7.1x)". This implies the 0.71ms is N-DGS, 0.67ms is dGS, and 0.10ms is dBS. The "7.1x" likely refers to dBS vs N-DGS. Let's look at C=4: "0.96 | 1.34 0.12 (7.7x)". Here N-DGS is 0.96ms, dGS is 1.34ms. dGS is slower than N-DGS in raw slicing time on A100 for 1M primitives in this specific harness. However, the text says "dGS is 2.0–2.3× faster than inference-cached N-DGS". This suggests the 0.71/0.96ms figures might be for a different setup or the "7.1x" refers to dBS. Let's stick to the explicit numbers: dGS slicing time is 0.67ms (C=3) and 1.34ms (C=4) on A100 with 1M primitives. In a separate harness with materialized inputs, dGS is 2.0–2.3× faster than inference-cached N-DGS and 1.8× faster than a factorized-query control. On Mip-NeRF 360, dGS achieves 61% faster rendering with +0.97 dB improvement. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Avoids query-block inversion and covariance correction. Exposes operational quantities directly. Better performance on dynamic scenes (D-NeRF, 7DGS-PBR) compared to opacity-only variants. Limitations: Slightly higher per-primitive parameter count than N-DGS for C=4 (26 vs 16). Raw slicing time on A100 can be slightly higher than optimized N-DGS for C=4 (1.34ms vs 0.96ms), but overall rendering is faster due to other optimizations. dGS was introduced in "Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting". It was developed to address the computational overhead of covariance-derived conditioning in N-DGS and UBS. It is used in UBS implementation experiments and compared against N-DGS under standard 3DGS densification. Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22778, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Conditional-coordinate parameterization
head: Proposition C.1, dGS conditional parameterization
body: Conditional-coordinate parameterization provides a non-redundant, smooth bijection between the space of joint Gaussian covariances and a set of operational quantities: conditional spatial covariance, query-space precision, and a regression operator. It solves the problem of efficiently representing and optimizing the cross-covariance between spatial and query dimensions in differentiable Gaussian splatting by avoiding the computational cost and instability of inverting the query covariance block during rendering. Unlike N-DGS, which derives the regression operator from a joint Cholesky factor, this method directly optimizes the regression operator and precision, treating the coupling as a block shear. Inputs and Outputs Input: A joint covariance matrix \Psi \in \mathbb{R}^{(p+C) \times (p+C)} that is symmetric positive-definite (SPD), where p is the spatial dimension and C is the query dimension. Output: A triplet (\Sigma{\text{cond}}, \mathbf{M}, \mathbf{V}{qq}) where: \Sigma{\text{cond}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p} is the conditional spatial covariance (SPD). \mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times C} is the effective query-to-position regression operator. \mathbf{V}{qq} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C} is the query-space precision matrix (SPD). Data Structures \Sigma{\text{cond}}: Stored as a symmetric matrix. In practice, only the lower triangular part is stored to save memory, requiring p(p+1)/2 parameters. \mathbf{M}: Stored as a dense rectangular matrix, requiring pC parameters. \mathbf{V}{qq}: Stored as a symmetric matrix. In dGS implementations, it is often factorized as \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top where \mathbf{L} is lower triangular with strictly positive diagonal entries to ensure positive definiteness. This requires C(C+1)/2 parameters. Formulas The joint covariance \Psi is parameterized by the triplet via the following block structure: \Psi = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{pp} & \Sigma{pq} \\ \Sigma{pq}^\top & \Sigma{qq} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{\text{cond}} + \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}\mathbf{M}^\top & \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} \\ \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}\mathbf{M}^\top & \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} \end{pmatrix} The blocks are defined as: 1. \Sigma{qq} = \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} 2. \Sigma{pq} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} 3. \Sigma{pp} = \Sigma{\text{cond}} + \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}\mathbf{M}^\top The inverse map, recovering the parameters from a given joint covariance \Psi, is: 1. \mathbf{V}{qq} = \Sigma{qq}^{-1} 2. \mathbf{M} = \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} 3. \Sigma{\text{cond}} = \Sigma{pp} - \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} \Sigma{pq}^\top Numbered Steps 1. Decompose Joint Covariance: Given \Psi, extract the blocks \Sigma{pp} (p \times p), \Sigma{pq} (p \times C), and \Sigma{qq} (C \times C). 2. Compute Query Precision: Invert \Sigma{qq} to obtain \mathbf{V}{qq}. 3. Compute Regression Operator: Multiply \Sigma{pq} by \mathbf{V}{qq} to obtain \mathbf{M}. 4. Compute Conditional Covariance: Subtract the Schur complement term \Sigma{pq} \mathbf{V}{qq} \Sigma{pq}^\top from \Sigma{pp} to obtain \Sigma{\text{cond}}. 5. Validation: Ensure \Sigma{\text{cond}} and \mathbf{V}{qq} are positive definite. If using the Cholesky factorization for \mathbf{V}{qq}, enforce strictly positive diagonal elements in \mathbf{L}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def jointtoconditionalparameters(Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq): """ Converts joint covariance blocks to conditional-coordinate parameters. Args: Sigmapp: (p, p) ndarray, symmetric positive-definite. Sigmapq: (p, C) ndarray. Sigmaqq: (C, C) ndarray, symmetric positive-definite. Returns: Sigmacond: (p, p) ndarray, conditional spatial covariance. M: (p, C) ndarray, regression operator. Vqq: (C, C) ndarray, query-space precision. """ # Step 2: Compute Query Precision Vqq = Sigmaqq^-1 Vqq = np.linalg.inv(Sigmaqq) # Step 3: Compute Regression Operator M = Sigmapq Vqq M = Sigmapq @ Vqq # Step 4: Compute Conditional Covariance Sigmacond = Sigmapp - Sigmapq Vqq Sigmapq^T # Note: Sigmapq @ Vqq is M, so M @ Sigmapq^T is equivalent to Sigmapq @ Vqq @ Sigmapq^T Sigmacond = Sigmapp - M @ Sigmapq.T return Sigmacond, M, Vqq def conditionalparameterstojoint(Sigmacond, M, Vqq): """ Reconstructs joint covariance blocks from conditional-coordinate parameters. Args: Sigmacond: (p, p) ndarray, conditional spatial covariance. M: (p, C) ndarray, regression operator. Vqq: (C, C) ndarray, query-space precision. Returns: Sigmapp: (p, p) ndarray. Sigmapq: (p, C) ndarray. Sigmaqq: (C, C) ndarray. """ # Invert Vqq to get Sigmaqq Sigmaqq = np.linalg.inv(Vqq) # Compute Sigmapq = M Vqq^-1 = M Sigmaqq Sigmapq = M @ Sigmaqq # Compute Sigmapp = Sigmacond + M Vqq^-1 M^T Sigmapp = Sigmacond + M @ Sigmaqq @ M.T return Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq Parameters p: Spatial dimension (typically 3). C: Query dimension (e.g., number of query features or dimensions). Typical values: For 3D Gaussian Splatting, p=3. C depends on the specific query space (e.g., frequency domain dimensions). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Singularity: The map is singular if \mathbf{V}{qq} approaches singularity (\det \mathbf{V}{qq} \to 0) or if \Sigma{\text{cond}} approaches its boundary (becomes singular). The construction \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top with strictly positive Cholesky diagonal keeps the parameterization in the interior of the SPD domain. Precision: Inverting \Sigma{qq} can be numerically unstable if \Sigma{qq} is ill-conditioned. Using the Cholesky factorization of \mathbf{V}{qq} directly avoids explicit inversion in some contexts, but the definition relies on \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}. A variant that directly optimizes the regression operator and precision without the joint Cholesky derivation. It avoids the computational cost of inverting the query covariance block during rendering. dGS Direct Regression Parameterization Time Complexity: The forward map involves matrix inversion (O(C^3)) and matrix multiplications (O(p^2 C + p C^2)). The inverse map involves similar operations. For fixed p and C, this is constant time per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: The parameter count is \frac{p(p+1)}{2} + pC + \frac{C(C+1)}{2} = \frac{(p+C)(p+C+1)}{2}, which is non-redundant and matches the number of parameters in the full joint covariance matrix. Strengths: Efficiency: Avoids repeated inversion of the query covariance block during rendering by optimizing \mathbf{V}{qq} and \mathbf{M} directly. Stability: The block shear interpretation provides a clear geometric understanding and stable optimization landscape when \mathbf{V}{qq} is kept positive definite. Non-redundancy: The parameterization is a smooth bijection, ensuring no loss of information. Limitations: Singularity Risk: If \mathbf{V}{qq} becomes singular, the parameterization breaks down. Strictly positive Cholesky diagonals are required. Complexity: The inverse map requires matrix inversion, which can be costly for large C. When to Use: Use when optimizing query-dependent Gaussian splats where the query-space precision and regression operator are natural optimization variables. Prefer over N-DGS when avoiding query covariance inversion during rendering is critical. The conditional-coordinate parameterization was introduced in the context of differentiable Gaussian splatting, specifically in the "Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting" paper. It formalizes the relationship between joint Gaussian covariances and their conditional components, providing a theoretical foundation for efficient optimization of query-dependent splats. The method leverages the Schur complement and block-triangular factorization to define a smooth bijection between the joint covariance space and the conditional parameters. Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22778, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian-based Representation
head: Gaussian mixture model, Gaussian splatting
body: Gaussian-based representation encodes signals, data, or geometric structures as an explicit, continuous sum (or mixture) of parameterized Gaussian functions. It solves the problem of representing high-dimensional data with a structure that allows for efficient, closed-form operations such as differentiation and convolution, enabling fast rendering and analysis. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is its use of explicit, analytically differentiable primitives rather than implicit neural fields or grid-based voxels; while 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Preliminaries focuses on the specific rasterization pipeline for novel view synthesis, this method generalizes to 2D image compression, vector search, and physics simulation. Inputs: A target signal or domain (e.g., a 2D image, a 3D scene, a vector dataset). A set of reference samples (e.g., pixel values, multi-view images, ground-truth vectors) for optimization. Outputs: A set of N Gaussian primitives, each defined by location, covariance, and amplitude/attributes. The reconstructed signal f(\mathbf{x}) evaluated at any point \mathbf{x}. The representation consists of a list of N Gaussians. The specific fields depend on the domain: 2D Image Domain (e.g., GaussianImage): Each Gaussian is parameterized by an 8-tuple: 1. Location \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^2: 2 floats. 2. Covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}: Stored via Cholesky decomposition, requiring 3 floats (since \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is symmetric positive-definite). 3. Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3 floats (RGB). 3D Scene Domain (e.g., 3DGS): Each Gaussian includes additional attributes to handle view-dependence and 3D geometry: 1. Mean \boldsymbol{\mu}n \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3 floats. 2. Rotation \mathbf{q}n \in \mathbb{R}^4: Unit quaternion (4 floats). 3. Scale \mathbf{s}n \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3 floats. 4. Opacity \alphan \in \mathbb{R}: 1 float. 5. Spherical Harmonics (SH) Coefficients: Variable size depending on order L (e.g., 3(L+1)^2 floats for RGB). 6. Covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}n: Constructed from rotation and scale as \boldsymbol{\Sigma}n = \mathbf{R}n \mathbf{S}n \mathbf{S}n^\top \mathbf{R}n^\top. The canonical primitive in d-dimensional Euclidean space is: Gn(\mathbf{x}) = an \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mun)^\top \boldsymbol\Sigman^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mun)\right) Where: \boldsymbol\mun \in \mathbb{R}^d is the center (mean). \boldsymbol\Sigman \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} is the symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix (shape). an is the amplitude or attribute vector (e.g., RGB color, opacity, semantic embedding). The total representation is the superposition: f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{n=1}^N Gn(\mathbf{x}) The physical or semantic meaning of f depends on context (image intensity, field value, feature embedding, etc.). N: The number of Gaussians in the mixture. d: The dimensionality of the Euclidean space (e.g., 2 for images, 3 for scenes). Loss Function: 2D Image: Typically L2 (MSE) or hybrid L2+D-SSIM over all pixels. 3D Scene: Photometric losses over multiple views or ray samples, combined with sparsity, density, or geometric constraints. 1. Initialization: Random/Iterative: Initialize N Gaussians with random locations and shapes. Vectorized: Use methods like EigenGS to map a principal-component eigenspace to Gaussian space for instant initialization. Feedforward: Use a predictive network to infer Gaussian parameters or densities in a single pass. 2. Optimization (Fitting): Define the loss function \mathcal{L} between the rendered/evaluated sum f(\mathbf{x}) and the reference signal. Optimize the parameters (\boldsymbol\mun, \boldsymbol\Sigman, an, and optional attributes like rotation/SH) using gradient descent. 3. Adaptive Deployment (Optional): Densification: Where residuals concentrate, create additional Gaussians (e.g., via SplitNet or confidence-aware splitting). Pruning: Remove Gaussians where coverage is redundant or negligible. Hierarchical Fitting: For large signals, establish a coarse, low-frequency backbone first, then add high-frequency residual Gaussians (Level-of-Gaussian fitting). 4. Rendering/Evaluation: 2D Image: Compute the permutation-invariant summation \sum Gn(\mathbf{x}) for each pixel. Alpha blending is unnecessary as occlusion is irrelevant. 3D Scene: Project each Gaussian to 2D, depth-sort, and alpha-blend front-to-back to yield correct occlusion and volumetric effects. name: Rendering and Lighting Pipelines
head: 3DGS Rendering, Gaussian Splatting Compositing, Volume Lighting in 3DGS
body: This family defines the differentiable rendering pipelines that convert a set of 3D Gaussian primitives (or their variants) into 2D images by projecting them onto the camera plane and compositing them. It solves the problem of efficiently rasterizing soft, view-dependent primitives while supporting inverse rendering tasks such as lighting estimation and physical parameter optimization. What sets these methods apart from standard rasterization is the use of alpha blending or weighted-sum compositing over sorted or spatially hashed primitives, often augmented with volume-based occlusion or explicit geometric intersection for sharp features. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of projecting 3D primitives into 2D screen space and accumulating color based on depth order or spatial locality. 1. Projection: Primitives are transformed from world space to camera space. For Gaussians, this involves computing the 2D covariance matrix in screen space using the Jacobian of the projection matrix and the 3D covariance. 2. Rasterization: Primitives are assigned to screen tiles. Visibility is determined by bounding boxes or projected extents. 3. Compositing: Color is accumulated using front-to-back alpha blending or order-independent techniques. The standard alpha blending equation is: C{out} = C{in} (1 - \alpha) + C{prim} \alpha where C{in} is the accumulated color, \alpha is the primitive's opacity, and C{prim} is the primitive's color. 4. Sorting: Most methods require sorting primitives by depth within tiles to ensure correct front-to-back compositing, although some variants (like Duplex-GS) use spatial hashing or cell-level sorting to approximate this or enable order-independent transparency. A dual-hierarchy framework for real-time order-independent Gaussian Splatting. It combines alpha-blending with reformulated Weighted-Sum Rendering (WSR) to eliminate popping and transparency artifacts. Unlike vanilla OIT, it reintroduces physical constraints via cell-level transmittance decay, allowing early termination. It differs from Sort-free GS by using cell-level sorting for physically grounded transmittance. Replaces Gaussian ellipsoids with convex polyhedra (octahedra/tetrahedra) to enable efficient volumetric rendering with bounded geometry. It solves the problem of reconstructing sharp geometric features by allowing gradients to backpropagate through explicit ray-triangle intersections (Möller-Trumbore), distinguishing it from methods relying on implicit density fields. Integrates volume occlusion directly into the per-splat lighting evaluation loop. It ray-marches through a 3D density texture to compute transmittance for shadows, combined with per-light attenuation. Unlike methods treating volume as a post-process, it shares the 3D density texture with the splat evaluation. Decomposes Gaussian Splatting features into diffuse, specular, and ambient components using a Blinn-Phong model. It supports inverse rendering via loss functions on depth, normals, and color sparsity. A two-stage pipeline for physically parameterized volume clouds. Stage 1 trains physical parameters (geometry, extinction, albedo, scattering) under a single sun. Stage 2 freezes these and trains a global environment network for arbitrary sun direction relighting and sky atmospheric scattering. A minor variant involving the extraction and conversion loop for alpha values from raw opacity parameters to ensure they are in the valid range for blending. After obtaining 2D Gaussian function values via adapted projection for non-pinhole cameras, alpha blending is performed to generate the final image, identical to the original 3D-GS compositing step. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The rendering pipeline relies on efficient rasterization of 2D Gaussians projected from 3D. Subsequent works have adapted this pipeline for differentiable rendering, volume lighting, and physical parameter estimation. The "unofficial" sources provide implementation details for JSplat, a Java-based 3DGS renderer. name: Duplex-GS
head: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting
body: Duplex-GS is a dual-hierarchy framework for real-time order-independent Gaussian Splatting that combines alpha-blending with reformulated Weighted-Sum Rendering (WSR) to eliminate popping and transparency artifacts while reducing sorting overhead. Unlike vanilla OIT-based Gaussian Splatting which lacks physical constraints and causes transparency artifacts, Duplex-GS reintroduces physical constraints via cell-level transmittance decay, eliminating transparency artifacts and enabling early termination. It differs from Sort-free Gaussian Splatting by using cell-level sorting to compute a physically grounded transmittance that decays rapidly upon encountering opaque objects, rather than using linear depth decay. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives organized into ellipsoidal cells (proxies), camera parameters (viewing direction \mathbf{r}n, viewing distance \deltan), and scene latent features. Output: A final rendered color image \mathcal{C}. Data Structures: 1. Cell (Proxy): Position: xn \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scales: Sn \in \mathbb{R}^3 Quaternion: Qn \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized) Calibration Scalar: vn (parameterized by spherical harmonic coefficients for directional variation) Latent Feature Vector: fn 2. Neural Gaussian (emitted by cell n, index k): Center: \mu{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity: \sigma{n,k} \in [0, 1] Color: \mathcal{C}{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale: s{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Quaternion: \mathbf{q}{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized) Learned Offset: \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}} \in [-1, 1]^3 Scale Ratio: \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} \in (0, 1) Parameters: K: Predefined number of neural Gaussians emitted per anchor/cell. \epsilon: Predefined threshold for early termination. Cell-level blending halts when Tn^{\text{cell}} < \epsilon. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize cells from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Each cell is centered according to the SfM point. 2. Gaussian Decoding (Layer I): For each cell n and each of its K emitted Gaussians k: Compute Gaussian center: \mu{n,k} = xn + \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}} \cdot Sn where \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}} is the learned offset and Sn is the cell scaling factor. Decode Opacity: \{\sigma{n,1}, \dots, \sigma{n,K}\} = F\sigma(\mathbf{f}n, \deltan, \mathbf{r}n) where F\sigma is a scene-wise MLP activated by Tanh. Decode Color: \{c^{n,1}, \dots, c^{n,K}\} = Fc(fn, \deltan, dn) where Fc is a scene-wise MLP. Decode Scale State: \{\mathcal{O}{n,1}^{\text{state}}, \dots, \mathcal{O}{n,K}^{\text{state}}\} = Fs(fn, \deltan, dn) where Fs is a scene-wise MLP activated by sigmoid. Decode Quaternion: \{\mathbf{q}{n,1}, \dots, \mathbf{q}{n,K}\} = Fq(fn, \deltan, dn) where Fq is a scene-wise MLP. Compute Gaussian Scale: s{n,k} = \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} Sn where \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} is the output of Fs. Clamp Scale Ratio to ensure Gaussian regions stay inside the cell: \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} = \min \left( \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}}, 1 - \|\mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}}\| \right). Update Cell Quaternion as the normalized weighted average of associated Gaussians' orientations: Qn = \text{norm}\left(\sumk^K q{n,k} \sigma{n,k}\right). 3. Cell Rasterization (Layer I): Assign visible cells to tiles. Apply radix sort to the cell sequence based on depth. This establishes a coarse spatial order for patches of Gaussians. 4. Physical OIT Blending (Layer II): Compute Cell-Level Transmittance: For each sorted cell n, compute the transmittance from preceding cells: Tn^{\text{cell}} = \prod{i=1}^{n-1} \prod{k=1}^{n-1} (1 - vi \cdot \alpha{i,k}) where vi is the learnable calibration scalar for cell i and \alpha{i,k} is the opacity of the k-th Gaussian in cell i. Note: The source formula indices for the product upper bound are written as n-1 in the notes, but logically refer to the preceding cells i < n. The implementation should iterate over all cells i preceding n in the sorted order. Compute Cell Weight: wn = vn \cdot Tn^{\text{cell}}. Early Termination: If Tn^{\text{cell}} < \epsilon, stop processing further cells for this ray/tile. Compute Final Rendered Color: \mathcal{C} = \frac{\sum{n=1}^N wn \sum{k=1}^K \alpha{n,k} \mathcal{C}{n,k}}{\sum{n=1}^N wn \sum{k=1}^K \alpha{n,k}} where \mathcal{C}{n,k} is the color of the k-th Gaussian in cell n. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def duplexgsrender(cells, cameraparams): """ Render a frame using Duplex-GS. cells: List of Cell objects. cameraparams: Dict containing viewing direction rn and distance deltan for each cell. Returns: Rendered color image. """ # Layer I: Cell Rasterization # 1. Assign visible cells to tiles visiblecells = assigncellstotiles(cells) # 2. Radix sort cells by depth sortedcells = radixsortbydepth(visiblecells) # Initialize output buffer coloraccumulator = 0.0 weightaccumulator = 0.0 # Layer II: Physical WSR for cell in sortedcells: # Early termination check if cell.transmittance < EPSILON: break # Decode Gaussians for this cell gaussians = decodegaussians(cell, cameraparams) # Compute cell weight # Note: cell.transmittance is precomputed or computed here based on previous cells cellweight = cell.calibrationscalar cell.transmittance # Aggregate Gaussians inside the cell (Order-Independent WSR) localcolorsum = 0.0 localweightsum = 0.0 for gaussian in gaussians: # alpha is the opacity sigma alpha = gaussian.opacity color = gaussian.color # Contribution to the weighted sum contribution = cellweight alpha color localcolorsum += contribution localweightsum += cellweight alpha coloraccumulator += localcolorsum weightaccumulator += localweightsum # Final normalization if weightaccumulator > 0: finalcolor = coloraccumulator / weightaccumulator else: finalcolor = 0.0 # Background color return finalcolor def decodegaussians(cell, cameraparams): """ Decode K neural Gaussians from a cell's latent feature. """ fn = cell.latentfeature deltan = cameraparams.viewingdistance rn = cameraparams.viewingdirection dn = cameraparams.viewingdirection # Assuming dn is viewing direction as per source # Decode attributes using shared MLPs # Fsigma, Fc, Fs, Fq are the learned MLPs # Opacity sigmas = Fsigma(fn, deltan, rn) # Output activated by Tanh # Clamp sigmas to [0, 1] if necessary, though Tanh maps to (-1, 1). # Source says "physically plausible range of [0, 1]", implying post-processing or specific activation. sigmas = torch.clamp(sigmas, 0, 1) # Color colors = Fc(fn, deltan, dn) # Scale State (Ratio) scaleratiosraw = Fs(fn, deltan, dn) # Output activated by sigmoid scaleratios = scaleratiosraw # Range (0, 1) # Quaternion quaternionsraw = Fq(fn, deltan, dn) quaternions = normalize(quaternionsraw) # Position Offset offsets = cell.offsets # Learned parameter Opos # Compute Gaussian Centers centers = cell.position + offsets cell.scales # Compute Gaussian Scales # sn,k = Oscalen,k Sn gaussianscales = scaleratios cell.scales # Clamp scale ratios to ensure Gaussians stay inside cell # Oscalen,k = min(Oscalen,k, 1 - ||Oposn,k||) offsetnorms = torch.norm(offsets, dim=-1, keepdim=True) scaleratios = torch.min(scaleratios, 1 - offsetnorms) # Recompute Gaussian Scales after clamping gaussianscales = scaleratios cell.scales # Update Cell Quaternion (for optimization, not rendering, but part of structure) # Qn = norm(sum(qn,k sigman,k)) # This is typically done during training/optimization steps. gaussians = [] for k in range(K): g = Gaussian( center=centers[k], opacity=sigmas[k], color=colors[k], scale=gaussianscales[k], quaternion=quaternions[k]) gaussians.append(g) return gaussians Time Complexity: Drastically reduces the overhead of global radix sorting compared to vanilla 3DGS because sorting is performed on the smaller population of cell proxies rather than individual Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Reduced memory consumption due to the smaller number of cells compared to Gaussians. Performance: Enables real-time performance on diverse real-world datasets. Strengths: Eliminates popping artifacts (locally order-independent) and transparency artifacts (physically grounded transmittance). Allows early termination for acceleration. Limitations: Order confusion caused by overlap among cells is a potential issue, addressed by the calibration scalar vn. When to use: When real-time rendering of Gaussian Splatting is required with high visual fidelity, specifically avoiding transparency and popping artifacts common in sort-free OIT methods. When not to use: If strict per-Gaussian depth ordering is required for specific physical effects not covered by the cell-level approximation. Duplex-GS was introduced in the paper "Duplex-GS: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon Scaffold-GS [20] which introduced anchors as local encoding proxies. Duplex-GS replaces point anchors with ellipsoidal cells to provide explicit geometric structure. It addresses limitations of vanilla OIT-based Gaussian Splatting [16] which lacks physical constraints and causes transparency artifacts. Duplex-GS: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2026.3666188, fetched 2026-10-30

name: LinPrim Differentiable Rendering Pipeline
head: LinPrim Rendering, LinPrim rasterizer, Linear Primitives Rendering, Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering
body: LinPrim is a differentiable rendering pipeline that replaces the Gaussian ellipsoids of 3D Gaussian Splatting with convex polyhedra (specifically octahedra and tetrahedra) to enable efficient, real-time volumetric rendering with bounded geometry. It solves the problem of reconstructing scenes with sharp geometric features and fine details by allowing gradients to backpropagate through explicit ray-triangle intersections, distinguishing it from sibling methods that rely on implicit density fields or Gaussian kernels. Unlike Duplex-GS which uses dual representations, or GsplatVolumeLighting which focuses on lighting integration, LinPrim explicitly constructs and rasterizes transparent polyhedral volumes. The pipeline operates in two main stages: per-primitive preprocessing and per-pixel rasterization/compositing. Inputs: Scene primitives defined by position, distances (vertex offsets), and rotation features. Camera pose (view and projection matrices). Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Outputs: Final rendered image with accumulated color and opacity. Each primitive stores the following parameters: 1. Geometric Features: Center position (\mathbf{c}). Distances from center to vertices. For octahedra, symmetry is enforced such that opposite vertices share the same distance, reducing complexity. For tetrahedra, 12 floats are required due to lack of full symmetry. Rotation features (quaternion or rotation matrix). 2. Color Features: 48 Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients (floats) to capture view-dependent reflectance. This accounts for the majority of memory per primitive. 1. Primitive Construction: Construct polyhedra (octahedra or tetrahedra) from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points in a fully differentiable manner. Enforce symmetry for octahedra so that opposite vertices share the same distance from the center, ensuring the center is the true geometric center. 2. Preprocessing (Per-Primitive): Transform primitives into the camera's coordinate system using the camera pose. Calculate view-dependent color based on the viewing direction using the stored SH coefficients. Project primitives into the 3D affine ray space approximation (EWA Splatting). This approximation error is negligible for small primitives. Compute each primitive's projected bounding box in screen space to determine visibility. 3. Global Sorting and Tiling: Tile the screen into regions. Sort primitives within each tile according to an approximate front-to-back order, leveraging techniques from 3DGS. 4. Rasterization (Per-Pixel): For each pixel ray, determine intersection with the convex primitive. Use the Möller-Trumbore intersection algorithm (MTIA) to find intersections. This algorithm is fully differentiable. If no intersections exist, the primitive is not visible for that pixel. If two intersections exist (entry and exit), calculate the distance between them. 5. Opacity and Density Calculation: Normalize intersection distances to handle scale ambiguity. Determine the smallest distance d among all primitives and scale all distance measurements accordingly. Calculate density \sigma based on the primitive opacity \alpha and the normalized distances dx, dy, dz. The formula for an octahedron is: \sigma(\alpha) = -\frac{\log(1 - 0.99 \cdot \alpha)}{2 \cdot \min(dx, dy, dz)} where \alpha is the primitive opacity and dx, dy, dz are the normalized distances. Note: The sources state that optimizing for unnormalized densities directly was experimented with but found to decrease interpretability without performance gains. 6. Compositing: Aggregate color contributions of all visible primitives via alpha blending in front-to-back order. Stop blending once the cumulative opacity reaches a threshold of 0.999. 7. Optimization (Backpropagation): Backpropagate image-space errors through the intersection calculations (MTIA) to distribute gradients onto the geometric features (position, distances, rotation) of each polyhedron. Adjust primitives' features and population based on gradient flow by comparing the rendered image with a known view. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linprimrender(primitives, camerapose, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Renders the scene using the LinPrim pipeline. primitives: List of Primitive objects. camerapose: Camera view and projection matrices. """ # 1. Preprocessing transformedprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: # Transform to camera space primcam = transformtocameraspace(prim, camerapose) # Calculate view-dependent color using SH # Note: SH evaluation depends on viewing direction, handled during rasterization or precomputed primcam.shcoeffs = prim.shcoeffs # Project to 3D affine ray space (EWA approximation) primcam.rayspace = projecttorayspace(primcam) # Compute screen-space bounding box primcam.bbox = computeboundingbox(primcam, imagewidth, imageheight) transformedprimitives.append(primcam) # 2. Global Sorting and Tiling # Tile screen and sort primitives front-to-back within tiles tiles = createtiles(imagewidth, imageheight) for tile in tiles: # Get primitives overlapping this tile's bbox tileprims = [p for p in transformedprimitives if intersectsbbox(p, tile.bbox)] # Sort by approximate depth (e.g., center depth) tileprims.sort(key=lambda p: p.centerdepth) tile.primitives = tileprims # 3. Rasterization and Compositing # Determine scale normalization factor (smallest distance d) mindist = min(p.getmindistance() for p in transformedprimitives) image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) opacityaccum = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) for tile in tiles: for prim in tile.primitives: # Check if primitive is already fully opaque for this tile region # (Optimization: skip if opacityaccum >= 0.999) # Rasterize primitive onto pixels in tile for pixel in tile.pixels: if opacityaccum[pixel.y, pixel.x] >= 0.999: continue # Ray-triangle intersection (Möller-Trumbore) # The primitive is a convex polyhedron (e.g., octahedron) # Find entry and exit points intersections = rayintersectpolyhedron(pixel.ray, prim) if len(intersections) == 2: dentry, dexit = intersections dist = dexit - dentry # Normalize distance normalizeddist = dist / mindist # Get opacity alpha from primitive parameters alpha = prim.opacity # Calculate density for this specific intersection segment # Using the formula provided in sources # Note: dx, dy, dz are normalized distances along axes or derived from dist # The source formula uses min(dx, dy, dz). # In implementation, this might be approximated by normalizeddist or axis-aligned extents. # Assuming normalizeddist represents the relevant scale metric here. dx, dy, dz = normalizeddist, normalizeddist, normalizeddist sigma = -log(1 - 0.99 alpha) / (2 min(dx, dy, dz)) # Compute color at intersection # Interpolate color between entry and exit or use entry point color = evaluatesh(prim.shcoeffs, pixel.viewdirection) # Alpha blending # Cout = Cin (1 - alphaeff) + Cprim alphaeff # Here alphaeff is derived from sigma and dist alphaeff = 1 - exp(-sigma dist) image[pixel.y, pixel.x] = ( image[pixel.y, pixel.x] (1 - alphaeff) + color alphaeff) opacityaccum[pixel.y, pixel.x] += alphaeff (1 - opacityaccum[pixel.y, pixel.x]) return image def backpropagategradient(loss, primitives, renderedimage, gtimage): """ Backpropagates error through the rendering pipeline to update primitive features. """ # Compute loss lossval = computeloss(renderedimage, gtimage) # Gradient w.r.t. image gradimg = computegradient(lossval, renderedimage) # Backprop through compositing and rasterization # The Möller-Trumbore intersection is differentiable # Gradients flow to intersection points, then to primitive vertices/geometry for prim in primitives: # Update geometric features (position, distances, rotation) # Update SH coefficients prim.updategradients(gradimg) SH Degree: 48 coefficients (typically degree 2 or 3, stored as floats). Opacity Threshold: 0.999 for stopping compositing. Normalization Factor: Smallest distance d among all primitives. Scale Ambiguity: Without normalization, appearance varies across different scene sizes. Handled by scaling distances relative to the smallest primitive distance d. Approximation Error: The 3D affine ray space approximation error grows with distance from center points but remains negligible for small primitives. Convexity: The rasterization assumes primitives are convex, ensuring at most two intersections per ray. Time Complexity: Real-time performance is achieved due to efficient parallelization in preprocessing and tiling-based rasterization. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of 48 SH coefficients per primitive. Reducing SH degree or primitive count lowers memory usage. Strengths: Bounded, triangular geometry allows for better handling of sharp features compared to Gaussian splats; fully differentiable; real-time speeds. Limitations: Approximation error in ray space projection; scale ambiguity requires global normalization. When to use: Scenes requiring high-fidelity reconstruction of fine geometry and sharp edges where Gaussian splats may blur details. LinPrim was introduced in the paper "LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering". It builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline but replaces Gaussian ellipsoids with transparent octahedron and tetrahedron primitives. The method was developed to provide an intuitive representation that can be easily understood and modified, while retaining real-time rendering speeds and comparable photometric reconstruction quality to existing methods.
