The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizepixel(surfelssorted, rcutsq): # Initialize accumulators for the current surface group Cg = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Wg = 0.0 zendmax = 0.0 layers = [] for surfel in surfelssorted: # 1. Ray-surfel intersection to get local coordinates (u, v) # Standard ray-surfel intersection solving for local (u, v) coordinates. uv = computeintersection(surfel) if uv is None: continue # 2. Evaluate MIP-filtered weight rhomip^2 via precomputed Sigmamip^{-1} # Standard Mahalanobis distance computation using inverse covariance. rhomipsq = computemipweight(surfel) # 3. Cutoff check if rhomipsq >= rcutsq: continue # 4. Calculate weight w nf = surfel.nf w = nf math.exp(-0.5 rhomipsq) # 5. Define depth interval zstarti = surfel.z - surfel.epsilonz zendi = surfel.z + surfel.epsilonz # 6. Gap detection and layer finalization if Wg > 0 and zstarti > zendmax: # Finalize current group via FLUSHLAYER (applies Shepard normalization) layer = flushlayer(Cg, Wg) layers.append(layer) Cg = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Wg = 0.0 zendmax = 0.0 # 7. Expand group extent zendmax = max(zendmax, zendi) # 8. Accumulate contribution Cg = [Cg[j] + w surfel.ci[j] for j in range(3)] Wg += w # Finalize the last group if it has content if Wg > 0: layer = flushlayer(Cg, Wg) layers.append(layer) # 9. Composite layers front-to-back using coverage-based opacity return compositelayers(layers) def computeintersection(surfel): # Standard ray-surfel intersection math. return None def computemipweight(surfel): # Standard covariance-based MIP weight math. return 0.0 def flushlayer(Cg, Wg): # Applies Shepard normalization to accumulated color Cg using weight Wg. return Layer(normalize(Cg, Wg)) def compositelayers(layers): # Standard front-to-back alpha blending using coverage-based opacity derived from Wg. return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-occlusion: Without depth-interval grouping, single-layer approaches produce self-occlusion errors at high-curvature concavities (e.g., inside ears, under chins) where distinct surface sheets project onto the same pixel. Silhouette Artifacts: Single-layer methods can produce "crusty" shells or aliased contours at silhouettes. This method avoids this by applying smooth coverage falloff independently on each layer. Precision: The gap detection relies on comparing z{\text{start}}^{(i)} with z{\text{end}}^{\max}. Precision issues in depth values could lead to incorrect gap detection or merging of distinct layers. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Sorting is done per-tile via radix sort. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Proportional to the number of surface layers per pixel. Strengths: Resolves self-occlusion at concavities; produces anti-aliased silhouettes without post-process edge detection; differentiable for inverse rendering. Limitations: Requires sorting and per-pixel state management; more complex than single-layer rasterization. When to use: When rendering unstructured surface representations (surfels) that require accurate self-occlusion handling and physically-based inverse rendering. 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS) was introduced in the paper "3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering". The rasterization method builds on the concept of depth-interval grouping to handle the challenges of rendering unstructured surfel clouds, particularly addressing the limitations of single-layer ternary depth tests and classical A-buffer approaches. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Radiometric Self-Calibration
head: Color Calibration, Exposure and Sensor Bias Estimation, Gain and Bias Calibration, Response Curve Optimization
body: Radiometric Self-Calibration optimizes per-camera and per-channel radiometric parameters (gain and bias) during the reconstruction process to correct for photometric errors and intensity mismatches between cameras. It addresses the problem where geometrically calibrated cameras still produce inconsistent pixel values for the same radiance due to sensor differences or lighting variations. Unlike Color Volume Optimization and Density Initialization which adjusts volume properties, this method adjusts the observation model. It typically improves reconstruction quality by approximately 1 dB. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground truth images I{\text{gt}}, camera poses, volume representation (e.g., neural field or voxel grid), and initial volume color estimates I{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}) and opacity I\alpha(\mathbf{p}) for each pixel \mathbf{p}. Outputs: Optimized per-camera, per-channel gain g and bias b, and optionally a static background image I{\text{rgb}}^{(\text{bg})}. Data Structures: Gain/Bias Parameters: A tensor of shape (N{\text{cameras}}, N{\text{channels}}) storing learnable parameters g and b. Background Image (Optional): A static RGB image tensor I{\text{rgb}}^{(\text{bg})} of resolution matching the camera sensor, stored as a learnable parameter. Steps: 1. Initialize: Initialize gain g to 1.0 and bias b to 0.0 for all cameras and channels. Initialize background image I{\text{rgb}}^{(\text{bg})} to black or zero if used. 2. Raymarch: For each camera view, raymarch through the volume to compute the accumulated volume color I{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}) and opacity I\alpha(\mathbf{p}) for each pixel \mathbf{p}. 3. Apply Radiometric Transform: Apply the per-camera, per-channel gain and bias to the volume color: I'{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}) = g \cdot I{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}) + b 4. Merge Background (Optional): If background estimation is enabled, blend the transformed volume color with the static background image based on the volume's opacity: \widehat{I}{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}) = (1 - I\alpha(\mathbf{p})) I{\text{rgb}}^{(\text{bg})}(\mathbf{p}) + I'{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}) If background estimation is disabled, \widehat{I}{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}) = I'{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}). 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the photometric loss (e.g., L1 or L2) between the rendered image \widehat{I}{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}) and the ground truth image I{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{p}). 6. Optimize: Update the gain g, bias b, and optionally the background image I{\text{rgb}}^{(\text{bg})} using gradient descent (e.g., Adam). Parameters: Learning Rate for Gain/Bias: 10^{-3}. Learning Rate for Background Image: 10^{-1}. Response Curve Optimization: Can be enabled to further improve quality, though specific implementation details are not provided in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def radiometricselfcalibration(volumemodel, cameras, gtimages, usebackground=False, lrgainbias=1e-3, lrbackground=1e-1): # Initialize learnable parameters # g: (numcameras, numchannels), b: (numcameras, numchannels) g = torch.oneslike(g) b = torch.zeroslike(b) if usebackground: # bgimages: (numcameras, H, W, numchannels) bgimages = torch.zeroslike(bgimages) optimizerbg = torch.optim.Adam([bgimages], lr=lrbackground) optimizergb = torch.optim.Adam([g, b], lr=lrgainbias) for iteration in range(numiterations): optimizergb.zerograd() if usebackground: optimizerbg.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 for camera, gtimage in zip(cameras, gtimages): # 1. Raymarch to get volume color and opacity # volumecolor: (H, W, C), opacity: (H, W, 1) volumecolor, opacity = volumemodel.raymarch(camera) # 2. Apply gain and bias # Apply per-camera gain/bias camidx = camera.id transformedcolor = g[camidx] volumecolor + b[camidx] # 3. Merge with background if enabled if usebackground: bg = bgimages[camidx] # alpha is assumed to be in [0, 1] rendered = (1.0 - opacity) bg + transformedcolor else: rendered = transformedcolor # 4. Compute loss loss = F.l1loss(rendered, gtimage) totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() optimizergb.step() if usebackground: optimizerbg.step() return g, b, bgimages if usebackground else None Optimizes geometric parameters, such as detector orientation and source position, during reconstruction to correct for calibration errors. It recovers from significant initial calibration errors, specifically recovering from a 15 dB degradation caused by Gaussian noise in position and rotation, outperforming the baseline. It is chosen when initial camera poses are inaccurate or noisy. Estimates a static per-camera background image I{\text{rgb}}^{(\text{bg})} to capture stationary objects outside the reconstruction volume, reducing artifacts caused by slight appearance differences from calibration errors or view-dependent effects. It is chosen when the scene contains static background elements that the volume reconstruction might otherwise try to model incorrectly, leading to smoke-like artifacts. Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead to the training loop as it involves only element-wise operations on the rendered images and optimization of a small number of parameters per camera. Memory Complexity: Negligible for gain/bias parameters. If background images are used, memory usage increases by N{\text{cameras}} \times H \times W \times 3 floats. Performance: Improves reconstruction quality by approximately 1 dB when enabled. Strengths: Robust to intensity mismatches between cameras; reduces artifacts from unmodeled background elements. Limitations: Assumes a static background if used; does not correct for non-linear response curves unless explicitly enabled. When to use: When cameras are geometrically calibrated but exhibit photometric inconsistencies. When static background elements cause reconstruction artifacts. Radiometric Self-Calibration originates from work on neural volume rendering and adaptive tomography. It was introduced in "Neural Volumes: Learning Dynamic Renderable Volumes from Images" (2019) and "Neural Adaptive Tomography" (2022). It is used in differentiable volume rendering pipelines to improve photometric consistency. name: Dynamic Appearance Features Modeling
head: Adaptive Sampling with K Feature Maps
body: Dynamic Appearance Features Modeling addresses the limitation of global feature embeddings in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which assume uniform environmental information (lighting, weather) across a scene. By extracting dynamic appearance features from a reference image and allowing each Gaussian point to sample from multiple feature maps, the method captures local details such as highlights and shadows that global embeddings miss. It sets itself apart from methods like NeRF-W and Ha-NeRF, which use global scene embeddings, and CR-NeRF, which integrates features at the 2D level without dynamic 3D environmental information. Inputs: Reference image I{gt} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. Known camera pose for the reference image, defining the projection matrix P. Set of N 3D Gaussian points, where each point i has a position coordinate Xi. Outputs: Dynamic appearance feature vector dfi \in \mathbb{R}^{16(K+1)} for each Gaussian point i. Data Structures: Feature Map F: A 2D tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{16(K+1) \times H \times W}. Projection Feature Map F^P: The first 16 channels of F, shape \mathbb{R}^{16 \times H \times W}. K Feature Maps (F^1, \dots, F^K): The remaining 16K channels of F, evenly divided into K maps, each of shape \mathbb{R}^{16 \times H \times W}. Sampling Coordinates sci: For each Gaussian point i, a set of K learnable 2D coordinates (sci^1, \dots, sci^K), where each sci^k \in [-1, 1]^2. Parameters: K: The number of additional feature maps for adaptive sampling. Typical value: 3. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass the reference image I{gt} through a U-Net model with a ResNet backbone to generate the combined feature map F \in \mathbb{R}^{16(K+1) \times H \times W}. 2. Map Division: Split F along the channel dimension into K+1 feature maps: the projection feature map F^P (first 16 channels) and K additional feature maps F^1, \dots, F^K (remaining 16K channels). 3. Projection Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian point i: Project its 3D position Xi onto the 2D image plane using the projection matrix P derived from the camera pose, resulting in coordinates \PiP(Xi). Sample the projection feature fi^P \in \mathbb{R}^{16} from F^P at \PiP(Xi) using bilinear interpolation. fi^P = BL(\PiP(Xi), F^P) \quad (6) where BL denotes bilinear interpolation sampling. 4. Adaptive Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian point i: Use the learnable sampling coordinates (sci^1, \dots, sci^K) to sample features from the K additional feature maps. Sample features (fi^1, \dots, fi^K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 16} from (F^1, \dots, F^K) using bilinear interpolation at the respective coordinates. (fi^1, fi^2, \dots, fi^K) = BL((sci^1, sci^2, \dots, sci^K), (F^1, F^2, \dots, F^K)) \quad (7) 5. Concatenation: Concatenate the projection feature and the K sampled features to form the dynamic appearance feature dfi. dfi = fi^P \oplus fi^1 \oplus fi^2 \oplus \dots \oplus fi^K \quad (8) where \oplus denotes concatenation. 6. Regularization: Apply a regularization loss L{sc} to prevent sampling coordinates from deviating beyond the effective sampling range [-1, 1]. L{sc} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \max\{0, |sci| - 1\} \quad (9) where N is the total number of Gaussian points and | \cdot | denotes the absolute value applied to each coordinate component. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def extractfeatures(referenceimage: torch.Tensor, unetmodel: torch.nn.Module) -> torch.Tensor: """Extracts the combined feature map F from the reference image using a U-Net with ResNet backbone.""" return unetmodel(referenceimage) def splitfeaturemaps(Fmap: torch.Tensor, K: int): """Splits the combined feature map F into projection feature map F^P and K additional feature maps.""" FP = Fmap[:16,:,:] FK = [Fmap[16 + k 16: 16 + (k + 1) 16,:,:] for k in range(K)] return FP, FK def sampleprojectionfeature(Xi: torch.Tensor, P: torch.Tensor, FP: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Samples the projection feature for a single Gaussian point.""" Xihom = torch.cat([Xi, torch.ones(1, device=Xi.device)]) projected = P @ Xihom u, v = projected[0], projected[1] grid = torch.tensor([[[[u, v]]]], device=Xi.device) FPbatch = FP.unsqueeze(0) return F.gridsample(FPbatch, grid, aligncorners=False).squeeze() def sampleadaptivefeatures(sci: list, FK: list) -> torch.Tensor: """Samples features from K feature maps using learnable sampling coordinates.""" features = [] for k in range(len(FK)): u, v = sci[k][0], sci[k][1] grid = torch.tensor([[[[u, v]]]], device=sci[k][0].device) Fkbatch = FK[k].unsqueeze(0) features.append(F.gridsample(Fkbatch, grid, aligncorners=False).squeeze()) return torch.stack(features, dim=0) def computedynamicappearancefeature(Xi: torch.Tensor, P: torch.Tensor, FP: torch.Tensor, sci: list, FK: list) -> torch.Tensor: """Computes the dynamic appearance feature dfi for a single Gaussian point.""" fiP = sampleprojectionfeature(Xi, P, FP) fiK = sampleadaptivefeatures(sci, FK) return torch.cat([fiP, fiK.flatten()]) def computeregularizationloss(scilist: list, N: int) -> torch.Tensor: """Computes the regularization loss Lsc for all Gaussian points.""" totalloss = torch.tensor(0.0, device=scilist[0][0].device) for sci in scilist: for sc in sci: totalloss += torch.sum(torch.clamp(torch.abs(sc) - 1, min=0)) return totalloss / N Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The projection matrix P must map 3D points to 2D coordinates compatible with the bilinear interpolation function's valid range. Boundaries: The regularization loss L{sc} is designed to keep sampling coordinates within [-1, 1]. If coordinates exceed this range, the loss penalizes them, but sampling outside this range may result in undefined behavior or zero-padding depending on the interpolation implementation. Degenerate Input: If the reference image I{gt} is not available or the camera pose is unknown, the projection feature map F^P cannot be computed, and the method fails. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method was trained on a single Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU for 70k steps, taking approximately 2 hours, with images downsampled twice during training and evaluation. Scaling: Increasing K beyond 3 yields no performance improvement while adding meaningless computational cost, establishing K=3 as optimal. Strengths: Captures local details such as highlights and shadows that global embeddings miss, aligning better with real-world varying environmental influences. Limitations: Limited by the single-view reference image I{gt}, where features sampled from the projection feature map are identical along the same ray, which is unreasonable under uneven lighting. Origin: Introduced in "Gaussian in the Wild: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unconstrained Image Collections". History and Development: Previous methods like NeRF-W and Ha-NeRF used global feature embeddings assuming uniform environmental information, while CR-NeRF integrated features at the 2D level without dynamic 3D environmental information. This method addresses these limitations by allowing each Gaussian point to independently learn its sampling positions. Usage: Used in the WildGaussians framework for 'in-the-wild' settings, integrating robust DINO features and a lightweight appearance modeling module within the 3DGS framework [Parent]. name: Densification Strategy
head: Gaussian Densification Strategies, 3DGS Densification
body: Densification strategies manage the population of Gaussian primitives during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models, addressing the issues of unpredictable model size, redundant primitives, and excessive training duration. Unlike the original 3DGS approach which relies on heuristic splitting and cloning based on position gradients and opacity, this family includes methods that use score-based constructive growth, temporal sensitivity pruning, and groupwise motion distillation to control model complexity and improve rendering efficiency. The core mechanism of densification in 3D Gaussian Splatting involves dynamically adjusting the number and distribution of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}i during the optimization process. The primary goal is to allocate more primitives in regions of high geometric or photometric complexity while removing or merging those that contribute little to the reconstruction. Common principles include: 1. Evaluation Metric: A score or metric is computed for each Gaussian to determine its contribution to the reconstruction quality. This metric often combines gradient information, saliency, and primitive properties. 2. Population Control: Strategies either add new Gaussians (densification), remove existing ones (pruning), or both, to reach a target model size or budget. 3. Temporal Aggregation: In dynamic scenes, metrics may be aggregated over multiple timesteps and poses to assess the stability and importance of a Gaussian over time. Link to [Gaussian Densification] Link to [Optimization and Densification Strategy] Link to [GroupFlow] Definition A purely constructive densification process that steers the addition of new Gaussians toward those that raise reconstruction quality, ensuring model size increases in a controlled manner towards an exact user-defined budget without requiring pruning or culling during training. Steps 1. Sample training views and compute per-pixel saliency to identify important regions. 2. Compute a per-Gaussian score Sg by combining gradient, saliency, and primitive properties into a scoring function F. 3. Densify new Gaussians in the vicinity of the top-scoring Gaussians according to a pre-defined budget. 4. Follow a growth curve that mimics 3DGS’ behavior and can be fitted to yield any desired model size after training. Comparison Unlike previous work that requires substantial pruning or culling of Gaussians during training, this method uses a purely constructive schedule, avoiding unnecessary peaks in optimization that could violate hardware or budget constraints. Definition Scales the densification gradient by the projected area in pixels, so a Gaussian that hurts many pixels is split first. Definition TSP is a pruning method that removes low-impact Gaussians by calculating a temporal sensitivity score approximating the second-order sensitivity to the L2 loss across all training views. Steps 1. For each Gaussian \mathcal{G}i, calculate the gradient of the rendered image I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) with respect to the projected Gaussian value gi for all training poses \phi and timesteps t in \mathcal{P}{gt}. 2. Square these gradients and sum them over all poses and timesteps to compute the cumulative sensitivity score \tilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i}. 3. Periodically prune Gaussians with low sensitivity scores during training to reduce neural inference load. Formula \tilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} \approx \nabla{gi}^2 L2 \approx \sum{\phi, t \in \mathcal{P}{gt}} \left( \nabla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) \right)^2 where \tilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} is the TSP score for Gaussian \mathcal{G}i, gi is the value of \mathcal{G}i projected onto image space, \mathcal{P}{gt} is the set of training poses and timesteps, and I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) is the rendered image at pose \phi and timestep t. Parameters \mathcal{P}{gt}: The set of training poses and timesteps used for sensitivity aggregation. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The original method used a heuristic densification process involving splitting and cloning Gaussians based on position gradients and opacity thresholds. However, this approach led to unpredictable model sizes and training durations, making it difficult to control for specific hardware or budget constraints. Subsequent works have proposed various densification strategies to address these limitations. "Taming 3DGS" introduced a score-based constructive densification method to control model size. "SpeeDe3DGS" introduced Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) for dynamic scenes to remove redundant primitives and improve rendering speed. Other variants like Pixel-GS and GaussianPro have also been proposed to improve densification efficiency and quality. name: Explicit Radiance Fields
head: Explicit Radiance Fields Reconstruction via Gauss-Newton, Non-linear least-squares volumetric reconstruction, PERF (Performant Explicit Radiance Fields), PERF reconstruction, Volumetric reconstruction with explicit voxels
body: Explicit Radiance Fields (also known as PERF) is a method for image-based 3D reconstruction of 360° scenes that formulates volumetric reconstruction as a non-linear least-squares problem solved explicitly without neural networks. It uses a voxel grid for the foreground and a hierarchical set of environment maps for the background, minimizing the sum of squared differences between accumulated ray colors and actual pixel colors. Unlike Plenoxels which uses fixed hierarchical structures, or Direct Voxel Grid Optimization which uses gradient descent, PERF employs a Gauss-Newton solver with Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient, achieving 2-3 orders of magnitude faster convergence than neural network-based methods like NERF. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of images of a scene with known camera poses. Outputs: A voxel grid containing color and differential opacity values, and a set of environment maps containing color and opacity values. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A 3D grid where each cell contains three color channels C = \{cr, cg, cb\} and differential opacity \sigma. Stored in a 3D surface for CUDA implementation. 2. Environment Maps: A hierarchical set of cubemap environment maps surrounding the object of interest, centered around it. Each texel contains color and opacity. Their distance increases with the square of the distance to the voxel grid. Stored in cube maps. 3. Backing Storage: For kernels using atomics, backing storage is copied to regular memory, as atomics are not supported for surfaces. CUDA texture objects are bound to surfaces for hardware trilinear interpolation. Parameters: \alpha: Geometrical decimation factor for line search, set to 0.7. \lambda: Weight for the auxiliary opacity penalty term, set to 0.1. Hierarchical Levels: Typically 4-5 levels. Resolution doubles per level. Initial resolution: 32^3 for voxel grid, 32 \times 32 for cubemaps. Iterations per level: N=30. PCG Iterations: Typically 1-3 iterations. Opacity Threshold: During rendering of converged scene, if (1.0 - \hat{T}) < 0.7, volume is considered fully transparent. Final Grid Resolution: Typically 256^3 or 512^3. Environment Maps Resolution: 256^2 or 512^2 per cubemap face. Image Resolution: Synthetic scenes run at half image resolution. 360° scenes run at quarter image resolution. Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with a low-resolution voxel grid (32^3) and environment maps (32 \times 32). Initialize with random colors and low opacity. 2. Hierarchical Optimization Loop: For each hierarchical level: a. Ray Integration (Voxel Grid): For each pixel, generate a ray. Ray origin jittering: Position within pixel chosen randomly using two uniformly distributed floats. Ray sample jittering: Randomize position of samples within half a raymarch step before and after uniform steps along the ray. Ray-march through the voxel grid using step length equal to the shortest side of a voxel cell. Compute accumulated color \hat{H} using the discrete volume rendering equation. b. Ray Integration (Environment Maps): After exiting the voxel grid, perform intersection tests with environment maps in order from inner to outer. Accumulate contribution similarly to the voxel grid. c. Residual Calculation: Compute residuals ri for each pixel. Each pixel has 3 residuals (one per color channel), defined as the difference between pixel color C and accumulated color \hat{H}. d. Auxiliary Term: Compute auxiliary penalty L = \lambda [-4(\hat{T} - 0.5)^2 + 1], where \hat{T} is accumulated opacity. This penalizes opacity deviations from 0 or 1 to mitigate view-dependent highlight artifacts. e. Derivative Computation: Compute partial derivatives of the first degree analytically using the iterative algorithm described below. f. Gauss-Newton Update: Solve the linear system A x = b where A = Jr^T Jr, x = \Delta, and b = -Jr^T r. Use Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (PCG) to solve for \Delta. Update x{i+1} = xi + \Delta. g. Line Search: Apply backtracking line search to scale the step size \gamma by \alpha = 0.7 if the error increases. h. Level Completion: When a level completes (after N=30 iterations), store result temporarily, reallocate buffers, populate new buffers with old data via linear interpolation, and resume optimization at the new level. Formulas: Discrete Volume Rendering Equation: \hat{H} = \sum{t=tn}^{tf} \hat{T}(t)(1 - e^{-\sigma(t)\delta(t)})c(t) where \hat{T}(t) = e^{-\sum{s=t}^{tf} \sigma(s)\delta(s)}. Expanded form: \hat{H} = e^{-\sum{j=1}^N \sigmaj \deltaj} (1 - e^{-\sigma1 \delta1}) c1 + e^{-\sigma1 \delta1} (1 - e^{-\sigma2 \delta2}) c2 + \dots + e^{-\sum{j=1}^{N-1} \sigmaj \deltaj} (1 - e^{-\sigmaN \deltaN}) cN. Objective Function: F[c(t), \sigma(t)] = 0.5 \sum{t=tn}^{tf} \sum{i=1}^{3} (\hat{H}i[ci(t), \sigma(t)] - Ci)^2. Non-linear Least-Squares General Form: S(x) = 0.5 \sum{i=1}^{m} ri(x)^2 where ri are residuals. Gauss-Newton Update: x{i+1} = xi - (Jr^T Jr)^{-1} Jr^T r(xi) = xi + \Delta. PCG System: A p = Jr^T Jr p = \sumi \nabla ri (\nabla ri^T p). Auxiliary Penalty: L = \lambda [-4(\hat{T} - 0.5)^2 + 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computederivatives(sigma, delta, c, N): # sigma, delta, c are arrays of length N for the ray samples # Returns dHdc and dHdsigma for each sample V = exp(-sum(sigma[i] delta[i] for i in range(N))) G = 0.0 dHdc = [0.0] N dHdsigma = [0.0] N for i in range(N - 1, -1, -1): V = V - sigma[i] delta[i] dHdc[i] = exp(-V) (1 - exp(-sigma[i] delta[i])) dHdsigma[i] = G + exp(-V) (1 - exp(-sigma[i] delta[i])) c[i] G = exp(-V) delta[i] exp(-sigma[i] delta[i]) c[i] - delta[i] G return dHdc, dHdsigma def pcgsolve(Apfunction, b, Minv, x0, eps=1e-6, maxiter=3): r = b - Apfunction(x0) Rprev = dot(r, r) z = Minv(r) p = z k = 0 while True: Ap = Apfunction(p) alphak = dot(r, z) / dot(p, Ap) xnext = x0 + alphak p rnext = r - alphak Ap R = dot(rnext, rnext) if R < eps or R / Rprev > 0.85: return xnext Rprev = R znext = Minv(rnext) betak = dot(rnext, znext) / dot(r, z) p = znext + betak p r = rnext x0 = xnext k += 1 if k >= maxiter: return xnext def linesearch(gamma, alpha, errorfunction): gammacurr = gamma muprev = float('inf') while True: mu = errorfunction(gammacurr) if mu > muprev: return gammacurr / alpha gammacurr = alpha gammacurr muprev = mu def gaussnewtonstep(x, rays, images, voxelgrid, envmaps): # 1. Compute residuals and gradients residuals = [] gradients = [] # Sum of Jr^T r for ray, pixelcolor in zip(rays, images): # Ray march voxel grid and env maps to get Hhat Hhat = renderray(ray, voxelgrid, envmaps) # Residuals (3 per pixel) r = Hhat - pixelcolor # Compute derivatives using Algorithm 1 dHdc, dHdsigma = computederivatives(...) # Accumulate gradient Jr^T r # Note: In practice, this is done efficiently by accumulating into global buffers # Here we show the conceptual accumulation for i in range(len(r)): gradients[i] += -r[i] dHdc[i] # Simplified for color channels residuals.append(r) # 2. Solve Ax = b using PCG # A = Jr^T Jr, b = -Jr^T r # Minv is diagonal Jacobi preconditioner: diag(Jr^T Jr) # Define Ap function: Ap = sumi gradri (gradri^T p) def Ap(p): Ap = zeroslike(p) for ray in rays: # Compute gradri for this ray gradr = computegradientforray(ray, p) Ap += gradr dot(gradr, p) return Ap # Preconditioner Minv def Minv(v): # Diagonal Jacobi: 1 / diag(A) diagA = computediagonalA() return v / diagA b = gradients # -Jr^T r x0 = x delta = pcgsolve(Ap, b, Minv, x0) # 3. Line Search gamma = 1.0 alpha = 0.7 newx = x + gamma delta errornew = computeerror(newx) errorold = computeerror(x) if errornew > errorold: gamma = linesearch(gamma, alpha, computeerror) newx = x + gamma delta return newx Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity: Jr is very sparse because only a fraction of voxels/texels are hit by a given ray. This sparsity is exploited to avoid explicit matrix inversion. View-Dependence: The method does not consider view-dependent effects, which can lead to smoke-like artifacts. Precision: The matrix A is too large to form explicitly (e.g., 4TB for a 32^3 grid). Boundaries: Environment maps are used to handle rays exiting the voxel grid, ensuring clean separation of foreground and background for 360° scenes. Time Complexity: 2-3 orders of magnitude faster than NERF reference. Example: Pinecone 24m:54s (Ours) vs 23h:21m (NERF) on 512^3 grid. Memory Complexity: The matrix A is too large to form explicitly. The method uses iterative solvers and sparse operations to manage memory. Measured Performance: On Nvidia Titan V GPU. Synthetic scenes run at half image resolution. 360° scenes run at quarter image resolution. Scaling: Uses a hierarchical scheme with 4-5 levels, doubling resolution per level. Initial resolution 32^3, final 256^3 or 512^3. Strengths: Fast convergence due to Gauss-Newton solver. Real-time rendering possible during training. Clean separation of foreground and background for 360° scenes. Limitations: Does not consider view-dependent effects. Quality is comparable to NERF without view-dependence but lower than full NERF or SNeRG. When to use: When fast reconstruction of 360° scenes is required and view-dependent effects are not critical. When not to use: When high-fidelity view-dependent effects are required. Explicit Radiance Fields (PERF) was presented by Sverker Rasmuson, Erik Sintorn, and Ulf Assarsson from Chalmers University of Technology in 2022. The method formulates volumetric reconstruction as a non-linear least-squares problem, solving it explicitly without neural networks. This allows the use of solvers with higher convergence rates than standard Stochastic Gradient Descent used for neural networks. The work builds on the NERF formulation but replaces the MLP and ADAM optimizer with explicit voxel/environment map representation and Gauss-Newton solver. name: NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields)
head: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis, Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)
body: NeRF is a neural rendering method that models a radiance field by incorporating both 3D position and view direction to correctly render specularities and transparency, which require view-dependent effects. It solves the problem of synthesizing novel views of complex 3D scenes from a sparse set of posed 2D images by learning a continuous 5D function that maps spatial coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and emitted color. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Explicit Radiance Fields and Plenoxels, is its use of a dense, fully-connected Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to represent the scene implicitly, allowing for high-fidelity reconstruction of complex geometry and appearance without explicit mesh or voxel structures. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N posed training images \{Ii\} with known camera poses (rotation Ri and translation ti) and intrinsics (focal length f). Outputs: A rendered RGB image, depth map, and accumulation (opacity) map for a target camera pose. Data Structures: The scene is represented by two MLPs (often sharing weights or architecture): a coarse network and a fine network. Positional Encoding: Inputs are transformed using sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{p}). For input vector \mathbf{v} and level L: \gamma(\mathbf{v}) = (\sin(2^0 \mathbf{v}), \cos(2^0 \mathbf{v}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \mathbf{v}), \cos(2^{L-1} \mathbf{v})) Position encoding (L=10): Input dimension 3 + 3 \times 2 \times 10 = 63. Direction encoding (L=4): Input dimension 3 + 3 \times 2 \times 4 = 27. MLP Architecture: Density Network: 8 fully-connected layers with 256 hidden units each, using ReLU activation. A skip connection concatenates the original encoded position input to the output of layer 4. Color Network: Takes the output of the density network (feature vector) and the encoded viewing direction. It consists of a few fully-connected layers (e.g., 128 units) followed by a final layer outputting 3 values (RGB). Output Dimensions: The final layer of the density network outputs 1 value (density \sigma) and a feature vector (e.g., 256 dims). The color network outputs 3 values (RGB). Total raw output per query is 4 values. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel (u, v) in the target image, generate a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Compute normalized image-plane coordinates: x = (u - W/2)/f, y = -(v - H/2)/f, z = -1. Transform direction to world space: \mathbf{d}{world} = R \cdot [x, y, 1]^T, then normalize. Set origin \mathbf{o} to the camera center. 2. Coarse Sampling: Sample Nc points along the ray within the interval [t{near}, t{far}]. Divide [t{near}, t{far}] into Nc equal bins. Draw one sample uniformly at random from each bin (stratified sampling). Typical values: Nc = 64, t{near} = 2.0, t{far} = 6.0 (for Blender datasets). 3. Coarse Network Query: Apply positional encoding to the 3D positions of the sampled points. Pass through the coarse MLP to predict raw density \sigmac and feature vectors \mathbf{f}c. Apply ReLU to \sigmac to ensure non-negativity. 4. Importance Sampling (Hierarchical Sampling): Compute weights for the coarse samples: wi = Ti \cdot (1 - \exp(-\sigma{c,i} \deltai)), where \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Normalize weights to form a Probability Density Function (PDF). Sample Nf additional points using inverse-CDF sampling based on this PDF, concentrating samples in regions of high density. Typical value: Nf = 128. 5. Fine Network Query: Combine coarse and fine sample points. Apply positional encoding to positions. Pass through the fine MLP to predict raw density \sigmaf and feature vectors \mathbf{f}f. Apply ReLU to \sigmaf. 6. Volume Rendering: For each sample i, compute opacity \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). Compute transmittance Ti = \prod{j<i} (1 - \alphaj). Compute rendering weights Wi = Ti \alphai. Concatenate feature vector \mathbf{f}i with the encoded viewing direction \gamma(\mathbf{d}). Pass through the color network head to get RGB color \mathbf{c}i. Apply Sigmoid to clamp RGB to [0, 1]. Compute final color: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sumi Wi \mathbf{c}i. Compute depth: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sumi Wi ti. Compute accumulation: \hat{A}(\mathbf{r}) = \sumi Wi. 7. Training: Minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the ground truth image color C(\mathbf{r}). Loss function: \mathcal{L} = \sum{\mathbf{r}} [\|\hat{C}{coarse}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|^22 + \|\hat{C}{fine}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|^22]. Use Adam optimizer with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, initial learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4} decaying exponentially to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def positionalencoding(v, numfrequencies, includeinput=True): """ Applies sinusoidal positional encoding to input vector v. v: Tensor of shape [..., D] numfrequencies: int L Returns: Tensor of shape [..., D (2L + 1)] if includeinput else [..., D 2L] """ freqbands = 2.0 torch.linspace(0, numfrequencies - 1, numfrequencies) # v[..., None] freqbands -> [..., D, L] # sin and cos -> [..., D, L, 2] encoded = torch.cat([torch.sin(v[..., None] freqbands), torch.cos(v[..., None] freqbands)], dim=-1) # Flatten last two dims -> [..., D 2 L] encoded = encoded.view(v.shape[:-1], -1) if includeinput: return torch.cat([v, encoded], dim=-1) return encoded def nerfmlpforward(xposenc, xdirenc, densitylayers, colorhead): """ Forward pass through the NeRF MLP. xposenc: Encoded position [..., 63] xdirenc: Encoded direction [..., 27] densitylayers: List of linear layers for density network colorhead: Linear layer for RGB output """ h = xposenc for i, layer in enumerate(densitylayers): h = layer(h) if i < len(densitylayers) - 1: # ReLU for hidden layers h = F.relu(h) if i == 3: # Skip connection at layer 4 (index 3) h = torch.cat([h, xposenc], dim=-1) # Last layer outputs density and feature vector # Assuming the last layer is defined to output 1 + featuredim rawdensity = h[...,:1] featurevec = h[..., 1:] # View-dependent color # Concatenate feature vector with direction encoding hcolor = torch.cat([featurevec, xdirenc], dim=-1) hcolor = F.relu(hcolor) rgb = colorhead(hcolor) return rawdensity, rgb def renderray(rayso, raysd, near, far, ncoarse, nfine, posencpos, posencdir, densitylayerscoarse, densitylayersfine, colorheadcoarse, colorheadfine): """ Renders a single ray (or batch of rays) using NeRF. """ # 1. Coarse Sampling tcoarse = torch.linspace(near, far, ncoarse) # Stratified sampling dt = (far - near) / ncoarse tcoarse = tcoarse + torch.randlike(tcoarse) dt - dt/2 # 2. Compute Coarse Weights for Importance Sampling deltas = tcoarse[..., 1:] - tcoarse[...,:-1] lastdelta = torch.fulllike(deltas[...,:1], 1e10) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, lastdelta], dim=-1) deltas = deltas raysd.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) sigmacoarse = F.relu(rawsigmacoarse) alphacoarse = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmacoarse deltas) # Transmittance transmittancecoarse = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alphacoarse[...,:1]), 1.0 - alphacoarse + 1e-10], dim=-1), dim=-1)[...,:-1] weightscoarse = transmittancecoarse alphacoarse # 4. Query Fine Network # Combine coarse and fine samples tall = torch.cat([tcoarse, tfine], dim=-1) posencall = positionalencoding(rayso + raysd.unsqueeze(-1) tall.unsqueeze(-1), 10) direncall = positionalencoding(raysd, 4) rawsigmafine, rawrgbfine = nerfmlpforward(posencall, direncall, densitylayersfine, colorheadfine) # 6. Volume Rendering # Re-calculate deltas for all samples tsorted, = torch.sort(tall, dim=-1) deltasfine = tsorted[..., 1:] - tsorted[...,:-1] lastdeltafine = torch.fulllike(deltasfine[...,:1], 1e10) deltasfine = torch.cat([deltasfine, lastdeltafine], dim=-1) deltasfine = deltasfine raysd.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) sigmafine = F.relu(rawsigmafine) alphafine = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmafine deltasfine) transmittancefine = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alphafine[...,:1]), 1.0 - alphafine + 1e-10], dim=-1), dim=-1)[...,:-1] weightsfine = transmittancefine alphafine # Compute RGB rgbfine = torch.sigmoid(rawrgbfine) rgbmap = torch.sum(weightsfine[..., None] rgbfine, dim=-2) # Compute Depth and Accumulation depthmap = torch.sum(weightsfine tsorted, dim=-1) accmap = torch.sum(weightsfine, dim=-1) # Optional: White background # rgbmap = rgbmap + (1.0 - accmap[..., None]) return rgbmap, depthmap, accmap Defines the optimization loop, data handling, and regularization strategies required to train a NeRF model. It distinguishes itself by focusing on the standard MLP architecture and training dynamics, unlike NeRF-SH which modifies the output representation. Replaces direct RGB output with spherical harmonic coefficients, enabling efficient storage of view-dependent appearance and faster rendering. Routes query points through a hierarchy of branch networks based on predicted uncertainty, adapting to scene complexity dynamically. Renders anti-aliased conical frustums instead of infinitesimal rays to reduce aliasing artifacts and improve fine detail representation. Represents scenes as a distribution of microflakes to recover physical attributes like shape and reflectance under unknown illumination. Adapts NeRF for large-scale, unbounded scenes captured via egocentric video using a balanced spherical feature grid. Decouples geometry, illumination, and material properties for intrinsic image decomposition without supervised labels. Time Complexity: Training is computationally expensive. A typical run on the 'Lego' scene (400x400) takes ~200k iterations, which can take ~20 hours on a single GPU (e.g., 2080 Ti). Rendering is slower than explicit methods because it requires querying the MLP for every sample point along every ray. Memory Complexity: The model weights are small (~5MB), but rendering requires storing intermediate tensors for all sample points along all rays, which can be memory-intensive. Chunking (e.g., 4096 rays per batch) is used to manage GPU memory. Performance: On the NeRF-Synthetic benchmark (400x400, 100k-200k iterations), NeRF achieves high fidelity: Lego (~32.5 dB PSNR, 0.961 SSIM), Chair (~33.0 dB PSNR, 0.967 SSIM), Drums (~25.0 dB PSNR, 0.925 SSIM). Strengths: High-quality novel view synthesis, handles complex geometry and view-dependent effects (specularity, transparency) naturally. Limitations: Slow training and rendering times compared to explicit methods. Sensitive to hyperparameters like positional encoding frequencies and sampling strategies. Can suffer from "floaters" or artifacts in unobserved regions if not regularized. NeRF was introduced by Ben Mildenhall, Pratul P. Srinivasan, Matthew Tancik, Jonathan T. Barron, Ravi Ramamoorthi, and Ren Ng in 2020 in the paper "NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" (arXiv:2003.08934). It builds on the concept of differentiable volume rendering and the use of Fourier features for neural networks. The method has become a foundational technique in neural rendering, inspiring numerous variants and applications in AR/VR, autonomous driving, and 3D reconstruction. name: NeRF Training Configuration
head: NeRF Training Loop Configuration, NeRF Training Setup, Sparsity Prior, Sparsity Regularization
body: NeRF Training Configuration defines the optimization loop, data handling, and regularization strategies required to train a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) model for novel view synthesis. It solves the problem of converging a continuous volumetric representation to match observed multi-view images while preventing the generation of arbitrary, non-photorealistic geometry in unobserved regions. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like NeRF-SH by focusing on the standard MLP architecture and training dynamics, and from NeuS Training Loss by relying on volumetric opacity rather than explicit surface constraints like the Eikonal equation. The training process involves loading datasets, initializing coarse and fine NeRF models, and optimizing them using a composite loss function that includes a sparsity prior. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of a static scene, camera poses (extrinsics and intrinsics), and bounding box defining the scene volume. Outputs: Optimized NeRF models (coarse and fine) and associated optimizer states. Data Structures: Dataset: Images are resized such that the shorter side is 400 pixels. Camera intrinsics are derived from height (H), width (W), and focal length (f). The intrinsic matrix K is: K = \begin{bmatrix} f & 0 & 0.5W \\ 0 & f & 0.5H \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. Checkpoint: Saved as a.pt file containing a dictionary with keys: 'epoch', 'coarsemodelstatedict', 'finemodelstatedict', and 'optimizerstatedict'. Note that model loading does not restore the epoch number from the checkpoint. Numbered Steps: 1. Data Loading: Load training, validation, and test datasets using a standard dataset loader (e.g., BlenderDataset) with the specified resolution. 2. Data Preparation: Create a DataLoader with batchsize=1 and shuffle=True for training. 3. Model Initialization: Initialize two NeRF models: a coarse model and a fine model. 4. Parameter Combination: Combine the parameters of the coarse and fine models into a single parameter set for optimization. 5. Optimizer Setup: Initialize the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-4} and betas (0.9, 0.999). 6. Loss Definition: Define the primary photometric loss as Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and target colors. 7. Sparsity Regularization: Compute the sparsity loss term to encourage empty space in unobserved regions. 8. Training Loop: Initialize a trainer with the models, optimizer, loss, and dataloader, then call trainer.train(). Formulas: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a combination of the RGB loss and the sparsity loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{RGB}} + \lambda{\text{sparsity}} \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} The RGB loss is the sum of squared errors over a batch of rays \mathcal{R}: \mathcal{L}{\text{RGB}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| C(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 \quad where C(\mathbf{r}) is the target color and \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) is the rendered color. The sparsity loss \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K |1 - \exp(-\lambda \sigmak)| \quad where: K is the number of uniformly random points sampled within the bounding box. \sigmak is the density value at the k-th random point. \lambda is a hyperparameter controlling the strength of the sparsity prior. Parameters: Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 1. Image Resolution: 400 pixels on the shorter side. Optimizer: Adam with betas (0.9, 0.999). Sparsity Hyperparameter: \lambda is used in the exponential term; specific value not given in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Solid Background: Without the sparsity prior, the model may converge to a solution where unobserved portions or the background are solid, which degrades the spatial resolution of subsequent octree-based representations (e.g., PlenOctrees). Checkpoint Epoch: When loading a checkpoint, the epoch number is not restored from the file, requiring manual handling or resetting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def computesparsityloss(densitysamples, lambdaparam): """ Computes the sparsity loss for NeRF training. Args: densitysamples (torch.Tensor): Tensor of density values sigmak at K random points. lambdaparam (float): Hyperparameter lambda for the sparsity prior. Returns: torch.Tensor: Scalar sparsity loss value. """ # Lsparsity = (1/K) sum{k=1}^K |1 - exp(-lambda sigmak)| expterm = torch.exp(-lambdaparam densitysamples) sparsityloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(1.0 - expterm)) return sparsityloss def trainnerf(config): """ Main training loop for NeRF configuration. Args: config (dict): Configuration dictionary containing dataset path, resolution, etc. """ # 1. Load datasets traindataset = BlenderDataset(resolution=config['resolution'], split='train') valdataset = BlenderDataset(resolution=config['resolution'], split='val') testdataset = BlenderDataset(resolution=config['resolution'], split='test') # 2. Create DataLoaders trainloader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader( traindataset, batchsize=1, shuffle=True) # 3. Extract camera intrinsics # Assuming dataset provides height, width, focallength H, W, f = traindataset.height, traindataset.width, traindataset.focallength K = torch.tensor([ [f, 0, 0.5 W], [0, f, 0.5 H], [0, 0, 1] ]) # 4. Initialize models coarsemodel = NeRFMLP() finemodel = NeRFMLP() # 5. Combine parameters allparams = list(coarsemodel.parameters()) + list(finemodel.parameters()) # 6. Create optimizer optimizer = optim.Adam(allparams, lr=5e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.999)) # 7. Create loss functions mseloss = nn.MSELoss() lambdasparsity = 1.0 # Example value, not specified in sources lambdargb = 1.0 # Weight for RGB loss # 8. Training loop numepochs = config.get('numepochs', 1000) for epoch in range(numepochs): coarsemodel.train() finemodel.train() for batch in trainloader: images = batch['image'] rays = batch['rays'] # Contains origins, directions, etc. optimizer.zerograd() # Render coarse and fine colors # Note: Actual ray marching and volume rendering logic is encapsulated in NeRFMLP.forward coarsecolor = coarsemodel(rays) finecolor = finemodel(rays) # Compute RGB loss lossrgb = mseloss(finecolor, images) # Compute sparsity loss # Sample random points in bounding box randompoints = samplerandompointsinbbox(config['bbox'], K=1000) randomdensities = coarsemodel.getdensity(randompoints) losssparsity = computesparsityloss(randomdensities, lambdasparsity) # Total loss loss = lambdargb lossrgb + losssparsity loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Validation and checkpointing would occur here # Checkpoint format: {'epoch': epoch, 'coarsemodelstatedict':...,...} The NeuS training loss is a composite objective function used to optimize neural implicit surface representations (specifically Signed Distance Fields or Unsigned Distance Fields) from multi-view images without 3D ground-truth supervision. It solves the problem of recovering high-fidelity open surfaces by combining photometric consistency with geometric regularization. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training NeRF Training Configuration by explicitly enforcing the Eikonal equation on the SDF/UDF gradients and using a mask-based binary cross-entropy loss to drive opacity toward binary values, thereby stabilizing the thin-surface approximation. Time Complexity: Training time is dominated by the volume rendering process, which requires sampling points along rays and querying the MLP. The addition of sparsity loss requires additional forward passes for random points, increasing computational cost slightly. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of parameters in the coarse and fine MLPs and the batch size. The sparsity loss does not significantly increase memory footprint as it operates on a fixed number of random points. Measured Performance: On NeRF-synthetic test scenes, the approach achieves comparable image quality to state-of-the-art methods like NSVF, with PSNR values around 31.71 and SSIM around 0.958 after fine-tuning. Strengths: The sparsity prior prevents the model from learning arbitrary geometry in unobserved regions, which is crucial for efficient octree-based compression and rendering. Limitations: Without the sparsity prior, the model may converge to solid backgrounds, degrading the quality of subsequent octree conversions. The method relies on careful tuning of the sparsity hyperparameter \lambda. When to use: Use when the goal is to train a standard NeRF model that will be converted to an octree-based representation (e.g., PlenOctrees) for real-time rendering. When not to use: Use NeuS Training Loss if explicit surface reconstruction is required rather than volumetric rendering. The NeRF Training Configuration, particularly the inclusion of the sparsity prior, was introduced in the context of PlenOctrees for real-time rendering of Neural Radiance Fields. The work demonstrated that while arbitrary geometry in unobserved regions does not directly worsen image quality metrics, it adversely impacts the conversion process to octree-based representations by occupying significant voxel space. The implementation details, such as the specific PyTorch training loop and data loading procedures, are documented in unofficial repositories. name: NeuS Training Loss
head: NeUDF loss, Neural Implicit Surface training objective, Training Loss, optimization objective
body:
The NeuS training loss is a composite objective function used to optimize neural implicit surface representations (specifically Signed Distance Fields or Unsigned Distance Fields) from multi-view images without 3D ground-truth supervision. It solves the problem of recovering high-fidelity open surfaces by combining photometric consistency with geometric regularization. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training NeRF Training Configuration by explicitly enforcing the Eikonal equation on the SDF/UDF gradients and using a mask-based binary cross-entropy loss to drive opacity toward binary values, thereby stabilizing the thin-surface approximation. The method optimizes a neural network that outputs a scalar field value (SDF or UDF) and an opacity value for any 3D point. The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of color, geometric, and mask losses. Inputs: Ground truth RGB images I{gt} for each camera pose. Ground truth binary foreground masks M{gt} (optional, but required for \mathcal{L}m). Ray origins o and directions d sampled from the image plane. Sample points xi along the rays, sampled according to the volume rendering integration strategy. Outputs: Rendered RGB images I{pred}. Rendered opacity/mask values \alpha{pred}. Network gradients 
abla S(x) at sample points. The implementation relies on tensors representing the batch of rays: raysvalid: Boolean mask indicating which rays have valid ground truth data (non-background). comprgbfull: Tensor of shape (N{rays}, 3) containing the accumulated RGB color for each ray. sdfgradsamples: Tensor of shape (N{samples}, 3) containing the gradient 
abla SDF for each sample point. opacity: Tensor of shape (N{rays}) or (N{samples}) depending on the specific accumulation step, representing the transmittance/opacity contribution. The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + \alpha \mathcal{L}e +  eta \mathcal{L}m Where: \mathcal{L}c: Color loss (photometric consistency). \mathcal{L}e: Eikonal loss (geometric regularization). \mathcal{L}m: Mask loss (binary opacity enforcement). \alpha: Weight for Eikonal loss.  eta: Weight for Mask loss. 1. Color Loss (\mathcal{L}c) Measures the difference between rendered and ground truth images. Sources indicate the use of L1 loss or MSE. The implementation in uses MSE masked by valid rays. \mathcal{L}c = 	ext{MSE}(I{pred}[rays\valid], I{gt}[rays\valid]) Parameter: lambdargbmse (weight for MSE component). 2. Eikonal Loss (\mathcal{L}e) Enforces that the gradient of the SDF/UDF has a unit norm everywhere, which is a property of distance fields. \mathcal{L}e = 	ext{mean}(\|
abla SDF(xi)\|2 - 1)^2 Parameter: lambdaeikonal (weight for Eikonal loss). 3. Mask Loss (\mathcal{L}m) Encourages the predicted opacity to match the ground truth foreground mask. It uses Binary Cross Entropy (BCE). To prevent numerical instability (\log(0)), opacity values are clamped to [10^{-3}, 1-10^{-3}]. \mathcal{L}m = 	ext{BCE}(	ext{clamp}(\alpha{pred}, 10^{-3}, 1-10^{-3}), M{gt}) Parameter: lambdamask (weight for mask loss). Applied only if masks are provided. 4. Additional Regularization Terms Source lists several additional terms used to improve stability and quality: Opaque Loss: Encourages opacity to be 0 or 1. \mathcal{L}{opaque} = 	ext{BCE}(\alpha{pred}, \alpha{pred}) Parameter: lambdaopaque. Sparsity Loss: Encourages the SDF to be positive (empty space) outside the surface. \mathcal{L}{sparsity} = 	ext{mean}(\exp(-\lambda{sparsity} \cdot |SDF|)) Parameter: sparsityscale (used as \lambda{sparsity} in the exponent). Curvature Loss: Uses the absolute mean of SDF Laplace samples. Requirement: Geometry model must compute sdflaplacesamples using finite differences (geometry.gradtype = 'finitedifference'). Parameter: lambdacurvature. Distortion Loss: Based on MipNeRF360, penalizing the distortion of the ray sampling intervals. Parameter: lambdadistortion. Background Distortion Loss: Similar to distortion loss but for learned background components. Parameter: lambdadistortionbg. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the core loss calculation and conditional optional terms as described in. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeneusloss(out, batch, config): """ out: dict containing 'comprgbfull', 'raysvalidfull', 'sdfgradsamples', 'opacity', 'sdfsamples', 'sdflaplacesamples' batch: dict containing 'rgb', 'mask' config: object containing system.loss parameters and hasmask flag """ loss = 0.0 # 1. Color Loss (MSE) validmask = out['raysvalidfull'][..., 0] predrgb = [out['comprgbfull'][i] for i in range(len(out['comprgbfull'])) if validmask[i]] gtrgb = [batch['rgb'][i] for i in range(len(batch['rgb'])) if validmask[i]] def mse(p, t): return sum((pv - tv)2 for pv, tv in zip(p, t)) / len(p) loss += mse(predrgb, gtrgb) config.lambdargbmse # 2. Eikonal Loss def l2norm(vec): return math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in vec)) gradnorms = [l2norm(out['sdfgradsamples'][i]) for i in range(len(out['sdfgradsamples']))] losseikonal = sum((g - 1.0)2 for g in gradnorms) / len(gradnorms) loss += losseikonal config.lambdaeikonal # 3. Mask Loss (BCE) if config.hasmask: def clamp(val, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, val)) def bce(pred, target): predc = [clamp(p, 1e-3, 1 - 1e-3) for p in pred] return -sum(t math.log(p) + (1 - t) math.log(1 - p) for p, t in zip(predc, target)) / len(target) opacityclamped = [clamp(out['opacity'][i], 1e-3, 1 - 1e-3) for i in range(len(out['opacity']))] gtmask = [batch['mask'][i] for i in range(len(batch['mask'])) if validmask[i]] loss += bce(opacityclamped, gtmask) config.lambdamask # 4. Opaque Loss lossopaque = bce(out['opacity'], out['opacity']) loss += lossopaque config.lambdaopaque # 5. Sparsity Loss sdfvalues = out['sdfsamples'] sparsityscale = config.sparsityscale losssparsity = sum(math.exp(-sparsityscale abs(s)) for s in sdfvalues) / len(sdfvalues) loss += losssparsity config.lambdasparsity # 6. Curvature Loss if 'sdflaplacesamples' in out: losscurvature = sum(abs(l) for l in out['sdflaplacesamples']) / len(out['sdflaplacesamples']) loss += losscurvature config.lambdacurvature # 7. Distortion Loss # Implementation details for MipNeRF360 distortion loss not provided in sources. if config.lambdadistortion > 0: pass # 8. Background Distortion Loss if config.lambdadistortionbg > 0: pass return loss Numerical Stability: Opacity values must be clamped away from 0 and 1 before computing Binary Cross Entropy to avoid \log(0) instability. Curvature Loss Prerequisite: The curvature loss requires the geometry model to explicitly compute SDF Laplace samples. The code must assert that geometry.gradtype is set to 'finitedifference' to ensure out['sdflaplacesamples'] is populated. Mask Availability: The mask loss \mathcal{L}m is only applied if foreground masks are provided in the dataset. The implementation checks self.dataset.hasmask before applying lambdamask. Dynamic Ray Sampling: Some implementations use a dynamic update rule for the number of rays N{rays} during training to balance computation and quality: N{rays}^{new} = \min\left(0.9 N{rays}^{old} + 0.1 \left\lfloor N{rays}^{old} \cdot  rac{N{samples}}{\sum N{samples}^{pred}} ightfloor, N{rays}^{max}ight). It distinguishes itself from siblings like RegSDF and TUVR by estimating point reliability during geometry optimization via uncertainty modeling rather than using uniform smoothing or external MVS confidence maps, enabling robust handling of noisy and sparse point data. The loss function combines photometric consistency (color loss) with geometric regularization (Eikonal loss) and mask supervision. The NeUDF variant extends this to Unsigned Distance Fields, maintaining the same loss structure but adapting the SDF properties. name: PG-NeuS
head: PG-NeuS: Point-Guided Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction by Volume Rendering, Point-NeuS
body: PG-NeuS is a point-guided neural implicit surface reconstruction method that enhances the base NeuS framework by modeling aleatoric uncertainty to capture point cloud noise distribution, using a Neural Projection module for geometric constraints, and employing a Bias Network to compensate for geometric bias between volume rendering and point modeling. It distinguishes itself from siblings like RegSDF and TUVR by estimating point reliability during geometry optimization via uncertainty modeling rather than using uniform smoothing or external MVS confidence maps, enabling robust handling of noisy and sparse point data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera center o, ray direction d, a noisy point cloud \{P\}, initial weights for the SDF network f, the Sigmoid parameter s, the Neural Projection module, the Bias Network, and observed pixel colors. Outputs: Reconstructed surface (zero-level set of f) and rendered colors. Data Structures: SDF Network (f): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D coordinates to signed distance values and aleatoric uncertainty. Neural Projection Module: A module that projects 3D points onto the implicit surface and then onto the 2D image plane to enforce photometric consistency. Bias Network: An MLP that takes high-fidelity points as input to output geometric corrections. Uncertainty Model: For each point pk \in P, the SDF value is modeled as a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(\muk, \sigmak^2), where \muk = f(pk) and \sigmak represents the aleatoric uncertainty. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling and Base Rendering: For each pixel, cast a ray p(t) = o + td for t > 0. Sample N points along the ray. Compute the discrete opacity \alphai for each sample point p(ti) using the NeuS formulation: \alphai = \max\left(\frac{\Phis(f(p(ti))) - \Phis(f(p(t{i+1})))}{\Phis(f(p(ti)))}, 0\right) where \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} is the Sigmoid function with trainable parameter s, and f is the SDF network output. Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) and the rendered color \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai ci, where ci is the color predicted by the network at p(ti). 2. Aleatoric Uncertainty Modeling: For each point pk in the input point cloud P, the SDF network predicts a mean value \muk = f(pk) and an uncertainty value \sigmak. The point's reliability is estimated based on \sigmak. 3. Neural Projection: The point data undergoes two projections within the Neural Projection module: a. Spatial Projection: Project the 3D point pk onto the implicit surface defined by f(x)=0. b. Image Projection: Project the spatially projected point onto the 2D image plane corresponding to the camera view. A photometric consistency constraint is imposed on these projected positions to serve as regularization for the SDF, ensuring the implicit surface aligns with the observed image colors. 4. High-Fidelity Point Filtering: Perform a filter operation utilizing the modeled uncertainty \sigmak to select high-fidelity points. 5. Bias Compensation: Feed the selected high-fidelity points into the Bias Network to compensate for the geometric bias between volume rendering and point modeling. 6. Optimization: Update the network weights (SDF, Projection, Bias) and parameter s by minimizing a combined loss function including photometric loss, geometric loss (from NeuS), uncertainty regularization, and photometric consistency constraints. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def pgneusrender(rayo, rayd, numsamples, sdfnet, sparam, colornet): # Ray parameterization: p(t) = o + td for t > 0 # Sample points along ray (simplified uniform sampling in t) tvals = [(i + 1) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples)] psamples = [[rayo[j] + t rayd[j] for j in range(3)] for t in tvals] # Query SDF network for mean and uncertainty # sdfnet(p) returns (sdfmean, sigma) sdfpreds = [sdfnet(p) for p in psamples] sdfmeans = [pred[0] for pred in sdfpreds] sdfuncert = [pred[1] for pred in sdfpreds] # Compute Phis(x) = (1 + exp(-sx))^-1 phis = [1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-sparam m)) for m in sdfmeans] # Opacity formula: alphai = max((Phis(ti) - Phis(t{i+1})) / Phis(ti), 0) alpha = [0.0] numsamples for i in range(numsamples - 1): phicurr = phis[i] phinext = phis[i + 1] if phicurr > 1e-6: alpha[i] = max((phicurr - phinext) / phicurr, 0.0) else: alpha[i] = 0.0 # Guard against division by zero # Transmittance: Ti = product{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) T = [1.0] numsamples for i in range(1, numsamples): T[i] = T[i - 1] (1.0 - alpha[i - 1]) # Color accumulation: Chat = sum{i=1}^N Ti alphai ci colors = [colornet(p) for p in psamples] renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): for c in range(3): renderedcolor[c] += T[i] alpha[i] colors[i][c] return renderedcolor, sdfuncert, psamples Parameters: s: A trainable parameter in the Sigmoid function \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} used to define opacity. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If the point cloud is extremely sparse, the Neural Projection module may fail to find valid surface projections. Precision: The uncertainty modeling requires the SDF network to output not just a value but a distribution parameter (\sigma). Boundary Conditions: The opacity formula involves division by \Phis(f(p(ti))). If \Phis is close to zero, numerical instability may occur. The base training objective combining photometric and geometric losses. PG-NeuS builds on this by adding uncertainty and projection losses. NeuS Training Loss Uses uniform smoothing for noise mitigation. PG-NeuS is preferred when noise characteristics vary significantly across regions, as RegSDF weakens precise point support. RegSDF Relies on MVS network confidence. PG-NeuS is preferred when depth camera data is used or when MVS confidence maps are unreliable, as PG-NeuS estimates reliability during optimization. TUVR Time Complexity: PG-NeuS achieves an 11x speedup compared to NeuS without masks. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Achieves a 33.3% improvement in accuracy compared to NeuS without masks on DTU and BlendedMVS datasets. Scaling: Benefits from lightweight networks, allowing efficient convergence while maintaining high accuracy. Strengths: Robust to noisy and sparse point data; balances accuracy and efficiency; handles region-specific noise via uncertainty modeling. Limitations: Requires a point cloud prior; complexity of implementing uncertainty modeling and bias compensation. When to use: When high-quality point clouds are available but contain noise, and computational efficiency is a concern. When not to use: When no point cloud prior is available, or when the point cloud is extremely sparse to the point where projection is ambiguous. PG-NeuS was proposed to address challenges in neural implicit surface reconstruction, specifically limited accuracy, excessive time complexity, and the impact of point cloud noise. It was introduced in the paper "Point-NeuS: Point-Guided Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction by Volume Rendering". The method improves upon prior point-guided methods like RegSDF and TUVR by introducing aleatoric uncertainty estimation and a Bias Network to handle geometric bias. name: NeRF-SH
head: NeRF with Spherical Harmonics, modified NeRF that predicts spherical harmonics coefficients
body: NeRF-SH is a variant of Neural Radiance Fields that replaces the direct RGB color output with spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, eliminating the need for viewing direction as a network input. This modification enables the efficient storage of view-dependent appearance in a sparse voxel-based octree (PlenOctree) and allows for faster training and real-time rendering compared to the original NeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and a vector of SH coefficients \mathbf{k} for the RGB color channels. Data Structures: The network f maps spatial position to coefficients: f(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{k}, \sigma) where \mathbf{k} = (k\ell^m){\ell: 0 \leq \ell \leq \ell{\max}}. Each coefficient k\ell^m \in \mathbb{R}^3 corresponds to the RGB components for a specific SH basis function indexed by degree \ell and order m. Spherical Harmonics Basis: Spherical Harmonics are used as a standard basis for functions defined on the surface of the sphere to model non-Lambertian materials and view-dependent effects. The color c at a point \mathbf{x} for a viewing direction \mathbf{v} (defined by angles \theta, \phi) is calculated by summing the weighted SH bases: c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum{\ell=0}^{\ell{\max}} \sum{m=-\ell}^{\ell} k\ell^m Y\ell^m(\theta, \phi) where Y\ell^m are the spherical harmonic basis functions evaluated at the viewing direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Network Definition: Define a neural network f that takes \mathbf{x} as input and outputs \sigma and \mathbf{k}. The view direction \mathbf{v} is not an input to f. 2. Training: Train the network using the standard NeRF volume rendering optimization procedure. 3. Sparsity Prior: Introduce a sparsity prior during training to improve the memory efficiency of the resulting octrees. 4. PlenOctree Construction: Densely sample the trained NeRF-SH model in the volume around the target object to tabulate density \sigma and SH coefficients \mathbf{k} into a sparse voxel-based octree (PlenOctree). 5. Optional Optimization: The values stored in the PlenOctree can be further optimized directly using training images, as the rendering procedure remains differentiable. Parameters: SH Degree (\ell{\max}): Not given in the sources. View-direction samples for projection: 10,000 per point (used only for the alternative projection method, not the main NeRF-SH method). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Projection Quality Loss: Directly projecting a trained standard NeRF (which outputs RGB) to SHs via Monte Carlo estimation (sampling random directions and multiplying by SH component values) imposes a quality loss of about 2 dB. Projection Cost: The Monte Carlo projection process takes several hours (e.g., ~2 hours for 10,000 samples per point). Comparison with Projection: With 10,000 view-direction samples per point, the PSNR of the projected method is 29.21, compared to 31.02 for the main NeRF-SH method prior to optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfshnetwork(x): """ NeRF-SH network that predicts SH coefficients and density. Input: x (3D spatial coordinates) Output: k (SH coefficients), sigma (density) """ # The network architecture is identical to standard NeRF except for the output layer. # It does NOT take viewing direction as input. # Let fneural be the underlying MLP. k, sigma = fneural(x) return k, sigma def rendercolor(k, theta, phi): """ Calculate color from SH coefficients and viewing direction. Input: k (SH coefficients vector), theta (polar angle), phi (azimuthal angle) Output: c (RGB color) """ c = 0 for l in range(0, lmax + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): # Ylm is the spherical harmonic basis function for degree l and order m ylm = sphericalharmonicbasis(l, m, theta, phi) # klm is the coefficient for this basis function (RGB vector) klm = getcoefficient(k, l, m) c += klm ylm return c def trainnerfsh(): """ Training loop for NeRF-SH. """ # Initialize network model = nerfshnetwork() # Add sparsity prior to loss function loss = reconstructionloss + sparsitypriorweight sparsityloss(model) # Optimize using standard NeRF volume rendering method # Note: View direction is NOT passed to the network optimize(model, loss) return model def buildplenoctree(model, volumesamples): """ Build PlenOctree from trained NeRF-SH model. Input: model (trained NeRF-SH network), volumesamples (dense 3D grid points) Output: octree (PlenOctree with density and SH coefficients) """ octree = SparseVoxelOctree() for x in volumesamples: k, sigma = model(x) octree.setleaf(x, sigma, k) return octree A sparse voxel-based octree that stores SH coefficients and density, enabling real-time rendering of NeRF-SH. General configuration settings for NeRF training, applicable to NeRF-SH. A sibling method using recursive neural networks for NeRF representation. A sibling method addressing aliasing by representing rays as cones. A sibling method for representing thin structures. A sibling method for ego-centric scene reconstruction. A sibling method for decomposing scene properties. Time Complexity: NeRF-SH training speed is similar to, but slightly faster than, standard NeRF (by about 10%). Memory Complexity: The use of a sparse voxel-based octree (PlenOctree) improves memory efficiency compared to dense voxel grids. Measured Performance: On the Synthetic NeRF Dataset, NeRF-SH achieves a PSNR of 31.69 and SSIM of 0.953, compared to 31.01 and 0.947 for the original NeRF. Strengths: Eliminates the need for view-direction input, enabling efficient storage in octrees and faster training; supports real-time rendering via PlenOctree. Limitations: Requires careful selection of SH degree; direct projection from standard NeRF to SHs results in significant quality loss and high computational cost. When to use: When real-time rendering or efficient storage of view-dependent effects is required, and training speed is a concern. When not to use: When extremely high-fidelity view-dependent effects beyond the capacity of the chosen SH degree are needed, or when converting an existing standard NeRF is preferred over retraining. NeRF-SH was introduced in the paper "PlenOctrees For Real-time Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)" by Yu et al.. It builds on the original NeRF method by incorporating spherical harmonics to handle view-dependent appearance, enabling the creation of PlenOctrees for real-time rendering.
