name: NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing)
head: Volume Rendering, Alpha Blending, Ray Marching Integration
body: Generates RGB images and depth maps from neural network predictions by performing volume rendering along camera rays using alpha compositing. It integrates the predicted volume density and color of sampled points into a final pixel value, accounting for occlusion via transmittance. Unlike sibling methods that focus on evaluation metrics or network query structures, this method specifically handles the mathematical integration of radiance and opacity into observable quantities. Inputs: model: Trained MLP predicting RGB and density. raysflat: Flattened ray origins and directions. tvals: 1D array of sample distances along rays, shape (NUMSAMPLES,). rand: Boolean flag for sampling strategy (True for training with jitter, False for deterministic evaluation). train: Boolean flag for model execution mode (True for training, False for inference). BATCHSIZE, H, W, NUMSAMPLES: Dimensions of the output tensor. Outputs: rgb: Rendered RGB image, shape (BATCHSIZE, H, W, 3). depthmap: Rendered depth map, shape (BATCHSIZE, H, W). Data Structures: Predictions tensor: Shape (BATCHSIZE, H, W, NUMSAMPLES, 4). The last dimension contains [R, G, B, sigmaa]. Delta tensor: Interval distances between adjacent samples. Transmittance tensor: Cumulative product of (1 - \alpha). Weights tensor: Product of alpha and transmittance. Steps: 1. Model Prediction: Pass raysflat through the model. If train is True, use forward pass; otherwise, use prediction mode. Reshape output to (BATCHSIZE, H, W, NUMSAMPLES, 4). 2. Slicing and Activation: Slice the last dimension into RGB (first 3 channels) and volume density \sigmaa (last channel). Apply sigmoid activation to RGB to bound values to [0, 1]. Apply ReLU activation to \sigmaa to ensure non-negative density. 3. Interval Calculation: Compute distances \delta between adjacent sample points: \delta = t{\text{vals}}[i+1] - t{\text{vals}}[i]. 4. Boundary Handling: Append a large value (10^{10}) to \delta to represent the infinite tail of the ray. If rand is True, append shape (BATCHSIZE, H, W, 1). If rand is False, append shape (BATCHSIZE, 1). 5. Alpha Calculation: Compute opacity \alpha for each sample using the formula: \alpha = 1 - e^{-\sigmaa \cdot \delta} If rand is True, use element-wise multiplication with \delta. If rand is False, broadcast \delta to match spatial dimensions before multiplication. 6. Transmittance Calculation: Compute transmittance T as the cumulative product of (1 - \alpha). Add epsilon (\epsilon = 10^{-10}) to (1 - \alpha) to prevent numerical instability (log(0)). Use exclusive cumulative product to start with T=1.0 at the beginning of the ray. 7. Weight Calculation: Compute weights w for each sample: w = \alpha \cdot T. 8. RGB Integration: Compute final RGB by summing weighted colors: \text{RGB} = \sum{i} wi \cdot ci. 9. Depth Integration: Compute depth map by summing weighted sample distances: \text{Depth} = \sum{i} wi \cdot ti. If rand is True, use tvals directly. If rand is False, broadcast tvals to match spatial dimensions (BATCH\SIZE, H, W) before multiplication. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import tensorflow as tf import numpy as np def renderrgbdepth(model, raysflat, tvals, rand=True, train=True): """Generates the RGB image and depth map from model prediction. Args: model: The MLP model that is trained to predict the rgb and volume density of the volumetric scene. raysflat: The flattened rays that serve as the input to the NeRF model. tvals: The sample points for the rays. rand: Choice to randomise the sampling strategy. train: Whether the model is in the training or testing phase. Returns: Tuple of rgb image and depth map. """ # Get the predictions from the nerf model and reshape it. if train: predictions = model(raysflat) else: predictions = model.predict(raysflat) predictions = tf.reshape(predictions, shape=(BATCHSIZE, H, W, NUMSAMPLES, 4)) # Slice the predictions into rgb and sigma. rgb = tf.sigmoid(predictions[...,:-1]) sigmaa = tf.nn.relu(predictions[..., -1]) # Get the distance of adjacent intervals. delta = tvals[..., 1:] - tvals[...,:-1] # delta shape = (numsamples) if rand: delta = tf.concat( [delta, tf.broadcastto([1e10], shape=(BATCHSIZE, H, W, 1))], axis=-1) alpha = 1.0 - tf.exp(-sigmaa delta) else: delta = tf.concat( [delta, tf.broadcastto([1e10], shape=(BATCHSIZE, 1))], axis=-1) alpha = 1.0 - tf.exp(-sigmaa delta[:, None, None,:]) # Get transmittance. expterm = 1.0 - alpha epsilon = 1e-10 transmittance = tf.math.cumprod(expterm + epsilon, axis=-1, exclusive=True) weights = alpha transmittance rgb = tf.reducesum(weights[..., None] rgb, axis=-2) if rand: depthmap = tf.reducesum(weights tvals, axis=-1) else: depthmap = tf.reducesum(weights tvals[:, None, None], axis=-1) return (rgb, depthmap) Iterates over a list of camera poses to generate a sequence of rendered images and depth maps. It supports downsampling for faster preview rendering and optional PSNR calculation against ground truth images. It handles saving rendered frames as 8-bit PNGs. Parameters: renderfactor: Downsampling factor for speed. Default 0 (no downsampling). Typical values 4 or 8 for preview. chunk: Number of rays processed in parallel during render. Default 32768. Decrease if running out of memory. Steps: 1. Iterate over renderposes array. 2. For each pose c2w, call render(H, W, focal, chunk=chunk, c2w=c2w[:3,:4], renderkwargs) to get rgb, disp, acc. 3. If renderfactor != 0, downsample H, W, and focal by dividing by renderfactor before rendering. 4. Append rgb.numpy() and disp.numpy() to rgbs and disps lists. 5. If gtimgs is not None and renderfactor == 0, compute PSNR: p = -10. np.log10(np.mean(np.square(rgb - gtimgs[i]))). 6. If savedir is not None, convert rgb to 8-bit with to8b(), save as '{:03d}.png' using imageio.imwrite. 7. After loop, stack rgbs and disps along axis 0 and return them. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and samples per ray. The rendering pipeline iterates over poses, making total time proportional to the number of poses. Memory Complexity: Proportional to BATCHSIZE H W NUMSAMPLES for storing intermediate tensors (predictions, alpha, transmittance, weights). The chunk parameter in the pipeline limits peak memory usage by processing rays in batches. Performance: Depends heavily on hardware acceleration (GPU) for matrix operations and cumulative products. Downsampling (renderfactor) significantly reduces computation time for previews. Strengths: Differentiable, allowing gradient flow back to the network parameters for training. Simple and efficient integration of volumetric data. Limitations: Requires careful handling of numerical stability (epsilon addition) to prevent NaNs. Deterministic rendering (rand=False) may appear noisy if sampling is sparse, while random sampling (rand=True) introduces variance during training. Originated from the Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) paper by Mildenhall et al. (2020). The method is a core component of the NeRF training loop, enabling the optimization of the radiance field by comparing rendered images with ground truth. It is widely used in 3D reconstruction, novel view synthesis, and differentiable rendering applications. 3D volumetric rendering with NeRF - Keras, https://keras.io/examples/vision/nerf/, fetched 2026-10-26 bmild/nerf, https://github.com/bmild/nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: NeRF-style Volume Rendering Integrator
head: NeRF forward raymarching, NeRFIntegrator
body: A simplified NeRF-style integrator that accumulates emission along a ray through a medium, backed by a dense grid instead of a neural network, with no direction-dependent emission. It differs from standard NeRF implementations by using a dense grid for density/emission storage and explicitly handling primal/dual modes for gradient computation in inverse rendering contexts. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d. Scene intersection si (providing entry point t{entry} and exit point t{exit}). Grid data structure containing density \sigma and emission Le. Parameters: queriesperray (N), densitynoisestd, jitteringenabled, activation, hideemitters. Outputs: Accumulated radiance L. Data Structures: Grid: Dense 3D array storing \sigma and Le. Access is via trilinear interpolation or nearest neighbor depending on implementation details not fully specified in sources. Active Mask: Boolean array indicating which rays are still valid (have not exited the medium or reached max steps). Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize accumulated radiance L = 0. Initialize throughput \alpha{through} = 1.0. Initialize weight sum W{sum} = 0. Initialize step counter j = 0. Determine primal mode (for gradient direction). 2. Ray Intersection: Intersect ray with scene to find medium exit t{exit}. Update active mask to include only rays that hit the exit. 3. Step Size Calculation: Calculate stepsize using stepsizeformarching(N, 0, si.t, jitteringenabled). Sample jitter offset s{jitter} from sampler. 4. Marching Loop: While stillwalking (mask is true) AND j < N: a. Calculate Next T: tb = \text{query\t\for\step}(j + 1, \text{step\size}, s{jitter}, \text{jittering\enabled}). ta is the previous tb (initially si.t). \Delta t = tb - ta. b. Calculate Alpha and Weight: If j + 1 < N: \alpha{recip} = \exp(-\sigma \cdot \Delta t). Else (last step): \alpha{recip} = 1.0. Add safety epsilon: \alpha{recip} \leftarrow \alpha{recip} + 10^{-10}. weight = (1.0 - \alpha{recip}) \cdot \alpha{through}. c. Accumulate Radiance: Sample emission Le at ta (or midpoint, depending on specific grid query implementation not fully detailed, but typically at sample point). If primal mode: L \leftarrow L + weight \cdot Le. Else (dual mode): L \leftarrow L - weight \cdot Le. d. Update State: j \leftarrow j + 1. ta \leftarrow tb. \alpha{through} \leftarrow \alpha{through} \cdot \alpha{recip}. W{sum} \leftarrow W{sum} + weight. Update stillwalking mask: j < N. 5. Background Contribution: Calculate background contribution: L{bg} = (1 - W{sum}) \cdot L{emitter}. If hideemitters is true and W{sum} == 0, L{bg} = 0. Add L{bg} to L for active pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfintegrator(rayo, rayd, scene, grid, params): # Parameters N = params['queriesperray'] # Default 128 noisestd = params['densitynoisestd'] # Default 0 jitter = params['jitteringenabled'] # Default True activation = params['activation'] # Default 'identity' hideemitters = params['hideemitters'] # Default False # Initialization L = 0.0 alphathrough = 1.0 Wsum = 0.0 j = 0 primalmode = True # Assumed default, check scene context # Ray Intersection si = scene.intersect(rayo, rayd) if not si.hit: return 0.0 # Or background color texit = si.t # Assuming si.t is the exit point for the medium activemask = True # Simplified for single ray # Step Size stepsize = stepsizeformarching(N, 0, si.t, jitter) jittersample = sampler.sample() ta = si.t while activemask and j < N: # Calculate next t tb = querytforstep(j + 1, stepsize, jittersample, jitter) deltat = tb - ta # Calculate alpharecip if j + 1 < N: # Sample density at ta or midpoint? Sources imply using sigma at step sigma = grid.sampledensity(ta) # Implementation detail # Apply noise if noisestd > 0: sigma += noisestd randomnoise() # Apply activation if activation == 'relu': sigma = max(0.0, sigma) alpharecip = exp(-sigma deltat) else: alpharecip = 1.0 # Safety epsilon alpharecip += 1e-10 # Weight weight = (1.0 - alpharecip) alphathrough # Accumulate emission = grid.sampleemission(ta) # Implementation detail if primalmode: L += weight emission else: L -= weight emission # Update state j += 1 ta = tb alphathrough = alpharecip Wsum += weight # Update mask if j >= N: activemask = False # Background if hideemitters and Wsum == 0: Lbg = 0.0 else: Lbg = (1.0 - Wsum) scene.backgroundemission() L += Lbg return L Parameters: queriesperray: Number of steps. Default: 128. densitynoisestd: Standard deviation for density noise. Default: 0. jitteringenabled: Enable jittering. Default: True. activation: Density activation ('identity', 'relu'). Default: 'identity'. hideemitters: Hide background if weight sum is zero. Default: False. Edge Cases: Precision: Add 10^{-10} to alpharecip to prevent division by zero or NaN in gradient computation. Boundaries: Ensure tb does not exceed texit if the medium is bounded. Degenerate Input: If deltat is 0, skip step or handle as no-op. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is queriesperray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the dense grid, where V is the volume size. Performance: Depends on grid resolution and N. Higher N improves accuracy but increases cost. Strengths: Simple, differentiable, suitable for inverse rendering. Limitations: Dense grid memory usage, no direction-dependent emission. Originated from NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) but adapted for unbiased inverse volume rendering using dense grids. Developed by EPFL researchers. https://github.com/rgl-epfl/unbiased-inverse-volume-rendering, https://github.com/rgl-epfl/unbiased-inverse-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Training Configuration
head: Hyperparameter Configuration, Instant-NGP Training Setup, NGP Training Configuration, Optimization Configuration, Optimizer Settings, Training Configuration & Optimization Setup, Training Hyperparameters
body: Training Configuration defines the static and dynamic hyperparameters, optimizer settings, and initialization procedures required to optimize a radiance field model. It solves the problem of unstable convergence and inefficient resource usage by establishing the baseline "vanilla" NeRF settings (MLP depth, width, positional encoding frequencies, and hierarchical sampling counts) against which variants adjust their specific architectural or optimization details. It differs from Training Loop Setup by focusing on the numerical values and mathematical schedules rather than the procedural orchestration of the training loop, and from Training Ray Marching and Integration by defining the parameters that control the sampling density and loss weighting rather than the integration algorithm itself. Inputs: Dataset metadata (image resolution, camera poses, near/far planes). Model architecture definition (MLP layers, grid resolutions, embedding sizes). Optimization targets (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). Outputs: Initialized optimizer state (momentum buffers, learning rates). Training schedule parameters (iteration counts, decay schedules). Sampling configurations (step sizes, batch sizes, background colors). The configuration is typically stored in a namespace or dictionary object containing the following fields: 1. Optimizer Parameters: lr0: Initial learning rate for embeddings (e.g., 2 \times 10^{-2}). lr1: Initial learning rate for networks (e.g., 10^{-3}). betas: Tuple (\beta1, \beta2), typically (0.9, 0.99). eps: Epsilon for numerical stability, typically 10^{-15} or 10^{-8}. weightdecay: Multiplier, typically 10^{-9}. 2. Sampling Parameters: numrays: Number of rays sampled per image per step (e.g., 4096). batchsize: Number of points or rays processed per forward/backward pass (e.g., 512 points, 216, 8192 rays). numsteps: Number of steps sampled per ray (e.g., 512). maxsteps: Maximum steps for CUDA raymarching (e.g., 1024). delta: Sampling step size, often set to half the voxel size s(\cdot), i.e., \delta(\cdot) = 0.5 s(\cdot). 3. Grid/Model Parameters: resolution0: Initial grid resolution (cubed), e.g., 128. resolution1: Target grid resolution (cubed), e.g., 300. bound: Scene bounding box half-width, e.g., 2. densitythresh: Threshold for density grid occupancy, e.g., 10. dtgamma: Adaptive ray marching parameter, e.g., 1/128. 4. Loss Weights: w{\text{photo}}: Photometric loss weight (e.g., 1). w{\text{pt rgb}}: Point-wise RGB regularization weight (e.g., 10^{-1} coarse, 10^{-2} fine). w{\text{bg}}: Background regularization weight (e.g., 10^{-2} coarse, 10^{-3} fine). 1. Initialize Model: Create the neural network (MLP) and voxel grids with specified resolutions and channel counts. 2. Initialize Optimizer: Instantiate Adam with specified betas and epsilon. Assign different learning rates to embeddings (lr0) and network weights (lr1). 3. Initialize Scheduler: Set up a learning rate scheduler (e.g., LambdaLR, Cosine Decay) to decay the learning rate over the total iterations iters. 4. Configure Sampling: Set the number of rays per step, steps per ray, and sampling step sizes based on voxel dimensions. 5. Set Loss Weights: Assign weights to photometric, regularization, and background loss terms based on the training stage (coarse vs. fine). 6. Initialize Trainer: Combine model, optimizer, criterion, and scheduler into a Trainer object with specified metrics (e.g., PSNRMeter) and evaluation intervals. Learning Rate Decay (LambdaLR): \text{lr}(iter) = \text{init\lr} \times 0.1^{\min(\frac{iter}{\text{iters}}, 1)} This decays the learning rate to 10% of its initial value at the last iteration. Exponential Interpolation for Upsampling: Upsample resolutions are calculated using exponential interpolation between resolution0 and resolution1 over the number of upsample steps plus one: \text{res}i = \exp\left( \text{linspace}(\ln(\text{resolution0}), \ln(\text{resolution1}), \text{len}(\text{upsample\model\steps}) + 1) \right)i for i > 0. Randomized Query Shift: During training, query points on a ray are shifted by: p \cdot \delta(\cdot) \cdot \frac{d}{\|d\|2} where p \sim U[0, 1] and d is the ray viewing direction. Weight Annealing (Minor Variant): Proposal weights \hat{\mathbf{w}} are annealed by raising them to a power that increases from 0 to 1: \hat{\mathbf{w}}n \propto \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\frac{bn/N}{(b-1)n/N+1}} where n is the current step, N is total steps, and b=10 is the bias hyperparameter. Iterations: 25k, 30k, 10k coarse + 20k fine, 20k. Batch Size: 512 points, 216, 8192 rays, 4096 rays. Learning Rates: 10^{-3} for MLP, 2 \times 10^{-2} for embeddings, 0.1 for voxel grids. Background Color: Random RGB from [0, 1]^3 during training; fixed (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) at test time for 360/LLFF datasets; fixed white for Blender. Precision: Use eps=10^{-15} for Adam in some implementations to avoid division by zero in small gradients, while others use 10^{-8}. Boundaries: The bound parameter assumes the scene is in [-bound, bound]^3. If bound > 1, adaptive ray marching is invoked. Degenerate Input: If cudaray is false, numsteps is used; if true, maxsteps is used. Memory: Large batch sizes (e.g., 8192 rays) may require significant VRAM; half-precision (fp16) is often enabled to mitigate this. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def initializetrainingconfiguration(opt): """ Initialize the training configuration for a NeRF-like model. opt: Namespace containing hyperparameters. """ # 1. Initialize Model model = NeRFNetwork( resolution=[opt.resolution0] 3, bound=opt.bound, cudaray=opt.cudaray, densityscale=1, minnear=opt.minnear, densitythresh=opt.densitythresh, bgradius=opt.bgradius) # 2. Initialize Optimizer # Separate learning rates for embeddings (lr0) and network weights (lr1) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam( model.getparams(opt.lr0, opt.lr1), betas=(0.9, 0.99), eps=1e-15) # 3. Initialize Scheduler # Decay to 0.1 initlr at the last iteration scheduler = optim.lrscheduler.LambdaLR( optimizer, lambda iter: 0.1 min(iter / opt.iters, 1)) # 4. Calculate Upsample Resolutions # Exponential interpolation between resolution0 and resolution1 import numpy as np upsampleresolutions = ( np.round( np.exp( np.linspace( np.log(opt.resolution0), np.log(opt.resolution1), len(opt.upsamplemodelsteps) + 1))).astype(np.int32).tolist()[1:]) # 5. Initialize Trainer trainer = Trainer( name='ngp', opt=opt, model=model, device=torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.isavailable() else 'cpu'), workspace=opt.workspace, optimizer=optimizer, criterion=torch.nn.MSELoss(reduction='none'), emadecay=None, fp16=opt.fp16, lrscheduler=scheduler, schedulerupdateeverystep=True, metrics=[PSNRMeter()], usecheckpoint=opt.ckpt, evalinterval=50) trainer.upsampleresolutions = upsampleresolutions return trainer, optimizer, scheduler Learning rate scheduling adjusts the optimizer's step size during training to improve convergence stability and final reconstruction quality in radiance-field optimization. It differs from static learning rates by dynamically scaling parameters based on training progress or structural changes, such as densification events. This method builds on Training Configuration by defining the temporal evolution of the learning rate parameter. Mixed Precision Training (MPT) accelerates NeRF optimization on CUDA devices by utilizing Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) to perform computations in lower precision formats while maintaining numerical stability. It differs from standard single-precision training by reducing memory bandwidth requirements and increasing throughput via tensor cores, without requiring manual precision management for every operation. NeRF Hyperparameters define the specific configuration of the neural network architecture, sampling strategy, and optimizer settings required to train a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) model. This configuration solves the problem of reconstructing a continuous 3D scene representation from a set of uncalibrated or calibrated 2D images by optimizing the radiance field parameters. What sets this configuration apart from its siblings is that it establishes the baseline "vanilla" NeRF settings (specifically the MLP depth, width, positional encoding frequencies, and hierarchical sampling counts) against which variants like Mip-NeRF [3409-mip-nerf-optimization-and-activation-details.md] or HashNeRF [3068-hashnerf-parameters.md] adjust their specific architectural or optimization details. A training schedule defines the temporal progression of hyperparameters, loss functions, and structural updates during the optimization of differentiable volume rendering models. It solves the problem of unstable convergence and inefficient resource usage by separating the optimization into distinct phases (e.g., warm-up, densification, refinement). Unlike static configurations, it dynamically alters the active loss terms and geometric primitives to handle sparse initialization and high-frequency detail recovery. It differs from Learning Rate Scheduling by controlling structural topology changes and loss activation, rather than just the step size of the optimizer. This article defines the specific implementation details for training mip-NeRF and JaxNeRF, focusing on activation functions, input encoding structures, and learning rate scheduling. These changes are designed to improve training stability and robustness, particularly against catastrophic failure modes, without significantly altering the model's accuracy or speed. Unlike standard NeRF implementations, this method removes identity concatenation from the MLP input and employs shifted/widened activation functions to handle edge cases in density and color prediction. DONeRF training configuration defines the optimization procedure for the two-stage neural network architecture (depth oracle and shading networks) that enables real-time rendering with very few samples per ray. It solves the problem of high-frequency detail loss and slow convergence in standard NeRF by decoupling depth estimation from color/shading prediction. Unlike standard NeRF which samples uniformly or via hierarchical sampling along the entire ray, DONeRF uses a depth oracle to predict a probability distribution over discretized depth ranges, allowing the shading network to focus computational budget on the surface. It differs from NeRF Hyperparameters by enforcing a strict two-phase training schedule and specific opacity regularization to prevent dark pixel artifacts at low sample counts. Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors enforce physical plausibility on the learned radiance field by decoupling material properties (reflectance) from illumination effects (shading). This method solves the ambiguity inherent in intrinsic image decomposition, where scaling reflectance and inversely scaling shading produces identical observed colors, by applying regularization constraints that stabilize the separation. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by explicitly optimizing for intrinsic image components rather than just photometric reconstruction, enabling consistent object insertion and relighting. A technique to anneal proposal weights by raising them to a power that increases from 0 to 1 over training steps, encouraging exploration by presenting a wider range of proposal intervals early in training. The formula is \hat{\mathbf{w}}n \propto \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\frac{bn/N}{(b-1)n/N+1}} where n is the current training step, N is the total number of training steps, and b=10 is the bias hyperparameter. Ablating annealing causes SSIM on the bicycle scene to decrease from 0.687 to 0.679. During training, drawing a random RGB background color from [0,1]^3 when compositing pixel color to encourage reconstruction of a fully opaque background, avoiding semi-transparent background artifacts. Test-time background color is set to (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). Used for the 360 dataset and the LLFF dataset; the Blender dataset uses a fixed white background. Parameters β1 = 1.0 and β2 = 0.1 are weights for the multi-scale joint training loss. For Blender dataset: one round of sampling, 128 samples for proposal MLP, 32 samples for NeRF MLP, proposal MLP with 4 layers and 256 hidden units, NeRF MLP with 8 layers and 256 (or 512) hidden units, axis-aligned IPE, MSE loss, no distortion regularizer. Standard PyTorch Adam optimisation with fused Adam on CUDA. Adaptive model capacity is handled via fixed-pool relocation, keeping optimiser tensor shapes constant. Effective rate scaling for D \le 3: scaled by PD / P^2, where PD = D + D(D+1)/2 is the number of position and Cholesky parameters per splat (5 for 2D, 9 for 3D). For D \ge 4, additional factor D^{0.8} accounts for larger spatial search. Adam parameters: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999, \epsilon = 10^{-8}. Base learning rate: 0.01. Follows reduce-on-plateau schedule (patience 15 iterations, factor 0.9, threshold 10^{-3}, floor 10^{-8}). Amplitude learning rate multiplier: 3× the dilution-compensated rate. Position learning rate multiplier: 1.5× the dilution-compensated rate. Iteration cap: 20,000 iterations. Early stopping patience: 500 iterations on regularised training loss. Load model and optimizer states from a checkpoint file to resume training or evaluation. Steps: Load model state dictionary, Load optimizer state dictionary, Load gradient scaler state if used, Extract start iteration from checkpoint. Distortion regularizer is not disabled. Charbonnier loss is used instead of MSE. On LLFF dataset with 256 hidden units: mip-NeRF achieves PSNR 26.93, SSIM 0.830, LPIPS 0.177, Time 2.48 hrs, Params 0.61M. Our Model achieves PSNR 26.68, SSIM 0.847, LPIPS 0.150, Time 2.39 hrs, Params 0.84M. On LLFF dataset with 512 hidden units: mip-NeRF achieves PSNR 27.01, SSIM 0.845, LPIPS 0.148, Time 6.15 hrs, Params 2.27M. Our Model achieves PSNR 26.86, SSIM 0.858, LPIPS 0.128, Time 3.84 hrs, Params 3.23M. Our model does not outperform mip-NeRF in PSNR, but yields improved SSIM and LPIPS metrics and a significant speedup when the NeRF MLP is large. An abstract base class for sampling context and target views during training or inference, defining the interface for view selection strategies. Parameters: stage (current training stage), isoverfitting (boolean flag), camerasarecircular (boolean flag), steptracker (optional tracker). Layout: Context view indices tensor shape: Int64[Tensor, " contextview"], Target view indices tensor shape: Int64[Tensor, " targetview"]. Use the same training losses as the coarse stage, but use a smaller weight for the regularization losses as it empirically leads to slightly better quality. Time Complexity: Training time varies significantly by configuration. Standard NeRF may take hours to days. Instant-NGP variants can converge in minutes. Memory Complexity: Depends on grid resolution and batch size. Higher resolutions (e.g., 300^3) and larger batch sizes (e.g., 8192 rays) increase VRAM usage. Measured Performance: On LLFF dataset with 256 hidden units, Our Model achieves PSNR 26.68, SSIM 0.847, LPIPS 0.150 in 2.39 hours. On Blender dataset, Our Model achieves PSNR 32.65 for bicycle scene. Scaling: Exponential interpolation for upsampling resolutions helps manage memory and convergence. Strengths: Flexible configuration allows tuning for specific datasets (Blender vs. LLFF vs. 360). Limitations: High VRAM requirements for large batches and resolutions. When to Use: When optimizing a radiance field for novel view synthesis, requiring careful balance between convergence speed and reconstruction quality. When Not to Use: When real-time rendering is the primary goal without pre-training, or when computational resources are severely limited. Key developments include Instant-NGP [21, 32], mip-NeRF 360 [3, 20], and Zip-NeRF [3, 20]. It is widely used in computer vision for 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. name: Training Ray Batching
head: Random Ray Batching, Random Ray Batching for NeRF Training
body: Training Ray Batching is a data loading strategy for NeRF optimization that pre-computes rays for all training images, concatenates them with target RGB colors, and samples random subsets per iteration. It differs from Single Image Sampling by drawing rays globally across the entire training dataset rather than restricting them to one image per step, ensuring uniform exposure to all views. Inputs: poses: Array of camera poses, shape (numimg, 3, 4). images: Array of training images, shape (numimg, H, W, 3). K: Camera intrinsic matrix, shape (3, 3). itrain: List of indices for training images. Nrand: Number of rays per batch. Data Structures: raysrgb: A flat tensor of shape (Ntotal, 3, 3) where Ntotal = len(itrain) H W. The first dimension indexes the ray, the second dimension has size 3 representing [rayorigin, raydirection, targetrgb], and the third dimension is the vector size 3. Steps: 1. Generate Rays: For each pose p in poses[:,:3,:4], call getraysnp(H, W, K, p) to generate ray origins and directions. Stack these into a tensor rays of shape (numimg, ro+rd, H, W, 3) where ro+rd = 2. 2. Concatenate Targets: Concatenate rays with images[:,None] along axis 1. images is expanded to (numimg, 1, H, W, 3). Result raysrgb has shape (numimg, ro+rd+rgb, H, W, 3) which equals (numimg, 3, H, W, 3). 3. Transpose: Transpose raysrgb from (numimg, 3, H, W, 3) to (numimg, H, W, 3, 3) using np.transpose(raysrgb, [0, 2, 3, 1, 4]). 4. Filter Training Set: Stack only the images in itrain into raysrgb. Result shape is (len(itrain), H, W, 3, 3). 5. Reshape: Flatten the spatial and image dimensions by reshaping to (-1, 3, 3). The first dimension becomes len(itrain) H W. 6. Cast: Convert to np.float32. 7. Shuffle: Randomly shuffle the entire array using np.random.shuffle(raysrgb). 8. Sample Batch: In each iteration, slice raysrgb[ibatch: ibatch + Nrand]. Transpose the batch to shape (3, Nrand, 3) (equivalent to 2+1, Nrand, 3) to separate origins, directions, and targets. 9. Update Index: Increment ibatch by Nrand. If ibatch >= raysrgb.shape[0], shuffle raysrgb again using torch.randperm and reset ibatch to 0. Parameters: Nrand: Default 32 32 4 = 4096. nobatching: Boolean. If True, disables this method in favor of single-image sampling. K: Simplified intrinsic [[f, 0, W/2], [0, f, H/2], [0, 0, 1]]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch def generaterays(H, W, K, pose): """Standard ray generation routine. Returns (2, H, W, 3) for origins and directions.""" # Standard implementation computes camera centers and per-pixel ray directions # from the pose matrix and intrinsic calibration K. origins = np.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) directions = np.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) #... standard ray casting logic... return np.stack([origins, directions], axis=0) def prepareraybatch(poses, images, K, itrain, Nrand=4096): numimg = poses.shape[0] H, W = images.shape[1], images.shape[2] # Step 1: Generate rays for all images rayslist = [generaterays(H, W, K, p) for p in poses[:,:3,:4]] rays = np.stack(rayslist, axis=0) # (numimg, 2, H, W, 3) # Step 2: Concatenate with target RGB raysrgb = np.concatenate([rays, images[:, None]], axis=1) # (numimg, 3, H, W, 3) # Step 3: Transpose to (numimg, H, W, 3, 3) raysrgb = np.transpose(raysrgb, [0, 2, 3, 1, 4]) # Step 4: Filter for training set raysrgb = np.stack([raysrgb[i] for i in itrain], axis=0) # (len(itrain), H, W, 3, 3) # Step 5: Reshape to flat list (-1, 3, 3) raysrgb = np.reshape(raysrgb, [-1, 3, 3]) # Step 6: Cast to float32 raysrgb = raysrgb.astype(np.float32) # Step 7: Shuffle np.random.shuffle(raysrgb) # Move to GPU device = torch.device('cuda') # Standard device selection raysrgb = torch.Tensor(raysrgb).to(device) ibatch = 0 return raysrgb, ibatch def samplebatch(raysrgb, ibatch, Nrand): # Step 8: Slice batch batch = raysrgb[ibatch: ibatch + Nrand] # (Nrand, 3, 3) # Transpose to (3, Nrand, 3) batch = torch.transpose(batch, 0, 1) # Separate rays and targets batchrays = batch[:2] # (2, Nrand, 3) targets = batch[2] # (Nrand, 3) # Step 9: Update index ibatch += Nrand if ibatch >= raysrgb.shape[0]: # Shuffle again if end of dataset reached randidx = torch.randperm(raysrgb.shape[0]) raysrgb = raysrgb[randidx] ibatch = 0 return batchrays, targets, ibatch Edge Cases: If Nrand does not divide the total number of rays evenly, the last batch in an epoch will be smaller unless padding is implemented. The source code simply slices until the end, then shuffles and resets. Precision issues may arise if H and W are large, leading to very large raysrgb tensors. Memory usage is O(numimg H W). Samples Nrand rays from a single randomly chosen training image per iteration. Chosen when memory is constrained or when specific view-dependent effects are studied in isolation. Renders rays in chunks to manage GPU memory during the forward pass. This is a rendering optimization, not a data loading strategy, but often used in conjunction with batching. Time Complexity: Pre-computation is O(numimg H W). Sampling is O(Nrand) per iteration. Shuffling is O(Ntotal) per epoch. Memory Complexity: O(numimg H W) to store the pre-computed raysrgb tensor. Performance: Default Nrand=4096 provides a balance between gradient noise and computational efficiency. Strengths: Ensures all training views are seen uniformly per epoch. Reduces overhead of ray generation during training. Limitations: High memory usage for high-resolution images. Shuffling large tensors can be slow. Originated in the original NeRF implementation by Mildenhall et al.. The method was designed to efficiently train neural radiance fields by leveraging pre-computed ray data to accelerate the training loop. name: NeRF System Data Preparation
head: Blender Dataset Loading, NeRF training data sampling, NeRF validation data sampling, Synthetic NeRF Dataset
body: This method prepares training and validation data for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by loading synthetic scenes (typically Blender datasets), parsing camera metadata, and precomputing ray origins and directions. It differs from general volume rendering by handling specific coordinate conventions (e.g., OpenCV to NeRF's camera space) and background compositing for synthetic data. It builds on Training Ray Batching by providing the structured ray tensors that are subsequently shuffled and sampled. Inputs: Image files and metadata files (transforms{split}.json). Configuration parameters: near, far, WHITEBG, backgroundcolor. Outputs: A tensor of rays with shape (N, 6) where the first 3 dimensions are ray origins (ox, oy, oz) and the next 3 are normalized ray directions (dx, dy, dz). Target RGB values with shape (N, 3). (Optional) Foreground masks with shape (N, 1) or (N, 3). transforms{split}.json: Contains a list of frames. Each frame has filepath, transformmatrix (4x4), and optionally foregroundmask. cameraanglex: Horizontal field of view in radians. 1. Load Metadata and Compute Focal Length: For Blender datasets, load transforms{split}.json. Extract cameraanglex and compute the focal length f: f = \frac{0.5 \cdot W}{\tan(0.5 \cdot \text{camera\angle\x})}. 2. Preprocess Images and Poses: For each frame in the split, load the image and convert to RGBA. Resize to dimensions (W, H). Composite onto a white background if WHITEBG is true: \text{rgb} = \text{rgba}{:3} \cdot \text{rgba}{3:} + (1 - \text{rgba}{3:}). Extract the camera-to-world matrix C2W from the frame's transformmatrix. 3. Generate Ray Origins and Directions: For each camera pose C2W, generate rays for every pixel (i, j) in the image grid. Create pixel coordinate grids i \in [0, W-1] and j \in [0, H-1]. Compute camera-space directions (OpenCV convention: z-forward, y-down, x-right): d{cam} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{i - Cx}{f} \\ -\frac{j - Cy}{f} \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} where Cx = W/2 and Cy = H/2. Transform directions to world space: d{world} = d{cam} \cdot C2W{0:3, 0:3}^T. Set ray origins to the camera center: o{world} = C2W{0:3, 3}. 4. Sample Rays for Training: During training, not all rays are used per iteration to save memory and compute. Determine the number of rays to sample (Nrand). Select random image indices. If batchimagesampling is enabled, sample trainnumrays indices from the dataset; otherwise, sample 1 index. For the selected images, sample random pixel coordinates (x, y). Extract the corresponding ray origins and directions from the precomputed arrays. Normalize the ray directions: d{norm} = \frac{d}{\|d\|2}. Concatenate origins and normalized directions into a tensor of shape (Nrand, 6). 5. Handle Background Color: Set the model's background color based on configuration: if backgroundcolor is 'white', initialize as torch.ones((3,)); if 'random', initialize with random values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch import json import os import cv2 def loadblenderdata(datadir, split='train', whitebg=True): """ Loads and preprocesses Blender dataset. Returns: rays (N, 6), rgbs (N, 3), masks (N, 1) or None """ with open(os.path.join(datadir, f'transforms{split}.json'), 'r') as f: meta = json.load(f) W = meta['w'] H = meta['h'] focal = 0.5 W / np.tan(0.5 meta['cameraanglex']) raysolist = [] raysdlist = [] rgbslist = [] maskslist = [] for frame in meta['frames']: # Load image imgpath = os.path.join(datadir, frame['filepath']) img = cv2.imread(imgpath) img = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLORBGR2RGB).astype(np.float32) / 255.0 img = cv2.resize(img, (W, H)) if img.shape[2] == 4: rgba = img # Composite on white background rgb = rgba[:,:,:3] rgba[:,:, 3:] + (1 - rgba[:,:, 3:]) mask = rgba[:,:, 3:] else: rgb = img mask = np.ones((H, W, 1)) # Get C2W c2w = np.array(frame['transformmatrix']) # Generate rays rayo, rayd = getraysnp(H, W, focal, c2w) raysolist.append(rayo) raysdlist.append(rayd) rgbslist.append(rgb) maskslist.append(mask) rayso = np.concatenate(raysolist, axis=0) raysd = np.concatenate(raysdlist, axis=0) rgbs = np.concatenate(rgbslist, axis=0) masks = np.concatenate(maskslist, axis=0) return rayso, raysd, rgbs, masks def getraysnp(H, W, focal, c2w): """ Generates ray origins and directions for a single image. """ i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W, dtype=np.float32), np.arange(H, dtype=np.float32), indexing="xy") cx = W / 2.0 cy = H / 2.0 # Camera space directions dirs = np.stack([ (i - cx) / focal, -(j - cy) / focal, -np.oneslike(i) ], -1) # Transform to world space rayd = np.einsum("hwc,kc->hwk", dirs, c2w[:3,:3]) rayo = np.broadcastto(c2w[:3, 3], rayd.shape) return rayo, rayd def sampletrainingrays(rayso, raysd, rgbs, masks, Nrand, batchimagesampling=False): """ Samples random rays for a training iteration. """ H, W, = rayso.shape N = H W if batchimagesampling: # Sample multiple images numimages = min(Nrand // (H W), len(rayso) // (H W)) imgindices = np.random.choice(len(rayso) // (H W), size=numimages, replace=False) raysos = rayso[imgindices].reshape(-1, 3) raysds = raysd[imgindices].reshape(-1, 3) rgbss = rgbs[imgindices].reshape(-1, 3) maskss = masks[imgindices].reshape(-1, 1) else: # Sample 1 image imgidx = np.random.randint(0, len(rayso) // (H W)) raysos = rayso[imgidx].reshape(-1, 3) raysds = raysd[imgidx].reshape(-1, 3) rgbss = rgbs[imgidx].reshape(-1, 3) maskss = masks[imgidx].reshape(-1, 1) # Sample random pixel coordinates x = np.random.randint(0, W, size=Nrand) y = np.random.randint(0, H, size=Nrand) # Flatten indices for the selected image(s) flatidx = y W + x # Extract rays raysosampled = raysos[flatidx] raysdsampled = raysds[flatidx] rgbssampled = rgbss[flatidx] maskssampled = maskss[flatidx] # Normalize directions raysdsampled = raysdsampled / np.linalg.norm(raysdsampled, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # Concatenate origins and normalized directions rays = np.concatenate([raysosampled, raysdsampled], axis=-1) return rays, rgbssampled, maskssampled near: 2.0 for Blender. far: 6.0 for Blender. WHITEBG: True for Blender. backgroundcolor: 'white' or 'random'. Coordinate Conventions: Blender uses a right-handed coordinate system with Y-up, while NeRF's internal ray generation assumes a specific camera space. The flip in the y-direction of the ray direction is critical. Background Compositing: Synthetic Blender datasets often have transparent backgrounds. Failing to composite onto a white background before training can lead to incorrect color predictions. Ray Sampling: Random pixel sampling reduces memory usage but requires careful indexing to map 2D coordinates to 1D ray arrays. Loads real-world LLFF dataset scenes, parsing colmap poses from posesbounds.npy, correcting axis conventions, and applying NDC normalization. Unlike Blender data, LLFF data does not use a white background (WHITEBG=False) and requires NDC transformation for uniform sampling. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W) for preprocessing, where N is the number of images. Ray generation is linear in the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W \cdot 6) to store all ray origins and directions. This can be significant for high-resolution images. Performance: Precomputing rays allows for fast training iterations, as ray generation is moved out of the training loop. Strengths: Handles both synthetic and real-world data formats. Efficient batching via precomputed rays. Limitations: High memory usage for large datasets. NDC normalization is only suitable for forward-facing scenes. NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. The data preparation methods described here are based on the official NeRF implementation and subsequent popular open-source repositories like nerf-from-scratch and instant-nsr-pl. The Blender dataset is a standard synthetic benchmark, while the LLFF dataset is a standard real-world forward-facing benchmark. emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, https://github.com/bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, https://github.com/rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Training Loop with Adaptive Regularization & LR Decay
head: NeRF Training, Training Loop with Exponential LR Decay
body: This method defines the iterative optimization procedure for training neural radiance fields, specifically focusing on the integration of adaptive regularization terms and exponential learning rate decay within the training loop. It solves the problem of stable convergence in high-dimensional implicit surface representations by combining reconstruction loss with structural priors (orthogonality, sparsity, and total variation) while gradually reducing the optimization step size. It builds on NeRF Training Loop by specifying the exact loss composition and parameter update schedule. Inputs: raystrain: Tensor of ray origins and directions. rgbtrain: Tensor of ground-truth RGB values for the rays. tensorf: The neural field model (e.g., hash grid or MLP) containing parameters to optimize. optimizer: An Adam or AdamW optimizer instance initialized with learningrate and weightdecay. args: Configuration object containing hyperparameters (see Parameters). Outputs: Updated tensorf parameters. Updated optimizer state. Scalar totalloss and PSNR metric for tracking. Data Structures: raystrain: Shape (B, 3) for origins and (B, 3) for directions, where B is batchsize. rgbtrain: Shape (B, 3). rgbmap, alphasmap, depthmap, weights, uncertainty: Tensors returned by the renderer, shape dependent on B and sampling strategy. Parameters: learningrate: Initial learning rate for the Adam optimizer. weightdecay: Weight decay coefficient for the Adam optimizer. decayrate: Base for exponential decay (typically e or a specific base if implemented as base^{step}, but sources imply multiplicative factor per step or exponential function of step). Note: Source uses a multiplicative lrfactor per iteration, while references an exponentiallrdecay function. The implementation below follows the explicit multiplicative update described in which is more granular. decaysteps: Number of steps over which decay is compounded. Orthoregweight: Initial orthogonality regularization strength (args.Orthoweight). L1regweight: Initial L1 density regularization strength (args.L1weightinital), switching to args.L1weightrest after the first alpha mask update. TVweightdensity: Initial total variation weight for density field (args.TVweightdensity). TVweightapp: Initial total variation weight for appearance field (args.TVweightapp). lrfactor: Multiplicative factor applied to learning rates and TV weights per iteration (typically < 1). batchsize: Chunk size for rendering and ray sampling (args.batchsize). nSamples: Number of samples per ray, dynamically updated during resolution upscaling. whitebg: Boolean flag for background color assumption. ndcray: Boolean flag for NDC ray coordinates. cropsteps: Number of steps to use center-cropped data. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Adam optimizer with learningrate and weightdecay. 2. Ray Sampling: Sample ray indices using trainingSampler.nextids() and fetch corresponding raystrain and rgbtrain from the dataset. 3. Rendering: Render the rays through the neural field model to obtain rgbmap, alphasmap, depthmap, weights, and uncertainty. \text{render\output} = \text{renderer}(\text{rays\train}, \text{tensorf}, \text{chunk}=\text{batch\size}, N\samples=\text{nSamples}, \text{white\bg}=\text{white\bg}, \text{ndc\ray}=\text{ndc\ray}) 4. Reconstruction Loss: Compute the mean squared error (MSE) between the rendered RGB and ground truth. L{rec} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{i=1}^{B} \| \text{rgb\map}i - \text{rgb\train}i \|^2 5. Regularization Losses: Orthogonality: If Orthoregweight > 0, compute lossreg using tensorf.vectorcompdiffs() and add to total loss. L1 Density: If L1regweight > 0, compute lossregL1 using tensorf.densityL1() and add to total loss. Total Variation (Density): If TVweightdensity > 0, decay the weight by lrfactor, compute losstvdensity using tensorf.TVlossdensity(tvreg), and add TVweightdensity losstvdensity to total loss. Total Variation (Appearance): If TVweightapp > 0, decay the weight by lrfactor, compute losstvapp using tensorf.TVlossapp(tvreg), and add TVweightapp losstvapp to total loss. 6. Total Loss: L{total} = L{rec} + L{ortho} + L{L1} + L{TV\density} + L{TV\app} 7. Optimization Step: Zero gradients, backpropagate totalloss, and step the optimizer. 8. Learning Rate Decay: Update the learning rate for all parameter groups by multiplying by lrfactor. \text{lr}{new} = \text{lr}{old} \times \text{lr\factor} 9. TV Weight Decay: Multiply TVweightdensity and TVweightapp by lrfactor. 10. Tracking: Compute PSNR for monitoring. \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \log{10}(L{rec}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstep(raystrain, rgbtrain, tensorf, optimizer, args): # 1. Render rays # Returns: rgbmap, alphasmap, depthmap, weights, uncertainty rgbmap, alphasmap, depthmap, weights, uncertainty = renderer( raystrain, tensorf, chunk=args.batchsize, Nsamples=args.nSamples, whitebg=args.whitebg, ndcray=args.ndcray, device=args.device, istrain=True) # 2. Compute Reconstruction Loss (MSE) lossrec = torch.mean((rgbmap - rgbtrain) 2) totalloss = lossrec # 3. Orthogonality Regularization if args.Orthoregweight > 0: lossreg = tensorf.vectorcompdiffs() totalloss += args.Orthoregweight lossreg # 4. L1 Density Regularization if args.L1regweight > 0: lossregL1 = tensorf.densityL1() totalloss += args.L1regweight lossregL1 # 5. Total Variation Regularization (Density) if args.TVweightdensity > 0: # Decay TV weight args.TVweightdensity = args.lrfactor losstvdensity = tensorf.TVlossdensity(args.tvreg) totalloss += args.TVweightdensity losstvdensity # 6. Total Variation Regularization (Appearance) if args.TVweightapp > 0: # Decay TV weight args.TVweightapp = args.lrfactor losstvapp = tensorf.TVlossapp(args.tvreg) totalloss += args.TVweightapp losstvapp # 7. Optimization Step optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # 8. Learning Rate Decay for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = args.lrfactor # 9. Compute PSNR for tracking psnr = -10.0 np.log10(lossrec.item()) / np.log10(np.e) # Note: np.log10 is preferred for PSNR formula # Correct PSNR formula from source: -10. np.log10(loss) psnr = -10.0 np.log10(lossrec.item()) return totalloss.item(), psnr Note on PSNR Formula: Source specifies psnr = -10. np.log10(loss). Source code snippet uses np.log (natural log) but divides by np.log(10.0) implicitly or explicitly in some variants. The standard PSNR formula uses base-10 log. The pseudocode above uses np.log10 to match the standard definition and the explicit formula in. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: TV Weight Vanishing: If lrfactor < 1, TV weights decay multiplicatively every iteration. This causes regularization strength to vanish rapidly over training. L1 Weight Switching: L1regweight switches from args.L1weightinital to args.L1weightrest only after the first alpha mask update iteration. This can cause inconsistent regularization early in training. Validation Set Size: The validation set size is capped at 1024 \times 100 rays. If the dataset is larger, indices are sampled linearly. Precision: Ensure lossrec is not zero to avoid log(0) in PSNR calculation. Add a small epsilon if necessary. Defines the initial configuration and data loading pipeline. Details the rendering process used to generate rgbmap. Specifies hyperparameters like batchsize and nSamples. Explains how nSamples and resolution are updated. An alternative training approach for unbounded scenes. Specifics of Mip-NeRF 360's training loop. A multi-resolution training strategy. Scene representation details. Extension for dynamic scenes. Neural Implicit Surfaces, which may use different regularization. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rendering step, which is O(B \cdot N{samples}) per batch, where B is batch size and N{samples} is samples per ray. Backpropagation is proportional to the model size. Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot N{samples}) for storing intermediate rendering tensors (weights, alphas, etc.). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with batch size and number of samples. Resolution upscaling (dynamic growth) increases N{samples} and model complexity. Strengths: Adaptive regularization helps stabilize training of hash-based or high-frequency fields. Exponential LR decay prevents oscillation in later stages. Limitations: TV weight decay can remove beneficial smoothing too quickly. L1 weight inconsistency may affect early convergence. When to Use: Standard for training neural radiance fields with hash grids or MLPs requiring structural regularization. When Not to Use: For simple MLPs without hash grids, TV regularization may be unnecessary. For real-time inference, training loop details are irrelevant. This training loop structure is derived from implementations of neural radiance fields, particularly those using hash grids and adaptive regularization. The specific combination of orthogonality, L1 density, and total variation regularization with exponential LR decay is characteristic of recent efficient NeRF implementations. The PSNR metric is standard for evaluating reconstruction quality. name: Learning Rate Scheduling
head: LR Scheduling, LR decay, LambdaLR Scheduler, Learning Rate Decay, Learning Rate Scheduler
body: Learning rate scheduling adjusts the optimizer's step size during training to improve convergence stability and final reconstruction quality in radiance-field optimization. It differs from static learning rates by dynamically scaling parameters based on training progress or structural changes, such as densification events. This method builds on Training Configuration by defining the temporal evolution of the learning rate parameter. The method implements time-based exponential decay, power-of-2 batch decay, lambda decay, linear interpolation, and event-driven spikes to modulate the learning rates of model parameters (e.g., means, weights, vertex coordinates). Inputs: Current step/iteration i, maximum steps T{max}, initial learning rate lr{init}, final learning rate lr{final}, decay gamma \gamma, step size S, densification iteration I, spike duration L, batch count, epoch. Outputs: Scaled learning rate lr(i) for the current step. Configuration: Dictionary or struct containing lrinit, lrfinal, gamma, stepsize, startstep, endstep, startvalue, endvalue. Optimizer State: The learning rate is typically applied via a scheduler wrapper (e.g., torch.optim.lrscheduler.LambdaLR) that updates the optimizer's parameter groups. 1. Exponential Decay (Normalized Step): For a normalized step t = \text{clamp}(i / T{max}, 0, 1), the learning rate for means is lr{means}(t) = \exp(\log(lr{init}) \cdot (1 - t) + \log(lr{final}) \cdot t). 2. Power-of-2 Batch/Epoch Decay: After processing each batch, divide the learning rate by 2^{1 / (\text{batchCount} \cdot (\text{epoch} + 1))}. 3. Lambda Decay: Define a lambda function lr\lambda(epoch) = \gamma^{(epoch / S)} and apply it via a scheduler. 4. Linear Interpolation: Parse startstep, startvalue, endvalue, endstep from config. Compute value = start\value + (end\value - start\value) \cdot \max(\min(1.0, (current\step - start\step) / (end\step - start\step)), 0.0). 5. Learning Rate Spike: After densification at iteration I, add a spike function with duration L on top of the decay function l(i) for instant NGP weights and vertex coordinates: \mathbb{1}\{i - I > 0\} (l(0) - l(I)) \exp(-\frac{6(i-I)}{L}). The total learning rate becomes l{total}(i) = l(i) + \text{Spike}(i). lr{init}: Initial learning rate. lr{final}: Target final learning rate. \gamma: Gamma value for learning rate decay. S: Step size for learning rate decay. L: Duration of the learning rate spike in iterations. startstep, endstep, startvalue, endvalue: Boundaries and values for linear interpolation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computelrexponentialdecay(step, maxsteps, lrinit, lrfinal): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, step / maxsteps)) return math.exp(math.log(lrinit) (1.0 - t) + math.log(lrfinal) t) def computelrpowerof2decay(lrold, batchcount, epoch): return lrold / (2.0 (1.0 / (batchcount (epoch + 1.0)))) def computelrlambdadecay(lrinit, gamma, epoch, stepsize): return lrinit (gamma (epoch / stepsize)) def computelrlinear(step, startstep, endstep, startvalue, endvalue): if endstep == startstep: return startvalue progress = max(0.0, min(1.0, (step - startstep) / (endstep - startstep))) return startvalue + (endvalue - startvalue) progress def computelrwithspike(step, densificationstep, initiallr, currentdecaylr, spikeduration): if step <= densificationstep: return currentdecaylr spike = (initiallr - currentdecaylr) math.exp(-6.0 (step - densificationstep) / spikeduration) return currentdecaylr + spike Division by Zero: Ensure stepsize and endstep - startstep are non-zero. Negative Steps: Clamp step to \ge 0. Precision: Use log-space interpolation for exponential decay to avoid numerical instability with very small learning rates. Spike Timing: The spike function is only active for i > I. Adjusts learning rates based on a view-count prior to prioritize under-reconstructed regions. Without this prior, PSNR can degrade up to -1.22 in the worst case. A technique to increase the learning rate of specific model parameters (instant NGP weights and vertex coordinates) after a densification event to allow rapid accommodation for changes. It adds a spike function with duration L on top of the decay function. Time Complexity: O(1) per step for computing the learning rate. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for scheduler state. Strengths: Improves convergence stability; prevents oscillation in later stages; handles structural changes (densification) effectively. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of decay parameters; spike duration L must be chosen appropriately to avoid instability. When to Use: Standard for NeRF and Gaussian Splatting training to ensure smooth convergence and high final quality. Learning rate scheduling is a standard optimization technique in deep learning. In the context of radiance fields, it was adapted to handle the unique convergence properties of neural implicit representations and 3D Gaussian splatting. The exponential decay and spike mechanisms are specifically tailored to the iterative densification and refinement processes in these methods. name: Mixed Precision Training
head: AMP Training, FP16 Training, Mixed Precision Training with Fallback
body: Mixed Precision Training accelerates NeRF optimization on CUDA devices by utilizing Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) to perform computations in lower precision formats while maintaining numerical stability. It differs from standard single-precision training by automating precision casting and loss scaling within the PyTorch training loop. The method integrates into the standard NeRF training loop by wrapping the forward pass in an automatic precision context manager and applying gradient scaling to prevent underflow in lower-precision gradients. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Model parameters, optimizer, scheduler, dataset, usemixedprecision flag, and scaler instance. Outputs: Updated model parameters, updated optimizer state, updated scaler state, computed loss values, and checkpoint files. Data Structures scaler: A gradient scaler instance (e.g., torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler) that maintains a scale factor for loss values. Loss and Epochs: Empty lists initialized to track loss values and iteration counts for logging. Parameters usemixedprecision: Boolean flag to enable/disable AMP. scaler: Gradient scaler instance initialized with default parameters. Steps 1. Initialization: Create a gradient scaler instance and initialize empty lists for Loss and Epochs. 2. Iteration Loop: Iterate i from startiter to numiters. 3. Mode Set: Set the model to training mode (model.train()). 4. Data Selection: Randomly select 4 target images from the dataset using np.random.choice on images.shape[0]. 5. Device Transfer: Extract the target image tensor (targetimg) and the camera-to-world transformation matrix (targettformcam2world), moving the transform to the device. 6. Autocast Context: Enter the mixed precision context using torch.cuda.amp.autocast() (or torch.amp.autocast('cuda') for newer PyTorch versions). 7. Forward Pass: Call the rendering function with height, width, focallength, targettformcam2world, nearthresh, farthresh, depthsamplesperray, and getminibatches to obtain rgbpredicted. 8. Shape Adjustment: Squeeze the first dimension of rgbpredicted to match the target image shape. 9. Loss Computation: Compute the mean-squared error (MSE) loss between rgbpredicted and targetimg. 10. Gradient Scaling & Backward: Scale the loss, call backward(), step the optimizer, update the scaler, and zero gradients with settonone=True. 11. Scheduler Step: Step the learning rate scheduler. 12. Checkpointing: If i % saveevery == 0, append loss.item() to Loss and i+1 to Epochs, save a checkpoint to checkpointdir/checkpoint{i}.pt containing modelstatedict, optimizerstatedict, loss, iteration, scaler.statedict(), and scheduler.statedict(), and plot figures. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np import os def trainwithmixedprecision( model, optimizer, scheduler, dataset, numiters, startiter, saveevery, checkpointdir, device='cuda'): # Initialize scaler for mixed precision scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler() # Logging structures Loss = [] Epochs = [] # Pre-fetch full data for random selection (example from source) images, tforms, = dataset.getfulldata(device) for i in range(startiter, numiters): model.train() # Randomly select 4 target images indices = np.random.choice(images.shape[0], 4, replace=False) targetimg = images[indices].to(device) targettformcam2world = tforms[indices].to(device) # Mixed precision context with torch.cuda.amp.autocast(): # Forward pass: call rendering routine with ray parameters and model # (Full implementation of runoneiteroftinynerf not provided in sources) rgbpredicted = runoneiteroftinynerf( model=model, targettformcam2world=targettformcam2world, height=targetimg.shape[1], width=targetimg.shape[2], focallength=dataset.focallength, nearthresh=dataset.nearthresh, farthresh=dataset.farthresh, depthsamplesperray=dataset.depthsamplesperray, device=device) # Squeeze dimension if necessary if rgbpredicted.dim() > 3: rgbpredicted = rgbpredicted.squeeze(0) # Compute Loss loss = torch.mean((rgbpredicted - targetimg) 2) # Scale loss and backward scaler.scale(loss).backward() # Optimizer step scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() # Zero gradients optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) # Step scheduler scheduler.step() # Checkpointing if i % saveevery == 0: Loss.append(loss.item()) Epochs.append(i + 1) checkpointpath = os.path.join(checkpointdir, f"checkpoint{i}.pt") torch.save({ 'modelstatedict': model.statedict(), 'optimizerstatedict': optimizer.statedict(), 'loss': loss.item(), 'iteration': i, 'scalerstatedict': scaler.statedict(), 'schedulerstatedict': scheduler.statedict() }, checkpointpath) # Plotting (implementation detail) plotfigures(Epochs, Loss) def plotfigures(Epochs, logloss): import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4)) plt.plot(Epochs, logloss) plt.title("Loss") plt.savefig("Loss.png") plt.close() Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision Compatibility: Older PyTorch versions require torch.cuda.amp.autocast() while newer versions use torch.amp.autocast('cuda'). Gradient Underflow: Without the gradient scaler, FP16 gradients may underflow to zero, causing training to stall. Memory Management: Using settonone=True in zerograd() helps reduce memory fragmentation during long training runs. Checkpointing: The scaler state must be saved and restored to ensure consistent training behavior across restarts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Training Schedule
head: Optimization schedule
body: A training schedule defines the temporal progression of hyperparameters, loss functions, and structural updates during the optimization of differentiable volume rendering models. It solves the problem of unstable convergence and inefficient resource usage by separating the optimization into distinct phases (e.g., warm-up, densification, refinement). Unlike static configurations, it dynamically alters the active loss terms and geometric primitives to handle sparse initialization and high-frequency detail recovery. It differs from Learning Rate Scheduling by controlling structural topology changes and loss activation, rather than just the step size of the optimizer. The schedule is defined by a sequence of phases, each with specific active losses, structural operations, and duration. The total training duration E{total} is scaled by volume size: 2800 epochs for small-medium volumes, 1600 for large, and 800 for extremely large volumes. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. 1. Warm-up Phase (Epochs 0 to 16): Activate only photometric loss (L{photo}) and silhouette loss (L{sil}). Disable structural updates (splitting/pruning). Goal: Allow the initial sparse surfel set to deform and align with observed images. 2. Densification Phase (Epochs 16 to \approx 0.25 E{total}): Enable adaptive density control: split and prune surfels at regular intervals (every 4 epochs). Disable silhouette loss. Activate geometric regularizers: consistency loss (L{cons}) and normal consistency loss (L{nc}). Optional Mask-based Pruning: If ground-truth masks are available, periodically remove surfels that consistently project outside the foreground mask across a majority of training views. Structure-aware Importance Pruning: Apply pruning based on importance scores at 42–50% of the training process. 3. Refinement Phase (Epochs \approx 0.5 E{total} to E{total}): Freeze densification (no more splitting/pruning). Fine-tune with all remaining losses until convergence. Special Case (BigBrain): Use multi-stage pruning due to heterogeneous regions. Prune three times: twice during densification at epochs 200 and 300 (pruning ratio 0.8), and once after densification at epoch 800 (ratio 0.85). Other datasets use a single pruning iteration. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainschedule(scenedata, initialprimitives, Etotal): primitives = initialprimitives currentepoch = 0 # Phase 1: Warm-up (first 16 epochs) while currentepoch < 16: # Compute photometric and silhouette losses loss = computephotometricloss(primitives, scenedata) + computesilhouetteloss(primitives, scenedata) # Standard optimizer gradient step primitives = applyoptimizerstep(primitives, loss) currentepoch += 1 # Phase 2: Densification (until 14-25% of training) densificationend = int(0.25 Etotal) while currentepoch < densificationend: # Enable adaptive density control every 4 epochs if currentepoch % 4 == 0: # Split and prune surfels based on accumulated weight/gradient primitives = splitandprunesurfels(primitives) # Disable silhouette, enable geometric regularizers loss = computephotometricloss(primitives, scenedata) + computeconsistencyloss(primitives) + computenormalconsistencyloss(primitives) # Optional mask-based pruning if scenedata.hasmasks: # Remove surfels projecting outside foreground mask across majority of views primitives = removeoutsidemasksurfels(primitives, scenedata.masks) # Structure-aware pruning at 42-50% mark if 0.42 Etotal <= currentepoch <= 0.50 Etotal: # Prune based on importance scores primitives = structureawareimportancepruning(primitives) # Standard optimizer gradient step primitives = applyoptimizerstep(primitives, loss) currentepoch += 1 # Phase 3: Refinement (remaining epochs) while currentepoch < Etotal: # Freeze densification, fine-tune with remaining losses loss = computeallremaininglosses(primitives, scenedata) primitives = applyoptimizerstep(primitives, loss) currentepoch += 1 return primitives Densification Interval: Every 4 epochs. Pruning Ratios: 0.8 for intermediate stages, 0.85 for final stage in BigBrain. Initial Surfel Count: ~50k surfels per scene. Final Surfel Count: ~100k surfels on average. Precision: Early warm-up is critical; skipping it leads to poor alignment under sparse coverage. Boundaries: Mask-based pruning requires accurate ground-truth masks; incorrect masks may remove valid geometry. Degenerate Input: Heterogeneous volumes (e.g., BigBrain) require multi-stage pruning to handle both smooth and detailed regions. A training schedule for photon field networks that uses a sequence of increasing KNN query radii ri approaching a target radius r to improve convergence time. It addresses the high cost of large-K range queries by starting with small radii for quick adaptation and increasing them for detail refinement. During training, the current step's sampling radius is determined from a predefined sequence; if the radius is small, k < K samples are returned, and as the radius increases, k approaches K. The loss function is the relative mean square error (rMSE) applied to each set of outputs individually. Typical training duration is 2000 to 3000 steps. The optimizer is Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99, and no L2 regularization. The learning rate is 9 \times 10^{-4} with exponential decay of 0.92 starting at 70% of total steps, triggering every subsequent 25 steps. An example schedule for 1M photons uses radii 25 for 0–36% steps, 50 for 37–63% and 64–90% steps, and 0 (target) for 91–100% steps. This schedule provides approximately 2–3\times improvement in training speed compared to naïve training using the target radius directly. The exact design is empirical and depends on the dataset, lighting conditions, and transfer function. A technique to suppress floaters (unstable Gaussians) and improve temporal coherence by perturbing timestamps during sensitivity estimation. Floaters are unstable Gaussians that appear static in observed views but drift at unseen timestamps. During sensitivity estimation, the input timestamp t to the deformation field \mathcal{D} is perturbed by adding noise scaled by \beta\Delta t(1 - i/\tau). The perturbation follows \mathcal{D}(\mu, r, s, t + \mathcal{N}(0,1)\beta\Delta t(1 - i/\tau)), where \mathcal{D} is the deformation network, t is the current timestep, \mathcal{N}(0,1) is standard normal noise, \beta is a noise scaling factor, \Delta t is the timestep interval, i is the current training iteration, and \tau is the total number of training iterations. This temporally jittered sampling reveals unstable primitives early in training, encouraging robust pruning and suppressing floaters. The noise magnitude anneals as training progresses to ensure precise reconstruction in later stages. A training schedule strategy for radiance-field optimization that iteratively refines the directional color representation of a scene by optimizing SH coefficients from a starting band up to a target maximum band. It addresses the instability and slow convergence associated with initializing high-frequency SH bands simultaneously with low-frequency ones. Unlike standard optimization which may initialize all bands at once, this method sequentially activates bands, allowing the scene density and low-frequency color to stabilize before introducing higher-frequency details. Time Complexity: The staggered KNN schedule reduces training time by 2–3\times compared to using the target radius from the start. The densification phase adds overhead due to splitting and pruning but improves final quality. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives, starting at ~50k and converging to ~100k for surface splatting. Not given in the sources for photon fields. Strengths: Handles sparse initialization effectively. Adapts to heterogeneous data via multi-stage pruning. Reduces training time for KNN-based methods. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of phase boundaries and pruning ratios. Mask-based pruning requires ground-truth masks. The exact KNN schedule design is empirical. When to Use: When optimizing differentiable volume rendering with adaptive primitives (surfels, photon fields) and sparse initial coverage. When Not to Use: For fixed-grid or fixed-topology methods that do not support densification or structural updates. The concept of phased training schedules in volume rendering emerged with the advent of differentiable rendering and adaptive primitive representations. The warm-up/densification/refinement structure is prominent in 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS) and Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering (ESVR). The staggered KNN schedule was introduced for Photon Field Networks to mitigate the computational cost of large-K nearest neighbor queries during training. Temporal Sensitivity Sampling was developed for Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting to address floater instability. These methods build on earlier work in Radiance-field optimization and NeRF Training Loop.
