name: Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics Optimization
head: Band-by-band optimization, SH Band Strategy
body: Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization is a training schedule strategy for radiance-field optimization that iteratively refines the directional color representation of a scene by optimizing SH coefficients from a starting band up to a target maximum band. It addresses the instability and slow convergence associated with initializing high-frequency SH bands simultaneously with low-frequency ones. Unlike standard optimization which may initialize all bands at once, this method sequentially activates bands, allowing the scene density and low-frequency color to stabilize before introducing higher-frequency details. The method controls the optimization of Spherical Harmonics coefficients by managing which bands are active and how their parameters are initialized during the training loop. It relies on specific configuration flags to determine the starting band and initialization behavior. Inputs: configs: A configuration object containing: sphericalHarmonicsBand: The maximum SH band index to optimize (integer). hierarchyBandStrategy: Boolean flag. If true, bands are optimized hierarchically. If false, all bands may be optimized together depending on other flags. SHsForTargetResoOnly: Boolean flag. If true and the current hierarchy level is not the minimum, the optimization resets to band 0. initialFromFile: Boolean flag. If true, density initialization is skipped for specific band transitions. learningRate: Base learning rate for scene parameters. shLearningRate: Learning rate specifically for SH coefficients. epochs: Total number of epochs per band stage. batchSize: Number of rays per batch. solidStrategy: Boolean flag. If false, self-sample offset is applied. varianceLossInterval: Interval (in batches) for applying variance loss. varianceCoefficient, shCoefficient: Weights for auxiliary losses. vairanceType, neighboorNums: Parameters for variance loss calculation. maskLossCoefficient, huberDelta: Parameters for RGB loss calculation. saveIntervals: Interval (in epochs) for saving model checkpoints. justModel: Boolean flag. If true, intermediate results are not saved. this->scene: The scene representation object, containing: optimizingBand: The current SH band being optimized. stepSize: The step size for ray marching. sparse: Boolean flag indicating sparse representation. grayImage: Boolean flag indicating if the scene is grayscale. setSelfSampleOffset(offset): Method to set sampling offset. this->sceneOptimizer: The optimizer object, containing: initialBand(band, densityInitialized): Initializes parameters for a specific band. initialAll(): Initializes all parameters at once. this->ray: Ray data, containing: totalRays: Total number of rays to process. RenderUtils: Rendering utilities, containing: renderRays(...): Renders rays for grayscale or basic loss. renderRayswithGradientsRGB(...): Renders rays with RGB gradients and loss computation. addVarianceLoss(...): Adds variance regularization loss. Optimizer: Optimizer utilities, containing: updateRGBScene(...): Updates RGB-specific scene parameters. lossesDevice, lossesHost: GPU and CPU arrays for storing per-ray losses. Outputs: Updated scene parameters (density, SH coefficients, RGB). Loss metrics (min, max, average) per epoch. Saved model checkpoints at specified intervals. The implementation relies on the following data structures as defined in the source code: 1. Camera Structure (Camera): w2cExternalMat[16]: World-to-camera transformation matrix (4x4). intrinsicMat[9]: Camera intrinsic matrix (3x3). alpha[2], principle[2]: Focal length and principal point parameters. translation[3]: Camera center position. rotationMat[9]: Rotation matrix. Device pointers (c2wExternalMatDevice, alphaDevice, etc.) for GPU transfer. 2. Configuration Structure (configs): Contains hyperparameters listed in Inputs. 3. Scene Structure (this->scene): optimizingBand: Integer tracking the current SH band. stepSize: Float for ray marching step size. sparse: Boolean. grayImage: Boolean. 4. Loss Arrays: lossesDevice: GPU array of double values, size actualBatchSize. lossesHost: CPU array of double values, size actualBatchSize. 1. Determine Starting Band: If configs->hierarchyBandStrategy is false, set startBand = configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand. Else, if configs->SHsForTargetResoOnly is true AND currentHierarchy is not minimumHierarchy, set startBand = 0. Else, startBand remains determined by the hierarchy strategy (typically 0 if hierarchy is active, or the max band if not). Note: The source logic implies startBand is set based on these conditions before the loop. 2. Iterate Through SH Bands: Loop optimizingBand from startBand to configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand (inclusive). 3. Set Current Band: Set this->scene->optimizingBand = optimizingBand. 4. Initialize Parameters: Check condition: If configs->hierarchyBandStrategy is true, OR (configs->hierarchyBandStrategy is false AND configs->SHsForTargetResoOnly is true AND currentHierarchy is not minimumHierarchy): Determine densityInitialized: If configs->initialFromFile is true AND optimizingBand == availableSHBand + 1, then densityInitialized = false. Otherwise, densityInitialized = true. Call this->sceneOptimizer.initialBand(optimizingBand, densityInitialized). Else (if configs->hierarchyBandStrategy is false AND NOT (configs->SHsForTargetResoOnly is true AND currentHierarchy is not minimumHierarchy)): Call this->sceneOptimizer.initialAll(). 5. Reset Learning Rates: Set configs->learningRate = rawLR (initial raw learning rate). Set configs->shLearningRate = rawSHLR (initial raw SH learning rate). 6. Epoch Loop: Loop epoch from 0 to configs->epochs (inclusive). 7. Batch Calculation: Calculate batchCount: \text{batchCount} = \lceil \frac{\text{this->ray.totalRays}}{\text{configs->batchSize}} \rceil = \frac{\text{this->ray.totalRays} + \text{configs->batchSize} - 1}{\text{configs->batchSize}} (Integer division rounding up). 8. Batch Loop: Loop batchIndex from 0 to batchCount - 1. 9. Sample Index and Batch Size: Calculate startSampleIndex = batchIndex configs->batchSize. Calculate actualBatchSize: If startSampleIndex + configs->batchSize < this->ray.totalRays, then actualBatchSize = configs->batchSize. Else, actualBatchSize = this->ray.totalRays - startSampleIndex. 10. Set Sampling Offset: If !configs->solidStrategy, call this->scene->setSelfSampleOffset(this->scene->stepSize / 2.0). 11. Render Rays (Grayscale/Basic): Call RenderUtils::renderRays(ray, scene, sampleRaysIndexGPU, startSampleIndex, actualBatchSize). 12. Render Rays (RGB/Gradients): If renderRes.grayImage is false: Call RenderUtils::renderRayswithGradientsRGB(sceneOptimizer, ray, scene, lossesDevice, sampleRaysIndexGPU, startSampleIndex, actualBatchSize, configs->maskLossCoefficient, configs->huberDelta). 13. Copy Losses to Host: Copy actualBatchSize doubles from lossesDevice to lossesHost: python cudaMemcpy(lossesHost, lossesDevice, sizeof(double) actualBatchSize, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost) 14. Compute Loss: Calculate loss = getMSEError(lossesHost, actualBatchSize). If isnan(loss): Print error. Free memory. Return (terminate training). 15. Update Loss Statistics: If loss > maxLoss, set maxLoss = loss. If minLoss > loss (or if minLoss is uninitialized), set minLoss = loss. Accumulate losses += loss. 16. Add Variance Loss: If !scene->sparse OR batchIndex % configs->varianceLossInterval == 0: Call RenderUtils::addVarianceLoss(scene, sceneOptimizer, configs->varianceCoefficient, configs->shCoefficient, configs->vairanceType, configs->neighboorNums). 17. Update RGB Scene: If scene->grayImage is false: Call Optimizer::updateRGBScene(sceneOptimizer, scene, timeStep). 18. Decay Learning Rates: Update configs->learningRate: \text{configs->learningRate} = \frac{\text{configs->learningRate}}{2^{(1.0 / \text{batchCount}) / (\text{epoch} + 1.0)}} Update configs->shLearningRate: \text{configs->shLearningRate} = \frac{\text{configs->shLearningRate}}{2^{(1.0 / \text{batchCount}) / (\text{epoch} + 1.0)}} 19. Store Epoch Losses: After the batch loop, store metrics in lossesPerEpochs array at indices epoch4 to epoch4+3: lossesPerEpochs[epoch4+0] = minLoss lossesPerEpochs[epoch4+1] = maxLoss lossesPerEpochs[epoch4+2] = losses / batchCount (Average loss) lossesPerEpochs[epoch4+3] = GPU elapsed time 20. Save Model: If !configs->justModel AND (epoch + 1) % configs->saveIntervals == 0: Save experiment results to directory named "Band%d" (where %d is the current optimizingBand). Unverified code. Typical values depend on desired detail (e.g., 3 or 4 for NeRF-like scenes). Not given in the sources. configs->hierarchyBandStrategy: Boolean. Controls hierarchical vs. flat optimization. configs->SHsForTargetResoOnly: Boolean. Resets start band to 0 if true and not at minimum hierarchy. configs->initialFromFile: Boolean. Skips density re-initialization if true and band matches availableSHBand+1. configs->learningRate, configs->shLearningRate: Base learning rates. Reset at each band start. configs->epochs: Number of epochs per band. configs->batchSize: Batch size for ray sampling. configs->solidStrategy: If false, applies self-sample offset. configs->varianceLossInterval: Interval for variance loss application. configs->varianceCoefficient, configs->shCoefficient: Weights for variance loss. configs->vairanceType, configs->neighboorNums: Parameters for variance loss. configs->maskLossCoefficient, configs->huberDelta: Parameters for RGB loss. configs->saveIntervals: Interval for saving models. configs->justModel: If true, skips saving intermediate results. NaN Loss: If the computed MSE loss is NaN, the training terminates immediately, freeing memory. Boundary Conditions: The last batch may have fewer rays than batchSize. The code explicitly calculates actualBatchSize to handle this. Density Initialization: The densityInitialized flag depends on initialFromFile and the relationship between optimizingBand and availableSHBand. If optimizingBand == availableSHBand + 1 and initialFromFile is true, density is not re-initialized. Learning Rate Decay: The decay factor is applied per batch, not per epoch, which can lead to significant decay over many batches. Time Complexity: The method adds overhead by iterating through SH bands. For each band, it runs a full training loop (epochs batches). If the maximum band is B, and each band requires E epochs and N batches, the total complexity is roughly O(B \cdot E \cdot N). However, since lower bands are simpler, the per-band cost may decrease, but the source does not provide specific timing data. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the scene representation and the SH coefficients. Optimizing bands sequentially allows for potential memory savings if lower bands are discarded, but the source does not specify memory management details beyond the standard scene and loss arrays. Performance: The method aims to improve convergence stability by avoiding the initialization of high-frequency bands too early. This can lead to better final quality but increases total training time due to the sequential nature. Strengths: Prevents instability from high-frequency SH coefficients; allows for controlled refinement of detail. Limitations: Increases training time; requires careful tuning of band transition parameters (hierarchyBandStrategy, SHsForTargetResoOnly). When to Use: When training radiance fields with SH representations and experiencing instability or poor convergence with high-frequency details. When Not to Use: When training time is critical and the scene does not require high-frequency detail; or when using a representation that does not support SH bands. Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics Optimization is a training schedule strategy used in differentiable volume rendering, specifically in the context of NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) and related radiance-field optimizations. It is implemented in the Clear-plenoxels repository. The method addresses the challenge of optimizing high-dimensional SH coefficients by breaking the problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems (bands). This approach is similar to other hierarchical optimization techniques in graphics, such as multi-resolution rendering or progressive refinement. nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, https://github.com/nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NeRF Hyperparameters
head: Blender Training Configuration, NeRF Model and Sampling Configuration, NeRF Training Hyperparameters, NeTF Training Configuration, TinyNeRF Training Setup, Training Loop Configuration
body: NeRF Hyperparameters define the specific configuration of the neural network architecture, sampling strategy, and optimizer settings required to train a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) model. This configuration solves the problem of reconstructing a continuous 3D scene representation from a set of calibrated 2D images by optimizing the radiance field parameters. What sets this configuration apart from its siblings is that it establishes the baseline "vanilla" NeRF settings (specifically the MLP depth, width, positional encoding frequencies, and hierarchical sampling counts) against which variants like Mip-NeRF [3409-mip-nerf-optimization-and-activation-details.md] or HashNeRF [3068-hashnerf-parameters.md] adjust their specific architectural or optimization details. The training process initializes an Adam optimizer and a NeRF model, loads a dataset (e.g., Blender synthetic scenes), and iteratively minimizes the difference between rendered and ground-truth images. The method relies on hierarchical sampling: a coarse proposal network samples points to identify high-density regions, and a fine network samples more densely in those regions. Inputs: Dataset: A collection of images with known camera poses (extrinsics) and intrinsics (focal length). Hyperparameters: Defined below (MLP layers, samples, learning rate, etc.). Outputs: Trained NeRF model weights (MLP parameters). Rendered images for validation/test sets. The model consists of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a Coarse MLP (proposal network) and a Fine MLP (final radiance field). Coarse MLP Structure: Input: 3D position (x, y, z) and viewing direction (\theta, \phi). Positional Encoding (PE): Axis-aligned PE applied to position and direction. Layers: 4 hidden layers. Hidden Units: 256 per layer. Output: Volume density \sigma and color c (RGB). Fine MLP Structure: Input: 3D position and viewing direction. Positional Encoding: Axis-aligned PE. Layers: 8 hidden layers. Hidden Units: 256 (standard) or 512 (larger capacity). Output: Volume density \sigma and color c (RGB). Positional Encoding: The positional encoding function \gamma(p) maps a scalar p to a vector of sines and cosines at different frequencies. For a position vector \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, the encoded vector has size 2 \times L \times \text{freqs}, where L is the dimensionality of the input (3 for position, 2 for direction in spherical coordinates). 1. Initialization: Initialize Adam optimizer with model parameters and learning rate. Load dataset images and normalize pixel values by dividing by 255.0. Reserve one image for validation/testing. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the training image batch, generate a ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Define near (tn) and far (tf) clipping planes along the ray. Typical values: tn = 2.0, tf = 6.0 for Blender scenes. 3. Coarse Sampling: Sample Nc points uniformly along the ray segment [tn, tf]. Default Nc = 64. Query the Coarse MLP at these points to get densities \sigmac and colors cc. Compute transmittance Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) and alpha \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). Render coarse color Cc = \sum{i=1}^{Nc} Ti \alphai c{c,i}. 4. Hierarchical Resampling: Use the coarse weights wi = Ti \alphai to construct a cumulative distribution function (CDF). Sample Nf points from this distribution (inverse CDF sampling) to concentrate samples in high-density regions. Default Nf = 128. Query the Fine MLP at these new points to get densities \sigmaf and colors cf. 5. Fine Rendering: Compute transmittance and alpha for the fine samples. Render fine color Cf = \sum{i=1}^{Nf} Ti \alphai c{f,i}. 6. Loss and Update: Compute Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between Cf and the ground-truth pixel color. Backpropagate and update model parameters using Adam. Decay learning rate exponentially. Volume Rendering Equation (Discrete Approximation): C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci Transmittance: Ti = \exp\left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right) Alpha (Opacity): \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) Delta (Distance between samples): \deltai = t{i+1} - ti Positional Encoding: For a scalar input p and frequency l: \gammal(p) = (\sin(2^l \pi p), \cos(2^l \pi p)) Coarse Samples (Nc): 64. Fine Samples (Nf): 128. Coarse MLP Layers: 4. Coarse MLP Width: 256. Fine MLP Layers: 8. Fine MLP Width: 256 or 512. Positional Encoding Frequencies (Position): 10. Positional Encoding Frequencies (Direction): 4. Learning Rate (\eta0): 5 \times 10^{-4} or 1 \times 10^{-3}. Learning Rate Decay: Exponential decay to 1 \times 10^{-4}. Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \epsilon = 1 \times 10^{-7}. Batch Size (Rays): 1024. Chunk Size (Inference): 4096 points processed per minibatch to avoid OOM. Near Plane: 2.0. Far Plane: 6.0. Total Iterations: 4096 or 200,000. Out of Memory (OOM): Processing all points for a batch simultaneously can exceed GPU memory. Solution: Split query points into chunks (e.g., 4096 points) and process sequentially. Precision: Use float32 for standard training. Mixed precision can be used but requires careful handling of loss scaling. Degenerate Input: If near/far planes are not set correctly relative to the scene scale, sampling may miss the object or include excessive empty space, leading to poor convergence. Distortion Regularization: Standard NeRF does not apply distortion regularization, unlike mip-NeRF which uses it to improve anti-aliasing [3409-mip-nerf-optimization-and-activation-details.md]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def positionalencoding(x, freqs): """Axis-aligned positional encoding.""" N, D = x.shape scales = 2.0 torch.arange(0, freqs, device=x.device) x = x.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, freqs) scales return torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1).reshape(N, -1) class NeRFMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, layers=8, width=256, posfreqs=10, dirfreqs=4): super().init() self.posfreqs = posfreqs self.dirfreqs = dirfreqs self.inputdim = 3 (2 posfreqs) + 2 (2 dirfreqs) self.layers = nn.ModuleList() self.layers.append(nn.Linear(self.inputdim, width)) for in range(layers - 1): self.layers.append(nn.Linear(width, width)) self.layers.append(nn.Linear(width, 4)) self.skipindices = [4] if layers > 4 else [] def forward(self, xpos, xdir): posenc = positionalencoding(xpos, self.posfreqs) direnc = positionalencoding(xdir, self.dirfreqs) x = torch.cat([posenc, direnc], dim=-1) for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): if i in self.skipindices: x = torch.cat([x, posenc], dim=-1) x = layer(x) if i < len(self.layers) - 1: x = torch.relu(x) sigma = torch.relu(x[..., 0]) color = torch.sigmoid(x[..., 1:]) return color, sigma def renderray(rayo, rayd, near, far, nsamples, model, perturb=True): """Render a single ray or batch of rays.""" tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nsamples, device=rayo.device) zvals = near (1.0 - tvals) + far tvals if perturb: mids = 0.5 (zvals[..., 1:] + zvals[...,:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, zvals[..., -1:]], -1) lower = torch.cat([zvals[...,:1], mids], -1) trand = torch.randlike(zvals) zvals = lower + (upper - lower) trand pts = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + rayd.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) chunksize = 4096 allcolors, allsigmas = [], [] for i in range(0, pts.shape[0], chunksize): chunkpts = pts[i:i+chunksize] chunkdirs = rayd[i:i+chunksize] colors, sigmas = model(chunkpts, chunkdirs) allcolors.append(colors) allsigmas.append(sigmas) colors = torch.cat(allcolors, dim=0) sigmas = torch.cat(allsigmas, dim=0) deltas = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] deltainf = 1e10 deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], -1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmas deltas) T = torch.cumsum(sigmas deltas, dim=-1) T = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(T[...,:1]), T], dim=-1) transmittance = torch.exp(-T) weights = alpha transmittance colorout = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) colors, dim=-2) return colorout, weights def trainstep(model, optimizer, images, poses, intrinsics, args): optimizer.zerograd() height, width = images.shape[1:3] focal = intrinsics[0, 0] y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(height), torch.arange(width), indexing='ij') dirs = torch.stack([(x - width/2)/focal, -(y - height/2)/focal, -torch.oneslike(x)], dim=-1) dirs = dirs / torch.norm(dirs, dim=-1, keepdim=True) origins = poses[...,:3, 3].unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1).expand(height, width, 3) rayso = origins.reshape(-1, 3) raysd = dirs.reshape(-1, 3) imagesflat = images.reshape(-1, 3) # Coarse sampling coarsecolor, coarseweights = renderray(rayso, raysd, args.near, args.far, args.nsamplescoarse, model.coarsemodel) # Hierarchical resampling: sample fine points based on coarse weights cdfs = torch.cumsum(coarseweights, dim=-1) cdfs = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdfs[...,:1]), cdfs], dim=-1) u = torch.randlike(cdfs) inds = torch.searchsorted(cdfs, u, right=True) inds = torch.clamp(inds, 1, args.nsamplescoarse - 1) zfine = torch.gather(coarseweights.newtensor(torch.linspace(args.near, args.far, args.nsamplescoarse)), 1, inds) finecolor, = renderray(rayso, raysd, args.near, args.far, args.nsamplesfine, model.finemodel) loss = torch.mean((finecolor - imagesflat) 2) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() Configures HashNeRF, which replaces the MLP with a multi-resolution hashed grid. It requires settings for hash map size and regularization, differing from the MLP-based NeRF hyperparameters. Details the specific changes to NeRF hyperparameters for Mip-NeRF, including cone tracing, different positional encoding, and distortion regularization. Specifies hyperparameters for DONeRF, which adapts NeRF for dynamic scenes, often involving temporal encoding and different sampling strategies. Time Complexity: Training time scales linearly with the number of iterations and the number of samples per ray (Nc + Nf). Quadrupling the sampling resolution (e.g., from 32x32 to 64x64 in NeTF context) quadruples training time. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the MLP weights and the intermediate activations during the forward pass. Chunking (e.g., 4096 points) limits peak memory usage. Measured Performance: On Blender dataset (Lego scene, 200k iterations): PSNR ~31-32 dB, SSIM ~0.96, Time ~12-15 hours on a single GPU. With 256 hidden units: 0.84M params, 1.86 hours training time, PSNR 32.96. With 512 hidden units: 3.23M params, 3.42 hours training time, PSNR 33.25. Comparison: The proposed model (with proposal networks) is significantly faster to train than mip-NeRF, with speedup increasing as model capacity rises. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust baseline, good quality on synthetic data. Limitations: Slow training for large scenes, requires many samples for high quality, sensitive to near/far plane selection. The hyperparameters described here are based on the original NeRF implementation and its common variants (like the "TinyNeRF" implementation and the "NeRF from Scratch"). The configuration has become a standard reference for differentiable volume rendering optimization. name: HashNeRF Parameters
head: HashNeRF Hyperparameters
body: HashNeRF parameters configure the training loop and model architecture for the HashNeRF method, which builds on NeRF Hyperparameters. Unlike standard NeRF which relies on positional encoding or fixed-resolution grids, HashNeRF uses a multi-resolution hashed embedding table indexed by voxel coordinates, requiring specific settings for the hash map size, loss regularization, and dataset-specific loading behaviors. The HashNeRF training configuration defines the inputs (dataset images, poses), the model structure (NeRFSmall with hashed embeddings), and the optimization schedule. When args.iembed==1, the model uses a hashed embedding table instead of standard positional encoding or fixed grids, with parameters stored in embeddingparams. The model architecture is NeRFSmall with fixed dimensions hiddendim=64 and geofeatdim=15. Non-hashed modes use the standard NeRF model with configurable depth and width. All values are defaults unless noted otherwise. Model and Embedding: finestres: Finest resolution for the hashed embedding grid. Default: 512. log2hashmapsize: Log2 of the hashmap size. Default: 19. rawnoisestd: Standard deviation of noise added to the regularized sigma output. Recommended: 1e0. tv-loss-weight: Weight for Total Variation loss applied to the embedding table. Default: 1e-6. sparse-loss-weight: Weight for sparse loss. Default: 1e-10. Optimizer: When args.iembed==1, the optimizer for embedding parameters uses RAdam with eps: 1e-15. Rendering and Crops: renderfactor: Downsampling factor for rendering to speed up previews. Set to 4 or 8 for fast preview. precropiters: Number of steps to train on central crops. Default: 0. precropfrac: Fraction of the image taken for central crops. Default: 0.5. Dataset and Scene Configuration: datasettype: Options: llff, blender, deepvoxels. Default: 'llff'. shape: Options: armchair, cube, greek, vase. Default: 'greek'. whitebkgd: Boolean flag to render synthetic data on a white background. halfres: Boolean flag to load Blender synthetic data at 400x400 instead of 800x800. scannetsceneID: Scene ID to load from ScanNet. Default: 'scene000000'. factor: Downsampling factor for LLFF images. Default: 8. nondc: Boolean flag to disable Normalized Device Coordinates (set for non-forward facing scenes). lindisp: Boolean flag to sample linearly in disparity rather than depth. spherify: Boolean flag to set for spherical 360 scenes. llffhold: Takes every 1/N images as the LLFF test set. Default: 8. testskip: Loads 1/N images from test/val sets. Default: 8. Logging and Checkpointing: iprint: Frequency of console printout and metric logging. Default: 100. iimg: Frequency of TensorBoard image logging. Default: 500. iweights: Frequency of weight checkpoint saving. Default: 10000. itestset: Frequency of testset saving. Default: 1000. ivideo: Frequency of renderposes video saving. Default: 5000. The forward pass iterates over multiple resolution levels, computes voxel indices via hashing, looks up embeddings, and interpolates features. The helper functions for voxelization and interpolation follow standard graphics routines. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch class HashedEmbedding(torch.nn.Module): def init(self, finestres=512, log2hashmapsize=19, nlevels=4, b=2.0, boundingbox=None): super().init() self.finestres = finestres self.log2hashmapsize = log2hashmapsize self.nlevels = nlevels self.b = b self.baseresolution = finestres / (b (nlevels - 1)) self.boundingbox = boundingbox self.embeddings = torch.nn.ModuleList([ torch.nn.Embedding(2log2hashmapsize, 4) for in range(nlevels) ]) def getvoxelvertices(self, x, resolution, log2hashmapsize): # Standard voxelization: normalize points, quantize to grid, hash coordinates, compute bounds if self.boundingbox is not None: xnorm = (x - self.boundingbox.min) / (self.boundingbox.max - self.boundingbox.min) else: xnorm = (x + 1.0) / 2.0 gridcoords = (xnorm resolution).long() keepmask = (gridcoords >= 0).all(dim=-1) & (gridcoords < resolution).all(dim=-1) hashedindices = (gridcoords[:, 0] 73856093) ^ (gridcoords[:, 1] 19349663) ^ (gridcoords[:, 2] 83492791) hashedindices = hashedindices % (2log2hashmapsize) voxelmin = gridcoords.float() / resolution voxelmax = (gridcoords + 1).float() / resolution return voxelmin, voxelmax, hashedindices, keepmask def trilinearinterp(self, x, voxelmin, voxelmax, voxelembedds): # Standard trilinear interpolation using fractional coordinates within the voxel frac = (x self.baseresolution) - voxelmin self.baseresolution w000 = (1 - frac[:, 0]) (1 - frac[:, 1]) (1 - frac[:, 2]) w100 = frac[:, 0] (1 - frac[:, 1]) (1 - frac[:, 2]) w010 = (1 - frac[:, 0]) frac[:, 1] (1 - frac[:, 2]) w110 = frac[:, 0] frac[:, 1] (1 - frac[:, 2]) w001 = (1 - frac[:, 0]) (1 - frac[:, 1]) frac[:, 2] w101 = frac[:, 0] (1 - frac[:, 1]) frac[:, 2] w011 = (1 - frac[:, 0]) frac[:, 1] frac[:, 2] w111 = frac[:, 0] frac[:, 1] frac[:, 2] # Simplified to center lookup for this context; full implementation gathers 8 corners return voxelembedds def forward(self, x): xembeddedall = [] for i in range(self.nlevels): resolution = torch.floor(self.baseresolution self.bi) voxelminvertex, voxelmaxvertex, hashedvoxelindices, keepmask = \ self.getvoxelvertices(x, resolution, self.log2hashmapsize) voxelembedds = self.embeddingsi xembedded = self.trilinearinterp(x, voxelminvertex, voxelmaxvertex, voxelembedds) xembeddedall.append(xembedded) keepmask = keepmask.sum(dim=-1) == keepmask.shape[-1] return torch.cat(xembeddedall, dim=-1), keepmask When args.iembed==1, the model uses a hashed embedding table instead of standard positional encoding or fixed grids. The embedding parameters are stored in embeddingparams and optimized with RAdam using eps: 1e-15. This configuration is paired with the NeRFSmall architecture (hiddendim=64, geofeatdim=15), whereas non-hashed modes use the standard NeRF model with configurable depth and width. name: Mip-NeRF Optimization and Activation Details
head: JaxNeRF Training Procedure, Mip-NeRF Misc. Changes
body: This article defines the specific implementation details for training mip-NeRF and JaxNeRF, focusing on activation functions, input encoding structures, and learning rate scheduling. These changes are designed to improve training stability and robustness, particularly against catastrophic failure modes, without significantly altering the model's accuracy or speed. Unlike standard NeRF implementations, this method removes identity concatenation from the MLP input and employs shifted and widened activation functions to handle edge cases in density and color prediction. The method modifies the standard NeRF training loop through four key components: input encoding structure, density activation, color activation, and learning rate scheduling. Inputs: Ray parameters (origin, direction), integrated positional encoding (IPE) features, and iteration index i. Outputs: Density \tau and color c for the ray segment. Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE): The MLP input consists solely of the IPE features derived from the ray's mean and covariance. The original position and view direction are not concatenated with the encoding. View Direction Encoding: The ray direction d is normalized, then processed with a standard positional encoding function with L=4 frequencies. 1. Input Preparation: Compute the IPE features for the ray segment. Pass these IPE features as the sole input to the MLP. 2. Density Prediction (\tau): The MLP produces a raw output value x\tau. Apply the shifted softplus activation to obtain density: \tau = \log(1 + \exp(x\tau - 1)) This is equivalent to initializing the bias of the density output layer to -1, ensuring initial \tau values are small. 3. View Direction Injection: Normalize the ray direction d. Apply positional encoding with L=4 to d. Inject these encoded view directions into the last layer of the MLP. This injection occurs after \tau is predicted but before the final color c is predicted. 4. Color Prediction (c): The MLP produces a raw output value xc. Apply the widened sigmoid activation to obtain color: c = \frac{1 + 2\epsilon}{1 + \exp(-xc)} - \epsilon Use \epsilon = 0.001. This allows the output to saturate slightly outside the [0, 1] range. 5. Optimization Loop: Use the Adam optimizer. Apply the learning rate schedule defined in the "Learning Rate Schedule" section below. Density Activation: \tau = \log(1 + \exp(x - 1)) x: Raw MLP output for density. Purpose: Prevents catastrophic failure where the MLP emits negative values everywhere, which would result in zero gradients for \tau and halt optimization. Color Activation: c = \frac{1 + 2\epsilon}{1 + \exp(-x)} - \epsilon, \quad \epsilon = 0.001 x: Raw MLP output for color. Purpose: Avoids optimization failure when explaining black or white pixels by allowing saturation slightly outside [0, 1]. Learning Rate Schedule: \etai = \left( \lambdaw + (1 - \lambdaw) \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \operatorname{clip}\left(\frac{i}{nw}, 0, 1\right)\right) \right) \times \left( \exp\left( (1 - \frac{i}{n}) \log(\eta0) + \frac{i}{n} \log(\etan) \right) \right) i: Current iteration index. n: Total number of iterations (1,000,000). nw: Warmup iterations (2,500). \eta0: Initial learning rate (5 \cdot 10^{-4}). \etan: Final learning rate (5 \cdot 10^{-6}). \lambdaw: Warmup scale factor, annealed from 0.01 to 1 during the warmup period. Optimizer: Adam. Total Iterations (n): 1,000,000. Batch Size: 4096. Warmup Iterations (nw): 2,500. Initial Learning Rate (\eta0): 5 \cdot 10^{-4}. Final Learning Rate (\etan): 5 \cdot 10^{-6}. Warmup Scale Factor Range: \lambdaw annealed from 0.01 to 1 during warmup. View Direction PE Frequencies (L): 4. Negative Density: Using standard ReLU for density can cause the MLP to emit negative values everywhere, leading to zero gradients and optimization failure. The shifted softplus prevents this. Black/White Pixel Saturation: Standard sigmoid saturation can cause training to fail when trying to explain extreme pixel values. The widened sigmoid mitigates this. Identity Concatenation: Concatenating original position/view direction with IPE is unnecessary and complicates the formalization of IPE features. Removing it simplifies the method without performance loss. Alternative PE: Concatenating positional encodings of mean and covariance square roots is sensitive to L hyperparameters and less compact than IPE. IPE is preferred. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def positionalencoding(x, L=4): """Standard positional encoding.""" scales = np.array([2.0 i for i in range(L)]) xexpanded = np.expanddims(x, axis=-1) scales return np.concatenate([np.sin(xexpanded), np.cos(xexpanded)], axis=-1).flatten() def shiftedsoftplus(x): """Density activation: log(1 + exp(x - 1)).""" return np.log(1.0 + np.exp(x - 1.0)) def widenedsigmoid(x, epsilon=0.001): """Color activation: (1 + 2eps)/(1 + exp(-x)) - eps.""" return (1.0 + 2.0 epsilon) / (1.0 + np.exp(-x)) - epsilon def computelearningrate(i, n=1000000, nw=2500, eta0=5e-4, etan=5e-6): """Learning rate schedule.""" clipval = min(max(i / nw, 0.0), 1.0) lambdastart = 0.01 warmupfactor = lambdastart + (1.0 - lambdastart) math.sin(math.pi / 2.0 clipval) logeta = (1.0 - i / n) math.log(eta0) + (i / n) math.log(etan) return warmupfactor math.exp(logeta) def mipnerfforward(mlp, ipefeatures, raydirection): """Forward pass following mip-NeRF activation and injection rules.""" # Step 1: Input is solely IPE features # Step 2: Density prediction rawtau = mlp(ipefeatures) tau = shiftedsoftplus(rawtau) # Step 3: View direction handling dnorm = raydirection / np.linalg.norm(raydirection) viewpe = positionalencoding(dnorm, L=4) # Step 4: Color prediction with view injection # The view PE is injected into the last layer before color prediction # Architecture-specific view injection implementation required rawc = mlpforwardviewdependent(ipefeatures, viewpe) c = widenedsigmoid(rawc) return tau, c Defines specific hyperparameters, network architectures, and loss functions for Mip-NeRF 360, using a multi-stage proposal sampling strategy and Charbonnier loss to stabilize optimization of unbounded, anti-aliased radiance fields. Training Time: Mip-NeRF is 13x faster to train than a brute-force supersampling baseline (16 rays/pixel). Evaluation Time: Mip-NeRF is 16x faster to evaluate than the supersampling baseline. Quality: Mip-NeRF outperforms the 16x supersampling baseline in quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). Stability: The activation functions and learning rate schedule improve training stability, particularly with large learning rates, though the core accuracy remains similar to standard NeRF. Memory: The removal of identity concatenation makes the IPE features more compact, reducing memory usage compared to concatenated PE approaches. Origin: This method is described in the "Mip-NeRF: A Multiscale Representation for Anti-Aliasing Neural Radiance Fields" paper. Development: These "miscellaneous" changes were identified to simplify the method and increase robustness during optimization, particularly for ablations and fair comparisons with JaxNeRF. Usage: Used in the training of mip-NeRF and JaxNeRF models. name: Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup
head: Mip-NeRF 360 Training Procedure
body: This article specifies the hyperparameters, network architectures, and loss functions used to train the Mip-NeRF 360 model. It stabilizes optimization by combining a two-stage proposal sampling strategy with a Charbonnier reconstruction loss and a stop-gradient operation that decouples proposal network updates from NeRF updates. It differs from standard NeRF training by enforcing strict separation between proposal and NeRF optimization via stop-gradient operations, and by using a Charbonnier loss instead of mean squared error to achieve more stable optimization. Inputs: A batch of rays \mathbf{t}, each defined by origin and direction, and their corresponding ground-truth pixel colors \mathbf{C}^. Outputs: Optimized weights for the proposal MLP (\Theta{\text{prop}}) and the NeRF MLP (\Theta{\text{NeRF}}). The method relies on two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Proposal MLP: Architecture: 4 layers, 256 hidden units per layer. Activations: ReLU for hidden layers, Softplus for the final density output \tau. Parameters: \Theta{\text{prop}}. 2. NeRF MLP: Architecture: 8 layers, 1024 hidden units per layer. Activations: ReLU for hidden layers, Softplus for the final density output \tau. Parameters: \Theta{\text{NeRF}}. 1. Proposal Sampling Stage 0: Evaluate the proposal MLP using 64 samples along each ray to produce the first set of weighted intervals (\hat{s}0, \hat{w}0). 2. Proposal Sampling Stage 1: Resample and evaluate the proposal MLP again using 64 samples to produce the second set of weighted intervals (\hat{s}1, \hat{w}1). 3. NeRF Sampling: Evaluate the NeRF MLP using 32 samples, resampled based on the proposal histograms, to produce the final set of weighted intervals (s, w). 4. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as the sum of reconstruction, distribution, and proposal losses, averaged over all rays in the batch: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{t}), \mathbf{C}^) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{w}) + \sum{k=0}^1 \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{w}, \hat{\mathbf{s}}^k, \hat{\mathbf{w}}^k) 5. Gradient Application: Apply stop-gradient to \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}} before backpropagating to \Theta{\text{NeRF}} to make the optimization of \Theta{\text{prop}} independent from \Theta{\text{NeRF}}. 6. Optimizer Update: Update both networks using the Adam optimizer. Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}): Charbonnier loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} = \sqrt{(x - x^)^2 + \epsilon^2} Where x is the predicted color, x^ is the ground truth color, and \epsilon = 0.001. Distribution Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}): Minimizes the weighted size of each individual interval. Regularization Weight (\lambda): Balances the data term \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} and the regularizer \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}, set to 0.01 in all experiments. Total Loss (\mathcal{L}): As defined in Step 4 above. Optimizer: Adam. \beta1 = 0.9 \beta2 = 0.999 \epsilon = 10^{-6} Learning Rate Schedule: Annealed log-linearly from 2 \times 10^{-3} to 2 \times 10^{-5}. Warm-up phase: 512 iterations. Gradient Clipping: Norm of 10^{-3}. Training Iterations: 250,000. Batch Size: 2^{14} rays. Regularization Weight (\lambda): 0.01. Z-aliasing: The proposal MLP may learn a non-smooth mapping from input coordinates to volumetric densities, causing rays to "skip" scene content. This artifact is particularly visible when the camera translates along the z-axis or when using high-capacity backends like iNGP. Interlevel Loss Artifacts: The standard Mip-NeRF 360 interlevel loss assigns equivalent loss to NeRF and proposal histogram bins regardless of overlap extent, penalizing only complete failures to overlap, which leads to non-smooth density maps. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmipnerf360(batchrays, batchgtcolors, numiterations=250000): # Initialize networks proposalmlp = MLP(layers=4, hiddenunits=256, activation='relu', densityactivation='softplus') nerfmlp = MLP(layers=8, hiddenunits=1024, activation='relu', densityactivation='softplus') # Initialize optimizer optimizer = Adam(params=[proposalmlp.parameters(), nerfmlp.parameters()], lr=2e-3, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-6) # Hyperparameters lrstart = 2e-3 lrend = 2e-5 warmupiters = 512 clipnorm = 1e-3 lambdareg = 0.01 epsiloncharb = 0.001 for iteration in range(1, numiterations + 1): # 1. Proposal Sampling Stage 0 t0 = uniformsamplet(numsamples=64) densities0 = proposalmlp(batchrays, t0) shat0, what0 = constructhistogram(t0, densities0) # 2. Proposal Sampling Stage 1 t1 = importancesamplet(histogram=(shat0, what0), numsamples=64) densities1 = proposalmlp(batchrays, t1) shat1, what1 = constructhistogram(t1, densities1) # 3. NeRF Sampling tnerf = importancesamplet(histogram=(shat1, what1), numsamples=32) densitiesnerf, colorsnerf = nerfmlp(batchrays, tnerf) s, w = constructhistogram(tnerf, densitiesnerf) # 4. Compute Losses renderedcolors = rendervolume(s, w, colorsnerf) reconloss = charbonnierloss(renderedcolors, batchgtcolors, epsiloncharb) distloss = intervalsizeloss(s, w) proploss0 = interlevelloss(s, w, shat0, what0) proploss1 = interlevelloss(s, w, shat1, what1) totalproploss = proploss0 + proploss1 # Total loss formula totalloss = reconloss + lambdareg distloss + totalproploss # 5. Gradient Application with stop-gradient on Lprop for NeRF # Compute gradients for proposal network (includes Lprop) gradsprop = computegradients(totalloss, proposalmlp.parameters()) # Compute gradients for NeRF network (excludes Lprop via stop-gradient) lossnerfonly = reconloss + lambdareg distloss gradsnerf = computegradients(lossnerfonly, nerfmlp.parameters()) # 6. Optimizer Update clipgradients(gradsprop, clipnorm) clipgradients(gradsnerf, clipnorm) optimizer.step(gradsprop, gradsnerf) # Update learning rate if iteration < warmupiters: currentlr = lrstart (iteration / warmupiters) else: progress = (iteration - warmupiters) / (numiterations - warmupiters) currentlr = lrstart (lrend / lrstart) progress optimizer.setlr(currentlr) def MLP(layers, hiddenunits, activation, densityactivation): """Standard feedforward network with specified activations.""" return Network(layers, hiddenunits, activation, densityactivation) def Adam(params, lr, beta1, beta2, eps): """Standard Adam optimizer with momentum and RMSprop scaling.""" return Optimizer(params, lr, beta1, beta2, eps) def uniformsamplet(numsamples): """Draws uniform samples from [0, 1].""" return random.uniform(0, 1, size=numsamples) def importancesamplet(histogram, numsamples): """Draws samples proportional to histogram weights.""" s, w = histogram cdf = cumulativesum(w) return inversecdfsample(cdf, numsamples) def constructhistogram(t, densities): """Converts raw samples to piecewise-linear histogram midpoints (s) and weights (w).""" s = (t[:-1] + t[1:]) / 2 w = densities (t[1:] - t[:-1]) return s, w def rendervolume(s, w, colors): """Renders color from histogram using standard volume rendering accumulation.""" return accumulatetransmittanceandcolor(s, w, colors) def charbonnierloss(pred, target, epsilon): """Computes Charbonnier loss.""" return sqrt((pred - target)2 + epsilon2) def intervalsizeloss(s, w): """Minimizes the weighted size of each individual interval.""" return mean(w (s[1:] - s[:-1])) def interlevelloss(snerf, wnerf, sprop, wprop): """Computes distance between NeRF and proposal histograms.""" return histogramdistance(snerf, wnerf, sprop, wprop) def computegradients(loss, params): """Computes gradients of loss with respect to parameters.""" return autograd.grad(loss, params) def clipgradients(grads, maxnorm): """Clips gradient norms to maxnorm.""" norm = sqrt(sum(g2 for g in grads)) if norm > maxnorm: scale = maxnorm / norm return [g scale for g in grads] return grads The Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss is a proposal supervision loss function that measures the distance between a NeRF histogram and a proposal histogram by blurring the NeRF histogram into a piecewise-linear spline and resampling it into the proposal's interval endpoints. Unlike the piecewise constant loss used in Mip-NeRF 360, which suffers from aliasing when NeRF histogram bins are narrow or translate relative to the proposal, this method produces a smooth loss surface that prevents aliasing artifacts during training. This method resolves z-aliasing artifacts in proposal networks by replacing the discrete interlevel loss with a continuous, smooth loss function that penalizes partial overlaps between proposal and NeRF histograms. It addresses the pitfall where the original Mip-NeRF 360 interlevel loss assigns equivalent loss to NeRF and proposal histogram bins regardless of overlap extent, penalizing only complete failures to overlap and leading to non-smooth density maps. The new loss prevents the proposal network from learning non-smooth mappings that occur with the previous loss, particularly when the proposal network has high capacity such as an iNGP backend. Time Complexity: The method uses a multi-stage sampling approach (2 proposal stages + 1 NeRF stage), increasing the number of forward passes per ray compared to single-stage NeRF. The proposal network is smaller (4 layers, 256 units) than the NeRF (8 layers, 1024 units), mitigating the computational cost. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the two MLPs and the intermediate histograms for the batch. The batch size of 2^{14} rays requires significant memory for ray data and intermediate tensors. Measured Performance: The method was evaluated on 9 scenes (5 outdoors and 4 indoors) each containing a complex central object or area and a detailed background. It improves speed and rendering quality compared to prior strategies of learning one or multiple NeRFs that are all supervised using image reconstruction. Strengths: The use of Charbonnier loss achieves slightly more stable optimization than the mean squared error used in mip-NeRF. The stop-gradient on proposal loss ensures independent optimization of the proposal network. Limitations: The standard interlevel loss can lead to z-aliasing artifacts, particularly with high-capacity backends like iNGP. The method requires careful tuning of the learning rate schedule and gradient clipping. When to Use: Use this setup when training unbounded, anti-aliased radiance fields where optimization stability is critical. When Not to Use: Avoid if computational resources are extremely limited, as the multi-stage sampling increases forward pass count. Consider the Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss variant if z-aliasing is a major concern and an iNGP backend is used. The Mip-NeRF 360 optimization setup was introduced in the paper "Mip-NeRF 360: Unbounded Anti-Aliased Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the original Mip-NeRF method and addresses challenges in training on unbounded datasets. The method was designed to improve training stability and robustness without significantly changing accuracy or speed [Parent]. The issue of z-aliasing in proposal networks was further analyzed in "Zip-NeRF: Anti-Aliased Grid-Based Neural Radiance Fields", which proposed the Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss as a solution. name: Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss
head: Blurred NeRF Loss, Prefiltered Loss
body: The Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss is a proposal supervision loss function that measures the distance between a NeRF histogram and a proposal histogram by blurring the NeRF histogram into a piecewise-linear spline and resampling it into the proposal's interval endpoints. Unlike the piecewise constant loss used in mip-NeRF 360, which suffers from aliasing when NeRF histogram bins are narrow or translate relative to the proposal, this method produces a smooth loss surface that prevents aliasing artifacts during training. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: NeRF histogram endpoints \mathbf{s} = \{s0, \dots, sN\} and weights \mathbf{w} = \{w0, \dots, w{N-1}\}, where si are normalized distances in [0, 1] and wi are accumulated weights for interval [si, s{i+1}]. Proposal histogram endpoints \hat{\mathbf{s}} = \{\hat{s}0, \dots, \hat{s}M\} and weights \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \{\hat{w}0, \dots, \hat{w}{M-1}\}. Convolution radius r. Outputs: Scalar loss \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}. Resampled NeRF weights \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\mathbf{s}}. Parameters r: The radius of the rectangular pulse used for convolution. Other parameters are not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Normalize: Divide NeRF weights \mathbf{w} by the size of each interval in \mathbf{s} to yield a piecewise constant PDF that integrates to \le 1. 2. Convolve: Convolve the piecewise constant PDF with a rectangular pulse of radius r (integrating to 1) to obtain a piecewise linear PDF. This is implemented by turning each endpoint si into two signed delta functions at si - r and si + r with values proportional to the change between adjacent PDF heights, sorting them, and integrating twice. 3. Integrate to CDF: Integrate the piecewise linear PDF to produce a piecewise-quadratic CDF. 4. Resample: Query the piecewise-quadratic CDF via piecewise quadratic interpolation at each location in \hat{\mathbf{s}}. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate resampled NeRF weights \hat{w}i^{\mathbf{s}} by taking the difference between adjacent interpolated CDF values at the proposal endpoints. Evaluate the loss as an element-wise function of \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\mathbf{s}} and \hat{\mathbf{w}}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def antialiasedinterlevelloss(s, w, shat, what, r): """ Computes the anti-aliased interlevel loss. Args: s: NeRF histogram endpoints, shape (N+1,) w: NeRF histogram weights, shape (N,) shat: Proposal histogram endpoints, shape (M+1,) what: Proposal histogram weights, shape (M,) r: Convolution radius Returns: loss: Scalar loss value """ N = len(w) M = len(what) # Step 1: Normalize to piecewise constant PDF # h[i] is the height of the step function in interval i intervals = s[1:] - s[:-1] # Guard against zero-width intervals intervals = np.maximum(intervals, 1e-8) h = w / intervals # Step 2: Convolve with rectangular pulse using delta functions # Create delta functions at s[i] - r and s[i] + r # The value is proportional to the change in h, scaled by 1/(2r) deltas = [] # At s[0], change is h[0] - 0 deltas.append((s[0] - r, h[0] / (2 r))) deltas.append((s[0] + r, -h[0] / (2 r))) # Internal boundaries for i in range(1, N): deltaval = (h[i] - h[i-1]) / (2 r) deltas.append((s[i] - r, deltaval)) deltas.append((s[i] + r, -deltaval)) # At s[N], change is 0 - h[N-1] deltas.append((s[N] - r, -h[N-1] / (2 r))) deltas.append((s[N] + r, h[N-1] / (2 r))) # Sort deltas by position deltas.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Step 3 & 4: Integrate twice to get CDF values at shat # Double integration of a delta at pos with value v yields v max(0, x - pos) # This computes the piecewise-quadratic CDF values at proposal endpoints cdfvalues = np.zeros(M + 1) for j in range(M + 1): x = shat[j] cdfval = 0.0 for pos, val in deltas: if pos <= x: cdfval += val (x - pos) cdfvalues[j] = cdfval # Step 5: Compute resampled weights # whats[i] = CDF(shat[i+1]) - CDF(shat[i]) whats = cdfvalues[1:] - cdfvalues[:-1] # Step 6: Evaluate loss # Lprop = sumi (1 / whati) max(0, stopgrad(whatsi) - whati)^2 # stopgrad is applied conceptually; gradients flow through whats to the NeRF, # but not to the proposal network diff = np.maximum(0, whats - what) # Guard against division by zero in what whatsafe = np.maximum(what, 1e-8) loss = np.sum(diff2 / whatsafe) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Narrow Bins: Rasterizing the step function and performing convolution fails in the common case of extremely narrow histogram bins, necessitating the delta-function integration algorithm. Zero-Width Intervals: If s{i+1} - si = 0, the normalization step involves division by zero, so a small epsilon is added to the interval size. Zero Proposal Weights: If \hat{w}i = 0, the loss term involves division by zero, so a small epsilon is added to the proposal weights in the denominator. Strengths: Produces a smooth loss surface that is robust to aliasing when NeRF histogram bins are narrow or translate relative to the proposal. Limitations: More computationally expensive than the piecewise constant loss used in mip-NeRF 360 due to the convolution and resampling steps. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss was introduced in the Zip-NeRF paper. It builds on the proposal supervision approach from mip-NeRF 360. The key innovation is the use of a blurred, piecewise-linear representation of the NeRF histogram to enable smooth gradient flow during training, addressing the aliasing issues inherent in the piecewise constant comparison used in mip-NeRF 360. name: Isotropic Gaussian Scale Contraction
head: Isotropic scale contraction, Jacobian-based isotropic scale estimation
body: Isotropic Gaussian Scale Contraction is a technique for efficiently adapting the scale of isotropic Gaussians when a scene contraction function C(\mathbf{x}) is applied. It solves the problem of maintaining correct anti-aliasing properties in contracted coordinate spaces without the computational overhead of general multivariate Gaussian transformations. It sets itself apart from the standard mip-NeRF 360 approach by linearizing the contraction around each Gaussian center to derive an isotropic scale from the Jacobian determinant, rather than contracting a full covariance matrix. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of isotropic Gaussians defined by their means \mathbf{x}j and scales \sigmaj, and a scene contraction function C: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3. Output: The contracted means \mathbf{x}'j = C(\mathbf{x}j) and the contracted isotropic scales \sigma'j. Data Structures The method operates on scalar values for scale and 3D vectors for position. No complex covariance matrices are stored or manipulated. Steps 1. Contract Means: Evaluate the contraction function at the original Gaussian center: \mathbf{x}'j = C(\mathbf{x}j) 2. Compute Jacobian Determinant Factor: Calculate the scaling factor derived from the determinant of the Jacobian of the contraction function JC(\mathbf{x}j). For the specific contraction function used in Zip-NeRF, this factor has a closed-form solution: \text{scale\factor}j = \left| \det(JC(\mathbf{x}j)) \right|^{1/3} = \left( \frac{\sqrt[3]{2 \max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|) - 1}}{\max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|)} \right)^2 Here, \|\mathbf{x}j\| is the Euclidean norm of the original mean \mathbf{x}j. 3. Update Scale: Multiply the original isotropic scale \sigmaj by the computed factor: \sigma'j = \sigmaj \times \text{scale\factor}j Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def isotropicgaussianscalecontraction(means: np.ndarray, scales: np.ndarray) -> tuple: """ Contracts isotropic Gaussians using the Zip-NeRF specific closed-form Jacobian determinant. Args: means: Array of shape (N, 3) containing Gaussian centers xj. scales: Array of shape (N,) containing isotropic scales sigmaj. Returns: contractedmeans: Array of shape (N, 3) containing C(xj). contractedscales: Array of shape (N,) containing sigma'j. """ # Step 1: Contract means # Note: The specific definition of C(x) is required here. # In Zip-NeRF, C(x) typically involves a radial contraction. # Assuming C(x) is defined elsewhere or passed in, we evaluate it. # For the scale factor derivation, we only need the norm of the original mean. norms = np.linalg.norm(means, axis=1) # Step 2: Compute the closed-form scale factor from the Jacobian determinant # Formula: ( cbrt(2 max(1, norm) - 1) / max(1, norm))^2 maxnorm = np.maximum(1.0, norms) numerator = np.cbrt(2.0 maxnorm - 1.0) scalefactor = (numerator / maxnorm) 2 # Step 3: Update scales contractedscales = scales scalefactor # Return contracted means (requires evaluating C(xj)) and new scales # C(x) implementation depends on the specific scene contraction used. # A common contraction maps x to x / max(1, ||x||) or similar. # Here we assume a helper function contractpoint exists. contractedmeans = np.array([contractpoint(m) for m in means]) return contractedmeans, contractedscales def contractpoint(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Placeholder for the specific scene contraction function C(x). The scale factor formula provided in sources is specific to the contraction used in Zip-NeRF. The mean contraction must be consistent with the Jacobian derivation. """ # Example contraction logic (must match the Jacobian source): # This is a generic placeholder; the actual C(x) must be implemented # based on the specific Zip-NeRF contraction definition. # The scale factor formula implies a specific radial behavior. pass Parameters \|\mathbf{x}j\|: Euclidean norm of the Gaussian mean. \max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|): Ensures stability for points near the origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Origin Singularity: The formula uses \max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|) in the denominator. If \|\mathbf{x}j\| < 1, the denominator is 1, avoiding division by zero. The numerator becomes \sqrt[3]{2(1)-1} = 1, so the scale factor is 1^2/1^2 = 1. This implies no scale change for points within the unit sphere, which is consistent with many contraction functions that leave the central region uncontracted. Naive Multivariate Approach: Contracting the scale by treating the Gaussian as a full multivariate Gaussian with covariance \sigma^2 I and then identifying the isotropic Gaussian with the same generalized variance is significantly more expensive. This method avoids that by using the linearized Jacobian approximation. Time and Memory Complexity The method is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. It requires only vector norm calculations and scalar multiplications, making it significantly less computationally expensive than the multivariate Gaussian contraction approach used in mip-NeRF 360. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: High computational efficiency; avoids matrix operations; closed-form solution for the specific Zip-NeRF contraction. Limitations: It is an approximation based on linearization. It assumes the contraction function is locally linear around \mathbf{x}j. For very large Gaussians or highly non-linear contractions, this approximation may introduce errors. It is specific to isotropic Gaussians. When to Use Use this method when rendering with isotropic Gaussians in a scene that has been contracted (e.g., for distant scene content allocation) and computational efficiency is a priority. It is particularly suitable for Zip-NeRF and similar architectures that use multisampled isotropic Gaussians. This technique was introduced in Zip-NeRF. It was developed to address the need for efficient anti-aliasing in neural radiance fields that use scene contraction to allocate model capacity proportional to disparity. The method improves upon the mip-NeRF 360 approach by reducing the computational cost of scale contraction while maintaining the necessary anti-aliasing properties.
