name: DONeRF
head: DONeRF Training Setup, Depth Oracle Network Training
body: DONeRF training configuration defines the optimization procedure for the two-stage neural network architecture (depth oracle and shading networks) that enables real-time rendering with very few samples per ray. It solves the problem of high-frequency detail loss and slow convergence in standard NeRF by decoupling depth estimation from color/shading prediction. Unlike standard NeRF which samples uniformly or via hierarchical sampling along the entire ray, DONeRF uses a depth oracle to predict a probability distribution over discretized depth ranges, allowing the shading network to focus computational budget on the surface. It differs from NeRF Hyperparameters by enforcing a strict two-phase training schedule and specific opacity regularization to prevent dark pixel artifacts at low sample counts. The method consists of two distinct training phases: training the Depth Oracle Network and training the Shading Network. The configuration assumes the presence of ground truth depth maps; if unavailable, a dense NeRF is trained first to generate pseudo-ground truth (see DONeRF Oracle Input Construction). Inputs: Camera poses, image pixels (RGB), and optionally ground truth depth maps. Outputs: RGB color values for novel views. Both the Depth Oracle Network and the Shading Network share the same architecture: Layers: 8 hidden layers. Hidden Units: 256 units per layer. Activation: Not specified in sources [G: Standard ReLU is implied for MLPs of this era, but not explicitly stated]. Depth Oracle Network: Input: 3D positions along the ray (see DONeRF Oracle Input Construction). Output: Probability distribution over discretized depth bins (classification). Shading Network: Input: 3D positions warped towards the view cell, features from the depth oracle. Output: RGB color and opacity (\delta) for each sample. The training is performed in two sequential stages, each lasting 300,000 iterations. 1. Phase 1: Depth Oracle Training Train the Depth Oracle Network for 300,000 iterations. Loss: Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) on the depth classification targets. Note: If ground truth depth is missing, a dense NeRF (12 layers, 512 hidden units, 128 samples/ray) is trained first to extract depth maps, which are then used as ground truth for this phase. 2. Phase 2: Shading Network Training Freeze the Depth Oracle Network. Train the Shading Network for 300,000 iterations using the oracle's predictions to guide sampling. Loss: Weighted sum of MSE and Opacity Loss (see Formulas). Optimizer: Adam [KB15]. Learning Rate: 0.0005. Batch Size: 4096 samples per iteration. Final Configuration Parameters: Neighborhood Filter Size (K): 5. Depth Smoothing Filter Size (Z): 5. Number of Oracle Inputs (I): 128. Samples per Ray (N): Variable (DONeRF-2, DONeRF-4, etc.). Opacity Loss (\text{loss}O): This term prevents "cheating" where the network mixes background color via opacity to satisfy RGB loss, causing dark pixels. It forces accumulated opacity to be at least 1. \text{loss}O = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } \sum{i=1}^X \deltai \geq 1 \\ \left( \left( \sum{i=1}^X \deltai \right) - 1 \right)^2, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where: X is the number of samples per ray. \deltai is the opacity of the i-th sample. Total Loss: \text{loss} = \alpha \cdot \text{loss}{\text{MSE}} + \beta \cdot \text{loss}{\text{O}} Where: \text{loss}{\text{MSE}} is the Mean Squared Error between predicted and ground truth RGB. \alpha = 1.0. \beta = 10.0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. NUMITERATIONS = 300000 LEARNINGRATE = 0.0005 BATCHSIZE = 4096 ALPHA = 1.0 BETA = 10.0 NUMHIDDENLAYERS = 8 HIDDENUNITS = 256 NUMSAMPLESRAY = 4 # Example for DONeRF-4 oraclenet = MLP(layers=NUMHIDDENLAYERS, units=HIDDENUNITS) optimizeroracle = Adam(oraclenet.parameters(), lr=LEARNINGRATE) for iteration in range(NUMITERATIONS): # Sample rays and get 3D positions (log-transformed, centered in depth bins) rays, positions = samplerays(batchsize=BATCHSIZE) # Get oracle predictions (probability distribution over depth bins) oraclepreds = oraclenet(positions) # Calculate BCE loss against ground truth depth bins lossoracle = BCELoss(oraclepreds, groundtruthdepthbins) optimizeroracle.zerograd() lossoracle.backward() optimizeroracle.step() shadingnet = MLP(layers=NUMHIDDENLAYERS, units=HIDDENUNITS) optimizershading = Adam(shadingnet.parameters(), lr=LEARNINGRATE) for iteration in range(NUMITERATIONS): # Sample rays rays, positions = samplerays(batchsize=BATCHSIZE) # Get depth distribution from frozen oracle depthdist = oraclenet(positions) # Warp positions and generate features (Space Warping) warpedpositions, features = warpandgeneratefeatures(positions, rays) # Get shading predictions (RGB and Opacity) rgbpred, opacitypred = shadingnet(warpedpositions, features) # Calculate MSE Loss lossmse = MSELoss(rgbpred, groundtruthrgb) # Calculate Opacity Loss accumulatedopacity = sum(opacitypred) if accumulatedopacity < 1.0: lossopacity = (accumulatedopacity - 1.0) 2 else: lossopacity = 0.0 # Total Loss loss = ALPHA lossmse + BETA lossopacity optimizershading.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizershading.step() The depth oracle network requires specific input construction to effectively guide the shading network. Inputs: 3D positions along the ray are provided as additional inputs to the first network layer. Positioning: These positions are placed at the centers of the discretized depth ranges. Transformation: A logarithmic transformation is applied to the classification steps (depth ranges) to align with the shading network's logarithmic sampling strategy. Encoding: Positional or Fourier encoding is not used for depth oracle inputs, as experiments showed it did not improve results. Parameter (I): The number of 3D input positions provided to the oracle. Tested values are 1 to 128. The final configuration uses I=128. Impact: Providing multiple samples along the ray as input adds approximately 1 dB to PSNR. Using a classification network (oracle) instead of predicting a single depth value adds 0.6 dB–1.5 dB to PSNR. Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 3090 at 800x800 resolution with 2 samples per ray, total inference time is 51.3 ms (~20 fps). Breakdown: Ray unification/feature gen (0.21 ms), Oracle network (12.64 ms), Space warping/second feature gen (3.46 ms), Shading network (34.9 ms), Final color gen (0.09 ms). Scaling: Shading network cost scales nearly linearly with the number of samples: 34.9 ms (2 samples), 65.4 ms (4 samples), 136.4 ms (8 samples), 270.4 ms (16 samples). Quality vs. NeRF: DONeRF achieves equal or better quality with 2–4 samples per ray compared to NeRF's 256. At 16 samples, DONeRF is up to 7 dB higher PSNR and 15–78x faster than NeRF. Quality vs. NSVF: NSVF-medium/large are similar in quality to DONeRF-2/4 but are 43x slower. NSVF requires 2x more memory for competitive quality and 6x longer training. Quality vs. LLFF: LLFF uses >1000x more memory and achieves lower quality. LLFF is faster for novel view generation due to simple blending but lacks neural representation capabilities. Quality vs. NeX: NeX is 45x faster but requires 25x more memory and is 3 dB lower quality than DONeRF-2. NeX-MLP is better quality but DONeRF is 10x faster and 25x more compact. Limitations: Reflective/Transparent Surfaces: Low sample counts and single depth estimates are insufficient for mirrors or refractive water. Dark Pixel Artifacts: Occur at low sample counts if opacity does not accumulate to 1. Remedied by the opacity loss term. No-GT Training: Without ground truth depth, background noise from the initialization NeRF can create high-frequency depth values in empty space, leading to zero-contribution samples. DONeRF was introduced in the paper "DONeRF: Towards Real‐Time Rendering of Compact Neural Radiance Fields using Depth Oracle Networks". The method addresses the computational bottleneck of standard NeRF by using a depth oracle to concentrate samples on surfaces. It builds on the concept of differentiable volume rendering but introduces a specialized training configuration involving a two-stage network and specific regularization to enable real-time performance on consumer hardware. DONeRF: Towards Real‐Time Rendering of Compact Neural Radiance Fields using Depth Oracle Networks, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14340, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors
head: Intrinsic Priors, Mean Reflectance Regularization, Shading Smoothness
body: Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors enforce physical plausibility on the learned radiance field by decoupling material properties (reflectance) from illumination effects (shading). This method solves the ambiguity inherent in intrinsic image decomposition, where scaling reflectance and inversely scaling shading produces identical observed colors, by applying regularization constraints that stabilize the separation. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by explicitly optimizing for intrinsic image components rather than just photometric reconstruction, enabling consistent object insertion and relighting. The method extends the standard NeRF training loop by introducing additional loss terms that constrain the reflectance \mathbf{R} and shading \mathbf{S} components of the predicted color. The total color \mathbf{C} is typically modeled as the product of reflectance and shading: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \odot \mathbf{S}, where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. Inputs: Camera poses, ray origins, ray directions, ground truth pixel colors, and the current state of the neural network parameters. Outputs: Updated neural network weights, decomposed reflectance \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{x}) and shading \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{x}) fields for any 3D point \mathbf{x}. The neural network outputs two additional channels or separate heads for each sampled point along a ray: 1. Reflectance \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{x}): A 3-dimensional vector (RGB) representing the intrinsic material color. 2. Shading \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{x}): A 3-dimensional vector (RGB) representing the illumination at that point. The total training loss \mathcal{L}{train} is a weighted sum of the photometric reconstruction loss and the intrinsic priors: \mathcal{L}{train} = \lambda0 \mathcal{L} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}d + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{mean,r} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{chro} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{rs} + \lambda5 \mathcal{L}{nrs} + \lambda6 \mathcal{L}s + \lambda7 \mathcal{L}{sn} Where: \mathcal{L} is the standard photometric loss (e.g., L1 or L2 between rendered and ground truth colors). \mathcal{L}d is a depth loss (if available). \lambdai are adjustable hyperparameters. The specific priors defined in the source are: 1. Mean Reflectance Regularization (\mathcal{L}{mean,r}): Constrains the maximum reflectance value across RGB channels to a target average brightness \beta{avg,r} to prevent unreasonable brightness scaling. \mathcal{L}{mean,r} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left| (\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}).max) - \beta{avg,r} \right| Here, \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}).max = \max(Rr, Rg, Rb) for the reflectance vector at ray \mathbf{r}, and \beta{avg,r} is a hyperparameter typically set to 0.6. 2. Shading Smoothness (\mathcal{L}s): Defined as the variance of shading values for all pixels in a single batch, encouraging spatially smooth illumination. \mathcal{L}s = \text{Var}(\{\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{x}) \mid \mathbf{x} \in \text{Batch}\}) Note: The exact mathematical formulation of the variance over the batch is not explicitly expanded in the source, but it is described as the variance of shading for all pixels in a single batch. 3. Shading-Normal Consistency (\mathcal{L}{sn}): Enforces consistency between shading and surface normals by penalizing large shading differences between nearby points with similar orientations. \mathcal{L}{sn} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \omegan(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') \cdot |\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}')| \cdot (1 - \tanh(\text{Dis}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'))) Where: \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}' are rays or sampling points. \omegan(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') measures the cosine similarity of the surface normals at \mathbf{r} and \mathbf{r}'. \text{Dis}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') is the Euclidean distance between the 3D points associated with \mathbf{r} and \mathbf{r}'. 4. Other Priors (Mentioned but not detailed in formulas): The source lists \mathcal{L}{chro} (reflectance chromaticities), \mathcal{L}{rs} (sparsity), and \mathcal{L}{nrs} (non-local sparsity) as common intrinsic image decomposition constraints used in the optimization, but does not provide their explicit mathematical definitions in the provided text. The following pseudocode illustrates the integration of these priors into a standard NeRF training step. It assumes a standard NeRF backbone that outputs color, density, and now reflectance and shading. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeintrinsicpriorsloss(renderedcolor, gtcolor, reflectancefield, shadingfield, normalfield, batchsize, betaavgr, lambdas): """ Computes the total loss including Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors. Args: renderedcolor: Tensor of shape (batchsize, 3), predicted RGB color. gtcolor: Tensor of shape (batchsize, 3), ground truth RGB color. reflectancefield: Tensor of shape (batchsize, 3), predicted reflectance R. shadingfield: Tensor of shape (batchsize, 3), predicted shading S. normalfield: Tensor of shape (batchsize, 3), predicted surface normals N. batchsize: Integer, number of samples in the batch. betaavgr: Float, target average max reflectance (default 0.6). lambdas: Dict of hyperparameters lambda0 to lambda7. Returns: totalloss: Scalar tensor. """ # 1. Standard Photometric Loss (L) # Assuming L1 loss as common in NeRF variants, though not explicitly defined in source lossphotometric = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedcolor - gtcolor)) # 2. Mean Reflectance Regularization (Lmean,r) # R(r).max is the max value across RGB channels for each sample maxreflectance = torch.max(reflectancefield, dim=1, keepdim=True)[0] lossmeanr = torch.mean(torch.abs(maxreflectance - betaavgr)) # 3. Shading Smoothness (Ls) # Variance of shading for all pixels in the batch # Variance is computed over the batch dimension for each channel, then averaged shadingvariance = torch.var(shadingfield, dim=0) lossshadingsmooth = torch.mean(shadingvariance) # 4. Shading-Normal Consistency (Lsn) # This requires pairwise comparisons or a local neighborhood. # The source formula sums over rays r, implying a comparison with neighbors r'. # In practice, this is often approximated using adjacent samples or a local grid. # Since the source does not specify the neighbor selection strategy, # we note this as a complex term requiring implementation details not in source. # Placeholder for Lsn calculation based on source formula (5): # lossshadingnormal = computesnloss(shadingfield, normalfield) # Implementation note: Typically involves computing cosine similarity of normals # and distance between 3D points for neighboring samples. lossshadingnormal = 0.0 # Placeholder: Not fully specified in source # 5. Other Priors (Lchro, Lrs, Lnrs) # Source mentions these but does not provide formulas. losschro = 0.0 # Placeholder lossrs = 0.0 # Placeholder lossnrs = 0.0 # Placeholder # 6. Depth Loss (Ld) # Placeholder if depth supervision is used lossdepth = 0.0 # Placeholder # 7. Total Loss totalloss = ( lambdas['lambda0'] lossphotometric + lambdas['lambda1'] lossdepth + lambdas['lambda2'] lossmeanr + lambdas['lambda3'] losschro + lambdas['lambda4'] lossrs + lambdas['lambda5'] lossnrs + lambdas['lambda6'] lossshadingsmooth + lambdas['lambda7'] lossshadingnormal) return totalloss \beta{avg,r}: Set to 0.6 for most scenes. Scale Ambiguity: A critical pitfall is the scale ambiguity between shading and reflectance. Scaling reflectance by k and shading by 1/k yields the same observed color. The Mean Reflectance Regularization helps mitigate unreasonable brightness changes but does not fully resolve the ambiguity without additional constraints or normalization. Sampling Density: The source notes that sparse sampling on objects can lead to missing details, which may affect the accuracy of the shading and normal consistency terms. Complexity: Adds computational overhead due to the calculation of variance and pairwise normal/shading consistency terms. The shading-normal consistency term \mathcal{L}{sn} is particularly expensive as it involves pairwise comparisons or local neighborhood searches. Performance: The regularization is described as "crucial, particularly for complex scenes," reducing noise in normal maps and improving the smoothness of intrinsic components. Use Case: Best suited for applications requiring object insertion, relighting, or physically plausible material decomposition. Not necessary for standard novel view synthesis where only photometric accuracy matters. This method originates from the work on "Relighting Scenes With Object Insertions in Neural Radiance Fields". It adapts traditional intrinsic image decomposition constraints (chromaticity, sparsity, non-local sparsity) to the NeRF backbone to enable the separation of scene and object intrinsic properties for compositing. Relighting Scenes With Object Insertions in Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/TCSVT.2025.3535599, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Dynamic Growth Parameters
head: NeRF Growth Steps, Recursive NeRF Growth
body: Dynamic Growth Parameters is an adaptive training strategy for Neural Radiance Fields that expands network capacity based on local scene complexity and prediction uncertainty. Unlike static architectures, it clusters high-uncertainty query points and grows parallel network branches to refine predictions in those regions, enabling coarse-to-fine representation without pre-defining the entire hierarchy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D query points X, their associated 2D image coordinates, viewing directions d, and ground-truth colors. Output: A recursively structured neural field with multiple branches, where each branch predicts color ci, density \sigmai, uncertainty \deltai, and a latent vector yi. Data Structures: Network Branch: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) taking parent output y{pi} and direction d as input. Cluster Centers: k centroids derived from k-means clustering of high-uncertainty points. Growth State: Tracks the current recursion depth and the set of active branches. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initial Training: Train a base NeRF branch for I1 iterations. 2. Uncertainty Estimation: Compute uncertainty \deltai for all sampled points xi using the current network. 3. Clustering: Identify points where \deltai > \tau (threshold). Apply k-means clustering with k \in [2, 4] to these points, yielding k cluster centers. 4. Network Growth: Instantiate k new child branches. Each child branch is initialized to predict residuals or refined features for its respective cluster. 5. Recursive Training: Jointly train the parent and new child branches. Points are routed to the child branch corresponding to their cluster center. 6. Early Termination: During rendering, if uncertainty \deltai is below a threshold, terminate recursion and use the current branch's output; otherwise, pass the latent vector yi to the appropriate child branch. 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–6. The total number of growth steps is limited to 3 by default. Parameters: k: Number of branches per growth step. Default: k=2. Total Growth Steps: Maximum 3. Threshold \tau: Uncertainty threshold for clustering. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamicgrowthtraining(points, directions, groundtruthcolors, maxsteps=3, k=2): # Initialize base branch branch = initializeneuralfield() for step in range(maxsteps): # 1. Train current branches branch.train(points, directions, groundtruthcolors) # 2. Estimate uncertainty for all points uncertainties = branch.predictuncertainty(points) # 3. Identify high-uncertainty points highuncertaintymask = uncertainties > THRESHOLD highuncertaintypoints = points[highuncertaintymask] if len(highuncertaintypoints) == 0: break # 4. Cluster high-uncertainty points # k-means with k clusters clustercenters = kmeans(highuncertaintypoints, k=k) # 5. Grow new branches newbranches = [] for center in clustercenters: # Initialize child branch child = initializechildbranch(parent=branch, center=center) newbranches.append(child) # 6. Assign points to branches for next iteration # Points are assigned to the branch whose center is closest assignments = assignpointstoclusters(highuncertaintypoints, clustercenters) # Update branch structure branch.children = newbranches branch.assignments = assignments return branch An adaptive strategy that clusters uncertain queries at the current stage and grows deeper networks according to the clustering result. After I1 iterations, points with uncertainty higher than a threshold are clustered using k-means with k \in [2, 4]. The network grows k branches according to the cluster centers. Time Complexity: Increases with each growth step due to additional network branches and clustering overhead. Total steps are capped at 3. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of branches. Each growth step adds k new sets of weights. Strengths: Efficiently allocates capacity to complex regions; early termination speeds up rendering. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of uncertainty thresholds and clustering parameters; training can be unstable if uncertainty estimates are noisy. When to Use: Scenes with varying levels of detail where uniform resolution is inefficient. When Not to Use: Simple scenes with uniform detail; real-time applications requiring fixed latency. Originated in Recursive-NeRF, published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics in 2022. The method addresses the inefficiency of static NeRF architectures by dynamically expanding network depth based on learned uncertainty, allowing for coarse-to-fine scene representation without manual hierarchy design. Recursive-NeRF: An Efficient and Dynamically Growing NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2022.3204608, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mip-NeRF 360
head: Unbounded Anti-Aliased Neural Radiance Fields
body: Mip-NeRF 360 is a method for synthesizing photorealistic views of unbounded, real-world scenes where the camera may rotate 360 degrees and content exists at arbitrary distances. It solves the problems of aliasing, training inefficiency, and geometric ambiguity inherent in standard NeRF and mip-NeRF when applied to large-scale environments. It sets itself apart from its parent NeRF Training Loop and sibling Mip-NeRF 360 Sampling and Training by introducing a non-linear scene parameterization, an online distillation training scheme using a proposal network, and a distortion-based regularizer. Inputs: A set of calibrated images with known camera poses and intrinsics. Outputs: A trained NeRF MLP (\Theta{\text{NeRF}}) and a proposal MLP (\Theta{\text{Prop}}) that can render images for new camera poses. Data Structures: 1. NeRF MLP: A coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron parameterized by \Theta{\text{NeRF}}. It takes integrated positional encodings of 3D coordinates and view direction as input. It outputs volumetric density \tau and color \mathbf{c}. 2. Proposal MLP: A smaller coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron parameterized by \Theta{\text{Prop}}. It takes the same inputs as the NeRF MLP but outputs only volumetric density \tau. It does not predict color. 3. Ray Representation: Rays are represented as conical frustums defined by mean position \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}. Non-linear Scene Parameterization: To handle unbounded scenes, 3D scene coordinates are mapped to a bounded domain using a non-linear parameterization. This allocates more MLP capacity to nearby content and less to distant content, addressing the unbalanced detail and scale of objects. The specific parameterization function is not detailed in the sources, but it is applied to the ray's mean and covariance before encoding. Integrated Positional Encoding: Instead of encoding infinitesimal points, mip-NeRF 360 encodes the conical frustum defined by the interval Ti. The mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} of the frustum are featurized using integrated positional encoding: \gamma(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} \left[ \sin(2^\ell \boldsymbol{\mu}) \exp\left(-2^{2\ell-1} \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\right) \right] \\ \left[ \cos(2^\ell \boldsymbol{\mu}) \exp\left(-2^{2\ell-1} \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\right) \right] \end{bmatrix} \right\}{\ell=0}^{L-1} where \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} are the mean and covariance of the conical frustum, and L is the number of frequency bands. This is the expectation of the standard NeRF positional encodings with respect to a Gaussian approximating the conical frustum. MLP Forward Pass: For each interval Ti along the ray, the NeRF MLP computes density and color: (Ti, \mathbf{c}i) = \text{MLP}(\gamma(\mathbf{r}(Ti)); \Theta{\text{NeRF}}) where \mathbf{r}(Ti) represents the parameterized ray segment, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and the view direction is also provided as input (omitted for simplicity). Volume Rendering: The final pixel color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) is approximated using numerical quadrature: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) = \sum wi \mathbf{c}i The alpha compositing weights wi are calculated as: wi = \left(1 - e^{-\taui(t{i+1}-ti)}\right)e^{-\sum{i'} \tau{i'}(t{i'+1}-t{i'})} where \taui is the density at interval i, ti and t{i+1} are the interval boundaries, and the sum is over all intervals i'. The weights w are guaranteed to sum to less than or equal to 1. Sampling Strategy: 1. Coarse Sampling: The ray is sampled using evenly-spaced "coarse" distances \mathbf{t}^c. During training, these are stochastic samples from a uniform distribution spanning the camera's near and far planes [tn, tf]: t^c \sim \mathcal{U}[tn, tf], \quad \mathbf{t}^c = \text{sort}(\{t^c\}) During evaluation, samples are evenly spaced. 2. Fine Sampling: After the NeRF MLP generates coarse weights \mathbf{w}^c, "fine" distances \mathbf{t}^f are sampled from the histogram defined by \mathbf{t}^c and \mathbf{w}^c using inverse transform sampling: t^f \sim \text{hist}(\mathbf{t}^c, \mathbf{w}^c), \quad \mathbf{t}^f = \text{sort}(\{t^f\}) This concentrates samples around scene content, improving efficiency. Online Distillation Training: Two MLPs are trained simultaneously: a proposal MLP and a NeRF MLP. 1. The proposal MLP predicts density only. 2. The NeRF MLP predicts density and color. 3. The proposal MLP is used to resample new intervals for the NeRF MLP. 4. Crucially, the proposal MLP weights are not supervised by image reconstruction loss. Instead, they are supervised using the histogram weights generated by the NeRF MLP. This "online distillation" allows the use of a large NeRF MLP evaluated few times, alongside a small proposal MLP evaluated many times. Distortion Regularizer: A distortion-based regularizer is applied to address ambiguity in unbounded scenes. It is designed to work with the continuous weights defined along each mip-NeRF ray, unlike point-based regularizers. Training Loss: The model is optimized via gradient descent to minimize a weighted combination of coarse and fine reconstruction losses: \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{1}{10} \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^c), \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r})) + \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^f), \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r})) where \mathcal{R} is the set of training rays, \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth color, and \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} is mean squared error. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def mipnerf360trainingloop(images, poses, intrinsics, numiterations=25000): """ Trains Mip-NeRF 360 model. """ # Initialize MLPs # ThetaNeRF: Large MLP for density and color # ThetaProp: Small MLP for density only thetanerf = initializemlplarge() thetaprop = initializemlpsmall() # Optimizer setup (Adam) optimizer = Adam([thetanerf, thetaprop], lr=1e-2, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.99, eps=1e-15) # Learning rate warm-up and decay parameters warmupiterations = 5000 maxlr = 1e-2 minlr = 1e-3 for iteration in range(1, numiterations + 1): # 1. Learning Rate Schedule if iteration <= warmupiterations: # Cosine decay from 1e-8 to 1 for warmup multiplier warmupmult = cosinedecay(iteration / warmupiterations, start=1e-8, end=1.0) currentlr = maxlr warmupmult else: # Logarithmic decay from 1e-2 to 1e-3 currentlr = logdecay(iteration, startlr=maxlr, endlr=minlr, totaliters=numiterations) optimizer.setlr(currentlr) # 2. Sample Batch of Rays rays = sampleraysfromimages(images, poses, intrinsics, batchsize=216) # 3. Coarse Sampling # Uniform sampling between near and far planes tcoarse = uniformsample(rays.near, rays.far, numsamplescoarse) tcoarse = sort(tcoarse) # 4. Proposal Network Forward Pass (Density Only) # Apply non-linear scene parameterization to ray coordinates paramscoarse = applysceneparameterization(rays, tcoarse) # Integrated positional encoding featurescoarse = integratedposencoding(paramscoarse.mean, paramscoarse.cov) # Proposal MLP predicts density tauprop = thetaprop(featurescoarse) # 5. Resampling for Fine Pass # Compute coarse weights from proposal density (assuming no color for proposal) # Note: The source says proposal is used to resample. # Standard volume rendering weights require density. # We assume a simple opacity calculation for resampling weights alphaprop = 1 - exp(-tauprop (tcoarse[1:] - tcoarse[:-1])) # Normalize or use as histogram for inverse transform sampling weightsprop = computecompositingweights(alphaprop) # Sample fine distances from histogram defined by tcoarse and weightsprop tfine = histogramsample(tcoarse, weightsprop, numsamplesfine) tfine = sort(tfine) # 6. NeRF Network Forward Pass (Density and Color) paramsfine = applysceneparameterization(rays, tfine) featuresfine = integratedposencoding(paramsfine.mean, paramsfine.cov) # NeRF MLP predicts density and color taunerf, colornerf = thetanerf(featuresfine) # 7. Volume Rendering (Fine) # Compute weights using NeRF density alphanerf = 1 - exp(-taunerf (tfine[1:] - tfine[:-1])) weightsnerf = computecompositingweights(alphanerf) colorrenderedfine = sum(weightsnerf colornerf) # 8. Volume Rendering (Coarse) - for supervision of proposal # Compute weights using proposal density alphaproprender = 1 - exp(-tauprop (tcoarse[1:] - tcoarse[:-1])) weightsproprender = computecompositingweights(alphaproprender) # Note: Proposal does not output color, so we might not render color from it directly # But we need the weights for distillation # 9. Compute Losses # Ground truth colors for the sampled rays gtcolors = getgtcolors(rays) # Reconstruction Loss for Fine Pass lossreconfine = meansquarederror(colorrenderedfine, gtcolors) # Reconstruction Loss for Coarse Pass (supervising NeRF coarse output if needed, # but source emphasizes fine loss and proposal distillation) # Source eq 7 includes coarse recon loss for NeRF. # We need to run NeRF on coarse intervals too or assume NeRF is evaluated on coarse tcoarse paramscoarsenerf = applysceneparameterization(rays, tcoarse) featurescoarsenerf = integratedposencoding(paramscoarsenerf.mean, paramscoarsenerf.cov) taunerfcoarse, colornerfcoarse = thetanerf(featurescoarsenerf) alphanerfcoarse = 1 - exp(-taunerfcoarse (tcoarse[1:] - tcoarse[:-1])) weightsnerfcoarse = computecompositingweights(alphanerfcoarse) colorrenderedcoarse = sum(weightsnerfcoarse colornerfcoarse) lossreconcoarse = meansquarederror(colorrenderedcoarse, gtcolors) # Total Reconstruction Loss lossrecon = 0.1 lossreconcoarse + lossreconfine # Distortion Loss (Regularizer) # Applied to NeRF weights/densities along the ray lossdistortion = computedistortionloss(tfine, weightsnerf, taunerf) # Online Distillation Loss # Supervise proposal MLP weights using histogram weights from NeRF # The source says: "supervised with the histogram weights generated by the NeRF MLP" # This implies matching the proposal's density distribution to the NeRF's weight distribution # A common implementation is MSE between proposal density (normalized) and NeRF weights # Or KL divergence. name: Zip-NeRF
head: Anti-Aliased Grid-Based Neural Radiance Fields
body: Zip-NeRF is a method that integrates scale-aware anti-aliased neural radiance fields with fast grid-based training to achieve lower error rates and faster convergence than prior techniques. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts in both spatial rendering and the loss function during online distillation, which are particularly prominent when rendering scenes across multiple scales or with sparse sampling. It sets itself apart from its parent Mip-NeRF 360 by replacing the large MLP with an Instant-NGP (iNGP) grid structure and introducing specific anti-aliasing mechanisms (multisampling, downweighting, and interlevel loss) to handle the high-frequency details of grid-based representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of posed images and a sparse initial point cloud (typically from COLMAP SfM). Output: A radiance field model capable of rendering anti-aliased images at various scales. Data Structures: Instant-NGP Structure (G\theta): A pyramid of voxel grids and hashes replacing the large MLP used in mip-NeRF 360. Feature Codes: Stored in the grids/hashes. Each level l has a resolution nl. Proposal Networks: Separate iNGP and MLP structures for each round of proposal sampling. NeRF MLP: Uses a larger view-dependent branch than the standard iNGP. Parameters: Sampling Budget: Two rounds of proposal sampling with 64 samples each, followed by 32 samples in the final NeRF sampling round. Anti-aliased Interlevel Loss Rectangular Pulse Width (r): r = 0.03 in the first proposal round; r = 0.003 in the second round. Anti-aliased Interlevel Loss Multiplier: 0.01. Normalized Weight Decay Multiplier: 0.1 (unless otherwise stated). Scale Factors: [1, 2, 4, 8] for multiscale dataset creation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Multiscale Dataset Creation: For each input image, generate four additional images by bicubically downsampling by scale factors s \in [1, 2, 4, 8]. These act as proxy training/test views with zoomed-out cameras. 2. Initialization: Initialize the scene representation using a set of 3D points \{vi\} from SfM and the Instant-NGP data structure G\theta. 3. Multiscale Training Loop: For each training iteration: a. Ray Sampling: Cast rays through the multiscale images. b. Downweighting: When querying the Instant-NGP grid at level l with resolution nl for a query with filter variance \sigma, apply the downweighting factor \phi(\sigma): \phi(\sigma) = \text{erf}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\sigma^2 nl^2}}\right) This convolves the output with a Gaussian, reducing the impact of higher-resolution features for larger queries. c. Multisampling: Use the anti-aliased multisampling strategy (hexagonal pattern or similar) to sample within the sub-frusta defined by mip-NeRF 360. d. Proposal Sampling: Perform two rounds of proposal sampling (64 samples each) using separate proposal iNGPs/MLPs. e. Final Sampling: Perform the final NeRF sampling round (32 samples). f. Loss Calculation: i. Data Term: Multiply the standard data term (reconstruction loss) by the scale factor s of the current ray/image. ii. Normalized Weight Decay: Calculate the loss \ell for feature codes in the pyramid: \ell = \text{mean}(Vl^2) where Vl is the set of grid/hash values at pyramid level l. Sum this mean across levels. This penalizes coarse scales more heavily than fine scales. Apply multiplier 0.1. iii. Anti-aliased Interlevel Loss: Impose the interlevel loss on both proposal rounds with pulse width r (0.03 for round 1, 0.003 for round 2) and multiplier 0.01. g. Optimization: Update parameters using JAX. 4. Evaluation: At test time, evaluate each scale factor s \in [1, 2, 4, 8] separately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Query Instant-NGP with downweighting # sigma is derived from the ray's cone size at the query point # nl is the resolution of grid level l def queryngpdownweighted(coord, sigma): value = 0 for l in range(numlevels): nl = gridresolution(l) rawval = Gtheta.query(coord, level=l) phi = erf(1.0 / sqrt(8 sigma2 nl2)) value += rawval phi return value # 2. Proposal Sampling Round 1 samples1 = proposalsample(Gprop1, ray, numsamples=64) # Apply anti-aliased interlevel loss with r=0.03 lossprop1 = computeinterlevelloss(samples1, r=0.03) # 3. Proposal Sampling Round 2 samples2 = proposalsample(Gprop2, ray, numsamples=64) # Apply anti-aliased interlevel loss with r=0.003 lossprop2 = computeinterlevelloss(samples2, r=0.003) # 4. Final NeRF Sampling samplesfinal = nerfsample(Mnerf, ray, numsamples=32) # 5. Compute Data Loss with scale weighting renderedcolor = render(samplesfinal, Mnerf) dataloss = meansquarederror(renderedcolor, imgs) scalefactor # 6. Compute Normalized Weight Decay weightdecayloss = 0 for l in range(numlevels): Vl = Gtheta.getvalues(level=l) weightdecayloss += mean(Vl2) weightdecayloss = 0.1 # 7. Total Loss totalloss = dataloss + \ 0.01 (lossprop1 + lossprop2) + \ weightdecayloss updateparameters(totalloss) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-aliasing: Disabling the anti-aliased interlevel loss causes z-aliasing artifacts in video results, though it may have little effect on single-image metrics. Sample Count: The baseline loss (without anti-aliasing) fails catastrophically if fewer than 16 samples are used, whereas the anti-aliased loss degrades gracefully. Weight Decay: Using non-normalized weight decay performs poorly; disabling it reduces accuracy significantly. View-Dependent Branch: Using iNGP’s small view-dependent MLP decreases accuracy; a larger branch is required. A querying scheme to mitigate aliasing where the output of instant-NGP is convolved with a Gaussian. It downweights higher resolution features for larger sized queries. The downweighting factor is \phi(\sigma) = \text{erf}\left(1/\sqrt{8\sigma^2 n\ell^2}\right), where \sigma is the filter variance and n\ell is the grid resolution of level \ell. This is combined with a regularizer that pulls all features towards 0 to reduce the impact of higher resolution features for larger sized queries. Time and Memory Complexity: Training Time: Zip-NeRF trains 24x faster than mip-NeRF 360 (0.89 hrs vs 21.69 hrs on the 360 dataset). It is ~6x slower to train than iNGP (0.89 hrs vs 0.15 hrs). Render Time: 0.9s per image, compared to 7.4s for mip-NeRF 360 and 0.2s for a naive mip-NeRF 360 + iNGP baseline. Measured Performance: 360 Dataset (Table 2): PSNR 28.54, SSIM 0.828, LPIPS 0.189. Outperforms mip-NeRF 360 (PSNR 27.57, SSIM 0.793, LPIPS 0.234) and iNGP (PSNR 25.68, SSIM 0.705, LPIPS 0.302). Multiscale 360 Dataset (Scale 1x): PSNR 28.25, SSIM 0.822, LPIPS 0.198. Multiscale 360 Dataset (Scale 8x): PSNR 32.52, SSIM 0.954, LPIPS 0.037. Error Reduction: 11% reduction in RMSE, 17% in DSSIM, 19% in LPIPS vs mip-NeRF 360 on the 360 dataset. 28% reduction in RMSE, 42% in DSSIM, 37% in LPIPS vs iNGP on the 360 dataset. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly faster training than mip-NeRF 360; superior image quality compared to iNGP; robust to low sample counts; handles multiscale generalization well. Limitations: Slower than raw iNGP; render time is higher than iNGP. When to Use: When high-quality, anti-aliased rendering is required for unbounded scenes, and training time is a constraint compared to pure MLP-based NeRFs, but quality is more important than the absolute fastest training time of iNGP. When Not to Use: When absolute minimum training time is required (use iNGP) or when rendering single images with high sample counts where z-aliasing is not a concern (mip-NeRF 360 may suffice, though Zip-NeRF is still better). Zip-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Zip-NeRF: Anti-Aliased Grid-Based Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the mip-NeRF 360 codebase and incorporates Instant-NGP's grid-based acceleration. The method addresses the divergence between scale-aware anti-aliased NeRFs and fast grid-based NeRF training, unifying them to handle aliasing in both spatial and loss domains. name: Mip-NeRF 360 Sampling and Training
head: Mip-NeRF 360 Training, Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling
body: Mip-NeRF 360 Sampling and Training extends the Mip-NeRF framework to unbounded, 360-degree scenes by introducing a disparity-based ray parameterization, a contraction function for coordinate space, and a coarse-to-fine training loop with a proposal network. It solves the artifacts of "floaters" and "background collapse" common in unbounded scene reconstruction by regularizing the density distribution and ensuring efficient sampling through online distillation. It differs from standard NeRF by using linear-in-disparity sampling and from basic Mip-NeRF by handling unbounded scenes via coordinate contraction and disparity parameterization. Inputs: Set of training rays \mathcal{R} with ground truth colors \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r}). Near and far clip distances tn, tf for each ray. Outputs: Rendered image colors \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}). Trained parameters for the Proposal MLP \Theta{prop} and the NeRF MLP \Theta{NeRF}. Data Structures: Proposal MLP (\Theta{prop}): A small MLP predicting volumetric density \hat{\sigma}, converted to proposal weights \hat{\mathbf{w}}. NeRF MLP (\Theta{NeRF}): A larger MLP predicting weights \mathbf{w} and color \mathbf{c}. Ray Samples: Sorted arrays of normalized distances \mathbf{s} and weights \mathbf{w}. Coordinate Transformation and Contraction: To handle unbounded scenes, input coordinates \mathbf{x} are mapped to a ball of radius 2 using the contraction function: \text{contract}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\| \le 1 \\ \left(2 - \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}\right) \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\| > 1 \end{cases} Gaussian intervals (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) are transformed using the linear approximation of the contraction function f (where f is contract): f(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \left(f(\boldsymbol{\mu}), \mathbf{J}f(\boldsymbol{\mu}) \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{J}f(\boldsymbol{\mu})^T\right) where \mathbf{J}f(\boldsymbol{\mu}) is the Jacobian of f at \boldsymbol{\mu}. Ray Parameterization: Ray distances are parameterized by an invertible mapping between Euclidean distance t and normalized distance s \in [0, 1]: s \triangleq \frac{g(t) - g(tn)}{g(tf) - g(tn)}, \quad t \triangleq g^{-1}(s \cdot g(tf) + (1-s) \cdot g(tn)) The function g(x) is set to 1/x to produce ray samples distributed linearly in disparity (inverse depth). Setting g(x) = \log(x) yields logarithmic spacing. Training Loop Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize \Theta{prop} and \Theta{NeRF} randomly. 2. Coarse Sampling: For each ray \mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}, sample Nc points uniformly in normalized disparity space s \in [0, 1]. Convert to t using the inverse mapping. Evaluate \Theta{prop} to get proposal weights \hat{\mathbf{w}}^c. 3. Fine Sampling: Resample Nf points from the proposal distribution \hat{\mathbf{w}}^c to get fine samples \mathbf{t}^f. Evaluate \Theta{NeRF} to get fine weights \mathbf{w}^f and colors \mathbf{c}^f. 4. Coarse NeRF Evaluation: Evaluate \Theta{NeRF} on the coarse samples \mathbf{t}^c to get coarse weights \mathbf{w}^c and colors \mathbf{c}^c. 5. Rendering: Compute rendered colors \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^c) and \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^f) using standard volume rendering integration. 6. Reconstruction Loss: Compute the weighted sum of reconstruction losses for coarse and fine rays: \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{1}{10} \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^c), \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r})) + \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^f), \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r})) where \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} is mean squared error. 7. Proposal Loss: Compute the proposal loss \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}} to ensure proposal weights bound NeRF weights. Define the bound function: \text{bound}(\hat{\mathbf{t}}, \hat{\mathbf{w}}, T) = \sum{j: T \cap \hat{T}j \neq \emptyset} \hat{w}j Compute the loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}(\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{w}, \hat{\mathbf{t}}, \hat{\mathbf{w}}) = \sumi \frac{1}{wi} \max(0, wi - \text{bound}(\hat{\mathbf{t}}, \hat{\mathbf{w}}, Ti))^2 Apply a stop-gradient on the NeRF MLP's outputs \mathbf{t} and \mathbf{w} when computing \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}. Compute \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}} efficiently using summed-area tables because \hat{\mathbf{t}} and \mathbf{t} are sorted. 8. Total Loss: Minimize \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}} (where \lambda is a weighting factor, typically 1) using gradient descent. Pitfalls: The proposal loss is asymmetric; it only penalizes proposal weights for underestimating the NeRF distribution. Overestimates are expected as proposal weights form an upper envelope. Floaters (small disconnected dense regions) and background collapse (distant surfaces modeled as close semi-transparent clouds) are mitigated by the regularization and parameterization. Time Complexity: The use of summed-area tables for the proposal loss allows efficient computation, scaling linearly with the number of samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storing weights and distances for both coarse and fine samples, plus the MLP parameters. Strengths: Handles unbounded scenes effectively; reduces floaters and background collapse; efficient sampling via disparity-based parameterization and proposal network. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the contraction function and disparity spacing; the proposal network adds complexity to the training loop. Mip-NeRF 360 was introduced by Barron et al. in 2022. It builds on the Mip-NeRF framework to address the challenges of unbounded, 360-degree scenes. The method introduces coordinate contraction and disparity-based sampling to improve reconstruction quality and efficiency. name: Coarse-to-Fine NeRF
head: Two-Stage NeRF, Coarse-Fine NeRF
body: Coarse-to-Fine NeRF is a hierarchical sampling strategy that improves the learning of high-frequency details in neural radiance fields by decoupling the search for opaque regions from the final rendering resolution. It addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling by first using a coarse network to identify where geometry exists, then clustering a denser set of samples around those opaque locations for a fine network. Unlike standard uniform sampling which distributes points evenly across the entire ray segment, this method concentrates computational budget on the visible surface, allowing the model to learn fine details without a proportional increase in coarse sampling cost. The method employs two separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), a coarse network and a fine network, which share the same architecture but maintain distinct parameters. Both networks are trained jointly to predict volume density and view-dependent color. Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for a batch of N rays. Near and far clipping plane distances, t{near} and t{far}. Hyperparameters: N{coarse} (coarse samples per ray), N{fine} (fine samples per ray), perturb (boolean), rawnoisestd (float), whitebkgd (boolean). Outputs: Dictionary containing: rgbcoarse: Rendered color from coarse pass, shape [N, 3]. depthcoarse: Depth from coarse pass, shape [N, 1]. rgbfine: Final rendered color from fine pass, shape [N, 3]. depthfine: Final depth from fine pass, shape [N, 1]. Coarse Samples (tc): Tensor of shape [N, N{coarse}] containing depth values along the ray. Fine Samples (t{fine}): Tensor of shape [N, N{fine}] containing depth values clustered near opaque regions. Concatenated Samples (tf): Tensor of shape [N, N{coarse} + N{fine}], sorted in ascending order. 3D Points (\mathbf{pts}): Tensor of shape [N, N{coarse} + N{fine}, 3], computed as \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. Raw Output: Tensor of shape [N, N{samples}, 4], where the first 3 channels are RGB (sigmoided) and the 4th channel is volume density \sigma. ncoarse: Number of samples in the coarse pass. Default: 64. nfine: Number of samples in the fine pass. Default: 128. perturb: If True, adds random jitter to coarse samples to break symmetry and reduce aliasing. Default: True. rawnoisestd: Standard deviation of uniform noise added to volume density \sigma before ReLU activation. Default: 0. whitebkgd: If True, adds unaccounted transmittance (1 - \alpha{total}) to the RGB map, assuming a white background. Default: False. poslevels: Number of frequency octaves for positional encoding. Default: 10. dirlevels: Number of frequency octaves for directional encoding. Default: 4. 1. Coarse Sampling: Generate N{coarse} samples tc uniformly along the ray between t{near} and t{far}. If perturb is enabled, stratify the samples by adding uniform noise \mathcal{U}[0, 1] within each bin to break symmetry. 2. Coarse Network Query: Convert tc to 3D points \mathbf{pts}c = \mathbf{o} + tc \cdot \mathbf{d}. Query the coarse MLP with \mathbf{pts}c and ray directions to obtain raw outputs \mathbf{raw}c of shape [N, N{coarse}, 4]. 3. Coarse Rendering (Alpha Compositing): Convert \mathbf{raw}c to weights wc using the raw2outputs logic (defined below). This involves: Computing distances \deltai = t{i+1} - ti, appending \infty to the last segment. Applying ReLU to the density channel \sigma and adding noise if rawnoisestd > 0. Computing opacity \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \delta). Computing transmittance T as the cumulative product of (1-\alpha), prepended with 1. Computing weights w = \alpha \cdot T. Rendering rgbcoarse and depthcoarse. 4. Hierarchical (Fine) Sampling: Use the coarse weights wc to define a probability distribution. Sample N{fine} new points t{fine} from this distribution using inverse transform sampling (or samplepdf). Pitfall: The sampling step is non-differentiable. The coarse weights wc and coarse samples tc must be detached from the computation graph (using.detach()) before being used to generate t{fine} to prevent cyclic gradients and ensure a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). 5. Concatenation and Sorting: Concatenate the coarse samples and fine samples: t{concat} = [tc, t{fine}]. Sort t{concat} in ascending order to produce tf of shape [N, N{coarse} + N{fine}]. 6. Fine Network Query: Convert tf to 3D points \mathbf{pts}f = \mathbf{o} + tf \cdot \mathbf{d}. Query the fine MLP with \mathbf{pts}f and ray directions to obtain raw outputs \mathbf{raw}f. 7. Fine Rendering: Apply the same raw2outputs logic to \mathbf{raw}f and tf to compute the final rgbfine and depthfine. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def raw2outputs(raw, zvals, raysd, rawnoisestd=0.0, whitebkgd=False): """ Converts raw MLP outputs to radiance, depth, and weights. Args: raw: Tensor of shape (raycount, samplecount, 4). Channels 0-2: RGB (linear), Channel 3: Density sigma. zvals: Tensor of shape (raycount, samplecount). Depth values. raysd: Tensor of shape (raycount, 3). Ray directions. rawnoisestd: Std dev for noise added to density before ReLU. whitebkgd: Boolean. Add background transmittance to RGB. Returns: rgbmap: (raycount, 3) depthmap: (raycount,) accmap: (raycount,) weights: (raycount, samplecount) """ # 1. Calculate distances between samples # deltai = z{i+1} - zi dists = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] # Append infinity to the last segment to force opacity of last segment to 1 # Shape: (raycount, samplecount) dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.fulllike(dists[...,:1], 1e10)], dim=-1) # Scale by ray direction norm (usually 1.0 for normalized rays) dists = dists torch.norm(raysd[..., None,:], dim=-1) # 2. Extract RGB and Density rgb = torch.sigmoid(raw[...,:3]) # (raycount, samplecount, 3) sigmaraw = raw[..., 3] # (raycount, samplecount) # 3. Add noise to density and apply ReLU noise = torch.zeroslike(sigmaraw) if rawnoisestd > 0.0: noise = torch.randnlike(sigmaraw) rawnoisestd # Note: In some implementations, noise overwrites the raw sigma data. # Here we add it to the raw sigma before activation. # Apply ReLU to density sigma = F.relu(sigmaraw + noise) # 4. Compute Opacity Alpha # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma dists) # 5. Compute Transmittance T and Weights # Ti = product{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) # Prepend 1.0 for T0. Discard the last column (T after last sample). ones = torch.oneslike(alpha[...,:1]) # cumprod of (1 - alpha + epsilon) transmittancecumprod = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([ones, 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10], dim=-1), dim=-1) # T is the cumulative product up to the previous sample T = transmittancecumprod[...,:-1] # Weights wi = alphai Ti weights = alpha T # 6. Render RGB and Depth rgbmap = torch.sum(weights[..., None] rgb, dim=-2) # (raycount, 3) depthmap = torch.sum(weights zvals, dim=-1) # (raycount,) accmap = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) # (raycount,) if whitebkgd: # Add unaccounted transmittance (1 - accumulated alpha) assuming white background rgbmap = rgbmap + (1.0 - accmap[..., None]) return rgbmap, depthmap, accmap, weights def stratifiedsample(near, far, Nc, rayo, rayd, perturb=True): """ Uniform stratified sampling along rays. Args: near: float. Near plane distance. far: float. Far plane distance. Nc: int. Number of coarse samples. rayo: Tensor (B, 3). Ray origins. rayd: Tensor (B, 3). Ray directions. perturb: bool. Add jitter. Returns: tvals: Tensor (B, Nc). Depth values. """ device = rayo.device # Create evenly spaced bins tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, Nc, device=device) # Expand to batch dimensions tvals = tvals.expand(rayo.shape[:-1], Nc) if perturb: # Jitter within each bin mid = (tvals[...,:-1] + tvals[..., 1:]) / 2.0 upper = torch.cat([mid, tvals[..., -1:]], dim=-1) lower = torch.cat([tvals[...,:1], mid], dim=-1) tvals = lower + (upper - lower) torch.randlike(tvals) return tvals def coarsetofinerender(rayso, raysd, coarsenet, finenet, near=0.0, far=1.0, ncoarse=64, nfine=128, perturb=True, rawnoisestd=0.0, whitebkgd=False): """ Implements the Coarse-to-Fine NeRF training/rendering loop. Args: rayso: Tensor (N, 3). Ray origins. raysd: Tensor (N, 3). Ray directions. coarsenet: Module. Coarse MLP. finenet: Module. Fine MLP. near: float. Near clip. far: float. Far clip. ncoarse: int. Coarse samples. nfine: int. Fine samples. perturb: bool. Perturb coarse samples. rawnoisestd: float. Noise std for density. whitebkgd: bool. White background flag. Returns: dict with 'rgbcoarse', 'depthcoarse', 'rgbfine', 'depthfine'. """ # 1. Coarse Sampling tc = stratifiedsample(near, far, ncoarse, rayso, raysd, perturb) # 2. Coarse Network Query # ptsc shape: (N, ncoarse, 3) ptsc = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) tc.unsqueeze(2) # coarsenet expects points and directions. # Assuming network takes (pts, dirs) and returns raw (N, ncoarse, 4) rawc = coarsenet(ptsc, raysd.unsqueeze(1).expandas(ptsc)) # 3. Coarse Rendering rgbcoarse, depthcoarse,, weightsc = raw2outputs( rawc, tc, raysd, rawnoisestd, whitebkgd) # 4. Hierarchical Sampling # Sample fine points based on coarse weights. # Note: weightsc must be detached to break the gradient flow from fine to coarse. # samplepdf is a helper that performs inverse transform sampling on weights. # Implementation of samplepdf: # zmid = (tc[...,:-1] + tc[..., 1:]) / 2.0 # zvalsfine = samplepdf(zmid, weightsc.detach(), nfine, detach=True) # For the purpose of this self-contained pseudocode, we assume samplepdf exists # or implement a simplified version if strictly required. # However, standard NeRF implementations use a specific PDF sampling routine. # We will denote this step as calling a standard hierarchical sampler. # Pseudocode for samplepdf (simplified inverse transform): # zmid = (tc[...,:-1] + tc[..., 1:]) / 2.0 # # Add eps to weights to avoid division by zero # weightscdetached = weightsc.detach() + 1e-5 # # Normalize weights to sum to 1 per ray # weightscdetached = weightscdetached / weightscdetached.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # # Cumulative sum # pdf = weightscdetached # cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, dim=-1) # cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # # Uniform samples in [0, 1] # u = torch.randlike(tc[...,:1]) # (N, 1) # # Inverse transform # indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='right') # # Clamp indices # indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, ncoarse - 1) # # Interpolate or pick? Standard NeRF picks indices and uses zmid or zvals. # # The original NeRF code uses tfp.distributions.Uniform and inverse CDF. # # Here we approximate by picking the zmid corresponding to the index. # tfine = torch.gather(zmid, -1, indices) # To ensure correctness without external libraries, we rely on the conceptual step: # tfine = samplepdf(zmid, weightsc.detach(), nfine) # We will assume a helper samplepdf is available or implemented as above. # For the sake of the "complete enough to implement" rule, we include the logic: zmid = (tc[...,:-1] + tc[..., 1:]) / 2.0 weightsdetached = weightsc.detach() + 1e-5 weightsdetached = weightsdetached / weightsdetached.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) pdf = weightsdetached cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) u = torch.randlike(tc[...,:1]) indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='right') indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, ncoarse - 1) tfine = torch.gather(zmid, -1, indices) # 5. Concatenate and Sort tconcat = torch.cat([tc, tfine], dim=-1) tfinesorted, = torch.sort(tconcat, dim=-1) # 6. Fine Network Query ptsfine = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) tfinesorted.unsqueeze(2) rawfine = finenet(ptsfine, raysd.unsqueeze(1).expandas(ptsfine)) # 7. Fine Rendering rgbfine, depthfine,, = raw2outputs( rawfine, tfinesorted, raysd, rawnoisestd, whitebkgd) return { 'rgbcoarse': rgbcoarse, 'depthcoarse': depthcoarse, 'rgbfine': rgbfine, 'depthfine': depthfine } Gradient Flow: The hierarchical sampling step is non-differentiable. The coarse weights wc and coarse samples tc must be detached from the computation graph before generating t{fine}. Failure to do so creates a cyclic definition in the compute graph, causing backpropagation to fail. Last Segment Distance: An infinite distance (1e10) is appended to the last segment's \delta to ensure the opacity of the last segment is 1, forcing the transmittance to 0 after the last sample. Noise Injection: Random noise is added to the volume density \sigma before ReLU if rawnoisestd > 0. This helps prevent the network from learning trivial solutions where density is zero everywhere except at exact sample points. This method constructs a multisampling pattern for a conical frustum by first generating a zero-mean, identity-covariance pattern for a cylinder and then warping it to match the frustum's analytical mean and covariance [3498-hexagonal-multisampling-pattern-derivation.md]. It ensures uniform distribution along the ray and in angles around the ray while minimizing the number of samples for efficiency [3498-hexagonal-multisampling-pattern-derivation.md]. It differs from DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering by explicitly matching statistical moments of the conical frustum rather than filtering depth estimates, and from Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts by using a fixed hexagonal geometry derived from cylindrical symmetry rather than hemispherical wavefronts [3498-hexagonal-multisampling-pattern-derivation.md]. DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering is a preprocessing step applied to the training targets of the depth oracle network in DONeRF to improve surface detection consistency and reduce false negatives. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Hexagonal Multisampling Pattern Derivation by operating on the classification targets in image and depth space rather than deriving sampling patterns directly, and from Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts by focusing on smoothing discontinuities in the oracle's one-hot encoding targets. This method is a coarse-to-fine sampling scheme for 2D hemispherical wavefronts used in Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging to balance reconstruction quality and computational overhead. It addresses the intractability of explicit volumetric resampling on a hemisphere by using a differentiable hierarchical approach, distinct from the 1D ray sampling used in NeRF. A network architecture using a single MLP with parameters \Theta for both coarse and fine sampling stages, enabled by IPE features which explicitly encode scale into input features. It uses a single MLP for both coarse and fine stages, querying it repeatedly in a hierarchical sampling strategy. The optimization problem is \min{\Theta} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left( \left\| \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}; \Theta, \mathbf{t}^c) \right\|2^2 + \left\| \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}; \Theta, \mathbf{t}^f) \right\|2^2 \right). The hyperparameter \lambda balances coarse and fine loss, with a default value of 0.1. Unlike NeRF which uses two distinct MLPs because PE features only model one scale, mip-NeRF uses one MLP because IPE encodes scale explicitly. This variant involves two rounds of proposal sampling to bound scene geometry and recursively generate new sample intervals, followed by one final NeRF round to render the final set of intervals into an image. The proposal NGP hierarchy is truncated at maximum grid sizes of 512 and 2048, and uses a single channel of features that predicts density only, not color. A sampling strategy that selectively increases the sampling rate only within the bounding box of an object area to ensure detailed sampling without significantly increasing overall computational cost. Direct composition in standard NeRF can lead to missing areas of the object in rendered images because the object NeRF size is smaller than the scene, causing sparse sampling points on the object. Sparse sampling on objects causes parts of the object to fall between two sampled points, leading to inaccurate probability density distribution (PDF) in the fine stage of NeRF sampling. Standard uniform sampling results in sparse points on small objects relative to the scene; segmented sampling fixes this by boosting density only in the object's bounding box. Time Complexity: The method requires two forward passes per ray (coarse and fine), effectively doubling the number of MLP evaluations compared to a single-pass uniform sampler with N{fine} samples. However, it achieves higher quality than a single pass with N{coarse} samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storing outputs for both coarse and fine passes, including weights, transmittance, and raw outputs for both networks. Performance: Improves detail learning by clustering samples near opaque regions, reducing aliasing and improving PSNR/SSIM metrics compared to uniform sampling. Strengths: Efficiently allocates samples to visible geometry; reduces artifacts from uniform sampling; allows for higher effective resolution without proportional increase in coarse cost. Limitations: Requires two separate MLPs (or careful parameter sharing); non-differentiable sampling step requires graph detachment; increased memory usage for intermediate tensors. When to Use: When high-frequency detail is important and uniform sampling is insufficient or inefficient. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and coarse detail is sufficient; or when the scene is entirely transparent/empty. Coarse-to-Fine NeRF was introduced in the original NeRF paper by Mildenhall et al. [2020] as a hierarchical sampling strategy to improve the quality of neural radiance field reconstructions. It was necessary because the positional encoding (PE) features used in the original NeRF architecture could only model a single scale of detail, necessitating separate coarse and fine networks to capture both global structure and fine details. The method has since been adapted in various forms, such as mip-NeRF which uses a single MLP with integrated positional encoding (IPE) to handle multiple scales, and other variants like Mip-NeRF 360 and Segmented Sampling for specific scene types. name: Hexagonal Multisampling Pattern Derivation
head: Conical frustum multisampling, Cylindrical multisampling pattern
body: This method constructs a multisampling pattern for a conical frustum by first generating a zero-mean, identity-covariance pattern for a cylinder and then warping it to match the frustum's analytical mean and covariance. It ensures uniform distribution along the ray and in angles around the ray while minimizing the number of samples for efficiency. It differs from siblings like DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering by explicitly matching statistical moments of the conical frustum rather than filtering depth estimates, and from Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts by using a fixed hexagonal geometry derived from cylindrical symmetry rather than hemispherical wavefronts. Inputs: n: Number of samples (fixed to 6). \mathbf{c}: Center of the conical frustum (mean position). \mathbf{\Sigma}: Covariance matrix of the conical frustum. \mathbf{R}: Rotation matrix aligning the cylinder's local z-axis with the ray direction. Outputs: \mathbf{x}j \in \mathbb{R}^3: The j-th sample position in world space, for j = 0, \dots, n-1. Data Structures: theta1: Array of 6 angles [0, 2\pi/3, 4\pi/3, \pi, 5\pi/3, \pi/3]. cylsamples: Array of 6 vectors \mathbf{y}j \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the canonical cylinder pattern. Steps: 1. Construct Canonical Cylinder Pattern: Generate n=6 points \mathbf{y}j in a local coordinate system where the cylinder axis aligns with the z-axis. The coordinates are defined as: \mathbf{y}j = \begin{bmatrix} \cos (\thetaj)/\sqrt {3} \\ \sin (\thetaj)/\sqrt {3} \\ \frac {j - (n-1)/2}{\sqrt {n(n^2-1)/12}} \end{bmatrix} where \thetaj are taken from theta1. This pattern has a mean of \mathbf{0} and a covariance of I3 (identity matrix). 2. Compute Warping Parameters: Determine the scaling and translation required to map the canonical cylinder to the target conical frustum. The target frustum has mean \mathbf{c} and covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}. The canonical cylinder has mean \mathbf{0} and covariance I3. 3. Warp Samples: Transform each canonical sample \mathbf{y}j to the world space sample \mathbf{x}j. The transformation aligns the cylinder's principal axes with the eigenvectors of \mathbf{\Sigma} and scales them by the square roots of the eigenvalues, then translates by \mathbf{c}. Specifically, if \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{\Lambda} \mathbf{Q}^T is the eigendecomposition, the transformation is: \mathbf{x}j = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{\Lambda}^{1/2} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{y}j where \mathbf{R} rotates the canonical cylinder's z-axis to align with the primary direction of the frustum (typically the ray direction). In the context of mip-NeRF, the frustum is oriented along the ray, so \mathbf{R} aligns the local z-axis with the ray direction vector. 4. Return Samples: Return the set \{\mathbf{x}0, \dots, \mathbf{x}{n-1}\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def hexagonalmultisamplingpattern(n=6): """ Generates the canonical hexagonal multisampling pattern for a cylinder. Returns the n sample coordinates in local cylinder space. """ # Angles from theta1 theta1 = np.array([0, 2np.pi/3, 4np.pi/3, np.pi, 5np.pi/3, np.pi/3]) samples = [] for j in range(n): # x component x = np.cos(theta1[j]) / np.sqrt(3) # y component y = np.sin(theta1[j]) / np.sqrt(3) # z component (along the cylinder axis) z = (j - (n - 1) / 2) / np.sqrt(n (n2 - 1) / 12) samples.append([x, y, z]) return np.array(samples) def warptoconicalfrustum(cylsamples, mean, cov, raydirection): """ Warps canonical cylinder samples to match a conical frustum defined by mean and covariance. Args: cylsamples: (n, 3) array of canonical cylinder samples. mean: (3,) array, center of the frustum. cov: (3, 3) array, covariance matrix of the frustum. raydirection: (3,) array, unit vector along the ray. Returns: (n, 3) array of warped samples in world space. """ # Eigendecomposition of the frustum covariance eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) # Square root of eigenvalues for scaling sqrteigenvalues = np.sqrt(eigenvalues) # Construct scaling matrix S = np.diag(sqrteigenvalues) # Rotation matrix to align canonical cylinder z-axis with ray direction canonicalz = np.array([0, 0, 1]) if np.allclose(raydirection, canonicalz): R = np.eye(3) elif np.allclose(raydirection, -canonicalz): # Rotate 180 degrees around x-axis R = np.diag([1, -1, -1]) else: # General case: rotate canonicalz to raydirection using Rodrigues' formula v1 = canonicalz v2 = raydirection cross = np.cross(v1, v2) dot = np.dot(v1, v2) skew = np.array([ [0, -cross[2], cross[1]], [cross[2], 0, -cross[0]], [-cross[1], cross[0], 0] ]) R = np.eye(3) + skew + skew @ skew (1 / (1 + dot)) # Combined transformation matrix: T = Q S R T = eigenvectors @ S @ R # Transform samples: x = mean + T @ y warpedsamples = (cylsamples @ T.T) + mean return warpedsamples Parameters: n=6: The number of samples. This is the smallest number that allows for a zero-mean, identity-covariance pattern with the specified angular distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No samples are placed exactly along the ray; they are distributed at a distance proportional to the cone radius. The full covariance matrices of the samples and the frustum are not necessarily identical, but variance along the ray and total variance perpendicular to the ray are equal. The mismatch goes to zero as t \gg \dot{r}. The pattern relies on specific angular choices (\theta1 or \theta2) to maintain the zero-mean and identity-covariance property for n=6. Using other angles or n values will break these properties. Filters depth estimates to improve sampling. Choose when depth uncertainty is high and analytical covariance is less reliable. Samples hemispherical wavefronts. Choose when rendering scenes with significant hemispherical illumination or when the conical frustum approximation is insufficient for large angles. Time Complexity: O(n) where n=6. The warping involves a fixed number of matrix-vector multiplications. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store the samples. Strengths: Efficient (only 6 samples), matches analytical moments of the conical frustum, ensures uniform angular and axial distribution. Limitations: Does not place samples on the ray axis, which may be suboptimal for some scenes. The covariance mismatch, though small, exists. When to use: When rendering with conical frustums and efficiency is critical, and the frustum is not extremely wide (t \gg \dot{r}). When not to use: When high accuracy on the ray axis is required, or when the frustum is very wide and the covariance mismatch becomes significant. The method was introduced in the context of Mip-NeRF to improve the accuracy of volume rendering by better approximating the integral over a conical frustum. It is based on the Unscented Transform, which uses a minimal set of samples to capture the mean and covariance of a random variable. The specific hexagonal pattern was derived to satisfy the criteria of uniform distribution and moment matching with the smallest number of points.
