name: DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering
head: Classified Depth Oracle, Depth smoothing filter, Neighborhood filter
body: DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering is a preprocessing step applied to the training targets of the depth oracle network in DONeRF to improve surface detection consistency and reduce false negatives. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Hexagonal Multisampling Pattern Derivation by operating on the classification targets in image and depth space rather than deriving sampling patterns directly, and from Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts by focusing on smoothing discontinuities in the oracle's one-hot encoding targets. The method filters the ground-truth classification targets generated for the depth oracle network. The oracle predicts a likelihood for each discretized segment along a ray, where a high value indicates the segment should receive samples and a low value indicates it should be skipped. Input: The unfiltered one-hot classification target C{x,y}(z) for each pixel (x,y) and discretized depth segment z. Output: The filtered classification target \hat{C}{x,y}(z) used for training the depth oracle network. Note: Filtering is applied only to training targets; no filtering is performed during inference. The classification target is a 3D tensor or array indexed by pixel coordinates (x,y) and depth segment index z. C{x,y}(z): Binary value (0 or 1). ds: Depth of the first surface along the ray. dz, d{z+1}: Discretization boundaries for segment z. The unfiltered target is a one-hot encoding: C{x,y}(z) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } dz \leq ds < d{z+1} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where ds is the depth of the first surface, and dz, d{z+1} are the boundaries of the discretized segment z. The filtering consists of two stages: a 2D spatial neighborhood filter and a 1D depth-axis smoothing filter. 1. 2D Neighborhood Filter (Radial): Applies a radial filter to include values from neighboring rays with a contribution weighted by their Euclidean distance. For a filter size K, the intermediate target \hat{C}{x,y}(z) is computed as: \hat{C}{x,y}(z) = \max{i,j \in \pm \lfloor K/2 \rfloor} \left( C{x+i,y+j}(z) - \frac{\sqrt{2+j^2}}{\sqrt{2 \cdot \lfloor K/2 \rfloor}} \right) Here, i and j are offsets in the x and y directions. The term \frac{\sqrt{2+j^2}}{\sqrt{2 \cdot \lfloor K/2 \rfloor}} represents the penalty for distance. Note that the source formula uses j in the numerator's square root but implies a radial distance; however, the text specifies "Euclidean distance" and gives examples for distances 0, 1, 2, 3 pixels. The provided formula in the source Eq. 7 uses j in the numerator, which appears to be a typo for radial distance \sqrt{i^2+j^2} or similar, but we must follow the source's explicit formula. The source states: "rays at a distance of 3, 2, 1, 0 pixels contribute 0, ≈ 0.30, ≈ 0.65, 1". Let's verify the source formula's behavior. If K=5, \lfloor K/2 \rfloor = 2. Denominator is \sqrt{2 \cdot 2} = 2. Distance 0 (i=0,j=0): 1 - 0/2 = 1. Distance 1 (i=1,j=0 or 0,1): \sqrt{1}/2 = 0.5. Contribution 1-0.5=0.5. Source says ≈0.65. Distance 2 (i=2,j=0 or 0,2 or 1,1): \sqrt{2}/2 \approx 0.707. Contribution 1-0.707=0.293. Source says ≈0.30. Distance 3 (i=3,j=0 etc, but K=5 limits to \pm 2). The source mentions distance 3 contributing 0. This implies the filter might be larger or the formula in the text has a specific interpretation. The source formula (7) uses \sqrt{2+j^2}. This seems inconsistent with "Euclidean distance" if i is ignored. However, the source explicitly provides Eq. 7. We will use Eq. 7 as the definition, noting the source's example values. For multiple depth values with the same discretization result (which shouldn't happen in one-hot, but may occur if smoothing creates overlaps or if the max is taken over multiple z), the maximum result is taken to ensure the largest value is placed at the actual surface. 2. 1D Depth Smoothing Filter: Applies a 1D triangle filter along the depth axis with kernel size Z: \hat{C}(z) = \min \left( \sum{i=-\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor}^{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor} \hat{C}(z+i) \frac{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor + 1 - |i|}{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor + 1}, 1 \right) This acts as label smoothing, blurring depth values to help the oracle predict consistent outputs at depth discontinuities. Filter Size K: Size of the 2D neighborhood filter. Example: K=5. Kernel Size Z: Size of the 1D depth filter. Example: Z=5. Loss Function: Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def filterdepthoracletargets(C, K, Z): """ Filters the depth oracle classification targets. Args: C: 3D array of shape (H, W, D) containing binary classification targets. C[x, y, z] is 1 if the surface is in segment z, else 0. K: Integer, size of the 2D spatial filter (must be odd). Z: Integer, size of the 1D depth filter (must be odd). Returns: filteredC: 3D array of shape (H, W, D) with filtered targets. """ H, W, D = C.shape filteredC = np.zeroslike(C) halfK = K // 2 halfZ = Z // 2 # Precompute radial weights for the 2D filter # The source formula uses sqrt(2+j^2) in the numerator, which seems specific. # However, standard radial distance is sqrt(i^2 + j^2). # The source text says "Euclidean distance" and gives specific values for K=5. # We implement the source's explicit formula (Eq. 7) but note the potential ambiguity. # Source Eq 7: max( C[x+i, y+j] - sqrt(2+j^2) / sqrt(2halfK)) # Note: The source formula in the text has 'j' in the numerator, not 'i' or 'sqrt(i^2+j^2)'. # We follow the source's explicit equation. denom2d = np.sqrt(2 halfK) for x in range(H): for y in range(W): for z in range(D): maxval = -np.inf # 2D Neighborhood Filter for i in range(-halfK, halfK + 1): for j in range(-halfK, halfK + 1): # Boundary check nx = x + i ny = y + j if 0 <= nx < H and 0 <= ny < W: # Source formula: sqrt(2+j^2) # Note: This formula in the source might be a typo for radial distance, # but we replicate it as written in Eq. 7. weight = np.sqrt(2 + j2) / denom2d val = C[nx, ny, z] - weight if val > maxval: maxval = val # Clamp to [0, 1] implicitly by the nature of max over binary - weight? # The source doesn't explicitly clamp the 2D step, but the 1D step clamps to 1. # We assume the result is the intermediate value. intermediateval = maxval # 1D Depth Smoothing Filter sumval = 0.0 for i in range(-halfZ, halfZ + 1): nz = z + i if 0 <= nz < D: # Triangle kernel weight weight = (halfZ + 1 - abs(i)) / (halfZ + 1) sumval += intermediateval weight # Note: intermediateval is scalar per (x,y,z) # Wait, the 1D filter is applied to the result of the 2D filter. # The 2D filter produces a value for each (x,y,z). # The 1D filter sums over z for a fixed (x,y). pass # Correction: The 1D filter should sum the filtered values from neighboring depths. # Let's restructure the loops for correctness. # Recompute for clarity # Step 1: Compute 2D filtered values for all z at (x,y) step1vals = np.zeros(D) for z in range(D): maxval = -np.inf for i in range(-halfK, halfK + 1): for j in range(-halfK, halfK + 1): nx = x + i ny = y + j if 0 <= nx < H and 0 <= ny < W: weight = np.sqrt(2 + j2) / denom2d val = C[nx, ny, z] - weight if val > maxval: maxval = val step1vals[z] = maxval # Step 2: Apply 1D triangle filter on step1vals sumval = 0.0 for i in range(-halfZ, halfZ + 1): nz = z + i # This z is the current z in the outer loop? No, we are computing for a specific z. # We need to compute the final value for each z. pass # Let's rewrite the inner loop properly finalvals = np.zeros(D) for z in range(D): # 1D filter centered at z sumval = 0.0 for i in range(-halfZ, halfZ + 1): nz = z + i if 0 <= nz < D: weight = (halfZ + 1 - abs(i)) / (halfZ + 1) sumval += step1vals[nz] weight finalvals[z] = min(sumval, 1.0) filteredC[x, y,:] = finalvals return filteredC Filter Size: Using an even larger filter size than recommended (e.g., K > 5) may reduce overall quality because it places many samples in empty space rather than on the surface. False Positives vs Negatives: Filtering increases false positives (sampling regions that do not need samples) but decreases false negatives (missing surfaces). This is acceptable because the local raymarching network handles empty space (no image contribution), while missing surfaces clearly reduces image quality. Inference: No filtering is done during inference; the filter is strictly for training target generation. Performance Gain: The neighborhood filter adds 1.3 dB–1.8 dB to PSNR, and the depth smoothing filter adds 0.1 dB, measured on test scenes with configuration K=5, Z=5, I=128 compared to the baseline. Cost: The filtering adds no inference cost as it is applied only to training targets. Scaling: The method scales with the filter sizes K and Z. Larger filters increase the computational cost of target generation but may degrade quality if too large. DONeRF (Depth Oracle Networks) was introduced to enable real-time rendering of compact neural radiance fields. The depth oracle filtering technique was developed to address the difficulty of training the oracle to predict consistent outputs at depth discontinuities by providing a multi-class target that is filtered in image-space and along the depth axis. DONeRF: Towards Real‐Time Rendering of Compact Neural Radiance Fields using Depth Oracle Networks, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14340, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts
head: Coarse-to-Fine Hemispherical Sampling, NeTF Hierarchical Sampling
body: This method is a coarse-to-fine sampling scheme for 2D hemispherical wavefronts used in Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging to balance reconstruction quality and computational overhead. It addresses the intractability of explicit volumetric resampling on a hemisphere by using a differentiable hierarchical approach, distinct from the 1D ray sampling used in NeRF. Inputs: Detection spot coordinates (x', y') and time t. Coarse network parameters. Fine network parameters. Number of coarse samples Nc^2. Number of fine samples Nf. Radius r of the hemispherical wavefront. Outputs: Estimated transient \tau(x', y', t). Data Structures: Coarse samples: Set of Nc^2 uniform points on the hemisphere, defined by spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi). Fine samples: Set of Nf points generated via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), defined by (\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f). PDF K(\theta, \phi): Probability density function estimated by the coarse network for importance sampling. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Sample Nc^2 uniform scene points in the hemisphere. 2. Coarse Evaluation: Evaluate the coarse network at these points using the estimated PDF k(\theta, \phi) to compute the coarse integral \tauc(x', y', t). 3. Fine Sampling (MCMC): Employ the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with a conditional Gaussian distribution for state transition of the Markov chain to produce Nf fine scene points K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f) along hemispherical wavefronts intersecting the NLOS scene. 4. Fine Evaluation: Compute the fine integral \tauf(x', y', t) using the fine samples and the PDF K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f). 5. Combination: Combine coarse and fine samples (Nc^2 + Nf) to re-evaluate reconstruction quality from the fine network, calculating the final transient as the average of the coarse and fine integrals. Formulas: The final transient is the average of the coarse and fine estimates: \tau(x', y', t) = \frac{\tauc(x', y', t) + \tauf(x', y', t)}{2} The fine integral is estimated as: \tauf(x', y', t) = \frac{1}{r^4} \sum{i,j} \frac{\sigma(r, \theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f) \rho(r, \theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f)}{K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f)} Where: \tauc(x', y', t) is the integral estimated with coarse samples Nc^2. \tauf(x', y', t) is the transient estimated with Nf samples from MCMC. K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f) is the PDF used for importance sampling in the MCMC fine sampling step. \sigma and \rho are volume density and emission/reflectance properties evaluated at the fine sample points. r is the radius of the hemispherical wavefront. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalsamplinghemisphere(xprime, yprime, t, r, Nc, Nf, coarsenet, finenet): """ Perform coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling on a hemispherical wavefront. Args: xprime, yprime: Detection spot coordinates. t: Time. r: Radius of the hemispherical wavefront. Nc: Integer, number of coarse samples is Nc^2. Nf: Integer, number of fine samples. coarsenet: Function evaluating the coarse network. finenet: Function evaluating the fine network. Returns: tau: Estimated transient value. """ # Step 1: Coarse Sampling # Sample Nc^2 uniform points on the hemisphere coarsepoints = sampleuniformhemisphere(Nc Nc) # Step 2: Coarse Evaluation # Evaluate coarse network with estimated PDF k(theta, phi) # Compute tauc tauc = evaluatecoarseintegral(coarsepoints, coarsenet) # Step 3: Fine Sampling (MCMC) # Use Metropolis-Hastings with conditional Gaussian distribution # to produce Nf fine points K(thetaij^f, phiij^f) finepoints = metropolishastingssampling( Nf, coarsepdfestimator=coarsenet, # K(theta, phi) derived from coarse net transitiondistribution="conditionalgaussian") # Step 4: Fine Evaluation # Compute tauf using importance sampling formula # tauf = (1/r^4) sum( (sigma rho) / K) finesamplessum = 0.0 for point in finepoints: thetaf, phif = point.theta, point.phi # Evaluate sigma and rho at fine point sigmaval = finenet.evaluatedensity(r, thetaf, phif) rhoval = finenet.evaluateemission(r, thetaf, phif) # Get PDF K for importance sampling Kval = coarsenet.evaluatepdf(thetaf, phif) # Accumulate term term = (sigmaval rhoval) / Kval finesamplessum += term tauf = (1.0 / (r 4)) finesamplessum # Step 5: Combination # Average of coarse and fine integrals tau = (tauc + tauf) / 2.0 return tau Parameters: Nc: Controls the number of coarse samples (Nc^2). Typical values not given in the sources. Nf: Number of fine samples generated by MCMC. Typical values not given in the sources. r: Radius of the hemispherical wavefront. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Explicit volumetric representations with fixed resolution make resampling on the hemisphere intractable for previous volume-based methods, unlike this differentiable hierarchical sampling. Spherical wavefronts only intersect with a very small portion of the NLOS scene, converging at specific patches, while contributions from the rest are negligible. A method for deriving multisampling patterns, potentially for different geometric configurations. A technique involving depth oracle filtering for differentiable volume rendering. Complexity: Uniform sampling complexity is O(N^2 L), where L is the number of hemispherical wavefronts and N^2 is the number of scene points per wavefront. The hierarchical scheme reduces overhead by focusing samples on regions where wavefronts intersect the NLOS scene. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Balances reconstruction quality and computational overhead; intrinsically differentiable; handles the 2D nature of hemispherical wavefronts unlike 1D ray sampling. Limitations: Previous explicit volume-based methods cannot easily apply this due to intractability of resampling on the hemisphere. When to Use: Use when performing NLOS imaging with neural transient fields where computational efficiency is critical and differentiability is required. Use when dealing with hemispherical wavefronts rather than linear rays. Origin: Introduced in the NeTF (Neural Transient Fields) paper. NeTF uses an MLP structure analogous to NeRF but with ReLU activations and simplified final layers. NeTF uses 2D sampling on a hemisphere, whereas NeRF uses 1D sampling along a ray. History and Development: The method was developed to address the high computational cost of uniform sampling in NLOS imaging, where denser samples lead to higher quality but also much higher overhead. It leverages the observation that under confocal settings, spherical wavefronts intersect only a small portion of the NLOS scene. Non-line-of-Sight Imaging via Neural Transient Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2021.3076062, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling
head: Modified Resampling, Proposal Sampling, midpoint resampling
body: Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling is a hierarchical sampling strategy used during the training of neural radiance fields to allocate samples efficiently in space. It solves the problem of aliasing and inefficient sampling by generating a second, finer set of sample intervals based on the opacity distribution of a coarse network. It sets itself apart from standard hierarchical sampling by using a "modified resampling" procedure that employs midpoints of adjacent samples as interval boundaries, which qualitatively reduces aliasing artifacts compared to using sampled points directly as endpoints. The method consists of two main phases: the generation of proposal intervals via modified resampling, and the configuration of the proposal networks. Input: A set of n sorted sample positions \{t1, t2, \dots, tn\} drawn from a coarse histogram, along with the coarse histogram's bin boundaries. Output: A set of n-1 fine intervals defined by their endpoints, which are used to sample a fine network. The proposal networks use a Hash Grid (NGP) structure. Hierarchy: Truncated at maximum grid sizes of 512 and 2048. Channels: Single channel of features is used for proposal networks, as they only predict density, not color. MLP: A view-dependent bottleneck of size 256 processed by a 3-layer MLP is used for the final round, though proposal rounds may use simpler structures. 1. Sample from Coarse Histogram: Draw n sorted values from the coarse histogram weights. Let these sorted values be t1, t2, \dots, tn. 2. Define Fine Intervals via Midpoints: Use the midpoints of adjacent sample pairs as the endpoints for the new set of n-1 fine intervals. For adjacent samples ti and t{i+1}, the midpoint is mi = \frac{ti + t{i+1}}{2}. 3. Handle Boundaries: Reflect the first sample t1 around the first endpoint and the last sample tn around the last endpoint to handle boundary conditions. This ensures the first and last fine intervals are properly bounded by the scene extent. 4. Proposal Rounds: Perform two rounds of proposal sampling to bound scene geometry and recursively generate new sample intervals. 5. Final Rendering: Perform one final NeRF round to render the final set of intervals into an image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def modifiedresampling(coarsesamples, firstendpoint, lastendpoint): """ Generates fine intervals from coarse samples using midpoint resampling. Args: coarsesamples: List of n sorted sample positions from coarse histogram. firstendpoint: The start of the first coarse bin. lastendpoint: The end of the last coarse bin. Returns: List of n-1 fine intervals, where each interval is (start, end). """ n = len(coarsesamples) fineintervals = [] # Step 1 & 2: Use midpoints of adjacent sample pairs as endpoints # We need n-1 intervals, so we compute n-1 midpoints midpoints = [] for i in range(n - 1): ti = coarsesamples[i] tnext = coarsesamples[i+1] midpoint = (ti + tnext) / 2.0 midpoints.append(midpoint) # Step 3: Handle boundaries by reflecting first and last samples # Reflect first sample around first endpoint reflectedfirst = 2 firstendpoint - coarsesamples[0] # Reflect last sample around last endpoint reflectedlast = 2 lastendpoint - coarsesamples[-1] # Construct intervals # The first interval starts at the reflected first sample and ends at the first midpoint fineintervals.append((reflectedfirst, midpoints[0])) # Intermediate intervals start at previous midpoint and end at current midpoint for i in range(1, len(midpoints)): fineintervals.append((midpoints[i-1], midpoints[i])) # The last interval starts at the last midpoint and ends at the reflected last sample fineintervals.append((midpoints[-1], reflectedlast)) return fineintervals def proposalsamplingpipeline(coarsehistogram, numsamples=64): """ Executes the two-round proposal sampling process. """ # Round 1: Coarse sampling # Sample n values from coarse histogram weights coarsesamples = samplefromhistogram(coarsehistogram, numsamples) coarsesamples.sort() # Generate fine intervals for Round 2 # Assuming firstendpoint and lastendpoint are known from scene bounds firstendpoint = coarsehistogram.bins[0].start lastendpoint = coarsehistogram.bins[-1].end fineintervalsround1 = modifiedresampling(coarsesamples, firstendpoint, lastendpoint) # Round 2: Recursive proposal # Sample from the fine intervals generated in Round 1 to create Round 2 intervals # This step is described as "recursively generate new sample intervals" # Implementation detail: Sample from the distribution defined by fineintervalsround1 round2samples = samplefromintervals(fineintervalsround1, numsamples) round2samples.sort() # Generate final intervals for the fine network finalintervals = modifiedresampling(round2samples, firstendpoint, lastendpoint) # Final Round: Render using the final intervals # Render the final set of intervals into an image image = renderneRF(finalintervals) return image Number of samples (n): Not explicitly fixed in the notes, but typical values in NeRF literature are 64 or 128. The sources mention sampling n values. Grid Sizes: Proposal NGP hierarchy truncated at maximum grid sizes of 512 and 2048. Channels: Single channel for proposal NGP. Aliasing: Using sampled points directly as endpoints can "erode" the coarse histogram because samples are unlikely to span the extent of each coarse bin, leading to aliasing. The midpoint resampling method mitigates this. Boundary Conditions: Without reflecting samples, the first and last intervals may not be properly bounded, leading to artifacts at the scene edges. Time Complexity: The resampling step is O(n \log n) due to sorting, where n is the number of samples. The subsequent rendering is proportional to the number of fine intervals. Memory Complexity: The proposal networks use truncated hash grids (max sizes 512 and 2048) and single-channel features, reducing memory usage compared to full-resolution NGP. Strengths: Qualitatively reduces aliasing artifacts. Efficiently bounds scene geometry through recursive proposal sampling. Limitations: Requires two rounds of proposal sampling before the final render, increasing training time per iteration. When to use: When training unbounded, anti-aliased neural radiance fields where aliasing is a concern. Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling was introduced in the Mip-NeRF 360 paper. It was later adopted and adapted in Zip-NeRF, which uses two rounds of proposal sampling to bound scene geometry and recursively generate new sample intervals. The method addresses the limitations of standard hierarchical sampling by modifying the resampling procedure to reduce aliasing. Mip-NeRF 360: Unbounded Anti-Aliased Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00539, fetched 2026-10-26 Zip-NeRF: Anti-Aliased Grid-Based Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.01804, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Volume Scene Setup
head: Mitsuba Scene Construction for Neural Volumes
body: Constructs a Mitsuba scene graph containing a volumetric cube and a custom neural radiance field integrator, initializing the density grid and spherical harmonics coefficients for differentiable volume rendering. It differs from generic training setup by specifically binding the neural network parameters (density grid, SH coefficients) to the Mitsuba scene graph's heterogeneous volume and integrator components, enabling end-to-end gradient flow through the ray marching process. Inputs: integratortype: String specifying the neural integrator variant. Supported values: 'prbvolpath', 'rfprb', 'rfprbrt', 'rfprbdrt', 'rfeikonal'. gridres: Integer base resolution for the density grid. Default: 16. shdegree: Integer degree for spherical harmonics basis. Default: 2. userelu: Boolean flag enabling ReLU activation in the network. Default: True. maxinitialdensity: Float upper bound for density scaling. Default: 5.0. Outputs: A configured Mitsuba Scene object ready for training. Data Structures: Density Grid: A 3D tensor of shape (gridres, gridres, gridres) storing the initial scattering coefficient \sigmat. Initialized to a constant value. Spherical Harmonics Coefficients: Parameters associated with the radiance field, determined by shdegree. Steps: 1. If integratortype is 'prbvolpath': Create a scene dictionary containing a 'cube' object. Define the cube's interior as 'heterogeneous'. Attach a 'gridvolume' to the interior for \sigmat. Initialize the grid volume values to 0.002 at resolution gridres^3. 2. If integratortype is 'rfprb', 'rfprbrt', 'rfprbdrt', or 'rfeikonal': Instantiate the corresponding integrator class (e.g., RadianceFieldPRB). Pass parameters: gridres, shdegree, userelu, and initialdensity. Calculate initialdensity as: \text{initial\density} = \frac{\text{max\initial\density}}{\text{grid\res}} Default maxinitialdensity is 5.0. 3. Load the scene dictionary with the created integrator and a constant emitter. 4. Return the constructed scene. Pitfalls: The 'rfeikonal' integrator is not implemented in the source codebase. The function falls back to 'RadianceFieldPRB' with a warning comment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createneuralvolumescene( integratortype: str, gridres: int = 16, shdegree: int = 2, userelu: bool = True, maxinitialdensity: float = 5.0) -> mi.Scene: """ Construct a Mitsuba scene for neural volume rendering. Args: integratortype: Type of neural integrator. gridres: Base resolution for density grid. shdegree: Degree of spherical harmonics. userelu: Whether to use ReLU activation. maxinitialdensity: Upper bound for density scaling. Returns: Configured Mitsuba Scene. """ # Calculate initial density parameter initialdensity = maxinitialdensity / gridres scenedict = {} if integratortype == 'prbvolpath': # Construct scene dict for volumetric path tracing scenedict['cube'] = { 'type': 'cube', 'interior': { 'type': 'heterogeneous', 'gridvolume': { 'type': 'gridvolume', 'resolution': gridres, 'values': 0.002 # Constant initial sigmat } } } # Note: Specific integrator instantiation logic for prbvolpath # is implied by the scene dict structure but not explicitly detailed # in the source beyond the dict creation. integrator = None # Placeholder for specific integrator creation logic elif integratortype in ['rfprb', 'rfprbrt', 'rfprbdrt', 'rfeikonal']: # Instantiate neural radiance field integrator if integratortype == 'rfeikonal': print("Warning: rfeikonal not implemented, falling back to RadianceFieldPRB") integratorclass = RadianceFieldPRB else: # Map string to class (implementation detail not fully specified in source) # Assuming a mapping exists or direct instantiation integratorclass = getintegratorclass(integratortype) integrator = integratorclass( gridres=gridres, shdegree=shdegree, userelu=userelu, initialdensity=initialdensity) # Construct scene dict for RF integrators scenedict['integrator'] = integrator scenedict['emitter'] = { 'type': 'constant' } # Cube and volume setup for RF integrators is handled by the integrator class # or implied by the scene structure. else: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported integratortype: {integratortype}") # Load scene with integrator and emitter # The exact mi.Scene.load() call depends on the scene dict structure # constructed above. For prbvolpath, the cube is in scenedict. # For RF types, the integrator is in scenedict. scene = mi.Scene(scenedict) return scene Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Proportional to gridres^3 for the density grid storage. Strengths: Provides a standardized way to initialize differentiable volume rendering scenes in Mitsuba with configurable neural network parameters. Limitations: Limited to specific integrator types supported by the tlir codebase; 'rfeikonal' is not functional. Originated in the tlir (Tensor Light Transport) repository by Jack Zhou. It is used to set up training environments for neural radiance fields and volume rendering optimization loops. JackZhouSz/tlir, https://github.com/JackZhouSz/tlir, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Neural Transient Field (NeTF)
body: NeTF is a neural modeling framework for Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging that recovers the 5D transient function (spatial location and direction) implicitly represented by a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Unlike NeRF, which parametrizes input training data along lines (rays), NeTF parametrizes input training data on spherical wavefronts. It addresses the challenge of sparse and unbalanced sampling in NLOS by using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and a two-stage training strategy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse set of detection spots on a relay wall, time-of-flight measurements (transients) at these spots, and camera geometry (confocal or non-confocal setup). Outputs: A 3D density volume implicitly represented by the MLP, which can be converted to a mesh via thresholding and Marching Cubes. Data Structures: MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron that takes 5D input (3D spatial coordinates + 2D direction) and outputs density and potentially other properties. Sampling Spots: A set of 2D coordinates on the relay wall (e.g., 256 \times 256 grid). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the MLP parameters. 2. Spherical Parametrization: Parametrize the input training data on spherical wavefronts rather than rays. 3. MCMC Sampling: Use Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to account for sparse and unbalanced sampling in the transient field. This enables more reliable volume density estimation. 4. Two-Stage Training (Optional but recommended for sparse data): Stage 1: Conduct training using all initial samples to obtain an initial reconstruction. Loss Calculation: Calculate the loss function between the predicted and measured transients at every measuring spot on the relay wall. PDF Formation: Normalize the calculated loss to form a probability density function (PDF). Resampling: Resample detection spots using the PDF: higher loss corresponds to higher PDF and is more densely sampled. Stage 2: Build a new training dataset from the resampled spots and retrain the network to refine reconstruction. 5. Reconstruction: The final reconstruction corresponds to a 3D density volume implicitly represented by the MLP. 6. Surface Extraction: Map the volume to surfaces, e.g., by thresholding followed by Marching Cubes. Formulas: The loss function L is calculated between predicted and measured transients at every measuring spot. The PDF P is formed by normalizing the loss: Pi = \frac{Li}{\sumj Lj}. Parameters: Sampling Grid: Typically 256 \times 256 spots on the relay wall. Sparse Sampling: Tested down to 4 \times 4 spots. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Confocal vs. Non-Confocal: NeTF does not separately treat confocal and non-confocal setups in its current form. Occlusions: Occlusion can lead to strong reconstruction artifacts if not handled properly; NeTF handles this better than Phasor Field. Noise: Brute-force implementation of Marching Cubes may lead to noise on smooth surfaces. A training strategy to address sampling bias (undersampling) in NLOS reconstruction by resampling detection spots based on reconstruction loss. It involves an initial training phase, loss calculation, PDF formation, resampling, and retraining. It is chosen when dealing with sparse or imbalanced sampling, such as recovering fine details like bunny ears that are missing in one-stage training. Accuracy: On the Bunny dataset (confocal), NeTF achieved a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 2.65 cm, compared to 2.38 cm for DLCT and 2.43 cm for F-K. On the Bunny dataset (non-confocal), NeTF achieved an MAE of 7.45 cm, compared to 3.77 cm for FBP and 7.02 cm for BP. Quality: NeTF produces sharper edges for both front and back planes in semi-occluded scenes compared to Phasor Field and DLCT/F-K. It manages to separate different parts of a mesh, whereas DLCT exhibits adhesion between different parts. Noise: NeTF reconstruction incurs much lower noise than State-of-the-Art (SOTA) methods, similar to NeRF. Computational Cost: Learning-based techniques like NeTF are substantially more computationally expensive than previous optimization techniques. Robustness: NeTF produces reasonable reconstructions even with very sparse sampling spots (e.g., 8 \times 8). NeTF was introduced as a novel neural modeling framework for NLOS imaging. It is analogous to NeRF but uses spherical wavefronts instead of rays. It was tested on synthetic and real NLOS data, including the Bunny, Lucy, Indonesian, Bike, Letter Z, and semi-occluded scenes. Non-line-of-Sight Imaging via Neural Transient Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2021.3076062, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Optimization Configuration (Adam + Exponential Decay + Selective L2)
head: Parameter update rule, Training optimizer setup
body: This configuration defines the specific hyperparameter setup and regularization strategy used to optimize neural radiance fields and volume rendering networks. It combines the Adam optimizer with a staircase exponential learning rate decay schedule and selective L2 weight decay applied only to specific network components (MLPs) while excluding positional encodings and appearance embeddings. This setup is distinct from standard NeRF training loops by explicitly masking L2 regularization to prevent divergence in embedding spaces and by using a specific decay schedule that holds the initial learning rate for 10,000 steps before decaying by a factor of 1/3 every 10,000 steps. The method configures the optimization process by initializing separate optimizers for different parameter groups, applying a global learning rate schedule, and defining a mask for L2 regularization. Inputs: lr: Initial learning rate scalar. params: Dictionary of network parameters, categorized into network (MLPs and encodings) and ae (appearance embeddings). step: Current training step integer. Outputs: updates: Dictionary of parameter updates. state: Optimizer state (momentum estimates, step count). paramlabels: A dictionary mapping parameter name prefixes to optimizer targets. Layout: {"nerf": "network", "bg": "network", "appearanceembeddings": "ae"}. mask: A dictionary defining which parameter groups receive L2 decay. Layout: {"nerf": {"densitymlp": True, "rgbmlp": True, "positionencoder": False}, "bg": True, "appearanceembeddings": False}. Note: True indicates L2 decay is applied; False indicates it is skipped. Learning Rate Schedule: initvalue: lr. transitionsteps: 10,000. decayrate: 1/3. staircase: True. transitionbegin: 10,000. endvalue: lr / 100. Adam Optimizer (Network): learningrate: Output of the schedule above. b1: 0.9. b2: 0.99. eps: 10^{-15}. epsroot: 10^{-15}. Adam Optimizer (Appearance Embeddings): learningrate: 10^{-4}. b1: 0.9. b2: 0.99. eps: 10^{-8}. epsroot: 0. L2 Regularization: weightdecay: 10^{-6}. 1. Initialize Learning Rate Schedule: Create an exponential decay scheduler with the parameters defined above. The schedule holds the initial lr for transitionbegin steps, then decays by decayrate every transitionsteps steps until it reaches endvalue. 2. Initialize Network Optimizer: Create an Adam optimizer instance using the scheduled learning rate and the specified Adam hyperparameters (b1, b2, eps, epsroot). 3. Initialize Appearance Embedding Optimizer: Create a separate Adam optimizer instance with a fixed learning rate of 10^{-4} and its specific hyperparameters. 4. Combine Optimizers: Use a multi-transform mechanism to map parameter groups to their respective optimizers based on paramlabels. Parameters labeled "network" use the network optimizer; parameters labeled "ae" use the appearance embedding optimizer. 5. Apply L2 Mask: During the update step, apply L2 weight decay with coefficient weightdecay only to parameters where the mask is True. Parameters where the mask is False (e.g., position encoders, appearance embeddings) are excluded from L2 decay. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp from jax import lax def initializeoptimizer(lr): """ Initializes the Adam optimizer and learning rate schedule. """ # Learning Rate Schedule Parameters initvalue = lr transitionsteps = 10000 decayrate = 1.0 / 3.0 staircase = True transitionbegin = 10000 endvalue = lr / 100.0 # Adam Hyperparameters for Network b1 = 0.9 b2 = 0.99 eps = 1e-15 epsroot = 1e-15 # Adam Hyperparameters for Appearance Embeddings lrae = 1e-4 b1ae = 0.9 b2ae = 0.99 epsae = 1e-8 epsrootae = 0.0 # L2 Regularization weightdecay = 1e-6 # Masks # paramlabels: {"nerf": "network", "bg": "network", "appearanceembeddings": "ae"} # mask: {"nerf": {"densitymlp": True, "rgbmlp": True, "positionencoder": False}, # "bg": True, "appearanceembeddings": False} return { "scheduleparams": { "initvalue": initvalue, "transitionsteps": transitionsteps, "decayrate": decayrate, "staircase": staircase, "transitionbegin": transitionbegin, "endvalue": endvalue }, "adamparamsnetwork": {"b1": b1, "b2": b2, "eps": eps, "epsroot": epsroot}, "adamparamsae": {"lr": lrae, "b1": b1ae, "b2": b2ae, "eps": epsae, "epsroot": epsrootae}, "weightdecay": weightdecay } def computelearningrate(step, scheduleparams): """ Computes the current learning rate using exponential decay. """ initvalue = scheduleparams["initvalue"] transitionsteps = scheduleparams["transitionsteps"] decayrate = scheduleparams["decayrate"] staircase = scheduleparams["staircase"] transitionbegin = scheduleparams["transitionbegin"] endvalue = scheduleparams["endvalue"] # Calculate the number of decay steps if staircase: # Integer division for staircase decay # Decay begins after transitionbegin steps stepssincebegin = jnp.maximum(0, step - transitionbegin) numdecays = stepssincebegin // transitionsteps else: # Continuous decay numdecays = step / transitionsteps lr = initvalue (decayrate numdecays) # Clamp to endvalue lr = jnp.maximum(lr, endvalue) return lr def adamupdate(params, grads, state, adamparams): """ Performs a single Adam update step. state: {"m": momentum, "v": velocity, "t": timesteps} """ b1 = adamparams["b1"] b2 = adamparams["b2"] eps = adamparams["eps"] epsroot = adamparams["epsroot"] lr = adamparams["lr"] # Current lr for this group t = state["t"] + 1 # Update biased first moment estimate m = lax.mul(b1, state["m"]) + lax.mul(1 - b1, grads) # Update biased second raw moment estimate v = lax.mul(b2, state["v"]) + lax.mul(1 - b2, lax.square(grads)) # Compute bias-corrected first moment estimate mhat = lax.div(m, 1 - b1 t) # Compute bias-corrected second raw moment estimate vhat = lax.div(v, 1 - b2 t) # Compute update # Adam update formula: lr mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + epsroot + eps) # Note: eps is added inside the sqrt term in some implementations, # but standard Adam adds eps to the denominator. # The source specifies eps and epsroot separately. # Standard JAX/Optax Adam: update = lr mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + epsroot) + eps? # Actually, Optax Adam uses: update = mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + epsroot) # And eps is often used for gradient clipping or inside the sqrt. # Given eps=1e-15 and epsroot=1e-15, we follow standard Adam: # thetanew = thetaold - lr mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + eps) # However, the source lists eps and epsroot. In Optax, eps is typically # added to the denominator to prevent division by zero, and epsroot # is often used in the RMSProp part. # Let's use the standard formula: update = lr mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + eps) # If epsroot is distinct, it might be: update = lr mhat / (sqrt(vhat + epsroot) + eps) # Given the small values, we assume standard Adam denominator: sqrt(vhat) + eps update = lax.mul(lr, lax.div(mhat, lax.sqrt(vhat) + eps)) newparams = lax.sub(params, update) newstate = { "m": m, "v": v, "t": t } return newparams, newstate def applyl2decay(params, grads, mask, weightdecay): """ Applies L2 weight decay to gradients based on the mask. """ # If mask is True, add weightdecay params to the gradient # If mask is False, do not add L2 decay # This requires knowing which part of params corresponds to the mask. # For simplicity, we assume grads and params are aligned and mask is applied element-wise or group-wise. # In practice, this is done per parameter group. # Example for a single parameter array where mask is a boolean array of same shape # decayedgrads = grads + weightdecay params mask # Since mask is hierarchical, this function would be called per group. # Here we return the modified gradients. return grads + weightdecay params mask def optimizestep(params, grads, state, mask, config): """ Main optimization step. """ step = state["t"] # 1. Compute Learning Rate lr = computelearningrate(step, config["scheduleparams"]) # 2. Separate parameters into Network and AE groups based on paramlabels # This is a logical separation. In implementation, params are passed in groups. # Group 1: Network (MLPs) # Use Adam with scheduled lr adamparamsnetwork = config["adamparamsnetwork"] adamparamsnetwork["lr"] = lr # Apply L2 decay to network params if mask is True # Note: mask["nerf"]["positionencoder"] is False, so L2 is not applied to encodings # This requires careful grouping. We assume the input params and grads # are already filtered to the "network" group. # For demonstration, we assume params and grads are for a specific masked group # where the mask value is known (e.g., densitymlp). # 3. Update # The actual implementation uses optax.multitransform which handles the routing. # Here we simulate the update for a single group. # Apply L2 decay if mask is True for this group # maskvalue = mask[groupname][subgroupname] # For the purpose of this pseudocode, we assume the mask has been applied # to the gradients before calling adamupdate, or adamupdate handles it. # The source says "Combine optimizers via optax.multitransform... and paramlabels". # And "Initialize network optimizer...". # And "weightdecay: L2 regularization coefficient applied to masked weights". # So, the gradient passed to Adam should include the L2 term if masked. # Let's assume grads are raw gradients. # We need to know the mask value for this specific parameter. # Since we don't have the full context of which parameter is being updated, # we will show the update step assuming L2 has been added if required. newparams, newstate = adamupdate(params, grads, state, adamparamsnetwork) return newparams, newstate Staircase Delay: With staircase=True and transitionbegin=10,000, the learning rate remains at lr for the first 10,000 steps. The first decay occurs at step 20,000 (since transitionbegin is the start of the decay period, and transitionsteps is the interval). This is a common pitfall if one expects decay to start immediately after transitionbegin. L2 Decay on Encodings: Applying L2 decay to position encoders or appearance embeddings can cause divergence or suboptimal convergence. The mask explicitly sets these to False. Precision: The use of eps=1e-15 and epsroot=1e-15 in the network Adam optimizer suggests a need for high numerical stability, possibly due to the small gradients or specific data types used. A variant used for tomographic reconstruction rather than neural radiance fields. It uses the BFGS quasi-Newton method with a Moreau envelope to smooth the L1 regularizer (GroupL1Norm) for total variation regularization. It requires an initial Hessian inverse estimate based on the operator norm and uses a limited memory approach (numstore=10). The FBP pseudoinverse must use the 'Hann' filter. A simpler protocol used for neural dual contouring and SDF reconstruction. It uses Adam with beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, and a fixed learning rate of 10^{-4}. The learning rate is halved every 100 epochs. It employs heavy data augmentation including random scaling, translation, and Gaussian noise (\mu=0.5) for noisy real scan reconstruction. Time Complexity: Adam is O(1) per parameter per step, making it efficient for large networks. The exponential decay calculation is negligible. Memory Complexity: Adam requires storing two moment estimates per parameter (2 \times parameter size). The multi-transform setup does not add significant overhead. Performance: This configuration is designed for long training runs (e.g., 100k+ steps) where a slow decay helps stabilize convergence. The exclusion of L2 decay from encodings and embeddings allows them to adapt freely to the data without being penalized for magnitude, which is crucial for high-frequency details in NeRFs. Strengths: Prevents divergence in embedding spaces; provides a robust learning rate schedule that avoids premature decay; simple to implement with standard optimizers. Limitations: The fixed decay schedule may not be optimal for all datasets; the specific hyperparameters (e.g., eps=1e-15) are sensitive to the implementation of the Adam optimizer. This configuration originates from the JAX-based implementation of Neural Graphics Primitives (NGP) or similar radiance field frameworks, as seen in the jaxngp repository. It is designed to optimize the MLPs and appearance embeddings in neural radiance fields. The use of selective L2 decay is a known technique in NeRF training to prevent over-regularization of positional encodings, which are critical for high-frequency detail representation. blurgyy/jaxngp, https://github.com/blurgyy/jaxngp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, https://github.com/adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Neural Dual Contouring, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01999v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gradient Descent Solver
head: Adam Optimizer Solver, L1/L2 Norm Solver
body:
The Gradient Descent Solver is a matrix-free iterative method for optimizing transfer functions in volume rendering, supporting both constant update rates and the Adam optimizer. It distinguishes itself from direct solvers like CGLS by avoiding the explicit formation of normal equations (A^T A), thereby offering numerical stability for ill-conditioned or rank-deficient systems while accumulating gradients via atomic additions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A differentiable rendering objective function (typically based on L2 or L1 norms), a learning rate schedule (constant \alpha or Adam parameters), and initial transfer function parameters. Output: Optimized transfer function parameters. Data Structures: The solver operates in a matrix-free manner. Gradients are accumulated directly into parameter buffers using atomic additions to handle parallel updates safely. No explicit Jacobian or Hessian matrices are stored. Parameters: \alpha: Constant update rate (learning rate). Adam parameters:  eta1,  eta2, \epsilon (standard Adam defaults are implied by the reference to [KB15], though exact values are not specified in the source text). Norm type: L2 (least squares) or L1 (least absolute deviations). Steps: 1. Initialize: Set initial transfer function parameters 	heta0. If using Adam, initialize first and second moment estimates m0 = 0, v0 = 0. 2. Forward Pass: Render the scene using current parameters 	hetat to compute the output image or scalar field. 3. Compute Residual: Calculate the residual r = y{target} - y{pred}. 4. Compute Gradient: Compute the gradient of the loss function with respect to 	hetat. For L2-norm (least squares): Loss J =  rac{1}{2} \|r\|2^2. Gradient 
abla J = -r \cdot  rac{\partial y{pred}}{\partial 	heta}. For L1-norm (least absolute deviations): Loss J = \|r\|1. Gradient 
abla J = -	ext{sign}(r) \cdot  rac{\partial y{pred}}{\partial 	heta}. 5. Accumulate Gradients: Accumulate the computed gradients into the solver's internal gradient buffer using atomic additions to ensure thread safety in parallel implementations. 6. Update Parameters: Constant Rate: 	heta{t+1} = 	hetat - \alpha \cdot 
abla J. Adam Optimizer: Update moments and apply Adam update rule as defined in [KB15]. 7. Repeat: Steps 2-6 until convergence or maximum iterations reached. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The solver is noted to show stable behavior for ill-conditioned systems, unlike direct matrix inversion methods. Norm Selection: The choice between L1 and L2 affects robustness to outliers. L2 penalizes large residuals quadratically, while L1 tolerates larger outliers better. The CGLS solver is a sparse linear least squares solver used to avoid the ill-conditioning of normal equations (A^T A), providing numerically stable results for large or rank-deficient problems. It differs from its parent Gradient Descent Solver by solving the linear system directly via conjugate gradients rather than iterative gradient updates, and from its siblings Partially Learned Gradient Descent by relying on the specific CGLS algorithm for least-squares minimization. Partially Learned Gradient Descent is an iterative reconstruction method that unrolls a fixed number of optimization steps into a neural network, combining a fixed physics-based gradient step with a learnable neural network update. It initializes the reconstruction with a filtered backprojection (FBP) estimate and, in its base form, does not use a regularization term in the network input. Unlike standard Gradient Descent which uses a fixed step size, this method learns the update rule via a convolutional network while retaining the physical forward model and gradient structure, making it more interpretable and robust to distribution shifts than fully learned end-to-end CNNs. It builds on Gradient Descent Solver. An ablation study variant that uses Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with a positive Student's t distribution. It replaces Gaussian distributions with Student's t distributions, removes negative components, and removes SGHMC (Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo). It adds a low-pass filter (0.3 diagonal offset) to ensure fair comparison with similar component counts. It is used in the Ablation Study to provide a fair comparison with similar component numbers against methods using the low-pass filter. Stability: Shows stable behavior for ill-conditioned systems, similar to CGLS. Performance: Generally slower than computing the matrix A^T A and vector A^T b explicitly, but avoids the numerical instability associated with forming A^T A for large or rank-deficient problems. Norm Impact: The choice of L1 vs L2 norm makes a minor difference in final results, with L2 penalizing larger residuals more strongly and L1 tolerating outliers. Complexity: Matrix-free implementation reduces memory overhead for storing large matrices, but requires careful handling of atomic operations for parallel gradient accumulation. The Gradient Descent Solver was implemented as part of a study on transfer function optimization for comparative volume rendering, specifically within the DiffDVR framework. It references the Adam optimizer from [KB15] and compares its performance against CGLS and other solvers using datasets such as those by Necker et al.. name: CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares)
head: Sparse Linear Least Squares Solver
body: The CGLS solver is a sparse linear least squares solver used to avoid the ill-conditioning of normal equations (A^T A), providing numerically stable results for large or rank-deficient problems. It differs from its parent Gradient Descent Solver by solving the linear system directly via conjugate gradients rather than iterative gradient updates, and from its siblings Partially Learned Gradient Descent by relying on the specific CGLS algorithm for least-squares minimization. Inputs and outputs: Input: Matrix A (implicitly defined via matrix-vector products), vector b. Output: Solution vector x minimizing \|Ax - b\|^2. Data structures: Vectors p, r, x of size n (dimension of the solution space). Scalar variables for step sizes and norms. Steps: 1. Initialize x0 = 0. 2. Compute initial residual r0 = b - A x0 = b. 3. Set initial search direction p0 = A^T r0. 4. Compute \rho0 = r0^T r0. 5. For k = 0, 1, \dots until convergence: a. Compute matrix-vector product q = A pk. b. Compute \alphak = \rhok / (pk^T q). c. Update solution: x{k+1} = xk + \alphak pk. d. Update residual: r{k+1} = rk - \alphak q. e. Apply Jacobi preconditioning to r{k+1} to achieve faster convergence. Let M be the diagonal of A^T A. The preconditioned residual is \tilde{r}{k+1} = M^{-1} r{k+1}. f. Compute new search direction: p{k+1} = A^T \tilde{r}{k+1} + \betak pk. g. Compute \rho{k+1} = \tilde{r}{k+1}^T r{k+1} (or r{k+1}^T r{k+1} depending on specific CGLS variant, but standard CGLS uses r^T r for \rho and preconditioning affects the direction update). Note: Standard CGLS does not use preconditioning in the \rho calculation, but applies it to the residual before computing the next p. The exact formula for \betak is \betak = \rho{k+1} / \rhok. h. Check convergence: if \|r{k+1}\| is sufficiently small, stop. Parameters: Tolerance for convergence: Not given in the sources. Maximum iterations: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: CGLS is preferred over normal equations for ill-conditioned systems. Rank deficiency: Provides more stable results for almost rank-deficient problems compared to normal equations. Performance: Generally slower than computing A^T A and A^T b explicitly for moderately sized problems. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cgls(Amatvec, Atmatvec, b, maxiter=1000, tol=1e-6): n = len(b) x = [0.0] n r = [b[i] for i in range(n)] # r = b - Ax, initially x=0 p = Atmatvec(r) # p = A^T r # Jacobi preconditioner: M = diag(A^T A) # We need to compute the diagonal of A^T A. # This requires computing A^T A ei for each basis vector ei. # For efficiency, this might be precomputed or approximated. # Let's assume we have a function to get the diagonal. Mdiag = getdiagonalAtA(Amatvec, n) Minvdiag = [1.0 / val if val != 0 else 0.0 for val in Mdiag] rho = dotproduct(r, r) for k in range(maxiter): q = Amatvec(p) pTq = dotproduct(p, q) if pTq == 0: break alpha = rho / pTq x = [x[i] + alpha p[i] for i in range(n)] r = [r[i] - alpha q[i] for i in range(n)] # Jacobi preconditioning rprecond = [Minvdiag[i] r[i] for i in range(n)] rhonew = dotproduct(rprecond, r) # Standard CGLS uses r^T r for rho, but preconditioned r for p update? # Actually, standard CGLS (without preconditioning) uses rho = r^T r. # With preconditioning, it's often PCGLS. The source mentions "Jacobi preconditioning" for CGLS. # Let's stick to the standard CGLS update but precondition the residual for the next p. # The source says "including Jacobi preconditioning to achieve faster convergence". # This implies PCGLS. # Recompute rho for beta rho = dotproduct(r, r) # Use unpreconditioned r for rho in standard CGLS? # Or preconditioned? Let's use standard CGLS with preconditioned residual for p. # The most common implementation of preconditioned CGLS: # rho = r^T r # beta = rho / rhoold # p = A^T (M^-1 r) + beta p # Let's assume the source implies standard CGLS with Jacobi preconditioning on the residual. # We need to be careful with the definition of rho. # Re-evaluating based on standard PCGLS: # rho = r^T r # p = A^T (M^-1 r) + beta p # But the source is vague. Let's use the standard CGLS formula with preconditioned residual for p. # Let's use the standard CGLS update for x and r, and precondition r for p. # rho = r^T r # beta = rho / rhoold # p = A^T (M^-1 r) + beta p # However, the source says "Jacobi preconditioning" for CGLS. # Let's assume the standard PCGLS algorithm. # Let's restart the loop logic with standard PCGLS: # x = 0, r = b, p = A^T M^-1 b # rho = r^T M^-1 r # for k=0.. # q = A p # alpha = rho / (p^T q) # x = x + alpha p # r = r - alpha q # z = M^-1 r # rhonew = r^T z # beta = rhonew / rho # p = z + beta p # rho = rhonew # This is the standard PCGLS. The source mentions Jacobi preconditioning. # Let's use this standard PCGLS implementation. pass # Placeholder for the loop body as defined above Note: The pseudocode above is incomplete due to ambiguity in the source regarding the exact preconditioned CGLS variant. The standard PCGLS algorithm is provided as a comment. This method recovers missing pixels in a rendered volume image by solving a regularized least-squares optimization problem using the Conjugate Gradient algorithm. It allows reconstruction from a subset of pixels, reducing total rendering time compared to full volume rendering. It differs from its parent CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) by explicitly defining the regularization term H via B-spline convolution and the sampling matrix S for pixel dropping, whereas the parent focuses on the general numerical stability of the least-squares formulation. The Symmetric Least Squares Solver computes the minimum-norm solution to the linear system Ax = b where A is a symmetric matrix, using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to construct the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. It is distinguished from its parent, the CGLS Solver, by its reliance on explicit spectral decomposition rather than iterative conjugate gradients, making it suitable for small, dense symmetric systems where direct inversion via SVD is computationally feasible and numerically robust against rank deficiency. Strengths: Numerically stable for very large or almost rank-deficient problems. Limitations: Generally slower than computing A^T A and A^T b explicitly. When to use: For ill-conditioned or rank-deficient systems where normal equations are unstable. When not to use: For moderately sized problems where speed is critical and normal equations are stable. The CGLS solver is based on the work by Paige and Saunders [PS82]. It is used in transfer function optimization for comparative volume rendering. name: Conjugate Gradient Solver for Compressive Volume Rendering
head: CG Solver, Compressive Volume Rendering with Conjugate Gradient Solver, Global CG Solver
body: This method recovers missing pixels in a rendered volume image by solving a regularized least-squares optimization problem using the Conjugate Gradient algorithm. It allows reconstruction from a subset of pixels, reducing total rendering time compared to full volume rendering. It differs from its parent CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) by explicitly defining the regularization term H via B-spline convolution and the sampling matrix S for pixel dropping, whereas the parent focuses on the general numerical stability of the least-squares formulation. Inputs: Y: The observed rendered image vector (size N \times 1, where N = \text{imageWidth} \times \text{imageHeight}). S: The binary sampling matrix (size N \times N). \lambda: Regularization parameter. \phi: The basis function (univariate uniform centered cubic B-spline \beta3(t)). Outputs: x: The reconstructed full-resolution image vector (size N \times 1). Data Structures: x, r, p, b: Vectors of size N (floats). A: Implicitly defined as S^T S + \lambda H. H: Convolution matrix defined by H{p,q} = \langle \phi(\cdot - jp), \phi(\cdot - jq) \rangle{L^2}. Formulas: The optimization problem is: \minx \|Sx - y\|2^2 + \lambda x^T H x The linear system to solve is: (S^T S + \lambda H)x = S^T y Let A = S^T S + \lambda H and b = S^T y. Steps: 1. Initialize x0 (e.g., zeros or interpolated guess). 2. Compute b = S^T Y. Note that S^T acts as an upsampling operator inserting zeros at missing pixel locations. 3. Initialize residual r0:= b - A x0 and search direction p0:= r0. 4. Iterate for k = 0, 1, \dots: a. Calculate step size \alphak:= \frac{rk^T rk}{pk^T A pk}. b. Update solution x{k+1}:= xk + \alphak pk. c. Update residual r{k+1}:= rk - \alphak A pk. d. If r{k+1} is sufficiently small (convergence criterion), exit loop. e. Calculate \betak:= \frac{r{k+1}^T r{k+1}}{rk^T rk}. f. Update search direction p{k+1}:= r{k+1} + \betak pk. g. Increment k. 5. Return x{k+1}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvecompressivevolumerendering(Y, S, lambdareg, phikernel, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): """ Solves (S^T S + lambda H) x = S^T Y using Conjugate Gradient. Y: observed image vector (N,) S: sampling matrix (N, N) - binary, rows are sampled pixels lambdareg: regularization weight phikernel: kernel for H (used in convolveH) """ N = len(Y) x = np.zeros(N) # b = S^T Y. S^T inserts zeros at missing pixels. # In practice, S is sparse. S^T Y places Y values at their original indices in a zero-filled vector. b = np.zeros(N) # Assuming S is defined such that S[i, j] = 1 if pixel j is observed in output i # Then (S^T Y)[j] = Y[i] if pixel j corresponds to observed pixel i, else 0. # Implementation detail: map observed pixels back to original coordinates. # For this generic implementation, we assume a helper applyStranspose exists. b = applyStranspose(Y, S) # Initial residual r0 = b - Ax0. Since x0=0, r0 = b. r = b.copy() p = r.copy() # Precompute r^T r rdot = np.dot(r, r) for k in range(maxiter): # Compute Ap = (S^T S + lambda H) p # S^T S p: downsamples p, then upsamples (inserts zeros) pdown = applyS(p, S) Ap = applyStranspose(pdown, S) # lambda H p: convolution with kernel phi Ap += lambdareg convolveH(p, phikernel) # alpha = (r^T r) / (p^T A p) pdotAp = np.dot(p, Ap) if pdotAp == 0: break # Zero search direction alpha = rdot / pdotAp # xnew = x + alpha p x += alpha p # rnew = r - alpha A p r -= alpha Ap rdotnew = np.dot(r, r) # Check convergence if np.sqrt(rdotnew) < tol: break # beta = (rnew^T rnew) / (r^T r) beta = rdotnew / rdot # pnew = rnew + beta p p = r + beta p rdot = rdotnew return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The global solver is too slow for real-time rendering due to high data transfer between CPU and GPU for FFT convolution and cuBLAS dot products. FFT-based convolution requires memory to be copied back and forth between CPU and GPU, decreasing performance. cuBLAS dot product operations require memory copy for each iteration, significantly reducing performance. The matrix S has size (imageWidth \times imageHeight) by (imageWidth \times imageHeight). Time Complexity: The reconstruction time is almost constant regardless of the number of features or pixels added, while total rendering time increases with features/pixels. However, the global solver is computationally expensive and performance depends on image size and iteration count. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for vectors x, r, p, b and intermediate results for S^T S and H operations. FFT-based convolution requires additional memory for transforms. Performance: Volume rendering using 100% of the pixels takes more time than the compressive rendering method. The global reconstruction process is too slow to interact with the volume renderer in real-time due to CPU-GPU data transfers. Strengths: Acceptable image quality for reconstructed images. Can significantly reduce rendering time by using a subset of pixels. Limitations: Poor performance for real-time interactive rendering due to data transfer overheads. This method is described in the thesis "GPU-based Compressive Volume Rendering". It builds on the concept of compressive sensing applied to volume rendering, utilizing the Conjugate Gradient solver to recover missing pixel data. The regularization term H is defined using cubic B-splines. GPU-based Compressive Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.11575/prism/5366, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Symmetric Least Squares Solver
head: Symmetric SVD Solver, Symmetric Pseudo-Inverse Solver
body: The Symmetric Least Squares Solver computes the minimum-norm solution to the linear system Ax = b where A is a symmetric matrix, using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to construct the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. It is distinguished from its parent, the CGLS Solver, by its reliance on explicit spectral decomposition rather than iterative conjugate gradients, making it suitable for small, dense symmetric systems where direct inversion via SVD is computationally feasible and numerically robust against rank deficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix A (stored as 6 floats: A{00}, A{01}, A{02}, A{11}, A{12}, A{22}), a 3D vector b, and parameters svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol. Output: The solution vector x, and the residual error ||Ax - b||^2. Data Structures: SMat3: Symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix. Fields: m00, m01, m02, m11, m12, m22. Mat3: General 3 \times 3 matrix. Fields: m00..m22 (9 floats). Vector3: 3D vector. Fields: x, y, z. Algorithm Steps: 1. SVD Decomposition: Compute the SVD of the symmetric matrix A. This yields the eigenvector matrix V and the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues D (stored as VTAV). The decomposition satisfies A = V D V^T. The implementation uses a Jacobi eigenvalue algorithm with svdsweeps iterations and convergence tolerance svdtol. 2. Pseudoinverse Construction: Compute the pseudoinverse A^+ using the formula A^+ = V D^+ V^T, where D^+ is the diagonal matrix with entries D^+{ii} = \text{pinv}(D{ii}, \text{pinv\tol}). 3. Solution Calculation: Compute x = A^+ b via matrix-vector multiplication. 4. Error Calculation: Return the squared residual error ||Ax - b||^2. Formulas: Pseudoinverse Thresholding: \text{pinv}(x, \text{tol}) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |x| < \text{tol} \text{ or } |1/x| < \text{tol} \\ 1/x & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This prevents division by zero or near-zero eigenvalues. Matrix Multiplication for Pseudoinverse: Given V (eigenvectors) and D (eigenvalues), the pseudoinverse matrix P is: P{ij} = \sum{k=0}^{2} V{ik} \cdot \text{pinv}(D{kk}, \text{tol}) \cdot V{jk} Specifically for 3 \times 3: P{00} = V{00} D^+0 V{00} + V{01} D^+1 V{01} + V{02} D^+2 V{02} (and similarly for other elements). Residual Error: \text{Error} = (Ax - b) \cdot (Ax - b) where \cdot is the dot product. Parameters: svdtol: Convergence tolerance for the Jacobi SVD iteration. Not given in the sources. svdsweeps: Number of Jacobi rotation sweeps. Not given in the sources. pinvtol: Threshold for inverting eigenvalues. Values near machine epsilon (10^{-7} for float) are typical. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvesymmetricleastsquares(Asym: SMat3, b: Vector3, svdtol: float, svdsweeps: int, pinvtol: float) -> (Vector3, float): # Step 1: SVD Decomposition # Asym is symmetric. V is orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors. # VTAV is diagonal matrix of eigenvalues (stored as SMat3). V = Mat3() VTAV = SMat3() getsymmetricsvd(Asym, VTAV, V, svdtol, svdsweeps) # Step 2: Compute Pseudoinverse pinvmatrix = computepseudoinverse(VTAV, V, pinvtol) # Step 3: Solve for x x = matvecmul(pinvmatrix, b) # Step 4: Calculate Residual Error residual = calcerror(Asym, x, b) return x, residual def getsymmetricsvd(A: SMat3, VTAV: SMat3, V: Mat3, tol: float, sweeps: int): """ Computes SVD for symmetric A using Jacobi eigenvalue algorithm. V contains eigenvectors as columns. VTAV contains eigenvalues on diagonal. """ # Initialize V as identity V.setidentity() # Copy A to VTAV VTAV.m00 = A.m00 VTAV.m01 = A.m01 VTAV.m02 = A.m02 VTAV.m11 = A.m11 VTAV.m12 = A.m12 VTAV.m22 = A.m22 # Perform Jacobi rotations for i in range(sweeps): # Find largest off-diagonal element # Apply Givens rotation to zero it out # Update VTAV and V # Check convergence against tol # Implementation details omitted: standard Jacobi algorithm for symmetric matrices pass def computepseudoinverse(D: SMat3, V: Mat3, tol: float) -> Mat3: """ Computes V D^+ V^T """ d0 = pinv(D.m00, tol) d1 = pinv(D.m11, tol) d2 = pinv(D.m22, tol) Out = Mat3() Out.m00 = V.m00 d0 V.m00 + V.m01 d1 V.m01 + V.m02 d2 V.m02 Out.m01 = V.m00 d0 V.m10 + V.m01 d1 V.m11 + V.m02 d2 V.m12 Out.m02 = V.m00 d0 V.m20 + V.m01 d1 V.m21 + V.m02 d2 V.m22 Out.m10 = V.m10 d0 V.m00 + V.m11 d1 V.m01 + V.m12 d2 V.m02 Out.m11 = V.m10 d0 V.m10 + V.m11 d1 V.m11 + V.m12 d2 V.m12 Out.m12 = V.m10 d0 V.m20 + V.m11 d1 V.m21 + V.m12 d2 V.m22 Out.m20 = V.m20 d0 V.m00 + V.m21 d1 V.m01 + V.m22 d2 V.m02 Out.m21 = V.m20 d0 V.m10 + V.m21 d1 V.m11 + V.m22 d2 V.m12 Out.m22 = V.m20 d0 V.m20 + V.m21 d1 V.m21 + V.m22 d2 V.m22 return Out def pinv(x: float, tol: float) -> float: if abs(x) < tol or abs(1.0 / x) < tol: return 0.0 return 1.0 / x def calcerror(Asym: SMat3, x: Vector3, b: Vector3) -> float: # Convert symmetric matrix to general for multiplication A = Mat3() A.setsymmetric(Asym) Ax = matvecmul(A, x) diff = b - Ax return dot(diff, diff) Computes the pseudoinverse of a symmetric matrix A given its SVD components V (eigenvectors) and D (eigenvalues). It inverts the eigenvalues in D, handling near-zero values via a threshold pinvtol to ensure numerical stability. It is chosen when the system is small (3 \times 3) and symmetric, allowing direct construction of the pseudoinverse without iterative refinement. The formula is A^+ = V D^+ V^T. Time Complexity: O(1) for 3 \times 3 matrices, dominated by the fixed number of Jacobi sweeps (svdsweeps). Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only 3 \times 3 matrices and vectors. Strengths: Numerically stable for rank-deficient or ill-conditioned symmetric matrices due to SVD. Direct solution avoids iterative convergence issues. Limitations: Only applicable to symmetric matrices. Computationally expensive for large matrices compared to iterative solvers like CGLS. When to use: Small, dense, symmetric linear systems in differentiable rendering pipelines where exact pseudoinverse is required. When not to use: Large sparse systems, non-symmetric matrices, or when iterative approximation is sufficient. The method is implemented in the DualContouringCSharp repository by tuckbone, used for dual contouring in 3D reconstruction. It leverages SVD-based pseudoinverse for solving symmetric least squares problems, a technique common in numerical linear algebra for handling ill-conditioned systems. tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, https://github.com/tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: General Least Squares Solver
head: Normal Equations Solver (via Symmetric Solver), Non-Symmetric Least Squares via Normal Equations
body: The General Least Squares Solver addresses the overdetermined linear system Ax = b for a non-symmetric matrix A by transforming it into a symmetric positive semi-definite system via the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b. It is distinguished from its parent, the Symmetric Least Squares Solver, by its preprocessing step of explicitly forming A^T A and A^T b, which squares the condition number of the original system, thereby gaining computational speed at the cost of numerical stability for ill-conditioned inputs. Inputs: A: A non-symmetric matrix of size M \times N (typically 3 \times 3 in the cited implementation context). b: A vector of size M. svd\tol: Tolerance for Singular Value Decomposition convergence. svd\sweeps: Number of Jacobi sweeps for SVD. pinv\tol: Tolerance for pseudoinverse calculation (singular value cutoff). Outputs: x: The solution vector of size N. Residual error (scalar). Data Structures: Mat3: A 3 \times 3 matrix structure. SMat3: A symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix structure (stores only upper/lower triangle). Vector3: A 3-element vector. Steps: 1. Transpose: Compute A^T from A. Let this be A^T. 2. Form Normal Matrix: Compute A^T A. Since A^T A is symmetric, store it in a symmetric matrix structure ATA. 3. Form Right-Hand Side: Compute A^T b. Let this be b'. 4. Solve Symmetric System: Call the Symmetric Least Squares Solver (SVD-based pseudoinverse) on ATA and b' to find x. The Symmetric Solver computes the SVD of ATA, calculates the pseudoinverse, and multiplies by b'. 5. Return: Return x and the residual error \|Ax - b\|. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvegeneralleastsquares(A, b, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol): # Step 1: Transpose A AT = transpose(A) # Step 2: Compute ATA = A^T A # Since ATA is symmetric, we can use a symmetric matrix structure ATA = matmulsymmetric(AT, A) # Step 3: Compute ATb = A^T b ATb = vmul(AT, b) # Step 4: Solve symmetric system ATA x = ATb using SVD pseudoinverse # This calls the Symmetric Least Squares Solver x = solvesymmetric(ATA, ATb, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol) # Step 5: Calculate residual error residual = calcerror(A, x, b) return x, residual def solvesymmetric(ATA, ATb, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol): # Compute SVD of symmetric matrix ATA # ATA = V D V^T (since symmetric, U=V) V, D = getsymmetricsvd(ATA, svdtol, svdsweeps) # Compute pseudoinverse of ATA # ATA^+ = V D^+ V^T ATApinv = pseudoinversesymmetric(ATA, V, D, pinvtol) # Solve for x x = vmul(ATApinv, ATb) return x def pseudoinversesymmetric(ATA, V, D, pinvtol): # D is diagonal matrix of singular values # Compute D^+ where 1/sigma if sigma > pinvtol else 0 Dinv = zeroslike(D) for i in range(len(D)): if D[i] > pinvtol: Dinv[i] = 1.0 / D[i] else: Dinv[i] = 0.0 # ATA^+ = V D^+ V^T ATApinv = matmul(V, matmuldiag(Dinv, transpose(V))) return ATApinv Parameters: svd\tol: Default not given in sources. Typical value 1e-6. svd\sweeps: Default not given in sources. Typical value 10-20 for 3 \times 3 matrices. pinv\tol: Default not given in sources. Typical value 1e-6. Edge Cases: Ill-conditioned A: Squaring the condition number (\kappa(A^T A) = \kappa(A)^2) can lead to significant numerical instability and loss of precision. Singular A^T A: The pseudoinverse handles this by zeroing out components corresponding to singular values below pinv\tol. The Normal Equations Solver addresses the overdetermined linear system Ax = b arising in radiance-field optimization by forming and solving the symmetric positive semi-definite system A^T A x = A^T b. It is distinguished from sibling methods like the General Least Squares Solver by explicitly squaring the condition number to gain computational speed, making it the fastest alternative for well-conditioned systems but prone to numerical instability when the matrix is ill-conditioned. Time Complexity: Dominated by matrix multiplication O(M^2 N) for forming A^T A and A^T b, and O(N^3) for SVD. For 3 \times 3 matrices, this is constant time but faster than iterative methods like CGLS for small systems. Memory Complexity: O(MN) to store A, A^T, ATA, and ATb. Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages highly optimized symmetric solvers; fast for small, well-conditioned systems. Limitations: Numerically unstable for ill-conditioned matrices due to squared condition number; not suitable for large sparse systems where forming A^T A is prohibitive. When to use: Small dense systems where speed is critical and A is well-conditioned. When not to use: Ill-conditioned systems or large sparse systems. The method is derived from the standard normal equations approach to least squares, implemented in the DualContouringCSharp repository. It builds on the Symmetric Least Squares Solver which uses SVD for robust pseudoinverse calculation. tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, https://github.com/tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
