name: Normal Equations Solver
head: A^T A Solver, Least Squares via Normal Equations
body: The Normal Equations Solver addresses the overdetermined linear system Ax = b arising in radiance-field optimization by forming and solving the symmetric positive semi-definite system A^T A x = A^T b. It is distinguished from sibling methods like the General Least Squares Solver by explicitly squaring the condition number to gain computational speed, making it the fastest alternative for well-conditioned systems but prone to numerical instability when the matrix is ill-conditioned. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse system matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} (where m \gg n) and vector b \in \mathbb{R}^m. Output: Solution vector x \in \mathbb{R}^n. Data Structures: Matrix A is stored in Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format to allow sequential querying of non-zero entries for the i-th voxel (row). Matrix A^T A is a band matrix. Due to the separate handling of RGB\alpha channels, non-zero entries exist only on the main diagonal and the two diagonals four rows/columns away from the main diagonal. Only the upper triangular part of A^T A is stored due to symmetry. Steps: 1. Assemble A^T A and A^T b: Compute the sparse matrix-matrix product A^T A and sparse matrix-vector product A^T b. This can be done using linear algebra libraries (e.g., Eigen on CPU, cuSPARSE on GPU) or custom matrix-free compute shaders. 2. Matrix-Free Assembly (Vulkan Compute Example): Iterate over all voxels i. For each voxel, determine the column indices j(Di) and j(Di)+1 and the interpolation weight w(i). Atomically add the following values to A^T A: (1-w(i))^2 to entry (j(Di), j(Di)) w(i)^2 to entry (j(Di)+1, j(Di)+1) (1-w(i))w(i) to entry (j(Di)+1, j(Di)). 3. Solve the System: Use a dense or sparse linear least squares solver (e.g., QR, LLT, LDLT) on the assembled A^T A and A^T b. 4. Constraint Handling: The ordinary least squares problem is convex with Hessian H(x) = 2A^T A. If the solver does not enforce box constraints 0 \le xi \le 1, apply truncation: x'i = \max\{\min\{xi, 1\}, 0\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvenormalequations(Acsr, b, numvoxels, getvoxelindicesandweight): """ Solves Ax = b via normal equations A^T A x = A^T b. Acsr: CSR format matrix A. b: Right-hand side vector. numvoxels: Number of voxels (rows in A). getvoxelindicesandweight: Function returning (j, jplus1, w) for voxel i. """ n = Acsr.numcolumns # Initialize symmetric matrix A^T A and vector A^T b # Using a dense array for A^T A is feasible as it is typically small ATA = zeros((n, n)) ATb = zeros(n) # Step 1: Assemble A^T A and A^T b # In a matrix-free GPU implementation, this loop runs in parallel over voxels # with atomic additions for ATA. Here we simulate the accumulation. for i in range(numvoxels): j, jplus1, w = getvoxelindicesandweight(i) # Compute contributions to A^T A # Entry (j, j) valjj = (1 - w) 2 ATA[j, j] += valjj # Entry (j+1, j+1) valjp1jp1 = w 2 ATA[jplus1, jplus1] += valjp1jp1 # Entry (j+1, j) - symmetric, so also affects (j, j+1) valjp1j = (1 - w) w ATA[jplus1, j] += valjp1j ATA[j, jplus1] += valjp1j # Maintain symmetry explicitly in dense storage # Compute contribution to A^T b # Assuming A is tall and skinny, and b corresponds to the voxel values # The specific row of A for voxel i is needed to compute (A^T b)k # However, the source notes imply A^T b is computed similarly or via library. # For completeness, if A is sparse CSR: # rowstart = Acsr.rowptr[i] # rowend = Acsr.rowptr[i+1] # for k in range(rowstart, rowend): # col = Acsr.colind[k] # val = Acsr.values[k] # ATb[col] += val b[i] # Note: The source emphasizes the atomic assembly of ATA for the specific # interpolation structure. A^T b assembly follows standard sparse mat-vec. pass # Step 2: Solve the symmetric system ATA x = ATb # Using a dense solver like LLT or LDLT try: # LLT requires positive definite; LDLT handles semi-definite better # QR is also an option but pivoting may be needed for stability x = solvelinearsystem(ATA, ATb, method='LDLT') except SingularMatrixError: # Fallback or error handling for rank deficiency x = solvelinearsystem(ATA, ATb, method='QR') # Step 3: Apply box constraints if not enforced by solver x = clip(x, min=0.0, max=1.0) return x Parameters: Memory usage for A: For a dataset with 1.76 \cdot 10^6 voxels using 32-bit floating point precision, the system matrix requires almost 7 GiB of memory. A^T A is usually small enough to be stored in dense format. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The condition number of the normal equations system is the square of the original matrix's condition number: \text{cond}(A^T A) = \text{cond}(A)^2. This leads to numerical instability for ill-conditioned matrices. Rank Deficiency: A^T A is often nearly rank deficient because certain transfer function values are hardly referenced by voxel values, or rank deficient if no values fall within a certain range. Solvers like QR may require pivoting for stability. A method to solve the box-constrained least squares problem \forall i \in [1,...,n]: 0 \le xi \le 1 by formulating it as a quadratic programming problem. It uses the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) via the OSQP solver library, exploiting sparsity. The quadratic programming problem is \minx \frac{1}{2} x^T Q x + c^T x, where Q = A^T A and c = -A^T b. While a GPU implementation of OSQP exists, no significant speed-up was observed compared to CPU for the small size of A^T A resulting from normal equations. Time Complexity: Generally the fastest alternative for solving the least squares problem due to the efficiency of forming and solving the symmetric system. Memory Complexity: A requires significant memory (e.g., ~7 GiB for 1.76 \cdot 10^6 voxels with 32-bit floats), but A^T A is typically small and fits in memory. Strengths: Fast assembly and solution for well-conditioned systems; leverages sparse matrix-matrix products efficiently. Limitations: Prone to stability issues if the matrix is ill-conditioned due to the squaring of the condition number. May require pivoting or alternative solvers (like QR) to handle near-rank deficiency. When to use: When computational speed is prioritized and the system matrix A is well-conditioned. When not to use: When the matrix is ill-conditioned or nearly rank deficient, as numerical errors may be amplified. The normal equations approach is a standard technique in linear algebra for solving least squares problems. In the context of volume rendering, it was applied to transfer function optimization, where the goal is to optimize RGB\alpha values subject to box constraints. The method was evaluated against other solvers like CGLS, noting that while normal equations are faster, they suffer from condition number squaring. The specific implementation details, including matrix-free Vulkan compute shaders for assembly, were described in recent work on transfer function optimization for comparative volume rendering. Transfer Function Optimization for Comparative Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2306.05885, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Symmetric Pseudo-Inverse Calculation
head: Pseudoinverse Calculation
body: Computes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of a symmetric matrix A using its singular value decomposition (SVD) or eigen-decomposition, specifically handling near-zero eigenvalues via a threshold to ensure numerical stability. It serves as the core linear algebra primitive for the Symmetric Least Squares Solver, enabling the solution of symmetric linear systems Ax=b where A may be singular or ill-conditioned. It differs from the General Least Squares Solver by exploiting the symmetry of A to use eigen-decomposition (A = V D V^T) rather than full SVD, reducing computational cost and memory footprint for symmetric inputs. Inputs: A: A 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix (represented as SMat3 or flattened array). V: The 3 \times 3 matrix of eigenvectors (columns), where A = V D V^T. D: The diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, represented as a vector d = [d{00}, d{11}, d{22}]^T or SMat3 diagonal. tol: A scalar threshold for singularity detection. Outputs: A^+: The 3 \times 3 pseudoinverse matrix. Data Structures: SMat3: Symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix storing 6 unique elements: m{00}, m{01}, m{02}, m{11}, m{12}, m{22}. Mat3: Full 3 \times 3 matrix storing 9 elements: m{ij} for i,j \in \{0,1,2\}. Vector3: 3-element vector. Steps: 1. Thresholded Inversion: For each eigenvalue dk (k \in \{0,1,2\}), compute the inverted value dk^+: dk^+ = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |dk| < tol \text{ or } |1/dk| < tol \\ 1/dk & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This prevents division by zero or amplification of noise when eigenvalues are near zero. 2. Reconstruction: Compute the pseudoinverse A^+ using the eigenvectors and inverted eigenvalues. Since A = V D V^T, then A^+ = V D^+ V^T. The elements of A^+ are calculated as: A^+{ij} = \sum{k=0}^{2} V{ik} dk^+ V{jk} Explicitly for a 3 \times 3 matrix: \begin{aligned} A^+{00} &= V{00}d0^+V{00} + V{01}d1^+V{01} + V{02}d2^+V{02} \\ A^+{01} &= V{00}d0^+V{10} + V{01}d1^+V{11} + V{02}d2^+V{12} \\ A^+{02} &= V{00}d0^+V{20} + V{01}d1^+V{21} + V{02}d2^+V{22} \\ A^+{11} &= V{10}d0^+V{10} + V{11}d1^+V{11} + V{12}d2^+V{12} \\ A^+{12} &= V{10}d0^+V{20} + V{11}d1^+V{21} + V{12}d2^+V{22} \\ A^+{22} &= V{20}d0^+V{20} + V{21}d1^+V{21} + V{22}d2^+V{22} \end{aligned} The remaining elements are filled by symmetry (A^+{ji} = A^+{ij}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pinv(x, tol): """Thresholded inverse of a scalar.""" if abs(x) < tol or abs(1.0 / x) < tol: return 0.0 return 1.0 / x def symmetricpseudoinverse(V, ddiag, tol): """ Computes pseudoinverse of symmetric matrix A = V diag(d) V^T. Args: V: Mat3, eigenvectors (columns). ddiag: Vector3 or SMat3 diagonal, eigenvalues [d0, d1, d2]. tol: Float, singularity threshold. Returns: Mat3, the pseudoinverse A+. """ # Step 1: Thresholded inversion of eigenvalues d0 = pinv(ddiag[0], tol) d1 = pinv(ddiag[1], tol) d2 = pinv(ddiag[2], tol) # Step 2: Reconstruct A+ = V diag(d+) V^T # Initialize output matrix Out = Mat3() # Row 0 Out.m00 = V.m00 d0 V.m00 + V.m01 d1 V.m01 + V.m02 d2 V.m02 Out.m01 = V.m00 d0 V.m10 + V.m01 d1 V.m11 + V.m02 d2 V.m12 Out.m02 = V.m00 d0 V.m20 + V.m01 d1 V.m21 + V.m02 d2 V.m22 # Row 1 Out.m10 = V.m10 d0 V.m00 + V.m11 d1 V.m01 + V.m12 d2 V.m02 Out.m11 = V.m10 d0 V.m10 + V.m11 d1 V.m11 + V.m12 d2 V.m12 Out.m12 = V.m10 d0 V.m20 + V.m11 d1 V.m21 + V.m12 d2 V.m22 # Row 2 Out.m20 = V.m20 d0 V.m00 + V.m21 d1 V.m01 + V.m22 d2 V.m02 Out.m21 = V.m20 d0 V.m10 + V.m21 d1 V.m11 + V.m22 d2 V.m12 Out.m22 = V.m20 d0 V.m20 + V.m21 d1 V.m21 + V.m22 d2 V.m22 return Out Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If an eigenvalue is exactly zero, pinv returns 0, effectively removing that dimension from the solution space. Numerical Stability: The condition |1/x| < tol handles cases where x is very small but non-zero, preventing overflow or extreme noise amplification. Symmetry Preservation: The output matrix must be explicitly symmetric. In implementation, only upper/lower triangular elements are computed, and the rest are mirrored. Computes the pseudo-inverse of a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix using eigen-decomposition, specifically designed for minimizing distance to a midpoint in dual contouring contexts. It uses auxiliary arrays w for inverse eigenvalues and u for eigenvectors. A key variant feature is the handling of degenerate cases: if two dominant eigenvalues are close (ratio > 0.2), it may return a pre-computed expectedNorm instead of computing the full inverse, optimizing for planar surfaces. Time Complexity: O(1) for fixed 3 \times 3 matrices. Dominated by the SVD/eigen-decomposition step (not included in this method) and the 9 multiplications/additions for reconstruction. Memory Complexity: O(1). Requires storage for the input V, D, and output A^+. Strengths: Numerically stable for symmetric matrices; handles singular systems gracefully via thresholding; efficient for small fixed-size matrices. Limitations: Only applicable to symmetric matrices; requires pre-computed SVD/eigen-decomposition; threshold selection (tol) is critical and problem-dependent. When to use: When solving symmetric linear systems Ax=b where A is derived from quadratic error functions (e.g., in dual contouring) and may be rank-deficient. When not to use: For non-symmetric matrices (use General Least Squares Solver) or when A is guaranteed to be full-rank and well-conditioned (direct inversion may suffice). Originated in the context of dual contouring and implicit surface reconstruction, where symmetric quadratic error functions are minimized. The method is implemented in open-source dual contouring libraries such as DualContouringCSharp and DualContouring. It leverages the mathematical property that the pseudoinverse of a symmetric matrix can be computed via its eigen-decomposition, avoiding the more expensive general SVD. tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, https://github.com/tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChessQian/DualContouring, https://github.com/ChessQian/DualContouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Partially Learned Gradient Descent
head: Learned Gradient Descent, Learned iterative reconstruction, Partially learned gradient descent without regularizer, Unrolled Optimization with Learned Updates, Unrolled optimization
body: Partially Learned Gradient Descent is an iterative reconstruction method that unrolls a fixed number of optimization steps into a neural network, combining a fixed physics-based gradient step with a learnable neural network update. It initializes the reconstruction with a filtered backprojection (FBP) estimate and, in its base form, does not use a regularization term in the network input. Unlike standard Gradient Descent which uses a fixed step size, this method learns the update rule via a convolutional network while retaining the physical forward model and gradient structure, making it more interpretable and robust to distribution shifts than fully learned end-to-end CNNs. It builds on Gradient Descent Solver. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Noisy projection data y, initial estimate x0 (typically FBP of y), and the forward operator \mathcal{A} (e.g., RayTransform). Output: Reconstructed image x after n{iter} steps. Data Structures: x: Current reconstruction estimate, shape [batch, height, width, 1]. s: Hidden state memory buffer, shape [batch, height, width, nmemory]. Initialized to zeros. y: Noisy projection data, shape [batch, projheight, projwidth, 1]. x{true}: Ground truth for loss calculation, shape [batch, height, width, 1]. Parameters: n{iter}: Number of unrolled iterations. Typical value: 10. n{memory}: Number of channels in the hidden state memory tensor s. Typical value: 5. \mu{water}: Attenuation coefficient of water for nonlinear forward models. Typical value: 0.02. photons{per\pixel}: Number of photons per pixel for noise simulation. Typical value: 10000. \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability in log operations. Value: 1/photons{per\pixel}. opnorm: Operator norm of \mathcal{A}, used for scale invariance. Convolutional Network Layout: The network takes a concatenated input tensor u and produces an update dx and new memory s{new}. Input channels: Concatenation of x, gradient(s), and s. Layer 1: Conv2D kernel W1 shape [3, 3, inchannels, 32], bias b1 shape [1, 1, 1, 32]. Activation: ReLU. Layer 2: Conv2D kernel W2 shape [3, 3, 32, 32], bias b2 shape [1, 1, 1, 32]. Activation: ReLU. Layer 3: Conv2D kernel W3 shape [3, 3, 32, nmemory + 1], bias b3 shape [1, 1, 1, nmemory + 1]. Activation: Linear. Output split: dx = h3[:,:,:, 0:1], s{new} = \text{ReLU}(h3[:,:,:, 1:]). Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute operator norm: opnorm = \|\mathcal{A}\|. Normalize operator: \mathcal{A}{norm} = \frac{1}{opnorm} \mathcal{A}. Normalize pseudoinverse: \mathcal{A}{pinv} = \mathcal{A}{pinv} \cdot opnorm. Initialize x0 = \mathcal{A}{pinv}(y) (FBP). Initialize s = 0 with shape [batch, height, width, nmemory]. 2. Iteration Loop (for i = 0 to n{iter}-1): Compute forward projection: Tx = \mathcal{A}{norm}(x). Compute data gradient g{data}: For linear models: g{data} = \mathcal{A}{norm}^(Tx - y). For nonlinear models (e.g., CT with attenuation): y{pred} = \exp(-\mu{water} \cdot Tx), then g{data} = \mu{water} \cdot \mathcal{A}{norm}^(y - y{pred}). Compute regularization gradient g{reg} (if using variant with regularizer): g{reg} = (\partial0^ \partial0 + \partial1^ \partial1)(x), where \partial0, \partial1 are partial derivatives. Concatenate inputs along channel axis to form u: Base variant: u = \text{concat}(x, g{data}, s). With regularizer variant: u = \text{concat}(x, g{data}, g{reg}, s). Apply convolutional network: h1 = \text{ReLU}(W1 u + b1) h2 = \text{ReLU}(W2 h1 + b2) h3 = W3 h2 + b3 Split output: dx = h3[:,:,:, 0:1] s{new} = \text{ReLU}(h3[:,:,:, 1:]) Update state: s = s{new} x = x + dx 3. Loss and Training: Loss function: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{b=1}^{N} \sum{i,j} (x{b,i,j} - x{true,b,i,j})^2. Optimizer: RMSProp with inverse time decay. Starter learning rate: 1e-3. Decay rate: 1.0. Decay steps: 500. Staircase: True. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import tensorflow as tf def partiallylearnedgradientdescent(y, xtrue, operator, operatoradjoint, operatornorm, niter=10, nmemory=5, muwater=0.02, useregularizer=False): """ Implements Partially Learned Gradient Descent. Args: y: Noisy projection data tensor [batch, projh, projw, 1] xtrue: Ground truth image tensor [batch, imgh, imgw, 1] operator: Forward projection function operatoradjoint: Adjoint projection function operatornorm: Scalar operator norm for scaling niter: Number of iterations nmemory: Number of memory channels muwater: Attenuation coefficient for nonlinear models useregularizer: Boolean flag for regularizer variant Returns: x: Reconstructed image """ # Normalize operator for scale invariance scaledoperator = lambda x: operator(x) / operatornorm scaledadjoint = lambda x: operatoradjoint(x) operatornorm # Initialize x0 via FBP (pseudoinverse applied to y) # Note: In practice, x0 is often precomputed or passed as input. # Here we assume a placeholder or initial value is provided. # For the sake of self-contained pseudocode, we assume x is initialized. # In the source, x0 is a placeholder. We simulate initialization. # x = pseudoinverse(y) # Not explicitly coded as a step in the loop, # but x0 is the input to the loop. # Initialize memory state s to zeros batchsize = tf.shape(y)[0] imgh, imgw = tf.shape(y)[1], tf.shape(y)[2] # Assuming square for simplicity, or use actual dims # Actually, x shape is [batch, size, size, 1]. We need to know size. # Let's assume size is derived from x0 if passed, or fixed. # For this pseudocode, we assume x is initialized to FBP result. # x = tf.zeros([batchsize, size, size, 1]) # Placeholder for x0 # Since x0 is an input, we start with it. # x = x0 (passed in or computed) s = tf.zeros([batchsize, size, size, nmemory]) # Define convolutional layers weights and biases # These are typically loaded from trained parameters or initialized. # For implementation, they must be defined. # w1, b1, w2, b2, w3, b3 shapes depend on input channels. for i in range(niter): # 1. Forward projection Tx = scaledoperator(x) # 2. Data gradient if usenonlinearmodel: ypred = tf.exp(-muwater Tx) gradx = scaledadjoint(y - ypred) muwater else: gradx = scaledadjoint(Tx - y) # 3. Regularization gradient (if applicable) if useregularizer: # Laplacian regularizer: partial0.adjoint partial0 + partial1.adjoint partial1 # Implemented as odlopregularizer(x) gradreg = regularizeradjoint(x) else: gradreg = None # 4. Concatenate inputs if useregularizer: updateinput = tf.concat([x, gradx, gradreg, s], axis=3) else: updateinput = tf.concat([x, gradx, s], axis=3) # 5. Convolutional Network # Layer 1 h1 = tf.nn.relu(conv2d(updateinput, w1) + b1) # Layer 2 h2 = tf.nn.relu(conv2d(h1, w2) + b2) # Layer 3 (Linear) h3 = conv2d(h2, w3) + b3 # 6. Split output dx = h3[:,:,:, 0:1] snew = tf.nn.relu(h3[:,:,:, 1:]) # 7. Update s = snew x = x + dx return x def conv2d(x, W, stride=(1, 1)): """Standard 2D convolution with SAME padding.""" return tf.nn.conv2d(x, W, strides=[1, stride[0], stride[1], 1], padding='SAME') Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nonlinear Model Stability: The exponential function in the nonlinear forward model (\exp(-\mu{water} \cdot Tx)) can saturate or become numerically unstable if the input is not scaled correctly or if \mu{water} is incorrect. Momentum Non-negativity: The momentum buffer s is updated using ReLU, ensuring it remains non-negative to prevent oscillatory behavior from negative momentum values. Scale Invariance: The operator and pseudoinverse must be normalized by the operator norm to ensure scale invariance. Input Shape: The input tensor to the convolutional network must have the correct channel dimension based on the variant (2 or 3 gradient channels + memory). A variant that includes a Tikhonov-like regularization term (adjoint of partial derivatives) in the network input concatenation. It computes the regularization gradient g{reg} = (\partial0^ \partial0 + \partial1^ \partial1)(x) and concatenates it with x, g{data}, and s. The input channel count is n{memory} + 3. Choose this variant when explicit regularization is needed to enforce smoothness or other priors in the reconstruction. A method for estimating velocity fields from density changes, using a proximal operator and momentum terms. It updates velocity estimates using auxiliary variables and error thresholds. This is distinct from the image reconstruction focus of Partially Learned Gradient Descent and is used in fluid modeling contexts. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of iterations n{iter} and the cost of the forward/backward projections and convolutional network passes per iteration. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the image size and n{memory} for the hidden state s, plus the memory for the convolutional network weights. Performance: Demonstrated on head CT and phantom data with 128x128 or 512x512 resolutions. Uses 30-1000 projection angles depending on the setup. Strengths: Retains physical interpretability by using the actual forward model and gradients, unlike end-to-end CNNs. The learned updates can converge faster or produce better quality than fixed-step gradient descent. Limitations: Requires training data and computational resources for training the network. The performance depends on the quality of the learned weights. The nonlinear forward model requires careful scaling. When to use: When you want the benefits of learned optimization dynamics but need to maintain physical consistency and interpretability. Suitable for medical imaging reconstruction tasks. When not to use: When computational resources for training are unavailable, or when a purely analytical solution (like FBP) is sufficient for the required quality. Partially Learned Gradient Descent was developed in the context of learned iterative reconstruction for medical imaging, specifically using the Open Data Library (ODL) and TensorFlow. It was introduced by Adler et al. in the repository learnedgradienttomography. The method unrolls optimization steps into a neural network, learning the update rules while keeping the physics-based gradient computation fixed. It has been applied to head CT reconstruction and phantom data. adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, https://github.com/adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Physics-Based Differentiable Rendering for Efficient and Plausible Fluid Modeling from Monocular Video, https://doi.org/10.3390/e25091348, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Deep Image Prior Reconstruction
head: DIP Reconstruction, DRP Denoising
body: Deep Image Prior Reconstruction (DIP Reconstruction) is an iterative inverse rendering method that uses a neural network as an implicit regularizer to solve for a volume or image from sparse or noisy projection data. It distinguishes itself from traditional iterative methods like SIRT by optimizing the network weights to fit the data while simultaneously updating a latent variable to maintain data consistency, leveraging the bias of convolutional architectures toward natural image structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse sinogram p (measured projections). Input: A differentiable projector (forward and backward projection operators). Input: A PriorModel (neural network architecture, e.g., U-Net or CNN). Output: Reconstructed image/volume x. Data Structures: The method maintains: z: Latent variable tensor, same shape as the reconstruction grid. \theta: Parameters of the PriorModel. Optimizer state for Adam. Parameters: epochs: Number of outer optimization epochs. Default: 250. innersteps: Number of Adam optimization steps on PriorModel weights per epoch. Default: 50. beta: Step size for the latent variable update. Default: 0.25. lr: Learning rate for the Adam optimizer on PriorModel weights. Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the PriorModel with random weights. Initialize the Adam optimizer with the PriorModel's parameters and learning rate lr. Compute an initial estimate of the reconstruction by applying Filtered Back Projection (FBP) to the sinogram p: z{init} = \text{FBP}(p). Detach z{init} from the computation graph to prevent gradients from flowing back through the FBP operation: z = z{init}.\text{detach()}. 2. Outer Loop (Epochs): For each epoch from 0 to epochs - 1: a. Data Consistency Update: Compute the current image estimate: x = \text{PriorModel}(z). Compute the forward projection of the estimate: \hat{p} = \text{projector.forward}(x). Compute the residual in projection space: r = p - \hat{p}. Compute the back-projected residual (gradient of the data fidelity term with respect to the image): \delta = \text{projector.backward}(r). Update the latent variable: z = x + \beta \cdot \delta. b. Network Optimization (Inner Steps): For each inner step from 0 to innersteps - 1: Compute the current image estimate: x = \text{PriorModel}(z). Compute the forward projection: \hat{p} = \text{projector.forward}(x). Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between the measured sinogram and the projected estimate: \mathcal{L} = \text{MSE}(\hat{p}, p). Perform backpropagation to compute gradients of \mathcal{L} with respect to the PriorModel parameters \theta. Perform one Adam optimizer step to update \theta. 3. Final Output: After all epochs, compute the final reconstruction: x{final} = \text{PriorModel}(z). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def deepimagepriorreconstruction( sinogram: torch.Tensor, projector: object, priormodel: nn.Module, epochs: int = 250, innersteps: int = 50, beta: float = 0.25, lr: float = 0.01, device: str = 'cpu') -> torch.Tensor: """ Performs Deep Image Prior Reconstruction. Args: sinogram: Measured projection data (torch.Tensor). projector: Object with methods forward(x) and backward(residual). priormodel: Neural network (nn.Module) mapping latent z to image x. epochs: Number of outer epochs. innersteps: Number of Adam steps per epoch. beta: Step size for latent variable update. lr: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. device: Device to run computation on. Returns: Reconstructed image/tensor. """ # Move prior model to device priormodel = priormodel.to(device) # Initialize Adam optimizer on prior model parameters optimizer = optim.Adam(priormodel.parameters(), lr=lr) # Initialize latent variable z using FBP # Note: FBP implementation is assumed to be available or provided by the user. # The result is detached to stop gradient flow through FBP. zinit = fbp(sinogram) # FBP function is not defined in sources; assumed available. z = zinit.detach().to(device) # Loss function mseloss = nn.MSELoss() for epoch in range(epochs): # --- Data Consistency Step --- # 1. Compute current image estimate from latent z x = priormodel(z) # 2. Forward project the estimate phat = projector.forward(x) # 3. Compute residual in sinogram space residualsinogram = sinogram - phat # 4. Back-project residual to image space # This acts as the gradient of the data fidelity term w.r.t x delta = projector.backward(residualsinogram) # 5. Update latent variable z = x + beta delta # --- Network Optimization Steps --- for in range(innersteps): # 1. Forward pass through prior model x = priormodel(z) # 2. Forward projection phat = projector.forward(x) # 3. Compute loss loss = mseloss(phat, sinogram) # 4. Backpropagation and optimizer step optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Final reconstruction output = priormodel(z) return output Edge Cases and Pitfalls: FBP Initialization: The quality of the initial z depends on the FBP implementation. If FBP is not available or inaccurate, the reconstruction may converge to a poor local minimum. Gradient Detachment: It is critical to detach z from the computation graph after FBP initialization. If not detached, gradients will flow through the FBP operator, which is typically non-differentiable or computationally expensive to differentiate. Precision: The method relies on floating-point arithmetic for the latent variable updates. Precision issues may arise if the residual \delta is very small or very large relative to x. Projector Implementation: The projector object must support both forward and backward projections. The backward projection is typically the adjoint of the forward projection (e.g., unweighted back-projection for a weighted forward projection). Uses dual-domain consistency for tomographic reconstruction. Adapts neural network architecture for tomography. Recovers volumes from compressive measurements. Uses gradient information for compressive rendering. Basic analytical reconstruction method. Framework for differentiable CT simulation. Classical iterative algebraic reconstruction technique. Generic optimization-based tomography. Fast Feldkamp-Davis-Kress algorithm for cone-beam CT. Color-based volume reconstruction from multi-view images. Implicit neural representation for holography. Renderer for emissive volumes. Reconstruction for ultrasound B-mode images. Gaussian-based reconstruction method. Time Complexity: The method is iterative and computationally expensive. Each epoch involves one forward/backward projection for the latent update and innersteps forward projections and backpropagations for the network optimization. Total complexity is roughly O(\text{epochs} \times \text{inner\steps} \times (\text{proj\cost} + \text{net\forward\cost})). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the latent variable z, the current image estimate x, and the gradients for the neural network. Memory usage is proportional to the size of the reconstruction grid and the neural network parameters. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Implicit regularization via the neural network architecture often leads to high-quality reconstructions from sparse or noisy data without explicit regularization parameters. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the need for many optimization steps. Convergence is not guaranteed and depends on the initialization and network architecture. When to Use: Suitable for sparse-view tomography or noisy data where traditional methods produce artifacts, and computational resources are available. When Not to Use: Not suitable for real-time applications or when computational efficiency is critical. Deep Image Prior Reconstruction was introduced as a method to leverage the structure of convolutional neural networks as a prior for inverse problems, specifically in the context of tomographic reconstruction. It builds on the Deep Image Prior concept, which suggests that the architecture of a neural network itself acts as a regularizer for natural images. The method was implemented in the DiffTomo repository, demonstrating its application to CT reconstruction. name: DuDoTrans
head: DuDoTransModel, Dual-Domain Transformer
body: DuDoTrans is a dual-domain transformer architecture designed for sparse-view CT reconstruction, addressing the ill-posed nature of tomographic recovery when projection data is limited. It distinguishes itself from standard self-attention methods by employing Window-based Multi-Head Self-Attention (W-MSA) to restrict global context to local windows, thereby reducing computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N \cdot Ws^2) while maintaining long-range dependency modeling through shifted windows. Input: A 4D tensor x of shape (B, H, W, C), where B is batch size, H and W are spatial dimensions (height and width), and C is the channel dimension (embedding dimension). Output: A 4D tensor of the same shape (B, H, W, C). The core component is the Swin Transformer block. Key internal structures include: 1. Relative Position Bias Table: Type: Parameter tensor. Shape: ((2Wh - 1)(2Ww - 1), \text{num\heads}). Initialization: Zeros, followed by truncated normal distribution with standard deviation \sigma = 0.02. 2. Relative Position Index: Type: Buffer tensor (non-trainable). Shape: (Wh Ww, Wh Ww). Content: Integer indices mapping spatial relative positions to the bias table. windowsize: Tuple (Wh, Ww) defining the height and width of the attention window. Default: (7, 7). shiftsize: Integer defining the shift amount for shifted window partitioning. If 0, non-shifted windows are used. Default: 0. mlpratio: Float ratio of the MLP hidden dimension to the embedding dimension. Default: 4.0. qkscale: Float overriding the default QK scaling factor. If None, defaults to head\dim^{-0.5}. Reshape the input tensor x into local windows to restrict attention scope. 1. Reshape x from (B, H, W, C) to (B, H/Ws, Ws, W/Ws, Ws, C). 2. Permute dimensions to (B, H/Ws, W/Ws, Ws, Ws, C). 3. Flatten the first and third spatial dimensions to produce (num\windows \cdot B, Ws, Ws, C), where num\windows = (H/Ws) \cdot (W/Ws). Compute indices to look up learned relative positional biases for attention scores. 1. Generate coordinates: coordsh = \text{arange}(Wh), coordsw = \text{arange}(Ww). 2. Create meshgrid and flatten to shape (2, Wh Ww). Let this be coords\flatten. 3. Compute relative coordinates: relative\coords = coords\flatten[:,:, \text{None}] - coords\flatten[:, \text{None},:]. Shape: (2, Wh Ww, Wh Ww). 4. Permute to (Wh Ww, Wh Ww, 2). 5. Shift indices to make them non-negative: relative\coords[:,:, 0] += Wh - 1 relative\coords[:,:, 1] += Ww - 1 6. Map to 1D index space: relative\coords[:,:, 0] = 2 Ww - 1. 7. Sum the last dimension to get the final index map: relative\position\index = \text{sum}(relative\coords, \text{axis}=-1). Shape: (Wh Ww, Wh Ww). Compute attention within each window. 1. Linear Projection: Compute qkv = \text{Linear}(x). Reshape to (B, N, 3, \text{num\heads}, C/\text{num\heads}) and permute to (3, B, \text{num\heads}, N, C/\text{num\heads}), where B = num\windows \cdot B and N = Ws^2. 2. Scale Q: Extract Q from qkv. Scale it: Q = Q \cdot \text{scale}, where \text{scale} = \text{qk\scale} or head\dim^{-0.5}. 3. Attention Scores: Compute attn = Q @ K^T. Shape: (B, \text{num\heads}, N, N). 4. Add Bias: Retrieve bias: bias = \text{relative\position\bias\table}[relative\position\index]. Shape: (N, N, \text{num\heads}). Reshape and permute bias to (\text{num\heads}, N, N). Add to attention scores: attn = attn + bias. 5. Softmax: Apply softmax along the last dimension: attn = \text{softmax}(attn). 6. Dropout: Apply attention dropout. 7. Output Projection: Compute V{out} = attn @ V. Shape: (B, \text{num\heads}, N, C/\text{num\heads}). Transpose and reshape to (B, N, C). Apply linear projection and projection dropout to get the final output for the window. Reconstruct the full image tensor from the processed windows. 1. Reshape windows from (num\windows \cdot B, Ws, Ws, C) to (B, H/Ws, W/Ws, Ws, Ws, C). 2. Permute to (B, H/Ws, Ws, W/Ws, Ws, C). 3. Flatten to (B, H, W, C). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F import math class WindowAttention(nn.Module): def init(self, dim, windowsize, numheads, qkvbias=True, qkscale=None, attndrop=0., projdrop=0.): super().init() self.dim = dim self.windowsize = windowsize # Wh, Ww self.numheads = numheads headdim = dim // numheads self.scale = qkscale or headdim -0.5 # Relative position bias table shape: (2Wh-1)(2Ww-1), numheads self.relativepositionbiastable = nn.Parameter( torch.zeros((2 windowsize[0] - 1) (2 windowsize[1] - 1), numheads)) # Get pair-wise relative coordinates index coordsh = torch.arange(self.windowsize[0]) coordsw = torch.arange(self.windowsize[1]) coords = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid([coordsh, coordsw])) # 2, Wh, Ww coordsflatten = torch.flatten(coords, 1) # 2, WhWw relativecoords = coordsflatten[:,:, None] - coordsflatten[:, None,:] # 2, WhWw, WhWw relativecoords = relativecoords.permute(1, 2, 0).contiguous() # WhWw, WhWw, 2 relativecoords[:,:, 0] += self.windowsize[0] - 1 # shift to start from 0 relativecoords[:,:, 1] += self.windowsize[1] - 1 relativecoords[:,:, 0] = 2 self.windowsize[1] - 1 relativepositionindex = relativecoords.sum(-1) # WhWw, WhWw self.registerbuffer("relativepositionindex", relativepositionindex) self.qkv = nn.Linear(dim, dim 3, bias=qkvbias) self.attndrop = nn.Dropout(attndrop) self.proj = nn.Linear(dim, dim) self.projdrop = nn.Dropout(projdrop) nn.init.truncnormal(self.relativepositionbiastable, std=.02) def forward(self, x, mask=None): """ x: shape (B, N, C) where N = Wh Ww mask: shape (B, numheads, N, N) or None """ B, N, C = x.shape qkv = self.qkv(x).reshape(B, N, 3, self.numheads, C // self.numheads).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4) q, k, v = qkv[0], qkv[1], qkv[2] # B, numheads, N, headdim q = q self.scale attn = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) # Add relative position bias relativepositionbias = self.relativepositionbiastable[self.relativepositionindex.view(-1)].view( self.windowsize[0] self.windowsize[1], self.windowsize[0] self.windowsize[1], -1) # WhWw, WhWw, nH relativepositionbias = relativepositionbias.permute(2, 0, 1).contiguous() # nH, WhWw, WhWw attn = attn + relativepositionbias.unsqueeze(0) if mask is not None: nW = mask.shape[0] attn = attn.view(B // nW, nW, self.numheads, N, N) + mask.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(0) attn = attn.view(-1, self.numheads, N, N) attn = self.attndrop(attn.softmax(dim=-1)) x = (attn @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, N, C) x = self.proj(x) x = self.projdrop(x) return x class SwinTransformerBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, dim, inputresolution, numheads, windowsize=7, shiftsize=0, mlpratio=4., qkvbias=True, qkscale=None, drop=0., attndrop=0., droppath=0.): super().init() self.dim = dim self.inputresolution = inputresolution self.numheads = numheads self.windowsize = windowsize self.shiftsize = shiftsize self.mlpratio = mlpratio if min(self.inputresolution) <= self.windowsize: # if window size is larger than input resolution, we don't partition windows self.shiftsize = 0 self.windowsize = min(self.inputresolution) assert 0 <= self.shiftsize < self.windowsize, "shiftsize must in 0-windowsize" self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(dim) self.attn = WindowAttention( dim, windowsize=(self.windowsize, self.windowsize), numheads=numheads, qkvbias=qkvbias, qkscale=qkscale, attndrop=attndrop, projdrop=drop) self.droppath = nn.Identity() self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(dim) mlphiddendim = int(dim mlpratio) self.mlp = Mlp(infeatures=dim, hiddenfeatures=mlphiddendim, actlayer=nn.GELU, drop=drop) def forward(self, x): H, W = self.inputresolution B, L, C = x.shape assert L == H W, "input feature has wrong size" shortcut = x x = self.norm1(x) x = x.view(B, H, W, C) # Pad feature map padl = padt = 0 padr = (self.windowsize - W % self.windowsize) % self.windowsize padb = (self.windowsize - H % self.windowsize) % self.windowsize x = F.pad(x, (0, 0, padl, padr, padt, padb)), Hp, Wp, = x.shape # cyclic shift if self.shiftsize > 0: shiftedx = torch.roll(x, shifts=(-self.shiftsize, -self.shiftsize), dims=(1, 2)) else: shiftedx = x # Partition windows xwindows = windowpartition(shiftedx, self.windowsize) # nWB, Wh, Ww, C xwindows = xwindows.view(-1, self.windowsize self.windowsize, C) # nWB, WhWw, C # W-MSA/SW-MSA attnwindows = self.attn(xwindows) # nWB, WhWw, C # Merge windows attnwindows = attnwindows.view(-1, self.windowsize, self.windowsize, C) shiftedx = windowreverse(attnwindows, self.windowsize, Hp, Wp) # B H' W' C # Reverse cyclic shift if self.shiftsize > 0: x = torch.roll(shiftedx, shifts=(self.shiftsize, self.shiftsize), dims=(1, 2)) else: x = shiftedx if padr > 0 or padb > 0: x = x[:,:H,:W,:].contiguous() x = x.view(B, H W, C) # FFN x = shortcut + self.droppath(x) x = x + self.droppath(self.mlp(self.norm2(x))) return x def windowpartition(x, windowsize): """ Args: x: (B, H, W, C) windowsize (int): window size Returns: windows: (numwindowsB, windowsize, windowsize, C) """ B, H, W, C = x.shape x = x.view(B, H // windowsize, windowsize, W // windowsize, windowsize, C) windows = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5).contiguous().view(-1, windowsize, windowsize, C) return windows def windowreverse(windows, windowsize, H, W): """ Args: windows: (numwindowsB, windowsize, windowsize, C) windowsize (int): Window size H (int): Height of image W (int): Width of image Returns: x: (B, H, W, C) """ B = int(windows.shape[0] / (H W / windowsize / windowsize)) x = windows.view(B, H // windowsize, W // windowsize, windowsize, windowsize, -1) x = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5).contiguous().view(B, H, W, -1) return x class Mlp(nn.Module): def init(self, infeatures, hiddenfeatures=None, outfeatures=None, actlayer=nn.GELU, drop=0.): super().init() outfeatures = outfeatures or infeatures hiddenfeatures = hiddenfeatures or infeatures self.fc1 = nn.Linear(infeatures, hiddenfeatures) self.act = actlayer() self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hiddenfeatures, outfeatures) self.drop = nn.Dropout(drop) def forward(self, x): x = self.fc1(x) x = self.act(x) x = self.drop(x) x = self.fc2(x) x = self.drop(x) return x Input Resolution vs Window Size: If the input spatial dimensions (H or W) are smaller than or equal to the windowsize, the shiftsize is forced to 0 and the windowsize is reduced to the minimum input dimension to avoid invalid partitioning. Precision: The relative position bias calculation relies on integer arithmetic for index mapping; ensure no overflow occurs for very large window sizes, though typical values (7x7) are safe. Boundary Handling: Padding is applied during window partitioning to handle cases where H or W are not divisible by windowsize. This padding must be removed before the final output is returned. Time Complexity: The window-based attention reduces complexity from O(N^2) to O(N \cdot Ws^2), where N is the number of tokens and Ws is the window size. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the relative position bias table of size ((2Wh - 1)(2Ww - 1), \text{num\heads}) and intermediate tensors for window partitioning. Strengths: Efficiently handles large images by limiting attention to local windows while capturing global context through shifted windows. Suitable for sparse-view CT where data is limited. Limitations: Performance depends heavily on the choice of windowsize and shiftsize. Not given in the sources. When to Use: Sparse-view CT reconstruction tasks where computational efficiency is critical and global context is needed. When Not to Use: Dense-view CT where standard attention might be feasible, or when real-time inference on extremely low-power hardware is required without optimization. DuDoTrans was introduced by Ce Wang, Kun Shang, Haimiao Zhang, Qian Li, and S. Kevin Zhou in the paper "DuDoTrans: Dual-Domain Transformer for Sparse-View CT Reconstruction", published in the International Workshop on Machine Learning for Medical Image Reconstruction in 2022. It adapts the Swin Transformer architecture, originally designed for natural images, to the domain of tomographic reconstruction, leveraging the dual-domain (spatial and frequency-like) properties of CT data. name: Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT)
body: Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT) is an adaptive, hierarchical neural rendering pipeline for multi-view inverse rendering, designed specifically for the tomographic reconstruction of semi-transparent volumetric scenes from X-ray images. It combines an adaptive explicit octree representation with neural features stored in leaf nodes to achieve efficient reconstruction and simultaneous self-calibration of geometric and photometric parameters. Unlike purely implicit neural representations or hybrid methods like ACORN, NeAT uses a purely explicit hierarchical structure optimized via differentiable volume rendering, which outperforms alternatives in both quality and compute time for tomographic tasks where samples are widely scattered. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N X-ray projection images I(p), where p denotes pixel coordinates. Initial estimates of camera poses (source and detector positions/orientations) and a reference image I0 (empty scan) are required but can be refined. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D volume represented by the optimized octree structure, neural feature grids, decoder weights, and calibrated camera parameters. Data Structures: The scene is represented as a sparse octree. Each node in the octree has the following layout: isleaf: Boolean flag. children: Array of 8 child nodes (if not a leaf). features: A uniform 3D grid of neural feature vectors (only if isleaf is true). The grid dimensions are fixed per node level (e.g., k \times k \times k). empty: Boolean flag indicating if the node contains no density; empty leaf nodes are pruned. Neural Decoder: A small multi-layer perceptron (MLP) decoder \Phi maps a feature vector f to a scalar density \mu: \mu = \Phi(f) The decoder is shared across all leaf nodes and is optimized during training. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize an octree with a single root node containing a coarse grid of random neural features. Initialize the neural decoder \Phi with random weights. Initialize camera parameters (poses) and photometric parameters (reference image I0, per-view exposure multipliers). 2. Ray Generation: For each training image and each pixel p, generate a ray rp(t) = op + t \cdot dp, where op is the X-ray source position and dp is the direction towards the detector pixel. 3. Ray-Octree Intersection: Trace ray rp through the octree. Identify the sequence of leaf nodes intersected by the ray. For each intersected leaf node, compute the entry and exit points tn, tf within the node's local space. 4. Neural Volume Sampling: Sample points ti along the ray segment within each leaf node. For each sample point x, determine its local coordinates within the leaf node's feature grid. Perform trilinear interpolation of the feature vectors from the grid to obtain the feature vector f(x) at x. 5. Density Decoding: Compute the density \mu(x) = \Phi(f(x)) using the shared decoder network. 6. Volume Rendering Integration: Integrate the density along the ray using a weighted sum (quadrature) to compute the estimated ray integral \hat{I}'p(p): \hat{I}'p(p) = \sum{i} wi \mu(xi) where wi are the quadrature weights determined by the sampling strategy and node boundaries. 7. Photometric Calibration: Apply the Beer-Lambert law to compute the final estimated pixel intensity \hat{I}(p): \hat{I}(p) = \hat{I}0(p) \exp \left( - \hat{I}'p(p) \right) where \hat{I}0(p) is the spatially varying source intensity (reference image) possibly modulated by per-view exposure multipliers. 8. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss L{total}: L{total} = \sump ||I(p) - \hat{I}(p)||^2 + \lambda{tv} L{tv} + \lambda{bc} L{bc} where I(p) is the measured intensity, \lambda{tv} and \lambda{bc} are hyperparameters. Total Variation (TV) Loss: Compute on feature vectors (preferred for speed/quality): L{tv} = \sumn \|\nabla fn\|1 where the gradient is computed over the feature grid indices of each leaf node. Boundary Consistency (BC) Loss: Minimize feature discontinuities between neighboring nodes n and m on their shared boundary surface \Lambda{bc}: L{bc} = \sum{(n,m) \in N} \sum{x \in \Lambda{bc}} |fn(x) - fm(x)| where N is the set of neighboring node pairs, and fn(x), fm(x) are the interpolated features at boundary point x from both nodes. 9. Optimization: Perform gradient descent to update: Neural feature grids in all leaf nodes. Decoder weights \Phi. Camera poses (geometric self-calibration). Reference image I0 and exposure multipliers (photometric self-calibration). 10. Octree Update (Adaptive Refinement): Compute volumetric error for each node n: E(n) = \rho{max}(n) \cdot \sum{(p,tn,tf) \in \Omegan} ||I(p) - \hat{I}(p)||^2 where \Omegan is the set of samples passing through node n, and \rho{max}(n) is the maximum density in node n. Solve a mixed-integer program (MIP) to determine the optimal tree structure (splitting nodes with high error, pruning empty nodes) based on E(n). Re-initialize features in newly split nodes and transfer/interpolate features from parent to children. 11. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-10 until convergence or maximum iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trainneat(Xrayimages, initialposes, initialI0, numiterations, lambdatv, lambdabc): """ Xrayimages: List of 2D arrays, shape (H, W), measured intensities. initialposes: List of camera parameters (source, detector). initialI0: 2D array, reference image (empty scan). """ # Initialize Octree octree = Octree(rootfeatures=randomgrid()) # Initialize Decoder decoder = MLP() # Initialize Calibration Parameters poses = copy(initialposes) I0 = copy(initialI0) exposures = np.ones(len(Xrayimages)) for iteration in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0 gradfeatures = [] graddecoder = [] gradposes = [] gradI0 = [] gradexposures = [] # Accumulate gradients for all pixels for viewidx, Imeasured in enumerate(Xrayimages): pose = poses[viewidx] exposure = exposures[viewidx] for p in pixels: # 1. Generate Ray ray = generateray(p, pose) # 2. Intersect Octree samples = octree.traceray(ray) # 3. Sample and Decode densities = [] for sample in samples: f = octree.interpolatefeatures(sample.position) mu = decoder.decode(f) densities.append(mu) # 4. Integrate (Simplified Riemann Sum) rayintegral = sum(d w for d, w in zip(densities, samples.weights)) # 5. Photometric Model I0val = I0[p] exposure Iestimated = I0val np.exp(-rayintegral) # 6. Loss Components mseloss = (Imeasured[p] - Iestimated) 2 # TV Loss (computed on features) tvloss = computetvloss(octree) # BC Loss (computed on boundaries) bcloss = computebcloss(octree) # Total Loss for this pixel (approximate for gradient accumulation) # Note: In practice, gradients are backpropagated through the differentiable renderer pixelloss = mseloss + lambdatv tvloss + lambdabc bcloss # Accumulate gradients (conceptual) # gradfeatures.append(backpropfeatures(pixelloss)) # graddecoder.append(backpropdecoder(pixelloss)) # gradposes.append(backpropposes(pixelloss)) # gradI0.append(backpropI0(pixelloss)) # gradexposures.append(backpropexposure(pixelloss)) totalloss += pixelloss # Update Parameters octree.updatefeatures(gradfeatures) decoder.updateweights(graddecoder) poses.update(gradposes) I0.update(gradI0) exposures.update(gradexposures) # Octree Refinement (every K iterations) if iteration % 10 == 0: octree.refine(lambdatv, lambdabc) return octree, decoder, poses, I0, exposures class Octree: def init(self, rootfeatures): self.root = Node(features=rootfeatures) def traceray(self, ray): # Returns list of Sample objects with position, weight, and leafnode reference pass def interpolatefeatures(self, position): # Find leaf node, compute local coords, trilinear interpolate pass def computetvloss(self): # Sum of L1 norms of gradients of feature grids pass def computebcloss(self): # Sum of L1 norms of feature differences at boundaries pass def refine(self, lambdatv, lambdabc): # Compute E(n) for each node # Solve MIP to split/prune # Re-initialize new nodes pass class Node: def init(self, features=None): self.features = features # 3D grid of vectors self.children = [None] 8 self.isleaf = features is not None Parameters: \lambda{bc}: Boundary Consistency regularizer strength. Typical value: 0.01. \lambda{tv}: Total Variation regularizer strength. Typical value: 0.00002 for sparse view problems, 0.00010 for limited angle problems. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Block-like Artifacts: If the Boundary Consistency regularizer is disabled, block-like artifacts appear at boundaries between neighboring octree nodes, especially with few images. Reference Image Validity: Adding or removing the object from the setup can disturb the validity of the reference image I0, causing reconstruction artifacts. NeAT mitigates this by optimizing I0 during training. Computational Cost: While NeAT is faster than other neural inverse rendering methods, it is still computationally intensive compared to traditional methods like SIRT or FDK. It is designed to handle high-resolution datasets and full 3D cone beam data better than previous neural methods. Sparse Views: The method is specifically designed to handle ill-posed geometric configurations (sparse views or limited angular coverage) where traditional methods fail. Time Complexity: The optimization process is iterative and involves differentiable volume rendering, ray tracing through an octree, and neural network decoding. The time complexity is dominated by the number of iterations, the number of pixels, and the depth of the octree. NeAT achieves reconstruction times far superior to existing neural inverse rendering methods. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of leaf nodes in the octree and the size of the feature grids. The sparse nature of the octree allows for efficient memory usage compared to dense voxel grids. Scaling: NeAT scales well with resolution due to the adaptive octree structure, which only refines regions with detail. It handles full 3D cone beam data effectively. Strengths: High-quality reconstruction for ill-posed configurations (sparse views, limited angles). Simultaneous geometric and photometric self-calibration. Faster than other neural inverse rendering methods. Outperforms purely implicit and hybrid explicit-implicit representations (like ACORN) in tomographic settings. Limitations: Still slower than traditional analytical methods (e.g., FDK, SIRT). Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (\lambda{tv}, \lambda{bc}). Sensitive to initial calibration; however, self-calibration mitigates this. When to Use: Use NeAT when dealing with sparse view or limited angle tomography, when high-quality reconstruction is needed despite ill-posed geometry, and when simultaneous calibration is beneficial. It is suitable when computational resources allow for iterative optimization. When Not to Use: Use traditional methods (e.g., Back-projection, FastFDK) when computational speed is critical and the geometry is well-posed (full angular coverage). Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT) was introduced by Darius Rückert, Yuanhao Wang, Rui Li, Ramzi Idoughi, and Wolfgang Heidrich from KAUST and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg. It was presented in 2022. The method addresses the limitations of existing neural inverse rendering frameworks, which suffer from long computing times, by introducing an adaptive, hierarchical neural representation specifically tuned for tomographic reconstruction. It builds on the concept of neural rendering [Mildenhall et al. 2020] and adaptive representations like ACORN [Martel et al. 2021], but adapts them for the specific challenges of X-ray tomography, such as scattered samples and the need for self-calibration. name: Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods
head: CS-Gradient, CS-Wavelet, Gradient Recovery via CS (Sen and Darabi), Least-Squares (SS), TV Minimization, TV Regularization, Total Variation (TV) Minimization
body: Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods are a set of techniques designed to reconstruct high-quality volume renderings from a sparse subset of pixels, treating the problem as an image restoration or inpainting task. Unlike standard iterative reconstruction methods that solve for voxel values directly via linear systems, these methods exploit prior knowledge about the signal's structure—specifically sparsity in transform domains (wavelet, gradient) or smoothness (Total Variation)—to recover the image from undersampled measurements. They are distinguished from siblings like SIRT by their reliance on non-linear optimization of sparsity-promoting regularizers rather than simple algebraic updates, and from Deep Image Prior Reconstruction by their use of explicit mathematical priors rather than neural network implicit biases. The core problem is recovering an image \mathbf{x} given a vector of rendered pixel values \mathbf{y}, where \mathbf{y} corresponds to only a fraction of the total pixels. The general formulation is a constrained optimization problem: \min{\mathbf{x}} R(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|2 \leq \epsilon where \mathbf{S} is the sampling matrix (selecting the observed pixels), R(\mathbf{x}) is a regularizer promoting the desired prior (sparsity or smoothness), and \epsilon is a noise tolerance. Image \mathbf{x}: A 2D vector of pixel values, size N \times 1, where N is the total number of pixels in the rendered image (e.g., 1200 \times 1200). Sampling Matrix \mathbf{S}: A binary matrix of size M \times N, where M is the number of observed pixels. S{ij} = 1 if pixel j is observed, 0 otherwise. Transform Matrices: \mathbf{W}^{-1}: Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) matrix. \Phi^{-1}: Gaussian blurring matrix (convolution kernel). Coefficients \hat{\mathbf{x}}b: The sparse representation of the blurred image in the transform domain. 1. Formulate the Measurement Equation: For methods exploiting wavelet sparsity (CS-Wavelet), the measurement model incorporates a blurring step to improve incoherence between the sampling matrix and the wavelet basis: \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{S}\Phi^{-1}\mathbf{W}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}b Here, \hat{\mathbf{x}}b is the DWT of the blurred image. The goal is to recover \hat{\mathbf{x}}b. 2. Solve the Optimization Problem: Depending on the specific variant, solve for the coefficients or the image directly using the appropriate solver and regularizer. CS-Wavelet / CS-Gradient: Minimize the L1 norm of the coefficients to promote sparsity. \min{\hat{\mathbf{x}}b} \|\hat{\mathbf{x}}b\|1 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\mathbf{S}\Phi^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}b - \mathbf{y}\|2 \leq \epsilon Use the NESTA solver [BBC11] to carry out L1 minimization. TV Minimization: Minimize the Total Variation seminorm of the image directly. \min{\mathbf{x}} \|\mathbf{x}\|{TV} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|2 \leq \epsilon The TV norm is defined as: \|\mathbf{x}\|{TV}:= \sum{i,j} |x{i+1,j} - x{i,j}| + |x{i,j+1} - x{i,j}| where x{i,j} is the pixel value at coordinates (i, j). Use the NESTA solver. Least-Squares (SS): Solve a regularized least-squares problem. \min{\mathbf{x}} \|\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|2^2 + \lambda \|\mathbf{x}\|2^2 Use Matlab's conjugate gradient solver. 3. Reconstruct the Image: For CS-Wavelet: Once \hat{\mathbf{x}}b is recovered, reconstruct the blurred image \mathbf{x}b = \mathbf{W}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}b. The final image \mathbf{x} is obtained by applying the inverse DWT to the recovered coefficients (effectively \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{W}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}b if \hat{\mathbf{x}}b represents the coefficients of the final image, or deblurring if \hat{\mathbf{x}}b is strictly for the blurred version; the source states "From the recovered coefficients \hat{\mathbf{x}}b, the final image is obtained according to \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{W}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}b"). For TV Minimization and SS: The solution \mathbf{x} from the optimization step is the final image. NESTA Tolerance/Stopping Criteria: 10^{-2} (Source text says "102", likely a typo for 10^{-2} or 1e-2, but explicitly cited as 102 in the parameter list). CS-Wavelet Blurring Filter Standard Deviation: 20. This value balances the trade-off between incoherence (higher sigma) and blurring effects (lower sigma). SS Regularization Parameter (\lambda): 102. Suggested by Xu et al. [XAE12]. Unverified code. Args: y: numpy array, shape (M,), observed pixel values. S: numpy array or sparse matrix, shape (M, N), sampling matrix. method: str, one of 'TV', 'CS-Wavelet', 'SS'. params: dict, optional parameters. 'blurringsigma': float, standard deviation for Gaussian blur (CS-Wavelet). 'tol': float, tolerance for NESTA/CG. 'lambda': float, regularization parameter for SS. Returns: x: numpy array, shape (N,), reconstructed image. """ if params is None: params = {} tol = params.get('tol', 1e-2) if method == 'TV': # Minimize TV subject to data fidelity # Using a simplified gradient descent or proximal method for TV minimization # Note: NESTA is referenced in source, but standard Python implementation # would use FISTA or ADMM for TV minimization. # Here we outline the structure. # Initialize x x = np.zeros(S.shape[1]) # Define TV norm gradient (subgradient) def tvgradient(ximg): # ximg is reshaped to 2D hdiff = np.diff(ximg, axis=0) vdiff = np.diff(ximg, axis=1) # Gradient of L1 norm of gradients # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation requires # handling of the L1 norm subgradient carefully. gradh = np.zeroslike(ximg) gradv = np.zeroslike(ximg) #... (Implementation of TV gradient via divergence of normalized gradients) return gradh + gradv # Optimization loop (e.g., FISTA) # x = optimizetvminimization(y, S, tol) # Placeholder for specific TV solver implementation as NESTA is Matlab-specific. # The source specifies using NESTA for TV minimization. raise NotImplementedError("TV minimization requires a specific solver like NESTA or FISTA. See source.") elif method == 'CS-Wavelet': sigma = params.get('blurringsigma', 20) # 1. Create Gaussian Blurring Matrix Phiinv # In practice, this is a convolution. For matrix form, it's a sparse Toeplitz-like matrix. # A = S @ Phiinv @ Winv # We need to solve for xhatb in y = A @ xhatb # Define the combined operator A # Note: Winv is Inverse DWT. Phiinv is Gaussian Blur. # We solve min ||xhatb||1 s.t. ||S @ Phiinv @ Winv @ xhatb - y||2 <= eps # Implementing NESTA in pure Python is complex. # We outline the linear system setup. # Create a function that applies A to a vector def applyA(v): # v is coefficients in wavelet domain # 1. "y = S Phiinv Winv xhatb". # If xhatb are coefficients of xb, then xb = Winv xhatb. # Then y = S xb. # The term Phiinv in the source equation y = S Phiinv Winv xhatb seems to # imply that the measurement is taken on the blurred image, but the coefficients # are of the blurred image. # Actually, the source says: "recover a blurred version xb... xb = Phi x". # And "y = S Phiinv Winv xhatb". # If xhatb is the DWT of xb, then xb = Winv xhatb. # So y = S xb. # The Phiinv term in the source equation (3.7) might be a typo or refers to # the relationship between the original image and the blurred image in the # optimization constraint. # Let's stick to the source's explicit equation: y = S @ Phiinv @ Winv @ xhatb. # This implies the measurement is S applied to (Phiinv applied to (Winv applied to xhatb)). # This is confusing. Phiinv would be deblur. # If y = S xb, then Phiinv is not needed in the forward model if xhatb is coeffs of xb. # However, the source explicitly writes: y = S Phiinv Winv xhatb. # We will implement the matrix-vector product as defined. # Step 1: Inverse DWT img = inversedwt(v) # Step 2: Apply Phiinv (Deblurring? Or is Phiinv the blur matrix itself?) # Source: "Phi^-1 is the Gaussian blurring matrix". This is contradictory notation. # Usually Phi is the blur. If Phi^-1 is the blur, then Phi is deblur. # Let's assume the matrix named Phiinv in the source is the Blur Matrix. imgblurred = applygaussianblur(img, sigma) # Step 3: Sample ypred = S @ imgblurred return ypred # Solve L1 minimization using NESTA-like algorithm # xhatb = nestsolve(applyA, y, tol) raise NotImplementedError("NESTA solver is Matlab-specific. See source.") elif method == 'SS': # Least Squares with L2 regularization # min ||Sx - y||^2 + lambda ||x||^2 # Normal equations: (S^T S + lambda I) x = S^T y lambdareg = params.get('lambda', 102) # Construct the linear system # A = S^T S + lambda I # b = S^T y # Using conjugate gradient def matvec(v): return S.T @ (S @ v) + lambdareg v Aop = LinearOperator((S.shape[1], S.shape[1]), matvec=matvec) b = S.T @ y x, status = cg(Aop, b, tol=tol) return x else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown method: {method}") def inversedwt(coeffs): # Placeholder for Inverse DWT # Use pywt.idwt or similar pass def applygaussianblur(image, sigma): # Placeholder for Gaussian Blur # Use scipy.ndimage.gaussianfilter pass Blurring Variance Sensitivity: The method is sensitive to the variance of the Gaussian blurring filter. It must be adjusted on a case-by-case basis to balance incoherence and blurring effects. High Missing Pixel Fraction: The method breaks down when the fraction of missing pixels is high. Pixel Distribution: The method is sensitive to the distribution of the observed pixels. A compressive volume rendering reconstruction approach where the image is reconstructed globally with the solver running the entire image at once. A technique to render a full image by using only a subset of pixels, reconstructed using an image representation model. Time Complexity: Depends on the solver. NESTA (used for TV and CS-Wavelet) and Conjugate Gradient (used for SS) are iterative. The source does not provide explicit Big-O complexity but notes that runtime is a factor in parameter tuning. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the sampling matrix \mathbf{S} and potentially the transform matrices. For 1200 \times 1200 images, this is manageable on the tested hardware (16GB RAM). Measured Performance: Tested on a Quad-core 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7-3770 CPU with 16GB RAM. Test images were 1200 \times 1200. Data resolution was \sim 256 \times 256 \times 256. Quality Metrics: Evaluated using PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio), SSIM (Structural SIMilarity), and CIELUV error images. Strengths: Can handle higher percentages of missing pixels compared to simple interpolation; produces high-quality recovery results by exploiting sparsity. Limitations: Sensitive to parameter tuning (blurring sigma, regularization); breaks down with very high missing pixel fractions; sensitive to pixel distribution. When to Use: When the volume rendering has sparse sampling and the image exhibits sparsity in wavelet or gradient domains. When Not to Use: When the fraction of missing pixels is extremely high, or when real-time performance is critical and iterative solvers are too slow. The methods are based on the work of Sen and Darabi [SD11], who introduced CS-Wavelet to handle incoherence between point sampling and the wavelet basis by recovering a blurred version of the image. The application of Total Variation (TV) minimization to compressive rendering was investigated as an image restoration problem, drawing on prior work in denoising and inpainting. The Least-Squares (SS) method references Xu et al. [XAE12]. The thesis provides a comprehensive comparison of these methods, including CS-Gradient (using DFT sparsity) and Dictionary Learning, within the context of compressive volume rendering. name: Local Solver
head: Block-based gradient solver, Block-wise CG Solver, Compressive Rendering (Local Solver), Local Conjugate Gradient Solver, Tiled CG Solver
body: The Local Solver is a parallel implementation of the conjugate gradient solver for compressive volume rendering that partitions the image into smaller, mutually exclusive blocks to reduce global memory access and improve performance using shared memory. It solves the inverse problem by reconstructing a full image through independent block-wise solutions that are subsequently merged. It differs from the Global Solver [4281-global-solver.md] by processing blocks independently, which allows for different numbers of iterations per block based on local convergence criteria, thereby optimizing computational cost. The method solves the linear system (S^T S + \lambda H)x = S^T y derived from the compressive rendering formulation, where S is the sampling matrix, H is the convolution filter, \lambda is a regularization parameter, and y is the given image with missing pixels. Inputs: The sampling matrix S, the convolution filter H, the regularization parameter \lambda, and the input image y containing missing pixels. Outputs: The reconstructed volume density field x. Shared Memory: Used per block to store intermediate vectors for the conjugate gradient algorithm. The amount of memory is limited, typically 48 KB per block. Ghost Elements: A padded region surrounding each image block containing known pixels from neighboring blocks to incorporate neighborhood information. Thread Configuration: The number of threads per block in the x and y dimensions, denoted as threadSizex and threadSizey. A configuration of 16 \times 16 threads produces the best results. Padding Size (P): The size of the ghost element border, defined as P = kernelWidth/2, where kernelWidth is the width of the convolution filter. The image is partitioned into blocks. The number of blocks in each dimension is calculated as: blockNumberx = \frac{imageWidth - P}{threadSizex + P} blockNumbery = \frac{imageHeight - P}{threadSizey + P} 1. Partition: Divide the image data into mutually exclusive blocks of size (threadSizex + P) \times (threadSizey + P), including the padding region. 2. Pad: For each block, populate the border region of size P with "ghost elements" (known pixels) from the neighboring blocks in the original image y. This ensures the convolution operation has access to neighborhood data. 3. Initialize: For each block, initialize the conjugate gradient vectors (r, p, x) based on the local sub-problem defined by the padded block data. 4. Iterate: Run the conjugate gradient solver locally for each block. Perform block-wise convolution using the shared memory. Perform vector dot product reductions using parallel reduction (complexity O(\log n)) within the block. Update vectors r, p, x. Check for convergence. Since blocks are independent, each block may require a different number of iterations to converge. 5. Synchronize: Use syncthreads() within each block to ensure correct execution order when writing to shared memory, as global fences do not apply. 6. Merge: Combine the reconstructed blocks into the final image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localsolver(imagewidth, imageheight, samplingmatrixS, convolutionfilterH, lambdaparam, inputimagey): """ Solves the compressive rendering problem using a block-wise conjugate gradient solver. """ # Parameters threadsizex = 16 threadsizey = 16 kernelwidth = len(convolutionfilterH) # Assuming 1D filter width for simplicity P = kernelwidth // 2 # Calculate block dimensions blockwidth = threadsizex + P blockheight = threadsizey + P # Calculate number of blocks numblocksx = (imagewidth - P) // blockwidth numblocksy = (imageheight - P) // blockheight # Initialize output image reconstructedimage = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) for bx in range(numblocksx): for by in range(numblocksy): # 1. Extract block coordinates xstart = bx blockwidth ystart = by blockheight xend = xstart + blockwidth yend = ystart + blockheight # 2. Create local block data with ghost elements # Local block size includes padding localblock = zeros((blockheight, blockwidth)) # Copy center data from input image (handling boundaries if necessary) # Note: Ghost elements are known pixels from neighbors # In a real implementation, this requires careful indexing to fetch # neighbors from inputimagey. centerxstart = bx threadsizex centerystart = by threadsizey # Fill center localblock[P:P+threadsizey, P:P+threadsizex] = \ inputimagey[ystart:ystart+threadsizey, xstart:xstart+threadsizex] # Fill ghost elements (padding) # Top padding if by > 0: localblock[0:P, P:P+threadsizex] = \ inputimagey[ystart-P:ystart, xstart:xstart+threadsizex] # Bottom padding if by < numblocksy - 1: localblock[threadsizey+P:, P:P+threadsizex] = \ inputimagey[ystart+threadsizey:ystart+threadsizey+P, xstart:xstart+threadsizex] # Left padding if bx > 0: localblock[P:P+threadsizey, 0:P] = \ inputimagey[ystart:ystart+threadsizey, xstart-P:xstart] # Right padding if bx < numblocksx - 1: localblock[P:P+threadsizey, threadsizex+P:] = \ inputimagey[ystart:ystart+threadsizey, xstart+threadsizex:xstart+threadsizex+P] # 3. Run Conjugate Gradient on local block # The system is (Slocal^T Slocal + lambda H) xlocal = Slocal^T ylocal # Slocal and H are restricted to the block dimensions. # Shared memory is used for vectors r, p, x. xlocal = conjugategradientlocal(localblock, samplingmatrixS, convolutionfilterH, lambdaparam) # 4. Store result back to global image (only the center part) reconstructedimage[ystart:ystart+threadsizey, xstart:xstart+threadsizex] = \ xlocal[P:P+threadsizey, P:P+threadsizex] return reconstructedimage def conjugategradientlocal(b, Amat, lambdaparam, Hmat): """ Standard Conjugate Gradient solver for the local block. Amat represents the system matrix derived from S and H. """ # Initialize x = zeroslike(b) r = b - matvecmul(Amat, x) p = r rsold = dotproduct(r, r) # Iteration for i in range(maxiterations): # maxiterations is a parameter Ap = matvecmul(Amat, p) pAp = dotproduct(p, Ap) if pAp == 0: break # Singular matrix alpha = rsold / pAp x = x + alpha p r = r - alpha Ap rsnew = dotproduct(r, r) if sqrt(rsnew) < tolerance: break p = r + (rsnew / rsold) p rsold = rsnew return x def matvecmul(M, v): """Matrix-vector multiplication.""" return M @ v def dotproduct(v1, v2): """Parallel reduction dot product.""" return sum(v1 v2) Boundary Artifacts: Without padding with ghost elements, the local solver generates incoherent results and boundary artifacts around the border of each block because the convolution lacks neighborhood information. Shared Memory Limits: The limited amount of shared memory (e.g., 48 KB) restricts the size of the blocks and the number of vectors that can be stored simultaneously. Race Conditions: Uncontrolled execution of threads may lead to race conditions if multiple threads try to read/write the same shared memory location without synchronization. Synchronization Scope: syncthreads() only synchronizes threads within a block. It does not act as a global fence, so care must be taken when merging results. Performance: The local solver significantly improves performance compared to the global solver by reducing global memory traffic. Using shared memory for block-level computations avoids the bottleneck of global memory access. Complexity: The parallel reduction for dot products has a complexity of O(\log n), which is more efficient than the O(n) complexity of sequential summation. Adaptivity: Since each block is solved independently, the solver can adapt the number of iterations per block based on local convergence, potentially reducing computational cost. Limitations: The method is constrained by the limited shared memory per block. It also requires careful handling of block boundaries via padding. The Local Solver was proposed as part of a parallel approach to GPU-based compressive volume rendering to address the poor performance of global solvers on GPUs due to high data transfer rates between CPU and GPU and global memory bottlenecks. It builds on the global solver approach [4281-global-solver.md] by decomposing the global problem into local problems. The method was detailed in a thesis by Liu and Alim et al., which compared CPU-based reconstruction times with parallel GPU approaches.
