name: Compressive Gradient Rendering
head: CS-Gradient
body: Compressive Gradient Rendering is a compressive sensing technique that renders discrete gradient components instead of pixel values to exploit sparsity in the Fourier domain, then reconstructs the image using a Poisson solver. It differs from standard volume rendering by optimizing for gradient coefficients in the frequency domain rather than direct pixel intensities, allowing for reconstruction from fewer samples than the Nyquist rate. Inputs: A set of m random pixel locations defined by a sampling matrix \mathbf{S}. A volume scene to render. A pixel reconstruction kernel (e.g., bilinear B-spline or Mitchell-Netravali cubic kernel). A noise tolerance parameter \epsilon. Outputs: The reconstructed image \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: \mathbf{y}1: An m \times 1 column vector containing the measured horizontal gradient components at the m sampled locations. \mathbf{y}2: An m \times 1 column vector containing the measured vertical gradient components at the m sampled locations. \hat{\mathbf{x}}1: The 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the horizontal gradient component. \hat{\mathbf{x}}2: The 2D DFT of the vertical gradient component. \mathbf{F}^{-1}: The inverse 2D DFT matrix. Steps: 1. Render Horizontal Gradient Component (x1): Compute the horizontal gradient measurements \mathbf{y}1. This is achieved by weighting incoming rays with the derivative of the pixel reconstruction kernel (e.g., the derivative of a bilinear B-spline or Mitchell-Netravali cubic kernel). Alternatively, one can use a box filter for rendering and apply a finite differencing scheme to obtain the gradient. The sensing mechanism is formulated as: \mathbf{y}1 = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}1 where \mathbf{y}1 is the measured gradient vector, \mathbf{S} is the sampling matrix, \mathbf{F}^{-1} is the inverse 2D DFT matrix, and \hat{\mathbf{x}}1 is the 2D DFT of the horizontal gradient. 2. Recover Horizontal Gradient DFT (\hat{\mathbf{x}}1): Solve the l1 minimization problem to approximate \hat{\mathbf{x}}1: \min \|\hat{\mathbf{x}}1\|1 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}1 - \mathbf{y}1\|2 \leq \epsilon This step exploits the sparsity of the gradient in the Fourier domain. 3. Render Vertical Gradient Component (x2): Compute the vertical gradient measurements \mathbf{y}2 using the same method as step 1 (weighting by the kernel derivative or finite differencing after box filtering). 4. Recover Vertical Gradient DFT (\hat{\mathbf{x}}2): Solve the analogous l1 minimization problem for the vertical component: \min \|\hat{\mathbf{x}}2\|1 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}2 - \mathbf{y}2\|2 \leq \epsilon. 5. Reconstruct Image (\mathbf{x}): Recover the pixel values from the gradient components by applying a Poisson solver with Dirichlet boundary conditions to the divergence of the gradient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.fft import fft2, ifft2, fftshift, ifftshift from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve from scipy.sparse import diags, kron def compressivegradientrendering(volume, samplingindices, epsilon, kernelderivativefunc): """ Reconstructs an image from compressive gradient measurements. Args: volume: 3D array representing the volume density. samplingindices: List of (row, col) tuples for the m sampled pixels. epsilon: Noise tolerance for the l1 minimization constraint. kernelderivativefunc: Function that returns the derivative of the reconstruction kernel at a given offset. Returns: x: Reconstructed 2D image. """ # 1. Render Horizontal Gradient Measurements (y1) # Weight incoming rays with the derivative of the pixel reconstruction kernel. # For a specific sample location (r, c), the gradient is computed by integrating # the volume along the ray, weighted by the kernel derivative. # Note: The exact ray marching integration depends on the volume representation. # Here we assume a helper rendergradientcomponent exists that performs # the weighted integration for a specific direction. y1 = np.zeros(len(samplingindices)) y2 = np.zeros(len(samplingindices)) for i, (r, c) in enumerate(samplingindices): # Render horizontal gradient component y1[i] = rendergradientcomponent(volume, r, c, direction='horizontal', kernelderivative=kernelderivativefunc) # Render vertical gradient component y2[i] = rendergradientcomponent(volume, r, c, direction='vertical', kernelderivative=kernelderivativefunc) # 2. Recover DFT of Horizontal Gradient (xhat1) # Solve: min ||xhat1||1 s.t. ||S F^-1 xhat1 - y1||2 <= epsilon # This is a Compressed Sensing problem. We use an iterative solver (e.g., ISTA or FISTA). # Let A = S F^-1. We want to solve A xhat1 approx y1. # Define the forward operator A for horizontal gradient # A is a partial Fourier matrix if sampling locations are random. # We construct the matrix A explicitly for small problems or use an operator for large ones. # For implementation clarity, we assume a solver function solvel1minimization # that handles the optimization. xhat1 = solvel1minimization(y1, samplingindices, epsilon, ishorizontal=True) xhat2 = solvel1minimization(y2, samplingindices, epsilon, ishorizontal=False) # 3. Reconstruct Image from Gradients # Apply Poisson solver with Dirichlet boundary conditions to the divergence of the gradient. # Divergence in spatial domain corresponds to multiplication by ik in frequency domain, # but we have gradients in frequency domain. # We need to convert xhat1 and xhat2 back to spatial gradients, then solve Poisson. # Inverse DFT to get spatial gradients gradx = np.real(ifft2(xhat1)) grady = np.real(ifft2(xhat2)) # Divergence of gradient (Laplacian of the image) # div(grad) = d(gradx)/dx + d(grady)/dy # We approximate derivatives using finite differences or spectral methods. # Using spectral method for consistency with DFT approach: # d/dx corresponds to multiplication by ikx, d/dy by iky. H, W = gradx.shape kx = np.fft.fftfreq(W) 2 np.pi ky = np.fft.fftfreq(H) 2 np.pi KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kx, ky) # Gradient in frequency domain: Gx = ikx X, Gy = iky X # We have Gx and Gy (which are gradx and grady in spatial domain, so their DFTs are xhat1, xhat2) # So X = Gx / (ikx) and X = Gy / (iky) # To avoid division by zero at DC component, we use a Poisson solver in spatial domain. # Construct Laplacian matrix for Poisson equation: div(grad) = Laplacian(x) # Using 5-point stencil for Laplacian N = H W maindiag = np.full(N, -4.0) offdiag1 = np.full(N - 1, 1.0) # horizontal neighbors offdiag2 = np.full(N - H, 1.0) # vertical neighbors # Remove connections across boundaries for r in range(H): for c in range(1, W): idx = r W + c offdiag1[idx - 1] = 0 # Break horizontal link at left boundary # Actually, simpler to build sparse matrix directly rows = [] cols = [] vals = [] for r in range(H): for c in range(W): idx = r W + c # Center rows.append(idx) cols.append(idx) vals.append(-4.0) # Neighbors if c > 0: rows.append(idx) cols.append(idx - 1) vals.append(1.0) if c < W - 1: rows.append(idx) cols.append(idx + 1) vals.append(1.0) if r > 0: rows.append(idx) cols.append(idx - W) vals.append(1.0) if r < H - 1: rows.append(idx) cols.append(idx + W) vals.append(1.0) Alaplacian = sps.csrmatrix((vals, (rows, cols)), shape=(N, N)) # Right hand side: divergence of gradient # div(grad) = d(gradx)/dx + d(grady)/dy # Approximate derivatives using finite differences on the spatial gradients rhs = np.zeros(N) for r in range(H): for c in range(W): idx = r W + c # d(gradx)/dx if c > 0 and c < W - 1: rhs[idx] += (gradx[r, c+1] - gradx[r, c-1]) / 2.0 elif c == 0: rhs[idx] += (gradx[r, 1] - gradx[r, 0]) # Forward diff elif c == W - 1: rhs[idx] += (gradx[r, c] - gradx[r, c-1]) # Backward diff # d(grady)/dy if r > 0 and r < H - 1: rhs[idx] += (grady[r+1, c] - grady[r-1, c]) / 2.0 elif r == 0: rhs[idx] += (grady[1, c] - grady[0, c]) elif r == H - 1: rhs[idx] += (grady[r, c] - grady[r-1, c]) # Solve A x = rhs # Dirichlet boundary conditions: assume boundary pixels are 0 or known. # For simplicity, we solve for interior points and set boundaries to 0. # This is a simplification. interiormask = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=bool) interiormask[1:-1, 1:-1] = True interiorindices = np.where(interiormask) interiorflatindices = interiorindices[0] W + interiorindices[1] Asub = Alaplacian[np.ix(interiorflatindices, interiorflatindices)] rhssub = rhs[interiorflatindices] xinterior = spsolve(Asub, rhssub) x = np.zeros((H, W)) x[interiormask] = xinterior return x def solvel1minimization(y, samplingindices, epsilon, ishorizontal): """ Solves the l1 minimization problem for gradient recovery. min ||xhat||1 s.t. ||S F^-1 xhat - y||2 <= epsilon """ # This is a compressed sensing problem. # We use a standard solver like ISTA or FISTA. # For brevity, we assume a library function or implementation exists. # Note: The matrix A = S F^-1 is a partial Fourier matrix. # Construct the measurement matrix A # F^-1 is the inverse DFT matrix. S selects rows. # We can compute A v = S ifft2(v) # Using a simple ISTA implementation H, W = 256, 256 # Assume fixed size for example, or infer from volume N = H W # Create sampling mask mask = np.zeros((H, W)) for r, c in samplingindices: mask[r, c] = 1 # Define the forward operator def forwardop(v): vimg = v.reshape(H, W) vifft = ifft2(vimg) vsampled = vifft mask return vsampled.flatten() # Define the adjoint operator def adjointop(yvec): yimg = yvec.reshape(H, W) yfull = yimg / mask # This is dangerous if mask is 0. # Correct adjoint for S F^-1 is F^-H S^H # S^H expands the vector to full size with zeros yexpanded = np.zeros((H, W)) yexpanded[samplingindices] = yvec # F^-H is the conjugate transpose of F^-1, which is F (forward DFT) yifft2 = fft2(yexpanded) return yifft2.flatten() # ISTA Iteration xhat = np.zeros(N) stepsize = 1.0 / (np.linalg.norm(forwardop(np.eye(N)[:, 0]), 2)2) # Approximate Lipschitz constant for iteration in range(100): residual = forwardop(xhat) - y grad = adjointop(residual) xhatnew = xhat - stepsize grad # Soft thresholding threshold = epsilon stepsize # Heuristic, exact threshold depends on formulation xhatnew = np.sign(xhatnew) np.maximum(np.abs(xhatnew) - threshold, 0) xhat = xhatnew return xhat Parameters: \epsilon: Noise tolerance. Typical values depend on the noise level of the rendering process. Not given in the sources. Sampling matrix \mathbf{S}: Should contain random pixel locations to ensure \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1} is a partial Fourier matrix. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The Poisson solver requires Dirichlet boundary conditions. The choice of boundary values affects the reconstruction. DC Component: The Fourier transform of the gradient at the DC component (0,0) is zero. This does not affect the gradient recovery but must be handled when reconstructing the image from gradients (the Poisson solver handles this implicitly by solving for the image relative to boundaries). Precision: The l1 minimization is sensitive to the choice of solver and parameters. Inaccurate recovery of \hat{\mathbf{x}}1 and \hat{\mathbf{x}}2 will lead to artifacts in the final image. Time Complexity: The method involves rendering m samples, solving two l1 minimization problems (which are iterative and computationally expensive), and solving a Poisson equation. The complexity is dominated by the l1 minimization, which is typically O(k \cdot N \log N) or worse depending on the solver, where k is the number of iterations and N is the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the volume, the gradient measurements, and the intermediate Fourier coefficients. The Poisson solver requires a sparse matrix of size N \times N. Strengths: Exploits sparsity in the gradient domain, allowing for reconstruction from fewer samples than the Nyquist rate. This can lead to significant computational savings in rendering. Limitations: The l1 minimization is computationally intensive. The method assumes the gradient is sparse in the Fourier domain, which may not hold for all images. When to Use: Suitable for applications where rendering is expensive and the image is known to be sparse in the gradient domain (e.g., MRI, certain types of volume data). When Not to Use: Not suitable for real-time rendering or when the image is not sparse in the gradient domain. Compressive Gradient Rendering was introduced in the thesis "Compressive Volume Rendering". It builds on the principles of Compressive Sensing (CS), which suggests that signals sparse in some domain can be reconstructed from a small number of measurements. The method adapts CS to volume rendering by rendering gradient components instead of pixel values, leveraging the sparsity of gradients in the Fourier domain. The approach is inspired by work in Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) where point measurements in the DFT domain are feasible. The image reconstruction from gradients uses a Poisson solver as described by Pérez et al.. Compressive Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.11575/prism/25391, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Back-projection
head: 2D → 3D Backward Projection, Adjoint Backprojection, Adjoint Projection, Adjoint of xrt_apply, Differentiable XRT Back-Projection, Fourier Backprojection
body: Back-projection is the mathematical adjoint (transpose) of the forward projection operator, used to accumulate 2D projection data into a 3D reconstruction volume. It solves the problem of mapping measured projection weights to volume expansion coefficients, serving as the core gradient computation step in differentiable tomographic reconstruction. Unlike direct methods like FDK which may suffer from artifacts with limited projections, back-projection provides the exact transpose required for stable iterative optimization over many iterations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D Fourier-space projections of shape [B, P, H, W/2+1]. Output: 3D reconstruction volume of shape [B, D, H{rec}, W{rec}/2+1], where D = H{rec} = W{rec} = H \cdot \text{oversampling}, forming a cubic volume. Parameters: rayspec: Tuple of ray anchors \mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^D and directions \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^D. knotspec: UniformSpec defining volume properties (\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{\Delta}, \mathbf{Q}). order: Integer 0, 1, or 2, selecting the basis function \psi for interpolation. data: Array of shape (L,) containing projections gl \in \mathbb{R}. buffer: Flattened C-ordered buffer of shape (Q1, \dots, QD) to accumulate weights f{\mathbf{q}} \in \mathbb{R}. mode: Differentiation mode. Data Structures: ArrayNf: Float array type (e.g., drjit.Array3f). ArrayNi: Int32 array type. ArrayNu: Uint32 array type. Float: Scalar value type. Bool: Mask type. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the accumulation buffer to zeros if None, or assert it matches the size math.prod(knotspec.num). Determine dimension D from ArrayNf size; assert D \in \{2, 3\}. 2. Coordinate Mapping (2D→3D): For each projection coordinate \mathbf{k}{proj} = (kr, kc), extend to 3D by setting the third coordinate to zero: \mathbf{k}{3D} = (kc, kr, 0). This implements the central slice through the origin. 3. Rotation Inverse: Compute the 3D sampling coordinate in the reconstruction \mathbf{k}{rec} using the inverse of the 3×3 rotation matrix \mathbf{R} used in forward projection: \mathbf{k}{rec} = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{k}{3D}. 4. Phase Modulation (if shifts present): If shifts are present, conjugate phase-modulate the projection data to ensure the mathematical adjoint relationship. 5. Interpolation and Accumulation: Accumulate the projection value into the reconstruction at \mathbf{k}{rec} using 3D interpolation kernels in transpose mode: Trilinear (Order 1): Distribute contributions to the 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighborhood around the fractional coordinate. Tricubic (Order 2): Spread contributions across the 4 \times 4 \times 4 neighborhood according to Catmull-Rom weights. Voxel (Order 0): Scatter add length L times data to the accumulator at the computed offset. 6. Weight Accumulation (Optional): Accumulate weights using the absolute values of the 3D interpolation kernel weights, handling 3D Friedel symmetry for real-valued reconstructions. Backward Pass (Gradient Computation): 1. Projection Gradients: Compute projection gradients using 3D→2D forward projection of reconstruction gradients, exploiting the adjoint relationship. 2. Rotation Matrix Gradients: Compute 3×3 rotation matrix gradients using Eq. 15, with spatial derivatives computed via Eqs. 16–18 (trilinear) or Eq. 19 (tricubic). 3. Shift Gradients: Compute shift gradients using Eq. 22, applied to the 2D projection coordinates: \frac{\partial P}{\partial \mathbf{s}} = -i2\pi\mathbf{k}{proj}P(\mathbf{k}{proj}) \quad (22). Pseudocode (2D→3D Adjoint Accumulation): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backproject2dto3d(projections, rotationmatrix, shifts, buffer, interpolationorder): """ Accumulates 2D Fourier projections into a 3D volume buffer. projections: [B, P, H, W/2+1] rotationmatrix: 3x3 matrix R shifts: optional shift array buffer: [B, D, Hrec, Wrec/2+1] initialized to 0 """ # 1. Extend 2D coords to 3D central slice # kproj = (kr, kc) -> k3D = (kc, kr, 0) k3d = extendto3d(projections) # 2. Apply inverse rotation krec = applyinverserotation(k3d, rotationmatrix) # 3. Handle shifts via conjugate phase modulation if shifts is not None: projections = conjugatephasemodulate(projections, shifts) # 4. Accumulate using interpolation kernel in transpose mode if interpolationorder == 1: # Trilinear accumulatetrilinear(buffer, krec, projections) elif interpolationorder == 2: # Tricubic accumulatetricubic(buffer, krec, projections) return buffer def accumulatetrilinear(buffer, krec, projections): """Distribute contributions to 2x2x2 neighborhood.""" # For each fractional coordinate in krec: # Compute weights for 8 neighbors # Scatter add: buffer[neighbor] += weight projectionvalue pass def accumulatetricubic(buffer, krec, projections): """Distribute contributions to 4x4x4 neighborhood using Catmull-Rom.""" # For each fractional coordinate in krec: # Compute Catmull-Rom weights for 64 neighbors # Scatter add: buffer[neighbor] += weight projectionvalue pass Pseudocode (3D Voxel Backprojection with DDA): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backprojectvoxel(rayspec, knotspec, data, buffer): """ Ray-traced backprojection for order=0 (voxel). rayspec: (rayt, rayn) knotspec: (x0, delta, Q) data: (L,) projection values buffer: (Q1, Q2, Q3) accumulation buffer """ rayt, rayn = rayspec x0, delta, Q = knotspec L = len(data) # Compute bounding box bboxll = x0 - (delta / 2) bboxur = x0 - (delta / 2) + (Q delta) # Stride for 3D buffer stride = ArrayNu(Q.y Q.z, Q.z, 1) # DDA Loop for i in range(L): t = rayt[i] n = rayn[i] # Ray-BBox Intersection active, t1, t2 = raybboxintersect(t, n, bboxll, bboxur) if not active: continue tmin = min(t1, t2) tmax = max(t1, t2) # Traverse grid cells currentt = tmin while currentt < tmax: # Get current cell index cellidx = getcellindex(t + currentt n, x0, delta) # Compute length of ray segment in this cell # Lseg = norm((pb - pa) delta) / prod(delta) # Simplified for voxel: contribution is proportional to path length pathlength = computepathlengthincell(t + currentt n, n, cellidx, x0, delta) # Scatter add offset = dot(cellidx, stride) buffer[offset] += pathlength data[i] # Advance currentt += steptonextcell(t + currentt n, n, cellidx, delta) return buffer An operator that generates 2D projections from a 3D Fourier-space reconstruction by sampling central slices through the 3D volume, implementing the Central Slice Theorem. A GPU-accelerated cone-beam CT reconstruction method that iterates over projection angles, loading each projection into global memory and accumulating contributions into a volume buffer using a single kernel launch per projection. GPU-based backprojection using OpenCL buffers for data storage. GPU-based backprojection using OpenCL image textures for data storage, likely leveraging hardware interpolation. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of projections P, volume resolution V, and interpolation kernel size K. For direct backprojection, O(P \cdot V \cdot K^D). Memory Complexity: O(V) for the reconstruction buffer plus O(P) for projections. Performance: Benchmarks on NVIDIA H100, Apple M4 CPU, and M4 Metal show throughput in thousands of projections per second, scaling with box size (32–256 pixels), batch size (1–8), and pose count (8–2048). Strengths: Provides the exact adjoint required for stable gradient-based optimization in differentiable rendering. Handles arbitrary 3D detector shifts and non-equispaced angles. Limitations: Direct methods like FDK (which uses backprojection) yield worse results than iterative methods (like SIRT) when projections are limited. Exact transposes may be less computationally efficient than approximate methods, though necessary for stability over many iterations. When to Use: Differentiable tomographic reconstruction, iterative optimization requiring stable gradients, cryo-EM reconstruction with CTF correction. When Not to Use: Real-time rendering where approximate methods suffice, or when limited projections make direct backprojection artifacts unacceptable without iterative refinement. Back-projection originates from the mathematical theory of the Radon transform and its inverse, forming the basis of filtered back-projection (FBP) algorithms in CT. In the context of differentiable rendering, it is formalized as the adjoint of the X-ray transform (forward projection), enabling gradient computation for volume parameters. The specific implementation described here, xrtadjoint, is part of the differentiablexrt library, designed for high-performance differentiable projection on GPUs using Dr.Jit. It addresses the need for matched projectors in iterative reconstruction to ensure stability over thousands of iterations, a requirement often violated by standard CT packages that prioritize speed over exact transposition. torch-projectors: A High-Performance Differentiable Projection Library for PyTorch, https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.03.10.710885, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) HaouchatY/differentiablexrt, https://github.com/HaouchatY/differentiablexrt, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Differentiable Forward Projector for X-ray Computed Tomography, https://differentiable.xyz/papers-2023/paper48.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Space-Time Tomographic Reconstruction of Deforming Objects, https://vccimaging.org/Publications/Zang2020Thesis/Zang2020Thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Forward Projection
head: 3D → 2D Forward Projection, Central Slice Theorem Projection, Fourier Slice Projection
body: Forward projection generates 2D projections from a 3D Fourier-space reconstruction by sampling central slices through the 3D volume, implementing the Central Slice Theorem. It serves as the differentiable forward operator in tomographic reconstruction pipelines, acting as the mathematical adjoint to back-projection. Unlike spatial-domain projection methods that integrate ray paths through density fields, this method operates directly in the frequency domain, enabling efficient gradient computation for rotation and translation parameters without explicit ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D reconstruction tensor in Fourier space with shape [B, D, H, W/2+1], where B is batch size, D is depth, H is height, and W is width (real-valued FFT output). Inputs: Rotation matrices with shape [B, P, 3, 3], where P is the number of projection poses. Inputs (Optional): 2D shift vectors with shape [B, P, 2]. Output: 2D projection tensor with shape [B, P, Hout, Wout/2 + 1]. Data Structures: The 3D reconstruction is stored as a complex-valued tensor (or real-valued tensor with conjugate symmetry for the last dimension) representing the 3D Fourier transform of the volume. Coordinates are defined in frequency space (kr, kc, kd). Parameters: Interpolation: Trilinear or tricubic (Catmull-Rom). Oversampling: The output dimensions H{out}, W{out} may differ from input H, W depending on the desired resolution of the projection. Forward Pass Steps: 1. Coordinate Extension: For each output projection coordinate \mathbf{k}{proj} = (kr, kc), extend it to 3D by setting the depth coordinate to zero: \mathbf{k}{3D} = (kc, kr, 0). This selects the central slice through the origin. 2. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the 3D coordinate into the reconstruction frame using the inverse of the rotation matrix \mathbf{R}: \mathbf{k}{rec} = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{k}{3D} where \mathbf{R} is the 3 \times 3 rotation matrix. 3. Interpolation: Sample the 3D reconstruction tensor F{rec} at \mathbf{k}{rec} using trilinear or tricubic interpolation. For trilinear interpolation, the value F{rec}(\mathbf{k}{rec}) is computed from the 8 surrounding voxels using linear kernel l(s) = 1 - |s| for |s| \le 1. For tricubic interpolation, the value is computed from the 64 surrounding voxels using the Catmull-Rom kernel w(s). 4. Phase Modulation: Apply the translation shift \mathbf{s} to the interpolated value: P(\mathbf{k}{proj}) = F{rec}(\mathbf{k}{rec}) \cdot e^{-i2\pi\mathbf{k}{proj}\cdot\mathbf{s}} where \mathbf{s} is the 2D shift vector. Backward Pass Steps: 1. Shift Gradient: Compute the gradient with respect to the shift vector \mathbf{s}: \frac{\partial P}{\partial \mathbf{s}} = -i2\pi\mathbf{k}{proj}P(\mathbf{k}{proj}). 2. Rotation Gradient: Compute the gradient with respect to the rotation matrix elements R{ij} using the chain rule: \frac{\partial P}{\partial R{ij}} = \frac{\partial F{rec}(\mathbf{k}{rec})}{\partial \mathbf{k}{rec}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{k}{rec}}{\partial R{ij}} The term \frac{\partial \mathbf{k}{rec}}{\partial R{ij}} is derived from the analytical derivative of the matrix inverse \mathbf{R}^{-1}. 3. Spatial Gradients: Compute the gradient of the interpolated value with respect to the coordinates \mathbf{k}{rec} = (d, r, c). For trilinear interpolation, the spatial derivatives are computed using the derivatives of the linear kernel l'(s) = \text{sign}(s) for |s| < 1: \frac{\partial F}{\partial d} = \sum{i=0}^1 \sum{j=0}^1 \sum{k=0}^1 p{ijk} \cdot l'(df - i) \cdot l(rf - j) \cdot l(cf - k) \frac{\partial F}{\partial r} = \sum{i=0}^1 \sum{j=0}^1 \sum{k=0}^1 p{ijk} \cdot l(df - i) \cdot l'(rf - j) \cdot l(cf - k) \frac{\partial F}{\partial c} = \sum{i=0}^1 \sum{j=0}^1 \sum{k=0}^1 p{ijk} \cdot l(df - i) \cdot l(rf - j) \cdot l'(cf - k) where p{ijk} are the sample weights and df, rf, cf are the fractional coordinates. For tricubic interpolation, the spatial derivatives use the derivative of the cubic kernel w'(s): \frac{\partial F}{\partial d} = \sum{i=-1}^2 \sum{j=-1}^2 \sum{k=-1}^2 p{ijk} \cdot w'(df - i) \cdot w(rf - j) \cdot w(cf - k) \frac{\partial F}{\partial r} = \sum{i=-1}^2 \sum{j=-1}^2 \sum{k=-1}^2 p{ijk} \cdot w(df - i) \cdot w'(rf - j) \cdot w(cf - k) \frac{\partial F}{\partial c} = \sum{i=-1}^2 \sum{j=-1}^2 \sum{k=-1}^2 p{ijk} \cdot w(df - i) \cdot w(rf - j) \cdot w'(cf - k). 4. Accumulation: Accumulate the reconstruction gradients into the 3D volume tensor at the transformed coordinates \mathbf{k}{rec} using transposed interpolation operations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def forwardprojection3dto2d(Frec, R, s=None): """ Frec: [B, D, H, W/2+1, 2] (Complex tensor as real/imag pairs) R: [B, P, 3, 3] s: [B, P, 2] (Optional) Returns: [B, P, Hout, Wout/2+1, 2] """ B, D, H, Whalf = Frec.shape[:4] P = R.shape[1] # Create output grid coordinates for the 2D projections # Assuming output resolution matches input H, W for simplicity # In practice, Hout, Wout might differ Hout, Wout = H, Whalf 2 - 1 # Approximate, depends on specific FFT layout # Note: The source uses W/2+1 for real FFT, so Wout/2+1 implies similar layout # Generate 2D projection coordinates (kr, kc) # kr corresponds to rows (height), kc to columns (width) # k3D = (kc, kr, 0) # Create meshgrid for kr (rows) and kc (cols) # kr ranges from -H/2 to H/2, kc from -W/2 to W/2 # This needs to be adapted to the specific frequency coordinate system # Assuming normalized coordinates or pixel indices mapped to frequency # For implementation, we iterate or vectorize over P projections # Vectorized approach: # 1. Generate 2D coordinates for each projection # Assuming output shape [B, P, Hout, Wout/2+1] # We need to map output indices to kproj # Let's assume we have pre-computed kproj grids for the output shape # kprojr: [B, P, Hout, Wout/2+1] # kprojc: [B, P, Hout, Wout/2+1] # 2. Extend to 3D: k3D = (kc, kr, 0) k3d = torch.stack([kprojc, kprojr, torch.zeroslike(kprojr)], dim=-1) # [B, P, Hout, Wout/2+1, 3] # 3. Transform to reconstruction frame: krec = R^-1 @ k3D # R is [B, P, 3, 3], k3D is [B, P, Hout, Wout/2+1, 3] # We need to apply R^-1 to each k3D vector Rinv = torch.inverse(R) # [B, P, 3, 3] # Matrix multiplication: [B, P, 3, 3] @ [B, P, Hout, Wout/2+1, 3] -> [B, P, Hout, Wout/2+1, 3] # Reshape for matmul k3dflat = k3d.view(B, P, -1, 3) # [B, P, N, 3] Rinvflat = Rinv.unsqueeze(2) # [B, P, 1, 3, 3] # krec = Rinv @ k3D.T? No, k3D is (x,y,z) # kreci = sumj Rinvij k3Dj krecflat = torch.matmul(Rinvflat.transpose(-2, -1), k3dflat.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # [B, P, N, 3] krec = krecflat.view(B, P, Hout, Wout//2 + 1, 3) # 4. Interpolate Frec at krec # Frec is [B, D, H, W/2+1] (Real/Imag) # We need to sample complex values # Using gridsample or custom interpolation # Extract real and imaginary parts Freal = Frec[..., 0] # [B, D, H, W/2+1] Fimag = Frec[..., 1] # Normalize coordinates to [-1, 1] for gridsample # This depends on the specific coordinate system of Frec # Assuming Frec coordinates are in frequency space indices # Custom trilinear interpolation for complex values #... (Implementation of trilinear/ tricubic interpolation in 3D) # 5. Apply phase modulation # P(kproj) = Frec(krec) exp(-i 2 pi kproj. s) if s is not None: # kproj. s = kr sr + kc sc phase = -2 torch.pi (kprojr s[..., 0] + kprojc s[..., 1]) expphase = torch.polar(torch.oneslike(phase), phase) # e^(i phase) # Frec is complex, so multiply Preal = Freal expphase.cos() - Fimag expphase.sin() Pimag = Freal expphase.sin() + Fimag expphase.cos() else: Preal = Freal Pimag = Fimag return torch.stack([Preal, Pimag], dim=-1) Time Complexity: Dominated by the interpolation step, which is O(P \cdot H{out} \cdot W{out}) per batch element, where P is the number of projections. The matrix inverse and coordinate transformation are O(P) or O(P \cdot H{out} \cdot W{out}) depending on implementation. Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot D \cdot H \cdot W) for the input volume and O(B \cdot P \cdot H{out} \cdot W{out}) for the output projections. Intermediate gradients require storing the interpolation weights and coordinates. Strengths: Efficient for differentiable tomography where the reconstruction is in Fourier space. Avoids the computational cost of ray casting. Analytical gradients for rotation and translation are available. Limitations: Requires the reconstruction to be in Fourier space. Interpolation artifacts (aliasing, blurring) can affect accuracy, especially with tricubic interpolation if not properly handled. The method assumes a specific coordinate system and central slice geometry. When to use: When performing differentiable tomographic reconstruction where the forward model is defined in the frequency domain. When not to use: When the reconstruction is in spatial domain and requires spatial-domain projection (e.g., for non-Fourier-based regularizers). The method is based on the Central Slice Theorem, which states that the 1D Fourier transform of a projection of a 2D object is a slice through the 2D Fourier transform of the object. In 3D, the 2D Fourier transform of a projection is a central slice through the 3D Fourier transform of the volume. This operator is implemented in the torch-projectors library, a high-performance differentiable projection library for PyTorch. It is used in differentiable tomographic reconstruction pipelines, such as those in. torch-projectors: A High-Performance Differentiable Projection Library for PyTorch, https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.03.10.710885, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Backprojection with Global Memory Buffer
head: GPU Backprojection Kernel Mapping, backproject
body: This method performs cone-beam CT reconstruction by mapping projection weights to volume expansion coefficients using a GPU-accelerated kernel that iterates over projection angles. It solves the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by accumulating contributions from filtered projections into a global memory volume buffer. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its use of a single kernel launch per projection angle with a 1D NDRange where each work-item corresponds to one voxel, avoiding complex local memory tiling or image texture sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of P filtered projection images, each of size W \times H. Geometric parameters: Source-to-Object Distance (sod), Source-to-Detector Distance (sdd), voxel size (voxelSize), and pixel size (pixelSize). Volume dimensions NX \times NX \times NY. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D volume buffer of size NX \times NX \times NY of type float. Data Structures: Volume Buffer: A 1D array of size V = NX \times NX \times NY allocated in global memory (CLMEMREADWRITE). Initialized to zero. Projection Buffer: A 1D array of size W \times H allocated in global memory (CLMEMREADONLY | CLMEMCOPYHOSTPTR) for the current projection angle. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize OpenCL context, command queue, and program from source file kernels/backprojectionbuffer.cl. 2. Allocate the volume buffer of size V \times sizeof(float) and fill with zeros. 3. Loop over each projection angle p from 0 to P-1: a. Calculate the rotation angle: \thetap = 2.0 \pi \frac{p}{P}. b. Create the projection buffer containing the p-th filtered projection slice. c. Set kernel arguments: projBuffer, volumeBuffer, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod, \thetap. d. Launch the backprojection kernel with a global size equal to V (1D NDRange). e. Release the projection buffer. 4. After all projections, read the volume buffer back to the host. 5. Scale the reconstructed volume by \frac{\pi}{P}. Kernel Logic (Per Work-Item): Each work-item with global ID gid corresponds to a unique voxel in the volume. The voxel coordinates (x, y, z) are derived from gid. The kernel computes the contribution of the current projection to this voxel: 1. Map the voxel (x, y, z) to the detector plane coordinates (u, v) using the cone-beam geometry defined by sod, sdd, and \thetap. 2. Sample the projection buffer at (u, v) using interpolation (e.g., bilinear). 3. Add the sampled value to the voxel at gid in the volumeBuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backprojectkernel(projbuffer, volumebuffer, W, H, NX, NY, voxelsize, pixelsize, sdd, sod, angle): gid = getglobalid(0) if gid >= NX NX NY: return # 1. Map 1D gid to 3D voxel coordinates (x, y, z) # Assuming row-major order: z = gid / (NXNX), rem = gid % (NXNX), y = rem / NX, x = rem % NX z = gid // (NX NX) rem = gid % (NX NX) y = rem // NX x = rem % NX # 2. Convert voxel indices to physical coordinates # Center of the volume is at (0,0,0) xphys = (x - (NX - 1) / 2.0) voxelsize yphys = (y - (NX - 1) / 2.0) voxelsize zphys = (z - (NY - 1) / 2.0) voxelsize # 3. Rotate voxel coordinates by -angle around Y-axis to align with projection frame # Rotation matrix for angle theta around Y-axis: # x' = xcos(theta) + zsin(theta) # z' = -xsin(theta) + zcos(theta) cosa = cos(angle) sina = sin(angle) xrot = xphys cosa + zphys sina zrot = -xphys sina + zphys cosa yrot = yphys # 4. Project to detector coordinates (u, v) # Using similar triangles: u = xrot (sdd / sod) # v = yrot (sdd / sod) # Note: zrot is used to determine if the voxel is within the cone beam, # but for simple backprojection into the volume, we assume valid geometry. scale = sdd / sod u = xrot scale v = yrot scale # 5. Map detector coordinates to pixel indices # Center of detector is at (W/2, H/2) uidx = u / pixelsize + W / 2.0 vidx = v / pixelsize + H / 2.0 # 6. Sample projection buffer # Check bounds if uidx < 0 or uidx >= W or vidx < 0 or vidx >= H: weight = 0.0 else: # Bilinear interpolation or nearest neighbor # For simplicity, using nearest neighbor or clamped access uint = int(round(uidx)) vint = int(round(vidx)) # Clamp to valid range uint = max(0, min(W - 1, uint)) vint = max(0, min(H - 1, vint)) weight = projbuffer[vint W + uint] # 7. Accumulate into volume buffer volumebuffer[gid] += weight def reconstructgpubuffer(projections, P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelsize, pixelsize, sdd, sod): # 1. Initialize OpenCL context, queue, program # 2. Allocate volume buffer (CLMEMREADWRITE) of size NXNXNY, fill with 0 volumebuffer = allocatebuffer(NX NX NY, 0.0) # 3. Loop over projections for p in range(P): angle = 2.0 PI p / P # 4. Create projection buffer with p-th projection projbuffer = allocatebuffer(W H, projections[p]) # 5. Set kernel arguments # 6. Launch kernel with global size NXNXNY launchkernel(projbuffer, volumebuffer, W, H, NX, NY, voxelsize, pixelsize, sdd, sod, angle) # 7. Release projection buffer releasebuffer(projbuffer) # 8. Read volume buffer back to host result = readbuffer(volumebuffer) # 9. Scale by PI / P result = [val PI / P for val in result] return result Parameters: P: Total number of projection angles. NX, NY: Volume dimensions. Volume size is NX \times NX \times NY. W, H: Projection image dimensions. voxelSize: Physical size of a voxel. pixelSize: Physical size of a pixel. sdd: Source-to-Detector Distance. sod: Source-to-Object Distance. Typical work-item count: 128 \times 128 \times 128 = 2,097,152. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors may occur if P is very large. Use double precision for intermediate geometric calculations if necessary. Boundaries: Voxel projections falling outside the detector bounds (0 \le u < W, 0 \le v < H) must be handled to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Clamp or check bounds before sampling. Degenerate Input: If sod = 0 or sdd = 0, division by zero occurs. Validate inputs before kernel launch. The adjoint operator to backprojection, mapping volume to projections. Uses OpenCL buffers for both input and output, similar to this method but potentially with different kernel optimization strategies. Uses image textures for projection data, leveraging hardware interpolation and caching. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot V), where P is the number of projections and V is the number of voxels. Each voxel is processed once per projection. Memory Complexity: O(V + W \cdot H). The volume buffer is stored in global memory, and one projection buffer is allocated and reused. Performance: The method is efficient for moderate resolution volumes due to the simplicity of the kernel and lack of complex synchronization. However, global memory bandwidth may become a bottleneck for very large volumes or high-resolution projections. Strengths: Simple implementation, no need for local memory management, easy to debug. Limitations: High global memory traffic as each voxel reads from the projection buffer. Not optimized for cache coalescing as effectively as tiled approaches. When to use: Suitable for prototyping, moderate resolution CT reconstruction, and when implementation simplicity is prioritized over maximum performance. When not to use: For very large volumes or real-time applications where memory bandwidth is a critical constraint. This method is part of the GPU-accelerated cone-beam CT reconstruction pipeline described in the ct-reconstruction-gpu repository. It serves as a baseline GPU implementation for backprojection, contrasting with more optimized versions using local memory or image textures. The approach follows the standard FDK (Feldkamp-Davis-Kress) algorithm structure, where filtered projections are backprojected into a volume. hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Buffers
head: Full GPU Path (Ramp Filter + Backprojection), GPU-Buffer Backprojection
body: A GPU-accelerated tomographic reconstruction pipeline that performs filtered backprojection (FBK) by storing projection data in OpenCL global memory buffers rather than image objects. It distinguishes itself from GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Image Textures by avoiding texture sampling hardware, and from GPU Backprojection with Global Memory Buffer by explicitly including the ramp filtering step in the GPU path (or CPU pre-filtering followed by GPU backprojection). It solves the problem of reconstructing a 3D volume from 2D projections by mapping projection weights to volume expansion coefficients, building on Back-projection. Inputs: projections: std::vector<float> of size P \times W \times H (column-major layout: psrc[u H + v] for each projection p). P: Number of projections. W, H: Detector width and height in pixels. NX, NY: Volume dimensions (NX \times NX \times NY voxels). voxelSize: Voxel size in mm. pixelSize: Pixel size in mm. sdd: Source-to-detector distance in mm. sod: Source-to-object distance in mm. Outputs: std::vector<float> representing the reconstructed volume of size NX \times NX \times NY. Data Structures: Volume Buffer: clmem with CLMEMREADWRITE, size sizeof(float) volumeSize where volumeSize = NX NX NY. Projection Buffer: clmem with CLMEMREADWRITE, size sizeof(float) projSize where projSize = W H (per projection, reused or copied per iteration). Steps: 1. Pre-filtering: Apply FDK pre-filter (ramp filter) on CPU to raw projections. 2. Volume Initialization: Fill volume buffer with zeros using clEnqueueFillBuffer. 3. Loop over projections: For each projection p from 0 to P-1: a. Calculate angle: \theta = 2.0f \times \pi \times p / P. b. Data Transposition: Convert projection data from column-major (psrc[u H + v]) to row-major (rowMajor[v W + u]) for memory coalescing in the kernel. c. Kernel Execution: Enqueue NDRange kernel with global size equal to volumeSize (NX \times NX \times NY). The kernel computes backprojection weights based on geometry and accumulates into the volume buffer. 4. Final Scaling: After reading the volume buffer back to host, multiply every voxel by scale = MPI / P. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructgpubuffer(projections, P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod): """ Reconstructs volume using GPU backprojection with OpenCL buffers. Assumes OpenCL context, command queue, and kernel 'backprojectkernel' are initialized. """ volumesize = NX NX NY projsize = W H # 1. Pre-filtering (CPU) # Apply FDK ramp filter to projections in-place or to a new buffer filteredprojections = applyfdkfilter(projections, W, H, voxelSize, sdd, sod) # 2. Volume Initialization volumebuffer = clCreateBuffer(context, CLMEMREADWRITE, volumesize sizeof(float), None, None) clEnqueueFillBuffer(queue, volumebuffer, 0, 0, volumesize sizeof(float), 0, None, None) # 3. Loop over projections for p in range(P): # Calculate angle angle = 2.0 math.pi p / P # Data Transposition: Column-major to Row-major # Input: filteredprojections[p projsize + u H + v] # Output: rowmajorproj[v W + u] rowmajorproj = transposecolumntorow(filteredprojections, p, W, H) # Create projection buffer for this iteration projbuffer = clCreateBuffer(context, CLMEMREADWRITE, projsize sizeof(float), None, None) clEnqueueWriteBuffer(queue, projbuffer, CLTRUE, 0, projsize sizeof(float), rowmajorproj, 0, None, None) # Set kernel arguments # kernel.setArg(0, volumebuffer) # kernel.setArg(1, projbuffer) # kernel.setArg(2, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod, angle) # Kernel Execution globalsize = [NX, NX, NY] clEnqueueNDRangeKernel(queue, kernel, 3, None, globalsize, None, 0, None, None) clFinish(queue) # Synchronize for correctness in this simple pipeline clReleaseMemObject(projbuffer) # 4. Final Scaling result = np.empty(volumesize, dtype=np.float32) clEnqueueReadBuffer(queue, volumebuffer, CLTRUE, 0, volumesize sizeof(float), result, 0, None, None) scale = math.pi / P result = scale clReleaseMemObject(volumebuffer) return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Expected MSE < 1e-4 against CPU reference. Boundaries: Ensure clEnqueueFillBuffer is used correctly to zero-initialize the volume. Memory: Large volumes may exceed global memory limits; not given in the sources. A GPU-accelerated tomographic reconstruction variant that optimizes memory access patterns by tiling the Z-axis reconstruction loop using OpenCL local memory. It reduces global memory bandwidth pressure by reusing projection data across threads within a work-group, distinguishing it from the parent GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Buffers which relies solely on global memory buffers for projection storage. Time Complexity: O(P \times NX \times NX \times NY), where P is the number of projections and NX, NY are volume dimensions. Memory Complexity: O(NX^2 \times NY + W \times H) for volume and projection buffers. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with number of projections and volume size. Strengths: Full GPU path for backprojection, avoids texture unit overhead. Limitations: Relies on global memory for projection data, which may cause bandwidth bottlenecks compared to local-memory tiling variants. When to use: When texture units are unavailable or when a simple buffer-based approach is preferred over image objects. When not: When memory bandwidth is a critical bottleneck and local memory tiling is feasible. Originated from the ct-reconstruction-gpu project by hardik0001. It is part of a suite of GPU reconstruction methods including CPU reference, image texture-based, and local-memory tiling variants. hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GPU Backprojection using Local-Memory Tiling
head: GPU Backprojection with Local Memory Tiling, GPU-Local
body: A GPU-accelerated tomographic reconstruction variant that optimizes memory access patterns by tiling the Z-axis reconstruction loop using OpenCL local memory. It reduces global memory bandwidth pressure by reusing projection data across threads within a work-group, distinguishing it from the parent GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Buffers which relies solely on global memory buffers for projection storage. Inputs: projections: std::vector<float> of size P \times W \times H. P: Number of projections. W, H: Detector width and height in pixels. NX, NY: Volume dimensions (NX \times NX \times NY). voxelSize: Voxel size in mm. pixelSize: Pixel size in mm. sdd: Source-to-detector distance in mm. sod: Source-to-object distance in mm. Outputs: std::vector<float> representing the reconstructed volume of size NX \times NX \times NY. Data Structures: Volume Buffer: Global memory buffer of size NX \times NX \times NY floats, initialized to zero. Projection Buffer: Global memory buffer containing pre-filtered projections. Local Memory Buffers: Two local memory buffers (col0, col1) of size H floats each, used to cache projection columns for interpolation. Parameters: TILEZ: Tile size along the Z-axis, defined as 64. Local Memory Requirement: 2 \times H \times \text{sizeof(float)} bytes. Steps: 1. Pre-filtering: Apply the FDK pre-filter (ramp filter and cosine weighting) on the CPU using applyFDKPreFilter before GPU execution. 2. Device Check: Check the device's local memory size. If insufficient, print an info message but proceed (no explicit fallback). 3. Kernel Loading: Load the kernel source from kernels/backprojectionlocal.cl. 4. Volume Allocation: Allocate the volume buffer and fill it with zeros. 5. NDRange Calculation: Local size: (1, 1, \text{TILE\Z}). Global Z size: Round up NY to the nearest multiple of TILEZ: gz = ((NY + \text{TILE\Z} - 1) / \text{TILE\Z}) \times \text{TILE\Z}. Global X, Y sizes: NX. 6. Projection Loop: Loop over projections p from 0 to P-1. Calculate the projection angle based on p and P. Create the projection buffer and set kernel arguments. Arguments 2 and 3 are local memory buffers (col0, col1) passed as size in bytes (address is nullptr). Launch the kernel with the calculated 3D NDRange (global size, local size). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructGPULocal(projections, P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod): TILEZ = 64 # 1. Pre-filter on CPU filteredprojections = applyFDKPreFilter(projections, P, W, H, voxelSize, sdd, pixelSize) # 2. Check local memory size (implementation detail omitted, proceed regardless) # 3. Load kernel from 'kernels/backprojectionlocal.cl' kernelsource = loadkernelsource('kernels/backprojectionlocal.cl') # 4. Allocate volume buffer and zero it volume = [0.0] (NX NX NY) # 5. Calculate NDRange localsize = (1, 1, TILEZ) gz = ((NY + TILEZ - 1) // TILEZ) TILEZ globalsize = (NX, NX, gz) # 6. Loop over projections for p in range(P): angle = calculateangle(p, P) # Create projection buffer from filteredprojections for current angle projbuffer = createbuffer(filteredprojections, p, W, H) # Local memory buffers for interpolation columns localmemcol0size = H 4 # sizeof(float) = 4 localmemcol1size = H 4 # Set kernel arguments # Arg 0: volume buffer # Arg 1: projbuffer # Arg 2: localmemcol0size (nullptr address) # Arg 3: localmemcol1size (nullptr address) # Arg 4-10: P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod, angle setkernelarguments(kernel, projbuffer, volume, localmemcol0size, localmemcol1size, P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod, angle) # Launch kernel launchkernel(kernel, globalsize, localsize) # Return volume return volume Kernel Logic (Conceptual): The kernel iterates over X and Y coordinates. For each voxel (x, y, z), it calculates the projection coordinates (u, v) on the detector. It uses local memory to cache two columns of the projection image (col0 and col1) to facilitate bilinear interpolation of the projection value at (u, v). The interpolated value is weighted by (sod \cdot sod) / u{proj}^2 and accumulated into the volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Memory Overflow: If 2 \times H \times \text{sizeof(float)} exceeds the device's local memory limit, the behavior is undefined or the kernel may fail. The source checks this but proceeds without fallback. Boundary Conditions: Projection coordinates outside [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1] are skipped. Precision: Uses float for volume accumulation. Large numbers of projections may lead to precision loss. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot NX \cdot NX \cdot NY), same as CPU backprojection, but optimized for GPU parallelism. Memory Complexity: O(P \cdot W \cdot H + NX \cdot NX \cdot NY + H) for global buffers and local memory. Performance: Reduces global memory bandwidth pressure by reusing projection data in local memory. Strengths: Efficient memory access pattern for Z-axis reconstruction. Limitations: Requires sufficient local memory (2 \cdot H \cdot 4 bytes). No fallback if local memory is insufficient. This method is part of a GPU-accelerated CT reconstruction toolkit, specifically optimizing the backprojection step using OpenCL local memory tiling. It builds on the FDK algorithm and CPU-based pre-filtering. hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Image Textures
head: GPU-Image Backprojection
body: This method accelerates the backprojection step of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm by leveraging OpenCL image objects (image2dt) for hardware-accelerated interpolation of pre-filtered projection data. It differs from the buffer-based sibling methods by offloading bilinear interpolation to the GPU's texture cache, which typically yields higher performance for large projection datasets. It builds on Back-projection and assumes pre-filtering has been performed on the CPU. The method processes each projection angle sequentially. For each angle, the raw projection data is transposed, loaded into an OpenCL image object, and used to backproject into the volume buffer. Inputs: projections: std::vector<float> containing raw projection data. P: Number of projections. W, H: Detector width and height in pixels. NX, NY: Volume dimensions. The volume is assumed to be cubic in X/Y, i.e., NX \times NX \times NY. voxelSize: Physical size of a voxel (mm). pixelSize: Physical size of a detector pixel (mm). sdd: Source-to-Detector Distance (mm). sod: Source-to-Object Distance (mm). Outputs: volume: std::vector<float> representing the reconstructed 3D volume, layout [0..NX-1, 0..NX-1, 0..NY-1]. OpenCL Image2D: Channel Order: CLR Channel Data Type: CLFLOAT Image Type: CLMEMOBJECTIMAGE2D Width: W Height: H Row Pitch: 0 (native alignment) Kernel Arguments: 1. clmem image: The projection image (CLMEMREADONLY). 2. clmem volumeBuffer: Output volume buffer. 3. int W, int H: Detector dimensions. 4. int NX, int NY: Volume dimensions. 5. float voxelSize, float pixelSize: Physical scales. 6. float sdd, float sod: Geometry distances. 7. float angle: Current projection angle in radians. 1. Pre-filtering (CPU): Apply FDK pre-filtering (cone weighting and ramp filter) to the raw projections on the CPU. The source notes specify this step occurs before GPU processing. 2. Data Transposition: For each projection p, convert the data from column-major (psrc[u H + v]) to row-major (dest[v W + u]) to match the image texture layout. 3. Loop over Projections: Iterate p from 0 to P-1. a. Calculate angle: \theta = \frac{2\pi p}{P}. b. Image Creation: Create an OpenCL image2dt from the transposed row-major data with flags CLMEMREADONLY | CLMEMCOPYHOSTPTR. c. Kernel Execution: Enqueue the backprojection NDRange kernel. Global Size: NX \times NX \times NY. Each work-item (x, y, z) computes the contribution of the current projection to that voxel. d. Cleanup: Release the image memory object. 4. Final Scaling: After reading the volume buffer back to the host, multiply every voxel by \frac{\pi}{P}. For each voxel (x, y, z) and projection angle \theta: t = y \cos(\theta) - x \sin(\theta) U = \text{sod} + y \sin(\theta) + x \cos(\theta) u{\text{proj}} = \text{sdd} \cdot \frac{t}{U} v{\text{proj}} = \text{sdd} \cdot \frac{z}{U} The contribution to the voxel is: \text{volume}[x, y, z] \ += \ \text{filtered\proj}(u{\text{proj}}, v{\text{proj}}) \cdot \frac{\text{sod}^2}{U^2} Where \text{filtered\proj}(u, v) is obtained via hardware bilinear interpolation from the OpenCL image object. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gpubackprojectionimage(projections, P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod): """ Simulates the logic of the GPU Image Backprojection method. Note: Actual OpenCL calls are abstracted; this shows the data flow and math. """ volume = [0.0] (NX NX NY) # Pre-filtering is assumed done on CPU before this function call # projections are now filtered for p in range(P): # 1. Transpose projection data from column-major to row-major # Original: psrc[u H + v] # Target: rowMajor[v W + u] projrowmajor = [0.0] (W H) for u in range(W): for v in range(H): srcidx = u H + v dstidx = v W + u projrowmajor[dstidx] = projections[p][srcidx] # 2. Create OpenCL Image2D (Abstracted) # image = clCreateImage2D(context, CLMEMREADONLY | CLMEMCOPYHOSTPTR,...) # imagedata = projrowmajor # 3. Calculate Angle angle = 2.0 math.pi p / P # 4. Kernel Execution: Backproject one projection # Global size: NX NX NY # Each work-item (x, y, z) runs the following logic: for x in range(NX): for y in range(NX): for z in range(NY): # Compute detector coordinates t = y math.cos(angle) - x math.sin(angle) U = sod + y math.sin(angle) + x math.cos(angle) # Avoid division by zero if U == 0: continue uproj = sdd t / U vproj = sdd z / U # Hardware interpolation of filtered projection # In OpenCL: readimagef(image, sampler, (float2)(uproj, vproj)) # We simulate bilinear interpolation here for completeness val = hardwareinterpolate(projrowmajor, uproj, vproj, W, H) # Accumulate with weighting weight = (sod sod) / (U U) idx = x NX NY + y NY + z volume[idx] += val weight # 5. Cleanup Image # clReleaseMemObject(image) # 6. Final Scaling scale = math.pi / P for i in range(len(volume)): volume[i] = scale return volume def hardwareinterpolate(data, u, v, W, H): """ Simulates OpenCL hardware bilinear interpolation. u and v are in continuous detector coordinates. """ # Clamp to valid range if u < 0 or u >= W - 1 or v < 0 or v >= H - 1: return 0.0 # Integer parts u0 = int(math.floor(u)) v0 = int(math.floor(v)) # Fractional parts fu = u - u0 fv = v - v0 # Neighbors # Layout is row-major: index = v W + u val00 = data[v0 W + u0] val01 = data[v0 W + (u0 + 1)] val10 = data[(v0 + 1) W + u0] val11 = data[(v0 + 1) W + (u0 + 1)] # Bilinear interpolation top = val00 (1 - fu) + val01 fu bottom = val10 (1 - fu) + val11 fu return top (1 - fv) + bottom fv Boundary Conditions: If u{\text{proj}} or v{\text{proj}} falls outside the detector bounds [0, W] or [0, H], the hardware interpolation typically returns 0.0. The pseudocode explicitly clamps and returns 0.0. Division by Zero: If U=0, the projection ray is parallel to the detector plane or originates from the source plane. The implementation must guard against this. Memory Management: The image object must be released after each projection to avoid memory leaks, as the loop creates a new image for each angle. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot NX \cdot NX \cdot NY). The dominant cost is the kernel execution for each projection. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H + NX \cdot NX \cdot NY). The projection image requires W \cdot H floats, and the volume requires NX^2 NY floats. Performance: Typically faster than buffer-based backprojection due to the GPU's texture cache handling interpolation, reducing global memory bandwidth pressure. Strengths: Efficient interpolation; leverages hardware acceleration. Limitations: Requires pre-filtering on CPU (as per source notes); sequential projection processing limits parallelism across angles compared to fully parallel GPU approaches. This method is part of a GPU-accelerated CT reconstruction toolkit. It specifically targets the backprojection stage using OpenCL image textures. name: WebSplatter
head: WebSplatter: Enabling Cross-Device Efficient Gaussian Splatting in Web Browsers via WebGPU
body: WebSplatter is a WebGPU-based renderer for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to achieve high-performance, stable, and cross-device compatibility for web-based applications. It solves the critical bottlenecks of previous web-based 3DGS implementations, specifically addressing the instability of Firefox WebGPU, excessive memory consumption on mobile devices, and severe performance degradation due to spin-wait-based sorting on Apple Silicon architectures. WebSplatter distinguishes itself from its siblings by employing a wait-free GPU-based radix sort and a highly optimized pre-processing pipeline that prevents the renderer from becoming sort-bound, ensuring consistent frame times and low variance across a wide spectrum of hardware, from high-end desktops to low-end integrated graphics and mobile phones. WebSplatter implements a complete 3DGS rendering pipeline within the WebGPU API. The method consists of three primary stages: pre-processing, sorting, and rasterization. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance/scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Outputs: A 2D color image (framebuffer) representing the rendered scene. The system processes raw splat data. While specific memory layouts for the Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients) follow the standard 3DGS format, WebSplatter optimizes the handling of these structures during the pre-processing stage to minimize memory bandwidth usage on low-end devices. 1. Pre-processing: Transform 3D Gaussian centers into clip space using the view and projection matrices. Project the 3D covariance matrix into 2D screen space to compute the 2D bounding box and screen-space covariance. Discard Gaussians that are outside the view frustum or have negligible screen-space extent. Compute the 2D screen-space center and the 2D covariance matrix determinant for depth sorting. Optimization: This stage is optimized to reduce memory throughput bottlenecks on low-end GPUs by efficiently scanning raw splats. 2. Sorting (Wait-Free GPU Radix Sort): Sort the visible Gaussians by their projected depth (z-coordinate) to ensure correct alpha blending. WebSplatter uses a GPU-based radix sort algorithm that is wait-free. This design avoids spin-waits, which are problematic on architectures like Apple M-series that lack guarantees for workgroup execution order. The sort key is the depth of the Gaussian center in clip space. 3. Rasterization (Rendering): Iterate through the sorted Gaussians. For each Gaussian, compute its 2D screen-space ellipse. Rasterize the ellipse, computing the contribution to the framebuffer pixels based on the Gaussian's opacity, color (from SH coefficients), and 2D covariance. Perform alpha blending to composite the final color. The following pseudocode outlines the core logic of the WebSplatter pipeline, focusing on the sorting and rendering stages. Note that WebGPU-specific buffer management and shader compilation are abstracted into standard compute and render pipeline calls. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def websplatterpipeline(gaussians, camera, width, height): """ Main rendering pipeline for WebSplatter. Args: gaussians: List of 3D Gaussian objects with attributes: center: vec3 scale: vec3 rotation: quat opacity: float shcoeffs: array (for color) camera: Object with viewmatrix (mat4) and projectionmatrix (mat4) width: int, framebuffer width height: int, framebuffer height Returns: ImageBuffer: Rendered 2D image """ # Step 1: Pre-processing # Transform and project Gaussians to screen space visiblegaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Transform center to clip space clipcenter = camera.projectionmatrix @ (camera.viewmatrix @ vec4(g.center, 1.0)) # Check frustum culling (simplified) if not isinfrustum(clipcenter): continue # Project covariance to 2D # Compute 2D bounding box and screen-space covariance # This step is optimized in WebSplatter to reduce memory bandwidth usage projectedg = projectgaussian(g, camera) if projectedg.isvalid: visiblegaussians.append(projectedg) # Step 2: Sorting # WebSplatter uses a wait-free GPU-based radix sort # Sort by depth (z-coordinate in clip space) # This avoids spin-waits on Apple Silicon and other architectures sortedgaussians = waitfreeradixsort(visiblegaussians, key=lambda g: g.clipcenter.z) # Step 3: Rasterization # Initialize framebuffer framebuffer = ImageBuffer(width, height, format='RGBA') # Render sorted Gaussians for g in sortedgaussians: # Compute 2D screen-space ellipse parameters # Compute contribution to each pixel within the bounding box rendergaussianellipse(g, framebuffer, width, height) return framebuffer def waitfreeradixsort(data, key): """ Wait-free GPU-based radix sort implementation. Uses atomic operations and barrier synchronization that does not rely on workgroup execution order guarantees, making it safe for Apple M-series chips. """ # Implementation details of the radix sort are handled by the WebGPU compute shader. # The key aspect is the absence of spin-waits. pass def rendergaussianellipse(g, framebuffer, width, height): """ Rasterize a single 2D Gaussian ellipse. """ # Compute bounding box of the ellipse in screen space bbox = compute2dboundingbox(g) # Iterate over pixels in the bounding box for y in range(bbox.miny, bbox.maxy): for x in range(bbox.minx, bbox.maxx): if isinsideellipse(x, y, g): # Compute alpha and color contribution alpha, color = computegaussiancontribution(x, y, g) # Alpha blend into framebuffer framebuffer.blendpixel(x, y, color, alpha) Sort Algorithm: GPU-based radix sort. WebGPU API: Used for all GPU operations. Scene Complexity: Tested with scenes ranging from 0.3M splats (van gogh) to 5.8M splats (garden). Apple Silicon Sorting: Spin-wait-based sorting (e.g., KeKsBoTer/web-splat) performs poorly on Apple M1 chips due to the lack of guarantees for workgroup execution order, leading to significant busy-waiting. WebSplatter's wait-free design avoids this. Memory Constraints: Baselines like KeKsBoTer/web-splat crash on devices with limited memory (e.g., Oppo Find X2) due to excessive memory requirements. WebSplatter's optimized pre-processing and sorting reduce memory pressure, allowing it to render on all tested devices. Firefox WebGPU Instability: Firefox WebGPU is unstable across tested devices, with crashes and blocklists. WebSplatter is tested on Google Chrome, which provides a more stable WebGPU implementation. Timestamp Query Discrepancies: On Intel NUC, Firefox WebGPU timestamp queries are unreliable (built-in queries: 2.8 ms vs JavaScript API: 258.36 ms). WebSplatter's performance measurements are robust against such API inconsistencies. Time Complexity: The system is never sort-bound across all tested hardware. On high-end GPUs (RTX 3070, Apple M-series, Redmi K70 Pro), the system is render-bound, with rasterization consuming 51.8% to 62.6% of frame time. On low-end GPUs (Nvidia MX350, Intel NUC iGPU), the system is pre-process-bound, consuming up to 47.2% of frame time due to limited memory throughput scanning raw splats. Memory Complexity: WebSplatter's optimized pre-processing and wait-free sorting reduce memory pressure, allowing it to run on devices with limited VRAM where other baselines crash. Nvidia RTX 3070: Median total frame time of 9.497 ms on the garden scene, a 1.52× speedup over the fastest competing WebGPU implementation. MacBook Air M4: 1.06× faster than baseline. On the garden scene (5.8M splats), standard deviation of 22.303 ms and P99 latency of 116.851 ms, indicating low variance and mitigation of micro-stuttering. Redmi K70 Pro: 1.18× faster than baseline. Renders the truck scene (2.5M splats) in 52.7 ms without crashing, while KeKsBoTer/web-splat crashes. Intel NUC (iGPU): 2.26× faster than baseline. MacBook Pro M1: Over 4.5× faster than KeKsBoTer/web-splat due to the avoidance of spin-wait-based sorting. Scalability: On Nvidia MX350, scaling from van gogh (0.3M splats) to garden (5.8M splats) increases WebSplatter frame time by ~143 ms, compared to >280 ms for KeKsBoTer/web-splat, yielding a 2.1× speedup on the largest scene. Strengths: High performance across a wide range of hardware, from high-end desktops to low-end mobile devices. Wait-free sorting ensures stability and performance on Apple Silicon. Low variance in frame times, reducing micro-stuttering. Successful rendering on all tested devices, including those with limited memory. Visual fidelity comparable to the official native CUDA implementation. Limitations: Performance is still bound by rasterization on high-end GPUs, limiting further speedups without algorithmic changes to the rendering stage. Pre-processing becomes a bottleneck on low-end GPUs, limited by memory throughput. Use WebSplatter for web-based 3DGS applications requiring high performance and stability across diverse hardware, especially when targeting Apple Silicon devices or low-end integrated graphics. Use when visual fidelity comparable to native implementations is required. Do not use if the target environment relies on Firefox WebGPU, due to known instability and blocklists. Do not use if the hardware has extremely limited memory and the scene complexity is very high, although WebSplatter is more memory-efficient than baselines, extreme cases may still be challenging. WebSplatter was introduced in the paper "WebSplatter: Enabling Cross-Device Efficient Gaussian Splatting in Web Browsers via WebGPU". The work addresses the growing need for efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering in web browsers, leveraging the WebGPU API for hardware-accelerated graphics. Previous web-based 3DGS implementations suffered from performance bottlenecks, particularly in sorting and memory management, and instability on certain hardware and browsers. WebSplatter's contributions include a wait-free GPU-based radix sort and an optimized pre-processing pipeline, enabling efficient and stable 3DGS rendering across a wide range of devices. name: ClearView (Unified) Renderer
head: ClearView, ClearView Unified Buffer, ClearView WebGL2 Spike
body: ClearView (Unified) is a 3-pass WebGL2 renderer for unstructured hexahedral meshes that uses a Parallel Prefix List (PPLL) to render wireframes and scalar fields on the GPU. It solves the problem of rendering complex volumetric meshes in web browsers by adapting a desktop GPU technique (which typically relies on Shader Storage Buffer Objects) to WebGL2's texture-only data storage model. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit 3-pass architecture (Clear, Gather, Resolve) and its use of atomic operations on image textures to build a linked list of fragments for depth-sorted alpha blending. The method consists of three sequential GPU passes. It operates on hexahedral meshes where each cell has 8 corners, 12 edges, and 6 faces. Input: A hexahedral mesh defined by vertex positions, cell connectivity (mapping 8 VTK-style corners to 8 STD corners), and per-vertex scalar attributes. Output: A final 2D image with depth-sorted, alpha-blended wireframes and scalar field visualizations. WebGL2 lacks Shader Storage Buffer Objects (SSBOs), so all mesh data is encoded into image2D textures with a fixed row width of TEXWIDTH = 4096. 1. Vertex Texture (vertexTex): Format: RGBA32F (Float32Array). Layout: 1 texel per vertex slot. Each texel stores (x, y, z, scalarattribute). Size: height = ceil(8 nCells / 4096). Corner Mapping: VTK corner indices [0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5, 7, 6] are mapped to STD indices [0..7] where 0=c000, 1=c100,..., 7=c111. 2. Face Texture (faceTex): Format: RG32UI (Uint32Array). Layout: 2 texels per face. Stores face-local corner indices and edge indices. Size: height = ceil(6 nCells / 4096). Enumeration: 6 faces per cell, defined in HEXFACES array with corners in face-local CCW order (viewed from outside) to ensure outward-facing normals. 3. Edge Texture (edgeTex): Format: RG32F (Float32Array). Layout: 1 texel per edge. Stores edge indices. Size: height = ceil(12 nCells / 4096). Definition: 12 edges per cell, defined as pairs of STD corner indices in HEXEDGES. 4. Cell Scalar Texture (cellScalarTex): Format: R32F (Float32Array). Layout: 1 texel per face. Stores scalar values associated with the face/cell. Size: height = ceil(6 nCells / 4096). 5. PPLL Structures: Start Offset Texture (startOffsetTex): R32UI image texture. Size matches the viewport. Stores the starting index in the fragment buffer for each pixel. Fragment Buffer Texture (fragmentBufferTex): RGBA32UI image texture. Fixed size 2048x2048 (4 million entries). Stores fragment data (position, color, depth, etc.). Atomic Counter Buffer: Single Uint32 value. Tracks the total number of fragments inserted into the buffer. 1. Initialization: Create startOffsetTex (viewport size) and fragmentBufferTex (2048x2048). Create and bind an atomic counter buffer (initial value 0). Upload mesh data to faceTex, vertexTex, edgeTex, and cellScalarTex using the TEXWIDTH = 4096 stride. 2. Pass 1: Clear: Bind startOffsetTex and fragmentBufferTex as image2D (read/write). Bind the atomic counter buffer. Render a full-screen triangle (or quad) to reset all values in startOffsetTex to -1. Disable depth testing and culling. 3. Pass 2: Gather: Bind startOffsetTex and fragmentBufferTex as image2D (read/write). Bind faceTex, vertexTex, edgeTex, and cellScalarTex as standard textures (units 0-3). Set uniforms: MVP matrix, ModelViewInverse, camera position, sphere parameters, LOD values, scalar range, and FOV. Render faceCount 6 triangles (representing the hexahedral faces). In the fragment shader: Compute ray-sphere and ray-plane intersections to determine visibility. Use atomicAdd on the atomic counter to get a unique index for the new fragment. Write fragment data to fragmentBufferTex at the obtained index. Update startOffsetTex for the corresponding pixel to point to this new fragment (building the linked list). 4. Pass 3: Resolve: Bind startOffsetTex and fragmentBufferTex as image2D (read-only). Render a full-screen triangle. In the fragment shader: Read the linked list of fragments for the current pixel from fragmentBufferTex using the start offset. Sort the fragments by depth (insertion sort if count \le 32, otherwise other method). Perform alpha blending of the sorted fragments to produce the final color. Ray-Sphere Intersection: Given ray origin O, direction D, sphere center C, and radius R: A = D \cdot D B = 2.0 \cdot D \cdot (O - C) C{val} = (O - C) \cdot (O - C) - R^2 \Delta = B^2 - 4AC{val} If \Delta < 0, no intersection. Otherwise: t0 = \frac{-B - \sqrt{\Delta}}{2A}, \quad t1 = \frac{-B + \sqrt{\Delta}}{2A} Intersection position: P = O + t0 D. Ray-Plane Intersection: Given ray origin O, direction D, plane point P{plane}, and normal N: ln = N \cdot D If |ln| < 10^{-4}, no intersection (parallel). t = \frac{N \cdot P{plane} - N \cdot O}{ln} Intersection position: P = O + t D. FRAGBUFFERW: 2048 FRAGBUFFERH: 2048 LINKEDLISTSIZE: 4,194,304 (2048 \times 2048) RESOLVECUTOFF: 32 fragments per pixel (threshold for insertion sort) TEXWIDTH: 4096 uMaxLodValue: 1.0 uSelectedLodValueFocus: 0.4 uSelectedLodValueContext: 0.7 uImportantLineBoostFactor: 0.5 SwiftShader Compatibility: SwiftShader's WebGL2 implementation does not support image2D or atomicuint, returning null/undefined for MAXIMAGEUNITS. Infinite Recursion: Shader include resolution must enforce a maximum depth (e.g., 10) to prevent infinite loops. Precision: Plane intersection uses a threshold of 10^{-4} for parallel detection. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resolveshaderincludes(src, sources, depth=0): if depth > 10: raise Error("Include depth exceeded") lines = src.split('\n') for i, line in enumerate(lines): match = re.match(r'^\s#include\s+"([^"]+)"\s', line) if match: name = match.group(1) if name not in sources: raise Error(f"Unknown shader include: {name}") lines[i] = resolveshaderincludes(sources[name], sources, depth + 1) return '\n'.join(lines) def buildclearviewbuffers(mesh): ncells = mesh.ncells facecount = 6 ncells vertexcount = 8 ncells edgecount = 12 ncells TEXWIDTH = 4096 # VTK to STD mapping VTKTOSTD = [0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5, 7, 6] # Vertex Buffer (RGBA32F) vertexheight = math.ceil(vertexcount / TEXWIDTH) verticestex = Float32Array(vertexheight TEXWIDTH 4) for c in range(ncells): for k in range(8): stdcorner = k vtkcorner = VTKTOSTD[stdcorner] pi = mesh.cellconn[c 8 + vtkcorner] linearidx = c 8 + stdcorner col = linearidx % TEXWIDTH row = linearidx // TEXWIDTH ti = (row TEXWIDTH + col) 4 verticestex[ti] = mesh.positions[pi 3] verticestex[ti+1] = mesh.positions[pi 3 + 1] verticestex[ti+2] = mesh.positions[pi 3 + 2] verticestex[ti+3] = mesh.scalars[pi] # Face, Edge, Cell Scalar buffers built similarly using HEXFACES and HEXEDGES #... (omitted for brevity, follows same pattern) return { 'faces': {'texels': facetex, 'width': TEXWIDTH, 'height': math.ceil(facecount / TEXWIDTH)}, 'vertices': {'texels': verticestex, 'width': TEXWIDTH, 'height': vertexheight}, 'edges': {'texels': edgetex, 'width': TEXWIDTH, 'height': math.ceil(edgecount / TEXWIDTH)}, 'cellscalar': {'texels': cellscalartex, 'width': TEXWIDTH, 'height': math.ceil(facecount / TEXWIDTH)}, 'facecount': facecount, 'vertexcount': vertexcount, 'edgecount': edgecount } def raysphereintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, spherecenter, sphereradius): A = dot(raydirection, raydirection) B = 2.0 dot(raydirection, rayorigin - spherecenter) C = dot(rayorigin - spherecenter, rayorigin - spherecenter) - sphereradius2 discriminant = B2 - 4.0 A C if discriminant < 0: return False, None, None sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) t0 = (-B - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 A) t1 = (-B + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 A) intersectionpos = rayorigin + t0 raydirection return True, t0, intersectionpos def rayplaneintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, planepoint, planenormal): ln = dot(planenormal, raydirection) if abs(ln) < 1e-4: return False, None pos = dot(planenormal, rayorigin) - dot(planenormal, planepoint) t = -pos / ln intersectionpos = rayorigin + t raydirection return True, intersectionpos A splatting-based renderer for point clouds and volumetric data in WebGL. It differs from ClearView by using additive blending of splats rather than explicit geometry rendering and linked lists. Choose WebSplatter for point-based data; choose ClearView for explicit mesh wireframes and scalar fields [1741-websplatter.md]. A method where the CPU manages rendering tasks and dispatches them to the GPU. It differs from ClearView's fully GPU-driven atomic PPLL approach. Choose CPU-Driven for complex culling logic or when GPU atomics are unsupported; choose ClearView for high-performance, self-contained GPU rendering [4397-cpu-driven-task-spawning.md]. Renderers that operate entirely in the browser without server-side processing. ClearView is a specific implementation within this category, optimized for WebGL2 mesh rendering. Choose Pure client-side for general web visualization; choose ClearView specifically for hexahedral mesh wireframes/scalars [5040-pure-client-side-renderers.md]. Time Complexity: The Gather pass is O(F) where F is the number of faces, dominated by atomic operations. The Resolve pass is O(P \cdot K \log K) or O(P \cdot K) where P is the number of pixels and K is the average number of fragments per pixel (capped at 32 for insertion sort). Memory Complexity: O(F + P \cdot K{max}). The fragment buffer is fixed at 4 million entries (64 MB for RGBA32UI). Mesh data scales with cell count. Measured Performance: Tuned for SPE-9 mesh (54,000 faces). The 2048x2048 buffer supports ~30-60 depth complexity per pixel efficiently. Strengths: Fully GPU-accelerated, no CPU-GPU synchronization during rendering, works in WebGL2 without extensions. Limitations: Fixed fragment buffer size limits maximum depth complexity. Not compatible with SwiftShader. Requires careful texture size management due to WebGL2 limitations. ClearView (Unified) is an implementation of a 3-pass WebGL2 renderer for hexahedral meshes, adapted from a C++ desktop renderer (ClearViewRendererFacesUnified). It was developed as part of the "geresim-spike" project to enable high-performance volumetric mesh visualization in web browsers, overcoming WebGL2's lack of SSBOs by mapping data to image textures.
