name: Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation
head: Direct volume rendering method for holograms, Approximate Volume Rendering Based CGH Calculation, Approximate Volume Rendering Based CGH Calculation with Elemental Holograms, Approximate volume rendering based CGH calculation method with elemental holograms
body: This method generates Computer-Generated Holograms (CGHs) for volumetric data by treating voxels as transparent objects with diffuse reflection, enabling the reconstruction of transparent and multi-layer objects. It differs from Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP)-based methods, which only display objects with maximum voxel values, by simulating light propagation and attenuation to preserve depth and transparency cues. The approximate variant reduces computational cost by dividing the hologram into elemental holograms and calculating final light propagation only once per elemental hologram using its center pixel. Inputs: Volume data: A 3D grid of voxels with scalar values I. Color map and Alpha (\alpha) map: Lookup tables mapping scalar values to RGB color components and opacity. Hologram parameters: Number of hologram pixels N, number of voxels M, number of viewpoints n, and number of elemental holograms Ne (for the approximate method). Optical parameters: Light source intensity I{d0}, wavelength (implicit in phase calculation), and geometry (light source position, viewpoint positions). Outputs: Complex amplitude distribution \mu(\xi, \eta) for the CGH, which is typically quantized to phase values 0 to 2\pi for display on an LCOS-SLM. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: 3D array of size Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Each voxel stores scalar value I. Color/Alpha Maps: Arrays mapping scalar indices to (R, G, B, \alpha) tuples. CGH Plane: 2D array of complex numbers or phase values. Steps: 1. Initialize Color and Opacity: For each voxel x with value Ix, calculate its color components Cx (where C \in \{R, G, B, \alpha\}) using linear interpolation between two known endpoints (I2, C2) and (I3, C3) from the map: Cx = C3 - \frac{(C3 - C2)(I3 - Ix)}{I3 - I2} This redefines each voxel as a transparent object with specific RGB and \alpha values. 2. Render Each Voxel (Diffuse Reflection Model): For each voxel eli and each viewpoint, calculate the light intensity in three parts: Part 1: Light Propagation from Source to Voxel: Calculate the incident light intensity I{di} reaching voxel eli after attenuation by preceding voxels j along the path from the light source: I{di} = I{d0} \times \prod{j=0} (1 - \alphaj) where I{d0} is the source intensity and \alphaj is the opacity of voxel j. Note that I{di} and the reflected intensity I{ri} are independent of the viewpoint direction. Part 2: Calculation of Reflected Light: Calculate the intensity of the reflected light I{ri} using the Lambertian diffuse reflection model: I{ri} = k{di} I{di} \max(0, \mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{N}) where k{di} is the Lambert light ratio, \mathbf{L} is the unit vector pointing to the light source, and \mathbf{N} is the normal unit vector derived from the gradient of \alpha in the x, y, z directions. Part 3: Light Propagation from Voxel to Viewpoint: Calculate the final reflected light intensity IrLi reaching the viewpoint, accounting for attenuation by subsequent voxels j between the voxel and the viewpoint: IrLi = I{ri} \times \prod{j=i+1}^{n} (1 - \alphaj) This step must be recalculated for each viewpoint. 3. Calculate Hologram Data (Point Light Source Method): Treat each voxel as a point light source. For a point light source i, calculate the complex amplitude distribution \mu(\xi, \eta) on the hologram plane: \mui(\xi, \eta) = \sqrt{I{rLi}} \exp(-j(k ri + \phii)) where I{rLi} is the intensity calculated in Step 2, ri is the distance from voxel i to the hologram pixel, k is the wavenumber, and \phii is the initial phase. The total CGH is the superposition of amplitudes from all voxels. 4. Approximate Calculation with Elemental Holograms (Optional): To reduce complexity, divide the hologram into Ne elemental holograms: Calculate the final light propagation IrLi only once for each elemental hologram using the center pixel of that elemental hologram to represent the entire region. The amplitude for voxel i in elemental hologram k is I{ek}^{rLi}. For all pixels in elemental hologram k, the amplitude of point light source i is assumed constant. Parameters: Number of iterations for CGH optimization (e.g., Gerchberg-Saxton): 50. Maximum spatial frequency: 4 lp/mm. Reflection Model: Lambertian diffuse reflection. Number of viewpoints n: Varies by application. Pitfalls: The calculation amount is very large, making the method computationally expensive compared to polygon-based or MIP-based methods. Output devices may not transfer the pattern to film at the required resolution, necessitating multiplex holograms or elemental hologram approximations. Holograms may require special lighting conditions, specifically a point monochrome light source at a specific angle, for reconstruction. Time Complexity: Standard Method: Incident light O(M^2), Reflected light O(M), Final light propagation O(M^2 \cdot N), CGH calculation O(M \cdot N). Approximate Method: Incident light O(M^2), Reflected light O(M), Final light propagation O(M^2 \cdot Ne), CGH calculation O(M^2 \cdot N). Note: Sources list CGH calculation complexity as O(M \cdot N) for the standard method and O(M^2 \cdot N) for the approximate method, which appears inconsistent with the text description of superposition. The text states "If Ne is small enough relative to N, the calculation time of final light propagation is greatly shortened. Generally, this method is 5 to 6 times faster than the standard proposed method". Measured Performance: Standard proposed method: 24.3 hours rendering, 3.8 minutes CGH calculation. Approximate method with Elemental Holograms: 3.6 hours rendering, 3.7 minutes CGH calculation. Comparison: Polygon-based (1.5s rendering, 0.3s CGH) and MIP-based (0.2s rendering, 0.6s CGH) are significantly faster but lack transparency/multi-layer detail. Strengths: Generates clear holograms for transparent and multi-layer objects. Parallel generation of focal points increases voxel density per frame (e.g., 4 focal points at 20 fps). Limitations: High computational cost. Requires high-resolution output devices or multiplexing/elemental approximations. Holography is a form of lensless photography based on recording the amplitude and phase of light. Computed holograms are created by calculating interference patterns, but output devices often cannot transfer these patterns to film at the required resolution. Multiplex holograms overcome this by rendering a series of perspective images stored on the same hologram using multiple exposures, with Benton's Alcove holograms using approximately 1000 images. The volume rendering based CGH calculation method was proposed to generate holograms for volume data using direct volume rendering and a point light source method, addressing the limitations of MIP-based methods which only show maximum voxel values. The approximate method with elemental holograms was introduced to reduce the huge computational load, based on the elemental hologram concept proposed by Dr. Ichikawa. name: Ray-box intersection
head: Slab Test, Slab Method, Smits' method, AABB Slab Method, Slab intersection, AABB Ray Intersection, Ray-AABB Intersection, Ray-BBox Intersection, Kay and Kajiya slab test, Smits' Ray-Box Intersection, Ray-Bounding Box Intersection, Ray-Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Intersection
body: The ray-box intersection method determines whether a ray intersects an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) by treating the box as the intersection of three pairs of parallel planes, known as slabs. It computes the entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) distances for each slab pair and checks for overlap across all three axes. Unlike general primitive intersection methods, this approach exploits the axis-aligned nature of the box to reduce the problem to simple scalar comparisons and vector operations, making it the dominant technique for bounding volume hierarchy traversal in ray tracing. Inputs: Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} = (ox, oy, oz) and direction \mathbf{v} = (vx, vy, vz), parameterized as \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v}. AABB: Defined by minimum corner \mathbf{p}0 = (x0, y0, z0) and maximum corner \mathbf{p}1 = (x1, y1, z1). Ray Interval (Optional): A valid hit distance interval [t{min}, t{max}] representing the range of t-values on the ray that count as a hit. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. If intersecting, the entry distance t{near} and exit distance t{far}. The method operates on scalar values or 3D vectors. Inverse Ray Direction: \mathbf{invV} = (1/vx, 1/vy, 1/vz). Interval Vectors: Vectors storing the computed t-values for the lower and upper bounds of each axis. The method can be implemented in two primary styles: the iterative scalar approach (Kay and Kajiya original) and the compact vector approach (widely used in modern kernels). This approach processes each axis (X, Y, Z) sequentially, updating global t{near} and t{far} values. 1. Initialize t{near} = -\infty and t{far} = \infty. 2. For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: a. Let oi be the ray origin component, vi be the ray direction component, mini be the box minimum coordinate, and maxi be the box maximum coordinate. b. Check for parallelism: If vi = 0: i. If oi < mini or oi > maxi, the ray is outside the slab. Return false (miss). ii. Otherwise, the ray is inside the slab along this axis; continue to the next axis. c. Compute intersection distances with the near and far planes of the slab: t1 = \frac{mini - oi}{vi} t2 = \frac{maxi - oi}{vi} d. Ensure t1 is the smaller value (entry) and t2 is the larger value (exit). If t1 > t2, swap t1 and t2. e. Update the global intersection interval: t{near} = \max(t{near}, t1) t{far} = \min(t{far}, t2) f. Check for miss: If t{near} > t{far}, the intervals do not overlap. Return false. g. Check if the box is behind the ray: If t{far} < 0, the entire box is behind the ray origin. Return false. 3. If the loop completes without returning false, the ray intersects the box. Return true. This approach computes all intersections in parallel using vector operations, often branchless. 1. Compute the inverse ray direction: \mathbf{invV} = (1/vx, 1/vy, 1/vz). 2. Compute the t-values for the lower and upper bounds of the box: \mathbf{t}{lower} = (\mathbf{p}0 - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{invV} \mathbf{t}{upper} = (\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{invV} where \odot denotes component-wise multiplication. 3. Determine the entry and exit t-values for each slab by taking the component-wise minimum and maximum of \mathbf{t}{lower} and \mathbf{t}{upper}: \mathbf{t}{min\slabs} = \min(\mathbf{t}{lower}, \mathbf{t}{upper}) \mathbf{t}{max\slabs} = \max(\mathbf{t}{lower}, \mathbf{t}{upper}) 4. Incorporate the ray's valid hit interval [t{min}, t{max}] as a fourth dimension (or separate scalar check). t{box\min} = \max(\mathbf{t}{min\slabs}.x, \mathbf{t}{min\slabs}.y, \mathbf{t}{min\slabs}.z, t{min}) t{box\max} = \min(\mathbf{t}{max\slabs}.x, \mathbf{t}{max\slabs}.y, \mathbf{t}{max\slabs}.z, t{max}) 5. The ray intersects the box if t{box\min} \le t{box\max}. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the robust compact vector approach, handling zero direction components and negative zeros correctly per IEEE 754 standards. def slabsboxtest(p0, p1, rayorigin, raydir, raytmin, raytmax): """ Determines if a ray intersects an AABB. Handles zero direction components and negative zeros robustly. """ tnear = float('-inf') tfar = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0.0: if rayorigin[i] < p0[i] or rayorigin[i] > p1[i]: return False, None, None continue invd = 1.0 / raydir[i] t1 = (p0[i] - rayorigin[i]) invd t2 = (p1[i] - rayorigin[i]) invd if invd >= 0.0: tnear = max(tnear, t1) tfar = min(tfar, t2) else: tnear = max(tnear, t2) tfar = min(tfar, t1) if tnear > tfar: return False, None, None if tfar < 0.0: return False, None, None return True, max(tnear, raytmin), min(tfar, raytmax) Ray Direction: Must be normalized in many applications, but the algorithm works with unnormalized directions as long as invraydir is computed correctly. Box Corners: \mathbf{p}0 and \mathbf{p}1 must satisfy p{0,i} \le p{1,i} for all i \in \{x,y,z\}. Ray Interval: The interval [t{min}, t{max}] represents the valid hit distances on the ray. Typical values are not given in the sources. Zero Direction Components: The algorithm produces correct results for rays with zero direction components (parallel to axes) provided the hardware is IEEE floating-point compliant. The division by zero in invraydir results in infinity, which is handled correctly by the min/max logic. Explicit checks for vi = 0 prevent NaN generation when the ray origin lies exactly on a box boundary. Negative Zero Direction: If a direction component is -0.0, testing the sign of the direction itself fails due to IEEE 754 rules. The robust implementation tests the sign of the reciprocal direction component instead. Ray Origin on Box Face: If the ray origin lies exactly on the box surface and the direction points along the face, naive implementations may result in NaN (Not a Number), causing the test to return false. This behavior can be modified if specific handling is required. Branchless Optimization: Removing early exit checks (like if tnear > tfar) creates a branchless implementation. While this performs more arithmetic operations, it significantly increases performance on modern hardware by avoiding branch mispredictions. Converts an inner bounding box to a list of bounds relative to an enclosing box, adding entries for sides where the inner box is strictly contained. It initializes a counter, loops over dimensions to count boundaries, allocates an array of ANNorthHalfSpace structs, and populates them with dimension index, cutting value, and sign (+1 or -1) based on whether the inner box's lower or upper bound is strictly inside the enclosing box. Computes entry and exit points of rays intersecting a bounding box by rendering the box geometry to textures using OpenGL, storing hit positions in 16-bit floating point textures. It creates a Framebuffer Object (FBO) with GLRGBA16F color attachments and a GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16 depth renderbuffer, enables face culling and depth testing, and draws the cube geometry using a hit shader program passing the MVP matrix as a uniform. The depth buffer must be cleared along with the color buffer, and correct depth writing from the geometry shader is required. Time Complexity: The algorithm performs a fixed number of arithmetic operations and comparisons regardless of scene complexity. Performance: The slabs test is the dominant method for AABB intersection due to its simplicity and efficiency. Branchless implementations are preferred in high-performance ray tracing kernels (e.g., Embree) to maximize throughput on SIMD units and GPUs. Strengths: Fast, robust, easy to implement, works well with SIMD/vectorization. Limitations: Only applicable to axis-aligned boxes. Origin: The method was introduced by T. L. Kay and J. T. Kajiya in their 1986 paper "Ray tracing complex scenes" presented at SIGGRAPH. Development: The algorithm has become the standard for AABB intersection in ray tracing. It is widely used in modern ray tracing kernels such as Embree and in astronomical simulation tools like raytheia. Usage: It is used for primary ray-scene intersection testing, shadow ray occlusion testing, frustum culling, and spatial traversal of octree and grid acceleration structures. name: Ray-Box Intersection via OpenGL Geometry Shaders
head: CubeIntersection, Front/Back Hit Textures
body: This method computes the entry and exit points of rays intersecting a volume's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) by rendering the box geometry to textures using OpenGL geometry shaders. It solves the problem of providing fragment shaders with precise start and end texture coordinates for volume traversal without complex CPU-side ray-box intersection calculations. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using a single-pass geometry shader approach to compute these points, whereas alternatives like Two-Pass Ray Entry/Exit Determination use a two-pass rendering approach with separate FBOs for front and back hits. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera projection matrix, model-view matrix, volume bounding box geometry (cube), and a boolean flag mbFront to select front (entry) or back (exit) hit computation. Outputs: Two 2D textures (TEXTUREFRONTHIT and TEXTUREBACKHIT) storing the 3D world-space hit positions (or texture coordinates) for each pixel. Data Structures: Hit Textures: 2D textures of size Width x Height (screen resolution). Format is GLRGBA16F, internal format GLRGBA16F, type GLFLOAT. Framebuffer Object (FBO): Contains a color attachment (the hit texture) and a depth renderbuffer of format GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16. Steps: 1. Create an FBO with a color attachment (TEXTUREFRONTHIT or TEXTUREBACKHIT) of format GLRGBA16F and a depth renderbuffer of format GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16. 2. Clear the color buffer and the depth buffer. 3. Enable GLCULLFACE and GLDEPTHTEST. 4. If mbFront is true, cull GLBACK faces; otherwise, cull GLFRONT faces. 5. Set up the geometry shader program. The vertex shader passes the vertex position and normal. The geometry shader receives the triangle vertices, computes the ray-box intersection for the ray defined by the camera origin and the fragment's screen position, and outputs the hit position. The fragment shader writes the hit position to the color attachment. 6. Draw the cube geometry using the hit shader program, passing the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix as a uniform. 7. Repeat steps 1-6 for the opposite hit (front or back) by toggling mbFront and using the other FBO/texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computerayboxhits(cameraorigin, cameradirection, mvpmatrix, cubevertices, width, height): # Create FBOs and textures for front and back hits frontfbo = createfbo(width, height, format=GLRGBA16F, depthformat=GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16) backfbo = createfbo(width, height, format=GLRGBA16F, depthformat=GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16) fronttexture = createtexture(width, height, format=GLRGBA16F, type=GLFLOAT) backtexture = createtexture(width, height, format=GLRGBA16F, type=GLFLOAT) attachtexturetofbo(frontfbo, fronttexture, attachment=GLCOLORATTACHMENT0) attachtexturetofbo(backfbo, backtexture, attachment=GLCOLORATTACHMENT0) # Load shader program with geometry shader shaderprogram = loadshaderprogram(vertexshadercode, geometryshadercode, fragmentshadercode) # Compute front hits (entry points) bindfbo(frontfbo) glclearcolorbuffer() glcleardepthbuffer() glenable(GLCULLFACE) glenable(GLDEPTHTEST) glcullface(GLBACK) # Cull back faces to get front hits useshader(shaderprogram) setuniform(shaderprogram, "mvpmatrix", mvpmatrix) setuniform(shaderprogram, "cameraorigin", cameraorigin) drawcube(cubevertices) # Compute back hits (exit points) bindfbo(backfbo) glclearcolorbuffer() glcleardepthbuffer() glcullface(GLFRONT) # Cull front faces to get back hits useshader(shaderprogram) setuniform(shaderprogram, "mvpmatrix", mvpmatrix) setuniform(shaderprogram, "cameraorigin", cameraorigin) drawcube(cubevertices) # Unbind FBOs bindfbo(0) return fronttexture, backtexture Geometry Shader Logic (Conceptual): The geometry shader receives a triangle. For each vertex, it computes the ray direction from the camera origin to the vertex. It then performs a ray-box intersection test (using the slab method from Ray-box intersection) to find the entry and exit points. The hit position is written to the output. The fragment shader then writes this position to the color attachment. Parameters: mbFront: Boolean flag determining whether to compute front (entry) or back (exit) hits. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The depth buffer is cleared along with the color buffer, but the depth test is enabled, requiring correct depth writing from the geometry shader. Precision issues may arise from using 16-bit floating point textures for storing hit positions. The method assumes the volume bounding box is axis-aligned and aligned with the world axes. This method determines the 3D volume texture coordinates for the entry and exit points of a ray passing through a volume's bounding box by rendering the box geometry to textures using OpenGL. It solves the problem of providing the fragment shader with the precise start and end texture coordinates required for volume traversal without complex CPU-side ray-box intersection calculations. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using a two-pass rendering approach where the first pass stores exit coordinates in a separate Framebuffer Object (FBO), and the second pass retrieves them, whereas alternatives like Ray-Box Intersection via OpenGL Geometry Shaders compute these points in a single pass using geometry shaders. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels in the screen resolution, as each pixel requires a ray-box intersection computation in the geometry shader. Memory Complexity: O(W H) for storing the hit textures, where W and H are the screen dimensions. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with screen resolution. Strengths: Offloads ray-box intersection computation to the GPU, reducing CPU overhead. Simple to implement using standard OpenGL features. Limitations: Requires OpenGL geometry shaders, which may not be available on all hardware. Precision issues with 16-bit textures. Limited to axis-aligned bounding boxes. When to use: When GPU-based ray-box intersection is desired and OpenGL geometry shaders are available. When not to use: When high precision is required (use 32-bit textures or CPU-side computation) or when geometry shaders are not supported. This method is described in the VRCUDA project, an unofficial implementation of volume rendering using CUDA and OpenGL. It is used in the context of GPU-accelerated volume rendering to efficiently compute ray-box intersections for volume traversal. franjaviersans/VRCUDA, https://github.com/franjaviersans/VRCUDA, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Two-Pass Ray Entry/Exit Determination
head: Front/Backface Buffer Raycasting, Ray Setup Pass, Ray casting setup rendering, Two-Pass Raycasting with Back-Face Depth Buffering
body: This method determines the 3D volume texture coordinates for the entry and exit points of a ray passing through a volume's bounding box by rendering the box geometry to textures. It solves the problem of providing the fragment shader with the precise start and end texture coordinates required for volume traversal without complex CPU-side ray-box intersection calculations. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using a two-pass rendering approach where the first pass stores exit coordinates in a separate Framebuffer Object (FBO), and the second pass retrieves them. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: The volume's bounding box geometry, the current camera view and projection matrices, and the volume texture dimensions. Outputs: Two 2D textures (or a single FBO with multiple attachments) containing the 3D texture coordinates for the ray entry and exit points for each pixel. Data Structures: Bounding Box Geometry: A cube defined by 8 vertices. Each vertex has a position and a color attribute representing its 3D texture coordinates. Framebuffer Object (FBO): A GPU-resident texture used to store the exit point coordinates from Pass 1. Vertex Shader Output: Contains clip-space position and interpolated texture coordinates (color). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Matrices: Compute the concatenated World-View-Projection matrix (M{WVP}). 2. Pass 1: Render Back Faces (Exit Points): Enable face culling to cull front faces: glEnable(GLCULLFACE) and glCullFace(GLFRONT). Bind the FBO texture for storing exit coordinates. Render the bounding box. The vertex shader transforms vertices using M{WVP}. The fragment shader outputs the vertex color (texture coordinates). The resulting texture contains the 3D texture coordinates of the exit point for each ray. 3. Pass 2: Render Front Faces (Entry Points): Disable face culling or cull back faces to render front faces. Bind the FBO texture from Pass 1 as a sampler in the fragment shader. Render the bounding box. The vertex shader transforms vertices using M{WVP}. The fragment shader receives the vertex color (texture coordinates of the entry point). The fragment shader samples the FBO texture at the current fragment's screen position to retrieve the exit point coordinates stored in Pass 1. The fragment shader now has both entry and exit 3D texture coordinates and computes the volume rendering integral. Formulas: Vertex Transformation: Pos{clip} = M{WVP} \times Pos{model}. Texture Coordinate Mapping: The vertices of the bounding box are assigned colors corresponding to their 3D texture coordinates. The axes map as follows: x goes from black (0) to red (1), y goes from black (0) to green (1), and z goes from black (0) to blue (1). The texture coordinates range from (0,0,0) at the lower-left-black corner to (1,1,1) at the upper-right-white corner. DirectX Specific Shift: If using DirectX-style model space coordinates in the range [-0.5, 0.5], they are shifted to normalized texture coordinates in [0.0, 1.0] using: output.Tex = Pos.xyz + float3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5). Parameters: M{WVP}: Concatenated world-view-projection matrix. Culling Mode: GLFRONT for Pass 1, GLBACK or disabled for Pass 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Coordinate Axes: The mapping of RGB channels to texture axes (x,y,z) must be consistent. x is Red, y is Green, z is Blue. Precision: Using 16-bit floating point textures for the FBO may introduce precision errors in the stored coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twopassraysetup(boundingbox, matrixwvp, width, height): # Initialize FBO texture to store exit point coordinates fboexitcoords = [[None] height for in range(width)] # Pass 1: Render back faces to FBO # Cull front faces so only back faces are processed for screeny in range(height): for screenx in range(width): # Standard rasterization pipeline transforms vertices by matrixwvp, # culls front faces, and interpolates vertex colors across fragments # The sources do not provide explicit rasterization code. fragment = rasterizepixel(screenx, screeny, boundingbox, matrixwvp, cullfront=True) if fragment is not None: # Vertex color attribute stores the 3D texture coordinate fboexitcoords[screenx][screeny] = fragment.color # Pass 2: Render front faces to default framebuffer outputtexture = [[None] height for in range(width)] # Cull back faces or disable culling to render front faces for screeny in range(height): for screenx in range(width): # Standard rasterization pipeline transforms vertices by matrixwvp, # culls back faces, and interpolates vertex colors across fragments fragment = rasterizepixel(screenx, screeny, boundingbox, matrixwvp, cullfront=False) if fragment is not None: entrytexcoord = fragment.color # Sample FBO at fragment position to retrieve exit point coordinates exittexcoord = fboexitcoords[screenx][screeny] # Fragment shader outputs the result of the volume rendering integral color = computevolumerenderingintegral(entrytexcoord, exittexcoord) outputtexture[screenx][screeny] = color return outputtexture Computes entry/exit in a single pass using geometry shaders. Choose when single-pass efficiency is critical and geometry shader support is available. Ray-Box Intersection via OpenGL Geometry Shaders Computes entry/exit on the CPU. Choose when GPU memory bandwidth for the FBO is a bottleneck or for simpler implementations. Ray-Box Intersection Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, performed twice (two passes). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for one additional FBO texture to store exit coordinates. Strengths: Simple to implement using standard OpenGL or DirectX rendering pipeline; avoids complex ray-box intersection math on the GPU. Limitations: Requires two rendering passes; precision loss with 16-bit textures. When to Use: When using OpenGL or DirectX and a two-pass approach is acceptable. When Not to Use: When single-pass performance is critical; when high precision is required and 16-bit textures are insufficient. This method was described in educational materials for GPU volume rendering, specifically in the CISC/CMPE 454 course notes. It is also implemented in the D3DVolumeRaycaster project, which uses a similar two-pass setup for DirectX. The technique leverages the rasterization pipeline to compute geometric intersections implicitly. name: Plane-AABB Overlap Test
head: Plane vs Bounds Intersection, Plane-AABB Intersection Test, Plane-Box Overlap Test, planeBoxOverlapCUDA
body: Determines if an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) overlaps with a plane defined by a normal vector and a point (or signed distance). It solves the problem of culling voxels or primitives that lie entirely on one side of a cutting plane. It differs from Ray-box intersection by testing a static infinite plane against a static box rather than a parametric ray, and from AABB Collision Detection by handling a single infinite half-space rather than two moving boxes. Inputs: planenormal: A 3D vector (nx, ny, nz) representing the plane's normal. planepoint: A 3D vector (px, py, pz) on the plane, OR planed: a scalar signed distance from the origin to the plane. aabbcenter: A 3D vector (cx, cy, cz) representing the center of the AABB. aabbextents: A 3D vector (ex, ey, ez) representing the half-widths of the AABB along each axis. Outputs: Boolean: true if the AABB intersects or touches the plane; false otherwise. Data Structures: Vector3: A struct with fields x, y, z of type float. Plane: A struct with fields normal (Vector3) and distance (float, where d = -\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p}). Bounds: A struct with fields center (Vector3) and max (Vector3). Extents are derived as \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{max} - \mathbf{center}. Formulas: 1. Signed Distance to Center (s): The signed distance from the plane to the AABB center. s = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{c} - d Where d is the plane's distance parameter. If defined by a point \mathbf{p}, d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p}. 2. Projected Radius (r): The maximum extent of the AABB projected onto the plane normal. r = ex |nx| + ey |ny| + ez |nz| 3. Overlap Condition: |s| \le r Steps: 1. Calculate the signed distance s from the plane to the AABB center using the dot product of the normal and center, minus the plane's distance parameter. 2. Calculate the projected radius r by summing the products of each AABB extent component and the absolute value of the corresponding normal component. 3. Return true if the absolute value of s is less than or equal to r; otherwise, return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planeaabboverlap(planenormal, planed, aabbcenter, aabbextents): """ planenormal: (nx, ny, nz) planed: float, signed distance from origin to plane aabbcenter: (cx, cy, cz) aabbextents: (ex, ey, ez) """ # Calculate signed distance from plane to AABB center # s = dot(normal, center) - d s = planenormal.x aabbcenter.x + \ planenormal.y aabbcenter.y + \ planenormal.z aabbcenter.z - planed # Calculate projected radius of AABB onto plane normal # r = ex|nx| + ey|ny| + ez|nz| r = (aabbextents.x abs(planenormal.x) + aabbextents.y abs(planenormal.y) + aabbextents.z abs(planenormal.z)) # Check if distance is within projected radius return abs(s) <= r Alternative Implementation (Corner Projection): Some implementations compute the minimum and maximum projections of the box corners onto the normal explicitly, avoiding absolute values in the radius calculation by selecting corners based on normal signs. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planeaabboverlapcorners(planenormal, planed, aabbcenter, aabbextents): """ Alternative method using explicit corner projection. Returns true if overlap exists. """ # Determine the corner that minimizes the dot product with the normal vmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Determine the corner that maximizes the dot product with the normal vmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for dim in range(3): if planenormal[dim] > 0.0: vmin[dim] = aabbcenter[dim] - aabbextents[dim] vmax[dim] = aabbcenter[dim] + aabbextents[dim] else: vmin[dim] = aabbcenter[dim] + aabbextents[dim] vmax[dim] = aabbcenter[dim] - aabbextents[dim] # Calculate dot products dotvmin = (planenormal.x vmin.x + planenormal.y vmin.y + planenormal.z vmin.z) dotvmax = (planenormal.x vmax.x + planenormal.y vmax.y + planenormal.z vmax.z) # The plane equation is dot(n, x) - d = 0. # We check if the range [dotvmin - d, dotvmax - d] contains 0. # If dotvmin - d > 0, the entire box is on the positive side (no overlap). if dotvmin - planed > 0.0: return False # If dotvmax - d >= 0, the box intersects or touches the plane. if dotvmax - planed >= 0.0: return True return False Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When |s| \approx r, floating-point inaccuracies may cause false negatives or positives. Using >= and <= with a small epsilon is recommended for robustness. Degenerate Box: If extents are zero, the test reduces to checking if the center lies on the plane. Normal Normalization: The normal vector must be normalized for the distance s and radius r calculations to be geometrically correct. If the normal is not normalized, r must be scaled by 1/|\mathbf{n}| or s by |\mathbf{n}|. The parent method. Use this when you need entry/exit distances for a ray. Use this when culling entire boxes against view frustum planes. Use this for dynamic collision between two boxes. Use this when preparing to sample volume data inside a box. Use this for specialized cube-shaped primitives. Use this when transforming rays into local box space. Use this for GPU shaders requiring branchless execution. Use this for 2D projections. Time Complexity: O(1). Requires a constant number of arithmetic operations (dot products, absolute values, comparisons). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures required. Performance: Extremely fast. Suitable for real-time voxelization and frustum culling. The corner-projection method may be slightly slower due to branching but avoids absolute value instructions on some architectures. The projected-radius method is branchless and often preferred for GPU implementation. Strengths: Simple, robust, and efficient. Handles arbitrary plane orientations. Limitations: Only tests against a single plane. Does not provide intersection points or normals. When to use: Voxelization of triangles, frustum culling, clipping volumes. When not to use: When ray-box intersection distances are needed, or when testing against multiple planes (use frustum culling instead). The plane-AABB overlap test is a fundamental primitive in computer graphics, particularly in voxelization and collision detection. It is widely used in GPU-based voxelizers to determine which voxels intersect with a triangle's plane. The method is derived from the separating axis theorem (SAT), where the plane normal serves as the separating axis. name: AABB Culling
head: 8-point frustum test, Box culling
body: AABB Culling determines if a box defined by 8 vertices is completely outside a viewing box along any axis, returning false if culled and true otherwise. It serves as a fast rejection test in volume rendering and ray tracing to avoid expensive intersection calculations for primitives that are clearly outside the view frustum or a specific spatial region. Unlike Ray-box intersection, which computes precise entry and exit distances for potential hits, this method performs a coarse binary check to discard objects early. Inputs: points: An array of 8 vectors [x, y, z] representing the vertices of the object box. box: A viewing box defined by 6 scalar values [minx, maxy, miny, maxx, minz, maxz] (indices 0-5) and potentially additional bounds at indices 3-5 depending on implementation specifics. Note: The source notation box[3], box[0], etc., implies a specific packing order where box[0] is min-x, box[3] is max-x, box[1] is min-y, box[4] is max-y, box[2] is min-z, and box[5] is max-z. Outputs: Boolean: true if the box intersects or overlaps the viewing box; false if it is completely outside. Data Structures: points: Array of 8 elements, each a 3-component vector. box: Array of 6 or more scalar values defining the axis-aligned viewing volume boundaries. Steps: 1. Initialize a counter out = 0. 2. Loop i from 0 to 7 (for each of the 8 vertices): a. If points[i][0] > box[3], increment out. b. If out == 8, return false (all points are outside the max-x bound). 3. Repeat the check for other axes: a. If points[i][0] < box[0], increment out. b. If points[i][1] > box[4], increment out. c. If points[i][1] < box[1], increment out. d. If points[i][2] > box[5], increment out. e. If points[i][2] < box[2], increment out. (Note: The source description implies a sequential check where out is incremented for each vertex that fails a specific bound check, and if all 8 vertices fail the same bound check, the object is culled. However, the pseudocode below clarifies the logic as checking if ALL points are outside a specific half-space.) Corrected Logic Interpretation: The source describes a test where out counts how many points are outside a specific boundary. If all 8 points are outside the same boundary (e.g., all x > maxx), the box is culled. The algorithm checks each of the 6 planes of the viewing box. If the box is completely outside any one plane, it returns false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbculling(points, box): """ points: list of 8 tuples (x, y, z) box: list of 6 scalars [minx, maxy, miny, maxx, minz, maxz] Note: Source indices are [0]=minx, [3]=maxx, [1]=miny, [4]=maxy, [2]=minz, [5]=maxz """ # Extract bounds for clarity minx = box[0] maxx = box[3] miny = box[1] maxy = box[4] minz = box[2] maxz = box[5] # Check if all points are outside the viewing box along any axis # X-axis: All points > maxx allabovemaxx = all(p[0] > maxx for p in points) if allabovemaxx: return False # X-axis: All points < minx allbelowminx = all(p[0] < minx for p in points) if allbelowminx: return False # Y-axis: All points > maxy allabovemaxy = all(p[1] > maxy for p in points) if allabovemaxy: return False # Y-axis: All points < miny allbelowminy = all(p[1] < miny for p in points) if allbelowminy: return False # Z-axis: All points > maxz allabovemaxz = all(p[2] > maxz for p in points) if allabovemaxz: return False # Z-axis: All points < minz allbelowminz = all(p[2] < minz for p in points) if allbelowminz: return False # If not completely outside any single plane, it intersects or overlaps return True Parameters: points: Array of 8 vectors [x, y, z] representing the vertices of the object box. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes the points array contains the 8 corners of the AABB. If the box is not axis-aligned, this simple component-wise test is invalid without transformation. Precision issues may arise if points lie exactly on the boundary; the strict inequality (>, <) may need adjustment to >= or <= depending on whether touching is considered an intersection or cull. Bounding Box Culling is a view-dependent pre-processing step that filters out 3D Gaussians whose projected 2D footprint does not intersect the camera viewport. It differs from general AABB Culling by operating on the projected 2D ellipse of a Gaussian rather than a static 3D axis-aligned box, thereby enabling early rejection of primitives that are off-screen in screen space. Subspace Culling reduces false-positive hits in ray-box intersection tests by embedding a binary voxel data structure into the volume, allowing cheap ray-voxel intersection via bitwise AND operations. It represents the ray as a conservative voxel volume and performs intersection checks using bitwise AND between the ray's voxel volume and the embedded voxel data structure. This method is applicable to hierarchical data structures such as Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVH) to reduce the number of intersections during traversal. It compresses the voxel data using a lookup table to achieve significant false-positive reductions with a small memory footprint. Unlike oriented bounding boxes which reduce false positives but are computationally expensive, this method uses cheap bitwise operations on voxel data. A pitfall of standard AABBs is that they produce extra empty space, leading to false-positive hits for thin and diagonal primitives, which this method aims to reduce. Time Complexity: O(1) per box, as it involves a fixed number of comparisons (8 vertices × 6 planes). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Extremely fast rejection test; minimal computational overhead. Limitations: Coarse approximation; does not provide intersection distances; assumes axis-aligned boxes. When to use: As a pre-filter before expensive ray-box intersection tests. When not to use: When precise intersection data is required or when boxes are not axis-aligned. The method originates from practical implementations in WebGL-based volume rendering and marching cubes algorithms, specifically noted in the webgl-marching-cubes repository. It is a standard technique in computer graphics for frustum culling of axis-aligned bounding boxes. name: Bounding Box Culling
head: 2D Gaussian Bounding Box Culling, Bounding Box Culling and Pre-processing, Viewport Culling via AABB
body: Bounding Box Culling is a view-dependent pre-processing step that filters out 3D Gaussians whose projected 2D footprint does not intersect the camera viewport. It differs from general AABB Culling by operating on the projected 2D ellipse of a Gaussian rather than a static 3D axis-aligned box, thereby enabling early rejection of primitives that are off-screen in screen space. Inputs: A list of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a 3D center position \mathbf{c} and a 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigma. Outputs: A buffer of alive primitives containing packed major/minor axes, depth, and color/opacity data. Data Structures: 1. Alive Primitive Buffer: Major/Minor Axes: Packed into two 32-bit unsigned integers. Each 32-bit integer stores a 2D vector component pair using 16-bit floats (half-precision) per component. Depth: Stored as a 32-bit floating-point value in a dedicated buffer. Color/Opacity: Packed into a single 32-bit unsigned integer using RGBA8 format (8 bits per channel). Steps: 1. Projection: For each Gaussian, project its 3D center \mathbf{c} and covariance matrix \Sigma into 2D screen space to yield a 2D ellipse. 2. Axis Calculation: Calculate the major and minor axes of the projected 2D ellipse. 3. AABB Calculation: Compute an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for the 2D ellipse. 4. Culling Test: Drop the Gaussian if its bounding box does not intersect the camera viewport. 5. Depth Storage: For alive primitives, calculate the depth and store it as a 32-bit floating point in a dedicated buffer. 6. Color Evaluation: Evaluate Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients based on the current viewing direction to compute the final RGB color. 7. Axis Packing: Compress and pack the major and minor axis vectors into a pair of 32-bit unsigned integers, using 16-bit floats for each vector component. 8. Color Packing: Compress and pack the resulting floating-point color and the splat’s opacity into a single 32-bit unsigned integer using an RGBA8 format. 9. Write: Write the alive primitives to the next stage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boundingboxculling(gaussians, viewprojmatrix, viewportbounds): aliveprimitives = [] depthbuffer = [] for g in gaussians: # 1. Project 3D center and covariance to 2D screen space clipc = viewprojmatrix @ np.append(g.center, 1.0) screenc = clipc[:2] / clipc[2] J = computeprojectionjacobian(g.center, viewprojmatrix) screencov = J @ g.covariance @ J.T # 2. Calculate major and minor axes of the projected 2D ellipse eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(screencov) majoraxis = eigenvectors[:, 1] np.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) minoraxis = eigenvectors[:, 0] np.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]) # 3. Compute AABB for the 2D ellipse extentx = np.abs(majoraxis[0]) + np.abs(minoraxis[0]) extenty = np.abs(majoraxis[1]) + np.abs(minoraxis[1]) aabbmin = screenc - np.array([extentx, extenty]) aabbmax = screenc + np.array([extentx, extenty]) # 4. Culling Test: Check intersection with camera viewport if aabbmin[0] > viewportbounds[1][0] or aabbmax[0] < viewportbounds[0][0] or \ aabbmin[1] > viewportbounds[1][1] or aabbmax[1] < viewportbounds[0][1]: continue # Drop the Gaussian # 5. Calculate depth and store as 32-bit float depth = clipc[2] depthbuffer.append(depth) # 6. Evaluate SH coefficients for RGB color viewdir = normalize(viewprojmatrix[:3, 3] - g.center) rgb = evaluatesh(g.shcoeffs, viewdir) # 7. Pack major/minor axes into pair of 32-bit uints (16-bit floats per component) packedaxes = pack16bitvectors(majoraxis, minoraxis) # 8. Pack color and opacity into single 32-bit uint (RGBA8) packedcolor = packrgba8(rgb, g.opacity) aliveprimitives.append({ 'axes': packedaxes, 'depth': depth, 'color': packedcolor, 'screencenter': screenc }) return aliveprimitives, depthbuffer def computeprojectionjacobian(center, viewproj): x, y, z = center w = viewproj[2, 0]x + viewproj[2, 1]y + viewproj[2, 2]z + viewproj[2, 3] f = 1.0 / w f2 = f f J = np.zeros((2, 3)) J[0, 0] = viewproj[0, 0] f - viewproj[0, 2] x f2 J[0, 1] = viewproj[0, 1] f - viewproj[0, 2] y f2 J[0, 2] = -viewproj[0, 2] z f2 J[1, 0] = viewproj[1, 0] f - viewproj[1, 2] x f2 J[1, 1] = viewproj[1, 1] f - viewproj[1, 2] y f2 J[1, 2] = -viewproj[1, 2] z f2 return J def evaluatesh(coeffs, direction): # Standard SH evaluation return np.clip(np.dot(coeffs, direction), 0.0, 1.0) def pack16bitvectors(major, minor): def pack2d(v): return (int(v[0] 65535) & 0xFFFF) | ((int(v[1] 65535) & 0xFFFF) << 16) return (pack2d(major), pack2d(minor)) def packrgba8(rgb, opacity): r = int(np.clip(rgb[0], 0, 1) 255) g = int(np.clip(rgb[1], 0, 1) 255) b = int(np.clip(rgb[2], 0, 1) 255) a = int(np.clip(opacity, 0, 1) 255) return (r << 24) | (g << 16) | (b << 8) | a Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of 16-bit floats for axis packing may introduce quantization errors for very small or very large splats. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian is projected to a point or line (degenerate ellipse), the AABB calculation must handle zero-area cases gracefully. Boundary Conditions: The intersection test must correctly handle Gaussians that are partially off-screen but still contribute to the visible area. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians O(N), as each Gaussian is processed independently. Memory Complexity: Requires additional buffers for depth, packed axes, and packed color/opacity, increasing memory bandwidth requirements during the pre-processing stage but reducing it during rasterization. Performance: Significantly reduces the number of primitives passed to the Sort and Rasterization stages, improving overall rendering efficiency. Strengths: Effective early rejection of off-screen primitives; reduces memory bandwidth for subsequent stages. Limitations: Requires projection and ellipse axis calculation for every Gaussian, even those culled. Bounding Box Culling is a key component of the pre-processing stage in WebSplatter, a system designed for efficient Gaussian Splatting in web browsers via WebGPU. It was introduced to address the computational bottleneck of sorting and rendering large numbers of Gaussians by filtering out invisible ones early. name: AABB Collision Detection
head: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Collision, Axis-Separated AABB Collision, Sliding Collision, AABB Collision Sliding, Axis-Aligned Collision Sliding, Axis-Separated Movement AABB Collision
body: AABB Collision Detection is a physics resolution method for voxel worlds that prevents entities (players, cameras, NPCs) from passing through solid blocks by separating movement into individual axis checks. Unlike single-step displacement checks, this method applies velocity along one axis, tests for intersection with the voxel grid, and commits or cancels that movement before proceeding to the next axis, enabling "sliding" along walls. It is distinct from Ray-box intersection, which determines if a ray hits a box, by focusing on resolving continuous entity motion against discrete voxel geometry. Inputs: Entity position P = (x, y, z), typically defined as the center of its AABB. Entity dimensions (half-extents or full width/height): W, H, D. Velocity or intended displacement vector V = (vx, vy, vz). Voxel world data structure (e.g., 2D/3D array worldMap) where BlockID > 0 indicates solid terrain. Outputs: Updated entity position P' that respects collision constraints. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A discrete array mapping integer coordinates to block types. Access is typically O(1). AABB: Defined by center P and half-dimensions hx, hy, hz. For a camera, typical dimensions are (0.8, 1.8, 0.8) or (0.8, 1.8, 0.2). For a player, typical dimensions are Width 0.3, Height 1.7. Steps: 1. Calculate Target Position: Compute the hypothetical new position if no collisions occurred: P{target} = P + V. 2. Compute Delta: Calculate the displacement vector \Delta = P{target} - P. 3. Axis-Separated Resolution: Iterate through axes (typically X, then Z, then Y to handle gravity/jumping): a. Apply Axis Movement: Create a tentative position P{tentative} by adding only the current axis component of \Delta to the current safe position P{safe}. b. Define AABB Bounds: Calculate the voxel grid indices covered by the entity's AABB at P{tentative}: mini = \lfloor P{tentative, i} - hi \rfloor maxi = \lceil P{tentative, i} + hi \rceil where i is the axis index (0, 1, 2). c. Collision Check: Method A (Voxel Sweep): Iterate through all voxels in the box defined by min and max. If any voxel has BlockID > 0, a collision is detected. Method B (Point Sampling): Sample specific points on the entity's boundary (e.g., Feet, Waist, Head) against the voxel grid. If any point intersects a solid voxel, a collision is detected. d. Resolve: If collision detected: Discard the movement for this axis. P{safe} remains unchanged for this axis. If no collision: Update P{safe} with the new coordinate for this axis. 4. Final Position: The resulting P{safe} is the new entity position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbcollisiondetection(position, velocity, world, entitydims): """ position: tuple (x, y, z) - center of AABB velocity: tuple (vx, vy, vz) - intended movement world: function voxel(x, y, z) -> int (0 for air, >0 for solid) entitydims: tuple (hx, hy, hz) - half-extents of AABB """ # Step 1 & 2: Calculate target and delta targetx = position[0] + velocity[0] targety = position[1] + velocity[1] targetz = position[2] + velocity[2] deltax = targetx - position[0] deltay = targety - position[1] deltaz = targetz - position[2] # Current safe position starts as original position safex = position[0] safey = position[1] safez = position[2] # Step 3: Axis-Separated Resolution (Order: X, Z, Y) # X Axis tentativex = safex + deltax # Define voxel bounds for X movement minx = floor(tentativex - entitydims[0]) maxx = ceil(tentativex + entitydims[0]) miny = floor(safey - entitydims[1]) maxy = ceil(safey + entitydims[1]) minz = floor(safez - entitydims[2]) maxz = ceil(safez + entitydims[2]) collidedx = False for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): if world(x, y, z) > 0: collidedx = True break if collidedx: break if collidedx: break if not collidedx: safex = tentativex # Z Axis tentativez = safez + deltaz minx = floor(safex - entitydims[0]) maxx = ceil(safex + entitydims[0]) miny = floor(safey - entitydims[1]) maxy = ceil(safey + entitydims[1]) minz = floor(tentativez - entitydims[2]) maxz = ceil(tentativez + entitydims[2]) collidedz = False for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): if world(x, y, z) > 0: collidedz = True break if collidedz: break if collidedz: break if not collidedz: safez = tentativez # Y Axis (Gravity/Jump) tentativey = safey + deltay minx = floor(safex - entitydims[0]) maxx = ceil(safex + entitydims[0]) miny = floor(tentativey - entitydims[1]) maxy = ceil(tentativey + entitydims[1]) minz = floor(safez - entitydims[2]) maxz = ceil(safez + entitydims[2]) collidedy = False for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): if world(x, y, z) > 0: collidedy = True break if collidedy: break if collidedy: break if not collidedy: safey = tentativey return (safex, safey, safez) Parameters: Gravity: Typically 18.0 units/s². Jump Force: Typically 8.0 units/s. Player Dimensions: Width 0.3, Height 1.7. Camera Dimensions: (0.8, 1.8, 0.8) or (0.8, 1.8, 0.2). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stuck Bug: Checking collision against the current cell (before moving) causes permanent sticking if the player starts inside a wall or moves into one. The solution is to check the next cell (the target position). Corner Penetration: Simple axis checks may allow corners to penetrate walls slightly if the step size is large, leading to "entombment" in doors or walls. This can be mitigated by testing all four corners of the AABB on both axis moves. A variant of AABB Collision Detection that tests all four corners of the player box on both axis moves to prevent overlap. It asserts that no corner ever enters a solid cell and ensures that pulling away from a wall works from the pressed position, solving the "entombment" bug where simple axis checks fail to escape narrow gaps. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the AABB's bounding box. For small entities in dense grids, this is small but constant per frame. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, assuming the voxel grid is accessed directly. Strengths: Simple to implement; allows smooth sliding along walls; prevents tunneling through thin walls if step sizes are small. Limitations: Can be computationally expensive if the AABB is large or the voxel grid is sparse but the AABB covers many empty voxels; prone to "stuck" bugs if not implemented with next-cell checks; may require corner checks for robustness in narrow passages. When to Use: Voxel-based games, simple physics engines, real-time applications where performance is critical and geometry is discrete. When Not to Use: Continuous physics with complex curved surfaces; scenes with large static objects where broad-phase culling is more appropriate. Originating from early raycasting engines and voxel games, AABB collision detection became a standard technique for player movement in 3D environments with grid-based worlds. It was popularized by games like Wolfenstein 3D and Minecraft clones, where simple, fast, and predictable collision resolution was essential for gameplay. The method is often cited in tutorials for building voxel engines from scratch. name: Mesh Bounding Box Calculation
head: axis-aligned bounding box, min-max vertex bounds
body: Computes the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of a mesh by determining the minimum and maximum coordinates across all vertex positions. It provides the foundational spatial extent for explicit geometry, serving as the input for subsequent ray-box intersection tests in raycasting Parent. Unlike methods operating on implicit point clouds or sample sets, this method specifically targets the vertex coordinates of explicit triangular or polygonal meshes. Inputs: A list of 3D vertices V = \{v0, v1, \dots, v{n-1}\}, where each vertex vi has coordinates (xi, yi, zi). Outputs: An AABB defined by two 3D vectors: min (mn) and max (mx). Data Structures: Vec3: A structure containing three floating-point components (e.g., x, y, z or an array mpos[3]). mn, mx: Vec3 instances initialized to the bounds. Steps: 1. Validation: Check if the vertex list V is empty. If empty, the method is undefined for this overload. 2. Initialization: Set mn and mx to the coordinates of the first vertex v0. mn = v0, \quad mx = v0 3. Iteration: For each vertex vi in V where i ranges from 1 to n-1: For each dimension d \in \{0, 1, 2\} (representing X, Y, Z): mn[d] = \min(vi[d], mn[d]) mx[d] = \max(vi[d], mx[d]) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemeshaabb(vertices): """ Computes the AABB for a list of 3D vertices. vertices: List of tuples or objects with x, y, z attributes. Returns: (minvec, maxvec) """ if not vertices: raise ValueError("Empty vertex list causes undefined behavior") # Initialize min and max with the first vertex first = vertices[0] mn = [first.x, first.y, first.z] mx = [first.x, first.y, first.z] # Iterate through remaining vertices for i in range(1, len(vertices)): v = vertices[i] # Update min and max for each dimension if v.x < mn[0]: mn[0] = v.x if v.x > mx[0]: mx[0] = v.x if v.y < mn[1]: mn[1] = v.y if v.y > mx[1]: mx[1] = v.y if v.z < mn[2]: mn[2] = v.z if v.z > mx[2]: mx[2] = v.z return mn, mx Parameters: EPSILON: A small constant (e.g., 10^{-9}) sometimes used in related precision contexts, though not explicitly applied in the basic min/max loop. precisiontype: Can be float or double. Edge Cases: Empty Input: Accessing v[0] on an empty list causes undefined behavior. Degenerate Geometry: The method works correctly for degenerate meshes (single point, line, or coplanar vertices) as it strictly computes the extent of the provided coordinates. Creates a cubic bounding box (AABox) by expanding the minimum bounding box dimensions to be equal in all axes, padding equally on both sides. Definition: Converts an arbitrary AABB into a cube centered at the same centroid. Steps: 1. Get the mesh's bounding box min and max. 2. Calculate axis lengths: Lx = maxx - minx, Ly = maxy - miny, Lz = maxz - minz. 3. Find the maximum length L{max} = \max(Lx, Ly, Lz). 4. For each axis i, calculate delta: \deltai = L{max} - Li. 5. Adjust bounds: mini = mini - \deltai / 2, maxi = maxi + \deltai / 2. When to choose: When a uniform spatial resolution or cubic voxelization grid is required, ensuring no axis is smaller than the largest dimension of the object. Link: Bounding Cube Creation Initializes positions of specific character primitives (S, A, N, G) and arcs, computing a surrounding bounding box to optimize sphere tracing queries. Definition: A specialized bounding box calculation for signed distance field (SDF) character rendering. Steps: 1. Define primitives (arcs for 'S', vertices for 'A', 'N', 'G'). 2. Compute global min/max x, y, z of all primitives. 3. Apply an offset (default 0.1) to the bounds to avoid missing points too close to the letters. 4. Create surroundingbbox with these coordinates. When to choose: Specifically for SDF-based text rendering where tight bounds improve ray marching efficiency. Link: Character Bounding Box Initialization Determines the coordinates of any of the 8 vertices of an AABB using a vertex index (0-7) and bit manipulation, avoiding floating-point arithmetic for coordinate selection. Definition: A lookup method for AABB corners based on binary encoding. Steps: 1. The AABB has 8 vertices. 2. Bit 0 of the index corresponds to X, Bit 1 to Y, Bit 2 to Z. 3. If the bit is 0, the coordinate is min; if 1, it is max. 4. Extract coordinates using bit masking: x = aabb.x\minmax[(i \& 1) >> 0] y = aabb.y\minmax[(i \& 2) >> 1] z = aabb.z\minmax[(i \& 4) >> 2] When to choose: When iterating over AABB corners for plane intersection tests or collision detection where floating-point branching is undesirable. Link: AABB Vertex Coordinate Encoding Computes the AABB enclosing two input AABBs by taking the component-wise minimum of their mins and maximum of their maxs. Definition: Merging two spatial bounds into one. Steps: 1. Given b0 and b1. 2. new\min = \min(b0.min, b1.min) 3. new\max = \max(b0.max, b1.max) When to choose: When combining multiple objects or sub-grids into a single parent bounding volume. Link: AABB Enclosure (Union) Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of vertices. Each vertex is visited exactly once. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space (excluding the input vertex list). Only two Vec3 structures are maintained. Strengths: Extremely fast, cache-friendly, and numerically stable for standard floating-point ranges. Limitations: Does not account for mesh normals or implicit surfaces; only bounds the explicit vertex positions. Empty inputs cause crashes in the basic implementation. When to use: As a first-pass culling step in raycasting or rasterization. When not to use: When tighter bounds are required (e.g., oriented bounding boxes) or when the mesh has no vertices (e.g., pure implicit volume). The method is a fundamental primitive in computer graphics, often referred to as computing "min-max vertex bounds". It is widely used in voxelization pipelines to determine the grid extent for sparse voxel DAGs and in raycasting models to define the initial search volume Parent. The specific implementation details, such as the empty-list pitfall, are documented in community-maintained voxelizer repositories. The bit-manipulation trick for vertex encoding is a known optimization in low-level graphics programming. kctess5/voxelizer, https://github.com/kctess5/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) prateekchandan/Advanced-CG-High-Resolution-Sparse-Voxel-DAGs, https://github.com/prateekchandan/Advanced-CG-High-Resolution-Sparse-Voxel-DAGs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) AlerianEmperor/SDF-Sphere-Tracing, https://github.com/AlerianEmperor/SDF-Sphere-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Couple 3D AABB Tricks, https://gpfault.net/posts/aabb-tricks.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Volume Bounds Computation
head: computeVolumeBounds
body: Computes an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) that encloses a set of 3D points, with optional padding. It serves as the foundational spatial extent definition for volume rendering grids, ensuring the voxelization domain tightly fits the data of interest. Unlike Mesh Bounding Box Calculation, which operates on vertex coordinates of explicit geometry, this method operates on arbitrary point clouds or sample sets, making it suitable for implicit representations or scattered data. Inputs: points: An array of 3D points, where each point is a tuple [x, y, z] of floating-point numbers. padding: A scalar value representing the padding to add to all sides of the bounding box in world units. Default is 0.0. Outputs: VolumeBounds: An object containing: min: [number, number, number] — The minimum coordinates of the AABB. max: [number, number, number] — The maximum coordinates of the AABB. size: [number, number, number] — The dimensions of the AABB (max - min). center: [number, number, number] — The center of the AABB ((min + max) / 2). Data Structures: VolumeBounds: min: Array of 3 floats. max: Array of 3 floats. size: Array of 3 floats. center: Array of 3 floats. Steps: 1. Initialize min and max arrays to infinity and negative infinity, respectively, for all three axes (x, y, z). 2. Iterate over each point p in points: a. For each axis i in {0, 1, 2}: i. Update min[i] = min(min[i], p[i]). ii. Update max[i] = max(max[i], p[i]). 3. Apply padding: a. For each axis i in {0, 1, 2}: i. min[i] = min[i] - padding. ii. max[i] = max[i] + padding. 4. Compute size[i] = max[i] - min[i] for each axis i. 5. Compute center[i] = (min[i] + max[i]) / 2.0 for each axis i. 6. Return the VolumeBounds object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevolumebounds(points, padding=0.0): # Initialize min and max to extreme values mincoords = [float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')] maxcoords = [float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf')] # Iterate over all input points to find min and max x, y, z coordinates for point in points: for i in range(3): if point[i] < mincoords[i]: mincoords[i] = point[i] if point[i] > maxcoords[i]: maxcoords[i] = point[i] # Apply configurable padding in world units to all sides for i in range(3): mincoords[i] = mincoords[i] - padding maxcoords[i] = maxcoords[i] + padding # Compute size and center sizecoords = [maxcoords[i] - mincoords[i] for i in range(3)] centercoords = [(mincoords[i] + maxcoords[i]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)] # Output VolumeBounds object return { 'min': mincoords, 'max': maxcoords, 'size': sizecoords, 'center': centercoords } Parameters: padding: Configurable padding in world units. Default value not specified, but 0.0 is implied if not provided. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty point set: If points is empty, min remains infinity and max remains negative infinity. The implementation should handle this case, potentially by returning a default bounds or raising an error. Not given in the sources. Precision: Use floating-point arithmetic consistent with the input data type. Not given in the sources. Computes an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) that encloses the visible geometry of a scene by projecting ground truth masks from training cameras. It serves as a robust initialization step for volume rendering, particularly when sparse representations are used, ensuring the bounding volume tightly fits the object of interest rather than the entire scene space. It differs from simple min-max point accumulation by using binary silhouette masks to determine visibility, making it resilient to background noise and sparse sampling artifacts. Computes a 3D bounding box for the scene by backprojecting silhouette masks from multiple training views to find the tightest volume containing all visible geometry. It differs from the basic point-based computation by using camera projections to infer 3D extent from 2D masks. Steps: 1. Iterate over training views. 2. For each view, extract binary silhouette mask. 3. Backproject mask pixels into 3D space using camera intrinsics/extrinsics. 4. Accumulate 3D points/volumes. 5. Compute min/max bounds along x, y, z axes. 6. Apply silhouetteRadius expansion. 7. Store bounds in scene.bboxdepth/width/heightmin/max. Parameters: traincameras: Array of camera poses. groundTruth: Array of ground truth images with masks. scene: Object scene structure to store computed bounds. datasetSize/viewCount: Number of training views. silhouetteRadius: Radius parameter for silhouette expansion. skipIndex/skips: Indices and strides for subsampling views. Time Complexity: O(N) for the basic method, where N is the number of points. For silhouette-based estimation, complexity depends on the number of views and pixels per mask. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the basic method, as it only stores min/max values. Silhouette-based estimation requires storing intermediate 3D points or volumes. Strengths: Simple, predictable performance for static datasets. Silhouette-based method is robust to background noise and sparse sampling. Limitations: Basic method is sensitive to outliers in the point cloud. Silhouette-based method requires accurate camera poses and masks. When to use: Use the basic method for known point clouds. Use silhouette-based estimation for sparse or noisy data where visibility is key. Originated in the context of 3D IDW interpolation volume and voxel visualization. Also used in NeRF-based methods like Clear-plenoxels for scene initialization. feat: 3D IDW interpolation volume and voxel visualisation, https://github.com/darkmine-oss/baselode/pull/50, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, https://github.com/nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Silhouette-based Bounding Box Initialization
body: Silhouette-based Bounding Box Initialization computes an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) that encloses the visible geometry of a scene by projecting ground truth masks from training cameras. It serves as a robust initialization step for volume rendering, particularly when sparse representations are used, ensuring the bounding volume tightly fits the object of interest rather than the entire scene space. It differs from simple min-max point accumulation by using binary silhouette masks to determine visibility, making it resilient to background noise and sparse sampling artifacts. The method is implemented as RenderUtils::bboxsilhouette. It takes training camera poses and corresponding ground truth silhouette masks to determine the spatial extent of the scene. Inputs: traincameras: Array of camera extrinsics and intrinsics. groundTruth: Array of binary silhouette masks (1 for foreground, 0 for background) corresponding to traincameras. scene: A temporary or target scene object containing the AABB fields (bboxdepthmax/min, bboxheightmax/min, bboxwidthmax/min). datasetSize: Number of training views. silhouetteRadius: Radius parameter for expanding the silhouette projection (used to account for depth uncertainty or anti-aliasing). skipIndex, skips: Parameters for subsampling views during initialization. Data Structures: The scene object contains AABB bounds. In the sparse case, a tempScene is initialized with specific parameters before calling the core function. The initialization of tempScene uses initSelf with arguments: sceneWidth, sceneHeight, sceneDepth, true, true, 0.1, -10., 0.5, 1. These likely correspond to spatial dimensions, flags for sparse/adaptive structures, and initial scale/offset parameters for the voxel grid or octree. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: If the scene is sparse, create a tempScene and initialize it with standard parameters. This temporary structure is used to compute the bounds safely before copying them to the final scene. 2. Projection: For each training camera i in traincameras: a. Retrieve the ground truth silhouette mask Mi. b. Project the 2D silhouette pixels into 3D space using the camera's projection matrix Pi. c. For each foreground pixel (u, v) in Mi, compute the ray direction di from the camera center. d. Intersect this ray with the current AABB bounds. If the ray passes through the volume, update the AABB to include the intersection points. e. Expand the bounds by silhouetteRadius to account for depth uncertainty. 3. Aggregation: The AABB is updated incrementally. The final bounds are the union of all rays passing through foreground pixels across all training views. 4. Post-processing: If a tempScene was used, copy its bbox fields to the final scene. Copy adaptiveLRDevice if applicable. Free tempScene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bboxsilhouette(traincameras, groundtruth, scene, datasetsize, silhouetteradius, issparse, skipindex, skips): # Initialize bounds to infinity/negative infinity bboxmin = [inf, inf, inf] bboxmax = [-inf, -inf, -inf] # Determine which cameras to use based on skip parameters camerastouse = [] for i in range(datasetsize): if i % skips == skipindex or skips == 1: camerastouse.append(i) for idx in camerastouse: camera = traincameras[idx] mask = groundtruth[idx] # Get camera projection matrix and intrinsics P = camera.projectionmatrix K = camera.intrinsics C = camera.center # Iterate over foreground pixels in the mask for u, v in mask.foregroundpixels(): # Back-project pixel to 3D ray # x = K^-1 [u, v, 1] raydircam = inv(K) @ [u, v, 1] raydirworld = camera.rotation @ raydircam raydirworld = normalize(raydirworld) # Intersect ray with current bounding box # Compute tmin and tmax for ray-box intersection tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(C, raydirworld, bboxmin, bboxmax) # If ray intersects, update bounds with intersection points if tmax > 0: # Point at tmax is further out, expand bounds pointfar = C + raydirworld tmax bboxmin = min(bboxmin, pointfar) bboxmax = max(bboxmax, pointfar) # Also consider point at tmin if it's outside current bounds if tmin > 0: pointnear = C + raydirworld tmin bboxmin = min(bboxmin, pointnear) bboxmax = max(bboxmax, pointnear) # Expand bounds by silhouette radius bboxmin = bboxmin - silhouetteradius bboxmax = bboxmax + silhouetteradius # Update scene bounds scene.bboxmin = bboxmin scene.bboxmax = bboxmax Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Scene: If the scene is sparse, a temporary scene must be used to avoid corrupting the final scene's internal state during initialization. The bounds are copied after computation. No Foreground: If no training views have foreground pixels, the bounds remain at initial values (infinity). This should be handled by a fallback to scene dimensions. Precision: Use double precision for intermediate calculations to avoid jitter in bounds updates. Silhouette Radius: A radius of 0 may result in tight but potentially incomplete bounds if the silhouette masks are noisy or undersampled. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of training views and P is the average number of foreground pixels per view. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot P) to store the silhouette masks. The bounding box itself is O(1). Strengths: Robust to background noise; works well with sparse data; provides a tight fit for the object of interest. Limitations: Requires ground truth silhouettes; sensitive to the silhouetteRadius parameter; may be slow for very high-resolution masks. When to Use: When initializing bounding boxes for novel view synthesis or NeRF-like methods where the object extent is unknown or sparse. When Not to Use: When ground truth silhouettes are unavailable; when the scene is dense and the bounding box can be computed from point clouds. This method is derived from the Clear-Plenoxels repository. It is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting and Plenoxels to initialize the spatial extent of the scene. The approach leverages the fact that silhouettes provide a strong constraint on the visible volume, allowing for efficient initialization without requiring dense point clouds. nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, https://github.com/nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: AABB Ray Distance
head: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Intersection Distance
body: Computes the distance along a ray direction from a given point to the nearest intersection with an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). It returns -1 if the starting point is inside the box or if the ray does not intersect the box. It differs from standard intersection tests by returning a scalar distance value rather than a boolean or hit point, which is useful for sorting or early-out optimizations in volume rendering pipelines. Inputs: point: The starting position of the ray (3D vector). direction: The ray direction vector (3D vector). boundingboxmin: Minimum coordinates of the AABB (3D vector). boundingboxmax: Maximum coordinates of the AABB (3D vector). Outputs: dist: The distance to the nearest intersection. Returns -1 if no valid intersection exists (point inside or ray misses). Data Structures: Vectors are treated as 3-element arrays or tuples (x, y, z). Coordinates are in world space. Steps: 1. Normalize the ray direction vector \vec{d} to unit length. Let \vec{d} = (dx, dy, dz). 2. Initialize dist to -1. 3. Iterate over each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: a. Let v be the coordinate of point on axis i. b. Let d be the component of direction on axis i. c. Let mini and maxi be the minimum and maximum extents of the AABB on axis i. d. If dist is -1: If v < mini and d > 0: Set dist = (mini - v) / d. If v > maxi and d < 0: Set dist = (maxi - v) / d. e. Else (dist is not -1): If v < mini and d > 0: Set dist = \max(\text{dist}, (mini - v) / d). If v > maxi and d < 0: Set dist = \max(\text{dist}, (maxi - v) / d). 4. Return dist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbraydistance(point, direction, boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax): # Normalize direction length = sqrt(direction.x2 + direction.y2 + direction.z2) if length == 0: return -1 dx = direction.x / length dy = direction.y / length dz = direction.z / length dist = -1 # Process X axis v = point.x d = dx if dist == -1: if v < boundingboxmin.x and d > 0: dist = (boundingboxmin.x - v) / d if v > boundingboxmax.x and d < 0: dist = (boundingboxmax.x - v) / d else: if v < boundingboxmin.x and d > 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmin.x - v) / d) if v > boundingboxmax.x and d < 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmax.x - v) / d) # Process Y axis v = point.y d = dy if dist == -1: if v < boundingboxmin.y and d > 0: dist = (boundingboxmin.y - v) / d if v > boundingboxmax.y and d < 0: dist = (boundingboxmax.y - v) / d else: if v < boundingboxmin.y and d > 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmin.y - v) / d) if v > boundingboxmax.y and d < 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmax.y - v) / d) # Process Z axis v = point.z d = dz if dist == -1: if v < boundingboxmin.z and d > 0: dist = (boundingboxmin.z - v) / d if v > boundingboxmax.z and d < 0: dist = (boundingboxmax.z - v) / d else: if v < boundingboxmin.z and d > 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmin.z - v) / d) if v > boundingboxmax.z and d < 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmax.z - v) / d) return dist Parameters: boundingboxmin/maxx/y/z: World coordinates defining the AABB extents. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The algorithm uses max (or fmaxf) to keep the largest positive distance when multiple axes yield intersections, effectively finding the entry point into the box. It returns -1 if the starting point is inside the box or if the ray points away from the box. Precision issues may arise if the ray direction is very close to zero on an axis; normalization handles this, but division by near-zero direction components should be guarded against in robust implementations.
