name: Near/Far Distance Precomputation Pass
head: Voxel Brick Distance Pass, tNear-tFar Rendering
body: The Near/Far Distance Precomputation Pass renders voxel bricks to a render target to compute the entry (t{Near}) and exit (t{Far}) distances of viewing rays intersecting the volume for each pixel. This prepares the bounds for the subsequent raymarching pass, allowing the main rendering pass to skip empty space and focus computation only on occupied regions. It differs from Homogeneous Volume Intersection by explicitly rasterizing the volume geometry to derive depth bounds rather than analytically solving for intersections with a homogeneous bounding box. Inputs: A flag volume texture (mpFlagVolumeSRV) indicating which bricks are active (occupied). Camera matrices (cbmView, cbmViewProj) and view position (cbf4ViewPos). Volume parameters: VOXELNUMX/Y/Z, VOXELBRICKRATIO, VOXELSIZE, gcf3VoxelReso, gcf3HalfBrickSize. A render target view (mpFarNearRTV) for output. Outputs: A render target where each pixel stores t{Near} in the RGB channels and t{Far} in the Alpha channel. Data Structures: Render Target (mpFarNearRTV): 32-bit floating-point format (RGBA32F). RGB channels: Store t{Near} (entry distance). Alpha channel: Store t{Far} (exit distance). Vertex Buffer (mpPassVB): Contains point primitives. Stride is sizeof(short). The content is effectively a list of primitive indices or dummy data, as the geometry is generated in the Geometry Shader. Flag Volume (texFlagVolume): A 3D texture where active bricks are marked with 1 and inactive with 0. Numbered Steps: 1. Clear Render Target: Clear mpFarNearRTV with {50.0f, 50.0f, 50.0f, -10.0f}. This sets an initial background value; RGB=50, Alpha=-10. 2. Set Topology: Set primitive topology to D3D11PRIMITIVETOPOLOGYPOINTLIST. 3. Bind Resources: Input layout: mpOutVL. Vertex Buffer: mpPassVB with stride sizeof(short). Shaders: Vertex Shader mpPassVS, Geometry Shader mpActiveCellAndSOGS, Pixel Shader mpFarNearPS. Constant Buffer: mpCBperFrame bound to GS. Shader Resource: mpFlagVolumeSRV bound to GS. 4. Set States: Rasterizer State: mpBackFaceRS (back-face culling enabled). Blend State: mpBlendState (configured for min/max operations, see below). 5. Draw: Issue a draw call for VOXELNUMX VOXELNUMY VOXELZ / VOXELBRICKRATIO^3 primitives. 6. Restore: Restore previous blend state. Blend State Configuration (mpBlendState): BlendEnable = true RGB Channels (t{Near}): SrcBlend = D3D11BLENDONE DestBlend = D3D11BLENDONE BlendOp = D3D11BLENDOPMIN Result: t{Near} = \min(t{Near}, \text{new\value}). Alpha Channel (t{Far}): SrcBlendAlpha = D3D11BLENDONE DestBlendAlpha = D3D11BLENDONE BlendOpAlpha = D3D11BLENDOPMAX Result: t{Far} = \max(t{Far}, \text{new\value}). RenderTargetWriteMask = D3D11COLORWRITEENABLEALL. Pseudocode (Geometry Shader Logic): The Geometry Shader iterates over active bricks, generates a cube for each, transforms it to clip space, and outputs it. The Pixel Shader calculates the depth. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct GSINPUT { uint primID; }; struct PSINPUT { float4 projPos; float4 Pos; // World/View space position for depth calculation }; cbuffer cbPerFrame { matrix cbmViewProj; float2 gcf3HalfBrickSize; // Half size of a brick in world units float4 gcf3VoxelReso; // Resolution of the flag volume uint gcuFlagVolSliceStep; uint gcuFlagVolStripStep; }; Texture3D gsrvFlagVolume; void main(inout LineStream<PSINPUT> lineStream, GSINPUT input) { uint primID = input.primID; // Decode brick coordinates from primitive ID uint u3Idx; u3Idx.z = primID / (gcuFlagVolSliceStep gcuFlagVolStripStep); u3Idx.y = (primID % (gcuFlagVolSliceStep gcuFlagVolStripStep)) / gcuFlagVolStripStep; u3Idx.x = primID % gcuFlagVolStripStep; // Check if the brick is active // Note: Source uses gsrvFlagVolume[u3Idx]. Assuming normalized or direct indexing. int active = gsrvFlagVolume[int3(u3Idx.x, u3Idx.y, u3Idx.z)]; if (active != 1) return; // Adjust Y coordinate (source flips Y) u3Idx.y = gcf3VoxelReso.y - 1 - u3Idx.y; // Calculate cell center in world space // VOXELSIZE VOXELBRICKRATIO is the brick size float3 brickSize = float3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) gcf3VoxelReso.x 0.5; // Approximation based on gcf3HalfBrickSize usage // More accurately from source: // f4CellCenterOffset = (u3Idx - gcf3VoxelReso 0.5f / VOXELBRICKRATIO + 0.5f) VOXELSIZE VOXELBRICKRATIO float3 centerOffset = (float3(u3Idx) - gcf3VoxelReso.xyz 0.5f / 1.0f + 0.5f) gcf3HalfBrickSize.xyz 2.0f; // Note: Source uses gcf3HalfBrickSize directly as scale factor for the -1..1 cube float4 f4HalfCellSize = float4(gcf3HalfBrickSize, 1.0f); // Define cube vertices in local space (-1 to 1) float3 verts[8] = { float3(-1, -1, -1), float3(-1, 1, -1), float3(1, 1, -1), float3(1, -1, -1), float3(-1, -1, 1), float3(-1, 1, 1), float3(1, 1, 1), float3(1, -1, 1) }; // Edges of the cube (indices into verts) int edges[12][2] = { {0,1}, {1,2}, {2,3}, {3,0}, // Front face {4,5}, {5,6}, {6,7}, {7,4}, // Back face {0,4}, {1,5}, {2,6}, {3,7} // Connecting edges }; for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) { PSINPUT output; // Vertex 1 float3 v1 = verts[edges[i][0]] gcf3HalfBrickSize.xyz + centerOffset; output.Pos = float4(v1, 1.0f); output.projPos = mul(output.Pos, cbmViewProj); lineStream.Append(output); // Vertex 2 float3 v2 = verts[edges[i][1]] gcf3HalfBrickSize.xyz + centerOffset; output.Pos = float4(v2, 1.0f); output.projPos = mul(output.Pos, cbmViewProj); lineStream.Append(output); lineStream.RestartStrip(); } } // Pixel Shader (mpFarNearPS) // Calculates tNear and tFar based on the depth of the projected cube faces float4 main(PSINPUT input): SVTarget { // Convert clip space position to view space depth // zclip is in [0, 1] or [-1, 1] depending on API. Assuming D3D11 [0,1]. float zclip = input.projPos.z / input.projPos.w; // Convert to view space Z (negative for forward) float zview = -(zclip 2.0 - 1.0); // Assuming standard D3D11 projection mapping // The depth value passed to the pixel shader is the depth of the fragment. // Since we are rendering wireframes/cubes, we need to determine the min/max depth // of the brick along the ray. // However, the source implies a simpler approach: // The blend state does MIN for RGB and MAX for Alpha. // This suggests the Pixel Shader outputs the depth of the current face. // For a cube, we need the min depth of all faces for tNear and max depth for tFar. // But rasterization processes fragments. // A common technique is to render the cube twice or use specific depth logic. // Given the blend state MIN(RGB) and MAX(Alpha), it implies: // tNear = min(all tNear candidates) // tFar = max(all tFar candidates) // The source code does not show the PS logic explicitly, but the blend state // dictates the accumulation. The PS likely outputs the depth of the current fragment. // To get correct tNear/tFar for the entire brick, the brick must be rendered // such that all its faces contribute to the min/max. // Since back-face culling is enabled, we only see front faces. // This pass likely relies on the fact that for a convex object like a cube, // the front faces define the entry, and if we rendered back faces too (or handled // the exit differently), we would get the exit. // However, with only front faces, we only get the entry depth (tNear). // The source clears Alpha to -10 and uses MAX. This suggests tFar might be // derived from the back faces or a separate pass, OR the "cube" rendering // includes both front and back faces in a way that the MAX accumulates the // furthest visible point. // Given the ambiguity in the PS code not being provided, we rely on the // blend state and clear value. // tNear (RGB) = MIN(currenttNear, fragmentdepth) // tFar (Alpha) = MAX(currenttFar, fragmentdepth) // Note: fragmentdepth must be in the same coordinate system as the ray distances. // Usually, this is view-space Z distance. float depth = input.projPos.z / input.projPos.w; // Convert to linear view space depth float linearDepth =...; // Implementation detail depends on projection matrix return float4(linearDepth, linearDepth, linearDepth, linearDepth); } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Back-Face Culling: The use of mpBackFaceRS means only front-facing triangles are rendered. This correctly identifies the entry point (t{Near}) but may fail to identify the exit point (t{Far}) if the exit is only visible from the back. The use of MAX on Alpha suggests that either back faces are also rendered (contradicting culling) or the geometry is constructed to ensure front faces contribute to both, or a separate pass handles t{Far}. Precision: Using float for depth calculations may introduce precision errors for large scenes. The clear value of 50.0 and -10.0 must be outside the expected range of valid depths to ensure correct min/max accumulation. Empty Bricks: Inactive bricks (flag != 1) are discarded, preventing unnecessary rendering and blending operations. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of active bricks. Each active brick generates a constant number of primitives (cube edges). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel for the render target. The flag volume requires O(V) memory, where V is the number of voxels. Performance: Depends on the number of active bricks and the resolution of the render target. Rasterizing wireframes can be expensive if the number of active bricks is high. Strengths: Efficiently culls empty space. Simple to implement using standard rasterization hardware. Limitations: Requires a second pass for raymarching. Accuracy depends on the rasterization of the cube geometry. Back-face culling may complicate t{Far} calculation. This method is part of the Dynamic Volume Raycasting project by pengliu916. It is used in real-time volume rendering applications where efficient culling of empty space is critical for performance. The technique leverages the GPU's rasterization pipeline to compute depth bounds, avoiding the need for complex CPU-side bounding volume hierarchy traversal or analytical intersection tests for every ray. pengliu916/DynamicVolumeRayCasting, https://github.com/pengliu916/DynamicVolumeRayCasting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Cube Intersection
head: box initialization
body: Ray-Cube Intersection computes the precise entry (t0) and exit (t1) points of a ray relative to an axis-aligned cube (AABB) defined by lower and upper bounds. It serves as the foundational primitive test for voxel-based volume rendering, determining whether a ray intersects the volume boundary and identifying the specific face of entry or exit. Unlike Ray-box intersection, which often returns a boolean or a generic hit structure, this method explicitly calculates the 3D intersection coordinates and the geometric face index, which are required to initialize the traversal state for brick-level methods like Ray-Cube Intersection (Brick/Slab). The method consists of two distinct calculations: one for the entry point (t0) and one for the exit point (t1). Both rely on computing intersection parameters along each axis and selecting the extremal value to determine the first or last face crossed. Inputs: raypos: The origin of the ray, a 3D vector (x, y, z). raydir: The direction of the ray, a 3D vector (dx, dy, dz). dirlower: The lower corner of the cube, a 3D vector (minx, miny, minz). dirupper: The upper corner of the cube, a 3D vector (maxx, maxy, maxz). Outputs: HitEntry: A structure containing the 3D position t0 and the entry face index inface. HitExit: A structure containing the 3D position t1 and the exit face index outface. The hit structure is defined as: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Hit: position: Vector3 # 3D float vector (x, y, z) face: int # Integer index identifying the face This step finds where the ray leaves the cube. 1. Compute Intersection Parameters (Qv): For each axis i \in \{0, 1, 2\} (corresponding to x, y, z), calculate: Qv[i] = \frac{dir\upper[i] - raypos[i]}{raydir[i]} 2. Identify Minimum Axis: Find the index i of the minimum component in Qv: i = \text{mincomponentf3index}(Qv) 3. Calculate Intersection Distance (Q): Q = Qv[i] 4. Calculate 3D Position (t1): t1 = raypos + raydir \times Q 5. Determine Exit Face (outface): Use a lookup table outfaces[i][direction], where direction is determined by the sign of the ray direction component: \text{direction} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } raydir[i] < 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} outface = outfaces[i][\text{direction}] Note: direction 0 corresponds to the negative face, and 1 to the positive face. 6. Clamp Position: To ensure numerical precision and exact boundary alignment, set the i-th component of t1 to the corresponding bound: t1[i] = dir\upper[i] 7. Return: Return Hit with position = t1 and face = outface. This step finds where the ray enters the cube. 1. Compute Intersection Parameters (Qv): For each axis i \in \{0, 1, 2\}, calculate: Qv[i] = \frac{dir\lower[i] - raypos[i]}{raydir[i]} 2. Handle Invalid Values: Coalesce any NaN values in Qv to negative infinity (-\infty) to handle division by zero or invalid inputs. 3. Identify Maximum Axis: Find the index i of the maximum component in Qv: i = \text{maxcomponentf3index}(Qv) 4. Calculate Intersection Distance (Q): Q = Qv[i] 5. Calculate 3D Position (t0): t0 = raypos + raydir \times Q 6. Determine Entry Face (inface): Use a lookup table infaces[i][direction], where direction is determined by the sign of the ray direction component: \text{direction} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } raydir[i] < 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} inface = infaces[i][\text{direction}] Note: The logic for inface maps direction 0 (negative ray dir) to the positive face of the cube, and direction 1 (positive ray dir) to the negative face, consistent with the ray entering from that side. 7. Clamp Position: To ensure numerical precision and exact boundary alignment, set the i-th component of t0 to the corresponding bound: t0[i] = dir\lower[i] 8. Return: Return Hit with position = t0 and face = inface. Unverified code. body: This method performs the primary hit resolution for a ray entering a 4×4×4 voxel brick, finding the entry point (t0) of the first solid voxel the ray crosses within a specified time interval [t{lo}, t{hi}]. It builds on Ray-Cube Intersection by extending the boundary check into a full traversal of the brick's interior voxels using the Amanatides-Woo Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA). Unlike the parent method which only identifies the cube entry face, this method returns the specific voxel index and normal of the first opaque (or non-transparent, if configured) voxel encountered, or -1 if the ray misses all solid voxels in the brick. Inputs: Ray origin o \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized or unnormalized, but non-zero). Brick lower bound bmin \in \mathbb{R}^3 (world coordinates of the brick's minimum corner). Time interval [t{lo}, t{hi}] defining the valid search range. Brick data structure bi containing voxel materials. Boolean flag skiptransparent: if true, voxels with transparent materials (e.g., water, glass, turf) are ignored. Outputs: Entry time t of the first solid voxel face. Voxel coordinates v and face normal n of that voxel. Return value: t if a hit is found, -1.0 otherwise. Data Structures: brickvoxelidx(x, y, z): Maps 3D voxel coordinates (x,y,z) \in [0,3]^3 to a linear index. brickvoxelsolid(bi, idx): Returns true if the voxel at idx in brick bi is not empty. brickvoxelmaterial(bi, idx): Returns the material ID of the voxel. rtistransparentmat(mat): Returns true if mat is transparent (e.g., IDs 5-12, 18, 35). rtfacenormal(axis, d): Returns the outward normal of the face crossed along axis (0, 1, or 2), consistent with ray direction d. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Inverse Direction: Calculate inv = \text{vec3}(rt\safe\inv(d.x), rt\safe\inv(d.y), rt\safe\inv(d.z)), where rt\safe\inv(x) = 1/x if |x| > \epsilon, else 10^{30}. 2. Compute Slab Times: Calculate entry and exit times for the brick boundaries: tb0 = (bmin - o) \cdot inv tb1 = (bmin + \text{vec3}(4.0) - o) \cdot inv Here, bmin + \text{vec3}(4.0) is the brick's upper bound. 3. Calculate Brick Entry/Exit: Determine per-axis entry times te = \min(tb0, tb1) and exit times tf = \max(tb0, tb1). The brick entry time tnear and exit time tfar are: tnear = \max(\max(te.x, te.y), te.z) tfar = \min(\min(tf.x, tf.y), tf.z) Note: The source formula uses \min for tnear components but \max for the final aggregation, consistent with standard slab intersection logic where tnear is the latest entry. 4. Clamp to Interval: Set t = \max(tnear, t{lo}) and t{end} = \min(tfar, t{hi}). If t > t{end}, return -1.0 (ray misses brick or interval). 5. Determine Entry Axis: Identify the axis of the first face crossed by comparing te components: If te.y > te.x, last\axis = 1. Else if te.z > \max(te.x, te.y), last\axis = 2. Else, last\axis = 0. This axis determines the initial face normal. 6. Initialize Voxel Position: Calculate the position just inside the brick: p = o + d \cdot (t + 10^{-4}) - bmin Clamp voxel coordinates to the brick bounds: v = \text{clamp}(\text{vec3}(\lfloor p \rfloor), \text{vec3}(0), \text{vec3}(3)) The small epsilon (10^{-4}) prevents precision errors at the entry face. 7. Determine Step Directions: Set step for each axis: 1 if d.axis > 0, else -1. 8. Calculate Next Boundary Times: For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: Calculate the next boundary coordinate: bnd = vi + (stepi + 1)/2 (effectively vi+1 if stepi=1, vi if stepi=-1). If brick\voxel\solid(bi, vi\q) is true AND (skiptransparent is false OR !rtistransparentmat(brickvoxelmaterial(bi, viq))): Set first\vox = v. Set first\normal = rt\face\normal(last\axis, d). Return t\cur. Find axis ax with minimum t\max. Update v.ax += step.ax. Update t\cur += t\delta.ax. Update t\max.ax += t\delta.ax. Update last\axis = ax. 10. Brick entry/exit te = min(tb0, tb1) tf = max(tb0, tb1) tnear = max(max(te.x, te.y), te.z) tfar = min(min(tf.x, tf.y), tf.z) # 4. Clamp t = max(tnear, tlo) tend = min(tfar, thi) if t > tend: return -1.0 # 5. Entry axis if te.y > te.x: lastaxis = 1 elif te.z > max(te.x, te.y): lastaxis = 2 else: lastaxis = 0 # 6. Initial voxel p = o + d (t + 1e-4) - bmin v = clamp(floor(p), vec3(0), vec3(3)) # 7. Step directions step = vec3( 1 if d.x > 0 else -1, 1 if d.y > 0 else -1, 1 if d.z > 0 else -1) # 8. Next boundary times tdelta = abs(inv) tmax = vec3( (v.x + (1 if step.x > 0 else 0) - (o.x inv.x)) tdelta.x, (v.y + (1 if step.y > 0 else 0) - (o.y inv.y)) tdelta.y, (v.z + (1 if step.z > 0 else 0) - (o.z inv.z)) tdelta.z) # Note: The above tmax calculation is a simplification. # Standard Amanatides-Woo: tmax[i] = (boundary - o[i]/d[i]) inv[i] # boundary is v[i] + (step[i] > 0 ? 1: 0) # o[i]/d[i] is o[i] inv[i] # So tmax[i] = (boundary - o[i]inv[i]) inv[i]? No. # t = (x - o)/d => x = o + td # tmax[i] = (boundary - o[i]) / d[i] = (boundary - o[i]) inv[i] # But we are at time t. The position is o + td. # The distance to boundary is boundary - (o[i] + td[i])? # No, tmax is the time to reach the boundary. # tmax[i] = (boundary - o[i]) / d[i] # But we already advanced to time t. # So we need the time from origin? No, tmax is the absolute time. # So tmax[i] = (boundary - o[i]) inv[i] # But we initialized v based on t. # So tmax should be the time to reach the NEXT boundary from origin. # tmax[i] = (v[i] + (step[i] > 0 ? 1: 0) - bmin[i] + o[i]?) No. # Let's use the standard formula: # tmax[i] = ( (v[i] + (step[i] > 0 ? 1: 0)) - (o[i] - bmin[i])? No. # The brick is at bmin. The voxel coordinates are local to the brick. # World coordinate of voxel v is bmin + v. # So boundary world coord is bmin + v + (step > 0 ? 1: 0). # tmax[i] = ( (bmin[i] + v[i] + (step[i] > 0 ? 1: 0)) - o[i]) inv[i] tmax = vec3( (bmin.x + v.x + (1 if step.x > 0 else 0) - o.x) inv.x, (bmin.y + v.y + (1 if step.y > 0 else 0) - o.y) inv.y, (bmin.z + v.z + (1 if step.z > 0 else 0) - o.z) inv.z) tcur = t # 9. Traverse for i in range(16): if tcur > tend: return -1.0 viq = brickvoxelidx(v.x, v.y, v.z) if brickvoxelsolid(brick, viq): if not skiptransparent or not rtistransparentmat(brickvoxelmaterial(brick, viq)): return tcur, v, rtfacenormal(lastaxis, d) # Find axis with smallest tmax if tmax.x < tmax.y: if tmax.x < tmax.z: ax = 0 else: ax = 2 else: if tmax.y < tmax.z: ax = 1 else: ax = 2 v[ax] += step[ax] tcur += tdelta[ax] tmax[ax] += tdelta[ax] lastaxis = ax return -1.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Components: Handled by rtsafeinv returning a large value, effectively making the ray never cross boundaries on that axis, which is correct for axis-aligned rays. Precision Errors: The epsilon 10^{-4} added to t prevents the ray from starting exactly on a voxel boundary, avoiding double-counting or missing voxels due to floating-point inaccuracies. Transparent Materials: If skiptransparent is true, the ray continues through transparent voxels. If all voxels in the brick are transparent, the method returns -1.0, which may be incorrect if the caller expects a hit on the brick boundary itself. This is a design choice to prioritize solid occlusion. A variant that visits all solid voxels within the brick to handle transparent or fringe cases, unlike this method which stops at the first solid voxel. Uses hardware RT cores for coarse BVH traversal and this method for in-brick resolution, replacing software beam pre-passes. Adapts the DDA logic to accept two explicit 3D points instead of a ray origin and direction, handling edge cases like zero deltas and negative traversal with higher precision. Time Complexity: O(1) per brick, as the brick size is fixed at 4×4×4 (16 voxels). The loop runs at most 16 times. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a few scalar variables for traversal state. Performance: Highly efficient for sparse or structured voxel grids where bricks are used as coarse bounds. The fixed-size traversal avoids dynamic memory allocation and branching overhead associated with hierarchical traversal. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory footprint, predictable performance. Limitations: Only suitable for fixed-size bricks. Does not handle empty-space skipping across multiple bricks (handled by the parent or caller). Precision issues at voxel boundaries if not handled with epsilon. name: In-Brick DDA for Occlusion
body: A Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) that marches through a 4×4×4 voxel brick to determine if any solid voxel occludes a shadow ray. Unlike primary hit resolution which stops at the first intersection, this method visits all solid voxels within the brick to correctly handle transparent or fringe cases. Inputs and Outputs: Ray origin o and direction dir (vec3<f32>). Brick bounds bmin and bmax (vec3<f32>), where bmax = bmin + vec3<f32>(4.0). Time bounds [tlo, thi] for the ray segment. Brick identifier bi and voxel data accessors brickvoxelidx and brickvoxelsolid. Shadow occlusion check function shadowvoxeloccludes. Output: Boolean true if any solid voxel occludes the ray, false otherwise. Data Structures: The brick is a fixed 4×4×4 grid of voxels. Voxel coordinates v are integers in [0, 3]. brickvoxelidx(x, y, z) maps 3D coordinates to a linear index. brickvoxelsolid(bi, vi) returns true if the voxel at index vi in brick bi is solid. Numbered Steps and Formulas: 1. Compute inverse direction components, handling zero division safely: inv = vec3<f32>(rtsafeinv(dir.x), rtsafeinv(dir.y), rtsafeinv(dir.z)). 2. Compute slab entry/exit times for the brick bounds: tb0 = (bmin - o) inv and tb1 = (bmin + vec3<f32>(4.0) - o) inv. 3. Calculate brick entry tnear and exit tfar times: tnear = max(max(min(tb0.x, tb1.x), min(tb0.y, tb1.y)), min(tb0.z, tb1.z)) and tfar = min(min(max(tb0.x, tb1.x), max(tb0.y, tb1.y)), max(tb0.z, tb1.z)). (Note: corrected tb3.z typo from source to tb0.z). 4. Clamp start time t and end time tend: t = max(tnear, 0.0) and tend = min(tfar, thi). If t > tend, return false. 5. Calculate initial voxel position and clamp voxel coordinates: p = o + dir (t + 1e-4) - bmin and v = clamp(vec3<i32>(floor(p)), vec3<i32>(0), vec3<i32>(3)). 6. Determine step direction for each axis: step.x = select(-1, 1, dir.x >= 0.0), step.y = select(-1, 1, dir.y >= 0.0), step.z = select(-1, 1, dir.z >= 0.0). 7. Calculate next boundary times and initial tmax for each axis, and tdelta = abs(inv). 8. Loop i from 0 to 15: Check bounds: if v.x < 0 or v.x > 3 or v.y < 0 or v.y > 3 or v.z < 0 or v.z > 3, return false. Check time: if tcur > tend, return false. Get voxel index: vi = brickvoxelidx(v.x, v.y, v.z). If brickvoxelsolid(bi, vi) is true, check shadowvoxeloccludes(worldbase + v, m, tcur, originworld, dir). If true, return true. Step to the next voxel along the axis with the smallest tmax. Update v, tcur, and tmax for that axis. 9. If loop completes without occlusion, return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inbrickddaocclusion(o, dir, bmin, tlo, thi, bi, brickvoxelidx, brickvoxelsolid, shadowvoxeloccludes, worldbase, m): # 1. Inverse direction (handles zero components safely) inv = vec3(1.0 / dir.x if dir.x != 0 else float('inf'), 1.0 / dir.y if dir.y != 0 else float('inf'), 1.0 / dir.z if dir.z != 0 else float('inf')) # 2. Slab entry/exit times tb0 = (bmin - o) inv tb1 = (bmin + vec3(4.0) - o) inv # 3. Brick entry/exit times tnear = max(max(min(tb0.x, tb1.x), min(tb0.y, tb1.y)), min(tb0.z, tb1.z)) tfar = min(min(max(tb0.x, tb1.x), max(tb0.y, tb1.y)), max(tb0.z, tb1.z)) # 4. Clamp to ray segment t = max(tnear, 0.0) tend = min(tfar, thi) if t > tend: return False # 5. Initial voxel position with epsilon offset p = o + dir (t + 1e-4) - bmin v = clamp(floor(p), vec3(0), vec3(3)) # 6. Step direction step = vec3(1 if dir.x >= 0 else -1, 1 if dir.y >= 0 else -1, 1 if dir.z >= 0 else -1) # 7. Delta and initial tmax (Amanatides-Woo standard initialization) tdelta = abs(inv) tmax = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if dir.x >= 0: tmax.x = (bmin.x + 1.0 - o.x) inv.x else: tmax.x = (bmin.x - o.x) inv.x if dir.y >= 0: tmax.y = (bmin.y + 1.0 - o.y) inv.y else: tmax.y = (bmin.y - o.y) inv.y if dir.z >= 0: tmax.z = (bmin.z + 1.0 - o.z) inv.z else: tmax.z = (bmin.z - o.z) inv.z tcur = t # 8. Fixed 16-iteration loop for i in range(16): if v.x < 0 or v.x > 3 or v.y < 0 or v.y > 3 or v.z < 0 or v.z > 3: return False if tcur > tend: return False vi = brickvoxelidx(v.x, v.y, v.z) if brickvoxelsolid(bi, vi): if shadowvoxeloccludes(worldbase + v, m, tcur, o, dir): return True # Step along axis with smallest tmax if tmax.x < tmax.y: if tmax.x < tmax.z: v.x += step.x tcur = tmax.x tmax.x += tdelta.x else: v.z += step.z tcur = tmax.z tmax.z += tdelta.z else: if tmax.y < tmax.z: v.y += step.y tcur = tmax.y tmax.y += tdelta.y else: v.z += step.z tcur = tmax.z tmax.z += tdelta.z return False Parameters: Brick size: 4×4×4 voxels. Loop limit: 16 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero direction components: handled by rtsafeinv which returns infinity. Ray not intersecting brick: handled by t > tend check. Voxel coordinates out of bounds: checked at the start of each loop iteration. Precision issues: small epsilon 1e-4 added to ray origin to avoid self-intersection. Time Complexity: O(1) per brick, as the loop runs a fixed 16 times. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. Strengths: Efficient for shadow testing within small bricks, handles transparency by checking all solid voxels. Limitations: Fixed brick size limits flexibility. When to use: Shadow testing in voxel-based rendering with small brick sizes. When not to use: Large bricks or when primary hit detection is sufficient. body: This method determines if a ray from origin to dir is occluded by any solid voxel within maxdist by using hardware ray-tracing cores to traverse a world BVH (TLAS/BLAS) to find candidate brick AABBs, then using a shared software Amanatides-Woo DDA within each candidate brick to resolve the exact first solid voxel. It replaces a software beam pre-pass and hierarchical-DDA empty-space skip with hardware traversal for the coarse search. It differs from the software variant by using hardware RT cores for coarse BVH traversal instead of a software beam pre-pass and hierarchical-DDA, while the in-brick resolution (Amanatides-Woo DDA) is shared between both variants. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin origin (world space), ray direction dir (normalized), maximum traversal distance maxdist, and the hardware acceleration structures (BLAS/TLAS) representing the voxel world. Outputs: Boolean true if occluded, false otherwise. In full intersection mode, it returns the nearest hit voxel index, material, and normal. Data Structures: The method relies on specific memory layouts to ensure compatibility with hardware BLAS build requirements. 1. Brick Structure: Represents the occupancy and material data for a single brick (4x4x4 voxels). wgsl struct Brick { occlo: u32, occhi: u32, materials: array<u32, 16>, }; occlo and occhi: Two 32-bit integers packing 64 bits total for the 4^3=64 voxels. materials: Array of 16 u32 values. Materials are packed 4 per 32-bit word (8 bits per material). 2. AABB Structure: Represents the bounding box of a brick. Scalar fields are used to maintain tight 24-byte packing, avoiding WGSL vec3 16-byte alignment padding which would break BLAS build compatibility. wgsl struct GpuAabb { minx: f32, miny: f32, minz: f32, maxx: f32, maxy: f32, maxz: f32, p0: f32, p1: f32, }; Total size: 36 bytes (9 floats). 3. Acceleration Structures: BLAS: Contains one GpuAabb per non-empty brick. The RT core skips empty space in hardware. TLAS: World Top-Level Acceleration Structure containing references to the BLAS. Brick Map: array<u32> mapping primitive indices from the BLAS to brick indices in the bricks array. Parameters: RTPRIMARY: An f32 override parameter. Default is 0.0 (off). If > 0.5, enables hardware RT primary trace instead of software DDA. VOXELGRT: Environment variable. Setting it to 1 enables hardware RT on a ray-query-capable adapter. Algorithm Steps: The method initializes a hardware ray query, iterates through candidate brick AABBs, checks brick activity, resolves the exact voxel hit via a shared DDA, and culls further traversal upon finding a closer hit. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwarertvoxelocclusion(origin, dir, maxdist, tlas, bricks, brickmap, aabbs, cameraworldorigin): # 1. Rebase world-space origin to window-local coordinates o = origin - cameraworldorigin # 2. Initialize hardware ray query against TLAS # RayDesc flags: 0 (no special flags), 0xFF (all hit types) # Distance range: [0.0, maxdist] rq = rayqueryinit(tlas, origin=o, direction=dir, tmin=0.0, tmax=maxdist, flags=0, hitmask=0xFF) bestt = 1e30 occluded = False # 3. Loop while the ray query proceeds while rayqueryproceed(rq): # 4. Get candidate intersection c = rayquerygetcandidate(rq) # 5. Check if candidate is an AABB (brick) if c.kind == RAYQUERYINTERSECTIONAABB: # 6. Retrieve brick index and AABB primitiveidx = c.primitiveindex bi = int(brickmap[primitiveidx]) a = aabbs[primitiveidx] # 7. Check if brick is active if not rtbrickactive(bi): continue # 8. Extract AABB min corner bmin = (a.minx, a.miny, a.minz) # 9. Resolve exact voxel hit using in-brick DDA # Calls shared Amanatides-Woo DDA from parent article bh = resolvebrickfull(bi, bmin, o, dir, origin, bestt, skiptransparent=False) # 10. Check if hit found and closer than current best if bh.hit and bh.t >= 0.0 and bh.t < bestt: bestt = bh.t occluded = True # 11. Cull further bricks by generating an intersection rayquerygenerateintersection(rq, bh.t) # Optimization: Return immediately for binary occlusion check return True # 12. If loop completes without finding a closer hit return occluded Edge Cases and Pitfalls: AABB Packing: Using vec3<f32> for AABB min/max in WGSL causes 16-byte alignment, breaking the tight 24-byte packing required by the BLAS build. Scalar fields are used instead. BVH Staleness: The BVH may be stale during async rebuilds. Correctness is maintained because the tile occupancy mask (rtbrickactive) is updated synchronously. Stale primitives render as sky, matching software DDA behavior. Precision: The committed intersection from the RT core is used only as a cross-check, not the source of truth for the voxel hit. The exact voxel hit is derived from the software DDA to ensure precision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Offloads coarse empty-space skipping to hardware RT cores, potentially offering significant speedups over software hierarchical DDA for primary rays and shadows. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated BVH traversal; consistent results with software path via shared DDA; handles async rebuilds gracefully. Limitations: Requires ray-query-capable hardware; overhead of software DDA per candidate brick; strict memory layout requirements for BLAS. When to Use: When hardware RT cores are available and primary ray/shadow performance is critical. Enabled via RTPRIMARY > 0.5 or VOXELGRT=1. When Not to Use: On hardware without ray-tracing support; when software fallback is required for correctness in all scenarios. Not given in the sources. This method originates from the voxelG project. It leverages modern GPU ray-tracing capabilities (specifically Vulkan Ray Query or WebGPU Ray Query) to optimize voxel traversal. The technique was developed to replace the software beam pre-pass and hierarchical-DDA empty-space skip with hardware traversal, improving performance for primary rays and occlusion queries. The in-brick DDA logic is shared with the software variant to ensure identical rendering results. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Amanatides and Woo Variation with 2-Point Input
head: 2-Point Voxel Traversal, Improved Amanatides and Woo
body: This method traverses a voxel grid by accepting two explicit 3D points (start and end) rather than a ray origin and direction vector. It is designed to handle edge cases such as zero coordinate deltas, exact edge hits, negative traversal, and non-0-based block centers with higher precision than standard face-to-face traversal. It builds on the Amanatides and Woo DDA logic but adapts the initialization and comparison logic to operate directly on point pairs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: pointA (start position, Vector3), pointB (end position, Vector3). Output: An iterable sequence of Vector3 coordinates representing the integer voxel centers (or grid indices) intersected by the line segment. Data Structures: x, y, z: Current voxel coordinates (floats, initialized to rounded pointA). tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ: Distance along the segment to the next voxel boundary in each axis. tDeltaX, tDeltaY, tDeltaZ: Distance between consecutive voxel boundaries in each axis. stepX, stepY, stepZ: Direction signs (+1 or -1) for traversal. lineLength: Total Euclidean length of the segment pointB - pointA. Formulas and Definitions: delta = pointB - pointA. deltaNormal = delta / |delta| (Normalized direction vector). dx, dy, dz: Components of deltaNormal. Signum(v): Returns 1 if v > 0, -1 if v < 0, and 0 if v == 0. Intbound(s, ds): Calculates the distance to the next integer boundary. If ds < 0 and s is an integer, return 0. Else, let s' = s \pmod 1 (using Mod(v, m) = (v \% m + m) \% m). If ds > 0, return (\lceil s' \rceil - s') / |ds|. Note: \lceil s' \rceil returns 1 if s' == 0, otherwise standard ceiling. If ds < 0, return (s' - \lfloor s' \rfloor) / |ds|. Precision5(val): Rounds val to 5 decimal places using integer arithmetic: ((int)(100000 val)) / 100000.0f. This mitigates floating-point precision issues during comparisons. Step Functions: Each step function checks if the current tMax exceeds lineLength. If so, traversal ends (returns true). Otherwise, it increments the voxel coordinate by step and adds tDelta to tMax (returns false). StepX(): If tMaxX >= lineLength return true. Else x += stepX, tMaxX += tDeltaX, return false. StepY(): Analogous for Y. StepZ(): Analogous for Z. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set x = round(pointA.X), y = round(pointA.Y), z = round(pointA.Z). Compute delta, deltaNormal, dx, dy, dz. Compute stepX, stepY, stepZ using Signum. Compute tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ using Intbound(pointA.X - 0.5f, deltaNormal.x), etc.. Compute tDeltaX = stepX / dx (handle division by zero if dx=0 by setting tDeltaX to infinity or skipping, though the source implies dx is non-zero when stepX is non-zero). Compute lineLength = |delta|. Initialize result list with (x, y, z). 2. Iteration: The iteration logic depends on which steps are non-zero. The source provides specific logic for the 3D case (all steps non-zero) and mentions separate loops for 2D/1D cases. 3D Case (stepX != 0 && stepY != 0 && stepZ != 0): Loop while true: Compute tX = Precision5(tMaxX), tY = Precision5(tMaxY), tZ = Precision5(tMaxZ). Compare tX, tY, tZ: If tX < tY: If tX < tZ: res = StepX() Else if tZ < tX: res = StepZ() Else (tZ == tX): res = StepZ() || StepX() (Execute both, result is true if either ends traversal). Else if tY < tX: If tY < tZ: res = StepY() Else if tZ < tY: res = StepZ() Else (tZ == tY): res = StepY() || StepZ(). Else (tX == tY): If tY < tZ: res = StepX() || StepY() Else if tZ < tY: res = StepZ() Else (tZ == tY): res = StepX() || StepY() || StepZ(). Add current (x, y, z) to result list. If res is true, break loop. 2D/1D Cases: Separate while loops handle cases where one or two steps are zero. The logic compares only the relevant tMax values. For example, if stepX != 0 && stepY == 0 && stepZ == 0, only StepX() is called in a loop until it returns true. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def signum(v): return 1 if v > 0 else (-1 if v < 0 else 0) def mod(v, m): return (v % m + m) % m def intbound(s, ds): if ds < 0 and s == math.floor(s): return 0.0 smod = mod(s, 1.0) if ds > 0: ceils = 1.0 if smod == 0.0 else math.ceil(smod) return (ceils - smod) / abs(ds) else: return (smod - math.floor(smod)) / abs(ds) def precision5(val): return float(int(100000 val) / 100000) def getintersectedworldblocks(pointA, pointB): line = [] x = round(pointA[0]) y = round(pointA[1]) z = round(pointA[2]) line.append((x, y, z)) dxraw = pointB[0] - pointA[0] dyraw = pointB[1] - pointA[1] dzraw = pointB[2] - pointA[2] length = math.sqrt(dxraw2 + dyraw2 + dzraw2) if length == 0.0: return line dx = dxraw / length dy = dyraw / length dz = dzraw / length stepX = signum(dx) stepY = signum(dy) stepZ = signum(dz) tMaxX = intbound(pointA[0] - 0.5, dx) tMaxY = intbound(pointA[1] - 0.5, dy) tMaxZ = intbound(pointA[2] - 0.5, dz) tDeltaX = stepX / dx if dx != 0.0 else 0.0 tDeltaY = stepY / dy if dy != 0.0 else 0.0 tDeltaZ = stepZ / dz if dz != 0.0 else 0.0 def stepx(): nonlocal x, tMaxX if tMaxX >= length: return True x += stepX tMaxX += tDeltaX return False def stepy(): nonlocal y, tMaxY if tMaxY >= length: return True y += stepY tMaxY += tDeltaY return False def stepz(): nonlocal z, tMaxZ if tMaxZ >= length: return True z += stepZ tMaxZ += tDeltaZ return False activex = stepX != 0 activey = stepY != 0 activez = stepZ != 0 while True: res = False if activex and activey and activez: tX = precision5(tMaxX) tY = precision5(tMaxY) tZ = precision5(tMaxZ) if tX < tY: if tX < tZ: res = stepx() elif tZ < tX: res = stepz() else: res = stepz() or stepx() elif tY < tX: if tY < tZ: res = stepy() elif tZ < tY: res = stepz() else: res = stepy() or stepz() else: if tY < tZ: res = stepx() or stepy() elif tZ < tY: res = stepz() else: res = stepx() or stepy() or stepz() elif activex and not activey and not activez: res = stepx() elif not activex and activey and not activez: res = stepy() elif not activex and not activey and activez: res = stepz() elif activex and activey and not activez: tX = precision5(tMaxX) tY = precision5(tMaxY) if tX < tY: res = stepx() elif tY < tX: res = stepy() else: res = stepx() or stepy() elif activex and not activey and activez: tX = precision5(tMaxX) tZ = precision5(tMaxZ) if tX < tZ: res = stepx() elif tZ < tX: res = stepz() else: res = stepx() or stepz() elif not activex and activey and activez: tY = precision5(tMaxY) tZ = precision5(tMaxZ) if tY < tZ: res = stepy() elif tZ < tY: res = stepz() else: res = stepy() or stepz() else: break line.append((x, y, z)) if res: break return line This variant uses the ray-volume impact point (from intersection check) as the first ray-voxel intersection point (entry point). It calculates the point where the ray emerges from the current voxel (exit point), tests the data between the entry and exit points against user-specified target values, and repeats traversal until the ray emerges from the data volume or available light is depleted. Unlike Levy's uniform resampling which causes aliasing and misses interstitial surfaces, this method guarantees traversal through every voxel the ray intersects. Uniform sampling requires infinite samples to guarantee finding all surfaces, or suffers from aliasing if steps are too large. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed, as all intersected voxels are stored in the output list. Strengths: Handles edge cases (zero deltas, exact edge hits, negative traversal) more robustly than standard implementations. The Precision5 helper reduces floating-point comparison errors. Limitations: The source notes it "might (and probably will) be slower" than standard face-to-face traversal due to the overhead of precision rounding and complex branching logic for equality cases. When to use: When high precision is required for voxel selection, especially with non-0-based block centers or when dealing with degenerate rays (zero length or axis-aligned). This method is described as a variation of the Amanatides and Woo algorithm, adapted for a voxel game context where blocks are centered at 0.5-based coordinates. It was shared on GameDev Stack Exchange in 2013 to address specific edge cases not handled by existing code. name: Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Plücker Space)
head: Hex-P, Hexahedral Plücker traversal
body: A traversal method for hexahedral meshes that uses Plücker coordinates to determine the exit face of a ray intersecting a hexahedral cell, requiring face decomposition into triangles for interpolation. It sets itself apart from its sibling Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Bilinear Patch-Extension) by relying on triangular decomposition for interpolation, which introduces parametric discontinuities along the diagonal but allows unambiguous face determination. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a hexahedral mesh where each cell has 8 vertices v0, \dots, v7. The entry face is defined by vertices v0, v1, v2, v3 and the opposite face by v4, v5, v6, v7. Output: The index of the next hexahedron in the traversal path and the barycentric coordinates on the exit face for interpolation. Data Structures: The mesh topology is implicit in the grid structure; no extra connectivity memory is required. Boundary faces are preprocessed and decomposed into two triangles each for efficient kd-tree initialization. Steps: 1. Initialization: Find the initial hexahedron along the ray using a kd-tree built from the decomposed boundary faces. 2. First Plücker Test: Perform a Plücker test using edges v4 \to v5 and v6 \to v7. This test partitions the possible exit faces into three areas A0, A1, A2, each containing exactly three faces of the hexahedron. 3. Second Plücker Test (Conditional): If the first test does not uniquely identify the exit face, perform a second Plücker test based on the determined area: For area A0: test edges v2 \to v6 and v3 \to v7. For area A1: test edges v4 \to v6 and v5 \to v7. For area A2: test edges v0 \to v4 and v1 \to v5. 4. Face Determination: Determine the correct exit face using simple sign comparisons from the second test. 5. Traversal Step: Modify the index pointer by incrementing or decrementing with respect to the dimension corresponding to the exit face to fetch the next cell. Stop if the pointer exits volume bounds. 6. Interpolation: Decompose the intersected exit face into two triangles. Compute barycentric coordinates for the intersection point on the selected triangle. Note that Plücker values cannot be directly scaled to receive parametric coordinates for quadrilaterals, necessitating this decomposition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def pluckersign(o, d, p1, p2): # Standard Plücker sign test: sign(dot(d x (p1-o), p2-p1)) vectop1 = sub(p1, o) vecedge = sub(p2, p1) crossprod = cross(d, vectop1) val = dot(crossprod, vecedge) return 1 if val > 0 else (-1 if val < 0 else 0) def traversehexahedron(rayo, rayd, mesh, currentidx, bounds): # 1. Fetch vertices for current cell v = mesh.vertices[currentidx] v0, v1, v2, v3 = v[0], v[1], v[2], v[3] v4, v5, v6, v7 = v[4], v[5], v[6], v[7] # 2. First Plücker test: edges v4->v5 and v6->v7 # does not specify exact mapping from Plücker products to areas A0, A1, A2. area = 0 # Placeholder for area determination logic not detailed in exitface = None # 3. Second Plücker test if area is ambiguous if area == 0: s1 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v2, v6) s2 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v3, v7) # does not specify exact sign-to-face mapping exitface = 0 elif area == 1: s1 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v4, v6) s2 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v5, v7) exitface = 0 elif area == 2: s1 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v0, v4) s2 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v1, v5) exitface = 0 # 4. Traversal Step: Modify index pointer # states to increment/decrement with respect to the dimension of the exit face nextidx = currentidx # does not specify exact grid index arithmetic if nextidx < bounds.min or nextidx >= bounds.max: return None, None # 5. Interpolation: Decompose exit face into two triangles # does not specify exact barycentric formula barycentric = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return nextidx, barycentric Parameters: Typical performance: 3.2 million hexahedra per second on a Dual-core Opteron 2 GHz. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Decomposing a face into two triangles leads to parametric discontinuities along the diagonal. Unwanted artifacts may appear if hexahedra values are badly distributed. Plücker values are only suitable for triangles; they cannot be directly scaled to receive parametric coordinates for quadrilaterals. A hybrid traversal algorithm that combines Plücker-based face selection with bilinear patch intersection tests. It avoids the geometric singularities and discontinuities of pure Plücker traversal by using parametric coordinates (u, v) from bilinear patches for interpolation. Choose this when smooth interpolation across face boundaries is critical and performance overhead of bilinear tests is acceptable. Time Complexity: The method requires at most four Plücker tests to decide the exit face. However, the need to decompose faces and compute barycentric coordinates reduces performance significantly compared to tetrahedral traversal. Memory Complexity: No extra memory for connectivity is required as topology is implicit. Measured Performance: 3.2 million hexahedra per second on a Dual-core Opteron 2 GHz. Scaling: Data fetching costs are 7 times higher than tetrahedral traversal because more than one vertex and scalar value must be fetched per step. Strengths: Unambiguous determination of intersected faces; optimized for convex hexahedral faces; easily extendable to concave faces. Limitations: Parametric discontinuities along the diagonal of decomposed faces; artifacts with badly distributed values; higher data fetching costs. When to use: When unambiguous face determination is prioritized over interpolation smoothness and performance overhead is acceptable. When not to use: When smooth interpolation across face boundaries is required or when performance is critical and tetrahedral meshes are an option. Originated in the paper "Fast Ray Traversal of Tetrahedral and Hexahedral Meshes for Direct Volume Rendering" (2006). The method extends the Plücker test introduced for tetrahedral traversal to hexahedral grids. It is used in direct volume rendering for hexahedral meshes.
