name: Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Bilinear Patch-Extension)
head: Bilinear Patch Traversal, Hex-H, Hybrid Hexahedral Traversal
body: This method is a hybrid traversal algorithm for hexahedral meshes that combines Plücker-based face selection with bilinear patch intersection tests. It solves the problem of geometric singularities and discontinuities inherent in pure Plücker traversal by utilizing the parametric coordinates (u, v) derived from bilinear patch intersections to compute interpolated scalar values directly. It sets itself apart from the parent Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Plücker Space) by avoiding the need to decompose exit faces into triangles for interpolation, thereby eliminating discontinuities at face boundaries. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, hexahedron vertices \mathbf{v}0 \dots \mathbf{v}7. Outputs: Exit face index, parametric coordinates (u, v) on the exit face, and interpolated scalar values at entry and exit points. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 8 3D vectors. Plücker Values: Three scalar areas A0, A1, A2 derived from cross products. Bilinear Patch Parameters: u, v \in \mathbb{R}. Steps: 1. Plücker Face Selection: Compute the Plücker values for the lines \mathbf{v}4 \to \mathbf{v}5, \mathbf{v}6 \to \mathbf{v}7, and the ray to determine the three areas A0, A1, A2. This identifies the three candidate exit faces. 2. Bilinear Patch Intersection: For each of the three candidate exit faces, perform a bilinear patch intersection test. A bilinear patch is defined by four vertices. 3. Exit Determination: Stop as soon as a patch is hit, i.e., when (u, v) \in [0, 1]^2. This provides the exit face and the parametric coordinates (u, v) for the exit point. 4. Numerical Consistency Check: If numerical inconsistencies occur due to insufficient floating-point accuracy, perform two additional Plücker tests equivalent to the second step of the pure Plücker method to resolve the correct exit face. 5. Interpolation: Use the known parametric coordinates (u, v) from the bilinear patch test to compute interpolated scalar values on the entry and exit faces. This avoids discontinuities associated with triangle-based interpolation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversehexahedron(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices): # hexvertices: list of 8 points [v0,..., v7] # Step 1: Compute Plücker areas for candidate faces # Lines: v4->v5, v6->v7, and ray direction v4, v5 = hexvertices[4], hexvertices[5] v6, v7 = hexvertices[6], hexvertices[7] edge1 = v5 - v4 edge2 = v7 - v6 # Compute Plücker areas A0, A1, A2 from edge1, edge2, and raydirection # Standard Plücker coordinate computation for ray-cell face intersection A0 = norm(cross(edge1, raydirection)) A1 = norm(cross(edge2, raydirection)) A2 = norm(cross(edge1, edge2)) # Identify candidate faces based on signs of A0, A1, A2 candidatefaces = [0, 1, 2] # Indices of the three candidate exit faces exitface = None u, v = 0.0, 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Check bilinear patch intersection for each candidate for faceidx in candidatefaces: # Perform bilinear patch intersection test # Fast and robust implementation described by Ramsey et al. [SDRH04] # Standard bilinear patch intersection solves P(u,v) = rayorigin + traydirection # Returns (hit, u, v) hit, u, v = solvebilinearpatchintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, faceidx) if hit and 0.0 <= u <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= v <= 1.0: exitface = faceidx break # Step 4: Handle numerical inconsistencies if exitface is None: # Perform two additional Plücker tests (pure Plücker fallback) # Equivalent to the second step of the pure Plücker method exitface = resolvepluckerfallback(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices) # Recompute (u, v) by projecting the exit point onto the exit face plane exitpoint = rayorigin + raydirection computetexit(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, exitface) u, v = projecttofaceuv(exitpoint, hexvertices, exitface) # Step 5: Interpolation # Compute scalar at entry point (previous cell exit or ray origin) # Compute scalar at exit point using u, v on exitface scalarexit = interpolatescalarbilinear(hexvertices, exitface, u, v) return exitface, u, v, scalarexit def solvebilinearpatchintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, faceidx): # Standard algebraic solution for ray-bilinear patch intersection return False, 0.0, 0.0 def resolvepluckerfallback(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices): # Two additional Plücker tests equivalent to pure Plücker method return 0 def computetexit(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, faceidx): # Standard ray-plane intersection return 1.0 def projecttofaceuv(point, hexvertices, faceidx): # Standard projection onto bilinear patch parameter space return 0.0, 0.0 def interpolatescalarbilinear(hexvertices, faceidx, u, v): # Standard bilinear interpolation return 0.0 Parameters: Floating-point precision: Standard double precision is recommended to minimize numerical inconsistencies. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes in Hexahedron: Bilinear patches are generally not flat, introducing holes in the hexahedron because the implicit edge representation depends on all four face vertices, unlike Plücker coordinates which depend solely on two edge points. This can cause rays to miss the exit face or produce invalid (u, v) coordinates. Numerical Inconsistencies: Insufficient floating-point accuracy can lead to incorrect face selection. The method requires a fallback to Plücker tests in these cases. Discontinuities: Pure Plücker traversal requires triangle decomposition, leading to discontinuities at face boundaries. This method avoids that by using bilinear patches. A method to calculate normals for hexahedral meshes using trilinear interpolation of vertex normals, converted from computational space to physical space via the Jacobian matrix. It is chosen when accurate shading is required for curvilinear hexahedral meshes. It differs from scalar interpolation by operating on vector fields and requiring Jacobian transformation. Steps: 1. Interpolate a vector at the entry and exit faces using the same parametric coordinates (u, v) used for scalar interpolation. 2. Perform a linear interpolation between the two interpolated vectors based on their distance to the isosurface to yield the final normal. 3. Calculate three vectors in physical space corresponding to the normal in computational space Nc and convert them to physical space Np using the Jacobian matrix. Formulas: Convert physical coordinates xi to computational coordinates \tilde{\rho}j using the Jacobian matrix J{ij}: xi = J{ij} \tilde{\rho}j J{ij} = \frac{\partial xi}{\partial \tilde{\rho}j} Approximate the Jacobian matrix J{ij} for a grid node n using central differences: J{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{xi(n) - xi(n-1)}{\tilde{\rho}j(n) - \tilde{\rho}j(n+1)} + \frac{xi(n+1) - xi(n)}{\tilde{\rho}j(n+1) - \tilde{\rho}j(n)} \right) A linear combination of the three vectors with the normal in computational space Nc results in the converted normal Np. Time Complexity: Raw traversal performance is 15% lower compared to the pure Plücker traverser due to the cost of bilinear patch intersection tests. However, overall performance gains 25% on average because time is saved in interpolation (no triangle decomposition needed). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The hybrid algorithm processes up to 4.5 million hexahedra per second on a Dual-core Opteron 2 GHz. Strengths: Better quality and significantly faster overall performance than the pure Plücker approach for hexahedral meshes due to avoided discontinuities and efficient interpolation. Limitations: Raw traversal is slower; numerical inconsistencies may require fallback tests, though this is rare. When to Use: Recommended for traversing curvilinear grids on a ray tracing basis, especially when high-quality rendering and continuous interpolation are prioritized over raw traversal speed. Originated in the paper "Fast Ray Traversal of Tetrahedral and Hexahedral Meshes for Direct Volume Rendering" (2006) by Ramsey et al.. The method was developed to address singularities and discontinuities in hexahedral mesh traversal for direct volume rendering. It builds on the Plücker-based traversal method but integrates bilinear patch tests to improve interpolation quality. Fast Ray Traversal of Tetrahedral and Hexahedral Meshes for Direct Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/eurovis06/235-242, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Point-in-Tetrahedron Test via Barycentric Coordinates
head: Barycentric Point-in-Tetrahedron Test
body: This method determines whether a set of query points lies inside a set of tetrahedra by solving for barycentric coordinates. It serves as the geometric core for the Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection algorithm, specifically handling the containment check after a ray has potentially intersected the tetrahedral volume. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on edge-based or Plücker coordinate formulations, this approach uses linear algebra to solve for the four barycentric weights directly, allowing for efficient vectorized processing of point clouds. Inputs: points: A tensor of shape (P, 3) containing P query points in 3D space. vertices: A tensor of shape (V, 3) containing the 3D coordinates of the mesh vertices. tetrahedra: A tensor of shape (T, 4) containing indices into vertices, defining T tetrahedra. Each row [i0, i1, i2, i3] refers to vertices v0, v1, v2, v3. Outputs: insidetet: A tensor of shape (P,) where each element is the index of the first tetrahedron containing the corresponding point, or -1 if no containing tetrahedron is found. barycentriccoords: A tensor of shape (P, 4) containing the barycentric weights [\lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3] for each point relative to its containing tetrahedron. If a point is not inside any tetrahedron, these values are zero. The implementation processes points in chunks to manage memory usage. chunksize: The number of points processed in a single batch. mat: A temporary tensor of shape (3, 3, \text{chunk\size}) representing the edge vectors of the tetrahedra. d: A temporary tensor of shape (3, \text{chunk\size}) representing the vector from the reference vertex to the query points. 1. Initialization: Initialize insidetet with -1 and barycentriccoords with 0. 2. Chunking: Iterate over the points in chunks of size chunksize. For each chunk, determine the start and end indices. 3. Vertex Retrieval: Retrieve the vertices for all tetrahedra using the tetrahedra index tensor. Let the vertices for a specific tetrahedron be v0, v1, v2, v3. 4. Edge Vector Computation: Compute the edge vectors originating from v3: a = v0 - v3 b = v1 - v3 c = v2 - v3 5. Point Vector Computation: Compute the vector from v3 to each query point p in the current chunk: d = p - v3 6. Barycentric Solve: The barycentric coordinates \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2 (relative to edges a, b, c) satisfy the linear system: \lambda0 a + \lambda1 b + \lambda2 c = d This is solved by constructing the matrix M = [a, b, c] and computing: [\lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2]^T = M^{-1} d In practice, this is done using a linear solver (e.g., torch.linalg.solve). 7. Lambda Extraction: Extract \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2 from the solution. Compute the fourth barycentric coordinate: \lambda3 = 1 - \lambda0 - \lambda1 - \lambda2 8. Containment Check: A point is inside the tetrahedron if and only if all barycentric coordinates are non-negative: \text{inside} = (\lambda0 \ge 0) \land (\lambda1 \ge 0) \land (\lambda2 \ge 0) \land (\lambda3 \ge 0) 9. Selection: For each point, if it is inside any tetrahedron, select the first one (lowest index). Update insidetet and barycentriccoords for the valid points in the chunk. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointintetrahedron(points, vertices, tetrahedra, chunksize=1024): """ Determine if points lie inside tetrahedra using barycentric coordinates. Args: points: Tensor of shape (P, 3) vertices: Tensor of shape (V, 3) tetrahedra: Tensor of shape (T, 4) chunksize: Integer, number of points to process at once Returns: insidetet: Tensor of shape (P,) with tetrahedron index or -1 barycentriccoords: Tensor of shape (P, 4) with barycentric weights """ P = points.shape[0] insidetet = torch.full((P,), -1, dtype=torch.int64) barycentriccoords = torch.zeros((P, 4), dtype=torch.float32) numtets = tetrahedra.shape[0] # Pre-fetch all tetrahedron vertices to avoid repeated indexing # Shape: (T, 4, 3) tetsvertices = vertices[tetrahedra] for start in range(0, P, chunksize): end = min(start + chunksize, P) chunkpoints = points[start:end] # Shape: (chunksize, 3) # Get vertices for all tetrahedra: (T, 4, 3) # Unpack into v0, v1, v2, v3: each (T, 3) v0, v1, v2, v3 = tetsvertices[:, 0], tetsvertices[:, 1], tetsvertices[:, 2], tetsvertices[:, 3] # Compute edge vectors: each (T, 3) a = v0 - v3 b = v1 - v3 c = v2 - v3 # Compute point vectors relative to v3: (chunksize, 3) # We need to broadcast v3 to match chunksize for the subtraction # v3 is (T, 3), chunkpoints is (chunksize, 3) # We want d to be (T, chunksize, 3) where d[t, p] = chunkpoints[p] - v3[t] d = chunkpoints.unsqueeze(0) - v3.unsqueeze(1) # Shape: (T, chunksize, 3) # Stack edge vectors to form matrix M: (T, 3, 3) # M[t] = [a[t], b[t], c[t]] M = torch.stack([a, b, c], dim=1) # Shape: (T, 3, 3) # Solve M lambda = d for each point # d is (T, chunksize, 3), we need to solve for each point independently # Reshape d to (T chunksize, 3) for batched solve, or use einsum/solve appropriately # torch.linalg.solve expects (..., N, N) and (..., N, K) # We want to solve for each of the T tetrahedra for each of the chunksize points # Reshape M to (T, 3, 3) and d to (T, chunksize, 3) # We need to solve M[t] @ x = d[t, p] for each t, p # This can be done by reshaping to (Tchunksize, 3, 3) and (Tchunksize, 3, 1) Mflat = M.reshape(-1, 3, 3) # (Tchunksize, 3, 3) dflat = d.permute(0, 2, 1).reshape(-1, 3, 1) # (Tchunksize, 3, 1) # Solve linear system sol = torch.linalg.solve(Mflat, dflat) # (Tchunksize, 3, 1) # Reshape back to (T, chunksize, 3) sol = sol.squeeze(-1).permute(1, 0, 2) # (chunksize, T, 3) # Extract lambdas: (chunksize, T) lambda0 = sol[:,:, 0] lambda1 = sol[:,:, 1] lambda2 = sol[:,:, 2] # Compute lambda3 lambda3 = 1.0 - lambda0 - lambda1 - lambda2 # Check inside condition: (chunksize, T) inside = (lambda0 >= 0) & (lambda1 >= 0) & (lambda2 >= 0) & (lambda3 >= 0) # Find first containing tetrahedron for each point # inside.any(dim=1) gives (chunksize,) boolean mask for valid points validtetexists = inside.any(dim=1) # Get indices of valid points in the chunk chunkvalidmask = validtetexists.nonzero(astuple=True)[0] if len(chunkvalidmask) > 0: # For valid points, find the first tetrahedron index # inside.float() is (chunksize, T) # argmax(dim=1) returns the first max index (which is the first True) chunkinsidetet = torch.where( validtetexists, inside.float().argmax(dim=1), torch.full((chunksize,), -1, dtype=torch.float32)).long() # Get the tetrahedron indices for valid points validtetidx = chunkinsidetet[chunkvalidmask] # Update insidetet insidetet[start:end][chunkvalidmask] = validtetidx # Update barycentriccoords # We need the lambdas corresponding to the selected tetrahedra # validtetidx is (numvalid,) # We need to gather lambda0, lambda1, lambda2 for these indices # Gather indices for each lambda # lambda0 shape: (chunksize, T) # We want lambda0[chunkvalidmask, validtetidx] # Create a grid of indices for gathering rowindices = torch.arange(len(chunkvalidmask), device=inside.device) colindices = validtetidx # Gather values l0 = lambda0[chunkvalidmask, colindices] l1 = lambda1[chunkvalidmask, colindices] l2 = lambda2[chunkvalidmask, colindices] l3 = lambda3[chunkvalidmask, colindices] barycentriccoords[start:end, 0][chunkvalidmask] = l0 barycentriccoords[start:end, 1][chunkvalidmask] = l1 barycentriccoords[start:end, 2][chunkvalidmask] = l2 barycentriccoords[start:end, 3][chunkvalidmask] = l3 return insidetet, barycentriccoords chunksize: Controls memory usage. Larger values improve throughput but increase peak memory. Typical values range from 1024 to 8192 depending on available GPU memory. Degenerate Tetrahedra: If the tetrahedron volume is zero (coplanar vertices), the matrix M is singular and the linear solver will fail or produce NaNs. Implementers should check for zero volume or use a pseudo-inverse if degenerate cases are expected. Precision: Barycentric coordinates should sum to 1.0. Floating-point errors may cause slight deviations. The condition \lambdai \ge 0 is robust, but strict equality checks for \sum \lambdai = 1 are not required if \lambda3 is computed as 1 - \sum{i=0}^2 \lambdai. Boundary Conditions: Points exactly on the boundary have \lambdai = 0. The condition \ge 0 includes them as "inside". Uses Plücker coordinates for intersection tests. Choose when working with line geometry primitives directly. A specific ray-intersection algorithm. Choose when using the IRIS framework. Optimizes ray intersection via skeleton parameters. Choose for skeleton-based representations. Intersects rays with cylinders. Choose for cylindrical primitives. Optimizes tetrahedron intersection on mesh shaders. Choose for GPU mesh shader pipelines. Handles cell-organized irregular volumes. Choose for structured irregular grids. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot T) in the worst case if checking all tetrahedra, but typically O(P) if spatial acceleration structures (like BVH or grid) are used to limit T to a small constant. The linear solve is O(1) per point per tetrahedron. Memory Complexity: O(P + T) for storing inputs and outputs. Chunking reduces peak memory to O(\text{chunk\size} \cdot T). Strengths: Vectorizable, numerically stable for non-degenerate tetrahedra, easy to implement with standard linear algebra libraries. Limitations: Requires solving a linear system for each tetrahedron-point pair, which can be expensive without acceleration structures. Degenerate tetrahedra cause numerical instability. When to Use: When high precision is needed for point containment in tetrahedral meshes, and acceleration structures are available to limit the search space. When Not to Use: For degenerate tetrahedra or when memory is extremely constrained and chunking is not feasible. This method is derived from the TetWeave project, which uses barycentric coordinates for resampling and optimization in tetrahedral grids. It is a standard technique in computational geometry for point-in-polyhedron tests. AlexandreBinninger/TetWeave, https://github.com/AlexandreBinninger/TetWeave, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Tetrahedron Face Extraction
body: Computes the four planar faces (unit normals and distances to the origin) from a four-vertex description of a tetrahedron. It serves as the geometric preprocessing step for Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection, converting vertex-based topology into half-space representations required for efficient ray-clipping. It differs from Plücker-based Tetrahedral Cell Intersection by using explicit plane equations rather than line geometry, and from Point-in-Tetrahedron Test via Barycentric Coordinates by outputting boundary definitions rather than containment tests. Inputs: verts: Array of four r3drvec3 vectors (v0, v1, v2, v3) defining the tetrahedron vertices. Outputs: faces: Array of four r3dplane structures. Each plane is defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n} and a scalar distance d from the origin, such that the plane equation is \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. Data Structures: r3drvec3: A 3D vector structure containing x, y, z components (typically float or double). r3dplane: A structure containing a normal vector n (r3drvec3) and a scalar d (float or double). Algorithm: For each of the four faces, identified by the vertex opposite to the face, the normal is computed via the cross product of two edge vectors lying on the face. The distance is computed by projecting the origin onto the normal relative to a point on the plane. 1. Define the four faces by their opposite vertices: Face 0: Opposite v0, defined by vertices v1, v2, v3. Face 1: Opposite v1, defined by vertices v0, v2, v3. Face 2: Opposite v2, defined by vertices v0, v1, v3. Face 3: Opposite v3, defined by vertices v0, v1, v2. 2. For each face i (where i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}): a. Identify the three vertices forming the face. Let these be a, b, c. b. Compute two edge vectors: \mathbf{e}1 = b - a and \mathbf{e}2 = c - a. c. Compute the unnormalized normal: \mathbf{n}{raw} = \mathbf{e}1 \times \mathbf{e}2. d. Normalize the normal: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{n}{raw}}{\|\mathbf{n}{raw}\|}. e. Compute the distance to the origin: d = -\mathbf{n} \cdot a. f. Store (\mathbf{n}, d) in faces[i]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tetrahedronfaceextraction(verts): """ verts: list of 4 vectors [v0, v1, v2, v3] returns: list of 4 planes [p0, p1, p2, p3] """ faces = [] # Mapping: face index i corresponds to the face NOT containing verts[i] # Face 0 uses v1, v2, v3 # Face 1 uses v0, v2, v3 # Face 2 uses v0, v1, v3 # Face 3 uses v0, v1, v2 faceindices = [ [1, 2, 3], [0, 2, 3], [0, 1, 3], [0, 1, 2] ] for i in range(4): idx = faceindices[i] a = verts[idx[0]] b = verts[idx[1]] c = verts[idx[2]] # Edge vectors e1 = [b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1], b[2]-a[2]] e2 = [c[0]-a[0], c[1]-a[1], c[2]-a[2]] # Cross product e1 x e2 nx = e1[1]e2[2] - e1[2]e2[1] ny = e1[2]e2[0] - e1[0]e2[2] nz = e1[0]e2[1] - e1[1]e2[0] # Magnitude magsq = nxnx + nyny + nznz # Guard against degenerate face (zero area) if magsq == 0: # Return a zero normal or handle error; standard implementation assumes valid tetrahedron nx, ny, nz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 mag = 0.0 else: mag = magsq 0.5 nx /= mag ny /= mag nz /= mag # Distance to origin: d = -n. a d = -(nxa[0] + nya[1] + nza[2]) faces.append({'n': [nx, ny, nz], 'd': d}) return faces Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Tetrahedron: If vertices are coplanar, the cross product magnitude is zero. The normal cannot be normalized. The source does not specify a fallback, but numerically this results in NaN or Inf if not guarded. Winding Order: The direction of the normal depends on the order of vertices a, b, c. The source implies a specific winding order consistent with the r3d library's expectations. Calculates the signed volume of a tetrahedron defined by four input vertices. The return value is the signed volume; a positive volume indicates a specific winding order, while a negative volume indicates the opposite. If the volume is negative, vertices may be swapped to ensure positive volume. Inputs: Four vertices pa, pb, pc, pd. Output: Scalar signed volume. Formula: V = \frac{1}{6} (pd - pa) \cdot ((pb - pa) \times (pc - pa)). The sign indicates orientation relative to the vertex order. Time Complexity: O(1), as it performs a fixed number of arithmetic operations (4 faces \times constant work). Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring storage for 4 plane structures. Strengths: Provides explicit plane equations suitable for standard ray-plane intersection tests. Simple to implement. Limitations: Requires non-degenerate input. Normalization introduces square roots, which may be slower than unnormalized tests if only sign checks are needed. Originated in the r3d library by Devon Powell. The method is part of the r3d geometric primitives suite, designed for ray tracing applications involving irregular volumes. It is used as a dependency in applications linking against libr3d. devonmpowell/r3d, https://github.com/devonmpowell/r3d, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Skeleton Parameter Minimization for Ray Intersection
head: Inverted Minima Computation, Rational Function Root Finding for SCALIS
body: This method computes the intersection of a ray with a Scale-Invariant Integral Surface (SCALIS) by minimizing the squared distance from the ray to the skeleton curve, normalized by the local radius, rather than solving the implicit surface equation directly. It replaces complex sphere-cone intersection logic with a robust root-finding procedure on a rational function, offering superior numerical stability and computational efficiency. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (unit vector). Skeleton segment defined by endpoints \mathbf{p}0 and \mathbf{p}1, with radii \tau0 and \tau1. Skeleton length L = \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0\|. Outputs: The ray parameter t{min} corresponding to the closest intersection point. The skeleton parameter s{min} \in [0, L] where the minimum occurs. Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{d} are 3D floating-point vectors. Scalars b, c, s{cand} are floating-point numbers. Definitions: \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0 is the skeleton direction vector. \Delta \tau = \tau1 - \tau0 is the radius change along the segment. \mathbf{m} = \mathbf{p}0 - \mathbf{o} is the vector from the ray origin to the skeleton start point. The skeleton point at parameter s is \mathbf{p}(s) = \mathbf{p}0 + \frac{s}{L}\mathbf{u}. The radius at parameter s is \tau(s) = \tau0 + \frac{s}{L}\Delta \tau. d{\mathbf{r}}(\mathbf{p}(s)) is the perpendicular distance from the ray to the point \mathbf{p}(s). Steps: 1. Precompute Geometric Terms: Compute the projection of \mathbf{m} onto the ray direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{m}{\perp} = \mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d} This vector \mathbf{m}{\perp} represents the component of \mathbf{m} orthogonal to the ray. 2. Compute Coefficients for the Linear Equation: Calculate the coefficients b and c for the linear equation bs + c = 0, which arises from setting the derivative of the objective function to zero: b = \tau0 L^2 (1 - (\mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{d})^2) - \Delta \tau L \mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{m}{\perp} c = \Delta \tau \|\mathbf{m}{\perp}\|^2 + \tau0 L \mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{m}{\perp} 3. Find Candidate Minimum: If |b| > \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small tolerance for numerical stability, e.g., 10^{-9}), solve for the critical point s{cand}: s{cand} = -\frac{c}{b} If |b| \le \epsilon, the derivative does not vanish within the interval (or is constant), so no internal critical point exists. Set s{cand} to None. 4. Evaluate Candidates: The global minimum of the objective function f(s) = \frac{d{\mathbf{r}}^2(\mathbf{p}(s))}{\tau(s)^2} must occur either at the boundaries s=0 or s=L, or at the internal critical point s{cand} if it lies within [0, L]. Define the objective function value at any s: f(s) = \frac{\|\mathbf{m}{\perp} + \frac{s}{L}\mathbf{u}{\perp}\|^2}{\tau(s)^2} where \mathbf{u}{\perp} = \mathbf{u} - (\mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d} is the component of the skeleton direction orthogonal to the ray. Note that \|\mathbf{m}{\perp} + \frac{s}{L}\mathbf{u}{\perp}\|^2 is the squared distance from the ray to \mathbf{p}(s). Evaluate f(s) at: s=0 s=L s=s{cand} (only if 0 \le s{cand} \le L) Select the s value that yields the minimum f(s). Let this be s{min}. 5. Compute Ray Intersection Parameter: The closest point on the skeleton is \mathbf{p}(s{min}). The ray parameter t{min} is found by projecting \mathbf{p}(s{min}) onto the ray: t{min} = \mathbf{p}(s{min})^T \mathbf{d} - \mathbf{o}^T \mathbf{d} (Assuming \mathbf{o}^T \mathbf{d} is subtracted if the ray is not parameterized from origin, or simply t{min} = (\mathbf{p}(s{min}) - \mathbf{o}) \cdot \mathbf{d}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def skeletonparamminimization(rayo, rayd, p0, p1, tau0, tau1): """ Finds the ray parameter tmin for intersection with a SCALIS primitive defined by a linear skeleton segment. Args: rayo: 3D vector, ray origin rayd: 3D vector, ray direction (assumed unit length) p0: 3D vector, skeleton start point p1: 3D vector, skeleton end point tau0: float, radius at p0 tau1: float, radius at p1 Returns: tmin: float, ray parameter of closest intersection smin: float, skeleton parameter of closest point """ L = norm(p1 - p0) if L < 1e-9: # Degenerate skeleton (point) # Distance from ray to point p0 m = p0 - rayo proj = dot(m, rayd) closestpointonray = rayo + proj rayd distsq = norm(p0 - closestpointonray)2 # For a point, the "intersection" is ambiguous without radius logic, # but typically treated as boundary case. # Assuming standard SCALIS logic, we return the projection. return proj, 0.0 u = p1 - p0 deltatau = tau1 - tau0 m = p0 - rayo # Precompute orthogonal components relative to ray direction udotd = dot(u, rayd) mdotd = dot(m, rayd) # uperp and mperp are vectors orthogonal to rayd uperp = u - udotd rayd mperp = m - mdotd rayd # Coefficients for linear equation bs + c = 0 # b = tau0 L^2 (1 - (u^T d)^2) - deltatau L (u^T mperp) # Note: u^T mperp = u^T (m - (m^T d)d) = u^T m - (u^T d)(m^T d) # However, the source formula uses u^T mperp directly. udotmperp = dot(u, mperp) term1 = tau0 (L2) (1 - (udotd2)) term2 = deltatau L udotmperp b = term1 - term2 # c = deltatau ||mperp||^2 + tau0 L (u^T mperp) mperpnormsq = dot(mperp, mperp) term3 = deltatau mperpnormsq term4 = tau0 L udotmperp c = term3 + term4 smin = 0.0 minf = float('inf') # Helper to evaluate objective function f(s) def evalf(s): # Radius at s taus = tau0 + (s / L) deltatau # Point at s ps = p0 + (s / L) u # Vector from ray origin to ps ms = ps - rayo # Orthogonal component to ray msperp = ms - dot(ms, rayd) rayd # Squared distance distsq = dot(msperp, msperp) # Objective function if taus < 1e-9: return float('inf') return distsq / (taus2) # Check boundaries f0 = evalf(0.0) if f0 < minf: minf = f0 smin = 0.0 fL = evalf(L) if fL < minf: minf = fL smin = L # Check internal critical point if abs(b) > 1e-9: scand = -c / b if 0.0 <= scand <= L: fcand = evalf(scand) if fcand < minf: minf = fcand smin = scand # Compute tmin psmin = p0 + (smin / L) u tmin = dot(psmin - rayo, rayd) return tmin, smin Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Skeleton: If L \approx 0, the skeleton is a point. The method should fall back to a point-ray intersection test. Zero Radius: If \tau(s) \approx 0, the objective function diverges. In practice, SCALIS fields often have a minimum radius or the intersection is determined by the boundary conditions if the minimum is at the endpoint. Numerical Stability: The source notes that this approach is more numerically stable than solving the implicit equation directly, which involves finding scaling factors for sphere-cone intersections. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive. The method involves a constant number of vector operations and a single linear solve. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Avoids iterative root-finding or complex geometric primitives (spheres/cones). It is analytically exact for linear skeletons and radii. Limitations: Assumes linear skeleton segments and linearly varying radii. End-point corrections may be needed for integral field accuracy near skeleton endpoints due to divergence in field variations. When to use: When rendering SCALIS fields with linear skeleton primitives. It is preferred over direct implicit surface solving for its stability and speed. This method was introduced in the context of ray tracing Scale-Invariant Integral Surfaces (SCALIS). SCALIS fields are defined by a skeleton curve and a radius field, representing smooth, tubular structures. The method inverts the order of minimization: instead of finding the ray parameter t for a fixed skeleton parameter s, it finds the skeleton parameter s that minimizes the normalized distance, then derives t. This avoids the complexity of handling sphere-cone intersections inherent in the direct formulation. Fast Ray Tracing of Scale‐Invariant Integral Surfaces, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14208, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mesh Shader Tetrahedron Intersection Optimization
head: Accelerated intersections using wave intrinsics within a mesh shader, Optimized Cyrus-Beck for tetrahedra
body: This method optimizes the computation of ray-tetrahedron intersections by leveraging mesh shader wave intrinsics to share geometric data between the four vertices of a single tetrahedron, thereby reducing redundant memory loads and arithmetic operations. It improves upon the naive per-vertex loading approach and the standard Cyrus-Beck algorithm by precomputing plane parameters in the mesh shader and interpolating them in the fragment shader, achieving a runtime cost of only 12 FLOPs for the intersection logic. The method splits the intersection calculation into two stages: a mesh shader stage that computes plane parameters for each face of the tetrahedron, and a fragment shader stage that solves the linear inequalities of the Cyrus-Beck algorithm using interpolated values. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}{ray} and direction \mathbf{d}{ray}. Vertex positions of the tetrahedron, accessible via wave intrinsics. tetVertexId: The index of the current vertex within the tetrahedron (0–3). Outputs: o.planeN: A vector of 4 floats containing the numerator of the plane equation for each face. o.planeD: A vector of 4 floats containing the denominator (dot product of normal and ray direction) for each face. Static Lookup Table: A constant array kTetTriangles of 4 uint4 vectors defines the vertex indices for the 4 faces of a tetrahedron. The indices are ordered to ensure outward-facing normals. \text{kTetTriangles} = \begin{bmatrix} 0, 2, 1, 3 \\ 1, 2, 3, 0 \\ 0, 3, 2, 1 \\ 3, 0, 1, 2 \end{bmatrix} Each row kTetTriangles[i] corresponds to the face opposite vertex i. The first three elements define the triangle vertices, and the fourth is unused in the cross product but part of the uint4 layout. 1. Retrieve Face Indices: In the mesh shader, for the current vertex tetVertexId, retrieve the face vertex indices from kTetTriangles[tetVertexId]. Let these be v0, v1, v2 (the first three components). 2. Access Vertices via Wave Intrinsics: Use wave read intrinsics (e.g., WaveReadLaneAt or WRTRV) to access the positions of the tetrahedron's vertices. Since all 4 vertices of the tetrahedron are processed in the same wave group, each lane can access any vertex's position. Let \mathbf{P}k be the position of vertex k. The vertices for the current face are \mathbf{P}{v0}, \mathbf{P}{v1}, \mathbf{P}{v2}. 3. Compute Outward Normal: Calculate the outward-facing normal \mathbf{n} for the current face using the cross product of two edge vectors: \mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{P}{v2} - \mathbf{P}{v0}) \times (\mathbf{P}{v1} - \mathbf{P}{v0}) This normal is computed in each lane but represents the same geometric plane for the tetrahedron face. 4. Compute Plane Numerator: Select the first vertex of the face, \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{P}{v0}. Compute the numerator for the plane equation: \text{num} = \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{o}{ray}) 5. Broadcast Numerator: Broadcast the scalar num to all lanes in the wave group to populate the output vector o.planeN. Specifically, lane i stores num in o.planeN[i]. 6. Compute Plane Denominator: For each lane i, compute the denominator by dotting the normal \mathbf{n} (which is identical across lanes for this face) with the ray direction \mathbf{d}{ray}: \text{planeD}i = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}{ray} Store these in o.planeD. 7. Fragment Shader Normalization: In the fragment shader, normalize the denominator by the length of the ray direction: \text{planeD}i \leftarrow \frac{\text{planeD}i}{\|\mathbf{d}{ray}\|} 8. Compute Intersection Parameters: For each plane i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}, compute the intersection parameter ti: ti = \frac{\text{planeN}i}{\text{planeD}i} 9. Determine Entry and Exit Distances: Initialize t{enter} = -\infty and t{exit} = +\infty. For each plane i: If \text{planeD}i > 0, the ray is entering the half-space. Update t{enter} = \max(t{enter}, ti). If \text{planeD}i < 0, the ray is exiting the half-space. Update t{exit} = \min(t{exit}, ti). If \text{planeD}i = 0, the ray is parallel to the plane; it does not contribute to entry/exit bounds in the standard Cyrus-Beck logic (handled by the conditional checks). 10. Result: The ray intersects the tetrahedron if t{enter} < t{exit} and t{exit} > 0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshshaderintersect(rayorigin, raydir, tetvertexpositions, tetvertexid): # Static lookup table for outward-facing faces # Each uint4 is (v0, v1, v2, unused) kTetTriangles = [ (0, 2, 1, 3), (1, 2, 3, 0), (0, 3, 2, 1), (3, 0, 1, 2) ] # Get face indices for the current tetrahedron vertex faceindices = kTetTriangles[tetvertexid] v0idx, v1idx, v2idx = faceindices[0], faceindices[1], faceindices[2] # Access vertex positions using wave intrinsics # WRTRV(pos, idx) returns the position of vertex idx from any lane in the wave Pv0 = WRTRV(tetvertexpositions, v0idx) Pv1 = WRTRV(tetvertexpositions, v1idx) Pv2 = WRTRV(tetvertexpositions, v2idx) # Compute outward normal n edge1 = Pv2 - Pv0 edge2 = Pv1 - Pv0 n = cross(edge1, edge2) # Compute numerator num = n. (v - rayOrigin) v = Pv0 num = dot(n, v - rayorigin) # Broadcast num to all lanes for planeN # Each lane i stores num in planeN[i] planeN = [WRTRV(num, i) for i in range(4)] # Compute denominator planeD = n. rayDir for each lane # Note: n is the same for all lanes in this wave group for this face planeD = [dot(WRTRV(n, i), raydir) for i in range(4)] return planeN, planeD def fragmentshaderintersect(planeN, planeD, raydir): # Normalize denominator by ray direction length raylen = length(raydir) normalizedplaneD = [d / raylen for d in planeD] # Compute t for each plane # Handle division by zero if necessary, though planeD=0 implies parallel allt = [] for i in range(4): if normalizedplaneD[i] == 0.0: allt.append(float('inf')) # Parallel, no intersection contribution else: allt.append(planeN[i] / normalizedplaneD[i]) # Compute tenter and texit tenter = float('-inf') texit = float('inf') for i in range(4): if normalizedplaneD[i] > 0.0: # Ray entering half-space if allt[i] > tenter: tenter = allt[i] elif normalizedplaneD[i] < 0.0: # Ray exiting half-space if allt[i] < texit: texit = allt[i] return tenter, texit kTetTriangles: Static constant array defining vertex indices for outward-facing normals. Wave Size: The method assumes a wave size of at least 4 to process all 4 vertices of the tetrahedron in a single wave group. Redundant Loads: The naive implementation loads tetrahedron data for each vertex separately. This optimization avoids that by sharing data via wave intrinsics, reducing memory loads by a factor of four. Perspective-Correct Interpolation: The source notes that interpolation between distances must be perspective-correct barycentric interpolation to ensure correctness, although the core Cyrus-Beck logic described here operates on precomputed plane parameters in the mesh shader. The 12 FLOP count applies to the optimized Cyrus-Beck steps. Parallel Rays: If planeD is zero, the ray is parallel to the plane. The algorithm handles this by excluding it from the max/min updates, which is correct for convex polyhedra. Time Complexity: The optimized implementation reduces the runtime cost to 12 FLOPs for the intersection calculation. Memory Efficiency: By sharing information between vertices in the mesh shader, the method reduces memory loads by a factor of four compared to the naive per-vertex approach. Strengths: Significant reduction in arithmetic and memory bandwidth usage. Suitable for high-performance volumetric rendering where tetrahedral meshes are dense. Limitations: Requires hardware support for mesh shaders and wave intrinsics (e.g., DirectX 12 Ultimate, Vulkan Mesh Shaders). The optimization is specific to tetrahedral primitives. This method was introduced in the paper "Radiance Meshes for Volumetric Reconstruction". It builds on the Cyrus-Beck algorithm for ray-convex polygon intersection, adapting it for tetrahedral meshes using modern GPU mesh shader capabilities. The goal was to accelerate the intersection test, which is a bottleneck in raytracing irregular volumes. name: Raytracing Cell-Organized Irregular Volumes
head: Cell-based volume raytracing, Raytracing irregular volume data
body: This method enables efficient ray traversal through irregular volumetric datasets composed of non-uniform cells (such as tetrahedra or hexahedra) by maintaining a current cell and stepping through adjacent cells via shared faces. It solves the problem of navigating complex, potentially concave geometries where standard grid-based traversal fails. Unlike Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection, which treats cells as isolated primitives, this approach explicitly manages cell connectivity to minimize redundant intersection tests. It differs from Plücker-based Tetrahedral Cell Intersection by relying on explicit face-sharing adjacency lists rather than geometric duality tests for navigation. Inputs: Ray origin d and direction vector c. Irregular volume dataset defined by cells (e.g., tetrahedra or hexahedra). Adjacency data structure mapping each face to its neighboring cells. Surface boundary information (list of exposed faces). Outputs: Sequence of cells intersected by the ray. Integration parameters (density, color) accumulated along the ray path within the volume. Data Structures: Cell: Contains vertex indices and material properties. Face: Defined by three vertex indices (a, b, c). Stores the precomputed normal vector N = Ab \times Ac, where Ab = b - a and Ac = c - a. Stores adjacency: a list of neighbor cell indices. If the list is empty, the face is an exposed boundary. Adjacency Map: Hash map or array linking Face ID to Neighbor Cell IDs. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initial Intersection: Intersect the ray against all exposed faces of the dataset to find the first entry point. Select the face with the smallest positive intersection parameter t. If no intersection is found, the ray misses the volume. 2. Cell Traversal Loop: While the ray has not exited the dataset: a. Identify Current Cell: Determine the cell containing the current intersection point. b. Intersect Cell Faces: For each of the four faces of the current tetrahedral cell (or six for hexahedra), compute the intersection parameter t{face} using the plane intersection formula. c. Verify Face Containment: For each candidate face with a positive t{face} > t{current}, verify if the intersection point lies within the triangular face boundaries using barycentric coordinates. d. Select Exit Face: Choose the face with the smallest valid t{face}. e. Check Adjacency: If the selected face has a neighbor cell, update the current cell to the neighbor and repeat step 2. If the selected face has no neighbor (exposed face), the ray has exited the current connected component. Proceed to Step 3. 3. Re-entry Check (Concavity Handling): Since irregular volumes can be concave, the ray may re-enter the dataset. Intersect the ray against all exposed faces again. Find the face with the smallest positive t{face} that is greater than the current exit t. If found, update the current cell to the neighbor of this new entry face and resume Step 2. If no such face exists, the ray has fully exited the dataset. Formulas: Plane Intersection Parameter: For a ray R(t) = d + t c and a plane defined by vertices a, b, c: t = \frac{(Ab \times Ac) \cdot a - (Ab \times Ac) \cdot d}{(Ab \times Ac) \cdot c} where Ab = b - a and Ac = c - a. The cross product N = Ab \times Ac is precomputed and stored with the face. Point-in-Triangle Test: To verify if the intersection point P = d + t c lies inside the triangle defined by a, b, c with ray direction e (where e is the normalized ray direction c): u = \frac{(Ac \times e) \cdot d - (Ac \times e) \cdot a}{(Ac \times e) \cdot b} v = \frac{(Ab \times e) \cdot d - (Ab \times e) \cdot a}{(Ab \times e) \cdot c} The point is inside the face if u > 0, v > 0, and u + v < 1. [G: Note that the denominator in the source text for v uses Ac in the dot product with c, which appears to be a typo in the source; standard barycentric derivation typically uses Ab \times Ac or consistent edge vectors. However, adhering strictly to the source formula provided: (Ab \times e) \cdot c is used in the denominator for v. Implementers should verify this against the specific coordinate system definition in.] Degenerate Cases: Coincident Vertices: If a tetrahedron has two coincident vertices, two faces have zero area. These faces are ignored. If the ray enters through a non-degenerate face, it exits through the other non-degenerate face. The distance difference dt = 0, so no integration is required. Planar Tetrahedron: If a tetrahedron is planar (no coincident vertices but zero volume), all face intersection distances are identical. The ray passes through the interior of two specific triangular faces (entry and exit). dt = 0, so no integration is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytraceirregularvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata): """ rayorigin: vector d raydirection: vector c volumedata: object containing cells, faces, and adjacency map """ currentt = 0.0 currentcell = None # Step 1: Initial Entry entryface = findfirstexposedfaceintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata.exposedfaces) if entryface is None: return [] # Ray misses volume currentt = entryface.t currentcell = entryface.neighbors[0] # Assuming entry face has one neighbor visitedcells = [currentcell] while True: # Step 2: Traverse current cell exitface = None mint = infinity for face in currentcell.faces: # Calculate intersection with plane N = face.normal # Precomputed Ab x Ac denom = dot(N, raydirection) if abs(denom) < epsilon: continue # Ray parallel to face t = (dot(N, face.vertexa) - dot(N, rayorigin)) / denom if t > currentt + epsilon: # Verify point is inside triangle intersectionpoint = rayorigin + t raydirection if ispointintriangle(intersectionpoint, face.vertexa, face.vertexb, face.vertexc, raydirection): if t < mint: mint = t exitface = face if exitface is None: break # Should not happen in valid convex cell currentt = mint # Check adjacency if len(exitface.neighbors) == 0: # Exited dataset, check for re-entry reentryface = findnextexposedfaceintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata.exposedfaces, currentt) if reentryface is not None: currentt = reentryface.t currentcell = reentryface.neighbors[0] visitedcells.append(currentcell) continue else: break # Fully exited else: # Move to neighbor # Select neighbor that is not the current cell (handle bidirectional adjacency) nextcell = None for neighbor in exitface.neighbors: if neighbor != currentcell: nextcell = neighbor break if nextcell is None: # Fallback: if adjacency is not strictly bidirectional or data error, # treat as exit and check re-entry reentryface = findnextexposedfaceintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata.exposedfaces, currentt) if reentryface is not None: currentt = reentryface.t currentcell = reentryface.neighbors[0] visitedcells.append(currentcell) continue else: break currentcell = nextcell visitedcells.append(currentcell) # Integration step would occur here using currentcell and previoust # previoust = currentt (before update) return visitedcells def ispointintriangle(point, a, b, c, raydir): Ab = b - a Ac = c - a e = raydir # Formula from denomu = dot(cross(Ac, e), b) if abs(denomu) < epsilon: return False u = (dot(cross(Ac, e), point) - dot(cross(Ac, e), a)) / denomu denomv = dot(cross(Ab, e), c) if abs(denomv) < epsilon: return False v = (dot(cross(Ab, e), point) - dot(cross(Ab, e), a)) / denomv return u > 0 and v > 0 and (u + v) < 1 Time Complexity: O(N) in the worst case where N is the number of cells intersected, but typically much faster than testing all cells due to adjacency traversal. Each cell visit requires 4 (for tetrahedra) or 6 (for hexahedra) plane intersections and containment tests. Memory Complexity: O(V + F) where V is vertices and F is faces, required to store the adjacency map and face normals. Strengths: Efficient for irregular meshes; avoids redundant intersection tests by following connectivity; handles concave volumes via re-entry logic. Limitations: Requires precomputed adjacency data; degenerate cells require special handling; re-entry checks can be expensive if the surface is complex. When to use: Ideal for unstructured grid volumes (e.g., finite element analysis data) where regular grid traversal is not applicable. This method was introduced by as a technique for raytracing irregular volume data. It addresses the limitations of regular grid traversal when applied to unstructured meshes. The approach relies on the geometric properties of the cells (tetrahedra or hexahedra) and their adjacency relationships. For hexahedra, if symmetric tessellation is not possible, the method suggests subdividing each hexahedron into twenty-four tetrahedra by adding a vertex at the center of each face. name: Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection
head: Kalra-Barr method, LG-implicit surface intersection
body:
Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection is a robust algorithm for finding the nearest intersection between a ray and an implicit surface f(\mathbf{x}) = 0. It solves the problem of missing fine surface details or grazing intersections inherent in standard discrete ray marching by guaranteeing numerical convergence to the nearest root without requiring fine-tuning or human choice of interactive parameters. It distinguishes itself from its parent Implicit Surface and SDF Intersection by providing a specific mathematical framework for "LG-implicit surfaces" that ensures no features are missed, and from its sibling Ray Tracing Implicit Surfaces by its reliance on global Lipschitz and gradient bounds rather than local sampling heuristics. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Implicit surface function f: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R}. Upper bound L: limits the net rate of change of f (Lipschitz constant). Upper bound G: limits the rate of change of the gradient 
abla f (bound on the Hessian norm). Search interval [t{min}, t{max}] along the ray. Outputs: Intersection distance t^ if a root exists in [t{min}, t{max}]. Failure status if no root is found or bounds are violated. Data Structures: Interval [ta, tb] representing the current search segment along the ray. Function value f(\mathbf{x}) and gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) at query points. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set current interval [ta, tb] = [t{min}, t{max}]. 2. Evaluation: Evaluate f(\mathbf{x}a) and f(\mathbf{x}b) where \mathbf{x}a = \mathbf{o} + ta \mathbf{d} and \mathbf{x}b = \mathbf{o} + tb \mathbf{d}. 3. Sign Check: If f(\mathbf{x}a) and f(\mathbf{x}b) have opposite signs, a root exists in [ta, tb]. Proceed to bisection. If not, the algorithm may terminate or expand the search, depending on implementation. 4. Bisection: Compute midpoint tm = (ta + tb) / 2. Evaluate f(\mathbf{x}m). If |f(\mathbf{x}m)| < \epsilon (tolerance), return tm. If f(\mathbf{x}a) and f(\mathbf{x}m) have opposite signs, set tb = tm. Else, set ta = tm. 5. Convergence Check: If tb - ta < \delta (precision threshold), return (ta + tb) / 2. Else, repeat Step 4. Formulas: Lipschitz condition: |f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{y})| \le L \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|. Gradient bound: \|
abla f(\mathbf{x}) - 
abla f(\mathbf{y})\| \le G \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|. Parameters: L: Not given in the sources. G: Not given in the sources. \epsilon: Not given in the sources. \delta: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If L or G are underestimated, the guarantee of finding the nearest intersection is lost. The algorithm assumes the surface is an "LG-implicit surface". Level-synchronized bisection ray casting is a robust algorithm for rendering the zero-level-set of an implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R} by processing all active rays in lockstep (batch) using interval arithmetic to guarantee no surface features are missed. It solves the problem of missing fine surface details or grazing intersections inherent in standard discrete ray marching by bounding the function value over continuous segments and iteratively bisecting intervals until convergence. It distinguishes itself from its parent Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection by explicitly leveraging interval arithmetic for inclusion testing and batch synchronization for performance, and from its sibling Bisection Ray Tracing with Interval Inclusion by its specific implementation of level-synchronized processing and Hermite-based root estimation. Bisection Ray Tracing with Interval Inclusion is a robust ray-surface intersection algorithm that guarantees finding the nearest intersection of an implicit surface with a ray without missing fine features. It solves the problem of precision loss and feature skipping inherent in fixed-step ray marching by using interval arithmetic to prune intervals that cannot contain a root, followed by bisection to narrow down the interval containing the sign change of the implicit function f. Unlike standard bisection which processes rays independently, this method processes rays in batches and uses front-to-back pruning to discard intervals that are behind already found hits, improving efficiency for scenes with multiple surfaces or occlusion. It builds on Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection by providing a specific batched, interval-arithmetic-based implementation strategy. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guaranteed to find the nearest intersection; guaranteed not to miss fine features; no fine tuning required. Limitations: Requires computation of L and G bounds; may be slower than heuristic methods if bounds are loose. When to use: When robustness and feature preservation are critical, and bounds L and G are known or can be estimated. When not to use: When performance is paramount and approximate results are acceptable. The algorithm was presented by Devendra Kalra and Alan Barr in July 1989. It significantly extends the ability to intersect rays with implicit surfaces in a guaranteed fashion, addressing limitations of existing schemes that worked only for limited sets of implicit functions or were ad-hoc. name: Level-synchronized bisection ray casting
head: Batch bisection, Iso-surface bisection, Ray Subdivision and Interval Processing
body: Level-synchronized bisection ray casting is a robust algorithm for rendering the zero-level-set of an implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} by processing all active rays in lockstep using interval arithmetic to guarantee no surface features are missed. It solves the problem of missing fine surface details or grazing intersections inherent in standard discrete ray marching by bounding the function value over continuous segments and iteratively bisecting intervals until convergence. It builds on Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection and differs from Bisection Ray Tracing with Interval Inclusion by its specific implementation of level-synchronized processing and Hermite-based root estimation. Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^R, directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^R (normalized). Scene bounds [\mathbf{b}{min}, \mathbf{b}{max}] \subset \mathbb{R}^3. Implicit function f(\mathbf{p}) and an InclusionFunction object providing bounds over 3D axis-aligned boxes. Parameters: maxdepth (integer, default 40), threshold (float, default 10^{-5}). Outputs: TraceResult dataclass containing: hit: boolean array (R,), true if surface found. t: float64 array (R,), distance to hit. position: float64 array (R, 3), world position of hit. normal: float64 array (R, 3), surface normal at hit. depthcount: int array (R,), number of bisection steps. tlo, thi: float64 arrays (R,), final interval bounds. Data Structures: rayidx: Array of active ray indices. ivtlo, ivthi: Arrays of interval endpoints for active rays. hitmask: Boolean mask identifying rays intersecting the scene AABB. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize resulthit to False, resultt to inf, resulttlo to inf, resultthi to inf, resultdepth to 0. Compute ray-AABB intersection for all rays. Identify active rays where intersection exists and t{max} > t{min}. Set rayidx to indices of active rays. Set ivtlo to t{min} and ivthi to t{max} for active rays. 2. Ray Subdivision (Pre-processing): Subdivide the ray parameter space [t{min}, t{max}] into intervals. Subdivide further when switching between areas overlapped by primitive supports and areas not overlapped by any primitive support to avoid processing empty areas. For each resulting interval [t{begin}, t{end}], proceed to interval processing. 3. Level-Synchronized Bisection Loop: Iterate depth from 0 to maxdepth. If len(rayidx) == 0, break. Convert to 3D Boxes: For each active ray i, compute 3D axis-aligned boxes corresponding to the current interval [iv\t\lo[i], iv\t\hi[i]]: \mathbf{p}0 = \mathbf{o}i + iv\t\lo[i] \cdot \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{p}1 = \mathbf{o}i + iv\t\hi[i] \cdot \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{lo}{3d} = \min(\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1) \mathbf{hi}{3d} = \max(\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1) Inclusion Test: Evaluate inclusion bounds using inclusionfn.evaluate(lo3d, hi3d) to get [f{lo}, f{hi}]. Filter Active Rays: Determine if zero level set is present: \text{has\zero}[i] = (f{lo}[i] \le 0.0) \land (f{hi}[i] \ge 0.0) Update rayidx, ivtlo, ivthi to keep only rays where haszero is true. If len(rayidx) == 0, break. 4. Interval Processing (Per Active Ray): For each active ray interval [t{begin}, t{end}] with Hermite data \mathbf{h}b at t{begin} and \mathbf{h}e at t{end}: Initialize n \leftarrow 0, saved \leftarrow None. While n < 32: n \leftarrow n + 1. Estimate root t{root} \leftarrow \text{Oracle}(t{begin}, t{end}, i) using quadratic interpolation of Hermite data. If t{root} = \infty and saved is None, return false, \infty (no hit in this interval). If t{root} < \infty: Evaluate Hermite data at root: \mathbf{h}r \leftarrow \text{HermiteData}(t{root}). If |\mathbf{h}r.\text{val}| < \varepsilon, return true, t{root} (hit found). Determine primitive sign change: b{prim} \leftarrow (\mathbf{h}r.\text{prim} > 0) \land (\mathbf{h}b.\text{prim} < 0). If saved is None and \mathbf{h}r.\text{val} \ge 0 and \mathbf{h}e.\text{val} < 0 and b{prim}, store potential backtrack: saved \leftarrow [(t{root}, \mathbf{h}r), (t{end}, \mathbf{h}e)]. Update interval: If \mathbf{h}r.\text{val} < 0 or b{prim}, set t{end}, \mathbf{h}e \leftarrow t{root}, \mathbf{h}r; else set t{begin}, \mathbf{h}b \leftarrow t{root}, \mathbf{h}r. Else if saved is not None: Restore interval: (t{begin}, \mathbf{h}b), (t{end}, \mathbf{h}e) \leftarrow \text{saved}, saved \leftarrow None. If loop completes without hit, return false, \infty. 5. Result Update: For each valid hit with distance t{valid}: If t{valid} < \text{result\t}[\text{ray\idx}[i]]: \text{result\hit}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow \text{True} \text{result\t}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow t{valid} \text{result\t\lo}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow t{lo} \text{result\t\hi}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow t{hi} This ensures front-to-back rendering by keeping only the closest hit. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class TraceResult: hit: np.ndarray t: np.ndarray position: np.ndarray normal: np.ndarray depthcount: np.ndarray tlo: np.ndarray thi: np.ndarray def levelsynchronizedbisectioncast(origins, directions, boundsmin, boundsmax, inclusionfn, maxdepth=40, threshold=1e-5): R = origins.shape[0] # Initialize results resulthit = np.zeros(R, dtype=bool) resultt = np.full(R, np.inf, dtype=np.float64) resulttlo = np.full(R, np.inf, dtype=np.float64) resultthi = np.full(R, np.inf, dtype=np.float64) resultdepth = np.zeros(R, dtype=np.int32) # Ray-AABB intersection safedirs = np.where(directions == 0, 1.0, directions) tminvals = (boundsmin - origins) / safedirs tmaxvals = (boundsmax - origins) / safedirs # Fix: use np.max/min over axis=1 to get scalar tmin/tmax per ray tminarr = np.max(tminvals, axis=1) tmaxarr = np.min(tmaxvals, axis=1) hitmask = (tminarr < tmaxarr) & (tmaxarr > 0) rayidx = np.where(hitmask)[0] ivtlo = tminarr[rayidx] ivthi = tmaxarr[rayidx] # Pre-subdivision handled by scene structure; initial AABB bounds serve as starting intervals. for depth in range(maxdepth): if len(rayidx) == 0: break # Convert intervals to 3D boxes p0 = origins[rayidx] + ivtlo[:, np.newaxis] directions[rayidx] p1 = origins[rayidx] + ivthi[:, np.newaxis] directions[rayidx] lo3d = np.minimum(p0, p1) hi3d = np.maximum(p0, p1) # Evaluate inclusion bounds flo, fhi = inclusionfn.evaluate(lo3d, hi3d) # Filter active rays: haszero if flo <= 0 <= fhi haszero = (flo <= 0.0) & (fhi >= 0.0) rayidx = rayidx[haszero] ivtlo = ivtlo[haszero] ivthi = ivthi[haszero] if len(rayidx) == 0: break validhits = [] validrayindices = [] validtlo = [] validthi = [] for i in range(len(rayidx)): tbegin = ivtlo[i] tend = ivthi[i] # Standard evaluation returning function value and derivative for Hermite interpolation hb = inclusionfn.gethermitedata(origins[rayidx[i]] + tbegin directions[rayidx[i]]) he = inclusionfn.gethermitedata(origins[rayidx[i]] + tend directions[rayidx[i]]) saved = None hitfound = False hitt = np.inf for n in range(32): troot = oraclehermiteinterpolation(tbegin, tend, hb, he) if troot == np.inf: if saved is None: break else: (tbegin, hb), (tend, he) = saved saved = None continue proot = origins[rayidx[i]] + troot directions[rayidx[i]] hr = inclusionfn.gethermitedata(proot) if abs(hr.val) < threshold: hitfound = True hitt = troot break bprim = (hr.prim > 0) and (hb.prim < 0) if saved is None and hr.val >= 0 and he.val < 0 and bprim: saved = [(troot, hr), (tend, he)] if hr.val < 0 or bprim: tend = troot he = hr else: tbegin = troot hb = hr if hitfound: validhits.append(hitt) validrayindices.append(rayidx[i]) validtlo.append(tbegin) validthi.append(tend) if validhits: validhits = np.array(validhits) validrayindices = np.array(validrayindices) validtlo = np.array(validtlo) validthi = np.array(validthi) mask = validhits < resultt[validrayindices] resulthit[validrayindices[mask]] = True resultt[validrayindices[mask]] = validhits[mask] resulttlo[validrayindices[mask]] = validtlo[mask] resultthi[validrayindices[mask]] = validthi[mask] resultdepth[validrayindices[mask]] = depth + 1 positions = np.zeros((R, 3)) normals = np.zeros((R, 3)) hitindices = np.where(resulthit)[0] if len(hitindices) > 0: positions[hitindices] = origins[hitindices] + resultt[hitindices][:, np.newaxis] directions[hitindices] normals[hitindices] = inclusionfn.getnormals(positions[hitindices]) return TraceResult( hit=resulthit, t=resultt, position=positions, normal=normals, depthcount=resultdepth, tlo=resulttlo, thi=resultthi) def oraclehermiteinterpolation(tbegin, tend, hb, he): dt = tend - tbegin if dt == 0: return np.inf c = hb.val b = hb.prim dt a = 2 (he.val - hb.val) - (hb.prim + he.prim) dt if abs(a) < 1e-12: if abs(b) < 1e-12: return np.inf t = -c / b else: discriminant = bb - 4ac if discriminant < 0: return np.inf sqrtdisc = np.sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) if 0 <= t1 <= 1: t = t1 elif 0 <= t2 <= 1: t = t2 else: return np.inf return tbegin + t dt Parameters: maxdepth: Maximum number of bisection iterations allowed per ray. Default value is 40 in the tracer, but examples use 48 or 52. threshold: Convergence width threshold. The bisection stops when the interval width (t{hi} - t{lo}) is less than this value. Default value is 10^{-5}. inclusionfn: An InclusionFunction object that implements the evaluate(lo, hi) method. name: Bisection Trace with Gradient Inclusion
head: Level-Synchronized Interval Bisection
body: Bisection Trace with Gradient Inclusion is a robust ray casting algorithm that renders the zero-level-set of an implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} by combining level-synchronized bisection with gradient-based inclusion functions. It solves the problem of missing surface features during ray traversal by using interval arithmetic to guarantee that no zero-crossings are pruned incorrectly. It distinguishes itself from standard bisection by using a Lipschitz constant derived from gradient norms to tighten the inclusion bounds, offering a configurable trade-off between generality and bound tightness. Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o}, directions \mathbf{d}, near/far clip planes t{min}, t{max}, implicit function f(\mathbf{x}), maximum bisection depth D{max}, convergence threshold \tau, and Lipschitz constant L (or 'auto'). Outputs: Hit mask and hit distances t. Data Structures: Ray Batch: Arrays of shape (N, 3) for origins and directions, (N,) for t{min}, t{max}, and hit status. Interval Box: Defined by lower bound \mathbf{lo} and upper bound \mathbf{hi}, both shape (N, 3). Inclusion Function: Implements evaluate(lo, hi) returning conservative bounds [f{min}, f{max}] for f over the box. Steps: 1. Initialize Inclusion Function: Create GradientInclusion(fnp, lipschitz=lipschitz). If L is 'auto', estimate it by sampling gradient norms \|\nabla f\| over the bounding box using automatic differentiation. 2. Batch Processing: Divide rays into batches of size B (default: process all if B=None) to manage memory. 3. Bisection Loop: For each active ray in the batch: a. Define current interval [t{curr\min}, t{curr\max}] along the ray. b. Construct axis-aligned box in \mathbb{R}^3 corresponding to the ray segment. c. Evaluate inclusion function: [f{min}, f{max}] = \text{Inclusion}(\text{box}). d. Pruning: If 0 \notin [f{min}, f{max}], the interval cannot contain a zero crossing and is pruned. e. Bisection: If 0 \in [f{min}, f{max}], compute midpoint t{mid} = (t{curr\min} + t{curr\max}) / 2. f. Refinement: Evaluate f at \mathbf{x}{mid} = \mathbf{o} + t{mid}\mathbf{d}. g. Convergence: If |f(\mathbf{x}{mid})| < \tau or interval width < \tau, record hit at t{mid}. h. Update: If not converged, update t{curr\min} or t{curr\max} based on the sign of f(\mathbf{x}{mid}) to maintain the zero crossing within the interval. i. Depth Check: If iteration count > D{max}, terminate with best estimate. 4. Newton Iteration (Optional): Apply k Newton steps for refinement if enabled. Parameters: maxdepth: Maximum bisection iterations. threshold: Convergence tolerance \tau. lipschitz: Lipschitz constant L. If 'auto', estimated via gradient sampling. batchsize: Number of rays per batch. None for all. Edge Cases & Pitfalls: Degenerate Intervals: If t{curr\max} - t{curr\min} falls below machine epsilon, the interval is treated as converged to avoid infinite loops. Precision Loss: Evaluating f at endpoints far from the origin can cause catastrophic cancellation; coordinate translation or higher precision is recommended for large bounding boxes. Lipschitz Underestimation: If L is too small, the inclusion bounds may incorrectly exclude the zero crossing, causing missed hits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def estimatelipschitz(ffunc, boxlo, boxhi, numsamples=16): """Estimate Lipschitz constant by sampling gradient norms over the bounding box. Sources specify using torch.autograd for exact gradient computation.""" pts = boxlo + np.random.rand(numsamples, 3) (boxhi - boxlo) gradnorms = np.zeros(numsamples) eps = 1e-5 for i in range(numsamples): grad = np.zeros(3) for j in range(3): pplus = pts[i].copy(); pplus[j] += eps pminus = pts[i].copy(); pminus[j] -= eps grad[j] = (ffunc(pplus) - ffunc(pminus)) / (2 eps) gradnorms[i] = np.linalg.norm(grad) return np.max(gradnorms) class GradientInclusion: """Inclusion function using gradient bounds.""" def init(self, ffunc, lipschitz): self.ffunc = ffunc self.L = lipschitz def evaluate(self, lo, hi): """Compute conservative range of f over box [lo, hi]. Uses mean value form: f(x) ≈ f(c) ± L ||x - c||.""" center = 0.5 (lo + hi) radius = np.max(hi - lo, axis=-1) / 2.0 fcenter = self.ffunc(center) fmin = fcenter - self.L radius fmax = fcenter + self.L radius return fmin, fmax def tracerays(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, hitmask, fnp, maxdepth=15, threshold=1e-5, newtoniter=0, batchsize=None): """Robust ray casting using level-synchronized bisection with gradient inclusion.""" nrays = origins.shape[0] if batchsize is None: batchsize = nrays # Initialize inclusion function if isinstance(hitmask, str) and hitmask == 'auto': boxlo = np.min(origins, axis=0) boxhi = np.max(origins, axis=0) lipschitz = estimatelipschitz(fnp, boxlo, boxhi) else: lipschitz = hitmask # Assume hitmask passed as lipschitz for 'auto' logic in sources # Adjusted to match source signature: hitmask is actually the inclusion object or lipschitz # Re-mapping to source signature: tracerays(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, hitmask, inclusion, fnp, maxdepth, threshold, newtoniter, batchsize) pass # Simplified to match source signature exactly def runtrace(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, inclusion, fnp, maxdepth, threshold, newtoniter, batchsize): nrays = origins.shape[0] hits = np.full(nrays, False) hitdistances = np.full(nrays, np.inf) for start in range(0, nrays, batchsize): end = min(start + batchsize, nrays) active = np.ones(end - start, dtype=bool) curtmin = tmin[start:end].copy() curtmax = tmax[start:end].copy() for in range(maxdepth): if not np.any(active): break ptsmin = origins[start:end][active] + curtmin[active][:, None] directions[start:end][active] ptsmax = origins[start:end][active] + curtmax[active][:, None] directions[start:end][active] lo = np.minimum(ptsmin, ptsmax) hi = np.maximum(ptsmin, ptsmax) fmin, fmax = inclusion.evaluate(lo, hi) containszero = (fmin <= 0) & (fmax >= 0) active &= containszero if not np.any(active): break tmid = 0.5 (curtmin[active] + curtmax[active]) xmid = origins[start:end][active] + tmid[:, None] directions[start:end][active] fval = fnp(xmid) converged = np.abs(fval) < threshold hitindices = np.where(converged)[0] if len(hitindices) > 0: hits[start + hitindices] = True hitdistances[start + hitindices] = tmid[hitindices] nonconverged = ~converged active &= nonconverged if not np.any(active): break maskpos = fval[nonconverged] > 0 curtmax[active] = np.where(maskpos, tmid, curtmax[active]) curtmin[active] = np.where(maskpos, curtmin[active], tmid) # Newton refinement step # if newtoniter > 0: apply Newton steps to hits return hits, hitdistances return runtrace(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, hitmask, fnp, maxdepth, threshold, newtoniter, batchsize) Computes conservative bounds on f over spatial domains. Distinguishes itself by offering a configurable trade-off between generality and bound tightness, spanning sampling-based estimates to analytic arithmetic. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D \cdot C), where N is number of rays, D is max depth, and C is cost of function evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(N) for ray state and batch processing. Strengths: Robust against missing features due to interval pruning; configurable accuracy via Lipschitz constant. Limitations: Slower than standard bisection due to inclusion function evaluation; requires gradient computation for 'auto' Lipschitz estimation. When to Use: High-quality rendering of complex implicit surfaces where robustness is critical. When Not to Use: Real-time applications with strict latency constraints or simple surfaces where standard bisection suffices. name: Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies
head: InclusionFunction strategies
body: Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies compute conservative bounds on an implicit function f over a spatial domain, enabling the bisection trace to prune intervals that cannot contain the zero-level set. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods by providing a configurable trade-off between generality (black-box compatibility) and bound tightness (performance/accuracy), spanning sampling-based estimates to analytic arithmetic. Every strategy constructs a conservative interval f = [f-, f+] guaranteeing that f(\mathbf{x}) \in [f-, f+] for all \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{B}. This bound is used to determine if the zero-level set (isosurface) can exist within the box \mathcal{B}. If 0 \notin [f-, f+], the box is pruned. The strategies generally rely on a Lipschitz constant \lambda or symbolic derivatives to bound the function's rate of change. SamplingInclusion requires only point evaluations and relies on \lambda to bound variation over the box diameter. GradientInclusion improves tightness by incorporating \nabla f directly. NaturalIntervalInclusion and AffineInclusion operate on the symbolic formula of f to produce progressively tighter bounds without sampling. Computes a conservative upper bound \lambda on the rate of change of f over a 3D bounding box. Choose this when you need a scalar bound for gradient-based or sampling-based inclusion, particularly for black-box functions where analytical gradients are unavailable. Computes valid, conservative bounds for a scalar field along a ray using first-order linear approximations. It sets itself apart by using linear bounds rather than quadratic ones, prioritizing computational simplicity. Choose this for basic sphere tracing or when gradient access is limited to local estimates. The approach formalizes robust iso-surface rendering via interval-arithmetic bisection for arbitrary implicit geometries, primarily targeting black-box functions where only point evaluations are available. The isoray library implements four distinct strategies: SamplingInclusion, GradientInclusion, NaturalIntervalInclusion, and AffineInclusion. These strategies were developed to guarantee no surface features are missed (e.g., thin shells, cusps, high-frequency surfaces) while optimizing performance through tighter bounds when analytic formulas are known. When only point evaluations are available, SamplingInclusion or GradientInclusion must be used, as the analytic strategies require symbolic formula access. name: Lipschitz Constant Estimation
body:
Lipschitz Constant Estimation computes a conservative upper bound \lambda on the rate of change of an implicit function f over a 3D bounding box \mathcal{B}. This constant bounds the function's variation over the box diameter, allowing interval inclusion strategies to prune boxes where the zero-level set cannot exist. It differs from symbolic strategies by relying on numerical gradient sampling, making it applicable to black-box implicit functions where analytical gradients are unavailable. Inputs: Implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 ightarrow \mathbb{R}. Bounding box \mathcal{B} defined by center \mathbf{c} and half-extents \mathbf{r}. Sampling configuration (number of points N, step size h). Not given in the sources. Outputs: Lipschitz constant \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^+. Data Structures: Sample points \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=1}^N uniformly distributed within \mathcal{B}. Gradient estimates 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i). Steps: 1. Sample Domain: Generate N points uniformly distributed within \mathcal{B}. 2. Estimate Gradients: For each \mathbf{x}i, compute 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i) using centered differences with step h: 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i) \approx \left[  rac{f(\mathbf{x}i + h\mathbf{e}1) - f(\mathbf{x}i - h\mathbf{e}1)}{2h},  rac{f(\mathbf{x}i + h\mathbf{e}2) - f(\mathbf{x}i - h\mathbf{e}2)}{2h},  rac{f(\mathbf{x}i + h\mathbf{e}3) - f(\mathbf{x}i - h\mathbf{e}3)}{2h} ight], where \mathbf{e}k are unit basis vectors. 3. Compute Norms: Calculate the Euclidean norm of each gradient: gi = \|
abla f(\mathbf{x}i)\|2. 4. Determine Constant: Set \lambda = \maxi gi. Formulas: The theoretical Lipschitz constant is defined as Lip(f) = \max{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}}  rac{|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{y})|}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|}. In practice, \lambda is approximated by the maximum observed gradient magnitude over the sample set. Parameters: lipschitz: Can be a float value or the string "auto". If "auto", the constant is estimated automatically using the sampling method. N, h: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Finite difference gradients are sensitive to h; too small h introduces numerical noise, while too large h underestimates local curvature. Boundaries: Samples near the boundary of \mathcal{B} may require gradient evaluations outside the box; clamping or reflection may be needed to prevent out-of-bounds access. Degenerate Input: If f is constant, \lambda = 0. Non-Lipschitz functions with unbounded gradients require regularization or will produce excessively large estimates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimatelipschitz(f, boxcenter, boxhalfextents, numsamples=100, h=1e-4): """ Estimate the Lipschitz constant for implicit function f over a bounding box. Args: f: Implicit function f(x: np.ndarray) -> float boxcenter: np.ndarray of shape (3,), center of the bounding box boxhalfextents: np.ndarray of shape (3,), half-extents of the bounding box numsamples: int, number of random samples to take h: float, step size for finite differences Returns: float: Estimated Lipschitz constant lambda """ import numpy as np # 1. Sample points uniformly within the bounding box randompoints = np.random.rand(numsamples, 3) samples = boxcenter + (randompoints - 0.5) (2.0 boxhalfextents) maxgradientnorm = 0.0 basisvectors = np.eye(3) # 2. Estimate gradients and compute norms for i in range(numsamples): x = samples[i] gradient = np.zeros(3) for j in range(3): # Centered difference for each dimension xplus = x + h basisvectors[j] xminus = x - h basisvectors[j] # Evaluate function fplus = f(xplus) fminus = f(xminus) gradient[j] = (fplus - fminus) / (2.0 h) # Compute Euclidean norm gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(gradient) # Update maximum if gradnorm > maxgradientnorm: maxgradientnorm = gradnorm return maxgradientnorm Time Complexity: O(N \cdot d) where d=3, requiring 2d function evaluations per sample. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store sample points and gradients. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Black-box compatible; requires only point evaluations. Limitations: The estimate is an approximation and may not be tight, leading to less aggressive pruning than symbolic methods. Insufficient samples may underestimate \lambda, causing incorrect pruning or missed intersections. When to Use: When analytical derivatives are unavailable or too complex to derive. When Not to Use: When tight bounds are critical for performance and symbolic derivatives are available. In volume rendering, Lipschitz continuity is used in sphere tracing to determine safe step sizes along rays. The specific application to interval arithmetic inclusion strategies for implicit surface rendering is described in recent works on robust iso-surface rendering.
