name: Local Lipschitz Bound Computation for Hierarchical Implicit Models
head: Hierarchical Lipschitz Bound Computation, Tree-based Lipschitz Bound
body:
This method computes the local Lipschitz bound \lambda(\mathbf{e}) for a segment \mathbf{e} within a hierarchical construction tree of implicit primitives and operators. It solves the problem of determining safe stepping distances in enhanced sphere tracing (Segment Tracing) by providing a tight bound on the gradient magnitude, which allows for larger, safe steps along the ray compared to conservative global bounds. It is distinguished from its parent Lipschitz Constant Estimation by operating on the specific geometric structure of the implicit model (the construction tree) rather than sampling the bounding box, and from its children by handling general hierarchical operators (Boolean, blending, affine, deformation) rather than specific primitive types. Inputs: A hierarchical construction tree where leaves are compactly supported skeletal primitives and nodes are operators (Boolean, blending, affine, deformation). A ray segment \mathbf{e} defined by parameter interval [t, t+\epsilon], with center c and radius r = \|\mathbf{e}\|/2. The ray direction unit vector \mathbf{u}. Outputs: The local Lipschitz bound \lambda(\mathbf{e}) for the segment \mathbf{e}. Data Structures: Hierarchical Construction Tree: A tree structure where leaves are compactly supported skeletal primitives and internal nodes store operator types and pointers to child nodes. Method: The computation traverses the tree recursively. For a node, the bound is computed based on the operator type. If the primitive or deformation is complex, coarser bounds may be used. 1. Base Case (Leaf Primitive): Compute \lambda(\mathbf{e}) for the skeletal primitive using the product of two terms: \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \|g' \circ d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e})\| \|
abla d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\| where: g is the falloff filter function. d is the Euclidean distance to the skeleton. \delta(\mathbf{e}) represents the ray parameterization over the segment. \mathbf{u} is the ray direction unit vector. Falloff Bound (\|g' \circ d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e})\|): Compute the interval image of the distance d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}). Approximate the distance interval using the 1-Lipschitz property of distance functions: d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \subset [d(c) - r, d(c) + r] where c is the segment center and r = \|\mathbf{e}\|/2. Bound g' using Interval Analysis on this distance interval. Gradient Bound (\|
abla d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\|): General Case: Use the bound 1, since \|
abla d\| = 1 for Euclidean distance to a skeleton (1-Lipschitz) and \|\mathbf{u}\|=1: \|
abla d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\| \leq 1 Tighter Bound (Points, Spheres, Line Segments): Compute the closed-form image of 
abla d \circ \delta \cdot \mathbf{u} over the segment \mathbf{e}. For a point primitive with center c, 
abla d(p) = (p-c)/\|p-c\|. The image is the interval [|
abla d \circ \delta(t) \cdot \mathbf{u}|, |
abla d \circ \delta(t+\epsilon) \cdot \mathbf{u}|]. 2. Coarser Bounds (Complex Primitives/Deformations): If exact computation is difficult, use global bounds for the supporting ray \Delta or bounding sphere S \supset \mathbf{e}: \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(\Delta) \quad 	ext{and} \quad \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(S) where \lambda(\Delta) and \lambda(S) are the Lipschitz bounds of f over the entire ray and sphere respectively. 3. Internal Nodes (Operators): Compute bounds for children and combine based on operator type: Blending (Additive): f = fA + fB \lambda(\mathbf{e}) = \lambdaA(\mathbf{e}) + \lambdaB(\mathbf{e}) Boolean Union/Intersection (Max/Min): fU = \max(fA, fB), fI = \min(fA, fB) \lambda(\mathbf{e}) = \max(\lambdaA(\mathbf{e}), \lambdaB(\mathbf{e})) Pasko Union: fU = fA + fB + \sqrt{fA^2 + fB^2} \lambda(\mathbf{e}) = 2(\lambdaA(\mathbf{e}) + \lambdaB(\mathbf{e})) 4. Affine Transformations: Let fD = fN \circ a, where a is the affine transformation. Transform segment \mathbf{e} to \mathbf{e}' = a^{-1}(\mathbf{e}). For translation/rotation (1-Lipschitz): \lambdaD(\mathbf{e}) = \lambdaN(\mathbf{e}') For scaling by factor \alpha: \lambdaD(\mathbf{e}) =  rac{1}{\alpha} \lambdaN(\mathbf{e}') 5. Deformations: Let fW = fN \circ \omega^{-1}, where \omega is the warping function. The gradient is 
abla fW = 
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}, where \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} is the Jacobian matrix of the inverse warping function. Bound the Lipschitz constant by bounding the gradient norm and Jacobian norm: \|
abla fW\| \leq \|
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1}\| \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}\| Compute two local bounds for the transformed segment \mathbf{e}' = \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{e}): 1. Bound of the norm of the gradient \|
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{e}')\|. 2. Bound of the norm of the Jacobian \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}(\mathbf{e}')\|. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computelipschitzbound(node, segmente, raydirectionu): """ Computes the local Lipschitz bound lambda(e) for a segment e in a hierarchical tree. """ if node.isleaf(): return computeprimitivelipschitz(node.primitive, segmente, raydirectionu) operatortype = node.operatortype lambdaleft = computelipschitzbound(node.leftchild, segmente, raydirectionu) lambdaright = computelipschitzbound(node.rightchild, segmente, raydirectionu) if operatortype == "BLEND": return lambdaleft + lambdaright elif operatortype in ["BOOLEANUNION", "BOOLEANINTERSECTION"]: return max(lambdaleft, lambdaright) elif operatortype == "PASKOUNION": return 2 (lambdaleft + lambdaright) elif operatortype == "AFFINE": segmenteprime = node.affinetransform.inversetransform(segmente) childbound = computelipschitzbound(node.child, segmenteprime, raydirectionu) alpha = node.affinetransform.getscalingfactor() return childbound / alpha elif operatortype == "DEFORMATION": segmenteprime = node.warpingfunction.inversetransform(segmente) lambdagrad = computelipschitzbound(node.child, segmenteprime, raydirectionu) # Sources do not specify the exact Jacobian norm computation for arbitrary warping functions. lambdajacobian = computejacobiannormbound(node.warpingfunction, segmenteprime) return lambdagrad lambdajacobian else: # Fallback to coarser bounds if operator type is not explicitly handled # Sources do not specify the exact fallback mechanism. return 1.0 def computeprimitivelipschitz(primitive, segmente, raydirectionu): """ Computes the Lipschitz bound for a leaf skeletal primitive. lambda(e) <= ||g' o d o delta(e)|| ||grad(d) o delta(e). u|| """ # 1. Falloff Bound: ||g' o d o delta(e)|| dcenter = primitive.distance(segmente.center) r = segmente.radius distanceintervalmin = dcenter - r distanceintervalmax = dcenter + r # Standard interval arithmetic evaluation of the falloff derivative g' over the interval falloffbound = max(abs(primitive.gprime(distanceintervalmin)), abs(primitive.gprime(distanceintervalmax))) # 2. Gradient Bound: ||grad(d) o delta(e). u|| if primitive.type == "POINT": pstart = segmente.startpoint pend = segmente.endpoint graddotustart = abs(dot(primitive.gradient(pstart), raydirectionu)) graddotuend = abs(dot(primitive.gradient(pend), raydirectionu)) gradientbound = max(graddotustart, graddotuend) else: gradientbound = 1.0 return falloffbound gradientbound def computejacobiannormbound(warpingfunction, segmente): # Sources do not specify the exact Jacobian norm computation for arbitrary warping functions. return 1.0 Parameters: Typical falloff functions: Wyvill's C^1 sextic, Wyvill's C^2 sextic, C^1 quartic. Scaling factor \alpha for affine transformations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Primitives/Deformations: Exact computation of \lambda(\mathbf{e}) may be very complex. Use coarser bounds \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(\Delta) and \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(S) to ensure correctness and efficiency. Distance Interval Approximation: The approximation d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \subset [d(c) - r, d(c) + r] relies on the 1-Lipschitz property of distance. This is valid but may be loose for complex skeletons. Gradient Bound Tightness: The general bound of 1 for \|
abla d \circ \delta \cdot \mathbf{u}\| is not accurate. Compute closed-form expressions for points, spheres, or line segments to obtain tighter bounds, especially when the ray is orthogonal to the gradient. This method computes the local Lipschitz bound \lambda for skeletal primitives by evaluating the maximum absolute value of the derivative of the falloff filter function g(x) over a specific interval [a, b]. It solves the problem of determining safe stepping distances in enhanced sphere tracing by providing a tight bound on the gradient magnitude, which allows for larger, safe steps along the ray compared to conservative global bounds. It is distinguished from generic interval arithmetic strategies by relying on closed-form analytical solutions for specific standard falloff functions, avoiding numerical approximation errors. Time Complexity: Depends on tree traversal depth and primitive/operator complexity. Coarser bounds are used for complex primitives/deformations to reduce computation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Reduces the number of field function queries (#f) and accelerates Segment Tracing compared to Sphere Tracing, which necessitates many smaller steps. Strengths: Local bounds are significantly smaller than global bounds, reducing queries and accelerating Segment Tracing. The structure implicitly implements a bounding volume hierarchy for efficient pruning during evaluation. Limitations: Exact computation is complex for some primitives or deformation operators. Requires interval analysis for falloff functions. When to Use: When rendering hierarchical implicit models with skeletal primitives and deformations, and when Segment Tracing is employed. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Described in "Segment Tracing Using Local Lipschitz Bounds". Adapts to hierarchical function representations such as procedurally defined scalar fields [RMD11] or function representations [PASS95]. name: Lipschitz Bound Computation for Skeletal Primitives
head: Falloff Filter Function Lipschitz Bound Computation
body: This method computes the local Lipschitz bound \lambda for skeletal primitives by evaluating the maximum absolute value of the derivative of the falloff filter function g(x) over a specific interval [a, b]. It solves the problem of determining safe stepping distances in enhanced sphere tracing by providing a tight bound on the gradient magnitude, which allows for larger, safe steps along the ray compared to conservative global bounds. It is distinguished from generic interval arithmetic strategies by relying on closed-form analytical solutions for specific standard falloff functions, avoiding numerical approximation errors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The falloff filter function g(x), the interval [a, b] representing the normalized distance range along the ray segment. Output: The Lipschitz bound \lambda, defined as \max{x \in [a,b]} |g'(x)|. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method relies on pre-computed analytical roots and derivative formulas for specific primitive types. Steps: 1. Identify the falloff function type (Wyvill, Quadric, or Blobs). 2. Compute the root x^0 of the second-order derivative g''(x) = 0 within the unit interval [0, 1]. 3. Determine the bound \lambda based on the position of x^0 relative to the input interval [a, b]: If a \geq 1, then \lambda = 0. If x^0 \in [a, b], then \lambda = |g'(x^0)|. Otherwise, \lambda = \max(|g'(a)|, |g'(b)|). Formulas: For all functions, g(x) is defined for x < 1 and 0 otherwise. The derivatives are evaluated as follows: Wyvill Function: g(x) = (1 - x^2)^3 g'(x) = -6x(1-x^2)^2 g''(x) = -6(1-x^2)(1-5x^2) Root: x^0 = 1/\sqrt{5}. Bound: \lambda0 = 96\sqrt{5}/125 \leq 1.72. Quadric Function: g(x) = (1 - x^2)^2 g'(x) = -4x(1-x^2) g''(x) = -4(1-3x^2) Root: x^0 = 1/\sqrt{3}. Bound: \lambda0 = 8\sqrt{3}/9 \leq 1.54. Blobs Function: g(x) = -\frac{4}{9}x^6 + \frac{17}{9}x^4 - \frac{22}{9}x^2 + 1 g'(x) = -\frac{4}{9}x(x^2 - 1)(6x^2 - 11) g''(x) = -\frac{4}{9}(30x^4 - 51x^2 + 11) Root: x^0 = \frac{51 - \sqrt{1281}}{2\sqrt{15}}. Bound: \lambda0 = (17\sqrt{1281} + 453)\sqrt{\frac{17}{2278125} - \frac{\sqrt{1281}}{6834375}} \leq 1.59. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computelipschitzboundwyvill(a, b): if a >= 1: return 0.0 xstar = 1.0 / math.sqrt(5.0) lambdastar = 96.0 math.sqrt(5.0) / 125.0 if a <= xstar <= b: return lambdastar else: def gprime(x): return abs(-6.0 x (1.0 - xx)2) return max(gprime(a), gprime(b)) def computelipschitzboundquadric(a, b): if a >= 1: return 0.0 xstar = 1.0 / math.sqrt(3.0) lambdastar = 8.0 math.sqrt(3.0) / 9.0 if a <= xstar <= b: return lambdastar else: def gprime(x): return abs(-4.0 x (1.0 - xx)) return max(gprime(a), gprime(b)) def computelipschitzboundblobs(a, b): if a >= 1: return 0.0 sqrt1281 = math.sqrt(1281.0) sqrt15 = math.sqrt(15.0) xstar = (51.0 - sqrt1281) / (2.0 sqrt15) term1 = 17.0 sqrt1281 + 453.0 term2 = 17.0 / 2278125.0 - sqrt1281 / 6834375.0 lambdastar = term1 math.sqrt(term2) if a <= xstar <= b: return lambdastar else: def gprime(x): return abs((-4.0/9.0) x (xx - 1.0) (6.0xx - 11.0)) return max(gprime(a), gprime(b)) Parameters: None. The method is deterministic based on the function type. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If a \geq 1, the bound is exactly 0, as the falloff function is 0 and its derivative is 0 outside the unit interval. Floating-point precision in evaluating g'(x) near boundaries should be handled carefully, though the analytical forms are stable. The root x^0 must be checked against the interval [a, b] correctly; if the interval does not contain the peak of the derivative, the maximum occurs at one of the endpoints. Computes the local Lipschitz bound \lambda(e) for a segment e within a hierarchical construction tree. This method provides the component-wise bound for skeletal primitives used within that larger hierarchical context. It is chosen when skeletal primitives are combined with other implicit operators in a construction tree, as it supplies the tight per-primitive gradient bounds required for the parent's hierarchical aggregation. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. The computation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the constants for the specific function type. Strengths: Provides tight, accurate bounds that enable larger stepping distances in sphere tracing, reducing the number of field function queries. It avoids the overhead of numerical root-finding or interval arithmetic propagation for these specific primitives. Limitations: Only applicable to skeletal primitives with the specific falloff functions defined (Wyvill, Quadric, Blobs). Not applicable to arbitrary implicit functions. When to use: When using enhanced sphere tracing with skeletal primitives and needing to optimize ray marching steps. When not to use: For non-skeletal primitives or when the falloff function does not match the predefined analytical forms. The method originates from the analysis of falloff filter functions used in soft object rendering. The Wyvill function was introduced by Wyvill in 1986. The Quadric function is a standard C^1 variant. The Blobs function, described in [WMW86], modifies the quadric to satisfy specific boundary conditions. The specific Lipschitz bound computation for these functions was detailed in the context of segment tracing using local Lipschitz bounds. name: Forward Linear Inclusion Function
head: Linear Bounding Function, Linear Inclusion Function
body: The Forward Linear Inclusion Function computes a conservative interval bound for a scalar field f along a ray, ensuring that the true function value lies within the calculated bounds for all points ahead of the current sample. It solves the problem of determining a safe maximum step size for sphere tracing by intersecting these linear bounds with the zero-level threshold. Inputs and Outputs Input: The current sample location on the ray t0, the function value at that location f(t0), and the Lipschitz constant \lambda for the function f. Output: An interval f = [f-(t), f+(t)] for t > t0, and the computed step size \Delta t to the next safe sample point. Data Structures The method requires no complex data structures; it operates on scalar values for t0, f(t0), and \lambda. Steps 1. Evaluate Function: Compute the scalar field value v = f(t0) at the current ray position t0. 2. Define Bounds: Construct the lower bound f-(t) and upper bound f+(t) as linear functions starting from v at t0. The slope of the upper bound is \lambda and the lower bound is -\lambda. f-(t) = f(t0) - \lambda(t - t0) f+(t) = f(t0) + \lambda(t - t0) This forms a bounding cone originating at (t0, f(t0)). 3. Compute Step Size: Determine the distance to the zero-level set by finding the intersection of the bounding lines with the threshold. Since the bounds are symmetric around f(t0), the step size is determined by the magnitude of the function value divided by the Lipschitz constant: \Delta t = \frac{|f(t0)|}{\lambda} If f(t0) = 0, the surface is hit exactly, and \Delta t = 0. 4. Advance Ray: Update the ray position to t{\text{new}} = t0 + \Delta t. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardlinearinclusionstep(f, t0, lambdaval): """ Computes the next step size for sphere tracing using forward linear inclusion. Args: f: A callable that evaluates the scalar field f(t) at position t. t0: The current position on the ray (scalar). lambdaval: The Lipschitz constant for f (scalar, >= 0). Returns: deltat: The safe step size to advance along the ray. """ # Evaluate the scalar field at the current position ft0 = f(t0) # Handle exact hit if ft0 == 0.0: return 0.0 # Compute step size: distance to zero crossing of the linear bound # The bound is f(t0) +/- lambda (t - t0) # Intersection with 0: 0 = f(t0) + lambda (t - t0) => t - t0 = -f(t0)/lambda # We take the absolute value for the forward step size deltat = abs(ft0) / lambdaval return deltat Parameters \lambda: The Lipschitz constant, which must be an upper bound on the magnitude of the gradient of f (\|\nabla f\| \leq \lambda). Typical values depend on the specific noise or implicit function being rendered. If \lambda is too small, the bound is invalid and the ray may tunnel through the surface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Lipschitz Constant: If \lambda = 0 and f(t0) \neq 0, division by zero occurs. Implementers should check for \lambda < \epsilon and handle it as an error or infinite step. Inaccurate Lipschitz Constant: The method assumes \lambda is a valid global or local Lipschitz constant. If the actual gradient exceeds \lambda, the inclusion property is violated, leading to visual artifacts (tunneling). Precision: For very small |f(t0)|, floating-point precision errors in the division may result in tiny step sizes. A minimum step size threshold may be applied to prevent infinite loops in flat regions. Uses second-order Taylor expansion to provide tighter bounds for functions with significant curvature, switching to linear bounds when the quadratic derivative exceeds the first-order limit. Choose this when the scalar field has high curvature and \lambda is large relative to the second derivative, allowing for larger steps than the linear method. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(1) per step. The calculation involves one function evaluation, one absolute value, and one division. Memory: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the scalar values. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and provides a rigorous guarantee of no tunneling if \lambda is valid. Limitations: The bounds are often loose for functions with high curvature, leading to smaller step sizes than necessary. It does not account for the second derivative of the function. When to Use Use when computational resources are limited or when the scalar field is relatively linear over the step size. It is also useful as a fallback or comparison baseline for more complex inclusion functions. The concept of forward inclusion functions was formalized in the context of sphere tracing for procedural volumetric noise. The specific formulation of the forward linear inclusion function is attributed to [AZ23] as cited in. It builds upon the general theory of interval arithmetic and Lipschitz continuity applied to ray marching. name: Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function
head: Hybrid quadratic-linear bound, Improved Quad. Bounds, Improved Quadratic Taylor
body: The Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function is a method for computing tighter, valid bounds on a scalar field function f(t) along a ray, used to determine safe step sizes in sphere tracing. It solves the problem where standard quadratic bounds violate the first-order Lipschitz constraint, causing the bound to grow too fast and result in smaller, inefficient step sizes than linear bounds. It sets itself apart by enforcing both first-order (\lambda) and second-order (\gamma) Lipschitz constraints simultaneously, switching to a linear bound when the quadratic derivative exceeds the first-order limit. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current ray parameter t0, function value f(t0), first derivative f'(t0), first-order Lipschitz constant \lambda, second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma. Output: Inclusion function f{\pm}(t) providing lower (f-) and upper (f+) bounds for t > t0. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the method relies on scalar arithmetic operations. Formulas: The improved inclusion function f{\pm}(t) is defined piecewise using a quadratic component q{\pm}(t) and a switch point t{\pm}: q{\pm}(t) = f(t0) + (t - t0) \cdot \left( f'(t0) \pm \frac{1}{2}\gamma(t - t0) \right) t{\pm} = t0 + \frac{\pm\lambda - f'(t0)}{\pm\gamma} The final bound is: f{\pm}(t) = \begin{cases} q{\pm}(t) & \forall t \in [t0, t{\pm}] \\ q{\pm}(t{\pm}) \pm \lambda \cdot (t - t{\pm}) & \forall t > t{\pm} \end{cases} Parameters: \lambda: First-order Lipschitz constant. \gamma: Second-order Lipschitz constant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def improvedquadraticinclusion(t0, ft0, fprimet0, lambdaval, gammaval): """ Computes the improved quadratic inclusion bounds for t > t0. Args: t0: Current ray parameter. ft0: Function value at t0. fprimet0: First derivative at t0. lambdaval: First-order Lipschitz constant. gammaval: Second-order Lipschitz constant. Returns: A function that takes t and returns (lowerbound, upperbound). """ # Calculate switch points for upper and lower bounds # tplus = t0 + (lambda - fprime) / gamma # tminus = t0 + (-lambda - fprime) / (-gamma) = t0 + (lambda + fprime) / gamma tplus = t0 + (lambdaval - fprimet0) / gammaval tminus = t0 + (lambdaval + fprimet0) / gammaval def bound(t): if t <= t0: return ft0, ft0 # Calculate quadratic components # qplus(t) = f(t0) + (t - t0) (f'(t0) + 0.5 gamma (t - t0)) # qminus(t) = f(t0) + (t - t0) (f'(t0) - 0.5 gamma (t - t0)) dt = t - t0 qplus = ft0 + dt (fprimet0 + 0.5 gammaval dt) qminus = ft0 + dt (fprimet0 - 0.5 gammaval dt) # Determine if we are past the switch point for upper bound if t > tplus: # Switch to linear bound # fplus(t) = qplus(tplus) + lambda (t - tplus) dtswitch = tplus - t0 qplusatswitch = ft0 + dtswitch (fprimet0 + 0.5 gammaval dtswitch) upper = qplusatswitch + lambdaval (t - tplus) else: upper = qplus # Determine if we are past the switch point for lower bound if t > tminus: # Switch to linear bound # fminus(t) = qminus(tminus) - lambda (t - tminus) dtswitch = tminus - t0 qminusatswitch = ft0 + dtswitch (fprimet0 - 0.5 gammaval dtswitch) lower = qminusatswitch - lambdaval (t - tminus) else: lower = qminus return lower, upper return bound Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard quadratic bounds that do not enforce the first-order Lipschitz constraint, potentially leading to loose bounds. Use when \gamma is small and \lambda is not a limiting factor. Time and Memory Complexity: The computational cost is the same as regular quadratic inclusion functions. Measured Performance: On the Sponge scene with all enhancements (SS, ES+1): Both Regular Quad and Improved Quad achieve 70.0 avg steps, 651.1 avg octaves, and 16.3 ms time, providing a \times 4.0 speedup vs Linear. On Sponge (far) scene with all enhancements (SS, ES+1): Regular Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.8 ms time. Improved Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.7 ms time. Both provide a \times 1.7 speedup vs Linear. Without enhancements, improved quadratic bounds allow \times 1.2 and \times 1.1 reduction in steps compared to naive methods, beating linear and regular quadratic bounds, but are slightly slower than linear bounds due to gradient computation overhead. When used with enhancements (Adaptive \gammaFn), the improved quadratic bound gives results similar to regular quadratic bounds, with performance gains too small to appear in tables. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Prevents the quadratic term from growing too fast by enforcing the first-order Lipschitz constraint, yielding bigger step sizes than regular quadratic bounds when the derivative would otherwise exceed \lambda. Limitations: Requires gradient computation, making it slightly slower than linear bounds in naive contexts. When to Use: Use when tighter bounds than linear are needed and the second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma is available, especially when regular quadratic bounds might violate the first-order constraint. The Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function was proposed to address the suboptimal performance of regular quadratic inclusion functions, which can perform worse than linear bounds because their derivative can exceed the first-order Lipschitz constant \lambda. It was introduced in the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". name: Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions
head: 2nd order Taylor bounds, Naive Quadratic Bounds, Quadratic bounds, Regular Quad. Bounds, Regular Quadratic Taylor Bounds
body: Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions (QTIF) are a method for adapting step size in sphere tracing by using quadratic forward inclusion bounds instead of linear ones, explicitly taking the ray direction into account. They require the function derivative to be computable on the fly and Lipschitz continuous. Without enhancements, they often perform worse than linear bounds due to the overhead of computing gradients and the exponential growth of the second-order Lipschitz constant in fractal Brownian motion (FBM). Inputs: Current position along the ray, t0. Function value at current position, Fn(t0). First derivative (gradient in ray direction) at current position, Fn'(t0). Second-order Lipschitz constant for the function sum, \gamma{Fn}. Target isosurface value (typically 0 or v). Outputs: Maximum safe step size \Delta t such that the inclusion function does not cross the isosurface threshold within the step. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar values for t0, Fn(t0), Fn'(t0), and \gamma{Fn}. \gamma{Fn} is computed as the sum of individual second-order Lipschitz constants of the constituent functions (octaves). Formulas: The forward quadratic Taylor inclusion function for a sum of functions Fn from position t0 is defined as: Fn = Fn(t0) + (t - t0) \left( Fn'(t0) \pm \frac{1}{2} \gamma{Fn} \cdot (t - t0) \right) Where: t is the candidate position along the ray. Fn(t0) is the value of the implicit function at the current step. Fn'(t0) is the derivative of the function in the ray direction at t0, calculated as \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla f(\boldsymbol{\delta}(t0)), where \mathbf{u} is the ray direction and \nabla f is the spatial gradient. \gamma{Fn} is the second-order Lipschitz constant of the sum Fn. For a sum of n functions fm, it is the sum of their individual constants: \gamma{Fn} = \sum{m=1}^n \gamma{fm}. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Compute Gradient: Calculate the first derivative Fn'(t0) by evaluating the gradient of the implicit function at the current position t0 and projecting it onto the ray direction \mathbf{u}. 2. Compute Lipschitz Constant: Determine \gamma{Fn} by summing the second-order Lipschitz constants of the active octaves. 3. Solve for Intersection: Find the smallest positive t > t0 where the inclusion function Fn intersects the target isosurface value V{target} (usually 0). The equation to solve is: V{target} = Fn(t0) + (t - t0) \left( Fn'(t0) \pm \frac{1}{2} \gamma{Fn} (t - t0) \right) Let \Delta t = t - t0. This is a quadratic equation in \Delta t: \frac{1}{2} \gamma{Fn} (\Delta t)^2 + Fn'(t0) \Delta t + (Fn(t0) - V{target}) = 0 The \pm in the inclusion function creates two bounds; the safe step size is determined by the bound that prevents crossing the surface. 4. Update Position: Set t{new} = t0 + \Delta t. 5. Sub-stepping (Optional/Advanced): If using sub-steps to improve accuracy or handle BVH levels, estimate the derivative at the new location t0 + \Delta t using the worst-case scenario for the derivative change: F'i(t0 + \Delta t) = F'i(t0) + (\gammai \cdot \Delta t) Then add the next derivative term f'{i+1}(t0 + \Delta t) to compute the new quadratic bound for the next sub-step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def quadratictaylorstep(t0, Fnt0, Fnprimet0, gammaFn, targetvalue): """ Computes the maximum safe step size using Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions. Args: t0: Current position along the ray. Fnt0: Value of the implicit function at t0. Fnprimet0: Derivative of the function in ray direction at t0. gammaFn: Second-order Lipschitz constant for the function sum. targetvalue: The isosurface value (e.g., 0). Returns: deltat: The maximum safe step size. """ # Coefficients for the quadratic equation: a(dt^2) + bdt + c = 0 # Derived from: target = F(t0) + dt (F'(t0) + 0.5 gamma dt) # Rearranged: 0.5 gamma dt^2 + F'(t0) dt + (F(t0) - target) = 0 a = 0.5 gammaFn b = Fnprimet0 c = Fnt0 - targetvalue # Handle degenerate case where gamma is 0 (linear behavior) if a == 0: if b == 0: # Function is constant, no root found or infinite roots. return 1e-6 else: # Linear case: bdt + c = 0 dt = -c / b return dt if dt > 0 else 1e-6 # Solve quadratic equation discriminant = b2 - 4 a c if discriminant < 0: # No real roots. The inclusion function does not cross the target. return 1e6 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) # We want the smallest positive root # Roots are (-b +/- sqrtdisc) / (2a) root1 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) root2 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) # Select the smallest positive root candidates = [] if root1 > 1e-9: candidates.append(root1) if root2 > 1e-9: candidates.append(root2) if not candidates: # No positive root found. return 1e6 return min(candidates) Parameters: \gamma{Fn}: Must be pre-computed or estimated. For FBM, this grows exponentially with the number of octaves n (\gamma{noise} \cdot (2^n - 1)). Target Value: Typically 0 for distance fields, or v for other implicit surfaces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exponential Growth of \gamma: For Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM), \gamma{Fn} grows exponentially with the number of octaves n. This makes the quadratic term \frac{1}{2} \gamma{Fn} (t-t0)^2 dominate quickly, leading to very small step sizes and poor performance. Gradient Cost: Requires computing f'(t) (the gradient projected on the ray) at each step, which is more expensive than just evaluating f(t). Lipschitz Continuity: Requires f'(t) to be Lipschitz continuous. If the derivative is not Lipschitz continuous, the bound is invalid. Performance: Without enhancements (like BVH or improved bounds), regular quadratic bounds result in worse step sizes (more steps) and added overhead, causing slowdowns (e.g., \times 0.6 and \times 0.4 on test scenes) compared to linear bounds. An improved inclusion function that enforces constraints from both first-order (\lambda) and second-order (\gamma) Lipschitz constants. It behaves as a regular quadratic bound as long as its derivative is within [-\lambda, \lambda], switching to a linear bound otherwise to prevent the quadratic term from growing too fast and providing loose bounds. Link A simpler inclusion function using only the first derivative and a first-order Lipschitz constant. It is less accurate for curved surfaces but cheaper to compute and does not suffer from the exponential \gamma growth in the same way. Link Time Complexity: O(1) per step for the bound calculation itself, but requires computing the gradient Fn'(t0), which is O(n) for n octaves if computed naively, or optimized via BVH. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per step. Measured Performance: On the "Sponge" scene without enhancements, Regular Quad bounds have 599.9 avg steps, 8969.0 avg octaves, and 181.8 ms time, resulting in a \times 0.6 slowdown vs Linear bounds. On the "Sponge (far)" scene, they have 416.6 avg steps, 4671.5 avg octaves, and 96.2 ms time, resulting in a \times 0.4 slowdown vs Linear bounds. Scaling: Performance degrades significantly with the number of octaves in FBM due to the exponential growth of \gamma{Fn}. Strengths: Provides tighter bounds for grazing rays compared to linear bounds when the function is smooth and \gamma is small. Can significantly reduce step count when combined with enhancements like BVH and sub-stepping (e.g., \times 4.0 speedup over linear bounds with enhancements). Limitations: High computational overhead for gradient calculation. Inefficient for high-frequency noise (FBM) without enhancements due to large \gamma. When to use: When high accuracy is needed for grazing rays and the function's derivative is cheap to compute and has a small Lipschitz constant. Best used with enhancements like BVH and sub-stepping. When not to use: For simple FBM without enhancements, or when gradient computation is prohibitively expensive. Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions were introduced by Aydinlilar et al. in the context of fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise. The method leverages the quadratic Taylor expansion to create forward inclusion functions that bound the implicit function's value along a ray. name: Bisection Ray Tracing with Interval Inclusion
head: Fast and robust ray intersection with arbitrary implicits, Interval/Affine Arithmetic Ray Tracing, IsoRay bisection tracer, Robust Ray Intersection with Arbitrary Implicits, Self-validated arithmetic ray tracing
body: Bisection Ray Tracing with Interval Inclusion is a robust ray-surface intersection algorithm that guarantees finding the nearest intersection of an implicit surface with a ray without missing fine features. It solves the problem of precision loss and feature skipping inherent in fixed-step ray marching by using interval arithmetic to prune intervals that cannot contain a root, followed by bisection to narrow down the interval containing the sign change of the implicit function f. Unlike standard bisection which processes rays independently, this method processes rays in batches and uses front-to-back pruning to discard intervals that are behind already found hits, improving efficiency for scenes with multiple surfaces or occlusion. It builds on Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection by providing a specific batched, interval-arithmetic-based implementation strategy. Inputs: origins: Array of shape (R, 3), ray origins. directions: Array of shape (R, 3), ray directions (normalized). tmin: Array of shape (R), near plane distances. tmax: Array of shape (R), far plane distances. hitmask: Boolean array of shape (R), rays that intersect the bounding volume. inclusion: An inclusion function object (e.g., SamplingInclusion) capable of evaluating bounds on the implicit field f over an interval [t{lo}, t{hi}]. f: The implicit surface function. maxdepth: Maximum number of bisection iterations allowed per ray. Default value is 40. threshold: The convergence width threshold for the bisection interval. Default value is 10^{-5}. Outputs: result: A TraceResult dataclass containing: hit: Boolean array (R), true if a surface was found. t: Float64 array (R), distance to the closest hit. position: Float64 array (R, 3), hit position (origin + t \cdot direction). normal: Float64 array (R, 3), surface normal (zeros if not hit). depthcount: Int32 array (R), number of bisection steps taken. tlo: Float64 array (R), lower bound of the final interval. thi: Float64 array (R), upper bound of the final interval. Data Structures: The algorithm maintains active intervals for rays. Key arrays include: rayidx: Indices of active rays. ivtlo: Lower bounds of intervals for active rays. ivthi: Upper bounds of intervals for active rays. resultt: Array storing the closest hit distance found so far for each ray (initialized to tmax or a large value). resulthit: Boolean array tracking if a hit has been recorded. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize resultt with tmax (or a large value) for all rays. Initialize resulthit to False. Initialize resultdepth to 0. Identify valid rays: validray = hitmask. Set initial intervals: ivtlo = tmin, ivthi = tmax for valid rays. rayidx contains indices of valid rays. 2. Bisection Loop: While len(rayidx) > 0 and current depth < maxdepth: a. Front-to-Back Pruning: Remove intervals that are entirely beyond the closest known hit. keep = ivtlo[rayidx] < resultt[rayidx]. Update rayidx, ivtlo, ivthi using the keep mask. If len(rayidx) == 0, break loop. b. Clip Far End: Ensure intervals do not extend past the closest known hit. ivthi[rayidx] = min(ivthi[rayidx], resultt[rayidx]). c. Interval Evaluation & Sign Change Detection: For each active interval [t{lo}, t{hi}], use the inclusion function to compute bounds on f(t). Identify intervals where the sign change occurs (i.e., the interval bounds contain 0, or f(t{lo}) and f(t{hi}) have opposite signs, depending on the specific inclusion function implementation). signchange = inclusion.containszero(ivtlo[rayidx], ivthi[rayidx]). validray = rayidx[signchange]. validtlo = ivtlo[signchange]. validthi = ivthi[signchange]. If no sign changes, break loop (no more hits to find). d. Convergence Check: Check if interval width is below threshold: converged = (validthi - validtlo) < threshold. The loop terminates when (t{hi} - t{lo}) < threshold. If converged, record hit: resulthit[validray] = True. resultt[validray] = (validtlo + validthi) 0.5. resulttlo[validray] = validtlo. resultthi[validray] = validthi. resultdepth[validray] = depth + 1. Mark these rays as converged to remove them from further bisection. e. Bisect Step: For non-converged valid rays: tmid = (validtlo + validthi) 0.5. Create new intervals: newrayidx = [validray, validray]. newtlo = [validtlo, tmid]. newthi = [tmid, validthi]. Update ivtlo, ivthi, rayidx with these new intervals. Increment depth. 3. Post-Processing (Optional Newton Refinement): For rays marked as hit, optional Newton refinement can be applied to converge the hit point to machine precision. This involves evaluating f and its gradient \nabla f at the hit position and iterating t{new} = t{old} - f(t{old}) / (\nabla f(t{old}) \cdot direction). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class TraceResult: hit: np.ndarray t: np.ndarray position: np.ndarray normal: np.ndarray depthcount: np.ndarray tlo: np.ndarray thi: np.ndarray def bisecttrace(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, hitmask, inclusion, f, maxdepth=40, threshold=1e-5): R = len(origins) resultt = np.full(R, np.inf) resulthit = np.zeros(R, dtype=bool) resulttlo = np.zeros(R) resultthi = np.zeros(R) resultdepth = np.zeros(R, dtype=np.int32) # Active intervals rayidx = np.where(hitmask)[0] ivtlo = tmin[rayidx] ivthi = tmax[rayidx] for depth in range(maxdepth): if len(rayidx) == 0: break # Front-to-back pruning: remove intervals beyond closest hit keep = ivtlo < resultt[rayidx] rayidx = rayidx[keep] ivtlo = ivtlo[keep] ivthi = ivthi[keep] if len(rayidx) == 0: break # Clip far end to closest hit ivthi = np.minimum(ivthi, resultt[rayidx]) # Evaluate inclusion function for sign change signchange = inclusion.containszero(ivtlo, ivthi) validray = rayidx[signchange] validtlo = ivtlo[signchange] validthi = ivthi[signchange] if len(validray) == 0: break # Check convergence converged = (validthi - validtlo) < threshold # Record hits for converged intervals hitindices = validray[converged] if len(hitindices) > 0: midt = (validtlo[converged] + validthi[converged]) 0.5 resulthit[hitindices] = True resultt[hitindices] = midt resulttlo[hitindices] = validtlo[converged] resultthi[hitindices] = validthi[converged] resultdepth[hitindices] = depth + 1 # Prepare next iteration for non-converged intervals notconverged = ~converged if np.any(notconverged): validraync = validray[notconverged] validtlonc = validtlo[notconverged] validthinc = validthi[notconverged] tmid = (validtlonc + validthinc) 0.5 # Concatenate new intervals newrayidx = np.concatenate([validraync, validraync]) newtlo = np.concatenate([validtlonc, tmid]) newthi = np.concatenate([tmid, validthinc]) # Update active intervals rayidx = newrayidx ivtlo = newtlo ivthi = newthi else: rayidx = np.array([], dtype=int) # Compute positions positions = origins + resultt[:, np.newaxis] directions # Compute normals using centered finite differences normals = np.zeroslike(directions) hitpositions = positions[resulthit] if len(hitpositions) > 0: eps = 1e-6 grad = np.zeroslike(hitpositions) for i in range(3): offset = np.zeroslike(hitpositions) offset[:, i] = eps fpos, = f(hitpositions + offset) fneg, = f(hitpositions - offset) grad[:, i] = (fpos - fneg) / (2 eps) norms = np.linalg.norm(grad, axis=1, keepdims=True) norms = np.maximum(norms, 1e-12) normals[resulthit] = grad / norms return TraceResult( hit=resulthit, t=resultt, position=positions, normal=normals, depthcount=resultdepth, tlo=resulttlo, thi=resultthi) Parameters: maxdepth: Maximum number of bisection iterations allowed per ray. Default value is 40. threshold: The convergence width threshold for the bisection interval. The loop terminates when (t{hi} - t{lo}) < threshold. Default value is 10^{-5}. batchsize: Number of rays to process per batch. None processes all rays at once. Positive integer splits rays into batches to limit peak memory usage. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision/Convergence: The algorithm uses a threshold (default 10^{-5}) to determine convergence. If the interval width is below this threshold, the ray is considered converged and removed from further processing. Smooth Blends: Reduced efficiency in the presence of shapes with many smooth blends, as interval evaluations may remain wide for many iterations. Self-Intersection: The algorithm handles self-intersecting surfaces (e.g., Whitney Umbrella) by finding the nearest intersection. Splits ray tracing into batches to limit peak memory usage. Processes each batch independently and merges results. If batchsize is None or \ge R, process all rays in a single call to bisecttrace. Otherwise, loop over start in range(0, R, batchsize), end = min(start + batchsize, R). Slice origins, directions, tmin, tmax, hitmask. Call bisecttrace on the slice. Apply Newton refinement if newtoniter > 0. Merge results into global result arrays. Parameter: batchsize: Number of rays to process per batch. None processes all rays at once. Positive integer splits rays into batches. Time Complexity: O(R \cdot D), where R is the number of rays and D is the average number of bisection steps. Each step involves interval evaluation and bisection. Memory Complexity: O(R) for storing active intervals and results. Batched processing reduces peak memory usage to O(B), where B is the batch size. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays. Batched processing allows handling larger scenes with limited memory. Strengths: Guarantees no surface features are missed, unlike fixed-step ray marching which can skip thin features or high-frequency detail. Robust for arbitrary function-based field definitions. Limitations: Reduced efficiency in the presence of shapes with many smooth blends. Interval arithmetic can be computationally expensive compared to direct evaluation. When to Use: When robustness and feature preservation are critical, and performance is secondary. Suitable for high-frequency surfaces, thin shells, and complex CAD meshes. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and the surface is simple or smooth. When memory is extremely constrained and batched processing is not feasible. Originated from the need for robust ray tracing of implicit surfaces. The method relies on iterative interval refinement and interval/affine arithmetics to compute bounds on field variation. It was implemented in the isoray library by narnia-ai-mason. The approach is discussed in the context of fast ray tracing of scale-invariant integral surfaces, where it is noted as a robust alternative to sphere tracing for arbitrary function-based field definitions. name: SDF Raycast Collision Detection
head: SDF Raycast, SDF Sign Change Check
body: This method detects collisions between a ray and a terrain represented by a Signed Distance Field (SDF) by evaluating the distance at the ray's origin and end points. It identifies collisions via sign changes in the distance values, indicating the ray has crossed the zero-level set (the surface). It distinguishes itself from continuous collision detection by relying on discrete time-step checks, which is simpler to implement but prone to tunneling at high velocities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D (assumed normalized), ray distance t{max}, and a distance evaluation function E(P) that returns the signed distance at point P. Output: Boolean indicating if a collision (sign change) occurred. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond the SDF evaluation function. The method operates on scalar distance values. Steps: 1. Normalize the direction vector D if it is not already normalized. 2. Calculate the end position of the ray: P{end} = O + D \cdot t{max}. 3. Evaluate the signed distance at the end position: d1 = E(P{end}). 4. Evaluate the signed distance at the origin: d2 = E(O). 5. Check for a sign change between d1 and d2. A collision is detected if one value is positive and the other is negative. 6. Return true if a sign change is detected, false otherwise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfraycastcollision(origin, direction, distance, evaluatedistance): # Step 1: Normalize direction direction = normalize(direction) # Step 2: Calculate end position endposition = origin + (direction distance) # Step 3: Evaluate distance at end position d1 = evaluatedistance(endposition) # Step 4: Evaluate distance at origin d2 = evaluatedistance(origin) # Step 5: Check for sign change # Collision if signs are different (one positive, one negative) if (d1 > 0 and d2 < 0) or (d1 < 0 and d2 > 0): return True # Step 6: Return false if no sign change return False Parameters: distance: The maximum length of the ray to test. Typical values depend on the scene scale and physics timestep. evaluatedistance: A function or method that queries the SDF. Implementation details vary by SDF representation (e.g., voxel grid, procedural function). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tunneling: At high velocities or large timesteps, the ray may pass completely through a thin surface without the endpoints straddling the zero-level set, resulting in a missed collision. Zero Distance: If the ray starts or ends exactly on the surface (d=0), the sign change check might fail depending on implementation. A robust implementation should handle d=0 as a collision or use a small epsilon. Non-normalized Direction: If the direction vector is not normalized, the calculated end position will be incorrect relative to the intended distance. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it requires exactly two SDF evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Extremely fast and simple to implement. No iterative search or complex data structure traversal is needed. Limitations: Prone to tunneling at high speeds or with thin geometry. Does not provide the exact intersection point or normal, only a boolean collision flag. When to Use: Suitable for simple collision detection in games or simulations where performance is critical and objects move slowly relative to the SDF resolution. When Not to Use: Unsuitable for continuous collision detection, high-speed physics, or when precise intersection points are required. This method is a basic technique used in terrain physics and simple collision detection systems involving SDFs. It is often found in game development tutorials and open-source projects dealing with voxel-based terrain. It serves as a foundational concept for more advanced SDF-based collision detection methods. 2JacT/Marching-Cubes-Terrain, https://github.com/2JacT/Marching-Cubes-Terrain, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Terrain SDF Collision Detection and Resolution
head: SDF Collision Detection, SDF Sign Change Collision
body: This method detects collisions between a moving object and a terrain represented by a Signed Distance Field (SDF) by evaluating the distance at the object's previous and current positions. It identifies collisions via sign changes in the distance values and estimates the surface normal to resolve penetration. Inputs: terrainSDFS: The terrain SDF evaluator. oldPosition: The object's position at the start of the time step. currentPosition: The object's position at the end of the time step. currentVelocity: The object's velocity vector. Outputs: justCollided: Boolean flag indicating if a collision occurred. resolution: A velocity correction vector to resolve the collision. Data Structures: float: Signed distance value. Positive values indicate outside the terrain and negative values indicate inside. Vec3: 3D position and normal vectors. Parameters: beta: Damping factor for collision resolution, typical value 0.1–0.3. contactOffset: Contact offset distance, typical value 3–10 mm. slop: Slop distance, typical value 1–3 mm. frictionMu: Friction coefficient, typical value 0.6f. Steps: 1. Evaluate the signed distance at the old position: d{\text{old}} = \text{terrainSDFS}.\text{EvaluateDistanceAt}(\text{oldPosition}) 2. Evaluate the signed distance at the current position: d{\text{new}} = \text{terrainSDFS}.\text{EvaluateDistanceAt}(\text{currentPosition}) 3. Check for collision by detecting a sign change: \text{collision} = (d{\text{old}} > 0 \land d{\text{new}} < 0) \lor (d{\text{old}} < 0 \land d{\text{new}} > 0) 4. If a collision is detected: a. Estimate the surface normal at the old position: \mathbf{n} = \text{EstimateGradient}(\text{terrainSDFS}, \text{oldPosition}) b. If the new distance is positive (object is now outside), invert the normal: \text{if } d{\text{new}} > 0: \mathbf{n} = -\mathbf{n} c. Set justCollided = true. d. Return the resolution result: \text{resolution} = -1 \times \text{currentVelocity} 5. If no collision is detected: a. Set justCollided = false. b. Return \mathbf{0}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, scalar): return Vec3(self.x scalar, self.y scalar, self.z scalar) def neg(self): return Vec3(-self.x, -self.y, -self.z) def truediv(self, scalar): return Vec3(self.x / scalar, self.y / scalar, self.z / scalar) def length(self): return (self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2)0.5 def normalized(self): l = self.length() return self / l if l > 0 else Vec3(0, 0, 0) @staticmethod def zero(): return Vec3(0, 0, 0) def TerrainSDFCollisionDetectionAndResolution(terrainSDFS, oldPosition, currentPosition, currentVelocity): oldDistance = terrainSDFS.EvaluateDistanceAt(oldPosition) newDistance = terrainSDFS.EvaluateDistanceAt(currentPosition) if (oldDistance > 0 and newDistance < 0) or (oldDistance < 0 and newDistance > 0): justCollided = True surfaceNormal = EstimateGradient(terrainSDFS, oldPosition) if newDistance > 0: surfaceNormal = -surfaceNormal resolution = -1 currentVelocity return justCollided, resolution else: justCollided = False return justCollided, Vec3.zero() def EstimateGradient(terrainSDFS, position): # Standard central difference approximation for gradient epsilon = 0.001 dx = terrainSDFS.EvaluateDistanceAt(position + Vec3(epsilon, 0, 0)) - terrainSDFS.EvaluateDistanceAt(position - Vec3(epsilon, 0, 0)) dy = terrainSDFS.EvaluateDistanceAt(position + Vec3(0, epsilon, 0)) - terrainSDFS.EvaluateDistanceAt(position - Vec3(0, epsilon, 0)) dz = terrainSDFS.EvaluateDistanceAt(position + Vec3(0, 0, epsilon)) - terrainSDFS.EvaluateDistanceAt(position - Vec3(0, 0, epsilon)) return Vec3(dx, dy, dz) / (2 epsilon) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A constraint-based method for resolving object penetration in terrain physics using Signed Distance Fields (SDF). It corrects positional drift via Baumgarte stabilization and eliminates inward velocity components to prevent tunneling. It distinguishes itself from simple positional correction by combining velocity damping with a proportional-derivative-like impulse application, ensuring stable contact without excessive jitter. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The specific implementation details, including the sign change check and the resolution logic, are found in the Marching Cubes Terrain project by 2JacT. 2JacT/Marching-Cubes-Terrain, https://github.com/2JacT/Marching-Cubes-Terrain, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: ERP/Baumgarte Collision Resolution
head: SDF Physics Collision, Terrain Collision Resolve
body: ERP/Baumgarte Collision Resolution is a collision resolution method that uses Signed Distance Fields (SDF) to determine depth and normal for correcting object penetration. It removes a fraction of penetration per step via Baumgarte stabilization and kills inward normal velocity. Inputs: pos: Current object position (vector). oldPos: Previous frame object position (vector). vel: Current object velocity (vector). mass: Object mass (scalar). contactOffset: SDF distance threshold for collision detection (scalar). slop: Allowed penetration depth before resolution triggers (scalar). beta: Baumgarte stabilization factor (scalar). frictionMu: Coefficient of friction (scalar). dt: Time step duration (scalar). Outputs: newVel: Updated velocity after collision resolution (vector). Data Structures: The method operates on standard vector and scalar types. It queries the terrain SDF via SDF(pos) for distance and EstimateGradient(pos) for the surface normal gradient at the old position. Steps: 1. Early Exit: If dt <= 0 or the magnitude of the SDF normal is near zero (< 10^{-10}), return vel unchanged. 2. Surface Normal: Normalize the SDF gradient at the old position to get the surface normal \mathbf{n}. 3. Penetration Depth: Calculate penetration as penetration = max(0, (contactOffset - sdfDistance) - slop), where sdfDistance is the SDF value at pos. If penetration <= 0, return vel unchanged. 4. Collision Detection: A collision is detected if the object crossed the surface boundary: (oldDistance > 0 && newDistance < 0) || (oldDistance < 0 && newDistance > 0). If no collision occurred, return vel unchanged. 5. Velocity Bias: Calculate incoming normal velocity vN = \mathbf{vel} \cdot \mathbf{n}. Calculate velocity bias \Delta vN: if vN < 0, set \Delta vN = -vN + \beta \cdot \frac{\text{penetration}}{\max(10^{-6}, dt)}; otherwise \Delta vN = 0. Apply the bias: \mathbf{vel} \leftarrow \mathbf{vel} + \Delta vN \mathbf{n}. 6. Inward Velocity Guard: If \mathbf{vel} \cdot \mathbf{n} < 0, subtract the inward component: \mathbf{vel} \leftarrow \mathbf{vel} - (\mathbf{vel} \cdot \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{n}. 7. Tangential Friction: Calculate normal impulse Jn = \text{mass} \cdot \max(0, \Delta vN). If frictionMu > 0 and Jn > 0, calculate tangential velocity \mathbf{v}T = \mathbf{vel} - (\mathbf{vel} \cdot \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{n}. If \|\mathbf{v}T\| > 10^{-6}, calculate max friction impulse J{t,\max} = \text{frictionMu} \cdot Jn and needed impulse J{t,\text{needed}} = \text{mass} \cdot \|\mathbf{v}T\|. Apply friction impulse magnitude Jt = \min(J{t,\text{needed}}, J{t,\max}) as a velocity change: \mathbf{vel} \leftarrow \mathbf{vel} - \frac{\mathbf{v}T}{\|\mathbf{v}T\|} \frac{Jt}{\text{mass}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resolvecollision(pos, oldpos, vel, mass, contactoffset, slop, beta, frictionmu, dt): if dt <= 0: return vel grad = estimategradient(oldpos) gradmag = (grad[0]2 + grad[1]2 + grad[2]2)0.5 if gradmag < 1e-10: return vel n = [grad[0]/gradmag, grad[1]/gradmag, grad[2]/gradmag] newdist = sdfdistance(pos) olddist = sdfdistance(oldpos) if not ((olddist > 0 and newdist < 0) or (olddist < 0 and newdist > 0)): return vel penetration = max(0.0, (contactoffset - newdist) - slop) if penetration <= 0: return vel vn = vel[0]n[0] + vel[1]n[1] + vel[2]n[2] dvn = 0.0 if vn < 0: dvn = -vn + beta (penetration / max(1e-6, dt)) vel = [vel[0] + dvnn[0], vel[1] + dvnn[1], vel[2] + dvnn[2]] dotvn = vel[0]n[0] + vel[1]n[1] + vel[2]n[2] if dotvn < 0: vel = [vel[0] - dotvnn[0], vel[1] - dotvnn[1], vel[2] - dotvnn[2]] jn = mass max(0.0, dvn) if frictionmu > 0 and jn > 0: vt = [vel[0] - dotvnn[0], vel[1] - dotvnn[1], vel[2] - dotvnn[2]] vtmag = (vt[0]2 + vt[1]2 + vt[2]2)0.5 if vtmag > 1e-6: jtmax = frictionmu jn jtneeded = mass vtmag jtmagnitude = min(jtneeded, jtmax) invvtmag = 1.0 / vtmag vel = [vel[0] - vt[0]invvtmag(jtmagnitude/mass), vel[1] - vt[1]invvtmag(jtmagnitude/mass), vel[2] - vt[2]invvtmag(jtmagnitude/mass)] return vel def estimategradient(pos): # Computes the gradient vector of the terrain SDF at pos # Standard central difference or analytical gradient evaluation return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def sdfdistance(pos): # Returns the signed distance value at pos return 0.0 Parameters: beta: Baumgarte stabilization factor. Not given in the sources. contactOffset: SDF distance threshold for collision detection. Not given in the sources. slop: Allowed penetration depth before resolution triggers. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Zero time step dt: Handled by early exit. Zero gradient magnitude: Handled by early exit. Zero penetration: Handled by early exit. Division by zero in Baumgarte term: Guarded by max(1e-6, dt). Not given in the sources. The method is described in the Marching-Cubes-Terrain repository. Baumgarte stabilization is a technique used in constraint solving to reduce positional drift by feeding back position errors into velocity corrections. 2JacT/Marching-Cubes-Terrain, https://github.com/2JacT/Marching-Cubes-Terrain, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Tracing Implicit Surfaces
head: Isosurface Ray Tracing, Ray Tracing General-Form Implicits, Ray Tracing Implicits, Ray casting isosurfaces
body: Ray tracing implicit surfaces renders a surface defined by a filter function f(\mathbf{x}) and an isovalue v by solving for the root where a viewing ray intersects the surface f(\mathbf{x}) - v = 0, without using a proxy triangle mesh. It distinguishes itself from rasterization of proxy geometry (e.g., Marching Cubes) by avoiding mesh extraction, thereby eliminating time complexity proportional to the number of samples and issues with proxy sampling rates beneath the Nyquist limit. Unlike SDF Raycast Collision Detection which often relies on distance-based stepping, this method formulates the intersection as a general root-finding problem for the parametric ray equation substituted into the implicit function. Inputs: Ray origin \vec{o} = (ox, oy, oz) and direction \vec{d} = (dx, dy, dz). Implicit surface function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}. Isovalue v (typically 0 for f(\mathbf{x})=v, or the function is pre-shifted to g(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) - v). Acceleration structure (e.g., grid, octree, kd-tree, BVH) specialized for the implicit data. Outputs: Intersection distance t > 0 (smallest root). Intersection point \vec{p} = \vec{o} + t\vec{d}. Data Structures: Acceleration Structure: A spatial hierarchy (grid, octree, etc.) that bounds the domain of f. For structured volume data, this is often a hierarchical grid storing min-max values of f to cull empty regions. Implicit Function: A callable routine f(\mathbf{x}) that evaluates the scalar field at any point \mathbf{x}. Steps: 1. Ray Formulation: Define the parametric ray equation: \vec{p}(t) = \vec{o} + t\vec{d} where t is the distance parameter. 2. Implicit Evaluation along Ray: Substitute the ray equation into the implicit function to create a unidimensional function ft(t): ft(t) = f(ox + t dx, oy + t dy, oz + t dz) The goal is to find the smallest t > 0 such that ft(t) = 0. 3. Acceleration Structure Traversal: Use the acceleration structure to determine a valid interval [t{min}, t{max}] where the ray might intersect the surface. This involves traversing the hierarchy (e.g., checking if the isovalue lies within the min-max bounds of a voxel or node) to skip empty space. 4. Root Finding: Solve ft(t) = 0 for the smallest t > 0 within the valid interval using an appropriate numerical method. The choice of method depends on the properties of f: Simple/Algebraic: Closed-form solutions or Newton-Raphson iterations. Complex/Multiple Roots: Robust techniques such as Lipschitz methods, bracketing, or self-validated arithmetic. Interval Arithmetic: Use interval arithmetic for root isolation, followed by a root refinement algorithm such as regula falsi, bounded Newton-Raphson, or another globally convergent numerical method. Differentiable Algebraics: Recursive root bracketing using Sturm sequences. GPU Approximation: Approximate implicit forms with piecewise Bernstein polynomials over local tetrahedral domains. 5. Refinement: If an approximate root t^ is found, refine it using the chosen numerical method to ensure |ft(t^)| < \epsilon for a desired precision \epsilon. 6. Secondary Rays: If the intersection is valid, proceed with shading calculations, potentially spawning secondary rays for shadows, reflections, or refractions, distinguishing this as "ray tracing" rather than simple "ray casting". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytraceimplicitsurface(rayorigin, raydirection, implicitfunc, isovalue, accelstruct): """ Ray trace an implicit surface defined by implicitfunc(x) = isovalue. Returns the smallest t > 0 where the ray intersects the surface, or None. """ # 1. Define the 1D function along the ray def ft(t): p = rayorigin + t raydirection return implicitfunc(p) - isovalue # 2. Use acceleration structure to find a candidate interval [tmin, tmax] # The accelstruct must support a query: findtinterval(ray) -> [tmin, tmax] # If no intersection is possible, return None tmin, tmax = accelstruct.findtinterval(rayorigin, raydirection) if tmin is None or tmax is None: return None # 3. Root finding within [tmin, tmax] # Choose a robust method based on the implicit function's properties. # Here we use a generic bracketing/refinement approach as an example. # Check if the interval contains a root # Note: Simple sign change check is insufficient for non-monotonic functions. # Robust methods (e.g., interval arithmetic, Sturm sequences) are preferred. # Example: Bounded Newton-Raphson with bracketing # Initialize with the midpoint or a point guaranteed to be inside the bracket tcurrent = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 # Iterative refinement for i in range(MAXITERATIONS): val = ft(tcurrent) # Check for convergence if abs(val) < EPSILON: return tcurrent # Compute derivative for Newton step # d/dt f(o + td) = gradf(p). d gradf = implicitfuncgradient(tcurrent, rayorigin, raydirection) deriv = dot(gradf, raydirection) if abs(deriv) < EPSILON: # Derivative is too small, fallback to bisection or regula falsi # For simplicity, we shift towards the midpoint of the bracket # In practice, a robust solver handles this internally tcurrent = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 else: tnext = tcurrent - val / deriv # Clamp to interval to ensure bracketing if tnext < tmin or tnext > tmax: tnext = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 # Update bracket based on sign of ft(tnext) # This is a simplified bracketing logic; robust implementations # use interval arithmetic or Sturm sequences for guaranteed isolation if ft(tmin) ft(tnext) < 0: tmax = tnext else: tmin = tnext tcurrent = tnext return None Parameters: EPSILON: Convergence tolerance for root finding. Typical value: 10^{-6} to 10^{-8}. MAXITERATIONS: Maximum number of iterations for the root finder. Typical value: 20-50. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Roots: Simple closed-form solutions or Newton-Raphson may fail for complex implicit functions with multiple roots or non-monotonic behavior along the ray interval. Robust techniques like interval arithmetic or Sturm sequences are required. Non-Convex Surfaces: The acceleration structure must correctly handle non-convex shapes to avoid missing intersections or returning false positives. Precision Issues: Floating-point precision errors in evaluating ft(t) can lead to incorrect root isolation, especially near the surface. Self-validated arithmetic or interval arithmetic can mitigate this. Time Complexity: With acceleration structures, each pixel is rendered at roughly O(\log N) cost with respect to the number of geometric primitives. Without acceleration, or for rasterization, the cost is O(N) for the entire frame. Memory Complexity: Depends on the acceleration structure. Hierarchical grids or octrees require memory proportional to the number of nodes, which can be significant for large structured volumes. Strengths: No mesh extraction required, avoiding time complexity on the order of the number of samples. Avoids issues with proxy sampling rates beneath the Nyquist limit. Enables on-the-fly changes in isovalue. Native support for secondary rays (shadows, refractions) and ray traversal of acceleration structures. Limitations: Root-solving process is not as fast as rasterization of simpler proxy geometry. Requires robust numerical methods for complex implicits, which can be computationally expensive. When to Use: Suitable for isosurface visualization of large structured data, particularly when dynamic isovalue changes are needed or when proxy mesh extraction is prohibitive. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the implicit surface is simple enough to be efficiently rasterized via proxy geometry. Ray tracing implicit surfaces was first explored by Hanrahan [39], using Descartes' rule of signs to determine if a given ray interval contained roots. Van Wijk [122] implemented a recursive root bracketing algorithm using Sturm sequences for differentiable algebraics, which is employed in the POV-Ray software [96]. Mitchell [82] suggested using interval arithmetic for root isolation followed by a root refinement algorithm. De Cusatis Junior et al. [16] extended the interval arithmetic technique to employ affine arithmetic. Loop and Blinn [72] implemented a GPU ray caster approximating implicit forms with piecewise Bernstein polynomials over local tetrahedral domains. Fryazinov and Pasko [27] employ rule-of-signs interval methods in ray tracing generalized implicit (FRep) surfaces on the GPU. Direct ray tracing of implicits interpolating volume data was first demonstrated by [115], with rendering times on the order of seconds per frame. Parker et al. [90, 89] implemented a tile-based parallel ray tracer on a 128-CPU SGI workstation, achieving interactive rendering of isosurfaces from large (1 GB) structured volumes. name: LevelSetHDDA
head: Hierarchical DDA for Level Sets, Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer for Level Set trees, LevelSet Hierarchical DDA
body: LevelSetHDDA is a specialized Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) designed for static intersection testing against level set trees, such as those used in signed distance field (SDF) representations. It recursively traverses the VDB tree hierarchy from a specified node level down to the leaf level (-1) to determine if a ray intersects the implicit surface. It differs from generic volume traversal methods by specializing in the binary occupancy test of level set nodes and terminating early upon finding the first valid voxel intersection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A TesterT object that encapsulates the ray, the tree structure, and the logic for node/voxel testing. The tester must provide: tester.ray(): Returns the ray being tested. tester.template hasNode<NodeT>(voxel): Returns true if the node at voxel is active/occupied. tester.setRange(tmin, tmax): Sets the valid time interval for the current traversal step. tester.init(t): Initializes the tester state at time t. tester(voxel, t): Returns true if the voxel at voxel is intersected at time t. Output: bool indicating whether an intersection was found. Data Structures: The method relies on the OpenVDB tree hierarchy. TreeT: The VDB tree type. ChainT: Defined as typename TreeT::RootNodeType::NodeChainType. NodeT: Defined as typename ChainT::template Get<NodeLevel>. This resolves to the specific node type at the current NodeLevel in the hierarchy. math::DDA: A Digital Differential Analyzer instance. It requires a ray and the total number of voxels along the node's side (NodeT::TOTAL for internal nodes, 0 for the leaf specialization). Algorithm Steps: The method is implemented as a template struct LevelSetHDDA<TreeT, int NodeLevel> with two specializations: the general recursive case and the base case for voxels (NodeLevel = -1). 1. General Case (NodeLevel > -1): 1. Create a DDA instance for the current node type: math::DDA<typename TesterT::RayT, NodeT::TOTAL> dda(tester.ray()). 2. Enter a loop controlled by dda.step(). 3. Check if the current voxel position dda.voxel() corresponds to an active node using tester.template hasNode<NodeT>(dda.voxel()). 4. If the node is active: Update the tester's valid time range to the current DDA interval: tester.setRange(dda.time(), dda.next()). Recursively call LevelSetHDDA<TreeT, NodeLevel-1>::test(tester). If the recursive call returns true, propagate true immediately. 5. Advance the DDA: dda.step(). If it returns false, exit the loop. 6. If the loop completes without finding an intersection, return false. 2. Base Case (NodeLevel = -1): 1. Create a DDA instance for voxels: math::DDA<typename TesterT::RayT, 0> dda(tester.ray()). 2. Initialize the tester with the starting time: tester.init(dda.time()). 3. Enter a loop controlled by dda.step(). 4. Test the current voxel: if (tester(dda.voxel(), dda.next())). 5. If the test returns true, return true immediately. 6. Advance the DDA: dda.step(). If it returns false, exit the loop. 7. If the loop completes without finding an intersection, return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def test(tester): # Determine node type and its total voxel count along one dimension ChainT = TreeT.RootNodeType.NodeChainType NodeT = ChainT.Get[NodeLevel] totalvoxels = NodeT.TOTAL # Initialize DDA for the current node level # Ray is obtained from tester dda = math.DDA(tester.ray(), totalvoxels) while True: # Check if the current voxel position has an active node if tester.hasNodeNodeT): # Set the time range for the recursive step tester.setRange(dda.time(), dda.next()) # Recurse to the next lower level if LevelSetHDDA[TreeT, NodeLevel-1].test(tester): return True # Step to the next voxel if not dda.step(): break return False def test(tester): # Initialize DDA for voxels (totalvoxels = 0 in this specialization context) dda = math.DDA(tester.ray(), 0) # Initialize tester state tester.init(dda.time()) while True: # Test the specific voxel at the current time if tester(dda.voxel(), dda.next()): return True # Step to the next voxel if not dda.step(): break return False Parameters: TreeT: The VDB tree type. NodeLevel: The current node level in the hierarchy being tested. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The DDA implementation relies on floating-point arithmetic for ray traversal. Precision issues may arise with very long rays or very small features, potentially causing missed nodes or voxels. Boundary Conditions: The DDA loop terminates when dda.step() returns false, which typically happens when the ray exits the bounding volume of the current node or voxel grid. Empty Trees: If the tree has no active nodes or voxels, the hasNode or tester calls will consistently return false, and the function will return false after traversing the entire ray extent within the bounds. A generic hierarchical DDA for ray intersections against a generic volume tree. Unlike LevelSetHDDA, it traverses down to the leaf node level (not the voxel level) and is designed for volumetric data rather than binary level set occupancy. VolumeHDDA Time Complexity: The complexity depends on the tree depth and the number of active nodes/voxels intersected by the ray. In the worst case, it traverses all active nodes down to the leaf level. The base case iterates through all voxels along the ray segment within the leaf node. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory is required beyond the recursion stack, which is proportional to the tree depth. Strengths: Efficient for sparse level set trees as it skips inactive nodes quickly. Early termination upon finding the first intersection makes it suitable for collision detection and surface finding. Limitations: Specialized for level sets; not directly applicable to dense volumetric data without modification. Performance degrades if the ray intersects many active nodes/voxels. When to use: Use for ray-casting against signed distance fields or level set representations where only the first intersection or occupancy is needed. When not to use: Use VolumeHDDA for dense volumetric data traversal where sampling values is required, not just occupancy. LevelSetHDDA is part of the OpenVDB library, developed by DreamWorks Animation and later maintained by the Academy Software Foundation. It is defined in openvdb/math/DDA.h. The method leverages the hierarchical structure of VDB trees to optimize ray traversal for level set data, which is commonly used in visual effects for fluid simulation, collision detection, and surface reconstruction.
