name: Ray-Ellipsoid Intersection
head: Ellipsoid Ray Intersection
body: Computes the intersection of a ray with an ellipsoid defined by a rotation matrix, translation vector, and scale factors, returning the existence of an intersection and the intersection point in world space. It differs from general implicit surface methods by exploiting the quadratic nature of the ellipsoid equation to solve for intersections analytically via a transformed coordinate system, offering a closed-form solution that is computationally cheaper than iterative root-finding. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} (3D vector) Ray direction \mathbf{d} (3D vector) Ellipsoid center \mathbf{t} (3D vector) Ellipsoid rotation matrix \mathbf{R} (3x3 matrix) Ellipsoid scale factors S = [Sx, Sy, Sz] (3D vector) Epsilon \epsilon for numerical stability (scalar, default 10^{-5}) Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection existence Intersection point \mathbf{p} in world space (3D vector) if intersection exists No complex data structures are required. The method operates on standard 3D vectors and 3x3 matrices. 1. Compute Inverse Transformation: Calculate the matrix that transforms world coordinates to the ellipsoid's local space. This matrix is the product of the inverse scale diagonal matrix and the transpose of the rotation matrix: \mathbf{M}{inv} = \text{diag}\left(\frac{1}{Sx}, \frac{1}{Sy}, \frac{1}{Sz}\right) \mathbf{R}^T 2. Transform Ray: Transform the ray origin and direction into the ellipsoid's local space: \mathbf{o}' = \mathbf{M}{inv} (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{t}) \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{M}{inv} \mathbf{d} 3. Handle Degenerate Direction: To prevent division by zero in the quadratic solver, check the first component of the transformed direction \mathbf{d}'. Let A be this component (or the magnitude of the direction vector squared in the standard quadratic form derivation, but here specifically referenced as a component for stability in the source). If |A| < \epsilon, set A = \epsilon. 4. Compute Discriminant: Calculate the discriminant of the resulting quadratic equation. Let B and C be the other coefficients derived from the transformed ray and ellipsoid equation (specifically, B = 2(\mathbf{o}' \cdot \mathbf{d}') and C = \mathbf{o}' \cdot \mathbf{o}' - 1 in the standard unit sphere intersection context, though the source implies a direct calculation). If \text{discriminant} < 0, there is no intersection. 5. Handle Near-Zero Discriminant: If |\text{discriminant}| < \epsilon, set \text{discriminant} = 0 to avoid numerical instability in the square root. 6. Compute Roots: Calculate the square root of the discriminant and the two potential intersection parameters t1 and t2: \sqrt{\text{discriminant}} = \sqrt{\text{discriminant}} t1 = \frac{-B - \sqrt{\text{discriminant}}}{2A} t2 = \frac{-B + \sqrt{\text{discriminant}}}{2A} 7. Check Ray Direction: If both t1 < 0 and t2 < 0, the intersections are behind the ray origin, so there is no valid intersection. 8. Select Valid t: Choose the smallest non-negative t. If t1 \ge 0, select t{intersect} = t1. Otherwise, select t{intersect} = t2. If |t1 - t2| < \epsilon, set t{intersect} = \min(t1, t2). 9. Compute Intersection Point in Local Space: \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{o}' + t{intersect} \mathbf{d}' 10. Transform Back to World Space: Transform the local intersection point back to world space using the forward transformation matrix \mathbf{M}{fwd} = \mathbf{R} \text{diag}(Sx, Sy, Sz): \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{M}{fwd} \mathbf{p}' + \mathbf{t} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def rayellipsoidintersection(o, d, t, R, S, eps=1e-5): """ Compute intersection of ray with ellipsoid. Args: o: Ray origin (3,) d: Ray direction (3,) t: Ellipsoid center (3,) R: Rotation matrix (3,3) S: Scale factors (3,) eps: Epsilon for numerical stability Returns: hit: Boolean p: Intersection point (3,) or None """ # Step 1: Compute inverse transformation matrix # invtransformmatrix = diag(1/S[0], 1/S[1], 1/S[2]) @ R.transpose() invscale = np.diag(1.0 / S) Minv = invscale @ R.T # Step 2: Transform ray to ellipsoid space otransformed = Minv @ (o - t) dtransformed = Minv @ d # Standard quadratic equation for ray-sphere intersection in local space: # At^2 + Bt + C = 0 # where A = d'.dot(d'), B = 2o'.dot(d'), C = o'.dot(o') - 1 A = np.dot(dtransformed, dtransformed) B = 2.0 np.dot(otransformed, dtransformed) C = np.dot(otransformed, otransformed) - 1.0 # Step 3: Handle degenerate direction (A near zero) if abs(A) < eps: A = eps # Step 4: Compute discriminant discriminant = BB - 4AC if discriminant < 0: return False, None # Step 5: Handle near-zero discriminant if abs(discriminant) < eps: discriminant = 0.0 # Step 6: Compute roots sqrtdiscriminant = math.sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-B - sqrtdiscriminant) / (2 A) t2 = (-B + sqrtdiscriminant) / (2 A) # Step 7: Check if both roots are negative if t1 < 0 and t2 < 0: return False, None # Step 8: Select valid t if t1 >= 0: tintersect = t1 else: tintersect = t2 if abs(t1 - t2) < eps: tintersect = min(t1, t2) # Step 9: Compute intersection point in transformed space intersectionpointtransformed = otransformed + tintersect dtransformed # Step 10: Transform back to world space # transformmat = R @ diag(S[0], S[1], S[2]) scalemat = np.diag(S) Mfwd = R @ scalemat intersectionpoint = Mfwd @ intersectionpointtransformed + t return True, intersectionpoint \epsilon: Epsilon for numerical stability, default 10^{-5}. Degenerate Direction: If the transformed direction vector has a near-zero component used in the denominator, it can cause division by zero. The source specifies clamping A to \epsilon. Near-Zero Discriminant: A discriminant very close to zero can lead to numerical instability in the square root. It is clamped to zero if |\text{discriminant}| < \epsilon. Back-Facing Intersections: Both roots being negative indicates the ellipsoid is behind the ray origin. This must be explicitly checked. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when the ray is tangent to the ellipsoid or when the ellipsoid is very small or large relative to the ray origin. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray-ellipsoid intersection, involving a constant number of matrix-vector multiplications and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Analytical solution is fast and robust for simple ellipsoids. No iterative convergence required. Limitations: Only applicable to ellipsoids. Requires transformation of the ray, which involves matrix multiplications. Numerical stability requires careful handling of edge cases (tangent rays, degenerate directions). When to Use: When rendering scenes with ellipsoidal primitives, such as in 3D Gaussian Splatting or other implicit surface representations where ellipsoids are the base primitive. When Not to Use: For complex non-ellipsoidal shapes or when higher-order primitives are needed. The method is based on the implementation found in the unofficial Taichi 3D Gaussian Splatting repository by wanmeihuali. It applies the standard technique of transforming the ray into the local coordinate system of the ellipsoid (where it becomes a unit sphere) to simplify the intersection calculation to a quadratic equation. wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: RayImplicitIntersection
head: ZeroCrossing, ZeroCrossingNode, nanovdb::ZeroCrossing
body: Detects if a ray intersects a zero-crossing (surface) at the voxel level of a Signed Distance Field (SDF) grid in an accessor. It performs empty-space ray-marching at all levels of the tree using a Hierarchical Distance Field Acceleration (HDDA). Unlike Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection which may traverse all active nodes, this method uses a leaf-only iterator to skip coarse tiles entirely, optimizing for the specific case of finding the first sign change in the narrow band. Inputs and Outputs: ray: The ray to test, containing origin, direction, and time bounds [t0, t1]. acc: The grid accessor providing voxel values and hierarchy traversal. ijk: Output coordinate of the closest voxel after the intersection point. v: Output grid value at ijk. t: Output time of the intersection along the ray. eps: Epsilon threshold for zero-crossing detection. If eps == 0.0f, a compile-time specialization (EpsZero) is used to drop the per-voxel deltaT < eps branch. startsinsidesurface: Parameter controlling behavior for rays starting inside the surface (defaults to reporting the exit crossing). Data Structures: HDDAValueIteratorImpl<AccT, ScalarT, bool LeafOnly>: A template class where LeafOnly is a compile-time gate. If LeafOnly is true, the iterator skips active coarse tiles. If false, it yields all active values (tiles and leaves). ScalarT: The data type of the SDF values. Supports fp32 and fp16 (c10::Half). For fp16 inputs, arithmetic is performed in fp32 (at::opmathtype<ScalarT>) and cast back only at store. Steps: 1. Clip Ray: Clip the ray to the bounding box of the grid root. If the ray does not intersect the bounding box or t1 exceeds a large threshold (e.g., 10^{20}), return false. python if not ray.clip(acc.root().bbox()) or ray.t1() > 1e20: return False 2. Seed Sign Reference: Find the first valid (non-NaN) voxel along the ray. This voxel's sign becomes the reference sign. This makes the method SDF-sign-agnostic and ensures rays starting inside the surface report the exit crossing. python ijk = RoundDown<Coord>(ray.start()) v0 = acc.getValue(ijk) if isnan(v0): # Advance to first valid voxel while isnan(acc.getValue(ijk)): ijk = nextvoxel(ijk, ray) if ijk out of bounds: return False v0 = acc.getValue(ijk) referencesign = sign(v0) 3. Initialize HDDA: Create an HDDA instance with the ray and the current dimension. Initialize lastT1 to track continuity for interpolation. python Delta = 1.0001f hdda = HDDA<RayT, Coord>(ray, acc.getDim(ijk, ray)) lastT1 = -inf 4. Traverse and Sample: Use the leaf-only iterator (HDDALeafVoxelIterator) to step through active leaf voxels. Skip active coarse tiles in a single coarse HDDA step, as tiles cannot contain the leaf-level zero crossing. python while hdda.step(): ijk = RoundDown<Coord>(ray(hdda.time() + Delta)) hdda.update(ray, acc.getDim(ijk, ray)) # Skip tiles or inactive voxels if hdda.dim() > 1 or not acc.isActive(ijk): continue v = acc.getValue(hdda.voxel()) # Detect sign flip voxelsign = sign(v) if voxelsign != referencesign: # Sign flip detected t0 = hdda.time() # Interpolate hit time if contiguous if t0 == lastT1: # Sub-voxel interpolate the hit time t = interpolatehittime(ray, lastT1, prevv, t0, v) else: # Fall back to bracket-entry time (gap between disjoint regions or NaN) t = t0 ijk = hdda.voxel() return True lastT1 = hdda.time() return False 5. Interpolation: If a sign flip is detected, sub-voxel interpolate the hit time. Only interpolate if the previous voxel was contiguous along the ray (t0 == lastT1). If not contiguous (e.g., gap between disjoint regions or NaN tile values), fall back to the bracket-entry time. Parameters: Delta: Static float constant set to 1.0001f, used to step slightly past the current hit time to avoid re-hitting the same voxel due to precision. eps: Epsilon threshold. If eps == 0.0f, the deltaT < eps branch is dropped. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inside-Surface Rays: Rays starting inside the surface must report the exit crossing. The convention-agnostic seed (first valid voxel) ensures this, avoiding spurious results from baked-in 'positive outside, negative inside' sentinels. Disjoint Regions/NaN Gaps: Interpolation across empty space (gaps between disjoint SDF regions or runs of NaN tile values) is prevented by checking t0 == lastT1 for continuity. Tile Skipping: The leaf-iterator switch is correct-by-construction for active tiles. The old iterator would have walked those into the per-voxel body (mis-indexing or reading gridScalars[-1]). The leaf iterator skips them. FP16 Dispatch: c10::Half is now dispatched. Code that caught NotImplementedError and fell back to fp32 conversion at the Python boundary should drop that branch. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the tree and the density of the narrow band. HDDA allows skipping empty space efficiently. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory per ray; uses cache hints to optimize L1/L2 usage. Performance: On RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, 1M rays, dragon dataset (267 MB SDF), fp32, eps=0: Speedup 1.95x (1.263ms -> 0.646ms). Instructions reduced by 50.6% (1.29e+08 -> 6.35e+07). Registers reduced from 80 to 78. On emu dataset (1.0 GB SDF): Speedup 1.73x. On crawler dataset (1.6 GB SDF): Speedup 1.67x. Strengths: High performance due to leaf-only traversal and cache hints. Correctness for inside-surface rays and disjoint regions. Limitations: Requires HDDA infrastructure. FP16 support requires careful arithmetic handling. Originated in the OpenVDB/fvdb-core project, specifically in the rayimplicitintersection kernel optimization. It is based on the nanovdb::ZeroCrossing method. The method was improved to fix correctness issues and enhance performance by reorganizing HDDA iterators and adding cache hints. name: Closed-form perspective-correct surfel rasterization
head: homography-based surfel projection, rational interpolation for surfels
body: A rasterization technique for planar surfels that computes screen-space texture coordinates (u, v) using an algebraically exact rational function of pixel position, avoiding per-pixel cross products and vector constructions. It sets itself apart from the reference 2DGS formulation by replacing the per-pixel cross-product-based inversion with a precomputed affine approximation, reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A surfel defined in camera space, the current camera projection matrix, and the screen-space bounding box of the surfel. Output: For each pixel (x, y) within the bounding box, the interpolated texture coordinates (u, v) and a validity flag. Data Structures: The method precomputates eight coefficients per surfel per frame. These are stored in a structure with the following layout: u0, v0: float16 (FP16). The intersection coordinates at the center of the screen-space bounding box. Ju, Jv: float16 (FP16). Elements of the Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J}, representing the rate of change of u and v per pixel offset. opacity, shape: float16 (FP16). Surfels' opacity and shape parameters (contextual, not part of the coordinate formula but stored alongside). dx, dy: float32 (FP32). Components of the perspective denominator gradient vector \mathbf{d}. Stored in FP32 because they span several orders of magnitude; errors here scale across the entire surfel. Numbered Steps: 1. Precomputation (per surfel, per frame): 1. Determine the screen-space bounding box of the surfel. 2. Compute the center of this bounding box, (xc, yc). 3. Evaluate the exact homography inversion at the center to find (u0, v0). 4. Compute the Jacobian \mathbf{J} and the denominator gradient \mathbf{d} at the center. This involves evaluating the partial derivatives of the rational function. Specifically, the solution p = k \times l (where k and l are linear constraints derived from the homography) is affine in (x, y) because the bilinear term xy(Tw \times Tw) vanishes. 5. Store the eight coefficients: (u0, v0), \mathbf{J}, and \mathbf{d}. 2. Rasterization (per pixel in bounding box): 1. Calculate the pixel offset from the center: \Delta = (x - xc, y - yc). 2. Compute the perspective denominator: denom = 1 + \mathbf{d}^{\top}\Delta. 3. Edge Case/Pitfall: If denom \le 0, the plane is parallel to or behind the camera for this pixel. Skip the fragment. 4. Compute the numerator corrections: numu = (\mathbf{J}\Delta)u numv = (\mathbf{J}\Delta)v 5. Evaluate the final coordinates: u = u0 + \frac{numu}{denom} v = v0 + \frac{numv}{denom} Formula: The core interpolation formula is: u = u0 + \frac{(\mathbf{J}\Delta)u}{1 + \mathbf{d}^{\top}\Delta}, \quad v = v0 + \frac{(\mathbf{J}\Delta)v}{1 + \mathbf{d}^{\top}\Delta} Where: \Delta is the pixel offset from the bounding box center. (u0, v0) is the intersection at the center. \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian (rate of change per pixel). \mathbf{d} is the gradient of the perspective denominator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputesurfelcoefficients(surfel, cameramatrix): """ Computes the 8 coefficients for a surfel. Returns: u0, v0, Ju, Jv, dx, dy """ # 1. Project surfel corners to screen space to find bounding box corners = projectcorners(surfel, cameramatrix) minx, miny, maxx, maxy = boundingbox(corners) # 2. Center of bounding box xc = (minx + maxx) / 2.0 yc = (miny + maxy) / 2.0 # 3. Evaluate exact homography inversion at center to get u0, v0 # The homography T maps surfel point q=(u,v,1) to screen (Tu·q, Tv·q)/(Tw·q) # We solve Tu · q = xc Tw · q and Tv · q = yc Tw · q # This yields linear constraints k·q=0 and l·q=0. Solution p = k x l. # u0 = px / pz, v0 = py / pz u0, v0 = exacthomographyinversion(surfel, cameramatrix, xc, yc) # 4. Compute Jacobian J and denominator gradient d # Since u(x,y) and v(x,y) are ratios of affine functions, # we can compute derivatives analytically or via finite differences around center. # The derivation shows p is affine in (x,y), so u and v are rational affine. # J is the rate of change of u and v per pixel offset. # d is the gradient of the denominator (1 + d^T Delta). # Analytical derivation from homography rows Tu, Tv, Tw: # k = xTw - Tu, l = yTw - Tv # p = k x l # u = px / pz, v = py / pz # Denominator of u is pz. Denominator of v is pz. # The shared denominator in the rational form is related to Tw·q. # Compute partial derivatives at (xc, yc) # du/dx, du/dy, dv/dx, dv/dy form J # dd/dx, dd/dy form d (gradient of the denominator term) # Note: The source states these 8 numbers depend only on surfel and camera. # We compute them once per surfel. # Implementation detail: Compute u and v at (xc+1, yc) and (xc, yc+1) # to estimate J, and analyze denominator structure for d. # However, exact analytical computation is preferred for stability. # Let D(x,y) = Tw·q(x,y). The rational form is u = Nu(x,y)/D(x,y). # The formula rewrites this around center. # For the purpose of implementation from text: # Ju = du/dx at center, Jv = dv/dy at center (diagonal elements if aligned, # but generally J is a 2x2 matrix. The formula uses (J Delta)u, implying # J is applied to Delta vector. So Ju and Jv in the coefficient list # likely refer to the relevant components or the matrix is stored. # The source lists "J" as a single entity in the coefficient list alongside u0,v0. # Given the formula (J Delta)u, J is a 2x2 matrix. # However, the precision section lists "J" as a single FP16 value? # "The coefficients (u0, v0), J, opacity, and shape are stored as FP16." # This implies J might be simplified or the text refers to the magnitude or # specific components. But the formula uses (J Delta). # Re-reading: "J its rate of change per pixel". # If J is 2x2, it has 4 elements. The text says "eight coefficients". # u0, v0 (2) + J (4?) + d (2) = 8. This fits. Juu, Juv, Jvu, Jvv = computejacobian(surfel, cameramatrix, xc, yc) dx, dy = computedenominatorgradient(surfel, cameramatrix, xc, yc) return u0, v0, Juu, Juv, Jvu, Jvv, dx, dy def rasterizesurfelpixel(x, y, u0, v0, Juu, Juv, Jvu, Jvv, dx, dy): """ Evaluates the closed-form formula for a single pixel. """ # Center is implicit in the coefficients (u0, v0 are at center) # We need the center coordinates to compute Delta. # However, the coefficients are precomputed for a specific bounding box center. # The caller must pass the center or the coefficients must include it. # The source says "Delta is the pixel offset from that center". # So the rasterizer needs to know the center or receive Delta directly. # Let's assume the rasterizer receives Delta. # If the rasterizer receives x, y, it needs xc, yc. # Let's assume the precomputed struct includes xc, yc or the rasterizer # is called with Delta. # For this pseudocode, we assume Delta is passed or computed by caller. # To make it self-contained, let's assume the function receives Delta. pass def evaluateclosedform(u0, v0, Juu, Juv, Jvu, Jvv, dx, dy, deltax, deltay): """ Evaluates u, v for a given pixel offset Delta. """ # Delta = (deltax, deltay) # Compute denominator denom = 1.0 + (dx deltax + dy deltay) # Edge case: skip if behind camera if denom <= 0.0: return None, None, False # Compute Jacobian product # (J Delta)u = Juu deltax + Juv deltay # (J Delta)v = Jvu deltax + Jvv deltay numu = Juu deltax + Juv deltay numv = Jvu deltax + Jvv deltay u = u0 + numu / denom v = v0 + numv / denom return u, v, True Parameters: Precision Split: (u0, v0), \mathbf{J}, opacity, and shape are stored as FP16. The denominator gradient \mathbf{d} is stored as FP32. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Denominator \le 0: Pixels with a non-positive denominator look at the plane from behind the camera and must be skipped. Floating-Point Reassociation: Near the alpha cutoff, floating-point reassociation can flip whether a fragment is drawn, causing non-byte-identical renders between the closed-form and reference methods (59–66 dB PSNR difference), though visual quality remains high. Precision Sensitivity: Errors in \mathbf{d} scale across the whole surfel, necessitating FP32 storage. Time Complexity: Per pixel, the method requires about 10 fused multiply-adds and one division, compared to roughly 15 fused multiply-adds and two divisions in the reference method. Memory Complexity: The precomputation stores 8 coefficients per surfel. The staging changes no arithmetic, only the shared-memory layout. Measured Performance: 32% higher mean frame rate than 2DGS on tested scenes. Quality: The renders match the 2DGS formulation to within 0.03 dB PSNR and 0.0002 LPIPS on 13 scenes. Strengths: No per-pixel cross product, making it computationally cheaper and numerically safer than packing plane rows at reduced precision (which costs 0.05–0.7 dB due to error amplification). Limitations: Not byte-identical to the reference method due to floating-point differences near alpha cutoffs. This method is described in "Bake It Till You Make It: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting". It builds on the homography projection properties of planar surfels, exploiting the fact that (u, v) is a ratio of two linear functions of the pixel position, similar to perspective-correct texturing in rasterizers. name: Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting (SPaGS)
head: Fast and Accurate 3D Gaussian Splatting for Spherical Panoramas, HTGS extended to spherical camera model, SPaGS (Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting), SPaGS Ray-Plane Intersection, omnidirectional Ray-Splat Intersection
body: SPaGS is a method for real-time volume rendering of 3D Gaussian splats on spherical panoramas, specifically equirectangular images, supporting arbitrary spherical camera models and distorted panoramic inputs. It solves the problem of rendering artifacts and numerical instability inherent in standard 3DGS when applied to wide-field-of-view (FoV) spherical projections, where the first-order affine approximation fails. Unlike standard 3DGS which relies on local affine approximations, SPaGS replaces rasterization with a numerically stable ray-splat intersection approach using perpendicular planes, avoiding matrix inversion of the covariance. It differs from ODGS by providing better rendering quality and speed, and from 3DGUT by using ray-splat intersection instead of the Unscented Transform. Inputs: A set of M 3D Gaussian splats representing the scene, and an equirectangular image of width W and height H. Outputs: A rendered equirectangular image with per-pixel color C. Data Structures: Each Gaussian splat i is defined by: position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), scale s{u,i}, s{v,i}, s{w,i} \in \mathbb{R}, opacity oi \in \mathbb{R}, and Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients of degree 3 for view-dependent color. The transformation from world to camera space is M \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, and the transformation from local splat coordinates to world space is T \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, defined by scaling, rotation, and position parameters. Steps: 1. Ray Direction Calculation: For each pixel (x, y) in the equirectangular image, compute the ray direction d in camera space. The image plane is defined as the surface of a unit sphere in camera space, mapped to the equirectangular plane. The direction components are: dx = \cos\left(\frac{2\pi x}{W}\right) \cos\left(\frac{\pi y}{H}\right) dy = \sin\left(\frac{\pi y}{H}\right) dz = \sin\left(\frac{2\pi x}{W}\right) \cos\left(\frac{\pi y}{H}\right) 2. Plane Normal Calculation: Compute the normals nx and ny of two perpendicular planes \pix and \piy that contain the ray direction d. These planes pass through the camera origin (0,0,0)^\top. The normals are computed directly in camera space: ny = \begin{pmatrix} -dy \\ dx \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} nx = \begin{pmatrix} -dx dz \\ -dy dz \\ dx^2 + dy^2 \end{pmatrix} (Standard orthogonal basis construction for planes containing a vector and the origin) 3. Plane Representation: Since the planes contain the camera origin, they are represented in homogeneous coordinates as \pix = (nx, 0)^\top and \piy = (ny, 0)^\top. 4. Transformation to Splat Local Space: Transform the planes from camera space into the local coordinate system of each 3D Gaussian using the world-to-camera matrix M and the local-to-world matrix T. The transformed planes are computed as \pi{local} = T^{-1} M^{-1} \pi{camera} (Standard homogeneous coordinate transformation for planes). 5. Ray-Splat Intersection: Perform the intersection test in the splat-local coordinate system to avoid matrix inversion of the covariance \Sigmai and handle degenerate Gaussians numerically stably. Compute the squared distance \rhoi(x)^2 from the ray origin to the Gaussian center, and the intersection point x \in \mathbb{R}^3. The alpha value \alphai is evaluated at x using the Gaussian's covariance \Sigmai and opacity oi: \alphai = oi \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \rhoi(x)^2\right) 6. Hybrid Transparency Blending: Split splats contributing to a pixel into a 'core' (first K depth-sorted splats) and a 'tail' (remaining splats). Core: Apply standard \alpha-blending for the first K splats. Tail: Combine remaining splats' colors ci and opacities \alphai without sorting to compute combined color c{tail} and remaining opacity T{tail}. Final Color: Compute the final pixel color as C = c{tail} + (1 - T{tail}) c{background}, where c{background} is the background color. Parameters: K: Number of depth-sorted splats in the core. SH Degree: 3. Pitfalls: Degenerate 3D Gaussians cause numerical instability in standard covariance-based rasterization. SPaGS avoids this by using ray-splat intersection via perpendicular planes, which avoids matrix inversion. Standard 3DGS uses a first-order affine approximation, leading to residual errors and artifacts in wide-FoV views. SPaGS avoids this by using exact ray-splat intersection. A two-stage method to calculate an axis-aligned screen-space bounding box for 3D Gaussians in spherical panoramas, addressing deformation caused by omnidirectional pixel distribution and non-linear spherical projection. It sets itself apart from standard affine approximations by projecting a tangent-space bounding box onto the equirectangular plane, ensuring validity despite spherical distortion. Time Complexity: The ray-splat intersection approach is more computationally expensive than the affine approximation of standard 3DGS but is optimized for real-time rendering on spherical panoramas. The use of hybrid blending and bounding box culling accelerates the process. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians M and the SH coefficients. Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves real-time rates for spherical panoramas. It is faster and provides better quality than ODGS. Strengths: Numerically stable for degenerate Gaussians. Handles arbitrary spherical camera models (e.g., equirectangular). Avoids artifacts from affine approximations in wide-FoV views. Supports hybrid transparency blending for efficient rendering. Limitations: More complex intersection logic than standard rasterization. Requires transformation of planes for each splat. When to use: Real-time rendering of 3D Gaussian splats on spherical panoramas, specifically equirectangular images, supporting distorted panoramic inputs. When not to use: Standard perspective cameras without distortion, where standard 3DGS affine approximation is sufficient and faster. SPaGS extends the approach of Hahlbohm et al. (HTGS) to a spherical camera model. The method addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS which only supports undistorted perspective camera models, restricting its application to 360° images. It is used for real-time rendering of 3D Gaussian splats on spherical panoramas. name: Tangent Plane-Based Bounding Box Calculation
head: SPaGS Bounding Box, Two-Stage Bounding Box
body: A two-stage method to calculate an axis-aligned screen-space bounding box for 3D Gaussians in spherical panoramas, addressing deformation caused by omnidirectional pixel distribution and non-linear spherical projection. It sets itself apart from standard affine approximations by projecting a tangent-space bounding box onto the equirectangular plane, ensuring validity despite spherical distortion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian splat parameters (mean \mathbf{m} in camera space, covariance \Sigma), camera intrinsic parameters (focal length f), and equirectangular image dimensions (W, H). Output: Axis-aligned bounding box (p{x,\min}, p{x,\max}, p{y,\min}, p{y,\max}) in equirectangular pixel coordinates. Data Structures: Tangent Space Basis: Vectors \hat{\mathbf{t}} (tangent), \hat{\mathbf{b}} (bitangent), \hat{\mathbf{n}} (normal) in \mathbb{R}^3. Tangent Box: Rectangle defined by t{x,\min}, t{x,\max}, t{y,\min}, t{y,\max} in tangent space. Camera Space Box: Derived from tangent box via transformation. Steps: 1. Define Tangent Space: For a splat with mean \mathbf{m} in camera space, determine the reference vector \mathbf{r}{\text{ref}} to avoid pole singularities. The mean \mathbf{m} is used as the reference, except when the splat lies on the vector of the two poles, in which case \mathbf{r}{\text{ref}} is used to avoid singularity. Compute the normal \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{m} / \|\mathbf{m}\|. Compute the tangent \hat{\mathbf{t}} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{r}{\text{ref}} \times \hat{\mathbf{n}}). Compute the bitangent \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \hat{\mathbf{t}}. The tangent plane is defined as z=1 with origin at the camera space origin. 2. Transform to Tangent Space: Construct the transformation matrix M from camera space to tangent space. The columns of M are \hat{\mathbf{t}}, \hat{\mathbf{b}}, \hat{\mathbf{n}}. Transform the Gaussian covariance \Sigma to tangent space: \Sigmat = M^T \Sigma M. Calculate the 2D bounding box (t{x,\min}, t{x,\max}, t{y,\min}, t{y,\max}) on the tangent plane using the standard 2D Gaussian projection method (e.g., as in HTGS [HFW25]), treating the tangent space as a local Euclidean plane. 3. Project to Camera Space: Map the tangent box corners back to camera space. A point in tangent space is \mathbf{t} = (tx, ty, 1)^T. The corresponding point in camera space \mathbf{c} is calculated using Eq. (17), where cx and cy are derived from the tangent coordinates. 4. Project to Equirectangular Plane (Stage 2): Convert camera space coordinates to spherical angles (longitude \phi, latitude \lambda) or directly to equirectangular coordinates (px, py). The equirectangular coordinates are proportional to \phi and \lambda. Due to the non-linear nature of \text{atan2} and \text{asin}, the bounding box in equirectangular space is not simply the projection of the tangent box corners. 5. Calculate py Bounds: Since \text{asin} is monotonically increasing, the minimum and maximum py are found by evaluating the function at the extreme values of the argument derived from the tangent box combinations. Calculate the range of cy / \|\mathbf{c}\| based on t{x,\min/max} and t{y,\min/max}. The bounds are computed using Eqs. (15), (16), and the monotonicity properties in Eqs. (22)-(23). 6. Calculate px Bounds: Directly using \text{atan2} is problematic due to discontinuity at the pole cut. Instead, calculate a maximized differential angle. Compute the range of longitude \phi covered by the box. The bounds are derived using Eqs. (24)-(25) to handle the wrap-around and singularity. 7. Handle Pole Coverage: Check if the projected bounding box covers the north or south pole. If it covers a pole: Set p{x,\min} = 0 and p{x,\max} = W (full image width). Recalculate p{y,\min} and p{y,\max} relative to the projection center on the respective sphere. If the projection center is exactly on a pole: Use the simplified calculation with negligible overhead. 8. Load Balancing: Apply a load balancing scheme similar to Radl et al. [RSP24] to mitigate the impact of occasional large bounding boxes on Gaussian/tile instance creation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def tangentplaneboundingbox(meancam, covcam, W, H): """ Calculate the equirectangular bounding box for a 3D Gaussian splat. Args: meancam: numpy array (3,), camera space mean of the Gaussian. covcam: numpy array (3,3), camera space covariance matrix. W: int, image width. H: int, image height. Returns: tuple: (pxmin, pxmax, pymin, pymax) in pixel coordinates. """ # 1. Define Tangent Space m = meancam normm = np.linalg.norm(m) if normm < 1e-8: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) nhat = m / normm # Reference vector to avoid singularity at poles if abs(nhat[2]) > 0.9: rref = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) else: rref = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) that = np.cross(rref, nhat) that = that / np.linalg.norm(that) bhat = np.cross(nhat, that) # Transformation matrix M (columns are that, bhat, nhat) M = np.columnstack((that, bhat, nhat)) # 2. Transform Covariance to Tangent Space covtan = M.T @ covcam @ M # 3. Calculate 2D Bounding Box in Tangent Space (HTGS approach) sigma2d = covtan[:2,:2] eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(sigma2d) k = 3.0 # 3-sigma coverage extents = k np.sqrt(eigenvalues) v1, v2 = eigenvectors[:, 0], eigenvectors[:, 1] dx = math.sqrt((v1[0] extents[0])2 + (v2[0] extents[1])2) dy = math.sqrt((v1[1] extents[0])2 + (v2[1] extents[1])2) # Center in tangent space (projection of mean onto z=1 plane) mproj = m / m[2] mtan = M.T @ mproj txmin, txmax = mtan[0] - dx, mtan[0] + dx tymin, tymax = mtan[1] - dy, mtan[1] + dy # 4. Project to Camera Space def tantocam(tx, ty): t = np.array([tx, ty, 1.0]) c = M @ t return c[0], c[1], c[2] # 5. Calculate py Bounds (arcsin monotonicity) def getpy(tx, ty): cx, cy, cz = tantocam(tx, ty) return math.asin(cy / math.sqrt(cx2 + cy2 + cz2)) pycandidates = [getpy(tx, ty) for tx in [txmin, txmax] for ty in [tymin, tymax]] pymin = min(pycandidates) pymax = max(pycandidates) # 6. Calculate px Bounds (maximized differential angle) def getpx(tx, ty): cx, cy, cz = tantocam(tx, ty) return math.atan2(cx, cz) pxcandidates = [getpx(tx, ty) for tx in [txmin, txmax] for ty in [tymin, tymax]] pxmin = min(pxcandidates) pxmax = max(pxcandidates) # Handle atan2 discontinuity by checking differential angles # Standard wrap-around handling for spherical coordinates if pxmax - pxmin > math.pi: pxmin = pxmax - math.pi elif pxmin - pxmax > math.pi: pxmax = pxmin + math.pi # 7. Handle Pole Coverage # Check if latitude exceeds threshold maxabslat = max(abs(math.asin(cy / math.sqrt(cx2 + cy2 + cz2))) for cx, cy, cz in [tantocam(tx, ty) for tx in [txmin, txmax] for ty in [tymin, tymax]]) if maxabslat > math.pi/2 - 1e-6: pxmin = 0.0 pxmax = float(W) # Recalculate py for projection center on respective sphere # Simplified clamping to hemisphere range pymin = 0.0 pymax = float(H) else: # Convert angles to pixel coordinates pxmin = (pxmin / (2 math.pi) + 0.5) W pxmax = (pxmax / (2 math.pi) + 0.5) W pymin = (pymin / math.pi + 0.5) H pymax = (pymax / math.pi + 0.5) H # 8. Load Balancing # Apply load balancing scheme similar to Radl et al. [RSP24] # In practice, clamp box dimensions to tile sizes or cap instance counts here return (pxmin, pxmax, pymin, pymax) Computes the screen-space bounding rectangle of a projected surfel by finding clip-space planes tangent to the unit sphere under the mapping \bar{h} = T^T h, using the inverse-transpose of the T-matrix for numerical stability with degenerate surfels. It stores the three non-degenerate rows of T as vectors T1, T2, T4 \in \mathbb{R}^3 and computes the screen-space center and half-extents using a closed-form expression involving dot products among these vectors. This method is particularly useful for handling degenerate (infinitesimally thin) surfels where tangent scales become very small during optimization. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat for the bounding box calculation, involving a constant number of matrix-vector multiplications and trigonometric functions. Memory Complexity: O(1) per splat, storing only the basis vectors and box coordinates. Performance: The method is designed for real-time rendering, avoiding the need for iterative intersection tests. The load balancing scheme helps mitigate the performance impact of large bounding boxes. Strengths: Handles spherical projection distortion accurately; numerically stable at poles; valid bounding boxes even with significant deformation. Limitations: The calculation of px bounds requires careful handling of the \text{atan2} discontinuity and pole coverage, which can be complex to implement correctly. The method was introduced in the SPaGS paper to enable real-time rendering of 3D Gaussian splats on spherical panoramas. It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS rasterization, which assumes a local affine approximation that fails under non-linear spherical projections. The approach builds on the tangent space formulation used in HTGS [HFW25] and extends it to the equirectangular domain. name: Linear Edge Intersection
head: Linear Edge Interpolation, Edge Crossing Linear Interpolation, Edge Intersection Vertex Interpolation, Linear Interpolation for Edge Intersection
body: Linear Edge Intersection calculates the exact position where an isosurface (defined by a scalar field threshold) intersects a straight edge connecting two grid vertices, assuming the scalar field varies linearly between those vertices. It solves the geometric problem of locating zero-crossings (or threshold crossings) on discrete grid structures, which is a fundamental step in algorithms like Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, and ray-marching volume rendering. Unlike Voxel selection via pick ray intersection, which determines which voxel a ray enters, this method determines where on a specific segment the surface lies. It is distinguished from Linear Intersection Approximation by using the actual scalar values at the endpoints rather than assuming the midpoint. Inputs: \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2: 3D coordinates of the two edge endpoints (vertices). v1, v2: Scalar field values (e.g., density, SDF, intensity) at \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2. isoLevel: The threshold value defining the isosurface. eps: A small tolerance for numerical stability checks (typically 10^{-5} to 10^{-7}). Outputs: \mathbf{p}: The 3D coordinate of the intersection point on the edge. Data Structures: Vectors/Points: 3-element arrays or structs containing (x, y, z) coordinates. Scalars: Floating-point numbers for values and thresholds. Steps: 1. Check for Degeneracy: Calculate the difference \Delta v = v2 - v1. If |\Delta v| < eps, the scalar values are effectively identical. Return \mathbf{p}1 as the intersection point. This prevents division by zero. 2. Calculate Interpolation Factor: Compute the normalized distance \mu along the edge where the scalar value equals isoLevel. The standard formula is: \mu = \frac{isoLevel - v1}{v2 - v1} Some implementations clamp \mu to the range [0.0, 1.0] to handle cases where the threshold is slightly outside the sampled range due to noise or precision errors. 3. Compute Intersection Point: Interpolate the position using \mu: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}1 + \mu (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}1) Alternatively, this can be expressed as a weighted average: \mathbf{p} = (1 - \mu)\mathbf{p}1 + \mu\mathbf{p}2 4. Alternative Formulation (Signed Distance/Plane): In clipping contexts (e.g., convex clipping), if d0 and d1 are the signed distances of \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2 to a clipping plane (where d0 > 0 and d1 \le 0), the intersection \mathbf{x}p is calculated as: \mathbf{x}p = \frac{d0 \mathbf{p}2 - d1 \mathbf{p}1}{d0 - d1} This form is numerically more stable when vertices lie very near the plane. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearedgeintersection(p1, p2, val1, val2, isolevel, eps=1e-7): """ Calculates the intersection point of an isosurface with the edge defined by p1 and p2. Args: p1: Tuple/Array (x, y, z) of the first vertex. p2: Tuple/Array (x, y, z) of the second vertex. val1: Scalar value at p1. val2: Scalar value at p2. isolevel: The threshold value for the isosurface. eps: Tolerance for degenerate cases. Returns: Tuple/Array (x, y, z) of the intersection point. """ # Step 1: Check for degeneracy (division by zero) diff = val2 - val1 if abs(diff) < eps: return p1 # Step 2: Calculate interpolation factor # Standard linear interpolation formula mu = (isolevel - val1) / diff # Optional: Clamp to [0, 1] if the threshold is outside the range [val1, val2] # This handles cases where the surface does not strictly cross the edge # but the threshold is slightly out of bounds due to noise. # mu = max(0.0, min(1.0, mu)) # Step 3: Compute intersection point # p = p1 + mu (p2 - p1) px = p1[0] + mu (p2[0] - p1[0]) py = p1[1] + mu (p2[1] - p1[1]) pz = p1[2] + mu (p2[2] - p1[2]) return (px, py, pz) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If v1 = v2, the denominator is zero. The method must check |v2 - v1| < eps and return an endpoint (typically p1). Threshold Outside Range: If isoLevel is not between v1 and v2, the mathematical intersection lies outside the segment [p1, p2]. Some implementations return p1 or clamp \mu to [0,1]. Others may return "No Hit" if strict geometric validity is required. Multiple Roots: In ray-marching contexts, if the scalar field has two roots within a voxel, linear interpolation between entry and exit points may fail to detect the intersection because the signs at the endpoints might be identical. This method assumes a single crossing per edge segment. Numerical Stability: When vertices are very close to the plane (in clipping applications), using signed distances directly in the weighted average formula is more stable than solving parametric equations. Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement is an iterative root-finding method used to refine the intersection position after a sign change has been detected during ray marching. It narrows down the interval [t{prev}, t{curr}] containing the isosurface by iteratively applying linear interpolation (bisection) within the segment. This approach solves the problem of geometric inaccuracy inherent in discrete sampling, providing a balance between computational speed and visual fidelity. Unlike closed-form algebraic solutions or higher-order root isolation techniques, it relies on repeated linear approximation. It builds on Linear Edge Intersection by applying similar linear interpolation principles within an iterative refinement loop over a ray segment rather than a single edge. Linear Intersection Approximation (also known as Midpoint Intersection) is a method for estimating the intersection point of an isosurface with a grid edge. It solves the problem of determining where a scalar field crosses a threshold value by calculating the geometric midpoint of the edge, rather than performing linear interpolation based on the scalar values at the endpoints. It is distinguished from its parent, Linear Edge Intersection, by ignoring the scalar field values entirely, and from its sibling, Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement, by using a single fixed step rather than recursive refinement. Approximates the zero-crossing position along an edge by sampling discrete points and selecting the one with minimum absolute density. Steps: 1. Initialize minValue to a large number (e.g., 100000.0), t to 0.0, currentT to 0.0, steps to 8, and increment to 1.0 / steps. 2. Loop while currentT \le 1.0: Compute point p = p0 + (p1 - p0) \times currentT. Compute density = |Density\Func(p)|. If density < minValue, update minValue = density and t = currentT. Increment currentT += increment. 3. Return p0 + (p1 - p0) \times t. Generates intersection points with snapping behavior for vertices close to the grid edge point. Steps: 1. If |v1| < snap, return p1. 2. If |v2| < snap, return p2. 3. If |v2 - v1| < snap, return p1. Formula: \mu = \frac{v2}{v2 - v1} point = \mu \mathbf{p}1 + (1 - \mu) \mathbf{p}2 Parameter: snap: Threshold to snap vertices when close to grid edge point. Default value is 0.01. Time Complexity: O(1). The calculation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (subtraction, division, multiplication, addition) regardless of grid size. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional data structures are required beyond the input variables. Performance: Extremely fast. It is the dominant operation in Marching Cubes and similar surface extraction algorithms, often executed millions of times per frame. Strengths: Exact solution under the linear assumption; numerically stable with proper epsilon checks; simple to implement. Limitations: Assumes linear variation of the scalar field, which is an approximation. It cannot resolve multiple intersections within a single edge segment. Accuracy is limited by the grid resolution; finer grids yield more accurate surface representations. When to use: When extracting surfaces from voxel data (Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring) or performing ray-marching with linear interpolation. When not to use: When the scalar field is known to be highly non-linear within the edge segment and higher-order interpolation (e.g., quadratic or cubic) is required for visual fidelity, or when multiple roots are expected within the segment. Linear Edge Intersection is a foundational technique in computer graphics, primarily associated with the Marching Cubes algorithm introduced by Lorensen and Cline in 1987. It is also used in Dual Contouring, ray-marching volume rendering, and various mesh reconstruction techniques. The method relies on the assumption that scalar fields vary linearly between grid points, which is a standard approximation in discrete field processing. Variations of this method, such as using signed distances for clipping or snapping for robustness, have been developed to address specific numerical stability and geometric consistency issues. name: Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement
head: Bisection Refinement, Intersection refined isosurface rendering, Iso Hit Bisection, Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement, Isosurface shader, Linear Interpolation Refinement
body: Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement is an iterative root-finding method used to refine the intersection position after a sign change has been detected during ray marching. It narrows down the interval [t{prev}, t{curr}] containing the isosurface by iteratively applying linear interpolation within the segment. This approach solves the problem of geometric inaccuracy inherent in discrete sampling, providing a balance between computational speed and visual fidelity. Unlike closed-form algebraic solutions or higher-order root isolation techniques, it relies on repeated linear approximation. It builds on Linear Edge Intersection by applying similar linear interpolation principles within an iterative refinement loop over a ray segment rather than a single edge. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Interval bounds [t{prev}, t{curr}] (or corresponding spatial points \mathbf{x}{prev}, \mathbf{x}{curr}) where the scalar field values d{prev} and d{curr} have opposite signs relative to the isovalue \rho (i.e., a sign change is detected). Scalar field values d{prev} = f(\mathbf{x}{prev}) and d{curr} = f(\mathbf{x}{curr}). Target isovalue \rho. Number of refinement iterations N (typically 4–10). Outputs: Refined intersection parameter t{hit} or point \mathbf{x}{hit}. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values and 3D vectors, storing only the current interval bounds and field values. Steps: 1. Initialization: Identify the interval [\mathbf{x}{near}, \mathbf{x}{far}] such that f(\mathbf{x}{near}) < \rho and f(\mathbf{x}{far}) \ge \rho (or vice versa, depending on convention). Let f{near} = f(\mathbf{x}{near}) and f{far} = f(\mathbf{x}{far}). 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat N times: a. Calculate the new sample position \mathbf{x}{new} using linear interpolation between \mathbf{x}{near} and \mathbf{x}{far} based on the ratio of the distance from f{near} to \rho over the total interval f{far} - f{near}: \mathbf{x}{new} = (\mathbf{x}{far} - \mathbf{x}{near}) \frac{\rho - f{near}}{f{far} - f{near}} + \mathbf{x}{near} b. Sample the scalar field value at the new position: f{new} = f(\mathbf{x}{new}). c. Update the interval bounds: If f{new} > \rho (the new point is "in front" of the isosurface, assuming higher values are inside), set \mathbf{x}{far} = \mathbf{x}{new} and f{far} = f{new}. Otherwise (f{new} \le \rho), set \mathbf{x}{near} = \mathbf{x}{new} and f{near} = f{new}. 3. Result: After N iterations, the refined intersection point is \mathbf{x}{hit} = \mathbf{x}{new}. Shade this point and return. 4. Edge Cases: If the initial detection does not find a sign change, or if the loop condition fails (e.g., ray leaves volume), advance to the next sampling step. Assumes direction is normalized. """ # Initialize interval bounds xnear = origin + tprev direction xfar = origin + tcurr direction fnear = dprev ffar = dcurr # Ensure correct ordering: fnear < isovalue <= ffar if fnear >= isovalue: xnear, xfar = xfar, xnear fnear, ffar = ffar, fnear xnew = xnear fnew = fnear for i in range(numiterations): # Guard against division by zero if ffar == fnear if ffar == fnear: break tratio = (isovalue - fnear) / (ffar - fnear) xnew = xnear + (xfar - xnear) tratio # Sample scalar field at xnew (implementation depends on volume data structure) fnew = samplescalarfield(xnew) # Update interval bounds if fnew > isovalue: xfar = xnew ffar = fnew else: xnear = xnew fnear = fnew # Return the refined parameter thit = dot(xnew - origin, direction) return thit Parameters: numiterations: The number of bisection steps to perform. Typical values range from 4 to 10. Source states that a fixed number of 4 steps is sufficient for high-quality positions. Source uses up to 10 iterations. Source mentions a parameter uRefinementIterations with a typical value of 5. More iterations improve accuracy at the cost of additional scalar field evaluations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If f{far} == f{near}, the interpolation ratio is undefined. This can occur if the scalar field is flat or if precision issues cause identical values. A guard should be added to break the loop or return the current estimate. Sign Convention: The method assumes a consistent sign convention (e.g., f < \rho is outside, f \ge \rho is inside). If the sign change detection logic uses a different convention, the update logic for xnear and xfar must be adjusted accordingly. Complex Topologies: In regions with high curvature or complex topology, linear interpolation may not accurately represent the surface, leading to artifacts. Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate, especially if the interval becomes very small. Using double precision for intermediate calculations may be beneficial in critical applications. Neubauer's algorithm is a method for finding the intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the problem of locating the precise root of the implicit function f(t) = \rho(R(t)) - \rho{iso} by using repeated linear interpolation to refine the intersection position within the ray segment containing the root. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on iterative linear approximation rather than closed-form algebraic solutions (like Schwarze's Analytic Inversion) or root isolation techniques (like Isolation and Iterative Root Finding), offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Fast Ray-Surface Intersection is an approximate method for determining the intersection point of a ray with an iso-surface within a volume rendering cell, trading geometric accuracy for computational speed. It solves the problem of finding the first-hit surface location without the high cost of inverting trilinear interpolation. Unlike exact intersection methods which compute all roots of the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation, this method subdivides the ray segment within the cell and uses linear interpolation to estimate the hit point, producing visually indistinguishable results in final renderings while being significantly faster. The Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the depth value d where a signed distance function (SDF) or occupancy logit crosses a threshold. It estimates the next intersection point using linear interpolation between two bracketing points. The Bisection Method is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the intersection position of a ray with an implicit surface within a specific segment identified by adaptive sampling. It serves as an alternative to the Secant method in ray marching pipelines, guaranteeing convergence by halving the search interval at each step. Unlike the Secant method, which uses linear interpolation between two points, the Bisection method relies solely on the sign of the field function evaluations to narrow the interval. name: Neubauer's Ray-Voxel Intersection Algorithm
head: Neubauer, Neubauer's Method, Repeated Linear Interpolation
body: Neubauer's algorithm is a method for finding the intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the problem of locating the precise root of the implicit function f(t) = \rho(R(t)) - \rho{iso} by using repeated linear interpolation to refine the intersection position within the ray segment containing the root. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on iterative linear approximation rather than closed-form algebraic solutions (like Schwarze's Analytic Inversion) or root isolation techniques (like Isolation and Iterative Root Finding), offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray R(t) = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}, where \mathbf{a} is the origin and \mathbf{b} is the direction. The interval [t{in}, t{out}] where the ray overlaps the voxel. The scalar field values \rho{ijk} at the eight vertices of the voxel. The iso-value \rho{iso}. The number of iterations N (typically 2-3). Output: The hit distance t{hit} along the ray, or a "NO HIT" status if no intersection is found within the voxel. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on scalar values representing the ray parameter t and the interpolated density \rho. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the search interval boundaries: t0:= t{in} t1:= t{out} Compute the density values at the boundaries: \rho0:= \rho(R(t0)) \rho1:= \rho(R(t1)) where \rho(R(t)) is computed via trilinear interpolation of the voxel's vertex data. 2. Initial Sign Check: If \text{sign}(\rho0 - \rho{iso}) = \text{sign}(\rho1 - \rho{iso}), return NO HIT. This indicates that the iso-surface does not cross the ray segment within the voxel, or crosses an even number of times, which the method cannot detect. 3. Iterative Refinement (Repeated Linear Interpolation): For i = 1 to N: a. Compute the candidate intersection parameter t using linear interpolation (secant step): t:= t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{\rho{iso} - \rho0}{\rho1 - \rho0} b. Evaluate the density at the candidate point: \rho{new}:= \rho(R(t)) c. Determine which sub-segment contains the root by comparing signs: If \text{sign}(\rho{new} - \rho{iso}) = \text{sign}(\rho0 - \rho{iso}): The root lies in the upper sub-segment [t, t1]. Update: t0:= t \rho0:= \rho{new} Else: The root lies in the lower sub-segment [t0, t]. Update: t1:= t \rho1:= \rho{new} 4. Final Result: After N iterations, compute the final hit distance: t{hit}:= t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{\rho{iso} - \rho0}{\rho1 - \rho0} Return t{hit}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def NeubauerRayVoxelIntersection(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelbounds, voxeldata, rhoiso, N=3): """ rayorigin: tuple (x, y, z) raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) voxelbounds: tuple (x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1) voxeldata: list/tuple of 8 floats representing density at voxel corners rhoiso: float, the iso-surface value N: int, number of interpolation iterations """ # 1. Calculate ray-voxel overlap interval [tin, tout] using slab method x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1 = voxelbounds tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for axis in range(3): p = rayorigin[axis] d = raydirection[axis] b0 = [x0, y0, z0][axis] b1 = [x1, y1, z1][axis] if abs(d) < 1e-12: if p < b0 or p > b1: return None else: t1 = (b0 - p) / d t2 = (b1 - p) / d if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None tin, tout = tmin, tmax # Helper to evaluate trilinear interpolation def evaluatedensity(t): px = rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0] py = rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1] pz = rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2] u = (px - x0) / (x1 - x0) v = (py - y0) / (y1 - y0) w = (pz - z0) / (z1 - z0) u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) w = max(0.0, min(1.0, w)) d000 = voxeldata[0]; d100 = voxeldata[1] d010 = voxeldata[2]; d110 = voxeldata[3] d001 = voxeldata[4]; d101 = voxeldata[5] d011 = voxeldata[6]; d111 = voxeldata[7] d00 = d000 (1 - u) + d100 u d10 = d010 (1 - u) + d110 u d01 = d001 (1 - u) + d101 u d11 = d011 (1 - u) + d111 u d0 = d00 (1 - v) + d10 v d1 = d01 (1 - v) + d11 v return d0 (1 - w) + d1 w # 2. Initialize interval t0 = tin t1 = tout rho0 = evaluatedensity(t0) rho1 = evaluatedensity(t1) # 3. Initial sign check def sign(val): if val > 0: return 1 elif val < 0: return -1 else: return 0 if sign(rho0 - rhoiso) == sign(rho1 - rhoiso): return None # 4. Iterative refinement for i in range(N): if abs(rho1 - rho0) < 1e-12: t = (t0 + t1) / 2.0 else: t = t0 + (t1 - t0) (rhoiso - rho0) / (rho1 - rho0) rhonew = evaluatedensity(t) if sign(rhonew - rhoiso) == sign(rho0 - rhoiso): t0 = t rho0 = rhonew else: t1 = t rho1 = rhonew # 5. Final result if abs(rho1 - rho0) < 1e-12: thit = (t0 + t1) / 2.0 else: thit = t0 + (t1 - t0) (rhoiso - rho0) / (rho1 - rho0) return thit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Intersections: The algorithm assumes a single root within the segment defined by differing signs. It can falsely return the last intersection point if three intersections are contained within a voxel but two of them are within the first ray segment. Complex Topologies: In cases where the function has two roots, the entry and exit densities may be on the same side of \rho{iso}, causing the initial sign check to return NO HIT incorrectly. SIMD Compatibility: The control flow involves conditional updates to t0, t1, \rho0, \rho1 based on sign comparisons. This inconsistent decision-making on which segment to handle makes the base algorithm less suitable for SIMD than methods with uniform control flow, although it is still functional and faster than Schwarze's method in SIMD contexts. Precision: As an iterative approximation, it is prone to approximation artifacts and image errors for complex voxel configurations compared to exact methods. Schwarze's Analytic Inversion is a method for computing the exact intersection of a ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the cubic polynomial resulting from substituting the ray equation into the trilinear interpolation function to find the precise root. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Neubauer's algorithm by its reliance on closed-form algebraic solutions (Cardano's formula) rather than iterative refinement or isolation techniques, offering mathematical exactness at the cost of significant computational expense and numerical instability. Isolation and Iterative Root Finding is a ray-voxel intersection algorithm for iso-surfaces that combines the speed of Neubauer's method with the correctness guarantees of Schwarze's method. It solves the problem of finding the first intersection of a ray with a cubic polynomial within a voxel by first isolating the root interval using the polynomial's extrema, then refining the location via iterative root finding. Unlike Neubauer's method, which can fail or return incorrect intersections when multiple roots exist in a segment, this method guarantees that the final interval contains exactly one root, ensuring the first valid intersection is found. It is roughly three times faster than Schwarze's method while maintaining superior numerical stability. Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection computes the point where a ray intersects an isosurface defined by trilinear interpolation within a 3D voxel cell. It solves for the first positive root of the cubic polynomial derived from the cell's corner values using an iterative bisection refinement strategy. Unlike analytical cubic solvers (e.g., Schwarze’s method), this approach is slightly faster and yields single-precision, numerically stable results. It builds on Neubauer's Ray-Voxel Intersection Algorithm by applying iterative root finding specifically to the reconstructed cell geometry. Time and Memory Complexity: The algorithm performs a fixed number of iterations N (typically 2-3). Each iteration requires one trilinear interpolation evaluation. Trilinear interpolation is O(1) with a constant number of arithmetic operations. Thus, the time complexity per ray-voxel intersection is O(N), which is effectively constant. Memory complexity is O(1) as it only stores a few scalar variables. Measured Performance: On a 1.8GHz AMD Opteron CPU, Neubauer achieves an average of 3.04 million ray-voxel intersections per second in synthetic setups (Table 1). In SIMD mode on synthetic setups, Neubauer achieves an average of 3.04 million ray-cell intersections per second (Table 2). On real-world datasets (Bonsai, Aneurism, Engine), Neubauer achieves approximately 2.93-2.94 million intersections per second (Table 3). In SIMD mode on real-world datasets, Neubauer achieves 6.94-7.65 million intersections per second, a speedup of factor 2.3-2.6 over sequential code (Table 4). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster than the accurate but slow Schwarze algorithm. Better suited for SIMD implementation than Schwarze due to simpler control flow (though still not ideal). Integrated into the OpenRT realtime ray tracing system. Limitations: Prone to approximation artifacts and image errors for complex voxel configurations. Can fail to locate valid intersections in cases with multiple roots or specific topological configurations. Less numerically stable than isolation-based methods. When to Use: Use when performance is critical and the voxel data topology is relatively simple, or when an approximate intersection is acceptable. It is a good baseline for SIMD-accelerated volume rendering where the overhead of exact solvers is prohibitive. When Not to Use: Avoid when high accuracy is required, especially for complex iso-surfaces with multiple intersections within a single voxel, or when numerical stability is paramount. Neubauer's algorithm was proposed by Neubauer et al. in 2002. It was analyzed and compared with other ray-voxel intersection techniques (including Schwarze's method and linear interpolation) in the context of iso-surface volume rendering by Wald et al. in 2004. The method is integrated into the OpenRT realtime ray tracing system for iso-surface volume rendering, where it serves as a fast, approximate intersection primitive. name: Schwarze's Analytic Inversion
head: Cardano's formula method, Exact Ray-Surface Intersection, Schwarze approach
body: Schwarze's Analytic Inversion is a method for computing the exact intersection of a ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the cubic polynomial resulting from substituting the ray equation into the trilinear interpolation function to find the precise root. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Neubauer's algorithm by its reliance on closed-form algebraic solutions (Cardano's formula) rather than iterative refinement or isolation techniques, offering mathematical exactness at the cost of significant computational expense and numerical instability. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, voxel corner values \rho{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}, iso-value \rho{iso}, voxel dimensions \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z, and traversal interval [t{in}, t{out}]. Output: The smallest ray parameter t \in [t{in}, t{out}] such that the interpolated density equals \rho{iso}, or None if no intersection exists in the interval. Data Structures: The method operates on the coefficients of the cubic polynomial f(t) = \rho(t) - \rho{iso} = 0. Let the ray be \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. The density \rho(t) is a cubic polynomial in t: \rho(t) = a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + d The coefficients a, b, c, d are computed from the voxel corner densities and ray direction components. The target polynomial is f(t) = a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + (d - \rho{iso}). Steps: 1. Compute Polynomial Coefficients: Calculate a, b, c, d based on the trilinear interpolation model and the ray parameters. 2. Check Special Cases: If |a| is negligible (below a threshold), the polynomial is quadratic or lower. Solve using the quadratic formula or linear equation. Note that even the quadratic case requires a costly square root operation. If |a| and |b| are negligible, solve the linear equation ct + (d - \rho{iso}) = 0. 3. Solve Cubic (Cardano's Formula): For the full cubic case (a \neq 0): Normalize the polynomial to x^3 + px + q = 0 by substituting t = x - \frac{b}{3a}. Calculate the discriminant D = (q/2)^2 + (p/3)^3. Apply Cardano's formula, which involves computing cosines and inverse cosines (arccos) to handle the trigonometric solution for the three real roots case when D \leq 0. Compute all three roots of the polynomial. 4. Filter Roots: Identify roots t that lie within the voxel traversal interval [t{in}, t{out}]. Select the smallest valid t as the intersection point. 5. Return Result: Return the smallest valid t. If no roots are in the interval, return None. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def schwarzeanalyticinversion(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelcorners, rhoiso, tin, tout, voxelsize): # voxelcorners: [rho000, rho100, rho010, rho110, rho001, rho101, rho011, rho111] # voxelsize: [dx, dy, dz] def cbrt(x): return math.copysign(abs(x)(1/3), x) def computetrilinearcoeffs(o, d, corners, vs): dx, dy, dz = vs u0, u1 = o[0]/dx, d[0]/dx v0, v1 = o[1]/dy, d[1]/dy w0, w1 = o[2]/dz, d[2]/dz # Basis coefficients for trilinear interpolation c00 = corners[0] c10 = corners[1] - corners[0] c01 = corners[2] - corners[0] c001 = corners[4] - corners[0] c11 = corners[3] - corners[1] - corners[2] + corners[0] c101 = corners[5] - corners[1] - corners[4] + corners[0] c011 = corners[6] - corners[2] - corners[4] + corners[0] c111 = corners[7] - corners[3] - corners[5] - corners[6] + corners[1] + corners[2] + corners[4] - corners[0] # Taylor expansion coefficients at t=0: rho(t) = d + ct + bt^2 + at^3 a = u1 v1 w1 c111 b = u1 v1 c11 + u1 w1 c101 + v1 w1 c011 c = (u1 (c10 + c11 v0 + c101 w0 + c111 v0 w0) + v1 (c01 + c11 u0 + c011 w0 + c111 u0 w0) + w1 (c001 + c101 u0 + c011 v0 + c111 u0 v0)) dval = (c00 + c10 u0 + c01 v0 + c001 w0 + c11 u0 v0 + c101 u0 w0 + c011 v0 w0 + c111 u0 v0 w0) return a, b, c, dval EPSILON = 1e-8 a, b, c, d = computetrilinearcoeffs(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelcorners, voxelsize) d -= rhoiso # 2. Handle special cases if abs(a) < EPSILON: if abs(b) < EPSILON: # Linear: ct + d = 0 if abs(c) < EPSILON: return None t = -d / c return t if tin <= t <= tout else None else: # Quadratic: bt^2 + ct + d = 0 disc = cc - 4bd if disc < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-c + sqrtdisc) / (2b) t2 = (-c - sqrtdisc) / (2b) valid = [t for t in (t1, t2) if tin <= t <= tout] return min(valid) if valid else None # 3. Full Cubic Case: at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d = 0 shift = b / (3a) p = (3ac - bb) / (3aa) q = (2bbb - 9abc + 27aad) / (27aaa) roots = [] D = (q/2)2 + (p/3)3 if D <= 0: # Three real roots using trigonometric formula if p >= 0: sqrtD = math.sqrt(D) u = cbrt(-q/2 + sqrtD) v = cbrt(-q/2 - sqrtD) roots.append(u + v + shift) else: r = math.sqrt(-p3 / 27.0) costheta = -q / (2 r) if abs(r) > EPSILON else 0.0 costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) theta = math.acos(costheta) for k in range(3): angle = (theta + 2 math.pi k) / 3.0 x = 2 math.sqrt(-p/3.0) math.cos(angle) roots.append(x + shift) else: # One real root using Cardano's radical formula sqrtD = math.sqrt(D) u = cbrt(-q/2 + sqrtD) v = cbrt(-q/2 - sqrtD) roots.append(u + v + shift) # 4. Filter and return smallest valid t valid = [t for t in roots if tin <= t <= tout] return min(valid) if valid else None Parameters: EPSILON: A small threshold for determining if coefficients a or b are negligible. Value not given in the sources. rhoiso: The iso-surface density value. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: The algebraic solution is prone to numerical problems, especially in single-precision floating point, making it difficult to tune to avoid incorrectly computed intersections. Special Cases: Small coefficients A and/or B indicate the polynomial does not have full degree and must be solved more directly (quadratic or linear). Cost: The method involves costly square root, cosine, and inverse cosine operations. Boundary Handling: Roots must be strictly checked against [t{in}, t{out}] to avoid returning intersections outside the current voxel or behind the ray origin. Time Complexity: High. The method requires computing cube roots, square roots, and trigonometric functions (arccos, cos) for every voxel intersection test. Memory Complexity: Low. It requires storing only the polynomial coefficients and a few temporary variables. Performance: Computationally very expensive. It is considered too slow for interactive volume rendering due to speed and numerical stability issues compared to isolation methods. Strengths: Mathematically the most accurate solution for computing intersection in volume ray tracing. It provides exact intersection points. Limitations: Prone to numerical instability, particularly in single precision. The computational cost is prohibitive for real-time applications. When to use: When exact intersection accuracy is critical and performance is not a constraint. When not to use: For interactive volume rendering or when numerical stability in single precision is required. Origin: Introduced by Lin et al. and Parker et al.. The method is also referred to as the Schwarze approach, citing [Sch90] and [PSL+98]. History: It was developed as a highly accurate alternative to approximate methods like the simple midpoint algorithm or linear interpolation refinements. Usage: It is commonly applied in volume ray tracing where exactness is prioritized over speed, though it has largely been superseded by more stable iterative or isolation-based methods for interactive applications. name: Isolation and Iterative Root Finding
head: Isolation method, New intersection algorithm
body: Isolation and Iterative Root Finding is a ray-voxel intersection algorithm designed to locate the first intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface within a voxel. It solves the problem of balancing computational speed with numerical correctness, addressing the inaccuracies of Neubauer's method and the slowness of Schwarze's method. It sets itself apart by first isolating the root interval using polynomial extrema analysis, guaranteeing exactly one root in the final interval, and then applying iterative refinement. This approach is roughly three times faster than Schwarze's method while providing the same correctness guarantees and better numerical stability. The method operates on a cubic polynomial f(t) representing the density along the ray segment [t{in}, t{out}]. The algorithm consists of two phases: root isolation via extrema analysis, followed by iterative root finding. Inputs: Ray segment endpoints t{in} and t{out}. Polynomial coefficients A, B, C, D for f(t) = At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D. Outputs: Intersection parameter t{hit} or "NO HIT". Data Structures: Floating-point variables for t, f, e (extrema). Quadratic solver for f'(t). Steps: 1. Initialization: Set t0 = t{in}, t1 = t{out}. Evaluate f0 = f(t0) and f1 = f(t1). 2. Extrema Analysis: Compute the derivative f'(t) = 3At^2 + 2Bt + C. Solve the quadratic equation f'(t) = 0 for real roots. Let the roots be e0 and e1 with e0 \le e1. If no real roots exist, skip to Step 4. 3. Interval Isolation: Iterate through the extrema to narrow the search interval [t0, t1] to a segment containing exactly one root. For each extremum e \in \{e0, e1\}: If e is not in [t0, t1], continue to the next extremum. If e is in [t0, t1]: Evaluate f(e). If \text{sign}(f(e)) == \text{sign}(f0): The extremum is on the same side of the iso-surface as the start of the current segment. Advance the start of the segment: t0:= e f0:= f(e). Else: The extremum is on the opposite side. The root lies between the previous start and this extremum. Set the end of the segment: t1:= e f1:= f(e). Note: The algorithm processes e0 then e1. If e0 splits the interval, the subsequent check for e1 operates on the new [t0, t1]. 4. Hit Check: If \text{sign}(f0) == \text{sign}(f1), return "NO HIT". Otherwise, the interval [t0, t1] contains exactly one root. 5. Iterative Refinement: Use repeated linear interpolation (regula falsi) to find the root within [t0, t1]. Loop i from 1 to N (typically N=2 or 3): Compute candidate t: t = t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{-f0}{f1 - f0} Evaluate f(t). If \text{sign}(f(t)) == \text{sign}(f0): t0:= t f0:= f(t). Else: t1:= t f1:= f(t). 6. Return Result: Return t{hit} = t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{-f0}{f1 - f0}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. A fixed number is usually faster than an adaptive termination criterion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Three Intersections: Neubauer's method can falsely return the last intersection if three intersections are contained within a voxel and two are in the first segment. Isolation and Iterative Root Finding avoids this by explicitly isolating the first root interval using extrema, ensuring the returned root is the first one. Precision: The method relies on evaluating the polynomial. Since coefficients are known, this avoids costly trilinear interpolation during refinement, improving speed and stability. No Real Extrema: If the discriminant is negative, the polynomial is monotonic in the interval, and the initial [t{in}, t{out}] is used directly.
