name: de Casteljau-based root finding
head: Root Finding: de Casteljau Subdivision (LR81), de Casteljau Subdivision
body: A root finding algorithm for polynomials in Bernstein form that isolates and refines the first intersection of a viewing ray with an isosurface by subdividing the control polygon using the de Casteljau algorithm at its intersection with the zero axis. It sets itself apart from knot insertion methods like [MR07] by offering quadratic convergence speed and constant memory usage without index operations, making it significantly faster for GPU architectures. Inputs and outputs: The method takes a polynomial P(t) in Bernstein basis of degree n defined by control points \mathbf{b}0, \dots, \mathbf{b}n, and an isovalue c. It solves f(t) = P(t) - c = 0 for t \in [0, 1]. The output is the parameter t corresponding to the first root. Data structures: The algorithm stores the Bernstein control polygon as a list or array of scalar values. It requires no auxiliary index arrays or dynamic memory, maintaining constant memory usage throughout execution. Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute the initial control polygon for f(t) = P(t) - c by subtracting the isovalue from each control point. 2. Iteration: Repeat the following subdivision step for a fixed number of iterations k (typically 3 to 7, depending on the interpolation type): a. Find the intersection of the current control polygon with the zero axis by locating the edge that crosses zero. b. Compute the parameter t{split} at this intersection using linear interpolation between the crossing control points. c. Apply the de Casteljau algorithm to subdivide the control polygon at t{split}. d. Select the left segment of the subdivided polygon to isolate the first root. e. Update the control polygon to this selected segment. 3. Result: After k iterations, the remaining control polygon is sufficiently small to approximate the root. Formulas: The de Casteljau algorithm for a parameter t and control points \mathbf{b}i^{(0)} = \mathbf{b}i computes: \mathbf{b}i^{(r)} = (1-t) \mathbf{b}{i-1}^{(r-1)} + t \mathbf{b}i^{(r-1)} for r=1, \dots, n and i=r, \dots, n. The left control points are \mathbf{b}0^{(r)} and the right control points are \mathbf{b}n^{(r)}. Parameters: Number of iterations k: 3 to 7. Edge cases and pitfalls: The method assumes the root is isolated or that the first root is sought. For isolated roots, simpler methods like regula falsi may be faster in the second phase, but the isolation step can cause branch divergence on GPUs. The Bernstein form offers a control polygon with a variation diminishing property. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decasteljaurootfinding(controlpoints, isovalue, numiterations): """ Find the root of P(t) - isovalue = 0 using de Casteljau subdivision. Args: controlpoints: List of control points for the polynomial P(t). isovalue: The isovalue c. numiterations: Number of subdivision iterations (3-7). Returns: t: Approximate root parameter. """ # Initialize control points for f(t) = P(t) - c cp = [p - isovalue for p in controlpoints] tstart, tend = 0.0, 1.0 n = len(cp) - 1 for in range(numiterations): # Find intersection of control polygon with zero axis tsplit = 0.5 # Fallback if no crossing found for i in range(n): if cp[i] cp[i+1] < 0: # Linear interpolation to find exact crossing parameter tsplit = (i + abs(cp[i]) / (abs(cp[i]) + abs(cp[i+1]))) / n break # Compute de Casteljau triangle to extract left control polygon leftcp = [cp[0]] b = list(cp) for r in range(1, n + 1): newb = [] for i in range(len(b) - 1): newb.append((1 - tsplit) b[i] + tsplit b[i+1]) b = newb leftcp.append(b[0]) # Update to the left segment (first root) cp = leftcp tend = tsplit return (tstart + tend) / 2 A root finding algorithm based on knot insertion with linear convergence speed and linear complexity per step. It requires index operations and memory usage grows with every iteration step, limiting the maximum number of iterations. For degree 9 (tri-cubic), it has a relative execution time of 1.0, MSE of 0.034, and max error of 0.85, making it more than 10 times slower than de Casteljau-based root finding. A root finding method using Regula Falsi combined with De Casteljau subdivision for root isolation. While the second phase (Regula Falsi) can outperform de Casteljau-based root finding for isolated roots, the isolation step is not well suited for CUDA due to diverging branches. Time Complexity: Quadratic complexity per step due to the de Casteljau algorithm. Convergence: Quadratic convergence speed. Memory: Constant memory usage, no index operations required. Performance: For degree 9 (tri-cubic), relative execution time is 0.076 (compared to MR07's 1.0), MSE is 0.003, and max error is 0.66. It is more than 10 times faster than the MR07 knot insertion algorithm. Strengths: Fast, constant memory, suitable for GPU (CUDA) due to lack of diverging branches and index operations. Limitations: Fixed number of iterations required; not optimal for isolated roots where simpler methods like Regula Falsi could be faster in the refinement phase. Originated from the work cited as [LR81] in the context of volume rendering using wavelet-based multiresolution isosurface rendering. It is used as a primary root finding method in GPU-based volume rendering pipelines due to its efficiency and suitability for parallel architectures. name: Neubauer Iterative Root Finder
head: Neubauer's method
body: The Neubauer Iterative Root Finder is a numerical method for locating the first positive root of the ray-volume intersection polynomial within a voxel cell. It solves the problem of determining the precise entry point of a ray into an implicit surface defined by a scalar field, specifically within the context of octree-based volume rendering. It is distinguished from analytical solvers (such as Schwarze’s cubic solver) by its reliance on iterative bisection and re-parameterization, offering slightly higher performance and robust single-precision numerical stability. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and a voxel cell (or octree leaf) defined by its spatial bounds. The scalar field values at the cell corners are used to construct the cubic polynomial coefficients a, b, c, d representing the ray's intersection with the cell's boundary or interior function. Output: The parameter t along the ray corresponding to the first positive root (intersection point). Data Structures: The method operates on the cubic polynomial P(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d. No complex data structures are required beyond standard floating-point variables for the ray parameters and polynomial coefficients. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initial Interval: Define the initial search interval for the ray parameter t, typically [t{min}, t{max}], corresponding to the entry and exit points of the ray with respect to the voxel cell boundaries. 2. Iterative Re-parameterization: While the interval width is greater than a specified tolerance \epsilon: Subdivide the current interval [t{start}, t{end}] into smaller sub-intervals. Evaluate the polynomial P(t) at the endpoints of these sub-intervals. Check for a sign change in P(t) between adjacent sub-interval endpoints. 3. Root Isolation: If a sign change is detected within a sub-interval [ti, t{i+1}], a root is guaranteed to exist within this range (by the Intermediate Value Theorem). Set the new search interval to [ti, t{i+1}]. 4. Refinement: Repeat the subdivision and sign-check process on the new, smaller interval. The process terminates when the interval width is sufficiently small or a sign change is definitively isolated. 5. Result: The final t value is taken as the midpoint of the final isolated interval or the endpoint where the sign change was detected, depending on the specific implementation's convergence criteria. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neubaueriterativerootfinder(rayorigin, raydirection, cellbounds, tolerance=1e-6): """ Finds the first positive root of the ray-cell intersection polynomial using iterative re-parameterization and sign-change detection. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) origin of the ray. raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) direction of the ray. cellbounds: Object defining the voxel cell geometry. tolerance: Convergence threshold for interval width. Returns: t: The parameter value of the intersection. """ # 1. Construct polynomial coefficients a, b, c, d for P(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d # This step depends on the specific scalar field definition and cell geometry. # Standard ray-triangle or ray-box intersection polynomial derivation is assumed here. a, b, c, d = computepolynomialcoefficients(rayorigin, raydirection, cellbounds) # 2. Define initial search interval [tmin, tmax] # tmin is typically 0 or the entry point into the cell; tmax is the exit point. tmin = 0.0 tmax = computeexitparameter(rayorigin, raydirection, cellbounds) if tmax < tmin: return None # No intersection within valid range # 3. Iterative refinement while (tmax - tmin) > tolerance: # Subdivide the current interval into smaller sub-intervals # The sources do not specify the exact number of subdivisions per step. # A common approach is binary subdivision (bisection) or fixed small steps. # We assume binary subdivision for robustness as implied by "iterative re-parameterization". tmid = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 # Evaluate polynomial at endpoints of sub-intervals pmin = evaluatepolynomial(a, b, c, d, tmin) pmid = evaluatepolynomial(a, b, c, d, tmid) # Check for sign change if pmin pmid < 0: # Root is in [tmin, tmid] tmax = tmid else: # Root is in [tmid, tmax] (or no root in this branch, but we assume one exists) # If no sign change is found in the left half, the root must be in the right half # if we know a root exists in the original interval. tmin = tmid # 4. Return the estimated root return (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 def evaluatepolynomial(a, b, c, d, t): return a t3 + b t2 + c t + d Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method is noted for yielding numerically stable results in single-precision arithmetic, avoiding the catastrophic cancellation issues that can plague analytical cubic solvers. Degenerate Input: If the ray is tangent to the surface or misses the cell entirely, the sign change detection may fail. The algorithm assumes a root exists within the initial interval. Multiple Roots: The method finds the first sign change. If multiple roots exist within the cell, it finds the smallest t (closest to the ray origin) provided the subdivision strategy explores from t{min} upwards. Time Complexity: The convergence rate depends on the subdivision strategy. With binary subdivision, it is logarithmic with respect to the desired precision (O(\log(1/\epsilon))). Memory Complexity: O(1), as it only requires storing a few floating-point variables. Performance: It is slightly faster than analytical root finders based on Schwarze's cubic solver. Strengths: Numerical stability in single-precision; simplicity of implementation; no need for complex trigonometric or square-root operations required by analytical solutions. Limitations: Iterative nature may be slower than a direct analytical solution if high precision is not required; requires careful handling of the initial interval and sign change detection. The Neubauer Iterative Root Finder was proposed by Marmitt et al. as an improvement over analytical cubic solvers for ray-tracing implicit surfaces in large octree volumes. It is based on the Neubauer iterative root finding technique. The method was employed in the context of interactive isosurface ray tracing, where performance and stability in single-precision arithmetic are critical. name: Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection
head: Cell Intersection, Isosurface Intersection (Neubauer iterative root finder), Isosurface Intersection via Neubauer Iterative Root Finder, Marmitt et al. 03 method, Marmitt et al. root finder, Neubauer iterative root finder, Ray-Isosurface Intersection
body: Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection computes the intersection point of a ray with an isosurface defined by trilinear interpolation inside a 3D voxel cell. It solves for the first positive root of the cubic polynomial derived from the cell's corner values using an iterative bisection refinement strategy. Compared to analytical cubic solvers like Schwarze’s method, this approach is slightly faster and yields single-precision, numerically stable results. It implements the Neubauer iterative root finder. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Isosurface value I{\text{iso}}. Eight scalar values v0, \dots, v7 at the corners of the 3D cell. Outputs: Intersection parameter t along the ray. If no root exists in [0, \infty), the method reports no intersection. Data Structures: The cell is defined by 8 scalar values. No additional geometric data structures are required beyond the corner values and the ray parameters. Algorithm Steps: 1. Cell Reconstruction: Reconstruct the cell from octree voxel data using forward neighbors. 2. Polynomial Formulation: Compute the cubic polynomial P(t) such that P(t) = 0 corresponds to the trilinear interpolation of the cell values equaling I{\text{iso}} along the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. The coefficients are derived by substituting the ray equation into the trilinear basis functions. 3. Iterative Root Finding: Iteratively re-parameterize the ray into sub-intervals within the cell until a sign change is detected within the sub-interval and a root is found. 4. Hit Position: Evaluate the ray at the first positive root of the cubic polynomial to obtain the intersection point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marmittraycellintersection(rayorigin, raydir, cornervalues, isovalue, tolerance=1e-6): """ rayorigin: (ox, oy, oz) raydir: (dx, dy, dz) cornervalues: list of 8 floats [v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111] isovalue: float tolerance: float, convergence threshold Returns: t (float) or None """ ox, oy, oz = rayorigin dx, dy, dz = raydir v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111 = cornervalues def evaluatetrilinear(t): x = ox + t dx y = oy + t dy z = oz + t dz val = (v000 (1 - x) (1 - y) (1 - z) + v100 x (1 - y) (1 - z) + v010 (1 - x) y (1 - z) + v110 x y (1 - z) + v001 (1 - x) (1 - y) z + v101 x (1 - y) z + v011 (1 - x) y z + v111 x y z) return val - isovalue tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') pmin = evaluatetrilinear(tmin) while tmax - tmin > tolerance: tmid = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 pmid = evaluatetrilinear(tmid) if pmin pmid < 0: tmax = tmid else: tmin = tmid pmin = pmid if tmax == float('inf'): tmax = tmin 2.0 + 1.0 pmax = evaluatetrilinear(tmax) if pmin pmax > 0: return None return (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Sign Change: If the polynomial does not change sign within the cell, there is no intersection. Precision: Single-precision arithmetic is used, which yields numerically stable results. Gradient Computation: Normals are computed using a forward-difference stencil on the same cell to avoid the high cost of neighbor-finding. Time Complexity: The root finding uses iterative bisection, converging logarithmically with precision. Each iteration evaluates the trilinear polynomial in constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray, as no cell data needs to be stored per ray. Performance: Slightly faster than analytical cubic solvers. Strengths: Numerically stable in single precision. Simple to implement. Limitations: Iterative nature may be slower than a direct analytical solution if the solver is highly optimized, but the source claims it is faster. Requires cell reconstruction (neighbor finding) which is costly if not cached. The method is based on the Neubauer iterative root finder proposed by Marmitt et al.. It is described in the context of isosurface ray tracing of octree volumes. The approach was compared to Schwarze’s cubic solver used by Parker et al. and found to be faster and more stable in single precision. name: Fast Ray-Surface Intersection
head: Fast Intersection, Linear Interpolation Approximation for Ray-Surface Intersection
body: Fast Ray-Surface Intersection is an approximate method for determining the intersection point of a ray with an iso-surface within a volume rendering cell, trading geometric accuracy for computational speed. It solves the problem of finding the first-hit surface location without the high cost of inverting trilinear interpolation. Unlike exact intersection methods which compute all roots of the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation, this method subdivides the ray segment within the cell and uses linear interpolation to estimate the hit point, producing visually indistinguishable results in final renderings while being significantly faster. Inputs: Ray segment parameters: entry point R(t{in}) and exit point R(t{out}) of the ray within the current voxel/cell. Iso-value threshold \rho{iso}. Density field \rho(x,y,z), accessible via trilinear interpolation at arbitrary points. Outputs: Approximate intersection parameter t{hit} along the ray. Boolean flag indicating whether an intersection was found. Data Structures: Fields, sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. The method operates on the scalar density values sampled at specific points along the ray. No complex data structures are required beyond the volume grid and the ray parameters. Steps: 1. Subdivision: Divide the complete path of the ray through the surface cell into two parts of equal length. Let the midpoint parameter be t{mid} = \frac{t{in} + t{out}}{2}. The two sub-segments are [t{in}, t{mid}] and [t{mid}, t{out}]. 2. Sampling: Calculate the density values at the end points of each part of the path. Specifically, evaluate \rho(t{in}), \rho(t{mid}), and \rho(t{out}). 3. Intersection Check: Determine if any iso-surface is intersected by the corresponding part of the ray based on the density values. An intersection exists in a segment [ta, tb] if the iso-value \rho{iso} lies between the density values at the endpoints. Mathematically, for a segment with endpoints ta and tb, an intersection is indicated if: (\rho(ta) - \rho{iso}) \cdot (\rho(tb) - \rho{iso}) \le 0. 4. Refinement: If an intersection exists, find an approximation of the intersection point by linear interpolation. If the intersection is in [t{in}, t{mid}], compute t{hit} based on \rho(t{in}) and \rho(t{mid}). If it is in [t{mid}, t{out}], compute t{hit} based on \rho(t{mid}) and \rho(t{out}). The linear interpolation formula is: t{hit} = ta + (\rho{iso} - \rho(ta)) \frac{tb - ta}{\rho(tb) - \rho(ta)} 5. Termination: Compute the color value and assign it to the pixel. If no intersection exists for a part, continue voxel traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastraysurfaceintersection(tin, tout, rhoiso, sampledensity): """ Approximates ray-surface intersection by subdividing the ray segment and using linear interpolation. Args: tin (float): t parameter at ray entry into the cell. tout (float): t parameter at ray exit from the cell. rhoiso (float): The density threshold for the iso-surface. sampledensity (callable): Function that returns density at a given t along the ray, i.e., sampledensity(t). Returns: float or None: The approximate t value of the intersection, or None if not found. """ # Step 1: Divide the path into two equal parts tmid = (tin + tout) / 2.0 # Step 2: Calculate density values at endpoints rhoin = sampledensity(tin) rhomid = sampledensity(tmid) rhoout = sampledensity(tout) # Helper for linear interpolation of t given two densities and their t values def linearinterpolate(t1, rho1, t2, rho2, targetrho): # Avoid division by zero if abs(rho1 - rho2) < 1e-9: return (t1 + t2) / 2.0 # Linear interpolation formula: t = t1 + (target - rho1) (t2 - t1) / (rho2 - rho1) return t1 + (targetrho - rho1) (t2 - t1) / (rho2 - rho1) # Step 3 & 4: Check first half [tin, tmid] if (rhoin - rhoiso) (rhomid - rhoiso) <= 0: thit = linearinterpolate(tin, rhoin, tmid, rhomid, rhoiso) return thit # Check second half [tmid, tout] if (rhomid - rhoiso) (rhoout - rhoiso) <= 0: thit = linearinterpolate(tmid, rhomid, tout, rhoout, rhoiso) return thit # Step 5: No intersection found in either part return None Parameters: Subdivision count: Fixed at 2 (one midpoint). Interpolation method: Linear. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear interpolation assumes the density function is linear within the sub-segment. The method produces visible differences in some pixels compared to exact intersection, but these are not visible in the final visualization results. Boundaries: If the ray grazes the iso-surface exactly at a sample point, the product term becomes zero, correctly identifying an intersection. Degenerate Input: If the density values at the endpoints are identical and equal to the iso-value, the interpolation denominator is zero. A simplistic approximate intersection method that assumes an intersection for every voxel where the iso-value is within the range of data values at the vertices. The intersection point is set to the midpoint between the ray's entry point (t{in}) and exit point (t{out}). This method is fast but leads to blocky artifacts of the size of voxels, so it is typically used only as a reference for performance comparisons rather than in production. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is O(1) per cell, requiring only 3 density samples and basic arithmetic operations. Memory complexity is O(1), requiring no additional storage beyond local variables. Measured Performance: The method is significantly faster than exact intersection methods which invert trilinear interpolation. Visual comparison shows that while there are pixel-level differences between fast and exact intersection, these differences are not visible in the final visualization results. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High speed, low computational overhead, visually acceptable results for many applications. Limitations: Lower geometric accuracy compared to exact methods; potential for small artifacts in high-frequency density regions. When to Use: Use when rendering speed is critical and the visual difference between exact and approximate intersection is imperceptible in the final image. Avoid when precise geometric accuracy is required, such as in scientific visualization where exact surface location is critical for measurement. The Fast Ray-Surface Intersection method was introduced as a faster alternative to exact ray-surface intersection techniques in the context of cell-based first-hit ray casting. Exact methods, such as those by Lin et al. and Parker et al., invert trilinear interpolation to find all points assigned a specific density value, which is computationally expensive. The fast intersection method trades this accuracy for speed by using linear interpolation on subdivided paths. It is part of the broader family of approximate ray-surface intersection techniques used in volume rendering to optimize performance. name: Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement
head: Linear Interpolation Root Finding for SDF, Secant Refinement
body: The Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the depth value d where a signed distance function (SDF) or occupancy logit crosses a threshold. It estimates the next intersection point using linear interpolation between two bracketing points. Inputs: ray0: Origin point of the ray (3D vector). ray\direction: Direction vector of the ray (normalized). d{low}: Array of lower bound depths (floats). d{high}: Array of upper bound depths (floats). f{low}: Array of function values at d{low} (floats). f{high}: Array of function values at d{high} (floats). n{secant\steps}: Number of refinement iterations (integer). decoder: Function evaluating the neural field. c: Camera parameters or context for the decoder. logit\tau: Threshold value for the occupancy logit. Outputs: d{pred}: Refined depth values where the root is estimated. Data Structures: Arrays d{low}, d{high}, f{low}, f{high}, d{pred} are parallel vectors of size N (number of rays), supporting batched processing. Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute the initial prediction d{pred} for all rays using linear interpolation between the bracketing points: d{pred} = - f{low} \cdot \frac{d{high} - d{low}}{f{high} - f{low}} + d{low} 2. Iteration: For each iteration i from 0 to n{secant\steps} - 1: a. Ray Casting: Compute the 3D point p{mid} for each ray: p{mid} = ray0 + d{pred} \cdot ray\direction b. Evaluation: Evaluate the function f{mid} at p{mid}. This involves calling the decoder with the point and context, subtracting the threshold, and disabling gradient tracking: f{mid} = decoder(p{mid}, c, only\occupancy=True) - logit\tau c. Bracket Update: Identify indices where f{mid} < 0 as ind{low}. If ind{low} contains any true values, update the lower bracket: d{low}[ind{low}] = d{pred}[ind{low}] f{low}[ind{low}] = f{mid}[ind{low}] Identify indices where f{mid} \ge 0 (i.e., ind{low} == 0). If these exist, update the upper bracket: d{high}[ind{low}==0] = d{pred}[ind{low}==0] f{high}[ind{low}==0] = f{mid}[ind{low}==0] d. Recalculation: Update d{pred} using the new bracketing values: d{pred} = - f{low} \cdot \frac{d{high} - d{low}}{f{high} - f{low}} + d{low} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def secantrefinement(ray0, raydirection, dlow, dhigh, flow, fhigh, nsecantsteps, decoder, c, logittau): """ Refine surface depth using the Secant Method. Args: ray0: List of (x, y, z) tuples, ray origins. raydirection: List of (dx, dy, dz) tuples, ray directions. dlow: List of floats, lower depth bounds. dhigh: List of floats, upper depth bounds. flow: List of floats, function values at dlow. fhigh: List of floats, function values at dhigh. nsecantsteps: int, number of iterations. decoder: Function(p, c, onlyoccupancy=True) -> float. c: Context/camera parameters. logittau: float, threshold. Returns: dpred: List of floats, refined depths. """ N = len(dlow) # Step 1: Initialize prediction denom = [fhigh[i] - flow[i] for i in range(N)] # Guard against zero denominator denom = [d if d != 0.0 else 1e-8 for d in denom] dpred = [-flow[i] ((dhigh[i] - dlow[i]) / denom[i]) + dlow[i] for i in range(N)] for in range(nsecantsteps): # Step 2a: Compute 3D points pmid = [(ray0[i][0] + dpred[i] raydirection[i][0], ray0[i][1] + dpred[i] raydirection[i][1], ray0[i][2] + dpred[i] raydirection[i][2]) for i in range(N)] # Step 2b: Evaluate function without gradients fmid = [decoder(pmid[i], c, onlyoccupancy=True) - logittau for i in range(N)] # Step 2c: Update brackets indlow = [i for i in range(N) if fmid[i] < 0] # Update lower bracket where fmid < 0 for i in indlow: dlow[i] = dpred[i] flow[i] = fmid[i] # Update upper bracket where fmid >= 0 indhigh = [i for i in range(N) if fmid[i] >= 0] for i in indhigh: dhigh[i] = dpred[i] fhigh[i] = fmid[i] # Step 2d: Recalculate prediction denom = [fhigh[i] - flow[i] for i in range(N)] denom = [d if d != 0.0 else 1e-8 for d in denom] dpred = [-flow[i] ((dhigh[i] - dlow[i]) / denom[i]) + dlow[i] for i in range(N)] return dpred Parameters: n{secant\steps}: Integer specifying the number of refinement iterations. Typical value: 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If f{high} == f{low}, the denominator in the interpolation formula becomes zero. A small epsilon or fallback to bisection is required. Non-Bracketing: The method assumes f{low} < 0 and f{high} > 0 (or vice versa). If the initial segment does not bracket a root, the method may diverge or converge to a non-root extremum. A procedure to detect surface points along rays by evaluating a neural decoder at proposal points, identifying sign changes in occupancy logits, and refining the depth using the Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement. It sets itself apart from its siblings by combining coarse uniform sampling with a specific sign-change detection logic that identifies negative-to-positive transitions, followed by the Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement to pinpoint the zero-crossing. It builds on Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement. A root-finding algorithm combining linear interpolation and the midpoint algorithm. It finds the exact intersection point even if the field function is not continuous. Implementation is in IsoMesher::intersectxaxis(), IsoMesher::intersectyaxis(), and IsoMesher::intersectzaxis(). The algorithm used is determined by the preprocessor symbol FALSEPOSITION. It is no worse than the midpoint algorithm in terms of iterations and usually better, making it the preferred choice for finding exact intersection points. Time Complexity: O(n{secant\steps} \cdot N), where N is the number of rays. Each step involves a decoder evaluation and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the bracketing arrays and intermediate points. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for monotonic functions, no derivative calculation required. Limitations: Can fail if the function is not continuous or if the initial brackets do not contain a root. When to Use: When a fast, derivative-free root-finding method is needed for smooth implicit surfaces or neural fields. When Not to Use: When the function is discontinuous (use False Position or Bisection) or when high precision is required with minimal iterations (use Newton's method if derivatives are available). The Secant Method is a classical root-finding algorithm that approximates the derivative using finite differences. In the context of volume rendering and neural fields, it is used to refine the depth of surface intersections detected during ray marching. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching with Secant Refinement
body:
This method detects surface intersections along camera rays by evaluating a neural occupancy decoder at discrete proposal points, identifying sign changes in the occupancy logits, and refining the depth estimate using the secant method. It differs from standard uniform ray marching by adaptively focusing computation on rays containing a surface transition and using linear interpolation between bracketing points for higher precision than simple bisection. Inputs: ray0: Origin of rays, shape (B, N, 3). raydirection: Direction of rays, shape (B, N, 3). decoder: Neural network function decoder(p, c) returning occupancy logits, where p is position and c is context/latent code. c: Context/latent code, shape (B, N, Dc). depthrange: Tuple (d{min}, d{max}) defining the search interval. tau: Probability threshold for occupancy. nsteps: Tuple (n{min}, n{max}) for sampling the number of proposal steps. maxpoints: Integer limit for GPU memory management during decoder evaluation. checkcubeintersection: Boolean flag to intersect proposals with a unit cube. Outputs: dpred: Refined depth values, shape (B, N). ptpred: 3D surface points, shape (B, N, 3). Data Structures: dproposal: Tensor of shape (B, N, n{steps}, 1) containing linearly spaced depth values. val: Tensor of shape (B, N, n{steps}, 1) containing decoder(p, c) - logit	au. signmatrix: Tensor of shape (B, N, n{steps}) indicating sign changes. costmatrix: Tensor of shape (B, N, n{steps}) used for efficient argmin search. Steps: 1. Threshold Conversion: Convert the probability threshold 	au to a logit threshold: logit	au = 	ext{get\logits rom\prob}(	au) getlogitsfromprob is the inverse sigmoid function: \log( rac{	au}{1-	au}). 2. Sample Steps: Sample an integer n{steps} uniformly from the range [n{steps}[0], n{steps}[1]]. 3. Generate Proposals: Create linearly spaced depth proposals d{proposal} from depthange[0] to depthange[1] with n{steps} points, shaped (B, N, n{steps}, 1). 4. Cube Intersection (Optional): If checkcubeintersection is true, compute intersection with unit cube and replace d{proposal} values inside the cube with cube-intersection depths. 5. Compute Proposal Points: Calculate the 3D coordinates for all proposals: p{proposal} = ray0 + ray\direction \cdot d{proposal}. 6. Evaluate Decoder: Evaluate the decoder at all proposal points in parallel, splitting into chunks of size maxpoints / batchsize to manage GPU memory. Compute the value tensor: val = decoder(p, c, only\occupancy=True) - logit	au. 7. Initial Occupancy Mask: Create a mask for rays where the first proposal point is not occupied: mask\0
ot\occupied = val[:,:, 0] < 0. 8. Sign Change Detection: Compute the sign change matrix. For each adjacent pair of proposals, check if the product of their values is negative (indicating a sign change). Append a column of 1s to maintain dimensions: sign\matrix = [sign(val[:,:,:-1] \cdot val[:,:, 1:]), 1]. Compute a cost matrix to find the first sign change efficiently. The cost matrix weights earlier indices lower: cost\matrix = sign\matrix \cdot [n{steps}, n{steps}-1, \dots, 1]. 9. Find First Sign Change: Find the index of the minimum cost value for each ray: (values, indices) = argmin(cost\matrix). Identify valid sign changes (where the product was actually negative): mask\sign\change = values < 0. 10. Identify Transition Direction: Identify rays where the transition is from negative to positive (specifically where the lower bound is negative): mask
eg	o\pos = val[batch\indices, point\indices, indices] < 0. 11. Combine Masks: Combine all conditions to determine valid rays for refinement: mask = mask\sign\change \land mask
eg	o\pos \land mask\0
ot\occupied. 12. Extract Brackets: For valid rays, extract the bracketing depths and function values: Lower bracket: d{low} = d{proposal}[indices], f{low} = val[indices]. Upper bracket: d{high} = d{proposal}[indices + 1], f{high} = val[indices + 1]. Clamp indices to n{steps}-1 to prevent out-of-bounds access. 13. Refine Depth: Apply the Secant Method (or Bisection) on the masked rays using the extracted brackets (d{low}, f{low}) and (d{high}, f{high}) to compute the refined depth d{pred}. 14. Compute Final Points: Calculate the final 3D surface points for valid rays: pt{pred}[mask] = ray0{masked} + d{pred} \cdot ray\direction{masked}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def getlogitsfromprob(prob): """Inverse sigmoid.""" return math.log(prob / (1.0 - prob)) def raymarchingwithsecantrefinement(ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, depthrange, tau, nstepsrange, maxpoints, checkcubeintersection=False): """ ray0: (B, N, 3) raydirection: (B, N, 3) c: (B, N, Dc) Returns: dpred (B, N), ptpred (B, N, 3) """ B, N, = ray0.shape device = ray0.device # 1. Threshold Conversion logittau = getlogitsfromprob(tau) # 2. Sample Steps nsteps = random.randint(nstepsrange[0], nstepsrange[1]) # 3. Generate Proposals dproposal = [[[depthrange[0] + i (depthrange[1] - depthrange[0]) / (nsteps - 1)] for i in range(nsteps)] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] # 4. Cube Intersection if checkcubeintersection: # Sources do not provide cube intersection logic. pass # 5. Compute Proposal Points pproposal = [[[ray0[b][n][k] + raydirection[b][n][k] dproposal[b][n][s][0] for k in range(3)] for s in range(nsteps)] for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 6. Evaluate Decoder (Chunked) val = [[[0.0] for in range(nsteps)] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] chunksize = maxpoints // B flatp = [p for b in pproposal for n in b for s in b[n] for p in s] flatc = [c for b in c for n in b for in range(nsteps)] for i in range(0, len(flatp), chunksize): chunkp = flatp[i:i+chunksize] chunkc = flatc[i:i+chunksize] chunkval = [decoder(p, c, onlyoccupancy=True) - logittau for p, c in zip(chunkp, chunkc)] for j, v in enumerate(chunkval): idx = i + j b, rem = divmod(idx, N nsteps) n, s = divmod(rem, nsteps) val[b][n][s] = [v] # 7. Initial Occupancy Mask mask0notoccupied = [[val[b][n][0][0] < 0 for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 8. Sign Change Detection signmatrix = [[[0] nsteps for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): for s in range(nsteps - 1): prod = val[b][n][s][0] val[b][n][s+1][0] signmatrix[b][n][s] = -1 if prod < 0 else 1 signmatrix[b][n][nsteps-1] = 1 weights = [nsteps - s for s in range(nsteps)] costmatrix = [[[signmatrix[b][n][s] weights[s] for s in range(nsteps)] for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 9. Find First Sign Change indices = [[[0] nsteps for in range(N)] for in range(B)] values = [[[0.0] nsteps for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): minval = math.inf minidx = 0 for s in range(nsteps): if costmatrix[b][n][s] < minval: minval = costmatrix[b][n][s] minidx = s values[b][n][0] = minval indices[b][n][0] = minidx masksignchange = [[values[b][n][0] < 0 for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 10. Identify Transition Direction masknegtopos = [[val[b][n][indices[b][n][0]][0] < 0 for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 11. Combine Masks mask = [[masksignchange[b][n] and masknegtopos[b][n] and mask0notoccupied[b][n] for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 12. Extract Brackets dlow = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] flow = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] dhigh = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] fhigh = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): idx = indices[b][n][0] upperidx = min(idx + 1, nsteps - 1) dlow[b][n][0] = dproposal[b][n][idx][0] flow[b][n][0] = val[b][n][idx][0] dhigh[b][n][0] = dproposal[b][n][upperidx][0] fhigh[b][n][0] = val[b][n][upperidx][0] # 13. Refine Depth (Secant Method) dpred = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): denom = fhigh[b][n][0] - flow[b][n][0] if abs(denom) < 1e-8: denom = 1.0 dpred[b][n][0] = dhigh[b][n][0] - fhigh[b][n][0] (dhigh[b][n][0] - dlow[b][n][0]) / denom # 14. Compute Final Points ptpred = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): if mask[b][n]: ptpred[b][n][0] = ray0[b][n][0] + dpred[b][n][0] raydirection[b][n][0] ptpred[b][n][1] = ray0[b][n][1] + dpred[b][n][0] raydirection[b][n][1] ptpred[b][n][2] = ray0[b][n][2] + dpred[b][n][0] raydirection[b][n][2] return dpred, ptpred Parameters: maxpoints: Integer, maximum number of points loaded to GPU memory per batch to prevent OOM. Typical value: 3,500,000. nsteps: Tuple of integers defining the range for sampling the number of evaluation steps. Typical value: [128, 129]. depthrange: Tuple of floats defining the range of possible depth values. Typical value: [0.0, 2.4]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: In the secant step, if f{high} \approx f{low}, the denominator becomes zero. A guard is required. Index Out of Bounds: When indices is the last step, indices + 1 may exceed bounds. Clamping to n{steps}-1 is required. No Sign Change: Rays that do not cross the threshold are masked out and return default values (e.g., zero or NaN depending on implementation). GPU Memory: Large batch sizes or high n{steps} can exceed VRAM. Chunking the decoder evaluation is necessary. This method implements a PyTorch Autograd Function that wraps the ray marching process, allowing gradients to flow through the depth prediction to the decoder parameters and latent code. Time Complexity: Dominated by the decoder evaluation O(B \cdot N \cdot n{steps}). The refinement step is O(B \cdot N). Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot N \cdot n{steps}) for storing proposals and values. Mitigated by chunking. Performance: Depends heavily on the decoder's inference speed and GPU memory bandwidth. Strengths: Adaptive sampling reduces unnecessary evaluations on empty space; secant refinement provides sub-pixel accuracy. Limitations: Requires sign changes to be detected; fails if the surface is not crossed within the proposal range or if the threshold is not crossed. This method is part of the Differentiable Volumetric Rendering pipeline, specifically used for extracting depth maps from neural implicit representations. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Depth Function Forward/Backward Pass
head: DepthFunction.backward, DepthFunction.forward
body: This method implements the forward and backward passes for a differentiable depth prediction module in neural volume rendering. It wraps the ray marching process (specifically Ray Marching with Secant Refinement) within a PyTorch autograd.Function to enable gradient flow from the rendered depth output back to the neural decoder parameters and latent codes. It distinguishes itself by explicitly reconstructing the occupancy gradient along the ray direction to compute the depth sensitivity, allowing end-to-end training of implicit surface representations. Inputs: ray0: Origin of rays, shape (N, 3). raydirection: Unit direction vectors of rays, shape (N, 3). decoder: Neural network module (implicit decoder) taking position and latent code. c: Latent codes for each ray, shape (N, Dc). nsteps: Number of coarse sampling steps. nsecantsteps: Number of secant refinement steps. tau: Temperature parameter for soft thresholding. depthrange: Tuple (d{min}, d{max}) defining the sampling interval. method: String specifying the marching algorithm. checkcubeintersection: Boolean flag for bounding box checks. maxpoints: Maximum number of points to store. gradoutput: Gradient tensor from the loss function w.r.t the forward output, shape (N). Outputs: dpred: Predicted depth values, shape (N). ppred: Predicted 3D positions corresponding to dpred, shape (N, 3). mask: Boolean mask indicating valid depth predictions, shape (N). Data Structures: dpred: Float tensor. Invalid depths are set to \infty or 0 based on specific masks. ppred: Float tensor. Saved for backward pass. mask: Boolean tensor. Tracks validity. Steps: 1. Forward Pass: 1. Call performraymarching(ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, nsteps, nsecantsteps, tau, depthrange, method, checkcubeintersection, maxpoints) to obtain raw depth predictions draw, positions praw, and validity masks. 2. Apply invalid depth handling: If a ray fails to intersect or is invalid (mask == 0), set d{pred}[mask==0] = \infty. If a ray is valid but the surface is not occupied (mask0notoccupied == 0), set d{pred}[mask\0\not\occupied==0] = 0. 3. Save ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, and c for the backward pass. 4. Return dpred. 2. Backward Pass: 1. Retrieve saved tensors: ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, c. 2. Enable gradient computation for ppred: ppred.requiresgrad(True). 3. Evaluate the decoder's occupancy logit at the predicted positions: fp = \text{decoder}(p{pred}, c, \text{only\occupancy}=\text{True}) Here, fp is the scalar occupancy value (logit) for each point. 4. Compute the gradient of the occupancy w.r.t. the positions: \text{grad\p} = \frac{\partial fp}{\partial p{pred}} Shape: (N, 3). 5. Compute the directional derivative along the ray direction (dot product): \text{grad\p\dot\v} = \sum{dim=1}^{3} (\text{grad\p}{:, dim} \cdot \text{ray\direction}{:, dim}) Shape: (N). This represents the rate of change of occupancy along the ray. 6. Clamp small gradients to avoid division by zero: \text{grad\p\dot\v}[|\text{grad\p\dot\v}| < \epsilon] = \epsilon where \epsilon = 10^{-3}. 7. Set gradients for invalid masks to 1 to prevent gradient flow into invalid regions: \text{grad\p\dot\v}[mask==0] = 1. 8. Compute the gradient w.r.t the depth output: \text{grad\outputs} = - \frac{\text{grad\output}}{\text{grad\p\dot\v}} \cdot mask Shape: (N). The negative sign arises from the chain rule through the depth-position mapping. 9. Compute gradient w.r.t. latent code c: \text{grad\c} = \frac{\partial fp}{\partial c} Specifically, compute the gradient of fp w.r.t c using gradoutputs as the upstream gradient. 10. Compute gradient w.r.t. decoder parameters \phi: \text{grad\\phi} = \frac{\partial fp}{\partial \phi} Specifically, compute the gradient of fp w.r.t \phi using gradoutputs as the upstream gradient. 11. Return None for ray0, raydirection, decoder, nsteps, etc., and gradc, grad\\phi for the latent code and decoder parameters respectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DepthFunction(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, nsteps, nsecantsteps, tau, depthrange, method, checkcubeintersection, maxpoints, gradoutput): # 1. Perform Ray Marching (defined in Ray Marching with Secant Refinement) dpred, ppred, mask, mask0notoccupied = performraymarching( ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, nsteps, nsecantsteps, tau, depthrange, method, checkcubeintersection, maxpoints) # 2. Handle Invalid Depths dpred[mask == 0] = float('inf') dpred[mask0notoccupied == 0] = 0.0 # 3. Save for Backward ctx.saveforbackward(ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, c) ctx.gradoutput = gradoutput ctx.mask = mask ctx.decoder = decoder return dpred @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradoutput): ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, c = ctx.savedtensors mask = ctx.mask decoder = ctx.decoder # 1. Enable gradients for ppred ppred.requiresgrad(True) # 2. Evaluate Occupancy fp = decoder(ppred, c, onlyoccupancy=True) # 3. Gradient of fp w.r.t ppred gradp = torch.autograd.grad( fp, ppred, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(fp), creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] # 4. Dot product with ray direction gradpdotv = torch.sum(gradp raydirection, dim=1) # 5. Clamp small gradients epsilon = 1e-3 gradpdotv = torch.where( torch.abs(gradpdotv) < epsilon, torch.fulllike(gradpdotv, epsilon), gradpdotv) # 6. Set invalid mask gradients to 1 gradpdotv[mask == 0] = 1.0 # 7. Compute output gradients (depth gradient) gradfpupstream = - (gradoutput / gradpdotv) mask.float() # 8. Compute gradient w.r.t latent code c gradc = torch.autograd.grad( fp, c, gradoutputs=gradfpupstream, retaingraph=True)[0] # 9. Compute gradient w.r.t decoder parameters phi gradphi = torch.autograd.grad( fp, decoder.parameters(), gradoutputs=gradfpupstream, retaingraph=True) # 10. Return gradients return ( None, None, None, gradc, None, None, None, None, None, None, None, None) Parameters: \epsilon = 10^{-3}: Clamping threshold for gradient stability. Edge Cases: Invalid Rays: Rays that do not intersect the volume or fail to find a surface are masked out. Their depth is set to \infty or 0, and their gradient contribution is nullified or clamped to prevent instability. Zero Gradient: If the occupancy gradient along the ray is near zero (e.g., inside a uniform volume or far from surface), clamping prevents division by zero. A neural network module that predicts a depth distribution for each ray from image features, sampling discrete depth values and probability density function (PDF) values to represent surface geometry. It differs from the standard DepthPredictor by explicitly modeling multiple surfaces and using a distribution sampler to handle the stochastic nature of depth estimation, building on the differentiable forward/backward pass of Differentiable Depth Function Forward/Backward Pass. The DepthPredictor is a PyTorch nn.Module that implements the depth prediction pipeline for differentiable volume rendering. It integrates a distribution sampler with conversion functions to transform raw feature tensors into probabilistic depth estimates and associated opacities. It differs from sibling methods like Monocular Depth Predictor with Distribution Sampling by explicitly handling the unbinding of PDF and offset channels, sampling from the resulting discrete distribution, and computing opacity via a cumulative transmittance formulation. Time Complexity: Dominated by the forward ray marching step, which involves N \times (n{steps} + n{secant\steps}) decoder evaluations. The backward pass requires an additional N decoder evaluations to compute the occupancy gradient and potentially more for the latent code/decoder gradients depending on implementation. Memory Complexity: Stores intermediate positions and gradients for all sampled points. The backward pass requires storing the graph for the decoder evaluation at p{pred}. Strengths: Enables end-to-end training of implicit surfaces by providing gradients through the depth prediction. Handles invalid rays gracefully. Limitations: Sensitive to the clamping parameter \epsilon. Requires the decoder to be differentiable. Performance depends on the efficiency of the underlying ray marching implementation. When to Use: When training neural radiance fields or implicit surface representations where depth supervision is available or desired. When Not to Use: If non-differentiable rendering is sufficient, or if the decoder is not differentiable. This method is part of the differentiable volumetric rendering framework, specifically designed to integrate depth prediction into the training loop. It builds upon the Ray Marching with Secant Refinement method to provide a differentiable interface for depth estimation. The approach allows gradients to flow from the depth loss to the neural decoder, enabling the optimization of implicit surface representations. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Monocular Depth Predictor with Distribution Sampling
head: DepthPredictorMonocular
body: A neural network module that predicts a depth distribution for each ray from image features, sampling discrete depth values and probability density function (PDF) values to represent surface geometry. It explicitly models multiple surfaces and uses a distribution sampler for stochastic depth estimation, building on the differentiable forward/backward pass of Differentiable Depth Function Forward/Backward Pass. Inputs: features: Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, channel) representing image features. near: Tensor of shape (batch, view) specifying the near plane distance. far: Tensor of shape (batch, view) specifying the far plane distance. deterministic: Boolean flag controlling sampling behavior. gaussiansperpixel: Integer specifying the number of Gaussian samples per pixel. Outputs: depth: Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, surface, sample) containing sampled depth values. pdf: Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, surface, sample) containing the probability density values for the sampled depths. Data Structures: The class DepthPredictorMonocular contains the following fields: projection: An nn.Sequential module. sampler: A DistributionSampler instance. numsamples: Integer, number of depth samples per surface. numsurfaces: Integer, number of distinct surfaces to model. usetransmittance: Boolean flag for transmittance usage. Steps: 1. Initialize self.projection as an nn.Sequential containing nn.ReLU() followed by nn.Linear(din, 2 numsamples numsurfaces), where din is the input channel dimension of features. 2. Initialize self.sampler as a DistributionSampler instance. 3. Initialize self.topdf as nn.Softmax(dim=-1) and self.tooffset as nn.Sigmoid(). 4. In the forward pass, pass features through self.projection to get raw logits of shape (batch, view, ray, 2 numsamples numsurfaces). 5. Rearrange the projected features from shape... name: DepthPredictor
body: The DepthPredictor is a PyTorch nn.Module that implements a depth prediction pipeline by integrating a distribution sampler with conversion functions. It transforms raw feature tensors containing probability density function (PDF) and offset channels into probabilistic depth estimates and associated opacities, differing from sibling methods by explicitly handling discrete distribution sampling and transmittance-based opacity computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: features tensor of shape Float[Tensor, "batch view ray surface depth 2"]. The last dimension contains two channels: raw PDF values and raw offset values. Outputs: depth: Float[Tensor, "batch view ray surface sample"]. opacity: Float[Tensor, "batch view ray surface sample"]. index: Int64[Tensor, "batch view ray surface sample"]. Data Structures: The method uses a sampler object that provides sample and gather methods to handle discrete sampling from the PDF and retrieval of corresponding offset values. Parameters: numdepths: Integer specifying the number of discrete depth buckets (size of the depth dimension in input). near: Near plane distance for depth conversion. far: Far plane distance for depth conversion. deterministic: Boolean flag controlling sampling mode. gaussiansperpixel: Integer specifying the number of samples to draw per pixel/ray. usetransmittance: Boolean flag controlling the opacity calculation method. Steps: 1. Unbind Features: Separate the last dimension of features into pdfraw and offsetraw tensors. 2. Normalize PDF: Apply a Softmax function to pdfraw to obtain the probability density function pdf. 3. Normalize Offsets: Apply a Sigmoid function to offsetraw to obtain bounded offsets offset. 4. Sample: Draw index and corresponding PDF densities pdfi from pdf using the sampler, with the sample count determined by gaussiansperpixel. 5. Gather Offsets: Retrieve the offsets corresponding to the sampled indices: offset = sampler.gather(index, offset). 6. Calculate Relative Disparity: Compute relative disparity using the sampled indices and offsets: \text{relative\disparity} = \frac{\text{index} + \text{offset}}{\text{num\depths}} 7. Convert to Depth: Map relative disparity to absolute depth using the near and far planes: \text{depth} = \text{relative\disparity\to\depth}(\text{relative\disparity}, \text{near}, \text{far}) 8. Compute Opacity: If usetransmittance is true: a. Compute cumulative sum of PDF: partial = pdf.cumsum(dim=-1). b. Shift cumulative sum to align with transmittance: partial = torch.cat((torch.zeroslike(partial[...,:1]), partial[...,:-1]), dim=-1). c. Compute opacity per bucket: opacityraw = pdf / (1 - partial + 1e-10). d. Gather opacity values: opacity = sampler.gather(index, opacityraw). If usetransmittance is false: a. Set opacity directly to the sampled PDF density: opacity = pdfi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DepthPredictor(nn.Module): def init(self, sampler, numdepths, near, far, usetransmittance=True): super().init() self.sampler = sampler self.numdepths = numdepths self.near = near self.far = far self.usetransmittance = usetransmittance def forward(self, features, deterministic=False, gaussiansperpixel=1): pdfraw, offsetraw = features.unbind(dim=-1) pdf = torch.softmax(pdfraw, dim=-1) offset = torch.sigmoid(offsetraw) index, pdfi = self.sampler.sample(pdf, deterministic, gaussiansperpixel) offset = self.sampler.gather(index, offset) relativedisparity = (index + offset) / self.numdepths depth = relativedisparitytodepth(relativedisparity, self.near, self.far) if self.usetransmittance: partial = pdf.cumsum(dim=-1) partial = torch.cat((torch.zeroslike(partial[...,:1]), partial[...,:-1]), dim=-1) opacity = pdf / (1 - partial + 1e-10) opacity = self.sampler.gather(index, opacity) else: opacity = pdfi return depth, opacity, index def relativedisparitytodepth(relativedisparity, near, far): # Standard linear mapping from normalized disparity to depth return near + relativedisparity (far - near) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The opacity calculation includes a small epsilon (1e-10) to prevent division by zero when 1 - partial approaches zero. Near/Far Plane Boundaries: The near and far parameters define the valid depth range; values outside this range produce invalid depth estimates. name: Bisection Method for Surface Depth Refinement
head: Bisection Method, Iterative Bisection, Midpoint (Bisection) Algorithm
body: The Bisection Method is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the intersection position of a ray with an implicit surface within a specific segment identified by adaptive sampling. It serves as an alternative to the Secant method in ray marching pipelines, guaranteeing convergence by halving the search interval at each step. Unlike the Secant method, which uses linear interpolation between two points, the Bisection method relies solely on the sign of the field function evaluations to narrow the interval. The method refines the intersection point on a line segment (typically an edge of a voxel or a ray step) where the implicit field function changes sign. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two endpoints of the search interval, P{low} and P{high}, such that the field function f(P{low}) and f(P{high}) have opposite signs. A maximum number of iterations N (optional, for termination). Output: The refined intersection point P{intersect} where f(P{intersect}) \approx 0. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the algorithm operates on scalar values (field evaluations) and vector positions. Steps: 1. Calculate the midpoint P{mid} of the current interval [P{low}, P{high}]: P{mid} = \frac{P{low} + P{high}}{2} 2. Evaluate the implicit field function at the midpoint: f{mid} = f(P{mid}). 3. Check for convergence: If f{mid} = 0 (or |f{mid}| < \epsilon for some tolerance \epsilon), the intersection is found. If the maximum number of iterations has been reached, return P{mid} as the best estimate. 4. Update the interval: If f{mid} has the same sign as f{low} (i.e., f{mid} \cdot f{low} > 0), the root lies in the upper half. Set P{low} = P{mid} and f{low} = f{mid}. Otherwise, the root lies in the lower half. Set P{high} = P{mid} and f{high} = f{mid}. 5. Repeat from Step 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bisectionrefine(plow, phigh, fieldfunc, maxiter=10, tol=1e-6): """ Refine ray-surface intersection using the bisection method. Args: plow: Vector3, start of interval where field sign is negative (or opposite to phigh). phigh: Vector3, end of interval where field sign is positive (or opposite to plow). fieldfunc: Function taking a Vector3 and returning a float. maxiter: Integer, maximum number of bisection steps. tol: Float, convergence tolerance for |f(mid)|. Returns: Vector3, the refined intersection point. """ flow = fieldfunc(plow) fhigh = fieldfunc(phigh) # Ensure the interval brackets the root if flow fhigh > 0: raise ValueError("Field function values at endpoints must have opposite signs.") for in range(maxiter): pmid = (plow + phigh) / 2.0 fmid = fieldfunc(pmid) # Check for exact zero or tolerance if abs(fmid) < tol: return pmid # Update interval based on sign if fmid flow > 0: plow = pmid flow = fmid else: phigh = pmid fhigh = fmid return (plow + phigh) / 2.0 Parameters: maxiter: Not given in the sources. tol: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sign Error: The method requires that the initial interval [P{low}, P{high}] brackets the root (i.e., f(P{low}) \cdot f(P{high}) < 0). Multiple Roots: If multiple roots exist within the interval, the method finds one of them, depending on the initial bracketing. Flat Regions: If the field function is flat near the root (f'(x) \approx 0), convergence may be slow, but the method remains stable. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guaranteed convergence; simple to implement; no derivative information required. Limitations: Slower convergence rate compared to interpolation-based methods; requires a bracketing interval. When to use it and when not: Use when guaranteed convergence is required and the field function is continuous; avoid when faster convergence is needed and the function is well-behaved. The Bisection Method is a classic root-finding algorithm. In the context of volume rendering and isosurface extraction, it is used as a refinement step after an initial coarse intersection is detected. It is often contrasted with the Secant method and the False Position method. The False Position method is described as a combination of linear interpolation and the midpoint algorithm, finding the exact intersection point even if the field function is not continuous, and is noted to be no worse than, and usually better than, the midpoint algorithm in terms of iteration count. The method is implemented in various isosurfacing libraries, such as IsoMesher, where it is selected via preprocessor symbols (e.g., BISECTION). It is also used in differentiable volumetric rendering pipelines, where it is called as an alternative to the Secant method for refining ray-surface intersections. Uses linear interpolation between two points to estimate the root. Faster convergence than bisection but not guaranteed to converge if the function is not well-behaved. Focuses on optimizing the initial intersection detection, often using spatial acceleration structures. name: Bracketed Newton Bisection
head: BNB
body: Bracketed Newton Bisection is a root-finding algorithm that combines bisection and Newton’s methods with a preliminary step that splits the polynomial into monotonic pieces. It finds all possible real roots of high-degree polynomials, ensuring no solutions are missed by guaranteeing at most one root per interval. Unlike simple numerical solvers that may converge to a single root or fail on high-degree cases, this method systematically partitions the domain using derivative roots to isolate and solve each root independently. Inputs: A polynomial P(x) of degree n, its first derivative P'(x), a list of higher-order derivative functions P^{(k)}(x) for k=2 \dots n-2, and a search domain [x{min}, x{max}]. Outputs: A list of all real roots of P(x) within the domain. Data Structures: A list of interval boundaries (initially [x{min}, x{max}]) and a list to accumulate found roots. Steps: 1. Base Interval Resolution: Start with the (n-2)-th derivative P^{(n-2)}, which is a quadratic polynomial (degree 2). Solve P^{(n-2)}(x) = 0 algebraically to find its real roots within the domain. These roots become the initial interval boundaries for the next level. If P^{(n-2)} has no real roots, the domain remains a single interval [x{min}, x{max}]. 2. Bottom-Up Interval Refinement: Iterate k from n-3 down to 1. For each derivative P^{(k)}, evaluate it at the current interval boundaries. If P^{(k)} changes sign between two adjacent boundaries, a root of P^{(k)} exists in that sub-interval. Find this root using the Bracketed Newton Bisection method. This root becomes a new boundary for the next derivative P^{(k-1)}. If P^{(k)} does not change sign, the existing boundaries are retained. 3. Final Root Finding: After reaching k=0, the boundaries define monotonic segments of P(x). For each segment [a, b] where P(a) \cdot P(b) < 0, apply the Bracketed Newton Bisection method to find the single root of P(x). Root Finding Formula (Mixture of Bisection and Newton): For a monotonic interval [x{min}, x{max}] with P(x{min}) \cdot P(x{max}) < 0: 1. Initialize x = (x{min} + x{max}) / 2. 2. Iterate until convergence: Compute f = P(x) and f' = P'(x). Compute Newton step: x{new} = x - f / f'. Bracketing Guard: If x{new} \notin [x{min}, x{max}] or the Newton step does not reduce |f| sufficiently, fall back to bisection: x{new} = (x{min} + x{max}) / 2. Update interval: If P(x{new}) \cdot P(x{min}) < 0, set x{max} = x{new}; else set x{min} = x{new}. Set x = x{new}. Parameters: Convergence tolerance and maximum iterations are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method can find at most 9 monotonic intervals for a degree-9 polynomial (e.g., tricubic SDFs). BNB does not offer an early skip strategy, unlike Affine Arithmetic tests. High-degree polynomials require evaluating multiple derivative chains, increasing computational cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bracketednewtonbisection(P, Pprime, derivs, domain, degree): """ Finds all real roots of polynomial P in the given domain. P: callable for P(x) Pprime: callable for P'(x) derivs: list of callables [P, P', P'',..., P^(n-2)] domain: tuple (xmin, xmax) degree: integer n """ xmin, xmax = domain # Step 1: Base case - solve quadratic P^(n-2) = 0 algebraically # Extract coefficients a, b, c for f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c from derivs[degree-2] c = derivsdegree - 2 b = (derivsdegree - 2 - derivsdegree - 2) / 2.0 a = (derivsdegree - 2 + derivsdegree - 2) / 2.0 - c quadroots = [] if abs(a) < 1e-12: if abs(b) > 1e-12: root = -c / b if xmin <= root <= xmax: quadroots.append(root) else: disc = b b - 4 a c if disc >= 0: sqrtd = disc 0.5 r1 = (-b + sqrtd) / (2 a) r2 = (-b - sqrtd) / (2 a) if xmin <= r1 <= xmax: quadroots.append(r1) if xmin <= r2 <= xmax: quadroots.append(r2) boundaries = sorted(list(set([xmin, xmax] + quadroots))) # Step 2: Bottom-up refinement from k = n-3 down to 1 for k in range(degree - 3, 0, -1): newboundaries = [] fk = derivs[k] fkplus1 = derivs[k + 1] for i in range(len(boundaries) - 1): aint, bint = boundaries[i], boundaries[i + 1] fa, fb = fk(aint), fk(bint) if fa fb < 0: root = findrootbnb(fk, fkplus1, aint, bint) newboundaries.append(root) else: newboundaries.append(aint) newboundaries.append(bint) boundaries = sorted(list(set(newboundaries))) # Step 3: Final root finding for P^(0) = P roots = [] for i in range(len(boundaries) - 1): aint, bint = boundaries[i], boundaries[i + 1] if P(aint) P(bint) < 0: root = findrootbnb(P, Pprime, aint, bint) roots.append(root) return roots def findrootbnb(f, fprime, xmin, xmax, tol=1e-7, maxiter=100): """Mixture of Bisection and Newton's method for a monotonic interval.""" x = (xmin + xmax) / 2.0 for in range(maxiter): fx = f(x) if abs(fx) < tol: return x fpx = fprime(x) if abs(fpx) < 1e-12: x = (xmin + xmax) / 2.0 continue xnew = x - fx / fpx # Bracketing Guard if xnew < xmin or xnew > xmax: xnew = (xmin + xmax) / 2.0 fxnew = f(xnew) if fxnew f(xmin) < 0: xmax = xnew else: xmin = xnew x = xnew return x The Analytic Ray-Intersection Polynomial Solver finds the intersection parameter t where a ray intersects the polynomial approximation of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) leaf node. It solves the problem of slow convergence in sphere marching when rays pass near parallel surfaces or graze the isosurface. Unlike sphere marching, which evaluates the SDF iteratively, this method computes a single polynomial in t per node and solves for its roots, offering a significant performance improvement near the surface at the cost of higher initial coefficient computation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: BNB provides an average 12% speedup over basic Sphere Marching in the narrow band for trilinear interpolation, primarily by skipping nodes early on silhouettes where Sphere Marching converges slowly. However, it is the slowest method for tricubic interpolation because it must search monotonic intervals of seven previous derivatives. Strengths: Guarantees finding all real roots of high-degree polynomials by splitting into monotonic intervals. Limitations: Requires computing and solving lower-degree derivative polynomials iteratively; lacks an early skip strategy. When to use: When high-degree polynomial approximations of SDFs are used and all real roots must be found. When not to use: When lower-degree polynomials are sufficient, analytical solutions are available, or an early skip strategy is required. Bracketed Newton Bisection is a root-finding algorithm named by Peters et al. and first proposed by Yuksel. name: Analytic Ray-Intersection Polynomial Solver
head: Polynomial SDF Intersection Solver
body: The Analytic Ray-Intersection Polynomial Solver finds the intersection parameter t where a ray intersects the polynomial approximation of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) leaf node. It solves the problem of slow convergence in sphere marching when rays pass near parallel surfaces or graze the isosurface. Unlike sphere marching, which evaluates the SDF iteratively, this method computes a single polynomial in t per node and solves for its roots, offering a significant performance improvement near the surface at the cost of higher initial coefficient computation. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{p} and direction \mathbf{v}. SDF leaf node coefficients defining the polynomial PN: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}. Node type: Trilinear (8 coefficients) or Tricubic (64 coefficients). Outputs: The smallest positive real root t of the intersection polynomial, representing the first intersection point. A boolean indicating if an intersection exists within the node. Data Structures: Trilinear Node: Array of 8 scalar coefficients c{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}. Tricubic Node: Array of 64 scalar coefficients c{ijkl} for i,j,k,l \in \{0,1,2,3\}. Intersection Polynomial Coefficients: Array of size 4 for trilinear (c{l3} \dots c{l0}) or size 10 for tricubic (c{c9} \dots c{c0}). Steps: 1. Compute Intersection Polynomial Coefficients: Substitute the ray equation \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}t into the node's polynomial PN(\mathbf{x}) and expand by powers of t. For Trilinear interpolation, the result is a cubic polynomial: c{l3}t^3 + c{l2}t^2 + c{l1}t + c{l0} = 0 Computing these 4 coefficients requires 26 multiplications. For Tricubic interpolation, the result is a degree 9 polynomial: c{c9}t^9 + c{c8}t^8 + \dots + c{c1}t + c{c0} = 0 Computing these 10 coefficients requires 492 multiplications. 2. Early Skip Test (Tricubic Only): For tricubic nodes, apply an Affine Arithmetic-based early skip test to detect non-collisions in constant time or provide a better starting point. Factorize the function as a degree 2 polynomial: PN(\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{v}t) \approx at^2 + bt + c = 0 where: a = c{c9}t^7 + c{c8}t^6 + \dots + c{c3}t + c{c2} b = c{c1} c = c{c0} Since a depends on t, approximate it with a fixed value (e.g., derived from coefficient bounds) to form a real quadratic equation. If starting outside the object, check if the quadratic evaluates to negative values; if it does not, return "No Intersection". 3. Identify Monotonic Intervals: Use the Bracketed Newton Bisection method to find all real roots of the derivative polynomials, which define the boundaries of monotonic intervals for the original polynomial. Start from the (n-2)-th derivative (degree 2), find its roots algebraically, and iteratively use them to bound the roots of the (n-3)-th derivative up to the original polynomial. Trilinear: The derivative is quadratic (degree 2) with at most 2 roots, creating at most 3 monotonic intervals for the cubic polynomial. Tricubic: The solver searches monotonic intervals of the seven previous derivatives, identifying up to 9 monotonic intervals for the degree 9 polynomial. 4. Root Finding: For each monotonic interval [t{min}, t{max}]: Evaluate the intersection polynomial P(t) at the endpoints. If P(t{min}) and P(t{max}) have opposite signs (sign change), a root exists in this interval. Apply Bracketed Newton Bisection to find the root within this interval. Discard analytical formulas like Cardano's method due to instability in certain situations. 5. Select Intersection: Return the smallest positive t found among all intervals. If no sign changes are detected in any monotonic interval, the node does not intersect the surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solveanalyticintersection(p, v, nodecoeffs, nodetype): """ p: list[float, float, float], ray origin v: list[float, float, float], ray direction (normalized) nodecoeffs: list[float], SDF node coefficients nodetype: 'trilinear' or 'tricubic' Returns: (t, hit) where t is the intersection distance and hit is a boolean """ # Step 1: Compute intersection polynomial coefficients if nodetype == 'trilinear': poly = expandtrilinear(p, v, nodecoeffs) degree = 3 elif nodetype == 'tricubic': poly = expandtricubic(p, v, nodecoeffs) degree = 9 else: raise ValueError("Unsupported node type") # Step 2: Early Skip Test (Tricubic only) if nodetype == 'tricubic': c9, c8, c7, c6, c5, c4, c3, c2, c1, c0 = poly # Approximate 'a' with a fixed bound for t in [0, nodesize] aapprox = sum(abs(c) for c in poly[:8]) b, c = c1, c0 # If quadratic at^2+bt+c has no real roots or stays positive for t>=0, skip disc = bb - 4aapproxc if disc < 0 or (aapprox > 0 and c >= 0 and -b/(2aapprox) < 0): return (float('inf'), False) # Step 3: Identify Monotonic Intervals intervals = findmonotonicintervals(poly, degree) # Step 4 & 5: Root Finding & Selection mint = float('inf') hit = False for tmin, tmax in intervals: if tmax <= 0: continue valmin = evaluatepoly(poly, tmin) valmax = evaluatepoly(poly, tmax) if valmin valmax < 0: troot = bracketednewtonbisection(poly, max(0, tmin), tmax) if troot < mint: mint = troot hit = True return (mint, hit) def expandtrilinear(p, v, c): # Expands trilinear basis with ray x(t)=p+vt. Requires 26 multiplications. # Standard polynomial composition of basis functions px, py, pz = p vx, vy, vz = v # Coefficients for t^3, t^2, t^1, t^0 c3 = vxvxvxc[7] + vxvxvyc[6] + vxvyvxc[5] + vxvyvyc[4] + vyvxvxc[3] + vyvxvyc[2] + vyvyvxc[1] + vyvyvyc[0] c2 = (3vxvxpxc[7] + vxvx(py+2px)c[6] + vxvx(pz+2px)c[5] + vxvxpyc[4] + vyvx(px+2py)c[3] + vyvxpyc[2] + vyvy(px+2py)c[1] + vyvypyc[0]) c1 = (3vxpxpxc[7] + vx(pypx+2pxpy)c[6] + vx(pzpx+2pxpz)c[5] + vxpypyc[4] + vy(pxpy+2pypx)c[3] + vypypyc[2] + vy(pxpy+2pypx)c[1] + vypypyc[0]) c0 = pxpxpxc[7] + pxpxpyc[6] + pxpxpzc[5] + pxpypyc[4] + pypxpxc[3] + pypxpyc[2] + pypypxc[1] + pypypyc[0] return [c3, c2, c1, c0] def expandtricubic(p, v, c): # Expands tricubic basis with ray x(t)=p+vt. Requires 492 multiplications. # Standard polynomial composition of basis functions # Returns array of 10 coefficients [cc9,..., cc0] # Implementation follows the same basis expansion pattern as trilinear but for degree 9 px, py, pz = p vx, vy, vz = v # Compute coefficients via nested polynomial multiplication def polymul(a, b): res = [0.0] (len(a) + len(b) - 1) for i, ai in enumerate(a): for j, bj in enumerate(b): res[i+j] += ai bj return res # Basis polynomials for each dimension: (1-(p+vt)) and (p+vt) # Tricubic basis is product of 1D cubic bases def dimbasis(pval, vval): # Returns coefficients for (1-p-vt)^3 and (p+vt)^3 etc. # Simplified to direct expansion for completeness return [pval3, 3pval2vval, 3pvalvval2, vval3] # Placeholder for full basis expansion # Full expansion requires convolving 1D bases across 3 dimensions return [0.0]10 # Sources do not provide exact coefficient formulas def findmonotonicintervals(poly, degree): # Iteratively finds derivative roots to bound monotonic intervals intervals = [[0.0, float('inf')]] currentpoly = poly for d in range(degree, 2, -1): deriv = getderivativecoeffs(currentpoly) roots = solvequadraticroots(deriv) if d == 3 else solvehigherderivativeroots(deriv) newintervals = [] for tmin, tmax in intervals: splitpoints = sorted([tmin] + [r for r in roots if tmin < r < tmax] + [tmax]) for i in range(len(splitpoints) - 1): newintervals.append([splitpoints[i], splitpoints[i+1]]) intervals = newintervals currentpoly = deriv return intervals def solvequadraticroots(deriv): # Returns real roots of quadratic derivative a, b, c = deriv[0], deriv[1], deriv[2] if a == 0: return [-c/b] if b != 0 else [] disc = bb -
