name: Ray Origin and Direction Setup
head: Camera Ray Generation, Camera Ray Setup, Primary Ray Generation, Ray Casting Vertex Shader, Ray Generation for Volume Ray Casting, Ray Origin/Direction Computation
body: Ray Origin and Direction Setup computes the 3D origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d} for a set of rays, typically one per pixel, to initialize volume rendering or ray tracing pipelines. It solves the problem of mapping discrete 2D raster coordinates (pixel indices or UVs) to continuous 3D world-space vectors defined by a specific camera model. Unlike Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation, which maintains parallel directions, this method generally constructs perspective rays that diverge from a viewpoint, though it encompasses the geometric basis for both. It differs from Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation by explicitly deriving geometry from camera parameters rather than reconstructing it from pre-computed payloads. The method transforms camera parameters and pixel coordinates into ray geometry. Implementations vary between GPU vertex/fragment shader approaches and CPU-based explicit construction, but share the core logic of basis vector definition and coordinate mapping. Inputs: Camera Position (\mathbf{e} or cameraPosition): The eye position, often in view space or world space. Camera Basis Vectors: Right (\mathbf{r} or uCamRight), Up (\mathbf{u} or uCamUp), and Forward (\mathbf{f} or uCamForward) vectors. Pixel Coordinates: Integer pixel indices (i, j) or normalized UV coordinates (u, v). Sub-pixel Offsets: Optional jitter or sampling offsets (sx, sy) for anti-aliasing. Camera Parameters: Viewport bounds (left l, right r, top t, bottom b), width, height, or Field of View (FOV) scales. Transformation Matrices: Model, View, and Projection matrices if transforming from view space to world space. Outputs: Ray Origin (\mathbf{o}): The starting point of the ray in world space. Ray Direction (\mathbf{d}): A normalized vector pointing from the origin through the pixel. Ray Structure: Typically a struct or pair containing origin (vec3) and direction (vec3). Uniforms/Parameters: cameraPosition: vec3. modelMatrix, modelViewMatrix: mat4. uCamRight, uCamUp, uCamForward: vec3. uResolution: vec2 (width, height). FOVSCALE: Scalar for field of view. 1. Determine Ray Origin (\mathbf{o}): If the camera position is provided in view space, transform it to world space. Multiply the homogeneous position vector by the inverse model matrix (or model-view inverse, depending on convention). \mathbf{o} = \text{xyz}(\text{inverse}(\mathbf{M}{\text{model}}) \cdot [\mathbf{e}{\text{view}}, 1]^T). Alternatively, if the camera position is already in world space or the basis vectors are defined in world space, use \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{e}{\text{world}} directly. 2. Compute 2D Image Plane Coordinates: Method A (UV/FOV based): Convert pixel UVs to a centered, aspect-corrected coordinate system. uvx = (u \cdot 2.0 - 1.0) \cdot \frac{\text{width}}{\text{height}} uvy = v \cdot 2.0 - 1.0 (Note: Y-axis orientation depends on convention; some systems use 1.0 - v). Method B (Viewport Bounds based): Map pixel indices (i, j) with sub-pixel offsets (sx, sy) to the view plane coordinates. vpx = l + (r - l) \cdot \frac{i + sx}{\text{width}} vpy = t - (t - b) \cdot \frac{j + sy}{\text{height}} (Note: The subtraction in vpy assumes a top-down Y-axis in screen space mapping to a bottom-up Y-axis in view space). 3. Compute Ray Direction (\mathbf{d}): Method A (Basis Vector Linear Combination): Construct the direction using the camera's right and up vectors scaled by the UV coordinates and the forward vector. \mathbf{d}{\text{raw}} = \mathbf{f} + \text{FOV\SCALE} \cdot (uvx \cdot \mathbf{r} + uvy \cdot \mathbf{u}) \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{d}{\text{raw}}). Method B (Viewport Vector Construction): Construct the direction vector from the view plane coordinates and the camera basis. \mathbf{d}{\text{raw}} = vpx \cdot \mathbf{u} + vpy \cdot \mathbf{v} - \text{dist} \cdot \mathbf{w} Here, \mathbf{u} is right, \mathbf{v} is up, and \mathbf{w} is forward (note: signs depend on coordinate system handedness; typically forward is negative Z in view space). \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{d}{\text{raw}}). Method C (Vertex Shader Difference): In some vertex-shader-based implementations, the direction is computed as the difference between the vertex position (in world space) and the camera origin. \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{\text{world}} - \mathbf{o}). 4. Assemble Ray: Return or store the pair (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}). Aspect Correction: uvx = (2u - 1) \frac{W}{H}. Viewport Mapping: vpx = l + \frac{i+sx}{W}(r-l), vpy = t - \frac{j+sy}{H}(t-b). Direction (FOV): \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{f} + k(ux \mathbf{r} + uy \mathbf{u})). Direction (Viewport): \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(vpx \mathbf{r} + vpy \mathbf{u} - d{\text{plane}} \mathbf{f}). FOVSCALE: Controls the field of view. In, this is a uniform scalar. In, HFOV and VFOV are used to derive similar scaling factors. Default HFOV/VFOV in is M\PI \cdot 160.0 / 180.0 (radians). Resolution: Width and height of the image plane. Sub-pixel Offsets: (sx, sy) for jittering. Normalization: The direction vector must be normalized to ensure consistent step sizes in ray marching. Coordinate System Handedness: The sign of the forward vector and the cross-product order for basis vectors (\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{f} \times \mathbf{up} vs \mathbf{up} \times \mathbf{f}) depend on whether the system is left-handed or right-handed. Y-Axis Orientation: Screen Y often increases downwards, while view space Y increases upwards. The mapping vpy = t - \dots or uvy = 1-v handles this inversion. Division by Zero: Ensure resolution dimensions are non-zero before aspect correction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateray(pixelu, pixelv, pixelwidth, pixelheight, cameraposworld, camright, camup, camforward, fovscale, useviewportbounds=False, l=0.0, r=1.0, t=1.0, b=0.0, dist=1.0, sx=0.0, sy=0.0): """ Generates a ray origin and direction. Args: pixelu, pixelv: Normalized UV coordinates in [0, 1]. pixelwidth, pixelheight: Image dimensions. cameraposworld: World space origin (vec3). camright, camup, camforward: Camera basis vectors (vec3). fovscale: Scalar for FOV (float). useviewportbounds: If True, use viewport mapping (S3), else UV/FOV (S2). l, r, t, b: Viewport bounds (floats). dist: Distance to view plane (float). sx, sy: Sub-pixel offsets (floats). Returns: origin (vec3), direction (vec3) """ # 1. Origin origin = cameraposworld # 2. Compute 2D coordinates if useviewportbounds: # Method B: Viewport bounds mapping # Note: pixel indices usually 0..W-1, 0..H-1. # Assuming pixelu, pixelv are integer indices i, j here for direct mapping, # or converted from UV. For UV input, we map to [0,1] range first. i = pixelu pixelwidth j = pixelv pixelheight vpx = l + (r - l) (i + sx) / pixelwidth vpy = t - (t - b) (j + sy) / pixelheight # 3. Direction # s = vpx u + vpy v - dist w # Assuming camright=u, camup=v, camforward=w rawdir = (vpx camright) + (vpy camup) - (dist camforward) else: # Method A: UV/FOV mapping # Aspect-corrected UV in [-1, 1] uvx = (pixelu 2.0 - 1.0) (pixelwidth / pixelheight) uvy = pixelv 2.0 - 1.0 # 3. Direction # rd = normalize(uCamForward + FOVSCALE (uv.x uCamRight + uv.y uCamUp)) rawdir = camforward + (fovscale ((uvx camright) + (uvy camup))) # 4. Normalize direction = normalize(rawdir) return origin, direction Constructs ray origins distributed on a grid perpendicular to the viewing direction and assigns identical normalized directions to all rays for an orthographic camera. It solves the problem of mapping pixel coordinates to physical ray vectors without perspective distortion, ensuring that parallel lines in the 3D scene remain parallel when drawn on the screen. It differs from perspective ray generation by maintaining parallel ray directions and linear spacing of origins across the image plane. Is a method for regenerating ray geometry (origins and directions) from discrete pixel indices and stored camera parameters, primarily used in streaming or deferred rendering pipelines where ray data is reconstructed on-demand rather than precomputed. It solves the problem of resuming ray tracing or computing shadow rays by mapping pixel coordinates to world space using either a direct pinhole camera model or an NDC unprojection approach. It differs from NDC Ray Transformation by explicitly handling the payload context (such as shadow vs. main view) and from Stochastic Jittering by generating deterministic primary or shadow rays without noise injection. A method for constructing ray origin and direction in object/local space rather than world space. This makes the raytraced object move, scale, and rotate with the mesh transform. This method generates per-pixel ray directions for volume rendering by encoding the index of pre-computed frustum corner vectors into the Z-coordinate of a full-screen quad's vertices, allowing the vertex shader to look up the correct ray direction from a uniform array. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding per-fragment matrix multiplications for direction calculation, instead using a discrete lookup based on vertex attributes. It differs from Basic GPU Ray Generation via Fragment Shader by performing the direction selection in the vertex shader rather than the fragment shader, reducing redundant calculations for adjacent pixels sharing the same vertex. Is a technique used in volume rendering to perturb the starting position of a ray march, thereby avoiding banding artifacts caused by the regular sampling grid. It differs from sibling methods like Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation or Camera Matrix Ray Generation, which define the geometric ray path, by adding a stochastic perturbation to the ray's origin or initial step. This method is distinct from Incremental Random Number Generation because it typically relies on spatial hashing to ensure deterministic, uncorrelated values for each pixel or sample, rather than maintaining a continuous state. Computes the origin and direction of a primary ray for each pixel in an image based on camera intrinsic parameters (focal length, principal point) and extrinsic parameters (camera-to-world pose). It solves the problem of mapping 2D raster coordinates to 3D world-space rays, enabling subsequent volume rendering or ray tracing operations. Unlike orthographic generation which uses parallel rays, this method constructs perspective rays that diverge from a single viewpoint. It differs from sample streaming payload methods by explicitly constructing the ray geometry from camera matrices rather than deriving it from pre-computed payloads or object-space offsets. This method generates camera rays for ray tracing by rendering a single quad (two triangles) to the screen, allowing the fragment shader to compute the ray origin and direction for each pixel using interpolated vertex coordinates. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding explicit matrix multiplications in favor of geometric basis vectors (side, up, forward) derived from camera parameters, and from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by supporting perspective projection through a viewing plane distance. It builds on Ray Origin and Direction Setup by providing a concrete GPU implementation pattern. Calculates the 3D position along a ray given a starting camera position, ray direction, and distance. Generates camera position, forward vector, and sun direction based on time and touch input for a moving camera system. Definition: A specific configuration for ray generation in a pinhole camera model, often used in Next-Best-View (NBV) planning or voxel-based simulations. Parameters: RES: Box resolution (voxel size). Default: 0.02f. RANGEMAX: Maximum sensor range. Default: 100000.0f. HFOV: Half horizontal field of view. Default: M\PI \cdot 160.0 / 180.0 radians. VFOV: Half vertical field of view. Default: M\PI \cdot 160.0 / 180.0 radians. HSIZE: Horizontal image size. Default: 6. VSIZE: Vertical image size. Default: 4. Orientation: Z-axis along the optical axis (orthogonal to the image plane), X-axis pointing towards the bottom/ground, Y-axis according to the right-hand rule. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray. The computation involves a constant number of vector operations and normalizations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, plus storage for camera parameters. Performance: On GPU, this is typically executed in vertex or fragment shaders, achieving high throughput by leveraging parallelism across pixels. CPU implementations are slower but allow for more complex camera paths or deferred generation. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and efficient. Provides a direct mapping from screen space to world space. Limitations: Does not handle depth-of-field or lens effects natively (requires extensions like Depth of Field and Lens Effects). Precision issues may arise with very large or very small scene scales if not using appropriate coordinate systems. When to use: Standard volume rendering, ray tracing, and visualization where a pinhole or simple perspective/orthographic camera model is sufficient. When not to use: When complex lens effects, non-pinhole projections, or interactive camera control with specific constraints are required. The method originates from fundamental computer graphics techniques for camera modeling and ray generation. It is widely used in volume rendering engines, ray tracers, and Next-Best-View planning systems. The specific implementations cited range from WebGL-based volume renderers to C++/CUDA-based scientific visualization tools and ROS-based robotic perception systems. name: Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation
head: Parallel Ray Generation
body: Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation constructs ray origins distributed on a grid perpendicular to the viewing direction and assigns identical normalized directions to all rays for an orthographic camera. It solves the problem of mapping pixel coordinates to physical ray vectors without perspective distortion, ensuring that parallel lines in the 3D scene remain parallel when drawn on the screen. It differs from perspective ray generation by maintaining parallel ray directions and linear spacing of origins across the image plane. Inputs: eye: Camera position in world space (3D vector). target: Look-at point in world space (3D vector). up: Up vector in world space (3D vector). width, height: Image dimensions in pixels (integers). extent: Half-size of the viewing region in world units along both right and up axes (float, default 1.0). Outputs: origins: Array of ray origins with shape (height, width, 3). directions: Array of ray directions with shape (height, width, 3). Data Structures: Vectors are 3D floating-point arrays. origins and directions are dense arrays matching the image resolution. Steps: 1. Compute the camera basis vectors (forward, right, camup) using the eye, target, and up vectors. The forward vector is normalized: \mathbf{f} = \text{normalize}(\text{target} - \text{eye}). The right vector is \mathbf{r} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{f} \times \text{up}). The camup vector is \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{f}. 2. Compute image plane dimensions based on aspect ratio. Let \text{aspect} = \text{width} / \text{height}. Then \text{half\w} = \text{extent} \times \text{aspect} and \text{half\h} = \text{extent}. 3. Generate pixel coordinates. Create a meshgrid of column indices j (from 0 to \text{width}-1) and row indices i (from 0 to \text{height}-1). Compute normalized coordinates u and v: u = \left( \frac{2.0 \cdot (j + 0.5)}{\text{width}} - 1.0 \right) \cdot \text{half\w} v = \left( 1.0 - \frac{2.0 \cdot (i + 0.5)}{\text{height}} \right) \cdot \text{half\h} This maps pixel centers to a centered coordinate system where the center is (0,0). 4. Compute origins. For each pixel (i, j), the origin is: \text{origin}{i,j} = \text{eye} + u{i,j} \cdot \mathbf{r} + v{i,j} \cdot \mathbf{u} This is implemented by broadcasting u and v to match the shape of eye and performing vector addition. 5. Set directions. The direction for all rays is the forward vector \mathbf{f}, broadcast to match the shape of origins. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def orthographicraygeneration(eye, target, up, width, height, extent=1.0): # Step 1: Compute camera basis forward = target - eye forward = forward / np.linalg.norm(forward) right = np.cross(forward, up) right = right / np.linalg.norm(right) camup = np.cross(right, forward) # Step 2: Compute image plane dimensions aspect = width / height halfw = extent aspect halfh = extent # Step 3: Generate pixel coordinates # Create meshgrid of indices j, i = np.meshgrid(np.arange(width), np.arange(height)) # Compute u and v coordinates u = (2.0 (j + 0.5) / width - 1.0) halfw v = (1.0 - 2.0 (i + 0.5) / height) halfh # Step 4: Compute origins # eye is (3,), u and v are (height, width) # Broadcast eye to (height, width, 3) eyebroadcast = np.broadcastto(eye, (height, width, 3)) # Broadcast right and camup to (height, width, 3) rightbroadcast = np.broadcastto(right, (height, width, 3)) camupbroadcast = np.broadcastto(camup, (height, width, 3)) # Reshape u and v for broadcasting ureshaped = u[:,:, np.newaxis] vreshaped = v[:,:, np.newaxis] origins = eyebroadcast + ureshaped rightbroadcast + vreshaped camupbroadcast # Step 5: Set directions directions = np.broadcastto(forward, (height, width, 3)) return origins, directions Parameters: extent: Half-size of the viewing region in world units along both right and up axes. Default value is 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If up is parallel to forward, the cross product for right will be zero, causing division by zero during normalization. A guard should ensure up is not parallel to the viewing direction. Precision issues may arise if extent is very large or very small relative to the scene scale, potentially affecting ray intersection accuracy. Viewing Plane Ray Generation constructs the initial ray origins and directions for an orthographic camera by defining a 2D grid of points in normalized screen space and transforming them into world space. It solves the problem of mapping pixel coordinates to physical ray vectors without perspective distortion. It differs from perspective ray generation by maintaining parallel ray directions and linear spacing of origins across the image plane. It builds on Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation. In the context of differentiable volume rendering for point clouds (e.g., VoGE), the camera type may be alternated from Orthographic to PerspectiveCamera with a similar viewing scope to enable rendering and improve boundary smoothness. Orthographic projection is a size-preserving projection where objects in the foreground take up the same amount of screen space as objects in the background, and parallel lines in the 3D scene remain parallel when drawn on the screen. It is defined by six clipping planes bounding the box in the orthographic projection: fleft, fright, fdown, fup, fnear, and ffar. In OpenGL, this is implemented via glOrtho. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to generate origins and directions, where W and H are image width and height. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to store the origins and directions arrays. Strengths: No perspective distortion; parallel lines remain parallel; uniform sampling density across the image plane regardless of depth. Limitations: No depth cueing via size reduction; not suitable for scenes requiring realistic depth perception. When to use: Technical visualization, CAD, scientific data visualization where accurate spatial relationships are critical. When not to use: Realistic rendering requiring depth cues, scenes with large depth ranges where perspective is needed for clarity. Orthographic projection is a fundamental concept in computer graphics, used to flatten the 3D scene onto a two-dimensional plane without perspective distortion. It is commonly used in technical drawing and visualization tools such as Smokeview for fire dynamics simulation data. The method is implemented in OpenGL via glOrtho. In modern differentiable rendering, orthographic cameras are used in methods like VoGE for point cloud rendering. name: Viewing Plane Ray Generation
body: Viewing Plane Ray Generation constructs initial ray origins and directions for an orthographic camera by defining a 2D grid of points in normalized screen space and transforming them into world space. It builds on Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation. Inputs: Image dimensions width, height (integers); transformation matrix mmat (4×4, typically translationmat × rotationmat × scalingmat); parameters sampleperiod (float, controls ray spacing or step size, typical value 2.0f) and CAMERASCALE (float, scaling factor applied to viewing plane dimensions, typical value 0.25). Outputs: rayorigins and raydirections arrays, containing one 3D vector per pixel. Data Structures: ViewingPlane stores mdata as a std::vector<vec3> of size width × height. Each element represents a 2D screen coordinate normalized to [-1, 1] for x and y, with z = 0. mmat stores the combined transformation matrix. Steps: 1. Initialize Grid Points: For each pixel (i, j) where 0 ≤ i < width and 0 ≤ j < height, compute normalized coordinates: x = (2.0 i / width) - 1.0, y = (2.0 j / height) - 1.0, z = 0.0. 2. Apply Transformation: Transform the grid points using mmat. 3. Compute Ray Direction: Transform three reference points via mmat: the origin a, the rightmost point b (e.g., vec3(1, 0, 0)), and the upmost point c (e.g., vec3(0, 1, 0)). Compute the direction: d = normalize(cross(b - a, c - a)). 4. Scale and Offset: Apply CAMERASCALE to the transformed viewing plane dimensions to adjust physical size. Use sampleperiod to control ray spacing or step size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateviewingplanerays(width, height, mmat, sampleperiod=2.0, camerascale=0.25): rayorigins = [] raydirections = [] # Transform reference points to compute direction a = mat4mulvec3(mmat, vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) b = mat4mulvec3(mmat, vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)) c = mat4mulvec3(mmat, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) direction = normalize(cross(b - a, c - a)) for j in range(height): for i in range(width): x = (2.0 i / width) - 1.0 y = (2.0 j / height) - 1.0 pointnorm = vec3(x, y, 0.0) pointworld = mat4mulvec3(mmat, pointnorm) pointworld = pointworld camerascale rayorigins.append(pointworld) raydirections.append(direction) return rayorigins, raydirections def mat4mulvec3(m, v): # Assumes column-major 4x4 matrix layout return vec3( m[0][0]v.x + m[1][0]v.y + m[2][0]v.z + m[3][0], m[0][1]v.x + m[1][1]v.y + m[2][1]v.z + m[3][1], m[0][2]v.x + m[1][2]v.y + m[2][2]v.z + m[3][2]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If b - a and c - a are collinear, the cross product yields a zero vector, making the direction undefined. Check for zero-length vectors and fallback to a default view direction. Precision: Ensure mmat is well-conditioned to avoid numerical instability in cross products and normalization. Boundaries: Handle width or height equal to zero by returning empty arrays. A camera mode that generates parallel rays for isometric views, defined by a height parameter. It is chosen when an isometric projection is required rather than perspective. See Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. body: org = transformpoint(wto, campos) dircam = forward + (screenx - 0.5) right + (screeny - 0.5) up dirworld = transformvector(wto, dircam / np.linalg.norm(dircam)) return {'org': org, 'dir': dirworld} ### Parameters and Typical Values Focal Length: Implicit in the camera basis vectors (horizontal, vertical) or explicit in NDC scaling. Image Dimensions: W, H are integers, typically 1920 \times 1080 or 1024 \times 1024. Pixel Centering: 0.5 offset is standard to align ray with pixel center. ### Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating point errors in normalization can cause slight direction drift; use normalize carefully. Boundary Pixels: The 0.5 offset ensures rays hit the center of the pixel, avoiding edge artifacts. Degenerate Camera: If horizontal or vertical are zero or parallel to direction, the ray direction is undefined. name: Custom Frustum Ray Generation via Vertex Z-Index
head: CustomGraphicsBlit, Frustum Corner Indexing, Ray Direction Assignment via Frustum Corners
body: This method generates per-pixel ray directions for volume rendering by encoding the index of pre-computed frustum corner vectors into the Z-coordinate of a full-screen quad's vertices, allowing the vertex shader to look up the correct ray direction from a uniform array. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding per-fragment matrix multiplications for direction calculation, instead using a discrete lookup based on vertex attributes. It differs from Basic GPU Ray Generation via Fragment Shader by performing the direction selection in the vertex shader rather than the fragment shader, reducing redundant calculations for adjacent pixels sharing the same vertex. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A full-screen quad (typically two triangles or one quad) with UV coordinates (u,v) \in [0,1]^2. The quad vertices carry a custom Z-coordinate representing an index. Uniforms: FrustumCornersES: A float4x4 (or array of float3) containing the eye-space coordinates of the four frustum corners. CameraInvViewMatrix: A float4x4 inverse view matrix to transform eye-space rays to world-space. MainTexTexelSize: A float4 containing texture dimensions, used to detect UV orientation. Output: A fragment shader input ray (world-space direction vector) and standard position/UV attributes. Data Structures: Vertex Buffer: Contains 4 vertices. Each vertex has: position: float3 (or float4). X and Y are screen-space UVs (0 or 1). Z is the corner index (0-3). uv: float2 (0 or 1). Uniform Array FrustumCornersES: Index 0: Top-Left (TL) corner direction in eye-space. Index 1: Top-Right (TR) corner direction in eye-space. Index 2: Bottom-Right (BR) corner direction in eye-space. Index 3: Bottom-Left (BL) corner direction in eye-space. Note: The mapping of indices to corners depends on the specific blit implementation. The source uses indices 3, 2, 1, 0 for vertices at (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1) respectively, mapping to BL, BR, TR, TL. Numbered Steps: 1. Prepare Frustum Corners (CPU Side): Calculate the four frustum corner directions in eye-space (or camera space) for the current camera. This is typically done using Camera.CalculateFrustumCorners with a full-screen rect (0,0,1,1). These vectors are normalized and passed to the shader as FrustumCornersES. 2. Issue Full-Screen Quad with Custom Z-Indices (CPU/GPU API Side): Draw a full-screen quad. For each of the four vertices, set the Z-coordinate of the vertex position to the index of the corresponding frustum corner. Vertex 1: UV (0,0), Z = 3 (BL) Vertex 2: UV (1,0), Z = 2 (BR) Vertex 3: UV (1,1), Z = 1 (TR) Vertex 4: UV (0,1), Z = 0 (TL) Note: The orthographic projection matrix is used to ensure these Z-values are passed through unchanged to the vertex shader. 3. Vertex Shader Processing: For each vertex: a. Extract the index from the vertex Z-coordinate: index = v.vertex.z. b. Reset the vertex Z-coordinate to a standard depth value (e.g., 0.1) to ensure correct projection and depth buffering: v.vertex.z = 0.1. c. Transform the vertex position using the model-view-projection matrix: o.pos = mul(UNITYMATRIXMVP, v.vertex). d. Pass the UV coordinates to the fragment shader. If the texture starts at the top (detected by MainTexTexelSize.y < 0), flip the Y-coordinate: o.uv.y = 1 - o.uv.y. e. Look up the eye-space ray direction using the extracted index: o.rayes = FrustumCornersES[(int)index].xyz. f. Transform the eye-space ray direction to world-space: o.rayws = mul(CameraInvViewMatrix, float4(o.rayes, 0)). Note: Since it is a direction, the translation component of the inverse view matrix should not affect it, but standard matrix multiplication is used. 4. Fragment Shader: Interpolate the ray vector across the screen. Use this world-space direction for raymarching. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def customgraphicsblit(sourcetexture, destinationtexture, material, passindex): # Set render target RenderTexture.active = destinationtexture # Bind material and pass material.SetPass(passindex) # Set uniforms material.SetMatrix("FrustumCornersES", getfrustumcornerseyespace()) material.SetMatrix("CameraInvViewMatrix", camera.inverseviewmatrix) # Draw full-screen quad # Using a low-level API like OpenGL/DirectX beginquads() # Vertex 1: Bottom-Left (UV 0,0), Index 3 setuv(0.0, 0.0) setvertex(0.0, 0.0, 3.0) # Vertex 2: Bottom-Right (UV 1,0), Index 2 setuv(1.0, 0.0) setvertex(1.0, 0.0, 2.0) # Vertex 3: Top-Right (UV 1,1), Index 1 setuv(1.0, 1.0) setvertex(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Vertex 4: Top-Left (UV 0,1), Index 0 setuv(0.0, 1.0) setvertex(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) endquads() # Reset state RenderTexture.active = None struct appdata { float4 vertex: POSITION; // x,y: UV, z: index float2 uv: TEXCOORD0; }; struct v2f { float4 pos: SVPOSITION; float2 uv: TEXCOORD0; float3 ray: TEXCOORD1; }; uniform float4x4 FrustumCornersES; uniform float4x4 CameraInvViewMatrix; uniform float4 MainTexTexelSize; v2f vert(appdata v) { v2f o; // 1. Extract index from Z int index = (int)v.vertex.z; // 2. Reset Z for standard projection v.vertex.z = 0.1; // 3. Transform position o.pos = mul(UNITYMATRIXMVP, v.vertex); // 4. Handle UV flipping if necessary o.uv = v.uv.xy; if (MainTexTexelSize.y < 0) { o.uv.y = 1.0 - o.uv.y; } // 5. Get eye-space ray direction float3 rayes = FrustumCornersES[index].xyz; // 6. Transform to world-space // Note: mul(matrix, vector) assumes column-major matrices o.ray = mul(CameraInvViewMatrix, float4(rayes, 0.0)).xyz; return o; } Parameters: FrustumCornersES: float4x4 uniform. Contains 4 vectors (columns or rows depending on convention) representing the eye-space directions to the four corners of the frustum. CameraInvViewMatrix: float4x4 uniform. The inverse of the camera's view matrix. MainTexTexelSize: float4 uniform. Used to detect UV orientation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: UV Orientation: On some platforms, textures may start at the top-left, requiring Y-flipping of UVs. This is handled by checking MainTexTexelSize.y < 0. Index Mapping: The mapping between vertex Z-index and frustum corner must be consistent between the CPU-side quad generation and the shader's lookup table. uses a specific mapping (3,2,1,0) that must be replicated. Precision: Using Z-coordinate for index storage relies on the vertex shader receiving the exact integer value. Floating-point precision issues are unlikely for small integers (0-3) in standard vertex formats. Degenerate Input: If the camera has no frustum (e.g., invalid projection), the corner vectors may be undefined. assumes a valid camera. A method to compute the four frustum corner directions in camera space using Camera.CalculateFrustumCorners with a full-screen rect (0,0,1,1), far clip plane, and mono eye. The corners are then transformed from camera space to world space using only rotation (via TransformDirection), as rays are directions, not points. The resulting four world-space direction vectors (FrustumCornerTR, FrustumCornerBR, FrustumCornerTL, FrustumCornerBL) are passed to the shader as uniform vectors. This variant pre-computes world-space directions directly, potentially simplifying the vertex shader by removing the need for CameraInvViewMatrix multiplication. A geometry shader-based approach that generates a full-screen quad representing the projection plane of the sensor (e.g., Kinect) in world space. The quad is generated by creating 4 vertices with normalized device coordinates (e.g., -1.0, 1.0, 0.01, 1.0) and calculating the world space position by multiplying half-window size coordinates with the inverse view matrix: Pos = mul(float4(-cb\f2HalfWinSize.x, cb\f2HalfWinSize.y, 1, 1), cb\mInvView). Texture coordinates are set to map screen space (0,0) to (WinReso.x, WinReso.y). Parameters include cbf2HalfWinSize (half resolution) and cbmInvView (inverse view matrix). This method is more explicit about world-space positioning but requires a geometry shader stage. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for ray direction calculation, as it is a simple array lookup and matrix multiplication in the vertex shader, interpolated to fragments. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the 4 frustum corner vectors and the inverse view matrix. Performance: Generally faster than per-fragment ray direction calculation because the lookup and transformation are done once per vertex (4 times per screen) rather than once per fragment. Strengths: Simple implementation, minimal GPU overhead, works well with standard image effect pipelines. Limitations: Only supports 4 discrete ray directions (corners), which may cause visible artifacts if the frustum is highly distorted or if high precision is required across the screen. It assumes a perspective camera with a standard frustum. When to use: When rendering volume data with a perspective camera and performance is critical, and the 4-corner approximation is sufficient for the visual quality required. When not to use: When high-precision ray directions are needed across the entire screen, or when using orthographic cameras (use Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation). This technique was popularized in the context of Unity game engine image effects and raymarching shaders. It is described in Adrian Bolboaca's blog post "Raymarching Distance Fields: Concepts and Implementation". The method leverages the flexibility of custom blit functions in Unity to pass additional data (the corner index) via the vertex Z-coordinate, which is otherwise unused in a standard orthographic blit. It is a common pattern in real-time raymarching for volumetric effects and distance field rendering. name: Ray Origin Offset Noise
head: Noise Generation for Ray Offset, Ray Offset Noise
body: Ray Origin Offset Noise is a technique used in volume rendering to perturb the starting position of a ray march, thereby avoiding banding artifacts caused by the regular sampling grid. It differs from sibling methods like Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation or Camera Matrix Ray Generation, which define the geometric ray path, by adding a stochastic perturbation to the ray's origin or initial step. This method is distinct from Incremental Random Number Generation because it typically relies on spatial hashing to ensure deterministic, uncorrelated values for each pixel or sample, rather than maintaining a continuous state. Inputs: uv: A 2D vector representing the normalized screen coordinates or spatial position of the sample/pixel. unitVector: A constant 2D vector used to break symmetry in the hash function. Outputs: r: A pseudo-random floating-point value in the range 0, 1). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. The method is stateless and computes the random value on the fly from the input coordinates. Steps: 1. Compute the dot product of the input coordinates uv and the scaled unitVector. 2. Apply the sine function to the result. 3. Multiply by the constant 43758.5453. 4. Extract the fractional part of the result to obtain the random value. Formula: r = \text{fract}(\sin(\text{dot}(uv, \text{unitVector} \times 79.30408)) \times 43758.5453) Where: \text{fract}(x) = x - \lfloor x \rfloor \text{dot}(a, b) = ax bx + ay by \text{unitVector} is a constant 2D vector, typically chosen to be irrational or non-integer to minimize correlation (e.g., (7.31, 2.13) or similar, though the specific vector is not defined in the source, only the scaling factor is provided). The constant 79.30408 scales the input vector. The constant 43758.5453 is a multiplier that exploits the chaotic nature of the sine function's tail to produce a uniform distribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayoriginoffsetnoise(uv: Vector2, unitvector: Vector2) -> float: """ Generates a pseudo-random value in [0, 1) for ray origin offsetting. Args: uv: 2D coordinates (e.g., normalized pixel coordinates). unitvector: 2D constant vector for hashing. Returns: A float in [0, 1). """ # Scale the unit vector by the constant factor scaledvector = unitvector 79.30408 # Compute dot product dotproduct = uv.x scaledvector.x + uv.y scaledvector.y # Apply sine sineval = math.sin(dotproduct) # Multiply by constant multiplied = sineval 43758.5453 # Extract fractional part randomvalue = multiplied - math.floor(multiplied) return randomvalue Parameters: unitVector: Not given in the sources. Typically a constant 2D vector. 79.30408: Scaling factor for the dot product. 43758.5453: Multiplier for the sine output. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the precision of the sine function and floating-point arithmetic. In low-precision environments, the output may exhibit patterns or reduced randomness. Boundary Conditions: The method is stateless, so boundary conditions are handled by the input uv. However, if uv is not normalized or scaled appropriately, the randomness may not be uniform across the screen. Correlation: If unitVector is not chosen carefully (e.g., if it has integer components), the output may exhibit banding or correlation artifacts. The source implies the use of a specific constant scaling factor to mitigate this, but the vector itself is not specified. A [hash-based pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) maps integer or floating-point coordinates to a deterministic pseudo-random value in the range [0, 1) or [-1, 1] using transcendental functions (typically sine) or bitwise/multiplicative mixing. It solves the problem of generating unique, seemingly random offsets for ray origins or noise sampling without storing large lookup tables, thereby avoiding banding artifacts in volume rendering. Unlike Incremental Random Number Generation, which generates a sequence of correlated random numbers for a single ray, this method generates independent values based on spatial coordinates, ensuring that the same coordinate always yields the same random value across different frames and devices. Incremental Random Number Generation is a method for producing low-discrepancy pseudo-random sequences by iteratively adding an irrational constant to a state variable and taking the fractional part. It solves the problem of generating uniformly distributed samples with minimal correlation between consecutive iterations, which is critical for avoiding banding artifacts in ray marching. It differs from hash-based generators by maintaining a continuous state that evolves deterministically, ensuring that the sequence covers the sampling space more evenly (quasi-Monte Carlo properties) than standard linear congruential generators, while being computationally cheaper than complex hash functions. A Linear Congruential Generator (LCG) producing deterministic pseudo-random floats in the range [-1, 1) using Numerical Recipes constants. Used for procedural sound synthesis. Steps: 1. Update state: Multiply current state by 6,364,136,223,846,793,005 and add 1,442,695,040,888,963,407 using wrapping arithmetic (mod 2^64). 2. Extract top 24 bits: Shift state right by 40 bits and cast to f32. Formula: x{n+1} = (xn \times 6364136223846793005 + 1442695040888963407) \mod 2^{64} v = \left(\frac{xn \gg 40}{8388608.0}\right) - 1.0 Parameters: Multiplier: 6,364,136,223,846,793,005 (u64). Increment: 1,442,695,040,888,963,407 (u64). State type: u64. Output range: [-1.0, 1.0). Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The computation involves a dot product, sine, multiplication, and fractional part extraction, all of which are constant-time operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the input coordinates and constant values. Performance: The method is computationally inexpensive and suitable for real-time applications. The use of transcendental functions (sine) may be slightly more expensive than bitwise operations, but modern GPUs optimize these well. Strengths: Deterministic, stateless, easy to implement, avoids banding artifacts. Limitations: The quality of randomness depends on the choice of constants and input coordinates. When to use: When avoiding banding artifacts in volume rendering is critical and computational resources are limited. When not to use: When high-quality statistical randomness is required, or when the input coordinates are not available or meaningful. name: Hash-based Pseudo-Random Number Generator
head: Hash Functions, Hash-based PRNG, Integer to Float Mapping, Pseudo-Random Number Generator (Hash), Random Number Generation for Noise, hash12, hash13
body: A hash-based pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) maps integer or floating-point coordinates to a deterministic pseudo-random value in the range [0, 1) or [-1, 1] using transcendental functions (typically sine) or bitwise/multiplicative mixing. It solves the problem of generating unique, seemingly random offsets for ray origins or noise sampling without storing large lookup tables, thereby avoiding banding artifacts in volume rendering. Unlike Incremental Random Number Generation, which generates a sequence of correlated random numbers for a single ray, this method generates independent values based on spatial coordinates, ensuring that the same coordinate always yields the same random value across different frames and devices. Input: A coordinate vector p. Common variants accept 2D (vec2) or 3D (vec3) inputs. The input is typically integer-based (e.g., voxel coordinates) or floating-point (e.g., ray origin). Output: A single floating-point scalar r \in 0, 1) or a vector of random values. No persistent data structures are required for the basic hash functions. The computation is stateless and depends only on the input coordinate p and hardcoded constants. Two primary families of hash functions are used: sine-based and sin-free. This is the most common implementation in shaders due to its brevity. 2D Variant (hash12 or rnd): r = \text{fract}(\sin(\text{dot}(p, \mathbf{a})) \times C) 3D Variant (hash13): r = \text{fract}(\sin(\text{dot}(p, \mathbf{b})) \times C) Constants: \mathbf{a} = (127.1, 311.7) for hash12. \mathbf{a}' = (12.9898, 78.233) for alternative rnd. \mathbf{b} = (127.1, 311.7, 74.7) for hash13. C = 43758.5453123. Definitions: \text{dot}(u, v): Dot product of vectors u and v. \sin(x): Sine function (radians). \text{fract}(x): Fractional part of x, defined as x - \lfloor x \rfloor. Used to avoid precision issues with sine on certain GPUs. 2D Variant (hash12): \begin{aligned} p3 &= \text{fract}(p{xyx} \times 0.1031) \\ p3 &= p3 + \text{dot}(p3, p3^{zyx} + 33.33) \\ r &= \text{fract}((p3.x + p3.y) \times p3.z) \end{aligned} Definitions: p{xyx}: Swizzle of p to (p.x, p.y, p.x). p3^{zyx}: Swizzle of p3 to (p3.z, p3.y, p3.x). Constants: 0.1031 and 33.33 are irrational/multiplicative constants chosen to spread bits. 1. Dot Product: Compute h = p.x \cdot a1 + p.y \cdot a2, where a1, a2 are the components of vector \mathbf{a}. 2. Sine: Compute s = \sin(h). 3. Scale: Compute scaled = s \cdot C. 4. Fraction: Compute r = scaled - \lfloor scaled \rfloor. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hash12sin(px, py): """ Generates a pseudo-random float in [0, 1) from 2D coordinates using sine. Constants from. """ # Constants a1 = 127.1 a2 = 311.7 C = 43758.5453123 # Step 1: Dot product h = px a1 + py a2 # Step 2: Sine s = sin(h) # Step 3: Scale scaled = s C # Step 4: Fractional part # floor() returns the largest integer <= x. # fract(x) = x - floor(x) r = scaled - floor(scaled) return r def hash12sinfree(px, py): """ Generates a pseudo-random float in [0, 1) from 2D coordinates using multiplicative mixing, avoiding sine for stability. """ # Step 1: Initial fract and swizzle # p3 is a 3-component vector (x, y, x) p3x = fract(px 0.1031) p3y = fract(py 0.1031) p3z = fract(px 0.1031) # Step 2: Add dot product mixing # dot(p3, p3.yzx + 33.33) # p3.yzx is (p3z, p3y, p3x) # p3.yzx + 33.33 is (p3z + 33.33, p3y + 33.33, p3x + 33.33) dotval = p3x (p3z + 33.33) + p3y (p3y + 33.33) + p3z (p3x + 33.33) p3x = p3x + dotval p3y = p3y + dotval p3z = p3z + dotval # Step 3: Final fract r = fract((p3x + p3y) p3z) return r Constants: The specific irrational constants (127.1, 311.7, 43758.5453123) are critical for bit dispersion. Changing them alters the statistical properties. Input Type: Integer inputs are preferred for [voxel grids to ensure exact reproducibility. Floating-point inputs may suffer from precision drift if not handled carefully. Precision Sensitivity: The sine-based hash is sensitive to floating-point precision differences between GPUs and CPUs. On some hardware, the sine function may produce slightly different results, leading to visual artifacts or non-deterministic behavior. Statistical Quality: The sine-based hash has known statistical shortcomings (e.g., correlations in higher dimensions). For high-quality renderers requiring rigorous randomness, integer/bitwise hashes (like Murmur) are recommended over sine-based ones. Negative Coordinates: Sine-based hashes handle negative coordinates via the sine function's periodicity, but bitwise hashes must explicitly handle sign extension or wrapping to ensure consistency. Source Uncertainty: The exact origin of the specific constants in the sine hash is unknown, possibly dating back to Rey 1998, cited by TestU01. Deterministic integer hashing provides a platform-independent method for generating pseudo-random integers from integer coordinates, ensuring identical bit-exact results between CPU (TypeScript/C++) and GPU (GLSL) environments. It solves the reproducibility problem in procedural content generation where floating-point sine-based hashing drifts due to library implementation differences. Unlike the standard Hash-based Pseudo-Random Number Generator which relies on transcendental functions, this method uses only 32-bit bitwise operations and multiplication, guaranteeing consistent wrapping behavior for negative coordinates. A permutation table is a shuffled array of integers used to index into a hash space without modulo operations, often used in gradient noise algorithms. Definition: Generates a shuffled permutation table of size 512 (SIZE + SIZE) using a seeded random shuffle, then duplicates the first 256 entries to avoid modulo operations. Steps: 1. Initialize mperm[0..255] with identity: mperm[i] = i. 2. Fisher-Yates shuffle: Decrement i from 255 to 1, swap mperm[i] with mperm[Random.Range(0, SIZE)]. 3. Duplicate first 256 entries to indices 256-511: mperm[SIZE + i] = mperm[i]. Parameters: SIZE: Constant 256. seed: Random seed passed to constructor. Layout: mperm is an integer array of size 512. Time Complexity: O(1) per coordinate. The sine-based hash involves a dot product, one sine, one multiplication, and one fractional part extraction. The sin-free hash involves several multiplications and additions but no transcendental functions. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the basic hash functions. No memory is allocated. Permutation tables require O(N) memory where N is the table size (e.g., 512 integers). Measured Performance: Sine-based hashes are extremely fast on GPUs due to hardware-accelerated sine instructions. Sin-free hashes are faster on hardware where sine is expensive or imprecise. Strengths: Extremely low memory footprint; deterministic; easy to implement in shaders; no pre-computation required. Limitations: Statistical quality is inferior to cryptographic or high-quality PRNGs (e.g., PCG, Murmur); precision-dependent on sine implementation; not suitable for applications requiring rigorous statistical randomness. When to Use: Ray origin offset noise, voxel world generation, procedural texture coordinate hashing. When Not to Use: Applications requiring high-quality statistical randomness, cryptographic security, or strict cross-platform bit-exactness without sin-free variants. The sine-based hash function fract(sin(dot(p, vec2(127.1, 311.7))) 43758.5453123) is a staple in shader programming, popularized by blogs and StackOverflow answers for its brevity and speed. Its origin is uncertain, possibly dating back to Rey 1998, as cited by TestU01. It is widely used in voxel world shaders, terrain generation, and procedural noise implementations. The sin-free variant was developed to address cross-platform precision issues. Permutation tables are a standard component of gradient noise algorithms like Perlin Noise, often generated via Fisher-Yates shuffle. name: Deterministic Integer Hashing
head: hashCell, hashToFloat, lowbias32
body: Deterministic integer hashing provides a platform-independent method for generating pseudo-random integers from integer coordinates, ensuring identical bit-exact results between CPU (TypeScript/C++) and GPU (GLSL) environments. It solves the reproducibility problem in procedural content generation where floating-point sine-based hashing drifts due to library implementation differences. Unlike its sibling Hash-based Pseudo-Random Number Generator which relies on transcendental functions, this method uses only 32-bit bitwise operations and multiplication, guaranteeing consistent wrapping behavior for negative coordinates. The system consists of three components: a base 32-bit mixer (uhash), a 3D coordinate hasher (hashCell), and a float converter (hashToFloat). Inputs and Outputs: uhash: Input x (32-bit unsigned integer), Output h (32-bit unsigned integer). hashCell: Inputs cx, cy, cz (32-bit signed integers), Output h (32-bit unsigned integer). hashToFloat: Input h (32-bit unsigned integer), Output f (32-bit float in 0, 1)). Data Structures: All intermediate values are 32-bit unsigned integers (uint32). Multiplication uses 32-bit wrapping semantics (modulo 2^{32}). Parameters: uhash multipliers: M{u1} = \text{0x7feb352d}, M{u2} = \text{0x846ca68b}. hashCell multipliers: M{cx} = \text{0x9e3779b9}, M{cy} = \text{0x85ebca6b}, M{cz} = \text{0xc2b2ae35}. computehash (byte slice variant) constants: M0 = 2860486313\text{U}, M1 = 3267000013\text{U}. Steps: 1. Base Mixer (uhash): Mix the input integer x using a sequence of XOR shifts and multiplications: \begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow x \oplus (x \gg 16) \\ x &\leftarrow x \times M{u1} \\ x &\leftarrow x \oplus (x \gg 15) \\ x &\leftarrow x \times M{u2} \\ x &\leftarrow x \oplus (x \gg 16) \\ \text{return } x \gg 0 \end{aligned} Note: >>> 0 or x >> 0 ensures the result is treated as an unsigned 32-bit integer, masking out any sign extension if the language treats shifts differently on signed types. 2. 3D [Coordinate Hashing (hashCell): Combine three integer coordinates into a single hash: \begin{aligned} h &\leftarrow \text{uhash}(cx \times M{cx}) \\ h &\leftarrow \text{uhash}(h \oplus (cy \times M{cy})) \\ h &\leftarrow \text{uhash}(h \oplus (cz \times M{cz})) \\ \text{return } h \gg 0 \end{aligned} Negative coordinates are handled naturally because the multiplication and XOR operations on 32-bit integers wrap identically to GLSL's uint(int) cast. 3. Float Conversion (hashToFloat): Map the integer hash to a float in [0, 1): f = \frac{h \gg 8}{16777216.0} Shifting right by 8 bits discards the lower 8 bits, leaving the top 24 bits. This ensures the value fits within the 24-bit mantissa of a 32-bit IEEE 754 float without precision loss during conversion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uhash(x: int) -> int: # Ensure 32-bit unsigned interpretation x = x & 0xFFFFFFFF x ^= (x >> 16) x = (x 0x7feb352d) & 0xFFFFFFFF x ^= (x >> 15) x = (x 0x846ca68b) & 0xFFFFFFFF x ^= (x >> 16) return x & 0xFFFFFFFF def hashCell(cx: int, cy: int, cz: int) -> int: # Constants MCX = 0x9e3779b9 MCY = 0x85ebca6b MCZ = 0xc2b2ae35 # Mix coordinates h = uhash(cx MCX) h = uhash(h ^ (cy MCY)) h = uhash(h ^ (cz MCZ)) return h def hashToFloat(h: int) -> float: # Shift top 24 bits down to 24-bit precision range # 16777216 = 2^24 return ((h >> 8) & 0xFFFFFF) / 16777216.0 def computehashbyteslice(data: list) -> int: """ Alternative hash for byte slices (e.g., from S1). data: list of integers 0-255 """ M0 = 2860486313 M1 = 3267000013 h = M0 for b in data: h = ((h ^ b) M1) & 0xFFFFFFFF return h Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Coordinates: Unlike sine-based hashing, integer hashing handles negative inputs correctly because 32-bit two's complement arithmetic wraps consistently across platforms. Precision Loss: Using the full 32-bit integer directly in a float conversion would lose precision because the mantissa only holds 24 bits. The >> 8 shift is critical. Platform Drift: Avoid sin() or cos() for hashing if CPU and GPU code share the same hash function, as math library implementations may differ slightly. Wraps the PCG32 fast random number generator, providing seeded streams per job. It seeds the engine for a specific job jid using a hash of the global seed and job ID: mengine.seed(hash(mseed, jid)). It generates uniform floats in [0, 1-\epsilon] via val = engine() and return min(0x1.fffffep-1, val 0x1p-32f). Time Complexity: O(1) for uhash and hashCell. O(N) for computehash where N is the number of bytes. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Extremely fast due to simple bitwise operations and multiplication. No transcendental function calls. Strengths: Bit-exact reproducibility across CPU/GPU boundaries; handles negative coordinates naturally; no precision loss in float conversion. Limitations: Not a cryptographic hash; statistical properties depend on the specific mixer constants. This method originates from the neon-raymarcher project, which required identical procedural generation on both a TypeScript CPU renderer and a GLSL GPU renderer. The computehash variant is sourced from the mc project. The use of specific constants like 0x9e3779b9 (related to the golden ratio) is common in hash functions to ensure good bit dispersion. nsf/mc, https://github.com/nsf/mc, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, https://github.com/PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Shibodd/volumepathtracer, https://github.com/Shibodd/volumepathtracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Permutation Table Generation
head: perm table
body: Generates a shuffled permutation table of size 512 using a seeded random shuffle, then duplicates the first 256 entries to avoid modulo operations during hash-based pseudo-random number generation. It serves as the foundational data structure for Hash-based Pseudo-Random Number Generator, ensuring deterministic yet uniformly distributed indices for noise functions. Unlike Deterministic Integer Hashing which computes hashes on the fly, this method pre-computes a lookup table, trading memory for computational speed and avoiding expensive bitwise operations or trigonometric functions during ray generation. Inputs: seed: Integer random seed passed to the constructor. Outputs: mperm: An integer array of size 512 containing a shuffled permutation of integers 0 \dots 255, with the first half duplicated. Data Structures: mperm: int[512]. The array stores indices. The first 256 entries are a permutation of 0 \dots 255. The next 256 entries are identical to the first 256. Parameters: SIZE: Constant integer 256. Steps: 1. Initialize the first SIZE entries of mperm with the identity permutation: m\perm[i] = i \quad \text{for } i \in [0, SIZE-1] 2. Perform a Fisher-Yates shuffle on the first SIZE entries using the provided seed to generate pseudo-random numbers. Iterate i from SIZE - 1 down to 1: a. Generate a pseudo-random integer j in the range [0, i] using the seeded RNG. b. Swap mperm[i] and mperm[j]. 3. Duplicate the shuffled first half to the second half to facilitate modulo-free indexing: m\perm[SIZE + i] = m\perm[i] \quad \text{for } i \in [0, SIZE-1] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatepermutationtable(seed, size=256): # Step 1: Initialize identity permutation perm = [i for i in range(size)] # Step 2: Fisher-Yates shuffle # Note: The specific PRNG implementation for Random.Range is assumed # to be provided by the context of the Hash-based PRNG. # Here we assume a standard linear congruential generator or similar # seeded RNG for the sake of completeness, though the source # references a specific 'Random.Range' helper. rng = SeededRNG(seed) for i in range(size - 1, 0, -1): # Generate random index j in [0, i] j = rng.nextint(i + 1) # Swap elements perm[i], perm[j] = perm[j], perm[i] # Step 3: Duplicate first half to second half fullperm = perm + perm return fullperm Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Seed Collision: Different seeds produce different permutations, but if the seed is not properly initialized, the table may be non-deterministic across runs. Modulo Avoidance: The duplication step is critical. When accessing the table with an index k, the code typically uses perm[k & 255] (bitwise AND) instead of perm[k % 256]. This requires the table to have at least 256 valid entries starting from index 0, which the duplication ensures. If the table were not duplicated, indices 256 \dots 511 would be out of bounds or require modulo. Precision: The values in mperm are integers. No floating-point precision issues arise during generation. Converts the CPU-side permutation array into GPU-readable textures for 1D and 2D noise lookups. The 1D permutation table is stored in a Texture2D of dimensions (SIZE, 1) with Alpha8 format. The pixel at coordinate (x, 1) is set to Color(0, 0, 0, mperm[x] / (SIZE - 1)). This normalization maps the integer indices 0 \dots 255 to the floating-point range [0, 1] suitable for GPU texture sampling. This allows the noise function to be evaluated entirely on the GPU using texture lookups, which can be faster than computing hashes in shader code on some hardware architectures. Time Complexity: O(N) where N=256. The Fisher-Yates shuffle is linear. This is a one-time cost per seed. Memory Complexity: O(N) integers. 512 integers = 2 KB. Negligible compared to volume data. Performance: Lookup is O(1) with bitwise AND. Faster than computing sine/dot product hashes per sample. Strengths: Deterministic, fast lookup, avoids modulo operations. Limitations: Requires memory allocation for the table. Less flexible than on-the-fly hashing if the hash function needs to change dynamically. Originated in the context of GPU-based marching cubes and noise generation, specifically in the Scrawk/Marching-Cubes-On-The-GPU repository. It is a standard technique in procedural noise generation to provide a fast, deterministic way to map integer coordinates to pseudo-random values. name: Incremental Random Number Generation
head: Golden Ratio Random, Quasi-Monte Carlo Random
body: Incremental Random Number Generation is a method for producing low-discrepancy pseudo-random sequences by iteratively adding an irrational constant to a state variable and taking the fractional part. It solves the problem of generating uniformly distributed samples with minimal correlation between consecutive iterations, which is critical for avoiding banding artifacts in ray marching. It differs from hash-based generators by maintaining a continuous state that evolves deterministically, ensuring that the sequence covers the sampling space more evenly (quasi-Monte Carlo properties) than standard linear congruential generators, while being computationally cheaper than complex hash functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar or vector state variable r (the previous random value). Output: A new scalar or vector random value r' in the range [0, 1). Data Structures: No external data structures are required. The method relies solely on the current state variable. Parameters: Golden Ratio (\phi): 0.6180339887. Pi (\pi): 3.1415926538. Formulas: The core operation is the fractional part function \{ x \} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor. 1. 1D Incremental Random: r{i+1} = \{ ri + 4 \phi \} Where ri is the previous scalar random value. 2. 2D Incremental Random: r{i+1} = \{ ri + (\phi, \pi) \} Where ri is the previous 2D vector random value. The addition is component-wise, and the fractional part is taken component-wise. Steps: 1. Retrieve the current state r (initially set to a small non-zero value or derived from pixel coordinates). 2. Add the precomputed constant(s) to r. For 1D: Add 4 \times 0.6180339887. For 2D: Add (0.6180339887, 3.1415926538). 3. Compute the fractional part of the result. 4. Return the result as the new random value and update the state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. GOLDENRATIO = 0.6180339887 PI = 3.1415926538 def fract(x): """Returns the fractional part of x.""" return x - math.floor(x) def incrementalrand1d(randstate: float) -> float: """ Generates the next 1D random number.:param randstate: The previous random value.:return: The new random value in [0, 1). """ return fract(randstate + 4.0 GOLDENRATIO) def incrementalrand2d(randstate: vec2) -> vec2: """ Generates the next 2D random number.:param randstate: The previous 2D random vector.:return: The new 2D random vector in [0, 1)^2. """ return fract(randstate + vec2(GOLDENRATIO, PI)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision limits the period of the sequence. If the state accumulates significant error or if the step size is not irrational enough relative to the precision, the sequence may repeat or cluster. Using fract ensures the value stays in [0, 1), mitigating overflow but potentially introducing correlation if the initial state is poorly chosen. Initialization: The initial state should not be zero, as adding an irrational constant to zero repeatedly might exhibit patterns if the constant's binary representation has regularities. A small random offset or coordinate-based seed is recommended. A variant that uses the golden ratio to precompute a low-discrepancy lookup table for spatial jitter, combined with temporal shifting for animation. It initializes a table of size N \times N (default 64) where table[i] = (i phi) % 1.0. To get jitter for pixel (x, y) at frameIndex, it calculates baseOffset = table[abs(floor(y)) % size size + abs(floor(x)) % size] and temporalShift = ((frameIndex % 16) phi) % 1.0, returning (baseOffset + temporalShift) % 1.0. It further refines subpixel jitter using a Halton sequence with bases 2 and 3, where halton(index, base) is computed by iteratively dividing the index by the base and summing f (i % base) with f starting at 1/base and halving each step. This approach provides blue-noise-like distribution properties for anti-aliasing. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. It involves only a few floating-point additions and a fractional part operation. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the basic method. The Blue Noise variant requires O(N^2) memory for the lookup table. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time ray marching where per-sample overhead must be minimized. Strengths: Low discrepancy (good coverage), simple implementation, no branching, stateful nature allows for smooth temporal evolution if desired. Limitations: The sequence is deterministic and periodic (though the period is very long for double precision). It is not suitable for cryptographic purposes or applications requiring statistical independence between non-consecutive samples without careful spacing. The method originates from the use of irrational constants, particularly the golden ratio, in quasi-Monte Carlo integration to ensure low-discrepancy sequences. It has been adopted in real-time ray tracing and voxel rendering to offset ray origins and directions, reducing banding artifacts caused by regular sampling patterns. The specific implementation using fract(rand + GOLDENRATIO 4) is documented in voxel ray demo repositories. The Blue Noise variant extends this concept to spatial-temporal jittering for cloud rendering. newDINO/voxelraydemo, https://github.com/newDINO/voxelraydemo, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, https://github.com/nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Camera Matrix Ray Generation
head: Camera Ray Generation, Raster-to-World Ray Construction, Ray Generation from Camera Matrix, Ray Initialization & AABB Intersection, getBound, initialRays
body: Camera Matrix Ray Generation computes the origin and direction of a primary ray for each pixel in an image based on camera intrinsic parameters (focal length, principal point) and extrinsic parameters (camera-to-world pose). It solves the problem of mapping 2D raster coordinates to 3D world-space rays, enabling subsequent volume rendering or ray tracing operations. Unlike orthographic generation which uses parallel rays, this method constructs perspective rays that diverge from a single viewpoint. It differs from sample streaming payload methods by explicitly constructing the ray geometry from camera matrices rather than deriving it from pre-computed payloads or object-space offsets. Inputs: Image dimensions: H (height), W (width). Camera intrinsic matrix K (3x3) or parameters: focal lengths fx, fy, principal point (cx, cy). Camera-to-world transformation matrix T{c2w} (4x4), where the upper-left 3x3 block is rotation \mathbf{R}{c2w} and the rightmost 3-column vector is translation \mathbf{t}{c2w} (camera origin). Optional: Axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the scene for early ray termination. Outputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o}: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) in world space. Ray directions \mathbf{d}: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) in world space (often normalized). Optional: Near and far t-values (t{min}, t{max}) for AABB intersection. Data Structures: Pixel coordinate grids: 2D arrays of shape (H, W) containing integer or float pixel indices i (column, width) and j (row, height). Intrinsic parameters: Extracted from K as scalars or vectors. Transformation matrices: Stored as 4x4 matrices or separate rotation/translation components. Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Coordinates: Create 2D meshgrids for pixel indices i \in [0, W) and j \in [0, H). 2. Center Pixel Coordinates (Optional): Add 0.5 to i and j to target pixel centers instead of corners. Note: Some implementations omit this if calibration accuracy is insufficient. 3. Compute Camera-Space Directions: Calculate unnormalized direction vectors in the camera coordinate system. The camera typically looks along the negative Z-axis (OpenGL convention) or positive Z-axis (OpenCV convention). For the standard OpenGL convention (looking down -Z): \mathbf{d}{cam} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{i - cx}{fx} \\ -\frac{j - cy}{fy} \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} where the negative sign on the Y-component accounts for the image Y-axis being opposite to the camera V-axis (down vs up). For OpenCV convention (looking down +Z), the Z component is 1 and Y sign may vary depending on image orientation. 4. Transform Directions to World Space: Rotate the camera-space directions into world space using the rotation part of the camera-to-world matrix: \mathbf{d}{world} = \mathbf{d}{cam} \cdot \mathbf{R}{c2w}^\top or equivalently \mathbf{d}{world} = \mathbf{R}{c2w} \mathbf{d}{cam} if \mathbf{d}{cam} is a column vector. 5. Set Ray Origins: The ray origin is the camera position in world space, extracted from the translation component of T{c2w}: \mathbf{o}{world} = \mathbf{t}{c2w} This origin is broadcast to match the shape of the directions (H, W, 3). 6. Normalize Directions (Optional): Normalize \mathbf{d}{world} to unit length if required by the renderer. 7. Compute AABB Intersection (Optional): If an AABB is provided, compute t{min} and t{max} for each ray to determine the valid marching range. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generaterays(H, W, K, c2w, usepixelcenters=True, computeaabb=False, aabbmin=None, aabbmax=None): """ Generate ray origins and directions for all pixels. Args: H: Image height W: Image width K: 3x3 intrinsic matrix [fx, 0, cx; 0, fy, cy; 0, 0, 1] c2w: 4x4 camera-to-world matrix usepixelcenters: Boolean, add 0.5 to pixel coordinates computeaabb: Boolean, compute tmin/tmax for AABB aabbmin: 3-vector, AABB minimum bounds aabbmax: 3-vector, AABB maximum bounds Returns: rayso: (H, W, 3) ray origins raysd: (H, W, 3) ray directions (normalized) tmin: (H, W) optional near t-values tmax: (H, W) optional far t-values """ # 1. Extract intrinsics fx = K[0, 0] fy = K[1, 1] cx = K[0, 2] cy = K[1, 2] # 2. Extract extrinsics Rc2w = c2w[:3,:3] # 3x3 rotation tc2w = c2w[:3, 3] # 3-vector translation (camera origin) # 3. Generate pixel coordinates # Create meshgrid with 'ij' indexing: i varies along rows (height), j along cols (width) # However, standard convention often uses i for x (width) and j for y (height) # Let's align with S10: j is rows (0..H-1), i is cols (0..W-1) j, i = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H, dtype=torch.float32), torch.arange(W, dtype=torch.float32), indexing='ij') # 4. Center pixel coordinates if usepixelcenters: i = i + 0.5 j = j + 0.5 # 5. Compute camera-space directions (OpenGL convention: look down -Z) # dcam = [(i - cx)/fx, -(j - cy)/fy, -1] # Note: Negative sign on Y because image Y is down, camera V is up dcamx = (i - cx) / fx dcamy = -(j - cy) / fy dcamz = -torch.oneslike(i) dcam = torch.stack([dcamx, dcamy, dcamz], dim=-1) # (H, W, 3) # 6. Transform directions to world space # dworld = dcam @ Rc2w.T dworld = torch.sum(dcam[..., None,:] Rc2w, dim=-1) # (H, W, 3) # 7. Normalize directions dworld = dworld / torch.norm(dworld, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # 8. Set ray origins # Broadcast tc2w to (H, W, 3) rayso = tc2w.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(H, W, 3) # 9. Compute AABB intersection if requested tmin = None tmax = None if computeaabb and aabbmin is not None and aabbmax is not None: # Ray-AABB intersection for each pixel # tmin = max((bboxmin - o) / d) for each axis, handling division by zero # tmax = min((bboxmax - o) / d) for each axis # Avoid division by zero by adding small epsilon or handling inf eps = 1e-8 dsafe = torch.where(torch.abs(dworld) < eps, eps, dworld) t1 = (aabbmin - rayso) / dsafe t2 = (aabbmax - rayso) / dsafe # tmin is max of mins, tmax is min of maxs tmin = torch.maximum(torch.minimum(t1, t2), dim=-1).values tmax = torch.minimum(torch.maximum(t1, t2), dim=-1).values # Filter out rays that don't intersect (tmin > tmax) # Or clamp to valid range valid = tmin < tmax tmin = torch.where(valid, tmin, torch.tensor(0.0)) tmax = torch.where(valid, tmax, torch.tensor(0.0)) return rayso, dworld, tmin, tmax Parameters: fx, fy: Focal lengths in pixels. cx, cy: Principal point coordinates in pixels. H, W: Image height and width in pixels. T{c2w}: 4x4 camera-to-world matrix. usepixelcenters: Boolean, default True. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If fx or fy is zero, or if ray direction components are zero during AABB intersection, division by zero occurs. IEEE 754 infinities may result, requiring explicit checks or clamping. Coordinate System Conventions: OpenGL cameras look down -Z, OpenCV down +Z. Image Y-axis is typically down, while camera V-axis is up. Signs in direction calculation must match these conventions. Pixel Centering: Omitting +0.5 offset can cause slight misalignment, but may be acceptable if calibration is inaccurate. AABB Intersection: If t{min} > t{max}, the ray does not intersect the AABB. This case must be handled to avoid invalid marching ranges. Generates rays for a pinhole camera model using field of view (FOV) and image size instead of explicit intrinsic matrices. It calculates ray directions based on normalized device coordinates (NDC) scaled by \tan(FOV/2). Choose this when camera intrinsics are not available but FOV and aspect ratio are known. It is a simplified variant of Camera Matrix Ray Generation that assumes a square pixel aspect ratio and zero skew. Time Complexity: O(H \times W) for generating rays for all pixels, as each pixel's ray is computed independently. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) to store ray origins and directions. Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPU using compute shaders or tensor operations. Performance is limited by memory bandwidth when storing large ray buffers. Strengths: Accurate perspective projection; supports arbitrary camera poses and intrinsics; efficient batch computation. Limitations: Requires accurate camera calibration; does not handle lens distortion or non-pinhole models without extension. When to Use: Standard perspective rendering, NeRF, volume rendering with known camera poses. When Not to Use: Orthographic rendering (use Orthographic Camera Ray Generation), real-time interactive rendering with dynamic camera where overhead is critical (though still efficient), or when lens effects are needed. Originating from standard computer graphics and photogrammetry, the method maps pixel coordinates to world rays using camera matrices. It is fundamental to NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) implementations, where accurate ray generation is critical for training and rendering. The approach is widely used in volume rendering, ray tracing, and 3D reconstruction pipelines. jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, https://github.com/jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Estudio de la compresión y la eficiencia del Sparse Voxel Octree en el cálculo de la Iluminación Global, https://hdl.handle.net/2117/445971, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kkhese/Volume-Rendering, https://github.com/kkhese/Volume-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Shibodd/volumepathtracer, https://github.com/Shibodd/volumepathtracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) yashbhalgat/HashNeRF-pytorch, https://github.com/yashbhalgat/HashNeRF-pytorch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, https://github.com/nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) an1pse/voxel-traversal, https://github.com/an1pse/voxel-traversal, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, https://github.com/rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, https://github.com/bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 7.6.
