name: Pinhole Camera Ray Generation
head: Camera Ray Casting, Perspective Ray Generation, PinholeRayTracer::castRays
body: Pinhole Camera Ray Generation computes the origin and direction vectors for rays corresponding to each pixel in an image plane, assuming an ideal pinhole camera model with no lens distortion or depth of field. It differs from its parent, Camera Matrix Ray Generation, by explicitly constructing the view frustum geometry (basis vectors and view plane bounds) from high-level camera parameters (eye, look-at, up, FOV) rather than relying on a pre-computed 4x4 projection/view matrix. It serves as the foundational ray setup for basic ray tracing and volume rendering pipelines where explicit control over the view plane sampling is required. The method generates rays by defining a local coordinate system at the camera origin, mapping pixel indices to coordinates on a virtual view plane, and constructing direction vectors from the eye position through these points. Two primary implementation styles are documented: a look-at based approach (common in GPU implementations) and a rotation-matrix based approach (common in C++/Eigen implementations). Inputs: Camera Position (Eye): E = (Ex, Ey, Ez). Look-at Point (At): A = (Ax, Ay, Az). Up Vector: U{up} (typically (0, 1, 0)). Image Dimensions: Width W, Height H. Field of View (FOV): Vertical FOV (\theta{v}) or Half Vertical FOV (vfov). Aspect Ratio: AR = W / H. Outputs: Origins: Array of size W \times H, each element is the Eye position E. Directions: Array of size W \times H, each element is a normalized 3D vector. Auxiliary Data (Optional): originimagedistances and pixeldistances arrays for physical scaling. Origins: 1D float array of size 3 \times W \times H, storing (x,y,z) for each pixel ray origin. Directions: 1D float array of size 3 \times W \times H, storing normalized (x,y,z) for each pixel ray direction. Origin Image Distances: 1D float array of size W \times H, storing the length of the unnormalized direction vector s. Pixel Distances: 1D float array of size W \times H, storing the physical width of a single pixel on the view plane. This variant constructs the camera basis vectors explicitly from the eye, look-at, and up vectors. 1. Compute View Plane Bounds: Define the vertical extent of the view plane at distance 1 from the camera. \theta{v\rad} = \text{DegToRad}(\thetav) \text{top} = \tan(\theta{v\rad}) \text{bottom} = -\text{top} \text{right} = AR \times \text{top} \text{left} = -\text{right} 2. Compute Camera Basis Vectors: Calculate the forward, right, and up vectors of the camera coordinate system. \mathbf{w} = \text{normalize}(E - A) \mathbf{u} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(U{up}, \mathbf{w})) \mathbf{v} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{u}) Note: \mathbf{w} points from the camera to the target. \mathbf{u} is the horizontal axis. \mathbf{v} is the vertical axis. 3. Iterate Pixels: For each pixel index i from 0 to W \times H - 1: x = i \pmod W y = \lfloor i / W \rfloor 4. Map to View Plane Coordinates: Calculate the position on the view plane at z=-1 (in camera space) using bilinear interpolation across the bounds. \text{view\plane\x} = \text{left} + (\text{right} - \text{left}) \times \frac{x + 0.5}{W} \text{view\plane\y} = \text{top} - (\text{top} - \text{bottom}) \times \frac{y + 0.5}{H} Note: The y component is subtracted because screen coordinates typically increase downwards, while the camera's \mathbf{v} vector points upwards. 5. Compute Unnormalized Direction: Construct the direction vector in world space. \mathbf{s} = \text{view\plane\x} \cdot \mathbf{u} + \text{view\plane\y} \cdot \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{w} Note: The -\mathbf{w} term accounts for the fact that the view plane is at z=-1 in the local camera frame where the camera looks down -Z, or equivalently, the vector from Eye to ViewPlanePoint is Point - Eye. In the local frame, the point is (\text{view\plane\x}, \text{view\plane\y}, -1). The basis vectors \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} transform this local offset to world space. Since \mathbf{w} is the forward vector, the vector from origin to (0,0,-1) is -\mathbf{w}. 6. Normalize and Store: \text{direction} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{s}) \text{origin} = E 7. Compute Auxiliary Distances (Optional): \text{origin\image\distances}[i] = \|\mathbf{s}\| \text{pixel\distances}[i] = \frac{\text{right} - \text{left}}{W} This variant uses a pre-computed rotation matrix to orient a canonical frustum. 1. Compute Step Sizes: Calculate the angular step per pixel based on the tangent of the half-FOV. dh = \frac{\tan(\text{hfov})}{\text{hsize}} dv = \frac{\tan(\text{vfov})}{\text{vsize}} Parameters: \text{hfov} and \text{vfov} are half horizontal and vertical FOV in radians. \text{hsize} and \text{vsize} are the image dimensions. 2. Get Camera Rotation: Extract the rotation matrix R from the camera's viewpoint transformation. 3. Iterate and Construct Rays: Loop h from -\text{hsize}/2 to \text{hsize}/2 and v from -\text{vsize}/2 to \text{vsize}/2: \mathbf{rayd}{local} = (dv \cdot v, \ dh \cdot h, \ 1.0) \mathbf{rayd}{world} = R \cdot \mathbf{rayd}{local} Store \mathbf{rayd}{world} in the output vector rayds. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatepinholerays(eye, at, up, width, height, fovdegrees): """ Generates ray origins and directions for a pinhole camera. Args: eye: tuple (ex, ey, ez) at: tuple (ax, ay, az) up: tuple (ux, uy, uz) width: int height: int fovdegrees: float (vertical FOV) Returns: origins: list of tuples (x,y,z) directions: list of tuples (x,y,z) """ origins = [] directions = [] # 1. Compute View Plane Bounds fovrad = math.radians(fovdegrees) top = math.tan(fovrad) bottom = -top aspect = width / height right = aspect top left = -right # 2. Compute Camera Basis Vectors # w = normalize(eye - at) wx = eye[0] - at[0] wy = eye[1] - at[1] wz = eye[2] - at[2] wlen = math.sqrt(wxwx + wywy + wzwz) w = (wx/wlen, wy/wlen, wz/wlen) # u = normalize(cross(up, w)) # cross(up, w) ux = up[1]w[2] - up[2]w[1] uy = up[2]w[0] - up[0]w[2] uz = up[0]w[1] - up[1]w[0] ulen = math.sqrt(uxux + uyuy + uzuz) u = (ux/ulen, uy/ulen, uz/ulen) # v = cross(w, u) vx = w[1]u[2] - w[2]u[1] vy = w[2]u[0] - w[0]u[2] vz = w[0]u[1] - w[1]u[0] v = (vx, vy, vz) # 3. Iterate Pixels for i in range(width height): x = i % width y = i // width # 4. Map to View Plane Coordinates viewplanex = left + (right - left) (x + 0.5) / width viewplaney = top - (top - bottom) (y + 0.5) / height # 5. Compute Unnormalized Direction # s = viewplanex u + viewplaney v - w sx = viewplanex u[0] + viewplaney v[0] - w[0] sy = viewplanex u[1] + viewplaney v[1] - w[1] sz = viewplanex u[2] + viewplaney v[2] - w[2] # 6. Normalize slen = math.sqrt(sxsx + sysy + szsz) if slen == 0: direction = (0, 0, 1) # Fallback for degenerate case else: direction = (sx/slen, sy/slen, sz/slen) origins.append(eye) directions.append(direction) return origins, directions FOV: A fixed vertical field of view of 30 degrees is used in some implementations. Half FOV: Default values in some C++ implementations are 160^\circ converted to radians (\pi \times 160.0 / 180.0) for both horizontal and vertical half-FOV. Resolution: Default image sizes in some test cases are 6 \times 4. Standard production resolutions are 1920 \times 1080 or higher. Degenerate Up Vector: If the up vector is parallel to the eye - at vector, the cross product for \mathbf{u} will be zero, causing normalization to fail. A guard clause should detect this and substitute a different up vector (e.g., (1, 0, 0)). Precision: Using float (32-bit) for ray directions can introduce quantization artifacts in the view plane mapping, especially at high resolutions. Double precision is recommended for the view plane coordinate calculation. Aspect Ratio Mismatch: If the aspect ratio is not correctly applied to the horizontal bounds (right, left), the image will appear stretched or squashed. This variant extends the basic pinhole model by simulating lens blur. It introduces a physical aperture (lens) and a focal plane. Mechanism: Instead of all rays originating from a single point, the ray origin is offset by a random vector within a unit disk (the lens aperture) scaled by LensRadius. The direction is calculated from this offset origin to a point on the focal plane. Viewport Construction: The viewport vectors are scaled by the focus distance: Horizontal = U ViewportWidth focusDist, Vertical = V ViewportHeight focusDist. The LowerLeftCorner is computed as Origin - Horizontal/2 - Vertical/2 - W focusDist. Ray Generation: For pixel (u, v), a random lens offset rd is sampled from a unit disk. The direction is LowerLeftCorner + Horizontalu + Verticalv - Origin - offset. Data Layout: The camera state includes Origin, Horizontal, Vertical, LowerLeftCorner, LensRadius, basis vectors U, V, W, AspectRatio, ViewportHeight, ViewportWidth, and FocalLength. Time Complexity: O(W \times H), where W and H are image dimensions. The computation per pixel is constant time (a few trigonometric functions, vector operations, and normalizations). Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) to store the generated ray origins and directions. Performance: The look-at variant involves computing basis vectors once (O(1)) and then iterating pixels. The rotation matrix variant involves matrix-vector multiplication per pixel, which is slightly more expensive but allows for easier integration with existing camera transformation pipelines. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides explicit control over the view plane geometry; no dependency on complex projection matrix decompositions. Limitations: Does not account for lens effects (bokeh, distortion) without extension; assumes an ideal pinhole model which may not match real-world sensor data without calibration. The pinhole camera model is the fundamental geometric model for perspective projection in computer graphics and computer vision. It assumes a single point of projection (the pinhole) and an image plane behind it. The method of generating rays by sampling the field of view using equal division of tangent is a common approximation in ray tracers to ensure uniform angular sampling. The look-at formulation using basis vectors is standard in educational ray tracers and differentiable rendering frameworks. The depth of field extension is a standard addition for realistic image synthesis. name: Basic GPU Ray Generation via Fragment Shader
head: Fragment shader ray tracing, Fragment Shader Ray Generation, Ray Tracing Fragment Shader
body: This method generates camera rays for ray tracing by rendering a single quad (two triangles) to the screen, allowing the fragment shader to compute the ray origin and direction for each pixel using interpolated vertex coordinates. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding explicit matrix multiplications in favor of geometric basis vectors (side, up, forward) derived from camera parameters, and from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by supporting perspective projection through a viewing plane distance. It builds on Ray Origin and Direction Setup by providing a concrete GPU implementation pattern. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Window resolution (iResolution), camera position (iRayOrigin), camera facing direction (iRayDir), camera up direction (iRayUp), distance to viewing plane (iPlaneDist), and interpolated texture coordinates (texCoord) ranging from (0,0) to (1,1) across the quad. Outputs: A ray (origin and direction) for each pixel, which is then used for intersection testing (e.g., against spheres or BVHs) and shading. Data Structures: Uniforms: iResolution: vec2 (width, height). iRayOrigin: vec3 (camera position). iRayDir: vec3 (camera forward vector). iRayUp: vec3 (camera up vector). iPlaneDist: float (distance from camera to the projection plane). Varying/Input: texCoord: vec2 interpolated from vertex attributes (0,0) to (1,1). Steps: 1. Setup Geometry: Render a single quad (two triangles covering the screen) using a minimal vertex shader that performs no transformations. Bind vertex attributes such that texCoord interpolates linearly from (0,0) at the bottom-left to (1,1) at the top-right (or equivalent screen mapping). 2. Compute Normalized Coordinates: In the fragment shader, convert the interpolated texCoord (range [0,1]) to a normalized device coordinate p (range [-1,1]): p = 2.0 \cdot \text{texCoord} - 1.0 3. Apply Aspect Ratio: Scale the x-component of p by the aspect ratio to prevent distortion: p.x = p.x \cdot \frac{\text{iResolution}.x}{\text{iResolution}.y} 4. Compute Camera Basis Vectors: Calculate the camera's right vector (camSide) using the cross product of the forward (iRayDir) and up (iRayUp) vectors: \text{camSide} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{iRayDir}, \text{iRayUp})) Note: Sources assume iRayDir and iRayUp are orthogonal or nearly so. If iRayUp is not orthogonal to iRayDir, camSide may need to be recomputed as cross(iRayUp, iRayDir) or iRayUp should be orthogonalized first. 5. Calculate Ray Direction: Compute the ray direction by combining the basis vectors scaled by p and the viewing plane distance: \text{raydir} = \text{normalize}(p.x \cdot \text{camSide} + p.y \cdot \text{iRayUp} + \text{iPlaneDist} \cdot \text{iRayDir}) Note: Source uses iRayUp in the final sum, while the code snippet in uses camUp. Assuming camUp is the input iRayUp. 6. Set Ray Origin: The ray origin is the camera position: \text{rayorig} = \text{iRayOrigin} 7. Trace and Shade: Use the generated ray to perform intersection tests (e.g., sphere tracing, BVH traversal) and compute the final color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. vec3 computeraydirection(vec2 texCoord, vec2 resolution, vec3 raydir, vec3 rayup, float planedist) { # Step 2: Normalize coordinates to [-1, 1] vec2 p = 2.0 texCoord - 1.0; # Step 3: Apply aspect ratio correction p.x = resolution.x / resolution.y; # Step 4: Compute camera side vector (right vector) # Note: Assumes raydir and rayup are roughly orthogonal. # If rayup is not orthogonal to raydir, cross product order matters for handedness. vec3 camside = normalize(cross(raydir, rayup)); # Step 5: Compute ray direction # p.x side + p.y up + planedist forward vec3 raydir = normalize(p.x camside + p.y rayup + planedist raydir); return raydir; } void main() { # Step 1: Ray generation (implicit via fragment shader execution per pixel) vec3 rayorig = iRayOrigin; vec3 raydir = computeraydirection(texCoord, iResolution, iRayDir, iRayUp, iPlaneDist); # Step 7: Trace ray against scene (example: sphere intersection) # This part depends on the specific scene representation (BVH, SDF, etc.) # See for sphere intersection example. Hit hit = tracescene(rayorig, raydir); # Compute color based on hit result vec3 color = vec3(0.0); if (hit.hit) { color = shade(hit.point, hit.normal, raydir); } else { color = backgroundcolor; } fragColor = vec4(color, 1.0); } struct Hit { vec3 point; vec3 normal; float t; bool hit; }; Hit tracesphere(vec3 rayorig, vec3 raydir, vec3 pos, float radius) { float OdotD = dot(rayorig - pos, raydir); float OdotO = dot(rayorig - pos, rayorig - pos); float base = OdotD OdotD - OdotO + radius radius; if (base >= 0.0) { float root = sqrt(base); float t1 = -OdotD + root; float t2 = -OdotD - root; # Select the closest positive t float t = -1.0; if (t1 >= 0.0 && t2 >= 0.0) { t = min(t1, t2); } else if (t1 >= 0.0) { t = t1; } else if (t2 >= 0.0) { t = t2; } if (t >= 0.0) { vec3 pt = rayorig + raydir t; vec3 normal = normalize(pt - pos); return Hit(pt, normal, t, true); } } return Hit(vec3(0), vec3(0), -1.0, false); } Parameters: iPlaneDist: Controls the field of view. A smaller value results in a wider FOV. Typical values depend on the scene scale and desired FOV. iResolution: Window dimensions in pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aspect Ratio Distortion: Failing to scale the x-coordinate by the aspect ratio (width/height) will distort the field of view, making circles appear as ellipses. Camera Basis Orthogonality: The camSide vector is computed via cross(iRayDir, iRayUp). If iRayUp is not orthogonal to iRayDir, the resulting basis is not orthonormal, leading to skewed rays. It is recommended to orthogonalize iRayUp against iRayDir before use or ensure the camera setup maintains orthogonality. Winding Order: The quad's vertex winding order determines the interpolation direction of texCoord. Ensure the quad covers the screen correctly (e.g., vertices at (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1)) and that the interpolation maps to screen space correctly (bottom-left to top-right). [1509-sample-streaming-payload-ray-computation.md]: Computes rays for streaming payloads, often used in advanced volume rendering. Choose for complex payload-based rendering. [1642-object-space-ray-setup.md]: Sets up rays in object space rather than camera space. Choose for object-local transformations. [1753-custom-frustum-ray-generation-via-vertex-z-index.md]: Uses vertex Z-index for custom frustum shapes. Choose for non-standard view volumes. [2118-ray-origin-offset-noise.md]: Adds noise to ray origins for anti-aliasing. Choose for reducing aliasing artifacts. [2172-camera-matrix-ray-generation.md]: Uses camera matrices to compute rays. Choose for standard matrix-based camera setups. [3931-interactive-camera-ray-generation.md]: Optimized for interactive camera movement. Choose for real-time applications. [4026-ray-structure.md]: Defines the data structure for rays. Choose for organizing ray data. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for ray generation. The total time is proportional to the number of pixels (W \times H) plus the cost of the ray tracing algorithm (intersection, shading). Memory Complexity: O(1) for uniforms and varyings. The geometry is minimal (a single quad). Performance: Very efficient for ray generation due to GPU interpolation. The bottleneck is typically the ray tracing and shading steps. Strengths: Simple to implement, leverages GPU interpolation, minimal geometry overhead. Limitations: Limited to perspective or simple orthographic projections. Not suitable for complex camera models without additional computation. When to Use: Simple ray tracing demos, educational purposes, or when a quick perspective camera setup is needed. When Not to Use: Complex camera models, non-perspective projections, or when high performance is critical and the ray tracing algorithm is the bottleneck. This technique is a fundamental approach to GPU ray tracing, popularized by educational resources and demos. It allows developers to implement ray tracing in the fragment shader without complex vertex transformations, making it accessible for learning and simple applications. The method is often introduced in the context of "Ray Marching" and "Signed Distance Fields". gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) mxbrt/svo, https://github.com/mxbrt/svo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Further Graphics - University of Cambridge, https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1819/FGraphics/1.%20Ray%20Marching%20and%20Signed%20Distance%20Fields.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Ray Marching with Signed Distance Fields - Scribd, https://www.scribd.com/document/831412915/1-Ray-Marching-and-Signed-Distance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Bundle
head: Ray Bundle Data Structure, Ray Bundle Generation
body: A Ray Bundle is a container data structure that groups ray origins, directions, and associated sampling parameters (sample points and lengths) into a single object, typically implemented as a collection of aligned tensors. It solves the problem of managing batched ray data for volume rendering and neural rendering pipelines, allowing efficient vectorized operations and memory transfers. It differs from a RayBatch container by explicitly bundling sampling metadata (sample points/lengths) alongside geometric ray data, and from a Hit Record Structure by focusing on input ray generation rather than output intersection results. Inputs: Tensors for ray origins, ray directions, sample points along rays, and distances of sample points from origins. Outputs: A structured object (class instance) containing these tensors, supporting indexing, reshaping, and device transfer. The RayBundle class wraps four per-ray tensors: 1. origins: Tensor of shape (N, 3), where N is the number of rays. Stores the 3D coordinates of ray origins. 2. directions: Tensor of shape (N, 3). Stores the normalized direction vectors of the rays. 3. samplepoints: Tensor of shape (N, n{pts}, 3), where n{pts} is the number of sample points per ray. Stores the 3D coordinates of sample points along each ray. 4. samplelengths: Tensor of shape (N, n{pts}, 1). Stores the distance of each sample point from the ray origin. 1. Initialization: Create a RayBundle instance by passing the four tensors (origins, directions, samplepoints, samplelengths) to the constructor. 2. Indexing: Access a subset of rays using getitem(idx). This returns a new RayBundle with sliced tensors for all four fields at index idx. 3. Reshaping: Use the reshape method to change the batch dimensions while preserving the last dimensions: origins and directions to (args, 3), sample points to (args, n{pts}, 3), and sample lengths to (args, n{pts}, 1). 4. Viewing: Use the view method to return a new RayBundle with viewed tensors, preserving the same last dimension constraints as reshape. 5. Replacement: Use replace(kwargs) to update specific attributes (e.g., origins) and return the modified bundle. 6. Device Transfer: Use to(device) to move all tensors to a specified device (e.g., GPU). 7. Property Access: shape: Returns origins.shape[:-1], representing the batch dimensions. sampleshape: Returns samplepoints.shape[:-1], representing the batch and sample dimensions. device: Returns samplepoints.device. name: NDC Ray Transformation
head: Normalized Device Coordinate Rays, Normalized Device Coordinate Ray Mapping, NDC Ray Conversion
body: NDC Ray Transformation maps camera-space rays into a bounded Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space, typically the cube [-1, 1]^3, enabling the rendering of forward-facing real-world scenes that extend to infinity within a fixed bounding volume. Unlike standard perspective ray generation which samples metric depth, this method converts perspective rays into parallel rays in NDC space and uses disparity (inverse depth) as the sampling parameter, allowing linear sampling in NDC space to correspond to linear sampling in disparity from the near plane to infinity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origins \mathbf{o} = (ox, oy, oz) and directions \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz) in camera space (where the camera looks down the -z axis), image width W, height H, focal length f{cam}, and near plane distance n. Output: NDC ray origins \mathbf{o}' and directions \mathbf{d}' in NDC space. Data Structures: Rays are typically stored as two arrays of shape (N, 3), where N is the number of rays (e.g., W \times H). rayso: Float32 array of shape (N, 3) containing (ox, oy, oz). raysd: Float32 array of shape (N, 3) containing (dx, dy, dz). Parameters: n: Near plane distance. Must be positive. f{cam}: Focal length in pixels. W, H: Image dimensions in pixels. f: Far plane distance. For real scenes extending to infinity, f \to \infty. Steps: 1. Shift Ray Origins to Near Plane (Implementation Detail): To ensure that linear sampling in NDC space corresponds to linear disparity sampling, the original ray origin \mathbf{o} is shifted to the intersection with the near plane z = -n before the NDC conversion. Calculate the shift parameter tn: tn = -\frac{n + oz}{dz} Update the origin: \mathbf{o}n = \mathbf{o} + tn \mathbf{d} Note: This step assumes dz \neq 0. If dz \approx 0, the ray is parallel to the near plane and does not intersect it in the forward direction; this is a degenerate case for forward-facing scenes. 2. Compute Projection Constants: Using the pinhole camera model and the assumption that the far plane is at infinity (f \to \infty), the projection constants simplify: ax = -\frac{f{cam}}{W/2} ay = -\frac{f{cam}}{H/2} az = 1 bz = 2n 3. Calculate NDC Origin \mathbf{o}': The NDC origin is calculated by projecting the original ray origin \mathbf{o} (not the shifted \mathbf{o}n): o'x = ax \frac{ox}{oz} o'y = ay \frac{oy}{oz} o'z = az + \frac{bz}{oz} = 1 + \frac{2n}{oz} 4. Calculate NDC Direction \mathbf{d}': The NDC direction is derived by factoring out the common term from the difference between the projected ray point and the projected origin: d'x = ax \left( \frac{dx}{dz} - \frac{ox}{oz} \right) d'y = ay \left( \frac{dy}{dz} - \frac{oy}{oz} \right) d'z = -\frac{bz}{oz} = -\frac{2n}{oz} 5. Reparameterization: The parameter t' in NDC space relates to the original parameter t by: t' = \frac{t dz}{oz + t dz} As t \to \infty, t' \to 1. Thus, sampling t' linearly from 0 to 1 covers the depth range from the near plane to infinity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def ndcrays(W, H, fcam, near, rayso, raysd): """ Transform camera-space rays to NDC space. Args: W (int): Image width. H (int): Image height. fcam (float): Focal length in pixels. near (float): Near plane distance. rayso (np.ndarray): Ray origins, shape (..., 3). raysd (np.ndarray): Ray directions, shape (..., 3). Returns: np.ndarray: NDC ray origins, shape (..., 3). np.ndarray: NDC ray directions, shape (..., 3). """ # 1. Shift ray origins to the near plane z = -near (implementation detail) dz = raysd[..., 2] oz = rayso[..., 2] tn = -(near + oz) / dz rayson = rayso + tn[..., np.newaxis] raysd # 2. Compute constants (assuming f -> infinity) ax = -fcam / (W / 2.0) ay = -fcam / (H / 2.0) bz = 2.0 near # 3. Calculate NDC Origin o' from the ORIGINAL origin rayso (not shifted) # o'x = ax ox / oz # o'y = ay oy / oz # o'z = 1 + bz / oz raysondc = np.zeroslike(rayso) raysondc[..., 0] = ax rayso[..., 0] / oz raysondc[..., 1] = ay rayso[..., 1] / oz raysondc[..., 2] = 1.0 + bz / oz # 4. Calculate NDC Direction d' # d'x = ax (dx/dz - ox/oz) # d'y = ay (dy/dz - oy/oz) # d'z = -bz / oz raysdndc = np.zeroslike(raysd) raysdndc[..., 0] = ax (raysd[..., 0] / dz - rayso[..., 0] / oz) raysdndc[..., 1] = ay (raysd[..., 1] / dz - rayso[..., 1] / oz) raysdndc[..., 2] = -bz / oz return raysondc, raysdndc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If dz = 0, the ray is parallel to the near plane and does not intersect it. If oz = 0, the shifted origin is at the origin, which should not happen if n > 0 and the shift is correct. Coordinate System: The derivation assumes the camera looks down the -z axis. If the camera looks down +z, signs must be adjusted. Far Plane: The simplification az=1, bz=2n relies on f \to \infty. Bounding Volume: The NDC space is a cube [-1, 1]^3. Points outside this volume may require clamping or culling, although the transformation maps the entire forward half-space to this volume. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of rays. The transformation involves basic arithmetic operations per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the transformed rays. Strengths: Allows rendering of scenes extending to infinity within a fixed bounding volume. Linear sampling in NDC space corresponds to linear sampling in disparity, which is often more natural for real-world scenes. Converts perspective rays to parallel rays in NDC space, simplifying some aspects of volume rendering or neural network input. Limitations: Only suitable for forward-facing scenes. Requires careful handling of the near plane and ray shifting. Not suitable for scenes with significant depth variation near the camera where disparity changes rapidly, potentially requiring dense sampling. When to Use: Ideal for forward-facing real-world scene reconstruction (e.g., LLFF, DeepVoxels) where the scene extends to infinity and a fixed bounding volume is desired. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with significant camera motion around the object (e.g., 360-degree rotation) or scenes with objects very close to the camera where disparity sampling becomes inefficient. The NDC Ray Transformation was introduced in the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for rendering real-world forward-facing scenes. The standard NeRF approach uses a synthetic scene bounded within a cube, but real-world captures can extend to infinity. The NDC space, commonly used in triangle rasterization pipelines, was adapted to map the depth range of real scenes into [-1, 1] using disparity instead of metric depth. This allows the neural network to learn a bounded representation of the scene. The method was used in experiments with datasets like DeepVoxels and LLFF. body: General NDC Ray Conversion maps camera-space rays into a normalized device coordinate (NDC) cube [-1, 1]^3 for general scenes, enabling uniform sampling in NDC space to correspond to inverse depth (disparity) sampling in the original world space. Unlike Blender-specific NDC conventions which assume a fixed focal length and aspect ratio, this method handles arbitrary camera intrinsics and extrinsics by explicitly shifting ray origins to the near plane and projecting them based on the camera's focal length and image dimensions. It is primarily used in forward-facing scene reconstruction to handle large depth ranges efficiently. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins in world/camera space, shape (..., 3). raysd: Ray directions in world/camera space, shape (..., 3). near: Distance to the near plane (scalar). Typically hardcoded to 1.0 in implementations. focal: Focal length of the camera (scalar). W: Image width (scalar). H: Image height (scalar). Outputs: raysondc: Transformed ray origins in NDC space, shape (..., 3). raysdndc: Transformed ray directions in NDC space, shape (..., 3). Data Structures: The method operates on batched tensors. The last dimension represents the 3D vector components (x, y, z). Steps: 1. Shift Ray Origins to Near Plane: The ray origins are shifted along the ray direction so that they lie exactly on the near plane. This ensures that the NDC transformation maps the near plane to a fixed coordinate (typically z' = -1 or 1 depending on convention, here mapped to 1 in the formula below with specific sign conventions) and handles the singularity at the camera center. Compute the shift parameter t: t = \frac{\text{near} - \text{rays\o}z}{\text{rays\d}z} Update the origin: \text{rays\o} \leftarrow \text{rays\o} + t \cdot \text{rays\d} Note: Source uses a slightly different formulation involving negative near plane logic or specific axis conventions (-(near + rays\o[..., 2:3]) / rays\d[..., 2:3]). Source uses the standard projection formula. We follow the explicit component-wise projection formulas provided in which assume the origin has been shifted or handles the shift implicitly in the projection logic for forward-facing scenes. Correction based on specific code logic: The source explicitly calculates t as -(near + rayso[..., 2:3]) / raysd[..., 2:3] and updates rayso. This implies a coordinate system where the camera looks along the negative Z axis or similar, and near is positive. However, the subsequent projection formulas in use rayso[..., 2:3] directly. To be implementable and consistent with the provided formulas in, we assume the inputs are pre-processed or the formula accounts for the shift. The most robust interpretation from is: t = \frac{-(\text{near} + \text{rays\o}z)}{\text{rays\d}z} \text{rays\o} \leftarrow \text{rays\o} + t \cdot \text{rays\d} (Note: If the camera looks along +Z, near might be negative or the sign flips. We stick to the exact arithmetic from) 2. Compute Transformed Origin Components: Project the shifted origins into NDC space. The x and y components are scaled by the inverse of the horizontal and vertical fields of view (derived from focal length and image size). The z component is mapped to the range [1, \infty) or similar, bounded by the near plane. o'x = -\frac{f}{W/2} \cdot \frac{\text{rays\o}x}{\text{rays\o}z} o'y = -\frac{f}{H/2} \cdot \frac{\text{rays\o}y}{\text{rays\o}z} o'z = 1 + \frac{2 \cdot \text{near}}{\text{rays\o}z} Where f is focal, W is W, H is H. 3. Compute Transformed Direction Components: Project the directions. The direction in NDC space is the difference between the projected direction endpoint and the projected origin endpoint. d'x = -\frac{f}{W/2} \cdot \left( \frac{\text{rays\d}x}{\text{rays\d}z} - \frac{\text{rays\o}x}{\text{rays\o}z} \right) d'y = -\frac{f}{H/2} \cdot \left( \frac{\text{rays\d}y}{\text{rays\o}z} \dots \text{Wait, check source} \right) Re-reading for direction: d0 = -\frac{1}{W / (2.0 \cdot \text{focal})} \cdot \left( \frac{\text{rays\d}x}{\text{rays\d}z} - \frac{\text{rays\o}x}{\text{rays\o}z} \right) d1 = -\frac{1}{H / (2.0 \cdot \text{focal})} \cdot \left( \frac{\text{rays\d}y}{\text{rays\d}z} - \frac{\text{rays\o}y}{\text{rays\o}z} \right) d2 = -\frac{2 \cdot \text{near}}{\text{rays\o}z} Note on d2: Source lists d2 = -2.0 \cdot \text{near} / \text{rays\o}z. This seems to represent the change in the mapped Z coordinate. Since o'z = 1 + 2 \cdot \text{near} / \text{rays\o}z, the derivative with respect to depth is complex. However, in NDC ray marching, the direction Z component often simplifies. We use the formula exactly as stated in. 4. Concatenate: Combine components to form the final NDC rays: \text{rays\o\ndc} = [o'x, o'y, o'z] \text{rays\d\ndc} = [d'x, d'y, d'z] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def generalndcrays(rayso, raysd, focal, W, H, near=1.0): """ Convert camera-space rays to NDC space for general scenes. Args: rayso: Tensor of shape (..., 3), ray origins in world/camera space. raysd: Tensor of shape (..., 3), ray directions in world/camera space. focal: Scalar, focal length. W: Scalar, image width. H: Scalar, image height. near: Scalar, near plane distance. Default 1.0. Returns: raysondc: Tensor of shape (..., 3), NDC origins. raysdndc: Tensor of shape (..., 3), NDC directions. """ # Ensure tensors are float32 rayso = rayso.float() raysd = raysd.float() # Extract z components raysoz = rayso[..., 2:3] raysdz = raysd[..., 2:3] # Step 1: Shift ray origins to the near plane # Formula from: t = -(near + rayso[..., 2:3]) / raysd[..., 2:3] # Note: This assumes a specific coordinate convention (likely OpenGL-like where camera looks -Z or similar adjustment) # If raysdz is 0, this will produce NaN/Inf. Guard against division by zero if necessary. t = -(near + raysoz) / raysdz # Update origins rayso = rayso + t raysd # Recompute z after shift for consistency in projection formulas raysoz = rayso[..., 2:3] # Precompute scaling factors # 1 / (W / (2 focal)) = 2 focal / W scalex = 2.0 focal / W scaley = 2.0 focal / H # Step 2: Compute transformed origin components # o0 = -scalex (raysox / raysoz) # o1 = -scaley (raysoy / raysoz) # o2 = 1 + 2 near / raysoz raysox = rayso[..., 0:1] raysoy = rayso[..., 1:2] invoz = 1.0 / raysoz o0 = -scalex raysox invoz o1 = -scaley raysoy invoz o2 = 1.0 + 2.0 near invoz raysondc = torch.cat([o0, o1, o2], dim=-1) # Step 3: Compute transformed direction components # d0 = -scalex (raysdx / raysdz - raysox / raysoz) # d1 = -scaley (raysdy / raysdz - raysoy / raysoz) # d2 = -2 near / raysoz raysdx = raysd[..., 0:1] raysdy = raysd[..., 1:2] invdz = 1.0 / raysdz d0 = -scalex (raysdx invdz - raysox invoz) d1 = -scaley (raysdy invdz - raysoy invoz) d2 = -2.0 near invoz raysdndc = torch.cat([d0, d1, d2], dim=-1) return raysondc, raysdndc Parameters: near: The near plane distance. In the reference implementation, this is hardcoded to 1.0. focal, W, H: Camera intrinsics. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If raysdz or raysoz is zero, the shift or projection will fail. This occurs if the ray is parallel to the image plane or if the origin is at the camera center (though shifting usually moves it away). Add a small epsilon to denominators if robustness is required. Coordinate System: The formulas in use specific signs (e.g., negative scaling for x/y). This assumes a specific camera convention (likely OpenGL NDC where Z is positive into the screen or similar). If using DirectX or other conventions, signs may need flipping. Forward-Facing Assumption: This method is designed for forward-facing scenes. It may not behave correctly for general 360-degree scenes with arbitrary camera orientations relative to the scene center. Converts 2D pixel coordinates to 3D rays, often feeding into this method. The parent technique describing the general concept of mapping rays to NDC for inverse depth sampling. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of rays. The operations are element-wise arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the transformed rays. Strengths: Enables uniform sampling in NDC space to approximate inverse depth sampling, which is crucial for efficient NeRF training on forward-facing scenes. Handles general camera intrinsics unlike Blender-specific NDC. Limitations: Assumes forward-facing scenes. Sensitive to the near plane definition. Performance depends on the efficiency of the tensor operations (e.g., in PyTorch/JAX). When to use: When training NeRF-like models on forward-facing datasets (e.g., LLFF) using general camera parameters. When not to use: For scenes with significant camera rotation around the object (non-forward-facing) or when using Blender's specific NDC conventions. name: Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates
head: Camera Ray Generation, Camera Raycasting, Pixel to Ray Unprojection, Ray Direction Calculation, Ray Generation from Camera/NDC, Ray Generation from Pixels, Ray Generation from Screen Coordinates
body: This method converts 2D screen pixel coordinates into 3D ray origins and directions in world space, serving as the foundational step for ray marching and volume rendering. It solves the problem of mapping discrete image samples to continuous 3D geometry by inverting the camera projection pipeline. Unlike Pinhole Camera Projection (Pixel to Camera), which outputs camera-space coordinates, this method typically targets world-space rays or handles the full transformation chain including the inverse Projection-View matrix. It differs from General NDC Ray Conversion by often assuming specific camera configurations (like Blender's or standard OpenGL/NDC conventions) and explicitly handling the generation of both origin and direction vectors for rasterization or marching. Inputs: Pixel coordinates (u, v) or a grid of indices. Image resolution: Width W, Height H. Camera parameters: Either an inverse Projection-View matrix M{inv} or intrinsic parameters like vertical Field of View (FOV). Near plane depth z{near} in NDC, typically 0 or 1. Outputs: Ray origins \mathbf{r}o \in \mathbb{R}^3 (usually the camera center). Ray directions \mathbf{r}d \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized vectors pointing from origin through the pixel). Pixel Grid: A tensor or array of shape (H, W, 2) or (N, 2) containing (u, v) coordinates. NDC Points: Homogeneous coordinates in Normalized Device Coordinates, shape (N, 4) or (N, 3) with appended w=1. RayBundle: A structure containing rayso (shape (N, 3)), raysd (shape (N, 3)), and zero-initialized samplepoints and samplelengths. This approach uses the inverse of the combined Projection and View matrices. It is standard in OpenGL-style pipelines where NDC ranges from [-1, 1]. 1. Convert to NDC: Map pixel coordinates (u, v) to NDC space (x{ndc}, y{ndc}). x{ndc} = \frac{2u}{W} - 1 y{ndc} = \frac{2v}{H} - 1 The z component is computed as z{ndc} = 2z{near} - 1 for the near plane. \mathbf{p}{ndc} = [x{ndc}, y{ndc}, z{ndc}, 1]^T 2. Transform to World: Multiply by the inverse Projection-View matrix M{inv}. \mathbf{p}{world\homo} = M{inv} \times \mathbf{p}{ndc} 3. Perspective Division: Convert to Cartesian coordinates. \mathbf{p}{world} = \left[ \frac{xw}{ww}, \frac{yw}{ww}, \frac{zw}{ww} \right]^T 4. Generate Origin and Direction: Calculate \mathbf{p}{world} for z{ndc}=0 (near plane) to get the ray origin \mathbf{r}o. Calculate \mathbf{p}{world} for z{ndc}=1 to get a second point \mathbf{p}{far}. Compute direction: \mathbf{r}d = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{far} - \mathbf{r}o). This approach is common in deep learning frameworks (e.g., PyTorch3D) and Metal shaders, using Field of View (FOV) and resolution. 1. Calculate Centered Coordinates: x{center} = u - \frac{W}{2} y{center} = v - \frac{H}{2}. Note that Metal's coordinate system places (0,0) at the top-left, requiring this centering adjustment. 2. Calculate Z-component (Depth): Using the vertical field of view FOV (in degrees): z = \frac{H}{\tan\left(\frac{FOV \cdot \pi}{360}\right)}. 3. Construct Ray Direction: The direction vector in camera space (assuming camera looks down negative Z) is: \mathbf{d}{cam} = [x{center}, y{center}, -z] \mathbf{r}d = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{d}{cam}). 4. Set Origin: The ray origin is the camera center \mathbf{C}. \mathbf{r}o = \mathbf{C} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generateraysmatrix(pixelu, pixelv, width, height, invprojview): """ Generate ray origin and direction using inverse Projection-View matrix. Args: pixelu: float, x-coordinate of pixel (0 to width-1) pixelv: float, y-coordinate of pixel (0 to height-1) width: int, image width height: int, image height invprojview: np.array, shape (4, 4), inverse of Projection View matrix Returns: origin: np.array, shape (3,) direction: np.array, shape (3,) """ # 1. Convert to NDC xndc = (2.0 pixelu) / width - 1.0 yndc = (2.0 pixelv) / height - 1.0 zndc = 0.0 # Near plane depth mapped to NDC # 2. Transform NDC to World Space (Near Plane) pndcnear = np.array([xndc, yndc, zndc, 1.0]) pworldhomonear = invprojview @ pndcnear origin = pworldhomonear[:3] / pworldhomonear[3] # 3. Transform NDC to World Space (Far Point for Direction) zndcfar = 1.0 pndcfar = np.array([xndc, yndc, zndcfar, 1.0]) pworldhomofar = invprojview @ pndcfar pfar = pworldhomofar[:3] / pworldhomofar[3] # 4. Compute Direction direction = pfar - origin direction = direction / np.linalg.norm(direction) return origin, direction def generateraysintrinsic(pixelu, pixelv, width, height, fovdeg): """ Generate ray direction using FOV and resolution. Origin is assumed to be (0,0,0) in camera space. Args: pixelu: float, x-coordinate pixelv: float, y-coordinate width: int height: int fovdeg: float, vertical field of view in degrees Returns: origin: np.array, shape (3,), typically [0,0,0] direction: np.array, shape (3,) """ # 1. Centered coordinates xcenter = pixelu - width / 2.0 ycenter = pixelv - height / 2.0 # 2. Z component fovrad = np.radians(fovdeg) z = height / np.tan(fovrad / 2.0) # 3. Direction in camera space (looking down -Z) direction = np.array([xcenter, ycenter, -z]) direction = direction / np.linalg.norm(direction) # 4. Origin origin = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) return origin, direction FOV: Vertical Field of View in degrees. Typical value: 45.0^\circ. Resolution: (W, H). Example: 1280 \times 720. name: Pinhole Camera Projection (Pixel to Camera)
head: Camera Ray Lifting, Inverse Projection, Pixel to Camera, Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates using Intrinsics
body: This method converts 2D pixel coordinates (u, v) and a depth value z into 3D camera-space homogeneous coordinates using the camera's intrinsic parameters. It serves as the inverse of the standard projection matrix, "lifting" a 2D pixel into 3D space relative to the camera origin. It differs from sibling methods like Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates by explicitly accepting a depth input z rather than generating a ray direction vector; it produces a specific point in camera space rather than a ray for further traversal. Inputs: Pixel coordinates: u, v (float arrays, shape [B, N]). Depth: z (float array, shape [B, N]). Intrinsics: A 3 \times 3 matrix K (float array, shape [B, 3, 3]). Data Structures: The intrinsic matrix K is structured as: K = \begin{bmatrix} fx & s & cx \\ 0 & fy & cy \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Where: fx = K{0,0}: Focal length in pixels (x-axis). fy = K{1,1}: Focal length in pixels (y-axis). cx = K{0,2}: Principal point x-coordinate. cy = K{1,2}: Principal point y-coordinate. s = K{0,1}: Skew coefficient. Steps: 1. Extract parameters fx, fy, cx, cy, s from the intrinsic matrix K. 2. Compute the camera-space x-coordinate x{lift}: x{lift} = \frac{u - cx + \frac{cy \cdot s}{fy} - \frac{s \cdot v}{fy}}{fx} \cdot z. Note: Source uses |z| while uses z. Implementers should verify if depth is signed or unsigned in their specific pipeline. 3. Compute the camera-space y-coordinate y{lift}: y{lift} = \frac{v - cy}{fy} \cdot z. 4. Construct the homogeneous coordinate vector by stacking x{lift}, y{lift}, z, 1 along the last dimension. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def pixeltocamera(u, v, z, intrinsics): """ Lifts pixel coordinates (u, v) with depth z to camera space homogeneous coordinates. Args: u: Tensor of shape [B, N], pixel x-coordinates. v: Tensor of shape [B, N], pixel y-coordinates. z: Tensor of shape [B, N], depth values. intrinsics: Tensor of shape [B, 3, 3], camera intrinsic matrix K. Returns: Tensor of shape [B, N, 4], homogeneous camera coordinates [x, y, z, 1]. """ # Extract intrinsic parameters fx = intrinsics[:, 0, 0] fy = intrinsics[:, 1, 1] cx = intrinsics[:, 0, 2] cy = intrinsics[:, 1, 2] skew = intrinsics[:, 0, 1] # Compute xlift # Formula: ((u - cx + cy skew / fy - skew v / fy) / fx) z # Note: Source uses abs(z), Source uses z. We follow for signed depth, # but check if your depth buffer is signed. xlift = ((u - cx + cy skew / fy - skew v / fy) / fx) z # Compute ylift # Formula: ((v - cy) / fy) z ylift = ((v - cy) / fy) z # Stack into homogeneous coordinates [x, y, z, 1] ones = torch.oneslike(z) result = torch.stack([xlift, ylift, z, ones], dim=-1) return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Skew Handling: If the camera has no skew (s=0), the term \frac{cy \cdot s}{fy} - \frac{s \cdot v}{fy} vanishes. Depth Sign: Source applies absolute value to z (|z|), while uses z directly. This discrepancy suggests that the sign convention of z (forward vs. backward in camera space) varies by implementation. If z represents distance from the camera, use |z|; if it represents a coordinate in a right-handed system where camera looks down -Z, use z. Division by Zero: Ensure fx and fy are non-zero. If fy=0, the skew terms and y{lift} calculation will fail. What it is: Generates a ray direction vector from pixel coordinates without depth, assuming a unit depth or normalized device coordinates. Difference: Returns a direction vector (ray) rather than a specific 3D point. When to choose: When performing ray marching or unbounded volume rendering where depth is determined by intersection, not input. Link: Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, involving constant-time arithmetic operations per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the output homogeneous coordinates. Strengths: Simple, differentiable, and directly invertible from projection if depth is known. Limitations: Requires depth input; does not account for extrinsic camera transformation (view matrix). When to use: When converting depth maps or pixel-wise depth estimates into 3D camera-space points for further processing (e.g., point cloud generation, volume rendering initialization). This method is a standard component in computer vision and graphics pipelines for inverse projection. It is derived from the pinhole camera model equations. The specific implementation details, including skew handling and depth sign conventions, are observed in modern deep learning-based 3D reconstruction and neural rendering frameworks. albertgassol1/vf-nerf, https://github.com/albertgassol1/vf-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) megvii-research/cv-master-ex, https://github.com/megvii-research/cv-master-ex, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: View Matrix Construction
head: LookAt Matrix, LookAt Matrix Construction, Camera Matrix Construction, gluLookAt
body: View Matrix Construction builds a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix that maps coordinates from world space to camera (view) space, or conversely transforms rays from view space to world space, given an eye position, a target (look-at) point, and an up vector. It solves the problem of defining a camera's extrinsic parameters in a 3D scene by establishing an orthonormal basis aligned with the viewing direction. It differs from NDC Ray Transformation by handling only the rigid body rotation and translation of the camera, not the projection into screen coordinates, and from Point to Camera Transformation by explicitly constructing the full basis vectors from geometric constraints rather than applying a pre-defined transform. Inputs: eye: A 3D vector representing the camera position in world space. center (or target): A 3D vector representing the point the camera is looking at in world space. up: A 3D vector indicating the camera's local "up" direction in world space. Outputs: A 4 \times 4 matrix. In the standard convention used by most sources, this matrix transforms view-space coordinates to world-space coordinates (camera-to-world). When used to transform world-space points to view-space, the inverse of this matrix is applied. The matrix layout places the basis vectors in the first three columns (or rows, depending on row-major/column-major storage interpretation, but logically forming the rotation component) and the eye position in the translation component. Data Structures: Vectors eye, center, up, f, s, u are 3-component floating-point vectors (e.g., float3 or vec3). The output matrix is a 4 \times 4 structure. The first three columns (in column-major layout) or rows (in row-major layout) contain the basis vectors s, u, and -f with a w-component of 0.0. The fourth column contains the eye position eye with a w-component of 1.0. Steps: 1. Calculate the forward vector f by normalizing the difference between the center and the eye: f = \text{normalize}(center - eye) This vector points from the camera to the target. Note that in view space, the camera looks down the negative z-axis, so the basis vector corresponding to the view direction is -f. 2. Calculate the side (right) vector s by taking the cross product of f and up, then normalizing: s = \text{normalize}(f \times up) This vector is orthogonal to the viewing plane. 3. Calculate the true up vector u by taking the cross product of s and f: u = s \times f This ensures u is orthogonal to both s and f, completing the orthonormal basis. Note that u is not normalized again if s and f are orthonormal, as the cross product of two orthonormal vectors is already unit length. 4. Construct the 4 \times 4 matrix. Using column-major storage (common in OpenGL and many graphics APIs), the matrix M is: M = \begin{bmatrix} sx & ux & -fx & 0 \\ sy & uy & -fy & 0 \\ sz & uz & -fz & 0 \\ eyex & eyey & eyez & 1 \end{bmatrix} Here, the first three columns are the basis vectors s, u, and -f, and the fourth column is the translation eye. If row-major storage is used, these vectors appear as rows. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def viewmatrix(eye, center, up): """ Constructs a 4x4 view matrix (camera-to-world) from eye, center, and up vectors. Args: eye: (3,) array-like, camera position in world space. center: (3,) array-like, target point in world space. up: (3,) array-like, up vector in world space. Returns: (4, 4) array-like, the transformation matrix. """ # Step 1: Forward vector (camera looks down -z in view space) f = normalize(center - eye) # Step 2: Side vector (right vector) s = normalize(cross(f, up)) # Step 3: True up vector u = cross(s, f) # Step 4: Construct matrix # Using column-major layout: columns are s, u, -f, eye # Row 0: s.x, u.x, -f.x, 0 # Row 1: s.y, u.y, -f.y, 0 # Row 2: s.z, u.z, -f.z, 0 # Row 3: eye.x, eye.y, eye.z, 1 matrix = [ [s[0], u[0], -f[0], 0.0], [s[1], u[1], -f[1], 0.0], [s[2], u[2], -f[2], 0.0], [eye[0], eye[1], eye[2], 1.0] ] return matrix Parameters: eye: Camera position. Typical values depend on the scene scale. center: Look-at target. Often the center of the volume or scene. up: Up vector. Typically (0, 1, 0) or (0, 0, 1) depending on the coordinate system. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If f and up are parallel (or anti-parallel), the cross product s becomes zero, leading to a degenerate matrix. This is a common pitfall when the camera is looking straight up or down relative to the global up vector. A guard should check for this condition and substitute a default up vector if necessary. The matrix assumes the camera looks down the negative z-axis in view space. When transforming direction vectors (rays), the w-component must be 0.0 to ensure rotation is applied but translation is not. The function assumes the center of the camera is aligned with the negative z-axis in view space when calculating ray marching directions. Computes a representative camera pose from a set of input camera poses by averaging their translations and rotations. It differs from simple vector averaging by using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to ensure the resulting rotation matrix remains orthogonal and valid, addressing the non-linear nature of rotation space. This method is primarily used to initialize a central view or create a canonical coordinate system for a scene. Camera Pose Transformation applies geometric transformations—specifically translation and rotation—to a point or coordinate system to define the camera's position and orientation within a 3D scene. It solves the problem of mapping local scene coordinates to the camera's view space or adjusting the camera's extrinsic parameters relative to the world. It sets itself apart from View Matrix Construction by operating on individual points or pose structures directly rather than constructing a full 4x4 matrix from basis vectors, and from Average Pose Calculation by performing a single rigid transformation rather than aggregating multiple poses. Computes an orthonormal camera basis (eye, forward, right, up) for an orbit camera looking at a target from a distance, oriented by yaw and pitch angles. The General Perspective Transformation is a camera model where both the eye point and the projection plane are positioned away from the world origin. It solves the problem of numerical instability in screen-z values that occurs when standard perspective projections (with the eye at the origin) are applied to scenes where the visibility bounding box (Vbb) is far from the origin. By shifting the eye and projection plane, it ensures the Jacobian of the transformation is the identity at the center of the Vbb, minimizing floating-point errors during the compositing of closely spaced geometry. It differs from standard textbook perspective matrices by explicitly decoupling the eye position from the origin to optimize precision for specific scene bounds. A custom implementation of 3D transformation matrices in JavaScript, providing native handling of translation, scaling, perspective projection, and look-at operations without external dependencies. It distinguishes itself by offering explicit, unoptimized implementations for small fixed-size matrices, prioritizing clarity and correctness over performance, serving as the computational core for view matrix construction and ray generation logic. Constructs a 3x3 rotation matrix that transforms world-space vectors into camera-local space, given a camera origin and look-at target. It builds an orthogonal camera coordinate system (basis) from a camera center and a look-at point by deriving an up vector orthogonal to the viewing direction, then computing the right vector via cross product. It differs from Orbit Camera Basis Computation by accepting an arbitrary look-at target rather than spherical angles, and from General Perspective Transformation by producing only the rotational component of the extrinsic transform, not the full projection matrix. View Transformations define the pipeline for mapping volume data from its native object coordinate system to the final image plane. This method manages four distinct transformation matrices (modeling, viewing, projection, and viewport) that collectively handle the geometric positioning of the volume, the camera orientation, and the final clipping and mapping to screen coordinates. It is distinct from sibling methods like Camera Look-at Basis Construction by managing the entire state stack of transformations rather than computing a single basis, and differs from View Matrix Construction by handling the full pipeline including projection and viewport stages. Copies the inverse view matrix (3 float4s, 12 floats) to device symbol for ray direction transformation. It involves copying 12 floats (representing the 3x4 rotation/translation part of the inverse matrix) to a device symbol invViewMatrix. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1), as it involves a fixed number of vector operations (subtraction, normalization, cross products) and matrix construction. Memory: O(1), storing a few 3D vectors and a 4 \times 4 matrix. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of cameras if constructing matrices for multiple views, but each individual construction is constant time. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple, efficient, and widely supported. Provides a clear geometric interpretation of camera pose. Limitations: Degenerates when the view direction is parallel to the up vector. Does not handle projection or field of view. When to use it and when not: Use when you need to define a camera's orientation and position in world space for ray generation or coordinate transformation. Do not use when you need to project 3D points to 2D screen coordinates (use NDC Ray Transformation or a projection matrix). The LookAt matrix is a standard concept in computer graphics, originally popularized by the OpenGL utility function gluLookAt. It is used to construct a view matrix that aligns the camera with a specified target and up vector. name: Average Pose Calculation
head: Average Pose Computation, mean pose via SVD
body: Computes a representative camera pose from a set of input camera poses by averaging their translations and rotations. It differs from simple vector averaging by using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to ensure the resulting rotation matrix remains orthogonal and valid, addressing the non-linear nature of rotation space. This method is primarily used to initialize a central view or create a canonical coordinate system for a scene. Inputs: poses: A list or array of N camera poses. Each pose is a 3 \times 4 or 4 \times 4 transformation matrix (camera-to-world). The first 3 \times 3 columns represent rotation, and the last column represents translation. Outputs: avgpose: A single 3 \times 4 or 4 \times 4 matrix representing the average pose. Data Structures: poses: Shape (N, 3, 4) or (N, 4, 4). center: Shape (3,), the averaged translation vector. meanrot: Shape (3, 3), the element-wise mean of the rotation matrices. avgrot: Shape (3, 3), the orthogonalized average rotation matrix. Steps: 1. Extract Translation: Calculate the average translation vector center by taking the mean of the translation columns (index 3) of all poses along the batch axis. \text{center} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \text{poses}i[:, 3] 2. Compute Mean Rotation: Calculate the element-wise mean of the rotation sub-matrices (indices 0-2) of all poses. \text{mean\rot} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \text{poses}i[:,:3,:3] 3. Orthogonalize Rotation: Perform Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on meanrot to obtain matrices U and V^T. U, \Sigma, V^T = \text{SVD}(\text{mean\rot}) Compute the average rotation matrix avgrot as: \text{avg\rot} = U V^T Note: If \det(U V^T) = -1, a correction is typically required to ensure a proper rotation (no reflection), though the sources do not explicitly detail this reflection handling. 4. Construct Average Pose: Concatenate avgrot and center (reshaped to a column vector) to form the final 3 \times 4 pose matrix. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def averageposecalculation(poses): """ Compute the average camera pose from a set of poses using SVD for rotation averaging. Args: poses: numpy array of shape (N, 3, 4) or (N, 4, 4) containing camera-to-world matrices. Returns: avgpose: numpy array of shape (3, 4) or (4, 4) representing the average pose. """ # Ensure poses are 3x4 for consistency if poses.shape[-2] == 4: poses = poses[:,:3,:] N = poses.shape[0] # Step 1: Calculate average translation (center) # Mean of the translation columns (index 3) center = np.mean(poses[:,:, 3], axis=0) # Step 2: Calculate mean rotation # Mean of the rotation sub-matrices (first 3 columns) meanrot = np.mean(poses[:,:,:3], axis=0) # Step 3: Orthogonalize rotation using SVD # Perform SVD on the mean rotation matrix U,, Vt = np.linalg.svd(meanrot) # Compute the orthogonal average rotation avgrot = U @ Vt # Step 4: Construct the average pose matrix # Concatenate rotation and translation avgpose = np.hstack((avgrot, center.reshape(-1, 1))) return avgpose Parameters: poses: Input poses, either [N, 3, 4] or [N, 4, 4]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reflection: If the determinant of U V^T is -1, the result is a reflection, not a rotation. Standard implementations often correct this by flipping the sign of the last column of U or V^T, but this specific correction is not detailed in the provided sources. Degenerate Input: If all poses are identical or collinear in rotation space, the mean rotation may be singular, leading to unstable SVD results. Precision: Floating-point errors in the mean rotation matrix can lead to slight non-orthogonality before SVD, which SVD corrects. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot d^2) where N is the number of poses and d=3 is the dimensionality of the rotation matrix. The dominant operation is SVD, which is constant time for fixed 3 \times 3 matrices. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot d^2) to store the input poses and intermediate mean rotation matrix. Strengths: Ensures the resulting rotation is valid (orthogonal) unlike simple averaging. Simple to implement using standard linear algebra libraries. Limitations: Does not account for the geodesic distance on the rotation manifold (SO(3)), which can be less accurate for large angular differences between poses compared to iterative methods. When to use: When a quick, central reference pose is needed for initialization or alignment. When not to use: When high precision in rotation averaging is required for widely varying camera orientations. The method originates from implementations in NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) pipelines, specifically for computing a canonical camera pose from a dataset of images. It is commonly referred to as posesavg in codebases like bmild/nerf and nerf-from-scratch. The use of SVD for rotation averaging is a standard technique in computer vision for handling rotation matrices. bmild/nerf, https://github.com/bmild/nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Camera Pose Transformation
head: Camera Offset and Rotation, Pose Transformation, RotateX
body: Camera Pose Transformation applies geometric transformations—specifically translation and rotation—to a point or coordinate system to define the camera's position and orientation within a 3D scene. It solves the problem of mapping local scene coordinates to the camera's view space or adjusting the camera's extrinsic parameters relative to the world. It sets itself apart from View Matrix Construction by operating on individual points or pose structures directly rather than constructing a full 4x4 matrix from basis vectors, and from Average Pose Calculation by performing a single rigid transformation rather than aggregating multiple poses. Inputs: A point p = (x, y, z) or a set of points in 3D space. A rotation angle \theta (float). A translation vector t (optional, e.g., [0, -1, -2.2]). A pose structure or matrix (optional, for recentering or rigid transformation contexts). Outputs: The transformed point p' or the adjusted camera pose. Data Structures: Points are represented as 3D vectors (x, y, z). For homogeneous transformations, points are extended to 4D vectors (x, y, z, w) where w=1 for points and w=0 for vectors. Poses may be stored as 3 \times 4 matrices (rotation R and translation t) or as quaternion + translation pairs. Steps: 1. Translation (Offset): If a translation vector t = (tx, ty, tz) is provided, add it to the point p: p{offset} = p + t Example: Offset by [0, -1, -2.2]. 2. Rotation: Apply rotation around a specified axis. RotateY: Rotate around the Y-axis by angle \theta. The x component remains unchanged. The y and z components are transformed using a 2D rotation matrix: \begin{aligned} y' &= y \cos(\theta) + z \sin(\theta) \\ z' &= -y \sin(\theta) + z \cos(\theta) \end{aligned} Note: The sign convention in uses -y \sin(\theta) for the new z, which corresponds to a specific handedness/rotation direction. Standard right-hand rule rotation around Y usually yields z' = y \sin(\theta) + z \cos(\theta) if y is up, but explicitly defines the formula as above. Implementers should follow the source's specific formula if replicating that effect. RotateX: Rotate around the X-axis. The y and z components are transformed: \begin{aligned} y' &= y \cos(\theta) - z \sin(\theta) \\ z' &= y \sin(\theta) + z \cos(\theta) \end{aligned} RotateZ: Rotate around the Z-axis. The x and y components are transformed: \begin{aligned} x' &= x \cos(\theta) - y \sin(\theta) \\ y' &= x \sin(\theta) + y \cos(\theta) \end{aligned} 3. Homogenization (for Matrix Multiplication): If applying a rigid transformation matrix T: Append 1 to points: ph = [x, y, z, 1]^T. Append 0 to vectors: vh = [x, y, z, 0]^T. 4. Matrix Application: Multiply the homogeneous point by the transformation matrix T: p'h = T \cdot ph Using einsum notation: einsum("ij, j -> i", T, ph). 5. Pose Recentering (Optional): To recenters a set of poses so their average is the identity: Compute the average pose P{avg}. Construct a 4 \times 4 identity-like matrix for P{avg} by appending [0, 0, 0, 1] to its 3 \times 4 rotation/translation part. Convert all input poses to 4 \times 4 matrices by appending [0, 0, 0, 1]. Left-multiply all poses by the inverse of P{avg}: P'{i} = P{avg}^{-1} \cdot P{i}. 6. RigidXform Construction (Optional): If building from a Pose: Dequantize and normalize the quaternion from the pose. Reject if orientation is zero. Combine with cell scale and translation. Based on. """ x, y, z = p cosa = math.cos(angle) sina = math.sin(angle) # Note: Formula from newy = cosa y + sina z newz = -sina y + cosa z return (x, newy, newz) def rotatex(p, angle): """ Rotates point p around the X-axis by angle (radians). Based on. """ x, y, z = p cosa = math.cos(angle) sina = math.sin(angle) newy = y cosa - z sina newz = y sina + z cosa return (x, newy, newz) def rotatez(p, angle): """ Rotates point p around the Z-axis by angle (radians). Based on. """ x, y, z = p cosa = math.cos(angle) sina = math.sin(angle) newx = x cosa - y sina newy = x sina + y cosa return (newx, newy, z) def transformpoint(p, translation=None, rotationaxis='y', rotationangle=0.0): """ Applies translation and rotation to point p. """ if translation: p = (p[0] + translation[0], p[1] + translation[1], p[2] + translation[2]) if rotationangle != 0.0: if rotationaxis == 'x': p = rotatex(p, rotationangle) elif rotationaxis == 'y': p = rotatey(p, rotationangle) elif rotationaxis == 'z': p = rotatez(p, rotationangle) else: raise ValueError("Unsupported rotation axis") return p def homogenizepoint(p): """ Converts 3D point to 4D homogeneous coordinates (w=1). Based on. """ return p + (1.0,) def applyrigidtransform(points, transformationmatrix): """ Applies a 4x4 rigid transformation matrix to a list of 3D points. Based on. """ transformedpoints = [] for p in points: ph = homogenizepoint(p) # Matrix-vector multiplication: T @ ph # Assuming transformationmatrix is a list of lists or 2D array newph = [ sum(transformationmatrix[i][j] ph[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4) ] # De-homogenize (assuming w=1 for points) transformedpoints.append((newph[0], newph[1], newph[2])) return transformedpoints Parameters: angle: Float representing the rotation angle in radians. translation: Vector (tx, ty, tz) for offsetting the origin. cellsizem: Uniform scale factor converting local cells to world metres (used in RigidXform). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors can accumulate in repeated transformations. Normalizing quaternions ensures the conjugate is the exact inverse. Zero Orientation: Reject poses with zero orientation to avoid undefined rotation. Boundary Conditions: In ray traversal, origins exactly on a boundary belong to the cell defined by the floor function. Handedness: Rotation formulas depend on the coordinate system's handedness. uses a specific sign convention for RotateY that may differ from standard right-hand rule implementations. Verify against the target rendering engine's conventions. RotateY is a geometric transformation primitive that rotates a point or shape around the Y-axis in 3D space. It serves as a fundamental building block for constructing camera poses and deforming Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). Unlike Rotation Transformation, which may imply a general rotation matrix, RotateY specifically isolates the Y-axis component, and unlike Twist, it applies a uniform rotation angle to the entire object rather than a spatially varying one. It is a sibling to RotateX and RotateZ. Similar to RotateX, but rotates around the z-axis instead. It takes a float input representing the angle of rotation. Recenters a set of poses such that their average pose becomes the identity transformation (origin at center, aligned axes). It involves computing the average pose, constructing a 4 \times 4 matrix, and left-multiplying all poses by the inverse of the average pose. A transformation structure that maps a volume's local cell space to world metres by applying a uniform cell scale, a rotation, and a translation. It is constructed from a Pose by dequantizing and normalizing the quaternion. The stored rotation is normalized, ensuring the conjugate is the exact inverse. A method to apply rigid transformations to camera coordinates by first homogenizing points (appending 1) and vectors (appending 0), then applying the transformation via matrix multiplication (einsum). Time Complexity: O(1) for single point transformation. O(N) for transforming N points. Memory Complexity: O(1) for single point. O(N) for storing transformed points. Performance: Very fast, as it involves basic arithmetic operations (multiplications and additions). Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient for real-time applications, flexible for various rotation axes. Limitations: Does not handle non-rigid transformations (scaling, shearing) unless explicitly added. Precision issues may arise with very large or very small coordinates. When to use: When defining camera positions, rotating objects in a scene, or adjusting SDFs. When not to use: When complex camera models (e.g., fisheye) or non-rigid deformations are required. It originates from basic linear algebra and geometry, where rotations and translations are used to transform coordinates between different spaces. name: RotateY
head: Y-axis rotation, Rotate around Y
body: RotateY is a geometric transformation primitive that rotates a point or shape around the Y-axis in 3D space. It serves as a fundamental building block for constructing camera poses and deforming Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). Unlike Rotation Transformation, which may imply a general rotation matrix, RotateY specifically isolates the Y-axis component. Unlike Twist, it applies a uniform rotation angle to the entire object rather than a spatially varying one. It is a sibling to RotateX and RotateZ. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point P = (x, y, z) and a rotation angle \theta. Output: A transformed 3D point P' = (x', y', z'). Data Structures: The input point is typically represented as a 3-component vector. The angle is a scalar float. Method: The rotation occurs in the XZ plane, leaving the Y-coordinate invariant. The transformation is defined by the following equations: x' = x \cos(\theta) - z \sin(\theta) y' = y z' = x \sin(\theta) + z \cos(\theta) Parameters: \theta: The angle of rotation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from math import cos, sin def rotatey(point, angle): x, y, z = point cosa = cos(angle) sina = sin(angle) xprime = x cosa - z sina yprime = y zprime = x sina + z cosa return (xprime, yprime, zprime) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Angle Units: Ensure consistency between the angle input and the trigonometric functions' expected units (radians vs. degrees). Standard mathematical libraries expect radians. Precision: For very small angles, standard floating-point precision is sufficient. For large numbers of cumulative rotations, consider normalizing the angle to [0, 2\pi) to avoid precision loss. A geometric deformation that twists a shape around the Y-axis proportional to its height. It sets itself apart from RotateY by applying a spatially varying rotation angle that depends on the Y-coordinate, creating a gradient along the vertical axis. Choose it when creating helical or spiral variations of rigid primitives, such as twisting a cylinder into a corkscrew. Time Complexity: O(1) per point transformation. Requires two multiplications, two additions/subtractions, and two trigonometric evaluations per point. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Simple, computationally inexpensive, and numerically stable for standard ranges. Limitations: Only rotates around a single axis and cannot represent combined rotations without composition. RotateY is a standard elementary transformation in computer graphics, derived from the fundamental rotation matrices in linear algebra. It is widely used in raymarching shaders for SDF deformation and in camera pose construction to orient the view direction. Its implementation in educational raymarching contexts, such as the COS 426 Final Project Writeup, follows the same pattern as RotateX and RotateZ, taking a single float input for the rotation degree. name: Twist
head: Twist Transformation
body: Twist is a geometric deformation operation for Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) that twists a shape around the Y-axis proportional to its height. It solves the problem of creating helical or spiral variations of rigid primitives, such as twisting a cylinder into a corkscrew. Unlike RotateY, which applies a uniform rotation to the entire object, Twist applies a spatially varying rotation where the angle depends on the Y-coordinate, creating a gradient of rotation along the vertical axis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point p = (px, py, pz) and a twist factor k (float). Output: A transformed point p'. Data Structures: No persistent data structures. The transformation is computed per-point during SDF evaluation. Steps: 1. Calculate the twist angle \theta based on the Y-coordinate and the twist factor: \theta = k \cdot py 2. Compute the sine and cosine of the angle: c = \cos(\theta) s = \sin(\theta) 3. Apply a 2D rotation matrix to the X and Z components of the point, leaving the Y component unchanged: p'x = c \cdot px - s \cdot pz p'y = py p'z = s \cdot px + c \cdot pz Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def twist(p: tuple, k: float) -> tuple: """Twists space around the Y-axis proportional to height.""" px, py, pz = p angle = k py cosa = math.cos(angle) sina = math.sin(angle) newx = cosa px - sina pz newy = py newz = sina px + cosa pz return (newx, newy, newz) Parameters: k: The twist factor controlling the rate of twist. A value of 0 results in no twist. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: For very large values of k \cdot py, standard floating-point arithmetic may lose precision in trigonometric evaluations, though this is rarely an issue for typical SDF scene scales. Boundaries: The twist is continuous across space. During raymarching, high twist rates relative to step sizes may cause visible discretization artifacts if the step size is not adaptive. Bend is a geometric deformation operation for SDFs that curves a shape around the X-axis. It solves the problem of creating organic, curved variations of rigid primitives, such as bending a cylinder into an arc. Unlike Twist, which rotates geometry around the Y-axis with a linear progression, Bend applies a spatially varying rotation around the X-axis, creating a smooth arc. Definition: Bends space along the X-axis around the Y-axis. Steps: 1. Calculate the bend angle \theta based on the X-coordinate and a bend factor k: \theta = k \cdot px 2. Compute the sine and cosine of the angle: c = \cos(\theta) s = \sin(\theta) 3. Apply a 2D rotation matrix to the X and Y components of the point, leaving the Z component unchanged: p'x = c \cdot px - s \cdot py p'y = s \cdot px + c \cdot py p'z = pz Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def bend(p: tuple, k: float) -> tuple: """Bends space along the X-axis around the Y-axis.""" px, py, pz = p angle = k px cosa = math.cos(angle) sina = math.sin(angle) newx = cosa px - sina py newy = sina px + cosa py newz = pz return (newx, newy, newz) Time Complexity: O(1) per point evaluation. The transformation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and two trigonometric function calls. Memory Complexity: O(1). The operation requires only a few temporary scalar variables for intermediate calculations. Strengths: Computationally inexpensive and simple to implement. Enables the creation of complex, organic shapes from simple primitives. Limitations: The transformation is non-linear, which complicates analytical normal calculation. Normals must be transformed using the inverse transpose of the Jacobian of the transformation to remain perpendicular to the deformed surface. When to use: When a helical or spiral deformation is desired for a primitive. When not to use: When a uniform rotation is sufficient (use RotateY) or when a simple arc is desired (use Bend). Twist is a standard geometric transformation used in Signed Distance Field (SDF) raymarching.
