name: Balanced-Load Minimized-Communication Assignment (BLMCA)
body: BLMCA is a load-balanced cell assignment method for tiled parallel volume rendering that simultaneously minimizes inter-processor communication volume and load imbalance. It improves upon pure Minimized-Communication Assignment (MCA) and pure Best-Fit Decreasing (BFD) load balancing by incorporating MCA’s greedy communication criterion into the BFD heuristic, prioritizing the assignment of heavily loaded mesh-cells to reduce communication overhead while maintaining balanced workloads. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of mesh-cells M, a set of processors P = \{P0, \dots, P{N-1}\}, the global ray-segment count Rm for each mesh-cell m \in M, and the local ray-segment count L{m,p} for each mesh-cell m on each processor p. The maximum allowable part size (bin capacity) C{max} is defined by the load balance criterion. Output: An assignment map A: M \rightarrow P, where A(m) is the processor assigned to mesh-cell m. Data Structures: Workload Vector: An array WL of size N, where WL[p] stores the current total load (sum of global ray-segment counts of assigned mesh-cells) of processor p. Initialized to zero for all p. Sorted Mesh-Cells: A list of mesh-cells sorted in decreasing order of their global ray-segment counts Rm. Pre-computation (Parallelization Step): Before the assignment algorithm runs, processors must determine the global ray-segment counts and the processor with the maximum local ray-segment count for each mesh-cell. This is achieved via a parallel global-sum and global-max operation on local workload matrices. After this "fold and expand" communication step, every processor possesses the complete global data required to run the assignment algorithm locally. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize WL[p] = 0 for all p \in P. 2. Sort mesh-cells M in descending order of Rm. 3. For each mesh-cell m in the sorted list: a. Identify the processor P{max} that has the maximum local ray-segment count for m (i.e., P{max} = \arg\max{p \in P} L{m,p}). b. Check if assigning m to P{max} keeps the load within bounds: if WL[P{max}] + Rm \le C{max}. c. If the condition is met, assign m to P{max} (A(m) = P{max}). d. Otherwise, assign m to the minimally loaded processor P{min} (i.e., P{min} = \arg\min{p \in P} WL[p]). This corresponds to the best-fit criterion in BFD. e. Update the workload: WL[A(m)] \leftarrow WL[A(m)] + Rm. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def BLMCA(meshcells, numprocessors, maxpartsize): """ meshcells: list of objects with attributes.id,.Rm (global ray-segment count), and.Lmp (dict mapping processorid -> local ray-segment count) numprocessors: int N maxpartsize: float Cmax Returns: assignment: dict mapping meshcell.id -> processorid """ # 1. Initialize workloads workload = [0.0] numprocessors # 2. Sort mesh-cells by global ray-segment count in descending order # Note: The global counts and max-local-processor indices must be pre-computed # via parallel global-sum and global-max operations before this function runs. sortedcells = sorted(meshcells, key=lambda c: c.Rm, reverse=True) assignment = {} for cell in sortedcells: # Find processor with maximum local ray-segment count for this cell # cell.Lmp is a dict {processorid: localcount} maxlocalproc = max(cell.Lmp, key=cell.Lmp.get) # Check if assigning to maxlocalproc violates capacity constraint if workload[maxlocalproc] + cell.Rm <= maxpartsize: # MCA criterion: assign to processor with max local data assignedproc = maxlocalproc else: # BFD criterion: assign to minimally loaded processor assignedproc = min(range(numprocessors), key=lambda p: workload[p]) # Assign and update workload assignment[cell.id] = assignedproc workload[assignedproc] += cell.Rm return assignment Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Capacity Constraint: If a single mesh-cell's global ray-segment count Rm exceeds C{max}, the load balance criterion is violated. The sources do not specify a fallback for this degenerate case. Tie Breaking: The sources do not specify tie-breaking rules for \arg\max or \arg\min operations. Implementers should choose a deterministic rule (e.g., lowest processor ID). Pre-computation Dependency: The algorithm assumes global data is available. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: BLMCA reduces communication volume compared to pure BFD by prioritizing local data locality for heavy mesh-cells, while reducing load imbalance compared to pure MCA. Strengths: Balances two conflicting objectives (communication and load) using a heuristic that prioritizes the most impactful assignments (heavy mesh-cells). Limitations: The load balancing sub-problem is NP-hard; BLMCA is a heuristic and may not find the optimal partition. BLMCA was proposed for tiled parallel volume rendering based on object-space decomposition. It addresses the limitations of using either communication-minimizing or load-balancing strategies in isolation for assigning mesh-cells to processors. name: Tile Boundary Computation Setup
head: Tile Boundary Buffer Setup, Tile Boundary Generation
body: This method initializes the data structures required for tiled parallel compositing by computing which triangles (or splats) overlap with each tile in the output framebuffer. It solves the problem of mapping spatial geometry to disjoint processing units without synchronization. It differs from its siblings by relying on a global radix-sort to organize triangle-tile relationships rather than per-tile queues or expensive coverage tests during setup. Inputs: Swapchain width and height (resolution). Number of instances (triangles/splats) to process. Sorted key buffer (sortKBufferEven) containing tile indices for each instance. Outputs: tileBoundaryBuffer: A storage buffer storing boundary indices for each tile. Data Structures: tileBoundaryBuffer: A storage buffer of size tileX tileY 2 sizeof(uint32t). It stores two uint32t values per tile, likely representing start and end indices into the sorted instance list. Parameters: tileX: Number of tiles in the x-direction, calculated as (width + 15) / 16. tileY: Number of tiles in the y-direction, calculated as (height + 15) / 16. numInstances: The total number of geometry instances (triangles/splats). Steps: 1. Calculate Tile Grid: Compute tileX and tileY using ceiling division by 16. tileX = \lceil \frac{width}{16} \rceil, \quad tileY = \lceil \frac{height}{16} \rceil 2. Allocate Buffer: Allocate tileBoundaryBuffer with size tileX tileY 2 sizeof(uint32t). 3. Initialize Buffer: Zero out tileBoundaryBuffer using a fill operation. 4. Barrier: Apply a pipeline barrier transitioning tileBoundaryBuffer from eTransfer to eComputeShader access. 5. Bind Descriptors: Bind sortKBufferEven and tileBoundaryBuffer to the compute pipeline descriptor set. 6. Dispatch: Bind tileBoundaryPipeline and dispatch compute shaders. Push constant: numInstances. Workgroup size: 256 threads per workgroup. Number of workgroups: (numInstances + 255) / 256. 7. Barrier: Apply a compute read/write barrier on tileBoundaryBuffer to ensure completion before subsequent reads. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setuptileboundaries(context, width, height, numinstances, sortkbuffereven): # 1. Calculate tile grid dimensions tilex = (width + 15) // 16 tiley = (height + 15) // 16 # 2. Allocate tile boundary buffer # Size: tileX tileY 2 sizeof(uint32t) tileboundarybuffer = context.createstoragebuffer( size=tilex tiley 2 4, name="tileBoundaryBuffer") # 3. Zero out the buffer context.fillbuffer(tileboundarybuffer, 0) # 4. Apply pipeline barrier: Transfer -> ComputeShader context.applypipelinebarrier( buffer=tileboundarybuffer, srcaccess=vk.AccessFlagBits.eTransferWrite, dstaccess=vk.AccessFlagBits.eShaderWrite, srcstage=vk.PipelineStageFlagBits.eTransfer, dststage=vk.PipelineStageFlagBits.eComputeShader) # 5. Bind descriptors descriptorset = context.createdescriptorset() descriptorset.bindbuffer(0, vk.DescriptorType.eStorageBuffer, vk.ShaderStageFlagBits.eCompute, sortkbuffereven) descriptorset.bindbuffer(1, vk.DescriptorType.eStorageBuffer, vk.ShaderStageFlagBits.eCompute, tileboundarybuffer) descriptorset.build() # 6. Dispatch compute pipeline # Pipeline: tileBoundaryPipeline # Push constant: numinstances # Workgroup size: 256 numworkgroups = (numinstances + 255) // 256 context.bindpipeline(tileboundarypipeline) context.binddescriptorset(0, descriptorset) context.pushconstant(numinstances) context.dispatchcompute(numworkgroups, 1, 1) # 7. Apply compute barrier context.applypipelinebarrier( buffer=tileboundarybuffer, srcaccess=vk.AccessFlagBits.eShaderWrite, dstaccess=vk.AccessFlagBits.eShaderRead | vk.AccessFlagBits.eShaderWrite, srcstage=vk.PipelineStageFlagBits.eComputeShader, dststage=vk.PipelineStageFlagBits.eComputeShader) Edge Cases: Zero Instances: If numinstances is 0, the dispatch should handle this gracefully or be skipped. Boundary Precision: Ceiling division ensures full coverage of the swapchain dimensions, even if not perfectly divisible by 16. Performs triangle setup and emits a conservative list of triangles touching each tile. It differs by using global radix-sort to avoid per-tile queues and expensive coverage tests during setup, minimizing inter-thread communication. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of instances for the dispatch, dominated by the preceding radix sort. Memory Complexity: O(tileX \times tileY) for the boundary buffer. Strengths: Zero synchronization between tiles during compositing; leverages GPU compute parallelism. Limitations: Requires a sorted input list; setup cost is non-trivial for very small tile counts or low instance counts. When to Use: When compositing large numbers of overlapping primitives on GPU where atomic operations are expensive or undesirable. This method is part of the Vulkan-based Gaussian Splatting implementation in 3DGS.cpp, utilizing Vulkan compute shaders for parallel processing. name: Coarse Raster
head: Coarse Rasterizer
body: The Coarse Rasterizer performs triangle setup and emits a conservative list of all triangles touching each tile in a tiled volume rendering pipeline. It differs from typical chunkers by avoiding per-tile queues and expensive tile coverage tests during the setup phase, instead relying on a global radix-sort to organize triangle-tile relationships. This approach minimizes inter-thread communication and leverages the high compute-to-bandwidth ratio of modern GPUs by recomputing setup data per tile rather than caching it. The method consists of three main phases: Triangle Setup, Tile Sorting, and Tile Splitting. Input: A list of triangles defined in world or voxel space. Output: A set of virtual tiles, each containing a bounded number of triangles, ready for the Fine Raster stage. 1. Triangle Descriptor: A word-sized integer used for sorting. Bits [0:1]: Dominant axis of the triangle (2 bits). Bits [2:31]: Tile ID (remaining bits). 2. Unsorted List: An array of pairs (triangleindex, descriptor). 3. Per-Tile Ranges: After sorting, a compact list of (begin, end) indices into the sorted list for each physical tile. 4. Virtual Tile Arena: Memory allocated per virtual tile during the fine raster stage. M{tile}: The maximum number of triangles allowed in a virtual tile. 1. Triangle Setup and Emission For each triangle, a single CUDA thread processes the triangle. a. Compute the integer bounding box of the triangle. b. Determine the dominant axis of the triangle. c. Identify all physical tiles whose voxel grid intersects the triangle's integer bounding box. This is a conservative estimate; expensive precise coverage tests are skipped. d. For each touched tile, compute the 12 floats required for the cheapest 6-separating triangle-voxel coverage test. These floats are recomputed for each tile rather than computed once and reused, optimizing for GPU compute-to-bandwidth ratios. e. Construct the descriptor: combine the dominant axis (2 bits) and the tile ID. f. Emit a pair (triangleindex, descriptor) to a global unsorted list. 2. Tile Sorting a. Perform a global radix sort on the unsorted list of (triangleindex, descriptor) pairs based on the descriptor. b. The sorting groups triangles by tile ID, and within each tile, by dominant axis. This grouping increases SIMD efficiency in the subsequent fine raster stage. c. Generate a compact list of per-tile (begin, end) ranges that point to the start and end indices of each tile's triangles in the sorted array. 3. Tile Splitting a. Iterate through the physical tiles. b. If a physical tile contains more than M{tile} triangles, split it into multiple virtual tiles. c. Each virtual tile contains at most M{tile} triangles. d. Virtual tiles may overlap on the voxel grid. During the fine raster stage, a separate memory arena is created for each virtual tile. A final merging pass blends the results of all virtual tiles mapping to the same physical framebuffer entry. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarseraster(triangles, Mtile): # Phase 1: Triangle Setup and Emission outputlist = [] for tri in triangles: # 1. Compute integer bounding box bboxmin = [int(tri.min[i]) for i in range(3)] bboxmax = [int(tri.max[i]) for i in range(3)] # 2. Determine dominant axis (0=x, 1=y, 2=z) extents = [bboxmax[i] - bboxmin[i] for i in range(3)] dominantaxis = max(range(3), key=lambda i: extents[i]) # 3. Find all tiles intersecting the bounding box touchedtiles = [] for x in range(bboxmin[0], bboxmax[0] + 1): for y in range(bboxmin[1], bboxmax[1] + 1): for z in range(bboxmin[2], bboxmax[2] + 1): touchedtiles.append((x, y, z)) # 4. Emit for each touched tile for tileid in touchedtiles: # Recompute 12 floats for this specific tile setupdata = computesetupfloats(tri, tileid) # Construct descriptor: 2 bits for axis, rest for tile ID descriptor = (tileid << 2) | dominantaxis outputlist.append((tri.id, descriptor)) # Phase 2: Tile Sorting # Represents the global radix sort counting and scattering phase sortedlist = sorted(outputlist, key=lambda x: x[1]) tileranges = {} currenttile = -1 startidx = 0 for i, (triidx, descriptor) in enumerate(sortedlist): tileid = descriptor >> 2 if tileid != currenttile: if currenttile != -1: tileranges[currenttile] = (startidx, i) currenttile = tileid startidx = i if currenttile != -1: tileranges[currenttile] = (startidx, len(sortedlist)) # Phase 3: Tile Splitting virtualtiles = [] for tileid, (start, end) in tileranges.items(): numtriangles = end - start if numtriangles <= Mtile: virtualtiles.append({ 'physicaltileid': tileid, 'triangles': sortedlist[start:end], 'isvirtual': False }) else: numsplits = (numtriangles + Mtile - 1) // Mtile for i in range(numsplits): chunkstart = start + i Mtile chunkend = min(start + (i + 1) Mtile, end) virtualtiles.append({ 'physicaltileid': tileid, 'triangles': sortedlist[chunkstart:chunkend], 'isvirtual': True, 'virtualindex': i }) return virtualtiles, tileranges def computesetupfloats(triangle, tileid): # Recompute the 12 floats required for the cheapest 6-separating triangle-voxel coverage test # for the specific tile. Implementation uses standard geometric calculations. return [0.0] 12 Low-resolution voxelizations: May have too few occupied tiles to fill the GPU machine, or skewed triangle distributions. Tile splitting addresses this by creating more virtual tiles to improve load balancing. Degenerate ranges: If a scanline range is degenerate, it does not intersect the triangle. The coarse rasterizer avoids this by using conservative bounding box tests, potentially emitting triangles to tiles they do not strictly intersect, which is handled by the fine rasterizer's precise tests. Time Complexity: Efficient due to low data amplification; triangles often touch one or a few tiles only. The sorting phase dominates complexity, typically O(N \log N) or O(N) with radix sort, where N is the number of triangle-tile pairs. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the unsorted list, sorted list, and per-tile ranges. Virtual tile arenas are allocated during fine raster. Strengths: Avoids inter-thread communication primitives like per-tile queues by using global radix-sort counting and scattering. The recomputation of setup data exploits high compute-to-bandwidth ratios. Sorting by dominant axis improves SIMD efficiency in the fine raster stage. Limitations: Conservative bounding box tests may emit more triangles than necessary, increasing the workload for the fine rasterizer. The need for a global sort adds latency compared to queue-based approaches if the number of triangle-tile pairs is small. When to use: When running on GPUs with high compute-to-bandwidth ratios and when tile sizes are large enough that triangles touch few tiles. Especially useful for low-resolution voxelizations where load balancing is critical. The Coarse Rasterizer is part of the VoxelPipe pipeline. It was designed to address the inefficiencies of previous tiled volume rendering approaches that relied on per-tile queues and inter-thread communication. The method leverages the parallel sorting capabilities of GPUs to efficiently organize triangle data for subsequent rasterization stages. name: Parallel Image Assembly
head: Final Image Assembly & Alpha Blending, Image Stitching, Z-Order Compositing
body: Parallel Image Assembly is the final stage of tiled parallel volume rendering where per-process or per-rank RGBA sub-images are collected and blended into a single final image. It solves the problem of reconstructing a coherent global view from disjoint spatial tiles processed independently. Unlike its siblings which handle tile distribution or boundary computation, this method focuses on the global accumulation of color and opacity, typically using front-to-back alpha compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Per-rank composited sub-images (color and opacity arrays), rank coordinates (px, py, pz), global image dimensions (X, Y), and the number of depth slices PZ. Outputs: A final RGBA image array and optionally total opacity map. Data Structures: finalimage: A numpy array of shape (X, Y, 4) with dtype np.float32, storing the final RGBA image. totalopacity: An array of shape (X, Y) or (X, Y, 1) storing accumulated opacity. zsplitimages: Intermediate storage for sub-images placed at spatial coordinates. Parameters: LOCATIONOFZ: Sorted unique z-start coordinates for each process chunk. PZ: Total number of depth slices. Steps: 1. Gather: Rank 0 gathers composited subdomain images and opacities from all other ranks. 2. Initialize: On Rank 0, initialize finalimage to zeros with shape (PX \times sub\height, PY \times sub\width, 4) and totalopacity to zeros. 3. Place: Iterate through all gathered ranks. For each rank, determine its (px, py, pz) coordinates. 4. Blend: For each z-slice (or specifically the middle depth slice pz == PZ // 2 as per some implementations), blend the sub-image into finalimage using front-to-back alpha compositing. Formula: C{final} = C{prev} + C{z} \cdot (1 - \alpha{prev}) \alpha{final} = \alpha{prev} + \alpha{z} \cdot (1 - \alpha{prev}) Where C is color (RGB) and \alpha is opacity. 5. Convert: Convert the finalimage from float32 to uint8 RGBA. 6. Save: Save the result as a PNG file. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelimageassembly(gatheredcolors, gatheredopacities, rankcoords, px, py, pz, subwidth, subheight, xdim, ydim): """ Assembles per-rank sub-images into a final image. Args: gatheredcolors: List of color arrays from all ranks. gatheredopacities: List of opacity arrays from all ranks. rankcoords: List of (px, py, pz) tuples for each rank. px, py, pz: Dimensions of the process grid. subwidth, subheight: Width and height of each sub-image. xdim, ydim: Total image dimensions. Returns: finalimage: numpy array of shape (xdim, ydim, 4) dtype uint8. """ # Initialize final image and opacity map finalimage = np.zeros((xdim, ydim, 4), dtype=np.float32) totalopacity = np.zeros((xdim, ydim), dtype=np.float32) # Iterate through all ranks for rankidx, (rpx, rpy, rpz) in enumerate(rankcoords): color = gatheredcolors[rankidx] opacity = gatheredopacities[rankidx] # Determine spatial coordinates in the final image # Assuming contiguous tiling xstart = rpx subwidth ystart = rpy subheight xend = xstart + subwidth yend = ystart + subheight # Extract RGB and A components # color shape: (subheight, subwidth, 3) or (subheight, subwidth, 4) # opacity shape: (subheight, subwidth) or (subheight, subwidth, 1) # Handle potential shape differences (e.g., opacity as 3D array) if opacity.ndim == 3: opacity = opacity[:,:, 0] # Front-to-back compositing # Cfinal = Cprev + Cz (1 - alphaprev) # alphafinal = alphaprev + alphaz (1 - alphaprev) # Get current alpha in the final image for the region currentalpha = finalimage[ystart:yend, xstart:xend, 3] currentalphaexpanded = currentalpha[:,:, np.newaxis] # Blend color # Note: color might be RGB or RGBA. Assuming RGB if shape is (H, W, 3) if color.shape[2] == 3: finalimage[ystart:yend, xstart:xend,:3] += color (1.0 - currentalphaexpanded) else: # If color is RGBA, use the alpha channel for blending zalpha = color[:,:, 3] zalphaexpanded = zalpha[:,:, np.newaxis] finalimage[ystart:yend, xstart:xend,:3] += color[:,:,:3] (1.0 - currentalphaexpanded) currentalpha = currentalpha + zalpha (1.0 - currentalpha) # Update alpha finalimage[ystart:yend, xstart:xend, 3] = currentalpha + opacity (1.0 - currentalpha) # Update total opacity map (optional, for debugging or specific use cases) totalopacity[ystart:yend, xstart:xend] += opacity (1.0 - totalopacity[ystart:yend, xstart:xend]) # Convert to uint8 finalimageuint8 = np.clip(finalimage, 0, 1).astype(np.uint8) return finalimageuint8 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use float32 for accumulation to avoid overflow and maintain dynamic range. Boundaries: Ensure sub-images are placed correctly without overlap or gaps. Degenerate Input: Handle cases where sub-images might be empty or have zero opacity. Handles compositing within a tile. Choose when memory is limited per tile. Distributes tiles dynamically. Choose when workload is uneven. Computes tile boundaries. Choose when tile sizes vary. Uses threads for tile processing. Choose for CPU parallelism. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, dominated by the compositing step. Memory Complexity: O(X \cdot Y) for the final image. Performance: Depends on network bandwidth for gathering and CPU speed for compositing. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, no synchronization needed during compositing. Limitations: Requires gathering all data to one rank, which can be a bottleneck for large images. When to Use: When a single final image is required and the image size fits in memory. When Not to Use: When the image is too large to fit in memory or when distributed final image generation is needed. Parallel Image Assembly is a standard technique in parallel volume rendering, often implemented using MPI for communication. It builds on the principles of tiled parallel compositing [Parent]. name: Multi-Threaded Tile-Based Rendering
head: threaded rasterization
body: Multi-Threaded Tile-Based Rendering is a CPU-based parallelization strategy that divides the screen height into disjoint horizontal tiles, assigning each tile to a separate thread to parallelize the rasterization workload. It builds on Tiled Parallel Compositing by providing the thread management and tile decomposition logic, allowing for lock-free, zero-synchronization processing of screen regions. Unlike Screen Parallel Rendering, which requires every processor to hold the entire volume in memory, this method allows for more flexible memory management as tiles are processed independently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Screen height (H), screen width (W), number of available hardware threads (N{hw}). Output: A fully rendered image (framebuffer) where each tile has been rasterized by its assigned thread. Data Structures: The core data structure is a Tile struct, which defines the rectangular region of the screen to be rendered by a specific thread. It contains four integer fields representing the boundaries: xmin: Left boundary (inclusive). xmax: Right boundary (exclusive or inclusive depending on implementation, typically exclusive for iteration). ymin: Top boundary (inclusive). ymax: Bottom boundary (inclusive). Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine the number of threads to use. If std::thread::hardwareconcurrency() returns 0 or is unavailable, default to 1 thread to prevent division by zero or empty thread vectors. THREADS = \max(1, \text{std::thread::hardware\concurrency}()) 2. Calculate the height of each tile. The screen height H is divided by the number of threads. The last tile may handle any remainder to ensure full coverage. tileH = \lfloor H / THREADS \rfloor 3. Create and launch worker threads. For each thread index i from 0 to THREADS - 1: Define the y-range for the tile. y{min} = i \times tileH y{max} = \begin{cases} H - 1 & \text{if } i == THREADS - 1 \\ (i + 1) \times tileH - 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Define the x-range. Typically, the tile spans the full width of the screen, so x{min} = 0 and x{max} = W - 1. Instantiate a Tile struct with these coordinates. Launch a new thread executing the renderTile function, passing the Tile struct as an argument. 4. Join all worker threads to ensure completion before proceeding. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading import math class Tile: def init(self, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax): self.xmin = xmin self.xmax = xmax self.ymin = ymin self.ymax = ymax def rendertile(tile, framebuffer, scenedata): """ Renders a single tile into the shared framebuffer. Assumes framebuffer is pre-allocated and thread-safe for writes (e.g., using atomic operations or disjoint memory regions per tile). """ for y in range(tile.ymin, tile.ymax + 1): for x in range(tile.xmin, tile.xmax + 1): # Perform rasterization/compositing for pixel (x, y) # This step is specific to the volume rendering method being used pixelcolor = computepixelcolor(x, y, scenedata) framebuffer[y][x] = pixelcolor def multithreadedtilerendering(width, height, scenedata): # Determine thread count try: numhwthreads = threading.activecount() # Placeholder for hardwareconcurrency check # In real C++ std::thread::hardwareconcurrency() returns unsigned int # If 0, treat as 1. Here we simulate the logic. threads = max(1, 4) # Example: assuming 4 cores if detection fails except: threads = 1 # Calculate tile height tileh = height // threads threadslist = [] for i in range(threads): ymin = i tileh if i == threads - 1: ymax = height - 1 else: ymax = (i + 1) tileh - 1 # Full width for each tile xmin = 0 xmax = width - 1 tile = Tile(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) # Create and start thread t = threading.Thread(target=rendertile, args=(tile, framebuffer, scenedata)) threadslist.append(t) t.start() # Join all threads for t in threadslist: t.join() return framebuffer Parameters: THREADS: Number of parallel workers. Typical value is std::thread::hardwareconcurrency(). tileH: Height of each tile. Determined by H / THREADS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If hardwareconcurrency() returns 0, the thread count must be clamped to 1 to avoid division by zero errors when calculating tileH or creating an empty thread vector. The last tile must explicitly handle the remainder of the height division to ensure the entire screen is covered without gaps or overlaps. A parallel scheme that divides the screen into p subscreens for p processors, where each processor takes responsibility for the entire ray for its subscreen. Tasks are assigned in a cyclic manner to statically balance workloads. It is suitable for small datasets that do not require data decomposition but requires large main memory because every processor must load the entire volume into memory. Time Complexity: O(N / T), where N is the total number of pixels and T is the number of threads, assuming uniform workload distribution. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the framebuffer, plus O(1) per thread for tile state. Unlike object-parallel schemes, it does not require distributing the volume data across processors if the volume is shared read-only. Strengths: Zero synchronization between tiles during rendering (no atomics or locks needed for pixel writes if tiles are disjoint), simple implementation, effective on CPUs. Limitations: Load imbalance if the scene has varying complexity across the screen (e.g., occlusion varies by tile). Requires careful handling of the last tile's boundaries. When to use: CPU-based volume rendering where memory bandwidth is not the primary bottleneck and the scene fits in memory. When not to use: Very large datasets that cannot fit in memory on each processor (see Screen Parallel Rendering for memory constraints) or when GPU acceleration is available. The concept of dividing the screen into subscreens for parallel processing was introduced in early parallel volume rendering schemes, specifically in the context of medical volume rendering. The specific implementation using std::thread and hardware concurrency detection is documented in the CPU-Rasterizer repository. whudsontosh/CPU-Rasterizer, https://github.com/whudsontosh/CPU-Rasterizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Medical Volume Rendering Techniques, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.07710v1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Register-form kernels with staged shell data
head: Staged shell data optimization
body: This method optimizes GPU compute shader kernels for volume rendering by staging shell metadata and coefficient data into groupshared memory, thereby eliminating dependent global memory loads during the inner loop evaluation. It builds on Compute Shader Kernel by restructuring data access patterns to improve occupancy and reduce latency for atomic orbital (AO) evaluations. Inputs: A list of Gaussian-type orbital (GTO) shells, each defined by centre, cutoff, angular momentum l, AO count, and primitive coefficients. A set of evaluation points (vertices or corners). Outputs: Evaluated function values and gradients at the points. Data Structures: Chunk: A subset of shells packed to at most 256 primitives. Groupshared Memory: Stores staged shell data (centre, cutoff, l, AO count, primitives) and rows of coefficient matrix C for the current chunk. Register Form: Vertex values are kept in registers during computation. Steps: 1. Pack Chunks: Group shells into chunks containing at most 256 primitives. Shells exceeding 64 primitives are refused by the set. 2. Stage Data: Load shell metadata and rows of C into groupshared memory for the current chunk. 3. Filter Shells: For each evaluation point, skip shells that are out of reach in all three dimensions (based on cutoff). 4. Evaluate: Execute the inner loop using the staged groupshared memory. This avoids dependent global loads per shell. 5. Accumulate: Accumulate contributions from primitives to the final value/gradient. Parameters: Maximum primitives per chunk: 256. Maximum primitives per shell: 64 (shells exceeding this are refused). Pitfalls: Shells with more than 64 primitives are refused. Precision issues may arise if not handled; however, specific precision guards are not detailed in the sources. This variant optimizes the evaluation of Cartesian monomials by computing them at once per angular momentum l in mdgto's order, with AO normalization folded into the staged rows of C, which are read as float4. A single function accumulates the shell's polynomial and multiplies by the radial part once. The groupshared rows are sized per F (number of channels), ensuring that narrow kernels maintain high occupancy. Performance: Eliminates dependent global loads in the inner loop, improving throughput. Memory: Uses groupshared memory for staging, reducing global memory bandwidth pressure. Occupancy: Row sizing per F helps maintain occupancy for narrow kernels. Limitations: Shells with >64 primitives are unsupported. This optimization is part of the mdgtoisogpu implementation in mdlib, focusing on efficient GPU isosurface extraction. It addresses the bottleneck of loading shell data from global memory for every evaluation point. mdgtoisogpu: optimized GPU isosurface extraction (non-blocking jobs, flood, one measured path), https://github.com/scanberg/mdlib/pull/15, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability
head: CUDA-GL Interop, CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability for 3D Textures, CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability for Raymarching, CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability for Volume Rendering, CUDA-OpenGL Interoperation via CUDA Array, OpenGL-CUDA Interoperability for Shared VBOs, Zero-Copy Volume Rendering, cudaGraphicsGLRegisterImage
body: CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability is a mechanism that allows CUDA kernels to read from and write to OpenGL resources (textures, buffers) directly in GPU memory, eliminating the need for CPU-mediated data transfers. It solves the bottleneck of copying rendered volume data or simulation results from CUDA device memory back to system memory for display. It sets itself apart from standard interop methods by supporting both read-only access (via mapped arrays/texture objects) and write access (via surface objects or direct buffer pointers), enabling zero-copy rendering pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: OpenGL resource IDs (Texture ID, Buffer ID), resource dimensions (width, height, depth), and CUDA graphics resource flags. Outputs: CUDA graphics resource handle (cudaGraphicsResourcet), mapped CUDA array (cudaArrayt), or device pointer (void). Data Structures: cudaGraphicsResourcet: Opaque handle returned by registration functions. cudaArrayt: Device memory structure representing the mapped OpenGL texture. cudaResourceDesc: Structure describing the resource type (Array, Buffer) and its properties. cudaSurfaceObjectt: Object allowing atomic writes to a mapped array. Numbered Steps: 1. Resource Registration: For Textures: Call cudaGraphicsGLRegisterImage with the OpenGL texture ID, target (GLTEXTURE2D or GLTEXTURE3D), and flags. Use cudaGraphicsRegisterFlagsSurfaceLoadStore if write access is required. For Buffers (VBO/PBO): Call cudaGraphicsGLRegisterBuffer with the VBO ID and flags (typically cudaGraphicsMapFlagsNone for read/write). Pitfall: Ensure the OpenGL context is current before registration. 2. Resource Mapping (Per Frame/Per Kernel Launch): Call cudaGraphicsMapResources with the resource handle count and array of handles to gain CUDA access. Pitfall: Accessing the mapped resource with OpenGL before unmapping causes program failure. 3. Resource Acquisition: For Textures: Call cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray to retrieve the cudaArrayt. For Buffers: Call cudaGraphicsResourceGetMappedPointer to retrieve the device pointer (void). 4. Binding (Optional but Recommended for Textures): For Read Access: Bind the cudaArrayt to a CUDA texture object using cudaBindTextureToArray. For Write Access: Initialize cudaResourceDesc with resType=cudaResourceTypeArray and res.array.array=array, then call cudaCreateSurfaceObject to create a cudaSurfaceObjectt. Alternatively, bind the array to a surface using cudaBindSurfaceToArray. 5. Kernel Execution: Launch the CUDA kernel. If using Surface: Pass the cudaSurfaceObjectt to the kernel. Use surfaceStore or atomic functions for writes. If using Pointer (VBO): Pass the device pointer obtained in Step 3. The kernel writes directly to the VBO memory. If using Texture Array (Read-only): Use standard texture fetch functions (tex3D, tex2D). 6. Unmapping: Call cudaGraphicsUnmapResources to release CUDA access, allowing OpenGL to use the resource again. 7. Cleanup (Optional): Destroy surface objects if created: cudaDestroySurfaceObject. Unregister resources on shutdown: cudaGraphicsUnregisterResource. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initopengltextureinterop(gltextureid, width, height, depth, iswritable=False): # Step 1: Register flags = cudaGraphicsRegisterFlagsSurfaceLoadStore if iswritable else cudaGraphicsRegisterFlagsReadOnly resourcehandle = cudaGraphicsGLRegisterImage(gltextureid, GLTEXTURE3D, flags) # Create surface object handle (initialized to 0) surfacehandle = 0 return resourcehandle, surfacehandle def initopenglbufferinterop(glvboid, sizebytes): # Step 1: Register Buffer resourcehandle = cudaGraphicsGLRegisterBuffer(glvboid, cudaGraphicsMapFlagsNone) return resourcehandle def renderframe(resourcehandle, surfacehandle, glvbohandle=None, width=1920, height=1080): # Step 2: Map Resources cudaGraphicsMapResources(1, resourcehandle) cudaarray = None deviceptr = None if glvbohandle is None: # Texture Path # Step 3: Get Mapped Array cudaarray = cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray(resourcehandle, 0, 0) if surfacehandle == 0: # Step 4: Create Surface for Writing resdesc = cudaResourceDesc() resdesc.resType = cudaResourceTypeArray resdesc.res.array.array = cudaarray surfacehandle = cudaCreateSurfaceObject(resdesc) # Step 5: Launch Kernel with Surface # launchkernel<<<blocks, threads>>>(surfacehandle, width, height) # Note: Kernel uses surf2Dwrite or atomicAdd on surface else: # Buffer Path # Step 3: Get Mapped Pointer deviceptr, bytescount = cudaGraphicsResourceGetMappedPointer(resourcehandle) # Step 5: Launch Kernel with Pointer # launchkernel<<<blocks, threads>>>(deviceptr, width, height) # Note: Kernel writes directly to deviceptr # Step 6: Unmap cudaGraphicsUnmapResources(1, resourcehandle) return surfacehandle def cleanup(resourcehandle, surfacehandle): if surfacehandle != 0: cudaDestroySurfaceObject(surfacehandle) cudaGraphicsUnregisterResource(resourcehandle) Parameters: blockdim: Typically dim3(16, 16, 1) for 2D image writing. griddim: Calculated as (Width + blockdim.x) / blockdim.x for x, (Height + blockdim.y) / blockdim.y for y, and 1 for z. constantWidth, constantHeight: CUDA constants storing viewport dimensions, updated via cudaMemcpyToSymbol. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Context Current: OpenGL context must be current when registering or mapping resources. Surface Creation Failure: If cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray fails, the surface object is not created, preventing kernel launch. Check cudaSuccess before creating the surface. Typo in Constants: Ensure variable names match exactly when using cudaMemcpyToSymbol (e.g., constantNCP vs cosntantNCP). Ray-Box Intersection: If NOTRAYBOX is defined, front/back hit positions are computed via OpenGL geometry shaders and stored in textures; otherwise, the inverse view matrix is passed to CUDA for GPU-side intersection. CUDA-OpenGL Interop Surface Write is a technique to render volume data by computing ray casting on the GPU (CUDA) and writing the final image directly into a texture that is registered with OpenGL, avoiding CPU-GPU data transfer for the final image [Parent]. It sets itself apart from standard interop methods by using CUDA surface objects (cudaSurfaceObjectt) for write access, which allows for atomic operations and potentially better performance for concurrent writes compared to standard texture memory writes or copies. Bindless Textures in CUDA is an object-oriented approach using the CUDA API to upload textures into VRAM and expose them via texture object descriptors, eliminating the need for per-frame binding and mapping required by OpenGL-CUDA interoperability for textures. It sets itself apart by allowing a dynamic number of textures specified at runtime and simultaneous exposure to the kernel, unlike the OpenGL mapping method which requires hardcoded global scope declarations and per-frame binding/unbinding. It is chosen when the number of textures is large or dynamic, and when the overhead of mapping/unmapping becomes a bottleneck. Time Complexity: O(1) for registration/unregistration (one-time). O(1) for map/unmap per frame. Kernel execution time depends on the rendering algorithm (e.g., raymarching). Memory Complexity: Zero-copy; no additional CPU memory allocation for the rendered image or texture data. Measured Performance: Eliminates four serial copies and four redundant texture objects compared to SFML-based approaches. Reduces frame latency from >20 ms (under 60 fps for 1080p) to significantly lower values, enabling real-time performance. Strengths: Eliminates CPU-GPU data transfer overhead; allows direct GPU-side rendering; supports atomic writes via surfaces. Limitations: Requires OpenGL context management; binding/unmapping overhead for textures (mitigated by Bindless Textures); limited simultaneous texture count in standard OpenGL interop (mitigated by Bindless Textures). When to Use: Real-time volume rendering, GPU-based simulations requiring visual feedback, avoiding CPU bottlenecks. When Not to Use: When CPU-side post-processing is required, or when using libraries that abstract away OpenGL/CUDA interop (e.g., SFML) where performance is not critical. CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability was introduced with CUDA 2.0. It has been widely used in volume rendering engines (e.g., VRCUDA, cuVRender) and fluid simulation visualizations (e.g., HZL-fluidEffectsStudio) to achieve real-time performance by bypassing the CPU. name: CUDA-OpenGL Interop Surface Write
head: Direct GL Texture Write from CUDA, Surface Write via CUDA Interop
body: CUDA-OpenGL Interop Surface Write is a technique to render volume data by computing ray casting on the GPU (CUDA) and writing the final image directly into a texture that is registered with OpenGL, avoiding CPU-GPU data transfer for the final image [Parent]. It sets itself apart from standard interop methods by using CUDA surface objects (cudaSurfaceObjectt) for write access, which allows for atomic operations and potentially better performance for concurrent writes compared to standard texture memory writes or copies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An OpenGL texture ID (created as RGBA8), CUDA device memory containing scene data (camera, volume, transfer function), and image dimensions (W, H). Output: The OpenGL texture updated with the rendered image pixels. Data Structures: cudaGraphicsResourcet: Handle to the registered OpenGL resource. cudaArrayt: Mapped array representation of the OpenGL texture in CUDA memory. cudaSurfaceObjectt: Surface object bound to the cudaArrayt for writing. Steps: 1. Create GL Texture: Generate an OpenGL texture with format GLRGBA8 and dimensions W \times H. 2. Register Resource: Register the GL texture with CUDA using cudaGraphicsGLRegisterImage. The registration flags depend on the access mode: Use cudaGraphicsRegisterFlagsSurfaceLoadStore if surface write is required (allows read/write). Use cudaGraphicsRegisterFlagsWriteDiscard if only writing and discarding previous content is sufficient. 3. Map Resource: Before the kernel launch, map the CUDA resource to make it accessible to CUDA kernels using cudaGraphicsMapResources. 4. Get Mapped Array: Retrieve the cudaArrayt handle for the mapped resource using cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray. 5. Bind Surface: Create a cudaSurfaceObjectt from the cudaArrayt using cudaCreateSurfaceObject. 6. Launch Kernel: Launch the CUDA kernel passing the surface object. Inside the kernel, use surfaceStore functions (e.g., surfaceStore<uchar4>(surfObj, coord, value)) to write pixels. 7. Unmap Resource: After the kernel completes (and any necessary synchronization), unmap the resource using cudaGraphicsUnmapResources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. gltextureid = creategltexturergba8(width, height) cudaresource = cudaGraphicsGLRegisterImage( gltextureid, GLTEXTURE2D, cudaGraphicsRegisterFlagsSurfaceLoadStore # or WriteDiscard) cudaGraphicsMapResources(1, cudaresource) cudaarray = cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray(cudaresource, 0, 0) surfaceobject = cudaCreateSurfaceObject(cudaarray) kernelraycast<<<grid, block>>>(scenedata, surfaceobject, width, height) cudaDeviceSynchronize() cudaDestroySurfaceObject(surfaceobject) cudaGraphicsUnmapResources(1, cudaresource) Parameters: width, height: Image dimensions. cudaGraphicsRegisterFlags: SurfaceLoadStore or WriteDiscard. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Synchronization: Ensure cudaDeviceSynchronize() or an event is used before unmapping if the OpenGL context needs to read the texture immediately, although cudaGraphicsUnmapResources is a blocking call for the CUDA side. Format Mismatch: The GL texture format must match the data type written by the surface (e.g., uchar4 for GLRGBA8). Resource Registration: The GL texture must be bound and valid at the time of registration. Copies a 3D volume of float data from device memory into a registered OpenGL 3D texture via CUDA interop, mapping the resource, performing a 3D memory copy, and unmapping. Steps: 1. Map resource: Call cudaGraphicsMapResources(1, &mresource). 2. Get mapped array: Call cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray(&array, mresource, 0, 0). 3. Configure copy parameters: Set srcPtr with makecudaPitchedPtr(sourcePointer, widthsizeof(float), width, height), dstArray=array, extent=makeextent(width, height, depth), kind=cudaMemcpyDeviceToDevice. 4. Execute copy: Call cudaMemcpy3D(&copy). 5. Unmap resource: Call cudaGraphicsUnmapResources(1, &mresource). Pitfall: Source pointer must not be null and resource must be registered; throws std::logicerror if either condition fails. Time Complexity: O(W \times H) for the ray casting kernel, plus overhead for mapping/unmapping resources. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the texture storage. Strengths: Eliminates the final CPU-GPU transfer bottleneck for the rendered image. Surface writes support atomic operations, beneficial for accumulation or blending. Limitations: Requires OpenGL-CUDA interop support. Surface writes may have different performance characteristics compared to texture writes depending on the hardware and access patterns. When to use: When real-time rendering of volume data is required and the final image needs to be displayed in an OpenGL context without CPU intervention. When not to use: If the rendering pipeline requires post-processing on the CPU or if the hardware does not support CUDA-OpenGL interop. Originated from the need to integrate CUDA compute capabilities with OpenGL rendering pipelines efficiently. The technique is demonstrated in the cuVRender project, which implements a CUDA-accelerated volume rendering engine. It is also referenced in fluid effects studios for texture management. name: Y-Bucket Parallelization
head: Y-bucket grouping
body: Y-Bucket Parallelization is a two-pass parallel algorithm for direct volume rendering that processes polygonal representations of isosurfaces or volume slices by grouping them into scanline-based "y-buckets". It solves the problem of efficiently rendering irregular and multiple grids in software by maximizing spatial coherence and avoiding the computational difficulties associated with ray-casting intersecting cells. Unlike tile-based parallelization methods that break scanlines and lose coherence, this method parallelizes on a scanline basis to limit duplication. The method operates on polygonal data representing volume slices or isosurfaces. The polygons are stored in counter-clockwise order when viewed from outside the grid, allowing the system to easily recognize boundaries and the last polygon in its grid within the visibility order. Inputs: A set of polygons representing the volume data. A set of processors (or threads). The image resolution (width and height). Outputs: A rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Y-Bucket Array: An array indexed by scanline (y-coordinate). Each entry stores the count of polygons intersecting that scanline. 2. Output Array: A common output array partitioned to store the final pixel values. 3. X-Bucket Structures: Associated with the leftmost pixel of a polygon's bounding box on a scanline. Contains a linked list of active polygons in front-to-back visibility order. Steps: 1. First Pass: Polygon Distribution Each processor iterates through the input polygons. For each polygon, determine the range of scanlines (y-coordinates) it intersects. Increment the counter in the Y-Bucket Array for each intersected scanline. Store the polygon in a temporary structure associated with its corresponding y-bucket, marking it as processed. 2. Second Pass: Bucket Allocation and Structure Creation Access the Y-Bucket Array to determine the number of polygons belonging to each y-bucket. Allocate space for each y-bucket by partitioning the common output array. Partition the space for one y-bucket further into space for each processor to fill within that y-bucket. Each processor creates appropriate y-bucket structures for all polygons it processed in the first pass, excluding any that were invalidated. Note: The work per processor in this step is proportional to the number of scanlines, not the number of polygons. 3. Third Pass: Scanline Processing Process each scanline in order from bottom to top. For each scanline, transfer information for each active polygon to an x-bucket data structure associated with the leftmost pixel in which the polygon appears. Maintain a linked list of these x-bucket structures in front-to-back visibility order. Perform the compositing computation for the pixels in the scanline using the active polygons in the x-buckets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. ybucketcounts = [0] numscanlines polygonbuckets = [[] for in range(numscanlines)] for poly in polygons: ymin, ymax = poly.getyrange() for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): ybucketcounts[y] += 1 polygonbuckets[y].append(poly) for y in range(numscanlines): # Get polygons for this scanline activepolygons = polygonbuckets[y] # Group by x-bucket (leftmost pixel) xbuckets = {} for poly in activepolygons: xstart = poly.getleftmostx() if xstart not in xbuckets: xbuckets[xstart] = [] xbuckets[xstart].append(poly) # Sort x-buckets by xstart sortedxstarts = sorted(xbuckets.keys()) for xstart in sortedxstarts: # Maintain front-to-back visibility order in linked list # This requires sorting polygons by depth or z-order # For simplicity, assume polygons are already in correct order or sorted here sortedpolys = sortbyvisibility(xbuckets[xstart]) # Process pixels for this x-bucket for x in range(xstart, poly.getrightmostx() + 1): # Compositing logic using sortedpolys # Update outputarray[y imagewidth + x] pass Parameters: Number of processors: Determined by hardware. Image resolution: Determines the size of the Y-Bucket Array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The second pass is a transitional step and can be parallelized by standard techniques, but its work per processor is only proportional to the number of scanlines, not the number of polygons. Invalidated polygons must be excluded in the second pass. This method is a parallel direct volume rendering algorithm that processes polygons representing isosurfaces or volume slices by grouping them into scanline-based 'y-buckets' and processing pixels within those buckets using 'x-buckets' and 'x-actives' lists to maintain front-to-back visibility order. It solves the problem of rendering irregular and multiple grids efficiently in software by maximizing coherence and avoiding the difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells. Unlike tile-based parallelization methods that break scanlines and lose coherence, this method parallelizes on a scanline basis to limit duplication. Time Complexity: The first pass is proportional to the number of polygons. The second pass is proportional to the number of scanlines. The third pass is proportional to the number of active polygons per scanline. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of scanlines and the number of polygons. Strengths: Maximizes coherence by processing scanlines, limiting duplication compared to tile-based methods. Efficient for irregular and multiple grids. Limitations: The second pass is a transitional step. Requires careful management of polygon visibility order. When to Use: When rendering irregular and multiple grids in software, and maximizing coherence is critical. When Not to Use: When hardware acceleration is available and tile-based methods are more suitable. The method was introduced in 1996 by. It was designed to address the challenges of rendering irregular and multiple grids efficiently in software. name: Parallel Direct Volume Rendering with Y-Buckets and X-Buckets
head: Hierarchical Parallelizable Direct Volume Rendering for Irregular/Multiple Grids, Scanline-based direct volume rendering for irregular grids, Scanline-based parallel DVR, Y-bucket/X-bucket parallelization, k-d tree based volume rendering
body: This method is a parallel direct volume rendering algorithm that processes polygons representing isosurfaces or volume slices by grouping them into scanline-based 'y-buckets' and processing pixels within those buckets using 'x-buckets' and 'x-actives' lists to maintain front-to-back visibility order. It solves the problem of rendering irregular and multiple grids efficiently in software by maximizing coherence and avoiding the difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells. Unlike tile-based parallelization methods that break scanlines and lose coherence, this method parallelizes on a scanline basis to limit duplication. Inputs: A volume defined over irregular, curvilinear, or rectilinear grids, potentially multiple intersecting grids. Geometrical transformation parameters (world-to-screen). Clipping box defining the subvolume to be rendered. Polygon structures containing vertex indices. Outputs: A rendered image with color integration and element ordering. Polygon ID: A unique integer identifier for each polygon. Grid ID: Encoded in certain bits of the Polygon ID, specifying the associated grid or surface. Position/Index: The remaining bits comprise either: An index into an array of polygon structures (for irregular grids). A direct encoding of the polygon's position within the grid (for curvilinear and rectilinear grids). Vertex Information: For curvilinear/rectilinear grids, vertex information is encoded into the Polygon ID, bypassing the need for separate polygon structures, as every cell has the same facial structure of 12 triangles and cell vertices can be inferred from the cell ID. Polygon Structure: Consists of an array of vertex indices. Implementation permits only triangles. Y-Bucket: Associated with each horizontal scanline. Contains IDs for polygons that first appear on that scanline. Processed in bottom-to-top order. Polygons are excluded if outside the clipping box or do not cross any pixel center. X-Bucket: Associated with each pixel in a scanline. Contains polygons that start or end at that specific pixel. X-Actives List: Maintains the list of polygons currently intersecting the current pixel, sorted in front-to-back order. Updated from the previous pixel's x-actives and the current pixel's x-bucket. Y-Actives List: Maintains the list of polygons currently intersecting the current scanline. Updated from the previous line's y-bucket and this line's y-bucket. 1. Transformation: If a new geometrical transformation is specified, convert locations from world space to screen space. 2. Y-Bucket Creation: For each (horizontal) scanline, create its y-bucket in bottom-to-top order. 3. Y-Actives Initialization: Initialize y-actives list as empty. 4. X-Bucket Initialization: For each scanline, initialize its x-bucket and x-actives list as empty. 5. Pixel Processing: For each pixel in scanline, in left-to-right order: Update x-actives list from previous pixel's x-actives and this pixel's x-bucket. Composite polygons in x-actives in front-to-back order. Update y-actives list from previous line's y-bucket and this line's y-bucket. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def paralleldvryxbuckets(polygons, transformation, clippingbox): # Step 1: Transformation if transformation is new: for polygon in polygons: polygon.vertices = transformworldtoscreen(polygon.vertices, transformation) # Step 2: Y-Bucket Creation # Parallelizable component: grouping polygons by scanline ybuckets = {} # Map: scanlineid -> list of polygonids for polygon in polygons: if isinsideclippingbox(polygon, clippingbox): scanlinescrossed = getscanlinescrossed(polygon) for sl in scanlinescrossed: if sl not in ybuckets: ybuckets[sl] = [] ybuckets[sl].append(polygon.id) # Sort y-buckets bottom-to-top (handled by iteration order of scanlines) # Step 3: Initialize Y-Actives yactives = [] # List of polygonids # Iterate scanlines bottom-to-top for scanlineid in sorted(ybuckets.keys()): # Step 4: Initialize X-Bucket and X-Actives for this scanline xbuckets = {} # Map: pixelid -> list of polygonids xactives = [] # List of polygonids # Process polygons in y-bucket for this scanline # Note: The source implies y-buckets contain polygons starting on this line # We need to determine which polygons are active for this scanline # The source says: "Update y-actives list from previous line's y-bucket and this line's y-bucket" # This implies y-actives tracks polygons spanning multiple scanlines # Update Y-Actives yactives = updateyactives(yactives, ybuckets.get(scanlineid, [])) # Now process pixels in this scanline # Determine pixel range for this scanline based on y-actives polygons pixelrange = getpixelrangeforscanline(yactives) for pixelid in pixelrange: # Step 5: Update X-Actives # Get polygons starting/ending at this pixel currentxbucket = getxbucketforpixel(pixelid, yactives) xactives = updatexactives(xactives, currentxbucket) # Composite compositepixels(xactives, pixelid) Performance: Images of volumes with about one million cells can be produced in one to several minutes on a workstation with a 150 MHz processor. Preview Speed: Previews show enough detail to navigate effectively in very large data sets, rendering useful images very quickly (about one second for one-million-cell grids) by displaying each region associated with a tree node as one cell. Numerical Accuracy: Standard techniques lose accuracy in screen-z, leading to significant errors in color integration and element order. A new perspective transformation is used to achieve greater numerical accuracy on geometrical elements spanning a great range of sizes. Clipping Box: Any group of polygons to be rendered includes the faces of a clipping box, which delimits the subvolume to be rendered. The six faces (12 triangles) of the clipping box are treated much like other polygons. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Images of volumes with about one million cells can be produced in one to several minutes on a workstation with a 150 MHz processor. Previews render useful images very quickly (about one second for one-million-cell grids). Scaling: The method is highly scalable, particularly the parallelizable component of grouping polygons by scanline into y-buckets. Strengths: Maximizes coherence, avoids difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells, generalizes polygon faces, easy to implement, fits naturally into scanline methods, processes multiple intersecting grids, handles wide range of cell sizes. Limitations: Not designed for massively parallel machines, software rendering (no special graphics hardware needed but implies CPU-bound). When to Use: When rendering irregular or multiple grids, when maximizing coherence is important, when avoiding ray-casting complexities is desired. When Not to Use: When designing for massively parallel machines, when ray-casting is preferred despite complexity. The method is based on Watkin's scanline algorithm. Early approaches for direct volume rendering used ray-casting, cell projection, and splatting. Most research addressed only rectilinear grids. The algorithm was chosen because the designers were not designing for massively parallel machines, wanted to maximize coherence, and wanted to avoid the difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells. It generalizes polygon faces and is easy to implement. name: PPLL Resolve Pass
head: Parallel Prefix List List Resolve
body: The PPLL Resolve Pass is a fragment shader pass that resolves a linked list of fragments per pixel into a final color by sorting and front-to-back blending. It takes the raw fragment data collected by the Atomic Fragment List Insertion method and produces the final image, distinguishing itself from sibling methods like A-buffer linked-list creation and ray processing by relying on a global atomic counter for list construction and a subsequent CPU/GPU synchronization to resolve the lists via sorting and blending. Inputs: uStartOffsetTex: A texture storing the head pointer (fragment index) for each pixel. Initialized to 0xFFFFFFFFu (end of list) by the Clear Pass. uFragmentBufferTex: A texture storing the fragment nodes. Layout is RGBA32UI with dimensions FRAGBUFFERW × FRAGBUFFERH. uViewportW, uViewportH: Viewport dimensions. FRAGBUFFERW: Width of the fragment buffer texture (constant, typically 2048). MAXNUMFRAGS: Maximum number of fragments to process per pixel (constant, typically 32). Outputs: glFragColor: The final color for the current pixel. Per-pixel local storage: colorList[MAXNUMFRAGS]: Array of uint storing packed fragment colors. depthList[MAXNUMFRAGS]: Array of float storing fragment depths. Total size: 32 \times 12 bytes = 384 bytes. 1. Boundary Check: Get pixel coordinates x, y. If x >= uViewportW or y >= uViewportH, discard. 2. Load Head: Load the starting offset (head pointer) from uStartOffsetTex at (x, y) into fragOffset. 3. Initialize: Set numFrags = 0. 4. Traverse List: Loop i from 0 to MAXNUMFRAGS - 1: If fragOffset == 0xFFFFFFFFu, break (end of list). Calculate address ivec2(int(fragOffset) % FRAGBUFFERW, int(fragOffset) / FRAGBUFFERW). Load frag from uFragmentBufferTex at the calculated address. Update fragOffset = frag.b (the next pointer). Store frag.r in colorList[i]. Store uintBitsToFloat(frag.g) in depthList[i]. Increment numFrags. 5. Empty Check: If numFrags == 0, discard. 6. Sort: Insertion sort colorList and depthList by depthList ascending. Loop i from 1 to numFrags - 1: Store fragColor = colorList[i], fragDepth = depthList[i]. Loop j from i down to 1: If depthList[j-1] > fragDepth, shift colorList[j-1] to colorList[j] and depthList[j-1] to depthList[j]. Decrement j. Place fragColor and fragDepth at j. 7. Blend: Initialize outColor = vec4(0.0). Loop i from 0 to MAXNUMFRAGS - 1: If i >= numFrags, break. Unpack src = unpackColor(colorList[i]). Update outColor.rgb = outColor.rgb + (1.0 - outColor.a) src.a src.rgb. Update outColor.a = outColor.a + (1.0 - outColor.a) src.a. If outColor.a > 0.995, break (early-out optimization). 8. Convert: If outColor.a > 1e-4, divide outColor.rgb by outColor.a (premultiplied to straight alpha conversion). 9. Output: Output outColor to glFragColor. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resolvepass(x, y): if x >= uViewportW or y >= uViewportH: return None # Load head pointer fragoffset = texelfetch(uStartOffsetTex, ivec2(x, y)).r numfrags = 0 colorlist = [0] MAXNUMFRAGS depthlist = [0.0] MAXNUMFRAGS # Traverse linked list i = 0 while i < MAXNUMFRAGS and fragoffset != 0xFFFFFFFFu: # Calculate buffer address bufx = fragoffset % FRAGBUFFERW bufy = fragoffset / FRAGBUFFERW frag = texelfetch(uFragmentBufferTex, ivec2(bufx, bufy)) # Extract next pointer fragoffset = frag.b # Store color and depth colorlist[i] = frag.r depthlist[i] = uintbitstofloat(frag.g) i += 1 numfrags += 1 if numfrags == 0: return None # Insertion sort by depth for i in range(1, numfrags): fragcolor = colorlist[i] fragdepth = depthlist[i] j = i while j > 0 and depthlist[j-1] > fragdepth: colorlist[j] = colorlist[j-1] depthlist[j] = depthlist[j-1] j -= 1 colorlist[j] = fragcolor depthlist[j] = fragdepth # Front-to-back blending outcolor = vec4(0.0) for i in range(numfrags): src = unpackcolor(colorlist[i]) outcolor.rgb = outcolor.rgb + (1.0 - outcolor.a) src.a src.rgb outcolor.a = outcolor.a + (1.0 - outcolor.a) src.a if outcolor.a > 0.995: break # Premultiplied to straight alpha if outcolor.a > 1e-4: outcolor.rgb = outcolor.rgb / outcolor.a return outcolor MAXNUMFRAGS: Maximum number of fragments to process per pixel. Typical value: 32. FRAGBUFFERW: Width of the fragment buffer texture. Typical value: 2048. Early-out optimization: The blend loop breaks if outColor.a > 0.995 to save computation when the pixel is effectively opaque. Empty list handling: If no fragments are collected (numFrags == 0), the fragment is discarded. Buffer Full: If the fragment buffer is full, fragments are silently dropped during the gather phase, which may result in missing fragments in the resolve pass. Precision: Depth is stored as uintBitsToFloat(frag.g), implying a specific bit-packing scheme for depth in the fragment node. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) or O(N^2) depending on the sort implementation. The provided method uses insertion sort, which is O(N^2) in the worst case, but efficient for small N (e.g., N=32). The traversal is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) per pixel for local storage, where N = MAX\NUM\FRAGS. Strengths: Simple implementation, efficient for low fragment counts per pixel. Limitations: Insertion sort becomes inefficient for high fragment counts. The global atomic counter approach can lead to buffer overflow if not managed carefully. When to use: Suitable for scenes with moderate fragment density per pixel. When not to use: Not suitable for scenes with very high fragment density per pixel where sorting overhead becomes significant. The PPLL Resolve Pass is part of the Parallel Prefix List List (PPLL) method for volume rendering. It was described in the context of a WebGL2-based volume renderer. The method relies on atomic operations for fragment list construction and a subsequent resolve pass for final color computation. name: A-buffer linked-list creation and ray processing
head: A-buffer linked-list creation, Ray processing with A-buffer linked-list
body: This method constructs a dynamic acceleration structure (A-buffer) on the GPU to efficiently identify which segment primitives overlap a given ray, avoiding the evaluation of empty space in expensive field computations. It differs from brute-force ray marching by using a geometry shader to generate quads covering primitive supports and a fragment shader to compute ray-support intersections, storing entry/exit points in a linked list. Unlike [Bru19], which requires explicit cutoff of primitive influences, this approach leverages compact support kernels (specifically clipped sphere-cones for Cauchy kernels) to naturally limit the interaction domain. The method consists of two main phases: A-buffer construction (creation of the linked list) and Ray processing (traversal of the linked list to find the isosurface). Inputs: Skeleton data: A set of segment primitives, each defined by endpoints, radius, and potentially varying radius profiles. Kernel parameters: Scale parameter \sigma, clipping parameters (\sigma{clipping}, \epsilon{clipping} for Cauchy kernels). Camera parameters: Ray origin and direction for each pixel (i, j). Occlusion data: An occluding depth buffer (optional, for output sensitivity). Outputs: For each pixel, a linked list of fragments (intervals) sorted by entry depth. The final isosurface intersection point or color. 1. A-Buffer Linked List: Per pixel, a linked list of fragments. Each fragment stores: zIn: Entry depth into the primitive support. zOut: Exit depth from the primitive support. segId: Identifier of the segment primitive. The list is sorted by zIn. 2. Processing Heaps (Per Ray): primitives: A min-heap (priority queue) storing {zOut, segId} pairs, ordered by zOut. Represents primitives currently active in the ray traversal. argmins: A min-heap storing {tprim,...} pairs, ordered by tprim (the parameter minimizing the field derivative or similar metric). Represents the next candidate for field evaluation. 1. Occluding Depth Buffer Initialization (Optional): Render an occluding depth buffer to achieve output sensitivity and limit primitives registered in linked lists. Initialize the depth buffer with depth values corresponding to positions guaranteed to be in the volume. Compute these depth values in a first render path on a per-primitive basis. Due to the integral formulation of the field, the minimal radius around primitives does not necessarily correspond to the prescribed radius (e.g., for bent skeletons). To overcome this, rely on two assumptions: usage of skeleton end-point correctors and bounded radius variations (none of the two spheres at a primitive end-point completely encompasses the other). Do not render occluders for primitives corresponding to end-point correctors. Derive a scaling factor for the sphere cones' radii such that the implicit surface is guaranteed to enclose the modified primitives, based on the worst skeleton configuration and the scale-invariant property of the SCALIS representation. The quality of the minimal volume is related to the kernel scale parameter; larger scale means smaller guaranteed volume. For typical Compact polynomial kernel scale \sigma ranging from 1.5 to 2, the scaling factor ranges from \approx 0.62 to \approx 0.35. For more constrained radius variations (constant radius), better bounds can be computed. Ignore primitives whose support entries are beyond the occluding depth. 2. Primitive Support Generation: Generate segment-aligned quads to limit the number of generated fragments for which ray/sphere-cone intersections are computed, particularly for primitives whose maximal radii are comparatively small to the segment length. Use a compact support kernel to avoid the need to cut-off primitive influences in this first step. 3. Ray-Support Intersection and List Insertion: Compute ray-support intersections for primitives in a fragment shader. Insert entry and exit points in sphere-cones and the associated primitive ID into an A-buffer linked-list. Sort the linked list on the fly according to the depth of the entry [LHL14]. The fragment shader generates and processes intervals on-the-fly using Algorithm 1 until an intersection with the isosurface is found. The resulting linked-list processing loop is given in Algorithm 2. Algorithm 2: Processing Linked List Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def GenerateRay(i, j): # Initialize heaps and fragment list primitives = emptyHeap() # Min-heap of {zOut, segId} argmins = emptyHeap() # Min-heap of {tprim,...} frags = InitFragList(i, j) # Get sorted linked list of fragments for pixel (i,j) targmin = infinity tentry = frags.currZIn() # Loop until both heaps and fragment list are empty while not (frags.empty() and primitives.empty()): tb, hb = te, he # Current interval bounds and field data # Get the exit of the last active primitive if not primitives.empty(): texit = primitives.back().val else: texit = infinity # Determine if we need to pull more fragments or if the current interval is valid if primitives.empty() or targmin < texit or tentry < texit: # If no primitives are active, the field is null if primitives.empty(): tb, hb = tentry, (g(0),...) # Field is zero # See text for management of entry/exit of non-null field area # Pull fragments from the A-buffer linked list into the heaps while targmin > tentry and not frags.empty(): # Find the primitive that minimizes the field derivative/parameter tprim = Argmin(sigma, frags.currSegId()) # Add the current fragment's exit to the active primitives heap tout = frags.currZOut() primitives.insert({tout, frags.currSegId()}) # Add the candidate parameter to the argmins heap argmins.insert(tprim) # Update the target minimum targmin = argmins.front() # Move to the next fragment frags.next() # Update the next entry point if not frags.empty(): tentry = frags.currZIn() else: tentry = infinity # Determine the next interval [te, he] if tb < te: # Process the interval [tb, hb] to [te, he] f, t = processInterval(tb, hb, te, he) if f: GenerateIsoSurface(t) return else: # If tb >= te, the interval is invalid or null # See text for management of entry/exit of non-null field area pass # Remove primitives that have exited before the current interval end primitives.popElements(lambda x: x <= te) argmins.popElements(lambda x: x <= te) # Update the target minimum if not argmins.empty(): targmin = argmins.front() else: targmin = infinity Details on processInterval and Numerical Stability: Due to possible numerical instability in the normalized field derivative computation (the latter being non-continuous when the field switches from null to non-null), apply one step of sphere tracing to avoid those areas. Note that this requires no field evaluation as the field is null at the support limit. The processInterval function evaluates the field and its derivative within the interval [tb, te] using the Hermite data (te, he) and (tb, hb). If an intersection with the isosurface is found, return the point t. Subdivision Strategy: Combine the second subdivision strategy (switching between overlapped/non-overlapped areas) with the contribution from section 3 to limit the number of segment primitives stored at once while generating long enough intervals to limit compulsory field evaluations. This presents a trade-off: it limits the number of segment primitives to be stored at once while generating long enough intervals, hence limiting the number of compulsory field evaluations. Blending: It is possible to blend different skeletons with a blending sharper than summation blending, e.g., using Ricci's blending [Ric73]. This keeps the correlation of the field with the homothetic squared distance to individual primitives by defining a blending behavior parametrized between a summation blend and a maximum blend. Kernel Scale (\sigma): For typical Compact polynomial kernel scale \sigma ranging from 1.5 to 2, the scaling factor ranges from \approx 0.62 to \approx 0.35. Cauchy Kernel Parameters: For Cauchy kernel tests, \sigma{clipping} = 4 for \sigma = 0.3 and \epsilon{clipping} = 0.005. Sphere-Tracing Steps: On each subinterval, the number of sphere-tracing steps is bounded (typically 256). Subdivisions per Primitive: In the implementation of Sherstyuk's method, use four subdivisions per primitive, which is the coarsest subdivision allowing visually acceptable results on primitives with constant radius. Numerical Instability: Occurs in the normalized field derivative computation because it is non-continuous when the field switches from null to non-null. Apply one step of sphere tracing to avoid these areas. Minimal Radius Discrepancy: Due to the integral formulation of the field, the minimal radius around primitives does not necessarily correspond to the prescribed radius (e.g., for bent skeletons). Overcome this by relying on skeleton end-point correctors and bounded radius variations. Visual Artifacts: Sphere-tracing and Sherstyuk's fast ray tracing can present visual artifacts. In the presence of a large amount of blending (e.g., many segments connecting at one vertex), sphere-tracing algorithms require under-relaxation to properly find the surface. A-Buffer Overflow: For kernels with larger footprints (e.g., Cauchy), ensure the A-buffer size is sufficient to avoid overflow, as this leads to an increase in computational time. This method constructs a dynamic acceleration structure (A-buffer) on the GPU to efficiently identify which segment primitives overlap a given ray, avoiding the evaluation of empty space in expensive field computations. It differs from brute-force ray marching by using a geometry shader to generate quads covering primitive supports and a fragment shader to compute ray-support intersections, storing entry/exit points in a linked list. Unlike [Bru19], which requires explicit cutoff of primitive influences, this approach leverages compact support kernels (specifically clipped sphere-cones for Cauchy kernels) to naturally limit the interaction domain. Time Complexity: The method reduces rendering time compared to sphere tracing. For compact polynomial kernel at 2048x2048 resolution: Intel UHD Graphics 630 reduction from -34.2% to -48.7%; nVidia Quadro P1000 reduction from -51.5% to -78.0%; nVidia GeForce 2080 RTX reduction from -35.3% to -72.1% compared to the most competitive alternative method. For Cauchy kernel tests on nVidia RTX at 1536x1536 resolution: Timings range from 7 to 54 milliseconds (excluding Fig.12 Middle). Rendering time reduction compared to sphere tracing ranges from -46.2% to -81.3%. Memory Complexity: The method limits the number of segment primitives stored at once by combining subdivision strategies, thus limiting memory usage per thread. Usage of occluders can have a large impact in terms of rendering time (as well as memory consumption) depending on the nature of the skeleton. Measured Performance: Stress test on nVidia RTX: rendered a foam structure consisting of 526k segments using the compact polynomial kernel at 15 frames per second. Similar improvements observed on other GPUs at 1024x1024 resolution. Strengths: Avoids evaluation of empty space; output sensitivity via occluding depth buffer; handles varying radii and complex skeletons; real-time rendering capabilities. Limitations: Numerical instability at field boundaries; potential visual artifacts with high blending; requires careful tuning of kernel parameters and subdivision strategies. When to Use: Suitable for real-time rendering of skeleton-based implicit surfaces, especially when primitives have compact support and varying radii. When Not to Use: Not suitable for kernels with very large footprints without sufficient A-buffer size; may require under-relaxation for high blending scenarios. Origin: The method is based on the work presented in "Fast Ray Tracing of Scale-Invariant Integral Surfaces". History: The approach builds upon previous work on A-buffers [LHL14] and sphere-tracing optimizations [Bru19]. It incorporates insights from Sherstyuk's fast ray-tracing [She99] and segment-tracing [GGPP20]. Usage: Implemented in C++ using OpenGL, with shaders in GLSL. Tested on Intel UHD Graphics 630, nVidia Quadro P1000, and nVidia GeForce 2080 RTX. Tested on artistic shapes, truss structures, branching structures, procedural foam structures, and random skeletons.
