name: Triton-accelerated Volume Raycasting
head: FlashDRR Triton Kernel, Triton-based Volume Raycasting, fused volume rendering
body: Triton-accelerated Volume Raycasting is a fused GPU rendering technique that uses the Triton compiler to perform volume raycasting, avoiding the materialization of intermediate ray-sample tensors in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to reduce memory footprint and increase speed. It sets itself apart from standard PyTorch-based raycasting by fusing the ray-marching loop into a single kernel, thereby eliminating the memory bandwidth bottlenecks and cache thrashing that cause super-linear performance degradation in non-fused implementations at high resolutions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 5D tensor representing the volume grid (shape: [1, C, D, H, W] where C is channels, e.g., 8 for density/opacity), a view matrix, and a coordinate transformation matrix (ras2ijk). Output: Rendered image tensors for RGB, depth, and opacity. Data Structures: The method relies on per-thread register accumulation to avoid global memory writes during the marching loop. accRgb: A stack-allocated array of size MAXVOLUMERENDERCHANNELS used to accumulate RGB values per ray. depth: A scalar variable for accumulating depth. opacity: A scalar variable for accumulating opacity. Parameters: triton: Boolean flag. If True, the fused Triton kernel is used; if False, the standard PyTorch implementation is used. raysamples: Number of samples per ray. Typical value is 384, configurable in the VolumeRaycaster. resolution: Output image resolution (e.g., 1024x1024 or 2048x2048). MAXVOLUMERENDERCHANNELS: Compile-time constant defining the maximum number of RGB channels supported in the accumulation register array. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each ray, initialize accRgb to zero, depth to 0, and opacity to 0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate through raysamples steps along the ray. Sample the volume grid at the current ray position. Compute the contribution (color, opacity, depth) for the current sample. Update accRgb, depth, and opacity using the volume rendering integral (alpha compositing). Note: The standard PyTorch implementation performs read-modify-write operations on global memory tensors (outRGB, outDepth, outOpacity) for every sample. The Triton implementation accumulates these values in per-thread registers. 3. Final Write: After the loop completes, write the final accumulated values from the per-thread registers (accRgb, depth, opacity) to the output tensors (outRGB, outDepth, outOpacity) exactly once per ray. 4. Inference Fast Path (Optional): If inference mode is enabled (backward pass not needed), skip storing intermediate weights (outWs) and depth/total samples, returning size-0 placeholder tensors to reduce global memory traffic further. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. @triton.jit def volumerenderkernel( gridptr, viewmatptr, ras2ijkptr, outrgbptr, outdepthptr, outopacityptr, H, W, raysamples, MAXCHANNELS): # 1. Identify ray pid = tl.programid(0) if pid >= H W: return # 2. Initialize registers accrgb = tl.zeros((MAXCHANNELS,), dtype=tl.float32) accdepth = 0.0 accopacity = 0.0 # 3. Ray marching loop for i in range(raysamples): # Compute sample position from ray origin and direction # Sample grid value at position (trilinear interpolation) # Compute weight and color contribution # Update registers accrgb += contributionrgb accdepth += contributiondepth accopacity += contributionopacity # 4. Write to global memory once if pid < H W: h = pid // W w = pid % W tl.store(outrgbptr + h W MAXCHANNELS + w MAXCHANNELS, accrgb) tl.store(outdepthptr + h W + w, accdepth) tl.store(outopacityptr + h W + w, accopacity) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Determinism: The Triton kernel uses tl.atomicadd (or similar parallel reduction mechanisms depending on implementation details not fully specified in the source, but the source explicitly mentions tl.atomicadd causing order-nondeterminism). This results in non-deterministic gradient outputs. Gradient Tolerance: Due to the nondeterminism, gradient checks require looser tolerances: atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-3, and nondettol=1e-6. Memory Scaling: Standard PyTorch execution degrades super-linearly beyond 1024x1024 resolution due to memory bandwidth limits and cache thrashing. A forward pass optimization where RGB, depth, and opacity are accumulated in per-thread registers (stack-allocated) rather than global memory, writing each per-ray output exactly once to eliminate per-sample global-memory read-modify-write operations. It differs from the baseline by eliminating per-sample global-memory read-modify-write on outRGB/outDepth/outOpacity, reducing global memory traffic. Choose this when global memory bandwidth is the bottleneck in the ray-marching loop. It is implemented in fvdb-core. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Standard PyTorch execution scales linearly with total samples (Rays × Samples/Ray), reaching ~12.4 GB at 1024x1024 resolution with 512 samples. Triton maintains a near-constant memory footprint below 430 MiB (specifically 110.7 MiB for evaluation and 121.6 MiB for training at 1024x1024 with 512 samples), achieving a 99.5% memory reduction at high workloads. Time: Triton maintains predictable linear scaling proportional to total rays rendered. Standard PyTorch suffers from non-linear degradation at high resolutions. Measured Performance: At 2048x2048 resolution with 256 ray samples: Triton iteration time is 9.16 ms compared to 1,804.32 ms for standard PyTorch, a 197x speedup. At 1024x1024 resolution with 512 samples: Triton training step time is 15.4 ms, while non-Triton evaluation time is 82.0 ms. Triton training adds ~3.05x overhead compared to its own evaluation, while standard PyTorch adds ~1.31x overhead. In a fire renderer at 256 spp, per-ray register accumulation reduced the volumerender stage time from 8772.5 ms to 6171.4 ms (-29.7%) and end-to-end walltime by 17.8%. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Drastic reduction in VRAM usage; significant speedup at high resolutions; linear scaling behavior. Limitations: Non-deterministic gradients due to atomic operations; requires Triton compiler support; potential precision differences between fp16/bf16 and fp32 (though sources indicate close matching with atol=1e-4). Triton-accelerated Volume Raycasting was introduced as part of the FlashDRR project to optimize direct volume rendering on GPUs using the Triton programming model. It addresses the limitations of standard PyTorch-based raycasting, which struggles with memory bandwidth at high resolutions. The technique is also discussed in the context of fvdb-core optimizations, where it is combined with per-ray register accumulation and inference fast paths to further reduce global memory traffic. pcarnah/flashdrr, https://github.com/pcarnah/flashdrr, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Optimizations for volumerender and move its autograd layer to Python, https://github.com/openvdb/fvdb-core/pull/640, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Efficient Ray Casting Pipeline
head: EfficientRayCast, Raycasting Rendering Pipeline
body: This article covers two distinct implementations sharing the name "Efficient Ray Casting Pipeline," which differ fundamentally in domain and technique. The first is a software-based 2D raycaster for unstructured grid visualization that minimizes per-pixel cost by rendering to a low-resolution internal framebuffer and upscaling. The second is a hardware-accelerated Direct Volume Ray Casting (DVR) pipeline for DirectX 11 that uses geometry shaders for active brick detection and ray generation. Both aim to optimize rendering performance by reducing redundant calculations, though they achieve this through resolution scaling versus hardware-specific shader stages respectively. This method casts one ray per screen column to render a 2D map, writing directly to the canvas buffer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D map grid (cells), camera position, camera direction, viewport dimensions. Output: Uint32Array view over the canvas’s raw pixel buffer. Data Structures: Map: 2D array of cell types (e.g., empty, wall). Framebuffer: Internal buffer of size 480x300 pixels. Steps: 1. Initialize the internal framebuffer at 480x300 resolution. 2. For each screen column x from 0 to viewport width: a. Calculate the ray direction based on camera orientation and column index. b. Perform ray traversal (e.g., DDA algorithm) to find intersections with grid cells. c. For each intersected pixel along the ray, perform a texture fetch and fog multiply. This operation consists of three integer multiplies and shifts. d. Write the resulting color exactly once into the internal framebuffer. 3. After all columns are processed, upscale the 480x300 framebuffer to fill the viewport using an integer scale factor and pixelated filtering (image-rendering: pixelated). Parameters: Internal Resolution: 480x300. Upscaling: Integer scale factor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of integer multiplies and shifts for fog calculation requires careful handling of overflow if values are large. Boundaries: The ray traversal must handle grid boundaries correctly to avoid out-of-bounds access. Degenerate Input: The algorithm assumes a valid 2D grid structure; empty or malformed grids may cause undefined behavior. This method uses a multi-pass D3D11 pipeline for volume raycasting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data (voxels), view/projection matrices, camera position, density range constants. Output: Final output texture (mpOutputTex). Data Structures: Constant Buffer (CBEfficientRayCastFrame): mInvView: XMMATRIX (Inverse View Matrix) mView: XMMATRIX (View Matrix) mViewProj: XMMATRIX (View-Projection Matrix) f4ViewPos: XMFLOAT4 (Camera Position) f2HalfWinSize: XMFLOAT2 (Half Window Size) f2WinReso: XMFLOAT2 (Window Resolution) f2MinMaxDensity: XMFLOAT2 (Density Range Constants: MINDENSITY, MAXDENSITY) NIU: float (Not Given in the sources) NIU1: float (Not Given in the sources) Textures: mpFarNearTex: Texture for storing near/far ray positions. mpOutputTex: Final output texture. mpBrickVolTex: Brick volume texture. mpVolTex: Volume texture. Shaders: mpActiveCellAndSOGS: Geometry shader for active brick check and cube mesh generation. mpRaymarchGS: Geometry shader for ray casting. name: CUDA-based Exclusive Prefix Sum for Vertex Indexing
head: Exclusive scan vertex indexing, Scan-based vertex deduplication
body: This method solves the duplicate vertex calculation problem in GPU-based parallel isosurface extraction by using an exclusive prefix sum (scan) to compute correct global vertex indices for vertices found by parallel threads. Unlike sibling methods that may only apply stream compaction to triangles, this approach applies scan-based indexing to both vertices and triangles, ensuring that vertices identified by different threads are assigned unique, non-overlapping global indices without requiring expensive post-processing merging. It builds on Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) Orchestration by providing the specific data structures and kernel orchestration required for volume rendering mesh generation. Inputs: A pair of volume slices (lower and upper) of size W \times H (typically 512 \times 512 to 2048 \times 2048). A grid of threads, where each thread processes one cell in the slice pair. Outputs: Compacted arrays of unique vertex coordinates (resvert) and triangle indices (restrinumvect). Global vertex indices assigned to each detected vertex. The method requires five sets of matrices for vertex coordinates and labels, and corresponding scan output matrices, plus triangle storage structures. All matrices are of size W \times H, corresponding to the number of cells in the slice pair. 1. Vertex Coordinate Matrices: xvert, yvert: Store coordinates for edges along the X and Y axes of the lower slice. Xvert, Yvert: Store coordinates for edges along the X and Y axes of the upper slice. zvert: Store coordinates for edges along the Z axis (connecting lower and upper slices). 2. Label Matrices: xlabel, ylabel, Xlabel, Ylabel, zlabel: Corresponding label matrices for the coordinate matrices above. Initially, all labels are set to 1 to indicate vertex presence. 3. Scan Output Matrices: xscan, yscan, Xscan, Yscan, zscan: Output of the exclusive prefix sum operation on the label matrices. These serve as input for stream compaction and index calculation. 4. Triangle Storage: trinumvect: Stores the number of triangles created for each cell. restrinumvect: Compacted array storing the number of created triangles. Triangle array size is proportional to slice size, as at most 5 triangles are created per cell. 1. Initialization: For each cell in the slice pair, a dedicated thread executes the VerticesCalc kernel. The thread identifies vertices on the cell's edges and writes their coordinates to the respective xvert, yvert, Xvert, Yvert, and zvert matrices. It also writes a label of 1 to the corresponding label matrix (xlabel, etc.) to mark the vertex's presence. 2. Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan): Perform an exclusive prefix sum operation on each of the five label matrices (xlabel through zlabel) using the CUDPP library. The output is stored in the corresponding scan matrices (xscan through zscan). The exclusive scan is defined as: V{out}[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} V{in}[j] Example: If xlabel contains \{5, 6, 2, 4, 0, 2, 0, 1\}, then xscan contains \{0, 5, 11, 13, 17, 17, 19, 19\}. 3. Index Assignment: The value in the scan matrix at a given cell's position indicates the number of vertices of that type found in all preceding cells. This value serves as the base global index for the vertices found in the current cell. If thread k finds N vertices, and the scan output for its cell is S, the global indices for these vertices are S, S+1, \dots, S+N-1. The total number of vertices is obtained by summing the last elements of the input label vector and the output scan vector (e.g., 1 + 19 = 20). 4. Stream Compaction (Vertices): Execute the VerticesCompact kernel to compact the vertex coordinate matrices into a single contiguous array resvert. The scan output matrices (xscan through zscan) are used to determine the write positions in resvert. Vertices are stored in a specific order: xvert, yvert, Xvert, Yvert, zvert. The global index of a vertex in the final mesh is calculated by summing the counts of previous edge types. For example, if 100 vertices were found previously, and the current cell has 10 X-edges, 20 Y-edges, and 7 Z-edges, the first Z-vertex gets global index 100 + 10 + 20 = 130. However, its position in the compacted resvert vector is based on local offsets within the current cell's contribution, specifically position 30 (10+20) relative to the start of the current cell's block in the compacted array. 5. Stream Compaction (Triangles): Execute a second compaction kernel to process the trinumvect array into restrinumvect. This step also uses the scan operation to determine write positions for triangle data, ensuring compact storage of triangle indices. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def VerticesCalc(celli, cellj, volumelower, volumeupper, xvert, yvert, Xvert, Yvert, zvert, xlabel, ylabel, Xlabel, Ylabel, zlabel): # Identify vertices on the 12 edges of the cell # Determine if a vertex exists on each edge based on isosurface criteria # Write coordinates to global memory matrices if vertexexistsonlowerxedge: xvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) xlabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: xlabel[celli, cellj] = 0 if vertexexistsonloweryedge: yvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) ylabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: ylabel[celli, cellj] = 0 if vertexexistsonupperxedge: Xvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) Xlabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: Xlabel[celli, cellj] = 0 if vertexexistsonupperyedge: Yvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) Ylabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: Ylabel[celli, cellj] = 0 if vertexexistsonzedge: zvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) zlabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: zlabel[celli, cellj] = 0 def VerticesCompact(celli, cellj, xvert, yvert, Xvert, Yvert, zvert, xscan, yscan, Xscan, Yscan, zscan, resvert): # Calculate base indices for this cell based on scan results basex = xscan[celli, cellj] basey = yscan[celli, cellj] baseX = Xscan[celli, cellj] baseY = Yscan[celli, cellj] basez = zscan[celli, cellj] # Determine how many vertices of each type were found in this cell countx = xlabel[celli, cellj] county = ylabel[celli, cellj] countX = Xlabel[celli, cellj] countY = Ylabel[celli, cellj] countz = zlabel[celli, cellj] # Write to compacted array in order: x, y, X, Y, z # The position in resvert is determined by the cumulative sum of counts # within the current cell's contribution, but the global index is derived from scan offset = 0 # Write X vertices for k in range(countx): resvert[basex + offset] = xvert[celli, cellj] # Assuming single vertex per edge for simplicity offset += 1 # Write Y vertices for k in range(county): resvert[basey + offset] = yvert[celli, cellj] offset += 1 # Write X (upper) vertices for k in range(countX): resvert[baseX + offset] = Xvert[celli, cellj] offset += 1 # Write Y (upper) vertices for k in range(countY): resvert[baseY + offset] = Yvert[celli, cellj] offset += 1 # Write Z vertices for k in range(countz): resvert[basez + offset] = zvert[celli, cellj] offset += 1 def main(): # 1. Launch VerticesCalc kernel for all cells # Grid size: (W, H, 1) VerticesCalc<<<grid, block>>>(...) # 2. Perform Exclusive Prefix Sum on label matrices using CUDPP # CUDPPscan(xlabel, xlabel, WH, ADD) # CUDPPscan(ylabel, ylabel, WH, ADD) #... repeat for Xlabel, Ylabel, zlabel # 3. Launch VerticesCompact kernel VerticesCompact<<<grid, block>>>(...) # 4. Perform Stream Compaction for triangles (similar scan + compact steps) #... Slice Size: Common dataset slice sizes are 512 \times 512 to 2048 \times 2048. Memory Occupancy: The auxiliary structures consume 78 to 1168 MB of GPU memory depending on slice size. Minimum GPU Memory: 512 MB is required to process 512 \times 512 slices. GPU Memory Limitation: The large size of auxiliary data structures for large slices (up to 1168 MB) necessitates processing one pair of slices at a time. Data Transfer Overhead: The effective number of vertices and triangles is much lower than the size of the data structures, leading to expensive data transfers. Stream compaction is critical to mitigate this. Search Structures: Search structures are disregarded because they also consume GPU memory, which is limited. Time Complexity: The method involves four kernels: two for vertex/triangle computation and two for stream compaction and scan operations. The scan operation is typically O(N) where N is the number of cells. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the slice size W \times H. For 512 \times 512 to 2048 \times 2048 slices, memory occupancy ranges from 78 to 1168 MB. Strengths: Solves the duplicate vertex calculation problem efficiently without post-processing merging. Reduces data transfer overhead via stream compaction. Compatible with standard CUDA devices with at least 512 MB of memory. Limitations: Memory-intensive, limiting the maximum slice size that can be processed at once. Data transfer between host and device remains a significant part of the execution time. When to Use: Suitable for GPU-based isosurface extraction where memory allows for processing slice pairs and high parallelism is desired. When Not to Use: Not suitable for volumes with very large slices that exceed available GPU memory, or when search structures are preferred despite memory costs. Origin: This method was introduced in the paper "A parallel isosurface extraction component for visualization pipelines executing on GPU clusters". Development: It extends previous work [25] which only used stream compaction for triangles, by applying it to both vertices and triangles to address duplicate vertex calculation. Usage: It is used in GPU-based visualization pipelines for isosurface extraction from volume data. name: Wait-Free Radix Sort
head: Hierarchical Blelloch Scan Sort
body: A parallel sorting algorithm designed for heterogeneous GPU environments (specifically WebGPU) that avoids inter-workgroup spin-waiting by using a hierarchical Blelloch scan to compute element positions. It solves the problem of stable, wait-free sorting across workgroups where scheduling order is not guaranteed, ensuring consistent behavior without busy-waiting. It sets itself apart from siblings like CUDA-based Exclusive Prefix Sum for Vertex Indexing by explicitly decoupling workgroup synchronization via a multi-level scan dispatch rather than relying on fixed scheduling assumptions or tile-based rasterizer constraints. Inputs: An array of N keys (e.g., 32-bit depth values) to be sorted. Outputs: A permutation of the input array sorted by key. Data Structures: input: Array of N keys. output: Array of N values (or indices) to be reordered. histogram: Local buffer per workgroup of size 256 (for 8-bit radix), storing counts of each digit value d \in [0, 255]. tilesums: Array of size N/wg, storing the sum of each workgroup's histogram for a specific digit. prefixes: Array of size N/wg, storing the exclusive prefix sums of tilesums. based: Scalar value representing the global offset for digit d. Parameters: N: Number of elements. wg: Workgroup size (tile size). B: Number of bits per pass (8). R: Radix size (2^B = 256). P: Number of passes (32/B = 4). Algorithm Steps: The full sort is performed by executing P consecutive passes of an 8-bit radix sort, starting from the least significant bits. In the k-th pass (k=0 \dots P-1), the algorithm processes bits k \times 8 to (k + 1) \times 8 - 1 of the key. Each pass consists of three steps: 1. Local Histogram: Each workgroup w computes a local histogram of the digit values extracted from its assigned elements. Let di be the digit value of element i. The workgroup increments histogram[di] for each element. 2. Prefix Scan: A hierarchical Blelloch scan is executed to compute two values: \text{base}d: The global offset for digit d, equal to the total count of all elements with a digit value less than d across all workgroups. \text{prefix}{wg}: The inter-workgroup rank, representing the total count of elements with digit d in all workgroups processed before the current workgroup w. The Blelloch scan is implemented as a two-phase process: Forward Pass (Upsweep): Level l0 performs an exclusive scan inside each workgroup tile of size wg over the indicator stream for digit d, producing tile sums forming an array of length N/wg. Level l1 runs the same Blelloch scan on this array to obtain prefixes across tiles, recursing until a single level remains. Backward Pass (Downsweep): The prefixes computed at the higher levels are added back to their corresponding l0 tiles, and then to individual elements, yielding the intra-workgroup ranks and the inter-workgroup offset \text{prefix}{wg}. \text{base}d is read from the last level of the upsweep as the sum of counts of digits smaller than d. 3. Scatter: Each element i is written to its new position in the output array. The position is calculated as: pos = \text{base}d + \text{rank}i where: \text{rank}i = \text{prefix}{wg} + \text{rank}{\text{local}i} Here, \text{rank}{\text{local}i} is the intra-workgroup rank (number of elements with digit d within the current workgroup before index i). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def waitfreeradixsort(inputkeys, N, wg): output = [None] N # 32-bit sort requires 4 passes of 8-bit radix sort for k in range(4): shift = k 8 # Extract digit d for each element digits = [(key >> shift) & 0xFF for key in inputkeys] # Step 1: Local Histogram # Each workgroup computes its local histogram # This is done in parallel by workgroups localhistograms = computelocalhistograms(digits, N, wg) # Step 2: Prefix Scan (Hierarchical Blelloch) # Compute tile sums from local histograms for the current digit d # Note: The scan is performed for each digit d independently or # aggregated. The source implies computing offsets for the digit # being processed. We assume the scan operates on the counts of # the specific digit d across workgroups. # Extract counts for digit d from each workgroup's histogram # tilecounts[d] = sum of counts of digit d in each workgroup tilecounts = [hist[d] for hist in localhistograms] # Perform Blelloch Scan on tilecounts to get prefixes # Returns array of length N/wg where prefix[i] is sum of tilecounts[0..i-1] prefixes = blellochscan(tilecounts) # based is the total sum of counts of digits < d # This requires running the scan for all digits or accumulating sums. # Based on source: "read based from the last level as the sum of counts # of digits smaller than d". # We assume based is precomputed or computed via a similar scan over # the cumulative sums of all digit counts. based = computebaseoffset(d, localhistograms, N, wg) # Step 3: Scatter for i in range(N): di = digits[i] w = i // wg idxinwg = i % wg # prefixwg is the prefix sum for workgroup w prefixwg = prefixes[w] # ranklocali is the count of elements with digit di in the # current workgroup before index i. # This requires a local scan within the workgroup. ranklocali = computelocalrank(i, di, localhistograms[w]) ranki = prefixwg + ranklocali pos = based + ranki output[pos] = inputkeys[i] # Update inputkeys for next pass inputkeys = output def blellochscan(data): """ Standard Blelloch Scan (Exclusive) on an array. Implemented as upsweep and downsweep. """ n = len(data) if n == 1: return [0] # Upsweep (reduce) # Build a tree of sums tree = [0] (2 n) tree[n:] = data[:] level = n while level > 1: for i in range(0, level, 2): tree[i // 2] = tree[i] + tree[i + 1] level //= 2 # Read based from the last level (root) if needed, # but for exclusive scan we need prefixes. # Downsweep tree[n] = 0 # Clear the root for exclusive scan logic if needed, # but standard Blelloch sets the root to 0 for exclusive scan? # Actually, for exclusive scan, the root of the downsweep # is set to 0. # Re-initialize tree for downsweep # The upsweep computed the total sum at tree[0]. # For exclusive scan, we set the root to 0. tree[0] = 0 level = 1 while level < n: for i in range(level 2 - 1, -1, -2): if i + 1 < 2 n: tree[i + 1] += tree[i] level = 2 return tree[n:] def computelocalrank(i, di, localhist): """ Compute the number of elements with digit di in the current workgroup before index i. """ # This requires scanning the local elements. # In a real implementation, this is done via a local scan within the workgroup. # Here we simulate it by counting. count = 0 # In practice, this is a local exclusive scan of the indicator vector # for digit di within the workgroup. return count # Placeholder for local scan logic Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The algorithm relies on integer arithmetic for counts. Ensure that the total count N fits within the data type used for offsets. Boundaries: The hierarchical scan must handle cases where N is not a multiple of wg. Padding or boundary checks are required in the local histogram and scan steps. Degenerate Input: If all keys are identical, the sort remains stable, and all elements are placed in their original relative order. The fundamental pass used in the wait-free radix sort. It sorts elements based on a single 8-bit digit of the key. It is chosen for its efficiency in parallel histogram computation and its compatibility with the hierarchical scan structure. Time Complexity: Linear work O(N) per pass, with P passes, resulting in O(P \cdot N) total work. The hierarchical scan adds a logarithmic factor in terms of workgroup count, but the total work remains linear in N. Memory Complexity: O(N/wg) auxiliary storage for the tile sums and prefixes. Performance: Avoids spin waiting across heterogeneous GPU schedulers, making it robust across different hardware. Strengths: Wait-free, stable, works on WebGPU and heterogeneous devices. Limitations: Requires multiple compute dispatches for the hierarchical scan levels, which may introduce overhead. Originating from the WebSplatter project, this method was designed to enable efficient Gaussian Splatting in web browsers via WebGPU. It addresses the limitations of CUDA-based approaches that assume fixed scheduling orders, which can degenerate into busy-waits on devices without such guarantees.
